description_generated: FOSL1 and FOSL2 are Fra-1 and Fra-2, AP-1 family partners of the Jun proteins, and the genes collected here are the transcriptional output they drive at AP-1 sites in promoters. The programme is one of tissue remodelling and inflammation: secreted cytokines and chemokines such as IL6, IL8, LIF and CCL2 recruit and activate leukocytes, while matrix metalloproteinases and the plasminogen activator PLAU degrade extracellular matrix and basement membrane. Structural and matrix-associated products including collagen, decorin and matrix Gla protein, together with the endothelial cofactor thrombomodulin, place this output in wound healing, fibrosis and vascular biology. Because the same genes support motility and invasion, sustained Fra-1 or Fra-2 activity downstream of growth factor and stress signalling contributes to tumour invasiveness, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and chronic inflammatory disease, whereas transient induction serves repair after injury.

Integrins are the principal receptors by which cells grip the extracellular matrix, and the interactions at the cell surface described here couple that grip to intracellular signalling, shape and survival. The set pairs matrix ligands — fibrillar and basement membrane collagens, fibronectin, laminin chains, tenascin — with the receptors that read them, notably the fibronectin receptor ITGA5 and the αV and β 3 subunits used by platelets and by angiogenic endothelium. Engagement clusters focal adhesion kinase, drives actomyosin contractility through myosin light chain, and cooperates with growth factor receptors such as EGFR, MET, KDR and the PDGF receptors, so adhesion and mitogenic signalling reinforce one another and gate cell cycle entry. This adhesive crosstalk underlies wound healing, platelet aggregation, vessel formation and the invasive, stiffened matrix of fibrosis and tumours; loss of the platelet αIIbβ 3 receptor causes a bleeding disorder.

Integrins read the extracellular matrix, and this collection represents the ligand side of those cell surface interactions: fibrillar collagen I, basement membrane collagen IV and laminins, fibronectin, fibrillin, tenascin C and von Willebrand factor. Engagement of these ligands anchors cells to their substratum, establishes basement membrane polarity beneath epithelia and endothelia, and converts matrix contact into signals for survival, spreading and directed migration during development, wound repair and angiogenesis. Von Willebrand factor additionally captures platelets at sites of vessel injury, linking the same adhesive chemistry to haemostasis. Because these proteins are both structural scaffold and receptor ligand, their mutation causes disease of tissue integrity rather than of signalling alone: collagen I defects give brittle bone, collagen IV defects hereditary nephritis, and fibrillin defects the connective tissue fragility of Marfan syndrome.

Genes induced when the transcription factor E2F1 is active, the state that commits a cell to duplicate its genome at the G1-to-S transition. This output explains why E2F1 sits at the centre of cell cycle control downstream of RB and CDK4/6 activity, and why its deregulation in tumours produces unscheduled proliferation and replication stress. The targets read as a replication toolkit: CDC6 and the MCM2/4/6 helicase subunits license and unwind origins, PCNA, POLE2 and RFC1 build and sustain the replication fork, DCK and UNG feed nucleotide supply and base excision repair, and RAD51 handles recombinational repair of damaged forks. Alongside them are brakes and timers, including WEE1, the licensing inhibitor geminin, the APC/C inhibitor FBXO5 and the repressive E2F7, so the same wave that starts S phase also restricts it to one round.

These genes are among the transcripts most strongly induced by E2F1, the transcription factor released when retinoblastoma protein is phosphorylated at the G1/S transition, and together they describe what a cell buys with that decision: the capacity to replicate its genome. Licensing and replisome components such as CDC6, MCM4, PCNA and the DNA polymerase alpha-primase subunits POLA2 and PRIM1 are switched on ahead of S phase, alongside histone supply through SLBP and NASP, homologous recombination via RAD51, and DNA damage processing. Mitotic and checkpoint regulators including WEE1, PKMYT1, FBXO5, SKP2 and the kinetochore component KNTC1 couple replication to the following division, while E2F7 provides negative feedback. Because RB-E2F control is disrupted in most human cancers, persistent expression of this programme is a signature of proliferating and transformed cells and a driver of replication stress.

Growth factor, antigen and cytokine receptors convert ligand binding into changes in proliferation, differentiation and cytoskeletal behaviour largely through small GTPases of the RAS family and the kinase cascades they trigger, and this RAS/MAPK signalling axis is the route by which such signals reach the nucleus. Its components are among the most frequently mutated in cancer, and gain-of-function lesions in the cascade also cause developmental disorders. Here the module includes guanine nucleotide exchange factors that load RAS-family and RAP GTPases in haematopoietic cells, the RAC GTPase that links signalling to actin remodelling, upstream MAP3K and MAP4K kinases, and MAP2K2, the MEK-level kinase that phosphorylates ERK. Also represented are parallel and modulatory inputs — AKT1 for survival signalling, TGFB1 as an extracellular cue, and scaffolding through filamin A and β-arrestin, which couples receptor desensitisation to kinase activation.

Phosphoinositides are minor membrane lipids whose phosphorylation state marks compartments and recruits effectors, and the phosphatidylinositol signaling system covers the kinases, phosphatases and inositol phosphate enzymes that write and erase those marks. It governs vesicle traffic, endosome and autophagosome identity, receptor signalling and calcium release, so its disruption produces defects in membrane turnover and synaptic recycling. Class II and class III PI 3-kinases, represented here by PIK3C2A and PIK3C3, generate PI3P pools that nucleate endosomal and autophagic machinery, PIKFYVE converts PI3P to PI(3,5)P2 for late endosome and lysosome maturation, and the synaptic polyphosphoinositide phosphatase SYNJ1 dephosphorylates PI(4,5)P2 to uncoat vesicles, with mutations causing early-onset parkinsonism. Inositol monophosphatase recycles free inositol for resynthesis of the lipid, a step inhibited by lithium, linking this route to neuronal signalling and mood stabilisation.

The strongest signal in this group is a mature B lymphocyte identity programme: CD79A forms the signal-transducing module of the B cell antigen receptor, STAP1 is a B cell adaptor that couples receptor engagement to downstream kinases, BTLA is an inhibitory receptor that raises the threshold for lymphocyte activation, and P2RX5 and prepronociceptin are expressed in B lineage cells and used to distinguish them. Together these support antigen recognition, tuned activation and the restraint that prevents autoreactivity. Alongside them sit components of cell-surface signalling and adhesion more broadly — caveolin-2 and the angiomotin-family scaffold AMOTL2 at membrane and junctional sites, a G protein gamma subunit, the growth hormone receptor, and SMAD1 carrying bone morphogenetic protein signals to the nucleus, with the secreted BMP antagonist chordin-like 1 opposing them. The set thus mixes lymphocyte receptor signalling with receptor-mediated growth and morphogenetic control.</description>

Orderly duplication and division of a cell depends on the cyclin-CDK engine described here, together with the checkpoints that license each transition only once. Cyclin D-CDK4 and cyclin E-CDK2 relieve repression of E2F-dependent transcription, allowing entry into S phase; the MCM2-7 helicase complex, CDC6 and CDC45 license and fire replication origins, with CDC7-DBF4 driving initiation and PCNA supporting the replication machinery. Cyclin A- and cyclin B-CDK1 activity drives mitosis, held in check by WEE1 and PKMYT1 phosphorylation and released by CDC25 phosphatases. The spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BUB1, BUB1B and MAD2L1 restrain the anaphase-promoting complex until chromosomes are attached, after which separase cleaves cohesin to allow segregation. ATR-CHEK1 and CHEK2 signalling and the CDK inhibitors p21, p27 and p16 arrest cycling after DNA damage; their loss underlies genomic instability and tumour growth.

These genes mark the megakaryocyte-platelet arm of haematopoiesis and the signalling that supports it. Platelet factor 4 is the archetypal alpha-granule chemokine released on platelet activation, junction plakoglobin anchors the cytoskeletal junctions and desmosomal-type adhesion used by these cells, and the G protein alpha-z subunit couples platelet ADP and adrenergic receptors to inhibition of adenylate cyclase, lowering cyclic AMP to permit aggregation. Monoacylglycerol lipase supplies arachidonic acid for eicosanoid production in the same setting. Alongside them sit regulators of progenitor commitment and marrow stromal support: the transcription factors MEF2C and ZNF423, the chromatin-associated MLLT3, and PDGFRA with the secreted modulators CRIM1 and FSTL1, which tune growth factor and BMP/TGF-beta input. Together the set describes how progenitors are specified toward thrombopoiesis and how the resulting platelets achieve haemostasis; its failure underlies bleeding and thrombotic disorders.

Granulocyte maturation in the bone marrow, and the antimicrobial cargo that neutrophils acquire as they mature, is the theme here. Promyelocytes and myelocytes load their granules with proteins that will later be deployed against bacteria: a lipopolysaccharide-binding bactericidal protein of the BPI family, the adipokine-like secreted factor resistin, prokineticin 2, the soluble pattern-recognition molecule pentraxin 3, and a haematopoietic growth factor of the CLEC11A type that supports progenitor expansion. Alongside them sit regulators that hold inflammatory signalling in check, including the kinase-dead IRAK family member IRAK3, and transport and lipid-remodelling enzymes such as the organic cation/ergothioneine transporter SLC22A4 and a lysophospholipid acyltransferase. A CDK inhibitor of the INK4 family and a linker histone variant point to the exit from proliferation that accompanies terminal differentiation. Together these define innate myeloid effector capacity, whose loss leaves recurrent bacterial infection.

Every molecule that moves between nucleus and cytoplasm passes through the nuclear pore complex, the channel embedded in the nuclear envelope that both permits transport of RNA and proteins and enforces the compartment boundary that makes nuclear regulation possible. The listed nucleoporins fall into recognizable modules: the Y-shaped scaffold ring built from NUP107, NUP133, NUP160, NUP85, SEH1L and NUP37 anchors the structure to the membrane, while phenylalanine-glycine repeat proteins such as NUP62 and NUP54 line the central channel and create the selective permeability barrier. Directional traffic depends on the RAN GTPase gradient, with RANBP1 helping recycle RAN and the exportin XPO1 carrying leucine-rich signal-bearing cargoes out of the nucleus. The complex is disassembled and rebuilt at each mitosis, and mutations in scaffold nucleoporins cause tissue-restricted disease including steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome.

During open mitosis the nuclear envelope breaks down and the nuclear pore complex is taken apart, then rebuilt around chromatin as daughter nuclei form. The core structural unit here is the Y-shaped Nup107 inety-160 scaffold inety- NUP107, NUP133, NUP160, NUP85, NUP37, NUP43 and SEH1L inety- which forms the outer rings of the pore and, once pores are disassembled, relocates to kinetochores and spindle poles, where it contributes to microtubule attachment and spindle assembly. The same subcomplex nucleates postmitotic pore reassembly, so its loss produces both chromosome segregation errors and defective nuclear envelope reformation. Also represented are cohesin (SMC1A) holding sister chromatids together, the CDK-activating kinase and transcription factor IIH components CCNH and GTF2H1 that couple cell cycle kinase activity to transcription, and SLBP, which governs replication-dependent histone mRNA supply. This links nucleocytoplasmic transport machinery directly to mitotic progression.

HOX genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the embryo, and this grouping draws on members of the HOXA and HOXB clusters spanning anterior paralogues such as HOXA2, HOXA3 and HOXB2 through to more posterior HOXA9, HOXA10 and HOXB9. Their ordered, colinear expression instructs hindbrain segmentation, branchial arch and craniofacial derivatives, vertebral and limb pattern, and the regionalisation of the urogenital tract. The same factors act after development in haematopoietic progenitors, where HOXA9 and HOXA10 sustain self-renewal and proliferation; their inappropriate reactivation, often through mixed-lineage leukaemia fusions, drives acute leukaemia, while loss-of-function mutations produce limb and genital malformations. Activity depends on retinoic acid signalling upstream and on chromatin-level control by Polycomb and trithorax complexes to keep cluster expression appropriately restricted, with cofactors shaping DNA-binding specificity.

Intestinal crypt epithelium maintained by Wnt signalling is what these genes describe: a stem and progenitor programme of the colonic crypt base together with markers of the differentiating epithelium above it. It sustains the continuous renewal of the gut lining, and its inappropriate reactivation underlies colorectal adenoma and carcinoma, where the same transcripts serve as tumour markers. Several members are direct Wnt/beta-catenin targets s ASCL2 specifies and reinforces stem cell identity, AXIN2 and RNF43 act as negative feedback on the pathway itself, RNF43 by ubiquitinating Frizzled receptors, and EPHB2 expression follows the crypt-axis gradient that sorts cells to their correct position. CDCA7 links the programme to proliferation, while GPX2, CEACAM5, MUC3B and TSPAN8 reflect mucosal antioxidant defence, mucin production and the apical surface of the absorptive epithelium.</description>

Leukocytes only work if they reach the right tissue, and this grouping covers the receptors and cytoskeletal machinery that read chemoattractant gradients and convert them into directed cell migration. Chemokine receptors such as CCR1, CCR2 and CCR7 guide monocytes into inflamed tissue and route naive T cells and dendritic cells into lymph nodes; the complement receptor C3AR1 adds an innate anaphylatoxin cue, while S1PR1 senses the sphingosine-1-phosphate gradient that licenses lymphocyte egress from lymphoid organs into blood. Downstream, coronin-1A and the HEM1 component of the WAVE regulatory complex control actin remodelling needed for motility and immune synapse formation, and nuclear envelope and transcriptional components including SYNE2, GATA3 and LEF1 tie migration to lineage identity and survival. Loss of these functions produces immunodeficiency with impaired T cell trafficking, and their overuse drives inflammatory tissue infiltration and tumour cell dissemination.</description

This is a transcriptional signature of monocytes, the circulating phagocytes that patrol blood, sense microbial and tissue-damage signals, and give rise to macrophages and inflammatory dendritic cells. The genes define the cell's identity and its effector toolkit: pattern-recognition receptors including TLR2, TLR4 and NOD2 alongside the inflammasome sensor NLRP3, the LPS co-receptor CD14, scavenger receptors CD36, CD163 and STAB1, and complement and immunoglobulin Fc receptors that drive phagocytosis and opsonic clearance. Signalling runs through TYROBP/FCER1G with Src-family kinases and SYK, while CSF1R and CSF3R read growth factor cues for survival and differentiation, and SPI1, CEBPA, KLF4 and MAFB enforce the myeloid programme. Also present are the NADPH oxidase subunits for respiratory burst, lysosomal proteases, and S100A8/A9 alarmins. Such genes rise in inflammation and sepsis and mark monocyte expansion in blood transcriptome studies.

Blood coagulation seals vascular injury by converting circulating precursors into a fibrin-platelet plug, and the same machinery restrains bleeding without occluding healthy vessels. Represented here is the cellular side of that response: factor V as a cofactor for thrombin generation, the transglutaminase subunit F13A1 that cross-links fibrin to stabilise the clot, and the platelet and monocyte receptors CD36, PECAM1, ITGAM and P2RX1 that mediate adhesion, activation and calcium entry at a damaged surface. Intracellular transmission runs through the tyrosine kinases LYN and SYK with the immune adaptor FCER1G and the scaffold DOK2, tying haemostasis to myeloid signalling. Fibrinolysis and its control appear as the plasminogen activator receptor PLAUR alongside the serpins SERPINA1 and SERPINB2. Imbalance produces bleeding, thrombosis, or the coagulopathy that accompanies severe inflammation and sepsis.

Neutrophils find infection by smelling it: bacterial N-formylated peptides and mitochondrial peptides released by damaged tissue bind formyl peptide receptors, and the resulting chemotactic and antimicrobial response is among the fastest arms of innate immunity. Engagement of FPR1 triggers directed migration, degranulation and assembly of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, whose cytosolic regulatory subunits NCF1 and NCF2 are needed for the respiratory burst that kills ingested organisms; loss of these subunits causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection. Cytoskeletal reorganisation for chemotaxis runs through PAK1, calcium-dependent signalling through CAMK1, and immunoglobulin-mediated phagocytosis through the low-affinity Fc receptor FCGR2A, while SLC11A1 restricts metal availability to microbes inside the phagosome. Inhibitory and accessory receptors of myeloid cells set thresholds so that this destructive output stays proportionate to the stimulus.

axon guidance is the process by which a growing axon steers toward its correct target, reading attractive and repulsive cues in the extracellular environment and translating them into directed movement of the growth cone. It builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system, and errors in it produce miswired circuits and defects in commissure formation and nerve pathfinding. Here the cues are semaphorin family ligands acting through neuropilin co-receptors, whose signals converge on cytoskeletal effectors: collapsin response mediator protein family members regulate microtubule assembly, while Rho and Ras small GTPases with focal adhesion kinase and non-muscle myosin II control actin contractility and adhesion turnover at the leading edge. Fibrillar collagens provide the substrate and mechanical context for that migration. The same machinery is reused outside the nervous system for cell migration, vascular patterning, and tumour cell invasion.

Growing axons find their targets by reading attractive and repulsive cues in the tissue they traverse, and this collection captures the guidance step where extracellular signals are converted into steering of the growth cone. Wiring of the nervous system depends on it, and comparable signalling directs migrating cells and sprouting vessels, so defects produce miswired circuits and disordered migration. A semaphorin ligand and the neuropilin co-receptor supply the directional cue; focal adhesion kinase and Ras- and Rho-family GTPases relay it to adhesion sites and the actomyosin cortex, with non-muscle myosin IIB and the CRMP family protein DPYSL3 acting on cytoskeletal dynamics to turn or collapse the growth cone. Fibrillar collagens here represent the substratum and adhesive environment through which the process occurs, linking guidance to cell-matrix interaction rather than to soluble signalling alone.

Cells detect viral nucleic acids and convert that detection into an interferon-driven defensive state, and this group represents the sensing arm together with genes controlled by the interferon regulatory factor IRF2. Its outputs matter for clearing viral infection and for setting the threshold at which innate immunity tips into inflammation: TLR7 reads single-stranded RNA in endosomes, ZBP1 senses nucleic acid in the cytosol and can trigger programmed cell death, and RIPK2 relays signals from intracellular bacterial sensors. Downstream effectors include BST2, which tethers budding virions at the plasma membrane, the immunoproteasome subunit PSMB8 and the peptide transporter TAP1, which together supply peptides for MHC class I presentation to cytotoxic T cells, and USP18, which removes ISG15 and restrains interferon signalling. Chemokine and B cell survival factors such as CXCL16 and TNFSF13B link this response to adaptive immunity and to myeloid inflammation.

Detection of viral nucleic acid inside infected cells and the interferon-driven gene programme that follows are captured here, with IRF2 acting as a transcriptional gatekeeper that tunes how strongly those antiviral genes are expressed. The products do the actual defending: a cytosolic RNA sensor initiates interferon induction, a Z-nucleic acid sensor couples infection to inflammatory and necroptotic death, and CASP1 processes inflammatory cytokines. Downstream effectors restrict virus release from the cell surface, recruit T cells and NK cells via CXCL10, block viral translation, and rebuild the antigen-processing machinery through immunoproteasome subunits and TAP1-dependent peptide loading onto MHC class I. USP18 supplies negative feedback by limiting interferon receptor signalling. Too little of this output leaves cells permissive to infection; unrestrained activity drives interferonopathy and autoimmune tissue damage, with B cell survival factor production linking it to antibody responses.

complement activation (I) is the humoral arm of innate immunity that marks pathogens and damaged cells for destruction, drives inflammation, and clears immune complexes and debris from the circulation. Loss of it leaves recurrent pyogenic infection and lupus-like autoimmunity; loss of its brakes causes hemolysis and kidney injury, as in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome and hereditary angioedema. The genes trace the classical route from the C1q recognition subunits through the C1r/C1s proteases and C2 to cleavage of C3, alongside the alternative amplification loop supplied by factor B and factor D. Cleavage fragments engage the C3a and C5a receptors on myeloid cells to recruit and activate leukocytes, while C7 contributes to the lytic terminal complex. Regulators including factor H, factor I, CR1 and C1 inhibitor restrict activation to intended surfaces and protect host tissue.

Complement activation is the humoral arm of innate immunity that marks microbes and debris for destruction and recruits inflammatory cells to the site. The genes here trace the classical route, where the C1q recognition subunits bind antibody-coated or altered surfaces and the C1r/C1s proteases cleave C4 and C2 to build a C3-cleaving enzyme, together with the alternative route sustained by factor B and factor D. Cleavage of C3 opsonises the target for phagocytes bearing CR1, while the released C3a and C5a act through their receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1 to drive chemotaxis, vascular leak and mast cell activation; C7 contributes to the lytic membrane pore. Restraint is built in: C1 inhibitor, factor H and factor I limit activation to intended surfaces, and their loss causes hereditary angioedema, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome or macular degeneration, whereas deficiency of early components predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and lupus-like autoimmunity.

Complement activation is the humoral arm of innate immunity that tags microbes and damaged cells for lysis and phagocytic clearance while amplifying inflammation. The genes here span both the triggering proteases and the brakes: C1R and C1S form the catalytic subunits of the C1 complex that initiates the classical route on antibody-coated surfaces, factor B (CFB) drives the alternative amplification loop, and C3 is the shared hub whose cleavage deposits opsonin on target membranes and releases chemotactic fragments. C7 contributes to the membrane attack complex that punches pores in target cells. Regulation is equally represented, with factor H and factor I restraining C3 convertase activity and clusterin inhibiting terminal complex assembly, alongside vitamin K-dependent protein S linking this chemistry to coagulation and apoptotic cell clearance. Loss of such restraint underlies atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and age-related macular degeneration, while IL33 ties the response to tissue-damage alarm signalling.

golgi membrane (I) groups proteins resident in or trafficking through the Golgi apparatus, where secreted and membrane-bound cargo is glycosylated, lipid-modified and sorted to its destination. This compartment determines the composition of the cell surface and the secretome, so its enzymes set the glycan and sphingolipid identity of a cell and the range of signals it can send. Here the glycosyltransferases build lactosylceramide-derived glycosphingolipids and chondroitin sulfate chains, while sphingomyelin synthase and a lysophospholipid acyltransferase remodel membrane lipids that shape Golgi structure and downstream inflammatory mediators. Other members handle cargo selection and export: sortilin routes proteins to lysosomes and regulates neurotrophin receptor traffic, WLS is the dedicated carrier that loads Wnt ligands for secretion, and PDGFC is itself Golgi-processed growth factor cargo. Defects in such Golgi steps disturb Wnt-dependent patterning, lysosomal delivery and glycolipid balance.

Proteins gathered here share residence in the Golgi membrane, the sorting and finishing station where newly made proteins and lipids are glycosylated, modified and dispatched to their destinations. The set spans the main jobs done at that membrane: glycan elaboration by B3GNT5, which extends lacto/neolacto glycolipid chains, and CSGALNACT1, which initiates chondroitin sulfate chains on proteoglycan core proteins; lipid remodelling and headgroup transfer by LPCAT2 and by SGMS2, which synthesises sphingomyelin; cargo sorting by the receptor SORT1; and dedicated secretion machinery such as WLS, the carrier that loads lipid-modified Wnt ligands for release. Also present are secretory clients and membrane proteins in transit, including the growth factor PDGFC and the endosomal nucleic-acid sensor TLR8. Together they illustrate how Golgi membrane composition determines extracellular matrix quality, membrane lipid identity and the reach of secreted signals.

This grouping describes the transcriptional programme of immature myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow, the stage at which granulocyte, mast cell and erythroid potential is still being resolved and primary granule proteins are first made. Its hallmark products are the azurophilic granule enzymes myeloperoxidase and neutrophil elastase, together with the mast cell protease carboxypeptidase A3 and the promyelocyte membrane marker MS4A3, so the signature marks promyelocytes and their close relatives rather than mature blood cells. Lineage transcription factors TAL1 and NFE2 act alongside proliferative drive from CDK6 and niche cues such as JAG1, PDGFC and the stem cell growth factor CLEC11A, while SLC40A1 exports iron for haem synthesis. Loss or distortion of this programme underlies congenital neutropenias and is the state in which acute myeloid leukaemia blasts are arrested.

Glycerophospholipids are the backbone of every cellular membrane, and their metabolism sets membrane fluidity, curvature and the supply of lipid second messengers. The core activity here is the cycle of deacylation and reacylation that remodels phospholipid acyl chains: a cytosolic phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from the sn-2 position, generating the precursor for prostaglandins and leukotrienes as well as a lysophospholipid, while lysophospholipid acyltransferases such as LPCAT2 and MBOAT2 re-esterify fatty acids to restore the diacyl species. An acylglycerophosphate acyltransferase contributes to de novo synthesis from lysophosphatidic acid, and an oxysterol-binding protein family member links this chemistry to lipid transfer between organelle membranes. Through the eicosanoid arm the pathway feeds inflammation and platelet-activating factor production, so its regulation matters for immune signalling as much as for membrane biogenesis.

This grouping of secreted immune mediators and their receptor chains describes how leukocytes talk to one another to set the size, type and duration of an immune response. Colony-stimulating factors CSF2 and CSF3 drive granulocyte and macrophage production from marrow progenitors; IL7R signalling sustains T and B lymphocyte development and naive T cell survival; IL15 presented in trans by IL15RA supports natural killer and memory CD8 T cells; IL2RA marks activated and regulatory T cells as the high-affinity IL-2 receptor subunit. IFNG and the IL23A subunit of IL-23 push type 1 and Th17 inflammatory programmes, IL6 and LIF act through the shared gp130 chain on acute-phase and stromal responses, and IL10 restrains all of this. Most signal via JAK-STAT to reprogram transcription, and imbalance among them underlies autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and immunodeficiency.</description>}

These genes outline a mesenchymal, mechanoresponsive fibroblast programme in which YAP and its paralogue TAZ (WWTR1) convert cytoskeletal tension and matrix stiffness into transcription of matricellular and adhesion genes. CYR61 is a canonical YAP/TAZ target, and alongside collagen III, follistatin-like 1, caveolin-1 and VCAM1 it marks cells that build and remodel connective tissue and support leukocyte and progenitor traffic. Growth factor and cytokine receptors such as PDGFRA and OSMR, together with the chemokine CXCL12, define the stromal niche signals these cells emit and receive, while ERRFI1 restrains EGF receptor output and EPS8 couples receptor signalling to actin. The same circuitry drives wound repair and alveolar and vascular stromal maintenance, and its persistent activation underlies fibrosis and the stiff, invasion-permissive stroma of tumours.

Cells must stick to surfaces, to matrix and to each other, and this cell adhesion programme captures that biology as it is used by leukocytes, where adhesion is the prerequisite for migration, antigen recognition and cell-cell communication rather than for tissue architecture alone. Most members are T cell and immune-cell molecules: CD6, CD96 and LY9 mediate contacts with antigen-presenting cells and target cells, SELPLG engages selectins for rolling on activated endothelium, and PTPRC (CD45) and the kinases ZAP70 and PRKCQ convert receptor engagement at the contact site into activation. Cytoskeletal and scaffolding components such as CORO1A and PSTPIP1 couple adhesion receptors to actin, allowing stable synapse formation and polarised movement, while CD40LG and CXCR3 tie adhesive contact to helper function and tissue homing. Loss of these functions produces immunodeficiency, defective lymphocyte trafficking, or autoinflammatory disease.

enriched in monocytes (IV) is a transcriptional signature of blood monocytes and the macrophage lineage they feed, marking the myeloid cells that patrol tissue for microbes and damage, present antigen, and clear debris. Its members define what a monocyte is functionally: pattern-recognition receptors and their accessory proteins (TLR1, LY96, CARD9, LGALS3) that sense bacterial and fungal ligands; lysosomal and degradative enzymes such as CTSS, LYZ and RNASE6 that support phagocytosis; adhesion and chemotaxis machinery including CXCR2, DOCK5, MYO1F and PAK1 for migration into inflamed tissue; and inflammatory effectors and cytokine receptors such as PTGS2, PTX3, IL1R2, TNFRSF1B and TNFSF13B that shape the local response and B cell survival. Lineage transcription factors including HHEX and BCL6, together with CD4, CD68 and EMR1 surface markers, place the programme downstream of myeloid commitment. Expression of these genes rises in sepsis and chronic inflammation and falls with monocyte depletion.

A blood transcriptional module whose expression marks monocytes and closely related myeloid cells, useful as a readout of monocyte abundance and activation state in whole-blood profiling of infection, inflammation and autoimmunity. The genes describe what these cells do: pattern recognition and innate sensing through TLR1, LY96 and the CARD9 adaptor, phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation via CD68, CTSS, LYZ and RNASE6, antigen presentation components such as HLA-DMB, and receptors for cytokines and chemoattractants including TNFRSF1B, IL1R2, LTBR and CXCR2 that position the cell in inflamed tissue. Prostaglandin synthesis by PTGS2, the acute-phase pattern-recognition molecule PTX3, and lipid-handling enzymes such as ACSL1 reflect the secretory and metabolic reprogramming that follows activation, while BCL6 and HHEX contribute transcriptional control of myeloid differentiation. Together these define the circulating precursors of macrophages and inflammatory dendritic cells.

enriched in monocytes (surface) describes the plasma-membrane protein signature that distinguishes blood monocytes from other leukocytes, providing the receptors through which these cells sense infection, migrate into tissue, and mature into macrophages and dendritic cells. Its members are the handles used to identify and sort monocyte populations and to gauge inflammatory state in disease. The set is dominated by innate immune receptors and adhesion molecules: CD4 and the adhesion GPCR EMR1 mark the lineage, TNFRSF1B and LTBR transduce tumour necrosis factor family signals, IL1R2 acts as a decoy that damps interleukin-1 responses, and TNFSF13B (BAFF) is released to support B cell survival. Alongside these sit MHC class II accessory machinery for antigen presentation, an ITAM-coupled activating receptor, and lactate and sphingosine-1-phosphate transport proteins that link glycolytic metabolism and chemotactic egress to monocyte effector function.

This is a monocyte-enriched surface signature: a group of membrane proteins whose expression marks circulating monocytes and their macrophage progeny rather than lymphocytes or granulocytes. Such markers underpin the identification and sorting of monocyte subsets and define how these cells sense inflammation, migrate into tissue, and present antigen. The collection spans innate immune receptors and receptor modifiers, including a decoy interleukin-1 receptor that dampens IL-1 signalling, TNF receptor family members that transduce TNF and lymphotoxin cues, a source of the B cell survival factor BAFF, an MHC class II-associated chaperone subunit, and CD4 itself, which monocytes express at lower levels than T cells. Transporters and a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor add metabolic and trafficking capacity, linking the profile to glycolytic support of activation and to recruitment during infection, atherosclerosis, and chronic inflammation.

This transcriptional signature marks dendritic cells that have received a maturation stimulus and switched from antigen sampling to antigen presentation, the step that licenses naive T cell priming and therefore the initiation of adaptive immunity. The genes read as a mature myeloid activation programme: CD83 and the costimulatory molecule CD86 appear on the surface as the cell prepares to engage T cells, CXCL2 recruits neutrophils and other myeloid cells to the inflamed site, while IL1RN and the amino acid oxidase IL4I1 act as brakes that limit interleukin-1 signalling and dampen T cell proliferation, so the same programme carries its own restraint. Additional members including PRKCD, the Ras-family regulators RGL1 and RIN2, and SLAMF8 support the signalling and membrane remodelling that accompany activation. Signatures of this kind are used to gauge dendritic cell maturation in inflammation, vaccination and tumour immunity.

A T cell that recognises antigen does not commit to a response unless it receives a second, confirmatory signal, and CD28 costimulation is that signal. Engagement of CD28 by B7 ligands on activated antigen-presenting cells lowers the threshold for T cell receptor triggering, driving interleukin-2 production, clonal expansion, metabolic reprogramming and survival; without it an antigen-engaged T cell becomes anergic instead, which is how peripheral tolerance is maintained and why blocking this axis is used therapeutically in transplantation and autoimmunity. The accompanying machinery is the proximal receptor signalling apparatus: the Src-family kinase LCK, the transmembrane adaptor LAT and related membrane-anchored adaptors that nucleate signalling complexes, and the cytosolic adaptor GRAP2 that couples them onward to kinase and calcium pathways. SH2D1A links related costimulatory receptor signalling and is mutated in X-linked lymphoproliferative disease.

These genes form a brake system on leukocyte activation, tuning how strongly lymphocytes and myeloid cells respond to antigen receptor, Toll-like and cytokine receptor engagement. Restraint of this kind sets thresholds for activation, prevents autoimmunity and chronic inflammation, and is also what tumours exploit to blunt T cell responses, making several members attractive immunotherapy targets. Mechanistically the set mixes activating and dampening arms: VAV1 is a Rac/Rho exchange factor downstream of antigen receptors, while ARHGAP15 and ARHGAP4 act as GTPase-activating proteins that switch such Rho-family signalling off. DGKZ consumes diacylglycerol to terminate protein kinase C and Ras signalling; MAP4K1 (HPK1) phosphorylates the adaptor SLP-76 to disassemble receptor signalosomes; SIGIRR blocks interleukin-1 and Toll-like receptor output. LYN, HCLS1, LPXN and beta-arrestin 2 couple these events to cytoskeletal and inhibitory-receptor responses, with GATA3 shaping lymphoid identity.

This grouping describes lymphocyte activation within organised lymphoid tissue, the process by which antigen-experienced B and T cells are positioned, co-stimulated and driven toward antibody secretion. It underlies germinal centre reactions and the generation of plasma cells, and its components are the surface markers used to identify activated and malignant lymphoid cells. A stromal chemokine and an oxysterol-sensing receptor guide migration into and within follicles, while CD27 and the SLAM-family receptors LY9 and SLAMF7 provide co-stimulatory contacts between lymphocytes. Downstream survival signalling through an NF-κB-associated ubiquitin ligase, IL-15 support, and the transcription factor IRF4 commit cells to effector and plasma-cell fates, reflected here in immunoglobulin kappa transcripts. Interferon-responsive elements including a peptide transporter for MHC class I loading tie the same tissue to cytotoxic T cell surveillance; loss of these interactions produces immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses.

This grouping describes the extracellular and signalling cues that make cells migrate, the process behind wound repair, vessel remodelling and leukocyte recruitment. Secreted chemoattractants such as CCL2 and CXCL12 establish directional gradients that draw monocytes, lymphocytes and progenitor cells toward sites of injury or inflammation, while IGF1 with its binding protein IGFBP5 and the growth factor TGFB2 provide promigratory and matrix-remodelling signals to stromal and smooth muscle cells. Guidance is read through co-receptors including NRP1, and traction depends on the actomyosin machinery activated by the myosin light chain kinase MYLK. Matrix and basement membrane components such as laminin alpha-4 and the proteoglycan podocan supply the substrate and set limits on movement, with the nuclear receptor NR2F2 contributing transcriptional control in vascular cells. Persistent activation of these cues underlies fibrosis, atherosclerotic lesion formation and tumour invasion.

This grouping marks the early stages of B lymphocyte development, the process by which bone marrow progenitors commit to the B lineage and assemble a working antigen receptor before leaving for the periphery. EBF1 is the lineage-determining transcription factor here, while VPREB1 and VPREB3 encode surrogate light chain components that pair with immunoglobulin heavy chain to form the pre-B cell receptor, the checkpoint that tests whether a productive rearrangement has occurred. Loss of these steps blocks antibody production and leaves humoral immunity absent. Other members place the programme in its niche and its competing alternatives: BCL11B drives T cell rather than B cell fate, DLL1 provides Notch ligand signals from stroma, ICOSLG supports later T-dependent responses, and GAB1 with the NR4A nuclear receptors couples receptor engagement to proliferation, survival and activation-induced gene expression.

A module enriched in membrane proteins drawn largely from blood cell biology, mixing erythroid transporters with neutrophil and innate immune surface receptors. The erythroid side is coherent and specific: the anion exchanger and Rh-associated glycoprotein of the red cell membrane handle bicarbonate/chloride and ammonium movement, aquaporin-1 provides water permeability, ferroportin exports iron, and ALAS2 commits glycine and succinyl-CoA to heme synthesis, so these genes together define oxygen carriage, gas exchange and iron handling. Alongside them sit ABC transporters that efflux porphyrins and xenobiotics, complement C3a and C5a receptors that convert complement activation into chemotaxis and degranulation, and neutrophil granule proteins such as elastase and lactoferrin. Loss of individual members produces hemolytic anemia, spherocytosis, iron overload or disordered granulocyte function, placing this collection at the interface of membrane transport and myeloid/erythroid differentiation.

This is a heterogeneous grouping rather than a single mechanism, but its members converge on the theme of cell-type-specific differentiation and the signalling that supports it. Transcriptional regulators dominate one arm: SOX15 and TCF15 act in mesodermal and skeletal muscle lineage specification, while CDKN2B encodes a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor of the INK4 family that restrains G1 progression and links differentiation to cell cycle exit, a function lost in many tumours. A neuronal arm includes the RNA-binding protein ELAVL3, which stabilises transcripts in neurons, the microtubule plus-end tracking protein MAPRE3, and the gamma isoform of protein kinase C, whose mutation causes spinocerebellar ataxia. Others reflect blood and vascular specialisation: GP1BB contributes to the platelet von Willebrand factor receptor, and FUT7 builds the fucosylated selectin ligands that let leukocytes roll on endothelium.

Double positive thymocytes are the CD4+CD8+ stage of T cell development in the thymic cortex, where a newly assembled αβ T cell receptor is tested against self peptide-MHC to decide whether the cell dies, becomes a helper lineage cell, or becomes a cytotoxic one. The genes here mark that stage and its signalling apparatus: CD3E and the adaptor LAT couple the receptor to downstream kinases, CD4 is the coreceptor read out during lineage choice, and UBASH3A dampens receptor signalling, tuning the strength that distinguishes positive from negative selection. BCL11B and TCF4 supply the transcriptional programme that commits and maintains T lineage identity, while SH2D1A links receptor engagement to later costimulatory responses. Failure of this checkpoint yields either an empty peripheral T cell repertoire or escape of self-reactive clones and autoimmunity, and the same programme is subverted in T lineage leukaemias.

Cells detect viral nucleic acid and respond by switching on a broad antiviral state; this is the type I interferon response, the first line of defence that restrains virus replication before adaptive immunity arrives. Sensing by the cytosolic RNA helicase IFIH1 and amplification through IRF7 and STAT1 drive transcription of interferon-stimulated genes whose products act directly on the infection: IFIT1 sequesters uncapped viral RNAs, RSAD2 (viperin) impairs budding and replication, IFITM1 blocks membrane fusion at entry, HERC5 conjugates ISG15 to newly made proteins, and TAP1 feeds peptides into MHC class I for display to cytotoxic T cells. USP18 removes ISG15 and dampens receptor signalling, a brake whose loss causes interferonopathy. Too little of this programme leaves severe viral susceptibility; chronic activation contributes to lupus and related autoimmune disease.

These genes converge on the regulation of gene expression at the steps between transcription and protein turnover. Cyclin T2 partners CDK9 in the elongation kinase that releases paused RNA polymerase II, while cyclin C works within the Mediator kinase module that gates promoter engagement, and ARID4A and SP3 act on chromatin and promoter DNA to set which genes are read. The CLK1 kinase phosphorylates SR-family splicing factors, and a splicing regulator of that family is present, linking transcriptional output to how transcripts are spliced. A second arm handles protein fate: RING ubiquitin ligases, a proteasomal ATPase subunit, and the deubiquitinase USP1, which removes monoubiquitin from FANCD2 and PCNA and so restrains DNA damage tolerance. Together the set reflects how proliferating cells couple transcriptional programmes, RNA processing, and regulated degradation, with membrane and mitochondrial components at the periphery.

inositol phosphate metabolism covers the making and breaking of phosphorylated inositol lipids and soluble inositol phosphates, the signalling currency that tells a membrane which compartment it is and which proteins may bind it. It matters because phosphoinositide identity governs endocytosis, autophagosome formation, endosome maturation and synaptic vesicle recycling, and because lithium's therapeutic action converges on inositol monophosphatase, which recycles free inositol for renewed lipid synthesis. The class II and class III PI 3-kinases generate PI3P on early endosomes and nascent autophagosomes, PIKFYVE converts it to PI(3,5)P2 to drive late endosome and lysosome function, and the synaptojanin phosphatase strips phosphates to release clathrin coats after vesicle budding. Effector modules such as FYVE-domain adaptors read these marks. Loss of this balance produces neurodegeneration, myopathy and lysosomal storage-like defects in membrane traffic.

Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and recycles the phosphorylated inositol species that mark membranes for identity and release calcium-mobilising second messengers. Its outputs govern how vesicles are sorted, how endosomes and autophagosomes mature, and how receptor signalling is terminated, so cells depend on it for membrane traffic as much as for signal transduction. Lipid kinases such as PIK3C2A, the class III enzyme PIK3C3 and the 5-kinase PIKFYVE phosphorylate inositol head groups on endosomal and autophagic membranes, while the polyphosphoinositide phosphatase synaptojanin removes phosphates to drive clathrin uncoating at synapses, and inositol monophosphatase completes the cycle by freeing myo-inositol for resynthesis. Loss of this turnover is damaging in neurons in particular: synaptojanin mutations cause parkinsonism and epileptic encephalopathy, and lithium acts partly by inhibiting the monophosphatase step.

DNA in the cytosol is a danger signal: it means a virus, an intracellular bacterium, or the cell's own damaged genome has breached a compartment boundary, and innate activation by cytosolic DNA sensing is how that breach is converted into an inflammatory response. The output is twofold. One arm assembles an inflammasome, in which the DNA receptor AIM2 recruits the adaptor ASC to activate caspase-1, maturing IL-1beta and driving pyroptotic death of the infected cell. The other arm is transcriptional, with NF-kB relieved of IkBalpha restraint and IRF7 driving type I interferon, which together induce IL-6 and the chemokines CXCL10, CCL5 and CCL4 that recruit monocytes, NK cells and activated T cells. ZBP1 links the same nucleic acid cues to necroptotic death. Chronic or self-DNA-driven activation of this axis underlies interferonopathies and contributes to autoimmune and sterile inflammation.

enriched in G-protein coupled receptors describes cell-surface receptor signalling through heterotrimeric G proteins, the route by which hormones, lipid mediators, chemokines and proteases are converted into second-messenger changes inside a cell. It matters because this receptor class governs vascular tone, platelet activation, inflammation and leukocyte traffic, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. The members span several arms of the system: a beta-adrenergic receptor and prostaglandin E and D receptors that raise cyclic AMP, a thrombin-activated protease receptor and a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor coupled to calcium and cytoskeletal responses, and chemokine ligands that recruit T and NK cells. Downstream effectors complete the circuit, with an inositol trisphosphate receptor releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores and a phosphodiesterase terminating cyclic AMP signals, so signal termination is as much a feature here as initiation.

This grouping is organised around signalling through G-protein coupled receptors, the largest family of cell-surface sensors and the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. Ligand binding here is diverse: catecholamines at the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, thrombin cleaving the protease-activated receptor F2R, prostaglandins D2 and E2 at PTGDR and PTGER2, sphingosine-1-phosphate at S1PR5, and the chemokines CCL5 and XCL1 acting on leukocyte receptors, with GPR18 as an orphan-like lipid-responsive member. Downstream components define the second-messenger arms: ITPR3 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores following phospholipase C activation, while PDE4D hydrolyses cAMP and so sets the duration of Gs-coupled responses. Together these mediate smooth muscle tone, platelet and endothelial responses to vascular injury, inflammatory mediator production, and the recruitment and trafficking of immune cells.

These genes mark the erythroid-megakaryocytic branch of hematopoiesis, the programme by which bone marrow progenitors commit to making red cells and platelets rather than lymphoid or granulocytic fates. Its transcriptional core is a TAL1-GFI1B axis that drives erythroid gene expression while restraining progenitor proliferation; loss of either blocks red cell production, and GFI1B mutation causes a bleeding disorder with malformed platelets. Downstream effectors give the lineage its identity: hemogen accompanies erythroid maturation, GMPR shapes the guanine nucleotide pool of erythroid cells, and the XK membrane protein partners with the Kell blood group antigen, its absence producing McLeod syndrome with acanthocytic red cells. Cytoskeletal and adhesion components such as ACTN1 and TNS1 support megakaryocyte and platelet structure, ACTN1 mutations causing inherited macrothrombocytopenia, while MS4A3 marks the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor compartment nearby.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to arrive at infected or damaged tissue, and their recruitment depends on a panel of chemoattractant receptors that read the chemical signature of injury and convert it into directed migration. Most of the members are G protein-coupled receptors tuned to distinct cues: complement C5a, bacterial and mitochondrial formylated peptides, short-chain fatty acids from microbial fermentation, platelet-activating factor, IL-8, thrombin-derived protease signals, and the chemokine PROK2, with a G protein gamma subunit representing the shared heterotrimeric transduction step. Receptor engagement drives actin remodelling and chemotaxis up the gradient, together with adhesion, degranulation and the oxidative burst once the cell arrives. Insufficient recruitment leaves bacterial and fungal infection unchecked; excessive or poorly resolved recruitment underlies tissue damage in sepsis, acute lung injury, gout and chronic inflammatory disease, making these receptors long-standing anti-inflammatory drug targets.

cell adhesion, membrane describes the junctional machinery that holds epithelial sheets together and gives them apical-basal polarity and barrier function. This organisation is what allows epithelia to line the gut, airway, breast and kidney, to separate compartments of differing composition, and to restrain cell movement; its loss during epithelial-mesenchymal transition accompanies carcinoma invasion and metastasis. E-cadherin and P-cadherin with the plakoglobin linker build adherens junctions anchored to the keratin and actin cytoskeleton, while claudins 3, 4 and 7 with the lipolysis-stimulated receptor seal tight junctions and set paracellular permeability. EPCAM and the protease inhibitor SPINT1 tune junction turnover and pericellular proteolysis, and the transcription factor EHF maintains the epithelial identity that sustains the whole program. Stratifin and BIK tie adhesion status to checkpoint control and apoptotic sensitivity, so that detached or disorganised cells are eliminated.

Epithelial sheets hold together through membrane-based cell adhesion, and this collection of junctional and surface proteins defines that organization. E-cadherin and P-cadherin with the plaque protein junction plakoglobin build calcium-dependent adherens and desmosomal contacts, while claudins 3, 4 and 7 together with the lipolysis-stimulated lipoprotein receptor seal tight junctions and set paracellular permeability; EPCAM and the keratin 19 cytoskeleton mark the epithelial state. EHF is a transcription factor that sustains this epithelial identity programme, and SPINT1 restrains membrane serine proteases that would otherwise remodel the surface. The result is a polarized, cohesive barrier separating tissue compartments, with 14-3-3 sigma and BIK linking adhesion status to proliferation and apoptosis. Loss of cadherin and claudin function underlies the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition seen in carcinoma invasion and in barrier failure of gut, lung and breast epithelium.

cell cell adhesion is the machinery that binds epithelial cells to one another and to their basement membrane, creating the sealed, polarized sheets that line skin, gut, lung and glands. Without it epithelia lose barrier function and cohesion: cells detach, tissues blister, and tumour cells acquire the migratory, invasive behaviour of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, which is why loss of E-cadherin is a classic marker of carcinoma progression. Three junction types are represented. Classical cadherins CDH1 and CDH3, linked through junctional plakoglobin to the cytoskeleton, mediate calcium-dependent homophilic contact; claudins CLDN3, CLDN4 and CLDN7 build the tight-junction strands that set paracellular permeability and apicobasal polarity; and laminin-332 with integrins β6β4 anchors basal keratinocytes to the matrix via hemidesmosomes. Mutations in the laminin-332 chains cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa, showing how directly adhesion translates into tissue integrity.

Epithelial sheets hold together and stay sealed through the adhesion machinery represented here, which keeps cells attached to their neighbours and polarised so that a tissue can act as a barrier. E-cadherin and P-cadherin mediate calcium-dependent contacts at adherens junctions, with junction plakoglobin linking the cadherin tails to the cytoskeleton, while claudin-3, -4 and -7 build the tight junction strands that control paracellular flux of ions and solutes. Laminin-332 subunits together with the integrins that bind it anchor basal keratinocytes and other epithelia to the basement membrane, so cell-cell and cell-matrix attachment are described together. Loss of E-cadherin and gain of these integrins accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and carcinoma invasion, and mutations in the laminin-332 chains cause junctional epidermolysis bullosa with fragile, blistering skin.

This grouping of membrane and endoplasmic reticulum proteins brings together products that reside in, or act at, cellular membranes and the early secretory pathway, and it reads as a snapshot of how cells build lipid-rich membranes, present receptors at the surface, and couple that surface to signalling. DHCR24 catalyses a late sterol reduction step in cholesterol synthesis on the ER membrane, supplying the lipid that sets membrane fluidity; TMED6 belongs to the p24 family of cargo receptors that shuttle secretory proteins between ER and Golgi; MRVI1 sits in the ER membrane and links cGMP signalling to inositol trisphosphate receptor calcium release in smooth muscle and platelets. Others are plasma-membrane receptors and adaptors: endoglin as a TGF-beta co-receptor in endothelium, CD72 on B cells, EMP2, and cytoplasmic partners such as focal adhesion kinase and Ras-family regulators that translate adhesion and receptor engagement into cytoskeletal and transcriptional responses.

The membrane-rich surface that defines the kidney proximal tubule is what this grouping of plasma membrane proteins describes: a brush border studded with endocytic receptors, peptidases and solute carriers that reclaims filtered protein and small molecules before urine leaves the nephron. Megalin and cubilin together form the multiligand receptor complex that retrieves albumin, vitamin-binding proteins and hormones from the filtrate, and their loss causes low-molecular-weight proteinuria and vitamin deficiency. Alongside them sit apical ectoenzymes such as aminopeptidase A, organic anion and urate-handling transporters of the SLC17 family, a sodium-dependent betaine/GABA carrier, and cytosolic enzymes of tubular amino acid and carnitine metabolism including AGXT2, BBOX1 and NAT8. PAX2 marks the developmental origin of this epithelium. Collectively the set links transepithelial reabsorption to systemic handling of urate, osmolytes and micronutrients.

This grouping of plasma membrane-enriched proteins reads as the transport and receptor machinery of the kidney proximal tubule, the epithelium that reclaims filtered solutes before urine leaves the nephron. Its members carry out apical uptake of amino acids, organic anions and proteins: the heavy subunit of the cystine and dibasic amino acid transporter, whose loss causes cystinuria with recurrent kidney stones; a sodium-phosphate-family organic anion exchanger linked to serum urate and gout risk; a betaine/GABA carrier; and the giant endocytic receptor cubilin, which with megalin retrieves albumin and vitamin-carrier complexes from the filtrate. Accompanying them are tubular metabolic and modifying enzymes, including an aminotransferase of the kynurenine pathway, an acetyltransferase acting on cysteine conjugates, a membrane aminopeptidase, and a potassium channel supporting basolateral membrane potential and thus the driving force for solute reabsorption.

This grouping centres on membrane traffic through the Golgi and the machinery that buds, tethers and fuses transport vesicles, the route by which secretory and lysosomal cargo reaches its destination. Its outputs are secretion, receptor recycling and delivery of hydrolases such as cathepsin D to lysosomes; when it falters, cargo is mislocalised and organelle identity degrades. A large GEF acting on ARF GTPases recruits the COPI coat for retrograde transport, a coat subunit is represented directly, and an NSF attachment protein supports SNARE complex disassembly after fusion, while a dynamin GTPase pinches off budding carriers. Heterotrimeric G protein subunits and phosphatase and kinase components add regulatory input, and lipid-modifying enzymes including a neuropathy target esterase-type lysophospholipase and an S-acyl protein thioesterase tune membrane lipid and palmitoylation states that govern where proteins reside.

This grouping centres on nuclear regulation of chromatin, transcription and genome maintenance, with a second arm in phosphoinositide-dependent membrane traffic and cytoskeletal signalling. The chromatin remodelling ATPase SMARCA5 positions nucleosomes for replication and repair, TLK1 couples histone chaperone activity to replication timing, and the deubiquitinase USP1 removes ubiquitin from PCNA and FANCD2 to terminate translesion synthesis and Fanconi anaemia-pathway repair; ZMYM2, ATF2 and the elongation/splicing regulators TCERG1 and SFRS12 shape transcriptional output and mRNA processing. Alongside these, PIKFYVE generates PI(3,5)P2 for endosome and lysosome maturation, ACBD3 and PLEKHF2 organise Golgi and endosomal membranes, and ROCK1 drives actomyosin contractility during cell shape change and apoptotic blebbing. Metabolic components including glycogen debranching and pantothenate kinase feed cofactor and carbohydrate supply, linking these regulatory activities to cell growth, division and stress recovery.

This grouping brings together nuclear regulators of chromatin and transcription with a smaller set of membrane and metabolic enzymes, and is best read as a broad housekeeping module supporting gene expression and genome maintenance. On the nuclear side, SMARCA5 is the ATPase of ISWI-type nucleosome remodelling complexes that space nucleosomes during replication and repair; TLK1 phosphorylates histone chaperones to couple chromatin assembly to S phase; USP1 removes ubiquitin from FANCD2 and PCNA to terminate DNA damage tolerance and interstrand crosslink repair; ATF2, TCERG1 and SFRS12 act on transcription and splicing, and ZMYM2 and RNF6 contribute transcriptional repression and ubiquitin ligation. Alongside these, PIKFYVE generates PI(3,5)P2 for endolysosomal membrane dynamics, ACBD3 organises Golgi signalling, and AGL and PANK3 serve glycogen debranching and coenzyme A synthesis. Loss of such functions impairs replication-coupled chromatin assembly, repair fidelity and basic metabolic supply.

This grouping centres on protein ubiquitination and its reversal, the tagging system that decides which proteins are degraded, relocalised or switched in activity. Ubiquitin ligases and conjugating enzymes here include an E3 that recognises destabilising N-terminal residues for proteasomal turnover, a RING-type ligase, and an E2 conjugating enzyme, while a deubiquitinase counteracts them by removing ubiquitin from substrates in DNA damage tolerance, where its loss disturbs translesion synthesis and Fanconi anaemia pathway regulation. Alongside these sit growth-signalling components — a small GTPase of the RAS family, a phosphoinositide 3-kinase, and the S6 kinase acting downstream of mTOR — linking ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover to the control of cell growth and proliferation. Also represented are RNA-binding and signal recognition particle functions, indicating that ubiquitination regulates proteins across transcription, splicing and cotranslational targeting rather than one route.

These are the proteins that make the endosomal-lysosomal system work as the cell's degradative compartment: acid hydrolases, lipid-binding cofactors, and the sorting machinery that delivers them. Cathepsins B, D, H and S are lysosomal proteases that break down internalised and autophagic cargo, acid alpha-glucosidase digests glycogen, and prosaposin gives rise to the saposins that present sphingolipids to their degrading enzymes, while NPC2 shuttles cholesterol out of the lumen. Delivery and trafficking depend on the mannose-6-phosphate receptor relative sortilin and on clathrin adaptor subunits, and CD68 marks the lysosomal membrane of macrophages, where SLC11A1 pumps divalent metals across the phagosome to restrict intracellular bacteria. Loss of individual hydrolases or lipid transporters produces lysosomal storage disease, linking this compartment to autophagy, antigen processing, cholesterol handling and innate defence.

T cell differentiation covers the developmental program that turns a thymic progenitor into a mature, antigen-responsive T lymphocyte, and the signalling machinery that decides at each step whether a cell survives, matures, or is deleted. It is what gives the body its helper and cytotoxic compartments; its failure produces immunodeficiency, while its miscalibration permits autoimmunity or T cell leukemia. The genes describe both control layers: transcriptional commitment through BCL11B and TCF7, which enforce T lineage identity and block alternative fates, and proximal receptor signalling through the tyrosine kinases ITK and TXK, the RasGRP1 exchange factor, and CD28 costimulation, which convert antigen and costimulatory input into activation. Negative regulators such as UBASH3A set the threshold for that response, and SH2D1A links receptor engagement to help delivered to B cells during antibody responses.

Thymic progenitors become functional T lymphocytes through a programme of lineage commitment and receptor-driven selection, and these genes mark that route. Its output is the naive T cell repertoire that underpins adaptive cellular immunity; failure produces immunodeficiency, while loss of the checkpoints on receptor signalling permits autoimmunity. BCL11B enforces T cell identity and prevents progenitors from diverting to other lineages, while TCF7 acts downstream of Wnt signals to sustain the naive and memory state. Signal transduction from the antigen receptor runs through the tyrosine kinases ITK and TXK and the Ras activator RASGRP1, converting receptor engagement into proliferation and differentiation decisions; CD28 supplies the costimulatory second signal and UBASH3A dampens receptor output. SH2D1A couples signalling in T cells to help for B cells, linking this developmental programme to antibody responses.

Secreted proteins that act in the space between cells, combining extracellular matrix structure and turnover with humoral innate immune recognition. Structural and matrix-binding components such as laminin alpha-2, latent TGF-beta binding protein 2, the adhesion molecule FLRT2 and IGFBP7 shape basement membranes and store growth factors, while MMP8 and MMP9 cleave collagen and other matrix substrates and TIMP2 restrains them, setting the balance that governs wound healing, leukocyte transit through tissue and tumour invasion. Alongside them are neutrophil-derived and mucosal secretory factors: proteinase 3, the protease inhibitor SLPI, ficolin-1 and properdin, which opsonise microbes and stabilise the alternative complement convertase, linking pathogen recognition to complement amplification. Together these activities describe an inflamed or repairing extracellular compartment, where granulocyte degranulation, complement activation and matrix degradation occur at the same site and failure of the inhibitory arm yields tissue destruction.

These genes mark the differentiated absorptive and secretory epithelium of the gastrointestinal tract, the barrier layer that absorbs nutrients, detoxifies luminal xenobiotics and presents a glycan-coated surface to the microbiota. Adhesion and junctional components such as EPCAM and FERMT1 hold the sheet together, while lineage transcription factors including FOXA3 and KLF5 drive and maintain the differentiated state; loss of these programmes underlies barrier failure, inflammatory bowel disease and the dedifferentiation seen in colorectal cancer, where CEACAM and galectin-4 expression is routinely used as an epithelial marker. A large glycosyltransferase and fucosylation component (B3GNT3, B3GNT5, FUT3, GMDS, ST3GAL6) builds the mucin and blood-group-related glycans of the apical surface. Additional members handle lipid binding and handling, iron export, oxidative defence through GPX2 and NOX1, and nuclear-receptor-driven drug metabolism.

A grouping of membrane transport proteins dominated by solute carriers that move anions, nutrients and organic solutes across epithelial membranes. Several members act in the kidney proximal tubule and liver, where SLC13A1 handles sulfate uptake, SLC17A1 and SLC17A3 export urate and organic anions into urine, SLC28A1 takes up pyrimidine nucleosides, and SLC6A13 moves GABA and betaine in a sodium- and chloride-dependent manner; variation in the urate transporters shifts serum urate and gout risk. Reabsorptive capacity is complemented by CUBN, the endocytic receptor that retrieves filtered vitamin B12 complexes and low-molecular-weight proteins, and by PAX2, the transcription factor that specifies kidney and urinary tract development. Other members reflect neural membrane biology, including the potassium channel-interacting protein KCNIP4 and the synaptic adhesion molecule neuroligin-1, so the collection spans transport in secretory epithelia and electrical signalling at synapses.

Messenger RNAs are capped, spliced and quality-checked in the nucleus, then handed through the nuclear pore to the cytoplasm, and these genes span both ends of that handoff. Structural nucleoporins of the Y-shaped outer ring and the inner ring, together with phenylalanine-glycine channel components, build the transport conduit through which ribonucleoprotein cargo and proteins pass, setting the permeability barrier that keeps nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments distinct. The RNA-side factors act at the cap and the 3' end: the small cap-binding subunit marks new transcripts for processing and export, the stem-loop binding protein handles the non-polyadenylated histone mRNAs made during S phase, and an exon junction complex-associated factor licenses nonsense-mediated decay of transcripts bearing premature stop codons. Together this couples transcript maturation and surveillance to nucleocytoplasmic traffic, gene expression output, and mitotic nuclear envelope reassembly.

This grouping brings together cell cycle regulators with nucleotide-binding and ATP-dependent activities, spanning the controls that license division, chromosome segregation and the destruction of regulatory proteins at defined transitions. Ordered progression depends on timed proteolysis, and several members supply it: proteasome subunits degrade cyclins and inhibitors, while a cullin scaffold and the NEDD8-activating enzyme subunit UBA3, together with a COP9 signalosome component, set ubiquitin ligase activity. Chromosome biology is represented by the cohesin subunit RAD21, which holds sister chromatids together until anaphase, by the mitotic kinases NEK7 and TLK1, and by histone deacetylase-dependent transcriptional repression. An AAA-ATPase involved in membrane scission links the programme to the final separation of daughter cells. Loss of such controls produces aneuploidy and unchecked proliferation, the route by which cell cycle failure becomes cancer.

Serum response factor, working with its coactivator myocardin and driven by changes in actin polymerization, switches on the contractile gene programme that defines smooth muscle cells. The genes here are that programme's output: smooth muscle actins, myosin heavy chain and its activating kinase MYLK, tropomyosins, and the actin-binding regulators caldesmon, transgelin, palladin and supervillin, together with calcium-handling and caveolar membrane components such as phospholamban and caveolin-2. Their expression gives vascular, airway and gut smooth muscle the ability to generate and sustain tone. Because the pathway reads the state of the actin cytoskeleton through G-actin sequestration of MRTF coactivators, mechanical and growth factor cues feed directly into contractile identity; loss of this output underlies the dedifferentiated, synthetic smooth muscle phenotype seen in atherosclerosis, restenosis and aortic aneurysm.

Serum response factor, partnered with myocardin-family coactivators, drives a battery of cytoskeletal and actin-associated genes that together build the contractile apparatus of smooth muscle. This programme defines the differentiated smooth muscle phenotype in vessels, gut and airway, and its loss underlies the switch to a proliferative, synthetic state seen in atherosclerosis, restenosis and vascular remodelling. The targets encode the machinery itself: smooth muscle actins, myosin heavy and light chains, tropomyosins, and the kinase that phosphorylates regulatory light chain to initiate contraction, alongside actin-binding regulators such as caldesmon, leiomodin and synaptopodin-2 and the adhesion proteins vinculin, tensin and sorbin-domain scaffolds that couple stress fibres to focal adhesions. Because actin polymerisation itself releases the coactivator to enter the nucleus, the pathway forms a feedback loop in which cytoskeletal tension and mechanical load sustain their own transcriptional output.

Antigen presentation and endosomal nucleic acid sensing are grouped here as the recognition arm of immunity. Class I molecules, including HLA-A, -B and -C plus the non-classical HLA-E, -F and -G, display peptides from within the cell to CD8 T cells and to NK receptors, while class II products of the HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP loci present exogenous peptides to CD4 T cells; the invariant chain CD74 chaperones class II and holds its groove until loading in the endosome, and CD4 itself stabilises the class II-T cell receptor encounter. TLR7 and TLR8 report single-stranded RNA from viruses and dying cells in the same endolysosomal compartment, driving interferon and inflammatory cytokine output. Together these determine self versus non-self discrimination, graft compatibility, and susceptibility to autoimmune disease, with TLR7 signalling implicated in lupus.

Intracellular transport covers the routing of proteins, membranes and nucleic acids between compartments, the logistics without which secretion, receptor turnover and nuclear-cytoplasmic communication all fail. The genes span the main stations of that route: signal recognition particle components and SEC63 that deliver nascent chains into the endoplasmic reticulum, clathrin adaptors and phosphoinositide kinases such as PIK3C2A and PIKFYVE that shape endosomal carriers, the ESCRT ATPase VPS4B that severs vesicles into multivesicular bodies, and exocyst subunit EXOC1 that tethers vesicles at the plasma membrane. Nucleoporins NUP107 and NUP133 form the scaffold through which macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope, while G3BP2 links transport to stress granule dynamics and mRNA localisation. Also represented are centrosomal and cytoskeletal regulators that position organelles. Disruption of these steps produces lysosomal storage, ciliopathy and secretory defects.

Moving proteins, membranes and cargo between compartments is the logistical backbone of a eukaryotic cell, and intracellular transport covers the steps by which newly made proteins enter the secretory pathway, vesicles bud and fuse, endosomes mature, and macromolecules cross the nuclear envelope. Without it, secretion and receptor turnover fail and misfolded protein accumulates. Distinct arms are represented here: a signal recognition particle subunit and the SEC63 translocon component direct cotranslational entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, where TMX1 assists oxidative folding; nucleoporins of the NUP107-133 scaffold form part of the nuclear pore for nucleocytoplasmic exchange; an exocyst subunit targets vesicles to the plasma membrane; clathrin-associated CLINT1 supports endocytic uptake. Phosphoinositide kinases PIK3C2A and PIKFYVE generate the lipid marks that specify endosomal identity, read by FYVE-domain proteins, while the AAA-ATPase VPS4B recycles ESCRT machinery during multivesicular body formation.

Membrane traffic and organelle remodelling form the common thread here: newly folded cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles built from SEC23A and SEC24B, is delivered through early endosomes marked by the tethering factor EEA1, and reaches the plasma membrane by SNARE-directed fusion, with STXBP3 acting among the Sec1/Munc18-family regulators of that step. Lipid composition and cytoskeletal geometry are managed alongside cargo flow: the inositol phosphatase SYNJ1 dephosphorylates PI(4,5)P2 to uncoat vesicles after endocytosis, TMEM30A serves as the accessory subunit that allows P4-ATPase flippases to translocate aminophospholipids across bilayers, and the microtubule-severing ATPase SPAST shapes tubules and axonal microtubule arrays. Additional members touch nuclear pore transport, transcriptional control by RB1, and ADAM9-mediated ectodomain shedding, linking secretory and endocytic capacity to cell surface signalling, neuronal maintenance and proliferation control.

These genes outline the transcriptional and structural programme that gives absorptive epithelium of the gut and kidney tubule its identity: a polarized brush-border cell that moves solutes across a sealed barrier. HNF4G, TFAP2C and SIX4 act as lineage-directing transcription factors, while CLDN2 builds a cation- and water-permeable tight junction pore that sets paracellular leakiness, and SLC3A1 supplies the heavy subunit of the transporter that reabsorbs cystine and dibasic amino acids — its loss causes cystinuria with kidney stones. Scaffolding and PDZ-domain proteins such as USH1C (harmonin), GIPC2 and the clarin-family membrane protein CLRN3 organize apical membrane and microvillar structure, and the E3 ligase RNF186 restrains inflammatory signalling in intestinal epithelium, a link that makes this module relevant to ulcerative colitis susceptibility and to barrier failure more broadly.

The Ran GTPase gradient that governs nuclear transport in interphase is reused in mitosis to tell a cell where chromosomes are, and this pathway covers that use. Because the nuclear envelope has broken down, RanGTP generated on chromatin marks the chromosomal neighbourhood, releasing importin-bound spindle assembly factors such as TPX2 from KPNA2 so that microtubule nucleation and branching occur near chromosomes rather than at random; RANBP1 helps keep the gradient steep. Released TPX2 activates Aurora A, while Aurora B, PLK1 and the kinesins KIF2C and KIF15 build and correct kinetochore-microtubule attachments, BUB1B enforces the spindle assembly checkpoint, and separase and the APC/C-associated UBE2S drive the transition to anaphase and mitotic exit. Loss of this spatial control gives multipolar or misaligned spindles, chromosome missegregation and the aneuploidy typical of tumour cells.</description>

Cells detect viral nucleic acid and respond before any antibody exists, and these genes are the effector arm of that innate antiviral response. Most are interferon-stimulated products whose induction converts an exposed cell into a hostile environment for replication: oligoadenylate synthetases sense double-stranded RNA and trigger RNase L-mediated RNA degradation, the kinase PKR shuts down cap-dependent translation through eIF2α phosphorylation, IFIT1 sequesters improperly capped viral transcripts, viperin interferes with viral replication at membranes, and an APOBEC3 cytidine deaminase hypermutates retroviral and other viral genomes.
