IRF7 provides the transcriptional amplification loop that raises type I interferon output, while TAP1 feeds viral peptides into MHC class I for CD8 T cell recognition, linking restriction to adaptive priming. Loss of these responses leaves hosts vulnerable to severe viral disease; chronic activation contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity.

These genes sketch a morphogen-driven programme that patterns mesenchymal tissue and steers progenitors toward bone, cartilage, skin and blood-supporting fates. BMP signalling sits at its centre: SMAD1 carries the receptor signal to the nucleus, ZNF521 acts as a nuclear cofactor tuning that output in skeletal and haematopoietic progenitors, while secreted GREM1 antagonises BMP ligands to keep niches permissive, and INHBA contributes an activin/TGF-beta arm through its own receptor-SMAD route. HHIP dampens Hedgehog signalling, so two major developmental gradients are held in check simultaneously by extracellular inhibitors. Downstream and in parallel, the Rac exchange factor TIAM1 and protein kinase C eta couple these cues to cytoskeletal remodelling and epithelial differentiation, ADAM12 remodels matrix and sheds surface proteins, and the transcriptional regulators RORA and BCL11B impose lineage identity. Imbalance here underlies skeletal dysplasia, fibrosis and tumour stroma behaviour.

Grouped as a B-cell-associated expression signature, these genes do not form a single mechanistic module, and the honest reading is of a marker set assembled from lymphocyte transcriptional profiling rather than a coordinated biochemical route. A few members do speak to immune function: MEFV encodes pyrin, the inflammasome sensor whose mutation causes familial Mediterranean fever; CCR9 is the chemokine receptor that directs lymphocyte homing to the small intestine; and interferon alpha genes such as IFNA10 and IFNA16 encode type I interferons that shape antiviral responses and B cell activation. Others belong to unrelated compartments entirely, including cancer-testis antigens of the GAGE and BAGE families, meiotic SYCP1, sperm-associated ZPBP, and neuronal or muscle products such as GABRB1, POU4F2 and triadin. The set is therefore best treated as a descriptive lymphocyte signature rather than a defined pathway.

This is a marker grouping derived from naive B cells, the resting, antigen-inexperienced lymphocytes that circulate after bone marrow development and before germinal centre entry, and whose activation initiates antibody responses. The genes assembled here do not form a coherent biochemical module: they span an innate immune regulator of pyrin-driven inflammasome activity and febrile inflammation, a type I interferon gene, a secreted metalloproteinase of the ADAMTS family, potassium channel tetramerisation-domain and transmembrane proteins, a POU-family transcription factor, a hepatic tyrosine aminotransferase, olfactory receptor and testis-expressed loci, and several pseudogene or low-confidence transcripts. The unifying theme is therefore expression pattern rather than shared mechanism, and the set is best read as a transcriptional signature distinguishing the naive B cell state from activated, memory and plasma cell stages, with interferon and inflammasome components hinting at the innate signalling context in which such cells are poised to respond.

This is a memory B cell expression signature rather than a mechanistically unified pathway: the genes it collects act in unrelated compartments and do not assemble into a single route. Memory B cells are the long-lived product of a germinal centre response, holding an affinity-matured, class-switched receptor in reserve so that a second encounter with the same antigen yields rapid, high-titre antibody; loss of this compartment is what makes vaccine-induced protection wane, and its dysregulated persistence underlies autoantibody-driven disease. Among the members, MEFV encodes pyrin, an inflammasome regulator whose mutation causes familial Mediterranean fever, and IFNA10 is a type I interferon with direct effects on B cell activation and differentiation; others, including a glycophorin blood-group antigen, a metalloproteinase and several metabolic enzymes, mark the heterogeneity of the signature rather than a shared complex.

No single process unites these genes; they instead sample several core housekeeping systems that any proliferating cell depends on. One arm is growth-factor signalling through small GTPases: NRAS relays receptor input to MAP kinase and PI3K routes, RAP2C acts in Ras-family signalling to cytoskeletal and polarity effectors, and PIK3C2A generates phosphoinositides that direct membrane traffic and endocytosis. A second arm handles protein biogenesis and secretion, with SRP9 targeting nascent chains to the endoplasmic reticulum and SEC23A forming part of the COPII coat that buds cargo toward the Golgi; loss of SEC23A activity underlies a craniofacial dysplasia. A third arm is nuclear and transcriptional: SP3 and TCF12 are DNA-binding regulators of developmental gene programmes, CCNC partners a kinase in transcriptional control, and AEBP2 associates with Polycomb repressive complex 2. RNF6 contributes ubiquitin-dependent turnover.

amino acid metabolishm and transport describes the handling of amino acids and their derivatives in the kidney proximal tubule and liver "" their reabsorption from filtrate, conjugation, and catabolism. This is the biology that keeps amino acids out of the urine and converts their carbon and nitrogen into usable or excretable forms; loss of it produces aminoacidurias such as cystinuria, caused by defects in the SLC3A1""SLC7A9 heteromeric cystine transporter, and disturbances of betaine, glycine and tryptophan metabolism. Apical and basolateral carriers for neutral and dibasic amino acids, betaine and organic anions work alongside scaffolds such as PDZK1 and collectrin that position them in the brush border. Metabolic components include betaine""homocysteine methyltransferase and dimethylglycine dehydrogenase in one-carbon and methionine metabolism, BBOX1 in carnitine synthesis, glycine and acetyl conjugating enzymes, and the kynurenine branch enzyme ACMSD, with bile acid""activated NR1H4 providing transcriptional control.

Amino acid metabolism and transport in this sense is largely the business of the liver and the kidney proximal tubule, where filtered amino acids and their derivatives are reabsorbed, conjugated, or degraded rather than lost in urine. The heterodimeric cystine and dibasic amino acid transporter formed by SLC3A1 with SLC7A9 is the clearest example: loss of either causes cystinuria and cystine stones, and TMEM27 and PDZK1 support apical transporter trafficking and scaffolding. Betaine and glycine handling appears through BHMT and BHMT2, which remethylate homocysteine to methionine, DMGDH, GLYAT and the betaine/GABA transporters SLC6A12 and SLC6A13, linking osmolyte accumulation to one-carbon metabolism. Other members degrade tryptophan and pyrimidine-derived intermediates, acylate or acetylate amino acids for excretion, and move urate, organic cations and anions across the tubular epithelium, tying nitrogen disposal to renal solute handling.

This cluster of solute carriers describes solute reabsorption and secretion across epithelial membranes, most recognisably in the renal proximal tubule, where filtered nutrients and ions are recovered and waste solutes and drugs are excreted. Members handle distinct substrate classes: glucose via a facilitative transporter and a sodium-coupled hexose carrier, cystine and dibasic amino acids through the heteromeric rBAT-b(0,+)AT pair, inorganic sulfate, nucleosides, urate and organic anions, organic cations, and betaine/GABA osmolytes that support medullary osmotic adaptation. A PDZ scaffold anchors several of these carriers in apical membrane complexes, and the FXYD2 subunit tunes the Na,K-ATPase that supplies the sodium gradient driving much of this uptake. Loss of individual components produces recognisable human disease, including cystinuria from defective cystine reabsorption, hypouricaemia or gout from altered urate handling, and glycosuria; collectively the group sets plasma solute composition and governs renal drug clearance.

This grouping of G protein coupled receptors collects cell-surface sensors for small inflammatory mediators, and its chief output is the recruitment and activation of leukocytes at sites of injury or infection. Receptors for the complement fragment C3a, bacterial and mitochondrial formylated peptides, leukotriene B4, platelet-activating factor and extracellular nucleotides drive neutrophil and monocyte chemotaxis, degranulation and oxidative burst, largely through Gi-coupled signalling that raises intracellular calcium and remodels the actin cytoskeleton. Others in the group bias the response the other way: prostaglandin D2 and E2 receptors here act through Gs and cyclic AMP to restrain or resolve inflammation, while a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor governs endothelial barrier tone and lymphocyte traffic. A parathyroid hormone-related receptor broadens the set beyond immunity to neuroendocrine signalling. Collectively these receptors set the threshold for innate immune activation and are heavily exploited as drug targets in asthma, allergy and vascular disease.

This signature marks the B lymphocyte lineage and its terminally differentiated antibody-secreting progeny, the plasma cells that sustain humoral immunity and long-lived serological memory. Much of it is immunoglobulin itself: heavy chain constant regions for IgM/IgD and IgG, kappa and lambda variable and constant segments, and the joining chain that links secretory IgA and IgM into polymers, so the set effectively reads out how much antibody a tissue is making. Around these sit surface and signalling components of B cells — the inhibitory co-receptor CD22, the Src-family kinase BLK, the adaptor STAP1, Fc receptor-like proteins, and the transcription factor SPIB — together with markers of plasma cell identity such as the BAFF/APRIL receptor TNFRSF17 and ER proteins supporting heavy secretory output. Expression of this kind dominates germinal centres and marrow plasma cell niches, tracks tumour-infiltrating B cells, and is the hallmark of myeloma.

Plasma cells are the terminally differentiated end of the B lineage, and their sole job is to secrete immunoglobulin in bulk; this signature captures that identity through heavy and light chain genes of every isotype and class, including IgM, IgD, IgG and IgA constant regions together with many kappa and lambda variable segments. Antibody output from these cells provides humoral immunity and long-lived serological memory after infection or vaccination. The supporting genes reflect what massive secretion demands: a thiol-disulfide oxidoreductase of the endoplasmic reticulum assists immunoglobulin folding, an ER-associated degradation component clears misfolded chains, and the transcriptional coactivator POU2AF1 drives the differentiation programme. Surface receptors such as CD27 and BCMA, the receptor for BAFF and APRIL, mark and sustain the cells in bone marrow niches. Malignant expansion of this compartment produces multiple myeloma, and BCMA is now a principal therapeutic target.

This grouping marks a natural killer cell signature, capturing genes whose expression is concentrated in cytotoxic innate lymphocytes and, to a lesser degree, in effector T cells. Such cells survey tissue for virus-infected and transformed targets without prior sensitisation, and their activity depends on balancing activating and inhibitory surface receptors. Here that balance is represented by an inhibitory KLR family member that reads HLA-E-presented peptides, together with TIGIT and PVRIG, checkpoint receptors that bind nectin and poliovirus receptor family ligands and restrain killing — both are targets of immunotherapeutic blockade. Downstream signalling components include the Src-family kinase MATK, the Ras-activating exchange factor RASGRP1, and the phosphatase PTPN4, while CX3CR1 and GPR18 direct migration and tissue positioning and CCL4 recruits other leukocytes to the site of recognition.

Type I interferon alpha signalling is the first line of antiviral defence: infected cells secrete these cytokines, neighbouring cells respond through a shared receptor and JAK-STAT relay, and hundreds of restriction factors are induced to block viral replication while dendritic cells and NK cells are mobilised. Several members of the clustered alpha interferon gene family are represented here, including IFNA4, IFNA7, IFNA10, IFNA14 and IFNA16, products of a tandemly duplicated locus whose individual genes differ in receptor affinity and in the strength of the antiproliferative versus antiviral output they drive; recombinant forms are used therapeutically in viral hepatitis and some malignancies. The remaining members point to matrix and epithelial biology, with basement membrane and adhesion components such as LAMC2 and ITGB4 and the remodelling proteases MMP12 and ST14, linking interferon exposure to tissue remodelling, wound repair and epithelial barrier behaviour.

This grouping is built around the clustered interferon alpha genes, the type I interferon ligands secreted chiefly by plasmacytoid dendritic cells and virus-infected cells to put neighbouring tissue into an antiviral state. The many near-identical IFNA subtypes here all converge on a single shared receptor and JAK-STAT signalling, inducing transcription of genes that block viral replication, raise antigen presentation, and activate natural killer and T cell responses; recombinant forms of these cytokines have been used to treat viral hepatitis and certain malignancies, while chronic overproduction drives the interferon signature of lupus and related autoimmunity. The remaining members sit outside this antiviral core, including the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor and prolactin, hormonal signalling components of reproductive physiology, so the set mixes interferon alpha response biology with endocrine and extracellular-matrix genes rather than describing one coherent cascade.

Many hormones, neurotransmitters and chemokines act through G protein-coupled receptors that raise intracellular calcium, and this pathway covers the relay from receptor-activated heterotrimeric G proteins to calcium-dependent enzymes. It is how a brief extracellular signal becomes secretion, contraction, gene transcription or synaptic change, and its components are drug targets across cardiovascular, neurological and inflammatory medicine. Gq-class subunits such as GNAQ and the hematopoietic GNA15 activate phospholipase C beta, which cleaves PIP2 to generate inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol and releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores; released calcium binds calmodulin, which in turn activates kinases including CAMK4 to drive nuclear transcriptional responses. Gi-class subunits and a Gγ subunit couple the same receptors to adenylate cyclase and thereby to cAMP and protein kinase A, so the two second-messenger arms are integrated rather than separate. Dysregulated Gq signalling underlies several cancers and cardiac hypertrophy.

TLR and inflammatory signaling is the innate-immune sensing program of myeloid cells, principally neutrophils and monocytes, that detects microbial products and host damage signals and converts them into an inflammatory response. It underlies the first line of antimicrobial defence, and its dysregulation drives septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and autoimmunity. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors, together with the LPS co-receptor MD-2, signal through MyD88 and IRAK kinases toward NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription, while IRAK3 imposes negative feedback and tolerance. Alongside them sit the effector receptors of myeloid activation: complement and formyl-peptide chemoattractant receptors that direct chemotaxis, Fc receptors and the ITAM adaptor TYROBP that trigger phagocytosis and Src-family kinase signalling, inhibitory LILR and Siglec receptors that restrain it, and NADPH oxidase and ALOX5 components that generate reactive oxygen species and leukotrienes. PADI4 links the same cells to neutrophil extracellular trap formation.

Innate immune cells detect microbial products and host-derived danger signals and convert that detection into inflammation, and this Toll-like receptor and inflammatory signalling programme is the sensing apparatus that does it. Surface and endosomal receptors for bacterial lipopeptides, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin and nucleic acids (TLR1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, TLR6, TLR7, TLR8) act with the LPS co-receptor MD-2 and signal through MyD88 and IRAK-family adaptors toward NF-κB-driven cytokine production; IRAK3 restrains this output to limit tissue damage and endotoxin tolerance. Alongside them sit the effector receptors of myeloid cells: complement and formyl-peptide receptors and the chemokine receptor CXCR2 that guide neutrophil recruitment, Fc gamma receptors and the DAP12 adaptor TYROBP for phagocytosis, inhibitory LILR and Siglec receptors that damp activation, plus leukotriene synthesis and the NADPH oxidase subunit NCF4. The composition reflects granulocyte and monocyte biology, host defence against infection, and the sterile inflammation underlying sepsis and autoimmunity.

Leukocyte differentiation covers the transcriptional programs that turn haematopoietic progenitors into the specialised white blood cells of innate and adaptive immunity, and that push mature cells into activated states. It determines the composition of the immune system: how many neutrophils, monocytes, dendritic cells and lymphocytes are produced, and whether they mature at all, with failures manifesting as immunodeficiency or leukaemic arrest. The genes here are largely inducible transcriptional regulators acting downstream of cytokine and antigen receptor signalling — NF-κB family members and their modulators such as NFKB2 and BCL3, immediate-early factors including JUNB, EGR2 and NR4A2, Krüppel-like factors, and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose disruption blocks myeloid maturation in promyelocytic leukaemia. Alongside them sit surface and secreted effectors such as CD83, ADAM8, IL1A and LIF, linking lineage decisions to inflammatory context and cell cycle exit.

Leukocyte differentiation is the process by which haematopoietic progenitors and activated immune cells commit to specialized fates anging from granulocytes and monocytes to dendritic cells and lymphocyte subsets, and it determines the composition of the immune system available to fight infection. The genes here are largely nuclear regulators that translate inflammatory and cytokine cues into lineage decisions: NF-κB family members and the IL-1-inducible modulator BCL3, immediate-early factors such as JUNB, EGR2, BTG2 and the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A2, Krüppel-like factors, and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose ligand drives granulocytic maturation and whose disruption by chromosomal translocation blocks it in acute promyelocytic leukaemia. Also represented are secreted signals including LIF and IL1A, the dendritic cell maturation marker CD83, the metalloprotease ADAM8, and the transcriptional coactivator MED1. Failure of this programme produces immunodeficiency or leukaemic arrest at an immature stage.

This grouping centres on control of cell survival and proliferation decisions during tissue growth and differentiation. Two hubs stand out: the retinoblastoma protein RB1, which restrains the G1/S transition by holding E2F-dependent transcription in check and whose loss underlies retinoblastoma and many sporadic cancers, and BCL2L1, an anti-apoptotic member of the BCL2 family that guards mitochondrial outer membrane integrity and blocks cytochrome c release. Around them sit transcriptional regulators (ATF1, SP3), the RNA-binding protein RBM38 and the splicing regulator MBNL3, which impose post-transcriptional layers on the same programme, alongside ubiquitin ligases such as RNF6 and HERC4 that set protein turnover. SLC7A5 imports large neutral amino acids to support anabolic growth, while SPAST severs microtubules, a function whose failure causes hereditary spastic paraplegia.

Epithelial cells seal into sheets by building specialized contacts at the plasma membrane, and this cell junction programme is the molecular signature of that epithelial state. It establishes the barrier and apicobasal polarity that let epithelia separate body compartments, and its loss is the defining feature of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in development, wound healing and carcinoma progression. E-cadherin anchors adherens junctions and links to plakophilin-containing desmosomal contacts, while claudins 3, 4 and 7 with the tight junction scaffold TJP3 set paracellular permeability. The transcription factors GRHL2, ELF3 and EHF and the splicing regulator ESRP1 maintain the epithelial expression pattern, and the membrane protease ST14 with its inhibitor SPINT1 controls pericellular proteolysis at the cell surface. EPCAM and MAL2 mark and traffic apical membrane domains, making this set a readout of epithelial identity and barrier integrity.

Epithelial cells seal themselves to their neighbours, and this cell junction programme supplies the adhesive and sealing structures that do it: E-cadherin-based adherens junctions, claudin-containing tight junctions with the scaffold ZO-3, and desmosomes built on desmoplakin and plakophilin-3. Together they create a selectively permeable barrier that separates apical from basolateral surfaces, restricts paracellular flux of ions and solutes, and anchors the keratin cytoskeleton so that sheets of cells resist mechanical stress. The same machinery establishes apicobasal polarity, with EPCAM and EPB41L5 acting at the lateral membrane and contributing to junction organisation. Loss of these contacts is a hallmark of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and of invasive carcinoma, where E-cadherin downregulation frees cells to migrate; inherited claudin and desmosomal defects instead cause leaky epithelia, ion-handling disorders and fragile skin and heart tissue.

This grouping of transcripts marks the neutrophil, the short-lived phagocyte that dominates the blood granulocyte pool and the first-responder wave of acute inflammation. Genes of this kind are expressed at much higher levels in neutrophils than in lymphocytes or monocytes, so their combined signal is used to read granulocyte content and activation state out of whole-blood expression data, where it rises in bacterial sepsis and other neutrophil-driven responses. The members touch several sides of phagocyte function: TYROBP is the ITAM-bearing adaptor that couples activating immunoreceptors to spleen tyrosine kinase signalling, ARAP3 and DENND3 regulate small GTPases controlling adhesion, spreading and membrane traffic, SLC40A1 exports iron across the plasma membrane, and complement factor D initiates the alternative pathway. Together they reflect innate immune recognition, chemotaxis and antimicrobial effector activity rather than one linear signalling route.

Xenobiotic metabolism is the chemical defence system by which cells modify drugs, dietary compounds and environmental toxins so they can be excreted, and it sets how long any given drug persists in the body. The genes here span the two classical arms: oxidative phase I attack by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP3A family, which handle a large share of clinically used drugs and whose polymorphic expression underlies interindividual differences in drug response, and phase II conjugation by a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that appends glucuronic acid to make metabolites water-soluble. Accompanying transporters and catabolic enzymes, including a cystine-dibasic amino acid carrier and the beta-alanine-generating pyrimidine breakdown steps of dihydropyrimidinase and ureidopropionase, place this activity in absorptive epithelia of gut, liver and kidney, where deficiencies cause fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxicity and impaired clearance.

Drugs, dietary chemicals and other foreign compounds must be chemically altered before they can be cleared, and xenobiotic metabolism is the set of enzymes that performs that conversion and disposal. Its capacity determines how long a drug persists, whether a pro-carcinogen is activated or detoxified, and how patients differ in response and toxicity. Two phases are represented here: cytochrome P450 monooxygenases of the CYP3A family carry out oxidative functionalisation of a broad range of substrates, while a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates sugar onto the products to make them water-soluble for excretion. Accompanying transporters and hydrolytic enzymes place this chemistry in absorptive epithelia of the intestine, liver and kidney, where amino acid and pyrimidine catabolic activities such as dihydropyrimidinase and beta-ureidopropionase overlap with handling of pyrimidine-analogue drugs. Loss of individual components shifts drug exposure and underlies inherited differences in clearance.

Dendritic cells that have sensed infection switch from antigen capture to antigen presentation and cytokine output, and this transcriptional programme marks that activated state. It matters because these cells set the size and flavour of the ensuing T cell response; blunting it weakens antiviral and vaccine responses, while its chronic engagement accompanies interferon-driven autoimmunity such as lupus and dermatomyositis. Much of the signature is type I interferon-inducible: the RNA sensor IFIH1 detects cytoplasmic double-stranded RNA, and IFIT family members, MX2, RSAD2 and PARP9 act as downstream restriction and amplification factors. Alongside these sit chemokines that recruit further leukocytes (CCL20, CCL8, CXCL11), the T cell polarising cytokine IL18, GM-CSF receptor subunits supporting myeloid survival, the anti-apoptotic BCL2A1, and LAMP3 and SIGLEC1 as maturation and macrophage-dendritic surface markers.

These genes mark the resident fibroblast and perivascular stromal compartment of connective tissue, the cell population that builds and remodels extracellular matrix and supplies growth signals to neighbouring epithelium, endothelium and immune cells. Matrix and matrix-associated products such as tenascin C, ECM2, OLFML3 and the BMP antagonist chordin-like 1 shape tissue architecture and the diffusion of morphogens, while locally produced complement components C1S and C7 give stroma a role in innate immune surveillance. Receptors for PDGF (PDGFRA, PDGFRB), growth hormone, oncostatin M and GDNF family ligands let these cells respond to injury, inflammatory and endocrine cues, and IGF2 provides paracrine growth support. Programmes of this kind underlie wound healing and tissue growth, and their persistent activation produces fibrosis and the tumour-supporting stroma of carcinomas.

This grouping reflects cell cycle control and the survival signalling that runs alongside it, the machinery that decides whether a cell divides, pauses, or dies. Several members sit in the growth-signalling arm: AKT1 promotes survival and growth, TSC2 restrains mTOR signalling as part of a GTPase-activating complex, and SESN3 links stress and nutrient status to that same axis. Others act directly on division and its fidelity — MAD1L1 is a spindle assembly checkpoint component that delays anaphase until chromosomes are correctly attached, while CDC34 and a proteasome subunit support the ubiquitin-dependent destruction of cyclins and inhibitors that makes cell cycle transitions irreversible. PPP2R1A provides a phosphatase scaffold opposing mitotic kinases, BCL2L1 sets the apoptotic threshold, and TGFB1 supplies an extracellular signal that arrests proliferation. Loss of such coordination underlies genomic instability and tumour growth.

enriched in dendritic cells marks the transcriptional signature of myeloid dendritic cells and closely related monocyte-derived antigen-presenting cells, the sentinels that sample tissue antigen and instruct T cell responses. Its members define how these cells recognise, ingest and process what they encounter: C-type lectin receptors such as CLEC10A and CLEC5A bind glycan and pathogen ligands, FCER1A confers high-affinity IgE capture on skin and blood DC subsets, DAB2 and CAPG support endocytic uptake and actin-dependent membrane remodelling, and the lysosomal cathepsins CTSB and CTSL degrade internalised protein for peptide loading onto MHC. Additional components tune the response to the tissue environment, including IL1R1 for inflammatory cytokine sensing, JAG1 for Notch-mediated instruction of neighbouring lymphocytes, and metabolic and glycosylation enzymes that accompany maturation. Together these genes distinguish dendritic cells in immune profiling and underlie the initiation of adaptive immunity and tolerance.

This grouping marks the transcriptional signature of dendritic cells, the antigen-presenting sentinels that sample tissue, migrate to lymph nodes and set the tone of T cell responses. Several members are the surface molecules by which these cells are recognised and by which they capture antigen: the high-affinity IgE receptor alpha chain FCER1A, and the C-type lectins CLEC10A and CLEC5A, which bind glycans on pathogens and damaged cells and feed signals into innate activation. Lysosomal cathepsins B and L supply the proteolysis needed to process internalised antigen for presentation and to mature invariant chain, while DAB2 supports endocytic uptake and CAPG remodels actin during migration and phagocytosis. Others contribute cytokine responsiveness through IL1R1, Notch ligand signalling to lymphocytes via JAG1, and metabolic support for activation. The set is useful chiefly for identifying and quantifying this lineage in tissue and blood.

This is a promoter-motif-defined module: genes sharing a CCAAT-containing upstream element that is characteristic of cell-cycle-regulated transcription, grouped here under mitosis. The members read as the machinery a cell needs to duplicate its genome and partition it faithfully, so their coordinated induction ties transcriptional timing to proliferation. Origin recognition complex subunits license replication origins, PCNA acts as the sliding clamp and processivity platform for replicative polymerases and repair, PMS1 contributes to mismatch repair of newly made DNA, and SMC1A forms part of the cohesin ring that holds sister chromatids together until anaphase. Others govern the nuclear compartment itself — a nucleoporin, the nuclear lamina-associated protein encoded by TMPO, and the karyopherin-dependent export factor XPO1, whose cargoes include spindle and checkpoint regulators. Loss of such coordination produces replication stress, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy.

Homeobox transcription factors of the clustered HOX family assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the embryo, and this grouping of HOXA and HOXB cluster members captures that patterning programme together with some of its cofactors and downstream targets. The genes are expressed in nested, colinear domains that specify vertebral, hindbrain, limb and gut segment identity; misexpression shifts one body region toward the character of another, and in the adult the same factors govern haematopoietic stem and progenitor output, where HOXA10 and HOXA9-region activity with the TALE-class partner MEIS1 is a recurrent driver of myeloid leukaemia. MEIS1 supplies DNA-binding cooperativity that sharpens otherwise degenerate HOX site selection. Additional members such as the tissue-restricted homeodomain factor NKX2-3, the transcriptional repressor ZNF503 and the laminin-binding integrin ITGA7 point to the mesenchymal and muscle differentiation outcomes that positional cues ultimately control.</description>

Hox transcription factors assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the embryo, and this grouping of HOXA and HOXB cluster members covers the central and posterior paralogues that specify cervical and thoracic segment identity. Their ordered, colinear expression tells cells in the somites, limb bud and branchial arches where they are, so that vertebrae, ribs, forelimb skeleton and associated nerves form in the right place; misexpression produces homeotic shifts in vertebral pattern and limb malformation, and several of these genes are reactivated in leukaemias and solid tumours. The homeodomain proteins act as sequence-specific regulators of downstream differentiation programmes, and the additional members here point to the effectors they intersect with: a zinc-finger transcriptional regulator controlling brown fat and cardiac development, a PDGF family ligand, and a secreted transport protein of the liver and choroid plexus.

Hox genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis, and this group of posterior and central paralogues from the A and B clusters, together with their MEIS cofactors, represents that patterning output. Their ordered, colinear expression specifies vertebral and limb segment identity and shapes the urogenital tract, where loss of HOXA10 or HOXA11 disturbs uterine and limb development. The same factors act repeatedly after embryogenesis in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, where HOXA9 with MEIS1 sustains self-renewal and blocks differentiation; their aberrant reactivation is a defining feature of MLL-rearranged and NPM1-mutant acute leukemias. MEIS proteins are TALE-class partners that bind Hox proteins and raise their DNA-binding selectivity, so target choice depends on cofactor availability as much as on which Hox protein is present.

Hox cluster IV is a set of homeodomain transcription factors from the HOXA and HOXB clusters that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the developing embryo. Their nested, colinear expression domains tell cells in the paraxial mesoderm, neural tube and limb bud where they are, and thereby which vertebral, rib, hindbrain or skeletal structure to build; loss or ectopic expression produces homeotic shifts in vertebral formulae and limb malformations. Central members such as HOXA5, HOXB4 and HOXB5 also pattern the respiratory and gut tube, while posterior genes including HOXA9, HOXB9 and HOXA11 specify lumbosacral segments and the distal limb, and govern hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal. Retinoic acid and CDX signals set their boundaries, and Polycomb and Trithorax complexes maintain them; misregulated posterior HOXA activity drives acute leukemias.

Hox genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the embryo, and this grouping draws on members of the A and B clusters spanning middle to posterior paralogue groups. Their nested, colinear expression domains tell cells in the paraxial mesoderm, neural tube and lateral plate which segment they occupy, so that vertebrae, limb segments, and hindbrain rhombomeres form in the right order. Loss or misexpression shifts structures to the identity of a neighbouring segment; in humans, HOXA11 mutation disrupts radius and ulna development and kidney formation, while several of these genes are also active in haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, where HOXA9 misregulation by chromosomal translocation drives leukaemia. Retinoic acid signalling and chromatin-level repression by Polycomb complexes set and maintain the boundaries of these expression domains during development.

These genes mark a perivascular stromal and endothelial compartment, the interface where capillaries meet connective tissue matrix. Secreted matrix components such as EFEMP1 (fibulin-3) and ECM2 organise the basement membrane and elastic fibre environment that keeps vessels and surrounding tissue mechanically coherent, while IL33 acts both as a nuclear factor in endothelium and, when released from damaged cells, as an alarmin that recruits type 2 immune responses. Several adhesion G protein-coupled receptors are represented, including ELTD1/ADGRL4, which is endothelial and shapes angiogenic sprouting, and GPR116/ADGRF5, required for alveolar surfactant homeostasis; GNG12 supplies a G protein gamma subunit for such signalling, and MPDZ scaffolds junctional complexes. Together the set describes matrix deposition, junction organisation and vascular-stromal crosstalk, processes underlying tissue remodelling, fibrosis and vessel integrity.

Heme is the iron-porphyrin cofactor that lets haemoglobin carry oxygen, and this route builds it from succinyl-CoA and glycine through the erythroid arm of porphyrin synthesis. The committed step is catalysed by the erythroid-specific ALAS2, whose product is condensed by ALAD and polymerised by HMBS; CPOX oxidises the ring and FECH inserts ferrous iron to complete protoheme. Because the flux is enormous in developing red cells, it is tightly coupled to globin supply and to the erythroid transcription factor GATA1, which drives both the enzymes and accessory genes such as HEMGN, TMOD1 and the alpha-haemoglobin stabilising protein AHSP that chaperones free globin chains. Loss or imbalance of individual steps produces sideroblastic anaemia and the porphyrias, in which accumulated intermediates cause photosensitivity or neurovisceral attacks, and E2F2 links the programme to the proliferative expansion of erythroid precursors.

enriched for TF motif TTCNRGNNNNTTC groups genes that share an upstream inverted nGAAn-repeat element of the kind read by heat shock factors, and the genes themselves form a coherent stress-and-injury response program rather than a metabolic route. They are classic immediate-early and inducible transcripts: FOSB and the zinc-finger EGR3 with the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A3 provide rapid transcriptional output, CXCL3 recruits neutrophils, EDN1 constricts vessels, and PLAU drives pericellular proteolysis for matrix remodelling and cell migration. Together they describe how cells respond within minutes to proteotoxic, inflammatory or mechanical stress by remodelling their transcriptome, signalling to the immune system, and altering vascular tone and tissue architecture. PHLDA2 and GJB2 add growth-restraining and gap-junction components, tying the program to wound healing, placental and epithelial biology, and to the inflammatory activation that accompanies tumour invasion.

Genes grouped by a shared upstream promoter element, TTCNRGNNNNTTC, an inverted repeat of TTC/GAA half-sites of the kind recognised by heat shock factors and related inverted-repeat binding transcription factors. The members are dominated by immediate-early and stress-responsive transcripts: the activator protein-1 component FOSB and the nuclear receptor-family factors EGR3 and NR4A3 are themselves transcription factors induced within minutes of growth factor, cytokine or stress stimulation, while endothelin-1, the chemokine CXCL3 and the plasminogen activator PLAU are secreted effectors that drive vasoconstriction, neutrophil recruitment and extracellular matrix proteolysis. PHLDA2 and GJB2 add imprinted growth regulation and gap-junction coupling to the collection. As a motif-defined group rather than a curated mechanism, its value is as a hypothesis about shared upstream control, linking rapid transcriptional responses to inflammation, wound repair and vascular tone.

Red cell production requires a committed progenitor to shut down proliferation, load itself with haemoglobin, and remodel its membrane and cytoskeleton, and erythrocyte differentiation is the programme that drives that conversion. Its output is the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood; failure produces anaemias, and several of the genes here are mutated in inherited red cell disorders. Lineage identity is set transcriptionally by GATA1 and KLF1, which together switch on the erythroid battery, including haem biosynthesis via HMBS and the membrane skeleton protein EPB42 that anchors band 3 to the spectrin network. BPGM supplies 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, tuning haemoglobin's oxygen affinity so the mature cell can unload oxygen in tissues. Additional regulators such as LYL1 and TRIM10 act on progenitor commitment and terminal maturation, linking this programme to haematopoietic stem cell fate decisions more broadly.

The dominant theme here is chromatin-based control of gene expression coupled to ubiquitin-dependent protein regulation. Polycomb components BMI1 and EED, the histone chaperone ANP32E, the chromatin remodeller SMARCA5 and the histone-binding MORF4L2 together repress or reposition nucleosomes at developmental and proliferation genes, keeping stem and progenitor identity stable and restraining tumour suppressor loci such as the CDKN2A region. Alongside them sit ubiquitin pathway components — the CUL5 scaffold and the RING ligases RNF6 and RNF138 — that set protein turnover and contribute to DNA damage responses, and a transcription-associated cyclin partner, CCNC. A second group acts in the secretory pathway and endoplasmic reticulum: SRP9 in cotranslational targeting, SEC63 in translocation, the thiol oxidoreductase TMX1, the selenoprotein SEP15 and the phosphoinositide phosphatase SACM1L. The set therefore spans nuclear gene silencing, regulated proteolysis and ER protein folding and quality control.

This grouping describes cell development in the sense of progenitor specification and differentiation within developing tissues, where signalling gradients assign identity and transcription factors lock it in. Wnt output dominates: AXIN2 reports and restrains pathway activity, SFRP2 sequesters Wnt ligands extracellularly, and ASCL2 is a Wnt-driven factor that maintains intestinal stem cells alongside CDX2, the master regulator of posterior gut identity. EPHB2 sorts cells along that gradient to position progenitors correctly. A second arm is hedgehog and BMP regulation, with IHH signalling and GREM1 and GAS1 modulating BMP and hedgehog reception, a combination central to skeletal growth and to the mesenchymal niche beneath the crypt. Collagens and CTHRC1 supply the matrix in which these decisions occur, while SATB2 and IRX3 set regional identity. Disruption produces patterning and skeletal malformation and, in the intestine, altered stem cell numbers and tumour predisposition.

These genes read as the secretory programme of a mesenchymal stromal or fibroblast-like cell that builds and maintains tissue architecture and supports the cells embedded in it. CXCL12 is the chemokine by which such stroma recruits and retains haematopoietic progenitors and lymphocytes, while IGF1 with its carrier IGFBP3 sets local growth-factor availability, FRZB tunes Wnt signalling as a secreted antagonist, and complement component C7 and the secreted nuclease DNASE1L3 contribute to clearance of extracellular debris and immune tone. Aquaporin-1 handles water permeability and connexin-43 couples neighbouring cells through gap junctions, features of perivascular and connective tissue. SNAI2 acts as the transcriptional regulator holding the mesenchymal state and driving epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and ALDH1A3 supplies retinoic acid for local patterning. Together this describes niche support, matrix remodelling and the fibroblast responses that turn into fibrosis or tumour stroma when sustained.

This pathway describes the surface receptors and survival machinery of circulating mononuclear leukocytes — monocytes and T lymphocytes — and the transcriptional programme that tunes their inflammatory responsiveness. Chemokine receptors CCR2 and CX3CR1 define the two major monocyte subsets and direct their exit from marrow and patrolling of the endothelium, making this biology the entry point for macrophage recruitment into inflamed tissue and atherosclerotic plaque. The GIMAP GTPases, expressed in lymphocytes, set the threshold for apoptosis and thereby peripheral T cell persistence. Signalling input arrives through the IL-1 receptor accessory protein and the TWEAK receptor TNFRSF12A, and is resolved by the immediate-early nuclear receptor NR4A3 and the MAP kinase phosphatase DUSP4, which restrains ERK and JNK output. Accompanying KRAB zinc-finger proteins, the transcriptional repressor HIC1 and the metabolic coactivator PPARGC1B shape the differentiated state, linking innate immune activation to mitochondrial and lipid metabolism.

A mixed immune-expression module centred on mononuclear leukocyte identity and trafficking, combining chemokine receptors, GTPase-of-immunity-associated proteins and transcriptional regulators. Monocyte and macrophage recruitment to inflamed tissue depends on CCR2 and CX3CR1, whose ligands direct patrolling and infiltrating cells to vessel walls and injured sites; loss of this axis blunts inflammatory monocyte egress from bone marrow and reshapes atherosclerotic and neuroinflammatory disease. The GIMAP proteins act in lymphocyte survival and homeostasis, linking the set to T cell persistence as well as myeloid function. Signalling and feedback components include the IL-1 receptor accessory protein required for interleukin-1 responses, the MAPK phosphatase DUSP4 that dampens kinase output, the TNF-family receptor FN14, and the immediate-early factor NR4A3. Numerous KRAB-type zinc finger proteins and the repressor HIC1 suggest accompanying transcriptional control, alongside metabolic and autophagy-related members.

This gene set centres on monocyte identity and chemotactic control of myeloid trafficking, the process that determines which circulating phagocytes leave the blood and where they go. CCR2 and CX3CR1 together define the two principal monocyte subsets: CCR2-high classical monocytes recruited to inflamed tissue in response to MCP-1, and CX3CR1-high patrolling monocytes that crawl the endothelium and give rise to resident macrophages and microglia. Loss of this axis blunts inflammatory recruitment in atherosclerosis, infection and neuroinflammation, while its overactivity drives chronic tissue damage. Accompanying immediate-early and orphan nuclear receptor transcription factors such as FOSL1 and NR4A3 provide the rapid transcriptional response downstream of chemokine and stress signalling, and a group of zinc-finger regulators, an immune-associated GTPase and cytoskeletal tropomodulin link this program to sustained gene control and the motility machinery migration requires.

Circulating monocytes find their way into tissue by reading chemokine gradients, and the two receptors that anchor this group, CCR2 and CX3CR1, are the pair that defines the classical and non-classical monocyte subsets and governs their recruitment to inflamed vessel walls, injured tissue and the brain, where they become macrophages or microglia. Loss or blockade of this axis limits atherosclerotic plaque myeloid influx and blunts inflammatory infiltration, which is why it is a longstanding drug target. Alongside the receptors sit immediate-early transcriptional responses, with the AP-1 component FOSL1 and the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A3 coupling receptor engagement to changes in gene expression that set monocyte activation state and survival. Additional zinc-finger factors and the immune-associated GTPase-like GIMAP6 suggest accompanying transcriptional and lymphoid-myeloid regulatory control rather than chemotaxis alone.

This is a computationally defined group of human genes sharing a CACGTG E-box-type element (NATCACGTGAY) in their promoters, the kind of site recognized by sterol regulatory element-binding factors and related basic helix-loop-helix leucine zipper proteins, and so its members are candidate SREBF1 targets rather than a validated pathway. SREBF1 is the transcription factor that couples membrane sterol and fatty acid status to gene expression, driving lipogenesis downstream of insulin and mTOR signalling and going awry in fatty liver disease and metabolic syndrome. The genes collected here are largely signalling and adaptor molecules — a receptor tyrosine kinase, protein kinase C epsilon, a calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase, Rho-family regulators, a cytokine signalling suppressor and a B cell linker protein — suggesting that shared promoter architecture may link growth-factor and calcium signalling components to lipogenic transcriptional control, a hypothesis the motif raises rather than establishes.\n

Genes grouped by a shared PAX3 transcription factor binding motif in their regulatory regions, a coregulation signature rather than a biochemical route. PAX3 is a paired-box factor that directs neural crest, myogenic and melanocyte development; loss-of-function underlies Waardenburg syndrome, and its fusion with FOXO1 drives alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, so the genes it may control are of interest as effectors of proliferative and developmental programmes. The members converge on nuclear housekeeping: chromatin repression by the Polycomb component BMI1, mismatch repair by PMS1, deubiquitination of the Fanconi anemia pathway by USP1, double-strand break end protection by the shieldin subunit encoded by FAM35A, nucleocytoplasmic traffic through NUP54 and a RAN-binding protein, single-stranded DNA and RNA binding by PURA, and apoptotic regulation via CASP8AP2 and TNFAIP8. The theme is genome maintenance and cell survival in dividing progenitors.

T cell differentiation via ITK and PKC describes the proximal signalling that converts antigen receptor engagement into T cell fate decisions, determining whether a thymocyte survives selection and which effector program a mature T cell adopts. It matters because these components set the threshold for activation: loss of ITK impairs helper T cell responses and causes an immunodeficiency with susceptibility to Epstein-Barr virus, and loss of the related adaptor SH2D1A produces X-linked lymphoproliferative disease. Mechanistically, ITK acts downstream of the T cell receptor to activate phospholipase C, generating diacylglycerol that recruits the T lineage-restricted kinases PRKCQ and PRKCH to the immunological synapse and drives transcription factors such as ETS1. Downstream outputs include BCL2-dependent survival and FASLG-mediated killing and activation-induced death, linking receptor signal strength to clonal expansion, contraction and tolerance.

T cell receptor engagement must be converted into decisions about survival, lineage identity and effector function, and the kinases ITK and the T cell-enriched protein kinase C isoforms sit at that conversion point. ITK is a Tec-family tyrosine kinase recruited to the activated receptor complex, where it drives phospholipase C-gamma activity and the calcium and diacylglycerol signals that follow; PRKCQ and PRKCH then read the diacylglycerol arm and feed NF-kB and AP-1 activation at the immunological synapse. The transcription factor ETS1 and the anti-apoptotic regulator BCL2 shape how thymocytes and peripheral T cells survive and commit to a lineage, while FASLG equips effector cells to kill and to be removed by activation-induced cell death. SH2D1A couples SLAM-family receptors into the same signalling network, and its loss causes X-linked lymphoproliferative disease; defective ITK signalling likewise produces combined immunodeficiency with poor control of Epstein-Barr virus.

Iron handling, hypoxic adaptation and membrane lipid composition converge here on a cell's vulnerability to iron-dependent oxidative death. Iron-regulatory protein 2 sets the labile iron pool by controlling ferritin and transferrin receptor messages post-transcriptionally, while ACSL4 activates polyunsaturated fatty acids for incorporation into phospholipids and thereby supplies the peroxidation substrate that commits a cell to ferroptosis. HIF1A couples the same chemistry to oxygen availability, and SIRT1, ATF2 and TCF12 provide NAD-dependent and transcriptional arms that tune stress responses and metabolic output. Additional members act on membrane and cytoskeletal traffic: SYNJ1 dephosphorylates phosphoinositides during synaptic vesicle recycling, OSTM1 partners the lysosomal chloride-proton exchanger required for bone resorption, and ROCK1 drives actomyosin contraction. The shared theme is redox- and iron-sensitive control of cell survival, relevant to neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury and tumour cell death.

Dividing cells need a supply of purine and pyrimidine precursors, and this set covers the biosynthetic core of nucleotide metabolism that makes them from small molecules rather than salvaging them. Most of the enzymes listed belong to de novo purine synthesis, where multistep proteins such as PPAT-linked GART, PFAS, PAICS, ADSL and the bifunctional ATIC build the inosine monophosphate ring, and GMPS then routes it toward guanine nucleotides. CAD carries the first three steps of pyrimidine synthesis, and CTPS makes CTP from UTP. Ribonucleotide reductase, the RRM1-RRM2 complex, converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides and so gates DNA replication and repair. Demand for this output rises sharply in proliferating and tumour cells, which is why several steps are targets of antifolate and antimetabolite chemotherapy; inherited defects cause neurological and immune disease.

A module of chromatin- and DNA-binding proteins whose shared business is copying and protecting the genome during S phase. Its members supply the substrates and machinery of replication and the surveillance that keeps forks stable: RRM1 provides the ribonucleotide reductase activity that makes deoxynucleotides, POLD3 is an accessory subunit of DNA polymerase delta, the BLM helicase resolves recombination intermediates and stalled forks, and DONSON acts at replication forks in genome maintenance. Alongside these sit chromatin and transcriptional regulators "" the histone H3K9 methyltransferase SUV39H1, the TFIID subunit TAF5, and TFDP1, the DP partner of E2F that drives expression of replication genes "" plus mitotic factors such as STIL and STMN1 that couple duplication to centrosome function and spindle assembly. Loss of such activities produces replication stress, chromosome instability and the cancer predisposition seen in Bloom syndrome, and makes the group a recurring signature of proliferating cells.

These genes mark the epithelial identity programme of stratified and glandular epithelia, particularly of the gastrointestinal tract, and its coordinated regulation of differentiation, adhesion and mucosal barrier function. Transcription factors set the programme: CDX1 specifies intestinal identity and is a determinant of intestinal metaplasia when expressed in stomach or oesophagus, while KLF5 and the ETS factor EHF drive proliferation and maturation of epithelial progenitors. Their downstream output includes structural components of cell-cell and cell-matrix junctions, with the plakophilin PKP3 in desmosomes and ladinin anchoring basal cells to the basement membrane, alongside the FXYD3 ion-transport modulator and glycosylation enzymes GALNT3 and GMDS that build mucin-type O-glycans and fucosylated surface glycans. TRIM29 ties the programme to keratinocyte differentiation and DNA-damage responses. Persistent activation of these factors is a recurring feature of carcinomas of epithelial origin, where they sustain tumour cell proliferation and lineage identity.

This grouping centres on TGF-β/BMP superfamily signalling and its downstream control of cell fate and growth arrest. BMP4 and the activin-like receptor ACVR1C transmit ligand binding into Smad-dependent transcription, with the repulsive guidance molecule RGMA acting as a BMP co-receptor, while CDKN2B encodes the p15 cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor that enforces the cytostatic response to these ligands in epithelial and haematopoietic cells. A parallel stress-kinase arm, built from MAP3K10 and the JNK-activating kinase MAP2K7, couples the same inputs to AP-1-type transcription and to FOXO4-mediated stress and survival control. Effectors of differentiation appear alongside: myocardin drives smooth muscle gene expression, WNT11 and FOXL1 pattern mesenchymal tissue, and DLG4 and APLP1 tie the module to synaptic scaffolding. Such signalling shapes vascular and mesenchymal development, and its loss contributes to tumour growth and fibrotic remodelling.

A heterogeneous module in which scaffolded stress-kinase signalling meets secretory and growth control. Its clearest core is a JNK pathway assembly: a mixed-lineage kinase of the MAP3K family together with a JNK-interacting scaffold protein organises upstream kinases into a complex, and such scaffolds concentrate stress signalling at defined membrane and synaptic sites, where the PDZ scaffold PSD-95 anchors receptors and channels in excitatory postsynaptic densities and an ARF6 guanine-nucleotide exchange factor directs membrane traffic and cortical remodelling. Other members tie this to endocrine and proliferative outcomes: insulin as the hormonal output of beta cells, a calcium-activated monovalent cation channel that shapes membrane depolarisation and excitability, a CARD-containing adaptor feeding NF-kB activation, a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor restraining G1 progression, and a Wnt ligand plus a forkhead factor acting in mesenchymal patterning. Failures in such couplings contribute to impaired insulin release, altered excitability, and dysregulated growth.

This grouping centres on regulators of neuronal and progenitor cell fate, linking chromatin-level transcriptional control to membrane and cytoskeletal signalling. Several members set how readily a cell proliferates or differentiates: the retinoblastoma protein restrains the G1-to-S transition, a histone deacetylase and a Paf1 complex subunit shape transcription elongation and repression, and a basic helix-loop-helix factor drives neural and mesenchymal differentiation programmes. Against that, a protein tyrosine phosphatase relays growth factor input into Ras-ERK signalling, while ATG5 commits membranes to autophagosome formation and a synaptic phosphoinositide phosphatase recycles vesicles at nerve terminals. The prion protein and a synaptic glycoprotein act at the neuronal surface. Metabolic and salvage enzymes supply the reducing and nucleotide chemistry these processes depend on, and loss of the purine salvage enzyme produces the neurological features of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

The grouping is anchored on post-transcriptional and transcriptional control of gene expression in neural and developing tissues. Three sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins carry much of its identity: the neuronal ELAV-family protein ELAVL3 and the cytoplasmic polyadenylation element binding protein CPEB3 govern stability, localisation and translation of mRNAs in neurons, where CPEB3 acts on transcripts encoding glutamate receptor subunits and contributes to synaptic plasticity and memory, while YBX1 is a broadly acting mRNA packaging and translational regulator. Their targets and partners appear alongside them: the obligatory NMDA receptor subunit GRIN1, which mediates calcium influx at excitatory synapses, and the ARF6 activator PSD, which drives membrane trafficking in neurites. Homeobox and SRY-box transcription factors such as EVX1, TCF15 and SOX15 place the same logic in embryonic patterning and muscle progenitors, and ARMC9 links the set to ciliary function, whose loss causes cerebellar malformation.

Mitochondria and peroxisomes divide the work of oxidising fatty acids and amino acid carbon skeletons, and this grouping covers enzymes and transporters of that shared chemistry, concentrated in liver and kidney. Omega-hydroxylation of fatty acids by CYP4A enzymes generates dicarboxylic acids that are handed to the peroxisomal beta-oxidation route, where the bifunctional enzyme EHHADH performs the hydration and dehydrogenation steps. Other members handle nitrogen-containing substrates: ACMSD diverts an intermediate of tryptophan catabolism away from quinolinate and de novo NAD synthesis, PRODH2 oxidises hydroxyproline, AGXT2 transaminates beta-alanine and related amines, and GLYAT conjugates glycine to acyl-CoAs for urinary excretion. Transporters for bile acids, nucleosides and glucose place the chemistry in the context of hepatic uptake and enterohepatic circulation. Defects here cause hyperoxaluria, bile acid malabsorption and disordered hepatic glucose sensing.

These genes mark the antimicrobial granule programme of neutrophils, the arsenal that granulocytes build during maturation in bone marrow and deploy against bacteria and fungi at sites of infection. BPI binds and permeabilises Gram-negative outer membranes through its affinity for lipopolysaccharide, lipocalin 2 sequesters bacterial siderophores to starve microbes of iron, and olfactomedin 4 defines a distinct subset of neutrophil specific granules; CEACAM8 is a surface glycoprotein used routinely to identify granulocytes and their precursors. Together they represent oxygen-independent killing and nutritional immunity rather than the respiratory burst. Supporting members point to vesicle handling and membrane lipid traffic during granule formation and exocytosis, while CARD11 contributes to antigen receptor-driven NF-κB signalling in lymphocytes. Loss or dilution of this granule content, as in myeloid maturation defects, leaves patients prone to recurrent pyogenic infection.

A grouping of secreted and cell-surface proteins that act in the extracellular space, where signalling molecules, matrix components and their remodelling enzymes together shape tissue structure and immune cell traffic. Chemokines such as CCL2, CCL18 and CCL23 recruit monocytes, macrophages and lymphocytes to sites of inflammation; BMP2 instructs bone and cartilage formation; growth hormone and neuropeptide Y act as endocrine and neuroendocrine messengers controlling growth and appetite. Structural and matrix elements including perlecan and ECM1 build basement membranes and regulate their permeability, while matrix metalloproteinases MMP19 and MMP28 cleave matrix substrates during remodelling and repair. Endoglin serves as a TGF-beta superfamily co-receptor on endothelium, CD34 marks haematopoietic and vascular progenitors, and selenoprotein P delivers selenium to peripheral tissues with antioxidant effect. Collectively these products govern how cells sense, modify and communicate through their surroundings.

Naive CD4 T cells commit to distinct helper fates, and this programme marks the Th2 branch, the arm of adaptive immunity that drives antibody class switching to IgE, eosinophil recruitment and defence against helminths, and whose overactivity underlies allergic asthma, atopic dermatitis and food allergy. The signature is dominated by proximal T cell receptor signalling: the CD3 chain and costimulatory receptor CD28 at the surface, the LCK kinase and the LAT and GRAP2 adaptors that nucleate the signalling complex, together with membrane organisers and negative regulators such as SIT1, TRAT1 and UBASH3A that set the activation threshold. GATA3 is the lineage-defining transcription factor, imposing the Th2 cytokine programme and suppressing alternative fates. Also present are surface and secreted markers of activated helper cells, including DPP4 and the cytokine-like IL32, reflecting cells that have engaged antigen and differentiated rather than resting naive precursors.

These genes outline the interface between proliferative arrest and inflammatory secretion that characterises cellular senescence. On the chromatin side, the Polycomb component BMI1 is part of the complex that ubiquitinates histone H2A to silence the CDKN2A locus and keep cells cycling, while the deubiquitinase USP16 removes that mark and opposes it, so the balance between them sets how readily a cell exits the cycle. Mitotic surveillance and division geometry are represented by the spindle checkpoint protein BUB3, the augmin subunit HAUS3, the phosphatase catalytic subunit PPP1CC and the p53-inducible cyclin CCNG1, linking damage and mis-segregation to arrest. Arrested cells then secrete IL1A, IL1B, oncostatin M and epiregulin, cytokines and growth factors that remodel the local tissue, recruit immune cells and can either reinforce tumour suppression or promote age-related inflammation and tumour progression.

This grouping centres on the movement of ions, solutes and lipids across membranes, the activity that lets epithelia secrete fluid, absorb nutrients and maintain the electrochemical gradients cells depend on. Its best-characterised members define intestinal and airway physiology: the chloride channel CFTR and the anion exchanger SLC26A3 drive salt and fluid secretion and chloride-bicarbonate exchange, with loss of the former causing cystic fibrosis and of the latter congenital chloride diarrhoea, while the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter SLC12A2 loads chloride for secretion and KCNQ1 and KCNK5 provide the potassium conductance that sustains it. Others handle distinct cargo: SLC19A2 imports thiamine, SLC35A3 supplies UDP-N-acetylglucosamine to the Golgi for glycosylation, and P4-ATPases such as ATP8A1 and ATP11C flip aminophospholipids to keep membrane asymmetry. Regulatory and trafficking proteins accompany the transporters, linking transport capacity to cellular signalling and metabolic state.

These genes converge on integrin-based adhesion and the cytoskeletal signalling that lets cells grip and respond to their extracellular matrix, with a supporting cast of metabolic and gene-regulatory proteins. Talin links activated integrin tails to actin, integrin-linked kinase couples the adhesion complex to downstream survival and contractility signalling, and a Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor restrains Rho-family GTPases so that actin remodelling is switched rather than constant; a microtubule-associated protein and the SNARE-recycling factor alpha-SNAP tie the same events to cytoskeletal turnover and membrane fusion. NBEAL2 is required for platelet alpha-granule biogenesis, and TGFB1 is a principal granule cargo and matrix-remodelling cytokine, placing part of this biology in platelet adhesion, secretion and wound repair. Additional components handle arginine methylation, NADPH and redox balance, oxidative carbon flux, and lipid-sensing transcriptional control, the metabolic backdrop on which adhesion and secretion depend.

These genes outline the terminal stages of erythroid differentiation, in which a committed progenitor remodels its membrane and cytoskeleton, condenses and expels its nucleus, and emerges as a deformable red cell able to survive repeated passage through capillaries and the spleen. Structural components dominate: beta-spectrin builds the membrane skeleton beneath the lipid bilayer, pleckstrin-2 and cortactin drive the actin rearrangements required for enucleation and cell shaping, and XK forms a disulphide-linked complex with the Kell glycoprotein at the erythrocyte surface. Transcriptional input from NFIA and PBX1 helps set the balance between erythroid and other myeloid fates, while GMPR and monoglyceride lipase reflect the nucleotide and lipid metabolism of maturing red cells. Loss of skeletal components causes hereditary spherocytosis and haemolytic anaemia; loss of XK produces acanthocytic red cells with neurological degeneration.

These genes converge on nuclear organisation and nucleocytoplasmic traffic: chromatin architecture, mRNA processing, ribosome biogenesis and export of cargo through the nuclear pore. CTCF and the cohesin subunit SMC1A together define chromatin loop boundaries and insulate promoters from inappropriate enhancers, which is how genome folding is translated into transcriptional output; ADNP and ATF1 act on transcription, the latter as a CREB-family factor responding to cAMP signalling. XPO1 exports proteins and ribonucleoprotein cargo out of the nucleus, NUP37 is a component of the nuclear pore scaffold, CRNKL1 contributes to spliceosomal function and NOC3L to pre-ribosome maturation, while centrin-3 links to centrosome duplication and a regulatory subunit of protein phosphatase 2A modulates mitotic progression. Collectively the set describes the interface between nuclear structure, gene expression and cell division, processes whose disruption drives developmental disorders and chromosomal instability in cancer.

muscle contraction, SRF targets describes the smooth muscle contractile program driven by serum response factor and its coactivator myocardin, the transcriptional switch that converts a mesenchymal cell into a differentiated, contractile smooth muscle cell. This program gives blood vessels, gut, bladder and airway their tone; when it is switched off, smooth muscle cells dedifferentiate into the proliferative, synthetic state that drives atherosclerotic plaque formation, restenosis and vascular remodelling. The genes are the structural output of that switch: smooth muscle myosin heavy chain and gamma-actin form the contractile apparatus, calponin, leiomodin and PGM5 organise and regulate the actin cytoskeleton, desmin builds the intermediate filament lattice, and phospholamban tunes calcium reuptake and therefore relaxation. Myocardin itself is included, since the pathway is self-reinforcing: actin dynamics feed back on SRF cofactor availability, coupling cytoskeletal state to contractile gene expression.

Smooth muscle cells maintain a contractile phenotype through a transcriptional program driven by serum response factor together with its muscle-restricted coactivator myocardin, and the genes here are the output of that program. They encode the contractile apparatus and its regulators: smooth muscle myosin heavy chain, gamma-actin, desmin, calponin, leiomodin and the calcium-handling modulator phospholamban, plus matrix and cytoskeletal components that couple force to surrounding tissue. Together they set the tone of blood vessels, airways, gut and bladder wall. Because actin polymerization itself releases the coactivators that license this transcription, the pathway acts as a feedback loop linking cytoskeletal state to contractile gene expression. Loss of the program underlies phenotypic switching of vascular smooth muscle toward proliferative, synthetic states in atherosclerosis and restenosis, while myocardin mutations impair visceral smooth muscle development.

When platelets encounter a damaged vessel wall they change shape, spread and clump, and this arm of platelet activation covers the link between surface receptors and the actin cytoskeleton that makes those changes possible. Integrin αIIbβ3, the fibrinogen receptor whose loss causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia, sits at the centre: outside-in signalling through it recruits Rho-family regulators such as a RhoGAP and a WASP-family nucleation promoting factor, while tropomyosins and an actin-binding LIM protein organise the filaments that drive lamellipodial spreading and clot retraction. Secreted and surface partners tune the response — thrombospondin and TGF-β from alpha granules, protein S as an anticoagulant cofactor, the thrombopoietin receptor governing megakaryocyte output, and a phosphodiesterase that degrades cyclic GMP and so opposes nitric oxide-mediated inhibition. Together these set the balance between effective haemostasis and thrombosis.

These genes outline an endothelial identity and blood-vessel morphogenesis programme, of the kind that distinguishes vascular endothelium and sets arterial versus venous character during angiogenic remodelling. Its output is a patent, correctly patterned vascular network: guidance receptors such as neuropilin-1 and the fibronectin leucine-rich repeat protein FLRT2 read angiogenic and adhesive cues, adhesion-family GPCRs enriched in endothelium (ADGRL4/ELTD1, ADGRL2) tune sprouting behaviour, and the soluble guanylate cyclase alpha subunit places nitric oxide-cGMP signalling and vessel tone in the same module. Downstream, the Hippo pathway transcriptional coactivators YAP1 and WWTR1/TAZ convert junctional and flow-derived mechanical information into growth and junction remodelling, while ARHGAP29 restrains RhoA to permit cytoskeletal and lumen formation and the scaffold MPDZ supports apical junction organisation. The nuclear receptor NR2F2 contributes venous specification, and failure of such regulation yields vascular malformation and impaired sprouting.

These genes converge on myeloid and platelet regulation, the arm of innate immunity and haemostasis in which surface receptor engagement is translated into inflammatory gene expression or into control of cell activation. LYN, the Src-family kinase that both initiates and dampens signalling from immunoglobulin and integrin receptors, together with the myeloid-restricted membrane protein LST1 and the transcription factor CEBPB, marks the monocyte/macrophage and granulocyte programme: CEBPB drives acute-phase and cytokine responses and is required for emergency granulopoiesis. MRVI1 anchors the nitric-oxide/cGMP brake on platelet calcium release, linking the set to inhibition of aggregation, while PDLIM7 and CPPED1 act on actin cytoskeletal and phosphatase-dependent remodelling that accompanies activation. Additional members contribute membrane phospholipid synthesis, autophagic trafficking, tRNA splicing and nuclear export, the housekeeping capacity such secretory, high-turnover cells depend on. Dysregulation here shifts the balance toward chronic inflammation or thrombosis.

These genes converge on myeloid and platelet function, where surface signalling is translated into changes in the actin cytoskeleton and in gene expression. The Src-family kinase LYN sits at the top of immunoreceptor and integrin signalling in leukocytes and platelets, setting both activating and inhibitory tone, while LST1 is an immune-cell transmembrane protein that shapes membrane protrusions and cell-cell contact. MRVI1 couples nitric oxide-driven cGMP signalling to inhibition of calcium release from intracellular stores, a brake on platelet activation. CEBPB provides the transcriptional arm, driving inflammatory and granulocyte-macrophage differentiation programmes, and PDLIM7 and XPO6 act on actin organisation, the latter exporting actin from the nucleus. Also represented are phospholipid synthesis, autophagy-related trafficking and tRNA splicing activities that support these cells, making the group a mixture of activation signalling, cytoskeletal control and housekeeping capacity.

Platelets stop bleeding by sticking to damaged vessel walls and then amplifying that contact into a clot, and the genes here cover both the adhesion step and its coupling to the coagulation cascade. The glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, encoded by GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9 and GP5, is the receptor for von Willebrand factor and captures platelets from flowing blood under high shear; GP6 binds exposed collagen and triggers the signalling that drives granule release and integrin activation. Loss of these receptors or of von Willebrand factor causes inherited bleeding disorders, while excessive engagement underlies arterial thrombosis, which is why this axis is a drug target. Other members temper or support the response: PROS1 acts as a cofactor for activated protein C in restraining thrombin generation, PCSK6 processes secreted precursors, and SEPT5 contributes to regulated granule exocytosis.

This is the fibroblast-type extracellular matrix programme: the set of genes that build and remodel the fibrillar collagen scaffold holding connective tissue together. It gives tissues tensile strength, provides the substrate cells adhere to and migrate along, and sequesters growth factors in a form that can be released on demand. Fibrillar collagens I, III and V are the structural core, with type VI and basement membrane components laminin and nidogens linking cells to the network; small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan and lumican, together with versican and fibrillin, control fibril diameter, spacing and elastic fibre assembly. A procollagen C-proteinase enhancer and matrix metalloproteinase 2 handle maturation and turnover, while PDGF ligand and its two receptors drive the mesenchymal cells that produce all of it. Persistent activation of this programme underlies fibrosis, wound scarring and the desmoplastic stroma of tumours.

This grouping describes the building and remodelling of the extracellular matrix, the fibrillar scaffold that gives tissues tensile strength and provides the surfaces on which cells adhere, migrate and receive growth factor cues. Fibrillar and basement membrane collagens together with fibrillin, laminin, nidogens, versican and the matricellular proteins SPARC, periostin, thrombospondin-2 and TGFBI form and organise that scaffold, while lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen, MMP2 and cathepsins degrade it, and HTRA1 and cystatin C act on matrix proteases and their substrates. Coordinated deposition and turnover underlie wound healing, vascular and skeletal integrity, and the stromal reaction around tumours; sustained excess deposition produces fibrosis, and mutations in the collagen and fibrillin components cause connective tissue disorders. A complement of neutrophil and macrophage granule and secreted products here links matrix turnover to inflammatory tissue remodelling.

This is a fibroblast-type extracellular matrix programme: the collagens, proteoglycans and glycoproteins that build interstitial connective tissue and the enzymes that remodel it. Such a matrix gives tissues tensile strength and elasticity, provides the scaffold on which cells migrate during wound healing, and stores growth factors that are released when it is degraded. Fibrillar collagens I, III and V assemble into the load-bearing fibrils, fibrillin-1 forms the microfibrils that organise elastic fibres, and laminin and nidogen contribute to basement membrane contacts, while decorin and versican regulate fibril diameter and tissue hydration. Matrix metalloproteinase 1 cleaves collagen to allow turnover, and cadherin-11 mediates the cell-cell adhesion typical of mesenchymal cells. Excess output from this programme underlies fibrosis and tumour stroma; mutations in its structural genes cause connective tissue disorders affecting skin, vessels and skeleton.

AP-1 is the dimeric transcription factor built from Jun and Fos family partners, and this network describes how its rapid induction converts growth factor, cytokine and stress signals into changes in gene expression. Because FOS, FOSB, JUN and JUNB are immediate-early genes, the response is fast and self-limiting, and it sets the transcriptional tone for proliferation, differentiation, wound repair and inflammation. Downstream targets in the network illustrate what the factor accomplishes: matrix metalloproteinases and urokinase plasminogen activator remodel extracellular matrix and support invasion, while chemokine and cytokine genes such as CCL2, IL6 and IL8 recruit and activate leukocytes. Additional stress-responsive regulators including ATF3 and EGR1 act alongside and feed back on the complex. Persistent AP-1 activity contributes to chronic inflammatory disease and to tumour invasion and metastasis, which is why this arm of immediate-early signalling is closely watched in cancer biology.

antigen processing and presentation is how cells display fragments of proteins and lipids on their surface so that T cells can inspect them, the step that lets the adaptive immune system distinguish self from pathogen. Without it, helper T cells are never primed, antibody responses fail, and tumour or microbial antigens go unseen.
