The genes centre on the MHC class II arm: HLA-DP and HLA-DQ heterodimers load peptides in the endosomal compartment of dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, while the HLA-DM chaperone catalyses removal of the placeholder CLIP peptide and edits the repertoire toward stable, high-affinity ligands. CD1D extends the same logic to lipid antigens recognised by invariant NKT cells, and WDFY4 is required for cross-presentation of cell-associated antigen by conventional dendritic cells to CD8 T cells. Variation here dominates genetic risk for autoimmune disease.

Immune surveillance depends on cells displaying fragments of what they have encountered, and this pathway covers the loading and surface display of antigen for recognition by T cells. The class II molecules here, including HLA-DP and HLA-DQ chains, present peptides taken up from outside the cell to CD4 helper T cells, an event that licenses antibody responses and macrophage activation; the HLA-DM heterodimer acts as a peptide-exchange catalyst in the endosomal loading compartment, releasing the invariant chain remnant and editing bound peptides for stability. CD1D instead presents lipid antigens to invariant natural killer T cells, and WDFY4 is required in dendritic cells for cross-presentation of cell-associated antigen to cytotoxic CD8 T cells. Variation in these loci underlies much of the genetic risk for autoimmune disease and shapes transplant compatibility, while loss of presentation lets tumours and intracellular pathogens escape detection.

The genes here sketch late erythroid differentiation and the assembly of the red cell surface. Erythropoiesis matters because it supplies the circulating oxygen carriers, and its transcriptional and membrane components determine both red cell mechanical resilience and the antigens that decide transfusion compatibility. Transcriptional regulators such as NFIA and PBX1 bias progenitors toward the erythroid rather than granulocytic fate, while cytoskeletal and adhesion proteins including the tropomodulin TMOD1, non-muscle myosin MYH10 and E-cadherin shape the actin-spectrin membrane skeleton and the erythroblastic island contacts with macrophages. Two membrane transporters carry clinically recognised blood group antigens: the urea transporter SLC14A1 and the xenobiotic efflux pump ABCG2, the latter also a marker of stem and progenitor populations. Loss of the structural arm of this programme produces fragile erythrocytes and haemolytic anaemia, while its surface proteins underlie alloimmunisation.

Connective tissue fibroblasts build and maintain the collagen-rich scaffold that gives organs their mechanical form, and this group of extracellular matrix and matrix-associated proteins marks that stromal programme. Secreted structural and regulatory components dominate: lumican and fibulin-1 bind collagen and elastic fibre networks, procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer promotes collagen maturation, and SFRP4 tunes Wnt signalling in the surrounding tissue. Alongside them sit mesenchymal identity factors such as TWIST1 and PRRX1, the PDGF receptor alpha that drives fibroblast proliferation and migration, and caldesmon, linking matrix output to actomyosin contractility. Together these activities govern wound healing, tissue stiffness and organ morphogenesis; sustained activation underlies fibrosis and the desmoplastic stroma of tumours, where such signatures mark cancer-associated fibroblasts and predict invasive behaviour.

This grouping centres on stress-activated transcriptional signalling and its supporting membrane and metabolic machinery. Its recognisable core is the kinase TAK1 (MAP3K7) acting upstream of the CREB/ATF family factors ATF1 and ATF2, a route by which cytokine, TGF-beta and stress inputs are converted into changes in gene expression governing inflammation, survival and differentiation; loss of TAK1 signalling causes inflammatory and developmental failure. Around this sit components of vesicular and secretory biology, including the early endosome tether EEA1 that organises incoming cargo on Rab5-positive membranes, the P4-ATPase ATP11C that flips phosphatidylserine to maintain plasma membrane asymmetry and is required for B lymphopoiesis and erythrocyte integrity, and the calcium-binding ER protein RCN2. Post-transcriptional and metabolic contributors include the splicing regulator MBNL2, the zinc-finger factors IKZF5 and ZBTB41, and glycogen debranching enzyme AGL, whose deficiency causes glycogen storage disease type III.

Newly synthesized polypeptides that cannot reach their native state unaided are folded inside barrel-shaped chaperonin cages, and this set captures that activity in both the cytosol and the mitochondrion. The eight-subunit cytosolic complex built from CCT2 through CCT8 folds actin and tubulin above all, so its output determines whether a cell can assemble a cytoskeleton, divide, and move; it also handles cell cycle regulators and other obligate clients. In mitochondria the HSPD1 ring works with its HSPE1 co-chaperonin to fold proteins after import across the inner membrane, supporting matrix enzymes of energy and nucleotide metabolism such as SUCLG1 and ATIC and the single-stranded DNA-binding protein SSBP1 that maintains the mitochondrial genome. ATP-driven cycles of substrate encapsulation and release provide a protected chamber in which folding proceeds without aggregation, and loss of these chaperonins causes proteostasis collapse and inherited neurodegeneration.

Newly synthesized actin and tubulin cannot reach their native shape on their own; they require the eukaryotic chaperonin, a double-ring ATP-driven folding chamber built from eight distinct CCT subunits. This route of chaperonin-mediated protein folding is what supplies the cell with polymerization-competent cytoskeletal monomers, so it underlies mitotic spindle assembly, cell motility and overall proteostasis, and its loss is not tolerated by dividing cells. Substrates are captured and delivered by prefoldin, a jellyfish-shaped hexameric cochaperone represented here by PFDN4, PFDN5 and VBP1, which binds nascent chains emerging from the ribosome and transfers them into the chaperonin cavity. Beyond actin and tubulin, the complex folds cell cycle regulators and assists assembly of multiprotein complexes, and its capacity is frequently co-opted by rapidly proliferating tumour cells.

This grouping centres on adaptor and scaffold proteins that set the gain of growth-factor and inflammatory signalling rather than carrying it themselves. Two arms dominate. One is NF- f0bB control: IKK f41 (CHUK) phosphorylates inhibitors of NF- f0bB to license inflammatory and survival transcription, while BAG4 and ZFAND6 act at TNF receptor complexes to restrain death-domain signalling. The other is BMP/TGF- f42 output, where the type II receptor BMPR2 initiates SMAD phosphorylation and the ubiquitin ligase RNF111 (Arkadia) degrades the inhibitory SMAD7 to sustain it; loss-of-function in BMPR2 underlies heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension. Linking these to cell-cycle and metabolic decisions are RB1, which enforces the restriction point, the mTOR effector kinase S6K1, and the NAD-dependent deacetylase SIRT1. Anchoring and GEF proteins such as AKAP11, ARFGEF2 and RAPGEF6 localise kinase and small-GTPase activity within this network.

Wnt signaling pathway refers to the intercellular signalling system that tells cells where they sit in a tissue, whether to divide, and which fate to adopt, and it governs stem cell maintenance, skeletal and neural patterning, and wound repair; its dysregulation drives fibrosis and cancer. The genes here emphasise extracellular tuning and mesenchymal output rather than the core destruction complex: secreted frizzled-related proteins FRZB and SFRP4 sequester Wnt ligands to set the strength and range of the signal, PDZRN3 acts as a ubiquitin ligase modulating receptor traffic and planar polarity, and YAP1 links the pathway to Hippo-dependent growth control. Matrix and guidance components such as LAMC1, LOXL2, NRP1 and CHL1, together with CXCL12 and KITLG, place this activity in the niche where migrating and differentiating cells read positional cues, with SOX4 carrying transcriptional output.

Wnt signalling tells cells where they are and what to become, controlling stem and progenitor self-renewal, body axis and limb patterning, bone mass and the mesenchymal programmes of tissue repair; its persistent activation drives cancers, while loss of tone in bone and cartilage contributes to degenerative disease. The genes here emphasise the extracellular and matrix-facing side of the pathway rather than the nuclear core: FRZB and SFRP4 are secreted Frizzled-related decoys that bind Wnt ligands and dampen receptor engagement, while laminin, LOXL2-dependent collagen crosslinking and adhesion molecules such as CHL1 and NRP1 shape the environment through which the ligand gradient is read. PDZRN3, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, tunes Wnt receptor and planar-polarity output, and SOX4 and the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 link the pathway to growth and cell-fate decisions downstream, alongside chemokine and growth-factor cues including CXCL12 and KITLG.

The dominant theme here is transmembrane solute handling in polarized epithelia of liver and kidney, coupled to regulated vesicular secretion. Several members are plasma-membrane carriers that set how nutrients and ions cross epithelial barriers: GLUT2 moves glucose across hepatocyte and beta-cell membranes and underlies glucose sensing, the organic cation transporter SLC22A2 clears cationic drugs and metabolites in the proximal tubule, SLC6A13 imports betaine and GABA, and the copper-transporting ATPase ATP7B loads copper onto ceruloplasmin and excretes excess into bile, its loss causing Wnson disease. LRP2/megalin retrieves filtered proteins and vitamin carriers by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Alongside these, Rab and active-zone-associated trafficking proteins direct granule and vesicle fusion, while the plasmin inhibitor SERPINF2 restrains fibrinolysis. Together the genes touch nutrient uptake, metal and xenobiotic excretion, and stimulus-coupled release.

This pathway centers on control of cell shape, adhesion and directed migration through Rho-family GTPase signalling and actin nucleation, coupled to transcriptional programs that specify tissue identity. ARHGAP5 inactivates RhoA to loosen adhesion and permit motility, SCAI restrains invasive migration by repressing MT1-MMP transcription downstream of RhoA-mDia, and JMY acts both as an actin nucleator at the leading edge and as a p53 cofactor linking cytoskeletal remodelling to DNA damage responses. HACE1, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that degrades active Rac1, suppresses tumour growth and reactive oxygen production, while TUBE1 seeds centriole assembly and thereby microtubule organisation. Homeodomain and NKX2-1 transcription factors impose regional and lung epithelial identity on these motile behaviours, and APP and CCL23 contribute adhesive and chemotactic cues. Together these activities govern morphogenesis, wound repair and the migratory steps that become tumour invasion when deregulated.

Cell migration and invasion are held in check by regulators that limit Rho-family GTPase activity and remodel the actin cytoskeleton, and several members here converge on that control point. ARHGAP5 accelerates GTP hydrolysis on RhoA, HACE1 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets active Rac1 for degradation, and SCAI restrains transcription-coupled invasion programmes, while JMY nucleates actin and also acts as a transcriptional cofactor for p53-dependent responses. Alongside these sit developmental transcription factors of the homeobox and NK2 families that specify regional and organ identity, notably NKX2-1 in thyroid and lung epithelium, plus APP and a chemokine ligand that influence adhesion and leukocyte recruitment. Taken together the grouping speaks to cytoskeletal and transcriptional restraint of motility and growth, biology whose loss contributes to tumour invasion and metastasis.

lysosome is the cell's acidic degradative compartment and the hydrolase set that works inside it, breaking down proteins, glycans and lipids delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis and autophagy so their building blocks can be recycled. Its capacity matters most in macrophages and other phagocytes, where CD68 marks the lysosomal membrane and cathepsins B, L and Z digest ingested material and process antigens; it also matters in neurons, where failure of these enzymes produces storage disease. The genes cover the main functional classes: cysteine protease hydrolases, glycosidases such as alpha-L-fucosidase and glucosamine-6-sulfatase that dismantle glycoconjugates and glycosaminoglycans, the lipid-hydrolase activators prosaposin and GM2 activator protein, and sortilin, a sorting receptor that traffics newly made hydrolases from the Golgi to the lysosome. Together they link membrane turnover and nutrient recovery to immune function.

Lysosomes are the acidic degradative compartment where proteins, glycans and lipids delivered by endocytosis, phagocytosis and autophagy are broken down and their building blocks returned to the cell. The genes here cover both the hydrolases and the machinery that supports them: cathepsins B, L, V and Z carry out bulk proteolysis, fucosidase and glucuronidase-type glycosidases trim sugar chains, and prosaposin and the GM2 activator protein act as lipid-transfer cofactors that present sphingolipid substrates to their enzymes. Sortilin sorts newly made hydrolases and other cargo from the Golgi toward this compartment, while CD68 is a heavily glycosylated lysosomal membrane protein used as a marker of macrophages and other highly phagocytic cells. Loss of single hydrolases or their activators causes lysosomal storage disease, with undigested substrate accumulating and neurodegeneration a frequent consequence.

Lymphocytes circulate continuously and must be captured out of the bloodstream at the right place, and this adhesion programme governs that homing into lymph nodes and other secondary lymphoid tissue. It is what allows naive T and B cells to meet antigen-presenting cells in organised follicles, so immune surveillance and the initiation of adaptive responses depend on it; the same steps are exploited by leukaemic and lymphoma cells that traffic to nodes. Rolling on high endothelial venules is initiated by L-selectin, while the chemokine receptor CCR7 and the B-cell-attracting chemokine CXCL13 provide the directional cues that position cells within distinct zones. Firm adhesion and arrest require cytoskeletal coupling through focal adhesion kinase and the Rho-family activator VAV1, linking receptor engagement to integrin-dependent attachment, junctional organisation and migration across the endothelium.

Connective tissue owes its tensile strength and elasticity to a collagen-rich extracellular matrix, and these genes cover its construction, decoration and controlled turnover. Fibrillar and network collagens of several classes are represented, including basement membrane COL4A1, the fibril-associated COL12A1 and COL14A1, and cartilage COL10A1 and COL11A1, alongside the crosslinking peroxidase PXDN and elastic-fibre and microfibril components such as EMILIN1, MFAP2/4/5 and fibulin-family EFEMP1 and EFEMP2. Small leucine-rich proteoglycans including decorin, osteomodulin and podocan bind collagen fibrils and set their diameter and spacing, while TIMP1 and TIMP3 restrain metalloproteinases and ADAMTS enzymes process procollagen and proteoglycans. CTGF and TGFB1I1 tie the programme to TGF-beta-driven fibrogenesis, and tenascin C marks remodelling matrix. Sustained activation of this output underlies fibrosis, scarring and tumour stroma; loss-of-function affects skeletal, vascular and corneal integrity.

This is a loosely connected housekeeping module whose members support cell growth control, membrane and organelle dynamics, and the damping of stress signalling rather than one linear route. Several components sit downstream of DNA damage and proliferative cues: cyclin G1 is a p53-responsive regulator of cell cycle progression and PP2A recruitment, BMI1 is a Polycomb repressive complex 1 subunit that silences the CDKN2A locus and sustains stem and progenitor self-renewal, and NEK7 serves both mitotic spindle assembly and inflammasome activation. Others handle infrastructure: ADD3 caps and links spectrin cytoskeleton at membranes, RAP1B controls integrin-mediated adhesion, SLC25A46 shapes mitochondrial and ER membrane dynamics with mutations causing optic atrophy and neuropathy, PLEKHF2 acts on endosomes, and RNF11 is a ubiquitin ligase component restraining NF-κB. CMPK1 supplies pyrimidine nucleotide phosphorylation for DNA and RNA synthesis and for activating nucleoside analogue drugs.

Purine nucleotide biosynthesis builds the adenine and guanine nucleotides that cells need for DNA and RNA synthesis, energy currency, and signalling, and demand for it rises sharply in proliferating cells such as lymphocytes and tumours. Several of the genes here carry out consecutive steps of the de novo route from phosphoribosylamine to IMP: a formylglycinamidine synthase, a bifunctional carboxylase/succinocarboxamide synthase, adenylosuccinate lyase and the bifunctional transformylase/IMP cyclohydrolase, with one-carbon units supplied by a trifunctional folate enzyme. Beyond IMP, IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthase commit flux to guanine nucleotides, which is why IMP dehydrogenase inhibition is used clinically as an immunosuppressant. The remaining members point to the physical organisation of this chemistry, since the pathway enzymes cluster into a multienzyme assembly whose folding and assembly depend on chaperonin subunits. Inherited loss of adenylosuccinate lyase causes severe neurodevelopmental disease.

A heterogeneous collection of transcriptional regulators and cofactors that set how RNA polymerase machinery is recruited and how much messenger RNA a gene yields, the layer of control that distinguishes one cell type from another and that tumours and developmental disorders routinely subvert. Several members act directly at promoters: BDP1 is a subunit of the RNA polymerase III initiation factor TFIIIB, BTAF1 modulates TBP binding to DNA, and MED23 is a Mediator subunit that couples signal-responsive activators to the core polymerase II apparatus. Others regulate transcription indirectly, through cyclin T2 in the CDK9-containing elongation kinase, CLK kinases that phosphorylate SR splicing factors, chromatin and cohesin-associated proteins such as ARID4B and STAG2, and zinc-finger and bZIP-type DNA-binding factors. Together they illustrate how initiation, elongation and co-transcriptional RNA processing are regulated as one connected process.

This grouping centres on membrane lipid organisation and the trafficking and signalling events built on it. Its clearest core is the aminophospholipid flippase machinery: ATP11B, a P4-ATPase, must partner with the accessory subunit TMEM30A (CDC50A) to fold, reach the plasma membrane and translocate phosphatidylserine to the cytosolic leaflet, which keeps this lipid hidden until apoptosis or platelet activation exposes it. LPGAT1 extends the theme by remodelling acyl chains during phospholipid synthesis, so bilayer composition and curvature are set here. The remaining members act on membrane-associated traffic and signal relay — STXBP3 in vesicle docking, SPAST in microtubule severing needed for membrane tubule and axonal maintenance, RP2 as a regulator of the small GTPase ARL3 in ciliary transport, and SOS2, PIK3CG, TGFBR1 and the IKK-family kinase CHUK transducing receptor signals from the membrane toward growth and inflammatory transcription.

Small GTPase mediated signal transduction is the switch-like relay by which Ras-superfamily GTPases convert receptor signals into changes in cytoskeletal shape, adhesion and motility. The genes here describe a specifically hematopoietic version of that relay, built around Rho-family members RAC2, RHOG and RHOH: the exchange factors VAV1 and FGD3 load them with GTP downstream of antigen and integrin receptors, while a large complement of RhoGAPs and the dissociation inhibitors ARHGDIA/ARHGDIB terminate and spatially confine the signal. This balance sets the timing of lymphocyte activation, leukocyte migration and phagocyte NADPH oxidase assembly; loss of RAC2 or VAV1 function produces immunodeficiency with defective T cell signalling and neutrophil chemotaxis. Because activation is transient by design, the abundance of negative regulators is the point rather than an accessory feature, and their disruption drives unchecked motility and invasion.

Small GTPase mediated signal transduction converts receptor engagement into changes in the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, adhesion and directed movement, and the genes here represent the Rho-family arm of that switching system as it operates in leukocytes. Rac2, RhoG and RhoH cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states; a nucleotide exchange factor such as VAV1 loads GTP downstream of immune receptor signalling, while numerous Rho GTPase-activating proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis to terminate the signal, and the guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors ARHGDIA and ARHGDIB sequester inactive GTPases in the cytosol. The balance of these opposing regulators sets how much and how long a cell can polarise, spread, phagocytose or migrate. Loss of RAC2 or VAV1 function compromises neutrophil chemotaxis, lymphocyte activation and immune synapse formation, and dysregulated Rho signalling contributes to invasive behaviour in cancer cells.

Aerobic ATP production depends on passing electrons from NADH and succinate along a chain of inner-membrane complexes to oxygen, using the released energy to pump protons and build the gradient that drives ATP synthesis. The genes here are accessory and small structural subunits spanning that entire route: several supernumerary subunits of complex I, two subunits of the cytochrome bc1 complex, a set of nuclear-encoded cytochrome c oxidase subunits, and two subunits of the ATP synthase stalk. Such subunits are largely peripheral to the catalytic cores but are needed for assembly, stability and supercomplex formation, so their loss lowers respiratory capacity rather than abolishing catalysis outright. Defects in this machinery underlie mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis, encephalomyopathy and cardiomyopathy, and its partial failure raises reactive oxygen species output and shifts cells toward glycolysis.

Despite the label, these genes describe a vascular stromal compartment rather than a lymphocyte programme: endothelial and perivascular cells together with the matrix they deposit. CDH5 forms the endothelial adherens junction that seals the vessel wall and restrains permeability, while LUM, MXRA5, ABI3BP and FLRT2 are secreted or matrix-associated proteins that organise collagen fibrils and guide adhesion of the surrounding mesenchyme. MEOX2 is a transcription factor of smooth muscle and pericyte-like lineages, and TMEM47 and PLSCR4 mark membrane specialisations of these mural cells. PROS1, an anticoagulant cofactor and also a ligand for TAM receptors, links the endothelium to control of clotting and clearance of dying cells, and FMO3 adds oxidative metabolism of amines. Collectively the set supports vessel integrity, tissue architecture and fibrotic remodelling, the stromal scaffolding on which immune tissue is built.

A loose assembly of housekeeping functions centred on nuclear gene expression and genome integrity, with additional arms in metabolism and membrane traffic. Transcription and chromatin components dominate: the Paf1-complex subunit CTR9 and the Elongator catalytic subunit ELP3 support RNA polymerase II elongation and co-transcriptional modification, GTF2H1 anchors the TFIIH complex used for both promoter opening and nucleotide-excision repair, and CSRP2BP contributes histone acetyltransferase activity. Genome maintenance is represented by the mismatch-repair protein PMS1, whose loss drives microsatellite instability, and by POT1, which caps the single-stranded telomeric overhang and prevents inappropriate DNA damage signalling at chromosome ends. Alongside these, ACADM performs the first step of medium-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation, ALG6 and nucleotide-sugar transporters serve glycosylation in the ER and Golgi, HPS5 builds lysosome-related organelles, and ATG4C processes autophagy proteins. Deficiencies in these genes produce unrelated disorders rather than one syndrome.

Oxidative phosphorylation depends on passing electrons from ubiquinol to oxygen, and the genes here build the two complexes that do it: the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, linked by the mobile carrier cytochrome c. Electron flow through these complexes pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthase, represented here by a subunit of its membrane stalk. Most of the members are small nuclear-encoded accessory subunits that assemble around the catalytic, mitochondrially encoded cores, stabilise them, and support the supercomplexes in which the respiratory chain is organised; COX7A2L in particular acts as an assembly factor for such higher-order associations. Loss of these subunits lowers respiratory capacity and produces mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and excess reactive oxygen production, since stalled electron carriers leak electrons to oxygen.

Correction of base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops left behind by DNA polymerases is what keeps the replicated genome faithful, and loss of this activity produces the microsatellite instability and hypermutation that underlie Lynch syndrome and a large fraction of sporadic colorectal and endometrial tumours. The recognition step here is the MSH2-MSH6 heterodimer, which scans newly made duplex DNA and, with the sliding clamp PCNA and the clamp loader subunits RFC2-RFC5, directs excision by EXO1 and resynthesis by replicative polymerases and primase. The wider membership places this repair squarely inside S-phase replication and chromosome dynamics: single-strand binding and replication-initiation factors, condensin and cohesin subunits, and the checkpoint proteins CHEK1, TOPBP1 and BUB1, reflecting how strand-discrimination signals are tied to the replication fork and to the checkpoints that halt division when damage persists.

Replication inserts the wrong base often enough that an error-correcting system is needed behind the fork, and DNA mismatch repair is that system: it finds base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops in newly made strands and replaces the daughter-strand segment. Loss of it raises mutation rates by orders of magnitude and destabilises short repeat tracts, the microsatellite instability seen in Lynch syndrome and in sporadic colorectal and endometrial tumours; the same defect makes tumours responsive to immune checkpoint blockade. Mismatches are recognised by MSH2 paired with MSH6, which recruits an MLH1-containing complex; the sliding clamp PCNA and its loader RFC provide the strand-discrimination signal, EXO1 excises the error-containing strand, RPA protects the exposed single-stranded gap, and polymerase delta resynthesises it. The pathway also contributes to damage signalling and to the toxicity of some chemotherapeutics.

Androgen receptor signalling toward luminal secretory epithelial identity is the coherent theme here, together with a minority of neuronal components. AR itself is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor whose transcriptional output specifies prostate luminal cells and drives their secretory programme; it is the therapeutic target in prostate cancer, and loss-of-function mutation causes androgen insensitivity. Alongside it sit transcription factors that pattern epithelia and glandular tissue components: SPDEF, which promotes secretory and goblet-cell differentiation, SOX9, required for chondrogenesis and ductal epithelium, and TFAP2A, acting in neural crest and surface ectoderm. SFN (14-3-3 csigma) links the group to p53-dependent growth arrest in stratified epithelia, while GRIN2B, KCNC3, NOS1AP and REEP1 reflect neuronal excitability and axonal membrane biology, genes mutated in spinocerebellar ataxia and hereditary spastic paraplegia. Hormone-responsive transcriptional control of differentiation is the unifying purpose.

No single process unites these genes; they sample several unrelated areas of biology, and the most useful reading is of the parts. Two type I interferon alpha genes encode secreted cytokines that place cells in an antiviral state through JAK-STAT signalling and shape innate and adaptive immune responses. MST1 encodes macrophage-stimulating protein, a plasminogen-related ligand for the RON receptor tyrosine kinase that influences macrophage motility and epithelial responses, and its variants associate with inflammatory bowel disease. ESCO2 is an acetyltransferase that modifies the cohesin complex to establish sister chromatid cohesion during S phase, and its loss causes Roberts syndrome. LBX1 and POU4F2 are homeodomain and POU transcription factors directing neuronal and muscle precursor fate, while RNF17 acts in germ cell piRNA-dependent silencing. Several remaining entries are non-coding or poorly characterised loci.

Heme biosynthesis supplies the iron-protoporphyrin cofactor that hemoglobin, cytochromes and catalase depend on, and in erythroid cells it runs at enormous scale to match globin production during terminal red cell maturation. The enzymatic core here covers the middle steps of the tetrapyrrole route: condensation of aminolevulinate by ALAD, assembly and cyclization of the linear tetrapyrrole via HMBS, and successive decarboxylation and oxidation by UROD, CPOX and PPOX that yield protoporphyrin IX for iron insertion. Partial loss of these activities causes the porphyrias, in which accumulated intermediates provoke neurovisceral attacks or photosensitivity. The accompanying erythroid context is explicit: KLF1 drives the red cell transcriptional programme, SPTA1 builds the membrane skeleton, RHD and RHCE encode blood group antigens, and BLVRB reduces biliverdin during heme turnover, tying synthesis to erythropoiesis and pigment catabolism.

This group of transcripts marks T lymphocytes, and its members read out the activities that distinguish resting and activated T cells from other blood leukocytes. Among them, CD40LG on activated helper T cells engages CD40 on B cells and dendritic cells to license antibody class switching and myeloid activation, and its loss causes hyper-IgM immunodeficiency; DPP4 (CD26) is a surface peptidase and costimulatory marker; CLEC2D is the ligand for the inhibitory receptor CD161; and a T-cell receptor gamma constant region reflects the gamma-delta compartment. Others, including HOPX, FGFBP2 and LRRN3, track effector and memory differentiation, with FGFBP2 typical of cytotoxic effector cells and LRRN3 of naive cells. Transport, trafficking and adaptor proteins such as SLC38A1, DENND2D and TC2N support the metabolic and membrane demands of lymphocyte activation, making the module useful for inferring T-cell content and activation state in tissue expression data.

A mixed group of membrane transport and excitability proteins that set ion gradients and electrical signalling across several tissues. Included are voltage-gated and ligand-gated channels (a retinal calcium channel subunit, an atrial potassium channel, a kainate-type glutamate receptor), solute carriers that move calcium, sodium, bicarbonate and glutamate, and a copper-transporting ATPase whose loss causes hepatic and neurological copper overload in Wilson disease. Others shape the membrane environment in which channels work: junctophilin couples surface membrane to sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release in cardiomyocytes, and dystrophin anchors the sarcolemma to the cytoskeleton, with its loss producing muscular dystrophy. Together these activities support cardiac and skeletal muscle contraction, photoreceptor and synaptic transmission, glutamate clearance, and intracellular pH and metal homeostasis, and mutations in individual members give rise to arrhythmia, retinal dystrophy and ataxia.

metabolism of steroids covers the enzymatic modification and disposal of steroid hormones and related lipophilic compounds, the step that terminates hormone action and allows androgens, estrogens and bile acid derivatives to be excreted in urine and bile. The dominant activity here is glucuronidation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT2A and UGT2B families conjugate glucuronic acid onto steroid hydroxyl groups, converting them into water-soluble products that no longer bind nuclear receptors. UGT2B15 and UGT2B17 act on testosterone and dihydrotestosterone metabolites, so their activity sets androgen tone in liver and prostate, and copy-number loss of UGT2B17 is a well-known source of variation in androgen clearance and drug metabolism. The remaining members point to the tissues where this chemistry happens — renal tubular and biliary epithelium, represented by PKHD1, HAVCR1 and myo-inositol oxygenase — linking steroid inactivation to excretory organ function and to xenobiotic detoxification more broadly.

Steroid hormones are cleared and inactivated as well as made, and this grouping centres on that disposal arm of steroid metabolism. Several UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT2B family attach glucuronic acid to hydroxysteroids, converting androgens and their metabolites into water-soluble conjugates that can be excreted in urine and bile; UGT2B15 and UGT2B17 are the main routes for testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, so their common deletion and coding polymorphisms shift circulating androgen levels and influence prostate biology and drug clearance. A related transferase acting on similar lipophilic substrates broadens the range of steroids and xenobiotics handled. The remaining members point to kidney and epithelial context, including a fibrocystin-encoding gene mutated in polycystic kidney disease, a kidney injury marker, an inositol oxygenase, a glycosyltransferase and a kinase, consistent with hormone conjugation occurring in liver and in the epithelia that complete excretion.

Regulated destruction of proteins by the proteasome is how cells terminate signalling, clear damaged or misfolded polypeptides, and impose the timed degradation of cyclins and transcription factors that drives cell cycle progression. The core of this module is the 20S particle, built from alpha-type subunits such as PSMA2 through PSMA6 that form the outer rings and gate substrate entry into the proteolytic chamber, together with 19S regulatory components: the AAA-ATPases PSMC2 and PSMC6 that unfold and translocate substrates, and PSMD14, the deubiquitinase that strips ubiquitin chains before degradation. Accompanying factors link this activity to nucleocytoplasmic transport and transcription, reflecting the fact that ubiquitin-dependent turnover acts on nuclear regulators and requires RAN-dependent trafficking. Loss of proteasome capacity causes proteotoxic stress, and its pharmacological inhibition is used therapeutically against plasma cell malignancies.

Translation initiation is the step at which ribosomes are recruited to an mRNA and positioned at the start codon, and it is the principal point where protein synthesis rates are set in response to nutrients, stress and growth signals. Core components here include the eIF2 complex subunits that deliver initiator methionyl-tRNA in a GTP-dependent manner, a subunit of the multiprotein eIF3 assembly that binds the small ribosomal subunit, and the RNA helicase accessory factor eIF4H that assists scanning through structured 5' untranslated regions. Phosphorylation of eIF2 alpha during the integrated stress response shuts down bulk initiation while permitting selective translation of stress-adaptive messages. Additional members link initiation to ribosome maturation through rRNA methylation, to deneddylation and proteasomal regulation, and to nuclear pore and mitochondrial respiratory functions, reflecting the coupling of protein synthesis to cellular energy supply and protein turnover.

Odour detection begins with olfactory receptors, the largest family of G protein-coupled receptors in the human genome, expressed on the cilia of olfactory sensory neurons in the nasal epithelium. Each neuron typically commits to a single receptor gene, and the combinatorial pattern of receptors activated by a volatile molecule is what the brain reads as a distinct smell; loss of this repertoire underlies anosmia and blunted flavour perception. Ligand binding drives Gs-type coupling to adenylate cyclase, cyclic nucleotide-gated channel opening, and depolarisation, a scheme shared with the guanylate cyclase activator machinery of photoreceptors represented here. Members such as OR2H1, OR2C3, OR7C2 and OR7D2 sit in clustered, highly polymorphic loci, and several are also transcribed outside the nose, where related receptors contribute to chemosensation in sperm, gut and kidney. The remaining entries reflect duplicated and pseudogene-rich sequence in these genomic neighbourhoods.

This grouping centres on transcriptional repression and chromatin-based silencing, the machinery that keeps developmental and proliferative genes switched off until they are needed. Polycomb components are the anchor: BMI1 is a core subunit of the PRC1 ubiquitin ligase complex that marks histone H2A to maintain silencing, while AEBP2 is a zinc-finger accessory factor that helps target the companion PRC2 methyltransferase to chromatin. Other members add repressive and regulatory context — MIER3 acts as a transcriptional corepressor, CRY1 represses the transcriptional output of the circadian clock, CCNC pairs with CDK8 in the Mediator kinase module, and CDKN2AIP links to p53/ARF-dependent growth control. Together these activities bear on stem and progenitor self-renewal, cell cycle exit and senescence; loss of Polycomb repression releases the CDKN2A locus and other targets, a route to both premature senescence and cancer.

Monocyte identity and output depend on the convergence of retinoic acid, WNT and colony-stimulating factor signals on a shared transcriptional programme. This network describes how growth factor receptors for M-CSF, GM-CSF and G-CSF, the Frizzled receptors of the WNT pathway, and nuclear retinoid receptors formed from RARA and RXRA heterodimers act together with the myeloid master regulators PU.1 and CEBPA to set commitment, proliferation and survival in the monocyte-macrophage lineage. Its output includes inflammatory effector genes such as the chemokine IL8 and the prostaglandin-generating enzyme encoded by PTGS2, with FOS providing immediate-early transcriptional coupling. The same receptors govern how monocytes are recruited and how they mature into macrophages and osteoclasts, so distortion of this circuitry contributes to myeloid leukaemias, chronic inflammation and bone remodelling disorders, and CSF1R blockade is used to manipulate macrophage numbers therapeutically.

Mitosis is the segment of the cell cycle in which a duplicated genome is condensed, attached to spindle microtubules, and split equally between two daughter cells; errors here produce aneuploidy and are a route to tumorigenesis and developmental failure. The genes here touch several requirements of that division. Kinetochore components such as the centromere protein CENPC and the MIS12 complex subunit build the chromosome-microtubule interface, while cohesin's SMC3 subunit holds sister chromatids together until anaphase. Nucleoporin-related factors including RANBP2 and ELYS contribute to nuclear envelope breakdown and reassembly and to kinetochore function, and tubulin epsilon supports centriole and centrosome organisation. Ubiquitin-pathway activity, via the NEDD8-activating subunit NAE1 and the HECT ligase HACE1, links protein turnover to mitotic progression, and p53-binding regulators tie division to damage checkpoints and apoptosis.

respiratory electron transport chain (mitochondrion) is the oxidative phosphorylation machinery of the inner mitochondrial membrane, the route by which electrons stripped from NADH and succinate are passed to oxygen and the energy released is captured as ATP. Nearly all aerobic ATP production depends on it, and loss of individual subunits causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and Leigh syndrome, with tissues of high energy demand such as brain, heart and muscle affected first. The genes span the chain from end to end: multiple accessory and core subunits of complex I, the Rieske iron-sulfur protein of complex III, a cytochrome c oxidase subunit, and subunits of the ATP synthase that converts the resulting proton gradient into chemical energy. Assembly is coordinated between nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, and the same electron flow is the principal cellular source of reactive oxygen species.

Oxidative phosphorylation is how most ATP in aerobic cells is made, and this is the mitochondrial inner-membrane machinery that does it: electrons stripped from NADH pass along the respiratory chain to oxygen while protons are pumped across the membrane, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthesis. The genes here span several of the complexes involved — numerous accessory and core subunits of complex I (including NDUFS3, NDUFA8 and the acyl carrier subunit NDUFAB1), the iron-sulfur subunit of complex III, a cytochrome c oxidase subunit, and subunits of the F1Fo ATP synthase. Tissues with high energy demand depend most heavily on this chain, and mutations in its subunits or their assembly factors cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome and optic neuropathies. The same electron flow is a principal source of reactive oxygen species, tying respiration to redox signalling and to apoptotic commitment.

A promoter-motif-defined grouping rather than a curated process: these genes share an upstream sequence resembling TNCATNTCCYR, the kind of shared cis-element that suggests coordinate transcriptional control by a common factor. The members converge on genome maintenance and basal transcription. RAD50 works within the sensor complex that detects double-strand breaks and initiates end resection, RAD51C supports homologous recombination and is a hereditary breast and ovarian cancer gene, and SMARCAL1 is an annealing helicase that stabilises stalled replication forks, its loss causing Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia. GTF2H1 is a core general transcription factor subunit also used in nucleotide excision repair, ELP4 belongs to the Elongator complex, and MEN1 encodes the menin tumour suppressor that scaffolds chromatin-modifying complexes. Others contribute peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, nucleotide signalling and vesicle tethering, so the set is best read as a regulatory module inferred from shared promoter architecture.

No single canonical route unites these genes; what they share is a bias toward developmental patterning and tissue-specific differentiation programmes. BMP4 is the signalling anchor, a secreted TGF-beta family ligand that instructs dorsoventral and organ-field patterning, limb and skeletal morphogenesis, and epithelial-mesenchymal dialogue. Acting with it are homeodomain regulators of positional identity along the body axis (HOXB13, HOXD10), the forkhead factor FOXN1 that specifies thymic epithelium and hair/nail keratinocytes and is required for T cell development, and the transcriptional repressor PRDM8 together with the neuronal RNA-binding protein ELAVL3, both tied to nervous system maturation. Other members point to differentiated cell functions: junctophilin-2 couples sarcolemmal and sarcoplasmic reticulum membranes in cardiomyocyte calcium release, BOK belongs to the BCL-2 family governing apoptotic commitment, and a secreted phospholipase and beta-crystallin serve immune and lens roles respectively.

transcription elongation, RNA polymerase II covers the productive phase of messenger RNA synthesis, in which polymerase II, having cleared the promoter, moves processively along the gene body to complete a full-length transcript. Rates of elongation set how quickly genes respond to stimuli and influence co-transcriptional splicing and termination, so defects here distort gene expression programmes broadly. The core here is the shared small subunits of the polymerase itself — POLR2E, POLR2I, POLR2J and POLR2L, which also serve RNA polymerases I and III — together with elongin B (TCEB2), a subunit of the elongin complex that suppresses transient pausing and, in a separate role, forms part of the VHL ubiquitin ligase. Accompanying mitochondrial respiratory subunits and small redox and iron-trafficking proteins link the transcriptional output to the energetic and metabolic state of the cell.

Once RNA polymerase II has initiated at a promoter, productive mRNA synthesis depends on it moving processively through the gene body, and the elongation step is where most regulation of transcript output is exerted. Several shared small subunits of the polymerase core, including POLR2E, POLR2I, POLR2J and POLR2L, hold the enzyme together and provide surfaces for elongation and termination factors, while elongin B (TCEB2) acts as the regulatory partner of the elongin complex, which stimulates the rate of elongation and is also the substrate-recognition module co-opted by the von Hippel-Lindau ubiquitin ligase. Failure of processive elongation stalls polymerase, promotes premature termination and distorts gene expression programmes. The remaining members are small respiratory chain and mitochondrial ribosome-associated proteins, tying transcriptional output to the energetic state of the cell rather than to the polymerase machinery itself.

This grouping of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes centres on matrix catabolism: medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase for fatty acid beta-oxidation, and a near-complete branched-chain amino acid route including 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase, 3-hydroxyisobutyrate dehydrogenase, methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase and a subunit of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, which together feed valine, leucine and isoleucine carbon into the TCA cycle. Alongside them sit a complex I accessory subunit, the mitochondrial co-chaperone DNAJA3 that supports import and matrix protein folding, and ALDH18A1, which commits glutamate to proline and ornithine synthesis. The shared theme is supplying acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA for oxidative ATP production and amino acid interconversion; loss of individual members causes inherited metabolic disease with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, organic acidurias or mitochondrial encephalopathy. Several remaining members are poorly characterised proteins whose co-regulation with these enzymes suggests mitochondrial function.

The dominant theme here is nuclear RNA production and maturation: an RNA polymerase I subunit supports ribosomal RNA transcription, a small-subunit processome component participates in pre-rRNA processing toward ribosome assembly, a general transcription factor subunit assists RNA polymerase II promoter opening, a spliceosome-associated crooked-neck-like factor acts in pre-mRNA splicing, and a core exosome subunit provides 3' to 5' exoribonuclease-mediated RNA trimming and surveillance; loss of that exosome subunit causes cerebellar hypoplasia with spinal motor neuron degeneration. Together these activities set the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and accurate mRNA output, and hence growth and protein synthesis. Accompanying members broaden the picture: a substrate receptor for a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase couples protein degradation to this machinery, GTPase-of-immunity-associated proteins regulate lymphocyte survival, a SNARE contributes to Golgi vesicle fusion, and zinc-finger proteins add transcriptional regulation.}

These are proteins that live in or act at the Golgi membrane, the sorting and modification station through which secretory and membrane cargo passes on its way from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell surface, endosomes and lysosomes. Several members build the glycan and lipid modifications that define Golgi output: a polypeptide GalNAc-transferase initiates mucin-type O-glycosylation, C1GALT1C1 acts as the chaperone required for core 1 synthase activity, sphingomyelin synthase converts ceramide at the trans-Golgi, and ZDHHC17 palmitoylates substrate proteins. Solute carriers of the SLC35 family import nucleotide sugars from the cytosol to feed these glycosyltransferases. The remainder handle membrane traffic and organelle architecture — COPI coat subunits, Rab GTPases, a PDZ scaffold and GOLPH3L linking Golgi membranes to cargo export and cisternal shape. Loss of such components disrupts glycosylation fidelity and secretion, the basis of congenital disorders of glycosylation.

Oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria depends on the respiratory electron transport chain, which passes electrons from NADH through a series of membrane complexes to oxygen and uses the released energy to pump protons across the inner membrane. The resulting electrochemical gradient drives ATP synthase, so this chemistry supplies most of the ATP used by heart, brain, and muscle. The genes here are mainly accessory and core subunits of complex I, including NDUFS7 and NDUFS8, which sit in the catalytic quinone-binding module, together with complex III subunits and several components of the ATP synthase stator and membrane sector. Loss of individual subunits causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies such as Leigh syndrome, and partial dysfunction raises reactive oxygen species production, linking this machinery to cellular redox balance and aging as well as to energy supply.

This grouping is built around proteins that handle or respond to calcium at the cell membrane and in the cytoskeleton, and it points to excitable and contractile tissues where calcium entry is translated into a change in activity. TRPC3 is a receptor-operated cation channel that admits calcium in response to phospholipase C signalling, notably in cerebellar Purkinje cells; GRIA4 is an AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunit carrying fast excitatory synaptic current; MYOZ2 (calsarcin-2) anchors calcineurin at the sarcomeric Z-disc, coupling calcium to hypertrophic gene programmes; and dystrophin links the muscle membrane to the actin cytoskeleton, with its loss in Duchenne muscular dystrophy producing calcium overload and fibre degeneration. Others, including EPHB1, SLITRK6 and SPOCK3, act in axon guidance and synapse organisation. Together the members connect calcium handling to synaptic transmission, muscle contraction and neuronal wiring rather than to a single signalling cascade.

cell activation (IL15, IL23, TNF) describes the inflammatory activation state of myeloid and stromal cells, in which pro-inflammatory cytokines are induced together with the NF-κB machinery that drives them and the brakes that limit them. This program mobilises innate and T cell responses — IL15 sustains NK and memory CD8 T cells, IL23 supports Th17 responses, and TNF amplifies local inflammation — and its unchecked persistence underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, which is why these cytokines are major drug targets. The gene complement captures the feedback logic as much as the output: NFKB2 and BCL3 shape late transcriptional responses, MAP3K8 relays signals toward cytokine production, and TNFAIP3 terminates NF-κB to prevent runaway signalling. Accompanying matrix and acute-phase components (FN1, COL3A1, SERPING1, A2M, TF) place the response in a tissue remodelling and wound-healing context, alongside CD83 marking activated antigen-presenting cells.

Inflammatory cell activation driven by the cytokines IL-15, IL-23 and TNF, a module that links innate stimulation to sustained NF- induced gene expression and to the tissue changes that accompany chronic inflammation. IL-15 supports natural killer and memory T cell survival, IL-23 sustains IL-17-producing T cells, and TNF amplifies both, so this combination underlies the cytokine networks targeted therapeutically in psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis. Signal relay runs through MAP3K8 to the MAP kinase cascade and through NFKB2, with BCL3, TNFAIP3 and SBNO2 acting as feedback restraints that limit how long activation persists; loss of such brakes predisposes to autoimmunity. Alongside these, CD83 marks activated dendritic cells, while fibronectin, collagen III, PDGFRA and acute-phase products such as A2M, SERPING1 and transferrin reflect the stromal remodelling and systemic response that follow prolonged activation.

chromosome Y linked collects genes carried on the male-specific portion of the Y chromosome, together with their X-linked counterparts, and it defines the small set of protein-coding functions unique to male cells. Its significance is twofold: these genes underlie spermatogenesis and male fertility, and their loss from blood cells with age is associated with cancer risk and cardiovascular disease. Several members are X-Y gene pairs that escaped degeneration and act in housekeeping roles -- the RNA helicase DDX3Y, the deubiquitinase USP9Y, and the histone demethylases KDM5D and UTY, which link Y-linked dosage to chromatin regulation and transcription. Deletions in this region cause azoospermia. The set also includes noncoding RNAs of sex chromosome regulation, notably XIST and its antisense partner, which govern X inactivation and thereby the broader problem of balancing sex chromosome gene dosage between males and females.

Genes carried on the male-specific portion of the Y chromosome, together with their X-linked counterparts, define the sex-chromosome dosage differences between male and female cells. Because the Y escapes the silencing that inactivates one X in females, its surviving genes are expressed from a single copy in males only, and several are ubiquitously transcribed housekeeping factors rather than testis-specific ones: an RNA helicase, a deubiquitinase, and the chromatin regulators that remove or read histone methylation marks, each with a closely related X-encoded paralogue. Others are restricted to germ cells and underlie spermatogenesis, so deletions of Y intervals produce azoospermia and male infertility, while age-related loss of the Y in blood cells is linked to cancer and cardiovascular risk. The presence of X-inactivation regulators here marks the counterpart process that balances expression from the other sex chromosome.

This grouping centres on a primate-specific gene family and the housekeeping functions that sit alongside it. The TBC1D3 paralogues, expanded by segmental duplication in the human lineage, encode Rab GTPase-activating domain proteins that act on endosomal trafficking and growth factor receptor recycling, amplifying signalling through the EGF receptor and insulin pathways, and their overexpression is oncogenic and has been linked to expansion of cortical progenitor pools during brain development. Other members reach into unrelated but broadly used processes: an HSP90 co-chaperone-like ATPase regulator supporting protein folding, a cyclin L family member that partners with CDK11 in pre-mRNA splicing, and a deadenylase complex subunit that trims poly(A) tails to control mRNA turnover. The calcitonin/CGRP locus contributes peptide hormones governing calcium handling and vasodilation, so the collection spans membrane traffic, RNA metabolism and endocrine signalling.

This is a heterogeneous grouping rather than a coherent signalling route, and the biology it points to is best read gene by gene. Several members are primate-specific TBC1D3 paralogues, products of a hominoid-expanded segmental duplication that carry a Rab-GAP-like domain, localise to endosomal membranes and modulate growth factor receptor trafficking and macropinocytosis; their amplification has been linked to transforming activity. CALCA encodes the precursor for calcitonin and CGRP, hormones that lower blood calcium and drive potent vasodilation and nociceptive signalling. PAN2 is the catalytic subunit of the Pan2-Pan3 deadenylase that trims mRNA poly(A) tails during the first phase of mRNA turnover, while CCNL2 is a cyclin-like partner of CDK11 acting in pre-mRNA splicing, so RNA processing and decay form one recognisable thread. AHSA2 is a co-chaperone-family relative of Hsp90 activators, with additional uncharacterised loci also included.</description>

These genes converge on the control of gene expression downstream of growth and stress signalling, linking receptor-proximal regulators to the transcriptional machinery and to the ubiquitin system that limits how long transcription factors persist. CREBBP and MED1 act as coactivators bridging DNA-bound factors to RNA polymerase II, REL carries NF- inkB-family transcriptional output, DYRK1A phosphorylates transcriptional and splicing substrates, and FBXW7 targets short-lived activators such as MYC, cyclin E and NOTCH for proteasomal destruction, setting the amplitude and duration of the response. RASA2 restrains Ras signalling, MAP3K2 feeds kinase cascades into it, and the sorting nexins and ACAP2 govern endosomal traffic and Arf-dependent membrane remodelling that determine where signalling receptors go. Dosage sensitivity in this circuitry underlies neurodevelopmental disorders with intellectual disability, and its loss of restraint is a recurrent route to tumour growth.

These genes converge on the braking and tuning of growth-factor signalling as it feeds into transcription, a control layer whose loss produces overgrowth, cancer and neurodevelopmental disease. Two GTPase-activating proteins, RASA2 for Ras and ACAP2 for an Arf-family GTPase, terminate signalling at the membrane, while MAP3K2 relays kinase input downstream and sorting nexins SNX13 and SNX14 govern endosomal trafficking and receptor fate. In the nucleus, the CREBBP acetyltransferase and the Mediator subunit MED1 couple activated signals to RNA polymerase II, and the NF-kappaB family member REL drives inflammatory and lymphoid transcription. Degradative and phosphorylation-based control comes from the FBXW7 ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor, which destroys short-lived growth regulators, and the DYRK1A kinase; STRN3 links the module to striatin-containing phosphatase complexes and Hippo pathway output. Many members are recurrently mutated in developmental disorders and tumours.

This grouping centres on the housekeeping machinery that keeps mitochondria energetically competent while proteins and metabolites are turned over. Two accessory subunits of respiratory complex I sit alongside the mitochondrial translation elongation factor TUFM, which delivers aminoacyl-tRNAs to the mitoribosome and so supplies the organelle-encoded core of the respiratory chain; PRELID1 participates in phospholipid transfer between mitochondrial membranes, and TMEM160 is an inner-membrane protein. Balancing these are degradative and biosynthetic functions: a proteasome beta subunit for ubiquitin-dependent turnover, the ER membrane protein BCAP31 that chaperones newly made membrane proteins and links to apoptotic signalling, APRT for adenine salvage into nucleotides, spermidine synthase for polyamine production, and tubulin cofactor B for tubulin folding. Together these represent the metabolic and proteostatic baseline on which oxidative ATP production, cytoskeletal assembly and cell growth depend.</description>

These genes converge on cyclic AMP as an intracellular messenger and on the cells that depend on it. Two calcium/calmodulin-stimulated adenylate cyclases, ADCY1 and ADCY8, generate cAMP in neurons in response to calcium entry, coupling synaptic activity to kinase signalling and long-term potentiation; the serotonin receptor HTR6 and a G protein gamma subunit sit upstream of the same second-messenger route, while CAMK2N1 restrains calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II and so tunes the calcium arm of the response. In kidney collecting duct, the vasopressin receptor AVPR2 uses cAMP to drive aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption, and its loss causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Other members act in muscle and germ cells, including a maternal-effect subcortical complex component and a tubulin-modifying enzyme, so the collection spans cAMP-dependent neuromodulation, water balance, and cell-type-specific cytoskeletal and developmental functions.

Cap-dependent protein synthesis begins when the eIF3 complex binds the small ribosomal subunit and organises the other initiation factors and mRNA into a functional 43S/48S preinitiation complex, so this assembly sets how much and which protein a cell makes. Several subunits are represented here — EIF3D, which can itself contact the mRNA cap for selective initiation, together with EIF3E, EIF3F, EIF3G, EIF3H and EIF3K — forming the multisubunit scaffold that prevents premature joining of the large subunit and helps scan to the start codon. Accompanying elongation factor subunits EEF1B2 and EEF1G, ribosomal protein RPL3 and the rRNA methyltransferase component fibrillarin place this activity within the broader translation and ribosome biogenesis machinery. Altered eIF3 subunit levels shift translation of growth- and proliferation-related mRNAs and are recurrently seen in cancer.

No single physiological programme unites these genes; the group is best read as a loose collection spanning lipid storage, growth-factor feedback, small RNA transcription and nutrient transport, several of whose members remain uncharacterised open reading frames or polymerase-related pseudogene sequences. The better-defined components point to distinct processes: a perilipin-family protein coats lipid droplets and governs regulated triglyceride mobilisation in oxidative tissues such as heart and muscle; a TGF-β- and androgen-inducible membrane protein acts in negative feedback on that signalling and is frequently overexpressed in prostate cancer; a Ras-association domain protein of the tumour-suppressor family couples Ras signalling to apoptosis; a sodium-coupled transporter carries short-chain fatty acids and lactate across the intestinal and renal epithelium; and a subunit of the snRNA-activating protein complex drives transcription of the spliceosomal snRNA genes. Shared membership here reflects co-expression or genomic proximity rather than a common mechanism.

enriched in nuclear pore complex interacting proteins points to the nuclear pore-interacting protein family, a primate-expanded group encoded in duplicated segments of chromosome 16 whose members associate with the nucleoporin scaffold that gates traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm. Nuclear pore complexes control the export of mRNA and ribosomal subunits and the import of transcription factors, so proteins docking at the pore influence how quickly regulatory signals reach chromatin. The set is dominated by NPIP-like genes and uncharacterised loci arising from the same low-copy repeats, alongside unrelated genes such as the pluripotency RNA-binding factor LIN28A, the histamine receptor HRH4 and the T helper 17 cytokine IL17A, reflecting the copy-number-variable, segmentally duplicated genomic neighbourhoods these sequences occupy rather than a single coherent biochemical route.

Nuclear pore complex interacting proteins are a primate-expanded family encoded near segmental duplications on human chromosome 16, and the grouping here is built around them together with a scattering of other loci. The NPIP-related members associate with the nucleoporin scaffold that forms the gateway between nucleus and cytoplasm, the channel through which mRNA, ribosomal subunits and transcription factors pass and through which nucleocytoplasmic traffic is regulated; their duplication history makes them useful markers of recent genome rearrangement rather than of a single defined biochemical step. The remaining members belong to unrelated processes — LIN28A is an RNA-binding regulator of let-7 microRNA maturation and stem cell self-renewal, IL17A a T cell cytokine driving mucosal inflammation, HRH4 a histamine receptor on immune cells — so the set is best read as a duplication-defined locus group with limited shared function.

This grouping centres on genome maintenance and the division machinery that protects it, linking interstrand crosslink repair to mitotic microtubule organisation and ubiquitin-dependent control of proliferation. Two of its members, FAAP100 and FAAP20, are accessory subunits of the Fanconi anaemia core complex, the E3 ligase assembly that monoubiquitinates FANCD2/FANCI at stalled replication forks; loss of this activity produces chromosome breakage, bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition. Alongside them sit regulators of the same cellular decisions from other angles: E4F1, an atypical ubiquitin ligase and transcription factor that couples p53 to cell-cycle arrest and mitochondrial metabolism; FBXL15, an SCF substrate adaptor; and SSNA1 and RASSF7, centrosomal and microtubule-associated proteins required for orderly spindle assembly. TBL3 adds ribosome biogenesis, tying growth capacity to the same proliferative checkpoints.

This grouping brings together proteins that have in common little more than a shared place in interaction screens, yet several of them converge on mitotic and genome-maintenance functions. SSNA1 is a microtubule-associated protein that promotes filament branching and localises to centrosomes and the midbody, and RASSF7 is likewise a centrosomal Ras-association domain protein required for orderly spindle formation and mitotic entry. Ubiquitin-dependent control is represented by E4F1, an atypical E3 ligase and transcription factor that acts on p53 and couples cell-cycle progression to metabolism, and by FBXL15, a substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF-type ligase. FAAP100 (C17orf70) belongs to the Fanconi anaemia core complex that ubiquitinates FANCD2 during interstrand crosslink repair, while TBL3 is a WD-repeat factor in small-subunit ribosome biogenesis. Together they mark proliferation-linked processes: spindle assembly, protein turnover, DNA crosslink repair and ribosome production.

These genes converge on white adipocyte biology and the endocrine control of fat storage. Adipose tissue must buffer nutrient excess by packaging triglyceride into lipid droplets and simultaneously report its own mass to the brain; failure of either function produces lipodystrophy, insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia. Leptin is the signal that adipose tissue sends to hypothalamic circuits regulating appetite and energy expenditure, while CIDEC and PLIN4 act at the droplet surface, driving droplet fusion and unilocular droplet formation and restraining lipolysis — loss of CIDEC causes partial lipodystrophy with multilocular adipocytes. CD300LG contributes to endothelial lipid handling and triglyceride clearance, TIMP4 restrains matrix metalloproteinases during adipose tissue remodelling, and heparan sulfate modification by HS2ST1 shapes lipoprotein and growth factor capture. Together the set describes adipocyte differentiation, lipid droplet architecture and systemic metabolic signalling.

These genes converge on the fat cell as a lipid-storing endocrine organ. Leptin is the adipocyte-derived hormone that reports fat mass to hypothalamic circuits controlling appetite and energy expenditure, and its loss causes severe hyperphagic obesity. CIDEC and PLIN4 act at the lipid droplet surface, the former promoting droplet fusion into the single large droplet characteristic of white adipocytes and the latter coating droplets to govern access by lipases; mutations in CIDEC cause partial lipodystrophy with insulin resistance. CD300LG is an endothelial transmembrane protein linked to triglyceride and HDL handling, TIMP4 restrains matrix metalloproteinases during adipose tissue remodelling, and HS2ST1 sulfates heparan sulfate chains that anchor lipases and growth factors to the cell surface. Together the group describes how triglyceride storage capacity, tissue expansion and metabolic signalling are coordinated, and how their failure produces dyslipidaemia and diabetes.

A monocyte/macrophage-centred module linking innate nucleic acid sensing to B cell support, built around the endosomal single-stranded RNA sensor TLR8 and the B cell survival cytokine BAFF (TNFSF13B). Myeloid cells that detect viral or self RNA in the endosome respond in part by secreting BAFF, which sustains B cell survival and maturation; chronic operation of this axis is a plausible route by which innate RNA sensing feeds autoantibody-producing B cells in lupus and Sjogren's syndrome. The accompanying genes mark the differentiated myeloid state rather than the signalling cascade itself: asialoglycoprotein receptor subunits and ferroportin reflect glycoprotein clearance and iron export by macrophages, thromboxane A synthase indicates eicosanoid output, a decoy IL-1 receptor damps inflammatory signalling, and BCL6 restrains inflammatory transcription. Together they describe the innate-to-adaptive interface that sets B cell numbers and tolerance thresholds.

Removing introns from pre-mRNA is the job of the spliceosome, and the genes here represent its core small nuclear ribonucleoprotein machinery. Without accurate splicing a cell cannot produce translatable messages, and defects in these components cause retinal degeneration, spinal muscular atrophy-like disease and myelodysplasia. The Sm proteins SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG form the sevenfold ring that assembles onto U-rich snRNAs to build U1, U2, U4 and U5 particles, while LSM3 and LSM5 belong to the related heptamer that caps U6 snRNA and also acts in cytoplasmic mRNA decay. SNRPA is the U1-specific protein that contacts the 5' splice site region, and RBMX contributes to splice site selection. MAGOH acts after the fact, as part of the exon junction complex deposited on spliced mRNA, linking splicing to export, translation and nonsense-mediated decay.

These genes define the differentiated intestinal epithelium, the absorptive lineage that lines the small bowel and colon and carries out nutrient uptake, barrier maintenance and fluid balance. The programme is set by a transcription factor core in which CDX1 and CDX2 specify intestinal identity and HNF4A and HNF4G drive enterocyte maturation; loss or ectopic activation of these factors underlies intestinal metaplasia and is used to distinguish gut-derived tumours. Downstream targets build the brush border and apical junctions, including villin, the atypical cadherins CDH17 and CDHR5, and the actin-based motor MYO1A, while FABP1 handles fatty acid transport, HMGCS2 supports ketogenesis from luminal substrates, and GUCY2C signals through cyclic GMP to control intestinal secretion. IL22RA1 places these cells downstream of mucosal cytokine signalling, and A1CF supports tissue-specific mRNA editing.

This grouping describes the differentiated absorptive epithelium of the intestine and liver, the tissue that takes up nutrients, forms a selective barrier, and performs first-pass metabolism of drugs and dietary xenobiotics. Its identity is set transcriptionally by the nuclear receptors HNF4A and HNF4G, which drive expression of brush border and apical junction components such as villin, CDHR5 and the harmonin scaffold USH1C, together with the lectin LGALS4 and the tetraspanin-like TM4SF5. A second arm is biotransformation: CYP3A4, CYP3A5 and CYP3A7 oxidise a large share of clinically used drugs, while a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates them for excretion, and A1CF contributes to mRNA editing characteristic of enterohepatic tissue. Loss of this programme underlies impaired barrier function and inflammatory bowel disease susceptibility, and variation in the CYP3A genes is a major source of interindividual differences in drug clearance.

These genes mark the differentiated intestinal and hepatic epithelium and the transcriptional programme that specifies it. HNF4A and HNF4G, with FOXA3, act as master regulators of enterocyte and hepatocyte identity, driving expression of the brush-border and junctional machinery that makes an absorptive epithelium possible: villin as the microvillar actin-bundling protein, claudin-2 setting paracellular cation and water permeability in the proximal intestine, and harmonin (USH1C) organising apical scaffolds. Others reflect specialised epithelial output, including galectin-4 in mucosal glycan handling, the mRNA-editing complementation factor A1CF acting with APOBEC1 on apolipoprotein B, DDC in amine synthesis, and CCL15 recruiting leukocytes to the gut mucosa. Loss of this regulatory axis impairs nutrient absorption and barrier function, and its reactivation or silencing accompanies colorectal and hepatic tumour differentiation states.

This grouping of chemokines defines the soluble guidance system that tells leukocytes where to go, and it is the core of how inflammation is localised to a particular tissue. Its members span the CC, CXC and C families together with interferon-gamma, which induces several of them, so the set covers both the recruitment signals and one of the cytokines that switches them on. Some are made rapidly by injured epithelium, endothelium and activated macrophages to draw in neutrophils and monocytes; others, including the platelet-derived factors, link clotting to inflammation; still others are made constitutively in lymphoid tissue to position T cells, B cells and stem cells in the correct microenvironment. Excessive or persistent output drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, atherosclerosis and tumour infiltration, while insufficient signalling leaves infected tissue uncleared.

chemokine cluster (II) is the inflammatory chemoattractant program that recruits leukocytes out of the blood and into infected or damaged tissue. It determines which cells arrive and when: monocytes and memory T cells follow CCL2, CCL5 and CCL7 through CCR1 and CCR5, neutrophils follow CXCL5 and CXCL6, and the interferon-inducible ligands CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 draw activated Th1 cells and NK cells to sites of viral infection, while CXCL13 organises B cells into follicles and ectopic lymphoid tissue. Sustained expression of these ligands underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, tumour-associated myeloid infiltration, and, in the case of the CCR5 ligands, competition with HIV entry. Annexin A1 marks the counter-regulatory side, restraining leukocyte adhesion and promoting resolution, so the set spans both the drive and the braking of inflammatory cell traffic.

This is a coordinated inflammatory chemokine module: a set of secreted chemoattractants and two of their receptors that recruit monocytes, T cells, neutrophils and dendritic cells out of the blood and into inflamed tissue. Its output determines which leukocytes arrive where, and so shapes the character of an immune response towards acute neutrophilic inflammation, chronic mononuclear infiltration, or organised lymphoid aggregates. CCL2, CCL7 and the CCL4/CCL5 pair act through CCR1 and CCR5 on monocytes and effector T cells; the interferon-inducible CXCL9, CXCL10 and CXCL11 draw in activated Th1 cells; CXCL5 and CXCL6 mobilise neutrophils, CXCL13 organises B cell follicles, and CCL20 targets immature dendritic cells and mucosal lymphocytes. Annexin A1 supplies a counter-regulatory, pro-resolving brake. Sustained expression of these ligands drives atherosclerosis, rheumatoid synovitis and tumour-associated inflammation, and CCR5 doubles as an HIV entry coreceptor.

Presentation of both lipid and protein antigens to T cells is the step that converts captured material into an adaptive immune response. The CD1 family loads self and microbial lipids "such as mycobacterial mycolates and glycolipids" and displays them to lipid-reactive and NKT cells, with CD1D the classic restricting element for invariant NKT cells and CD1E acting inside the endosome as a lipid-transfer helper rather than a surface display molecule. In parallel, class II heterodimer chains present peptides from internalised proteins to CD4 T cells, while CD8A marks the cytotoxic partner that reads class I. Supporting genes reflect how antigen reaches these molecules and where presentation occurs: CD36 is a scavenger receptor taking up lipids and apoptotic material, and CCR7 directs loaded dendritic cells to draining lymph nodes. Loss of this axis impairs antimycobacterial defence and tolerance alike.

This is the core output of an activated innate immune cell: the secreted proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines that convert detection of infection or tissue damage into a recruited, systemic inflammatory response. Macrophages, monocytes and epithelial cells release TNF, IL1A and IL1B to raise local vascular permeability and adhesion molecule expression, IL6 to drive the hepatic acute-phase response and fever, and the chemokines IL8 and CCL20 with CCL3 to bring neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes to the site along a gradient read by their chemokine receptors. Complement C3 and the soluble pattern-recognition molecule PTX3 add opsonisation and microbial clearance to the same programme. Transient induction clears pathogens and initiates repair; sustained or excessive output produces septic shock, and chronic low-level signalling through these mediators underlies rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and other conditions treated by TNF and IL6 blockade.</description>

Cells rarely respond to a cue in an all-or-nothing way; the strength, duration and outcome of signalling is set by modulators, and this collection represents the regulation of signal transduction across several receptor systems. It matters because the same ligand can drive proliferation, differentiation or inflammation depending on which brakes and amplifiers are present, and loss of that tuning underlies chronic inflammation, fibrosis and malignant growth. Included are secreted antagonists and matrix modifiers such as IL1RN, TIMP2, APCDD1 and the sulfatase SULF2 that adjust ligand availability; Wnt and BMP components including WLS, FZD8 and BMP2; innate immune receptors TLR2, TLR5 and NOD2 with the kinases LYN, SYK and PRKCD that propagate their signals; adaptors and GTPase regulators such as GAB1, ASAP2 and TIAM2 that shape cytoskeletal and adhesion responses; and transcription factors FOXO1, KLF4, GATA3 and BCL6 that determine the eventual output.

Platelets adhere to damaged vessel wall, change shape and secrete their granules, and this group of genes covers the adhesion and cytoskeletal machinery that lets them do it together with related motility signalling in vascular cells. Loss of these functions causes bleeding, while their excess drives thrombosis and the cellular remodelling that follows vessel injury. Collagen sensing through the GP6 receptor and outside-in signalling through the integrin beta-3 subunit, which pairs with alpha-IIb on platelets and alpha-v elsewhere, converge on focal adhesion kinase and the Gab1 adaptor to reorganise actin; caldesmon, tropomyosin and tensin link those adhesions to contractile filaments. P-selectin displayed after granule release recruits leukocytes, ALOX12 generates 12-lipoxygenase eicosanoids, and growth factors such as PDGF and HB-EGF act on the surrounding wall, tying haemostasis to migration, matrix deposition and wound repair.</description>
