Cells that have been stressed or stimulated by inflammatory signals must pause division while they respond, and this cell cycle and growth arrest programme is the immediate-early transcriptional output that enforces that pause and then limits the response. Its members are classic stress-response and NF- inhibitory genes: GADD45B and PPP1R15A (GADD34) couple genotoxic and unfolded-protein stress to growth arrest and translational recovery, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases to terminate p38 and JNK signalling, TNFAIP3 (A20) acts as a brake on NF- B downstream of TNF and Toll-like receptors, and JUNB and RARA provide transcriptional control of proliferation. Alongside them sit secreted mediators IL1A, IL1B, IL8 and OSM that propagate inflammation to neighbouring cells, plus THBS1, which restrains angiogenesis. Together they describe the coupling of inflammatory and stress signalling to a reversible halt in proliferation, a decision central to wound healing, immune activation and tumour suppression.

Platelets respond to vessel injury by switching from a passive discoid state to an adhesive, spreading, granule-secreting cell that plugs the breach, and this module captures the cytoskeletal and signalling machinery behind that switch. Its output is haemostasis; too little gives bleeding, too much gives arterial thrombosis, which is why the integrin activation step here is the target of antiplatelet drugs. Talin and filamin bind the beta integrin tail to couple inside-out activation with mechanical anchoring, while actinin, zyxin, coronin and profilin remodel and control actin filament turnover during shape change and spreading. Heterotrimeric G protein subunits relay signals from purinergic and thrombin receptors, AKT1 and the phosphatase catalytic and scaffolding subunits set the threshold for secretion, and TGFB1 represents the growth factor cargo released from alpha granules to act on the vessel wall.

Circulating platelets must switch from a quiescent state to a spread, adherent, secretory one within seconds of vessel injury, and this arm of platelet activation covers the cytoskeletal and membrane machinery that executes that switch. It is the basis of primary haemostasis, and its failure produces bleeding while its inappropriate engagement drives arterial thrombosis. Talin and filamin bind the integrin beta cytoplasmic tail and convert inside-out signalling into high-affinity fibrinogen binding, while actinin, profilin and zyxin remodel actin for shape change and clot retraction. Heterotrimeric G protein subunits relay agonist receptor input, and AKT1 with a MAP kinase kinase supports the downstream phosphorylation events. Clathrin adaptor and dynamin components, together with NBEAL2, connect the programme to granule biogenesis and release; loss of NBEAL2 causes gray platelet syndrome, in which alpha granules fail to form. TGFB1 released from those granules links activated platelets to wound repair and fibrosis.

Centred on coronin-1A and the SLP76-family adaptor DEF6 (IBP/SWAP-70-like), this interaction network describes the actin- and small-GTPase-linked machinery that lymphocytes use to organise their cytoskeleton and secretory traffic after antigen receptor engagement. Coronin-1A regulates F-actin turnover and is required for T cell survival and egress from the thymus; its loss in humans causes a T-lymphopenic combined immunodeficiency, while DEF6 acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor toward Rho-family GTPases to shape immune synapse formation and cytokine output. Accompanying members point to the effector arms that such signalling controls: SIPA1 as a Rap1 GTPase-activating protein, ACAP1 in ARF6-dependent endosomal recycling, STXBP2 in granule exocytosis, HGS in endosomal sorting, and TSC2 in mTOR-dependent growth control, with TGFB1 as an immunoregulatory input. Together they sketch how adhesion, migration and receptor signalling are coupled in immune cells.

KLF12 is a Kruppel-like zinc finger transcription factor that represses target promoters through GC-rich binding sites, and the genes assembled here represent its downstream regulatory output rather than a single biochemical route. The collection is functionally mixed, which is typical of a transcription factor target network: small GTPases and their partners (GNAI2, GNB2, RHOG) with an Arf GAP and endosomal sorting components point to heterotrimeric G protein signalling and membrane traffic; CORO1A and DGKZ tie into actin remodelling and lipid second messenger control in leukocytes; PPP2R1A, CNOT3 and UBE2M place phosphatase, mRNA deadenylation and neddylation-dependent protein turnover under the same regulatory umbrella. Also included are a nuclear liver X receptor partner and a latent TGF-beta binding protein, linking the network to lipid-sensing and extracellular growth factor availability. KLF12 activity has been studied in epithelial proliferation, cardiac and renal development, and tumour cell behaviour.

Centred on coronin-1A and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor DEF6, this protein network links actin cytoskeletal remodelling to antigen receptor signalling in lymphocytes. Coronin-1A restrains F-actin turnover and is required for T cell survival and egress from the thymus; its loss in humans causes a combined immunodeficiency with T cell lymphopenia, while DEF6 acts on Rho-family GTPases at the immune synapse and shapes cytokine production and autoimmune susceptibility. Associated members extend the module into membrane and lipid signalling — a diacylglycerol kinase that terminates DAG-based second messenger signals, an ARF GAP with a BAR domain implicated in receptor recycling, an ESCRT-associated sorting protein, and the heterotrimeric G protein beta subunit — alongside adaptors such as SH2B1 and nuclear regulators of transcription and mRNA turnover. Together they sketch how cell surface cues are converted into cytoskeletal polarisation, receptor traffic and changes in gene expression.

A heterogeneous grouping of housekeeping regulators that link membrane traffic, chromatin-based transcriptional repression, and reversible protein modification. Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is represented by the AP-2 mu subunit and dynamin-2, whose GTPase-driven scission releases coated vesicles and whose loss impairs receptor uptake and causes myopathy and neuropathy. Chromatin and RNA regulation appear through HMG20B, a partner of the LSD1-CoREST demethylase corepressor complex, the transcription factor MAZ, the Groucho/TLE-family corepressor AES, and the hnRNP-type RNA-binding proteins RALY and ACIN1, the latter acting in splicing and in apoptotic chromatin condensation. Signalling output is tuned by serine/threonine phosphatase machinery, including the PP2A scaffolding A subunit and the PP1-targeting protein spinophilin, alongside the protein kinase PKN1 and the NEDD8-conjugating enzyme UBE2M, which primes cullin ubiquitin ligases. Together these activities support vesicle budding, gene silencing, and proteostasis rather than one linear route.

This pathway describes growth-factor signal transduction coupled to receptor endocytosis, the arm of cell signalling in which ligand-bound receptors are internalised and sorted so that the strength and duration of downstream kinase output is set rather than left to run unchecked. It matters for cell survival, proliferation and the cytostatic and fibrogenic responses to TGF-beta, and its imbalance underlies tumour growth and tissue fibrosis. The clathrin adaptor subunit AP2M1, the fission GTPase DNM2 and the ESCRT-0 component HGS carry cargo from the plasma membrane through endosomes toward degradation, while AKT1 with its co-chaperone CDC37 and the kinase PKN1 transmit the surviving signal; PPP2R1A supplies phosphatase-mediated damping and PSMD3 links the route to proteasomal turnover. Calcium- and lipid-binding proteins such as CPNE1 and NUCB1 tie membrane traffic to intracellular calcium, placing receptor fate at the intersection of trafficking and phosphorylation control.

This grouping centres on the coupling of clathrin-mediated receptor internalisation to intracellular kinase signalling, the step that determines how long a growth factor signal lasts and whether the receptor is recycled or degraded. Adaptor and scission components, including the AP-2 mu subunit and dynamin-2, capture cargo at the plasma membrane and pinch off vesicles, while the ESCRT-0 protein HGS sorts ubiquitinated receptors toward the lysosome. On the signalling side, AKT1 and the related kinase PKN1 transmit survival and cytoskeletal cues, CDC37 works with HSP90 to fold and stabilise client kinases, and the scaffolding subunit of protein phosphatase 2A opposes them by dephosphorylation. TGFB1 provides a ligand whose receptors are themselves controlled by endocytic trafficking. Together these activities set signal amplitude and duration, processes that when deregulated drive growth factor independence in cancer and fibrotic tissue remodelling.

This is a mixed regulatory module centred on growth control, chromatin and protein turnover rather than a single linear route. Its clearest axis is nutrient- and energy-sensing restraint of cell growth: the kinase STK11 (LKB1) acts upstream of AMPK signalling, and TSC2 is the GTPase-activating component that switches off Rheb and thereby mTORC1, with EIF4G1 representing the cap-binding translation initiation step that mTORC1 ultimately controls. Loss of either tumour suppressor causes hamartoma syndromes and predisposes to cancer. A second strand concerns protein and receptor fate: HGS sorts ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation, while UBE2M (UBC12) conjugates NEDD8 to cullins and DCAF15 serves as a substrate receptor for a cullin-RING ligase. MAP2K2 provides MEK-ERK mitogenic input, and BRD2 and the linker histone variant H1FX place part of this regulation on chromatin.

Cells change shape, adhere, and migrate by continually rebuilding their actin scaffolding, and this cytoskeletal remodeling programme couples adhesion receptors and growth-factor signals to that rebuilding. It underlies wound healing, immune cell motility, platelet spreading and tissue stiffness sensing, and its deregulation contributes to fibrosis and to tumour invasion. Focal adhesion components link integrins to actin and transmit mechanical force: talin bridges integrin tails to filaments, zyxin concentrates at stress fibres and adhesion sites where tension is sensed, and filamin A cross-links actin while binding numerous membrane partners. A spectrin-family scaffold supports cortical membrane organisation, clathrin adaptor machinery couples remodeling to endocytic turnover of surface receptors, and AKT1 and TGFB1 supply the signalling input that drives cytoskeletal reorganisation, survival and contractile gene expression during migration and matrix remodeling.

inflammatory response is the coordinated reaction of innate immune cells to infection, tissue damage and modified self-molecules, producing the cytokine output and phagocytic clearance that contain a threat and then set the stage for repair. The genes here sit largely in the myeloid compartment: TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CARD9 relays signals from C-type lectin and other pattern receptors to NF-κB, and FCER1G with its partner adaptor TYROBP couples immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs to Syk in macrophages, dendritic cells and microglia, where AIF1 marks activated states. Counterweights are present too — β-arrestin-2 dampens receptor signalling, glutathione peroxidase limits oxidative injury, and the scavenger receptor STAB1 clears modified lipoproteins and apoptotic debris. TNFSF13 links this innate activity to B cell help. Unrestrained, the same circuitry drives sepsis, atherosclerosis and chronic neuroinflammation.

The inflammatory response is the innate reaction to infection and tissue damage, in which myeloid cells detect microbial and host-derived signals, release cytokines, recruit further leukocytes, and then help resolve the reaction; too little leaves infection unchecked, too much drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. The genes here are largely macrophage and dendritic-cell machinery: TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide, CARD9 couples pattern-recognition receptors to NF- cebB-dependent cytokine transcription, and the TYROBP/FCER1G pair provides the ITAM-bearing signalling subunits shared by Fc and immunoreceptor-like receptors, with AIF1 marking activated microglia and macrophages. Counterbalancing elements are present too: arrestin beta 2 dampens receptor signalling, STAB1 is a scavenger receptor for clearance of damaged material, and glutathione peroxidase 1 limits oxidative damage from the respiratory burst. Together they span recognition, amplification, scavenging and restraint.

cytoskeletal remodeling (enriched for SRF targets) describes the contractile actin program that lets fibroblasts, smooth muscle and endothelial cells stiffen, spread, adhere and pull on their surroundings. It sets the contractile phenotype of vascular smooth muscle, drives wound closure and myofibroblast conversion, and when it runs unchecked it feeds fibrosis, vascular remodeling and tumor stroma stiffening. The members are the output of actin-MRTF-SRF signaling: filament stabilizers and crosslinkers such as tropomyosins, alpha-actinin and caldesmon, the focal adhesion protein vinculin, and myosin light chain kinase, which generates the actomyosin tension that in turn frees MRTF to sustain transcription. Secreted matrix components CTGF and thrombospondin-1 export the same program to the extracellular environment, coupling it to TGF-beta signaling, while lipid phosphatase and nuclear receptor components tune the upstream Rho and differentiation inputs. Mechanotransduction and gene expression are thereby locked in a feedback loop.

Cells that must generate or resist mechanical force keep a transcriptional programme on standby that rebuilds the actin cytoskeleton and its attachments, and this cytoskeletal remodeling module — dominated by targets of serum response factor and its actin-sensing MRTF coactivators — is that programme. Its output defines the contractile phenotype of smooth muscle cells, myofibroblasts and activated fibroblasts, and drives wound closure, vascular tone and, when sustained, fibrosis and tumour stroma stiffening. The genes encode the machinery itself rather than the signals: tropomyosins and caldesmon that tune actomyosin interaction, myosin light chain kinase that triggers contraction, alpha-actinin and vinculin that anchor filaments at focal adhesions, and secreted matrix regulators such as CTGF and thrombospondin-1 that feed force back through integrins. Because monomeric actin controls MRTF availability, the pathway is a feedback loop in which cytoskeletal state dictates its own reinforcement.

When a T cell receptor engages antigen, the cell converts that recognition into a burst of new transcription and then into effector function; this is the signalling output that distinguishes an activated T cell from a resting one. Immediate-early transcription factors of the AP-1 family and their partners, including FOS, FOSB, JUN, JUNB, EGR1 and ATF3, are induced within minutes and set up the gene programme that follows. Its products are the tools of cell-mediated immunity and costimulation: interferon gamma and TNF for macrophage activation and inflammation, perforin and granzyme B for granule-mediated killing, FAS ligand for death-receptor-induced apoptosis of targets, the high-affinity IL-2 receptor chain for clonal expansion, and the TNF receptor family members OX40 and 4-1BB for sustained survival signals. Too little of this response leaves infections and tumours unchecked; too much drives cytokine-mediated tissue damage and autoimmunity.

Once a T cell has recognised antigen and committed to an effector response, it acquires the tools to kill target cells and to inflame tissue, and this arm of T cell signalling captures that activated state. Cytotoxic output is represented by granzyme B and perforin, which together breach a target cell membrane and trigger apoptosis, alongside Fas ligand for receptor-mediated killing; interferon gamma and TNF provide the inflammatory and macrophage-activating output. Sustained expansion depends on high-affinity interleukin-2 receptor subunits, while the costimulatory TNF receptor family members OX40, 4-1BB and GITR reinforce survival and proliferation after the initial activation signal, with AP-1 component FOSL1 among the transcriptional responders. This programme drives antiviral and antitumour immunity, is the effector limb manipulated by checkpoint and agonist immunotherapies, and when poorly restrained contributes to autoimmune tissue damage and cytokine-driven pathology.

This grouping describes the surface molecules through which T cells recognise antigen, adhere to partner cells, and set their activation threshold. Signalling chains of the T cell receptor complex together with the CD8 coreceptor couple peptide-MHC recognition to intracellular kinase cascades, while CD40 ligand on activated T cells licenses dendritic cells and drives B cell help and immunoglobulin class switching. Adhesion is supplied by an integrin alpha-4 subunit and its endothelial counter-receptor VCAM1, the pair that lets lymphocytes arrest on inflamed vessels and enter tissue. Balancing these positive inputs, the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptors LILRB1-LILRB4 deliver inhibitory ITIM signals on recognition of MHC class I, and TYROBP is the ITAM-bearing adaptor for related activating receptors. Together these determine whether an encounter yields effector differentiation, tolerance, or exhaustion, and they are the handles used by checkpoint and adhesion-blocking therapies.

A broad transcriptional signature of immune activation in blood, dominated by myeloid effector biology with a counterposed lymphocyte arm. Its practical value is as a readout of inflammatory state: neutrophil granule proteins such as elastase, proteinase 3, azurocidin, defensins, lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and matrix metalloproteinases mark granulopoiesis and degranulation, while pattern-recognition and chemotactic receptors including several Toll-like receptors, formyl peptide and complement receptors, CXCR2, TREM1 and inflammasome components NLRP3 and NLRC4 report on pathogen sensing and recruitment. Fc receptors, integrin CD11b and C-type lectins support phagocytosis and antibody-dependent killing. Alongside these sit T and B lineage markers -- CD3 chains, LAT, BCL11B, CD19, PAX5, EBF1, BTK, surrogate light chains -- and MHC class II with its transactivator, plus proliferation and DNA replication machinery reflecting expanding leukocyte populations. Such coordinated shifts accompany sepsis, autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.

enriched in neutrophils (I) is a transcriptional signature of mature blood neutrophils, the first-responding phagocytes of innate immunity, and the genes in it define how those cells are recognised, mobilised and licensed to kill. Loss or dysfunction of these products underlies recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, while their excess drives the tissue damage of sepsis and chronic inflammation. The set is dominated by chemoattractant receptors that steer migration to infected tissue — formyl peptide receptors, the complement C5a receptor, interleukin-8 receptor CXCR1 and the platelet-activating factor receptor — alongside immunoglobulin Fc receptors that mediate opsonophagocytosis, the G-CSF receptor that governs granulopoiesis, and NCF4 of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase that generates the respiratory burst. Also present are granule and metabolic enzymes, short-chain fatty acid and niacin receptors sensing microbial metabolites, and inflammasome regulators such as NLRP12 that restrain the response.

This is a neutrophil-enriched expression signature: the genes it collects are the ones that distinguish circulating granulocytes from other blood leukocytes, and together they define how these cells are recruited, activated and armed for antimicrobial defence. Loss or dysregulation of this programme underlies impaired bacterial and fungal killing, while its overexpansion marks the inflammatory neutrophilia seen in sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease. Much of it is receptor machinery for danger sensing and chemotaxis — formyl peptide receptors, the C5a receptor, IL-8 receptor CXCR1, the platelet-activating factor receptor and short-chain fatty acid receptor FFAR2 — alongside Fc gamma receptors including the neutrophil-specific FCGR3B that drive opsonic phagocytosis, and the G-CSF receptor CSF3R that supports granulopoiesis. Additional members support the respiratory burst, leukotriene metabolism, glycogen and glycolytic fuelling, inflammasome regulation and lineage transcription, reflecting the metabolic and secretory specialisation of a short-lived effector cell.

These genes mark proteins that reside in or act on the endoplasmic reticulum, the membrane network where lipids are made, membrane and secreted proteins are folded and glycosylated, and calcium is stored. Much of the group is lipid-metabolic: a stearoyl-CoA desaturase and a very-long-chain fatty acid elongase shape membrane fatty acid composition, a sterol reductase completes cholesterol synthesis, an acyl-CoA synthetase activates fatty acids for downstream use, and cytochrome P450 and thromboxane synthase activities generate eicosanoid and fatty acid oxidation products on the ER face. Another arm reflects ER control of protein trafficking and innate immunity, where an ER-resident chaperone delivers nucleic acid-sensing Toll-like receptors to endosomes, and a cargo receptor and vesicle protein serve secretory transport. Loss of ER homeostasis in this compartment produces stress responses and, for the wolframin gene, diabetes with neurodegeneration.

cell division covers the machinery that duplicates a genome and partitions it faithfully into two daughter cells, the process underlying tissue growth, renewal and, when deregulated, tumour proliferation. The genes span the sequence of events: cyclin E driving the G1-to-S transition and licensing DNA replication, the BLM helicase and the nuclease partner CtIP resolving recombination intermediates and processing broken ends so that replication finishes without chromosome fusions, condensin subunits compacting sister chromatids into transportable rods, and spindle- and kinetochore-associated factors together with a nucleoporin that must be redeployed once the nuclear envelope breaks down. VRK1 kinase couples envelope disassembly and chromatin condensation to mitotic entry. Failure at any of these steps produces aneuploidy, micronuclei or mitotic arrest, and several components are hallmarks of proliferating cells used as markers of tumour growth fraction.

Cell division requires that a replicated genome be condensed, resolved into separate sister chromatids, and partitioned equally, and the genes here span those steps. Cyclin E with CDK2 drives the G1-to-S transition and licenses replication origins, setting the pace at which cells commit to a division cycle. Condensin subunits shape mitotic chromosomes, while the Bloom syndrome helicase and the CtIP nuclease cofactor resolve recombination intermediates and stalled forks so that entangled or broken DNA does not reach anaphase; loss of BLM causes chromosome instability and cancer predisposition. A microtubule-associated protein contributes to spindle function, a nucleoporin to nuclear envelope reassembly, and the VRK1 kinase to chromatin and envelope changes at mitotic entry and exit. Together these activities couple genome duplication and repair to accurate chromosome segregation, and their failure yields aneuploidy or proliferative arrest.

Chemokines and their receptors direct where leukocytes go, converting local inflammatory cues into oriented migration across endothelium and into tissue. The ligands here span monocyte- and T cell-attracting CC chemokines such as CCL2, CCL4 and CCL5 and the neutrophil chemoattractant IL8, matched to receptors including CCR5, CXCR4 and CXCR6; ICAM1 provides the adhesive counter-receptor that lets a responding cell arrest and crawl, and TNF drives expression of many of these genes. Downstream, the hematopoietic guanine nucleotide exchange factor DOCK2 activates Rac to remodel actin for polarized movement, with the Src-family kinase HCK contributing to myeloid activation. This axis underlies infection control, wound healing, atherosclerotic and arthritic inflammation, hematopoietic stem cell retention in marrow, and the entry of HIV, which uses CCR5 and CXCR4 as coreceptors.

integrin mediated leukocyte migration describes how circulating white blood cells stick to blood vessel walls and crawl out of them into tissue, the step that delivers immune cells to sites of infection and inflammation. Without it leukocytes remain in the bloodstream and cannot mount local defence, the basis of leukocyte adhesion deficiency and recurrent bacterial infection; when it runs unchecked it drives the tissue infiltration of autoimmune disease, which is why blocking the α4 integrin is therapeutic in multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease. Mechanistically, integrins such as LFA-1 (ITGAL/ITGB2) and α4β1 engage endothelial counter-receptors including VCAM1, and inside-out activation converts chemokine and antigen receptor signals into high-affinity adhesion. The signalling module is lymphocyte-specific: TEC-family kinases ITK and TXK, PI3Kδ, PLCγ1, protein kinase Cβ and the Rho-family exchange factor VAV1 link receptor engagement to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

Leukocytes leave the bloodstream by gripping the inflamed endothelium and then crawling across it, and integrin-mediated leukocyte migration is the adhesion-and-motility step that makes this possible. Without it, immune cells circulate but cannot reach infected or injured tissue, the defect seen in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, where recurrent bacterial infection follows from failed extravasation. The pathway centres on the beta-2 integrin chain ITGB2 paired with ITGAL to form LFA-1, and on the alpha-4 integrin that binds endothelial VCAM-1; both must switch from a low- to a high-affinity conformation on cue. Antigen and chemokine receptors deliver that cue through Tec-family kinases ITK and TXK, PI3K delta, phospholipase C gamma and protein kinase C, with the Rho-family exchange factor VAV1 remodelling actin to generate traction. The same machinery is targeted therapeutically to block lymphocyte trafficking in multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease.

Two coordinated programmes dominate here: the proliferative machinery that duplicates and segregates a genome, and the transcriptional output of myeloid differentiation, a pairing typical of haematopoietic tissue where dividing progenitors give rise to non-dividing phagocytes. The cell cycle arm covers origin licensing and replication (MCM subunits, CDC6, CDT1, GINS, PCNA, POLA1, primase), nucleotide supply (RRM1/RRM2, TYMS, TK1, DHFR), homologous recombination repair (BRCA1, RAD51, FANCD2, EXO1), and mitosis through cyclin–CDK1 activity, kinetochore and centromere components, condensins, kinesins and the spindle checkpoint, with FOXM1, MYBL2 and E2F factors driving the associated transcription. Against this, SPI1, CEBPA, KLF4 and MAFB specify monocyte and macrophage identity, supporting pattern recognition and phagocytosis through TLRs, Fc and lectin receptors, the NADPH oxidase, and SYK–TYROBP signalling. The balance between expansion and maturation set here underlies normal myelopoiesis and is subverted in leukaemia.

Proliferating cells duplicate their genome and then partition it equally, and this coordinated cell cycle programme supplies the machinery for both halves of that task. Its coherent expression defines dividing tissue, and its inappropriate activation is the proliferative signature seen in tumours, which is why many of these proteins are drug targets or grading markers. One arm builds and licenses replication origins and synthesises DNA: the MCM helicase core, GINS and CDC45, polymerase and primase subunits, PCNA and replication factor C, together with nucleotide supply enzymes such as RRM2 and TYMS. The other arm assembles centromeres and kinetochores, builds and pulls the spindle through kinesins and Aurora kinases, drives condensin-mediated chromosome compaction, and completes cytokinesis. Cyclin-CDK pairs, CDC25 phosphatases, anaphase-promoting complex activity and the spindle checkpoint impose order, while checkpoint and homologous recombination factors respond to replication stress and breaks.

This grouping captures the proliferative core of the cell division cycle, specifically the transitions into S phase and into mitosis that decide whether a cell duplicates its genome and divides. Cyclin E partners with CDK2 to drive the G1/S switch, while B-type cyclins activate CDK1 to trigger mitotic entry, and CDC25A removes the inhibitory phosphates that keep those kinases off until the cell is ready. Alongside the drivers sit the machinery of replication and its surveillance: a replicative helicase subunit, the ribonucleotide reductase subunit RRM2 that supplies deoxynucleotides, a CRL4 substrate receptor controlling licensing factor turnover, and CHEK1 and BRCA1 linking damaged or stalled forks to checkpoint arrest and repair. Coordinated expression of these genes is the hallmark of dividing tissue and of tumours, and its deregulation is a route to genomic instability.

Antigen-stimulated CD4 T cells exit quiescence and undergo rapid clonal expansion, and this set captures the mitotic cell cycle machinery that expansion depends on. Without it, helper T cell responses cannot generate the numbers of effector and memory cells needed to support B cell antibody production and macrophage activation. The genes span the transitions of proliferation itself: cyclin A2 driving S phase and mitotic entry with its partner kinases, Aurora B acting at the kinetochore and midbody to ensure faithful chromosome segregation and cytokinesis, and Shugoshin-like regulation of the spindle checkpoint. Replication demands are met by thymidine kinase 1 supplying nucleotide precursors and by RAD51C and RAD54L repairing replication-associated breaks through homologous recombination, while SUV39H1-mediated heterochromatin methylation and stathmin-dependent microtubule turnover couple chromatin and cytoskeletal remodelling to division.

MYC is a transcription factor that couples growth signals to the biosynthetic and proliferative capacity a dividing cell needs, and the genes it drives form a recognisable proliferation signature in tumours. The targets gathered here read as the output of that network: replication licensing through MCM6, nucleotide supply through thymidine kinase and nucleoside diphosphate kinase, chromatin and centromere components such as HMGA1 and CENPA, mitotic machinery including cyclin B1, the kinesin KIF11 and topoisomerase II alpha, and survivin, which both restrains apoptosis and acts at the mitotic spindle midbody. Branched-chain aminotransferase BCAT1 ties in amino acid catabolism. Because MYC amplification or deregulation is among the most common events in human cancer, sustained expression of this programme marks cells locked into cycle, and it explains why MYC-driven tumours are unusually dependent on nucleotide and metabolic flux.

Cell junctions are the sites where a cell is physically coupled to its neighbours or to the matrix, and where those contacts are converted into cytoskeletal and signalling responses. Their integrity determines epithelial sheet formation, barrier function, migration and contact-dependent growth control; loss of junctional adhesion is a hallmark of tumour invasion. The genes here converge on the actin-linked face of such contacts: alpha-catenin tethers the cadherin complex to actin filaments, tensin-3 links integrin-based adhesions to the cytoskeleton, the membrane skeleton protein EPB41L3 organises submembrane scaffolds, and actin-bundling and scaffolding proteins shape the junctional cortex. Regulation is supplied by kinases acting on this machinery, including the Rho-family effector PAK1, protein kinase C delta, and the Src-family and Fes non-receptor tyrosine kinases prominent in haematopoietic cells, placing adhesion remodelling downstream of both mechanical and immune signalling.

Rho GTPase cycle is the switching of Rho-family GTPases between active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound states, and here it is the mitotic face of that cycle: the spatial control of RhoA activity that positions and drives the cleavage furrow. Without it cells fail to complete cytokinesis, generating binucleate and aneuploid progeny. The centralspindlin components ECT2 and RACGAP1 pair a Rho activator with a Rho inactivator at the central spindle, where PRC1 crosslinks antiparallel microtubules and CEP55 recruits the abscission machinery to the midbody. Additional GAPs such as ARHGAP11A and ARHGAP19, together with DEPDC1 and DEPDC1B, restrict Rho signalling in time and space, while E2F2 links their expression to cell cycle entry. The whole module is a proliferation signature, and its genes are broadly overexpressed in aggressive tumours.

Rho family GTPases switch between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and the cycling itself — loading by exchange factors, inactivation by GTPase-activating proteins — is what converts signals into localized actomyosin contraction. The genes here tie that cycle to cell division: ECT2 is the exchange factor that activates RhoA at the equatorial cortex, while RACGAP1, its partner in the centralspindlin complex, provides GAP activity and helps position the cleavage furrow. PRC1 crosslinks antiparallel midzone microtubules and CEP55 recruits abscission machinery to the midbody, so the pathway spans furrow ingression through the final severing of the daughter cells. Several ARHGAP and DEPDC1 members add further inactivating or regulatory input, and E2F2 links the whole programme to S-phase entry. Loss of control here produces failed cytokinesis, binucleate cells and aneuploidy, and these genes are recurrently overexpressed in proliferative tumours.

This is a monocyte-enriched expression module: a small group of transcripts whose abundance marks cells of the monocyte/macrophage lineage and distinguishes them from lymphocytes and granulocytes in blood. Such signatures are used to infer myeloid content in tissue and blood profiling and to track monocyte activation in inflammation. The genes fit that identity: the Src-family kinases HCK and FES transduce signals from Fc and growth factor receptors toward phagocytosis, adhesion and myeloid differentiation; the galectins LGALS1 and LGALS3 are abundant secreted lectins that modulate cell adhesion and immune cell activation; TNFSF13 (APRIL) is a monocyte-derived TNF-family ligand supporting plasma cell survival and antibody production; and a copper transporter and cytoskeletal or membrane-skeleton components round out the phenotype. Together they reflect the phagocytic, antigen-presenting and cytokine-secreting functions on which innate immune defence and tissue remodelling depend.

Polo-like kinase 1 sits at the centre of mitotic entry and exit, and the events organised around it determine whether a dividing cell builds a bipolar spindle, attaches its chromosomes correctly, and separates them on schedule. Loss or inhibition of this activity arrests cells in mitosis and drives apoptosis, which is why the kinase is a target in proliferating tumours; the same genes are a recurrent proliferation signature in cancer expression profiles. The activity depends on Aurora A and its activator TPX2 for centrosomal activation, on CDC25C and WEE1 for the phosphatase-kinase switch that releases CDK1, and on the anaphase-promoting complex adaptor CDC20 with its inhibitor FBXO5 for timing of securin cleavage by separase. Kinetochore and spindle-checkpoint components including NDC80, BUB1, BUB1B and CENPE, central spindle and midbody proteins such as ECT2, KIF23 and PRC1, and centromeric chromatin factors like HJURP place this signalling across chromosome segregation and cytokinesis.

Monocytes, macrophages and related phagocytes carry a distinctive surface and membrane-transport repertoire, and this collection of myeloid-enriched receptors and transporters captures it. These proteins let innate immune cells sense microbes and damaged self, take up ligands, present lipid antigen and communicate with lymphocytes, so the programme underlies pathogen recognition, scavenging and inflammatory activation in tissues. Pattern recognition is represented by CD14 and Toll-like receptors responding to bacterial products, scavenging by MARCO, and inhibitory tuning by sialic-acid-binding SIGLEC and LILR family members that set thresholds for activation. CD1D presents lipids to NKT cells while CD86 provides costimulation to T cells. Solute carriers handle amino acid, sugar and cation fluxes across plasma and endolysosomal membranes, including the SLC7A7 transporter whose loss causes lysinuric protein intolerance, and chemokine receptor CCR1 directs recruitment to inflamed sites.

Duplicating the genome once and only once per division is the defining task of S phase, and these genes cover the route from licensing an origin to running a replication fork. Origin recognition and loading factors place the MCM2-7 helicase on chromatin in G1, then CDC7 and CDK2 activity triggers firing, recruiting CDC45 and MCM10 to convert the loaded helicase into an active unwinding machine. The polymerase alpha-primase complex lays down RNA-DNA primers, PCNA clamps processive synthesis, and replication protein A coats the exposed single strands. Loss of control here produces re-replication, stalled forks and the DNA damage that drives genome instability in cancer, which is why replication licensing is tightly restricted to a single window of the cell cycle. Also present are centriole duplication factors such as PLK4 and STIL, and mitotic spindle proteins including TPX2 and KIF15, reflecting coordination of chromosome and centrosome copying with the subsequent division.

When a CD4 T cell recognises antigen, it stops being quiescent and begins dividing, and this programme is the proliferative machinery that clonal expansion depends on: without it an antigen-specific helper population cannot be built and effector or memory responses fail. The genes are largely those of the mitotic cell cycle proper cdash DNA replication and nucleotide supply through MCM6, RRM2 and TYMS, spindle assembly and chromosome segregation through KIF11, NDC80, NUF2, TOP2A and TACC3, and the spindle checkpoint and anaphase-promoting complex activator MAD2L1 and CDC20, with CDK1 driving mitotic entry. Alongside them sit markers of activated helper cells themselves: IFNG, the inhibitory receptor LAG3, the chemokine receptor CXCR6, and the miR-155 host gene, tying division to differentiation. Dysregulated versions of this proliferative signature recur in lymphoid malignancy and in chronically activated T cells.

When a CD4 T cell is activated by antigen, it converts from a quiescent state into a rapidly dividing effector, and this programme covers the replication and mitotic machinery switched on during that clonal expansion. Without it there is no proliferative burst and no adequate helper T cell response. The genes here fall into two connected groups: DNA replication and replication-associated repair, including the GINS components of the CMG helicase, a polymerase epsilon subunit, and the Fanconi anaemia factors FANCD2, FANCI, FANCL and UBE2T together with BRCA1 and BRCA2, which protect stressed forks during repeated rounds of S phase; and chromosome segregation and cytokinesis, with condensin, centromere and midbody proteins such as NCAPG2, CENPM, ANLN and CEP55. The same modules drive proliferation in tumours, which is why these transcripts mark dividing cells generally.

mitotic cell cycle covers the machinery that drives a cell from DNA replication licensing through chromosome segregation and division, the process by which tissues grow, renew and repair themselves. Its control determines whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome; loss of that control produces aneuploidy and is a hallmark of tumours, which is why several of these components are drug targets. Mitotic entry is set by cyclin B/CDK1, held in check by the inhibitory kinases WEE1-family PKMYT1 and released by CDC25 phosphatases, with FOXM1 and E2F factors supplying the transcriptional wave of cyclins and mitotic kinases. Downstream, PLK1 and NEK2 organise centrosome separation and spindle assembly, PLK4 and the CEP proteins license centriole duplication, gamma-tubulin and CKAP5 build and stabilise spindle microtubules, and shugoshin protects centromeric cohesion until anaphase.

Somatic cells duplicate their chromosomes and partition them equally into two daughters, and this mitotic cell cycle module covers the commitment to division and the machinery that executes it. Getting it wrong produces aneuploidy, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability that characterises tumours; sustained overexpression of these genes is one of the most consistent proliferation signatures in cancer tissue. Mitotic cyclins partnered with CDK1 drive entry into mitosis, opposed by the inhibitory kinases WEE1-family member PKMYT1 and reversed by CDC25 phosphatases that remove the restraining phosphates. FOXM1 supplies the transcriptional programme for the G2/M genes. Downstream, PLK1 and NEK2 coordinate spindle assembly and centrosome separation, PLK4 and centriolar proteins such as CEP152 license centriole duplication, gamma-tubulin nucleates microtubules, and shugoshin protects centromeric cohesion until anaphase.

Passage through the G1/S boundary commits a cell to divide, and the E2F transcription network is the programme that carries out that commitment by switching on the genes needed to copy and segregate the genome. Its targets here span the replication machinery itself — the MCM helicase subunits that license origins, PCNA and replication factor C for polymerase loading, thymidylate kinase and ribonuclease H2 for nucleotide supply and primer removal — together with DNMT1 for maintenance methylation of newly made DNA, damage-response components such as TOPBP1, PRKDC and H2AX, and mitotic factors including MAD2L1, ZWINT and KIF4A for spindle checkpoint and chromosome function. E2F7 acts as a repressive family member that dampens the response once S phase is under way. Loss of restraint over this network, typically through retinoblastoma protein inactivation, underlies uncontrolled proliferation in cancer.

When a naive CD4 T cell meets antigen, it must convert activation into rapid clonal expansion, and this set marks the mitotic cell cycle programme that stimulated CD4 T cells switch on to do so. Loss of it leaves helper T cell responses unable to build the numbers needed for effective antibody production and cell-mediated immunity. The genes cover successive demands of a dividing cell: licensing and restraint of replication origins through CDC6 and its inhibitor geminin, replication fork support and nucleotide supply by DONSON and RRM1, homologous recombination repair of replication-associated damage via RAD51 and the nuclease partner encoded by RBBP8, and then chromosome segregation through centromere-associated motors, condensin, the spindle assembly checkpoint, and centriole duplication by PLK4. EZH2-mediated repression and MASTL-dependent phosphatase control link the proliferative burst to the epigenetic and mitotic-entry states that accompany it.

complement and other receptors in DCs describes the surface sensing and antigen-presenting apparatus of dendritic cells and related myeloid antigen-presenting cells, the machinery by which they detect pathogens, tissue damage and dying cells and convert that detection into T cell activation. Its components span three jobs: local production of complement C1q subunits, which opsonise debris and apoptotic cells for clearance; innate pattern receptors such as TLR8 with its MD-2 cofactor and the scavenger receptor OLR1, which read microbial RNA and modified lipoproteins; and the CD11c integrin, SIRPA-TYROBP signalling module and MHC class II with CD86 and CD58, which together set the threshold for costimulation and adhesion at the immunological synapse. This combination defines dendritic cell identity in tissue transcriptomes and links innate recognition to the initiation of adaptive immunity, self-tolerance and clearance of immune complexes.

Dendritic cells sample tissue for pathogens and debris and then instruct T cells, and this receptor repertoire is what lets them do both jobs at once. Complement C1q, assembled from its A, B and C chains, binds immune complexes and apoptotic cell surfaces and marks them for uptake, while a scavenger receptor for oxidised lipoprotein and the LPS co-receptor MD-2 with endosomal TLR8 add recognition of modified self and of microbial nucleic acid. The output of that sensing is antigen presentation and costimulation: class II HLA-DQ molecules display peptide, CD86 and CD58 engage T cell CD28 and CD2. Complement receptor 2, the integrin chain CD11c, SIRP-alpha and the signalling adaptor TYROBP set adhesion, phagocytic threshold and the 'don't eat me' restraint imposed by CD47. Loss of C1q function predisposes to lupus-like autoimmunity, reflecting failed clearance of dying cells.

No single mechanism unites these genes; they are better read as a collection of tissue-restricted and developmentally regulated products drawn from several unrelated processes. One recurring theme is epithelial and mucosal defence: alpha-defensin 5 is the antimicrobial peptide secreted by intestinal Paneth cells, a secretory protein of upper airway glands contributes to innate protection of mucosal surfaces, a colonic CEACAM adhesion molecule marks differentiated gut epithelium, and a type I interferon gene belongs to the antiviral response. A second theme is patterning and growth control, with posterior HOXC transcription factors specifying axial position, a Sprouty family member damping receptor tyrosine kinase output, and an imprinted zinc-finger gene acting in growth regulation. The remainder cover solute transport, including cystine import that sustains glutathione synthesis and ferroptosis resistance, plus chromatin, cytoskeletal and membrane-shaping components.

No single coherent process unites these genes; they span secreted signalling, metal handling, steroid synthesis, muscle structure and mucosal defence, so the grouping is best read as a heterogeneous collection rather than one mechanism. Individual members do have well-defined roles: ATP7B loads copper onto ceruloplasmin and excretes excess copper into bile, and its loss causes Wilson disease with hepatic and neurological copper overload; CYP11B1 performs the final 11-beta-hydroxylation step of cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex, and its deficiency produces congenital adrenal hyperplasia; DMD encodes dystrophin, the sarcolemmal link between cytoskeleton and extracellular matrix whose absence causes muscular dystrophy. Others contribute to neuropeptide signalling through the pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating peptide, ERBB4 receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, Paneth cell antimicrobial defence, imprinted growth control, and type I interferon antiviral responses.

This pathway centers on neuronal differentiation and survival signaling, with a secondary thread of solute transport and stress defense. Neurotrophic and peptide cues dominate: pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide acts through cAMP to promote neuronal survival and neurosecretion, GFRA3 presents artemin to RET in sensory and sympathetic neurons, and ERBB4 receives neuregulin to shape interneuron migration and synapse formation. Downstream identity is set transcriptionally by POU4F2, which specifies retinal ganglion cells and sensory neurons, while GRID2 and TUBB4 support cerebellar Purkinje cell synapses and the microtubule cytoskeleton of axons; mutations in these cause ataxia and dystonia. Alongside, SLC7A11 imports cystine for glutathione synthesis and guards against ferroptosis, SLC17A1 handles phosphate and organic anion transport, and PEG3 links imprinted growth control to apoptotic signaling. Failure of these cues yields defective neural wiring and neurodegeneration.

The dominant theme here is neuronal specification and neurotrophic signalling, with several components that shape how developing neurons find their targets and survive. A secreted neuropeptide of the PACAP family acts through G protein-coupled receptors to promote neuronal survival and neuroendocrine responses to stress; a GDNF-family co-receptor transmits artemin signals in sensory and sympathetic neurons; ERBB4 receives neuregulin at synapses and in interneuron development; the delta-2 glutamate receptor subunit is a Purkinje cell synaptic organiser whose loss causes ataxia; and POU4F2 is the transcription factor that commits retinal ganglion cells to their fate. A beta-tubulin isotype supplies the microtubule lattice for axonal structure, and a cystine/glutamate antiporter links glutamate handling to glutathione synthesis and ferroptosis resistance. Other members, including an imprinted zinc-finger regulator, a Paneth cell defensin and a renal anion transporter, sit outside this neural core.

This pathway groups regulators of tissue patterning and secretory differentiation rather than a single metabolic route, centring on developmental transcription factors and receptor tyrosine kinases that shape epithelial and neural structures. TFAP2A and HOXC10 assign positional and lineage identity in neural crest, surface ectoderm and posterior axial tissues, while the imprinted regulator PEG3 links this control to growth and placental function. EPHB1 and ERBB4 transduce contact and neuregulin cues that guide axon targeting, cell sorting and epithelial morphogenesis, and NPR3 clears natriuretic peptides to set vascular tone and skeletal growth. Terminal specialised functions appear alongside: CYP11B1 completes cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex, DEFA5 provides Paneth cell antimicrobial defence in the small intestine, and dystrophin anchors the muscle membrane to its cytoskeleton. Loss of individual members produces craniofacial defects, adrenal steroid deficiency, or muscular dystrophy.

This is a heterogeneous grouping whose members share little beyond being tissue-restricted effectors and regulators of differentiated cell function, so it is best read as a composite of developmental patterning and organ-specific specialisation rather than a single mechanism. Transcriptional regulators dominate one side of it: TFAP2A directs neural crest and surface ectoderm derivatives such as craniofacial structures and epidermis, HOXC10 contributes positional identity along the posterior body axis, and the imprinted PEG3 acts in growth control and maternal behaviour. Receptor signalling makes up another arm, with the Eph receptor EPHB1 guiding axons and cell sorting and ERBB4 responding to neuregulins in neural and cardiac development, while NPR3 clears natriuretic peptides and thereby tunes blood pressure and skeletal growth. The remainder are terminal specialisations: dystrophin anchoring the muscle sarcolemma, CYP11B1 completing adrenal cortisol synthesis, and DEFA5 providing Paneth cell antimicrobial defence in the small intestine.

This is a set of candidate downstream targets of the ATF/CREB family of basic-leucine-zipper transcription factors, which bind cAMP- and stress-response elements to convert signals such as raised cAMP, endoplasmic reticulum stress and amino acid deprivation into changes in gene expression. Rather than a single biochemical route, the collection describes a transcriptional output: what the cell builds once these factors are engaged. Many of the members are neural or neuroendocrine, including the pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating neuropeptide ADCYAP1, which itself feeds back onto cAMP signalling, the brain lipid-binding protein FABP7 of radial glia and astrocytes, the brain-enriched sulfotransferase SULT4A1, and the endoplasmic reticulum-shaping protein REEP1 whose loss causes hereditary spastic paraplegia. Others cover copper export by ATP7B, Wnt-linked cytoskeletal control by DAAM2, imprinted growth regulation by PEG3 and positional patterning by HOXC10, indicating a regulatory network touching differentiation, metal handling and secretory signalling.

Platelets must switch from a quiescent circulating state to an adhesive, aggregating one within seconds of vessel injury, and this arm of platelet activation covers the tyrosine-kinase route that does it. Collagen exposed in damaged subendothelium engages the glycoprotein VI receptor, whose signal passes through the immune receptor gamma chain FCER1G, the Src-family kinase LYN and the spleen tyrosine kinase SYK, then through the adaptor LCP2 and the exchange factor VAV1 to phospholipase C-gamma2 and PI3K. The resulting inositol phosphate and calcium signals, reinforced by Gq-family alpha subunits GNAQ and GNA15 acting downstream of thrombin and thromboxane receptors, drive granule secretion, integrin activation and shape change. Loss of PLCG2 or SYK function causes bleeding, while overactivity of the same route contributes to arterial thrombosis, making these kinases antiplatelet drug targets.

Dendritic cells and other myeloid cells convert pathogen detection into a T cell-stimulating state, and this is the NF- tkB-driven arm of that switch. Its output defines the mature dendritic cell: raised surface CD83, adhesion molecules ICAM1 and VCAM1 for firm contact with lymphocytes, a fucosyltransferase that builds selectin ligands for tissue entry, and secreted TNF, CCL5 and the IL-23/IL-27 subunits IL23A and EBI3 that recruit and polarise effector T cells. The transcriptional core is the non-canonical branch f NFKB2 and RELB f together with the kinase MAP3K8 upstream and the atypical inhibitors BCL3 and NFKBID, which shape and limit the response rather than simply amplify it. Loss of this activation leaves antigen presentation tolerogenic; excess drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune tissue damage.

When myeloid cells and dendritic cells meet a pathogen signal, NF-kB drives a transcriptional programme that converts them into effective antigen-presenting and cytokine-secreting cells; these genes represent that activation output. The set is dominated by the non-canonical arm and its own feedback: NFKB2 and RELB form the p52/RelB dimer, while NFKBIA, BCL3 and TNIP3 restrain or redirect signalling so that inflammation is self-limiting. Downstream products shape the ensuing immune response — IL23A pairs with EBI3-associated subunits to influence T helper polarisation, CCL5 recruits T cells and monocytes, ICAM1 and FUT7-dependent glycans support adhesion and trafficking, LTB contributes to lymphoid tissue organisation, and BIRC3 blocks apoptosis so activated cells survive. IL1RN acts as a competitive antagonist at the IL-1 receptor, damping the same axis. Dysregulation here underlies chronic inflammatory disease and B cell lymphoma.

T cell signaling and costimulation covers the events by which a T cell converts antigen recognition into a decision to proliferate, differentiate, or remain quiescent, and the accessory inputs that set the threshold for that decision. It is what allows adaptive immunity to respond only to genuine antigen presentation; weakened signalling produces immunodeficiency, while unrestrained signalling drives autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation. The Src-family kinases LCK and FYN initiate phosphorylation at the engaged receptor, feeding into stress- and mitogen-activated kinase cascades through MAPK14, while cytoskeletal and adaptor proteins such as LCP1 and the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor ARHGDIB reorganise the actin network at the contact site. Cytokine input via IL7R sustains survival and homeostatic expansion, TCF7 imposes the transcriptional programme of naive and memory states, and IL23A links the response to inflammatory T helper differentiation.

T cells commit to proliferation and differentiation only when antigen receptor engagement is accompanied by costimulatory and cytokine input, and this combination of signalling and costimulation sets the threshold for that decision. The genes here span the proximal kinases that initiate receptor signalling, LCK and FYN, which phosphorylate receptor chains and adaptors to launch downstream cascades; MAPK14 carries stress- and cytokine-driven signals into transcriptional responses. Survival and homeostatic cues arrive through the IL-7 receptor, indispensable for thymocyte development and peripheral T cell persistence, while IL23A supports inflammatory effector programmes. TCF7 acts in the transcriptional network that specifies T cell identity and sustains stem-like memory states. Cytoskeletal and membrane organisers such as LCP1, ARHGDIB and the tetraspanin CD37 shape the immune synapse and adhesion. Loss of these inputs produces immunodeficiency; their excess drives autoimmunity.

Leukocyte activation and migration couples adhesive contact with the surrounding tissue and with other immune cells to intracellular signalling that licenses the cell to respond and to move. This is how T cells and myeloid cells roll on endothelium, arrest, cross into inflamed tissue, and form stable conjugates with antigen-presenting or target cells; loss of the adhesion arm causes immunodeficiency with defective leukocyte trafficking. Integrins ITGAL and ITGA4 mediate firm attachment to endothelial and matrix ligands, while SELPLG supports selectin-dependent tethering under flow. Engagement of CD2 by CD48 and of receptors bearing the FCER1G signalling chain triggers the Src-family kinases LCK and FYN, and the resulting tyrosine phosphorylation is opposed by the phosphatase PTPN6 and the inositol phosphatase INPP5D, setting activation thresholds. SIRPG contributes further contact-dependent regulation at the immune synapse.

When a CD4+ T cell recognises antigen, it leaves quiescence and undergoes rounds of rapid division that expand a clone of helper cells; this programme is the proliferative arm of that response, and without it there is no clonal expansion and no effective adaptive immunity. The genes are those a dividing lymphoblast switches on: origin licensing and replisome components such as CDT1, CDC45 and GINS1, the cyclin-dependent kinases CDK6 and CDK1 that drive entry into S phase and mitosis, nucleotide-supplying enzymes RRM2 and TYMS, homologous recombination repair through RAD51, chromosome segregation factors TOP2A, KIF4A, KIF20A and the kinetochore protein ZWINT, plus UHRF1 for propagating DNA methylation to daughter cells. MYB supports the proliferative state. The same signature marks proliferating cells generally and is the basis for reading lymphocyte activation, and for targeting dividing T cells with antimetabolites and immunosuppressants.

enriched in B cells (I) is a transcriptional signature of the B lymphocyte lineage: the set of genes expressed far more highly in B cells than in other blood cells, useful for identifying B cell content in tissues and tumours and for tracking B cell depletion or expansion. Its members span the antigen receptor itself and its proximal signalling apparatus — surface immunoglobulin heavy and light chains, the CD79A/CD79B module, CD19, CD22, BLK, BANK1 and STAP1 — together with the transcription factors PAX5, EBF1, SPIB and TCF4 that commit progenitors to the lineage and maintain B cell identity. Also represented are co-receptors and inhibitory regulators (CD72, BTLA, FCER2, complement receptor CR2), the follicular homing receptor CXCR5, and markers of immature and naive stages such as VPREB3 and TCL1A. Loss of these programs abolishes antibody-mediated immunity; their dysregulation underlies B cell lymphomas and autoimmunity.

This is a B lymphocyte identity signature: the genes whose expression marks cells of the B lineage and distinguishes them from other leukocytes in blood, lymph node and tumour samples. It captures what a B cell is built to do carry a surface immunoglobulin receptor, sense antigen, and mature into an antibody-secreting or memory cell and its components are the markers used clinically to type B cell leukaemias and lymphomas and the targets of depleting antibody therapy. Antigen receptor subunits and their proximal signalling adaptors appear alongside immunoglobulin heavy and light chain loci, the surface tetraspanin CD20, and co-receptors such as CD19, CD22 and CD72 that tune receptor output. Lineage commitment is enforced by the transcription factors PAX5, EBF1, BCL11A and SPIB, while CXCR5 directs homing into follicles where germinal centre responses occur.

This is a B-cell identity signature: the genes mark cells of the B lineage and together define what a B cell is and does in humoral immunity. Antigen receptor components and their proximal adaptors, together with co-receptor and accessory surface molecules, transmit antigen binding into activation, while an inhibitory Fc receptor for IgG raises the threshold for that response and guards against autoreactivity. Lineage-determining transcription factors commit progenitors to B-cell fate and sustain the programme, with a co-activator and helix-loop-helix partners supporting immunoglobulin gene expression; immunoglobulin heavy and light chain loci and secreted isotypes reflect antibody production itself. A chemokine receptor for follicular homing places these cells in germinal centres, and MHC class II-associated machinery supports antigen presentation. Loss or dysregulation of these components causes antibody deficiency, and their persistence identifies B-cell malignancies and the targets of depleting therapy.

This is a B-cell signature: a group of transcripts whose coordinate expression marks the B lymphocyte lineage in blood and lymphoid tissue, useful for gauging B cell abundance and activation state in bulk expression data. Its members span the machinery of humoral immunity — immunoglobulin heavy, kappa and lambda loci including IgD and IgA constant regions, the B cell receptor signalling kinase BTK, Fc receptor-like molecules and the inhibitory low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, the LPS-responsive TLR homologue CD180, and MHC class II components involved in antigen presentation to T cells. Transcription factors such as MEF2C and HHEX, together with pre-B markers VPREB3 and CD24, reflect lineage commitment and maturation, while CD69 indicates recent activation. Loss or depletion of these cells removes antibody production and class switching, causing humoral immunodeficiency; their expansion characterises B cell malignancies and autoantibody-driven disease.

enriched in B cells (IV) is a transcriptional signature of the B lymphocyte compartment, the set of genes whose expression in blood or tissue reports how many B cells are present and how mature they are. It matters because such modules let B cell content be read out of bulk expression data in vaccination, autoimmunity and lymphoma, where B cell abundance tracks disease activity and response to depleting therapy. The members span the antigen receptor signalling apparatus, notably the kinase BTK whose loss blocks B cell development and causes agammaglobulinaemia, the innate co-receptors CD180 and TLR10 that shape B cell activation thresholds, the MHC class II machinery CIITA and HLA-DOA underlying antigen presentation to helper T cells, the survival receptor FAIM3, the lineage transcription factor MEF2C, and immunoglobulin heavy chain transcripts marking antibody-secreting differentiation.

This is a B cell signature module: a group of genes whose expression in blood or tissue marks the presence and activity of B lymphocytes, useful for reading out humoral immune compartments from bulk expression data. Several members define B cell identity directly — BTK transmits antigen receptor signals to survival and proliferation programmes and is lost in X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, CD180 and TLR10 are innate receptors that shape B cell responses to microbial ligands, and FAIM3 encodes the IgM Fc receptor. Immunoglobulin heavy chain genes for IgA and IgG report the antibody output of plasma cells and memory B cells. Antigen presentation is also represented, with the MHC class II transactivator CIITA controlling class II gene expression and HLA-DOA modulating peptide loading, while MEF2C supports B lineage transcriptional programmes.

This grouping marks the B lymphocyte compartment, collecting surface molecules that identify B cells and tune how strongly they respond to antigen and to microbial cues. Antibody responses depend on exactly this kind of tuning: FCGR2B is the inhibitory Fc receptor that raises the threshold for B cell activation by immune complexes, and its loss is associated with autoantibody production and lupus-like autoimmunity. CD180 and TLR10 sit in the Toll-like receptor family and link innate recognition to B cell activation, while the FCRL proteins carry cytoplasmic motifs that modulate receptor signalling in naive and memory subsets. The tetraspanin CD37 organises membrane complexes and supports survival signalling, CD69 appears rapidly on activation and restrains tissue egress, and LY9 mediates homotypic contacts between lymphocytes. Together the set is useful for scoring B cell content and activation state in tissue and blood expression data.

These genes outline the myeloid identity and activation program of monocytes and macrophages, the cells that patrol tissue for microbes and debris and set the tone of an inflammatory response. The transcription factor SPI1 (PU.1) specifies this lineage together with HHEX, while TLR4 senses bacterial lipopolysaccharide and PTAFR responds to platelet-activating factor, coupling through the Src-family kinase LYN, the phospholipase PLCB2 and the ITAM-bearing adaptor TYROBP (DAP12) to calcium mobilization and cytoskeletal change; DOK2 acts as a brake on this kinase signaling. Scavenger and lipoprotein receptors such as STAB1 and APOB48R support clearance of modified ligands and lipid uptake, linking the same cells to foam cell formation in atherosclerosis. TNFSF13 (APRIL) released by these cells feeds back on B cell survival and immunoglobulin production, tying innate activation to humoral immunity.

Transcriptional control of blood cell development, centred on the erythroid lineage, links a lineage-specifying set of factors to the cell-cycle and cytoskeletal machinery that terminal differentiation depends on. GATA1, TAL1 and KLF1 drive the erythroid programme, switching on globin and red cell membrane skeleton genes such as spectrin chains, ankyrin-1 and protein 4.2, whose loss produces hereditary spherocytosis and anaemia; CEBPA, KLF4 and RXRA add myeloid and nuclear receptor input to lineage choice. Alongside these, mitotic regulators including CDK1-cyclin B, CDC20, EMI1 and aurora-pathway substrates control the final divisions, and cytokinetic and actomyosin components such as ECT2, MYH10, PAK1 and gelsolin support the cytoskeletal remodelling that culminates in enucleation of the erythroblast. The combination illustrates how differentiation programmes must coordinate gene expression with proliferative exit and morphological change to yield functional circulating cells.

Adaptive immune responses begin when peptide antigen is displayed to T cells and the resulting signal is tuned up or down, and this pathway covers both halves of that process. Class II molecules and their peptide-loading chaperones HLA-DM and HLA-DO, together with cathepsin-dependent processing, generate the displayed peptides on dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, while CD86 and innate sensing through Toll-like receptors and MyD88 set how strongly the presenting cell licenses a response. On the T cell side the receptor complex, CD3 chains and CD4 recruit LCK, ZAP70, LAT2 and PLCG1 to activate NF-kB and AP-1 target genes; CSK, PTPN6, PTPN22, CTLA4 and BTLA restrain the same circuit. Loss of these brakes drives autoimmunity, whereas defects in receptor proximal kinases such as BTK, SYK or ZAP70 cause immunodeficiency and failed lymphocyte activation.

T cells commit to a response only when their antigen receptor reads a peptide-MHC complex, and this module covers the receptor itself and the proximal signalling that follows engagement. It underlies adaptive cellular immunity: antigen discrimination, helper T cell activation, clonal expansion and cytokine responsiveness, and its loss produces severe combined immunodeficiency. The T cell receptor alpha chain genes pair with the invariant CD3 delta, epsilon and gamma subunits and the CD247 zeta chain, whose phosphorylated tails recruit the ZAP70 kinase; LCK, held in position by the CD4 coreceptor and regulated by the CD45 phosphatase, initiates that phosphorylation, and ITK propagates the signal toward calcium flux and transcription. Adhesion and costimulatory molecules such as CD2 lower the activation threshold, CCR7 directs naive cells to lymph nodes where antigen is presented, and the shared IL2RG chain plus IL12RB1 couple activation to cytokine-driven proliferation and differentiation.

Dendritic cells and monocyte-derived antigen-presenting cells are defined largely by the surface receptors they display, and this grouping collects the CD1 family together with other dendritic cell markers and growth factor receptors that shape their development and function. The CD1 proteins present lipid and glycolipid antigens rather than peptides, allowing T cells to recognise mycobacterial cell wall components and self lipids; CD1a, CD1b and CD1c are surface presenting molecules while CD1e acts intracellularly to assist lipid loading. Alongside them, receptors for macrophage and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factors drive differentiation and survival of the myeloid lineage, and the interleukin-1 receptor pair sets inflammatory responsiveness, with one member acting as a decoy that dampens signalling. Together these molecules underpin lipid antigen surveillance and the myeloid arm of innate-to-adaptive immune handoff.

cell adhesion covers the molecular contacts that let cells grip the extracellular matrix, each other, and circulating blood cells, holding tissues together and letting them be remodelled. Its outputs are connective tissue integrity, vascular wall stability, leukocyte recruitment to inflamed endothelium, and platelet plug formation at sites of injury; loss of these functions produces bleeding disorders, fibrosis, and unchecked tumour invasion. The genes span the matrix itself — fibrillar and network collagens, fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, thrombospondins and periostin — and the receptors that read it, notably the integrin αIIbβ3 and GPIb-IX complexes through which platelets bind von Willebrand factor. Endothelial and junctional components such as VCAM1, P-selectin, ESAM and JAM3, together with CXCL12 and inflammatory cytokines, couple adhesion to immune trafficking, while SNAI2 links it to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and migratory behaviour.

Cells attach to each other and to the matrix around them, and this cell adhesion programme supplies both the ligands and the receptors that make those contacts. It underlies tissue architecture, wound healing, leukocyte recruitment and platelet plug formation, and its dysregulation contributes to fibrosis, thrombosis and tumour invasion. Fibrillar and network collagens together with fibronectin, laminins, nidogen, tenascin, periostin and thrombospondins build the adhesive substrate, while integrins such as the platelet fibrinogen receptor pair ITGA2B/ITGB3, the von Willebrand factor receptor complex GP1BA/GP9, and endothelial adhesion molecules VCAM1, SELP and junctional JAM3/ESAM mediate binding under flow. Chemokines CXCL12 and IL8 and the cytokine IL1B activate these receptors on circulating cells, and SNAI2 links the same machinery to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, coupling adhesion to migration and matrix remodelling.

T cell activation (IV) describes the machinery by which a T cell recognises antigen through its receptor and converts that recognition into proliferation, cytokine output and effector differentiation. It matters because this step licenses adaptive immunity to pathogens and tumours, and because its thresholds determine whether a response is protective or autoimmune. The genes span the proximal receptor module and its tuning: the CD3 epsilon chain of the receptor complex, the Src-family kinase LCK that initiates phosphorylation, and the phosphatases PTPN6 and CD45 that set signal gain, alongside inhibitory surface receptors CD5 and LAG3 that damp overactivation. Transcriptional regulators including GATA3, GFI1 and SPI1 direct lineage choice and helper-subset commitment, while L-selectin governs entry into lymph nodes and XCL1 recruits dendritic cells. Together these define both the sensitivity and the outcome of antigen encounter.

T cells commit to an immune response only when the T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC, and this module covers the proximal machinery and transcriptional context of that activation step. It matters because the same components set the threshold between productive immunity and either anergy or autoimmunity, and several are the basis of clinical T cell markers and checkpoint blockade. Receptor-proximal signalling runs through the CD3 epsilon chain and the Src-family kinase LCK, which is regulated by the phosphatases CD45 and SHP-1 acting as brakes on tyrosine phosphorylation; LAG3 provides further inhibitory tuning, while CD5 dampens receptor sensitivity. Lineage and effector output are shaped by transcription factors including GATA3 and GFI1, with L-selectin governing lymph node entry of naive cells and the chemokine XCL1 recruiting dendritic cells to the responding T cell.

Inflammasome receptors and their signalling convert detection of microbial products and cellular damage into inflammatory output: cytosolic sensors such as NLRP3, NLRC4 and NOD2 oligomerize on recognizing bacterial flagellin, peptidoglycan fragments, pore-forming toxins or disturbances in ion and organelle homeostasis, driving caspase-1 activation, maturation of IL-1 family cytokines and pyroptotic cell death. The same sensors also feed transcriptional inflammation through the RIPK2 kinase and CARD9 adaptor, and through surface recognition by TLR4, converging on NF-κB with IkB-alpha and the ubiquitin-editing brakes A20, BIRC2 and BIRC3 setting the amplitude and duration of the response. This machinery gives macrophages and intestinal epithelium their capacity to raise fever, recruit neutrophils and restrict invasive bacteria; gain-of-function in NLRP3 causes hereditary periodic fever syndromes, NOD2 variants predispose to Crohn's disease, and chronic activation contributes to gout, atherosclerosis and metabolic inflammation.

When antigen binds the B cell receptor, the signal must be converted into decisions about proliferation, survival, antibody production or tolerance, and this is the proximal machinery that does it. Receptor engagement activates the Src-family kinase LYN and the tyrosine kinase SYK on receptor tails, which recruit the adaptor BLNK and the kinase BTK, and together they turn on phospholipase C-gamma-2 to generate the calcium and diacylglycerol signals that drive transcriptional change, while class IA PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits generate PIP3 at the membrane and VAV1 activates RAC2 for cytoskeletal remodelling. Restraint is built in: the inositol phosphatase INPP5D (SHIP1) degrades PIP3 and the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN6 (SHP-1) reverses activating phosphorylation, setting signalling thresholds. Loss of BTK blocks B cell development and causes agammaglobulinaemia; sustained signalling through this route supports B cell malignancies and autoimmunity, and BTK and SYK are drug targets accordingly.

Granulocyte development and activation is the theme here: a transcriptional core that commits myeloid progenitors to the neutrophil lineage, a cytokine receptor that drives their expansion, and signalling and cytoskeletal components that let mature cells respond. PU.1 and the retinoic acid receptor set and maintain myeloid identity, which is why blockade of retinoid signalling in promyelocytic leukaemia arrests cells short of maturity and why pharmacological retinoid treatment restores it. The G-CSF receptor transmits the principal proliferative and survival signal for neutrophil production, with mutations in it causing severe congenital neutropenia and predisposing to leukaemic transformation. Downstream, protein kinase C delta, a myeloid Ras activator and the adaptor DOK3 shape activation thresholds, while Rho-family GTPase signalling and actin-associated LIM-domain proteins support adhesion, shape change and migration to infected tissue.

MAPK cascades must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this grouping collects the brakes that terminate ERK, JNK and p38 signalling once a stimulus has been transduced. Without such damping, growth-factor and inflammatory inputs would drive sustained kinase activity, unchecked proliferative signalling and prolonged cytokine output. Dual-specificity phosphatases act directly on the kinases, removing the activating phosphates on the TEY/TGY motif; DUSP6 is selective for ERK, while DUSP1 also restrains stress-activated kinases and is itself induced as a delayed-feedback gene alongside immediate-early targets such as FOS. In parallel, the arrestins uncouple activated G protein-coupled receptors from their transducers and scaffold signalling complexes, and a decoy interleukin-1 receptor sequesters IL-1 without signalling. The result is negative feedback that sets the duration and amplitude of MAPK output in inflammatory and mitogenic settings.

immuregulation - monocytes, T and B cells describes the crosstalk by which myeloid cells, T cells and B cells tune each other's activation, setting the threshold between productive immunity and inflammatory damage. It matters because the same molecules that amplify a response also restrain it: CTLA4 delivers the inhibitory counter-signal that terminates T cell costimulation, and CD200 engages its myeloid receptor to keep monocytes and macrophages quiescent, while IL1A, IL23A, OSM, CSF3 and the chemokine CCL4 drive recruitment, granulopoiesis and T helper polarisation. B cell identity is represented by the antigen receptor adaptor CD79A, surface IgD and the low-affinity IgE receptor FCER2, linking antibody responses to this network. KIT ties in progenitor and mast cell output. Loss of the inhibitory arm produces autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; excess suppression permits chronic infection and tumour escape, which is why these checkpoints are drug targets.

Immune responses are tuned by signals passed between monocytes and lymphocytes, and this collection of immunoregulatory mediators spans all three compartments: B cell receptor components and surface markers, T cell inhibitory receptors, and monocyte- and macrophage-derived cytokines. Together they set the balance between activation and restraint that determines whether an encounter with antigen produces effective immunity, tolerance, or inflammatory tissue damage.
