CTLA4 delivers the inhibitory counterweight to costimulation and restrains T cell expansion; CD200 engages its myeloid receptor to dampen macrophage activation; CD79A and BLK carry antigen receptor signalling in B cells, while FCER2 and secreted IgD reflect their activation state. Inflammatory and growth-promoting outputs including IL1A, IL23A, CCL4, OSM and CSF3 recruit and expand myeloid cells and shape helper T cell polarisation, linking this circuitry to autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.</description>

B cells must build a working antigen receptor and then translate its engagement into survival and proliferation, and this cluster covers both the developmental and activation arms of that process. Its output is humoral immunity: without it, progenitors stall before maturity and antibody responses fail, as in the agammaglobulinaemia caused by loss of BTK, while inappropriate survival signalling contributes to B cell malignancy. Receptor-proximal signalling runs through the Src-family kinase LYN, the adaptor BLNK and the kinase BTK, with GAB2 and the leukocyte-restricted PI3K catalytic subunit PIK3CD amplifying the signal, DUSP6 restraining ERK output and NEDD4 marking components for ubiquitin-dependent turnover. BCL2 sets the apoptotic threshold that decides which cells persist, while SPIB and TCF4 act transcriptionally in lymphoid lineage specification and later plasmacytoid differentiation.

Chemokine receptors guide leukocytes to the tissues and lymphoid compartments where they are needed, and this grouping links two of them to the intracellular circuitry that shapes the response. CCR1 draws monocytes, neutrophils and other myeloid cells toward inflamed tissue in response to CCL3 and CCL5, while CCR7 directs dendritic cells and naive T cells into lymph nodes along CCL19 and CCL21 gradients, making it the basis of adaptive immune priming and lymphoid architecture. Downstream, p38 MAPK signalling is transmitted by MAPK14 and restrained by the phosphatase DUSP6, while CISH and SOCS2 terminate cytokine receptor signalling and TRIB1 tunes kinase output. BCL6 imposes transcriptional control on lymphocyte differentiation, and TIMP2 inhibits matrix metalloproteinases, connecting migration to remodelling of the tissue being entered. Dysregulation underlies chronic inflammatory infiltration and altered immune cell trafficking.

mitotic cell division is the machinery that attaches chromosomes to spindle microtubules and delays anaphase until every attachment is correct, so that each daughter cell inherits one exact copy of the genome. When it fails, chromosomes missegregate and cells become aneuploid, a hallmark of tumours and a cause of embryonic lethality. The genes describe the kinetochore itself, from the CENP-A-marked centromeric chromatin and its inner constitutive components through the outer NDC80/NUF2 microtubule-binding complex and the SKA subunits that stabilise attachment. Layered on this are the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BUB1, MAD2L1 and the RZZ components, which restrain CDC20 and hence the anaphase-promoting complex, and the error-correcting kinases Aurora B and PLK1 acting with the chromosomal passenger complex. Depolymerising kinesins and shugoshin-mediated cohesion protection complete the control of chromosome movement and separation.

Faithful segregation of duplicated chromosomes during mitotic cell division depends on building a kinetochore at each centromere and attaching it correctly to spindle microtubules. The genes here define that machinery: centromere-specific histone and constitutive centromere-associated proteins that mark and assemble the platform, the outer kinetochore complex including NDC80 and NUF2 that grips microtubules, and microtubule-depolymerising motors that tune attachment stability. Overlaid on this is the spindle assembly checkpoint, in which BUB1, BUB1B and MAD2L1 restrain CDC20 and thus the anaphase-promoting complex until every chromosome is bioriented. Aurora B kinase with survivin and its partners corrects erroneous attachments, while PLK1 coordinates mitotic progression. Loss of these controls produces lagging chromosomes, missegregation and aneuploidy, a route to chromosomal instability in cancer; many components are also proliferation markers and drug targets.

A co-expression grouping that marks lymphocytes as a population rather than any single signalling route, mixing B cell and T cell identity genes and so tracking the abundance of infiltrating or circulating lymphocytes in a tissue sample. Its B cell side includes the surface antigen receptor coreceptor CD19, the adaptor BANK1 and the transcription factor MEF2C, which supports B cell proliferation and survival; its T cell side includes CD2 and the costimulatory receptor CD28, required alongside antigen recognition for full activation, together with the T cell-restricted adaptor SH2D2A and the scaffold GAB1 that couples receptor engagement to downstream kinase cascades. PRKCZ contributes to lymphocyte polarity and activation signalling. Signatures of this kind are read as immune-cell content in tumour, blood and inflamed-tissue expression data, where high scores indicate lymphocytic infiltration.

These genes mark natural killer cells, the innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization and shape immune responses through cytokine release. The signature is dominated by the receptors that set the NK activation threshold: inhibitory and activating killer immunoglobulin-like receptors that read HLA class I on target cells, NKG2D recognizing stress-induced ligands, and the NKp80 and CD161 lectin-like receptors, with CD247 supplying the ITAM-bearing chain that couples activating receptors to intracellular signalling. Cytotoxic granule protein NKG7, the IL-2/IL-15 receptor beta chain that drives NK survival and proliferation, and the trafficking receptors S1PR5 and GPR56 place these cells in circulation and in tissue. Loss of the balance encoded here permits tumour escape and failed antiviral control, while excessive activation contributes to pregnancy complications and haemophagocytic disease.

Natural killer cells decide whether to kill a target by reading its surface HLA class I, and the killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor cluster provides the receptors that make that judgement. These genes sit together in a highly polymorphic, variably haplotyped region on chromosome 19 and are expressed in a clonally variegated pattern across NK cells and some effector T cells, so each cell carries its own combination. Long-tailed forms such as KIR2DL1, KIR2DL3 and KIR3DL1 carry inhibitory cytoplasmic motifs that recruit phosphatases and veto cytotoxicity when self HLA is intact; short-tailed forms signal activation instead. Loss of class I on virus-infected or transformed cells removes the inhibitory signal and licenses killing, the basis of missing-self recognition. Inherited receptor and HLA combinations shape susceptibility to viral infection, autoimmunity, pregnancy complications, and outcomes after stem cell transplantation.

enriched in NK cells (receptor activation) describes the surface receptor repertoire by which natural killer cells decide whether a target cell lives or dies. NK cells patrol for virus-infected and transformed cells that have downregulated MHC class I, and this receptor set encodes both halves of that decision: inhibitory killer immunoglobulin-like receptors and CD94/NKG2A-type lectins that read self MHC and restrain killing, and activating receptors such as NKG2D and 2B4 that detect stress ligands and tumour-associated markers. Engagement is transduced through the CD3 inth-chain zeta adaptor and ZAP70, then through ITK, PKC-theta and the CARD11 scaffold toward NF-kB activation, degranulation and cytokine release. The same components serve cytotoxic T cells, and the balance of inhibitory versus activating input underlies missing-self recognition, tumour immune surveillance, and the therapeutic logic of KIR-mismatched transplantation and checkpoint blockade.

Natural killer cells decide whether to kill a target by summing activating and inhibitory signals from surface receptors, and this receptor repertoire is what defines that decision. It underlies surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells that have lost MHC class I, and its inhibitory arm enforces tolerance to healthy self tissue. Killer immunoglobulin-like receptors read HLA class I ligands, with long-tailed forms delivering inhibition and short-tailed forms contributing activation; NKG2D paired with CD94/NKG2 family partners detects stress-induced ligands, while CD244 and CD96 tune adhesion and co-stimulation. Signals converge on ITAM-bearing CD3 zeta and the kinases ZAP70 and ITK, with protein kinase C-theta and the CARD11 scaffold linking receptor engagement to transcriptional activation and cytotoxic granule release. Skewed receptor-ligand combinations affect antiviral control, transplant outcome and susceptibility to autoimmunity.

Lymphocyte identity depends on a programme of development and activation that equips T and B cells with antigen receptors and the signalling machinery to respond to them, the basis of adaptive immunity and of the immunodeficiencies that follow when it fails. T-lineage components here include the CD3 epsilon and gamma chains of the T cell receptor complex, CD7, and the TCR-associated regulators TRAT1 and UBASH3A, which tunes receptor-proximal tyrosine phosphorylation. On the B side, EBF1 commits progenitors to the lineage while VPREB1 and VPREB3 contribute to the surrogate light chain that tests whether a functional receptor has been assembled, and TCL1A supports early B cell survival. Costimulation is represented by ICOSLG, and SH2D1A couples SLAM-family receptors to downstream kinases; its loss causes X-linked lymphoproliferative disease. Adaptors and kinases such as GAB1 and PTK2 carry these signals toward proliferation, differentiation and adhesion.

This is a promoter-motif-defined grouping rather than a known signalling route: the genes share an uncharacterised transcription factor binding site (CTCNANGTGNY) in their regulatory regions, and the presumption is coordinate control by a common, unidentified regulator. The members themselves span unrelated cellular jobs dash EBF1 as a transcription factor that commits progenitors to the B cell lineage, PTK2 (focal adhesion kinase) transducing integrin engagement into cytoskeletal remodelling and migration, ENG (endoglin) as an accessory receptor for TGF-beta family ligands in endothelium, SMPD3 hydrolysing sphingomyelin to ceramide, ELOVL4 elongating very-long-chain fatty acids, and HHIP sequestering Hedgehog ligands. Sets of this kind are useful as hypotheses about shared upstream transcriptional input, and gain meaning only when the motif's cognate factor and the conditions under which it acts are identified; the biology they report is gene regulation itself.

regulation of localization covers the control layer that decides where proteins, vesicles and lipids end up inside a cell and at its surface, rather than how much of them is made. This positional control determines whether a receptor reaches the plasma membrane, whether a secretory granule fuses, and whether cholesterol is exported instead of stored, so its failure shows up as mistrafficking, defective secretion and unrestrained growth signalling. The genes here span several arms of that control: AKT1 and TSC2 couple growth-factor input to the localization of metabolic and mTOR-pathway components; SNX17 retrieves integrins and receptors from endosomes for recycling; NAPA and STXBP2 execute SNARE-dependent membrane fusion, and STXBP2 loss causes familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis through failed cytotoxic granule release; ARHGDIA, FLNA, ARAP1 and PKN1 tie Rho- and Arf-family GTPase activity to cytoskeletal anchoring, while NR1H2 governs sterol redistribution.

Cells constantly decide where proteins, vesicles and lipids should be, and this collection covers the control of that positioning rather than transport itself. The genes span several routes by which a signal changes a molecule's location: kinase signalling that drives effectors to membranes, as with AKT1 and its substrate TSC2 or the MAP2K2 arm of the MAPK cascade; small GTPase regulation, where ARHGDIA sequesters Rho GTPases in the cytosol and ARAP1 acts as a GTPase-activating protein toward Arf and Rho family members; sorting and recycling of internalised receptors through the endosomal adaptor SNX17; and membrane fusion steps needed for regulated secretion, including SNAP-alpha and the Munc18 family member STXBP2 required for cytotoxic granule release. Filamin A anchors receptors to actin, while TGFB1 and the nuclear receptor NR1H2 link extracellular and lipid cues to these placement decisions.}</description>

This is a transcriptional signature of activated dendritic cells and monocytes, the myeloid antigen-presenting and inflammatory cells that convert detection of microbial or tissue-damage signals into recruitment of other leukocytes. Its members mark cells that have already responded to stimuli such as lipopolysaccharide or inflammatory cytokines, so the signature is used to read out myeloid activation in tissue and blood. It combines secreted mediators that drive fever, endothelial activation and neutrophil chemotaxis "IL1B together with the chemokines CXCL1 and IL8 " with the natural antagonist IL1RN that restrains interleukin-1 signalling, a built-in brake on the same response. Alongside these sit cell-surface receptors including SIRPA and ANPEP, membrane and cytoskeletal regulators such as MARCKS and NINJ1, lysosomal transporters, and SOD2, which handles the mitochondrial superoxide generated by sustained inflammatory metabolism. Persistent expression accompanies chronic inflammatory and infectious disease.

T cells depend on two kinds of signal: antigen recognition through the T cell receptor, and cytokine support through the interleukin-2 and interleukin-7 receptors, and this network links both. Together they set the size, survival and responsiveness of the peripheral T cell pool, and loss of the shared cytokine receptor gamma chain or the kinase that works beneath it causes severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T cells. The rearranged receptor alpha and beta chain segments provide antigen specificity, while the Src-family kinase LCK and the downstream kinase ITK propagate that recognition into activation, with CD45-associated PTPRCAP tuning the threshold. IL7 receptor signalling through JAK3 sustains naive cells and induces BCL2 to block apoptosis. CCR7 directs those cells to lymph nodes, tying survival and antigen encounter to lymphoid homing and organisation.

This pathway is the differentiated tissue macrophage program — the transcriptional and enzymatic identity that lets monocyte-derived cells phagocytose debris and pathogens, present antigen, and locally restrain T cell responses. It matters for infection control, iron and heme turnover, and the immunosuppressive myeloid states found in tumours and in the inflamed brain. The genes trace several arms of that phenotype: FCER1G with BTK and ADAP2 couple Fc and immune receptors to phagocytic and cytoskeletal responses; CYBB drives the NADPH oxidase respiratory burst whose loss causes chronic granulomatous disease; HMOX1 degrades heme to release iron and carbon monoxide; and IFI30, CPVL and CST3 handle lysosomal proteolysis for antigen processing. IDO1, KMO and KYNU run tryptophan down the kynurenine route, depleting tryptophan and generating metabolites that suppress effector lymphocytes, with MAFB reinforcing macrophage commitment."TBA" aside, this is macrophage effector biology.

These genes mark the differentiated tissue macrophage and microglial state, the resident phagocyte programme that clears debris and dying cells, handles iron and heme, and shapes local immune tone. Fc receptor gamma chain and the Tec kinase BTK couple immunoglobulin and immune-complex recognition to phagocytosis, while CYBB encodes the NADPH oxidase catalytic subunit gp91phox that generates the respiratory burst; its loss causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection. Heme oxygenase-1 degrades heme to biliverdin, carbon monoxide and free iron, linking these cells to erythrocyte recycling and to copper and amino acid transport by SLC31A2 and SLC7A7. IDO1 with KMO and KYNU carries tryptophan down the kynurenine route, producing metabolites that suppress T cell responses and, in brain, act on neurons. MAFB sustains the macrophage identity underlying all of it.

Dendritic cells that have sensed infection switch from quiet surveillance to an activated state, presenting antigen and broadcasting cytokines that set the direction of the ensuing T cell response. The genes marking this state are dominated by nucleic-acid sensing and type I interferon output: the cytosolic RNA helicases RIG-I and MDA5 detect viral double-stranded RNA, IRF7 drives transcription of interferon genes, and interferon-stimulated effectors such as viperin and DDX60 restrict viral replication. Complement components and the C1q chain point to a parallel opsonisation and clearance role, while CD38 and BIRC3 reflect the surface activation marker and the NF-kB-dependent survival signalling that let an activated cell persist long enough to prime lymphocytes. This activation state links innate viral recognition to adaptive immunity, and its inappropriate persistence contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity.

Cytosolic sensing of viral RNA by RIG-I-like receptors is how most cells detect an RNA virus replicating inside them, and it triggers the type I interferon and inflammatory response that limits spread before adaptive immunity arrives. RIG-I (DDX58) and MDA5 (IFIH1) recognize different classes of duplex and 5'-triphosphate RNA, while LGP2 (DHX58) modulates their activity; ubiquitination by TRIM25 licenses RIG-I signalling through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS. The output is activation of IRF7-driven interferon transcription and, in parallel, NF-kB relief from its inhibitor IkBa to induce TNF, IL8 and the chemokine CXCL10, recruiting leukocytes. Interferon-stimulated products such as ISG15 feed back on both the virus and the sensors themselves. Too little signalling permits uncontrolled viral replication; gain-of-function or failed restraint produces interferonopathies and autoinflammatory disease.

enriched in B cells (VI) is a transcriptional signature of the mature B lymphocyte, the cell type responsible for antibody-mediated immunity and antigen presentation to helper T cells. Its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted, including CD19, CD20 (MS4A1), CD22 and the complement receptor CR2, together with the antigen receptor's signalling subunits CD79A and CD79B, which couple immunoglobulin binding to intracellular kinase cascades. Also present are inhibitory co-receptors such as BTLA, CD72 and CD200 that set thresholds for activation and prevent autoreactivity, the follicular homing receptor CXCR5 that positions cells in germinal centres, and HLA-DOB, a modulator of MHC class II peptide loading. Expression of this program marks B cell content in tissue and blood, and its loss accompanies B cell depletion or immunodeficiency.

This grouping captures the transcriptional signature of mature B cells, the antibody-producing lineage of adaptive immunity, and its members are the surface proteins by which B cells are recognised and therapeutically targeted. The core is the antigen receptor complex and its immediate modulators: CD79A and CD79B transmit immunoglobulin engagement into intracellular signalling, while CD19 amplifies that signal and CD22, CD72 and BTLA restrain it, setting the threshold at which a B cell responds to antigen rather than ignoring it or reacting to self. Complement receptor CR2 links innate opsonisation to B cell activation, CXCR5 directs homing into follicles and germinal centres, and HLA-DOB tunes peptide loading for presentation to helper T cells. MS4A1, the CD20 target of depleting antibodies, and Fc receptor-like proteins complete a profile that distinguishes B cells in tissue and blood expression data.

This T-cell-enriched signature marks the presence and activity of mature T lymphocytes in a tissue or blood sample, the cells that provide antigen-specific adaptive immunity and cytotoxic defence against virus-infected and tumour cells. Its core is the T cell receptor itself, with rearranged alpha, beta and delta chain genes, the CD3 subunits and CD247 that couple the receptor to the cytoplasm, and the proximal kinases and adaptors LCK, ZAP70, ITK, LAT and RASGRP1 that convert antigen recognition into calcium flux and Ras signalling. Costimulatory and inhibitory receptors such as CD28, ICOS and TIGIT set the activation threshold; IL7R supports survival; and lineage transcription factors including BCL11B, GATA3, LEF1 and EOMES specify and maintain T cell identity. Cytotoxic effector genes -- granzymes, perforin, granulysin, NKG7 -- and chemokines such as CCL5 and XCL1 indicate the killing and recruitment functions these cells carry out.

Engagement of the T cell receptor by peptide-MHC, reinforced by costimulation, is what converts a resting lymphocyte into a proliferating effector, and these genes define that activation programme. It underlies adaptive cellular immunity: without it infections go uncleared, and when its brakes fail autoimmunity follows, which is why a phosphatase variant here is one of the broadest autoimmune risk alleles. The receptor complex and its CD3 chains, together with CD8 coreceptors, recruit Src- and Syk-family kinases such as LCK and ZAP70; adaptors and guanine-nucleotide exchange activity feed into PKC-theta, calcium release through inositol trisphosphate receptors, and calmodulin-dependent kinase signalling. Costimulatory and inhibitory receptors including CD28, ICOS and TIGIT set the threshold, while transcription factors such as BCL11B, TCF7, LEF1, GATA3 and EOMES specify lineage and differentiation state. Cytokine receptors for IL-7 and IL-21 sustain survival and expansion, and chemokine components direct trafficking to lymphoid tissue.

enriched in NK cells (I) is a transcriptional signature of natural killer cells and closely related cytotoxic effector lymphocytes, the innate arm of lymphoid immunity that kills virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation and shapes the response through interferon-gamma and chemokine output. Loss of these cells leaves patients vulnerable to herpesvirus disease and impairs tumour surveillance. The genes trace the whole effector programme: granule contents and delivery machinery such as perforin, granulysin and multiple granzymes; germline-encoded recognition receptors of the killer lectin-like family including NKG2D and NKG2A that weigh activating ligands against MHC class I; proximal signalling through CD247, ZAP70 and ITK; and the transcription factors T-bet, EOMES and STAT4 that impose cytotoxic identity. Trafficking and tissue-exit cues appear as S1PR5 and the chemokines XCL1/XCL2 and CCL5, which recruit dendritic cells to sites of killing.

This is a natural killer cell signature: the transcripts that mark circulating cytotoxic innate lymphocytes and distinguish them from other leukocytes. NK cells kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization and shape immune responses through chemokine and cytokine output, so this programme underlies antiviral defence and tumour surveillance. Much of it is the killing apparatus itself — perforin, granulysin and a set of granzymes stored in cytotoxic granules, together with FASLG for death-receptor-mediated lysis. Target recognition runs through germline-encoded activating and inhibitory receptors of the killer lectin-like family, including NKG2D and CD94/NKG2 partners signalling via CD3-zeta, ZAP70 and ITK. Transcription factors EOMES, TBX21 and STAT4, with IL-2 and IL-18 receptor subunits, set the lineage and its interferon-gamma response, while S1PR5 governs egress into blood. CCL5 and the XCL chemokines recruit dendritic cells.

Antigen recognition by T cells converts a resting lymphocyte into an effector, and this programme captures that transition in its effector-differentiated form. The T cell receptor complex and its CD3 subunits, together with the invariant zeta chain, transmit antigen binding through the kinases LCK, ZAP70 and ITK to the transcriptional machinery that commits a cell to inflammation; STAT4 acting downstream of IL-12 and IL-18 receptors drives interferon-gamma production and a type 1 effector phenotype. Cytotoxic and trafficking components -- granzyme A, NKG7, CCL5 with CCR5, and CXCR3 -- place these cells at sites of infection and give them killing capacity. Costimulatory and coinhibitory receptors including ICOS, SLAM-family members and TIGIT set the threshold and duration of the response, so that loss of restraint yields autoimmunity while failure of activation leaves intracellular pathogens and tumours uncontrolled.

T cell activation (III) covers the proximal signalling and transcriptional machinery that converts antigen recognition by the T cell receptor into proliferation, cytokine output and lineage commitment. Without it, thymocytes fail selection and peripheral T cells cannot mount effective responses, leaving both immunodeficiency and, when regulation is lost, autoimmunity. The kinase LCK initiates the cascade at the receptor, PRKCQ and RASGRP1 propagate it to NF-kB and Ras-ERK, and THEMIS tunes signal strength during positive and negative selection in the thymus. Calcium-dependent CAMK4 relays activation to the nucleus, where LEF1, ETS1, RORA and KLF12 set quiescence, survival and helper-subset identity, with chromatin readers such as ZMYND11 and GLYR1 shaping the accessible state. CD96 contributes adhesion-based costimulation. Together these define naive-to-effector transition and the thresholds that keep self-reactive cells in check.

Engagement of the T cell receptor must be converted into a decision to proliferate, differentiate or remain quiescent, and this module captures one arm of that T cell activation programme, dominated by proximal signalling and the transcriptional identity of naive T lymphocytes. LCK initiates receptor-proximal tyrosine phosphorylation, PRKCQ relays signals from the immunological synapse toward NF- theB-dependent transcription, RASGRP1 couples diacylglycerol to Ras-ERK activation, and CAMK4 transmits calcium signals into the nucleus. THEMIS sets the signalling thresholds that govern positive and negative selection in the thymus, while LEF1, ETS1 and RORA shape lineage commitment and effector differentiation. CD96 contributes adhesion and co-signalling. Loss of these functions produces immunodeficiency with impaired antigen responses, whereas failures of thresholding and selection permit autoreactive clones, linking this biology to both host defence and tolerance.

This grouping has no single coherent pathway identity; the genes converge loosely on vascular and inflammatory tissue biology together with transcriptional control of differentiation. Several members mark the acute-phase response and innate immune activation, including the serum amyloid A proteins SAA1 and SAA2 that rise sharply in plasma during inflammation, complement factor B of the alternative pathway, and the leukotriene B4 receptor LTB4R2 that directs granulocyte chemotaxis. Endothelial and platelet functions are represented by claudin-5, a tight junction protein of the blood-brain barrier, the collagen COL16A1, and the GP1BB subunit of the von Willebrand factor receptor, whose loss causes Bernard-Soulier bleeding. Other members act in the nucleus or on growth control: CDKN2B restrains cyclin-dependent kinases, TCF15 and MSC are lineage transcription factors, and NUP62 forms part of the nuclear pore transport channel.

A small, mixed regulatory collection whose centre of gravity is the decision between proliferation, growth arrest and death. The PI3K catalytic subunit p110delta and the forkhead factor FOXO4 sit on opposite ends of one axis: signalling through phosphoinositide 3-kinase keeps FOXO factors out of the nucleus, and when that signal weakens FOXO-driven transcription pushes cells toward quiescence, stress resistance and apoptosis. The cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p15 reinforces arrest at the G1 restriction point downstream of TGF-beta, while BOK, a Bcl-2 family relative of BAX and BAK, acts at mitochondria in cell death. Around this core sit tissue-restricted regulators: the neuronal RNA-binding protein ELAVL3, the homeobox factors SIX5 and SOX15 active in muscle, a fucosyltransferase that builds selectin ligands for leukocyte rolling, and cytoskeletal and membrane-trafficking adaptors.

This grouping marks cells engaged in presenting peptides to CD4 T cells via MHC class II. The core of it is the class II locus itself — DR, DP and DQ alpha and beta chains together with CD74, the invariant chain that chaperones nascent class II molecules, blocks premature peptide loading and directs them to endosomal compartments where its degradation frees the groove. Expression of these products defines dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells and sets the threshold for helper T cell activation, autoimmunity and transplant rejection; loss of class II expression produces severe combined immunodeficiency of the bare lymphocyte type. Accompanying genes point to the activated myeloid state in which presentation occurs: heme oxygenase and cyclooxygenase-2 shape the inflammatory and oxidative milieu, the urokinase receptor supports migration, and lipid-handling enzymes reflect the metabolic reprogramming of maturing antigen-presenting cells.

No single canonical route unites these genes; together they sketch a broad regulatory module spanning nuclear gene control, ubiquitin-dependent signalling, and membrane and cytoskeletal dynamics of proliferating cells. Chromatin-associated factors such as ADNP, ARID4B, DEK, MORC3 and the zinc-finger repressor ZBTB11 shape transcriptional programmes, while FMR1 restrains translation of target mRNAs in neurons, linking this group to neurodevelopment, where ADNP and FMR1 loss cause intellectual disability syndromes. Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like enzymes, including the E3 ligases RNF138 and RNF6 and the NEDD8-activating subunit UBA3, couple protein modification to DNA repair and cullin-based degradation. Kinase and phosphatase components such as NEK7, MST4, ROCK1 and PTPN11 feed growth-factor and cytoskeletal signalling, and ORC4 ties the set to replication licensing, with phosphoinositide and lipid-flippase proteins supporting organelle membrane identity.

This pathway describes a set of broadly expressed housekeeping regulators that keep transcription, RNA handling, and membrane trafficking coordinated during cell growth and division. Its members touch several general control layers: chromatin and transcription (the ARID4B repressor complex component, the SP3 transcription factor, cyclin C as a partner of CDK8 in Mediator-associated transcriptional control, and the chromatin architectural protein DEK), post-transcriptional regulation (FMR1 and MBNL1 governing translation and alternative splicing of neuronal and muscle transcripts, with G3BP2 nucleating stress granules), and endomembrane dynamics (VPS4B disassembling ESCRT complexes for multivesicular body formation and abscission, SACM1L controlling phosphoinositide levels, ITSN2 and PLEKHF2 in endocytic trafficking). NEK7 links the group to mitotic spindle assembly and inflammasome activation, while PPP1R12A targets myosin phosphatase to the actin cytoskeleton. Together these activities support proliferation, cytokinesis, and cellular responses to stress.

A mixed group of broadly expressed regulators that keep housekeeping functions of the cell running: chromatin-associated and transcriptional components, RNA-binding proteins, and machinery for endosomal membrane traffic and cytoskeletal contractility. Several members act on gene expression — a chromatin-interacting subunit of a histone deacetylase-containing repressor complex, a cyclin partner of the CDK8 kinase module of Mediator, and the zinc-finger transcription factor SP3. Others control the fate of mRNAs after they are made: MBNL1 governs alternative splicing of muscle and neuronal transcripts, FMR1 represses translation at synapses and its loss causes fragile X syndrome, and G3BP2 nucleates stress granules when translation stalls. A third arm handles membranes and organelles, including the ESCRT-associated ATPase VPS4B in multivesicular body formation, a phosphoinositide phosphatase acting at the Golgi and ER, and a myosin phosphatase targeting subunit that tunes actomyosin tension.

This is a loosely connected group of regulatory proteins rather than a single biochemical route, spanning chromatin, RNA metabolism, membranes and the cytoskeleton, and it is best read as a set of general-purpose control points on gene expression and protein localisation. Nuclear members include a cohesin subunit required for accurate sister chromatid cohesion and chromosome segregation, a chromatin-associated ARID-family corepressor component, a zinc-finger transcription factor of the Sp family, and the inner nuclear membrane lamin B receptor that tethers heterochromatin to the nuclear envelope. In the cytoplasm, the fragile X protein represses translation of target mRNAs in neurons and partners with a stress-granule scaffold, while a phosphoinositide phosphatase, a PH-domain endosomal protein, a palmitoyltransferase and the myosin phosphatase targeting subunit govern membrane traffic, protein lipidation and actomyosin contractility. A RING ubiquitin ligase links the group to turnover of transcriptional repressors downstream of TGF-beta family signalling.

This is a blood transcriptional module whose expression marks monocytes, the circulating phagocytes that traffic into tissue and become macrophages or dendritic cells. Its members define the monocyte's readiness to sense inflammatory cues and move: a chemokine receptor for MIP-1alpha and RANTES that guides recruitment to inflamed sites, a receptor for hydroxycarboxylic acid ligands typical of myeloid cells, and a metalloproteinase inhibitor shaping the matrix the cell migrates through. The transcriptional component is the myeloid-biased CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein beta together with a MiT-family factor and BCL6, balancing differentiation against inflammatory gene output. Immediate-early and stress-response genes such as FOS and IER3 and the ERK-directed phosphatase DUSP6 mark how rapidly these cells respond to stimulation. Changes in this signature track monocyte abundance and activation state in infection, sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease.

Glucocorticoids act largely by changing gene expression: hormone-bound glucocorticoid receptor enters the nucleus and either binds response elements directly or tethers to other transcription factors, and the genes collected here are among its transcriptional outputs. The mix captures why steroids are used clinically and why they have broad side effects. Several members are immune genes — the B cell kinase BTK, the T cell receptor component CD3E, the MHC class II-related HLA-DOA, and a regulator of inflammatory transcript stability — consistent with the suppression of lymphocyte signalling and antigen presentation that underlies glucocorticoid immunosuppression. Others point to connective tissue and metabolic remodelling, including the matrix signalling factor CTGF, the collagen crosslinking enzyme LOXL1, the desmosomal protein junction plakoglobin, and the lipogenic enzyme SCD. Together they illustrate hormone-driven reprogramming of immunity, tissue structure and lipid synthesis during stress responses and steroid therapy.

Cells that detect viral nucleic acid switch on a coordinated transcriptional programme, and this antiviral interferon signature is the readable output of that switch. It is what limits early viral replication in infected and neighbouring cells, and it is the same module measured in blood as a marker of acute viral infection and of interferonopathies and lupus, where chronic induction drives inflammation and tissue damage. Cytosolic RNA sensors such as RIG-I and IFIH1, aided by the regulatory helicase DHX58, signal through IRF7 to induce type I interferon; the induced effectors then act directly on the virus, with OAS enzymes activating RNase L, IFIT1 blocking translation initiation, RSAD2 perturbing viral budding and replication, and HERC5 and PML contributing ISG15 conjugation and nuclear body restriction. Chemokine and complement components, notably CXCL10 and IL1B, recruit and prime the accompanying inflammatory and myeloid response.

DNA repair is the set of surveillance and correction activities that keep the genome intact as cells replicate and encounter damage, and its failure is the direct route to the mutation load and chromosomal instability that drive cancer. The genes gathered here cover the recombinational arm most closely tied to replication: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex that senses and resects double-strand breaks, RAD51 with BRCA1 and BRCA2 loading it onto RPA-coated single-stranded DNA for strand invasion, and the Fanconi anaemia proteins that resolve interstrand crosslinks stalling forks. Repair synthesis then reuses the replication machinery itself — PCNA, the RFC clamp loader, polymerases delta and epsilon, FEN1 and ligase I. Phosphorylated H2AX marks damaged chromatin to recruit these factors. Germline loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or Fanconi components causes hereditary breast and ovarian cancer and bone marrow failure syndromes.

Genomes are damaged continuously by replication errors, crosslinking agents and double-strand breaks, and this DNA repair programme is the machinery that detects those lesions and restores the duplex before a cell divides. Its failure is the origin of hereditary cancer predisposition and of bone marrow failure syndromes, and its partial loss is what makes tumours sensitive to crosslinking chemotherapy and to inhibitors that force reliance on a single repair route. The genes here cover homologous recombination, with BRCA1 and BRCA2 loading RAD51 onto resected single-stranded DNA coated by replication protein A; end sensing and resection by the MRE11-RAD50 complex; crosslink repair through the Fanconi anaemia proteins FANCD2 and FANCI; and the shared synthesis and ligation steps that finish repair, using clamp loader subunits, PCNA, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1. Histone H2AX marks damaged chromatin to recruit these factors.

Fibrous connective tissue depends on a coordinated programme in which mesenchymal cells secrete collagens and organize them into matrix while TGF-beta family signals control how much is made. The genes here combine structural output — interstitial and basement membrane collagens such as COL1A2, COL3A1 and COL4A1/COL4A2 together with fibronectin — with the receptors and modulators that drive it, including the BMP2 ligand, the TGF-beta co-receptor endoglin, and the PDGF receptors that mobilize fibroblasts and pericytes. Adhesion and mechanotransduction components such as focal adhesion kinase, junctional proteins and THY1 couple matrix engagement back to gene expression, while SNAI2 and TCF4 support mesenchymal identity and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. This axis builds vessel walls, dermis and stroma during development and wound repair, and its persistent activation underlies organ fibrosis and the desmoplastic stroma of tumours.

This grouping captures the secreted output of activated myeloid cells: inflammatory and counter-regulatory cytokines alongside basement membrane components and matrix-degrading enzymes. Macrophages and dendritic cells shape an inflammatory response not only by releasing IL6 and the Th17-promoting IL23A subunit but by restraining it, through IL10 and the receptor antagonist IL1RN that blocks IL-1 signalling without triggering it. At the same time they remodel the tissue they infiltrate, with MMP9 and MMP19 cleaving collagen and other matrix substrates to open routes for migration and to liberate matrix-bound signals, while laminin beta-3 and gamma-2 chains contribute the epithelial anchoring laminin-332 of the basement membrane being crossed. Vasoactive endothelin-1, the actin-severing protein gelsolin and stratifin place this activity at the interface of inflammation, wound healing and epithelial repair, biology that is co-opted in tumour invasion and chronic fibrosis.

These genes mark the mature myeloid compartment, particularly monocytes, macrophages and neutrophils, and the secretory and degradative capabilities that make those cells useful in innate immunity and tissue remodelling. Surface ectoenzymes such as aminopeptidase N and maltase-glucoamylase digest peptides and carbohydrates at the plasma membrane, an aquaglyceroporin channel moves water and small solutes during phagocyte activation and swelling, and a secreted sulfatase edits heparan sulfate on the extracellular matrix to release bound growth factors and chemokines. Thromboxane A synthase directs arachidonate toward a potent vasoconstrictive and platelet-aggregating eicosanoid, while a CXC chemokine recruits further neutrophils to inflamed tissue. A macrophage-associated transcription factor and a secreted kinase that phosphorylates extracellular substrates add regulatory and matrix-directed layers. Together the set describes inflammatory effector output, matrix turnover and the local lipid mediators that shape leukocyte recruitment.

The E2F transcription factor network is the switch that commits a cell to divide, coupling growth signals received in G1 to the burst of gene expression needed for DNA replication. When retinoblastoma protein releases E2F1 and E2F2, they turn on the genes that license and fire replication origins — CDC6 and the origin recognition subunits ORC1 and ORC6 — together with CDC25A and cyclin A2, which drive the kinase activity that carries cells through S phase. The same programme supplies factors for homologous recombination and replication-associated repair, including BRCA1 and RAD54L, and for chromosome segregation and cohesion later in the cycle. Because this network sets the restriction point, its deregulation through loss of retinoblastoma control is a common route to unchecked proliferation in cancer, while excess E2F1 activity can instead trigger apoptosis.

This pathway couples cell-surface receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and transcriptional responses in two settings that share the same wiring: lymphocyte activation and endothelial/mesenchymal adhesion. On the immune side, the B cell adaptor BLNK, the T cell receptor-associated TRAT1, the gut-homing chemokine receptor CCR9 and the transcription factor MEF2C tie antigen and chemokine sensing to survival, differentiation and tissue-selective trafficking, functions whose loss produces immunodeficiency and impaired mucosal immunity. On the adhesion side, focal adhesion kinase PTK2, the GAB1 scaffold, phospholipase C beta and a G protein gamma subunit relay integrin and growth factor input into calcium and Ras-family signalling, while endoglin and CTGF tune TGF-beta responses in vessel wall and matrix remodelling, the axis disrupted in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Glycosyltransferases such as LARGE and NDST3 modify the ligand-binding sugars these receptors depend on."TBA" is not used here.

These genes converge on receptor-proximal signalling that converts extracellular cues into changes in cell adhesion, migration and tissue remodelling. One arm is vascular and mesenchymal: endoglin acts as a TGF-beta superfamily co-receptor in endothelium, CCN2/CTGF and CRIM1 shape growth-factor availability in the matrix, and focal adhesion kinase with GAB1, PLCB1 and the Ral activator RGL1 relay integrin and growth-factor input to the cytoskeleton and to Ras-family GTPase output. A second arm is lymphoid: the adaptor BLNK couples the B cell receptor to downstream kinases, TRAT1 associates with the T cell receptor complex, the chemokine receptor CCR9 directs gut-homing of lymphocytes, and MEF2C acts as a transcriptional regulator in both haematopoietic and cardiovascular lineages. Together the members read as a module supporting vascular integrity and immune cell positioning, with LARGE-dependent glycosylation contributing basement-membrane attachment.

A transcriptional signature of the myeloid compartment, marking monocytes and their close relatives among blood and tissue cells. Its members define how these cells sense microbes and damage and how they are recruited: CD14 with TLR4 detects bacterial lipopolysaccharide, TLR7 senses single-stranded RNA, CCR2 guides monocyte egress from marrow into inflamed tissue, and CSF1R transmits the growth factor signal that sustains monocyte and macrophage survival and differentiation. NLRP3 links the same sensing to inflammasome assembly and interleukin-1 release, the step that turns detection into fever and sterile inflammation. A parallel set of megakaryocyte-platelet genes — ITGA2B with ITGB3, SELP, THBS1, MMRN1 — reflects the shared myeloid origin of platelets and the overlap between thrombosis and inflammation. Such signatures are used to quantify monocyte content in tissue and blood expression data, where they rise in infection, atherosclerosis and tumour infiltration.

Signal transduction at the plasma membrane is represented here in its mesenchymal form: fibroblast surface receptors reading cues from the surrounding matrix and converting them into migration, contraction and matrix deposition. The programme builds connective tissue and drives wound healing, and when it persists it produces fibrosis and the activated stroma of tumours. Platelet-derived growth factor receptors alpha and beta receive the ligands that recruit and expand fibroblasts and pericytes, while the collagen I chains, fibronectin and laminin they induce form the matrix that engages adhesion receptors in turn. Cytoplasmic relays set the tone of the response, with DLC1 acting as a Rho GTPase-activating protein that lowers Rho signalling and DOCK4 activating Rac during cell motility. A secreted Wnt-modulating factor, an IGF-binding protein and the transcriptional regulators SNAI2 and NR2F2 tie surface signalling to mesenchymal identity, and cell-surface FAP marks the activated state.

enriched in naive and memory B cells marks the resting, antigen-inexperienced and recirculating memory compartments of the B lineage, the cells that populate follicles and lymph node mantle zones and stand ready to respond to antigen without yet secreting antibody. The genes are the surface identity of such cells: the tetraspanin CD37 and CD20 organise membrane microdomains and receptor signalling thresholds, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B restrains activation by immune complexes, LY86 supports innate receptor responsiveness, and the adaptor BANK1 tunes antigen receptor calcium signalling. MEF2C provides transcriptional control of B cell proliferation after receptor engagement. Together these define a state biased toward restraint and survival rather than plasma cell differentiation, and their expression distinguishes naive and memory B cells from germinal centre and antibody-secreting cells in tissue and blood profiling.

This signature marks resting B cells of the naive and memory compartments, the circulating pool that carries immunological memory and stands ready to respond to antigen without yet having become an antibody-secreting plasma cell. Its members are the surface proteins and regulators by which such cells are recognised in blood and tissue: MS4A1 (CD20), the tetraspanin CD37, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B that raises the threshold for antigen receptor activation, the scaffold BANK1 that dampens B cell receptor signalling, and the pattern-recognition accessory molecule LY86. MEF2C supplies transcriptional control of B cell proliferation and germinal centre responses. Loss of these restraints on receptor signalling predisposes to autoimmunity, while the same markers make this population the target of depleting antibody therapy. The adhesion molecules and other regulators present suggest additional roles in homing and quiescence rather than effector secretion.

Leukocytes only reach the tissues where they are needed if they can stick to blood vessel walls and to one another, and this set of integrins and adhesion receptors is how they do it. L-selectin initiates the tethering and rolling of circulating lymphocytes on endothelium and directs their entry into lymph nodes, after which the beta-2 integrin LFA-1 (ITGAL with ITGB2) engages ICAM ligands to arrest the cell and firmly adhere, and alpha-4 partners with beta-1 or beta-7 to bind VCAM1 and gut endothelial ligands for tissue-selective homing. The same contacts build the immunological synapse and stabilise antigen presentation, with JAML and CD96 contributing junctional and NK-cell adhesion and an inhibitory receptor tuning the response. Loss of beta-2 integrin function causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency, with recurrent infection despite abundant circulating neutrophils; blocking alpha-4 is used therapeutically to keep lymphocytes out of inflamed tissue.

When a vessel wall is breached, platelets adhere, activate and empty their granules, releasing adhesive and regulatory proteins that recruit more platelets and set up a fibrin clot; this activation and degranulation programme is what converts circulating platelets into a haemostatic plug, and its failure causes bleeding while its inappropriate triggering drives thrombosis. The genes here describe the released and matrix-facing side of that response: von Willebrand factor bridges platelets to collagen at high shear, fibronectin and thrombospondins provide adhesive scaffolding, and tissue factor initiates the extrinsic coagulation cascade on the exposed surface. Collagen chains supply the subendothelial ligand that activates platelets in the first place. Alongside these, protease and plasminogen-activation inhibitors such as SERPINE1 and TIMP1 restrain fibrinolysis and matrix turnover, linking platelet secretion to wound healing, matrix remodelling and fibrosis rather than clotting alone.</response>

Monocytes, macrophages and neutrophils respond to infection or tissue damage by switching on a burst of chemokine and inflammatory gene expression, and this myeloid inflammatory programme is what recruits further leukocytes to the site and sets the tone of acute inflammation. Its output includes TNF and IL1B as master cytokines, neutrophil-attracting CXCL1 and CXCL2, and CCL4 and CCL20 for monocytes, T cells and dendritic cells. Most of these genes are direct NF-kB targets, and the same program encodes its own brakes: NFKBIA sequesters NF-kB, TNFAIP3 restrains upstream ubiquitin signalling, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases, and adenosine and cyclic-nucleotide signalling through ADORA2A and PDE4B damp activation further. Survival factors such as BCL2A1 and TRAF1 keep activated cells alive. Failure to resolve this response underlies septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease, which is why several of these molecules are drug targets.

proinflammatory dendritic cell, myeloid cell response describes the activated state of dendritic cells and macrophages that converts detection of microbes or tissue damage into an inflammatory, T cell–stimulating program. This is the step that decides whether an immune response is mounted at all: the same genes drive protective host defence and, when sustained, the tissue injury of inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis and sepsis. The output is a burst of cytokines and chemokines — IL1B, TNF, CCL4 and CCL20 — that recruit neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes, alongside CD80-mediated costimulation that licenses naive T cells. IFNG and STAT4 mark the reciprocal Th1 amplification loop feeding back on myeloid cells, while GCH1 supports tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent nitric oxide production. Adenosine receptor and phosphodiesterase components set the cAMP tone that restrains the response, and TNFAIP6 and SERPINB9 limit collateral damage and self-killing.

This programme captures the proinflammatory activation state of dendritic cells and other myeloid cells as they sense microbial or tissue-damage signals and convert them into a T cell-recruiting, T cell-stimulating response. It underlies acute innate defence and the initiation of adaptive immunity, and when sustained it drives the tissue damage of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. Activated cells secrete TNF, IL1B and the chemokines CCL4 and CCL20 to draw monocytes and lymphocytes into the site, while CD80 provides the costimulation that licenses responding T cells. GCH1 supplies tetrahydrobiopterin for nitric oxide production, SERPINB9 protects the activated cell from its own granzyme B exposure, and ADORA2A and PDE4B set cyclic AMP-dependent brakes on cytokine output. STAT4 and IFNG mark the type 1 polarised feedback loop that reinforces the response.

Solute movement across membranes in blood and immune cells, covering the channels, exchangers and pumps that set cytosolic ion, water and metabolite composition. Erythrocyte identity depends heavily on this: the band 3 anion exchanger SLC4A1 couples bicarbonate/chloride exchange to CO2 carriage, the Rh-associated glycoprotein RHAG handles ammonium, AQP1 provides water permeability and SLC14A1 urea flux, while ATP1B2 supports Na/K-ATPase activity. A second arm serves phagocytes, where SLC11A1 depletes divalent metals from the phagosome to starve intracellular bacteria, SLC15A3 moves histidine and peptide fragments out of lysosomes to support nucleic-acid sensing, and ABC transporters such as ABCB6 and ABCG2 export porphyrins and xenobiotics. Innate sensors and effectors including TLR2, TLR4, NLRP3, CD36 and HMOX1 link this transport capacity to pathogen recognition, heme turnover and oxidative stress handling.

leukocyte migration is represented here by a coherent intestinal epithelial programme: the genes define the differentiated enterocyte and colonocyte, the polarised absorptive cell that forms the gut's selective barrier and its first line of defence against luminal microbes. Loss of this programme underlies barrier failure in inflammatory bowel disease and its reactivation marks intestinal metaplasia and colorectal cancer. The CDX1/CDX2 and FOXA3 transcription factors impose intestinal identity, driving expression of brush border and apical machinery (VIL1, MYO1A, MYO7B, PLS1, MEP1A, GUCY2C), tight junction claudins with EPCAM to seal the paracellular route, and secreted mucins and galectins that maintain the protective glycocalyx. Fucosyltransferases and GMDS glycosylate surface adhesion molecules such as CEACAM5 and GPA33, while RNF43 restrains Wnt signalling in the crypt, coupling barrier maintenance to controlled epithelial renewal, lipid handling and xenobiotic sensing.

These genes mark the differentiated intestinal and colonic epithelium, the absorptive barrier that takes up nutrients, excludes luminal bacteria and renews itself continuously from crypt stem cells. The master transcription factors CDX1 and CDX2, with FOXA3, impose hindgut identity, while EPCAM, CDH17 and the claudins CLDN3, CLDN4 and CLDN7 build adherens and tight junctions that seal the paracellular space. Brush border and apical organisation depend on villin, myosins MYO1A and MYO7B, PLS1 and POF1B; mucins MUC13 and MUC3B, galectin-4 and fucosyltransferases glycosylate the surface; FABP1 and ACSL5 handle absorbed lipid, and GUCY2C transduces guanylin signals controlling fluid secretion. RNF43 restrains Wnt activity in the crypt. Loss of this programme underlies barrier failure in inflammatory bowel disease, congenital diarrhoeas, and the aberrant expression of CEACAM5 and KRT20 seen in colorectal cancer and gastric intestinal metaplasia.

enriched in hepatocyte nuclear factors (I) describes the transcriptional program that gives endoderm-derived epithelia — liver, pancreatic duct and islet, intestine and kidney tubule — their identity and their differentiated metabolic output. It matters because these factors set up bile and lipid handling, glucose-responsive insulin secretion and intestinal absorptive character; loss-of-function mutations in HNF4A and HNF1B cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young, renal cysts and pancreatic hypoplasia, and the same regulators are re-expressed in gastrointestinal and hepatic tumours. FOXA2 and FOXA3 open chromatin at endodermal enhancers and act with HNF4A, HNF4G and HNF1B in a cross-regulating, self-reinforcing loop, while MNX1 contributes to pancreatic endocrine specification. Their downstream targets appear here as the effectors of that identity: apical mucins and glycosyltransferases such as MUC13 and GMDS, the brush-border lectin LGALS4, CEACAM5, and cytoskeletal and lipid-signalling components of polarised epithelial cells.

Hepatocyte nuclear factors are the transcriptional regulators that give liver, pancreas, intestine and kidney epithelium their identity, and this grouping centres on that circuitry: FOXA2 and FOXA3 act as pioneer factors that open chromatin at endoderm-specific enhancers, while HNF1B, HNF4A and HNF4G drive the downstream programmes of bile acid and lipid handling, glucose metabolism, and apical epithelial differentiation. The factors cross-regulate one another in a reinforcing network, so loss of a single member destabilises the whole state — heterozygous HNF1B or HNF4A mutation causes maturity-onset diabetes of the young and renal cystic disease, and MNX1 loss disrupts pancreatic beta cell specification. Accompanying targets such as the intestinal lectin LGALS4, the membrane mucin MUC13 and CEACAM5 mark the differentiated brush-border epithelium these factors specify, alongside fucose-donor synthesis by GMDS for glycan production.

This grouping captures the transcriptional identity of endoderm-derived epithelium, built around the hepatocyte nuclear factor family: FOXA2 and FOXA3, HNF1B, and the nuclear receptors HNF4A and HNF4G. Together these factors specify and maintain liver, pancreas, and intestinal epithelial fate, driving expression of the differentiated gene programme rather than merely responding to it. Their targets here are characteristic epithelial and brush-border products — the adhesion molecules EPCAM and CDH17, the carcinoembryonic antigen CEACAM5, and the guanylate cyclase receptor GUCY2C that governs intestinal fluid secretion. Loss of HNF1B causes renal cysts and maturity-onset diabetes of the young, and HNF4A mutations likewise disturb pancreatic beta cell function and hepatic metabolism. In tumours, retention of this module marks gastrointestinal and hepatic lineage, making these genes useful for assigning the tissue of origin of carcinomas.

PAX3 is a paired-box transcription factor that directs neural crest and myogenic progenitor specification, and its fusion to FOXO1 drives alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma; the genes gathered here as putative PAX3 targets read as the transcriptional output measured downstream of that factor. Strikingly, they are the classic immediate-early response programme: the EGR zinc-finger family, the orphan nuclear receptors NR4A1 and NR4A2, the AP-1 partner MAFF, the growth arrest regulator CDKN1A, the small GTPase GEM, and the MAP kinase phosphatase DUSP2 that feeds back to dampen ERK signalling. Secreted members such as HBEGF, CXCL2 and IL8 extend the response to neighbouring cells and to inflammatory recruitment. Collectively these genes convert a transient signalling event into decisions about proliferation, survival, differentiation and paracrine communication, the cellular programmes that PAX3 dysregulation subverts in tumours.

PAX3 is a paired-box transcription factor that directs neural crest and skeletal muscle development, and the genes grouped here as its putative targets are the downstream transcripts whose levels shift when its activity changes. Notably, they form a coherent immediate-early module rather than a myogenic one: activating transcription factors and zinc-finger factors such as ATF3, EGR2, EGR3 and the orphan nuclear receptors NR4A1 and NR4A2 are induced within minutes of stimulation, while DUSP1 and DUSP2 encode phosphatases that dephosphorylate MAP kinases and so terminate the signal that switched them on. RGS1 similarly dampens G protein signalling, and CD83 and INHBA link the response to immune activation. The set therefore reads as a rapid, self-limiting transcriptional response to extracellular cues, of interest because PAX3 misregulation underlies Waardenburg syndrome and the fusion oncoprotein of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma.

B cell development covers the signals and transcriptional regulators that guide progenitors through the B lineage and shape the mature B cell compartment, the basis of antibody production and humoral memory. Its failure yields immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses, while dysregulation feeds autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy. The genes span several layers of that control: the ETS factor SPI1 (PU.1) sets haematopoietic lineage output with partners such as HHEX, CEBPE and the transcriptional corepressor CBFA2T3, while the Src-family kinase LYN transmits and dampens antigen receptor signalling, setting thresholds for tolerance. Cytokines of the TNF family, including lymphotoxin-alpha and the survival factor TNFSF13/APRIL, together with LIF, act on the stromal niches and germinal centre architecture that support maturation, and CCR7 directs migration into lymphoid tissue. TLR4 links innate recognition to B cell activation.

B cell development spans the commitment of haematopoietic progenitors to the B lineage, their maturation in bone marrow, and their positioning and activation in secondary lymphoid tissue, and it underwrites antibody-mediated immunity. Lineage-determining transcriptional regulators are represented here: SPI1 (PU.1) sets myeloid versus lymphoid output in a dose-dependent way, while HHEX and CBFA2T3 act as transcriptional regulators of early progenitor fate. Signalling contributions come from LYN, a Src-family kinase that both propagates and dampens antigen receptor output so that autoreactive responses are held in check, and from innate sensing through TLR4. Cytokines of the tumour necrosis factor family, including TNF, LTA and TNFSF13 (APRIL), support B cell survival, plasma cell maintenance and the lymphoid microenvironment, and CCR7 directs chemotactic homing to lymph node and spleen. Disruption of these steps yields immunodeficiency, impaired antibody responses, or loss of self-tolerance.

These genes together mark the differentiated absorptive epithelium of the intestine, the cell layer that takes up nutrients, senses dietary and xenobiotic chemicals, and forms a barrier to gut contents. Lineage-defining transcription factors such as CDX1 and HNF4G impose regional intestinal identity on gut endoderm and drive expression of the enterocyte's working machinery: a brush border built with the unconventional myosin MYO1A, apical solute carriers including SLC3A1 for cystine and dibasic amino acids and the zinc transporter SLC39A5, and HMGCS2 for ketogenesis from fatty acids in a tissue with high energetic turnover. Retinoid handling by CRABP2 and xenobiotic sensing through the nuclear receptor NR1I2 couple luminal contents to gene expression and detoxification. Loss of this differentiation programme underlies malabsorption and barrier failure, and its components are reactivated in intestinal metaplasia and colorectal tumours.

Leukocytes only work if they can be told where to go, and this adhesion, migration and chemotaxis module is the directional cue system that moves them. Secreted chemokines and their G protein-coupled receptors set up gradients that recruit neutrophils to infected or injured tissue, guide monocytes and T cells along inflamed endothelium, and steer naive T cells and dendritic cells into lymph node zones, where the CCL19/CCL21-CCR7 axis organises lymphoid architecture and CXCL13 positions B cells in follicles. Downstream signalling reshapes the actin cytoskeleton and switches integrins to a high-affinity state so cells arrest, crawl and cross vessel walls. Other cues here broaden the theme: thrombin acting through its protease-activated receptor and platelet factor 4 link coagulation to leukocyte recruitment, while annexin A1 and adrenergic signalling restrain it. Defects produce immunodeficiency, impaired lymphocyte homing, or chronic inflammatory tissue damage; the same receptors serve as HIV entry cofactors and as drug targets.

Lipid-modifying enzymes anchored in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane oxidise fatty acids, eicosanoids and other lipophilic substrates, shaping both inflammatory signalling and the clearance of hydrophobic compounds. Several cytochrome P450 monooxygenases here act on arachidonic acid and leukotrienes: the CYP4F enzymes hydroxylate leukotriene B4 and other fatty acids to terminate their signalling activity, while CYP3A family members oxidise steroids, bile acid precursors and a large share of clinically used drugs, making this compartment a determinant of drug exposure and interactions. Prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2, the inducible cyclooxygenase targeted by anti-inflammatory drugs, and thromboxane A synthase route the same arachidonate pool toward prostanoids that drive pain, fever and platelet aggregation. A microsomal glutathione transferase contributes conjugation and peroxidase activity at the same membrane. Together these activities set the balance between generating and inactivating lipid mediators.

This grouping centres on inflammatory cytokine output from activated lymphocytes and the signalling that licenses it. Tumour necrosis factor, the IL-6-family members LIF and oncostatin M, and the p19 subunit of IL-23 are secreted effectors that drive acute inflammation, acute-phase and stromal responses, and the expansion and stabilisation of Th17-type responses; excess of these mediators underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, and TNF and IL-23 are themselves targets of biologic therapy. Upstream, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase IV and protein kinase C alpha couple antigen-receptor and calcium signals to the transcription of these genes, while CRTAM mediates cell-cell contact that sustains cytotoxic and helper effector differentiation. Also represented are modulators of the surrounding tissue response: urokinase plasminogen activator in pericellular proteolysis, a TGF-beta co-receptor that sequesters ligand, and the Hedgehog receptor Patched.

This is the immediate-early transcriptional burst that cells mount within minutes of growth factor, serum or stress stimulation, dominated by the NR4A family of orphan nuclear receptors (NR4A1, NR4A2, NR4A3) together with other rapidly induced genes such as EGR3, DUSP1, CYR61 and ID1. Its output determines whether a stimulated cell proceeds into the cycle, pauses, differentiates or dies: CDKN1A imposes a p21-dependent brake on cyclin-dependent kinases, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases to terminate the very signal that induced it, and PPP1R15A feeds back on translational stress responses. CYR61 is a secreted matricellular protein linking the response to adhesion and angiogenesis, while IL6 couples it to inflammation. Because these genes are transcribed without new protein synthesis, the module serves as a fast, self-limiting relay between receptor signalling and durable changes in cell fate, and its persistent activation is a feature of tumours and of neuronal activity-dependent plasticity.

This grouping marks the presence and activity of professional antigen-presenting cells, chiefly macrophages, microglia, dendritic cells and B cells, that display peptides on MHC class II to CD4 T cells and so set the threshold for adaptive immune responses. Several class II alleles and the peptide-loading catalyst HLA-DM are present alongside IRF8, a transcription factor that specifies dendritic cell and monocyte identity and drives class II gene expression. The remainder of the signature is myeloid and lymphoid membrane hardware: the pan-leukocyte phosphatase PTPRC, the tetraspanin CD53, beta-2 integrins ITGAL, ITGAM and ITGB2 with ITGA4 for adhesion and transmigration, L-selectin for lymph node homing, and cytoplasmic adaptors such as FYB, HCLS1 and PLEK that couple receptor engagement to the actin cytoskeleton. IL10RA provides the anti-inflammatory brake. Tissue expression of these genes usually reports immune infiltration, and loss of class II presentation produces bare lymphocyte syndrome with profound CD4 T cell deficiency.

enriched in antigen presentation (III) describes the machinery by which professional antigen-presenting cells display peptides to CD4+ T helper cells, the step that licenses adaptive immune responses and antibody production. Its core is the MHC class II locus BA/DRB heterodimers, together with HLA-DM, which catalyses the exchange of invariant chain-derived CLIP peptide for antigenic peptide in the endolysosomal loading compartment. Around this sits the myeloid and lymphoid membrane apparatus needed for productive contact: the integrin LFA-1 beta chain and ICAM1 forming the adhesive ring of the immunological synapse, the phosphatase CD45 and adaptors FYB and PLEK tuning receptor signalling, and macrophage- and microglia-associated proteins such as AIF1, CD53 and LAPTM5. Expression of these genes marks tissue macrophage and dendritic cell infiltration, and their variation at the class II locus underlies susceptibility to many autoimmune diseases.

This module marks the professional antigen-presenting compartment of the immune system, where extracellular proteins are displayed on MHC class II to CD4 T cells so that helper responses, antibody production and immunological memory can be initiated. Its core is the class II locus itself — HLA-DR alpha and beta chains together with the HLA-DM chaperone that catalyses exchange of the invariant chain-derived placeholder peptide for high-affinity antigenic peptides in the late endosome. Around this sit the adhesion and signalling components that make a productive contact with the T cell and sustain it: ICAM1 with the integrin beta-2 chain, the pan-leukocyte phosphatase CD45, CD53, and the myeloid adaptors AIF1, FYB and PLEK. Expression of this programme in monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and B cells defines their competence to present; loss of class II expression causes profound combined immunodeficiency, while its inappropriate induction contributes to autoimmunity and transplant rejection.

Hox transcription factors give cells a positional address along the head-to-tail axis, and this grouping of paralogues drawn from the A and B clusters represents that combinatorial code. Their nested, colinear expression domains in the embryo specify vertebral identity, hindbrain segment character, limb proximodistal segments and the regional identity of the gut, and misexpression produces homeotic shifts — ribs on the wrong vertebra, altered branchial arch derivatives, limb malformations. Anterior members such as HOXA2, HOXA4 and HOXB2/B3 pattern the pharyngeal and rostral domains, while posterior HOXA9 and HOXA11 act in caudal skeleton, limb and urogenital development; HOXA9 also governs self-renewal in haematopoietic progenitors and is a recurrent driver when deregulated in leukaemia. Accompanying regulators including the homeodomain factor NKX2-3 and the chromatin-associated PRDM16 extend the programme into gut lymphoid tissue and mesenchymal cell fate decisions.

This grouping marks genes whose expression tracks with SMAD2/3 signalling, the intracellular arm through which TGF-beta and activin/nodal ligands reach the nucleus. Receptor-activated SMAD2 and SMAD3 partner with SMAD4 and with lineage transcription factors to set differentiation state, restrain proliferation, and drive extracellular matrix output, which is why this axis governs wound repair and fibrosis and is subverted in tumour progression and immune suppression. The members read as downstream effectors rather than signalling components: matrix and matrix-modifying genes such as the laminin gamma-1 chain and the collagen prolyl hydroxylase P4HA2, the cell-surface peptidase MME, and transcriptional regulators including GATA3, MEF2C and RUNX2 that direct lymphoid, muscle and osteoblast programmes. TCL1A and VPREB1 point to a B-lineage context, where TGF-beta family input shapes maturation and antibody class switching.

These genes read as candidate loci for alcohol use and dependence, spanning the two ends of that biology: how ethanol is handled chemically and how the brain responds to it. Alcohol dehydrogenase 7 oxidises ethanol to acetaldehyde in the upper gastrointestinal tract and mucosa, while a bitter taste receptor of the TAS2R family shapes the aversive sensory response that limits intake. The remainder are neural: the mu opioid receptor, target of naltrexone in dependence treatment, mediates the rewarding component of drinking; an NMDA receptor subunit and a serotonin type-3 receptor subunit govern the glutamatergic and serotonergic signalling altered by chronic exposure; RBFOX1, ERBB4, NOS1AP and VSNL1 act in neuronal splicing, synapse development and calcium-dependent signalling. Together they frame addiction risk as an interaction of metabolic capacity, taste-mediated aversion and reward circuitry rather than a single mechanism.

No coherent biology links these genes, which span unrelated compartments and organ systems, so the set is best read as a heterogeneous grouping rather than a functional module. Its members touch adrenal steroid synthesis, where a mitochondrial cytochrome P450 performs the 11-beta-hydroxylation step that yields cortisol and whose loss causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia with hypertension; muscle membrane integrity through dystrophin, absent in Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy; and excitatory neurotransmission through an NMDA receptor subunit and a neuronal splicing regulator that shapes brain-specific transcript isoforms. Others contribute innate defence at mucosal surfaces, an alpha interferon of the antiviral type I family, a cystine-glutamate antiporter that supplies cysteine for glutathione and restrains ferroptosis, and a beta-tubulin isotype used to build microtubules. The unifying theme is therefore breadth rather than a shared pathway.

This grouping describes a mesenchymal, fibroblast-like programme in which mechanical and growth-factor cues are converted into matrix remodelling and stromal activation. Its hallmark outputs, the secreted matricellular proteins CCN1 and CCN2, are canonical readouts of YAP/TAZ activity downstream of cell stretch, stiffness and Rho signalling, and caveolin-1 links plasma-membrane mechanics to that response. Alongside them sit secreted modulators of TGF-beta superfamily signalling — the activin A subunit INHBA, follistatin-like 1, and the BMP antagonist gremlin-1 — together with the Wnt pathway inhibitor DACT1, so the ensemble both sends and tunes morphogen signals in the stroma. PDGFRA marks the responding fibroblast and pericyte populations, while EPHA2 contributes contact-dependent guidance. Sustained activity of this axis drives wound healing and tissue fibrosis, and is a feature of cancer-associated fibroblasts supporting tumour growth.

T cell surface signature is the set of membrane proteins that mark a cell as a T lymphocyte and equip it to read antigen and costimulatory cues. It defines the identity used to enumerate T cells in blood and tissue, and its components are the handles by which T cell responses are amplified or shut down therapeutically. The core is the T cell receptor signalling apparatus -- CD3E and CD3G, the adaptor SIT1, and the CD45-associated phosphoprotein PTPRCAP -- flanked by adhesion and costimulatory receptors CD2, CD6, CD28 and ICOS that set the threshold for activation, and by inhibitory LAG3 and SIRPG that restrain it. Chemokine receptors such as CXCR6 direct tissue homing, while MAL organises raft microdomains at the immunological synapse. Amino acid and cofactor transporters appear alongside, reflecting the metabolic reprogramming that accompanies activation and clonal expansion.

A surface signature of T lymphocytes, comprising the membrane proteins that define the lineage and set the threshold for its activation. These molecules are the basis of T cell identification by flow cytometry and the targets of both stimulatory and blocking immunotherapies. The core is the antigen receptor signalling apparatus, with CD3E and CD3G transducing T cell receptor engagement and the adaptors SIT1 and PTPRCAP tuning it at the membrane; costimulation is supplied through CD28 and ICOS, adhesion and synapse formation through CD2 and CD6, and inhibitory restraint through LAG3 and SIRPG. Chemokine and cytokine receptors including CXCR6 direct tissue positioning, while MAL and ITM2A shape raft organisation and trafficking. Coordinate expression of this module underlies antigen recognition, helper and cytotoxic function, and tolerance; its loss or depletion leaves cell-mediated immunity absent.

Natural killer cells are cytotoxic innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization, and the membrane proteins gathered here form the surface signature by which they are recognized and by which they decide whether to kill. Their identity rests on a balance of receptors: inhibitory and activating killer immunoglobulin-like receptors read HLA class I on potential targets, while NKG2D, NKp46, NKp80 and CD16-associated machinery detect stress ligands and antibody-coated cells; NCAM1 (CD56) remains the canonical marker. Cytokine receptors for IL-2/IL-15, IL-12 and IL-18 license effector function and interferon-gamma output, and FASLG and TNFSF14 deliver death signals. Chemoattractant and lipid receptors such as CX3CR1 and S1PR5 govern egress and tissue patrolling, while TGFBR3, HAVCR2 and PVRIG mark inhibitory tone exploited by tumours. Loss of this programme leaves patients prone to herpesvirus disease and impaired tumour surveillance.

Immature, steady-state dendritic cells display a distinctive set of membrane proteins that equips them to sample tissue antigen and await activating signals, and this resting surface signature captures that phenotype. It matters because these cells are the sentinels that decide whether an encountered antigen provokes immunity or tolerance, and the same molecules are used to identify myeloid dendritic cells and to target them therapeutically. The collection is dominated by antigen-presenting machinery, including the CD1 family that presents lipid antigens alongside MHC class II components, together with the high-affinity IgE receptor chain FCER1A and the C-type lectin CLEC10A for glycan uptake. Integrin ITGAX, growth factor receptor CSF1R, scavenger receptors such as STAB1 and TREM2, tetraspanins, and numerous solute carriers round out a surface tuned for endocytosis, adhesion, migration cues and metabolic support before maturation reprogrammes it.

When dendritic cells encounter bacterial lipopolysaccharide they remodel their plasma membrane, and this surface signature captures the mature, T cell-stimulating phenotype that results.
