The change is what converts a tissue sentinel into an antigen-presenting cell able to prime naive T lymphocytes in lymph nodes, and it simultaneously sets the ceiling on that response. Costimulatory ligands CD40, CD80 and CD58 provide the second signals T cells require, while the PD-1 ligands CD274 and PDCD1LG2 restrain them, so activation and checkpoint inhibition are induced together. Cytokine and growth factor receptor chains including IL3RA, CSF2RB and IL13RA1 tune responsiveness to the surrounding milieu, TNFSF13B supports B cell survival, and lectins such as SIGLEC1 and LY75 mediate antigen capture. Interferon-inducible products, solute carriers and integrin and semaphorin receptor components round out a membrane geared for migration and immune synapse formation.

This is a catalogue of plasma-membrane proteins whose expression marks the B lymphocyte lineage, the set of receptors and surface antigens by which B cells are identified, sorted and therapeutically targeted. Its core is the antigen-receptor apparatus and its co-receptors: CD19, MS4A1 (CD20), the CD79A/CD79B signalling subunits, the inhibitory regulators CD22 and CD72, complement receptor CR2, the Fc receptor FCGR2B, and the FCRL family, together with MHC class II molecules and accessory chaperone-like subunits that equip these cells for antigen presentation to T cells. Chemokine receptors such as CXCR5 and CCR6 place them in germinal centres and mucosal follicles, while inhibitory ligands like BTLA and CD200 tune activation thresholds. The remainder spans adhesion molecules, channels, solute carriers and orphan GPCRs, reflecting a surface profile assembled by expression comparison rather than by shared signalling mechanism.

Terminally differentiated, antibody-secreting plasma cells can be recognised by a distinctive set of proteins at and within their plasma membrane, and this surface signature is how they are identified, sorted and targeted — most familiarly by syndecan-1 (CD138), the canonical plasma cell marker exploited in myeloma diagnosis and in tracking antibody responses after vaccination or infection. Adhesion and homing molecules such as ICAM2 and the chemokine receptor CCR10 support residence in mucosal and bone marrow niches where long-lived plasma cells survive. Solute carriers for choline and monocarboxylates, together with membrane-embedded components of the secretory pathway including HM13, TRAM2 and TXNDC15, reflect the extreme demands of immunoglobulin synthesis, folding and export in a cell given over almost entirely to protein secretion, alongside potassium channels and lipid-handling proteins that tune membrane properties.

The plasma-membrane repertoire that distinguishes blood monocytes collects the receptors these cells use to patrol tissue, sense infection, and differentiate into macrophages and inflammatory dendritic cells. It explains how monocytes are identified by flow cytometry and how they act: pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2 and TLR4 detect bacterial products, complement and chemoattractant receptors including C5AR1, FPR1 and CCR2 direct migration out of the circulation, and Fc receptors together with the integrin ITGAM support phagocytosis and antibody-dependent clearance. Scavenger and lectin receptors such as CD36, MARCO, CD163 and LRP1 take up lipids, haemoglobin complexes and modified ligands, linking these cells to iron handling through SLC40A1 and to atherosclerotic foam-cell formation through cholesterol efflux via ABCA1. Inhibitory LILRB receptors and cytokine receptors for IL-6, IL-1 and TNF set the threshold of the resulting inflammatory response.

Dendritic cells are the professional antigen-presenting cells that bridge innate detection of pathogens to T cell priming, and this collection of membrane proteins is what distinguishes their surface from that of other myeloid cells. The molecules here do the jobs that define the cell type: lipid antigen presentation by CD1 family members, MHC class II peptide display, costimulation and maturation marking through CD83 and CD58, and counter-regulation through the PD-1 ligands CD274 and PDCD1LG2, which restrain T cell responses and are exploited by tumours. Scavenger and lectin-type receptors such as MSR1, OLR1, COLEC12, SIGLEC1 and TREM2 capture material for processing, while transferrin receptor, amino acid and organic anion transporters support the metabolic demand of antigen uptake. Also present are receptors for GM-CSF, IL-1 and neuropilins that shape differentiation, migration and interaction with lymphocytes.

Activated CD4 helper T cells that have committed to the Th1 fate display a distinctive set of plasma membrane and membrane-associated proteins, and this surface signature of stimulated Th1 cells is useful both as a marker panel for identifying the subset and as a source of targets for modulating it. Th1 responses drive macrophage activation and clearance of intracellular pathogens, and when unrestrained they contribute to autoimmune tissue damage. The genes here include the inhibitory checkpoint receptor LAG3, which is induced on activated T cells and dampens further responses, the thrombin receptor F2R, orphan G protein-coupled receptors, a tetraspanin, a synaptic vesicle protein and an adaptor of the NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligase network that tunes receptor turnover. Together they mark the shift in surface composition that accompanies antigen-driven activation and effector differentiation rather than a single signalling cascade.

Surface molecules marking activated Th2-polarized CD4 T cells, the helper subset that drives IgE class switching, eosinophil recruitment and mucosal responses to helminths, and whose overactivity underlies allergic asthma, atopic dermatitis and rhinitis. The signature includes the core T cell receptor and costimulatory apparatus needed for antigen-driven activation — a CD3 signalling chain and CD28 — together with membrane adaptors such as SIT1 and MAL that organize receptor-proximal signalling in lipid rafts and tune the strength of activation. Receptors for cytokine and orphan ligands, notably the IL-25 receptor subunit IL17RB, link these cells to epithelial alarmins that amplify type 2 inflammation, while chemoattractant-type receptors including GPR15 bias trafficking toward gut and skin. Several solute carriers and small transmembrane proteins reflect the metabolic and membrane remodelling that accompanies helper T cell differentiation.

This is a membrane-protein signature intended to mark naive B cells — mature, antigen-inexperienced lymphocytes circulating between blood and secondary lymphoid follicles before they encounter antigen and differentiate into germinal centre, memory or plasma cells. The immunologically interpretable members fit that state well: CD72, CD37 and TSPAN13 organise B cell receptor signalling at the plasma membrane, BTLA and CD200 impose inhibitory restraint that keeps resting cells unresponsive, CXCR4 and CCR6 direct homing to marrow and mucosal follicles, HVCN1 supports the proton flux accompanying receptor-triggered oxidative signalling, and HLA-DMA with HLA-DOA shape peptide loading for antigen presentation. Many remaining entries are receptors, channels and transporters with no established B cell role, so the set is best read as a transcript-based surface phenotype for distinguishing resting B cells from activated or differentiated descendants, rather than a mechanistic signalling module.

Memory B cells are the long-lived antigen-experienced lymphocytes that allow a second encounter with a pathogen or vaccine to produce a faster, higher-affinity antibody response, and this collection marks the surface proteins by which they can be distinguished from naive and germinal-centre B cells. The identity-carrying members are receptors for B cell survival and differentiation cytokines of the BAFF/APRIL family, whose loss causes common variable immunodeficiency and impaired class-switched memory, together with an inhibitory Fc receptor that raises the threshold for reactivation by immune complexes, and broadly expressed lymphocyte glycoproteins and adhesion molecules that govern trafficking and homing to gut and lymphoid tissue. Many remaining entries are adhesion, channel and orphan receptor genes with no established B cell role, so the set is best read as a surface phenotype signature rather than a coherent signalling cascade.

Single strand break repair removes nicks and gaps in one strand of the DNA duplex before they can be converted into far more dangerous double-strand breaks or stall transcription and replication. Single-strand breaks arise constantly from oxidative attack, abortive topoisomerase reactions and the incision steps of base excision repair, and cells that cannot seal them accumulate persistent damage; inherited defects in this machinery cause cerebellar degeneration and neurological syndromes, reflecting how dependent long-lived neurons are on it. Mechanistically it uses the same enzymes as base excision repair: damaged or blocked break ends are cleaned up by end-processing factors such as aprataxin and tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase, gaps are filled, and XRCC1 acts as the scaffold coordinating end processing with ligation. Related activities include glycosylase-initiated base removal, transcription-coupled repair, and chromatin and telomere contexts that shape access to lesions.

Single-strand breaks are the most frequent DNA lesion in cells, arising from oxidative attack, abortive topoisomerase action, and the incision steps of base excision repair; repairing them prevents replication fork collapse and the double-strand breaks and transcription blocks that follow. Detection recruits a scaffold, XRCC1, which organises end-processing and ligation at the nick. End-cleaning enzymes prepare chemically damaged termini: aprataxin removes abortive ligation adducts, TDP1 resolves trapped topoisomerase I-DNA intermediates, and APLF contributes nuclease and scaffolding activity, while uracil-DNA glycosylase and NEIL3 generate nicks through excision of damaged bases. Coupling to transcription is represented by the CSB and CSA proteins, which handle lesions encountered by elongating RNA polymerase. Because neurons are long-lived and highly oxidative, defects in this repair route produce hereditary cerebellar ataxias and neurodegeneration rather than cancer predisposition, and the pathway also intersects chromatin regulation and telomere protection.

Recombination must be permitted where it is useful and suppressed where it is dangerous, and this regulatory layer sets the frequency, location and outcome of homologous exchange and of programmed rearrangement at immunoglobulin loci. It matters because too little leaves double-strand breaks unrepaired and too much, or recombination between the wrong repeats, produces translocations, telomere loss and cancer predisposition. Control operates at several levels: break sensing and resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, loading and stabilisation of RAD51 filaments, anti-resection and end-protection by 53BP1, RIF1 and the shieldin subunits that push repair toward end joining, helicases such as BLM and RTEL1 that dismantle joint molecules, and mismatch repair proteins that police heteroduplex fidelity. Chromatin contributes through linker histones, NuA4/TIP60-type acetylation, H4K20 methyltransferases and PRDM9, which designates meiotic hotspots. Cytokine and receptor components reflect the B-cell signals that license class switch recombination.

regulation of mitotic recombination controls how often and how far homologous recombination proceeds in dividing somatic cells, keeping repair of broken or stalled replication forks accurate rather than allowing crossovers, loss of heterozygosity and gross rearrangements. Too little recombination leaves double-strand breaks unrepaired; too much, or recombination between the wrong repeats, drives translocations and the genome instability characteristic of cancer. The genes span the steps where that balance is set: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex that senses and resects breaks, the mismatch repair factor MLH1 that rejects mismatched heteroduplexes and limits recombination between diverged sequences, ANKLE1 nuclease activity resolving joint molecules late in the process, and TERF2 shielding chromosome ends from being read as breaks. ZSCAN4 links this control to telomere recombination and elongation. The pathway therefore sits within DNA damage response and chromosome maintenance rather than meiotic exchange.

Recombination between homologous sequences is a safe way to repair a broken chromosome in a dividing cell, but unrestrained exchange produces loss of heterozygosity, translocations and rearrangements between repeats. Regulation of mitotic recombination sets how often and how far such exchange proceeds during somatic cell divisions, and its loosening is a route to genome instability and cancer predisposition. The genes here act at several control points: the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex senses and processes double-strand break ends to commit them to homology-directed repair, the mismatch repair factor MLH1 polices heteroduplex fidelity and rejects recombination between diverged sequences, TERF2 shields telomeres from being treated as broken ends, and ANKLE1 is a nuclease that resolves branched recombination intermediates late in the process. Together they link break repair, telomere protection and repeat stability to faithful chromosome transmission.

Separating chromosomes requires the two spindle poles to be driven further apart, and this lengthening of the mitotic spindle from prophase through anaphase B is what sets the final distance between the daughter genomes and the position of the cleavage furrow. The genes here centre on two machines: the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B or its meiotic counterpart Aurora C partners with INCENP, survivin and borealin to phosphorylate substrates at centromeres and the spindle midzone, and a midzone crosslinking module in which PRC1 and the kinesins KIF4A and KIF23 organise antiparallel microtubule overlaps. NUMA1 anchors and focuses microtubules at the poles, while RACGAP1 links midzone assembly to RhoA-directed cytokinesis. Loss of coordination here yields lagging chromosomes, failed furrow placement and aneuploid progeny, connecting spindle mechanics to genome stability and tumourigenesis.

Large ribosomal subunit assembly is the step in ribosome biogenesis where ribosomal RNA is folded, modified and packaged with large-subunit proteins into a functional particle capable of peptide bond formation. Cells tune it to their growth rate, and defects in it cause ribosomopathies and trigger p53 stabilisation through the RPL5/RPL11 surveillance route, which links assembly failure to cell cycle arrest. The genes here cover both compartments: nucleolar factors such as BOP1, BRIX1, RPF2 and RRS1 chaperone 5S RNP incorporation and pre-rRNA processing, EIF6 blocks premature subunit joining, and MDN1 drives large remodelling steps. A parallel mitochondrial arm assembles the mitoribosomal large subunit, with rRNA methyltransferases MRM2, MRM3 and NSUN4, GTPases MTG1 and MTG2, and MALSU1 acting as an anti-association factor, supporting synthesis of respiratory chain subunits inside the organelle.

Building the small ribosomal subunit means folding its rRNA, loading the structural proteins onto it, and chemically maturing the region that will read mRNA — the step that sets how many ribosomes a cell can make and therefore its capacity for growth. Both cytoplasmic and mitochondrial versions are represented here: nucleolar factors and small-subunit proteins such as RPS6, RPS14, RPS19 and RPSA assemble the 40S particle, while ERAL1 chaperones mitochondrial 12S rRNA and TFB1M and METTL15 install methyl marks required for a functional mitoribosomal decoding centre. RBFA and NOA1 act as late-stage maturation factors. Defects in this process are a recognised cause of ribosomopathies, with impaired erythropoiesis and developmental malformation, and mitochondrial small-subunit failure impairs respiratory chain translation. Several components double as regulators of p53 and of nucleolar stress responses.

Very long-chain fatty acid metabolic process covers the synthesis and breakdown of fatty acids longer than 22 carbons, the lipids that build myelin, skin barrier ceramides, retinal photoreceptor membranes and sperm membranes. Its failure is directly disease-causing: defective peroxisomal import of these substrates underlies X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, and mutations in the elongase acting on retinal species cause macular dystrophy. Elongation proceeds by iterative cycles on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, with ELOVL enzymes setting chain-length and substrate specificity, followed by 3-hydroxyacyl dehydratase and trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase steps. Because mitochondrial beta-oxidation cannot handle such long chains, catabolism requires ATP-binding cassette transporters to deliver activated substrates into peroxisomes, where acyl-CoA oxidase, a bifunctional enzyme and thiolase shorten them. Fatty acid transport proteins and acyl-CoA synthetases supply activation, and thioesterases release free acid, linking this route to membrane lipid composition and lipid signalling.

Fatty acids longer than 22 carbons are made and broken down by a dedicated set of enzymes, and the balance between the two determines the lipid composition of myelin, skin barrier ceramides, retinal photoreceptor membranes and sperm. Elongases together with the reductase and dehydratase steps of the microsomal elongation cycle add two carbons at a time to acyl-CoA substrates, while peroxisomes handle the catabolic side: transporters of the ABCD family import very-long-chain acyl-CoAs, which are then shortened by acyl-CoA oxidase, the multifunctional D-bifunctional protein and thiolase, with acyl-CoA synthetases and thioesterases setting substrate availability. Loss of this capacity is directly pathogenic causing X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy when peroxisomal import fails, Stargardt-like macular dystrophy from elongase mutations, and ichthyosis when barrier lipids cannot be assembled.

Iron, zinc, copper and manganese are needed as enzyme cofactors but are toxic in excess, so cells move them across membranes under tight control; transition metal ion transport covers the importers, exporters, ferroxidases, carriers and storage proteins that set those internal concentrations. Iron enters via transferrin and its receptor or through the divalent metal transporter SLC11A2, is exported by ferroportin under hepcidin control, stored in ferritin, and delivered to mitochondria for heme and iron-sulfur cluster synthesis. Zinc flux depends on the complementary ZIP importer and ZnT exporter families, while ATP7A and ATP7B load copper onto secreted cuproenzymes and excrete the excess. Endosomal and lysosomal channels, vesicle trafficking adaptors and TRP channels provide additional routes. Failures produce hemochromatosis, anemia, Menkes and Wilson disease, acrodermatitis enteropathica, and manganese neurotoxicity, and pathogen iron withholding by lactoferrin and lipocalin-2 links this biology to innate immunity.

urea cycle is the liver's route for disposing of waste nitrogen, converting ammonia generated by amino acid breakdown into urea for excretion by the kidney. Without it ammonia accumulates in blood and brain, and inherited deficiencies of any step present as hyperammonemic encephalopathy in newborns or after protein loads. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, activated by N-acetylglutamate from NAGS, condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and ornithine/citrulline exchange across the inner membrane by ORNT carriers links this to the cytosolic steps in which argininosuccinate is built from aspartate, cleaved to arginine and fumarate, and hydrolysed by arginase to release urea and regenerate ornithine. The fumarate produced ties nitrogen disposal to the citric acid cycle, while arginine output feeds nitric oxide and polyamine metabolism; hepatocyte expression is set by transcription factors such as CEBPA.

Protein turnover releases ammonia, which is toxic to the brain, and the urea cycle is how the liver converts it into a harmless, excretable form. Running largely in periportal hepatocytes, the route fixes ammonia and bicarbonate into carbamoyl phosphate, condenses it with ornithine, and adds a second nitrogen from aspartate to build argininosuccinate; cleavage yields arginine and fumarate, and hydrolysis of arginine liberates urea while regenerating ornithine for another turn. Mitochondrial and cytosolic steps are linked by ornithine/citrulline exchange across the inner membrane, and flux is tuned by N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory activator of the first committed enzyme, and by transcriptional control of hepatic gene expression. Loss of any component causes an inherited urea cycle disorder, with hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and coma. The cycle also supplies arginine and connects nitrogen disposal to fumarate entry into the citric acid cycle.

Citrulline sits at the junction of two nitrogen-handling routes: the urea cycle, which disposes of ammonia from amino acid breakdown, and the recycling of arginine for nitric oxide synthesis. Its metabolism matters because the intermediate is made in liver mitochondria from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate by ornithine transcarbamylase, exported, and condensed with aspartate by argininosuccinate synthetase toward arginine and urea; loss of either step causes hyperammonaemia with neurological injury, the basis of OTC deficiency and citrullinaemia. Carbamoyl phosphate supply comes from CPS1 in the mitochondrial arm and from the multifunctional CAD enzyme in cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis, while pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase links the pathway to proline and ornithine supply. DDAH1 feeds in by degrading methylarginines to citrulline, relieving inhibition of nitric oxide synthases and so connecting this amino acid chemistry to vascular tone.

ribosomal large subunit export from nucleus is the final nuclear step of ribosome biogenesis: the newly assembled 60S subunit is escorted through nuclear pores into the cytoplasm, where it joins 40S subunits to translate mRNA. Cells depend on it to sustain protein synthesis and growth, and blocking it stalls translational capacity and triggers nucleolar stress responses that stabilise p53. The adaptor NMD3 binds the maturing 60S and presents a leucine-rich export signal to the exportin CRM1, whose cargo release is driven by the RAN GTPase gradient across the nuclear envelope; passage occurs through nucleoporin channels including NUP88. Nucleolar chaperones such as nucleophosmin and assembly factors like SDAD1 couple export competence to correct late maturation, so that only properly built subunits leave the nucleus. This links nucleolar ribosome assembly to cytoplasmic translation and to proliferative control in rapidly dividing and cancer cells.

Ribosome production begins in the nucleolus but translation happens in the cytoplasm, and export of the assembled large subunit is the step that bridges the two. Without it, pre-60S particles accumulate in the nucleus, ribosome supply falls, and cells lose the capacity to sustain growth and protein synthesis; such defects underlie ribosomopathies and impose nucleolar stress that engages p53. The adaptor NMD3 binds the maturing 60S particle and presents a leucine-rich export signal to the exportin XPO1, whose cargo release depends on the RanGTP gradient set across the nuclear envelope; passage occurs through nuclear pore channels built from nucleoporins such as NUP88, while NPM1 and SDAD1 act in nucleolar assembly and maturation of the particle before and during transit. Final maturation steps, including release of the adaptor, occur once the subunit reaches the cytoplasm.

Ribosome production ends in the nucleus only for the small subunit's precursor; the pre-40S particle must be delivered through nuclear pores to the cytoplasm, where its final maturation and first translation-competent assembly occur. Export of the ribosomal small subunit from the nucleus therefore sets how fast a growing cell can build translation capacity, and it couples nucleolar assembly to protein synthesis demand. Carrier-mediated transport does the work: the exportin XPO1 and the RAN GTPase gradient provide directionality, and nucleoporins such as NUP88 form the channel the particle passes through. Riding along are assembly factors that keep the particle immature and export-competent, including LTV1 and the atypical kinase RIOK2, which are released in the cytoplasm before 40S joins the pool. NPM1 and the RNA-binding factor NOP9 act earlier, on rRNA processing and pre-40S quality, linking nucleolar surveillance to export.

Every mitosis must deliver one complete copy of the genome to each daughter cell, and mitotic sister chromatid segregation is the machinery that accomplishes it. Errors produce aneuploidy, micronuclei and chromosome instability, a hallmark of tumours and a cause of developmental and microcephaly syndromes. Condensin complexes compact the replicated chromosomes while cohesin rings, released by separase and WAPL, hold sisters together until anaphase. Kinetochores built on centromeric CENP-A chromatin, with the NDC80, MIS12 and SKA components, capture spindle microtubules; unattached kinetochores recruit MAD1, MAD2, BUB1 and BUBR1 to restrain the anaphase-promoting complex through CDC20 until biorientation is achieved. Aurora B within the chromosomal passenger complex corrects erroneous attachments, kinesins and dynein generate the forces that move chromosomes, and ESCRT proteins complete the final abscission of the daughter cells.

Cells only divide if their DNA is intact and their chromosomes are correctly attached, and cell cycle checkpoint signaling is the surveillance that enforces those conditions. Damage or stalled replication is detected at the fork and at breaks, where the ATM and ATR kinases, with partners such as ATRIP, TOPBP1, CLSPN and the 9-1-1 clamp, phosphorylate CHEK1, CHEK2 and p53 to arrest progression, stabilise forks and buy time for repair by homologous recombination factors including BRCA1, BRCA2, MRE11-RAD50-NBN and RAD51. In mitosis, the spindle assembly checkpoint uses kinetochore components such as MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1, BUB3 and the NDC80 complex to hold CDC20 and the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until every chromosome is bipolarly attached. Loss of these controls permits replication of damaged templates and missegregation, producing the mutations and aneuploidy characteristic of cancer, and many components are tumour suppressors or targets of checkpoint-inhibitor drugs.

Cells must not divide until every chromosome has been copied, and DNA replication checkpoint signaling is the surveillance system that enforces that order. Stalled or damaged replication forks are detected and converted into a signal that halts entry into mitosis, stabilizes the fork so replication can resume, and restrains firing of additional origins until the problem is resolved. Sensor and scaffold components such as the RAD9A-HUS1-RAD17 clamp and clamp loader, the replication factor C subunits, TOPBP1, MDC1 and the TIMELESS-TIPIN complex couple fork status to kinase activation, with claspin relaying the signal onward to effector kinases. Replication licensing and initiation factors including ORC1, CDC6, CDT1, CDC45, CDC7-DBF4 and TICRR place this monitoring directly on the origin firing machinery. Loss of the checkpoint produces under-replicated DNA, chromosome breakage and the genome instability that fuels tumorigenesis and developmental microcephaly syndromes.

Cyclin-dependent kinases only fire when their regulators permit it, and this pathway covers the inputs that set that threshold: cyclin availability, inhibitor binding, activating and inhibitory phosphorylation, and chaperone-assisted assembly. It is the control layer that decides whether a cell crosses from G1 into S phase, commits to mitosis, or arrests after DNA damage, and its loss is a standard route to unchecked proliferation in cancer. Activating phosphatases such as CDC25A and CDC25C strip the inhibitory phosphates placed by the kinase PKMYT1, while CDKN1B and CDKN2A restrain cyclin-CDK complexes directly and GADD45A links damage signalling to mitotic delay. Other members act outside the cell cycle proper: CDK5R1 and CDK5R2 activate CDK5 in neurons, and cyclins T and K partner CDKs that regulate transcription elongation rather than replication.

sulfur amino acid metabolic process covers the making, breaking and recycling of methionine, cysteine and their derivatives, the chemistry that links dietary protein to methylation capacity, glutathione supply and sulfide handling. It matters because these reactions set the cell's redox buffer and its universal methyl donor: loss of cystathionine beta-synthase or methionine synthase activity causes homocystinuria and megaloblastic anemia, while failure of glutamate-cysteine ligase leaves cells unable to detoxify oxidants. The genes trace the transmethylation cycle (MAT1A, GNMT, MTR, MTRR, MTHFR, BHMT), transsulfuration to cysteine (CBS, CTH), the methionine salvage route from methylthioadenosine (MTAP, APIP, ENOPH1, MRI1), and cysteine's fates in taurine synthesis (CDO1, CSAD), glutathione assembly, and sulfurtransferase-mediated disposal of sulfide and cyanide. Cystine import by SLC7A11 ties the pathway to ferroptosis resistance and tumour redox adaptation.

Handling of the sulfur-containing amino acids methionine and cysteine underpins methylation capacity, glutathione supply and sulfide detoxification. Methionine is activated to S-adenosylmethionine by MAT1A for methyl transfer, and homocysteine is either remethylated by the folate- and betaine-dependent routes (MTR, MTRR, MTHFR, BHMT) or committed to cysteine by the transsulfuration enzymes CBS and CTH; loss of CBS causes homocystinuria, and impaired remethylation raises homocysteine with vascular and neural consequences. Cysteine obtained this way or imported by the SLC7A11 antiporter feeds glutathione synthesis via GCLC/GCLM and taurine formation through CDO1 and CSAD, linking the pathway to redox defence and bile salt conjugation. Salvage of methylthioadenosine regenerates methionine from polyamine synthesis, while sulfurtransferases such as MPST and TST dispose of cyanide and hydrogen sulfide, and MSRA repairs oxidised methionine residues in proteins.

Sulfur amino acid biosynthesis is how cells make and regenerate methionine and cysteine, the pair that supplies nearly all biological methyl groups and the sulfur used for glutathione, taurine and iron-sulfur chemistry. Homocysteine sits at its centre: it can be remethylated back to methionine, either by the folate- and cobalamin-dependent route using methionine synthase with its reductase and the MTHFR-generated methyl donor, or by betaine-dependent transfer, or it can be committed irreversibly to cysteine through the transsulfuration enzymes cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase. A parallel salvage arm recycles methylthioadenosine, the byproduct of polyamine synthesis, back to methionine. Loss of these reactions causes homocystinuria, raises plasma homocysteine with its vascular consequences, and constrains the S-adenosylmethionine supply on which DNA and histone methylation depend. Cysteine dioxygenase directs excess cysteine toward taurine and sulfate rather than allowing it to accumulate.

Breakdown of sulfur-containing amino acids disposes of excess methionine and cysteine while generating useful products: cysteine sulfinate and taurine for bile salt conjugation and osmotic balance, sulfate for conjugation reactions, and sulfide-derived sulfur for cofactor and thiol chemistry. Cysteine is toxic in excess, so flux through this catabolic route sets the cell's cysteine ceiling. Transsulfuration links the two amino acids, with cystathionine beta-synthase committing homocysteine to cysteine synthesis; its loss causes classical homocystinuria with thrombosis, lens dislocation and skeletal changes. Cysteine dioxygenase and sulfinoalanine decarboxylase then direct cysteine toward taurine, while sulfurtransferases including rhodanese and mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase transfer sulfur and detoxify cyanide. Methionine adenosyltransferase and methionine synthase reductase tie the pathway to the methylation cycle, making sulfur amino acid catabolism a hub linking one-carbon metabolism, glutathione supply and antioxidant defence, prominently in liver.

Cells must import cystine, cysteine and methionine to build proteins, synthesise glutathione and feed one-carbon metabolism, and this transport step sets how much sulfur amino acid is available. The carriers involved span the plasma membrane and the lysosomal membrane: heteromeric complexes built on the heavy chains SLC3A1 and SLC3A2 pair with light chains such as SLC7A9 and SLC7A11 to exchange cystine for intracellular glutamate or neutral amino acids, SLC7A5 and SLC43A2 handle methionine and other large neutral amino acids, and CTNS exports cystine from the lysosome after protein degradation. Loss of CTNS causes cystinosis, with cystine crystals destroying kidney and eye; defective renal reabsorption through the SLC3A1-SLC7A9 pair causes cystinuria. Cystine uptake via SLC7A11 supplies glutathione and determines sensitivity to ferroptosis, linking this transport to redox defence and tumour cell survival.

Genes are kept off as deliberately as they are switched on, and this collection covers the machinery that restrains RNA polymerase II transcription: sequence-specific repressors, corepressor complexes, chromatin modifiers that close promoters, and factors that stall the polymerase after initiation. Such repression defines cell identity, since lineage commitment depends as much on silencing alternative programmes as on activating the chosen one, and its loss underlies developmental malformation and cancer. The members span KRAB zinc fingers and their TRIM28 partner, Polycomb components such as EZH2, SUZ12 and RNF2, histone deacetylases with the NCOR, SIN3 and NuRD scaffolds, DNA methyltransferases and methyl-CpG readers like MECP2, Groucho/TLE and CtBP corepressors, HES/ID and SNAI/ZEB factors, and negative regulators of elongation including HEXIM proteins acting on P-TEFb. Also here are repressive arms of p53, Notch, TGF-beta, nuclear receptor and circadian control.

Ribosomal RNA leaves the polymerase as a plain transcript and is then chemically decorated before it can fold into a working ribosome. These modifications — 2'-O-methylation of riboses, base methylation, acetylation and conversion of uridine to pseudouridine — stabilise rRNA structure, tune the decoding centre and peptidyl transferase site, and act as checkpoints that license successive steps of subunit maturation. Much of the methylation and pseudouridylation is guided by small nucleolar RNAs working with the fibrillarin methyltransferase or with a pseudouridine synthase complex built around DKC1, GAR1, NHP2 and NOP10; other enzymes act alone on defined nucleotides, and a separate set of methyltransferases modifies mitochondrial rRNA for mitoribosome assembly. Loss of function causes ribosomopathies, with dyskeratosis congenita arising from DKC1 mutation, and links altered translational fidelity to bone marrow failure, developmental defects and cancer.

Mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades are the relay by which cells convert surface signals into decisions about proliferation, differentiation, stress adaptation, inflammation and death. Signalling runs through tiers: a MAP3K (or an upstream MAP4K) phosphorylates a MAP2K, which in turn phosphorylates the terminal MAPK, producing the ERK, JNK and p38 branches that phosphorylate transcription factors such as JUN and ATF2 and downstream kinases like MAPKAPK2. Input comes from an enormous range of receptors represented here "u2014 receptor tyrosine kinases for growth factors (EGFR, FGFRs, PDGFRs, NTRKs, INSR), cytokine and Toll-like receptors, integrins and G protein-coupled receptors "u2014 funnelled through adaptors such as GRB2, SHC1 and RAS-RAF modules. Output is tuned by dedicated brakes: DUSP phosphatases, SPRY and SPRED proteins, and scaffolds including KSR1 and MAPK8IPs that dictate specificity. Hyperactivation through RAS or RAF underlies many cancers and developmental RASopathies.

nuclear-transcribed mRNA catabolic process, nonsense-mediated decay is the surveillance system that destroys messenger RNAs carrying a premature stop codon, preventing the accumulation of truncated proteins that would act as dominant-negative or toxic species. It sets the severity of many nonsense mutations in human disease and also tunes the normal transcriptome, clearing transcripts with upstream open reading frames, retained introns, or unproductive alternative splicing. Recognition depends on the exon junction complex deposited during splicing — EIF4A3, MAGOH, RBM8A and CASC3 — which, if it lies downstream of a terminating ribosome, recruits UPF1, UPF2 and UPF3B. The SMG1 kinase then phosphorylates UPF1, licensing SMG6 endonucleolytic cleavage and SMG5/SMG7-directed deadenylation, decapping and exonucleolytic degradation by the exosome and the SKI complex. Release factors ETF1 and GSPT1 couple the decision to translation termination itself, and mutations in UPF3B cause X-linked intellectual disability.

Messenger RNAs carrying a premature stop codon are recognized and destroyed rather than translated, and nonsense-mediated decay is the surveillance system that does it. This protects cells from truncated, dominant-negative proteins, shapes the severity of nonsense mutations in inherited disease, and also tunes the abundance of normal transcripts that contain upstream open reading frames or retained introns. Recognition depends on a stalled terminating ribosome with its release factors and the helicase UPF1 together with UPF2 and UPF3; the exon junction complex, including MAGOH, RBM8A and EIF4A3, marks spliced junctions downstream of the stop. The SMG1 kinase and the SMG5-SMG7 and SMG6 branches then commit the transcript to decay, which proceeds by decapping and 5' exonucleolysis, deadenylation, endonucleolytic cleavage, and exosome-dependent degradation. The pathway is thus coupled to splicing, nuclear export and translation termination.

protein polyubiquitination is the tagging of proteins with ubiquitin chains, the mark that commits a substrate to proteasomal destruction or, with different chain linkages, to signalling and membrane trafficking outcomes. It sets the lifetime of most regulatory proteins, so it governs cell cycle progression, DNA damage responses, quality control of misfolded proteins, and the switching on and off of inflammatory signalling. E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2 family work with E3 ligases of several architectures: multisubunit cullin-RING complexes with their F-box and BTB substrate receptors, the anaphase-promoting complex that degrades mitotic cyclins and securin, HECT and RBR ligases such as ITCH, NEDD4 and parkin, and RING and TRIM proteins including RNF8 and RNF168 that build chains at damaged chromatin. Linear and K63 chains assembled by RNF31, SHARPIN and TRAF6 propagate NF- influenced innate immune and IL-17 receptor signalling, while TNFAIP3 reverses them. Loss of individual ligases causes neurodegeneration, developmental syndromes and cancer.

Tagging a protein with a chain of ubiquitins rather than a single moiety is how cells mark substrates for destruction by the proteasome, and how they encode non-degradative signals such as the linkage types that drive inflammatory signalling and DNA damage responses. Protein polyubiquitination is carried out by E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2 family working with RING, HECT and RBR E3 ligases, including cullin-RING complexes built on CUL1-SKP1-RBX1 with interchangeable F-box or BTB substrate adaptors, and the anaphase-promoting complex that destroys cyclins and securin to allow mitotic exit. Through it, cells time cell cycle transitions, clear misfolded proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, restrain WNT and NF-kB signalling, and mark damaged mitochondria for autophagy. Loss of individual ligases causes cancer predisposition, neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease, and dysregulated immune activation, reflecting how much regulatory information is written in ubiquitin chains.

Meiotic spindle organization is the building, positioning and eventual disassembly of the microtubule spindle in oocytes and spermatocytes, the apparatus that must segregate homologous chromosomes and then sister chromatids without error. Because oocytes divide acentrosomally and asymmetrically, spindle assembly here is unusually error-prone, and its failure produces aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and infertility — mutations in the oocyte-specific β-tubulin TUBB8 cause human oocyte maturation arrest. The genes involved span tubulin supply and nucleation (TUBG1/TUBG2 γ-tubulin, the microtubule-severing-related KATNAL2), spindle pole and spindle-size determination (ASPM), kinetochore–microtubule attachment through the NDC80 complex and the SKA coupling complex, and the cell cycle timers that license division: Aurora A kinase, cyclin B2, the MOS kinase driving oocyte maturation, separase and cohesin release via WAPL. Together they couple spindle mechanics to meiotic progression and gamete quality.

Microtubule cytoskeleton organization covers the nucleation, growth, stabilization, severing and spatial arrangement of microtubules and the proteins that decorate them. It underlies mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation, centriole and centrosome duplication, cilium and sperm flagellum construction, neuronal polarity and axonal transport, and epithelial cell shape. Tubulin isotypes are polymerized from gamma-tubulin ring complexes at centrosomes, then tuned by plus-end trackers, minus-end CAMSAP proteins, kinesins and cytoplasmic dynein, katanin and spastin severing enzymes, and tubulin tyrosine ligase and acetylation or deacetylation activities that write the tubulin code. Mitotic kinases such as AURKA and PLK1 with TPX2 and the augmin complex direct spindle microtubules, while kinetochore and dynein adaptors couple them to chromosomes and cargo. Defects cause microcephaly, ciliopathies and primary ciliary dyskinesia, male infertility, lissencephaly and tubulinopathies, and shape the response to antimitotic drugs.

Every round of pre-mRNA splicing consumes a U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP, and this assembly route rebuilds it so the spliceosome can act again on the next intron. It matters because intron removal is required for essentially all protein-coding gene expression, and because the pathway serves both the major spliceosome and the minor, U12-dependent one that uses U4atac, U6atac and their snRNP partners. Base-paired U4 and U6 snRNAs released from a disassembled spliceosome are reannealed with help from a recycling factor, Sm and LSm protein rings stabilise the snRNAs, and U5 with its scaffolding components PRPF8, EFTUD2 and the BRR2 helicase SNRNP200 joins to complete the particle, aided by PRPF3, PRPF4, PRPF6, PRPF31 and assembly chaperones such as AAR2 and TSSC4. Mutations in several of these proteins cause retinitis pigmentosa, and U4atac defects underlie severe developmental syndromes.

Nearly every human protein-coding transcript must have its introns removed, and this is the stepwise construction of the machine that does it. Small nuclear RNAs (U1, U2 and the minor-class U11/U12/U4atac/U6atac) are packaged with a seven-membered Sm core ring assembled by the SMN complex, then recruited to a pre-mRNA in an ordered series: branch-point and 3' splice site recognition by SF1, U2AF2 and the U2-associated SF3A and SF3B subcomplexes, followed by delivery of the tri-snRNP and DEAD-box helicase-driven rearrangements that create the catalytic center. SR proteins and their SRPK kinases, CELF and PTB-family regulators, and LUC7L paralogs bias which sites are chosen, linking assembly to alternative splicing. Failure is consequential: SMN1 loss causes spinal muscular atrophy, SF3B1 and ZRSR2 mutations drive myelodysplastic syndromes, and minor-spliceosome snRNA defects cause developmental syndromes.

Allantoin metabolism sits at the far end of purine catabolism, where the nitrogen-rich rings of adenine and guanine nucleotides are dismantled for disposal. The upstream steps are the ones that matter most in human tissue: cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases strip phosphate from nucleoside monophosphates, purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves the resulting nucleosides to free bases, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase performs the two oxidations that yield urate. In most mammals urate is oxidised further and degraded through allantoin to allantoate and urea, but humans have lost functional urate oxidase, so urate is the excreted end product and the downstream allantoin-handling enzymes are vestigial. Failure of this route is clinically familiar: purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency causes combined immunodeficiency, and excess flux through xanthine oxidase drives hyperuricaemia and gout, the reason that enzyme is a drug target. Nucleotide salvage and deoxynucleotide turnover feed the same steps.

Mitochondria continually divide, and this fission machinery splits one mitochondrion into separate compartments, which lets the network be partitioned during cell division, distributed along cytoskeletal tracks to where ATP and calcium buffering are needed, and pruned of damaged segments for mitophagy. The central event is recruitment of the cytosolic GTPase DRP1 to the outer membrane by receptors including MFF, FIS1 and the MID49/MID51 adaptors, followed by constriction and scission at sites pre-marked by ER contacts and actin polymerization through INF2 and the SPIRE1/MYO19 machinery. Quality-control kinases and ligases such as PINK1, parkin and MARCHF5 couple fission to the removal of depolarized mitochondria, while OPA1 governs the opposing fusion and cristae state. Imbalance here drives neurodegeneration, peripheral neuropathy caused by GDAP1 mutation, and lethal encephalopathy from defective DRP1.

Peptidoglycan is a bacterial cell wall polymer that animals do not make but must detect and degrade, and this peptidoglycan metabolic process covers the host enzymes and receptors that do so. It is a component of innate antimicrobial defence at epithelial and mucosal surfaces, in secretions such as saliva, sweat and gut mucus, and in neutrophil granules, and it also shapes the commensal microbiota. The g-type lysozyme-like proteins hydrolyse the glycan backbone between N-acetylmuramic acid and N-acetylglucosamine, lysing bacteria directly. The peptidoglycan recognition proteins bind muropeptides; one of them, PGLYRP2, is an N-acetylmuramoyl-L-alanine amidase that cleaves the peptide stem from the sugar chain and thereby limits the inflammatory signalling that free peptidoglycan fragments would otherwise drive, while the others kill bacteria and modulate host responses. Loss of this activity is associated with altered susceptibility to infection and with inflammatory disease of the skin and intestine.

Cells store and export sugar in polymeric form, and this is the biosynthetic machinery that builds those polysaccharides. The dominant theme is glycogen: glycogenin self-glucosylates to prime a chain, glycogen synthase extends it from UDP-glucose supplied by UGP2 and phosphoglucomutase, and a branching enzyme introduces the alpha-1,6 branch points that make the granule soluble and rapidly mobilizable. Control is hormonal and reciprocal — insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT inactivates GSK3 and directs PP1 to glycogen via the PPP1R3 targeting subunits, dephosphorylating and switching on synthase. Laforin and malin restrict aberrant branching, and their loss causes the polyglucosan inclusions of Lafora disease, while synthase and branching enzyme defects cause glycogen storage disease. Related activities build extracellular polysaccharides, including hyaluronan synthases and the EXT heparan sulfate copolymerases.

Breaking long sugar polymers back down into usable monosaccharides is how cells and whole organisms draw on stored fuel and digest dietary carbohydrate. This polysaccharide catabolic process is dominated by glycogen mobilisation: phosphorylases in muscle, liver and brain cleave glucose units from the polymer, a debranching enzyme handles the branch points, phosphoglucomutase and phosphorylase kinase subunits complete and control the route, and hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase releases free glucose to the blood under hormonal direction from insulin and pituitary-derived peptides. A second, lysosomal arm uses acid alpha-glucosidase together with a glycogen-binding receptor and core autophagy machinery to deliver glycogen for degradation, while intestinal maltase-glucoamylase and chitinases act on dietary and environmental polysaccharides. Loss of individual steps produces the glycogen storage diseases, with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly or exercise intolerance depending on which tissue's enzyme fails.

mitotic cell cycle is the ordered program by which a somatic cell duplicates its genome and divides it equally between two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M. It underlies all tissue growth, renewal and repair, and its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer, while errors in chromosome partitioning generate aneuploidy. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F switch, and made irreversible by ubiquitin-mediated destruction through the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases. Aurora and Polo kinases, the gamma-tubulin ring complex and kinetochore components including the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes build and correct the spindle, with the spindle assembly checkpoint holding anaphase until attachment is complete. Cohesin and condensin shape the chromosomes, ESCRT machinery severs the midbody, and ATM/ATR damage checkpoints impose delay when replication or DNA integrity is compromised.

Cell proliferation depends on an ordered progression through the mitotic cell cycle — G1, S, G2 and M — in which the genome is replicated once and then partitioned equally into two daughter cells. The programme is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27 and by the retinoblastoma–E2F switch that licenses S-phase entry, and reset by ubiquitin-mediated destruction of cyclins and securin through the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases. Origin licensing by MCM proteins, checkpoint kinases responding to DNA damage or replication stress, kinetochore and spindle assembly checkpoint components, condensin and cohesin, centrosomal and microtubule machinery, and ESCRT-dependent abscission at the cleavage furrow each govern a distinct step. Loss of these controls produces aneuploidy, genome instability and unchecked growth, which is why the pathway is central to cancer and to development.

Mitotic cytokinesis is the final step of cell division, physically splitting one cell's cytoplasm into two daughters after the chromosomes have separated; when it fails, cells become binucleate and tetraploid, a route to genome instability and tumorigenesis. Position is set by the central spindle and the chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B, INCENP, survivin and borealin, which restrict the RhoA activator ECT2 and its partner centralspindlin to the cell equator. Active RhoA, with ROCK kinases, anillin, septins and non-muscle myosin, builds and constricts the actomyosin ring, while Rab11- and exocyst-dependent vesicle delivery supplies membrane to the furrow. The residual intercellular bridge is resolved at the midbody, where CEP55 recruits ALIX and ESCRT-III subunits and the VPS4 ATPases to sever the membrane, with spastin clearing residual microtubules. Abscission timing is checked by the Aurora B-CHMP4C pathway when chromatin lags in the bridge.

Most cytoplasmic mRNAs are destroyed by first trimming their poly(A) tail, and this deadenylation-dependent decay route sets how long a transcript survives and therefore how much protein it makes. It is the main way cells shut off inflammatory cytokine, cell-cycle and developmental messages after they are no longer needed; its failure leaves unstable transcripts persisting, a defect linked to autoimmunity and oncogenic overexpression. Shortening proceeds in two stages, an initial PAN2-PAN3 trim followed by the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose CNOT6/CNOT7 nuclease modules are recruited by sequence-specific factors: AU-rich element binders such as ZFP36 and its paralogues, constitutive decay element binders RC3H1/RC3H2, and miRNA-loaded AGO2 with TNRC6 scaffolds. The stripped body is then capped for destruction by the LSM1-7 ring, PATL1 and DDX6, decapped by DCP2 with EDC4, and degraded 5' to 3' by XRN1 or from the 3' end by the exosome. Much of this occurs in P-bodies.

The lifespan of a cytoplasmic mRNA is largely set by how fast its poly(A) tail is trimmed, and poly(A) tail shortening of nuclear-transcribed mRNAs is the committing step that silences a transcript and hands it on to decapping and decay. This is how cells switch off inflammatory and proliferative messages on schedule, and how translational timing is imposed during oocyte maturation and early development; loss of control leaves cytokine and cell-cycle transcripts inappropriately stable. Two deadenylase systems do most of the work: the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, built around the CNOT1 scaffold with CNOT7/CNOT8 and CNOT6/CNOT6L nuclease modules, and the PAN2-PAN3 pair that performs earlier, poly(A)-binding-protein-dependent trimming, with PARN acting on selected targets. Sequence-specific recruiters give the process its selectivity: AU-rich-element proteins of the ZFP36 family, BTG/TOB antiproliferative factors, Smaug-like repressors, and microRNA-loaded Argonaute with TNRC6 partners.

As cisternae mature and move forward through the Golgi stack, resident enzymes and membrane components must be retrieved and returned to earlier compartments; this intra-Golgi retrograde recycling, carried out by COP I vesicles, is what keeps each cisterna's glycosylation machinery in place. Without it, glycosyltransferases and nucleotide-sugar transporters are lost to the secretory flow and glycans on secreted and surface proteins are truncated or abnormal, the basis of the congenital disorders of glycosylation caused by mutations in the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex. The eight COG subunits form a tethering complex, organized as two lobes, that captures incoming retrograde vesicles at the Golgi membrane and couples them to SNARE-mediated fusion, while a golgin coiled-coil protein contributes to vesicle capture and stack architecture. The pathway therefore sustains Golgi enzyme compartmentalization, cisternal identity and overall Golgi structure.

Cells continuously encounter superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants from respiration, inflammation and drug metabolism, and the response to reactive oxygen species is how they sense that burden and adjust to it. The immediate work is enzymatic disposal and thiol maintenance: superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space, catalase, glutathione peroxidase, peroxiredoxins and the thioredoxin system. Transcriptional arms follow, with NFE2L2 driving antioxidant and detoxification genes such as HMOX1 and NQO1, FOXO3 and SIRT1 tuning stress resistance, and HIF1A linking oxidant signals to hypoxic adaptation. Stress-activated kinases, mitochondrial quality control through PINK1 and BNIP3, and DNA repair activities including OGG1 and ATM handle damage that escapes scavenging; when the load exceeds them, apoptosis or necroptosis ensues. Chronic imbalance underlies neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, vascular disease and ageing phenotypes.

response to oxygen radical is the set of cellular reactions triggered by superoxide, hydroxyl and related free-radical species, allowing cells to survive the unavoidable leakage of partially reduced oxygen from respiration, phagocyte oxidases and xenobiotic metabolism. When it fails, radicals oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA, driving vascular disease, neurodegeneration and premature senescence. Detoxification is handled by the superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondrion and extracellular space, with copper delivery by CCS and ATP7A, downstream peroxide removal by peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin reductase, and quinone handling by NQO1. Transcriptional adaptation runs largely through NFE2L2, which induces antioxidant and detoxifying enzymes, while PARK7 senses oxidative damage and ERCC6 links the response to repair of oxidised DNA lesions. Uncoupling proteins and endothelial nitric oxide synthase with its GCH1-dependent cofactor tie redox tone to mitochondrial proton leak and vascular signalling.

Cells detect and respond to oxygen radicals such as superoxide and hydroxyl radical, mounting a defence that limits damage to lipids, proteins and DNA and keeps redox-sensitive signalling within a usable range. The response matters because unchecked radical flux drives atherosclerosis, neurodegeneration and ageing phenotypes, and because motor neuron disease follows from mutation of superoxide dismutase. Three superoxide dismutases dispose of superoxide in cytosol, mitochondrial matrix and extracellular space, with a dedicated copper chaperone loading the cytosolic enzyme; peroxiredoxins and mitochondrial thioredoxin reductase then clear the resulting peroxide. The transcription factor NFE2L2 induces detoxifying enzymes including NQO1, while uncoupling proteins lower mitochondrial radical production, metallothionein and globins buffer metals and oxygen, and GCH1 and NOS3 tie the response to nitric oxide and vascular tone. DNA repair and PARP-linked components handle the oxidative lesions that escape.

Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases are switched on by attachment of the ubiquitin-like modifier NEDD8 and reset by its removal, and protein deneddylation is that removal step. It matters because cullin ligases would otherwise remain locked in a single substrate-loaded state; cyclical deneddylation allows exchange of substrate receptors so that a cell can retarget its degradation machinery as cell cycle regulators, transcription factors and damaged proteins come and go. The bulk of the activity resides in the COP9 signalosome, an eight-subunit complex whose COPS5 subunit carries the metalloprotease active site while the other subunits, including COPS2, GPS1 and the paralogous COPS7A and COPS7B, form the scaffold. A separate isopeptidase, SENP8, strips NEDD8 from cullins and other substrates. Loss of this control destabilises ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis, with consequences for proliferation, DNA damage responses and development.</br>

Trans-splicing joins a short spliced leader (SL) exon, donated from a separate small RNA, onto the 5' end of a pre-mRNA, and the reaction begins when the SL RNP docks with the U4/U6-U5 tri-snRNP to make a quadruple particle. This assembly step is the trans-splicing counterpart of the tri-snRNP recruitment that builds a conventional spliceosome, and it determines whether the leader exon can later be transferred to an acceptor transcript. The U-rich small nuclear RNAs listed here supply the structural core: U4 and U6 are held in a base-paired duplex that must be unwound for catalysis, U5 tethers exon sequence across the splice junction, and pairing between U6 and the SL RNA helps position the 5' splice site. The RNAs themselves, not proteins, provide the recognition and catalytic scaffold on which nuclear pre-mRNA processing depends.

Removing introns from precursor mRNA by two sequential transesterification reactions is the step that turns a primary transcript into a translatable message, and alternative choices of splice site multiply the protein output of a limited gene count. The spliceosome carries this out: U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 snRNAs with their Sm and LSm cores, the SF3A/SF3B branch-point recognition complexes, U2AF and SF1 at the 3' splice site, the DEAD/DEAH-box helicases that drive conformational rearrangements, the Prp19/CDC5L complex that activates the catalytic centre, and SLU7 and PRPF18 for exon ligation. SR proteins and hnRNPs bias site selection, SRPK and CLK kinases tune them, the SMN-Gemin machinery assembles snRNPs, and a minor spliceosome with U11/U12 handles rare introns. Deposition of the exon junction complex links splicing to export and nonsense-mediated decay. Mutations here cause retinitis pigmentosa, spinal muscular atrophy and myelodysplastic syndromes.

Some tRNA precursors carry an intron that must be excised before the tRNA can be charged and used in translation, and this step is the recognition and cleavage half of that process. The tRNA splicing endonuclease, a heterotetramer of two catalytic subunits and two structural ones, reads the tertiary fold of the precursor rather than a sequence motif, measuring the intron against the mature domain of the tRNA, then cuts precisely at both the 5' and 3' splice sites to release the intron and leave exon halves for a downstream ligation step. The associated RNA kinase links the endonuclease to broader RNA end-processing. Loss of endonuclease subunit function causes pontocerebellar hypoplasia, a severe inherited neurodegenerative disorder, showing how dependent developing neurons are on an intact tRNA maturation pathway.

A single gene can yield many proteins because the spliceosome does not always join the same exons, and alternative splicing is the regulated choice of which exons are kept. It multiplies proteome diversity from a limited gene count and defines tissue identity: neuron-specific isoform programmes, muscle sarcomere and ion channel variants, and epithelial versus mesenchymal states all depend on it. Sequence-specific RNA-binding regulators bind enhancer and silencer elements near splice sites to promote or block their recognition, with SR proteins and hnRNPs acting as broadly opposing families and tissue-restricted factors such as NOVA, RBFOX, CELF, PTBP1 and RBM20 setting particular exon choices; kinases and exon junction-associated components couple the decision to signalling and to downstream mRNA fate. Mutation or misregulation of these factors causes cardiomyopathy, neurodevelopmental disorders and aberrant isoform switching in cancer.

Most human genes yield more than one mRNA, and the choice of which exons are kept is made by sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins that bias spliceosome assembly at competing splice sites. This regulation of alternative splicing expands proteome diversity and sets tissue identity: RBFOX and NOVA proteins and SRRM4 drive neuronal exon programmes, RBM20 and RBM24 shape sarcomere and cardiac transcripts such as titin, and CELF and PTBP1 proteins act antagonistically during muscle and neural differentiation. SR proteins and hnRNPs (SRSF1-SRSF7, HNRNPA1, HNRNPL, PTBP1) provide the general activator-repressor balance, with kinases like DYRK1A and the m6A reader YTHDC1 coupling signalling and RNA modification to splice-site selection. Loss or mutation of these regulators causes dilated cardiomyopathy, neurodevelopmental disease, and the splicing shifts seen in fragile X syndrome and cancer.

Before any pre-mRNA intron can be removed, the small nuclear ribonucleoproteins that recognise and excise it must themselves be built, and spliceosomal snRNP assembly is that construction programme. It supplies the U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 particles, plus their minor-spliceosome counterparts, on which essentially all nuclear gene expression depends; its failure is behind spinal muscular atrophy and inherited retinal degeneration. A methylosome containing PRMT5 with its partners symmetrically dimethylates Sm protein tails, and the SMN-Gemin complex then loads the Sm ring onto each snRNA, while Lsm proteins form the analogous ring on U6. Cap hypermethylation and nuclear import follow, with Cajal bodies marked by coilin serving as the maturation site. Tri-snRNP-specific factors such as PRPF31, PRPF6, PRPF8 and SART3 complete assembly and recycling after each round of splicing.

mRNA 3'-splice site recognition is the step in pre-mRNA splicing at which the spliceosome identifies the downstream end of an intron, fixing exactly where the exons will be joined. Accurate choice of this site determines the reading frame of the mature transcript and, through alternative selection of competing sites, which protein isoform a gene produces; errors generate frameshifted or intron-retaining messages and underlie splicing-driven disease. Branch point binding by SF1 together with the SF3A subunits of the U2 snRNP defines the intron's 3' region during early assembly, while SLU7 acts later to ensure the correct AG dinucleotide is used in the second transesterification. The same logic applies to the minor U12-type spliceosome acting on its rarer introns. This is part of nuclear mRNA maturation, upstream of export and translation.

Every intron must be located precisely before it can be removed, and recognition of the 3' end of the intron is how the assembling spliceosome fixes one of those boundaries. Errors here shift the reading frame or retain intronic sequence, so the fidelity of this step determines whether a transcript yields functional protein. In both the major U2-type and the minor U12-type systems, branch-point recognition by SF1 together with the U2 snRNP-associated SF3A complex (SF3A1, SF3A2, SF3A3) commits the intron 3' region to splicing, while SLU7 acts later to ensure the correct 3'-splice site is selected during the second catalytic step. This branch-site and 3'-site selection is also where regulated alternative splicing operates, expanding proteome diversity; mutations in these components are associated with myelodysplastic syndromes and other splicing-factor diseases.

Before a spliceosome can cut an intron out of a pre-mRNA, it must remodel itself: the assembled particle is catalytically inert and only becomes an active ribozyme after a series of choreographed rearrangements. This activation step underlies accurate splicing of nearly every human transcript, and mutations in its components cause retinitis pigmentosa, craniofacial disorders such as mandibulofacial dysostosis, and myelodysplastic syndromes. ATP-dependent RNA helicases including SNRNP200 and DDX23 unwind U4 from U6 so that U6 can pair with U2 and the 5' splice site, releasing the U4/U6 proteins PRPF3, PRPF4 and PRPF31 while the tri-snRNP scaffold PRPF8 and EFTUD2 position the catalytic RNA core. SF3B subunits occlude the branch point until displacement frees it for attack, and Sm proteins hold the snRNPs together throughout. The same machinery governs branch-site selection, making it a point of control over alternative splicing.

A minority of introns are removed not by the spliceosome but by a protein endonuclease that cuts at both splice sites and a ligase that seals the exons, the route used for intron-containing pre-tRNAs and for the unconventional cytoplasmic splicing of XBP1 mRNA. This chemistry is what makes many tRNAs translatable and what switches on the transcription factor arm of the unfolded protein response when misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum. A four-subunit endonuclease of TSEN2, TSEN34, TSEN15 and TSEN54 recognises the folded substrate and cleaves it; the IRE1 endoribonuclease ERN1 performs the equivalent cut on XBP1; and the RTCB-containing ligase complex, with DDX1, FAM98A/B and RTRAF, joins the exon halves, with kinase and phosphotransferase activities handling the terminal phosphates. Mutations in the endonuclease subunits cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia, tying tRNA maturation to neuronal survival.

Splicing begins with a decision about where an intron starts, and this pathway covers recognition of the 5'-splice site by the earliest components of the assembling spliceosome. Accurate marking of that boundary determines which exons are joined, sets the reading frame of the mature message, and underlies the alternative splicing that diversifies proteomes; errors at donor sites are a common route by which point mutations cause disease. The work is done largely by base pairing between the pre-mRNA and the U1 snRNA, present here as multiple U1 gene copies and variants, together with the U1-specific protein SNRPC and the U1-associated factor PRPF39. SR proteins such as SRSF1 bind exonic sequences and help commit nearby donor sites for use. Minor-class snRNAs, including U11 and the U4atac and U6atac species, provide the parallel recognition system for the rare U12-type introns.

Autophagy of mitochondrion is the selective clearance of mitochondria by the autophagy machinery, the quality-control system that removes organelles that have become depolarised, damaged, or surplus to requirement. It sets mitochondrial number during erythrocyte and cardiomyocyte maturation, limits release of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and DNA, and its failure underlies recessive Parkinson disease through loss of PINK1 or the ubiquitin ligase parkin. Damage-sensing occurs on the organelle itself: PINK1 accumulates on unimported precursors, parkin ubiquitinates outer-membrane proteins, and receptors including BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1, FKBP8 and BCL2L13 recruit LC3 and GABARAP family adaptors, with OPTN and SQSTM1 bridging ubiquitin to nascent membrane. Downstream steps use the general core machinery -- ULK1 with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG14-containing PI3K complex, WIPI and ATG9 lipid delivery, and the ATG7-ATG5-ATG12 conjugation cascade -- to build the engulfing autophagosome for lysosomal degradation. USP30 opposes the process.

Cells dispose of damaged or surplus mitochondria by wrapping them in autophagosomes and delivering them to lysosomes for degradation, the quality-control route known as mitophagy. It limits release of reactive oxygen species and apoptogenic factors, adjusts mitochondrial mass during differentiation and metabolic change, and clears paternal mitochondria and erythroid mitochondria during maturation. Loss of this clearance underlies recessive Parkinson disease, where the kinase PINK1 accumulates on depolarized outer membranes and activates the ubiquitin ligase parkin, tagging substrates such as VDAC1 and mitofusin for recognition by receptors including optineurin and SQSTM1; USP30 opposes this by removing ubiquitin. Receptor-mediated routes act independently of ubiquitin, with BNIP3, BNIP3L/NIX, FUNDC1 and BCL2L13 binding LC3 and GABARAP directly. Downstream, the ULK1 kinase complex, BECN1-ATG14 lipid kinase machinery, WIPI and ATG2 proteins and the ATG5-ATG12-ATG7 conjugation system build the engulfing membrane.

Mitophagy is the quality-control route by which whole mitochondria are captured in autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes, letting cells cull organelles that are depolarised, damaged, or simply surplus. It sets mitochondrial number during reticulocyte maturation and after metabolic remodelling, and its failure allows damaged organelles to accumulate and leak reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial DNA, a defect central to autosomal recessive Parkinson disease. The best-defined arm is ubiquitin-driven: the kinase PINK1 accumulates on depolarised outer membranes, activates the ligase Parkin, and the resulting ubiquitin chains recruit OPTN and SQSTM1, with USP30 opposing the mark. Receptor-mediated arms act independently, through BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1, BCL2L13 and inner-membrane prohibitin, binding LC3 and GABARAP directly. Core autophagy machinery, ULK1 initiation, ATG conjugation, and fission by DNM1L then execute engulfment, tying this pathway to hypoxia, iron handling and metabolic reprogramming.

Mitochondria that are damaged, depolarised or simply surplus are removed by mitophagy, a selective form of macroautophagy in which an individual organelle is captured in an autophagosome and delivered to lysosomes. This is how cells keep their respiratory network functional, how reticulocytes clear mitochondria during maturation, and how neurons limit oxidative damage; its failure underlies familial Parkinson disease. The best-characterised route begins with the kinase PINK1 accumulating on depolarised membranes and recruiting the ubiquitin ligase parkin, whose ubiquitin chains -- opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30 -- recruit receptors such as OPTN and SQSTM1 to bridge the organelle to ATG8-family proteins. Receptors embedded in the outer membrane, including BNIP3, BNIP3L and FUNDC1, provide ubiquitin-independent capture under hypoxia and during development. Downstream, the core autophagy initiation, elongation and lipidation machinery builds and closes the engulfing membrane.

Cells tune which genes they transcribe according to which fuel is available, and in mammals this carbon catabolite regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription is largely the glucose-sensing arm of hepatic and adipose metabolism. When glucose is abundant, its metabolites drive transcription of glycolytic and de novo lipogenic genes so that excess carbon is converted to fat rather than left to accumulate; blunting or overdriving this response contributes to hepatic steatosis, hypertriglyceridemia and the lipid abnormalities of insulin resistance. The carbohydrate-response element binding factor MLXIPL, partnered with MLX, and the upstream stimulatory factor USF1 occupy sugar-responsive promoters, while the acetyltransferase KAT2B and the coactivator NCOA1 remodel chromatin and bridge to the basal machinery. OGT adds O-GlcNAc to transcriptional regulators using UDP-GlcNAc derived from nutrient flux, making the modification itself a direct readout of carbon supply.

Ribosome production begins with a single long precursor transcript carrying the small subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large subunit rRNA in tandem, and that precursor must be cut apart before either subunit can mature. Cleavage within the first internal transcribed spacer is the step that physically separates the small subunit pathway from the 5.8S/large subunit pathway, committing each to its own assembly route in the nucleolus. The proteins involved are components of the small subunit processome and associated nucleolar factors — including UTP20, NOP14, FCF1, KRI1, RCL1 and NOP9 — which fold the pre-rRNA, position the endonucleolytic activity and coordinate cutting with assembly of early small subunit particles. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and cell growth, defects here cause nucleolar stress and underlie ribosomopathies.

Cleavage in ITS2 between 5.8S rRNA and LSU-rRNA of tricistronic rRNA transcript (SSU-rRNA, 5.8S rRNA, LSU-rRNA) is a step in making the large ribosomal subunit: the single polymerase I transcript carrying 18S, 5.8S and 28S sequences must be cut apart, and this reaction separates the 5.8S end from the 28S body by an endonucleolytic incision within the second internal transcribed spacer. Ribosome output, and therefore the cell's capacity to grow and proliferate, depends on it. The genes form the PELP1-TEX10-WDR18-LAS1L complex together with the SUMO protease SENP3 and the polynucleotide kinase NOL9, which prepare the cleaved ends for exonucleolytic trimming; the AAA-ATPase MDN1 and the PES1-BOP1-WDR12 module then drive nucleolar pre-60S maturation. Defects here stall pre-rRNA processing, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathy-like phenotypes.

Ribosomal RNA is transcribed as one long precursor carrying the small subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large subunit rRNA in tandem, and the spacers between them must be removed for functional ribosomes to be made. This step is the endonucleolytic cut inside internal transcribed spacer 2, which separates the 5.8S rRNA from the large subunit rRNA and commits the pre-60S particle to maturation; blocking it stalls large subunit assembly, triggers nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlies ribosomopathy-like growth defects. The genes here form the PELP1-TEX10-WDR18 nucleolar complex together with the SUMO protease SENP3, the endonuclease LAS1L paired with the polynucleotide kinase NOL9, the AAA-ATPase MDN1 and the pre-60S factor BOP1. Their coordination links spacer processing to nucleolar quality control and to the proliferative demand for new ribosomes.

Newly transcribed ribosomal RNA is chemically decorated before it can fold into a working ribosome, and 2'-O-methylation of its ribose sugars is one of the most abundant of these modifications. The methyl marks stabilise rRNA folding, guide processing of the precursor transcript, and tune the accuracy and efficiency with which the finished ribosome decodes mRNA; altered methylation patterns change translation of specific transcripts and are seen in cancer and in ribosomopathies. The reaction is carried out by fibrillarin-type methyltransferases acting within box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complexes, in which NOP56, NOP58 and the 15.5K protein encoded by SNU13 assemble around a guide snoRNA that base-pairs with the target site to select the nucleotide to be modified. A parallel set of mitochondrial enzymes methylates the mitoribosomal large subunit rRNA, linking this chemistry to both nucleolar and mitochondrial ribosome assembly.

Ribosomal RNA is chemically decorated as ribosomes are built, and isomerization of uridine to pseudouridine is the most abundant of those modifications, stabilizing rRNA folding and tuning the decoding and peptidyl transferase centers so that translation is accurate and efficient. In the enzyme-directed route, a standalone pseudouridine synthase recognizes its own target site in the rRNA rather than being positioned by a base-pairing guide RNA, which distinguishes it from the small nucleolar RNA-dependent machinery. The RPUSD family members contribute such site-specific activity in the nucleolus and, for at least one of them, on mitochondrial ribosomal RNA, linking this chemistry to mitochondrial translation as well as cytoplasmic ribosome assembly. TSR3 acts downstream of one such modified residue in 18S rRNA, adding an aminocarboxypropyl group during late small-subunit maturation. Defects in rRNA pseudouridylation, notably through DKC1, impair ribosome function and cause bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition.

The large ribosomal subunit carries a short 5.8S rRNA alongside 28S, and this pathway covers the trimming of its precursor into the mature species during ribosome biogenesis in the nucleolus. Ribosome output sets the cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth, and defects in these processing steps cause nucleolar stress, p53 stabilisation and the ribosomopathy phenotypes of bone marrow failure and skeletal defects. Mechanistically, internal transcribed spacer 2 is cleaved and the resulting extension is shortened from the 3' end by the exosome complex, whose subunits and catalytic partners are prominent here, with the RNA helicase MTREX and the exonuclease EXOSC10 supplying processivity and specificity. A pre-60S module including PES1, BOP1 and WDR12 organises the intermediate particles, while endonucleolytic and kinase-associated activities such as LAS1L and NOL9 act at the spacer cleavage site.
