Ribosome production begins with a single long polymerase I transcript carrying the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs in tandem, and this pathway covers the cleavage and folding steps that release mature small subunit rRNA from that tricistronic precursor. It sets the cell's capacity for protein synthesis, and its disruption stalls 40S production, triggers nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlies ribosomopathies and craniofacial and growth defects. Much of the work is done by a large nucleolar particle assembled on the 5' end of the pre-rRNA, including UTP-family subunits, PWP2, WDR43, TBL3 and HEATR1, which organises cleavage at the 5' external and first internal spacer sites. RNA helicases such as DHX37, the endonuclease-like components FCF1 and UTP23, RCL1 and RRP36 act at specific cut sites, while TSR1 and TSR2 accompany pre-40S particles and small subunit proteins including RPS8, RPS16 and RPS19 are incorporated as maturation proceeds toward the cytoplasm.

Ribosome biogenesis begins with a single long polymerase I transcript carrying the small subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large subunit rRNA in tandem, and this pathway covers the cleavage, trimming and modification steps that release and mature the 28S large subunit rRNA from that tricistronic precursor. Its output is the catalytic core of the 60S subunit, so a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth depends on it, and defects in these nucleolar factors cause ribosomopathy-like phenotypes and are exploited by proliferating tumour cells. Mechanistically it is carried out in the nucleolus by the PELP1-TEX10-WDR18-SENP3 complex, the PeBoW module of PES1, BOP1 and WDR12, endonuclease and kinase activities in LAS1L and NOL9 that process the internal spacer, RNA helicases and GTPases such as DDX18 and GTPBP4, the 2'-O-methyltransferase FTSJ3, and assembly factors that load early large subunit proteins.

Ribosomes begin as a single polymerase I transcript carrying the small-subunit rRNA, 5.8S rRNA and large-subunit rRNA in tandem, and this pathway covers the cuts and trims that release a mature 5.8S species for the large subunit. It matters because 5.8S processing is a checkpoint on ribosome supply and therefore on cell growth; defects cause nucleolar stress, p53 stabilisation and ribosomopathy-like phenotypes, and several components are amplified in proliferating tumours. Internal transcribed spacers are cleaved endonucleolytically and then shortened by 3'-to-5' exonucleases, with the RNA exosome and its catalytic subunit EXOSC10 performing the final trimming. The PeBoW complex (PES1, BOP1, WDR12) and the Rix1-type module with LAS1L, NOL9 and SENP3 act on ITS2 removal, while the huge AAA-ATPase MDN1 drives remodelling and release of assembly factors from pre-60S particles in the nucleolus.

Ribosome assembly requires that each rRNA be trimmed to an exact length, and this step finishes the 3' end of 5.8S rRNA after it is released from the long precursor transcript that carries the small-subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large-subunit rRNA in tandem. Endonucleolytic cuts leave 5.8S with extra nucleotides at its 3' end, and 3'-to-5' exonucleases remove them to yield the mature species incorporated into the large ribosomal subunit. Most of the activity here comes from the RNA exosome, whose core subunits form a barrel that channels substrate to the catalytic subunit EXOSC10, assisted by dedicated 3' exonucleases of the ERI family. Because the exosome also degrades aberrant transcripts, this trimming doubles as quality control: incomplete processing yields extended 5.8S forms, stalls subunit maturation, and underlies ribosomopathy-like defects in growth and protein synthesis capacity.

Ribosome production requires the 28S/5.8S ribosomal RNAs of the large subunit to be cut out of a long polycistronic precursor, chemically modified and folded, and maturation of LSU-rRNA is the set of nucleolar steps that accomplish this. Its output sets the cell's capacity for protein synthesis, which is why the machinery is upregulated in growing and transformed cells and why defects in it cause ribosomopathies with bone marrow failure and craniofacial phenotypes. Members include the PeBoW complex (PES1, BOP1, WDR12) and the related NOL9-LAS1L-PELP1-TEX10-SENP3 module that processes internal transcribed spacer 2, RNA helicases such as DDX18 and DDX55 that remodel pre-rRNA, methyltransferases including FTSJ3 and NOP2, GTPases such as GTPBP4, and assembly factors RPF1, RPF2 and EIF6 that load ribosomal proteins and block premature subunit joining. Failure stalls pre-60S particles and triggers nucleolar stress signalling to p53.

Ribosome production begins with a single long precursor RNA carrying the small-subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large-subunit rRNA in tandem, and endonucleolytic cleavage of this tricistronic transcript is how those three mature species are separated from each other and from the spacers between them. Cutting must be accurate and ordered, because each incision commits the precursor to either the small-subunit or the large-subunit assembly route; errors stall ribosome biogenesis, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathies. The genes here are nucleolar processing factors rather than metabolic enzymes: components of the U3-associated small-subunit processome such as UTP20, UTP23, NOP14 and BMS1, the endonuclease-bearing LAS1L-NOL9 module that cleaves within internal transcribed spacer 2 and phosphorylates the resulting end, the SUMO protease SENP3, and the AAA-ATPase MDN1 that drives assembly-intermediate remodelling.

Ribosome production begins with a single long polymerase I transcript carrying the small-subunit rRNA, 5.8S and the large-subunit rRNA separated by spacers, and the first trimming events remove the leader ahead of the 18S sequence. Endonucleolytic cleavage in the 5' external transcribed spacer of this tricistronic precursor is an early, conserved checkpoint that commits the transcript to maturation and sets up later cuts that separate the small- and large-subunit branches; failure stalls 18S production and triggers nucleolar stress and p53 activation. The proteins involved assemble into the small-subunit processome, a large nucleolar particle built on the nascent transcript around U3 snoRNA. Members such as FCF1, UTP23 and the atypical RNA cyclase-like protein RCL1 contribute to or license the cleavage itself, while NOP14, NOP9, TBL3 and UTP20 organise the particle. Defects in this machinery underlie ribosomopathies with growth and developmental consequences.

small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein complex assembly builds the box C/D and H/ACA particles that guide 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation of ribosomal RNA, and so determines whether a cell can make functional ribosomes at all. Assembly is not spontaneous: dedicated chaperones and assembly factors capture nascent core proteins before they meet RNA, with SHQ1 holding dyskerin and NAF1 placing it on H/ACA RNAs, while ZNHIT3, ZNHIT6 and NUFIP1 chaperone the box C/D core protein SNU13 onto its RNA. The AAA+ ATPases RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, together with PIH1D1 and the R2TP adaptor machinery, provide the energy-dependent remodelling that licenses these handovers. The same route supplies telomerase, which shares an H/ACA core. Loss of these factors impairs ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar function, and mutations in the pathway cause ribosomopathies and neurodevelopmental disease.

Small nucleolar RNAs do not work as bare transcripts; each must be loaded with a defined set of core proteins before it can guide modification or cleavage of ribosomal RNA, and snoRNP complex assembly is the chaperoned process that builds those particles. Because box C/D and box H/ACA snoRNPs carry out the 2'-O-methylation, pseudouridylation and pre-rRNA processing steps that precede ribosome maturation, a failure here limits ribosome production and cell growth, and telomerase — itself an H/ACA particle — depends on the same route. Dedicated assembly chaperones act on each class: SHQ1 and NAF1 hand off to H/ACA cores, while ZNHIT3, ZNHIT6 and NUFIP1 deliver C/D proteins. The R2TP machinery, comprising the RUVBL1–RUVBL2 AAA+ ATPase ring with PIH1D1 and its partners, provides the ATP-dependent remodelling that places proteins onto the RNA in the nucleolus.

Box C/D small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins are the guides that direct 2'-O-methylation of ribosomal RNA, and they must be built before they can act, so their assembly sets the pace of ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar function. The core proteins — a 15.5K-type RNA-binding subunit that recognises the box C/D motif, plus the fibrillarin methyltransferase and NOP56/NOP58 scaffold — do not load onto the snoRNA spontaneously. Instead the AAA+ ATPases RUVBL1 and RUVBL2, an adaptor of the R2TP class containing PIH1D1, and zinc-finger HIT proteins together with NUFIP1 act as a dedicated assembly chaperone system, holding immature protein–RNA intermediates and delivering subunits in order. Loss of these factors starves cells of methylation-competent guide particles and impairs ribosome maturation and growth; mutations in ZNHIT3 cause a severe developmental disorder, linking snoRNP construction to human disease.

Long noncoding RNAs can act after a transcript is made, pairing with or sequestering mRNAs and microRNAs to decide how much protein a gene actually yields. This lncRNA-mediated post-transcriptional gene silencing adds a layer of control on top of promoter regulation, and its members are frequently deregulated in cancer, where loss of a competing transcript releases a microRNA to suppress a tumour suppressor. Several mechanisms converge here: nuclear retention and sequestration of RNA-binding proteins, as in the paraspeckle scaffold NEAT1; competing endogenous RNA behaviour, illustrated by a PTEN pseudogene antisense transcript; and duplex-dependent decay routed through STAU1, which recognises double-stranded RNA structures and triggers degradation. The RNA-binding protein ELAVL1 links these transcripts to mRNA stability control, tying the pathway to proliferation, differentiation and stress responses.

Embryonic axis specification is how a ball of early cells acquires direction s anterior–posterior, dorsal–ventral and left–right s so that head, trunk and internal organs form in the right places and in the right order. Failure produces axis duplication, truncation, laterality defects and failed gastrulation, and milder disturbance underlies segmentation disorders of the vertebral column. Nodal/TGF-beta signalling through SMAD2 and SMAD4 with the coreceptor CRIPTO, and Wnt signalling through beta-catenin and Frizzled receptors, set up the primitive streak and mesoderm, with SMAD6 and CXXC4 acting as brakes on these same routes. Downstream transcription factors including TBXT, MESP1/2, TBX6 and LHX1 assign mesodermal identity, while RIPPLY1 and RIPPLY2 terminate that programme to define somite boundaries. Hedgehog reception, cilium-associated components and Tudor-domain germline factors tie patterning to left–right asymmetry and germ cell specification.

During meiosis, crossover intermediates pair strands from homologous chromosomes that are not identical in sequence, and meiotic mismatch repair is the machinery that recognises and corrects the resulting base-base mismatches, small insertion-deletion loops and stretches of heterology in heteroduplex DNA. Because correction can convert one allele to the other, it produces gene conversion and non-Mendelian segregation of alleles in the resulting gametes, and it also shapes how many crossovers form and where. The MutS-family recognition component MSH6 binds mismatched DNA, while MutL-family heterodimers built from MLH1 with MLH3, PMS2 or PMS1 provide the downstream nicking and processing activity; MLH1-MLH3 in particular is required to resolve recombination intermediates into mature crossovers. Loss of these functions causes chromosome mis-segregation, reduced fertility, and, in somatic tissue, the microsatellite instability underlying Lynch syndrome cancers.

Meiotic recombination leaves the two homologous chromosomes physically joined by branched DNA structures, and resolving those intermediates is what converts them into two intact molecules carrying exchanged genetic material. This step is what allows homologues to separate cleanly at the first meiotic division; without it chromosomes remain entangled or break, producing aneuploid gametes, and failures in the human genes involved are a recognised cause of infertility and azoospermia. Resolution depends on structure-selective nucleases and their scaffolds — MUS81 with its partners EME1 and EME2, ERCC4 and the SLX4 platform, plus the ANKLE1 endonuclease — while FANCM and the RMI1-containing complex channel intermediates toward non-crossover outcomes. MLH1 marks sites destined to mature into crossovers, meiosis-specific factors such as HFM1, SHOC1, MEIOB and TEX11 act earlier in strand exchange and crossover designation, and topoisomerases relieve the accompanying topological strain.

Telomere maintenance via recombination keeps chromosome ends long enough to be replicated and protected when telomerase is absent or insufficient, using homologous recombination to copy sequence from one telomere to another. This is the basis of the alternative lengthening of telomeres programme that roughly one in ten cancers uses to escape replicative senescence, and it also salvages ends that have shortened or become damaged in normal cells. RAD51 and its paralogues, with BRCA2 as the loader, invade a donor telomeric repeat; the SMC5/6 complex with the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase promotes recombination-dependent telomere clustering, while ERCC1-XRCC4 nucleolytic and XRCC1-dependent repair activities process the resulting joints. TERF2 restrains inappropriate recombination at intact ends, so the pathway sits at the interface of end protection, double-strand break repair and cellular immortalisation.

Chromosome ends shorten with every division, and when telomerase is absent or insufficient cells can instead copy sequence from another telomere by homologous recombination to keep ends long enough to be protected. This break-induced replication route is the basis of the alternative lengthening of telomeres programme used by a subset of cancers, and it also determines whether cells escape crisis or enter senescence when telomeres erode. Strand invasion and repair synthesis depend on RAD51 with its paralogues RAD51C and XRCC3 and the mediator BRCA2, while the RAD50-containing nuclease complex processes ends and the ERCC1-ERCC4 structure-specific endonuclease trims recombination intermediates. The SMC5/6 complex with the SUMO ligase NSMCE2 resolves and relocalises recombining telomeres, and shelterin's TERF2 normally suppresses this activity so that ends are not treated as double-strand breaks. Failure of the balance produces telomere fusions, rearrangements and genome instability.

Double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks are repaired accurately by copying an intact homologous sequence, and recombinational repair is the machinery that carries out that exchange of genetic material. It preserves genome stability in dividing cells, permits crossing over in meiosis, and underlies tumour suppression: loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or the RAD51 paralogues predisposes to breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer and creates the dependency exploited by PARP inhibitors. Breaks are sensed and signalled by ATM, CHEK1 and phosphorylated H2AX; the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease resects DNA ends, RPA coats the resulting single strand, and mediators load RAD51 (or meiotic DMC1) to form the invading filament. Helicases, structure-specific nucleases and the SMC5/6 complex resolve the resulting joint molecules, while chromatin remodellers, ubiquitin ligases and shieldin components determine whether a break is resected at all or instead sealed by end joining.

Break-induced replication rescues a double-strand break that has only one usable end, such as a collapsed replication fork or an eroded telomere, by using strand invasion into a homologous template to restart processive DNA synthesis that runs to the end of the chromosome. Without it a one-ended break cannot be sealed by conventional homologous recombination and the chromosome arm is lost. The gene complement here is essentially the replicative helicase machinery redeployed for repair: the MCM2-7 ring together with CDC45 and GINS subunits forms the CMG helicase, and CDC7 kinase licenses its activation, so the invading 3' end is extended by a bona fide replisome rather than by repair polymerases alone. The structure-specific endonuclease MUS81 resolves the branched intermediates that result. In cancers lacking telomerase, this route underlies alternative lengthening of telomeres, and its mutagenic side effects include template switching and loss of heterozygosity.

When both strands of DNA break, a cell must decide how to mend them, and the nucleolytic chewing back of the 5' strands is the step that commits the break to homologous recombination rather than end joining. The resulting 3' single-stranded tail is what RAD51 and its mediators coat to search for a sister chromatid template, so this processing determines repair fidelity and, with it, genome stability, chromosome integrity and resistance to radiation and crosslinking agents. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP (RBBP8) initiates short-range resection and activates ATM signalling; DNA2 and helicases including BLM and HELB extend or limit it; chromatin remodelling and ubiquitin conjugation by UBE2N-UBE2V2 and RNF138 tune access to the ends. The same machinery processes programmed meiotic breaks made by SPO11. Loss of these functions underlies cancer predisposition and hypersensitivity to DNA-damaging therapy.

DNA synthesis involved in DNA repair is the gap-filling step that finishes a repair reaction: once a broken 3' end has invaded a homologous duplex, a polymerase copies the intact template to restore the missing sequence. Without it, recombination intermediates cannot be completed, double-strand breaks persist, and cells accumulate the genomic instability that drives cancer and premature ageing syndromes. The genes cover the replicative machinery redeployed for repair — polymerase alpha, delta and epsilon subunits with the clamp loader — plus translesion polymerase eta for damaged templates, ribonucleotide reductase subunits that supply dNTP precursors, and the WRN helicase-exonuclease whose loss causes Werner syndrome. Meiotic recombination components such as SPATA22, SYCP1 and TEX12 tie the same synthesis step to crossover formation during gametogenesis, while SIRT1 and CDKN2D link it to cell cycle and chromatin control.

When a double-strand break is resected to leave a 3' single-stranded end, that end invades an intact homologous duplex and is extended by new DNA synthesis — the repair-associated synthesis step that converts a strand invasion intermediate into restored sequence. Without it, homologous recombination cannot be completed, breaks are shunted into error-prone end joining, and cells accumulate translocations and chromosome loss. The polymerases that carry out this extension include the replicative enzymes Pol delta and Pol epsilon with their clamp loader subunits, alongside the primase-associated Pol alpha and the translesion enzyme Pol eta; ribonucleotide reductase subunits supply the deoxynucleotide pools required. The RecQ helicase WRN and its interacting partner WRNIP1 process and stabilise recombination and stalled fork intermediates. Several members act in meiotic recombination, where the same synthesis chemistry generates crossovers during germ cell development.

Once DNA is replicated, the two copies of each chromosome must be held together, attached to opposite spindle poles, and then released simultaneously so that each daughter cell receives exactly one copy. Sister chromatid segregation is that process, and errors in it produce aneuploidy, micronuclei and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours and of miscarriage. Cohesin rings with their loader and the releasing factor WAPL keep sisters paired until separase cleaves the RAD21 subunit; condensin compacts the arms while topoisomerase II resolves catenanes. Kinetochore assembly on centromeric CENPA chromatin builds the NDC80 and SKA microtubule interface, and the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUB3) restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until every kinetochore is attached. Aurora B within the chromosomal passenger complex corrects faulty attachments, and kinesins, dynein and midbody components complete anaphase and cytokinetic abscission.

cell morphogenesis is the process by which a cell acquires and maintains its shape, size and polarity as it differentiates, and it is what distinguishes a neuron with a long axon from a hair cell with a stereocilia bundle or an epithelial cell with an apical surface. Without it tissues cannot be wired or organized, and defects produce cortical malformations, axon guidance disorders, hearing loss and neurodegeneration. The genes converge on remodelling of the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton: Rho-family GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, WAVE/Arp2/3 regulators, formins, cofilin and myosins, together with tubulins and MAPs that build and steer growth cones. Layered on top are the guidance and adhesion systems that tell a cell which way to grow — semaphorin-plexin, ephrin-Eph, netrin-DCC/UNC5, slit-Robo, cadherins, integrins and planar cell polarity components — plus transcription factors that specify shape as part of cell fate.

Cells acquire their characteristic size and shape during development, and this morphogenetic programme is what turns an unpolarised progenitor into a neuron with an axon and dendrites, an epithelial cell with an apical brush border, or a hair cell with an ordered stereocilium bundle. Actin and microtubule machinery does the building — actins, cofilin, formins, WAVE/Arp regulators, tubulins and the microtubule-associated proteins MAP2 and MAPT — while Rho-family GTPases such as RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 with their many GEFs, GAPs and PAK/ROCK effectors decide where protrusion and contraction occur. Guidance and adhesion cues including semaphorins with their plexin receptors, ephrins and Eph kinases, slits with Robo, netrins with DCC and UNC5, cadherins and integrins orient the process, and transcription factors plus Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog and neurotrophin signalling couple it to cell fate. Disruption underlies neurodevelopmental malformations, hereditary spastic paraplegia and syndromic deafness.

Cytokinesis is the final step of cell division, in which the cytoplasm and plasma membrane are physically split so that each daughter cell receives one genome and a working complement of organelles. Getting it wrong produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and chromosome instability, a route toward tumorigenesis, and its controlled incompletion is what creates the intercellular bridges of germ cell syncytia. Positional information from the anaphase spindle, delivered by the central spindle kinesin and its RhoGAP partner and by the aurora kinase-containing chromosomal passenger complex, activates RhoA to assemble an actomyosin ring; septin filaments, anillin and IQGAP proteins organise the furrow cortex. Rab11 and exocyst-directed vesicle traffic then feeds membrane to the midbody, where ESCRT components recruited by CEP55 and the VPS4 ATPases sever the last connection. Phosphatases, PLK1 and cullin-based ubiquitin ligases time each transition.

Cytokinesis is the final step of cell division, partitioning cytoplasm and plasma membrane so that each daughter cell receives one genome and a complete set of organelles; when it fails, cells become binucleate or tetraploid, a route to aneuploidy and tumorigenesis, and in male germ cells its deliberate incompleteness creates the intercellular bridges of the syncytium. RhoA, activated at the equator by the ECT2/RACGAP1 module, drives assembly and constriction of an actomyosin ring built from non-muscle myosin II, anilin and septin filaments, while kinesins and PRC1 organise the central spindle. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin times the events and monitors the furrow, and Rab11 vesicle traffic plus the exocyst deliver membrane to the cleavage site. Final abscission of the intercellular bridge depends on CEP55 recruiting ESCRT components, IST1 and VPS4 ATPases, with spastin severing the residual microtubules.

Every messenger RNA made in the nucleus is eventually destroyed, and the rate at which that happens sets how much protein a gene yields; the catabolism of nuclear-transcribed mRNAs is therefore as much a part of gene regulation as transcription is. It also serves quality control, clearing transcripts with premature stop codons, stalled ribosomes or no stop codon at all so that truncated and aberrant proteins are not made. Decay typically begins with shortening of the poly(A) tail by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 deadenylases, followed by removal of the cap by DCP2 with its activators and degradation by the 5'-to-3' exonuclease XRN1 or by the exosome with its helicase partners. Surveillance branches built on UPF1, UPF2 and SMG proteins recognise faulty translation termination, while miRNA-loaded Argonaute complexes, ZFP36 family AU-rich element binders and RNA-binding proteins target individual transcripts, tuning inflammatory and proliferative messages.

Mitochondrial gene expression produces long polycistronic transcripts, antisense RNAs and processing by-products, and the organelle must destroy them as fast as it makes them; mitochondrial RNA catabolism is that disposal arm, setting the steady-state level of each mitochondrially encoded mRNA, rRNA and tRNA and so the supply of respiratory chain subunits. The core activity is a degradosome in which the helicase SUPV3L1 unwinds structured and duplex RNA for the exoribonuclease PNPT1 to digest processively, with REXO2 clearing short oligonucleotide products and PDE12 trimming mRNA poly(A) tails to shorten transcript lifetimes. Opposing and shaping this turnover are RNA-binding stabilisers and granule components such as LRPPRC, SLIRP and GRSF1, which sequester or protect transcripts. Loss of balance leaves double-stranded mitochondrial RNA that escapes to the cytosol and triggers interferon responses, and underlies combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency and deafness phenotypes.

Mitochondria transcribe their own genome as long polycistronic RNAs, and the resulting mRNAs must be degraded as well as made if the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded there are to be produced in the right amounts. Turnover of mitochondrial mRNA sets transcript half-life and clears aberrant, antisense and double-stranded RNA species that would otherwise accumulate and, if released to the cytosol, trigger interferon responses. A degradosome built from the RNA helicase SUPV3L1 and the phosphorolytic exoribonuclease PNPT1 unwinds and digests these transcripts, while the LRPPRC-SLIRP complex binds and stabilises mature mRNAs and supports their polyadenylation, opposing decay; PDE12 trims poly(A) tails to modulate stability. Loss of LRPPRC causes a French-Canadian form of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, and PNPT1 mutations produce combined oxidative phosphorylation defects with deafness and neurological disease.

The thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA are made from a single polycistronic transcript, and mitochondrial RNA metabolism is what converts that transcript into usable mRNAs, rRNAs and tRNAs. Without it oxidative phosphorylation fails, which is why defects here cause encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis, deafness and cardiomyopathy. A dedicated polymerase with its transcription factors and elongation factor reads the genome; an endonuclease pair cleaves tRNA ends to release flanking mRNAs; then polyadenylation, CCA addition, and extensive tRNA and rRNA modification—methylation, pseudouridylation, thiolation, threonylcarbamoylation—mature the products. RNA-binding proteins including LRPPRC with SLIRP, GRSF1 and the FASTKD family stabilise transcripts and organise RNA granules, while exonucleases and a degradosome helicase set turnover rates. Mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge the tRNAs, coupling this processing directly to organellar translation and cellular energy supply.

regulation of mitochondrial RNA catabolic process controls how quickly transcripts made from the mitochondrial genome are destroyed, and thereby sets how much of each respiratory chain subunit a cell can build. Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic units from both strands, so degradation, not initiation, is the main determinant of steady-state mRNA levels and the means of clearing antisense and double-stranded byproducts that would otherwise leak into the cytosol and trigger interferon responses. The degradosome formed by the helicase SUPV3L1 with the exoribonuclease PNPT1 performs the turnover, while GRSF1 sequesters transcripts in RNA granules and the LRPPRC-SLIRP complex stabilises and polyadenylates mature mRNAs against it. Loss of this balance depletes specific mitochondrial mRNAs and causes oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, as in LRPPRC-linked Leigh syndrome.

Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, and the steady-state level of each mature transcript depends as much on how fast it is degraded as on how fast it is made; this pathway covers the control of that turnover of mitochondrially encoded RNA. It matters because the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by the organellar genome must be supplied in balance with nuclear-encoded partners, and because non-coding and antisense products of the same genome would otherwise accumulate and form RNA duplexes. Degradation activity resides in a helicase-exoribonuclease pair, SUPV3L1 with PNPT1, which forms the degradosome that resolves and digests aberrant and antisense species. GRSF1 melts structured transcripts within RNA granules, while LRPPRC with its partner SLIRP binds and stabilises mature mRNAs, protecting them from this machinery; loss of LRPPRC causes a French-Canadian form of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency.

The mitochondrial genome is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, and mitochondrial RNA processing is what converts them into usable mRNAs, tRNAs and rRNAs; without it the organelle cannot translate the thirteen subunits it contributes to the respiratory chain, and oxidative phosphorylation fails. Excision begins at the embedded tRNAs, cut at their 5' ends by a protein-only RNase P complex (PRORP with TRMT10C and HSD17B10) and at their 3' ends by ELAC2, after which TRNT1 adds CCA and polymerase MTPAP appends mRNA poly(A) tails. The transcripts are then chemically decorated by methyltransferases and pseudouridine synthases, and by modifiers such as MTO1 and GTPBP3 that build the wobble-base modifications tRNAs need for accurate codon reading. FASTK-family proteins and LRPPRC-SLIRP bind and stabilise specific mRNAs, while SUPV3L1 and PNPT1 degrade aberrant and antisense RNA. Mutations across these steps cause encephalomyopathies, deafness and cardiomyopathy.

Mitochondrial transcription produces long polycistronic precursors, and maturation of their 3' ends is what converts that continuous transcript into usable tRNAs, rRNAs and messengers. Without it, mitoribosomes lack the tRNAs and templates needed to translate the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded in the organelle, and the result is combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency. Punctuation at tRNA boundaries is performed by a ribonuclease that cuts precisely at the tRNA 3' side, working alongside the methyltransferase-containing complex with HSD17B10 and TRMT10C that also acts on the 5' side; CCA is then added to the tRNA end by TRNT1 for aminoacylation. Messenger 3' ends are extended by a mitochondrial poly(A) polymerase, while PNPT1 and the SUPV3L1 helicase together degrade aberrant and antisense transcripts, so end formation and surveillance are coupled. Mutations in these components cause sideroblastic anaemia, deafness and infantile mitochondrial disease.

Forming a mature 5' end is one of the first things that happens to a new transcript, and it determines whether the RNA is stable, translatable, and recognised as self. Nascent polymerase II transcripts receive a guanosine cap from the capping enzyme and cap methyltransferases, with additional 2'-O-methylation of the first transcribed nucleotides marking the message as endogenous and preventing innate immune sensing; the nuclear cap-binding complex then escorts the capped RNA through splicing and export. A separate branch cleaves 5' leaders from precursor tRNAs, carried out both by the RNase P ribonucleoprotein and by a protein-only mitochondrial enzyme acting with its methyltransferase and dehydrogenase partners. Further activities trim ribosomal RNA precursors, hypermethylate small nuclear and nucleolar RNA caps, and generate histone mRNA ends. Loss of these steps destabilises transcripts, impairs ribosome and tRNA maturation, and triggers interferon responses against the cell's own RNA.

rRNA 5'-end processing trims the precursor ribosomal RNA transcript to generate the exact 5' terminus of mature rRNA, a prerequisite for building functional ribosomes and therefore for all protein synthesis and cell growth. The genes here belong to the small subunit processome, the large nucleolar assembly that folds and cleaves the 47S/45S pre-rRNA en route to 18S rRNA. UTP20 and TBL3 are core processome scaffolds, NOP14 and NOP9 are RNA-binding factors that position cleavage sites, and ABT1 associates with the transcription and early processing machinery. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on proliferation, this step is a control point coupling nucleolar activity to growth signalling; defects impair 18S maturation, trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathies characterised by tissue-specific developmental failure.

Ribosome production begins with a long polycistronic rRNA precursor that must be cut and trimmed at defined points, and forming the mature 5' end of rRNA is one of those steps. The genes here act in the small-subunit processome, the large nucleolar assembly that folds and cleaves the 5' portion of the pre-rRNA destined for the 40S subunit. NOP14, NOP9, TBL3 and UTP20 are processome components that bind the nascent transcript and coordinate cleavage with assembly of early ribosomal proteins, while ABT1 contributes to the same nucleolar maturation events. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on cell growth, defects in these steps stall proliferation and provoke nucleolar stress signalling; comparable processome lesions in humans underlie ribosomopathies with growth and developmental consequences.

Where a gene sits inside the nucleus is part of how it is regulated, and this process anchors actively transcribed RNA polymerase II genes to the nuclear periphery in a manner that depends on their own transcription. Promoter elements, activators bound to them and sequences in the transcript's 3' end recruit the locus to the nuclear envelope, coupling gene positioning to mRNA synthesis and export. The genes here point to two contributing machines: structural nucleoporins of the nuclear pore scaffold, including NUP107, NUP133, NUP155 and NUP98, and the mRNA export factors RAE1 and PCID2, the latter a component of the TREX-2 complex that docks transcribing genes at pores. LDB1 adds a chromatin-looping transcriptional regulator. Peripheral tethering of this kind supports efficient export, transcriptional memory on reinduction, and the spatial organization of chromosomes relative to the envelope.

Cells and tissues respond to acidic chemical species -- amino acids, organic and inorganic acids, protons at the cell surface -- by reshaping metabolism, gene expression and excitability, and the response to acid chemical stimulus collects these adaptations. A large part of the gene complement is the amino acid sensing arm of mTORC1 signalling: Rag GTPases, the Ragulator subunits, the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 and the leucine and methionine sensors, together with Sestrins, CASTOR proteins and the GATOR/CUL3-based regulators that couple nutrient sufficiency to growth, translation and autophagy. Other members handle acid load and its consequences: ureagenesis enzymes such as CPS1 and ASS1, glutathione synthesis and NFE2L2-driven antioxidant defence, acid-sensitive ion channels and glycine, glutamate and GABA receptors, aquaporin-2 and vasopressin signalling in the kidney, and collagens and matrix metalloproteinases remodelling tissue under acidic stress. Failure of such sensing underlies disordered growth control, acidosis intolerance and inflammatory tissue damage.

Getting RNA polymerase II off the promoter and into productive elongation is a distinct step from assembling the initiation complex, and promoter clearance is the transition between them: the enzyme sheds initiation-only factors, escapes the promoter DNA, and adopts an elongation-competent conformation. How efficiently this happens sets how much of a gene's output is real message rather than abortive short transcripts, and it is a major control point for genes regulated at the level of paused polymerase. Much of the regulation is written on the polymerase C-terminal domain as phosphorylation: the PNUTS-PP1 phosphatase module, comprising a regulatory subunit with the catalytic phosphatase, TOX4 and WDR82, reverses CTD marks, while RPRD1A and RPRD1B read the phosphorylated CTD and scaffold these events. CDK11 kinases and the coactivator PC4 act at the initiation-to-elongation boundary, linking clearance to capping and to downstream RNA processing.

Ribosome production begins with the loading of RNA polymerase I onto rDNA promoters, and this assembly step sets how many ribosomes a cell can make. Because rRNA synthesis consumes much of a growing cell's transcriptional output, the rate of preinitiation complex formation is a direct readout of growth signalling, and it is suppressed during stress, quiescence and nucleolar disruption. Assembly is ordered: the HMG-box factor UBTF binds and bends promoter and upstream control element DNA, the SL1 complex of TBP with TAF1B and TAF1C is recruited to select the transcription start site, and RRN3 tethers polymerase I itself, here represented by the subunit POLR1E, to the promoter for the first nucleotide additions. Chromatin-directed components including BAZ2A and SWI/SNF subunits set how many rDNA repeats are available, silencing a fraction of copies. Dysregulation of this step accompanies hypertrophic growth and tumour cell proliferation.

Extrachromosomal circular DNA arises when a chromosomal segment is excised and its ends joined, most often by recombination between direct tandem repeats. The process is a recognised source of genome instability: circles made from telomeric repeats (t-circles) accompany telomere trimming and the recombination-based ALT pathway used by some cancers to maintain chromosome ends, while circular DNA elsewhere in the genome can amplify oncogenes or delete the region left behind. The genes here are the resection and resolution machinery that make such excision possible — the RecQ helicases BLM and WRN with the nucleases DNA2 and EXO1 to process ends, the SLX4 scaffold with its SLX1 and ERCC1 partners to cut branched joint molecules, RAD51 paralogue XRCC3 for strand invasion, NBN for damage sensing, and the shelterin proteins TERF1 and TERF2 that restrain unwanted recombination at telomeres.

Guanine nucleotides act outside the cell as well as inside it, and moving GTP, GDP, GMP and cyclic derivatives across membranes is what links intracellular purine pools to extracellular purinergic signalling and to the disposal of nucleotide-based drugs. Vesicular loading of nucleotides for regulated release is handled by SLC17A9, which fills secretory vesicles with ATP and related nucleotides for exocytosis, while ABCC4 and ABCC5 pump cyclic nucleotides and nucleotide analogues out across the plasma membrane and so shape cAMP/cGMP gradients and resistance to antiviral and antimetabolite therapy. Volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits provide a conductive route for bulky anions including cyclic dinucleotides, feeding STING-dependent innate immune sensing. Folate and antifolate carriers such as SLC19A1 and SLC46A2 additionally import cyclic dinucleotides. Together these routes govern extracellular nucleotide availability, purinergic receptor stimulation, and chemotherapeutic drug efflux.

Skeletal system development covers the whole trajectory of the vertebrate skeleton, from patterning of mesenchymal condensations through cartilage and bone formation to the remodelling that maintains bone mass in adult life. It determines limb and vertebral proportion, craniofacial shape and skull suture closure, and its disruption produces chondrodysplasias, osteogenesis imperfecta, craniosynostosis and osteopetrosis. Positional identity is set by HOX clusters and homeodomain and paired-box regulators, while SHH, WNT, FGF, BMP and TGF-beta signals drive condensation and growth-plate progression, with SOX9 governing chondrocyte and RUNX2 osteoblast differentiation. Chondrocytes and osteoblasts build a specialised matrix of collagens, aggrecan and proteoglycans that is mineralised by alkaline phosphatase and later degraded by matrix metalloproteinases and cathepsin K. Osteoclast recruitment through RANKL and its decoy receptor osteoprotegerin, together with parathyroid hormone, vitamin D receptor and IGF1 signalling, couples bone turnover to mineral homeostasis and growth.

Cartilage condensation is the step where loosely dispersed mesenchymal cells committed to the chondrocyte fate pack together into dense aggregates that prefigure every future cartilage element, and through endochondral ossification most of the skeleton. Getting it wrong shortens and distorts limbs and skull elements, and several of the genes here underlie human chondrodysplasias. Adhesion and matrix cues drive the aggregation itself, with type II and type XI collagens and the matricellular protein CCN2 building the early cartilage matrix and MGP restraining premature mineralization. SOX9, acting with SOX5 and SOX6, is the master transcriptional trio that switches on cartilage matrix genes and locks in chondrocyte identity. BMP signalling through BMPR1B, TGF-beta, FGF and WNT ligands set condensation boundaries and size, coupling the process to limb bud patterning, joint formation and skeletal growth.

Ossification is how bone tissue is made — mineralized matrix laid down directly by osteoblasts in membranous bone, or replacing a cartilage template during endochondral growth of the long bones. It builds the skeleton in the embryo, drives longitudinal growth at the growth plate, repairs fractures, and continues lifelong in balance with osteoclastic resorption; its failure or excess underlies osteoporosis, osteopetrosis, chondrodysplasias, craniosynostosis and heterotopic bone. Commitment of mesenchymal progenitors runs through RUNX2 and SP7 acting under BMP/TGF-beta receptor and SMAD signalling, Wnt/beta-catenin input tuned by LRP5 and the antagonists sclerostin and DKK1, and hedgehog and FGF cues that pattern chondrocyte hypertrophy. Osteoblasts then secrete type I collagen, osteocalcin and bone sialoprotein and control mineral deposition via alkaline phosphatase, PHEX, ENPP1 and phosphate transport, while PTH, vitamin D activation and RANKL/RANK/TRAF6 coordinate remodelling and calcium homeostasis.

Synaptic signalling is terminated largely by clearing transmitter from the extracellular space, and neurotransmitter uptake is the transport machinery that does it, returning glutamate, GABA, glycine, dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin to neurons and glia for reuse or degradation. Excitatory amino acid carriers such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3, expressed mainly by astrocytes and coupled to sodium gradients maintained by ATP1A2 and potassium buffering through KCNJ10, keep glutamate below excitotoxic levels; sodium- and chloride-dependent SLC6 family carriers recover monoamines and inhibitory transmitters. Vesicular transporters of the SLC18 and SLC17 families then repackage the recovered transmitter for release, linking uptake to the vesicle cycle alongside SNAP25 and synaptic regulators. These carriers are the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants and anticonvulsants, and their dysfunction contributes to excitotoxic injury, movement disorders and monoamine-related psychiatric disease.

Excitable cells signal by driving their membrane potential through a stereotyped cycle: a threshold-triggered depolarizing spike followed by repolarization and recovery. This underlies nerve impulse conduction, skeletal and cardiac muscle contraction, and the rhythmic pacemaking of the sinoatrial node, so its components are the targets of antiarrhythmic and anticonvulsant drugs and the genes behind long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, epilepsy and myotonia. Voltage-gated sodium channels and their beta subunits generate the upstroke, L-type and T-type calcium channels sustain the plateau and couple excitation to contraction, and a large family of potassium channels with accessory subunits sets threshold, repolarization rate and afterhyperpolarization. Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels and background leak conductances produce pacemaker depolarization, while sodium-potassium ATPases, sodium-calcium exchange and calcium release from ryanodine receptor stores restore ionic gradients. Anchoring proteins, gap junction connexins and cytoskeletal scaffolds position these channels so that excitation spreads reliably between coupled cells.

Almost every class of cellular RNA is chemically decorated after it is made, and RNA methylation is the most common of those modifications: a methyl group, nearly always donated by S-adenosylmethionine, is placed on a base or on the 2'-O position of ribose. The marks tune RNA folding, stability, translational efficiency and decay rather than change the coded sequence. Distinct enzyme families handle distinct substrates: the METTL3-METTL14 complex with its adaptors installs N6-methyladenosine on mRNA, RNMT caps transcripts, fibrillarin and its snoRNP partners methylate ribose in ribosomal RNA, NSUN and TRMT enzymes modify cytosines and bases in tRNA and mitochondrial RNA, and MEPCE caps the 7SK snRNA that restrains transcription elongation. Loss of individual writers causes intellectual disability, microcephaly and mitochondrial translation defects, and m6A machinery is recurrently deregulated in leukaemia, linking these marks to ribosome biogenesis, protein synthesis fidelity and gene expression control.

Pseudouridine is the most abundant modified nucleotide in cellular RNA, made by isomerizing a uridine already in place rather than by inserting a new base, and the resulting change in base pairing and backbone rigidity tunes how ribosomal RNA folds, how tRNAs read codons, and how spliceosomal snRNAs recognize their substrates. Two routes converge here: stand-alone synthases acting directly on their targets, including the tRNA enzymes PUS1, PUS3 and TRUB1, cytoplasmic and mitochondrial members such as the RPUSD proteins, and the spliceosomal RNA modifier PUS7; and a guide-RNA-dependent route in which the catalytic subunit DKC1 works with GAR1, NHP2, NOP10 and the assembly factor NAF1 to place modifications at sites specified by box H/ACA small RNAs. Loss of DKC1 function causes X-linked dyskeratosis congenita, with impaired telomerase RNA stability, bone marrow failure and defective ribosome biogenesis.

Beating cilia and flagella generate the forces that propel sperm, clear mucus from the airways, circulate cerebrospinal fluid and set left-right body asymmetry, and this pathway covers the axonemal machinery that makes that movement possible. Its failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, situs inversus, hydrocephalus and male infertility. The genes encode the parts of the 9+2 axoneme and its regulators: outer and inner dynein arm heavy and intermediate chains and their cytoplasmic assembly factors, nexin-dynein regulatory complex subunits, radial spoke heads, tektin filaments and central apparatus proteins, together with tubulin polyglutamylases that tune dynein activity along the doublets. Sperm-specific components add motility control and energy supply, including the CatSper calcium channel complex that drives hyperactivation, A-kinase anchoring proteins of the fibrous sheath, and glycolytic enzymes such as GAPDHS and PGK2. Intraflagellar transport and basal body factors supply and position the organelle.

Ovarian follicle development is the staged maturation of a primordial follicle into an ovulatory structure, and it sets a woman's reproductive lifespan: the size of the resting pool, the rate at which follicles are recruited, and how many are lost to atresia together determine fertility and the timing of menopause. Pituitary gonadotrophins acting through their receptors drive granulosa proliferation and steroidogenesis, while locally produced inhibins, activins and anti-Mullerian hormone feed back to restrain recruitment and select a dominant follicle. Oocyte-granulosa dialogue via KIT ligand and its receptor, natriuretic peptide signalling that holds meiosis arrested, zona pellucida assembly, and FOXL2- and FOXO3-dependent transcriptional control coordinate the two cell types. Meiotic recombination and DNA damage response genes police oocyte quality, and matrix remodelling plus angiogenic factors build the vasculature and permit follicle rupture. Failure produces premature ovarian insufficiency or anovulatory infertility.

Ovulation is the final step of the ovarian follicular cycle, in which the wall of a mature preovulatory follicle is broken down so the oocyte and its surrounding cumulus cells can be released into the oviduct for fertilization. Failure of this rupture leaves a trapped oocyte and unruptured luteinized follicles, a cause of anovulatory infertility. The event is triggered by the luteinizing hormone surge and executed largely through progesterone receptor signalling, which induces proteases that remodel the follicular extracellular matrix, including ADAMTS1 and matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP2 and MMP19. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase contributes vasodilatory and inflammatory-like changes at the apex, while nuclear receptor coregulators and metabolic sensors including NRIP1, SIRT1 and leptin signalling tie ovulatory competence to hormonal coactivation and nutritional state. FOXO3 acts in the wider control of follicle activation and ovarian reserve.

Antral follicle growth is the final, gonadotropin-dependent phase of ovarian folliculogenesis, in which a fluid-filled antrum expands and granulosa cells proliferate to produce an oocyte competent for ovulation. It sets how many follicles reach maturity each cycle and therefore underlies fertility, cycle regulation, and the ovarian reserve; its disruption contributes to anovulation, premature ovarian insufficiency, and polycystic ovary phenotypes. Oocyte-derived signals acting through the BMP type I receptor BMPR1B coordinate granulosa behaviour, while estrogen acting on ESR1 sustains proliferation and the CNP/NPR2 pair (NPPC and its guanylyl cyclase receptor) generates the cGMP that holds the oocyte in meiotic arrest until the luteinizing surge. Epiregulin relays that surge to cumulus cells, and matrix components such as PTX3 and TNFAIP6 cross-link the hyaluronan-rich cumulus matrix. FOXO3 restrains excessive follicle activation, linking growth to reserve depletion.

After ovulation the emptied follicle does not disperse; its theca and granulosa cells are remodelled into a transient endocrine gland, the corpus luteum, and this luteinization programme is what makes progesterone available to prepare and maintain the uterus for implantation. Failure of the transition shortens the luteal phase and causes infertility and early pregnancy loss. The change involves hypertrophy and steroidogenic reprogramming of follicular somatic cells, controlled by the nuclear receptor NR5A1 driving steroidogenic gene expression, by prolactin- and cytokine-responsive STAT5A and STAT5B transcription factors, and by oocyte- and TGF-beta-family signals such as GDF9 and inhibin/activin subunit INHBA. Wnt receptor FZD4 and PDGFRA support the accompanying vascularisation and stromal reorganisation, while matrix metalloproteinase MMP2 degrades the follicular basement membrane so that capillaries and luteal cells can invade the collapsed follicle.

Luteolysis is the regression of the corpus luteum at the end of a non-fertile ovarian cycle, and it sets the length of the luteal phase. It proceeds in two linked steps: progesterone output falls first, then the steroidogenic and vascular cells of the gland are actually cleared, so the ovary can begin a new follicular cycle. If an embryo implants, this programme must be blocked, and failure to suppress it withdraws the progesterone support that pregnancy depends on. The genes here point to regulated cell death and tissue disassembly rather than hormone synthesis: executioner and initiator caspases dismantle luteal cells, a matrix metalloproteinase remodels the extracellular scaffold, and Notch receptors together with Slit ligands and a Robo receptor act as survival and guidance cues over the luteal vasculature, controlling whether the gland is maintained or dismantled.

Oocyte maturation is the final preparation of an arrested egg for fertilization: meiosis resumes, the germinal vesicle breaks down, and the oocyte proceeds to a second arrest at metaphase II with a competent spindle and a store of maternal mRNA ready for use. Without it there is no fertilizable egg, and human mutations in components such as the oocyte-specific tubulin TUBB8 or the kinase WEE2 cause spindle assembly failure or fertilization arrest and infertility. Meiotic arrest is held by cyclic nucleotide signalling from the follicle, with natriuretic peptide acting through NPR2 and PDE3A controlling cAMP hydrolysis; release activates the MOS dash MAPK route and cyclin B dash CDK1, with CDC25B and FBXO5 tuning the transition. In parallel, cytoplasmic maturation depends on translational control of stored transcripts by ZAR1, DAZL, and uridylation and decay factors, and on cohesin and recombination proteins that ensure accurate chromosome segregation.

Cell growth — the increase in cell size and biomass — is set by nutrient supply, growth factors and mechanical cues, and this collection covers the machinery that raises or lowers that rate. Its outputs determine organ size, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy, neuronal process extension and the decision to arrest rather than enlarge; loss of restraint contributes to tumour growth, while excess restraint yields growth failure and atrophy. The mTOR complexes and their regulators, with RPTOR, RICTOR, MLST8 and the LAMTOR scaffolds, couple nutrient and insulin/IGF1 input to biosynthetic capacity, opposed by STK11, sestrins and the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors CDKN1A and CDKN1B acting under TP53 and RB1. TGF-beta and BMP receptors signalling through SMAD proteins, Hippo components LATS2 and YAP1, Wnt ligands, IGF-binding proteins, and axon guidance cues including semaphorins, slits and netrins supply the extracellular and contact-dependent instructions that scale growth up or down.

fatty acid alpha-oxidation removes a single carbon from the front end of branched-chain fatty acids so that they can be handled by the ordinary beta-oxidation machinery. It exists because dietary phytanic acid, derived from chlorophyll, carries a methyl group at carbon 3 that blocks the dehydrogenation step of beta-oxidation; shortening the chain by one carbon shifts the branch to an even position and unblocks the route. The reactions occur in peroxisomes, where phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase introduces a 2-hydroxyl group and HACL1 cleaves the bond to release formyl-CoA and pristanal, en route to pristanic acid. Substrate entry and cofactor supply depend on peroxisomal transporters and on the import machinery of the organelle. Loss of phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase causes Refsum disease, with phytanic acid accumulation producing retinitis pigmentosa, peripheral neuropathy and ataxia.

Branched-chain fatty acids such as phytanic acid, released from chlorophyll-derived dietary lipids, carry a methyl group at carbon 3 that blocks the dehydrogenation step of ordinary beta-oxidation; alpha-oxidation shortens them by one carbon so the remainder can be degraded conventionally. The chemistry is peroxisomal: a long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase activates the substrate, a 2-hydroxylase introduces a hydroxyl at the alpha carbon, and a thiamine-pyrophosphate-dependent 2-hydroxyacyl-CoA lyase cleaves off formyl-CoA, yielding pristanal and then pristanic acid for entry into beta-oxidation. Delivery of enzymes into the organelle and transport of substrates and cofactors across its membrane are part of the route, which is why generalised peroxisome biogenesis defects impair it. Loss of the hydroxylase step causes phytanic acid accumulation with retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia and peripheral neuropathy, linking this catabolic route to dietary lipid handling and neurological health.

Response to protozoan covers the host reaction to parasites such as Plasmodium, Leishmania and Toxoplasma, and it determines whether an infection is contained in the tissue or spreads systemically. It matters because these organisms live inside macrophages and other host cells, so control depends on cell-autonomous killing plus tightly balanced inflammation; too little causes uncontrolled parasitaemia, too much causes cerebral malaria and immunopathology. The genes describe both arms. Pattern recognition through Dectin-1 and MyD88 drives IL-12 and interferon-gamma-dependent programmes, and the guanylate-binding proteins then disrupt the parasitophorous vacuole to expose the parasite to killing. Transcription factors including IRF8, IRF4 and the BATF proteins set macrophage and dendritic cell activation states, while arginase-1, IL-10 and phagosomal metal transport by SLC11A1 tune the balance between nitric oxide production, nutrient deprivation and resolution of inflammation. Defensins and platelet factor 4 add direct antiparasitic activity.

Protozoan parasites such as Plasmodium, Toxoplasma and Leishmania provoke a distinctive host response, and this pathway covers the cellular and organismal changes triggered by that encounter. It matters because control of intracellular protozoa depends on interferon-driven macrophage activation rather than antibody alone, and defects here lead to uncontrolled parasite replication or, at the other extreme, immunopathology from excessive inflammation. Pattern recognition through a C-type lectin for fungal and parasite glycans and the adaptor MyD88 initiates signalling; transcription factors including IRF8, IRF4 and the BATF family drive dendritic cell and macrophage programmes and IL12B production, steering T cells toward interferon-gamma output. Guanylate-binding proteins then disrupt parasite-containing vacuoles, while SLC11A1 restricts phagosomal metal availability and arginase and IL-10 restrain the response. Antimicrobial defensins and CD40 costimulation link innate detection to adaptive immunity.

Vascular networks are not built as single tubes but by repeated sprouting and branching of existing vessels, and this branching arm of blood vessel morphogenesis determines how dense, well-patterned and appropriately perfused a tissue's capillary bed becomes. It underlies embryonic vascular patterning, wound healing and the pathological neovascularisation of tumours and retinopathy; too little yields ischaemic, poorly perfused tissue, while unchecked sprouting gives leaky, disorganised vessels. VEGFA acting through KDR and the co-receptor NRP1 drives endothelial tip cell selection, which Notch signalling through DLL4, NOTCH4 and the feedback regulator NRARP restrains so that only a fraction of cells lead a sprout. Repulsive guidance by SEMA3E and PLXND1 steers the growing branch, BMP and TGF-beta inputs via ENG, GDF2 and ACVR1 stabilise it, and Wnt, hedgehog and endothelin signals, together with transcription factors such as FOXC2 and SRF, couple branching to surrounding tissue cues.

The first blood vessels of an embryo are not sprouted from existing ones but built from scratch: mesodermal progenitors commit to endothelial fate, coalesce, and hollow out into patent tubes. Vasculogenesis in this sense establishes the dorsal aorta, cardinal veins and yolk sac plexus, and without it the embryo cannot perfuse its tissues and dies early; defective versions of the same machinery underlie cavernous malformations, arteriovenous shunts and hereditary telangiectasia. VEGFA acting through KDR and NRP1 drives progenitor specification and survival, while SOX17 and SOX18 with NOTCH1, HEY1/HEY2 and the ephrin receptor EPHA2 impose arterial versus venous identity. BMP and TGF-beta receptors including ENG and TGFBR2, apelin signalling via APLNR, and junctional and lumen-forming factors such as CCM2, HEG1 and RASIP1 govern tube formation, while PDGFRB recruits mural support.

Gangliosides are sialic acid-bearing glycosphingolipids that dominate the outer leaflet of neuronal plasma membranes, where they organise lipid rafts, tune receptor signalling, mediate cell adhesion and myelin contacts, and serve as receptors for toxins and pathogens. Their metabolism is a balance of stepwise synthesis and lysosomal breakdown. Sialyltransferases and glycosyltransferases build the series from lactosylceramide: ST3GAL5 makes GM3, B4GALNT1 adds N-acetylgalactosamine to form GM2 and GD2, B3GALT4 extends to GM1, and ST8SIA family enzymes add further sialic acids for b- and c-series species. Degradation runs in reverse in the lysosome, where sialidases remove sialic acid, beta-hexosaminidase subunits HEXA and HEXB with the GM2 activator protein strip terminal GalNAc, and GLB1 cleaves galactose. Loss of these catabolic steps causes storage diseases including Tay-Sachs, Sandhoff and GM1 gangliosidosis, with progressive neurodegeneration; synthetic defects produce severe infantile epilepsy and developmental failure.

Gangliosides are sialylated glycosphingolipids concentrated in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, most abundantly in neurons, where they organize lipid rafts, modulate receptor signalling, and mediate cell-cell recognition and myelin-axon adhesion. Their biosynthesis proceeds stepwise in the Golgi: ceramide is glucosylated and then galactosylated by B4GALT5 and B4GALT6 to lactosylceramide, ST3GAL5 adds the first sialic acid to make GM3, B4GALNT1 adds N-acetylgalactosamine, and B3GALT4 completes the tetrasaccharide core, which further sialyltransferases of the ST3GAL, ST6GALNAC and ST8SIA families extend into the a-, b- and c-series species. Because each enzyme competes for shared intermediates, their relative expression sets the ganglioside profile of a cell and changes with neural development and tumour progression. Loss of ST3GAL5 or B4GALNT1 causes infantile epilepsy syndromes and hereditary spastic paraplegia, and these glycolipids serve as receptors for bacterial toxins and targets of autoimmune neuropathy antibodies.

Bundling microtubules into parallel arrays is how cells build the stiff, organised scaffolds that motile cilia, sperm flagella, neuronal axons and the mitotic spindle all depend on. The axonemal contingent dominates here: outer and inner dynein arms and their cytoplasmic assembly factors, radial spoke and nexin-dynein regulatory complex subunits, and central-pair proteins together hold the nine-plus-two arrangement in register and convert dynein stepping into a coordinated beat. Loss of these components causes primary ciliary dyskinesia, situs defects, hydrocephalus and male infertility, while retinal axoneme genes underlie photoreceptor degeneration. A second group acts in the cytoplasm, where plus-end tracking and crosslinking proteins, doublecortin, MAP1B and tubulin polyglutamylases tune lattice spacing and stability for axon and dendrite shaping, and spindle and midbody factors organise microtubules during division.

Bone is built by osteoblasts, and this programme describes how mesenchymal and neural crest progenitors commit to that fate and acquire the machinery to deposit and mineralize matrix. Its output is skeletal mass: too little activity gives osteopenia, delayed ossification and craniofacial or limb malformation, while its balance against bone resorption sets adult bone remodelling. Commitment runs through a transcriptional hierarchy in which RUNX2 with its CBFB partner and the downstream factor SP7 drive expression of matrix and mineralization genes such as COL1A1, ALPL, BGLAP, IBSP and SPP1. Upstream, BMP ligands acting through type I and II receptors and SMAD1/5/9, Wnt signals via LRP5 and beta-catenin, hedgehog, Notch, FGF, IGF and parathyroid hormone receptor input converge on that hierarchy, opposed by secreted antagonists including noggin, gremlin, chordin and sclerostin-like inhibitors, and tuned by numerous microRNAs. Related programmes divert the same progenitors toward chondrocytes or adipocytes.

Kidneys, ureters, bladder, gonads and the ducts that connect them all arise from a shared intermediate mesoderm field, and urogenital system development is the programme that patterns that field into functioning excretory and reproductive organs. Its failure produces congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, hypospadias, duct regression defects and disorders of sex development. Nephric lineage specification depends on PAX2, PAX8, LHX1 and OSR1, while ureteric budding and branching run on GDNF-independent inputs such as FGF10 and FGFR2 signalling alongside BMP4, BMP7, SHH-PTCH1-GLI1 and WNT5A/WNT11. Posterior HOX genes of the 9-13 paralogue groups position the ducts and external genitalia. Sexual differentiation enters through SOX9, AMH, androgen receptor and the steroidogenic enzymes CYP19A1 and SRD5A1, and several members also govern prostate epithelial identity, including NKX3-1 and FOXA1.

The metanephros is the third and final embryonic kidney, and its development produces the permanent adult organ that filters blood, balances salt and water, and secretes renin and erythropoietin. Development begins when metanephric mesenchyme signals to the nephric duct to evoke a ureteric bud, which then branches repeatedly to build the collecting system while inducing nested cap mesenchyme to form nephrons. GDNF acting through RET drives bud outgrowth, with sprouty and BMP signals restraining it; SIX2, WT1, SALL1, PAX2 and EYA1 maintain or commit the progenitor pool, and WNT9B and WNT4 convert mesenchyme into epithelial tubules. Stromal, vascular and podocyte programmes follow, yielding glomerular and tubular transport proteins such as nephrin-associated podocin, aquaporins and organic anion carriers. Disruption causes renal agenesis, hypodysplasia, duplex or obstructed ureters, and reduced nephron number that predisposes to later hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

Mammals hold core body temperature within a narrow range whatever the ambient conditions, and this is the machinery that senses thermal challenge and generates or conserves heat in response. Its main effector arm is brown and beige adipose tissue: sympathetic noradrenaline acting on beta-adrenergic receptors drives lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation, while UCP1 uncouples the mitochondrial proton gradient so that substrate oxidation yields heat rather than ATP. Transcriptional regulators such as PRDM16, EBF2, PPARGC1A and the thyroid hormone activator DIO2 specify and maintain thermogenic adipocytes, and skeletal muscle contributes through sarcolipin-dependent futile calcium cycling. Thermosensitive TRP channels report cold and heat, while hypothalamic signals including leptin, orexin and prostaglandin E2 set the defended temperature and mediate fever. Loss of these responses causes cold intolerance, and their chronic engagement raises energy expenditure, linking thermoregulation to obesity and metabolic disease.

Fever is the regulated rise of body temperature above its normal set point, most often triggered by infection, and this is the circuitry that raises that set point rather than simply producing heat. Pyrogenic cytokines released by activated innate immune cells — interleukin-1 alpha and beta, TNF, and RANKL signalling through its receptor — act on the vasculature and glia of the hypothalamic preoptic region. There they induce cyclooxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E synthase, so that locally made prostaglandin E2 engages EP3 receptors on thermoregulatory neurons; the consequence is sympathetic drive to brown fat thermogenesis, cutaneous vasoconstriction, and shivering. TRPV1 contributes thermosensation, and endothelin signalling modulates vascular tone. Because prostaglandin synthesis is the obligatory step, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are antipyretic. Fever aids host defence, but unchecked pyrogen signalling drives the malaise, cachexia, and hypotension of sepsis.

Cells that crawl rather than remain anchored move by repeatedly extending a pseudopodium, adhering weakly, and retracting the rear, and this ameboidal-type migration is how gastrulating mesoderm, neural crest, endothelial tip cells, immune cells and invading tumour cells relocate through tissue. The machinery is built around Rho-family GTPase control of the actin cortex: CDC42 and RAC1 with their activators DOCK1 and ARHGEF7, WAVE-complex components, and the severing and barbed-end proteins cofilin and profilin, with ROCK1 and PAK1 driving contractile retraction. Integrins, talin-like and kindlin adaptors, FAK and SRC couple the cytoskeleton to fibronectin and laminin, while matrix metalloproteinases clear a path. Direction comes from extracellular guidance cues — a large semaphorin–neuropilin/plexin repertoire, endothelins, TGF-beta/BMP/Nodal ligands acting through SMAD2/3, SHH, WNT5A and VEGFA. Loss of this coordination underlies neural crest and cardiac outflow malformations, Hirschsprung disease, defective wound closure and metastatic dissemination.

Acrosome assembly is the step in spermiogenesis that converts Golgi-derived proacrosomal vesicles into the single large cap covering the anterior sperm nucleus, the secretory organelle whose hydrolases and adhesion proteins let a sperm penetrate the zona pellucida and fuse with the egg. Without it spermatozoa are globozoospermic — round-headed, acrosome-less and infertile — a recognised cause of male infertility treatable only by assisted fertilisation. The genes here cover vesicle trafficking and tethering from the Golgi, a Rab GAP and Golgi-associated tethering factors, membrane fusion and docking, and the acroplaxome/acrosome–acroplaxome anchoring machinery built on actin-related proteins that also couples the acrosome to nuclear shaping and manchette function. Transcriptional regulators active in round spermatids drive the haploid programme, while zona-binding and sperm–egg interaction proteins are the cargo whose correct packaging is the point of the whole process.

Long-chain fatty acids of thirteen to twenty-two carbons are the cell's main fuel reserve, membrane building blocks, and the precursors of lipid signalling molecules, and this metabolic programme covers their uptake, activation, elongation, desaturation, oxidation and conversion into bioactive mediators. Transporters and acyl-CoA synthetases charge incoming fatty acids with coenzyme A so they can be esterified or burned; carnitine palmitoyltransferases hand them to mitochondrial beta-oxidation, while peroxisomal transporters and thioesterases handle branched and very long species. Elongases and desaturases tailor chain length and double bonds to produce arachidonate and related polyunsaturates, which phospholipases release for cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases and cytochrome P450 enzymes to convert into prostaglandins, leukotrienes and epoxy- and hydroxy-fatty acids. Endocannabinoid turnover by diacylglycerol lipases, FAAH and monoacylglycerol lipase belongs here too. Defects cause peroxisomal and fatty acid oxidation disorders, and dysregulation drives inflammation, steatosis and insulin resistance.

Cells must keep their internal glucose and glucose-derived flux within narrow limits, both to fuel themselves and, in specialised cells, to read blood glucose as a signal. This programme couples glucose sensing to hormone secretion and to transcriptional adjustment of metabolism, and its failure underlies diabetes: loss of pancreatic beta cell function, impaired insulin release, and unrestrained hepatic glucose output. Sensing begins with transport and phosphorylation — the GLUT2 transporter with glucokinase and other hexokinases setting the rate of entry into glycolysis — which changes ATP levels and closes the KATP channel subunit encoded by ABCC8, triggering calcium-dependent exocytosis through syntaxin and Munc13 machinery. Beta cell identity factors such as PDX1, NKX6-1 and RFX6 maintain the secretory phenotype, while FOXO1, PPARGC1A, SIRT1, AMPK subunits and ChREBP tune gluconeogenic and lipogenic gene expression; insulin/IGF receptor signalling through IRS2 and PI3K closes the loop, with additional microRNA-level control.

Every tRNA is transcribed with an extra stretch of nucleotides at its 5' end, and removing that leader is the first processing step that turns a precursor into a functional adaptor for translation. The cut is endonucleolytic and precise, defining the mature 5' terminus that must pair correctly with the acceptor stem for aminoacylation and ribosome use. In the nucleus the job is done by a ribonucleoprotein RNase P built from an RNA subunit and a set of protein partners including POP1, POP4, POP5, POP7 and RPP21, RPP25, RPP30 and RPP38, while PRORP is a protein-only enzyme that performs the same reaction on mitochondrially encoded tRNAs. La protein binds the UUU-OH ends of nascent polymerase III transcripts and protects them during this maturation. Defective processing starves cells of usable tRNA and underlies mitochondrial translation disorders.

Histamine is an amine signal that drives allergic inflammation, gastric acid secretion, and neurotransmission, and its levels are set by how fast it is made, moved, and destroyed. This metabolic route covers that balance: histidine decarboxylase generates histamine in mast cells, basophils, enterochromaffin-like cells of the stomach, and histaminergic neurons, while histamine N-methyltransferase terminates its action by methylating it to an inactive product. Transport steps matter as much as chemistry, since carriers of the organic cation and plasma membrane monoamine type clear extracellular histamine into cells for degradation, limiting how long receptors are stimulated. Insufficient inactivation prolongs vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, itch, and increased vascular permeability, and variation in the methyltransferase has been linked to asthma and histamine intolerance. The pathway therefore sits upstream of both immediate hypersensitivity responses and physiological control of acid output.

Gastric acid secretion is the release of hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen by parietal cells, the step that lowers gastric pH enough to activate pepsin, kill ingested microbes, and liberate dietary iron and vitamin B12. Too little acid causes hypochlorhydria with bacterial overgrowth and malabsorption; too much drives peptic ulceration and reflux disease. Secretion is switched on by gastrin acting through CCKBR, by histamine through the H2 receptor, and by muscarinic input from the vagus, and restrained by prostaglandin E2 receptors, somatostatin and peptides such as secretin and ghrelin. Downstream, the proton pump is trafficked to the apical canalicular membrane in a process requiring HIP1R and SNX10, while KCNQ1 recycles potassium and SLC26A7 and SLC9A4 handle the accompanying anion and sodium fluxes. TFF2 provides mucosal protection against the acid produced.

Gastric acid secretion is the controlled release of hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen by parietal cells, which lowers luminal pH enough to activate pepsin, kill ingested microbes and liberate dietary iron and vitamin B12. Secretion is driven by the proton pump at the apical membrane, supported by anion and cation transport that recycles chloride and potassium, with SLC26A7 supplying chloride, KCNQ1 providing potassium conductance and SLC9A4 handling sodium-proton exchange. Stimulation comes through receptors for gastrin, acetylcholine and histamine, while prostaglandin E and somatostatin-like signals restrain it; ghrelin, secretin and neuromedin U add endocrine control tied to feeding. Trafficking proteins including HIP1R and SNX10 govern the tubulovesicle rearrangements that deliver pumps to the canaliculus. Too much acid produces peptic ulceration and reflux disease, while achlorhydria causes malabsorption and bacterial overgrowth, and TFF2 marks the protective mucous response.

This grouping covers the genes whose loss halts progression of the embryo in the uterus, from zygote through organogenesis to birth, and it is defined empirically by embryonic lethality rather than by one mechanism. What it captures is the minimum set of processes a mammalian conceptus cannot do without: specification of the early lineages by pluripotency and trophoblast factors such as POU5F1, CDX2 and TEAD4; placental and vascular assembly requiring VEGFA, HIF1A, ANGPT1 and GCM1; and patterning by the major morphogen routes, with Nodal/BMP/TGF-beta signalling through SMAD2/3/4, Wnt/beta-catenin, Notch and Hedgehog all represented. Alongside these sit housekeeping demands that are simply heavier in a rapidly dividing embryo: DNA replication and repair (BRCA2, PALB2, LIG4), chromatin and imprinting control (TRIM28, CTCF, SIN3A), transcription elongation and mRNA processing. Hypomorphic defects in the same genes underlie congenital malformation syndromes, ciliopathies and placental insufficiency.

Gastrulation in deuterostomes, where the blastopore formed by the first invagination becomes the anus and the mouth arises later at the opposite end, is the step that converts a simple epithelial ball into a three-layered embryo with a defined head-to-tail and left-right axis. Everything built afterwards depends on it: mesoderm and endoderm are set aside, the primitive streak and node form, and cells move through them to their final positions. The genes here are the classical axis-inducing signals and their readouts, including NODAL with its activin-type receptors and SMAD4, WNT5A with beta-catenin and LRP5, and the transcription factors TBXT, FOXA2, LHX1, OTX2 and ZIC3 that specify streak, node and anterior endoderm identity. Planar cell polarity components such as PRICKLE1 direct the convergent-extension movements that elongate the body axis. Loss of these activities causes failed mesoderm formation, situs defects and early embryonic lethality.

Gastrulation converts a uniform epiblast into the three primary germ layers initial ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm from which every tissue of the body is later built, and its failure arrests embryogenesis outright.
