Desmosome assembly builds the rivet-like junctions that anchor neighbouring cells to each other through the intermediate filament cytoskeleton, giving epidermis, mucosa and myocardium the mechanical resilience to withstand shear and repeated contraction. Desmosomal cadherins such as desmoglein 3 engage in trans across a widened intercellular space, while plakoglobin and the plakophilins (PKP1, PKP2, PKP3) form the dense cytoplasmic plaque that clusters the cadherin tails and couples them to keratin or desmin filaments; classical E-cadherin contacts help position nascent junctions before the desmosomal plaque matures. Protein kinase C signalling modulates plaque assembly and disassembly, allowing junctions to be remodelled during wound healing and differentiation. Loss or autoantibody-mediated disruption of these components produces blistering skin disease such as pemphigus vulgaris, palmoplantar keratoderma, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy when cardiomyocyte adhesion fails.

Protein synthesis in the cytoplasm converts messenger RNA sequence into polypeptide, supplying essentially every cellular activity with its protein output and consuming a large share of cellular energy. The core machinery here is the 80S ribosome itself, with the full complement of large and small subunit proteins, joined by initiation factors that cap-dependently recruit and scan mRNA, elongation and release factors, and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that charge tRNAs. Regulation is prominent: the guanine nucleotide exchange complex acting on initiation factor 2 sets the rate of ternary complex formation and is the node at which stress responses throttle translation, while mTOR signalling, poly(A)-binding protein and sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins such as FMRP, CPEBs and YTHDF2 tune which transcripts are read and how often. Ribosomal protein mutations cause ribosomopathies including Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, and dysregulated initiation drives oncogenic growth.

cytoplasmic translational elongation is the processive phase of protein synthesis in which the ribosome adds one amino acid at a time to a growing polypeptide, setting the rate at which cells convert transcripts into functional protein and thereby governing growth, secretory output and the speed of stress responses. Charged tRNAs supplied by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as AARS1 are delivered by elongation factor complexes, with the eEF1B subunit EEF1D recycling the GTPase and the ribosomal stalk protein RPLP2 recruiting factors to the ribosome. Elongation is also a control point: CPEB family proteins tune translation of specific mRNAs in neurons and oocytes, while NEMF surveys stalled ribosomes and marks incomplete nascent chains for degradation. Defects in these steps cause protein aggregation, ribosome collision stress, and neurological disease.

Cytoplasmic translational elongation is the processive phase of protein synthesis in which the ribosome adds one amino acid after another to a growing polypeptide, setting the rate at which cells convert transcripts into protein and therefore how quickly they grow, secrete and respond to stimuli. Charged tRNA supply comes from aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as the alanyl enzyme AARS1, while elongation factor subunits and ribosomal stalk proteins like RPLP2 support factor recruitment and repeated cycles of tRNA delivery and translocation. Quality control is part of the same process: NEMF recognises stalled ribosomes carrying incomplete chains and helps mark them for degradation, preventing accumulation of truncated products. Cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding proteins impose message-specific control, repressing or activating elongation on particular mRNAs, a mode of local translational regulation prominent in neurons and in synaptic plasticity.

Cytoplasmic translational initiation is the rate-limiting first step of protein synthesis, in which a small ribosomal subunit loaded with initiator methionyl-tRNA is delivered to an mRNA and positioned on its start codon. Because initiation is where most translational control is exerted, this step sets how much protein a cell makes from each transcript and is the point at which growth factor and stress signals are converted into changes in proteome output. The genes cover cap recognition and scaffolding through eIF4A/eIF4G and the nuclear cap-binding proteins, the multisubunit eIF3 complex that binds the 40S subunit and promotes scanning, the eIF2 ternary complex with its eIF2B guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and mTOR- and AKT-dependent regulation. Also present are reinitiation and non-canonical factors such as DENR-MCTS1 and eIF2D, m6A readers, and DHX29 for structured 5' leaders. Impaired eIF2B function causes leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter.

Translational initiation in the cytoplasm is the step at which a message is chosen for protein synthesis: the small ribosomal subunit, loaded with initiator methionyl-tRNA, is recruited to an mRNA, scans to a start codon, and joins the large subunit before the first peptide bond forms. Because it is rate-limiting, it is the main point at which growth signals and stress set the cell's protein output. The eIF3 multisubunit complex, the cap-binding and helicase activities of eIF4A/eIF4G and the nuclear cap-binding proteins, eIF5 and the eIF2 subunits with their eIF2B guanine-nucleotide exchange factor form the core machinery, and eIF2B loss causes leukoencephalopathy. mTOR-dependent signalling, phosphorylation-driven eIF2 inhibition during the integrated stress response, and m6A readers or DENR-MCTS1 for reinitiation tune which transcripts are translated; failure produces stress granules, arrested growth, and ribosomopathy-like disease.

Most protein synthesis in human cells begins at the 5' m7G cap, where cap-binding proteins mark the site at which the 40S ribosomal subunit is loaded before scanning in the 5' to 3' direction to the first suitable AUG. Cap-dependent initiation sets the rate of translation for the great majority of mRNAs, so it is the step at which growth factor and nutrient signalling is converted into protein output, and its deregulation raises the synthesis of growth-promoting proteins in cancer. Scaffolding by EIF4G1 bridges the cap complex to the small subunit through EIF3D, the nuclear cap-binding heterodimer NCBP1-NCBP2 escorts newly exported transcripts into a pioneer round, and MIF4GD with SLBP directs the specialised, non-polyadenylated histone mRNAs into this same machinery during S phase. Kinase input from AKT2 links initiation to upstream survival and metabolic cues.

Somatic diversification of immune receptors generates antigen receptor variety that the germline genome does not encode, so that lymphocytes can collectively recognise essentially any pathogen. It covers V(D)J recombination in developing B and T cells, and class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation in activated B cells that mature antibody affinity and switch effector isotype. Loss of these steps produces severe combined immunodeficiency or hyper-IgM syndromes; their misfiring underlies lymphoid translocations. The genes trace a deliberate DNA damage strategy: RAG1/RAG2 or AID-initiated uracil lesions processed by uracil glycosylase and mismatch repair, then resolved by non-homologous end joining and translesion polymerases, with ATM, 53BP1 and the shieldin complex directing repair choice. Cytokine and costimulatory signals such as IL-4, CD40L and TGF-beta, read out through STAT6, BATF and BCL6, determine which B cells undergo the process and which isotype they adopt.

Antigen receptor diversity is not inherited but built in each developing lymphocyte, and this somatic diversification of immune receptors is how a limited germline repertoire yields antibodies and T cell receptors against essentially any pathogen. The same DNA-breaking chemistry also switches antibody isotypes and refines affinity in germinal centres. RAG1 and RAG2 initiate V(D)J recombination, and the resulting breaks are sealed by non-homologous end joining involving DNA-PKcs, Artemis, LIG4, XRCC4 and the shieldin complex under 53BP1 control; AID deaminates cytosine in immunoglobulin loci, and uracil glycosylase plus mismatch repair factors convert those lesions into mutations or class switch recombination. Cytokine and costimulatory inputs such as IL4, CD40 ligation and TGFB1 direct which isotype is chosen. Loss of these steps produces severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgM syndromes, or radiosensitivity with lymphoid malignancy.

Innate immunity begins when germline-encoded receptors detect conserved microbial structures or misplaced host molecules and switch on a defensive transcriptional and inflammatory programme; this is the set of events that triggers that switch. It underlies the first hours of antimicrobial defence, fever and cytokine production, and when it misfires it drives autoinflammatory disease, septic shock and interferonopathies. Toll-like receptors at the surface and in endosomes signal through MYD88, TIRAP and TICAM1 to IRAK kinases, TRAF6 and the IKK complex, releasing NF-kB and activating MAP kinases; cytosolic sensing runs in parallel, with RIG-I-like receptors and MAVS, and cGAS with STING1, converging on TBK1 and IRF3 to induce type I interferon. NOD1/NOD2 and NLRP3-family inflammasomes with PYCARD and caspase-1 add peptidoglycan sensing and IL-1 maturation. Ubiquitin editors such as TNFAIP3, CYLD and OTULIN, plus decoy and regulatory proteins, keep the response proportionate.

Detection of microbes at the plasma membrane is the first step in innate defence, and this pathway covers the signalling that runs from a cell surface receptor engaging its ligand to the transcriptional output of an activated innate immune response. It licenses macrophage and dendritic cell inflammatory activation, cytokine and type I interferon production, phagocyte recruitment, and the priming of adaptive immunity; too little of it leaves hosts vulnerable to bacterial and fungal infection, while too much drives sepsis and chronic inflammation. Toll-like receptors with co-receptors such as CD14, LBP and the MD-2 adaptor recognise lipopolysaccharide and lipopeptides, recruiting MyD88 and TRIF-family adaptors to the IRAK kinases, TRAF6 and TAK1 and thence to IKK-driven NF-κB release or TBK1-dependent IRF3 activation. C-type lectins like Dectin-1 and Dectin-2 signal instead through SYK and PLCγ2, and NK receptor complexes signal through DAP12. Collectins, ficolins and MASP proteases add complement-linked opsonic recognition, and A20, TNIP proteins and several microRNAs restrain the response.

Toll-like receptors are the innate immune system's first-line sensors of conserved microbial structures — bacterial lipopeptides and lipopolysaccharide at the cell surface, viral and bacterial nucleic acids in endosomes — and the signalling they initiate decides whether a tissue mounts an inflammatory response. Recognition drives inflammatory cytokine and type I interferon production, recruits phagocytes, and licenses dendritic cells to prime adaptive immunity; loss of core components causes recurrent pyogenic or herpesvirus infection, while unrestrained signalling contributes to sepsis and autoimmune inflammation. Receptor engagement recruits the adaptors MYD88 or TICAM1 with TIRAP and TICAM2, assembling IRAK1/IRAK4 kinase complexes that act through TRAF6 and MAP3K7 to activate IKK–NF-κB and stress kinases, or through IRF3 and IRF7 to switch on interferon genes. Much of the pathway is devoted to restraint: decoy kinases, deubiquitinases, NF-κB inhibitors and microRNA feedback limit the response, and UNC93B1 controls delivery of nucleic acid sensors to endosomes.

Mucosal surfaces of the gut, airway and urogenital tract face constant microbial load, and the innate immune response mounted in those tissues is the first chemical barrier that keeps commensals contained and pathogens from invading the epithelium. Much of it is secreted antimicrobial protein: alpha- and beta-defensins from Paneth and epithelial cells, cathelicidin, iron-sequestering lactoferrin, eosinophil-derived ribonucleases, a secreted phospholipase and a BPI-fold protein of airway mucus. Inducible nitric oxide synthase adds a reactive-nitrogen arm, while a claudin points to the tight-junction barrier these defences protect. Histone H2B proteins and ribosomal proteins appear because their fragments and cationic surfaces carry intrinsic membrane-permeabilizing activity. Loss or reduced expression of this repertoire predisposes to bacterial overgrowth, chronic inflammation and inflammatory bowel disease, placing it upstream of adaptive immunity in mucosal homeostasis.

Natural killer cells kill virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation and shape the wider response by secreting cytokines, and this is the machinery that lets them do it. Their decision to kill is a balance of signals: inhibitory receptors that read self MHC class I, including killer immunoglobulin-like receptors and the CD94/NKG2A pair with HLA-E, are opposed by activating receptors such as NKG2D reading stress ligands of the MICA and ULBP families, natural cytotoxicity receptors, DNAM-1, SLAM-family receptors and the Fc receptor that mediates antibody-dependent killing. Signals pass through ITAM adaptors like DAP12 and DAP10, PI3K, VAV1 and SH2D1A, while SHP-1 enforces inhibition. Killing itself requires polarised transport and fusion of granzyme- and perforin-bearing lytic granules, depending on RAB27A, UNC13D and LYST; mutations in these cause familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. IL-12, IL-18 and IL-21 drive interferon-gamma output, and checkpoint receptors such as TIGIT and TIM-3 restrain antitumour activity.

Host cells detect viral nucleic acids and then amplify the response that follows, and this pathway covers the processes that push that antiviral programme upwards rather than damping it. Its output is interferon and inflammatory cytokine production, restriction of viral replication, and recruitment of adaptive immunity; blunting it leaves cells permissive to infection, while excessive activity drives interferonopathy and autoinflammation. Cytosolic sensors for DNA and RNA are central here, with cGAS and STING handling DNA and RIG-I signalling through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, alongside the inflammasome components AIM2 and PYCARD. Downstream, STAT1 carries interferon signalling into transcription, a PARP9-DTX3L pair and several tripartite-motif proteins tune sensing and add restriction of their own, APOBEC3 deaminases mutate viral genomes, and IL-12 and IL-23 family cytokines and their receptors link innate detection to T cell effector responses.

Inflammation depends on getting leukocytes out of the blood and into tissue at the right place, and this pathway covers the directed migration of those cells toward inflammatory cues. Without it, bacteria and damaged tissue go uncleared; in excess, it drives the neutrophil and monocyte infiltration that damages joints, lung and vessel wall. The cues themselves are chemically diverse: ALOX5 initiates leukotriene synthesis from arachidonic acid to generate lipid chemoattractants, FFAR2 senses short-chain fatty acids from gut microbes, and LBP transfers bacterial lipopolysaccharide to its receptor complex to raise endotoxin sensitivity. The growth factors midkine and pleiotrophin act here as recruitment signals rather than mitogens, while SLAM-family receptors tune myeloid activation and NINJ1 contributes at the point where dying cells rupture and release further inflammatory material. Together they link pathogen and damage detection to cell movement.

response to molecule of bacterial origin is the cellular reaction to bacterial products such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, flagellin and peptidoglycan fragments, and it is how the innate immune system detects infection before any antibody exists. It sets the tempo of inflammation: too little and bacteria disseminate unchecked, too much and the same mediators produce sepsis, tissue injury and chronic inflammatory disease. Recognition runs through surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their accessory proteins CD14, LBP and LY96, and through cytosolic sensors such as NOD2 and the NLRP3 inflammasome, converging on MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 signalling to NF-kB, MAP kinases and interferon regulatory factors. The output is transcription of TNF, IL1B, IL6 and chemokines, inducible nitric oxide and antimicrobial peptides, phagocyte recruitment and antigen-presenting cell maturation. Negative regulators including A20, IRAK3, SIGIRR, ZC3H12A and several microRNAs enforce resolution and tolerance.

Host cells detect conserved bacterial products — lipopolysaccharide, lipoproteins, peptidoglycan fragments, flagellin, CpG DNA — and this response to molecules of bacterial origin converts that detection into inflammation, antimicrobial defence and tissue repair. It is the front line of innate immunity at epithelial surfaces and in macrophages and neutrophils; too little of it permits invasive infection, while too much drives sepsis, endotoxic shock and chronic inflammatory disease. Recognition runs through Toll-like receptors with CD14, LBP and the MD-2 partner LY96, and through the cytosolic sensor NOD2, feeding MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 into NF-κB, MAP kinase and interferon-regulatory transcription. Output includes IL-1β, IL-6, TNF and chemokines such as CXCL8, inflammasome-dependent caspase-1 processing, inducible nitric oxide synthase, and secreted antimicrobials including lactoferrin, lipocalin-2, cathelicidin and defensins. Negative regulators — TNFAIP3, IRAK3, SIGIRR, IL18BP, IL36RN, ZC3H12A and several microRNAs — restrain and terminate the reaction.

Detecting fungi depends on recognising their cell wall carbohydrates, and this response to molecules of fungal origin is how myeloid cells convert that recognition into inflammation and killing. Dectin-1, encoded by CLEC7A, binds β-glucan on Candida and Aspergillus and recruits spleen tyrosine kinase, which with the transmembrane adaptor SCIMP and the cytoplasmic kinase BTK builds a signalling module driving reactive oxygen production, phagocytosis, cytokine release and Th17-skewing of the subsequent adaptive response. MYD88 adds the parallel Toll-like receptor arm, so fungal lipopeptides and nucleic acids reinforce the same NF-κB output. Loss of these components in humans produces susceptibility to mucocutaneous and invasive fungal disease, and the same receptors shape responses to fungal components in asthma and inflammatory bowel disease. The pathway sits at the interface of pattern recognition, phagocyte effector function and antifungal immune instruction.

Hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation describes how mesoderm-derived precursors and hematopoietic stem cells acquire the identity of committed myeloid and lymphoid progenitors, the step that sustains lifelong production of blood and immune cells. Its failure underlies bone marrow failure syndromes, immunodeficiency and leukemia, since the same regulators that specify progenitors are recurrently mutated in transformed blood cells. Lineage choice is set by a core transcriptional network -- TAL1, MYB, SPI1, GATA3, SOX4, MLLT3 and HOX factors such as HOXB4 -- acting downstream of niche cues delivered through KIT and its ligand, FLT3, NOTCH1, BMP4 and TGF-beta family signals. Cytokine receptors couple to LYN, PTPN6 and RAS-ERK components to control progenitor proliferation and self-renewal, while m6A writers and readers, DNA repair and replication factors, and TP53 maintain genome integrity during rapid expansion.

All blood and immune cells descend from stem cells that first commit to intermediate progenitors, and hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation is the step in which a precursor acquires that restricted myeloid or lymphoid identity. It sets the output of the bone marrow for life; its failure underlies aplastic marrow syndromes, immunodeficiency and leukaemic transformation, since blocked or misdirected commitment is a recurring theme in myeloid malignancy. Lineage-determining transcription factors do much of the work — TAL1, MYB, SPI1, GATA3, SOX4 and the HOXB4/MLLT3 axis that sustains self-renewal — acting downstream of cytokine receptors such as KIT with its ligand KITLG, and FLT3, alongside Notch, BMP, TGF-beta/activin and Hedgehog cues from the niche. Chromatin and m6A RNA modification machinery, including METTL3/METTL14 and YTHDF2, plus genome-maintenance factors, tune how rapidly progenitors expand and differentiate.

wound healing involved in inflammatory response covers the repair of damaged tissue as it proceeds under, and is driven by, inflammation — the phase in which clotting, immune cell recruitment, and matrix remodelling are coordinated so that a breach is sealed and rebuilt rather than left open or scarred. It matters for skin and vascular injury, ulcer closure in diabetes, and fibrotic outcomes when the inflammatory phase fails to resolve. Damage-associated signals acting through TLR4 and the receptor for advanced glycation end products alert resident cells; thrombin acting on F2R links coagulation to that alert; IL1A amplifies it. Hypoxia sensing via HIF1A and the cytoprotective enzyme HMOX1 adapt cells to the wound's low-oxygen, oxidant-rich environment, while TGFB1 and TIMP1 drive fibroblast activation and restrain matrix degradation. PPARG provides an anti-inflammatory brake that steers macrophages toward resolution.

Tissue injury triggers repair and inflammation together, and this is the arm of wound healing that feeds into the inflammatory response: the events that restore barrier integrity while recruiting and instructing immune cells. It matters for how cleanly a wound closes — too little and healing stalls, as in chronic diabetic ulcers, too much and the result is fibrosis or scarring. Damage-associated signals sensed through TLR4 and AGER, together with thrombin acting on its receptor F2R, link clotting and innate immune activation to cytokine output such as IL1A. TGFB1 drives matrix deposition and myofibroblast behaviour, while TIMP1 restrains metalloproteinase-mediated matrix turnover. Hypoxia in the wound bed acts through HIF1A, and HMOX1 and PPARG temper oxidative and inflammatory tone, placing resolution alongside repair as part of the same programme.

When damaged tissue cannot regenerate its original cell types, or when fibrinous exudate persists at an inflamed site, the defect is filled instead with collagenous scar. This replacement of lost parenchyma by connective tissue during inflammatory wound healing restores mechanical integrity at the cost of function, and its unchecked continuation is fibrosis of the lung, liver, kidney and heart. Injury signals such as IL1A and thrombin acting through its protease-activated receptor, together with hypoxia sensed via HIF1A and advanced glycation end-product signalling through AGER, drive fibroblast recruitment and myofibroblast conversion. TGFB1 is the dominant fibrogenic cue, inducing matrix deposition while TIMP1 blocks metalloproteinase-mediated turnover so that collagen accumulates. Opposing inputs, including PPARG activity and miR-17 family repression of fibrogenic transcripts, restrain the response, and their loss favours persistent scarring over resolution.

Lymphocyte anergy is the state in which a T or B cell that has encountered antigen becomes functionally silent rather than activated, a form of peripheral tolerance that keeps self-reactive cells from causing autoimmunity while limiting damage from chronic stimulation. Cells enter this state when antigen receptor engagement occurs without adequate costimulation, and it is enforced actively: the E3 ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH mark receptor-proximal signalling components for degradation, and the phosphatase PHLPP1 dampens AKT-dependent survival and proliferative signalling downstream. Inhibitory surface receptors of the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like family contribute by raising the threshold for activation, while FOXP3 links the process to regulatory T cell-imposed suppression. Loss of these brakes yields hyperresponsive lymphocytes and autoimmune disease, whereas their sustained action underlies tolerance to self tissue, transplants, and tumour antigens.

Lymphocyte-based immunity that recognises antigen through somatically diversified receptors and remembers it, so that a second encounter with the same pathogen is met faster and harder — the basis of vaccination, and of autoimmunity and transplant rejection when it misfires. The gene complement spans the whole arc: recombining immunoglobulin and T cell receptor variable, joining and constant segments; the RAG1 and non-homologous end-joining machinery that cuts and repairs them; AICDA-driven class switching and affinity maturation; antigen processing and presentation by class I and class II HLA molecules, the peptide-loading transporters TAP1/TAP2, aminopeptidases and lysosomal cathepsins; and proximal receptor signalling through CD3 chains, ZAP70, SYK, BTK and LAT. Costimulatory and inhibitory checkpoints such as CD28, CTLA4 and PDCD1, cytokine–STAT circuits, and master transcription factors including TBX21, GATA3, RORC, BCL6 and FOXP3 set helper and regulatory fates, while complement and Fc receptors link antibody to effector clearance.

Immunity mounted locally within a particular organ or tissue differs from systemic responses: epithelial surfaces of the gut, airway, kidney and liver defend themselves with secreted antimicrobials and tissue-restricted lymphocytes rather than relying on circulating effectors. Much of the effector output here is chemical — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, lactoferrin, eosinophil-derived ribonucleases and bactericidal lipid-binding proteins secreted onto mucosal surfaces — alongside histone-derived antimicrobial activity. The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor ferries secretory antibody across epithelium, while interferon lambda acting through its epithelium-biased receptor gives barrier cells an antiviral state that spares systemic inflammation. Short-chain fatty acid sensing links microbial metabolites to local responses, and transcription factors such as RORC and ZBTB16 specify the innate-like and group 3 lymphoid cells that reside in these tissues. IL6 signalling and inducible nitric oxide synthase supply the inflammatory arm, whose dysregulation drives colitis, hepatic and neuroinflammatory disease.

Immune effector processes are the business end of an immune response: once lymphocytes and myeloid cells have been activated, these are the activities that actually destroy pathogens, kill infected or transformed cells, and clear debris. The programme spans complement activation and the lytic pore, cytotoxic granule exocytosis with perforin and granzymes, antibody production and class switching, phagocyte oxidative and proteolytic killing by neutrophil elastase and myeloperoxidase, and cytokine output including type I and type II interferons, interleukins and tumour necrosis factor. Antigen presentation on MHC class I, class II and CD1 molecules, Fc and complement receptors, natural killer activating and inhibitory receptors, and the co-stimulatory and checkpoint ligands that tune the strength of the attack are all represented. Too little of this activity leaves immunodeficiency and recurrent infection; too much, or misdirected, drives autoimmunity, allergy and tissue damage.

This is the set of processes that switch an immune response on, spanning the first detection of a threat through the signalling that commits cells to respond. It underlies host defence against bacteria, viruses and damaged self, and its miscalibration produces autoinflammatory disease, autoimmunity or failure to clear infection. Pattern recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like and RIG-I-like families, together with cytosolic DNA sensing through cGAS and STING, feed adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1 and MAVS into NF-kB and interferon regulatory factor activation; inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 drive IL1B maturation. In parallel, antigen receptor complexes on T and B cells signal via LCK, ZAP70, SYK and BTK with costimulatory and checkpoint receptors setting the threshold, while complement cascades and their regulators opsonise targets and amplify inflammation. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and phosphatases tune the strength and duration of activation.

The size of the peripheral lymphocyte pool stays remarkably constant, and lymphocyte homeostasis is the balance of survival, proliferation and deletion that holds it there without antigenic stimulation. Too little deletion gives lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity; too much, or loss of survival signals, gives immunodeficiency. Survival is set by cytokine input through IL2, its high-affinity receptor chain and JAK3-STAT5, and by BAFF-family ligands and receptors that support B cell persistence, with the BCL2 family acting as the intracellular rheostat between BCL2 and pro-apoptotic BAX, BAK1, BIM and NOXA. Death receptor signalling through FAS and FADD to caspases removes excess and self-reactive cells, while FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells and TGF-beta impose dominant restraint. Thymic selection, antigen receptor rearrangement by RAG1, thymoproteasome subunits and peptide loading contribute the developmental side, and negative regulators such as TNFAIP3 and the roquin proteins limit chronic activation.

Blood counts stay steady because the production of myeloid cells is balanced against their clearance, and myeloid cell homeostasis is the regulatory programme that keeps that balance in the absence of infection or bleeding. Most of the machinery here concerns the erythroid arm: lineage transcription factors such as GATA1, TAL1, KLF1 and SPI1 specify progenitors, the erythropoietin receptor acting through JAK2 and STAT5 sets survival and expansion, and heme synthesis enzymes, globins, iron transporters and red cell membrane proteins equip the mature cell. Counterbalancing this, apoptotic regulators including BAX, BAK1, BCL2L11 and CASP3, together with phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and AXL, remove excess or aged cells. Megakaryocyte and granulocyte output is represented too, via MPL and myeloid signalling kinases. Disturbance produces anemias, cytopenias, or myeloproliferative expansion.

Immune responses begin when a lymphocyte, myeloid cell or granulocyte switches from a resting to an effector state, and this pathway covers that transition: the receptor engagement, costimulation and cytokine cues that change a cell's shape, gene expression and secretory behaviour so that an immune reaction can be started and sustained. Antigen receptor proximal kinases and adaptors such as SYK, BTK, LYN, LAT and PLCG2 convert ligand binding into calcium and PI3K signalling; costimulatory pairs including CD28, CD80/CD86, CD40 with CD40LG and ICOS/ICOSLG set the threshold; interferons, interleukins and their JAK-STAT circuits, with lineage transcription factors such as TBX21, GATA3, RORC, FOXP3, IRF4 and SPI1, commit cells to particular effector programmes. Also present are mast cell and granule release machinery, class-switch recombination and DNA repair components, and inflammasome parts. Loss of these steps produces immunodeficiency, while unrestrained activation drives allergy and autoimmunity.

Neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, mast cells and basophils sit quiet until a ligand tells them otherwise; myeloid leukocyte activation is the shift in shape and behaviour that follows, converting a circulating cell into one that adheres, degranulates, phagocytoses and secretes. It underlies innate defence against bacteria and fungi, allergic and asthmatic responses, and the tissue damage of sepsis and chronic inflammation. Recognition comes through pattern receptors such as TLR4 and TLR9 signalling via MYD88 and TRAF6, Fc and immunoglobulin-E receptors, complement and formyl-peptide receptors, and lectin-like receptors coupled to TYROBP; these converge on SYK, BTK, LYN and SRC family kinases, PLCG2 and PI3K isoforms, restrained by phosphatases like PTPN6. Cytokine inputs including IL-33, IL-4, GM-CSF and interferon-gamma tune the response, while SNARE and UNC13D-dependent machinery executes granule release, and lineage factors SPI1 and CEBPA set the competence to respond.

Myeloid cells respond to microbial products, immune complexes, damage signals and soluble mediators by switching into an activated state, and this activation is what converts recognition into inflammation: degranulation, cytokine release, phagocytosis and recruitment of further leukocytes. It underlies innate defence and allergic hypersensitivity alike, and its dysregulation drives anaphylaxis, chronic inflammatory disease and cytokine-driven tissue damage. Recognition runs through immunoglobulin and pattern receptors coupled to the FCER1G/TYROBP adaptors and MYD88, with SYK, LYN, FGR, BTK, PLCG2 and PI3K isoforms carrying the signal to calcium flux and RAC2-dependent cytoskeletal change. Secretion of preformed granules depends on SNARE and regulatory machinery including VAMP proteins, STX4, STXBP2 and UNC13D, whose loss causes uncontrolled haemophagocytic syndromes. Transcription factors SPI1, GATA1 and GATA2 set the myeloid and mast cell background on which these responses occur, and inhibitory receptors such as CD300A, MILR1 and HAVCR2 restrain them.

Mast cell activation during an immune response is the switch from a resting tissue sentinel to a degranulating effector cell, and it underlies immediate hypersensitivity, allergic asthma, anaphylaxis and much of antiparasite defence, as well as itch and drug-induced pseudoallergic reactions. Antigen crosslinking of IgE bound to the high-affinity receptor, whose alpha and gamma chains are present here, triggers Src- and Syk-family kinases such as LYN, FGR and SYK, the adaptors LAT and GAB2, PI3K catalytic subunits and BTK, and calcium-dependent activation of RAS and PKC pathways. SNARE and Munc proteins including SNAP23, STXBP2, UNC13D and several VAMPs then drive fusion of histamine-loaded granules, while prostaglandin D synthase and IL13 add lipid and cytokine mediators. Inhibitory receptors such as CD300A and MILR1 and the phosphatase PTPN6 set the threshold; KIT signalling supports survival. MRGPRX2 provides an IgE-independent route.

Macrophage activation involved in immune response is the switch that turns a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell: on encountering a cytokine, microbial product, or damage signal it changes shape, ramps up phagocytosis, and begins secreting inflammatory mediators that recruit and instruct other immune cells. This step sets the tone of innate immunity and of the tissue response that follows, and its misregulation drives chronic inflammation, sepsis pathology, and neurodegenerative microglial states. The genes cover the triggering inputs (IFNG, IL1B, IL33, HMGB1 as an alarmin, LBP delivering bacterial lipopolysaccharide), the receptors and adaptors that read them (IL1R1 with IL1RAP, TICAM1 downstream of Toll-like receptors, TREM2 signalling through TYROBP and SYK), and the phospholipase and kinase relays that convert them into transcription. TNF and IL1B are the principal outputs, while TREX1 and SBNO2 restrain the response.

Macrophages are not fixed in one state: exposure to cytokines, microbial products, damage signals or cellular ligands converts a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell that phagocytoses, secretes inflammatory mediators and shapes the wider immune response. This activation drives host defence against infection, clearance of dying cells and debris, and the inflammatory tone of tissues, and its dysregulation underlies chronic inflammation, autoinflammatory disease and neurodegeneration. The genes here span the stimuli and their receivers: interferon gamma, TNF and IL-1 family cytokines with their receptor and accessory chains, the alarmin HMGB1 and lipopolysaccharide-binding protein, the metabolite sensor SUCNR1, and the TLR adaptor TICAM1. Downstream, the TREM2/TYROBP pair signals through SYK and PLCG2 to sustain microglial and macrophage responses to lipids and damaged tissue, while granulin and TREX1 restrain excessive activation.

Microglia are the resident macrophages of the brain, and their activation in the course of an immune response converts a surveying, ramified cell into a motile, phagocytic, cytokine-secreting one. This switch clears debris, dying neurons and misfolded protein aggregates, prunes synapses, and recruits other immune effectors; when it is mistuned the same programme drives chronic neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. The genes here mark the signals that trigger and restrain it: interleukin-1 beta acting through its receptor and the accessory subunit IL1RAP, the alarmin IL33 released from damaged tissue, and the fractalkine receptor CX3CR1 through which neurons hold microglia in a quiescent state. TREM2 with its obligate signalling adaptor TYROBP, together with progranulin, sets the phagocytic and lipid-handling response to damage, and loss-of-function alleles in these genes cause or predispose to frontotemporal dementia and Alzheimer disease.

Neutrophils patrol blood as pre-armed cells, and activation during an immune response is the switch that converts them from circulating bystanders into adherent, degranulating killers at a site of infection. Without it, bacteria and fungi are not cleared; with it running unchecked, released granule contents and chromatin damage host tissue, as in vasculitis and lupus-associated autoimmunity. Cytokines, chemokines and opsonised particles are sensed through integrin CD11b/CD18 pairs and immune receptors coupling via FCER1G and TYROBP to SYK and, for Toll-like receptor input, MYD88. The output is cytoskeletal change, adhesion, and regulated fusion of granules with the plasma membrane, executed by SNARE and SNARE-binding machinery including VAMP2, VAMP7, VAMP8 and STXBP2; loss of STXBP2 causes a haemophagocytic degranulation defect. SPI1 sets the myeloid transcriptional background, while secreted DNases limit the extracellular DNA that activated neutrophils leave behind.

When a lymphocyte meets antigen, cytokine or cellular ligand, it changes shape and behaviour and commits to an effector programme; this activation step converts recognition into a working immune response. It underlies protective immunity, vaccine responses and, when misdirected, autoimmunity and lymphoproliferative disease. Costimulatory and inhibitory surface pairs such as CD28 with CD80/CD86, CD40 with its ligand, ICOS with ICOSLG, and MHC class II presentation set the threshold for a response, while JAK1/JAK3 relay interleukin signals to STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A and STAT6. Lineage-defining transcription factors, including TBX21, GATA3, RORC, BCL6, FOXP3 and IRF4, then fix helper and regulatory identities. Also represented are the class switch and repair machinery of activated B cells, notably AICDA, UNG and mismatch-repair and end-joining factors, plus proteasome subunits and immunoproteasome components supporting antigen processing and NF- inkappaB-dependent gene expression.

T cell activation involved in immune response describes how a resting T cell, on encountering peptide-MHC together with costimulation and cytokines, changes shape, proliferates, and acquires an effector programme that drives host defence. It sets the tone of adaptive immunity: too little gives susceptibility to intracellular pathogens, too much gives autoimmunity and inflammatory disease. The genes span the recognition step -- class II MHC and its chaperone, CD80/CD86 and ICOS ligands, adhesion via ICAM1 and LFA-1 -- and the signalling that follows through PI3K-mTOR, PKC-MALT1-NF-κB, and JAK1/JAK3-STAT modules. Cytokine inputs including IL-2, IL-6, IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-27 and the interferons feed master transcription factors such as TBX21, GATA3, RORC, EOMES, BCL6 and FOXP3 that fix helper and regulatory lineage identity. Proteasome subunits, SOCS proteins, ZC3H12A and the roquin ligases restrain the response, and antigen processing supplies it.

When a T cell meets antigen presented on MHC together with costimulation, it changes shape, upregulates activation markers, proliferates and commits to an effector programme; this is the step that converts specific recognition into an actual immune response. The genes here span the antigen-presentation and costimulatory interface (HLA class II, CD74, CD80/CD86, ICOS and its ligand, ICAM1 and the integrin LFA-1), the cytokine and JAK-STAT circuitry that instructs lineage choice, and the transcription factors that define the resulting subsets — TBX21 for Th1, GATA3 for Th2, RORC for Th17, BCL6 for follicular helper and FOXP3 for regulatory T cells. Immunoproteasome subunits, IL-12/IL-23/IL-6 receptor components and negative regulators such as SOCS3, SMAD7 and the roquin proteins set the threshold and duration of the response. Too little yields immunodeficiency; unchecked activation drives autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.

T cell activation via T cell receptor contact with antigen bound to MHC molecule on antigen presenting cell describes the licensing step of adaptive immunity: a T cell changes shape and behaviour after its receptor engages peptide displayed on MHC by a dendritic cell, macrophage or B cell, committing it to proliferate and mount a response. Without productive contact the T cell remains naive or is tolerized, and the balance of stimulatory and inhibitory input here sets the difference between protective immunity, autoimmunity and tumour escape. The genes cover the physical side of the immunological synapse — integrin LFA-1 with ICAM-1 and the adaptor RIAM that clusters it, tetraspanin and MHC class II peptide-loading support — alongside checkpoint receptors such as TIM-3 and its galectin-9 ligand, LILRB1, and TREM2–TYROBP signalling in the presenting cell, plus semaphorin–plexin cues that tune contact duration.

T cells commit to an immune response only when their receptor engages a peptide displayed on MHC by an antigen-presenting cell, and this pathway covers the accessory contacts at that interface that decide whether the encounter activates, tunes down, or fails to move the T cell. It underlies antigen-specific adaptive immunity and, when misregulated, contributes to autoimmunity or to the exhausted, unresponsive T cells found in tumours and chronic infection. Adhesion and cytoskeletal components such as the integrin LFA-1 chain ITGAL, its ligand ICAM1, and the RAP1 effector APBB1IP stabilise the immunological synapse; HLA-DMB supports peptide loading onto class II MHC. Countering these are inhibitory inputs, notably the galectin-9/HAVCR2 axis and the MHC class I-binding receptor LILRB1, while TREM2 with its adaptor TYROBP and semaphorin-plexin contacts modulate the presenting cell side.

When a naive T cell meets antigen, it must choose what kind of cell to become: a helper of one flavour or another, a cytotoxic effector, a suppressive regulatory cell, or a long-lived memory cell. This differentiation step during an immune response sets the character of host defence, and its miscalibration underlies autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and failed responses to infection. Cytokine receptors and their JAK-STAT couplings feed into master transcription factors that lock in each fate, with TBX21 and STAT4 for type 1 responses, GATA3 and STAT6 for type 2, RORC with STAT3 downstream of IL-6, IL-21 and IL-23 for the IL-17 programme, FOXP3 for regulatory cells, and BCL6 for follicular helpers. Costimulation through CD80, CD86 and ICOS ligation, immunoproteasome-dependent antigen processing, mTOR-linked metabolic rewiring, and brakes such as SOCS3 and the RC3H RNA-binding repressors tune the outcome.

T-helper cell lineage commitment is the decision point at which an activated CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell locks into one of the helper fates that direct the rest of an immune response — Th1, Th2, Th17 and related subsets — determining whether the body mounts an antiviral, antiparasitic or antifungal defence, and whether that response tips into autoimmunity or allergy. Cytokines encountered at priming set the outcome: IL-12 and IL-23 receptors, IL-6 signalling through IL6R and gp130, and the JAK1/JAK3 kinases funnel into STAT3, STAT5A, STAT6 and the master transcription factors TBX21, IRF4 and BATF, which open subset-specific enhancers with the help of EP300 and BET proteins. SOCS3 restrains the same signals, while SLAM-family contacts, mTOR-dependent metabolic reprogramming and mitochondrial remodelling through OPA1 couple commitment to the energetic demands of clonal expansion and stable effector identity.

A naive CD4 T cell that has recognised antigen must choose which kind of helper cell to become, and T-helper lineage commitment is that decision: the point at which cytokine cues are converted into a stable, self-reinforcing transcriptional identity. The choice determines whether the ensuing response favours intracellular pathogens, worms and allergy, or mucosal defence, and skewed commitment underlies asthma, autoimmune inflammation and susceptibility to mycobacteria. Cytokine receptors for IL-6, IL-12 and IL-23 signal through JAK1 and JAK3 to STAT3, STAT5A and STAT6, which induce master regulators including TBX21 and IRF4; SOCS3 restrains this signalling. Chromatin readers and the acetyltransferase EP300 open the relevant cytokine loci, BATF cooperates with IRF4 at enhancers, and mTOR couples metabolic state to the outcome. SLAM-family receptors provide the T-T contact cues that accompany the decision.

When a mature B cell meets its antigen, it changes shape, proliferates, and remodels its immunoglobulin genes; this activation step during an immune response is what converts a naive lymphocyte into an antibody-secreting or memory cell. It depends on antigen receptor signalling through CD19 and PLCG2, costimulation by CD40 engaging CD40 ligand from helper T cells, and cytokine input including IL-4, IL-21, IL-6 and type I interferons acting via transcription factors such as STAT6, BCL6, BATF and POU2AF1. A large part of the machinery here serves class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation: AICDA deaminates cytosine in switch and variable regions, uracil-DNA glycosylase and mismatch repair proteins process the lesions, and 53BP1 with the shieldin complex and LIG4 channel the resulting breaks into end joining. XBP1 supports the secretory expansion of plasma cells. Defects give hyper-IgM syndromes, antibody deficiency, or lymphomagenesis from misrepaired breaks.

After antigen encounter, activated B cells in secondary lymphoid tissue enter a specialized, rapidly cycling state in which they undergo somatic hypermutation and affinity selection; germinal center B cell differentiation is the acquisition of that state, marked by loss of surface IgD and high peanut agglutinin binding. It is the step that converts a naive repertoire into high-affinity antibody and long-lived memory, so its failure leaves poor vaccine responses and defective class-switched immunity, while its dysregulation underlies lymphomas of germinal center origin. T follicular helper-derived IL21 and the inflammatory cytokine IL6 provide the extrinsic signals, and transcriptional regulators including the B cell coactivator POU2AF1 together with the ETS and interferon-regulatory factors SPI1 and IRF8 enforce the program intrinsically. The pathway sits downstream of antigen receptor and T cell help within humoral immunity.

Marginal zone B cells sit at the interface between blood and splenic white pulp, where they respond quickly to blood-borne bacteria and produce early, largely T-independent antibody against polysaccharide antigens and oxidised self-components. Their differentiation diverts transitional splenic B cells away from the follicular fate, and losing it leaves mice and people poorly protected against encapsulated bacteria. The decisive input is Notch: NOTCH2 signalling driven by the DLL1 ligand, with fringe glycosyltransferases such as LFNG and MFNG tuning receptor responsiveness to particular ligands, commits cells to the marginal zone programme. Downstream, the NF-κB regulator BCL3 supports the transcriptional outcome, while DOCK10 and DOCK11 act as Cdc42-directed exchange factors and PTK2B as a cytoplasmic kinase, linking commitment to the migration and positioning that keep these cells in their anatomical niche.

The end point of a B cell response is a plasma cell: a short-lived or long-lived factory that secretes large quantities of antibody, and plasma cell differentiation is the transition that produces it. Without it there is no durable humoral immunity or serum antibody; in excess or when unchecked it underlies myeloma and autoantibody-driven autoimmune disease. Activated B cells remodel their secretory apparatus, and XBP1 links the unfolded protein response to expansion of the endoplasmic reticulum needed for immunoglobulin output. Cytokines shape the decision from outside, with IL10 and IL2 acting on activated B cells to promote antibody-secreting fates, while transcriptional regulators such as NFKBIZ and NKX2-3 contribute downstream of activation and within the splenic and mucosal niches where the cells arise. Galectins and other surface and adhesion molecules influence the homing and survival of the differentiating cell.

Myeloid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which a multipotent haematopoietic precursor commits to the myeloid side of blood formation, generating the progenitors that later give rise to granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages, erythrocytes, and platelets. Without it the marrow cannot replenish innate immune cells or oxygen-carrying cells, and its deregulation is the basis of myeloid leukaemias and myelodysplasia. The commitment is enforced transcriptionally by PU.1, whose dose determines myeloid versus lymphoid fate, with chromatin remodelling subunits such as DPF2 shaping the accessible enhancer landscape. Receptor tyrosine kinases KIT and FLT3, acting through RAS-RAF signalling, supply the proliferation and survival cues that expand the committed pool, which is why activating mutations in these genes drive acute myeloid leukaemia. Adhesion molecules such as JAM3 tie progenitor behaviour to the marrow niche.

Myeloid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which multipotent haematopoietic precursors commit to the lineages that produce granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages, erythrocytes, megakaryocytes and mast cells, and it sets the supply of blood and innate immune cells for life. Two receptor tyrosine kinases, KIT and FLT3, read stem cell factor and FLT3 ligand from the marrow niche and drive progenitor survival and expansion, with BRAF carrying the signal into the MAP kinase cascade; SPI1 (PU.1) acts as the transcriptional master switch that specifies myeloid over lymphoid fate, assisted by chromatin regulators such as DPF2. Adhesive contact with the niche, mediated in part by JAM3, and regulators such as MLF1 tune whether progenitors proliferate or mature. Disruption of these signals underlies bone marrow failure, and constitutive activation of KIT, FLT3 or BRAF is a recurrent driver of myeloid leukaemia and mastocytosis.

Lymphoid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which a multipotent haematopoietic precursor commits to the lineages that give rise to T cells, B cells and innate lymphoid cells, and it sets the size and breadth of the adaptive immune system. Cytokine receptors such as FLT3 and KIT, relayed through RAS exchange factors, sustain progenitor survival and expansion, while Notch signalling and its HES targets, together with transcription factors including SPI1, GATA3, SOX4 and BATF, impose lineage choice; BCL2 keeps committed cells alive. Morphogens like BMP4 and Sonic hedgehog supply niche instruction. Because these progenitors immediately begin antigen receptor gene rearrangement, DNA double-strand break repair factors such as PRKDC and LIG4 are part of the same programme, and their loss produces severe combined immunodeficiency rather than a general growth defect.

B cell proliferation involved in immune response is the clonal expansion step that turns a few antigen-specific B cells into a population large enough to mount a useful antibody response. Without it, humoral immunity is quantitatively inadequate: germinal centre reactions fail and protective antibody titres never accumulate, while unrestrained proliferation of the same kind underlies B cell lymphomas and autoantibody-driven disease. The genes cover both the drive and the brake. Antigen receptor co-receptor CD19 and the kinase ABL1 amplify signals into cell cycle entry, and the Toll-like receptors CD180 and TLR4 provide microbial co-stimulation that lowers the threshold for division. Countering these, GAPT and the phospholipase C-like adaptor PLCL2 dampen receptor output and limit expansion, so the pathway sits at the junction of antigen recognition, innate sensing and proliferative control in the humoral arm of adaptive immunity.

Following antigen encounter, activated B cells must expand into a clone large enough to supply antibody, and this proliferative burst is what turns recognition into a useful humoral response. Its regulation sets the magnitude of antibody output; too little leaves poor protection after infection or vaccination, while unrestrained expansion contributes to autoantibody production and lymphoproliferation. The genes here sit on both sides of that balance: CD19 amplifies antigen receptor signalling to lower the threshold for division, while GAPT and PLCL2 act as brakes on B cell receptor-driven responses. CD180 and TLR4 add innate sensing of bacterial lipopolysaccharide, so microbial context can drive proliferation alongside antigen, and ABL1 kinase links receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and cell cycle machinery. The result couples antigen specificity, innate danger signals and negative feedback to clonal expansion during an immune response.

Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes that kill virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation, and their activation during an immune response converts a resting circulating cell into a degranulating, interferon-gamma-secreting effector. The trigger can come from cytokines, from antibody-coated targets sensed through the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR3A, or from receptor engagement of ligands on stressed cells, including recognition of HLA-F and signalling through CD160, CD244 and KLRC2; type I interferons and IL-12 provide the soluble priming context. Much of the gene content concerns the lytic granule itself: RAB27A, UNC13D, the granule membrane proteins LAMP1 and NKG7, and VAMP-family SNAREs govern granule transport, docking and fusion at the immune synapse, while CORO1A shapes the actin cytoskeleton needed to form it. Loss of the granule release machinery causes familial haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, in which failed cytotoxicity leads to uncontrolled immune activation.

Commitment of a lymphoid progenitor to the B cell lineage is the decision point at which a multipotent precursor gives up other fates and begins building an antibody-producing cell. Without it there are no B cells, no immunoglobulin, and no humoral immunity, and the arrest of this step underlies forms of severe combined immunodeficiency and agammaglobulinaemia. The genes here span the two demands of the transition: transcriptional specification, in which E-protein activity from TCF3 (E2A) drives expression of the early B cell programme, and V(D)J recombination of the immunoglobulin loci, where RAG2 introduces the double-strand breaks that DNA-PK catalytic subunit PRKDC helps repair through non-homologous end joining. BCL2-dependent survival keeps the newly committed precursor alive while these breaks are made and resolved, coupling lineage choice to controlled genome rearrangement.

The step at which a B cell precursor first becomes an immature B cell, expressing surface IgM after successful rearrangement of its immunoglobulin genes, is the gate through which all antibody-producing cells must pass. RAG1 and RAG2 cut and rejoin V, D and J segments, ATM oversees repair of the resulting double-strand breaks, and the assembled mu heavy chain paired with light chain gives the first true antigen receptor; cells that fail these tests are deleted or re-edited. Lineage transcription factors including SPI1 and SPIB commit progenitors to the B cell programme, while KIT signalling, FNIP1-dependent metabolic control and the survival cytokine BAFF set how many cells survive expansion and selection. Defects here produce severe combined immunodeficiency or agammaglobulinaemia, and the same recombination chemistry, when misdirected, drives translocations that initiate lymphoid leukaemia and lymphoma.

pro-B cell differentiation covers the earliest committed step of B lymphopoiesis, in which a bone marrow lymphoid progenitor takes on pro-B identity and begins joining diversity and joining segments of the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus. It sets the size and diversity of the antibody repertoire, and its failure produces arrest at the pro-B stage with absent mature B cells and immunodeficiency. Recombination intermediates are resolved by the non-homologous end joining machinery, with DNA-PKcs and DNA ligase IV sealing the coding and signal joins, so defects here cause radiosensitive severe combined immunodeficiency. Cytokine and receptor input through FLT3 and RAS activation via SOS1/SOS2 drives progenitor expansion, while Notch signalling and its HES targets bias progenitors toward or away from the T lineage. Folliculin and FNIP1 couple metabolic and mTOR-linked checkpoints to passage through this stage, and SOX4 supports the transcriptional program.

Pro-B cell differentiation is the first committed step of B lymphopoiesis, in which a lymphoid progenitor acquires pro-B identity and begins rearranging the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus by joining D and J segments. Without it there are no mature B cells and no antibody response, and the severe combined immunodeficiency caused by defective DNA repair at this stage illustrates the dependence directly: DNA-PKcs and DNA ligase IV complete the non-homologous end joining that seals the breaks made during V(D)J recombination. Cytokine input through the FLT3 receptor and the RAS exchange factors SOS1 and SOS2 drives progenitor expansion, while Notch signalling and its HES targets bias cells away from the B lineage toward T cell fates, so commitment requires that this pressure be relieved. SOX4 and the folliculin-FNIP1 nutrient-sensing module are further requirements for progression past this checkpoint.

pre-B cell differentiation is the developmental step in the bone marrow at which a pro-B cell, having rearranged and expressed an immunoglobulin heavy chain, becomes a pre-B cell and is tested for productive receptor assembly. It sets the size and diversity of the antibody repertoire, and its failure produces agammaglobulinemia and severe combined immunodeficiency. The recombinase components RAG1 and RAG2 introduce the double-strand breaks that join V, D and J segments, while ATM coordinates the DNA damage response that holds broken intermediates together and prevents translocations that would otherwise seed lymphoid malignancy. Surface expression of the mu heavy chain with surrogate light chain signals successful rearrangement and licenses proliferation and light chain recombination, with LAPTM5 and LRRC8A shaping receptor turnover and lymphocyte survival. The pathway couples programmed genome rearrangement to checkpoint control during lymphopoiesis.

Pre-B cell differentiation is the stage at which a pro-B cell rearranges its immunoglobulin heavy chain V, D and J segments and displays the resulting mu chain, the step that decides whether a developing lymphocyte can go on to make antibody. Everything downstream of it — a diverse antibody repertoire, mature B cells, humoral immunity — depends on this recombination succeeding, and its failure produces B cell aplasia and agammaglobulinaemia. The recombinase encoded by RAG1 and RAG2 introduces the double-strand breaks at recombination signal sequences, and ATM couples those breaks to the DNA damage response so that joining is completed faithfully and cells with unrepaired breaks are arrested or removed; defects here cause immunodeficiency with genomic instability. Expression of membrane IGHM marks successful rearrangement, while other components support the surface signalling and trafficking that accompany the transition.

Transitional B cells arriving in the spleen must choose a fate and finish maturing, and this final differentiation step generates the follicular and marginal zone populations that mount antibody responses to blood-borne antigen. Without it the peripheral B cell pool is incomplete, marginal zone compartments fail to form, and responses to encapsulated bacteria and to T cell help are impaired. Notch signalling through NOTCH2, its ligand DLL1 and the fringe glycosyltransferases that tune ligand binding directs marginal zone commitment, while tonic antigen receptor signalling via CD19, PLCG2, PTK2B and the NF-kB arm through MALT1 and BCL3 sets survival and positioning thresholds; FCGR2B and GPR183 shape inhibitory input and follicular migration. Transcriptional regulators including SPI1, IRF8, POU2AF1 and NKX2-3 maintain lineage identity and splenic architecture, and cytokines such as IL2, IL6, IL10 and IL21 push cells toward antibody secretion, with XBP1 preparing the secretory apparatus.

This is the set of cellular changes triggered when an immune cell or tissue encounters a tumour cell, spanning recognition, cytotoxic attack, and the inhibitory feedback that limits it. It matters because it determines whether a nascent tumour is cleared or tolerated, and its inhibitory arm is the target of checkpoint blockade immunotherapy. Recognition runs through MHC class I and class II molecules, the stress-induced ligand MICA, and nectin-family ligands such as PVR and NECTIN2 read by activating receptors including CD226 and CRTAM. Killing is executed by perforin and granule proteins and by death receptor and gasdermin-dependent lysis. Counterbalancing this, PDCD1, CTLA-4-like and TIM-3/LAG-3 receptors together with the ligand CD274 and TGFB1 dampen effector function, while HMGB1 and heat shock proteins act as danger signals that recruit and mature antigen-presenting cells.

Immune surveillance and cell-intrinsic tumour suppression converge in the defense response to tumour cells, the set of reactions an organism mounts when a transformed cell appears. Its effectiveness determines whether nascent tumours are eliminated or escape to grow, and its loss is a step in carcinogenesis. Two arms are represented: cytotoxic killing, where perforin delivers pore-forming attack from lymphocyte granules and the death receptor TNFRSF10B triggers apoptosis on engagement by its TRAIL ligand; and growth-suppressive control within the target cell, where the kinase DAPK1 promotes apoptosis and the transcription factor KLF4 restrains proliferation. Myeloid and lymphoid identity factors such as SPI1, the endolysosomal protein LAPTM5 and the NF-kB subunit RELA place much of this activity in immune cells, linking inflammatory transcription to antitumour effector function and tumour immune evasion.

T cell lineage commitment is the step at which a multipotent lymphoid progenitor loses access to B, myeloid and NK fates and is fixed on a T cell path, a decision made in the thymus and prerequisite for all adaptive cell-mediated immunity. Thymic epithelial cues, including the FOXN1-dependent stromal niche, IL-7 signalling through JAK1/JAK3 and STAT5, and Notch-associated inputs drive survival and proliferation of committed progenitors while RAG2 and PRKDC carry out and repair the DNA breaks of antigen receptor gene rearrangement. Transcriptional regulators such as TOX, IRF4, BATF and the bromodomain proteins BRD2/BRD4, together with the acetyltransferase EP300, remodel chromatin to lock in identity. Downstream cytokine circuits involving IL-6, IL-12, IL-23 and STAT3 bias effector differentiation, with FOXP3 and TBX21 specifying regulatory and Th1 programmes. Failure yields severe combined immunodeficiency or thymic aplasia; deregulation contributes to T cell leukaemia and autoimmunity.

Regulatory T cells enforce peripheral tolerance, restraining effector responses to self and to harmless antigens, and this pathway covers the differentiation of CD4-positive, CD25-positive alpha-beta T cells into that suppressive lineage. Loss of the programme is not subtle: mutation of the lineage-defining transcription factor FOXP3 causes early, systemic autoimmunity affecting gut, endocrine organs and skin, while excessive regulatory T cell induction blunts antitumour and antiviral immunity. Commitment follows T cell receptor engagement of peptide presented on MHC class II together with cytokine input through the common gamma chain shared by the IL-2 receptor, with transcriptional regulators such as TOX shaping the differentiating state. Galectin-9 and selectin-ligand fucosylation link the emerging cells to inhibitory receptor engagement and tissue homing, so differentiation here is inseparable from where these cells later act.

Immune cells communicate largely by secreting cytokines, and this pathway covers the induction of that output after a cell detects infection, damage or a signal from another leukocyte. It sets the size and flavour of an immune response: too little leaves pathogens unchecked, too much drives fever, septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern recognition receptors for microbial nucleic acids, lipopolysaccharide and fungal glucans, together with RNA sensors and their adaptors, feed through kinases and ubiquitin ligases to transcription of interferons, tumour necrosis factor, interleukin-1 beta and interleukin-6. An inflammasome component controls maturation and release of interleukin-1 family members. Lineage-defining transcription factors such as T-bet, GATA3, BCL6 and FOXP3 direct which cytokines a T cell makes, while transforming growth factor beta, interleukin-10 and inhibitory receptors restrain production, and MHC class I molecules and metabolic enzymes tune the threshold.

Effector T cells act largely by secreting cytokines, and this pathway covers the inputs and regulators that determine how much of which cytokine a T cell makes. The output sets the character of an immune response: interferon-gamma-dominated defence against intracellular pathogens, type 2 cytokines driving allergy and helminth immunity, or restraint that prevents autoimmunity and cytokine-driven tissue damage. Lineage transcription factors including TBX21, GATA3 and FOXP3 commit cells to distinct cytokine programmes; MHC class I molecules and costimulatory or coinhibitory receptors such as SLAMF1, TNFSF4 and BTLA tune the strength of the activating signal; and MALT1, MAP3K7, TRAF2 and TRAF6 relay receptor engagement to NF-kB-dependent transcription. Innate signals feed in as well, with IL-18 and IL-1 receptor signalling and inflammasome-derived cytokines amplifying T cell output, while SMAD7 and ARG1 mark suppressive influences on it.

Natural killer cells respond to infection and tumour cells not only by killing them but by secreting cytokines, above all interferon-gamma and TNF, which recruit and instruct macrophages and shape the ensuing T cell response. This pathway covers the receptor inputs and intracellular relays that set how much cytokine an NK cell makes. Activating receptors such as CD226 (DNAM-1) engage stress-induced ligands of the RAET1/ULBP family, while non-classical MHC molecules HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G, together with the receptors CD160 and KIR2DL4, report on the health and identity of the target cell and can either license or restrain the response; KIR2DL4 recognition of HLA-G is notable at the maternal-fetal interface. The adaptor CLNK couples receptor engagement to secretion, and IL21 from helper T cells amplifies it. Tuning here determines whether inflammation is protective or damaging.

Dendritic cells translate detection of microbial material into the cytokine signals that instruct T cells, and this pathway covers how that output is generated. Interferons and interleukins released by these cells set the direction of the ensuing adaptive response, so too little leaves infection unchecked while excess drives autoimmunity and inflammatory pathology. Sensing is distributed across compartments: surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors for lipopolysaccharide, double-stranded RNA and CpG DNA, the C-type lectin CLEC7A for fungal beta-glucan, and cytosolic RNA recognition by RIG-I signalling through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, with TICAM1 carrying the TRIF-dependent arm. Several DEAD/DEAH-box helicases act as additional nucleic acid sensors. Downstream, PLCG2 and calcium-dependent CAMK4 signalling, JAK3, and the transmembrane adaptor SCIMP shape the transcriptional response, while BST2 links interferon-induced antiviral restriction back to this circuitry.

Myeloid dendritic cells are the sentinels that convert detection of a pathogen into an instructive cytokine signal, and cytokine production by these cells sets the tone of the ensuing T cell response — type I interferon for antiviral defence, and inflammatory cytokines that shape helper cell polarisation. The genes here mark the nucleic acid sensing routes that trigger that output: the RNA helicase RIG-I signalling through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, the TRIF adaptor relaying Toll-like receptor engagement, and a DDX1–DDX21–DHX36 complex together with DHX36 acting as sensors of double-stranded and CpG DNA-associated ligands. Calcium\/calmodulin-dependent kinase IV links receptor-proximal calcium flux to transcription factor activation in the same cells. Too little of this activity leaves viral infection unchecked and vaccine adjuvants inert; too much feeds interferon-driven autoimmunity.

Antibody output by B cells is the effector arm of humoral immunity, and this pathway covers the signals, transcriptional programmes and DNA transactions that raise immunoglobulin levels inside and outside the cell. T cell help through CD40/CD40LG and cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21, IL-6 and IL-10 licenses activation, while STAT6, BATF, BCL6, TCF3 and XBP1 steer germinal centre reactions and the secretory expansion of plasma cells. Class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation begin with AICDA-induced uracils processed by UNG and mismatch repair factors, then resolved by non-homologous end joining and shieldin-dependent end protection involving TP53BP1, RIF1, LIG4 and XRCC4, with translesion polymerases introducing mutations. Inhibitory receptors such as CD22 and FCGR2B restrain the response. Loss of these steps produces hyper-IgM syndromes, common variable immunodeficiency and poor vaccine responses; unchecked activity contributes to autoantibody disease and lymphomagenesis.

Antibody output during an immune response depends on B cells not only secreting immunoglobulin but first remodelling the antibody genes that encode it, and this pathway covers both the induction of immunoglobulin production and the DNA transactions that shape it. Its failure produces hyper-IgM syndromes and broader antibody deficiency, with recurrent infection and poor vaccine responses; excessive activity contributes to autoantibody disease. T cell help through CD40-CD40L and costimulation, together with cytokines such as IL-4, IL-10, IL-21-family signals and TGF-beta acting via STAT6 and transcription factors including BCL6 and BATF, licenses class switching. AICDA deaminates cytosine in switch and variable regions; uracil glycosylase and mismatch repair proteins convert these lesions to breaks, which 53BP1, RIF1, the shieldin complex and non-homologous end joining resolve, coupling DNA damage signalling to isotype diversification and affinity maturation.

Immune responses mounted in gut-associated lymphoid tissue — Peyer's patches, the appendix and solitary lymphoid follicles — are how the intestine samples luminal contents and decides between tolerance to food and commensals and defence against pathogens. The output is secretory antibody, resident innate-like lymphocytes and a locally imprinted memory pool, and its failure contributes to mucosal infection and inflammatory bowel disease. The genes here point to two requirements. First, homing: the integrin pair ITGA4 and ITGB7 forms α4β7, which binds MAdCAM-1 on intestinal endothelium and directs lymphocytes into gut tissue, a route blocked therapeutically in colitis. Second, lineage specification: RORC drives the RORγt-dependent programme of Th17 cells, group 3 innate lymphoid cells and lymphoid tissue inducer cells that build these follicles, ZBTB16 specifies innate-like T cells, and ZBTB46 marks conventional dendritic cells that present sampled antigen.

Dendritic cells only work as antigen-presenting cells if they can travel: from blood into inflamed tissue, and then out again through lymphatics to the T cell zones of lymph nodes. Directed migration along chemokine gradients is what makes that journey possible, and losing it leaves antigen stranded in the periphery and T cell priming impaired. Immature cells respond to inflammatory cues through receptors such as CCR1, CCR2, CCR5 and CCR6, while maturation switches them to CCR7, which reads the CCL19 and CCL21 gradients laid down by lymphoid stroma; CXCR4 and the oxysterol receptor GPR183 provide additional positional cues. Downstream, PI3K-gamma and Rho-family GTPase exchange factors convert receptor engagement into cytoskeletal polarity, and TRPM channels contribute the calcium signals that motility requires. Damage-associated signals including HMGB1 and calreticulin recruit these cells to dying tissue, linking chemotaxis to the initiation of adaptive immunity.

Myeloid dendritic cell chemotaxis describes the directed migration of antigen-bearing dendritic cells out of peripheral tissues and into draining lymph nodes, the step that physically connects innate antigen capture to T cell priming. Without it, antigen stays in the periphery, lymph node T cell zones are poorly populated, and adaptive responses to infection and vaccination fail to be initiated; the same axis is exploited by tumours and by metastasising cells to reach lymphoid tissue. Mechanistically, maturing dendritic cells upregulate CCR7 and follow gradients of the lymphoid chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 produced by stromal and lymphatic endothelial cells, with receptor engagement converted into polarised actin remodelling through Rho-family exchange factors such as ARHGEF5. The myeloid identity of the migrating cell is set upstream by the transcription factor SPI1, tying leukocyte lineage specification to this trafficking programme.

Myeloid dendritic cells only present antigen usefully if they can leave the tissue where they captured it and find the T cell zones of a draining lymph node, and this directed migration is what the chemotaxis programme provides. Stromal and lymphatic endothelial cells lay down the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, which the receptor CCR7 reads on the maturing dendritic cell surface, converting a gradient into polarized crawling toward and along lymphatic vessels. Downstream, a Rho-family guanine nucleotide exchange factor couples that signal to cytoskeletal rearrangement, while the myeloid transcription factor PU.1 specifies the cell type in which this machinery is expressed. Loss of the receptor or its ligands strands antigen-loaded cells in the periphery, blunting priming of naive T cells and tolerance induction; the same axis is exploited by tumour cells for nodal metastasis.

Tumours are recognised and attacked by the immune system, and this immune response to tumour cells covers both the killing machinery and the checkpoints that restrain it. Cytotoxic lymphocytes and NK cells detect transformed cells through MHC class I and class II molecules, the stress-induced ligand MICA, and the nectin-family ligands PVR and NECTIN2 read by the activating receptor CD226; perforin and NKG7-dependent granule release then deliver lethal hits, with gasdermin E converting caspase cleavage into pyroptotic tumour death. Opposing this, inhibitory receptors including PD-1, LAG3, TIM-3, BTLA and CD160, together with the ligand PD-L1, CEACAM1 and TGF-beta, dampen T cell activation and underlie immune evasion; they are the targets of checkpoint blockade therapy. IL-12 subunits and released HMGB1 amplify the response, while ubiquitin-pathway components such as FBXO38 control receptor turnover on effector cells.

Natural killer cells recognise and kill transformed cells without prior sensitisation, and this pathway describes the receptor-ligand decisions and cytokine inputs that determine whether a tumour cell is destroyed or tolerated. Killing depends on the balance of activating and inhibitory contacts at the immune synapse: DNAM-1 (CD226) and CRTAM engage nectin-family ligands such as PVR and nectin-2 that are frequently upregulated on tumours, while CEACAM1 and TIM-3 (HAVCR2) deliver restraining signals and CD160 contributes to recognition of MHC class I-related ligands. Interleukin-12, formed from the IL12A and IL12B subunits, licenses cytotoxicity and interferon-gamma output, whereas TGF-beta suppresses it, a major route by which tumours escape surveillance. Granule protein NKG7 supports degranulation and target lysis. The same axes are targets of checkpoint-directed cancer immunotherapy, and their subversion permits outgrowth of otherwise immunogenic tumours.

Tumours are visible to the immune system because T cells read peptides displayed on MHC molecules, and this pathway covers the recognition and effector arm of that response along with the brakes that limit it. Its outcome determines whether a nascent tumour is eliminated or escapes, and it is the biology exploited by checkpoint blockade therapy. Class I and class II molecules together with the non-classical antigen-presenting molecule MR1 supply the ligands; PD-1 and its ligand CD274, together with LAG3 and BTLA with its ligand TNFRSF14, deliver inhibitory signals that dampen T cell activation and underlie exhaustion in the tumour microenvironment. Ubiquitin-pathway components including FBXO38 and KLHL22 control the abundance of these receptors, while released HMGB1 and HSPD1 act as danger signals and IL4I1 and AHR contribute tryptophan-derived immunosuppression. Failure here permits immune evasion and tumour outgrowth.

Antigen processing and presentation of peptide antigen via MHC class Ib is the display of peptides on non-classical class I molecules such as HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G, rather than on the classical HLA-A/B/C molecules that prime conventional cytotoxic T cells. This arm of antigen presentation speaks mainly to innate lymphocytes: HLA-E loaded with leader peptides from other class I proteins reports on the integrity of the whole presentation system to NK cell receptors, and HLA-G at the maternal-fetal interface enforces tolerance toward the trophoblast. Like the classical molecules, these heavy chains require beta-2 microglobulin and peptide delivered through the transporter associated with antigen processing. Related surface ligands of the RAET1/ULBP family are recognised by the same innate effectors as stress signals. Loss or tumour-driven remodelling of this axis lets cancers and viruses evade NK surveillance.
