Non-classical MHC class Ib molecules display peptides and related ligands at the cell surface to report a cell's internal state to lymphocytes, complementing the classical class I route that presents to conventional cytotoxic T cells. Presentation via HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G tunes natural killer and T cell responses rather than simply flagging foreign peptides: HLA-G restrains maternal immune attack on trophoblast at the placental interface, and HLA-E signals whether normal class I synthesis is intact. All of these heavy chains require beta-2-microglobulin for assembly and depend on transporter-mediated delivery of peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum. The accompanying ULBP and RAET1 stress-induced ligands share the class I fold but engage activating NK receptors instead of presenting peptide. Loss or subversion of this axis contributes to viral immune evasion, tumour escape from NK surveillance, and pregnancy disorders.

Complement activation generates fragments that are not just opsonins but ligands, and complement receptor mediated signalling is how cells read them. Binding of C3a, C5a or C3b-coated surfaces to their receptors tells phagocytes and other leukocytes where inflammation is, driving chemotaxis, degranulation, oxidative burst and phagocytic uptake, and it links innate recognition to adaptive responses when complement-tagged antigen engages B cells. The anaphylatoxin receptors C3AR1, C5AR1 and C5AR2 act through G protein-coupled cascades converging on kinases such as AKT1, while CR1 and CR2 handle bound C3 fragments and the integrin CD11b (ITGAM) mediates iC3b-dependent adhesion and ingestion. Related formyl peptide and chemerin receptors share this chemoattractant signalling logic, including receptors for resolution-phase lipid mediators. Excessive signalling here contributes to sepsis, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and autoimmune tissue damage, making these receptors sought-after anti-inflammatory drug targets.

Antibody-coated targets are recognized by immune cells through Fc receptors, and the stimulatory signalling that follows converts that binding into phagocytosis, degranulation, respiratory burst and cytokine release. This is how immunoglobulin specificity is translated into effector action, underlying clearance of opsonized microbes, antibody-dependent killing of tumour cells, and the tissue damage of immune-complex disease. Receptor engagement clusters the ITAM-bearing gamma chain, which recruits the kinase SYK and Src-family members such as LYN, FYN, HCK and FGR; downstream VAV exchange factors, RAP1A and PAK1/LIMK1 drive cytoskeletal remodelling, while phospholipases and protein kinase C isoforms generate lipid second messengers. Output includes inducible nitric oxide synthase and interferon gamma. The same list carries the brakes: CSK, the phosphatases CD45 and PTPRJ, and the CD47 axis set thresholds so that activation stays proportionate to the antibody signal.

Phagocytes engulf antibody- or complement-coated microbes and debris, and this is the receptor-proximal signalling that licenses engulfment: surface immune receptors detect bound particles and convert that contact into local actin remodelling and membrane extension around the target. It underlies clearance of bacteria, apoptotic cells and immune complexes, and its failure leaves opsonised pathogens uningested and debris uncleared, a contributor to infection susceptibility and autoimmune inflammation. Src-family kinases such as LYN, FGR, HCK, FYN and SRC together with SYK phosphorylate receptor tails and adaptors; VAV family exchange factors activate Rho-family GTPases, and PAK1 with LIMK1 drives cytoskeletal reorganisation at the forming phagocytic cup. Protein kinase C isoforms, phospholipases and phosphatidic acid metabolism contribute lipid second messengers, while IFNG priming and inducible nitric oxide synthase tie ingestion to subsequent microbial killing.

Antibodies bound to antigen form lattices that must be taken out of circulation before they lodge in vessel walls, glomeruli and joints; immune complex clearance is the disposal route that keeps this from happening. It matters most where it fails: persistent complexes drive the glomerulonephritis, vasculitis and serum-sickness-like inflammation seen in lupus and other antibody-mediated disease. The genes here span the steps involved. Complement receptor 1 on erythrocytes captures complement-opsonised complexes and ferries them to hepatic and splenic phagocytes; the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B binds IgG and raises the threshold for activation, so that uptake occurs without runaway inflammation; a chemokine receptor recruits monocytes to sites of deposition; and clusterin acts as an extracellular chaperone limiting precipitation of aggregated material. The pathway thus links humoral immunity to phagocytic housekeeping and to tolerance.

Inflammation triggered by antigen recognition is how the adaptive immune system converts epitope-specific sensing into the local tissue changes of swelling, leukocyte recruitment and mediator release, and it underlies both protective immunity and allergic and autoimmune disease. Antigen presented on MHC class II engages T cells whose costimulation and receptor-proximal signalling run through Src-family kinases, SYK, BTK, PLCG1 and RASGRP1, while immunoglobulin-bound antigen is read by IgE and IgG receptors on mast cells, basophils and phagocytes to drive degranulation and complement-assisted clearance. Cytokine output and receptor usage here define the type 2 arm in particular, with GATA3 directing the transcriptional programme and IL5, IL25 and IL31 receptor components marking eosinophil and pruritic effector routes, balanced by IL10. Alarmins such as HMGB1, TNF and lymphotoxin amplify the response, and stress-activated MAPK14 signalling sustains it.

When an antigen is encountered by a primed immune system, the response mounted within minutes to hours is antibody-driven rather than purely innate, and this pathway covers that acute inflammatory reaction. It underlies immediate hypersensitivity and allergy, serum sickness and immune-complex disease, as well as protective clearance of opsonised targets. IgE and IgG bound to antigen engage Fc receptors: the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells and basophils triggers degranulation through its signalling gamma chain and the kinase BTK, while activating and inhibitory IgG receptors set the threshold for phagocyte and neutrophil activation, with complement C3 amplifying the reaction. Downstream effects include neutrophil elastase release, selectin ligand-dependent leukocyte trafficking, and chemokine-guided migration to lymph nodes. GATA3 links the response to type 2 T helper polarisation, which drives the IgE class switching that makes this loop self-sustaining and, if unresolved, chronic.

Immune responses work largely through secreted and surface-displayed molecules, and this pathway covers the making and release of those mediators — cytokines, immunoglobulins, antimicrobial peptides and MHC-presented ligands — so that their levels rise where a response is needed. Loss or excess of this output underlies immunodeficiency on one side and inflammatory, allergic and autoimmune disease on the other. Two arms dominate the gene membership. One is cytokine production driven by innate sensing (Toll-like receptors, nucleic-acid sensors such as cGAS and RIG-I, inflammasome components including NLRP3) and by helper T cell programmes set by TBX21, GATA3, FOXP3 and BCL6, yielding interferons, TNF, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-17 and the type 2 cytokines IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13. The other is antibody production in B cells: AICDA-initiated class switching and somatic hypermutation handled by mismatch repair, uracil processing and non-homologous end joining, with XBP1 and MZB1 supporting secretory plasma cell differentiation.

Leukocyte mediated immunity covers the effector arms of immune defence that white blood cells actually carry out: killing infected and transformed cells, degranulating against microbes, opsonising and lysing pathogens, and secreting antibody. It is what converts immune recognition into clearance, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, uncontrolled infection and impaired tumour surveillance, while its excess drives autoimmunity and hyperinflammation. The genes span cytotoxic granule contents and their release machinery (perforin, granzymes, RAB27A, UNC13D, syntaxins and VAMPs), neutrophil azurophil proteases such as elanase and cathepsin G, the complement cascade with its regulators, Fc and NK receptor families (FCGR, KLR, KIR, NCR) signalling through SYK, BTK and ITAM adaptors, MHC and CD1 antigen presentation, and immunoglobulin loci with the class-switch and somatic hypermutation machinery. Cytokine receptors and lineage transcription factors set which effector program a leukocyte adopts.

Leukocyte mediated immunity covers the effector work that white blood cells actually perform once mobilised: killing infected and tumour cells, degranulating, phagocytosing opsonised targets, and secreting antibody and cytokines. It is what converts recognition into clearance of pathogens, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, haemophagocytic syndromes and recurrent infection, while its excess drives autoimmunity and tissue damage. The genes span several effector arms: cytotoxic granule contents and the machinery that releases them, including perforin, granzymes and the exocytosis regulators UNC13D, STXBP2 and RAB27A; activating and inhibitory receptors of NK and T cells such as KLRK1, KIR and PDCD1, signalling through SYK, LYN, BTK, VAV1 and PI3K subunits; Fc and complement receptors that couple immunoglobulin and the complement cascade to myeloid ingestion; neutrophil granule proteases; MHC class I, class II and CD1 lipid presentation; and the immunoglobulin loci with the class-switch and somatic hypermutation apparatus, AICDA and mismatch and end-joining repair factors, that diversify antibody effector function.</description>

Neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, mast cells and basophils execute immunity through phagocytosis, degranulation and release of inflammatory mediators, and this myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity is the arm of host defence that handles bacteria and fungi and drives allergic inflammation. Recognition is largely through Fc receptors for IgG and IgE, complement receptors and integrins such as CD11b/CD18, plus innate sensors signalling via MYD88, IRAK4, CARD9 and RIG-I-like receptors. Engagement is transduced by ITAM adaptors FCER1G and TYROBP into SYK, LYN, FGR, BTK and PI3K signalling, culminating in NADPH oxidase assembly through NCF1 and RAC2 and in granule exocytosis using SNAREs and the UNC13D/STXBP2 machinery. Granule cargo includes elastase, cathepsin G and azurocidin, while lineage factors SPI1, GATA1 and GATA2 and the KIT receptor specify the cells themselves. Defects cause recurrent infection, impaired killing, haemophagocytic syndromes or mast cell-driven hypersensitivity.

Antibody-dependent destruction of the body's own cells is the hallmark of type II hypersensitivity: IgG or IgM bound to antigens on a cell surface marks that cell for complement attack, for phagocytosis, or for killing by Fc receptor-bearing effectors, and antibodies against cellular receptors can instead block or inappropriately stimulate them. This is the basis of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, transfusion reactions, Graves' disease and myasthenia gravis, and also of the mechanism by which therapeutic antibodies clear target cells. Complement component C3 deposition opsonises the target, while activating Fc gamma receptors on macrophages, neutrophils and NK cells, together with the shared FCER1G signalling chain, drive phagocytosis and cytotoxic granule release; FCGR2B provides the inhibitory counterweight that raises the threshold for effector activation. The pathway sits at the interface of humoral immunity and innate effector function.

Neutrophils are the first responders of innate immunity, and this programme covers the effector functions they carry out once recruited to infected or damaged tissue: adhesion and transmigration, phagocytosis, degranulation, oxidative burst and release of extracellular traps. Loss of these functions produces recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, as seen in congenital neutropenia and chronic granulomatous disease, while unrestrained activity drives tissue injury in sepsis and inflammatory disease. The genes cover granule proteases stored in azurophilic granules such as elastase, cathepsin G and azurocidin, the SNARE and Munc18 machinery that docks granules for fusion, the beta-2 integrin pair that mediates firm adhesion, NADPH oxidase subunit NCF1 for superoxide generation, and receptor-proximal signalling through SYK, MYD88, IRAK4 and CARD9. Transcriptional identity is supplied by SPI1, and extracellular DNases limit the persistence of released chromatin.

Eosinophils carry out immunity against helminths and contribute to the tissue damage of allergic disease, and this pathway covers how they are recruited and how they release their armament. Recruitment depends on chemokine signalling, with CCR2 and CCL3 drawing cells from blood into inflamed tissue; activation can also come through IgE bound to its high-affinity receptor and through protease-activated receptor signalling, linking mast cell-type allergic triggers and local proteases to eosinophil responses. The output is degranulation: SNARE proteins including syntaxin 4 and several VAMP isoforms drive fusion of crystalloid granules and secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane, discharging cationic proteins, cytokines and lipid mediators. TRAF3IP2 couples IL-17-family receptor input to NF-κB-driven inflammatory transcription. Excessive activity of this axis underlies asthma, eosinophilic esophagitis and hypereosinophilic syndromes.

Lymphocyte mediated immunity covers the effector arms by which T, B and NK cells eliminate infected or transformed cells and neutralise pathogens, and it is what vaccination exploits and what fails in primary immunodeficiency. Three themes dominate the membership. Antigen presentation and recognition: classical and non-classical MHC molecules, CD1 lipid-presenting proteins, and the activating and inhibitory receptors of NK cells, including KLRK1 with its ULBP and MICA ligands, balanced against checkpoint receptors such as PDCD1, HAVCR2, LAG3 and TIGIT. Cytotoxic killing: perforin and granzymes delivered by a granule secretion machinery requiring RAB27A, UNC13D and LYST, whose loss causes haemophagocytic syndromes. Humoral output: immunoglobulin heavy and light chain genes, AICDA-driven class switch recombination with its DNA repair partners, complement components that opsonise and lyse antibody-coated targets, and Fc receptors. Cytokines and lineage transcription factors such as TBX21, GATA3 and FOXP3 set which effector programme is used.

Antibodies secreted into blood and lymph protect by binding pathogens and then recruiting effector machinery, and the humoral immune response mediated by circulating immunoglobulin is that arm of adaptive immunity. Its core output is opsonisation and lysis: immunoglobulin heavy chains of the IgM, IgG, IgA, IgD and IgE classes, together with the classical pathway initiators C1q, C1r and C1s, trigger a proteolytic cascade through C2, C3, C4 and C5 that ends in the C6-C9 membrane attack complex. Lectin-pathway recognition via mannose-binding lectin and MASP2 feeds the same route. Because unchecked complement damages host tissue, regulators such as C4b-binding protein, factor I, CD46, CD55 and clusterin restrain it, while complement receptors CR1 and CR2 and the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B link deposition back to B cell activation thresholds. Deficiencies cause recurrent encapsulated bacterial infection; regulator loss underlies complement-mediated haemolysis and immune complex disease.</description>Instruction

T cell mediated immunity covers the effector arm of adaptive immunity in which T cells recognise antigen presented on host cells and act on it, killing infected or transformed targets and directing the behaviour of other immune cells. It underlies defence against viruses and tumours, and its miscalibration produces autoimmunity at one extreme and immune evasion at the other. Presentation is supplied by classical and non-classical MHC molecules together with lipid- and metabolite-presenting CD1 proteins and MR1; recognition is modulated by costimulatory ligands such as CD80 and CD70 and by inhibitory checkpoints including PDCD1, CD274, LAG3 and BTLA, the targets of current immunotherapy. Cytotoxicity depends on perforin and granule release machinery, while cytokine axes centred on IL12, IL18, IL23 and IL4 with the transcription factors TBX21, GATA3 and FOXP3 determine helper and regulatory fates. AIRE-dependent tolerance sets the repertoire that this response can draw on.

T cells are usually thought of as the recipients of antigen, but they can also display peptide or lipid antigen on their own surface in complex with MHC, allowing T cells to present to one another and modulate activation, tolerance and regulatory feedback within an immune response. The genes here point to the cytoskeletal and membrane organisation that such presentation requires: the actin regulator WAS, whose loss causes immunodeficiency with defective immune synapse formation, and the lipid raft scaffold RFTN1, which organises receptor-proximal signalling platforms. Adhesion through ICAM1 stabilises contacts between lymphocytes so that MHC-peptide complexes can be scanned, while the DNA exonuclease TREX1 limits self-nucleic-acid-driven inflammation that would otherwise distort antigen display. Together these functions place T cell antigen presentation at the interface of cell adhesion, membrane trafficking and control of lymphocyte activation.

Vertebrate adaptive immunity rests on lymphocytes whose antigen receptors are assembled by somatic recombination of germline segments encoding immunoglobulin superfamily domains, producing T cell receptors and antibodies of essentially unlimited specificity. This is what allows a first, slow primary response to leave behind memory cells that make later encounters with the same pathogen fast and decisive, and it underlies vaccination; its failure gives immunodeficiency, while loss of its restraints gives autoimmunity. The genes here span the whole arc: immunoglobulin variable and constant segments, MHC class I and II molecules plus proteasome subunits and peptide transport for antigen presentation, costimulatory and inhibitory receptors such as CD28, CD40, PD-1 and LAG3, cytokines and STAT-coupled receptors that steer helper T cell fates through GATA3, TBX21, RORC and FOXP3, and the deaminase AICDA with non-homologous end joining and mismatch repair factors that mediate class switching and affinity maturation. Complement components link these responses to effector clearance.

Peripheral tolerance requires an active immune response rather than its absence: mature T and B cells that encounter antigen can be switched off, deleted, or converted into suppressors, and tolerance induction dependent upon an immune response covers that outcome. It is what keeps self-reactive lymphocytes that escaped thymic screening from causing autoimmunity, and what allows a mother's immune system to accept a semi-allogeneic fetus. Inhibitory receptors such as BTLA and HAVCR2 and their ligand partners raise the threshold for activation and drive anergy, FOXP3 specifies and maintains regulatory T cells, and non-classical HLA-G together with pregnancy-specific glycoproteins contributes to maternal-fetal and placental tolerance. AIRE governs self-antigen display that shapes which clones survive. Failure yields autoimmune disease; excessive engagement of the same inhibitory receptors lets tumours evade immunity, which is why they are checkpoint blockade targets.

Self-reactive lymphocytes that escape thymic selection must be restrained where they encounter antigen, and peripheral tolerance induction is the set of mechanisms that does this in blood, lymph nodes, spleen and mucosal lymphoid tissue. Its failure produces autoimmunity; its excess allows tumours and chronic infections to evade attack, and its deliberate exploitation underlies transplant acceptance and fetal-maternal tolerance. The genes here span the main routes: FOXP3 specifies regulatory T cells, which suppress neighbouring effector responses; BTLA signalling through its ligand HTLV entry mediator (TNFRSF14) delivers an inhibitory co-receptor signal that raises the threshold for lymphocyte activation; the non-classical MHC molecule HLA-G engages inhibitory receptors on T and NK cells and is prominent at the placenta. AIRE, best known for driving promiscuous self-antigen expression in thymic epithelium, also acts in extrathymic antigen-presenting cells that present tissue antigens to circulating T cells.

Germinal center formation is the step that turns an activated B cell response into a high-affinity, class-switched antibody response: activated B cells enter lymphoid follicles and build a specialized microenvironment where they proliferate intensely, undergo somatic hypermutation, and are selected on the basis of antigen affinity. Without it, memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells are not generated, leaving durable humoral immunity and effective vaccine responses impossible; when its controls fail, autoantibodies and B cell lymphomas follow. The transcriptional repressor BCL6 defines the germinal center B cell state, while CXCL13 organizes the follicle by attracting B cells to follicular dendritic cell networks, and BAFF and NF- criptB-family signalling provide survival and activation input. Negative regulators such as TNFAIP3 and RC3H1 restrain the reaction, limiting the duration and magnitude of follicular B cell expansion.

Dendritic cells are the professional link between innate detection of a pathogen and the adaptive response, and this is the programme by which they capture antigen, load it onto MHC molecules, and display it at the surface for T cell inspection. Without it, naive T cells are never primed and antigen-specific immunity fails to start; excessive or misdirected presentation drives autoimmunity. Class II molecules and the invariant chain CD74 handle peptide loading in endosomal compartments, while lysosomal and phagosomal proteins support uptake and degradation of engulfed material. Intracellular sensors such as NOD1 and NOD2 recognise bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and supply the maturation signal, and the chemokine receptor CCR7, with its ligands CCL19 and CCL21, guides the loaded cell out of tissue into lymph node T cell zones. Inhibitory receptors including FCGR2B and CLEC4A set the threshold for activation.

Every nucleated cell continuously advertises samples of its internal protein content to cytotoxic T cells, and this is the machinery that builds those displays: presentation of peptide antigen on MHC class I. It is how virus-infected and tumour cells are recognised and killed, and how self-tolerance is calibrated during thymic selection. Proteasome-derived peptides are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to the right length by aminopeptidases such as ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains paired with beta-2 microglobulin by a peptide-loading complex including tapasin, calreticulin and the thiol oxidoreductase PDIA3. Classical HLA-A, -B and -C molecules carry the display to the surface, alongside non-classical relatives and NKG2D ligands of the ULBP and RAET1 families that report cellular stress to natural killer cells. Defects here yield immune evasion and bare lymphocyte syndrome.

Non-classical MHC class I molecules present cargo that the classical class I system cannot: lipids and glycolipids rather than peptides, plus signals of cellular stress. This pathway covers loading and surface display on CD1 family proteins and on HLA-E, -F and -G, together with the related ULBP and RAET1 stress ligands. It gives rise to lipid-reactive T cells, including invariant NKT cells that respond to CD1D-presented glycolipids, and to innate surveillance in which NK cells read HLA-E and ULBP surfaces to decide whether a cell is healthy, infected or transformed. Beta-2 microglobulin partners the heavy chains, while endosomal adaptor complexes of the AP-3 type and transporters route CD1 molecules through lipid-sampling compartments. HLA-G contributes to maternal-fetal tolerance, and tumours exploit the same molecules to suppress NK attack.

Non-classical class I molecules such as HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G present peptides to a distinct set of immune receptors, and this route describes how an antigen-presenting cell loads peptide derived from proteins taken up from outside the cell onto those complexes and displays them at the surface. What is shown here matters less for conventional T cell killing than for restraint: HLA-E engages NKG2A on natural killer cells and HLA-G suppresses NK and T cell attack, so the same display machinery that arms cytotoxicity can also license tolerance, as it does at the maternal-fetal interface and in tumours that upregulate these molecules to escape immune clearance. Assembly depends on beta-2 microglobulin as the obligate light chain and on transporter-mediated delivery of peptide into the endoplasmic reticulum, the shared steps that also serve the classical HLA-A, -B and -C heavy chains.

Antigen-presenting cells take up proteins from outside themselves and display fragments of them on MHC molecules, which is how the immune system learns what pathogens and vaccines look like. This is the step that lets helper T cells recognise extracellular bacteria, and, through cross-presentation onto class I molecules, lets cytotoxic T cells respond to material they never encountered directly. Internalised protein is degraded by endosomal and lysosomal proteases including cathepsins S, L and D and the asparaginyl endopeptidase legumain, while the invariant chain CD74 escorts class II heterodimers and HLA-DM edits the peptides loaded into them. Uptake is aided by Fc receptors for immune complexes, and the endosomal environment depends on PIKFYVE and UNC93B1. Defective presentation weakens antibody and T cell responses, whereas particular HLA class II alleles predispose to autoimmunity.

Antigen processing and presentation of endogenous peptide antigen is how a cell advertises its internal protein contents to the immune system, displaying fragments of self-made proteins on MHC class I molecules at the surface. This is the surveillance mechanism by which cytotoxic T cells detect virus-infected and tumour cells, and by which healthy cells prove their normality; loss of it allows tumours and viruses to escape killing. Proteasome-derived peptides are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto HLA-A, -B and -C heavy chains paired with β2-microglobulin, with tapasin holding the complex until a high-affinity peptide binds. Non-classical relatives such as HLA-E and HLA-G, together with the stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands, extend the same display logic to natural killer cell recognition.

Every nucleated cell continuously advertises samples of its own protein content on its surface, and this display of endogenously derived peptides is how cytotoxic T cells distinguish healthy cells from ones harbouring a virus or expressing mutated tumour proteins. Proteasomal fragments are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains paired with beta-2-microglobulin, with tapasin holding the complex in a peptide-receptive state. Classical HLA-A, -B and -C molecules carry the peptides to the surface, while the non-classical relatives HLA-E and HLA-G and the stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands instead signal cell status to NK receptors. Loss of loading machinery lets tumours and viruses escape surveillance; particular allotypes and ERAP variants predispose to autoinflammatory disease.

peptide antigen assembly with MHC protein complex is the loading step of antigen presentation: peptides are placed into the binding groove of class I and class II MHC molecules so that T cells can inspect what a cell contains. This is what allows cytotoxic T cells to detect virally infected or tumour cells and helper T cells to recognise material taken up by dendritic cells and macrophages, and it sets the repertoire of self peptides against which tolerance is established. Class I loading depends on a peptide-loading complex in which tapasin, calreticulin and the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57 edit peptides onto HLA-A heavy chains paired with beta-2-microglobulin; class II loading requires HLA-DM to exchange the invariant chain remnant for antigenic peptide, with HLA-DO tuning that exchange. Polymorphism in these HLA genes underlies transplant matching and much of the genetic risk for autoimmune disease.

Loading a peptide into the binding groove of an MHC molecule is the step that determines what the immune system sees. Without it, class I and class II molecules reach the cell surface empty or unstable, T cells cannot be selected in the thymus or activated in the periphery, and infected and tumour cells escape recognition; the same chemistry underlies transplant rejection and the strong HLA associations of autoimmune disease. Class I assembly occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum, where beta-2 microglobulin, calreticulin, the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57 and tapasin hold the heavy chain receptive until a suitable peptide binds. Class II molecules, built from the paired alpha and beta chains of the DR, DQ and DP isotypes, acquire peptides in endosomal compartments, with HLA-DM catalysing exchange and HLA-DO tuning it. Groove occupancy thus sets both the stability and the antigenic content of surface MHC.

Cytotoxic T cells survey the interior of every nucleated cell by reading peptides displayed on MHC class I molecules, and this pathway is the loading step that puts those peptides in place. A newly synthesised class I heavy chain pairs with beta-2 microglobulin in the endoplasmic reticulum and is held in a peptide-receptive state by a peptide-loading complex that includes calreticulin, the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57 and the dedicated chaperone tapasin, with its relative TAPBPL acting as a peptide editor that removes poorly bound cargo. Proofreading here determines which epitopes reach the cell surface, so it sets the threshold for recognition of virus-infected and tumour cells and for natural killer cell inhibition. Loss of loading components leaves empty, unstable complexes, low surface class I and blunted CD8 T cell responses a failure route also exploited by viruses and by tumours escaping immune surveillance.

Loading a peptide into the groove of an MHC class II molecule is the step that determines what CD4 T cells will see, and so what antigens the adaptive immune system responds to. It takes place in the late endosomal compartments of dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, where fragments of internalised protein are exchanged onto the class II heterodimer after the invariant chain placeholder is degraded. The DM heterodimer catalyses that exchange and edits the repertoire toward stably bound peptides, while the DO heterodimer restrains DM activity and tunes selection in B cells and thymic epithelium. The classical DP, DQ and DR heterodimers, encoded by the most polymorphic genes in the human genome, carry the peptides themselves; their allelic variation is the strongest genetic association known for type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, rheumatoid arthritis and multiple sclerosis.

Antigen-presenting cells display peptide or polysaccharide fragments on MHC class II molecules so that CD4 T cells can recognise what has been taken up from outside the cell; this is how helper T cell responses, antibody class switching and tolerance to self are set in motion, and variation in the class II locus is the strongest genetic contributor to many autoimmune diseases. Internalised antigen is degraded in acidic endosomes by cathepsins and legumain, while the invariant chain CD74 escorts newly made class II dimers and blocks the groove until HLA-DM catalyses peptide exchange, a step modulated by HLA-DO. Ubiquitin ligases MARCHF1 and MARCHF8 control surface levels of the complexes, and endosome maturation and trafficking factors such as PIKFYVE position the loading compartment. Receptor-mediated uptake through Fc and innate receptors feeds antigen into the route.

Tolerance induction is the set of processes that teach the immune system not to attack the body's own tissues or harmless introduced antigens, and its failure produces autoimmunity while its excess allows tumours and chronic infections to escape. Central tolerance depends on AIRE, which drives promiscuous expression of tissue-restricted self antigens in the thymus so that self-reactive thymocytes are deleted or diverted. In the periphery, FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells with high-affinity IL2RA and TGFB1 output suppress effector responses, while inhibitory receptors including PDCD1, BTLA, HAVCR2 and its ligand LGALS9 raise the threshold for T cell activation. E3 ligases such as CBLB and ITCH and the ubiquitin-editing enzyme TNFAIP3 enforce anergy and damp NF-kB signalling from within. Tolerogenic antigen-presenting cells contribute through IDO1-mediated tryptophan catabolism and non-classical HLA-E and HLA-G engagement of inhibitory receptors, a mechanism also used at the maternal-fetal interface.

The immune system must learn not to attack the body's own tissues, and tolerance induction to self antigen is how that restraint is established and maintained. Without it, lymphocytes bearing self-reactive receptors escape into the periphery and cause autoimmune disease; loss of AIRE produces multi-organ autoimmune endocrinopathy, and loss of FOXP3 produces the severe systemic autoimmunity of IPEX syndrome. Two arms are represented: thymic display of otherwise tissue-restricted self proteins so that developing T cells reactive to them are deleted or diverted, and the differentiation of regulatory T cells that suppress self-reactive cells in the periphery. TGF- cbeta signalling through its type II receptor supports that suppressive programme, LYN sets inhibitory thresholds for antigen receptor signalling in B cells, and phospholipid scrambling on dying cells channels self antigen into non-inflammatory, tolerogenic clearance.

T cell tolerance induction covers the mechanisms that stop T cells from attacking self tissue, operating both during thymic development and in the periphery once cells have matured. Without it, autoreactive clones expand and drive autoimmune disease; too much of it, and tumours or chronic infections escape immune control. In the thymus, AIRE drives ectopic expression of tissue-restricted antigens so that self-reactive thymocytes can be deleted or diverted into the regulatory lineage. Peripherally, FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells with high-affinity IL2RA and ICOS costimulation enforce suppression, TGF-beta signalling reinforces it, and inhibitory receptors such as BTLA with its ligand TNFRSF14 and the LILRB family raise the activation threshold. Cell-intrinsic anergy is imposed by E3 ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH and by phosphatase-mediated damping of receptor signalling, while IDO1-driven tryptophan catabolism starves responding T cells locally.

Building a functioning immune system means both constructing the organs that house immune cells — thymus, spleen, lymph nodes, gut-associated tissue — and generating lymphocytes with diverse, self-tolerant antigen receptors. Failure at either step produces immunodeficiency, thymic aplasia with DiGeorge-like malformations, or autoimmunity. Transcription factors including FOXN1, GATA3, BCL11B, TCF3, PAX-related and homeobox regulators such as HOXA3 and TBX1 pattern lymphoid tissue and commit progenitors to T and B lineages, while IL7R, IL2RA and STAT5 signalling drives their expansion and survival. RAG1 and RAG2 initiate V(D)J recombination and AICDA drives class switching, so the double-strand break repair machinery — DNA-PK, LIG4, XRCC4, NHEJ1, ATM, the shieldin complex — is intrinsic to receptor assembly rather than incidental. AIRE and FOXP3 enforce tolerance centrally and peripherally, and checkpoint receptors such as PDCD1, CTLA-4 pathway members and BTLA calibrate mature responses.

leukocyte differentiation is the broad developmental program by which hematopoietic progenitors commit to and mature into the white blood cell lineages — T and B lymphocytes, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, granulocytes, osteoclasts and innate lymphoid subsets. It builds the entire cellular basis of immunity, and its failure produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or leukemia. Lineage choice is enforced by transcription factor networks acting in mutually antagonistic pairs, such as SPI1 and GATA1, PAX5 and EBF-driven B cell commitment, BCL11B and TCF7 in thymocytes, and CEBPA/CEBPE in granulopoiesis, with chromatin remodelers and polycomb components setting the accessible landscape. Cytokines and their receptors (IL7R, KIT, FLT3, CSF1R, TNFSF11) plus JAK–STAT and NOTCH signaling supply the instructive extrinsic cues, while antigen receptor assembly by RAG1/RAG2 and thymic selection through peptide–MHC and costimulatory molecules impose checkpoints that couple differentiation to self-tolerance.

White blood cells of every kind arise from hematopoietic precursors that progressively lose potency and acquire lineage-specific machinery, and leukocyte differentiation is the collection of programmes that make this happen. It supplies the myeloid and lymphoid cells of innate and adaptive immunity, and its disruption produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or leukemia when progenitors are frozen at an immature stage. Lineage-determining transcription factors such as SPI1, GATA1, PAX5, CEBPA, FOXP3 and TBX21 set and maintain identity, acting alongside chromatin remodelling complexes and Notch, Wnt and TGF-beta inputs. Cytokines and their receptors, including IL7R, KIT, FLT3, CSF1R and the JAK-STAT machinery they engage, drive survival and expansion, while antigen receptor assembly and thymic selection impose checkpoints on lymphocyte maturation. Osteoclast-forming genes extend the same logic to bone-resorbing macrophages.

Leukocyte migration involved in inflammatory response is the recruitment step of innate immunity: the directed movement of neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes out of blood and through tissue toward a site of infection or injury. Without it, pathogens are not cleared and wounds do not resolve; in excess, it drives the tissue damage of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease. The genes trace the adhesion cascade itself — E-selectin and the fucosyltransferase that builds its glycan ligand for tethering, the beta-2 integrin chain shared by LFA-1 and Mac-1 for firm adhesion, and junctional adhesion molecules for passage between endothelial cells. Alongside these are chemoattractant systems, including the leukotriene-generating 5-lipoxygenase, short-chain fatty acid sensing, fractalkine and the CCR6 axis, plus neutrophil alarmins S100A8/A9 and granule proteases that amplify further influx. Loss of integrin function causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with recurrent bacterial infection.

Inflammation depends on leukocytes leaving the circulation and moving into damaged or infected tissue, and this is the arm of the inflammatory response that directs that traffic. Without it, bacteria are not cleared and abscesses cannot form; in excess it drives the neutrophil-rich infiltrates of arthritis, colitis, atherosclerosis and acute lung injury. Endothelial E-selectin and the fucosyltransferase that builds its glycan ligands capture flowing cells, the beta-2 integrin subunit shared by LFA-1 and Mac-1 converts capture into firm adhesion, and junctional adhesion molecule C governs passage between endothelial cells. Chemotactic cues come from a chemokine receptor used by memory lymphocytes, a membrane-anchored chemokine, leukotriene products of 5-lipoxygenase, and a short-chain fatty acid receptor sensing microbial metabolites. Neutrophil-derived S100A8/A9 and elastase amplify recruitment, linking migration to granulocyte activation and tissue damage.

Hypersensitivity is the damaging face of adaptive immunity: an antigen that is harmless in itself, whether inhaled pollen, a drug, or a self protein, is recognised by antibody and T cells and triggers inflammation out of proportion to any threat. It underlies allergy, asthma, anaphylaxis, and immune-complex and autoantibody-driven tissue injury. The genes here mark the antibody effector arm, with IgE and IgG bound by the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells and basophils and by a family of Fc gamma receptors that includes both activating forms and the inhibitory FCGR2B that raises the threshold for degranulation; the shared FCER1G chain and BTK carry the resulting signal, and complement C3 amplifies it. GATA3 directs the type 2 T helper programme that licenses IgE class switching, while chemokine and selectin-ligand components bring the responding cells into the affected tissue.</br>

The acute inflammatory response is the body's immediate reaction to injury or infection, unfolding over minutes to hours and either resolving or giving way to chronic inflammation. It brings fluid, plasma proteins and granulocytes to the affected tissue, producing the familiar swelling, heat and pain, and it underlies fever, the clinical acute-phase blood profile, and the tissue damage of sepsis when it runs unchecked. Cytokines such as IL1A, IL1B, IL6 and TNF, generated in part through inflammasome assembly involving NLRP3, act on hepatocytes via IL6R and STAT3 to induce acute-phase reactants including CRP, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin and serine protease inhibitors. Parallel arms supply prostaglandins through PTGS2 and PTGES, complement and coagulation activation, Fc receptor-dependent recognition of immune complexes, neutrophil effectors like elastase and lipocalin-2, and sensory neuropeptide and TRPV1 signalling that links inflammation to pain. Negative regulators including IL1RN and SIGIRR restrain the response.

production of molecular mediator involved in inflammatory response covers how cells manufacture and release the signals that create inflammation — cytokines, eicosanoids, reactive nitrogen species and antimicrobial peptides — after an inflammatory stimulus is sensed. It is the output arm of innate immunity: it recruits leukocytes to infected or damaged tissue, and when it runs unchecked it produces the autoinflammatory syndromes, septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease that follow loss of restraint on cytokine output. Pattern recognition receptors such as TLR4, NOD2 and CLEC7A feed through MYD88, SYK and CARD9 into NF-κB and p38 signalling to drive transcription of TNF, IL6 and the IL-17 and IL-36 families; inflammasome components including PYCARD and MEFV control maturation of IL-1-family mediators, while ALOX5 with its activating protein and secreted phospholipases generate leukotrienes. Vesicle proteins mediate release, and numerous microRNAs plus ZFP36, ZC3H12A and PDCD4 impose post-transcriptional damping.

Inflammation works through diffusible messengers, and this pathway covers the making and releasing of those mediators once a cell detects an inflammatory stimulus. It sets the amplitude and duration of host defence: too little and infection goes unchecked, too much and the result is sepsis, chronic inflammatory disease, or the periodic fevers caused by mutations in genes such as MEFV. Pattern-recognition receptors including TLR4, TLR3, NOD2 and the fungal sensor CLEC7A signal via MYD88, TICAM1, SYK and CARD9 into NF-κB subunits and stress kinases, driving transcription of TNF, IL6, IL17 family members and inducible nitric oxide synthase. Lipid mediators come from ALOX5 with its activating protein and secreted phospholipases, and inflammasome adaptors process IL-1 family cytokines. Release depends on vesicle fusion machinery, while negative regulators—NFKBIA, DUSP10, ZFP36, ZC3H12A and numerous microRNAs—restrain output and resolve the response.

Inflammation is executed largely through the cytokines that inflamed cells make, and this pathway covers the induction and release of those mediators after an inflammatory stimulus. It sets the amplitude of host defence against bacteria and fungi, and its miscalibration underlies septic shock at one extreme and chronic autoinflammatory or autoimmune disease at the other. Pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4, NOD2 and the C-type lectin dectin-1 with its adaptor CARD9 signal through MYD88 and TRIF to p38 and IKK, releasing NF-κB subunits from the inhibitor NFKBIA to transcribe TNF, IL6, NOS2 and the IL-17 and IL-36 family members; inflammasome components including pyrin and ASC handle IL-1 maturation. Restraint is built in: decoy and inhibitory receptors, the mRNA-destabilising proteins ZFP36 and Regnase-1, and numerous microRNAs including miR-146a and miR-21 limit how long and how loudly cytokine output continues.

When phagocytes encounter microbes or inflammatory stimuli, they sharply increase oxygen consumption and convert it into superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals — the respiratory burst that accompanies an inflammatory response. This oxidative output kills ingested bacteria, shapes the local redox environment and feeds back onto leukocyte signalling; losing it leaves patients unable to clear catalase-positive organisms and prone to granuloma formation, while unrestrained bursting damages host tissue. Genes here span the reaction itself and its control: NCF1 is a cytosolic component of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, S100A9 and LBP link pattern recognition and calcium-binding alarmin signalling to activation, and PRDX2, a peroxiredoxin, reduces peroxide and limits the response. Progranulin and SLAMF8 act as negative regulators, illustrating that this biology is as much about restraining oxidant production as generating it during innate immune defence.

Inflammation is shaped chemically by lipid mediators, and this pathway covers the stimulus-triggered production and release of arachidonic acid metabolites that raise mediator levels inside and around an activated cell. The products — leukotrienes above all — recruit and activate neutrophils and eosinophils, contract airway smooth muscle, and increase vascular permeability, which is why this arm of lipid signalling underlies asthma, and why its blockade is a therapeutic strategy. The committed step is carried out by 5-lipoxygenase acting with its membrane-anchored activating protein ALOX5AP, which presents substrate liberated from phospholipids; a fatty acid desaturase supplies and remodels the polyunsaturated precursor pool. Antimicrobial and fibrinolytic components in this grouping point to the broader innate response in which the mediators are made, linking eicosanoid output to host defence peptide release and to control of plasminogen activation during tissue injury.

Inflammation that persists for weeks or months, with destruction and attempted repair running alongside continuing immune activation, is the setting for granuloma formation, fibrosis, atherosclerosis, and the tissue damage of autoimmune and inflammatory bowel disease. Unlike a resolving acute response, it is often low-grade and asymptomatic at onset, and it depends as much on brakes as on drivers. Tumour necrosis factor and lymphotoxin alpha sustain activation, chemokines such as CCL5, CCL11 and CXCL13 recruit lymphocytes and eosinophils and organise lymphoid aggregates, and VCAM1 holds leukocytes at activated endothelium. S100A8 and S100A9 released from myeloid cells amplify the response, while IL10, FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells, IDO1-mediated tryptophan catabolism and the NF-kB inhibitor TNFAIP3 restrain it. Loss of these counter-regulatory arms converts a contained response into persistent, damaging inflammation.

Monocytes leave the bloodstream and travel toward damaged or infected tissue by following gradients of secreted attractants, and this directed migration determines how quickly macrophages accumulate at a site of injury. It underlies innate defence and wound repair, but the same recruitment drives atherosclerotic plaque growth, chronic inflammatory disease and the infiltration of tumours by monocyte-derived cells. The gradients are largely set by CC chemokines such as CCL2, CCL3, CCL5 and CCL7 acting on the receptors CCR1, CCR2 and CX3CR1, with additional cues from formyl peptide and other G protein-coupled receptors, alarmins including HMGB1 and S100 proteins, galectin-3, and cytokines such as IL6. Downstream kinases and adaptors, together with membrane remodelling and adhesion components, convert receptor occupancy into polarised movement, while negative regulators including DUSP1 and ANXA1 restrain the response so that recruitment resolves.

Antibody affinity maturation depends on deliberately mutating immunoglobulin genes in activated B cells, and somatic diversification of immune receptors via somatic mutation is that controlled mutagenesis. Without it, germinal centre B cells cannot improve antigen binding or switch effectively between antibody classes, and patients develop hyper-IgM immunodeficiency; misdirected activity contributes to lymphoma-associated translocations. The reaction begins when a cytidine deaminase acting on single-stranded DNA at transcribed variable regions creates uracils; base excision by uracil-DNA glycosylase and mismatch recognition by MSH2-MSH6 and MLH1-PMS2 then convert these lesions into nicks and gaps rather than repairing them faithfully. Error-prone polymerases and translesion synthesis enzymes such as REV1, POLQ and POLB fill the gaps, while HMCES shields abasic sites, so DNA repair machinery is repurposed here to generate diversity instead of restoring sequence.

Myeloid leukocyte differentiation is the route by which unspecialized bone marrow progenitors acquire the identities of neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, mast cells, eosinophils and osteoclasts. It supplies the cells of innate immunity and of bone remodelling, and its failure produces congenital neutropenia, impaired antimicrobial defence, or osteopetrosis when osteoclasts do not form. Lineage choice is set by transcription factors including SPI1, CEBPA, CEBPE, GATA1, GATA2, RUNX1, IRF4/IRF8-family partners such as BATF3 and ZBTB46 for dendritic cells, and MITF and NFATc/TRAF6 signalling downstream of RANKL and its receptor TNFRSF11A for osteoclasts. Cytokines and their receptors instruct output and expansion, notably CSF1 acting through CSF1R, CSF2, CSF3, KIT and interleukin-1 family signals, with TGFB1 and SOCS1 restraining it. Downstream kinases LYN, FES, SRC, PIK3CD and MAPK14 couple these cues to granule gene expression, fusion into multinucleated osteoclasts, and mature effector function.

Platelet degranulation is the release of preformed mediators from platelet secretory granules at sites of vascular injury, converting an initial adhesion event into a self-amplifying haemostatic response. Dense granules discharge ADP, ATP, calcium and serotonin, while alpha granules deliver adhesive and growth-promoting proteins that recruit further platelets and support wound repair; blunting this step causes bleeding tendency, while excessive release drives thrombosis and vascular inflammation. The genes cover the sequence from receptor to secretion: immune receptor and collagen receptor signalling through FCER1G, the Src-family kinase LYN and SYK, purinergic ATP-gated P2RX1 and phosphoinositide-dependent calcium mobilisation, the cytoskeletal adaptor PLEK, and the SNARE chaperone STXBP1 that licenses granule membrane fusion. Loading of the granules is also represented, with TPH1 synthesising serotonin and the transporter ABCC4 concentrating nucleotides and other small mediators.

When platelets adhere at a site of vascular injury, they release the contents of preformed storage granules, and platelet degranulation is that regulated exocytosis step. The secreted cargo — serotonin, ADP, calcium, adhesive and coagulation proteins — recruits and activates further platelets, so this release amplifies a local activation signal into a stable haemostatic plug; too little causes bleeding, too much promotes thrombosis. Activation signals converge through immunoreceptor-type tyrosine kinase signalling, with the Src-family kinase LYN and the spleen tyrosine kinase SYK acting downstream of an FcR gamma-chain-coupled collagen receptor, alongside purinergic calcium entry through the P2RX1 channel. STXBP1 contributes to the SNARE-dependent fusion of granules with the membrane, while TPH1 generates the serotonin and ABCC4 transports mediators into dense granules for storage.

Antigen presentation is not a fixed property of a cell but a tunable one, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower how much antigen is processed and displayed to T cells. Tuning it sets the threshold between productive immunity and tolerance, and its disturbance contributes to autoimmunity, chronic infection and tumour immune escape. Several members act directly on the loading machinery: CD74 occupies the MHC class II groove until peptide exchange, the HLA-DO heterodimer restrains that exchange, and cathepsin S degrades the invariant chain to permit it. Others set the context in which presentation happens — CCR7 with its chemokines draws dendritic cells into lymph nodes, inhibitory receptors such as LILRB2 and FCGR2B damp activation, and intracellular sensors including NOD2 and the inflammasome adaptor PYCARD couple pathogen detection to enhanced display.

Antigen processing and presentation must be dialled down as well as up, and this collection of brakes restrains how much peptide reaches the surface on MHC molecules and how strongly presenting cells stimulate T lymphocytes. The restraint keeps immune responses proportionate and helps maintain self-tolerance; losing it favours autoimmunity, while tumours and chronic infections exploit it to escape surveillance. The mechanisms are varied: HLA-DOA and HLA-DOB form a non-classical dimer that inhibits HLA-DM and so limits peptide exchange onto class II molecules; TAPBPL acts as a tapasin-like peptide editor for class I; HFE competes with transferrin-binding-related class I chemistry; LILRB2 delivers inhibitory signals through ITIM motifs on myeloid cells, as does the low-affinity Fc receptor FCGR2B. FGL2 and THBS1 contribute immunosuppressive signals from macrophages and the matrix, tuning dendritic cell and macrophage activation.

Positive regulation of antigen processing and presentation covers the signals that increase how much antigen a cell loads onto MHC molecules and displays to T cells, setting the strength with which adaptive immunity is initiated. It matters because T cell priming depends on dendritic cells and macrophages reaching lymphoid tissue and upregulating presentation machinery; when these inputs fail, pathogens persist and tolerance is poorly calibrated. The genes span the steps involved: chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 to bring antigen-bearing dendritic cells into lymph nodes, CD74 chaperoning MHC class II and protecting its peptide groove until loading, intracellular pattern recognition by NOD1 and NOD2 and inflammasome assembly via PYCARD that license maturation, phagosomal metal transport by SLC11A1 supporting degradation, and TREM2 tuning myeloid activation. The pathway therefore links innate sensing and cell trafficking to antigen display.

Antigen processing and presentation converts intact proteins into peptides displayed on MHC molecules for inspection by T cells, and the genes here act to increase that activity rather than to carry it out directly. Boosting presentation is how innate sensing translates into adaptive immunity: without it, dendritic cells and macrophages fail to prime naive T cells and infections are cleared poorly, while excessive enhancement contributes to autoimmunity. The chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 bring antigen-bearing dendritic cells and naive lymphocytes together in lymph node T cell zones, and CD74 chaperones MHC class II and shields its peptide groove during transit. Intracellular bacterial sensors NOD1 and NOD2, the inflammasome adaptor PYCARD, the phagosomal metal transporter SLC11A1 and the myeloid receptor TREM2 tie pathogen detection and phagosome maturation to stronger presentation.

MHC class II molecules display peptides from internalised antigens to CD4+ helper T cells, and this regulatory layer sets how much of that display occurs in dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells. Tuning it determines the strength of helper T cell priming, and so the balance between effective antibody and cell-mediated responses and the risk of autoimmunity or, at the other extreme, failed immunity. The non-classical class II-like subunits HLA-DOA and HLA-DOB assemble into a dimer that modulates HLA-DM-catalysed peptide exchange in the MHC class II compartment, biasing which peptides survive to reach the cell surface. Other members act from the sensing and phagocytic side: TREM2 on myeloid cells and the inflammasome adaptor PYCARD couple innate cues to antigen-presenting capacity, while thrombospondin-1 provides extracellular signals that dampen dendritic cell activation.

Whether a cell displays a given peptide to T cells is itself controlled, and this pathway covers the modulators that tune how much peptide antigen is processed and presented. It sets the threshold for CD4 and CD8 T cell recognition, shaping both protective immunity and the risk of autoreactivity. Several members act directly on the loading machinery: HLA-DOA and HLA-DOB form a non-classical MHC class II dimer that restrains HLA-DM and so biases which peptides survive editing in the endosomal compartment, while TAPBPL is a tapasin-related peptide editor that proofreads class I loading in the secretory pathway. HFE, better known for its role in iron sensing, competes with transferrin at its receptor and also engages class I molecules. TREM2 and the inflammasome adaptor PYCARD link myeloid activation state to presentation capacity, connecting innate sensing in macrophages and microglia to adaptive priming.

Dendritic cells decide how much antigen reaches T cells, and this regulatory layer sets the frequency and extent of their antigen processing and presentation. It matters because the same machinery that primes protective T cell responses can, if left unchecked, drive autoimmunity, while too little presentation leaves infections uncontrolled. Several components act on dendritic cell trafficking: the chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 and their receptor CCR7 direct antigen-bearing cells from tissue into lymph node T cell zones, where presentation occurs. Others tune the loading step itself, including CD74, the invariant chain that chaperones MHC class II and blocks premature peptide binding. Inhibitory and immunomodulatory receptors and secreted factors such as FCGR2B, FGL2 and THBS1 damp activation, while NOD1 and NOD2 sense bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and raise it. Phagosomal proteins including SLC11A1 link microbial handling to peptide generation.

positive regulation of dendritic cell antigen processing and presentation covers the signals that push dendritic cells to display captured antigen more effectively to T cells, the step that converts innate detection of a pathogen into an adaptive immune response. Without it, priming of naive T cells in lymph nodes fails and vaccination or infection generates weak cellular immunity. The genes span the two requirements for this to happen: chemokine guidance, in which CCL19 and CCL21 from lymphoid stroma act through CCR7 to bring antigen-loaded dendritic cells into T cell zones, and intracellular sensing, in which the cytosolic peptidoglycan receptors NOD1 and NOD2 and the phagosomal metal transporter SLC11A1 report on microbial presence and shape the maturing compartment. CD74 chaperones MHC class II and controls when peptide loading occurs, linking these cues to antigen display itself.

Dendritic cells only prime T cells effectively once they have been instructed to load and display antigen, and this pathway covers the signals that raise the rate and extent of that processing and presentation. It sits at the junction between innate detection of microbes and the onset of adaptive immunity: without it, antigen captured in tissue is never converted into productive T cell priming in lymph nodes, and tolerance or unchecked infection follows. Chemokine signalling through CCR7 with its ligands CCL19 and CCL21 draws activated dendritic cells into lymphoid tissue where presentation occurs, while the cytosolic sensors NOD1 and NOD2 detect bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and license maturation. CD74 chaperones MHC class II and controls peptide loading, and SLC11A1 acts in the phagosome, linking divalent metal transport to antimicrobial handling of ingested antigen.

Germinal centers are the transient structures in lymphoid follicles where activated B cells proliferate, mutate their immunoglobulin genes and are selected for higher affinity, producing memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells. Regulating how readily and how extensively these centers form sets the balance between effective antibody responses and autoimmunity or lymphomagenesis, and several of these genes are classic tuners of that balance. BCL6 is the transcriptional repressor that specifies the germinal center B cell state, while BAFF (TNFSF13B) supplies the survival signal that sustains follicular B cells. Restraint comes from negative regulators of NF-kB and of activation transcripts: TNFAIP3 terminates receptor-driven NF-kB signalling, and the RNA-binding protein RC3H1 destabilises costimulatory messages such that its loss drives spontaneous germinal centers and autoantibodies. MEF2C contributes to B cell proliferative responses downstream of antigen receptor engagement.

regulation of immunoglobulin production sets how much antibody a B cell makes and of which class, tuning humoral immunity between protective responses and the excesses seen in allergy, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency. Control operates at several levels. T cell help through CD40-CD40L, CD28/OX40 costimulation and cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21, IL-6 and IL-10 drives activation, while IL-13/STAT6 biases toward IgE and TGFB1 toward other isotypes; inhibitory receptors CD22 and FCGR2B, together with BCL6 and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells, damp the response. Class switch recombination requires resolution of AID-induced DNA breaks by mismatch repair and the 53BP1-RIF1-shieldin end-joining axis, so mutations here restrict the antibody repertoire. Terminal differentiation into plasma cells depends on XBP1, MZB1 and DNAJB9 expanding secretory capacity to sustain high-rate immunoglobulin synthesis and folding.

Antibody output by B cells is tuned rather than simply switched on, and the regulation of immunoglobulin production covers the signals and machinery that set how much antibody of which class a response generates. It matters for vaccine responses and mucosal defence, and its dysregulation gives hypogammaglobulinaemia at one extreme and autoantibody disease or IgE-driven allergy at the other. T cell help provides much of the input: costimulatory and TNF-family ligand-receptor pairs such as CD40 with its ligand, CD28-CD86 and OX40 engagement, together with cytokines including IL-4, IL-21, IL-6, IL-10 and TGF-beta acting through STAT6 and lineage factors like BCL6, TBX21 and FOXP3. Inhibitory receptors including CD22 and the low-affinity Fc gamma receptor IIB damp the response. Class switching and somatic diversification require double-strand break repair and mismatch repair components, notably the shieldin complex, 53BP1, RIF1 and MLH1-MSH2-PMS2, while XBP1, MZB1 and DNAJB9 support the secretory expansion of plasma cells.}

Antibody output has to be capped as well as switched on, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that stop or reduce immunoglobulin production by B cells. Without such restraint, plasma cell differentiation and class switching run unchecked, contributing to hypergammaglobulinaemia, autoantibody formation and allergic IgE responses. The genes here act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CD22 and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B raise the threshold for B cell activation and deliver negative signals from immune complexes, while complement receptor CR1 tunes complement-dependent stimulation. BCL6 holds germinal centre B cells in a proliferative, differentiation-blocked state, opposing terminal plasma cell commitment. FOXP3 marks regulatory T cells that suppress the helper signals B cells require, and NDFIP1 promotes ubiquitin-mediated limitation of lymphocyte responses. Cytokine-side components, including an IL-33 and decoy IL-13 receptor pairing, link tissue signals to restraint of type 2 antibody responses.

Antibody output by B cells is tuned up by signals from helper T cells, cytokines and innate receptors, and this positive regulation of immunoglobulin production determines how much antibody, and of which class, an immune response delivers. Loss of the co-stimulatory arm — CD40 and its partners CD28, CD86 and OX40/OX40L — or of B cell receptor signalling through BTK gives hypogammaglobulinaemia and recurrent infection, while excess drives autoantibody disease and allergy. Cytokines act as the dial: IL-4, IL-13 and IL-5 signalling through IL13RA1 and STAT6 push IgE and IgG1, whereas IL-21, IL-6 and IL-10 support plasma cell differentiation. That differentiation requires the XBP1–MZB1 secretory programme to expand the endoplasmic reticulum for high-rate secretion. Class switching depends in parallel on mismatch repair and end-joining factors including MLH1, MSH2, 53BP1, RIF1 and the shieldin complex, which channel AID-induced lesions into productive switch recombination.

Immune tolerance is the state in which lymphocytes meet an antigen and do not attack it, and this pathway covers the signals that set how readily that state is established. It matters in both directions: too little tolerance gives autoimmunity and graft rejection, too much lets tumours and chronic infections persist. Regulatory T cells are central, and the genes here include the lineage factor FOXP3 and the high-affinity IL-2 receptor chain IL2RA on which they depend, along with TGF-beta receptor signalling. Coinhibitory receptors such as PD-1, BTLA and TIM-3 raise the threshold for T cell activation, while E3 ligases including CBLB and ITCH enforce anergy by degrading activation machinery. Non-classical HLA-G and inhibitory leukocyte receptors, together with tryptophan catabolism by IDO1, extend the same restraint to antigen-presenting cells and the maternal-fetal interface.

Immune tolerance keeps lymphocytes from attacking self tissue, harmless antigens, or a fetus, and this pathway covers the processes that promote its establishment. Loss of it produces autoimmunity and inflammatory disease; excessive engagement of the same machinery lets tumours and chronic infections escape immune attack. Several routes converge here: FOXP3 specifies regulatory T cells and TGF-beta receptor signalling sustains their induction, while the E3 ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH raise the threshold for T cell activation and enforce anergy in cells that see antigen without adequate costimulation. Getting white blood cells out of the bloodstream and into tissue is how inflammation becomes localized, and this pathway covers the signals that increase the rate and extent of that movement. Without it, infections go uncontained and wounds heal poorly; in excess, it drives the leukocyte influx of atherosclerosis, arthritis and chronic inflammatory disease. Inside the cell, RHOA, RAC1/RAC2, PTK2 and PTK2B remodel the cytoskeleton, converting these cues into polarized crawling and tissue entry.

Leukocytes only reach infected or injured tissue if they can read a chemical gradient, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that set how strongly and in which direction they move. Tuning it determines the size of an inflammatory infiltrate: too little and wounds fail to clear pathogens, too much and the same recruitment drives atherosclerosis, arthritis and tumour-associated myeloid accumulation. Inflammation must be resolved as well as started, and this is the braking side of leukocyte chemotaxis — the set of activities that damp or halt the directed migration of neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes toward chemoattractant gradients. positive regulation of leukocyte chemotaxis covers the signals that recruit white blood cells out of the bloodstream and steer them toward sites of infection, injury or tumour growth. It is how inflammation is localised: without it, host defence and wound healing fail, and when it is excessive it drives chronic inflammatory disease, atherosclerosis and leukocyte infiltration of tumours. The bulk of the activity is chemokine-based, with ligands such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8 and CXCL12 acting through G protein-coupled receptors including CCR2, CCR7, CX3CR1 and the complement receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1. Alarmins like HMGB1, lipid and peptide chemoattractants, and growth factors of the VEGF and CSF1 families add further recruiting cues. Downstream, ERK signalling, focal adhesion kinases, Rac GTPases and the WNK-OXSR1/STK39 module remodel the actin cytoskeleton and adhesion so cells polarise and crawl up the gradient.

Leukocytes only reach infected or damaged tissue if something tells them where to go, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that increase the rate and extent of that directed migration. Leukocytes leave the bloodstream at sites of infection or injury by rolling, arresting and squeezing between endothelial cells, and this pathway sets how readily that happens. Leukocytes reach infected or injured tissue by crossing the vessel wall, and this pathway comprises the signals that increase that movement. Immune effector processes are the business end of immunity — cytokine secretion, antibody production, complement-mediated lysis, cytotoxic killing, degranulation and phagocytosis — and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and how long they run. Immune effector processes are the business ends of immunity inflammatory cytokine release, cytotoxic killing, antibody production, complement-mediated lysis, phagocytosis and this collection covers the signals that turn them up. Immune responses have to be dialled down as well as switched on, and this pathway collects the brakes that limit how much antibody, cytokine and other soluble mediator gets made. Leukocytes kill infected and transformed cells, phagocytose pathogens, and release granule contents, and this pathway covers the controls that set how strongly and how often they do so. T cell mediated immunity has to be tuned as well as triggered, and this pathway covers the processes that set how strongly and for how long effector T cells respond. negative regulation of T cell mediated immunity is the set of brakes that limit how strongly and how long T cells attack, protecting tissues from collateral damage and enforcing tolerance to self and to fetal tissue. Costimulatory and stress ligands including OX40L, nectins and the ULBP/RAET1 family engage NKG2D and related receptors to lower the threshold for cytotoxic killing.

T cells only attack what they are shown, and this pathway covers the events that raise the strength, speed and reach of T cell mediated immunity. It matters for clearing intracellular pathogens and tumour cells, and its excess drives autoimmunity and inflammatory tissue damage. Antigen presentation supplies the trigger: classical class I and class II molecules together with beta-2 microglobulin and the peptide transporter, plus the lipid-presenting CD1 family and the metabolite-presenting MR1 that serve unconventional T cells. Stress-induced ULBP and RAET1 ligands and nectin-family surface proteins engage activating receptors, while costimulation and cytokines including IL-12, IL-18, IL-23, IL-1 and IL-6 push differentiation toward effector states, with T-bet and GATA3 fixing helper lineage choice. Adaptor and kinase components such as MALT1, TRAF6 and MAP3K7 carry receptor engagement into transcription, and FOXP3 marks the regulatory arm that counterbalances it.

Antibody responses must be tuned in magnitude, isotype and affinity, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that set how much B cell mediated immunity a host mounts. Too little gives poor humoral protection and immunodeficiency; too much drives autoantibody disease, and several components here are the brakes — an inhibitory Fc receptor for IgG, the phosphatase SHP-1, regulatory T cell programmes through FOXP3 and TGFB1, and complement regulators such as C4BP and CD46. Positive input comes from T cell help via CD40 and costimulation, cytokines including IL-4 acting through STAT6, IL-2, IL-10 and BAFF-family ligands, and BTK-dependent receptor signalling. A large DNA repair contingent — mismatch repair proteins, 53BP1 with RIF1 and the shieldin complex — directs class switch recombination, linking double-strand break end-joining choice to which antibody isotype a plasma cell ultimately secretes.

negative regulation of B cell mediated immunity is the set of brakes that keep antibody responses proportionate and self-tolerant, limiting how much antibody is made and how far complement-mediated damage proceeds. Without these restraints, autoantibody production and immune complex disease follow, which is why several of these genes are lupus and glomerulonephritis susceptibility loci. Restraint operates at three levels: inhibitory surface receptors such as FCGR2B, which raises the threshold for B cell activation by immune complexes, and the phosphatase PTPN6 that dampens antigen receptor signalling; soluble and membrane complement regulators including C4b-binding protein, CD46 and CR1, which prevent convertase amplification on host cells; and transcriptional control, where BCL6 constrains plasma cell differentiation while FOXP3 regulatory T cells and NDFIP1-directed ubiquitination suppress helper signals that would otherwise sustain the response.

Antibody responses must be damped as well as launched, and this set covers the braking processes that limit B cell mediated immunity so that self-tissue is spared and responses resolve once antigen is cleared. Several routes converge: inhibitory receptor signalling through the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B and the phosphatase PTPN6, which raises the threshold for B cell activation and drives apoptosis of low-affinity clones; complement restraint by regulators such as C4BPA/C4BPB, CD46 and CR1, which prevent amplification of the classical cascade on host membranes; and transcriptional control, where BCL6 restrains differentiation and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells suppress help to B cells. Loss of these controls permits autoantibody production, immune complex disease and lupus-like autoimmunity, while ubiquitin-pathway regulators including NDFIP1 contribute by curbing lymphocyte activation. The biology sits at the interface of peripheral tolerance, complement homeostasis and germinal centre regulation.

Antibody responses are amplified when B cells receive help, switch isotype, and mature their receptors, and this is the biology that turns up the frequency and extent of B cell mediated immunity. Costimulatory and cytokine inputs dominate one half of the list: CD40 ligation, CD28 engagement, and interleukins such as IL4 acting through STAT6 drive proliferation, germinal centre help, and the choice of antibody class, with BAFF/APRIL-family and TNF-superfamily members sustaining survival. The other half is the DNA end-joining machinery of class switch recombination — 53BP1 with RIF1 and the shieldin complex, plus mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2 and PMS2 — which channels AID-initiated lesions toward productive switching rather than resection. Loss of these arms produces hyper-IgM and antibody deficiency syndromes; BTK mutation abolishes B cell output entirely. Complement and Fc receptor components extend the response to effector clearance of opsonised targets.

Natural killer cells kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization, and this pathway covers the tuning of that killing — how strongly, how often, and against which targets. The balance is set by opposing surface receptors: inhibitory receptors read MHC class I molecules such as HLA-A/B/C and HLA-E and their partner B2M so that healthy self cells are spared, while activating receptors including NKG2D and the natural cytotoxicity receptors detect stress-induced ligands like MICA and the RAET1 family. Nectin and CD226/TIGIT interactions, along with checkpoint proteins such as TIM-3 and LAG3, further raise or lower the threshold. Downstream adaptors and signalling proteins (VAV1, GRB2, the SLAM-associated proteins, the phosphatase SHIP1) convert receptor engagement into degranulation, and cytokines including IL-12, IL-18 signalling and IL-21 amplify it while TGF-beta suppresses it. Loss of restraint yields autoimmune and hemophagocytic pathology; loss of activation permits tumours and herpesvirus infection to escape.

Natural killer cells must be restrained as well as armed, and this is the braking system that keeps their cytotoxicity off healthy self tissue. Inhibitory receptors read MHC class I molecules on target cells — classical HLA-A and HLA-B, the non-classical HLA-E recognised by the KLRC1/KLRD1 heterodimer, and HLA-G at the maternal-fetal interface — so that cells displaying normal self are spared while those that have lost it are killed. Additional checkpoints act through TIGIT and CD96 binding nectin-family ligands, TIM-3 engaging galectin-9, and CEACAM1 and LILRB1, with signals converging on the inositol phosphatase SHIP1 and adaptors such as GRB2 and CRK to dampen activating input; TGFB1 suppresses NK function in the surrounding milieu. Tumours exploit these brakes to evade lysis, which is why they are targeted therapeutically, while their loss favours autoimmunity and pregnancy failure.

Natural killer cells kill virally infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization, and this is the biology that raises the threshold-crossing signals that license them to do so. Enhancing NK-mediated immunity matters for tumour surveillance, control of herpesvirus infection, and the maternal-fetal interface, where NK recognition of HLA-C, HLA-E and HLA-G shapes trophoblast tolerance. Activating receptors such as NKG2D (KLRK1) paired with CD94/KLRD1, the nectin-binding receptors CD226 and CRTAM, and the SLAM-family adaptors SH2D1A and SH2D1B feed into VAV1 and RASGRP-dependent signalling that triggers cytotoxic granule release, with LAMP1 marking the degranulating lytic compartment. Cytokines add a second tier: IL-12 subunits, IL-18 receptor accessory signalling and IL-21 drive STAT5-dependent proliferation and interferon-gamma output. Stress-induced ULBP/RAET1 ligands on damaged cells supply the target-side cues that make this activation tumour-selective.
