Immune responses have to be damped as well as launched, and this pathway covers the braking processes that stop or reduce cytokine output once an immune response is underway. Without such restraint, inflammatory mediators accumulate and drive tissue damage, cytokine storm, and autoimmunity. The suppression works through several routes: secreted immunosuppressive cytokines such as IL10 and the TGF-beta family, which signal through SMAD intermediates including the inhibitory SMAD7; inhibitory surface receptors on lymphocytes and myeloid cells, including BTLA, CD96 and the LILRB family of MHC class I-binding receptors; transcriptional control by FOXP3, which specifies regulatory T cells, and BCL6; and intracellular negative feedback on Toll-like receptor signalling by the pseudokinase IRAK3. Arginase and lipoprotein components contribute further metabolic and lipid-dependent dampening, tying inflammatory tone to macrophage polarisation and plasma lipid status.

Immune cells commit to a response largely by deciding how much cytokine to make, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that output upward. It sets the magnitude of inflammation and the flavour of T helper differentiation, so its overactivity underlies autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease while its failure leaves infections uncontrolled. Pattern-recognition receptors for bacterial and viral ligands, including a lipopolysaccharide-sensing Toll-like receptor, a cytosolic peptidoglycan sensor, a fungal beta-glucan receptor and RNA helicase sensors, feed through adaptors and kinases such as TRAF6, MAP3K7, MALT1 and BCL10 to switch on transcription of IL1B, IL6, IL18 and IL21. Inflammasome assembly via NLRP3 handles the maturation step for interleukin-1 family members. Lineage transcription factors GATA3 and TBX21 bias output toward type 2 or type 1 cytokines, while MHC class I molecules and NK receptors tune lymphocyte activation thresholds.

T cells that have been activated must also be restrained, and this is the set of brakes that lowers how much cytokine an activated T cell makes. Dampening interleukin and interferon output limits collateral tissue damage during infection, enforces peripheral tolerance, and is exploited by tumours to blunt local immunity; losing it produces autoimmunity and cytokine-driven inflammatory disease, as the FOXP3 mutations that abolish regulatory T cell function show. The mechanisms are mixed. Inhibitory surface receptors such as BTLA, signalling through its ligand HVEM, and the leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor LILRB4 deliver negative signals at the immune synapse; arginase depletes the arginine that T cells need; SMAD7 sits in the transforming growth factor beta arm; and type I interferons can suppress as well as stimulate. Transcriptional control appears too, since TBX21 shapes which cytokines a helper T cell is licensed to produce.

Effector T cells do their work largely by secreting cytokines, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the amount they make. Its outputs determine whether an immune response is inflammatory, antiviral, or allergic, and excessive signalling here drives autoimmune and atopic disease while too little leaves infections uncleared. Antigen presentation components and costimulatory ligands such as OX40 ligand and SLAMF1 deliver the initial signals, while receptors for interleukin-1 and interleukin-18 amplify them; the inflammasome component NLRP3 and IL1B supply the innate cytokines that license this amplification. Downstream, MALT1, TRAF2/TRAF6 and MAP3K7 carry receptor engagement into NF-κB activation, and the lineage transcription factors TBX21 and GATA3 direct which cytokines are produced, specifying type 1 versus type 2 helper T cell output. IL4 and IL6 act as both products and feed-forward signals.

Natural killer cells respond to infection and malignant transformation not only by killing targets but by secreting interferon-gamma and other cytokines that shape the wider immune response, and this is the set of inputs that raises that output. Engagement of activating surface receptors such as CD226 and CD160, and of the non-classical MHC molecules HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G by their cognate NK receptors, tips the balance of activating versus inhibitory signals toward cytokine transcription; KIR2DL4 recognition of HLA-G is a notable example at the maternal-fetal interface, where NK-derived cytokines support spiral artery remodelling rather than cytotoxicity. Stress-induced ligands of the RAET1 family mark damaged cells for the same recognition, and the cytoplasmic adaptor CLNK couples immunoreceptor signalling to downstream activation. Interleukin-21 provides the accessory cytokine input that amplifies the response.

Dendritic cells decide how strong and what kind of an immune response follows an encounter with a pathogen, and much of that decision is transmitted as cytokine output. Raising dendritic cell cytokine production amplifies interferon and inflammatory mediator release, which in turn licenses T cell priming and shapes helper cell polarisation; too little leaves infections unchecked, while too much drives autoinflammation. The genes here mark the sensing routes that feed this output: the fungal beta-glucan receptor CLEC7A signalling through PLCG2 and the transmembrane adaptor SCIMP, Toll-like receptor signalling via the adaptor TICAM1, and cytosolic RNA recognition by RIGI and DEAD/H-box helicases converging on the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS. Calcium-dependent signalling through CAMK4 and growth factor input from KIT modulate the response, linking pattern recognition at the cell surface and in the cytosol to transcriptional induction of cytokines.

Innate immune cells detect microbes before any antibody exists, and signalling from cell surface pattern recognition receptors is how that detection becomes a response. Toll-like receptors at the plasma membrane, aided by co-receptors and lipid-binding accessory proteins such as CD14, LBP, LY96 and CD36, recognise conserved microbial structures including lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides and flagellin, while a C-type lectin arm (CLEC7A, TREM2) and collectin/ficolin-MASP components sense fungal glucans and surface carbohydrates. Ligand binding recruits MYD88 or TICAM adaptors, activates IRAK kinases, TRAF6 and MAP3K7, and drives NF-kB (RELA, restrained by NFKBIA, TNFAIP3 and TNIP proteins) plus IRF3/TBK1-dependent interferon output, yielding cytokines, chemokines and antimicrobial effectors. Host danger signals such as HMGB1 feed into the same receptors. Several microRNAs, notably MIR146A, damp the cascade; insufficient restraint produces sepsis, chronic inflammation and autoimmune tissue damage, while loss of signalling leaves recurrent bacterial infection.

cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signaling pathway is the intracellular arm of innate immune surveillance: sensors sitting in the cytosol detect microbial nucleic acids, peptidoglycan fragments and other conserved pathogen structures that have breached the membrane, and convert that detection into interferon production, inflammatory cytokine release and inflammasome-driven cell death. It is how cells recognise viral replication and invasive bacteria from within, and its misfiring underlies interferonopathies, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and Crohn-associated inflammation. DNA sensing runs through cGAS and STING to TBK1 and IRF3; RNA sensing through RIG-I and MDA5 to MAVS; peptidoglycan through NOD1/NOD2 and RIPK2 to NF- cB; and NLRP3, NLRP1 and pyrin assemble with ASC to activate caspase-driven maturation of IL-1 family cytokines. Layered onto these are ubiquitin editors, palmitoyl transferases, endolysosomal transporters and negative regulators such as TREX1 and A20 that keep the response from turning on self.

Intracellular sentinels detect microbial nucleic acids and cell wall fragments that have breached the plasma membrane, and this cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signaling underlies the first line of antiviral and antibacterial defence in essentially every cell type, not just professional immune cells. Cytosolic DNA is read by cGAS and IFI16 feeding STING, RNA duplexes by RIG-I and MDA5 feeding the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, and bacterial peptidoglycan by NOD1 and NOD2 through RIPK2, converging on TBK1-IRF3 to drive type I interferon or on TAK1-IKK-NF-κB to drive inflammatory cytokines. A parallel arm assembles inflammasomes around NLRP3, NLRP1 or pyrin with ASC, activating caspase-mediated IL-1 release and pyroptosis. Ubiquitin editing by A20, CYLD and OTULIN, TRIM ligases, palmitoylation, and nucleases such as TREX1 keep the output proportionate; loss of restraint produces interferonopathies and hereditary periodic fever syndromes, while loss of sensing leaves hosts vulnerable to infection.

Toll-like receptors recognise conserved microbial patterns, and the MyD88-dependent branch is the route by which most of them convert that recognition into inflammatory gene expression. It underlies the innate response to bacterial lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides and microbial DNA, and its loss in humans causes recurrent pyogenic infection, while excessive output drives septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease. Receptor engagement recruits MyD88 together with the bridging adaptor TIRAP to form a scaffold on which IRAK4 activates IRAK1 and IRAK2; TRAF6 then acts as a ubiquitin ligase to engage MAP3K7 and the IKK complex, releasing NF-kB and, through IRF7, type I interferon transcription. Brakes are built in: IRAK3 is a catalytically inactive decoy kinase and TNIP1 restrains NF-kB, while inhibitory receptors such as CD300A tune the threshold. Downstream effectors include antimicrobial products like REG3G at mucosal surfaces.

Some Toll-like receptors sense microbial patterns and signal without the MyD88 adaptor, instead routing through the TRIF adaptor TICAM1 and its bridging partner TICAM2 to produce type I interferon alongside inflammatory gene expression. This MyD88-independent branch is what allows lipopolysaccharide-engaged TLR4, after endocytosis, to trigger an antiviral-type transcriptional response rather than only NF-kB-driven cytokines, and it shapes how strongly and for how long macrophages and dendritic cells respond to infection. TRAF3 and TRAF6 partition the output, TBK1/IKK activity with IRF3 and IRF7 drives interferon transcription, and MAP3K7 and IKBKB feed the NF-kB arm; SARM1 and TNIP3 restrain it. Trafficking components such as RAB11FIP2 place the receptor in the endosomal compartment where this signalling occurs. Too little leaves innate defence blunted; too much contributes to endotoxin shock and sterile inflammation.

Secreted antimicrobial molecules — defensins, cathelicidin, lysozyme and related peptides — form a chemical barrier on skin, mucosa and glandular surfaces, and this pathway covers the processes that tune how much of that response is mounted. Tight control matters because too little permits bacterial and fungal colonisation while too much drives inflammatory skin and gut disease. The set spans several layers of that control: the cathelicidin precursor CAMP as an effector whose production is regulated; the T helper 17 cytokines IL17A and IL17F, which drive epithelial antimicrobial peptide expression and keep mucosal surfaces protected against Candida and extracellular bacteria; the protease inhibitor SPINK5, which restrains epidermal serine proteases and thereby barrier and peptide processing; and the transcription factor GATA6, which shapes epithelial and macrophage programmes. Loss of such regulation underlies chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and Netherton syndrome, linking innate epithelial defence to inflammatory pathology.

Secreted antimicrobial molecules form a first line of chemical defence at epithelial surfaces and in body fluids, and this pathway covers the signals and factors that raise their production and activity. Enhancing this antimicrobial humoral response helps clear bacteria and fungi at barrier sites such as skin, gut, lung and the urogenital tract, and its failure predisposes to mucocutaneous infection and chronic candidiasis. The T cell cytokines IL17A and IL17F act on epithelial and stromal cells to drive expression of defensins, cathelicidin and other effectors, while cathelicidin itself, encoded by CAMP, is processed into a membrane-permeabilising peptide. ACOD1 contributes by generating itaconate in activated macrophages, linking immunometabolism to antimicrobial output. Other members reflect proteolytic and acid-protease activities of glandular secretions, placing this biology at the interface of innate immunity, epithelial biology and inflammation.

Blood monocytes, granulocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, megakaryocytes and osteoclasts all arise from a common myeloid progenitor, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast and how far that differentiation proceeds. Getting the balance right determines innate immune capacity, bone remodelling and platelet output; losing it produces neutropenia, osteopetrosis or osteoporosis, and blocked maturation is the defining lesion of myeloid leukaemia. Lineage-instructive transcription factors such as RUNX1, GATA2, TAL1, CEBPB, MAFB, MITF and RARA act as the core switches, with ZFPM1 and PIAS3 tuning their output and microRNAs including MIR223 and MIR125B1 adding a post-transcriptional layer. Cytokines and their receptors supply the external cues: CSF1 and IL34 drive macrophage and microglial programmes, while RANKL signalling through TNFRSF11A, TRAF6, TREM2 and TYROBP directs osteoclast fusion, opposed by the decoy receptor TNFRSF11B. Inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IFNG and IL23A shift the same decisions during infection.

Blood cell output has to be held in check as well as driven, and this pathway collects the brakes on myeloid leukocyte differentiation " s" the signals and factors that slow or block progenitors from becoming granulocytes, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells or osteoclasts. Restraint matters because unchecked myeloid maturation depletes the stem cell pool, and because loss of these brakes features in myeloid leukaemia and in inflammatory bone loss. Transcriptional regulators such as RUNX1, GATA2, MAFB, RARA and PRDM16 set thresholds for lineage commitment, while inhibitory receptors of the LILRB family and the phosphatase-adaptor INPP5D dampen the signalling that would otherwise push cells forward. Secreted inhibitors including osteoprotegerin, activin/inhibin subunits, SFRP1 and IL4, together with ubiquitin ligase components FBXW7 and CUL4A and the microRNA miR-125b, provide extrinsic and post-translational layers of the same control.</br>

Granulocytes, monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and osteoclasts all arise from myeloid progenitors, and this grouping covers the signals that push those progenitors toward differentiation rather than self-renewal. It matters for steady-state blood production, for the emergency output of phagocytes during infection, and for bone remodelling, since osteoclasts are a myeloid end-product; loss of these cues underlies neutropenia and impaired host defence, while unbalanced signalling contributes to myeloid leukaemia and to pathological bone loss. Growth factors and cytokines including CSF1, IL34, LIF, TGFB1, TNF and the IL23–IL17 axis act through receptors and adaptors such as TNFRSF11A with TRAF6, TREM2 with TYROBP, and FES kinase, converging on transcription factors RUNX1, STAT5A, FOS, CREB1 and ID2. Fusion machinery including DCSTAMP and OCSTAMP marks the osteoclast arm, and death-domain proteins CASP8, FADD and RIPK1 contribute non-apoptotic differentiation signals.

Immune responses begin when a receptor meets its ligand, and this collection covers the receptor-proximal signalling that decides whether that encounter activates, sustains, or damps an immune reaction. It spans antigen receptor complexes and their kinases and adaptors — CD3 chains with LCK, ZAP70, LAT and LCP2, the B cell receptor with CD79A/B, SYK and BTK — alongside pattern recognition by Toll-like receptors through MYD88 and IRAK proteins, cytosolic nucleic acid sensing via cGAS–STING and RIG-I–MAVS, and inflammasome assembly around NLRP3, PYCARD and caspase-1. Equally represented are the brakes: inhibitory checkpoint receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1 and LAG3, killer-cell inhibitory receptors, phosphatases including PTPN6 and PTPN22, and ubiquitin editors like TNFAIP3. Loss of this balance produces immunodeficiency, autoinflammation or autoimmunity.

Immune cells need brakes as well as triggers, and immune response-inhibiting signal transduction is how receptor engagement is converted into damping rather than activation of effector function. It sets the threshold at which natural killer cells and myeloid cells attack, protects healthy tissue and the fetus from destruction, and is the axis tumours and chronic viruses exploit to evade killing; its loss contributes to autoimmunity and inflammatory tissue damage. Most members are inhibitory surface receptors of the killer-cell immunoglobulin-like and leukocyte immunoglobulin-like families, together with the lectin-like CD33, CLEC12B, LAIR1 and the CD94-associated KLRC1, which read MHC class I and related ligands including the non-classical HLA-G. Their cytoplasmic tails recruit phosphatases through tyrosine-based motifs, with the Src-family kinase LYN acting in the same circuitry, so that activating signals are opposed at the level of proximal phosphorylation.

Immune cells decide whether to attack, tolerate, or stand down on the basis of what their surface receptors encounter, and this pathway covers the signalling that follows such engagement and sets the strength and direction of the response. It spans antigen receptors on T and B cells with their CD3 and Ig-alpha/Ig-beta modules, Fc receptors for antibody, Toll-like receptors and C-type lectins sensing microbial patterns, complement and formyl peptide receptors, and the NK cell KIR and NKG2 families. Engagement is transduced by Src and Syk/ZAP70 kinases onto adaptors such as LAT, LCP2, BLNK and MYD88, converging on PI3K, phospholipase C-gamma, NF-kB and MAPK output. Coinhibitory receptors including CTLA4, PDCD1, BTLA and phosphatase-recruiting ITIM proteins such as PTPN6 and INPP5D damp the same circuits; their loss drives autoimmunity, while their exploitation by tumours is the basis of checkpoint blockade.

Immune cells need a brake on antibody-triggered activation, and inhibitory Fc receptor signalling supplies it. When a receptor bearing cytoplasmic ITIM motifs engages the constant region of an immunoglobulin or an MHC class I ligand, it recruits phosphatases that strip activating phosphorylation from nearby kinase cascades, damping degranulation, phagocytosis, cytokine release and antibody-dependent killing. The leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptors LILRB1, LILRB2 and LILRB4 are the receptor arm here, and the Src-family kinase LYN phosphorylates their ITIMs to nucleate the inhibitory complex, the same kinase that also drives activating signals — so the balance of receptor occupancy, not the kinase alone, sets the outcome. This restraint keeps effector responses proportionate and limits autoimmune tissue damage; tumours and some pathogens exploit the same receptors to render myeloid cells tolerant, which is why they are pursued as checkpoint targets.

Epithelial surfaces and phagocytes defend themselves chemically, and this pathway covers the making and release of antimicrobial peptides that kill or restrain bacteria, fungi, viruses and protozoa at those barriers. Much of the regulation is proteolytic: defensins and cathelicidins are produced as inactive precursors and must be cleaved to become microbicidal, work carried out by neutrophil elastase in granulocytes, matrilysin in intestinal Paneth cells, and kallikreins in skin, where the inhibitor SPINK5 restrains that proteolysis — its loss causes Netherton syndrome with barrier breakdown and inflammation. The T helper 17 cytokines IL17A and IL17F drive epithelial transcription of these effectors, linking adaptive immunity to mucosal antimicrobial output. Together these activities set the antimicrobial tone of gut, airway and skin surfaces, and their failure predisposes to chronic candidiasis and bacterial colonisation.

Antimicrobial peptides are small cationic effectors of innate defence at epithelial and mucosal surfaces, and most are made as inactive precursors that must be cut to become bactericidal. This pathway covers that production step, which sets how much active peptide reaches the gut lumen, the airway or the skin surface, and so shapes the composition of the resident microbiota and resistance to invading bacteria and fungi. Neutrophil elastase and matrilysin are proteases that process precursor forms, matrilysin being the enzyme that converts pro-defensins into active alpha-defensins in Paneth cells of the small intestine; the kallikreins KLK5 and KLK7 act in the stratum corneum, where the inhibitor SPINK5 restrains them. Loss of that restraint causes Netherton syndrome, with barrier breakdown and inflammation, illustrating that antimicrobial peptide generation is inseparable from control of epithelial protease activity.</description>

Antibacterial peptide production covers the making and liberation of small microbicidal peptides that defend epithelial and mucosal surfaces, giving skin, gut and secretory tissues a chemical barrier against bacteria before adaptive immunity engages. Much of the regulation is proteolytic: many antimicrobial peptides are synthesised as inactive precursors and must be cleaved to become active. Neutrophil elastase and matrilysin (MMP7) process pro-defensins, kallikreins such as KLK5 and KLK7 act in the stratum corneum, and the serine protease inhibitor SPINK5 restrains that kallikrein activity, a brake whose loss causes Netherton syndrome with barrier failure and infection. Other members reflect the tissue setting rather than the chemistry, including cornified envelope and gastric secretory components. Output of this pathway shapes the commensal microbiota as well as pathogen killing, and its dysregulation contributes to inflammatory skin and intestinal disease.

Epithelial surfaces defend themselves chemically, secreting defensins, cathelicidins and other antimicrobial peptides onto skin, gut and airway linings, and this pathway sets how much of that output is made. Tuning matters in both directions: too little leaves barriers open to bacterial and fungal colonisation, as in the chronic Candida infections seen when interleukin-17 signalling fails, while excess drives the inflammatory lesions of psoriasis. IL17A and IL17F, released by T cells and innate lymphocytes, act on keratinocytes and other epithelia to induce peptide expression, while the protease inhibitor SPINK5 and the cornified envelope protein EVPL tie the response to the integrity of the skin barrier itself, where unrestrained protease activity causes Netherton syndrome. The remaining members link secreted peptide production to glandular and gastric epithelia, placing this control at the interface of innate immunity and barrier maintenance.

Hormone-secreting cells must be able to switch off as well as on, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that reduce or halt release of peptide hormones. Much of it is pancreatic islet biology: the KATP channel subunits SUR1 and Kir6.2 hold the beta cell hyperpolarized and suppress insulin granule fusion until glucose metabolism closes them, while uncoupling protein 2, SIRT4 and HADH limit the metabolic signal that couples fuel to secretion. Inhibitory G-protein-coupled input through alpha-2 adrenergic, dopamine D2, melatonin and ghrelin receptors, transduced by Gi/Go-class subunits, dampens secretion in islets and neuroendocrine tissue, and CRH-binding protein and leptin act as extracellular restraints. Loss of this restraint produces hyperinsulinism and hypoglycaemia; excessive restraint contributes to type 2 diabetes, several of these genes being diabetes risk loci.

Peptide hormones are stored in dense-core granules and released only on demand, and this pathway covers the signals that raise the rate of that release. Its dominant theme is the pancreatic islet beta cell: glucose entry through GLUT2 and phosphorylation by glucokinase raise ATP, close the KATP channel subunit encoded by ABCC8, and trigger calcium-dependent exocytosis of insulin, with granule proteins such as the zinc transporter SLC30A8 and SNARE/Rab machinery including STX4, DOC2B and MYRIP completing the step. Amplifying inputs come from incretin and free fatty acid receptors, cAMP through adenylate cyclase, protein kinase A and the exchange factors RAPGEF3/4, and protein kinase C. Transcription factors PDX1, NEUROD1, NKX6-1, ISL1 and RFX6 build and maintain the secretory cell itself. Beyond the islet, glucagon, ghrelin, CRH, growth hormone-releasing hormone and urocortins place the same logic in gut and neuroendocrine tissue; blunted secretion underlies type 2 diabetes.

Adaptive immunity has to be tuned as well as triggered, and this collection covers the processes that set how strongly, how long and in which direction a lymphocyte response proceeds. Antigen presentation molecules, including classical and non-classical MHC class I, class II and the CD1 lipid-presenting family, determine what T cells see, while costimulatory and coinhibitory receptors such as CD28, CD40, PD-1 and its ligand CD274, CTLA-family relatives, LAG3, TIM-3 and BTLA raise or lower the activation threshold. Cytokines and their receptors, notably the IL-12/IL-23/IL-27 axis, IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, TGF-beta and IL-10, together with lineage transcription factors TBX21, GATA3, BCL6, FOXP3 and RORgt-associated regulators, steer helper subset choice and tolerance. Negative regulators including TNFAIP3, PTPN6, SOCS5 and the roquin ribonucleases restrain signalling; class-switch and repair factors support antibody diversification. Loss of this control produces autoimmunity, chronic inflammation, immunodeficiency or tumour immune escape.

Adaptive immunity must be damped as well as launched, and this collection of brakes limits how strongly and how long lymphocytes respond to antigen — the difference between clearing an infection and destroying host tissue. Loss of these restraints produces autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; their deliberate exploitation by tumours and their blockade by checkpoint antibodies is the basis of modern immunotherapy. Inhibitory surface receptors such as PDCD1 with its ligand CD274, BTLA with TNFRSF14, LAG3, HAVCR2 and CD160 raise the threshold for T cell activation, while PTPN6 and DUSP22 dephosphorylate signalling intermediates downstream. FOXP3 specifies regulatory T cells, BCL6 constrains helper differentiation, and the RNA-binding proteins RC3H1, RC3H2 and ZC3H12A degrade transcripts encoding costimulators and cytokines. Complement regulators including CD46 and C4BP, plus tolerogenic HLA-G, extend the same restraint to humoral and fetal-maternal contexts.</description>

Adaptive immunity is amplified as well as initiated, and this collection captures the processes that raise the magnitude, speed or persistence of lymphocyte responses to antigen. It matters for effective vaccination and pathogen clearance, and its dysregulation drives autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and immunodeficiency. Antigen is displayed by classical and non-classical MHC molecules together with lipid-presenting CD1 proteins and MR1, while costimulatory receptors such as CD28, CD40 and CD226 and their ligands lower the threshold for T cell activation. Cytokines including IL-2, IL-4, IL-6, IL-12, IL-18 and IL-23 act through receptor chains and STAT signalling to expand and polarise effector subsets, with lineage transcription factors GATA3, TBX21 and FOXP3 fixing helper and regulatory fates. Innate sensors, NF-κB adaptors and class switch recombination and mismatch repair machinery feed into antibody diversification and sustained effector output.

regulation of T-helper 1 type immune response tunes the strength of the IFN-γ-dominated arm of adaptive immunity, the response that clears intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses by arming macrophages and cytotoxic cells. Too little of it leaves patients with disseminated mycobacterial and Salmonella infection; too much drives autoimmune tissue damage and granuloma formation. Control is exerted mostly at the point where innate cytokines instruct a naive CD4 T cell: IL-12 and IL-18, amplified by IL-1 and IL-23 and shaped by IL-27, signal through paired receptor chains and JAK-STAT to induce the lineage transcription factor TBX21, with HLX and ARID5A reinforcing commitment. Counter-regulators set the ceiling, including the decoy IL-18BP, SOCS5, and the inhibitory receptor pair TIM-3 and galectin-9 that deletes activated Th1 cells. Costimulation, chemokine-guided positioning in lymph nodes, and eicosanoid signalling complete the circuit.

Type 1 helper T cell responses drive defence against intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses, and this pathway covers the signals that raise or damp that response. Interferon-gamma-producing Th1 cells depend on it; too little leaves susceptibility to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection, while too much contributes to autoimmune and granulomatous inflammation. The core mechanism is cytokine instruction of naive T cells: IL-12 and its shared receptor subunits, IL-18 with its receptor and the decoy binding protein IL-18BP, and related IL-12 family members including IL-23 and IL-27 acting through shared chains such as IL6ST and downstream JAK3. TBX21 is the lineage-defining transcription factor, with HLX reinforcing the programme and SOCS5 restraining it. Costimulation via CD80 and TNFSF4, inhibitory input through HAVCR2 and its ligand LGALS9, chemokine-guided positioning, and inflammasome-linked IL-1 signalling set the response's magnitude and its resolution.

Th1 responses drive interferon-gamma-dependent defence against intracellular pathogens, but unchecked they cause tissue damage and autoimmunity, so they must be actively restrained; this pathway covers the brakes applied to T-helper 1 type immunity. Several mechanisms appear together. IL-27, formed from EBI3 with its partner chain and signalling through IL27RA with the shared IL6ST subunit, limits Th1 and Th17 differentiation and promotes regulatory programmes. The checkpoint receptor HAVCR2 (TIM-3) engaged by galectin-9 (LGALS9) triggers exhaustion or death of interferon-gamma-producing effector T cells. A soluble binding protein sequesters IL-18, neutralising a cytokine that would otherwise amplify interferon-gamma output, while IL-33 acting through IL1RL1 skews responses toward type 2 immunity. Loss of such restraint underlies chronic inflammatory disease, whereas its excess in tumours blunts protective antitumour T cell activity.

Type 1 immunity is the arm of adaptive defence that arms macrophages and cytotoxic cells against intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses, and the genes here act to amplify it. Their combined effect is to push naive CD4 T cells toward the IFN-gamma-producing T-helper 1 fate and to sustain that program once established; loss of the axis leaves people susceptible to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection, while excess drives autoinflammatory and autoimmune tissue damage. Mechanistically, myeloid-derived IL-12, IL-18, IL-23 and IL-1 engage their matched receptor chains on responding lymphocytes, with IL12RB1 shared across the IL-12 and IL-23 receptors and RIPK2 relaying intracellular bacterial sensing from NOD receptors. TBX21 is the lineage-defining transcription factor that locks in IFN-gamma competence, while chemokine signals such as CCR2 and XCL1 recruit the monocytes and dendritic cells that deliver these cues.

Type 2 immunity is the arm of adaptive defence directed at helminths and allergens, and this regulatory programme sets how strongly and how long it runs. Gain of function shows up as allergic asthma, atopic dermatitis and eosinophilic inflammation; loss leaves the host unable to expel parasites or repair damaged epithelium. The core axis is IL4 acting through STAT6 to induce GATA3, which commits CD4 T cells to the Th2 fate; SOCS5 and the ubiquitin adaptor NDFIP1 dampen that signal, while TBX61-type opposing factors, here TBX21 and BCL6, drive cells toward alternative helper programmes. Epithelial IL33 alarms the system, type I and type III interferons and IL18 restrain it, and arginases mark alternatively activated macrophages downstream. Costimulation via CD86 and TNFSF4 on dendritic cells determines whether a naive T cell is polarised this way at all.

Type 2 immunity drives IgE production, eosinophilia and mucus secretion, and restraining it is what keeps antiparasite and barrier defence from tipping into allergy and asthma. Negative regulation of the type 2 immune response covers the brakes applied at several levels: transcription factors that impose alternative fates on differentiating CD4 T cells, notably TBX21 for the Th1 programme and BCL6 for follicular helper cells, with HLX and ASCL2 reinforcing non-Th2 identity; cytokine signalling that cross-inhibits, including type I and type III interferons and the IL-27 receptor; and intracellular dampers such as SOCS5 and the ubiquitin ligase adaptor NDFIP1, which limits effector T cell cytokine output. Arginase isoforms tie the response to arginine availability in myeloid cells, and annexin A1 contributes anti-inflammatory tone. STAT6, the central Th2 transducer, is the node most of this circuitry converges on.

Type 2 immunity is the arm of adaptive defence directed against helminths and allergens, characterised by IL-4-driven B cell class switching to IgE, eosinophil recruitment and mucus production; its positive regulation describes the signals that initiate and amplify this programme. The genes here act at several tiers: GATA3 is the master transcription factor committing CD4 T cells to the Th2 lineage, IL4 is the defining effector cytokine, and IL33 is an epithelial alarmin released on barrier damage that licenses Th2 and innate lymphoid responses. Antigen-presenting molecules and costimulatory ligands such as CD74, CD86 and TNFSF4 (OX40L) bias T cell priming toward this fate, while inflammasome and pattern-recognition components including NLRP3 and NOD2 link tissue insult to cytokine output. Excessive amplification underlies asthma, atopic dermatitis and food allergy, whereas insufficiency impairs antiparasite clearance and tissue repair.

Detecting a microbe is only half the problem; setting the size of the reply is the other half, and this is the tuning layer that modulates responses to biotic stimuli such as bacteria, viruses and fungi. Too little output permits invasive infection, too much drives septic shock, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and autoimmunity, so the same genes recur in susceptibility to both. Sensors of the Toll-like, NOD-like, RIG-I-like and cytosolic DNA classes feed adaptors including MYD88, TICAM1, MAVS and STING1 toward NF- fB and interferon regulatory factors, while brakes act at every step: negative-feedback deubiquitinases and ubiquitin ligases such as TNFAIP3, CYLD, OTULIN and TRIM family members, decoy and inhibitory receptors, phosphatases, inhibitory immune checkpoints, microRNAs, complement regulators, and pyrin-domain decoys that restrain inflammasome assembly and interleukin-1 release. Natural killer and T cell recognition receptors set thresholds for cytotoxicity within the same framework.

Immune responses to microbes and other organisms must be damped as well as launched, and this collection of braking mechanisms is what keeps antiviral and antibacterial activation proportionate and self-limited. Loss of such restraint underlies interferonopathies, autoinflammation and autoimmunity, while its exaggeration by tumours or chronic infection produces immune evasion and lymphocyte exhaustion. The brakes act at several levels: inhibitory receptor–ligand pairs such as PD-1 with CD274, TIGIT and its nectin ligands, LAG3, HAVCR2 with LGALS9, and HLA class I molecules read by killer-cell receptors; intracellular negative regulators including TNFAIP3, USP18, SIGIRR, IRAK3, TREX1, SAMHD1 and the NLR family members NLRC3 and NLRX1 that curb innate nucleic-acid sensing and NF-κB signalling; phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPN2; and suppressive programmes driven by TGFB1 and FOXP3. Arginine-depleting enzymes, serpins, microRNAs and m6A readers add metabolic and post-transcriptional layers of dampening.

Detecting microbes and other organisms is only useful if the detection is amplified, and this is the machinery that turns up the gain on responses to biotic stimuli such as bacteria, viruses, fungi and their molecular signatures. It underlies innate immune defence, inflammation and the priming of lymphocyte responses; excess activity drives autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, while loss leaves hosts prone to recurrent infection. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their adaptors MYD88 and TICAM1, cytosolic nucleic acid sensors including CGAS, RIGI and IFIH1 signalling through STING1 and MAVS, and NOD-like receptors such as NOD2 and NLRP3 all feed into IRAK and TRAF6-dependent kinase cascades that activate NF-kB and the IRF transcription factors, inducing type I interferon and cytokines. Inflammasome components, ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, palmitoyltransferases and microRNAs set the threshold and amplitude of these responses, as do natural killer cell receptors and antigen-presenting molecules that couple innate sensing to cytotoxicity.

regulation of response to tumor cell governs how strongly the immune system attacks transformed cells, setting the balance between effective tumor clearance and the tolerance that lets cancers grow. It is the biology exploited by checkpoint blockade: PD-1 with its ligand PD-L1, LAG3, TIM-3, BTLA and CD160 with the herpesvirus entry mediator, and the CD226/TIGIT axis competing for the nectin ligands PVR and NECTIN2 all tune the activation threshold of cytotoxic T and NK cells. Counterbalancing signals promote attack, including IL-12 driving type 1 differentiation, MR1-restricted and MHC class II antigen presentation, and immunogenic release of HMGB1 or gasdermin-mediated pyroptotic death. Suppressive arms act through TGF-beta, the tryptophan-metabolising IL4I1 and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling. Ubiquitin-pathway components such as FBXO38 and KLHL22 control checkpoint receptor turnover, determining how long inhibition persists on the cell surface.

Immune recognition and killing of tumour cells is tunable, and this pathway covers the processes that set how strong that antitumour response becomes. Its components are the checkpoints exploited by cancers to escape immunity and the targets of checkpoint blockade therapy: PD-1 with its ligand PD-L1, LAG3, TIM-3 (HAVCR2), BTLA and its ligand TNFRSF14, CD160, and the nectin-family ligands PVR and NECTIN2 that engage the activating receptor CD226. Counterbalancing signals come from IL-12 subunits and HMGB1, which promote cytotoxic and NK responses, while TGFB1, AHR and IL4I1 impose immunosuppression through metabolite and cytokine cues. Regulators of checkpoint protein stability, including the ubiquitin machinery acting on PD-1, determine surface receptor levels. Also represented are intrinsic death routes such as gasdermin E-dependent pyroptosis, linking target-cell killing mode to the resulting inflammation and immune escape.

Immune attack on transformed cells is held in check by inhibitory signals, and this collection of brakes on the response to tumor cells describes how that restraint is imposed. It matters in both directions: the same circuits that prevent autoimmunity and limit collateral tissue damage are co-opted by tumours to escape killing, which is why several members are the targets of checkpoint blockade therapy. PD-1 and its ligand PD-L1, together with LAG3, TIM-3 and CEACAM1, deliver coinhibitory signals that dampen T and NK cell activation and cytotoxicity. TGF-beta suppresses effector differentiation and favours regulatory phenotypes, while the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and the tryptophan-metabolising enzyme IL4I1 generate an immunosuppressive metabolic environment through ligand-driven transcription. The net result is reduced tumour cell recognition, blunted effector output, and tolerance of a growing malignancy.

Immune recognition and killing of transformed cells is amplified by this set of activating processes, which raise the frequency or magnitude of the antitumour response and underpin natural immunosurveillance as well as the efficacy of checkpoint and cell-based cancer therapies. Activating receptors on NK and T cells, including CD226 and CRTAM, engage nectin-family ligands such as PVR and NECTIN2 on tumour cells to trigger cytotoxicity, while CD160 contributes to NK effector function and MR1 and class II MHC molecules present antigen to unconventional and helper T cells. The IL12 heterodimer drives interferon-gamma production and Th1 polarisation. Intracellular regulators tune this output: FBXO38 and KLHL22 act through ubiquitin-dependent control of checkpoint receptor levels, and GSDME converts caspase cleavage into pyroptotic, immunogenic tumour cell death. Loss of such amplification permits immune escape and tumour outgrowth.

Tumours survive immune attack in part by actively damping the T cells sent to kill them, and this braking of the T cell mediated response to tumour cells is the process exploited by checkpoint blockade therapy. PD-1 on activated T cells, engaged by its ligand PD-L1 displayed on tumour and myeloid cells, attenuates T cell receptor signalling and cytotoxic effector function, while LAG-3 imposes a parallel inhibitory signal and marks exhausted tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes. A metabolic arm also contributes: IL4I1 oxidises aromatic amino acids to generate ligands for the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, whose transcriptional output favours tolerance over effector differentiation. Loss or blockade of these restraints restores tumour killing, which is why they are the main drug targets in cancer immunotherapy; conversely, their overactivity in the tumour microenvironment permits immune escape and progression.

Tumours are recognised and killed by T cells, and this pathway covers the events that raise the strength of that attack, either by improving how tumour antigen is displayed or by keeping cytotoxic T cells functional inside the tumour. Its output matters directly for immune surveillance and for the success of checkpoint blockade: when it is weakened, tumour-specific T cells become exhausted or blind to their target and the tumour escapes. Class II histocompatibility molecules and the related presentation molecule MR1 supply the antigen-display arm, presenting peptide and metabolite ligands to helper and unconventional T cells. Other members act inside the T cell itself, where ubiquitin ligase components such as FBXO38 and KLHL22 control turnover of inhibitory surface receptors, and the AMPK catalytic subunit PRKAA1 links nutrient stress in the tumour microenvironment to T cell metabolic fitness.

Natural killer cells kill transformed cells without prior sensitization, and the tuning of that antitumour killing determines whether a nascent tumour is cleared or escapes. The genes here represent both arms of the control: activating receptor ligation and cytokine priming on one side, inhibitory checkpoints and suppressive cytokines on the other. Nectin-family and poliovirus receptor ligands on the tumour surface engage the activating receptor DNAM-1 (CD226), while CEACAM1 and TIM-3 (HAVCR2) deliver inhibitory signals, and CD160 and CRTAM modulate cytotoxic engagement and conjugate stability. Interleukin-12, as its two subunits, licenses NK cytotoxicity and interferon-gamma output, whereas TGF-beta blunts it. Tumours exploit this balance by upregulating inhibitory ligands and secreting TGF-beta, which is why several of these molecules are pursued as checkpoint targets for restoring innate tumour surveillance.

Natural killer cells recognise and lyse transformed cells that have lost or altered the signals marking them as normal, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise that antitumour killing. Activating receptors on the NK cell engage ligands displayed on tumour cells: DNAM-1 (CD226) and CRTAM bind the nectin-family ligands CD155 (PVR) and CD112 (NECTIN2), while CD160 provides an additional activating input through MHC class I contacts, together tipping the balance of stimulatory and inhibitory signals toward degranulation and cytokine release. The two subunits of interleukin-12 supply the cytokine arm, licensing NK cells for interferon-gamma production and enhanced cytotoxicity. Because the same nectin ligands are frequently upregulated on tumours and can also engage inhibitory TIGIT, this axis sits at the centre of tumour immune surveillance and is actively pursued as an immunotherapy target; its loss permits tumour escape from innate immune control.

Inflammation triggered by antigen must be tuned in both directions: strong enough to clear the challenge, restrained enough to avoid tissue damage, autoimmunity or anaphylaxis. This set of regulators sets the gain on that response. Immunoreceptor signalling dominates — Src-family kinases such as LYN, FYN, HCK and FGR together with SYK, BTK and PLCG1 transduce signals from Fc receptors and the FCER1G adaptor, while the inhibitory receptor FCGR2B imposes a negative threshold on activating Fc receptor output. Antigen presentation through MHC class II and costimulation via CD28 set the T cell contribution, and cytokines including TNF, lymphotoxin-alpha and IL12B amplify the response while IL10 dampens it. Additional brakes come from cyclic AMP-dependent protein kinase regulatory subunits, p38 MAPK signalling, complement C3, and inflammasome-associated NLRP6. Loss of such restraint underlies allergic, arthritic and other chronic inflammatory disease.

Inflammation triggered by antigen must be damped once it has served its purpose, and this braking programme limits the magnitude and duration of that response so that tissue damage and autoimmunity do not follow. Several routes converge: the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B raises the threshold for immune-complex-driven activation through ITIM signalling engaging Src-family kinases such as LYN, FGR and HCK together with SYK and PLCG1; interleukin-10 acts as the canonical anti-inflammatory cytokine restraining myeloid activation; cAMP-dependent protein kinase regulatory subunits hold PKA inactive until cAMP-elevating receptors such as GNAS-coupled ones signal; and TREM2 tunes microglial and macrophage reactivity. Antioxidant and proteostatic components including GPX1, SELENOS and proteasome subunits temper oxidative and ER-stress-driven cytokine output, while several microRNAs add post-transcriptional restraint. Loss of these checks predisposes to lupus-like autoimmunity, chronic inflammatory disease and neuroinflammation.

Antigen recognition by the adaptive and innate arms of immunity can be amplified into overt inflammation, and this pathway covers the signals that raise the intensity of that response. It matters because the same amplification that clears pathogens and drives protective immunity also underlies allergy, autoimmune tissue damage and transplant rejection. Fc receptor components such as FCER1G and the high-affinity IgG receptor FCGR1A couple immune complexes to cellular activation, with the kinase BTK carrying signals from these receptors and from the B cell receptor toward cytokine output. Complement C3 opsonizes and generates inflammatory peptides, while TNF and lymphotoxin alpha act as the effector cytokines. Costimulation through CD28 and chemokine-guided trafficking via CCR7 position T cells for full activation, so the pathway links antigen encounter to leukocyte recruitment, cytokine release and inflammatory swelling.

Antigen encounter can trigger a rapid inflammatory burst — mast cell and basophil degranulation, complement activation, immune complex clearance, vascular leak and leukocyte influx — and this pathway sets how strong and how prolonged that burst becomes. Tuning matters because unrestrained acute responses to antigen produce anaphylaxis, serum sickness and immune complex tissue injury, while insufficient response leaves antigen uncleared. Fc receptors for IgE and IgG transmit the activating signal, with the inhibitory low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B raising the threshold and BTK carrying signalling downstream of receptor engagement; complement component C3 amplifies opsonisation and mediator release. Additional restraint comes from a secreted phospholipase, a neuropeptide arm linking neural input to inflammation, and molecules controlling leukocyte homing and adhesion such as CCR7, FUT7 and SPN, placing this regulation at the interface of innate effector cells and antigen-specific immunity.

negative regulation of acute inflammatory response to antigenic stimulus is the braking system on antigen-triggered acute inflammation, the set of processes that limit how fast and how far an immediate hypersensitivity or immune-complex reaction can escalate. It matters because unchecked responses of this type produce anaphylaxis, serum sickness and tissue-damaging immune-complex disease, and because loss of these brakes predisposes to autoantibody-driven autoimmunity. The best-defined component is the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B, whose ITIM-based signalling raises the threshold for immune-complex activation of B cells, mast cells and phagocytes; sialophorin (SPN, CD43) similarly restrains leukocyte adhesion and activation. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors supplies neural input that dampens mast cell and leukocyte reactivity, while SELENOS links endoplasmic reticulum stress handling to cytokine output. Together these represent receptor-level inhibition, neuroimmune modulation and cytokine receptor competition converging on resolution rather than initiation of inflammation.

Acute inflammation triggered by antigen must be actively damped, or immune complexes and mast cell activation drive tissue injury, anaphylaxis and autoantibody-driven disease; the genes here restrain that response rather than initiate it. The clearest example is the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, the only inhibitory Fc gamma receptor, which carries an inhibitory signalling motif and raises the threshold for B cell, mast cell and phagocyte activation by immune complexes; loss of its function predisposes to systemic autoimmunity. Neuropeptide Y acting through its receptors links neural output to immune tone, illustrating neuroimmune brake on local inflammatory responses, while sialophorin (SPN, CD43) shapes leukocyte adhesion and contact-dependent activation. Other members contribute cytokine receptor signalling and endoplasmic reticulum stress handling. Collectively this is the negative arm of hypersensitivity control, setting how strongly and how long an antigen-provoked inflammatory episode proceeds.

Amplification of the acute inflammatory response to an antigenic stimulus covers the steps that make an early immune reaction to foreign material stronger or faster, driving the vascular leakage, mast cell and granulocyte activation, and complement-dependent effects that produce immediate hypersensitivity and rapid pathogen clearance. Excessive activity here underlies anaphylaxis and immune complex disease, while blunted activity leaves antigen poorly cleared. The genes involved span several arms of the response: complement component C3 opsonises antigen and generates inflammatory fragments, the immunoglobulin receptor gamma chain FCER1G and the high-affinity IgG receptor FCGR1A couple antibody-bound antigen to phagocyte and mast cell activation, and the kinase BTK carries those receptor signals forward inside the cell. CCR7 and HLA-E connect the reaction to lymphocyte trafficking and antigen surveillance, linking acute inflammation to the adaptive response that follows.

Hypersensitivity is an immune response that overshoots, damaging tissue in reaction to an antigen that poses little threat, as in allergy, asthma and immune complex disease. Setting the frequency and severity of such reactions is what this regulatory biology does, and the balance it strikes determines whether an encounter with allergen or antibody-coated antigen is quiet or inflammatory. Antibody receptors supply both arms of that control: the high-affinity IgG receptor and the IgE receptor gamma chain couple immune complexes to mast cell and phagocyte activation, while the inhibitory FCGR2B receptor raises the threshold for triggering, and BTK transmits the activating signal downstream. Complement component C3 amplifies effector responses, and leukocyte trafficking determinants such as CCR7 and fucosyltransferase-dependent selectin ligands position responding cells. Loss of the inhibitory limb favours autoantibody-driven and allergic disease.

Myeloid effector cells — neutrophils, monocytes and macrophages, mast cells and eosinophils — kill microbes and clear debris by degranulating, phagocytosing and releasing mediators, and this pathway covers the controls that set how strongly they do so. Tuning matters in both directions: too little leaves pyogenic infection unchecked, too much drives tissue damage in asthma, vasculitis and sepsis. Activating and inhibitory receptors are balanced against each other, with Fc receptors and the ITAM adaptors FCER1G and TYROBP feeding Src- and Syk-family kinases such as LYN, FGR, HCK-like FES, BTK and SYK through adaptors like GAB2 and RAC2, while ITIM-bearing CD300A and FCGR2B damp the same circuits. Granule release requires dedicated fusion machinery — UNC13D, STXBP2, VAMP7 and VAMP8 — whose loss causes haemophagocytic syndromes. Chemokine receptors, complement C3, integrins and the transcription factors SPI1 and GATA2 position and differentiate the cells that execute these responses.

Myeloid cells such as neutrophils, macrophages and mast cells carry out powerful effector functions, and this pathway covers the brakes that keep those functions from causing collateral tissue damage. Negative regulation of myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity restrains degranulation, phagocytosis, oxidative burst and inflammatory cytokine output, and its loss underlies chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and allergic disease. Much of the control comes from inhibitory surface receptors: CD300A binds exposed phosphatidylserine on apoptotic and activated cells, FCGR2B acts as the low-affinity IgG receptor that dampens immune-complex-driven activation through an inhibitory cytoplasmic motif, and the galectin LGALS9 engages glycoprotein partners to limit cell activation and survival. Chemokine receptors CCR2 and CX3CR1 place monocyte and macrophage recruitment under regulation, while the myeloid master transcription factor SPI1 and the RAB-directed exchange factor RABGEF1 set the intrinsic activation threshold of these lineages.

positive regulation of myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity describes the signals that ramp up the effector output of neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and mast cells — degranulation, phagocytosis, oxidative burst and cytokine release — during infection and inflammation. Its strength sets whether pathogens are cleared efficiently or whether tissue is damaged by excessive myeloid activation, as in sepsis, vasculitis and allergic disease. The genes span the main activating inputs: Fc receptors and their shared ITAM adaptors FCER1G and TYROBP feeding into BTK-dependent kinase cascades, complement C3 and the CD11b/CD18 integrin pair driving opsonic phagocytosis and adhesion, protease-activated and neuropeptide receptors, and innate nucleic acid sensors such as RIG-I and MAVS with the TLR adaptor TICAM1. SPI1 supplies the transcriptional program that specifies myeloid identity in the first place, while STX4 supports the membrane fusion that delivers granule contents.

Myeloid effector cells — neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, mast cells — kill microbes and clear opsonised targets by degranulation, phagocytosis and oxidative burst, and this pathway covers the signals that turn that activity up. Enhanced myeloid leukocyte mediated immunity is what makes acute antibacterial and antifungal defence possible, while unchecked amplification drives tissue damage in sepsis and inflammatory disease. The genes point to several converging inputs: Fc receptor engagement of complement-opsonised or antibody-coated particles through FCGR1A with the FCER1G and TYROBP signalling chains, the CD11b/CD18 integrin pair mediating adhesion and complement receptor function, and BTK relaying these to granule release, with STX4 supplying the fusion machinery for exocytosis. Innate nucleic acid sensing via RIGI, MAVS and TICAM1 and the lineage transcription factor SPI1 set the responsiveness of these cells, while C3 and POMC-derived peptides act as extracellular modulators.

Type II hypersensitivity is tissue damage caused by IgG or IgM antibodies bound to antigens on a cell's own surface, which recruit complement and Fc receptor-bearing effector cells to destroy that cell; it underlies autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, immune thrombocytopenia, Goodpasture syndrome and transfusion reactions. The genes here set the threshold of that reaction rather than initiating it. Complement component C3 amplifies opsonisation and lysis of antibody-coated targets, while the Fc receptor gamma chain and high-affinity IgG receptor FCGR1A transmit activating signals for phagocytosis and antibody-dependent cytotoxicity. Opposing them, the inhibitory receptor FCGR2B raises the threshold for effector activation and restrains autoreactive B cells, and HLA-E engages inhibitory receptors on NK cells to mark a target as self. Balance between these activating and inhibitory inputs determines whether antibody binding is tolerated or destroys the tissue.

B cell numbers are set as much by which cells are allowed to die as by which divide, and this regulatory layer tunes how readily a B cell undergoes programmed death. It governs removal of self-reactive and non-productive cells during development, survival of germinal centre B cells while they mutate their receptors, and the size of the mature repertoire; loss of restraint on either side yields autoimmunity or lymphoma. Antigen receptor signalling components such as BTK and LYN couple receptor engagement to survival decisions, the transcriptional repressor BCL6 permits germinal centre B cells to tolerate DNA damage, and MYC links proliferative drive to death sensitivity, with BAX acting at the mitochondrial commitment step. Cytokines including IL2 and IL10, the MIF-CD74 axis, and metabolic regulators such as FNIP1 and the zinc transporter SLC39A10 adjust the threshold from outside and inside the cell.

B cells are produced in excess and most die; survival signals that block apoptosis decide which ones persist, and this negative regulation of B cell death shapes the size of the peripheral B cell pool, the germinal centre reaction, and the lifespan of memory and plasma cell precursors. Loss of these brakes causes lymphopenia and poor antibody responses, while their excess underlies autoimmunity and lymphoma. The genes here act at several levels: BCL6 represses apoptotic and DNA-damage response programmes so germinal centre B cells can tolerate somatic hypermutation, FOXP1 sustains transcriptional survival programmes, BCL10 relays antigen receptor engagement toward NF-"κB-dependent survival, CD74 transduces signalling by the cytokine MIF, and zinc import through SLC39A10 supports B cell persistence. Adenosine deaminase deficiency conversely kills lymphocytes, linking purine metabolism to the same decision.

Lymphocyte anergy is the functional silencing of a T or B cell that has seen antigen without adequate costimulation, and processes that increase it enforce peripheral tolerance to self and harmless antigens. Promoting anergy restrains autoimmunity and limits transplant rejection, but the same brake is exploited by tumours and chronic infections to blunt effector responses. The genes here act at two levels: E3 ubiquitin ligases such as CBLB and ITCH ubiquitinate proximal T cell receptor signalling components and transcription factors, raising the threshold for full activation, while the CD3 epsilon chain marks the receptor complex through which that tuned signal passes. FOXP3 links the programme to regulatory T cells, which impose unresponsiveness on neighbouring cells, and the inhibitory receptor LILRB4 delivers suppressive signals from antigen-presenting cells. Loss of these controls yields lymphoproliferation and autoantibody-driven disease.

Regulation of humoral immune response tunes the arm of immunity that acts through soluble mediators — complement, antibodies and antimicrobial peptides — setting how strongly and for how long these systems attack a target. Its main business is restraint: membrane and fluid-phase complement regulators such as CD46, CD55, CD59, factor H, factor I and the C4b-binding proteins prevent the cascade from damaging host tissue, and their loss causes haemolytic disease, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and hereditary angioedema. On the other side sit activators and amplifiers, including C3, MASP1, properdin and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, LTA, IL1B and IL-17. Antibody output itself is modulated by inhibitory receptors like FCGR2B and phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPRC, while CXCL13 and CCR7 position B cells in lymphoid follicles where responses are generated.

Humoral immunity — antibodies, complement and soluble antimicrobial factors acting in blood and mucosal fluid — must be tuned so that it clears pathogens without damaging host tissue, and this pathway covers the processes that raise or dampen its magnitude and duration. Much of the control is exerted on the complement cascade: membrane and fluid-phase regulators such as CD46, CD55, CD59, factor H, factor I and C4b-binding protein restrain C3 and C5 convertase activity and protect self cells from lysis, while properdin stabilises the alternative pathway and MASP1 initiates the lectin arm. Complement receptors CR1 and CR2 link opsonised antigen to B cell activation, and FCGR2B together with the phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPRC sets the threshold for antibody-mediated feedback. Cytokines including TNF, lymphotoxin-alpha, IL1B and IL17, plus the follicular chemokine CXCL13, shape the lymphoid environment in which antibody responses develop. Loss of these brakes underlies complement-driven haemolysis, nephropathy and autoantibody disease.

Antibody and complement responses in body fluids have to be damped and confined, and this is the braking system that does it: negative regulation of the humoral immune response keeps complement activation off healthy host surfaces and raises the threshold for B cell antibody production. Membrane regulators such as CD55, CD46 and CD59 accelerate decay of C3/C5 convertases, act as cofactors for cleavage of deposited C3b and C4b, and block assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex, while fluid-phase inhibitors including C4b-binding protein, C1-inhibitor and clusterin restrain the classical and lectin arms. On B cells, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B recruits the phosphatase SHP-1 to attenuate antigen receptor signalling when immune complexes accumulate. Loss of these controls produces intravascular haemolysis, hereditary angioedema, complement-driven kidney disease and autoantibody-mediated autoimmunity, showing that self-tissue protection depends on continuous inhibition rather than the absence of activation.

positive regulation of humoral immune response describes the processes that amplify immunity carried by soluble mediators — antibodies, complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides — rather than by direct cell contact. Boosting this arm speeds opsonisation and lysis of extracellular bacteria and helps clear immune complexes, while unchecked amplification drives autoantibody disease and complement-mediated tissue injury. The genes span several amplifying inputs: complement components and the properdin-dependent alternative pathway with its receptors CR1 and C3, inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, lymphotoxin-alpha, IL1B and the IL-17 family that promote germinal centre organisation and antibody output, chemokine-driven lymphocyte homing through CCR7, and antimicrobial effectors including cathelicidin. Regulators such as the inhibitory receptor FCGR2B and the phosphatase CD45 set the threshold at which B cells respond, tying humoral output to inflammatory and innate signalling context.

Humoral immunity is the arm of defence carried by soluble factors in blood and tissue fluids — antibodies, complement proteins and antimicrobial peptides — and this grouping covers the signals that raise its output. Enhancing it speeds opsonisation and lysis of bacteria and helps clear immune complexes; excessive drive contributes to autoantibody disease and complement-mediated tissue injury. Several members act directly in the cascade, with C3 as the central convertase substrate, C6 in the lytic terminal complex, properdin stabilising the alternative pathway, and CR1 and FCGR2B tuning how opsonised particles and antibody complexes are handled on cell surfaces. Cytokines including TNF, lymphotoxin alpha, IL1B and the IL-17 family amplify the response and support the lymphoid architecture where antibody is made, while CCR7 positions lymphocytes and dendritic cells for that encounter. Cathelicidin and haem-binding hemopexin extend the effect to direct antimicrobial and sequestering activity.

Antibody circulating in blood only protects if its downstream effects are kept in proportion: this pathway covers the controls that tune how strongly a humoral response mediated by circulating immunoglobulin proceeds, chiefly by setting thresholds on complement activation and on B cell signalling. Much of the restraint is complement regulatory: C4b-binding protein subunits, membrane cofactor protein CD46 and complement receptor 1 promote decay or factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b/C4b, sparing host surfaces from lysis and opsonisation, while CR2 links complement-tagged antigen to B cell activation. On the lymphocyte side, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B and the phosphatases SHP-1 and CD45 damp antigen receptor output, curbing autoantibody production. TNF and lymphotoxin-alpha supply the inflammatory and lymphoid-organising context. Loss of such braking underlies complement-driven tissue injury, haemolytic disease and systemic autoimmunity.

Antibody in the circulation kills by fixing complement, and this braking programme keeps that destruction aimed at pathogens rather than at host tissue. Its failure underlies complement-driven disease — atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, age-related macular degeneration, and lupus-like autoimmunity — while its deliberate exploitation lets some pathogens and tumour cells evade lysis. Two arms are represented. Soluble and membrane regulators such as C4b-binding protein, membrane cofactor protein CD46 and complement receptor 1 dismantle the C3 and C5 convertases, accelerating their decay and acting as cofactors for factor I cleavage of C3b and C4b. Separately, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B recruits the phosphatase SHP-1 through an ITIM, raising the activation threshold of B cells and myeloid cells so that immune-complex binding dampens rather than amplifies antibody output and effector responses.

Antibody circulating in blood clears pathogens only if the responses that generate and amplify it are turned up at the right moment, and this pathway covers the signals that increase the magnitude, rate or frequency of such circulating immunoglobulin-mediated humoral immunity. It sits at the interface of innate signalling and B cell output: the tumour necrosis factor family members lymphotoxin alpha and TNF drive lymphoid tissue organisation and germinal centre reactions that support antibody production, the receptor-type phosphatase CD45 sets antigen receptor signalling thresholds in lymphocytes, and a myeloid immunoreceptor plus the plasma heme scavenger hemopexin link inflammatory and tissue-damage cues to the same output. Enhancement of this arm underlies protective responses to encapsulated bacteria and to vaccination, while unchecked amplification contributes to autoantibody-driven disease and immune complex pathology.

When blood supply to a tissue falls short, cells mount a coordinated response to ischemia that determines whether they survive the oxygen and nutrient deficit or die, and whether reperfusion adds further injury. This biology underlies infarct size in heart and brain, ischemic preconditioning, and the neuroinflammatory aftermath of stroke. Several arms are represented: ATP-sensitive potassium channels formed with KCNJ11 and KCNJ8 couple metabolic state to membrane excitability; mitochondrial gatekeepers including PPIF, PINK1, ATP5IF1 and AIFM1 govern permeability transition, mitophagy and caspase-independent death, with CASP9 and BCL2 setting the apoptotic threshold; NFE2L2 and STAT3 drive protective transcription while HK2 and TIGAR shift glucose handling. Purinergic receptors and pannexin channels release and sense extracellular ATP as a damage signal, recruiting microglia and macrophages through CSF1R, CX3CR1 and TREM2. Caveolins and RCAN1 tune the surviving cell's signalling.

Adding a hydroxyl group to a fatty acyl chain converts inert lipids into signalling molecules and into substrates for further oxidation and excretion, and lipid hydroxylation is the enzymatic step that does it. The cytochrome P450 monooxygenases collected here use molecular oxygen and NADPH-derived electrons to oxidise fatty acids and related lipids at specific carbons, generating hydroxy and epoxy derivatives that act on vascular tone, renal sodium handling and inflammation. Omega-hydroxylation of arachidonic acid by a CYP4A-family enzyme yields a potent vasoconstrictor, while CYP2C8 and CYP2E1 contribute epoxide and hydroxy products with opposing effects; CYP3A and CYP1A1 members handle overlapping lipid and xenobiotic substrates in liver and extrahepatic tissue. Because the same enzymes clear drugs, their activity links dietary and pharmacological exposure to blood pressure regulation, lipid turnover and hypertension risk.

Desmosomes are the rivet-like junctions that let epithelia and cardiac muscle withstand mechanical stress, and their organization covers how these patches are built, arranged and taken apart. Desmosomal cadherins such as the desmogleins and desmocollins bridge the intercellular space, while plakoglobin, plakophilins and desmoplakin build the cytoplasmic plaque that anchors keratin or desmin intermediate filaments, coupling the cytoskeletons of neighbouring cells into a continuous network. Transcriptional inputs including GRHL1 and SNAI2 set how many junctions a cell makes, and PRKCA-dependent phosphorylation shifts adhesion between stable and remodelling states during wound healing. Loss or autoantibody-mediated blockade of these components produces blistering skin disease such as pemphigus, palmoplantar keratoderma, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy when PKP2 or desmoplakin fail. The same machinery intersects with adherens junction adhesion and with epithelial-mesenchymal transition, where desmosome disassembly accompanies loss of epithelial cohesion.

Fibroblast-like type B synoviocytes line the joint cavity, secrete lubricating hyaluronan and matrix components, and are normally a quiescent, sparse population. Their expansion is the defining event of synovial hyperplasia in rheumatoid arthritis, where a thickened, invasive pannus erodes cartilage and bone and sustains local inflammation. The regulators here act at several levels: tumour necrosis factor delivers the inflammatory cytokine signal that drives proliferation and matrix-degrading gene expression, a B cell-associated tyrosine kinase links immune receptor signalling to this response, and a long non-coding RNA and a microRNA provide transcriptional and post-transcriptional control of the proliferative state. Because synoviocyte outgrowth converts a transient immune response into persistent joint destruction, this proliferative programme is a target of anti-cytokine and kinase-inhibitor therapy in inflammatory arthritis.

tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine modification installs the t6A mark at position 37, immediately 3' of the anticodon, on every tRNA that reads an ANN codon. This bulky modification stabilises codon-anticodon pairing and enforces reading-frame maintenance, so without it ribosomes misread and frameshift, translational fidelity collapses, and cells show growth and stress-response defects; in humans, loss-of-function mutations in the complex cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome and microcephaly. YRDC first makes the threonylcarbamoyl-AMP intermediate from threonine, bicarbonate and ATP, and the KEOPS complex — the OSGEP catalytic subunit with TPRKB, GON7 and their partners — transfers that moiety onto the adenine amino group in the cytoplasm and nucleus, while OSGEPL1 performs the equivalent reaction on mitochondrial tRNAs. The pathway thus links amino acid and one-carbon availability to the accuracy of protein synthesis.

Accurate decoding of ANN codons depends on a bulky modification at position 37, immediately 3' of the anticodon, and tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine modification is how it is installed. The mark stabilises codon-anticodon pairing and suppresses frameshifting and near-cognate misreading, so its loss degrades translational fidelity across a large share of the genetic code. Threonine, bicarbonate and ATP are first condensed into a threonylcarbamoyl-adenylate intermediate by YRDC, which then serves as donor for the transfer step carried out by the KEOPS complex: the metallo-hydrolase-fold catalytic subunit OSGEP together with the accessory subunits TPRKB and GON7, with OSGEPL1 acting on mitochondrial tRNAs. Beyond translation, KEOPS components have been tied to telomere maintenance and transcriptional regulation, and biallelic mutations in OSGEP, TPRKB or GON7 cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, combining steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome with microcephaly and brain malformation.

developmental process involved in reproduction covers the progressive changes in germline and reproductive somatic tissues that give an organism the capacity to produce offspring, from gonad specification through gamete maturation. It underlies fertility, and its disruption causes disorders of sex development, premature ovarian insufficiency, azoospermia and teratozoospermia. The genes span sex determination and gonadal differentiation (SRY, SOX9, WT1, NR5A1, FOXL2, AMH), pituitary and steroid hormone signalling that drives puberty and gametogenesis (FSHB, LHCGR, AR, ESR1, CYP19A1, inhibins and activins), and meiotic entry and recombination (STRA8, SPO11, DMC1, SYCP1-3, MSH4, REC8). A large sperm-specific module builds the acrosome, flagellar axoneme and sperm head, compacts chromatin with protamines and transition proteins, and equips the cell for capacitation via CatSper channels. Oocyte factors, piRNA-pathway TDRD and PIWIL proteins, and imprinting DNA methyltransferases link gamete quality to the epigenetic state inherited by the embryo.

Making offspring requires more than gamete production: gonads must be specified and built, germ cells must complete meiosis, and gametes must be shaped into functional sperm and eggs. This broad developmental programme of reproduction covers sex determination and gonad morphogenesis, germline specification, meiotic recombination and gametogenesis, together with the hormonal control that coordinates them. Transcriptional regulators such as SRY, SOX9, NR5A1, WT1, FOXL2 and the DMRT family set gonadal fate, while gonadotropin and steroid signalling through FSHR, LHCGR, AR and ESR1 drive maturation. Meiosis depends on SPO11-initiated recombination and synaptonemal complex components including SYCP1-3, and piRNA factors with PIWI proteins silence transposons in the germline. Spermiogenesis contributes flagellar axoneme and outer dense fibre proteins, protamine-based chromatin remodelling, and CatSper channels for sperm motility and fertilization. Failure at any stage yields disorders of sex development, premature ovarian insufficiency, azoospermia or infertility.

heart morphogenesis is the construction of the heart during embryonic development: the specification of cardiac progenitors, their assembly into a beating tube, and the looping, chamber ballooning, septation, valve formation and outflow tract remodelling that convert that tube into a four-chambered pump. Its failure is the origin of congenital heart disease, the commonest class of birth defect, including septal defects, valve malformations and laterality-associated malposition. A core transcriptional network of NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND1/2 and MEF2C reads out inductive signalling from BMP, TGF-beta/Nodal, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog and FGF8, while left-right cues from cilia and PITX2 orient the looping heart. Downstream, sarcomeric and cytoskeletal genes such as MYH6, TNNT2 and TTN build contractile myocardium, and endothelial and neural crest contributions supply endocardium, cushions and great vessels. Cell migration, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and extracellular matrix remodelling shape each step.

Heart morphogenesis covers the shaping of the heart from mesodermal precursors into a four-chambered pump: specification of cardiac progenitors, looping of the linear tube, septation, valve formation, outflow tract remodelling and buildup of the conduction system and working myocardium. Failure at any step produces the congenital heart defects that are the commonest birth malformations, and the same genes underlie inherited cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia when they act later in life. Core transcription factors such as NKX2-5, TBX5, GATA4 and HAND1/2 set chamber identity, while BMP, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog, TGF-beta and FGF8 signalling from surrounding endocardium, epicardium and pharyngeal mesoderm pattern the tissue; retinoic acid synthesis and cilium-dependent left-right cues fix asymmetry. Endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition builds the cushions that become valves, and sarcomeric genes including MYH6, TNNT2 and TTN give the growing chambers contractile function.

Voluntary movement, posture and breathing all depend on skeletal muscle contraction, in which an action potential at the neuromuscular junction is converted into sarcomere shortening. Acetylcholine receptor subunits transduce motor nerve input, the voltage-gated sodium channel SCN4A propagates the resulting depolarisation, and excitation-contraction coupling proteins including STAC3, the ryanodine receptor modulator FKBP1A and the calcium-buffering protein calsequestrin release and manage sarcoplasmic calcium; the SERCA1 pump ATP2A1 reclaims it to allow relaxation. Calcium binding to the troponin complex, together with titin, telethonin and alpha-actinin as the structural scaffold, permits myosin heads to hydrolyse ATP and generate force against actin. Myoglobin and carbonic anhydrase 3 support the metabolic demands of repeated cycles. Mutations across these components cause muscular dystrophy, congenital myasthenic syndromes, myotonia, periodic paralysis and central core disease, so the pathway defines both the myofibre and its clinical vulnerabilities.
