Voluntary skeletal muscle contraction is the conscious generation of force by limb and trunk muscles, the process that converts motor neuron commands into movement, posture and breathing effort. Force arises in the sarcomere, where myosin heads cycle on actin filaments using ATP hydrolysis, shortening the fibre and changing muscle geometry. The genes here span the steps that make this ordered and controllable: a slow-twitch myosin heavy chain (MYH7) as the motor itself, troponin T (TNNT1) as the thin-filament switch that renders contraction calcium-dependent, alpha-actinin-3 anchoring actin at the Z-disc, synemin linking the sarcomere to the cytoskeletal lattice, and the fast-twitch sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump ATP2A1, which reclaims cytosolic calcium so the muscle can relax. Defects in these components cause myopathies, distal arthrogryposis and cardiomyopathy, and impair relaxation as much as contraction.

muscle system process covers the work that muscle tissue performs as an organ system: generating force in skeletal muscle for movement and posture, pumping blood through rhythmic cardiac contraction, and setting the tone of smooth muscle in vessels, airways and gut. The genes span the whole chain from excitation to force. Voltage-gated sodium, calcium and potassium channels and the neuromuscular acetylcholine receptor set membrane excitability; dihydropyridine receptors coupled to ryanodine receptors, junctophilins, calsequestrin, triadin and SERCA/phospholamban handle calcium release and reuptake; actin, myosin heavy and light chains, troponins, tropomyosins and titin form the contractile apparatus, with myosin light chain kinase and RhoA-ROCK tuning smooth muscle sensitivity. Also present are the myogenic regulators MYOD1, MYOG, MEF2A and cardiac factors such as NKX2-5 and GATA4, plus dystrophin-glycoprotein complex members and atrophy controls like FBXO32 and myostatin. Failure produces muscular dystrophy, myopathy, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

Muscle system processes are the organ-level functions of contractile tissue: skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation, the cardiac beat and its rhythm, and the tone of smooth muscle in vessels, airways and gut. They underlie locomotion and posture, cardiac output, blood pressure control and visceral motility, and their failure produces myopathy, cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia, and vascular or airway dysregulation. The genes span the sarcomere itself (actins, myosin heavy and light chains, titin, tropomyosins and the troponin complexes), the calcium cycling machinery that times contraction (ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps, calsequestrins, phospholamban, junctophilins, triadin, dihydropyridine channel subunits), and the sodium and potassium channels that shape excitability and conduction. Alongside these sit the neuromuscular junction acetylcholine receptor subunits, dystrophin-associated costameric proteins linking sarcomere to membrane, and adrenergic, endothelin and purinergic receptors that set tone, plus transcriptional and microRNA regulators that specify and remodel muscle.

Moving blood and extracellular fluid through the body requires a pump, tubes that can change their diameter, and barriers that control what leaves the vessel; the circulatory system process covers all three. Its outputs are cardiac rate and contractility, vascular tone and blood pressure, and the permeability of the endothelium, and its failure underlies arrhythmia, heart failure, hypertension, oedema and stroke. Cardiac excitation and contraction are handled by voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, ryanodine receptor calcium release with phospholamban-regulated SERCA reuptake, sarcomeric troponins and myosins, and transcription factors such as NKX2-5 and TBX5 that specify the conduction system. Tone is set by opposing vasoconstrictor and vasodilator signalling -- renin-angiotensin and endothelin against nitric oxide synthases, natriuretic peptides and cyclic GMP effectors -- alongside adrenergic, purinergic and vasopressin receptors. Endothelial junction and transporter components govern barrier function and solute exchange.

Kidney function comes down to filtering blood and then selectively reclaiming what the body needs, and this renal system process covers the transport, signalling and filtration-barrier machinery that accomplishes it. The output is stable plasma volume, sodium and potassium concentration, pH and excretion of nitrogenous waste; its failure produces hypertension, salt-wasting or salt-retaining tubulopathies, nephrotic syndrome and renal acidosis. Glomerular podocyte and slit-diaphragm proteins such as NPHS2, CD2AP and PTPRO set what is filtered, while segment-specific transporters -- the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter SLC12A3, the epithelial sodium channel subunit SCNN1B, glucose reabsorbing SLC5A2, urate and organic anion carriers, and aquaporin water channels -- determine what returns. Vasopressin acting through AVPR2 and cyclic AMP, the renin-angiotensin system, natriuretic peptides, endothelins and WNK-OXSR1/STK39 kinase signalling tune this reabsorption to systemic fluid and blood pressure demands.

The heart works by contracting rhythmically to keep blood moving, and this pathway gathers the machinery that generates, times and tunes each beat. Pacemaker and conduction properties come from ion channels and transporters — HCN4 and voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits, potassium channels including KCNQ1 and KCNH2, and L-type calcium channels — while calcium cycling through the ryanodine receptor RYR2, SERCA2 with its regulator phospholamban, and the sodium/calcium exchanger couples excitation to force. Contraction itself is delivered by sarcomeric myosins, troponins, titin and associated Z-disc and desmosomal proteins, and output is adjusted beat to beat by adrenergic, muscarinic, angiotensin, endothelin and natriuretic peptide signalling. Transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4 and TBX5 specify chamber and conduction identity. Disruption produces arrhythmia, long QT and Brugada syndromes, cardiomyopathy and heart failure.

Breathing and gas exchange depend on more than lungs: the respiratory system process covers the coordinated activity of airway tissues, respiratory muscles and the brainstem circuits that drive ventilation. The genes here fall into recognisable arms of that biology. Motile cilia components such as DNAH9, CFAP43, CFAP54, SPAG16, ODAD4 and TTLL1 generate the beat that clears mucus from airways, and their loss causes primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic airway infection. A neural arm including PHOX2B, MECP2, GLRA1, TLX3 and PBX3 specifies and operates the central respiratory rhythm generator; mutation of PHOX2B underlies congenital central hypoventilation, and MECP2 loss produces the irregular breathing of Rett syndrome. Others contribute lung branching and lymphatic patterning, muscle integrity and chemosensory tone. Failure across any arm presents as apnoea, hypoventilation or impaired mucociliary clearance rather than a single molecular defect.

Blood vessels do more than carry blood: they set their own diameter and control what crosses their walls, and these vascular processes in the circulatory system determine tissue perfusion and blood pressure. Vasoconstrictor and vasodilator signalling dominates the gene content — angiotensin and endothelin systems, adrenergic, purinergic, serotonergic and bradykinin receptors, natriuretic peptides acting through particulate guanylate cyclase, endothelial nitric oxide synthase with soluble guanylate cyclase and PRKG1, and downstream RhoA/ROCK and potassium and calcium channels in smooth muscle. A second arm is barrier function and transendothelial exchange: claudin-5, occludin and tight junction scaffolds, PECAM1 and VE-cadherin at endothelial junctions, MFSD2A and PLVAP, and a large complement of solute carrier and ABC transporters that move nutrients, ions and xenobiotics across the endothelium. Loss of this control underlies hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, oedema and blood–brain barrier breakdown.

Cells must know how much oxygen is available in order to adjust metabolism, iron handling and vascular growth, and oxygen detection is the step in which a change in oxygen tension is converted into an intracellular signal. Its outputs govern erythropoiesis, angiogenesis and the antioxidant response, so failure leaves tissues unable to adapt to hypoxia or to limit oxidative damage. The genes here connect oxygen sensing to several downstream arms: a cytochrome b5 reductase-type flavoprotein implicated in redox-linked sensing, a divalent metal transporter that brings iron into cells for oxygen-dependent enzymes and heme, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase that disposes of the superoxide generated when respiration encounters low oxygen, and endoglin with a TGF-beta ligand, which couple the signal to endothelial responses and vessel remodelling.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure mediated by a chemical signal is the hormonal and locally released chemistry that sets vascular tone and blood volume, keeping perfusion pressure within limits from beat to beat and across days. Its failure produces hypertension, and with it heart failure, stroke and renal damage; several of its members are the targets of the most widely used antihypertensive drugs. The core is the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis, in which renin and angiotensin-converting enzyme generate angiotensin II acting through AGTR1, while ACE2 and MAS1 form an opposing degradative arm and aldosterone synthase couples the system to sodium handling. Around it sit vasoconstrictors and vasodilators acting in parallel -- endothelins and their receptors, vasopressin, adrenergic and thrombin receptors, tachykinins, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase -- together with mast cell proteases and peptidases that process the peptide ligands, and redox enzymes that modulate endothelial responsiveness.

Systemic arterial blood pressure is set moment to moment by circulating and locally released chemical signals acting on vessel tone, cardiac output and renal salt and water handling. This hormonal, autocrine and paracrine control is what keeps perfusion adequate on standing or after blood loss, and its derangement underlies essential hypertension, pre-eclampsia and heart failure. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis dominates: renin cleaves angiotensinogen, angiotensin-converting enzyme generates angiotensin II for AT1 and AT2 receptors, while ACE2 and a Mas receptor arm oppose it and aldosterone synthase drives mineralocorticoid production. Vasopressin and oxytocin receptors, endothelins with their converting enzyme, adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors, substance P and tachykinin signalling, and thrombin-activated protease receptors add further inputs, balanced against endothelial nitric oxide synthase-derived vasodilation and modulated by NADPH oxidase-generated superoxide and mast cell proteases.

Blood pressure and regional blood flow are set largely by how hard the smooth muscle in arterial walls squeezes, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower that tone. Vasoconstrictor signals arriving through adrenergic and purinergic receptors such as ADRA2B and the ATP-gated channel P2RX1 raise cytosolic calcium, while RhoA-dependent kinase signalling sensitises the contractile apparatus to a given calcium level; ARHGAP42 acts as a brake on RhoA and is a locus associated with blood pressure variation. Opposing elements include the plasma membrane calcium pump ATP2B1, which extrudes calcium to promote relaxation, and Rac-directed DOCK guanine nucleotide exchange factors. Palmitoylation and ubiquitin-dependent turnover tune receptor and effector availability. Persistent imbalance here contributes to hypertension, vasospasm and the arterial remodelling that accompanies them.

Cardiac output is adjusted moment to moment by raising or lowering the force each beat generates, and here that adjustment is driven by circulating hormones and locally released mediators rather than by stretch or rate alone. Catecholamines acting on beta-adrenergic and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors increase contractile force by altering calcium handling in the myocyte, endothelin provides a paracrine inotropic input, and nitric oxide generated by endothelial nitric oxide synthase supplies an opposing, cGMP-mediated brake. Desensitisation by G protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 and scaffolding of receptors and signalling enzymes in caveolae set how strongly each stimulus is transmitted. This inotropic control matches perfusion to demand during exercise and stress; its chronic overdrive, with receptor downregulation and impaired nitric oxide signalling, is a feature of heart failure and hypertensive remodelling, and it is the target of beta-blocker therapy.

Heart rate is set not only by the sinoatrial pacemaker's intrinsic rhythm but by chemical messengers — hormones, neuropeptides and locally released paracrine and autocrine factors — that tune how fast cardiomyocytes depolarize and repolarize. This chemical control matches cardiac output to circulatory demand, and its failure produces inappropriate tachycardia, bradycardia or repolarization instability. The repolarizing potassium channel KCNH2 carries the rapid delayed-rectifier current that ends the ventricular action potential; loss-of-function variants cause long QT syndrome and risk of torsades de pointes, and NOS1AP variants modify QT interval through nitric oxide signalling near the channel. Contractile and regulatory proteins such as TPM1 couple electrical activity to force, a microRNA of the muscle-specific miR-133 family restrains excitability and hypertrophic remodelling, and the neuropeptide precursor CARTPT acts on autonomic circuits influencing cardiovascular tone.

The kidney sets long-term arterial pressure by controlling how much sodium and water are retained and how much vasoconstrictor tone is imposed on the vasculature, and this renal contribution to systemic blood pressure regulation is why hypertension is so often a kidney disease. Renin released from juxtaglomerular cells cleaves angiotensinogen to launch the renin-angiotensin cascade, whose peptides act through AGTR1 to constrict vessels and through AGTR2 and the MAS1 receptor to oppose that action; aldosterone synthase provides the mineralocorticoid arm, while HSD11B2 protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol, its loss causing apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4A/CYP4F family generate 20-HETE in the tubule and microvasculature, and endothelin, adenosine, succinate and podocyte- and glomerular-expressed regulators tune afferent and efferent tone. The balance of pressor and depressor limbs determines pressure natriuresis and volume homeostasis.

Long-term arterial blood pressure is set largely by the kidney, which adjusts the tone of peripheral resistance vessels and thereby the force opposing blood flow. This renal contribution to peripheral vascular resistance is built around angiotensinogen, the liver-derived precursor cleaved to angiotensin II, which constricts arterioles through the type 1 receptor and raises systemic pressure, while the type 2 receptor and the MAS1 receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) oppose that action with vasodilation. RHOA links receptor engagement to calcium sensitization of smooth muscle contraction, and the MRGPRD receptor for beta-alanine contributes vasoactive signalling. Overactivity of this axis produces hypertension and its downstream vascular and cardiac remodelling, which is why receptor blockers and inhibitors of the converting enzyme are mainstays of treatment; insufficient signalling causes hypotension and renal hypoperfusion.

Arterial blood pressure is held within a narrow range by opposing vasoconstrictor and vasodilator influences acting on vascular tone, cardiac output and renal sodium handling; systemic arterial blood pressure regulation is the balance between them, and its failure produces hypertension, orthostatic intolerance or shock. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone axis is prominent here, with renin, angiotensinogen, angiotensin-converting enzymes and the AT1 and AT2 receptors setting vasoconstriction and aldosterone synthesis, countered by ACE2 and the Mas receptor. Endothelins and their receptor, adrenergic and vasopressin receptors, and kallikreins push pressure up; endothelial nitric oxide synthase, the natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP with their processing protease corin, and adrenomedullin push it down. Renal tubular transporters and the WNK kinase pathway tie pressure to salt and volume status, while smooth muscle RhoA signalling and potassium channels tune myogenic contraction directly.

Systemic arterial blood pressure is set in part by a circulating hormonal cascade in which renin cleaves angiotensinogen, angiotensin-converting enzyme generates angiotensin II, and receptor engagement drives vasoconstriction, aldosterone release and renal sodium retention. This renin-angiotensin control of vascular tone determines long-term fluid balance and perfusion, and its overactivity underlies hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy and progressive kidney disease, which is why ACE inhibitors and AGTR1 blockers are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Counter-regulatory branches are represented too: ACE2 and carboxypeptidases generate angiotensin-(1-7) acting through MAS1, opposing AGTR1-mediated constriction, as does AGTR2. Peptidases including aminopeptidases, neprilysin, chymase and cathepsin G provide alternative routes of peptide generation and degradation, while NADPH oxidase subunits and RHOA link receptor signalling to oxidative stress and smooth muscle contractility. Related vasoactive receptors for endothelin, thrombin, substance P and succinate act alongside this axis.

Mean arterial pressure is defended by mechanisms that raise it when perfusion falls, and the genes here represent that pressor arm of cardiovascular homeostasis: vasoconstriction, sodium and water retention, and increased vascular tone. Their failure or excess is the substance of clinical hypertension and of hypotensive shock. Angiotensin-converting enzyme generates angiotensin II, while aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) drives mineralocorticoid production and renal sodium reabsorption; HSD11B2 protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol, and its loss causes apparent mineralocorticoid excess. Vasopressin acting through V1A receptors constricts vessels and through V2 receptors concentrates urine, and WNK1 tunes renal sodium-chloride cotransport, with gain of function producing familial hyperkalaemic hypertension. Smooth muscle contractility is set by RhoA signalling and modulated by NADPH oxidase-derived reactive oxygen species, linking neuroendocrine input to endothelial and myocyte responses.

negative regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure covers the signals that lower arterial pressure, opposing vasoconstrictor and volume-retaining drives so that perfusion stays within a range the heart and vasculature can tolerate. Loss of this depressor arm underlies hypertension and its sequelae: left ventricular hypertrophy, stroke, and renal damage. The genes span several convergent mechanisms. Cardiac natriuretic peptides released on atrial stretch promote natriuresis and vasodilation; the angiotensin II type 2 receptor and the MAS receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) counterbalance the classical pressor arm of the renin-angiotensin system; adrenergic beta receptors, adenosine A1, and neuropeptides such as substance P and CRH act on vascular tone, renal handling, and central autonomic outflow. Smooth muscle contractility is tuned by a Rho GAP, potassium channel activity, and antioxidant control of nitric oxide availability, with Klotho linking the pathway to vascular ageing.

Blood pressure is held within a narrow range by opposing influences, and this pathway covers the arm that lowers it — reducing the force with which blood travels through the systemic arterial circulation. It matters because loss of these depressor mechanisms leaves vasoconstriction and sodium retention unchecked, the setting for hypertension and its downstream damage to heart, kidney and vessel wall. The natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP, released from stretched cardiac myocytes, promote vasodilation and renal sodium excretion; the angiotensin II type 2 receptor and MAS1 oppose the classical pressor axis of the renin–angiotensin system; adrenergic and adenosine receptors, tachykinins and MRGPRD-linked sensory signalling relax smooth muscle or damp sympathetic outflow. Also represented are regulators of vascular tone and remodelling such as ARHGAP42, BMPR2 and Klotho, tying this control to endothelial function, oxidative stress and pulmonary as well as systemic vascular disease.

The kidney sets how much water the body retains, and renal water homeostasis is the loop by which plasma osmolality is held nearly constant despite variable drinking and losses. Vasopressin released from the hypothalamus acts on its V2 receptor in the collecting duct, which couples through Gs and adenylate cyclases to cAMP and protein kinase A; phosphorylated aquaporin-2 is then trafficked to the apical membrane, with myosin Vb and anchoring proteins directing the vesicles, while basolateral AQP3 completes transepithelial water flow into the hypertonic interstitium. Medullary tonicity depends on urea and salt handling, and uromodulin from the thick ascending limb contributes to concentrating capacity. Loss of receptor or channel function causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with massive dilute urine, whereas excessive vasopressin signalling produces hyponatraemia; sorbitol synthesis and vacuolar H+-ATPase link the same segments to osmolyte accumulation and urinary acidification.

regulation of glomerular filtration covers the signals that tune how fast plasma is filtered across the glomerular capillary wall into the renal tubule, setting the kidney's clearance of water and solutes and, through it, salt balance and blood pressure. Filtration rate depends on capillary hydraulic pressure and on the integrity of the podocyte-endothelial barrier, and both are targets here: adenosine acting through ADORA1 mediates tubuloglomerular feedback and afferent arteriolar constriction, thrombin and trypsin receptors F2R and F2RL1 couple coagulation proteases to mesangial and endothelial tone, PDGFB sustains mesangial cell recruitment, and gap junction connexin GJA5 propagates vasoconstrictor signals along the arteriole. Podocyte-restricted proteins such as PTPRO, CORO2B and EMP2 maintain foot process architecture and slit diaphragm function. Loss of these controls produces proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis and declining filtration rate in chronic kidney disease.

The kidney sets how fast plasma is filtered across the glomerular capillary wall, and this regulation determines urine output, solute clearance and salt and water balance across the whole body. Filtration rate is tuned both by vascular tone in the afferent and efferent arterioles and by the contractile and structural state of mesangial cells and podocytes that support the capillary loops. Adenosine acting through ADORA1 mediates tubuloglomerular feedback, constricting the afferent arteriole when distal salt delivery rises, while thrombin receptors F2R and F2RL1, PDGFB and GAS6 signal to mesangial and endothelial cells, and gap junction protein GJA5 helps propagate vasomotor signals along the arteriole. PTPRO, EMP2 and CORO2B act in the podocyte, where their loss produces foot process effacement, proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome; CYBA-dependent superoxide production modulates the same tone. Dysregulation underlies hyperfiltration injury in diabetes and hypertension.

Renal sodium ion transport is how the kidney sets the body's salt balance and, through it, extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure. Filtered sodium is reclaimed along the nephron by apical transporters and channels whose activity is continuously tuned: the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter SLC12A3 in the distal convoluted tubule, the ROMK potassium channel KCNJ1 that recycles K+ to sustain reabsorption, and basolateral chloride exit through CLCNKB. A kinase cascade provides the control layer, with WNK4 and WNK3 acting through the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39 to phosphorylate cotransporters, while KLHL3 targets WNK proteins for degradation and aldosterone-induced SGK1 raises transport capacity. Endothelin signalling through EDNRA and EDNRB, guanylin peptides, and tubular uromodulin modulate the same set point. Mutations in these components cause Gitelman and Bartter syndromes, distal renal tubular acidosis, and familial hyperkalaemic hypertension.

Renal water transport is how the kidney decides how much of the water filtered at the glomerulus is returned to the blood, setting urine concentration and defending plasma osmolality and blood volume. Its failure produces diabetes insipidus, with large volumes of dilute urine and thirst that cannot keep pace. Water crosses tubular epithelium through aquaporin channels: a constitutive channel in proximal tubule and descending limb supports bulk reabsorption, while in the collecting duct a regulated channel is shuttled from storage vesicles into the apical membrane and a basolateral partner completes the exit route. The hormonal arm is vasopressin acting on its type 2 receptor, a Gs-coupled receptor that raises cAMP and drives that trafficking step; receptor mutations cause the nephrogenic form of the disease. Hyaluronan synthesis and turnover in the medullary interstitium modulate the osmotic gradient this transport depends on.

regulation of systemic arterial blood pressure by endothelin describes how the vascular endothelium raises vascular tone and blood pressure through the endothelin peptides, one of the most potent vasoconstrictor systems in the body. It sets basal arterial resistance and is recruited in hypertension, pulmonary arterial hypertension, heart failure and chronic kidney disease, which is why endothelin receptor antagonists are used clinically. Endothelin-1 is synthesised as a precursor and activated by endothelin-converting enzyme at the endothelial surface, then acts on adjacent smooth muscle to trigger calcium entry and RhoA-dependent sensitisation of the contractile apparatus, sustaining constriction. The same pathway is balanced against endothelial nitric oxide synthase, so the net diameter of a vessel reflects opposing vasoconstrictor and vasodilator signals from the same cell layer. Related endothelin isoforms additionally act in neural crest and craniofacial development.

Endothelin is the endothelium's most potent vasoconstrictor, and its control of systemic arterial blood pressure sets vascular tone from moment to moment as well as over the long term through vessel wall remodelling. The peptide precursors encoded by EDN1, EDN2 and EDN3 are matured by the endothelin-converting enzyme ECE1 and then act on smooth muscle receptors, raising intracellular calcium and engaging RhoA-dependent contractile signalling that sensitises the myofilaments and sustains constriction. The same endothelial cells oppose this through endothelial nitric oxide synthase, so arterial diameter reflects a balance between endothelin-driven constriction and nitric oxide-driven relaxation. Loss of that balance, with excess endothelin tone, contributes to pulmonary arterial and systemic hypertension, and receptor blockade is an established therapy. Endothelin signalling also shapes neural crest derivatives during development, linking blood pressure control to craniofacial and enteric nervous system formation.

Before a heart can form, a patch of lateral mesoderm must be assigned cardiac identity, and heart field specification is that assignment: the delineation of first and second heart field progenitor territories from surrounding mesoderm. Everything downstream — chamber formation, outflow tract elongation, looping — depends on the size and position of these fields, and their mis-specification underlies congenital heart malformations. Positional information arrives as opposing secreted cues, with BMP2 and BMP4 promoting cardiogenic fate while Wnt pathway components and the antagonist DKK1 restrict or refine it; AXIN2 marks feedback control of that Wnt input. Within the responding cells, MESP1 acts at the top of the cardiac mesoderm hierarchy and ISL1, GATA5, MEF2C and the chromatin subunit SMARCD3 establish and stabilise progenitor gene expression. Notch signalling through RBPJ and Robo guidance receptors add boundary and migration control to the specified field.</description>

Specification of the secondary heart field sets aside a pool of lateral mesoderm distinct from the first heart field, and its descendants build most of the right ventricle together with the outflow tract at the arterial pole and part of the inflow tract at the venous pole. Because these are precisely the structures malformed in conotruncal and right-heart congenital heart disease, the delineation step underlies tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle and persistent truncus arteriosus. Mesodermal progenitors marked by MESP1 are directed into this territory by BMP4 and by non-canonical WNT5A and WNT11 signalling, with canonical Wnt output tuned through AXIN2 and Notch input relayed by RBPJ. ISL1 identifies the undifferentiated progenitor state, while MEF2C and the chromatin-remodelling subunit SMARCD3 drive the transcriptional programme that commits these cells to cardiomyocyte fate and later cardiac morphogenesis.

Vertebrate organs are placed asymmetrically, and this is the step that tells the lateral plate mesoderm which side it is on, so that the heart loops in one direction and the gut, lungs and spleen adopt their normal handedness. Left-sided Nodal signalling is the core event: NODAL acts through SMAD2 with the forkhead partner FOXH1 to switch on left-specific transcription, while the secreted antagonist DAND5 restricts that activity on the right side of the embryo. Hedgehog input via SHH and its transducer SMO, together with the nicalin–NOMO membrane complex that tempers Nodal responsiveness, sets the threshold and timing of the response, and CITED2 links the cue to downstream cardiac patterning. Disruption produces situs inversus, heterotaxy and complex congenital heart malformations, connecting this decision to node and cilia function upstream.

The first recognizable heart is a simple epithelial tube, and its formation and patterning set up every later cardiac structure: inflow and outflow poles, chamber identity, and the looping that converts a midline tube into a left-right asymmetric organ. Failure here underlies congenital heart disease, including outflow tract and septal defects and heterotaxy with situs inversus. Cardiac mesoderm is specified by MESP1 and then by a core transcriptional module including NKX2-5, GATA4, MEF2C, TBX20 and the HAND factors, which drives myocardial differentiation and regional gene expression. Laterality information arrives through nodal cilia and left-right signalling, so many components are ciliary or intraflagellar transport proteins whose loss randomizes looping. Overlying this are Nodal/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog, canonical and planar-cell-polarity Wnt, FGF8 and Hippo-YAP inputs that coordinate progenitor proliferation, migration and epithelial organization during heart tube morphogenesis.

The single embryonic outflow vessel must be divided into aorta and pulmonary trunk, and outflow tract septum morphogenesis is the building of that partition. When it fails, the result is the conotruncal group of congenital heart defects — persistent truncus arteriosus, double outlet right ventricle, tetralogy of Fallot, and the outflow lesions of DiGeorge syndrome, where TBX1 haploinsufficiency disturbs pharyngeal mesoderm and neural crest contributions. The genes converge on a few instructive signals: BMP ligands acting through type I and II receptors and SMAD4, TGF-beta signalling, FGF8 from the pharyngeal endoderm, and retinoic acid receptors, all interpreted by cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, ISL1, GATA6, ZFPM2 and TBX20. Semaphorin-plexin and neuropilin cues, together with Robo receptors, guide cardiac neural crest cells into the cushions that fuse to form the septum, linking cell migration to chamber and great-vessel alignment.

The ventricular septum closes the heart's two pumping chambers off from one another, and its upper portion, the membranous septum, is the last part to form; shaping it correctly is what separates systemic from pulmonary circulation. Failure leaves a perimembranous ventricular septal defect, the commonest form of congenital heart malformation, often together with outflow tract and valve anomalies. The genes here place this morphogenesis downstream of BMP and TGF-beta signalling, with BMP4 and its extracellular antagonist noggin setting the balance of growth signals, TGFB2 acting through TGFBR2 in the endocardial cushion mesenchyme that contributes the septal tissue, and ID2 relaying transcriptional output. Frizzled receptors and the planar cell polarity protein VANGL2 add Wnt-dependent control of cell orientation and movement, while the chromatin methyltransferase NSD2 links the process to the cardiac defects of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.

Morphogenesis of the muscular septum shapes the thick, myocardial lower portion of the wall that divides the left and right ventricles, completing the separation of systemic from pulmonary circulation. When it fails, the result is a muscular ventricular septal defect, one of the commonest congenital heart malformations, allowing left-to-right shunting and volume overload of the lungs. The genes involved point to instructive signalling between myocardium and the growing septal ridge: BMP4 provides a transforming growth factor-beta family cue and TGFBR3 modulates such signals, while FZD1 and FZD2 receive Wnt ligands and VANGL2 contributes planar cell polarity, orienting cell movement and trabecular coalescence. HEY2 is a Notch-responsive transcriptional repressor that patterns compact ventricular myocardium and distinguishes chamber identity. The pathway sits within broader cardiac chamber and outflow development, coupling growth factor gradients to oriented myocardial growth.

Outflow tract morphogenesis builds the exit channel of the developing heart and divides it into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, so that systemic and pulmonary circulations are separated at birth. Its failure produces the common conotruncal malformations — tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, transposition and persistent truncus arteriosus — and is the basis of the cardiac defects in 22q11 deletion and Alagille syndromes. The process depends on second heart field progenitors marked by ISL1 and TBX1 adding myocardium to the arterial pole, and on cardiac neural crest cells migrating in along semaphorin, plexin and slit-robo cues to septate the vessel and pattern the aortic arch arteries. BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, WNT and FGF8 signalling coordinate these populations with endocardial cushion remodelling, valve formation and smooth muscle differentiation, under transcriptional control by NKX2-5, GATA6, HAND2, PITX2 and TBX20.

The outflow tract is the single vessel leaving the embryonic heart that must be septated, rotated and remodelled into separate aorta and pulmonary trunk with their valves. Getting this wrong produces the common conotruncal malformations — tetralogy of Fallot, double-outlet right ventricle, transposition, persistent truncus arteriosus — and it is the developmental step disrupted in DiGeorge/22q11 deletion through TBX1 and CRKL. Building it requires second heart field progenitors marked by ISL1 and NKX2-5, cardiac neural crest guided by SEMA3C–PLXND1 and Robo signals, and endocardial cushion cells undergoing endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition. BMP, FGF8, Notch–JAG1–RBPJ, TGF-beta, retinoic acid and non-canonical Wnt/planar polarity inputs converge on transcription factors including TBX20, HAND2, GATA6, PITX2 and TWIST1 to pattern septation, valve formation and great-artery identity.

Organs begin as inductive interactions between epithelium and mesenchyme, and this pathway covers the signals that tune how strongly and how quickly those rudiments form. Its output determines whether a kidney, limb, heart or genital structure is initiated at the right place and size; too little or too much signalling produces agenesis, hypoplasia, or duplicated and misplaced structures, and several members are mutated in congenital malformation syndromes. The logic is a small set of secreted cues read at graded strength: bone morphogenetic proteins, hedgehog, fibroblast growth factors acting through FGFR1 and the adaptor FRS2, and WNT ligands feeding β-catenin, with DKK1 and SPRY1 damping WNT and FGF output respectively. Transcriptional regulators such as WT1, SIX1, GATA5 and posterior HOX genes set the competence of the responding tissue, while GDNF and ROBO receptors position branching and boundary formation.

The endocardium is the endothelial lining of the heart chambers, and its development produces both a non-thrombogenic inner surface and a signalling layer that instructs the myocardium and builds the valves and cardiac cushions. Without it, trabeculation and valve septation fail, giving congenital defects such as bicuspid aortic valve and septal and outflow tract malformations. Endothelial specification depends on VEGF signalling through KDR and on SOX17 and SOX18, while NOTCH1 acting with its transcriptional partner RBPJ patterns the endocardium and drives endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition in cushion-forming regions. BMP signalling via ACVR1 and SMAD4 and endocardium-derived NRG1 relay instructions to adjacent myocardium, and the Hippo kinases STK3 and STK4 restrain growth. PROX1 and OVOL2 contribute transcriptional control, linking this programme to valve morphogenesis and chamber maturation.

Blood vessels, lymphatics and the heart are lined by a single sheet of endothelial cells, and endothelium development covers how that layer is specified from mesoderm and matured into a selective, non-leaky barrier. It determines whether a vessel becomes arterial, venous or lymphatic, and its failure underlies vascular malformations, oedema and defective barrier function. Transcription factors such as ETV2, SOX17/SOX18, NR2F2 and PROX1 assign endothelial identity and lineage fate, while VEGFA-KDR, Notch ligands DLL4 and JAG1 with HEY1/HEY2, and BMP/TGF-beta receptors including ACVRL1 and BMPR2 pattern arteriovenous specification and sprouting. Junction proteins VE-cadherin, PECAM1, claudin-5 and the zonula occludens family, coupled to RhoA-ROCK and Rap1-linked signalling, close the paracellular seal; sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors and the CCM complex stabilise it. Inflammatory inputs such as TNF, IL1B and ICAM1 remodel the same junctions during leukocyte traffic.

morphogenesis of an endothelium is the shaping of the single-cell layer that lines blood vessels, lymphatics and heart chambers into a continuous, correctly patterned sheet. It determines whether a vascular tube forms a lumen of the right diameter with stable cell-cell junctions, and its failure produces the vascular malformations seen in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and cerebral cavernous malformation, where ACVRL1 and CCM2 act respectively. The genes span the inputs and effectors of this remodelling: Notch components DLL4 and RBPJ set arterial versus venous and tip versus stalk identity during sprouting, beta-catenin couples junctional adhesion to transcription, and RhoA, RhoB and the RhoGAP STARD13 drive the cytoskeletal contractility that bends and elongates cells. Growth factor and chemokine cues such as FGF1 and CXCL10 tune the process, linking endothelial architecture to angiogenesis, barrier integrity and inflammation.

Blood and lymphatic vessels work only if their endothelial lining is built into the right shape: a continuous, correctly polarized monolayer enclosing a lumen of appropriate calibre. Morphogenesis of an endothelium covers the sculpting of that layer during vascular development and remodelling, and its failure produces malformed, leaky or shunting vessels. Notch components such as DLL4 and its transcriptional partner RBPJ set tip-versus-stalk identity and restrain excessive sprouting, while ACVRL1 transduces BMP9/10 signals that stabilize arterial endothelium and is mutated in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Junctional and cytoskeletal control runs through beta-catenin, RHOA and RHOB with the RhoGAP STARD13, and CCM2 loss produces cerebral cavernous malformations by disrupting endothelial junction integrity. Additional inputs from FGF1, chemokine signalling and transcriptional regulators such as FOXP1 tune proliferation, migration and tube formation during angiogenesis and vessel maturation.

The endocardium is the endothelial and matrix lining of the heart chambers, and shaping it into a continuous inner layer is what allows valves, trabeculae and the cushions of the atrioventricular canal to form. Endocardium morphogenesis therefore sits upstream of septation and valvulogenesis, and its disruption produces congenital heart disease of the bicuspid aortic valve and septal defect type. Notch signalling through its receptor and the transcriptional partner RBPJ instructs endocardial cells to remodel, delaminate and support cushion formation, while SOX17 and SOX18 act with the wider SoxF group in arterial and endothelial identity. PROX1 and OVOL2 supply transcriptional control that restrains inappropriate epithelial-to-endothelial character during chamber growth. The biology is a specialised branch of endothelial development, coupling regional patterning of endothelium to the mechanics of a beating, blood-filled heart.

The heartbeat originates in a small population of specialized cardiomyocytes, and cardiac conduction system development is how those cells are set aside from working myocardium and wired into a pacemaker-to-ventricle relay. It produces the sinoatrial node, atrioventricular node and His-Purkinje network, so that electrical impulses arise rhythmically and are delayed appropriately between atria and ventricles; failure gives sick sinus syndrome, conduction block, accessory pathways and inherited arrhythmia. Transcription factors including NKX2-5, TBX5, TBX3, SHOX2 and ISL1 specify nodal identity and repress the chamber programme, while BMP and Notch signalling through SMADs and HEY factors partition conductive from compact myocardium. The functional readout is electrophysiological: the pacemaker channel HCN4, the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A, and gap junction connexins such as GJA5 and GJA1 that determine whether tissue conducts rapidly or slowly.

The atrioventricular node is the electrical relay of the heart: it receives the impulse generated by the sinoatrial node, delays it long enough for the atria to empty, then passes it to the His-Purkinje system so the ventricles contract in sequence. Building this small population of specialised conduction myocytes depends on the genes collected here, and when the programme fails the result is heart block, conduction delay and arrhythmia, often alongside septal defects. Notch receptors and the Mastermind-like coactivator pattern the AV canal myocardium and set conduction-cell identity, while BMP receptor signalling and the cardiac transcription factors NKX2-5, TBX5, GATA4 and GATA6 act combinatorially to specify and maintain the node; mutations in several of them cause familial congenital heart disease with progressive atrioventricular conduction abnormalities. KCNJ8 contributes potassium channel function to the resulting cells.

The heart's pacemaker arises from a small region of right sinus venosus myocardium that must escape the working-myocardium programme and instead acquire spontaneous, rhythmic automaticity. Sinoatrial node development produces the cells that set heart rate and hand the impulse on toward the atrioventricular node; failure of the programme underlies sick sinus syndrome, sinus bradycardia and inherited arrhythmia. Transcriptional repressors such as SHOX2 and TBX3 suppress the atrial gene programme, including the fast connexins and chamber markers driven by TBX5 and GATA6, while TBX18 marks the head of the node and ISL1 maintains the progenitor state; MESP1 and BMP4 place the whole structure within early cardiac lineage specification and patterning. The output is a distinctive electrophysiology, with the HCN4 funny current and low-voltage-activated calcium entry through CACNA1G generating diastolic depolarisation, and POPDC1 tuning the response to sympathetic stimulation.

Ventricular contraction is coordinated by a specialized conduction network, and the development of the His-Purkinje system is how that network is carved out of working myocardium. The bundle of His, its branches and the Purkinje fibers carry the impulse relayed from the AV node rapidly to the ventricular apex, so that the chambers contract in the correct sequence; failure of the programme produces bundle branch block, conduction delay and arrhythmia, and mutations in several of these genes cause congenital heart disease with conduction defects. Transcriptional control dominates: NKX2-5 and TBX5 act together to specify and maintain conduction-cell identity, TBX3 and ID2 repress the working myocardial programme in cells destined to conduct, and IRX3 sets the fast-conduction gene expression pattern of the peripheral fibers. Desmosomal adhesion via DSG2 supports the mechanical and electrical coupling of these cells to surrounding myocardium.

Cardiac valves form from endocardial cushions and then remodel into thin, fibrous leaflets that keep blood moving in one direction through the heart; incomplete or disordered valve development underlies bicuspid aortic valve, mitral valve prolapse, and valve stenosis or regurgitation in congenital heart disease. The programme begins when myocardial BMP and TGF-beta signals, acting through type I and II receptors and SMAD effectors, induce a subset of endocardial cells to undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition driven by SNAI1/SNAI2 and TWIST1. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, JAG1, DLL4 and RBPJ with HEY-family repressors specifies which endocardial cells delaminate, while NFATC1, GATA4/5, TBX5, TBX20 and NKX2-5 provide transcriptional context. Later steps remodel the cushion matrix: SOX9 and SCX drive a tendon-like fibrous programme, elastin and ADAMTS proteases sculpt proteoglycan-rich leaflets, and Slit-Robo and Rho-ROCK signalling shape valve morphology.

The mitral and tricuspid valves that separate atria from ventricles begin as endocardial cushions, and atrioventricular valve development tracks that tissue from cushion formation through remodelling into thin, layered fibrous leaflets. It matters because the mature valve must open and close for a lifetime without regurgitation; disrupted development gives valve dysplasia, mitral valve prolapse, atrioventricular septal defects and bicuspid or insufficient valves. Cushion cells arise by endocardial-to-mesenchymal transition driven by BMP and TGF-beta signalling through their receptors and SMAD effectors, with SMAD6 restraining the response, while NOTCH1 and HEY factors pattern endocardium and set the boundary between valve and myocardium. Cardiac transcription factors including GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, TWIST1 and PITX2 specify cushion mesenchyme and left-right asymmetry, and matrix components such as DCHS1 and ADAMTS19 organise the extracellular matrix on which leaflet mechanics depend.

mitral valve development builds the left atrioventricular valve, the two-leaflet structure that keeps blood moving forward from left atrium to ventricle under the highest pressures in the heart. Its failure produces some of the commonest structural heart disease in humans, from myxomatous leaflet prolapse and regurgitation to atrioventricular septal defects. The process begins with endocardial cushions: BMP and activin receptor signalling through SMAD effectors, restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6, drives endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, while NOTCH1, TWIST1 and SOX4 govern cushion cell migration, proliferation and remodelling into thin fibrous leaflets. Planar cell polarity through DCHS1 orients the mesenchymal cells that lay down organised extracellular matrix, and ADAMTS19 and glycosaminoglycan turnover shape that matrix as the valve matures. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of cardiac morphogenesis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and connective tissue patterning.

The mitral valve separates the left atrium from the left ventricle and must form leaflets thin enough to open freely yet strong enough to seal against systolic pressure; this developmental programme takes it from an endocardial cushion of the atrioventricular canal to that mature, layered structure. Its failure underlies myxomatous degeneration and mitral valve prolapse, one of the commonest causes of valve surgery, as well as congenital atrioventricular septal defects. Endocardial cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and populate the cushions under BMP receptor signalling through ACVR1, BMPR1A and BMPR2, restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6, with NOTCH1 and transcriptional regulators including TWIST1 and SOX4 driving mesenchymal identity. Planar cell polarity through DCHS1 orients the migrating cells, and later remodelling organizes extracellular matrix into the stratified leaflets and tension apparatus that give the valve its mechanical competence.

The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle and must form as a thin, layered leaflet apparatus that opens and closes without leaking for a lifetime of heartbeats. Its development begins with endocardial cushions in the atrioventricular canal, where endocardial cells undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, invade the cardiac jelly and then remodel into compact, matrix-organised leaflets and supporting chordae. Bone morphogenetic protein and TGF-beta receptor signalling through BMPR1A, BMPR2 and TGFBR2 drives cushion formation and mesenchymal outgrowth, while the transcriptional regulators TBX20, HEY2 and ZFPM1 pattern chamber and valve identity, and the secreted protease ADAMTS19 shapes the extracellular matrix during leaflet maturation. Disruption of these steps produces congenital right-sided valve disease such as Ebstein anomaly, tricuspid atresia and dysplastic, regurgitant valves, and links this programme to broader cardiac septation and outflow morphogenesis.

Formation of the pulmonary valve turns the outflow tract cushions of the embryonic heart into thin, layered leaflets that keep blood from regurgitating back into the right ventricle. When the programme goes wrong the result is clinically familiar congenital disease: pulmonary stenosis or atresia, dysplastic or thickened leaflets, and valve lesions that appear as part of syndromic heart malformation. The genes involved trace the signalling that patterns the endocardial cushions and their remodelling: Notch receptors with their ligand JAG1, the RBPJ transcriptional effector and HEY-family repressors, BMP and TGF-beta ligands with SMAD transducers and the inhibitory SMAD6, NFATC1-dependent endocardial gene expression, SLIT-ROBO guidance cues, and ADAMTS proteases that sculpt the proteoglycan-rich valve matrix. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase and the transcription factor TBX20 tie leaflet growth to endocardial and myocardial cues from the surrounding outflow tract.

Heart valves begin as swellings of extracellular matrix in the embryonic atrioventricular canal and outflow tract, and this morphogenetic programme converts them into the thin, layered, fibrous leaflets that enforce one-way blood flow. Failure produces bicuspid aortic valve, valve stenosis or regurgitation, and myxomatous mitral prolapse, among the commonest congenital and adult structural heart diseases. Endocardial cells overlying the cushions undergo an endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition driven by BMP and TGF-beta signalling through SMAD effectors and by NOTCH1 with its HEY targets, with SNAI1/SNAI2 and TWIST1 executing the change in cell state. NFATC1, GATA4/5, TBX5, TBX20 and NKX2-5 pattern the endocardium and myocardium that instruct it, while SOX9, elastin, EMILIN1 and ADAMTS proteases remodel the matrix into stratified leaflets. Slit-Robo guidance, planar polarity through DCHS1, and Rho-ROCK cytoskeletal control shape and elongate the growing valve.

Shaping of the aortic valve turns endocardial cushion tissue at the left ventricular outflow into three thin, layered, collagen- and elastin-rich leaflets that open and close without regurgitation for a lifetime. When the programme goes wrong the result is bicuspid aortic valve, the most common congenital cardiac malformation, predisposing to calcific stenosis and ascending aortic aneurysm. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, its ligands JAG1 and DLL4 and HEY-family targets specifies valve endocardium and restrains calcification, while TGF-beta/BMP inputs relayed by SMAD2 and tempered by the inhibitory SMAD6 drive endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition through SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1. Cardiac transcription factors GATA4, GATA5, NKX2-5 and TBX20 set the outflow tract context, SOX9 and ADAMTS proteases with elastin and EMILIN1 remodel the leaflet matrix, and SLIT-ROBO with RHOA-ROCK signalling guides cushion cell migration and elongation.

Pulmonary valve morphogenesis builds the three-leaflet valve that separates the right ventricle from the pulmonary artery and enforces one-way flow into the lungs. Errors here produce pulmonary stenosis, dysplastic or bicuspid pulmonary valves, and are part of the outflow tract malformations seen in Tetralogy of Fallot and Alagille syndrome. The valve arises from endocardial cushion tissue: NOTCH1/2 with JAG1 and the HEY family transcriptional repressors specify endocardium and restrain myocardial fate, while TGFB2, BMP4 and SMAD2 drive endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, with SMAD6 limiting it. NFATC1 and endothelial nitric oxide signalling coordinate leaflet elongation and proliferation, SLIT-ROBO guidance cues shape cushion patterning, and ADAMTS proteases including ADAMTS19 remodel the proteoglycan-rich matrix so leaflets thin into flexible cusps. TBX20 supplies the underlying cardiac transcriptional program, linking this process to outflow tract septation and general heart valve development.

The pulmonary valve guards the outflow from the right ventricle into the lung circulation, and its formation from endocardial cushion tissue determines whether blood leaves the heart in one direction only. Failure of this morphogenetic programme produces pulmonary stenosis, atresia or dysplastic thickened leaflets, lesions common in congenital heart disease and in syndromes such as Alagille. Notch receptors with their Jagged ligand and HEY-family transcriptional repressors pattern the cushion endocardium and drive endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, while TGF-beta and BMP4 signalling through SMAD2 is restrained by the inhibitory SMAD6 to set leaflet size. Calcineurin-NFATC1 signalling and endothelial nitric oxide synthase couple valve endothelium to cushion remodelling, SLIT-ROBO guidance cues shape the outflow tract, and ADAMTS proteases with versican turnover sculpt the extracellular matrix into thin, elongated leaflets. TBX20 supplies the upstream cardiac transcriptional context.

Heart valve formation covers the earliest steps by which valve rudiments appear in the developing heart, beginning with the specification of endocardial cushion tissue and ending when a recognizable valve primordium exists. These structures enforce one-way blood flow, so errors here produce bicuspid aortic valve, valve stenosis or regurgitation, and mitral valve prolapse. Endocardial cells overlying the cushions undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invade the cardiac jelly, a step driven by NOTCH1 signalling with its HEY1 and HEY2 targets, TGF-beta/BMP transduction through SMAD4, and the transcription factors GATA4, TBX20, TWIST1 and SOX9 that control mesenchymal proliferation and matrix production. Cadherin- and protocadherin-mediated adhesion, including DCHS1, together with RHOA-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling, shapes the growing leaflet, while SCX and SOX9 push cushion mesenchyme toward the fibrous, tendon-like matrix of the mature valve.

atrioventricular valve formation is the embryonic construction of the mitral and tricuspid valves, the structures that enforce one-way flow between atria and ventricles. Its failure produces some of the commonest congenital heart defects — atrioventricular septal defects, valve dysplasia, regurgitation — and milder disruption of the same program underlies degenerative mitral valve prolapse in adults. The process begins in the atrioventricular canal, where endocardial cells receive myocardial cues, undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and invade the cardiac jelly to form the endocardial cushions that later remodel into thin fibrous leaflets. Notch signalling through NOTCH1 and its HEY1/HEY2 targets sets the boundary of the valve-forming region, GATA4 with its cofactor ZFPM1 and BMP/TGF-beta signals transduced by SMAD4 drive cushion mesenchyme formation, and DCHS1 governs the planar organisation and extracellular matrix of the maturing leaflet.

The mitral and tricuspid valves begin as endocardial cushions in the atrioventricular canal, and this pathway covers the steps that turn that swelling into a recognizable valve rudiment. Without it, the heart cannot separate atrial from ventricular blood or prevent regurgitation, and defects here underlie atrioventricular septal defects, valve dysplasia and myxomatous mitral valve disease. Endocardial cells overlying the cushion undergo endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invade the cardiac jelly, a decision governed by NOTCH1 signalling and its transcriptional effectors HEY1 and HEY2, by TGF-beta/BMP signals routed through the common mediator SMAD4, and by the GATA4-ZFPM1 (FOG2) transcription factor partnership that patterns the atrioventricular canal. DCHS1, a protocadherin mutated in mitral valve prolapse, orders the migration and polarity of the resulting valve interstitial cells. The programme links cardiac chamber specification to the mechanics of unidirectional flow.

Endocardial cushion development is the step in heart morphogenesis that produces the mesenchymal swellings in the atrioventricular canal and outflow tract from which the cardiac valves and the septa separating the chambers are built. Without it the heart cannot be divided into a systemic and pulmonary circuit, and failure of individual components underlies septal defects, valve malformations and abnormal outflow tract septation, among the most common congenital heart malformations. The core event is an endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition in which endocardial cells delaminate and invade the underlying matrix, driven by BMP and TGF-beta ligands signalling through type I and type II receptors to SMAD2/SMAD4, with NOTCH1-RBPJ and its HEY targets and the SNAI1/SNAI2 and TWIST1 transcription factors executing the change in cell state. Cardiac transcription factors including GATA4, TBX5 and TBX20, BMP antagonism by noggin, and remodelling of cushion matrix set the timing and extent of the response.

The valves and membranous septa of the heart begin as swellings of extracellular matrix lined by endocardium, and they only become tissue when endocardial cells delaminate and invade. In this cardiac epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, endocardial cells lose apical-basolateral polarity, break intercellular junctions, degrade the underlying basement membrane and migrate into the cushion matrix, where their descendants form valve leaflets and septal tissue. Failure produces congenital malformations such as septal defects and dysplastic, regurgitant valves. The conversion is driven by TGF-beta ligands acting through TGFBR1/TGFBR2 and SMAD4, by BMP4 and FGF8 from the adjacent myocardium, and by NOTCH1 signalling via RBPJ with HEY-family repressors; these converge on SNAI1 and SNAI2, which repress epithelial adhesion genes, with MSX1/MSX2 and the endothelial co-receptor endoglin shaping the response.

The endocardial cushions are swellings of mesenchyme in the atrioventricular canal and outflow tract of the embryonic heart that go on to form the cardiac valves and the septa dividing the chambers. Their morphogenesis converts a simple tube into a four-chambered pump with one-way flow, and its failure underlies much of congenital heart disease: septal defects, valve dysplasia, bicuspid and myxomatous valves. Cushion formation begins when overlying endocardial cells undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, driven by TGF-beta and BMP ligands acting through type I and type II receptors and SMAD effectors, together with NOTCH1-RBPJ signalling and the HEY transcriptional repressors. Downstream regulators including SNAI1/SNAI2, TWIST1, TBX2/TBX3, MSX1/MSX2 and SOX9 control delamination, migration, proliferation and subsequent remodelling of the cushion extracellular matrix into mature valve leaflets, with BMP antagonism and guidance cues shaping the boundaries.

Cardiac chamber development converts the simple looping heart tube into distinct atria and ventricles with defined walls, septa, trabeculae and conduction properties, and it is the process whose failure produces most congenital heart disease — septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, outflow malformations and non-compaction. Chamber identity is set by transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, HAND1/2, MEF2C and ISL1, with TBX2 and TBX3 repressing chamber gene programmes in the atrioventricular canal and nascent conduction tissue. BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, Wnt and FGF signalling, together with Notch effectors HEY1/HEY2 and RBPJ, coordinate myocardial growth with endocardial and cushion morphogenesis. Downstream, sarcomeric and calcium-handling genes such as MYH6, MYH7, MYL2, TNNT2 and RYR2 give each chamber its contractile character, linking developmental patterning directly to later cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia risk.

cardiac chamber morphogenesis is the developmental program that carves the early heart tube into discrete atria and ventricles with walls, trabeculae and septa of the right size and shape. It determines whether a newborn has a normally partitioned four-chambered heart, and its disruption underlies much of congenital heart disease — septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, valve and outflow malformations — as well as later cardiomyopathy. Chamber identity is set by a core of transcription factors, including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, HAND1/2 and MEF2C, acting on regional patterning cues from BMP, TGF-beta, Notch, WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling. Endocardial–myocardial crosstalk through NOTCH1, JAG1, HEY2 and NRG1 drives trabeculation and compaction, while sarcomeric genes such as MYH6, MYH7, TNNT2 and MYL2 give each chamber its contractile character. Laterality and cushion genes coordinate looping with septation.

The four-chambered heart is built by carving distinct atrial and ventricular cavities out of a simple tube, and cardiac chamber morphogenesis is the programme that generates and shapes those chambers. It determines wall thickness, trabeculation, septation and the atrioventricular boundary, and its failure produces the commonest human birth defects "septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, non-compaction and valve malformations. Cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, HAND1/2 and MEF2C set chamber identity and regional gene expression, with TBX2 and TBX3 repressing chamber programmes in the canal and conduction regions. They act downstream of BMP, TGF-beta/SMAD, Notch-Jagged, Wnt/Frizzled and neuregulin signals passing between endocardium and myocardium, and converge on sarcomeric output "MYH6, MYH7, MYL2, troponins, tropomyosin " so that each chamber acquires the contractile properties its workload demands.

The heart tube must be partitioned into discrete pumping cavities, and cardiac chamber formation is the step that converts a linear tube into atria and ventricles with distinct identities. Without it the embryo cannot establish separated inflow and outflow circuits, and the resulting defects — hypoplastic chambers, septal and valve malformations — account for much of congenital heart disease. Transcriptional regulators drive the process: a mesodermal progenitor determinant marks the earliest cardiac cells, while NKX2-5, MEF2C, TBX5 and TBX20 act combinatorially to specify chamber myocardium and switch on sarcomeric and conduction genes, with the bHLH factors HAND1 and HAND2 biased toward left and right ventricular growth. TBX2 conversely suppresses chamber differentiation to keep atrioventricular canal tissue non-working, and BMP, endothelin and Notch inputs pattern this regional decision. Chromatin remodelling through SMARCD3 supports the underlying transcriptional programme.

The pumping chambers of the heart acquire their shape, wall thickness and trabecular architecture through cardiac ventricle morphogenesis, the programme that turns cardiomyocyte progenitors into a compact myocardium capable of ejecting blood into the great arteries. Its disruption underlies much of congenital heart disease — ventricular septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, non-compaction cardiomyopathy — and the same genes recur in inherited cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia. Core cardiac transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20, MEF2C and the HAND proteins specify and pattern chamber myocardium, while Notch signalling through NOTCH1, JAG1, DLL4 and the HEY repressors coordinates endocardial–myocardial crosstalk and trabeculation, and BMP and TGF-beta receptor signalling drives growth and outflow tract remodelling. Downstream, sarcomeric and calcium-handling genes such as MYH6, MYH7, MYL2, TNNT2 and RYR2 provide contractile output, and desmosomal components maintain ventricular wall integrity.

The atria are the receiving chambers of the heart, taking venous return and delivering it to the ventricles, and their shaping during embryogenesis is what this pathway covers. Getting it wrong produces atrial septal defects, abnormal left-right patterning of the chambers, and conduction abnormalities such as atrial fibrillation and heart block. Cardiac progenitors marked by MESP1 and ISL1 are specified and then assigned a chamber identity by a transcription factor network including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5 and TBX20, with PITX2 imposing left-sided asymmetry and HEY2 restricting ventricular fate. Atrium-specific output includes the myosin heavy chain MYH6 and the gap junction connexin GJA5 that supports rapid atrial conduction. BMP, Notch, TGF-beta, Wnt and hedgehog signalling coordinate myocardial growth with endocardial and epicardial contributions, linking chamber morphogenesis to septation and to the venous inflow tract.

Cardiac ventricle formation is the step in heart development that builds the thick-walled pumping chambers which receive blood from the atria and drive it into the systemic and pulmonary circulations. Without it there is no functional pump: embryos fail at the point where circulation must support growth, and partial failure in humans gives ventricular septal defects, hypoplastic chambers and conduction abnormalities. The genes here define the regulatory circuit that specifies chamber myocardium from mesoderm and shapes it, with an early mesodermal determinant upstream of cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, TBX5, MEF2C and the paired bHLH factors HAND1 and HAND2, which are differentially deployed between left and right ventricles. A chromatin remodelling subunit couples these factors to their target promoters, and Notch signalling patterns the endocardium and trabeculae, linking chamber growth to valve and septal morphogenesis.

Shaping of the left ventricle is the step that turns a looped embryonic heart tube into the chamber that must later drive systemic circulation, and it fixes wall thickness, trabeculation and outflow alignment. Failure produces hypoplastic left heart, ventricular septal defects and cardiomyopathy presenting in infancy. Chamber identity is set transcriptionally: TBX5 and HAND1 pattern the left ventricular myocardium, while NOTCH1 acting through the transcription factor RBPJ and its target HEY2 separates compact myocardium from trabeculae and coordinates endocardial-myocardial crosstalk. TGF-beta signalling via TGFBR2 and SMAD4 drives the cushion and septal remodelling that divides the chambers, with endothelin and Wnt-modulating inputs tuning growth. Contractile and calcium-handling components such as RYR2 tie chamber maturation to the onset of function, so cardiac left ventricle morphogenesis links developmental patterning directly to pump performance.</description

The right ventricle is built largely from second heart field progenitors, and shaping it into a chamber that can drive blood into the pulmonary circulation is what right ventricular morphogenesis achieves. When it fails, the result is congenital malformation: hypoplastic or double-outlet right ventricle, tetralogy of Fallot, tricuspid and outflow tract defects that require surgical correction in infancy. Progenitor identity and chamber regionalization are set by transcription factors including ISL1, NKX2-5, TBX20, GATA4 and the bHLH pair HAND1 and HAND2, with HEY2 helping distinguish ventricular compact myocardium. BMP and TGF-beta ligands acting through BMPR1A, Notch signalling via JAG1 and NOTCH1, and SEMA3C-guided outflow tract remodeling coordinate growth, trabeculation and septation, while chromatin regulators such as CHD7 and SMARCD3 license the underlying cardiac transcriptional programme. Several of these genes are mutated in human syndromic heart disease.

Shaping of the left ventricular myocardium determines how the heart's main pumping chamber is built: the thickness of its compact wall, the arrangement of trabeculae, and the alignment of cardiomyocytes that lets the chamber generate systemic pressure. Failure of this morphogenetic programme produces congenital defects such as a hypoplastic or non-compacted left ventricle and thin-walled, poorly contractile chambers. The contributing genes span signalling and excitation: endothelin receptor type A transmits endothelin signals that drive myocardial growth and vascular tone, SMAD4 carries transforming growth factor beta and bone morphogenetic protein signals into transcriptional programmes that pattern chamber wall and septum, and the ryanodine receptor RYR2 releases calcium from cardiomyocyte sarcoplasmic reticulum, linking contractile activity to proper chamber development. This biology sits at the intersection of cardiac chamber specification, cardiomyocyte proliferation and growth control during embryonic and postnatal heart development.

Trabeculae are the sponge-like muscular ridges that project from the ventricular wall into the chamber lumen, and their formation lets the early heart contract forcefully and oxygenate itself before a coronary circulation exists. Ventricular trabecular myocardium morphogenesis converts a smooth-walled myocardial tube into this ridged architecture, and its failure produces thin, non-compacted ventricles, embryonic heart failure, and congenital defects resembling left ventricular non-compaction. Endocardium instructs the underlying muscle: Notch signalling through NOTCH1, its ligand DLL4 and the transcriptional partner RBPJ induces HEY2 and drives neuregulin production, while NRG1 acts on the myocardium to promote trabecular outgrowth. TGF-beta and BMP arms, including ENG, TGFBR1 and BMPR1A, and cardiac transcriptional regulators such as NKX2-5, FOXH1 and CHD7 set chamber identity and the balance between trabeculation and later compaction. HEG1 links the programme to endocardial and cardiac chamber growth.

The ventricular wall is built in two layers, and the formation of the outer compact myocardium determines how thick and mechanically competent the ventricle becomes. Cardiomyocytes in this zone proliferate and organize into dense circumferential sheets rather than the loose trabecular meshwork lining the chamber, so failure of the process leaves a thin, poorly contracting wall and underlies noncompaction and thin-myocardium phenotypes with embryonic or perinatal heart failure. Signalling from the overlying epicardium and endocardium drives the growth: BMP and TGF-beta receptors, together with the BMP antagonist noggin, set the balance between proliferation and differentiation, while a chromatin remodeller and a POU-domain transcription factor act in the transcriptional programmes of cardiac and neural crest-derived cells. Desmoplakin contributes the intercalated disc junctions that let the compacted layer transmit force.

Atrial cardiac muscle tissue development builds the thin-walled upper chambers of the heart and gives them an identity distinct from the ventricles, including the specialized conduction tissue that sets heart rate. It determines atrial wall growth, left-right asymmetry of the atria, and the formation of the sinoatrial node; its disruption underlies atrial septal defects, atrial fibrillation, sick sinus syndrome and laterality defects such as heterotaxy. Cardiac progenitors marked by MESP1 and ISL1 are directed by NKX2-5, GATA6, TBX5 and PITX2, with PITX2 enforcing left atrial character and TBX3/SHOX2 repressing working-myocardial genes to carve out pacemaker tissue expressing HCN4. BMP10 and BMP4, tuned by the antagonist noggin and by endoglin, drive chamber myocardial proliferation, while MYH6 and gap junction and Popeye-domain proteins provide contractile and electrical coupling. The pathway sits within broader cardiac morphogenesis and cardiac conduction.

Atrial cardiac muscle tissue development covers the specification, growth and maturation of the thin-walled upper chambers of the heart, the compartment that fills the ventricles and houses the pacemaking and conduction tissue. Its outcome determines atrial identity as distinct from ventricular myocardium, marked by chamber-specific contractile and gap junction proteins such as MYH6, and it sets left-right asymmetry of the atria through PITX2 and ZIC3 activity. Transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA6, TBX5, ISL1 and MESP1 act with BMP and WNT signals, the BMP antagonist NOG among them, to drive cardiac progenitors into atrial myocytes, while TBX3, SHOX2 and the HCN4 pacemaker channel carve out the sinoatrial node within this territory. Disruption produces septal defects, atrial isomerism, sinus node dysfunction and a predisposition to atrial fibrillation.

Formation of the heart's ventricular walls turns a simple cardiac tube into the thick-walled pumping chambers that drive systemic and pulmonary circulation, and errors here produce the commonest congenital heart defects — septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, non-compaction — as well as inherited cardiomyopathy. Ventricular cardiac muscle tissue development couples chamber-specific transcriptional identity, set by factors such as NKX2-5, TBX5, HAND1, HEY2 and IRX3, to signals from the endocardium and epicardium: Notch ligands and RBPJ, neuregulin, and BMP and TGF-beta receptor pathways feeding SMAD outputs that pattern trabeculation and compaction. Downstream, the sarcomere itself is specified, with ventricular myosin, troponin and tropomyosin isoforms (MYH7, MYL2, MYL3, TNNI3, TNNT2, MYBPC3) plus RYR2-dependent calcium release establishing contractile competence, while desmosomal genes secure the mechanical junctions between working myocytes.

Cardiac atrium development covers the emergence of the blood-receiving chambers of the heart, from specification of atrial progenitors in the early mesoderm through to chambers with their own myocardial identity, conduction properties and venous connections. It matters because atrial patterning sets left-right asymmetry of the inflow region and builds the substrate for sinus node and internodal conduction; its disruption underlies atrial septal defects, anomalous venous return, heterotaxy and inherited atrial fibrillation. Transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, TBX20 and ISL1 drive chamber gene programmes such as the atrial myosin MYH6 and the gap junction connexin GJA5, while PITX2 and SHOX2 impose laterality and restrain pacemaker fate in the left atrium. Superimposed on this are BMP, Notch, TGF-beta and non-canonical WNT signals that coordinate myocardial growth with endocardial and epicardial cues, HEY2 helping separate atrial from ventricular identity.

The ventricles are the pumping chambers of the heart, and their construction from early cardiac progenitors through trabeculation, chamber ballooning, septation and compaction determines whether blood can be driven into the systemic and pulmonary circuits. Failure at these steps produces much of congenital heart disease: ventricular septal defects, hypoplastic chambers, noncompaction and conduction abnormalities. Cardiac ventricle development couples lineage-specifying transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, MEF2C, HAND1 and HAND2 to intercellular signalling by BMP10 and other BMPs, TGF-beta receptors, Notch ligands and receptors with HEY2 output, and Wnt and Slit-Robo guidance cues that pattern chamber versus non-chamber myocardium. In parallel, sarcomeric and excitability genes including MYH7, MYL2, TNNT2, MYBPC3, RYR2 and SCN5A give the maturing chamber its contractile and electrical properties; many are also loci for inherited cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia.

growth involved in heart morphogenesis is the tissue growth that gives the developing heart its shape — the expansion and remodelling of myocardium, chambers and outflow tract that turns a simple tube into a four-chambered pump. When this growth is misproportioned, the result is congenital heart disease: hypoplastic chambers, valve and septal defects, or thin, poorly trabeculated ventricular walls. The genes span the stages of that process. A mesoderm transcription factor specifies the cardiac progenitors that supply the growing heart, Notch signalling patterns endocardium and trabeculae and instructs myocardial proliferation, and sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor signalling couples vascular and endocardial cues to growth of the surrounding tissue. A cardiac-enriched ADP-ribosylhydrolase-like protein acts in the sarcomeric apparatus of growing cardiomyocytes, and a microRNA tunes proliferative output. Together they link cell cycle control in cardiomyocytes to organ-level form.

Growth that contributes to shaping the heart couples cell proliferation and tissue expansion to the sculpting of chambers, valves and outflow structures during cardiac development. Timing matters: too little growth leaves hypoplastic chambers or thin ventricular walls, while misplaced growth distorts septa and valves, and defects in this process underlie much of congenital heart disease. The genes here span the sequence from specification to remodelling. MESP1 marks the earliest cardiogenic mesoderm that gives rise to the heart tube, NOTCH1 signalling patterns endocardium and is required for valve and outflow tract formation, and S1PR1 links sphingosine-1-phosphate sensing to endothelial behaviour and vascular integrity within the growing myocardium.
