It matters because it links dietary and xenobiotic detoxification to the supply of membrane lipids, steroid hormones and signalling molecules. Alcohol dehydrogenases and aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidise ethanol and related substrates to aldehydes and acids, while aldo-keto reductases and short-chain dehydrogenases run the reverse chemistry on sugars, retinoids and steroid intermediates. A large sterol arm runs from HMG-CoA reductase and squalene epoxidase through the post-squalene steps to cholesterol, under feedback control by the SREBP–SCAP–INSIG system, with lipoproteins, LDLR and cytochrome P450 hydroxylases handling transport, oxysterol formation and bile acid output. Inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases, glycerol kinase and sphingolipid enzymes complete the picture. Defects cause hypercholesterolaemia, alcohol intolerance, retinal dystrophy and inborn sterol synthesis disorders.

Ethanol metabolism is the route by which the body clears drinking alcohol, converting it to acetaldehyde, then to acetate, and finally to acetyl-CoA that feeds ordinary intermediary metabolism. It matters because the intermediate acetaldehyde is toxic and mutagenic: when its removal is slow, flushing, nausea and raised risk of upper gastrointestinal cancer follow, and chronic flux through this route reshapes hepatic redox balance and promotes fatty liver. An alcohol dehydrogenase carries out the first oxidation, mitochondrial and cytosolic aldehyde dehydrogenases including ALDH2 and ALDH1B1 detoxify the aldehyde, and acyl-CoA synthetases ACSS1 and ACSS2 activate acetate for lipid synthesis and acetylation reactions. Accompanying sulfotransferases conjugate sulfate onto phenolic and steroid substrates, linking this chemistry to the broader phase II detoxification and xenobiotic clearance capacity of liver and gut.

Glycerol metabolic process handles the three-carbon backbone released when fats are broken down, deciding whether it is burned, converted to glucose, or re-esterified into new lipid. It links adipose tissue lipolysis to hepatic gluconeogenesis, and so supports blood glucose during fasting; loss of glycerol kinase activity causes glycerol kinase deficiency with hyperglycerolaemia and metabolic decompensation. Glycerol entering a cell is phosphorylated by GK and oxidised by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, feeding the triose phosphate pool through TPI1 and the gluconeogenic step catalysed by PCK1 and PCK2. The opposite direction is also represented: monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol acyltransferases rebuild triacylglycerol, while phospholipase and lipid-binding proteins supply and traffic the substrates. Hormonal control by leptin and ANGPTL3 ties the route to whole-body energy balance and plasma triglyceride handling.

Glycerol sits at the junction of fat storage and glucose production: released when triglycerides are broken down in adipose tissue, it travels to the liver and kidney to be phosphorylated and fed into glycolysis or gluconeogenesis, or re-esterified back into lipid. Handling it properly is how the body converts stored fat into circulating fuel during fasting, and glycerol kinase deficiency causes hypoglycaemia, acidosis and developmental problems. Glycerol kinase performs the committing phosphorylation, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase links the product to the mitochondrial shuttle that reoxidises cytosolic NADH, and triose phosphate isomerase channels the carbons into central metabolism. Acyltransferases such as the monoacylglycerol and diacylglycerol enzymes run the opposite direction, rebuilding triacylglycerol, while PCK1 and PCK2 commit the carbon skeleton to glucose synthesis. Leptin and ANGPTL3 place the whole process under systemic control of lipolysis and lipoprotein handling.

Glycerol-3-phosphate sits at the junction of glucose metabolism, fat storage and redox balance, and the reactions that make and consume it decide whether a cell burns, stores or exports the carbon. Glycerol kinases phosphorylate free glycerol so that glycerol taken up from blood can enter glycolysis or gluconeogenesis, most notably in liver. Cytosolic and mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases work as a shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents from cytosolic NADH into the respiratory chain, regenerating NAD+ for continued glycolysis and contributing to thermogenesis in brown fat. Acyltransferases of this set commit glycerol-3-phosphate to the first acylation step of glycerolipid synthesis, the entry point for triacylglycerol and phospholipid production. Loss of glycerol kinase causes hyperglycerolaemia, and the dehydrogenase step is tied to insulin secretion and, for GPD1L, to cardiac sodium channel function.

Aldehydes are reactive intermediates generated by alcohol oxidation, lipid peroxidation, sugar metabolism and vitamin A turnover, and cells must make, interconvert and above all detoxify them; this metabolic programme does that work. Its failure allows protein and DNA adducts to accumulate, and the human consequences are concrete: the common aldehyde dehydrogenase variant behind alcohol flushing, seizures from impaired lysine-pathway aldehyde clearance, and oxalate stone disease when glyoxylate is mishandled. Broad families dominate: aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidising aldehydes to acids, aldo-keto and short-chain dehydrogenase/reductases reducing them to alcohols, and the glyoxalase system disposing of methylglyoxal from glycolysis. Retinaldehyde handling links the same enzymes to retinoic acid signalling and to the visual cycle, while transketolase, transaldolase and triosephosphate isomerase tie aldehyde flux to pentose phosphate and central carbohydrate metabolism.

Organic acid metabolism covers the interconversion, breakdown and synthesis of carbon-containing acids "amino acids, fatty acids, keto acids, bile acids and the carboxylic acid intermediates of central carbon metabolism" and so underlies almost all cellular energy production and biosynthesis. The genes here span glycolysis and the citric acid cycle, fatty acid activation, mitochondrial and peroxisomal beta-oxidation, branched-chain and aromatic amino acid catabolism, one-carbon and folate metabolism, urea cycle nitrogen disposal, bile acid and eicosanoid formation, and the cytochrome P450, sulfotransferase and glutathione transferase enzymes that modify acidic metabolites for excretion. Regulatory layers are included too: nuclear receptors such as the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors and bile acid receptor, sterol regulatory factors, AMP-activated protein kinase and mTOR components, which tune flux to nutrient supply. Inherited defects in these steps produce the classical organic acidemias, urea cycle disorders and fatty acid oxidation diseases.

acetyl-CoA metabolic process governs the production and consumption of the two-carbon currency that links sugar, fat and amino acid breakdown to energy generation and biosynthesis. Whether a cell burns acetyl units in the TCA cycle, stores them as fatty acids, or diverts them into cholesterol and isoprenoids determines its metabolic state; loss of control here produces lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration on the catabolic side and dyslipidaemia on the anabolic side. The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its regulatory kinases and phosphatase form the central switch, gating glycolytic carbon entry into mitochondria. Citrate export and cleavage by ACLY supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA, which acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit to fatty acid synthesis via FASN or HMGCS1 and HMGCR commit to the mevalonate route. Ketogenesis, acetate activation, thioesterase-mediated release and sirtuin deacylation adjust the pool, which also sets the substrate supply for protein acetylation.

Acetyl-CoA sits at the junction of catabolism and biosynthesis, and the reactions that make and consume it decide whether a cell burns fuel or builds with it. Sugars enter through the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its regulatory kinases and phosphatase, which switch oxidation of pyruvate on and off according to nutrient supply; amino acid breakdown and mitochondrial citrate export via ATP-citrate lyase, plus direct acetate activation, feed the same pool. Downstream, acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit it to malonyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis, HMG-CoA synthase and reductase route it into cholesterol and isoprenoids, and a ketogenic arm supplies fuel during fasting. Because the cytosolic and nuclear pool also supplies acetyl groups for protein acetylation, this metabolism links energy status to gene regulation. Inherited defects in the pyruvate dehydrogenase subunits cause lactic acidosis and neurological disease.

Acetyl-CoA is the hub metabolite where sugar, fat, amino acid and ketone breakdown converge, feeding the TCA cycle for ATP production while also supplying carbon for lipid synthesis and acetyl groups for protein acetylation. Its biosynthesis is dominated here by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, whose catalytic and structural subunits decarboxylate pyruvate imported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier; flux through it is set by opposing kinases and a phosphatase, so cells can switch between glucose and fatty acid oxidation. Alternative routes are represented too: ATP-citrate lyase generates cytosolic acetyl-CoA for lipogenesis and histone acetylation, acetyl-CoA synthetases activate free acetate, and thiolase supplies acetyl units from ketone and fatty acid catabolism. Thiamine pyrophosphate is the required cofactor. Loss of pyruvate dehydrogenase activity causes lactic acidosis and severe neurological disease, reflecting the brain's dependence on glucose oxidation.

The irreversible oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is the committed step that hands the products of glycolysis to the TCA cycle, and it is where cells decide whether sugar carbon is burned or spared. The mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex does the chemistry: a thiamine-dependent decarboxylase core (PDHA1/PDHA2 with PDHB), a dihydrolipoyl transacetylase that transfers the acetyl group to coenzyme A, and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase that reoxidises lipoamide using NAD+, with a binding protein anchoring the subunits and a thiamine pyrophosphokinase supplying the cofactor. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation, PDK1-4 inactivating the complex and PDP1 with its regulatory subunit reactivating it, while a carrier subunit delivers pyruvate across the inner membrane. Loss of activity causes congenital lactic acidosis and neurological disease, and kinase-driven suppression of the complex is a feature of tumour glycolytic metabolism.

Lactate is the endpoint of glycolysis when pyruvate cannot be oxidized fast enough, and its production, consumption and shuttling between cells let tissues keep making ATP under low oxygen or high glycolytic flux. The lactate dehydrogenase family sits at the centre, interconverting pyruvate and lactate with NADH so that cytosolic redox balance is maintained; a distinct D-isomer dehydrogenase and related enzymes handle the D-lactate and methylglyoxal-derived pool, including the glyoxalase step that detoxifies a reactive glycolytic by-product. Control comes largely from hypoxia sensing: HIF1A and a hypoxia-induced microRNA push flux toward lactate, while phosphofructokinase-2 activity and TIGAR tune glycolytic intermediates, and a circadian component links the pathway to daily metabolic rhythms. This chemistry underlies muscle performance, the Warburg-type metabolism of tumours, and lactic acidosis when the balance fails.

Pyruvate metabolic process covers the production and disposal of pyruvate, the hub metabolite where glycolysis meets mitochondrial oxidation, lactate production and gluconeogenesis. It determines whether a cell burns glucose aerobically or ferments it, and so underlies muscle performance, hepatic glucose output, the Warburg-like shift of proliferating and hypoxic cells, and the lactic acidosis and encephalopathy that follow enzyme deficiency. The genes span the full glycolytic chain from hexokinase and phosphofructokinase through GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase, the lactate dehydrogenases and monocarboxylate transporters that export or import lactate, the mitochondrial carrier and pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its PDK kinases and PDP phosphatases, malic enzymes, and the PCK1/FBP1 gluconeogenic exits. Layered on top is regulation: HIF1A and MYC-like transcriptional control, insulin and IGF1 input, AMPK and mTOR nutrient sensing, and sirtuin and acetylation-dependent tuning of flux.

Pyruvate sits at the junction between glucose breakdown and oxidative metabolism, and the reactions that make, consume and dispose of it determine whether a cell burns sugar aerobically or ferments it to lactate. The glycolytic chain from hexokinases through phosphofructokinases, aldolases, enolases, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase and pyruvate kinase generates the pyruvate pool; lactate dehydrogenases and monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16A1 and SLC16A3 handle its reduction and export; the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its dedicated kinases and phosphatase commit it to acetyl-CoA and the TCA cycle; and PCK1/PCK2 with fructose-bisphosphatase run the gluconeogenic direction. Layered on top are hypoxic, hormonal and nutrient controls through HIF1A, insulin signalling, AMPK and mTOR that set flux according to oxygen and fuel supply. Disturbance underlies lactic acidosis, inherited glycolytic enzyme deficiencies with haemolytic anaemia or myopathy, and the fermentative shift of tumour metabolism.

This is the cell's core energy economy: the reactions that break down sugars, glycogen, fatty acids and ketone bodies into precursor metabolites and then extract usable energy from them. It covers glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, the pentose phosphate shunt, glycogen synthesis and breakdown, pyruvate oxidation, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, with the full complement of respiratory chain and ATP synthase subunits, including mitochondrially encoded ones, plus succinate dehydrogenase, isocitrate and oxoglutarate dehydrogenases, and hexokinases and phosphofructokinases. Hormonal and nutrient-sensing control is embedded alongside the enzymes: insulin signalling through its receptor and IRS adaptors, AMP-activated kinase subunits, mTOR complex components, HIF1A, PPARs and PPARGC1A, and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases and phosphatases that gate carbon entry into mitochondria. Tissue fuel choice, thermogenesis and redox balance depend on it; defects cause glycogen storage diseases, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and metabolic syndrome.

The pentose phosphate shunt diverts glucose-6-phosphate away from glycolysis to make NADPH and five-carbon sugars, and cells depend on it for two things glycolysis cannot supply: reducing power for antioxidant defence and lipid synthesis, and ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotides and nucleic acids. Its oxidative branch runs through glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, whose NADPH keeps glutathione reduced; deficiency of the first enzyme is the commonest human enzymopathy and causes haemolysis under oxidative stress. A reversible non-oxidative branch, using transketolase, transaldolase and the ribose/ribulose isomerase and epimerase steps, interconverts pentoses with fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate so flux can be matched to demand. Regulation ties the route to growth and stress signalling: p53 and its target TIGAR steer carbon into it, while mTOR complex components link it to anabolic states, which is why proliferating and tumour cells rely on it heavily.

The tricarboxylic acid cycle is the central oxidative hub of mitochondrial metabolism, taking the acetyl group delivered by acetyl-CoA and oxidizing it to two molecules of CO2 while loading electrons onto NADH and FADH2 for the respiratory chain. It is how carbohydrate, fat and amino acid carbon is converted into usable energy, and its intermediates double as precursors for amino acids, heme, lipids and nucleotides, so flux through the cycle is continually topped up and drained by anaplerotic and biosynthetic reactions. Citrate synthase condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate, and successive steps through isocitrate dehydrogenases, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, succinyl-CoA ligase, succinate dehydrogenase, fumarase and malate dehydrogenase regenerate oxaloacetate; the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex feeds it from glycolysis. Loss of succinate dehydrogenase or fumarase subunits causes paraganglioma and renal cancer through oncometabolite accumulation, and defects in the dehydrogenase complexes produce severe lactic acidosis and encephalopathy.

Isocitrate sits at a branch point of central carbon metabolism, and the reactions that consume and regenerate it determine both how much energy a cell extracts from citrate and how much reducing power it has for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Isocitrate metabolism here is carried by the isocitrate dehydrogenases, which oxidatively decarboxylate isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate. The heterotrimeric NAD-dependent enzyme built from IDH3A, IDH3B and IDH3G performs this step inside the TCA cycle proper, feeding electrons to the respiratory chain. The NADP-dependent forms, cytosolic IDH1 and mitochondrial IDH2, instead supply NADPH for lipid synthesis and glutathione and thioredoxin regeneration, and can run in reverse for reductive carboxylation when respiration is limited. Mutant IDH1 and IDH2 in gliomas and acute myeloid leukaemia acquire a neomorphic activity that produces 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and blocks differentiation.

2-oxoglutarate sits at the junction of energy metabolism and nitrogen handling, and the reactions that make and consume it determine how carbon skeletons and amino groups are exchanged. It is generated by isocitrate dehydrogenases and by transaminases that strip amino groups from aspartate and alanine onto oxaloacetate and pyruvate, and it is consumed by the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, whose E1, E2 and shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase subunits feed succinyl-CoA into the TCA cycle. It also serves as co-substrate for dioxygenases such as the phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase of peroxisomal fatty acid breakdown, and the D- and L-2-hydroxyglutarate dehydrogenases return stray hydroxyacids to the pool. Loss of those dehydrogenases causes 2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria with neurological damage, while mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase in glioma and leukaemia diverts the metabolite into an oncometabolite that blocks demethylation and differentiation.

Succinyl-CoA sits at the junction of the citric acid cycle, amino acid and odd-chain fatty acid catabolism, and heme synthesis, and the reactions that make and consume it are what this metabolic process covers. It is generated in the mitochondrion by the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, whose E1, E2 and dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase subunits are all represented, and by the propionate route in which propionyl-CoA carboxylase, methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase and the B12-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase feed carbon in from valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine. Succinyl-CoA ligases then couple its conversion to succinate with substrate-level ATP or GTP synthesis, while acyl-CoA thioesterases and Nudix hydrolases release free acid and CoA to balance the pool. Loss of individual steps causes methylmalonic acidemia, propionic acidemia and mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes with lactic acidosis.

Succinate sits at a junction between energy metabolism and neurotransmitter turnover, and the reactions that make and consume it are described here. In the citric acid cycle succinate is oxidised to fumarate by succinate dehydrogenase, whose flavoprotein and iron-sulfur subunits SDHA and SDHB also serve as complex II of the respiratory chain, coupling this oxidation directly to the electron transport chain. Loss of these subunits causes succinate to accumulate, which inhibits dioxygenases and stabilises hypoxia-inducible factor, the basis of paraganglioma, pheochromocytoma and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy. A second route enters from GABA: glutamate decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2 generate the inhibitory neurotransmitter, and succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH5A1) completes the GABA shunt into succinate, so that defects produce succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency with elevated GABA and neurological impairment.

Oxaloacetate metabolic process governs the turnover of a four-carbon hub metabolite that sits at the junction of the TCA cycle, gluconeogenesis, amino acid interconversion and lipid synthesis. Because oxaloacetate condenses with acetyl-CoA to keep the citric acid cycle turning, its supply sets the anaplerotic capacity of mitochondria; its withdrawal by PCK1 and PCK2 into phosphoenolpyruvate commits carbon to glucose production during fasting, a step whose dysregulation contributes to hyperglycaemia in diabetes. Cytosolic and mitochondrial malate dehydrogenases and the aspartate aminotransferases GOT1 and GOT2 shuttle oxaloacetate-derived carbon and reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane through the malate-aspartate shuttle, linking glycolytic NADH to respiration. ATP-citrate lyase releases oxaloacetate while generating cytosolic acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, and FAHD-family decarboxylases dispose of it, tuning mitochondrial oxidative flux.

Oxaloacetate sits at the junction of the citric acid cycle, gluconeogenesis and amino acid metabolism, and the enzymes that make and consume it decide whether carbon is burned for energy, exported as glucose, or shuttled between cytosol and mitochondrion. The reactions represented here include reversible transamination with aspartate by cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases, interconversion with malate by malate dehydrogenase, and decarboxylation to phosphoenolpyruvate by the cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of PEPCK, the committed step of gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney. The malate-aspartate shuttle built from these same activities moves reducing equivalents into mitochondria and supports redox balance. Oxaloacetate decarboxylase activity of the FAHD family and ATP-citrate lyase, which cleaves citrate to acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate for lipogenesis, further tune the pool. Loss of PEPCK function causes hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis during fasting.

Malate sits at the junction of mitochondrial and cytosolic carbon handling, and the reactions that make and consume it — malate metabolism — set the pace of the citric acid cycle while also moving reducing equivalents and carbon between compartments. Fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate; the malate dehydrogenases MDH2 and MDH1 interconvert malate and oxaloacetate in mitochondria and cytosol, the paired reactions that constitute the malate–aspartate shuttle carrying NADH equivalents into mitochondria. Malic enzymes ME1, ME2 and ME3 decarboxylate malate to pyruvate, generating NADPH for fatty acid synthesis and supporting glutamine-fuelled anaplerosis in proliferating cells. Succinyl-CoA ligase subunits tie the route to the cycle's substrate-level phosphorylation step. Because these steps govern both respiration and biosynthetic reducing power, loss of fumarase causes metabolite accumulation with oncogenic consequences, and defects in the ligase produce mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with mtDNA depletion.

regulation of carbohydrate metabolic process covers the control layer that decides how fast cells make, store, and burn sugars, matching fuel use to nutritional state. It is the biology of blood glucose homeostasis: insulin, glucagon, leptin and adiponectin signalling through their receptors into IRS1/IRS2, AKT, GSK3 and mTOR complexes, with AMPK subunits and sirtuins reading energy and NAD status. Downstream, glycogen handling is tuned by the PPP1R3 family of glycogen-targeting phosphatase subunits, phosphorylase kinase subunits, and by glucokinase and fructose-bisphosphatase at the glycolytic/gluconeogenic switch, while pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases gate entry into oxidation. Transcriptional and epigenetic regulators including FOXO1, HIF1A, PPARGC1A, MLXIPL, TCF7L2 and TP53 set longer-term capacity, and microRNAs fine-tune it. Failure of this control produces insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and glycogen storage disease.

Cells and whole organisms must match glucose use and storage to fuel availability, and this collection captures the control layer over carbohydrate metabolism rather than its enzymatic steps. It sets whether glucose is burned, stored as glycogen, or made anew, and its failure underlies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and glycogen storage disease. Hormonal inputs dominate: insulin and glucagon acting through their receptors, IRS adaptors, AKT and GSK3, opposed by glucocorticoid, leptin and adiponectin signalling. Energy-sensing arms run through AMPK subunits, mTOR with RPTOR and MLST8, and sirtuins. Glycogen phosphatase targeting subunits of the PPP1R3 family direct PP1 onto glycogen enzymes, while pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases gate entry of pyruvate into oxidation. Transcriptional regulators including FOXO1, HIF1A, PPARGC1A, MLXIPL and TCF7L2, plus several microRNAs, provide slower adjustment of glycolytic and gluconeogenic gene expression.

Cells must match the rate at which they burn glucose to their oxygen supply, growth signals and nutrient state, and this is the control layer that sets glycolytic flux rather than carrying it out. Hormonal input through insulin and its receptor, IGF1 and the mTOR complex components raptor and mLST8 raises glucose use during growth, while the AMP-activated kinase subunits sense low energy charge and reset it. Oxygen sensing enters through HIF1A with its partner ARNT and the coactivator EP300, driving the shift to fermentative metabolism in hypoxia and in tumours; SIRT6 and corepressors such as NCOR1 restrain it. Dedicated metabolic nodes appear too: glucokinase as the hepatic and beta-cell glucose sensor, FBP1 running the opposing gluconeogenic step, PFKFB1 controlling fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, and TIGAR lowering it downstream of p53.

Fasting requires the liver to make glucose from pyruvate, lactate, glycerol and amino acids, and this pathway covers the hormonal and transcriptional control that sets how fast it runs. Getting the set point wrong is a direct route to disease: too much output gives the fasting hyperglycaemia of type 2 diabetes, too little gives hypoglycaemia. Insulin and glucagon are the opposing inputs, with leptin and adiponectin reporting nutritional state; downstream, FOXO1 and the coactivator PPARGC1A drive the gluconeogenic gene programme, glucocorticoid receptor signalling amplifies it, and the AMPK regulatory subunits, SIK1 and the sirtuins restrain or retune it. Acetyltransferases such as EP300 and KAT2B, O-GlcNAcylation by OGT, and the circadian factor CRY1 add post-translational and daily timing control, while FBP1 and GCK mark the committed enzymatic steps of glucose production versus disposal.

energy reserve metabolic process covers how cells build up and draw down stored fuel — chiefly glycogen and fat — so that blood glucose and ATP supply are maintained between meals and during exercise. It defines the metabolic behaviour of liver, muscle and adipose tissue, and its failure produces glycogen storage diseases, Lafora disease, and the impaired glucose handling of insulin resistance and diabetes. Glycogen synthesis and breakdown are carried out by glycogenin, glycogen synthase, branching and debranching enzymes and the phosphorylase kinase complex, all switched by protein phosphatase 1 targeting subunits and glycogen synthase kinase 3. Insulin, glucagon and leptin signalling through insulin receptor substrates, AKT and mTOR set the direction, while autophagy components including WIPI proteins and glycophagy receptor STBD1 deliver stored glycogen and lipid to lysosomes. Fatty acid oxidation and circadian regulators tie the process to whole-body energy balance.

Between meals or during exercise, cells draw on stored fuel rather than circulating nutrients, and energy reserve metabolism covers the making and breaking of those stores. It centres on glycogen: synthases and branching enzymes build the polymer from UDP-glucose on a glycogenin core, while phosphorylases and their phosphorylase kinase subunits, debranching enzyme and lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase release glucose again. Protein phosphatase 1 catalytic and glycogen-targeting subunits, together with glycogen synthase kinase 3, set the balance, and insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT tips it toward storage while glucagon and adrenergic signals tip it toward mobilisation. Autophagy components provide a parallel route for degrading glycogen and lipid stores in the lysosome. Leptin, POMC and clock proteins link the process to whole-body energy balance. Defects cause glycogen storage diseases, Lafora body epilepsy, hypoglycaemia and exercise intolerance.

Fermentation lets cells regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running when oxygen or respiration is unavailable, producing ATP solely by substrate-level phosphorylation rather than through the electron transport chain. The payoff is speed and independence from mitochondria: fast-twitch skeletal muscle sustains bursts of contraction this way, and proliferating or hypoxic cells, including tumours, rely on it to maintain glycolytic flux. Lactate dehydrogenase A performs the committing step, reducing pyruvate to lactate and returning oxidized NAD+ to the pathway; a hypoxia-induced microRNA and a p53-responsive regulator of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels shape how much carbon is routed this way versus into oxidative metabolism or the pentose phosphate pathway. Genetic variation in a fast-fibre structural protein links the same shift toward glycolytic energy supply to muscle performance and fibre-type composition, while excess lactate output acidifies tissue and blood.

Oxidative phosphorylation is the process that supplies most of the ATP used by human cells, coupling the oxidation of NADH and succinate to the synthesis of ATP at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Tissues with high energy demand — heart, brain, skeletal muscle — depend on it, and inherited defects in its subunits or assembly factors produce mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome and optic neuropathies. Electrons pass through complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, pumping protons whose return through the F1Fo ATP synthase drives phosphorylation of ADP; both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded subunits are required, so the two genomes must be coordinated. Also represented are cofactor and assembly steps, iron-sulfur cluster supply through ISCU and frataxin, and regulators such as SIRT3, PINK1 and the inhibitory factor ATP5IF1 that tune output, quality control and mitochondrial apoptotic signalling.

Aerobic ATP production is completed here: electrons stripped from nutrients pass down the mitochondrial respiratory chain to oxygen, pumping protons across the inner membrane, and the resulting gradient drives ATP synthase. Nearly every energy-demanding process in the cell depends on this output, and its failure produces the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, with tissues of high oxidative demand such as brain, heart and muscle affected first. The gene complement spans all five complexes, including the many NDUFA/NDUFB/NDUFS subunits of complex I, the succinate dehydrogenase tetramer linking the pathway to the TCA cycle, cytochrome bc1 and cytochrome c oxidase subunits, mobile cytochrome c, and the F1FO ATP synthase with its inhibitory factor. Both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded subunits appear, so assembly requires coordination between the two genomes, aided by dedicated assembly factors, metal and iron-sulfur cofactor delivery, and regulators including SIRT3 and PINK1 that tie respiration to quality control.

The first step of the respiratory chain, in which electrons stripped from NADH by complex I are passed through flavin and a chain of iron-sulfur clusters to ubiquinone, with protons pumped across the inner mitochondrial membrane to build the gradient that drives ATP synthesis. This reaction also regenerates NAD+ for the TCA cycle and glycolysis, so its failure stalls oxidative metabolism and forces cells toward lactate. The genes encode the complex's core subunits from both genomes: mitochondrially encoded membrane arm subunits, the nuclear NDUFA, NDUFB, NDUFS and NDUFV families that form the matrix and accessory arms, and assembly and cofactor factors including an iron-sulfur scaffold and an enzyme of ubiquinone synthesis. Inherited complex I deficiency causes Leigh syndrome and other encephalomyopathies, and the presence of PINK1, PARK7 and SNCA reflects the link between complex I impairment, oxidative stress and Parkinson disease.

Succinate dehydrogenase is the one enzyme shared by the citric acid cycle and the respiratory chain, and this step is what it does electrically: electrons stripped from succinate as it is oxidized to fumarate are passed to ubiquinone in the inner mitochondrial membrane, feeding the pool that supplies complexes III and IV. Unlike the other respiratory complexes it pumps no protons, so its contribution to ATP synthesis is indirect, through the quinone pool and through keeping the cycle turning. A flavoprotein subunit carries the FAD that accepts the electrons, an iron-sulfur subunit relays them, and two membrane subunits anchor the heme and quinone site, with a dedicated assembly factor required for flavinylation. Loss-of-function mutations cause succinate accumulation that stabilizes HIF signalling, underlying paraganglioma, pheochromocytoma and severe mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

Oxidative phosphorylation depends on a middle step in which electrons pass from ubiquinol to cytochrome c, the reaction carried out by respiratory complex III. It matters because this transfer pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, sustaining the electrochemical gradient that ATP synthase uses, and because it links the dehydrogenases feeding the quinone pool to the terminal oxidase. The complex is built from a mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b together with nuclear-encoded cytochrome c1, a Rieske iron-sulfur protein, core proteins and several small supernumerary subunits, with dedicated assembly factors required to mature the holoenzyme. Electron bifurcation at the quinol oxidation site makes this site a principal source of superoxide, and the soluble carrier cytochrome c released from the membrane also triggers apoptosis. Loss of subunits or assembly factors causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy.

The final step of the respiratory chain passes electrons from reduced cytochrome c to molecular oxygen, reducing it to water and pumping protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane. This reaction sets the terminus of oxidative phosphorylation: the proton-motive force it helps build drives ATP synthesis, and without it cells depend on glycolysis, with lactic acidosis, encephalomyopathy and Leigh syndrome among the consequences of cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. Complex IV is a hybrid assembly, with the mitochondrially encoded catalytic core carrying the heme and copper centres surrounded by nuclear-encoded subunits that modulate activity and stabilise the complex; some exist as tissue- or hypoxia-specific isoforms that tune respiration to local oxygen supply. Cytochrome c itself shuttles electrons from complex III, and its release into the cytosol links this machinery to apoptotic signalling.

Cells hold nucleotide pools—ATP, GTP, cyclic nucleotides and NAD-linked intermediates—within narrow limits, and this control layer sets how fast those molecules are made, consumed and interconverted. It matters because ATP supply is the cell's energy currency and cyclic nucleotides are second messengers: losing the balance leaves cells unable to match biosynthesis to fuel availability, a failure that shows up in insulin resistance, tumour metabolism and neurodegeneration. Much of the regulation runs through energy sensing and growth signalling, with AMPK subunits reading adenylate charge and mTOR complex components, HIF1A, TP53 and TIGAR steering glycolytic and pentose-phosphate flux toward or away from nucleotide precursors. Hormonal inputs from insulin and IGF1, cyclase and PKA activity governing cAMP, mitochondrial quality control via PINK1 and parkin, and NAD-consuming enzymes such as PARP1 and SIRT6 all feed into the same pool management.

Purine nucleobase metabolism supplies and recycles the adenine and guanine rings used for DNA, RNA, ATP and GTP, and balances their synthesis against degradation to uric acid. Cells build purines de novo from ribose-5-phosphate through a multistep route requiring PRPS1, PPAT, GART and PAICS, but most day-to-day demand is met by salvage, where HPRT1 and APRT reattach free bases to phosphoribosyl groups and ADK phosphorylates adenosine. The catabolic arm, through ADA, guanine deaminase and xanthine dehydrogenase, disposes of excess bases. The medical consequences of failure are unusually well defined: loss of HPRT1 causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and neurological disease, ADA deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency by poisoning lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine, and overproduction of urate underlies gout. Proliferating cells depend heavily on this supply, which is why several enzymes here are antimetabolite drug targets.

Purine nucleoside catabolism disposes of adenosine, inosine, guanosine and their deoxy forms, converting them through deamination and phosphorolysis toward hypoxanthine and xanthine and ultimately to uric acid for excretion. It sets the balance between salvage and degradation of purines, and its failure is unusually consequential for immunity: loss of adenosine deaminase allows deoxyadenosine nucleotides to accumulate and kill developing lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency, while purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency produces a related T-cell defect. Downstream, xanthine dehydrogenase generates urate and is the enzyme targeted in gout therapy. Guanine deaminase and related deaminases feed guanosine-derived bases into the same funnel, and a nucleotide hydrolase sanitises oxidised purine nucleotides so that damaged bases are degraded rather than incorporated into nucleic acids. The pathway also governs extracellular adenosine levels, linking purine turnover to immunosuppressive signalling.

Rather than building purine rings from scratch, cells recover them from the breakdown products of nucleic acids and nucleotides, and purine ribonucleoside salvage is the set of reactions that converts those bases and nucleosides back into usable nucleotides. It is far cheaper in ATP than de novo synthesis and is the dominant route in tissues such as brain and erythrocytes that cannot synthesise purines well. Phosphoribosyltransferases attach a ribose phosphate to hypoxanthine, guanine or adenine, adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine directly, and a phosphorylase interconverts nucleosides and free bases; a methylthioadenosine-specific step ties salvage to polyamine synthesis and methionine recycling. Loss of the hypoxanthine-guanine enzyme causes uric acid overproduction with gout and the severe neurological phenotype of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, while the phosphorylase deficiency produces T cell immunodeficiency, showing how strongly some cell types depend on recycled purines.

AMP is the entry point to the adenine nucleotide pool, and its biosynthesis supplies the precursors from which ADP and ATP, plus the adenine moiety of nucleic acids and cofactors, are made. Two routes converge here. The de novo arm builds the purine ring on ribose-5-phosphate through a series of steps beginning with the amidophosphoribosyltransferase reaction and running through glycinamide ribonucleotide and AICAR intermediates to IMP, which adenylosuccinate synthetase and adenylosuccinate lyase then convert to AMP. The salvage arm recovers preformed bases and nucleosides instead: APRT reattaches adenine to a ribose phosphate, HPRT1 handles hypoxanthine and guanine, and adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine directly. Salvage is cheaper and dominates in tissues such as brain and erythrocytes, which is why HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Nucleotide supply of this kind paces proliferation, and the de novo enzymes are long-standing antifolate and immunosuppressant targets.

cAMP biosynthetic process is the generation of cyclic AMP, the second messenger that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at the cell surface into intracellular action through protein kinase A and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels. It sets the tone for glycogen and lipid mobilisation, cardiac contractility and heart rate, hormone secretion, olfactory and taste transduction, and the synaptic plasticity underlying memory. The core of the pathway is the family of adenylyl cyclases, which convert ATP to cAMP downstream of stimulatory and inhibitory G proteins; individual isoforms are tuned differently, some by calcium and calmodulin, and the soluble form ADCY10 responds instead to bicarbonate and is required for sperm capacitation and motility. Upstream input comes from receptors such as those for PACAP and neurotensin, together with neuropeptide ligands, which couple external cues to cAMP output. Dysregulated cyclase activity contributes to endocrine tumours, heart failure and movement disorders.

Formation of cyclic AMP from ATP is the step that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at the cell surface into an intracellular second messenger, setting the tone for protein kinase A activity, ion channel gating, gene transcription and metabolic switching such as glycogenolysis and lipolysis. The pathway is carried chiefly by a family of membrane adenylyl cyclases with distinct regulation -- some stimulated by calcium and calmodulin, others inhibited by it, all subject to control by Gs and Gi proteins -- plus a soluble, bicarbonate-sensitive cyclase that operates independently of G proteins and is required for sperm motility and capacitation. Upstream input comes from receptors for peptide ligands, including the pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide receptor and the neurotensin receptor. Deficient or excessive cAMP production distorts neuronal plasticity, endocrine output and cardiac contractility.

ADP biosynthesis here is the work of the adenylate kinase family, which interconverts adenine nucleotides so that a cell can buffer its energy charge: transferring a phosphate between ATP and AMP yields two molecules of ADP, and running the reaction in reverse salvages AMP back into usable ATP. This keeps the ATP/ADP/AMP ratio near equilibrium across compartments and feeds ADP to the respiratory chain and to glycolytic kinases, while the AMP produced acts as the signal that activates AMP-sensing metabolic control. The isoforms occupy distinct niches — cytosolic AK1 in muscle and other high-turnover tissues, AK2 in the mitochondrial intermembrane space, AK3 and AK4 in the matrix where they prefer GTP — so nucleotide shuttling is compartment-specific. Loss of AK2 causes reticular dysgenesis, a severe immunodeficiency with deafness, and AK1 deficiency produces haemolytic anaemia.

Guanine nucleotides for RNA synthesis, DNA replication, G-protein signalling and glycosylation all originate as GMP, and this is the route that makes it. Most of the enzymes listed build the purine ring de novo from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate through a multistep assembly line — the amidophosphoribosyltransferase that commits ribose-5-phosphate to purine synthesis, the multifunctional GART and PAICS proteins, and ATIC, which closes the ring to yield IMP. From that branch point, IMP dehydrogenase oxidises IMP to XMP and GMP synthase aminates it, a step whose flux limits proliferation and which is the target of immunosuppressive and antiviral drugs. Salvage through HPRT1 recycles guanine and hypoxanthine and spares the costly de novo route; its loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. AMP deaminases feed adenine nucleotides back toward IMP, balancing the two purine pools according to demand.

Cyclic GMP is the second messenger that relaxes smooth muscle, tunes salt and water handling, and carries the light signal in photoreceptors, and its biosynthetic process is the set of guanylate cyclases that make it from GTP. Two architectures are represented: the soluble nitric oxide-sensitive heterodimer built from alpha and beta subunits, which converts endothelial NO into vasodilation and platelet inhibition, and membrane receptor cyclases whose extracellular domains bind ligands directly. Natriuretic peptides secreted by heart atria and ventricles act through their receptor cyclases to lower blood pressure and promote natriuresis, while a related receptor and its C-type ligand drive endochondral bone growth, and retinal cyclases resynthesize cGMP to reset the phototransduction cascade. Loss of these activities causes hypertension, skeletal dysplasias, secretory diarrhoea and inherited retinal degeneration.

GTP biosynthetic process supplies the cell with guanosine triphosphate, the nucleotide that fuels RNA and DNA synthesis, translation elongation, G protein signalling, tubulin polymerisation and countless GTPase switches. Because proliferating cells demand far more guanine nucleotide than resting ones, this route sets a limit on lymphocyte activation and tumour growth, and its rate-limiting enzyme IMPDH is the target of immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate; mutations in IMPDH1 cause retinitis pigmentosa. IMPDH1 and IMPDH2 oxidise inosine monophosphate to xanthosine monophosphate, committing purine flux toward guanine rather than adenine, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinases of the NME family transfer phosphate from ATP to GDP to complete the triphosphate pool. These kinases act in distinct compartments, including mitochondria, coupling local GTP supply to organelle function, and NME1 additionally acts as a metastasis suppressor.

GTP biosynthesis supplies the guanine nucleotide pool that fuels RNA synthesis, protein translation, G protein and small GTPase signalling, and tubulin polymerisation, so its output sets how fast a cell can grow and divide. Two committed steps dominate here: IMP dehydrogenase oxidises inosine monophosphate to xanthosine monophosphate, the rate-limiting and feedback-controlled entry into guanine nucleotide synthesis and the target of immunosuppressive drugs used to restrain lymphocyte proliferation, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinase family transfers a phosphate from ATP to GDP to regenerate GTP, including within mitochondria and at sites of local nucleotide demand. Proliferating and secretory tissues depend on this flux; loss of the retinal IMP dehydrogenase isoform causes dominant retinitis pigmentosa, and nucleoside diphosphate kinase members double as metastasis suppressors and regulators of membrane dynamics, linking nucleotide supply to cell behaviour.

Inosine monophosphate is the branch point from which both adenine and guanine nucleotides are made, and its formation is what this pathway delivers. Cells build IMP two ways, and genes here cover both: the ten-step de novo route from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate, in which PPAT commits the sugar, multifunctional enzymes such as GART, PAICS and ATIC carry out several consecutive steps, and ADSL and the final cyclohydrolase close the purine ring; and salvage, where HPRT1 reclaims hypoxanthine and guanine from turnover rather than paying the full biosynthetic cost. The AMP deaminases feed AMP back to IMP, linking adenylate charge to purine pools. Demand is highest in proliferating cells, which makes these steps a target of antifolate and antimetabolite drugs, while HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and neurological disease, and muscle AMP deaminase deficiency causes exercise intolerance.

Purine nucleotides for DNA, RNA, ATP and GTP can be salvaged or built from scratch, and de novo IMP biosynthesis is the route that builds them, assembling the purine ring atom by atom on a ribose 5-phosphate backbone to yield inosine monophosphate, the branch point to AMP and GMP. Proliferating cells depend heavily on it, which is why the pathway is a target of antifolate and antimetabolite chemotherapy. An amidophosphoribosyltransferase commits ribose 5-phosphate and glutamine to the pathway and is the main regulated step, feedback-inhibited by the end-product nucleotides; subsequent multifunctional enzymes carry out formyltransfer, ring closure and carboxylation steps that consume glycine, aspartate, bicarbonate and folate-borne one-carbon units. Loss of adenylosuccinate lyase or of the final bifunctional cyclohydrolase step causes inherited neurodevelopmental disease with accumulation of partially assembled intermediates, tying the pathway to nitrogen and folate metabolism as well as nucleotide supply.

Breakdown of AMP is the exit route from the adenine nucleotide pool, converting surplus monophosphate into adenosine, inosine, hypoxanthine and ultimately uric acid, and it sets how much adenosine a tissue releases as a signalling molecule. AMP deaminase deaminates AMP to IMP, cytosolic and ecto-5'-nucleotidases strip the phosphate to give adenosine, adenosine deaminase converts that to inosine, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase carries the purine ring through to urate. The balance matters in two ways: adenosine generated at the cell surface acts on purinergic receptors to dampen inflammation and dilate vessels, while the terminal oxidase step is the source of urate that crystallises in gout and a generator of reactive oxygen species. Defects in adenosine deaminase cause severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic deoxyadenosine accumulation in lymphocytes, and muscle AMP deaminase deficiency impairs exercise energetics.

cAMP catabolic process terminates cyclic AMP signalling by hydrolysing the second messenger to 5'-AMP, and so sets how strongly and how long a cell responds to hormones, neurotransmitters and other stimuli acting through G protein-coupled receptors. Without this degradative arm, protein kinase A activity would remain switched on after the receptor signal has passed, and the spatial compartmentalisation of cAMP into discrete microdomains would collapse. The work is done by cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases with distinct tissue distributions and affinities: PDE4 family members dominate in inflammatory cells and brain, PDE8 isoforms act at very low cAMP concentrations, and PDE10A is enriched in striatal medium spiny neurons. These enzymes are drug targets in asthma and COPD, depression, and psychiatric and movement disorders, making cAMP breakdown a practical control point for tuning inflammation, cardiac contractility and neuronal excitability.

Signals carried by cyclic AMP have to be terminated as well as started, and this pathway is the off switch: cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases hydrolyse cAMP to 5'-AMP, setting how high and how long a cAMP signal rises after a receptor engages adenylate cyclase. The rate of breakdown, more than the rate of synthesis, defines local cAMP gradients and therefore how much protein kinase A activity a cell experiences. The enzymes here are the cAMP-preferring families, differing in affinity, regulation and where they sit in the cell: PDE4 isoforms dominate in inflammatory and airway cells and are the target of anti-inflammatory inhibitors, PDE10A is enriched in striatal neurons and manipulated for psychiatric and movement disorders, and PDE8 forms contribute to steroidogenic and immune cell control. Loss of this catabolism leaves cells persistently stimulated, distorting metabolism, secretion and contractility.

Breakdown of inosine monophosphate is the route by which purine nucleotides are disposed of rather than recycled, and it sets the pace at which cells generate uric acid. Cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases dephosphorylate IMP to inosine, purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves the ribose to release hypoxanthine, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase then oxidises hypoxanthine through xanthine to urate, the terminal excretory product of purine metabolism in humans. The pathway matters because its flux competes with salvage: the same intermediates can be re-phosphorylated for nucleotide supply, so IMP catabolism is a control point for the adenine and guanine nucleotide pools, particularly in muscle and erythrocytes during energy stress. Excess flux underlies hyperuricaemia and gout, while loss of purine nucleoside phosphorylase causes a severe combined immunodeficiency from toxic accumulation of deoxynucleosides in lymphocytes.

Pyrimidine nucleobase metabolism supplies and disposes of the uracil, thymine and cytosine rings that DNA and RNA are built from, balancing de novo synthesis, salvage and catabolism against the demands of cell growth. The de novo arm runs from carbamoyl phosphate through the multifunctional CAD enzyme and the mitochondrial dehydrogenase DHODH to UMP, then to CTP via the CTP synthases, while thymidylate synthase with DHFR and SHMT1 regenerates the one-carbon units needed for dTMP. Degradation proceeds through DPYD, DPYS and downstream steps, and cytidine deaminase and thymidine phosphorylase feed salvage. Growth signalling through mTOR couples this output to proliferation, which is why the pathway is the target of antifolates, fluoropyrimidines and DHODH inhibitors; inherited DPYD deficiency causes severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity, and urea-cycle-linked CPS1 loss connects the same nitrogen chemistry to ammonia handling.

Cells that are growing or dividing need a supply of pyrimidines for RNA, DNA and membrane lipid synthesis, and de novo pyrimidine nucleobase biosynthesis builds the ring from scratch rather than salvaging it. The route begins with carbamoyl phosphate and aspartate condensed by the multifunctional CAD enzyme, proceeds through the mitochondrial inner-membrane dehydrogenase DHODH, whose oxidation of dihydroorotate couples the pathway to the respiratory chain, and is completed by UMPS to give UMP, which CMPK1 phosphorylates onward. Thymidylate supply is linked through thymidylate synthase with folate cofactors regenerated by dihydrofolate reductase and serine hydroxymethyltransferase, which is why antifolates and DHODH inhibitors are used against cancer, autoimmunity and proliferating lymphocytes. mTOR signalling raises flux through the pathway to match nucleotide output to growth. Inherited defects cause developmental and metabolic disease, and the urea-cycle enzyme CPS1 links the chemistry to nitrogen disposal.

pyrimidine nucleobase catabolic process is the route by which uracil and thymine are dismantled rather than salvaged, converting them through dihydro intermediates and ring opening to β-alanine, β-aminoisobutyrate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. It sets the balance between nucleotide reuse and degradation in liver and other tissues, and it is the same route that clears fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics: loss of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity, while inherited deficiency of this enzyme or of dihydropyrimidinase produces neurological and developmental disease from accumulated pyrimidines. The first, rate-limiting reduction is followed by hydrolytic ring cleavage and a methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase step that feeds carbon into central metabolism. Several dihydropyrimidinase-like proteins here retain the fold but not the catalytic function, acting instead as collapsin response mediators that steer axon guidance and cytoskeletal remodelling in neurons.

Breakdown of the pyrimidine nucleobases uracil and thymine disposes of bases released by nucleic acid turnover and returns their carbon and nitrogen to central metabolism as beta-alanine, beta-aminoisobutyrate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. The route runs in three steps: dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase reduces the ring, dihydropyrimidinase hydrolyses it open, and a beta-ureidopropionase step completes the degradation, with a methylmalonate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase linking the thymine branch onward to propionyl-CoA. This chemistry sets how much of a pyrimidine analogue drug survives in the body, and loss of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity causes severe, sometimes fatal fluoropyrimidine toxicity, while inherited defects in the first two enzymes produce neurological and developmental disease. Several family members here, the collapsin response mediator proteins, are catalytically inactive relatives that instead regulate microtubules and axon guidance in neurons.

Cells obtain the cytidine, uridine and thymidine building blocks of RNA and DNA either by synthesising them anew or by recycling nucleosides released from degraded nucleic acids, and pyrimidine nucleoside metabolism covers the salvage, interconversion and breakdown arms of that supply. It sets the size of the dTTP pool that replication and repair draw on, so its enzymes are also the gatekeepers for fluoropyrimidine and nucleoside-analogue drugs. Kinases such as TK1 and TK2 phosphorylate thymidine to commit it to the nucleotide pool, cytosolic and mitochondrial activities dividing the task between proliferating and resting cells, while a nucleotidase reverses that step; phosphorylases including TYMP and UPP1 cleave nucleosides to free bases, and DPYD and UPB1 catabolise uracil and thymine. Loss of these activities causes mitochondrial DNA depletion, pyrimidine degradation disorders, and severe toxicity from 5-fluorouracil.

Cytosine, uracil and thymine nucleotides are needed in balanced supply for DNA replication, RNA synthesis, phospholipid and glycosylation chemistry, and pyrimidine nucleotide metabolism is the network that makes, recycles and degrades them. De novo synthesis runs from glutamine and aspartate through the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the mitochondrial dehydrogenase DHODH, and UMPS to UMP, which kinases such as CMPK1, DTYMK and the NME family phosphorylate onward to di- and triphosphates; CTPS1/2 aminate UTP to CTP, while TYMS supplies dTMP. Salvage through DCK, UCK1/2, UPRT and thymidine phosphorylase reuses preformed bases and nucleosides, and DPYD initiates catabolism. Sanitising enzymes including DUT and DCTPP1 keep dUTP and dCTP from corrupting DNA, which links this metabolism to the uracil and base excision repair activities of UNG, SMUG1 and TDG. Defects cause mitochondrial DNA depletion, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency with fluoropyrimidine toxicity, and underlie antifolate and nucleoside analogue chemotherapy.

Pyrimidine nucleotides supply the CTP, UTP and dTTP that DNA replication, RNA synthesis, phospholipid head-group activation and protein glycosylation all draw on, so this biosynthetic route sets how fast a cell can divide. De novo synthesis begins with the multifunctional CAD enzyme building carbamoyl aspartate, passes through the inner mitochondrial membrane flavoenzyme DHODH that couples orotate oxidation to the respiratory chain, and is completed by UMPS to give UMP; CTP synthetases then aminate UTP, while thymidylate synthase with serine hydroxymethyltransferase supplies dTMP for DNA. Parallel salvage kinases such as UCK1/2, DCK and UPRT recycle preformed bases and nucleosides, and NME and adenylate kinase family members handle the phosphorylation steps to triphosphates. Because proliferating lymphocytes and tumour cells depend heavily on this output, DHODH and thymidylate synthase are established targets of immunosuppressive and antineoplastic drugs, and inherited UMPS deficiency causes orotic aciduria.

UDP is the immediate precursor of UTP and the carrier of sugars destined for glycosylation, glycogen and glycolipid synthesis, so making it sets the pace for how much RNA a cell can transcribe and how much of its glycan output it can support. Formation of uridine 5'-diphosphate begins with de novo pyrimidine synthesis: a multifunctional enzyme performs the first three steps from glutamine and bicarbonate, a mitochondrial dehydrogenase linked to the respiratory chain oxidises dihydroorotate, and a bifunctional transferase-decarboxylase yields UMP. A nucleoside monophosphate kinase then phosphorylates UMP to UDP, the committed step for the diphosphate pool. Proliferating cells depend heavily on this route, which is why the dehydrogenase is a drug target in autoimmune disease and cancer; inherited loss of the UMP-forming enzyme causes hereditary orotic aciduria with megaloblastic anaemia.

UTP is the pyrimidine nucleotide that RNA polymerases use for uridine incorporation and that cells spend on sugar activation, glycogen and glycoprotein synthesis, and phospholipid head-group transfer, so its supply is tied to both transcription and anabolic metabolism. Production runs in two stages here: the multifunctional CAD enzyme carries out the first committed steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis, generating carbamoyl aspartate en route to the uridine nucleotide backbone, while the nucleoside diphosphate kinase family transfers a terminal phosphate from ATP onto UDP to complete UTP. The several NME isoforms differ in localization, including mitochondrial and membrane-associated members, letting nucleotide pools be balanced in separate compartments. Because proliferating cells demand large pyrimidine pools, this route is a target of antimetabolite chemotherapy, and deficiency of pyrimidine synthesis impairs growth and immune cell expansion.

dTTP is one of the four nucleotides DNA polymerases require, and its synthesis sets the pace at which cells can replicate and repair their genomes. Thymidylate synthase commits the pathway by converting dUMP to dTMP using a folate-derived methyl group, after which thymidylate kinase phosphorylates dTMP to dTDP and nucleoside diphosphate kinase activity completes the step to dTTP. Because this route is the only source of thymine nucleotides, blocking it starves replication of dTTP and drives uracil misincorporation and strand breaks — the basis for fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Balanced output also matters for mitochondrial DNA maintenance, and imbalance in the deoxyribonucleotide pools is mutagenic. Related kinases here broaden the picture to pyrimidine nucleotide phosphorylation generally, linking dTTP supply to folate metabolism upstream and to S-phase demand downstream.

Pyrimidine nucleotide catabolism dismantles cytosine-, uracil- and thymine-containing nucleotides, recovering ribose and phosphate and feeding the ring carbons toward beta-alanine and central metabolism. Its practical importance is dosage control: nucleotidases and pyrophosphatases such as NT5C, NT5M, DUT and DCTPP1 sanitise the precursor pools so that dUTP and other miscoding species are not incorporated into DNA, while phosphorylases and deaminases including TYMP, UPP1 and CDA recycle nucleosides. The same chemistry sets the fate of pyrimidine analogue drugs; loss of DPYD, the first step of uracil and thymine ring reduction, causes severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity, and DPYS deficiency disrupts the same route. Coupled to this are uracil and oxidised-base DNA glycosylases -- UNG, SMUG1, TDG, MBD4, OGG1, NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes -- which excise damaged or inappropriate bases, linking nucleotide turnover to base excision repair and genome fidelity.

DNA metabolic process covers everything a cell does to its own genome: replicating it, repairing it, recombining it, packaging it and degrading it when a cell dies. Together these activities keep the genetic material accurate across divisions, and their failure produces the mutation, chromosome breakage and cancer predisposition seen in inherited genome instability syndromes. Replication is represented by origin licensing and helicase components, the polymerases, primase, clamp loaders and ligases; repair by base and nucleotide excision, mismatch correction, interstrand crosslink resolution, homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining, with damage sensing through ATM, ATR, checkpoint kinases and p53-dependent arrest or apoptosis. Also here are chromatin remodellers and histone chaperones that open and restore the template, telomerase and shelterin components that protect chromosome ends, meiotic recombination and synaptonemal machinery, programmed rearrangement in lymphocytes, and nucleotide pool enzymes supplying precursors.

DNA replication is the duplication of the genome that must happen once, and only once, before every cell division, so that each daughter cell inherits a complete and accurate copy. Failure produces under-replicated or rearranged chromosomes, and the human syndromes of replication failure feature growth retardation, bone marrow failure, premature ageing and cancer predisposition. Origins are licensed by the origin recognition complex with CDC6 and CDT1, loading MCM2-7 helicase, which CDC7-DBF4 and cyclin-dependent kinases convert into an active CMG helicase at a fired origin; primase, polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon with PCNA and RFC then synthesise and mature the new strands while chromatin is reassembled behind the fork. Also here are the checkpoint and fork-protection responses -- ATR, CHEK1, RPA, TOPBP1 -- together with translesion polymerases, nucleases and helicases that restart stalled forks, plus the nucleotide supply and mitochondrial replication machinery.

Duplicating the genome once and only once each cell cycle is the task captured here, and it underwrites proliferation, tissue renewal and the faithful inheritance of genetic information; its failure produces replication stress, chromosome rearrangement and the genome instability that drives cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Origins are licensed by the origin recognition complex with CDC6 and CDT1, loaded with MCM2-7 helicase subunits, then fired under CDK and CDC7-DBF4 control, with geminin and licensing inhibitors preventing re-replication. Unwinding by the CMG helicase with GINS and CDC45 feeds primase-polymerase alpha, the processive polymerases delta and epsilon, PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, while RPA coats single strands. Also present are nucleotide supply enzymes, Okazaki maturation and ligation, chromatin assembly and cohesion factors, ATR-CHEK1 fork surveillance, translesion and fork-restart activities, and the separate mitochondrial replication machinery.

Copying the genome before division depends on using each parental strand as a template for DNA-dependent polymerases, and this is the machinery that does it. Origins are licensed by the origin recognition complex with CDC6 and CDT1, the MCM2-7 helicase is loaded and then activated by CDC7-DBF4 and CDK2-cyclin E at a single opportunity per cycle, with geminin preventing relicensing. Primase and polymerase alpha initiate, polymerases delta and epsilon extend behind PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, and FEN1 with LIG1 matures and joins nascent strands; separate polymerase gamma and mitochondrial factors replicate mitochondrial DNA. When forks stall, ATR-TOPBP1 signalling, RPA, fork remodellers such as SMARCAL1 and ZRANB3, and helicases including BLM and WRN protect and restart them. Loss of fidelity or licensing control produces genome instability, developmental disorders and cancer predisposition.

Each mitochondrion carries its own small circular genome encoding respiratory chain subunits and the tRNAs and rRNAs needed to make them, and mitochondrial DNA replication is how that genome is copied and kept at adequate copy number in every tissue. Loss of this capacity produces mtDNA depletion and multiple-deletion syndromes, with hepatocerebral disease, progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myopathy and neuropathy following the tissues that depend most on oxidative phosphorylation. Replication runs on a dedicated apparatus rather than the nuclear one: the polymerase gamma catalytic and accessory subunits synthesize DNA, the TWNK helicase unwinds the template, SSBP1 coats the displaced strand, and the mitochondrial RNA polymerase supplies the primers that initiate synthesis. Flap removal and ligation finish each nascent strand, while RRM2B supplies the deoxyribonucleotide pool that non-dividing cells need to replicate mtDNA outside the cell cycle.

Every process that tracks along DNA "unwinding replication forks, transcribing genes, condensing and segregating chromosomes" generates torsional strain and tangles that must be removed, and DNA topological change is the controlled alteration of helix linking number that resolves them. Type I enzymes such as TOP1 and its mitochondrial counterpart TOP1MT nick one strand to relax supercoils, while type II enzymes TOP2A and TOP2B pass a duplex through a transient double-strand break to decatenate and unknot chromosomes; TOP3A and TOP3B act on single strands and RNA, resolving recombination intermediates. Architectural HMG-box proteins bend and distort DNA to facilitate these transactions, and TDRD3 helps recruit topoisomerase activity to transcribed regions. Failure produces replication stress, transcription-associated R-loops, chromosome missegregation and genome instability; TOP1 and TOP2 are also the targets of widely used anticancer drugs that convert these enzymes into DNA-damaging lesions.

DNA polymerases cannot start a chain from scratch, so every new strand at a replication fork begins with a short primer laid down on single-stranded template. Synthesis of that primer is the committing step of replication initiation and of each Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand, and it sets how often lagging-strand synthesis must be restarted, proofread and ligated. The polymerase alpha-primase complex does the work: the PRIM1 catalytic and PRIM2 regulatory subunits make a short RNA with a free 3'-OH, which POLA1 with its POLA2 partner extends as an RNA-DNA hybrid before handoff to the processive replicases. PRIMPOL provides an alternative, repriming downstream of lesions and stalled forks so replication can continue and be completed later, while the helicase HELB contributes to unwinding and to restraining resection. Defects here cause replication stress, genome instability and developmental disorders.

DNA replication initiation is the step that decides where and when a genome starts copying itself, licensing each origin exactly once per cell cycle so that daughter cells inherit one complete, unduplicated copy. Loss of that control produces re-replication, amplification and the genome instability that drives tumorigenesis. The origin recognition complex marks chromatin, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer, and cyclin E-CDK2 together with CDC45, GINS and MCM10 converts it into an active replisome that unwinds duplex DNA for priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase. Licensing is restricted by geminin and by CRL4-DDB1-CDT2 mediated degradation of CDT1, while TOPBP1 and TICRR couple firing to checkpoint state. The same machinery is redeployed in multiciliated cell differentiation through GMNC and MCIDAS, linking origin control to centriole amplification.

Before a cell divides it must copy its genome exactly once, and replication initiation is the step that decides where and when copying starts. Origin recognition complex subunits mark origins in G1, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase to license them, and rising cyclin E-CDK2 activity together with CDC45, GINS and TOPBP1/TICRR converts licensed origins into unwound, primed forks where the polymerase alpha-primase complex lays down RNA-DNA primers. Licensing is confined to G1 by geminin, which sequesters CDT1, and by CRL4-DTL-mediated degradation of CDT1 after firing, so that no origin fires twice; loss of this restraint causes re-replication, amplification and genome instability of the kind that drives cancer. The same machinery is redeployed developmentally, as MCIDAS and GMNC direct centriole amplification in multiciliated cells.

Once replication origins have fired, the replisome must copy the genome accurately and at speed, and DNA strand elongation during DNA replication is that synthetic phase: nucleotides are added to the 3' end of a growing strand templated by the parental DNA. Everything about genome duplication in S phase depends on it, and errors or stalling here generate the double-strand breaks and mutations that drive genome instability and cancer. The MCM subunits with GINS components unwind the duplex ahead of the fork; polymerase alpha primes synthesis, while polymerase delta and epsilon subunits extend the lagging and leading strands. The sliding clamp PCNA, loaded by replication factor C subunits, tethers polymerases processively. Okazaki fragment maturation requires the nuclease DNA2 to trim displaced flaps and ligase I to seal the remaining nicks into continuous daughter strands.

Cells must copy their genome exactly once per division, and this control layer sets when replication starts, how fast forks move, and whether origins are allowed to fire again. Its failure produces re-replication, amplified regions, stalled and collapsed forks, and the genome instability that underlies tumourigenesis. Licensing runs through origin loading of the MCM helicase by CDC6 and CDT1, restrained by geminin and by ubiquitin ligase complexes built on CUL4-DDB1 and cullin-RBX1 scaffolds; kinases including CDC7-DBF4, CDK2 and CDK1 drive firing, while WEE1, CDKN1A and CDKN1B and the ATR-mediated replication checkpoint oppose or delay it. Chromatin remodelling by INO80 and ISWI-type complexes, histone acetylation modules, cohesion factors such as ESCO1/2 and WAPL, and telomere and single-strand binding proteins couple fork progression to chromatin state, sister chromatid cohesion and chromosome end protection.

Using RNA as a template to make DNA is, in human cells, essentially the job of telomerase, and this collection of genes describes that reaction and its regulation. Chromosome ends shorten with every round of replication, and telomerase — the reverse transcriptase TERT bound to its integral RNA template TERC — copies that template into new telomeric repeats, allowing stem, germline and most cancer cells to divide indefinitely; its loss underlies telomere shortening syndromes such as dyskeratosis congenita, while its reactivation is one of the commonest events in tumours. Accessory H/ACA proteins including DKC1, NOP10, NHP2 and GAR1, together with WRAP53 and chaperone complexes, assemble and traffic the enzyme, and RNA exonucleases and poly(A) machinery set TERC levels. Shelterin components and the CST complex, with ATM, ATR and the MRN nuclease, control access to the 3' overhang and couple telomere length to damage signalling.

DNA repair is the collective machinery that keeps the genome intact against damage from radiation, chemical mutagens, oxidative and alkylating byproducts of metabolism, and errors made during replication. Without it cells accumulate mutations and chromosomal rearrangements, and the human consequences are cancer predisposition, immunodeficiency, developmental syndromes and premature ageing, as seen in the excision-repair, Fanconi anaemia and helicase disorders. The genes span all of its branches: direct reversal by alkyltransferases and dioxygenases, base excision through glycosylases with APEX1, LIG3 and XRCC1, nucleotide excision with XPC and the transcription-coupled TFIIH helicases, mismatch correction by MSH and MLH complexes, translesion synthesis by Y-family polymerases, and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination with BRCA1/2 and RAD51 or by nonhomologous end joining. Overlaid are damage sensing and checkpoint signalling through ATM, ATR and TP53, chromatin remodelling, and ubiquitin and PARP-dependent recruitment that organise repair at the lesion.

Genomes are continuously damaged by radiation, chemical mutagens, endogenous oxidants and alkylating agents, and by errors made during replication; DNA repair is the collective response that restores the original sequence and keeps cells viable and non-mutagenic. Its failure produces cancer predisposition and progeria-like and immunodeficiency syndromes, as seen with mutations in BRCA1/BRCA2, the Fanconi anaemia genes, mismatch repair genes such as MLH1 and MSH2, and the nucleotide excision repair factors XPA and XPC. Distinct routes are represented: direct reversal by alkyltransferases and dioxygenases, base excision initiated by DNA glycosylases and APEX1, nucleotide excision coupled to transcription, mismatch correction, translesion synthesis by Y-family polymerases, and double-strand break repair by homologous recombination or end joining. Sensing and signalling through ATM, ATR and checkpoint kinases coordinate arrest with repair, while chromatin remodellers, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases control access to damaged DNA.

Damage repair is not simply switched on; its rate, choice of pathway and shutdown are actively tuned, and this regulatory layer determines whether a break is mended faithfully, mended badly, or left to kill the cell. Much of it is chromatin work: SWI/SNF and INO80 remodellers, NuA4/TIP60 and SAGA acetyltransferase modules, and methyltransferases and sirtuins open damaged chromatin and mark it for the machinery that follows. Signalling by ATM, ATR and DNA-PK spreads phosphorylated H2AX, while RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitylation, the BRCA1-A complex and deubiquitinases recruit or evict effectors; 53BP1 with shieldin and RIF1 restrains resection to favour end joining, whereas BRCA1-BARD1 and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease license homologous recombination. Loss of this control produces genome instability, hypersensitivity to radiation and crosslinkers, hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition, and altered response to chemotherapy.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky lesion such as a UV photoproduct or a crosslink, transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair removes the block so that transcription of active genes can resume. This is the branch of excision repair that reads the stalled polymerase itself as the damage sensor, giving preferential repair of the transcribed strand and handling some lesions the genome-wide surveillance route never detects. Loss of it causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with photosensitivity, neurodegeneration and premature ageing. Mechanistically, CSB (ERCC6) engages the arrested polymerase, the CSA-containing ubiquitin ligase module with RBX1 and the stabilising factors UVSSA and USP7 controls its ubiquitination and turnover, and the elongation factor ELOF1 and splicing-related XAB2 act at the polymerase interface. Repair then converges on the shared incision machinery, including the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 and the structure-specific nuclease ERCC5.

base-excision repair is the cell's routine maintenance system for small, non-helix-distorting DNA lesions — oxidised, deaminated, alkylated or mismatched bases and the abasic sites and single-strand breaks they generate. It handles the thousands of such damages arising daily from normal metabolism, and its failure raises mutation rates: inherited defects in MUTYH or NTHL1 cause colorectal polyposis and cancer predisposition. A damage-specific glycosylase such as OGG1, UNG, TDG or MPG excises the offending base, APEX1 incises the resulting abasic site, and PNKP or the polymerase's lyase activity cleans the ends.
