POLB fills short patches sealed by LIG3 with XRCC1 as scaffold, while long-patch repair uses PCNA, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1. PARP1 and PARP2 detect the strand break and recruit the machinery, which is why this pathway underlies the synthetic lethality exploited by PARP inhibitors.

Base-excision repair handles the most common kind of everyday DNA damage: single bases that have been oxidised, deaminated, alkylated or mismatched, such as the 8-oxoguanine left by reactive oxygen species or the uracil left by cytosine deamination. Without it, these lesions become point mutations at every round of replication, and inherited defects in the glycosylases MUTYH and NTHL1 predispose to colorectal cancer. A damage-specific glycosylase (OGG1, UNG, TDG, MPG, SMUG1, MBD4, the NEIL enzymes) excises the base; the AP endonuclease APEX1 cuts the abasic sugar-phosphate backbone; polymerase beta fills the single-nucleotide gap, or FEN1 with PCNA and replicative polymerases performs longer-patch synthesis; and LIG3 with its scaffold XRCC1 seals the nick. PARP1 and PARP2 sense the strand break and recruit repair factors, which is why PARP inhibition is exploited therapeutically in tumours already deficient in other repair routes.

base-excision repair, AP site formation is the opening step of the pathway that removes the small chemical lesions DNA sustains constantly from oxidation, deamination, alkylation and spontaneous base loss. It matters because these damaged bases are mutagenic if left in place: loss of OGG1 or MUTYH activity lets oxidised guanine mispair and drive G:C to T:A transversions, and inherited MUTYH or NTHL1 defects cause colorectal cancer and polyposis syndromes. Each of these DNA glycosylases surveys the duplex for a particular class of altered base, flips it out of the helix, and hydrolyses the N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic sugar that the downstream endonuclease incises so the gap can be filled and ligated. Substrate specificities overlap and complement one another, covering uracil from cytosine deamination, thymine glycol and other ring-fragmented purines and pyrimidines, and alkylated bases, including lesions in methylated CpG contexts.

Bases in DNA are constantly damaged by oxidation, deamination and alkylation, and this first step of base-excision repair is how the offending base is found and cut out, leaving an abasic (AP) site for downstream processing. Without it, oxidised and deaminated bases persist through replication and generate point mutations; loss of the adenine glycosylase MUTYH, which removes adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine, causes an inherited colorectal adenomatous polyposis, and germline NTHL1 defects likewise predispose to tumours. Each glycosylase has its own substrate preference: UNG and SMUG1 excise uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation, TDG and MBD4 act on deaminated 5-methylcytosine at CpG sites, MPG removes alkylated purines, and OGG1 with the NEIL enzymes handles oxidative lesions. The resulting AP site is then incised and the gap resynthesised, linking this chemistry to genome stability, mutation avoidance and control of cytosine methylation turnover.

Base excision repair removes the small chemical lesions that arise constantly from oxidation, deamination and alkylation of bases, and the gap-filling step is where the resulting gap in the damaged strand is resynthesised and sealed. After a glycosylase and AP endonuclease activity leave a nicked abasic site, ends are made ligatable — a polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase cleans 3'-phosphate and 5'-hydroxyl termini, and poly(ADP-ribose) turnover by PARG and ADP-ribosylhydrolase activity resolves the scaffolding signal that recruits repair factors. DNA polymerase beta inserts one or a few nucleotides; longer patches use replicative polymerases with PCNA, with FEN1 trimming the displaced flap, and ligase I or ligase III completes the strand. This machinery keeps mutation rates low in nuclear and, through the mitochondrial polymerase, mitochondrial DNA, and its loss drives genomic instability and sensitises cells to alkylating agents and oxidative stress.

nucleotide-excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions "such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts, intrastrand crosslinks and chemical adducts" by excising a short oligonucleotide around the damage and resynthesising the strand with DNA polymerase and ligase. It is the pathway that protects skin and neurons from sunlight and genotoxins; its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy, with extreme skin cancer risk or neurodegeneration. Lesions are found either by XPC-RAD23 and the DDB1-DDB2-CUL4 ubiquitin ligase scanning the genome, or by stalled RNA polymerase II with CSA/CSB and UVSSA during transcription. XPA and RPA verify the damage, TFIIH with its XPB and XPD helicases opens the duplex, and ERCC1-XPF and XPG incise. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling, histone acetylation and p53 make the damage accessible and couple repair to cell cycle arrest.

Bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, 6-4 photoproducts and chemical adducts are removed by nucleotide-excision repair, which excises a short damage-containing oligonucleotide and refills the gap by DNA polymerase and ligase action. This is the pathway that protects skin and other exposed tissues from sunlight-induced mutation; its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum with extreme UV sensitivity and skin cancer, or Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes when the transcription-coupled branch fails. Damage is recognized either globally, through XPC with RAD23 partners and the DDB1/DDB2 complex acting with a CUL4-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, or by RNA polymerase II stalling, sensed via ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. TFIIH subunits including the ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases open the duplex, XPA and RPA stabilize the bubble, and ERCC1-ERCC4 and ERCC5 incise it. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits and p53 make the lesion accessible and couple repair to damage signalling.

Ultraviolet light fuses adjacent pyrimidines into cyclobutane dimers and 6-4 photoproducts that block transcription and replication, and pyrimidine dimer repair is how cells remove or tolerate these lesions. Without it, sunlight-exposed skin accumulates mutations, the outcome seen in xeroderma pigmentosum and in UV-driven carcinoma. Damage is recognised in the genome at large by XPC together with the DDB2 damage-binding subunit, and in transcribed strands by stalled RNA polymerase with ERCC6, feeding lesions into nucleotide excision repair where the ERCC1 endonuclease partner incises the damaged strand and gap-filling synthesis restores the duplex. When a dimer escapes excision and reaches a replication fork, the translesion polymerase POLH copies past thymine dimers accurately, and its loss causes a variant form of xeroderma pigmentosum. Chromatin factors and SIRT1-dependent regulation tune access to the lesion within nucleosomal DNA.

After a bulky, helix-distorting lesion such as a UV photoproduct or chemical adduct has been excised as a short oligonucleotide, nucleotide-excision repair leaves a single-stranded gap that must be resynthesised and sealed before the chromosome can be replicated or transcribed. This gap-filling step restores the original sequence using the intact complementary strand as template, and its failure leaves persistent nicks and gaps that collapse replication forks and drive the photosensitivity and skin cancer predisposition seen when excision repair is defective. Replicative polymerases delta and epsilon, loaded behind a sliding clamp, carry out most of the synthesis, with polymerase beta and the translesion-capable polymerase kappa contributing in particular contexts; a ligase then joins the new patch to the existing strand. The pathway sits at the junction of DNA damage removal, DNA synthesis, and genome stability maintenance.

Mismatch repair corrects the base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that DNA polymerases leave behind, acting after replication to raise the fidelity of the newly synthesised strand by orders of magnitude. Its loss produces microsatellite instability and a hypermutator phenotype, and germline defects in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome with its excess of colorectal and endometrial cancer; tumours lacking the system are also the ones that respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Recognition complexes built from MSH2 with MSH6 or MSH3 detect the lesion, MutL homologues license strand incision, and EXO1, RPA, PCNA, POLD and LIG1 excise and resynthesise the error-containing tract. Related activities extend the theme: MSH4 and MSH5 act in meiotic recombination, MUTYH removes oxidised-base mispairs, and the RNase H2 complex handles ribonucleotides embedded in DNA.

DNA polymerases make mistakes, and mismatch repair is the proofreading system that finds and removes them after replication, restoring the correct base by excising and resynthesizing a stretch of the newly made strand. Its loss leaves cells with microsatellite instability and a mutation rate orders of magnitude too high; inherited defects in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome and predispose to colorectal and endometrial cancer, while tumours that lose the system accumulate neoantigens and respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Mismatch recognition by MSH2-containing heterodimers is coupled through MLH1 partners to strand discrimination, with EXO1 excision, RPA-coated single-stranded intermediates, PCNA-dependent resynthesis by polymerase delta and ligation by LIG1. Related components act in meiotic recombination, where MSH4-MSH5 and MLH3 promote crossover formation, and in other lesion-removal routes such as oxidized-base and nucleotide excision repair.

Replication forks routinely meet base damage that a high-fidelity polymerase cannot copy, and DNA damage tolerance lets the fork finish the genome anyway by bypassing the lesion rather than repairing it. This buys cell survival at some cost in mutation, and it underlies much of the mutational burden of chemotherapy-treated tumours as well as the sunlight sensitivity of xeroderma pigmentosum variant patients, who lack the polymerase that copies UV photoproducts accurately. The switch is run by ubiquitin: RAD18 with UBE2A/UBE2B monoubiquitinates PCNA at stalled forks, recruiting translesion polymerases such as POLH, POLI, POLK and the REV1-REV3L complex, while USP1 reverses the mark to restore normal synthesis. Polyubiquitination through UBE2N and the UBE2V partners instead directs error-free template switching. PRIMPOL repriming downstream of lesions, SPRTN-mediated protein-crosslink proteolysis and VCP extraction complete the routes available.

Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous form of DNA damage, and repairing them restores a continuous helix before a broken chromosome is lost, fused or translocated. The pathway covers both major routes: end joining, in which a DNA-dependent protein kinase, a ligase IV complex with XRCC4 and accessory factors seal ends directly, and homologous recombination, in which nuclease-mediated end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex generates single-stranded DNA, RPA is replaced by RAD51 with help from BRCA2 and PALB2, and a homologous template is copied. Layered on top are damage sensing and signalling by ATM, ATR and the checkpoint kinases, ubiquitin and PARP-dependent marking of chromatin around the break, chromatin remodelling and histone modification that grant access, and shieldin and 53BP1-dependent choice between the two routes. Related machinery processes programmed meiotic breaks made by SPO11. Loss of these functions causes chromosomal instability, immunodeficiency, infertility and hereditary cancer predisposition, and underlies the sensitivity of tumours to radiation and PARP inhibition.

When both strands of DNA are severed, the fastest way to restore continuity is to ligate the ends back together with little or no homology, and nonhomologous end joining is the route that does it. It operates throughout the cell cycle, keeps chromosomes from fragmenting or fusing, and is the mechanism that seals the programmed breaks made during antigen receptor gene rearrangement, so its loss produces radiosensitivity with immunodeficiency. Broken ends are detected and the damage signal amplified through ATM and ubiquitin-dependent chromatin marking, with 53BP1, RIF1 and the shieldin complex blocking resection so that end joining wins out over homologous recombination. The Ku heterodimer of XRCC5 and XRCC6 with DNA-PKcs holds the ends, nucleases and end-processing enzymes such as Artemis and PNKP trim them, template-independent polymerases fill gaps, and XRCC4-LIG4 with PAXX and NHEJ1 completes the seal. Alternative microhomology-driven joining using LIG3 and POLQ is more mutagenic and generates translocations.

DNA modification covers the enzymatic chemistry that changes bases in place rather than replacing them, and the machinery that reads those changes as damage. It matters because the same reactions serve two opposite ends: deliberate mutation, as when activation-induced deaminase and the APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases edit immunoglobulin genes or hypermutate viral genomes, and genome defence, as when a spectrum of DNA glycosylases excises deaminated, oxidised or alkylated bases to start base excision repair. UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 handle uracil and thymine mismatches, OGG1, NTHL1, NEIL1-3 and MUTYH handle oxidative lesions, and PARP enzymes signal the resulting strand breaks and recruit repair factors. Terminal transferase adds untemplated nucleotides during receptor assembly. Loss of control here drives APOBEC mutational signatures in cancer, colorectal tumour predisposition, and autoinflammation when cytosolic DNA is not cleared.

Covalent DNA modification, the enzymatic alteration of bases in place, is used both as a deliberate mutagenic tool and as the entry point to repair. Activation-induced deaminase converts cytosine to uracil in immunoglobulin genes to drive somatic hypermutation and class switching, while the APOBEC3 deaminases edit retroviral and retroelement DNA as an innate restriction mechanism — and, when misdirected, leave characteristic mutation signatures across many cancers. The resulting lesions are recognised by uracil and thymine DNA glycosylases such as UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4, alongside oxidative-damage glycosylases OGG1, NTHL1, MUTYH and the NEIL enzymes, which excise the damaged base and commit the site to base excision repair; loss of MUTYH predisposes to colorectal adenomas. PARP enzymes add ADP-ribose at breaks to recruit repair factors, and TREX1 degrades cytoplasmic DNA. Together these activities set the balance between programmed diversification and genome stability.

Alkylating agents, from endogenous methyl donors to chemotherapeutics such as temozolomide, leave methyl and other alkyl adducts on DNA bases that block replication or mispair and cause mutation; DNA alkylation repair removes them and so protects genome stability and determines how well tumour cells survive alkylating drugs. Three chemically distinct strategies are represented. MGMT transfers a methyl group off O6-methylguanine directly onto its own cysteine, a suicide reaction whose silencing by promoter methylation predicts temozolomide response in glioma. MPG excises alkylated purines to launch base excision repair. The AlkB-family dioxygenases ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 oxidatively demethylate 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine, with ALKBH3 recruited to lesions through the ASCC helicase complex; FTO is a related demethylase acting mainly on RNA. Deubiquitinases including OTUD4, USP7 and USP9X regulate the stability and assembly of these repair factors.

Degradation of DNA into nucleotides is how cells dispose of genomes they no longer need or must not keep, and this DNA catabolic process covers both the regulated destruction of chromatin during cell death and the routine clearance of DNA debris. Its most visible output is the internucleosomal laddering of apoptosis, driven by caspase-3 cleavage of the DFFA inhibitor to release the DFFB nuclease, with mitochondrial ENDOG and lysosomal DNASE2 acting in parallel on engulfed nuclei. Secreted and intracellular deoxyribonucleases including DNASE1, DNASE1L3 and the 3' exonuclease TREX1 clear extracellular and cytosolic DNA, and their loss provokes interferon-driven autoimmunity such as lupus and Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. Structure-specific nucleases like MUS81 instead resolve branched intermediates, linking DNA breakdown to replication fork repair and to the erasure of damaged or foreign nucleic acid.

Apoptotic DNA fragmentation is the terminal dismantling of the genome in a dying cell, the step that produces the nucleosomal ladder used for decades as a hallmark of apoptosis. Chromatin is first cut into large 50 kbp domains and then between nucleosomes into ~200 bp multiples, ensuring that a cell destined for clearance cannot pass on intact genetic material and that its DNA is degraded before it becomes an inflammatory or autoimmune stimulus. Mitochondrial permeabilization by BAX and apoptosome-driven caspase-3 activity release the nuclease DFFB from its inhibitory partner DFFA, while lysosomal and secreted DNases such as DNASE2 and DNASE1L3 finish the job in the dying cell and in phagocytes that engulf it. Loss of these nucleases leaves undigested DNA that triggers interferon-driven autoimmunity, including lupus-like disease.

Recombination reshuffles DNA sequences to create new gene combinations, and the same chemistry that generates genetic diversity also repairs broken chromosomes. Two arms dominate here. In meiosis, SPO11 makes deliberate double-strand breaks at PRDM9-marked hotspots, DMC1 and RAD51 with their mediators invade homologous duplexes, and synaptonemal complex proteins such as SYCP1-3 and SYCE1-3 hold homologues together so crossovers form and chromosomes segregate; loss of these steps causes infertility and aneuploid gametes. In somatic and immune cells, RAG1/RAG2-mediated V(D)J rearrangement and AICDA-driven class switching build antibody and T cell receptor diversity, while MRE11-RAD50-NBN, BRCA1/BRCA2, resolvases and end-joining factors including LIG4 and the Ku proteins restore broken ends. Chromatin remodellers, cohesins, helicases and SMC5/6 license and constrain these exchanges; their failure underlies cancer predisposition, immunodeficiency and chromosome instability syndromes.

Mitotic recombination is homologous recombination as it operates in dividing somatic cells, where its job is to repair double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks using an intact sister chromatid as template. This is the high-fidelity arm of break repair, and its loss underlies chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition, most familiarly through BRCA2 deficiency and the sensitivity to PARP inhibition that follows. Mechanistically, the MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex resects broken ends, mediators load RAD51 and its paralogues onto single-stranded DNA to drive strand invasion, and structure-specific nucleases such as MUS81-EME1 and GEN1 resolve the resulting joint molecules; the SMC5/6 complex with the NSMCE2 SUMO ligase restrains and disentangles recombination intermediates. Mismatch repair proteins police heteroduplex fidelity, while a telomere-associated branch supports recombination-based telomere maintenance in cells lacking telomerase activity.

Somatic cells use homologous recombination during mitotic growth to repair double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks accurately, copying sequence from an intact homologous duplex rather than joining broken ends. This is what keeps dividing tissues from accumulating deletions and translocations, and its loss underlies the genomic instability of BRCA2-mutant cancers and Fanconi-type repair disorders. The MRE11-RAD50 nuclease complex processes broken ends, BRCA2 and RAD52 load RAD51 and its paralogues onto single-stranded DNA to invade the donor template, and structure-selective nucleases such as MUS81-EME1 and GEN1 resolve the resulting joint molecules; the SMC5/6 complex with the SUMO ligase NSMCE2 restrains and disentangles recombination intermediates. Mismatch repair proteins police heteroduplex fidelity, and telomere factors link the same machinery to recombination-based telomere maintenance.

chromatin organization covers the assembly and continual remodeling of the nucleosomal packaging of DNA, the layer of regulation that decides which genes a cell can read and how faithfully its genome is copied and repaired. It defines cell identity and differentiation, and its disruption underlies cancers, imprinting disorders and neurodevelopmental syndromes. The genes span the core and variant histones themselves, histone chaperones such as ASF1 and the CAF-1 subunits that deposit them behind the replication fork, and ATP-dependent remodelers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80 families that slide and evict nucleosomes. Layered on top are the writers, erasers and readers of histone marks — acetyltransferases and HDACs, SET-domain and PRDM methyltransferases, JmjC and LSD demethylases, bromo- and chromodomain readers — together with DNA methylation machinery, Polycomb complexes, cohesin and CTCF-based genome folding, and specialized centromeric and germline-specific packaging.

Chromatin organization covers how DNA is packaged with histones into nucleosomes and how that packaging is built, moved, marked and dismantled so that genes can be read, replicated and repaired at the right time. It sets which parts of the genome are accessible, underlies cell identity and its inheritance through division, and its failure produces developmental syndromes, imprinting disorders and many cancers. Core and linker histones plus variants such as H2A.Z, macroH2A, H3.3 and the centromeric CENP-A are deposited by chaperones like ASF1, HIRA, NPM1 and CAF-1, then repositioned by ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80/SRCAP families. Writers, erasers and readers of acetylation, methylation, phosphorylation and ubiquitylation control Polycomb and heterochromatin silencing, DNA methylation via DNMTs, TETs and UHRF1, cohesin- and CTCF-based genome folding, and the chromatin response to double-strand breaks.

DNA replication-dependent chromatin assembly rebuilds nucleosomes on daughter DNA strands as the replication fork advances, so that a newly copied genome is packaged and epigenetically re-marked rather than left as naked DNA. This coupling protects fork stability, restrains cryptic transcription, and propagates histone modification patterns to both daughter cells; when it falters, cells accumulate replication stress, DNA damage and loss of heritable gene expression states. Histone H3-H4 dimers are escorted by the chaperones ASF1A and ASF1B and the histone-binding protein NASP, then handed to the CAF-1 complex of CHAF1A, CHAF1B and RBBP4, which is recruited to the fork through PCNA and deposits the tetramer before H2A-H2B completes the particle. The same chaperones buffer soluble histone pools, linking histone supply to S-phase progression and to chromatin restoration after DNA repair synthesis.

As a replication fork passes, the DNA it leaves behind must be repackaged into nucleosomes within minutes, and replication-dependent chromatin assembly is the machinery that does it. Without it, newly copied DNA stays naked and vulnerable, forks stall, and the epigenetic state of the parent chromatin is not restored in the daughter cells. Histone H3-H4 dimers are escorted from their point of synthesis by soluble chaperones, handed to ASF1A and ASF1B, and delivered to the CAF-1 complex, whose CHAF1A and CHAF1B subunits are recruited to the fork through PCNA and deposit the H3-H4 tetramer onto nascent DNA before H2A-H2B completes the particle. RBBP4 links this histone handling to chromatin-modifying and remodelling complexes that mature the new nucleosomes. The result couples S-phase histone supply to DNA synthesis and underlies heritable chromatin organisation and genome stability.

Chromatin remodeling covers the enzymatic reorganization of nucleosomes and their chemical marks that makes DNA accessible, or keeps it closed, for transcription, replication, recombination and repair. It defines which genes a cell expresses and so underlies differentiation, genomic imprinting, X inactivation and heterochromatin maintenance; its disruption is among the most common features of developmental syndromes and of cancer. The machinery here spans ATP-dependent remodelers of the SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD and INO80 families, histone chaperones and the core histones and variants they deposit, and the writers, readers and erasers of histone marks—acetyltransferases and HDACs, SET-domain and PRMT methyltransferases, JmjC and LSD demethylases, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases. DNA methylation and demethylation enzymes, Polycomb and HP1-type repressive complexes, CTCF and cohesin loading, and damage-responsive kinases link the same nucleosome surface to genome organization and checkpoint signalling.

Constitutive heterochromatin keeps repetitive DNA, pericentromeric satellites and transposable elements permanently silent, and one route to that state begins with cytosine methylation of the underlying DNA. This matters most where a mobile element would otherwise damage the genome: in the germ line, piRNA-guided factors including PIWIL2, PIWIL4, MOV10L1 and several Tudor-domain proteins direct de novo methylation of transposon promoters via DNMT3A with its catalytically inactive partner DNMT3L, and loss of this arm causes retrotransposon activation and infertility. Methylated CpGs are then read by MBD-family proteins, which recruit histone deacetylases and the H3K9 methyltransferases EHMT2 and SETDB1 together with TRIM28, while DNMT1 and chromatin remodellers such as HELLS and SMARCA5 propagate the mark through replication. The result is compact, transcriptionally inert chromatin that stabilises repeat regions and contributes to imprinting and long-term gene silencing.

Every gene's expression begins with the same committed step: recruiting RNA polymerase to a promoter, melting the DNA, and making the first phosphodiester bonds before the enzyme clears the promoter and elongates. This is where most regulation of gene expression is exerted, so the machinery here sets cell identity, growth rate and stress responses, and its components are recurrent targets of oncogenic mutation and of transcription-directed drugs. All three nuclear polymerases are represented alongside their own initiation factors ation TBP and TAFs with the general factors for class II promoters, SL1/UBTF and RRN3 for ribosomal RNA, and BRF/BDP1 for tRNA genes ation plus the mitochondrial polymerase with TFAM and its methyltransferase-derived factors. Mediator couples sequence-specific activators such as MYC, TP53, CREB1 and nuclear receptors to the preinitiation complex, while chromatin remodellers, histone acetyltransferases, KDM1A and TET enzymes make promoters accessible. TFIIH doubles as a nucleotide excision repair helicase and its CDK7 kinase licenses promoter escape.

DNA-templated transcription termination is the step that ends transcription: polymerase halts, the RNA-DNA hybrid melts, and both transcript and enzyme are released from the template. Getting this right sets where genes stop, prevents polymerase from running into neighbouring genes or replication forks, and keeps the polymerase pool available for reinitiation; failure produces read-through transcripts, R-loop accumulation and transcription-replication collisions that damage the genome. The genes cover all three nuclear polymerases plus the mitochondrial termination factors, together with the effectors that act on them: the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2 and cleavage factor PCF11 for torpedo-style termination of protein-coding genes, the helicase senataxin for resolving RNA-DNA hybrids, TTF1 and TTF2 for ribosomal and stress-induced release, and phosphatases such as SSU72 and PP1 that reverse polymerase tail phosphorylation. Premature termination through ZC3H4 and SCAF proteins also shapes non-coding transcription.

Transcription must stop as reliably as it starts, and DNA-templated transcription termination is the step that halts elongating polymerase, releases the nascent RNA from the RNA-DNA hybrid, and recycles the enzyme for reuse. It sets the 3' boundaries of genes, prevents read-through into neighbouring transcription units, and resolves collisions between transcription and replication; failure leaves persistent R-loops and genome instability, as seen with mutations in the RNA-DNA helicase senataxin. All three nuclear polymerases are represented, together with the mitochondrial termination factors that define rRNA and mRNA ends in the organelle. Mechanistically, CTD phosphatases such as SSU72 and the PP1 holoenzyme with its PNUTS regulatory subunit, cleavage factor PCF11, the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2, and the ATPase TTF2 cooperate to dismantle elongation complexes, linking termination to 3' end processing, chromatin state and polymerase turnover.

Once a polymerase has cleared a promoter, the rate and processivity with which it extends the nascent RNA sets how much of each gene is actually made, and this elongation step is where most regulated control of transcript output is exerted. Paused polymerase near the promoter is held by NELF and DSIF and released when CDK9 within P-TEFb phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and DSIF, a step itself restrained by the 7SK snRNP with HEXIM1 and LARP7 and promoted by BRD4 and the super elongation complex containing AFF and ELL proteins. Mediator couples activators to the machinery, the PAF1 complex and SUPT6H/FACT coordinate chromatin passage and co-transcriptional histone marking such as SETD2 methylation, elongation factors relieve backtracking, and the Integrator complex terminates unproductive transcripts prematurely. Members include all RNA polymerase subunits. Misregulation here drives leukemic fusions, and coupling to capping and splicing links elongation to mRNA maturation.

Ribosomal RNA is made by RNA polymerase I in the nucleolus, and controlling how fast it is made sets the ceiling on ribosome production and therefore on cell growth. Regulation of this polymerase links nutrient and stress signalling to growth capacity: mTOR promotes rRNA synthesis when conditions permit, while stress arms such as the PERK/ATF4 axis and the repressor MAF1 restrain it, and excessive output is a hallmark of proliferating tumour cells. Mechanistically the genes here act at the ribosomal DNA promoter and through chromatin: UBTF is the core DNA-binding transactivator, ATP-dependent remodellers including SMARCA5 and BAZ2A-containing complexes silence or open rDNA repeats, and histone modifiers such as PHF8, CARM1, CREBBP and the deacetylase SIRT7 tune activity. Additional nucleolar factors including nucleolin, MYBBP1A, DDX21 and small subunit processome components couple transcription to nascent rRNA processing.

RNA polymerase III makes the cell's tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA and other short non-coding transcripts, so controlling how often it fires sets the ceiling on translational capacity and growth. Tuning this output couples ribosome and tRNA supply to nutrient status and proliferative demand, and its deregulation is a recurring feature of transformed cells, while loss-of-function in the polymerase and its factors causes hypomyelinating leukodystrophies. Promoter recognition runs through TBP-containing complexes with BRF1 or BRF2 and BDP1, which select type 1/2 versus type 3 promoters, and ZNF143 contributes sequence-specific activation at snRNA-type genes. MAF1 is the conserved repressor, held inactive by mTOR signalling through RPTOR so that growth factor and amino acid availability raise transcription. Chromatin remodellers such as SMARCA5 and CHD8 and subunits POLR3C, POLR3F and POLR3G further modulate accessibility and enzyme composition.

Ribosome production begins with transcription by RNA polymerase I, which copies the tandem rRNA gene repeats in the nucleolus into the 47S precursor that yields the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs. Because this single job consumes most of a growing cell's transcriptional output, it is the step at which growth signals are converted into ribosome supply, and its rate is set by nutrient and stress inputs through mTOR, ATF4 and the repressor MAF1. The multisubunit enzyme (POLR1A/B and shared small subunits) is recruited to rRNA promoters by the TBP-containing SL1 complex, the activator UBTF and the initiation factor RRN3, with TTF1 acting in termination and chromatin remodellers, SIRT7 and PHF8 tuning nucleolar chromatin. Treacle, encoded by TCOF1, links this machinery to craniofacial development, and defects cause Treacher Collins syndrome; excessive activity supports tumour cell proliferation.

Ribosome production begins here: transcription initiation at the RNA polymerase I promoter commits a cell to making new rRNA, and because rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus sets the ceiling on ribosome number, this step effectively sets the cell's capacity for growth and protein synthesis. Its rate is tuned to nutrient and growth-factor signals, is raised in proliferating and transformed cells, and mutations in the polymerase and its initiation factors cause acrofacial dysostoses and other ribosomopathies. Mechanistically, the multisubunit polymerase I enzyme (POLR1A/POLR1B catalytic core plus subunits shared with polymerase II) is recruited to ribosomal DNA promoters by the selectivity factor built on TBP with TAF1A-C, by the HMG-box architectural factor UBTF, and by RRN3, which bridges polymerase to the committed complex. Chromatin context matters: BAZ2A-dependent silencing and SWI/SNF remodelling subunits determine how many rDNA repeats are available, while TTF1 acts at promoter and terminator regions.

Transcription elongation by RNA polymerase I is the productive synthesis phase of ribosomal RNA, in which Pol I moves processively along ribosomal DNA repeats in the nucleolus after clearing the promoter. Because pre-rRNA output sets the ceiling on ribosome production, this step largely determines a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth, and it is throttled down under nutrient stress or DNA damage and driven up in rapidly proliferating and tumour cells. The catalytic core POLR1A/POLR1B, together with the shared subunits POLR1C, POLR1D and several small Pol II-common subunits, forms the enzyme; associated factors such as POLR1F and POLR1G couple it to the initiation machinery. Also present are the repair helicases ERCC2 and ERCC6 with a TFIIH component, reflecting how lesions in rDNA stall elongation and recruit transcription-coupled repair. Mutations in these subunits cause ribosomopathies affecting craniofacial development.

Ribosome production begins with the synthesis of the large ribosomal RNA precursor, and transcription elongation by RNA polymerase I is the processive phase in which that long transcript is actually made after the enzyme has cleared the rDNA promoter. Because rRNA output sets the ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can build, the rate of this step is tied directly to growth capacity, nucleolar size, and the response to nutrient and growth-factor signals; it is also a pressure point exploited by drugs that block nucleolar transcription in rapidly dividing tumours. The polymerase itself is represented here by its catalytic core subunits POLR1A and POLR1B together with the subunits it shares with the other nuclear polymerases, while ERCC6, ERCC2 and GTF2H5 link elongation to the repair of lesions that stall the enzyme on ribosomal DNA. Defects in these components underlie ribosomopathies and craniofacial malformation syndromes.

Ribosome production begins with a single long pre-rRNA transcript, and this pathway defines where that transcript ends. Termination of RNA polymerase I transcription releases the enzyme at defined sites downstream of the rRNA gene, freeing it for reinitiation and preventing read-through into downstream sequences; the efficiency of this step helps set how much ribosomal RNA a cell makes, which in turn scales nucleolar size, protein synthesis capacity and growth rate. Termination requires a terminator protein, TTF1, which binds specific downstream elements and stalls the elongating polymerase so that release and transcript processing can follow. The polymerase itself is represented by its full catalytic and subunit complement, including subunits shared with RNA polymerases II and III. Because ribosome biogenesis is tightly coupled to proliferation, changes in this step are linked to nucleolar stress responses and to the altered rRNA output of cancer cells.

rRNA processing converts the long primary ribosomal RNA transcripts made in the nucleolus into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species that build the ribosome, and so sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity to make protein and grow. Endonucleases and exonucleases trim the precursor at defined sites, snoRNP components such as fibrillarin, dyskerin, NOP56 and NHP2 direct site-specific methylation and pseudouridylation, and DEAD-box helicases, GTPases and large scaffolds of the U3 small subunit processome remodel the pre-ribosome as assembly factors and ribosomal proteins load onto it. The exosome complex degrades excised spacers and discards defective intermediates, while parallel enzymes mature mitochondrial rRNA. Imbalance here triggers nucleolar stress and p53 activation through free ribosomal proteins, and inherited defects in factors such as SBDS or dyskerin cause ribosomopathies with bone marrow failure and cancer predisposition.

Ribosomes cannot be built until the long primary transcript made in the nucleolus is trimmed, chemically modified and folded into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species, and rRNA processing is that conversion. It sets the ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can make, so it tracks growth rate and is a major consumer of nuclear energy; when it stalls, unassembled ribosomal proteins stabilise p53 and trigger the nucleolar stress response, and inherited defects cause ribosomopathies such as Shwachman-Diamond syndrome and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia. The work is done by large small-nucleolar RNP-guided machines: pseudouridine synthases and the fibrillarin methyltransferase modify specific nucleotides, UTP-containing processome subunits and numerous DEAD-box helicases remodel the pre-rRNA, and endo- and exonucleases including the exosome complex and XRN2 make the cleavages and degrade discarded spacers. Related enzymes serve the parallel maturation of mitochondrial rRNA.

Every mRNA begins with the assembly of a functional initiation complex on an RNA polymerase II promoter, and this is the step at which most regulation of gene expression is imposed. TBP and the TAFs of TFIID recognise promoter sequence and chromatin, the general factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH load the twelve-subunit polymerase and open the DNA, and the CDK7-containing kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase tail to license promoter escape. Mediator, with its many MED subunits and the CDK8-type regulatory arm, relays instructions from sequence-specific activators such as p53, MYC, CREB1, NF-κB, SPI1 and nuclear receptors, while SWI/SNF remodellers, WDR5-containing methyltransferase complexes, acetyltransferases, demethylases and TET enzymes set the chromatin state that permits or blocks initiation. The Integrator complex terminates and recycles paused transcripts. Mutations in these components cause developmental syndromes and are widespread in cancer.

transcription elongation by RNA polymerase II covers everything that happens after polymerase II clears a promoter: the release of paused polymerase, its processive movement through the gene body, and the coupling of that movement to chromatin and RNA processing. It sets how fast and how completely genes are expressed, and its control by CDK9 within P-TEFb, restrained by the 7SK snRNP with HEXIM1 and LARP7, is the step at which many growth and developmental programmes are actually decided. NELF and DSIF impose the pause; BRD4 and Mediator recruit the kinase that lifts it; the PAF1 complex, SPT6, TFIIS and the ELL-containing elongation factors keep the enzyme moving and rescue backtracked complexes; SETD2 and the Integrator complex link elongation to histone methylation and premature termination. Loss of these controls underlies leukaemias, VHL-associated renal cancer and CDK12-mutant tumours.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it typically stalls just downstream, and the transition into productive elongation is the step that decides whether a gene is actually expressed. This control point governs inducible and developmental gene programmes, and its subversion by enhancer-associated bromodomain proteins and CDK9 is the basis of transcriptional addiction in cancer. The negative elongation and DSIF factors hold paused polymerase in place; P-TEFb, itself sequestered in an inhibitory complex with 7SK RNA, HEXIM1 and LARP7, phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the pausing factors to release it. The PAF1 complex, SPT6, TFIIS and ELL-containing complexes then sustain processive synthesis, the Integrator complex offers an opposing route of premature termination and snRNA 3' processing, and SETD2-dependent histone methylation couples elongation to chromatin state and co-transcriptional splicing.

termination of RNA polymerase II transcription is the step that tells an elongating polymerase where a gene ends, releasing the finished pre-mRNA and clearing the template so that transcription units do not run into their neighbours. Without it, read-through transcription generates chimeric and antisense RNAs, interferes with downstream promoters, and leaves stalled polymerase and RNA:DNA hybrids that threaten genome stability. Termination is coupled to 3' end processing: cleavage factors such as PCF11 recognise poly(A) signals via the polymerase C-terminal domain, the exonuclease XRN2 degrades the downstream RNA to chase the enzyme off the DNA, and the helicase senataxin resolves R-loops at pause sites. Phosphatase activity, notably SSU72 and PP1 with its regulator PNUTS, reverses CTD and Spt5 phosphorylation to convert elongation into termination, while TTF2 strips polymerase from chromatin. The pathway also shapes gene looping, transcriptional recycling and mitotic silencing.

Ending a transcription cycle is as regulated as starting one: termination of RNA polymerase II transcription releases the polymerase and the finished pre-mRNA from the gene, defining where transcripts stop and preventing read-through into neighbouring genes or regulatory elements. It is coupled to 3' end processing, so the same events that cleave and hand off the nascent RNA also dismantle the elongation complex. Recognition of poly(A) signals and cleavage by PCF11-containing machinery is followed by exonucleolytic chase of the downstream RNA by XRN2, while the helicase SETX resolves RNA:DNA hybrids that would otherwise stall polymerase and provoke DNA damage. The phosphatase SSU72 and PP1 with its regulator PPP1R10 reset phosphorylation marks on the polymerase C-terminal domain, and TTF2 can strip stalled polymerase from chromatin. Failure produces read-through transcription, R-loop accumulation and genome instability.

Every RNA polymerase II transcript acquires a protective 5' cap within moments of initiation, and this capping reaction is what marks an RNA as messenger RNA. The cap shields the transcript from 5' exonucleases, recruits the nuclear cap-binding complex that licenses splicing and export, and is later read by translation initiation machinery, so a transcript that fails to be capped is degraded rather than expressed. A bifunctional triphosphatase-guanylyltransferase removes the gamma phosphate of the first nucleotide and transfers GMP through an inverted 5'-5' linkage; a guanine-N7 methyltransferase acting with its activating subunit then completes the m7G structure. Further cap-adjacent ribose 2'-O-methylation on the first and second transcribed nucleotides refines the cap, contributing to the distinction between self and viral RNA sensed by innate immune receptors, and influences translation efficiency.

Before an intron can be removed, the spliceosome must decide exactly where it begins and ends, and mRNA splice site recognition is that decision. Getting it right sets the reading frame and the protein isoform produced; getting it wrong produces frameshifted or exon-skipped transcripts, and mutations in splice site recognition components underlie retinal, neurodevelopmental and haematological disease. U1 snRNA and its associated protein SNRPC base-pair with the 5' splice site, while the minor spliceosome uses U11 and U4atac/U6atac snRNAs for the rarer AT-AC introns. Branch point and 3' end selection involve SF1, the U2-associated SF3A subunits, PUF60 and SLU7. Layered over this core, SR proteins such as SRSF1 and SRSF6, the CELF family and PTBP2 bind exonic and intronic elements to promote or suppress individual sites, which is how alternative splicing patterns are made tissue-specific and developmentally regulated.</description>}

Adenosine-to-inosine editing rewrites RNA after it is transcribed, deaminating adenosine so that the ribosome and the splicing machinery read the position as guanosine. This recoding diversifies protein products from a single gene, most famously in glutamate receptor subunits where it tunes calcium permeability and channel kinetics, and it also alters splice sites, microRNA targeting and the base-pairing of repeat-derived duplexes. Editing of endogenous double-stranded RNA marks it as self, so loss of the main nuclear deaminase triggers interferon-driven autoinflammation, while brain-enriched family members shape neuronal excitability. The genes here span the catalytic double-stranded RNA adenosine deaminases and their catalytically inactive relatives, which bind RNA and modulate editing rather than performing it, together with a tRNA-specific adenosine deaminase subunit that edits the wobble position to broaden codon reading.

transcription by RNA polymerase III produces the small untranslated RNAs that the rest of gene expression runs on — tRNAs, 5S ribosomal RNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other short transcripts — so its output sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth. Output scales with nutrient and growth-factor status: mTOR signalling through raptor relieves the repressor MAF1, linking ribosome and tRNA supply to anabolic demand, and its deregulation contributes to transformation. Mechanistically the multisubunit polymerase, which shares several subunits with the other nuclear polymerases, is recruited by distinct promoter architectures: TFIIIC and TFIIIB with BRF1 and BDP1 at internal gene-type promoters, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex plus TBP at upstream snRNA-type promoters. Chromatin remodellers, ZNF143 and assorted helicases modulate access, while RO60 surveys the resulting nascent transcripts.

Cells need a constant supply of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and other short untranslated transcripts, and RNA polymerase III transcription is the machinery that makes them. Because these products set the ceiling on translational capacity and spliceosome assembly, output is tuned to growth: nutrient and mTOR signalling, acting through the repressor MAF1, restrains the polymerase when biosynthesis must slow, and its de-repression supports proliferation and transformation. The multisubunit enzyme, which shares several small subunits with the other nuclear polymerases, is recruited by distinct initiation routes — TFIIIC and TFIIIA with TFIIIB components BRF1 and BDP1 at gene-internal promoters, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex and ZNF143 at upstream snRNA-type promoters — all requiring TBP. Chromatin remodellers and RNA helicases assist elongation and template access. Mutations in polymerase subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, and the transcripts are also sensors in innate immune nucleic acid detection.

Every cell needs a constant supply of tRNAs, 5S ribosomal RNA and other small non-coding RNAs, and these come from transcription initiation at RNA polymerase III promoters. The output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis capacity, which is why this step is tightly coupled to growth signalling and is raised in proliferating and transformed cells. Assembly begins with promoter recognition by the multisubunit TFIIIC complex, which recruits TFIIIB — including BDP1 and the TBP-associated factor BRF1 — to position the polymerase over the start site; a SNAPc subunit contributes at the distinct promoters of certain small RNA genes. The polymerase itself is a seventeen-subunit enzyme built from dedicated POLR3 catalytic and specificity subunits together with subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Mutations in POLR3A and POLR3B cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, and the cytosolic enzyme also senses DNA to trigger interferon responses.

RNA polymerase III makes the small, abundant, untranslated RNAs a cell runs on — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and vault RNAs — and this step defines where each of those transcripts ends. Accurate termination sets the 3' end that downstream processing and nuclear export machinery recognise, and it releases the polymerase so it can be recycled onto the next gene, coupling termination to reinitiation and thus to the overall rate of tRNA synthesis. The genes here are the enzyme itself: the POLR3A–POLR3B catalytic core, the subcomplexes that read the terminator and mediate release, shared subunits borrowed from the Pol I and Pol II machineries, and the alternative POLR3G/POLR3GL subunits that vary with proliferative and stem-cell state. Termination is intrinsic to the polymerase, triggered by a run of template T residues. Mutations in these subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies.

Mitochondrial DNA carries the genes for core respiratory chain subunits and the rRNAs and tRNAs needed to translate them, and mitochondrial transcription is how those genes are read. Because the organelle uses its own dedicated machinery, the whole output of oxidative phosphorylation depends on it, and defects produce mitochondrial depletion syndromes, deafness and encephalopathy. A single-subunit polymerase, POLRMT, is recruited to the promoters in the displacement loop by TFAM, which also packages and bends the genome, together with the transcription factors TFB2M and TFB1M; TEFM converts the polymerase to a processive elongating form. Members of the mitochondrial termination factor family set where transcription stops and how rRNA synthesis is balanced against the rest of the transcript, and nuclear inputs such as FOXO3 and AMPK-alpha link the programme to energy demand, coupling mitochondrial gene expression with biogenesis and replication.

Primary transcripts emerge from RNA polymerase as precursors and must be cut, joined, trimmed, capped, tailed and chemically modified before they can act; RNA processing is the collection of steps that converts them into functional mature RNAs. It determines which protein isoforms a cell makes, how much ribosome and tRNA capacity it has, and how transcripts are surveyed and destroyed when defective. The machinery represented here includes the spliceosomal snRNPs and their U-rich snRNAs with SR and hnRNP splicing regulators, cleavage and polyadenylation and Integrator complexes acting on mRNA 3' ends, capping and cap methylation enzymes, snoRNA-guided pseudouridylation and 2'-O-methylation during ribosome biogenesis, tRNA end maturation, splicing and base modification, and small RNA maturation by Drosha and Dicer feeding Argonaute and PIWI proteins. The exosome and nonsense-mediated decay factors provide quality control. Mutations in these components cause retinitis pigmentosa, spinal muscular atrophy, myotonic dystrophy and myeloid malignancies.

Newly made pre-mRNA is not translatable until it has been capped, spliced, cleaved and polyadenylated, and mRNA processing covers the whole of that conversion into a mature, exportable message. It determines which protein isoforms a cell makes, how stable each transcript is, and whether nonsense-bearing messages are destroyed rather than translated. The machinery here includes the major and minor spliceosomes with their snRNAs, Sm and LSm cores and SF3B and U2AF branch-site recognition factors; hnRNP and SR proteins plus tissue-restricted regulators such as NOVA, RBFOX, MBNL and CELF that set alternative exon choice; capping and cap-methylation enzymes; the CPSF/CSTF cleavage and polyadenylation complexes; exon junction and export factors; and editing and methylation activities including ADAR deaminases and the METTL3-METTL14-WTAP m6A writer. Mutations in these components cause retinitis pigmentosa, spinal muscular atrophy, myotonic dystrophy and myelodysplastic syndromes.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are the exception to the rule that eukaryotic messages end in a poly(A) tail; they instead terminate in a conserved stem-loop generated by endonucleolytic cleavage, and this specialized 3'-end processing by stem-loop binding and cleavage is what makes histone supply switch on and off with S phase. The stem-loop binding protein recognizes the six-base-pair stem and four-nucleotide loop and, together with a U7 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein built on distinctive Sm-like subunits LSM10 and LSM11 that base-pairs with a downstream element, positions the CPSF73 endonuclease and its CPSF100 partner for cleavage a few nucleotides past the stem. The same nuclease and scaffold subunits serve canonical cleavage and polyadenylation, so this route is a redirection of general 3'-end machinery. The retained stem-loop then governs histone mRNA export, translation and rapid degradation when replication halts, coupling nucleosome production to DNA synthesis and genome stability.

Every codon read during translation depends on a tRNA that has been transcribed, trimmed, edited, chemically decorated and charged with the correct amino acid, and tRNA metabolism covers that whole life cycle. It matters because accuracy and speed of protein synthesis rest on it: mutations in the enzymes here cause neurodevelopmental disorders, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, peripheral neuropathies and anaemias. Polymerase III with its general factors makes the precursors; endonucleases and the ribonuclease P complex generate mature 5' and 3' ends; splicing endonuclease subunits remove introns before a ligase seals the halves; a nucleotidyltransferase adds CCA. A large share of the members are modification enzymes — methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, dihydrouridine synthases, thiouridylases, queuosine and wybutosine machinery, and the elongator and threonylcarbamoyl complexes — which tune anticodon decoding and tRNA stability. Cytoplasmic and mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, with their accessory and deacylase proofreading factors, complete the cycle by supplying charged tRNA to the ribosome.

Transfer RNAs leave transcription as bare sequences and are only made functional by a dense set of chemical decorations, and this collection of enzymes installs them. The modifications fall into two broad jobs: those in the anticodon loop, especially at the wobble position, set how accurately and how fast a codon is read, while those in the body of the molecule stabilise the fold and protect against degradation. Methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, dihydrouridine synthases, thiolation and taurinomethylation enzymes, queuosine and wybutosine pathways, and the Elongator and KEOPS complexes all contribute, in both cytosol and mitochondria. Loss of individual steps distorts translational fidelity and frameshifting, and in humans causes intellectual disability, microcephaly and mitochondrial encephalomyopathies; wobble thiolation defects also link this chemistry to insulin secretion and type 2 diabetes risk. The pathway sits upstream of essentially all protein synthesis and of stress-responsive translational control.

mRNA catabolic process is the controlled destruction of messenger RNA, the step that sets how long each transcript persists and therefore how much protein it makes. Without it, transcriptomes cannot be remodelled during differentiation, inflammatory messages are not switched off, and faulty transcripts are translated into truncated proteins. Degradation begins with deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 complexes, followed by decapping through DCP2 with LSM-PATL1 partners and 5'-to-3' digestion by XRN1, or 3'-to-5' attack by the exosome and SKI complex. Specificity comes from sequence- and modification-reading factors: AU-rich element proteins such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1, m6A writers and YTHDF readers, endonucleases of the ZC3H12 family, and microRNAs acting through Argonaute and TNRC6 scaffolds. Surveillance branches recognise premature stop codons via UPF1 and SMG proteins, or stalled ribosomes, linking decay to translation quality control, germ cell mRNA storage and immune homeostasis.

Every transcript has a lifespan, and controlled mRNA degradation sets it, determining how much protein a message yields and how fast expression can be switched off. Deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 complexes initiates decay, followed by decapping through DCP2 with its LSM-PATL1 partners and 5'-to-3' digestion by XRN1, or 3'-to-5' attack by the cytoplasmic exosome and SKI complex; DIS3L2 clears uridylated targets. Quality-control arms remove faulty messages: UPF1 with SMG proteins and the endonuclease SMG6 execute nonsense-mediated decay, while PELO-HBS1L rescue stalled ribosomes. Sequence-specific recognition comes from AU-rich element binders such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1, the ZC3H12 endoribonucleases, m6A readers of the YTHDF family, and microRNAs acting through Argonaute-TNRC6 complexes. This machinery shapes inflammatory cytokine output, germ cell and oocyte transcript storage, and stress responses, and its failure underlies immune dysregulation and tumour-associated gene expression changes.

Where an RNA ends up determines whether and where its protein is made, so cells invest heavily in getting transcripts to the right compartment and holding them there. This RNA localization programme spans nuclear export through the pore, cytoplasmic transport along the cytoskeleton, and sequestration into granules. A large nucleoporin set plus the Ran GTPase system and the RAN-binding and exportin proteins build and power the export route, while the TREX complex, the export receptor NXF1 with its NXT1 partner, the cap-binding proteins and the exon junction complex mark spliced, processed mRNA as ready to leave. In the cytoplasm, RNA-binding proteins such as STAU1/2, IGF2BP family members, FMR1, QKI and G3BP2 assemble transport granules moved by kinesin and dynein adaptors, supporting local translation in neuronal dendrites and axons and asymmetric protein production. Surveillance factors including UPF1 and SMG proteins couple localization to quality control, and defects underlie fragile X syndrome and motor neuron disease.

Transcripts made in the nucleus are useless until they reach ribosomes, and RNA export from the nucleus is the licensing step that moves only properly processed RNA across the nuclear envelope. It couples transcription, splicing and 3' end formation to translation: the exon junction complex, the cap-binding complex and the TREX complex mark a finished mRNA, adaptors such as ALYREF and CHTOP load the NXF1-NXT1 carrier, and translocation through the nuclear pore is completed by DDX19 helicase activity at GLE1, which strips the carrier and confers directionality. Nucleoporins and the RAN gradient, with exportins for tRNA, miRNA precursors and snRNA, supply the transport framework, while nonsense-mediated decay factors and m6A readers determine which messages survive the journey. Loss of these steps causes nuclear retention of mRNA, stalled gene expression, and neurodegenerative and developmental disease; several pore proteins are also recurrent leukaemia fusion partners.

mRNA export from nucleus is the step that licenses a transcript to be translated: only fully processed, correctly packaged mRNAs are handed through the nuclear pore to the cytoplasm, so this pathway couples gene expression to quality control. Blocking it silences protein synthesis regardless of how much transcription occurs. Capping, splicing and 3' end formation leave marks that recruit the TREX complex and its adaptor ALYREF, which load the export receptor NXF1-NXT1 onto the messenger ribonucleoprotein; the exon junction complex and cap-binding proteins mark spliced transcripts, while the nuclear pore basket, TPR and NUP214, together with the helicase DDX19 and GLE1, give directionality by stripping receptors on the cytoplasmic face. Retained or aberrant transcripts are instead degraded, and the same first round of translation feeds nonsense-mediated decay through UPF1 and SMG proteins. Methylation readers such as YTHDC1 bias which transcripts leave.

Gene expression only counts once a transcript reaches the ribosome, and mRNA export from the nucleus is the licensing step that moves finished, correctly processed transcripts through the nuclear pore to the cytoplasm. It couples transcription, splicing and 3' end formation to translation: the TREX complex and its ALYREF adaptor load onto spliced mRNA, the exon junction complex (MAGOH, RBM8A, EIF4A3) marks splice sites, and the NXF1-NXT1 receptor carries the ribonucleoprotein to nucleoporins such as NUP214 and TPR, where the DEAD-box helicases DDX19A/B with GLE1 strip adaptors and impose directionality. Cap-binding proteins, methylation readers and modification enzymes bias which transcripts leave and when, while the surveillance factors UPF1 and SMG1-7 destroy those bearing premature stop codons. Defects in pore and helicase components produce motor neuron degeneration and inherited arthrogryposis, and export is a common target of viral shutoff strategies.

translation is protein synthesis itself: the decoding of mature mRNA by the ribosome into a polypeptide, together with the machinery that decides which messages are read, how fast, and when reading stops. Every cell depends on it for growth, and its regulation is where nutrient, stress and growth-factor signals converge — mTOR and the 4E-BP/eIF4E axis set cap-dependent initiation, while eIF2α kinases such as PERK and GCN2 shut initiation down during the integrated stress response. The genes span cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, initiation, elongation and release factors, tRNA and mRNA modification enzymes, and quality-control systems that rescue stalled ribosomes and degrade faulty nascent chains. Overlaid on this are repressive controls: microRNAs with their Argonaute–TNRC6 effectors, deadenylation by the CCR4–NOT complex, and sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins that store or silence transcripts. Defects underlie ribosomopathies, neurodegeneration and oncogenic growth.

Translation is the step where the information in a mature mRNA is read out as protein, and this collection spans the whole of it: cytoplasmic and mitochondrial ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that charge tRNAs, initiation, elongation and release factors, and the tRNA-modifying enzymes that keep decoding accurate. Because protein synthesis consumes much of a cell's energy, it is also a major control point for growth and stress adaptation: mTOR and S6 kinases raise output, eIF4E-binding proteins restrain cap-dependent initiation, and eIF2alpha kinases such as PERK and GCN2 shut initiation down during the integrated stress response while favouring ATF4. Also represented are quality-control and mRNA-fate systems that decide whether a message is translated at all, including nonsense-mediated decay, ribosome-associated ubiquitin ligases, deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex, and microRNA/Argonaute repression. Defects cause ribosomopathies, neuropathies and mitochondrial translation disorders.

Translational initiation is the step at which a ribosome is recruited to an mRNA and positioned on a start codon with the first methionyl-tRNA in place, and it is the main point at which cells decide how much of each protein to make. Because it is rate-limiting, it is the hub through which growth signalling and stress converge on protein output: mTOR and its kinases relieve 4E-BP inhibition of the cap-binding factor eIF4E to license cap-dependent initiation, while stress kinases such as PERK, GCN2, HRI and PKR phosphorylate the eIF2 alpha subunit to shut initiation down and induce ATF4. Multisubunit eIF3, the eIF4F cap complex with its helicases, eIF5 and eIF5B, poly(A)-binding partners, and mitochondrial initiation factors carry the mechanics; m6A readers, FMRP and Argonaute impose message-specific control. Dysregulation drives tumour growth, and defects in eIF2B cause leukoencephalopathy.

Elongation is the phase of protein synthesis in which the ribosome repeatedly decodes mRNA and adds amino acids to a growing polypeptide, and it is where most of a cell's energy and translational fidelity is spent. The canonical machinery here includes the eEF1 complex that delivers aminoacyl-tRNAs, eEF2 and its inhibitory kinase eEF2K, hypusinated eIF5A that helps ribosomes through difficult sequences, and separate mitochondrial factors such as TUFM and TSFM for organellar translation. Specialised branches insert selenocysteine, requiring SEPSECS, SECISBP2 and the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC. Much of the rest concerns what happens when elongation stalls: ribosome collision sensing by ZNF598, splitting and rescue by PELO, HBS1L and ABCE1, and ribosome-associated quality control through NEMF and the ubiquitin ligase LTN1 with VCP-dependent extraction. Failures cause aggregation-prone truncated proteins and neurodegeneration.

Translational termination ends protein synthesis: when a stop codon enters the ribosomal A site, the nascent polypeptide is hydrolysed from tRNA and released, freeing the ribosome for reuse. Accurate stop-codon recognition sets the C-terminus of every protein and guards against readthrough that would append aberrant extensions, while coupling to recycling and to mRNA surveillance determines how quickly ribosomes return to the pool. In the cytosol, the release factor ETF1 reads all three stop codons with the GTPase GSPT1/GSPT2, and the ATPase ABCE1 then splits the post-termination ribosome; UPF1 links premature termination to degradation of nonsense-containing transcripts. Mitochondria use their own factors, MTRF1L and MTRFR among them, for the separately encoded translation of respiratory chain subunits. Modifications of the factors themselves — methylation by HEMK1, hydroxylation by JMJD4 — tune termination efficiency, as does hypusinated EIF5A, which resolves stalling at the peptidyl transferase centre.

Cells decide not only which mRNAs to make but how much protein to draw from each one, and this control of translation sets that output. It lets a cell respond within minutes to amino acid shortage, ER stress, growth factors or viral infection without changing transcription, and it underlies germ cell mRNA storage, synaptic plasticity, and the translational reprogramming that supports tumour growth. Several layers are represented: initiation factor availability, where mTOR-directed phosphorylation of 4E-BP proteins frees eIF4E and eIF2alpha kinases such as PERK and GCN2 shut down initiation during stress; sequence-specific repressors including Pumilio, CPEB, ZFP36 family AU-rich element binders and IGF2BP proteins; microRNAs acting with Argonaute and TNRC6 scaffolds; deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex; m6A readers; tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes; and quality-control steps that rescue stalled or nonsense-containing transcripts.

How often a ribosome is loaded onto an mRNA sets how much protein a cell makes, and the regulation of translational initiation is the main point at which growth signals, nutrient supply and stress are converted into changes in protein output. Two hubs dominate. One is the initiation factor eIF2 and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B: stress-activated kinases such as the heme-regulated, double-stranded-RNA-activated, ER-resident and amino-acid-sensing kinases phosphorylate eIF2α to shut down general initiation while favouring ATF4, with GADD34-directed phosphatase activity reversing it. The other is mTOR acting through S6 kinases, 4E-BP repressors and LARP1 to control cap-dependent scaffolding by eIF4G and eIF4E. Layered on top are poly(A)-binding protein regulators, m6A readers, RNA-binding repressors such as FMR1 and CSDE1, and GIGYF-ZNF598 surveillance of stalled ribosomes. Dysregulation underlies the integrated stress response, tumour growth and inherited neurodevelopmental and white-matter disease.

Once a ribosome has initiated, how fast and how faithfully it moves along an mRNA is itself a regulated variable, and this control over translational elongation sets protein output independently of initiation. It matters for coping with difficult sequences: polyproline stretches and other stalling motifs would otherwise arrest ribosomes, and eIF5A, uniquely modified by hypusination, resolves these pauses to keep synthesis moving. Other members act on the machinery rather than the message — methyltransferases such as METTL18 and SMYD5 modify ribosomal and elongation factor components, RACK1 sits on the 40S subunit as a scaffold linking signalling to the elongating ribosome, and SRP9 imposes elongation arrest while a nascent signal peptide is engaged for targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum. CPEB proteins and tRNA-modifying activities add further layers. Dysregulated elongation control contributes to stress responses, neuronal local translation, and tumour cell growth.

Ribosomes must stop precisely at a stop codon, release the finished polypeptide, and be recycled; regulation of translational termination sets how efficiently that happens and therefore how much readthrough, frameshifting or premature stop tolerance a cell allows. The core release machinery here is the stop-codon-recognizing release factor ETF1 working with the GTPase GSPT1, whose activity is tuned by post-translational modification — hydroxylation by OGFOD1 and JMJD4-dependent hydroxylation of the release factor sharpen termination fidelity. EIF5A and its paralogues, uniquely modified by hypusination, help ribosomes resolve difficult sequences and promote peptide release. UPF1 couples termination at premature stop codons to nonsense-mediated decay, so faulty transcripts are destroyed rather than translated into truncated protein. Because stop-codon readthrough also governs viral and cellular recoding events, this control point links protein synthesis quality to mRNA surveillance and antiviral defence.

Accurate protein synthesis depends on continual proofreading of which amino acid is attached to which tRNA and how codons are read, and this regulation of translational fidelity covers the activities that keep the genetic code faithfully interpreted. Errors here produce statistically mistranslated proteins that misfold and aggregate, and defects in these components cause neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy and other tissue-specific disease. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases for alanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine and threonine act in both cytosolic and mitochondrial pairs, and their editing domains hydrolyse misacylated products; dedicated D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylases remove the wrong stereoisomer. An amidotransferase subunit corrects misacylated tRNA-Gln in mitochondria, while enzymes that modify anticodon-adjacent nucleosides, including a threonylcarbamoyladenosine pathway component, tune codon-anticodon pairing. A small ribosomal subunit protein contributes to decoding accuracy on the ribosome itself.

Some UGA codons are not stop signals but instructions to insert selenocysteine, and this recoding is how translational readthrough builds the selenoprotein family. Without it, cells cannot make glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases or the deiodinases that convert thyroxine to active thyroid hormone, so redox defence and thyroid hormone metabolism both fail; loss of the SECISBP2 reader causes a multisystem disorder with abnormal thyroid hormone levels, myopathy and azoospermia. Mechanistically, a selenocysteine insertion sequence in the 3' untranslated region is bound by SECISBP2, which recruits the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC and the selenocysteinyl-tRNA; that tRNA is charged first with serine by seryl-tRNA synthetase and then converted by SEPSECS. The output includes DIO2 and the ER-resident SELENOT, placing this specialised decoding step upstream of hormone activation and oxidative stress handling rather than within general protein synthesis.

Protein folding is the chaperone system that gets newly made and stress-damaged polypeptides into their correct three-dimensional shapes and assembles them into complexes, the prerequisite for essentially every protein's activity. Without it cells accumulate misfolded and aggregated species, the outcome behind neurodegenerative proteinopathies, cataract, and secretory-cell stress. The genes span the major machines and their compartments: HSP70s with their DNAJ co-chaperones and nucleotide-exchange factors, HSP90 with CDC37 and the FKBP/PPI immunophilins, the cytosolic CCT/TRiC chamber with prefoldin for actin and tubulin, mitochondrial HSPD1/HSPE1, and small heat-shock proteins that hold unfolded clients soluble. In the endoplasmic reticulum, BiP, calnexin/calreticulin lectin cycles, UGGT1 quality control, and protein disulphide isomerases with ERO1 oxidases fold and proofread secretory and membrane proteins, linking this activity to the unfolded protein response, degradation triage, and collagen and antigen-presentation maturation.

Newly made polypeptides do not reach their functional shape unaided, and this is the machinery that guides them there and keeps them there. It sustains the proteome under heat, oxidative and metabolic stress, and its failure produces misfolded, aggregation-prone protein — the basis of chaperonopathies, cataract from mutant lens crystallins, and the aggregate burden of neurodegeneration. The work is done by ATP-driven chaperone families and their cofactors: HSP70s with their J-domain partners and nucleotide exchange factors, HSP90 with co-chaperones such as CDC37 and the immunophilins, the mitochondrial HSP60/HSP10 chamber, small heat shock proteins that hold unfolded clients soluble, and the CCT/TRiC and prefoldin system that folds actin and tubulin. In the endoplasmic reticulum, calnexin and calreticulin, protein disulfide isomerases and oxidases, and glycan-based quality control ensure correct disulfide bonding and release only properly folded secretory cargo. Peptidyl-prolyl isomerases and dedicated assembly factors handle rate-limiting isomerization and subunit-specific folding.

Newly synthesised polypeptides emerge from the ribosome unfolded and aggregation-prone, and de novo protein folding is the chaperone-assisted process that guides them to their native tertiary structure before they can misfold or be degraded. Without it, nascent chains aggregate, the secretory pathway accumulates defective cargo, and cells mount stress responses that can end in death. Ribosome-associated components such as the HSPA14 nascent-chain complex and its DNAJC2 co-chaperone engage chains co-translationally, while the mitochondrial HSPD1 chaperonin folds imported proteins in the matrix. Peptidyl-prolyl isomerases of the FKBP family catalyse the cis-trans proline switching that is often rate-limiting for folding, and in the endoplasmic reticulum UGGT1 reglucosylates incompletely folded glycoproteins to return them to lectin chaperones for another attempt. Tubulin folding illustrates the dependence of cytoskeletal assembly on this quality-control machinery.

Proteins destined for secretion, the plasma membrane, or the mitochondrial intermembrane space carry an N-terminal signal or targeting sequence that must be cut off once translocation has begun, and signal peptide processing is that cleavage step. Without it, nascent chains stay tethered to the translocation channel and cannot fold, mature, or traffic onward, so secretory output and membrane protein biogenesis both fail. The endoplasmic reticulum signal peptidase complex does the bulk of the work, with catalytic SEC11A/B/C subunits assembled alongside the accessory SPCS1, SPCS2 and SPCS3 proteins; IMMP1L and IMMP2L perform the equivalent cut on imported mitochondrial precursors. Liberated signal peptides are then cleared from the membrane by the intramembrane protease HM13, a step that can also generate bioactive fragments. Related proteolytic maturation of secretory cargo by FURIN links this processing to hormone and growth factor activation, and loss of CLN5 causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

Phosphorylation is only a switch if it can be turned off, and protein dephosphorylation is the reversal arm that sets the duration and amplitude of kinase signalling. Without it, growth factor and immune receptor cascades stay on, cell cycle transitions lose their ordering, and metabolic enzymes remain locked in one state. The genes span the major catalytic families: serine/threonine phosphatases built from a shared catalytic subunit plus regulatory partners, including the PP1, PP2A and calcineurin holoenzymes; classical receptor and non-receptor tyrosine phosphatases such as CD45 and SHP-1/SHP-2 that gate lymphocyte and cytokine signalling; dual-specificity enzymes that inactivate MAP kinases; and lipid-directed members such as PTEN and the myotubularins, which act on phosphoinositides rather than proteins. Also present are regulators of RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain phosphorylation and pyruvate dehydrogenase. Loss of individual members underlies tumour predisposition, myotubular myopathy and immune dysregulation.

Transfer of an acetyl group onto amino acid side chains or protein N-termini is one of the most widespread protein modifications, and it sets how tightly chromatin is packed, how stable a newly made protein is, and how transcription factors, tubulin and actin behave. Histone acetyltransferases such as CREBBP, EP300, KAT2A/KAT2B, KAT5 and the MYST enzymes KAT6A and KAT7 open chromatin at active promoters and enhancers and acetylate non-histone substrates including p53 and FOXO1, while SIRT1 removes such marks to couple gene expression to metabolic state, notably within the CLOCK-BMAL1 circadian machinery. A separate branch of N-terminal acetyltransferases modifies nascent chains co-translationally, and specialised members acetylate tubulin or actin. Cohesin acetylation by ESCO1 and ESCO2 licenses sister chromatid cohesion; its loss causes Roberts syndrome, and dysregulated acetyltransferases recur in developmental disorders and cancer.

Most proteins are acetylated on their very first residue, usually as they emerge from the ribosome, and N-terminal protein amino acid acetylation is the machinery that performs this irreversible modification. The mark alters protein half-life, folding and complex assembly, and can serve as a degradation signal recognised by ubiquitin ligases, so the composition of the proteome depends on it.
