Distinct N-terminal acetyltransferases handle different substrate classes according to the identity of the first residues: catalytic and auxiliary subunits acting co-translationally, a Golgi-membrane-anchored enzyme serving transmembrane proteins, and a dedicated enzyme that acetylates actin and thereby tunes cytoskeletal dynamics and cell motility. Also represented are lysine acetyltransferases such as CREBBP, EP300 and KAT2B, better known for chromatin and transcription factor acetylation, and the serotonin N-acetyltransferase step of melatonin synthesis.

Acetylation of internal amino acid side chains differs from N-terminal acetylation in being reversible, and it works as a switch that changes protein charge, interaction surfaces and stability. The best known substrates are histone lysines, where acetyl marks loosen chromatin and mark promoters and enhancers as active, so transcriptional programmes for growth, differentiation and DNA damage response depend on this chemistry. Lysine acetyltransferases here include the coactivator EP300, the GCN5-related enzymes KAT2A and KAT2B, the MYST-family KAT7, and HAT1, which acetylates newly synthesised histone H4 before deposition into chromatin. Non-histone targets matter too: ATAT1 acetylates alpha-tubulin lysine 40 inside the microtubule lumen, altering mechanical resilience and motor-based transport. BAG6 contributes as part of a chaperone complex that presents substrates for modification. Loss or imbalance of these activities disrupts gene expression control and is recurrent in cancer.

Protein deacetylation strips acetyl groups from lysine residues on histones and thousands of non-histone proteins, and in doing so sets how tightly chromatin is packed, how long transcription factors survive, and how metabolic enzymes are tuned to nutrient supply. Because acetylation is reversible, this reaction is the off switch that makes lysine acetylation a signal rather than a permanent mark; its loss deregulates gene expression, mitochondrial fuel choice, and genome maintenance, and its enzymes are drug targets in cancer. Zinc-dependent histone deacetylases such as HDAC3 and HDAC7 act within corepressor complexes on promoters, HDAC6 works in the cytoplasm on tubulin and misfolded protein cargo, and the NAD+-dependent sirtuins couple deacetylation directly to cellular energy state, with SIRT3, SIRT4 and SIRT5 acting inside mitochondria. Acetyltransferases and shared adaptor subunits are present as the opposing arm that this activity balances.

Protein deacetylation strips acetyl groups from lysine residues, reversing the marks left by acetyltransferases and thereby setting how tightly chromatin is packed, how stable and active many enzymes are, and how cells read their metabolic state. Because acetyl-CoA supplies the acetyl group and NAD+ is consumed by the sirtuin class, this chemistry links nutrient availability to gene expression, and its loss contributes to genome instability, metabolic disease and features of ageing. Classical zinc-dependent enzymes such as HDAC3 act in corepressor complexes on histones, while HDAC6 works in the cytoplasm on tubulin and chaperones and SIRT3-SIRT5 operate inside mitochondria on fatty acid oxidation and urea cycle enzymes. Counterpart acetyltransferases and their partner subunits appear here too, since deacetylation is meaningful only as one half of a reversible cycle whose balance is continuously adjusted.

Attaching sulfate as an ester to protein acceptors is a late Golgi modification that tunes how secreted and surface proteins recognise their partners. The tyrosylprotein sulfotransferases TPST1 and TPST2 transfer sulfate from the donor PAPS onto tyrosine residues of proteins passing through the secretory pathway, a change that strengthens binding of chemokine receptors to their ligands, of P-selectin glycoprotein ligand to selectins during leukocyte rolling, and of coagulation and hormone-processing substrates; loss of both enzymes in mice impairs fertility and postnatal growth. The carbohydrate sulfotransferases here act on the glycan chains carried by glycoproteins, with CHST4 generating sulfated ligands for L-selectin on lymph node high endothelial venules and thereby directing lymphocyte homing, and HS3ST5 modifying heparan sulfate. Together these reactions govern adhesion, immune cell trafficking and extracellular ligand recognition.

Protein methylation covers the transfer of methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto amino acid side chains and protein termini, a modification that tunes protein interactions, stability and activity without changing sequence. It sets the histone marks that define transcriptional states — H3K9 by EHMT1/EHMT2, H3K36 by SETD2, H4K20 by KMT5A, H3K4 by SETD7 — and equally modifies non-histone substrates: arginine methylation by the PRMT family regulates Sm proteins and spliceosome assembly, actin histidine methylation by SETD3 shapes cytoskeletal function, and dedicated methyltransferases mark translation factors eEF1A, eEF2 and the release factor, chaperones, ATP synthase and respiratory complex I subunits. Related activities methylate protein N-termini, prenylated C-termini for membrane anchoring, and repair isoaspartyl damage. Loss of individual enzymes causes developmental syndromes, congenital insensitivity to pain, myopathy and cancer, reflecting how broadly gene expression, RNA processing and mitochondrial assembly depend on this chemistry.

Protein methylation is the enzymatic transfer of a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine onto amino acid side chains or protein termini, and it is one of the main ways a cell tunes a protein's interactions without changing its sequence. The genes here cover the breadth of that chemistry: lysine methyltransferases acting on histones (EHMT1/2, KMT5A, SETD2, SETD7, SMYD2) to set chromatin states and direct transcription and DNA repair; arginine methyltransferases of the PRMT family that mark histones and RNA-binding proteins, including Sm proteins of the spliceosome, and depend on methylosome partners; N-terminal and non-histone methyltransferases that modify translation factors, chaperones, respiratory chain assembly factors and ATP synthase; and prenylcysteine carboxyl methylation that completes membrane anchoring of small GTPases. TRMT112 serves as an obligate activating subunit for several of these enzymes. Loss of individual activities causes intellectual disability syndromes, mitochondrial dysfunction and cancers driven by aberrant chromatin marking.

Most proteins that enter the secretory pathway are decorated with sugars attached to asparagine side chains, and this N-linked glycosylation determines whether they fold correctly, survive quality control, and behave properly at the cell surface. The route begins with a lipid-linked oligosaccharide built stepwise on dolichol by the ALG enzymes, transferred en bloc to nascent chains by the oligosaccharyltransferase complex (STT3A/STT3B with RPN1, RPN2, DDOST and accessory subunits), then trimmed by glucosidases and mannosidases. Trimming intermediates feed the calnexin cycle, where UGGT re-glucosylates incompletely folded proteins for another attempt, and MAN1B1 marks persistent failures for degradation. Golgi branching by MGAT enzymes and capping by fucosyl- and sialyltransferases generate the mature complex glycans that mediate cell adhesion, receptor signalling and immune recognition. Defects across these steps produce congenital disorders of glycosylation, with multisystem neurological, hepatic and coagulation disease; GNPTAB lesions instead misroute lysosomal enzymes.

Every N-linked glycoprotein begins as a fourteen-sugar precursor built on a lipid carrier in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and dolichol-linked oligosaccharide biosynthesis is the assembly line that makes it. Without an intact precursor, glycosylation of secreted and membrane proteins fails, and the resulting congenital disorders of glycosylation present with developmental delay, seizures, coagulopathy and multisystem disease. The route starts with the carrier itself: DHDDS and NUS1 form the cis-prenyltransferase that elongates the polyprenyl chain, and SRD5A3 reduces it to dolichol. DPAGT1 then transfers the first GlcNAc, and successive ALG glycosyltransferases add GlcNAc, mannose and glucose residues, with RFT1 involved in flipping the intermediate to the luminal face and MPDU1 and DPM1 supplying dolichol-linked mannose and glucose donors. The finished glycan is handed to the oligosaccharyltransferase complex for transfer onto nascent polypeptides, linking this lipid chemistry to secretory protein folding and quality control.

After a preassembled oligosaccharide is transferred onto a nascent protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, it is trimmed and rebuilt into the mature glycans that decorate secreted and membrane proteins. This N-glycan processing determines whether a glycoprotein folds correctly, is retained for another attempt or is dispatched for degradation, and it sets the surface sugar code that governs cell adhesion, receptor signalling and serum protein clearance. Glucosidase II subunits and ER mannosidases perform the conserved early trimming tied to the calnexin folding cycle; Golgi mannosidases and branching transferases then generate complex antennae, which fucosyltransferases and polysialyltransferases cap, the latter adding polysialic acid that keeps neural adhesion molecules from sticking during brain wiring. Phosphotransferase subunits instead mark lysosomal hydrolases with mannose-6-phosphate for delivery, and loss of that step causes mucolipidosis; defects elsewhere in the route underlie congenital disorders of glycosylation and lysosomal storage disease.

protein O-linked glycosylation builds the sugar chains attached through serine, threonine, hydroxylysine or tyrosine hydroxyls, generating the mucin coats of epithelial surfaces, the glycosaminoglycan chains of proteoglycans, the O-mannose glycans that let dystroglycan grip laminin, and the O-fucose and O-glucose marks that tune Notch. Loss of individual steps causes congenital muscular dystrophies with brain malformation, skeletal dysplasias, bleeding and immune-cell trafficking defects, so the pathway underlies basement membrane adhesion, cartilage and bone matrix assembly, and leukocyte homing. Polypeptide GalNAc transferases initiate mucin-type cores that are elongated by C1GALT1 with its chaperone, branched by GCNT enzymes, then capped with sialic acid and fucose; xylosyltransferases and EXT enzymes start heparan and chondroitin chains, which sulfotransferases and epimerases then decorate. Nucleotide-sugar transporters supply donors, and cytoplasmic OGT and OGA add and remove O-GlcNAc as a nutrient-responsive regulatory modification.

Sugars attached to serine, threonine, tyrosine or hydroxylysine side chains give secreted and membrane proteins their bulk, charge and binding specificity, and protein O-linked glycosylation covers all of the routes by which these chains are initiated and extended. Mucin-type synthesis begins with a large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases and the core-1 galactosyltransferase with its chaperone, then branches, sialylates and fucosylates to build selectin ligands and mucus barriers. Separate arms make O-mannose glycans on dystroglycan, whose loss causes congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye involvement; O-fucose and O-glucose on EGF repeats, which tune Notch; collagen galactosyl-hydroxylysine; and the xylose-primed linker that nucleates heparan and chondroitin sulfate chains, with sulfotransferases and epimerases setting their sulfation patterns. Nucleotide-sugar transporters and the nucleocytoplasmic O-GlcNAc cycle of OGT and OGA complete the picture, linking nutrient status to signalling.

N-terminal protein lipidation attaches fatty acids to the amino terminus of newly made proteins, converting soluble polypeptides into membrane-associating ones and thereby setting where they act in the cell. Its best-known outputs are N-myristoylation of hundreds of substrates by the myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2, which anchors Src-family kinases, ARF GTPases and G protein alpha subunits to membranes, and N-palmitoylation of Hedgehog by HHAT, a modification without which the morphogen cannot be secreted or signal to Patched during development. The modification also creates the exposed myristoyl groups recognised during apoptotic protein relocalisation and pathogen effector targeting. Loss of this lipidation misroutes signalling proteins to the cytosol, degrades growth factor patterning, and is exploited pharmacologically, since myristoyltransferase and Hedgehog acyltransferase inhibitors are pursued as anticancer agents. It belongs to the wider set of co-translational and post-translational lipid modifications governing membrane trafficking.

Attaching a lipid to a protein's amino terminus converts a soluble polypeptide into one that docks onto membranes, and this modification determines where many signalling proteins can act. The dominant reaction is N-myristoylation, in which the N-myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2 transfer myristate from myristoyl-CoA onto an N-terminal glycine exposed after initiator methionine removal; substrates include Src-family kinases, ARF GTPases and calcineurin-associated proteins, whose membrane targeting and stability depend on it. A distinct branch is N-terminal palmitoylation of Hedgehog proteins by the acyltransferase HHAT, a step required for Sonic hedgehog to signal during embryonic patterning; HHATL is a related inactive homolog. Loss of these activities misdirects proteins away from membranes, blunts developmental signalling, and myristoylation is exploited as a drug target in cancer and parasitic infection.

GPI anchor metabolic process builds and remodels the glycolipid tether that fastens a large family of proteins to the outer face of the plasma membrane, among them CD55 and CD59, alkaline phosphatases, folate receptors and prion protein. Loss of the pathway strips cells of these surface proteins: somatic mutation of PIGA in haematopoietic stem cells causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria through complement-mediated lysis, while inherited hypomorphic defects in PIGV, PIGN or PGAP3 produce intellectual disability syndromes with raised serum alkaline phosphatase. Assembly begins on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum with GlcNAc transfer to phosphatidylinositol, proceeds through mannosylation using dolichol-phosphate-mannose and addition of ethanolamine phosphate side chains, and ends when a transamidase complex including PIGK, GPAA1 and PIGT swaps the anchor for a protein's C-terminal signal. Subsequent lipid and glycan remodelling in the ER and Golgi determines anchored-protein sorting, raft association and stability.

Many surface proteins have no transmembrane domain and are tethered to the outer face of the plasma membrane by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor; the metabolic pathway that makes, attaches and remodels these anchors is what puts them there. Its products include CD59 and CD55, alkaline phosphatases, folate receptors and numerous ectoenzymes, so the pathway supports complement regulation on blood cells, nutrient uptake and membrane microdomain organisation. Stepwise glycosylation of phosphatidylinositol by the PIG enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum builds the core glycan, with mannose donated as dolichol-phosphate-mannose; a transamidase complex including GPAA1, PIGK, PIGS, PIGT and PIGU then cleaves a nascent protein's C-terminal signal and joins it to ethanolamine phosphate. Later lipid and side-chain remodelling by PGAP enzymes matures the anchor for transport. Somatic loss of PIGA causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, while inherited defects give intellectual disability and seizure syndromes.

Breaking peptide bonds is how cells destroy, mature and reshape proteins, and this broad proteolysis programme covers both the destructive turnover of unwanted polypeptides and the precise cleavages that switch proteins on. One arm is the ubiquitin-proteasome system: E1, E2 and E3 enzymes including cullin-RING, HECT and RBR ligases mark substrates, deubiquitinases reverse the mark, and the 26S proteasome degrades them, with allied routes for ER-associated degradation, autophagic and lysosomal cathepsin digestion, and mitochondrial AAA proteases. The other arm is limited, regulatory cleavage: signal peptidases and proprotein convertases mature secreted proteins, caspases execute apoptosis and inflammasome signalling, matrix metalloproteinases and ADAMTS enzymes remodel extracellular matrix under serpin and TIMP restraint, coagulation and complement cascades amplify through serine proteases, and secretase complexes release signalling fragments. Failures cause bleeding or thrombotic disorders, neurodegeneration, pancreatitis, immune dysregulation and cancer.

Many cell-surface proteins are switched off, switched on, or converted into soluble signals by having their extracellular portion clipped away, and membrane protein ectodomain proteolysis is that shedding step. It converts membrane-anchored TNF into a circulating cytokine, releases cytokine receptors as decoys, sheds Notch ligands and adhesion molecules, and generates the amyloid precursor protein fragments whose further processing underlies Alzheimer disease. The main sheddases here are ADAM metalloproteinases, notably ADAM10 and ADAM17, whose trafficking and activity are governed by tetraspanin partners and opposed by TIMP inhibitors; BACE1 and BACE2 and the proprotein convertase furin cleave their own substrate sets. Remnant stubs left in the bilayer are then cut within the membrane by the presenilin–nicastrin complex or by SPPL intramembrane proteases, coupling shedding to release of intracellular signalling fragments. Dysregulated shedding drives inflammation, unchecked growth factor signalling and neurodegeneration.

Attaching a single ubiquitin to a substrate, rather than a polyubiquitin chain, is a signalling event rather than a degradation order: monoubiquitination marks histones for transcriptional regulation, licenses DNA lesion bypass, routes receptors into endosomes, and flags stalled ribosomes. The genes here span the enzymatic relay that performs it — E2 conjugating enzymes such as UBE2W, UBE2T and the UBE2E group that favour single-ubiquitin transfer, cullin–RING assemblies built on CUL1/CUL3 with SKP1, RBX1 and interchangeable substrate adaptors, and RING or HECT ligases including FANCL, RAD18, TRIM37, NEDD4, ITCH, HUWE1 and PRKN. Individual outputs are well defined: RAD18 monoubiquitinates PCNA to recruit translesion polymerases, FANCL modifies FANCD2 in interstrand crosslink repair, and ZNF598 marks ribosomal proteins during quality control of collided ribosomes. Loss of these activities underlies Fanconi anaemia, genome instability, peroxisome biogenesis defects and parkinsonism.

Cells continuously generate proteins that fail to fold, stall during synthesis, or are left without a partner subunit, and this quality control programme recognises those species and destroys them before they aggregate. Its failure underlies protein aggregation disease, mitochondrial dysfunction and the toxicity of ribosome stalling. Two arms are represented: cytosolic ubiquitin-dependent degradation, in which the chaperone-linked ligase STUB1, the E2 enzyme UBE2W, N-recognin ligases such as UBR4, and cullin-RING complexes built on CUL3 with substrate adaptors mark defective proteins, while the AAA-ATPase VCP extracts them from membranes and complexes and deubiquitinases including ATXN3 edit the signal; and organellar proteolysis by the ATP-dependent proteases LONP1, CLPP, AFG3L2, YME1L1 and OMA1 within mitochondria. Dedicated factors handle products of stalled translation and mistargeted tail-anchored or peroxisomal proteins, coupling protein triage to organelle biogenesis and stress signalling.

Glycoproteins and proteoglycans are eventually dismantled, and this catabolic programme is how both their sugar chains and their polypeptides are returned to the cell as reusable monosaccharides and amino acids. Much of it is lysosomal: exoglycosidases and sulfatases such as HEXA/HEXB, GLB1, MAN2B1, IDUA, GUSB, SGSH and GALNS strip terminal residues from glycans and glycosaminoglycans in ordered steps, while cathepsin L and matrix or ADAMTS proteases degrade the protein backbone and remodel extracellular matrix. A parallel arm acts before the lysosome, in the endoplasmic reticulum, where EDEM mannosidases trim misfolded glycoproteins for disposal, NGLY1 removes N-glycans from proteins retrotranslocated to the cytosol, and F-box proteins including FBXO2 and FBXO6 recognise exposed glycans to direct ubiquitin-dependent degradation. Because each glycosidase step is non-redundant, loss of single enzymes causes storage of undegraded substrate and the lysosomal storage diseases, including Tay-Sachs and the mucopolysaccharidoses.

Sugars added to proteins are not permanent, and their removal serves both quality control and signalling. The genes here cover two distinct arms: trimming of N-linked glycans in the endoplasmic reticulum, where mannosidases and the EDEM family clip mannose residues to mark terminally misfolded glycoproteins for disposal, and removal of O-GlcNAc from nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins by OGA, which together with O-GlcNAc addition tunes metabolic and transcriptional responses to nutrient supply. The ER arm is coupled to degradation: UGGT1 and UGGT2 re-add glucose to give a slow-folding protein another chance at the calnexin cycle, while membrane ubiquitin ligases such as SYVN1, RNF5 and MARCHF6 commit failed substrates to retrotranslocation and proteasomal destruction. Lysosomal AGA completes breakdown of glycoasparagines; its loss causes aspartylglucosaminuria, a storage disease with progressive intellectual disability.

Peptide metabolic process covers the making and breaking of short amino-acid chains, from the maturation of prohormones to the destruction of signalling peptides and the synthesis and turnover of glutathione. It determines how long a hormone or vasoactive peptide persists, what fragments are loaded onto MHC class I for immune surveillance, and how much reduced thiol a cell has to buffer oxidative stress. Proprotein convertases such as FURIN and PCSK1 cleave precursors at basic residues, carboxypeptidases and aminopeptidases trim the products, and PAM amidates peptide C-termini to give them activity. Membrane ectoenzymes including ACE, MME and ECE1 terminate peptide signals at the cell surface, controlling blood pressure and natriuretic tone. In parallel, GCLC, GCLM and GSS build glutathione while gamma-glutamyl transferases degrade it, with NFE2L2 driving that arm. Trimming steps in the endoplasmic reticulum shape the antigenic repertoire presented to T cells.

amino acid metabolic process covers the synthesis, interconversion and breakdown of amino acids, the reactions that let cells build protein, dispose of excess nitrogen, and feed carbon skeletons into the citric acid cycle. It underlies whole-body nitrogen balance and is the origin of many inborn errors of metabolism: phenylketonuria from PAH, urea cycle defects from OTC, CPS1 or ASS1, maple syrup urine disease from the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, and homocystinuria from CBS. The genes span transaminases and dehydrogenases such as GOT1/2 and GLUD1, serine and proline biosynthetic enzymes, tryptophan degradation through the kynurenine route, sulfur amino acid and methionine cycling, glutathione synthesis, and mitochondrial and cytosolic aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases that commit amino acids to translation. Also included are transporters and transcriptional controls such as ATF4, which link amino acid supply to stress signalling, and the decarboxylases producing neurotransmitters and polyamines.

Amino acids are the building blocks of protein, but they are also nitrogen carriers, neurotransmitter precursors and fuels, and this broad collection of reactions covers their synthesis, interconversion and breakdown. It sets how the body disposes of surplus nitrogen through urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1, how branched-chain and aromatic amino acids are catabolised toward the TCA cycle and ketone bodies, and how serine, glycine and methionine feed one-carbon and glutathione chemistry. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases link the same pools to translation, while decarboxylases and hydroxylases generate dopamine, serotonin, GABA, histamine and nitric oxide. Loss of individual steps produces the classical inborn errors of metabolism — phenylketonuria, tyrosinaemia, maple syrup urine disease, homocystinuria, hyperammonaemia — and dedicated transporters and transcriptional regulators such as ATF4 adjust flux when particular amino acids run short.

Cells must tune how fast amino acids are made, broken down and interconverted, and regulation of amino acid metabolic process covers the controls that set those rates rather than catalysing the reactions themselves. Such control matters for nitrogen balance, neurotransmitter precursor supply and redox homeostasis: the cystine importer SLC7A11 governs how much cysteine enters the cell for glutathione synthesis, and losing that supply sensitises cells to oxidative death. Other regulators act transcriptionally, as with the hepatocyte factor HNF4A and the bile-acid receptor NR1H4 shaping liver amino acid handling, or enzymatically, as with ACMSD diverting tryptophan degradation away from quinolinate and toward picolinate. PARK7 and CLN3 link the same regulation to neuronal stress responses, which is why perturbations here surface as metabolic liver disease and neurodegeneration rather than as isolated enzyme deficiencies.

Alanine sits at the junction of amino acid and carbohydrate metabolism, and the reactions that make and consume it let tissues move nitrogen and carbon between organs. Muscle disposes of amino groups by transferring them onto pyruvate, and liver reverses the step to feed gluconeogenesis, the basis of the glucose-alanine cycle that supports fasting blood glucose. Cytosolic and mitochondrial alanine aminotransferases carry out this reversible transamination, and their release into serum is the standard clinical readout of hepatocyte injury. Related aminotransferases handle alanine as an amino donor in glyoxylate detoxification, where loss of the peroxisomal enzyme causes primary hyperoxaluria with calcium oxalate kidney stones, while a D-amino acid oxidase degrades the D-enantiomer. Together these activities link nitrogen handling, pyruvate flux and peroxisomal detoxification.

Arginine sits at the junction of nitrogen disposal, polyamine synthesis and nitric oxide signalling, and the reactions that make and consume it determine how a cell handles ammonia and how blood vessels, neurons and macrophages generate NO. The urea cycle enzymes here — carbamoyl phosphate synthetase activator NAGS, OTC, ASS1 and ASL — build arginine from citrulline and then release urea via arginase, and inherited loss of any step produces hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy. The same amino acid is cleaved by arginases into ornithine, feeding ornithine aminotransferase and ODC1 toward proline and the polyamines needed for growth, with antizyme inhibitors AZIN1/2 tuning that flux. Alternatively, the nitric oxide synthases oxidise arginine to citrulline and NO for vasodilation, neurotransmission and antimicrobial defence, a route restrained by DDAH1 clearance of methylarginine inhibitors. Arginase induction in myeloid cells depletes arginine and suppresses T cell responses.

Arginine is made from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate, and in humans the same chemistry doubles as the urea cycle, which is how the liver disposes of waste nitrogen from amino acid breakdown. Arginine itself is the precursor for nitric oxide, creatine and polyamines, so its synthesis links nitrogen clearance to vascular signalling and growth. Ornithine transcarbamylase condenses ornithine with carbamoyl phosphate to give citrulline; argininosuccinate synthase joins citrulline to aspartate, and argininosuccinate lyase cleaves the product to arginine and fumarate, feeding carbon back to the TCA cycle. N-acetylglutamate synthase supplies the allosteric activator that switches on carbamoyl phosphate production and thus sets flux through the whole route. Loss of any step causes hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy, the inherited urea cycle disorders, and arginine becomes dietarily essential.

Arginine sits at a junction between nitrogen disposal, polyamine and proline synthesis, and nitric oxide signalling, and the catabolic routes that consume it decide which of those outputs a cell gets. Arginase channels arginine to ornithine and urea, feeding the urea cycle in liver and, via ornithine aminotransferase, the proline and glutamate pools; the nitric oxide synthases instead oxidise it to citrulline and NO for vasodilation, neurotransmission and macrophage antimicrobial killing. Because the two branches compete for one substrate, arginase induction limits NO output, a switch that shapes macrophage polarisation, endothelial function and tumour immune suppression. Methylarginine turnover by DDAH1 removes an endogenous inhibitor of the synthases and so raises NO capacity. Loss of arginase activity causes hyperargininaemia with spastic diplegia and cognitive impairment, while dysregulated flux through this catabolism contributes to hypertension and impaired wound repair.</description>

Aspartate sits at the junction of amino acid, nitrogen and energy metabolism, and the reactions that make and consume it link the citric acid cycle to urea synthesis, purine synthesis and the transfer of reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane. Cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases interconvert aspartate and oxaloacetate with glutamate and 2-oxoglutarate, the core step of the malate-aspartate shuttle and of transamination-based nitrogen handling; the mitochondrial enzyme is also the clinically measured marker of liver and muscle injury. Argininosuccinate synthase consumes aspartate to dispose of ammonia as urea, and adenylosuccinate synthase feeds its amino group into AMP synthesis. Catabolic arms include D-aspartate oxidase and aspartoacylase, whose loss of function causes Canavan disease through failure to cleave N-acetylaspartate in the brain. A solute carrier contributes amino acid transport to the pathway.

Cysteine sits at the junction of sulfur amino acid metabolism and antioxidant defence, and the reactions that make, use and dispose of it set the cell's capacity for glutathione synthesis and its handling of sulfide. Cysteine is generated from homocysteine and serine by the transsulfuration enzymes cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase, imported as cystine by the SLC7A11 antiporter, and consumed by the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits GCLC and GCLM in the rate-limiting step of glutathione production, with gamma-glutamyl transferase recycling extracellular glutathione back to its constituents. Alternative fates include oxidation by cysteine dioxygenase toward taurine and hypotaurine via CSAD, and sulfurtransferase-mediated detoxification of cyanide and mobilisation of persulfides by MPST. Loss of transsulfuration causes homocystinuria, while limiting cysteine supply starves cells of glutathione and predisposes them to oxidative death, a vulnerability exploited by ferroptosis-inducing therapies.

Glutamate sits at the crossroads of nitrogen handling, energy metabolism and neurotransmission, and the reactions that make and consume it set how a cell disposes of amino groups and fuels the TCA cycle. Glutamine synthetase builds glutamine from ammonia while glutaminases run the reverse, glutamate dehydrogenases interconvert glutamate and 2-oxoglutarate to feed anaplerosis, and transaminases such as GOT1 and GOT2 shuttle amino groups between aspartate and glutamate across the mitochondrial membrane. Related branches degrade histidine and proline, synthesise proline and ornithine, supply N-acetylglutamate for urea-cycle control, and commit glutamate to glutathione via GCLC and GCLM or to GABA via the decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2. Loss of individual steps produces hyperammonaemia, urea-cycle and amino-acid disorders, seizure phenotypes, and impaired antioxidant defence, and tumours often lean on glutaminolysis for carbon and nitrogen.

Glutamate is the body's main excitatory neurotransmitter and the central hub of amino acid nitrogen metabolism, and this is the set of reactions that make it. Glutaminase enzymes deamidate glutamine to glutamate, supplying the transmitter pool that neurons load into synaptic vesicles after astrocytes recycle released glutamate back as glutamine; the liver-type and kidney-type isoforms serve very different jobs, from ammoniagenesis in renal acid-base handling to anaplerotic fuelling of the TCA cycle in proliferating cells. Glutamate dehydrogenase interconverts glutamate and 2-oxoglutarate with free ammonium, linking amino acid catabolism to energy supply and to insulin secretion, while a cytosolic aspartate aminotransferase moves amino groups between aspartate and glutamate as part of the malate-aspartate shuttle. A folate hydrolase releases glutamate from folylpoly-gamma-glutamates and from the neuropeptide NAAG. Dysregulation contributes to hyperinsulinism, excitotoxic neuronal injury, and glutamine addiction in tumours.

Glutamate sits at the junction of nitrogen handling, neurotransmission and the citric acid cycle, and its catabolism determines whether the amino acid is burned for energy, converted into an inhibitory signal, or disposed of as glutamine. Oxidative deamination by glutamate dehydrogenase yields alpha-ketoglutarate and free ammonia, feeding carbon into mitochondrial oxidation and linking amino acid breakdown to insulin secretion and hepatic ureagenesis. Transamination by the cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases moves amino groups onto oxaloacetate, and the pair also carries reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane. Decarboxylation by the two glutamate decarboxylases produces GABA, so this chemistry defines inhibitory neurons and pancreatic islet cells; glutamine synthetase instead amidates glutamate, the step astrocytes use to clear synaptic transmitter. Loss or dysregulation of these enzymes causes hyperinsulinism with hyperammonaemia and contributes to epilepsy and excitotoxic injury.

Glutamine is the body's main nitrogen carrier and a major fuel for proliferating cells, and the reactions that make and break it set the balance between nitrogen disposal, ammonia detoxification and anaplerotic supply to the TCA cycle. Glutamine synthetase builds it from glutamate and ammonia, while the glutaminases GLS and GLS2 release that ammonia again, feeding glutamate dehydrogenase and, in liver, the urea cycle through carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and argininosuccinate lyase. The same amide nitrogen is donated to purine and pyrimidine synthesis via CAD and PFAS and to serine-linked one-carbon metabolism, which is why tumours become glutamine-dependent. Regulation runs through mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT4, which restrains glutamate dehydrogenase, and through uncoupling and bile-acid receptor signalling. Loss of these steps causes hyperammonaemia and urea cycle disease, and disturbed glutamine handling contributes to hepatic encephalopathy and excitotoxic glutamate imbalance in brain.

Glycine sits at the junction of amino acid catabolism, one-carbon metabolism and conjugation chemistry, and the reactions that make and dispose of it keep both nitrogen and folate-bound methyl groups in balance. Serine hydroxymethyltransferases in cytosol and mitochondria interconvert serine and glycine while loading one-carbon units onto tetrahydrofolate for nucleotide and methionine synthesis, with PHGDH feeding serine in from glycolysis. The mitochondrial glycine cleavage system, comprising GLDC, AMT and the lipoate-carrying GCSH, is the main route of glycine breakdown; its loss causes nonketotic hyperglycinemia, with glycine accumulation, encephalopathy and seizures. Transaminases acting on glyoxylate route that intermediate back to glycine rather than to oxalate, and AGXT deficiency produces primary hyperoxaluria with kidney stones. Other members conjugate glycine to bile acids and acyl-CoAs for excretion.

Glycine biosynthesis supplies the simplest amino acid, which cells need far beyond protein synthesis: as the donor of one-carbon units for purine and thymidylate production, as a precursor of heme, creatine and glutathione, and as an inhibitory neurotransmitter. The dominant route converts serine to glycine through cytosolic and mitochondrial serine hydroxymethyltransferases, transferring the released one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate and thereby coupling amino acid interconversion to folate-dependent nucleotide synthesis; the mitochondrial isoform is strongly induced in proliferating and tumour cells. A second route transaminates glyoxylate to glycine, with peroxisomal and mitochondrial aminotransferases and a glycolate oxidase generating and disposing of glyoxylate. Loss of this detoxifying step diverts glyoxylate to oxalate, causing primary hyperoxaluria with renal stones and nephrocalcinosis, which places glycine formation at the junction of one-carbon metabolism and glyoxylate handling.

Histidine is an essential amino acid that is either degraded for energy and one-carbon units or diverted into signalling and buffering molecules, and this metabolic route covers both fates. The catabolic arm runs from histidine ammonia-lyase through urocanate and imidazolonepropionate to formiminoglutamate, which a bifunctional transferase-cyclodeaminase hands to tetrahydrofolate as a one-carbon donor, linking the pathway to folate status and glutamate production; inherited defects at these steps cause histidinaemia and urocanic aciduria. Separately, histidine decarboxylase makes histamine, the mediator of gastric acid secretion, allergic responses and neurotransmission, and a methyltransferase inactivates histamine to terminate that signal. Carnosine synthase joins histidine to beta-alanine to form the dipeptide buffer abundant in skeletal muscle and brain, which a dedicated methyltransferase converts to anserine. Together these reactions set tissue levels of histamine, carnosine and the folate-linked intermediates.

Isoleucine, one of the three branched-chain amino acids obtained from diet, is handled by a catabolic route that lets muscle and liver use it as fuel and as a source of acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. The first step is reversible transamination by a mitochondrial aminotransferase, after which the branched-chain keto acid dehydrogenase complex commits the carbon skeleton irreversibly to oxidation; a dedicated kinase restrains that complex by phosphorylation, tuning how much isoleucine is burned versus spared for protein synthesis. Downstream, a short/branched-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, a hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase and a thiolase complete the conversion. Defects in these steps cause organic acidurias and ketothiolase deficiency, with accumulation of toxic intermediates, metabolic crises and neurological damage, linking this pathway to amino acid disposal, ketone body metabolism and nutrient signalling.

Leucine is an essential branched-chain amino acid that cells either build into protein or break down for energy, and this catabolic route handles the second fate. A mitochondrial aminotransferase first removes the amino group to give the ketoacid, which the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex decarboxylates; that committed step is held in check by a dedicated kinase, BCKDK, whose phosphorylation of the complex switches it off when leucine is scarce. The carbon skeleton then passes through isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a biotin-dependent carboxylase, a hydratase and HMG-CoA lyase to yield acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate, linking leucine to ketogenesis and the citric acid cycle. Inherited blocks at successive steps cause isovaleric acidemia, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaric aciduria, presenting as metabolic acidosis and hypoglycemia during catabolic stress. Leucine abundance is also read as a nutrient signal by growth control machinery.

Leucine, one of the branched-chain amino acids obtained from diet and protein turnover, is degraded through a mitochondrial route that ends in acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate, feeding the citric acid cycle and ketone body production during fasting or high protein load. After transamination, the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex commits the carbon skeleton irreversibly, and its kinase BCKDK phosphorylates and inhibits that complex to set flux according to leucine supply. Downstream steps include isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, the biotin-dependent 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase formed by MCCC1 and MCCC2, a hydratase, and HMG-CoA lyase, which splits HMG-CoA in the last reaction shared with ketogenesis. Inherited defects at each step cause organic acidurias — isovaleric acidemia, 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, 3-methylglutaconic aciduria and HMG-CoA lyase deficiency — presenting with metabolic acidosis and hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

Lysine is an essential amino acid that cannot be resynthesised, so its handling is essentially a matter of controlled disposal: surplus lysine is degraded to acetyl-CoA, feeding energy metabolism and ketogenesis, while intermediates are kept from accumulating to toxic levels. The dominant route runs through saccharopine, formed and then cleaved by the bifunctional enzyme AASS, and continues via 2-aminoadipate semialdehyde, transamination by AADAT, and oxidative decarboxylation by a 2-oxoadipate dehydrogenase complex sharing the DLST and DLD subunits of related keto acid dehydrogenases, with glutaryl-CoA handed on to GCDH. A mitochondrial carrier moves oxoadipate across the inner membrane, and ALDH7A1 detoxifies the reactive semialdehyde. Loss of these steps causes inherited metabolic disease: GCDH deficiency produces glutaric aciduria with striatal injury, and ALDH7A1 mutation underlies pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy, in which accumulating intermediates deplete active vitamin B6.

Methionine sits at the junction of protein synthesis and cellular methylation, and its metabolism keeps both supplied. The amino acid is activated to S-adenosylmethionine by methionine adenosyltransferase, spent as the methyl donor for DNA, RNA, protein and small-molecule methylation "including glycine N-methyltransferase, which buffers excess SAM" and then regenerated. Remethylation runs by two routes: the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase with its reductase, which draws methyl groups from folate supplied by MTHFR and the MTHFD enzymes, and betaine-dependent transfer by BHMT in liver and kidney. A parallel salvage arm recovers methionine from the methylthioadenosine left over when spermine synthase and its relatives make polyamines. Oxidised methionine residues in proteins are repaired by methionine sulfoxide reductase. Disruption raises homocysteine and causes neural tube defects, megaloblastic anaemia and vascular disease, while MTAP loss is a recurrent event in cancer.

Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid that must be either incorporated into protein or broken down, and this metabolic route handles the degradative fate. Phenylalanine hydroxylase converts it to tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin, which a quinoid dihydropteridine reductase regenerates so the reaction can continue; tyrosine is then transaminated and passed through hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, homogentisate dioxygenase, a maleylacetoacetate isomerase and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase to yield fumarate and acetoacetate for central metabolism. Loss of individual steps causes a well-known series of inherited disorders: phenylketonuria with its neurotoxic accumulation of phenylalanine, tyrosinemia from the terminal hydrolase defect, and alkaptonuria from homogentisate build-up. An amino acid oxidase acting on aromatic side chains links the same substrate to immune regulation, where phenylalanine and tryptophan catabolism restrains lymphocyte responses. The pathway is largely hepatic and central to nitrogen and aromatic amino acid handling.

Proline sits at a junction between amino acid pools, the urea cycle and mitochondrial redox balance, and L-proline metabolic process covers both its synthesis from glutamate or ornithine and its degradation back to glutamate. Because each direction consumes or produces NAD(P)H and feeds electrons to the respiratory chain, the cycle acts as a redox shuttle that supports collagen-rich tissues, proliferating cells and tumours with high proline demand. ALDH18A1 commits glutamate to the route, the PYCR reductases complete ring formation, and proline dehydrogenase and ALDH4A1 run the reverse steps; ornithine aminotransferase links the pathway to arginine and ornithine handling, while D-amino acid oxidase and hydroxyproline dehydrogenase handle related substrates. Loss of ALDH18A1 or PYCR1 causes cutis laxa with developmental defects, OAT deficiency causes gyrate atrophy of the retina, and proline dehydrogenase loss underlies hyperprolinemia.

L-serine sits at a junction between glycolysis, one-carbon metabolism and lipid synthesis, and the reactions that make and consume it keep cells supplied with glycine, folate-borne methyl groups, cysteine and the serine headgroups of sphingolipids and phosphatidylserine. The de novo route diverts 3-phosphoglycerate through PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH, and proliferating and neural cells depend on it heavily; loss of these three enzymes causes serine deficiency syndromes with microcephaly, seizures and hypomyelination, while their amplification supports tumour growth. Cytosolic and mitochondrial serine hydroxymethyltransferases interconvert serine and glycine while loading tetrahydrofolate for nucleotide synthesis, CBS commits serine to transsulfuration with homocysteine, and serine racemase generates D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors. Catabolic serine dehydratase and the glyoxylate-handling aminotransferase AGXT link the amino acid to gluconeogenic and hepatic disposal routes.

L-serine catabolism disposes of surplus serine and links it to one-carbon and sulfur metabolism, so that amino acid supply from diet and gluconeogenic precursors is balanced against demand. Serine dehydratase, expressed mainly in liver, deaminates serine to pyruvate and ammonia, feeding carbon into gluconeogenesis and the citric acid cycle; a related dehydratase-like protein accompanies it. Cytosolic serine hydroxymethyltransferase transfers the side-chain carbon of serine to tetrahydrofolate, yielding glycine and 5,10-methylene-THF, the entry point for nucleotide synthesis and methylation. Cystathionine beta-synthase instead condenses serine with homocysteine in the transsulfuration route toward cysteine and glutathione, and its loss causes homocystinuria with thrombosis and skeletal and ocular disease. Flux through these steps is sensitive to hormonal and dietary protein status, tying serine disposal to hepatic nitrogen handling.

Threonine is an essential amino acid that humans cannot synthesise, so the relevant biology is its catabolism and disposal once dietary protein is digested. Breakdown feeds the amino acid's carbon into glycine, aminoacetone and pyruvate, linking it to one-carbon metabolism, gluconeogenesis and energy production in liver and kidney. The enzymes here cover both routes: a serine/threonine dehydratase pair converts threonine to 2-oxobutyrate and ammonia, while 2-amino-3-ketobutyrate CoA ligase acts in the glycine-producing arm together with a reactive-intermediate deaminase that handles the unstable enamine/imine products of dehydratase chemistry and prevents their damaging other enzymes. Phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase ties this activity to serine biosynthesis, with which threonine catabolism shares substrates and products. Flux through these reactions rises with high protein intake and during fasting, and disturbances affect glycine supply and nitrogen handling.

Tryptophan is the only amino acid that feeds directly into NAD synthesis, and its metabolism decides whether the indole ring is burned for energy, converted to nicotinamide nucleotides, or turned into immunologically active breakdown products. Most of the flux runs down the kynurenine route, opened by the heme dioxygenases IDO1, IDO2 and TDO2 and continued through formamidase, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase and kynureninase to 3-hydroxyanthranilate; ring cleavage by HAAO and decarboxylation by ACMSD set the branch point between complete oxidation and quinolinate, which QPRT and the downstream NAD-forming enzymes convert to the dinucleotide. The route matters twice over: local tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation suppress T cell responses and support tumour immune evasion, while intermediates such as quinolinic acid are neuroactive and implicated in neurodegeneration and mood disorders. Deficiencies in the pathway cause pellagra-like NAD insufficiency or organic acidurias.

L-tryptophan catabolic process degrades the essential amino acid tryptophan, chiefly through the kynurenine route, which both disposes of excess tryptophan and generates the precursors for de novo NAD+ synthesis. Its outputs matter well beyond metabolism: local tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation suppress effector T cells and favour regulatory T cell induction, making this a checkpoint on immune tolerance at the placenta and within tumours, while neuroactive intermediates such as kynurenic and quinolinic acid influence glutamatergic signalling. The first and rate-limiting oxidation is performed by IDO1, IDO2 and hepatic TDO2, with IL4I1 offering an alternative indole route; downstream formamidase, kynureninase, KMO and HAAO steps carry flux toward quinolinate, and ACMSD diverts intermediates to complete oxidation instead. Dysregulation contributes to inflammatory neurodegeneration and to immune evasion by cancers.

Tryptophan is the only amino acid degraded largely through the kynurenine route, and this catabolic pathway both disposes of surplus tryptophan and generates the precursors for de novo NAD+ synthesis. Its first and rate-limiting step is oxidative ring cleavage, performed in liver by TDO2 and in immune and inflamed tissues by the interferon-inducible IDO1 and IDO2; downstream, formamidase, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, kynureninase and HAAO produce kynurenine, 3-hydroxykynurenine and quinolinate, while ACMSD diverts intermediates toward complete oxidation instead of NAD+. Because depleting tryptophan and accumulating kynurenines suppress effector T cells and promote regulatory ones, this route is a major mechanism of immune tolerance in pregnancy and of immune escape by tumours, with IL4I1 contributing an alternative oxidation. The same intermediates are neuroactive, linking the pathway to excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration.

Tyrosine sits at a junction between amino acid catabolism and the synthesis of pigments and catecholamines, and the reactions that consume it are handled here. Most dietary tyrosine is degraded in liver through transamination and a chain of ring-opening steps involving hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, homogentisate dioxygenase, an isomerase and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, ending in fumarate and acetoacetate for energy use; blocks along this route cause tyrosinemia and alkaptonuria, while loss of phenylalanine hydroxylase or its pterin cofactor regeneration machinery causes phenylketonuria. In melanocytes the same amino acid is oxidised by tyrosinase and its related enzyme, with copper delivery and melanosomal transporters such as OCA2 and SLC45A2 supporting the reaction, so defects here produce albinism. Tyrosine hydroxylase commits tyrosine instead to dopamine and the other catecholamines, and iodotyrosine deiodinase recycles iodide during thyroid hormone turnover.

L-tyrosine catabolic process degrades the aromatic amino acid tyrosine to fumarate and acetoacetate, feeding its carbon skeleton into the citric acid cycle and ketone body metabolism. It matters most in liver and kidney, where dietary and protein-turnover tyrosine must be disposed of; blocking any step traps reactive intermediates that damage tissue rather than simply accumulating. Transamination by tyrosine aminotransferase begins the route, followed by hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase, homogentisate dioxygenase, the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and finally fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Loss of these enzymes causes the classic tyrosinemias and alkaptonuria: FAH deficiency produces hepatorenal disease driven by succinylacetone, while homogentisate build-up pigments and destroys cartilage. An amino acid oxidase, IL4I1, provides an alternative immune-cell route of tyrosine deamination linked to lymphocyte regulation. The pathway ties amino acid disposal to gluconeogenic and ketogenic fuel supply.

Tyrosine catabolism disposes of the aromatic amino acid taken in from diet and protein turnover, converting it in the liver and kidney to fumarate and acetoacetate that feed the citric acid cycle and ketogenesis. The route runs through transamination to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate by tyrosine aminotransferase, dioxygenase-mediated conversion to homogentisate by HPD, ring cleavage by homogentisate dioxygenase, isomerization by the maleylacetoacetate isomerase activity of GSTZ1, and final hydrolysis by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. Blocks at each step cause recognizable inherited disease: HPD or FAH deficiency gives tyrosinemia with hepatorenal damage from accumulated reactive intermediates, while loss of homogentisate dioxygenase causes alkaptonuria, in which homogentisate polymerizes and pigments cartilage. IL4I1, an L-amino acid oxidase secreted by myeloid cells, oxidizes tyrosine and other aromatic amino acids in the immune microenvironment rather than for energy, linking this chemistry to local amino acid depletion and T cell suppression.

Valine is a branched-chain amino acid that cannot be made by human cells, so what happens to it is a matter of disposal and fuel: its carbon skeleton is stripped down to propionyl-CoA and fed into the citric acid cycle, while its nitrogen is transferred for reuse. Valine metabolism begins with mitochondrial transamination by BCAT2 and oxidative decarboxylation of the resulting keto acid by the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, whose activity is set by the inhibitory kinase BCKDK. Downstream steps — acyl-CoA dehydrogenation, hydration, thioester hydrolysis and successive oxidations by HIBCH, HIBADH and a methylmalonate semialdehyde dehydrogenase — are each a site of inherited metabolic disease, producing developmental delay, encephalopathy and organic acid accumulation. The route also links dietary protein intake to mitochondrial energy supply and to signalling that senses branched-chain amino acid abundance.

Amino acids are not only building blocks for protein; cells convert them into cofactors, antioxidants, hormones and energy-buffering metabolites, and this modified amino acid metabolism covers that downstream chemistry. Several distinct arms are represented: glutathione synthesis, conjugation and recycling through the gamma-glutamyl cycle, with glutamate-cysteine ligase, glutathione synthetase, the glutathione transferases and reductase defending against electrophiles and oxidative damage; one-carbon and folate metabolism via serine hydroxymethyltransferase, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase, thymidylate synthase and methionine synthase, supplying methyl groups and nucleotide precursors; betaine, sarcosine and glycine methylation; carnitine synthesis and the palmitoyltransferases that use it to move fatty acids into mitochondria; creatine synthesis and the creatine kinases that buffer ATP in muscle and brain; and thyroid hormone production and deiodination from iodinated tyrosine. Dedicated transporters move folate, carnitine, creatine and cystine across membranes, and defects in these routes cause homocystinuria, cystinosis, creatine deficiency syndromes and hypothyroidism.

Betaines are N-trimethylated amino acid derivatives, and this metabolic process covers both their synthesis and their consumption in two connected jobs: osmotic and methyl-group balance in the kidney and liver, and fatty acid transport into mitochondria. Choline oxidation via choline dehydrogenase and an aldehyde dehydrogenase yields glycine betaine, which donates a methyl group to homocysteine through betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, linking this chemistry to the methionine cycle and to homocysteine control; the resulting dimethylglycine is demethylated onward to glycine. In parallel, lysine-derived trimethyllysine is hydroxylated and cleaved to carnitine by gamma-butyrobetaine hydroxylase, and carnitine palmitoyltransferases and acyl-CoA dehydrogenases then drive the carnitine shuttle and beta-oxidation. Transport by an organic cation/carnitine carrier distributes these zwitterions. Loss of flux here impairs fatty acid oxidation during fasting and disturbs one-carbon metabolism.

Betaines are N-trimethylated amino acid derivatives, and their synthesis serves two ends in human physiology: osmotic protection with one-carbon donation, and fatty acid transport into mitochondria. Choline dehydrogenase oxidises choline in the mitochondrial inner membrane, and aldehyde dehydrogenases including ALDH7A1 and ALDH9A1 convert betaine aldehyde to glycine betaine, which stabilises cells against osmotic and oxidative stress in kidney medulla and liver and feeds methyl groups into homocysteine remethylation alongside folate-linked enzymes such as SHMT1. A parallel branch builds carnitine, itself a betaine, from trimethyllysine: TMLHE hydroxylates the precursor and BBOX1 catalyses the final step, supplying the carrier needed for long-chain acyl transfer to the beta-oxidation machinery that ACADM serves. Loss of these activities disturbs methyl group supply, cellular osmolyte balance, and fatty acid oxidation, and TMLHE deficiency has been studied in relation to neurodevelopmental disorders.

Thyroid hormone generation is the sequence by which follicular cells of the thyroid build thyroxine and triiodothyronine, the circulating regulators of basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, growth and brain development; its failure causes congenital hypothyroidism, goitre and cretinism. Iodide is concentrated from blood by the sodium-iodide symporter and passed to the follicular lumen through anion transporters such as SLC26A7, where thyroid peroxidase, using hydrogen peroxide supplied by the DUOX oxidases and their maturation factors, iodinates tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin and couples them. Lysosomal proteases including cathepsins B and K liberate the hormones from that scaffold. Deiodinases DIO1 and DIO2 convert thyroxine to the more active triiodothyronine, while MCT8 and OATP1C1 move hormone across cell membranes, including into the brain. Lineage transcription factors PAX8, FOXE1 and GATA3 maintain the differentiated follicular state on which all of this depends.

Ornithine is not used to build proteins but sits at the junction of nitrogen disposal and the synthesis of arginine, proline and polyamines, so its metabolism determines how efficiently the liver clears ammonia and how readily cells make the precursors for growth and collagen. Mitochondrial handling dominates here: a carrier imports ornithine across the inner membrane, where ornithine transcarbamylase condenses it with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline and commit nitrogen to the urea cycle. Loss of that enzyme produces the most common inherited urea cycle disorder, with hyperammonaemia and neurological injury in early life. Flux is also routed toward proline via a bifunctional synthase, toward polyamines through regulation of ornithine decarboxylase activity, and the hepatocyte transcription factor HNF4A supports expression of the urea cycle programme itself.

Putrescine, spermidine and spermine are small polycations that cells need for proliferation, chromatin and nucleic acid stability, translation and ion channel modulation, and polyamine metabolism is the set of reactions that makes, modifies and disposes of them. Levels are held within a narrow window because excess is toxic and depletion arrests growth, so the pathway is unusually tightly autoregulated. Ornithine decarboxylase commits ornithine to putrescine and is the rate-limiting step; antizymes target it for degradation while antizyme inhibitors relieve that repression. Decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine supplies aminopropyl groups for spermidine and spermine synthases, and a back-conversion arm of acetylation followed by oxidation, together with spermine oxidase and diamine oxidase, returns or exports polyamines and generates hydrogen peroxide. Spermidine is also the obligate donor for hypusine modification of eIF5A. Elevated flux through this route is characteristic of tumours and is the target of difluoromethylornithine.

polyamine biosynthetic process builds putrescine, spermidine and spermine, the small polycations that cells require for growth, ribosome function and chromatin compaction. Proliferating tissues, spermatogenesis and wound repair depend on it, and its deregulation is a hallmark of tumours, which is why ornithine decarboxylase inhibition is pursued therapeutically. Ornithine decarboxylase commits ornithine to putrescine, while adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supplies the aminopropyl donor used by spermidine and spermine synthases. Flux is held under unusually tight control: antizymes target ornithine decarboxylase for proteasomal destruction without ubiquitin, antizyme inhibitors relieve that block, and acetylation by SAT1 followed by oxidation by PAOX or SMOX either exports or recycles the higher polyamines in a back-conversion loop. An agmatinase route offers an alternative entry from arginine. The pathway ties amino acid and methionine metabolism to translational control, including polyamine-dependent hypusination and eIF5A activity.

Putrescine, spermidine and spermine are small polycations that bind nucleic acids and stabilise chromatin, and their synthesis supports proliferation, translation, and hypusine modification of eIF5A; tumours raise this flux, and its inhibition is the basis of ornithine decarboxylase-targeted therapy. Ornithine decarboxylase (ODC1) makes putrescine, S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase (AMD1) supplies the aminopropyl donor, and spermidine and spermine synthases (SRM, SMS) extend the chain, with an alternative route from agmatine via agmatinase. Because excess polyamines are toxic, the pathway is held under unusually tight control: antizymes (OAZ1-3) direct ODC to proteasomal degradation while antizyme inhibitors (AZIN1, AZIN2) relieve that block, and acetylation by SAT1 plus oxidation by SMOX and PAOX feed a back-conversion and export cycle that sets steady-state pool sizes.

Muscle and brain need to hold ATP concentration steady through sudden swings in demand, and phosphocreatine is the buffer that lets them do it. Creatine kinases catalyse reversible transfer of a phosphoryl group between ATP and creatine, so phosphocreatine accumulates when energy is plentiful and regenerates ATP within milliseconds when contraction or neuronal firing draws it down. The isoenzymes named here divide the work by compartment and tissue: mitochondrial forms sit at the inner membrane and couple oxidative phosphorylation to phosphocreatine synthesis, while cytosolic brain-type and muscle-type enzymes release the phosphate at sites of consumption such as the myofibril and the sarcolemmal pump. Together they form a spatial energy shuttle rather than a simple reservoir. Loss of creatine or its phosphorylated form produces muscle weakness and neurological impairment, and release of the muscle isoform into blood is a standard marker of myocardial and skeletal muscle injury.

Protein targeting is the sorting problem every cell must solve: newly made proteins carry address information that must be read so each one ends up in the right membrane, lumen or organelle. Getting it right builds the secretory pathway, mitochondria, peroxisomes and lysosomes; getting it wrong causes mislocalisation diseases, peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal enzyme deficiency. The genes cover the main delivery routes: signal recognition particle and its receptor with the Sec61 translocon and signal peptidase for co-translational entry into the ER, a GET/SGTA route for tail-anchored proteins, TOM and TIM translocases with processing peptidases for mitochondrial import, PEX factors for peroxisomal matrix and membrane proteins, mannose-6-phosphate tagging and receptors for hydrolase delivery to lysosomes, and adaptor, HOPS/GARP and ESCRT complexes for vesicular sorting. ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases add lipid anchors that direct membrane association, while ubiquitin ligases and autophagy receptors clear proteins that fail to reach their destination.

Newly made proteins have to reach the compartment where they work, and protein targeting is the collection of recognition and delivery steps that gets them there, usually by reading a sorting signal built into the polypeptide. Without it, secretory and membrane proteins never enter the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and peroxisomes cannot import their proteomes, and lysosomal enzymes are secreted instead of stored. The signal recognition particle and its receptor deliver ribosomes to the Sec61 translocon, where signal peptidase removes the cleaved sequence; tail-anchored proteins use a separate insertion route; TOM and TIM translocases with matrix processing peptidases handle mitochondrial precursors; PEX proteins recognise peroxisomal targeting signals; and mannose-6-phosphate tagging routes hydrolases to lysosomes. Palmitoyltransferases, adaptor and retromer-like complexes, ubiquitin ligases and autophagy receptors then position or redirect cargo, linking targeting to organelle quality control and diseases such as peroxisome biogenesis disorders and lysosomal storage.

Proteins made in the cytoplasm but needed in the nucleus carry a short basic nuclear localization signal, and this route is how that signal is read and acted upon. It sets the nuclear proteome: transcription factors, histones, replication and repair enzymes reach chromatin only through it, so signal-dependent responses such as NF- cB or STAT activation ultimately depend on regulated cargo entry. An importin-alpha adaptor family (KPNA1-KPNA7, with distinct cargo preferences) binds the signal and docks onto importin-beta or the related IPO5, which ferries the complex through the pore by contacting nucleoporins and the RANBP2/RGPD cytoplasmic filaments. RanGTP in the nucleus releases the cargo and drives directionality, making transport dependent on the Ran gradient across the envelope. Altered adaptor abundance, KPNA2 in particular, accompanies proliferation and tumour progression, and viruses exploit the same machinery to reach the nucleus.

Protein export from nucleus moves proteins out of the nucleus through the nuclear pore, the return leg of nucleocytoplasmic transport that lets a cell decide where a regulator acts. Because localisation is itself a switch, this pathway controls transcription factor activity, cell cycle progression, tumour suppressor function and stress responses: forced nuclear retention or premature export changes gene expression without changing protein levels. Exportins including XPO1 and the CSE1L importin-recycling route capture cargo bearing leucine-rich export signals, and directionality comes from the RanGTP gradient maintained by RanGAP1, RanBP3 and NUTF2, with docking at pore components such as NUP214 and TPR. Kinases and 14-3-3 proteins including GSK3B, PRKACA and YWHAE gate export by phosphorylating cargo, while p14ARF and SMAD-linked factors tune it. XPO1 inhibition is exploited therapeutically in myeloma to trap tumour suppressors in the nucleus.

Proteins made in the cytoplasm but working in the nucleus must eventually be returned, and regulated export across the nuclear envelope is how cells control where a protein acts. It underlies signal-dependent relocalization: transcription factors, cyclin-dependent kinase regulators, and tumour suppressors are switched off by being moved out of the nucleus, and blocking this traffic is the basis of exportin-targeted cancer therapy. Cargo recognition is carried out by karyopherin-family exportins, chief among them XPO1, which bind leucine-rich export signals together with RanGTP; directionality comes from the Ran gradient, maintained by cytoplasmic RanGAP1 and its nuclear guanine-nucleotide exchange, with RanBP3 and NXT1 acting as export cofactors. Nucleoporins such as NUP214 and TPR provide the docking sites at the pore where complexes disassemble. Phosphorylation by kinases including GSK3B and PKA, and 14-3-3 binding, gate individual cargoes, linking export to growth, stress and DNA damage responses.

Membranes acquire their protein content only because newly made polypeptides carry sorting information that is read and acted on, and protein targeting to membrane covers the machinery that interprets those signals. Without it, secreted and integral membrane proteins never reach the endoplasmic reticulum, receptors and channels never reach the cell surface, and misdirected proteins accumulate in the cytosol. Co-translational routing is handled by the signal recognition particle and its receptor, which deliver ribosome-bound chains to the Sec61 translocon with Sec62/Sec63, TRAM and signal sequence receptor subunits assisting insertion; BAG6, SGTA and UBL4A triage tail-anchored and mistargeted substrates, and a GET-dependent route inserts tail-anchored proteins. A large family of ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases and the prenylation-related enzymes ICMT and Rab escort proteins attach lipid anchors that tether peripheral proteins such as Ras to membranes. Downstream consequences include receptor trafficking, ion channel surface delivery and ER protein quality control.

Cotranslational protein targeting to membrane routes newly made secretory and membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, the entry step for roughly a third of the proteome, including antibodies, hormones, receptors and lysosomal enzymes. As a signal sequence emerges from the ribosome, the signal recognition particle — an RNA-protein complex built on 7SL RNA with SRP9, SRP14, SRP54 and the SRP68/72 heterodimer — binds it, pauses elongation, and docks the ribosome onto the SRP receptor at the ER membrane. Translation then resumes directly through the Sec61 translocon, assisted by SEC62/SEC63, the translocon-associated signal sequence receptor subunits, TRAM proteins and the BiP nucleotide exchange factor SIL1, which drive insertion, topology and lumenal folding. Loss of these components disturbs secretory capacity and ER proteostasis, and underlies conditions ranging from Marinesco-Sjögren syndrome to polycystic liver disease and immunodeficiency.

Secretory and membrane proteins must reach the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being made, and this cotranslational targeting route is how that happens: the signal recognition particle binds an emerging signal sequence, pauses elongation, and delivers the ribosome-nascent chain complex to its receptor at the ER membrane. Handover to the Sec61 translocon channel, assisted by Sec62/Sec63, the translocon-associated signal sequence receptor subunits and the TRAM proteins, allows the chain to cross the bilayer or integrate into it, after which lumenal folding factors take over. The RNA component of the particle is contributed by 7SL genes. Everything downstream depends on it — antibody and hormone secretion, receptor and channel biogenesis, glycosylation — and failures produce ER stress and translocation disease; mutations in the main translocon subunit cause immunodeficiency and polycystic kidney disease.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane delivers nascent secretory and membrane proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, and is the entry step for essentially everything a cell secretes or displays on its surface. A signal sequence emerging from the ribosome is captured by the signal recognition particle, built around the 7SL RNA and the SRP9/14, SRP19, SRP54 and SRP68/72 proteins; SRP54 binding pauses elongation until the complex docks on the heterodimeric SRP receptor at the ER membrane. The ribosome is then transferred to the Sec61 translocon, with SEC63, TRAM proteins and the translocon-associated subunits assisting insertion of transmembrane segments and translocation of soluble domains into the lumen. Loss of this route strands hydrophobic precursors in the cytosol, triggering proteotoxic stress and failure of secretion, antibody production and membrane biogenesis.

Secreted and membrane proteins must reach the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being made, and this is the route that gets them there. The signal-recognition particle, a complex of the 7SL RNA with SRP9, SRP14, SRP54 and the SRP68/72 heterodimer, binds an emerging signal sequence, pauses elongation, and delivers the ribosome-nascent chain complex to the SRPRA/SRPRB receptor on the ER membrane. The nascent chain is then transferred into the SEC61 translocon channel, with SEC63, TRAM proteins and the signal sequence receptor subunit assisting insertion and translocation of hydrophobic segments. This targeting step defines the entire secretory pathway: without it, antibodies, hormones, receptors and ion channels would be synthesised in the cytosol and degraded, and secretory cells such as plasma cells and pancreatic acinar cells could not function. Translocon mutations cause immunodeficiency and polycystic kidney disease.

Secreted and membrane proteins are made by ribosomes in the cytosol but must reach the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, and this is the step where the nascent chain actually crosses the bilayer. After the signal recognition particle and its receptor deliver the translating ribosome to the ER surface, SRP releases the chain to the translocon, a protein-conducting channel formed by the Sec61 alpha, beta and gamma subunits, with TRAM proteins assisting insertion of signal sequences and transmembrane segments. The growing polypeptide passes directly from the large ribosomal subunit into the channel, never seeing the cytosol, and folds only once inside the lumen where glycosylation and disulphide formation await. Everything downstream depends on it: antibody and hormone secretion, receptor and transporter biogenesis, lysosomal enzyme delivery. Mutations in SEC61A1 cause tubulointerstitial kidney disease and antibody deficiency, and failed translocation feeds substrates back into ER stress and degradation routes.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane, signal sequence recognition is the first decision point in the secretory pathway: as a ribosome begins translating a protein bearing an N-terminal signal sequence, the signal recognition particle captures that sequence and commits the nascent chain to the endoplasmic reticulum. Everything a cell secretes or displays on its surface — hormones, antibodies, receptors, lysosomal enzymes — depends on this recognition step being accurate. The particle is a ribonucleoprotein built on 7SL RNA with a set of protein subunits: SRP54 binds the hydrophobic signal, the SRP9/SRP14 Alu domain transiently arrests elongation so the chain cannot fold or emerge prematurely, and the SRP68/72 core mediates handoff to the heterodimeric SRP receptor at the ER membrane, where translation resumes into the translocon. Loss of components causes ribosomopathy-like bone marrow failure and neutropenia.

Secreted and membrane proteins must be delivered to the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being made, and this step is where that decision is taken: the signal recognition particle binds the hydrophobic signal sequence as it emerges from the ribosome exit tunnel, pauses elongation, and holds the nascent chain translocation-competent until the complex docks at the ER membrane. The particle is built from the 7SL RNA scaffold together with SRP9, SRP14, SRP19, SRP54, SRP68 and SRP72, with SRP54 making the direct contact with the signal peptide and the GTPase handshake with the heterodimeric SRP receptor formed by SRPRA and SRPRB. Recognition failure misroutes secretory and membrane cargo into the cytosol, so this early sorting event underlies secretion, glycoprotein biogenesis and the composition of every downstream compartment of the secretory route.

Not every protein destined for the endoplasmic reticulum is threaded into it while still being made; short secretory proteins and tail-anchored membrane proteins finish translation in the cytosol and must be delivered afterwards. Post-translational targeting to the ER membrane handles them, and it matters because these clients — SNAREs, many single-pass tail-anchored proteins, small hormones and peptides — would otherwise aggregate or be degraded. A cytosolic holdase complex built around BAG6 with UBL4A and the co-chaperone SGTA captures the hydrophobic segment and keeps it insertion-competent, deciding between delivery and ubiquitin-dependent disposal. GET1 and GET4 mediate insertion of tail-anchored substrates into the lipid bilayer, while fully translated secretory precursors cross through the Sec61 channel assisted by SEC62, SEC63 and the luminal chaperone BiP, with the translocon-associated protein subunits supporting translocation. Loss of this route causes mislocalized membrane proteins and proteotoxic stress.

Soluble chaperones and folding enzymes work only if they stay in the endoplasmic reticulum, and protein retention in the ER lumen is how the cell keeps them there. Escaped residents that reach the cis-Golgi are recognised by KDEL receptors, which bind the C-terminal KDEL or HDEL signal and return the cargo to the ER by retrograde transport, then recycle back; the same receptors also signal to adjust secretory capacity when the ER is stressed. A parallel arm retains cargo that should not leave at all: transmembrane-domain-based retrieval keeps unassembled subunits out of the secretory route, and lectin-based recognition of misfolded glycoproteins commits them to degradation rather than export. Together these mechanisms preserve the oxidising, chaperone-rich folding environment of the ER and enforce quality control on everything the cell secretes, including proteins destined for GPI anchoring and disulfide-bond formation.

Lysosomes only work if their hydrolases and membrane proteins actually arrive there, and this is the sorting machinery that reads targeting signals and delivers cargo to the lysosomal lumen or membrane. The canonical route begins in the Golgi, where an N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase complex (GNPTAB/GNPTG with its accessory factor LYSET) tags newly made hydrolases with mannose-6-phosphate; the cation-dependent and cation-independent receptors M6PR and IGF2R then bind these tags and hand cargo to endosomes, with GGA and AP-3 adaptors, retromer-like and GARP subunits, and sortilin-family receptors routing other cargo.
