Late endosome-lysosome fusion and maturation depend on RAB7A and ESCRT/VPS4 activity, and class III PI3K components link the same compartment to autophagosome delivery. Loss of the phosphotransferase causes mucolipidosis, and receptor or adaptor defects produce lysosomal storage, pigmentation and immune disorders, since undelivered enzymes are secreted instead of degrading substrates.

Newly made hydrolases and membrane proteins reach the lysosome, the animal cell's vacuolar compartment, only if they carry the right sorting signal and meet the machinery that reads it; this targeting is what gives the lysosome its degradative content. Mannose-6-phosphate tagging by the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase subunits and the receptors that bind that tag, together with sortilin and SORL1, divert acid hydrolases out of the secretory route, while adaptor complexes, retromer- and GARP-related components, ESCRT subunits and RAB7A-directed maturation steps deliver cargo through endosomes. Related activity supports autophagosome formation and cargo capture, via the PIK3C3-BECN1-ATG14 lipid kinase complex and receptors such as SQSTM1 and NCOA4 for ferritin. Loss of these steps causes lysosomal storage disease, pigment and platelet granule defects, and neurodegeneration, linking the pathway to cellular clearance, organelle biogenesis and iron handling.

Peroxisomes have no internal genome, so every enzyme they contain must be made in the cytosol and imported after folding; protein targeting to the peroxisome is that delivery system. It supplies the organelle with the catalase, beta-oxidation and ether-lipid enzymes that handle very-long-chain fatty acids, branched-chain lipids, plasmalogen synthesis and hydrogen peroxide, and its failure causes the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, with neuronal migration defects and early death. Cargo bearing a C-terminal type 1 signal is captured by the PEX5 receptor and cargo with an N-terminal type 2 signal by PEX7, which dock at the membrane and release their load into the matrix; the PEX1-PEX6 AAA-ATPase pair then recycles the receptor using ATP, while PEX19 and PEX16 handle insertion of membrane proteins and organelle formation. Matrix residents such as HACL1 and the protease LONP2 are among the imported clients.

protein targeting to mitochondrion covers the delivery of nuclear-encoded proteins to mitochondria and their translocation across the outer and inner membranes, the route by which almost the entire mitochondrial proteome is built since the organelle's own genome encodes only a handful of subunits. Cytosolic precursors bearing targeting signals are recognised by outer-membrane receptors and passed through the TOM channel, then handed to small intermembrane-space chaperones or the TIM23 translocase and pulled inward by a matrix motor; presequences are then clipped by processing peptidases and degraded, and rhomboid and AAA proteases mature or clear substrates. Import efficiency doubles as a quality-control readout: PINK1 stalled on depolarised mitochondria recruits Parkin and ubiquitin machinery to trigger mitophagy, linking this pathway to fission, apoptotic priming, and the neurodegeneration seen when import or its surveillance fails.

Nearly all mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol and must be delivered to the correct submitochondrial compartment, and protein targeting to the mitochondrion is the recognition-and-import step that makes this possible. Presequences are read by outer-membrane receptors and the translocation pore (TOMM20, TOMM22, TOMM40 and partners), passed to inner-membrane carriers of the TIMM family with the TIMM44 motor, and then clipped by matrix processing peptidases (PMPCA/PMPCB, MIPEP) or intramembrane proteases such as PARL and HTRA2 to yield mature protein. Import efficiency doubles as a quality-control sensor: stalled or unimported precursors stabilise PINK1 at the outer membrane, recruiting parkin and ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes to mark damaged organelles for mitophagy, alongside fission and fusion factors including FIS1, MFF and MFN2. Failures compromise oxidative metabolism and underlie neurodegenerative and neuropathic disease, including parkinsonism and Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2A.

protein processing involved in protein targeting to mitochondrion describes the proteolytic maturation steps that finish mitochondrial protein import. Most proteins made in the cytosol for mitochondria carry N-terminal targeting signals that must be clipped off after translocation, and only then do they fold, assemble into respiratory complexes, or reach their correct sub-compartment. The matrix processing peptidase, built from the catalytic PMPCB and regulatory PMPCA subunits, removes the presequence, and the mitochondrial intermediate peptidase trims a residual octapeptide from a subset of substrates; the inner membrane peptidase subunits IMMP1L and IMMP2L cleave signals from proteins sorted into the intermembrane space. UQCRC1 is a structural relative of the processing peptidase within complex III. Loss of these activities strands unprocessed precursors, impairs oxidative phosphorylation, and causes mitochondrial disease with cardiomyopathy and neurodegeneration.

Most mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol with an N-terminal targeting signal that must be cut off once the protein arrives, and this proteolytic maturation is what completes import and lets the mature protein fold, assemble and function. The matrix processing peptidase, a heterodimer of PMPCA and PMPCB, removes the presequence from incoming precursors, and MIPEP trims residual octapeptides from a subset of them, including subunits of the respiratory chain. The inner membrane peptidase subunits IMMP1L and IMMP2L cleave signals from proteins routed to the intermembrane space. Loss of these steps leaves unprocessed precursors that cannot mature, causing respiratory chain deficiency and neurodegenerative and ataxic disease; PMPCA and MIPEP mutations give cerebellar ataxia and cardiomyopathy. The presence of LRRK2 and the complex III core subunit UQCRC1 links this processing to mitochondrial quality control and assembly of oxidative phosphorylation complexes.

This is the broad territory of lipid metabolism: the synthesis, modification, transport and breakdown of fatty acids, glycerolipids, phospholipids, sphingolipids, sterols and isoprenoids, together with the regulatory machinery that sets their rates. It supplies membrane bilayers, energy stores, signalling molecules and steroid hormones, so its failure spans dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis, fatty liver, lipodystrophy, lysosomal storage disease, peroxisomal disorders and skin barrier defects. Represented here are de novo fatty acid synthesis and elongation, mitochondrial and peroxisomal beta-oxidation with carnitine-dependent import, cholesterol synthesis from mevalonate and its sterol-sensing control through SREBP factors, bile acid and steroid hydroxylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes, glycerophospholipid and inositol phosphate turnover by phospholipases and kinases, ceramide and glycosphingolipid handling, eicosanoid production from arachidonate, GPI anchor assembly, lipoprotein assembly and receptor-mediated uptake, and hormonal and nuclear receptor control by insulin, AMPK, PPARs and liver X and farnesoid receptors.

Fatty acid metabolism covers the making, breaking, activation and chemical modification of long-chain carboxylic acids, and it determines whether a cell stores energy as lipid or burns it. Its reach extends from the acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase steps of de novo lipogenesis, through elongation and desaturation that set membrane fluidity, to carnitine-dependent import and the mitochondrial and peroxisomal beta-oxidation spirals that feed the respiratory chain during fasting. Acyl-CoA synthetases and thioesterases set the activated acyl pool; lipases and phospholipases liberate substrate from stores and membranes; cytochromes P450, lipoxygenases and cyclooxygenases convert released arachidonate into prostaglandins, leukotrienes and related signals. Nutrient sensors including AMPK subunits, PPARs, SREBP with SCAP, and insulin-responsive IRS proteins tune the whole system. Defects cause hypoglycaemia with sudden infant death, peroxisomal and leukodystrophy syndromes, fatty liver and insulin resistance.

Cells build their own fatty acids for membrane lipids, energy storage, protein acylation and signalling molecules, and this biosynthetic programme is where carbon from citrate is committed to that purpose. The core route runs from ATP-citrate lyase through acetyl-CoA carboxylase, whose malonyl-CoA product is condensed by the multidomain fatty acid synthase into palmitate; elongases and desaturases then extend and unsaturate the chain to give the very long chain, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated species membranes require, while acyl-CoA synthetases activate fatty acids for further use. Output is tuned to nutritional state by AMP-activated protein kinase, the SREBP-regulating proteins SCAP and INSIG, carbohydrate-responsive and liver X receptor transcription factors, and a set of microRNAs. Downstream branches convert released polyunsaturated acids into prostaglandins, thromboxane and leukotrienes. Dysregulation underlies hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance, and the lipogenic enzymes are markedly upregulated in tumours; peroxisomal transporter defects cause demyelinating disease.

Breaking fatty acids down two carbons at a time is how heart, muscle, liver and other tissues generate ATP when glucose is scarce, and how the liver makes ketone bodies during fasting. Beta-oxidation begins with activation of the fatty acid to its CoA thioester; long chains are then shuttled across the mitochondrial inner membrane by the carnitine palmitoyltransferase system with CPT1 as the rate-limiting, malonyl-CoA-sensitive step, while very-long-chain and branched substrates are pre-shortened in peroxisomes by acyl-CoA oxidases and imported by ABCD transporters. Each mitochondrial cycle runs dehydrogenation, hydration, oxidation and thiolysis, feeding electrons through the electron transfer flavoprotein to the respiratory chain and acetyl-CoA to the TCA cycle. PPAR transcription factors and insulin signalling tune capacity to nutritional state. Inherited defects in the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, the trifunctional protein or carnitine transfer cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis; peroxisomal failure underlies adrenoleukodystrophy.

Cells build monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids to keep membranes fluid, to store energy, and to supply the precursors of lipid signalling molecules. Desaturases introduce double bonds into saturated chains, with stearoyl-CoA desaturase generating oleate and the FADS1/FADS2 pair carrying out the delta-5 and delta-6 steps that convert dietary linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid into arachidonic acid and long-chain omega-3 species; ELOVL enzymes alternately elongate the growing chains, and peroxisomal transporters and reductases handle very long chain products. Much of the downstream output feeds eicosanoid production: phospholipases release arachidonate, cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases oxygenate it, and terminal synthases make prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane, linking this biosynthetic capacity to inflammation, platelet function and vascular tone. Defects in chain elongation cause retinal and neurological disease, and the desaturation steps are closely tied to hepatic lipogenesis and insulin resistance.

Acyl-CoA thioesters are the activated form in which fatty acids, acetate and the carbon skeletons of amino acids enter metabolism, and this pathway covers their formation, interconversion and hydrolysis. It sets the balance between burning and storing fat: long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases charge free fatty acids with coenzyme A, thioesterases release them again to tune the free acyl-CoA pool, and acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA for fatty acid synthase and the elongase cycle that extends chains in the ER. The same currency feeds mitochondrial oxidation, cholesterol synthesis via HMG-CoA reductase, triglyceride assembly by diacylglycerol acyltransferases, bile acid and glycine conjugation, and branched-chain and lysine catabolism. Pyruvate dehydrogenase with its kinases and phosphatases governs entry of glucose-derived carbon. Defects produce organic acidaemias, peroxisomal disease and disturbed lipid handling.

Neutral lipids — triacylglycerols, diacylglycerols, cholesteryl esters and retinyl esters — are the cell's and the body's energy and sterol reserve, and this pathway covers their synthesis, storage and breakdown. It determines how dietary fat is absorbed and packaged into lipoproteins, how adipocytes store fat and release it as fatty acids during fasting, and how much triglyceride accumulates in liver and muscle; its dysregulation underlies hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver disease and insulin resistance. Glycerolipid synthesis proceeds through acyltransferase and phosphatidate phosphatase steps to diacylglycerol and then to triacylglycerol by DGAT1 and DGAT2, while lipases such as LPL, PNPLA2, LIPE and MGLL hydrolyse stored and circulating esters, with perilipins and ABHD5 governing access to the lipid droplet surface. Apolipoproteins, CETP, MTTP and receptors including LDLR and SCARB1 handle interorgan transport, and SREBF1, INSIG proteins and liver X receptors provide transcriptional control.

Monoacylglycerol biosynthesis produces glycerol esterified with a single fatty acid, the intermediate that links dietary fat absorption to triglyceride storage and also the precursor of signalling lipids such as 2-arachidonoylglycerol. In enterocytes, fatty acids and monoacylglycerol taken up from the gut lumen are re-esterified on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane by acyl-CoA-dependent acyltransferases, and the monoacylglycerol acyltransferases and diacylglycerol acyltransferases in this group carry out sequential acylation steps that rebuild triglyceride for chylomicron assembly. A phospholipase-mediated route contributes by releasing acyl chains from glycerophospholipids. Flux through these enzymes sets how efficiently fat is absorbed and deposited, which is why diacylglycerol acyltransferase activity is a target in obesity, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance; loss of DGAT1 in humans causes congenital diarrhoea with protein-losing enteropathy.

Triglyceride metabolic process covers the synthesis, storage, transport and breakdown of the triesters of glycerol that serve as the body's main energy reserve. It determines how dietary fat is absorbed, how much lipid is deposited in adipocytes and liver, and how fatty acids are released to fuel other tissues; its dysregulation underlies hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver disease, lipodystrophy and pancreatitis. Synthesis runs through the glycerol-3-phosphate and monoacylglycerol routes, with acyltransferases, phosphatidate phosphatases of the lipin family and the terminal diacylglycerol acyltransferases DGAT1/2 building triglyceride for packaging into lipid droplets coated by perilipins and CIDE proteins. Mobilisation depends on hormone-sensitive lipase, ATGL with its activator ABHD5, and monoacylglycerol lipase under protein kinase A control. Secreted lipoproteins and their apolipoprotein regulators, together with lipoprotein lipase and its endothelial anchor GPIHBP1, deliver plasma triglyceride to tissues, all under transcriptional control by SREBP and liver X receptors.

Triglyceride metabolism is how the body stores surplus fatty acids as neutral lipid and releases them again when fuel is needed, and it links dietary fat absorption, adipose storage, hepatic lipid handling and plasma lipoprotein transport into one continuous economy. Synthesis proceeds through glycerol-3-phosphate acylation by GPAT and AGPAT enzymes, dephosphorylation of phosphatidate by lipins, and final esterification by DGAT1 and DGAT2; monoacylglycerol acyltransferases provide the intestinal re-esterification route after pancreatic lipases digest dietary fat. Mobilisation runs the other way through ATGL (PNPLA2) with its activator ABHD5, hormone-sensitive lipase and monoacylglycerol lipase acting on perilipin-coated droplets under protein kinase A control. Circulating triglyceride is delivered by apoB-containing particles and hydrolysed by lipoprotein lipase with its APOC2 activator and GPIHBP1 anchor, while SREBF1, INSIG and liver X receptors set transcriptional tone. Defects cause hypertriglyceridaemia, lipodystrophy, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance.

Membrane lipid metabolism covers the synthesis, remodelling and breakdown of the lipids that build biological membranes, here dominated by sphingolipids, glycosphingolipids and GPI anchors. It sets membrane fluidity and raft organisation, supplies the ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate messengers that decide between apoptosis and proliferation, builds the skin permeability barrier, and provides the glycolipid coats used for cell recognition. Serine palmitoyltransferase subunits begin de novo synthesis, ceramide synthases and desaturases elaborate the backbone, very-long-chain fatty acid elongases and reductases supply acyl chains, and glycosyltransferases and sialyltransferases decorate the headgroups. Lysosomal hydrolases such as glucocerebrosidase, hexosaminidases, arylsulfatase-related activators and acid ceramidase, with their saposin activators, return lipids to their parts; their loss causes sphingolipidoses including Gaucher and Tay-Sachs disease. A parallel arm assembles GPI anchors that tether surface proteins, and kinases and phosphatases tune sphingosine-1-phosphate gradients guiding lymphocyte trafficking.

Phospholipid metabolic process covers the synthesis, remodelling and breakdown of the phosphate-containing lipids that build every cellular membrane and serve as the substrate pool for lipid signalling. It sets membrane composition, curvature and fluidity, supplies surfactant in the lung and myelin in nerve, anchors GPI-linked proteins to the cell surface, and generates the second messengers that relay receptor activation. The genes span de novo glycerophospholipid synthesis through glycerol-3-phosphate acylation and the Kennedy pathway, the Lands cycle acyltransferases and phospholipases that swap acyl chains, cardiolipin production and tafazzin-dependent remodelling in mitochondria, the stepwise assembly of GPI anchors, and the phosphoinositide kinases, phosphatases and phospholipase C enzymes that mark organelle identity and drive calcium and PI3K signalling. Also included are lipid transfer and transport proteins and lipoprotein-associated enzymes. Defects cause Barth syndrome, myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, surfactant deficiency and dyslipidaemia.

Phospholipids are the structural backbone of every cellular membrane and the source of most lipid second messengers, and this metabolic programme builds, remodels, degrades and interconverts them. It sets membrane fluidity and curvature, supplies surfactant and lipoprotein lipids, and generates the signals that drive growth, secretion and inflammation; its failure underlies myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, surfactant deficiency, Barth syndrome and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria. Glycerophosphate acyltransferases and CDP-choline/ethanolamine enzymes assemble the major classes, while lysophospholipid acyltransferases and diverse phospholipases remodel acyl chains and release arachidonate for eicosanoid synthesis. A large phosphoinositide arm—PI kinases, PIP5 and PIP4 kinases, myotubularin and INPP/OCRL phosphatases, and phospholipase C isoforms—writes and erases the lipid codes that mark organelle identity and recruit trafficking and signalling proteins. Further branches handle cardiolipin for mitochondrial function, GPI anchor assembly, sphingomyelin exchange, and lipid transfer between membranes.

Phosphatidylethanolamine is one of the most abundant lipids in cellular membranes, and its biosynthesis supplies the cone-shaped lipid that lets bilayers curve, fuse and divide — needed for cytokinesis, mitochondrial fission and fusion, and autophagosome formation, where it is the anchor conjugated to LC3. Two routes converge on it: the cytidine pathway, in which ethanolamine kinases phosphorylate ethanolamine, PCYT2 forms the CDP-ethanolamine intermediate, and a membrane aminoalcohol phosphotransferase (CEPT1 or SELENOI) transfers the head group to diacylglycerol; and decarboxylation of phosphatidylserine by mitochondrial PISD, which generates the inner-membrane pool. The choline kinases present here reflect the shared enzymology with phosphatidylcholine synthesis. Loss of these steps is damaging in proportion to how much membrane a cell must build — SELENOI and PCYT2 defects cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and neurodevelopmental disease, and the pathway also furnishes substrate for lipid peroxidation during ferroptosis.

Phospholipids are made largely in the endoplasmic reticulum but must reach the plasma membrane and other destinations, and this transfer to membranes is how lipid is moved between bilayers and how membrane composition is set rather than left to bulk vesicle flow. It matters for membrane identity, for the asymmetric distribution of lipid between leaflets, and for lipid-dependent signalling at organelle contact sites. Oxysterol-binding protein family members here act as lipid transfer proteins that shuttle sterols and phospholipids such as phosphatidylserine between apposed membranes, linking ER contact zones to the plasma membrane. Other members contribute transport and metabolic steps: an ABC transporter that moves retinoid-phosphatidylethanolamine conjugates across photoreceptor disc membranes, an enzyme acting on phosphoethanolamine, and a purinergic receptor whose activation drives phospholipid scrambling and exposure. Failure of such handling disrupts retinal function and membrane lipid homeostasis.

Glycerophospholipid metabolism builds, remodels and breaks down the phospholipids that make every cellular membrane, and it also generates most of the lipid second messengers cells use to signal. Its outputs set membrane curvature, fluidity and surface charge, supply lung surfactant and lipoprotein lipids, anchor proteins to the cell surface through GPI attachment, and mark organelle identity. Synthesis proceeds from glycerol-3-phosphate through acyltransferases and cytidine-nucleotide steps to phosphatidylcholine, ethanolamine, serine, inositol and cardiolipin, while phospholipases, lysophospholipid acyltransferases and serine hydrolases remodel acyl chains and release arachidonate. A large kinase and phosphatase network writes and erases phosphoinositide codes that recruit trafficking and autophagy machinery, with PTEN and phosphoinositide 3-kinases governing growth signalling. Defects cause surfactant deficiency, myotubular and demyelinating neuropathies, GPI-anchor deficiencies, and cardiolipin-linked cardiomyopathy.

Diacylglycerol sits at the junction of fat storage and lipid signalling, and this is the set of reactions that generate it. Cells make it by two routes represented here: stepwise acylation of the glycerol backbone, where a mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferase initiates the pathway and monoacylglycerol acyltransferases add the second acyl chain, and phospholipase C cleavage of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate, which liberates diacylglycerol as a membrane-bound second messenger alongside inositol trisphosphate. Lipolytic release from stored triglyceride by adipose triglyceride lipase also yields it, while DGAT2 consumes it to complete triglyceride synthesis. The output therefore feeds both protein kinase C activation and neutral lipid deposition, and the intestinal and adipose enzymes involved connect dietary fat absorption to hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance when flux through them is excessive.

Phosphatidylglycerol biosynthesis supplies the anionic phospholipid that inner mitochondrial membranes need, both as a membrane lipid in its own right and as the obligatory precursor of cardiolipin; in the lung it is also a major component of surfactant. The route begins with phosphatidic acid, which an acyltransferase such as GPAM helps generate, and proceeds through CDP-diacylglycerol made by CDS2 at the endoplasmic reticulum or by TAMM41 inside mitochondria. PGS1 condenses that intermediate with glycerol-3-phosphate, and the phosphatase PTPMT1 dephosphorylates the product to yield phosphatidylglycerol, which cardiolipin synthase CRLS1 then converts to cardiolipin. Because cardiolipin organises respiratory chain supercomplexes and supports cristae architecture, defects here compromise oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial morphology, linking this short lipid pathway to cellular energy metabolism, apoptotic signalling and inherited mitochondrial disease.

Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in mammalian membranes, and its synthesis sets membrane bulk, curvature and the capacity to export lipid in bile, lipoproteins and lung surfactant. Loss of it causes hepatic steatosis and surfactant deficiency, because cells cannot package neutral lipid or make a functional air-liquid interface. Production runs mainly through the CDP-choline route: choline enters on SLC44 family transporters, is trapped by choline kinases CHKA and CHKB, converted to CDP-choline by the rate-setting cytidylyltransferases PCYT1A and PCYT1B, and condensed with diacylglycerol by CHPT1 or the dual-specificity CEPT1. The liver adds an alternative supply by trimethylating phosphatidylethanolamine via PEMT. Remodelling enzymes such as LPCAT1 and LPCAT3 reacylate lysophosphatidylcholine to set fatty acyl composition, MFSD2A imports lysophosphatidylcholine-bound docosahexaenoic acid, and LCAT and apolipoproteins link the pool to plasma lipoprotein metabolism.

Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in mammalian membranes, and the CDP-choline pathway is the main route by which cells make it from dietary and recycled choline. The output supplies bulk membrane lipid for growth and division, surfactant in the lung, bile phospholipid, and the lipoprotein surface needed to export triglyceride from liver, so failure of the route causes hepatic steatosis and impaired VLDL secretion. Choline kinases phosphorylate choline first; the rate-limiting step is the conversion of phosphocholine to CDP-choline by CTP:phosphocholine cytidylyltransferase, an enzyme regulated by reversible association with membranes that senses lipid demand. Cholinephosphotransferase then transfers the phosphocholine head group onto diacylglycerol, an activity shared with a dual-specificity enzyme that also produces phosphatidylethanolamine. Mutations in the muscle-associated choline kinase cause a congenital muscular dystrophy with abnormal mitochondria.

Phosphatidylserine is a minority membrane lipid with outsized jobs: kept on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane it recruits and activates signalling proteins such as protein kinase C and small GTPase effectors, and when exposed on the outer leaflet it becomes the "eat me" signal that marks apoptotic cells for phagocytosis and provides the surface for blood coagulation reactions. This metabolic programme covers its synthesis, remodelling, transport and turnover. Base-exchange synthases build it from other phospholipids in a specialised ER domain, acyltransferases of the MBOAT and LPCAT families re-acylate lysophospholipids to set fatty acyl composition, phospholipases and serine hydrolases including ABHD12 degrade it and its lyso forms, oxysterol-binding-related proteins move it between organelle membranes at contact sites, and scramblases collapse leaflet asymmetry. Loss of these steps disturbs membrane identity, lipid signalling and clearance of dying cells.

Phosphatidylinositol biosynthesis supplies the lipid backbone from which all phosphoinositide signals are made, and the genes here cover both its synthesis and the kinase/phosphatase cycles that interconvert its phosphorylated forms. CDS1 and CDIPT build the lipid from phosphatidic acid and myo-inositol, while inositol monophosphatases and inositol polyphosphate phosphatases recycle the inositol headgroup. From this pool, class I, II and III PI3Ks, PI4Ks, PIP5Ks and PIKFYVE generate the pool-specific messengers that mark plasma membrane, Golgi and endosomes, opposed by PTEN, OCRL, SACM1L, the myotubularins and synaptojanins. Downstream consequences include growth factor and receptor signalling, autophagosome initiation through the BECN1-PIK3C3-ATG14 complex, membrane traffic, and GPI anchor assembly by the PIG and PGAP enzymes, which use phosphatidylinositol as substrate. Loss of individual steps causes myopathy, neuropathy, Lowe syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and cancer-associated PI3K/PTEN dysregulation.

Sphingolipids are built on a long-chain amino alcohol backbone and serve both as structural components of membranes and as signalling molecules, so their synthesis and breakdown sets membrane order, skin barrier integrity and cell fate decisions. Synthesis begins with serine palmitoyltransferase subunits, restrained by ORMDL proteins, and proceeds through ceramide synthases that attach fatty acids of defined length; ceramide is then converted to sphingomyelin, glucosyl- and galactosylceramide, and onward to the many gangliosides made by sialyl- and galactosyltransferases. Catabolism runs through sphingomyelinases, glucocerebrosidase, ceramidases and lysosomal glycosidases with their activator proteins, and defects here cause the sphingolipidoses, including Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, Krabbe, Fabry and Tay-Sachs disease. Sphingosine kinases and the lyase control the balance between pro-apoptotic ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate, a secreted mediator of lymphocyte trafficking and vascular barrier function. Very-long-chain fatty acid elongation and omega-hydroxylation feed the ceramides required for epidermal waterproofing.

Ceramide sits at the hub of sphingolipid metabolism, and the reactions that make, modify and destroy it determine both the structural lipids of membranes and a signalling lipid that pushes cells toward growth arrest, stress responses and apoptosis. Synthesis begins with serine palmitoyltransferase and its regulatory subunits, passes through reduction and N-acylation by a family of ceramide synthases with distinct acyl-chain preferences, and is desaturated to ceramide; alternatively, sphingomyelinases and glycosidases regenerate ceramide from sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids. Ceramidases and sphingosine kinases convert it onward to sphingosine-1-phosphate, setting the balance between pro-death and pro-survival lipid signals. Downstream glycosylation and sialylation build gangliosides and galactosylceramide for myelin. Loss of individual steps causes lysosomal storage diseases such as Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs and Krabbe, while defects in very-long-chain ceramide production disrupt the skin permeability barrier in ichthyosis.

Glycosylceramide metabolism covers the making and breaking of the simplest glycosphingolipids, the glucosyl- and galactosylceramides that seed the entire glycosphingolipid series and build the lipid rafts and myelin sheaths of the nervous system. Synthesis begins when ceramide is glucosylated by UGCG or galactosylated by UGT8, after which galactosyltransferases, sialyltransferases and a sulfotransferase extend or sulfate the head group; fatty acid 2-hydroxylation tunes the ceramide backbone. Degradation runs through lysosomal and cytosolic glycosidases, including acid beta-glucosidase and galactosylceramidase, with SCARB2 required to deliver the former to the lysosome. Loss of these catabolic steps causes sphingolipidoses — Gaucher, Krabbe and Fabry disease — in which undegraded glycolipid accumulates and damages macrophages, oligodendrocytes or vascular endothelium. The balance also feeds into membrane signalling, energy sensing and ceramide-dependent stress responses.

Glucosylceramide is the simplest glycosphingolipid and the gateway metabolite from which most complex glycolipids are built, so its synthesis and breakdown set the composition of membrane lipid rafts, the skin permeability barrier and myelin. Ceramide glucosyltransferase (UGCG) makes it at the Golgi; galactosyltransferases extend it toward lactosylceramide and higher gangliosides, while glucocerebrosidases degrade it either in the lysosome (GBA1, delivered there by its trafficking receptor SCARB2) or in the cytosol-facing non-lysosomal route (GBA2). Failure of lysosomal degradation causes Gaucher disease, with glucosylceramide-laden macrophages, and the same deficiency is among the strongest genetic risks for Parkinson disease. Hydroxylation of the fatty acyl chain by FA2H diversifies the ceramide backbone, and kinase and microRNA regulators tie flux through this route to cellular energy state and stress signalling.

Glucosylceramide sits at the junction of sphingolipid recycling, and its catabolism releases glucose from the ceramide backbone so that membrane lipid turnover can be completed and ceramide reused or degraded further. The lysosomal acid β-glucosidase encoded by GBA1 performs this step inside the lysosome, and its loss causes Gaucher disease, with glucosylceramide accumulating in macrophages and producing hepatosplenomegaly, bone disease and, in severe forms, neurodegeneration; the same gene is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Parkinson disease. Delivery of that enzyme to the lysosome depends on the membrane protein encoded by SCARB2 rather than on mannose-6-phosphate targeting. A non-lysosomal, cytosol-facing glucosylceramidase and a cytosolic glucosidase provide activity in other compartments, while protein kinase C signalling and several microRNAs modulate the pathway's output. Sphingolipid flux through this route shapes membrane composition, ceramide-dependent stress signalling and macrophage lipid handling.

Galactosylceramide biosynthesis builds the simplest glycosphingolipid of myelin, attaching galactose to a ceramide backbone and then decorating it further. These lipids, together with their sulfated form sulfatide, make up a large fraction of the myelin sheath and of oligodendrocyte and Schwann cell membranes, where they stabilize lipid rafts, support axon-glia adhesion and maintain the integrity of compact myelin. UGT8 performs the committed galactosyl transfer from UDP-galactose to ceramide, GAL3ST1 sulfates the product at the galactose 3-position to give sulfatide, and FA2H generates the 2-hydroxylated fatty acyl chains characteristic of these lipids; galactosyltransferase activities can extend the head group. Loss of these steps disturbs myelin architecture and nerve conduction, and defective 2-hydroxylation causes a hereditary spastic paraplegia with leukodystrophy, linking sphingolipid head-group chemistry to nervous system function.

Sphingomyelin is the major sphingolipid of the plasma membrane and of myelin, where together with cholesterol it forms the ordered, detergent-resistant domains that organise receptor signalling and insulate axons. Its metabolic turnover both builds membranes and generates messengers: synthesis condenses ceramide with phosphocholine at the Golgi via sphingomyelin synthases, while acid and neutral sphingomyelinases hydrolyse it back to ceramide, a pro-apoptotic and stress-signalling lipid released in response to cytokines and other insults. Serine palmitoyltransferase subunits supply the initiating step of de novo sphingoid base formation, and ceramide transfer and oxysterol-binding proteins with their ER-anchoring VAP partner move substrate between organelles at membrane contact sites. Loss of acid sphingomyelinase causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, with lysosomal sphingomyelin storage, neurodegeneration and organomegaly; neutral sphingomyelinase deficiency disturbs bone mineralisation.

Sphingomyelin catabolic process is the hydrolysis of sphingomyelin, the major sphingolipid of the plasma membrane and lysosomal membranes, into ceramide and phosphocholine. This single step converts a structural lipid into a potent signalling molecule: ceramide generated here drives apoptosis, stress responses, senescence and membrane microdomain reorganisation, and it feeds the wider sphingolipid network toward sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate. The reaction is carried out by sphingomyelinases distinguished by pH optimum and location — acid sphingomyelinase in the lysosome, neutral enzymes at the plasma membrane, Golgi and nuclear envelope, and an alkaline intestinal enzyme that digests dietary sphingomyelin. Protein kinase C signalling couples receptor stimulation to this ceramide release. Loss of the lysosomal enzyme causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B, in which undegraded sphingomyelin accumulates with neurodegeneration and organomegaly, while the neutral enzymes shape bone mineralisation and membrane vesicle release.

Sphingomyelin catabolism converts an abundant membrane phospholipid into ceramide and phosphocholine, and because ceramide is itself a signalling lipid, the reaction couples membrane composition to decisions about stress responses, growth arrest and apoptosis. The sphingomyelinases here work in distinct settings: an acid enzyme in the lysosome, whose loss causes Niemann-Pick disease types A and B through massive sphingomyelin storage and neurodegeneration, and neutral, magnesium-dependent enzymes at the plasma membrane, Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum that generate ceramide locally in response to cytokines and stress, with roles in bone and cartilage mineralisation. Related phosphodiesterases act on the intestinal brush border to digest dietary sphingomyelin or on extracellular substrates in macrophages, and a protein kinase C isoform links receptor signalling to enzyme activation. The ceramide produced feeds onward into sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate metabolism.

Sphingomyelin biosynthetic process builds the most abundant sphingolipid of the plasma membrane, the lipid that together with cholesterol forms ordered membrane domains and gives the myelin sheath and the epidermal barrier their physical properties. It begins with serine palmitoyltransferase, whose SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 subunits condense serine and palmitoyl-CoA to commit the cell to sphingoid base synthesis; mutations here cause hereditary sensory neuropathy. Ceramide made in the endoplasmic reticulum is then carried to the Golgi by CERT1 working against VAP anchors at membrane contact sites, where sphingomyelin synthases transfer phosphocholine from phosphatidylcholine onto ceramide, SGMS1 in the Golgi lumen and SGMS2 at the cell surface. Because that reaction consumes ceramide and releases diacylglycerol, it sets the balance between two potent lipid second messengers and thereby links membrane construction to apoptosis and growth signalling.

Sphingomyelin biosynthesis produces the abundant choline-containing sphingolipid of plasma membranes and myelin, where it pairs with cholesterol to form ordered, raft-like domains and sets membrane rigidity and permeability. The route begins with serine palmitoyltransferase (SPTLC1/SPTLC2) condensing serine and palmitoyl-CoA to launch de novo sphingoid base synthesis, and ends when a sphingomyelin synthase transfers phosphocholine onto ceramide: SGMS1 acting in the Golgi and SGMS2 largely at the cell surface, with SAMD8 a related ceramide phosphoethanolamine synthase. Because ceramide is made in the endoplasmic reticulum, delivery depends on ceramide transfer by CERT1 tethered through VAPA, alongside lipid-transfer and membrane-contact roles for OSBP. The balance struck here governs how much ceramide accumulates as a pro-apoptotic signal versus being consumed; mutations in serine palmitoyltransferase subunits cause hereditary sensory neuropathy, and the pathway also feeds cellular cholesterol and choline handling.

Glycosphingolipid metabolism builds and breaks down the sugar-bearing lipids that decorate the outer face of the plasma membrane, where they organize membrane microdomains, define blood group and ganglioside antigens, and modulate receptor signalling and cell adhesion. Synthesis begins with serine palmitoyltransferase subunits and ceramide synthases making the sphingoid backbone, after which glucosylceramide or galactosylceramide synthases add the first sugar and a large set of galactosyl-, N-acetylgalactosaminyl-, fucosyl- and sialyltransferases elaborate globo-, lacto- and ganglioside series; ST8SIA enzymes add the polysialic linkages typical of brain gangliosides. Catabolism runs in the lysosome through glucocerebrosidase, galactosylceramidase, alpha-galactosidase, beta-hexosaminidases with their GM2 activator, sphingomyelinase and sialidases. Because neurons are especially dependent on this turnover, loss of individual hydrolases produces the sphingolipidoses " template" group of storage diseases, including Gaucher, Fabry, Krabbe and Tay-Sachs disease, with progressive neurodegeneration.

Glycosphingolipid biosynthesis builds the sugar-capped lipids that populate the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, where they organise membrane microdomains, define blood group and tumour-associated antigens, and serve as receptors for toxins and pathogens. The route begins with de novo ceramide synthesis — serine palmitoyltransferase subunits, ketosphinganine reductase, a desaturase and ceramide synthases — and diverges when ceramide is either glucosylated by UGCG or galactosylated by UGT8, the latter feeding galactosylceramide and its sulfated form for myelin. Sequential Golgi glycosyltransferases then elaborate the lacto-, globo- and ganglioside series, with sialyltransferases and polysialyltransferases adding the acidic residues that dominate neural membranes. Loss of individual steps causes hereditary spastic paraplegia, infantile epileptic encephalopathy and severe neurodegeneration, underscoring how much neuronal and glial membrane function depends on this glycolipid output.

Gangliosides are sialylated glycosphingolipids concentrated in neuronal plasma membranes, and their catabolism is the stepwise dismantling of those glycan headgroups in the lysosome so that sugars, sialic acid and ceramide can be recycled. Because neurons turn over membrane lipid continuously, blockage anywhere along this route causes progressive storage disease: deficiency of the hexosaminidase subunits HEXA or HEXB, or of their obligatory lipid-binding cofactor GM2A, causes GM2 gangliosidoses such as Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff disease, while loss of the beta-galactosidase GLB1 gives GM1 gangliosidosis, both presenting as neurodegeneration in infancy. Sialidases initiate breakdown by removing sialic acid, with NEU1 acting in the lysosome and NEU3 at the plasma membrane, where its remodelling of ganglioside patterns also influences cell signalling, adhesion and differentiation rather than degradation alone.

Eicosanoids are the C20 fatty acid signalling lipids — prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes and related oxygenated products — that drive inflammation, fever, pain, platelet aggregation, vascular tone, bronchoconstriction and renal salt handling, and their synthesis and breakdown are the reactions collected here. Arachidonate is first released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipases such as PLA2G4A, then committed down one of three branches: cyclooxygenases PTGS1 and PTGS2 feed prostaglandin and thromboxane synthases; lipoxygenases with the ALOX5-activating protein generate leukotrienes, with LTC4S adding glutathione and LTA4H yielding LTB4; and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases produce epoxy- and hydroxyeicosatrienoic acids. Dehydrogenases, reductases, glutathione transferases and dipeptidases terminate or interconvert the products, while transporters export them. This chemistry is the target of aspirin, other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and anti-asthma leukotriene blockade, and its dysregulation underlies chronic inflammatory disease and thrombosis.

Leukotrienes are lipid mediators of inflammation that drive bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leak and leukocyte recruitment, and their metabolism determines the intensity and duration of asthmatic and allergic responses. Synthesis begins when phospholipases release arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; 5-lipoxygenase, working with its nuclear membrane partner ALOX5AP, converts it to the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. From there the pathway branches: LTA4H hydrolyses it to the chemotactic leukotriene B4, while LTC4S and related membrane glutathione transferases conjugate glutathione to form cysteinyl leukotriene C4, which ABCC1 exports and gamma-glutamyl transferases and dipeptidases process successively to LTD4 and LTE4. Termination depends on omega-hydroxylation by CYP4F enzymes and reduction steps that inactivate LTB4. Kinase and phagocyte oxidase components reflect the activation of this route in stimulated myeloid cells, and it is the target of leukotriene-modifying asthma drugs.

Prostanoid metabolism covers the making, interconversion and disposal of prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane, the short-lived lipid mediators that set vascular tone, platelet aggregation, fever, pain sensitisation and mucosal protection in the stomach and kidney. It begins with release of arachidonate from membrane phospholipids by phospholipases such as PLA2G4A, after which the cyclooxygenases PTGS1 and PTGS2 generate the unstable endoperoxide PGH2. Competing terminal synthases then decide the output: PTGES for PGE2, PTGDS and the haematopoietic HPGDS for PGD2, PTGIS for prostacyclin and TBXAS1 for thromboxane. Levels are limited by oxidation through HPGD and by reductases including PTGR1 and several aldo-keto reductases, which convert or inactivate individual prostanoids. Because inflammatory signals such as IL1B induce the inducible cyclooxygenase, this route is the target of aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and its dysregulation underlies inflammatory pain, thrombosis and tumour-associated PGE2 signalling.

Steroids share a four-ring nucleus, and the steroid biosynthetic process covers both its construction from acetyl-CoA and the subsequent tailoring that turns one sterol into another. It supplies membrane cholesterol, bile acids, vitamin D metabolites, and the adrenal and gonadal hormones that set salt balance, stress responses, and sexual development, so defects here cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia, disorders of sex development, and skeletal dysplasias from blocked post-squalene sterol synthesis. The mevalonate arm runs from HMGCS1 and HMGCR through squalene epoxidation and lanosterol demethylation, under feedback control by the SREBF transcription factors with SCAP and the ER sensors INSIG1/2. Downstream, STAR delivers cholesterol into mitochondria for side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1, and cytochrome P450s with hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and reductases generate cortisol, aldosterone, androgens and oestrogens. Trophic hormones and their receptors, including LHCGR and MC2R, place the whole programme under endocrine command.

Bile acid biosynthesis converts cholesterol into the amphipathic acids that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the intestine, and it is the body's principal route for disposing of excess cholesterol. Hepatic CYP7A1 sets the rate of the classic pathway, with CYP8B1 determining how much cholic acid is made, while CYP27A1, CYP7B1 and CYP39A1 feed an alternative route through oxysterols; AKR1D1, HSD3B7 and AKR1C4 remodel the steroid nucleus, peroxisomal beta-oxidation with AMACR, ACOX2 and SCP2 shortens the side chain, and BAAT plus SLC27A5 conjugate the product before ABCB11 exports it into bile. Output is restrained by feedback: bile acids activate the nuclear receptor FXR, inducing intestinal FGF19 that signals through hepatic FGFR4, with circadian and sterol-transport inputs layered on. Failure produces cholestasis, fat malabsorption and progressive liver disease in infancy.

C21-steroid hormone biosynthesis produces progesterone, glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids, the steroids that sustain pregnancy, regulate stress metabolism and control sodium balance and blood pressure. The rate-limiting step is delivery of cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane, carried out by STAR with the outer-membrane translocator protein TSPO and lipid-transfer proteins such as STARD3 and SCP2; side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1 then yields pregnenolone, which HSD3B1 converts to progesterone and the CYP11B1 and CYP11B2 enzymes finish as cortisol and aldosterone in the adrenal cortex. Output is set by pituitary gonadotropins LHB and FSHB and by angiotensin- and potassium-driven depolarisation through channels including CACNA1H and CLCN2, whose mutation causes familial hyperaldosteronism. Local BMP and WNT signals together with transcriptional regulators such as EGR1 and REST tune steroidogenic gene expression; loss of these steps underlies adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Progesterone biosynthesis is the steroidogenic route that converts cholesterol into the hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation and sustains early pregnancy, and that also supports luteal function and negative feedback on the reproductive axis. Loss or insufficiency of this output causes luteal phase defects and pregnancy failure. The committed chemical step is the conversion of pregnenolone to progesterone by a 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase, acting on substrate delivered to mitochondria by cholesterol-binding and lipid-transfer proteins such as SCP2 and a StAR-related domain carrier. Upstream, pituitary gonadotropins built from the LH and FSH beta subunits drive the granulosa and luteal cells that carry out the synthesis, with immediate-early transcriptional control by EGR1 and modulation by locally acting peptides including adrenomedullin. The pathway therefore links endocrine signalling to intracellular cholesterol trafficking and steroid enzymology.

Androgen biosynthetic process builds testosterone and dihydrotestosterone from steroid precursors, the hormones that drive masculinisation of the fetal genitalia, pubertal virilisation, spermatogenesis and the growth of prostate and hair follicles. It operates mainly in testicular Leydig cells and the adrenal cortex, with peripheral tissues finishing the job: CYP17A1 performs the hydroxylase and lyase steps that divert pregnenolone away from cortisol toward C19 steroids, 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and HSD17B3 complete testosterone synthesis, and SRD5A2 reduces it to the far more potent dihydrogenase-resistant dihydrotestosterone in target tissues. Nuclear receptor coactivation by MED1 and gonadal patterning input from WNT4 link hormone output to the transcriptional programme of the steroidogenic cell. Loss of individual enzymes causes disorders of sex development, 46,XY undervirilisation, or congenital adrenal hyperplasia, while excess flux underlies hyperandrogenism and fuels prostate cancer growth.

Androgen biosynthesis converts cholesterol-derived precursors into testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, the hormones that masculinize the fetal genital tract and drive puberty, spermatogenesis, and prostate growth. Loss of individual steps causes disorders of sex development: CYP17A1 performs the 17"a-hydroxylation and 17,20-lyase cleavage that commit pregnenolone to the C19 series, HSD3B2 supplies the adrenal and gonadal 3"b-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase activity, and HSD17B3 completes testicular testosterone synthesis by reducing androstenedione. Peripheral 5"a-reductases encoded by SRD5A1 and SRD5A2 amplify signalling by converting testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone, the step blocked pharmacologically in benign prostatic hyperplasia and androgenetic alopecia. Regulatory input is represented by the nuclear receptor coactivator MED1 and by WNT4, which restrains steroidogenic differentiation during gonadal development. The route operates chiefly in Leydig cells, adrenal cortex, and androgen target tissues such as skin and prostate.

Estrogen biosynthetic process produces the C18 steroid hormones that drive female sexual development, ovarian cycling, endometrial and mammary growth, and, in both sexes, bone maturation and closure of the growth plate. Its centrepiece is aromatase, CYP19A1, which converts androgens to estrogens in granulosa cells, placenta, adipose tissue and brain and sets the local estrogen supply that feeds nuclear receptor signalling. Flanking it are the 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, which interconvert weak and potent forms: HSD17B1 generates estradiol from estrone, while HSD17B2 reverses that step, so the balance of these oxidoreductases determines hormone potency in a given tissue. Upstream 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase activity supplies precursors from the common steroidogenic route. Loss of aromatase causes virilisation and skeletal defects, while excess local synthesis sustains hormone-dependent breast and endometrial tumours, the rationale for aromatase inhibitors.

Estrogen biosynthesis converts androgen precursors into the C18 steroid hormones that drive female sexual development, ovarian cycling, endometrial and breast growth, and, in both sexes, bone maturation and lipid and brain function. The committed step is aromatization of androgens to estrogens by aromatase (CYP19A1), the only enzyme able to make the aromatic A ring; its loss causes estrogen deficiency with tall stature and unfused epiphyses, and its inhibition is the basis of endocrine therapy for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. Interconversion of potency is handled by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, with HSD17B1 favouring reduction of estrone to the more active estradiol and HSD17B2 oxidizing it back, so local ratios of these enzymes set tissue estrogen exposure. HSD3B1 and additional short-chain and aldo-keto reductases supply and recycle precursors, linking this route to the wider steroidogenic pathway from cholesterol.

Glucocorticoid biosynthesis is the adrenal cortex pathway that converts cholesterol into cortisol, the hormone that sustains blood glucose, blood pressure and the stress response and restrains inflammation. Its output is controlled from above by hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone and pituitary ACTH derived from proopiomelanocortin, acting through the melanocortin 2 receptor to drive cholesterol delivery into mitochondria by STAR and its side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1. Successive hydroxylations by CYP17A1, CYP21A2 and CYP11B1 complete the C21 steroid, while CYP11B2 diverts flux toward mineralocorticoid synthesis in the outer zone; the transcription factor NR5A2 and secreted WNT and BMP signals pattern the steroidogenic cells themselves. Circulating hormone is carried by corticosteroid-binding globulin and feeds back through the glucocorticoid receptor. Enzyme deficiencies here cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia and adrenal insufficiency.

Mineralocorticoid biosynthesis produces aldosterone and related C21 steroids from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex, and it is the endocrine arm of sodium retention, potassium excretion and blood pressure control. The committed enzymatic steps belong to mitochondrial and microsomal cytochromes P450: CYP21A2 hydroxylates at C21, CYP11B1 generates cortisol, and CYP11B2 carries out the final oxidations that make aldosterone unique to the zona glomerulosa. Because glomerulosa cells respond to angiotensin II and extracellular potassium through membrane depolarization, calcium entry via channels such as CACNA1H and chloride conductance through CLCN2 couple electrical signalling to steroid output; gain-of-function changes in either drive primary aldosteronism. WNT4, DKK3 and BMP ligands, together with REST, shape adrenocortical zonation and maintain the glomerulosa phenotype. Enzyme deficiency instead causes salt-wasting and adrenal hyperplasia, while excess aldosterone produces hypertension and hypokalemia.

Steroids are not excreted intact; they must be hydroxylated, reduced, conjugated or ring-cleaved first, and steroid catabolism is the set of reactions that dismantles them. This determines how long a hormone acts, how cholesterol leaves the body, and how vitamin D signalling is terminated. Cytochrome P450 enzymes do most of the oxidative work: CYP7A1 commits cholesterol to bile acid synthesis, CYP46A1 converts brain cholesterol into a form that can cross the blood-brain barrier, and CYP24A1 inactivates active vitamin D under FGF23 control. Reductases and dehydrogenases such as AKR1D1, SRD5A1/2 and HSD11B1 modify the steroid nucleus and reset androgen and glucocorticoid potency, while sulfotransferase and steryl sulfatase activities interconvert sulfated reservoirs with free hormone. Lipoprotein receptors including SCARB1 supply substrate. Loss of individual steps causes bile acid synthesis disorders, hypercalcaemia, or disordered sex steroid exposure.

Cholesterol cannot be oxidised to carbon dioxide, so the body disposes of it by converting it into bile acids and oxysterols that can be excreted — the catabolic route described here. It sets whole-body sterol balance: bile acid synthesis in the liver is the main exit path for cholesterol, and in the brain, where the blood-brain barrier blocks lipoprotein exchange, hydroxylation provides the only meaningful outflow. Cytochrome P450 enzymes commit the sterol nucleus and side chain to degradation, with CYP7A1 performing the rate-limiting 7α-hydroxylation, CYP27A1 acting on the side chain, and CYP46A1 generating the brain-specific 24S-hydroxycholesterol; a reductase then shapes the bile acid ring system. Scavenger receptors and apolipoprotein E deliver and recycle the substrate lipoprotein cholesterol. Loss of these steps causes bile acid synthesis disorders, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, and sterol accumulation in tissues.

Androgen catabolism is how tissues dispose of or divert testosterone and related C19 steroids, setting the local concentration of hormone that reaches the androgen receptor rather than merely the amount made by the gonads. Because target-tissue exposure governs male sexual differentiation, prostate growth, sebaceous and hair follicle activity, and the feedback that tunes gonadotropin output, this clearance arm matters wherever androgen signalling must be limited. Aromatase (CYP19A1) removes androgens from the pool irreversibly by converting them to estrogens, the main source of estrogen in adipose tissue, bone and brain; the 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases here act oxidatively to interconvert active hormones with weaker 17-keto forms, and 5alpha-reductase activity channels substrate toward reduced metabolites. Loss or excess of these steps produces disorders of sex development, gynecomastia and estrogen deficiency, and the same enzymes are pharmacological targets in hormone-dependent cancer.

Isoprenoid metabolism builds and disposes of the branched five-carbon-unit compounds that cells need for membrane sterols, respiratory quinones, protein prenylation and glycosylation, and vision. Two arms dominate here. The mevalonate arm runs from HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA reductase through mevalonate kinase and decarboxylase to isopentenyl diphosphate, then branches via farnesyl and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthases toward squalene and lanosterol for cholesterol, toward polyprenol and dolichol for N-glycosylation, and toward coenzyme Q side chains. The retinoid arm cleaves dietary carotenoids, esterifies and reduces retinol through lecithin retinol acyltransferase and short-chain dehydrogenases, regenerates 11-cis-retinal for opsin, and oxidises retinaldehyde to retinoic acid for nuclear receptor signalling before cytochrome P450 hydroxylases and glucuronosyltransferases clear it. Binding proteins and lipoprotein receptors handle transport. Defects cause mevalonate kinase deficiency, congenital glycosylation disorders, retinal dystrophies and statin-sensitive cholesterol dysregulation.

Tetrahydrobiopterin is the redox cofactor that aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthases cannot work without, so its synthesis determines whether a cell can make dopamine, serotonin, tyrosine and nitric oxide. Loss of it produces hyperphenylalaninaemia together with catecholamine and serotonin deficiency, causing dystonia and developmental regression that phenylalanine restriction alone does not correct; partial deficiency of the rate-limiting enzyme underlies dopa-responsive dystonia, and reduced cofactor availability uncouples endothelial nitric oxide synthase. The de novo route proceeds from GTP through GTP cyclohydrolase I, 6-pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase and sepiapterin reductase, with a pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase step regenerating the cofactor after each hydroxylation. Dihydropteridine reductase and dihydrofolate reductase return oxidized pterin to the active tetrahydro form, linking this biology to folate metabolism and to salvage as well as synthesis.

One-carbon metabolism supplies the activated methyl and formyl groups that cells use to build nucleotides and to methylate DNA, RNA, proteins and lipids, linking folate and methionine chemistry to growth and epigenetic state. Folate-bound carbon units are generated by serine hydroxymethyltransferases in cytosol and mitochondria, shuttled through the interconverting dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase activities of the MTHFD family, reduced by MTHFR, and consumed by thymidylate synthase for dTMP synthesis and by purine synthesis; DHFR regenerates tetrahydrofolate and FPGS adds the polyglutamate tail that retains folates in the cell. On the methionine side, MAT enzymes make S-adenosylmethionine, GNMT disposes of excess methyl groups, and AHCY hydrolyses S-adenosylhomocysteine to keep methyltransferases from being inhibited. Mitochondrial serine transport by sideroflexins feeds the cycle. Failure causes megaloblastic anaemia, hyperhomocysteinaemia and neural tube defects, and the route is the target of antifolate chemotherapy.

NADP+ metabolism supplies and recycles the phosphorylated nicotinamide coenzyme whose reduced form, NADPH, pays for reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids and cholesterol and for antioxidant defence through the glutathione and thioredoxin systems. Cells that cannot keep NADPH reduced suffer oxidative damage, as in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and haemolysis under oxidant stress. The main supply route is the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, with G6PD and PGD feeding a non-oxidative arm of transketolase, transaldolase and ribose-phosphate isomerases that also yields sugar phosphates for nucleotide synthesis; cytosolic and mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenases, malic enzymes and the inner-membrane transhydrogenase NNT provide additional reducing equivalents. NAD kinases phosphorylate NAD+ to make NADP+ itself, linking this pool to salvage enzymes such as NAMPT. Flux is tuned by nutrient signalling through mTOR complex components and by p53 acting via TIGAR to divert glucose toward NADPH production.

NADPH regeneration replenishes the cell's pool of reducing power, the currency that supports reductive biosynthesis of fatty acids, cholesterol and nucleotides and that keeps glutathione and thioredoxin reduced against oxidative damage. Cells that cannot regenerate NADPH fail to detoxify peroxides, as in erythrocytes lacking G6PD, where oxidant stress causes haemolysis. Several routes converge on NADP+: the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway through G6PD, PGLS and PGD, with the non-oxidative transketolase and transaldolase arm recycling carbon back to glycolysis; cytosolic IDH1; mitochondrial folate-linked ALDH1L2; and the inner-membrane transhydrogenase NNT, which draws on the proton gradient. Flux is regulated rather than constitutive: p53 and its target TIGAR shift glucose away from glycolysis toward the pentose phosphate route, while mTOR complex components tie NADPH supply to anabolic growth signalling and redox demand in proliferating and tumour cells.

NADPH is the cell's reducing currency for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence, and this pathway covers the reactions that refill its pool wherever it is consumed. Without adequate regeneration, glutathione and thioredoxin cannot be re-reduced, reactive oxygen species accumulate, and fatty acid and nucleotide synthesis stall; red cells are especially vulnerable, as glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency and drug-induced haemolysis illustrate. The oxidative pentose phosphate branch, with G6PD and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase, is the dominant cytosolic source, feeding a non-oxidative arm of transketolase, transaldolase and pentose isomerases that also supplies ribose for nucleotides. Cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase and the folate-linked ALDH1L enzymes provide additional reducing equivalents, while nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase regenerates NADPH across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Flux is tuned by p53 and its target TIGAR, and by mTOR complex components, tying redox supply to growth and stress signalling.

NADP+ biosynthesis converts NAD+ into the phosphorylated coenzyme that cells depend on for reductive rather than oxidative chemistry. Where NAD+ collects electrons for catabolism, NADPH donates them to fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, nucleotide and amino acid production, cytochrome P450 reactions, and the glutathione and thioredoxin systems that neutralise peroxides, so the size of this pool sets a cell's capacity for both biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. The committed step is ATP-dependent phosphorylation of NAD+ by NAD kinase, carried out in the cytosol and, by a separate mitochondrial enzyme, inside the organelle, keeping the two compartments independently supplied. Upstream salvage enzymes regenerate the NAD+ substrate from nicotinamide, linking this route to overall pyridine nucleotide turnover. Proliferating and oxidatively stressed cells raise flux through it, and tumour metabolism frequently exploits the same demand.

Glutathione metabolism maintains the cell's principal thiol buffer, the tripeptide that keeps protein cysteines reduced, disposes of peroxides, and conjugates electrophiles for export. Its capacity sets how much oxidative and xenobiotic stress a cell can survive, which is why it governs drug and carcinogen detoxification in liver and kidney, chemotherapy resistance in tumours, and neuronal vulnerability when cystine supply fails. Synthesis runs through glutamate-cysteine ligase, whose catalytic and modifier subunits are induced by NRF2, followed by glutathione synthetase; the gamma-glutamyl cycle recovers constituent amino acids via extracellular gamma-glutamyl transferases and cytosolic cyclotransferases. Reduced pools are regenerated by glutathione reductase using NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway, while glutathione peroxidases and glutaredoxins consume them. Broad glutathione S-transferase families conjugate reactive compounds, and multidrug resistance transporters pump the conjugates out. Related side reactions handle methylglyoxal and persulfides.

Glutathione is the cell's main thiol antioxidant, and its catabolism is what turns that tripeptide back into free amino acids, closing the gamma-glutamyl cycle and recovering cysteine for resynthesis. Two routes appear here. Membrane-bound gamma-glutamyltransferases, exemplified by GGT1 and GGT5, act on the outer face of the cell and cleave extracellular glutathione and glutathione S-conjugates, transferring the gamma-glutamyl group and leaving cysteinylglycine, which dipeptidase DPEP1 splits at the renal and intestinal brush border. Inside the cytosol, CHAC1 degrades glutathione directly to 5-oxoproline and cysteinylglycine, a step induced during amino acid starvation and endoplasmic reticulum stress that lowers thiol buffering and can sensitise cells to ferroptosis. Together these activities govern cysteine supply between tissues, the final stage of mercapturic acid detoxification, and the redox tone a cell can sustain.

ATP biosynthesis is how cells convert nutrient-derived reducing equivalents and glycolytic intermediates into the nucleotide that powers essentially all energy-requiring work, from ion pumping to biosynthesis to motility. Most of the genes here build the mitochondrial machinery: the many NDUFA/NDUFB/NDUFS subunits and mitochondrially encoded ND proteins of complex I, the four succinate dehydrogenase subunits, and the full F1Fo ATP synthase with its catalytic ATP5F1 head, c-ring and peripheral stalk, which uses the proton-motive force to phosphorylate ADP. Glycolytic contributors such as aldolase A, enolase 1 and lactate dehydrogenase provide substrate-level phosphorylation. Regulation and quality control are represented too, including the ATP synthase inhibitory factor, assembly factors, cardiolipin remodelling by tafazzin, and PINK1/parkin-dependent removal of damaged mitochondria. Loss of these components causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome, paraganglioma and parkinsonism, and limits the energy supply of neurons and muscle first.

Folate metabolism supplies the one-carbon units that cells use to make thymidylate and purines and to regenerate methionine for methylation reactions, so this is the chemistry behind DNA synthesis, repair and the methyl economy of the cell. Dietary folate must be taken up by receptors and transporters, reduced by dihydrofolate reductase, and retained intracellularly by polyglutamylation, a tag that gamma-glutamyl hydrolase removes to allow efflux. Interconversion among tetrahydrofolate species by the cytosolic and mitochondrial dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase and serine hydroxymethyltransferase enzymes sets the balance between formyl donors for purine synthesis, methylene-THF for thymidylate synthase, and methyl-THF used by methionine synthase with its reductase partner. Deficiency or inherited defects cause megaloblastic anaemia, hyperhomocysteinaemia and neural tube defects, and the same route is exploited by antifolate chemotherapy and by thymidylate synthase inhibitors.

Vitamins must be absorbed, converted to their active coenzyme or hormone forms, and then degraded, and this vitamin metabolic process covers all three steps for both fat- and water-soluble classes. Because the products serve as cofactors for transaminases, decarboxylases and one-carbon enzymes, or as nuclear receptor ligands, disruption here produces deficiency states rather than defects of any single pathway. Cytochrome P450 enzymes dominate: CYP2R1 and CYP27B1 hydroxylate vitamin D toward the active hormone while CYP24A1 inactivates it, CYP26 family members clear retinoic acid, and CYP4F enzymes act on vitamin K and tocopherols. BCO1 cleaves carotene to retinal, and RDH10 oxidises retinol. Kinases including PDXK, RFK, TPK1 and THTPA generate pyridoxal phosphate, FAD precursors and thiamine phosphates, with SLC19A2/3 and SLC25A19 importing thiamine and folate. FGF23 and LRP2 link this chemistry to renal handling of vitamin D and mineral balance.

Riboflavin metabolism converts dietary vitamin B2 into the flavin coenzymes FMN and FAD, without which the cell cannot run the flavoenzymes of fatty acid beta-oxidation, the respiratory chain, amino acid catabolism and folate and glutathione redox chemistry. Because humans cannot synthesise riboflavin, the pathway begins with uptake: a family of plasma membrane riboflavin transporters handles absorption in the intestine, placental and tissue delivery, and neuronal supply. Inside the cell, riboflavin kinase phosphorylates the vitamin to FMN and a bifunctional FAD synthase adenylylates FMN to FAD, which is then loaded onto apo-flavoproteins. Loss of transporter function causes Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, with pontobulbar palsy, deafness and motor neuron degeneration, while FAD synthase deficiency presents as a riboflavin-responsive multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Both are treatable with high-dose riboflavin, making this cofactor supply route directly relevant to metabolic and neurological medicine.

Vitamin A metabolic process converts dietary carotenoids and retinyl esters into the active retinoids the body needs: retinoic acid for gene regulation, and 11-cis-retinal for vision. Its failure causes night blindness and retinal degeneration, and disrupts the retinoid signalling that patterns developing limbs, heart, and nervous system. Beta-carotene is first cleaved by BCO1 to retinal, while LIPA liberates retinol from stored esters and LRAT re-esterifies it for storage in liver stellate cells and the retinal pigment epithelium. Because retinoids are hydrophobic and reactive, each intermediate is escorted by a dedicated binding protein such as RBP1, RBP2, or RLBP1. In the visual cycle RPE65 isomerizes retinyl ester to 11-cis-retinol for regeneration of rhodopsin chromophore, whereas ALDH1A2 commits retinal irreversibly to retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoid receptors controlling differentiation.

Vitamin A metabolism converts dietary carotenoids and retinyl esters into the two forms the body actually uses: retinal for vision and retinoic acid for gene regulation. Without it, animals lose photoreceptor function and develop night blindness, and embryonic patterning of the heart, hindbrain and limbs fails because retinoic acid gradients cannot be built. Beta-carotene is cleaved to retinal, esterified retinol is mobilised by lysosomal and cytosolic ester hydrolysis, and lecithin retinol acyltransferase stores retinol back as retinyl esters in liver and retinal pigment epithelium. In the visual cycle, an isomerohydrolase regenerates 11-cis-retinal for opsin, with dedicated binding proteins escorting these insoluble, reactive retinoids between compartments and cells. A dehydrogenase step commits retinal irreversibly to retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoid receptors that control differentiation of epithelia and immune cells. Mutations in the visual-cycle components cause inherited retinal dystrophies.

Porphyrin-containing compound metabolic process covers the synthesis, transport and breakdown of heme and related tetrapyrroles, the cofactors that let hemoglobin carry oxygen and let cytochromes, catalases and P450 enzymes perform redox chemistry. Erythroid precursors depend on it most heavily, and defects in individual steps cause the porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia, and jaundice from failed bilirubin handling. The eight-enzyme route runs from succinyl-CoA and glycine through aminolevulinic acid synthases and the cytosolic enzymes to ferrochelatase in mitochondria, supported by glycine and intermediate transporters and by iron delivery. Catabolism proceeds through heme oxygenases and biliverdin reductases to bilirubin, which is glucuronidated and exported by hepatic transporters. Regulation ties the pathway to iron status and to translational control of globin synthesis, so that heme and its apoproteins are made in matched amounts.

Metabolism of porphyrin-containing compounds covers the making, transport and breakdown of the tetrapyrrole ring that becomes heme, the cofactor of hemoglobin, cytochromes and catalases. Its output sets the oxygen-carrying capacity of red cells and the electron-transfer capacity of mitochondria and the cytochrome P450 system, so blocked or unbalanced flux causes the porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia and jaundice. Eight enzymes, from the rate-setting ALAS1 and erythroid ALAS2 through HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX to ferrochelatase, build protoporphyrin and insert iron, with mitochondrial carriers such as SLC25A38 and ABCB10 supplying glycine and moving intermediates. Heme oxygenases HMOX1 and HMOX2 open the ring to biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases and UGT1A1 convert to excretable bilirubin. Related branches feed heme a synthesis for cytochrome oxidase and couple synthesis to cellular iron sensing and translational control.

Protoporphyrinogen IX is the last colourless intermediate on the route to heme, and its synthesis covers the steps from glycine and succinyl-CoA through the tetrapyrrole ring. The output feeds hemoglobin production in erythroid precursors and cytochrome and catalase synthesis everywhere else, so the throughput of these reactions sets how much oxygen a person can carry. Aminolevulinate synthase begins the pathway, with a housekeeping form and an erythroid-specific form whose translation is controlled by iron regulatory protein binding, linking heme output to iron availability; dehydratase, deaminase, and the uroporphyrinogen and coproporphyrinogen enzymes then build and decarboxylate the ring before protoporphyrinogen oxidase completes the step to protoporphyrin. Defects in individual enzymes cause the porphyrias, in which accumulated intermediates produce neurovisceral attacks or photosensitivity, while erythroid synthase loss causes sideroblastic anemia.

Heme A biosynthetic process produces the specialized heme variant that sits in the catalytic core of cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the respiratory chain. Without it, complex IV cannot assemble or transfer electrons to oxygen, and cells lose oxidative phosphorylation capacity — the basis of infantile cardiomyopathy, Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies caused by mutations in the farnesyltransferase COX10 and the monooxygenase COX15. The route begins with the shared tetrapyrrole pathway, in which succinyl-CoA and glycine are condensed by ALAS1 and successive enzymes build the porphyrin ring, ending with ferrochelatase inserting iron to give heme B. Heme B is then modified inside mitochondria: COX10 farnesylates a vinyl group to yield heme O, and COX15 hydroxylates a methyl group to give heme A. The pathway thus links iron and porphyrin metabolism directly to respiratory chain biogenesis.

Cytochrome c oxidase cannot function without heme A, a specialized heme bearing a farnesyl side chain and a formyl group, and heme A biosynthesis is the route that makes it. The pathway begins as the common porphyrin route: ALAS1 condenses glycine and succinyl-CoA, ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX elaborate and oxidize the tetrapyrrole, and ferrochelatase inserts iron to give heme B. Two mitochondrial inner-membrane enzymes then commit that heme to respiration, COX10 transferring a farnesyl group to form heme O and COX15 oxidizing its methyl substituent to the formyl of heme A. Without this tailoring, complex IV fails to assemble and oxidative phosphorylation collapses, causing infantile cardiomyopathy, Leigh syndrome and other mitochondrial disease, while defects in the upstream porphyrin steps instead produce porphyrias and anemia.

Heme B is the iron-protoporphyrin cofactor of hemoglobin and myoglobin, of catalases and peroxidases, of cytochromes P450 and the b-type cytochromes, and its biosynthesis supplies oxygen transport, drug metabolism and respiration with the prosthetic group they depend on. Synthesis begins in mitochondria with condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA by an aminolevulinate synthase coexisting in a housekeeping form and an erythroid-specific form, continues through cytosolic steps that build and decarboxylate the porphyrin ring, and returns to the mitochondrion where protoporphyrinogen is oxidized and ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron.
