Because intermediates are photoreactive and neurotoxic, partial enzyme deficiencies cause the porphyrias, with cutaneous or acute neurovisceral attacks depending on the blocked step, while failure of iron insertion or of erythroid initiation produces sideroblastic anemia. Flux is tightly matched to iron availability and globin demand.

sulfur compound metabolic process covers the handling of sulfur in the cell, from the sulfur amino acids methionine and cysteine through glutathione, coenzyme A, thiamine, lipoate, sulfate esters and hydrogen sulfide. It supplies the reducing thiols that buffer oxidative stress, the methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine, and the acyl carrier and cofactor chemistry on which fatty acid and energy metabolism depend; its failure produces homocystinuria, cystinosis, glutathione deficiency and sulfide toxicity. The genes trace transsulfuration and methionine recycling (CBS, CTH, MAT2A, MTR), glutathione synthesis, conjugation and recycling by the glutathione transferases and gamma-glutamyl cycle, coenzyme A biosynthesis through the pantothenate kinases, sulfate activation by PAPSS1/2 with the sulfotransferases that modify hormones, xenobiotics and glycans, and sulfide clearance by SQOR and ETHE1. Much of it is transcriptionally coordinated by NFE2L2 as part of the antioxidant and detoxification response.

Sulfur compound metabolism covers the handling of the element in all its cellular forms: the sulfur amino acids methionine and cysteine, glutathione, coenzyme A and thioester acyl carriers, thiamine and lipoate cofactors, sulfate esters, and inorganic sulfide. It underwrites methylation capacity, redox buffering and detoxification, and it is why defects here produce homocystinuria, cystinosis, glutathione deficiency and sulfite oxidase disease. Transmethylation and transsulfuration link methionine through homocysteine to cysteine via CBS and CTH, feeding glutathione synthesis by GCLC/GCLM and GSS and taurine production through CDO1 and CSAD. Glutathione is then consumed by transferases and gamma-glutamyl enzymes to conjugate electrophiles, and regenerated by reductase and peroxidase activity. Sulfate activated by PAPSS1/2 supplies cytosolic sulfotransferases and carbohydrate and tyrosine sulfation, while MPST, TST and SQOR dispose of hydrogen sulfide. Coenzyme A and thioesterase reactions place fatty acid metabolism within the same thiol economy.

Phosphorus metabolic process gathers the reactions that make, break and transfer phosphate-containing compounds, the chemistry on which cellular energy currency, signalling and nucleic acid synthesis all depend. It spans ATP production by glycolytic enzymes, the mitochondrial respiratory chain and ATP synthase; nucleotide salvage and de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis; phospholipid and inositol phosphate turnover through kinases, phospholipases and phosphatases; and sugar phosphate handling in the pentose phosphate pathway. A large share of the genes are protein kinases and phosphatases, so reversible phosphorylation of proteins is part of the same chemistry, linking this metabolism directly to growth factor and cytokine signalling, cell cycle checkpoints, and nutrient sensing through AMPK and mTOR complexes. Because phosphate transfer underlies both bioenergetics and information flow, defects in individual steps produce mitochondrial disease, metabolic disorders, immunodeficiency and cancer, and the pathway also connects to systemic phosphate homeostasis via PTH and PHEX.

Phosphorus metabolic processes encompass every reaction that makes, breaks, or transfers phosphate-containing compounds, and they underlie the chemistry of energy, information, and membranes. The nucleotide and sugar-phosphate arms shown here build purines and pyrimidines, run glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, and feed oxidative phosphorylation through respiratory complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, and the ATP synthase, so that cells can store and spend energy as ATP. A second arm turns phosphate into a reversible regulatory mark: hundreds of protein kinases (receptor tyrosine kinases, MAP kinase cascades, AMPK and mTOR components, cyclin-dependent kinases) paired with phosphatases such as the PTP and DUSP families and PP1/PP2A catalytic subunits, governing growth, division, and stress responses. Lipid kinases, phosphoinositide phosphatases, phospholipases, and phosphatidylinositol-anchor biosynthesis enzymes generate membrane phosphate species that recruit proteins and define organelle identity. Loss of individual steps causes metabolic, neurological, and oncogenic disease.

Superoxide metabolism covers the deliberate production of the O2- radical and its rapid disposal, and the balance between the two decides whether the anion serves as a weapon and signal or as a source of oxidative damage. Its best-known use is the phagocyte respiratory burst: the membrane flavocytochrome formed by CYBB and CYBA, assembled with the cytosolic factors NCF1, NCF2, NCF4 and a Rac GTPase, reduces oxygen to superoxide inside the phagosome for microbial killing, and loss of these components causes chronic granulomatous disease. Related NADPH oxidases and dual oxidases generate superoxide or peroxide for thyroid hormone synthesis, mucosal defence and redox signalling in vascular and other tissues. Superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space, supported by peroxiredoxins and NRF2-driven antioxidant gene expression, clear the radical; uncoupled nitric oxide synthases add to the load, linking this chemistry to endothelial function, inflammation and neurodegeneration.

Handling of foreign chemicals taken in from diet, drugs, plants and pollution is what xenobiotic metabolism accomplishes: it converts lipophilic compounds into water-soluble derivatives that can be excreted, and it is the main determinant of drug dose, duration of action and toxicity. The work is organised in phases. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and organic cation families deliver substrates into hepatocytes and enterocytes; cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, flavin monooxygenases, aldehyde oxidase, esterases and epoxide hydrolase oxidise or hydrolyse them; glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione transferases, N-acetyltransferases and thiopurine methyltransferase conjugate the products; and ATP-binding cassette pumps export conjugates to bile or blood. Ligand-activated transcription factors including the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, pregnane X receptor and HNF4A induce these enzymes on exposure, so the system is inducible and highly polymorphic. Bioactivation of procarcinogens by the same enzymes explains why detoxification can also generate reactive, mutagenic metabolites, and variants here underlie much interindividual variation in drug response.

Every cell must move simple ions such as sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, protons, zinc, iron, copper and magnesium across membranes, and monoatomic ion transport is the collected machinery that does it. These fluxes set the resting membrane potential and fire action potentials, drive secretion and reabsorption in kidney, gut and stomach, acidify lysosomes, load calcium stores for muscle contraction and synaptic release, and keep trace metals available but non-toxic. The work is done by voltage- and ligand-gated channels of the sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride families, transient receptor potential and store-operated calcium entry components, aquaporins and gap junction and pannexin channels, pumps including the sodium/potassium and calcium ATPases and the vacuolar proton pump, and a very large complement of solute carriers and mitochondrial carriers. Layered on top are regulatory kinases, calmodulin, auxiliary subunits and scaffolds that gate and localise transport. Mutations in these genes underlie channelopathies of heart, brain, muscle and kidney, cystic fibrosis, deafness and disorders of metal overload.

Every cell maintains steep gradients of single-atom positive ions across its membranes, and monoatomic cation transport is the collected machinery that builds and exploits them. It sets resting membrane potential, fires action potentials in neurons, heart and muscle, acidifies lysosomes and the stomach lumen, drives nutrient uptake by secondary active transport, and delivers iron, zinc, copper and manganese to enzymes while keeping them below toxic levels. The players span voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels with their auxiliary subunits, TRP and ASIC sensors, ryanodine receptors and store-operated entry via STIM and ORAI, P-type pumps such as the Na+/K+ ATPase and SERCA, vacuolar H+-ATPase subunits, respiratory complexes that pump protons, and numerous exchangers and solute carriers. Failure produces arrhythmias, epilepsies, deafness, renal salt-wasting and metal overload disorders.

Potassium is the ion that sets a cell's resting membrane potential, and its directed movement across membranes underlies electrical excitability, stimulus-secretion coupling and epithelial salt and water handling. The machinery here spans voltage-gated, inward-rectifier, two-pore-domain leak, calcium-activated and hyperpolarization-activated channels together with their accessory beta, KCNE, KChIP and DPP-like subunits, the Na+/K+-ATPase pumps and their FXYD modulators, gastric H+/K+ pumps, and cation-chloride cotransporters with their WNK-OXSR1/STK39 kinase regulators. Anchoring and trafficking proteins such as ankyrins, AKAPs, caveolins and NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligases determine where channels sit and how long they last. Outputs range from repolarizing the cardiac action potential and shaping neuronal firing to insulin release through ATP-sensitive channels, potassium recycling in the cochlea and renal tubular reabsorption. Mutations produce long QT syndromes, epilepsies and ataxias, deafness, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, and neonatal diabetes or hyperinsulinism.

Sodium ion transport covers every route by which Na+ crosses membranes, and the electrochemical gradient it builds is the currency the rest of the cell spends. The Na+/K+-ATPase subunits and their FXYD regulators set that gradient; voltage-gated channels then exploit it to fire action potentials in nerve, skeletal muscle and heart, while HCN and NALCN channels set pacemaker and resting excitability. Epithelial sodium channels with their WNK-SGK-NEDD4L regulatory network reabsorb Na+ in kidney and airway, fixing blood pressure and fluid balance. A large family of secondary transporters harnesses the same gradient to move glucose, amino acids, neurotransmitters, phosphate, bile acids, protons and calcium, coupling salt handling to nutrient uptake, pH control and Ca2+ extrusion. Mutations produce epilepsies, pain and arrhythmia syndromes, myotonia, and inherited hypertension or salt-wasting disease.

Calcium ion transport covers the movement of Ca2+ across membranes and between compartments, the basis of one of the most widely used intracellular signals. Cells hold cytosolic calcium extremely low so that brief, localized rises can trigger muscle contraction, neurotransmitter and hormone release, fertilization, immune activation, gene transcription and apoptosis. The machinery here spans voltage-gated channels of the CACNA/CACNB families, ligand- and stimulus-gated entry through NMDA receptors, purinergic P2X receptors and TRP channels, store-operated entry in which STIM proteins sense endoplasmic reticulum depletion and gate ORAI, release through inositol trisphosphate receptors and ryanodine receptors, and clearance by SERCA and plasma membrane pumps, sodium/calcium exchangers and mitochondrial uniporter subunits. Downstream, calmodulin, CaMKII and calcineurin decode the signal. Mutations in these channels and pumps cause arrhythmias, malignant hyperthermia, migraine, epilepsy, immunodeficiency and deafness.

Phosphate is needed for ATP, nucleic acids, membrane lipids and bone mineral, and cells and tissues move it across membranes against steep gradients by dedicated carriers. This transport activity spans several families: sodium-dependent type II cotransporters such as SLC34A1 and SLC34A3 reclaim filtered phosphate in the kidney proximal tubule and SLC34A2 supplies lung surfactant synthesis, the type III carriers SLC20A1 and SLC20A2 handle ubiquitous cellular uptake, SLC25A3 imports phosphate into mitochondria for oxidative phosphorylation, and XPR1 provides an efflux route. Regulation is endocrine as much as molecular, with FGF23 acting through FGFR1 and with vitamin D receptor signalling setting renal and intestinal handling; ANKH controls pyrophosphate and phosphate flux at mineralizing surfaces. Failure produces hypophosphatemic rickets, tumoral calcinosis, nephrolithiasis, brain calcification and mitochondrial energy deficits, linking this traffic to skeletal mineralization and systemic mineral balance.

Movement of simple single-atom anions — chloride above all, along with iodide, bicarbonate-linked fluxes, and sulfate — across membranes sets cell volume, drives transepithelial fluid and salt secretion, acidifies intracellular compartments, and determines whether a neurotransmitter response is inhibitory. The machinery spans ligand-gated channels (GABA-A and glycine receptors, whose chloride influx hyperpolarizes neurons), the cAMP-regulated CFTR channel of airway and gut epithelium, calcium-activated anoectamins, bestrophins, the CLC family of channels and chloride/proton exchangers that acidify endosomes and lysosomes, volume-regulated LRRC8 heteromers, and secondary-active carriers including cation-chloride cotransporters, SLC4 and SLC26 exchangers, and the thyroidal sodium-iodide symporter. Loss of individual members produces cystic fibrosis, Bartter syndrome, myotonia, osteopetrosis, deafness with goitre, and hyperekplexia, so this transport underlies epithelial secretion, renal salt handling, neuronal inhibition, and organelle pH control.

Chloride is the most abundant permeant anion in the body, and its directed movement across membranes sets epithelial fluid secretion, cell volume, intracellular pH and the resting excitability of neurons. The machinery here spans several unrelated families: CFTR and the CLC channels and chloride/proton antiporters, calcium-activated anoctamins and bestrophins, volume-regulated LRRC8 channels, intracellular CLICs, and ligand-gated GABA-A and glycine receptors, whose chloride influx is the basis of fast synaptic inhibition. Coupled cotransporters and exchangers of the SLC12, SLC26 and SLC4 families move chloride against bicarbonate, sodium and potassium, driving salt reabsorption in the nephron and loop of Henle and secretion in airway and gut. Failure of individual members produces cystic fibrosis, Bartter syndrome, congenital chloride diarrhoea, osteopetrosis, myotonia and epilepsy, making anion flux the shared substrate of secretory, renal and neuronal physiology.

Cobalt reaches human cells almost entirely as the metal centre of cobalamin, so directed movement of cobalt ions is largely the story of vitamin B12 handling plus a set of broad-specificity divalent metal carriers. Intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells and the haptocorrin and transcobalamin binding proteins escort dietary cobalamin through the gut lumen, bloodstream and into tissues, where it becomes the cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; loss of this route causes pernicious anaemia and neurological degeneration. The transporters here are promiscuous metal channels rather than cobalt-dedicated pumps: SLC11A2 imports ferrous iron and other divalent cations across endosomal and apical membranes, SLC39A8 and SLC30A5 move zinc and manganese, and SLC41A2 handles magnesium, meaning cobalt distribution is coupled to the wider economy of divalent cation uptake and can compete with iron absorption.</description

Copper is needed as a cofactor by cytochrome c oxidase, lysyl oxidase, superoxide dismutase and ceruloplasmin, yet free copper is toxic, so cells move it along protein-to-protein relays rather than letting it diffuse. This transport pathway covers uptake at the plasma membrane, delivery within the cell, and export or loading into the secretory route. A high-affinity importer of the SLC31 family brings reduced copper across the membrane, cell-surface reductases of the STEAP family supply Cu(I), the ATOX1 chaperone hands metal to the P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B, and those pumps either load cuproenzymes in the trans-Golgi or traffic to membranes to excrete surplus copper. Loss of ATP7A causes Menkes disease with systemic copper deficiency, while loss of ATP7B blocks biliary excretion and produces the hepatic and neurological copper overload of Wilson disease.

Iron ion transport moves iron across membranes and between tissues, supplying haem synthesis, iron-sulfur cluster assembly and oxygen carriage while keeping free iron low enough to avoid Fenton chemistry and ferroptosis. Dietary uptake begins with ferric reduction at the brush border and apical import through a divalent metal transporter, with export to plasma via ferroportin coupled to ferroxidase activity; hepcidin binding to that exporter sets systemic iron availability, and loss of this control underlies haemochromatosis, while overactive signalling contributes to anaemia of inflammation. Transferrin and its receptors deliver iron by receptor-mediated endocytosis, with endosomal reductases, clathrin and dynamin supporting the cycle. Ferritin subunits store iron safely, mitochondrial carriers such as mitoferrin and an ABC transporter feed the organelle, and haem and siderophore-binding proteins including haemopexin, lactoferrin and lipocalin-2 handle iron outside cells and during infection.

Manganese ion transport moves manganese across membranes to keep this trace metal available as an enzyme cofactor while preventing its accumulation to neurotoxic levels. Manganese is required by mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, arginase, and the Golgi glycosyltransferases that build glycans, so cells must supply it to the right compartments; excess manganese damages the basal ganglia and produces a parkinsonian syndrome. Uptake transporters of the SLC39 family, notably SLC39A8 and SLC39A14, import manganese at the intestine and liver, while SLC30A10 exports it for biliary excretion, and loss-of-function mutations in these genes cause inherited manganese deficiency with skeletal dysplasia or hypermanganesemia with dystonia. Secretory-pathway calcium/manganese ATPases and TMEM165 load the Golgi lumen to support glycosylation, and divalent metal transporters such as SLC11A2 couple manganese handling to iron uptake, linking this pathway to systemic metal homeostasis and macrophage antimicrobial defence.

Manganese is needed as a cofactor by glycosyltransferases, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and arginase, yet it is neurotoxic in excess, so cells and the body must move it with precision. This transport system handles uptake, compartmentalisation and disposal: divalent metal importers of the SLC11 and SLC39 families bring manganese across the plasma membrane and into hepatocytes and enterocytes, secretory-pathway calcium/manganese ATPases and TMEM165 load it into the Golgi where glycosylation enzymes use it, and SLC30A10 exports it for biliary excretion. Failure at either end causes recognisable disease: loss of efflux or of SLC39A14 produces manganese accumulation in the basal ganglia with dystonia and parkinsonism, while defective Golgi delivery gives congenital disorders of glycosylation. The pathway therefore links trace-metal homeostasis to protein glycosylation, antioxidant defence and neurological function.

Zinc is required by hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, yet free zinc is toxic, so cells move it across membranes under tight control. This transport system sets cytosolic zinc concentration and fills the compartments that need it: two opposing solute carrier families do most of the work, with ZIP proteins importing zinc into the cytosol from outside the cell or from organelles, and ZnT exporters moving it the other way into secretory vesicles, the Golgi, and granules. Specialised members serve specific physiology insulin granule loading in pancreatic beta cells, zinc uptake from the intestine, and delivery into synaptic vesicles while metallothionein buffers the labile pool and channels such as TRPM7 provide an additional route. Loss of individual transporters causes acrodermatitis enteropathica, transient neonatal zinc deficiency, and skeletal and connective tissue disease, and several also carry manganese or iron.

Cells cannot pump water directly, so osmotic water movement depends on channels and on the solute gradients that drive it; water transport is the machinery that makes rapid, regulated water flux across membranes possible. It underlies urine concentration in the kidney, tear and saliva secretion, cerebrospinal fluid balance in the brain, and lens transparency. The aquaporin family provides the pores, several also conducting glycerol or urea, while the vasopressin hormone and its renal V2 receptor control the trafficking of one of them to the collecting duct apical membrane in response to dehydration. Urea and glucose carriers and a chloride channel supply the coupled osmotic gradients, and matrix and cytoskeletal components shape the surrounding tissue barrier. Loss of function causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, congenital cataract, corneal dystrophy, and altered brain oedema after injury.

Dicarboxylic acid transport moves two-carboxylate solutes "such as glutamate, aspartate, succinate, citrate, malate, oxaloacetate, sulfate-coupled substrates and folates" across plasma and mitochondrial membranes, linking neurotransmission, renal handling of organic anions, and the exchange reactions that keep the citric acid cycle and redox shuttles running. Excitatory amino acid carriers of the SLC1 family clear synaptic glutamate into astrocytes and neurons, while vesicular glutamate transporters load it for release; loss of this clearance produces excitotoxic neuronal death. Mitochondrial carriers of the SLC25 family run the malate/aspartate and oxoglutarate shuttles and import glutamate for oxidation, and citrate and dicarboxylate carriers of the SLC13 family feed hepatic and renal metabolism. Multidrug resistance pumps, sulfate/anion exchangers of the SLC26 family, organic anion transporters and volume-regulated LRRC8 channels extend the same chemistry to secretion, reabsorption and osmotic release of anionic metabolites.

neurotransmitter transport covers the whole logistical chain that moves chemical messengers where they are needed: loading them into synaptic vesicles, releasing them at the active zone, and clearing them from the synaptic cleft afterwards. Without it chemical synaptic transmission fails, and the genes involved are the ones mutated in epilepsy, dystonia, paroxysmal movement disorders and parkinsonism, and the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants and anticonvulsants. Vesicular transporters of the SLC17, SLC18 and SLC32 families concentrate glutamate, monoamines, acetylcholine and GABA against a proton gradient; SNARE proteins with syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMP2, together with the calcium sensors synaptotagmin and complexin and the priming factors UNC13 and STXBP1, execute regulated exocytosis; plasma membrane SLC1 and SLC6 carriers in neurons and astrocytes then recapture transmitter to terminate signalling and recycle substrate. Presynaptic scaffolds such as piccolo and RIM organise the release site, linking this pathway to synaptic vesicle cycling and calcium channel coupling.

Chemical signalling between neurons depends on moving transmitter molecules into the right compartment at the right moment, and this pathway covers both halves of that job: loading and clearing transmitters across membranes, and releasing them from synaptic vesicles. Vesicular carriers of the SLC17, SLC18 and SLC32 families concentrate glutamate, monoamines, acetylcholine and GABA into vesicles, while plasma-membrane SLC6 and SLC1 transporters recapture GABA, glycine, dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and glutamate from the cleft, terminating signalling and protecting against excitotoxicity. Release itself runs through calcium-triggered fusion: syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMPs form the fusion complex, synaptotagmins and complexins gate it, and Munc13, Munc18, RIMs and the active-zone scaffolds piclo and bassoon-like proteins organise vesicle priming. Loss of these components produces epilepsy, movement disorders, paroxysmal dyskinesia and neurodegeneration, and the reuptake transporters are the direct targets of antidepressants and psychostimulants.

Serotonin acts as a neurotransmitter in the brain and as a signalling molecule in gut, platelets and blood vessels, and its movement across membranes determines how much is available to receptors and how quickly signalling ends. Transport here has two arms: vesicular loading, carried out by the vesicular monoamine transporters that package serotonin and other monoamines for regulated release, and plasma-membrane uptake, dominated by the high-affinity serotonin transporter SLC6A4 with lower-affinity, broadly selective organic cation and plasma membrane monoamine carriers providing uptake in liver, kidney and other tissues. Accessory and modulatory components, including serotonin autoreceptors such as HTR1A and HTR1B, integrin and immune signalling proteins, and alpha-synuclein, shape transporter surface expression and clearance. This machinery sets synaptic serotonin tone, underlies platelet serotonin stores, and is the direct target of SSRI antidepressants, amphetamines and reserpine.

mitochondrial transport covers the movement of metabolites, ions, proteins and whole organelles into, out of and within mitochondria, the traffic that lets a compartment sealed by two membranes participate in cellular metabolism. Carrier families dominate: the SLC25 solute carriers exchange ADP/ATP, ornithine, carnitine-acylcarnitines, citrulline and glutathione, MPC1/MPC2 import pyruvate for oxidation, sideroflexins and TMEM14C handle serine and porphyrin intermediates, and uncoupling proteins dissipate the proton gradient for thermogenesis. Outer-membrane channels VDAC1/2 and MTCH2 set the permeability that carnitine shuttle enzymes CPT1/CPT2 depend on for fatty acid oxidation. The same channels are commandeered by the BCL2 family, so permeabilization by BAX and BAK converts transport into apoptotic release of cytochrome c. Miro GTPases RHOT1/2 move mitochondria along cytoskeletal tracks, and PINK1-PRKN marks damaged ones for mitophagy; failures here underlie Parkinson's disease, neuropathy and metabolic disorders.

Mitochondria are metabolically sealed off from the cytosol, so almost everything they consume or release has to be carried across their membranes, and this transport biology covers that traffic. It supplies the matrix with pyruvate, fatty acyl groups, amino acids, serine and one-carbon units, ornithine and glycine for heme synthesis, adenine nucleotides and metal ions, and it exports ATP and metabolic intermediates back to the cell. Carrier families dominate the list: the SLC25 exchangers, the sideroflexins, the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier subunits, uncoupling proteins that dissipate the proton gradient as heat, and outer-membrane porins. Carnitine shuttle enzymes feed fatty acid oxidation. The same membranes govern release of apoptogenic proteins, so BCL2-family regulators, permeability transition components and the PINK1-parkin mitophagy pair appear alongside Miro GTPases that move organelles along the cytoskeleton. Defects cause metabolic, neurodegenerative and hematologic disease.

Tricarboxylic acid transport moves citrate and related tri- and dicarboxylic acids across membranes, linking the mitochondrial matrix, the cytosol, and the bloodstream. This traffic sets the supply of cytosolic citrate that is cleaved to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and for protein acetylation, and it governs how much citrate the kidney reabsorbs rather than excretes. The mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 exports citrate in exchange for malate, while the sodium-coupled transporters SLC13A5 and SLC13A3 import citrate and succinate at the plasma membrane of hepatocytes, neurons, and renal tubule cells; SFXN5 handles citrate at the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of these activities has clear consequences: SLC25A1 deficiency causes combined D,L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, SLC13A5 mutations cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and reduced urinary citrate promotes calcium stone formation.

Citrate and related tricarboxylic acids must cross membranes to move between the compartments that make and use them, and this transport is what couples mitochondrial oxidative metabolism to cytosolic lipid and sterol synthesis. The mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 exports citrate in exchange for malate, supplying the acetyl-CoA and NADPH-generating steps of de novo lipogenesis; its loss causes a severe neurometabolic disorder with D-2- and L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria. At the plasma membrane, sodium-dependent dicarboxylate/citrate transporters of the SLC13 family take up citrate from blood, intestine and renal tubular fluid, where SLC13A5 shapes hepatic and neuronal citrate supply and mutations cause early infantile epilepsy, while renal handling of citrate influences urinary calcium stone formation. A sideroflexin family member and the kidney-secreted protein uromodulin place this transport activity in both mitochondrial carrier biology and tubular solute handling.

pyruvate transport moves pyruvate across membranes, linking glycolysis in the cytosol to oxidative metabolism in the mitochondrion and allowing cells to exchange this three-carbon fuel with one another. Without it, pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle, so cells fall back on lactate production regardless of oxygen supply — the metabolic state that characterises proliferating tumour cells. Two arms are represented: the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, an inner-membrane heterocomplex of MPC1 and MPC2 that governs how much pyruvate is available for oxidation and gluconeogenesis, and plasma-membrane monocarboxylate transporters such as SLC16A1 and SLC16A3 that co-transport pyruvate and lactate with protons, supporting lactate shuttling between glycolytic and oxidative tissues. SLC5A8 adds sodium-coupled uptake in kidney and gut epithelium. Loss of carrier function causes lactic acidosis and developmental disease, and MPC activity sets the balance between glucose and fatty acid use in muscle, liver and pancreatic beta cells.

Pyruvate sits at the junction between glycolysis and oxidative metabolism, but it cannot cross membranes unaided, so its directed movement across the plasma membrane and the inner mitochondrial membrane is what decides whether a cell burns it, exports it as lactate, or shunts it elsewhere. Two families do the work here: monocarboxylate transporters of the SLC16 group carry pyruvate and lactate across the plasma membrane along proton gradients, allowing lactate export from glycolytic tissue and uptake by oxidative tissue, while the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, a heterocomplex of MPC1 and MPC2, delivers pyruvate to the matrix for oxidation by pyruvate dehydrogenase or carboxylation for gluconeogenesis. A sodium-coupled monocarboxylate transporter additionally absorbs short-chain monocarboxylates in gut and kidney epithelium. Loss of carrier function causes lactic acidosis and developmental disease, and these transporters shape the metabolic flexibility exploited by tumours.

Mitochondrial calcium ion transmembrane transport moves Ca2+ into and out of mitochondria, linking cytosolic calcium signals to the control of energy metabolism, cell death and redox balance. Matrix Ca2+ activates dehydrogenases of the citric acid cycle and thereby matches ATP output to demand, while overload opens the permeability transition pore and triggers necrotic and apoptotic death, a route implicated in ischemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration. Uptake occurs through the inner-membrane uniporter, a pore of MCU and MCUB with the essential regulator EMRE and the gatekeeping MICU1/2/3 subunits that set a cytosolic Ca2+ threshold, fed by VDAC1 across the outer membrane at contacts with ER release sites bearing IP3 receptors and presenilin. Efflux runs through the mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger SLC8B1 and LETM1, and quality-control proteases such as AFG3L2 and SPG7 govern uniporter assembly and stability.

Mitochondria take up calcium from the cytosol and release it again, and this traffic sets the pace of oxidative metabolism, shapes cytosolic calcium signals, and decides whether a stressed cell survives. Uptake runs through the inner-membrane uniporter channel, whose pore subunit MCU works with the regulatory subunit EMRE and the paralogue MCUB, while MICU1, MICU2 and MICU3 act as calcium-sensing gatekeepers that keep the channel shut at resting concentrations and open it during signalling. Calcium enters the matrix down the membrane potential and stimulates dehydrogenases that feed the respiratory chain; efflux via the sodium/calcium exchanger SLC8B1 and LETM1 returns the matrix to baseline. VDAC1 and ER-resident IP3 receptors supply calcium at contact sites, and AFG3L2 and SPG7 control maturation of uniporter components. Overload triggers permeability transition and cell death, linking this transport to ischaemic injury and neurodegeneration.

Cells must move drugs and other foreign chemicals across their membranes, and xenobiotic transmembrane transport is the combined import and export machinery that determines which compounds get in, how long they stay, and how they leave. It sets drug disposition in liver, kidney, intestine and the blood-brain barrier, and it is a common route to therapeutic failure: overexpression of the ATP-driven efflux pumps here confers multidrug resistance in tumours, while loss of hepatobiliary transporters such as ABCB11 or ABCC2 causes cholestasis and hyperbilirubinaemia. ATP-binding cassette proteins of the ABCB and ABCC families pump substrates out against a gradient, often after conjugation to glutathione or glucuronide; solute carriers work in the opposite direction, with SLC19A1 taking up folates and antifolate chemotherapeutics, SLC28 and SLC29 members handling nucleosides and nucleoside analogues, and SLC47A1 mediating organic cation efflux. Lipid flippase subunits and accessory factors support this transport at the membrane.

Short peptides of two to twenty residues are not simply digestive waste; they are a nutritional currency, a source of drug delivery, and cargo that must be moved across membranes intact. Oligopeptide transport describes the carriers and pumps that perform this movement, and it determines how much dietary protein is actually absorbed and how many peptide-like drugs reach the bloodstream. The proton-coupled peptide transporters of the SLC15 family carry di- and tripeptides across the intestinal brush border and the renal proximal tubule, and their intracellular relatives deliver bacterial peptides to endosomal innate immune sensors. Members of the ABCC family export glutathione and glutathione conjugates, linking this traffic to detoxification and to the cysteine supply maintained by the SLC7A11 antiporter, while a lysosomal transporter returns peptide antigens toward the presentation machinery. The set therefore spans nutrient uptake, xenobiotic efflux and immune surveillance.

Movement of material outside the cell surface — mucus along airways, cerebrospinal fluid through the ventricles, ova along the oviduct, and the sperm cell through its surroundings — is generated by beating motile cilia and flagella, and this extracellular transport function is what the genes here build. Loss of it produces primary ciliary dyskinesia and related ciliopathies: chronic sinopulmonary infection and bronchiectasis, hydrocephalus, infertility, and randomized left-right body asymmetry arising from failed nodal flow. Axonemal dyneins such as DNAH5, DNAH11 and DNAI1 provide the motors, a large cytoplasmic preassembly group of DNAAF chaperones loads them onto the axoneme before transport into the cilium, and radial spoke and central apparatus components including RSPH4A, SPAG6 and SPAG17 convert motor activity into a coordinated waveform. Transcriptional regulators such as RFX3 and GMNC specify multiciliated cell fate upstream.

Nucleotides carry energy, signalling information and the building blocks of nucleic acids, but they are charged and cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells depend on dedicated carriers to move them between compartments and out into the extracellular space. This transport underlies mitochondrial ATP export in exchange for ADP by the adenine nucleotide translocases, delivery of NAD, CoA, FAD and folate cofactors into the mitochondrial matrix, and import of nucleotide sugars and PAPS into the Golgi and ER for glycosylation and sulfation. At the plasma membrane, pannexin and calcium homeostasis modulator channels, volume-regulated anion channels and ABC-family efflux pumps release ATP and cyclic nucleotides that act as purinergic signals on receptors such as P2RX7, coordinating inflammation, taste transmission and vascular tone. Vesicular loading of ATP for regulated secretion depends on SLC17A9. Loss of these carriers produces mitochondrial myopathies, thiamine-responsive disorders, ectopic mineralization and defective glycoconjugate synthesis.

Amino acids cross membranes only through carriers, and this transport underpins protein synthesis, nitrogen handling, neurotransmission and nutrient sensing. Carriers of the SLC1, SLC7, SLC38, SLC36, SLC6 and SLC43 families move glutamate, neutral and cationic amino acids, glycine and proline across plasma membranes, often coupled to sodium, protons or exchange; mitochondrial carriers of the SLC25 group shuttle glutamate, aspartate, ornithine and glycine for the urea cycle, the malate-aspartate shuttle and heme synthesis, while vesicular transporters load glutamate and GABA for synaptic release. Astrocytic glutamate uptake terminates excitatory signalling and prevents excitotoxicity; intestinal and renal reabsorption by SLC6A19 with SLC3A1/SLC7A9 explains Hartnup disorder and cystinuria, and lysosomal cystine export loss causes cystinosis. Leucine entry through SLC7A5 and lysosomal arginine sensing by SLC38A9 tie this transport to mTORC1-dependent growth control.

Glutamine is the body's main carrier of nitrogen between tissues and a preferred fuel and biosynthetic precursor for rapidly dividing cells, so moving it across membranes determines which cells can use it. This transport step supplies substrate for glutaminolysis, nucleotide and hexosamine synthesis, glutathione production, and the glutamate-glutamine cycle that recycles neurotransmitter between astrocytes and neurons, and it feeds renal and hepatic ammonia handling. The carriers here are sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporters of the SLC38 family together with SLC1A5 and SLC1A4, working at the plasma membrane and, for SLC38A7 and SLC38A9, at the lysosome, where efflux of glutamine and arginine links amino acid sufficiency to mTORC1 activation. Tumour cells upregulate SLC1A5 to sustain glutamine addiction, and the pathway also intersects with leptin-dependent metabolic signalling.

Intracellular copper ion homeostasis keeps cellular copper at a level that supplies cuproenzymes without allowing free copper to catalyse oxidative damage. Copper is required by cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase and ceruloplasmin, yet an unbuffered ion is toxic, so cells import, chaperone, store and export it along tightly controlled routes. High-affinity transporters of the CTR family bring copper across the plasma membrane, metallothioneins and the chaperone ATOX1 buffer and route it, SCO1 and SCO2 deliver it to the respiratory chain, and the P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B load copper onto secreted enzymes in the Golgi and traffic to membranes for efflux when copper rises. Loss of these ATPases causes Menkes disease and Wilson disease, showing how systemic copper distribution depends on cell-level handling; the same machinery is linked to prion protein and amyloid precursor protein biology.

Copper is needed as a catalytic cofactor yet is toxic when free, so cells keep intracellular copper ion homeostasis by importing, chaperoning and exporting it without ever letting an unbound pool accumulate. The high-affinity importer SLC31A1 brings copper across the plasma membrane, metallothionein and small chaperones such as ATOX1 buffer it and hand it on, and the two copper-transporting ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B load it onto secreted cuproenzymes including ceruloplasmin or excrete the excess, with trafficking regulators shifting them between Golgi and membrane as copper rises. A separate branch delivers copper to cytochrome c oxidase through SCO1, SCO2 and COX19, linking this balance to respiration. Loss of the exporters causes Menkes disease and Wilson disease, the classic copper deficiency and copper overload disorders, and the same chemistry underlies copper-dependent cell death and the copper binding attributed to prion protein and APP.

Iron is indispensable for heme, iron-sulfur clusters and oxygen transport, yet free iron drives Fenton chemistry and oxidative damage, so cells hold it within a narrow range. This homeostatic programme couples uptake, storage, use and export: transferrin and its receptors deliver iron to acidified endosomes, ferrireductases and divalent metal transporters move it into the cytosol, ferritin heavy and light chains sequester it, and ferroportin provides the sole cellular exit. Sensing runs through the iron-regulatory proteins ACO1 and IREB2 acting on mRNA iron-responsive elements, with FBXL5-directed degradation tuning that switch, while NCOA4 delivers ferritin to lysosomes for ferritinophagy. At the organismal level, BMP6-SMAD signalling through hemojuvelin and HFE sets hepcidin output, which internalises ferroportin. Failure produces hemochromatosis, anaemias, and iron-dependent cell death, and links this chemistry to hypoxia signalling and heme catabolism.

Zinc is required by hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors yet is toxic when free, so cells hold cytosolic zinc at vanishingly low free concentrations while keeping a buffered, mobilizable store. This balancing act depends on two transporter families pulling in opposite directions: importers of the SLC39/ZIP group bring zinc into the cytosol from outside the cell or from organelles, while SLC30/ZnT exporters move it out of the cytosol into secretory vesicles, insulin granules, milk or the extracellular space. Metallothioneins provide the buffering capacity, binding and releasing zinc in response to demand and oxidative stress. Lysosomal and endosomal components, including a cation channel and trafficking adaptors, contribute compartmental storage. Loss of individual carriers causes acrodermatitis enteropathica, spondylocheirodysplastic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, transient neonatal zinc deficiency and impaired insulin granule maturation, linking this homeostasis to immunity, skin integrity, skeletal growth and glucose control.

Cells keep internal sodium far below the extracellular level, and that gradient is the currency used to drive secondary transport, set membrane excitability, control cell volume and pH, and move salt and water across epithelia. Intracellular sodium ion homeostasis is the balancing act that maintains it: Na+/K+-ATPase catalytic and beta subunits continuously export sodium in exchange for potassium, tuned by the small FXYD regulators, while entry routes such as the epithelial sodium channel subunits, the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter, and Na+/H+ exchangers admit sodium for reabsorption, pH regulation and osmotic adjustment. Calcineurin B homologues act as accessory regulators of exchanger activity, and sodium-coupled glutamate uptake ties the gradient to neurotransmitter clearance. Loss of this balance produces the salt-wasting and hypertensive syndromes of renal tubule transport, impaired gastric acid secretion, and neuronal and muscular disorders in which failure of pump subunits causes hemiplegic migraine, dystonia or periodic paralysis.

Cells hold their volume nearly constant despite continual osmotic challenge, and cell volume homeostasis is the set of transport and signalling events that restores it after swelling or shrinkage. The mechanism is largely coupled fluxes of salt and water: aquaporin channels provide the water route, cation-chloride cotransporters of the SLC12 family either accumulate or extrude KCl, and volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits together with chloride channels such as CLCN3 open on swelling to release osmolytes. Calcium- and stretch-activated channels including TRPV4, KCNN4 and KCNMA1 link mechanical strain to potassium efflux, while WNK kinases and their downstream targets OXSR1 and STK39 phosphorylate the cotransporters to set the direction of net transport. This regulation underlies epithelial salt handling in kidney and secretory tissues, neuronal chloride gradients, apoptotic cell shrinkage, and blood pressure control, and its failure contributes to inherited salt-wasting and hypertensive syndromes.

Cells and tissues hold hydrogen ion concentration within narrow limits, and this pH regulation sets enzyme activity, membrane transport, and the acidity of compartments and body fluids. Two arenas dominate here: the plasma membrane, where sodium-proton exchangers, bicarbonate and chloride-bicarbonate transporters of the SLC4 and SLC26 families, gastric H+/K+-ATPases and carbonic anhydrase II interconvert CO2 and bicarbonate to buffer cytosol, secrete acid into the stomach, and let the kidney reclaim base; and the endomembrane system, where the multi-subunit vacuolar ATPase, with its assembly factors and accessory subunits, pumps protons to acidify endosomes, lysosomes, melanosomes and secretory vesicles. Counter-ion channels and lysosomal membrane proteins dissipate the charge and tune the set point. Failure produces distal renal tubular acidosis, deafness with enlarged vestibular aqueduct, osteopetrosis from defective osteoclast acid secretion, pigmentation defects, and lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disease.

Proteins are made in one place and must work in another, and intracellular protein transport is the collective machinery that gets them there: across membranes into the ER, mitochondria and peroxisomes, through the nuclear pore in both directions, and between compartments in coated vesicles. Without it secretion, lysosome biogenesis, receptor recycling and organelle identity all collapse, which is why defects underlie peroxisome biogenesis disorders, lysosomal storage and pigmentation syndromes, and hereditary spastic paraplegias. The genes here span the recognisable modules of this traffic: the SEC61 translocon with signal recognition particle receptors, TIMM and TOMM import components, PEX receptors and docking factors, karyopherins, importins, exportins and nucleoporins operating on the RAN gradient, COPI, COPII, clathrin and adaptor coats, RAB GTPases with ARF and SAR1, SNAREs and NSF, retromer and sorting nexins, HOPS and ESCRT complexes, plus ER-associated degradation factors that retrieve misfolded cargo for destruction.

Exocytosis is how cells release cargo packaged in membrane-bounded vesicles eady to fuse with the plasma membrane — neurotransmitters at synapses, hormones and peptides from endocrine granules, granzymes and cytokines from immune cells, and matrix or lipid components from secretory epithelia. The genes trace the whole sequence: Rab GTPases and their effectors plus the exocyst complex tether and target vesicles, syntaxins, SNAP25/23 and VAMPs form the fusion SNARE complex, and NSF with SNAPs recycles it afterwards. Regulation is largely calcium-driven, through synaptotagmins, complexins, Munc13 and Munc18 proteins, CAPS and Doc2 sensors acting together with voltage-gated channels and store-operated entry. Loss of individual steps causes epilepsies and movement disorders, familial hemophagocytic syndromes and pigment-granule diseases, platelet and neutrophil secretion defects, and impaired mast cell degranulation, placing this biology behind synaptic transmission, immune killing and endocrine output alike.

Everything a cell secretes or puts on its surface leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in coated carriers, and this is the export step that moves newly folded cargo from the ER to the cis-Golgi. It sets the throughput of the secretory pathway, so defects produce bleeding disorders from poor clotting factor secretion, skeletal and craniofacial disease from failed collagen export, and broad ER stress. A small GTPase and the inner and outer COPII layers (SAR1A/B, SEC23/24 and SEC13/SEC31, organised at exit sites by SEC16) select cargo and bud the vesicle; cargo receptors such as LMAN1 with MCFD2, SURF4 and the TMED family concentrate specific clients, while an ubiquitin ligase pair enlarges carriers for procollagen. Delivery requires RAB1, the tethers USO1 and the TRAPP complex, and SNAREs including STX5, BET1, SEC22B and GOSR2, with COPI components returning escaped residents.

Secretion is not a one-way street: proteins and lipids that move forward to the Golgi must be balanced by return traffic, and retrograde vesicle-mediated transport from Golgi back to the endoplasmic reticulum is that return arm. It recycles cargo receptors and SNAREs for reuse, retrieves escaped ER-resident proteins bearing KDEL signals through KDEL receptors, and keeps the size, lipid composition and glycosylation enzyme content of Golgi cisternae stable. COPI coat subunits, recruited by ARF GTPases acting under the exchange factor GBF1, bud the carriers; Rab6 and dynein/kinesin-linked adaptors move them; the COG complex and an ER-localised SNARE set including STX18, USE1, BNIP1 and SEC22B, with the NRZ tether, complete fusion. Loss of these components collapses Golgi organisation and causes congenital glycosylation and skeletal disorders, and the route is also exploited by bacterial toxins travelling to the cytosol.

Proteins and lipids traversing the Golgi must be moved between cisternae and returned from later to earlier compartments, and intra-Golgi vesicle-mediated transport is the carrier traffic that does this. It keeps glycosylation enzymes in the cisternae where they belong, so its failure scrambles glycan processing; defects in the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunits cause congenital disorders of glycosylation with developmental and neurological consequences. COPI coat subunits bud retrograde carriers from Golgi membranes, Rab6 and Rab33B with the tethering factors of the COG and TRAPP complexes select and capture them at the acceptor cisterna, and Golgi SNAREs such as GOSR1, GOSR2, VTI1A and VTI1B pair to drive fusion, after which NSF and its SNAP adaptors disassemble the complexes for reuse. The same machinery maintains cisternal identity, Golgi ribbon architecture and the flow of secretory cargo.

post-Golgi vesicle-mediated transport is the sorting step that decides where newly made membrane proteins, secreted cargo and lysosomal enzymes actually end up. After the Golgi, vesicles must be budded, loaded with the right cargo, moved along cytoskeletal tracks and fused with a specific target, and this pathway supplies each of those activities: clathrin adaptor complexes (AP-1 through AP-4) and GGA proteins select cargo, ARF GTPases and their regulators such as GBF1 initiate budding, Rab GTPases with motors like MYO5A and KIF13A direct delivery, and SNAREs including VAMP2/3 with NSF drive fusion. Retromer-like and commander/retriever components recycle receptors back from endosomes. The output is cell surface polarity, regulated secretion, lysosome biogenesis and receptor recycling; sortilin-family receptors here also route neurotrophin and lipoprotein cargo, and defects cause lysosomal storage disease, pigmentation and platelet disorders, and neurodegeneration.

Cargo leaving the Golgi must be sorted into vesicles and delivered to the right destination "u2014 endosomes, lysosomes, secretory granules, or a particular face of the plasma membrane "u2014 and post-Golgi vesicle-mediated transport is that delivery system. It sustains secretion, receptor and transporter surface levels, lysosome biogenesis and the polarity of epithelial and neuronal cells; defects produce lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disease, pigmentation and coagulation disorders. Adaptor complexes and GGA proteins recognise sorting signals and recruit clathrin at the trans-Golgi, sortilin-family receptors select hydrolase and neurotrophin-receptor cargo, and Arf and Rab GTPases with their regulators specify carrier identity. Kinesins and myosin motors move carriers along cytoskeletal tracks, while exocyst, SNARE and NSF-dependent fusion machinery completes tethering and membrane merger. Retromer-like and commander/retriever components recycle receptors back for reuse, coupling outward traffic to endosomal retrieval.

The final leg of the secretory route, carrying cargo from the trans-Golgi network to the cell surface in transport vesicles that then fuse during exocytosis. It determines which receptors, channels, transporters and secreted proteins reach the plasma membrane, and in polarized cells it decides whether they arrive at the apical or basolateral face — so epithelial polarity, ciliary protein delivery, insulin-responsive glucose transport and neurotransmitter release all depend on it. Rab GTPases such as RAB10, RAB11A and RAB13 with their effectors specify carrier identity and routing, GGA adaptors and Golgi scaffolds sort cargo at the exit face, motors and spectrin/actin linkers move carriers along cytoskeletal tracks, the exocyst complex tethers them at the target membrane, and VAMP SNAREs with NSF drive fusion. A retrieval branch including COMMD and CCDC93 components recycles receptors rather than letting them be degraded. Defects produce ciliopathies, keratinization and skin disorders, and neurodegenerative disease.

Traffic from the Golgi to endosomes is the route by which newly made lysosomal enzymes, sorting receptors and membrane proteins leave the secretory pathway and enter the endocytic system, rather than continuing to the cell surface. It keeps lysosomes supplied with hydrolases and returns cargo receptors for reuse, so its failure produces missorted enzymes and defective degradative compartments. Clathrin-coated carriers bud from the trans-Golgi network with adaptor complexes such as AP-1 and AP-4 and accessory factors including an AP-1 binding regulator and EPS15, while sortilin serves as a cargo receptor for lysosomal and neurotrophin-related ligands. Arf-family control through a GBF1-type exchange factor, the Mon2/DOPEY module, RAB14 and kinesin-driven movement of early endosomes position and direct the carriers. The pathway sits at the junction of secretion, endosomal sorting, lipid flippase activity and autophagy-related membrane supply.

Golgi to vacuole transport is the route by which newly made hydrolases, membrane proteins and lipids are delivered from the Golgi to the lysosome (the vacuolar compartment of animal cells), building and maintaining the cell's degradative organelle. Without it, acid hydrolases are missecreted, lysosomes fail to mature, and storage disease follows. Sorting begins at the trans-Golgi network, where receptors such as sortilin capture cargo and clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3 concentrate it into budding carriers, with GAK and the GGA-associated factor CCDC91 supporting coat assembly and uncoating. Vesicles then travel through endosomal intermediates, guided by Rab effectors including ANKFY1 and rabenosyn-5 and the GARP complex, and fuse using the SNAREs VTI1A and VTI1B. Cargo delivered this way includes LAMP1 and CLN3, whose loss causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, tying this traffic to lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic turnover and antigen processing.

Newly made lysosomal enzymes, membrane proteins and pigment-granule cargo leave the Golgi by carriers directed specifically to the vacuolar or lysosomal compartment, and this route is what gives a cell a functional degradative organelle. The clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3, with their accessory factors, select cargo at the trans-Golgi network and at endosomes; sortilin acts as a sorting receptor that captures ligands for delivery and is then retrieved, while SNAREs such as VTI1A and VTI1B and retromer-associated subunits VPS52 and VPS54 handle fusion and recycling steps. LAMP1 marks the destination membrane. Failures of this traffic underlie lysosomal storage and pigmentation disorders, including the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis caused by loss of CLN3 and Hermansky-Pudlak-type defects in AP-3, and they compromise antigen processing and melanosome and platelet granule formation.

Endocytosis is how cells internalise nutrients, receptors, pathogens and patches of their own plasma membrane, pulling the membrane inward to bud off a vesicle that is then sorted, recycled or degraded. It sets how long a signalling receptor stays active at the surface, supplies cholesterol and iron through lipoprotein and transferrin uptake, retrieves synaptic vesicle components after release, and lets macrophages engulf microbes and dying cells. Clathrin with the AP-2 adaptor complex, accessory proteins such as EPS15, PICALM and epsins, and the dynamins that sever the neck define the best-characterised route, while caveolins, flotillins and actin regulators support clathrin-independent and phagocytic uptake. Rab GTPases, sorting nexins, ESCRT components and ubiquitin ligases then direct cargo between early endosomes, recycling routes and lysosomes. Defects contribute to hypercholesterolaemia, immune deficiency, and neurodegeneration linked to impaired synaptic vesicle recycling and protein clearance.

Cells take up specific macromolecules from outside by having a surface receptor bind its ligand and then internalizing that patch of membrane as a vesicle, leaving most other plasma membrane proteins behind. This receptor-mediated endocytosis supplies cholesterol and iron, clears hormones and growth factors, downregulates activated receptors, and is the route by which many viruses and toxins enter; its failure underlies familial hypercholesterolaemia, iron overload and proteinuric kidney disease. Cargo-selective receptors such as the LDL receptor family, transferrin receptor, mannose and scavenger receptors, and megalin-cubilin recruit adaptors including the AP-2 complex, DAB2, PICALM and ARH to clathrin-coated pits, where FCHO and epsin-like proteins shape the bud, actin regulators assist, and dynamins pinch off the vesicle. Rab5 and sorting nexins then direct cargo to early endosomes for recycling or lysosomal degradation, with ubiquitin ligases and arrestins marking receptors for downregulation. A caveolar and clathrin-independent arm operates in parallel.

Membrane traffic begins with vesicle budding from a membrane: a patch of bilayer is deformed outward, loaded with cargo, and pinched off as a discrete carrier. This step supplies the secretory pathway with COPII vesicles leaving the endoplasmic reticulum, generates clathrin-coated endocytic vesicles at the plasma membrane, and produces intralumenal vesicles during endosomal sorting, so its failure blocks protein secretion, receptor downregulation and cargo delivery to lysosomes. Coat subunits such as SEC23/24, SEC13 and SEC31 are recruited by the SAR1 GTPases and shape the bud, adaptor complexes AP-2 and AP-3 select cargo, and dynamins sever the neck. ESCRT-III components including the CHMP proteins with the VPS4A ATPase drive budding away from the cytosol, while TRAPP subunits and p24 family cargo receptors couple budding to downstream tethering, collagen export and lipid homeostasis.

Transport vesicles do not form spontaneously: a protein coat is recruited to the donor membrane, bends it into a bud, selects the cargo to be carried, and marks the resulting vesicle for its destination. Vesicle coat assembly is the step that makes secretion, endosomal sorting and organelle biogenesis possible, and its components define where a cargo goes. Here the COPII arm dominates: the small GTPase SAR1A/SAR1B, activated at the endoplasmic reticulum, drives coat polymerisation at exit sites organised by SEC16A, with p24-family membrane proteins (TMED2, TMED9, TMED10) acting as cargo receptors and ARFGAP2/3 promoting coat turnover. TRAPP subunits tether and activate Rab GTPases on the emerging carriers, while the AP-3 adaptor complex builds coats for lysosome- and melanosome-directed traffic. Ubiquitin ligase activity via CUL3-KLHL12 enlarges carriers for bulky cargo such as procollagen; loss of individual subunits causes skeletal dysplasias, pigmentation defects and neurodevelopmental disease.

Vesicle targeting is the step that gives membrane traffic its specificity: once a transport vesicle has budded, it must be delivered to the correct destination membrane rather than any membrane it encounters. This selectivity keeps the secretory pathway organised, sustains polarised delivery to the cell surface, and underlies regulated secretion and neurotransmitter release; its failure produces broad trafficking disease, including skeletal and neurodevelopmental disorders linked to tethering-complex mutations. The genes describe the machinery involved -- COPII coat and cargo receptors such as SAR1A/B, SEC16A and the TMED p24 proteins for ER exit, the multisubunit TRAPP and exocyst tethering complexes that capture vesicles at Golgi and plasma membrane, golgins and microtubule plus-end tracking proteins that position them, and SNAREs including SNAP23, SNAP29 and YKT6 that commit tethered vesicles to fusion. Kinases, ubiquitin ligases and calcium sensors tune the process.

Vesicle targeting is the step that gives membrane traffic its specificity: a budded carrier must be steered to the one destination membrane whose cargo and identity match it, rather than fusing indiscriminately. The genes here cover the machinery that does this at successive stations. COPII budding and ER exit involve SAR1A/SAR1B, SEC16A, TFG and the p24 family cargo receptors, while ARFGAP2/3 and GBF1 govern Arf-dependent coat dynamics on Golgi membranes. The multisubunit TRAPP complexes and the exocyst act as tethers that capture arriving vesicles and license SNARE pairing, with SNAP23, SNAP29, YKT6 and synaptotagmin/complexin components carrying the process through to fusion; CLASP proteins and TRIP11 link carriers to microtubules. Before a secretory vesicle can fuse and release its contents, it must first be tethered and held against the correct patch of plasma membrane; this docking step in exocytosis sets where and how fast release occurs. It underlies neurotransmitter release at synapses, hormone and granule secretion, and delivery of transporters and channels to the cell surface. The eight-subunit exocyst complex provides tethering to defined membrane domains under control of Rab and Ral GTPases, while active-zone proteins of the RIM and Munc13 families capture vesicles and prime them by opening syntaxin, working with Munc18-type chaperones, SNAP25 and complexins to render the SNARE machinery fusion-ready. Loss of priming and docking components produces severe synaptic transmission defects and epileptic encephalopathies, and related failures impair platelet and immune-cell granule release.

Pinocytosis is the bulk uptake of extracellular fluid and its dissolved solutes: the plasma membrane ruffles and invaginates to enclose a droplet in a vesicle, or pinosome, which is then delivered into the endosomal system. Literally cell drinking, it lets cells sample their surroundings for nutrients and antigens, retrieve membrane, and internalise macromolecules that no dedicated receptor transports, and it is a route exploited by pathogens and by therapeutic macromolecules. Actin remodelling under CDC42 control drives the ruffle, caveolin and sorting nexins shape the forming vesicle, and endosomal adaptors such as APPL1 and APPL2 and Rab-pathway regulators direct the resulting cargo toward recycling or degradation. Lysosomal components including PPT1 and CLN3 link the pathway to eventual breakdown of the imbibed material, tying fluid-phase uptake to nutrient scavenging and lysosomal function.

Phagocytosis is how macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and microglia physically eat particles cells, bacteria, dying and deliver them to lysosomes for destruction. It clears apoptotic corpses to prevent autoimmunity, removes pathogens as a first line of innate defence, and provides antigen for presentation; its failure underlies recurrent infection, chronic inflammation, defective tissue remodelling and neurodegeneration. Recognition comes from opsonins and receptors: complement components and collectins coat targets, Fc receptors and integrins bind antibody and complement, and scavenger and phosphatidylserine receptors such as MERTK, TIMD4, MFGE8 and TREM2 read "eat-me" signals, while CD47 SIRPA marks self as off-limits. Engagement drives Src-family and SYK signalling to Rho-family GTPases through VAV and DOCK ELMO modules, remodelling actin and phosphoinositides to close the cup. Rab GTPases, SNAREs and the NADPH oxidase then mature the phagosome into a degradative, microbicidal compartment.

Phagocytosis is how macrophages, neutrophils, dendritic cells and microglia swallow microbes, dying cells and debris and route them to the lysosome for destruction. It underlies innate defence against bacteria and fungi, the silent clearance of apoptotic cells that prevents autoimmunity, surfactant and lipid turnover in the lung, and synaptic pruning in the brain. Recognition comes from opsonins and their receptors complement components with integrin partners, IgG-binding Fc receptors, collectins and pentraxins and from direct sensors of exposed phosphatidylserine such as MERTK, TIMD4 and MFGE8, while CD47 SIRPA signals self and spares healthy cells. Receptor engagement activates Src-family and SYK kinases, PLCG2, and Rho-family GTPase exchange through VAV and DOCK ELMO modules to drive actin remodelling and cup closure. Phosphoinositide turnover and a RAB cascade then mature the phagosome, coupling it to NADPH oxidase assembly, antigen presentation and cytokine output.

Before a phagocyte can engulf anything it must first decide what to grab, and this recognition step is where that decision is made. Target binding underlies clearance of bacteria, immune complexes and dying cells; when it fails, microbes go unchecked and apoptotic debris accumulates, driving autoimmunity and inflammation. Two broad strategies appear here. Opsonins coat the particle: complement components and their regulators, C-reactive protein, pentraxin 3, collectins and ficolins that engage the lectin pathway through MASP proteases, and surfactant protein A in the airway, with Fc receptor engagement reading out bound antibody. Alternatively, receptors read the surface directly — scavenger receptors CD36 and SCARB1 bind modified lipids and phosphatidylserine, MEGF10 and TREM2 mediate corpse and debris uptake, and dectin-1 detects fungal beta-glucan. Binding then triggers signalling that reorganises the actin cortex for internalisation and sets the inflammatory tone of the response.

Phagocytes finish the job of recognition by physically swallowing their target, and the engulfment step of phagocytosis is that act: extension or invagination of plasma membrane around bacteria, immune complexes, debris or apoptotic cells until the particle is enclosed in a phagosome. It underlies innate antimicrobial defence and the silent clearance of dying cells that keeps tissue from becoming inflammatory or autoimmune. Recognition comes from scavenger and opsonin receptors such as MSR1, MARCO, CD36, TIMD4, MEGF10 and TREM2, complement and Fc receptors with integrin partners, and bridging molecules; these converge on Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 with the DOCK1/ELMO1 module and their GAPs to drive actin remodelling, while myosin, gelsolin and VAMP7-dependent membrane delivery supply contractile force and extra surface. Scramblases of the XKR family and ANO6 expose the phosphatidylserine that marks targets for uptake. Defective clearance contributes to chronic inflammation, lupus-like disease and neurodegeneration.

The execution phase of apoptosis is the point at which a condemned cell is physically taken apart, and this is the dismantling step: nuclear and cytoskeletal structures, chromatin and organelles are cleaved into fragments that can be packaged into apoptotic bodies and cleared by phagocytes without inflammation. It matters because orderly disassembly keeps cell death immunologically silent; failure to degrade apoptotic DNA releases self-nucleic acids and drives autoimmunity, as loss of DNASE1L3 does in lupus-like disease. Executioner caspase activity, licensed by mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation through BAX and BOK and apoptosome formation with APAF1, cleaves DFFA to free the DFFB nuclease, while ENDOG, EXOG and lysosomal DNASE2 complete internucleosomal and mitochondrial DNA degradation. ACIN1 contributes to chromatin condensation, linking substrate cleavage to the morphology that defines apoptotic corpses.

After an immune response clears its antigen, the expanded T cell pool must be culled, and activation-induced cell death is how re-stimulation through the T cell receptor converts a proliferating effector into an apoptotic one. This is a principal mechanism of peripheral tolerance and of contraction at the end of clonal expansion; when it fails, autoreactive and chronically activated clones persist, producing lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity. The death signal is largely extrinsic: Fas engaged by its ligand recruits FADD to assemble a death-inducing complex and activate initiator caspases, with SIVA1 and the mitochondrial chaperone DNAJA3 feeding pro-apoptotic input and RIPK3 offering an alternative, necroptotic route when caspase activity is blocked. Survival and threshold-setting signals oppose this, including AKT1, IL2 receptor signalling through its alpha chain, TGF-beta and the glucocorticoid-induced regulator TSC22D3, so the outcome reflects the balance between restimulation and trophic support.

Inflammation must be switched off as well as switched on, and the programmed death of the cells that mediate it — neutrophils, macrophages, eosinophils and recruited lymphocytes — is how resolution happens. Apoptosis of inflammatory cells allows their intact, non-leaky clearance by phagocytes, which both removes the source of proteases and oxidants and triggers anti-inflammatory signalling in the engulfing macrophage; when it fails or is delayed, tissue damage persists and chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease follows. Death receptor input through FASLG, glucocorticoid-associated ANXA1 signalling, the niacin receptor HCAR2, and innate sensors such as NOD2 and the interferon regulators IRF3 and IRF7 set the threshold, while PI3K catalytic subunits and SIRT1 modulate survival in the opposite direction. Cytokine and chemokine members, including IL6 and CCL5 with CCR5, tie the decision to the inflammatory milieu itself.

Cells crawl by gripping something: substrate-dependent cell migration is the orderly translocation of a cell along the extracellular matrix, in which a leading protrusion extends, adheres to the substrate, and pulls the cell body forward. This is how neural crest and immune cells disperse in development, how fibroblasts close wounds, how axons and growth cones advance, and how tumour cells invade when the same machinery is redeployed. The genes here cover the whole cycle: fibronectin and fibulin as substrate ligands, integrin alpha subunits and their cytoplasmic partners as the adhesive grip, cortactin and non-muscle myosin heavy chain for actin protrusion and contractility, and adaptors such as NCK1, SDCBP and shootin-1 that link receptors to the cytoskeleton. Guidance cues including netrin-1, SLIT2 with ROBO1, neuropilin-1 and an ephrin receptor steer the direction taken, while SNAI2 sets the transcriptional state that makes a cell motile.

Cells crawling over a substrate move by first pushing out a protrusion at the front, and this cell extension step is where a migrating cell commits to a direction. Lamellipodia and filopodia formed this way underlie axon pathfinding, microglial process extension toward injury, endothelial sprouting and wound closure; without them cells lose polarity and directed motility. The genes here span the machinery that couples guidance cues to actin at the leading edge: cortactin and an adaptor set including NCK1, CD2AP and syntenin nucleate and organise branched actin near adhesions, non-muscle myosin IIB provides contractile force, the Rho-family regulator OPHN1 tunes cytoskeletal turnover, and shootin-1 links actin flow to adhesion for traction. Netrin-1 with neuropilin-1 supplies the extracellular direction signal, while purinergic P2RY12 orients process extension toward nucleotides released by damaged tissue.

A crawling cell only advances if its leading-edge protrusions are anchored, and this step — cell attachment to the substrate during substrate-dependent migration — provides that anchorage. Integrins engage extracellular matrix ligands, cluster, and recruit structural and signalling components into nascent adhesions, which convert actin protrusion into traction and set the direction and speed of movement. Fibronectin and fibulin supply the matrix ligands being gripped, while EPB41L5 links adhesion and polarity machinery to the cytoskeleton, and the TWEAK receptor TNFRSF12A and the kinase STK4 couple adhesion state to downstream survival, cytoskeletal and Hippo-related signalling. The same machinery operates in gastrulation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, in wound closure, and in the invasive migration of tumour cells; without stable substrate attachment, protrusions retract and net migration fails.

muscle contraction is the generation of force by actin and myosin filaments sliding past one another at the expense of ATP, the process behind every heartbeat, every voluntary movement, and the tone of blood vessels, airways and gut. The genes span all three muscle types: sarcomeric myosins, actins, troponins and tropomyosins with their scaffolds titin, desmin and dystrophin-associated proteins; the excitation-contraction coupling apparatus of dihydropyridine receptors, ryanodine receptors, junctophilins, triadin, calsequestrin and the SERCA-phospholamban pump; and the voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels that shape the action potential in cardiac and neuronal excitability. Smooth muscle is represented by myosin light chain kinase, RhoA-ROCK signalling and receptors for endothelin, adrenaline and acetylcholine that set vascular tone. Mutations here cause the cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophies, arrhythmia syndromes and malignant hyperthermia, linking calcium handling directly to contractile output.

Muscle contraction is the conversion of chemical energy into mechanical force, shortening or stiffening skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle to move the skeleton, pump blood, and set the tone of airways, gut and blood vessels. The core machinery is the sarcomere actin and myosin heavy and light chains, titin, tropomyosin and the troponin complex whose ATP-driven cross-bridge cycling is switched on by calcium. Excitation contraction coupling supplies that calcium: voltage-gated sodium, potassium and L-type calcium channels shape the action potential, dihydropyridine receptors signal to ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and SERCA pumps with phospholamban and calsequestrin restore resting levels. In smooth muscle, myosin light chain kinase and Rho-kinase set sensitivity to calcium downstream of adrenergic, muscarinic and endothelin receptors. Mutations here cause cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias, congenital myopathies and muscular dystrophies.

Regulation of muscle contraction sets how strongly, how fast and how often cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle shorten, tuning heartbeat, vascular tone, airway and gut motility, and voluntary movement to physiological demand. Its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, hypertension and myopathy. Control converges on calcium: voltage-gated channels and their auxiliary subunits trigger release through ryanodine receptors held in junctional membranes by junctophilins, triadin and calsequestrin, while SERCA pumps, phospholamban, sodium-calcium exchangers and calmodulin set removal and the duration of the transient. Sensitivity of the myofilaments themselves is adjusted at troponin, tropomyosin and myosin light chains through kinase and phosphatase activity. Layered on top are neurohumoral inputs -- adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting via cAMP, PKA, PKG and RhoA -- plus transcriptional and microRNA programs that fix contractile phenotype, and channels including HCN4 and KCNQ1 that govern pacemaking and repolarisation.

Whether a muscle cell contracts, how strongly and how fast, is set by processes that tune calcium delivery to the sarcomere and the sensitivity of the sarcomere to it; this regulation of muscle contraction covers cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle alike. It determines cardiac output and rhythm, vascular tone and blood pressure, gut and airway motility, and skeletal muscle force, and its failure produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia-type disorders and hypertension. Voltage-gated calcium and sodium channels, potassium and pacemaker channels, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum release and uptake machinery (ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps with phospholamban, calsequestrin, triadin and junctophilins) shape the calcium transient, while troponins, tropomyosin, myosin light chains and their kinases translate it into force. Layered on top are G protein-coupled inputs from adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, purinergic and tachykinin receptors acting through cyclic nucleotides, calmodulin and RhoA, plus transcriptional and microRNA control of the contractile programme.

Smooth muscle contraction is the force-generating program of the involuntary muscle that lines blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis, bronchial calibre and continence. Its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthma, vasospasm and intestinal dysmotility. Force comes from actin and a high ratio of myosin rather than sarcomeres, with contraction switched on by myosin light chain kinase acting on smooth muscle myosin, and switched off by nitric oxide-cGMP signalling through soluble guanylate cyclase and protein kinase G. Sensitivity to calcium is tuned by RhoA-ROCK and phosphatase inhibition, while calcium entry, extrusion pumps, sodium-calcium exchange and BK channels shape the underlying calcium and membrane-potential cycles. A broad set of adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, tachykinin, purinergic and prostanoid receptors provides the inputs, and myocardin with serum response factor and microRNAs such as miR-143/145 maintain the differentiated contractile phenotype.
