Smooth muscle contraction generates force in the walls of blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis, bronchial calibre and parturition; its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthmatic bronchoconstriction, vasospasm and intestinal dysmotility. Unlike striated muscle it lacks sarcomeres and contracts over a wide length range, using calcium-calmodulin activation of myosin light chain kinase to phosphorylate the regulatory light chain of smooth muscle myosin and drive actin-based force with ATP hydrolysis. Rho-ROCK signalling sensitises the apparatus by suppressing myosin phosphatase, while nitric oxide acting through soluble guanylate cyclase and PRKG1 promotes relaxation. Contractile tone is tuned by a large repertoire of surface receptors for adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, tachykinin, purinergic and prostanoid ligands, and by calcium handling through sodium-calcium exchange, plasma membrane pumps and large-conductance potassium channels. Myocardin and SRF, with miR-143/145, maintain the differentiated contractile phenotype.

Smooth muscle in blood vessels, airways, gut and uterus sets its tone by tuning how strongly and how often it contracts, and this regulatory layer determines blood pressure, bronchial calibre, peristalsis and labour. Contractile agonists act through G protein-coupled receptors for adrenaline, acetylcholine, endothelin, thrombin, tachykinins and thromboxane, converging on calcium entry and on RhoA-driven inhibition of myosin phosphatase, which sensitises the myofilaments to a given calcium level. Relaxation runs the other way: nitric oxide stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase, and cGMP-dependent protein kinase acting with its membrane partner lowers calcium and desensitises the machinery, while beta-adrenoceptors and RGS2 dampen the contractile arm. Transcriptional control by myocardin and serum response factor, reinforced by miR-143/145, maintains the differentiated contractile phenotype; loss of it accompanies vascular remodelling, hypertension and asthma.

striated muscle contraction is the force-generating program of skeletal and cardiac muscle, in which sarcomeric actin and myosin convert ATP into shortening and thereby produce movement, posture, and the cardiac output that sustains circulation. Its logic is excitation-contraction coupling: voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels and their accessory subunits depolarise the sarcolemma and T-tubules, dihydropyridine receptors signal through junctional proteins such as STAC3, junctophilins and triadin to ryanodine receptors, and released calcium binds troponin C to relieve tropomyosin inhibition of the thin filament. Relaxation follows from SERCA pumps, phospholamban, calsequestrin buffering, sodium-calcium exchange, and repolarising potassium channels. Titin, dystrophin, myosin-binding protein C and the sarcomeric myosins and myosin light chains set mechanical properties and tune contractility, while adrenergic and calmodulin-kinase signalling adjust it to demand. Mutations here cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, arrhythmia syndromes, congenital myopathies, and muscular dystrophy.

Striated muscle contraction is the force-generating programme of skeletal and cardiac muscle, in which sarcomeres arranged in register shorten as myosin heads cycle on actin using ATP. It underlies locomotion, posture, breathing and the heartbeat, and its components are the genes mutated in cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies and inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Excitation begins with acetylcholine receptors or pacemaker and sodium channel activity, spreads through voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels, and is coupled at triad and dyad junctions, where dihydropyridine receptors, junctophilins and ryanodine receptors release stored calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium binds troponin C, shifting tropomyosin to permit crossbridge formation; relaxation follows reuptake by SERCA pumps under phospholamban control and sodium-calcium exchange. Titin, dystrophin and associated costameric proteins transmit and buffer the resulting force, while adrenergic and calmodulin-kinase signalling tunes contractile strength.

Cardiac and skeletal muscle cells must grade how hard and how often they contract, and this regulation of striated muscle contraction covers the machinery that sets that output beat by beat. It matters because the same components tune cardiac output to sympathetic drive and set skeletal force, and their mutation causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia syndromes and myopathy. Depolarization by voltage-gated sodium and L-type calcium channels is coupled through junctional membrane proteins such as junctophilins, triadin and calsequestrin to ryanodine receptor calcium release, while the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pumps and their inhibitor phospholamban, together with sodium-calcium exchange, determine relaxation. Beta-adrenergic receptors acting through Gs, adenylate cyclase and protein kinase A, opposed by phosphodiesterases, phosphorylate troponin I, myosin-binding protein C and phospholamban to adjust myofilament calcium sensitivity. Desmosomal and dystrophin-associated proteins transmit the resulting force, and several microRNAs modulate the programme.

Cell-cell fusion producing a syncytium initially, a single plasma membrane enclosing many nuclei underlies skeletal muscle fibre formation, the placental syncytiotrophoblast, osteoclast generation and sperm-egg fusion. Distinct fusogens serve these settings: myomaker and myomixer drive myoblast fusion downstream of the myogenic factors MYOD1 and MYOG; captive retroviral envelope proteins acting with the transcription factor GCM1 fuse trophoblasts; DC-STAMP and OC-STAMP with the TREM2-TYROBP module support multinucleated osteoclasts; and IZUMO1 mediates gamete membrane fusion. Common requirements include integrin- and tetraspanin-based adhesion (ITGB1, CD9, CD81), Rac activation through DOCK exchange factors, actomyosin and membrane-remodelling activity, calcium and NFAT signalling, and metalloproteinase-mediated surface processing. Failure of these steps impairs muscle regeneration and myotube growth, placental hormone production and nutrient exchange, bone resorption, and fertilisation; the same machinery is exploited by fusogenic viruses.

Infection or tissue injury triggers a systemic change in the protein composition of blood plasma, and this acute-phase response is that change: hepatocytes switch their secretory output toward defence proteins while inflammatory cytokines act on the brain and bone marrow to produce fever, sickness behaviour and the anaemia of inflammation. The circulating readouts of inflammation used clinically, including C-reactive protein, serum amyloid A, haptoglobin, orosomucoid and fibrinogen-associated clotting factors, are products of this programme, as are antiproteases such as SERPINA1 and SERPINA3 that limit collateral damage from neutrophil enzymes. IL-6 acting through its receptor and STAT3, together with IL-1 and TNF and the transcription factor CEBPB, drives the hepatic switch; IL1RN and SIGIRR restrain it. Iron and heme sequestration by haptoglobin, CD163, lactoferrin-like LCN2 and transferrin receptor starves pathogens of nutrients. Sustained activation underlies amyloidosis and chronic inflammatory wasting.

Inflammatory response is the body's immediate defensive reaction to infection or tissue injury, producing the local vasodilation, plasma leakage and leukocyte influx that clear pathogens and damaged cells and set the stage for repair. Without it, hosts cannot contain microbes; when it fails to resolve, the result is chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, fibrosis and septic shock. Pattern-recognition receptors such as the Toll-like receptors, NOD proteins and NLRP inflammasome sensors detect microbial and damage signals and route through MyD88, IRAK kinases, MAP kinases and NF-kB to induce cytokines including TNF, IL-1, IL-6 and IL-17 family members. Chemokines and their receptors direct neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes along selectin- and integrin-dependent adhesion routes, while eicosanoids, complement, kinins and acute-phase proteins amplify the response. Caspase-1-driven pyroptosis, negative regulators such as A20 and IL-10, and lipid mediator switching enforce resolution.

The immediate defensive reaction of vertebrate tissue to infection or injury, marked by local vasodilation, leakage of plasma into interstitial spaces, and recruitment of neutrophils and macrophages to the site. It clears pathogens and damaged tissue and initiates repair; when it fails to resolve, the same machinery drives sepsis, autoinflammatory fevers, atherosclerosis and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors including Toll-like receptors and NOD-like sensors, acting through MYD88, IRAK kinases and NF-kB, induce cytokines such as IL1B, IL6 and TNF; inflammasome assembly on NLRP3 and PYCARD activates caspase-1 and gasdermin-dependent release of mature IL-1 family cytokines. Chemokines and their receptors direct leukocyte traffic, selectins and integrins mediate adhesion to endothelium, complement, eicosanoids, bradykinin and acute-phase proteins amplify the response, and negative regulators including IL10, IL1RN, TNFAIP3 and SOCS3 terminate it.

Complement activation is the humoral arm of innate immunity that marks and destroys microbes, clears immune complexes and apoptotic debris, and recruits inflammatory cells. Three initiating routes converge: the classical pathway, in which C1q bound to antibody activates the C1r/C1s proteases; the lectin pathway, in which mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins engage MASP1/MASP2; and the alternative pathway, sustained by factor B, factor D and properdin amplification on surfaces. All three cleave C3 and C5, generating opsonins and chemotactic peptides and assembling C6-C9 into the lytic membrane attack complex. Because the cascade is indiscriminate, host tissue depends on regulators such as C1 inhibitor, factor H and the factor H-related proteins, factor I, C4-binding protein, CD46, CD55 and CD59; their loss or dysregulation underlies hereditary angioedema, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and complement-driven glomerular and macular disease.

The alternative complement pathway is the arm of complement that turns over continuously without needing antibody or a lectin trigger, providing immediate surveillance of microbial and altered host surfaces. Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 lets factor B be cleaved by factor D to form a C3 convertase, which is stabilised on foreign surfaces by properdin and amplifies deposition of C3b; the cascade then recruits C5 and the terminal components C7, C8 and C9 into the pore-forming membrane attack complex that lyses targets, while C3b fragments opsonise them for receptor-bearing phagocytes. Because the trigger is indiscriminate, restraint is built in: factor H, factor I, CR1 and related regulators dismantle convertases and inactivate C3b on host membranes. Loss of that control drives atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, C3 glomerulopathy and age-related macular degeneration, whereas deficiency of terminal components predisposes to Neisserial infection.

Antibody bound to a target is turned into a signal for destruction by the classical complement pathway, which lyses microbes, clears immune complexes and apoptotic debris, and shapes downstream immune and inflammatory responses. Recognition begins when the C1q subunits engage clustered immunoglobulin Fc regions, activating the associated C1r and C1s proteases; these cleave C4 and C2 to build a C3 convertase, and the cascade proceeds through C5 to assemble the C6-C9 membrane attack complex. Opsonised surfaces are then recognised through complement receptors such as CR1 and CR2, linking innate clearance to B cell activation. Regulators including C4b-binding protein, factor I, CD46, CD55 and clusterin restrain the cascade so that host cells are spared; their loss causes haemolytic and renal complement-mediated disease, while deficiency of early components predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and lupus-like autoimmunity. C1q also supports synaptic pruning in the brain alongside TREM2.

Immunity carried in blood, mucus, saliva and other body fluids relies on secreted molecules rather than direct cell contact, and this humoral immune response gathers that machinery: antibodies, complement, chemokines, cytokines and antimicrobial peptides. It provides the first soluble barrier to microbes at epithelial surfaces and the systemic opsonisation and lysis that clears bloodborne pathogens. Immunoglobulin heavy chains with the polymeric-Ig joining chain supply secreted antibody, while B-lineage factors such as POU2AF1, POU2F2 and BLNK support the cells that make it. Complement runs through classical, lectin and alternative routes (C1q subunits, MBL2 and the MASP proteases, factors B and D) onto the lytic C5-C9 pore, restrained by regulators including CD55, CD59 and factor H so that host tissue is spared. Defensins, lysozyme, lactoferrin, cathelicidin, S100 and WFDC proteins kill or sequester microbes directly, while CC and CXC chemokines recruit leukocytes. Loss of individual components causes recurrent infection, complement-mediated renal disease or hemolytic disorders.

cellular defense response covers the effector arm of innate and cytotoxic immunity: how leukocytes detect microbes, injured tissue and abnormal cells, migrate to them, and destroy them. It is what makes neutrophil and macrophage killing, natural killer cell surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells, and the recruitment of these cells into inflamed tissue possible; its failure produces recurrent infection, and its excess produces inflammatory tissue damage. The genes span the steps in sequence: chemokine receptors such as CCR2, CCR5 and CXCR2 with the complement receptor C5AR1 guide cells to the site; LBP and LY96 hand endotoxin to Toll-like receptor signalling, which reaches NF-κB through BCL10 and RELA; NADPH oxidase subunits NCF1 and NCF2 build the respiratory burst; and perforin, granulysin, NCR1/NCR2 and killer-cell inhibitory receptors set the threshold for granule-mediated cytotoxicity. Adhesion, phagosome acidification and autophagy components complete the killing machinery.

Cell-mediated defense against microbes and damaged or transformed cells, carried out largely by neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages and natural killer cells rather than by antibodies. Loss of these functions leaves a host prone to recurrent bacterial and viral infection and impairs clearance of infected or stressed targets. The genes cover the main effector steps: chemokine receptors such as CCR2, CCR5 and CX3CR1 that steer leukocytes to inflamed tissue; pattern and complement sensing through LY96, LBP and the C5a receptor; NADPH oxidase subunits NCF1 and NCF2 that generate the microbicidal oxidative burst; and cytotoxic granule proteins perforin and granulysin that lyse targets. Killer-cell immunoglobulin-like and NKG2 receptors with the TYROBP adaptor, together with HLA-G and NCR ligand recognition, set the activating versus inhibitory balance that licenses NK killing, while NF-kB components including RELA and BCL10 drive the accompanying inflammatory transcription.

Cells must defend their volume when extracellular solute concentration shifts, and the response to osmotic stress is the coordinated set of transport, signalling and transcriptional changes that restores it. Without it, cells swell or shrink irreversibly, and tissues exposed to steep osmotic gradients dash the renal medulla, brain and cornea dash fail first; brain oedema, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and corneal dystrophy follow from defects in members of this programme. Sensing feeds into WNK kinases and their targets OXSR1 and STK39, which set the activity of cation-chloride cotransporters, while volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits release chloride and organic osmolytes during swelling and aquaporins move water. NFAT5 drives transcription of osmolyte-accumulating genes such as the aldose reductase AKR1B1. Parallel stress-activated MAP kinase, mTOR complex and inflammasome components link osmotic insult to growth control, apoptosis and cytokine release.

Cells exposed to a hypotonic environment swell as water enters, and the hypotonic response is the detection of that dilution and the corrective effort to restore volume and ionic balance. Without it, epithelial and neural cells lyse or lose the ion gradients on which transport and excitability depend. Sensing involves stretch- and osmolarity-gated channels, notably the mechanosensitive cation channel TRPV4, together with a volume-regulated chloride conductance provided by CLCN2 and water permeation through the aquaporin AQP5. The osmotic stress kinases OXSR1 and STK39, with their MO25 partner CAB39, phosphorylate the cation-chloride cotransporters SLC12A5 and SLC12A6 to shift the balance between ion loading and extrusion, driving regulatory volume decrease. Downstream effects include cytoskeletal and adhesion changes via myosin light chain kinase, and metabolic adjustment. This biology matters for corneal and kidney epithelial fluid handling, neuronal chloride homeostasis, and secretory gland function.</br>

Cells exposed to a solute-rich environment shrink as water leaves, and the hyperosmotic response is how they sense that loss and restore volume before macromolecular crowding damages protein folding and DNA. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where tubular cells work in an osmolarity no other tissue tolerates, and in any cell facing hypertonic stress. Sensing feeds into a kinase cascade in which WNK1 and WNK3 activate the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39, which in turn stimulate the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter SLC12A2 to drive ion uptake. In parallel, the transcription factor NFAT5 turns on genes for compatible organic osmolytes, including the aldose reductase AKR1B1 that makes sorbitol, together with the glucose transporter SLC2A1 and aquaporin water channels. Mechanosensitive TRPV4 and Rho-family signalling through RAC1 and ARHGEF2 couple the change in cell shape to cytoskeletal remodelling, while mitochondrial calcium handling adjusts metabolic output.

Genomes are damaged continuously by radiation, chemicals, replication errors and oxidative metabolism, and the DNA damage response is the cell's coordinated reaction to that damage: detect the lesion, halt the cell cycle, repair it, or kill the cell if repair fails. Loss of this surveillance produces the mutator phenotypes behind cancer predisposition, immunodeficiency and premature ageing syndromes. Sensor kinases ATM, ATR and DNA-PK are activated at breaks and stalled forks and signal through CHEK1, CHEK2 and TP53 to induce CDKN1A-mediated arrest or apoptosis via BAX and PMAIP1. Downstream lie every major repair route — base and nucleotide excision, mismatch correction, non-homologous end joining, homologous recombination with BRCA1/BRCA2 and RAD51, Fanconi anaemia crosslink repair and translesion polymerases — supported by chromatin remodellers, ubiquitin and PARP signalling at damage sites, and by replication fork protection and telomere maintenance.

Aerobic metabolism, phagocyte respiratory bursts and xenobiotic exposure all generate superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals, and the response to oxidative stress is the coordinated defence that keeps these species from oxidizing lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the limits on cell survival in ischaemia-reperfusion, inflammation and ageing, and its erosion underlies neurodegeneration, with several members mutated in familial parkinsonism and motor neuron disease. Sensing runs largely through KEAP1 release of NFE2L2, which drives glutathione synthesis, NQO1 and HMOX1, alongside FOXO and TP53 arms that induce sestrins and catalase. Detoxification is carried out by superoxide dismutases, peroxiredoxins, glutathione peroxidases and the thioredoxin system, supported by G6PD-derived NADPH. Downstream branches repair oxidized DNA and methionine residues, clear damaged proteins through the proteasome, remove injured mitochondria by PINK1/PRKN mitophagy, and, when damage is irreparable, commit the cell to apoptosis, necroptosis or ferroptosis.

When protein accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum beyond its folding capacity, cells mount an ER overload response that couples the stress to inflammatory transcription through NF-kappaB, distinct from but overlapping with the classical unfolded protein response. It matters because it links secretory-pathway stress to cytokine production and cell-fate decisions, and its chronic activation contributes to beta cell failure in diabetes, neurodegeneration, and inflammatory tissue injury. Sensing depends on the ER chaperone BiP (HSPA5) and the kinase PERK (EIF2AK3), which attenuates translation and, via ATF4, induces CHOP (DDIT3) to drive apoptosis when adaptation fails; PPP1R15B restores eIF2alpha dephosphorylation to reset translation. Other members support ER calcium handling and quality control, including WFS1, whose loss causes Wolfram syndrome, the channel-associated TMCO1, and SELENOS in ER-associated degradation, with GSK3B and TP53 tying the response to survival signalling.

The endoplasmic reticulum reports its own condition to the nucleus, and this ER-to-nucleus signalling is how cells match protein-folding capacity and lipid supply to demand. It underlies secretory cell function, insulin-producing beta cell survival, and the adaptation of tumour and stressed cells to hypoxia and nutrient limitation; chronic failure drives apoptosis, and loss of individual components causes diabetes with neurodegeneration. Unfolded protein accumulation is sensed at the membrane and relayed by three arms: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to throttle translation while permitting ATF4 and CHOP synthesis, ATF6 travels to the Golgi for cleavage by site-1 and site-2 proteases, and XBP1 mRNA is processed into an active transcription factor, with GADD34-containing phosphatase complexes resetting the response. The same proteolytic machinery, governed by SCAP and INSIG sterol sensing, releases SREBP transcription factors to control cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis.

Cells monitor how much sterol their membranes contain and, when supply falls, switch on the genes that make and import cholesterol and fatty acids. This response to sterol depletion keeps membrane composition and plasma lipoprotein levels in range; its chronic activation drives hepatic steatosis and hypercholesterolaemia, and it is the circuit that statin therapy engages. The sensing step occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum, where SCAP binds the SREBP precursors and, under sterol-replete conditions, is retained by the INSIG proteins; depletion releases the complex for transport to the Golgi and proteolytic liberation of the SREBF1 and SREBF2 transcription factors. Sterol-dependent turnover of INSIG1 and of HMG-CoA reductase runs through ER-associated degradation components including the ubiquitin ligase AMFR and the ERLIN proteins, while NPC1L1 mediates dietary sterol uptake, tying transcriptional output to degradation and absorption.

Building, arranging and taking apart the nucleus is what this pathway covers: the nuclear envelope and its lamina, the pore complexes that perforate it, the tethers that link chromatin and cytoskeleton across it, and the nucleolus within. It matters because the envelope must be disassembled at mitotic entry and rebuilt around segregated chromosomes in each daughter cell, a job performed by mitotic kinases such as CDK1 and PLK1 together with BANF1, LEM-domain proteins and ESCRT-III subunits including CHMP7 and CHMP4B, which seal the reforming membrane with VPS4 ATPases. Lamins and the LINC complex proteins SUN1/2 and nesprins position the nucleus and transmit mechanical force; mutation of LMNA or of the processing protease ZMPSTE24 causes laminopathies and premature ageing syndromes. Sperm chromatin remodelling by protamines and transition proteins, and meiotic chromosome attachment, represent specialised versions of the same nuclear reorganisation.

The double membrane that separates chromatin from cytoplasm must be taken apart at mitotic entry and rebuilt around each daughter nucleus, and nuclear envelope organization covers that assembly, arrangement and disassembly. It determines nuclear shape and stiffness, anchors chromatin at the periphery, and reseals holes that would otherwise expose the genome to the cytoplasm; when it fails, cells acquire micronuclei, ruptured nuclei and DNA damage. Lamins A/C and B form the underlying meshwork, with inner-membrane partners such as emerin, LEMD2 and the LAP1/torsin system tethering it, while ZMPSTE24 carries out the final processing step of prelamin A. Mitotic kinases including CDK1, PLK1 and VRK1 drive disassembly by phosphorylating lamins and BAF, and ESCRT-III subunits with VPS4 ATPases and CHMP7 perform membrane sealing. Mutations in the lamin and processing genes cause muscular dystrophies, lipodystrophy and premature ageing syndromes.

Nuclear pore organization covers the building, spatial arrangement and dismantling of the channels that perforate the nuclear envelope and control all traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm. Without it a cell cannot re-establish nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization after mitosis, and transport of mRNA, ribosomal subunits and karyopherin cargoes fails. Assembly proceeds through modular subcomplexes: the Y-shaped scaffold built on NUP107, NUP133 and SEH1L is targeted to chromatin by ELYS (AHCTF1) as the envelope reforms, inner-ring components such as NUP93, NUP205 and NUP35 close the channel wall, and transmembrane proteins including NDC1 and TMEM170A anchor the structure in the membrane. Phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins such as NUP98, NUP54 and NUP153 line the permeability barrier, while TPR forms the nuclear basket. Reticulon-mediated membrane shaping contributes to pore insertion during interphase growth, linking pore biogenesis to endoplasmic reticulum and envelope morphology.

The nucleolus is built around actively transcribed ribosomal RNA genes, and its assembly, internal arrangement and disassembly determine how much ribosome production a cell can sustain. Organizing this compartment couples growth control to chromatin state: RNA polymerase I subunits and its transcription factor RRN3 drive rRNA synthesis, while nucleolar chromatin remodelling by SMARCA5 with BAZ2A, together with the histone methyltransferase SUV39H1 and macroH2A deposition, silences a fraction of the repeats as heterochromatin. Histone demethylases PHF2 and PHF8 and the deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT2 tune this balance to nutrient and stress signals, and NOLC1 and USP36 act as scaffolding and ubiquitin-removing regulators within the compartment. Because nucleolar integrity reports on ribosome biogenesis stress, its disruption feeds into p53 activation, senescence and the altered nucleolar morphology characteristic of tumour cells.

mitochondrion organization covers everything cells do to build, shape, position and dismantle their mitochondria, and it determines whether the organelle can sustain oxidative phosphorylation, buffer calcium, and serve as the platform for apoptosis. Its breadth is reflected in the machinery involved: import translocases of the outer and inner membranes, cristae-shaping MICOS and OPA1 complexes, assembly factors that chaperone respiratory complex I, III and IV subunits into place, mitochondrial DNA maintenance and transcription factors such as TFAM and SSBP1, and quality-control proteases including LONP1, CLPP and AFG3L2. Opposing fission and fusion activities (DRP1, MFF, MFN1/2) set network morphology, while PINK1-parkin, BNIP3 and FUNDC1 mark damaged organelles for mitophagy and BCL2-family proteins govern outer membrane permeabilization. Biogenesis is driven transcriptionally through PPARGC1A. Defects here produce optic atrophies, spastic paraplegias, cardiomyopathy, and neurodegeneration.

Mitochondria are built, shaped, positioned and turned over continuously, and mitochondrion organization covers the whole of that housekeeping: import of nuclear-encoded proteins, assembly of the respiratory complexes, maintenance of cristae architecture, fusion and fission, movement along the cytoskeleton, replication of the mitochondrial genome, and selective removal of damaged organelles. Its outputs are oxidative energy supply, calcium buffering and control of apoptosis, so failures surface as mitochondrial myopathy and encephalopathy, optic atrophy, peripheral neuropathy and parkinsonism. The machinery includes outer- and inner-membrane translocases, the cristae-organizing scaffold with its mitofilin and MICOS components, dedicated assembly factors for complexes I, III, IV and the ATP synthase, the dynamin-related fission GTPase with its receptors opposing the fusion GTPases mitofusin and OPA1, motor-adaptor proteins for trafficking, matrix chaperones and proteases, and the PINK1-parkin mitophagy axis. Outer-membrane BCL2-family proteins couple organelle state to permeabilization and cell death.

Mitochondria depend on the shape and integrity of their two membranes: cristae must be folded to hold the respiratory chain, the outer membrane must admit imported proteins, and its controlled breach commits a cell to apoptosis. Building and remodelling those membranes is what this pathway covers. Cristae junctions are held by the MICOS complex with mitofilin, CHCHD3 and CHCHD6, tethered to the outer membrane through SAMM50, while OPA1 and MFN2 govern inner- and outer-membrane fusion and OMA1 cleaves OPA1 when the organelle is stressed. Import channels formed by TOM and TIM subunits, along with OXA1L, insert and sort new membrane proteins; tafazzin remodels cardiolipin to give the bilayer its curvature. The same membranes are where BAX, BAK1 and BCL2 family members decide permeabilization, and where PINK1 marks damaged organelles for mitophagy. Disruption causes optic atrophy, neuropathy and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

Inner mitochondrial membrane organization builds and maintains the folded architecture of the mitochondrial inner membrane, the surface on which oxidative phosphorylation happens. Cristae shape sets respiratory efficiency, so its loss lowers ATP output, destabilises supercomplexes, releases cytochrome c and predisposes to optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and neurodegeneration. The MICOS complex, anchored by mitofilin and the CHCHD3/CHCHD6 subunits, holds crista junctions in place and, through SAMM50 and the metaxins, tethers the inner membrane to the outer membrane at contact sites. OPA1 and the AFG3L2/OMA1 proteases regulate crista remodelling and fusion, while the TIM22 and TIM8/13 carrier import machinery, OXA1L and TAFAZZIN insert and lipidate the membrane's proteins and cardiolipin. PINK1 links this architecture to quality control, marking damaged organelles for mitophagy.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae, and the shaping and maintenance of that architecture is what this pathway describes. Cristae geometry sets how densely respiratory complexes can pack, how much cytochrome c is sequestered, and therefore how much ATP a cell makes and how readily it commits to apoptosis; its collapse underlies optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and mitochondrial encephalopathy. Central to it is the MICOS complex at cristae junctions, built around mitofilin (IMMT) with CHCHD3, CHCHD6, APOO and APOOL, tethered to the outer membrane through SAMM50 and the metaxins. OPA1 controls inner membrane fusion and junction tightness and is cleaved by the stress proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2. Carrier-pathway TIM chaperones and the insertases OXA1L and COX18 deliver membrane proteins into the bilayer, while tafazzin remodels cardiolipin, the lipid that stabilises the curvature these proteins impose.

The outer mitochondrial membrane is the organelle's interface with the cytosol, and its organization determines how proteins get in and how the membrane itself is shaped and connected to the inner membrane. Nearly all mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol, so the import pore and its receptors — the TOM complex, with TOMM40 forming the channel and TOMM20, TOMM22 and TOMM70 recognizing targeting signals alongside small assembly subunits — set the capacity of the whole organelle for biogenesis. SAMM50 works with the metaxins to insert beta-barrel proteins into the membrane and anchors contact sites that hold cristae architecture in place, while MTCH1 and MTCH2 act as insertases for tail-anchored and other outer membrane proteins and influence apoptotic permeabilization. Loss of these activities compromises respiratory capacity, mitochondrial morphology and the threshold for cell death.

Plasma membrane organization covers how a cell builds, shapes, repairs and remodels its outer boundary, determining cell shape, polarity, and the ability to fuse, divide, or seal a wound. Loss of these activities underlies muscular dystrophies with defective sarcolemma repair, failures of sperm-egg fusion and infertility, and defects in apoptotic cell clearance. The genes span the main machineries involved: BAR-domain and caveolar proteins (BIN1, PACSIN, CAV1-3, EHD2) that impose curvature and form membrane invaginations; ESCRT-III subunits with VPS4 ATPases that scission and patch membrane; spectrin, ankyrin and IQGAP-actin linkages that tether bilayer to cytoskeleton; scramblases and flippases (ANO6, PLSCR, XKR, ATP8B1) that control phospholipid asymmetry and phosphatidylserine exposure; and dedicated fusogens such as IZUMO1, MYMK and MYMX for gamete and myoblast fusion. Together they make the membrane a dynamic, repairable, compositionally patterned structure rather than a passive barrier.

How a cell builds, shapes and repairs its outer boundary is captured here as plasma membrane organization: the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of the lipid bilayer and its associated scaffolds. It determines cell shape and polarity, the formation of caveolae and membrane microdomains, wound resealing after sarcolemmal injury, and the membrane fusion events of myoblast and sperm-egg fusion. Caveolins and cavin, flotillin, and BIN/amphiphysin and PACSIN family proteins generate and stabilise curvature, while dynamin, sorting nexins and the ESCRT-III subunits with VPS4 ATPases sever and reseal membrane necks. Spectrin, ankyrin, plectin and myosin link the bilayer to the cortical cytoskeleton, and scramblases and flippases of the XKR, PLSCR and ATP8B/ATP10 families redistribute phospholipids to expose or conceal surface signals such as phosphatidylserine. Loss of these activities underlies muscular dystrophies, cholestasis, peripheral neuropathies and defects in fertilisation.

Cells build and continually remodel an internal scaffold of actin filaments, microtubules and intermediate filaments, and cytoskeleton organization covers the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of those structures. It determines cell shape and polarity, provides tracks for intracellular transport, drives migration, cytokinesis and chromosome segregation, and anchors junctions and contractile machinery in muscle, epithelia and neurons. Actin nucleators such as the Arp2/3 complex, formins and WASP-family activators work with capping, severing and monomer-binding proteins like cofilin, profilin and gelsolin, while Rho-family GTPases with their exchange factors and GAPs, and kinases including ROCK, PAK and LIM kinase, set where filaments grow. Tubulins, gamma-tubulin ring components, centrosomal and ciliary proteins, kinesins, dynein and plus-end trackers organize microtubules and axonemes; keratins, lamins, spectrins and plakins give mechanical resilience. Defects underlie ciliopathies, microcephaly, cardiomyopathies, skin fragility and neurodegeneration.

Cell shape, movement and mechanical strength all depend on how actin filaments are built, bundled and taken apart, and actin filament organization covers that whole repertoire: nucleation, elongation, capping, severing, cross-linking into bundles or branched meshworks, and anchoring to membranes and adhesions. It underlies lamellipodial and filopodial protrusion during migration, phagocytosis and immune cell chasing of chemokines, sarcomere assembly in muscle, stereocilia and microvilli in sensory and absorptive epithelia, podocyte foot processes, and the contractile ring and junctional belts of epithelial sheets. Branched networks arise from the Arp2/3 complex with its WAVE and WASP activators, linear filaments from formins and Ena/VASP proteins, while cofilin, gelsolin, profilin, tropomyosins and capping proteins set filament length and turnover. Rho-family GTPases with their GEFs, GAPs and kinases such as ROCK and LIMK route external signals onto this machinery; failures produce immunodeficiency, deafness, nephrotic syndrome, cardiomyopathy and invasive tumour behaviour.

Microtubules underlie mitosis, intracellular transport, cell shape and the beating of cilia and sperm flagella, and this collection spans every process that builds, remodels or uses them. Alpha/beta tubulin isotypes and their cofactors supply the polymer; gamma-tubulin ring components and centrosomal and pericentriolar scaffolds nucleate and anchor it; plus-end trackers, severing enzymes and kinesin and dynein motor complexes with dynactin set filament length, polarity and cargo traffic. A large cilium-associated contingent covers intraflagellar transport, axonemal dynein assembly, radial spokes and dynein regulatory complex parts, and motile ciliary transcription programmes. Mitotic modules include the kinetochore, spindle assembly and abscission machinery. Failure in any branch produces recognisable disease: primary microcephaly and lissencephaly from spindle and neuronal migration defects, ciliopathies with situs inversus, cystic kidney or retinal degeneration, asthenozoospermic infertility, and chromosome missegregation in cancer.

Microtubule-based movement covers the transport and sliding driven along microtubule tracks, and it underlies how cells position organelles, segregate chromosomes, and beat cilia and flagella. Kinesins moving largely toward microtubule plus ends and cytoplasmic dynein with its dynactin, Lis1/NDEL1 and adaptor partners (BICD, HOOK, TRAK, FHIP) carry vesicles, lysosomes, mitochondria, autophagosomes and mRNA granules over long distances, a requirement that makes axons especially dependent on it; mutations in motor and adaptor subunits cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and motor neuron disease. A second arm is axonemal: outer and inner dynein arms, radial spokes, the nexin-dynein regulatory complex, docking and assembly factors, and intraflagellar transport machinery generate ciliary and sperm motility, so defects give primary ciliary dyskinesia, situs abnormalities, male infertility and ciliopathies. Spindle motors and microtubule depolymerases add the mitotic dimension, linking this transport to chromosome movement and cytokinesis.

Microtubules are not static polymers, and controlled loss of tubulin heterodimers from their ends is what lets a cell remodel its cytoskeleton on the timescale of mitosis, neurite growth, or cell migration. Depolymerization sets microtubule length and turnover, corrects erroneous kinetochore attachments, trims spindle and midbody arrays, and releases tubulin for reuse; when it is unbalanced, chromosomes missegregate and axons fail to remodel. Kinesin-13 family motors such as KIF2A, KIF2C and KIF18B actively peel subunits from ends, stathmins sequester free heterodimers to promote catastrophe, and severing enzymes including spastin and katanin subunits cut within the lattice. Opposing these are plus-end regulators and lattice-binding proteins such as CKAP5, the CLASPs and CAMSAP2, together with kinases and deacetylases that tune stability. The balance underlies spindle assembly, neuronal morphogenesis and cilium disassembly, and is the point of attack for tubulin-targeting drugs.

Every microtubule in a cell has to be started somewhere, and this is the step that creates a new seed from free alpha/beta tubulin dimers rather than extending an existing filament. Control over where and when nucleation happens sets the geometry of the spindle in mitosis, the radial array that positions organelles in interphase, and the noncentrosomal arrays built at the Golgi and along existing microtubules. The core machinery is the gamma-tubulin ring complex — gamma-tubulin with its TUBGCP subunits plus the small MZT adaptors and the activator NEDD1 — recruited to sites by pericentrin, ninein, AKAP9 and CEP192, or to microtubule walls by the eight-subunit augmin complex. TPX2 and CKAP5 promote branched and spindle nucleation, while CLASPs and SLAIN proteins couple new seeds to processive growth. Defects disrupt centrosome and cilium assembly and cause microcephaly and chromosome missegregation.

Microtubules are built from a single building block, the alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimer, and tubulin complex assembly is the chaperoned folding and pairing process that produces it. Newly translated tubulin monomers cannot dimerize unaided: they pass through a cytosolic chaperonin ring related to TCP1 and are then handed to a series of dedicated cofactors, TBCA through TBCE, which capture the individual subunits, bring them together, and use GTP hydrolysis to release a polymerization-competent dimer. The same cofactors work in reverse to dissociate dimers, so they also set the size of the soluble tubulin pool. Small heat shock proteins such as CRYAB contribute general chaperone support. Because every mitotic spindle, cilium, axonal transport track and cell shape change depends on this supply, defects are damaging; loss of TBCE function causes hypoparathyroidism with growth retardation and dysmorphism.

post-chaperonin tubulin folding pathway finishes the job of making usable tubulin: after the CCT chaperonin releases partially folded alpha- and beta-tubulin, a set of dedicated cofactors completes folding and assembles the two into the heterodimer that microtubules are built from. Everything that depends on microtubules — mitotic spindles, cilia and flagella, intracellular transport, neuronal axons — depends on this supply step, and the same cofactors also dismantle dimers, so the pathway sets the size of the free tubulin pool. Cofactors A and B capture the monomers, C, D and E form the complex in which GTP hydrolysis validates and releases the dimer, and RP2 acts as a GTPase-activating partner for TBCC. Mutations cause retinitis pigmentosa, cortical malformations, and hypoparathyroidism with encephalopathy, linking dimer quality control to neurodevelopment and photoreceptor survival.

Alpha- and beta-tubulin emerge from the chaperonin only partly folded, and this post-chaperonin step finishes the job and joins the two monomers into the heterodimer that polymerises into microtubules. Without it a cell cannot build spindles, cilia or axonal tracks, and the supply of assembly-competent dimer sets the size of the usable tubulin pool. Dedicated cofactors each capture one subunit or the other, bring them together, and then hydrolyse GTP to release a native dimer; the same cofactors can run in reverse to dissociate dimers, so the pathway also governs tubulin turnover and degradation. RP2 acts as a GTPase-activating protein for ARL3 and shares activity with the cofactor C domain, and its loss causes X-linked retinitis pigmentosa, while mutations in TBCE cause hypoparathyroidism with dysmorphism and encephalopathy, and TBCD mutations give early-onset neurodegeneration.

Microtubules constantly grow and shrink, and stabilising them against depolymerization is how a cell holds a shape, keeps a spindle intact, or extends an axon. Negative regulation of microtubule depolymerization covers the proteins that cap, coat, or rescue microtubule ends so that filaments persist rather than catastrophically disassemble. CLASP1 and CLASP2 promote rescue at growing plus ends, CAMSAP2 binds and protects free minus ends of non-centrosomal arrays, and TPX2 stabilises microtubules nucleated around chromatin during spindle assembly, while MAP1B and other lattice-binding proteins shield the polymer along its length. Links to cortical and adhesion machinery, through APC and Rho-pathway components, tie stabilised microtubules to directed cell migration and polarity. The same activities underlie neuronal process outgrowth and ciliary and centrosomal organisation, and their loss produces disorganised spindles, shortened neurites, and defective polarised transport.

Cytoplasm organization covers the building, spatial arrangement and dismantling of the cell's non-nuclear contents, including the assembly of membraneless granules and the cytoskeletal and motor systems that position organelles. The genes here point strongly to germ cell and germline granule biology: several Tudor-domain proteins, together with a mitochondrial phospholipase and a peptidyl-arginine deiminase of the oocyte cytoplasmic lattices, build the nuage and piRNA-processing compartments that silence transposons and stockpile maternal RNA for early embryogenesis, and their loss causes infertility and cataract in the case of one lens-expressed Tudor protein. Other members contribute motor-driven transport along microtubules, actin capping in the sperm head, lysosomal glycan degradation, and transcriptional control, reflecting how cytoplasmic architecture is set by a mix of phase-separated granules, cytoskeletal scaffolds and the gene expression programmes that supply their components.</description

The endoplasmic reticulum is a single continuous membrane system spanning the cell as flattened sheets near the nucleus and a branching tubular network toward the periphery, and this pathway builds, shapes, fuses and prunes that network. Its geometry determines where proteins are inserted and folded, where lipids are made, and where the ER contacts mitochondria, endosomes and the plasma membrane to exchange lipids and calcium. Reticulon and REEP proteins impose tubule curvature, atlastin GTPases fuse tubules into three-way junctions, lunapark stabilises those junctions, and FAM134/RETREG receptors target ER fragments for selective autophagy. Membrane protein insertion complexes, the Sec61 translocon, tail-anchored protein targeting factors and ER exit site components tie network architecture to secretory capacity. Mutations in the tubule-shaping and fusion machinery cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, reflecting the demands long axons place on ER continuity.

The Golgi apparatus is not self-assembling scaffolding but a structure actively built, stacked, ribboned and, at mitosis, taken apart and rebuilt in the daughter cells; Golgi organization covers all of that. Its geometry sets the order in which secretory cargo is glycosylated and sorted, so loss of organization scatters the ribbon into ministacks and degrades secretion and glycan quality. Golgins and GRASP proteins tether cisternae to one another, the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex and TRAPP subunits support retrograde tethering and vesicle capture, and Rab1, Rab2, Rab6 and their effectors together with syntaxin-5, p115 and TMED/p24 members drive the membrane fusion that maintains cisternal identity. Microtubule and actin linkers such as CLASPs, CAMSAPs and myosin-18A position the organelle near the centrosome, while mitotic kinases including CDK1 and PLK1 trigger its ordered disassembly. Mutations in several components cause skeletal dysplasias, congenital glycosylation disorders and neurodegeneration.

Peroxisome organization builds and maintains the small oxidative organelle where very-long-chain fatty acids are beta-oxidized, plasmalogens are made, and hydrogen peroxide is generated and destroyed. Loss of it causes the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, with severe neurological and hepatic disease, while defects in single cargo transporters cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Peroxins do the core work: membrane proteins are inserted via PEX3, PEX16 and PEX19, while PEX5 and PEX7 recognize matrix proteins carrying targeting signals and deliver them through the PEX13/PEX14 docking site, after which ubiquitin ligases and the PEX1-PEX6-PEX26 AAA-ATPase complex recycle the receptor. Growth and division are handled by PEX11 isoforms together with the fission machinery shared with mitochondria, including DNM1L, FIS1 and MFF. ABCD transporters import fatty acyl-CoA substrates, and ACOX1 initiates their oxidation.

Material taken into a cell by endocytosis is sorted, concentrated and either recycled to the surface or committed to lysosomal degradation, and endosome organization is the set of activities that builds and shapes the compartments where this happens. Its output determines how long growth factor receptors signal, how membrane transporters are turned over, and how pathogens and autophagic cargo reach degradative compartments. Early endosome identity is set by Rab5 GTPases and the tethering factor EEA1, with phosphoinositide kinases marking membranes for effector recruitment; conversion to late endosomes involves RAB7A and its adaptor RILP for dynein-based transport. Ubiquitinated cargo is captured by HGS and STAM and passed to ESCRT complexes, whose CHMP subunits and the VPS4 ATPases bud intralumenal vesicles to form multivesicular bodies. Sorting nexins and the WASH and retromer-associated machinery form recycling tubules, while vacuolar ATPase subunits acidify the lumen. Defects cause lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disease.

Vacuole organization covers the making, shaping, filling and remodelling of lysosomes and related acidic compartments in human cells, the degradative hub on which protein and lipid turnover, nutrient sensing and immune defence all depend. The genes span V-ATPase subunits that acidify the lumen, lysosomal hydrolases such as cathepsin D, GBA1, HEXA/HEXB and TPP1, mannose-6-phosphate tagging enzymes that route those hydrolases, membrane proteins LAMP1/LAMP2 and the channels MCOLN1, TMEM175 and TPCN2, plus tethering, fusion and fission machinery including HOPS subunits, ESCRT-III/VPS4, RAB7A and STX17. Autophagosome formation and its fusion with lysosomes are embedded here through the ULK1-ATG13 and ATG12-ATG5 modules, LC3/GABARAP lipidation, and PIK3C3-BECN1, while mTORC1 on the lysosomal surface with LAMTOR1, FLCN-FNIP1 and TFEB/TFE3 links compartment status back to growth. Loss of these functions causes lysosomal storage disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and neurodegeneration linked to LRRK2, GRN and C9orf72.

Vacuolar transport covers the routes by which proteins, lipids and solutes are delivered into, out of and within the lysosome or vacuole, the degradative compartment on which cellular clearance depends. It determines whether receptors are downregulated, whether damaged mitochondria and protein aggregates are digested, and whether hydrolases reach the organelle at all; its failure produces lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration and immune dysfunction. Cargo is sorted by clathrin adaptor complexes and mannose-6-phosphate receptors, packaged into intralumenal vesicles by ESCRT subunits, and carried along microtubules by motor adaptors before tethering complexes and Rab7-dependent machinery drive fusion. Acidification by the vacuolar ATPase, phosphoinositide signalling through the class III PI3K complex, and autophagy receptors such as SQSTM1 and NCOA4 couple delivery to degradation. Mutations in many members, including LRRK2, GRN, NPC1 and PRKN, cause Parkinsonism, frontotemporal dementia and storage disorders.

Lysosomes and related vacuolar compartments only work when their interior is kept acidic, and this pathway is the pumping and regulatory machinery that lowers that pH. The acidic lumen activates cathepsins and other hydrolases, drives degradation of endocytosed and autophagic cargo, and powers secondary transport of metals and amino acids out of the organelle. The core is the vacuolar H+-ATPase, built from a cytosolic ATP-hydrolysing V1 sector and a membrane-embedded V0 proton pore, with accessory and assembly factors such as ATP6AP1, ATP6AP2, VMA21 and RNASEK required for its maturation, together with lysosomal membrane proteins LAMP1 and LAMP2 and regulators including CLN3, GRN and TMEM106B. Loss of individual subunits causes osteopetrosis, distal renal tubular acidosis with deafness, or neurodegeneration, and defective acidification is a shared lesion in lysosomal storage disease.

Proteins delivered to the lysosome (the animal cell's counterpart of the yeast vacuole) are degraded to amino acids by acid hydrolases, and this catabolic route is how cells dispose of endocytosed cargo, autophagic substrates and turned-over membrane proteins. Its failure underlies the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses and related storage and neurodegenerative diseases, in which undigested material accumulates and neurons die. The genes here span the whole chain: endocytic receptors such as LRP1, LRP2 and LDLR that bring substrates in, sorting and trafficking machinery including retromer, GGA3, AP-5 and ubiquitin-dependent steps mediated by USP8 and membrane-bound E3 ligases, the V-ATPase subunit TCIRG1 that acidifies the compartment, and the proteases themselves — cathepsin H, tripeptidyl peptidase 1, dipeptidyl peptidase 7. Progranulin, TMEM106B, CLN3 and MFSD8 tune lysosomal integrity and are recurring risk loci in frontotemporal dementia and Parkinson disease.

Lysosomes only work if the right cargo reaches them, and lysosomal transport covers the directed delivery of hydrolases, membrane proteins and substrates into, out of and within the organelle. It underlies degradation of endocytosed and autophagic cargo, membrane protein turnover, iron and zinc handling, and antigen and lipid processing; its failure produces lysosomal storage disease and neurodegeneration. Newly made acid hydrolases are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate by GNPTAB/GNPTG and captured by M6PR or IGF2R for sorting from the Golgi, while sortilin and SORL1 route other cargo. RAB7A with RILP and kinesin adaptors positions lysosomes along microtubules, HOPS and related tethers drive fusion, ESCRT components package ubiquitinated cargo into intraluminal vesicles, and retromer and sorting nexins recycle receptors out. Transporters and channels such as NPC1, MFSD1 and TPCN2 move solutes across the limiting membrane. Mutations in GRN, CLN3, LRRK2 and ATP13A2 link this traffic to neuronal survival.

Lysosomes only digest their contents when their interior is kept strongly acidic, and this pathway is the pumping and regulatory machinery that establishes that gradient. The acidic lumen sets the pH optimum for cathepsins and other acid hydrolases, drives amino acid and metal export, and allows lysosomes to act as signalling platforms for nutrient sensing. The core is the vacuolar H+-ATPase: a membrane-embedded V0 sector containing the proton-translocating subunits together with the cytosolic V1 ATP-hydrolysing sector, assisted by accessory and assembly factors including ATP6AP1, ATP6AP2 and dedicated ER chaperones such as VMA21. Membrane proteins including LAMP1/LAMP2, TMEM106B, progranulin and several neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis proteins tune luminal pH and lysosome biogenesis. Loss of acidification produces undigested storage material, seen in lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative disease, while defects in the osteoclast-specific pump subunit TCIRG1 cause osteopetrosis by blocking bone resorption.

Epithelia and endothelia only work as barriers because their cells are physically bonded to one another, and this pathway covers the building of those contacts: tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes and gap junctions. Without it, sheets leak, paracellular transport is uncontrolled, and cells detach and become motile — the hallmark of epithelial-mesenchymal transition and of invasive carcinoma. Classical cadherins engage in trans and are linked through beta-catenin, alpha-catenin and vinculin to the actin cytoskeleton, while claudins, occludin and JAM family proteins seal the apical belt with scaffolds such as ZO-1 and MPDZ. Polarity complexes containing PARD3 and PARD6 position junctions apically, and Rho GTPase signalling through RHOA, RAC1 and ROCK kinases supplies the contractile force that matures them. Connexins add direct cytoplasmic coupling, and transcriptional repressors SNAI1 and SNAI2 dismantle the whole programme during development, wound healing and tumour progression.

cell cycle covers the ordered program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it into daughter cells, the process behind all tissue growth, renewal and repair, and the process whose deregulation underlies cancer and developmental disorders. The genes span every stage: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases with their CDK-inhibitor brakes and E2F/RB transcriptional switches that license S phase; origin licensing and replication machinery such as MCMs, CDC45, PCNA and DNA polymerases; ATM/ATR-CHEK1/CHEK2 damage and replication checkpoints converging on p53; cohesins, condensins and kinetochore-spindle assembly checkpoint components that ensure faithful chromosome segregation; centrosome duplication, tubulins and mitotic kinases such as PLK1 and Aurora; and ESCRT-dependent abscission at cytokinesis. Ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF impose irreversibility by timed proteolysis. Also included is the meiotic variant, with recombination, synaptonemal complex and germ-cell factors required for gametogenesis.

Cell division requires that a cell duplicate its genome once and only once, then partition the copies equally, and this pathway encompasses the whole ordered sequence from growth-factor-driven commitment through DNA replication, mitosis and cytokinesis, including the meiotic variant used in the germ line. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with successive cyclins, opposed by CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27 and gated by the retinoblastoma protein and E2F transcription factors; ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF impose irreversibility by timed proteolysis. Checkpoints sensing DNA damage, replication stress or unattached kinetochores act through ATM, ATR, CHEK1/2 and p53 to delay progression, while centrosomes, spindle microtubules, kinesins, cohesin, condensin and ESCRT-dependent abscission execute segregation and division. Meiosis-specific recombination and synapsis components support gamete formation. Loss of this control underlies aneuploidy, infertility and the unchecked proliferation of cancer.

Spindle organization builds, shapes and disassembles the bipolar microtubule array that segregates chromosomes at each division, and it determines whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome and where the division plane falls. Loss of fidelity here produces aneuploidy, chromosomal instability in tumours, and, through mutations in centrosomal and spindle-pole components such as ASPM and WDR62, microcephaly from depleted neural progenitor pools. The genes cover nucleation by the γ-tubulin ring complex and the augmin/HAUS branching machinery, RAN-GTP release of TPX2 to activate Aurora A, motor-driven pole separation and antiparallel sliding by kinesins and dynein, plus-end regulation by CKAP5, CLASPs and EB proteins, kinetochore attachment through NDC80 and SKA complexes, and cortical force generation that orients the spindle. Chromosomal passenger, PLK1 and cohesin components couple spindle geometry to error correction, anaphase onset and midbody abscission.

Before a dividing cell can separate its chromosomes it must build a bipolar microtubule array, and spindle organization covers the assembly, shaping, positioning and eventual disassembly of that structure. Get it wrong and chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploid daughters, or the division plane is misplaced, which in neural progenitors causes microcephaly. Nucleation begins at centrosomes and on pre-existing microtubules through the gamma-tubulin complex and the augmin subunits, while RAN-GTP gradients and TPX2 activate Aurora A to promote assembly near chromatin. Motors such as the kinesin KIF11 push poles apart, kinetochore-associated NDC80 and SKA modules couple chromosomes to microtubule tips, and CKAP5 and CLASP proteins regulate plus-end dynamics. Aurora B within the inner-centromere complex corrects faulty attachments, PLK1 and cyclin B-CDK1 time the whole programme, and cortical cues orient the spindle to set the axis of division.

Every mitosis depends on building a bipolar microtubule array that can capture chromosomes and pull them apart, and mitotic spindle organization covers the assembly, arrangement and eventual disassembly of that array. Get it wrong and cells missegregate chromosomes, producing aneuploidy, micronuclei and the genome instability characteristic of tumours; in neural progenitors, defects in spindle positioning genes such as WDR62 cause microcephaly. The genes here span centrosome duplication and maturation (SASS6, STIL, PCNT, CEP192), microtubule nucleation from γ-tubulin complexes, plus-end and crosslinking factors including CKAP5, CLASP1/2, TPX2 and PRC1, and the kinesin motors KIF11 and KIF15 that drive pole separation. Aurora kinases, PLK1 and the RAN-importin system impose spatial control, the NDC80 complex links microtubules to kinetochores, and dynein-dynactin with NUMA1 and GPSM2 orients the spindle relative to the cell cortex. ESCRT components and VPS4B act at the final abscission step.

Spindle assembly involved in female meiosis builds the microtubule apparatus that segregates chromosomes in the oocyte, the step that determines whether an egg carries the correct chromosome number. Because oocyte spindles form without canonical centrosomes and must hold chromosomes through long arrest, this process is error-prone, and its failure is the main source of aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and maternal age-related infertility; mutations in the oocyte-specific tubulin TUBB8 cause oocyte maturation arrest in women. The genes cover microtubule nucleation and pole organisation under Aurora A kinase, kinetochore-microtubule attachment through the NDC80 and SKA complexes, cohesin release by WAPL, and control of anaphase timing via cyclin B and the APC/C inhibitor FBXO5. It therefore sits at the intersection of meiotic cell cycle regulation, cytoskeletal organisation and reproductive competence.

Oocytes divide without centrosomes and must build a bipolar spindle from scratch, and spindle assembly in female meiosis is the process that does it, positioning chromosomes for the asymmetric divisions that produce a single egg and its polar bodies. Errors here are a principal source of aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and trisomy, and mutations in the oocyte-specific β-tubulin TUBB8 cause oocyte maturation arrest and female infertility. Aurora A kinase organises acentrosomal microtubule nucleation and spindle poles, while the NDC80 complex with the SKA1–SKA3 subcomplex couples kinetochores to dynamic microtubule ends. Cyclin B2 and the APC/C inhibitor FBXO5 time the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, and cohesin regulation through WAPL governs how sister chromatid linkages are resolved across two sequential divisions. The pathway sits at the intersection of cytoskeletal organisation, chromosome segregation and the oocyte-specific control of meiotic progression.

Chromosome segregation is the machinery that divides replicated genetic material equally between daughter cells, in both mitosis and meiosis. Its accuracy determines ploidy: failure produces aneuploidy, micronuclei and chromosome instability, drives tumourigenesis, and in the germline causes infertility, miscarriage and trisomic offspring. The genes cover the whole sequence — condensin-driven chromosome compaction and topoisomerase-mediated decatenation, cohesin loading and its protection at centromeres by shugoshin, assembly of the CENP-A-marked centromere and the outer kinetochore that grips spindle microtubules, and the bipolar spindle built by gamma-tubulin complexes, augmin, kinesins and dynein. Aurora and Polo kinases with the spindle assembly checkpoint license anaphase only when attachments are correct, at which point the anaphase-promoting complex destroys securin and cyclin B to release separase. A meiosis-specific arm adds synaptonemal complex formation, programmed double-strand breaks and crossover control, plus ESCRT-dependent abscission at the end of division.

Accurate partitioning of duplicated chromosomes into daughter cells is what keeps genomes stable across divisions; when it fails, cells acquire aneuploidy and structural rearrangements that drive tumourigenesis, miscarriage and developmental disorders. The genes here cover the whole sequence: condensin and cohesin complexes compact chromosomes and hold sister chromatids together, centromeric CENP proteins and the HJURP chaperone define the kinetochore platform, and the NDC80, MIS12 and SKA modules couple that platform to spindle microtubules nucleated from gamma-tubulin complexes and augmin. Aurora kinases, PLK1, BUB1 and MAD2 monitor attachment through the spindle assembly checkpoint, delaying anaphase-promoting complex activation until separase can cleave cohesin. Kinesins and dynein generate the forces that move chromosomes poleward, while ESCRT components finish abscission. A meiotic arm — synaptonemal complex proteins, SPO11, PRDM9, REC8 and the MSH4/MSH5 machinery — adapts the same problem to recombination and reductional division in germ cells.

After replication, the two copies of each chromosome must stay physically tethered until anaphase so that the spindle can attach them to opposite poles and divide them evenly; sister chromatid cohesion is that tethering. The ring-shaped cohesin core of SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and a STAG subunit is loaded onto chromatin by NIPBL-MAU2, stabilised by acetylation of SMC3 through ESCO1 and ESCO2, and opposed by WAPL and by HDAC8-mediated deacetylation, while PDS5 proteins and shugoshins protect centromeric cohesion from premature release. Separase, held in check until the spindle checkpoint is satisfied, finally cleaves the kleisin subunit to trigger sister separation. Meiosis substitutes REC8, RAD21L1, SMC1B and STAG3 for stepwise loss of cohesion across two divisions. Failure produces aneuploidy and chromosome instability, and germline defects in loaders and acetyltransferases cause Cornelia de Lange and Roberts syndromes; cohesin also organises chromatin loops with CTCF beyond division itself.

Sister chromatids must stay physically linked from replication until anaphase so that the spindle can pull one copy of each chromosome to each pole; this pathway sets how tightly and how long that linkage is held. Too little cohesion produces premature chromatid separation and aneuploidy, too much blocks segregation, and defects in the machinery underlie cohesinopathies and chromosome instability in cancer. Cohesin subunits such as RAD21 are loaded onto chromatin, the releasing factor WAPL opens the ring to allow turnover, and the separase protease ESPL1 cleaves cohesin at anaphase onset, while the BUB1 kinase contributes centromeric protection through checkpoint signalling. Additional inputs come from architectural and chromatin factors including CTCF and ATRX, the DDX11 helicase acting at replication forks, and the SMC5/6 complex with its SUMO ligase activity, linking cohesion control to replication and DNA repair.

From the moment a chromosome is replicated until metaphase, its two sister chromatids must stay physically linked so that the spindle can attach to them as a unit and pull one copy to each pole; this is mitotic sister chromatid cohesion, and it sets the fidelity of chromosome transmission. Loss of it produces missegregation, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability seen in tumours, and hypomorphic defects in the loading and acetylation machinery cause developmental disorders such as Cornelia de Lange and Roberts syndromes. A ring of SMC1A, SMC3 and RAD21 with STAG1 or STAG2 encircles the sisters; NIPBL with MAU2 loads it, ESCO1 and ESCO2 acetylate SMC3 while HDAC8 reverses this, and sororin stabilises the engaged state. Shugoshin proteins with kinases including BUB1 and Haspin protect centromeric cohesion until CDC20-driven anaphase release.</description>

Before a cell divides, its chromatin must be reorganised from diffuse interphase fibres into discrete, mechanically stiff rods that spindle microtubules can segregate without tangling or breakage. Mitotic chromosome condensation accomplishes this compaction, and its failure produces anaphase bridges, chromosome breakage and aneuploidy. The core machinery is the condensin complexes, built on the SMC2-SMC4 ATPase heterodimer with distinct kleisin and HEAT-repeat subunits (NCAPH and NCAPD2/NCAPG for one form, NCAPH2 and NCAPD3 for the other) that loop DNA processively. Mitotic kinase activity, notably PLK1, times and drives the transition, while chromatin remodelling and histone-modifying activities such as SMARCA5, BAZ1B and the H4K20 monomethyltransferase KMT5A prepare the underlying nucleosome template. Microtubule- and matrix-associated factors including NUSAP1 and the AKAP8 proteins link condensed chromosomes to the spindle and to nuclear envelope breakdown, tying compaction to the wider mitotic programme.

Open mitosis requires the nuclear envelope to be taken apart so that spindle microtubules can reach chromosomes, and mitotic nuclear membrane disassembly is the regulated breakdown that permits this. Without it, chromosome capture and segregation fail and the cell cannot complete division. The trigger is largely phosphorylation by mitotic kinases: CDK1 with its cyclin partner, PLK1, NEK6 and VRK1 phosphorylate lamins, nuclear pore components and inner nuclear membrane proteins, dissolving the lamina and the links that tether chromatin to the envelope, while protein kinase C isoforms contribute to lamin B disassembly. Mechanical force also participates, with dynein and its dynactin subunit DCTN1 tearing the envelope along microtubules. The phosphatase regulator CTDNEP1 and the lipin phosphatidate phosphatase it activates connect this to membrane lipid synthesis, linking envelope breakdown to the later reassembly of the nucleus in daughter cells.

Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be captured by microtubules from opposite spindle poles and brought to the spindle equator; mitotic metaphase chromosome alignment is that positioning step, and it is what allows the subsequent anaphase pull to give each daughter an identical chromosome complement. Failure produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and micronuclei, the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. The machinery spans the centromere and its kinetochore, where CENPA-marked chromatin supports the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes and the SKA complex stabilises attachment to dynamic microtubule ends; motors such as CENPE, KIF18A, KIF22 and KIF2C generate and damp movement along the spindle. The chromosomal passenger complex built around AURKB, INCENP, BIRC5 and CDCA8 corrects erroneous attachments, while MAD1L1, TTK and ZW10 hold the spindle checkpoint until alignment is complete and CDK1-cyclin B activity is licensed for release.

Mitotic nuclear division is controlled so that chromosomes are segregated only once, accurately, and only when a cell is licensed to divide; loss of this control produces aneuploidy, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. Two control layers dominate here. The spindle assembly checkpoint — kinetochore components such as NDC80, NUF2, KNL1 and SKA1 together with BUB1, BUB1B, BUB3, MAD1L1 and MAD2L1 and the RZZ proteins ZW10, ZWILCH and ZWINT — senses unattached kinetochores and restrains the anaphase-promoting complex and its activator CDC20, delaying separase-driven cohesin cleavage. Mitotic kinases including PLK1, AURKA, AURKB with the chromosomal passenger partners INCENP, BIRC5 and CDCA8, plus CDK5RAP2 and NEK2, organise spindle poles and correct attachments, while CDC25C, PKMYT1, CCNB1, CHEK1 and ATM set entry timing. Growth factor and cytokine inputs and RB1 couple division to extracellular cues.

mitotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is the surveillance system that halts cell division until DNA is intact and chromosomes are correctly attached to the spindle, so that daughter cells receive one accurate copy of the genome. Its failure produces aneuploidy, structural rearrangements and the genomic instability that drives tumour formation, which is why several components are inherited cancer predisposition genes. Two arms dominate. Damage and replication stress are sensed by the ATM and ATR kinases with their mediators and clamp loaders, which activate CHEK1/CHEK2 and p53 to impose G1/S and G2/M arrest and stabilise stalled forks. At mitosis, kinetochore-based signalling through MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1 and the NDC80 complex sequesters CDC20 and restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until biorientation is achieved, with Aurora B correcting faulty attachments and an abscission checkpoint delaying the final cut.

Cells that divide with damaged or unreplicated DNA, or with chromosomes not properly attached to the spindle, produce aneuploid and mutated progeny, and mitotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is what delays division until those conditions are corrected. It underlies genome stability, and its components are classic tumour suppressors whose loss drives chromosome instability and cancer predisposition. Two broad arms are represented. Damage and replication-stress sensing runs through the ATM and ATR kinases, the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, TOPBP1, CLSPN and the CHEK1/CHEK2 effectors to p53 and CDKN1A, restraining CDK activity and origin firing. The spindle assembly checkpoint uses kinetochore components including BUB1, BUB1B, BUB3, MAD1L1, MAD2L1, the NDC80/NUF2 complex and the ROD-ZW10-Zwilch module to sequester CDC20 and block anaphase-promoting complex activity until attachments are correct. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin corrects errors, while abscission checkpoint proteins delay the final cut.

Cells that suffer DNA damage in G2 must not enter mitosis with broken chromosomes, and this checkpoint is what holds them back. Delaying the G2/M transition buys time for repair and prevents mis-segregation, aneuploidy and the chromosomal rearrangements that drive cancer; germline loss of its components causes radiosensitivity and cancer predisposition syndromes. Double-strand breaks are sensed by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, which activates ATM, while replication-associated lesions signal through TOPBP1, claspin and CHEK1. The output is suppression of CDK1 activity and of PLK1-driven mitotic entry, reinforced transcriptionally by p21 induction and by FOXO- and FOXN3-dependent repression. A BRCA1-containing ubiquitin ligase and deubiquitinase module, with ABRAXAS1, BABAM1/2 and BRCC3, couples damage recognition to repair choice, and TAOK kinases and CDC14B contribute to arrest and to eventual checkpoint recovery.

Leaving mitosis is not simply the end of division but a controlled switch: mitotic CDK activity must collapse, mitotic phosphorylations must be reversed, and the cell must reset into G1 with a single intact genome. Regulation of exit from mitosis covers the steps between anaphase/telophase and G1 that enforce this conversion from high to low CDK activity. Central to it is destruction of mitotic cyclins and securin by the anaphase-promoting complex, represented here by the CDC23 subunit and the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2C, together with CDC14-family phosphatases that undo CDK-directed phosphorylation, and CDK inhibitors of the CIP/KIP class that keep kinase activity low. Also present are spindle-checkpoint silencing and kinetochore components, which ensure exit waits until chromosomes are correctly attached, plus cytokinesis and midbody factors such as anillin and survivin. Premature or failed exit yields aneuploidy and genomic instability.

During meiotic prophase each chromosome must find its homologue, align with it along its length, and lock the pairing in place before the first division separates them. This homologous chromosome pairing is what makes accurate reduction of ploidy and genetic recombination possible; when it fails, oocytes and spermatocytes arrest or produce aneuploid gametes, and the human outcome is infertility or miscarriage. Programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11 at hotspots marked by PRDM9 are resected and loaded with the meiosis-specific recombinase DMC1, which searches for the homologue; HORMAD proteins and IHO1/MEI4 govern where breaks are made and monitor unpaired axes. Telomeres are tethered through a nuclear-envelope bridge of TERB1/TERB2/MAJIN with SUN1 and KASH5 so that cytoskeletal forces move chromosome ends. Cohesins REC8 and STAG3 build the axis, SYCP1-3 and the SYCE proteins zip the synaptonemal complex together, and MSH4/MSH5 with MLH1/MLH3 and RNF212 mature a subset of joint molecules into crossovers.

Spermatocytes halve their chromosome number through two specialized divisions, and this male meiotic nuclear division programme is what makes fertile sperm possible; its failure produces meiotic arrest, aneuploid gametes and non-obstructive azoospermia. Programmed double-strand breaks introduced by SPO11 are repaired as crossovers using the meiosis-specific recombinase DMC1 together with BRCA2, MEIOB and RAD51C, while MLH1 and MLH3 mark the crossover sites that hold homologues together. Axial element and cohesin components such as SYCP2, SYCP3 and REC8 build the synaptonemal chromosome axis, ATM and TRIP13 police break formation and checkpoint progression, and CCNA1 with SPDYA drives the meiotic divisions themselves. A piRNA arm including MOV10L1, MAEL, TDRD9 and DNMT3L silences transposons so that recombination occurs on a stable genome, linking germline epigenetic control to chromosome segregation and spermatid differentiation.

male meiosis I is the reductional division of spermatocytes, the step that halves chromosome number and shuffles parental alleles before sperm are made; when it fails, spermatocytes arrest and are cleared, producing azoospermia and male infertility. The genes trace its defining events: SPO11 introduces programmed double-strand breaks, DMC1, MEIOB, BRCA2, RAD51C and HSF2BP direct their repair by homologous recombination onto the homologue rather than the sister chromatid, SYCP3 and REC8 build the synaptonemal complex and hold cohesion until anaphase, and TRIP13 governs checkpoint release and crossover maturation. Layered on this are germline transcriptional and chromatin programmes -- MYBL1, BRDT, DNMT3L and the piRNA factors MOV10L1 and TDRD9 that silence transposons -- together with CCNA1 and HSPA2 driving the meiotic G2/M transition. The pathway thus links genome recombination, chromosome segregation and spermatogenic differentiation.

Spermatocytes halve their chromosome number in the first meiotic division, and this male-specific programme covers the events that get them through it: double-strand break formation, homologous pairing and recombination, sister chromatid cohesion, and the transcriptional switch that licenses progression.
