Its output is haploid, genetically recombined spermatids; failure causes spermatocyte arrest, apoptotic loss of germ cells and azoospermic infertility, and mis-segregation yields aneuploid sperm. SPO11 initiates programmed breaks that DMC1, MEIOB, BRCA2 and RAD51C resolve using the homologue as template, TRIP13 governs checkpoint turnover of repair intermediates, REC8 and SYCP3 build the cohesion and synaptonemal axis that holds bivalents together, and MYBL1 and CCNA1 drive the meiotic transcriptional and cell cycle machinery. A piRNA arm including MOV10L1 and TDRD9 silences transposons, protecting the germline genome while recombination leaves it transiently broken.

Oocytes halve their chromosome number through two specialized divisions, and female meiotic nuclear division covers the nuclear events that make this possible: homologue pairing and crossover formation in prophase I, the long arrest that follows, and the asymmetric spindle-driven segregation at maturation. Errors here are the dominant source of human aneuploidy, underlying miscarriage, trisomic pregnancy and age-related infertility. Recombination machinery such as MEIOB, HSF2BP and the MLH1-MLH3 resolvase pair ensures each bivalent receives a crossover, while cohesion regulators and TRIP13 govern how long chiasmata hold. Meiotic resumption depends on kinase-phosphatase balance, with WEE2, MASTL and PP2A subunits setting CDK1-cyclin B activity, and AURKA, PLK1, TTK and the NDC80-SKA kinetochore components executing chromosome capture. Actin nucleators FMN2 and the spire proteins drive the off-centre spindle positioning that produces a polar body and conserves ooplasm for the embryo.

Female meiosis I is the reductional division in the oocyte that separates homologous chromosomes, and it is the step at which human eggs most often go wrong: errors here produce aneuploid eggs, miscarriage and trisomic pregnancy, and the risk rises steeply with maternal age. The genes involved span the two things this division must get right. Homologue pairing and crossover formation depend on meiotic recombination factors such as MEIOB, HSF2BP and BRME1, with MLH3 resolving crossovers so that homologues stay physically linked until anaphase. The other arm is cell cycle control and chromosome segregation: cyclin B2 with CDC25B drives maturation-promoting factor activity, FBXO5 restrains the anaphase-promoting complex during prolonged prophase arrest, and NDC80 with TRIP13 governs kinetochore attachment and spindle checkpoint silencing on the acentrosomal oocyte spindle.

Cell adhesion covers the molecular machinery by which cells attach to one another and to the extracellular matrix, the basis of tissue architecture, epithelial barriers, immune cell trafficking, wound healing and neural wiring. Loss of adhesion control underlies metastasis, blistering skin disease, leaky epithelia and inflammatory pathology. The genes span the major adhesion receptor families — cadherins and protocadherins at adherens junctions and desmosomes, claudins and tight-junction scaffolds such as TJP1 and F11R, integrins with their talin, kindlin and paxillin-linked focal adhesion complexes, selectins and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors (ICAMs, VCAM1, NCAM1, nectins, CADMs) used for leukocyte rolling and immune synapse formation — together with their matrix ligands: collagens, laminins, fibronectin and thrombospondins. Downstream, Src, FAK, Rho-family GTPases and catenin–actin linkages convert attachment into cytoskeletal remodelling, migration, survival signalling and transcriptional change, coupling adhesion to development and differentiation.

Cell adhesion is how cells attach to one another and to the extracellular matrix, and it underlies almost every multicellular arrangement: epithelial sheets that seal a lumen, endothelium that retains blood, synapses that pair the right neurons, and leukocytes that stick to vessel walls before entering tissue. The machinery falls into recognisable families here dash cadherins, protocadherins and catenins at adherens junctions; claudins, occludin partners and tight-junction scaffolds such as ZO proteins; desmosomal cadherins with plakophilins and desmoplakin; integrins with talin, kindlin, paxillin and focal adhesion kinase linking matrix ligands like fibronectin, laminins and collagens to the actin cytoskeleton; and selectins, ICAMs and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors mediating immune contacts. Adhesion complexes also signal, controlling survival, polarity, migration and differentiation. Loss of adhesive integrity produces blistering skin and kidney disease, barrier failure, immunodeficiency, and the detachment and invasion that accompany tumour metastasis.

Homophilic cell-cell adhesion is the binding of a surface molecule on one cell to the same molecule on its neighbour, a like-binds-like rule that lets tissues sort themselves into layers, boundaries and compartments without any external instruction. It builds epithelial sheets and junctions, keeps endothelial barriers sealed, and in the nervous system supplies the recognition code by which axons choose partners, tile dendritic fields and avoid their own sister branches. The classical and desmosomal cadherins anchor adherens junctions and desmosomes to the cytoskeleton, while the clustered protocadherin locus generates combinatorial identities that give individual neurons a distinguishing surface signature. Immunoglobulin-superfamily members such as nectins, CADMs, DSCAM and L1CAM, and guidance receptors including the ROBO family, extend the same principle to synapse formation and axon guidance. Loss of this adhesion underlies blistering skin disease, deafness, retinal degeneration, and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas after cadherin downregulation.

Tissues hold together in part by like-binding-like: an adhesion molecule on one cell engages an identical molecule on its neighbour, so that cells of the same type sort into coherent sheets, layers and boundaries. This homophilic cell-cell adhesion underlies epithelial integrity, endothelial barrier function, and the wiring specificity of neurons, and its failure shows up as loss of epithelial cohesion in cancer invasion, blistering skin disease when desmosomal components are attacked, and neurodevelopmental disorders. The classical cadherins, including the epithelial and neural forms, couple such binding to the actin cytoskeleton at adherens junctions, while desmogleins and desmocollins anchor desmosomes. The very large clustered protocadherin families, expressed in stochastic combinations, give individual neurons a recognition identity used for self-avoidance and dendritic patterning. Nectins, CADMs, contactins, receptor tyrosine phosphatases and the atypical FAT and CELSR cadherins extend the same logic to synapse formation, planar polarity and tissue growth control.

Cells can bind neighbours through matched pairs of unlike surface receptors, and heterophilic cell-cell adhesion covers exactly those asymmetric partnerships: one molecule on one cell engaging a different molecule on the cell opposite. Such pairings encode directionality and cell-type identity in ways that like-binds-like adhesion cannot, which is why they organise immune cell traffic, synapse assembly and epithelial architecture. Selectins and endothelial ligands such as ICAM1 and VCAM1 capture leukocytes from flowing blood and hand them to integrin partners including ITGAL and ITGA5; neurexin-neuroligin and nectin-afadin type contacts specify and align synaptic and junctional membranes; IgLON and CADM family proteins guide axon tract formation; Fat and Dachsous cadherins with Crumbs components set planar polarity and apical organisation. Loss of these interactions underlies immunodeficiency with defective leukocyte recruitment, retinal degeneration, synaptic disorders, and the adhesion changes that accompany tumour invasion.

Neurons stick to other cells through dedicated adhesion molecules, and this attachment is how migrating neuroblasts travel along glia, how axons select their partners, and how synapses form and are held in register. Neurexins on the presynaptic side pair with postsynaptic neuroligins to build and specify excitatory and inhibitory contacts, a transsynaptic bridge whose disruption is repeatedly linked to autism spectrum disorders and intellectual disability. Astrotactins mediate glia-guided neuronal migration during cortical and cerebellar lamination, while contactin and NCAM-family immunoglobulin proteins support axon fasciculation and guidance. Telencephalin, a dendritically enriched adhesion molecule, can engage leukocyte integrins, connecting neurons to immune cell contacts. CDK5R1 supplies the activator that couples adhesion and cytoskeletal signalling to migration. Together these interactions determine where neurons settle, which cells they touch, and how stable those contacts remain.

Leukocytes do their work by touching other cells: rolling on and sticking to endothelium before entering tissue, and forming the immunological synapse with antigen-presenting cells. This adhesion determines whether an infection is cleared, how inflammation is localized, and whether tolerance or autoimmunity follows; loss of the integrin-activating machinery causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency, with recurrent bacterial infection and impaired pus formation. Selectins and their fucosylated glycan ligands mediate the initial tether, while beta-2 and beta-1/beta-7 integrins engaging ICAMs, VCAM1 and MADCAM1 provide firm arrest, with FERMT3 and talin-linked inside-out signalling switching integrins to high affinity. At the synapse, MHC class I and II molecules, the T cell receptor complex with LCK and ZAP70, and costimulatory and checkpoint pairs such as CD28, CTLA4, PD-1 and its ligands set the strength and outcome of contact. Chemokines, cytokines and actin regulators coordinate polarity and migration.

Cells anchor themselves to the extracellular matrix through receptor-ligand engagement, and this attachment governs whether a cell survives, migrates, spreads or differentiates. The pathway underlies tissue architecture, wound healing, leukocyte trafficking and angiogenesis; its loss detaches cells from survival cues, and its dysregulation contributes to fibrosis, blistering skin disease and tumour invasion and metastasis. Integrin alpha-beta heterodimers dominate the receptor repertoire, binding fibronectin, collagens, vitronectin, laminins and fibrinogen, while kindlins, talin and ILK-containing complexes link the receptor tails to actin through vinculin, alpha-actinin and filamin-like scaffolds. Clustering recruits focal adhesion kinase and Src, activating Rho- and Rac-directed cytoskeletal remodelling and PI3K signalling, with phosphatases and GAPs such as PTEN and DLC1 restraining the output. Matrix-remodelling proteases and secreted matrix components in the same programme make adhesion a two-way conversation with the surrounding tissue.

Cells must be able to let go as well as stick: this is the set of processes that stop, reduce or reverse cell adhesion, whether to neighbouring cells or to matrix. Loosening contacts permits leukocytes to detach and migrate, epithelia to remodel during development and wound repair, and neurons and growth cones to be repelled rather than held. The genes span several routes to that end: repulsive guidance receptors and ligands of the ephrin, semaphorin-plexin and Slit-like families; proteases such as ADAM10, MMP2 and MMP14 that shed cadherins and other adhesion receptors; phosphatases and kinase brakes including CSK, PTEN and PTPN6 that damp integrin and Src signalling; Rho-pathway regulators such as DLC1 and RHOA effectors controlling adhesion turnover; and inhibitory immune receptors like CTLA4, PDCD1 and TIGIT that weaken immunological synapse contacts. Loss of these constraints stabilises inappropriate adhesion, while excess detachment favours invasion and metastasis.

Most cells are not symmetric: epithelia have an apex and a base, neurons have an axon and dendrites, a migrating cell has a front and a rear, and a dividing cell orients its spindle relative to its neighbours. Establishing and maintaining cell polarity is what creates and sustains that asymmetry, and it underlies epithelial barrier formation, directional migration, ciliogenesis, and the choice between symmetric and asymmetric division; its loss contributes to tissue disorganisation and tumour invasion. The core machinery comprises conserved complexes acting antagonistically at the cortex — PARD3/PARD6 with atypical PKC, Crumbs with PALS1 and PATJ, and Scribble with DLG and LLGL — read out through Rho-family GTPases such as CDC42 and RAC1 and their effectors on actin and microtubules. Planar signals from WNT5A, VANGL2 and PRICKLE1 align polarity across a tissue, while spindle orientation factors and LKB1/MARK kinases couple polarity to division and cytoskeletal organisation.

Cells within a sheet must agree on a common axis in the plane of the tissue, and establishment of tissue polarity is how that shared orientation is set up and propagated. It determines which way hair cells of the inner ear point, the uniform slant of skin hairs, the directional beating of motile cilia in airway and ependyma, and the convergent-extension movements that close the neural tube and elongate the body axis; loss of it produces neural tube defects, deafness, hydrocephalus and cystic kidneys. The core machinery is the non-canonical, beta-catenin-independent branch of Wnt signalling: Wnt5a and secreted Frizzled-related antagonists provide the tissue-level cue, while asymmetrically localized Vangl2, Frizzled3/6, the atypical cadherin Celsr1 and the pseudokinase PTK7 partition to opposite cell edges and communicate across junctions. Effectors including Fuzzy, Inturned and WDPCP link this polarity to ciliogenesis and cytoskeletal remodelling, with vesicle trafficking components delivering the relevant proteins to the surface.

Cells read their environment largely through receptors that are themselves enzymes, and this pathway covers that entire mode of communication: ligand binding to a catalytic receptor, or to one tightly coupled to a kinase, and the cascade that ends in changed transcription, growth, migration or metabolism. It encompasses receptor tyrosine kinase families for growth factors and their ligands — EGF/ERBB, FGF, PDGF, VEGF, insulin/IGF, HGF-MET, neurotrophin-TRK, EPH — the serine/threonine receptor kinases of the TGF-beta, BMP and activin systems signalling through SMAD complexes, cytokine receptors working via JAK-STAT, and receptor guanylate cyclases for natriuretic peptides. Adaptors such as GRB2, SHC, IRS and GAB link them to RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR, while phosphatases, SOCS, SPRED/SPRY and ubiquitin ligases including CBL and SMURF set signal duration. This wiring builds tissues during development, maintains metabolic and vascular homeostasis, and is the ground on which most oncogenic driver mutations and receptor-targeted therapies act.

Receptor guanylyl cyclase signaling pathway covers hormone and peptide signals that are transduced by cell-surface receptors which are themselves cyclase enzymes, generating cGMP directly rather than through G proteins. It sets blood pressure and fluid balance, controls intestinal fluid secretion, drives skeletal growth at the growth plate, and resets photoreceptors after light. Natriuretic peptides ANP, BNP and CNP bind NPR1 and NPR2 to raise cGMP and activate protein kinase G, relaxing vascular smooth muscle and promoting natriuresis; guanylin-family peptides acting on intestinal GUCY2C regulate salt and water movement and epithelial turnover; retinal GUCY2D and GUCY2F, tuned by calcium-sensing activator proteins, restore cGMP to gated channels in phototransduction. Phosphodiesterases such as PDE2A and PDE10A terminate the signal. Loss of these components causes hypertension and heart failure, secretory diarrhoea, skeletal dysplasia, and inherited retinal degeneration.

Some hormone receptors are themselves enzymes: binding of a peptide ligand to the extracellular domain switches on an intracellular guanylyl cyclase domain that makes cGMP from GTP, and this receptor guanylyl cyclase route converts that second messenger into changes in ion transport, tone and gene expression. Two arms dominate. Natriuretic peptides secreted by the heart and vasculature act through their cyclase-linked receptors to lower blood pressure, promote natriuresis and, via a separate receptor, drive the chondrocyte proliferation that sets long bone growth. An intestinal receptor responds to guanylin-family peptides to control fluid secretion and is the target hijacked by bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin in secretory diarrhoea. Retina-specific cyclases, regulated by calcium-sensing activator proteins, restore cGMP after photon absorption and are mutated in inherited retinal degeneration. Output is read by cGMP-dependent protein kinase and terminated by cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases.

Growth factors, insulin and related ligands act on the cell surface through receptors that phosphorylate tyrosines, and this collection covers that whole mode of communication: ligand binding, receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, recruitment of adaptors, and the cytoplasmic cascades that end in changed transcription, metabolism, motility or survival. It underlies proliferation and tissue growth, angiogenesis and lymphatic patterning, axon guidance and neurotrophic support, and glucose handling, and its inappropriate activation is one of the commonest routes to cancer, which is why many of these receptors are drug targets. Represented families include EGFR/ERBB, FGFR, PDGFR, VEGFR, insulin and IGF1 receptors, TRK neurotrophin receptors, MET, KIT, RET and the large EPH/ephrin group. Phosphotyrosine docking sites engage GRB2, SHC, IRS and GAB adaptors to drive RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR output, while CBL-mediated ubiquitination, endosomal sorting, SPRY and SOCS proteins and phosphatases set signal duration.

Assembly of signalling complexes is the step at which receptors and adaptors are brought together into a physical unit able to relay a signal inward, so that occupancy of a receptor becomes a biochemical event rather than a binding measurement. The genes here point to two settings where this matters. At integrin-based adhesions, focal adhesion kinase and the related PTK2B, paxillin and the Src tyrosine kinase nucleate a scaffold on the cytoplasmic face of attachment sites, converting mechanical engagement of the matrix into control of cytoskeletal remodelling, cell spreading and migration. The NCK adaptors couple phosphorylated receptor tails to actin regulators, while CD3E contributes to the T cell receptor complex and MAPK8IP2 scaffolds JNK-pathway kinases. Common to all is that proximity and correct arrangement, not the presence of the parts, determines whether signalling proceeds.

Signalling through the EGF receptor drives proliferation and survival, so cells need ways to shut it off; this is the braking side of that system, dampening EGF-activated receptor activity once ligand has been sensed. Loss of these brakes prolongs receptor output and is a route to epithelial hyperproliferation and tumour growth, which is why several members behave as tumour suppressors. Two broad strategies appear here. ERRFI1 (Mig6) binds the receptor kinase domain and blocks its activation directly, while SOCS4 and SOCS5 promote receptor ubiquitination and turnover. The remainder act on trafficking: TSG101 and VPS25 are ESCRT subunits, CHMP6 works at the ESCRT-III step, and SNX6 and ZFYVE28 influence endosomal sorting, together committing internalised receptor to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling. ZGPAT adds transcriptional repression of receptor expression, so attenuation operates at kinase activity, protein level, and gene output.

cell surface receptor protein serine/threonine kinase signaling pathway is essentially the TGF-beta superfamily axis: ligands such as TGF-beta, the BMPs, activins, inhibins, nodal, GDFs and anti-Mullerian hormone binding type II receptors that recruit and phosphorylate type I receptors, which in turn phosphorylate receptor-SMADs for transport to the nucleus with SMAD4. It patterns the embryo, specifies left-right asymmetry, builds bone and cartilage, drives epithelial-mesenchymal transition and fibrosis, restrains epithelial proliferation, and sets hepcidin-dependent iron balance; its loss underlies skeletal dysplasias, vascular malformations such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and tumour progression. Output is heavily tuned rather than simply transmitted: secreted antagonists like noggin, chordin, gremlin and follistatin sequester ligands, latent complexes and integrins control activation, inhibitory SMAD6/7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases terminate signalling, and SKI/SnoN with histone deacetylase complexes and numerous microRNAs shape the transcriptional response.

Signalling through cell surface receptors that are themselves serine/threonine kinases is essentially the TGF-beta superfamily system: ligands such as TGF-beta isoforms, activins, inhibins, nodal, anti-Mullerian hormone, myostatin and the many BMPs and GDFs bind paired type I and type II receptors, whose kinase activity phosphorylates SMAD transcription factors that partner with SMAD4 and reach the nucleus to reprogramme gene expression. The outputs shape embryonic patterning and left-right asymmetry, bone and cartilage formation, muscle mass, fibrosis and extracellular matrix deposition, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, immune suppression and iron homeostasis via hepcidin control. Much of the gene content is regulatory: secreted antagonists like noggin, follistatin, gremlins and chordin, latent complex and matrix binding proteins, decoy receptors, inhibitory SMAD6/SMAD7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases, phosphatases, corepressors such as SKI and TGIF, and numerous microRNAs. Loss of restraint underlies skeletal dysplasias, vascular malformations, pulmonary hypertension, cancer progression and organ fibrosis.

Cells read TGF-beta family cues to decide whether to divide, differentiate, migrate, or deposit matrix, and this receptor-initiated cascade is how those cues reach the nucleus. Its outputs include growth arrest of epithelial cells, immune suppression, wound healing, and the fibrotic and epithelial-to-mesenchymal programmes that follow chronic injury; loss of restraint contributes to fibrosis, vascular malformations, aortic disease, and tumour progression, where the pathway switches from tumour suppressor to invasion promoter. Ligands such as TGFB1, activins, nodal and BMPs are released from latent complexes held by latent-binding proteins and matrix components, then engage type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors with accessory co-receptors including betaglycan and endoglin. Receptor-phosphorylated SMAD2/3 or SMAD1/5/9 partner with SMAD4 and recruit CREBBP/EP300 or Sin3/HDAC complexes at target genes, while inhibitory SMAD6/7, SKI/SKIL, SMURF ubiquitin ligases, phosphatases, deubiquitinases and numerous microRNAs set signal strength and duration.

Tyrosine phosphorylation is set not only by kinases but by phosphatases that strip the same marks, and a subset of those phosphatases sit in the plasma membrane with extracellular domains that read cues from outside the cell. Signalling through these cell surface receptor protein tyrosine phosphatases lets contact with matrix, neighbouring cells, or soluble ligands such as pleiotrophin reset the phosphorylation state of adhesion and growth factor effectors, tuning axon guidance, synapse formation, cell adhesion and adhesion-coupled growth control. The receptor-type enzymes here, including PTPRD, PTPRF, PTPRE and PTPRU, have large ectodomains of immunoglobulin and fibronectin repeats; ligand engagement or dimerisation modulates their catalytic output, which converges on cytoskeletal and Rho-family regulators such as TRIO and on adaptors like FRS2 that couple receptor tyrosine kinases to downstream transcription. Loss of these brakes is recurrent in nervous system development disorders and in cancer.

Cells read most of their chemical environment through G protein-coupled receptors, the largest receptor family in the genome and the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. Odorants, tastants, photons, neurotransmitters, peptide and glycoprotein hormones, chemokines, nucleotides, lipids such as sphingosine-1-phosphate and prostanoids all act here, so this signalling underlies smell and vision, neurotransmission, leukocyte chemotaxis, endocrine control of metabolism, vascular tone and platelet activation. Ligand binding drives GDP-to-GTP exchange on a heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunit, which separates from the beta-gamma dimer; Gs and Gi subunits raise or lower adenylate cyclase output and cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity, Gq members activate phospholipase C beta to release calcium and diacylglycerol, and G12/13 members engage Rho exchange factors. Regulators of G protein signalling accelerate GTP hydrolysis, while receptor kinases and arrestins desensitise and internalise the activated receptor, terminating and redirecting the response.

G protein-coupled receptor signaling pathway, coupled to cyclic nucleotide second messenger is the route by which hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines and drugs change the intracellular concentration of cAMP or cGMP, converting an extracellular ligand into a graded, amplified change in kinase activity and gene expression. It sets heart rate, smooth muscle tone, steroid and thyroid hormone output, lipolysis, pigmentation, mood and nociception, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed medicines. Receptors here couple through Gs to stimulate adenylate cyclase or through Gi/Go to inhibit it, with cAMP acting mainly on protein kinase A and Epac. The membership spans adrenergic, muscarinic, serotonergic, histaminergic, opioid, cannabinoid, somatostatin, melanocortin and glycoprotein hormone receptors, so receptor pairs on the same cell can push cyclase in opposite directions and tune the response. Loss or constitutive activation of individual receptors causes endocrine and metabolic disease.

Many hormones, neurotransmitters and drugs act on cells without entering them, and this is the route by which they do it: a receptor at the surface engages a heterotrimeric G protein that turns adenylate or guanylate cyclase up or down, and the resulting change in cyclic nucleotide concentration sets protein kinase activity, ion channel behaviour and gene expression. The receptors named here span the pharmacology of the nervous and endocrine systems — muscarinic acetylcholine, serotonin, histamine, dopamine, opioid, cannabinoid, somatostatin and melanocortin receptors, together with peptide hormone receptors for thyrotropin, parathyroid hormone, luteinizing hormone and VIP. Stimulatory coupling raises cAMP and mobilises steroidogenesis, glycogenolysis or lipolysis; inhibitory coupling lowers it and damps neuronal firing and transmitter release. Because this signalling is dose-graded and reversible, it is the most heavily drugged interface in medicine, and activating receptor mutations cause endocrine hyperfunction such as familial hyperthyroidism and precocious puberty.

Much of how cells read hormones, neurotransmitters and local mediators comes down to whether a receptor raises or lowers cyclic AMP. This adenylate cyclase-modulating branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling covers receptors that couple through stimulatory Gs or inhibitory Gi/Go proteins to the transmembrane adenylyl cyclases, setting cAMP levels that are read out by protein kinase A, anchoring proteins that localise it, Rap-activating exchange factors, and phosphodiesterases that terminate the signal. The receptor repertoire spans adrenergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic, muscarinic, opioid, adenosine, prostanoid, melanocortin and peptide hormone families, so the same chemistry drives cardiac contractility, glucose and lipid mobilisation, water reabsorption in the kidney, steroidogenesis, pigmentation, neuronal excitability and platelet behaviour. Mutations in the pathway cause endocrine tumours, hormone resistance syndromes and obesity, and its receptors are among the most heavily drugged targets in medicine.

Many hormones, neurotransmitters and lipid mediators act by raising cyclic AMP, and this is the route they take: receptor occupancy activates a stimulatory G protein, which switches on adenylyl cyclase, and the cAMP produced engages protein kinase A and cAMP-activated exchange factors to alter metabolism, secretion, contractility and gene transcription. The breadth of receptors here — beta-adrenergic, glucagon and incretin, parathyroid hormone, melanocortin, TSH and gonadotropin, prostaglandin, adenosine, VIP/PACAP and secretin — shows how central the second messenger is to fight-or-flight responses, glucose homeostasis, calcium balance, pigmentation, thyroid and gonadal function, and appetite control. Phosphodiesterases hydrolyse cAMP to terminate the signal and are drug targets in heart failure and inflammation, while A-kinase anchoring proteins confine kinase activity to microdomains. Inactivating or activating mutations in the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit, PKA regulatory subunits or melanocortin receptors cause endocrine resistance syndromes, tumours and obesity.

Turning on adenylate cyclase is the step that converts an extracellular signal into cyclic AMP, the second messenger that drives protein kinase A and thereby hormone-responsive metabolism, secretion, and gene expression. Most of the genes here are receptors that couple to the stimulatory G protein: vasopressin V2 receptor for renal water reabsorption, GLP-1 and GIP receptors for glucose-dependent insulin release, adenosine A2B and a purinergic receptor for nucleotide sensing, corticotropin-releasing hormone and PACAP receptors for neuroendocrine stress responses. GNAS encodes the G alpha subunit that directly stimulates the cyclase, and inactivating or activating mutations in it cause pseudohypoparathyroidism and fibrous dysplasia respectively, showing how tightly physiology depends on the set point of cAMP production. Adenylate cyclase-associated proteins and calcitonin peptide signalling extend the same output to cytoskeletal and calcium-handling responses.

Dopamine acting through D1-class receptors raises cyclic AMP, and this is the excitatory arm of dopaminergic signalling that shapes movement, reward learning, and renal sodium handling. D1 and D5 receptors couple through stimulatory G proteins, including the neuronal Gs-like alpha subunit encoded by GNAL together with beta and gamma subunits, to activate adenylate cyclases such as ADCY5; the resulting cAMP drives protein kinase A and phosphorylation of downstream channels and transcriptional regulators in striatal neurons. Scaffolding by the sodium-hydrogen exchanger regulatory factor organises receptor trafficking and crosstalk at the membrane. Loss or distortion of this signalling underlies parkinsonian motor deficits and dyskinesia, dystonia arising from GNAL mutations, and altered blood pressure control, and it is the route through which psychostimulants and antipsychotic drugs exert much of their effect.

Adenylate cyclase-activating serotonin receptor signaling pathway is the excitatory, cAMP-raising branch of serotonin signalling, used when serotonin needs to increase rather than dampen the activity of a target cell. It governs gut motility and secretion, mood, cognition and sleep-wake regulation, and its receptors are drug targets: 5-HT4 agonists are prokinetics for constipation, while 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 antagonism is pursued for cognitive and psychiatric indications. Mechanistically, serotonin binds 5-HT4, 5-HT6 or 5-HT7, which couple through the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS to adenylate cyclase, so that ATP is converted to cAMP; the resulting rise in cAMP activates protein kinase A and alters ion channel conductance, neurotransmitter release, smooth muscle contraction and gene expression. It stands in functional opposition to the Gi-coupled serotonin receptors that inhibit the same cyclase.

Serotonin does not act through a single mechanism; one branch of its signalling raises intracellular cAMP, and that is what this adenylate cyclase-activating serotonin receptor pathway describes. Receptors of the 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 classes couple through the stimulatory G protein subunit encoded by GNAS to membrane adenylyl cyclase, so that serotonin binding increases cAMP and activates protein kinase A and downstream transcriptional and channel targets. The consequences are regional: enhanced neuronal excitability and neurotransmitter release in cortex and hippocampus, modulation of mood, cognition and circadian and thermoregulatory output, and stimulation of peristalsis in the gut, where 5-HT4 agonists are used as prokinetic drugs. The same receptors are pursued as targets in depression, schizophrenia-associated cognitive deficits and irritable bowel syndrome, placing this arm of serotonergic transmission at the interface between neuromodulation and cyclic nucleotide second-messenger control.

Many hormones and neurotransmitters act by turning cAMP production down rather than up, and this Gi/Go-coupled arm of G protein-coupled receptor signalling is how that happens: receptor activation releases inhibitory G alpha subunits that suppress adenylyl cyclase, lowering cyclic AMP and reducing protein kinase A activity, while the released beta-gamma subunits act on channels and other effectors. The output is restraint — presynaptic inhibition of neurotransmitter release, slowing of the heart by muscarinic receptors, dampened platelet activation, reduced lipolysis and hormone secretion. The receptor complement here is broad, spanning opioid, dopamine D2-class, alpha-2 adrenergic, somatostatin, metabotropic glutamate and GABA-B, adenosine, chemokine and chemoattractant receptors, and includes the drug targets of opioid analgesics, antipsychotics and antiplatelet agents. Adenylyl cyclase isoforms, Gi/Go subunits, phosphodiesterase and PKA, scaffolding AKAPs and RGS proteins set the amplitude and duration of the response.

Cyclic AMP levels set the tone of countless cellular responses, and turning adenylate cyclase down is how cells terminate or oppose stimulatory signalling. This negative regulation is carried largely by Gi-coupled receptors: chemokine, endothelin, galanin, leukotriene B4 and metabotropic glutamate receptors together with the GABA-B receptor subunit GABBR2 all signal through inhibitory G proteins, and GNAI2 and GNAI3 are the alpha subunits that directly suppress the cyclase. Lowering cAMP restrains protein kinase A, which changes neuronal excitability and neurotransmitter release, dampens smooth muscle and immune cell responses, and shapes how strongly a tissue reacts to hormones that raise cAMP. The scaffold AKAP5 contributes by tethering the relevant signalling components near the membrane, so that inhibition is local rather than cell-wide. Loss of this braking arm leaves adenylate cyclase output unopposed, with presynaptic inhibition and receptor desensitisation among the functions most affected.

Dopamine acting through D2-class receptors lowers rather than raises cyclic AMP, and this inhibitory arm of dopaminergic signalling sets the tone of movement control, reward learning, prolactin release and working memory. Binding of dopamine to D2, D3 or D4 receptors couples to Gi/Go, which suppresses adenylate cyclase — including the striatally enriched AC5 encoded by ADCY5 — so that protein kinase A activity and phosphorylation of downstream targets fall. The same receptors act presynaptically as autoreceptors, damping further dopamine synthesis and release, and their signalling is shaped by scaffolding and trafficking partners such as the actin-binding protein filamin A, which influences receptor surface delivery, and by arginine methylation. This is the pathway targeted by antipsychotic drugs, which block D2 receptors, and by dopamine agonists used in Parkinson disease and hyperprolactinaemia; its dysregulation contributes to dyskinesias and addiction.

Glutamate does more than open ion channels: acting through metabotropic receptors coupled to inhibitory G proteins, it lowers cyclic AMP and thereby dampens neuronal excitability and transmitter release. This adenylate cyclase-inhibiting arm of glutamate receptor signalling is largely the work of group II and group III metabotropic receptors, which sit presynaptically on glutamatergic and GABAergic terminals and act as autoreceptors that restrain further release when synaptic glutamate rises. Reduced cAMP means less protein kinase A activity, altered channel phosphorylation, and changes in synaptic strength that contribute to long-term depression and to the tuning of cortical, hippocampal, striatal and retinal circuits. Because this negative feedback limits excitotoxic glutamate accumulation, these receptors are pursued as drug targets in anxiety, schizophrenia, epilepsy and Parkinson's disease, while a retina-enriched member underlies signalling in ON bipolar cells and congenital stationary night blindness.

Acetylcholine acting through muscarinic receptors coupled to inhibitory G proteins lowers cAMP, and this braking arm of cholinergic signalling is what slows the heart, damps neuronal excitability and restrains transmitter release. The M2 and M4 receptors are the canonical Gi/Go-coupled members: M2 in cardiac pacemaker and atrial tissue mediates vagal slowing of heart rate and is the target of atropine, while M4 in striatum opposes dopaminergic drive and is of interest in psychosis and Parkinson's disease. Falling cAMP reduces protein kinase A activity, and the liberated G protein subunits also open potassium channels and inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels, producing hyperpolarization and presynaptic autoinhibition. Histamine H3 and H4 receptors and the mu opioid receptor share the same inhibitory output, placing cholinergic tone alongside histaminergic and opioid modulation as convergent suppressors of cyclase activity in neurons and immune cells.

Serotonin can either raise or lower cAMP depending on which receptor it meets, and this is the inhibitory arm: receptors of the 5-HT1 family, together with 5-HT5A, couple through Gi/Go proteins to suppress adenylate cyclase and lower cyclic AMP in the responding neuron. The consequence is dampened excitability and reduced transmitter release, since many of these receptors sit on serotonergic cell bodies and terminals as autoreceptors that feed back on raphe firing and 5-HT output. This restraint underlies the therapeutic logic of triptans in migraine, which act on 5-HT1B/1D receptors on cranial vessels and trigeminal afferents, and of 5-HT1A-directed anxiolytics and antidepressant augmentation. Downstream of Gα inhibition, released Gβγ and falling protein kinase A activity alter potassium and calcium channel behaviour, linking monoamine signalling to mood, anxiety, sleep and vascular tone.

This is the calcium-mobilizing arm of G protein-coupled receptor signalling: receptors coupled through Gq-family subunits activate phospholipase C-beta, which cleaves PIP2 into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing stored calcium through IP3 receptors and activating protein kinase C and protein kinase D. Through it, cells convert an enormous range of external cues — acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, catecholamines at alpha-1 adrenoceptors, angiotensin, endothelin, thrombin, serotonin, chemoattractants such as C5a and formyl peptides, purinergic nucleotides and metabotropic glutamate — into contraction, secretion, platelet activation, neutrophil chemotaxis and changes in neuronal excitability. Diacylglycerol kinases and inositol phosphatases terminate the signal, and store-operated entry sustains it. Its outputs govern vascular tone, smooth muscle and exocrine function, and inflammatory cell recruitment, which makes these receptors among the most heavily drugged in medicine.

Cytosolic calcium is held at very low resting levels so that its rise can act as a signal, and this collection covers the receptors, channels and transporters that raise it. Such elevations trigger secretion, smooth muscle and cardiac contraction, leukocyte chemotaxis, synaptic plasticity, fertilization and, at the extreme, cell death. Two broad routes appear: release from internal stores through inositol trisphosphate receptors and ryanodine receptors following G protein-coupled receptor activation by chemokines, prostanoids, endothelin, angiotensin, vasopressin and neuropeptides; and entry across the plasma membrane through voltage-gated L- and P/Q-type channels, purinergic P2X receptors, TRP channels and ionotropic glutamate receptors. Junctophilins couple surface membrane to store, sodium-calcium exchangers set the balance, and apoptotic regulators such as BAX and BCL2 tune store release. Dysregulated calcium loading contributes to arrhythmia, excitotoxicity and inflammatory tissue injury.

Phospholipase C-activating G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor signaling pathway is the excitatory arm of muscarinic cholinergic transmission, in which acetylcholine acting through Gq-coupled receptors mobilises intracellular calcium rather than altering cyclic AMP. It drives smooth muscle contraction in airway, gut and bladder, glandular secretion, and slow depolarising responses in neurons that support learning and memory; blocking it is the basis of bronchodilator and antispasmodic anticholinergic drugs. Ligand binding to M1, M3 or M5-type receptors activates Gq/G11 family alpha subunits, which stimulate phospholipase C beta to cleave PIP2 into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol. IP3 opens receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum to release stored calcium, while diacylglycerol and calcium together activate protein kinase C, whose substrates carry the signal to contractile machinery, ion channels and transcriptional programs.

Acetylcholine acts through two receptor families, and this route covers the muscarinic arm that raises intracellular calcium: agonist binding to M1, M2 or M3 receptors couples to Gq-family subunits, which activate phospholipase C beta to cleave PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate. IP3 opens its receptor channel on the endoplasmic reticulum to release stored calcium, while DAG and calcium together engage protein kinase C, converging on contraction, secretion and changes in gene expression. This is the signalling underlying parasympathetic control of smooth muscle tone, glandular secretion and gastric acid release, and in the brain the M1 pathway shapes cortical and hippocampal excitability and memory. Muscarinic antagonists and agonists acting here treat overactive bladder, COPD, and glaucoma, and loss of M1-mediated signalling is implicated in cognitive decline. The presence of M2, normally Gi-coupled, reflects promiscuous coupling to Gq at high receptor density.

Serotonin acts on several receptor subtypes, and one branch of that signalling works through phospholipase C to raise intracellular calcium and activate protein kinase C. This route carries serotonin's effects on mood, appetite, sleep, vascular and gut smooth muscle tone, and platelet behaviour, and it is the target engaged by hallucinogens, atypical antipsychotics and appetite suppressants; the same receptors underlie the valvular fibrosis caused by some of those drugs. Ligand binding to 5-HT2A, 5-HT2B or 5-HT2C couples through Gq to a beta isoform of phospholipase C, which cleaves membrane PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing calcium from internal stores and driving downstream changes in gene transcription and neuronal excitability. The 5-HT1B receptor is included as a serotonin receptor that also modulates this phosphoinositide arm alongside its canonical inhibitory coupling.

Tachykinin peptides such as substance P and neurokinin B act on neurons, smooth muscle, and immune cells to drive pain transmission, neurogenic inflammation, gut motility, vasodilation, and reproductive neuroendocrine control; when tachykinin receptors signal through phospholipase C, those peptide messages become intracellular calcium and protein kinase C activity. Ligands encoded by TAC1 and TAC3 bind the receptors TACR1, TACR2 and TACR3, which couple through the Gq alpha subunit GNAQ to phospholipase C, generating inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol and releasing calcium from internal stores to alter excitability, contraction, secretion, and gene transcription. The neurokinin B to TACR3 arm sets GnRH pulse frequency, and loss-of-function mutations there cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with delayed puberty; the substance P to TACR1 arm is blocked therapeutically by antagonists used against chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting.

Serotonin released from raphe neurons, enterochromaffin cells and platelets acts on a family of receptors that set mood, appetite, sleep, gut motility, vascular tone and nausea, and this receptor signalling is what converts that ligand into cellular responses. Most members are G protein-coupled: HTR1A couples to inhibitory G proteins and dampens neuronal firing as a somatodendritic autoreceptor, the HTR2A/2B/2C group works through Gq and phospholipase C to raise intracellular calcium, and HTR4, HTR6 and HTR7 engage Gs and adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP. HTR3 subunits are different in kind, forming a ligand-gated cation channel related to nicotinic receptors, which explains the presence of nicotinic-type subunits alongside them. Clinically this is the target space of antidepressants, atypical antipsychotics, triptans, prokinetics and antiemetics, and disturbances here accompany depression, anxiety, migraine and irritable bowel syndrome.

Dopamine released at synapses acts through this G protein-coupled receptor pathway to set the excitability of striatal and cortical neurons, shaping movement initiation, reward learning, motivation and prolactin release. Five receptors divide into D1-like (DRD1, DRD5), which couple through Gs/Golf to adenylyl cyclases such as ADCY5 to raise cAMP, and D2-like (DRD2, DRD3, DRD4), which couple through Gi/Go to lower it and to act on ion channels; RGS proteins including RGS4 and RGS9 accelerate G protein deactivation and thereby limit the response. Scaffolds and trafficking factors such as filamin A, NHERF1 and the retromer subunit VPS35 govern receptor surface delivery and recycling. Loss or distortion of this signalling underlies the motor deficits of Parkinson's disease, and the receptors are the direct targets of antipsychotics, dopamine agonists and psychostimulants; LRRK2 and VPS35 link it to inherited parkinsonism.

G protein-coupled acetylcholine receptor signaling pathway covers the slow, modulatory arm of cholinergic transmission, in which acetylcholine acts through muscarinic receptors rather than ion channels to reset the excitability, secretion and contractile tone of a target cell. It is the basis of parasympathetic control of heart rate, smooth muscle and glandular output, of cholinergic modulation of learning and memory in cortex and hippocampus, and of the actions of atropine-like and pro-cholinergic drugs. The five muscarinic receptors split by G protein coupling: M1, M3 and M5 engage Gq/G11 to activate phospholipase C-beta, releasing inositol trisphosphate, calcium through ITPR1, and protein kinase C, while M2 and M4 act through Gi to lower cyclic AMP and open potassium channels. Kinases such as GRK2 and RGS proteins terminate the signal, and receptor output feeds into transcriptional and synaptic plasticity programs.

Acetylcholine acts not only through fast ionotropic channels but also through the five muscarinic receptors, and this slower, G protein-coupled arm of cholinergic transmission sets the tone of parasympathetic control and of cortical and hippocampal circuits. It slows the heart, drives glandular secretion and smooth muscle contraction, and shapes attention, learning and memory; loss of this signalling contributes to cognitive decline, and its receptors are the targets of atropine-like antimuscarinics and of bronchodilator therapy. The odd-numbered receptors couple through Gq/G11 to phospholipase C beta, generating inositol trisphosphate that opens ITPR1 channels and releasing calcium alongside protein kinase C activation, while the even-numbered ones signal through Gi to lower cyclic AMP and act via beta-gamma subunits. Receptor kinases and RGS proteins terminate the response, and shared downstream components link the cascade to histamine and opioid receptor signalling and to transcriptional change.

GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian brain, and gamma-aminobutyric acid signaling is how its release is converted into reduced excitability in a target neuron. Without it, excitation goes unchecked, which is why loss-of-function in these receptors produces epilepsy and developmental encephalopathies, and why benzodiazepines, barbiturates, anaesthetics and alcohol act at this site. Two receptor classes are represented: pentameric chloride channels assembled from alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, theta, pi and rho subunits, which mediate fast phasic and tonic inhibition; and the metabotropic GABA-B heterodimer, which couples through inhibitory G proteins to potassium and calcium channels for slower, longer-lasting suppression of transmitter release. Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter of the vertebrate nervous system, and glutamate receptor signaling is how its release is converted into postsynaptic depolarization, calcium entry, and lasting changes in synaptic strength and gene expression. It underlies learning and memory, and its dysregulation produces excitotoxic neuronal death in stroke and neurodegeneration as well as the synaptic deficits seen in autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. Ionotropic AMPA, kainate and NMDA receptor subunits, together with delta receptors, form the ligand-gated channels; metabotropic receptors act through Gq and phospholipase C to mobilize intracellular calcium. Scaffolds such as PSD-95, Homer and Shank proteins organize these receptors in the postsynaptic density, where adhesion molecules including neurexin and neuroligins align them with presynaptic release sites, and kinases such as Fyn and PYK2 relay activity to downstream transcriptional regulators including MEF2C. Retinal ON-bipolar signalling through mGluR6 and TRPM1 is a specialized branch.

Glutamate acts not only through fast ionotropic channels but also through metabotropic receptors that couple to G proteins, and this slower arm tunes how strongly synapses respond rather than carrying the signal itself. The eight metabotropic glutamate receptors split by function: group I receptors such as GRM1 and GRM5 couple through Gq to phospholipase C, raising intracellular calcium and driving forms of long-term depression, while group II and III receptors act largely presynaptically to lower cyclic AMP and restrain further glutamate release. Homer scaffolds tether group I receptors to intracellular calcium stores and to postsynaptic density proteins, and the Src-family kinase FYN links receptor activation to phosphorylation of synaptic substrates. In retinal ON bipolar cells, GRM6 signalling gates the TRPM1 channel to invert the photoreceptor signal, and its loss causes congenital stationary night blindness. Dysregulation elsewhere is implicated in anxiety, addiction and fragile X syndrome.

Tachykinins are short secreted neuropeptides — substance P and neurokinin A from TAC1, neurokinin B from TAC3, and the hemokinins/endokinins of TAC4 — and this pathway covers how they act on their target cells through the G protein-coupled receptors TACR1, TACR2 and TACR3. It underlies pain and itch transmission by primary sensory neurons, neurogenic inflammation and plasma extravasation, smooth muscle contraction in gut and airway, emesis, and the hypothalamic control of GnRH pulses that sets reproductive timing, where loss of neurokinin B signalling causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Receptor engagement couples largely through Gq, with GNAQ driving phospholipase C, inositol phosphate production and calcium release to depolarize neurons or contract muscle. Signalling is then curtailed by G protein-coupled receptor kinases, which phosphorylate the activated receptor and promote arrestin recruitment, desensitization and internalization. Substance P receptor antagonists exploit this axis clinically as antiemetics.

Neuropeptides are small secreted messengers that tune neuronal and endocrine activity over slower timescales than fast synaptic transmission, and this signalling route covers their action from release to receptor to intracellular response. It sets appetite and body weight, sleep and arousal, stress responses, pain thresholds, reproduction and gut motility, and its receptors are among the most exploited drug targets in medicine. Precursors such as POMC, proenkephalin, prodynorphin, NPY, orexin and galanin are processed by carboxypeptidase E and related secretory-granule machinery, then bind seven-transmembrane receptors including the melanocortin, opioid, somatostatin, NPY and orexin families, which couple through Gi or Gq to adenylate cyclase, phospholipase C and downstream calcium and kinase cascades. Sortilin-family receptors handle sorting and trafficking of propeptides and neurotrophic ligands. Disruption of the AGRP-POMC-MC4R arm causes hyperphagic obesity, while opioid receptor signalling underlies analgesia and addiction.

Notch signalling lets a cell take instruction directly from its neighbour's surface, and it is the main way tissues decide that adjacent cells should adopt different fates. It patterns the nervous system, the intestinal and airway epithelium, somite boundaries, T cell development and arterial versus venous identity in the vasculature; disrupted signalling underlies Alagille syndrome, CADASIL, spondylocostal dysostosis and T-lineage leukaemia. Membrane-bound ligands of the Delta and Jagged families engage Notch receptors, triggering shedding by ADAM proteases and cleavage by the gamma-secretase complex to release the intracellular domain, which enters the nucleus and converts RBPJ with Mastermind coactivators into an activator of HES and HEY repressors. Output is tuned by glycosylation of the receptor by fringe enzymes and O-fucosyltransferases, ubiquitin ligase-driven ligand endocytosis and turnover of activated receptor, making signal strength and duration as regulated as the switch itself.

Notch receptor processing converts a membrane-bound Notch receptor into a transcriptional signal by cutting it apart in a defined order, and it is the step that makes juxtacrine cell-cell communication possible. Neighbouring cells use this to decide between alternative fates during neurogenesis, somite and vascular patterning, gut and skin stem cell renewal, and T cell development; when the cleavages run unchecked the released intracellular domain drives leukaemic and other cancers, which is why the enzymes here are drug targets. Ligand binding exposes an extracellular site cut by the ADAM17 metalloprotease, and the remaining stub is cleaved within the membrane by gamma-secretase, whose catalytic presenilin subunit works with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 to liberate the intracellular domain for nuclear entry. Glycosylation and ligands such as DNER modulate which cells receive the signal.

Notch is a receptor that signals by being cut apart: ligand binding triggers successive proteolytic cleavages that release its intracellular domain to travel to the nucleus and switch on transcription, so receptor processing is the activating step rather than a preliminary to it. This is how neighbouring cells make divergent fate choices, and it underlies lateral inhibition during neurogenesis, boundary formation in somites, intestinal and haematopoietic progenitor decisions, and vascular patterning; loss or gain of cleavage efficiency shifts all of these at once. A metalloprotease of the ADAM family performs the ectodomain shedding step, after which the gamma-secretase complex — presenilin as the catalytic aspartyl protease together with nicastrin, APH-1 and PEN-2 — cuts within the transmembrane region. Glycosylation of the extracellular repeats tunes ligand responsiveness. The same protease complex also processes amyloid precursor protein, linking this machinery to Alzheimer disease.

positive regulation of transcription of Notch receptor target is the nuclear endpoint of Notch signalling, the step at which contact between neighbouring cells is converted into a change in gene expression. It governs binary cell-fate decisions throughout development and adult tissue renewal — neurogenesis, T-lymphocyte specification, vascular and intestinal patterning — and its deregulation drives T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while loss of pathway components causes vascular and skeletal malformation. After ligand binding and proteolysis, the released Notch intracellular domain enters the nucleus and binds RBPJ, displacing corepressors; recruitment of a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1, MAML2 or MAML3) completes a ternary complex that engages histone acetyltransferases and stimulates target transcription, including HES and HEY repressors. RBM15 links the same machinery to RNA-level control. The output is inherently transient, since the complex is rapidly phosphorylated and degraded.

When a Notch receptor is cleaved, its intracellular domain travels to the nucleus and switches on target genes, and this is the transcriptional output step of that pathway. It is how cell-fate decisions are executed during development: lateral inhibition between neighbouring cells, boundary formation, maintenance of stem and progenitor pools, and lineage choice in the nervous system, gut, skin and blood. The released Notch1 or Notch4 intracellular domain binds the DNA-binding factor RBPJ, converting it from a repressor into an activator, and recruits a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1, MAML2 or MAML3) to assemble the ternary complex that drives transcription of HES and HEY family targets. Because the receptor itself is the transcription cofactor, signalling is short-lived and dose-sensitive. Fusions and mutations affecting these coactivators and receptors recur in leukaemias and salivary gland tumours.

Not all Wnt signals go through beta-catenin; the calcium-modulating branch of Wnt signalling instead raises intracellular calcium and turns on protein kinase C, and it is the arm that governs cell polarity, movement and tissue morphogenesis rather than proliferative target-gene transcription. Ligands such as WNT5A and WNT11 acting through Frizzled receptors including FZD4 couple to G protein-dependent phospholipase C activity, releasing calcium from internal stores and engaging calcium-sensitive effectors; the downstream kinase NLK links this output back to transcriptional control and can antagonise the canonical branch. DKK1 sets the tone of the system by blocking Wnt access to co-receptors. This signalling shapes gastrulation and convergent extension movements, heart and vascular development, and when misdirected contributes to tumour cell invasion, where WNT5A is repeatedly implicated in migratory behaviour.

Smoothened signaling is the transducing arm of the Hedgehog pathway, the patterning system that tells cells in a developing embryo where they are and what to become. Its output builds the neural tube's ventral cell types, the limb skeleton, the face and the gut, and its failure causes holoprosencephaly, polydactyly and skeletal dysplasias, while inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Ligands such as SHH, IHH and DHH bind the receptor PTCH1, relieving its inhibition of SMO; SMO then accumulates in the primary cilium, where a suppressor (SUFU), kinases including PKA catalytic subunits, and the ubiquitin machinery are overcome so that GLI1-GLI3 transcription factors escape proteolytic processing and degradation and enter the nucleus. The prominence of intraflagellar transport components, transition zone proteins and cilium-localized GPR161 reflects how completely this signalling depends on an intact primary cilium.

Cells read the composition and mechanics of their surroundings through integrins, heterodimeric receptors that bind extracellular matrix ligands such as fibronectin, laminins, collagens and vitronectin, or counter-receptors on other cells, and convert that engagement into intracellular signals controlling adhesion, spreading, migration, survival and gene expression. This adhesion signalling anchors epithelia to basement membrane, lets leukocytes arrest on endothelium and enter tissue, and drives platelet aggregation; its loss underlies blistering skin disease, bleeding disorders and leukocyte adhesion deficiency, and its misuse supports tumour invasion. Alpha and beta subunits pair combinatorially and are switched to high affinity from inside the cell by talin and kindlins binding the beta tail. Clustered receptors nucleate focal adhesions where FAK, Src-family kinases, ILK, paxillin-like scaffolds and p130Cas assemble, activating Rho-family GTPase exchange factors and linking the actomyosin cytoskeleton to matrix remodelling by proteases.

Cells must sense changes in external osmolarity and respond before they swell or shrink past tolerance, and osmosensory signaling is the route from that physical cue to a corrective response. It matters for systemic water balance, blood pressure control and the volume regulation of every epithelium, and in the kidney and brain it underlies the thirst and vasopressin responses to hypertonicity. Mechanosensitive and osmotically gated cation channels of the TRPV family provide an entry point for calcium, while the WNK-OXSR1 kinase module couples tonicity to phosphorylation of cation-chloride cotransporters and thus to ion and water movement; a sodium channel subunit implicated in sodium-level sensing acts in the same context. Hypotonic or hypertonic stress also converges on the NLRP3 inflammasome with ASC and caspase-1, linking cell volume disturbance to interleukin-1 processing and inflammatory signalling.

Inflammatory and immune gene expression is switched on largely through canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction, the route by which cytokine and pattern-recognition receptors at the cell surface change transcription in the nucleus. It drives production of TNF, IL-1 and chemokines, supports lymphocyte activation and lymphoid organ development, and blocks apoptosis; chronic activity underlies autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease and sustains tumour survival, while loss of components causes immunodeficiency or ectodermal dysplasia. Ligands acting on TNF receptors, IL-1 receptor, TLRs and NOD-like sensors recruit adaptors such as MYD88, TRADD and the TRAF proteins, which build polyubiquitin scaffolds that engage TAK1 and the IKK complex of CHUK, IKBKB and IKBKG. IKK phosphorylation of IkappaB proteins including NFKBIA marks them for ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, freeing RELA, REL and NFKB1 dimers to enter the nucleus. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD and TNFAIP3, plus IkappaB resynthesis, restrain the response.

activation of NF-kappaB-inducing kinase activity describes how upstream receptors switch on NIK, the kinase that drives the non-canonical NF-kappaB route to processing of p100 into p52. This is the arm of NF-kappaB signalling that builds and maintains lymphoid tissue: lymphotoxin alpha/beta acting through the lymphotoxin beta receptor organises lymph node and spleen architecture and germinal centre stroma, and its loss leaves secondary lymphoid organs malformed. Tumour necrosis factor receptors, death receptors and Toll-like receptors feed into the same output, coupling infection and inflammatory cues to transcription of survival and chemokine genes. Activation works largely by relieving constitutive degradation, with the ubiquitin ligase ZFP91 stabilising NIK, while CARD10 and CARD14 scaffold receptor-proximal signalling in epithelium and skin, where gain-of-function mutations cause psoriasis. Sustained NIK activity is a feature of multiple myeloma and other lymphoid malignancies.

NF-kappaB-inducing kinase sits at the head of the non-canonical NF-kappaB branch, and its activation is the step that licenses processing of the p100 precursor into active p52 for genes controlling lymphoid tissue organisation, stromal chemokine production and inflammatory survival signalling. Because the kinase is constitutively degraded in resting cells, stimulation depends on receptor engagement stabilising and phosphorylating it: the lymphotoxin ligands and their receptor, TNF receptor family members including TNFRSF1A/1B and the death receptors TNFRSF10A/10B, and Toll-like receptors such as TLR3 and TLR6 all feed in, with CARD10 and CARD14 scaffolding downstream complex assembly and ZFP91 acting as a ubiquitin ligase that spares the kinase from turnover. Loss of this input compromises lymph node and Peyer's patch development and germinal centre responses, while excessive activity drives chronic inflammation, psoriatic skin disease and lymphoid malignancy.

The JNK cascade is the stress-activated arm of MAP kinase signalling, converting insults such as UV damage, oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress, inflammatory cytokines and developmental cues into changes in gene expression that determine whether a cell proliferates, differentiates, mounts an inflammatory response or dies. Signals from Toll-like receptors, TNF-family receptors, WNT/Frizzled, and growth factor and adhesion receptors converge on MAP4K and MAP3K tiers, including MAP3K5 and the mixed-lineage kinases, which activate MAP2K4 and MAP2K7; these dual kinases phosphorylate JNK1-3 (MAPK8, MAPK9, MAPK10), which in turn phosphorylate JUN and ATF2 to drive AP-1-dependent transcription. Scaffolds of the MAPK8IP family and SH3RF1 organise the tiers, while DUSP phosphatases and inhibitory adaptors set signal duration. The output shapes innate immune activation, neuronal stress responses and apoptosis, and persistent or defective signalling contributes to neurodegeneration, insulin resistance and tumour biology.

Cytokines act at the cell surface but change transcription in the nucleus, and the JAK-STAT route is how that happens in one step: a ligand dimerizes its receptor, receptor-bound Janus kinases trans-phosphorylate, and recruited STAT factors are phosphorylated, dimerize, move to the nucleus and set target gene expression. This is the output arm for interferons, interleukins, colony-stimulating factors, growth hormone, prolactin and leptin, so it determines T helper subset polarization, antiviral defence, haematopoiesis, growth and appetite. Specificity comes from receptor-kinase pairing and from which STAT is engaged, with shared subunits such as the common gamma chain and gp130 pooling many ligands onto JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2. Negative feedback through SOCS proteins, CISH, PIAS inhibitors and phosphatases including PTPN2 limits the response. Loss of JAK3 or the gamma chain causes severe combined immunodeficiency, and constitutive signalling drives leukaemias and myeloproliferative disease.

Cytokine receptors convert an extracellular signal into transcription by phosphorylating a tyrosine on a STAT protein, which dimerises, enters the nucleus and switches on target genes. This step is the switch point for most interleukin, interferon and colony-stimulating factor responses: it sets T helper cell polarisation, drives lymphocyte survival and proliferation, and shapes antiviral and anti-inflammatory programmes. Shared receptor subunits and their associated Janus kinases, notably JAK2 and JAK3, perform the phosphorylation; receptor tyrosine kinases such as KIT, FLT3, CSF1R and ERBB4 and cytoplasmic kinases including FER and PTK6 feed in the same modification, while the phosphatase PTPN2 removes it to limit signalling duration. Loss of components causes severe combined immunodeficiency and defective interleukin-10-dependent tolerance, whereas constitutive activation through mutated kinases underlies myeloproliferative disease and leukaemia.

Nitric oxide is a diffusible gas used as a messenger between and within cells, and this signalling cassette covers its production, detection and the responses it drives. Its best-known output is vascular smooth muscle relaxation: endothelial and neuronal nitric oxide synthases generate NO, soluble guanylyl cyclase subunits sense it and raise cGMP, and cGMP-dependent protein kinase relaxes the vessel, so loss of this arm underlies hypertension, endothelial dysfunction and erectile failure. The same chemistry supports neuronal messaging and, through the inducible synthase, macrophage killing of pathogens. Upstream control appears here as VEGF acting through its receptor on endothelium, angiotensin signalling, and scavenger receptors with thrombospondin modulating the response; DDAH1 sustains output by degrading methylarginine inhibitors of the synthases. cGMP-independent effects on channels and calcium handling extend the signal beyond the classical cyclase route.

small GTPase-mediated signal transduction covers the nucleotide-switch relays that convert receptor and adhesion cues into decisions about cell shape, movement, growth and membrane traffic. These switches set cytoskeletal architecture during neuronal outgrowth, immune cell migration and epithelial junction assembly, drive vesicle budding and endosomal sorting, and gate proliferative signalling; their deregulation underlies RASopathies, cancer and neurodevelopmental disease. The logic is uniform across families: guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as SOS1, VAV and DOCK proteins load GTP, GTPase-activating proteins including NF1, DLC1 and the ARHGAP family terminate the signal, and GDIs sequester inactive pools. Effectors then execute the output, as when RHOA acts through ROCK on actomyosin, RAC1 through WAVE complexes on lamellipodia, RAS through RAF-MEK on transcription, RHEB on mTOR-dependent growth, and RAB and ARF proteins on compartment identity. Guidance receptors, integrins and G protein-coupled receptors feed into the same cassettes.

Small monomeric GTPases act as nucleotide-dependent switches that convert receptor activation into defined cellular outputs, and this signalling cassette covers the Ras, Rho, Rap, Ral, Rab and Arf families together with the regulators that set their timing. Because these switches control cytoskeletal remodelling, cell shape and polarity, adhesion, migration, vesicle traffic and growth-factor-driven proliferation, they determine how cells crawl, divide, extend neurites and organise epithelial and vascular junctions. Activation state is governed by exchange factors that load GTP, GTPase-activating proteins that accelerate hydrolysis, and dissociation inhibitors that sequester the inactive GDP-bound form, illustrated here by large families of Rho GEFs and GAPs, DOCK-ELMO modules, SOS and RasGRP exchange factors, and NF1 and TSC2 as GAPs for Ras and Rheb. Downstream effectors include ROCK kinases, WASP/WAVE actin nucleation machinery and the RAF-MEK cascade. Mutations in these switches and their regulators underlie cancers, RASopathies, and neurodevelopmental and vascular malformation syndromes.

Ras proteins are the switch that converts receptor activation at the cell surface into decisions about proliferation, differentiation and survival, and this relay is among the most frequently corrupted circuits in cancer and in developmental syndromes. Growth factor and antigen receptors recruit adaptors such as GRB2 and LAT, which bring exchange factors of the SOS and RASGRP families to the membrane so that HRAS, KRAS, NRAS and their relatives RRAS, MRAS and RIT1 load GTP. GTPase-activating proteins including NF1 and the RASA and SYNGAP families reverse this, terminating the signal; loss of that braking drives tumour growth. Active Ras engages effectors such as RAF with its scaffolds KSR1 and SHOC2, and RalGDS-family exchange factors, while Sprouty proteins impose feedback inhibition. Downstream consequences converge on cell cycle entry through CDK2, cyclin A and RB1, opposed by p53 and p21.

Rho-family GTPases act as switches that convert surface signals into changes in the actin cytoskeleton, and this signalling cassette covers the whole switch cycle: exchange factors that load GTP, GAPs that turn it off, dissociation inhibitors that hold the inactive pool in the cytosol, and effectors such as the ROCK kinases and LIM kinase that stiffen actomyosin and regulate cofilin. The output is cell shape, adhesion, contractility and directed movement, so this biology underlies cytokinesis, leukocyte migration, platelet and endothelial barrier responses, axon guidance and neurite retraction. Upstream inputs arrive from G protein-coupled receptors through Gα12/13, from integrins, and from guidance receptors including plexins, Robo and the Nogo receptor. Loss or hyperactivation of these switches distorts tissue architecture and contributes to tumour invasion, while mutations in components cause immunodeficiency and neurodevelopmental disease.

Cell-cell signaling covers every route by which one cell informs another: diffusible hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and growth factors, contact-dependent cues delivered by adhesion molecules, and direct cytoplasmic coupling through gap junction channels. It is what allows tissues to behave as organs rather than collections of cells, coordinating neural transmission, endocrine control of metabolism, immune recruitment and developmental patterning. The genes here span the whole arc of information transfer: peptide and monoamine synthesis, packaging and vesicular release machinery such as synaptotagmins, SNAREs, RIMs and Munc13 proteins; ligand families including Wnts, FGFs, BMPs, neurotrophins and chemokines; receptors from glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, dopamine and opioid systems through G protein-coupled and tyrosine kinase classes; connexins and pannexins forming intercellular channels; and the kinases, calcium channels, scaffolds and postsynaptic density proteins that interpret the signal in the receiving cell. Disruption underlies epilepsy, neurodegeneration, diabetes and inflammatory disease.

Chemical signalling between neurons depends on the regulated release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic terminal, and this pathway covers the machinery that loads vesicles, docks them at the active zone, and fuses them with the plasma membrane when calcium enters. It sets the speed and reliability of synaptic transmission, and its disruption underlies epilepsies, movement disorders, and synaptic failure in neurodegeneration. Vesicular transporters fill vesicles with acetylcholine, GABA or glycine; priming factors such as UNC13 proteins and STXBP1 prepare the SNARE proteins SNAP25, VAMP2 and syntaxin-1 for fusion; synaptotagmins act as the calcium sensors, with complexins clamping premature release. Scaffolds including piccolo, RIMS and liprins organise release sites opposite the postsynaptic membrane, while presynaptic receptors and channels tune output. Mutations in LRRK2, PRKN, SNCA and PSEN1 connect this biology to neurodegenerative disease.

Chemical communication between one neuron and the next is the basis of all circuit function, and neuron-to-neuron synaptic transmission covers the release, reception and modulation of transmitter at those contacts. Loss of control over it produces the phenotypes seen in epilepsy, autism spectrum conditions and movement disorders. The genes here touch several layers of the process: a scaffold of the postsynaptic density organises receptor and signalling complexes; a dopamine receptor and an opioid-family receptor with its nociceptin precursor act as G protein-coupled modulators that dampen or tune release probability; a kinesin motor carries synaptic vesicle precursors down the axon; and a lipid phosphatase constrains growth and plasticity signalling in neurons. Cytoskeletal and mitochondrial outer-membrane components link synaptic structure and local energy supply to transmission, which depends on tight spatial coupling between vesicle pools and metabolism.

Cholinergic synaptic transmission covers the release of acetylcholine from a presynaptic terminal and its action on receptors across the cleft, setting the postsynaptic membrane potential and ion fluxes in target neurons, muscle fibres and secretory cells. It is the basis of neuromuscular contraction, autonomic output, and the attentional and arousal modulation of cortical circuits, so its loss produces paralysis, and its receptors are the targets of nicotine, curare and myasthenic autoantibodies. A choline transporter and a vesicular acetylcholine transporter supply and load the neurotransmitter, acetylcholinesterase terminates the signal, and its anchoring at the synaptic cleft depends on a collagen tail and basement membrane components. Postsynaptically, diverse nicotinic subunits assemble into pentameric cation channels whose folding and clustering require dedicated chaperone and scaffold proteins, alongside muscarinic G protein-coupled signalling.

Axons conduct rapidly and survive long-term only because glia wrap around them, and this ensheathment programme covers both myelinating and non-myelinating glial envelopment of neuronal cell bodies and axons. Oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system and Schwann cells in the periphery are specified by transcription factors such as SOX10, OLIG2, MYRF, EGR2 and POU3F1, then produce a lipid-rich compact membrane whose structural proteins include MBP, PLP1, MPZ, PMP22, MAG and CLDN11. Glial-axonal contact is read out through adhesion and receptor systems including CNTN1/CNTNAP1, NFASC, ADGRG6 and the neuregulin receptors ERBB2/ERBB3, feeding PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MAPK signalling that scales myelin sheath thickness, with PTEN and NF1 restraining it. Galactolipid and sphingolipid enzymes such as UGT8, GAL3ST1, FA2H and GALC supply the membrane. Loss of these functions underlies leukodystrophies, demyelinating peripheral neuropathies and the failure of remyelination after injury.

Neuromuscular synaptic transmission is how a motor neuron tells a muscle fibre to contract, and it is the step that converts nerve impulses into movement, breathing and posture. Its failure produces weakness and fatigability, as in myasthenic syndromes, and it is the target of curare-like blockers and organophosphates. Presynaptically, choline is taken up by a high-affinity transporter and acetylated by choline acetyltransferase, packaged, and released by a calcium-triggered vesicle fusion machinery that includes STXBP1, RAB3A and RIM-binding proteins tethering release sites to calcium channels. Postsynaptically, nicotinic receptor subunits such as CHRNA1 and CHRNB1 cluster with RAPSN and the dystrophin-associated protein DTNA in the glycosylated, LARGE1-dependent synaptic membrane, while STAC3 links depolarisation to excitation–contraction coupling. Neurexin–neuroligin adhesion and activity-dependent transcription factors build and maintain the junction.

Male fertility depends on a self-renewing pool of spermatogonia that divide mitotically before entering meiosis, and spermatogonial cell division is the amplifying step that converts a small stem population into the many primary spermatocytes needed for continuous sperm output.
