Loss of these divisions, or errors within them, depletes the germline reserve and produces oligospermia or azoospermia, a common cause of male infertility. The genes here point to several requirements of the process: a germline-restricted histone H3 variant that shapes the specialised chromatin of male germ cells, a DNA helicase partner of the BRCA1 repair machinery that guards replication and interstrand crosslink resolution during rapid proliferation, and an m6A reader that clears maternal-style transcripts to time developmental transitions. Together they link cell cycle progression, genome integrity and post-transcriptional control to germ cell expansion in the testis.

Sperm motility depends on building the flagellar axoneme, the nine-plus-two bundle of microtubules with its dynein arms, radial spokes and nexin-dynein regulatory complex that generates the beat driving a spermatozoon through the female tract. When assembly fails, men present with asthenozoospermia or multiple morphological abnormalities of the sperm flagellum — short, coiled or absent tails — and infertility, a phenotype linked to many cilia- and flagella-associated proteins here such as CFAP43, CFAP44 and CFAP65. Axonemal dyneins including DNAH1 supply the motor force, SPAG6 and SPAG16 contribute to the central apparatus and radial spokes, and SPEF2 with MEIG1 delivers cargo along the growing tail via intramanchette transport. Tubulin tyrosine ligase-like enzymes add polyglutamate marks that tune dynein activity. Because the same machinery builds motile cilia, several components also affect airway and ependymal ciliary function.

As a round spermatid becomes a sperm cell, its nucleus condenses, elongates and shuts down transcription, and this remodelling of the spermatid nucleus is what makes the paternal genome compact enough to be delivered at fertilization. Failure produces malformed heads, retained histones, DNA damage and male infertility. The core event is a genome-wide exchange of chromatin proteins: testis histone variants and the bromodomain reader BRDT prime hyperacetylated nucleosomes, KAT5 acetylation and RNF8-dependent ubiquitination license their removal, transition proteins TNP1 and TNP2 act as intermediates, and protamine PRM1 finally packages DNA into toroids, with SRPK1 phosphorylation tuning protamine deposition. Chromatin remodellers, the demethylase KDM3A and the testis-specific transcription factor TBPL1 control the late spermiogenic gene programme, while PIWIL1 links piRNA silencing of transposons to this differentiation.

Oogenesis produces the haploid female gamete, an oocyte that must not only halve its chromosome number correctly but also stockpile the RNAs, proteins and organelles that will drive the first divisions of an embryo. Its failure underlies primary ovarian insufficiency, oocyte maturation arrest, aneuploid eggs and infertility. Germ cells enter meiosis under retinoic acid-responsive control, generate programmed double-strand breaks through SPO11 with its accessory REC114/MEI4 partners, pair and recombine homologues on a synaptonemal framework, and resolve crossovers using MLH1/MLH3; cohesin and kinetochore components then enforce the reductional division. In parallel, granulosa-oocyte dialogue via GDF9, BMP15 and their receptors, gonadotropin signalling through FSHR, and natriuretic peptide control of cyclic nucleotides hold the oocyte in prophase arrest until maturation. Maternal-effect factors such as ZAR1, NPM2 and TUBB8, together with m6A readers and cytoplasmic polyadenylation machinery, set egg quality and competence.

Oocyte construction covers the loading of an ovarian germ cell with the RNAs, proteins and organelles it must carry before meiosis produces a functional ovum. What defines this set of genes is the machinery that builds and staffs germ granules, the phase-separated RNA-protein bodies where maternal transcripts are stored, silenced and handed on to the next generation. Several Tudor-domain proteins act as scaffolds that read symmetrically methylated arginines on PIWI proteins and recruit them, together with their small RNA cargo, into these granules; PLD6 is a mitochondrial surface nuclease that generates piRNA precursor ends. The shared purpose is transposon silencing and controlled maternal mRNA storage during gametogenesis, so that the egg enters meiosis with a stable genome and an intact maternal contribution. Loss of these factors disrupts germ granule assembly and causes infertility.

Insemination is the delivery of sperm into the female genital tract, and it depends as much on the smooth muscle mechanics of seminal emission and ejaculation as on the sperm themselves. The genes here cover both sides of that event. Oxytocin acting through its receptor, along with substance P from the tachykinin precursor and its receptor, drives contraction of the vas deferens and seminal vesicle, while the P2X1 purinergic receptor mediates the sympathetic purinergic contraction that propels sperm forward; loss of this channel in males causes infertility despite normal sperm. Semenogelin forms the seminal coagulum that is later liquefied, and the serpins protein C inhibitor and protease nexin-1 restrain the proteases involved and protect sperm during transit. Failure at these steps produces anejaculation or retrograde ejaculation rather than defective spermatogenesis.

Fertilization by exactly one sperm is the event that creates a diploid zygote and starts development, and the genes here cover the steps from sperm reaching the egg to the block that keeps a second sperm out. Sperm must first bind and penetrate the zona pellucida built from ZP1-ZP4, aided by hyaluronidases and acrosomal proteases such as acrosin, then undergo the acrosome reaction; ABHD2 and CatSper-associated signalling together with calcium entry through TRP and IP3-receptor channels drive hyperactivated motility and exocytosis. Gamete fusion itself depends on the IZUMO1-JUNO pair with ADAM family sperm surface proteins, tetraspanins CD9 and IGSF8, and SPACA6 and TMEM95. The fusing sperm delivers PLCZ1, whose phosphoinositide cleavage triggers the calcium oscillations that release the oocyte from meiotic arrest, while ASTL cleaves ZP2 to prevent polyspermy. Defects in these factors cause male and female infertility and fertilization failure.

Fertilization begins when a capacitated sperm recognizes and attaches to the zona pellucida, the glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte, and this binding step sets species specificity and limits fertilization to a single sperm. The egg side is built from ZP1-ZP4, which polymerize into the matrix that sperm must engage and then penetrate; ZP2 cleavage by the oocyte protease astacin-like ovastacin underlies the block to further sperm binding after fertilization. On the sperm side, surface and acrosomal proteins mediate adhesion and passage: hyaluronidase and acrosin act on the cumulus and zona, ADAM family disintegrin proteins and zona pellucida binding proteins localize to the acrosomal region, chaperones including calmegin and the CCT/TRiC complex ensure these proteins fold and traffic correctly, and IZUMO1 is positioned for the subsequent fusion with the egg plasma membrane. Loss of these components produces male infertility despite otherwise normal sperm.

Acrosome reaction is the single-shot exocytotic event that licenses a sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida and fuse with the egg; sperm that cannot complete it are fertilization-incompetent, a recognized cause of male infertility. Binding to zona glycoproteins ZP2, ZP3 and ZP4 triggers calcium entry and a phospholipase-driven second messenger cascade, with progesterone acting through ABHD2 to open the CatSper-associated pathway while proton and calcium channels alkalinize and depolarize the cell. The outer acrosomal membrane then fuses with the plasma membrane using conventional SNARE and priming machinery -- syntaxin, Munc18, Munc13, synaptotagmins and RAB3A -- releasing hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase, restrained by their cognate serine protease inhibitors. Exposure of inner acrosomal and equatorial proteins including SPESP1 and EQTN remodels the sperm surface for gamete membrane fusion, linking regulated secretion to sexual reproduction.

Fertilisation requires a sperm to shed the contents of its single anterior secretory granule at the moment it meets the egg coat, and the acrosome reaction is that regulated exocytotic event. Zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP2, ZP3 and ZP4 provide the binding cue; calcium entry and lipid signalling through phospholipases, adenylate cyclase and progesterone-responsive ABHD2 convert it into membrane fusion, with the outer acrosomal membrane joining the sperm plasma membrane and releasing acrosin and hyaluronidase-type hydrolases that digest a path through the zona. The release machinery is the same SNARE and synaptotagmin apparatus used at synapses, here anchored by sperm-specific scaffolds and RAB3A. Protease inhibitors of the SPINK family and proprotein convertase processing restrain premature activation. Sperm that cannot complete the reaction, or complete it too early, fail to fuse with the oocyte, a recognised cause of male infertility and a target for contraception.

Penetration of zona pellucida is the step of fertilization in which a capacitated sperm drills through the glycoprotein coat surrounding the oocyte so that the two plasma membranes can meet. Without it fertilization fails outright, and defects in the sperm head structures involved are a recognized cause of male infertility. The work depends on the acrosome, a modified lysosome capping the sperm nucleus, whose regulated exocytosis releases hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase together with glycosidases that cleave zona sugars; a sperm-surface galactosyltransferase contributes to recognition of zona glycoproteins. Other members reflect the sperm-specific architecture that makes this possible — acrosomal and inner-acrosomal membrane proteins, the mitochondria-associated cysteine-rich protein of the flagellum that supports the motility needed for mechanical thrust, and the calcineurin subunit and protamine that mark spermatid remodelling into a fertilization-competent cell.

Fertilization requires a sperm to breach the glycoprotein coat surrounding the egg, and penetration of the zona pellucida is the step that grants access to the oocyte plasma membrane for fusion. Failure at this point is a cause of male infertility even when sperm counts and motility appear normal. The work is done largely by the acrosome, a secretory organelle derived from lysosomes that caps the sperm head and releases hydrolases on contact with the zona: acrosin, a trypsin-like protease, along with glycosidases such as beta-hexosaminidase and hyaluronidase activity that loosen the matrix. Other contributors reflect the specialized architecture and signalling of the sperm head and tail, including sperm mitochondria-associated cysteine-rich protein, acrosomal membrane proteins, a testis-specific calcineurin regulatory subunit, and the chromatin-compacting transition protein laid down during spermiogenesis.

Fertilization does not simply join two genomes; it switches a quiescent oocyte into a metabolically active embryo, and egg activation is that switch. The arrested egg resumes meiosis, begins protein and DNA synthesis, and remodels its cortex and cytoplasm so that only one sperm contributes a genome. Sperm-derived phospholipase C zeta and the related factor encoded by WBP2NL trigger the calcium oscillations that drive this transition, with phosphoinositide signalling through PLCB1 feeding the same second messenger. Cortical granule release then delivers the protease ovastacin, which cleaves ZP2 in the zona pellucida built from ZP1, ZP2 and ZP4 to harden the coat and block further sperm binding. Cytoskeletal reorganization involving myosin heavy chain and maternal-effect factors such as NLRP5 support the earliest cleavage divisions; defects here cause fertilization failure and arrested preimplantation development.

regulation of mitotic cell cycle governs whether and how fast a cell commits to division, ensuring that DNA is replicated once and chromosomes are segregated accurately; its failure produces aneuploidy, genome instability and the unchecked proliferation typical of cancer. The controls act at several decision points: cyclin-CDK pairs with their CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F switch set the restriction point for S-phase entry; CDC25 phosphatases opposed by WEE1 and MYT1 time mitotic entry; ATM/ATR, CHEK1/2 and p53 impose damage and replication checkpoints; and the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD2, BUB1/BUB3, kinetochore NDC80 and KNL1 complexes) restrains the anaphase-promoting complex until attachment is complete, whereupon APC/C-CDC20 ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction of cyclin B and securin trigger sister chromatid separation. Aurora, PLK and NEK kinases, chromatin remodellers and numerous microRNAs tune these transitions to growth-factor and stress input.

Cells divide only when conditions permit, and the regulation of the mitotic cell cycle is the control layer that decides when to advance, when to pause, and when to abandon division altogether. It sets proliferation rates in development and tissue renewal, and its loosening is the route to genomic instability and cancer, which is why so many of its members are tumour suppressors and oncogenes. Cyclin–CDK pairs with their inhibitors drive the transitions, Rb–E2F gates entry into S phase, and CDC25 phosphatases oppose WEE1/MYT1 to license mitotic entry. DNA damage and replication stress feed in through ATM, ATR and CHEK1/2 to TP53, arresting progression until lesions are repaired. Spindle assembly checkpoint proteins including MAD2L1, BUB1 and the kinetochore NDC80 complex hold the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until chromosomes attach, and ubiquitin–proteasome degradation makes each transition irreversible. Chromatin remodellers, microRNAs and growth factor signalling tune the whole programme.

Blastoderm segmentation names the hierarchical subdivision of the early embryo along its anterior-posterior axis, the process by which a uniform sheet of cells is progressively partitioned into ordered domains that later become the repeating units of the trunk. The genes here point to the signalling and transcriptional inputs that set up axial pattern in vertebrate embryos: WNT5A and FZD5 in non-canonical Wnt signalling and convergent extension, TBXT and TBX3 as T-box factors specifying mesoderm and posterior axial identity, a HOXD family member conferring positional value, NEUROG1 marking early neural commitment, and neuropilins with SEMA3F guiding the migration of cells across the forming axis. A cluster of Tudor-domain proteins ties the same interval to germline specification and piRNA-mediated silencing in primordial germ cells. Disruption of axial patterning at this stage produces caudal and axial malformations rather than localized defects.

Head-to-tail patterning of the early embryo depends on genes transcribed by the zygote itself, rather than on maternally deposited products, and this zygotic arm of anterior/posterior axis determination sets where along the body axis each structure will form. In insects the paradigm is a cascade in which gap genes subdivide the embryo into broad domains, pair-rule genes refine these into periodic stripes, and segment polarity genes fix orientation within each segment; in vertebrates the equivalent work establishes rostrocaudal identity of the axis and its derivatives. The genes assembled here reflect the transcriptional and signalling side of that process, including a proneural basic helix-loop-helix factor and a zinc-finger transcription factor required for urogenital development, together with a proprotein convertase that matures secreted patterning ligands and cytoskeletal regulators acting during early morphogenesis. Failure of axial specification produces severe, often lethal, malformations.

This is an anterior-posterior patterning function borrowed from insect embryology: the specification of trunk segments — thorax and anterior abdomen — by gap genes, of which Krüppel is the canonical example, acting on positional information laid down by maternal gradients to divide the embryo into broad domains that later resolve into segments. In vertebrates the corresponding annotation collects zinc-finger and bHLH transcriptional regulators rather than a conserved segmentation cascade, and the genes here are better understood through their own developmental roles: WT1 governs urogenital and kidney development and is a Wilms tumour gene, while NEUROG1 is a proneural factor driving neuronal commitment in sensory ganglia and brain. The theme that unites them is regional transcriptional control of embryonic cell fate, in which loss of a single regulator deletes or misspecifies an entire body region or cell lineage.

Gastrulation is the embryonic reorganisation that converts a simple epiblast into the three germ layers — ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm — and establishes the body axes on which all later organogenesis depends. Failure at this stage is lethal or produces axis and laterality defects such as holoprosencephaly, caudal dysgenesis and heterotaxy. The genes describe how it is run: Nodal, BMP and WNT gradients, restrained by antagonists such as CER1, NOG, DKK1 and SFRP, signal through SMAD2/3, SMAD1/4 and β-catenin to switch on primitive-streak transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, GSC, FOXA2, MESP1 and SOX17, while POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 mark the pluripotent state being exited. Cells then execute epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and directed migration, using SNAI1, planar cell polarity components, integrins, laminins and collagens, and matrix metalloproteinases to ingress through the streak and pattern the nascent mesoderm.

Gastrulation converts a simple epiblast into a three-layered embryo, generating ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm and setting up the body axes on which all later organogenesis depends. Failure at this stage is embryonic lethal, and partial defects produce axis duplication, situs abnormalities, caudal truncation and heart and node malformations. The genes here trace the signalling logic: Nodal, BMP and Activin ligands acting through type I/II receptors and SMAD2/3 or SMAD1, WNT ligands with Frizzled receptors, beta-catenin and LEF1, FGF8 through FGFR1, and secreted antagonists such as Cerberus, Noggin and DKK1 that carve out the organizer. Transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, GSC, FOXA2, SOX17 and MESP1/2 specify primitive streak and germ-layer fates, while planar-cell-polarity components, integrins, laminins, collagens and matrix metalloproteinases drive the epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell migration that physically reorganize the embryo.

Segment specification is the step at which repeating body segments stop being equivalent and take on distinct positional identities along the head-to-tail axis, the process classically defined by homeotic gene action in insects and carried out in vertebrates by the somites and hindbrain rhombomeres. It determines which vertebrae, ribs, muscles and cranial nerve territories form where, and errors produce homeotic transformations, fused or extra vertebrae, and craniofacial defects. Positional identity is encoded by HOX genes such as HOXA2 and read out with MEOX1/MEOX2, IRX and OSR1 transcription factors, while MAFB marks specific rhombomeres. Polycomb components BMI1 and MTF2 keep identity codes stably repressed once set, and Notch-linked players including DLL1 and HES5, together with MSGN1 and RIPPLY1, couple segmentation clock output and boundary formation to the assignment of segment identity in presomitic mesoderm.

Embryonic segments are not uniform; each is subdivided into compartments whose cells adopt distinct fates, and this regionalization sets the anterior-posterior polarity that patterns vertebrae, ribs, and the segmental routing of nerves and blood vessels. Notch signalling does most of the work: the ligands DLL1 and DLL3 acting on NOTCH1, with the glycosyltransferase LFNG modifying Notch receptors to tune ligand sensitivity, generate and then stabilize the oscillatory and boundary-forming activity that separates rostral from caudal halves of a somite. The homeodomain cofactor PBX3 contributes by partnering Hox proteins to give positional identity along the body axis. When this compartment pattern specification fails, somite boundaries form in the wrong place or not at all, producing the fused and misshapen vertebrae of spondylocostal dysostosis and related axial skeletal malformations.

Embryos acquire their body plan by dividing initially uniform tissue into territories with distinct positional identities, and this pattern specification process is what tells a cell where it is and therefore what to become. It sets the head-to-tail order of vertebrae and hindbrain segments, the left-right placement of heart and viscera, the dorsoventral identity of spinal neurons, and the axes of developing limbs; failures produce holoprosencephaly, situs inversus, vertebral segmentation defects, polydactyly and congenital heart malformation. Graded secreted cues from Sonic hedgehog, Wnt, BMP/Nodal and FGF families, read out through GLI, beta-catenin and SMAD effectors and modulated by antagonists such as Noggin, chordin and Lefty, are interpreted by HOX, PAX, SIX and DLX transcription factors. Notch-driven oscillations time somite formation, motile and primary cilia transduce hedgehog signalling and break left-right symmetry, and Polycomb complexes lock the resulting identities into stable chromatin states.

Ectoderm development covers the fate and maturation of the embryo's outer germ layer after gastrulation, the layer that gives rise to skin and its appendages, and to the neural plate and its derivatives. What depends on it is the formation of an intact epidermal barrier, hair, teeth and glands, and the patterning of the eye and forebrain; disruption produces neural tube defects, ectodermal dysplasias and epidermal fragility. The genes here span the signalling systems that specify and pattern this layer canonical Wnt through a Frizzled receptor and beta-catenin, BMP receptor signalling, and Hedgehog together with transcriptional regulators that drive epithelial differentiation and keratinocyte identity, such as GRHL3 and ELF5, and homeodomain factors patterning the eye field and anterior structures. Cell adhesion and polarity components including an integrin subunit and NF2 link the programme to epithelial architecture and the control of proliferation during morphogenesis.

The size of the mature brain is set largely by how many rounds of division neural progenitors undergo before they differentiate, and neuroblast proliferation is that expansion step. Its regulation determines cortical surface area and neuron number, and its failure in humans produces microcephaly and lissencephaly, while its inappropriate continuation contributes to glioma and neuroblastoma. Patterning and mitogenic signals — Sonic hedgehog acting through its receptor and the Gli transcription factors, Wnt/β-catenin with LEF1, FGF receptor signalling via FRS2, and Notch with the Numb adaptors that bias asymmetric division — converge on progenitors whose identity is fixed by transcription factors such as PAX6, FOXG1, ASCL1 and SIX3. A second group acts on the mitotic apparatus itself: ASPM, WDR62, LIS1/NDE1 and ZNF335 govern spindle orientation and centrosome function, coupling the geometry of division to the choice between renewal and neurogenesis.

Brain development requires that dividing neural progenitors stop dividing on schedule, and negative regulation of neuroblast proliferation covers the signals that restrain or terminate their expansion so cells can exit the cycle and differentiate. Loss of this brake enlarges progenitor pools and predisposes to childhood brain tumours, medulloblastoma in particular. The genes involved act through several routes: adherens junction and cadherin-linked adhesion via CTNNA1 couples progenitor density to growth arrest, KCTD11 opposes Hedgehog-driven proliferation in cerebellar granule precursors, and neurofibromin restrains Ras signalling downstream of growth factor receptors, with its loss causing the glial and neural overgrowth of neurofibromatosis. A secreted growth factor and TGF-beta-family cytokine signalling contribute extrinsic limits, a microRNA imposes post-transcriptional control favouring neuronal differentiation, and a homeodomain factor supplies regional transcriptional context. Together these constrain progenitor number, timing of neurogenesis, and final brain size.

Axonal fasciculation is the gathering of growing axons into bundles, or fascicles, so that pioneer axons can guide followers along shared trajectories and nerve tracts form as coherent cables rather than scattered fibres. It underlies the stereotyped wiring of commissures, peripheral nerves and long projection tracts, and its failure produces misrouted or defasciculated axons, mistargeted connections and malformed tracts such as an absent corpus callosum. Adhesion between neighbouring axolemmas is supplied by immunoglobulin-domain and contactin-family recognition molecules including NRCAM, NCAM2, CNTN2 and CNTN4, while ephrin-Eph pairs, semaphorin and neuropilin signalling and the Nogo receptor ligand RTN4 provide the repulsive cues that keep bundles separate and confine them to permitted corridors. These surface signals converge on Rho-family and CDK5 regulators that remodel the growth cone cytoskeleton, and pruning of surplus axons links the process to developmental apoptotic machinery.

Synapse assembly is the process by which an axon terminal and a postsynaptic membrane recognise each other, align their machinery and mature into a transmitting contact. It sets the number, type and location of connections in a developing nervous system, and its disruption is repeatedly implicated in autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia; at the neuromuscular junction the same logic builds motor endplates via agrin, LRP4 and MUSK. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs do the recognition work — neurexins with neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs, cadherins, protocadherins and teneurin-like adhesion GPCRs — while secreted cerebellins and C1q-like proteins bridge specific partners. Their cytoplasmic tails recruit scaffolds such as SHANK proteins, gephyrin, bassoon and piccolo to cluster glutamate and GABA-A receptors and the release apparatus. Guidance and growth-factor cues (semaphorins with plexins, ephrin receptors, Wnts, netrins, neurotrophins) and Rho-family GTPase regulators remodel the actin cytoskeleton as the contact stabilises.

Building a brain and spinal cord from neuroepithelium is the business of central nervous system development, and it dictates how many neurons of which identity are made, where they settle, and how they are wired and insulated. Patterning signals — Sonic hedgehog, Wnts, BMPs, FGFs and retinoic acid — set positional coordinates that are read out by homeodomain and bHLH transcription factors such as PAX6, OTX2, the LHX and NKX families, and the neurogenins, while Notch signalling holds progenitors in reserve. Radial glial scaffolds, centrosomal and microtubule proteins, and the reelin–VLDLR–DAB1 axis govern neuronal migration and cortical lamination; guidance receptors of the Robo, DCC, Eph, plexin and netrin systems steer axons, and oligodendrocyte factors including OLIG2, SOX10 and MYRF produce myelin. Disruption at any stage yields neural tube defects, microcephaly, lissencephaly, holoprosencephaly, intellectual disability and leukodystrophy.

Ventral midline development produces the floor plate, the specialised strip of cells at the base of the neural tube that patterns the nervous tissue around it. Its signals assign ventral neuronal identities such as motor neurons and interneurons and guide commissural axons across the midline, so failure of this programme collapses dorsoventral organisation of the spinal cord and brain, as in holoprosencephaly. The genes here place Sonic hedgehog signalling at the centre: the secreted ligand acts through the receptor-coupled transducer Smoothened to relieve repression of the GLI transcription factors, which then switch on ventral identity genes including GLI1 itself. Because this transduction happens in the primary cilium, ciliary trafficking and kinase components are equally part of the pathway, linking midline specification to ciliogenesis and explaining why ciliopathies disturb neural tube patterning.

Building the peripheral nervous system means generating sensory, autonomic and enteric neurons from neural crest, extending their axons to distant targets, and wrapping those axons in myelin so that impulses travel quickly. The genes here span both halves of that task. Neurotrophic signalling through NGF and GDNF family ligands with their receptors, transmitted by RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK and AKT cascades, supports neuronal survival and target innervation, while transcription factors such as ISL1, POU4F1, RUNX1 and RUNX3 assign sensory neuron subtype identity. Schwann cell development runs on NRG1 acting via ERBB2/ERBB3 and on SOX10, EGR2 and POU3F1, with PMP22, PRX, NDRG1 and SH3TC2 maintaining compact myelin and the node-paranode architecture set by NFASC and CNTNAP1. Disruption produces inherited demyelinating and axonal neuropathies, congenital aganglionic megacolon, and loss of sensation or autonomic control.

Vision, hearing and balance depend on organs built during embryogenesis from placodal and neural ectoderm, and sensory organ development covers that whole trajectory from field specification to a functioning eye and inner ear. Eye components appear as lens crystallins and their regulators PAX6, FOXE3 and PITX3, photoreceptor identity factors CRX, NRL and NR2E3, phototransduction proteins such as rhodopsin and the PDE6 subunits, and retinal pigment epithelium genes including RPE65 and MERTK. Ear components include the hair-cell fate determinant ATOH1, stereocilia and mechanotransduction proteins such as MYO7A, USH2A, PCDH15, TMC1 and STRC, and otic patterning factors EYA1, SIX1 and POU4F3. Retinoic acid, Wnt, BMP, FGF, Hedgehog and Notch signalling pattern the fields and, with ciliary trafficking machinery, sequence progenitor proliferation against differentiation. Mutations here produce congenital cataract, anophthalmia, retinal dystrophies, Usher and Bardet-Biedl syndromes, and hereditary deafness.

Salivary glands arise as branched exocrine organs of the oral cavity, and their development sets up the acinar and ductal architecture that produces saliva for lubrication, digestion and oral antimicrobial defence; disrupted gland formation or later loss of these structures underlies dry mouth and the vulnerability of the gland to radiation injury. Formation begins as an epithelial bud invades condensed mesenchyme and undergoes repeated clefting and branching, driven by fibroblast growth factor signalling through FGFR1 and FGFR2, with FGF10 from mesenchyme sustaining epithelial outgrowth. Ectodysplasin signalling through EDA and EDAR, hedgehog, TGF-beta family ligands, EGF and HGF cues, and semaphorin-plexin and neuropilin guidance coordinate epithelium, nerves and vasculature, while basement membrane laminins and BTBD7 control cleft formation. Transcriptional regulators including ASCL3, NFIB and TFCP2L1 specify progenitor and secretory cell identity during maturation.

Shaping of the foregut is the embryonic step that converts the anterior endoderm tube into the primordia of the pharynx, oesophagus, trachea and lung buds, stomach, liver and pancreas. Getting it wrong produces some of the commonest structural birth defects, including oesophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula and congenital diaphragmatic hernia. The genes here trace the signalling that patterns this region: Nodal-type ligands acting through the ACVR2B receptor and SMAD2/SMAD3 to specify definitive endoderm alongside SOX17, hedgehog signalling from the endoderm instructing surrounding splanchnic mesoderm, Wnt/beta-catenin and Notch input, and the transcription factors FOXF1 and GATA4 driving mesenchymal and cardiac-adjacent responses. Cytoskeletal and polarity components such as EPB41L5 and NCKAP1 supply the epithelial rearrangement and apical-basal organisation that turn patterning into tube shape, separation and outgrowth of organ buds.

endoderm development tracks the innermost germ layer from its specification at gastrulation to the mature tissues it builds — the gut tube and its derivatives, including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. Getting it right determines whether an embryo forms a digestive and respiratory system at all, and the same signalling logic is exploited to direct pluripotent stem cells toward hepatic and pancreatic fates. Nodal and its downstream SMAD2/3–SMAD4 relay, tuned by BMP4, GDF3, FGF8 and the antagonists NOG and DKK1, drives POU5F1/NANOG-positive epiblast cells through EOMES, MIXL1 and SOX17 into definitive endoderm, after which HNF1B, GATA4/6, ONECUT1 and NKX2-1 impose regional and organ identity. Wnt–CTNNB1 input, PAF1 complex and chromatin regulators such as SETD2 and HDAC1 set transcriptional competence, while laminins, collagens, integrins and matrix metalloproteinases provide the adhesive and remodelling context for the cell movements involved.

During gastrulation the innermost germ layer is specified and then elaborated into the epithelia of the gut tube, liver, pancreas, thyroid and lungs, and endoderm development covers that whole trajectory from germ-layer formation to organ primordia. Nodal and GDF signals acting through SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 drive the transition, opposed by the antagonists Noggin and DKK1, while BMP4 and FGF8 pattern the emerging sheet. Pluripotency and mesendoderm transcription factors including POU5F1, NANOG, EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA4/6, HNF1B and ONECUT1 hand off in sequence to commit and regionalise cells, with NKX2-1 marking thyroid and lung endoderm. Cell movement depends on integrins, laminins and fibronectin, remodelled by matrix metalloproteinases, and chromatin and transcription-elongation machinery such as the PAF complex, SETD2 and HDAC1 licenses the switches. Failure yields gastrulation arrest and malformed foregut-derived organs.

Midgut development traces the middle portion of the gut tube, from the distal stomach and bile duct outlet through the small intestine to the proximal colon, from its early specification to a functioning absorptive and secretory organ. Its failure explains a family of congenital gut disorders: aganglionic bowel when enteric neural crest cells fail to colonize the intestine, and malformations of gut rotation, lumen formation and vascular investment. Reciprocal signalling between endoderm and surrounding splanchnic mesenchyme drives the process, with retinoic acid produced by ALDH1A2, hedgehog reception through SMO, non-canonical WNT5A cues and mesenchymal transcription factors FOXF1 and FOXL1 patterning the gut wall, while RET and EDNRB govern migration and survival of enteric neurons. The accompanying urea-cycle and ketogenic enzymes mark the metabolic differentiation that intestinal and hepatic epithelium acquires as the midgut matures toward nutrient handling.

Mesoderm development covers the birth and maturation of the middle germ layer, the source of skeletal and cardiac muscle, bone and cartilage, kidney, blood and vasculature, and connective tissue. Cells ingress through the primitive streak under Nodal, BMP and WNT signalling, with SMAD transducers, FOXH1 and secreted antagonists such as CER1, NOG and DKK1 shaping the gradients that decide how much mesoderm forms and where. Lineage transcription factors including TBXT, EOMES, MIXL1, MESP1 and MSGN1 commit cells to mesodermal fate, while TBX6, HES7 and Notch-related components drive segmentation into somites and downstream regulators such as ETV2, TAL1 and HAND1 divert progenitors toward endothelium, blood and heart. Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, integrin-mediated migration and left-right patterning are integral to the process. Disruption causes gastrulation arrest, axial and somite defects, congenital heart disease and renal malformation.

Early in gastrulation, cells of the primitive streak are steered toward mesoderm rather than neural or endodermal fates, and mesodermal cell fate specification is the reversible commitment step that makes them capable of forming muscle, heart, blood, bone and kidney. The decision is made by graded extracellular signals: NODAL and BMP signalling through BMPR1A, WNT3A, and FGFR1-mediated FGF input converge on transcriptional responses, while DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain WNT to sharpen the boundary in space and time. MESP1 marks and drives nascent mesoderm toward cardiac and somitic derivatives, HOXA11 imparts positional identity along the body axis, and the EYA/SIX/PAX2 module specifies intermediate mesoderm destined for the nephric lineage. Because the state is not yet locked in, it is the stage exploited to direct pluripotent stem cells to mesodermal tissues; its disruption in the embryo causes axial, cardiac and kidney malformations.

Gonadal mesoderm development traces the intermediate mesoderm territory that gives rise to the gonads, from the genital ridge through commitment to testis or ovary. It matters because sexual differentiation of the whole body follows from what this tissue becomes: the somatic cells formed here host germ cells and secrete the hormones that pattern the reproductive tract, and disruption produces gonadal dysgenesis and disorders of sex development. The genes involved include a transcriptional cofactor that partners GATA4 in supporting SRY-dependent testis determination, mutations in which cause 46,XY sex reversal and congenital diaphragmatic hernia, and anti-Mullerian hormone, a TGF-beta family signal from Sertoli cells that drives regression of the Mullerian ducts. Y-linked testis-specific proteins expressed in the male germline are also represented, linking gonadal somatic development to spermatogenic potential.

Heart development is the program that builds a four-chambered pump from mesoderm and keeps it beating, covering cardiac progenitor specification, chamber and valve morphogenesis, conduction system patterning, and the maturation of contractile muscle. Its failure is the origin of congenital heart disease, the commonest birth defect, and of cardiomyopathies and arrhythmias that appear later. A core of transcription factors including NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, MEF2C, HAND1/2 and ISL1 acts with Notch, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog and FGF signalling to assign cells to first and second heart fields, drive endocardial cushion epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and remodel outflow tract and septa. Nodal, laterality determinants and ciliary and intraflagellar transport components set left-right asymmetry before looping. Downstream, sarcomeric and cytoskeletal proteins such as TTN, MYH6/7 and TNNT2, calcium handling machinery, gap junctions and cardiac microRNAs establish rhythmic, force-generating myocardium and its vascular supply.

Cardiogenesis takes mesodermal progenitors through specification, looping of the linear heart tube, chamber and valve formation, septation, conduction system patterning and coronary vascularization, ending in a four-chambered pump that contracts rhythmically for life. Failure at any step underlies congenital heart disease, laterality defects and cardiomyopathy. Lineage transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND1/2, MEF2C and ISL1 act with chromatin regulators and Notch, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog, FGF and Nodal signalling to assign chamber identity and left-right asymmetry; motile and primary cilia genes set the initial laterality cue. Endocardial cushions form by endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition and remodel through matrix proteins and metalloproteinases into valves, while neural crest and second heart field cells build the outflow tract. Differentiation converges on sarcomere assembly and excitation-contraction coupling components including MYH6, TNNT2, TTN, RYR2 and SCN5A, alongside microRNAs and Hippo-YAP control of cardiomyocyte growth.

Adult heart development covers the maturation of the heart from its embryonic form into the mature four-chambered organ and the maintenance of that structure, determining chamber size, wall thickness and contractile competence in the adult animal. The genes involved span the layers this requires: cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, HAND2 and MEF2D that specify and sustain cardiomyocyte identity, the chromatin regulator CHD7, the sarcomeric myosin heavy chains MYH6 and MYH7 together with the Z-disc protein telethonin, and secreted cues including BMP10 and apelin acting through its receptor APLNR to drive cardiomyocyte proliferation and growth. Adrenergic input via ADRA1A links contractile performance to hypertrophic remodelling. Disruption of these factors underlies congenital heart malformation, cardiomyopathy and the failure of the adult ventricle to compensate for increased load.

Muscle organ development covers the whole trajectory by which mesodermal progenitors become contractile tissue, from specification and myoblast fusion through sarcomere assembly to the mature, innervated, force-generating organ, and it encompasses skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle alike. It is what gives an animal locomotion, posture, a beating heart and vascular tone, and its disruption underlies congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophies and cardiomyopathy. The core myogenic transcription factors MYF5, MYOD1, MYOG and MYF6 act with MEF2 proteins, PAX3/PAX7 progenitor regulators and SIX1/SIX4 to drive lineage commitment, while Wnt, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch and Hedgehog inputs pattern where and when muscle forms. Fusion itself requires the myomaker and myomixer membrane proteins. Downstream come the structural and calcium-handling products that define the fibre: titin, nebulin, dystrophin and the sarcoglycan complex, troponins and myosin light and heavy chains, and the RYR1-DHPR machinery of excitation-contraction coupling. Myostatin and IGF signalling then set muscle mass.

Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated because mononucleate myoblasts leave the cell cycle and fuse with one another and with existing myotubes, and this fusion programme is what builds muscle during development and rebuilds it after injury. Loss of the core machinery produces mononucleated, non-functional muscle: the dedicated fusogens myomaker and myomerger drive membrane hemifusion and pore formation, while the myogenic transcription factors MYOD1 and MYOG, together with NFATC2, commit cells to differentiation and sustain nuclear accretion. Recognition and adhesion steps use cadherin-like and immunoglobulin receptors such as CDON and NEO1, integrin beta-1, and tetraspanins including CD9 and CD81; DOCK proteins direct Rac-dependent actin remodelling at the fusion site, and metalloproteases such as ADAM12 remodel the surrounding matrix. Ribosomal protein genes here reflect the surge in translational capacity accompanying myotube growth, and endogenous retroviral envelope fusogens link this process to syncytium formation more broadly.

Neuromuscular junction development builds and maintains the synapse through which motor neurons command skeletal muscle, the structure whose failure produces myasthenia, congenital myasthenic syndromes and the denervation seen in motor neuron disease. Assembly is instructed from the nerve: neurally released agrin binds the muscle receptor complex LRP4-MuSK, which through DOK7 and downstream kinase cascades clusters acetylcholine receptors and anchors them via rapsyn to the underlying spectrin and ankyrin cytoskeleton. A specialised synaptic basal lamina of laminins, collagen IV and the collagen tail that tethers acetylcholinesterase, read by dystroglycan and its glycosyltransferases, aligns pre- and postsynaptic elements. Voltage-gated calcium channel subunits and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter equip the nerve terminal for release, while ubiquitin ligases and axonal transport components prune and refine contacts. The pathway therefore couples synaptogenesis, extracellular matrix organisation and postsynaptic receptor trafficking to voluntary movement.

The synapse between a motor neuron and skeletal muscle must be built, aligned and maintained for voluntary movement to occur, and neuromuscular junction development covers its assembly, patterning and remodelling. Nerve-derived agrin binds the muscle receptor LRP4, which activates the kinase MuSK through the adaptor DOK7; rapsyn then anchors clustered acetylcholine receptors beneath the nerve terminal, while synaptic basal lamina components including laminins, collagen IV and the collagen tail that tethers acetylcholinesterase organise the cleft. Dystroglycan and its glycosylation machinery link the postsynaptic membrane to that matrix, spectrin and ankyrin scaffolds stabilise it, and ubiquitin ligases prune excess innervation. Loss of these steps produces congenital myasthenic syndromes with fatigable weakness, and the same junction is the target of autoimmune myasthenia; several genes here also underlie motor neuron degeneration and muscular dystrophy.

Sex determination is the decision that commits a bipotential gonad to become a testis or an ovary, and the hormonal consequences that then masculinise or feminise the rest of the body. It matters because the choice is made once, early, and irreversibly: disruption produces gonadal dysgenesis, sex reversal and disorders of sex development, with infertility as the common endpoint. A Y-linked transcription factor acts with SOX9, FGF9, DMRT1 and nuclear receptor cofactors to drive Sertoli cell differentiation, while WNT4 and FOXL2 support the granulosa cell fate and actively suppress the testicular programme, so the two arms are mutually antagonistic rather than merely alternative. Downstream, anti-Mullerian hormone regresses the female duct system and androgens acting through their receptor, with 5-alpha-reductase supplying the more potent ligand, build male internal and external genitalia. WT1 and NR5A1 are also required for the earlier step of building the gonad and adrenal primordium at all.

Sex differentiation is the process by which a genetically determined embryo acquires the gonads, ducts and external genitalia of one sex, and it underlies fertility, hormonal physiology and the clinical spectrum of disorders of sex development. A bipotential gonad is first specified by factors such as WT1, NR5A1 and GATA4, then committed: SRY and SOX9 with FGF9 drive testis formation, while WNT4, FOXL2 and R-spondin/β-catenin signalling support ovarian fate, the two programmes mutually antagonistic. Sertoli-derived anti-Müllerian hormone acting through AMHR2 regresses the Müllerian ducts, whereas androgens made via CYP17A1 and HSD17B3, reduced by 5α-reductase and read by the androgen receptor, masculinise the urogenital sinus; aromatase and oestrogen receptor signalling act on the female side. Also represented are germ cell survival and meiotic components, gonadotropin and inhibin/activin control, and apoptotic regulators that shape germ cell number.

Pregnancy begins only if the blastocyst attaches to a receptive endometrium and invades it, and embryo implantation is the narrow window in which that happens; failure underlies much early pregnancy loss and infertility, while excessive or misplaced invasion contributes to ectopic implantation and placental disorders. The genes here span both partners in the encounter. Uterine receptivity depends on LIF acting through its receptor complex with IL11RA signalling, prostaglandin synthesis via PTGS2, and decidual remodelling by MMP2 and MMP9 with their inhibitors TIMP1 and RECK. Adhesion and trophoblast attachment involve integrins, osteopontin, trophinin and basigin, alongside gap-junction coupling and laminin-rich basement membrane. Nodal and activin receptors feeding SMAD2/SMAD3 pattern the early embryo, while VEGFA drives the angiogenesis that converts attachment into a functioning maternal-fetal interface.

Parturition is the transition of the pregnant uterus from a quiescent, stretch-tolerant organ to a coordinated contractile one that expels the fetus, and its timing determines whether birth occurs at term or prematurely. The genes here cover the endocrine and paracrine signals that set that switch: corticotropin-releasing hormone and its receptor form a placental clock whose output rises toward labour, oxytocin and prostaglandin F receptors drive myometrial contraction, and relaxin signalling through RXFP1 contributes to cervical and pelvic softening. Prostaglandin availability is set by phospholipase A2 enzymes that release arachidonate and by the dehydrogenase HPGD that inactivates prostaglandins locally. Endothelin-1 adds vasoconstrictive and contractile tone, while matrix metalloproteinase activity remodels cervical and membrane extracellular matrix to permit dilation. Dysregulation of these signals underlies preterm labour, post-term pregnancy and failed induction.

Cells and tissues continually adjust metabolism and gene expression to the nutrients available, and this response to nutrient stimulus collects the sensors, transcription factors and effector enzymes that carry out that adjustment. It determines whether fuel is stored or burned, how minerals and vitamins are absorbed and disposed of, and how growth is licensed only when building blocks are present. Amino acid and energy status converge on mTOR with its regulators, while lipid-sensing nuclear receptors such as PPARA, PPARG and their RXR partners, together with SREBP and its SCAP escort, ChREBP and USF1, set programmes for fatty acid synthesis, oxidation and ketogenesis through targets including FASN, CPT1A and HMGCS2. Retinoid and vitamin D arms act via RARA, VDR and the CYP26 and CYP27B1/CYP24A1 hydroxylases, alongside calcium and phosphate control by PTH, FGF23, CASR and Klotho. Leptin and adiponectin feed systemic energy signals in, and oxidative and folate one-carbon responses accompany them; derangement underlies obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and rickets.

Gas exchange by the respiratory system is the physiological end point of breathing: oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide release across a thin, ventilated alveolar surface. The genes here span the several layers that make this possible. Surfactant proteins and the phospholipid-associated machinery lower surface tension so alveoli stay open, and their loss causes neonatal respiratory distress and interstitial lung disease. Elastin and collagen set lung compliance, while endothelin signalling and lymphangiogenic receptors govern pulmonary vascular and lymphatic tone and structure. Axonemal dyneins and cilia-associated proteins drive mucociliary clearance, with defects producing ciliary dyskinesia. A neural arm, including the autonomic transcription factors PHOX2A and PHOX2B and bombesin-family peptides and receptors, patterns the brainstem circuits that generate and chemically regulate respiratory rhythm; disruption underlies central hypoventilation. Together these elements couple airway development, ventilation control and alveolar mechanics to systemic oxygenation.

digestion is the coordinated breakdown of ingested food into absorbable units and their uptake across the gut epithelium, the process that converts a meal into circulating nutrients. Its failure produces malabsorption, steatorrhoea, pancreatic insufficiency and nutritional deficiency. Pancreatic zymogens and lipases such as trypsinogens, chymotrypsinogen, colipase and PNLIP, together with gastric pepsinogens and brush-border enzymes like sucrase-isomaltase, perform the hydrolysis, while transporters including SLC5A1, SLC2A5, NPC1L1 and the ABCG5/ABCG8 sterol pump, plus fatty acid handlers CD36 and FABP2, move products into enterocytes. Secretion and motility are set by gut hormones — cholecystokinin, secretin, gastrin signalling, somatostatin, ghrelin and leptin — acting alongside cholinergic receptors. Mucins, trefoil factors and tight junction proteins maintain the barrier and paracellular ion flux, bile acid synthesis and nuclear receptors such as VDR and the LXRs adjust lipid and sterol handling to intake.

Digestion is how an animal converts food into absorbable molecules, and the genes here span the whole sequence: secretion of enzymes, acidification and buffering of the lumen, motility and appetite control, mucosal protection, and transport across the intestinal epithelium. Pancreatic acinar products such as trypsinogens, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, colipase and pancreatic lipase hydrolyse protein, starch and triglyceride, while gastric pepsinogens and the H+-handling and chloride/bicarbonate transporters set luminal pH. Gut hormones including cholecystokinin, secretin, ghrelin, somatostatin and motilin-like peptides coordinate enzyme release, gallbladder and gastric emptying with feeding, acting alongside muscarinic, histamine and serotonin receptor signalling. Brush-border sucrase-isomaltase, sugar transporters, fatty acid binding proteins, NPC1L1 and the ABCG5/ABCG8 sterol exporter govern uptake of sugars, lipids and cholesterol, and trefoil factors and mucins shield the epithelium. Failure produces malabsorption, pancreatitis, ulceration and inflammatory bowel disease.

Excretion is how the body rids itself of metabolic waste — water, carbon dioxide and nitrogenous end products such as urea and urate — largely through the kidney, and its failure produces uremia, acidosis, gout and fluid overload. The genes here converge on renal handling of solutes and volume: organic anion transporters and the urate transporter encoded by SLC22A12 move urate and drugs across tubular membranes, ABCG2 effluxes urate into the gut and urine, and uromodulin is secreted by the thick ascending limb. Vacuolar ATPase subunits in intercalated cells acidify urine, and their loss causes distal renal tubular acidosis. Layered on top are systemic controls of salt and water balance: the angiotensinogen–AT1 receptor axis, natriuretic peptide signalling through corin and NPR1, endothelin, and neural and dopaminergic input that adjusts filtration and tubular reabsorption to body needs.

Glands and epithelia release fluids onto surfaces and into lumens, and this pathway covers the controlled secretion of those body fluids — milk, saliva, tears, mucus, intestinal and airway surface liquid. Its output keeps the eye and airway moist, lubricates the gut, delivers nutrition to the newborn, and sets luminal salt and water balance; impaired secretion underlies dry eye, xerostomia, and defective mucus clearance, while unrestrained secretion produces secretory diarrhoea. Muscarinic, purinergic and peptide receptors raise intracellular calcium to open chloride channels such as ANO1 and calcium-activated potassium channels, with aquaporins AQP1 and AQP5 providing the water route and sodium transport by SCNN1B and the WNK–STK39 kinase module tuning ion flux. Prolactin acting through PRLR and STAT5 drives the milk protein programme including caseins, and vesicle SNAREs deliver secretory granules to the apical membrane.

Lactation is the phase in which the mammary gland secretes milk to feed offspring, and the genes here cover both the hormonal control of that period and the secretory differentiation that makes it possible. Prolactin acting through its receptor and the STAT5A/STAT5B transcription factors, with coactivators such as MED1 and NCOA1 and repression by NCOR2, drives expression of milk protein genes including the caseins CSN2 and CSN3; SOCS2 restrains this signalling. Oxytocin acting on OXTR triggers the milk ejection reflex by contracting myoepithelial cells. Alveolar epithelium must expand its secretory apparatus and metabolic capacity, reflected in XBP1-dependent secretory pathway function, glucose and nutrient transport, lipid synthesis, copper loading of milk by ATP7B, and VEGFA- and HIF1A-supported vascular and glycolytic adaptation. Failure of these steps produces lactation insufficiency, while the same signalling axis is implicated in mammary tumorigenesis.

Clotting can be triggered by contact of blood with a negatively charged surface, and the intrinsic pathway is that route to fibrin formation. Factor XII, prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen assemble on the surface, with factor XII and kallikrein activating each other reciprocally; factor XIIa then cleaves factor XI, factor XIa activates factor IX, and factor IXa with its cofactor factor VIII converts factor X to Xa, feeding the common pathway that generates thrombin. Loss of factor VIII or factor IX causes haemophilia A and B, with bleeding into joints and muscles, while factor XII deficiency prolongs clotting tests without causing bleeding, marking this arm as more relevant to thrombosis than to haemostasis. The platelet glycoprotein Ib-V-IX complex anchors the reaction to the adhering platelet surface, and APOH modulates contact activation.

hemostasis is the body's response to vascular injury: the arrest of bleeding by plugging a damaged vessel wall while keeping blood fluid everywhere else. Its failure in either direction is clinically obvious, giving haemophilia and von Willebrand disease when clotting is insufficient and thrombosis, stroke or myocardial infarction when it is excessive. The genes cover the whole sequence: von Willebrand factor and the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V and GPVI receptors that capture platelets on exposed collagen; thrombin, tissue factor and the vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors that convert fibrinogen to fibrin; integrin αIIbβ3 with talin, filamin and the actomyosin machinery that retracts the clot; and dense- and alpha-granule secretion, which amplifies recruitment through ADP and thromboxane receptors. Balancing them are anticoagulant and fibrinolytic controls — antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, TFPI, plasminogen activators and their serpin inhibitors — plus endothelial nitric oxide and ADAMTS13, which limit clot growth to the site of damage.

Hemostasis is how the body seals a breached vessel and stops blood loss while keeping the rest of the circulation fluid, and its failure produces either bleeding disorders or pathological thrombosis. Injury exposes collagen and tissue factor, so platelets tether through von Willebrand factor to the GP1b-IX-V complex, engage collagen via GP6 and integrin alpha2beta1, then spread and aggregate through integrin alphaIIbbeta3 with talin and kindlin-3 completing activation. Thromboxane, ADP acting on P2RY1 and P2RY12, and thrombin acting on PAR receptors amplify the response through G protein, kinase and phospholipase signalling and granule release. In parallel the coagulation cascade generates thrombin to convert fibrinogen into a crosslinked fibrin clot, while antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor and the plasminogen activators restrain and eventually dissolve it. Vitamin K handling by GGCX and VKORC1, and platelet granule biogenesis, keep the system provisioned.

Sensory perception covers how the nervous system detects stimuli from the outside world and converts them into neural signals the brain can interpret. It defines the specialized receptor cells of the eye, ear, nose, tongue and skin, and its failure produces the common sensory disorders: retinitis pigmentosa and macular degeneration, congenital and progressive deafness, anosmia, cataract, and inherited insensitivity or hypersensitivity to pain. Mechanistically it spans distinct transduction logics united by a common plan of receptor, ion channel and amplifying cascade -- rhodopsin and cone opsins feeding transducin, phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels in photoreceptors; a very large odorant receptor repertoire with taste and vomeronasal receptors acting through gustducin and phospholipase C; hair-cell mechanotransduction built from cadherin-23, protocadherin-15, myosins and TMC channels; and nociceptor TRP, ASIC, PIEZO and voltage-gated sodium channels. Developmental regulators such as PAX6, CRX and POU4F3 specify these cells, while ciliary trafficking and retinoid recycling maintain them.

Sensory perception covers the machinery by which the nervous system captures a physical or chemical stimulus, transduces it into an electrical signal, and encodes its quality and intensity. The gene list spans the major modalities: visual phototransduction through rhodopsin and cone opsins, transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase subunits, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the retinoid cycle enzymes that regenerate chromophore; a very large olfactory receptor repertoire with its trafficking cofactors and the vomeronasal and trace-amine receptors; sweet, umami and bitter taste receptors coupled to gustducin and PLC signalling; hair-cell mechanotransduction and stereocilia architecture via myosins, cadherin 23, protocadherin 15, usherin and whirlin; and somatosensory channels such as TRPV1, TRPM8, PIEZO2 and sensory sodium channels for pain, temperature and touch. Also present are lens crystallins and eye and ear developmental transcription factors. Failure of these components produces retinal degeneration, inherited deafness, cataract, anosmia and congenital insensitivity to pain.

Vision begins when a photon is converted into an electrical signal by a photoreceptor, and this is the cascade that performs that conversion. Rhodopsin in rods and the cone opsins absorb light, activate the G protein transducin, and stimulate a cGMP phosphodiesterase; the resulting fall in cGMP closes cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and hyperpolarizes the cell. Recovery and adaptation are equally part of the pathway: rhodopsin kinase and arrestin shut off activated opsin, recoverin and calcium-binding proteins report the calcium drop, guanylate cyclase activators restore cGMP through retinal guanylate cyclases, and sodium/calcium-potassium exchangers extrude calcium. Chromophore recycling and outer-segment transport proteins keep the system supplied and correctly built. Mutations in these components cause retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, cone dystrophies and colour blindness. Related non-visual opsins support circadian and other light responses.

Vision begins when a photon of visible light is converted into an electrical change in a photoreceptor, and this is the cascade that performs that conversion in rods and cones. Absorption by rhodopsin or a cone opsin activates the photoreceptor-specific G protein transducin, which relieves inhibition of cyclic GMP phosphodiesterase; the resulting fall in cGMP closes cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and hyperpolarises the cell. Recovery and adaptation matter as much as excitation: rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates activated opsin, arrestin caps it, and retinal guanylate cyclases resynthesise cGMP to reset sensitivity. Chaperone and lipid-modification steps, including N-myristoylation and the AIPL1 chaperone for phosphodiesterase, keep the components folded and correctly targeted to outer segments, while a retinal-clearing transporter limits toxic retinoid adducts. Mutations across these steps cause congenital stationary night blindness, Leber congenital amaurosis, retinitis pigmentosa and macular degeneration.

Chemosensation lets an animal detect volatile and dissolved chemicals in its environment, and this pathway covers the whole arc from receptor binding to a coded neural signal. It underlies smell, taste and pheromone-like detection, guiding food choice, avoidance of spoiled or toxic material, and, in humans, the loss of which presents as anosmia or altered taste with consequences for appetite and safety. The bulk of the machinery is a very large family of odorant receptors together with bitter and sweet/umami taste receptors, trace amine-associated and vomeronasal receptors, all G protein-coupled. Their signals run through dedicated transducins and cyclase steps, notably GNAL, GNAT3, ADCY3 and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels, or through phospholipase C and the TRPM-adjacent components including ITPR3 and CALHM channels for transmitter release. Sour and salt sensing add acid-sensing and epithelial sodium channels, while chaperones such as the RTP proteins and ciliary BBSome components deliver receptors to the sensory membrane.

Smell begins when volatile chemicals dissolve in nasal mucus and bind receptors on the cilia of olfactory sensory neurons, and this pathway covers that detection and its conversion into electrical signals. It gives animals the ability to find food, avoid spoilage and toxins, and read social and environmental cues; its loss produces anosmia, with the attendant loss of flavour perception and hazard detection. The bulk of the machinery is the very large family of odorant G protein-coupled receptors, each neuron expressing essentially one, together with trace amine-associated receptors tuned to amines. Receptor activation works through the olfactory-specific G protein subunit encoded by GNAL and adenylate cyclase ADCY3 to raise cAMP, opening CNGA2-containing cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and chloride conductances that depolarize the cell; sodium-calcium exchange and phosphodiesterase activity restore sensitivity. Ciliary trafficking proteins of the Bardet-Biedl complex, odorant-binding proteins and xenobiotic-metabolizing enzymes support and terminate the response.

behavior covers the nervous-system-dependent actions an animal takes in response to internal states and external cues tion — feeding, sleep, mating, locomotion, learning, fear and social interaction — and the molecules that generate them. It matters because these outputs define an animal's fitness, and their disruption produces autism, addiction, obesity, anxiety and movement disorders. The genes span the layers that build such responses: neurotransmitter systems (dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, GABA, opioid and cholinergic receptors and their transporters), synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins such as neurexins, neuroligins and SHANK family members that specify circuit wiring, activity-dependent immediate-early transcription (FOS, EGR1, ARC, NPAS4) that converts firing into lasting change, and hypothalamic peptide signalling — leptin, melanocortin, orexin, oxytocin, NPY — that sets appetite, arousal and social drive. Circadian regulators and ion channels controlling excitability tie these outputs to timing and state.

Behaviour is the coordinated output of the nervous system — feeding, sleep and circadian timing, locomotion, learning and memory, social interaction, reproduction, nociception and reward — and this broad collection captures the molecules through which those actions are generated and tuned. Neurotransmitter systems dominate: dopamine, serotonin, opioid, glutamate and GABA receptors, transporters such as SLC6A3 and SLC6A4, and synthetic enzymes including TH and GAD1. Neuropeptide circuits for energy balance and arousal are prominent, with POMC, AGRP, NPY, leptin and its receptor, orexins, oxytocin and CRH acting on hypothalamic targets. Synaptic adhesion and scaffolding proteins (neurexins, neuroligins, SHANK family, SYNGAP1), activity-induced transcription factors such as FOS and NPAS4, ion channels and clock components complete the picture. Disruption of these genes underlies autism and intellectual disability, addiction, obesity, sleep disorders and neurodegenerative disease, linking molecular synaptic function to whole-organism conduct.

Learning and memory describe how nervous systems acquire information, encode it as lasting changes in synaptic strength, and retrieve it later; this capacity underlies adaptive behaviour, and its erosion defines intellectual disability, autism-spectrum conditions and dementia. The genes here converge on the glutamatergic synapse, where NMDA receptor subunits (GRIN1, GRIN2A/B), AMPA receptor trafficking, and postsynaptic scaffolds such as DLG4 and the SHANK family translate coincident activity into calcium signals. Those signals feed calcium/calmodulin kinases, adenylate cyclases, calcineurin and CREB-dependent transcription, producing immediate-early gene products including FOS, EGR1, ARC and NPAS4 that consolidate plasticity. Neuromodulatory tone from dopamine, serotonin, cholinergic and neuropeptide receptors gates when encoding occurs, while trans-synaptic adhesion molecules such as neurexins, neuroligins and reelin signalling shape circuit wiring. Several members, notably APP, PSEN1, MAPT and APOE, tie this biology directly to neurodegenerative memory loss.

Learning is the set of processes by which experience produces lasting changes in behaviour, and at the cellular level it depends on activity-driven remodelling of synaptic strength in the hippocampus, cortex and striatum. The genes here span the machinery of that remodelling: glutamate receptors and their scaffolds, including NMDA receptor subunits GRIN1 and GRIN2A, the postsynaptic density protein DLG4, SHANK family scaffolds and the synaptic GAP SYNGAP1; adhesion molecules such as neurexins and neuroligins that specify and stabilise synapses; and neuromodulatory inputs through dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, neuropeptide and monoamine systems that gate when plasticity occurs. Calcium signalling, CREB1- and FOS-dependent transcription, and NPAS4-driven activity programmes convert stimulation into durable change. Disruption of these components underlies intellectual disability, autism, and the memory loss of Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease, linking synaptic plasticity directly to cognition.

Memory is the brain's capacity to register, store and later retrieve experience, and the genes supporting it span the whole arc from encoding through consolidation to recall. Its loss defines the clinical picture of Alzheimer's disease and of intellectual disability syndromes, and several members here — APP, PSEN1, APOE, MAPT, TREM2, MECP2 — are among the best-known risk or causal loci for those conditions. Mechanistically the set is built around activity-dependent synaptic plasticity: glutamate receptor subunits such as GRIA1 and GRIN2A, calcium and cyclic-AMP signalling through calcineurin, CAMK4 and adenylate cyclases, and the immediate-early transcriptional response of FOS, EGR1, ARC and NPAS4 acting with CREB1 to convert transient activity into lasting change. Postsynaptic scaffolds, Reelin signalling, neuromodulatory dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline and cholinergic components, and local translational control set the threshold at which experience becomes a stable trace.

Short-term memory holds information for seconds to minutes, long enough to guide an ongoing behaviour, and depends on transient second-messenger-driven changes in synaptic strength rather than the lasting transcriptional and structural remodelling that consolidates long-term traces. The biology here spans the excitability and plasticity of hippocampal and cortical circuits: calcium handling and buffering by calbindin and the calcineurin regulators RCAN1 and RCAN2, cholinergic modulation of attention and encoding through the alpha-7 nicotinic receptor, activity-dependent transcription via NPAS4 that tunes inhibitory input onto active neurons, and developmental patterning factors such as CUX2, ADNP, MDK and BRINP1 that set up the interneuron and pyramidal populations the process runs on. Glucose delivery by the transporter SLC2A4 links neuronal energy supply to performance. Disruption of these components produces working-memory deficits seen in intellectual disability, schizophrenia, Down syndrome and Alzheimer disease.

Memories that last weeks to years require more than transient synaptic change: they depend on transcription and new protein synthesis triggered by second messenger cascades, and this long-term memory programme is what converts activity into durable circuit modification. Calcium entry during strong synaptic activity engages adenylate cyclases and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase signalling, which activate transcription factors including EGR1, SRF, NPAS4 and NFATC4 to induce plasticity genes such as ARC. Chromatin and translational regulators, among them MECP2, the acetyltransferase KAT2A and the polyadenylation factor CPEB3, set how persistently those programmes run, while AMPA receptor subunits and postsynaptic scaffolds like SHANK1 execute the change at the synapse. Failure of these steps underlies memory deficits in Rett syndrome, and APOE and RELN link the same biology to age-related and Alzheimer-type cognitive decline.

Mating behavior covers the coordinated courtship, partner recognition, copulatory and pair-bonding interactions through which animals achieve fertilization, and it sits at the intersection of neuroendocrine signalling and reproductive physiology. The genes here span the neuropeptide axis that shapes sexual and affiliative behaviour — oxytocin and vasopressin with their receptors, substance P and its receptor — alongside the monoamine systems that supply motivation and reward, including tyrosine hydroxylase for catecholamine synthesis, dopamine D1 and D5 receptors, the serotonin transporter and the striatal signalling proteins DARPP-32 and spinophilin. Hormonal context is set by thyroid hormone receptors and a nuclear receptor coactivator, while melatonin receptor signalling ties behaviour to photoperiod. A separate arm acts in the reproductive tract and semen, where semenogelin and protease inhibitors govern coagulation and liquefaction. Disruption impairs courtship, erectile and ejaculatory function, and social bonding.

Copulation covers the neural, endocrine and reproductive-tract events that bring about sexual union and the delivery of sperm, a behaviour on which fertilisation and reproductive success depend. The genes span its separate layers: oxytocin and vasopressin receptor signalling together with tachykinin/substance P and its receptor set sexual arousal, mating behaviour and the smooth muscle contractions of ejaculation; purinergic receptors and endothelin signalling drive contraction of vas deferens and vascular smooth muscle underlying erectile and emission responses; and seminal proteins such as semenogelin, kallikrein 14, protein C inhibitor and serpin E2 govern coagulation and liquefaction of semen, sperm motility and capacitation. Amino acid and nucleoside catabolic enzymes modulate the neurotransmitter tone behind these reflexes. Disruption produces erectile and ejaculatory dysfunction, altered mating behaviour, and infertility arising from defective seminal plasma rather than from the sperm themselves.

Copulation, the sexual union that delivers sperm to the female tract, depends on coordinated neural, smooth-muscle and seminal-fluid events rather than on a single tissue. Genes here span the behavioural and the mechanical: oxytocin and vasopressin receptor signalling, substance P acting through its receptor, and GABA transaminase shape the central and spinal circuits controlling arousal, erection and ejaculatory reflex, while purinergic receptors and endothelin receptor signalling drive contraction of vas deferens and vascular smooth muscle that propels semen. Accessory-gland products such as semenogelin and epididymal secretory proteins, together with the serine protease inhibitors of the SERPIN family and kallikrein activity, govern coagulation and liquefaction of the ejaculate and protect spermatozoa during transit. Disruption at any level manifests as erectile or ejaculatory dysfunction, altered semen viscosity, or impaired fertility, linking reproductive behaviour to the biochemistry of the seminal plasma.

Behaviours that repeat on a fixed schedule — sleep and wakefulness, feeding bouts, locomotor activity rhythms, hormone release — are organised by the machinery collected here, which links the molecular clock to the neural circuits that execute rhythmic behavior. Core clock and clock-output components such as PER3, the nuclear receptors NR1D1 and NR1D2, CIART, ID2 and ZFHX3 impose daily timing on transcription, while co-regulators including NCOR1 and NCOA2 couple that timing to chromatin. Output is behavioural: adenosine signalling through ADORA1 and ADORA2A tracks sleep pressure, melatonin acts via MTNR1B, orexin signalling through HCRTR2 stabilises arousal, and dopamine, CRH, ghrelin and GHRH connect the clock to motivation, stress and appetite. Ion channels set the firing patterns of the pacemaker and target neurons. Disruption produces insomnia, restless legs, shifted sleep phase and metabolic consequences of mistimed feeding.

circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour internal clock that anticipates the day-night cycle and schedules sleep, feeding, hormone release, body temperature and metabolism accordingly. Its disruption underlies jet lag, shift-work intolerance, familial advanced sleep phase, and contributes to metabolic and mood disorders. At its core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK/NPAS2 and BMAL1 drive expression of PER and CRY, whose proteins return to inhibit their own activators; timing is set by phosphorylation through casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and GSK3B and by ubiquitin-mediated degradation via FBXL3 and beta-TrCP complexes. Nuclear receptors such as REV-ERB and ROR, plus chromatin modifiers, sirtuins and NAMPT, couple the loop to redox and nutrient state, while AMPK and mTOR relay feeding cues. Light input through melanopsin and retinal opsins entrains the suprachiasmatic pacemaker, which broadcasts phase to peripheral tissues via melatonin, glucocorticoid and neuropeptide signalling.

Circadian rhythm is the roughly 24-hour internal timing programme that aligns sleep and wake, hormone release, feeding and metabolism with the solar day. Its core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK and BMAL1 drive expression of the PER and CRY repressors, which in turn shut down their own activators; kinases such as CSNK1D/E and the ubiquitin ligase adaptor FBXL3 set the period by timing repressor degradation, while nuclear receptors of the REV-ERB and ROR families and chromatin modifiers add further feedback. Melatonin synthesis and its receptors, opsins including melanopsin, and neuropeptide signalling convey light and behavioural cues to the clock, and outputs reach lipid and glucose metabolism through PPARs, SIRT1, AMPK and NAMPT. Disruption underlies sleep-phase disorders and contributes to metabolic syndrome, mood disturbance and altered drug and tumour behaviour.

Grooming is a stereotyped, self-directed motor routine that keeps fur and skin free of dirt and parasites, and in mammals it doubles as a readout of arousal, stress and repetitive-behaviour circuitry. The genes here converge on striatal and hypothalamic control of that routine: dopamine receptors DRD1 and DRD2 set the excitability of the basal ganglia loops that initiate and terminate bouts, while oxytocin, vasopressin with its V1a receptor, neuromedin U and QRFP act as neuropeptide modulators of arousal-linked behaviours. Synaptic scaffolds and adhesion proteins including DLG4, SLITRK5 and CNTNAP4 shape corticostriatal transmission, and loss of SLITRK5 or of the glutamate transporter SLC1A1 produces excessive grooming resembling compulsive behaviour. Purine salvage defects in HPRT1 and lysosomal disease genes such as CTNS and PPT1 link the same output to self-injurious over-grooming, making this behaviour a sensitive index of striatal dysfunction.
