Locomotory behavior is the coordinated movement of an animal from place to place in response to internal state and external cues, and the genes grouped here span the whole arc from motor circuit construction to the neurotransmitter signalling that sets activity level and gait. Its failure is recognisable clinically: loss of dopaminergic control produces parkinsonism, spinal interneuron and motor neuron defects produce spasticity, ataxia or paralysis, and lysosomal storage defects produce progressive movement decline. Dopamine synthesis and packaging, the receptors and striatal effectors that read it, and modulatory opioid, adenosine and neuropeptide inputs tune how much an animal moves. Alongside these sit neuronal migration and axon guidance components, inhibitory glycinergic and GABAergic transmission, ion channels that set excitability, and synaptic release machinery. Several familiar neurodegeneration genes appear because locomotion is the behavioural readout on which their loss is measured.

Feeding behavior encompasses the neural and hormonal control of appetite, meal initiation and termination, and the intake of food that keeps energy stores matched to expenditure. Its failure underlies obesity, cachexia and eating disorders, and several of its components are the best-validated monogenic causes of human hyperphagia. Peripheral signals of nutritional state — leptin from fat, insulin, ghrelin from the stomach, and gut peptides such as CCK, GLP-1/glucagon, PYY and GDF15 acting through GFRAL — converge on hypothalamic neurons expressing the orexigenic peptides AgRP, NPY and melanin-concentrating hormone or the anorexigenic POMC-derived melanocortins. Melanocortin receptors MC3R and MC4R, with the accessory protein MRAP2 and processing enzymes, set the balance, while orexin, galanin, CART and oxytocin circuits, dopaminergic reward signalling and leptin-STAT3 transcriptional output tune motivation and satiety. Ciliary and body-weight-associated genes modulate the same circuitry.

Seeing is only useful if it changes what an animal does, and visual behavior covers the responses an organism makes to visual stimuli — orienting to light, tracking moving objects, optomotor and startle responses, visually guided learning and place preference. The genes here span the whole arc from photon capture to motor output: transducin subunits of rod and cone phototransduction and melanopsin for irradiance detection, ciliary and intraflagellar transport components whose loss degenerates photoreceptors, glutamatergic synaptic machinery including NMDA receptor subunits and SYNGAP1 for relaying and plasticity in visual circuits, and dopaminergic and cholinergic signalling that sets arousal, attention and reward value on what is seen. Failure at any level produces behavioral blindness, impaired visual acuity or attentional deficits, which is why this readout is used to phenotype retinal degeneration and neurodevelopmental disorders such as those involving MECP2 and NF1.\n

Chemosensory behavior covers the responses an animal makes after detecting chemicals in its environment — sniffing out food, avoiding bitter or irritant compounds, withdrawing from noxious stimuli. It underlies olfactory-guided feeding and social behaviour, taste aversion, and chemical nociception, and its loss shows up clinically as anosmia or as insensitivity to painful irritants. The genes here span the sensory chain: odorant-binding and bitter taste receptors that capture the stimulus, an adenylate cyclase and protein kinase C that transduce it, and TRPV1 and a sodium channel that convert chemical irritants into firing in sensory neurons. Others act earlier, building the apparatus itself — ciliary and transcription factor components whose mutation disrupts olfactory neuron cilia or olfactory bulb development, as in Bardet-Biedl and CHARGE syndromes. Trophic signalling through NTRK1 maintains the nociceptive neurons that this behaviour depends on.

Responding to touch, vibration or sound requires that a mechanical stimulus be converted into neural activity and then into a behavioural output, and mechanosensory behavior names that whole arc from stimulus to movement. Genes here act mostly on the wiring and synaptic side rather than on transduction itself: the neurexins NRXN1 and NRXN2 with SHANK3 and SLITRK6 build and specify synapses in sensory and central circuits, NEUROG1 and ETV1 drive differentiation of sensory neuron subtypes, and SLC1A3 clears glutamate around them. FOXP2 and CNTNAP2 tie the same circuits to vocal and auditory processing, and HTT links the pathway to striatal degeneration. Loss of these components shows up as altered startle and acoustic responses, impaired hearing, and the sensory abnormalities that accompany autism spectrum and neurodevelopmental disorders, making this biology a readout of sensory circuit assembly as much as of behaviour.

The heart must beat at a rate and force matched to demand, and this is the collected machinery that sets those parameters. Pacemaker currents carried by HCN channels and T-type calcium channels set firing rate in nodal tissue, while gap junction connexins and sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits propagate the impulse; repolarizing potassium channels including KCNQ1, KCNH2 and their KCNE partners determine action potential duration. Beat-to-beat force depends on calcium handling — release through RYR2 with triadin, junctophilin and calsequestrin, reuptake by SERCA2 under phospholamban control, and extrusion by sodium-calcium exchange — feeding troponin and myosin in the sarcomere. Adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, natriuretic and angiotensin signalling tune all of this, and cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, TBX5 and GATA4 specify the conduction and chamber identities involved. Mutations here cause arrhythmia syndromes, cardiomyopathy and sudden death.

tRNA processing converts newly transcribed pre-tRNAs into the mature adaptors that decode mRNA, so every round of protein synthesis depends on it. Precursors must be trimmed at both ends by the RNase P complex and by 3' endonucleases, have CCA added by a nucleotidyltransferase, and in the case of intron-containing tRNAs be cut by the splicing endonuclease and rejoined by an RNA ligase complex. Dozens of modification enzymes then decorate the body and anticodon loop — pseudouridine synthases, methyltransferases, dihydrouridine and queuosine enzymes, thiolation and wybutosine machinery, and the elongator and KEOPS complexes acting at the wobble position — tuning decoding accuracy, translational speed and tRNA stability. Both nuclear and mitochondrial tRNA pools are served. Loss of individual enzymes causes intellectual disability, microcephaly, mitochondrial disease and anaemia, and altered wobble modification reshapes codon-biased translation in cancer and stress responses.

Freshly transcribed tRNAs are not usable; they must be trimmed, tailored and chemically decorated before an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase can charge them and the ribosome can read them accurately. This maturation pathway covers 5' leader removal by the ribonuclease P complex and its protein-only mitochondrial counterpart, 3' trailer cleavage by tRNase Z enzymes, CCA addition, and splicing of intron-containing precursors by the TSEN endonuclease complex followed by RTCB-dependent ligation. Layered on top is an extensive set of base and ribose modifications — pseudouridines, methylations, dihydrouridines, queuosine and wybutosine, thiolated and adenosine-deaminated wobble bases, and threonylcarbamoyl groups added by the KEOPS/EKC and Elongator machineries — which stabilise tRNA folding and set codon reading fidelity and frameshift avoidance. Both cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNAs are substrates, so defects impair global translation and oxidative phosphorylation, causing pontocerebellar hypoplasia, intellectual disability, microcephaly, mitochondrial myopathy and altered diabetes risk.

Cell recognition is how a cell reads the identity of the surfaces and cues around it and decides whether to adhere, fuse, turn away, or engulf. Three arms dominate here. In reproduction, sperm and egg recognise each other through zona pellucida glycoproteins, IZUMO1 and its oocyte receptor, and acrosomal proteases and ADAM-family surface proteins, without which fertilisation fails. In the nervous system, contactins, protocadherins, DSCAM, neural cell adhesion molecules and the Robo, Eph/ephrin and semaphorin-plexin receptor systems let growth cones distinguish self from non-self and steer axons to correct targets. In immunity, complement components, ficolins, collectins, C-type lectins and receptors such as TREM2, CD36 and scavenger receptors tag pathogens and dying cells for clearance. Shared downstream machinery includes cytoskeletal adaptors and Rho-family regulators that convert recognition into adhesion or motility.

Developing neurons must read the identity of the cells and surfaces they touch in order to grow axons along the right tracks, select synaptic partners, and avoid sticking to themselves. This recognition capacity shapes wiring of the nervous system: midline crossing, topographic mapping of projections, dendrite self-avoidance and tiling, and the pruning of inappropriate contacts. It is carried largely by cell-surface adhesion and guidance receptors — contactins and their partner CNTNAP2, IgLON family members such as OPCML and neurotrimin, DSCAM and DSCAML1, NCAM2 and NRCAM — together with Eph receptors reading ephrin gradients, Robo receptors responding to Slit repulsion, semaphorin and plexin/neuropilin signalling, and RTN4-mediated growth inhibition. Cytoskeletal and signalling effectors including GAP43, CDK5R1 and Rho regulation translate surface contact into growth-cone steering. Disruption of these recognition molecules is linked to autism spectrum disorders, epilepsy and cortical malformation.

Motor axons leaving the spinal cord must reach the correct muscle, and this guidance programme steers their growth cones there using attractive and repulsive cues read at the tip of the extending axon. Its output is the basic wiring of voluntary movement: limb innervation, correct dorsal-ventral choices at the plexus, and midline crossing decisions. Class 3 semaphorins acting through neuropilin and plexin receptors, together with Slit ligands and EphA4, repel axons from inappropriate territory, while LIM-homeodomain transcription factors such as LHX3 and LHX4 assign motor neuron subtype identity and thus which receptors a neuron displays. Cytoskeletal effectors including Rac GTPases, the Rac-inactivating GAP CHN1, CDK5 and kinesin-mediated transport convert those signals into directed motility. Mutation of CHN1 or EPHA4 in humans and mice produces misrouted cranial or corticospinal projections and abnormal eye or limb movement.

Mitochondria are not fixed organelles; they merge with one another so that membrane potential, metabolites and mitochondrial DNA can be shared across a connected network. Mitochondrial fusion buffers damage by diluting it, supports oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and maintains mtDNA integrity, and its loss causes fragmented mitochondria, mtDNA depletion and neurodegeneration "" mutations in MFN2 give Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and OPA1 mutations dominant optic atrophy. Outer-membrane fusion is driven by the dynamin-family GTPases MFN1 and MFN2 tethering adjacent organelles, while OPA1 handles inner-membrane fusion and cristae shape; its activity is set by proteolytic processing through OMA1, YME1L1, AFG3L2 and PARL, coupling fusion to stress and bioenergetic state. Ubiquitin ligases and the deubiquitinase USP30 tune mitofusin levels, linking fusion to mitophagy and to apoptotic control by BCL-2 family members, with adaptors such as CHCHD3, MIGA1/2 and PLD6 assisting membrane remodelling.

Toll signaling pathway is the innate immune signalling module that converts recognition of microbial and damage-associated molecules at Toll-like and interleukin-1 receptors into new gene transcription, chiefly the inflammatory programme driven by NF- cappaB and interferon regulatory factors. It gives cells their first-response capacity against infection, and its miscalibration produces septic shock at one extreme and recurrent pyogenic infection at the other. Ligand binding nucleates a receptor-proximal complex in which MyD88 recruits the IRAK kinases, IRAK4 and IRAK1 acting as the activating core while IRAK3 serves as a brake; Pellino E3 ligases and TRAF adaptors then build the ubiquitin scaffolds that propagate the signal to downstream kinases. Negative regulators such as SIGIRR and NLRP12 restrain output, reflecting how tightly this pathway must be tuned to avoid chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

Toll and Toll-like receptors detect conserved microbial structures at the cell surface and in endosomes, and the signalling cascade described here converts that detection into transcriptional programmes for inflammation and host defence. Ligand binding recruits the adaptor MyD88, which assembles a receptor-proximal complex with the IRAK kinases; IRAK4 activates IRAK1 and IRAK2, and the Pellino E3 ligases ubiquitinate IRAK substrates to propagate signalling toward NF-kB and interferon regulatory factors. Output is tuned by built-in brakes: IRAK3 is a catalytically inactive pseudokinase that dampens the cascade, SIGIRR acts as a decoy receptor restraining Toll-like receptor responses, and TRAF3 biases output toward type I interferon. Because this circuit sets the threshold for innate immune activation, too little signalling leaves patients vulnerable to pyogenic bacterial infection, while unchecked activity drives septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease.

During gastrulation, cells that have taken on mesodermal fate must leave the primitive streak and travel to the positions where heart, somites, blood and vessels will form; mesodermal cell migration is that orderly movement. It sets the body plan, and when it fails embryos show defective heart tube formation, disorganised somites and failed vascular patterning. The genes here span the layers that make such movement possible: a transcription factor that specifies nascent mesoderm and licenses its emigration, FGF8 signalling that provides directional cues and keeps cells moving away from the streak, a FERM-domain protein that remodels cell adhesion and apical-basal organisation during the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, a WAVE complex subunit that drives actin-based protrusion at the leading edge, and a secreted peptide ligand acting on Aplnr that guides cardiac mesoderm. Together they link fate specification to motility and morphogenesis.

Neurons are geometrically extreme cells, and almost nothing a synapse needs is made where it is used, so cargo must be ferried along microtubules out into axons and dendrites and back to the soma. Axo-dendritic transport covers this directed movement of organelles, vesicles, mRNAs and protein complexes, and it determines whether synaptic vesicle precursors, mitochondria, lysosomes and autophagosomes reach their destinations. Kinesins of the KIF1, KIF5 and KIF3 families drive anterograde traffic while cytoplasmic dynein with its dynactin subunits moves retrograde; adaptors such as TRAK2 and syntabulin link motors to mitochondria and vesicles, BLOC-1 and AP-3 complexes sort cargo, and microtubule regulators including MAPT, MAP2, TRIM46 and the severing enzyme spastin shape the tracks and their polarity. Mutations in these motors, adaptors and microtubule proteins cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and motor neuron degeneration, where distal axons fail first.

Neurons build and maintain axons that can extend far beyond the cell body, and anterograde axonal transport is how the materials they need get there: the outward, plus-end-directed movement of organelles, vesicles, mitochondria and protein cargo along axonal microtubules toward synapses and growth cones. Kinesin motors of the KIF1 and KIF5 families provide the force, adaptors such as MAPK8IP3, FEZ1 and HAP1 couple specific cargoes to them, and BORC together with ARL8 GTPases drives lysosome-related organelles distally; the BLOC-1 and AP-3 complexes supply the vesicles being moved. Microtubule-associated proteins, tubulin carboxy-terminal processing enzymes and TRIM46 shape the tracks themselves. Because axons cannot survive on local synthesis alone, defects here produce length-dependent degeneration, and mutations in KIF5A, SPAST, KIF1A, HSPB1, NEFL and SOD1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, peripheral neuropathy and motor neuron disease.

Neurons must move cargo from distant axon terminals back to the cell body, and retrograde axonal transport is the motor-driven traffic that does it: signalling endosomes carrying neurotrophin receptor complexes, damaged mitochondria, autophagosomes and injury signals all travel this route along microtubules. It tells the soma what is happening at the synapse and clears material that cannot be degraded locally, so neurons depend on it for survival signalling, injury responses and axon maintenance over lengths of up to a metre. Cytoplasmic dynein heavy chain provides the minus-end-directed force, with dynactin components, LIS1 and NDEL1 acting as processivity and cargo-adaptor factors, while HAP1 and SNAPIN link vesicles to the motor; neurofilament and spectraplakin cytoskeletal proteins shape the track. Kinesins in the same axon carry anterograde loads that must be balanced against it. Mutations in these motors and in SOD1 cause motor neuron disease and hereditary neuropathies.

Cells change shape, crawl, divide and build protrusions by continuously lengthening and shortening actin filaments, and this pathway covers the addition and removal of monomers at filament ends. Its output determines lamellipodial and filopodial protrusion, phagocytosis, immune cell chemotaxis, podocyte foot process integrity and the spectrin-based membrane skeleton of erythrocytes; loss of individual components causes immunodeficiency, nephrotic syndrome, deafness and nemaline myopathy. Nucleation and branching are driven by an Arp2/3 complex with WASP-family and WAVE regulatory activators downstream of Rho-family GTPases, while formins elongate unbranched filaments and profilin charges monomers for addition. Opposing activities set the balance: capping proteins and tropomodulins block ends, cofilin and destrin sever and depolymerize filaments under control of slingshot phosphatases and LIM-kinase-linked signals, and gelsolin and thymosin sequester or cut. Together they make the cytoskeleton a rapidly remodelled, signal-responsive structure rather than a static scaffold.

Cells must license each origin of replication exactly once per cycle and must halt fork progression when the genome is damaged; the restraining side of that control is what this pathway describes. Losing it produces re-replication, amplified copy number and stalled or collapsed forks, the kind of genomic instability that seeds cancer. Geminin sequesters CDT1 to block reloading of the replicative helicase onto origins already fired, and an F-box protein of the anaphase-promoting complex pathway limits the licensing factors CDC6 and CDT1 further; a cullin-RING module with elongin B/C and RBX1 targets replisome components for ubiquitin-dependent removal. ATR with the RAD17 clamp loader and the TIMELESS-TIPIN fork protection complex slows replication in response to stress, while telomeric TERF1 and cohesin-associated PDS5A and WAPL restrain replication through repetitive and chromatin-organised regions.

Steroid metabolism covers the making, modification, transport and disposal of all molecules built on the fused four-ring sterol nucleus cholesterol, bile acids, vitamin D metabolites, glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids. It sets membrane composition, supplies signalling hormones that control salt balance, stress responses, reproduction and calcium handling, and provides the detergents that allow dietary fat absorption. Cholesterol is assembled through the mevalonate route by HMGCR, squalene epoxidase and downstream sterol-modifying enzymes, under feedback control by SREBP factors with SCAP and INSIG sensors and by PCSK9 and the LDL receptor at the uptake step. Mitochondrial delivery via STAR feeds side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1, after which cytochromes P450, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and reductases such as SRD5A generate individual hormones, while sulfotransferases and UGT enzymes conjugate them for excretion. Nuclear receptors including NR1H4, NR1H3 and NR3C1 close the regulatory loop. Defects produce congenital adrenal hyperplasia, cholestasis, hypercholesterolaemia and sterol synthesis malformation syndromes.

Bile acids are the detergent end products of cholesterol breakdown, and their synthesis, conjugation, export and feedback control constitute the bile acid metabolic process. It is the body's main route for disposing of cholesterol, it makes dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins absorbable, and its products double as hormones that regulate lipid and glucose handling. Hepatic hydroxylation by CYP7A1 and the alternative CYP27A1 route feeds ring modification and peroxisomal side-chain shortening, after which BAAT amidates the acid with glycine or taurine and canalicular transporters including ABCB11 pump the salts into bile. Nuclear receptors, chiefly the bile acid sensor FXR acting with intestinal FGF19 and its hepatic receptor FGFR4, restrain synthesis when bile acids are plentiful. Defects cause cholestasis, pruritus, fat malabsorption and progressive liver injury, and several steps are pharmacological targets.

C21 steroids — progesterone, the glucocorticoids and the mineralocorticoids — are made and broken down by the reactions collected here, and this chemistry sets circulating cortisol and aldosterone levels, sustains pregnancy, and underlies the adrenal cortex's response to stress and to salt and volume depletion. Cholesterol is delivered to the inner mitochondrial membrane by STAR with TSPO and sterol carriers, and side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1 commits it to steroid synthesis; 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, CYP17A1 and the terminal 11-beta-hydroxylases CYP11B1 and CYP11B2 then generate cortisol and aldosterone, while aldo-keto reductases and 5-alpha/5-beta reductases reduce and inactivate ring A. Pituitary gonadotropins, BMP and WNT ligands and transcriptional regulators tune steroidogenic output. Loss of individual enzymes produces congenital adrenal hyperplasia, aldosterone synthase deficiency or apparent mineralocorticoid excess, with salt wasting, hypertension and disordered sexual development.

Androgen metabolism covers the enzymatic steps that make, interconvert and dispose of C19 steroid hormones such as testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, the signals that drive male sexual differentiation, prostate and hair follicle biology, and muscle and bone maintenance. Synthesis begins with CYP17A1 cleaving the C17-C20 bond of pregnane precursors, followed by 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases that set the balance between weak and potent androgens; HSD17B3 supplies testicular testosterone, while steroid 5alpha-reductases convert testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone. Termination routes include oxidative and reductive inactivation by aldo-keto reductases, hepatic CYP3A4 hydroxylation, glucuronidation, and aromatization to estrogens by CYP19A1, linking androgen and estrogen pools. Loss of 17beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 or 5alpha-reductase 2 causes 46,XY disorders of sex development, and the same enzymes are pharmacological targets in benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer.

Estrogen metabolism sets how much active hormone reaches estrogen receptors in ovary, breast, endometrium, bone, brain and adipose tissue, and it also determines how estrogens are disposed of. Aromatase, encoded by CYP19A1, converts androgens into estrone and estradiol, and 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases interconvert the weak and potent forms, HSD17B1 favouring estradiol synthesis and HSD17B2 its inactivation. Hepatic cytochromes P450, including CYP1A1, CYP1A2, CYP1B1 and CYP3A4, hydroxylate the steroid nucleus, generating catechol estrogens that can be further oxidised to DNA-reactive quinones. Conjugation by sulfotransferases such as SULT1E1 and by the UGT1A and UGT2B glucuronosyltransferases blocks receptor binding and permits excretion. The balance among these steps underlies estrogen-dependent proliferation in breast and endometrial cancer, is the target of aromatase inhibitors, and influences bone density and reproductive function; local synthesis in peripheral tissues supplies hormone after the ovaries cease production.

Glucocorticoid metabolic process covers the making, interconversion and clearance of the C21 steroids that set daily rhythms of glucose production, protein catabolism and immune restraint. It matters because too little cortisol causes adrenal insufficiency and salt wasting while too much drives Cushingoid obesity, hypertension, muscle wasting and immunosuppression. Synthesis begins with cholesterol delivery to the inner mitochondrial membrane by STAR and its side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1, followed by the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial hydroxylations of CYP17A1, CYP21A2 and CYP11B1 that yield cortisol; CYP11B2 diverts the same backbone to aldosterone. Output is driven from above by hypothalamic CRH and pituitary POMC-derived ACTH acting through MC2R, with adrenocortical identity maintained by nuclear receptor transcription factors. In target tissues, HSD11B2 inactivates cortisol to protect mineralocorticoid receptors, SERPINA6 buffers the circulating pool, and NR3C1 transduces the hormonal signal.
