Mineralocorticoid metabolism covers the making and turnover of the C21 steroids, chiefly aldosterone, that the adrenal cortex releases to control sodium retention, potassium excretion and extracellular fluid volume, and therefore blood pressure. The biosynthetic core is adrenal: CYP21A2 hydroxylates precursors on the route from cholesterol-derived pregnenolone, while the closely related mitochondrial enzymes CYP11B1 and CYP11B2 split the pathway toward cortisol and toward aldosterone respectively, with CYP11B2 carrying out the final oxidation steps unique to aldosterone. Output is set by the membrane potential of glomerulosa cells, so channels such as CACNA1H and CLCN2 tune calcium entry and hence steroidogenic gene expression; somatic mutations in these channels and in CYP11B2 drive aldosterone-producing adenomas and primary aldosteronism. Developmental and paracrine signals from BMP and WNT family members, along with endothelin receptor signalling, shape adrenal zonation and responsiveness. Loss of enzyme activity instead causes salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Spermine is the most highly charged of the cellular polyamines, and its metabolic process governs how much of it a cell holds — enough to neutralise and compact nucleic acids, stabilise ribosomes and chromatin, and permit DNA replication and growth, but not so much that it becomes toxic. Flux begins with ornithine decarboxylase, the rate-limiting step that converts ornithine to putrescine, while adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supplies the decarboxylated aminopropyl donor used by spermidine and spermine synthases to build the higher amines. Catabolism runs the other way: spermine oxidase acts directly on spermine, and acetylation followed by peroxisomal polyamine oxidase returns it to spermidine, generating hydrogen peroxide and aldehydes in the process. Because proliferating and tumour cells depend on this supply, the biosynthetic enzymes are long-standing drug targets, and loss of spermine synthase causes an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome.

spermidine metabolic process covers the synthesis, modification and breakdown of spermidine, the polyamine that cells depend on for translation, chromatin compaction, autophagy and proliferation. Ornithine decarboxylase and S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase supply putrescine and the aminopropyl donor, spermidine synthase joins them, and catabolism proceeds through acetylation by spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferase followed by polyamine oxidase, a back-conversion and export route that lets cells rapidly lower polyamine levels when they are in excess. Spermidine is also the sole donor for hypusine formation on eIF5A by deoxyhypusine synthase, linking this pathway directly to the translation of proline-rich proteins. Polyamine pools are tightly autoregulated because both depletion and excess are toxic; sustained flux through ornithine decarboxylase downstream of MYC supports tumour growth, making these enzymes long-standing chemoprevention targets. Related deacetylases act on polyamine-derived substrates and on tubulin.

Spermidine is the polyamine cells depend on for proliferation, and the reactions that make, modify and degrade it keep its concentration within a narrow window. Synthesis starts from ornithine decarboxylation, one of the most tightly regulated steps in metabolism, and requires the decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine made by AMD1 as the aminopropyl donor for spermidine synthase. Catabolism runs through acetylation by spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferases, which both targets the polyamine for export and feeds oxidation by polyamine oxidase, generating hydrogen peroxide. Spermidine also serves as the sole substrate for hypusination of eIF5A by DHPS, linking this metabolic process to translation elongation, autophagy and cell growth; deacetylases of the HDAC6 family contribute a further layer of polyamine-linked regulation. Dysregulated flux through these steps accompanies tumour growth, and dietary spermidine is studied for effects on autophagy and ageing.

Arterial pressure is held within a narrow range by opposing vasoconstrictor and vasodilator influences, renal handling of sodium and water, and neurohumoral reflexes; the genes here span all of those arms. Renin, angiotensinogen, the converting enzymes and angiotensin receptors set the dominant pressor axis, countered by natriuretic peptides and their receptors, kallikreins, adrenomedullin and apelin, and by nitric oxide synthases acting on vascular smooth muscle tone. Endothelins with their receptors drive constriction, while epithelial sodium channel subunits with WNK kinases, SGK1 and uromodulin govern tubular salt reabsorption. Adrenergic, vasopressin, oxytocin, tachykinin and dopamine receptors couple autonomic and endocrine signals to resistance vessels, and steroidogenic enzymes plus HSD11B2 tune mineralocorticoid action. Disruption produces hypertension, salt-wasting or pressure-dependent target organ damage, linking this regulation to stroke, heart failure and renal disease.

Opsonization is the tagging of microbes and other particles with soluble serum proteins so that phagocytes can recognize and engulf them, converting a poorly adherent target into one bound avidly by complement and Fc receptors on neutrophils and macrophages. It is the arm of innate humoral defence that clears encapsulated bacteria, fungi and apoptotic debris, and its failure predisposes to recurrent pyogenic infection and to persistence of uncleared dead cells. The coats themselves come from several families: complement components and the alternative pathway proteins C3, C2, C4, factor B and properdin; the collagenous lectins and ficolins that bind microbial sugars and activate MASP1 and MASP2; and pentraxins such as CRP and PTX3 that recognize altered self and bacterial surfaces. Regulators including C4b-binding protein restrain deposition on host tissue, while surfactant protein A extends the same recognition to the airway lining.

G protein-coupled receptors are the largest family of cell-surface sensors, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and for how long they signal. Tuning matters because unchecked receptor output desensitises tissues or drives disease: the same logic underlies tachyphylaxis to beta-adrenergic drugs, light adaptation in photoreceptors, and dopamine receptor regulation in the brain. Receptor kinases of the GRK family phosphorylate activated receptors so that arrestins can bind, uncoupling them from G proteins and routing them to internalisation; visual arrestin and rhodopsin kinase perform this step in rods and cones. RGS proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis on G alpha subunits to shorten signalling bursts, while phosphodiesterases degrade the cyclic nucleotide second messengers produced downstream. Accessory proteins such as the RAMPs and MRAPs alter receptor trafficking and ligand preference, and ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and palmitoyltransferases control receptor stability and membrane anchoring.

Cells divide only when instructed to, and this collection captures the many inputs that push them to do so — growth factors, cytokines, hormones, morphogens and the intracellular machinery that converts those signals into cell cycle entry. It underlies embryonic growth, tissue repair, immune expansion after antigen challenge, and haematopoiesis, and its inappropriate activation is a hallmark of cancer and hyperplastic disease. Ligand families such as the FGFs, VEGFs, PDGFs, EGF-like factors and interleukins act through receptor tyrosine kinases and cytokine receptors that recruit PI3K–AKT, RAS–MAPK and JAK–STAT modules; these converge on MYC, cyclin D and E2F to license CDK activity and S-phase entry. Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, TGF-beta/BMP and nuclear receptor routes contribute, alongside chromatin remodellers and numerous microRNAs that set proliferative thresholds. Balance against growth arrest is maintained by counterparts such as PTEN, CDKN1A and CDKN1B.

Tissues need brakes on cell division as much as accelerators, and this collection of growth-suppressing activities is what stops, slows or limits expansion of a cell population. It underlies organ size control, wound resolution, terminal differentiation and immune self-restraint; when it fails, hyperplasia and cancer follow. The machinery is broad: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors and the retinoblastoma-p53 axis impose cell cycle arrest, tumour suppressors such as PTEN, NF1, NF2, VHL, STK11 and the Hippo kinases restrain growth-factor and mTOR signalling, and secreted cues including TGF-beta family ligands, BMPs, Wnt antagonists such as the SFRPs, and somatostatin acting through its receptors deliver antiproliferative signals from outside. Antiproliferative RNA-binding and BTG/TOB proteins and many microRNAs damp growth transcripts, while inhibitory immune receptors like CTLA4, PD-L1 and PTPN6 curb lymphocyte clonal expansion.

Insulin binding to its receptor tells cells that nutrients are abundant, and this signalling pathway converts that message into glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, protein translation and suppression of gluconeogenesis. Its blunting is the molecular definition of insulin resistance and underlies type 2 diabetes, while excessive flux through the same wiring drives growth and survival in tumours. The activated receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylates IRS adaptors, which recruit PI3K to generate the lipid signal that activates PDK1 and AKT; downstream, GSK3 is inhibited, FOXO transcription factors are excluded from the nucleus, and mTOR with its S6 kinase targets raises translation. A parallel Ras-RAF-MEK-ERK branch through GRB2 and SHC1 handles mitogenic output. Negative regulators are prominent: protein tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN1, GRB10 and GRB14 adaptors, SOCS proteins, TRIB3 and the insulin-degrading enzyme all damp or terminate the response, and the related IGF1/IGF1R axis shares much of the machinery.

Acetylcholine metabolism covers the making and breaking of the transmitter that drives neuromuscular contraction, autonomic output, and cholinergic modulation of attention and memory. Its supply is rate-limited by choline uptake: a high-affinity sodium-coupled choline transporter feeds choline into the nerve terminal, where choline acetyltransferase joins it to acetyl-CoA, and this enzyme defines cholinergic neurons wherever they occur. Termination of the signal falls to acetylcholinesterase, anchored in the synaptic basal lamina by a collagenous tail subunit whose loss causes congenital myasthenic syndrome with prolonged endplate potentials; butyrylcholinesterase provides broader plasma hydrolysis of esters, including several anaesthetics. The same chemistry is exploited pharmacologically by cholinesterase inhibitors in dementia and myasthenia gravis and is the target of organophosphate poisoning. Non-neural cholinergic signalling, including in epithelia and reproductive tissue, relies on the same enzymes acting in a paracrine fashion.

Where a messenger RNA sits inside a cell determines where its protein appears, and intracellular mRNA localization is the set of activities that move transcripts to a defined site or hold them there. This underlies local translation in neuronal dendrites and axons, the asymmetric protein distributions that polarize cells, and the delivery of transcripts to mitochondria and other organelles; when it fails, synaptic plasticity and myelination suffer. RNA-binding proteins recognize sequence and structure elements in untranslated regions and package transcripts into transport granules, exemplified by the double-stranded RNA-binding Staufen proteins, the Pumilio-family repressor PUM2, and QKI, whose targets include myelin transcripts. Coupling to kinesin motors and adaptors such as KIF5C and BICD1 provides microtubule-based movement, while ZFP36 family proteins link localization to translational silencing and mRNA decay, so transport, storage and turnover are managed together.

Isoprenoid biosynthesis builds the five-carbon building blocks from which cells assemble sterols, prenyl groups, dolichols, ubiquinone side chains and retinoids, so it sits upstream of membrane cholesterol, protein lipidation, N-glycosylation and mitochondrial electron transport all at once. The mevalonate route runs from acetyl-CoA through HMGCS1 and the rate-limiting reductase HMGCR to mevalonate, which MVK, PMVK and MVD convert to isopentenyl pyrophosphate; isomerases and the prenyltransferases FDPS and GGPS1 then extend it to farnesyl and geranylgeranyl diphosphate for sterol synthesis via lanosterol synthase, for coenzyme Q assembly by PDSS1/PDSS2 and COQ2, and for dolichol made by DHDDS and used by the dolichol-phosphate mannose synthase subunits. A parallel arm handles carotenoid cleavage and retinol oxidation by RDH10, RPE65 and aldehyde dehydrogenases to generate retinoic acid and visual chromophore. Loss of individual steps causes periodic fever syndromes, ubiquinone deficiency, glycosylation disorders, muscular dystrophy and retinal degeneration.

Isoprenoid catabolism disposes of isoprene-derived compounds, most visibly the carotenoids and retinoids that the body cannot afford to let accumulate. Its main output in humans is control of retinoic acid concentration: the carotenoid oxygenases cleave dietary β-carotene to retinal centrally or at an eccentric position, while a set of cytochrome P450 enzymes dedicated to retinoic acid hydroxylate it to 4-hydroxy and 4-oxo forms that are cleared. Because retinoic acid is a nuclear receptor ligand that patterns the embryonic axis and drives epithelial differentiation, losing this degradative arm produces excess signalling and developmental malformation, and the same enzymes shape responsiveness to retinoid therapy. Aldo-keto reductases interconvert retinaldehyde and retinol, contributing a further layer of flux control. Related activities act on polyprenyl phosphates, linking the process to the lipid intermediates used in protein glycosylation.

Associative learning is the process by which an animal links a stimulus to the outcome that follows it, the basis of conditioning, and the behavioural readout of synaptic plasticity in hippocampus, amygdala and striatum. Its failure underlies memory deficits in neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease, and many of these genes are mutated in intellectual disability or autism. Glutamate receptors and their scaffolds set the strength of excitatory synapses, with NMDA and AMPA subunits such as GRIN1, GRIN2A and GRIA1 acting alongside SHANK family postsynaptic scaffolds and the synaptic GAP SYNGAP1. Dopaminergic and neuropeptide signalling, through D1-D5 receptors, DARPP-32 and neurotransmitter transporters, supplies the reinforcement and neuromodulatory context, while activity-dependent transcription via CREB1, FOS and SRF converts transient stimulation into lasting change. Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases, CDK5 and MECP2 tune the persistence of that change.</description>

Oocytes and spermatocytes arrest in an extended G2 before the first meiotic division, and the G2-to-metaphase I transition is the switch that ends that arrest and commits the cell to reductional division. In oocytes this is meiotic resumption " germinal vesicle breakdown " and its timing determines whether a fertilizable egg is produced; premature or failed activation contributes to oocyte maturation failure and aneuploid gametes. The core event is activation of the cyclin B–CDK1 complex: B-type cyclin accumulates, the membrane-associated kinase PKMYT1 holds CDK1 inhibited by phosphorylating its ATP-binding and adjacent residues, and CDC25 family phosphatases remove those inhibitory phosphates to trigger the switch. Downstream, kinetochore components such as NDC80 prepare chromosomes for spindle capture, linking the decision to enter meiosis I with the machinery that will segregate homologous chromosomes.

Material taken up at the cell surface or marked for destruction must be delivered from endosomes to lysosomes, and this transport route is how that delivery happens. It sets the lifetime of signalling receptors, clears internalized ligands and damaged membrane, and supplies hydrolases and their cargo to the degradative compartment; when it fails, undegraded material accumulates and lysosomal storage and neurodegenerative phenotypes follow. Maturation depends on the RAB7A switch and its effector RILP, on tethering by HOPS-type complexes containing VPS11, VPS16, VPS18 and VPS39, and on ARL8B with kinesin adaptors and HOOK-family linkers that move vesicles along microtubules. ESCRT-III subunits and the VPS4 ATPases drive cargo sorting into multivesicular bodies, while sorting nexins and receptors such as sortilin and the mannose 6-phosphate receptor recycle or retrieve components. Membrane fusion contributes VAMP7, and LIPA represents the hydrolase payload.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are the one major class of metazoan messages that carry no poly(A) tail, and this pathway covers how they are made, stabilised and destroyed so that histone supply matches DNA synthesis during S phase. Their 3' ends are generated not by polyadenylation but by an endonucleolytic cleavage that leaves a conserved stem-loop, carried out by the U7 snRNP (with LSM10, LSM11 and ZNF473) together with cleavage and polyadenylation factors such as CPSF3, CPSF2 and symplekin borrowed from the canonical machinery. SLBP binds the stem-loop and licenses export and translation. When replication stops or finishes, the same transcripts are oligo-uridylylated by terminal transferases and degraded by ERI1, the exosome and XRN1, with UPF1 and ATM signalling coupling decay to replication stress. Failure to clear them causes histone imbalance, chromatin defects and genome instability.

Determination of adult lifespan covers the genetic inputs that set how long an animal survives after reaching maturity, and the genes gathered here point to genome maintenance, chromatin state, metabolic signalling and lysosomal function as the main levers. DNA repair and damage response components — ATM, TP53, the mismatch repair proteins MSH2 and MSH6, nucleotide excision repair factors, WRN and RAD54 paralogues — link accumulated lesions to senescence and premature ageing syndromes, while SIRT6, SUV39H1 and ZMPSTE24 tie heterochromatin integrity and nuclear lamina processing to the same outcome; loss of ZMPSTE24 or WRN function causes progeroid disease. Endocrine and nutrient-sensing inputs act through leptin, growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor and Klotho, and ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits couple metabolic state to excitability. Lysosomal hydrolase deficiencies and mitochondrial ubiquinone synthesis further connect proteostasis and respiration to longevity and to neurodegeneration.

Adult feeding behavior is the hypothalamic control of when a mature animal eats and how much, translating peripheral energy signals into hunger or satiety and setting long-term body weight. Circulating hormones report nutritional state: leptin from adipose tissue signals repletion, while ghrelin acting through its receptor GHSR signals an empty stomach and drives meal initiation. These converge on arcuate neurons whose orexigenic peptides NPY and AgRP stimulate intake, opposed by anorexigenic CART, with further modulation through the prolactin-releasing peptide receptor and the bombesin-like receptor BRS3, which also influences energy expenditure. A developmental transcription factor and a deubiquitinase contribute to building and tuning the circuits involved. Loss of leptin signalling or of melanocortin-pathway balance produces hyperphagia and early-onset obesity, placing this appetite circuitry at the centre of metabolic disease and of the physiology exploited by anti-obesity drugs.

Coordinated walking, running and posture in the mature animal depends on intact motor circuitry from spinal interneurons up through the basal ganglia, and the genes grouped here under adult locomotory behavior are those whose loss produces ataxia, tremor, spasticity, dystonia or paralysis. Several arms of that circuitry are represented: dopaminergic control of movement initiation and reward, via dopamine receptors, the midbrain identity factors NR4A2, EN1 and FOXA2, and the Parkinson's disease proteins SNCA, PRKN, PARK7 and UCHL1; glycinergic inhibition through the receptor subunits GLRA1 and GLRB, whose failure causes startle disease; myelination and axon guidance; and neuronal excitability set by SCN1A, CACNB4 and KCNJ10. Lysosomal and neurodegenerative genes such as NPC1, HEXA, CSTB, PPT1 and FXN contribute the progressive gait disorders. The set therefore spans circuit development, synaptic transmission and neuronal maintenance, read out as a whole-organism motor phenotype.

Glial cell migration is the directed movement of astrocytes, oligodendrocyte precursors, radial glia and microglia through developing and injured nervous tissue, positioning the cells that myelinate axons, buffer ions, support synapses and clear debris. Without it, myelination fails, cortical layering is disturbed, and microglia cannot reach sites of damage. The genes here combine guidance and chemotactic cues with the cytoskeletal and nuclear machinery that moves a cell body: Reelin signalling through LRP8 and DAB1 and the CDK5/p35 kinase pair control migration and nucleokinesis, LIS1 and LINC-complex proteins (SUN1, SUN2, SYNE2) couple the nucleus to the cytoskeleton, and Eph and Slit-Robo GAP components steer the leading edge. Chemokine axes such as CCL2-CCR2 and CX3CL1-CX3CR1, with TREM2 and purinergic receptors including P2RY12, recruit microglia, while CSPG4, VCAN and MMP14 handle the proteoglycan-rich matrix through which these cells travel.

Germ cells are specified early and far from where the gonad will form, so the lineage that produces eggs and sperm must travel through the embryo to reach the genital ridges; this migration of primordial germ cells is what populates the gonad and sets the size of the future germline. Failure leaves ectopic germ cells that die or, if they survive outside the gonad, can seed extragonadal germ cell tumours, and leaves the gonad depleted, causing infertility. Guidance depends on KIT receptor signalling toward its stem cell factor ligand laid down along the route, integrin-mediated adhesion to extracellular matrix for motility, and TGF-beta signalling through its type I receptor shaping directional movement and survival. Transcriptional regulators including DMRT1 and FOXC1 act in the germ cells and the somatic gonad that receives them, linking migration to sex-specific gonad development.

Asymmetric cell division is how one mother cell produces two daughters with different fates, and it is the basic way a tissue generates diversity rather than more of the same. Stem and progenitor pools depend on it: a neural progenitor that divides symmetrically expands but does not differentiate, so the balance between the two modes sets brain size and the timing of neurogenesis. The machinery works by polarizing the cortex and orienting the spindle relative to it, so that fate determinants segregate unequally. Polarity scaffolds such as PARD3 and the spindle-orientation adaptor INSC couple cortical cues to the mitotic apparatus, actin nucleation by the ARP2/3 subunits ACTR2 and ACTR3 and Rho-pathway regulators remodel the cortex, and ASPM acts at spindle poles. Transcription factors including PAX6, POU5F1 and ZBTB16 then read out the resulting difference as distinct developmental potential. Mutation of these spindle components causes microcephaly.

Cells acquire and maintain their form by continuously remodelling the actin cortex and its attachments to the plasma membrane, and this control of cell shape underlies epithelial apicobasal organisation, erythrocyte deformability, neurite and dendrite morphology, immune cell spreading and migration, and the lumen formation of blood vessels. Much of the machinery here is Rho-family: Rac and atypical Rho GTPases with their FGD-type exchange factors and RhoGAPs such as ARHGAP35, CDC42 effector proteins, and downstream formins, WAVE-complex members and cofilin that set filament nucleation and turnover. Non-muscle myosin II heavy chains generate the contractility, while spectrin, protein 4.1, dematin, ezrin/radixin/moesin and merlin link the network to membrane and junctions, and integrin-associated parvins, kindlin and focal adhesion kinases couple it to extracellular matrix. Semaphorin-plexin and growth factor receptor cues feed in, so shape change becomes the output of guidance and adhesion signalling; its failure produces fragile red cells, disordered morphogenesis and invasive behaviour.

Cells set and defend a characteristic size, balancing growth against osmotic water and ion fluxes, and this regulation determines whether a neuron extends a long axon, whether a muscle or kidney cell hypertrophies, and whether a swollen cell recovers its volume. Two themes dominate here. Growth control runs through mTOR complex 1 and its partners raptor, the LAMTOR subunits, DEPTOR and PRAS40, restrained by the TSC1/PTEN axis and coupled to autophagy initiation via ULK1/2 and RB1CC1, so that biosynthetic capacity matches nutrient supply. Volume regulation runs through cation-chloride cotransporters of the SLC12 family with their WNK-OXSR1/STK39 kinase cascade, volume-sensitive LRRC8 anion channels, aquaporins and stretch-activated TRPV channels. Superimposed on both is cytoskeletal and guidance signalling by semaphorins, netrins, slits, ephrins, Rho GTPase regulators and microtubule-associated proteins that shapes neuronal soma and process size. Loss of this control contributes to cardiac and renal hypertrophy, tumour overgrowth and neurodevelopmental disease.

Most human genes are transcribed as precursors containing introns, and RNA splicing is the reaction that excises those introns and ligates the flanking exons to produce translatable mRNA. Because exons can be included or skipped, this step also multiplies the proteome, generating tissue-specific isoforms that define neurons, muscle and epithelium, and its misregulation underlies spinal muscular atrophy, retinitis pigmentosa and myelodysplastic syndromes carrying SF3B1 or U2AF1 mutations. The machinery is the spliceosome: U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 small nuclear RNAs with their Sm and LSm cores, assembled cytoplasmically by the SMN-gemin complex, together with SF3 branch-point recognition, PRPF8 and the DEAH-box helicases that drive stepwise remodelling. Splice site choice is tuned by SR proteins and hnRNPs and by tissue-restricted regulators such as RBFOX, NOVA, MBNL, PTBP and ESRP, with SRPK and CLK kinases controlling their activity. A minor U12-dependent spliceosome, cap binding, export and nonsense-mediated decay factors link splicing to the wider mRNA lifecycle.

Cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, passes electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen and pumps protons to sustain the membrane potential that drives ATP synthesis; building it requires a large cast of dedicated assembly factors beyond its own subunits. This maturation programme joins mitochondrially encoded core subunits such as the MT-CO3 product with nuclear-encoded partners in a staged, membrane-embedded process. Copper is delivered through soluble chaperones including COX17 and the metallochaperones SCO1 and SCO2, heme a is made and inserted by COX10 and COX11, and factors such as SURF1, COX20, PET100 and the COA proteins stabilise intermediates, while TACO1 acts at the level of mitochondrial translation. Loss of these steps causes isolated complex IV deficiency, presenting as Leigh syndrome, encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy or hepatic failure, and links the pathway to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial gene expression.

Fibroblast growth factors acting on their receptor tyrosine kinases drive limb and skeletal patterning, branching morphogenesis of lung and kidney, wound repair, and stem cell self-renewal; the same axis controls phosphate and bile acid homeostasis through endocrine ligands. Ligand binding to FGFR1-4 requires heparan sulfate, so chain-synthesizing and editing enzymes and the co-receptors Klotho and beta-Klotho set which cells can respond, while secreted binding proteins and decoys tune ligand availability. Activated receptors recruit FRS2, GRB2, SOS1, SHP2 and SHOC2 to fire RAS-ERK output, with Sprouty proteins and microRNAs imposing negative feedback; downstream transcription factors such as RUNX2 translate the signal into osteoblast differentiation. Activating receptor mutations cause achondroplasia and craniosynostosis syndromes, loss of FGF23 signalling causes phosphate-wasting rickets, and receptor amplification is a recurrent oncogenic driver.

Epidermis development covers the formation and maturation of the skin's outer epithelium, from a single-layered surface ectoderm into a stratified, continuously renewing barrier with its appendages. What it produces is a waterproof, mechanically tough surface that excludes microbes and prevents fluid loss; when it fails, the result is ichthyosis, epidermolysis bullosa, atopic or psoriatic inflammation, or ectodermal dysplasia with missing hair and teeth. Basal progenitors held in an undifferentiated state by TP63 commit to terminal differentiation as keratin pairs switch from KRT5/KRT14 to KRT1/KRT10, and cornified envelope precursors such as involucrin, loricrin, filaggrin and the small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases. Ceramide and very-long-chain lipid synthesis supplies the intercellular lipid seal, while desmosomal and basement membrane adhesion anchors the sheet. Wnt, Notch, Hedgehog, BMP, EDAR and FGF signalling, read out by GRHL, KLF4, OVOL and ZNF750 transcription factors, pattern appendages and time each differentiation step; protease-antiprotease balance controls desquamation.

Motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres must build a synapse precisely where they meet, and this regulatory programme sets how much and how fast that neuromuscular junction is assembled. Its output is reliable neuromuscular transmission: nerve-derived agrin acting through the muscle receptor tyrosine kinase MuSK drives clustering of acetylcholine receptors beneath the nerve terminal, while a collagen-tailed subunit anchors acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft so that transmitter is cleared after each impulse. Transcription factors of the SIX family contribute to the muscle differentiation context in which the postsynaptic apparatus forms, and scaffolding and ubiquitin-ligase components tune synaptic protein localisation and terminal growth. Loss of agrin-MuSK signalling, or autoantibodies against it, produces congenital myasthenic syndromes and myasthenia gravis, with fatigable weakness from failed postsynaptic organisation.

Hedgehog ligands act through the receptor Patched and the transducer Smoothened to pattern the embryo and maintain adult stem cell niches, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and how long that signal runs. Tuning matters because too little gives holoprosencephaly, polydactyly and skeletal dysplasias, while sustained activity drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Much of the control is built into the primary cilium: intraflagellar transport subunits, transition zone components and retrograde dynein move Smoothened and GLI proteins in and out, while GPR161 and TULP3 hold the pathway off in the absence of ligand. SUFU and kinesin KIF7 restrain GLI transcription factors, protein kinase A subunits phosphorylate them toward repressor forms, and ubiquitin ligases and KCTD adaptors set their turnover. Secreted antagonists such as HHIP and GAS1, along with PTCH2, adjust ligand availability at the cell surface.

Toll-like receptor signalling has to be turned up and shut off on cue, and this is the layer of control that sets how strongly and how long the pathway fires after microbial ligands are detected. Getting it wrong is costly: too little restraint gives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune activation, too much leaves innate defence blunted. Pellino family E3 ubiquitin ligases act positively within the receptor-proximal complex, ubiquitinating IRAK kinases and shaping downstream NF-kB and interferon output, while SIGIRR is a decoy-type single immunoglobulin receptor that sequesters IRAK and MyD88 components to dampen responses, notably in intestinal epithelium. NLRP12 contributes further negative regulation of inflammatory NF-kB signalling, and mutations in it cause hereditary periodic fever. The overall theme is proportionate innate immune activation and resolution rather than initiation of pathogen sensing itself.

regulation of Notch signaling pathway controls how strongly and how long the Notch receptors signal, tuning a juxtacrine system that decides cell fate between neighbouring cells. Because Notch output sets the balance between progenitor maintenance and differentiation, its regulation shapes neurogenesis, somite segmentation, angiogenesis and arterial-venous specification, T cell development and gut epithelial renewal; loss of restraint drives leukaemia and Alagille- or CADASIL-type vascular disease. Control is exerted at every step: glycosyltransferases such as POFUT1, POGLUT1 and the fringe enzymes modify the receptor to bias ligand preference, ADAM10 with its tetraspanin partners performs the activating cleavage, ligands including DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 and the non-signalling DLK1 set input strength, ubiquitin ligases DTX1, FBXW7 and WWP2 limit receptor lifetime, and HES/HEY repressors plus NRARP close feedback loops. Crosstalk with BMP, WNT, YAP and STAT3 integrates Notch with other fate decisions.

Notch signalling decides cell fate between neighbouring cells, and this collection covers the many ways its output is tuned up or down. Because the pathway has no amplification step, dose matters: small shifts in ligand or receptor availability change whether a progenitor becomes a neuron, an arterial endothelial cell, or a secretory intestinal cell, and misregulation drives T-cell leukaemia, Alagille syndrome, CADASIL and aberrant angiogenesis. Control is exerted at every level. Glycosyltransferases such as POFUT1, POGLUT1 and the fringe enzymes modify receptor EGF repeats to bias ligand preference; tetraspanins and ADAM10 govern the proteolytic release of the intracellular domain; ubiquitin ligases including FBXW7, DTX1 and WWP2 set its lifetime. Downstream, HES and HEY repressors and the feedback inhibitor NRARP shape the transcriptional response, with additional input from BMP, Wnt, Hippo and microRNA regulation.

Photoreceptor cell morphogenesis builds the elaborate architecture that lets a rod or cone capture light: the stacked outer-segment discs, the connecting cilium that links them to the cell body, and the synaptic terminal that passes the signal on. This shaping happens as an immature retinal cell acquires its sensory identity, and it must be maintained for life, since outer segments are continuously renewed. Failure produces inherited retinal degeneration — retinitis pigmentosa, cone-rod dystrophy and the retinal component of ciliopathy syndromes. The genes point to the machinery involved: ciliary trafficking and basal body components such as BBS1, TMEM216 and CFAP418, the photoreceptor-specific cadherin CDHR1 that tethers nascent discs, a calcium-binding protein organizing the ribbon synapse, and a lipid transporter supplying the docosahexaenoic acid that outer-segment membranes are built from.

Rod and cone photoreceptors are among the most elaborately shaped cells in the body, and photoreceptor cell morphogenesis is the process by which an unspecialized retinal cell builds those structures: a stacked outer segment packed with visual pigment, the connecting cilium that supports it, and the specialized synaptic terminal that passes light responses to bipolar cells. The genes here converge on ciliary and membrane architecture, with a BBSome subunit and ciliary transition-zone and cilia-associated proteins governing transport into the outer segment, a photoreceptor-specific cadherin-related adhesion protein maintaining the link between outer segment and cilium, a lysophospholipid transporter supplying the docosahexaenoic acid that outer segment membranes require, and a calcium-binding protein serving the ribbon synapse. Loss of these functions causes retinal degeneration, from cone-rod dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa to syndromic ciliopathies with blindness.

Faithful chromosome segregation depends on every kinetochore capturing microtubules from the correct spindle pole, and this is the biology of making and testing those attachments. Without it cells missegregate chromosomes, producing the aneuploidy and chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. The outer kinetochore provides the load-bearing interface: the MIS12 complex with DSN1, NSL1 and PMF1 links the inner centromere protein CENPC to the NDC80/NUF2/SPC24/SPC25 complex, while the SKA complex and astrin-SKAP stabilise mature end-on binding and CENPE and KIF2C contribute motor and depolymerase activity to error correction. Aurora B within the chromosomal passenger complex, together with INCENP, survivin and borealin, destabilises attachments that lack tension, and unattached kinetochores retain MAD1, BUB3 and the RZZ components to sustain spindle checkpoint signalling until anaphase is safe. Shugoshin and cohesin regulators maintain the centromeric geometry that biorientation requires.

This is the cell's lipid-making capacity taken as a whole: the synthesis of fatty acids, glycerolipids and triglycerides, phospholipids, sphingolipids and glycosphingolipids, cholesterol and its steroid and bile acid derivatives, isoprenoids, ether lipids, eicosanoids and phosphoinositides. It supplies membrane bilayer material for growth and division, energy stores in adipose tissue, the skin permeability barrier, myelin, lung surfactant, lipid second messengers, and the substrates for steroid hormone and prostaglandin production. Committed steps include acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, elongases and desaturases, the mevalonate route through HMG-CoA reductase and squalene epoxidase, serine palmitoyltransferase and the ceramide synthases, and the GPI-anchor and inositol phosphate machinery. Output is set by sterol- and nutrient-responsive transcription factors and kinases such as the SREBPs, liver X and PPAR receptors, AMPK and mTOR complexes. Dysregulation underlies fatty liver, dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis, while loss of individual enzymes causes ichthyosis, leukodystrophy, lipodystrophy and congenital steroid or GPI-anchor deficiencies.

Cells can be instructed to die by their neighbours, and death domain receptors are how that instruction is delivered. Ligands such as FASLG, TNF and TRAIL engage FAS, TNFRSF1A and the TRAIL receptors, which recruit adaptors including FADD and TRADD to nucleate a death-inducing complex that activates caspase-8; cleavage of BID then links the surface signal to mitochondrial permeabilisation by BAX, release of cytochrome c and DIABLO, and the execution phase of apoptosis. This extrinsic route removes virus-infected and damaged cells, allows cytotoxic lymphocytes to kill targets, and enforces immune contraction and tissue turnover. It is held in check by decoy receptors, the caspase-8 pseudosubstrate CFLAR, BCL2-family survival proteins, and the IAPs BIRC2/BIRC3 with TRAF2, whose activity also diverts the same receptors toward NF- cB signalling. Loss of this control contributes to autoimmunity and to tumour resistance to death ligand therapy.

intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to osmotic stress is the route by which a cell that has lost control of its ion and water balance commits to self-destruction from within. It matters because tissues exposed to shifting tonicity — kidney medulla, vascular endothelium, neurons during ischaemia — must eliminate cells whose volume regulation has failed rather than let them lyse and inflame the surrounding tissue. Disturbed intracellular ion homeostasis is sensed and relayed through stress kinase and Rho-GEF scaffolding to the BCL-2 rheostat, where BAD tips the balance toward mitochondrial permeabilisation, cytochrome c release and caspase-3-driven execution. Counterbalancing survival inputs, including erythropoietin receptor signalling and prostaglandin synthesis via COX-2, set the threshold, while ubiquitin-editing and RNA-binding regulators tune how readily the decision is made. It is one input branch of the mitochondrial apoptotic program.

Cells that cannot restore ion and water balance after an osmotic insult commit suicide, and this is the intrinsic route by which that decision is executed. It matters wherever tonicity swings are physiological or pathological — renal medulla, blood volume regulation, ischaemic and inflammatory tissue — because the alternative to controlled death is lytic rupture and inflammation. Disturbed intracellular ion homeostasis is sensed and converted into mitochondrial permeabilisation, with the BH3-only protein BAD tipping the balance toward cytochrome c release and caspase-3-mediated demolition. Counter-signals set the threshold: erythropoietin acts as a survival factor, bradykinin receptor and prostaglandin-synthase signalling couple osmotic and inflammatory cues, and cytoskeletal and ubiquitin-pathway regulators modulate stress kinase output. The outcome is a graded choice between osmoadaptation and elimination of cells whose volume regulation has failed.

Hormones can instruct a target cell to die, and hormone-mediated apoptotic signalling covers the route from receptor engagement by a circulating peptide to commitment to the execution phase of apoptosis. This kind of control shapes tissue turnover in endocrine-responsive organs: parathyroid hormone acting on bone cells influences osteoblast and osteocyte survival, somatostatin acting through its receptors, including SSTR3, restrains proliferation and can drive death in neuroendocrine and tumour cells, and corticotropin-releasing hormone couples stress-axis activation to neuronal and immune cell fate. The common logic is that a receptor at the cell surface, rather than internal damage sensing, supplies the initiating signal, which then converges on the caspase machinery shared with other apoptotic routes. Such hormone-triggered death matters for skeletal remodelling, for involution of hormone-dependent tissues, and for the antiproliferative effects exploited by somatostatin analogue therapy.

When genomic damage is too severe to repair, a cell can choose to kill itself, and this is the route by which that decision is executed from inside the cell. It removes cells carrying mutagenic lesions and so acts as a tumour-suppressive barrier; its loss underlies both oncogenesis and resistance to genotoxic chemotherapy and radiation. Damage sensing through ATM and CHEK2 converges on p53 and its relatives p63 and p73, together with coactivators and modifiers such as EP300, HIPK2, PML and SIRT1, to induce BH3-only proteins including PUMA, NOXA and BIM. These neutralise BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 and license BAX and BAK1 to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane, releasing factors that activate caspase-9 and the executioner cascade. CASP2 provides an alternative damage-responsive initiator, and CDKN1A-mediated arrest competes with the death outcome, so the balance between repair, senescence and apoptosis is set here.

When reactive oxygen species overwhelm a cell's antioxidant defences, oxidative damage is converted into a decision to die through the intrinsic, mitochondrial route of apoptosis. This pathway limits the propagation of cells with damaged DNA, lipids and proteins, and its dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and the survival of tumour cells under redox stress. Sensing arms include antioxidant enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2 and GPX1 and the NFE2L2 transcriptional programme, whose failure allows the signal to proceed; the redox-regulated kinase MAP3K5 relays stress to JNK/p38 branches. Commitment is set at the mitochondrion by the balance of BCL2 and MCL1 against pro-apoptotic activity, with outer membrane permeabilisation releasing DIABLO and the protease HTRA2 to relieve inhibitor-of-apoptosis restraint on caspases. PINK1, PRKN and PARK7 link the same stress to mitochondrial quality control, and survival inputs such as AKT1 and SIRT1 raise the threshold.

Mitochondria are the decision point of the intrinsic death pathway, and the apoptotic changes they undergo — outer membrane permeabilization, loss of membrane potential, cristae remodelling and fragmentation — commit a cell irreversibly to dying. This is how developmental sculpting, removal of damaged cells and chemotherapy-induced killing are executed; too little leaves transformed cells alive, too much drives neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury. The balance is set by the BCL-2 family: BAX, BAK1 and BOK form the pore, BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 restrain them, and BH3-only proteins such as BID, BBC3, PMAIP1 and BCL2L11 relay stress signals including p53-dependent transcription. Fission and fusion machinery (DNM1L, FIS1, OPA1, PARL) reshapes the organelle, adenine nucleotide carriers and PPIF govern permeability transition, and PINK1–PRKN links the same membrane events to mitophagy, so quality control and death share this ground.

carbohydrate transport moves sugars across membranes, the step that lets cells obtain glucose and related hexoses from blood and gut lumen and that sets whole-body glycaemic control. Its failure produces glucose-galactose malabsorption, renal glycosuria, and the insulin resistance underlying type 2 diabetes. Two transporter families carry most of the traffic: facilitative GLUT carriers (SLC2A1-14) that equilibrate glucose down its gradient, and sodium-coupled SGLTs (SLC5A1, SLC5A2) that concentrate sugar against a gradient in intestinal and kidney epithelium, alongside aquaglyceroporins that pass glycerol and sucrose-type SLC45 carriers. Much of the pathway is regulatory rather than structural: insulin acting through INSR, IRS1/2, PI3K and AKT2 triggers exocytosis of GLUT4 storage vesicles via RHOQ, STXBP4 and TBC-associated trafficking factors, while leptin, adiponectin, FGF21, inflammatory cytokines and microRNAs tune transporter abundance in muscle, adipose and liver.

Sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells depend on dedicated carriers to take up glucose, fructose and related solutes and to move them between tissues. Carbohydrate transport of this kind sets blood glucose, fuels the brain and red cells, allows the intestine and kidney to absorb and reclaim dietary sugar, and fails visibly in diabetes and in inherited glucose transporter deficiencies causing seizures or renal glycosuria. Two carrier families dominate: facilitative GLUT-type uniporters that follow the concentration gradient, and sodium-coupled cotransporters that drive uptake against it, the target of modern glycosuric drugs. Much of the remainder is regulation. Insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT triggers translocation of the storage transporter to the plasma membrane of muscle and fat, with Rab and SNARE-associated trafficking proteins executing the step, while leptin, adiponectin, growth hormone and inflammatory cytokines tune sensitivity. Aquaporin channels contribute glycerol and related permeability.

Cells must make many of their own amino acids rather than importing them, and this biosynthetic capacity supplies protein synthesis, one-carbon and nitrogen metabolism, and neurotransmitter pools. The genes here cover the serine route from glycolytic intermediates through PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH, its handoff to glycine and folate-linked one-carbon units via SHMT1/SHMT2 and methionine regeneration by MTR, transsulfuration to cysteine through CBS and CTH, proline synthesis by pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases, asparagine formation by ASNS, and glutamate and glutamine interconversion by GLUD1, GLUL and the glutaminases. Aminotransferases such as GOT1/GOT2 and the branched-chain BCAT enzymes redistribute amino groups, while selenocysteine and D-serine are generated for selenoprotein synthesis and NMDA receptor signalling. Urea cycle enzymes including CPS1, OTC, ASS1 and ASL link arginine synthesis to ammonia disposal, and their loss causes hyperammonaemia; PAH deficiency causes phenylketonuria.

Phospholipid biosynthetic process builds the glycerophospholipids that make up cellular membranes and the signalling lipids derived from them, so it determines membrane identity, organelle shape, and the platforms on which signalling complexes assemble. Its outputs are structural (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylserine, cardiolipin for mitochondrial inner membranes) and regulatory (phosphoinositides that mark compartments for trafficking and autophagy). The genes cover glycerol-3-phosphate acylation and lysophospholipid acyltransferases that set fatty acyl composition, the CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine arms via choline/ethanolamine kinases and phosphotransferases, phosphatidylserine synthesis and decarboxylation, and the kinase-phosphatase pairs, including PI3Ks, PIP5Ks, PTEN and myotubularins, that interconvert phosphoinositide species. A large GPI-anchor branch attaches lipid anchors to surface proteins. Failures cause lipodystrophy, myopathy, neurodegeneration and inherited GPI-anchor deficiencies, and dysregulated phosphoinositide turnover drives oncogenic growth signalling.

Membranes are built from phospholipids, and this biosynthetic programme supplies them: the glycerophospholipids that form every bilayer, the phosphoinositides that mark organelle identity, cardiolipin for mitochondrial cristae, and the GPI anchors that tether proteins to the cell surface. Glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases and acylglycerophosphate acyltransferases build the diacylglycerol backbone, which CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine branches convert to phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while CDP-diacylglycerol synthases feed phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylserine and cardiolipin synthesis. Lysophospholipid acyltransferases remodel acyl chains, and a large set of kinases, phosphatases and inositol phosphate enzymes interconverts phosphoinositides to control vesicle traffic, autophagy and growth signalling. Loss of individual steps causes lipodystrophy, neuropathy, myopathy and, for GPI anchor defects, congenital disorders of glycosylation with seizures and developmental delay. Sterol and sphingolipid enzymes present here reflect coordinated membrane lipid supply.

Cells can rebuild pyrimidine nucleotides from breakdown products rather than paying the energetic cost of making rings from scratch, and pyrimidine-containing compound salvage is that recycling route. It sustains DNA and RNA synthesis in tissues with limited de novo capacity, and it matters clinically because it is the entry route for pyrimidine analogue drugs: kinases and phosphorylases here decide whether cytarabine, gemcitabine or capecitabine become active or are inactivated. Uridine-cytidine kinases phosphorylate salvaged uridine and cytidine to their monophosphates, uridine phosphorylases interconvert uracil and uridine with ribose-1-phosphate, cytidine deaminase converts cytidine to uridine, and a mitochondrial thymidine kinase supplies deoxythymidine monophosphate for mitochondrial DNA replication; loss of that step causes mitochondrial DNA depletion with myopathy. Nucleoside-diphosphate kinase activity completes the conversion to triphosphates feeding nucleic acid metabolism.

Female cells carry two X chromosomes but need only one dose of X-linked gene product, and dosage compensation by X-chromosome inactivation solves this by silencing one X in its entirety early in development. The silenced copy is converted into a compact heterochromatic body that persists through every subsequent cell division, so failures of the process cause aberrant X-linked gene expression and skewed silencing associated with developmental and immune phenotypes. The long noncoding RNA Xist is the organizing agent, and the proteins here are its interpreters: SPEN recruits histone deacetylase activity to strip acetylation from the nascent silent X, Polycomb components including SUZ12 with PCGF3/PCGF5 deposit repressive histone marks, macroH2A variants replace canonical H2A in chromatin, and SMCHD1 enforces the compacted higher-order architecture. RNA-binding proteins and m6A machinery, including METTL3 and YTHDC1, act on Xist itself, while LBR helps tether the inactive X to the nuclear lamina.

The non-oxidative branch of the pentose-phosphate shunt interconverts sugar phosphates so that a cell can balance its need for ribose against its need for glycolytic intermediates. Starting from ribulose 5-phosphate, an epimerase and an isomerase generate xylulose 5-phosphate and ribose 5-phosphate, and transketolase and transaldolase then shuffle two- and three-carbon units to yield fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. Because these steps are reversible, they can also run backwards to make ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis when NADPH is not required, and they feed erythrose 4-phosphate toward aromatic amino acid-related metabolism. Transketolase depends on thiamine, linking this route to thiamine-responsive disease, and transaldolase deficiency causes a congenital multisystem disorder with liver and kidney involvement. Proliferating and tumour cells lean heavily on this branch for ribose supply.

Cells must dismantle their own large molecules as well as build them, and this collection of macromolecule catabolic processes covers the routes by which proteins, RNAs, polysaccharides and glycoconjugates are taken apart. It is how short-lived regulators are cleared on schedule, how damaged or misfolded products are removed, and how nutrients are recovered during starvation; its failure underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and the accumulation of oncogenic proteins. Much of the machinery is ubiquitin-dependent: E1, E2 and cullin-RING or HECT ligases, F-box and BTB substrate adaptors, deubiquitinases, and the 26S proteasome, with the anaphase-promoting complex driving mitotic exit. Parallel arms include ERAD with retrotranslocation through VCP, autophagy and ESCRT-mediated lysosomal delivery, cathepsin and glycosidase hydrolysis, glycogen breakdown, and mRNA decay through deadenylases, decapping, exosome, nonsense-mediated surveillance and microRNA-directed silencing.

Fatty acid catabolism is how cells extract energy from lipid stores, and it becomes the dominant fuel source during fasting, exercise and in tissues such as heart and liver. Activated fatty acids are shuttled into mitochondria by the carnitine palmitoyltransferase system and degraded by successive rounds of beta-oxidation using chain-length-specific acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, hydratase, dehydrogenase and thiolase activities, with electrons passed to the respiratory chain through the electron transfer flavoprotein pair and its dehydrogenase. Very long chain, branched and dicarboxylic substrates are handled first in peroxisomes, which depend on the ABCD transporters, acyl-CoA oxidases, the bifunctional enzyme and peroxisomal import machinery; alpha-oxidation via phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deals with phytanic acid. The whole programme is transcriptionally driven by PPAR nuclear receptors and tuned by insulin signalling and adipokines. Inherited defects cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and peroxisomal leukodystrophies.

Amino acids surplus to protein synthesis are dismantled here, their nitrogen routed to urea and their carbon skeletons fed into the citric acid cycle or ketone body production, which makes amino acid catabolism the link between dietary protein, gluconeogenesis during fasting, and nitrogen disposal. Transaminases such as GOT1/2 and GPT strip amino groups onto glutamate, glutamate dehydrogenase and glutaminase release ammonia, and OTC and ARG1 commit it to urea. Branched-chain degradation runs through BCAT1/2 and the BCKDH complex with its regulatory kinase and phosphatase; phenylalanine and tyrosine flow through PAH, HPD, HGD and FAH; tryptophan proceeds down the kynurenine route via IDO1, TDO2 and KMO toward NAD precursors. Blocks at individual steps cause phenylketonuria, tyrosinemia, maple syrup urine disease, urea cycle defects and glutaric aciduria, with neurological damage from accumulated substrates or ammonia. Several products, including GABA, histamine and nitric oxide, are signalling molecules in their own right.

Metabolism of the glutamine family of amino acids — glutamine, glutamate, proline and arginine — sits at the junction of nitrogen disposal, neurotransmission and biosynthesis, supplying carbon to the TCA cycle through alpha-ketoglutarate and nitrogen to urea. Glutaminase and glutamine synthetase set the glutamine/glutamate balance; glutamate dehydrogenase and the aminotransferases GOT1/GOT2 link it to oxidative metabolism; glutamate decarboxylases make GABA, and glutamate cysteine ligase subunits commit it to glutathione synthesis. Ornithine and arginine handling feeds the urea cycle (CPS1, OTC, ASS1, ASL, ARG1), polyamine production via ornithine decarboxylase, and nitric oxide output by the three NO synthases, while PYCR and PRODH enzymes cycle proline for collagen and redox buffering. Defects cause hyperammonaemia and urea cycle disease, proline and histidine metabolic disorders, and are exploited by tumours dependent on glutamine anaplerosis.

Formation of aspartate and the amino acids derived from it defines this biosynthetic route, which in human cells centres on aspartate itself, asparagine and methionine. Cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases interconvert oxaloacetate and glutamate with aspartate, linking the pathway to the malate-aspartate shuttle, nitrogen handling and nucleotide synthesis, while asparagine synthetase amidates aspartate in an ATP-dependent reaction whose loss causes congenital asparagine synthetase deficiency and whose expression sets sensitivity to asparaginase therapy in leukaemia. Methionine is regenerated rather than made de novo: methylthioadenosine salvage enzymes recycle the thioether carbon skeleton released during polyamine synthesis, and homocysteine is remethylated either by cobalamin- and folate-dependent methionine synthase with its reductase partner, or by betaine-dependent methyltransferases, tying the pathway to one-carbon metabolism and methylation capacity. Collagen lysyl hydroxylases connect lysine chemistry to extracellular matrix maturation.

Serine family amino acid biosynthesis builds L-serine from the glycolytic intermediate 3-phosphoglycerate and converts it onward to glycine, cysteine and selenocysteine. It supplies the one-carbon units that feed folate metabolism, purine and thymidylate synthesis, methylation and glutathione production, which is why proliferating and tumour cells often amplify its entry enzymes. Three sequential steps, a dehydrogenase, an aminotransferase and a phosphatase (PHGDH, PSAT1, PSPH), commit carbon to serine; cytosolic and mitochondrial hydroxymethyltransferases interconvert serine and glycine while loading tetrahydrofolate. Transsulfuration through cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase disposes of homocysteine and yields cysteine, and selenophosphate synthetases with a tRNA-dependent synthase divert serine into selenocysteine for selenoproteins. Peroxisomal and mitochondrial aminotransferases link the route to glyoxylate handling. Loss of function causes serine deficiency syndromes with microcephaly and seizures, homocystinuria, or primary hyperoxaluria.

Aromatic amino acid metabolic process covers the degradation and conversion of phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and histidine, routes that both dispose of dietary amino acids and generate signalling molecules and cofactors. Its failure is the classic cause of inborn errors of metabolism: PAH deficiency gives phenylketonuria, FAH and HGD defects give tyrosinaemia and alkaptonuria, and HAL loss gives histidinaemia, while pigmentation genes such as TYR, DCT and OCA2 tie tyrosine catabolism to melanin synthesis and albinism. Hydroxylation by PAH, TH and TPH requires tetrahydrobiopterin, regenerated by PCBD1 and QDPR, and commits tyrosine and tryptophan instead to catecholamine and serotonin production. The kynurenine branch, opened by IDO1, IDO2 and TDO2 and continued through KMO, KYNU and QPRT, feeds de novo NAD synthesis and shapes immune tolerance. Histidine decarboxylation yields histamine, inactivated by HNMT.

Handling of the ring-bearing amino acids phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and histidine determines whether they are burned for energy or diverted into signalling molecules and cofactors. Phenylalanine hydroxylase, with its tetrahydrobiopterin recycling partners, converts phenylalanine to tyrosine, and the downstream tyrosine catabolic route through HPD, HGD and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase feeds carbon into the TCA cycle; blocks at these steps cause phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria and tyrosinaemia. The same tyrosine pool supplies tyrosinase, DCT and pigment transporters for melanin synthesis in melanocytes, where loss produces albinism, and tyrosine hydroxylase for catecholamine production. Tryptophan is split between serotonin synthesis by TPH1 and TPH2 and the kynurenine pathway run by TDO2, IDO1/2, KMO and KYNU, which generates immunosuppressive metabolites, neuroactive quinolinate, and de novo NAD+. Histidine degradation and histamine formation complete the set.}

Breakdown of amino acids carrying an aromatic ring — phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan and histidine — feeds their carbon into fumarate, acetoacetate and glutamate rather than letting the amino acids and their intermediates accumulate to toxic levels. The tyrosine arm runs from hydroxylation of phenylalanine by PAH, with its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor regenerated in part by QDPR, through HPD, HGD and FAH; loss of these steps gives phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria and hepatorenal tyrosinaemia. Tryptophan is opened by IDO1, IDO2, IL4I1 or TDO2 into the kynurenine route via KMO, KYNU and HAAO toward quinolinate and NAD synthesis, a branch that also dampens T cell responses and shapes tumour immune evasion. Histidine degradation proceeds through HAL, UROC1, AMDHD1 and FTCD, linking to one-carbon folate metabolism, while HDC and HNMT handle decarboxylation to histamine and its inactivation.

Leucine, isoleucine and valine cannot be made by human cells but must still be disposed of, and their catabolism links dietary protein to mitochondrial energy metabolism. Branched-chain amino acid metabolism begins with reversible transamination by cytosolic and mitochondrial aminotransferases, then commits the resulting keto acids to irreversible oxidative decarboxylation by the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, whose activity is set by a kinase that inhibits it and a phosphatase that restores it. Subsequent dehydrogenation, hydration and thiolysis steps feed acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, with biotin-dependent carboxylases handling the leucine and valine branches. Loss of individual steps causes maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric and propionic acidemias and related organic acidurias, with neurological crisis from accumulated keto acids. Elevated circulating branched-chain amino acids also track insulin resistance, and leucine availability is itself a nutrient signal for growth.

Glutamate sits at the hub of nitrogen metabolism, and this biosynthetic route builds it and the amino acids made from it — glutamine, proline and arginine. It matters for ammonia disposal, for collagen synthesis, and for supplying nitrogen donors to nucleotide and polyamine production. Glutamate dehydrogenase and transaminases interconvert glutamate with α-ketoglutarate, linking the pathway directly to the citric acid cycle, while glutamine synthetase and the glutaminases set the balance between glutamine and glutamate that detoxifies ammonia in liver and brain. A dedicated branch reduces glutamate through glutamate-5-semialdehyde, made by ALDH18A1 and reduced by the pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases, to proline; ornithine aminotransferase and the urea cycle enzymes OTC, ASS1 and ASL route the same intermediate toward arginine and citrulline. Defects cause hyperammonaemia, gyrate atrophy of the retina, and cutis laxa with connective tissue fragility.

methionine biosynthetic process covers the reactions that regenerate L-methionine rather than obtain it from the diet, sustaining the supply of S-adenosylmethionine on which all cellular methylation of DNA, histones, phospholipids and small molecules depends. Two routes are represented. Remethylation of homocysteine is carried out either by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase with its reductase partner, drawing methyl groups from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supplied by MTHFR and the folate one-carbon enzymes, or by the betaine-dependent transferases active in liver and kidney. The second route is the methionine salvage cycle, in which MTAP cleaves methylthioadenosine left over from polyamine synthesis and MRI1, ENOPH1, ADI1 and APIP convert the thiomethyl group back into methionine. Loss of these steps causes hyperhomocysteinaemia with vascular and neural tube consequences, and links folate, vitamin B12 and choline status to epigenetic regulation.

Humans cannot synthesise methionine from scratch, so they regenerate it, and the reactions grouped here as methionine biosynthesis are the two routes that do so. Homocysteine is remethylated either by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase, using 5-methyltetrahydrofolate supplied by MTHFR and the folate one-carbon enzymes and kept active by its reductase partner, or by betaine-homocysteine methyltransferases in liver and kidney, which draw a methyl group from betaine instead. In parallel, the methylthioadenosine salvage route recovers methionine from the by-product of polyamine synthesis through MTAP, MRI1, ENOPH1, APIP and ADI1. Together these keep S-adenosylmethionine available for methylation of DNA, histones, phospholipids and small molecules, and prevent homocysteine accumulation; inherited defects cause homocystinuria with neurological and vascular disease, and loss of MTAP is a common feature of tumours.

Cysteine is both a sulfur donor and a potential toxin, so cells degrade surplus cysteine rather than let it accumulate; cysteine catabolism is the route that disposes of it and converts its sulfur into useful products. The dominant step is oxidation of cysteine to cysteinesulfinate by cysteine dioxygenase, an iron enzyme whose abundance in liver rises sharply with dietary sulfur amino acid load. Cysteinesulfinate is then decarboxylated toward hypotaurine and taurine, supplying the taurine needed for bile salt conjugation and osmotic balance, or transaminated to yield pyruvate and sulfite that feeds into sulfate excretion. An alternative branch through cystathionine beta-synthase links the same amino acid to transsulfuration and hydrogen sulfide generation. Loss of control over this flux underlies homocystinuria on one side and the cysteine elevations seen in some neurodegenerative and hepatic disease.

Most secreted and membrane proteins carry sugars, and glycoprotein metabolism covers how those glycans are built, remodelled and finally degraded. It determines protein folding and quality control, cell adhesion, receptor signalling, blood group and selectin-ligand identity, and lysosomal turnover, so its failure produces congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies and the mucopolysaccharidoses. Dolichol-linked precursors assembled by the ALG enzymes are transferred to asparagine by the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, then trimmed by glucosidases and mannosidases while calnexin-cycle sensors and EDEM proteins route misfolded glycoproteins to ER-associated degradation. Golgi branching and capping enzymes add N-acetylglucosamine, galactose, fucose and sialic acid; GALNT enzymes initiate mucin-type O-glycans; POMT and LARGE enzymes O-mannosylate dystroglycan; xylosyl- and galactosyltransferases start proteoglycan chains that sulfotransferases then modify. Nucleotide-sugar synthesis and Golgi transporters supply the donors, and lysosomal glycosidases complete the catabolic arm.

glycoprotein biosynthetic process builds the sugar coats that most secreted and membrane proteins carry, determining whether they fold, exit the ER, reach the right compartment, and are recognised by other cells. It underlies blood group and selectin ligand identity, extracellular matrix assembly, muscle membrane integrity and neural development; its failure produces the congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies from defective dystroglycan O-mannosylation, and lysosomal enzyme mistargeting. The genes cover dolichol-linked precursor synthesis and the oligosaccharyltransferase complex that transfers N-glycans, ER quality control by glucosidases and UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferases, Golgi mannose trimming and branching by mannosidases and MGAT enzymes, and terminal capping by fucosyl-, sialyl- and sulfotransferases. Parallel arms make mucin-type O-glycans through GALNT enzymes, O-fucose and O-glucose on Notch, and proteoglycan chains initiated by xylosyltransferases, all supported by nucleotide-sugar synthesis and Golgi transporters.

Most proteins that reach the cell surface or the extracellular space carry sugars, and this is the machinery that builds them. Glycoprotein biosynthesis determines protein folding and quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, secretion, receptor half-life, cell adhesion and immune recognition; its failure produces the congenital disorders of glycosylation, with multisystem developmental, neurological and coagulation defects, and the dystroglycanopathy muscular dystrophies. Assembly begins with nucleotide- and dolichol-linked sugar donors and the lipid-linked precursor made by the ALG enzymes, which the oligosaccharyltransferase complex (STT3A/STT3B, DDOST, RPN1/2) transfers to asparagine residues; trimming by glucosidases and mannosidases feeds calnexin-cycle folding checks, then Golgi GlcNAc-, galactosyl-, fucosyl- and sialyltransferases elaborate mature branches. Parallel routes install mucin-type O-GalNAc chains, O-mannose on dystroglycan, O-fucose on Notch, proteoglycan xylose linkers with heparan and chondroitin chains, and cytoplasmic O-GlcNAc. Sugar transporters, Golgi structural proteins and ion homeostasis factors keep these compartments competent.

Humans cannot synthesise most vitamins de novo, but they must still convert dietary precursors into the active cofactor or hormone forms that enzymes and receptors actually use, and this activation chemistry is what the vitamin biosynthetic process covers. Cytochrome P450 steps generate 25-hydroxyvitamin D and then the active hormone 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, with CYP24A1 providing the catabolic off-switch; loss of these activities causes rickets or hypercalcaemia. A carotenoid cleavage enzyme releases retinal from beta-carotene, UBIAD1 makes menaquinone-4 for vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, and kinases plus an oxidase convert pyridoxine to pyridoxal 5'-phosphate and riboflavin to FAD precursors. Thiamine reaches cells and mitochondria through dedicated transporters before pyrophosphorylation, and defects there cause thiamine-responsive anaemia and biotin-thiamine-responsive encephalopathy. Inflammatory mediators and transcriptional regulators tune the output, linking cofactor supply to immune and developmental states.

Vitamins must be cleared as well as acquired, and this catabolic branch sets how long each active form persists in a cell. Most of the work is oxidative: cytochrome P450 enzymes hydroxylate retinoic acid (the CYP26 family), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and 25-hydroxyvitamin D (CYP24A1), and tocopherols and phylloquinone (the CYP4F enzymes), committing them to further oxidation and excretion. Because the same substrates are hormones and morphogens, degradation is a patterning and endocrine control, not mere disposal: CYP26 activity shapes retinoid gradients in the developing hindbrain and limb, while the balance between CYP27B1 synthesis and CYP24A1 breakdown, tuned by the phosphaturic hormone FGF23, governs calcium and phosphate homeostasis. Other members handle water-soluble vitamins, including dephosphorylation of pyridoxal phosphate and folate-related turnover. Loss of this clearance causes hypercalcaemia, retinoid toxicity and developmental malformation.

Nucleobase metabolism supplies and disposes of the purine and pyrimidine rings that nucleic acids, energy carriers and many cofactors are built from, balancing de novo synthesis, salvage and degradation against the demands of DNA replication and RNA turnover. Proliferating cells depend on it, which is why several of its enzymes are drug targets: dihydrofolate reductase, thymidylate synthase and dihydroorotate dehydrogenase are blocked by antifolates, fluoropyrimidines and immunosuppressants respectively. The multifunctional enzymes CAD, GART and PAICS carry out the committed steps of pyrimidine and purine ring assembly, while HPRT1 and APRT recover free bases, and adenosine deaminase, xanthine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase route nucleobases toward catabolism. Loss of these activities causes distinct human disease: HPRT1 deficiency produces Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, adenosine deaminase deficiency abolishes lymphocyte development, and defective pyrimidine catabolism underlies severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity. Nutrient signalling through mTOR tunes flux to growth.

Adenine and guanine are half the alphabet of DNA and RNA, and this is the biology that makes them. Cells build purine rings stepwise on a ribose phosphate backbone, starting when an amidophosphoribosyltransferase commits PRPP — itself made by PRPS1 — to the pathway, with multidomain enzymes such as GART and PAICS carrying out several of the ten synthetic steps and GMPS branching the product toward guanine nucleotides. One-carbon units from folate metabolism, supplied via serine hydroxymethyltransferase, feed two of those steps. Running alongside is salvage, in which HPRT1 and APRT recover free bases rather than paying the full biosynthetic cost, while adenosine deaminase routes nucleosides toward degradation. The balance matters clinically: HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with urate overproduction, ADA deficiency destroys lymphocytes and causes severe combined immunodeficiency, and proliferating cells depend on flux here for replication.

Nucleoside metabolism is the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of the ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides — adenosine, guanosine, inosine, cytidine, uridine, thymidine and their deoxy forms — that sit between nucleotide pools and the free bases. It matters because most cells recover far more of their purines and pyrimidines than they synthesise anew, and because balanced deoxynucleoside triphosphate pools determine whether DNA is replicated and repaired accurately. Kinases such as adenosine kinase, thymidine kinase and deoxyguanosine kinase phosphorylate nucleosides back toward nucleotides, while 5'-nucleotidases run the reverse dephosphorylation and phosphorylases including PNP, TYMP and UPP1 cleave the glycosidic bond to release bases and ribose-1-phosphate for recycling. Catabolism continues through deaminases and xanthine dehydrogenase to urate. Loss of these steps causes severe combined immunodeficiency, mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes and gout, and the enzymes are the activating route for many nucleoside analogue drugs.

Nucleotide metabolic process covers the synthesis, salvage, interconversion and breakdown of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, the molecules that supply DNA and RNA precursors, carry cellular energy as ATP, and act as second messengers. Its output sets the pace of proliferation, and its failures cause hyperuricaemia and gout, immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase loss, and mitochondrial DNA depletion when deoxyribonucleotide pools are unbalanced. The genes span de novo synthesis from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPS1, PPAT, CAD, UMPS), salvage kinases and phosphorylases (HPRT1, APRT, DCK, TK2), ribonucleotide reduction, and the nucleotidases and Nudix hydrolases that sanitise damaged nucleotides. Tightly coupled to it are glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway supplying ribose and reducing power, oxidative phosphorylation regenerating ATP, NAD biosynthesis, and cyclases and phosphodiesterases governing cyclic AMP and GMP signalling, with AMPK and mTOR reading nucleotide status.

Nucleotides are the currency of energy transfer, the substrates of DNA and RNA synthesis, and the carriers of intracellular signals, and this broad metabolic programme makes, recycles, interconverts and degrades them. It covers de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis from ribose-phosphate through enzymes such as PPAT, GART, ATIC, CAD, DHODH and UMPS; salvage of bases and nucleosides by HPRT1, APRT, ADK, TK2 and the uridine-cytidine kinases; reduction to deoxyribonucleotides by ribonucleotide reductase; and catabolism via nucleotidases, deaminases and xanthine oxidase to urate. Interlocking with it are glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway supplying PRPP, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthase, NAD biosynthesis, and cyclic nucleotide signalling through adenylate and guanylate cyclases opposed by phosphodiesterases. Balanced pools matter: imbalance drives mutagenesis and replication stress, and inherited defects cause immunodeficiency, gout, anaemia and neurological disease, while these enzymes are long-standing targets of antimetabolite chemotherapy and immunosuppression.

Ribonucleoside metabolic process covers the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of ribose-linked purine and pyrimidine nucleosides, the step that decides whether adenosine, inosine, guanosine and uridine are recycled into nucleotide pools or degraded to waste. It matters because it keeps nucleotide supply cheap for dividing and non-dividing cells alike, and because its failures are classic inborn errors: adenosine deaminase loss causes severe combined immunodeficiency by poisoning lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine, HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and xanthine oxidase activity sets urate output and gout risk. Ecto-5'-nucleotidases and cytosolic counterparts dephosphorylate nucleotides to nucleosides, kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases run the reverse salvage arm, and phosphorylases release the ribose moiety into central carbon metabolism. Extracellular adenosine generated by CD73 also acts as an immunosuppressive signal, linking this metabolism to purinergic receptor signalling and tumour immune evasion.

Ribonucleoside metabolism covers the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of nucleosides built on ribose, and it is how cells recycle adenosine, inosine, guanosine and uridine rather than making purines and pyrimidines from scratch.
