This economy matters most in tissues that cannot afford de novo synthesis: loss of HPRT1 salvage causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with urate overproduction, ADA deficiency poisons lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine metabolites and produces severe combined immunodeficiency, and XDH at the end of purine catabolism sets the uric acid load underlying gout. Kinases such as ADK and DGUOK phosphorylate nucleosides back into the nucleotide pool, while 5'-nucleotidases including NT5C2 and ecto-enzyme NT5E run the reverse step, and phosphorylases PNP, UPP1 and MTAP cleave nucleosides to free bases. The extracellular arm of this chemistry generates adenosine as a signalling molecule that dampens inflammation and modulates vascular tone.

Deoxyribonucleosides sit at the junction between DNA breakdown and DNA synthesis, and their metabolism decides whether a cell can refill its dNTP pools from salvage rather than making everything de novo. This matters most in resting and post-mitotic tissue and in mitochondria, where the enzymes here supply thymidine and purine deoxynucleotides for mitochondrial DNA replication; loss of the mitochondrial thymidine or deoxyguanosine kinases causes mtDNA depletion with myopathy and liver failure. Cytosolic thymidine kinase and thymidylate kinase phosphorylate salvaged nucleosides toward dTTP, while adenosine deaminase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase degrade deoxyadenosine and other deoxyribonucleosides to bases, and xanthine dehydrogenase carries the products to urate. Because deoxyadenosine accumulation is lymphotoxic, deficiency of adenosine deaminase or the phosphorylase produces severe combined immunodeficiency, and these same enzymes activate or inactivate nucleoside analogue drugs.

Nucleoside monophosphate metabolism is the hub where cells make, recycle and dispose of the AMP, GMP, UMP, CMP and dTMP units that feed into DNA and RNA synthesis and into the adenylate energy pool. De novo arms are represented by the glutamine-dependent phosphoribosylamine route through PPAT, GART, PAICS and ATIC to IMP, by CAD, DHODH and UMPS to UMP, and by TYMS with SHMT1 supplying thymidylate; salvage runs through HPRT1, APRT, ADK and the deoxyribonucleoside kinases DCK, TK1, TK2 and DGUOK. Adenylate kinases interconvert mono-, di- and triphosphates, 5'-nucleotidases and deaminases such as ADA, AMPD and PNP direct flux toward catabolism and urate via XDH, and IMPDH and GMPS commit IMP to guanine nucleotides. Losses here cause immunodeficiency, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and orotic aciduria, and the enzymes are the targets of antifolate, thiopurine and nucleoside analogue chemotherapy.

Every round of DNA replication, transcription and nucleotide-dependent metabolism draws on a pool of nucleoside monophosphates, and their biosynthesis is how cells fill that pool. Two routes converge here: de novo synthesis, in which phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate made by PRPS enzymes is elaborated through the ten-step purine pathway (PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS, ATIC) to IMP and through CAD, DHODH and UMPS to UMP; and salvage, in which preformed bases and nucleosides are recycled by HPRT1, APRT, adenosine and deoxynucleoside kinases, and uridine-cytidine kinases. Branch enzymes then commit IMP toward AMP via adenylosuccinate steps or toward GMP via IMPDH and GMPS, while TYMS supplies dTMP. Proliferating lymphocytes and tumours depend on this output, which is why several of these enzymes are antifolate, immunosuppressant and antimetabolite drug targets; inherited defects cause gout, immunodeficiency and neurological disease.

Breaking down nucleoside monophosphates is how cells dispose of surplus nucleotides, recycle bases through salvage, and set the size of intracellular nucleotide pools. It matters because the balance between degradation and salvage determines purine and pyrimidine supply for DNA replication, controls uric acid production, and governs the toxicity and efficacy of nucleoside analogue drugs. Cytosolic and membrane 5'-nucleotidases strip the phosphate to yield nucleosides; the ecto-enzyme among them generates extracellular adenosine, an immunosuppressive signal at adenosine receptors. Phosphorylases and deaminases then cleave or convert the freed nucleosides, with xanthine dehydrogenase carrying purines to urate and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase initiating pyrimidine ring breakdown. Salvage enzymes such as HPRT1 recapture bases rather than waste them. Loss of individual steps causes recognizable disease: adenosine deaminase deficiency destroys lymphocyte development, HPRT1 loss produces Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and DPYD variants underlie severe fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxicity.

Purine nucleoside monophosphate metabolism keeps cells supplied with AMP, IMP and GMP, the immediate precursors of the nucleotides used for DNA and RNA synthesis, energy currency and signalling. Both routes are represented: de novo construction of IMP on a ribose-phosphate backbone by PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS and ATIC, and salvage of free bases and nucleosides through HPRT1, APRT, ADK and PNP. IMP is then committed to adenylate nucleotides via adenylosuccinate synthetase and lyase, or to guanylates via IMPDH and GMPS, while 5'-nucleotidases, deaminases such as ADA and AMPD, and xanthine dehydrogenase drain the pool toward catabolism and urate. Adenylate kinases interconvert mono-, di- and triphosphates to buffer the energy charge. Defects cause severe combined immunodeficiency, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, myopathy and gout, and these enzymes are the targets of antimetabolite and immunosuppressive drugs. Several MAGUK scaffolds with guanylate kinase-like domains are included by homology.

Purine nucleoside monophosphate biosynthesis supplies the AMP, IMP and GMP that cells need for RNA and DNA synthesis, energy currency, and signalling nucleotides, and it operates by two complementary routes. The de novo arm builds the purine ring stepwise on ribose-5-phosphate through a series of multifunctional enzymes, starting with the committed amidotransferase step and running through the formyltransferase and carboxylase-synthetase activities to IMP, which is then branched to AMP by adenylosuccinate synthetase and lyase or to GMP by IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthase. The salvage arm recovers preformed bases and nucleosides using phosphoribosyltransferases and nucleoside kinases, which is how most resting and differentiated cells meet demand cheaply. Loss of HPRT1 salvage causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and deficiencies of adenosine deaminase or the mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase cause immunodeficiency and mitochondrial DNA depletion respectively. Deaminases and nucleotidase-like activities drain the pool, balancing adenylate and guanylate supply.

Breakdown of purine nucleoside monophosphates is how cells dispose of AMP, IMP and GMP and their deoxy forms, either recycling the base back into nucleotide pools or committing it to excretion as uric acid. The route sets the size of the adenylate pool and thus the energy charge, and its failure is clinically loud: loss of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine metabolites, while loss of the salvage enzyme HPRT1 causes hyperuricaemia with the neurological features of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Mechanistically, 5'-nucleotidases in the cytosol and the ecto-enzyme NT5E strip the phosphate, deaminases convert adenylate and guanine derivatives toward inosine and xanthine, purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves the glycosidic bond, and xanthine dehydrogenase performs the terminal oxidations. The extracellular arm also generates adenosine, linking purine catabolism to immunosuppressive signalling in tumours and inflamed tissue.

Cytidine, uridine and thymidine monophosphates are the immediate precursors of RNA and DNA pyrimidines, and the reactions that make, interconvert and degrade them set the size and balance of the cellular pyrimidine pool. The de novo arm builds the ring on carbamoyl phosphate through CAD, DHODH at the inner mitochondrial membrane, and UMPS to yield UMP, while salvage kinases such as UCK1/UCK2 and DCK rephosphorylate nucleosides recovered from turnover, and CMPK1 carries monophosphates onward to the di- and triphosphate level. Opposing these, 5'-nucleotidases, deaminases, phosphorylases and the DPYD-DPYS catabolic route drain the pool. TYMS with SHMT1 supplies dTMP for replication, and DUT keeps dUTP out of DNA. Because these enzymes activate or inactivate fluoropyrimidines and nucleoside analogues, their activity governs proliferation and the response to antimetabolite chemotherapy; inherited deficiencies cause severe drug toxicity and metabolic disease.

Pyrimidine nucleoside monophosphate biosynthetic process builds the UMP, CMP and dTMP units from which RNA and DNA are assembled, supplying the nucleotide pools that proliferating cells draw on during S phase and that lymphocytes expand rapidly on activation. Two routes converge here: de novo synthesis, in which the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the mitochondrial inner-membrane dehydrogenase DHODH and UMPS generate UMP from glutamine and aspartate, and salvage, in which uridine, cytidine and deoxycytidine are rephosphorylated by kinases such as UCK1/2, DCK and CMPK1. Thymidylate is made separately by TYMS using folate one-carbon units provided by SHMT1, linking pyrimidine supply to folate metabolism. Because tumour cells depend heavily on this flux, its enzymes are the targets of fluoropyrimidines, methotrexate, leflunomide and cytarabine, and inherited UMPS or dihydroorotate defects cause orotic aciduria and metabolic disease.

Pyrimidine nucleoside monophosphates are the immediate precursors of the CTP, UTP and dTTP pools used for DNA replication, RNA synthesis, phospholipid head-group activation and protein glycosylation, and this pathway is how cells make them. Two routes converge: de novo synthesis, where the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the inner-membrane flavoenzyme DHODH and the bifunctional UMPS produce UMP from glutamine, bicarbonate and aspartate, and salvage, where nucleoside and base kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases such as UCK1/UCK2, DCK and UPRT recycle uridine, cytidine and deoxycytidine. Thymidylate is generated separately by TYMS with methyl groups supplied through serine hydroxymethyltransferase and folate metabolism. Because proliferating cells depend on this output, the enzymes are classic drug targets inhibited by antifolates and fluoropyrimidines and by DHODH inhibitors used in autoimmune disease, while DCK and CDA determine activation and inactivation of nucleoside analogue chemotherapies. Imbalance distorts nucleotide pools and destabilises the genome.

Breakdown of pyrimidine nucleoside monophosphates dismantles CMP, UMP, dTMP and dUMP back toward free bases, balancing nucleotide pools against salvage and de novo synthesis and preventing distorted dNTP ratios that corrupt DNA replication. The route begins with 5'-nucleotidases that strip the phosphate: cytosolic enzymes acting on pyrimidine monophosphates and a mitochondrial counterpart that protects the organellar dTMP pool. The resulting nucleosides are then cleaved by uridine and thymidine phosphorylases to release uracil or thymine, while cytidine deaminase feeds cytidine into the uridine branch, and the released bases are reduced and ring-opened by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase for disposal. This catabolic capacity has direct clinical weight: it determines clearance of fluoropyrimidine and nucleoside analogue drugs, so dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency causes severe fluorouracil toxicity, and loss of thymidine phosphorylase produces mitochondrial DNA instability from nucleoside imbalance.

Nucleoside diphosphates sit at the junction between energy metabolism and nucleotide supply, and this collection of reactions covers both their generation and their conversion to mono- and triphosphate forms. Adenylate kinases interconvert ATP, ADP and AMP across cytosol and mitochondria, setting the adenylate charge that AMP-activated protein kinase subunits read out as an energy alarm; nucleoside diphosphate kinase and the pyrimidine kinases keep balanced pools of UDP, CDP and dTDP for RNA, DNA and glycoconjugate synthesis. Ribonucleotide reductase subunits reduce ribonucleoside diphosphates to the deoxy forms that replication and repair consume. A large glycolytic contingent -- hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, the PFKFB bifunctional enzymes, GAPDH, enolases and pyruvate kinase -- both consumes and regenerates these nucleotides, while ectonucleotidases hydrolyse extracellular species to shape purinergic signalling. Disturbance impairs erythrocyte and muscle energetics, nucleotide-pool fidelity, and growth control through mTOR and HIF1A.

Nucleoside diphosphates sit one phosphorylation step away from the triphosphates used for RNA and DNA synthesis, and their biosynthesis keeps the nucleotide pool balanced across compartments. The adenylate kinases interconvert AMP, ADP and ATP in cytosol, mitochondrial intermembrane space and matrix, so they also set the adenylate energy charge that AMP-sensing enzymes read. Nucleoside monophosphate kinases specific to each base supply the rest: guanylate kinase for GDP, cytidylate kinases for CDP and its mitochondrial counterpart, and thymidylate kinase for dTDP, the committed step toward dTTP for replication and repair. De novo pyrimidine synthesis feeds the same pool through the multifunctional carbamoyl-phosphate/aspartate transcarbamoylase enzyme, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase at the inner mitochondrial membrane, and UMP synthase. Proliferating and immune cells depend on this flux, which is why dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and thymidylate kinase are drug targets in cancer and autoimmunity.

nucleoside diphosphate catabolic process covers the enzymatic removal of phosphate from nucleoside diphosphates such as ADP, UDP and GDP, a step that both salvages nucleotides and terminates their signalling. Extracellular ADP and UDP are potent agonists of platelet and purinergic receptors, so the ectonucleotidases of the ENTPD/CD39 family, working with CD73, set the balance between pro-thrombotic, pro-inflammatory nucleotide signals and immunosuppressive adenosine; loss of this control drives thrombosis and inflammation, while its excess in tumours blunts T cell responses. Intracellular NUDIX hydrolases perform analogous housekeeping on modified and damaged nucleotides. The bulk of the genes here, however, are glycolytic: hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, PGK, enolases and pyruvate kinase consume and regenerate ADP, together with their insulin, AMPK, mTOR and HIF1A regulators, tying nucleoside diphosphate turnover to cellular energy charge and glucose flux.

Nucleoside diphosphates are consumed as well as made, and this catabolic branch covers their hydrolysis to monophosphates plus inorganic phosphate together with the glycolytic reactions that spend and regenerate ADP. It matters for purinergic signalling at the cell surface, where ectonucleotidases of the ENTPD family and NT5E stepwise degrade extracellular ATP and ADP to adenosine, switching an inflammatory, platelet-activating signal into an immunosuppressive one; loss of this control alters thrombosis, T cell responses and tumour immune evasion. Intracellularly, hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, aldolase, GAPDH, PGK and pyruvate kinase transfer phosphate between nucleotides and sugar intermediates, with NUDT hydrolases clearing diphosphate nucleotides and damaged species. Overlaying this are the regulators that set glycolytic flux to nucleotide supply and demand: AMP-activated protein kinase, mTOR complex components, HIF1A and insulin signalling, linking nucleotide turnover to energy sensing and growth.

Purine nucleoside diphosphate biosynthesis is the step that converts purine monophosphates into diphosphates, supplying the ADP and GDP pools from which triphosphates are regenerated. It links nucleotide salvage and de novo synthesis to energy metabolism, since ADP is the substrate for oxidative phosphorylation and glycolytic ATP production, and GDP feeds G protein cycling, translation, and tubulin dynamics. The adenylate kinase family carries out reversible phosphoryl transfer between ATP and AMP to yield two ADP, with distinct members occupying cytosol, mitochondrial intermembrane space and matrix so that adenylate charge can be sensed and buffered in each compartment; AK4 sits in the matrix and is induced under hypoxia. Guanylate kinase phosphorylates GMP to GDP and is the obligatory activating step for thiopurine and acyclic guanosine analogue prodrugs. Loss of the erythroid or mitochondrial kinases causes haemolytic anaemia and reticular dysgenesis respectively.

Pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphate metabolism sits in the middle of the route from simple precursors to the CDP, UDP and dTDP pools that feed RNA and DNA synthesis, phospholipid head-group activation and sugar nucleotide production. Cells that cannot keep these intermediates flowing cannot replicate their genomes or proliferate, which is why the route is a long-standing target in cancer and autoimmune therapy. De novo synthesis begins with the multifunctional carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase/aspartate transcarbamoylase/dihydroorotase enzyme, passes through mitochondrial dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, which couples pyrimidine ring oxidation to the respiratory chain, and is completed by UMP synthase. Dedicated kinases then set the diphosphate level: CMPK1 phosphorylates UMP and CMP, DTYMK makes dTDP for thymidine triphosphate supply, and the interferon-inducible CMPK2 supports mitochondrial nucleotide needs and antiviral responses. Nucleoside diphosphatases of the ENTPD family drain the pool, balancing synthesis against hydrolysis.

Pyrimidine nucleoside diphosphates are the immediate precursors of the triphosphates used for RNA and DNA synthesis, and their formation keeps replication, transcription, phospholipid head-group activation and protein glycosylation supplied with substrate. Two stages are represented: de novo construction of the pyrimidine ring, in which a multifunctional synthetase generates carbamoyl phosphate and dihydroorotate, a mitochondrial dehydrogenase oxidises dihydroorotate in a step linked to the respiratory chain, and a bifunctional enzyme produces UMP; then phosphorylation of monophosphates by nucleoside monophosphate kinases, with UMP-CMP kinase and thymidylate kinase raising UMP, CMP and dTMP to the diphosphate level. Flux here sets deoxynucleotide pool balance, so deficiency causes nucleotide imbalance and genome instability, and blocking the dehydrogenase step suppresses lymphocyte proliferation. A mitochondrial kinase in this group also contributes antiviral nucleotide signalling.

Nucleoside triphosphate metabolism covers the making, interconversion and breakdown of ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP and their deoxy counterparts, the currency that powers essentially every energy-requiring reaction and supplies the precursors for DNA and RNA synthesis. The genes here span glycolysis from hexokinases and phosphofructokinases through pyruvate kinase, the respiratory chain complexes and the F1Fo ATP synthase that generate most cellular ATP, and kinases that shuttle phosphates between nucleotides, including adenylate kinases and the nucleoside diphosphate kinases. Salvage and sanitation enzymes such as adenosine and deoxyguanosine kinases, thymidylate kinase, dUTPase and the dNTP hydrolases SAMHD1 and DCTPP1 keep nucleotide pools balanced and free of mutagenic species. Sensors including AMP-activated protein kinase and mTOR complex components read nucleotide charge and adjust growth accordingly. Defects cause mitochondrial disease, nucleotide pool imbalance, genome instability and inherited metabolic myopathies.

nucleoside triphosphate biosynthetic process covers the reactions that produce ATP, GTP, CTP, UTP and dTTP, the energy currency and polymerisation substrates on which essentially all cellular work depends. Two arms dominate. One is oxidative phosphorylation: the complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, the mitochondrially encoded ATP synthase subunits and the full F1Fo assembly, together with quality-control and assembly factors such as PINK1, PRKN and TAFAZZIN, which couple respiration to ATP output. The other is nucleotide salvage and interconversion, where adenylate and nucleoside diphosphate kinases, thymidylate kinase, uridine-cytidine kinases, CTP synthetases, IMPDH isoforms and thymidylate synthase raise mono- and diphosphates to the triphosphate level and balance the pools needed for DNA replication and transcription. Loss of the respiratory arm causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy; the nucleotide arm sets proliferative capacity and is a longstanding target of antimetabolite chemotherapy.

Cells must continuously regenerate the triphosphorylated nucleotides that fuel work and supply the substrates for RNA and DNA synthesis, and this is the set of reactions that makes them. The dominant contribution comes from oxidative phosphorylation: complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, and the F1Fo ATP synthase together convert the proton-motive force into ATP, with glycolytic enzymes providing a substrate-level route. Alongside ATP production, kinases interconvert and top up the other triphosphates, including adenylate kinases, nucleoside diphosphate kinases, thymidylate and uridine-cytidine kinases, and the CTP and IMP dehydrogenase enzymes that commit flux toward pyrimidine and purine pools. Mitochondrial quality-control and assembly factors are included because ATP output depends on intact organelles. Loss of these activities produces mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis and neuromuscular failure, while the nucleotide-synthesizing arm is a long-standing target of antiproliferative and immunosuppressive drugs.

Nucleoside triphosphate catabolic process degrades ATP, GTP, dUTP, dCTP and their non-canonical relatives, and its main service is quality control of the nucleotide pool. Cells cannot afford to let dUTP, dITP or oxidised and halogenated triphosphates reach DNA polymerases, so hydrolases such as DUT, ITPA, DCTPP1 and the NUDT sanitising enzymes clear them before incorporation; loss of this surveillance produces uracil-laden or mutagenic DNA. A second arm sets the size of the dNTP supply itself: SAMHD1 depletes dNTPs and thereby restricts retroviral reverse transcription, and its failure causes the interferon-driven Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. Ectonucleotidases including ENPP1 and the ENTPD family act outside the cell, stepping ATP down toward adenosine and so converting a pro-inflammatory purinergic signal into an immunosuppressive one. The same chemistry governs how thiopurine drugs are detoxified, making NUDT15 a pharmacogenetic determinant of chemotherapy toxicity.

Nucleoside triphosphate catabolism removes NTPs and dNTPs from the cell's pools, both to size those pools for accurate DNA replication and to clear damaged or non-canonical nucleotides that would otherwise be incorporated into nucleic acids. Hydrolases here act at different sites: dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase limit uracil and modified cytosine misincorporation, ITPA removes deaminated inosine and xanthosine triphosphates, and NUDT15 and NUDT16 sanitise nucleotide pools, which is why NUDT15 variants cause severe toxicity from thiopurine drugs. SAMHD1 depletes cellular dNTPs and thereby restricts retroviral reverse transcription; its loss causes Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome with chronic interferon activation. Ecto-enzymes of the ENPP and ENTPD families degrade extracellular ATP and related nucleotides, terminating purinergic receptor signalling and generating adenosine, while adenosine deaminase links this catabolism to immune function.

Breakdown of purine nucleoside triphosphates keeps the cell's pool of DNA and RNA precursors balanced and free of damaging or non-canonical species. The hydrolases here act as a sanitation system: ITPA removes inosine and xanthosine triphosphates that would otherwise be misincorporated into nucleic acids, NUDT15 and NUDT16 hydrolyse modified or excess nucleotides including thiopurine-derived metabolites, and SAMHD1 depletes the dNTP pool by cleaving deoxynucleoside triphosphates to nucleoside plus triphosphate, which restrains retroviral reverse transcription and limits accumulation of cytoplasmic nucleic acids. Adenosine deaminase contributes to downstream purine turnover toward inosine and hypoxanthine. The clinical stakes are direct: SAMHD1 loss causes an interferon-driven autoinflammatory encephalopathy, NUDT15 and ITPA variants predict thiopurine toxicity, and adenosine deaminase deficiency abolishes lymphocyte development. Together these reactions link nucleotide quality control to genome stability, innate immune tone and drug metabolism.

Cells need a supply of UTP, CTP, dTTP and dUTP to transcribe RNA, replicate DNA, glycosylate proteins and build membrane lipids, and the metabolism of pyrimidine nucleoside triphosphates is where those pools are made, interconverted and kept in correct proportion. A first committed step by the multifunctional CAD enzyme feeds de novo synthesis, while uridine-cytidine kinases salvage circulating nucleosides; CTP synthetases aminate UTP to CTP, thymidylate synthase and thymidylate kinase supply the dTTP branch, and a family of nucleoside diphosphate kinases performs the final phosphate transfer to the triphosphate level. Housekeeping hydrolases matter as much as the synthetic steps: dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase destroy nucleotides that would otherwise be misincorporated and provoke mutation. Imbalance in these pools stalls replication forks and causes genome instability, and the same enzymes determine the activity of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapeutics.

Cells need UTP, CTP and dTTP in bulk to transcribe RNA, replicate DNA and build membrane lipids and glycoconjugates, and pyrimidine nucleoside triphosphate biosynthesis is the final stretch that supplies them. The route begins either de novo, where the multifunctional CAD enzyme carries out the first committed steps of the pyrimidine ring, or by salvage, where uridine-cytidine kinases phosphorylate recycled nucleosides. Monophosphates are then raised to diphosphates by kinases such as CMPK2 and DTYMK, and a family of nucleoside diphosphate kinases (NME1-NME7 and relatives) completes the transfer to the triphosphate level, while CTP synthases aminate UTP to CTP and thymidylate synthase feeds the deoxythymidine branch. Proliferating cells and activated lymphocytes depend heavily on this output, and it is the target of antimetabolite chemotherapy; CTPS1 loss causes a T and B cell immunodeficiency.

Purine deoxyribonucleotide metabolism sets the supply of dATP and dGTP available for DNA replication and repair, and balances it by degrading the same nucleotides back to bases for salvage or excretion. Salvage kinases such as deoxycytidine kinase and the mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase phosphorylate deoxyadenosine and deoxyguanosine, guanylate kinase and adenylate kinases carry them to diphosphates, while 5'-nucleotidases, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, adenosine deaminase and xanthine dehydrogenase run the catabolic direction toward hypoxanthine and urate. SAMHD1 hydrolyses dNTPs to limit the pool, restraining replication stress and retroviral reverse transcription, and NUDT-family hydrolases sanitize damaged or non-canonical nucleotides before they are incorporated. Because lymphocytes are unusually sensitive to deoxynucleotide imbalance, loss of adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase causes severe immunodeficiency, and these same enzymes determine how nucleoside-analogue and thiopurine drugs are activated or inactivated.

Cells build the deoxyadenosine and deoxyguanosine nucleotides that DNA replication and repair consume, and much of that supply comes from salvaging preformed purine deoxyribonucleosides rather than making them from scratch. Purine deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis of this kind matters most where de novo synthesis is limited: in resting lymphocytes, in post-mitotic tissue, and inside mitochondria, which must maintain their own dNTP pool to replicate mitochondrial DNA. The chemistry is sequential phosphorylation. Deoxycytidine kinase and the mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase carry out the committing first step on deoxynucleosides, adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine, and guanylate and adenylate kinases raise monophosphates to diphosphates for the final step to triphosphate. Loss of the mitochondrial kinase depletes mitochondrial dNTPs and causes hepatocerebral mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome, and the same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs used in cancer and antiviral therapy.

Breakdown of purine deoxyribonucleotides disposes of dAMP, dGMP and their triphosphate forms, keeping deoxynucleotide pools balanced and clearing damaged or non-canonical species that would otherwise be incorporated into DNA. Nucleotidases such as NT5C, NT5C1A and NT5C2 strip the phosphate to give deoxynucleosides, which purine nucleoside phosphorylase and adenosine deaminase convert onward toward hypoxanthine and xanthine, and xanthine dehydrogenase oxidises to uric acid for excretion. SAMHD1 hydrolyses dNTPs directly, limiting the substrate supply available to reverse transcription and to replication, while NUDT-family hydrolases sanitise oxidised and mutagenic nucleotides. Loss of function here has clear clinical consequences: adenosine deaminase deficiency destroys lymphocytes and causes severe combined immunodeficiency, SAMHD1 mutation causes an interferon-driven autoinflammatory disease, and these same enzymes determine the activation and toxicity of thiopurine and nucleoside analogue drugs.

Ribonucleoside monophosphate biosynthetic process builds the immediate precursors of RNA and of the nucleotide cofactors that power metabolism, supplying AMP, GMP, UMP and CMP to dividing cells. Proliferating tissues, lymphocytes above all, depend on it, and its enzymes are long-standing drug targets: inhibition of inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase is used to suppress immune responses, and thiopurines act through the salvage route. Two arms are represented. De novo synthesis starts from ribose-5-phosphate via PRPS-generated PRPP, then proceeds through the multistep purine assembly line (PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS, ATIC, ADSL) or the pyrimidine route through CAD and UMPS. Salvage enzymes such as HPRT1, APRT, ADK and the uridine-cytidine kinases recycle preformed bases and nucleosides far more cheaply, while deaminases and AMP deaminases balance the pools. Loss of individual steps causes gout, immunodeficiency and neurological disease.

Cells need a steady supply of ribonucleoside monophosphates as the immediate precursors of RNA, DNA and the nucleotide cofactors of metabolism, and this biosynthetic process is how they make them. Two routes converge: de novo synthesis builds purine rings stepwise on phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate through the multifunctional enzymes GART, PAICS and ATIC to reach IMP, which is then committed either to AMP via adenylosuccinate synthase and lyase or to GMP via IMPDH and GMP synthase, while CAD and DHODH feed the pyrimidine arm toward UMP. Salvage routes recycle preformed bases and nucleosides through HPRT1, APRT, adenosine kinase and uridine-cytidine kinases, and deaminases with AMP deaminases drain flux back out. Rapidly dividing cells depend heavily on this output, which is why several steps are antimetabolite drug targets; inherited defects cause gout, immunodeficiency and Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

Deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate biosynthesis supplies the immediate precursors of DNA, feeding the dNTP pools that replication and repair draw on; when the supply is unbalanced, cells misincorporate uracil, stall forks, and accumulate mutations, and in mitochondria the result is depletion of mitochondrial DNA. Two routes converge here. Salvage kinases phosphorylate preformed nucleosides — thymidine kinase in the cytosol during S phase and its mitochondrial counterpart, deoxycytidine kinase for purine and pyrimidine deoxynucleosides, deoxyguanosine kinase in mitochondria — while de novo methylation of dUMP by thymidylate synthase, using folate one-carbon units generated by serine hydroxymethyltransferase, produces dTMP. A dUTP pyrophosphatase keeps uracil out of DNA, and deoxycytidylate deaminase routes dCMP toward dUMP. These same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs, and inherited loss of the mitochondrial kinases causes hepatocerebral and myopathic DNA depletion syndromes.

Breakdown of ribonucleoside monophosphates is how cells dispose of, recycle, or re-use nucleotides once they are no longer needed, and it sets the balance between salvage and complete degradation to waste products. Cytosolic and ecto-5'-nucleotidases strip the phosphate to give nucleosides; deaminases acting on adenosine, cytidine, guanine and AMP redirect flux; phosphorylases and uridine phosphorylase then cleave the glycosidic bond, releasing ribose-1-phosphate and a free base that HPRT1 can return to the nucleotide pool or that xanthine dehydrogenase can oxidise to urate. Pyrimidine bases are instead opened by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase. The route matters clinically: adenosine deaminase loss causes severe combined immunodeficiency, HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, DPYD variants underlie fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxicity, and NT5E activity generates extracellular adenosine that dampens immune responses.

Deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate catabolic process dismantles dNMPs back to bases and sugars, and by doing so it sets the size and balance of the deoxynucleotide pools that DNA replication and repair draw upon. Its output matters twice over: it prevents accumulation of imbalanced or damaged nucleotides that would drive mutagenesis, and it feeds salvage and terminal degradation routes that dispose of purine and pyrimidine rings. Cytosolic and mitochondrial 5'-nucleotidases strip the phosphate, phosphorylases and deaminases such as PNP, ADA, TYMP and CDA cleave or convert the resulting nucleosides, and XDH or the dihydropyrimidine enzymes complete breakdown to urate or beta-amino acids. Failure at individual steps produces severe disease -- immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase or PNP loss, mitochondrial DNA depletion from thymidine phosphorylase deficiency -- and these same enzymes govern the activation and clearance of nucleoside analogue chemotherapeutics.

Breakdown of deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates keeps the deoxynucleotide pools that feed DNA replication and repair in balance, disposing of excess or damaged precursors and recycling their bases and sugars. The first committed step is dephosphorylation by 5'-nucleotidases acting in cytosol and mitochondria, including NT5C2 and the mitochondrial NT5M, releasing nucleosides that are then cleaved phosphorolytically by purine nucleoside phosphorylase or thymidine phosphorylase, deaminated by adenosine, cytidine or guanine deaminases, and finally degraded to uric acid by xanthine dehydrogenase or through the pyrimidine catabolic route via dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase. The balance matters clinically: loss of adenosine deaminase or of purine nucleoside phosphorylase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through accumulation of toxic deoxynucleotides in lymphocytes, thymidine phosphorylase deficiency drives mitochondrial DNA instability, and these same enzymes determine activation and clearance of nucleoside analogue chemotherapeutics.

Nucleoside biosynthesis supplies the purine and pyrimidine ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides that feed into nucleotide pools for DNA replication, RNA synthesis and energy metabolism, and much of it runs through salvage rather than building bases from scratch — a cheaper route that proliferating cells, lymphocytes and neurons depend on. Phosphoribosyltransferases such as HPRT1 and APRT recapture free bases, phosphorylases and hydrolases including PNP and MTAP interconvert nucleosides with their bases, and kinases such as ADK, TK1, TK2 and DTYMK return the products to the nucleotide pool; deaminases including ADA and DCTD route flux between purine and pyrimidine species, while a 5'-nucleotidase acting outside the cell releases nucleosides from nucleotides. Loss of these steps has clear clinical consequences: adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, HPRT1 loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and MTAP deletion is a recurrent vulnerability in cancer.

Nucleotide biosynthesis supplies the building blocks for DNA replication, RNA synthesis, the cell's energy currency, redox cofactors and second messengers, so proliferating tissues, immune cells and neurons all depend on it. De novo routes assemble purine and pyrimidine rings from amino acids and one-carbon units through multistep enzymes such as PPAT, GART, ATIC, CAD, DHODH and UMPS, while salvage kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases including HPRT1, APRT, ADK and thymidine kinase recycle preformed bases. Ribonucleotide reductase and thymidylate synthase commit precursors to deoxyribonucleotides, nucleoside diphosphate and adenylate kinases interconvert phosphorylation states, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation complexes regenerate ATP. Related branches build NAD from tryptophan and nicotinamide, and adenylyl and guanylyl cyclases generate cyclic nucleotide signals. Deficiencies cause immunodeficiency, gout, and mitochondrial DNA depletion, and these enzymes are prime chemotherapy targets.

Purine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate metabolism sets the size and balance of the dAMP and dGMP pools that feed DNA replication and repair, and it decides whether a deoxynucleoside is salvaged back into DNA precursors or degraded to uric acid. The salvage arm phosphorylates deoxyadenosine and deoxyguanosine, with cytosolic deoxycytidine kinase and mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase supplying the first phosphate and guanylate kinase raising dGMP to the diphosphate; opposing 5'-nucleotidases dephosphorylate the monophosphates, and adenosine deaminase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase and xanthine dehydrogenase route the freed bases toward catabolism. The balance matters clinically: loss of adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase allows deoxynucleotides to accumulate and kill lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency, while deoxyguanosine kinase deficiency depletes mitochondrial DNA. These same enzymes activate or inactivate nucleoside analogue drugs, making the pathway a determinant of chemotherapy and antiviral response.

Breakdown of purine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphates dismantles dAMP and dGMP and their derivatives, keeping deoxynucleotide pools balanced and feeding bases into salvage or terminal oxidation. This matters because deoxynucleotide imbalance is mutagenic and because accumulation of intermediates is directly toxic to lymphocytes: loss of adenosine deaminase, which deaminates adenosine and deoxyadenosine, causes severe combined immunodeficiency, while purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency produces a T cell-predominant immune defect. The route begins with 5'-nucleotidases, including cytosolic and muscle-type isoforms that dephosphorylate the monophosphate, and a dedicated 2'-deoxynucleoside 5'-monophosphate N-glycosidase that cleaves the base directly from dNMPs. Liberated nucleosides are then phosphorolysed, deaminated by adenosine or guanine deaminase, and the resulting hypoxanthine and guanine either salvaged or oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to urate, linking this catabolism to nitrogen excretion and hyperuricaemia.

Pyrimidine ribonucleoside monophosphate metabolism covers the making, salvaging and breaking down of UMP and CMP, the precursors from which all cellular UTP, CTP and their deoxy counterparts derive, and therefore the nucleotides needed for RNA synthesis, DNA replication, glycosylation via UDP-sugars and phospholipid synthesis via CDP-intermediates. The de novo arm runs through a multifunctional carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase/aspartate transcarbamylase enzyme, a mitochondrial dihydroorotate dehydrogenase that couples the route to the respiratory chain, and a bifunctional UMP synthase that decarboxylates orotidine monophosphate; loss of the latter causes hereditary orotic aciduria. Salvage kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases recover uridine, cytidine and free bases, while nucleotidases and phosphorylases run the reverse direction, and catabolism proceeds through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase. These same enzymes activate or inactivate fluoropyrimidine and cytarabine chemotherapeutics, so their variation governs both drug response and toxicity.

Cells obtain pyrimidine ribonucleoside monophosphates — chiefly UMP and CMP — either by building the ring from scratch or by recycling preformed bases and nucleosides, and both routes converge here. The output feeds RNA synthesis, DNA replication via ribonucleotide reduction, phospholipid and glycosylation chemistry through UDP-sugars and CDP-choline, so proliferating tissues depend heavily on it. De novo synthesis runs through the multifunctional CAD enzyme, the mitochondrial inner-membrane dehydrogenase DHODH that couples orotate formation to the respiratory chain, and the bifunctional UMPS that yields UMP; CMPK1 then phosphorylates UMP and CMP onward. Salvage enzymes such as uridine-cytidine kinases, uracil phosphoribosyltransferase and the phosphorylases and deaminase that interconvert uridine and cytidine species provide the alternative supply. This chemistry is the target of antiproliferative and antiviral drugs, and it activates nucleoside analogue prodrugs; DHODH loss causes Miller syndrome.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate metabolic process governs the supply and turnover of dCMP and dTMP, the immediate precursors of the cytosine and thymine nucleotides that DNA replication and repair consume. Its output sets the size and balance of the deoxynucleotide pool, and imbalance here is directly mutagenic: loss of dUTPase allows uracil misincorporation and futile excision repair, while thymidylate synthase and its serine hydroxymethyltransferase-supplied folate one-carbon units are the target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Deaminases and phosphorylases feed the salvage route by recycling cytidine, uridine and thymidine, and 5'-nucleotidases run the reverse dephosphorylation step that tunes pool levels. Catabolism through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase disposes of excess bases and determines patient tolerance to 5-fluorouracil, linking this metabolism to proliferating tissues, mitochondrial DNA maintenance and drug toxicity.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside monophosphate metabolism governs the supply and turnover of dCMP and dTMP, the immediate precursors of the DNA building blocks dCTP and dTTP. Because DNA replication and repair stall when thymidylate runs short, this chemistry sets both the rate of proliferation and the fidelity of the genome, and it is the target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Thymidylate synthase methylates dUMP to dTMP using folate one-carbon units supplied by serine hydroxymethyltransferase, while dCMP deaminase feeds dCMP into the same node and a dUTP-hydrolysing pyrophosphatase prevents uracil misincorporation. Opposing 5'-nucleotidases and nucleoside phosphorylases dephosphorylate and degrade these monophosphates, and the pyrimidine catabolic enzymes including dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase dispose of the released bases. Loss of these steps causes nucleotide pool imbalance, mitochondrial DNA depletion, and severe toxicity from pyrimidine analogue drugs.

Cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP are the two second messengers that let hormones, neurotransmitters and gases act inside a cell without entering it, and this pathway covers their synthesis and breakdown. Adenylate cyclases, including the bicarbonate-sensitive soluble form required for sperm motility, generate cAMP downstream of G protein-coupled receptors, while soluble guanylate cyclase makes cGMP in response to nitric oxide and membrane-bound receptor guanylate cyclases respond to natriuretic peptides and guanylin-type ligands. Phosphodiesterases set the amplitude and duration of these signals by hydrolysing them, which is why they are drug targets in erectile dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension, heart failure, inflammation and psychiatric disease. Ligands and receptors here link the chemistry to physiology: natriuretic peptides to blood pressure and cardiac load, parathyroid hormone and its related peptide to calcium handling and bone growth, and retinal cyclases to photoreceptor recovery, where mutation causes inherited blindness.

Cells must keep nucleoside diphosphates available as the immediate precursors of the triphosphates used for RNA synthesis, energy transfer and signalling, and this is the step that makes them. Adenylate kinases interconvert ATP, ADP and AMP across cytosol, mitochondrial intermembrane space and matrix, buffering the adenylate pool and acting as a sensor arm of cellular energy charge; loss of the mitochondrial form causes reticular dysgenesis with severe immunodeficiency and deafness. Parallel kinases raise the monophosphates of the other bases to the diphosphate level, with guanylate kinase handling GMP and a UMP-CMP kinase serving the pyrimidines, a step also required to activate many nucleoside analogue drugs. Upstream, the multifunctional CAD enzyme, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and UMP synthase build the pyrimidine ring de novo, feeding this phosphorylation network and linking it to proliferation and nucleotide supply.

Cells convert extracellular signals into intracellular second messengers by synthesising cyclic nucleotides, and this biosynthetic route is where cAMP and cGMP are made. The output sets the tone of hormone and neurotransmitter responses: cAMP produced by the adenylate cyclase family drives protein kinase A signalling in neurons, cardiac myocytes, and secretory epithelia, while cGMP made by soluble and membrane-bound guanylate cyclases mediates nitric oxide-dependent vasodilation, natriuretic peptide signalling, and phototransduction in retinal photoreceptors. Natriuretic peptides acting through their receptor guanylate cyclases link cardiac wall stress to renal sodium handling and blood pressure control, and a related receptor in intestinal epithelium governs fluid secretion. Failure of individual members causes distinct disease: retinal guanylate cyclase mutations underlie inherited blindness, and natriuretic receptor loss disrupts skeletal growth. Upstream, G protein-coupled receptors for peptides and neuropeptides gate how much cyclase activity is engaged.

Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate metabolism supplies and balances the dNTP pool that DNA replication and repair draw on, in both the nucleus and the mitochondrion. Pool size and composition must be held within narrow limits: too little and replication forks stall, mitochondrial DNA is depleted and muscle, liver and brain fail; too much or too skewed and mutation rates rise. The genes here span both directions of flux. Salvage kinases such as DGUOK and GUK1 phosphorylate deoxyribonucleosides and guanine nucleotides toward the triphosphate level, and RRM2B provides the p53-inducible ribonucleotide reductase subunit that makes deoxyribonucleotides in resting and post-mitotic cells. Opposing them, SAMHD1 hydrolyses dNTPs and restrains retroviral reverse transcription, while ITPA, NUDT15 and NUDT16 sanitise the pool by removing non-canonical or damaged nucleotides. ADA and NUDT15 variants shape thiopurine and purine-drug toxicity, and loss of several of these enzymes causes mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes or immune dysregulation.

Ribonucleoside triphosphate catabolism strips phosphates from ATP, GTP and related nucleotides, and it serves two quite different purposes: clearing extracellular nucleotides that act as signals, and cleansing the intracellular nucleotide pool of species that would corrupt nucleic acid synthesis. The ectonucleotidases here are membrane-anchored enzymes that hydrolyse nucleoside triphosphates and diphosphates on the cell surface or in the secretory and lysosomal system, terminating purinergic receptor signalling and setting the balance of ATP against adenosine that shapes platelet activation, vascular tone and immune responses. ITPA works inside the cell, hydrolysing the non-canonical triphosphates ITP and dITP so they are not incorporated into RNA and DNA; its loss causes accumulation of these metabolites and, in severe cases, early-onset encephalopathy, and its variants alter tolerance of thiopurine and ribavirin therapy.

UTP and CTP are the ribonucleoside triphosphates that RNA synthesis, phospholipid head-group activation and protein glycosylation all draw on, and this is the metabolism that makes and interconverts them. Cells obtain them by de novo synthesis, where a single multifunctional enzyme carries out the first steps of the pyrimidine route, and by salvage, where uridine and cytidine kinases phosphorylate recycled nucleosides. CTP synthetases convert UTP to CTP using glutamine, a step that sets the balance between the two bases and is amplified in proliferating cells; nucleoside diphosphate kinases of the NME family transfer phosphate to raise diphosphates to triphosphates in cytosol and mitochondria, while nucleotidases of the ENTPD family hydrolyse them back. Supply here limits lymphocyte proliferation and makes these enzymes targets for antiproliferative and antiviral drugs.

Cells need UTP and CTP not only for RNA synthesis but for phospholipid head-group activation, protein glycosylation and sugar-nucleotide metabolism, and this route supplies them. It combines de novo and salvage inputs: the multifunctional CAD enzyme carries out the first committed steps of pyrimidine ring construction, while uridine-cytidine kinases phosphorylate salvaged nucleosides taken up from the circulation, and a family of nucleoside diphosphate kinases transfers the terminal phosphate to yield the triphosphates. CTP synthetases then aminate UTP to CTP, a step that sets the balance between the two pools and is rate-limiting for lymphocyte proliferation; loss of CTPS1 causes a immunodeficiency with impaired T and B cell expansion. Because rapidly dividing cells depend on this flux, its enzymes are longstanding targets of antimetabolite and antiproliferative drugs.

pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphate metabolic process supplies and balances the dCTP and dTTP pools that DNA replication and repair draw on, and keeps them free of the wrong nucleotides. Its output determines whether a cell can enter and complete S phase; imbalance or contamination of these pools causes misincorporation, replication stress and mutagenesis, which is why the pathway is a target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy. Thymidylate synthase commits folate-derived one-carbon units to dTMP, thymidylate kinase and NME-family phosphotransferases carry it to the triphosphate, and dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase act as sanitising enzymes that destroy dUTP and modified dCTP before polymerases can use them. CMPK2, induced by interferon, links this nucleotide chemistry to innate immune signalling and mitochondrial DNA maintenance. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of nucleotide biosynthesis, genome stability and proliferative control.

Metabolism of pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates supplies and polices the dCTP and dTTP used for DNA replication and repair. Balanced pools matter as much as abundance: excess dUTP leads to uracil misincorporation, and skewed dTTP/dCTP ratios drive mutagenesis and replication stress. Thymidylate synthase generates dTMP from dUMP, thymidylate kinase phosphorylates it onward, and a nucleoside diphosphate kinase completes conversion to the triphosphate, while dUTP pyrophosphatase and a dCTP pyrophosphatase sanitize the pool by hydrolysing dUTP and excess or damaged dCTP back to monophosphates. A mitochondrial cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase contributes to nucleotide supply for mitochondrial DNA and is induced by interferon. These enzymes are classic chemotherapy targets, and inherited defects cause mitochondrial DNA depletion and neurological disease, placing the pathway at the junction of genome stability and nucleotide salvage.

Signals carried by cAMP and cGMP must be terminated as well as generated, and cyclic nucleotide catabolism is the step that does it, hydrolysing the cyclic phosphodiester to the linear 5'-monophosphate and setting how long and how far a second-messenger signal spreads. Because the phosphodiesterases involved differ in substrate preference, affinity and subcellular anchoring, they shape local nucleotide gradients rather than simply lowering whole-cell levels: PDE4 family members and PDE8s act on cAMP, PDE5A and PDE9A on cGMP, and PDE2A on both. This makes them the practical drug targets for smooth muscle relaxation and erectile dysfunction, inflammatory airway disease, and striatal signalling disorders, where PDE10A is enriched. Loss of hydrolytic capacity leaves protein kinase A and G signalling persistently active, degrading the temporal precision on which hormone, neurotransmitter and phototransduction responses depend. A 2',3'-cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase acting on a distinct substrate is included among these activities.

Cells must hold dATP and dGTP at concentrations high enough for DNA replication and repair but low enough to avoid mutagenesis, and this is the metabolism of purine deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates that sets that balance. Salvage kinases build the pools: deoxyguanosine kinase phosphorylates deoxypurine nucleosides inside mitochondria, adenosine kinase and guanylate kinase feed the corresponding nucleotide routes, while adenosine deaminase disposes of deoxyadenosine. Degradative activities work in the opposite direction, with SAMHD1 hydrolysing dNTPs to nucleoside plus triphosphate and NUDT enzymes clearing hydrolysed or damaged nucleotides before they are incorporated. The consequences of failure are well defined: adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency through dATP accumulation in lymphocytes, deoxyguanosine kinase loss depletes mitochondrial DNA, and NUDT15 variants determine thiopurine toxicity. The same pools limit retroviral reverse transcription in non-dividing cells.

Pyrimidine ribonucleotide metabolism supplies the UTP and CTP that cells need for RNA synthesis, phospholipid and glycosyl donor chemistry, and, after reduction, for DNA replication, so its output scales with proliferation and is a long-standing target of antimetabolite chemotherapy. De novo synthesis runs through the multifunctional CAD enzyme and the mitochondrial inner-membrane enzyme DHODH, which couples orotate formation to the respiratory chain, before UMPS completes UMP; CTPS1 and CTPS2 aminate UTP to CTP, and loss of CTPS1 causes a severe T and B cell immunodeficiency. Salvage routes recapture nucleosides and bases through uridine-cytidine kinases, uridine phosphorylases and UPRT, while CDA and the DPYD/DPYS catabolic arm degrade them; DPYD variants determine fluoropyrimidine toxicity. Stepwise phosphorylation by CMPK1 and the NME nucleoside diphosphate kinases, balanced by nucleotidases and ENTPD hydrolases, sets the final nucleotide pool sizes.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotide metabolism supplies and balances the dCTP and dTTP pools that DNA replication and repair draw on, and it disposes of the same nucleotides when they are damaged or in excess. Getting the balance wrong is mutagenic: thymidylate synthase and thymidylate kinase build dTTP with folate-derived one-carbon units from serine hydroxymethyltransferase, while dUTPase and the dCTP pyrophosphatase sanitise the pool by clearing dUTP and non-canonical triphosphates before they are inserted. Deaminases, nucleoside phosphorylases and 5'-nucleotidases run salvage and catabolism through to ring opening by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, whose deficiency causes severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity. The uracil and thymine DNA glycosylases here, including UNG, SMUG1 and TDG, excise misincorporated or deaminated bases and feed them back as free pyrimidines, tying nucleotide supply directly to base excision repair. These enzymes are also the targets and activators of antimetabolite chemotherapy and antiviral nucleoside analogues.

Pyrimidine ribonucleotides are the building blocks of RNA, the precursors of DNA precursors, and the sugar-activating carriers of phospholipid and glycan synthesis, so cells must make and maintain a supply of UMP, UTP and CTP. Two routes converge here: de novo synthesis, in which a multifunctional carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase/aspartate transcarbamoylase/dihydroorotase enzyme initiates the ring, the mitochondrial inner-membrane flavoenzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase oxidises dihydroorotate, and UMP synthase completes UMP; and salvage, in which uridine and cytidine kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases recycle preformed bases and nucleosides. Nucleoside-diphosphate kinases and CTP synthetases then supply the triphosphates. Proliferating lymphocytes depend heavily on this output, which is why dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibition is used as an immunosuppressive and antiproliferative strategy; inherited UMP synthase deficiency causes orotic aciduria, and the salvage kinases activate cytarabine and related nucleoside analogue drugs.

Replicating cells must supply dCTP and dTTP in balanced amounts, and pyrimidine deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis is how those precursors are made and phosphorylated to the triphosphate level used by DNA polymerases. Thymidylate synthase builds dTMP by transferring a one-carbon unit from folate, with cytosolic serine hydroxymethyltransferase regenerating the folate donor; thymidylate kinase and nucleoside diphosphate kinase activity then raise dTMP to dTTP, while dCMP deaminase feeds cytosine nucleotides into the thymidine branch. A pyrophosphatase acting on dUTP keeps uracil out of DNA by preventing its misincorporation. Because pool sizes and ratios govern replication fidelity, imbalance here produces mutagenesis, strand breaks and stalled forks. The route is the target of widely used antimetabolite chemotherapy, and its enzymes also determine how much nucleotide is available for mitochondrial DNA maintenance and for DNA repair synthesis.

Pyrimidine ribonucleotide catabolism dismantles cytidine and uridine nucleotides back to their constituent base, sugar and phosphate, recovering carbon and nitrogen and keeping nucleotide pools balanced rather than letting them skew replication fidelity. Nucleoside diphosphatases and a pyrimidine-preferring 5'-nucleotidase strip phosphates, cytidine deaminase converts cytidine to uridine, and uridine phosphorylases cleave the nucleoside to release uracil, which dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase then reduce and ring-open toward beta-alanine and ammonia. This route matters clinically because it is the same machinery that clears fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics: loss-of-function variants in dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase cause severe, sometimes fatal 5-fluorouracil toxicity, while deaminase and phosphorylase activity govern the activation and inactivation of cytarabine and capecitabine. Inherited defects further downstream produce neurological disease with accumulation of dihydropyrimidines, linking the pathway to both drug metabolism and beta-alanine supply.

Nucleotide-sugar metabolic process builds the activated sugar donors -- UDP-, GDP- and CMP-linked monosaccharides -- that every glycosyltransferase in the cell depends on, and so sets the supply line for N- and O-glycosylation, proteoglycan and glycolipid synthesis, and glycogen metabolism. Interrupting it causes congenital disorders of glycosylation: defects in phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase produce multisystem disease and dystroglycanopathy, while loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase underlies galactosemia. The genes trace the individual branches -- the hexosamine route through glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase and PGM3 to UDP-GlcNAc, GDP-fucose synthesis by GMDS and its salvage counterpart, sialic acid production via GNE, NANS and CMAS, and UDP-glucuronate and UDP-xylose generation for glycosaminoglycan chains. Dedicated transporters then move these donors into the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum lumen, coupling nutrient flux from glucose to the glycan code displayed on cell surfaces.

Every glycan a cell makes is built from activated sugar donors, and nucleotide-sugar metabolism is the set of reactions that produces, interconverts and delivers them. It supplies UDP-GlcNAc, UDP-Gal, UDP-GlcA, UDP-xylose, GDP-mannose, GDP-fucose and CMP-sialic acid for N- and O-glycosylation, proteoglycan and glycolipid synthesis, so its output determines the composition of the cell surface and secreted proteins. Hexosamine entry is controlled by glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminase (GFPT1/2) and continued through GNPNAT1, PGM3 and UAP1; parallel branches run through phosphomannomutase PMM2 and GMPPA/GMPPB to mannose and fucose donors, while CMAS activates sialic acid for transfer. Dedicated transporters such as SLC35A3 and SLC35C1 move donors into the Golgi lumen. Defects in these steps cause congenital disorders of glycosylation and congenital myasthenic syndromes, and blocked galactose handling through GALT underlies galactosemia; flux here also links nutrient supply to glycan-based signalling.

Glycosylation depends on a supply of activated sugar donors, and nucleotide-sugar biosynthesis is how cells make them. These pathways convert glucose and salvaged monosaccharides into UDP-GlcNAc, GDP-mannose, GDP-fucose, CMP-sialic acid, UDP-glucuronic acid and UDP-xylose, the donors used by glycosyltransferases in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi to build N- and O-glycans, glycolipids, proteoglycans and the hexosamine-dependent O-GlcNAc modification. Dedicated branches handle each sugar: glutamine-fructose-6-phosphate transaminases open the hexosamine route toward UDP-GlcNAc, phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase feed mannose and fucose donors, and sialic acid synthesis proceeds through NANS and CMAS before nuclear activation. Because the donors and their Golgi transport are shared by all glycoconjugates, defects here cause congenital disorders of glycosylation and muscular dystrophies, as seen with PMM2, GMPPB and the GDP-fucose transporter. Flux through these routes also links nutrient availability to cell surface glycan composition.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) is useless to a cell until it is phosphorylated, and this route converts the imported vitamin into thiamine diphosphate, the cofactor required by pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase. Without it, oxidative decarboxylation stalls, lactate accumulates and the pentose phosphate pathway loses its non-oxidative arm, which is why deficiency strikes brain and heart hardest. Dedicated carriers bring thiamine across the plasma membrane, thiamine pyrophosphokinase adds the diphosphate group, and a mitochondrial carrier delivers the finished cofactor to the matrix where the ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes work; a further phosphatase activity sets the balance with the triphosphate form. Loss-of-function mutations in these steps cause thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia, biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease and Amish microcephaly, disorders that link vitamin handling directly to central energy metabolism.

Vitamin K2, or menaquinone, is the form of vitamin K supplied largely by intestinal bacteria and by conversion within our own tissues, and its handling determines how much active cofactor is available for the gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein. Two opposing activities are represented. UBIAD1 is the prenyltransferase that builds menaquinone-4 from menadione and geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, the step that lets extrahepatic tissues make their own vitamin K2; loss of its function causes Schnyder corneal dystrophy and it also participates in the sterol-sensing control of HMG-CoA reductase degradation. The CYP4F enzymes, including CYP4F2, omega-hydroxylate the isoprenoid side chain and so initiate catabolism, setting vitamin K turnover and contributing to variation in warfarin dose requirement. Together they place menaquinone metabolism at the junction of coagulation, bone mineralisation and vascular calcification.

Vitamin B12 cannot be made by human cells, so it must be captured from food, ferried across membranes, stripped of its upper ligand and converted into the two cofactor forms the body actually uses; this is the cobalamin metabolic process. Its output supports methionine synthase in the cytosol, which remethylates homocysteine and sustains folate cycling and methylation, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in mitochondria, which lets propionate from odd-chain fatty acids and branched-chain amino acids enter the citric acid cycle. Cubilin with amnionless mediates receptor-mediated uptake in ileum and kidney, a lysosomal transporter releases cobalamin to the cytosol, and dedicated processing and chaperone proteins handle decyanation, adenosylcobalamin synthesis and cofactor delivery. Inherited defects at each step produce methylmalonic acidaemia, homocystinuria or both, with failure to thrive, neurological damage and megaloblastic anaemia.

Isopentenyl diphosphate is the five-carbon building block from which every isoprenoid is made, and its biosynthesis in humans runs through the mevalonate route. Output from this segment feeds cholesterol and steroid hormone synthesis, dolichol for protein glycosylation, ubiquinone for respiration, heme A, and the farnesyl and geranylgeranyl groups that anchor Ras-family GTPases to membranes, so the flux set here constrains membrane biogenesis and signalling alike. Acetyl-CoA is condensed by HMG-CoA synthase and reduced by HMG-CoA reductase, the sterol-regulated, statin-inhibited committed step; mevalonate is then phosphorylated twice and decarboxylated by mevalonate kinase, phosphomevalonate kinase and diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase, and isopentenyl-diphosphate isomerases interconvert the product with its dimethylallyl isomer to supply chain elongation. Mevalonate kinase deficiency causes periodic fever with hyperimmunoglobulinemia D, illustrating how impaired prenylation drives inflammasome activation.

Attaching sugars to lipids builds the glycolipid classes that decorate the outer face of the plasma membrane, and this biosynthetic programme covers both major routes. One branch makes sphingolipid-based glycolipids: serine palmitoyltransferase and ceramide synthases supply the ceramide backbone, glucosylceramide and galactosylceramide synthases add the first sugar, and successive galactosyl-, GalNAc-, fucosyl-, sulfo- and sialyltransferases elaborate the globo-, lacto- and ganglioside series, including the polysialylated structures made by ST8SIA enzymes. The other branch assembles glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors through the PIG and PGAP enzymes, which build the glycan on phosphatidylinositol, transfer it onto nascent proteins and remodel its lipid tails. The products define blood group and tumour-associated antigens, myelin and neuronal membrane composition, and lipid raft organisation; loss of individual steps causes GPI-anchor deficiency syndromes, leukodystrophy and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

Protein lipoylation attaches lipoic acid to specific lysine residues on the handful of mitochondrial enzymes that require it, and without this modification oxidative metabolism of pyruvate, branched-chain ketoacids and glycine collapses. The recipients are the E2 subunits of the pyruvate, alpha-ketoglutarate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes plus the H protein of the glycine cleavage system, so the pathway sits directly upstream of entry into the citric acid cycle and of one-carbon metabolism. An octanoyl chain is transferred from the mitochondrial acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1 by LIPT2, sulfurated by the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS using its own iron-sulfur clusters, and finally transferred to target apoproteins by LIPT1; BOLA3 supports cluster handling. Because of this dependence, defects in these steps or in iron-sulfur cluster supply cause lipoic acid synthesis disorders with lactic acidosis, hyperglycinaemia and severe infantile neurological disease.

Four mitochondrial enzyme systems — pyruvate dehydrogenase, 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and the glycine cleavage system — are inert unless a lipoyl group is covalently attached to a specific lysine on their carrier subunits, and protein lipoylation is the route by which that cofactor is installed. Without it, pyruvate and branched-chain amino acids cannot enter oxidative metabolism and glycine accumulates, producing the lethal infantile lactic acidosis and hyperglycinemia of lipoic acid synthesis defects. The octanoyl precursor is delivered from the mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis machinery via the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1, transferred to the substrate lysine by LIPT2 and LIPT1, and converted to lipoate by the radical SAM enzyme LIAS, which depends on iron–sulfur clusters supplied with help from BOLA3. The pathway therefore links fatty acid synthesis, cluster assembly and central carbon oxidation.

In humans the glucan that matters is glycogen, and this is the biosynthetic route that stores dietary glucose as branched polymer in liver and muscle so that blood sugar can be defended between meals and working muscle can draw on local fuel. Glucose is phosphorylated by hexokinases including glucokinase, activated as UDP-glucose by UGP2, primed on glycogenin, elongated by glycogen synthase in liver or muscle isoforms, and branched by GBE1. Control is largely hormonal: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT relieves GSK3-mediated inhibition of glycogen synthase, while a family of PPP1R3 targeting subunits directs protein phosphatase 1 onto the granule. Circadian and energy-sensing inputs tune the flux. Loss of the laforin and malin quality-control pair yields poorly branched, insoluble polyglucosan and progressive myoclonic epilepsy, and other component defects cause glycogen storage diseases.

10-formyltetrahydrofolate is the one-carbon donor used for purine ring synthesis and for formylation of mitochondrial initiator tRNA, and this set of reactions determines how much of it a cell holds. Interconversion with other folate forms runs through the trifunctional cytosolic enzyme MTHFD1 and its mitochondrial counterparts MTHFD1L and MTHFD2L, which link formate exchange between compartments to the methylenetetrahydrofolate pool feeding thymidylate and methionine synthesis. Disposal is equally deliberate: the 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases ALDH1L1 and ALDH1L2 oxidise the formyl group to CO2, regenerating tetrahydrofolate and acting as a brake on nucleotide biosynthesis; loss of ALDH1L1 is common in tumours. Because folate-dependent one-carbon flux supports DNA replication and mitochondrial translation, disturbance here affects proliferation, neural tube closure and antifolate drug response.

Nucleotides are not only building blocks but a currency that must be spent, recycled and disposed of, and ribonucleotide catabolism covers the breakdown of ribose-containing nucleotides back to nucleosides, free bases and ultimately excretable end products. It sustains purine and pyrimidine salvage, sets the size of nucleotide pools available for RNA synthesis and signalling, and clears cyclic and triphosphate species once their message is delivered. Ecto-nucleotidases and 5'-nucleotidases strip phosphates from extracellular and cytosolic nucleotides, generating adenosine that damps inflammation through purinergic signalling; a family of cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases terminates cAMP and cGMP signals; adenosine deaminase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase and xanthine dehydrogenase carry purines toward uric acid, while HPRT1 returns bases to the pool. Because ATP turnover is set by glycolysis and by AMPK and mTOR-dependent energy sensing, glycolytic enzymes and these kinases appear alongside. Loss of individual steps causes immunodeficiency, gout, and hyperuricaemia.

deoxyribonucleotide metabolic process supplies and polices the dNTP pool that DNA replication and repair draw on, keeping the four precursors balanced in the right amounts at the right time. Too little limits replication fork progression; too much or too skewed a pool drives mutagenesis, and loss of individual enzymes causes mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes, immunodeficiency, or the interferon-driven autoinflammation of Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. De novo synthesis runs through ribonucleotide reductase and thymidylate synthase with folate-linked one-carbon input, while salvage kinases such as DCK, DGUOK and TK-type activities recycle deoxyribonucleosides, notably in mitochondria. Opposing them are catabolic and sanitising enzymes -- nucleotidases, deaminases, phosphorylases, SAMHD1 and NUDT hydrolases -- that degrade excess or damaged nucleotides. The associated uracil and oxidised-base glycosylases connect pool quality to base excision repair. These enzymes also determine the activation and toxicity of nucleoside analogue chemotherapies and antivirals.

Supplying DNA replication and repair with balanced pools of the four dNTPs is the job of deoxyribonucleotide metabolism, and the size and proportion of those pools sets both the speed and the fidelity of genome duplication. Ribonucleotide reductase subunits convert ribonucleotides to their deoxy forms, thymidylate synthase and thymidylate kinase build the thymidine arm, and deoxyribonucleoside and nucleoside monophosphate kinases salvage bases from turnover. Countervailing activities keep pools in check and remove hazardous species: 5'-nucleotidases and deaminases degrade nucleotides, SAMHD1 hydrolyses dNTPs, dUTPase and pyrophosphohydrolases clear dUTP and oxidised or modified precursors, and DNA glycosylases excise the mispaired or damaged bases that escape. Imbalance here drives mutagenesis and replication stress; inherited defects cause mitochondrial DNA depletion and immunodeficiency, and these enzymes determine the activation and toxicity of nucleoside analogue and antifolate chemotherapy.

DNA replication and repair consume deoxyribonucleotides, and their biosynthesis is how cells supply balanced dNTP pools at the right time. The committed step is reduction of ribonucleotides at the ribonucleotide reductase complex, whose large subunit pairs with a proliferation-associated small subunit or with a p53-inducible partner that serves resting and post-mitotic cells, including mitochondria; loss of the latter depletes mitochondrial DNA. Thymidylate is made by thymidylate synthase using one-carbon units from serine hydroxymethyltransferase, the route targeted by fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy, while a pyrophosphatase removes dUTP to keep uracil out of DNA. Salvage kinases acting on deoxycytidine and deoxyguanosine recover nucleosides and activate nucleoside analogue drugs, and successive phosphorylation by nucleoside monophosphate and diphosphate kinases yields the triphosphates. Imbalance here causes replication stress, mutagenesis and mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes.

Deoxyribonucleotide catabolism disposes of DNA precursors and their damaged or excess forms, keeping the dNTP pool balanced and free of building blocks that would be miscoded into DNA. Nucleotidases such as NT5C, NT5C2 and NT5M strip phosphates, phosphorylases and deaminases including PNP, ADA, CDA and TYMP break the resulting nucleosides down to bases and sugars, and pyrimidine ring degradation through DPYD and DPYS feeds the carbon skeletons onward while xanthine oxidase completes purine disposal to urate. A house-cleaning arm removes hazardous species: DUT and DCTPP1 hydrolyse dUTP and dCTP analogues, SAMHD1 drains dNTPs and restrains retroviral replication and innate immune activation, and NUDT enzymes sanitise oxidised or drug-derived nucleotides. Glycosylases such as UNG, OGG1, TDG and NEIL1 excise the damaged bases that enter this route from DNA. Loss of individual steps causes immunodeficiency, gout, thiopurine toxicity or interferonopathy.

Cells and whole organisms must sense temperature and react to it, and the response to temperature stimulus gathers the sensing, signalling and protective arms of that reaction. Three themes dominate. Thermosensation runs through TRP channels such as TRPV1, TRPM8 and TRPA1 together with sensory sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A, which convert heat and cold into nociceptive and thermoregulatory firing; loss of these components produces insensitivity to painful heat. Heat shock signalling through HSF1 drives HSPA1A, HSP90, small chaperones such as HSPB1 and CRYAB, and a large DNAJ co-chaperone family, refolding and triaging proteins destabilised by heat, with translational arrest imposed by eIF2 dB1 phosphorylation. Adaptive thermogenesis supplies the effector side, with beta-adrenergic receptors, uncoupling proteins UCP1-UCP3, CIDEA and fatty acid oxidation enzymes generating heat in brown and beige adipose tissue. Cold-inducible CIRBP and cold-shock regulation round out the response.

cellular response to starvation is how a cell detects that nutrients have run short and rewires itself to survive until they return. It preserves viability during fasting, ischaemia and amino acid limitation, and its failure underlies both neurodegeneration from defective autophagy and the unchecked growth signalling seen in tumours. Two sensors dominate: mTORC1 with its Rag GTPases, GATOR/KICSTOR regulators, sestrins and amino acid detectors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR, and AMPK, which reads falling energy charge. Their inactivation and activation converge on autophagy initiation through ULK-BECN1-PIK3C3 complexes, ATG conjugation and LC3/GABARAP lipidation, then autophagosome-lysosome fusion via STX17 and VAMP8. In parallel, GCN2-eIF2α-ATF4 and the ER stress arm reprogramme translation, TFEB drives lysosomal biogenesis, and FOXO, PPARA, p53 and SREBP outputs shift metabolism toward catabolism, gluconeogenesis and lipid droplet turnover.

When nutrients run short, cells stop building and start recycling, and this starvation response is the switch that makes that happen. It preserves viability through fasting and ischaemia, supports amino acid and glucose homeostasis at the organismal level, and when it fails cells either die or, in tumours, exploit it to survive nutrient-poor microenvironments. Two sensors dominate: the mTOR complex 1 machinery, with its Rag GTPases, GATOR and TSC regulators and sestrins reporting amino acid and energy status, and AMPK, activated when ATP falls. Their combined output releases autophagy initiation through ULK-associated ATG14, beclin and PI3KC3, drives LC3 and GABARAP lipidation, and directs autophagosome-lysosome fusion by STX17 and VAMP8. In parallel, eIF2α kinases and ATF4 reprogramme translation and induce amino acid synthesis and transport, while TFEB and FOXO transcription factors expand lysosomal and catabolic capacity.
