Cells sense and react to acidity, and this response to pH covers both the detectors of extracellular protons and the machinery that restores internal balance. It matters for nociception, taste, breathing control, renal acid handling and the behaviour of immune cells in acidic tumour or inflamed tissue. Proton-gated cation channels of the acid-sensing family, together with TRPV1 and the PKD2L1/PKD1L3 sour-taste pair, convert falling pH into depolarising current, while proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptors such as GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68 signal through Gq/Gs cascades. Two-pore potassium channels are silenced by acid, shifting excitability. Balancing this, the NHE1 exchanger extrudes protons, HVCN1 conducts them out of activated phagocytes, and lysosomal transporters and acid hydrolases operate only at low pH. Loss of these components disturbs pain sensitivity, osteoclast function and organellar degradation.

GDP-mannose is the activated sugar donor that supplies mannose to N-linked glycans, O-mannosylated proteins, GPI anchors and glycosphingolipids, so its synthesis sets the ceiling on how much glycosylation a cell can perform. The route begins with hexokinase-phosphorylated glucose or with free mannose, converts fructose-6-phosphate and mannose-6-phosphate through a phosphomannose isomerase step, isomerises mannose-6-phosphate to mannose-1-phosphate via phosphomannomutase, and caps it with GTP through the GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase subunits. Loss of these steps causes congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 deficiency is the most common such disease, with cerebellar hypoplasia and multisystem involvement, while GMPPB mutations produce dystroglycanopathy with muscular dystrophy because O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan fails. The pathway therefore links central carbohydrate metabolism to the secretory glycosylation machinery and to muscle and neural development.

Messenger RNA synthesis from a DNA template is the step at which a cell decides which proteins it will make, and essentially every adaptive response, differentiation decision and growth programme depends on it. The core machinery here is the RNA polymerase II apparatus and its general initiation factors: TBP together with a large family of TAF subunits forms TFIID, which recognises promoter DNA and nucleates preinitiation complex assembly on the POLR2A-containing polymerase. Mediator subunit MED1 and the coactivators NCOA1 and NCOA2 relay signals from sequence-specific regulators to that complex, including nuclear receptors for thyroid hormone, vitamin D, retinoids, oxysterols and fatty acids, and stimulus-driven factors such as CREB1, ATF4, STAT3, IRF3 and TP53. Nascent transcripts are captured by the nuclear cap-binding complex, coupling initiation to downstream processing and export. Mutations in these components cause developmental and metabolic disease.

Spliceosomal and other small nuclear RNAs are made by a specialized transcription programme distinct from ordinary mRNA synthesis, and without it a cell cannot assemble the spliceosome or process the U6 and 7SK RNAs that control splicing and elongation. Promoter recognition at snRNA genes depends on the multi-subunit SNAPc complex, whose components direct either RNA polymerase II or, for U6-type genes, polymerase III. Transcription is coupled to a dedicated termination and 3'-end formation step: CDK7 phosphorylates the polymerase carboxy-terminal domain, RPAP2 removes that mark, and the little elongation complex built on ELL family proteins with ICE1 and ICE2 supports elongation at these short genes. LARP7 and MEPCE stabilize and cap 7SK, while USPL1 acts in Cajal bodies where snRNA transcription is organized. Defects disrupt splicing fidelity and, through the 7SK arm, global elongation control.

Making ribosomes begins with transcribing ribosomal RNA, and this pathway covers the synthesis of rRNA from the tandem rDNA repeats in the nucleolus plus the 5S rRNA genes transcribed elsewhere. Because rRNA output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis, the pathway is the point at which growth signals are converted into ribosome supply: mTOR-dependent input, chromatin regulators and nucleolar factors such as nucleolin, treacle protein and SIRT7 tune polymerase loading at rDNA promoters. RNA polymerase I subunits together with the TAF1B-containing selectivity factor and UBF-type activators build the initiation complex, while topoisomerase I relieves torsional stress during elongation; the general transcription factor IIIC complex and TFIIIA-like zinc finger factor direct polymerase III to 5S genes. Loss of these functions causes ribosomopathies, including craniofacial malformation in Treacher Collins syndrome, and nucleolar stress that stabilises p53.

Every protein-synthesising cell must continuously replenish its pool of transfer RNAs, and tRNA transcription is the step that makes them from DNA templates. Output of this pathway sets the ceiling on translational capacity, so it is tuned to growth signals and nutrient status and is elevated in rapidly dividing and tumour cells. RNA polymerase III does the synthesis, with catalytic and accessory subunits including POLR3A and POLR3D plus subunits shared with the other nuclear polymerases. Promoter recognition falls to the multisubunit TFIIIC complex, which binds internal control regions in tRNA genes and recruits TFIIIB, whose BRF1 subunit delivers the polymerase to the start site. Mutations in polymerase III subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, and the same enzyme also senses cytosolic DNA during antiviral responses.

Amine metabolism covers the synthesis, interconversion and breakdown of weakly basic nitrogenous compounds, and here it spans two families that matter most to human physiology: the biogenic amine neurotransmitters and the polyamines. Dopamine, noradrenaline, adrenaline, serotonin and histamine are made by a chain of hydroxylases and decarboxylases including PAH, TH, DDC, DBH, PNMT and HDC, with GCH1 supplying the tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor, then inactivated by monoamine oxidases, COMT, HNMT and sulfotransferases, and cleared from the synapse by transporters such as SLC6A3. Loss of these dopaminergic neurons, and the handling of alpha-synuclein by PRKN, PARK7 and VPS35, defines Parkinson disease. In parallel, ODC1, AMD1, SRM and SMS build spermidine and spermine for proliferation and chromatin binding, under tight feedback through antizymes and antizyme inhibitors, while SAT1 and the amine oxidases return polyamines to catabolism.

Small nitrogenous bases — catecholamines, histamine, melatonin and the polyamines — are made by a handful of decarboxylation and hydroxylation steps, and this amine biosynthetic programme covers both branches. One arm builds neurotransmitters and hormones: tyrosine hydroxylase and DDC give dopamine, DBH converts it to noradrenaline and PNMT to adrenaline, while HDC yields histamine and AANAT with ASMT convert serotonin to melatonin; GCH1 supplies the tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor that PAH and TH require. The other arm produces putrescine, spermidine and spermine through ODC1, AMD1, SRM and SMS, with antizymes and their inhibitors setting ODC1 stability and acetylation and oxidation by SAT1, SMOX and PAOX returning flux, so polyamine pools stay matched to growth. Transcription factors including GATA3, HAND2 and INSM1 impose the noradrenergic and neuroendocrine identity in which these enzymes are expressed. Loss of individual steps causes phenylketonuria, dopa-responsive dystonia and catecholamine deficiency.

Amine catabolic process is the set of reactions that dispose of biogenic amines and polyamines once they have acted, keeping neurotransmitter, histamine and polyamine pools within safe limits. It matters because unchecked amine signalling drives hypertension, migraine and psychiatric disturbance, while polyamine excess promotes proliferation and oxidative stress; drugs that block these enzymes, notably monoamine oxidase inhibitors, work precisely by interrupting the route. Monoamine oxidases MAOA and MAOB oxidatively deaminate dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline in the outer mitochondrial membrane, with COMT and the sulfotransferases providing parallel methylation and conjugation routes, and HNMT terminating histamine action. A second arm handles polyamines: SAT1 acetylates spermidine and spermine for oxidation by PAOX or direct back-conversion by SMOX. Choline and betaine oxidation feeds the related one-carbon and osmolyte metabolism, linking amine turnover to methyl group supply and to catecholamine reuptake by DAT.

Amine catabolism is the set of reactions that dispose of biogenic amines, polyamines and choline-derived betaines, terminating their signalling activity and preventing accumulation of reactive or toxic nitrogenous compounds. Its importance is clearest in the nervous system, where monoamine oxidases A and B oxidatively deaminate dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and related transmitters, catechol O-methyltransferase methylates catechols, and histamine N-methyltransferase inactivates histamine; loss or variation in these steps alters mood, blood pressure and susceptibility to parkinsonism, and MAO inhibitors are used as antidepressants. Sulfotransferases of the SULT1A family conjugate phenolic amines for excretion, while spermine oxidase, polyamine oxidase and spermidine/spermine acetyltransferase run the polyamine back-conversion route that generates hydrogen peroxide and aminoaldehydes. Choline and dimethylglycine dehydrogenases feed choline degradation into one-carbon metabolism, and a dopamine transporter delivers substrate for intracellular turnover.

Oligosaccharide metabolism covers the making and breaking of short sugar chains, from the dietary starch and disaccharides we digest in the gut to the glycan branches that decorate proteins and lipids. Two themes run through it. Digestive and lysosomal hydrolases trim sugars for absorption or degradation: salivary amylases, sucrase-isomaltase, lactase, maltase-glucoamylase and trehalase release monosaccharides in the intestine, while acid alpha-glucosidase, beta-hexosaminidase, alpha-galactosidase, mannosidases and sialidases dismantle glycoconjugates in lysosomes. Loss of these activities gives lactose or sucrose intolerance at one end and storage diseases such as Pompe, Fabry and Sandhoff at the other. Working in the opposite direction, families of fucosyltransferases, galactosyltransferases, sialyltransferases and polysialyltransferases build the terminal structures that determine blood group and Lewis antigens, selectin ligands for leukocyte adhesion, ganglioside headgroups and neural polysialic acid. Oligosaccharide biosynthesis builds the short sugar chains, two to about twenty residues long, that decorate glycoproteins, glycolipids and milk. The products are what cells display to each other: blood group antigens, the sialyl Lewis structures that let leukocytes roll on endothelium, and the gangliosides and mucin-type glycans of epithelial surfaces. Assembly is stepwise in the Golgi, each glycosyltransferase adding one residue from a nucleotide-sugar donor: galactosyltransferases extend the backbone, sialyltransferases cap it with negatively charged sialic acid, and fucosyltransferases add the fucose that completes H antigen and selectin ligands. FUT1 and FUT2 determine ABO/H and secretor status, FUT7 governs selectin ligand formation on leukocytes, and lactalbumin partners with B4GALT1 to make lactose for milk. Altered glycan capping accompanies tumour progression and inflammatory adhesion, while mutations in individual transferases cause congenital glycosylation defects.

Short sugar chains, whether taken in with food or released from glycoproteins and glycolipids during turnover, must be cut down to single monosaccharides before they can be absorbed or reused, and that is what oligosaccharide catabolism accomplishes. Two settings dominate. At the intestinal brush border, lactase, sucrase-isomaltase, maltase-glucoamylase and trehalase hydrolyse dietary disaccharides and starch-derived oligomers into glucose, galactose and fructose; loss of lactase activity after weaning produces lactose intolerance, and sucrase-isomaltase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhoea. In lysosomes and at the cell surface, exoglycosidases trim glycans residue by residue: sialidases remove terminal sialic acid, mannosidases release mannose, a chitobiase acts on the chitobiose core, and beta-hexosaminidase with its GM2 activator protein degrades gangliosides. Defects in these degradative steps cause storage diseases including sialidosis, beta-mannosidosis and GM2 gangliosidosis, linking the pathway to both nutrient assimilation and glycoconjugate recycling.

Cells and organisms sense electromagnetic radiation across a wide range of energies, and the response to radiation gathers the machinery that detects it and limits the damage it causes. At the ionizing end, the ATM/ATR and DNA-PK kinases, checkpoint effectors CHEK2 and CDKN1A, and p53 with its targets BAX, BBC3 and GADD45A halt the cell cycle, direct double-strand break repair by homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining, or commit damaged cells to apoptosis; loss of these functions underlies radiosensitivity syndromes and cancer predisposition. Ultraviolet exposure recruits nucleotide excision repair (XPA, XPC, the ERCC helicases, DDB2) and pigmentation responses through TYR and MC1R, whose failure produces xeroderma pigmentosum and skin cancer. At visible wavelengths, opsins, transducins, phosphodiesterases and guanylate cyclases convert photons into retinal signals supporting vision, while melanopsin and the PER/CRY/CLOCK machinery entrain circadian rhythms to light.

Membrane phospholipids are not permanent structures; their controlled breakdown supplies signalling lipids, remodels membranes, and feeds fatty acids back into metabolism. Phospholipid catabolism covers the hydrolases that cut these molecules at each position: phospholipases A2 of the cytosolic, secreted and calcium-independent families release arachidonic acid for eicosanoid production, phospholipase C isoforms generate diacylglycerol and inositol phosphates downstream of receptors, phospholipase D yields phosphatidic acid, and sphingomyelinases such as SMPD1 liberate ceramide. Serine hydrolases including ABHD6, ABHD12 and NAPEPLD control endocannabinoid and N-acylethanolamine levels, while glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterases and ENPP enzymes complete degradation of headgroup-containing intermediates and produce lysophosphatidic acid. Lipases acting at lipoproteins, with apolipoprotein cofactors and receptors, extend the same chemistry to circulating particles. Loss of individual steps causes lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration and disordered inflammatory signalling.

folic acid-containing compound biosynthetic process builds and maintains the pool of reduced folate cofactors that carry one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis and methylation. Cells cannot make the pterin ring's dietary equivalent without uptake, so this biology combines receptor- and transporter-mediated acquisition of folate (FOLR1, the proton-coupled intestinal transporter SLC46A1) with reduction by dihydrofolate reductase, polyglutamylation by FPGS to retain folates intracellularly, and interconversion of formyl, methylene and methenyl derivatives by MTHFD1 and MTHFS. GCH1 supplies GTP-derived pterin, linking the pathway to tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism. The output feeds purine synthesis directly through ATIC, thymidylate production, and methionine and S-adenosylmethionine regeneration. Insufficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neural tube defects, and the dependence of proliferating cells on this route is the basis of antifolate chemotherapy, where DHFR inhibition starves DNA synthesis of thymidine and purines.

Folate derivatives carry one-carbon units for purine and thymidylate synthesis, methionine regeneration and methylation, so the biosynthesis and interconversion of folic acid-containing compounds sets the supply of these cofactors. Mammals cannot make the pterin ring into a complete folate and must take up dietary folate, which is why a receptor and a proton-coupled intestinal transporter belong here alongside the enzymes; poor uptake or reduced activity produces megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects. Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate and is the target of methotrexate, while polyglutamylation by FPGS retains folates inside cells and mitochondria. GTP cyclohydrolase I supplies dihydroneopterin triphosphate for the related pterin route, and MTHFD1 with its mitochondrial counterpart MTHFD1L generate and interconvert formyl and methylene forms that ATIC consumes during purine synthesis.

Handling of toxins covers the enzymatic conversion of poisonous compounds — whether ingested, inhaled, or produced by other organisms — into forms that can be excreted, and this chemistry determines whether an exposure is cleared or turned into something more damaging. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases such as CYP1A1, CYP1A2, CYP1B1 and CYP3A4 introduce reactive oxygen-containing groups, flavin monooxygenases oxidise nucleophilic heteroatoms, and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases conjugate the products for elimination; an arsenic methyltransferase and an aflatoxin aldehyde reductase act on specific environmental poisons. The transcription factor NFE2L2 coordinates induction of this defensive capacity under electrophilic and oxidative stress. Because oxidation frequently generates epoxides and other electrophiles before conjugation removes them, the same machinery underlies both detoxification and the metabolic activation of procarcinogens, making it central to chemical carcinogenesis, drug clearance and inter-individual variation in drug response.

Cells survive exposure to poisons by chemically converting them into less reactive, more water-soluble products that can be excreted, and this toxin catabolic activity is the basis of hepatic and intestinal detoxification and of resistance to dietary carcinogens. An aldo-keto reductase reduces reactive aldehydes, notably the aflatoxin B1 dialdehyde, while UDP-glucuronosyltransferases conjugate glucuronic acid onto phenolic and other electrophilic substrates to mark them for elimination. Coordinating this response is NFE2L2, the transcription factor that senses electrophilic and oxidative stress and induces batteries of phase II conjugating and antioxidant enzymes; protein kinase C signalling feeds into its activation. Loss or polymorphic variation in these steps raises the burden of DNA-damaging adducts and underlies susceptibility to chemical carcinogenesis, while the same enzymes determine the clearance rate of many drugs.

response to heat is the cell's emergency programme for surviving temperatures above its optimum, when proteins begin to unfold and aggregate. It preserves proteome integrity under thermal, oxidative and metabolic stress, and its capacity determines whether a cell recovers or dies; the same machinery is co-opted by tumours to buffer misfolded protein loads and declines with age in neurodegeneration. The core is transcriptional: HSF1, held in check by HSP90 and HSBP1, trimerises on heat shock elements to induce HSPA1A/B, HSPB1 and a large family of DNAJ co-chaperones that refold or triage damaged substrates, with CHIP/STUB1 and VCP routing the irreparable to degradation. In parallel, eIF2α and its eIF2B guanine-nucleotide exchange factor arrest bulk translation and drive stress granule assembly. Thermosensation is represented too, through TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPM2 and TRPA1 channels in sensory neurons that convert noxious heat into pain signalling.

Cells and organisms exposed to temperatures above their optimum mount a coordinated defence against protein unfolding, and this heat response is what keeps the proteome soluble and functional during fever, exercise or environmental stress. Its core is transcriptional and chaperone-based: HSF1 drives induction of inducible HSP70 family members, HSP90 isoforms, small heat shock proteins such as HSPB1 and the alpha-crystallins, and a large set of DNAJ co-chaperones that direct substrate selection, with HSPBP-like regulators and nuclear import factors controlling where chaperones act. Parallel arms suppress translation through eIF2 and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor subunits, route terminally damaged proteins to degradation via CHIP, VCP and HDAC6, and trigger antioxidant and heme oxygenase defences. Sensory thermoreception is also represented, with TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPA1 and TRPM2 channels converting heat into neuronal signalling and pain. Loss of this capacity underlies heat-sensitive myopathies and aggregation-prone neurodegeneration.

Exposure to temperatures below the thermal optimum triggers a coordinated defence of body temperature and cellular integrity, and this cold response is what allows mammals to maintain core temperature and what fails in cold intolerance. Peripheral sensing involves cold- and menthol-activated channels TRPM8 and TRPA1 in sensory neurons alongside the sodium channel SCN11A, while sympathetic output acting through β1–β3 adrenergic receptors and protein kinase A mobilises stored triacylglycerol from lipid droplets coated by PLIN1 and CIDEA. Fatty acids are then activated, imported and β-oxidised by ACADM and ACADVL to fuel uncoupled respiration through UCP1 in brown and beige adipocytes, with thyroid hormone receptor α, PRKAA1 and ZNF516 shaping the thermogenic transcriptional programme. In parallel, cold-inducible RNA binding protein, heat shock chaperones and the eIF2α kinases PERK and GCN2 adjust translation and protein folding to low-temperature stress.

Cells and tissues must sense and dispose of chemicals they did not make — drugs, plant toxins, pollutants, industrial compounds — and the response to xenobiotic stimulus covers the whole reaction, from ligand sensing through enzymatic conversion, export and downstream changes in gene expression and physiology. This determines how drugs are cleared and dosed, why some individuals are sensitive to carcinogens, and how reactive intermediates cause liver injury. Ligand-activated transcription factors such as the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and the pregnane X receptor induce oxidative phase I cytochromes P450, followed by conjugation through glutathione transferases, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and N-acetyltransferases, with ABC and SLC transporters handling uptake and efflux into bile and urine. Oxidative by-products engage antioxidant defences under NFE2L2 control, while DNA damage sensing, p53 signalling, apoptotic and inflammatory responses are recruited when detoxification is overwhelmed.

Ultraviolet light damages DNA directly, creating cyclobutane dimers and other photoproducts, and cells answer with a coordinated response to UV that decides between repair, arrest and death. Failure of this response underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne and UV-sensitive syndromes and the mutational burden that drives skin cancer. Much of the gene content is nucleotide excision repair: damage recognition by XPC and the DDB1-DDB2-CUL4 ubiquitin ligase, unwinding by the ERCC2/ERCC3 helicases of the transcription factor IIH complex, incision by ERCC1-ERCC4 and ERCC5, and gap filling by replicative polymerases. Stalled forks are rescued by translesion synthesis through POLH and POLK and by PRIMPOL repriming, while ATR signalling and TP53 impose checkpoint arrest via CDKN1A or apoptosis via BAX and the caspases. Stress kinases, the integrated stress response, matrix metalloproteinases and pigmentation genes such as MC1R and TYR extend the reaction to tissue-level photoprotection and photoaging.

Prolonged lack of water forces an organism to conserve what it has, and this response to water deprivation covers the cellular and transcriptional changes that follow dehydration. Its central output is renal: vasopressin released from the hypothalamus acts on collecting duct cells, and AQP2 water channels are trafficked to the apical membrane so that water is reabsorbed from urine rather than lost, concentrating the urine and defending plasma osmolality. AVPR1A mediates the complementary vascular and smooth muscle actions of vasopressin, raising vascular tone and supporting blood pressure when volume falls, while UMOD, the major protein secreted by thick ascending limb cells, participates in generating the medullary concentrating gradient. Accompanying changes in gene expression, including AP-1 family factors such as JUND, adapt tubular cells to hypertonic stress. Failure of this axis produces diabetes insipidus and an inability to concentrate urine.

response to water covers how cells and tissues sense and react to water availability and osmotic state, the basis of body fluid homeostasis. In humans this is most visible in the kidney, where vasopressin acting through its receptor drives insertion of the aquaporin-2 water channel into collecting duct membranes to concentrate urine; loss of this axis produces diabetes insipidus and dehydration. Other members report on the mechanical and ionic consequences of water movement: polycystin channels transduce flow and osmotic cues in renal cilia and are mutated in polycystic kidney disease, uromodulin shapes tubular salt handling, and calcium pumps and cytoskeletal linkers such as plectin buffer the resulting volume and tension changes. Downstream, transcriptional and kinase signalling adjust gene expression so that transport capacity matches hydration status.

Cells and whole organisms adjust their behaviour to the presence, absence or concentration of water, and in mammals this response is largely about defending body fluid osmolality and blood volume. The kidney carries most of the burden: vasopressin receptor signalling drives insertion of the water channel aquaporin-2 into collecting duct apical membranes so that free water is reabsorbed rather than lost in urine, while uromodulin shapes salt handling and the concentrating capacity of the thick ascending limb. Osmotic and mechanical cues are also read directly, through polycystin channels of the TRPP family that sense flow and tonicity, and through calcium pump and phosphoinositide kinase activity that translate these cues into intracellular signals and altered gene expression. Failure of this water response produces diabetes insipidus, dysnatraemia, and impaired urine concentration, and the same sensing machinery contributes to cyst formation in polycystic kidney disease.

Light is both information and insult, and the response to light stimulus gathers the ways cells and tissues react to it. One arm is vision: rod and cone opsins coupled to transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels convert photons into a change in photoreceptor membrane potential, with arrestin, rhodopsin kinase and guanylate cyclase activators resetting the cascade and RPE65 regenerating chromophore; mutations in these and in outer-segment structural genes cause retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis and colour-vision defects. A second arm entrains physiology to the day, where melanopsin input drives the clock loop of CLOCK, the period and cryptochrome genes and their ubiquitin-dependent turnover, and pineal AANAT times melatonin output. A third handles ultraviolet damage, coupling nucleotide excision repair and translesion polymerases to p53-dependent arrest or apoptosis, alongside melanin synthesis and pigmentary tanning responses.

Cells must continuously make NAD+, the hydride carrier for glycolysis, the TCA cycle and respiration and the consumed substrate of sirtuins, PARPs and CD38, so its supply sets both redox capacity and the budget for signalling that cleaves it. Synthesis runs by two routes converging on the same adenylyl transfer step: de novo degradation of tryptophan through the kynurenine pathway, where IDO1/IDO2, KMO, KYNU and HAAO generate quinolinate that QPRT decarboxylates, and salvage from vitamin B3 forms, with NAMPT phosphoribosylating nicotinamide, NAPRT handling nicotinic acid and NMRK1/2 phosphorylating nicotinamide riboside. NMNAT1, NMNAT2 and NMNAT3 then adenylylate the mononucleotides in nucleus, cytosol and mitochondria respectively, and NADSYN1 amidates NAAD. ACMSD diverts kynurenine intermediates away from NAD+. Declining flux is linked to axon degeneration, where loss of NMNAT2 triggers programmed axon death, and to metabolic and age-related dysfunction.

Carnitine metabolism supplies and uses the carrier that lets long-chain fatty acids reach the mitochondrial matrix for beta-oxidation, so it governs how tissues fuel themselves during fasting and sustained exercise. Heart and skeletal muscle depend on it most, and defects in the carrier enzymes cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Two arms are represented: biosynthesis from trimethyllysine, where a dioxygenase and gamma-butyrobetaine hydroxylase complete the route to carnitine, and the shuttle itself, in which outer-membrane carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 isoforms esterify acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine and the inner-membrane CPT2 reverses the step for oxidation by acyl-CoA dehydrogenases. Carnitine acetyltransferase and a peroxisomal octanoyltransferase buffer the acetyl-CoA pool and move medium-chain acyl groups between compartments, while a plasma-membrane organic cation transporter handles cellular carnitine uptake. CPT1 inhibition by malonyl-CoA ties the whole system to nutritional state.

Methylglyoxal is a reactive dicarbonyl formed as an unavoidable by-product of glycolysis, largely from the triose phosphates, and it attacks arginine and lysine side chains and DNA bases to form advanced glycation end products. Handling it keeps proteins and the genome from accumulating glycation damage, and failure of this detoxification is linked to diabetic complications, neurodegeneration and cellular ageing. The main route is glutathione-dependent: glyoxalase I converts the hemithioacetal to S-D-lactoylglutathione, which glyoxalase II hydrolyses to D-lactate and regenerates glutathione. Additional glutathione-independent deglycase and glyoxalase-like activities, including that of DJ-1/PARK7, repair or remove dicarbonyl adducts directly, tying this chemistry to oxidative stress defence and to Parkinson disease biology. Triose phosphate isomerase sets the supply side, since its deficiency raises methylglyoxal formation from glycolytic intermediates.

Putrescine is the entry point of polyamine metabolism, the diamine from which spermidine and spermine are built, and cells guard its supply tightly because polyamines are required for proliferation, translation of specific mRNAs, chromatin compaction and ion channel regulation. Ornithine decarboxylase makes putrescine from ornithine and is one of the most rapidly turned-over enzymes known; its stability is set by antizymes, which are in turn neutralised by the antizyme inhibitors in this group. An alternative route runs from agmatine via agmatinase. Catabolism balances synthesis: spermidine/spermine N1-acetyltransferases acetylate higher polyamines for export or for oxidation back toward putrescine by polyamine oxidase, while a copper-containing amine oxidase degrades putrescine itself, generating hydrogen peroxide. Dysregulated flux through this axis accompanies MYC-driven tumour growth and makes ornithine decarboxylase a chemoprevention target.

Putrescine biosynthesis opens the polyamine pathway, supplying the diamine from which spermidine and spermine are built; because polyamines are required for ribosome function, chromatin compaction and rapid proliferation, flux through this step sets how much growth a cell can support, and it is characteristically elevated in tumours and in regenerating tissue. Ornithine decarboxylase performs the committed decarboxylation of ornithine and is one of the shortest-lived enzymes in the cell, held under tight control by antizyme-mediated degradation; the antizyme inhibitors AZIN1 and AZIN2 sequester antizyme and thereby raise decarboxylase activity. An alternative arginine-derived route proceeds through agmatine, which agmatinase hydrolyses to putrescine and urea. Putrescine is also regenerated by back-conversion, in which polyamine oxidase cleaves acetylated spermidine, making the pool a balance of synthesis, catabolism and recycling rather than a one-way route.

GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian brain, and its metabolism sets how much of it is available to dampen neuronal firing. Glutamate decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2 synthesise GABA from glutamate in inhibitory neurons, while GABA transaminase (ABAT) and succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH5A1) degrade it back through succinate semialdehyde into the TCA cycle, linking neurotransmitter turnover to mitochondrial energy metabolism. Astrocytes contribute the other half of the cycle: the glutamate transporter SLC1A3 clears released transmitter and glutamine carriers return precursor to neurons. Loss of the degradative arm causes succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency, with GABA accumulation, developmental delay and seizures, whereas impaired synthesis shifts cortical excitation-inhibition balance toward epilepsy. The same enzymes are the targets of antiepileptic drugs that raise synaptic GABA by blocking its breakdown.

GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian brain, and its biosynthesis sets the balance between excitation and inhibition that keeps cortical and subcortical circuits from running away into seizure. The committed step is decarboxylation of glutamate by the two glutamate decarboxylase isoforms, one supplying a cytosolic metabolic pool and the other coupled to vesicle filling at the synapse; loss or autoimmune attack on these enzymes produces epilepsy and stiff-person syndrome. Supply of precursor depends on the glutamate–glutamine cycle, with astrocytic glutamate uptake by the EAAT1 transporter and neuronal glutamine import by SNAT1 feeding the reaction. An alternative route through aldehyde dehydrogenase generates GABA from putrescine-derived aldehyde, while GABA transaminase returns the transmitter to succinate semialdehyde, linking inhibitory signalling to the TCA cycle through the GABA shunt.

After transcription, nucleotides within RNA are chemically decorated — methylated, pseudouridylated, deaminated, thiolated or otherwise rewritten — and this RNA modification landscape determines how stable, how translatable and how accurately decoded a transcript will be. Transfer RNAs are the most heavily modified species here, with anticodon-loop and wobble-position changes from the elongator complex, thiouridylases and pseudouridine synthases setting codon reading fidelity; ribosomal RNA is methylated and pseudouridylated by fibrillarin- and dyskerin-containing small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins during ribosome biogenesis. Messenger RNA carries N6-methyladenosine installed by a METTL3–METTL14–WTAP writer complex, cap methylation, and C-to-U or A-to-I editing by APOBEC and ADAR deaminases that recodes proteins and marks self double-stranded RNA. Mitochondrial RNAs have their own dedicated enzymes. Loss of these activities causes intellectual disability, mitochondrial disease, bone marrow failure and interferon-driven autoinflammation, and several writers are recurrently altered in cancer.

Fertilization is the sequence of events by which a sperm and an egg recognise each other, fuse, and produce a diploid zygote, the starting point of every new individual; failure at any step causes infertility or early developmental arrest. The genes trace the whole itinerary: sperm capacitation and hyperactivated motility through CatSper channels, ABHD2 and axonemal/flagellar accessory proteins; binding to and penetration of the zona pellucida built from ZP1-ZP4, aided by acrosomal proteases such as acrosin, ZAN and SPAM1; and gamete membrane adhesion and fusion through the IZUMO1-JUNO pair with TMEM95, SPACA6 and DCST1/2. After fusion, PLCZ1 triggers the calcium oscillations that release the oocyte from meiotic arrest via WEE2, while ASTL cleaves ZP2 to block polyspermy, and sperm chromatin packaged by transition proteins is remodelled by NPM2 for pronuclear formation.

Fertilization is the meeting of sperm and egg that creates a zygote, and the genes here cover the whole sequence from sperm capacitation to egg activation. Sperm must cross the cumulus and bind the zona pellucida glycoprotein coat (ZP1-ZP4), undergo the acrosome reaction to release hydrolases such as acrosin and hyaluronidase, then fuse with the oolemma through the IZUMO1-JUNO receptor pair together with SPACA6, TMEM95 and DCST1/2. Progesterone-stimulated calcium entry via CatSper channels, with ABHD2 as the lipid sensor, steers hyperactivated motility and chemotaxis. After fusion, sperm-delivered PLCZ1 triggers oocyte calcium oscillations that release the meiotic arrest maintained by WEE2, while ASTL cleaves ZP2 to block additional sperm, and protamine removal with NPM2 remodels the paternal genome. Defects in these steps are a common cause of male and female infertility and of failed in vitro fertilization.

Sensory cells convert physical features of the environment — light, mechanical force, temperature, sound, osmotic and chemical irritants — into electrical and second-messenger signals, and this detection of abiotic stimulus is the first step of vision, hearing, touch and nociception. The phototransduction arm is heavily represented: rod and cone opsins, transducin subunits, cGMP phosphodiesterase, guanylate cyclases with their calcium-sensing activators, rhodopsin kinase and arrestin for shutoff, plus retinoid recycling by RPE65 and outer-segment structural proteins whose loss causes retinitis pigmentosa and Leber congenital amaurosis. Mechanotransduction contributes hair-cell channel components such as TMC1 and LHFPL5 with stereocilia proteins linked to deafness, and the PIEZO stretch channels. Thermal, acidic and irritant stimuli act through TRPV1, TRPA1, acid-sensing channels and sensory sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A, mutations in which alter pain perception. Downstream, calcium- and cyclic-nucleotide-gated conductances set receptor potential and adaptation.

Vision begins with the conversion of absorbed photons into a neural signal, and this phototransduction machinery is what performs that conversion in rod and cone photoreceptors. Opsins bound to retinal — rhodopsin in rods, the long-, middle- and short-wavelength cone pigments — isomerize on light capture and activate transducin, which stimulates cyclic GMP phosphodiesterase; the resulting fall in cGMP closes cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and hyperpolarizes the cell. Recovery depends on rhodopsin kinase and arrestin quenching the activated receptor, on recoverin and guanylate cyclase activators reporting calcium, and on guanylate cyclases restoring cGMP. Parallel components regenerate chromophore in the pigment epithelium, build the outer segment disc rim, and relay the signal to bipolar cells through a metabotropic glutamate receptor. Mutations across these steps cause retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, stationary night blindness, macular dystrophy and colour vision defects. Non-visual opsins extend the same chemistry to circadian photoentrainment.

Vision begins when a photon striking an opsin in a rod or cone is turned into an electrical change, and this is the phototransduction machinery that performs that conversion. It sets the sensitivity and speed of sight, and mutations in its components cause retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, congenital stationary night blindness, Stargardt disease and colour vision defects. Rhodopsin and the long-, middle- and short-wavelength cone opsins activate rod and cone transducins, which stimulate cGMP phosphodiesterase and close cGMP-gated channels; guanylate cyclases resynthesise cGMP, rhodopsin kinases and arrestin quench the activated receptor, and a chaperone and retinoid transporter keep the cycle running. Non-visual opsins including melanopsin extend light detection to circadian and irradiance signalling, while metabotropic glutamate signalling transmits the resulting message to bipolar cells.

Cells and organisms must sense the chemical composition of their surroundings, and this detection of chemical stimulus biology covers the receptors and transduction machinery that turn a bound molecule into an intracellular signal. Its largest component is the odorant receptor repertoire, several hundred G protein-coupled receptors expressed in olfactory sensory neurons together with the accessory proteins (RTP family) that traffic them to the surface and the transduction elements (GNAT1/GNAT2, CNGB1, SLC24A4) that convert binding into depolarization. Taste is represented by sweet and umami heterodimers of TAS1R subunits, the bitter TAS2R family, and downstream PLCB2, alongside candidate sour channels PKD2L1 and PKD1L3. Chemical irritants and acid act through TRPV1, TRPA1 and ASIC3, extracellular calcium through CASR, and microbial products through Toll-like receptors, NOD2 and TREM2. Together these define smell, taste, chemical nociception, nutrient sensing and innate immune recognition; loss produces anosmia, altered taste perception and impaired danger detection.

detection of biotic stimulus is the front end of innate immunity: the sensing step by which cells recognise molecules made by microbes and other organisms and convert that recognition into an intracellular signal. It sets the threshold for inflammation, determines whether an infection is contained or becomes sepsis, and shapes what antigen is later shown to T cells. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their accessory proteins LBP and LY96 read lipopeptide, LPS and CpG DNA; C-type lectins such as CLEC7A and CLEC6A detect fungal glucans and mannans; cytosolic NOD1, NOD2 and the NLRC4 and NLRP3 inflammasomes respond to peptidoglycan fragments and to bacterial secretion systems by driving caspase-1 activation. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins and scavenger receptors bind and clear microbial ligands directly, while MHC and CD1D molecules link detection to lymphocyte presentation.

Host cells must recognise that a microbe is present before they can respond to it, and detection of biotic stimulus covers the receptors and accessory proteins that convert microbial molecules into intracellular signals. This is the sensing step of innate immunity: without it, bacterial and fungal invaders replicate unchecked, while inappropriate or excessive sensing drives septic shock and autoinflammatory disease. Surface Toll-like receptors, aided by LBP and the LY96 co-receptor, detect lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides and microbial DNA; C-type lectins such as CLEC7A and CLEC6A bind fungal glucans and mannans; cytosolic NOD1 and NOD2 sense peptidoglycan fragments; and NLRP3 or NLRC4 with NAIP nucleate inflammasomes that mature IL-1 family cytokines. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins and complement components add direct antimicrobial and opsonic activity, while MHC and CD1D molecules link recognition to lymphocyte activation and adaptive immunity.

Response to symbiont covers how a host cell or tissue changes its behaviour when it detects another organism living in close association with it, from commensal gut bacteria to invading microbes and parasites. It matters because barrier surfaces must tolerate a resident microbiota while still restraining it, and the response determines whether that relationship stays benign or becomes infection and inflammation. The genes here point to several arms of that adjustment: C4BP subunits restrain complement activation on host surfaces, a control point that microbes themselves exploit to evade lysis; glutathione peroxidase buffers the oxidative burst that accompanies microbial encounters; and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases together with the carnitine transporter SLC22A5 handle conjugation and transport of small molecules at mucosal epithelium. Together they describe host defence and detoxification tuned to microbial exposure rather than to sterile injury.

This is the host side of living with a smaller partner organism: the changes in gene expression, secretion and enzyme activity that follow contact with a symbiont or other closely associated microbe. Such responses set the terms of colonisation, deciding whether a resident microbe is tolerated, contained, or cleared, and they shape mucosal chemistry at the interfaces where microbes are encountered. The genes here point to three arms of that adjustment: restraint of complement activation on host surfaces by the C4b-binding protein subunits, which keeps an inflammatory cascade from damaging host tissue; antioxidant defence against hydrogen peroxide by glutathione peroxidase 1; and conjugative detoxification of small lipophilic compounds by UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the olfactory and airway mucosa, alongside a carnitine and organic cation transporter that supports epithelial metabolism.

Tissue damage triggers a coordinated organismal program, and the response to wounding encompasses everything from sealing a breached vessel to rebuilding the injured tissue. Its first phase is haemostasis: fibrinogen chains, thrombin and the coagulation factors, von Willebrand factor and the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, balanced by anticoagulant and fibrinolytic regulators such as antithrombin, protein C, tissue factor pathway inhibitor and plasminogen activators. Platelet granule biogenesis and secretion, membrane repair by annexins and ESCRT components, and inflammatory signalling through interleukin-1, IL-6, TNF and Toll-like receptors follow. Repair then requires growth factor and integrin-dependent signalling, cytoskeletal remodelling and cell migration, keratinocyte and endothelial proliferation, angiogenesis driven by VEGF and angiopoietins, and TGF-beta-directed matrix deposition with matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors. Failure gives bleeding or thrombotic disorders, chronic non-healing ulcers, or fibrotic scarring.

response to mechanical stimulus is how cells and tissues sense physical force — stretch, pressure, shear, touch, sound — and convert it into altered ion flux, gene expression and secretion. It underlies hearing and touch sensation, blood pressure and flow sensing by endothelium, load-dependent bone remodelling, cartilage and tendon maintenance, and the hypertrophic growth of stretched cardiac muscle; its failure produces deafness, insensitivity to pain, polycystic kidney disease and maladaptive cardiac remodelling. Force is transduced at the membrane by mechanosensitive channels such as PIEZO1/2, TRPV4, TMC1/2 and the polycystins, and at adhesions and the cytoskeleton through integrins, focal adhesion kinase, dystrophin–sarcoglycan links and titin-associated sarcomeric proteins including TCAP, CSRP3 and ANKRD1. Downstream MAPK, NF-κB and β-catenin signalling drives immediate-early transcription (FOS, JUN, MYC), inflammatory cytokine output, matrix remodelling by collagens and MMPs, and osteocyte signals such as sclerostin and osteocalcin.

Cells continually sense physical force "u2014 stretch, pressure, shear, sound and touch "u2014 and convert it into electrical, transcriptional and secretory responses; this is the response to mechanical stimulus. It underlies hearing and balance, touch and mechanical pain, blood pressure and flow sensing in vessels, bone remodelling under load, and the hypertrophic adaptation of heart and skeletal muscle. Force is transduced at the membrane by mechanosensitive channels such as PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, TRPV4, potassium channels of the two-pore family, acid-sensing channels, and the hair-cell machinery built around TMC1/TMC2 and their tip-link partners, and at adhesions where integrins, cadherins, focal adhesion kinase and the cytoskeleton relay tension inward. Downstream, MAPK cascades, NF-"u03baB and immediate-early factors such as FOS and JUN reprogram gene expression, while sarcomeric and costameric proteins including titin, dystrophin and CSRP3 report muscle load. Defects give deafness, polycystic kidney disease, cardiomyopathy and skeletal fragility.

Cells detect viral infection and reprogramme themselves to block replication, alert neighbours, and if necessary die — the broad response to virus that underlies antiviral immunity and, when miscalibrated, drives interferonopathies and cytokine-driven pathology. Nucleic acid sensors distinguish viral RNA and DNA from host material: RIG-I and MDA5 signal through MAVS, cGAS makes a cyclic dinucleotide that activates STING, and endosomal Toll-like receptors recruit MyD88 or TRIF, converging on TBK1/IKK kinases and IRF3, IRF7 and NF-κB to induce type I, II and III interferons. Interferon receptors then act through STAT1/STAT2 and IRF9 to switch on effectors that degrade RNA, halt translation, restrict entry or tether virions — the OAS/RNase L and PKR arms, MX GTPases, IFIT and IFITM families, tetherin, APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases and SAMHD1. Parallel branches include TRIM and ISG15 ubiquitin-like control, inflammasome assembly with caspase-1, autophagy, chemokine secretion, and apoptotic or necroptotic death of infected cells.

This is the host's integrated reaction to bacteria and their products, spanning recognition, killing, and the inflammatory and repair programmes that follow, and it determines whether a mucosal or systemic bacterial encounter is contained or becomes sepsis or chronic inflammatory disease. Surface and cytosolic sensors such as the Toll-like receptors, NOD1/NOD2 and inflammasome scaffolds including NLRP3, NLRC4 and PYCARD detect conserved microbial structures, signalling through MYD88, IRAK kinases, TRAF6 and MAP kinases to NF-kB-driven transcription of TNF, IL1B, IL6 and chemokines, while caspase-1 and caspase-4 mature IL-18 and cleave gasdermin D for pyroptotic release. In parallel, effector arms deliver direct antimicrobial force: alpha- and beta-defensins, lysozymes, RNases, lactoferrin, calprotectin subunits, complement, peptidoglycan-recognition proteins, phagocyte oxidase and nitric oxide synthases, plus iron and zinc withholding by hepcidin and lipocalin-2. Negative regulators such as TNFAIP3, IRAK3, SIGIRR and several microRNAs restrain the response so that antimicrobial defence does not damage tissue.

Detecting fungi and mounting a defence against them is what this response covers, and its failure is visible in humans as chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and invasive fungal disease in the immunocompromised. Recognition begins with C-type lectin receptors of the myeloid surface — dectin-1, dectin-2, Mincle and their relatives — which read fungal β-glucan and mannan and signal through Syk, PLCγ2 and the CARD9–BCL10–MALT1 module to activate NF-κB, with TLR4 and MyD88 contributing a parallel input. The output is phagocyte recruitment and killing plus a type 17 cytokine programme: IL-17A acting through IL17RA/IL17RC drives epithelial production of antimicrobial effectors. Those effectors dominate the gene list — α- and β-defensins, cathelicidin, histatins, lactoferrin, calprotectin subunits S100A8/A9, and the neutrophil granule enzymes myeloperoxidase and elastase — linking innate sensing to mucosal and skin barrier immunity.

Infection by parasitic nematodes provokes a characteristic type 2 immune reaction, and this response encompasses the cellular and secretory changes triggered by worm-derived stimuli. Its outcome is expulsion of helminths from the gut and airway, tissue repair after the damage they cause, and, when misdirected against harmless antigens, the allergic inflammation of asthma and atopy. The epithelial alarmin IL25 alerts innate lymphoid cells and Th2 lymphocytes, which produce IL13 to drive mucus secretion, smooth muscle contraction and goblet cell hyperplasia. Macrophages adopt an alternatively activated state marked by arginase-1, diverting arginine from nitric oxide synthesis toward polyamine and proline production for repair. Lipid mediators contribute through prostaglandin synthase activity and prostaglandin D2 generation, acting on receptors such as PTGER2, while intelectin binds carbohydrate structures on the parasite surface. The programme links mucosal barrier defence to inflammation and wound healing.

Cells and tissues must sense and survive the non-living features of their environment — light, temperature, oxygen tension, osmolarity, pH, mechanical force, radiation and chemical insult — and this response to abiotic stimulus gathers the sensors and downstream programmes that make that possible. It spans phototransduction in retinal photoreceptors and hair-cell mechanotransduction, circadian entrainment through the clock machinery, hypoxia sensing by prolyl hydroxylases and the HIF transcription factors, osmotic and pH regulation through ion channels, transporters and kinases, thermal and noxious detection by TRP and acid-sensing channels, and heat-shock and oxidative-stress defences built on chaperones and antioxidant enzymes. Genotoxic stress converges on DNA repair and p53-directed arrest or apoptosis. The shared logic is a stimulus converted into altered ion flux, transcription or protein quality control, so the cell either adapts or dies; loss of individual branches produces blindness, deafness, insensitivity to pain, cancer predisposition and failure to tolerate ischaemia.

response to gravity covers how cells and tissues sense and adapt to gravitational load, a stimulus that shapes bone mass, muscle bulk and the vestibular sense of head position. Its relevance is clearest when gravity is removed: in microgravity or during prolonged unloading, bone mineral is lost and skeletal muscle wastes, changes traceable to the mechanotransduction and endocrine components represented here. Osteocalcin marks the osteoblast response to mechanical loading, growth hormone receptor and myostatin set the anabolic and catabolic balance of muscle, and immediate-early transcription through FOS, downstream of Ras signalling, converts a mechanical cue into altered gene expression. Otopetrin 1 and an NADPH oxidase are required for otoconia formation in the inner ear, the dense particles that let the utricle and saccule register linear acceleration, with synaptic transmission relaying that information onward for balance and postural control.

Gravity is a constant mechanical and sensory input, and cells respond to it by changing gene expression, growth and signalling output. Two distinct arms are represented here. In the inner ear, the otoconia of the vestibular system transduce linear acceleration and head tilt: OTOP1 is required for otoconia formation, NOX3 supplies the oxidase activity needed for their assembly, and STX1A supports transmitter release at hair cell synapses; loss of these leaves animals unable to sense which way is down, with balance and righting defects. In bone and muscle, mechanical loading against gravity governs tissue mass, with osteocalcin marking osteoblast activity, growth hormone receptor and RAS signalling relaying anabolic cues, immediate-early FOS induction reporting the load itself, and myostatin restraining muscle growth. Unloading, as in disuse or spaceflight, causes bone loss and muscle atrophy through these same routes.

response to herbicide covers the cellular and organismal reactions triggered by exposure to plant-killing chemicals, which in humans and other animals act as xenobiotic toxicants rather than as intended targets. It matters because agricultural herbicides such as paraquat and glyphosate cause oxidative injury, dopaminergic neuron loss and porphyrin-pathway disturbance, and this response determines how much damage exposure produces. The genes trace several arms of that reaction: induction of a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that oxidises the foreign compound, changes in the first and third enzymes of heme biosynthesis, which are classic readouts of chemically induced porphyria, secretion of the iron-sequestering stress protein lipocalin-2, and the mitochondrial serine protease HTRA2, which links herbicide-driven mitochondrial stress to apoptosis. Together they place this biology at the intersection of xenobiotic metabolism, heme synthesis and mitochondrial cell death signalling.

Herbicides such as paraquat, glyphosate and the diphenyl ethers reach animal cells as xenobiotic and oxidative insults, and this grouping collects the cellular responses they provoke: altered gene expression, induction of detoxifying enzymes, and adjustments to heme synthesis and stress handling. Its relevance is toxicological rather than developmental, since herbicide exposure in humans is linked to oxidative tissue injury and, for paraquat, to dopaminergic neuron loss and parkinsonism. The members point to the mechanisms involved: a xenobiotic-inducible cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that metabolises aromatic compounds, the first and second enzymes of the heme biosynthetic route whose activity is sensitive to porphyrinogenic chemicals, a mitochondrial serine protease that participates in stress-induced apoptosis, and a secreted iron-siderophore-binding protein induced during inflammation and cellular damage.</br>

Cells and tissues respond to poisons, drugs, reactive metabolites and heavy metals by inducing the machinery that detoxifies them, expels them, and repairs the damage they cause. This response to toxic substance determines chemical tolerance in the liver, kidney and gut, sets drug pharmacokinetics, and when overwhelmed leads to oxidative injury, apoptosis and cell death. Xenobiotic-sensing transcription factors such as AHR and the oxidative-stress regulator NFE2L2 drive cytochrome P450 oxidation, glutathione S-transferase and UGT conjugation, and NQO1-mediated quinone reduction, while ABC and SLC transporters import and efflux the products. Parallel antioxidant systems — superoxide dismutases, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin reductases — buffer reactive oxygen species, and metallothioneins with zinc, copper and manganese transporters sequester and distribute metals. Persistent damage engages p53-linked stress genes, DNA repair, and mitochondrial apoptotic and mitophagy responses.

response to blue light covers the cellular changes triggered by short-wavelength visible light, from circadian timing to pigment production and metabolic adjustment. In humans this is the biology behind light entrainment of the body clock and the effects of daylight and screen exposure on sleep, mood and skin. The cryptochromes CRY1 and CRY2 sit in the core clock feedback loop, repressing CLOCK/BMAL1-driven transcription and setting the phase of downstream rhythms, while OPN3 is an opsin photoreceptor expressed outside the retina, in skin melanocytes and adipose tissue, where blue light stimulates calcium signalling. Downstream effectors include the melanogenic enzymes tyrosinase and DCT, linking irradiation to pigmentation, and CPT1B, tying photic input to fatty acid oxidation. Loss of this responsiveness disrupts sleep-wake alignment and the peripheral rhythms that follow it.

Blue light in the 440-500 nm range is the strongest entraining signal for the mammalian circadian clock and also a stress stimulus for skin and eye, and this pathway covers the cellular responses it triggers. The cryptochromes CRY1 and CRY2, core repressors of the clock's transcriptional feedback loop, and the opsin OPN3 provide light-responsive components, while tyrosinase and dopachrome tautomerase link short-wavelength exposure to melanin synthesis and pigmentation in melanocytes. Downstream consequences extend to metabolic and inflammatory output, including fatty acid oxidation capacity through the carnitine palmitoyltransferase CPT1B and secretion of lipocalin-2. Disruption of these responses contributes to misaligned sleep-wake timing, altered metabolic rhythms, and light-driven skin damage, placing blue light detection at the interface of photobiology, circadian timing and energy balance.

Cells and organisms adjust their behaviour and gene expression according to how bright the light is, and in vertebrates this response to light intensity is dominated by the photoreceptors of the retina, which must work across many orders of magnitude of illumination without saturating. The genes here trace that circuitry: rhodopsin captures photons, transducin subunits and the regulator RGS9 set the speed at which the phototransduction cascade switches on and off, sodium/calcium-potassium exchangers extrude calcium from the outer segment to drive light adaptation, and peripherin-2 maintains the disc membranes that house the pigment. Retinoid handling, catalase-dependent protection against light-driven oxidative damage, and potassium channel activity shaping downstream signalling also contribute. Loss of these functions produces retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness and defective recovery from bright light.

Bright illumination is both a signal and a hazard for the retina, and this response covers how cells adjust to and survive high light intensity. Excess photon flux drives sustained photopigment bleaching, retinoid turnover and oxidative stress, and failure to buffer it contributes to photoreceptor degeneration and light-induced retinal damage. Several of the genes here act in photoreceptors: potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchangers extrude calcium from outer segments, which is how phototransduction terminates and how sensitivity is reset during light adaptation, while a retinol dehydrogenase handles retinaldehyde produced during the visual cycle, limiting the accumulation of reactive retinoid intermediates. Survival kinase signalling through AKT2 supports cells under the resulting metabolic and oxidative load. The theme is protective adaptation to strong light rather than vision itself, linking sensory transduction, calcium homeostasis and stress resistance.

Photoperiodism is the ability of an organism to read day length and change its physiology accordingly, so that reproduction, metabolism, pigmentation and seasonal behaviour are timed to the time of year rather than to the moment. In humans the same machinery sets sleep-wake timing and the nocturnal melatonin signal, and its disruption underlies seasonal mood change, jet lag and shift-work disorders. Light information enters through retinal photoreceptors and opsins, including the UV-sensitive OPN5, and is converted into a nightly melatonin pulse by AANAT. Interpretation depends on the core clock loop, where CLOCK drives transcription that PER1-3 and CRY1/2 feed back to repress, with FBXL3 and USP2 setting repressor lifetime and phosphatase and kinase activity tuning phase. Downstream hypothalamic peptides such as AGRP, NPY and NMU translate the seasonal signal into altered feeding and energy balance.

Internal circadian clocks run near but not exactly at 24 hours, so they must be reset daily by external cues; entrainment of the circadian clock is the process that locks the oscillator to environmental time, principally the light-dark cycle. Without it, sleep-wake timing, hormone release and metabolic rhythms drift out of phase with the solar day, the basis of jet lag, shift-work intolerance and non-24-hour sleep disorders. Light detected by retinal photoreceptors and opsins such as OPN5 feeds through G protein signalling and CREB coactivation to acutely induce the PER genes, shifting clock phase. Stability of the negative limb sets the magnitude of that shift: FBXL3 targets CRY1 and CRY2 for degradation, USP2 acts as a deubiquitinase on clock proteins, and phosphatase and kinase activities including protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits and SIK1 tune PER turnover so the resetting signal is damped appropriately.

Ultraviolet light damages DNA directly, by forming pyrimidine dimers and bulky adducts, and indirectly through reactive oxygen species, and this pathway covers the defences that let cells survive repeated exposure. Much of it is nucleotide excision repair: XPA recognises the distorted duplex, the ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases of the transcription/repair factor open it, ERCC1-ERCC4 and its partner nucleases incise the damaged strand, and FEN1 processes flap intermediates during resynthesis. Loss of these steps causes xeroderma pigmentosum and extreme sunlight sensitivity with early skin cancer. Antioxidant enzymes such as catalase and glutathione peroxidase dispose of the peroxides UV generates, while MC1R signalling in melanocytes sets the balance of eumelanin pigment that absorbs incoming photons in the first place. Together these arms explain why pigmentation and repair capacity both determine photocarcinogenesis risk.

Response to salt stress is the set of adjustments a cell or organism makes when external salt concentration rises or falls, protecting cells from osmotic swelling, shrinkage and ionic damage. In humans this matters most in the kidney medulla, where cells routinely face extreme sodium chloride and urea gradients, and in systemic control of water balance: vasopressin release, aquaporin-mediated water permeability, and sodium transport by Na/K-ATPase regulatory subunits and cation-chloride cotransporters together set urine concentration and blood volume. Downstream responses include accumulation of compatible osmolytes through aldose reductase, mechanosensitive calcium entry via TRPV4, chaperone induction, mitochondrial calcium handling, and mRNA destabilisation programmes that reshape gene expression. When the stress exceeds adaptive capacity, apoptotic and inflammatory routes engage, linking hypertonicity to tubular cell death, cytokine release and impaired concentrating ability.

Cells and tissues exposed to changing external salt concentration must defend their volume and internal ion balance, and the response to salt stress is the coordinated set of adjustments that makes this possible. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where cells survive osmolarities that would kill other tissue by accumulating compatible osmolytes, remodelling transport, and blunting the DNA damage and apoptosis that hypertonicity provokes. Aldose reductase generates sorbitol as an organic osmolyte, aquaporin water channels and cation-chloride cotransporters move water and ions across the membrane, vasopressin drives systemic water retention, and a stretch-sensitive TRPV4 channel reports cell swelling. Mitochondrial calcium uptake components and the cell death machinery set the threshold between adaptation and loss of the cell. Failure of these adaptations contributes to renal injury and to disturbances of sodium and blood pressure homeostasis.

Humans do not synthesise phenylpropanoids, but they ingest them constantly in plants, spices and tobacco smoke, and the reactions grouped here are how aromatic derivatives of cinnamic acid — coumarin, eugenol, safrole and related compounds — are chemically handled and cleared. The route matters for dietary and drug safety: the same oxidations that detoxify these molecules can also convert them into reactive epoxides and quinones that damage DNA, which is why some naturally occurring flavour compounds are carcinogens. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, including the coumarin 7-hydroxylase CYP2A6 and its relatives CYP2A13 and CYP1A1, introduce hydroxyl groups, and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT1A family then conjugate the products with glucuronic acid to make them excretable. Common variation in these enzymes, particularly CYP2A6 and CYP2D6, produces large person-to-person differences in clearance.

Catechol-containing compounds — chiefly the catecholamine neurotransmitters dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline — are made, stored, released and broken down by this metabolic programme, which sets the tone of motor control, reward, mood, blood pressure and the sympathetic stress response. Synthesis runs from tyrosine through the rate-limiting hydroxylase TH, with GCH1 supplying its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor, then decarboxylation by DDC, beta-hydroxylation by DBH in vesicles, and N-methylation by PNMT to adrenaline in chromaffin cells. Degradation and inactivation proceed through monoamine oxidases MAOA and MAOB, O-methylation by COMT, aldehyde handling by ALDH2, and sulfonation by SULT1A enzymes. Reuptake via the dopamine transporter SLC6A3 terminates signalling, while receptors DRD1–DRD4 transduce it, and transcription factors such as NR4A2, HAND2 and GATA3 specify the neurons and chromaffin cells involved. Failure of dopamine handling and of associated proteins including SNCA, PRKN and PARK7 underlies parkinsonism and other movement and neuropsychiatric disorders.

Formation of catechol-bearing small molecules is essentially the biosynthesis of catecholamine neurotransmitters and hormones — dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline — which drive movement control, reward, mood, sympathetic cardiovascular tone and the adrenal stress response. The route runs from tyrosine through the rate-limiting hydroxylase TH, which requires the tetrahydrobiopterin made by GCH1, then aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine, dopamine β-hydroxylase (a copper enzyme dependent on ATP7A for metal loading) to noradrenaline, and PNMT to adrenaline. Transcription factors including GATA3, HAND2, INSM1 and NR4A2 specify and maintain the noradrenergic, adrenal chromaffin and midbrain dopaminergic identities that express these enzymes, while SLC6A3 recaptures released dopamine. Loss or degeneration of these neurons, and the handling of dopamine by SNCA, PARK7 and VPS35, ties this chemistry directly to Parkinson disease; upstream defects in PAH or biopterin supply cause inherited neurotransmitter deficiencies.

Cells constantly adjust their behaviour to signals generated inside the body rather than outside it, and the response to endogenous stimulus collects that whole repertoire: reacting to hormones, growth factors, cytokines, neuropeptides, steroids and metabolites produced by the organism itself. It is the basis of endocrine and paracrine control of growth, metabolism, reproduction, development and tissue repair, and its miscalibration underlies diabetes, obesity, infertility, fibrosis and hormone-dependent cancers. Represented here are ligands and their receptors (insulin and IGF signalling, TGF-beta/BMP family members with SMAD transducers, FGFs and their kinase receptors, WNTs, leptin, corticotropin-releasing hormone and pituitary hormones), the intracellular relays that carry them — PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK cascades, JAK/STAT with SOCS feedback, cyclic AMP and protein kinase C — and the nuclear receptors, coactivators, chromatin modifiers and microRNAs that convert these inputs into changes in gene expression, secretion and cell fate.

Hormones coordinate physiology between distant tissues, and this collection covers how cells detect and respond to them: changes in gene expression, secretion, enzyme activity, growth and metabolism triggered by an endocrine signal. It spans both major receptor classes. Nuclear receptors for steroids, thyroid hormone, retinoids and vitamin D (ESR1, AR, PGR, NR3C1, THRA/B, VDR, RARs, RXRs) act with coactivators and corepressors such as NCOA1-3, EP300, NCOR1/2 and chromatin modifiers to reprogramme transcription. Peptide hormone receptors for insulin, growth hormone, leptin, glucagon, GnRH, TSH and somatostatin signal through adenylate cyclases and PKA, PI3K-AKT-mTOR with IRS adaptors, and JAK-STAT with SOCS feedback. Downstream effectors include gluconeogenic and lipogenic enzymes, glucose and ion transporters, and circadian clock components. Failure at these nodes underlies insulin resistance and diabetes, hormone-dependent cancers, hormone resistance syndromes, and disorders of growth, calcium balance and reproduction.

Cells and tissues sense dietary and circulating sugars and respond by adjusting secretion, metabolism and gene expression, and this response to carbohydrate is what keeps blood glucose within a narrow range after a meal. Its core is the pancreatic beta cell: glucokinase sets the threshold for glucose metabolism, the GLUT2 transporter and the KATP subunit SUR1 couple that metabolism to membrane depolarization, and SNARE and Rab11 trafficking machinery drives insulin granule exocytosis, while PDX1, MAFA, NKX6-1, NEUROD1 and RFX6 maintain the secretory identity that makes it possible. Downstream and in parallel, incretin receptors, adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin, and the transcription factors ChREBP, SREBF1, HNF4A and TXNIP redirect hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycogen synthesis and lipogenesis. Chronic overload contributes to glucotoxicity, ER stress and beta cell failure, and loss of these components underlies monogenic and type 2 diabetes.

Sucrose in the diet is sensed both metabolically and behaviourally, and the response to a sucrose stimulus covers the changes in gene expression, hormone release and neural signalling that follow a sugar load. The genes here span those levels: adiponectin links adipose tissue to insulin sensitivity and is suppressed as sugar-driven adiposity develops; PNPLA3 acts in hepatic lipid droplet turnover, and its activity connects high carbohydrate intake to fat accumulation in the liver; oxytocin and an AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunit place part of the response in central circuits for appetite, reward and satiety, where sweet intake modulates synaptic drive; a calcitonin receptor-like receptor contributes peptide signalling that shapes feeding and vascular tone. Together they illustrate how sugar consumption is translated into endocrine, hepatic and neural adjustments relevant to obesity, fatty liver disease and sugar preference.

Fructose arriving from diet or from fruit sugars must be sensed, taken up and metabolically routed, and the response to fructose covers the cellular and systemic changes that follow that stimulus. It matters because chronic high fructose intake drives hepatic lipid accumulation, insulin resistance and hyperuricaemia, and the genes here mark the steps where that happens. Uptake across intestinal and hepatic membranes depends on the facilitative transporter SLC2A5 (GLUT5), while GCKR sets how much sugar carbon is committed to glycolytic and lipogenic flux in liver. The transcriptional arm couples the sugar load to fat synthesis and oxidation through SREBF1 and the nuclear receptor PPARA, with XBP1 linking endoplasmic reticulum stress signalling to lipogenic gene expression. Inflammatory output, represented by TNF and the secreted iron- and stress-responsive protein LCN2, ties fructose exposure to metabolic inflammation, connecting this response to nutrient sensing and lipid homeostasis generally.

Hormones released by one tissue are detected by another and converted into changes in gene expression and physiology; this pathway covers that detection and the signalling that follows. It underlies reproduction, growth, metabolic balance, stress responses and circadian timing, and its failure produces endocrine disease from infertility and hypothyroidism to hormone-driven cancers of breast and prostate. Much of the machinery is nuclear receptor based: steroid, thyroid, retinoid, vitamin D and lipid-sensing receptors such as ESR1, AR, PGR, NR3C1, THRA, RARA, VDR and PPARG bind ligand and recruit coactivators including NCOA1/3, MED1 and EP300, or corepressors NCOR1/2 with HDAC1/2, while chromatin modifiers and cytochrome P450 enzymes that make or clear ligands tune the output. Cell-surface arms are also present, with pituitary glycoprotein hormones and their G protein-coupled receptors, growth hormone and prolactin receptors signalling through JAK2, and somatostatin and corticotropin-releasing hormone receptors feeding hypothalamic-pituitary control loops.

Carbohydrate mediated signaling covers the cellular responses triggered when a sugar or glycan is detected, whether as a nutrient or as a marker of foreign material. It links dietary carbohydrate to metabolic gene expression and links microbial sugars to innate immune activation, so its outputs range from insulin secretion and lipogenesis to antifungal defence. One arm is glucose sensing in the pancreatic beta cell and liver, where PDX1 and NKX6-1 maintain beta cell identity and glucose-responsive transcription factors such as MLXIPL and the USF proteins, acting with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, drive lipogenic and glycolytic programmes. The other arm is lectin-based recognition: CLEC7A binds fungal beta-glucan to initiate phagocyte signalling, while AGER responds to advanced glycation end products, tying chronic hyperglycaemia to inflammatory signalling and diabetic tissue damage.

Cells read sugars as information, and carbohydrate-mediated signalling covers the routes by which detection of a carbohydrate ligand or a rise in glucose is converted into a cellular response. Two distinct arms are represented. One is nutrient sensing: transcription factors such as MLXIPL and the USF proteins, together with chromatin remodelling subunits SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 and the islet regulators PDX1 and NKX6-1, couple glucose availability to lipogenic and beta-cell gene programmes and to insulin secretion, with adenylate cyclase amplifying the secretory signal. The other is innate recognition: the lectin receptors CLEC7A and COLEC12 and the advanced glycation end-product receptor AGER bind fungal beta-glucans, glycosylated ligands and modified sugars to trigger phagocytosis and inflammatory responses. Failure on the metabolic side underlies diabetes and dysregulated lipogenesis; failure on the recognition side impairs antifungal defence.

Asymmetric cell division lets one mother cell produce two daughters with different fates, and its regulation sets how often a dividing progenitor self-renews versus generates a differentiating daughter. This balance governs the size and cellular composition of developing tissues, most visibly in the neural progenitors of the cortex, where loss of spindle-orientation control shrinks the brain: mutations in ASPM, a spindle pole protein needed for accurate mitotic spindle positioning, cause primary microcephaly. Control operates at two levels represented here — the machinery that orients the division axis and distributes fate determinants, including the polarity adaptor INSC, and transcriptional and secreted signals such as PAX6, POU5F1 and a WNT ligand that determine whether asymmetric outcomes are favoured. The pathway therefore links mitotic geometry to stem and progenitor cell maintenance, differentiation, and organ growth.

Embryo development covers everything between the fertilized egg and birth: cleavage of the zygote, formation of the germ layers, laying down the body axes, and the organogenesis that produces a viable fetus. Its failure is the commonest cause of early pregnancy loss, and partial failure gives the congenital malformation syndromes of the heart, skeleton, face, kidney and neural tube. The genes gathered here span the machinery that does this work: maternal-effect and pluripotency factors such as NANOG and POU5F1; the Nodal, BMP/TGF-beta, Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, FGF and retinoic acid signalling systems that pattern tissues; ciliary and intraflagellar transport components through which Hedgehog output is read; HOX, SOX, PAX, TBX, DLX and FOX transcription factors that assign regional identity; chromatin remodellers and Polycomb components that lock those choices in; and extracellular matrix, integrin and planar polarity proteins that let cells move and reshape epithelia.
