Post-embryonic development covers everything that happens between the end of embryogenesis and the mature organism: postnatal growth, organ maturation, tissue remodelling and the acquisition of adult physiology. Failure at this stage shows up as growth retardation, skeletal and craniofacial defects, neurodevelopmental disorders and postnatal lethality rather than as early patterning errors. The genes involved span the machinery that sustains and directs late development: morphogen signalling through bone morphogenetic protein, transforming growth factor beta and fibroblast growth factor receptors; transcription factors such as GATA3, KLF4, FOXP2 and BCL11B that specify or maintain differentiated cell identities; chromatin regulators including MECP2, DNMT3A, ATRX and mixed-lineage leukaemia methyltransferases that keep expression programmes stable; and apoptotic and growth-control components — BAX, BAK1, BCL2 and mTOR signalling — that balance cell survival against tissue expansion, together with metabolic and DNA-repair functions needed for continued growth.

Embryonic development from the fertilized zygote through to birth is covered here as a single programme: the sequence of cleavage, implantation, gastrulation, axis formation, somitogenesis and organogenesis that builds a whole animal before it must live independently. Failure at almost any step is lethal in utero or produces congenital malformation, so these genes dominate the catalogue of syndromic birth defects. The machinery spans the major developmental signalling systems — Nodal, BMP and TGF-beta acting through SMAD2/3 and SMAD4, WNT ligands with beta-catenin and LEF1, Hedgehog through PTCH1, SMO and GLI factors, and Notch with DLL ligands and RBPJ — read out by HOX clusters, SOX, PAX, TBX and FOX transcription factors that assign positional identity. Supporting these are maternal-effect and pluripotency regulators such as POU5F1, primary cilium and intraflagellar transport components that transduce Hedgehog, planar cell polarity proteins, extracellular matrix and chromatin remodellers.

Axis specification is the embryonic patterning work that turns a symmetric ball of cells into an organism with head and tail, back and front, left and right, and it fixes the coordinates within which every later organ forms. The genes here are the classic axial signalling systems and their readouts: Nodal, BMP4 and their SMAD transducers, Wnt ligands with the Axin-beta-catenin axis and secreted antagonists such as CER1 and SFRP1, Hedgehog through SHH, PTCH1 and SMO, and Notch-Delta feedback with RIPPLY factors that drives somite segmentation. Downstream, CDX, TBXT, MESP, OTX2, SIX3 and PITX2 impose regional identity, while ciliary and left-right determinants including ARL13B, IFT172 and LEFTY establish asymmetry. Loss or mistiming of these cues produces axial truncations, vertebral segmentation defects, holoprosencephaly, eye malformations and laterality disorders such as situs inversus and heterotaxy.

Vertebrate embryos look outwardly symmetric but place the heart, gut and lungs asymmetrically, and this pathway covers how that body plan is specified: the initial breaking of left-right symmetry at the embryonic node and the downstream patterning that follows it. Motile cilia at the node generate directional flow, sensed through a polycystin channel complex, and the signal is converted into asymmetric Nodal activity restrained on the right by Lefty and Dand5 antagonists, with Pitx2 acting as the left-side transcriptional output. Ciliary assembly and dynein-arm genes, Sonic hedgehog and Notch inputs, and Wnt-dependent segmentation all feed in, alongside cardiac transcription factors such as Nkx2-5 and the Hand and Tbx families that read asymmetry into looping. Loss of these steps produces situs inversus, heterotaxy with complex congenital heart defects, and primary ciliary dyskinesia.

Flavonoids from fruit, tea, soy and vegetables are not human biosynthetic products, so in people this metabolism is essentially the disposal route for dietary polyphenols: absorbed aglycones are oxidised and then conjugated to water-soluble forms for biliary and urinary excretion. The chemistry determines how little of an ingested flavonoid ever reaches tissues as free compound, and it explains why these dietary constituents interfere with drug clearance. A cytochrome P450 introduces or shifts hydroxyl groups on the flavan skeleton, a broad family of UDP-glucuronosyltransferases in the gut and liver adds glucuronic acid, and cytosolic sulfotransferases add sulfate, with several enzymes competing for the same substrates at different affinities. Intestinal lactase-phlorizin hydrolase contributes by cleaving flavonoid glucosides at the brush border so the aglycone can be absorbed. The same enzymes handle drugs, bilirubin and steroid hormones, placing flavonoid handling within general phase I and phase II xenobiotic metabolism.

In humans, alkaloid metabolism covers two linked activities: the handling of plant-derived nitrogenous compounds taken in as drugs or dietary constituents, and the turnover of nicotinamide, the pyridine alkaloid backbone of NAD. Hepatic oxidases such as CYP1A2, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4/5 together with the esterases BCHE and CES2 oxidise and hydrolyse caffeine, nicotine, morphine-type and other alkaloids, setting their clearance rate and accounting for much of the person-to-person variation in drug response and toxicity. In parallel, NAMPT and the nicotinamide riboside kinases NMRK1/2 salvage nicotinamide into NAD, NNMT methylates it for disposal, and NAD-consuming enzymes including CD38 and several PARP family members release nicotinamide again, while a mitochondrial carrier moves NAD across the inner membrane. The pathway therefore connects xenobiotic detoxification to cellular redox and signalling cofactor supply.

Humans encounter alkaloids as plant-derived drugs and poisons, and this alkaloid catabolic route is how the body dismantles them. It is essentially xenobiotic detoxification carried out by liver and plasma enzymes: butyrylcholinesterase and carboxylesterase 2 hydrolyse ester bonds in compounds such as cocaine and heroin, while cytochrome P450 monooxygenases oxidise, demethylate and hydroxylate substrates including codeine, morphinans and related alkaloids using NADPH and molecular oxygen. The products are more polar and readily conjugated and excreted. Because CYP2D6 and CYP3A4/5 differ widely between individuals in expression and sequence, the rate of this breakdown determines both drug efficacy and toxicity — a poor metaboliser gains no analgesia from codeine, an ultrarapid one risks overdose. The same chemistry is the basis for many drug–drug interactions and for succinylcholine sensitivity when cholinesterase activity is deficient.

Embryonic pattern specification lays down the spatial map that tells cells in an early embryo what to become, converting a nearly uniform ball of cells into an organism with a head-to-tail axis, a left-right asymmetry, and a segmented trunk. Its failure produces some of the most severe congenital malformations: holoprosencephaly and midline defects when hedgehog signalling through SHH and PTCH1 breaks down, laterality defects and heterotaxy when NODAL, ZIC3 or ciliary components fail, and vertebral segmentation disorders when the somite clock genes TBX6, MESP2 and the RIPPLY repressors are disturbed. The work is done by a small number of secreted cues — Nodal and BMP ligands read out by SMAD transcription factors, Wnts acting through beta-catenin, FGFs, Delta-Notch — whose graded and oscillating activity is interpreted by CDX, HOX, MEIS and TBXT transcription factors. Germline-associated Tudor-domain proteins tie this to the maternal legacy of the oocyte.

post-embryonic animal morphogenesis covers the shaping of anatomical structures after embryogenesis is complete, during larval, juvenile and postnatal growth when tissues continue to be patterned, remodelled and matured. It matters because many organs — retina, brain, skeletal muscle, gut-associated lymphoid tissue — acquire their final architecture only in this window, and disruption produces developmental malformation rather than early lethality. The genes point to distinct arms of that process: a chromatin remodeller required for proper growth and brain development, an apical polarity protein that maintains photoreceptor and retinal layer organisation, an immunoglobulin-family adhesion receptor guiding axon and dendrite wiring, a glycosyltransferase that matures dystroglycan for muscle and neuronal migration, a homeobox factor patterning spleen and gut lymphoid tissue, and a vesicle-trafficking subunit whose loss causes progressive motor neuron degeneration. Together they link cell adhesion, glycosylation, transcriptional control and trafficking to postnatal tissue form.

Shaping of anatomical structures does not end at birth: tissues continue to grow, remodel and organize their layers through juvenile stages, and post-embryonic animal morphogenesis covers that later construction and patterning of organs. The genes grouped here point to several arms of it. A chromatin remodeller of the SWI/SNF-like family, ATRX, sustains the transcriptional programmes behind postnatal growth and brain development, and its loss causes a syndromic intellectual disability with genital and skeletal anomalies. CRB1 maintains apical polarity and adhesion at the outer limiting membrane of the retina, where failure produces progressive photoreceptor degeneration. DSCAM guides axon and dendrite arborization and self-avoidance; LARGE1 glycosylates dystroglycan so that muscle and neurons engage basement membrane laminin, and its mutation gives congenital muscular dystrophy with brain malformation. NKX2-3 patterns gut and spleen mesenchyme, while VPS54 supports motor neuron maintenance.

Organ morphogenesis is the process by which embryonic tissues are shaped into functioning structures such as the heart, kidney, limb, tooth, inner ear, eye, lung and skin. It links patterning information to physical tissue rearrangement, and its failure produces the large family of congenital malformations: cardiac septal and outflow defects, renal agenesis, cleft palate, polydactyly, deafness and retinal dysplasia. A small number of secreted cues are used repeatedly in different combinations — WNT ligands with FZD receptors and beta-catenin, Hedgehog through PTCH1, SMO and GLI factors, BMP and TGF-beta acting on SMADs, FGFs, Notch ligands and receptors — interpreted by HOX, PAX, SOX, TBX, FOX and DLX transcription factors that assign regional identity. Downstream, cells execute the shape changes: epithelial–mesenchymal transition, planar cell polarity, adhesion and cytoskeletal remodelling, primary cilium signalling, and matrix deposition and proteolysis by collagens and metalloproteinases.

Cells must constantly decide how fast to tear things down — proteins, RNAs, lipids, glycogen, whole organelles — and this collection covers the regulatory layer that sets those rates rather than the breakdown chemistry itself. Control of catabolism matches degradation to nutrient supply, stress and developmental need; when it slips, misfolded proteins and damaged mitochondria accumulate, as in neurodegeneration, or growth signalling runs unchecked, as in cancer. The major arms are visible in the membership: nutrient sensing through mTORC1 with its Rag GTPases, regulators and AMPK, autophagy initiation via ULK1–ATG13–RB1CC1 and the class III PI3K complex with BECN1, selective cargo receptors such as SQSTM1 and OPTN, lysosomal V-ATPase subunits and the transcription factor TFEB, ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and proteasome subunits, plus extensive mRNA-decay control through CCR4–NOT, decapping, nonsense-mediated decay, RNA-binding proteins and microRNAs. Lipolysis and glycogen breakdown are likewise tuned here.

Breakdown is as tightly controlled as synthesis, and this grouping collects the brakes: factors that stop, slow or limit degradative routes for proteins, RNA, lipids and stored carbohydrate. Restraining catabolism lets cells hold onto biosynthetic capacity during growth, protect mRNAs and organelles from premature destruction, and avoid the wasting of muscle and fat that follows unchecked proteolysis and lipolysis. Several arms are visible. Nutrient-sensing through mTOR with its Rag GTPases, raptor and the TSC complex suppresses autophagy when amino acids and growth signals are plentiful, while Rubicon and a transcriptional repressor of lysosomal genes act as further autophagy brakes. Deubiquitinases such as USP7, USP14 and USP5 counteract proteasomal targeting, TIMP family inhibitors block matrix metalloproteinases, and RNA-binding proteins and poly(A) polymerases stabilise transcripts against decay. Perilipins shield lipid droplets. Loss of such restraint contributes to atrophy, neurodegeneration and metabolic disease.

Cells actively dial up their degradative machinery when nutrients run short, proteins misfold, damaged organelles accumulate, or a transcript must be silenced, and this collection captures the regulators that push those breakdown routes faster. The effect spans several destruction systems: autophagy initiation and cargo selection through the ULK1/ATG13 complex, ATG5/ATG7 conjugation machinery, receptors such as SQSTM1, OPTN and CALCOCO2, and mitophagy via PINK1, PRKN, BNIP3 and BNIP3L; ubiquitin-proteasome targeting by cullin-RING and HECT ligases, TRIM proteins and CHIP; lysosomal biogenesis under TFEB with mTORC1, AMPK and sestrins setting the nutrient threshold; cytoplasmic mRNA decay through decapping, CCR4-NOT and exonucleolytic deadenylation, guided by microRNAs, Argonautes, AU-rich element binding proteins and m6A readers; plus lipolysis and lipoprotein turnover. Sustained turnover of this kind underlies proteostasis, energy balance, immune signal termination and protection from neurodegeneration.

Keratinocytes leaving the basal layer of the skin execute a terminal differentiation programme that converts them into the flattened, cross-linked corneocytes of the stratum corneum, producing the barrier that keeps water in and microbes and allergens out. Loss of this programme underlies ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, Netherton syndrome and the barrier defects of atopic dermatitis and psoriasis. Basal keratins such as KRT5 and KRT14 give way to suprabasal KRT1 and KRT10, while filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin and the small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases and enclosed by a lipid envelope built from ceramide and long-chain fatty acid enzymes and the lipid transporter ABCA12. Protease/antiprotease balance (KLK5 with SPINK5) controls desquamation, and Notch, Hedgehog, Wnt, Hippo/YAP and transcription factors including KLF4, IRF6, GRHL and OVOL family members time the switch. Related keratins and cadherins extend the same logic to hair follicle and inner-ear epithelia.

Hormones only act if they reach their targets, and hormone transport covers the machinery that moves them across membranes and out of the cells that make them. Much of the collection is secretory: SNARE and synaptotagmin-family proteins, complexins, Rab GTPases and their effectors, and dense-core granule components such as chromogranin A and carboxypeptidase E, which together drive regulated exocytosis of peptide hormones. Insulin release from pancreatic beta cells is the best-represented example, with glucose sensing through glucokinase and GLUT2, ATP-sensitive potassium channels, and the transcription factors that specify the islet lineage. Carrier proteins are also present, including thyroid hormone transporters of the monocarboxylate and organic anion families and retinol-binding protein. Failures produce diabetes, hypothyroidism and defects in growth, reproductive and stress-axis signalling, linking vesicle trafficking and solute carrier biology to whole-body endocrine control.

anterior/posterior axis specification is the embryonic patterning program that establishes the head-to-tail axis and then elaborates it into ordered segments and organ fields. It is what allows a radially symmetric early embryo to acquire a body plan, and its disruption produces gastrulation failure, axis duplication or truncation, caudal malformations and laterality defects. The genes trace the signalling that sets it up: Nodal and BMP4 with their antagonists Lefty and Cerberus, canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands acting through beta-catenin and Frizzled, and Sonic hedgehog from midline tissue. These inputs converge on transcription factors that read positional value — Brachyury, CDX1/2/4, OTX2 and FOXA2 for axial level, and MESP2 with the RIPPLY repressors and TBX6 for the segmentation clock that partitions presomitic mesoderm into somites. Related activities include primitive streak formation, mesoderm induction and left-right asymmetry.

The head-to-tail body plan is laid down in the early embryo, and anterior/posterior axis specification is the process that establishes it, maintains it, and elaborates it into regionally distinct tissues. Its failure produces axis duplication, truncated or missing posterior structures, and laterality defects, and the same machinery is reused later to segment the trunk. Nodal and its feedback antagonists Lefty1/2 and Cerberus-like signalling set the organiser and break symmetry, while Wnt3, Wnt8A and stabilised beta-catenin with Wnt secretion machinery drive posterior identity through the CDX factors and the mesodermal transcription factors TBXT, MESP1/2 and TBX6. Anterior character is protected by FOXA2, OTX2 and LHX1, and RIPPLY1/2 provide the periodic repression that positions somite boundaries. BMP4, SHH and Polycomb-type chromatin repression coordinate this with dorsoventral patterning and HOX gene deployment along the growing axis.

Early embryos must decide which side becomes back and which becomes belly, and dorsal/ventral axis specification is the patterning programme that makes that choice and then holds it. It sets the coordinate frame on which neural tube, somite and eye patterning are later built; disruption produces axial duplications, failed neural patterning and ocular coloboma. Two opposing morphogen systems dominate. Canonical Wnt signalling through WNT3 and WNT8A stabilises beta-catenin, with AXIN1/AXIN2 and the secreted antagonist SFRP1 restraining it and CXXC4 and CAPRIN2 tuning the output. BMP signalling through BMPR1A and SMAD transducers ventralises, while the inhibitory SMAD6 limits that arm. Downstream transcription factors including PAX6 and VAX2 translate the resulting gradients into regional identity, notably along the dorsoventral axis of the developing retina and optic fissure.

Anterior/posterior pattern specification is the embryonic process that assigns positional identity along the head-to-tail axis, so that vertebrae, somites, limb segments, gut regions and brain subdivisions each form in the right place. Its output is read out by the HOX clusters, whose collinear expression encodes axial level; CDX factors and retinoic acid metabolism set the posterior boundaries, while Polycomb components and histone methyltransferases keep the code stable once established. Layered on top are the gradient-forming signals that organize the axis: WNT ligands with beta-catenin and LEF/TCF output, NODAL and BMP with SMAD transducers and their antagonists NOGGIN, CERBERUS and DKK1, SHH, and FGF8. A Notch-driven oscillator built from HES/HEY repressors, LFNG, DLL1/DLL3 and MESP/RIPPLY segments the presomitic mesoderm. Failure produces vertebral and rib malformations, spondylocostal dysostosis, caudal and laterality defects, and homeotic shifts in segment identity.

Dorsal/ventral pattern formation sets up the back-to-belly axis of the embryo, so that cells at different positions along it adopt different fates — floor plate versus roof plate in the neural tube, ventral versus dorsal forebrain, limb and somite polarity. Failure produces holoprosencephaly, neural tube and skeletal malformations. Three opposing gradients do most of the work: BMP signals from the dorsal side acting through BMPR1A/B and ACVR1, antagonised by secreted binders such as chordin, noggin, gremlins and NBL1; Wnt ligands with beta-catenin and Axin-based regulation; and Sonic hedgehog from notochord and floor plate, transduced by PTCH1, SMO, SUFU and GLI factors within the primary cilium, which explains the presence of intraflagellar transport components, ARL13B and TULP3. These gradients are read out by position-specific transcription factors including NKX2-2, PAX6, PAX7, DBX1, GSX2 and LHX genes, which fix regional identity and subsequent differentiation.

Limbs, kidneys and other outgrowths must know how far from the body they are, and proximal/distal pattern formation is the regionalization that assigns cell fates along that axis, from shoulder to fingertip. It explains why a limb bud produces stylopod, zeugopod and autopod in the right order, and why its disruption yields shortened or duplicated segments and digit malformations. Positional identity is encoded largely by posterior HOX genes of the A, C and D clusters acting with PBX cofactors, while opposing retinoic acid signalling from ALDH1A2 and its degradation by CYP26B1 set a proximal-to-distal gradient. Mesenchymal FGF10 sustains outgrowth, hedgehog transduction through GLI factors and BMP antagonism by GREM1 feed back on it, and Wnt/beta-catenin, Notch ligands and IRX and DLX transcription factors refine the resulting territories. The same logic patterns branching epithelia and the developing kidney.

Cells identify appropriate partners before committing to adhesion or fusion, and cell-cell recognition covers the surface molecules that make such discrimination possible. The dominant theme here is gamete recognition: zona pellucida glycoproteins form the egg coat that sperm must bind and penetrate, acrosomal enzymes and serine proteases remodel that coat, and the IZUMO1-JUNO receptor pair licenses sperm-egg plasma membrane fusion, with tetraspanins CD9 and CD81 and testis-restricted factors such as TEX101, SPACA6 and ZPBP required for sperm to become fusion-competent. Loss of these steps causes infertility without affecting gamete production. A second arm concerns immune recognition, where chemokine receptor CCR7 and its ligands guide lymphocytes and dendritic cells into contact, and lectins and adaptors shape the resulting synapse. Both arms depend on carbohydrate modification and on cytoskeletal adaptors that stabilise the contact once made.

Intracellular water homeostasis keeps cell volume and osmolarity within tolerable limits, allowing cells to survive osmotic challenge without swelling, shrinking, or lysing. It matters wherever fluid moves across epithelia and membranes in bulk: kidney tubules concentrating urine, brain astrocytes buffering the perivascular space, and secretory tissues handling large water fluxes. The core machinery is the aquaporin water channels, which provide selective transmembrane pores rather than relying on slow diffusion through the lipid bilayer; AQP1 serves vascular and tubular water flow, AQP4 dominates astrocyte endfeet and shapes brain water content and oedema, and AQP11 maintains intracellular and endoplasmic reticulum compartments, with its loss producing renal cyst formation. Hormonal input from secretin and its receptor links water transport to ductal fluid secretion, while CLN3 ties lysosomal and vacuolar volume control into the same regulatory picture.

Cells must hold their water content steady against osmotic swings, because volume changes distort membrane tension, cytoskeletal organisation and solute concentrations, and unchecked swelling kills. Intracellular water homeostasis covers the channels and signals that set how fast water crosses membranes and how the cell responds to osmotic stress. Aquaporins provide the conduits: AQP1 in capillary endothelium and other absorptive epithelia, AQP4 at astrocyte endfeet where it governs brain water movement and contributes to cerebral oedema, and AQP11 in an intracellular position in kidney proximal tubule and other tissues, where its loss causes vacuolated cells and polycystic kidney disease. Hormonal input arrives through G protein-coupled receptors, including the secretin receptor, whose ligand drives fluid secretion. CLN3, mutated in juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, links lysosomal function and cell volume regulation to the same balance.

Oocyte differentiation is the maturation of a female germ cell into a fertilizable egg, the step that determines a woman's reproductive lifespan and the developmental competence of the embryo that follows. Its failure underlies premature ovarian insufficiency, oocyte maturation arrest and infertility. The genes trace the whole trajectory: transcription factors such as FIGLA, SOHLH1/2, ZGLP1 and FOXL2 commit and sustain the oocyte program; meiotic recombination and cohesion factors including DMC1, REC8, BRCA2 and ATM execute and monitor prophase I; and MOS, CCNB1, CDC25B, WEE2 and FBXO5 drive meiotic arrest and resumption downstream of NPPC-NPR2 and PDE3A control of cyclic nucleotides. In parallel, piRNA-associated TDRD proteins and maternal RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, ZAR1, YBX2, TUT4/7 and YTHDF2 silence transposons and store, extend and time the destruction of maternal mRNAs. Granulosa communication via GDF9 and follicle growth signals couple oocyte quality to the surrounding follicle.

Oocyte differentiation is the maturation of a female germ cell into a fertilizable egg, and it determines both the size of the ovarian reserve and the quality of the maternal contribution to the embryo. Transcription factors such as FIGLA, SOHLH1/2, NOBOX-like regulators, FOXL2 and ZGLP1 commit and sustain the oocyte programme, while meiotic components including DMC1, REC8, TRIP13 and MEIOC execute recombination and chromosome cohesion. Because the growing oocyte is transcriptionally quiescent, much of the control is post-transcriptional: Tudor-domain proteins and piRNA factors silence transposons, and TUT4/TUT7, YTHDF2, YBX2 and ZAR1 manage maternal mRNA storage, tailing and timed decay. Cell-cycle arrest and release depend on CCNB1, MOS, WEE2, FBXO5 and CDC25B, with granulosa-derived signals such as GDF9, NPPC-NPR2 and IGF1 coordinating follicle growth. Defects cause premature ovarian insufficiency, oocyte maturation arrest and early embryonic failure.

Glial cell differentiation is the route by which neural progenitors and Schwann cell precursors become astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia-supporting partners and peripheral myelinating glia, the cells that insulate axons, buffer extracellular potassium and glutamate, and sustain neuronal metabolism. Its failure or misdirection underlies dysmyelinating leukodystrophies, impaired nerve regeneration, and the reactive gliosis and glioma phenotypes seen in injured or transformed brain. Lineage choice is set by transcription factors including OLIG1/2, SOX10, SOX9, NKX2-2, NFIA and MYRF, acting against the Notch effectors HES1 and HES5 and the inhibitory ID proteins, and instructed by Sonic hedgehog, BMP, FGF and gp130 cytokines such as CNTF, LIF and IL6. Axon-derived neuregulin acting through ERBB2/ERBB3 drives Schwann cell myelination, while downstream PI3K-AKT-mTOR and MAPK cascades, chromatin regulators and RNA-binding factors such as QKI convert these cues into expression of myelin proteins like PLP1, MAG and CNP.

Cardioblast differentiation is the step at which mesodermal cells commit to a cardiac fate while remaining proliferative precursors rather than finished muscle. It sets the size and patterning of the heart fields from which chambers, valves and outflow tract later form, and disruption of these regulators underlies congenital heart malformations such as septal and conduction defects. Mesendoderm factors including EOMES and TBXT feed into a core cardiac transcriptional programme built on NKX2-5, ISL1, TBX5, TBX2 and the SRF cofactor MYOCD, which together drive expression of contractile and cardiac identity genes. Signalling inputs set the boundaries: NOTCH1 acting through RBPJ, TGFB2 and neuregulin instruct neighbouring cells, GREM1 antagonises BMP, and REST restrains neuronal genes. Planar polarity via PRICKLE1 links commitment to the oriented cell behaviours that shape the forming heart tube.

Before meiotic divisions can segregate chromosomes cleanly, chromatin must be compacted into discrete, mechanically robust rods, and that compaction is what meiotic chromosome condensation provides. Without it, chromosomes tangle, anaphase bridges form, and gametes inherit broken or aneuploid genomes. The genes here are the condensin machinery: an SMC2-SMC4 heterodimer forms the ATPase core that entraps and loops DNA, while distinct kleisin and HEAT-repeat subunits define the two holocomplexes, with NCAPH and NCAPD2 building condensin I and NCAPH2 and NCAPD3 building condensin II. Loop extrusion by these complexes shortens and stiffens chromosome arms and helps resolve sister chromatids and homologue pairs once recombination is complete. The same complexes act in mitosis, but in meiosis their output must accommodate a reductional first division, linking chromatin architecture directly to fertility and to the prevention of chromosomally abnormal offspring.

Cells sense and react to fluctuations in metal ion levels, and this response to metal ion stimulus covers the sensing, buffering, transport and transcriptional adjustments that keep iron, zinc, copper, calcium and toxic heavy metals within tolerable limits. Without it, free metals catalyse oxidative damage or mislocalise, producing iron overload and anaemia, copper toxicosis, and the metal-associated protein aggregation seen in neurodegeneration. The metal-responsive transcription factor MTF1 drives metallothionein genes that chelate zinc and cadmium, while hepcidin, transferrin receptors and divalent metal transporters set systemic iron availability and the copper-transporting ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B handle secretion and excretion. Zinc and calcium fluxes run through SLC30 exporters, store-operated and TRP channels, ryanodine receptors and calmodulin-dependent effectors, feeding into kinase, NFAT and stress-response signalling. Antioxidant and detoxification arms, including NFE2L2 targets, superoxide dismutases and heme oxygenase, limit the resulting redox injury.

Cells and tissues sense iron availability and adjust uptake, storage, use and disposal accordingly, and this adaptive response to iron ion levels keeps a redox-active metal useful rather than toxic. Too little iron starves haem synthesis and oxidative metabolism; too much drives Fenton chemistry, lipid peroxidation and organ damage, as in haemochromatosis and iron-loading anaemias. Systemic control runs through the hepatocyte axis in which HFE, TFR2 and BMP6 signalling set hepcidin output, while transferrin and its receptor deliver iron to cells and DMT1 and the ferrireductase CYBRD1 move it across membranes. Intracellularly, the iron-regulatory RNA-binding aconitase ACO1 couples cytosolic iron to mRNA fate, haem enzymes such as ALAD and CPOX consume the metal, and hypoxia signalling through HIF1A links iron to oxygen sensing. Autophagy components contribute to ferritin turnover and iron recycling, and iron-driven oxidative stress in dopaminergic neurons connects this biology to neurodegeneration.

Cells must react to the arrival of ferrous iron, which is both a needed cofactor and a source of damaging free radicals through Fenton chemistry. This response to iron(II) couples sensing of the labile iron pool to changes in gene expression, iron sequestration and autophagic turnover, and its failure contributes to iron overload toxicity, oxidative injury and iron-dependent cell death. Cytosolic aconitase doubles as an iron-regulatory RNA-binding protein, switching between enzymatic and post-transcriptional roles depending on iron availability so that transferrin receptor and ferritin messages are adjusted accordingly. Lipocalin 2 binds siderophore-bound iron extracellularly and limits its availability. Core autophagy components including BECN1, ATG5 and an LC3 isoform support ferritin turnover and organelle clearance under iron stress, while alpha-synuclein and the beta-cell factor PDX1 link this biology to neuronal and pancreatic vulnerability to excess iron.

Manganese is needed as a cofactor for enzymes such as mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, yet in excess it is a neurotoxin, and the cellular response to a manganese ion stimulus determines which of those outcomes prevails. The genes here mark the two main arms of that response: metal handling and transport, including a lysosomal polyamine/cation transporter mutated in juvenile parkinsonism and the transferrin receptor route that manganese shares with iron, and stress signalling through the PERK kinase, its substrate eIF2α, and ATF4, the integrated stress response branch of the unfolded protein response that reports on endoplasmic reticulum and redox strain. Mitochondrial and quality-control factors including parkin and LRRK2 link manganese overload to oxidative damage and to the dopaminergic neuron loss of manganism and Parkinson's disease, while amyloid precursor protein and its processing enzymes tie metal exposure to neurodegenerative proteostasis more broadly.

Zinc is both an obligate cofactor and a potential toxin, so cells sense its level and respond by changing gene expression, buffering, and transport. This response to zinc ion stimulus protects against metal overload while supplying zinc to metalloenzymes, and its failure contributes to neuronal zinc toxicity after ischaemia or seizure, to defective insulin granule storage, and to disordered metallothionein induction. The metal-responsive transcription factor MTF1 drives expression of the metallothionein family, which chelates excess zinc, and of the exporter SLC30A1; other members of that efflux family load zinc into synaptic vesicles, insulin granules, and milk. Zinc also acts as a signal: it modulates ligand-gated channels including glycine and GABA-A receptors and P2X purinoceptors, gates proton and potassium channels, and alters enzymes such as ALAD and PARP1. Related processes include oxidative stress defence and neurotransmission.

During embryogenesis a group of cells must be told not merely to form an organ but which organ to form, and the specification of animal organ identity is that decision: a primordium is assigned the aggregate of characteristics that make it a kidney rather than a lung, a heart rather than a limb. The genes here are the signalling systems that regionalize embryonic fields — WNT ligands with beta-catenin, AXIN2 and the antagonist DKK1; FGF ligands acting through FGFR1 and the adaptor FRS2 under SPRY1 feedback; BMP2 and BMP4; Notch via RBPJ; and hedgehog output through GLI3 — read out by organ-selective transcription factors such as PAX2 and PAX8 in the nephric lineage, ISL1, MEF2C and MESP1 in cardiac progenitors, SIX1, and posterior HOX genes. GDNF and ROBO receptors couple identity to subsequent branching and axon guidance. Errors produce organ agenesis, duplication, or structures with the wrong regional character, as in renal and cardiac congenital malformation.

Proton movement across membranes sets gastric acid secretion, lysosomal and endosomal acidification, and the electrochemical gradients that drive ATP synthesis, and this regulatory layer tunes how fast and how far those protons are pumped. The genes involved span distinct settings: the gastric H+/K+-ATPase alpha subunit responsible for acidifying the stomach lumen, and a subunit of the vacuolar-type ATPase whose loss blocks osteoclast acidification of the bone resorption lacuna and causes infantile malignant osteopetrosis. A mitochondrial prohibitin-family protein and a sphingosine kinase contribute to organellar and lipid-signalling control of pump activity, while a cytokine input indicates that inflammatory signalling can modulate epithelial acid handling. Collectively this biology determines luminal and organellar pH, with consequences for digestion, bone remodelling, and degradative compartment function.

X-rays deposit energy that breaks both strands of DNA, and the cellular response to X-ray exposure determines whether an irradiated cell repairs the damage, arrests, or dies. This is the biology that sets tissue radiosensitivity, underlies the toxicity and efficacy of radiotherapy, and when defective produces the radiation hypersensitivity and cancer predisposition seen in ataxia-telangiectasia and related breakage syndromes. ATM heads the damage-sensing arm, signalling to checkpoint and apoptotic effectors including caspase-3 and to cyclin D-dependent control of cell cycle entry. Repair proceeds by two routes represented here: homologous recombination using RAD51 with BRCA2, BLM and the RAD51 paralogue XRCC2, and non-homologous end joining through LIG4, XRCC4 and the Ku subunit XRCC6. Nucleotide excision and mismatch repair factors handle base damage, while stress-induced genes such as LCN2 mark the wider transcriptional reaction to irradiation.

Shaping the body of the embryo requires that fields of cells be told where they are and then told to grow, fold, or fuse accordingly, and this set covers the signalling and transcriptional machinery that builds and organizes the anatomical structures of the soma. Its outputs are the skeleton, craniofacial structures, palate, limbs and connective tissue; loss of individual members produces recognizable human malformation syndromes, including cleft palate, craniofacial and cardiac outflow defects, and skeletal dysplasia. Morphogen pathways dominate: WNT3 and LEF1 with the antagonist DKK1, hedgehog signalling through IHH and its co-receptor CDON, BMP inhibition by NOG and GREM2, and all three TGF-beta ligands. These act on homeodomain and T-box regulators such as MSX1, DLX5, PAX9 and TBX1, on chromatin factors including EP300, NIPBL and ANKRD11, on RAS-pathway components, and on ciliary and planar-polarity proteins that orient tissue growth. Extracellular matrix remodelling by COL1A1 and MMP2 executes the resulting form.

Shaping the embryonic soma means turning an unpatterned early embryo into a body with an axis, a closed neural tube, and correctly positioned organ fields. Failure produces some of the most severe congenital malformations: holoprosencephaly, neural tube defects, skeletal and craniofacial anomalies, and laterality disturbances. Several of the genes here converge on the primary cilium and the Hedgehog signalling it supports, including an intraflagellar transport component, a centriolar and basal body protein mutated in oral-facial-digital syndrome, a planar cell polarity effector required for ciliogenesis, and a cell-surface Hedgehog co-receptor. Others act through cytoskeletal remodelling during the collective cell movements of gastrulation and neurulation, through BMP antagonism that tunes dorsoventral patterning, or through transcriptional control of early lineage commitment. Together they link ciliary signalling, morphogen gradients, and coordinated cell movement to the construction of body form.

Cells read the ambient concentration of sugars and convert that reading into changes in gene expression, so that metabolic and developmental programmes match nutrient supply. This sugar-mediated signalling underlies the switch between fed and fasted transcriptional states in liver and the glucose responsiveness of pancreatic beta cells; when it fails, lipogenic and insulin-secretory gene programmes are set inappropriately, contributing to hypertriglyceridaemia and diabetes. The carbohydrate response element binding factor encoded by MLXIPL drives glycolytic and lipogenic genes when sugar metabolites accumulate, while USF1 and USF2 bind related E-box elements in the same promoters. PDX1 and NKX6-1 specify and maintain beta cell identity and link glucose sensing to insulin gene transcription, and chromatin remodelling subunits such as SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 provide the promoter accessibility these factors require. The overall theme is nutrient-controlled transcription rather than a single hormone cascade.

Ionizing radiation from X-rays, gamma rays or decaying isotopes breaks both strands of DNA and generates reactive oxygen species, and the cellular response to that insult decides whether a cell repairs itself, arrests, or dies. This determines tissue tolerance of radiotherapy and underlies the cancer predisposition seen when its components are lost. Damage sensing runs through the ATM and ATR kinases, which phosphorylate histone H2AX and CHEK2 and stabilise p53; downstream, CDKN1A enforces cell cycle arrest while BAX, BAK1 and PUMA commit irreparably damaged cells to apoptosis. Repair proceeds by homologous recombination using BRCA1, BRCA2 and RAD51, or by non-homologous end joining through DNA-PK, LIG4 and XRCC4. Ubiquitin signalling at break sites, antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and GPX1, and inflammatory cytokine output complete a response spanning genome maintenance, redox defence and cell fate control.

Ultraviolet-B wavelengths penetrate the epidermis and generate cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and other helix-distorting lesions, and the response to UV-B is the coordinated cellular reaction that follows: damage recognition and repair, cell cycle arrest, inflammation, and a decision between survival and death. It matters because its failure underlies sunburn, photoaging and keratinocyte carcinogenesis; inherited defects in the nucleotide excision repair components here, XPC and the transcription-coupled repair helicase ERCC6, cause extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition. Lesion detection feeds into p21-mediated arrest downstream of p53, while BCL2 sets the apoptotic threshold and mismatch repair contributes to lesion processing. In parallel, stress-activated p38 kinases and NF-κB signalling drive cytokine output, an inflammasome sensor triggers keratinocyte inflammatory death, and hyaluronidases and matrix-associated proteins remodel the dermal extracellular environment after irradiation.

response to UV-C is the cellular reaction to short-wavelength ultraviolet light, the most genotoxic part of the UV spectrum, which forms pyrimidine dimers and other helix-distorting lesions that stall replication forks and block transcription. Cells that cannot mount this response accumulate mutations and die or transform, and inherited defects in its components underlie photosensitivity and cancer-prone syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and Werner syndrome. The genes span lesion removal and tolerance: the nucleotide excision repair endonuclease ERCC5 excises damaged DNA, POLH performs translesion synthesis across dimers, and BRCA2 and the WRN helicase restart or protect damaged forks. Chromatin factors including HMGN1 open damaged templates for repair, while MAP3K4 signalling and transcriptional regulators such as YY1 and BCL3 couple damage sensing to stress kinase activation, altered gene expression, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

Short-wavelength ultraviolet light in the UV-C band is absorbed directly by DNA, producing cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and other helix-distorting photoproducts, and this response is how a cell detects that damage and decides between repair, arrest and death. What it enables is genome stability after photodamage; failure of its components underlies sun-sensitivity syndromes, premature ageing and cancer predisposition. Several members act on the lesions themselves: a nucleotide excision repair endonuclease removes damaged strands, a translesion polymerase copies past dimers that would otherwise stall replication forks, and helicase and recombination factors such as WRN and BRCA2 handle the broken or collapsed forks that follow. Alongside repair, chromatin proteins and transcriptional regulators including HMGN1 and YY1 reshape gene expression, while a stress-activated kinase cascade feeds into checkpoint and apoptotic decisions, linking photodamage sensing to cell fate.

Response to lithium ion covers the cellular and transcriptional changes triggered by exposure to Li+, the ion used therapeutically as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder and known for its narrow therapeutic window and effects on kidney and thyroid. The genes trace lithium's two best-understood molecular targets: glycogen synthase kinase-3, inhibited by lithium to alter Wnt and insulin signalling and downstream programs of proliferation and differentiation, and inositol monophosphatase, whose blockade depletes inositol and dampens phosphoinositide second-messenger cycling. Downstream consequences appear as altered adenylate cyclase and calcineurin-NFAT signalling, changed glutamate receptor function at synapses, and shifts in differentiation-linked transcription factors governing adipocyte, myogenic and hepatic programs. Sodium-dicarboxylate transporters and chaperone-mediated stress responses place ion handling and cellular homeostasis alongside neuronal excitability in the overall reaction to lithium.

Cells and tissues exposed to lithium ions mount a characteristic set of transcriptional and signalling changes, and this response underlies both the mood-stabilising action of lithium in bipolar disorder and its side effects on kidney, thyroid and bone. The best-understood targets appear here: glycogen synthase kinase-3 alpha, which lithium inhibits and whose inhibition reshapes Wnt, insulin and circadian outputs, and inositol monophosphatase, whose blockade depletes the inositol pool that supports phosphoinositide second-messenger cycling. Downstream consequences include altered adenylate cyclase signalling, calcineurin-NFAT-dependent transcription, glutamate receptor availability at synapses, and shifts in differentiation programmes for adipocytes, muscle and epithelium through factors such as CEBPA, MYOG, ID2 and hedgehog signalling. Dicarboxylate transporters and cell-cycle regulators round out the cellular adjustment to the ion.

Vascular transport is the movement of nutrients, ions, drugs and signalling molecules across the endothelial and perivascular cells that line blood vessels, determining what reaches a tissue from the circulation and what is returned to it. It is the basis of blood-tissue barrier function, most conspicuously at the blood-brain barrier, where influx carriers such as the glucose transporter SLC2A1, the thyroid hormone carrier SLCO1C1 and the lipid transporter MFSD2A admit required substrates while efflux pumps of the ABC family, including ABCB1 and ABCG2, expel xenobiotics and limit drug penetration. Amino acid, monocarboxylate, nucleoside and organic ion carriers set the composition of the interstitial space, receptor-mediated routes such as transferrin receptor and LRP1 handle iron, lipoproteins and protein clearance, and ATPase pumps maintain the ion gradients these carriers depend on. Loss of selectivity here underlies barrier breakdown, oedema and altered drug delivery.

Cells spend a large share of their ATP keeping ion concentrations different on the two sides of a membrane, and this pathway covers the pumps and accessory subunits that establish or maintain that transmembrane electrochemical gradient. The resulting sodium and potassium gradients set the resting potential of excitable cells, drive secondary active transport of sugars, amino acids and drugs, and support gastric acid secretion by a related proton pump. Catalytic alpha subunits of the Na+/K+-ATPase pair with beta subunits and with small FXYD proteins that tune pump kinetics in a tissue-specific way, while an organic cation transporter exploits the gradient for uptake of cationic substrates. Mutations in the neuronal and glial alpha isoforms cause hemiplegic migraine, alternating hemiplegia and dystonia-parkinsonism, and the presence of BAX and BAK links gradient loss to mitochondrial membrane permeabilization during apoptosis.

The interior of a eukaryotic cell is partitioned into interconnected membrane compartments, and endomembrane system organization covers the building, shaping and remodelling of those compartments: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi stacks, endosomes, lysosomes, secretory vesicles and the nuclear envelope. It underlies secretion, membrane protein biogenesis, cargo sorting, organelle inheritance during division, and the repair and sealing of damaged membranes. Reticulon and REEP proteins together with atlastin GTPases curve and fuse ER tubules; COPII components and Sec16 organize export sites; golgins, GRASPs and the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex hold Golgi architecture; Rab GTPases, SNAREs and their regulators direct tethering and fusion; ESCRT subunits and CHMP proteins deform membranes for multivesicular body formation, nuclear envelope resealing and abscission. Mutations in these components cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, Hermansky-Pudlak pigment and platelet defects, congenital glycosylation disorders and lysosomal storage disease, and several members act in sperm acrosome formation and membrane fusion at fertilization.

Complex I, the NADH dehydrogenase of the respiratory chain, is the largest entry point for electrons into oxidative phosphorylation, and building it requires that roughly forty subunits encoded by two genomes be joined in the correct order within the inner mitochondrial membrane. Assembly proceeds through modular intermediates: mitochondrially encoded subunits such as ND1, ND2 and ND5 are inserted into the membrane with help from insertases and translocase-associated factors, while nuclear-encoded core subunits form the matrix arm that carries the flavin site and the iron-sulfur relay, with dedicated chaperones handling cofactor delivery and methylation steps. Assembly factors act transiently and are not retained in the finished enzyme. Failure at almost any step lowers complex I activity and causes infantile mitochondrial disease, including Leigh syndrome, encephalomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, reflecting how strictly proton pumping and NAD+ regeneration depend on complete assembly.

Selenium is a trace element that cells must sense and respond to, both because selenoproteins depend on it and because excess is toxic. This response encompasses the changes in gene expression and enzyme activity that follow exposure to selenium ions, tuning antioxidant capacity and inflammatory output. Several members are selenoproteins themselves: glutathione peroxidase GPX1 reduces hydroperoxides, thioredoxin reductase TXNRD2 maintains mitochondrial thiol redox balance, SELENOP serves as the plasma carrier that distributes selenium to tissues, and SELENOM resides in the endoplasmic reticulum. Alongside them sit the mitochondrial superoxide dismutase SOD2 and the prostaglandin-generating enzymes PTGS2 and HPGDS, with IL13 linking the response to type 2 immune signalling, and ALAD in haem synthesis is a known target of metal ion inhibition. The pathway connects dietary micronutrient status to oxidative stress defence, eicosanoid production and inflammation.

Detoxification of copper ion protects cells from the redox chemistry of free copper, which catalyses hydroxyl radical formation and displaces metals from the active sites of other proteins. Cells need copper as an enzyme cofactor but can tolerate almost none of it unbound, so excess is buffered or exported. The bulk of this capacity comes from the metallothionein family, small cysteine-rich proteins induced by metal load that clamp copper in thiolate clusters and hold it in an inert pool; ATP7A moves copper out of the cytosol into the secretory pathway for efflux or delivery to cuproenzymes, and DJ-1 contributes antioxidant defence against copper-driven damage. Loss of this buffering underlies copper toxicity in liver and brain, links to Wilson and Menkes disease physiology, and modulates sensitivity to copper-dependent cell death; the same metallothioneins also handle zinc and cadmium.

Copper is needed as an enzyme cofactor but is dangerous when free, since redox cycling of the ion generates reactive oxygen species and displaces other metals from their binding sites. Detoxification of copper ion keeps the cytosolic free pool near zero by buffering the metal in high-affinity thiol-rich proteins and exporting the excess. The metallothionein family, represented here by many closely related MT1 genes along with MT2A, MT3 and MT4, provides cysteine clusters that sequester copper and zinc and are induced when metal levels rise. The ATP7A copper-transporting ATPase moves copper across membranes for efflux and for loading onto cuproenzymes; its loss causes Menkes disease, while related transport failure underlies hepatic copper overload. DJ-1 contributes an oxidative-stress-protective arm, linking metal handling to redox homeostasis and neuronal survival.

Cells and whole organisms survive repeated or sustained high temperature by raising their heat tolerance in advance, and heat acclimation is that adaptive adjustment. It matters because unfolded and aggregated proteins accumulate quickly at elevated temperature; acclimated cells resist damage that would otherwise kill them, and the same capacity underlies thermotolerance in tissues such as skeletal muscle and the vasculature during heat stress. The core effectors here are inducible HSP70 chaperones, which bind exposed hydrophobic surfaces on heat-denatured proteins and support refolding or degradation. Their induction is limited by heat shock factor binding proteins, which restrain the transcriptional response so it resolves rather than persists, and a chromatin-associated component links the response to transcriptional regulation. Together this represents a negative-feedback-controlled proteostasis programme rather than an open-ended stress reaction, and its loss leaves cells vulnerable to proteotoxic collapse.

Lead is a non-essential heavy metal that cells cannot excrete efficiently, and the response to lead ion stimulus covers the changes in gene expression, enzyme activity and metabolism that follow exposure. Its most direct victims are the heme biosynthetic enzymes: delta-aminolevulinate dehydratase and coproporphyrinogen oxidase are inhibited by lead, so heme synthesis falters and porphyrin precursors accumulate, which accounts for the anaemia of lead poisoning. In the nervous system, exposure shifts amyloid precursor protein processing through BACE1 and alters tau, links that underlie the developmental neurotoxicity and cognitive deficits seen in exposed children. Other members point to the downstream consequences: catalase and the uncoupling protein UCP2 against oxidative stress, autophagy components such as beclin 1 and an LC3 family member, DNA methyltransferase activity for epigenetic reprogramming, and parathyroid hormone with a renal phosphate transporter for disturbed bone and kidney handling.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a signalling molecule and a source of oxidative damage, so cells control how much of it is made and how fast it is removed; this regulatory layer sets that balance. Its outputs matter for thyroid hormone synthesis, mucosal antimicrobial defence, redox-dependent kinase and transcription factor signalling, and protection of mitochondria from oxidative injury. Control operates on both sides: maturation factors and cytosolic organizer and activator subunits, together with small Rho-family GTPases, govern assembly and output of NADPH oxidase complexes, while mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and a thiol peroxidase determine how much peroxide accumulates and how quickly it is reduced. PINK1 links the process to mitochondrial quality control, and altered peroxide handling in this setting, along with alpha-synuclein and metallothionein involvement, connects the pathway to neurodegeneration and to inflammatory tissue damage.

Membrane invagination — the infolding of a bilayer to internalize material or bud a vesicle inward — is the shared geometric step behind phagocytosis, apoptotic cell clearance, endocytic uptake and autophagosome formation. It matters because macrophages and microglia rely on it to remove dying cells, debris and pathogens without provoking inflammation, and failure of that clearance contributes to autoimmunity, atherosclerosis and neurodegeneration. Recognition receptors such as scavenger and phosphatidylserine-binding proteins, immunoglobulin Fc receptors, integrins and TREM2 mark the target, then Rho-family GTPases including RAC1, CDC42 and RHOA, with their regulators and the DOCK1-ELMO1 module, drive actin remodelling beneath the deforming membrane. Sorting nexins with BAR domains and clathrin adaptors bend the bilayer, myosin and gelsolin supply mechanical force, and ESCRT components complete scission. Scramblases of the XKR and ANO6 families expose the lipid signals that initiate engulfment, while BECN1 links the same curvature machinery to autophagy.

Ionising gamma radiation shatters DNA and floods cells with reactive oxygen, and the response to gamma radiation is the coordinated programme that detects this damage, halts the cell cycle, repairs what it can and kills cells that are beyond saving. It determines tissue tolerance to radiotherapy and diagnostic exposure, and its failure underlies radiosensitivity syndromes and radiation-induced cancer. Damage sensing runs through the ATM and ATR kinases and CHEK2 to stabilise p53, which imposes arrest via the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A and is itself restrained by MDM2. Double-strand breaks are rejoined by non-homologous end joining components including PRKDC, LIG4 and the Ku subunits XRCC5 and XRCC6, or repaired by homologous recombination using RAD51 and BRCA2, while PARP1 and POLB handle base damage. Apoptotic commitment is set by the balance of BAX, BAK1 and BCL2, and antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and GPX1 buffer oxidative injury.

The COP9 signalosome is an eight-subunit complex that removes the ubiquitin-like modifier NEDD8 from cullin scaffolds, and this pathway concerns how its subunits come together into that functional assembly. Because deneddylation resets cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, the intact complex governs how quickly substrates such as cell cycle inhibitors, transcription factors and damaged-DNA sensors are marked for proteasomal destruction; without it, ligase remodelling stalls and protein turnover becomes inflexible. Paralogous subunits COPS7A and COPS7B, together with COPS8, occupy positions in the horseshoe-shaped core, so their availability shapes which version of the complex a cell builds. Assembly is therefore an upstream determinant of ubiquitin-proteasome throughput, with consequences for proliferation, development and signalling outputs including Wnt pathway activity, and for lymphocyte biology where complex components influence receptor-driven responses.

Most fatty acids are degraded from the carboxyl end, but when that route is saturated or blocked the cell can attack the opposite methyl terminus instead. Omega-oxidation converts that terminal carbon stepwise to an alcohol, an aldehyde and finally a second carboxyl group, producing a dicarboxylic acid that can then be shortened by beta-oxidation, largely in peroxisomes. The committed hydroxylation is performed by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4 family, including CYP4F2 and CYP4F3, with alcohol dehydrogenases such as ADH4 and ADH7 carrying out the subsequent oxidation. Beyond its role as a salvage route for long-chain substrates in fatty acid oxidation disorders, this chemistry inactivates signalling lipids, and CYP4F-mediated hydroxylation of leukotriene B4 and of 20-HETE links it to inflammation resolution and vascular tone. Loss of CYP4V2 causes Bietti crystalline retinal dystrophy.</description>

Cells and tissues sense extracellular acidification and respond to it, a capacity that shapes pain perception, taste, immune behaviour in inflamed or tumour tissue, and systemic acid-base handling. Falling pH is detected by two broad classes of receptor: proton-gated cation channels of the acid-sensing family and related degenerin/epithelial sodium channel subunits, which depolarize sensory neurons, and proton-activated G protein-coupled receptors such as GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68 that signal through Gq and Gs to change cAMP and calcium. Acid-sensitive two-pore potassium channels are closed by protons, adding excitability, while TRPV1 integrates acid with heat and capsaicin at nociceptor terminals. Downstream adjustments include sodium/proton exchange by SLC9A1 to restore intracellular pH, trafficking of transporters, and release of mediators such as somatostatin. Low pH also favours the acidic proteases cathepsin S and legumain. Chronic tissue acidosis in ischaemia, inflammation and tumours engages these same sensors.

Development depends not only on cells choosing a fate but on how tightly and when that choice is enforced, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the threshold for cell fate commitment. Secreted morphogens and their receptors provide positional information — BMP4 acting through BMPR1A, WNT3A via FZD7, FGF2 through FGFR1 — while DKK1, SFRP2 and SOSTDC1 restrain those same signals to keep neighbouring progenitors uncommitted. Chromatin machinery converts the decision into a heritable state: the NuRD complex (CHD3/CHD4, MTA1-3, MBD3, RBBP4/7, HDAC1/2) closes off alternative programmes, and EP300 with BRD2/BRD4 sustains the chosen one. Lineage transcription factors including SOX17, MESP1, PAX7, TBX21 and NKX6-2, plus muscle-specific microRNAs, mark the endpoints, spanning germ layer specification, myogenesis, neural patterning and helper T cell polarisation through IL-12 and IL-23 signalling.

negative regulation of cell fate commitment covers the braking signals that keep progenitor cells uncommitted, delaying or blocking their assignment to a particular differentiated identity. This restraint preserves stem and progenitor pools during development and in adult tissues; losing it causes premature differentiation, exhaustion of progenitors, and patterning defects. Much of the mechanism is secreted Wnt antagonism — DKK1, SFRP2 and SOSTDC1 sequester ligands or block receptor engagement, tuning the same Frizzled receptors that drive commitment — alongside Notch-driven HES1, a transcriptional repressor that suppresses proneural and lineage-determining factors to sustain a progenitor state. Other members act in immune lineage decisions, where JAK3–STAT5 signalling and the transcription factors TBX21 and SPDEF bias helper T cell and secretory epithelial fates by repressing alternatives. The theme throughout is inhibition of differentiation programmes so that timing and position, not chance, determine identity.

Development requires not only pushing cells toward a fate but holding them back from one, and this is the repressive side of cell fate commitment: processes that block, delay or damp the rate at which progenitors lock into a particular identity, keeping pools uncommitted and boundaries between territories sharp. Several members act as extracellular brakes on Wnt signalling, with DKK1, SFRP2 and SOSTDC1 sequestering or blocking ligand-receptor engagement and so restraining fate decisions in skin appendages, bone and neural tissue. HES1 supplies the Notch-driven transcriptional repression that sustains progenitors and prevents premature neuronal or secretory differentiation. Others operate in lymphoid commitment, where JAK3-STAT5A signalling and lineage factors such as TBX21 bias helper T cell identity while suppressing alternatives. Loss of such restraint causes progenitor exhaustion, mispatterned tissue and, in adult epithelia, the aberrant differentiation seen in metaplasia and cancer.

Cells become committed to a particular fate when signalling and chromatin inputs converge to lock in a differentiation programme, and this collection covers the influences that push that commitment forward rather than restrain it. Such reinforcement decides how many cells of a given type a tissue acquires, and it matters in muscle formation, secretory epithelial differentiation, oligodendrocyte specification and the choice of T helper lineage. Secreted cues such as WNT3A and FGF2 supply positional information, while the IL12 and IL23 cytokine and receptor subunits bias helper T cell commitment toward defined effector states. Transcriptional and chromatin regulators including the histone acetyltransferase EP300, the bromodomain proteins BRD2 and BRD4, the goblet-cell factor SPDEF and the homeodomain protein NKX6-2 implement commitment, and muscle-enriched microRNAs including MIR206 and MIR133A1 stabilise it by silencing alternative programmes.

Centriole-centriole cohesion keeps the mother and daughter centriole of a centrosome tethered together from the end of mitosis until the next G2, so that a cell presents a single microtubule-organizing centre through interphase rather than two independent ones. The link is a proteinaceous tether anchored at the proximal centriole ends, built from rootletin and C-Nap1 (CEP250) with CEP68, CEP44, centlein and ninein-family docking proteins, and stabilized by CEP135 and the appendage component ODF2. Loss of the tether causes premature centrosome splitting, which alters spindle geometry, cilium positioning and the direction of microtubule-based transport. Timed dissolution is the point of regulation: NEK2 kinase phosphorylates the tether proteins to drive centrosome disjunction before bipolar spindle assembly, while shugoshin and dynactin-associated factors contribute to keeping the pair engaged. The same machinery links centrosome number control to accurate chromosome segregation.

Leaving M phase is a commitment step: once anaphase is complete, a cell must dismantle the mitotic state, reverse the phosphorylation that built the spindle and condensed chromosomes, and re-establish an interphase nucleus and cytoplasm as it enters G1. Exit from mitosis depends on destruction of mitotic regulators by the anaphase-promoting complex together with its ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S, on release of the spindle assembly checkpoint through factors such as MAD2L1BP and the ZW10/KNTC1 machinery, and on phosphatases including CDC14 family members and PP1/PP2A regulatory subunits that undo CDK substrate phosphorylation. Completion also requires physical separation of the daughters, with anillin at the cleavage furrow, ESCRT-III components and the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin resolving the intercellular bridge. Failure produces cytokinesis defects, tetraploidy and chromosome instability, and CDK inhibitors here couple exit to G1 arrest and differentiation.

Heart rate is set by the pacemaker activity of sinoatrial cells and continuously trimmed by signals that slow it, and this braking arm—negative regulation of heart rate—keeps output matched to demand, permits diastolic filling, and protects the myocardium from the energetic cost of sustained tachycardia. Its effectors act at several levels: calcium handling proteins such as phospholamban, which restrains the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, together with sorcin and the ryanodine receptor-associated FKBP1B, shape the amplitude and timing of each beat; connexin-family and spectrin components influence conduction and the localisation of ion channels at the axon initial segment and cardiac membranes. Neuropeptides and humoral mediators including neuropeptide FF, spexin, substance P precursor TAC1, angiotensin II type 2 receptor signalling and the secreted amine oxidase renalase contribute chronotropic and blood-pressure-linked restraint, while TNF depresses contractile and pacemaker function during inflammation. Loss of such restraint favours arrhythmia and heart failure.

Cardiac output is adjusted beat to beat by raising the firing rate of the sinoatrial pacemaker, and this positive chronotropic control is what allows circulation to match exercise, stress, blood loss or hypotension. Sympathetic input through the beta-1 adrenergic receptor and alpha-1A receptor, together with circulating and locally released peptides such as adrenomedullin, endothelins, natriuretic peptide and neuromedin U, converges on cyclic nucleotide signalling that is shaped by phosphodiesterase 4D and by regulators of G protein signalling. The resulting change in rate depends on calcium handling and repolarization in pacemaker and working myocardium: ryanodine receptor RYR2 releases sarcoplasmic calcium, SERCA2 pumps it back, and channels including KCNQ1, TRPM4 and the sodium channel subunit SCN3B set the action potential. Loss of balance here produces bradycardia, inappropriate tachycardia or arrhythmia, and chronic overdrive contributes to heart failure.

Mesenchymal cells build organs as three-dimensional masses rather than epithelial sheets, and controlling how many of them accumulate sets the size and shape of limbs, craniofacial structures, lung, kidney and heart. This programme covers the expansion of those populations during development: BMP ligands and their type I receptor, hedgehog signalling through SMO and IHH, FGF ligands acting on FGFR1 and FGFR2, PDGF, and WNT/beta-catenin input all drive proliferation, while chordin sequesters BMPs and CTNNBIP1 restrains beta-catenin to keep growth bounded. Lineage transcription factors including PRRX1, SIX1, SIX2, SOX9, TBX1, HAND2, ISL1 and FOXF1 determine which mesenchyme responds, and MYC and MYCN carry the signal into cell cycle entry. Reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signalling depends on it, and loss or misregulation produces skeletal and limb malformations, lung and kidney hypoplasia, and overgrowth syndromes.

Mesenchyme is the loose, three-dimensional cell mass from which skeleton, connective tissue, and the supporting layers of lung, gut and limb are built, and controlling how fast those cells divide sets organ size and shape during development. Regulation of mesenchymal cell proliferation gathers the signals that epithelium and mesenchyme exchange: hedgehog ligands acting through SMO, BMP4 with its receptor BMPR1A and the antagonist chordin, FGF9 read by FGFR1 and FGFR2, PDGFA, and WNT inputs converging on CTNNB1 and LRP5. These feed transcription factors such as FOXF1, PRRX1, SIX1, TBX1, SOX9, MYC and MYCN that license or restrain cell cycle entry. Too little proliferation gives limb, palate, craniofacial and lung hypoplasia; unchecked activity contributes to fibrosis and to mesenchymal tumours, and MYCN amplification illustrates how the same circuitry drives embryonal cancers.

Proteolysis has to be contained, and negative regulation of peptidase activity covers the inhibitors that set where and for how long a protease is allowed to act. Without such restraint, released enzymes degrade extracellular matrix, basement membrane and plasma proteins indiscriminately, which is the route to tissue destruction in inflammation, emphysema and tumour invasion. Several classes are represented here: serpins such as SERPINB1 inhibit neutrophil serine proteases including elastase and cathepsin G; TIMP1 and TIMP2 block matrix metalloproteinases and so govern matrix turnover and angiogenesis; testicular and plasma proteins such as EPPIN and FETUB restrain proteases in reproductive fluids, with EPPIN controlling semen liquefaction and sperm motility. Complement receptor CR1 and matrix components ECM1 and SPOCK3 add extracellular control, making this biology part of matrix remodelling, immune damage limitation and fertilisation.

Cells tune how strongly they respond to a given ligand, and this regulation of signaling receptor activity covers the accessory proteins, trafficking machinery and feedback inhibitors that set receptor abundance, sensitivity and lifetime at the membrane. It matters because the same hormone or neurotransmitter can produce quite different outputs depending on how many competent receptors are present and how quickly they are silenced. Several distinct mechanisms appear together: auxiliary subunits such as the transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory proteins, cornichon homologues and SHISA7 control glutamate receptor trafficking and gating in neurons; SOCS proteins and ERRFI1 impose negative feedback on cytokine and EGF receptor signalling; ESCRT components including TSG101, VPS25 and CHMP6 sort activated receptors toward lysosomal degradation, while proteasome subunits complete their turnover. Secreted modulators such as CRH-binding protein and gremlin act by sequestering ligands before they reach a receptor at all.

Gastrulation converts a single-layered embryo into the three germ layers, and the genes here tune how fast and how far that rearrangement proceeds rather than simply permitting it. Getting the timing and extent right sets the body axes and the founder populations for gut, notochord, heart and nervous system; disturbing it causes early lethality or midline defects such as holoprosencephaly, which follows loss of NODAL pathway restraint by the TGIF repressors. NODAL is the central inductive signal, and its output is bounded by transcriptional corepressors and by downstream factors including FOXA2, LHX1 and OTX2 that specify anterior endoderm and organizer derivatives. Other members act on the cells themselves: the apical polarity protein CRB2 shapes epithelial behaviour during ingression, and POGLUT1 glucosylates Notch-type EGF repeats. Together these represent the control layer over morphogenetic movement in the early embryo.

Substances passing directly from one cell to its neighbour, rather than through the extracellular space, is what intercellular transport describes, and the genes here point to two ways cells manage it. Most are connexins that oligomerise into gap junction channels, allowing ions, metabolites and second messengers to diffuse between coupled cells; GJA3 and GJA8 together with the water channel MIP sustain the transparent, avascular lens, while GJB2 and GJB6 couple cochlear supporting cells and their loss is a common cause of inherited deafness, and GJB2 mutations also disrupt epidermal differentiation. CLDN16 instead governs paracellular passage, forming the tight junction pore for magnesium and calcium reabsorption in the renal thick ascending limb. ARC and PEG10 retain retroviral-like capsid activity and can package RNA for transfer between neurons, a route for intercellular signalling distinct from channel-mediated coupling.

Regulated destruction of proteins by the proteasome is how cells terminate signalling, clear damaged or misfolded polypeptides, and impose the timed decay of regulatory proteins on which cell cycle progression and differentiation depend. Substrates are marked with ubiquitin by E2 enzymes and a large family of E3 ligases, including cullin-RING complexes built on CUL1-5 with SKP1, RBX1 and interchangeable F-box, KLHL, SPSB and DCAF substrate receptors, plus the anaphase-promoting complex that destroys cyclins and securin at mitotic exit. Tagged proteins are delivered by shuttle factors such as the ubiquilins and RAD23 proteins to the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory subunits hydrolyse them, while deubiquitinases like USP14 and UCHL5 edit the signal. A specialised branch retrotranslocates misfolded glycoproteins from the endoplasmic reticulum through SEL1L-SYVN1 and VCP. Failure underlies neurodegenerative aggregate diseases and unrestrained oncogenic signalling.

Proteasomal ubiquitin-independent protein catabolic process is the arm of proteasome-mediated degradation that destroys substrates without first tagging them with ubiquitin chains. It disposes of oxidatively damaged, intrinsically disordered and unstructured proteins, and provides a rapid route for turning over short-lived regulators, so that protein quality control does not depend entirely on the ubiquitin ligase machinery. The genes centre on the 20S core particle itself, both the outer alpha ring that gates substrate entry and the beta ring carrying the caspase-, trypsin- and chymotrypsin-like catalytic sites, together with the immunoproteasome subunit PSMB10 and the PA200 activator. Regulators such as midnolin and ENC1 deliver or restrain specific clients, and NFE2L2 links this route to oxidative stress, being itself degraded in this manner while also driving expression of proteasome subunits during antioxidant responses.

Not every protein destroyed by the proteasome is tagged with ubiquitin first. This route covers degradation in which the 20S core particle, built from the alpha rings (PSMA1-7) and the catalytic beta subunits (PSMB1-7, plus the immunoproteasome subunit PSMB10), directly engages intrinsically disordered or oxidatively damaged substrates and hydrolyses their peptide bonds without prior ubiquitin conjugation. Activators and adaptors shape the process: PSME4 caps the core and promotes degradation of unstructured substrates, while MIDN and ENC1 deliver or present clients, and NFE2L2, the master transcription factor of the antioxidant response, is itself a well-known ubiquitin-independent proteasome substrate. The pathway matters for rapid disposal of damaged and short-lived regulatory proteins, for tuning oxidative stress responses, and for protein quality control when the ubiquitin conjugation machinery is overwhelmed or bypassed.

Autophagy lets a cell digest its own cytoplasm to survive starvation and to clear damaged organelles and aggregated proteins, and the machinery here sets how much of it happens and when. Nutrient and energy sensing dominates the control: the mTOR complex with its Rag GTPase and TSC/Rheb regulators suppresses initiation, while AMPK subunits and the upstream kinase STK11 activate ULK1/2 at the initiation complex with ATG13 and RB1CC1. Downstream, the PIK3C3/BECN1 lipid kinase complex, its inhibitor RUBCN, and ATG5-ATG12-ATG16L1 build the autophagosome, cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, OPTN and CALCOCO2 select substrates, PINK1 and PRKN mark mitochondria for mitophagy, and lysosomal v-ATPase subunits with TFEB tie degradative capacity to transcription. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, sirtuins and stress pathways tune the balance. Loss of this regulation underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease, Crohn's disease and tumour metabolic adaptation.

Autophagy must be restrained as well as induced, and this collection covers the brakes: processes that stop, prevent or reduce the rate and extent of self-digestion of cytoplasm. Keeping the pathway off when nutrients are plentiful preserves biosynthetic capacity and prevents excessive degradation of organelles and cytosol, while failure of these brakes contributes to muscle wasting, neurodegeneration and altered tumour cell survival. The dominant node is mTOR complex 1 — MTOR with RPTOR and MLST8, activated at the lysosome by the Rag GTPases and held in check by the TSC1/TSC2 complex — acting downstream of growth factor and AKT1 signalling to suppress autophagy initiation. Anti-apoptotic BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 sequester BECN1, RUBCN dampens autophagosome maturation, and transcriptional repressors such as ZKSCAN3 limit expression of autophagy and lysosomal genes.

Cells survive starvation, damaged organelles and intracellular microbes by degrading their own cytoplasm in lysosomes, and this collection covers the inputs that switch that self-digestion on or raise its rate. The upstream logic is nutrient and energy sensing: AMPK subunits and the upstream kinase STK11 respond to low energy, TSC2, sestrins and GATOR/FLCN-related components restrain mTORC1, and the transcription factors TFEB, FOXO1/3 and HIF1A expand lysosomal and autophagy gene expression for the longer term.
