Downstream, ULK1 with ATG13 and RB1CC1 initiates, BECN1 with AMBRA1 and UVRAG directs lipid kinase activity to the forming phagophore, and ATG5/ATG16L1 conjugation plus WIPI and SNX proteins build the membrane. Selective arms are prominent: PINK1 and parkin with BNIP3L flag mitochondria, while receptors such as SQSTM1, OPTN and CALCOCO2, TBK1, STING1 and NOD-like receptors couple innate immune sensing to capture of pathogens. Failure of these controls underlies neurodegeneration, Crohn's disease susceptibility and impaired stress tolerance.

Control over how much phosphatidylinositol a cell makes sets the size of the lipid pool that supplies PIP2, and therefore the capacity of cells to generate the second messengers inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol for calcium release and protein kinase C activation. The genes here are upstream receptor inputs rather than the biosynthetic enzymes themselves: the Gq-coupled serotonin receptors of the 5-HT2 family, expressed in neurons, smooth muscle and platelets, and the platelet-derived growth factor ligands acting through receptor tyrosine kinases on mesenchymal cells. Both routes drive phosphoinositide turnover and feed back on synthesis to replenish what signalling consumes. This link matters for neuromodulation and for 5-HT2 antagonism by antipsychotics, for vascular tone and platelet responses, and for growth-factor-driven proliferation, wound repair and fibrosis, where sustained phosphoinositide signalling depends on adequate precursor supply.

Cytosolic calcium is a signal, and it only means something if its entry is controlled; this pathway covers the factors that tune how fast calcium is admitted into the cytosol, whether from outside the cell or from internal stores. The setpoint matters because sustained calcium loading triggers mitochondrial permeabilization and cell death, while too little blunts neurotransmission, secretion and contraction. Ligand-gated entry is represented by ATP-activated P2X receptors and the NMDA receptor subunit GRIN1, with TRPC3 providing store- and receptor-operated influx at the plasma membrane. Release from the endoplasmic reticulum is modulated by junctate/aspartyl hydroxylase and by TMBIM6, and the BCL2 family sets ER calcium content so that BAX and BAK-driven apoptosis is either favoured or restrained. Caveolin-1 and neuronal nitric oxide synthase place this control in membrane microdomains, linking calcium handling to nitric oxide signalling, neuropeptide action and apoptotic commitment.

negative regulation of calcium ion transport into cytosol restrains the release of calcium into the cytoplasm, keeping this potent second messenger below the thresholds that trigger contraction, secretion, or death. Sustained cytosolic calcium overload opens the mitochondrial permeability transition pore and activates calpains, so damping calcium entry is one way cells survive ischaemia, excitotoxicity, and endoplasmic reticulum stress. The genes act at several control points: BCL2 and the ER membrane protein TMBIM6 limit calcium leak and IP3 receptor-mediated efflux from internal stores, tuning the ER-mitochondrial calcium transfer that commits a cell to apoptosis, while nitric oxide generated by NOS1 nitrosylates and inhibits channels including the ryanodine receptor. Circulating factors such as calcitonin gene-related peptide and erythropoietin impose the same restraint from outside the cell, linking this control to vascular tone, neuroprotection, and cell survival signalling.

Cytosolic calcium is a signal that must be kept transient, and this pathway covers the braking processes that limit how fast calcium enters the cytosol from internal stores or across the plasma membrane. Restraining that influx protects cells from the sustained calcium overload that triggers mitochondrial permeabilisation, calpain activation and death, so these activities sit upstream of apoptosis control, excitotoxic injury and cardiovascular tone. The members act by distinct routes: BCL2 at the endoplasmic reticulum dampens release through inositol trisphosphate receptors, while TMBIM6 similarly reduces ER calcium leak and buffers store content; neuronal nitric oxide synthase generates NO that feeds back on channel and receptor activity; and secreted factors including calcitonin gene-related peptide and erythropoietin signal through their receptors to lower calcium entry in target cells. Together they define the inhibitory side of calcium signalling rather than its initiation.

Cytosolic calcium is kept low so that its rise can be used as a signal, and this pathway covers the processes that increase calcium entry into the cytosol, whether across the plasma membrane or out of internal stores. The resulting transients drive neurotransmitter release, synaptic plasticity, secretion, contraction and immune activation, and unchecked calcium loading is a route to cell death. Ligand-gated and store channels carry much of the flux: ATP-gated P2X receptors open a cation-permeable pore, the NMDA receptor subunit GRIN1 admits calcium at excitatory synapses, and TRPC3 supports receptor-operated entry. Release from the endoplasmic reticulum is promoted by the junctate/aspartyl hydroxylase protein ASPH, while BAX and BAK1 couple calcium redistribution to apoptotic commitment. Caveolin-1 scaffolds these channels in membrane microdomains, and a G protein-coupled neuropeptide receptor links extracellular cues to the same rise.

Platelets must switch from quiescent circulation to adhesion, spreading and aggregation the moment vessel wall collagen and subendothelial matrix are exposed, and this is the set of inputs that tunes how readily that switch is thrown. Getting the balance wrong produces either bleeding or thrombosis, so these regulators sit behind haemostasis, arterial thrombosis and stroke risk. Positive drive comes through the von Willebrand factor receptor complex (GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9, GP5) and the collagen receptor GP6, which signal via FCER1G, LYN, SYK and phospholipase-mediated calcium and protein kinase C activation, with thrombin acting through G-protein-coupled routes. Restraint is imposed by endothelial nitric oxide and cyclic GMP-dependent kinase signalling, thrombomodulin, and phosphatases such as PTPRJ and UBASH3B. Adhesion molecules, thromboxane-pathway lipid enzymes, and cytokine inputs including interleukin-6 signalling and JAK2 modulate the threshold further, linking inflammation to thrombotic tendency.

Negative regulation of platelet activation is the braking system that keeps circulating platelets quiescent and confines clotting to sites of genuine vessel injury. Without it, spontaneous aggregation and thrombus propagation cause arterial and venous thrombosis, stroke, and consumptive coagulopathy; healthy endothelium therefore actively suppresses the platelets flowing over it. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase supplies NO, which raises cyclic GMP and engages PRKG1 to blunt integrin activation and granule release, while thrombomodulin redirects thrombin toward protein C activation instead of platelet stimulation and serpin inhibitors quench residual protease activity. Inhibitory receptors such as CEACAM1 and CD9, the adaptor SH2B3, the phosphatase UBASH3B, and PKC-delta dampen GPVI and ITAM-linked signalling from within, and thiol-oxidoreductase and metalloprotease activities at the surface limit von Willebrand factor- and collagen-driven adhesion. This restraint is the counterweight to procoagulant signalling in haemostasis.

Platelets must stay quiescent in flowing blood and respond only where vessel wall is breached, and the brakes on platelet activation set that threshold. Losing them favours spontaneous aggregation, arterial thrombosis and consumptive platelet loss; too much restraint prolongs bleeding. Endothelium supplies much of the signal: nitric oxide from the endothelial synthase NOS3 raises cyclic GMP and acts through the kinase PRKG1 to suppress integrin activation and granule release, while thrombomodulin redirects thrombin toward anticoagulant protein C activation rather than platelet stimulation. Inhibitory receptors and adaptors such as CEACAM1, SH2B3 and UBASH3B damp immunoreceptor- and GPVI-linked tyrosine kinase signalling, and a serpin plus a metalloprotease-family member limit protease and von Willebrand factor-dependent stimulation. The result is negative control layered onto haemostasis, tuning clot formation, vascular tone and the interface between thrombosis and inflammation.

positive regulation of glycoprotein biosynthetic process covers the signals that push cells to make more glycosylated protein, whether that is mucin and matrix proteoglycan output, surface receptor glycoforms, or the glycoprotein hormones and enzymes a differentiating tissue needs. Because glycans dictate protein folding, secretion, adhesion and receptor half-life, raising their synthesis changes how a cell communicates with its environment; sustained upregulation contributes to fibrotic matrix deposition and to the altered glycosylation seen in tumours. The genes are mostly upstream regulators rather than glycosyltransferases: chemokine signalling through CCL19, CCL21 and CCR7, growth factor input from IGF1, the IL33 alarmin, phospholipase C and calcium relays, and Wnt-responsive transcription via CTNNB1 and TCF7L2. Others act nearer the biosynthetic machinery, including nicastrin as part of the gamma-secretase complex and transporters supplying sugar and lipid precursors, linking developmental and inflammatory cues to secretory pathway throughput.

Glycoproteins — mucins, proteoglycans, receptors and secreted matrix components — require coordinated upregulation of the enzymes and precursors that attach sugars to protein backbones, and this pathway covers the signals that push that output upward. Increased glycoprotein synthesis supports cartilage and mucosal barrier function, airway secretion, matrix deposition during growth and repair, and the display of glycosylated receptors at the cell surface; excessive drive contributes to mucus hypersecretion and fibrotic matrix accumulation. The genes represented act largely as upstream inputs rather than glycosyltransferases themselves: growth factor and cytokine signalling through IGF1 and IL33, chemokine receptor engagement by CCR7 with its ligands CCL19 and CCL21, phospholipase C–calcium signalling, and Wnt-responsive transcription via CTNNB1 and TCF7L2. Cells raise the flux of phosphate-transfer chemistry whenever they need to convert an external cue into an internal decision, and positive regulation of phosphorus metabolic processes covers the proteins that push that chemistry upward — mostly by increasing protein phosphorylation, but also nucleotide and lipid phosphate turnover. The membership is dominated by growth factor and cytokine receptors (EGFR, ERBB2, FGFR1, KIT, FLT3, VEGF receptors, INSR, IL4R, PRLR) together with the kinase relays they feed: RAF1/BRAF to MAP2K1/2 and MAPK1, PIK3CA to AKT1 and the mTOR complex components MTOR, RPTOR and MLST8, and JAK2–STAT3. Also present are adenylate cyclases and protein kinase A subunits that raise cyclic nucleotide signalling, AMPK catalytic subunits with the STK11 activating module, and TRAF/RIPK adaptors that initiate inflammatory kinase cascades. Through these routes the pathway drives proliferation, survival, metabolic switching and immune activation, and its sustained elevation underlies much of oncogenic signalling.

Cells hold their phosphorylation-driven signalling and phosphate-handling metabolism in check as deliberately as they switch it on, and this collection of brakes on phosphorus metabolic processes captures that restraint. Losing it gives unopposed growth-factor and nutrient signalling, which is why many members are tumour suppressors: PTEN reverses phosphoinositide 3-kinase output, TP53, RB1, CDKN1A and CDKN2A arrest the cycle, LATS1/LATS2 relay Hippo-dependent growth suppression, and DEPTOR and the tuberous-sclerosis-related FLCN and NPRL2 components damp mTOR complex activity toward nutrient sensing. Classical protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPN1, PTPN2, PTPN22, PTPRC, PTPRJ), dual-specificity DUSP7, SOCS adaptors and PPP2CA remove or block activating phosphorylations on receptors and kinases, tuning immune and metabolic responses. Other members constrain phosphorylated-sugar and lipid flux through glycolysis and phosphatidate metabolism, linking kinase control to intermediary metabolism.

Cell division must be timed, ordered and reversible when something goes wrong, and this collection covers the regulators that modulate individual steps of the cell cycle rather than executing them. Its outputs determine whether a cell commits to replication, pauses to repair damage, or divides its chromosomes accurately, and its failure underlies genome instability and tumour growth as well as microcephaly and infertility syndromes. Cyclin-CDK pairs driven by CDC25 phosphatases and opposed by WEE1 and CDKN inhibitors set the phase transitions; the retinoblastoma protein and E2F factors gate S-phase entry; ATM, ATR, CHEK1/2 and TP53 impose damage and replication checkpoints; and the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2L1, BUB1 and BUB3 restrain the anaphase-promoting complex until kinetochores are attached. Aurora and Polo-like kinases, ESCRT components and condensins regulate spindle assembly, centrosome duplication, chromosome condensation and abscission, with meiotic regulators handling germline divisions.

regulation of ketone metabolic process governs how much acetyl-CoA the body diverts into ketone bodies and related carbonyl metabolites, the fuel switch that keeps the brain and heart supplied during fasting, prolonged exercise, and carbohydrate restriction. Its failure underlies diabetic ketoacidosis at one extreme and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia at the other. Control is largely transcriptional and hormonal: nuclear receptors such as PPARA, PPARD and the LXR and FXR family, together with SREBP/SCAP and ChREBP, coordinate fatty acid uptake and beta-oxidation with hepatic ketogenesis, while insulin acting through IRS proteins and AKT, and the opposing sirtuin and AMPK arms, set the rate. Downstream effectors include carnitine palmitoyltransferase, acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, peroxisomal transporters, and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases that gate flux between glucose and lipid oxidation. Adipokines, microRNAs and bile acid signalling tune the response to nutritional state.

Control over ketone body production and use links fasting, insulin signalling and fatty acid oxidation to the fuel supply of brain, heart and muscle. When glucose is scarce, hepatic mitochondria convert fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate; setting the rate of that conversion is what this regulation accomplishes, and losing the restraint produces diabetic ketoacidosis while losing the capacity causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Regulation operates largely at the level of transcription and substrate delivery: nuclear receptors and their coregulators such as PPARA, PPARGC1A, the liver X and farnesoid X receptors and NCOR1/2 drive the oxidative programme, SREBF1 with SCAP and the insulin-responsive INSIG proteins oppose it, CPT1A governs mitochondrial fatty acid entry, and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases divert pyruvate away from oxidation. Hormones including insulin, adiponectin, FGF19 and GDF15, sirtuins, AMPK subunits and several microRNAs tune the response to nutritional state.

This grouping covers the control points that set how fast cells make ketone-containing metabolites, from hepatic ketone bodies used as fuel during fasting to steroid and quinone-type ketones made in peripheral tissues. Such regulation matters because ketogenic output has to track nutrient supply: too little leaves brain and muscle without an alternative to glucose during starvation, while unrestrained flux drives ketoacidosis. The members act mostly as upstream modulators rather than as the synthetic enzymes themselves — transcriptional regulators including CREB1, EGR1 and the repressor REST, secreted morphogens of the BMP and WNT families with their DKK antagonists, and mitochondrial factors such as the sirtuin SIRT5 and the phosphatase PPTC7 that tune enzyme activity post-translationally. Steroid-modifying oxidoreductases like AKR1C3 and H6PD supply the ketosteroid arm, linking this regulation to hormone metabolism as well as energy homeostasis.

Homologous recombination restores broken chromosomes accurately by copying an intact sister or homologous template, and this collection of factors sets how often and how far that route is used rather than performing the strand exchange itself. The balance matters because the alternatives — end joining and microhomology-mediated repair — leave mutations, and tipping it either way causes genome instability, replication stress and the chemosensitivity seen in recombination-deficient tumours. Regulation acts at several levels: chromatin is remodelled and marked around the break by the NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase complex with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, together with methyltransferases such as SETD2 and KMT5A; ubiquitin and SUMO ligases including RNF8 and PIAS4 recruit downstream effectors; and 53BP1 with the shieldin subunits SHLD1–3 and RIF1 restricts end resection to oppose recombination. Helicases, RAD51 loaders such as RAD51AP1, and antirecombinases then tune filament assembly, coupling repair choice to cell cycle position.

Cells only duplicate their genome once per division, and the steps that activate and accelerate nuclear DNA replication during the cell cycle determine when licensed origins actually fire. The core event is origin firing itself: the CDC7 kinase, together with its activating subunits DBF4 and DBF4B, phosphorylates the MCM helicase to convert a loaded pre-replication complex into an active replisome, a step that sets replication timing and is required for S phase entry. Chromatin context is equally decisive, with the INO80 remodelling complex and the chromatin remodeller ATRX shaping nucleosome organisation at origins and in repetitive or heterochromatic regions where replication is otherwise difficult. Growth signals feed in as well, linking proliferative cues to replication onset. Excessive activation drives replication stress and genome instability, which is why this activating arm is tightly restrained in normal tissue and frequently deregulated in cancer.

When the endothelium is breached, platelets must switch rapidly from a quiescent circulating state to an adhesive, secretory one, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that switch harder and faster. It underlies primary haemostasis and, when overactive, arterial thrombosis and the platelet contribution to inflammation; when weak, it produces bleeding. Central to it is the von Willebrand factor receptor complex, whose subunits GP1BA, GP1BB, GP5 and GP9 capture platelets onto exposed subendothelium under shear and signal inward, with FLNA linking the receptor to the actin cytoskeleton. Downstream amplification involves JAK2, the cytosolic phospholipase PLA2G4A liberating arachidonic acid for thromboxane synthesis, and PKC substrate pleckstrin. PEAR1 reinforces contact-dependent aggregation, P-selectin mediates platelet-leukocyte adhesion after granule release, and TLR4 couples innate immune stimuli to platelet reactivity.

Vascular endothelial growth factor production is the step at which a tissue signals that it needs new blood or lymphatic vessels, controlling how much VEGF is synthesised and released rather than how endothelial cells respond to it. Output rises with hypoxia through the HIF1A–ARNT transcriptional response, with ER stress through the PERK–ATF4 arm of the unfolded protein response, and with inflammation via IL1, IL6–STAT3, TNF–NF-κB, prostaglandin synthesis and complement anaphylatoxin receptors. A large set of microRNAs tunes the message downward, giving post-transcriptional brakes on angiogenic drive. Processing enzymes such as ADAMTS3 with CCBE1 mature VEGFC for lymphangiogenic signalling through FLT4, while heparanase and sulfatases liberate matrix-bound growth factor. The balance set here governs wound healing, placental and cardiac development, and retinal vessel growth, and its excess sustains tumour vascularisation and diabetic eye disease.

Blood vessel growth is driven largely by how much vascular endothelial growth factor a tissue makes, and this collection of upstream inputs describes the signals that raise VEGF output. It matters for wound healing, placental and cardiac development, and the adaptation of tissue to low oxygen; the same circuitry is hijacked in tumours to build a blood supply and drives pathological neovascularisation in the retina. The central route is hypoxic: HIF1A with its partner ARNT transcribes VEGF when oxygen is scarce. Inflammatory and stress inputs converge on the same output, with IL1B, IL6 through IL6ST and STAT3, prostaglandin synthesis via PTGS2, complement activation through C3AR1 and C5AR1, NF-κB signalling, and the PERK-ATF4 arm of the integrated stress response. Developmental transcription factors such as GATA4 and ISL1, TGFB1, and heparan sulfate modifying enzymes that alter growth factor availability contribute additional control.</br>

microRNAs set the quantitative tone of gene expression, and this pathway covers their whole life cycle: transcription of primary hairpins, nuclear cropping by DROSHA, export through XPO5, DICER1 cleavage, loading into Argonaute effectors, and the tailing, trimming and decay steps that destroy them. Because a single miRNA can damp hundreds of transcripts, control over miRNA abundance shapes differentiation, proliferation, angiogenesis and inflammatory output, and its distortion is a recurrent feature of cancer and fibrosis. Much of the gene content here is regulatory rather than catalytic: transcription factors such as TP53, MYC, SMAD4, STAT3 and hypoxia-inducible HIF1A drive or repress specific miRNA genes, while LIN28A/B block processing of the let-7 family, terminal uridylyl transferases and DIS3L2 route precursors to degradation, and ZSWIM8 triggers target-directed turnover of Argonaute-bound miRNAs. Signalling ligands including TGFB1, BMPs and VEGFA feed into this layer, coupling extracellular cues to post-transcriptional silencing.

Mature microRNAs are not permanent; controlled degradation sets their half-lives and lets cells change post-transcriptional programmes quickly, and this miRNA catabolic process is the route by which they are destroyed. It matters most in development and stem cell states, where clearing a microRNA is how a differentiation programme is released. Two logics appear here. One is tailing and trimming of the small RNA itself: terminal nucleotidyltransferases add uridine or adenosine to precursors and mature species, marking them for the 3'-5' exonucleases DIS3L2, PARN and PNPT1, with LIN28A and LIN28B recruiting uridylation to block let-7 maturation. The other is target-directed decay, in which a ZSWIM8-containing cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, with the elongin subunits ELOB and ELOC, destroys Argonaute so its bound microRNA is lost. Several long noncoding RNAs and RNA-binding proteins modulate the same turnover.

Migrating cells push forward on lamellipodia, flat sheets of branched actin at the leading edge, and this pathway covers the signals that set how readily those sheets are built and how far they extend. The output governs directed cell movement in wound healing, immune cell chemotaxis, axon guidance and tumour invasion, and its misregulation shows up as defective immune surveillance or excessive metastatic spread. Rho-family GTPases such as CDC42, RAC1 and RAC2 relay receptor input to the WAVE regulatory complex, whose subunits including CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2 and BRK1 present nucleation-promoting activity to the ARP2/3 complex so that new filaments branch from existing ones. Phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling positions these events at the membrane, while cofilin, twinfilin and fascin remodel and bundle the resulting network. Guidance cues such as SLIT2 and ephrin receptor signalling tune the response, making this the point where external direction becomes protrusion.

Migrating cells push forward by building a lamellipodium, the flat sheet of branched actin at the leading edge, and this is the signalling and assembly activity that increases its formation. It underlies directed cell migration in wound healing, immune cell chemotaxis, neuronal process outgrowth and tissue morphogenesis, and its dysregulation contributes to tumour cell invasion. Rho-family GTPases, chiefly RAC1, RAC2 and CDC42, act downstream of PI3K signalling to engage the WAVE regulatory complex, whose subunits CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2, BRK1 and WASF2 relieve autoinhibition and present the Arp2/3 complex (ACTR2, ACTR3, ARPC2) for nucleation of new actin branches. Accessory actin regulators including cofilin, twinfilin, advillin and fascin control filament severing, capping and bundling to sustain protrusion, while CARMIL2 tunes capping protein activity at the membrane.

Migrating cells push forward by building lamellipodia, thin sheets of branched actin at the leading edge; restraining that assembly is how a cell stops spreading, changes direction, or holds still. Negative regulation of lamellipodium assembly limits protrusion and so shapes axon guidance, wound repair, angiogenesis and the invasiveness of tumour cells. The genes act at several levels: cofilin severs and depolymerises actin filaments to turn over the network, an ABI family member dampens WAVE-complex-driven Arp2/3 nucleation, and repulsive guidance cues acting through plexin and Slit receptors collapse protrusions by reducing Rac-dependent actin polymerisation. Histidine-rich glycoprotein contributes an extracellular anti-angiogenic, anti-migratory influence, and two microRNAs tune the same output post-transcriptionally. Loss of such restraint gives persistent, poorly directed motility, as seen when guidance signalling fails during neural wiring or when carcinoma cells acquire migratory freedom.

Blood vessels grow, remodel and repair by having endothelial cells detach from an existing vessel wall and move directionally through extracellular matrix, and this pathway covers the positive and negative control of that movement. It underlies sprouting angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour vascularization, and its dysregulation contributes to ischaemic disease, vascular malformation and pathological neovascularization in retina and tumour. Growth factor and guidance inputs dominate: VEGFA acting through KDR and neuropilins, FGF2 through FGFR1, angiopoietins through TEK, plus DLL4-NOTCH1 tip/stalk selection and TGF-beta family signalling via ACVRL1 and GDF2. These converge on PI3K-AKT, focal adhesion kinase, integrin-linked adhesion turnover and Rho-family GTPases to steer lamellipodia and matrix attachment. Transcriptional regulators such as HIF1A, KLF4, GATA2 and PROX1, class IIa deacetylases, cerebral cavernous malformation proteins, and a large complement of microRNAs tune migratory output up or down.

Blood and lymphatic vessels grow by moving endothelial cells through the surrounding matrix, and this pathway covers the inputs that speed or extend that movement. It underlies wound healing, tissue repair and the vascularisation of developing organs, and is exploited by tumours to recruit their own blood supply; too little of it impairs collateral vessel formation in ischaemic tissue. Secreted cues such as VEGFA, VEGFC, angiopoietins and fibroblast growth factors act through receptors including KDR, FLT4, FGFR1, TEK and the neuropilin co-receptors, converging on PI3K-AKT, phospholipase C and p38 signalling to remodel the actin cytoskeleton via RAC1, RHOJ and integrin-adhesion adaptors like BCAR1. Transcriptional regulators including HIF1A, GATA2, ETS1, PROX1 and FOXC2 set the migratory and lymphatic-versus-blood endothelial programme, while numerous microRNAs tune the response. Matrix and adhesion modifiers such as SPARC, THBS1 and ADAM17 shape the path taken.

Blood vessels only grow where and when they are needed, and restraining endothelial cell migration is how sprouting is held in check so that vessels stabilise into a quiescent, barrier-competent endothelium. Loss of this braking causes pathological neovascularisation in tumours and retinopathy, while defects in specific brakes produce vascular malformations: mutations in the BMP9/ALK1 axis and in the cerebral cavernous malformation complex of KRIT1 and PDCD10 both act here, as does Notch signalling driven by DLL4 to suppress excess tip-cell behaviour. Matrix-derived inhibitors such as thrombospondin-1 and decorin, the secreted regulators multimerin-2 and vasohibin, and transcription factors including KLF4 and MEOX2 impose quiescence, and a large complement of microRNAs tunes migratory and cytoskeletal output through RHOA, integrin-binding and Slit-Robo guidance. The pathway is thus the negative arm of angiogenesis and vascular homeostasis.

P-bodies are cytoplasmic granules where translationally silenced mRNAs are stored, remodelled or committed to decay, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how readily they form and how large they grow. Their assembly follows from the deadenylation step of mRNA turnover: the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, through its scaffold and its two nuclease subunits, and the PAN2-PAN3 deadenylase shorten poly(A) tails, stripping mRNAs of poly(A)-binding protein and freeing them to condense with decapping and repression factors. A Pat1-family protein bridges deadenylated transcripts to that granule core, while a small regulatory peptide tunes the interaction network. The balance matters for how long maternal and other stored transcripts persist, for silencing by microRNAs, and for the stress-responsive partitioning of the transcriptome between translation and storage; mutations in the oocyte-enriched Pat1-like component cause oocyte maturation failure.

Cells park translationally repressed mRNAs in cytoplasmic processing bodies, granules where transcripts are stored, silenced or committed to decay, and this pathway covers the inputs that drive their formation. The genes here are the two major cytoplasmic deadenylases: the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, with its scaffold CNOT1, the CNOT2 structural subunit and the CNOT6/CNOT6L nucleases, together with the PAN2-PAN3 pair that trims long poly(A) tails. Shortening the poly(A) tail strips mRNAs of poly(A)-binding protein and translation initiation factors, and the resulting repressed messenger complexes coalesce by condensation into visible foci. Promoting P-body assembly therefore links deadenylation-dependent mRNA turnover to the phase-separated compartments that concentrate decapping and decay machinery, shaping how quickly cells silence transcripts during stress, development and microRNA-directed repression.

Once a transcript has been made, its fate is still open: how long it survives, whether it is translated, where in the cell it is stored, and whether it carries chemical marks that change its behaviour. Post-transcriptional regulation of gene expression covers that entire layer of control, and it lets cells respond to stress, differentiation cues and developmental timing faster than new transcription allows. The components here include microRNAs and their Argonaute and TNRC6 effectors, Dicer and Drosha-associated processing factors, deadenylases of the CCR4-NOT complex, decapping and exonucleolytic decay machinery, nonsense-mediated decay factors, and AU-rich element binding proteins such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1 that set inflammatory mRNA half-lives. Translation initiation factors, eIF2alpha kinases and mTOR-responsive 4E-BPs tune output globally, while m6A writers and readers, pseudouridine synthases and stress-granule proteins add transcript-specific control. Germline regulators such as DAZL, PUM and CPEB proteins govern stored maternal mRNAs.

The heart remodels in response to workload, hormones and fuel supply, and this pathway governs how far and how fast that remodelling goes. It sets the boundary between physiological growth, as in exercise or pregnancy, and pathological hypertrophy with fibrosis and dilation that ends in heart failure and arrhythmia. Calcium-dependent signalling through calcineurin and the TRPC3 channel drives the hypertrophic transcriptional programme, while FOXO1, PPARG and SMAD3 tie growth control to metabolic substrate switching and fibrotic gene expression. A striking share of the regulation is post-transcriptional: cardiac microRNAs including the myosin-encoded miR-208a and miR-199a tune contractile isoform choice and stress responses. Nuclear envelope and interacting proteins such as LMNA and MLIP link mechanical load to the nucleus, and LMNA mutation causes dilated cardiomyopathy with conduction disease.

The heart remodels itself in response to workload, stretch, neurohormonal input and nutrient supply, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that adaptation forward — driving cardiomyocyte growth, altered contractile gene expression and changes in chamber geometry. Such adaptation is protective in exercise but becomes pathological hypertrophy and a route to heart failure when pressure overload persists. Calcium is the central signal: TRPC3 provides a receptor-operated cation entry route that feeds the calcium-dependent phosphatase calcineurin, whose catalytic subunit PPP3CA dephosphorylates NFAT transcription factors to switch on the hypertrophic gene programme. The apelin receptor APLNR couples peptide hormone signalling to contractility and myocardial load. A set of microRNAs, including the cardiac-enriched miR-208a encoded within a myosin heavy chain gene, tunes myosin isoform switching, fibrosis and stress-responsive transcription, placing post-transcriptional control alongside signalling in cardiac remodelling.

The heart remodels in response to pressure overload, exercise, altered substrate supply and neurohormonal input, and this pathway covers the restraints placed on that remodelling — brakes that limit how far cardiomyocytes grow, change gene programmes and reorganise contractile structure. Such negative regulation of cardiac muscle adaptation keeps physiological growth from tipping into pathological hypertrophy, fibrosis and heart failure, and its loss underlies decompensated remodelling. The genes involved act at several levels: transcriptional control through FOXO1, PPARG and the TGF-beta effector SMAD3; nuclear envelope and lamina signalling through LMNA and its partner MLIP, where mutations cause dilated cardiomyopathy and conduction disease; calcium handling at the plasma membrane via the PMCA pump ATP2B4; growth-factor receptor damping by ERRFI1; apelin receptor signalling; and post-transcriptional tuning by microRNAs. Together they connect mechanical and metabolic stress sensing to limits on cardiomyocyte size and phenotype.

Development builds tissues partly by removing cells, and this pathway covers the genetically encoded death that is part of a cell's normal developmental programme rather than a response to injury. Sculpting of the nervous system, turnover of haematopoietic precursors and elimination of neurons that fail to secure trophic support all depend on it, and when it is blocked or excessive the result is malformation, retained supernumerary cells, or degeneration. The core decision is set by the balance between pro-apoptotic BAX and anti-apoptotic BCL2 at the mitochondrion, with CASP2 acting as an initiator caspase. Survival signals from neurotrophic and growth factor receptors such as NTRK1, KIT and the CNTF and FGF2 axes suppress that death, while inflammatory cytokines can promote it; DNASE1L3 degrades chromatin from dying cells, and PRKDC links the outcome to DNA damage signalling.

Schwann cells must stop dividing before they can wrap and myelinate peripheral axons, and restraining their proliferation is how the peripheral nervous system converts an expanding pool of precursors into a stable population of differentiated myelinating and non-myelinating glia. Loss of this brake produces the hyperproliferative Schwann cells of nerve sheath tumours and impairs myelin formation and nerve repair after injury. The genes involved act at several levels: microRNA processing by DICER1 is required for the exit from proliferation into the myelination programme, the transcription factor SOX10 and the transcriptional corepressor SKI shape the glial differentiation state, and sphingolipid synthesis through CERS2 supplies the ceramide backbone of myelin lipids. Together they link cell cycle withdrawal to the onset of axon ensheathment rather than to growth signalling alone.

This is the broad collection of activities that increase the frequency, rate or extent of gene expression, from transcriptional initiation through RNA stability and translation into mature product. It matters because almost every inducible response — inflammation, stress adaptation, differentiation, growth-factor signalling — is enacted by turning particular genes up, and the same machinery drives oncogenic programmes when it is misdirected. The members span sequence-specific activators and lineage factors such as MYC, STAT1/3, RELA, SMADs, GATA and SOX proteins; chromatin and DNA-modifying enzymes including histone acetyltransferases, KMT2A with its WDR5–RBBP5–ASH2L partners, and the TET dioxygenases; and post-transcriptional regulators — ELAVL1, IGF2BP and LARP proteins, m6A writers and YTHDF readers, microRNAs and translation initiation factors. Also prominent are upstream receptor and adaptor routes, notably Toll-like receptors with MYD88 and TRAF6 and cytosolic nucleic-acid sensing, that couple external cues to induced cytokine and interferon output.

Cells must switch genes off as precisely as they switch them on, and the negative regulation of gene expression gathers the machinery that lowers the rate or extent at which a coding sequence yields mature RNA or protein. It spans repression at every level: DNA methylation and reading by MECP2 and MBD proteins, histone deacetylases and Polycomb complexes that compact chromatin, transcriptional repressors such as REST, BCL6 and ID factors, and a large post-transcriptional arm built from microRNAs with Dicer, Drosha and Argonaute-TNRC6 silencing complexes, deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex, decapping and exosome-mediated decay, nonsense-mediated decay through UPF and SMG proteins, and translational brakes including 4E-BP and ZFP36-family destabilisers of cytokine mRNAs. This restraint sets differentiation boundaries, keeps inflammatory and growth-factor programmes transient, silences transposons in the germline, and maintains imprinting; its loss drives oncogenic overexpression, autoinflammation and developmental defects.

Epithelial sheets move as coordinated collectives during wound closure, gut and kidney tube morphogenesis, and gland branching, and this pathway covers the inputs that speed up, slow down or redirect that movement. Its outputs matter clinically at both extremes: too little epithelial motility leaves skin and corneal wounds unhealed, while unrestrained motility accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and carcinoma invasion. Growth factors and cytokines such as FGF7, FGF10, HBEGF, TGFB2 and interferon gamma feed through receptor tyrosine kinases, TGF-beta receptors and phospholipase C isoforms onto the adhesion and cytoskeletal machinery, where integrin ITGA2, focal adhesion kinase PTK2, SRC, profilins and microtubule-plus-end proteins of the CLASP family set lamellipodial protrusion and turnover of attachments. Rab11 and Rab25 traffic adhesion receptors forward, ARF6 and DOCK family Rac activators steer the leading edge, and PTEN and various phosphatases, plus several microRNAs, impose the restraint. Hypoxia acting through HIF1A and matrix remodelling by MMP9 and hyaluronan synthase link the response to tissue context.

Epithelial sheets must migrate during wound healing and morphogenesis, but that movement has to be restrained afterwards; this is the braking side of epithelial cell migration, keeping cells anchored in an intact sheet and limiting invasive behaviour. Loss of the brake contributes to tumour cell dissemination, which is why several members are tumour suppressors: PTEN degrades the PIP3 signal that drives leading-edge protrusion, DAB2IP restrains Ras and PI3K signalling, and MCC and PTPN23 act as negative regulators of growth and motility signalling. Protein tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPRG and PTPRR, and the MAPK phosphatase DUSP10, damp kinase cascades that would otherwise promote migration, while junctional and cytoskeletal proteins including MARVELD3, EPPK1, EVL, PFN2 and CORO1C set actin dynamics and cell-cell adhesion. Cytokine and microRNA inputs add extracellular and post-transcriptional control.

Epithelial sheets move during wound closure, tube formation and organ morphogenesis, and this pathway covers the inputs that push epithelial cell migration up in rate and extent. It matters for re-epithelialisation of skin and cornea, branching of glands and lung, and — when inappropriately sustained — for the invasive behaviour of carcinomas. Growth factor and cytokine cues (FGF7, FGF10, HBEGF, TGFB2 acting through TGFBR2) converge on SRC and focal adhesion kinase, PLCG and protein kinase C signalling, and on integrin-based adhesion through ITGA2. Downstream, Rho- and Rac-directed exchange factors and adaptors such as DOCK1 and DOCK5, ARF6 with RAB11A/RAB25-dependent recycling of adhesion receptors, and microtubule-plus-end proteins CLASP1/CLASP2 set lamellipodial protrusion and turnover of contacts. Matrix remodelling by MMP9 and hyaluronan synthesis clear a path, while HIF1A, JUN and SOX9 provide transcriptional reinforcement.

Mitochondria repeatedly merge and divide, and the controls on merging set how interconnected the network becomes, which in turn determines how efficiently membrane potential, metabolites and mitochondrial DNA are shared across the organelle population. Tilting this balance toward fragmentation is a prelude to mitophagy and apoptosis, while excessive or unregulated fusion blunts quality control; the regulators here act on both sides. Proteases of the inner membrane and intermembrane space, including OMA1 and YME1L1, process the fusion machinery and thereby govern whether inner-membrane fusion can proceed, ubiquitin ligases such as MUL1, HUWE1 and parkin mark fusion and fission proteins for degradation, and PLD6 generates phosphatidic acid at the outer membrane to promote merging. Outer-membrane and adaptor proteins including BNIP3, MTCH2 and MIEF1 couple this to mitophagy and to organelle positioning, linking network shape to cellular energy state and stress.

positive regulation of mitochondrial fusion covers the inputs that push the mitochondrial network toward a connected, tubular state rather than a fragmented one. Fusion lets mitochondria share matrix contents, mtDNA and membrane components, buffering damage in individual organelles and supporting oxidative metabolism, and its loss produces fragmented networks, mtDNA instability and neuromuscular and optic nerve disease. The genes act at several levels: a mitochondria-localised phospholipase D generates phosphatidic acid on the outer membrane to promote mitofusin-driven tethering, an intermembrane-space protease processes the inner-membrane fusogen OPA1 to balance long and short isoforms, a cytosolic adaptor is required for normal network morphology in muscle, and Parkin-dependent ubiquitylation couples fusion status to mitochondrial quality control. Together they tie organelle shape to metabolic demand, mitophagy and cell fate decisions.

Mitochondria continually merge and divide, and the pathway that promotes fusion tips this balance toward a connected network, allowing membrane potential, metabolites and mitochondrial DNA to be shared between organelles and damaged content to be diluted rather than accumulated. A cell that cannot upregulate fusion ends up with a fragmented, functionally heterogeneous mitochondrial population, a state linked to neurodegeneration and to the dominant optic atrophy and neuropathy syndromes caused by defects in the core fusion GTPases. The regulators here act on the outer and inner membranes: a mitochondrial phospholipase D generates phosphatidic acid from cardiolipin to favour outer-membrane tethering, MSTO1 supports fusion from the cytosolic face, and the inner-membrane protease YME1L1 processes OPA1, determining whether cristae and inner membranes can join. Such control is tightly coupled to mitochondrial quality surveillance and to fission machinery acting in the opposite direction.

Mitochondrial shape is set by a balance between fusion and division, and the processes that restrain fusion tip that balance toward fragmentation — a prerequisite for segregating damaged organelles and clearing them by mitophagy. Suppressing fusion matters during stress, hypoxia and depolarization, when keeping a damaged mitochondrion joined to the healthy network would spread the damage. Several routes converge on the fusion machinery itself: the inner-membrane protease OMA1 cleaves OPA1 to inactivate it, while ubiquitin ligases including MUL1, HUWE1 and parkin target mitofusins for degradation, and BNIP3 links hypoxic signalling to fragmentation and organelle turnover. The outcome is smaller, more numerous mitochondria that can be separated from the network and degraded. Loss of this restraint yields hyperfused, unsegregated mitochondria and impaired quality control, a defect relevant to neurodegeneration where parkin-dependent mitophagy fails.

Organelles are built, positioned, remodelled and taken apart on cue, and this grouping collects the activators that drive those events forward rather than restraining them. It spans the machinery that promotes actin filament nucleation and branching through Arp2/3 regulators and WAVE-complex members, microtubule and centrosome duplication controlled by polo-like and Aurora kinases, centriole assembly factors and plus-end tracking proteins, and chromosome condensation by condensin and cohesin complexes during mitosis. A second arm accelerates mitochondrial fission and mitophagy, with DNM1L, its receptors MFF and FIS1, and the PINK1-Parkin axis targeting damaged mitochondria for clearance, alongside autophagosome formation via ATG5, BECN1 and ULK1 and the release of mitochondrial apoptotic factors by BAX and BAK1. Telomere capping and nucleolar and PML body organization also appear. Because these steps set spindle fidelity, organelle turnover and cell death thresholds, their misregulation underlies chromosome instability and neurodegeneration.

Organelles and cytoskeletal structures are built, positioned and taken apart continuously, and this collection captures the braking side of that balance: processes that slow, cap, sever, sequester or dismantle organelle assembly rather than promote it. Restraint matters because unchecked polymerisation or unchecked division is as damaging as failure to build. Actin filament growth is limited by capping proteins, cofilin-family severing and profilin, with tropomodulins blocking pointed ends; microtubule dynamics are damped by stathmins, katanin regulatory subunits and centriole duplication brakes such as CCP110 and CEP97. The spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1, NDC80 complex members) holds anaphase back until kinetochores are attached, while shelterin components cap telomeres to prevent inappropriate DNA end processing. Mitochondrial fission and mitophagy factors including PINK1, PRKN, OPA1 and BNIP3 limit or remodel that organelle. Loss of such restraint drives aneuploidy, genome instability and disordered cell shape.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptors drive proliferation and migration of mesenchymal cells during wound healing, vascular smooth muscle investment of vessels, and fibrosis, so the strength and duration of their signalling must be held within limits; unchecked output contributes to intimal hyperplasia, glioma and fibrotic disease. The genes here set that ceiling by several routes. Ubiquitin ligases CBL and CBLB mark activated receptors for degradation, endosomal sorting and trafficking proteins such as HGS, HIP1, HIP1R and IFT20 govern receptor internalisation and delivery to the primary cilium, and receptor-type and cytoplasmic tyrosine phosphatases including PTPRJ, PTPN2 and PTPN12 reverse the phosphorylation that SRC and the receptor itself create. Other members act upstream or in parallel, with LRP1 and APOE influencing ligand and receptor availability and MYOCD linked to the smooth muscle differentiation state that PDGF signalling opposes.

PDGF receptor signalling drives the proliferation, migration and survival of mesenchymal cells — fibroblasts, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle — during wound healing, vessel maturation and tissue fibrosis, and the processes gathered here raise the amplitude or duration of that signalling. Several act on receptor availability rather than ligand supply: the huntingtin-interacting proteins HIP1 and HIP1R couple the receptor to clathrin-mediated endocytic trafficking, and a microRNA limits degradative sorting so that receptor levels at the surface are sustained. The Src kinase transduces and amplifies signals from the activated receptor tyrosine kinase, while tissue factor with coagulation factor VII, and interleukin-1 acting through its type I receptor, link haemostatic and inflammatory cues to growth factor responsiveness. Excessive output from this axis contributes to intimal hyperplasia, fibrotic remodelling and tumour stromal recruitment.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptors drive proliferation, migration and survival in fibroblasts, pericytes and vascular smooth muscle, and this dampening arm sets when and for how long that signal is allowed to run. Restraint matters because unchecked PDGF receptor activity contributes to intimal hyperplasia, fibrosis, glioma growth and pathological angiogenesis, while the same braking keeps smooth muscle in a contractile rather than synthetic state. The mechanisms are varied: receptor tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPRJ, PTPN2 and PTPN12 strip activating phosphotyrosines, HGS sorts activated receptors into the endosomal degradation route, and LRP1 promotes receptor internalisation and clearance. Secreted lipid-handling factors including APOE, APOD and adiponectin lower responsiveness from outside the cell, a scaffolding adaptor constrains receptor localisation, and transcriptional regulators such as MYOCD limit receptor expression, together tuning growth factor input to tissue repair rather than continuous growth.

Cell communication by electrical coupling is direct electrical continuity between neighbouring cells: current passes from one cytoplasm to the next through gap junction channels, so that a tissue behaves as a functional syncytium rather than a collection of independent cells. This is what allows the heart to contract as a coordinated unit and permits synchronised firing and metabolic sharing in neurons, glia and the cochlea. Connexins such as GJA1 and GJA5 form the channels, while their placement depends on intercalated disc and cytoskeletal partners including PKP2, ANK3 and TMEM43. Coupling is only useful if the coupled cells generate current in the first place, so the pathway also draws in the machinery of the cardiac action potential and calcium cycling: sodium pumps, L-type calcium channels, the ryanodine receptor with triadin and calsequestrin, the sodium-calcium exchanger, and transcriptional regulators like TBX5. Loss of these components produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, deafness and demyelinating neuropathy.

Electrical coupling lets adjacent cells share current directly, so that a tissue responds as a unit rather than as isolated cells. In the heart it is what allows a wave of depolarisation to spread from the sinoatrial node through atria and ventricles as a coordinated contraction, and in glia and cochlear supporting cells it synchronises populations and equalises ion loads. Connexins such as GJA1, GJA5 and GJC1 form the intercellular channels, docking at junctional plaques whose integrity depends on partners including PKP2 and TMEM43. Coupling is only useful alongside the machinery that generates and shapes the current: sodium pump subunits, the L-type calcium channel CACNA1C, ryanodine receptor RYR2 with triadin and calsequestrin, the sodium-calcium exchanger, and calmodulin-CaMKII and PKA regulation. Loss or mislocalisation of these components underlies arrhythmia and conduction block, deafness from GJB2 and GJB6 mutations, and hypomyelinating disease from GJC2.

Signalling between cells has to be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this collection covers the braking machinery: the inhibitors, feedback loops and decoys that reduce the strength, duration or spread of intercellular communication. Without them, responses to growth factors, cytokines, neurotransmitters and morphogens run unchecked, which underlies tumour growth, chronic inflammation, fibrosis and developmental patterning defects. The mechanisms are diverse but recognisable: secreted antagonists of WNT, BMP and Hedgehog such as DKKs, SFRPs, noggin and HHIP; intracellular destruction complex and pathway repressors including AXIN1, APC, SUFU, SMAD6/7 and the SOCS proteins; phosphatases and dual-specificity MAP kinase phosphatases that reverse activating phosphorylation; RGS proteins and phosphodiesterases that terminate G protein and cyclic nucleotide signals; immune checkpoint receptors such as CTLA4 and PDCD1; ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases that set receptor lifetime; and numerous microRNAs tuning transcript levels.

Adjacent cells that are electrically coupled share current directly through gap junction channels, and this pathway covers the processes that tune how strongly and how fast that coupling occurs. It matters most in the heart, where coordinated conduction between myocytes turns individual excitable cells into a synchronously contracting organ; disturbed coupling underlies conduction slowing, arrhythmia and sudden death. The genes point to two linked layers of control: connexin channels themselves, including the atrial and conduction-system channel encoded by GJA5, and the calcium-handling and signalling machinery that sets excitability around them — calmodulin isoforms, CAMK2D, the sodium–calcium exchanger SLC8A1, and sarcoplasmic reticulum proteins such as triadin, calsequestrin and sorcin. Transcription factors TBX5 and IRX3 pattern the conduction system and set regional channel expression, while ANK3 organises ion channels at specialised membrane domains.\n

Muscle cells are long-lived and largely post-mitotic, so their survival determines the working mass of heart and skeletal muscle; suppressing apoptosis in cardiomyocytes and myofibres is what keeps contractile tissue intact after ischaemia, mechanical overload or oxidative stress, and its failure contributes to heart failure, cardiomyopathy and muscle wasting. The genes here restrain caspase activation at several levels: CFLAR blocks death receptor signalling at the DISC, NOL3 and BAG3 act as anti-apoptotic chaperone and caspase-inhibitory factors supporting sarcomere maintenance, and IGF1 acting through PDPK1 delivers a survival signal. Cardiac transcription factors such as GATA4, NKX2-5, HAND2 and MYOCD couple survival to the differentiated muscle programme, while NFE2L2 buffers oxidative injury. A large set of microRNAs, including muscle-enriched MIR133A1 and MIR21, tunes the same decision post-transcriptionally, linking survival control to cardiac remodelling and regeneration.

Programmed death of mature contractile cells is the route by which cardiomyocytes and skeletal or smooth myocytes are lost after ischaemia, pressure overload, oxidative injury or dystrophic membrane damage, and because adult muscle regenerates poorly, this loss translates directly into heart failure, cardiomyopathy and muscle wasting. The genes here cover both the executioner machinery and its restraints: an apoptosome adaptor and caspase-recruiting step, calpain-mediated proteolysis, and inhibitors such as a caspase-8 decoy, an ARC-type repressor, and BAG-family and HSP90 chaperones that hold death signalling in check. Survival inputs arrive through insulin-like growth factor, neuregulin, adrenergic receptors and BMP/SMAD signalling, converging on FOXO1, ATF4, NRF2 and SIRT1 to balance stress adaptation against elimination. Mitochondrial quality control, superoxide dismutase and calcium handling by the sarcoplasmic reticulum set the threshold, and a large complement of microRNAs tunes it.

Cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle fibres are largely post-mitotic, so their death by apoptosis is effectively permanent tissue loss, and this programme is the route by which striated muscle cells are dismantled following ischaemic, mechanical, oxidative or metabolic stress. Its control underlies infarct expansion, adverse remodelling toward heart failure, and cachectic muscle wasting. Core machinery includes the apoptosome adaptor APAF1 acting with mitochondrial outer-membrane and mitophagy-linked proteins such as BNIP3 and AMBRA1, while calcium handling through the sarcoplasmic reticulum pump ATP2A2 and CaMK-dependent signalling couples excitation and stress to death decisions. Much of the content is protective: caspase decoys and inhibitors such as CFLAR and NOL3, chaperone and co-chaperone activity including HSP90AA1 and BAG3, NFE2L2-driven antioxidant defence, and survival input from NRG1. Cardiac transcription factors and numerous microRNAs set the threshold, tying survival to the differentiation programme itself.

Muscle fibres and cardiomyocytes are long-lived cells whose loss is poorly compensated, so signals that raise the rate of muscle cell apoptosis shape outcomes in heart failure, ischaemic injury, cachexia and muscular dystrophy. This pro-apoptotic arm gathers the stimuli that push a myocyte past the caspase threshold: sustained beta-adrenergic stimulation through ADRB1 and ADRB2 with downstream CaMKII activity, disturbed sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium handling via ATP2A2, mitochondrial stress and fission responses involving BNIP3 and MFN2, integrated stress signalling through ATF4, and inflammatory cytokines such as interferon gamma and IL-12. Transcriptional effectors including FOXO1, SMAD4, PPARG and the CDKN2A locus couple metabolic and growth-factor status to death commitment, while a large complement of microRNAs, among them miR-1 and miR-34a, tunes survival protein levels. The result is myocyte dropout, fibrotic replacement and declining contractile reserve.

Cardiac and skeletal muscle cells are long-lived and poorly replaced, so signals that push them into apoptosis set the pace of muscle loss in heart failure, ischaemic injury and myopathy. This programme covers the inputs that raise the rate of striated muscle cell death by caspase-dependent dismantling. Much of it runs through adrenergic and calcium handling: β-adrenergic receptors and the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases CAMK2A and CAMK2D couple chronic catecholamine drive to death signalling, while the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump ATP2A2 and the calcium-activated protease calpain CAPN2 link disturbed calcium cycling to the execution machinery. BNIP3 acts at mitochondria under hypoxic stress, TIGAR shifts glucose flux toward antioxidant defence, and a set of microRNAs including MIR34A, MIR195 and MIR16-1 tune apoptotic thresholds post-transcriptionally. Sustained activation contributes to adverse remodelling and contractile failure.

Cardiomyocytes and skeletal myofibres are largely post-mitotic, so any that dies by apoptosis is not replaced; suppressing that death is what allows the heart and skeletal muscle to tolerate ischaemia, mechanical load and oxidative stress without losing contractile mass. Genes here act as brakes on caspase-dependent programmed cell death in striated muscle: caspase-8 recruitment is blocked at the death receptor level by CFLAR, NOL3 restrains caspase activity in cardiac myocytes, and the co-chaperone BAG3 couples proteostasis and sarcomere maintenance to survival, with its loss causing dilated cardiomyopathy. Cardiac transcription factors such as GATA4, NKX2-5, HAND2 and HEY2, growth and trophic signals including NRG1, BMP7 and midkine, and stress-response regulators such as NFE2L2 and small heat-shock proteins feed into the same outcome, as do numerous microRNAs. The balance set here determines the extent of myocyte loss after infarction and in heart failure and muscular dystrophy.

Ectodermal cell differentiation describes how uncommitted embryonic cells take on the identity of the outer germ layer, the source of skin and its appendages, mammary and other ectodermal glands, and neural tissue. Its outputs are the epithelia that form the body's barrier and the placodes that give rise to hair, teeth and sweat glands; disrupted signalling here produces ectodermal dysplasias, in which those structures fail to form. The genes point to the signals and transcriptional outputs that drive this commitment: a TNF-family receptor of the ectodysplasin axis, Frizzled-mediated Wnt reception, ETS-family transcription factors including ELF5 that specify secretory mammary epithelium, and integrin-based attachment to basement membrane that keeps progenitors in their niche. A microRNA component adds post-transcriptional restraint, tuning the switch between progenitor self-renewal and terminal epithelial specialization during development and tissue renewal.

Ectodermal cell differentiation is the commitment and maturation of unspecialized cells into the derivatives of the embryonic ectoderm — epidermis and its appendages, mammary and other surface epithelia, and neural tissue. It determines the barrier and glandular structures of the skin, and its disruption produces ectodermal dysplasias with sparse hair, missing teeth and absent sweat glands. The genes here span the layers of that decision: a tumour necrosis factor family receptor of the ectodysplasin system relays the signal that specifies appendage placodes, a Frizzled receptor receives Wnt cues that pattern surface ectoderm, ETS-family transcription factors including ELF5 drive commitment to secretory and mammary epithelial fates, and integrin-mediated attachment to basement membrane keeps progenitors in their niche. A microRNA adds post-transcriptional restraint, tuning how quickly progenitors exit the proliferative state and differentiate.

Epithelia must hold their sheet architecture together while continuously renewing, and this homeostatic programme is what keeps that structure intact. It matters most at mucosal surfaces, where loss of barrier integrity leads to inflammatory bowel disease, ulceration and impaired wound repair. Several strands converge here: junctional and polarity components such as SCRIB, PKP3, LSR, ILDR1 and CXADR organise cell-cell contacts and apicobasal orientation; the FRAS1-FREM complex anchors epithelium to underlying basement membrane, and its failure produces congenital fusion defects; secreted mucins and trefoil factors build and restitute the protective mucus layer over gut and gastric epithelium. Innate immune sensors including TLR4, NOD2 and IL10RA signalling tune the epithelial response to microbial contact, while SOX9, NEUROD1 and SRF direct differentiation of the cell types that replenish the sheet. Damage, inflammation and repair are therefore inseparable from structural maintenance.

Sympathetic nerve terminals limit their own output, and the negative regulation of norepinephrine secretion is the brake that keeps noradrenergic drive from running away. It sets resting sympathetic tone, blood pressure and heart rate, and is the target of clonidine-type drugs used for hypertension, and of the presynaptic feedback lost in states of sympathetic overactivity. The core mechanism is autoinhibition: the three alpha-2 adrenergic receptor subtypes sit on the presynaptic membrane, sense released norepinephrine, and couple through inhibitory G proteins to close calcium channels and open potassium channels, damping vesicle fusion. Purinergic and neuropeptide receptors provide parallel presynaptic restraint, so co-released ATP and hypothalamic signals feed into the same set point. This places the pathway within autonomic control of cardiovascular function and within the stress axis rather than in transmitter synthesis itself.

Connective tissue strength depends on how much collagen is made, how it is processed and when it is degraded, and this pathway covers the controls that set those rates. It matters wherever matrix turnover must be tuned: wound healing, bone and tendon formation, vascular remodelling, and the fibrotic scarring that follows chronic injury in liver, lung, heart and kidney. TGFB1 and TGFB3 signalling, along with activin, BMP and WNT inputs, drives fibroblast collagen transcription, while IL6 signalling, thrombin acting through its receptor F2R, and integrin and discoidin-domain collagen receptors such as ITGA2/ITGB1 and DDR2 feed matrix and inflammatory cues back into the same output. Regulation is not only transcriptional: LARP6 controls collagen mRNA translation, CREB3L1 supports secretory capacity, and several microRNAs including the miR-29 family repress collagen transcripts directly. Transcription factors such as SCX and RUNX1 place this control within lineage-specific matrix programmes.

Connective tissue only holds its shape if collagen deposition is restrained as well as driven, and this is the braking side of collagen metabolism — processes that lower the rate or extent of collagen synthesis, maturation and turnover. Its failure is fibrosis: excess matrix in liver, lung, kidney, skin and heart, and stiffening of vessel walls and valves. The restraint is imposed at several levels. Micro-RNAs of the miR-29 family directly repress collagen and other matrix transcripts, making them among the best-characterised antifibrotic regulators. Transcriptional inputs including KLF15, PPARD and NOTCH1 tune fibroblast and smooth muscle matrix output, while IL6 signalling through its receptor links inflammatory tone to collagen handling. Secreted components such as EMILIN1 and the protease inhibitor CST3 act extracellularly, and ERRFI1 dampens growth factor receptor signalling that would otherwise promote matrix production.

Collagen is the load-bearing protein of skin, bone, tendon and vessel wall, and this pathway covers the signals that push its production and turnover upward. Raising collagen output is how tissues heal wounds, mineralize bone and remodel after mechanical loading; when the same drives persist, the result is fibrosis, stiffened arteries and scarring. The inputs are largely secreted morphogens and injury signals — TGF-beta family ligands including TGFB1, TGFB3, BMP4 and INHBA, hedgehog and WNT cues, and thrombin acting through its protease-activated receptor — converging on fibroblast, osteoblast and tenocyte programmes. Transcriptional effectors such as CREB3L1, RUNX1 and the tendon factor SCX raise collagen gene expression, while LARP6 binds collagen mRNA to control its translation and DDR2 and integrin alpha-2 read the existing fibrillar matrix back as a feedback signal. The pathway sits at the interface of growth factor signalling, extracellular matrix assembly and repair.

Tissues remodel by breaking down the matrix they sit in, and this pathway covers the controls that set how fast and how far that breakdown goes. Balanced disassembly permits wound repair, angiogenesis, immune cell migration and mammary or vascular remodelling; unchecked, it underlies tumour invasion and metastasis, fibrotic turnover and cartilage loss, while excessive restraint leaves matrix accumulating. Control acts at several levels. Inhibitors such as TIMP3, RECK and the cysteine protease inhibitor cystatin C hold matrix proteases in check, whereas surface proteases and glycosidases including FAP, DPP4 and heparanase cleave collagen and heparan sulfate directly. Collagen-binding receptors DDR1 and DDR2 sense fibrillar collagen and feed back onto protease expression, and cytokine signalling through TGFB1 and IL6-STAT3 tunes the programme transcriptionally. Several microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, repress matrix and remodelling transcripts, and LRP1 clears proteases and matrix fragments by endocytosis.

Connective tissue only holds its shape if matrix breakdown is restrained, and negative regulation of extracellular matrix disassembly covers the brakes that limit proteolytic turnover of collagen, proteoglycans and basement membrane. Restraint of this kind keeps tissue architecture intact during wound healing and remodelling; when it fails, matrix is degraded too freely, favouring tumour invasion, metastasis, aneurysm and emphysematous lung destruction, while excess restraint contributes to fibrosis. The effectors act at several levels: TIMP3 directly inhibits matrix metalloproteinases and ADAM-family sheddases, RECK is a membrane-anchored inhibitor of MMP activity, cystatin C blocks cathepsin-type cysteine proteases, and TGFB1 signalling shifts the balance toward matrix deposition and protease inhibitor expression. Several microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, add post-transcriptional control over matrix and protease gene output, so the pathway sits at the interface of proteolysis and matrix homeostasis.

Epithelial cells can be licensed to abandon their polarity and junctions and move, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how readily that switch is thrown. Controlled epithelial-to-mesenchymal conversion builds the heart valves, palate and neural crest derivatives in development and drives wound repair; when it is inappropriately sustained it underlies fibrosis of kidney, lung and liver and gives carcinoma cells invasive and stem-like properties. The dominant driver arm here is TGF-beta and BMP signalling through TGFBR1/2 and receptor SMADs, restrained by SMAD7, BAMBI, noggin and gremlin, and converging with WNT/beta-catenin-LEF1/TCF, Notch and receptor tyrosine kinase output damped by Sprouty and SPRED proteins. Transcriptional execution runs through SNAI1, TWIST1 and TAZ, opposed by OVOL2 and ZNF750, with chromatin regulators such as EZH2, KDM1A and HDAC2 and an extensive set of microRNAs tuning the balance.

Epithelial cells can be driven to abandon apical-basal polarity, dissolve their junctions, breach basement membrane and move as mesenchymal cells; the genes here act to increase the rate and extent of that conversion. The programme builds the heart cushions, palate and neural crest during development, drives wound repair and organ fibrosis, and when reactivated in carcinoma supplies invasiveness, stem-like traits and drug resistance. TGF-beta ligands acting through TGFBR1/TGFBR2 and SMAD2/3/4, BMP signalling via ACVR1 and endoglin, Wnt output through beta-catenin with LEF1 and TCF7L2, and Notch and inflammatory cytokines such as IL1B and IL6 converge on the transcription factors SNAI1 and TWIST1, which repress epithelial adhesion genes. Chromatin regulators including EZH2, HDAC2 and the demethylase KDM1A entrench the new state, while LOXL2, collagen I and focal adhesion kinase remodel the matrix the cell must cross.

Epithelial cells can be driven to lose polarity, break their junctions and become migratory mesenchymal cells; the restraints collected here hold that conversion in check and so preserve epithelial sheets, barrier function and differentiated tissue architecture. Their loss permits fibrosis and the invasive, metastatic behaviour of carcinomas, and the same brakes limit stemness and drug resistance in tumour cells. Mechanistically they act at several levels: extracellular antagonists of BMP and Wnt such as NOG, SFRP1 and SFRP2, intracellular inhibitors of TGF-beta and receptor tyrosine kinase output including SMAD7, DACT3, the SPRED and SPRY proteins, PTEN and GSK3B, and transcription factors that enforce epithelial identity such as FOXA1, FOXA2, GATA3, OVOL2 and ZNF750. Numerous microRNAs, the miR-200-like miR-145 and miR-29 among them, repress mesenchymal transcripts post-transcriptionally, while desmosomal DSG2 and ephrin-Eph contacts stabilise cell-cell adhesion.

This grouping collects the signals and regulators that accelerate or extend cell development — the maturation of an already specified cell into its finished form — rather than the commitment decisions that assign fate. Its outputs are the differentiated cell types that tissues depend on: neurons extending axons and dendrites under guidance cues such as netrin, slit and semaphorin receptors, oligodendrocytes and myelin regulators including SOX10 and MYRF, skeletal muscle driven by the myogenic factors MYOD1, MYOG and MYF5, and lymphoid and myeloid cells shaped by interleukins, antigen receptor kinases like LCK, SYK and ZAP70, and osteoclast induction through RANKL and its receptor. Chromatin remodelling subunits of the BAF complex, Notch, Wnt, Hedgehog and BMP signalling, and neurotrophin–TRK support converge on transcriptional programmes of maturation. Loss of such positive regulation underlies neurodevelopmental disorders, immunodeficiency, dysmyelination and failed muscle or bone remodelling.

Differentiation has to be held back as well as driven, and this collection covers the brakes: processes that slow or restrain the maturation of a cell once its fate has been assigned, without deciding that fate. Restraint of this kind keeps progenitor pools from being exhausted, sets the timing of maturation, and prevents inappropriate activation or overgrowth. Two arenas dominate. In the nervous system, growth-cone inhibitors and guidance repellents — semaphorins, slits, netrin receptors, myelin-associated MAG and RTN4 with its receptor — limit neurite outgrowth and differentiation, while Notch-HES signalling, ID factors, REST and microRNAs such as miR-137 and LIN28A hold neural progenitors immature. In the immune system, FOXP3, CTLA4, LAG3, SOCS1, PTEN and inhibitory Fc and LILRB receptors curb lymphocyte and myeloid maturation. BMP antagonists, WNT and SHH modulators, TGF-beta family inhibitors like SMAD7, and proteasome subunits that degrade differentiation factors add further layers. Loss of such restraint contributes to autoimmunity, developmental malformation and tumour formation.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a signalling molecule and a source of oxidative damage, so cells restrain how much of it is made and how long it persists; this pathway covers the influences that lower peroxide production and turnover. Damping peroxide protects membranes, iron-sulfur proteins and DNA from oxidation, and it tunes redox-sensitive signalling rather than abolishing it, which matters for inflammation, neuronal survival and tissue responses to haemolysis. The genes here act through varied routes: haptoglobin sequesters free haemoglobin so that heme iron cannot drive peroxide chemistry, metallothionein-3 buffers zinc and copper and scavenges reactive species in brain, a mitochondrial inner-membrane protein of the MPV17 family limits organellar reactive oxygen output, and the kinase FYN, the deacetylase HDAC6 and the transcription factor STAT3 link redox state to signalling and gene expression. Loss of such restraint contributes to oxidative stress in neurodegeneration and vascular injury.

regulation of hydrogen peroxide biosynthetic process controls how much H2O2 a cell makes, balancing its use as a signalling molecule and antimicrobial weapon against its capacity to oxidise DNA, lipids and protein thiols. Setting this level matters for thyroid hormone synthesis, mucosal host defence, and redox-dependent control of growth signalling; too little leaves hypothyroidism and poor epithelial defence, too much drives oxidative damage and inflammation. The maturation factors DUOXA1 and DUOXA2 escort dual oxidases from the endoplasmic reticulum to the apical membrane, where they generate peroxide extracellularly, while superoxide dismutase 2 produces H2O2 in the mitochondrial matrix from respiratory superoxide. Kinase and transcriptional inputs such as FYN and STAT3 tune this output, linking peroxide production to cytokine and growth factor signalling rather than leaving it a passive byproduct of aerobic metabolism.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a damaging byproduct of aerobic metabolism and a deliberate signalling molecule, and the processes that set how much of it a cell makes determine which of those roles dominates. Control over hydrogen peroxide biosynthesis matters for thyroid hormone synthesis, where peroxide generated at the apical membrane of thyrocytes is the oxidant used to iodinate thyroglobulin, and for the oxidative burst that epithelia and phagocytes direct at microbes. The maturation factors DUOXA1 and DUOXA2 are required for the dual oxidases to fold, traffic to the plasma membrane and produce peroxide rather than superoxide, so their loss causes congenital hypothyroidism. Other components act as brakes or tuners: mitochondrial superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to peroxide and shapes the mitochondrial oxidant pool, while kinase and transcription-factor input from FYN and STAT3 couples oxidant output to growth-factor and cytokine signalling and to redox-dependent gene expression.

regulation of macrophage derived foam cell differentiation controls whether a macrophage in the arterial wall becomes a lipid-engorged foam cell, the defining cell of atherosclerotic plaque. Because foam cells drive lesion growth, necrotic core formation and plaque instability, the balance set here determines cardiovascular risk. Two opposing arms are represented: uptake of modified lipoproteins through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and MSR1, aided by lipoprotein lipase, apolipoprotein B particles and secreted phospholipases that make lipoproteins more atherogenic; and cholesterol efflux through ABCA1 and ABCG1, transcriptionally driven by the liver X receptors NR1H2/NR1H3 and PPAR nuclear receptors. Inflammatory input from TNF, IL1B, IL18 and NF-kB signalling, together with CSF1-dependent macrophage differentiation, angiotensin signalling and adiponectin, tunes the outcome, linking lipid handling to innate immune activation and to metabolic and endocrine control of vascular inflammation.

Foam cells are lipid-engorged macrophages that form the fatty streaks of atherosclerotic plaque, and this pathway covers the signals that push macrophages toward that fate or hold them back. The balance set here determines whether an artery wall clears deposited lipoprotein or accumulates it, making it one of the proximate controls on atherosclerosis, plaque inflammation and its thrombotic consequences. Uptake is driven by scavenger receptors such as CD36 and MSR1 acting on modified LDL, together with lipases and secreted phospholipases that process lipoprotein substrates. Opposing this, cholesterol efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1, induced by the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 and by PPAR family factors, unload cholesterol onto acceptors. Inflammatory cytokines including TNF, IL1B and IL18, NF-kB signalling, and angiotensin-system components tune the outcome, linking innate immune activation to lipid handling in the vessel wall.

Foam cells are the lipid-engorged macrophages that fill atherosclerotic plaques, and this pathway covers the signals that push macrophages further and faster into that state.
