It matters because foam cell accumulation drives fatty streak formation, plaque growth and eventual rupture in coronary and carotid disease. Scavenger receptors such as CD36 and MSR1 take up modified and aggregated lipoprotein particles carrying apolipoprotein B, while lipoprotein lipase and secreted phospholipases of the PLA2 family modify those particles to make them more avidly internalized. Inflammatory cytokines including TNF, IL1B and IL18, the macrophage growth factors CSF1 and CSF2, platelet-derived PF4, and angiotensin acting through its type 1 receptor all amplify uptake, with NFKB1-dependent transcription and kinase signalling relaying the input. The result links innate immune activation and lipid handling to vascular inflammation.

Macrophages in the artery wall take up modified lipoproteins and, if they cannot dispose of the cholesterol they ingest, become lipid-laden foam cells that form the core of atherosclerotic plaque. This pathway covers the brakes on that conversion, and its output is essentially cholesterol efflux: the transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1 move cellular cholesterol and phospholipid onto apolipoprotein A-I and HDL particles, keeping the macrophage from accumulating cytoplasmic lipid droplets. Much of the control is transcriptional, through the sterol-sensing nuclear receptors LXRa and LXRb together with PPARa and PPARg, which induce the efflux machinery when cholesterol loading rises. Adipokine signalling via adiponectin, restraint of NF-kB-driven inflammatory activation, and microRNA-mediated tuning add further layers. Loss of these controls, as in ABCA1 deficiency, leaves macrophages engorged and accelerates plaque formation and cardiovascular disease.

How much long-chain fatty acid a cell takes up from the blood is not set by the transporter alone; it is tuned by insulin signalling and by metabolic trapping inside the cell, and this regulation of long-chain fatty acid import across the plasma membrane determines whether muscle, heart and adipose tissue burn or store lipid. Acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL1 and ACSL5 esterify newly arrived fatty acids to CoA, keeping the free intracellular pool low so that net inward flux continues and the fatty acid is committed to oxidation or triglyceride synthesis. Insulin acting through IRS2 and the AKT1/AKT2 kinases promotes transporter availability at the surface, while the matricellular protein THBS1 links extracellular cues to uptake. Excessive flux through this route contributes to ectopic lipid accumulation, lipotoxicity and insulin resistance in obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Nitric oxide diffuses from endothelium into neighbouring cells and is read out by soluble guanylate cyclase, which raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle; controlling the gain of this NO-mediated signal transduction sets vascular tone, blood pressure and platelet reactivity. Both catalytic subunits of the NO receptor guanylate cyclase appear here as the direct sensor, and several of the remaining genes act upstream on how much signal is generated or permitted. Growth factor input through VEGFA and its receptor KDR stimulates endothelial NO output, insulin does likewise via metabolic signalling to endothelium, and the matricellular protein thrombospondin-1 acts as a brake, restraining NO-cGMP responses through CD47. Cystathionine beta-synthase links the pathway to sulfur amino acid metabolism and hydrogen sulfide crosstalk. Loss of this regulation contributes to endothelial dysfunction, hypertension, impaired angiogenesis and defective wound perfusion.

Nitric oxide released by endothelium acts on neighbouring smooth muscle and platelets, and this pathway covers the inputs that strengthen that signal, raising the amount of cGMP made in response to NO. The output is vasodilation, restrained platelet aggregation and blood pressure control, and its loss is a defining feature of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension, diabetes and atherosclerosis. Two of the genes encode alpha subunits of soluble guanylate cyclase, the heme-containing NO receptor that converts the gas into cGMP for downstream kinase and channel targets. The others are upstream stimuli acting on endothelial cells: insulin, the VEGF receptor KDR, and the HDL receptor SCARB1, each capable of activating endothelial NO synthase through kinase signalling and so amplifying flux through the NO-cGMP axis.

Receptor guanylyl cyclases generate cGMP in response to natriuretic peptides or gut peptides such as guanylin, driving vasodilation, natriuresis and intestinal fluid secretion; damping that signal is how cells set the duration and amplitude of the response rather than leaving it switched on. The genes here act as brakes. Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases hydrolyse cGMP back to GMP, with PDE2A stimulated by cGMP itself to form a feedback loop, and PDE10A and PDE11A providing dual cAMP/cGMP degradation in striatum and other tissues. Thrombospondin-1 acts extracellularly through CD47 to suppress cGMP production and blunt nitric oxide- and peptide-driven relaxation, while melatonin receptor signalling through inhibitory G proteins lowers cyclase output. Loss of this negative control shifts vascular tone, platelet reactivity and secretory balance, and phosphodiesterases of this class are long-standing drug targets.

Plasmin is the protease that dissolves fibrin clots and degrades extracellular matrix, and control over how fast plasminogen is converted into it sets the balance between clot persistence and bleeding, and between tissue remodelling and invasion. Regulation of plasminogen activation covers both sides of that balance: tissue-type and urokinase plasminogen activators cleave the zymogen, the urokinase receptor concentrates that reaction at the cell surface, and cell-surface docking sites such as the annexin A2 u2013S100A10 complex and PLGRKT localise plasminogen where activation is efficient. Opposing them are serpins, including plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and alpha-2 antiplasmin, which quench activators and plasmin itself, while thrombospondin-1 and tetranectin modulate the reaction. Through these steps the pathway shapes fibrinolysis, wound healing, angiogenesis, pericellular proteolysis during tumour invasion, and the thrombotic risk that follows excess inhibitor activity.

Plasmin is the protease that degrades fibrin and activates matrix-remodelling enzymes, and this pathway covers the events that increase the conversion of circulating plasminogen into it. Enhanced plasminogen activation clears thrombi, opens paths for cell migration and invasion, and releases growth factors from matrix; unchecked, it promotes bleeding and tumour spread, while insufficient activation favours fibrin persistence. Much of the control is surface-based: annexin A2 in complex with S100A10 forms a cell-surface receptor that co-localises plasminogen with its activators, and PLGRKT and enolase-1 similarly present plasminogen through C-terminal lysine binding, accelerating cleavage at the membrane. Coagulation factor XII links the contact activation system to fibrinolysis, and the transmembrane serine protease hepsin contributes proteolytic activity. Tetranectin binds plasminogen kringle domains, coupling this regulation to matrix and bone biology.

Plasmin is the protease that dissolves fibrin clots and degrades extracellular matrix, and restraining its generation from plasminogen sets how long a clot survives and how far tissue remodelling proceeds. Negative regulation of plasminogen activation is carried out largely by serpins: SERPINE1 (PAI-1) inhibits both tissue-type and urokinase-type plasminogen activators, SERPINE2 acts on related serine proteases, and SERPINF2 (alpha-2-antiplasmin) neutralises plasmin itself, while thrombospondin-1 binds and modulates activator activity at the cell surface and in matrix. The plasminogen activators PLAT and PLAU appear here as the targets of this control. Too little inhibition produces bleeding and excessive matrix breakdown; too much favours thrombosis and fibrosis, and elevated PAI-1 is a feature of metabolic syndrome and of tumour invasion, where the same axis governs pericellular proteolysis and cell migration.

Macrophages only reach infected or damaged tissue if their directed migration is tuned, and this pathway covers the signals that raise or damp the rate and extent of macrophage chemotaxis. It sets how much myeloid infiltrate an inflamed site accumulates, and so shapes wound healing, atherosclerotic plaque growth, tumour-associated macrophage recruitment and the resolution of infection. Chemoattractants act through G protein-coupled receptors — complement fragments via C3AR1 and C5AR1, CCL2 and CCL5 via chemokine receptors, and chemerin via CMKLR1 — while CSF1 and IL34 signalling through the shared receptor CSF1R supports macrophage survival, differentiation and movement. Inside the cell, focal adhesion kinases PTK2 and PTK2B and the ERK kinases MAPK1 and MAPK3 convert these cues into cytoskeletal steering, with MIF, midkine and thrombospondin adding further attractant or modulatory input and phosphatases such as PTPRJ restraining the response.

Macrophages must be told where to go, and this is the set of signals and receptors that increase their directed migration toward a site of infection, injury or tissue remodelling. It underlies inflammatory infiltration, wound repair, and the recruitment of tumour-associated macrophages, and its excess drives chronic inflammatory and fibrotic disease. Chemokines such as CCL2 and CCL5 act through classical receptors, complement fragments act through the C3a and C5a receptors, and chemerin signals via CMKLR1; CSF1 and the related ligand IL34 engage CSF1R to support both survival and movement. Downstream, ERK1/2 and the focal adhesion kinase PTK2 couple receptor input to cytoskeletal remodelling and adhesion turnover, with the mechanosensitive channel TRPV4 and matricellular THBS1 modulating responsiveness. Positive regulation here sits at the interface of innate immune signalling and cell motility control.

Macrophages are recruited to tissues by chemotactic gradients, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven, or inflammatory infiltrate persists and causes collateral tissue damage. Negative regulation of macrophage chemotaxis covers the signals that slow or stop that directed migration, restraining how many macrophages arrive at a site of injury or infection and how far they move once there. The genes involved act at several levels: secreted cytokine-like mediators and their receptor engagement, a complement component whose cleavage products are themselves chemoattractants and therefore a point of gradient control, a matrix metalloproteinase implicated in limiting macrophage recruitment, a signalling adaptor, and an immune-cell surface receptor of the SLAM family. An estrogen-synthesising enzyme links steroid hormone status to the strength of the response, one route by which sex hormones shape inflammation and the resolution phase of wound healing.

Fibroblasts crawl through connective tissue by protruding and retracting pseudopodia, and this motility is what closes wounds, remodels collagen-rich matrix during development, and drives the fibrotic scarring and desmoplastic stroma of chronic disease. Movement requires coupling of integrin-based adhesions to the actin cytoskeleton: beta1 and beta3 integrins with talin-like and tensin adaptors, ILK and focal adhesion kinase transmitting adhesion signals inward, and Rac1 with PAK1 and the exchange factor ARHGEF7 setting the direction of lamellipodial protrusion. Growth factor and cytokine cues, notably FGF2 and TGFB1, license migration and can convert fibroblasts to contractile, smooth-muscle-actin-expressing myofibroblasts, while matrix components such as thrombospondin, syndecan-4, hyaluronan synthase and the collagen receptor DDR2 tie locomotion to the substrate being traversed. Several microRNAs and transcriptional regulators including ZEB2 tune the whole programme.

Fibroblasts crawl into wounds, deposit collagen and remodel the surrounding matrix, and the control of that movement sets the pace of tissue repair, scarring and fibrosis. This pathway covers the signals that speed up, slow down or redirect fibroblast migration, which depends on cycles of pseudopodial extension and retraction driven by actin remodelling. Integrins such as ITGB1 and ITGB3, with the co-receptor syndecan-4 and adaptors including ITGB1BP1, couple matrix contact to focal adhesion kinase PTK2, while RAC1 and its regulators ARHGEF7 and ARHGAP4 act through PAK1 to shape the leading edge. Growth factor and cytokine inputs, notably FGF2 and TGFB1, plus matrix cues from thrombospondin and hyaluronan turnover, feed into AKT1 and BRAF signalling; several microRNAs and the transcription factor ZEB2 tune the response. Excessive activity contributes to fibrotic remodelling and myofibroblast persistence, while impairment delays wound closure.

positive regulation of fibroblast migration covers the signals that drive fibroblasts to crawl into and across tissue, the movement that closes wounds, remodels connective tissue and, when sustained, produces fibrosis and scarring. Fibroblast motility supplies the collagen-secreting cells that granulation tissue and healing skin depend on; in tumours the same programme generates the invasive stroma. The genes describe the machinery that converts adhesive and growth-factor cues into directed pseudopodial extension: integrin β1 and β3 receptors and the collagen receptor DDR2 sense matrix, focal adhesion kinase and the Rac/Cdc42 exchange factor ARHGEF7 with PAK1 relay to the actin cytoskeleton, and scaffolds such as AKAP12 organise PKC and Akt signalling at the leading edge. TGFβ1 and thrombospondin-1 act as extracellular drivers, coupling this behaviour to myofibroblast differentiation, while miR-145 tunes the cytoskeletal output.

Fibroblasts crawl toward sites of tissue injury to deposit and remodel matrix, and this pathway covers the signals that raise the rate and extent of that movement. It matters most in wound healing and in its pathological extension: sustained stimulation drives fibrosis of lung, liver and heart, and contributes to tumour stroma invasion, while too little impairs wound closure. Adhesion to collagen and fibronectin through integrin beta subunits and the collagen receptor DDR2 is transmitted by focal adhesion kinase, PAK1 and the Rho-family exchange factor ARHGEF7 to reorganise actin and cycle pseudopodial protrusion against retraction, with smooth muscle actin marking the contractile myofibroblast state. TGFB1 and the matricellular protein thrombospondin-1 supply extracellular cues, AKT1 and protein kinase C epsilon relay survival and motility signalling, and a microRNA component provides post-transcriptional restraint on the same cytoskeletal programme.

Fibroblasts crawl toward sites of injury to deposit matrix and close wounds, and the restraint of that movement sets how far and how fast they go. Braking fibroblast migration limits scarring and fibrosis; when the brakes fail, wound repair tips into excessive matrix deposition and tissue stiffening, while excessive braking delays healing. The genes here act at several levels of the motile machinery: a Rho-family GTPase and a Rho GTPase-activating protein govern actin protrusion at the leading edge, an integrin beta-1 binding protein tunes adhesion turnover, hyaluronan synthesis and its degradation alter the pericellular matrix the cell must pull against, and growth factor and transcriptional inputs including FGF2 and ZEB2 reset the migratory programme. Microt RNAs of the miR-19 family contribute post-transcriptional control, linking this negative regulation to broader control of cell shape, adhesion and tissue remodelling.

positive regulation of sodium ion transport covers the mechanisms that increase sodium movement across membranes, tuning both electrical excitability and whole-body salt and water balance. It matters because the same regulatory steps set cardiac and neuronal firing thresholds and determine renal sodium reabsorption, so its disturbance produces arrhythmia, altered nerve conduction, and hypertension. Two arms are evident. One consists of accessory and modulatory subunits of voltage-gated sodium channels and the sodium pump — SCN1B–SCN4B, the FXYD family, ATP1B isoforms — together with cytoskeletal and junctional partners such as ANK3 and PKP2 that place channels at nodes of Ranvier and cardiac intercalated discs, and intracellular FGF12/FGF13 that shift SCN5A gating. The other is a kinase network, including WNK2/WNK3, STK39 and AKT1, that activates sodium-coupled cotransporters and epithelial sodium channels in response to volume and hormonal cues, with proteolytic activation by PRSS8 and transcriptional input from NKX2-5.

Sodium gradients drive electrical excitability in nerve and muscle, salt reabsorption in kidney, and secondary transport of nutrients and other ions, and this pathway covers the agents that increase sodium movement rather than carrying it themselves. Much of the content is accessory: FXYD family proteins tune the Na+/K+-ATPase by associating with its catalytic pump and beta subunits, while SCN1B-SCN4B and fibroblast growth factor homologous factors FGF12 and FGF13 modify the gating and surface density of voltage-gated sodium channels such as cardiac SCN5A. A second arm is regulatory kinase signalling, where WNK kinases and the downstream STK39 activate sodium-coupled cotransporters, and AKT1 and the protease PRSS8 raise epithelial sodium channel activity. Failure or excess here produces cardiac conduction disease and arrhythmia, epilepsy, and disordered blood pressure and salt handling.

Sodium movement across membranes sets epithelial salt handling, extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure, as well as the excitability of nerve and muscle, so the braking mechanisms that restrain it are as consequential as the channels themselves. Negative regulation of sodium ion transport collects the processes that lower channel and transporter activity or abundance. Ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family tag the epithelial sodium channel for removal from the apical surface, curbing renal Na+ reabsorption; loss of that control underlies a hereditary hypertension. WNK kinases together with the downstream STK39 and OSR1 kinases set the activity of cation-chloride cotransporters, while scaffolds such as NHERF1 and signalling through angiotensinogen-derived peptides, protein kinase C and CaMKII adjust exchanger and channel behaviour. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional restraint. The net output is tuned sodium flux in kidney, vasculature and excitable tissue.

Differentiating cells must physically remodel themselves — extending processes, elaborating branches, expanding surfaces — and this is the arm of that programme that drives such shape change forward rather than restraining it. In the nervous system, where most of these genes act, it determines dendrite arborization, axon guidance and the formation and stabilization of dendritic spines, and so sets the wiring capacity of a circuit; loss of members such as CDKL5, RELN, PAFAH1B1 or TBC1D24 produces epileptic encephalopathy, cortical malformation and intellectual disability. Mechanistically it links surface receptors and guidance cues — ephrin receptors EPHA4 and EPHB2, a Frizzled receptor, the reelin receptor LRP8, PTPRD — to actin and microtubule regulators including drebrin, BAIAP2 and a plus-end tracking protein, with calcium/calmodulin kinase signalling, RNA-binding proteins that localize transcripts to growing processes, and a cullin–RING ubiquitin module tuning the response.

Messenger RNA must be licensed and delivered through nuclear pores before it can be translated, and this regulatory layer sets how fast and how selectively that delivery happens. It couples the history of a transcript to its fate: co-transcriptional marks left by chromatin and elongation factors, such as the histone methyltransferase SETD2 acting with the elongation-associated IWS1, help load export machinery onto nascent mRNA, while RNA modifications laid down or removed by NSUN2 and the m6A demethylase ALKBH5 alter which messages leave and when. Structural components contribute directly — a subunit of the TREX export complex and the nuclear basket protein TPR, which retains incompletely processed transcripts — alongside nuclear-retained long noncoding RNA scaffolding of paraspeckles. Through these steps the pathway tunes cytoplasmic protein output, shapes stress and developmental responses, and when deregulated contributes to aberrant gene expression in cancer.

Phosphorylation on threonine residues is a switch used throughout signalling, and this pathway covers the upstream inputs that raise or lower how much of it happens on a given substrate. Controlling the extent of threonine phosphorylation determines whether kinase cascades stay on, how polarity complexes are assembled, and how cells respond to growth factors and stress. The members act at several removes from the chemistry itself: a growth factor ligand and the ERK-family kinase MAPK1 feed activating signals inward, the scaffold PARD3 positions kinases within apical-basal polarity complexes, the deacetylase SIRT2 tunes kinase and substrate activity through acetylation, and WNK3 belongs to a kinase family that phosphorylates downstream threonines on ion transporter regulators. Because the targets include cell cycle, cytoskeletal and transport proteins, altered regulation here shifts proliferation, epithelial organisation and ion homeostasis rather than one narrow output.

Threonine residues are a major target of regulatory phosphorylation, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of such modification on substrate proteins. Because threonine phosphorylation sits at activation loops and docking sites of kinases and at the control points of transporters and transcription factors, increasing it shifts cells toward proliferation, survival, migration or altered ion handling. The contributors here are heterogeneous rather than a single cascade: a growth factor and a secreted glycoprotein act through receptor signalling to drive downstream kinase activation, MAPK1 itself is both a threonine-phosphorylated kinase and a kinase acting on substrates, WNK3 belongs to a family controlling chloride-dependent cation cotransport, and ubiquitin-pathway and immunity-related components modulate kinase activity indirectly. Such positive regulation matters in inflammation, autophagy control and tumour cell behaviour, where sustained phosphorylation replaces transient signalling.

Threonine phosphorylation on target proteins is a reversible switch, and this pathway covers the braking side of it — processes that lower the rate or extent of peptidyl-threonine modification, either by restraining the kinases responsible or by sequestering their substrates. Damping such phosphorylation matters for keeping kinase output transient rather than constitutive, which is how cells maintain junctional stability, cytoskeletal organisation and polarity rather than locking into a signalling state. The genes involved point to several routes: a cell adhesion molecule and a polarity scaffold that position signalling complexes at membranes and cell contacts, a cytoskeletal adaptor linking membrane to actin, and a NAD-dependent deacetylase whose substrate modification alters downstream kinase activity. Loss of this restraint biases cells toward sustained kinase signalling, with consequences for epithelial architecture and cell division control.

Tumor necrosis factor binding to its receptors can drive inflammation, cell survival or death, and the balance between those outcomes is set by the regulatory layer described here. Tuning TNF-mediated signalling matters because unrestrained output produces chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, while excessive restraint blunts host defence; several components are also checkpoints against inappropriate cell death. Control acts at every step: metalloproteinases such as ADAM17 shed TNF and its receptor from the surface, receptor-proximal complexes assemble around TNFRSF1A, TRAF2, RIPK1 and SHARPIN, and ubiquitin editing by TNFAIP3, CYLD with SPATA2, and OTULIN determines whether signalling proceeds to NF-kB activation or to caspase-8-dependent death. IAP family members including XIAP restrain caspases, inhibitory kappaB kinase regulators and NKIRAS proteins gate transcription, and inflammasome adaptors such as PYCARD and CASP1 couple the pathway to cytokine maturation. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional damping.

Tumour necrosis factor engagement of its receptors drives inflammatory gene expression and, if unchecked, caspase-8-dependent death; this collection defines the brakes that limit how strongly and how long that signalling runs. Restraint matters because persistent TNF signalling underlies chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and tissue destruction, while too much brake permits infection and tumour survival. Several mechanisms appear together: ubiquitin-editing and NF-κB-restricting adaptors such as TAX1BP1 and TANK dampen receptor-proximal complexes, caspase inhibitors and decoy CARD/pyrin proteins including XIAP, NOL3 and CARD16 block apoptotic and inflammasome output, a phosphatase (PTPN2) and PP2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylation, and the soluble decoy receptor TNFRSF11B sequesters ligand before it reaches a receptor. Microenvironmental and metabolic signals feed in through adiponectin, apolipoprotein A-I and the bile acid receptor NR1H4, and a set of microRNAs adds post-transcriptional tuning.\n

Before a synaptic vesicle can release neurotransmitter it must be made fusion-competent, and this pathway tunes how many vesicles reach that primed, release-ready state. Because priming sets the size of the readily releasable pool, its regulation determines release probability, short-term plasticity and the fidelity of fast synaptic transmission; loss of the machinery produces severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathies and movement disorders. Regulation acts on assembly of the SNARE complex that docks vesicle and presynaptic membranes: syntaxin-1A and -1B provide the plasma membrane SNARE, Munc18-1 chaperones syntaxin and is required for its productive engagement, a Munc13 isoform catalyses transition to the primed state, and tomosyn restrains priming by forming a non-fusogenic SNARE complex. NSF-associated alpha- and beta-SNAP recycle SNAREs for further rounds, while synaptophysin and synaptogyrin shape the vesicle membrane, and a presynaptic kinase adds phosphorylation-dependent control.

Cells attach to the extracellular matrix through integrin-based contacts, and this pathway covers the machinery that tunes how strong, how numerous and how long-lived those attachments are. Controlled adhesion to substrate underlies cell migration, wound healing, angiogenesis, immune cell trafficking and epithelial tissue integrity; when it is misregulated, cells detach and invade, or fail to spread and die by anoikis. Integrins such as ITGB1BP1-bound and ITGB3 receptors are activated from inside the cell by talin and kindlin proteins, linked to actin through vinculin, filamin, alpha-actinin and ILK, and signal outward through focal adhesion kinase and SRC to Rho-family GTPases RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 with their ROCK effectors. Matrix ligands including fibronectin, collagens, vitronectin, thrombospondin and fibrinogen provide the substrate, while phosphatases, proteases, GAPs such as DLC1, and PTEN restrain the response. Growth factor and Wnt inputs bias the balance toward adhesion or release.

Cells attach to the extracellular matrix through integrin-based contacts, and this pathway covers the signals and structural components that increase the strength, frequency or extent of that attachment. Firm substrate adhesion is what allows epithelia to remain anchored, leukocytes to arrest and spread on vessel walls, platelets to engage fibrinogen and vitronectin, and migrating cells to generate traction; loss of adhesive control contributes to anoikis, defective wound healing, and tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes here span matrix ligands such as fibronectin, fibrinogen chains, nidogen and fibulins, integrin subunits and their intracellular activators kindlin-2 and ILK, and the focal adhesion signalling machinery including CRK adaptors, NEDD9, PTK2B and the Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 with ROCK1, which remodel actin to reinforce nascent contacts. Growth factor and chemokine inputs, including VEGFA, PDGFB and CCR7 ligands, feed into the same adhesive response.

negative regulation of cell-substrate adhesion covers the processes that loosen or dismantle a cell's grip on the extracellular matrix, which is what allows cells to migrate, round up for division, remodel tissue, or detach during wound healing, angiogenic sprouting and metastasis. Adhesion strength must be actively turned down as often as it is built up: integrin activation is antagonised at the cytoplasmic tail by ITGB1BP1 and KANK1, focal adhesion turnover is driven by SRC and by phosphatases such as PTEN and PTPN1, and RHOA-directed GAPs including DLC1, ARHGAP6 and RASA1 tune contractility and adhesion disassembly. Matrix itself is cleared by MMP14, MMP12 and plasminogen, while SERPINE1 and THBS1 act as anti-adhesive matricellular signals. Guidance and morphogen cues from ephrins, semaphorins, Notch and Wnt receptors, together with several microRNAs, feed into the same output. Loss of this restraint yields rigid, poorly motile cells or, when overactive, invasive behaviour.

Cells must let go of their extracellular matrix as often as they grip it, and this collection covers the processes that dampen cell-substrate adhesion instead of building it. Loosening focal contacts is what permits migration during wound healing, angiogenic sprouting and immune cell trafficking, and its deregulation contributes to tumour invasion and metastasis. Several routes converge here: Rho-family regulators such as DLC1 and ARHGAP6 turn off adhesion-promoting contractility signals, PTEN and PTPN1 remove phosphorylation marks that SRC and integrin-proximal kinases deposit, and MMP14 and MMP12 proteolytically remodel or clear the matrix and its receptors. Integrin activity itself is modulated from inside by ITGB1BP1 and by adaptors including KANK1, ACTN4 and CLASP2 that link adhesions to actin and microtubules. Neuropeptide signals must be terminated as well as sent, and neuropeptide catabolism is the proteolytic arm that does it, degrading transmitter and hormone peptides so that receptor stimulation is brief and local. The enzymes here are largely cell-surface and secreted metallopeptidases plus a lysosomal cysteine protease: neprilysin and endothelin-converting enzyme cleave enkephalins, substance P, natriuretic peptides and amyloid-beta; angiotensin-converting enzyme and the leucyl/cystinyl aminopeptidase act on angiotensins, bradykinin and oxytocin/vasopressin. Because several of these peptidases both generate and destroy active peptides, the same reactions set blood pressure, fluid balance, pain thresholds and appetite, which is why they are drug targets in hypertension and heart failure. Reduced clearance capacity also matters in the brain, where failure to degrade amyloidogenic peptides contributes to plaque accumulation, linking peptide turnover to neurodegeneration.

Bradykinin is a short-lived vasodilator and pain mediator released during inflammation and tissue injury, and its degradation sets how long and how strongly those effects last. Several peptidases with overlapping specificity clear it: angiotensin-converting enzyme removes C-terminal dipeptides, carboxypeptidase N trims the terminal arginine to give des-Arg metabolites that act on a different kinin receptor, neprilysin and endothelin-converting enzyme cleave internally, aminopeptidase P attacks the N-terminus, and insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin H contribute further hydrolysis. Because the same enzymes shape angiotensin and other vasoactive peptides, this catabolism links kinin turnover to blood pressure control and vascular permeability. Loss of clearance is clinically visible: inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme, or reduced aminopeptidase P activity, allows bradykinin to accumulate and produce cough and angioedema, while kinin excess drives plasma leakage and swelling.

Endocrine signalling depends not only on receptors but on how much hormone is present, and this collection covers the processes that set and reset those concentrations: synthesis, prohormone processing, storage and regulated secretion, transport, and inactivation or clearance. Steroidogenic cytochrome P450s and hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases build and interconvert androgens, oestrogens and corticosteroids from cholesterol; thyroperoxidase, thyroglobulin and the deiodinases make thyroid hormone and tune its local potency; retinaldehyde dehydrogenases and retinol dehydrogenases balance retinoic acid against its CYP26-mediated breakdown. Proprotein convertases cleave precursors such as proopiomelanocortin and proinsulin, while SNARE and Rab machinery with ATP-sensitive potassium channels governs insulin and peptide hormone release from islet and neuroendocrine granules. Sulfotransferases, UGTs and peptidases including ACE, DPP4 and insulin-degrading enzyme terminate signals. Imbalance here underlies diabetes, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, thyroid disease, hypertension and disorders of growth and reproduction.

T cells only work if they arrive in the right place, and directed migration along chemokine gradients is how they reach lymph nodes, inflamed tissue and tumours. The chemoattractants here span homeostatic homing and inflammatory recruitment: CCL21 guides naive T cells into lymphoid tissue through high endothelial venules, CXCL12 retains and positions cells in marrow and stroma, while interferon-induced CXCL10 and CXCL11 acting on CXCR3 pull effector and memory T cells into sites of infection. Receptors such as CCR2 and the oxysterol sensor GPR183 add further positioning cues, and membrane sheddases ADAM10 and ADAM17 release surface-anchored ligands like CXCL16. Signal transmission runs through PI3K isoforms PIK3CD and PIK3CG to cytoskeletal remodelling, with the WNK1-OXSR1/STK39 axis and the NKCC1 cotransporter coupling cell volume regulation to motility. Disrupted T cell chemotaxis leaves immunodeficiency or, when misdirected, drives autoimmune tissue infiltration.

T cells must be steered to the right tissue at the right time, and this pathway covers the signals that dial that directed migration up or down. It governs how naive T cells home to lymph nodes and how effector cells are recruited into inflamed or tumour tissue, so its output shapes immune surveillance, graft rejection and autoimmune infiltration. Secreted chemoattractants such as CCL21, CCL5, CXCL10, CXCL13 and XCL1 set the gradients, while receptors including CCR2 read them. The membrane metalloproteinases ADAM10 and ADAM17 tune availability of chemokines and adhesion or cytokine substrates by shedding them from the cell surface, and TNFSF14 and WNT5A act as additional extrinsic modifiers. Intracellularly, the WNK1 kinase with its downstream OXSR1 and STK39 relays chemokine signals into cytoskeletal and ion-transport changes needed for migration and adhesion, making this a key control point of lymphocyte trafficking.

SORL1 contributes through receptor-mediated handling of lipoproteins. Failure of this negative control drives excessive fatty acid release, lipotoxicity and insulin resistance.

Stored triglyceride must be mobilised on demand, and this regulatory theme covers the signals and cofactors that raise the rate of triglyceride breakdown, both inside cells and in the circulation. Within adipocytes and other lipid-droplet-bearing cells, PNPLA2 (adipose triglyceride lipase) initiates hydrolysis and is strongly stimulated by its coactivator ABHD5, while protein kinase A catalytic activity links catecholamine and cAMP signalling to lipolytic release of fatty acids for oxidation. In plasma, APOC2 serves as the obligatory activator of lipoprotein lipase, with APOA5 and APOA4 further promoting clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Loss of these activating functions produces severe hypertriglyceridaemia and pancreatitis, whereas failure of the intracellular arm causes neutral lipid storage disease with myopathy or ichthyosis. The pathway thus sits at the junction of energy mobilisation during fasting and exercise and the handling of dietary fat.

regulation of very-low-density lipoprotein particle remodeling controls how quickly triglyceride-rich lipoproteins secreted by the liver are stripped of their fat cargo in the circulation, and therefore sets plasma triglyceride levels. It matters because too little lipolysis produces hypertriglyceridemia, chylomicronemia and pancreatitis, while the pathway's set point also shapes atherosclerotic risk and the delivery of fatty acids to muscle and adipose tissue. The regulators work mainly by tuning lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase: APOC2 is the obligatory activator and APOA5 enhances lipolysis, while APOC3 and the angiopoietin-like proteins ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit it, the latter in a tissue- and fasting-dependent way that partitions lipid between organs. Exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA1 and APOA2 alter particle surface composition during remodeling, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 provides transcriptional control, linking this step to nutrient and bile acid status. These proteins are prominent lipid-lowering drug targets.

Very-low-density lipoprotein carries triglyceride from the liver to muscle and adipose tissue, and this pathway sets how quickly those particles are stripped of their triglyceride cargo and converted toward remnants and LDL. Control is exerted largely on lipoprotein lipase: APOC2 is its required activator and APOA5 promotes its action, while APOC3 and the angiopoietin-like proteins ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit lipolysis, the latter in a tissue- and nutritional-state-dependent way that partitions fatty acids between storage and oxidation. The bile acid receptor NR1H4 links this tuning to hepatic transcriptional control of apolipoprotein genes, and exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA1 and APOA2 move between particles as remodeling proceeds. Loss of restraint on lipase activity lowers plasma triglyceride, whereas excess inhibition produces hypertriglyceridaemia, chylomicronaemia and pancreatitis risk, making these regulators prominent lipid-lowering drug targets.

Very-low-density lipoprotein particles delivered into the circulation are stripped of triglyceride by lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase; restraining that remodeling keeps triglyceride-rich particles in the blood longer and sets fasting triglyceride levels. The brake is applied mainly by secreted lipase inhibitors and by apolipoproteins carried on the particle surface: ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit lipoprotein lipase, and APOC3 blocks lipase access and receptor-mediated clearance, while APOA1 and APOA2 also modulate lipolytic processing. Bile-acid-activated nuclear receptor signalling through NR1H4 links this control to hepatic lipid and bile acid metabolism. Loss-of-function variants in these inhibitors lower triglycerides and cardiovascular risk, which is why they are drug targets, whereas excess inhibition produces hypertriglyceridemia. The pathway sits at the interface of fatty acid partitioning between adipose storage and oxidative tissues.

Blood glucose must be used, stored, or made as conditions demand, and this pathway covers the controls that set the rate of glucose metabolism rather than the catabolic steps themselves. It links hormonal signals to hepatic, muscle and adipose fuel choice: insulin and glucagon, insulin receptor signalling through IRS1/IRS2 and AKT to FOXO1, adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin acting via their receptors, and glucocorticoid and PPAR-family transcriptional programmes. Glucokinase sets hepatic glucose sensing, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase gates gluconeogenesis, pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases shunt pyruvate away from oxidation, and protein phosphatase 1 glycogen-targeting subunits together with phosphorylase kinase components determine glycogen storage. AMPK subunits, sirtuins, PPARGC1A and circadian factors including CRY1 and RORA impose energy-status and time-of-day control. Failure of this regulation underlies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and glycogen storage disorders.

Cells and whole organisms raise the rate of glucose handling on demand, and this positive regulation of glucose metabolic process collects the signals that push glucose into glycolysis, glycogen synthesis or, in liver, gluconeogenesis. It underlies how a meal is converted into stored fuel and how fasting blood sugar is defended; its failure is the core lesion of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Insulin and glucagon act through their receptors and the insulin receptor substrates IRS1 and IRS2 to AKT1/AKT2, which inactivate FOXO1 and so reset the gluconeogenic and glycolytic gene programmes, while glucokinase sets the threshold for glucose sensing in beta cells and hepatocytes. Protein phosphatase 1 targeting subunits and phosphorylase kinase subunits control glycogen turnover, and AMPK subunits, PPARGC1A, PPARA and SIRT1 couple the same flux to nutrient and circadian state.

Triglyceride-rich very-low-density lipoprotein particles must be taken up by the liver and degraded once their lipid cargo has been delivered, and this regulatory layer sets how fast that removal happens. Tuning it determines how long remnant particles circulate, and persistent delay produces the hypertriglyceridaemia and remnant accumulation that accompany atherogenic dyslipidaemia and pancreatitis risk. The small exchangeable apolipoproteins carried on the particle surface act as the tuning knobs: APOC1 and APOC3 impede receptor-mediated uptake and lipolytic processing, whereas APOC2 serves as the cofactor that permits lipoprotein lipase to hydrolyse the triglyceride core, a step that precedes clearance. LRPAP1 chaperones the LDL receptor family members that perform endocytosis, and a microRNA input indicates transcriptional and post-transcriptional control over apolipoprotein levels. The pathway therefore links plasma lipid transport to hepatic receptor-mediated endocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

Mitochondria hold a charge across their inner membrane, and this grouping covers the processes that build or strengthen that potential. The gradient is the currency of oxidative phosphorylation: it drives ATP synthase, powers protein import and calcium uptake, and its collapse is the signal that marks an organelle for destruction. Contributors here span several levels. Respiratory chain assembly and function are represented by a complex I subunit and by mitoregulin, a small inner-membrane peptide that supports supercomplex organisation and fatty acid oxidation. Mitofusin-1 promotes outer membrane fusion, keeping the network connected and energetically buffered. Quality control enters through parkin and VCP, which clear damaged proteins and depolarised mitochondria. BAD and BID normally push the other way as BCL-2 family apoptotic effectors, linking membrane potential to commitment to cell death and, when dysregulated, to neurodegeneration.

Inositol phosphates, chiefly IP3 generated when phospholipase C cleaves PIP2, are the messengers that release calcium from intracellular stores, so controlling how fast they are made sets the gain on calcium signalling in many cell types. This regulatory layer is dominated by receptors that couple to Gq: the PACAP receptor, vasopressin V1B, the neurotensin and luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptors, the purinergic P2RY1 and P2RY6 nucleotide receptors, and the G protein-coupled estrogen receptor. Parathyroid hormone acting through PTH1R illustrates the physiology, where the same ligand-receptor pair tunes inositol phosphate output alongside cAMP to regulate calcium and phosphate handling in bone and kidney. Intracellular modulators are also represented, including pleckstrin and alpha-synuclein, which restrain or shape phosphoinositide turnover. Through these inputs the pathway governs hormone secretion, smooth muscle tone, platelet and immune cell activation, and neuronal excitability.

regulation of phosphatase activity covers the control of enzymes that remove phosphate groups from proteins and lipids, setting the duration and amplitude of every signal that a kinase initiates. Because dephosphorylation resets signalling, its regulation determines whether growth factor, calcium and stress inputs are transient or sustained, and its failure produces uncontrolled or prematurely terminated responses. The genes act largely as inhibitors, targeting subunits and scaffolds rather than catalytic enzymes themselves: PPP1R17 and URI1 restrain protein phosphatase 1 and 2A holoenzymes, CHP1 and CHP2 are calcineurin-homologous calcium binding proteins that modulate calcineurin and Na+/H+ exchange, and MTMR9 partners with catalytically active myotubularins to control phosphoinositide turnover. EPM2A, the laforin glucan phosphatase, links this control to glycogen metabolism, and its loss causes Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

Phosphatases reverse the work of kinases, and their activity must itself be controlled if phosphorylation-based signalling is to be switched off at the right time and place. Regulation of phosphatase activity covers the modulators that raise or lower the rate of phosphoester hydrolysis rather than the catalytic enzymes themselves. The genes here act largely through binding partners and targeting subunits: calcineurin-interacting proteins that tune calcium-dependent dephosphorylation and downstream transcription, an inhibitor of protein phosphatase 1 in neurons, a catalytically inactive myotubularin-family member that partners active phosphoinositide phosphatases, and a prefoldin-like subunit of a phosphatase-containing complex that restrains gene expression. Also represented is laforin, a glycogen phosphatase whose loss causes Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy through accumulation of poorly branched polyglucosan. Collectively these activities set the duration of signals in calcium, growth factor and glycogen metabolic pathways.

Building a cell's characteristic structure is part of how it acquires its shape, and this collection covers the assembly steps that give differentiating cells their final form. Three programmes dominate. Sarcomere assembly in cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle organises titin, nebulin, myosins, tropomodulins and Z-disc proteins such as telethonin, myotilin-related LIM proteins and filamin C into contractile arrays; failure produces cardiomyopathy, nemaline and other structural myopathies. Myelin sheath formation by Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes depends on myelin basic protein, PMP22, MAG and plasmolipin, and its disruption underlies demyelinating neuropathy. Spermatid differentiation contributes acrosome biogenesis and flagellar/manchette components, with zona-binding and acrosomal proteins required for fertility. Transcriptional inputs including NKX2-5, SRF, SMAD4 and RFX2 couple these structural outputs to developmental commitment, linking cytoskeletal and membrane assembly directly to organ and gamete morphogenesis.

macrophage cytokine production describes the induction and release of cytokines by macrophages after they sense a stimulus, the step that converts pattern recognition into inflammation. It sets the tone of innate immune responses: too little and infections go uncontrolled, too much and tissues suffer the damage of sepsis, atherosclerosis or chronic inflammatory disease. Recognition inputs are represented by TLR4 and the scavenger receptor CD36, which together read bacterial lipopolysaccharide and modified lipids, while PLCG2 couples receptor engagement to calcium and kinase signalling. Restraint is equally represented: IRAK3 acts as a decoy kinase that dampens Toll-like receptor output, SIRT1 deacetylates inflammatory transcription factors, inhibitory receptors such as LILRB1 read HLA-G, and the TGFB ligands enforce a suppressive, resolving phenotype. The balance of these arms determines macrophage polarisation and whether an inflammatory episode resolves.

Macrophages translate sensing of microbes, damaged tissue and immunoregulatory ligands into the release of cytokines, and this pathway covers the synthesis and secretion that raise those cytokine levels after stimulation. The output sets the tone of innate immunity and of inflammation generally: too little leaves infection unchecked, too much drives septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and fibrosis. Both the triggering and the braking arms are represented. Surface recognition through TLR4, the scavenger receptor CD36 and the MHC class II chaperone CD74 initiates signalling, with PLCG2 relaying receptor input, while IRAK3 acts as a negative regulator of Toll-like receptor signalling, SIRT1 restrains inflammatory transcription, and the inhibitory receptor LILRB1 and the non-classical HLA-G it binds damp activation. TGF-beta ligands feed back as anti-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic signals, linking macrophage output to tissue remodelling and repair.

Macrophages amplify inflammation by secreting cytokines, and this braking arm keeps that output proportionate, limiting collateral tissue damage and allowing resolution once a threat is cleared. Loss of such restraint underlies septic shock, chronic inflammatory disease and fibrosis, while excessive restraint leaves macrophages tolerant and poorly responsive to infection. The negative regulation of macrophage cytokine production operates at two levels represented here: an intracellular checkpoint on Toll-like receptor signalling, where IRAK3 acts as a catalytically inactive decoy kinase that blocks downstream NF-κB activation, and CUEDC2 dampens inflammatory transcriptional responses; and secreted control, where the three TGF-beta ligands act on macrophages in an autocrine and paracrine fashion to suppress pro-inflammatory gene expression and push cells toward a reparative, immunosuppressive state. Together these mechanisms set the threshold and duration of innate immune activation.

Some transcriptional repression works not by recruiting silencing machinery but by occupancy: a factor binds the same promoter element that an activator requires, and the activator is simply excluded. This competitive mode of negative regulation shapes circadian output, developmental fate choices and inflammatory gene programmes, and its loss allows target promoters to stay inappropriately active. The proteins here illustrate the range of the mechanism: BHLHE41 competes for E-box sites that drive clock and myogenic genes, HHEX and OVOL2 are homeodomain and zinc-finger repressors that occupy sites used by related activators, SMAD7 blocks productive SMAD complexes on TGF-beta responsive promoters, and DACH1 antagonises activating transcription factors at shared elements. Chromatin modifiers such as HDAC2, HDAC4 and the demethylase KDM2A reinforce the repressed state once binding is established, linking direct site competition to durable promoter silencing.

Cells divide only when conditions permit, and negative regulation of cell cycle processes is the collective brake that holds or slows progression. It matters because unchecked division propagates damaged genomes: loss of these restraints underlies tumour formation, while their enforcement produces quiescence, differentiation and senescence. The brakes act at several points. DNA damage and replication stress sensors such as ATM, ATR with ATRIP, CHEK1, CHEK2 and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex signal through TP53 and CDKN1A to inhibit cyclin-dependent kinases, while WEE1 and PKMYT1 phosphorylate CDK1 to delay mitotic entry and RB1 with its relatives represses E2F-driven S-phase genes. Licensing inhibitors including GMNN prevent re-replication, and the spindle assembly checkpoint -- MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1B, BUB3 and the kinetochore-associated ZW10 and ZWILCH -- restrains APC/C until chromosomes attach correctly. Ubiquitin ligase modules and numerous microRNAs add further dampening of cyclin and CDK abundance.

Proteases that cut internal peptide bonds are held under tight restraint, and this grouping covers the inputs that raise their activity — increasing how often, how fast or how extensively endopeptidases cleave their substrates. The consequences are diverse because the enzymes are: complement convertases that amplify innate immune attack on microbes and damaged cells, the gamma-secretase complex that performs intramembrane cleavage of Notch and amyloid precursor protein, and semen-derived substrates and regulators acting on seminal plasma proteolysis during liquefaction and sperm activation. PSENEN contributes to gamma-secretase assembly and activity, while CR1 engages complement components and shapes their processing. Because unchecked proteolysis damages tissue and misdirected cleavage generates pathogenic peptides such as amyloid-beta, positive regulation here sits opposite the serpins and other inhibitors, and the balance between them determines immune tone, receptor signalling and reproductive function.

Proteases that cut within a polypeptide chain must be held in check, and this pathway covers the inhibitory side of that balance: dampening endopeptidase activity so that proteolysis stays local, timed and proportionate. It matters wherever uncontrolled cleavage would be destructive u2014 complement activation on host cell surfaces, neutrophil granule serine proteases released at sites of inflammation, matrix metalloproteinases remodelling connective tissue, and the acrosomal and fertilisation-associated proteases restrained by fetuin-like inhibitors. Serpins such as SERPINB1, SERPINB8 and SERPINB13 act as suicide-substrate inhibitors of serine proteases and protect the cells that make them, while TIMP1 blocks metalloproteinase catalytic sites and a testican-family proteoglycan contributes inhibitory activity in the extracellular matrix. Loss of this restraint drives tissue damage in emphysema, inflammatory disease and tumour invasion, linking protease inhibition to matrix integrity and immune homeostasis.

Proteases are held in check by default, and this pathway covers the events that raise peptidase activity above baseline — zymogen conversion, cofactor supply, and relief of inhibition — so that proteolysis happens where and when it is needed. Positive regulation of peptidase activity matters wherever cleavage is the committing step: complement activation on cell surfaces, extracellular matrix and growth factor processing, semen liquefaction, and regulated intramembrane cleavage of substrates such as Notch and amyloid precursor protein, where PSENEN is a subunit of the gamma-secretase complex. Members include a serine protease of the tryptase family, a collagen prolyl hydroxylase-associated ER protein, secreted seminal vesicle proteins, and progranulin, whose cleavage into granulins couples this activity to lysosomal function and, when lost, to frontotemporal dementia. Setting protease output too high drives tissue destruction and inflammation; too low leaves substrates unprocessed.

Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation inside cells, required for ATP to be biologically usable, for ribosome and nucleic acid stability, and for hundreds of kinases and phosphatases; magnesium ion homeostasis is the set of transport and regulatory activities that hold its intracellular and whole-body levels steady. Uptake and efflux are handled by channels and transporters such as the channel-kinase TRPM7, the CNNM family of magnesium efflux regulators, and SLC41A1, a Na+/Mg2+ exchanger, with reabsorption in the kidney and intestine setting systemic balance. Hormonal and electrical inputs tune it: parathyroid hormone links magnesium handling to calcium and phosphate control, and the potassium channel KCNA1 contributes through effects on renal tubular transport. Loss of these functions produces hypomagnesemia with seizures, tetany, cardiac arrhythmia and secondary disturbances of calcium and potassium.

Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation inside cells, where it is required for ATP binding, ribosome function and hundreds of kinase and phosphatase reactions, so its intracellular concentration is held within narrow limits. This homeostatic balance depends on channels and transporters that set influx against efflux: TRPM7, a channel fused to a kinase domain, carries Mg2+ (and other divalent cations) into the cell and is needed for embryonic development and cell proliferation, while SLC41A1 works as a Na+-dependent Mg2+ extruder at the plasma membrane. Additional members, including the Kell blood group protein with its partner XK and the endothelin peptide EDN3, connect magnesium status to erythroid membrane biology and to vascular and neural crest signalling. Loss of magnesium handling impairs energy metabolism, excitability and growth, and mutations in these transporters are linked to hypomagnesaemia and neurological disease.

Control of how much phosphate crosses membranes sets serum phosphate levels and, through them, bone mineralization and energy metabolism. Regulation of phosphate transport is the tier of control acting on transporters such as the kidney proximal tubule sodium-phosphate cotransporter SLC34A1, whose abundance at the apical membrane determines how much filtered phosphate is reclaimed. The bone-derived hormone FGF23 signals through FGFR1 with Klotho as cofactor to suppress that reabsorption and promote phosphate excretion; excess FGF23 activity causes hypophosphatemic rickets, while loss produces hyperphosphatemia and ectopic calcification. Additional inputs include the secreted Wnt modulator SFRP4, circadian regulation via CRY2, and transcription factors ATF4 and CEBPB that couple phosphate handling to stress and differentiation programmes. Claudin-mediated paracellular permeability contributes to epithelial ion flux alongside the transcellular route.

New microtubules do not appear at random: they are born at defined sites, and this pathway sets how fast and how often that happens. Control over nucleation determines how many spindle microtubules form during mitosis, how centrosomal and non-centrosomal arrays are organized in interphase, and ultimately whether chromosomes segregate accurately, so its loss produces spindle assembly defects and aneuploidy. The full eight-subunit augmin complex (HAUS1-HAUS8) supplies branched nucleation from the walls of existing microtubules, amplifying spindle mass without a centrosome; CKAP5 (ch-TOG) stabilizes nascent polymer ends, while myomegalin (PDE4DIP) and NME7 act at centrosomal and Golgi-associated nucleating sites. A GIT1-ARHGEF7-PAK1 module links Rho-family GTPase signalling and cytoskeletal scaffolding to nucleation rate, connecting cell shape and adhesion cues to microtubule array formation alongside dynein-dynactin anchoring through DCTN1.

regulation of neuron projection development controls how far, how fast and in which direction neurons extend axons and dendrites, and therefore determines how the nervous system is wired. Its outputs are the growth cone's decisions during development and the capacity for neurite regrowth or collapse after injury, where inhibitory myelin signals through Nogo receptors and RTN4 block repair. Guidance cue families dominate the set — netrins and DCC, slits and ROBOs, semaphorins with plexins and neuropilins, ephrins with Eph receptors — acting alongside neurotrophins and their TRK receptors, Reelin–VLDLR/DAB1 signalling, and Wnt ligands. These converge on Rho-family GTPase regulators, PAK and LIMK kinases, CDK5, GSK3 and cofilin to remodel actin, and on MAPT, MAP1B and katanin-associated factors to reorganise microtubules. Disrupted regulation underlies cortical malformations, intellectual disability and autism-spectrum disorders, and constrains recovery from central nervous system damage.

Neurons acquire their shape by extending axons and dendrites, and this pathway covers the signals that speed up, slow down, redirect or terminate that outgrowth. Getting it right determines how far an axon travels, where it branches, and how dendritic arbours are sized, so it underlies wiring of cortex, retina and peripheral nerve, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, epilepsy and failure of regeneration after injury. Guidance cues and their receptors provide the instructions — netrins with DCC and neogenin, slits with ROBOs, semaphorins with plexins, ephrins with EPH kinases, myelin-derived RTN4 acting through Nogo receptors — while neurotrophins signalling through TRK receptors promote growth. These inputs converge on Rho-family GTPase regulators, PAK and LIM kinases, cofilin and microtubule-associated proteins such as MAPT, MAP1B and CRMPs, remodelling the growth cone cytoskeleton, with CDK5, GSK3 and reelin signalling tuning the response.

positive regulation of neuron projection development gathers the signals and effectors that drive neurons to extend and elaborate axons and dendrites, the step that converts a postmitotic neuron into a wired component of a circuit. It underlies developmental axon outgrowth and guidance, dendritic arborisation, synapse formation, and the regenerative sprouting attempted after nerve injury; its failure produces malformed cortical wiring, intellectual disability and impaired repair. Neurotrophins acting through TRK receptors, together with FGF, GDNF-RET, ALK and BMP inputs, converge on Src- and Abl-family kinases, Rho-family GTPase regulators and small GTPase exchange factors, which in turn remodel the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton through stathmin, drebrin, cofilin-family and katanin components. Guidance and adhesion receptors including plexins, ephrin receptors, Robo, contactins and the Reelin receptors position growth cones, while transcriptional and microRNA regulators set the permissive growth state.

Neurons acquire their shape by extending axons and dendrites, and this grouping covers the signals and effectors that accelerate or extend that outgrowth. It underlies wiring of circuits during development, collateral sprouting and regeneration after injury, and the dendritic elaboration that supports synapse formation; when it is weak or misdirected, connectivity defects and neurodevelopmental disorders follow. Neurotrophins acting through their receptor tyrosine kinases, together with other growth factor and guidance receptors and the Reelin pathway acting via its lipoprotein receptors, converge on Src- and Abl-family kinases, Rho-family regulators and Rap guanine nucleotide exchange factors. These in turn reorganise actin and microtubules through actin-binding and severing proteins, tubulin, and microtubule-associated regulators, while membrane trafficking and lipid-modifying components supply material to the growing tip. Transcriptional regulators and microRNAs set how strongly the programme runs.

Neurons must stop growing as well as grow, and this collection of brakes on neuron projection development sets where axons and dendrites halt, retract, or are forbidden to enter. Repulsive guidance cues and their receptors dominate: semaphorins with plexins and neuropilin, ephrins with Eph receptors, slits, netrin acting through DCC, draxin, and the RGM/Nogo system, in which myelin-derived inhibitors signal through Nogo receptors to collapse growth cones. Downstream, Rho-family regulators, CDK5, collapsin response mediator proteins and stamins remodel the cytoskeleton, while receptor phosphatases, PTEN and Wnt/DKK components tune growth competence. The same inhibitory tone that sculpts precise circuits during development becomes an obstacle afterwards, since myelin-associated glycoprotein, Nogo and the reactive glial environment marked by GFAP block axon regeneration after central nervous system injury; APOE, PSEN1 and LRRK2 link the process to neurodegeneration.</description>}

regulation of high-density lipoprotein particle clearance controls how quickly HDL particles are taken out of circulation and catabolised, and so sets steady-state HDL levels and the efficiency of reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues back to the liver. Because HDL turnover determines how much cholesterol is offloaded from macrophages and vessel walls, changes here shift atherosclerosis risk. The regulators act at several levels: endothelial lipase and phospholipase activity remodel HDL lipids and phospholipid content, generating particles that are more readily cleared; apolipoprotein C-III alters particle composition and lipase accessibility; and a set of microRNAs, notably the sterol-responsive miR-33 family, tunes the transporters and receptors that mediate cholesterol efflux and hepatic uptake. Macrophage lipid handling contributes through TREM2, linking HDL catabolism to innate immune cells in lipid-rich tissue and to disorders of lipoprotein metabolism.

How long an HDL particle circulates before being taken up and degraded sets the steady-state level of plasma HDL cholesterol, and this regulatory layer tunes that removal rate. It matters for reverse cholesterol transport: faster clearance shortens the window in which HDL can accept cholesterol from peripheral tissues and macrophages, while slowed clearance raises circulating HDL. Control is exerted both on the particle and on the liver's uptake machinery. Endothelial lipase hydrolyses HDL phospholipid and accelerates catabolism of the remodelled particle, apolipoprotein C-III alters lipoprotein composition and lipase access, and a phospholipase D releases GPI-anchored surface proteins. A set of microRNAs, among them the cholesterol-responsive miR-33 family and miR-144, adjusts expression of hepatic transporters and receptors that govern HDL handling. Disturbance of this balance contributes to dyslipidaemia and atherosclerotic risk.

HDL particles are taken out of circulation when receptors on liver and other tissues bind them and route their lipid and protein cargo for degradation, and this arm of the pathway speeds that removal, lowering plasma HDL levels and setting the tempo of reverse cholesterol transport. Because HDL concentration reflects the balance between particle production and disposal, accelerating clearance shifts lipid handling toward hepatic uptake rather than continued cholesterol efflux from peripheral cells, with consequences for atherosclerosis risk. Endothelial lipase remodels HDL by hydrolysing its phospholipids, generating smaller particles that are catabolised more rapidly, while a phospholipase D acting on GPI anchors also modifies particle surfaces. Several microRNAs, including the miR-33 family embedded in the sterol-regulatory transcription factor genes, tune the expression of cholesterol transport and lipase components, linking HDL turnover to broader sterol homeostasis and macrophage lipid metabolism.

How fast lipoproteins are pulled out of the circulation sets plasma cholesterol and triglyceride levels, and this regulatory layer tunes that rate. Its central node is the LDL receptor together with its endocytic adaptor LDLRAP1: PCSK9 binds the receptor and routes it to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, the E3 ligase MYLIP (IDOL) ubiquitinates it, and a large complement of microRNAs including the miR-33 pair and miR-148a represses receptor and transporter expression post-transcriptionally. Apolipoprotein C family members act on the triglyceride-rich side, modulating lipolysis and hepatic uptake of remnant particles, while GPIHBP1 positions lipoprotein lipase at the capillary endothelium. Loss or gain of function here produces familial hypercholesterolaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia and accelerated atherosclerosis, and the PCSK9-LDLR step is the basis of cholesterol-lowering antibody therapy.

Circulating lipoproteins are normally pulled out of plasma by receptor-mediated endocytosis in the liver, and the processes gathered here work in the opposite direction, damping that removal and so raising plasma cholesterol and triglyceride. This is the biology that sets LDL levels and, when it dominates, drives atherosclerosis; it is also the biology that drugs target. Restraint is imposed at several levels: secreted PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor and directs it to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, the E3 ligase MYLIP (IDOL) ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail, and LRPAP1 chaperones receptor family members in the secretory pathway. Apolipoproteins of the C cluster, notably APOC1 and APOC3, shield particles from lipase action and hepatic uptake. Numerous microRNAs and the RNA-binding protein KHSRP add post-transcriptional control over receptor and apolipoprotein abundance, tuning how fast lipoprotein particles are cleared.

Circulating lipoproteins are taken out of the blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis and broken down, and this pathway covers the influences that push that removal faster or further. It sets how long LDL, remnants and triglyceride-rich particles persist in plasma, so it bears directly on plasma cholesterol levels and atherosclerotic risk; loss of the clearance machinery produces hypercholesterolaemia. The genes span several levels of control: an adaptor that couples the LDL receptor to clathrin-coated pits, an endothelial lipase and a GPI-anchored transporter that position lipoprotein lipase on the capillary surface, a phospholipase that releases GPI-anchored proteins, and a lipid-sensing receptor of myeloid cells that mediates uptake of lipid and lipoprotein debris. Several microRNAs act as post-transcriptional brakes and modulators of cholesterol handling, linking receptor abundance to overall lipid homeostasis.

Circulating LDL is removed from blood mainly by hepatic LDL receptors, which bind the particle, internalise it by endocytosis and deliver its cholesteryl esters for lysosomal degradation; how fast this happens sets plasma cholesterol and, with it, atherosclerotic risk. The genes here modulate that rate rather than perform the uptake itself. Receptor supply is controlled at several levels: an adaptor is needed for efficient endocytosis in hepatocytes, a secreted protease-like chaperone directs the receptor to lysosomal destruction instead of recycling, and an E3 ubiquitin ligase induced by nuclear receptor signalling degrades the receptor when sterols are abundant. RNA-binding proteins and numerous microRNAs tune receptor and apolipoprotein transcript levels, while an apolipoprotein that inhibits lipolysis slows particle remodelling and clearance. Loss-of-function in the receptor or its adaptor causes familial hypercholesterolaemia, and pharmacological blockade of the degradative arm lowers LDL therapeutically.

Circulating LDL is removed from plasma when hepatic LDL receptors bind the particle and internalize it for lysosomal degradation; the processes gathered here push in the opposite direction, damping that clearance and so raising plasma cholesterol. This braking arm sets the level at which LDL sits in blood and, when it dominates, favours atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease — the reason two of its components are drug targets. PCSK9 binds the LDL receptor at the cell surface and routes it to lysosomal destruction rather than recycling, while the E3 ubiquitin ligase MYLIP (IDOL) ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail to trigger its degradation; APOC3 impairs lipoprotein handling and clearance from the circulation. A set of microRNAs adds post-transcriptional repression of receptor and lipoprotein-uptake mRNAs, alongside an RNA-binding destabilizer of LDL receptor transcripts, making receptor abundance the principal control point.

Ubiquitin is a finite, reusable currency: chains must be trimmed from substrates and disassembled back into monomers before those substrates are degraded, or the free pool collapses and the cell loses its ability to tag anything new for turnover. Maintaining that steady state of ubiquitin monomers and unanchored chains, largely at proteasome-bound ubiquitinated intermediates, keeps protein quality control, cell cycle proteolysis and selective autophagy running. The genes here span both sides of the balance — E2 conjugating enzymes such as UBE2C, UBE2S and UBE2K that build chains, E3 ligases and adaptors including FBXW7, TRIM32 and the mitophagy pair PINK1 and PRKN that mark targets, and cofactors like PLAA that assist chain disassembly and extraction. Failure shows up as depleted free ubiquitin, stalled degradation and accumulation of damaged mitochondria and aggregation-prone proteins, a theme in neurodegeneration.

Ubiquitin is usually attached to a substrate, but some ligases and E2 enzymes also build free, unanchored polyubiquitin chains, and this polymerization of ubiquitin chains that are not conjugated to any protein produces signalling molecules in their own right. Unanchored chains act as ligands rather than degradation tags: they can activate kinases and innate immune signalling, prime proteasome and deubiquitinase activity, and be recycled back into monomeric ubiquitin. The enzymes here span several chain linkages and contexts — the mitochondrial pair PINK1 and parkin, which links ubiquitin polymerization to clearance of damaged mitochondria; RNF135 and TRIM family ligases that generate chains supporting antiviral RIG-I signalling; and E2 enzymes including UBE2S and UBE2C, associated with anaphase-promoting complex activity and cell cycle progression. Chain-type specificity determines which downstream effector reads the product.

Hearing is not just transduction in the cochlea but a whole-organism reaction: startle, orienting, arousal, and the changes in gene expression and behaviour that follow a sound. This grouping covers cellular and systemic responses to auditory stimulation, spanning the hair cells that detect sound, the neurons that relay it, and the circuits that interpret it. Outer hair cell electromotility depends on prestin (SLC26A5), while the alpha9/alpha10 nicotinic receptor pair mediates efferent olivocochlear feedback that tunes cochlear gain and protects against noise. Potassium channels such as KCNQ3 and KCNC1 set the fast, precisely timed firing that auditory neurons require, and synaptic organizers including neurexins, SHANK3, CNTNAP2 and FOXP2 link sound processing to vocal learning and language. Disruption produces deafness, altered acoustic startle, and the auditory processing deficits seen in autism and neurodegenerative disease.

Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cells, and their development from committed precursors into functional, branched cells is what gives neurons their metabolic support, potassium and glutamate buffering, blood-brain barrier induction, and synaptic modulation. Loss or distortion of this programme leaves neurons poorly supported and contributes to leukodystrophy, neurodegeneration and gliotic scarring after injury. Gliogenic commitment and maturation are driven by cytokine signalling through CNTF and IL-6 family receptors, Notch ligand DLL1, Sonic hedgehog transduction via SMO, and transcriptional regulators including POU3F2 and ZEB2, while GFAP and vimentin mark the maturing intermediate filament cytoskeleton. Many members instead reflect reactive astrogliosis, the injury-induced state in which TNF, IL-1B, interferon-gamma, complement and TLR4 signalling reshape astrocyte phenotype alongside microglial cues such as TREM2 and progranulin, linking this biology to neuroinflammation and to tauopathy and Alzheimer-associated proteins.

Oligodendrocyte development is the route by which a committed glial progenitor of the central nervous system becomes a mature myelinating cell, wrapping axons in lipid-rich membrane so that impulses travel quickly and axons remain metabolically supported. The programme sets the timing of myelination in the developing brain and its reactivation governs remyelination after demyelinating injury; failure produces hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and contributes to the chronic deficits of multiple sclerosis. Lineage identity is imposed by transcription factors including SOX10, OLIG1, NKX2-2, NKX6-2 and the myelin regulatory factor MYRF, with HES5 and ID2/ID4 holding progenitors undifferentiated until differentiation is permitted. Sonic hedgehog and other extrinsic cues specify progenitors, axonal contactins and their associated proteins mediate recognition of the target axon, and structural and lipid-synthetic genes such as PLP1, MAG and FA2H build the sheath itself. Mutations in the translation initiation factor EIF2B subunits disrupt this maturation, causing white matter disease.

Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain, and this programme describes how progenitors acquire their specialized identity and homeostatic phenotype. Mature microglia survey the neuropil, prune synapses, clear apoptotic debris and mount innate immune responses, so failure of their differentiation or maintenance leaves the CNS with defective phagocytic surveillance and skewed neuroinflammation. TGFB1 signalling is the dominant instructive cue, with NRROS controlling its local availability and thereby the survival and identity of microglia in the brain parenchyma; loss of either produces profound microglial defects. Innate immune sensing through TLR2, TLR4 and the adaptor MYD88 shapes activation state, while glucocorticoid signalling through NR3C1 restrains it. Lysosomal and trafficking genes such as GBA1, NAGLU and MFSD8 link the pathway to the degradative capacity microglia need, and their mutation causes neurodegenerative and storage disease with prominent microglial pathology.

Glial cell proliferation expands the non-neuronal populations of the nervous system — astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and their precursors, Schwann cells, and microglia — during development, after injury, and in disease. Controlled division supplies myelinating cells to axons and reactive astrocytes and microglia to damaged tissue; uncontrolled division underlies gliomas and schwannomas, as loss of the tumour suppressor NF2 illustrates. Mitogenic input arrives through cytokine and growth factor receptors, with CSF1 and IL34 acting on CSF1R to sustain microglial numbers and LGI4 signalling driving Schwann cell expansion, while fractalkine, IL1B, IL6, TNF and IL33 couple proliferation to inflammatory state. Lineage transcription factors including SOX10, NFIA, NFIB, HES1 and NOTCH1 set glial identity alongside division, and E2F1, CREB1 and several microRNAs tune the cell cycle response. GFAP and CLU mark the reactive astrocyte output of this programme.

Peripheral nerves depend on Schwann cells to myelinate axons and to repopulate the nerve after injury, and the control of Schwann cell proliferation sets how many of these glia are available. Expansion must be matched to axon number: too little and myelination and regeneration fail, too much and the result is schwannoma or neurofibroma, as seen when the merlin tumour suppressor encoded by NF2 is lost. The genes here span lineage specification by SOX10, small RNA processing through DICER1 with the miR-221/222 pair acting on cell cycle brakes, transcriptional repression by SKI, and sphingolipid synthesis via CERS2 that supplies myelin lipids.
