This chemistry links respiratory gas exchange to acid-base homeostasis and renal ammonium handling; loss of haemoglobin subunits causes the thalassaemias, and carbonic anhydrase II deficiency produces osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis.

Oxygen transport is the carriage of molecular oxygen from the lungs to respiring tissues and its local buffering within cells, the function that allows large aerobic animals to exist at all. Its core is the globin family: adult haemoglobin tetramers assembled from alpha- and beta-type chains, the embryonic and fetal variants that adapt oxygen affinity to placental exchange, myoglobin storing oxygen in muscle, and cytoglobin and neuroglobin acting in neurons and other tissues. Affinity is tuned rather than fixed, and the erythrocyte bisphosphoglycerate mutase that generates 2,3-BPG sets how readily haemoglobin releases its cargo. Because loading and unloading depend on cooperative haem chemistry, mutations and imbalanced globin expression produce sickle cell disease and the thalassaemias, while the switch from fetal to adult globins is a long-standing therapeutic target. The pathway sits upstream of all oxidative metabolism and of systemic responses to hypoxia.

Aerobic tissues need oxygen delivered from the lungs faster than diffusion allows, and oxygen transport is the carrier-based system that does it. Globins bind O2 reversibly through a heme iron: the adult alpha and beta chains of hemoglobin in erythrocytes carry the bulk of the load, embryonic and fetal chains (zeta, epsilon, gamma) substitute during development and confer higher oxygen affinity in utero, and myoglobin buffers and shuttles oxygen inside muscle. Neuroglobin and cytoglobin serve smaller local roles in neurons and other tissues. Affinity is tuned rather than fixed, and bisphosphoglycerate mutase supplies 2,3-BPG, the allosteric effector that lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity so O2 is released where tissue demand is high. Defects in the globin chains underlie sickle cell disease and the thalassemias, in which impaired or unstable carriers cause anemia and tissue hypoxia.

Copper is needed as a cofactor by cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase and dopamine beta-hydroxylase, but is toxic when free, so cells acquire it through a small dedicated set of transporters that constitute copper ion import. Uptake across the plasma membrane is carried out by the high-affinity carrier SLC31A1 and its lower-affinity relative SLC31A2, which take up the reduced Cu(I) form; the STEAP family metalloreductases supply that substrate by reducing Cu(II) at the membrane, an activity they share with their role in iron handling. The P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B then pump copper into the secretory pathway, loading cuproenzymes and directing excess to export or biliary excretion. Loss of these ATPases causes Menkes disease and Wilson disease, the two poles of copper deficiency and copper overload, illustrating how tightly this route must be balanced.

Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation inside cells, required for ATP binding, nucleic acid stability and hundreds of enzyme reactions, and this pathway covers the channels and carriers that move it across membranes and set its concentration in cells and body fluids. Renal and intestinal uptake through the TRPM6 and TRPM7 channels, paracellular reabsorption via the tight-junction protein claudin-16, and efflux through SLC41 exchangers together determine systemic magnesium balance; their loss produces hypomagnesaemia with secondary hypocalcaemia, seizures and renal magnesium wasting. CNNM proteins and Mrs2, the mitochondrial inner-membrane channel, handle intracellular and organellar distribution, while MAGT1 and TUSC3 double as subunits of the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, linking magnesium handling to protein N-glycosylation and, in the case of MAGT1 deficiency, to immunodeficiency. NIPA-family transporters extend the same function to neurons, where mutation causes hereditary spastic paraplegia.

Many metabolites, neurotransmitters and drugs carry a positive charge at physiological pH and cannot cross membranes unaided; organic cation transport is the collective carrier activity that moves them across plasma and organelle membranes. It underlies renal and hepatic clearance of xenobiotics, loading of neurotransmitters into synaptic vesicles, reuptake of monoamines and choline at synapses, and delivery of carnitine, polyamines, thiamine and cationic amino acids to cells. The work is done largely by solute carrier families: the classic organic cation transporters and multidrug-extrusion antiporters of kidney and liver epithelium, vesicular monoamine and acetylcholine transporters, sodium-coupled monoamine and amino acid symporters, choline-like transporters, and mitochondrial carriers handling carnitine, ornithine and coenzyme A. Loss of individual members causes carnitine deficiency, thiamine-responsive disorders, aminoacidurias and altered drug disposition, making this transport capacity a determinant of both neurotransmission and pharmacokinetics.

Quaternary ammonium group transport moves permanently charged organic cations — carnitine, choline, betaine, thiamine, ergothioneine and many cationic drugs — across membranes that they cannot cross unaided. It sets whether the liver and kidney can take up and excrete cationic xenobiotics, and whether muscle and heart receive the carnitine needed to import fatty acids into mitochondria for beta-oxidation. Organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family handle hepatic and renal uptake of metformin and related drugs, while SLC22A5 is the high-affinity carnitine carrier whose loss causes systemic carnitine deficiency with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy. Mitochondrial members carry carnitine-conjugated acyl groups and thiamine pyrophosphate across the inner membrane, and sodium-dependent carriers accumulate betaine as an osmolyte in the renal medulla. A scaffold protein anchors several of these transporters at the apical membrane, linking their surface delivery to polarised epithelial function.

Cells must move chloride, bicarbonate, sulfate, phosphate, iodide and nitrate across membranes to set their volume, internal pH and electrical excitability, and inorganic anion transport is the collective machinery that does it. The pathway spans several structurally unrelated families: CFTR and the CLC chloride channels and transporters, calcium-activated anoctamins, bestrophins, volume-regulated LRRC8A channels, the SLC4 and SLC26 bicarbonate/chloride exchangers, SLC12 cation-chloride cotransporters, and SLC34/SLC20 phosphate carriers, alongside ligand-gated anion channels such as GABA-A and glycine receptors that hyperpolarize neurons. Regulatory input comes from calcium sensing, WNK kinase signalling, and vitamin D and FGF23 control of phosphate handling. The consequences of failure are correspondingly varied: cystic fibrosis, Bartter and Pendred syndromes, congenital chloride diarrhoea, osteopetrosis, macular dystrophy, epilepsy and disorders of thyroid iodide uptake and renal mineral balance.

Bicarbonate transport moves HCO3- across membranes and so sets the pH of blood, cytoplasm and secreted fluids. It is how the kidney reclaims filtered bicarbonate and excretes acid, how the pancreas, duodenum and airway produce alkaline fluid, how the red cell carries CO2 as bicarbonate, and how corneal endothelium and inner ear maintain their specialised fluids; loss of individual carriers causes distal renal tubular acidosis, congenital chloride diarrhoea, corneal dystrophy and deafness. The work is shared between the SLC4 family of Na+- and Cl--coupled exchangers and cotransporters, including the erythrocyte anion exchanger AE1, and the SLC26 anion exchangers that pair with CFTR at secretory apical membranes. Carbonic anhydrase supplies substrate locally, and anion-permeable bestrophin channels provide a parallel conductive route. The pathway therefore ties acid-base homeostasis to epithelial fluid secretion, gas transport and cell volume regulation.

Moving bicarbonate across membranes is how cells and tissues set pH, and this transport underlies acid-base balance in blood, kidney, gut, pancreas and brain. Red cell band 3 (SLC4A1) exchanges chloride for bicarbonate to let haemoglobin carry CO2, while carbonic anhydrase activity supplies the substrate by hydrating CO2; sodium-coupled cotransporters such as SLC4A4 and SLC4A5 reclaim bicarbonate in the proximal tubule and secrete it into pancreatic and duodenal fluid, where SLC26 anion exchangers and the CFTR channel work together to alkalinise and hydrate secretions. Loss of these activities produces distal and proximal renal tubular acidosis, hereditary spherocytosis, corneal dystrophy, congenital chloride diarrhoea and the thickened mucus of cystic fibrosis. Intracellular pH set this way also governs neuronal excitability, epithelial fluid secretion and, through associated bestrophin channels and zinc-transporting proteins, broader ion homeostasis.

Iodide transport is the movement of iodide across cell membranes by transporters and channels, and in humans it exists chiefly to concentrate iodide in the thyroid follicular cell so that thyroid hormone can be made. The sodium-iodide symporter takes up iodide from blood at the basolateral surface against a steep gradient, driven by the sodium gradient, while pendrin and related anion exchangers together with anion channels move it across the apical membrane into the follicular lumen, where it is organified onto thyroglobulin. A potassium channel subunit supports the electrical driving force for uptake. Loss of these steps causes dyshormonogenetic congenital hypothyroidism and goitre, with Pendred syndrome adding sensorineural deafness; the same symporter makes radioiodine uptake possible in thyroid imaging and cancer therapy. Related solute carriers here also handle lactate, vitamins and other monocarboxylates.

Negatively charged carbon-containing molecules travel across membranes only with help, and organic anion transport covers the carriers, channels and binding proteins that move them into, out of and within cells. The traffic it handles is the everyday chemistry of physiology: bile acids recycled by the liver and gut, urate and drug conjugates cleared by the kidney proximal tubule, lactate and pyruvate shuttled between glycolytic and oxidative tissues, fatty acids, folate, prostaglandins, neurotransmitter glutamate and GABA, and citrate and malate across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Large solute-carrier families dominate, including the organic anion transporting polypeptides, multidrug resistance-associated ABC efflux pumps, monocarboxylate and dicarboxylate carriers, bile-acid transporters and mitochondrial carriers, alongside anion channels and cytosolic lipid- and retinoid-binding proteins. Loss of individual members produces cholestasis, gout, chloride and bicarbonate secretion defects, and altered disposition of many prescribed drugs.

Phosphorylated sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so moving hexose phosphates between compartments requires dedicated carriers, and this transport step links cytosolic glucose metabolism to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Its best-understood use is the final stage of glucose production: SLC37A4 carries glucose-6-phosphate into the ER, where glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunits hydrolyse it so free glucose can be released into the blood during fasting. Loss of either the transporter or the liver enzyme causes glycogen storage disease type I, with fasting hypoglycaemia and hepatic glycogen accumulation, while defects in the ubiquitously expressed G6PC3 cause neutropenia, showing that the same chemistry serves neutrophil survival as well as hepatic glucose output. Related sugar-phosphate exchangers of the SLC37 family, together with a phosphate-handling SLC17 carrier, broaden the substrate range beyond glucose-6-phosphate and connect this transport to glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway.

Lactate, pyruvate, ketone bodies, short- and long-chain fatty acids, bile acids and prostaglandins all carry a single carboxylate group and cannot cross membranes unaided; monocarboxylic acid transport is the collection of carriers, pumps and binding proteins that move them across plasma membranes and into mitochondria and peroxisomes. It underwrites the lactate shuttle between glycolytic and oxidative tissues, hepatic uptake and biliary export of bile salts and drugs, fatty acid delivery for beta-oxidation, and renal handling of organic acids. Proton-coupled monocarboxylate transporters, organic anion transporters and uptake carriers, sodium-bile acid cotransporters, ATP-binding cassette export pumps, fatty acid transport proteins and cytosolic fatty-acid- and retinol-binding proteins provide the routes, while the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier and a carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase govern entry into oxidative metabolism. Nuclear receptors including the PPARs and the bile-acid sensor FXR tune capacity to nutrient supply; loss of individual carriers causes cholestasis, hyperuricaemia, thyroid hormone transport defects and altered drug disposition.

Bile acids made in the liver must be exported into bile, reclaimed from the gut, and returned to hepatocytes, and this transport machinery is what makes that enterohepatic circulation possible. It sustains fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption while keeping detergent-like bile salts from accumulating inside cells; when it fails, the result is cholestasis, pruritus, and hepatocyte injury, as in the progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis syndromes caused by loss of the canalicular bile salt export pump ABCB11 or the flippase ATP8B1. Sinusoidal uptake uses the sodium-dependent taurocholate cotransporter SLC10A1 and organic anion transporting polypeptides such as SLCO1B1, ileal reuptake uses SLC10A2, and basolateral efflux via the SLC51A/SLC51B heterodimer and several multidrug resistance-associated proteins returns bile salts to portal blood. The bile acid receptor NR1H4 senses the returning pool and feeds back on synthesis and transporter expression.

Prostaglandins are made and act locally, but because they are charged organic anions at physiological pH they cannot cross membranes freely; carrier-mediated prostaglandin transport is what moves newly synthesised mediator out of the producing cell and later pulls it back in for degradation. This traffic sets how long and how far a prostaglandin signal reaches, and it matters for fever, inflammatory pain, renal salt and water handling, uterine contraction at labour, and closure of the ductus arteriosus after birth. Efflux is driven by an ATP-binding cassette pump, while organic anion transporting polypeptides such as SLCO2A1 and organic anion transporters of the SLC22 family mediate uptake in kidney, liver and other epithelia. Upstream, phospholipases release arachidonate, and cyclooxygenase-2 with prostaglandin E synthase generate the ligand, linking transport to inflammatory stimuli such as interleukin-1 beta and to RANKL-driven bone remodelling.

Four-carbon dicarboxylates — succinate, malate, oxaloacetate, aspartate and glutamate among them — must cross membranes to link cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolism, and C4-dicarboxylate transport is the collection of carriers that moves them. It underpins the malate-aspartate shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents into mitochondria, renal and intestinal reabsorption of citric acid cycle intermediates, and clearance of synaptically released glutamate and aspartate by astrocytes. Sodium-dependent plasma membrane carriers of the SLC13 and SLC1 families handle uptake, while inner mitochondrial membrane carriers including the dicarboxylate and 2-oxoglutarate exchangers and the aspartate-glutamate carriers SLC25A12 and SLC25A13 couple matrix pools to the cytosol. Loss of these steps has clear consequences: citrin deficiency disrupts ureagenesis and the redox shuttle, SLC13A5 mutations cause early infantile epilepsy, and failed glutamate clearance produces excitotoxic neuronal injury.

Alpha-ketoglutarate sits at the junction of the citric acid cycle, amino acid metabolism and oxygen sensing, and moving it across membranes is what lets different compartments and organs share it. Carriers of the dicarboxylate transporter family take up alpha-ketoglutarate and related di- and tricarboxylates with sodium at the apical and basolateral surfaces of kidney tubule and intestinal epithelium, generating the intracellular dicarboxylate gradient that organic anion transporters then use as a counter-substrate to secrete drugs, toxins and metabolites into urine. A mitochondrial carrier exchanges alpha-ketoglutarate for malate, the outward-facing step of the malate-aspartate shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents from cytosol to matrix, while a related carrier handles oxoadipate in lysine and tryptophan degradation. Loss of these routes impairs renal handling of citrate and xenobiotics and disturbs cytosolic redox balance.

Humans lack urate oxidase, so serum urate levels are set almost entirely by how much of it the kidney and gut reabsorb versus excrete, and the transporters that move urate across epithelial membranes are what perform that balancing act. Reabsorption at the renal proximal tubule brush border is driven by exchangers such as URAT1 (SLC22A12), with basolateral exit through the facilitative carrier GLUT9 (SLC2A9) returning urate to the blood; secretion runs the other way through ABCG2 and ABCC4 and the sodium-phosphate-related SLC17 family transporters at the apical surface. Loss-of-function in the reabsorptive arm causes renal hypouricemia, while impaired secretion, notably common ABCG2 variants, raises urate and predisposes to gout and urate nephrolithiasis. Uromodulin, secreted by the thick ascending limb, influences urate handling indirectly and links this transport biology to tubular function and chronic kidney disease.

Phosphate-ester-containing metabolites and lipids rarely cross membranes unaided, and this transport programme covers the carriers, pumps, flippases and channels that move them between compartments, across the plasma membrane and between cells. It sustains phospholipid asymmetry, nucleotide and cofactor supply to mitochondria, sugar-nucleotide delivery to the Golgi for glycosylation, lipoprotein-borne lipid traffic in plasma, and release of ATP as an extracellular signal. P4-type ATPases with their CDC50 subunits flip aminophospholipids inward, scramblases and XKR family members collapse that asymmetry to expose phosphatidylserine during apoptosis and platelet activation, and ABC transporters export lipids and organic anions. Mitochondrial carriers exchange ADP for ATP and import NAD, FAD, CoA and folate, while lipid-transfer proteins and apolipoproteins shuttle phospholipids at contact sites and in circulation. Failures produce cholestasis, dyslipidaemia, bleeding disorders, congenital glycosylation defects and peroxisomal disease.

monosaccharide transmembrane transport moves glucose, fructose, galactose and related sugars across membranes, the step that lets cells obtain fuel and the body distribute it. Nothing about carbohydrate metabolism works without it: intestinal absorption, renal glucose reclamation, brain glucose supply, and insulin-stimulated uptake by muscle and fat all depend on these carriers, and their failure produces glucose-galactose malabsorption, renal glycosuria, De Vivo disease and insulin resistance. Two carrier families do the work — facilitative GLUT/SLC2 uniporters driven by concentration gradients and sodium-coupled SLC5 symporters that concentrate sugar against them. Much of the remaining biology is regulatory: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT triggers RAB- and syntaxin-binding-protein-dependent trafficking of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane, while leptin, adiponectin, FGF21, growth hormone and inflammatory cytokines tune transporter abundance and thus whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells depend on dedicated carriers to bring glucose, fructose, galactose and related monosaccharides into the cytoplasm and across epithelia. This transport sets the fuel supply for glycolysis, enables intestinal and renal absorption and reabsorption of dietary and filtered glucose, and is the step that insulin regulates to clear sugar from blood. Two carrier families dominate: facilitative GLUT-type transporters that move sugar down its concentration gradient, and sodium-coupled cotransporters that drive uptake against a gradient using the sodium electrochemical gradient. Layered on top is the hormonal control machinery — insulin and its receptor, IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT, and the trafficking proteins that shuttle the insulin-responsive transporter to the cell surface — together with adipokines and hepatic factors that tune it. Failure produces glucose transporter deficiency syndromes, renal glycosuria, malabsorption, and the insulin resistance of type 2 diabetes.

Fructose cannot cross membranes unaided, so its uptake from the diet and its distribution between tissues depend on carrier proteins that move the sugar across the plasma membrane. This transport step sets how much dietary fructose reaches the liver for conversion to glucose, glycogen and lipid, and its failure in the intestine produces fructose malabsorption with osmotic diarrhoea and bloating. Most of the carriers here belong to the facilitative glucose transporter family: SLC2A5 is the principal apical fructose entry route in enterocytes, SLC2A2 provides basolateral exit and hepatic uptake, and several relatives including SLC2A7, SLC2A8, SLC2A9 and SLC2A11 carry fructose with differing affinity and tissue distribution. SLC2A9 doubles as a urate transporter, linking this sugar transport to serum uric acid and gout, and excess fructose flux is tied to hepatic steatosis and metabolic syndrome.

Dietary galactose, released mainly from lactose in the gut, must cross cell membranes before it can be phosphorylated and funnelled into glycolysis or used to build galactosylated glycans and glycolipids, and galactose transmembrane transport is the carrier-mediated step that gets it there. The transporters involved work in two modes: the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 drives uptake against a gradient at the intestinal brush border using the sodium electrochemical gradient, while facilitative GLUT-family carriers such as GLUT2 and GLUT3 allow passive equilibrative movement, GLUT2 handling basolateral export from enterocytes and hepatic uptake and release. Additional members contribute in brain and connective tissue, including a sugar transporter of the SLC45 family and GLUT10, whose loss causes arterial tortuosity syndrome. The pathway therefore links intestinal sugar absorption and hepatic handling to galactose metabolism, and its capacity sets how quickly a galactose load is cleared from blood.

Glycosylation happens inside the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum, but the activated sugar donors are made in the cytosol, so every glycan depends on carriers that move nucleotide-sugars across those membranes in exchange for the nucleoside monophosphate left behind. The SLC35 family supplies this antiport activity, each member with its own donor preference: CMP-sialic acid, UDP-galactose, UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, GDP-fucose and UDP-glucuronic acid among them. Their importance is visible in disease, since loss of the CMP-sialic acid transporter or of the Golgi GDP-fucose transporter causes congenital disorders of glycosylation with immune and leukocyte adhesion defects, and loss of a UDP-sugar transporter serving proteoglycan synthesis produces skeletal dysplasia. The pathway therefore sets the substrate supply limit on protein and lipid glycosylation, glycosaminoglycan assembly, and the cell-surface carbohydrate code used in adhesion and recognition.

polyol transmembrane transport moves sugar alcohols such as glycerol, sorbitol, myo-inositol and mannitol across cell membranes, a step cells depend on for osmotic balance and for trafficking metabolic fuel between tissues. Its main effectors are the aquaglyceroporins, a branch of the water channel family whose wider pore admits small uncharged polyols: AQP3 and AQP9 supply the skin and liver with glycerol, AQP7 exports glycerol from adipocytes during lipolysis for hepatic gluconeogenesis, and AQP10 serves the same role in human fat. Alongside them, sodium-coupled carriers accumulate myo-inositol and related polyols against a gradient, allowing kidney medulla and neural cells to build up compatible osmolytes and survive hypertonic stress. Loss of these routes disturbs epidermal hydration, adipose glycerol release and renal osmoregulation, linking the pathway to lipid metabolism, water handling and osmotic adaptation rather than to any single organ.

Polyols such as glycerol, sorbitol and myo-inositol cross membranes only through dedicated channels and carriers, and this transmembrane transport determines how cells buffer osmotic stress and how glycerol moves between fat and liver. The aquaglyceroporin branch of the water channel family carries most of the traffic: AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 conduct glycerol as well as water, releasing it from adipocytes during lipolysis and taking it up in hepatocytes for gluconeogenesis, while AQP3 also supports skin hydration and AQP2 provides the vasopressin-regulated water route in the kidney collecting duct. Sodium-coupled carriers of the SLC5 family accumulate myo-inositol and related polyols as compatible osmolytes, which matters in renal medulla and brain where cells must survive large swings in tonicity. Loss of these routes alters glycerol handling, fat mass, urinary concentrating ability and osmotic tolerance.

Glycerol transmembrane transport moves glycerol across cell membranes through aquaglyceroporin channels, linking the tissues that release glycerol to those that consume it. This traffic underlies whole-body energy balance: adipocytes export glycerol generated by triglyceride lipolysis through AQP7, and hepatocytes take it up through AQP9 as a substrate for gluconeogenesis during fasting. The same channels hydrate the skin, where AQP3 supplies glycerol to keratinocytes of the epidermis, and contribute to water handling in kidney and gut, since most family members conduct water as well as small uncharged solutes such as glycerol and urea. Transport is passive and gradient-driven, with selectivity set by the pore architecture of each aquaporin and regulation achieved largely by trafficking channels to and from the plasma membrane. Disrupted aquaglyceroporin function alters adiposity, insulin sensitivity and skin barrier integrity.

Glycerol is the backbone of triglycerides and a substrate for gluconeogenesis, so moving it across membranes links fat stores to hepatic glucose production. This transport is carried out by aquaglyceroporins, a branch of the aquaporin channel family whose pore accommodates small uncharged solutes such as glycerol and urea in addition to water. Adipocyte channels release glycerol generated by lipolysis into the blood, and hepatocyte channels take it up for conversion to glucose during fasting; skin and gut members contribute to hydration and osmotic balance. Because the channels are passive, flux follows concentration gradients set by hormonal control of lipolysis rather than by the transporters themselves. Loss or reduced expression of individual members has been linked to altered adiposity, impaired fasting glucose output, and defective skin water and glycerol content, while related family members handle water permeability in kidney collecting duct.

Movement of acidic amino acids — chiefly glutamate and aspartate — across membranes determines how much excitatory transmitter sits in the synaptic cleft and how fast it is cleared. This is the basis of glutamatergic neurotransmission and of the astrocyte's protective role: excitatory amino acid transporters such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 take glutamate up into glia, vesicular transporters SLC17A6/7/8 load it back into synaptic vesicles, mitochondrial aspartate–glutamate and glutamate carriers feed the malate–aspartate shuttle, and the cystine–glutamate exchanger SLC7A11 couples export to glutathione synthesis. Failure to clear glutamate produces excitotoxic neuronal death, a mechanism implicated in ischaemia, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Volume-regulated anion channels, potassium channels and gap junction proteins that shape glial ion and osmotic homeostasis accompany the transporters, together with receptors and release machinery that regulate transport, linking amino acid handling to energy metabolism, nitrogen balance and redox defence.

Aromatic amino acid transport moves phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan across membranes, supplying cells with precursors for protein synthesis and for catecholamine, thyroid hormone, serotonin and kynurenine production. The carriers here work in several compartments and configurations: the heterodimeric partner SLC3A2 pairs with light chains SLC7A5 and SLC7A8 to exchange large neutral amino acids at the plasma membrane and blood-brain barrier, SLC16A10 moves aromatic amino acids without an exchange partner, SLC6A14 couples uptake to sodium and chloride, and lysosomal and mitochondrial transporters such as SLC66A1 and SLC25A29 handle intracellular pools. ACE2 acts here as a chaperone required for intestinal neutral amino acid uptake rather than as a transporter itself, and its loss produces tryptophan malabsorption with pellagra-like disease. Tumour cells depend on this route for leucine and tryptophan entry that sustains mTORC1 signalling and growth.

Arginine, lysine and ornithine must be moved across membranes to be absorbed from the diet, reclaimed from urine, delivered to the urea cycle and sensed as a signal of nutrient sufficiency, and basic amino acid transport is the carrier system that does this. Cationic transporters of the SLC7 family, some working alone and some as heterodimers with the heavy chains SLC3A1 or SLC3A2, handle uptake at the plasma membrane; loss of the renal and intestinal pair causes cystinuria and kidney stones, while defects in the intestinal partner underlie lysinuric protein intolerance. Mitochondrial carriers import ornithine for urea synthesis, and mutation of one of them produces hyperornithinaemia with hyperammonaemia. Lysosomal members, including the arginine sensor SLC38A9 and the transporter mutated in Batten disease, couple amino acid efflux from that compartment to mTORC1 activation and to cellular growth control.

Leucine, isoleucine and valine must be carried across membranes before they can be used for protein synthesis, oxidized for energy, or read as a nutrient signal, and branched-chain amino acid transport is the set of carriers that moves them into cells, out again, and into organelles. It underlies intestinal and renal reabsorption of dietary amino acids, delivery of leucine across the blood-brain barrier, and the leucine supply that mTORC1 senses to license growth. Heteromeric exchangers pair the SLC3A2 heavy chain with light chains such as SLC7A5 and SLC7A8, swapping a branched-chain amino acid inward for another neutral amino acid; sodium-dependent SLC6 family members and the SLC43 uniporters add facilitated and concentrative routes, SLC38A9 works at the lysosome, and SLC25A44 imports these substrates into mitochondria for catabolism. Loss of SLC7A7 causes lysinuric protein intolerance, illustrating how transport failure becomes systemic metabolic disease.

Neutral amino acid transport moves uncharged amino acids such as glutamine, glycine, alanine, serine, proline and the branched-chain and aromatic amino acids across membranes, supplying cells with substrates for protein synthesis, nitrogen handling and neurotransmitter turnover. Families here span sodium-coupled system A and N carriers (SLC38), the SLC1 glutamate and ASCT transporters, proton-coupled PAT carriers (SLC36), SLC6 members including the glycine transporters and the intestinal and renal broad-scope carrier SLC6A19, and heteromeric exchangers built on the SLC3A2 heavy chain with SLC7 light chains. Mitochondrial and lysosomal components extend the same chemistry to organelles, with SLC38A9 reporting lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 and aspartate-glutamate carriers running the malate-aspartate shuttle. The transporters matter physiologically: loss of SLC6A19 or its chaperone ACE2 causes Hartnup aminoaciduria, SLC3A1 and SLC7A9 defects cause cystinuria, and glial glutamate uptake by SLC1A2 limits excitotoxicity.

L-amino acid transport moves amino acids across membranes, the step that lets cells acquire nitrogen and carbon skeletons, load neurotransmitters into vesicles, clear glutamate from synapses, and reabsorb filtered amino acids in kidney and gut. Its failure is directly pathogenic: cystinuria and lysinuric protein intolerance from defective dibasic amino acid carriers, cystinosis from lysosomal cystine export failure, and excitotoxic injury when glial glutamate uptake falters. The work is done by families of solute carriers with distinct logic — sodium-dependent excitatory amino acid transporters, heterodimeric light chains paired with the 4F2 heavy chain for exchange of neutral and cationic substrates, proton-coupled lysosomal and vesicular carriers, and mitochondrial carriers serving the urea cycle and aspartate-malate shuttle. Beyond nutrition, these transporters feed cystine into glutathione synthesis and allow lysosomal arginine sensing to activate mTORC1, linking amino acid flux to growth control and redox defence.

Cells cannot make all the amino acids they need, so carriers must move L-amino acids across the plasma membrane and across organellar membranes, and this transport activity sets the supply for protein synthesis, neurotransmission, nitrogen disposal and nutrient signalling. Distinct families do distinct jobs: excitatory amino acid carriers such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 clear glutamate from synapses, vesicular glutamate transporters load it for release, heterodimers built on the SLC3A2 heavy chain with SLC7A5, SLC7A11 or SLC7A8 exchange large neutral or cystine/glutamate pairs, SLC38 members drive sodium-coupled glutamine flux, proton-coupled SLC36 transporters recover amino acids from lysosomes, and mitochondrial SLC25 carriers run the aspartate-glutamate shuttle and ornithine entry into the urea cycle. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, cystinosis, urea cycle failure and excitotoxic injury, and lysosomal arginine sensing by SLC38A9 links amino acid availability to mTORC1-dependent growth control.

Alanine moves constantly between tissues — from muscle to liver in the glucose–alanine cycle, across the intestinal and renal brush border during absorption and reabsorption, and into mitochondria for one-carbon and serine metabolism — and none of that happens without carriers. L-alanine transport describes this directed movement across membranes, and the proteins involved define how cells acquire nitrogen and gluconeogenic carbon. The set spans several families with distinct logic: proton-coupled amino acid transporters of the SLC36 group, whose loss in the kidney underlies iminoglycinuria-type phenotypes; sodium-coupled system A and N carriers of the SLC38 family that also handle glutamine and serve hepatic ammonia handling; the heterodimeric exchanger formed by SLC3A2 with SLC7A8; the neutral amino acid exchanger SLC1A4; and SLC — sideroflexin SFXN1, which delivers serine into mitochondria. Together they couple amino acid supply to metabolism, growth signalling and nitrogen disposal.

Aspartate must cross membranes to serve as an excitatory transmitter, a nitrogen carrier, and a shuttle for reducing equivalents, and this transport biology provides the carriers that move it. At the plasma membrane, sodium-dependent excitatory amino acid carriers such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 clear glutamate and aspartate from the synaptic cleft into astrocytes, limiting excitotoxic damage, while neutral amino acid exchangers of the same family and volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits allow release or flux down electrochemical gradients. Inside mitochondria, the aspartate-glutamate carriers SLC25A12 and SLC25A13 complete the malate-aspartate shuttle and feed ureagenesis, and their loss causes citrin deficiency and a severe infantile neurodevelopmental disorder. Related kidney transporters handle dibasic and acidic amino acid reabsorption. The astrocytic marker GFAP marks the cell type where much of this clearance occurs.

Cystine, the oxidized dimer of cysteine, must be moved across membranes before cells can use it, and the carriers that do this work set both antioxidant capacity and renal amino acid handling. At the kidney and intestinal brush border, a heterodimeric transporter built from a heavy chain and its light-chain partner reabsorbs cystine and dibasic amino acids; loss of either subunit causes cystinuria, in which poorly soluble cystine precipitates as kidney stones. In most other cells an exchanger takes up cystine in return for glutamate, supplying the cysteine needed for glutathione synthesis, which makes it a determinant of ferroptosis sensitivity and a target in tumour redox biology. A lysosomal transporter exports cystine generated by protein degradation out of the lysosome; its failure produces nephropathic cystinosis, with crystal accumulation and renal tubular damage.

gamma-aminobutyric acid transport moves the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter across membranes: packaging it into synaptic vesicles, clearing it from the synaptic cleft, and shuttling it between neurons and glia. Without this traffic, inhibitory tone collapses or persists inappropriately, and the resulting excitation-inhibition imbalance manifests as epilepsy, spasticity and altered anxiety states; the plasma-membrane carriers are direct drug targets, as tiagabine's action on SLC6A1 shows. The vesicular inhibitory transporter SLC32A1 loads GABA and glycine for regulated release, while sodium- and chloride-coupled SLC6 family carriers in neurons and astrocytes terminate signalling and recycle transmitter toward degradation by the mitochondrial transaminase ABAT. Release and reuptake are tuned by presynaptic scaffolds, calcium channel subunits, metabotropic GABA-B receptors and glial channels such as BEST1, linking transport capacity to synaptic strength and network rhythm generation.

GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian brain, and its movement across membranes sets how much inhibition a synapse delivers and how quickly it ends. Transport works at two levels: a vesicular carrier (SLC32A1) loads GABA together with glycine into synaptic vesicles for release, while plasma membrane sodium- and chloride-coupled carriers of the SLC6 family — GAT1, GAT3 and betaine/GABA transporter among them — clear it back into neurons and astrocytes, where ABAT degrades it into the succinate arm of the TCA cycle. Regulators and release-modulating receptors, including presynaptic GABA-B autoreceptors, calcium channel subunits and scaffolding adaptors, tune the process. Losing GAT1 function causes epileptic encephalopathy, and the same transporters are the targets of antiepileptic reuptake inhibitors, placing this traffic at the centre of the excitation–inhibition balance and of osmolyte handling in kidney and retina.

L-glutamate transmembrane transport moves the brain's principal excitatory neurotransmitter and a central metabolic amino acid across membranes, both to load it into synaptic vesicles and to clear it from the synaptic cleft. This traffic sets the amplitude and duration of excitatory signalling; when clearance fails, extracellular glutamate accumulates and kills neurons by excitotoxicity, a mechanism invoked in stroke, epilepsy and motor neuron disease. Vesicular transporters such as SLC17A6/7/8 fill glutamatergic vesicles using a proton gradient, while the EAAT family (SLC1A1-A3, SLC1A6) performs sodium-dependent uptake largely into astrocytes, supported by the Na+/K+-ATPase and potassium channel Kir4.1 that maintain the driving ion gradients. Mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate and glutamate carriers feed the malate-aspartate shuttle and nitrogen metabolism, and the cystine/glutamate antiporter SLC7A11 couples glutamate efflux to glutathione synthesis and ferroptosis resistance. Regulatory and trafficking partners tune transporter surface expression.

Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter and also a hub metabolite, so moving it across membranes determines both how fast synapses are silenced and how nitrogen and carbon are shuttled between compartments. This transmembrane transport of L-glutamate covers vesicular loading by the VGLUT proteins SLC17A6/7/8, high-affinity reuptake from the synaptic cleft by the excitatory amino acid carriers SLC1A1-SLC1A7 — SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 doing most of the astrocytic clearance — cystine/glutamate exchange through SLC7A11 that supplies cysteine for glutathione, and mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate and glutamate carriers of the SLC25 family that feed the malate-aspartate shuttle and ureagenesis. Associated accessory and regulatory proteins, including ARL6IP5 and the potassium channel KCNJ10 that sets the astrocyte driving force, tune the process. When clearance fails, extracellular glutamate rises and excitotoxic neuronal death follows, a mechanism implicated in ischaemia, epilepsy and motor neuron disease.

Glycine transport moves this small amino acid across membranes, and where it happens determines whether glycine acts as a nutrient, a heme precursor, or a neurotransmitter. In the spinal cord and brainstem, plasma membrane carriers clear glycine from inhibitory synapses and reload the presynaptic pool, while a vesicular transporter loads glycine together with GABA into synaptic vesicles; loss of the neuronal clearance route causes hyperekplexia, with exaggerated startle and muscle rigidity. Other members supply glycine for metabolism: a mitochondrial carrier imports glycine for the first step of heme synthesis, and its failure produces sideroblastic anemia, while proton-coupled and sodium-coupled carriers handle intestinal and renal absorption, lysosomal efflux of amino acids released by proteolysis, and reabsorption whose defect gives iminoglycinuria. Associated regulators of G protein signalling modulate transporter activity, linking glycine handling to receptor-driven control.

Isoleucine transport moves this branched-chain essential amino acid across cell membranes, supplying it for protein synthesis, branched-chain amino acid catabolism, and as a signal that nutrients are available. Because isoleucine cannot be synthesised, cells depend entirely on carrier proteins to import it from blood, gut lumen and cerebrospinal fluid, and the same carriers set the intracellular leucine/isoleucine pool that activates mTORC1 and thereby controls cell growth. The heterodimeric transporter formed by SLC7A5 with its chaperone subunit SLC3A2 exchanges branched-chain and aromatic amino acids across the plasma membrane and at the blood-brain barrier, and is strongly upregulated in proliferating tumour cells; SLC43A1 and SLC43A2 provide sodium-independent uptake of the same substrates. Loss or excess of this transport capacity distorts amino acid balance, neurotransmitter precursor delivery to brain, and growth signalling in cancer.

Isoleucine is a branched-chain essential amino acid that cells cannot make, so its uptake across membranes sets how much is available for protein synthesis and for signalling to the growth machinery. The carriers here move isoleucine and related large neutral amino acids: the heterodimer of SLC7A5 with its chaperone subunit SLC3A2 exchanges them for intracellular substrates, while SLC43A1 and SLC43A2 provide facilitated, sodium-independent transport. This traffic supplies leucine and isoleucine to mTORC1, which senses them to license translation and cell growth, and it underlies branched-chain amino acid entry across the blood-brain barrier and the placenta. Rapidly proliferating and tumour cells raise SLC7A5 to meet that demand, making the transporter a route for amino acid-mimetic drugs. Loss of such transport impairs amino acid homeostasis and nutrient-dependent growth control.

Leucine cannot be made by human cells and must be carried across membranes, and this transport activity supplies it to tissues and to the nutrient sensors that read it. Because leucine is the amino acid that activates mTORC1, its uptake couples extracellular supply to protein synthesis, cell growth and insulin secretion, and it also feeds branched-chain amino acid catabolism. The work is done largely by heteromeric and facilitative carriers: SLC7A5 and SLC7A8 pair with the chaperone subunit SLC3A2 to exchange large neutral amino acids, SLC43A1 and SLC43A2 mediate sodium-independent facilitated diffusion, and SLC6A15 and SLC6A17 handle neutral amino acid uptake in neurons. SLC7A7 mutations cause lysinuric protein intolerance, and LLGL2 contributes to the polarised placement of such transporters in epithelia, which determines whether absorption is apical or basolateral.

Ornithine sits at the junction of the urea cycle and polyamine synthesis, but the enzymes that consume it are split between mitochondrial matrix and cytosol, so the amino acid must be carried across membranes for either route to work. The carriers here do that job: mitochondrial inner-membrane transporters exchange cytosolic ornithine for matrix citrulline, delivering substrate to ornithine transcarbamylase and returning the cycle intermediate for argininosuccinate synthesis, while plasma-membrane cationic amino acid transporters of the SLC7 family take up ornithine, arginine and lysine into the cell. Loss of the mitochondrial ornithine/citrulline exchanger SLC25A15 causes hyperornithinaemia-hyperammonaemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome, in which ammonia detoxification fails despite intact cycle enzymes. The same transport also governs arginine supply for nitric oxide production and ornithine flux toward putrescine and downstream polyamines, linking nitrogen disposal to cell growth.

Phenylalanine transport moves the aromatic amino acid phenylalanine across cell membranes, supplying tissues with a substrate they cannot synthesise and that is needed for protein synthesis and for catecholamine and melanin precursor pools. Uptake at the blood-brain barrier, intestine, liver and placenta depends on it, and the same carriers export phenylalanine when intracellular levels rise, so their capacity shapes how neural tissue is exposed to the amino acid excess of phenylketonuria. The genes encode the two main routes: the heterodimeric system L exchanger, in which a light chain such as SLC7A5 or SLC43A2 pairs with the SLC3A2 heavy chain to trade large neutral amino acids across the plasma membrane, and the facilitative aromatic amino acid transporter SLC16A10, which permits net efflux. Both feed amino acid sensing and mTORC1 activation as well as nutrition.

Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid that cells must import from blood for protein synthesis, for conversion to tyrosine and thence to catecholamines and melanin, and as a signal of amino acid sufficiency. This transport activity moves it across plasma membranes through facilitative and exchange carriers. SLC7A5 pairs with the glycoprotein heavy chain SLC3A2 to form a heterodimeric antiporter that takes up large neutral and aromatic amino acids in exchange for intracellular glutamine, a route that also carries thyroid hormone and L-DOPA and supplies leucine to activate mTORC1; SLC43A2 and SLC16A10 provide sodium-independent uptake and efflux, the latter important in liver, kidney and intestine. Such carriers govern amino acid delivery across the blood-brain barrier, so their failure distorts brain aromatic amino acid balance, and their high expression supports the anabolic demands of proliferating tumour cells.

Proline transport moves this imino acid across membranes, supplying it for protein synthesis, collagen production, osmotic balance and, in the brain, for the neuronal pools handled by proline-preferring carriers. The genes encode sodium- and proton-coupled neutral amino acid transporters: lysosomal and apical proton/amino acid symporters of the SLC36 family, the SLC6 members that take up proline and other small neutral amino acids at the plasma membrane and in synaptic vesicles, the broadly expressed SLC38A2 system A carrier, and the heterodimeric partner SLC3A2 with its exchanger SLC7A5. ACE2 and its relative CLTRN act as accessory proteins that traffic and stabilise SLC6A19/SLC6A20-type carriers in kidney and intestinal brush border. Loss of this machinery produces renal iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria, and altered brain proline handling has been linked to neuropsychiatric phenotypes, placing the pathway at the junction of epithelial amino acid reabsorption and neurotransmitter-related metabolism.

Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that cells cannot make, so its movement across membranes sets the supply for protein synthesis and for the serotonin, melatonin and kynurenine pathways that branch from it. The carriers here move tryptophan and other large neutral amino acids: the heterodimeric exchangers formed by SLC7A5 or SLC7A8 with the SLC3A2 heavy chain, which trade intracellular amino acids for extracellular tryptophan at the blood-brain barrier, placenta and activated lymphocytes; an aromatic amino acid facilitator, SLC16A10; and a lysosomal amino acid transporter. ACE2 acts not as a transporter itself but as a chaperone required for surface expression of the intestinal neutral amino acid carrier, and its loss causes the tryptophan malabsorption of Hartnup-like disease with pellagra-type skin and neurological signs. Restricting tryptophan uptake is also how kynurenine-driven immune suppression starves responding T cells.

Peptide transport covers the directed movement of di- and oligopeptides and of peptide hormones across membranes and out of cells, whether by carriers and pores or by regulated secretion. Two distinct arms are represented. One is carrier-mediated uptake: the proton-coupled oligopeptide transporters of the SLC15 family move dietary and bacterially derived peptides across intestinal and renal brush borders and across endosomal membranes, where they also deliver peptidoglycan fragments to innate immune sensors, while TAP1 and TAP2 pump cytosolic peptides into the endoplasmic reticulum for loading onto MHC class I. The larger arm is hormone exocytosis, dominated by pancreatic islet biology: glucose sensing through GCK and SLC2A2, KCNJ11/ABCC8 channels, incretin and somatostatin receptors, islet transcription factors such as PDX1, MAFA and NEUROD1, and the SNARE, synaptotagmin and Rab machinery that fuses insulin and glucagon granules. Failure of these steps produces diabetes and endocrine deficiency.

Amines must be moved across membranes to be used, stored, or cleared, and this transport biology covers that directed movement of monoamines, polyamines, choline, ammonium and related amino-group compounds by carriers, channels and vesicular pumps. Its most visible role is in neurotransmission: vesicular monoamine and acetylcholine transporters load dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline and acetylcholine into secretory vesicles, while exocytotic machinery such as syntaxin, synaptotagmins and STXBP1 releases them, and presynaptic receptors for dopamine, adrenaline, adenosine and glutamate tune how much is released. Other members handle ammonium and amino-acid amines across epithelia and erythrocyte membranes, or export choline and organic cations in kidney and liver. Loss of control here has clear consequences — disrupted vesicular dopamine handling and alpha-synuclein aggregation feature in parkinsonian degeneration, and impaired ammonium clearance compromises nitrogen balance.

Betaine and related trimethylated amino acid derivatives such as carnitine must be moved across membranes, and this transport underpins two distinct jobs: defending cells against osmotic stress and delivering carnitine for mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. Kidney medulla and brain cells accumulate betaine as a compatible osmolyte through the sodium- and chloride-coupled carrier SLC6A12, while SLC22A5 imports carnitine at the plasma membrane and SLC25A20 shuttles acylcarnitines across the inner mitochondrial membrane; loss of either produces systemic carnitine deficiency with cardiomyopathy, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and muscle weakness. Broader-specificity organic cation and amino acid carriers of the SLC22, SLC6, SLC38 and SLC7 families contribute overlapping uptake in intestine, kidney and liver, where they also handle drugs and xenobiotics. The scaffold PDZK1 anchors several of these transporters at the apical surface, coupling their trafficking and activity to epithelial polarity.

Urea is the nitrogenous end product of amino acid breakdown, and moving it across membranes is what allows the kidney to excrete nitrogen while simultaneously using urea to build the medullary osmotic gradient that concentrates urine. Transport is carried out by dedicated urea transporters of the SLC14 family, expressed in collecting duct epithelium and in the descending vasa recta, together with several aquaglyceroporins such as AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 that conduct urea and glycerol alongside water. Loss of this permeability produces a urine-concentrating defect, since urea recycling in the loop of Henle is required for water reabsorption under vasopressin control. Associated factors point to the surrounding renal tubule context: a POU-domain transcription factor patterning nephron segments, uromodulin secreted by the thick ascending limb, and uroplakin of the urothelial permeability barrier that keeps stored urine from equilibrating with blood.

Monoamine transport moves dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and histamine across membranes, and it sets how much neurotransmitter reaches a receptor and for how long. Two steps dominate: vesicular monoamine transporters load amines into secretory vesicles for regulated release, while plasma membrane carriers such as the dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin transporters recapture them into neurons; organic cation transporters and related carriers handle lower-affinity uptake and clearance in peripheral tissues. Release itself depends on synaptotagmins, syntaxin and vesicle trafficking proteins, and the whole process is tuned by presynaptic autoreceptors -- adrenergic, dopaminergic, serotonergic and muscarinic -- that feed back on further release. This biology underlies mood, reward, arousal and motor control; it is the target of antidepressants, psychostimulants and antihypertensives, and its disruption, together with alpha-synuclein and PINK1/parkin handling of monoaminergic neurons, features in Parkinson's disease and psychiatric disorders.

polyamine transport moves putrescine, spermidine and spermine across membranes, letting cells top up or dispose of a pool of small polycations that they otherwise have to make from ornithine. Because polyamines are required for proliferation, translation, chromatin compaction and ion channel modulation, cells guard their internal concentration tightly, and transport is one of the two levers they use alongside biosynthesis. The genes cover both the carriers and their control: P5B-type ATPases such as ATP13A2 and ATP13A3 export polyamines from lysosomes and endosomes into the cytosol, organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and vesicular SLC18B1 handle uptake and sequestration, while antizymes and their inhibitors couple uptake to degradation of ornithine decarboxylase. Loss of ATP13A2 causes juvenile parkinsonism with lysosomal dysfunction, and cancer cells frequently exploit uptake to sustain growth, making these carriers drug targets.

Polyamines such as spermidine and spermine are required for growth, translation and chromatin function, but cells cannot make them freely and instead balance synthesis against uptake and export. Polyamine transport is the movement of these amines across membranes, and it matters because intracellular polyamine levels must be held within a narrow range: excess is toxic, depletion arrests proliferation. The P5B-type ATPases ATP13A2 and ATP13A3 export polyamines from lysosomes into the cytosol, and loss of ATP13A2 causes juvenile parkinsonism with lysosomal dysfunction. Organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and the multidrug extruder SLC47A1 carry polyamines alongside other cations, linking this traffic to drug disposition. Antizymes (OAZ1-3) and their inhibitors (AZIN1, AZIN2) feed back on both uptake and ornithine decarboxylase degradation, coupling transport to biosynthetic control of the polyamine pool.

Putrescine, the diamine made by decarboxylating ornithine and the starting point for spermidine and spermine synthesis, must cross membranes to reach the cells and compartments that use it, and this transport activity is what supplies it. Polyamines are needed for proliferation, chromatin and nucleic acid stabilisation, and translation via hypusination, so cells that cannot import them slow their growth; conversely, tumours often upregulate uptake to bypass inhibition of their own synthesis, which is why polyamine transport is pursued alongside synthesis blockade as a therapeutic target. The carriers here span distinct families: a P5B-type ATPase, ATP13A3, pumps polyamines out of endolysosomes into the cytosol and its loss causes lysosomal polyamine trapping, while organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and a multidrug and toxin extrusion antiporter move diamines across plasma membranes in liver and kidney, linking this route to drug and xenobiotic handling.

Spermidine transport moves this polyamine across membranes, letting cells acquire spermidine from the diet and gut microbiota rather than making it all themselves, and letting them dispose of it when it accumulates. Because polyamines are required for translation, chromatin compaction, autophagy and proliferation, and are toxic in excess, carrier-mediated uptake and vesicular sequestration set the size of the intracellular pool alongside synthesis from putrescine and decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine. The carriers here are mostly organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family, which are polyspecific and also handle drugs such as metformin and cisplatin in liver, kidney and intestine, so polyamine handling shares machinery with xenobiotic disposition. SLC18B1 instead loads spermidine and spermine into vesicles, supplying regulated release. Tumours that depend on imported polyamines exploit these routes, which is why blocking uptake is combined with inhibition of polyamine synthesis.

Organic acid transport covers the carrier-mediated movement of carboxylate-bearing metabolites — amino acids, monocarboxylates such as lactate and pyruvate, fatty acids, bile acids, urate, folate and prostanoids — across plasma and organelle membranes, and it is what allows tissues to exchange fuels, clear waste anions and terminate chemical signalling. Much of the work falls to solute carrier families: glutamate and GABA transporters that clear neurotransmitters from synapses, proton-coupled monocarboxylate carriers that move lactate between glycolytic and oxidative cells, sodium-dependent bile acid and organic anion uptake transporters that drive enterohepatic circulation, and mitochondrial carriers for citrate, malate, pyruvate and carnitine-conjugated acyl groups. ABC pumps and fatty-acid binding and activating proteins handle efflux and intracellular trafficking, while nuclear receptors of the PPAR family and bile-acid sensing tune capacity to demand. Loss of individual carriers produces aminoacidurias, cystinuria, bile salt export failure and cholestasis, or drug-handling and urate disorders.

Alcohols and other hydroxyl-bearing organic molecules rarely cross membranes unaided, and this transport programme covers the carriers, channels and lipid-shuttling proteins that move them between compartments, cells and tissues. It underpins cholesterol and bile salt handling, monoamine neurotransmitter storage and reuptake, glycerol and water-solute flux, and hepatic drug and xenobiotic clearance, so its failure produces hypercholesterolaemia, cholestasis, sterol storage disease and disturbed neurotransmission. Sterol movement dominates: ABC transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG5/8 export cholesterol and plant sterols, apolipoproteins and lipases remodel the particles that ferry them, NPC1 and NPC1L1 handle lysosomal egress and intestinal uptake, and oxysterol-binding and StAR-related proteins carry sterols between organelles under the control of liver X and SREBP-driven transcription. Solute carriers, aquaporins, vesicular monoamine transporters and organic anion transporters provide the membrane steps, with numerous microRNAs tuning the lipid arm.

Nucleobases and their nucleosides cannot cross membranes unaided, so carriers must move purines and pyrimidines across the plasma membrane and between compartments. This traffic feeds the salvage arm of nucleotide metabolism, which many cell types depend on rather than making bases from scratch, and it is the route by which nucleoside-analogue drugs such as gemcitabine, cytarabine and antiretrovirals enter their target cells. Equilibrative carriers of the SLC29 family move nucleosides down their gradients and also govern extracellular adenosine available to purinergic receptors, while sodium-coupled SLC28 transporters drive concentrative uptake across absorptive epithelia; SLC23 members carry ascorbate and nucleobases, and a purine-selective carrier handles free bases. Mitochondrial and channel-forming proteins, including adenine nucleotide translocases and a porin, extend the same logic to organelle membranes, linking nucleotide supply to energy metabolism.

Adenine and its nucleoside and nucleotide derivatives must cross membranes rather than be synthesised wherever they are needed, and this transport activity covers that movement across the plasma membrane and the mitochondrial envelope. It supports the salvage arm of purine metabolism, letting cells recover adenine-containing bases instead of paying the cost of de novo synthesis, and it determines cellular uptake of nucleoside and nucleobase analogue drugs used in cancer and antiviral therapy. Equilibrative nucleoside transporters SLC29A1 and SLC29A2 carry adenosine and related nucleosides down their gradients, thereby also setting extracellular adenosine available to purinergic receptors, while SLC43A3 handles nucleobases directly. At the inner mitochondrial membrane the adenine nucleotide translocases SLC25A4 and SLC25A5 exchange ADP for ATP, coupling oxidative phosphorylation to cytosolic energy demand, with the outer-membrane porin VDAC3 providing passage across the second barrier.

Cells that cannot make purines and pyrimidines from scratch, and cells recovering nucleosides released by neighbours, depend on carrier proteins to move these molecules across membranes. Nucleoside transport covers that directed movement, and it sets both the salvage supply of precursors for nucleotide synthesis and the extracellular concentration of adenosine, the signal read by adenosine receptors such as ADORA1 to slow heart rate and dampen neuronal excitability. Two families do the work: equilibrative carriers of the SLC29 group, which move nucleosides down their gradient, and concentrative sodium-coupled carriers of the SLC28 group, which accumulate them against a gradient with distinct purine and pyrimidine preferences. The same proteins determine uptake of nucleoside-analogue drugs used in cancer and antiviral therapy, so transport capacity shapes chemosensitivity. Related carriers handle nucleotide-derived cofactors across the inner mitochondrial membrane, linking this traffic to mitochondrial methylation chemistry.

Cells that cannot synthesise purines de novo depend on salvaging adenosine, inosine and deoxyadenosine from the extracellular space, and purine nucleoside transmembrane transport is the step that brings them in. The carriers involved set how much adenosine reaches its receptors, so they shape vascular tone, cardiac conduction, sleep pressure and inflammatory signalling as well as nucleotide supply. Two mechanisms operate side by side: sodium-coupled concentrative transporters accumulate nucleosides against a gradient, notably in intestine, kidney and liver, while equilibrative transporters such as SLC29A1 move them bidirectionally down their concentration gradient and are the target of adenosine-uptake inhibitors like dipyridamole. The same proteins carry nucleoside-analogue drugs, making them determinants of antiviral and cytotoxic chemotherapy uptake. A mitochondrial carrier is also represented, extending the theme to transport across internal membranes.

Cells that cannot make pyrimidines de novo, and tissues that salvage nucleosides for economy, depend on carrier proteins to bring uridine across the plasma membrane. Uridine transmembrane transport is carried out here by two families: sodium-coupled concentrative carriers that drive uptake against a gradient using the inward sodium electrochemical potential, and equilibrative carriers that move nucleosides down their concentration gradient in either direction. Together they feed the salvage route to UMP and the pyrimidine nucleotide pool, and they set intracellular and extracellular nucleoside levels that in turn shape adenosine receptor signalling. The same carriers determine cellular entry of nucleoside analogue drugs such as gemcitabine and cytarabine, so their expression influences chemotherapy response; loss of the lysosomal equilibrative member causes histiocytosis and related inherited disease. Transport activity also links to organ-level handling of nucleosides in intestine, kidney and liver.

Purine nucleotide transport moves ATP, ADP, cAMP, cGMP and related phosphorylated purines across membranes, since these molecules are too charged to cross lipid bilayers on their own. Two purposes dominate. One is release of ATP to the extracellular space, where it acts as a signal on purinergic receptors to drive inflammation, taste transmission, mechanosensation and nucleotide-mediated cell death; pannexin and CALHM channels, volume-regulated LRRC8 anion channels, and a vesicular nucleotide transporter that loads secretory vesicles all contribute, with P2RX7 both responding to extracellular ATP and promoting further release. The other is compartmental supply: mitochondrial carriers exchange ADP for ATP across the inner membrane, and related carriers import NAD+, CoA and adenine nucleotides that mitochondria cannot synthesise. ABCC-family pumps export cyclic nucleotides and conjugates. Loss of individual members causes mitochondrial myopathy, pseudoxanthoma elasticum-like calcification and disordered purinergic signalling.

ADP transport moves adenosine diphosphate across membranes, and in mitochondria it is the step that closes the loop of oxidative phosphorylation: cytosolic ADP must reach the matrix for ATP synthase to use it, and the ATP made must leave. The adenine nucleotide translocases that carry out this exchange are among the most abundant inner-membrane carriers, with tissue-restricted forms in heart and muscle, testis and liver; loss or mutation of the muscle isoform causes mitochondrial myopathy and cardiomyopathy, and the same carriers participate in permeability transition during cell death. Related members of the same carrier family import ATP-Mg in exchange for phosphate to set matrix adenine nucleotide content, deliver CoA and adenine nucleotides to peroxisomes, or supply ATP to the endoplasmic reticulum for chaperone function, while a vesicular transporter loads nucleotides for release as purinergic signals.

ATP does not cross membranes unaided, so its movement between compartments and out of cells depends on dedicated carriers and channels, and this transport underlies both cellular energetics and purinergic signalling. Inside the cell, mitochondrial carriers of the SLC25 family exchange ATP for ADP across the inner membrane, coupling oxidative phosphorylation to cytosolic demand, while a related transporter supplies ATP to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen for chaperone function. Vesicular loading by SLC17A9 packages ATP for regulated secretion, and large-pore channels including pannexin 1 and the calcium homeostasis modulator family release it into the extracellular space, where it acts as a danger signal and neurotransmitter at purinergic receptors, contributing to taste transmission, inflammation and pain. Loss of extracellular ATP release, as with ANKH or ABCC6 dysfunction, disturbs pyrophosphate balance and promotes ectopic calcification.

Choline cannot be synthesised de novo in useful amounts, so cells depend on carrier proteins to bring it across membranes for two distinct fates: phosphatidylcholine synthesis, which supplies most membrane phospholipid, and acetylcholine synthesis at cholinergic nerve terminals. Choline transport is carried out here by several families with different kinetics and locations: the high-affinity, sodium-dependent transporter SLC5A7 concentrates choline into presynaptic terminals and sets the ceiling on acetylcholine release, so its loss produces congenital myasthenic syndrome with impaired neuromuscular transmission; the SLC44 choline transporter-like proteins handle lower-affinity uptake in most tissues, with SLC44A1 also serving mitochondrial and myelin-related demands; SLC22A2 moves choline and other organic cations in renal tubules. FLVCR1 and FLVCR2 have been identified as plasma-membrane choline importers, and SLC25A48 delivers choline into mitochondria for oxidation to betaine, linking this transport to one-carbon metabolism.

Dopamine transport covers the movement of this catecholamine transmitter into vesicles, out of neurons and back across the plasma membrane, setting how much dopamine reaches receptors and for how long. It underlies reward signalling, motor control and motivation, and is the point of action of psychostimulants and of the vesicular blockers used to treat hyperkinetic movement disorders. Vesicular monoamine transporters load dopamine into synaptic vesicles, the plasma membrane dopamine transporter and noradrenaline transporter retrieve it, and organic cation carriers provide lower-affinity uptake in brain and periphery; synaptotagmins and Rab proteins handle the calcium-triggered release step. Release is tuned presynaptically by autoreceptors and by cholinergic, GABAergic, glutamatergic, serotonergic and opioid inputs, while COMT degrades released transmitter. Several Parkinson's disease proteins, including alpha-synuclein, parkin, PINK1 and DJ-1, are tied to this machinery, and its loss produces dopaminergic denervation and parkinsonism.

Movement of norepinephrine across membranes governs how long and how strongly the transmitter acts, both at sympathetic nerve terminals and in central noradrenergic tracts. Vesicular loading by the monoamine transporter SLC18A1 packages newly synthesised norepinephrine for exocytotic release, a step requiring syntaxin-dependent vesicle fusion, while the plasma membrane norepinephrine transporter SLC6A2 recaptures released transmitter into the neuron; organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and plasma membrane monoamine transporters provide lower-affinity uptake in peripheral tissues, and COMT degrades what escapes. Presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors, adenosine and purinergic receptors restrain further release, forming a feedback loop over sympathetic tone. This traffic sets blood pressure, heart rate and arousal, and is the target of antidepressants and stimulants; it also underlies epinephrine synthesis in adrenal chromaffin cells and is perturbed in synucleinopathies affecting catecholaminergic neurons.

Fatty acids cannot reach the mitochondrial matrix for beta-oxidation unless carnitine is available inside the cell and able to shuttle acyl groups across membranes, and carnitine transport is what supplies and distributes it. The carriers involved span two compartments: plasma membrane solute carriers absorb carnitine from diet and reclaim it from urine, with SLC22A5 the high-affinity sodium-dependent transporter whose loss causes primary systemic carnitine deficiency, presenting as hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and skeletal muscle weakness. Related organic cation transporters and a monocarboxylate-family carrier handle uptake in kidney, intestine and testis, while a scaffold protein anchors and regulates them at the apical membrane. Inside the mitochondrion, SLC25A20 exchanges acylcarnitine for free carnitine across the inner membrane, completing the carnitine shuttle that feeds long-chain fatty acids into energy production during fasting and sustained exercise.

Folic acid transport moves folate across membranes so that cells can obtain the one-carbon units needed to make purines, thymidylate and methionine. Folate cannot be synthesised by humans, so uptake from the diet and its delivery to tissues sets the ceiling on nucleotide synthesis and methylation capacity; failure causes megaloblastic anaemia, and inadequate maternal supply causes neural tube defects. Three routes are represented: the reduced folate carrier SLC19A1, which handles systemic uptake at physiological pH; the proton-coupled transporter SLC46A1, which absorbs folate in the acidic small intestine and whose loss causes hereditary folate malabsorption; and the GPI-anchored folate receptors FOLR1 and FOLR2, which bind folate with high affinity and internalise it by endocytosis, aided by megalin at the renal and choroid plexus surfaces. SLC25A32 completes the route by importing folate into mitochondria, and ABCC5 exports it. These carriers also determine antifolate chemotherapy uptake.

Cells cannot make folate and must import it, so folic acid transport determines the supply of one-carbon units for purine and thymidylate synthesis, methionine regeneration and DNA methylation. Three routes are represented: high-affinity folate receptors that bind the vitamin and internalise it by endocytosis, often with the endocytic receptor megalin at absorptive epithelia such as kidney and placenta; the reduced folate carrier, an antiporter that handles folate uptake at physiological concentrations in most tissues; and the proton-coupled transporter of the acidic intestinal surface, whose loss causes hereditary folate malabsorption with megaloblastic anaemia and neurological disease. A mitochondrial carrier delivers folate to the matrix for formate-generating one-carbon reactions, while an ABC efflux pump exports folate and antifolates. Because methotrexate and pemetrexed enter cells through these same carriers, transport capacity shapes antifolate chemotherapy response, and inadequate folate in pregnancy leads to neural tube defects.

Heme is indispensable as a cofactor but toxic when free, so cells move it between compartments and between tissues under tight control rather than letting it diffuse. This transport biology supports erythropoiesis, hepatic and macrophage heme recycling, and the delivery of heme to mitochondrial and cytosolic hemoproteins; its failure causes hemolysis, oxidative injury from labile heme, and disorders such as posterior column ataxia with retinitis pigmentosa. Exporters of the FLVCR family relieve cells of excess heme or import it, plasma hemopexin scavenges heme released by red cell lysis and routes it to receptor-mediated hepatic uptake, and ABC transporters at mitochondrial and other membranes move heme, porphyrin intermediates and related substrates. Endosomal and lysosomal steps return heme or its iron to the cytosol, linking this traffic to iron homeostasis, porphyrin synthesis and folate transport at the same membranes.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) cannot be synthesised by human cells, so its uptake across membranes sets the supply of the cofactor thiamine pyrophosphate required by pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenases and by transketolase. Thiamine transport is carried out by dedicated carriers SLC19A2 and SLC19A3 at the intestinal, renal and blood-brain interfaces, while SLC25A19 moves thiamine pyrophosphate into mitochondria to serve the matrix dehydrogenases. Organic cation transporters and a multidrug-and-toxin extrusion carrier contribute to handling and renal disposition of thiamine and structurally similar cations. Loss of these routes produces recognisable disease: thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia with diabetes and deafness, biotin- or thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease with encephalopathy, and microcephaly with lactic acidosis, reflecting how quickly oxidative carbohydrate metabolism fails when the vitamin does not reach its enzymes.

Vitamin B12 cannot be made by human cells, so the body relies on a relay of binding proteins and receptors to move dietary cobalamin from the gut lumen to the enzymes that need it. This transport route sets the supply for methionine synthase in the cytosol and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in mitochondria, and its failure produces megaloblastic anaemia, homocystinuria and demyelinating neurological disease. Intrinsic factor secreted by gastric parietal cells escorts the vitamin to the ileum, where the cubilin-amnionless receptor complex, with megalin, mediates uptake; haptocorrins and transcobalamin then carry it in plasma for delivery through the CD320 receptor. Inside the cell, lysosomal export by ABCD4 releases free cobalamin for cofactor processing. Inherited defects at individual steps cause selective B12 malabsorption and transcobalamin deficiency, linking this pathway to one-carbon metabolism and erythropoiesis.

Fatty acids are poorly soluble and cannot simply diffuse to where they are burned or stored, so cells use dedicated carriers, binding proteins and activating enzymes to move them across membranes and through the cytosol. This transport underlies energy supply to heart and muscle, lipid storage in adipocytes, intestinal absorption of dietary fat, and delivery of essential fatty acids to the brain. Uptake at the plasma membrane involves CD36 and the SLC27 transporter family, coupled to acyl-CoA synthetases that trap fatty acids intracellularly; cytosolic FABPs shuttle them to organelles, carnitine palmitoyltransferases with the carnitine/acylcarnitine carrier deliver acyl groups into mitochondria for beta-oxidation, and ABCD transporters import very-long-chain substrates into peroxisomes. PPAR transcription factors tune the whole programme. Phospholipases liberate arachidonate for eicosanoid synthesis. Loss of ABCD1 causes adrenoleukodystrophy, and defective carnitine shuttling produces hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy.

Long-chain fatty acids are poorly soluble and cannot simply diffuse where they are needed, so cells rely on dedicated carriers and channels to move them across membranes and through the cytosol. This transport determines whether a cell burns fat, stores it, or builds membranes from it, and it feeds substrate into mitochondrial beta-oxidation for energy production. Scavenger receptor CD36 and the SLC27 family capture fatty acids at the plasma membrane, cytoplasmic FABPs shuttle them while bound, and acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL1 trap them as thioesters so uptake remains unidirectional.
