Carnitine palmitoyltransferases with the carnitine/acylcarnitine carrier SLC25A20 deliver acyl groups into mitochondria, while peroxisomal ABCD transporters handle very long chains; loss of ABCD1 causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Phospholipases liberate fatty acids from lipid stores and membranes, and PPARG coordinates the transcriptional side of lipid handling in adipocytes.

Cells that burn or store fat must first get it across the plasma membrane, and this pathway covers the uptake of long-chain fatty acids from the extracellular space into the cytosol. It supplies substrate for beta-oxidation in muscle and heart, for triglyceride storage in adipocytes, and for hepatic lipid handling; too much flux through it contributes to lipid overload, insulin resistance and steatosis, while loss of the scavenger receptor CD36 impairs fatty acid uptake and cardiac fuel selection. Transport involves CD36 at the cell surface together with SLC27 family fatty acid transport proteins, and is made effectively unidirectional by acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL1 and ACSL5, which trap incoming fatty acids as CoA thioesters. Insulin signalling through IRS2 and AKT regulates transporter trafficking, linking nutrient uptake to hormonal control of metabolism.

Phospholipids are made in only a few membranes but needed everywhere, and this pathway covers the machinery that moves them between membrane leaflets, between organelles and between cells. It sets membrane asymmetry, supplies lipid to growing autophagosomes, and drives reverse cholesterol transport and plasma lipoprotein remodelling. Flippases of the P4-ATPase family, working with their CDC50 subunits, use ATP to pull aminophospholipids inward, while scramblases and the XKR and anoctamin proteins collapse asymmetry to expose phosphatidylserine as an eat-me signal on apoptotic cells and a procoagulant surface on platelets. ABC transporters export phospholipid to nascent HDL or into bile; soluble carriers including the PITP, ORP and PRELI/TRIAP families ferry single lipids across the cytosol and at membrane contact sites, and apolipoproteins with transfer proteins handle traffic in plasma. Failure causes cholestasis, ichthyosis, retinal degeneration, respiratory distress and disordered lipoprotein metabolism.

Aminophospholipid transport is the work of moving phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine across membranes, and it is what keeps these amino-headgroup lipids confined to the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane. That asymmetry is a signal in its own right: loss of it exposes phosphatidylserine on the cell surface, marking apoptotic cells for phagocytic clearance and providing the surface on which coagulation complexes assemble. The P4-ATPases here are ATP-driven inward flippases that require a CDC50 partner subunit, encoded by TMEM30A and TMEM30B, for folding and delivery to their target membranes. Their specificities and locations differ, and the consequences of failure are correspondingly varied — cholestatic liver disease from ATP8B1 loss, retinal and neurological degeneration from ATP8A2 loss, and anemia and B cell defects when ATP11C is absent. The pathway thus links lipid bookkeeping to membrane trafficking, bile secretion, and cell-surface recognition.

Cholesterol and related sterols are nearly insoluble in water, so cells and tissues depend on dedicated carriers, pumps and membrane contact sites to move them where they are needed; sterol transport covers that directed movement into, out of and within cells as well as between organs. It sustains membrane and lipid-raft composition, bile acid and steroid hormone synthesis, and reverse cholesterol transport from peripheral tissues to the liver, and its failure underlies atherosclerosis, familial hypercholesterolaemia and lysosomal storage disease. Lipoproteins built around apolipoproteins such as APOA1 and APOB are loaded by ABC transporters and unloaded through receptors including LDLR and SCARB1, with PCSK9 setting receptor abundance; NPC1 and NPC2 export sterol from lysosomes, while OSBP-related and STARD proteins and the GRAMD1 aster proteins ferry it between membranes. Liver X receptors, SREBF2 and a set of microRNAs including the MIR33 family tune the whole system to cellular sterol load.

Nucleobase-containing compound transport covers the directed movement of nucleobases, nucleosides, nucleotides and whole nucleic acids across membranes and through pores, and it links where these molecules are made to where they are used. Two broad arms dominate. One is nuclear export of RNA: nucleoporins of the pore complex, the Ran GTPase system with its importins and exportins, the TREX/THO and cap-binding complexes, and the NXF1-NXT1 carrier deliver mRNA, tRNA and small RNAs to the cytoplasm, with mRNA-binding proteins and surveillance factors coupling export to quality control and translation. The other is carrier-mediated solute movement: equilibrative and concentrative nucleoside transporters, mitochondrial carriers for ATP/ADP, NAD, folate and thiamine pyrophosphate, Golgi nucleotide-sugar transporters, and ABCC efflux pumps, plus channels such as pannexin and connexin-like proteins that release ATP for purinergic signalling. Defects cause nucleoporopathies, mitochondrial disease, and altered handling of nucleoside analogue drugs.

Coenzyme A metabolic process builds, recycles and degrades the universal acyl carrier that makes fatty acid oxidation, the citric acid cycle, ketone and cholesterol synthesis, and countless acyl-transfer reactions possible. Cells cannot import coenzyme A intact, so they must synthesise it from pantothenate through a committed five-step route: pantothenate kinases (PANK1-4) set the rate-limiting step, PPCS and PPCDC generate pantetheine phosphate, and the bifunctional COASY completes adenylylation and phosphorylation. Balance is maintained by degradation and salvage, with Nudix hydrolases cleaving CoA and acyl-CoA esters and vanin releasing pantothenate from pantetheine, while thioesterases free fatty acids from their CoA thioesters. Genes such as ACLY, HMGCR and ACAT1 mark the biosynthetic demands that draw on this pool. Loss of PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration, and COASY mutations produce a related brain iron accumulation disorder.

Coenzyme A is the universal carrier of acyl groups, and this is the set of reactions that make it, recycle it, and dispose of it. Nearly every route through central metabolism depends on the supply — fatty acid oxidation and synthesis, the citric acid cycle, ketone and cholesterol synthesis, and protein acetylation all run on acyl-CoA thioesters. Synthesis begins with pantothenate phosphorylation by the pantothenate kinases, continues through cysteine conjugation and decarboxylation by PPCS and PPCDC, and is completed by the bifunctional COASY. Countervailing activities set the pool size and composition: Nudix hydrolases degrade CoA and its esters, thioesterases such as ACOT7 and CROT release free fatty acids and regenerate free CoA, and vanin-1 recovers pantothenate from pantetheine. Loss of PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, marking neurons as particularly intolerant of a failing CoA supply.

Coenzyme A biosynthetic process builds the universal acyl carrier that virtually all of intermediary metabolism depends on, from fatty acid oxidation and synthesis to the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling, amino acid catabolism and protein acetylation. Cells cannot make its pantothenate precursor and must salvage vitamin B5, so the committed step is its phosphorylation by pantothenate kinases; PANK2 acts in mitochondria and its loss causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation. Downstream, cysteine is conjugated and decarboxylated by PPCS and PPCDC to form pantetheine phosphate, and the bifunctional COASY adds and phosphorylates adenosine to complete coenzyme A; mutations here also produce childhood neurodegeneration. Flux is tuned by feedback from acyl-CoA thioesters, with thioesterases such as ACOT7 and transferases like ACAT1 setting the balance between free and acylated pools, coupling cofactor supply to lipid and energy demand.

Coenzyme A is the universal acyl carrier of intermediary metabolism, and its biosynthetic process converts dietary pantothenate into the thiol-bearing cofactor on which fatty acid oxidation, the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling, cholesterol synthesis and protein acetylation all depend. Pantothenate kinases carry out the committed first step and set the flux through the route; the pathway then proceeds by cysteine ligation and decarboxylation to yield pantetheine phosphate, with a bifunctional adenylyltransferase/kinase enzyme completing the molecule. Because the kinases are feedback-inhibited by CoA and its acyl thioesters, the pathway is tuned to the cell's own acyl load, and thioesterase activity that liberates free CoA feeds back into the same pool. Loss of the neuronally important kinase PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and mutations in the downstream synthase produce a related neurodegenerative disorder.

Pantothenate, vitamin B5, is the obligatory precursor of coenzyme A, and its metabolism determines how much CoA a cell can make for fatty acid synthesis and oxidation, the citric acid cycle, and every acetylation and acylation reaction that depends on acyl-CoA thioesters. Handling of the vitamin begins with its phosphorylation by pantothenate kinases, the committed and feedback-regulated step of CoA biosynthesis, while pantetheinase enzymes recycle pantothenate from pantetheine and release cysteamine, linking the route to oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in gut and blood. Mitochondrial carriers import CoA and related nucleotides across the inner membrane so that the matrix pool matches the demands of oxidative metabolism, and a phosphopantetheinyl transferase transfers the CoA-derived prosthetic arm onto acyl carrier proteins. Loss of the neuronal pantothenate kinase causes brain iron accumulation with progressive dystonia.

Formate is the smallest one-carbon unit a cell handles, and its production and consumption tie histidine breakdown to the folate pool that supplies methyl and formyl groups for nucleotide synthesis. The catabolic arm degrades histidine through histidase, urocanase and imidazolonepropionase to formiminoglutamate, which a bifunctional transferase-cyclodeaminase converts by handing the one-carbon group to tetrahydrofolate; loss of these steps causes histidinaemia and urocanic aciduria. On the folate side, mitochondrial serine hydroxymethyltransferase and the dehydrogenase-cyclohydrolase activities generate formate that is exported to the cytosol, where it is recaptured onto tetrahydrofolate for purine and thymidylate biosynthesis. This mitochondrial-to-cytosolic formate shuttle is a major carbon source for proliferating cells, and the enzymes involved are upregulated in tumours and required for normal neural tube closure.

Cells hold their nucleotides in a shifting balance of mono-, di- and triphosphate forms, and this interconversion chemistry keeps each pool supplied without new synthesis from scratch. It is what allows adenylate, guanylate and pyrimidine nucleotides to be rephosphorylated for DNA and RNA synthesis, signalling and energy transfer, and it sets the adenylate energy charge that many metabolic enzymes read. Adenylate kinases equilibrate AMP, ADP and ATP in distinct compartments, with a mitochondrial intermembrane-space form coupling matrix ATP export to cytosolic demand; guanylate kinase and a cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinase perform the equivalent step for GMP and pyrimidine monophosphates, including phosphorylation of nucleoside-analogue drugs. A nudix hydrolase acting on NAD-related dinucleotides and a glutaredoxin contribute cofactor turnover and redox-linked regulation. Loss of individual kinases causes haemolytic anaemia and mitochondrial disease.</description>

Diadenosine polyphosphates such as Ap3A and Ap4A are made as by-products of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase chemistry and act as intracellular alarmones, accumulating under oxidative, heat and DNA-damage stress and modulating transcription, purinergic signalling at cell surfaces, and platelet and vascular responses. Their metabolism keeps these signals transient. Glycyl- and lysyl-tRNA synthetases generate the dinucleotides during amino acid activation, while hydrolases dispose of them: the histidine triad enzyme FHIT cleaves Ap3A to AMP plus ADP, and several Nudix family members degrade diadenosine and diphosphoinositol polyphosphates, linking this chemistry to inositol pyrophosphate turnover. The balance matters clinically because FHIT sits at a common fragile site and is lost early in lung, oesophageal and cervical carcinomas, where its tumour-suppressive activity depends on binding these dinucleotides rather than simply hydrolysing them, tying nucleotide signalling to genome stability and growth control.

Diadenosine polyphosphates such as ApppA and Ap4A accumulate as by-products of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase reactions and other adenylylating enzymes, and act as intracellular alarmones that influence transcription, nucleotide signalling and stress responses. Their catabolism keeps these messengers from building up, and the hydrolases involved do double duty on related phosphorylated substrates. FHIT is a bis(5'-adenosyl)-triphosphatase whose gene sits at a fragile chromosomal site and is frequently deleted early in lung, oesophageal and other epithelial cancers, making it one of the better-studied tumour suppressors linked to nucleotide turnover. The Nudix-motif hydrolases in this group cleave diadenosine polyphosphates and also inositol pyrophosphates, connecting this degradative route to inositol phosphate signalling and phosphate homeostasis. Loss of these activities alters nucleotide-derived signalling rather than bulk energy metabolism, and in the case of FHIT removes a brake on epithelial transformation.

Most of the ATP a human cell uses is made by chemiosmosis, and this is the machinery that does it: proton motive force-driven ATP synthesis couples respiratory electron transfer to phosphorylation of ADP. Complex I subunits, both nuclear-encoded and the mitochondrially encoded ND proteins, oxidise NADH and pump protons across the inner membrane, while the succinate dehydrogenase subunits feed electrons in from the TCA cycle. The resulting electrochemical gradient drives the F1Fo ATP synthase, whose F1 catalytic head, c-ring rotor and peripheral stalk are represented here, together with the inhibitory factor ATP5IF1 that limits wasteful ATP hydrolysis when the membrane depolarises, and assembly factors such as DNAJC30. Loss of these components causes mitochondrial disease -- Leigh syndrome and optic neuropathy from complex I defects, paraganglioma and pheochromocytoma from succinate dehydrogenase mutations -- and defines cellular dependence on oxidative rather than glycolytic metabolism.

Viral process covers the whole of the host-virus interface: the host molecules a virus exploits to enter, replicate and leave a cell, and the countermeasures the cell mounts against it. It matters because these proteins set susceptibility to infection and determine whether an exposure becomes disease, and they are the targets of antiviral drugs and vaccines. Entry receptors and priming proteases such as ACE2, CD4, CCR5, NPC1, TMPRSS2, furin and the cathepsins define tropism; endosomal trafficking, glycosylation and ER-associated machinery support virion maturation; translation initiation factors, RNA-binding proteins and nuclear import carriers are commandeered for viral gene expression; and the ESCRT complexes are hijacked for budding and membrane scission. Opposing this are intrinsic and interferon-induced restriction factors -- APOBEC3 deaminases, TRIM proteins, IFITMs, tetherin, the OAS-RNase L arm and autophagy components -- which degrade viral nucleic acid, trap particles and trigger innate signalling.

Viruses cannot replicate alone, so every stage of their life cycle borrows host machinery, and this collection of host-virus interactions covers the whole of it: attachment and entry, genome replication and translation, assembly, and budding. The host factors here are the ones that determine susceptibility and tropism, including entry receptors and proteases such as ACE2, CD4, CCR5, NPC1, TMPRSS2 and the cathepsins, glycosylation enzymes that build receptor and envelope sugars, translation initiation and RNA-binding proteins commandeered for viral protein synthesis, and the ESCRT machinery with VPS4 and TSG101 that pinches off enveloped particles. Opposing them are restriction and sensing factors — APOBEC3 deaminases, tetherin, IFITMs, MX1, OAS-RNase L, TRIM proteins and RIG-I-like sensors — so the same processes underlie both permissiveness and innate antiviral defence. The balance sets whether infection is cleared, becomes persistent, or drives pathology.

Vision begins when a photon is captured by an opsin pigment in a retinal photoreceptor, and these genes encode the human visual pigments that perform that first step. Rhodopsin serves the rods and supports dim-light and peripheral vision, while the long-, middle- and short-wavelength cone opsins tile the visible spectrum and make trichromatic colour discrimination possible. Each is a G protein-coupled receptor bound to 11-cis-retinal; absorption isomerises the chromophore, switching the receptor into a form that activates transducin and launches the phototransduction cascade that hyperpolarises the cell. The spectral tuning of the apoprotein sets which wavelengths each photoreceptor reports. Loss or rearrangement of the tandem long- and middle-wavelength genes on the X chromosome produces red-green colour blindness, and rhodopsin mutations are a common cause of retinitis pigmentosa, linking photon reception directly to inherited blindness.

Lipid catabolism is how cells and whole organisms liberate energy and signalling molecules from fats, membrane phospholipids and sphingolipids, and it underlies fasting tolerance, dietary fat absorption and lysosomal turnover of membrane debris. Dietary and circulating triglycerides are hydrolysed by pancreatic and lipoprotein lipases acting with apolipoproteins and receptors; stored triacylglycerol in adipocytes is mobilised by a lipase cascade under hormonal control, with insulin and catecholamine signalling, cyclic-AMP-dependent kinase, phosphodiesterase and perilipins setting the rate. Released fatty acids are activated, carried into mitochondria by the carnitine palmitoyltransferase system and degraded by beta-oxidation, while very-long-chain and branched substrates are handled in peroxisomes; ketone body metabolism and the nuclear receptors PPARA and PPARD tie output to systemic fuel use. Phospholipases and phosphatases generate diacylglycerol, lysophospholipids, arachidonate and endocannabinoids as second messengers. Failures cause lysosomal storage diseases, fatty acid oxidation disorders, peroxisomal disease, lipodystrophy and dyslipidaemia.

Detection of bacterium is the sensing step of antibacterial immunity: the recognition of conserved microbial structures and their conversion into intracellular signals that launch inflammation. It determines whether a bacterium is tolerated or attacked, and defects in its components predispose to invasive infection or, when signalling is unrestrained, to inflammatory disease such as Crohn's disease and inherited autoinflammatory syndromes. Recognition happens in two compartments. At the surface, Toll-like receptor heterodimers of TLR2 with TLR1 or TLR6 bind lipopeptides and lipoteichoic acid, while peptidoglycan recognition proteins and scavenger-type receptors bind and in some cases directly kill bacteria. In the cytosol, NOD1 and NOD2 detect peptidoglycan fragments, and NAIP paired with NLRC4 detects flagellin and type III secretion components to assemble an inflammasome. Antigen-presenting molecules, including CD1d for bacterial lipids, hand the detected material to T cells, linking innate sensing to adaptive responses.

Host cells recognise bacteria by sensing conserved microbial structures and converting that encounter into an immune signal, the first step in mounting defence against infection. Surface Toll-like receptors, acting as TLR1/2 and TLR2/6 heterodimers, detect bacterial lipopeptides and lipoteichoic acid and trigger inflammatory gene expression, while cytosolic NOD1 and NOD2 respond to peptidoglycan fragments that reach the cytoplasm of invaded cells. NAIP and NLRC4 sense bacterial flagellin and secretion-system components to assemble an inflammasome, driving caspase-1 activation, interleukin-1 release and pyroptotic death of infected macrophages. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins bind and in some cases directly kill bacteria or degrade their cell wall, and MHC class I, class II and CD1D molecules present bacterial peptides and lipids to T cells, linking this detection of bacterium to adaptive immunity. Loss-of-function variants, notably in NOD2, predispose to Crohn's disease and other inflammatory conditions.

Sensing hot and cold begins when a temperature stimulus is converted into an electrical and molecular signal in peripheral sensory neurons, the first step in thermal perception and in the protective withdrawal from damaging heat or cold. The genes here outline that transduction and the neurons that perform it: heat-activated TRPV1 and acid-sensing ASIC3 open at noxious stimuli, while voltage-gated sodium channels SCN9A and SCN11A set threshold and convert receptor currents into action potentials; loss-of-function mutations in these channels or in the transcriptional regulator PRDM12 cause congenital insensitivity to pain, and gain-of-function produces burning pain syndromes. Nerve growth factor signalling through NTRK1 and NGFR specifies and maintains the nociceptive lineage, alongside the developmental factor DRGX. Neuropeptides such as substance P relay the signal centrally, and modulators including adenosine and serotonin receptors tune sensitivity during inflammation and injury.

Cells enlarge irreversibly by accumulating protein, membrane and cytoplasm faster than they are degraded, and this growth programme sets organ and body size, drives cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy, and extends neuronal axons and dendrites. Nutrient and growth-factor inputs converge on mTOR complexes, whose components here include the catalytic kinase, RPTOR, RICTOR, MLST8 and the lysosomal LAMTOR scaffolds, with ribosomal S6 kinases, eIF4G initiation factors and SGK kinases as output arms; sestrins, STK11 and ULK kinases restrain growth when energy is scarce. Extracellular cues arrive through IGF1 with its binding proteins, TGF-beta/BMP, WNT, neuregulin and natriuretic peptide receptors, while semaphorin, slit, netrin and ephrin guidance systems coordinate directed enlargement of neurites. Cell cycle inhibitors such as CDKN1A, RB1 and TP53 couple size increase to division, and Hippo components LATS2, NF2 and YAP1 link it to organ size control. Dysregulation underlies tumour growth, cardiac hypertrophy and overgrowth syndromes.

Vesicle organization covers how cells build, shape, load, dock and dismantle the membrane carriers that move cargo between compartments and to the cell surface. It underlies secretion, endocytic uptake and degradation, neurotransmitter release, pigment and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis, and the release of extracellular vesicles; its failure produces Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, neurodegeneration and defective immune granule secretion. The genes trace each step: COPII and TRAPP components budding carriers from the ER, clathrin adaptors and dynamins pinching vesicles from membranes, sorting nexins and Rab GTPases with their effectors specifying identity and destination, HOPS and syntaxin/VAMP SNARE pairs with synaptotagmin calcium sensors driving fusion, ESCRT subunits and the vacuolar ATPase generating and acidifying multivesicular bodies, and BLOC/HPS complexes routing cargo to melanosomes and secretory granules. Sperm acrosome formation is treated here as a specialised instance of the same vesicle-shaping machinery.

Membrane traffic depends on vesicles being built, loaded, docked and taken apart again, and vesicle organization covers that whole life cycle: budding from a donor membrane, acquisition of the right coat and cargo, tethering and fusion, and the inward budding that creates multivesicular bodies. It underlies secretion, endosome and lysosome maturation, autophagy, neurotransmitter release and the biogenesis of specialized granules such as melanosomes and platelet dense bodies. COPII components and SEC24 paralogues select cargo at the ER, adaptor complexes and sorting nexins sort at the Golgi and endosomes, dynamins pinch off buds, TRAPP and HOPS complexes tether, syntaxins with VAMPs and synaptotagmins drive calcium-triggered fusion, and ESCRT subunits with VPS4 deform membranes into intralumenal vesicles. Vacuolar ATPase subunits acidify the resulting compartments. Failure produces Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes, lysosomal storage disease, and neurodegeneration linked to LRRK2, alpha-synuclein and C9orf72.

Carbohydrate biosynthesis covers the routes by which cells build sugars and sugar polymers rather than burn them: gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol and amino acids, glycogen synthesis for storage, and the transfer of sugars onto glycoproteins, glycolipids and glycosaminoglycans. Together these determine whether blood glucose is maintained during fasting, how muscle and liver bank fuel, and what carbohydrate structures decorate the cell surface. The gluconeogenic arm runs through pyruvate carboxylase, PCK1, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase with glucose export via SLC37A4, while glycogenin, glycogen synthase and branching enzyme build glycogen under the control of glycogen synthase kinase-3, protein phosphatase-1 targeting subunits and AMP-kinase subunits. Insulin, glucagon, leptin and glucocorticoid signalling, with transcriptional regulators such as FOXO1, CREB-coactivator CRTC2, PPARGC1A and circadian factors, set the direction. Glycosyltransferases and sulfotransferases handle glycan assembly. Defects cause glycogen storage diseases, Lafora disease, hypoglycaemia and diabetic dysregulation.

Carbohydrate catabolism is how cells extract energy and biosynthetic precursors from sugars, and it underpins everything from red cell ATP supply to muscle contraction during exercise and hepatic glucose output between meals. The core route is glycolysis, represented here in full from the hexokinases through phosphofructokinases, aldolases, the enolases and pyruvate kinase to lactate dehydrogenase, flanked by glycogen mobilisation via the phosphorylases and their phosphorylase kinase subunits, lysosomal acid maltase and glycogen-directed autophagy, and by entry routes for galactose, fructose, mannose and dietary disaccharides digested by sucrase-isomaltase, lactase and maltase-glucoamylase. Flux is set by insulin and its receptor, AMP-activated protein kinase, mTOR complex components, HIF1A under hypoxia, and p53 acting through TIGAR. Inherited defects in these steps produce the glycogen storage diseases, galactosaemia, fructose intolerance and haemolytic anaemia, while rewiring toward lactate is characteristic of tumour metabolism.

organic acid biosynthetic process gathers the reactions by which cells build carboxylic acids — fatty acids, eicosanoids, bile acids, amino acids and their keto-acid relatives — the small molecules that serve as membrane building blocks, fuels, signalling mediators and nitrogen carriers. Its breadth explains why defects here surface as such varied disease: urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1 prevent ammonia toxicity, PAH and CBS failures cause phenylketonuria and homocystinuria, and peroxisomal ACOX1 and ABCD1 lesions produce leukodystrophy. Fatty acid synthesis through ACACA, FASN, SCD and the ELOVL/FADS elongation and desaturation series is coordinated with lipolysis and beta-oxidation by AMPK subunits, SREBP regulators and nuclear receptors including LXR and FXR, while cytochrome P450s and the prostaglandin and leukotriene synthases convert cholesterol and arachidonate into bile acids and inflammatory lipid mediators. Together these routes tie carbon, nitrogen and one-carbon folate metabolism to nutrient sensing and immune signalling.

Organic acid biosynthesis gathers the routes by which cells build carboxylic acids and related acidic metabolites: fatty acids and their very-long-chain and desaturated derivatives, bile acids, eicosanoids, amino acids, and the intermediates of urea and one-carbon metabolism. Together these supply membrane lipids, fuel for oxidation, nitrogen disposal, dietary lipid absorption, and signalling molecules, so defects surface as urea cycle crises, phenylketonuria, hyperoxaluria, peroxisomal disease, or dyslipidaemia. Mechanistically it spans cytosolic de novo synthesis by acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, ER elongation and desaturation steps, peroxisomal beta-oxidation and bile acid conjugation, cytochrome P450 oxidations that initiate bile acid formation from cholesterol, and prostaglandin and leukotriene generation from arachidonate released by phospholipases. Regulation runs through nutrient and lipid sensors including AMP-activated protein kinase subunits, SREBP-pathway proteins, and nuclear receptors such as the bile acid and oxysterol receptors, linking output to nutritional and circadian state.

Breakdown of organic acids brings amino acid carbon skeletons, fatty acids and keto acids into pathways that feed the TCA cycle, gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis, and it is what allows tissues to draw energy and nitrogen from protein and lipid stores during fasting. The genes span branched-chain amino acid transamination and the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, mitochondrial and peroxisomal beta-oxidation with their acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and trifunctional enzymes, carnitine shuttling through CPT1 and CPT2, tryptophan degradation along the kynurenine route, and the tyrosine and phenylalanine pathway through PAH, HPD, HGD and FAH. Peroxisome biogenesis factors and ABC transporters deliver very-long-chain and branched substrates to their oxidizing compartment, while PPAR transcription factors and insulin-responsive signalling set flux according to nutritional state. Inherited defects at almost any step produce organic acidurias, hyperammonaemia, hypoketotic hypoglycaemia or neurological decompensation during catabolic stress.

Wnt signaling pathway is the cell-cell communication system that patterns the embryo and sustains stem cell compartments in adult tissues such as the intestinal crypt, bone and hair follicle. Secreted Wnt ligands, lipid-modified by PORCN and exported via WLS, engage Frizzled receptors with LRP5/6 or alternative co-receptors including ROR1/2, RYK and PTK7. In the canonical branch this inactivates the AXIN-APC-GSK3-CK1 destruction complex so that beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF, displacing TLE corepressors to drive MYC, CCND1 and AXIN2. Non-canonical branches instead direct planar cell polarity and convergent extension through Dishevelled, VANGL, PRICKLE, CELSR and small GTPases. Tuning comes from DKK, SFRP, WIF1, NOTUM, and the RNF43/ZNRF3-RSPO-LGR module that sets receptor abundance. Loss of restraint, as in APC mutation, causes colorectal cancer, while insufficient signalling underlies bone density and limb patterning defects.

Wnt signalling tells a cell where it is, what to become, and whether to keep dividing, and it does so from embryonic patterning through to the maintenance of adult stem cells in gut, skin and bone. Secreted Wnt ligands, lipid-modified by porcupine and exported with the help of Wntless, engage Frizzled receptors together with LRP5/6 or alternative receptors such as ROR and RYK. In the canonical branch, receptor engagement disables the destruction complex built on APC, Axin, CK1 and GSK3, so beta-catenin escapes ubiquitin-mediated degradation, enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF and Pygopus/BCL9 to drive targets including MYC and cyclin D1, while Groucho/TLE repressors hold those promoters off in the unstimulated state. Non-canonical arms acting through Dishevelled, Vangl, Prickle and Rho-family GTPases orient cells during planar polarity and convergent extension. Secreted antagonists (DKKs, SFRPs, sclerostin, NOTUM) and the RSPO-LGR-RNF43/ZNRF3 module set signal strength; loss of this control underlies colorectal and other cancers, skeletal disease and developmental malformation.

Vision begins when a photon isomerizes the retinal chromophore bound to an opsin, and this light-activated G protein-coupled receptor cascade is how that single-photon event becomes a change in neurotransmitter release at the photoreceptor synapse. Rhodopsin couples to the rod transducin alpha subunit GNAT1, which lowers cyclic GMP and closes the cation channels that keep the outer segment depolarized; guanylate cyclases GUCY2D and GUCY2F resynthesize cyclic GMP to restore the dark current, while rhodopsin kinase GRK1 phosphorylates activated opsin and arrestin (SAG) caps it so the cell can recover and adapt. Chaperone and modification enzymes such as AIPL1 and the N-myristoyltransferases support folding and membrane targeting of the phototransduction machinery. Different Galpha classes serve cone and non-image-forming opsins. Loss of these components causes stationary night blindness, Leber congenital amaurosis and retinal degeneration.

Type I hypersensitivity is the immediate allergic reaction: within minutes of re-exposure, antigen cross-links IgE already bound to mast cells and basophils, and the cells degranulate, releasing histamine and other preformed and newly made mediators. This is the biology of hay fever, allergic asthma, urticaria, food allergy and anaphylaxis, where vasodilation, bronchoconstriction and oedema can become life-threatening. Sensitization requires IgE heavy chain production, and the response depends on the high-affinity IgE receptor, whose alpha chain binds the antibody while the associated gamma subunit carries the signalling motifs that recruit kinases; BTK then propagates the tyrosine kinase cascade toward calcium mobilization and granule exocytosis. An inhibitory Fc receptor sets the threshold, so the outcome reflects a balance between activating and restraining receptor input rather than antigen exposure alone.

Everything that happens to a messenger RNA between transcription and its destruction is covered here: capping, splicing, 3' end cleavage and polyadenylation, export, methylation and editing, translational control, and decay. This mRNA metabolism sets how much protein each gene actually makes and which protein isoform is produced, so it shapes cell identity as much as transcription does. The spliceosomal snRNPs and SR and hnRNP proteins choose exons; cleavage and polyadenylation factors define transcript ends; m6A writers such as METTL3-METTL14 with WTAP and YTH readers mark transcripts for fate; deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex, decapping, exosome and XRN nucleases, microRNA-Argonaute silencing, and UPF1-dependent nonsense-mediated decay remove them. Mutations in splicing factors underlie retinitis pigmentosa, myelodysplasia and neurodegeneration.

Ribosomal RNA is the catalytic and structural core of the ribosome, and this pathway covers its entire life cycle: transcription, chemical modification, processing of precursors into mature species, and turnover. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and growth, the nucleolar machinery here is tightly coupled to growth signalling through MYC and mTOR, and its disruption triggers a p53-dependent nucleolar stress response. RNA polymerase I subunits and its initiation factors synthesize the 47S precursor, which is then cleaved by endo- and exonucleases including the exosome complex and XRN2, methylated and pseudouridylated by snoRNP-guided enzymes such as fibrillarin and dyskerin, and folded by numerous DEAD-box helicases and assembly factors. Mitochondrial rRNA modification enzymes are included as well. Mutations in these components underlie ribosomopathies -- Diamond-Blackfan anemia, Treacher Collins syndrome, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome and dyskeratosis congenita.

Spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs must be transcribed, 3'-end processed, chemically modified and quality-controlled before they can be assembled into snRNPs, and snRNA metabolism covers that whole life cycle. Without it pre-mRNA splicing fails, and mutations in several components cause poikiloderma with neutropenia, dyskeratosis congenita and neurodevelopmental disease. A dedicated promoter-recognition complex built on SNAPC subunits directs RNA polymerase II and III to snRNA genes; the multisubunit Integrator complex, whose INTS11-INTS9 pair supplies the endonuclease, cleaves nascent snRNA 3' ends and terminates transcription, with associated phosphatase activity restraining elongation. Trimming and tailing enzymes such as TOE1, USB1 and TUT1 mature the ends, methyltransferases including METTL16 and pseudouridine synthase components modify bases, and the nuclear exosome with its NEXT adaptors degrades misprocessed transcripts. LARP7 and MEPCE instead stabilise and cap 7SK, linking this biology to control of transcriptional elongation.

Small nucleolar RNAs guide the site-specific modification of ribosomal RNA and other transcripts, and this metabolic pathway covers how those guide RNAs are made, trimmed, tailed and degraded. Its output determines whether ribosomes are correctly pseudouridylated and 2'-O-methylated, so defects reverberate through translation capacity and ribosome biogenesis; mutations in the pseudouridine synthase DKC1 cause X-linked dyskeratosis congenita, with bone marrow failure and impaired telomerase RNA stability. Maturation involves 3' end trimming by the deadenylase-family nuclease PARN and by the multisubunit exosome, whose catalytic and ring components are represented here alongside the nuclear adaptor ZCCHC7 that recruits substrates for polyadenylation-stimulated decay. Fibrillarin supplies the methyltransferase activity of box C/D particles, LARP7 chaperones a related small RNA, and non-canonical polymerase and Nudix-family activities add or remove terminal nucleotides and caps, setting guide RNA abundance.

Ribosomal RNA is the most abundant RNA in the cell, and its controlled destruction is how cells dispose of misassembled pre-ribosomal intermediates, discard excess or damaged ribosomes, and eliminate spacer fragments left over from rRNA processing. The core machinery here is the RNA exosome, whose barrel of EXOSC subunits channels substrates to the ribonucleases DIS3 and DIS3L for 3'-to-5' degradation, complemented by the 5'-to-3' exonuclease XRN1. Quality control of translating ribosomes feeds into the same outcome: PELO acts in the rescue of stalled and subunit-split ribosomes, marking defective particles for turnover. Several Schlafen proteins contribute endoribonucleolytic cleavage activity that can attack rRNA and tRNA, linking this catabolism to interferon-driven restriction of viral replication and to translational shutdown. Failure to clear aberrant rRNA leaves cells with defective ribosomes and imbalanced protein synthesis capacity.

Small nuclear RNAs are the catalytic core of the spliceosome, but they are made in excess and often as extended or misprocessed precursors, and snRNA catabolism is how the nucleus destroys the surplus and the defective. Removing these species keeps spliceosomal snRNP assembly accurate and prevents aberrant transcripts from accumulating in the nucleoplasm. The work is done by the nuclear RNA exosome together with its RNA helicase MTREX and the NEXT complex, in which RBM7 recognises unstable and poorly processed RNA and ZCCHC8 scaffolds the helicase to it; EXOSC10 provides the 3'-to-5' exoribonuclease activity that trims and degrades the substrate. ZCCHC7 links the same machinery to the nuclear poly(A) polymerase route, where oligoadenylation marks an RNA for decay. The same surveillance clears promoter-associated and other short-lived nuclear transcripts, so snRNA turnover sits within general nuclear RNA quality control.

Transfer RNAs are not indefinitely stable: damaged, hypomodified or surplus tRNAs are recognised and destroyed, and this decay sets tRNA abundance and quality alongside synthesis. The pathway matters because mature tRNA pools determine translation capacity and codon-specific decoding, and because the fragments released are themselves signals — angiogenin cleaves tRNA anticodon loops during stress to generate tRNA halves that dampen protein synthesis, with an intracellular ribonuclease inhibitor restraining it until stress arrives. Nuclear surveillance routes aberrant transcripts to the exosome complex, whose subunits and the catalytic RNase EXOSC10 degrade them 3'-to-5', with a zinc-knuckle adaptor delivering substrates. Methyltransferases such as METTL1, NSUN2 and TRDMT1 install modifications whose absence makes tRNA vulnerable to this destruction, while processing enzymes including ELAC2, the RNase P subunit POP1 and the CCA-adding enzyme TRNT1 mark the boundary between maturation and turnover. Loss of these activities causes anaemia, neurodevelopmental disease and translational stress.

Chemical neurotransmission depends on a vesicle full of transmitter fusing with the presynaptic membrane at the moment an action potential arrives, and this is the machinery that accomplishes it. It sets the speed and precision of synaptic signalling, and its components are the targets of antiepileptic drugs and the sites of mutations causing epilepsy, movement disorders and intellectual disability. Voltage-gated calcium channels admit calcium into the active zone, where synaptotagmins act as the calcium sensors and complexins clamp a partially assembled fusion complex until release is triggered. Fusion itself is driven by SNAREs — syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMP2 — chaperoned by STXBP1 and primed by UNC13 proteins, with scaffolds such as piccolo, RIMs and liprins tethering vesicles near channels. NSF and its SNAP attachment proteins recycle the SNARE complex, while Rab3, synapsins and synaptophysin manage the vesicle pool for repeated rounds of release.

Before a nerve terminal can release transmitter, synaptic vesicles must be brought into physical contact with the presynaptic active zone; this docking step sets how many vesicles are release-ready and therefore how reliably and quickly a synapse responds to an action potential. Active zone scaffolds such as RIM proteins and their liprin partner position vesicles near calcium channels, while UNC13/Munc13 priming factors catalyse the transition from a loosely tethered vesicle to one whose SNARE machinery is partly assembled. Syntaxin-1A/1B and SNAP-25 supply the plasma membrane half of that fusion apparatus, complexin and syntaphilin act as clamps or brakes that restrain premature fusion, and a BLOC-1 subunit links the process to vesicle biogenesis and trafficking. Loss of these components collapses evoked release and causes severe developmental epileptic and movement disorders.

Before a synaptic vesicle can release neurotransmitter within a millisecond of calcium entry, it must be made fusion-competent, and priming is the step that does this. It sets the size of the readily releasable pool at the active zone and so determines how much transmitter a synapse can release and how it behaves during repeated firing; loss of the machinery abolishes evoked release and causes severe epileptic and neurodevelopmental encephalopathies. Munc13 proteins open syntaxin-1 from its closed complex with Munc18, allowing partial zippering of a SNARE complex with SNAP-25 and the vesicular partner, while RIM proteins tether Munc13 and calcium channels to the active zone scaffold. Accessory factors including SV2A, synaptophysin, CAPS and complexin-like regulators tune the primed state, and alpha-synuclein and synaptojanin link priming to vesicle cycling and recycling. This is the immediate prelude to calcium-triggered exocytosis.

Humans encounter monoterpenoids constantly as dietary and inhaled plant constituents — menthol, limonene, camphor, thymol, eucalyptol — and this pathway covers their handling and clearance. The C10 terpene skeleton is lipophilic and would otherwise accumulate in membranes, so hepatic cytochrome P450 monooxygenases hydroxylate and epoxidize these substrates, adding oxygen to create handles for subsequent glucuronidation or sulfation and excretion. The enzymes involved are the major drug-metabolizing P450s of the liver, including CYP2E1, CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and CYP1A2, which explains why monoterpenoid-rich foods, herbal preparations and essential oils can compete with prescription drugs for the same catalytic sites and shift their clearance. Common polymorphisms in several of these genes make the rate of monoterpenoid oxidation vary between individuals, and some oxidation products are more reactive than their parent compounds, linking this chemistry to both detoxification and bioactivation.

diterpenoid metabolic process is, in human cells, essentially retinoid metabolism: the uptake of dietary carotenoids and vitamin A, their conversion to retinol, retinaldehyde and retinoic acid, and the disposal of excess. It supplies the visual chromophore that makes photoreception possible and the nuclear receptor ligand that patterns embryos and maintains epithelial differentiation, so its failure causes night blindness, retinal degeneration and developmental malformation. Carotenoid cleavage enzymes and lipases release retinol from esters, binding proteins and transthyretin carry it through blood and cytosol, and reversible dehydrogenase and reductase steps interconvert retinol and retinaldehyde before aldehyde dehydrogenases commit it to retinoic acid. In the eye, an esterification and isomerohydrolase cycle regenerates 11-cis-retinal for opsin. Dedicated CYP26 enzymes, other cytochromes P450 and glucuronosyltransferases then inactivate retinoic acid, keeping its concentration within the narrow range that gene regulation requires.

Vitamin A and its derivatives are the diterpenoid compounds this pathway handles, and the chemistry runs from dietary carotenoid cleavage through storage, transport, oxidation to retinoic acid, and finally inactivation. It matters because retinoic acid is the ligand for nuclear receptors that pattern the embryo and maintain epithelia, while 11-cis-retinal is the chromophore of the visual pigments. Carotenoid oxygenases split provitamin A, lecithin retinol acyltransferase esterifies retinol for storage in lipid droplets, lipases and esterases mobilise it, and retinol dehydrogenases plus retinaldehyde dehydrogenases generate the acid; CYP26 enzymes and glucuronidation terminate the signal. Binding proteins and transthyretin carry the hydrophobic ligands between compartments, and receptor-mediated uptake delivers them to cells. The visual cycle isomerase RPE65 and photoreceptor dehydrogenases place retinal regeneration in this route, so failures produce blindness, and excess or deficiency produces developmental malformation.

Diterpenoid biosynthetic process in human cells is effectively the making of retinoic acid, the vitamin A-derived hormone that patterns the embryo and maintains epithelial differentiation, spermatogenesis and immune tolerance. Deficiency causes night blindness and epithelial keratinization, while excess is teratogenic, so flux through this route is tightly controlled. Dietary carotene is cleaved by BCO1 to retinal, retinol is bound and trafficked by RBP1, and reversible oxidation by RDH10 and DHRS9 feeds the irreversible step catalysed by the aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH1A2, ALDH1A3 and ALDH8A1, which fix the tissue-specific domains of retinoic acid production. CYP1A1 and AKR1C3 modulate the pool by catabolism and by competing carbonyl reduction. The product acts as a ligand for nuclear retinoic acid receptors, linking this metabolic pathway directly to developmental gene transcription.

In humans this diterpenoid biosynthetic route is essentially retinoid production: dietary carotenoids and retinol are converted into retinoic acid, the ligand for nuclear retinoic acid receptors that patterns the embryo and maintains epithelia, germ cells and immune tissue. BCO1 cleaves beta-carotene to retinal, cellular retinol-binding protein RBP1 delivers retinol to the oxidative steps, and dehydrogenases/reductases such as RDH10 and DHRS9 interconvert retinol and retinal; aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH1A2 and ALDH1A3 then perform the irreversible oxidation to retinoic acid, with ALDH8A1 favouring 9-cis substrate and CYP1A1 contributing oxidative turnover. Because the retinoic acid gradient acts as a morphogen, too little or too much disrupts limb, eye, heart and neural tube development, and altered flux is linked to vitamin A deficiency, night blindness and to differentiation therapy in leukaemia.

Terpenoid biosynthesis builds the isoprenoid backbone that the cell converts into sterols, prenyl anchors, dolichol-linked sugar donors and retinoids, so it sits upstream of membrane composition, protein lipidation and vitamin A signalling at once. The mevalonate arm runs from acetyl-CoA through HMG-CoA synthase and the rate-limiting reductase HMGCR, the target of statins, to mevalonate kinase, decarboxylation and isomerisation of isopentenyl units, then chain elongation by farnesyl and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthases; lanosterol synthase commits flux to cholesterol, while dolichol-phosphate mannose subunits feed glycosylation. A parallel arm cleaves carotenoids and oxidises retinol through retinol dehydrogenases and aldehyde dehydrogenases to retinoic acid, with RPE65 and RBP1 supporting the visual cycle. Loss of mevalonate kinase causes periodic fever and severe metabolic disease, and defects in the retinoid arm impair vision and developmental patterning.

Terpenoid catabolic process is the breakdown of isoprenoid-derived compounds, most consequentially retinoids and carotenoids, so that their signalling activity is terminated and their levels held within a narrow window. This matters because retinoic acid is a morphogen: too much or too little disrupts hindbrain patterning, limb and craniofacial development, germ cell entry into meiosis, and epithelial differentiation in the adult. The CYP26 family of cytochrome P450 enzymes performs the committed step, hydroxylating all-trans retinoic acid to 4-oxo and 4-hydroxy products destined for excretion, and their expression is itself retinoic acid-inducible, forming a negative feedback loop that shapes gradients across tissue. Carotenoid cleavage by BCO2 within mitochondria and aldo-keto reductase-mediated reduction of retinal and related carbonyls supply parallel routes, while a polyprenol phosphatase acts on longer isoprenoid chains. Loss of these clearance enzymes produces retinoid excess phenotypes.

Terpenoids, the isoprenoid-derived compounds that include carotenoids, retinoids and polyprenyl phosphates, are broken down by this catabolic route so that their signalling and cofactor activity is terminated at the right time and place. Its best-understood job is limiting retinoic acid: the CYP26 enzymes hydroxylate all-trans retinoic acid toward inactive metabolites, and the steep degradation gradients they create pattern the hindbrain, limb bud and germ cells, while their loss causes retinoid excess and severe developmental malformation. Carotenoid cleavage by BCO2 disposes of non-provitamin A xanthophylls in mitochondria, preventing their accumulation in tissue, and aldo-keto reductases reduce retinaldehyde and related carbonyls. PLPP6 dephosphorylates presqualene diphosphate, turning over an isoprenoid phosphate that restrains neutrophil signalling. Together these steps couple isoprenoid turnover to nuclear receptor signalling, vitamin A homeostasis and embryonic patterning.

Sterol metabolism covers everything cells do with cholesterol and its relatives: making it, taking it up, storing it, moving it between membranes, and disposing of it. It sets membrane fluidity and raft composition, supplies the precursor for bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D, and when it is mismanaged produces hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. The biosynthetic arm runs from acetyl-CoA through the mevalonate route, with HMG-CoA reductase and squalene epoxidase as rate-limiting steps and post-squalene enzymes such as DHCR7 and EBP finishing the ring system; defects here cause malformation syndromes. Supply is matched to demand by SREBP transcription factors with SCAP and INSIG sensing ER sterol levels, while LDLR, PCSK9 and NPC1/NPC2 govern uptake and lysosomal egress, and ABCA1, ABCG1 and apolipoproteins drive efflux onto HDL. Cytochrome P450 hydroxylases and sulfotransferases generate oxysterols and bile acids for excretion and nuclear receptor signalling.

Cholesterol and the other sterols that give membranes their fluidity and serve as precursors to bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D are built by this route, which converts acetyl-CoA through mevalonate and squalene to lanosterol and then, over roughly nineteen further steps, to cholesterol. Because sterol is both indispensable and toxic in excess, flux is held under tight feedback: sterol-sensing in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane controls whether SCAP escorts SREBF2 to the Golgi for proteolytic activation by site-1 and site-2 proteases, while INSIG proteins retain it and direct degradation of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme and the target of statins. AMP-activated kinase subunits add a further energy-status brake, and transporters and lipoproteins distribute the product. Loss of individual post-squalene enzymes such as DHCR7, EBP or NSDHL causes malformation syndromes, underscoring the demand for sterol during development.

Glycoside metabolic process covers the making and, mostly, the breaking of compounds in which a sugar is linked to another molecule through oxygen, sulfur or selenium. In humans this chemistry matters in two settings: turnover of glycolipids and glycoconjugates in the lysosome, and the handling of dietary and xenobiotic glycosides in liver and gut. Glycosidases here cleave specific terminal residues — glucocerebrosidase releases glucose from glucosylceramide, alpha-galactosidase A acts on globotriaosylceramide, and fucosidases and alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase trim their own linkages — and loss of these steps causes storage diseases such as Gaucher, Fabry, fucosidosis and Schindler disease. Alongside them, aldo-keto reductases and a sulfotransferase reduce and conjugate the aglycone products, tying glycoside breakdown to phase I and II detoxification, prostaglandin and steroid metabolism, and clearance of reactive carbonyls.

Glycoside metabolism covers the making and breaking of bonds between a sugar and an aglycone, and here the emphasis falls on hydrolysis of such linkages and on the reduction of sugar-derived carbonyls. Lysosomal glycosidases dominate: acid beta-glucosidase releases glucose from glucosylceramide, alpha-galactosidase A cleaves globotriaosylceramide, alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase and the two alpha-L-fucosidases trim terminal residues from glycolipids and glycoproteins. Loss of these activities causes lysosomal storage disease, with Gaucher and Fabry disease the clearest examples, and undigested substrate accumulating in macrophages, kidney and nerve. Alongside them, a family of aldo-keto reductases uses NADPH to reduce aldehydes and ketones, including glucose to sorbitol by aldose reductase, linking this chemistry to polyol formation in hyperglycaemia as well as to steroid and prostaglandin turnover and detoxification of reactive carbonyls.

Breakdown of glycosides — sugars joined through a glycosidic bond to a lipid, protein or small-molecule aglycone — depends on a set of glycosidases that cleave off the terminal sugar so both halves can be recycled. This chemistry keeps glycolipid and glycoprotein turnover moving in lysosomes and at the membrane, and its failure is the basis of several storage diseases: loss of acid beta-glucosidase causes Gaucher disease with glucosylceramide accumulation in macrophages, alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease with globotriaosylceramide deposition in vascular endothelium, and alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase deficiency causes Schindler disease. Alpha-L-fucosidases remove fucose from glycoconjugates, and fucosidase deficiency likewise produces progressive neurodegeneration. A non-lysosomal beta-glucosidase acting at the cytosolic face broadens the same reaction beyond the acidic compartment, linking glycoside catabolism to sphingolipid signalling and to dietary glucoside handling.

Small nuclear RNAs are made as longer primary transcripts that must be trimmed, capped, modified and stabilised before they can work, and snRNA processing is the set of steps that produces the mature forms. Without it the spliceosomal U snRNAs cannot be assembled, so pre-mRNA splicing fails across the transcriptome. The Integrator complex, built around a cleavage module in which INTS11 is the endonuclease and INTS9 and INTS4 complete the catalytic core, attenuates RNA polymerase II near snRNA genes and generates the 3' end; the nuclear RNA exosome and the deadenylase-like TOE1 trim and quality-control the products, while USB1 acts on U6. Methyltransferases and a pseudouridine synthase complex containing DKC1, NHP2 and NOP10 add modifications, and LARP7 with MEPCE caps and stabilises 7SK, the noncoding RNA that restrains transcription elongation. Defects underlie splicing-related neurodevelopmental disease and poikiloderma with neutropenia.

Recycling of synaptic vesicles at the nerve terminal begins with coating: adaptor complexes gather at the presynaptic endocytic zone, recognise the membrane proteins left behind after exocytosis, and build a coated pit around them before the bud pinches off. Without this cargo-selective step, neurotransmitter transporters and vesicle SNAREs are not retrieved efficiently and terminals cannot sustain repeated release. Here the work is done by the heterotetrameric AP-3 adaptor, whose beta, delta, mu and sigma subunits assemble on membranes downstream of ARF activation; the neuron-enriched beta subunit gives the complex a specialised role in generating synaptic vesicles from endosomal intermediates. The same adaptor family sorts cargo to lysosomes and lysosome-related organelles, and loss of its subunits causes pigmentation and platelet defects alongside neurological phenotypes, linking presynaptic vesicle biogenesis to general endosomal protein sorting.

A newly budded synaptic vesicle cannot release transmitter until it has been acidified and loaded, and synaptic vesicle maturation covers those finishing steps that turn an initiated vesicle into a release-competent one. Neurotransmission depends on it: without a proton gradient across the vesicle membrane there is no driving force for transmitter uptake, and quantal release fails. The bulk of the machinery here is the vacuolar H+-ATPase, whose V1 and V0 sectors pump protons into the vesicle lumen, with a chloride channel providing the counter-ion flux that lets the gradient build. A vesicular glutamate transporter then exchanges lumenal protons for glutamate, while Rab3A, synaptophysin, SNAPIN and the Munc18 protein STXBP1 govern trafficking, priming and docking. Palmitoyl transferases anchor vesicle proteins to membranes, and PICALM contributes to the clathrin-dependent budding that generates new vesicles for this cycle.

vesicle-mediated transport is the cell's internal courier system: cargo is packaged into membrane-bounded vesicles, budded from a donor compartment, moved along cytoskeletal tracks, and fused with a target membrane. Nearly every aspect of cell physiology depends on it — secretion of hormones, antibodies and neurotransmitters, uptake of nutrients and receptors by endocytosis, delivery of lysosomal enzymes, recycling of plasma membrane transporters, and antigen presentation. The genes span the whole itinerary: COPII and COPI coats and TRAPP/Golgi tethers for early secretory traffic, clathrin with AP adaptors and dynamins for budding and scission, Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs specifying compartment identity, SNAREs, synaptotagmins and NSF driving fusion, and retromer, WASH, ESCRT and HOPS complexes sorting cargo toward recycling or degradation. Loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration, immune deficiency, pigmentation and lysosomal storage disorders, reflecting how specialised secretory and phagocytic cells are.

Membrane traffic moves proteins and lipids between compartments inside sealed vesicles, and vesicle-mediated transport covers the whole itinerary: cargo selection, budding with a coat, movement along cytoskeletal tracks, then tethering and fusion with the target membrane. This is how secreted proteins leave the cell, how receptors are internalised and either recycled or sent to lysosomes for degradation, and how neurons release neurotransmitter and phagocytes engulf and digest microbes. The machinery here spans COPI, COPII, clathrin and adaptor complexes, Rab GTPases with their activating and inactivating regulators, SNAREs and their SM-protein and NSF partners, ESCRT subunits for multivesicular body formation, retromer and WASH for endosomal recycling, tethering assemblies such as TRAPP, HOPS, COG and the exocyst, plus motors and lipid kinases that set compartment identity. Failures produce lysosomal storage and pigmentation disorders, immunodeficiencies, neurodegeneration and defective lipoprotein and hormone secretion.

Endosomal transport is the sorting system that decides the fate of everything a cell internalises: receptors and transporters are either recycled to the plasma membrane, returned to the Golgi, or committed to lysosomal degradation. It sets how long growth factor and nutrient receptors signal, maintains surface levels of channels and adhesion molecules, and underlies antigen handling, cholesterol uptake and synaptic receptor turnover; its failure causes neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disease. Rab GTPases with their exchange factors and GAPs mark successive endosomal compartments, phosphoinositide kinases and phosphatases define membrane identity, and tethering complexes with SNAREs execute fusion. Retromer and the related retriever and commander assemblies, working with sorting nexins and the WASH actin nucleation machinery, retrieve cargo from degradation, while ubiquitin-directed ESCRT components bud cargo into intraluminal vesicles of multivesicular bodies. Motor adaptors move these carriers along microtubules to position them within the cell.

Growing axons do not navigate continuously; they pause at defined decision points, read local guidance molecules, and commit to one path. Axon choice point recognition is that reading step, and it determines whether tracts cross the midline, turn, or stop, thereby setting the wiring plan of the nervous system. The Slit receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 make midline crossing unattractive once a commissural axon has traversed it, while ROBO3 transiently suppresses this repulsion to permit crossing in the first place; loss of ROBO3 in humans causes horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis from uncrossed hindbrain tracts. Ephrin-B3 supplies a complementary repulsive cue at the midline, GAP43 links guidance signals to growth cone cytoskeletal remodelling, and FOXG1 shapes the forebrain territory in which these decisions are made. Failures here produce commissural agenesis and miswired circuits rather than loss of neurons.

Commissural axons in the developing central nervous system must decide whether to cross the midline, and this recognition event at the midline choice point is where the growth cone reads that decision. Getting it right builds the commissures that link the two halves of the brain and spinal cord; getting it wrong produces mirror movements, horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, and failures of callosal and corticospinal tract formation. Roundabout receptors on the growth cone detect Slit repellents emanating from midline glia, with ROBO1 and ROBO2 enforcing expulsion after crossing while ROBO3 modifies this responsiveness so that pre-crossing axons can approach and traverse the floor plate. Amyloid precursor protein contributes to growth cone guidance signalling, and the forebrain transcription factor FOXG1 sets the regional identity in which these projections are specified, tying axon guidance to earlier patterning of the telencephalon.

Chromosome ends look like broken DNA, and telomere capping is what stops the cell from treating them that way. Without it, telomeres are nucleolytically degraded, fused end-to-end, and reported to the DNA damage machinery, producing dicentric chromosomes, bridge-breakage cycles and the genome instability that drives cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Protection is built on the shelterin complex, where TERF1 and TERF2 bind duplex telomeric repeats and POT1 with ACD coats the single-stranded 3' overhang, suppressing ATM-dependent signalling and end joining. The CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 governs overhang processing and replication of the terminal repeats, DCLRE1B and RTEL1 resolve t-loops and secondary structures, and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease shapes the overhang rather than resecting it destructively. Capping thereby sits at the junction of telomere length homeostasis, DNA repair choice and replicative senescence.

Macroautophagy is the bulk degradative route by which a cell encloses cytoplasm, damaged organelles, protein aggregates and intracellular microbes in a double-membraned autophagosome and delivers the contents to lysosomes for breakdown and recycling. It sustains amino acid supply during starvation, clears mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum that have failed quality control, and protects neurons and other long-lived cells; its decline underlies neurodegeneration, myopathy, lysosomal storage disease and defective antibacterial defence, as seen with Crohn's-associated ATG16L1 and Parkinson's-associated PINK1, PRKN and LRRK2. Nutrient and energy status converge on mTORC1, AMPK and the ULK1 initiation complex, which activate the class III PI3K with BECN1 to nucleate a phagophore; two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems lipidate LC3 and GABARAP proteins onto the growing membrane, cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN select ubiquitinated substrates, and SNAREs, HOPS and ESCRT machinery complete fusion with acidified lysosomes.

Macroautophagy is the bulk degradative route in which a double-membrane autophagosome engulfs cytoplasm, damaged organelles or protein aggregates and delivers them to the lysosome for breakdown and recycling. It sustains cells through nutrient starvation, clears mitochondria and other cargo that would otherwise become toxic, and its decline underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and impaired control of intracellular bacteria. Nutrient and stress signals converge on mTORC1 and AMPK to release the ULK1 kinase complex, which with Beclin-1-associated PI3KC3 generates phosphoinositide at the growing phagophore; ATG7, ATG3 and the ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 machinery conjugate LC3 and GABARAP proteins to its membrane, while ATG9A and lipid transfer proteins supply membrane. Cargo receptors such as p62, NBR1, OPTN and NDP52, together with PINK1-Parkin ubiquitination, select substrates, and SNAREs, Rab7 and HOPS-linked tethering complete fusion with acidified lysosomes.

Microautophagy is the route by which lysosomes and late endosomes swallow small portions of cytosol directly, by pinching their own limiting membrane inward rather than building a separate autophagosome around the cargo. It gives cells a low-cost, continuous way to turn over soluble proteins, organelle fragments and damaged membrane components, contributing to amino acid supply during nutrient stress and to the quality control of the endolysosomal system itself. The genes span the core autophagy machinery — the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system, ATG7, the ATG4 proteases that process lipidated LC3, and the lipid-transferring ATG2 proteins with the scramblase ATG9 — together with sorting nexins and the ESCRT-associated ATPases VPS4A/VPS4B that drive membrane scission after invagination. Loss of this capacity leaves cells with impaired proteostasis and accumulating lysosomal damage.

Microautophagy delivers cytosolic material into the lumen of late endosomes or lysosomes without building a separate autophagosome: the limiting membrane of the degradative compartment invaginates directly, pinches off, and the cargo is degraded still wrapped in a single membrane derived from that invagination. It provides a route for turnover of proteins and portions of cytoplasm, and for remodelling the lysosomal membrane itself, complementing the larger-scale macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated uptake pathways in maintaining protein and organelle quality control. The machinery overlaps heavily with canonical autophagy: the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinases with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system with the E1-like enzyme ATG7, ATG4 proteases that process and delipidate ATG8-family proteins, lipid-transfer proteins ATG2A/ATG2B and the transmembrane lipid scramblase ATG9A. Membrane scission draws on the ESCRT-associated AAA-ATPases VPS4A and VPS4B, and sorting nexins contribute membrane recognition.

Cells raise the rate of macroautophagy when nutrients run short, when mitochondria are damaged, or when protein aggregates and intracellular bacteria must be cleared, and this pathway collects the inputs that turn that bulk degradation route up. The output is delivery of cytosolic cargo to the lysosome for breakdown and recycling, which supports survival during starvation, limits proteotoxic and oxidative stress, and underlies the quality control lost in neurodegeneration. Amino acid and energy sensing converge through TSC2, AMPK signalling and sestrins onto the ULK1 kinase and the BECN1-AMBRA1-UVRAG nucleation machinery; PINK1 and PRKN tag depolarised mitochondria, while OPTN, CALCOCO2, TBK1 and SQSTM1-like receptors select ubiquitinated cargo. C9orf72-SMCR8, WDR45 and WIPI1 act at phagophore formation, and mutations in several of these genes cause familial ALS, parkinsonism and other neurological disease.

Autophagy only completes degradation when a closed autophagosome is brought into contact with a lysosome or late endosome, and autophagosome membrane docking is the initial tethering step that holds the two membranes close enough for their surface proteins to engage before fusion. Without it, autophagosomes accumulate undegraded, cargo such as damaged mitochondria and aggregated protein persists, and cells lose the recycling route they depend on during starvation and proteotoxic stress. The docking machinery here is a SNARE-based apparatus: an autophagosomal SNARE and its partner assemble with an endolysosomal SNARE into a trans-complex, while calcium and calmodulin, a sarcoplasmic/endoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, and membrane-shaping regulators including ATG14 and VMP1 modulate when and where tethering occurs. This links autophagosome maturation to ER-derived membrane contact and calcium signalling, and its failure contributes to neurodegenerative and myopathic disease.

Macroautophagy engulfs cytoplasmic cargo in double-membraned autophagosomes for lysosomal degradation, and this collection concerns the inputs that set how much of it happens. Tuning matters because autophagic flux supplies amino acids during starvation, clears damaged mitochondria and aggregated proteins, and restrains inflammation; too little underlies neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease, while its regulators are frequently subverted in cancer. Nutrient and energy sensing through mTOR with its TSC1/TSC2-RHEB switch, AMPK and sestrins converges on the ULK1 kinase complex and the BECN1-PIK3C3-ATG14 lipid kinase, with AMBRA1, RUBCN and UVRAG shifting the balance. Selective mitophagy is regulated by PINK1, PRKN, USP30, BNIP3 and BNIP3L, while adaptors such as OPTN, CALCOCO2 and TBK1 link ubiquitinated cargo to the growing membrane. Vacuolar ATPase subunits, sorting nexins and retromer components govern acidification and the membrane traffic that completes degradation.

Macroautophagy must be held in check when nutrients are plentiful, and this is the braking side of that balance: the processes that stop or slow bulk sequestration of cytoplasm into autophagosomes. Restraint matters because unchecked self-digestion wastes biosynthetic capacity, destroys mitochondria a cell still needs, and in some settings drives cell death, while too much braking leaves damaged organelles and aggregates in place — a recurring theme in neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease. Growth-factor signalling through class I PI3K, AKT and mTOR is the dominant off switch, coupling amino acid and insulin status to suppression of autophagy initiation. Other members act closer to the machinery: Rubicon dampens the lipid kinase complex and autophagosome maturation, deubiquitinases such as USP30 oppose ubiquitin-driven mitophagy, and further regulators tune membrane delivery and cargo recognition. Several are mutated in parkinsonism and myopathy.

Many surface proteins, including CD59, alkaline phosphatases and folate receptors, reach the plasma membrane not as transmembrane proteins but tethered by a lipid glycan; attachment of the GPI anchor to protein is the step that installs that tether. In the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, a five-subunit transamidase complex recognises a C-terminal GPI signal sequence on the nascent chain, cleaves it, and joins the new C-terminus to the preassembled glycolipid in one concerted reaction. PIGK provides the catalytic cysteine protease-like subunit, while GPAA1, PIGS, PIGT and PIGU complete the complex; PGAP1 then remodels the anchor by removing an inositol-linked acyl chain, a prerequisite for efficient export from the ER. Loss of these activities strands substrates in the secretory pathway and causes inherited GPI deficiency syndromes with developmental delay, seizures and skeletal anomalies, and somatic failure of anchor synthesis underlies paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic bridges between neighbouring cells, channels that let ions, metabolites and second messengers under about a kilodalton pass while excluding proteins and nucleic acids. This electrical and metabolic coupling is what allows cardiac muscle to contract as a synchronised unit, the cochlea and epidermis to maintain ionic homeostasis, and Schwann cells to nourish myelinated axons; mutations in the connexins listed here cause deafness, palmoplantar keratoderma, X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and cardiac conduction disease. Connexin hexamers are trafficked to the plasma membrane, docked with partner hemichannels in the apposed cell, and stabilised at junctional plaques through adherens-junction and caveolar components such as CTNNA1 and CAV1. Transcriptional regulators including TBX5, IRX3 and HOPX pattern which connexin is expressed where, setting up the fast-conducting versus slow-conducting regions of the heart.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic bridges between neighbouring cells, channels that let ions, metabolites and second messengers under about a kilodalton pass freely while excluding proteins and nucleic acids. This coupling is what allows cardiac myocytes to propagate an action potential as a syncytium, Schwann cells to nourish the inner myelin layers, and cochlear support cells to recycle potassium; loss of it causes arrhythmia and conduction block, X-linked demyelinating neuropathy through connexin 32, and hereditary deafness and skin disease through connexin 26 and 30. Assembly requires connexin hexamers to be trafficked, docked with a partner hemichannel in the apposing membrane and stabilised at junctional plaques, a step that depends on adherens junction and caveolar components such as alpha-catenin and caveolin-1. Cardiac transcriptional regulators including TBX5 and IRX3 set which connexins a cell expresses, patterning conduction velocity across the heart, while inflammatory and renin-angiotensin signals remodel coupling.

Mucin-type O-linked glycosylation begins when a GalNAc residue is attached in alpha linkage to serine or threonine hydroxyls of secreted and membrane proteins, and continues as that core sugar is extended into branched O-glycans. This decoration gives mucins their gel-forming, water-binding character in the gut and airway, shields protein backbones from proteases, and builds the carbohydrate ligands that mediate leukocyte rolling and blood-group and tumour-associated antigen display. A large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases (GALNT1-18) chooses the acceptor sites, setting substrate specificity; branching enzymes such as GCNT1 and GCNT3 and beta1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases elaborate core structures, while sialyltransferases including ST3GAL1 and ST6GALNAC2 and sulfotransferase capping terminate the chains. Loss of individual transferases alters FGF23 processing and phosphate handling, lipoprotein metabolism, and mucosal barrier integrity, and aberrant truncated O-glycans are a hallmark of carcinoma cells.

phosphorylation is the transfer of phosphate onto proteins, sugars and lipids, the most widespread reversible modification cells use to switch enzymes on and off and to relay information from the cell surface to the nucleus. Nearly every regulated process depends on it: growth factor and cytokine responses, cell cycle progression, metabolic commitment of glucose, apoptosis and innate immune signalling. The genes here span the machinery that does this work — receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs and PDGFRs; cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases including SRC, SYK, BTK and the JAK family; serine/threonine cascades through RAF–MEK–ERK, AKT–mTOR, GSK3B and the CDKs and Aurora, PLK and NEK mitotic kinases — alongside sugar kinases such as hexokinases and phosphofructokinases, regulatory subunits and cyclins, scaffolds, and the phosphatases and inhibitors that reverse or restrain the reaction. Dysregulated kinase activity here drives much of oncogenesis and is the target of many drugs.

Attaching a phosphate group to a protein, sugar or lipid substrate is the cell's most widely used switch, and this collection spans essentially the whole enzymology of that reaction. Protein kinases dominate: receptor tyrosine kinases for growth factors and cytokines (EGFR, FGFRs, PDGFRs, KIT, INSR), the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinases and JAK family that relay them, and serine/threonine cascades running through RAF-MEK-ERK, PI3K-AKT-MTOR, the polo, aurora, NEK and cyclin-dependent kinases that time mitosis, and checkpoint kinases such as ATM and CHEK1/2. Alongside them sit metabolic phosphotransferases -- hexokinases, phosphofructokinase-2 family enzymes, galactokinase, nucleotide and sugar kinases -- that trap and commit substrates to glycolysis and other routes.
