Also present are the phosphatases, pseudokinase decoys and inhibitory subunits that reverse or restrain the reaction, since the biological information lies in the balance. Deregulated kinase activity underlies much of oncogenesis and is the target of a large share of modern drugs.

Dephosphorylation is the removal of phosphate groups from proteins, lipids and small molecules, the counterweight to kinase action that makes phosphorylation a reversible switch rather than a one-way mark. Without it signalling cannot be terminated or reset, and cells lose the timing that governs growth factor responses, cell cycle progression, immune activation and membrane traffic. The genes span the major phosphatase families: serine/threonine holoenzymes built on PP1, PP2A, calcineurin and PPM catalytic subunits with their regulatory partners; classical and receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN6 and CD45 that set thresholds in receptor signalling; dual-specificity enzymes that inactivate MAP kinases; and inositol- and phosphoinositide-directed phosphatases including PTEN, OCRL, myotubularins and synaptojanins that shape membrane lipid identity. Loss-of-function in individual members causes cancer predisposition, myopathies, neuropathies and autoimmunity, reflecting how broadly this chemistry is used.

Phosphate removal is the counterpart to kinase action, and this collection of dephosphorylation activities sets how long a phosphorylation signal lasts on proteins, lipids and small molecules. Serine/threonine phosphatase catalytic subunits and their regulatory partners (PP1, PP2A, calcineurin, PP5, PP6, the metal-dependent PPM family) reverse kinase marks on cytoskeletal, transcriptional and cell cycle substrates, while classical and receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN11, PTPN6, PTEN and CD45 tune growth factor and immune receptor signalling. Dual-specificity phosphatases inactivate MAP kinases, terminating ERK, JNK and p38 output. A large lipid phosphatase contingent — myotubularins, inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases, synaptojanins, OCRL and phospholipid phosphate phosphatases — remodels phosphoinositides and sphingolipid phosphates to control membrane identity and trafficking. Loss of these activities underlies tumour suppression failure, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy, myotubular myopathy, Lowe syndrome and Noonan syndrome, and unrestrained inflammatory signalling.

The endoplasmic reticulum is a single continuous membrane network, and that continuity has to be actively maintained by fusing tubules together wherever they meet. This homotypic membrane fusion builds and repairs the polygonal ER tubular network, allowing lumenal contents, calcium and newly made proteins to diffuse throughout the cell and permitting the ER to be remodelled during growth and after division. The atlastin GTPases ATL1, ATL2 and ATL3 drive the fusion step directly, tethering apposed tubule tips and merging their bilayers through GTP-dependent conformational change, while accessory factors including a SNARE-associated component and a deubiquitinating enzyme contribute to membrane joining and its regulation. Mutations in ATL1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, and ATL3 defects cause sensory neuropathy, linking ER shape to the maintenance of long axons.

Oocytes must halve their chromosome number in two successive divisions, and female meiotic chromosome segregation is the step that physically separates homologues and then sister chromatids into the egg and its polar bodies. Errors here are the dominant source of human aneuploidy, producing miscarriage and trisomic conceptions, and they rise sharply with maternal age. The genes involved span the tasks the division requires: a mismatch repair factor that also stabilises crossovers so homologues stay linked until anaphase, condensin subunits that compact and resolve chromosome arms, a meiosis-specific kinetochore protein that dictates mono-orientation of sister kinetochores in the first division, and mitotic kinases acting at centromeres and spindle poles. Together they couple recombination-derived physical connections to kinetochore geometry and spindle attachment, so that each division segregates the intended units.

Early nervous systems are built with an excess of axon branches, dendrites and synapses, and neuron remodeling is the developmentally scheduled retraction and elimination that trims this surplus into a functional circuit. Getting it right sets receptive field size, sensory map refinement and the balance of excitation a mature neuron receives; too little pruning leaves redundant connections, while excessive or mistimed pruning strips synapses and is implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders and in early synapse loss during neurodegeneration. Much of the work is done by tagging branches for removal and recruiting phagocytes: complement components such as C1QA and C3 opsonize weak synapses for microglial engulfment, scavenger receptors mediate uptake, and neuronal CX3CL1 signals to microglia. Repulsive and cytoskeletal cues, including ephrin receptor signalling and Rho-family GTPase regulators, drive the local collapse and retraction of the branches themselves.

Embryonic epithelia are the sheets from which the neural tube, kidney, limb ectoderm, gut and skin are built, and their morphogenesis is the process that folds, elongates and patterns those sheets into organ-shaped structures. Failure produces some of the commonest birth defects: neural tube closure defects, cleft palate, renal agenesis and limb malformation. The genes here span the signalling centres that instruct epithelia — Shh with its receptor Patched and the Sufu brake, BMPs opposed by Noggin and Gremlin, FGF8/FGF10 acting through FGFR2, and retinoic acid synthesis via ALDH1A2 and RDH10 — together with the planar cell polarity machinery (VANGL2, CELSR1, PRICKLE1, FZD3/FZD6, PTK7) that orients cells for convergent extension. Apicobasal polarity complexes, intraflagellar transport and ciliary proteins, actin regulators, and transcription factors such as GRHL2/GRHL3, PAX2 and TFAP2A translate these cues into coordinated sheet bending, fusion and branching.

Cells can hold onto one another without calcium, and the dominant example is the claudin family, which seals epithelial and endothelial sheets at the tight junction. This adhesion defines the paracellular barrier: claudin strands encircle each cell, joining neighbours and determining which ions and small solutes may pass between them, so that epithelia can sustain the gradients that transport depends on. Different family members build pores selective for cations or anions or make junctions essentially impermeable, which is why loss of the renal magnesium-handling claudins causes hypomagnesaemia with nephrocalcinosis, and why the blood-brain barrier and myelin junctions depend on their own members. Also represented is fractalkine, a membrane-anchored chemokine whose extended stalk lets endothelium capture leukocytes directly. Barrier formation, epithelial polarity, and regulated permeability all rest on this class of contact.

Tissues hold together because neighbouring cells grip one another through adhesion receptors whose binding depends on bound calcium ions. This calcium-dependent cell-cell adhesion is what gives epithelia their sheets, endothelium its barrier, and developing neurons their selective partner recognition; losing it underlies the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasive behaviour of carcinomas, where E-cadherin is a classic tumour suppressor. The bulk of the machinery here is the cadherin superfamily: classical cadherins such as E-, N-, VE- and P-cadherin forming homophilic junctions linked to the actin cytoskeleton, atypical and large cadherins including those required for stereocilia tip links and planar polarity, and clustered protocadherins that generate combinatorial neuronal identity codes. Selectins contribute the calcium-dependent lectin binding that tethers leukocytes to vessel walls. Supporting proteins govern junction assembly, trafficking and secretory-pathway calcium supply, linking adhesion to morphogenesis, barrier maintenance and synapse formation.

Dendrite development covers the whole life history of a neuron's receptive arbor, from the first outgrowth of a nascent branch to a stable, appropriately sized and oriented tree bearing spines. Because dendritic geometry sets how many inputs a neuron can receive and where, this programme determines cortical layering, circuit wiring and synaptic capacity; its disruption underlies intellectual disability, autism and the dendritic simplification seen in Rett syndrome and fragile X. Extracellular cues acting through Reelin receptors, ephrin receptors, semaphorins, netrin and Wnt signalling are converted by Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42, their regulators and WAVE-complex and actin effectors including CFL1 and drebrin into local cytoskeletal remodelling, while MAP2 and other microtubule-associated proteins build the shaft. Calcium- and activity-dependent kinases, MEF2 transcription factors, MECP2 and local mRNA-binding proteins such as FMR1 tune branching to experience.

B cells broaden the antibody repertoire after they leave the bone marrow by deliberately mutating and rearranging their own immunoglobulin genes, and this somatic diversification of immunoglobulins is what allows affinity maturation and class switching to isotypes suited to a given infection. The initiating enzyme AICDA deaminates cytosine in transcribed switch and variable regions; the resulting uracil is processed by UNG and mismatch repair factors such as MSH2/MSH6 and MLH1/PMS2, and the breaks are sealed by non-homologous end joining involving PRKDC, XRCC4, LIG4 and the 53BP1-shieldin axis, with translesion polymerases introducing point mutations. T cell help through CD40-CD40L and cytokines including IL-4, IL-10 and IL-21 receptor signalling, with BCL6 and BATF, sets the germinal centre context. Loss of these steps causes hyper-IgM syndromes and antibody deficiency, while misdirected breaks drive lymphoma translocations.

Cell migration is the guided, self-propelled movement of cells toward a destination, and it underlies gastrulation and organ formation, axon and neuron guidance, angiogenesis and lymphatic patterning, wound repair, leukocyte trafficking to inflamed tissue, and the invasion and metastasis of tumour cells. The genes here cover the whole chain from cue to movement: chemokines and their receptors, growth factors such as HGF, VEGF and PDGF with their kinases, and guidance ligand families including semaphorins with plexins, netrins, slits with Robo receptors, ephrins and cadherins. These converge on Rho-family GTPases, their GEFs and GAPs, PAK and ROCK kinases, and integrin-based adhesions containing talin-like FERMT proteins, paxillin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase, which couple to actin nucleation and myosin contractility. Matrix metalloproteinases clear a path, while transcription factors and microRNAs set migratory competence and epithelial-mesenchymal state.

Ribosomal RNA genes are transcribed by RNA polymerase I, and damping that output is how cells match ribosome production to growth conditions and nutrient supply. Restraining polymerase I transcription conserves a large share of the cell's biosynthetic budget, and its loss is associated with nucleolar hypertrophy and the elevated ribosome biogenesis typical of transformed cells. Much of the control is chromatin-based: a nucleolar remodelling complex built around BAZ2A and the ATPase SMARCA5 establishes silenced rDNA copies, macroH2A histone variants mark repressed chromatin, and acetyltransferase activity tunes the promoter state. Other components act on the polymerase machinery itself, with MAF1 serving as a growth-signal-responsive repressor and the nucleolar proteins DDX21 and NOP53 feeding back on rRNA synthesis. Together these inputs couple nucleolar activity to stress, growth signalling and p53-linked surveillance.

Membrane cargo does not diffuse to its destination; it is packaged, moved along cytoskeletal tracks and delivered to a specific compartment, and cytosolic transport covers that directed traffic of vesicles and organelles between endosomes, the Golgi and the cell surface. It determines whether receptors are recycled or degraded, whether lysosomes mature, and whether neurons can supply distant synapses, so its failure produces neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage disease. Clathrin and adaptor complexes select cargo, Rab GTPases with their TBC-family regulators and the GARP, retromer and WASH machinery mark and remodel compartments, SNAREs such as STX5, STX6 and VAMP3 execute fusion, and kinesins with dynactin provide the motive force. Several members are disease genes in their own right: LRRK2 and VPS35 in Parkinson disease, CLN3 and CLN5 in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and SORL1 in Alzheimer disease.

Protein processing covers the limited proteolytic cuts that convert inactive precursors into working proteins, a maturation step that many secreted and membrane proteins cannot bypass. It determines whether a hormone is bioactive, whether a clotting cascade fires, whether a receptor reaches the surface, and whether an imported mitochondrial protein is correctly trimmed; failures produce bleeding and thrombotic disease, hypertension, amyloid deposition and lysosomal storage phenotypes. The chemistry is carried by distinct protease families acting in defined compartments: signal peptidase and the proprotein convertases furin, PCSK1 and PCSK9 in the secretory route; ADAM and matrix metalloproteinases together with the presenilin- gamma-secretase complex performing ectodomain shedding and regulated intramembrane cleavage; trypsin-like serine proteases of the coagulation, complement and kallikrein cascades; caspases in inflammasome and apoptotic maturation; and mitochondrial processing peptidases and AAA proteases at the import site. Cleavage is thus a switch, irreversible and self-amplifying.

Many proteins are synthesised as inactive precursors and become functional only when a peptide bond is cut in the right place, and this maturation by limited proteolysis is what these genes carry out. It converts prohormones, growth factors, clotting factors and receptors into active molecules, and removes targeting sequences from newly made proteins. Signal peptidase and mitochondrial processing peptidases trim presequences after translocation; proprotein convertases such as FURIN and PCSK1/2 cleave at basic residues in the secretory pathway; and membrane-anchored serine proteases, ADAM sheddases and the gamma-secretase complex release ectodomains and intracellular fragments. The coagulation cascade, complement activation, angiotensin generation by ACE, Hedgehog ligand autoprocessing and caspase maturation during apoptosis all depend on it. Mutations in individual steps cause bleeding disorders, hormone deficiencies, iron overload and neurodegeneration, and several of these proteases are exploited by viruses for entry.

Some proteins mature by cleaving themselves rather than waiting for another enzyme, and protein autoprocessing covers this self-cleavage step that converts a precursor into its active or released form. It matters because the activity in question is held latent until the cell needs it: inflammatory caspases such as CASP1 and CASP4 autocleave on inflammasome assembly to drive interleukin maturation and pyroptosis, PCSK9 autoprocesses in the secretory pathway before it can direct LDL receptor degradation, and hedgehog ligands including SHH, IHH and DHH use an intramolecular reaction that splits the precursor and attaches cholesterol to the signalling domain. Other members are proteases and mitochondrial peptidases—HTRA2, OMA1, AFG3L2, CTSL, KLK6—that trim their own zymogen or propeptide, alongside factors such as MYRF, which self-cleaves to liberate a transcription factor for myelin gene expression. The theme is timed, self-limited activation of proteolysis, signalling and quality control.

RNA base conversion or substitution editing rewrites genetic information after transcription, changing individual nucleotides so that a transcript's coding potential, splicing, or base-pairing behaviour differs from the gene that encoded it. Two chemistries dominate: adenosine deaminases acting on RNA, including ADAR and ADARB1, convert adenosine to inosine in double-stranded regions, which is read as guanosine and recodes proteins such as glutamate receptor subunits while also marking endogenous duplex RNA as self so that it does not trigger interferon responses. Cytidine deaminases of the APOBEC family, with cofactors A1CF and RBM47, deaminate cytidine to uridine, the classic example creating a stop codon in apolipoprotein B mRNA to produce the intestinal short form. Related deaminases act on tRNA wobble bases or, in the case of AICDA, on immunoglobulin DNA during antibody diversification. Loss of editing causes autoinflammatory disease, and misdirected deaminase activity is a source of mutations in cancer.

Cytidine to uridine editing rewrites RNA after transcription by deaminating a cytosine base, so that a transcript encodes something its gene does not. The best-understood example is intestinal editing of apolipoprotein B mRNA, where APOBEC1 acting with its cofactors A1CF or RBM47 creates a stop codon and yields the shorter ApoB-48 protein required for dietary lipid absorption and chylomicron assembly. The related APOBEC3 deaminases target single-stranded nucleic acid in innate defence, restricting retroviruses and retroelements by introducing lethal C-to-U changes in viral cDNA, while AICDA initiates antibody diversification through deamination at immunoglobulin loci. Because the chemistry is mutagenic, these enzymes are tightly compartmentalised and regulated; their misdirection onto genomic DNA leaves characteristic mutation signatures that contribute to tumour evolution in breast and other cancers.

Messenger RNAs are not simply transcribed copies of DNA; they are chemically edited and decorated after synthesis, and mRNA modification covers the enzymes that rewrite or tag individual nucleotides. The consequences are functional: adenosine-to-inosine editing by ADAR enzymes recodes transcripts and marks endogenous double-stranded RNA as self, preventing interferon-driven autoinflammation, while APOBEC1 with its cofactor A1CF deaminates cytidine in apolipoprotein B mRNA to create a truncated protein needed for intestinal lipoprotein assembly. The METTL3-METTL14-WTAP complex installs N6-methyladenosine, the mark that sets transcript stability, splicing and translation rates and shapes stem cell and germline programmes. Pseudouridine synthases and box C/D and H/ACA components add isomerized uridines and 2'-O-methyl groups, altering base pairing and decoding. Together these reversible marks form an epitranscriptomic layer of gene regulation, and their loss causes developmental, haematopoietic and autoimmune disease.

Peroxisomes multiply not only by budding from the ER but by dividing existing organelles, and peroxisome fission is the step that splits one mature compartment into two. It sets peroxisome number and size in response to metabolic demand, so that cells such as hepatocytes expanding their fatty acid oxidation capacity can scale up their complement of organelles; loss of the machinery produces abnormally few, elongated peroxisomes and impaired handling of very long chain fatty acids. The organelle is first elongated and constricted by the PEX11 family of membrane-shaping proteins, then severed by the dynamin-related GTPase DNM1L recruited through the tail-anchored receptors FIS1 and MFF, components shared with mitochondrial division and thus coordinating the two organelles. PEX19 supplies the chaperone route that inserts these tail-anchored proteins into the peroxisomal membrane, while resident enzymes such as ACOX1 mark the lipid-oxidising cargo being partitioned.

protein import into peroxisome matrix, receptor recycling is the recovery step of peroxisomal protein import: after the shuttling receptor PEX5 delivers PTS1-bearing cargo across the membrane, it must be released and returned to the cytosol so that further rounds of import can occur. Without this export step receptors become trapped in the membrane, matrix enzymes such as those for beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids and ether lipid synthesis fail to reach the organelle, and empty peroxisomal ghosts accumulate — the basis of Zellweger spectrum disorders. Mechanistically the RING-finger complex of PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 ubiquitinates PEX5, and the AAA-ATPases PEX1 and PEX6, anchored by PEX26, extract it using ATP hydrolysis; deubiquitination by USP9X rescues the receptor from degradation. The logic parallels ubiquitin-driven retrotranslocation at the ER, coupling cofactor-free protein translocation to an ATP-powered recycling cycle.

Peroxisomal matrix enzymes are made in the cytosol and delivered by shuttling receptors, so the import cycle can only continue if those receptors are released from cargo and returned for reuse. Receptor recycling is that recovery step: after PEX5 deposits its cargo at the membrane it is ubiquitinated by the RING-finger ligases PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12, then extracted back into the cytosol by the AAA-ATPases PEX1 and PEX6, which are tethered to the membrane by PEX26; the deubiquitinase USP9X reverses the tag so the receptor can be used again rather than degraded. Loss of these components blocks matrix protein import altogether and produces the Zellweger spectrum disorders, with failed ether lipid synthesis and very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation, severe neurological and hepatic disease. The logic parallels ATPase-driven retrotranslocation used elsewhere in protein quality control.

Rac protein signal transduction is the relay in which Rho-family GTPases of the Rac subfamily, switched on by nucleotide exchange factors and switched off by GTPase-activating proteins, convert receptor and adhesion cues into remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton. It is how cells build lamellipodia and ruffles, and so underlies migration, phagocytosis, neurite and dendritic spine growth, neuromuscular junction assembly and endothelial tube formation. Activation typically follows engagement of growth factor, chemokine or Wnt receptors, with adaptors such as GRB2 and CRK and exchange factors including TIAM1 and DOCK–ELMO complexes loading GTP onto RAC1 or RAC3; deactivation is imposed by ARHGAP-family proteins and by neurofibromin. Active Rac then drives the WAVE regulatory complex – WASF1/2 with CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2 and BRK1 – to nucleate branched actin through Arp2/3, while PI3K arms feed back into the cycle. Dysregulation contributes to tumour invasion and to neurodevelopmental disorders.

Sumoylation attaches the small ubiquitin-like modifier SUMO to lysine residues of target proteins, a reversible tag that alters where a protein goes, what it binds, and whether it is stable rather than simply marking it for destruction. It shapes transcriptional repression, nuclear body formation, chromosome segregation and the repair of replication-associated DNA damage. The pathway runs through a single E1 heterodimer (SAE1-UBA2) and one E2 conjugating enzyme, UBE2I, with substrate choice imposed by E3 ligases including the PIAS proteins, RANBP2 at the nuclear pore, ZNF451 and the NSMCE2 subunit of the SMC5/6 complex. SENP isopeptidases strip the modification, making the mark dynamic. Sumoylated targets here include PML, which nucleates nuclear bodies, the NF-κB subunit RELA, MDM2 and β-catenin, linking the system to stress responses, innate immune signalling and growth control.

SUMO modification is reversible, and protein desumoylation is the step that removes the modifier from its target, returning substrates to their unmodified state and recycling free SUMO for reuse. Because conjugation is continuous, the isopeptidases here set the steady-state level of SUMOylation on transcription factors, nuclear body components, chromatin regulators and DNA repair proteins, and they also mature SUMO precursors by trimming their C-termini. The SENP family carries most of this activity with distinct preferences and locations: some act mainly at the nuclear envelope and nucleoplasm, others in the nucleolus on ribosome biogenesis substrates, and the SENP6/SENP7 pair dismantles polySUMO chains. Additional hydrolases such as DESI1 and USPL1 act through unrelated catalytic folds. Loss of this reversibility disturbs mitosis, hypoxic and inflammatory gene programmes, and nuclear body dynamics, and SENP1 in particular influences transcriptional responses driven by hypoxia-inducible factors.

poly(A)+ mRNA export from nucleus moves finished, polyadenylated messenger RNAs through the nuclear pore into the cytoplasm, the step that licenses a transcript for translation and couples gene expression to protein output. It matters because export is a quality-control checkpoint: only mRNAs that have been correctly spliced, capped and polyadenylated acquire the adaptors needed to leave, so unprocessed transcripts are retained and degraded. The TREX complex and associated adaptors such as SARNP, POLDIP3 and ENY2 load the NXF1-NXT1 export receptor onto mRNA during transcription and splicing, and the receptor then shuttles through pores built from nucleoporins including NUP93 and NUP133. At the cytoplasmic face, the DEAD-box ATPases DDX19A/B, activated by GLE1 and inositol hexakisphosphate, strip the receptor to give directionality and release the message. Loss of these steps blocks mRNA availability and causes motor neuron and developmental disease.

Polyadenylated mRNAs made in the nucleus are useless until they reach the ribosome, and this route carries them through the nuclear pore into the cytoplasm. Export is coupled to the preceding steps of mRNA maturation, so only properly capped, spliced and polyadenylated transcripts are released; retention of defective messages is part of nuclear quality control, and blocking export shuts down gene expression as effectively as blocking transcription. Transcripts are loaded with export adaptors and handed to the NXF1-NXT1 heterodimer, which shuttles cargo through the pore channel formed by nucleoporins such as NUP93 and NUP133. Directionality comes from terminal-side remodelling: GLE1 stimulates the DDX19 helicases to strip the receptor from mRNA at the cytoplasmic face, preventing return. Associated transcription-export and THO-related components link elongation and 3' end processing to release, and PABPN1 marks the poly(A) tail itself.

Heme-containing redox proteins only work once they are folded, loaded with their cofactors and slotted into a multi-subunit complex, and cytochrome complex assembly is the set of chaperone and metallation steps that accomplishes this — chiefly for cytochrome c oxidase and the cytochrome bc1 complex of the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Without it electron transport stalls, ATP output falls, and infants present with Leigh syndrome, cardiomyopathy or lactic acidosis. Dedicated factors handle each requirement: COX10 and COX15 synthesise heme a, COX17 with SCO1 and SCO2 deliver copper to the catalytic core, COX18 and COX20 manage membrane insertion and maturation of newly translated subunits, TACO1 promotes translation of a mitochondrially encoded subunit, and the UQCC and LYRM7 proteins chaperone Rieske and cytochrome b subunits into complex III. HCCS attaches heme covalently to cytochrome c itself, linking cofactor chemistry to assembly.

Proteins made outside a cell or outside an organelle must be recognised and moved across a membrane to reach the place where they work, and this import activity groups those targeting and translocation events. Several distinct routes appear together: receptor-mediated uptake at the cell surface, where the endocytic receptor LRP2 and ligands such as APOE and clusterin carry cargo into cells; delivery of lipoprotein lipase across capillary endothelium by GPIHBP1; and lysosomal entry of substrate proteins in chaperone-mediated autophagy, where the cytosolic chaperone HSPA8 hands cargo to LAMP2 at the lysosomal membrane. Perforin illustrates the extreme case, forming pores that let cytotoxic granule contents enter a target cell. Because these steps determine which compartment a protein reaches, they bear on renal protein reabsorption, triglyceride clearance, selective protein degradation and immune killing.

Complex III of the respiratory chain, the cytochrome bc1 complex, passes electrons from reduced coenzyme Q to cytochrome c while pumping protons, and it cannot function until its subunits, haems and iron-sulfur cofactor are brought together in the inner mitochondrial membrane. This assembly route builds that machine: dedicated chaperones stabilise nascent subunits and hold intermediates, the AAA-ATPase BCS1L inserts the Rieske iron-sulfur protein UQCRFS1 into the maturing complex, LYRM7 chaperones that subunit beforehand, and TTC19 clears its processed fragments afterwards. Iron-sulfur cluster supply links the process to frataxin and mitochondrial iron handling. Because oxidative phosphorylation depends on a fully matured complex, defects in these factors cause isolated complex III deficiency, with lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, tubulopathy and the GRACILE and Björnstad phenotypes, illustrating how assembly factors rather than structural subunits often underlie mitochondrial disease.

Insecticides used against insect nervous systems also reach human cells, and this grouping covers the cellular changes that follow such exposure: altered gene expression, shifts in enzyme activity, and adjustments to proliferation and neuronal signalling. Its relevance is toxicological, since organophosphate and pyrethroid exposure is linked to neurodevelopmental harm, porphyria-like disturbances of haem synthesis, and endocrine disruption. Several members point to concrete routes of response. A cytochrome P450 monooxygenase inducible through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor handles oxidative metabolism of xenobiotics; coproporphyrinogen oxidase places haem biosynthesis among the affected routes, consistent with chemically provoked porphyria. An auxiliary sodium channel subunit and a microtubule-associated protein reflect the neuronal targets on which pyrethroid-class compounds act, while a mitotic cyclin and a ubiquitin fusion protein tie the response to cell cycle progression and protein turnover after chemical stress.

plasma membrane phospholipid scrambling is the collapse of the normal lipid asymmetry of the plasma membrane, moving phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine from the inner leaflet to the cell surface. That exposed phosphatidylserine is a signal read by other cells and enzymes: it marks apoptotic cells for recognition and engulfment by phagocytes, provides the catalytic surface for the coagulation cascade on activated platelets, and licenses membrane fusion events. Scrambling is energy-independent and bidirectional, carried out by distinct families of scramblases — calcium-activated anoctamins such as ANO6, whose loss causes the bleeding disorder Scott syndrome, caspase-cleaved XKR8 acting downstream of apoptotic signalling, and the phospholipid scramblases PLSCR1-5. Related lipid-mobilising proteins including ATG9A, TMEM41B and VMP1 link the same chemistry to autophagosome membrane expansion, while SERINC proteins alter viral envelope lipid composition and restrict infectivity.

A resting plasma membrane keeps phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine confined to the inner leaflet; scrambling collapses that asymmetry and moves them bidirectionally to the outer surface. The exposed phosphatidylserine is a signal read by other cells: it marks apoptotic corpses for engulfment by phagocytes, provides the catalytic surface for clotting factor assembly during platelet activation, and contributes to membrane fusion events in myoblasts and bone. The work is done by several unrelated families of energy-independent lipid scramblases, including the calcium-activated anoctamins, the caspase-activated XKR proteins that partner with the apoptotic machinery, the phospholipid scramblase family, and lipid-mobilising proteins such as ATG9A, TMEM41B and VMP1 that also support autophagosome membrane expansion. Calcium entry through purinergic and TRP channels can trigger the process acutely. Loss of the platelet scrambling route causes Scott syndrome, a bleeding disorder, while failed apoptotic exposure leaves dead cells uncleared and promotes inflammation.

Tissue maintenance depends on stem cells dividing in a way that replaces the daughter that differentiates while keeping a stem cell behind, and this self-renewing mode of division is what keeps blood, gut, skin and neural compartments stocked for a lifetime. Too little of it causes marrow failure and premature exhaustion of progenitor pools; too much, or division uncoupled from differentiation, is the route to leukaemia and other cancers. The genes involved combine niche signalling with chromatin control and division geometry: Wnt ligands and Frizzled receptors, Notch, and TGF-beta relay positional cues, while polycomb repression by BMI1 and the opposing CDKN2A locus set the balance between proliferation and senescence. Transcriptional regulators such as HOXB4, MYB, MLLT3, ZBTB16 and ESRRB sustain the undifferentiated state, and planar polarity proteins orient the spindle so that fate is partitioned asymmetrically between daughters.

Cells routinely shut protein synthesis down or throttle it on particular messages, and this collection of repressors is how they do it. Global control runs through the integrated stress response, where kinases responding to amino acid shortage, heme deficiency, double-stranded RNA or ER stress phosphorylate the initiation factor eIF2 alpha subunit, and through 4E-binding proteins that sequester the cap-binding factor eIF4E downstream of growth signalling. Message-specific control uses microRNAs loaded into Argonaute proteins with GW182-family scaffolds, which recruit the CCR4-NOT deadenylase and decapping machinery, alongside RNA-binding repressors such as ZFP36 family tristetraprolins, CPEBs, Pumilio-like and IGF2BP proteins that act on untranslated regions. Ribosome quality control and stress granule assembly add further braking. The outputs matter for iron homeostasis, oocyte and germ cell dormancy, synaptic plasticity, inflammatory transcript turnover, and tumour suppression.

Neurotransmitters, peptide hormones and granule contents are released on demand when cytosolic calcium rises, and this calcium-regulated exocytosis is what converts an electrical or receptor signal into secretion. It underlies synaptic transmission, insulin and catecholamine release, mast cell and platelet granule discharge, and the cortical granule reaction at fertilization; loss of its components causes epileptic encephalopathy, movement disorders and bleeding or immune secretory defects. Vesicles are tethered and primed at release sites by RIM and Munc13 proteins with Munc18 and CAPS, then fuse through the SNARE complex of syntaxin-1, SNAP25 and VAMP2. Synaptotagmins act as the calcium sensors that trigger fusion, with DOC2 isoforms supporting slower asynchronous release, while voltage-gated and store-operated calcium entry, Rab3 cycling, calcineurin and CDK5 set the timing and replenishment of the releasable pool.

Exocytosis releases neurotransmitters, hormones, granule contents and membrane proteins by fusing vesicles with the plasma membrane, and the control layered on top of it sets how much is released, when, and in response to which stimulus. This regulation makes synaptic transmission graded and plastic, allows mast cells, neutrophils, platelets and cytotoxic lymphocytes to discharge their granules only on receptor engagement, and shapes endocrine secretion. Calcium sensing by synaptotagmins and complexins gates the fusion machinery built from SNAREs and their chaperones such as STXBP1 and NSF; active-zone scaffolds including piccolo, RIMs and CADPS organise vesicles for release; Rab GTPases and their regulators, notably RAB27A and UNC13D, direct granule docking. Kinases, G protein-coupled and immune receptors tune the output. Loss of components causes familial hemophagocytic syndromes, bleeding and pigmentation defects, epileptic encephalopathy, and contributes to neurodegeneration.

Neurotransmitter and hormone release is triggered when calcium entering a stimulated cell is sensed at the site of vesicle fusion, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how readily and how strongly that release occurs. It determines synaptic strength and short-term plasticity, insulin and catecholamine secretion, and the timing precision on which neural circuits depend. Synaptotagmins act as the calcium sensors that couple ion binding to fusion of the SNARE complex formed with syntaxin-1A and its regulator STXBP1/Munc18, while Rab3 and its effectors rabphilin and RIM-associated proteins govern vesicle priming and docking. Calcium supply itself is tuned by presynaptic N-type channels and their regulators, by SERCA-mediated store refilling, and by presynaptic autoreceptors signalling through inhibitory G proteins; CDK5 and calcineurin add phosphorylation-dependent control. Disrupted regulation here underlies epilepsy, movement disorders and impaired secretory responses.

Hydroxylation of lysine residues in proteins, producing peptidyl-hydroxylysine, serves two quite different ends: it licenses the crosslinking and glycosylation chemistry that gives collagen fibrils their tensile strength, and it tunes the activity of factors in mRNA splicing and translation. In the endoplasmic reticulum, prolyl 3-hydroxylase family members P3H3 and P3H4 act together with lysyl hydroxylase activity on procollagen telopeptides, and the VPS33B/VIPAS39 trafficking complex is required for normal collagen lysine modification; loss of either VPS33B or VIPAS39 causes arthrogryposis-renal dysfunction-cholestasis syndrome, with defective collagen crosslinking and bile canalicular polarity. The nuclear and cytoplasmic JmjC-domain enzymes JMJD4, JMJD6 and JMJD7 are 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent oxygenases that hydroxylate lysines in substrates including translation termination and elongation factors and splicing regulators, linking oxygen and metabolite availability to protein synthesis fidelity and RNA processing.

Adding one, two or three methyl groups to lysine side chains is a reversible mark that changes how a protein is read without changing its sequence, and the enzymes here cover both the histone and the non-histone sides of that chemistry. On chromatin, EHMT1 and EHMT2 deposit repressive marks on histone H3, KMT5A monomethylates H4K20 to influence replication and damage responses, and SETD2 generates H3K36 trimethylation co-transcriptionally, guiding splicing and mismatch repair. Beyond histones, a family of seven-beta-strand and SET-domain methyltransferases modifies the translation apparatus and other abundant substrates: elongation factors 1A and 2, ribosomal and chaperone proteins, actin via SETD3, ATP synthase subunits, citrate synthase and the VCP/p97 ATPase. Loss of individual members causes intellectual disability syndromes and is common in cancer, reflecting roles in gene silencing, transcription elongation fidelity and protein quality control.

Trimethylation of specific lysine residues installs a permanent, bulky positive charge that alters how a protein folds, binds partners or is read by effector modules, and this set covers the enzymes that carry peptidyl-lysine to the N6,N6,N6-trimethyl state. Several act on single non-histone substrates: dedicated methyltransferases modify the mitochondrial adenine nucleotide translocase and the ATP synthase c-subunit, citrate synthase, the translation elongation factor eEF2, and the AAA-ATPase VCP/p97, linking the modification to oxidative phosphorylation, the citric acid cycle, protein synthesis and ubiquitin-dependent protein extraction. SETD2 trimethylates histone H3 on lysine 36 in transcribed chromatin, coupling elongation to splicing, DNA repair and mismatch repair, and its loss is a driver event in clear cell renal carcinoma. The group as a whole shows methylation acting beyond chromatin, as a tuning mechanism for mitochondrial and cytoskeletal machinery.

Adding a single methyl group to a lysine side chain is one of the smallest covalent changes a protein can carry, yet peptidyl-lysine monomethylation redirects how the modified protein is read and what binds it. On histones, the mono-methyl marks placed by the enzymes here distinguish active from silenced chromatin: KMT5A methylates histone H4 lysine 20 and links chromatin state to DNA replication and damage response, while EHMT1 and SETD7 act on H3 lysines and are required for normal neurodevelopment and for tuning transcription factor activity. Other members act on non-histone substrates, methylating transcriptional regulators such as NF-kB components and p53 to change their interactions, or modifying translation machinery and mitochondrial proteins. Collectively this chemistry represents a writer layer of the protein methylation code, with methyl-lysine binding modules translating the mark into changes in gene expression, protein stability, and cell proliferation.

Adding two methyl groups to the same lysine side chain creates a distinct mark, and peptidyl-lysine dimethylation covers the enzymes that produce it on histones and on non-histone substrates. The best-characterised activity here is the G9a/GLP pair, EHMT2 and EHMT1, which dimethylate lysine 9 of histone H3 to establish repressive chromatin over developmental and lineage-inappropriate genes; loss of EHMT1 causes a neurodevelopmental syndrome, and both enzymes are recurrently exploited by tumours to silence differentiation programmes. SMYD2 and SETD7 methylate histone tails and also modify regulatory proteins such as p53, tuning transcriptional output rather than packaging DNA, while CSKMT acts in mitochondria on citrate synthase, showing that the chemistry is not confined to the nucleus. Because these marks are read by chromodomain and other effector proteins and erased by demethylases, the pathway forms part of reversible epigenetic control of gene expression.

Polyglutamylation attaches chains of glutamate residues to the carboxyl group of an existing glutamate in a target protein, most conspicuously on the acidic C-terminal tails of tubulin. The resulting negative charge marks subsets of microtubules and tunes how strongly motors, severing enzymes and microtubule-associated proteins bind them, which matters most in structures that must last: axonemes of cilia and flagella, centrioles, and neuronal axons. The TTLL family supplies the glutamylases, with different members acting as chain initiases or elongases and preferring alpha- or beta-tubulin, so their combined output sets the tail code on a given microtubule population. CEP41 governs delivery of glutamylation activity to the ciliary axoneme and is mutated in Joubert syndrome, and loss of this modification more generally disturbs sperm motility, photoreceptor maintenance and ciliary beating. Non-tubulin substrates, including nucleosome assembly proteins, are also modified.

peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation covers the transfer of phosphate onto threonine residues in proteins, one of the core reversible modifications by which cells encode information about their state. Threonine phosphorylation switches enzyme activity, creates or destroys binding surfaces, and marks proteins for degradation, so it sits underneath cell cycle progression, growth factor responses, stress signalling and ion transport; loss of control over the responsible kinases is a recurrent theme in cancer and in hypertension. The genes span the kinase classes that do this work: cyclin-dependent kinases such as CDK1 that drive mitotic entry, checkpoint and DNA damage kinases including CHEK1 and PRKDC, the MAP kinase cascades acting through MAPK1 and MAPK8, calcium- and lipid-activated kinases like CAMK2A and PRKCD, the AKT1 and STK11 axis of metabolic control, and WNK and STK39 kinases governing epithelial salt handling, together with substrates such as ATF2.

Adding a phosphate to a threonine residue in a protein is one of the basic switches cells use to change enzyme activity, protein interactions and localisation on a fast timescale. Peptidyl-threonine phosphorylation gathers the kinases and regulators that carry out and control this modification, and through it cell cycle progression, stress responses, growth factor signalling and ion transport are all set. The genes span several kinase families: cyclin-dependent kinases and the checkpoint kinase CHEK1 that time mitotic entry and arrest damaged cells, AKT1 and MAPK1/MAPK8 acting downstream of growth factor and stress inputs, the LKB1 kinase STK11 in energy sensing, WNK3 and STK39 in regulating cation-chloride cotransporters, and TBK1 in innate immune signalling. Substrates include transcription factors such as ATF2, linking threonine phosphorylation to changes in gene expression. Misregulation of these kinases underlies tumour growth, hypertension and impaired damage responses.

Protein hydroxylation is the enzymatic addition of hydroxyl groups to specific amino acid side chains, a modification that both stabilises structural proteins and acts as a signal reporting on oxygen availability. Most of the enzymes here are 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent dioxygenases that consume molecular O2, which makes their activity an intrinsic oxygen sensor: the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN2 and EGLN3 mark HIF-alpha for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so their inhibition in hypoxia switches on the adaptive transcriptional response driving erythropoiesis and angiogenesis. Other members hydroxylate collagen prolyl and lysyl residues, and prolyl 3-hydroxylases together with the VPS33B-VIPAS39 complex support collagen folding, crosslinking and secretion; their loss produces brittle bone and connective tissue disease. Ribosomal and translation-factor hydroxylation by OGFOD1, RIOX1/2 and JmjC-family enzymes tunes protein synthesis, linking oxygen status to ribosome function and cell growth.

Hydroxylation of amino acid side chains is a post-translational modification that tunes protein stability, folding and translation, and most of the enzymes that install it are 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent dioxygenases whose activity tracks oxygen availability. That oxygen dependence is the basis of cellular oxygen sensing: prolyl hydroxylases such as EGLN2 and EGLN3 mark the hypoxia-inducible factor alpha subunits for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so the hypoxic transcriptional response is switched on by loss of hydroxylation rather than by a ligand. Other members act on the translational apparatus and on ribosomal proteins, including OGFOD1 and the JmjC-domain and ribosomal oxygenase enzymes, while the prolyl 3-hydroxylases and the protein disulfide isomerase subunit P4HB serve collagen maturation in the endoplasmic reticulum, where defective hydroxylation produces brittle-bone and connective tissue disease. VPS33B and VIPAS39 link the pathway to lysosome-related organelle trafficking.

Covalent peptide cross-linking joins protein chains through bonds that cannot be undone by ordinary proteolysis, giving tissues mechanical toughness and insolubility. The transglutaminase family dominates here, catalysing calcium-dependent isopeptide bonds between glutamine and lysine side chains. Their best-known product is the cornified envelope of the epidermis, in which loricrin, involucrin and small proline-rich proteins are lashed together beneath the plasma membrane with desmosomal components such as desmoplakin and envoplakin to form the skin's water barrier; loss of the keratinocyte enzyme TGM1 causes lamellar ichthyosis. Related reactions stabilise other structures: factor XIII cross-links fibrin to consolidate blood clots, a red cell enzyme acts on the membrane skeleton, and the widely expressed TGM2 modifies extracellular matrix proteins including collagen. The same chemistry contributes to wound healing, tissue fibrosis and the generation of deamidated gluten peptides in coeliac disease.

Oxidation of amino acid side chains converts inert residues into reactive or functional groups, and the examples here span both structural and catalytic ends of that chemistry. The copper-dependent lysyl oxidase family deaminates lysine and hydroxylysine in collagen and elastin to reactive aldehydes, the first committed step in the covalent crosslinking that gives connective tissue, vessel walls and bone their tensile strength; loss of this activity produces fragile aortas and skin, while its induction in tumour stroma stiffens matrix and promotes invasion and metastasis. A separate reaction, carried out by the formylglycine-generating enzyme, oxidizes an active-site cysteine of newly made sulfatases to formylglycine, the residue those enzymes need for catalysis, and its failure causes multiple sulfatase deficiency with lysosomal storage disease. The apolipoproteins of HDL contribute residues that are themselves oxidized, linking this modification to lipoprotein function and oxidative stress.

peptidyl-amino acid modification is the broad business of chemically altering amino acid residues after a protein has been made, which is how cells expand a fixed genome into a far larger range of protein behaviours. These marks decide whether an enzyme is active, where a protein sits, how long it survives, and which partners it binds, so signalling, chromatin regulation and metabolic control all depend on them. The genes span most of the major chemistries: tyrosine and serine/threonine kinases from growth factor and cytokine receptors through to nuclear substrates; SUMO conjugation and the SENP proteases that reverse it; lysine acetyltransferases and sirtuin deacetylases; arginine and lysine methyltransferases and demethylases; palmitoyl and myristoyl transferases that anchor proteins to membranes; tubulin glutamylation and detyrosination; prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation and collagen cross-linking; lipoylation, diphthamide synthesis, and vitamin K-dependent carboxylation. Loss of individual enzymes produces phenotypes from cancer to connective tissue and neurodevelopmental disease.

Post-translational modification of amino acid residues within proteins, covering the enzymes that add, remove and read chemical marks on polypeptides after synthesis. Such modification expands protein function far beyond the genetic code: it switches enzymes on and off, creates docking sites for partners, targets proteins for degradation, and anchors them to membranes. Represented chemistries include phosphorylation by tyrosine and serine/threonine kinases acting downstream of growth factor and cytokine receptors, reversal by phosphatases, lysine acetylation by histone acetyltransferases and its removal by sirtuins, lysine and arginine methylation, SUMO conjugation and its cleavage by SENP proteases, S-palmitoylation by ZDHHC acyltransferases, N-myristoylation, tubulin polyglutamylation and detyrosination, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylation of collagen, vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, tyrosine sulfation, lipoylation and diphthamide formation. Loss of individual writers or erasers causes developmental syndromes, bleeding disorders, ciliopathies and cancer.</description>Also note that the ,

Arginine residues in proteins carry a bulky guanidinium group that can be decorated enzymatically, and peptidyl-arginine modification covers the writing and reversal of those marks. Methylation is the dominant chemistry here: type I enzymes such as PRMT1 and its neuronal relative PRMT8 generate asymmetric dimethylarginine, PRMT5 produces the symmetric form, and PRMT7 leaves residues monomethylated. The consequences reach across gene regulation and RNA biology, because methylated arginines in histone tails and in the glycine-arginine-rich regions of RNA-binding proteins dictate chromatin state, splicing, and the assembly of ribonucleoprotein granules; PRMT5 activity is also a dependency exploited in cancer therapeutics. Beyond the nucleus, NDUFAF7 methylates an arginine in a core subunit during assembly of respiratory complex I, and the Jumonji-family enzyme KDM8 acts on arginine-containing substrates, linking this residue-level chemistry to mitochondrial biogenesis and cell proliferation.

Cysteine side chains are uniquely reactive, and covalent modification of them converts sequence information into changes in protein localisation and activity. The dominant activity here is S-acylation: a large family of DHHC-motif palmitoyltransferases, working in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi with the accessory subunit GOLGA7, attaches fatty acyl chains to cysteines and thereby tethers otherwise soluble proteins to membranes, sorting signalling molecules into rafts and controlling receptor trafficking and synaptic protein turnover; a related transferase palmitoylates Hedgehog ligands, a step required for their secreted signalling. A second arm is redox-based, with nitric oxide generated by inducible nitric oxide synthase forming S-nitrosothiols on targets such as glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, linking inflammatory signalling to metabolic enzyme regulation. Loss of individual palmitoyltransferases causes intellectual disability and neuropsychiatric phenotypes, underlining how much membrane-protein organisation depends on this chemistry.

Glutamate residues within proteins can be enzymatically decorated, and peptidyl-glutamic acid modification covers the two major ways this happens in human cells. One branch is polyglutamylation, in which tubulin tyrosine ligase-like enzymes add glutamate chains onto the acidic tails of tubulin and other substrates, tuning how motors and microtubule-associated proteins read the surface of axonemes, centrioles and neuronal microtubules; cytosolic carboxypeptidases of the AGBL family and AGTPBP1 trim those chains back, and loss of this balance causes cilia and flagella defects, sperm immotility and neurodegeneration. The second branch is vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, where the carboxylase GGCX converts glutamate to gamma-carboxyglutamate so that clotting factors and bone matrix proteins can bind calcium, with VKORC1 regenerating reduced vitamin K and serving as the target of warfarin. Together these reactions link cytoskeletal regulation to haemostasis through a shared residue chemistry.

peptidyl-histidine modification covers the enzymatic tailoring of histidine residues within proteins, a rare class of post-translational modification whose best-characterised examples are diphthamide formation on translation elongation factor 2 and histidine methylation of actin. Both alter the mechanics of the cytoskeleton and of protein synthesis. The diphthamide route proceeds through several steps: an iron-sulfur enzyme pair transfers an aminocarboxypropyl group to a single histidine of eEF2, followed by methylation and amidation, and the finished residue is the target ADP-ribosylated by diphtheria toxin. Loss of these steps disrupts translational fidelity and causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature. Separately, methylation of a conserved actin histidine tunes filament polymerisation kinetics and is required for normal smooth muscle contraction, including uterine function during labour.

Modification of histidine residues in proteins is rare but decisive, and the genes here carry out the two best-characterised examples in human cells. Most of them build diphthamide, an elaborately modified histidine unique to translation elongation factor 2: a radical SAM step transfers an aminocarboxypropyl group, followed by methylation and amidation to complete the residue. Diphthamide keeps translational elongation accurate, guards against ribosomal frameshifting, and is the target attacked by diphtheria toxin and related ADP-ribosylating toxins; loss of these enzymes causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature. SETD3 represents the other branch, methylating histidine 73 of actin to stabilise filaments, with consequences for smooth muscle contraction and labour. Together these reactions link an unusual post-translational chemistry to protein synthesis fidelity and cytoskeletal function.

Lysine side chains are the cell's most heavily decorated amino acid, and this collection covers the enzymes that write and erase those marks: acetylation, methylation, SUMOylation, lipoylation, hydroxylation and oxidative cross-linking. The consequences are broad, because lysine modification is how chromatin state, protein stability, localisation and enzyme activity are set. Acetyltransferases such as EP300, CREBBP, KAT2A and KAT5 and the sirtuin deacetylases together tune histone and transcription-factor activity; SETD and EHMT methyltransferases mark histones and selected non-histone substrates; a SUMO branch built on SUMO1-3, the SAE1-UBA2 activating enzyme, UBE2I, PIAS ligases and SENP proteases controls nuclear body formation, DNA repair through the SMC5/6 complex, and transcriptional repression. Lysyl oxidases act outside the cell, cross-linking collagen and elastin for tissue tensile strength, while lipoyltransferases attach lipoate to mitochondrial dehydrogenases. Loss of individual components produces developmental syndromes, connective tissue fragility and cancer predisposition.

Proline residues in proteins are chemically altered after synthesis, and these modifications control protein folding, stability and signalling in ways sequence alone cannot. Peptidyl-proline modification covers two distinct chemistries: hydroxylation of proline by 2-oxoglutarate- and iron-dependent dioxygenases, and cis-trans isomerisation of the peptide bond preceding proline. Prolyl 4- and 3-hydroxylases acting in the endoplasmic reticulum generate hydroxyproline that stabilises the collagen triple helix, while the related oxygen-sensing enzymes tag hypoxia-inducible factor subunits for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, making this chemistry the cell's oxygen sensor. Ribosomal hydroxylation by OGFOD1 tunes translational fidelity. Separately, cyclophilin-type and parvulin-type isomerases, including PIN1, which acts on phosphorylated Ser/Thr-Pro motifs, flip proline bonds to accelerate folding and switch the activity of cell cycle and signalling proteins. Loss of these activities causes connective tissue fragility and deranged hypoxic responses.

peptidyl-serine modification covers the covalent alteration of serine residues in proteins, overwhelmingly their phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases, which is the most common switch cells use to change protein activity, localisation and stability within seconds of a stimulus. Reversible serine phosphorylation is what allows growth factor, cytokine and stress signals to be converted into decisions about proliferation, survival, metabolism and cell death, and its deregulation underlies much of oncogenesis. The genes span the major kinase families that carry out this chemistry: RAF-MEK and AKT/mTOR effectors downstream of receptor tyrosine kinases, casein kinase 2 and GSK3 as constitutive modifiers, DNA damage-responsive kinases such as ATM, PRKDC and SMG1, mitotic and polarity kinases including AURKA and BRSK1, and inflammatory kinases IKBKB, TBK1 and RIPK1. Counter-regulators such as PTEN and SPRY2, and cytokine inputs including IL6, LIF and IFNG, place the modification within signalling networks rather than a single route.

Covalent modification of serine residues in proteins — overwhelmingly phosphorylation by serine/threonine kinases — is the most common way cells convert signals into changes in protein activity, localisation and stability. The kinases here span the major growth and stress routes: AKT1 and RPS6KB1 downstream of growth factor and mTOR signalling, RAF1, BRAF, ARAF and MAP2K2 in the MAPK cascade, GSK3B and CSNK2A1 as constitutively active multi-substrate kinases, IKBKB and TBK1 driving inflammatory transcription, ATM, PRKDC and SMG1 responding to DNA damage, AURKA and CDK2 timing mitosis and S phase, and ULK1 initiating autophagy. PTEN and SPRY2 act as brakes on the lipid and receptor inputs feeding these kinases. Because serine phosphorylation gates proliferation, apoptosis, cytokine responses and metabolic enzyme activity, misregulated kinases of this type are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers and the most heavily pursued drug targets.

Adding or removing a modification on a tyrosine side chain is how cells convert extracellular cues into intracellular decisions, and peptidyl-tyrosine modification covers that chemistry and its regulators. Most of it is phosphorylation: receptor kinases for growth factors and cytokines such as EGFR, ERBB2, the FGF, PDGF and VEGF receptor families, KIT, FLT3 and IGF1R, cytoplasmic kinases of the SRC, ABL, SYK/ZAP70 and JAK classes, and the phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPN2 together with SOCS proteins that terminate signalling. Ligands are included as well, from interleukins and interferons to angiopoietins and neuregulin, placing the pathway upstream of proliferation, survival, migration, angiogenesis and lymphocyte activation. Tyrosylprotein sulfotransferases TPST1 and TPST2 contribute a distinct secretory-pathway modification affecting ligand recognition. Because these kinases set growth and immune thresholds, their mutation or constitutive activation drives cancers and immunodeficiency, and they are among the most heavily drugged targets in medicine.

Arginine methylation marks proteins with methyl groups on guanidino nitrogens, a modification that tunes protein-protein and protein-nucleic acid interactions without changing charge. It shapes chromatin through histone arginine marks, governs assembly of spliceosomal Sm proteins and the behaviour of RNA-binding proteins, and controls signalling adaptors and transcriptional coactivators. The enzymes here span the major classes: PRMT1 as the dominant asymmetric dimethyltransferase, PRMT5 producing symmetric dimethylarginine in complex with its cofactor partner, PRMT7 restricted to monomethylation, and the neuronally enriched, membrane-associated PRMT8. NDUFAF7 acts on a different substrate class, methylating an arginine in NDUFS2 during assembly of respiratory complex I. Loss of these activities disrupts splicing fidelity, DNA damage responses and stem cell maintenance, and PRMT5 dependence has made this chemistry a target in cancers with deletions affecting methionine salvage.

S-palmitoylation of cysteine residues attaches a 16-carbon fatty acid through a labile thioester bond, giving otherwise soluble proteins a membrane anchor and steering them into particular membranes and lipid microdomains. Because the linkage is reversible, it acts as a switch: Ras and other small GTPases, receptors, ion channels and synaptic scaffolds are shuttled between compartments and turned on or off according to their palmitoylation state, which also affects protein stability and raft partitioning. The reaction is catalysed by a family of multipass membrane acyltransferases bearing the DHHC cysteine-rich domain, distributed across the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and plasma membrane, with GOLGA7 serving as an accessory subunit that supports enzyme stability and activity. Individual enzymes have distinct substrate preferences and tissue biases; loss of ZDHHC9 causes X-linked intellectual disability, and ZDHHC8 has been linked to schizophrenia risk, underscoring the dependence of neuronal signalling on this lipid modification.

Most secreted and membrane proteins carry sugars attached to asparagine within an Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequon, and N-linked glycosylation via asparagine is how that attachment is made and elaborated. The modification governs folding, quality control, secretion, receptor half-life and cell-surface recognition; its failure underlies congenital disorders of glycosylation with multisystem developmental and neurological disease. In the endoplasmic reticulum a multisubunit oligosaccharyltransferase built around the catalytic subunits STT3A or STT3B, with accessory components such as DDOST, RPN1, OST4, OSTC, DAD1 and the magnesium-binding oxidoreductases MAGT1 and TUSC3, transfers a preassembled oligosaccharide from dolichol-linked donor to the nascent chain; ALG5 and ALG8 supply and extend that donor. Glucosyltransferases UGGT1 and UGGT2 reglucosylate incompletely folded glycoproteins to retain them in the folding cycle, while Golgi enzymes including MGAT1, MGAT2, MGAT5, FUT8 and ST6GAL1 branch, fucosylate and sialylate the mature glycans.

Protein geranylgeranylation attaches a 20-carbon isoprenoid lipid, derived from the mevalonate pathway, to C-terminal cysteines of small GTPases so that they can dock onto membranes and work where their targets are. Without it, Rho, Rac and Rab proteins stay soluble and inert, and vesicle traffic, cytoskeletal remodelling and secretion fail; this dependence explains part of the cellular effect of statins and of bisphosphonates, which starve the reaction of substrate. Two enzyme classes carry it out: geranylgeranyltransferase type I, which shares a subunit with the farnesyltransferase alpha chain, and Rab geranylgeranyltransferase, which acts on Rab GTPases only after they are presented by a Rab escort protein. Attaching a 16-carbon palmitoyl group to cysteine residues gives proteins a reversible membrane anchor, and protein palmitoylation is how cells control where many signalling proteins sit and how long they stay there. Because the modification can be removed, it acts as a switch: it targets Ras and other small GTPases to the plasma membrane, clusters receptors and channels at synapses, and directs trafficking through the Golgi. The ZDHHC family of DHHC-motif acyltransferases carries out the transfer, with accessory subunits such as GOLGA7 and SELENOK required for the stability or activity of particular enzymes, while HHAT instead palmitoylates Hedgehog ligands to make them signalling-competent for developmental patterning. Loss of individual enzymes has clear consequences: ZDHHC9 mutations cause X-linked intellectual disability, and ZDHHC8 and ZDHHC17 are tied to neuronal and Huntingtin-related biology, placing this chemistry upstream of synaptic function and morphogenesis.

Peptidyl-lysine acetylation is the transfer of acetyl groups onto lysine side chains of proteins, a reversible modification that neutralises the residue's positive charge and creates docking sites for bromodomain readers. It is the chemistry behind histone acetylation and therefore behind open chromatin and transcriptional activation, but it extends far beyond the nucleus: acetylation of tubulin by ATAT1 marks stable microtubules, and acetylation of metabolic enzymes and transcription factors tunes their activity to acetyl-CoA availability. The genes span the major acetyltransferase families, from the CREBBP/EP300 coactivators that couple signal-responsive transcription factors to the general machinery, through GCN5/PCAF and the MYST enzymes KAT5 and KAT7 that act in DNA damage response and replication licensing, to ESCO1, which acetylates cohesin to establish sister chromatid cohesion. SIRT1 provides the opposing deacetylase activity, making the mark a dynamic, nutrient-sensitive switch.

Acetylation of lysine side chains is one of the most widespread reversible protein modifications, and this pathway covers the enzymes that place the acetyl group and the factors that direct them to substrates. On histones it loosens chromatin and marks active promoters and enhancers, so transcriptional programmes for growth, differentiation and stress responses depend on it; on non-histone targets it tunes protein stability, localisation and enzyme activity. The transferases here span several families: the paralogous coactivators CREBBP and EP300, the GCN5/PCAF pair, and KAT5 and KAT7, which acetylate histones in the context of DNA damage signalling and replication licensing. ESCO1 acetylates the cohesin subunit SMC3 to establish sister chromatid cohesion, while ATAT1 acetylates α-tubulin to mark long-lived microtubules. Loss or mutation of these writers causes developmental syndromes and is recurrent in cancer, and the opposing deacetylase activity of SIRT1 keeps the mark dynamic.

Many proteins acquire their final functional form only after their last residue is altered, and C-terminal modification covers the enzymes that trim, methylate or conjugate lipids to that terminus. The consequences are concrete: cytosolic carboxypeptidases of the AGBL family and AGTPBP1 remove glutamates and tyrosine from tubulin tails, tuning microtubule-based transport so that loss of AGTPBP1 causes Purkinje cell degeneration and motor neuron loss. ICMT carboxyl-methylates prenylated CaaX proteins such as Ras family GTPases, completing the membrane anchor needed for their signalling, while LCMT1 methylates the C-terminal leucine of the protein phosphatase 2A catalytic subunit to govern which regulatory subunits assemble with it. ATG7 and ATG16L1 act in the conjugation of a C-terminal glycine on ATG8 proteins to membrane lipid during autophagosome formation, and GPLD1 cleaves GPI anchors to release proteins from the cell surface.

Phenolic metabolites dominate several hormone and pigment pathways, and handling compounds with a hydroxylated aromatic ring is what this metabolic process covers. Tyrosine is the common precursor: ring hydroxylation by tyrosine hydroxylase and phenylalanine hydroxylase, with tetrahydrobiopterin supplied via GCH1, feeds dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline synthesis, and degradation follows through monoamine oxidases, COMT-mediated O-methylation, aldehyde dehydrogenases and SULT-family sulfotransferases. The same precursor supports melanin production in melanosomes through tyrosinase, TYRP1, DCT and pigment transporters such as OCA2 and SLC45A2, and iodinated thyronines made on thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase and dual oxidases, then activated or inactivated by deiodinases and carried by SLC16A2 and SLCO1C1. Dopamine receptors and transporters place the output in neurotransmission. Loss of individual steps produces phenylketonuria, tyrosinaemia, albinism, congenital hypothyroidism, and, through catecholamine handling, susceptibility to parkinsonism.

Viral latency is the dormant phase after initial infection, during which a virus persists in the host cell without producing progeny, ending only when a reactivation signal restarts replication. Latency is what allows herpesviruses and retroviruses to remain in the body for life and to recur, and it is the reason antivirals that block replication cannot clear infection. The genes here point to the host side of that switch: a cellular coactivator that is recruited to immediate-early viral promoters and is a well-studied determinant of lytic reactivation, transcription factors of the bZIP and interferon-regulatory families that couple stress and innate immune signalling to viral gene expression, and a non-homologous end-joining ligase that acts in the joining of DNA ends, relevant to maintaining and circularising viral genomes. Together they connect host transcriptional control and DNA repair to whether a genome stays silent or resumes replication.

Viruses have no metabolism of their own, so every stage of the viral life cycle — attachment, entry, uncoating, translation of viral mRNA on host ribosomes, genome replication, assembly and budding — is executed with host proteins, and this collection maps the human side of that dependency. One arm is the entry apparatus: receptors and attachment factors such as ACE2, CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4, DPP4, nectins, CXADR, transferrin receptor and NPC1, together with the proteases TMPRSS2, furin and cathepsins B and L that cleave viral glycoproteins, and endosomal trafficking through RAB7A and LAMP1. Budding and egress co-opt the ESCRT machinery — TSG101, CHMP subunits, VPS4 ATPases and ALIX — plus NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligases. Opposing these are restriction factors and innate sensors: APOBEC3 deaminases, tetherin, IFITMs, MX1, OAS–RNase L, ISG15 and TRIM5. The balance between permissive host factors and this antiviral arsenal sets tropism, and determines whether infection is productive or aborted.

Many viruses do not fuse at the plasma membrane but are taken into the cell inside vesicles after binding a surface receptor, and this receptor-mediated endocytic uptake is the step that determines host range and tissue tropism for coronaviruses and several other enveloped viruses. Entry receptors such as ACE2 and DPP4, and the lectins CLEC4M and SIGLEC1 that capture virions and hand them on, define which cells can be infected at all. After internalisation, clathrin adaptors and caveolins shape the carrier, while endosomal maturation supplies the acidic, protease-rich environment in which cathepsin L cleaves viral glycoproteins to trigger fusion. Ion flux and lipid signalling across the endolysosomal membrane, through the channel TPCN2 and the kinase PIKFYVE, govern whether the particle progresses or is stalled, which is why both are drug targets for blocking viral entry.

Virion assembly is the late step of infection in which viral structural proteins, genome and membrane come together at a defined site in the cell and a nascent particle is formed and pinched off. Host machinery does much of this work, and the genes here are dominated by the ESCRT system — TSG101 and the VPS37/MVB12 subunits, the CHMP proteins that polymerise on membrane necks, ALIX, and the VPS4 ATPases that recycle them. Enveloped viruses such as HIV recruit these factors through short late-domain motifs to catalyse the membrane scission that releases budding virions, the same reaction used for multivesicular body formation and cytokinetic abscission. Additional components point to secretory and trafficking contributions: RAB1 and RAB43 GTPases with their regulators, signal peptidase subunits, and NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligases that mark budding substrates. APOE and DDX6 link particle maturation and infectivity to lipoproteins and cytoplasmic RNA granules.

The last step of a viral life cycle is getting finished particles out of the cell, and viral release from host cell covers that exit — budding through membranes, scission of the nascent particle, or lysis — which determines how efficiently infection spreads to neighbouring cells. Many enveloped viruses accomplish this by hijacking the host machinery that normally buds vesicles away from the cytoplasm: ESCRT components including TSG101 and the VPS37 subunits recruit the CHMP proteins that polymerise at the neck of a budding particle, and the AAA-ATPases VPS4A and VPS4B disassemble those filaments to complete membrane cutting. Trafficking factors such as RAB7A and ARL8B position the relevant compartments, the cyclophilin PPIA acts on retroviral capsid, and TRIM25 and related ubiquitin ligases work at the interface with innate antiviral restriction, so release is simultaneously a target of host defence and of antiviral drug design.

viral genome replication covers the host processes that support or restrict copying of a viral genome inside an infected cell, including the nucleotide supply and RNA-handling steps replication depends on. It matters because the same machinery decides whether an infection is productive or aborted, and mutations in it shape susceptibility to hepatitis, HIV and influenza. Much of the gene content is antiviral: interferon-induced effectors such as MX1, ISG15, the OAS-RNase L system and IFITM proteins, cytosolic sensors including IFI16 and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, and the APOBEC3 and ADAR deaminases that mutate viral nucleic acid. Against these sit host factors that viruses co-opt -- cyclophilins, PCBP and PABPC1 RNA-binding proteins, VAP proteins and TMEM41B for replication-organelle membranes, SMC5/6 and topoisomerases for episomal DNA. Autophagy components and translational control through PKR link replication to broader stress responses.

Replication of a viral genome inside a host cell depends on borrowed nucleotide pools, host RNA-binding proteins and membrane platforms, and it is also the step the innate immune system works hardest to block. The genes here span both sides of that contest: cyclophilins, poly(C)-binding proteins, DDX3X, PABPC1 and membrane factors such as TMEM41B and VAP proteins that support replication complexes, alongside restriction and sensing machinery that limits it. Cytosolic sensors including IFIH1 and IFI16 signal through MAVS to induce interferon, whose effectors — the OAS–RNase L arm, MX1, IFIT and IFITM proteins, ISG15 and RSAD2 — degrade viral RNA or stall its synthesis, while APOBEC3 deaminases and ADAR edit viral nucleic acid. The balance struck here sets whether an infection is cleared, becomes persistent, or drives the mutational drift underlying viral escape.

Viruses have no ribosomes or polymerases of their own for most steps, so converting a viral gene into protein or mature RNA depends on host transcription, RNA processing, translation and post-translational maturation — and on host factors that try to block each step. Represented here are the transcriptional machinery and elongation controls that read viral templates, including a general transcription factor, a cyclin T subunit and the 7SK complex components HEXIM1 and LARP7 that restrain it; RNA-binding proteins such as PTBP1, PCBP2, DHX9 and CSDE1 that direct IRES use, frameshifting and RNA stability; and cap-independent initiation factors including eIF3 subunits, DENR and MCTS1. Downstream, signal peptidase, glucosidase and glycosyltransferase activities mature viral envelope glycoproteins, and furin cleaves them. Opposing all of this, interferon-induced restriction factors and numerous TRIM ubiquitin ligases intercept viral messages and proteins, making this pathway the main battleground of antiviral defence.

Viruses carry no ribosomes, so viral mRNA must be translated into viral protein by the host's own machinery, and this pathway covers that hijacking and the cell's attempts to block it. The genes reflect the unconventional initiation strategies viruses depend on: internal ribosome entry driven by RNA-binding proteins such as PTBP1, PCBP2 and CSDE1, cap-independent and reinitiation events served by DENR, MCTS1 and EIF2D, and core scanning through the multisubunit eIF3 complex. Programmed ribosomal frameshifting and stop-codon readthrough, illustrated by the antizymes and the retrotransposon-derived PEG10, allow one transcript to yield several products. Against this, interferon-induced IFIT1 sequesters improperly capped viral mRNA and SHFL restricts frameshifting, while EIF2AK4 links amino acid stress to translational shutdown. The balance struck here determines whether an infection produces progeny virions or stalls.

Viruses have no biosynthetic machinery of their own for maturing envelope and structural proteins, so they borrow the host secretory pathway, and proteolytic maturation of viral polyproteins and glycoprotein precursors is the step that converts inert precursors into fusion-competent, infectious particles. Cleavage by the proprotein convertase furin at multibasic sites, and signal peptide removal by the endoplasmic reticulum signal peptidase complex, prime viral glycoproteins for membrane fusion; the efficiency of this cleavage is a determinant of tropism and virulence for influenza and coronaviruses.
