Accompanying the cleavage steps are calnexin-assisted folding and quality control, oligosaccharyltransferase-linked trimming by glucosidase and mannosidases, and branching and terminal sialylation by GlcNAc-, fucosyl- and sialyltransferases, which build the glycan shield that masks antibody epitopes. Host kinases and ADP-ribosyltransferases modulate these events, making the pathway both a requirement for viral fitness and a target for antiviral intervention.

Transcription of a viral genome inside an infected cell depends on host machinery, and this collection captures both the factors viruses recruit and the host restriction that opposes them. Retroviral and lentiviral promoters are read by host RNA polymerase II with general factors such as GTF2B and the transcription factors USF1, USF2 and UBP1 binding viral enhancer elements, while CCNT2 provides the cyclin partner of the P-TEFb kinase that releases paused polymerase for elongation; HEXIM1 and LARP7 sequester that kinase in the inactive 7SK complex, setting the balance between viral latency and active replication. Opposing this, an array of TRIM ubiquitin ligases, the nuclear body protein SP100 and the interferon-induced IFITM3 restrict viral gene expression, linking the process to innate antiviral immunity. The interplay determines whether an integrated provirus stays silent or produces virus, a central question in HIV persistence.

Reproductive behaviour covers the mating, courtship, copulatory and parental acts by which animals actually reproduce, and it is organised by neuroendocrine circuits that read hormonal state and translate it into motivated action. Oxytocin and vasopressin with their receptors underlie pair bonding, mating and maternal care; dopaminergic and serotonergic components including tyrosine hydroxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, D1-type receptors and the serotonin transporter supply the reward and arousal signals that drive sexual motivation and ejaculatory control. Steroid and thyroid hormone receptors and the coactivator NCOA1 make these circuits responsive to gonadal and metabolic status, while GABAergic and tachykinin signalling shape the output. Peripheral contributors act on the gametes themselves, with semenogelin and protease inhibitors of seminal plasma governing coagulation and sperm function. Disruption alters libido, mating success, and maternal nurturing, linking this behaviour to fertility and to neuropsychiatric conditions affecting social bonding.

Some peptides are built by dedicated enzymes rather than by ribosomes, and in human cells the dominant product of this nonribosomal peptide biosynthetic route is glutathione, the tripeptide that buffers oxidative and electrophilic stress. Glutamate-cysteine ligase, a catalytic and a modifier subunit, joins glutamate to cysteine, and glutathione synthetase adds glycine; gamma-glutamyl transferases break the bond again at the cell surface to recycle precursors through the gamma-glutamyl cycle. Cysteine supply limits the whole process, which is why cystine and glutamate transporters, including the exchanger SLC7A11, appear alongside the synthetic enzymes, and why NFE2L2 coordinately induces them when cells sense oxidant load. Loss of this capacity leaves cells vulnerable to peroxides, xenobiotics and ferroptotic death, and inherited deficiencies produce haemolytic anaemia with neurological disease. A siderophore-type ligase and 2-oxoglutarate-derived chemistry point to related non-template amide bond formation.

Cells and whole organisms must match lipid synthesis, storage, transport and breakdown to nutritional state, and this collection of controls over lipid metabolic processes is how that balance is set. Its failure underlies obesity, fatty liver, dyslipidaemia, atherosclerosis and insulin resistance. Much of the regulation is transcriptional: sterol-responsive factors with their escort and retention partners SCAP and INSIG govern cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis, nuclear receptors including PPARs, LXRs, the bile acid receptor NR1H4, RXRA and HNF4A tune oxidation and bile acid output, and coregulators such as NCOR1, PPARGC1A and sirtuins set their activity. Superimposed are hormonal and kinase inputs from insulin signalling, AMPK and mTOR complexes, lipid droplet proteins of the perilipin and CIDE families with the lipase ATGL and its activator ABHD5, apolipoproteins and lipoprotein receptors that direct circulating lipid, and numerous microRNAs including the cholesterol-linked miR-33.

regulation of fatty acid metabolic process covers the control layer that decides whether a cell burns fatty acids or stores and synthesises them, matching lipid flux to nutritional state. It sets the balance struck between feeding and fasting in liver, adipose tissue, heart and muscle, and its derangement produces hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance and lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. Transcriptional control dominates: the PPAR family with PGC-1α drives β-oxidation and mitochondrial fatty acid entry through CPT1A, while SREBP-1c with SCAP, INSIG proteins and ChREBP drives lipogenesis, and liver X receptors and NCOR1 tune both. Superimposed are insulin signalling through IRS-AKT, AMPK and sirtuin-dependent nutrient sensing, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and malonyl-CoA turnover, microRNAs such as miR-33a, and secreted regulators including adiponectin, ANGPTL4 and the apolipoprotein C cluster that govern lipoprotein lipase activity and fatty acid delivery to tissues.

Cells must match fatty acid synthesis, oxidation and storage to nutrient supply and energy demand, and this regulatory layer sets the balance. It matters because failure of the controls produces hepatic steatosis, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and lipotoxic damage to heart and muscle. Nuclear receptors and lipogenic transcription factors -- PPARA, PPARD, PPARG with its coactivator PPARGC1A, the liver X receptors, and SREBF1 under SCAP and INSIG control -- switch the transcriptional programme between fat burning and fat making. Insulin acting through IRS and AKT, AMP-activated kinase subunits, sirtuins and the CPT1A/malonyl-CoA node provide acute regulation, while secreted signals such as adiponectin, ANGPTL4 and apolipoprotein-mediated modulation of lipase activity coordinate tissues. Several microRNAs, notably MIR33A, tune the same targets post-transcriptionally, and peroxisomal import and processing components extend the control to very-long-chain fatty acid handling.

Steroid metabolism has to be held within narrow limits: cholesterol supply must match membrane and hormone demand, bile acid synthesis must not exceed what the liver can tolerate, and adrenal and gonadal steroid output must track endocrine signals. This regulatory layer sets those rates. Sterol sensing in the ER, through SCAP, INSIG proteins and the site-1 and site-2 proteases that release SREBP transcription factors, tunes cholesterol uptake via the LDL receptor and de novo lipid synthesis, while nuclear receptors including the bile acid receptor NR1H4, NR5A1 and the glucocorticoid receptor control CYP7A1, STAR and downstream steroidogenic genes. Trophic hormone signalling through MC2R, LHCGR and PKA drives cholesterol delivery to mitochondria for pregnenolone formation, and several microRNAs impose additional restraint. Failure of this control underlies hypercholesterolaemia, cholestatic and gallstone disease, and disorders of adrenal steroid production.

cytokine-mediated signaling pathway is how cells talk to one another during immune responses, blood cell production and inflammation: a secreted cytokine binds its surface receptor and the message is converted into changes in gene transcription, survival or motility. It defines immune cell identity and behaviour, and its failures produce immunodeficiency, autoinflammatory disease, cytokine storm and leukaemia. The genes span the major receptor families and their downstream logic — interleukin, interferon and colony-stimulating factor receptors coupled through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, with SOCS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN2 imposing negative feedback; tumour necrosis factor and interleukin-1 family receptors acting through TRAF adaptors, IRAK kinases and MYD88 to activate NF-κB or caspase-8-dependent death; chemokines and their G protein-coupled receptors directing leukocyte trafficking; and inflammasome components maturing IL-1β. Hormone-like ligands including leptin, growth hormone, erythropoietin and thrombopoietin use the same receptor architecture to control metabolism and haematopoiesis.

Cells coordinate immune defence, inflammation, haematopoiesis and tissue repair by secreting cytokines and reading them at the surface, and this pathway covers that whole transmission process, from ligand binding through to changes in gene transcription. It spans the major cytokine families and their receptors — interleukins and their shared chains such as IL2RG and IL6ST, type I, II and III interferons, colony-stimulating factors, erythropoietin and thrombopoietin, chemokines with their G protein-coupled and atypical scavenger receptors, and the tumour necrosis factor superfamily. Downstream, receptor-associated JAK kinases phosphorylate STAT transcription factors, while TRAF and IRAK adaptors converge on NF-kB and MAP kinase activation; SOCS proteins, phosphatases and deubiquitinases such as TNFAIP3 and CYLD impose negative feedback. Loss of individual components produces immunodeficiency or cytopenia, whereas failed restraint underlies autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, and the same receptors are the targets of biologic anti-cytokine therapy.

Nerve impulse transmission is the core operation of the nervous system: an electrical signal is generated and propagated along an axon and then converted into chemical signalling at a synapse so that information reaches the next cell. Voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN1A and SCN2A with their beta subunits set excitability and are classic loci for epilepsy and pain disorders, while potassium and HCN channels, a leak sodium channel complex built around NALCN with UNC79 and UNC80, and calcium channel subunits shape firing rate and repolarisation. Ankyrin-G, beta-IV spectrin and contactin-associated proteins organise the axon initial segment and nodes of Raxon, and myelin components support saltatory conduction. Ionotropic glutamate and acetylcholine receptors, glycine receptors, neuropeptides such as orexin and enkephalin, and their G protein-coupled receptors carry the signal across synapses. Loss of these components produces epilepsy, ataxia, neuropathy and disordered nociception.

Neurons encode and propagate information as action potentials, all-or-none voltage spikes generated when depolarization opens voltage-gated sodium channels and terminated as potassium channels repolarize the membrane. The genes here cover that cycle: sodium channel pore and accessory subunits such as SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN9A and SCN4B, a broad set of potassium channels including Kv1 and Kv4 members, KCNQ3, two-pore leak channels and large-conductance channel beta subunits, the hyperpolarization-activated HCN1 that sets rhythmic firing, and the NALCN sodium leak channel with its UNC79/UNC80 partners that fixes resting potential and basal excitability. Ankyrin-G clusters sodium channels at the axon initial segment and nodes, while FGF12 and neuromodulatory receptors tune channel availability and firing threshold. Mutations in these components shift excitability in either direction, producing epilepsies, pain and channel-related movement and sensory disorders, and underlie sensory transduction and neuronal rhythm generation.

Blood pressure and regional blood flow depend on continuous adjustment of arterial calibre, and this set covers the signals that set how strongly and how often vessels narrow. Vasoconstriction is tuned by circulating and locally released agonists acting on smooth muscle G protein-coupled receptors: adrenergic receptors for sympathetic catecholamines, angiotensin II via AGTR1, vasopressin, endothelins, thromboxane, serotonin, histamine and substance P, opposed by vasodilatory inputs such as adrenomedullin and the ACE2 arm of the renin-angiotensin system. Downstream, RhoA and its regulators, calcium handling by plasma membrane pumps and cation channels, and potassium channel subunits set myosin light chain phosphorylation and contractile tone. Peptide-generating enzymes including ACE, ECE1 and DBH supply the ligands. Dysregulation underlies hypertension, pulmonary arterial hypertension (as with BMPR2 loss), vasospasm and impaired tissue perfusion, linking this control to cardiovascular and renal homeostasis.

Proprioception is the body's internal sense of limb position, muscle length and movement, carried by specialized sensory neurons whose endings sit in muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint capsules. Without it, coordinated gait, posture and limb placement fail even when vision and strength are intact, which is why sensory ataxia rather than weakness dominates conditions affecting these afferents; loss of frataxin in Friedreich ataxia degenerates exactly this population of dorsal root ganglion neurons. The genes here span the specification and function of proprioceptive afferents: transcriptional regulators including a POU-domain factor and a homeobox gene that help set sensory neuron identity and connectivity in the dorsal root ganglion and spinal cord, an ion channel component contributing to mechanically activated currents in these endings, and MECP2, whose loss disturbs sensory as well as central circuits. The pathway links mechanotransduction to motor control reflexes.

Nociception is how the body detects stimuli that threaten tissue damage and converts them into the conscious experience of pain, a protective system whose loss leaves people injuring themselves unnoticed and whose sensitization produces chronic and neuropathic pain. Transduction begins at peripheral sensory endings, where heat- and irritant-sensing channels such as TRPV1 and TRPA1, acid-sensing ASIC3 and purinergic P2RX receptors depolarize the terminal; voltage-gated sodium channels SCN9A and SCN11A then set firing threshold, and mutations in them cause congenital insensitivity or inherited pain syndromes, as do defects in the transcription factor PRDM12. Neurotrophin signalling through NGF and its receptor NTRK1 specifies and maintains these neurons. Inflammatory mediators including TNF, prostaglandins and chemokines lower thresholds after injury, while opioid receptors, endogenous enkephalin and nociceptin peptides, and potassium channels provide the inhibitory arm that dampens transmission centrally.

response to pheromone is the cellular detection of chemical signals released by one individual that alter the physiology or behaviour of another, the basis of social and reproductive chemosensation in mammals. In humans the pathway is largely vestigial but its parts remain: the vomeronasal type 1 receptors are G protein-coupled receptors of the sensory neuron surface, several of them pseudogenes, coupled through G protein subunits such as GNG8 to depolarisation of chemosensory neurons and transmission to the accessory olfactory system. Downstream, such signals influence hypothalamic control of mating, aggression, territorial marking and oestrous timing rather than conscious odour perception. The pathway illustrates how sensory receptor repertoires expand and decay with lifestyle, and it sits alongside olfactory and taste reception as one branch of chemical sensing coupled to neuroendocrine output.

Pheromones are chemical signals passed between members of a species, and the response to pheromone describes how a cell or animal changes its behaviour, secretion or gene expression when it detects one. In mammals this chemosensation is largely the province of the vomeronasal organ, and the vomeronasal type 1 receptors here (VN1R1 through VN1R5, plus a pseudogene relic) are the G protein-coupled detectors expressed by its sensory neurons, coupled through G protein subunits such as GNG8 to depolarising transduction cascades. Downstream, these signals reach accessory olfactory and hypothalamic circuits that govern mating, aggression, territorial marking and maternal behaviour, and can influence neuroendocrine output. In humans the system is much reduced, with most vomeronasal receptor genes pseudogenised, so this biology is best understood as an evolutionarily contracted chemosensory route for social and reproductive cues.

Citrulline is made by condensing carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine, and its formation is the committed step that channels waste nitrogen into the urea cycle. In periportal liver hepatocytes, mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 fixes ammonia into carbamoyl phosphate, and ornithine transcarbamylase transfers the carbamoyl group to ornithine; the citrulline produced is exported to the cytosol for argininosuccinate synthesis and ultimately urea. Intestinal enterocytes run the same chemistry to supply circulating citrulline that the kidney converts to arginine. Loss of either enzyme causes hyperammonaemia with neurological crisis in the newborn, the commonest inherited urea cycle disorders. The related pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase links this chemistry to proline and ornithine supply from glutamate, while the cytosolic multienzyme carbamoyl phosphate source serves pyrimidine synthesis, placing citrulline formation at the junction of nitrogen disposal, arginine provision and nucleotide metabolism.

Lactate formation is the terminal step of glycolysis when pyruvate cannot be fully oxidised, regenerating NAD+ so that ATP production can continue without oxygen. It supports contracting muscle, proliferating cells and the Warburg-type metabolism of tumours, and the lactate produced is exported as fuel and as a signalling molecule for neighbouring cells. Lactate dehydrogenase isoforms carry out the reduction itself, including a testis-enriched form active in sperm energetics. Flux into the pathway is set upstream: a phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-bisphosphatase enzyme controls the fructose-2,6-bisphosphate signal that drives glycolytic rate, while a circadian transcriptional repressor links lactate output to daily metabolic cycles. The presence of DJ-1 connects this chemistry to glycation and oxidative stress control, a reminder that reactive glycolytic intermediates must be managed as lactate is made.

N-acetylneuraminate catabolic process dismantles sialic acid, the terminal sugar of most cell-surface glycans, so that its carbon can be recycled into glycolysis rather than accumulating. This matters because sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids turn over constantly in lysosomes, and the freed sialic acid must be degraded or re-used; blocked flux through this route causes sialic acid storage and free sialic acid excretion, while the same enzymes let cells salvage amino sugars from dietary and mucosal sources. Mechanistically, an aldolase cleaves N-acetylneuraminate to pyruvate and N-acetylmannosamine, which is epimerised to N-acetylglucosamine, phosphorylated by NAGK, deacetylated by AMDHD2, and finally deaminated by glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases to fructose-6-phosphate. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of glycan turnover, hexosamine biosynthesis and central carbon metabolism, balancing supply of UDP-sugar precursors against catabolic disposal.

Sialic acid released from turned-over glycoproteins and glycolipids must be disposed of, and N-acetylneuraminate catabolism is the route that dismantles it and returns its carbon to central metabolism. The free sugar is cleaved by an N-acetylneuraminate pyruvate lyase into pyruvate and N-acetylmannosamine; an epimerase interconverts that sugar with N-acetylglucosamine, which is phosphorylated by N-acetylglucosamine kinase, deacetylated by a GlcNAc-6-phosphate deacetylase, and finally deaminated by glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases to fructose-6-phosphate plus ammonia, feeding glycolysis. The same intermediates are shared with amino sugar salvage and with the hexosamine pathway that supplies UDP-GlcNAc for glycosylation, so flux here sets the balance between recycling and degradation. Lysosomal or transport defects upstream cause sialic acid storage disease, and the pathway also governs how much free sialic acid is available for re-use on newly made glycans.

Isopentenyl diphosphate is the five-carbon building block from which every isoprenoid is made, and the mevalonate pathway is how animal cells build it from acetyl-CoA. Everything downstream depends on this output: cholesterol and the steroid hormones and bile acids derived from it, dolichol for protein glycosylation, ubiquinone for respiration, heme A, and the farnesyl and geranylgeranyl groups that anchor Ras-family GTPases and other prenylated proteins to membranes. HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA reductase produce mevalonate, the committed and rate-limiting step and the target of statins; mevalonate kinase, phosphomevalonate kinase and the diphosphomevalonate decarboxylase then phosphorylate and decarboxylate it to the final product. Flux is tuned to sterol supply through SREBP-driven transcription and regulated degradation of the reductase. Partial loss of mevalonate kinase causes periodic fever with hyperimmunoglobulinemia D, linking the route to inflammatory signalling.

Although labelled as fucose breakdown, the genes assembled here carry out the opposite chemistry: transfer of fucose from GDP-fucose onto glycans, the step that terminates and decorates N-glycans, O-glycans and glycolipids. This fucosylation determines the ABO-related H and Lewis blood group antigens on red cells and secretions, builds the sialyl-Lewis x ligands that let leukocytes roll on endothelial selectins, and installs the core fucose on antibody Fc regions that tunes antibody-dependent cytotoxicity. Distinct enzymes specialise by linkage: alpha1,2 transferases create H antigen and secretor status, alpha1,3/1,4 enzymes generate Lewis and selectin ligands, and core alpha1,6 fucosylation modifies growth factor receptors and immunoglobulins. Loss of these activities impairs leukocyte recruitment and Notch-dependent signalling, while their overexpression accompanies tumour progression and metastatic spread. GDP-fucose supply from salvage and de novo routes limits the whole process.

Five-carbon sugars are handled by a small set of kinases, dehydrogenases and isomerases that feed them into central carbohydrate metabolism, and pentose metabolism is the collective name for that traffic. Its main output is ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis, together with the NADPH that supports reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase perform the oxidative steps, while ribose-5-phosphate isomerase and ribokinase interconvert and salvage the sugars themselves. Dietary and metabolic pentoses such as xylulose and L-xylulose are dealt with by dedicated kinases and a carbonyl reductase, and UXS1 decarboxylates UDP-glucuronate to UDP-xylose for proteoglycan and glycan assembly, linking this chemistry to glycosylation of matrix and muscle proteins. Loss of the oxidative branch causes haemolytic anaemia on oxidant stress; defects in xylose handling produce pentosuria or disordered glycosylation.

Phenol-containing compound catabolic process is the set of reactions that inactivate and dispose of hydroxylated aromatic molecules, a class that includes the catecholamine neurotransmitters, thyroid hormones, tyrosine-derived metabolites and many dietary and drug phenols. It matters because signalling by dopamine, noradrenaline and thyroxine is terminated by degradation rather than by dilution, and because incomplete breakdown of tyrosine catabolites is directly toxic. Monoamine oxidases and aldehyde dehydrogenase oxidise the amine side chain, catechol O-methyltransferase and the sulfotransferases mask the phenolic hydroxyl for excretion, the dopamine transporter delivers substrate into cells for turnover, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase and related copper monooxygenases interconvert the catecholamines. Iodothyronine deiodinases perform the analogous inactivation of thyroid hormone, while fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase completes ring cleavage in tyrosine degradation; its loss causes hepatorenal tyrosinemia. The pathway therefore links neurotransmitter clearance, endocrine control and xenobiotic detoxification.

Phenolic compounds — catecholamines, thyroid hormones and tyrosine-derived metabolites — must be inactivated and cleared once they have acted, and this catabolic route does that work. It terminates dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline signalling and sets how long these transmitters persist in brain and at sympathetic synapses, which is why its enzymes are targets of antidepressants and of drugs for Parkinson's disease. A dopamine transporter first retrieves the amine, monoamine oxidases A and B oxidatively deaminate it to an aldehyde that an aldehyde dehydrogenase converts to acid, while catechol O-methyltransferase caps the ring hydroxyl and sulfotransferases conjugate phenols for excretion. Iodothyronine deiodinases strip iodine from thyroxine to activate or inactivate thyroid hormone locally, and fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase closes the tyrosine degradation route — its loss causes hereditary tyrosinaemia with liver and kidney damage.

Transsulfuration converts homocysteine into cysteine through the intermediate cystathionine, linking methionine metabolism to the supply of cysteine for glutathione, taurine and protein synthesis. It is the route by which cells dispose of homocysteine, and its failure raises homocysteine to levels that damage vessels and connective tissue: loss of cystathionine beta-synthase causes classical homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, skeletal abnormality and thrombosis. Cystathionine beta-synthase condenses homocysteine with serine, and cystathionine gamma-lyase cleaves the product to cysteine, ammonia and alpha-ketobutyrate; both enzymes also generate hydrogen sulfide, a gaseous signalling molecule affecting vascular tone. A sulfurtransferase contributes to persulfide and sulfide handling downstream, while folate-dependent one-carbon metabolism feeds the remethylation branch that competes for homocysteine. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of sulfur amino acid catabolism, antioxidant capacity and one-carbon flux.

Cells recycle nicotinamide, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide riboside back into NAD rather than building the dinucleotide from tryptophan, and this pyridine nucleotide salvage supplies most of the NAD that redox metabolism, sirtuins, PARPs and CD38 consume. Because NAD is continuously cleaved by those consumers, salvage sets the cellular NAD pool and with it glycolytic and mitochondrial flux, deacetylase-dependent gene regulation, DNA repair capacity and axon survival; loss of the axonal adenylyltransferase NMNAT2 triggers Wallerian-type degeneration, and declining salvage capacity is a feature of ageing tissue. NAMPT phosphoribosylates nicotinamide, NAPRT handles nicotinic acid, and nicotinamide riboside kinases phosphorylate the riboside; the resulting mononucleotides are adenylylated by nuclear, cytosolic and mitochondrial NMNAT isoforms, with NADSYN1 amidating the acid route. Compartment-specific isoforms let each organelle maintain its own NAD supply.

Cells extend saturated fatty acyl chains two carbons at a time in the endoplasmic reticulum, producing the long and very-long-chain species that membranes, sphingolipids and specialized lipids require. The condensation step that commits a malonyl-CoA unit to the growing chain is carried out by a family of elongases with distinct substrate preferences: one favours palmitate and shorter chains, others act on already long substrates to make the C24 and beyond acyl groups found in ceramides, myelin lipids and retinal and skin barrier lipids. A ketoacyl reductase supplies the first reduction of the four-step cycle. Output from this elongation determines membrane fluidity, skin barrier competence and myelin composition, and defects in individual elongases cause macular dystrophy, spinocerebellar ataxia and ichthyosis. The route also links dietary and de novo lipogenic flux to the long-chain pools that downstream desaturation and complex lipid synthesis draw upon.

Arachidonate metabolism is the route by which a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid stored in membrane phospholipids is released and converted into the lipid mediators that drive inflammation, pain, fever, platelet aggregation, bronchial and vascular tone. Phospholipases such as PLA2G4A liberate arachidonate from phospholipids, while diacylglycerol lipases and hydrolases including MGLL and FAAH generate or clear it from endocannabinoid precursors. Three enzymatic branches then act: cyclooxygenases PTGS1 and PTGS2 with downstream synthases make prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane; lipoxygenases from ALOX5 to the skin-specific ALOX12B and ALOXE3 make leukotrienes, hydroxy fatty acids and barrier lipids; and cytochrome P450s of the CYP2C, CYP2J and CYP4F families make epoxy- and hydroxyeicosatrienoic acids affecting renal and vascular function. Glutathione peroxidases and epoxide hydrolase terminate signalling. This chemistry is the target of aspirin, NSAIDs and anti-leukotriene drugs, and its dysregulation underlies asthma, thrombosis, ichthyosis and tumour-associated inflammation.

Leukotriene biosynthetic process builds the lipid mediators that drive bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, vascular leak and leukocyte recruitment, making it the pathway behind asthma and other allergic inflammation and the target of drugs such as zileuton and montelukast. It begins when phospholipases release arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, after which 5-lipoxygenase, docked at the nuclear envelope by its activating protein, converts it to the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. That intermediate is then routed one of two ways: a hydrolase makes the chemotactic leukotriene B4, while conjugation to glutathione by leukotriene C4 synthase or related microsomal transferases yields the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which are exported by MRP1 and progressively trimmed by gamma-glutamyl transferases to LTD4 and LTE4. Expression is largely restricted to myeloid and mast cells, where receptor signalling through kinases including SYK triggers calcium-dependent enzyme translocation.

Leukotrienes are lipid mediators that drive bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and leukocyte recruitment, and their biosynthesis is the reason asthma and allergic inflammation are treated with drugs aimed at this route. Arachidonic acid is first released from membrane phospholipids by cytosolic and secreted phospholipases such as PLA2G4A, then presented by the membrane protein ALOX5AP to 5-lipoxygenase, which forms the unstable epoxide leukotriene A4. From there the pathway branches: LTA4H hydrolyses it to the chemotactic leukotriene B4, while LTC4 synthase and related microsomal glutathione transferases conjugate glutathione to make the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which ABCC1 exports and gamma-glutamyl transferases trim to LTD4. Output is largely a property of myeloid and mast cells, where receptor and kinase input including SYK couples immune activation to mediator production. Excess flux underlies aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease and chronic airway inflammation.

Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators that set vascular tone, platelet behaviour, fever, pain sensitivity and the inflammatory response, and the cyclooxygenase pathway is how they are made from arachidonic acid released from membrane phospholipids. The committed step is carried out by prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase, in constitutive (PTGS1) and inducible (PTGS2) forms, which converts arachidonate to the unstable endoperoxides PGG2 and PGH2; this is the step blocked by aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Downstream terminal synthases then decide which mediator a given cell makes: PTGES and PTGES2 for PGE2, PTGDS and the haematopoietic HPGDS for PGD2, and PTGIS for prostacyclin. Because these enzymes are distributed differently across endothelium, platelets, mast cells and brain, the same substrate yields opposing outcomes, and selective inhibition of one branch shifts the balance toward thrombosis, gastric injury or resolution of inflammation.

Oxygenation of arachidonic and related polyunsaturated fatty acids by lipoxygenases generates the hydroperoxide intermediates from which leukotrienes, lipoxins and hepoxilins are made, giving cells a second branch of eicosanoid signalling alongside the cyclooxygenase route. The products drive leukocyte recruitment and bronchoconstriction in asthma and allergic inflammation, and also the resolution phase that ends it, so the balance of these enzymes shapes whether inflammation persists. A phospholipase releases free fatty acid from membrane phospholipid to start the process; ALOX5 initiates leukotriene synthesis in myeloid cells, ALOX12 acts in platelets, and ALOX15 oxygenates both free and esterified substrates. Glutathione peroxidases reduce the hydroperoxides, limiting flux and protecting membranes from lipid peroxidation, linking this chemistry to ferroptotic cell death. Epidermal isoforms including ALOXE3 and ALOX12B instead build the skin permeability barrier, and their loss causes congenital ichthyosis.

Arachidonic acid released from membranes can be oxidised by cytochrome P450 enzymes instead of by cyclooxygenases or lipoxygenases, and this epoxygenase branch generates epoxyeicosatrienoic acids and their hydrolysis products, the dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acids, along with hydroxylated eicosanoids. These lipid mediators relax vascular smooth muscle, act as endothelium-derived hyperpolarising factors, modulate renal sodium handling and blood pressure, and temper inflammatory signalling, so altered flux through this route is linked to hypertension, ischaemic injury and vascular disease. The enzymes involved span several P450 families: CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP2J2 favour epoxidation across the double bonds, while CYP4A11 and CYP4F2 hydroxylate the terminal carbon to yield 20-HETE with largely opposing vascular effects. Many of these same monooxygenases, including CYP1A2 and CYP2E1, handle drug and xenobiotic oxidation, tying eicosanoid production to hepatic metabolic capacity and to common pharmacogenetic variation.

Galactolipid metabolism covers the synthesis and breakdown of glycolipids carrying galactose or N-acetylgalactosamine, chemistry that matters most in the nervous system because galactosylceramide and its sulfated derivative are the dominant lipids of compact myelin. UGT8 transfers galactose onto ceramide to make galactocerebroside, GAL3ST1 sulfates it to sulfatide, and FA2H supplies the 2-hydroxylated fatty acyl chains that give these lipids their unusual stability in the myelin sheath; the same products help organize oligodendrocyte and Schwann cell membranes and axo-glial junctions. Degradation runs the other way, with the lysosomal galactosylceramidase GALC releasing galactose from galactosylceramide and related glycosphingolipids. Loss of that enzyme causes Krabbe disease, a demyelinating leukodystrophy, while galactosyltransferases such as B3GALT2 and B4GALT3 extend glycolipid and glycoprotein sugar chains more broadly, linking this route to glycosphingolipid biosynthesis and membrane lipid turnover generally.

Glycolipid catabolism dismantles the sugar-bearing lipids of membranes, stripping terminal carbohydrates and then cleaving the lipid backbone so that ceramide, sphingosine and monosaccharides can be recycled. Most of the work is lysosomal and stepwise: sialidases remove sialic acid from gangliosides, beta-hexosaminidase A with its GM2 activator protein removes N-acetylgalactosamine, and glucocerebrosidase and galactosylceramidase cleave the final sugar from glucosyl- and galactosylceramide, while acid sphingomyelinase and alpha-galactosidase A handle related substrates. Accessory factors matter as much as the hydrolases: SCARB2 delivers GBA1 to the lysosome, mannose-6-phosphate receptors route newly made enzymes there, and SUMF1 activates the sulfatases. Loss of single steps produces the sphingolipidoses — Gaucher, Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff, Krabbe, Fabry, GM1 gangliosidosis — in which undegraded glycolipid accumulates and neurons degenerate, and reduced glucocerebrosidase activity also predisposes to Parkinson's disease.

Galactose catabolism converts dietary galactose, released mostly from the lactose in milk, into glucose-1-phosphate so it can enter glycolysis or glycogen synthesis. The route matters from the first days of life: infants depend on it to handle their principal sugar, and its failure causes galactosemia, with cataracts, liver damage and developmental injury from accumulated galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol. The classical Leloir steps are represented here — a mutarotase interconverting the anomers, a kinase phosphorylating galactose, a uridylyltransferase exchanging the sugar onto UDP, an epimerase regenerating UDP-glucose, and a phosphoglucomutase feeding the product into central carbon metabolism. Beta-galactosidase activity liberates terminal galactose from glycoconjugates and glycosphingolipids upstream of this, linking the pathway to lysosomal turnover, while UDP-galactose supply ties it back to glycosylation.

Alditol biosynthetic process covers the reduction of sugars to their polyol counterparts, of which the dominant human example is the production of glycerol from carbohydrate carbon. This matters for whole-body fuel handling: glycerol released by adipose tissue is a substrate for hepatic gluconeogenesis, and its synthesis in the fasting or insulin-resistant state links triglyceride turnover to blood glucose. The genes point specifically to glyceroneogenesis, in which the cytosolic and mitochondrial forms of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase divert pyruvate and amino acid carbon toward triose phosphates, aspartate aminotransferase feeds the malate-aspartate shuttle that supplies those precursors, and a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase completes the route by dephosphorylating the intermediate to free glycerol. Leptin signalling sets the hormonal context, tying polyol output to adipose energy stores and to the futile cycling of fatty acids that buffers lipotoxicity.

Alditols are sugar alcohols formed by reducing the carbonyl group of a monosaccharide, and the best known product of this route in mammals is glycerol, the backbone of triacylglycerols and a substrate that moves between fat and liver during fasting. The genes here point specifically at glyceroneogenesis: cytosolic and mitochondrial phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase divert oxaloacetate from non-carbohydrate precursors toward triose phosphates, aspartate aminotransferase feeds that carbon through the malate-aspartate shuttle, and a glycerol-3-phosphate phosphatase releases free glycerol. Leptin links the flux to whole-body energy status, since the balance between glycerol release and re-esterification of fatty acids in adipose tissue determines how much lipid escapes into the circulation. Distortion of this balance contributes to insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis and dyslipidaemia, placing alditol synthesis at the junction of gluconeogenic carbon flow and lipid storage.

Sugar alcohols such as glycerol and sorbitol are useful fuels only after they are converted into glycolytic intermediates, and alditol catabolism performs that conversion. It links adipose lipolysis to hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycolysis: glycerol released from triglyceride is phosphorylated by glycerol kinase and oxidised by a mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, feeding both the glycerophosphate shuttle and the triose phosphate pool, where triose-phosphate isomerase and a triokinase handle interconversion of dihydroxyacetone and glyceraldehyde units. Sorbitol dehydrogenase completes the polyol route by oxidising sorbitol to fructose, the second step of the pathway implicated in diabetic complications when flux through it is excessive. Loss of these activities causes glycerol intolerance and hyperglycerolaemia, and impaired sorbitol disposal contributes to osmotic damage in lens, nerve and kidney.

Triglyceride catabolism releases fatty acids from stored or circulating triesters of glycerol, supplying fuel for oxidation and substrate for membrane and signalling lipids. It operates in two arenas. In the gut and bloodstream, pancreatic lipases digest dietary fat while lipoprotein lipase, anchored to capillary endothelium by GPIHBP1 and modulated by apolipoproteins such as APOC2 (an activator) and APOC3 (an inhibitor), hydrolyses triglyceride carried in chylomicrons and VLDL; hepatic and endothelial lipases act on remnant particles. Inside adipocytes, sequential action of ATGL (PNPLA2) with its coactivator ABHD5, hormone-sensitive lipase, and monoacylglycerol lipase strips the glycerol backbone, controlled by PKA phosphorylation of perilipin at the lipid droplet surface. Loss of function produces severe hypertriglyceridaemia and pancreatitis, while impaired droplet lipolysis causes neutral lipid storage disease; the same reactions set fatty acid supply during fasting and exercise.

Most dietary tryptophan that is not used for protein synthesis is degraded along the kynurenine route, and this set covers its opening steps: conversion of L-tryptophan to N-formylkynurenine and then to L-kynurenine. The rate-limiting dioxygenases differ in context, with the hepatic enzyme TDO2 handling bulk amino acid turnover and the inducible IDO1 and IDO2 responding to interferon-gamma and other inflammatory signals in dendritic cells, macrophages and tumours. AFMID hydrolyses the formyl group to release kynurenine, and KYNU acts further downstream in the same route toward anthranilate and ultimately NAD precursors. Beyond nutrient catabolism, local tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation suppress effector T cells and promote regulatory T cell differentiation, which is why this chemistry is exploited for immune tolerance in pregnancy and by tumours evading immune attack, and why its metabolites are studied in neuroinflammation and mood disorders.

Lysine is an essential amino acid that cannot be recycled once its amino groups are removed, so excess lysine is degraded to acetyl-CoA for oxidation or ketogenesis. The main route, saccharopine-dependent lysine catabolism, condenses lysine with 2-oxoglutarate and proceeds through saccharopine, 2-aminoadipate semialdehyde, 2-aminoadipate and glutaryl-CoA, with AASS carrying the first bifunctional step, ALDH7A1 oxidising the semialdehyde, AADAT transaminating 2-aminoadipate, and GCDH dehydrogenating glutaryl-CoA; a shared 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase core contributes DLST and DLD, while PIPOX acts on pipecolate from the alternative route. The clinical importance is stark: loss of ALDH7A1 causes pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy through accumulation of a piperideine intermediate that sequesters vitamin B6, and GCDH deficiency causes glutaric aciduria with striatal injury. The pathway thus links amino acid disposal to mitochondrial energy metabolism and neurological health.

Polyamine synthesis consumes decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine and discards 5'-methylthioadenosine as a by-product; the methionine salvage route recovers the sulfur and carbon skeleton of that by-product and regenerates L-methionine, so that rapidly proliferating cells can keep making polyamines without draining their methionine and S-adenosylmethionine pools. It also clears methylthioadenosine itself, an inhibitor of methyltransferases and polyamine enzymes. The cycle begins with phosphorolysis of methylthioadenosine to methylthioribose-1-phosphate by MTAP, followed by isomerase, dehydratase, enolase-phosphatase and dioxygenase steps that convert the sugar to the 2-oxo acid, which is transaminated to methionine. MTAP lies in a chromosomal region frequently co-deleted with the CDKN2A tumour suppressor, and the resulting loss of salvage capacity leaves such tumours dependent on de novo methionine and sensitive to methyltransferase-directed treatment. The pathway ties sulfur amino acid economy to methylation and growth control.

Oxalate transport moves oxalate, a metabolic dead-end anion that the body cannot degrade, across epithelial membranes so it can be secreted into the gut and excreted in urine rather than accumulating. This matters because oxalate binds calcium avidly: when handling fails, calcium oxalate crystals form kidney stones and, in primary hyperoxaluria, deposit throughout the body and destroy renal function. The work is carried out largely by the SLC26 family of anion exchangers, which swap oxalate for chloride, sulfate or bicarbonate at intestinal and renal tubular brush borders; SLC26A6 and SLC26A1 dominate oxalate flux, while related members serve chloride, iodide and sulfate transport in thyroid, airway and cochlea. Upstream of transport, the peroxisomal enzyme AGXT limits how much oxalate is generated from glyoxylate in hepatocytes, tying this pathway to amino acid metabolism and systemic mineral balance.

Oxalate is a metabolic dead end in humans: it cannot be broken down, and it precipitates with calcium to form kidney stones, so handling it depends on moving it across epithelial membranes for excretion. This transport activity is carried largely by the SLC26 family of anion exchangers, which swap oxalate against chloride, sulfate or bicarbonate at the apical and basolateral surfaces of intestinal and renal tubular cells; SLC26A1 and SLC26A6 are the principal oxalate carriers, while other members of the family specialise in chloride, iodide or bicarbonate movement in the thyroid, airway, gut and inner ear. Alongside them, the liver enzyme AGXT limits how much oxalate is generated in the first place by transaminating glyoxylate, and its loss causes primary hyperoxaluria with progressive nephrocalcinosis. The pathway therefore links glyoxylate metabolism to epithelial anion secretion and stone risk.

Glucuronate metabolism links detoxification chemistry to sugar catabolism. Its best-known output is glucuronidation: UDP-glucuronosyltransferases such as UGT1A1 transfer glucuronic acid onto bilirubin, drugs, steroids and dietary phenols, converting them into water-soluble conjugates that the liver and gut can excrete. Loss of UGT1A1 activity causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, from mild Gilbert syndrome to the severe jaundice of Crigler-Najjar, and variation across the UGT1A genes shapes how individuals clear particular drugs. A deglucuronidating hydrolase activity, attributed to ABHD10, reverses acyl glucuronide formation and so tunes the balance. The remaining enzymes carry glucuronate through the glucuronate-xylulose route, reducing and decarboxylating it via L-gulonate and 3-keto-L-gulonate to xylitol and xylulose, which SORD, DCXR and a xylulokinase step feed back into the pentose phosphate pool, connecting uronic acid turnover to central carbohydrate metabolism and polyol handling.

catechol-containing compound catabolic process is the inactivation and clearance of catecholamines and related catechols, the chemistry that terminates dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline signalling and protects tissues from their reactive oxidation products. It sets how long a monoamine signal lasts at a synapse and how much of an ingested or circulating catechol survives first-pass metabolism, so its capacity shapes mood, movement, attention and blood pressure. Degradation proceeds by O-methylation, oxidative deamination by the outer mitochondrial membrane monoamine oxidases, and sulfonation by cytosolic sulfotransferases, with the dopamine transporter first recapturing transmitter from the extracellular space and dopamine beta-hydroxylase interconverting substrates within the biosynthetic route. Loss or variation of these steps produces monoamine excess states and behavioural phenotypes, and the same enzymes are the targets of MAO inhibitors and COMT inhibitors used in depression and Parkinson disease.

Catecholamines such as dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline must be cleared quickly once released, and the catabolism of catechol-containing compounds is how signalling is terminated and how these reactive molecules are kept from generating quinones and oxidative damage. Catechol-O-methyltransferase caps one hydroxyl of the catechol ring, monoamine oxidases A and B oxidatively deaminate the amine side chain at the outer mitochondrial membrane, and sulfotransferases of the SULT1A family conjugate sulfate to phenolic substrates including dopamine, generating excretable metabolites. A dopamine transporter provides the reuptake step that delivers transmitter back into neurons for degradation, coupling clearance to synaptic recovery. The same enzymes act on dietary catechols, catechol estrogens and drugs such as L-DOPA, which is why their inhibitors are used in Parkinson's disease and depression, and why variants affect prefrontal dopamine tone and blood pressure control.

Short-chain fatty acid catabolism breaks down aliphatic acids of fewer than six carbons, the fuels delivered by gut microbial fermentation and produced by the final rounds of mitochondrial beta-oxidation. It lets liver, colonic epithelium and muscle recover energy from butyrate and related acids and feeds their carbon into the citric acid cycle. Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase performs the first oxidation of butyryl-CoA, while propionate is handled by a separate carboxylation route in which propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunits, a methylmalonyl-CoA epimerase and downstream isomerisation convert it to succinyl-CoA, an anaplerotic entry point. Esterase activity releases free acids from esters, and phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase links the pathway to branched-chain lipid degradation. Inherited loss of these steps causes propionic acidemia and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, with organic acid accumulation, acidosis and neurological injury.

organophosphate metabolic process is the broad set of reactions that make, interconvert and break down phosphate-bearing organic molecules — nucleotides, sugar phosphates, phospholipids, phosphoinositides, coenzymes and cyclic nucleotide messengers. Because phosphorylated intermediates are the currency of both energy metabolism and signalling, this chemistry underwrites nearly every cellular activity, and inherited defects in individual steps cause glycolytic anaemias, mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, myopathies, and lipid storage and GPI-anchor deficiencies. The genes span glycolysis and the pentose phosphate route, purine and pyrimidine synthesis and salvage, nucleoside and nucleotide kinases and phosphatases, oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthase, NAD and coenzyme A biosynthesis, glycerolipid and cardiolipin assembly, sphingolipid turnover, GPI anchor construction, and the phosphoinositide cycle with its lipid kinases, phospholipases and inositol polyphosphate enzymes. Cyclases, phosphodiesterases and AMPK/mTOR components link this flux to hormonal and nutrient control.

Organophosphate metabolic process gathers the reactions that make, modify and break down phosphate-bearing organic molecules, which is most of the chemistry a cell uses to store energy, signal and build membranes. Its breadth is reflected in the genes: glycolytic and pentose phosphate enzymes plus mitochondrial ATP synthase and respiratory complex subunits handle phosphorylated sugars and ATP turnover; nucleoside and nucleotide kinases, phosphatases and nucleotidases (adenylate kinases, NME family, 5'-nucleotidases, ribonucleotide reductase) supply and balance nucleotide pools; phosphoinositide kinases and phosphatases such as PTEN, OCRL and the myotubularins, together with phospholipases, acyltransferases and choline/ethanolamine pathway enzymes, generate membrane lipids and lipid second messengers; adenylate and guanylate cyclases with cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases set cAMP and cGMP levels. Also included are GPI anchor assembly, coenzyme A and NAD synthesis, and sulfation. Defects across these routes cause mitochondrial disease, myopathy, nucleotide-pool disorders and cancer-associated growth signalling.

Glucuronate released from the turnover of glycosaminoglycans and from glucuronide conjugates is not discarded but fed back into central carbon metabolism, and this route converts it stepwise into D-xylulose 5-phosphate, an entry point to the pentose phosphate pathway. An aldo-keto reductase reduces glucuronate to L-gulonate, which is oxidised and decarboxylated to L-xylulose; a dicarbonyl/L-xylulose reductase and sorbitol dehydrogenase interconvert the xylulose and xylitol intermediates, and a xylulokinase phosphorylates D-xylulose to the sugar phosphate. The pathway therefore links uronic acid salvage to NADPH-generating and ribose-supplying metabolism, and it is the same chemistry that produces ascorbate in species able to synthesise it. Loss of the reductase step causes pentosuria, a benign condition marked by urinary L-xylulose, illustrating how these sugar interconversions govern renal handling of rare pentoses.

GDP-mannose metabolic process supplies the activated sugar donors that glycosylation depends on, converting mannose and fructose-6-phosphate into GDP-mannose and, from it, GDP-fucose. Without this route cells cannot properly build N-linked glycans, O-mannosyl glycans or fucosylated ligands, and the consequences are the congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 deficiency causes the commonest form, with cerebellar and multisystem disease, while GMPPB and GMPPA mutations produce dystroglycanopathy-type muscular dystrophy and alacrima-achalasia syndrome. The sequence runs from hexokinase and mannose phosphate isomerase through phosphomannomutase and GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase, with GMDS and GFUS diverting flux to fucose donors and a Golgi transporter importing GDP-fucose for fucosyltransferases; loss of that transporter impairs selectin ligand synthesis and leukocyte adhesion. The pathway thus links central carbohydrate metabolism to protein quality control, muscle integrity and immune cell trafficking.

GDP-mannose is the activated sugar donor that feeds nearly all protein glycosylation, and its metabolism is the supply line that keeps N-linked glycans, O-mannosylation and GPI anchors supplied with mannose. The route converts fructose-6-phosphate to mannose-6-phosphate via phosphomannose isomerase, isomerises it to mannose-1-phosphate through phosphomannomutase, and caps it with GTP using the GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase subunits GMPPA and GMPPB. A branch handled by GMDS and GFUS dehydrates and epimerises GDP-mannose into GDP-fucose, which SLC35C1 then imports into the Golgi for fucosyltransferases. Loss of these steps causes congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 deficiency is the commonest form, GMPPB mutations produce dystroglycanopathy with muscular dystrophy, and defective fucose transport impairs selectin ligand synthesis and leukocyte adhesion. Hexokinase and guanylate kinase link the pathway to glycolytic and nucleotide pools.

NAD+ metabolic process covers the synthesis, recycling and consumption of the central redox coenzyme that carries electrons in glycolysis, the TCA cycle and fatty acid oxidation, and that also serves as substrate for signalling enzymes. Cells replenish it two ways: de novo from tryptophan through the kynurenine route (IDO1, KMO, KYNU, QPRT) and by salvage of nicotinamide and nicotinamide riboside via NAMPT, NAPRT, NMRK kinases and the NMNAT isoforms that act in nucleus, cytosol and mitochondria. Consumers such as PARPs and sirtuin-linked deacetylation couple NAD+ levels to DNA damage responses and metabolic gene regulation, while SARM1-driven NAD+ destruction executes axon degeneration after injury. Malate-aspartate shuttle components and glycerophosphate dehydrogenases move reducing equivalents across the mitochondrial membrane, and NADK diverts the pool toward NADP+ for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Declining NAD+ accompanies aging, neurodegeneration and metabolic disease.

NAD+ is the electron carrier that makes catabolism possible, and this metabolic process covers both how cells build and destroy it and how they cycle it between oxidised and reduced states. Supply comes by two routes: de novo synthesis from tryptophan through the kynurenine pathway (IDO1, KMO, KYNU, HAAO, QPRT) and salvage of nicotinamide or nicotinamide riboside via NAMPT, NAPRT, NMRK kinases and the NMNAT adenylyltransferases, with NADSYN1 completing amidation and NADK producing NADP+. Consumption and turnover run through ADP-ribosylation and the SARM1 hydrolase, whose activation collapses axonal NAD+ and drives Wallerian degeneration. Redox balance is maintained by malate dehydrogenases, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases, transaminases and mitochondrial carriers that constitute the shuttles moving reducing equivalents across the inner membrane. Falling NAD+ availability impairs oxidative metabolism, sirtuin signalling and DNA repair, and underlies pellagra and axon loss.

NAD+ is consumed as well as recycled, and this catabolic branch covers the enzymes that cleave or divert it rather than use it as a redox carrier. How fast NAD+ is degraded sets the cellular NAD+ pool, and that pool governs sirtuin-dependent deacetylation, ADP-ribosylation, and the metabolic fitness of neurons and ageing tissue. SARM1 is the injury-activated NAD+ hydrolase whose engagement triggers axon degeneration after nerve damage, making its restraint the basis of axon-protective strategies. PARP14 consumes NAD+ to transfer ADP-ribose onto protein targets in immune and interferon-linked signalling. Nudix hydrolases cleave NAD(P)H to yield NMN or AMP, contributing to cofactor turnover and quality control, while methylation of nicotinamide shunts the salvage precursor away from resynthesis and out of the cell. Together these reactions balance NAD+ supply against demand.

Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate sits at the hub where glycolysis, gluconeogenesis and the sugar-rearranging arm of the pentose phosphate pathway meet, and its metabolic turnover determines whether three-carbon units are burned for ATP, rebuilt into glucose, or traded for the pentoses needed for nucleotide synthesis. Aldolase B cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to this triose plus dihydroxyacetone phosphate, and triosephosphate isomerase interconverts the two; the transketolase and transaldolase reactions, together with ribose-5-phosphate isomerase and ribulose-phosphate 3-epimerase, exchange it for erythrose-4-phosphate, ribose and ribulose phosphates. Triokinase/FMN cyclase and glycerate kinase feed in fructose- and glycerate-derived carbon, while cytosolic PEPCK and a mitochondrial dicarboxylate carrier link the node to gluconeogenic flux. Loss of individual steps produces defined metabolic disease, including hereditary fructose intolerance, triosephosphate isomerase deficiency with haemolytic anaemia, and transaldolase deficiency, underscoring how narrow the tolerance is for imbalance at this intermediate.

ribose phosphate metabolic process covers the making, interconversion and breakdown of phosphorylated ribose sugars and the nucleotides built on them, the currency that powers essentially every cellular transaction. It supplies ATP and GTP for work and signalling, purine and pyrimidine precursors for DNA and RNA, and cofactors such as NAD, FAD and PAPS. PRPP synthetases feed the de novo purine assembly line and the salvage enzymes HPRT1 and APRT, while nucleoside kinases, nucleotidases and deaminases balance synthesis against degradation toward urate. Most ATP itself comes from the glycolytic enzymes and the respiratory chain and ATP synthase subunits represented here, with adenylate kinases, NME phosphotransferases and AMPK sensing the resulting energy charge. Cyclic nucleotide cyclases and phosphodiesterases divert the same metabolites into second-messenger signalling. Defects cause gout, immunodeficiency, hemolytic anemia and mitochondrial disease.

Ribose phosphate metabolism sits at the junction of sugar breakdown and nucleotide supply: phosphorylated ribose sugars derived from glycolysis and the pentose phosphate route are activated to PRPP and used to build purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, which in turn become ATP, GTP, cyclic nucleotides and cofactors. The gene complement spans PRPP synthetases and their associated proteins, de novo purine synthesis enzymes such as PPAT, GART, PAICS, ATIC and ADSL, pyrimidine enzymes including CAD, DHODH and UMPS, and the salvage route through HPRT1, APRT, ADA and PNP. Alongside these sit the glycolytic enzymes that feed carbon in, and the machinery that produces and consumes the nucleotides themselves — respiratory complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, ATP synthase, adenylate and nucleoside-diphosphate kinases, adenylyl and guanylyl cyclases, phosphodiesterases and AMPK. Deficiencies cause gout, immunodeficiency, anaemia and neurodevelopmental disease, and the pathway is a standing target for antiproliferative drugs.

In humans the alkanesulfonate handled in quantity is taurine, and this pathway covers its synthesis from cysteine and its use downstream. Taurine supports bile acid conjugation, osmoregulation, calcium handling and antioxidant defence, and dietary or genetic shortfall is linked to retinal degeneration and cardiomyopathy in mammals. Cysteine dioxygenase oxidises cysteine to cysteine sulfinate, which cysteine sulfinic acid decarboxylase converts toward hypotaurine and then taurine; serine supplied by phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase feeds the upstream cysteine pool. Bile acid-CoA:amino acid N-acyltransferase then conjugates taurine to bile acids, giving the taurocholates that emulsify dietary lipid. Flavin-containing monooxygenases contribute sulfur and amine oxidation chemistry in the same hepatic setting, and growth hormone receptor signalling through STAT5A and STAT5B places the liver's capacity for this sulfur metabolism under endocrine control.

Choline sits at the junction of membrane lipid supply, one-carbon metabolism and cholinergic signalling, and the reactions that handle it determine whether the nutrient is burned for methyl groups, built into phospholipid, or recovered after neurotransmitter breakdown. The genes here cover transport into cells, hydrolytic release from choline-containing esters, and stepwise oxidation: choline dehydrogenase converts choline to betaine aldehyde, an aldehyde dehydrogenase yields betaine as a methyl donor and osmolyte, and dimethylglycine dehydrogenase carries the carbon onward into the folate-linked one-carbon pool. Butyrylcholinesterase clears choline esters in plasma and is the enzyme behind variable sensitivity to muscle relaxants such as succinylcholine, while a phosphodiesterase acting on glycerophosphocholine liberates free choline from membrane turnover. Inadequate choline handling manifests as hepatic steatosis, altered homocysteine methylation and disturbed osmotic balance in kidney.

Calcium-mediated signaling is the use of a transient rise in cytosolic Ca2+ as the message that couples a receptor at the cell surface to a change in what the cell does — contracting, secreting, proliferating, or switching on a transcriptional programme. It underlies the heartbeat and skeletal muscle contraction, lymphocyte activation, chemotaxis of leukocytes, and neuronal plasticity, and its dysregulation contributes to arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia, immunodeficiency and neurodegeneration. Chemokine and other G protein-coupled receptors, ionotropic glutamate and purinergic channels, and immune receptor complexes signalling through SYK, ZAP70 and phospholipase Cγ generate the signal; inositol trisphosphate receptors and ryanodine receptors release stores, ORAI1 and TRP channels admit extracellular Ca2+, and SERCA, the sodium–calcium exchanger and plasma membrane pumps end it. Downstream, calmodulin, CaMKII, protein kinase C and the phosphatase calcineurin acting on NFAT convert the ion flux into lasting cellular responses.

B cell mediated immunity is the effector arm of humoral immunity: the production of antibodies of appropriate class and affinity, and the downstream destruction or clearance of what those antibodies bind. It protects against extracellular bacteria, viruses and toxins, and its failure produces immunodeficiency with recurrent infection, while its misdirection produces autoantibody disease. The genes span the whole output chain. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable and constant regions supply the antibody repertoire itself; AICDA acting with uracil processing, mismatch repair and non-homologous end joining factors such as UNG, MSH2, LIG4 and the shieldin complex drives somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination. T cell help through CD40, CD40LG and cytokines including IL4, IL21 and IL10, with BCL6 and BATF, licenses germinal centre reactions. Secreted antibody is then translated into effector action by Fc receptors and the complement cascade, from C1q through the membrane attack complex, under regulators such as CD55 and CFI.

B cell mediated immunity covers the effector arm of humoral defence: antibody production, isotype diversification, and the downstream systems that translate antibody binding into pathogen clearance. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain constant and variable segments dominate here, and with them the machinery of class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation — AICDA deaminates cytosine in switched loci, uracil-DNA glycosylase and mismatch repair proteins process the lesion, and non-homologous end joining with 53BP1, RIF1 and the shieldin complex resolves the resulting breaks. Costimulation through CD40 and its ligand plus cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21 and IL-10 direct which isotype is made, while BCL6 and BATF shape germinal centre fate. Secreted antibody then engages Fcγ and Fcε receptors and the complement cascade, from C1q recognition to the lytic C5b-C9 pore, with regulators like CD55, CD46 and factor I restraining self-damage. Defects produce hyper-IgM syndromes, antibody deficiency and lupus-like autoimmunity.

Cells survive only by holding their internal chemistry within narrow limits, and cellular homeostasis is the collective machinery that does so: buffering ion concentrations, metal availability, redox state and pH against constant flux across membranes. The genes here span the major regulated variables. Calcium is handled by SERCA and plasma-membrane pumps, ryanodine and inositol-trisphosphate receptors, store-operated STIM proteins and the mitochondrial uniporter with its MICU gatekeepers. Sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate are set by Na/K-ATPase subunits, cation-chloride cotransporters, WNK kinases, anion exchangers and TRP and CLC channels, while vacuolar ATPase subunits acidify endolysosomes. Iron and copper traffic through transferrin receptors, ferritin, ferroportin, hepcidin and ATP7A/B; zinc through SLC30 and SLC39 families; oxidative balance through peroxiredoxins, thioredoxins, glutathione enzymes and NRF2. Loss of such control underlies neurodegeneration, cardiac arrhythmia, iron-overload and lysosomal storage disease, and links this biology to stress responses, secretion and cell death.

Body fluids that bathe epithelial surfaces — mucus, saliva, tears, airway lining fluid, milk, semen, plasma — carry a chemical defence that kills or restrains microbes before infection is established, and this antimicrobial humoral response is that layer of immunity. It is mostly secreted effectors rather than cells: alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, lysozyme, lactoferrin, bactericidal permeability-increasing protein, histatins, S100 proteins, regenerating-islet-derived lectins, RNase family members with ribonuclease-independent killing activity, and peptides released from neutrophil granules such as elastase, cathepsin G and azurocidin. Protease–antiprotease balance (kallikreins against SLPI, elafin and WFDC/SPINK inhibitors) tunes peptide maturation and limits tissue damage, hepcidin withholds iron from pathogens, and secreted immunoglobulins with J chain provide specificity. A large chemokine component recruits phagocytes to reinforce the response. Loss or misregulation underlies skin and gut barrier disease, recurrent infection, and inflammatory conditions such as psoriasis and Netherton syndrome.

Antibacterial humoral response is the soluble, secreted arm of innate defence against bacteria: the antimicrobial peptides, proteins and antibodies released into mucus, saliva, sweat, milk, seminal fluid and plasma that kill or immobilise microbes before an infection takes hold. It defines the barrier competence of skin, gut and airway epithelia and the killing capacity of neutrophil granules; its loss underlies recurrent infection, and its dysregulation contributes to inflammatory skin and bowel disease. The effectors act largely by permeabilising bacterial membranes or starving microbes of nutrients — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, dermcidin, lactoferrin and transferrin sequestering iron, lysosomal proteases such as elastase and cathepsin G, RNase family members, and WFDC/SLPI protease inhibitors that restrain collateral tissue damage. Secreted immunoglobulins with J chain link this fluid-phase defence to adaptive immunity, while histone and neuropeptide components broaden it further.

Body fluids and mucosal secretions carry a standing chemical defence against bacteria, and this antibacterial humoral response is that defence: soluble effectors in plasma, saliva, tears, milk, airway and gut fluid, sweat and seminal plasma that kill or restrain microbes before an adaptive response is mounted. It combines pore-forming and membrane-disrupting peptides such as the alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin and dermcidin with iron-sequestering lactoferrin and transferrin, bactericidal RNases, secretory phospholipases, and the antimicrobial and protease-inhibitory WFDC and SLPI/elafin families, alongside neutrophil granule proteases including elastase and cathepsin G. Secreted immunoglobulins and the J chain that polymerises IgA add antigen-specific opsonisation at mucosal surfaces, and several neuropeptides contribute direct antimicrobial activity. Loss of these effectors, as in impaired defensin output or SPINK5 deficiency, produces recurrent bacterial infection and barrier inflammation.

Fungi that land on skin or mucosa are met first by soluble antimicrobial factors secreted into surface fluids and plasma, and the antifungal humoral response describes this cell-free arm of defence against yeasts and moulds. It matters because it acts before phagocytes arrive and shapes whether commensal Candida remains harmless; deficiency in these peptides is linked to chronic mucocutaneous and skin infections. The effectors here are mostly small cationic or metal-sequestering proteins: cathelicidin and neutrophil defensin permeabilize fungal membranes, lactoferrin withholds iron, and angiogenin and amyloid precursor protein contribute ribonuclease and peptide-derived killing activity. A striking feature is the number of neuropeptides among them — adrenomedullin, calcitonin gene-related peptide, substance P, VIP and NPY — which couple sensory and endocrine signalling to barrier immunity, alongside chemerin and an interleukin-36 receptor antagonist that tune the accompanying inflammation.

Nitrogen utilization covers how cells sense the availability of usable nitrogen and adjust the transport and metabolism of nitrogen-containing compounds so that amino groups are captured rather than lost. In humans the dominant problem is ammonia, which is toxic at low concentrations and must be fixed into glutamine, glutamate or urea; argininosuccinate lyase acts in the urea cycle to release arginine and fumarate, and its loss causes argininosuccinic aciduria with hyperammonaemia and neurological injury. Lengsin, a glutamine synthetase-family protein of the lens, marks the tissue-specific side of amino-group handling. Regulatory and survival components link nitrogen status to transcriptional control and cell fate: the bile acid-activated nuclear receptor FXR coordinates hepatic nitrogen and lipid metabolism, while the BAX/BCL2 pair sets the apoptotic threshold in cells that must tolerate metabolic stress. The pathway therefore connects amino acid catabolism to hepatic detoxification.

Secondary metabolism covers chemistry that is not needed for basic growth but serves the organism in other ways, and in humans two such branches dominate this grouping: pigment synthesis and the disposal of foreign or reactive small molecules. Melanin production in melanocytes and retinal pigment epithelium depends on tyrosinase and its related enzymes, the melanosomal transporters that set organelle pH and ion content, and the melanocortin receptor signalling that switches cells between eumelanin and pheomelanin; loss of these steps causes albinism and altered UV protection, while their misregulation accompanies melanoma. In parallel, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, aldo-keto reductases, flavin monooxygenases, sulfotransferases and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases oxidise and conjugate drugs, carcinogens and endogenous carbonyls for excretion, with NFE2L2 driving this detoxification response under oxidative stress. Both arms handle reactive intermediates that would otherwise damage the cell.

Polyols are sugar alcohols and related multi-hydroxyl compounds, and this collection of reactions covers their synthesis, interconversion and breakdown inside cells. Three arms dominate. Glycerol metabolism links triglyceride turnover to energy supply through glycerol kinase, glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, monoacylglycerol acyltransferases and gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and TPI1. Inositol metabolism supplies the backbone of phosphoinositide signalling, with inositol synthase and the inositol monophosphatases making free inositol, kinases such as ITPKA/B and IPMK and the inositol pyrophosphate kinases elaborating higher phosphates, and phosphatases including OCRL, SYNJ1 and the INPP enzymes reversing them. Sphingoid base handling via serine palmitoyltransferase subunits, ceramidases and sphingosine kinases connects the same chemistry to membrane lipid signalling, while sorbitol dehydrogenase links the polyol route of glucose disposal implicated in diabetic complications. Additional members handle tetrahydrobiopterin, the cofactor for nitric oxide synthase and aromatic amino acid hydroxylases.

Small one-carbon solutes — carbon dioxide, urea, ammonia — must cross membranes far faster than simple diffusion allows, and this transport biology provides the channels that let them. It underlies respiratory gas exchange in the blood, ammonia handling and acid excretion in the kidney, and the urinary concentrating mechanism. Aquaporins form the water and glycerol pores, with several also conducting CO2 and urea; Rh-associated glycoproteins move ammonia/ammonium across erythrocyte and renal tubular membranes; urea transporters of the SLC14 family recycle urea across collecting duct and vasa recta to sustain the medullary osmotic gradient. Haemoglobin chains and carbonic anhydrase II couple the process to bicarbonate chemistry, converting CO2 for carriage in plasma and reversing it at the lung. Loss of these carriers produces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, impaired urea concentration, and defective ammonia disposal.

Cytolysis is the destructive rupture of a cell membrane and spilling of cytoplasm, used both as a weapon of host defence against microbes and as the terminal step by which a dying cell releases its contents. It matters because it converts an infected or damaged cell into an inflammatory signal: without controlled membrane rupture, dying cells stay intact and the alarmins and cytokines that recruit immune cells are never released. The genes cover two arms. Antimicrobial effectors such as cathelicidin, RNASE7 and the chemokine CCL28 permeabilise bacterial and fungal membranes at epithelial and skin surfaces, while interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins coat intracellular pathogens and their vacuoles to expose them to lysis and inflammasome activation. NINJ1 and its relative execute the final plasma-membrane break during pyroptosis and other lytic death, making rupture an actively driven event rather than passive swelling.

Cytolysis is the destruction of a cell by rupture of its membrane and spilling of cytoplasm, used both as a weapon against microbes and as the final step by which a dying host cell releases its contents. The genes here cover both sides of that outcome. Cathelicidin and RNASE7 are secreted antimicrobial effectors that permeabilise bacterial membranes at epithelial and skin surfaces, and CCL28 is a mucosal chemokine with comparable direct antimicrobial activity. Guanylate-binding proteins, induced by interferon, coat intracellular bacteria and pathogen-containing vacuoles, breaking them open and exposing ligands that drive inflammasome activation. NINJ1 acts at the end of lytic cell death, polymerising in the plasma membrane to cause the rupture that releases inflammatory contents. Together these define membrane breach as an immune mechanism, linking host defence to inflammation and, when unrestrained, to tissue damage.

Vitamin C metabolism covers the handling of L-ascorbate as both an enzyme cofactor and a water-soluble antioxidant: humans cannot synthesise it, so uptake, recycling and redox interconversion determine how much is available to the collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, to catecholamine synthesis, and to the scavenging of reactive oxygen species. Sodium-coupled transporters bring reduced ascorbate into cells and concentrate it in tissues such as intestine, kidney and brain, while glucose transporters carry the oxidised form, dehydroascorbate, which must then be reduced again intracellularly. Glutathione supplies the reducing equivalents for that regeneration, so glutamate-cysteine ligase and glutathione transferase omega members tie ascorbate recycling to thiol metabolism; endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductases connect the same pool to disulfide bond formation and oxidative folding. Loss of dietary ascorbate causes scurvy through failed collagen hydroxylation, and impaired transport or recycling narrows antioxidant reserve in oxidatively stressed tissues.

Formation of the pyrimidine ring supplies the uracil-, cytosine- and thymine-based nucleotides needed for DNA replication, RNA synthesis, phospholipid head groups and sugar activation, so demand for it rises sharply in proliferating cells. The de novo route begins with a multifunctional enzyme carrying carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, aspartate transcarbamoylase and dihydroorotase activities, continues through the inner mitochondrial membrane flavoenzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, which couples ring oxidation to the respiratory chain, and is completed by UMP synthase; kinases and CTP synthetases then elaborate UMP toward CTP. Thymidylate is produced separately by thymidylate synthase using folate one-carbon units supplied by serine hydroxymethyltransferase and regenerated by dihydrofolate reductase. Growth signalling through mTOR raises flux through this route. These steps are the targets of antifolates, fluoropyrimidines and immunosuppressive dihydroorotate dehydrogenase inhibitors, and inherited defects cause orotic aciduria.
