Antigen processing and presentation is how cells display fragments of proteins and lipids on their surface so that T cells can inspect them, and it is the basis of adaptive immune recognition, self-tolerance, transplant rejection and tumour immune surveillance. Two routes dominate: cytosolic proteins are degraded by immunoproteasomes, trimmed by aminopeptidases, and loaded onto class I molecules in the endoplasmic reticulum with help from TAP transporters, tapasin, calreticulin and beta-2-microglobulin; endocytosed material is cleaved by cathepsins and legumain in acidified vesicles and loaded onto class II molecules after the invariant chain is removed under HLA-DM control. CD1 and MR1 proteins present lipids and metabolites instead. Rab GTPases, AP-3 adaptors and phagosome maturation machinery direct the trafficking, including cross-presentation by dendritic cells, and loss of these steps lets viruses and cancers escape detection.

T cell surveillance depends on antigen-presenting cells displaying fragments of proteins, lipids or metabolites at the surface bound to MHC and MHC-like molecules, and this pathway covers how those complexes are generated and delivered. Class I loading uses immunoproteasome subunits, the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, ERAP aminopeptidase trimming and a tapasin-calreticulin-PDIA3 chaperone step with beta-2-microglobulin; class II loading depends on the invariant chain CD74, lysosomal cathepsins and legumain, and peptide exchange catalysed by HLA-DM with HLA-DO as its modulator. CD1 family members and MR1 present lipids and microbial metabolites instead. Vesicular traffic through Rab GTPases, AP-3 and phagosomal machinery supports cross-presentation, while MARCH ubiquitin ligases tune surface MHC levels. Failures cause immunodeficiency, allow viral and tumour immune evasion, and underlie HLA-linked autoimmunity and transplant rejection.

Antigen processing and presentation of endogenous antigen is how a cell advertises what it is making inside itself, displaying peptides or lipids derived from its own cytosolic and membrane proteins on surface MHC molecules for inspection by T cells and NK cells. This is the basis of immune surveillance against viruses and tumours: cells expressing altered or foreign proteins are recognised and killed, while loss of presentation is a common route to immune escape. Mechanistically, proteasomal peptides are pumped into the ER by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains with beta-2 microglobulin and tapasin. Related molecules extend the repertoire: CD1 proteins present lipid antigens, HLA-E and HLA-G modulate NK responses, and ULBP/RAET1 ligands signal stress. Autophagy machinery routes cytosolic material toward class II loading.

Cells continually advertise samples of their own protein and lipid contents on the surface, and this display of endogenous antigen is how cytotoxic T cells and NK cells distinguish healthy cells from infected or transformed ones. Peptides generated in the cytosol are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed to length by the aminopeptidases ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto class I heavy chains with beta-2-microglobulin and tapasin; lipid antigens take a parallel route on CD1 molecules. Non-classical relatives such as HLA-E, HLA-G and the ULBP/RAET1 stress-induced ligands instead tune NK cell activation and maternal-fetal tolerance, while autophagy machinery can divert cytoplasmic cargo onto class II. Loss of this surveillance lets tumours and viruses escape T cell killing, and its misdirection against self peptides underlies HLA-linked autoimmunity.

Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells capture material from outside themselves and display fragments of it on the cell surface, and this handling of exogenous antigen is how the adaptive immune system learns about pathogens, vaccines and transplanted tissue. Internalised proteins are delivered to acidic endosomes and lysosomes, where cathepsins, legumain and the thiol reductase IFI30 unfold and cleave them; the invariant chain CD74 chaperones class II molecules until HLA-DM catalyses peptide exchange, with HLA-DO tuning that step. Loaded HLA-DR, -DQ and -DP complexes then stimulate CD4 T cells, while CD1 proteins present lipid antigens and MR1 presents microbial metabolites, and some cargo is cross-presented on class I with B2M. Receptor-mediated uptake through Fc receptors, endosomal trafficking via AP-3 and PIKfyve, and TLR signalling through UNC93B1 and TRAF6 link antigen capture to the decision to present it.

Antigen-presenting cells sample proteins taken up from outside the cell and display fragments of them on MHC class II molecules, the step that allows CD4 T cells to recognise bacteria, parasites and vaccines and to license antibody responses and macrophage activation. Dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells internalise antigen through receptors such as the Fc gamma and Fc epsilon receptor chains, then degrade it in increasingly acidic endosomes using cathepsins, the asparaginyl endopeptidase legumain and the thiol reductase IFI30. Newly made class II heterodimers, chaperoned and blocked by the invariant chain CD74, traffic to these compartments, where HLA-DM catalyses exchange of the residual invariant chain fragment for antigenic peptide and HLA-DO tunes that editing. The resulting complexes reach the surface for T cell inspection. Failures cause bare lymphocyte syndrome and immunodeficiency, while the same peptide display underlies the strong HLA class II associations of autoimmune disease.

Neurons must deliver mitochondria from the soma to distant axon terminals and synapses, and retrieve damaged ones, so axonal transport of mitochondria sets where ATP and calcium buffering are available along an axon that may be a metre long. Loss of this trafficking starves synapses of energy and is a recurring theme in axonal degeneration, hereditary spastic paraplegia, optic atrophy and tauopathy. Movement is motor-driven along axonal microtubules: dynactin-associated and kinesin-linked adaptors, including syntabulin and FEZ1, couple organelles to motors, while outer-membrane ARMCX/mitochondrial-anchoring proteins regulate their attachment and arrest. The track itself is tuned by tubulin modification and by the microtubule-severing ATPase spastin, and by tau, which competes with motors when hyperphosphorylated. Neurofilament and ubiquitin-pathway components tie transport to axonal cytoskeletal integrity and mitochondrial quality control, with OPA1 linking transport to fusion and cristae maintenance.</description>}Fusion

Sexual reproduction joins the haploid genomes of two gametes into a diploid zygote, and the genes here cover the whole arc that makes this possible: germ cell specification, meiosis, gamete differentiation, fertilization and the transition to embryonic development. Meiotic machinery dominates — SPO11 and PRDM9 initiate programmed double-strand breaks, synaptonemal complex proteins such as SYCP1-3 and SYCE1-3 pair homologues, meiosis-specific cohesins and recombinases (REC8, STAG3, DMC1, MSH4/5) execute crossover formation, and telomere-nuclear envelope bridges anchor chromosome movement. Spermiogenesis contributes protamines, outer dense fibre and flagellar axoneme components, and CatSper channels for sperm motility and capacitation; oocyte and fertilization factors include zona pellucida glycoproteins, IZUMO1 and its receptor, PLCZ1 for egg activation, and maternal-effect gene products. piRNA pathway factors and DNA methyltransferases silence transposons and set imprints in the germline. Defects cause infertility, aneuploidy and pregnancy loss.

Hemoglobin metabolism spans the making, loading and eventual breakdown of the oxygen carrier that defines the red blood cell, and the genes here cover the whole arc. Heme synthesis supplies the prosthetic group, with the erythroid-specific delta-aminolevulinate synthase ALAS2 starting the pathway and ferrochelatase inserting iron at the end; a mitochondrial iron importer and an ABC transporter feed that reaction, while a dedicated chaperone stabilises free alpha-globin until it pairs with beta-globin. Transcriptional regulators and a kinase that restrains translation when heme is scarce keep globin output matched to heme supply, and erythropoietin under hypoxic control sets how many precursors are made at all. Downstream, biliverdin reductase and a plasma heme-binding protein handle catabolism and scavenging. Imbalance produces sideroblastic anaemia, porphyria, or the globin-chain excess that underlies thalassaemia.

The spinal cord is the conduit carrying sensory information to the brain and motor commands to muscle, and its development converts a segment of neural tube into precisely arranged pools of motor neurons and dorsoventral interneuron classes. Graded signals set position: sonic hedgehog from the floor plate acting through patched, smoothened and GLI factors, opposed dorsally by BMP and WNT ligands and their antagonists noggin and chordin, with retinoid and GDF11 inputs conferring rostrocaudal identity read out by HOX genes. Progenitor domains expressing OLIG2, NKX2-2, PAX6, DBX1 and LBX1 give rise to neurons specified by LIM-homeodomain and ISL factors, and MNX1-positive motor neurons extend axons guided by DCC, slit and netrin cues while reelin signalling positions cells. Ciliary trafficking components tune hedgehog reception. Disruption produces neural tube and axon guidance defects and motor neuron disease phenotypes.

Patterning of the spinal cord assigns positional identity along its dorsoventral and rostrocaudal axes, so that motor neurons, interneurons and glia arise in the right places to wire reflex and locomotor circuits. Graded Sonic hedgehog from the notochord and floor plate, read through Smoothened and the Gli transcription factors with Sufu and cilium-associated components such as IFT122 and Inturned setting pathway output, specifies ventral progenitor domains marked by NKX2-2 and LHX3, while Chordin antagonises BMP dorsally and GDF11 contributes to rostrocaudal identity. Progenitor transcription factors including DBX1, FOXN4, ASCL1, DMRT3 and SOX1 define discrete interneuron classes, among them the commissural neurons that coordinate left-right stepping; Reelin guides subsequent neuronal positioning. Disruption of this regionalization produces holoprosencephaly-spectrum and neural tube defects, loss of motor neuron subtypes, and abnormal gait patterning.

The ventral spinal cord houses the interneurons that relay signals between sensory input and motor output, and this differentiation programme is how neuroepithelial progenitors in the ventral neural tube commit to those identities rather than to motor neurons. Its output is the local circuitry behind reflexes and the rhythmic left-right and flexor-extensor coordination of locomotion; disturbed specification changes gait and reflex behaviour. Graded ventral patterning signals set up progenitor domains marked by homeodomain and related transcription factors such as DBX1, NKX2-2 and LHX3, while proneural and cofactor activity from ASCL1, FOXN4, GATA2 and LMO4 drives progenitors out of the cycle into defined interneuron classes, including the DMRT3-dependent commissural population. Notch ligand signalling keeps some progenitors undifferentiated, so the pathway couples neurogenic timing to positional identity along the dorsoventral axis.

The spinal cord is built by assigning progenitors along the dorsoventral axis to distinct neuronal and glial identities, and this differentiation programme is what produces motor neurons, the interneuron classes that wire reflex and locomotor circuits, and oligodendrocytes. Graded Sonic hedgehog from the floor plate, read through its receptor Patched and the Gli transcription factors, specifies ventral progenitor domains, while Wnt and BMP-family signals from the roof plate pattern dorsal ones; Notch signalling and the proneural factor ASCL1 then time the switch from progenitor division to neurogenesis. Homeodomain and bHLH codes make the identities concrete — OLIG2 for motor neuron and oligodendrocyte progenitors, ISL1/ISL2 with LHX3 and MNX1 for motor neurons, DBX1, GSX1/2, PAX7, LBX1 and DMRT3 for interneuron subtypes, with HOX genes fixing rostrocaudal position. Disruption underlies neural tube patterning defects and motor neuron malformation.

dorsal spinal cord development builds the sensory half of the spinal cord — the dorsal horn interneurons that receive input from sensory ganglia and relay touch, pain, temperature and proprioceptive information toward the brain. Without correct dorsal patterning, sensory circuits miswire and reflex and nociceptive processing fail. Roof plate signals, chiefly WNT1, WNT3A and the BMP family member GDF7, set up a dorsal-to-ventral gradient that specifies successive progenitor domains marked by PAX7, GSX1 and GSX2, while proneural ASCL1 drives them to differentiate. Combinatorial LIM-homeodomain and related transcription factors, including LHX1, LHX5, LHX3, DRGX and PROX1, then assign the distinct dorsal interneuron identities. Guidance and adhesion components such as DRAXIN, MDGA1 and GDNF steer commissural and sensory axons across and along the cord, linking neuronal specification to circuit assembly in the developing nervous system.

The dorsal half of the spinal cord is where sensory information from skin, muscle and viscera first enters the central nervous system, and its development produces the interneuron classes that sort touch, pain and proprioceptive input before relaying it onward. Patterning begins with roof plate signals — WNT1, WNT3A and the BMP family member GDF7 — which impose dorsoventral positional identity, while DRAXIN restrains axon growth across the midline. Progenitor domains are demarcated by transcription factors including PAX7, GSX1 and GSX2, and ASCL1 drives them toward neurogenesis; LHX1, LHX5, LMO4, PROX1 and TAL1 then fix the identities and settling positions of individual dorsal interneuron subtypes. Related factors such as DRGX act in the sensory ganglion neurons that supply this circuitry. Disruption skews subtype proportions and miswires sensory relay, with consequences for reflex control and nociception.

The ventral half of the spinal cord is where motor neurons and the interneurons that govern locomotion are born, so its development sets up the output side of the entire motor circuit. A gradient of Sonic hedgehog from the floor plate, read out through its receptor Patched and the Gli transcription factors, subdivides the ventral neural tube into progenitor domains marked by combinations of NKX2-2, OLIG2, PAX6 and DBX1. Those domains then express identity codes — ISL1, ISL2, MNX1, LHX3 and LHX4 for motor neurons, DMRT3, LBX1 and LHX1 for defined interneuron classes — that fix neurotransmitter phenotype, columnar position and axon target. Reelin signalling through its lipoprotein receptors and DAB1 helps position the resulting neurons, and cilium-dependent trafficking is required for hedgehog transduction. Disruption gives loss or mispatterning of motor neurons, abnormal limb innervation and disturbed locomotor rhythm.

Spinal cord motor neuron cell fate specification is the step at which a ventral neural tube progenitor becomes committed to a motor neuron identity, before it grows an axon out to muscle. Getting it right determines whether the spinal cord can drive movement at all, and the same transcription factors are used to make motor neurons from stem cells in the laboratory and are implicated in congenital disorders of limb innervation and eye movement. Commitment is executed by combinatorial transcription factor codes: LIM homeodomain proteins ISL1, ISL2 and LHX3 with the cofactor LMO4 form the complexes that impose generic motor neuron identity, MNX1 stabilises and maintains that choice, and posterior HOX genes such as HOXC10 and HOXD10 assign rostrocaudal position, so that lumbar motor pools project to the correct hindlimb muscles. Patterning along the dorsoventral axis, reflected here by OLIG3, sets the progenitor territory from which these neurons arise.

Spinal cord motor neuron differentiation is the program by which progenitors in the ventral neural tube become the motor neurons that connect the central nervous system to muscle. It establishes the final common pathway for all voluntary movement, and its disruption underlies congenital motor disorders, arthrogryposis and syndromes of abnormal eye and limb innervation. A ventral-to-dorsal Sonic hedgehog gradient, read out through Patched and Gli repressors, partitions the progenitor domains marked by OLIG2, NKX2-2 and LBX1; primary cilium and intraflagellar transport components are required for that readout. Committed progenitors then switch on the LIM homeodomain and homeobox code -- ISL1, ISL2, LHX3, MNX1 -- that fixes motor neuron identity, while HOX genes assign columnar and pool identity along the rostrocaudal axis so that axons reach the correct muscle targets. Related factors specify visceral and cranial motor subtypes.

Motor neurons of the spinal cord are born in the ventral neural tube, where graded Sonic hedgehog signalling from the floor plate patterns progenitors and assigns them a motor fate; without this programme there is no functional link from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle. Hedgehog transduction components including SHH, PTCH1 and GLI3, together with cilium and intraflagellar transport proteins, set the ventral-dorsal gradient, while OLIG2 defines the progenitor domain and NKX2-2 and LBX1 restrict neighbouring interneuron identities. Commitment and maturation then depend on LIM-homeodomain and homeobox factors -- ISL1, ISL2, LHX3, LHX4 and MNX1 -- which drive cholinergic identity and, with HOX factors such as HOXC10 and HOXD10, specify rostrocaudal columnar and pool identity for correct muscle innervation. Disruption of these steps underlies neural tube patterning defects and contributes to motor neuron vulnerability in degenerative disease.

Somatic motor neurons are the output cells that connect the central nervous system to skeletal muscle, and their differentiation converts neuroepithelial progenitors in the ventral neural tube into cells capable of driving voluntary movement, breathing and eye movement. Loss of these neurons, or failure to specify them, produces paralysis and the weakness seen in motor neuron disease. Specification depends on graded Sonic hedgehog signalling from the floor plate and notochord, which patterns progenitor domains along the dorsoventral axis; ciliary transduction machinery such as TCTN1 shapes how that gradient is read. Downstream, LIM-homeodomain factors LHX3 and LHX4 and the homeobox factor PHOX2A assign subtype identity and columnar organisation, distinguishing cranial from spinal motor populations. Survival and growth signalling through AKT1 supports the newly generated neurons as they extend axons toward muscle targets and form neuromuscular junctions.

Dorsal interneurons of the spinal cord are the relay cells that receive incoming sensory information and pass it to motor circuits and ascending tracts, and this programme is how neuroepithelial progenitors of the dorsal neural tube become them. Its outputs define the circuitry underlying touch, pain and proprioceptive processing, and shape the dorsal horn laminae. Roof plate signals, including WNT1, WNT3A and the BMP-family ligand GDF7, pattern the dorsal progenitor domains, where homeodomain factors such as PAX7, GSX1 and GSX2 and the proneural factor ASCL1 set progenitor identity and drive neurogenesis. Postmitotic subtype identity is then fixed by combinations of LIM-homeodomain and LIM-only proteins, LHX1, LHX5, LHX3 and LMO4, together with the bHLH factor TAL1, which distinguishes inhibitory from excitatory association neuron fates. Cell-surface proteins such as MDGA1 contribute to the migration and settling of the newly born neurons. Disrupted dorsal specification alters sensory gating.

Oligodendrocytes wrap central axons in myelin, and in the spinal cord they arise from ventral neural tube progenitors that must first be specified and then driven toward a glial fate. This differentiation programme supplies the myelinating cells on which rapid saltatory conduction in ascending and descending tracts depends; its failure leaves axons unmyelinated and is the developmental counterpart of demyelinating disease and of the repair attempted after spinal injury. The transcription factors here act combinatorially along the dorsoventral axis: OLIG2 marks the progenitor domain that yields both motor neurons and oligodendrocyte precursors, NKX2-2 and ASCL1 help switch that domain from neuronal to glial output, and SOX6 restrains premature maturation so precursors proliferate and migrate before differentiating. The pathway sits at the intersection of neural tube patterning, lineage commitment and myelination.

The early neural tube is subdivided into territories that will become forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain and spinal cord, and along its circumference into floor plate, motor neuron and dorsal interneuron domains. This patterning fixes where each class of neuron is born, so its failure produces holoprosencephaly, ventralization defects and other structural brain and spinal malformations. Ventral identity is set by SHH acting through PTCH1 and SMO, with signal strength tuned in the primary cilium: intraflagellar transport and transition zone components, the ciliary GTPase ARL13B, and the negative regulators GPR161 and TULP3 determine how much GLI activity a cell sees. Dorsal and boundary cues come from BMP4, WNT1 and WNT3A, while FGF8 with GBX2 and EN1 organizes the midbrain-hindbrain junction. Graded signalling is read out as transcription factor domains such as PAX6 and PAX7, reinforced by Polycomb repression through BMI1 and KDM2B.

The hindbrain gives rise to the cerebellum, pons and medulla, and this pathway covers the steps by which its unspecialized progenitors commit to and mature into the neuron types those structures depend on " Purkinje cells, granule cells, and the visceromotor and branchiomotor neurons that control breathing, swallowing and autonomic reflexes. Transcriptional regulators set identity: PHOX2B specifies visceral motor neurons and its loss underlies congenital central hypoventilation, RORA and SKOR2 are required for Purkinje cell maturation, PROX1 acts in granule cell differentiation, and LHX1, LHX5, GATA2, FOXP2 and the cofactor LDB1 partition interneuron and projection neuron fates. Secreted cues such as WNT7A and the BMP antagonist noggin pattern the field, while synaptic and adhesion proteins including CBLN1, GRID2 and NRXN1 consolidate the resulting circuits. Failure produces cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia and disordered motor and autonomic control.

Expansion of the progenitor pools that build the hindbrain — cerebellum, pons and medulla — depends on this proliferative programme, which sets how many granule cells, Purkinje cells and brainstem neurons a brain will contain. Too little proliferation gives cerebellar hypoplasia and ataxia; failure to stop it underlies medulloblastoma, which arises from these same dividing precursors. Secreted mitogens drive the process: SHH from Purkinje cells sustains granule cell precursor division in the external germinal layer, while FGF2, EGF and IGF1 act on neuroepithelial and glial progenitors. Regional identity is imposed in parallel by transcriptional regulators such as GBX2, which specifies anterior hindbrain territory near the midbrain boundary, and by RORA and SKOR2 acting in Purkinje cell differentiation. Counterbalancing factors including CEND1 push cells out of the cycle toward neuronal differentiation, so the pathway is fundamentally about timing the switch from division to maturation.

Hindbrain neurons are largely born far from where they finally work, so building the brainstem depends on the orderly migration of cells into and within the hindbrain. This movement positions precerebellar nuclei, pontine and inferior olivary neurons, branchiomotor and visceral motor pools, and the autonomic centres that set breathing rhythm; when it fails, nuclei end up ectopic and reflex and respiratory circuits are miswired. Guidance comes from Eph receptors and semaphorin–plexin pairs that constrain rhombomeric territories, from Reelin signalling through DAB1 that tells neurons where to stop, and from integrin and cadherin-catenin adhesion to substrate and neighbouring cells. Cytoskeletal and ciliary components including filamin A, ARL13B and TTBK2 couple these cues to motility, while transcriptional regulators such as PHOX2B, POU4F1 and NHLH2 specify which cells migrate and what identity they carry. It combines neuronal fate specification with directed cell motility.

The diencephalon arises from the caudal forebrain and gives rise to thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and subthalamus, so its development sets up the relay of sensory information to cortex and the neuroendocrine and autonomic control centres that govern feeding, stress responses, growth and water balance. Regional identity is imposed by graded signalling — SHH acting through SMO, PTCH and GLI effectors, WNT/beta-catenin, FGF8 from local organizers, and BMPs opposed by the antagonist Noggin — which is read out by transcription factors such as SIX3, RAX, PAX6, OTX1, GBX2, ARX and SOX2 to set boundaries and specify neuronal subtypes. A parallel arm builds the pituitary and its hormone axes through HESX1, PROP1, POU1F1, LHX3 and NKX2-1, while semaphorin–plexin and neuropilin signalling guides emerging axons. Mutations here cause holoprosencephaly, septo-optic dysplasia and combined pituitary hormone deficiency.

telencephalon development builds the forebrain structures that carry out perception, movement planning, memory and cognition — the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, olfactory bulb, basal ganglia and amygdala — from the anterior neural tube. Its failure produces microcephaly, lissencephaly, heterotopia, holoprosencephaly and intellectual disability, and many of its genes are recurrent autism and schizophrenia candidates. Patterning transcription factors such as FOXG1, EMX2, PAX6, GLI3 and the DLX/GSX2 pair, acting under SHH, WNT, BMP and FGF8 signals, divide the vesicle into dorsal cortical and ventral ganglionic-eminence territories that generate excitatory and GABAergic neurons respectively. Neural progenitors then proliferate with spindle and centrosome machinery (ASPM, WDR62, MCPH1), and newborn neurons migrate along RELN–DAB1 and LIS1/NDEL1 routes to form layers specified by TBR1, BCL11B and FEZF2. Axon guidance through SLIT–ROBO, semaphorin, ephrin and NOGO receptor systems completes wiring, while glial transporters support the mature tissue.

The telencephalon is the forebrain division that gives rise to the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, olfactory structures, and the basal ganglia and other subcortical nuclei, and its development converts a patch of anterior neuroepithelium into layered, regionally specified circuitry. Patterning factors such as FOXG1, PAX6, EMX2, GLI3 and SIX3 set dorsal-ventral and area identity, with SHH, FGF8, WNT and BMP signals from local organizers; GSX2, ASCL1 and the DLX genes drive ventral progenitors toward GABAergic interneurons that migrate tangentially into cortex. Radial glial proliferation, spindle and centrosome components such as ASPM, WDR62 and MCPH1, and a RELN-DAB1-LIS1 module control neuron number and inward radial migration, while SLIT, ROBO, semaphorin and ephrin cues build axon tracts and the TBR1-BCL11B-FEZF2 hierarchy assigns laminar fate. Disruption underlies microcephaly, lissencephaly, holoprosencephaly, epilepsy and intellectual disability.

The corpus callosum is the great commissure of the mammalian forebrain, and its morphogenesis is the process by which callosal neurons extend axons across the midline and organize them into the fibre bundle that links the two cerebral hemispheres. Without it, interhemispheric communication fails: agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum is one of the most common brain malformations seen on imaging and a recurring feature of intellectual disability and epilepsy syndromes. The genes here act at several stages of that construction, from neuronal proliferation and migration to midline guidance and axon targeting. PAFAH1B1 governs nuclear translocation during cortical neuron migration and is the lissencephaly gene; ZEB2 encodes the transcriptional repressor lost in Mowat-Wilson syndrome; SZT2 and C12orf57 are linked to recessive disorders combining callosal defects with seizures. Together they connect cortical development to the wiring of long-range projections.

The dentate gyrus is the input gate of the hippocampus, a layered sheet of granule cells that relays entorhinal information onto CA3 pyramidal neurons and remains one of the few sites of adult neurogenesis; its construction is the biology captured here. Building it requires patterning of the hippocampal primordium, migration of progenitors along a glial scaffold into the granule layer, and terminal differentiation into granule neurons. Transcriptional control dominates the gene set: PROX1 and NEUROD1 specify granule cell identity, EMX2 and LEF1 tie dorsal telencephalic patterning and Wnt signalling to progenitor expansion, and NR2E1 maintains the neural stem cell pool, with Hedgehog input through SMO. Glycosylation enzymes acting on dystroglycan anchor the pial basement membrane, so their loss disorganises the layer as in dystroglycanopathy. Defects produce granule cell dispersion, disrupted spatial memory and pattern separation, and susceptibility to epilepsy and intellectual disability.

The pallium is the dorsal roof of the telencephalon that becomes the cerebral cortex and hippocampus, and its development turns a pseudostratified neuroepithelium into a layered sheet of excitatory projection neurons. Patterning factors such as FOXG1, EMX2, PAX6, LHX2 and GLI3, responding to FGF and WNT signals from the rim, set areal identity, while EOMES, NEUROD6 and TBR1 mark the progenitor-to-neuron transition. Radial glia divide with tightly controlled spindle orientation and centrosome function, and mutations in ASPM, WDR62, MCPH1 or PAFAH1B1 curtail progenitor output or derail migration. Newborn neurons climb radial fibres under reelin signalling through LRP8 and DAB1, with CDK5 and its activators, RHOA/RAC1 and the tubulin cytoskeleton driving nucleokinesis. Failure at these steps produces microcephaly, lissencephaly, cobblestone malformations and heterotopia, and milder disruption underlies intellectual disability and autism-spectrum phenotypes.

Subpallium development builds the ventral half of the telencephalon, the source of the basal ganglia and of nearly every cortical GABAergic interneuron. It matters because the structures it generates control action selection, habit and reward learning; disruption of its patterning or of the striatal projection neurons it produces underlies movement disorders, dystonia and neurodevelopmental conditions with autistic and obsessive-compulsive features. Ventralising cues from FGF8 and retinoid signalling, opposed by GLI3-dependent limits on hedgehog output, establish progenitor domains in which GSX2 and ASCL1 drive neurogenesis and the DLX1/DLX2 pair specifies GABAergic identity. Downstream, BCL11B, FOXP1 and FOXP2 differentiate medium spiny neurons into direct and indirect pathways marked by DRD1 and DRD2, while synaptic organisers such as SHANK3, SLITRK5 and CNTNAP2 assemble their circuits. Ciliary BBSome components link the pathway to hedgehog transduction in progenitors.

The subpallium is the ventral floor of the embryonic telencephalon, and its development gives rise to the basal ganglia and to the GABAergic interneurons that migrate from it into cortex, hippocampus and olfactory bulb. Without it, inhibitory tone in the forebrain and the striatal circuits controlling movement, motivation and habit learning fail to form. Patterning depends on ventralising signals opposed by dorsal cues, with GLI3 and FGF8 setting positional boundaries and GSX2 specifying progenitors that ASCL1 and the DLX1/DLX2 pair drive toward a GABAergic fate. Later steps involve striatal identity and projection-neuron programmes carried by BCL11B, FOXP1 and FOXP2 and the dopamine receptors DRD1 and DRD2 that define the direct and indirect pathways. Retinoid signalling contributes to regional identity. Mutations in members such as FOXP2, SHANK3 and CNTNAP2 link this developmental programme to speech, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders.

The twelve pairs of cranial nerves carry vision, hearing, smell, taste, facial and jaw movement, and parasympathetic control of head and visceral organs, and their development builds these circuits from hindbrain and neural crest precursors. Loss of this programme produces congenital cranial dysinnervation — squint and gaze palsies, deafness, facial weakness, feeding and swallowing failure — as seen in CHARGE and DiGeorge-type syndromes linked to CHD7 and TBX1. Hox genes together with EGR2 and MAFB assign rhombomere identity and motor nucleus position; PHOX2A and PHOX2B specify branchiomotor and visceromotor neurons; ISL1, NEUROG1, POU4F1 and POU4F3 drive sensory and hair-cell neurogenesis in the associated ganglia and inner ear. Axons then navigate by semaphorin, neuropilin, plexin and ephrin receptor cues, while placodal factors SIX1 and SIX4 and retinal determinants such as ATOH7 tie the process to sensory organ formation.

The hindbrain is built as a series of repeating transverse segments, and rhombomere development covers their formation, boundary maintenance and acquisition of distinct identities. Each segment is a lineage-restricted compartment whose cells cannot mix with neighbours, and the identity it takes fixes which cranial motor nuclei, branchial nerves and neural crest streams arise from that axial level. The genes here form the classic segmental code: a graded set of anterior Hox factors assigns position along the rostrocaudal axis, EGR2 marks and specifies alternating segments, MAFB acts in the more caudal rhombomeres, and GBX2 sets the anterior limit of hindbrain territory at the midbrain junction. These factors cross-regulate one another to sharpen initially fuzzy expression domains into crisp segmental borders. Disruption produces malformations of cranial nerve and inner ear patterning, and the same regulatory logic illustrates how positional information is converted into regional neuronal fate.

The pons is the hindbrain segment lying between the medulla and midbrain, relaying motor information from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum and housing nuclei for facial and eye movement, hearing, breathing and sleep control. Its development converts rhombomere-stage neuroepithelium into these organised nuclei and transverse fibre tracts. Segmental identity is set by Hox-dependent patterning, with HOXB1 marking the rhombomere that gives rise to facial branchiomotor neurons, while ASCL1 drives neurogenic commitment and PHOX2A specifies visceral and cranial motor neuron fates. CDK5 activators p35 and p39 support the neuronal migration that positions pontine nuclei, and planar-polarity and trafficking proteins such as SCRIB and SEC24B guide the tangential migration and neural tube closure on which hindbrain architecture depends; BCL2 limits apoptosis among newly born neurons. Disrupted pontine development underlies congenital cranial nerve palsies, hypoventilation syndromes and pontocerebellar hypoplasias.

The sense of smell depends on olfactory sensory neurons in the nasal epithelium projecting axons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, and this pathway covers the formation and maturation of that first cranial nerve. When it fails, the nerve and bulb are hypoplastic or absent, producing anosmia and, because gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons migrate along the same axonal scaffold, the hypogonadotropic hypogonadism seen in Kallmann syndrome and CHARGE syndrome, where CHD7 chromatin remodelling is disrupted. Guidance is contributed by plexin receptors that transduce semaphorin repulsion to sort and target incoming axons, while neurotrophin signalling through NTRK1 supports sensory neuron survival, and SALL1 acts in the transcriptional programme of craniofacial and neural patterning. Genes of the olfactory transduction machinery, including a cyclic nucleotide-gated channel subunit and a sodium/potassium/calcium exchanger, tie odorant-evoked activity to proper wiring.

Optic nerve development builds the cable that carries vision from the eye to the brain, from the first retinal ganglion cells through axon outgrowth, midline decision-making at the optic chiasm, and myelinated maturation of the optic tract. Without it there is no route for visual information: failures produce optic nerve hypoplasia, atrophy, coloboma, and the abnormal chiasmal crossing seen in albinism and foveal hypoplasia. The genes cover the successive steps. ATOH7 specifies the ganglion cell fate that supplies every optic axon; PAX2 and GLI3 pattern the optic stalk and fissure; EPHB1 and EPHB2, with heparan sulfate made by EXT1, guide growth cones and set the ipsilateral/contralateral choice at the midline; SLC38A8 links to chiasmal misrouting. Potassium channel subunits tune conduction in the mature nerve, while SLC25A46 and TMEM126A tie mitochondrial function to the hereditary optic neuropathies.

Formation of the optic nerve turns retinal ganglion cell axons into an organised tract that carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It matters because vision depends on these axons leaving the retina through the optic disc, sorting correctly at the chiasm, and surviving; its disruption underlies optic nerve hypoplasia, coloboma, achiasmia and inherited optic atrophy. A proneural transcription factor, ATOH7, specifies the retinal ganglion cells that supply the axons, while PAX2, GLI3 and NKX2-2 pattern the optic stalk and disc region. Guidance at the midline involves EPHB1 and EPHB2 receptors with heparan sulfate made by EXT1, determining which fibres cross. Potassium channel subunits and cholinergic signalling shape axonal excitability and activity-dependent refinement, and mitochondrial proteins such as SLC25A46 and TMEM126A support the metabolic demands of these long projections, linking this developmental programme to optic neuropathy.

Formation of the trigeminal nerve builds the main sensory supply of the face and the motor supply to the muscles of mastication, so that touch, temperature, pain and corneal protection from the forehead, cheek and jaw reach the brainstem and chewing can be controlled. The genes here cover two phases: specification of trigeminal sensory neurons from placodal and neural crest precursors by transcription factors including NEUROG1, ISL1, POU4F1, DRGX and TFAP2A, and the subsequent guidance of their axons into the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular branches. Secreted class-3 semaphorins SEMA3A and SEMA3F signal through neuropilin co-receptors NRP1 and NRP2 with plexin-A partners to repel growing axons, sculpting branch trajectories and preventing aberrant projection. Disrupted development leaves facial anaesthesia, feeding difficulty and abnormal cranial nerve patterning, and the same guidance logic operates broadly in peripheral nervous system wiring.

Hearing and balance depend on a sensory nerve that links the inner ear to the brainstem, and vestibulocochlear nerve development is the programme that builds it. Its cochlear branch carries auditory information from hair cells of the cochlear duct, while its vestibular branch reports head position and movement from the vestibular apparatus; failure of the programme produces congenital sensorineural deafness and vestibular dysfunction. Neurogenin-driven neurogenesis specifies the statoacoustic ganglion neurons, PAX2 patterns the otic vesicle and its cochlear derivatives, and POU4F3 is required for survival of the hair cells that these neurons contact. Guidance and trophic cues, including neuropilin receptors and the transmembrane leucine-rich protein SLITRK6, direct axons to their targets and sustain innervation, so the pathway couples otic patterning to axon guidance and neuronal survival.

Hindbrain morphogenesis shapes the medulla, pons and cerebellum from the posterior neural tube, producing the circuits that run breathing, heart rate, balance and coordinated movement; when it fails the result is cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia and the malformations seen in Dandy-Walker and Joubert-type syndromes. Patterning inputs from WNT1 and hedgehog signalling through SMO and the GLI factors drive proliferation of granule cell precursors, while Notch ligand DLL1 with HES1 and transcriptional regulators such as LHX1, LHX5, PROX1, RORA and SKOR2 assign Purkinje, granule and interneuron identities. Reelin signalling via DAB1 and cytoskeletal and motor components including CDK5, TUBA1A and SPTBN2 position migrating neurons into their final laminae, and synaptic organizers such as CBLN1 and GRID2 wire the resulting cerebellar cortex. Mutations in several of these genes cause inherited ataxias and developmental delay.

Hindbrain maturation is the final step by which the medulla, pons and cerebellum become functional after their basic shape is set, independent of further morphogenesis. It matters because these territories run breathing, heart rate and other autonomic reflexes as well as balance and motor coordination, so incomplete maturation leaves brainstem and cerebellar circuits structurally present but physiologically inadequate. The genes here point to neuronal differentiation and cell cycle exit as the substance of that maturation: the CDK5 activators p35 and p39 direct CDK5 kinase activity toward cytoskeletal and migratory substrates in postmitotic neurons, CEND1 couples withdrawal from the cell cycle to terminal differentiation, and RERE acts as a nuclear receptor co-regulator of developmental transcription. A coatomer subunit implicates secretory trafficking in supplying the membrane and surface proteins that maturing neurons require.

The brain's ventricular system is the set of interconnected cavities that hold cerebrospinal fluid, produced by the choroid plexus and circulated over the ependymal lining; its development sets the size and patency of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles and the aqueducts between them. When it fails, fluid accumulates and hydrocephalus follows, with ventricular dilation compressing the developing cortex. Much of the genetic requirement here is ciliary: motile axonemal components such as DNAH5, HYDIN and ODAD2 drive the ependymal flow that keeps channels open, while ciliopathy genes including BBS1, BBS4, RPGRIP1L and TTC21B couple cilia to hedgehog-dependent patterning. Other members act on neuroepithelial behaviour template u2014 NUMB and NUMBL in progenitor fate, MYH10 in apical cytoskeletal organisation, AQP1 and ATP1B2 in fluid and ion transport across the choroid plexus epithelium.

The twelve pairs of cranial nerves supply motor and sensory innervation to the head, neck and viscera and carry vision, hearing, olfaction and taste as well as parasympathetic output to autonomic ganglia; cranial nerve morphogenesis is how those nerves are specified, positioned and wired during hindbrain development. Failure produces congenital cranial dysinnervation — misrouted or absent nerves, ocular motility disorders, deafness and the craniofacial and pharyngeal defects seen in DiGeorge-like syndromes. Hox genes acting with EGR2, MAFB and HOXA1/HOXB1 assign rhombomere identity and determine which motor nuclei form where, while NEUROG1, PHOX2A, PAX2, SIX1 and TFAP2A specify sensory ganglion and branchiomotor neurons. Axon trajectories are then sculpted by repulsive semaphorin signalling through neuropilin and plexin receptors and by ephrin receptor guidance, and TBX1 and GLI3 couple this wiring to pharyngeal arch patterning.

The twelve pairs of cranial nerves carry vision, hearing, smell and taste, provide motor and sensory innervation of the head and neck, and supply parasympathetic output to visceral ganglia; their initial formation from hindbrain neural tissue and adjacent placodes is what this programme accomplishes. Regional patterning factors set the rhombomeric address in which each nerve nucleus arises, with HOXA1 and MAFB acting on hindbrain segmentation and PAX2 and TFAP2A on placodal and otic contributions. NEUROG1 drives the neurogenesis that generates cranial sensory ganglion neurons, while PHOX2A specifies the oculomotor and trochlear motor neurons. Axon guidance receptors of the plexin family, responding to semaphorins, then steer the growing nerves along stereotyped trajectories to their peripheral targets. Disruption produces congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders such as fixed strabismus, facial palsy and deafness.

The twelve pairs of cranial nerves carry vision, hearing, smell, taste, general sensation from the head and neck, motor control of facial and jaw muscles, and parasympathetic output to visceral ganglia, and this pathway covers the shaping of those nerves from rudimentary axon bundles into their stereotyped adult form. Getting it right determines whether axons exit the hindbrain at the correct rhombomere, stay bundled, and reach their peripheral targets; errors produce congenital cranial dysinnervation, strabismus, facial weakness and deafness. Hindbrain segmental identity set by HOXB1, HOXB2 and EGR2 assigns motor neurons to the right nerve, while secreted semaphorins SEMA3A and SEMA3F signalling through neuropilin co-receptors and plexins repel growth cones to keep trajectories separated and prune inappropriate branches. PAX2 contributes to the sensory placodal and optic components.

facial nerve morphogenesis builds the seventh cranial nerve, the mixed sensory and motor nerve that drives the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the anterior tongue, and supplies lacrimal, nasal and oral secretory glands through its parasympathetic branches. Its failure produces congenital facial palsy and the branchio-oto-renal and Moebius-like syndromes in which facial weakness accompanies ear and jaw defects. The genes describe two linked layers of control: a hindbrain patterning program in which Hox factors and Egr2 assign rhombomere 4 identity and specify facial branchiomotor neurons, with Six1 required for their survival and migration, and a guidance layer in which class 3 semaphorins signalling through neuropilin and plexin receptors steer motor axons and dendrites along stereotyped exit and branching routes. Together they place cranial nerve assembly within segmental hindbrain development and axon pathfinding.

Formation of the facial nerve builds the seventh cranial nerve that drives the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the anterior tongue, and supplies lacrimal, nasal and oral secretory glands. Its assembly depends on giving branchiomotor neurons the right hindbrain identity and then guiding their axons along stereotyped branches out of the second pharyngeal arch. Hox factors together with EGR2 specify rhombomere-level identity and the facial motor neuron programme, and SIX1 contributes to cranial placode and ganglion development, while secreted semaphorins acting through neuropilin and plexin receptors repel growing axons to keep the trunk and its branches in place. Disrupted patterning yields misrouted or hypoplastic nerves and congenital facial palsy, as seen in disorders of hindbrain segmentation affecting eye movement and facial weakness, linking axon guidance to craniofacial function.

Shaping of the facial nerve into its mature form gives rise to the seventh cranial nerve, which drives the muscles of facial expression, carries taste from the anterior tongue, and routes parasympathetic output to lacrimal, nasal and oral secretory glands; disrupted development underlies congenital facial palsy and syndromes of impaired eye closure and feeding. Two processes are represented here. Hindbrain patterning transcription factors specify the rhombomere identity from which the facial branchiomotor neurons arise and control their characteristic caudal migration, with a regulatory cascade linking Hox factors to Krox20/EGR2. In parallel, secreted class 3 semaphorins signalling through neuropilin co-receptors and plexin-A partners repel growth cones, sorting facial nerve branches away from inappropriate territory so that each peripheral projection reaches its target muscle or gland.

Once the brain and spinal cord have taken shape, they must still be made to work, and central nervous system maturation covers that final functional tuning: neurons differentiate terminally, extend and refine processes, and microglia prune and sculpt synapses so that circuits carry signals reliably. Failure at this stage produces intellectual disability, epilepsy and neurodevelopmental syndromes in structurally normal-looking brains. The genes here span several routes to that endpoint. CDK5R1 and CDK5R2 encode the neuronal activators p35 and p39 that switch on CDK5, the kinase governing cytoskeletal dynamics, migration and neurite outgrowth, and CEND1 pushes neuroblasts out of the cycle toward differentiation. CX3CR1 lets microglia read neuronal fractalkine during synaptic refinement, while RERE acts as a nuclear receptor coregulator of transcription and ATP6AP2 supports lysosomal acidification and Wnt responsiveness in developing neurons.

Shaping of the optic nerve turns retinal ganglion cell axons into an organized tract that carries visual information from the eye to the brain. It determines where axons exit the eye at the optic disc, how the optic stalk closes and is patterned, and which fibres cross the midline at the chiasm versus staying ipsilateral "" the arrangement that makes binocular vision possible. Failure produces optic nerve hypoplasia, coloboma, and misrouted projections with corresponding visual field loss. A transcription factor programme including PAX2 and the GLI3 arm of hedgehog patterning sets the boundary between optic stalk and retina, while EPHB1 and EPHB2 read midline ephrin cues to sort crossed from uncrossed axons. Cholinergic and potassium channel subunits point to the spontaneous retinal waves and electrical activity that refine these projections before eye opening.

Hearing and balance depend on a nerve that carries signals from the inner ear to the brainstem, and this pathway covers the generation and shaping of that vestibulocochlear nerve. Its vestibular branch reports head position and motion from the labyrinth, while its auditory branch relays sound transduced by the cochlear duct; failure of the programme produces congenital deafness and vestibular dysfunction. Neurogenin-1 specifies the otic neuroblasts that delaminate from the otic vesicle to form the statoacoustic ganglion, and PAX2 patterns the otic placode and cochlear compartment in which those neurons arise. Neuropilin-1 and neuropilin-2, as co-receptors for class 3 semaphorins and VEGF, guide the outgrowing axons and shape their fasciculation and target selection. The pathway therefore links placodal neurogenesis to axon guidance in the service of sensory innervation of the ear.

Vestibulocochlear nerve formation is the building of the eighth cranial nerve, the sensory cable that carries hearing and balance information from the inner ear to the brainstem. Without it, sound never reaches the auditory pathway and the head cannot register its orientation relative to gravity, producing congenital deafness and vestibular dysfunction. The nerve has two branches with distinct targets: a vestibular branch supplying the maculae and cristae of the membranous labyrinth, and a cochlear branch supplying the sensory epithelium of the cochlear duct, where sound-induced fluid movement is transduced. Formation depends on the specification of statoacoustic ganglion neuroblasts from the otic placode and their outgrowth toward both peripheral hair cells and central nuclei. The proneural factor NEUROG1 commits otic progenitors to this neuronal fate, while PAX2 patterns the otic vesicle and its neurogenic domain, linking inner ear morphogenesis to neuronal identity.

Hearing and balance depend on a dedicated cranial nerve linking the inner ear to the brainstem, and vestibulocochlear nerve formation is the developmental step that builds it. Neurons delaminating from the otic epithelium and neighbouring ganglionic region must be specified, then extend peripheral processes to hair cells of the cochlear duct and the vestibular end organs while projecting centrally; failure yields congenital deafness, cochlear nerve aplasia or vestibular dysfunction, and limits the benefit of cochlear implantation, which requires surviving nerve fibres. The genes here point to early neurogenic specification: a proneural transcription factor of the neurogenin class initiates commitment of otic neuroblasts, and a paired-box transcription factor patterns the otic placode and vesicle from which both sensory epithelia and their innervating neurons derive. The process sits within cranial sensory ganglion development and peripheral neurogenesis generally.

The lateral ventricles are the paired fluid-filled cavities of the cerebral hemispheres, carved from the lumen of the embryonic neural tube, and their formation determines the geometry of the developing forebrain and the flow of cerebrospinal fluid through it. Shaping them requires a properly polarized neuroepithelium, a functioning ependymal lining, and choroid plexus secretion: aquaporin-1 and a sodium pump subunit support fluid transport across the plexus and ventricular surface, ciliary and ciliopathy-associated components such as DNAH5 and RPGRIP1L give ependymal cells motile cilia and keep hedgehog signalling in check, and NUMB with its paralogue NUMBL controls asymmetric division and adherens junction integrity in ventricular zone progenitors. Proliferative control through CDK6 and chromatin regulation set progenitor number. Disruption collapses or dilates the cavity, producing hydrocephalus, ventriculomegaly and loss of the septum pellucidum.

Nerve development covers the progression of a nerve from its initial formation to a mature, functional structure, and it is what gives the peripheral and cranial nervous systems their stereotyped wiring: sensory ganglia, motor and autonomic nerves, and the optic and auditory projections. The genes here span the sequence of events that builds a nerve. Transcription factors including Neurog1, Isl1, Phox2a/Phox2b, Pou4f1 and a set of Hox proteins specify neuronal identity and hindbrain segment origin; neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF, NT-3 and neurturin, acting through TrkA and p75, sustain survival and target innervation; and semaphorin, plexin, neuropilin and ephrin receptor families steer and prune growing axons. Additional components supply myelination and glial support, dystroglycan-linked basement membrane glycosylation, and ion channels that mature excitability. Disruption yields congenital sensory and autonomic neuropathies, cranial nerve and eye movement disorders, hearing loss, and optic atrophy.

Third ventricle development covers the shaping and maintenance of the cerebrospinal fluid-filled cleft that lies in the midline of the diencephalon, bounded by the thalami, floored by the hypothalamus and roofed by ependyma. Its patency matters because CSF must pass from the lateral ventricles through it to the cerebral aqueduct; failure of this morphogenesis produces ventricular dilatation and hydrocephalus, and midline defects here accompany malformations of the corpus callosum and hypothalamic structures. The genes involved point to several contributing processes: a non-muscle myosin heavy chain provides the actomyosin contractility needed for neuroepithelial shape change and midline fusion, a Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunit supports the ion transport that drives fluid movement across ependymal and choroid surfaces, a chromatin-modifying histone demethylase contributes transcriptional patterning, and factors linked to ciliary function bear on ependymal CSF flow.

Purkinje cells are the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex, and the formation of the single-cell-thick layer they occupy is what makes that output possible. Development of the cerebellar Purkinje cell layer covers the specification of these GABAergic neurons from the ventricular zone, their migration into an orderly monolayer, and the elaboration of their planar dendritic trees onto granule cell parallel fibres. Transcriptional regulators including RORA, SKOR2, FOXP2, LHX1/LHX5 and LDB1 drive lineage identity and dendritic maturation, while cytoskeletal and membrane proteins such as SPTBN2, MYH10 and the SEZ6 family shape arbor and synapse architecture. Loss of these functions produces degeneration or maldevelopment of the layer, manifesting as ataxia and impaired motor coordination; several members are mutated in human spinocerebellar ataxia and in lysosomal or mitochondrial disorders with prominent cerebellar involvement.

The granular layer is the innermost sheet of the cerebellar cortex, packed with the small granule neurons whose parallel fibers drive Purkinje cell dendrites and whose dendrites receive mossy fiber input at glomeruli. Building it requires that proliferating precursors of the external germinal layer exit the cycle, migrate inward past the Purkinje cells, and then wire correctly, so failures of this programme produce cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia and impaired motor learning. The genes here span those steps: cell cycle and differentiation control through a kinesin and neuronal differentiation factors, Wnt and midkine signals guiding proliferation and migration, and synaptic organizers such as cerebellin, its partner glutamate receptor delta-2, and a neurexin that assemble the parallel fiber–Purkinje synapse. Mutations in several, including the delta-2 receptor and a tau-tubulin kinase, cause inherited ataxias in humans.

Cerebellar granular layer morphogenesis builds the innermost layer of the cerebellar cortex, the densely packed sheet of granule neurons that relays mossy fiber input to Purkinje cells and thereby supports motor coordination and learning. Its failure produces cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia, and intellectual disability. The process spans proliferation and inward migration of granule precursors from the external germinal zone, extension of parallel fibers into the molecular layer, and assembly of glomerular synapses with mossy fiber terminals and Golgi cell axons. Trans-synaptic bridges built from cerebellin and the delta-type glutamate receptor GRID2 with presynaptic neurexins specify parallel fiber-Purkinje cell contacts, while WNT7A shapes presynaptic terminal remodeling, PROX1 drives granule cell differentiation, and OPHN1, a Rho-GAP mutated in X-linked intellectual disability, tunes dendritic and spine architecture. Cell cycle and cytoskeletal regulators such as KIF14 control precursor expansion.

The cerebellar granular layer is the densely packed innermost sheet of the cerebellar cortex, and its morphogenesis is how granule neurons are generated, migrate inward past the Purkinje cell layer, and arrange their parallel fibres and mossy fibre glomeruli into the circuit that feeds all cerebellar computation. Getting this wrong produces hypoplastic cerebellum, ataxia and impaired motor learning. The genes here span the steps involved: proliferation and cell division control in granule precursors, transcriptional specification of the granule fate by PROX1, and synapse assembly in which secreted CBLN1 bridges neurexins to the glutamate receptor delta-2 subunit GRID2 to build parallel fibre-Purkinje cell contacts. WNT7A remodels presynaptic mossy fibre terminals, while OPHN1, a Rho-family regulator mutated in X-linked intellectual disability, links the process to dendritic and spine morphology more broadly.

Formation of the cerebellar granular layer builds the innermost sheet of the cerebellar cortex, where granule cells are packed more densely than neurons anywhere else in the brain and relay mossy fibre input from the pons upward as parallel fibres onto Purkinje dendrites. Getting this layer built and wired correctly underlies motor coordination and cerebellar learning; disruption produces ataxia and, in humans, contributes to intellectual disability and cerebellar hypoplasia. The genes here span the steps involved: a transcription factor that specifies granule cell identity, secreted Wnt7a acting on axon and synapse remodelling at glomeruli, and a synaptic organizing module in which cerebellin-1 bridges neurexin on granule cell parallel fibres to the delta2 glutamate receptor on Purkinje cells. Rho-linked regulators such as OPHN1 shape dendrite and spine maturation, tying layer assembly to activity-dependent circuit refinement.

The cerebellar cortex delivers all of its output through Purkinje cells, and this programme builds the single-cell-thick monolayer in which those neurons sit, with dendrites fanning into the molecular layer to receive granule cell parallel fibres and axons projecting into white matter. Correct specification, migration and alignment of these cells sets up the inhibitory circuitry underlying motor coordination and learning; disruption produces ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia and Purkinje cell degeneration. Transcriptional regulators including RORA, SKOR2, LHX1/LHX5 with the cofactor LDB1, and FOXP2 drive Purkinje identity and dendritic maturation, while Notch ligand DLL1 patterns neighbouring progenitors. Cytoskeletal and trafficking components such as the spectrin SPTBN2, tubulin-modifying enzymes, and mitochondrial and lysosomal proteins sustain dendritic architecture and survival, linking this morphogenesis to inherited spinocerebellar ataxias and neurodegenerative disease.

Formation of the cerebellar Purkinje cell layer organizes the sole output neurons of the cerebellar cortex into a single-cell-thick sheet whose planar dendritic arbors receive granule cell parallel fibers and whose inhibitory axons carry cerebellar computation into the deep nuclei. When it fails, the result is ataxia, tremor and impaired motor learning, and Purkinje cells are among the neurons most vulnerable to degeneration in humans. Transcriptional control dominates the early steps: the nuclear receptor RORA drives Purkinje dendritic maturation and its loss produces the staggerer phenotype, while SKOR2, FOXP2, LHX1 and LHX5 with the cofactor LDB1 specify and maintain Purkinje identity. Later survival and arborization depend on cytoskeletal and housekeeping functions, including tubulin polyglutamylation and its reversal by AGTPBP1, copper transport, lysosomal glucocerebrosidase and mitochondrial membrane dynamics, linking layer formation to long-term neuronal maintenance.

Formation of the cerebellar cortex turns a proliferative rhombic-lip and ventricular-zone territory into the layered sheet that coordinates balance, gait, eye movements and motor learning, and its disruption underlies cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia and dysmorphic foliation. Granule cell precursors expand under Sonic hedgehog signalling relayed by SMO and the GLI transcription factors from Purkinje cells, then migrate inward past a Purkinje layer whose identity depends on factors such as SKOR2, RORA and LHX1/LHX5. Purkinje dendrites arborise and are wired to parallel fibres and climbing fibres through CBLN1 and the glutamate receptor delta-2 subunit GRID2, with SPTBN2 supporting membrane organisation in these cells. Cytoskeletal, migration and metabolic components including CDK5, TUBA1A and mitochondrial enzymes act alongside, and mutations in many of these genes cause inherited ataxias and cerebellar malformation syndromes.

Shaping of the cerebellar cortex turns a simple neuroepithelium into the foliated, layered sheet that supports motor coordination, balance and motor learning. Purkinje cells must be specified, positioned in a monolayer and elaborate their planar dendritic arbors, while granule cells proliferate in the external germinal layer and migrate inward past them; failure at any step produces ataxia, hypoplasia and dysmorphic folia. Sonic hedgehog transduction through SMO and the GLI transcription factors drives granule precursor expansion, RORA and SKOR2 enforce Purkinje cell identity, and CBLN1 with its postsynaptic partner GRID2 builds the parallel fibre synapse. Cytoskeletal and trafficking components such as TUBA1A, SPTBN2 and CDK5 support migration and dendrite growth. Mutations in several of these genes underlie inherited cerebellar ataxias and developmental malformations, linking this morphogenesis to lifelong motor control.

Building the layered cortex of the cerebellum requires granule cell precursors to proliferate, migrate inward past Purkinje cells, and wire into a stereotyped circuit that supports motor coordination, balance and motor learning. Failure of this programme produces cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia and, in humans, developmental motor and speech deficits. Transcriptional determinants including RORA, SKOR2, LHX1/LHX5 and PROX1 specify Purkinje and granule cell identities and drive their dendritic maturation, while Notch ligand DLL1 and WNT7A regulate progenitor behaviour and mossy fibre-granule cell synapse remodelling. Synaptic organizers such as CBLN1, GRID2 and NRXN1 assemble the parallel fibre-Purkinje cell connections whose loss causes ataxia, and CDK5 together with Rho-regulatory and cytoskeletal factors controls neuronal migration and process outgrowth. Tubulin-modifying enzymes and protein turnover components influence Purkinje cell survival, linking cortical construction to long-term degeneration phenotypes.

Building a structure is not the same as making it work, and developmental maturation covers the final steps by which a cell, tissue or organelle acquires full function after its shape is essentially set. The genes assembled here span several such endpoints: sperm capacitation and motility, where CatSper channel subunits and ROPN1/TDRD-family proteins equip the mature gamete; oocyte competence, via maternal factors such as ZAR1, MOS and TUBB8; synapse and axon maturation, with postsynaptic scaffolds, neurexins, RELN-DAB1 signalling and myelin-related SOX10 and LGI4; erythrocyte, osteoclast and lysosome-related organelle maturation, including vacuolar ATPase subunits and BLOC1 components; and vascular and skeletal functional maturation through KDR, SOX18, RUNX2 and IHH-PTH1R signalling. Transcriptional regulators including GATA2, CEBPA, ASCL1 and XBP1 drive the terminal differentiation programmes involved. Failure yields structures of correct anatomy but inadequate function, as in infertility, secretory insufficiency and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Striatum development covers the formation and maturation of the caudate, putamen and associated ventral forebrain structures that gate voluntary movement, habit learning and reward-guided behaviour. The genes involved specify medium spiny neurons and equip them to respond to dopamine: transcriptional regulators such as BCL11B, FOXP1 and FOXP2 drive striatal projection neuron identity, retinoid signalling through RARB and ALDH1A3 patterns the region, and the D1 and D2 dopamine receptors define the two output pathways that balance direct and indirect basal ganglia circuits. Synaptic organizers including SHANK3, SLITRK5 and CNTNAP2 build and refine corticostriatal connections. Disruption of this programme underlies striatal contributions to autism spectrum and obsessive-compulsive phenotypes, speech and language disorder, and movement disease, with HPRT1 loss and LRRK2 mutation causing striatal dysfunction in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Parkinson disease respectively.

Formation of the limbic system produces the interconnected structures into which emotion, motivation, reward and the affective coloring of memory are built: the hippocampus and dentate gyrus, amygdala, hypothalamic nuclei and their cortical partners. Building them requires sequential neurogenesis, migration of newborn neurons along radial and tangential routes, and precise axon guidance. Reelin signaling through its receptors and the downstream adaptor DAB1, together with the CDK5 kinase and its neuronal activators and the LIS1/YWHAE motility machinery, positions neurons in their proper layers; WNT/beta-catenin activity with LEF1, hedgehog transduction through SMO and GLI3, and regional transcription factors such as EMX2, LHX5, PROX1, TBR1, DLX1/2 and NEUROD1 specify the fields and their neuron types. Semaphorins, plexins, neuropilins and EPHA5 wire the resulting circuits, while dopamine and serotonin receptors and GABAergic markers mark their mature signaling. Disruption underlies lissencephaly, hippocampal malformation, epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism-spectrum phenotypes.

The formation and maturation of the substantia nigra, the midbrain grey matter comprising the pigmented dopaminergic pars compacta and the GABAergic pars reticulata, which together supply striatal dopamine and relay basal ganglia output for the control of movement; degeneration of its dopaminergic neurons underlies the motor signs of Parkinson's disease. The genes here point less to a single signalling cascade than to the cellular capacities this region must acquire: growth factor cues such as FGF2 and FGF9, cytoskeletal and morphogenetic regulators including RHOA, CDC42 and the neuronal intermediate filament INA, calmodulins and 14-3-3 adaptors for calcium and phosphoprotein signalling, and myelin proteins PLP1, MAG and CNP reflecting oligodendrocyte support of nigral projections. Also represented is the high oxidative and energetic demand of these neurons, through respiratory chain subunits, GLUD1, G6PD and the dopamine-degrading enzyme MAOB.

Formation of the amygdala, the almond-shaped nuclear complex of the medial temporal lobe that assigns emotional value to sensory experience and drives fear learning, threat responses and aspects of reward and social behaviour. Its construction depends on correct specification and migration of glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons into distinct nuclei and on their wiring to cortex, hippocampus and hypothalamus; disruption is linked to anxiety disorders, autism and the behavioural features seen in neurofibromatosis. The genes involved span transcriptional control of telencephalic regional identity and projection neuron fate, exemplified by the nuclear receptor NR2E1 and the T-box factor TBR1, alongside a Ras GTPase-activating protein that restrains growth factor signalling, a peptidase that degrades neuropeptide signals, an astrocytic sodium-potassium pump subunit and a transporter, tying maturation to local ionic and neuropeptide environments.

Hippocampus development is the construction of the brain's memory and spatial-navigation circuitry, from patterning of the medial pallium through neurogenesis, migration and lamination to the mature dentate gyrus and Ammon's horn. Its failure produces cortical malformation, epilepsy and intellectual disability, and the same programs are redeployed in adult dentate neurogenesis. Wnt and Shh signalling with transcription factors such as EMX2, LEF1, LHX5, ZIC and PROX1 specify the hippocampal field and dentate granule identity, while NEUROD1 and NEUROD6 drive neuronal differentiation. Radial migration and layer formation depend on the Reelin pathway acting through DAB1 and LRP8 and on the LIS1-YWHAE-CDK5 cytoskeletal module, whose loss causes lissencephaly. Additional genes govern axon guidance, mossy fibre targeting and synaptic partner matching, interneuron supply from ventral progenitors, and growth control through PTEN and TSC1.

The hippocampus is built over development from a patterned region of dorsomedial telencephalon into the layered dentate gyrus and cornu ammonis fields that support spatial navigation and the encoding of episodic memory; disrupted formation underlies epilepsy, intellectual disability and lissencephaly-type malformations. The genes here span the sequence of events: transcriptional regionalisation and progenitor identity through EMX2, LHX5, ZIC factors, GLI3 and Wnt/Hedgehog signalling; dentate granule cell specification via PROX1 and NEUROD1; and radial migration governed by Reelin acting through its receptor LRP8 and the DAB1 adaptor, with CDK5 and its activators, LIS1 and tubulin providing the cytoskeletal machinery. Later steps include axon guidance by ephrin and semaphorin receptors, synaptic target selection by KIRREL3, glycosylation-dependent dystroglycan function, and mTOR restraint by PTEN and TSC1 that sets neuronal size and connectivity.

Glial cell fate specification is the step at which a neural progenitor commits, reversibly, to becoming a glial cell rather than a neuron, setting the balance of astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and neurons produced from the developing brain and spinal cord. Without it the nervous system lacks the cells that myelinate axons, buffer extracellular ions and potassium, support synapses and form the blood-brain barrier interface. The genes here are transcriptional regulators acting in the progenitor: OLIG2 and NKX2-2 pattern the ventral neural tube and drive oligodendrocyte precursor identity, the nuclear factor I proteins NFIA and NFIB switch progenitors toward astrocyte gene expression and gliogenic competence, and PAX6 and the bHLH factor ASCL1 position cells along the neurogenic-to-gliogenic transition. Their misregulation is a recurring theme in glioma, where progenitor-like fate programmes are reactivated.

Glial cell fate commitment is the step at which a multipotent neural progenitor stops being able to become a neuron and is locked into an astrocyte or oligodendrocyte path, setting the ratio of neurons to glia that a developing brain and spinal cord ends up with. Without it there is no myelination, no astrocytic support of synapses or the blood-brain barrier, and gliogenesis timing defects; the same regulators reactivate in glioma, where progenitor-like states are maintained inappropriately. The commitment is transcriptional: SOX9 and the nuclear factor I proteins NFIA and NFIB initiate the astrocyte programme, OLIG2 and NKX2-2 specify oligodendrocyte precursors along the ventral neural tube, and HES5 represses proneural ASCL1 to block neurogenic differentiation. SOX2 and PAX6 maintain the progenitor pool upstream, while Wnt signalling through CTNNB1 and positional patterning determine when and where the switch to glia occurs.

Glial cell development covers the path from a committed neural progenitor to a functional astrocyte, oligodendrocyte, Schwann cell or microglial cell, and it determines whether axons are myelinated, whether extracellular potassium and glutamate are buffered, and whether the CNS has resident immune surveillance. Lineage transcription factors including SOX10, OLIG1, ASCL1, NKX2-2, POU3F1 and MYRF drive fate choice and the switch to myelin gene expression, while Notch effectors and ID proteins hold progenitors undifferentiated. Axon-derived and matrix cues acting through ERBB2/ERBB3, adhesion GPCR signalling, laminins, dystroglycan and PTEN-regulated PI3K/AKT and MAPK cascades control glial survival, ensheathment and radial sorting; polarity proteins such as PARD3 organise the myelinating membrane. Structural products such as PLP1, MAG, PRX and GFAP mark the mature states. Disruption underlies leukodystrophies, hereditary peripheral neuropathies, and reactive gliosis with microglial activation in neurodegeneration.

Branchiomotor neurons in the hindbrain send axons out of the brainstem to innervate muscles derived from the branchial arches, the muscles that move the jaw, produce facial expression, and operate the larynx and pharynx. Getting those axons to the right arch is what makes chewing, swallowing, blinking and vocalisation possible, and misrouting shows up as cranial nerve palsies and feeding difficulty. Guidance here is largely repulsive: secreted class 3 semaphorins such as SEMA3A and SEMA3F act on growth cones through neuropilin co-receptors and plexin-A signalling subunits, steering axons away from inappropriate territory and keeping exit points and nerve trunks separated. The ubiquitin ligase MYCBP2 acts intracellularly to shape how growth cones respond, linking receptor engagement to cytoskeletal remodelling and to the pruning of aberrant branches during motor axon pathfinding.

Thalamus development covers the formation and maturation of the diencephalic relay nucleus that routes sensory, motor and limbic information to the cortex and shapes arousal and attention. Regional identity is set by transcription factors such as GBX2, FOXB1 and TAL2, which mark the prethalamic and thalamic territories and specify neuronal fate, while OLIG2 contributes to progenitor patterning. Sonic hedgehog signalling through its receptor PTCH1's partner SMO provides the positional cue from the zona limitans that separates prethalamus from thalamus and governs neurogenic timing. Later steps involve circuit refinement and thalamocortical connectivity, with CNTNAP2 and the nicotinic receptor subunit CHRNB2 acting in axon organisation and activity-dependent wiring; mitochondrial and metabolic components support the energetic demands of this growth. Disruption of these steps underlies thalamocortical miswiring associated with intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy.

Building the layered cerebral cortex requires newborn neurons to travel from proliferative zones to their final positions, and this migratory programme sets that itinerary. When it fails, cortical lamination is disrupted, producing lissencephaly, subcortical band heterotopia, periventricular nodular heterotopia and epilepsy with intellectual disability. Reelin secreted by early-born neurons acts through the receptors LRP8 and DAB1 to instruct radially migrating pyramidal cells where to stop, while CDK5 with its neuronal activators p35 and p39 and the LIS1-NDEL1 module control microtubule dynamics and nucleokinesis; LINC complex proteins SUN1, SUN2 and nesprin couple the nucleus to the cytoskeleton so it can be towed. Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and RHOA, SRGAP2, and SLIT-ROBO guidance cues shape leading-process extension, and transcription factors including FOXG1, ARX, LHX6 and NKX2-1 specify the interneurons that migrate tangentially from the ganglionic eminences.

The cerebral cortex is not uniform: motor, somatosensory and visual areas occupy fixed positions, and that map is laid down in the embryonic neuroepithelium before neurons arrive. Cortical regionalization establishes graded positional identity across the dorsal telencephalon, so that progenitors in each domain generate the right neuron types and migrating neurons settle in the right area. Transcription factors do most of the work: PAX6 and EMX2 are expressed in opposing gradients that set anterior-posterior and medial-lateral coordinates, EMX1 and DMRTA2 mark and maintain the dorsal pallial territory, and EOMES marks the intermediate progenitors that expand the excitatory neuron output. Adhesion signalling through ADGRG1 anchors the pial basement membrane and constrains how far neurons travel. When patterning or its downstream migration fails, the result is malformed cortex with disordered layers and, clinically, epilepsy and intellectual disability.
