positive regulation of cell-cell adhesion covers the signals and surface molecules that make cells stick together more tightly or more often, a step that underlies tissue integrity, platelet aggregation, leukocyte recruitment and, above all, the stable contacts immune cells must form to communicate. Much of the content is immunological: MHC class I and II molecules, T cell receptor components and their kinases (LCK, FYN, ZAP70, SYK), costimulatory and checkpoint ligands of the CD28/B7 and TNF superfamilies, and the selectins, integrins and glycosyltransferases that build homing receptor ligands for rolling and firm arrest on endothelium. Cytokines and chemokines amplify these contacts, while junctional and cytoskeletal proteins such as catenin, ZO-1, JAM-A, RHOA and PTK2 convert receptor engagement into mechanically stable adhesion. Chromatin remodelling and lineage transcription factors set the adhesion programme during lymphocyte development. Loss of this regulation impairs immune synapse formation, antigen priming and inflammatory cell trafficking.

Cells stick to one another on cue, and this is the set of regulators that raise the rate or extent of that sticking. Much of the biology here is immunological: antigen presentation by MHC class I and class II molecules, costimulatory and coinhibitory receptor pairs such as CD28 with CD80/CD86 and ICOS with its ligand, and the proximal T cell kinases LCK, FYN, ZAP70 and SYK that convert receptor engagement into integrin activation and stable immunological synapses. Selectins, their fucosyl- and sulfotransferase-dependent ligands, junctional adhesion molecule F11R, VCAM1 and ITGA4/ITGB2 support leukocyte rolling, firm arrest and transmigration, while chemokines including CCL19, CCL21 and CXCL13 position cells for contact. Cytokine, Wnt, Hedgehog, ephrin and TGF-beta inputs, together with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits and lineage transcription factors, set adhesive competence transcriptionally. Such control underlies lymphocyte development, inflammation, wound repair and tissue integrity, and its dysregulation contributes to autoimmunity and tumour immune evasion.

Cells constantly take structures apart, and cellular component disassembly gathers the machinery that does so across very different scales: severing and depolymerising cytoskeletal filaments, dismantling extracellular matrix, stripping stalled ribosomes of their nascent chains, resolving membrane and chromatin assemblies. Controlled breakdown is what allows a mitotic spindle to turn over, a cell to change shape and migrate, a tissue to be remodelled or invaded, and damaged organelles to be cleared. Representative activities include actin-filament severing and capping by cofilin, gelsolin, tropomodulins and capping proteins, microtubule destabilisation by katanin, spastin and kinesin-13 family members, matrix proteolysis by matrix metalloproteinases, ADAMs and cathepsins, autophagic and ESCRT-mediated membrane scission with ATG8 proteins and CHMP subunits, ribosome-associated quality control and translational termination, and caspase-driven nuclear dismantling during apoptosis. Loss of such turnover underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and tumour invasion.

cellular process involved in reproduction in multicellular organism covers the cell-level events that make gametes and allow them to unite, and so underlies fertility itself; loss of these functions produces azoospermia, oocyte maturation arrest, premature ovarian insufficiency and failed fertilisation. It spans germ cell specification and survival (NANOS, DAZL, DND1, KIT), the meiotic program with its double-strand break machinery, synaptonemal complex and recombination checkpoints (SPO11, REC8, SYCP1/3, DMC1, MLH1), and the piRNA and RNA-binding systems that silence transposons and store maternal transcripts. Later steps build the sperm itself: chromatin remodelling into protamines, acrosome formation, and axonemal and outer dense fibre assembly, with CATSPER channels and ABHD2 conferring the hyperactivated motility and capacitation needed to reach the egg. Fertilisation is completed by zona pellucida proteins and the IZUMO1-JUNO recognition pair, followed by egg activation and oocyte-to-embryo transition.

Sexual reproduction in animals depends on specialized cell-level programmes that build gametes and allow them to meet, and this collection covers those events from germ cell specification through meiosis, sperm and oocyte maturation, and fertilization. Loss of these functions produces infertility rather than systemic disease: azoospermia, teratozoospermia with malformed sperm heads or tails, premature ovarian insufficiency, and oocytes that fail to activate after sperm entry. Mechanistically it spans meiotic recombination and synapsis (SPO11, DMC1, SYCP1/SYCP3, REC8, MLH1), piRNA-directed silencing of transposons in germ cells (PIWIL1/2, MOV10L1, TDRD family), chromatin remodelling in which transition proteins and protamines replace histones during spermiogenesis, axonemal and flagellar assembly, and sperm motility control through CatSper calcium channels. Sperm-egg recognition and fusion requires IZUMO1 with its egg receptor and the tetraspanin CD9, while zona pellucida proteins and maternal-effect factors prepare the oocyte for embryogenesis.

Producing offspring requires a dedicated biology that runs alongside ordinary somatic physiology, and this reproductive programme spans germ cell specification, meiosis, gamete maturation, fertilization, and the hormonal and uterine support of pregnancy. Its failure is the molecular basis of infertility: azoospermia, oocyte maturation arrest, gonadal dysgenesis, recurrent pregnancy loss. Meiotic recombination and synapsis machinery such as SPO11, DMC1, the SYCP synaptonemal complex proteins and MSH4/MSH5 generates crossovers and haploid genomes, while piRNA factors including PIWIL1 and MOV10L1 silence transposons in the germline. Sperm are built and powered by axonemal, outer dense fibre and CATSPER channel components, protamines replace histones to compact the paternal genome, and IZUMO1 with its egg receptor and the zona pellucida glycoproteins mediate sperm-egg recognition. Gonadotropins, steroid receptors, TGF-beta/BMP ligands such as GDF9 and BMP15, and sex-determining regulators including SRY and SOX9 coordinate gonad development, folliculogenesis and implantation.

Digestion converts a meal into absorbable molecules and moves them into metabolism, and this collection of activities spans the secretory, motor, barrier and transport functions of the gut and its accessory glands. Pancreatic lipase and carboxyl ester lipase hydrolyse dietary fat, while intestinal transporters and lipid-binding proteins such as SLC5A1 for glucose, SLC2A5 for fructose, NPC1L1 and CD36 for sterols and fatty acids, and FABP1/FABP2 handle uptake; ABCG5/ABCG8 pump excess sterol back into the lumen, and apolipoproteins package absorbed lipid for export. Gut hormones including ghrelin, secretin, leptin and their receptors, together with muscarinic and serotonergic receptors, tune gastric acid, motility and appetite. Mucins and trefoil factors protect the epithelium, claudins and tight-junction proteins set paracrine permeability, and WNK-SPAK kinases with anion exchangers control fluid and electrolyte flux. Failure produces malabsorption, diarrhoea, or inflammatory and cholestatic disease.

ovulation cycle process covers the recurring events of the female reproductive cycle by which ovarian follicles grow, select a dominant follicle, release a mature oocyte, and remodel into a corpus luteum that prepares the endometrium for implantation. It sets fertility and cycle length, and its disruption underlies anovulation, premature ovarian insufficiency and polycystic ovary phenotypes. The genes trace the gonadotropin axis from FSHB through the FSH and LH receptors into STAT5- and steroid-receptor-dependent transcription, with ESR1, PGR, NR5A1 and FOXO3 governing granulosa cell fate and the resting follicle pool. Oocyte-derived GDF9 and BMP/TGF-beta family ligands coordinate granulosa proliferation, while NPPC-NPR2 signalling holds meiosis in arrest until the ovulatory surge. Follicle rupture and cumulus expansion require matrix remodelling by ADAMTS1, MMP2, PTX3 and TNFAIP6, and atresia of unselected follicles proceeds through caspase-mediated apoptosis. Metabolic signals such as leptin link nutritional state to cycling.

The ovulation cycle process covers the recurring events by which ovarian follicles grow, select a dominant follicle, release a mature oocyte and remodel the ovary afterwards, together with the hormone-driven changes in the uterus that prepare it for implantation. It is the basis of female fertility, and its disruption underlies anovulatory infertility, polycystic ovary syndrome and premature ovarian insufficiency. Gonadotropins acting through FSHR and LHCGR drive granulosa cell proliferation and steroidogenesis, with STAT5 signalling and nuclear receptors including ESR1, PGR and NR5A1 relaying the response; oocyte-derived GDF9 and BMP receptor signalling coordinate the surrounding somatic cells, while NPPC-NPR2 signalling holds the oocyte in meiotic arrest until the ovulatory surge. Follicle rupture requires proteolytic and matrix remodelling by metalloproteinases and the cumulus matrix proteins PTX3 and TNFAIP6, and atresia of non-selected follicles proceeds by caspase-dependent apoptosis under FOXO3 control.

regulation of anatomical structure morphogenesis covers the control layer over how tissues and organs acquire their shape during development and repair — setting how fast and how far processes like branching, tube formation, axon outgrowth and blood vessel sprouting proceed. Its outputs define body plan and organ architecture, and mis-tuning underlies congenital malformations, vascular anomalies, neurodevelopmental disorders and the aberrant angiogenesis and invasion of tumours. Mechanistically it draws together the morphogen systems that pattern tissues (WNT, BMP/TGF-beta, Hedgehog, Notch, FGF and their inhibitors such as NOG, DKK1 and SPRY), guidance cue families that steer growing axons and vessels (ephrins, semaphorins, slits, netrins, VEGF/angiopoietin receptors), and the Rho-family GTPases, actin regulators and cadherin-integrin adhesion complexes that execute cell shape change and migration. Lineage transcription factors and numerous microRNAs set the quantitative thresholds at which these programs run.

Shaping tissues and organs during development requires not only the machinery that builds them but control over how fast and how far that building goes, and this broad regulatory programme covers the modulation of anatomical structure morphogenesis. It governs how epithelia branch, how blood vessels sprout and remodel, how neurons extend and steer axons and dendrites, and how mitochondria and cell shape are reorganized to permit those movements. The effectors are correspondingly varied: Rho-family GTPases with their exchange factors and GAPs acting on the actin cytoskeleton, guidance cues and receptors such as netrins, slits, semaphorins, ephrins and their plexin, Robo and Eph partners, angiogenic ligands including VEGFA and angiopoietins with KDR, TEK and NRP1, and morphogen inputs from WNT, BMP, TGF-beta, FGF and Hedgehog families, layered with transcription factors and microRNAs that tune the response. Misregulation underlies congenital malformations, vascular anomalies and abnormal tissue remodelling in disease.

Cells acquire and maintain their shapes by controlling where actin filaments are built, where membrane is pushed out, and where adhesions anchor the cortex, and this set gathers the regulators that set the pace and extent of that shaping. It matters wherever shape is function: neurons extending axons and dendritic spines, epithelia forming junctions and apical belts, erythrocytes holding a deformable biconcave membrane skeleton, endothelial cells forming tubes, and immune cells spreading and migrating. Much of the control converges on Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42 together with their activators, GAPs and effectors, on formins and Arp2/3-associated nucleation promoters, on non-muscle myosins and actin-severing and capping proteins, and on spectrin-ankyrin and ezrin-radixin-moesin cortical linkers. Guidance receptors of the plexin, ephrin and semaphorin families, integrin-associated kinases and Wnt pathway components feed positional cues in. Loss of this regulation produces neurodevelopmental disease, fragile red cells, and disordered epithelial architecture.

Mammalian oogenesis proceeds through defined stages in which a primordial female germ cell grows, arrests in meiosis, and is finally released as a fertilizable ovum, and the genes here mark the ovarian signals that time those transitions. Their output determines how many follicles are recruited from the resting pool, how long an oocyte is held in prophase arrest, and whether ovulation yields a competent egg; disruption produces anovulation, premature ovarian insufficiency, or altered litter and ovulation rate. Granulosa-derived natriuretic peptide acting on its guanylyl cyclase receptor sustains the cyclic nucleotide tone that keeps the oocyte arrested, anti-Mullerian hormone restrains primordial follicle activation, and BMP receptor signalling plus EGF-family ligands such as epiregulin drive cumulus expansion, with secreted matrix organizers building the expanded cumulus. RNA-binding and splicing-associated factors contribute to the oocyte's stored maternal transcript programme.

Glands form by budding an epithelium into surrounding mesenchyme and then branching, elongating and hollowing it into a secretory tree, and gland morphogenesis covers the generation and organization of those structures. It builds the mammary, prostate, salivary and lacrimal glands and the skin appendages, so its disruption produces ectodermal dysplasias with missing or hypoplastic glands, while its reactivation in adult tissue underlies hormone-driven proliferation in breast and prostate. Reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signalling drives it: hedgehog, FGF, EGF-family, WNT, BMP and TGF-beta ligands with their receptors, ectodysplasin signalling through EDAR, and hormone receptors for androgen, oestrogen, progesterone and glucocorticoid that read systemic cues into local branching decisions. Transcription factors such as FOXA1, SOX9, NFIB and the posterior HOX proteins specify regional identity, while laminins, matrix metalloproteinases, cell polarity and adhesion components and selective apoptosis shape cleft formation and lumen clearance.

Every RNA that works as part of a machine rather than a message must first be folded, modified and packaged with proteins, and ribonucleoprotein complex biogenesis covers that construction work: making the RNA and protein subunits, chemically modifying them, and assembling them into functional particles. The output is the cell's core expression machinery — ribosomes, spliceosomal snRNPs, telomerase and RNase P, microRNA effector complexes and the mitochondrial translation apparatus. Nucleolar processing factors, small nucleolar RNP components such as the pseudouridine synthase DKC1 with NOP10 and GAR1, methyltransferases including fibrillarin, exosome ribonucleases and AAA-ATPase assembly chaperones build and proofread pre-ribosomes, while SMN with its Gemin partners loads Sm proteins onto snRNAs and splicing factors of the SF3B and PRPF families complete spliceosome assembly. Defects here cause ribosomopathies, spinal muscular atrophy and Treacher Collins syndrome, reflecting how sensitive growth and differentiation are to assembly capacity.

Before two cells or two membrane compartments can fuse, signal, or transfer material, their bilayers must first be tethered close enough for surface proteins to engage, and membrane-to-membrane docking is that initial attachment step. The genes here point to its best-characterised physiological setting: leukocyte capture on activated endothelium, where the immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptors ICAM1 and VCAM1 protrude from the endothelial surface and grip integrins on a rolling leukocyte. Holding that contact requires mechanical anchoring, supplied by ezrin and moesin, which crosslink the cytoplasmic tails of transmembrane adhesion receptors to the cortical actin cytoskeleton, with ROCK1 controlling actomyosin tension and the phosphorylation state of these linkers. Docking of this kind governs inflammatory recruitment and immune surveillance; excessive or misplaced adhesion contributes to chronic inflammation and atherosclerotic lesion formation.

Protein to membrane docking is the first committed step by which a soluble or vesicle-borne protein is captured at the surface of its destination membrane, held there by receptors and tethers that project from the target bilayer. This initial adhesion sets the specificity of downstream events: only after docking can a cargo be inserted, translocated, or a vesicle be primed for fusion. The genes span several arenas where this occurs. Peroxisomal membrane proteins are recognised and docked by PEX16 and PEX26, without which peroxisomes fail to form and severe developmental disease follows. RAB7A and SNX3 mark late endosomal and retromer-associated membranes, recruiting effectors to define where sorting and maturation take place, while STXBP3 acts with SNARE machinery to position vesicles before membrane fusion. Together they represent the recognition and tethering stage that precedes protein insertion and vesicle fusion in intracellular trafficking.

Docking is the first committed step by which a soluble or peripherally associated protein is captured at a target membrane, held there by proteins that project from the membrane surface long enough for downstream tethering, translocation or fusion to proceed. It matters because it determines where cargo, coats and fusion machinery act: peroxisomal membrane biogenesis depends on PEX16 and the tail-anchored PEX26, which recruits the AAA-ATPase receptor-recycling complex to the peroxisome; endosomal identity and cargo sorting depend on the small GTPase RAB7A and the phosphoinositide-binding sorting nexin SNX3, which recognises PtdIns3P-rich membranes; and STXBP3, a Munc18-family SM protein, engages SNARE complexes to prepare vesicles for fusion in regulated exocytosis and glucose transporter trafficking. Loss of such docking events derails organelle formation and membrane traffic, as in the peroxisome biogenesis disorders arising from PEX gene mutations.

DNA strand elongation is the productive phase of DNA synthesis, in which polymerases extend a primed 3' end to copy the genome ahead of cell division and to complete repair patches. Without it replication forks stall and collapse, generating breaks, chromosomal rearrangements and the genome instability that underlies cancer. The genes cover the core replisome and its accessory machinery: the MCM helicase with GINS, priming by polymerase alpha, processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon on a PCNA clamp loaded by RFC, and Okazaki fragment maturation through DNA2 and ligase I. Elongation happens on chromatin, so the INO80 remodelling complex with its RUVBL ATPases repositions nucleosomes at the fork. Telomeric components, including telomerase and the shelterin protein POT1 with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, extend and protect chromosome ends where conventional replication cannot finish.

Extending a DNA strand by adding nucleotides to its 3' end is the productive step of replication, and the machinery here covers both the polymerases that do it and the factors that keep forks moving through chromatin. Without it cells cannot duplicate their genomes on schedule, and stalled or collapsed forks become the source of the chromosomal breaks and rearrangements that drive cancer. Replicative polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon work behind an MCM helicase and GINS, with PCNA as the sliding clamp loaded by RFC subunits, DNA2 and LIG1 processing and sealing Okazaki fragments. The INO80 chromatin remodelling complex, with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, clears nucleosomes ahead of the fork and aids restart. MRE11-RAD50-NBN handles damaged forks, while TERT and POT1 extend and protect the chromosome ends that conventional elongation cannot finish.

Tissues remodel by cutting apart the protein scaffold their cells sit in, and extracellular matrix disassembly is the controlled proteolysis that does it. It underlies wound repair, bone and cartilage turnover, ovulation, mammary and vascular remodelling, and leukocyte passage through basement membrane; when it runs unchecked it enables tumour invasion, metastasis, aneurysm and the cartilage loss of arthritis. Matrix metalloproteinases, including the membrane-anchored MMP14, degrade collagens, gelatin and elastin, while aggrecanases such as ADAMTS4 and ADAMTS5 clear cartilage proteoglycan and heparanase cleaves heparan sulfate chains. Cysteine and serine proteases from macrophages, osteoclasts, neutrophils and mast cells contribute, and plasminogen and furin activate latent enzymes. Inhibitors such as TIMP3, RECK and cystatin C restrain the process, cytokines including TGF-beta and IL6 set its level, and collagen receptors DDR1 and DDR2 report matrix state back to the cell.

Transporters and channels rarely act alone: their opening, conductance, trafficking and turnover are set by accessory subunits, calcium sensors and kinases, and this regulation of transmembrane transporter activity is what tunes ion flux to the needs of excitable and secretory cells. The consequences are concrete — cardiac repolarization, skeletal muscle excitation–contraction coupling, synaptic strength and store-operated calcium entry all depend on it. Calmodulin and CaMKII relay intracellular calcium back onto channels, phospholamban and sarcolipin restrain the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, KCNE subunits reshape KCNQ1 potassium currents, STAC proteins and calcium channel gamma/beta subunits govern voltage-gated calcium and AMPA receptor behaviour, and STIM1/STIM2 sense store depletion to gate ORAI channels. Regulatory proteasome subunits and ubiquilin add degradative control of channel abundance, while WNK kinases and TRPC6 link the system to osmotic and hormonal signals; failure produces arrhythmia, myopathy and epilepsy.

Electron transport chain is the set of membrane-embedded carriers that pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 down a redox gradient to oxygen, pumping protons and building the electrochemical potential that ATP synthase uses. It supplies most of the ATP in aerobic tissues, and its failure produces the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and exercise intolerance seen when complex I or cytochrome oxidase subunits are mutated. The core is complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, with cytochrome c and ubiquinone as mobile shuttles, together with assembly factors, iron-sulfur and heme cofactor pathways, and the electron transfer flavoprotein route that feeds in electrons from fatty acid oxidation. Output is regulated transcriptionally through PGC-1alpha and hypoxia-responsive signals, and the same components govern superoxide production, redox stress handling and release of cytochrome c during apoptosis.

Cells recover most of the energy in nutrients by passing electrons down a chain of carriers to a terminal acceptor, and this electron transport chain is that machinery. Coupled to proton pumping, it builds the inner-membrane gradient that ATP synthase uses, so its failure collapses oxidative phosphorylation and causes the mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, lactic acidosis and neurodegeneration seen when respiratory subunits are mutated. Nuclear- and mitochondrially encoded subunits of complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase assemble with cytochrome c, ubiquinone and iron-sulfur or copper cofactors supplied by dedicated assembly and metallation factors. Flavoprotein dehydrogenases feed electrons in from fatty acid oxidation. Quality control and biogenesis regulators such as PINK1, PARK7 and the transcriptional coactivator PPARGC1A tune chain content, while leaked electrons generate superoxide, countered here by SOD2.

Signal transduction feeding into regulation of gene expression captures the step where an extracellular cue is converted into a change in transcription, and the genes here are dominated by the developmental version of that logic: patterning the early embryo. Secreted antagonists such as CER1 and DAND5 restrain Nodal and BMP signalling, FGF8 and FGF5 supply growth factor input, PDGFRA and the purinergic receptor P2RY1 transduce surface signals, and SMAD3 carries TGF-beta family signals to DNA. The transcription factors they converge on -- GSC, SOX17, MESP1, TBX6, PAX6, MSX1/MSX2, NEUROD1, HNF4A -- assign germ layer identity, somite boundaries, neural and endodermal fates. Because position in the embryo is read out as gene expression, disruption of this signal-to-transcription coupling produces axis and mesoderm defects, craniofacial and eye malformations, and failures of endoderm-derived organ specification.

CD40 is a tumour necrosis factor receptor family member on B cells, dendritic cells, macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells, and its engagement by CD40 ligand on activated T cells is how helper T cells license antibody responses and myeloid activation. Signalling through it drives germinal centre formation, immunoglobulin class switching and costimulatory molecule upregulation; loss of the ligand causes hyper-IgM syndrome with absent class switching and poor responses to protein antigens. Receptor clustering recruits TRAF adaptors, including TRAF2, TRAF5 and TRAF6, which nucleate ubiquitin-dependent assembly of kinase complexes leading to NF-kB and MAP kinase activation and changes in transcription. Linear ubiquitin chain components such as RNF31 and SHARPIN support this output, while TNFAIP3 and TNIP2 restrain it, so the pathway also illustrates how ubiquitin editing sets the duration of inflammatory gene expression.

Neuronal signal transduction covers the step in which an activated receptor on a neuron converts an external cue into an intracellular change, altering excitability, growth or connectivity. The genes here point to the synapse and the axon surface rather than to a single cascade: neurexin and neuroligin form a trans-synaptic adhesion pair that specifies and aligns pre- and postsynaptic compartments, olfactomedin-like secreted proteins modulate synaptic receptor composition, and the Nogo receptor transmits myelin-derived inhibitory cues that restrict axon regrowth and stabilise mature circuits. A voltage-gated potassium channel subunit shapes the electrical response that follows, a purinergic receptor reads extracellular nucleotides, and clusterin acts as a secreted chaperone in the extracellular environment. Together these support synapse formation and plasticity; disruption of the adhesion and growth-inhibitory arms underlies neurodevelopmental disorders and the limited repair seen after central nervous system injury.

This is a very broad collection of genes whose activity increases the strength, duration or frequency of cell signalling, spanning essentially every major communication system a human cell uses. Represented here are ligands and receptors of the WNT, Hedgehog, Notch, TGF-beta/BMP, receptor tyrosine kinase, cytokine, chemokine, G protein-coupled and innate immune Toll-like receptor families, together with the adaptors, kinases, phosphatases, GTPases, ubiquitin ligases, scaffolds and microRNAs that amplify their output. Positive regulation of signalling of this kind sets how strongly cells respond to growth factors, hormones, neurotransmitters and pathogen-derived cues, and so underlies development, immune activation, metabolic control, synaptic transmission and tissue repair. Because amplification is inherently dangerous, many of the same components are proto-oncogenes or inflammatory drivers, and their unchecked activity contributes to cancer, autoimmunity, fibrosis and neurodegeneration.

Cells communicate by exporting messengers, and signal release covers the regulated discharge of neurotransmitters, peptide hormones, cytokines and lipid mediators into the extracellular space. It underlies synaptic transmission, glucose homeostasis through insulin and glucagon secretion, neuroendocrine control of stress, appetite and reproduction, and inflammatory mediator output; its failure produces epilepsy, neurodegeneration, diabetes and endocrine disease. The core machinery is calcium-triggered vesicle exocytosis: voltage-gated calcium channels and intracellular calcium sensors of the synaptotagmin family act on SNARE complexes built from syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMPs, with Munc13 and Munc18 proteins priming vesicles at active zones scaffolded by RIMs and piccolo. Layered on top are the cues that decide when to secrete: G protein-coupled receptors for monoamines, opioids and incretins, ATP-sensitive potassium channels, protein kinase A and C cascades, transcription factors specifying secretory cell identity, and circadian clock components timing hormone output.

Cells must move metal ions across membranes against steep gradients, and this broad transport programme covers that directed movement of calcium, sodium, potassium, zinc, copper, iron, magnesium and manganese into, out of and within cells. It underlies electrical excitability in neurons, cardiac and skeletal muscle, secretion and contraction triggered by calcium rise, nutrient metal acquisition, and protection against metal toxicity. The machinery spans voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels with their accessory subunits, ligand- and stimulus-gated channels such as glutamate receptors and TRP family sensors, P-type pumps including the Na/K-ATPase and sarcoplasmic calcium ATPases, exchangers and solute carriers, store-operated entry through STIM and ORAI, mitochondrial uptake via the MCU complex, and iron and zinc handlers such as transferrin receptor, ferroportin and the ZIP and ZnT families. Mutations here cause channelopathies, arrhythmia, deafness, epilepsy, renal salt-wasting and disorders of copper, iron and zinc balance.

Cells hold their internal chloride at a set point, and that set point determines whether opening a chloride channel depolarises or hyperpolarises the membrane, how much water follows salt across an epithelium, and how far a cell can swell or shrink. This is intracellular monoatomic anion homeostasis, and chloride is the anion that matters most. Cation-chloride cotransporters do the loading and unloading: NKCC1 accumulates chloride against its gradient, while the neuronal KCC2 extrudes it, and the developmental switch between them is what makes GABA inhibitory in mature neurons. A WNK kinase module with the downstream kinase SPAK senses chloride and cell volume and phosphorylates these transporters to set transport direction. Potassium channel subunits including KCNQ1 with KCNE3 supply the recycling conductance that sustains secretion. Disruption causes hypertension, salt-wasting tubulopathies, and epilepsy.

Cells hold potassium far above its extracellular concentration, and intracellular potassium homeostasis is the set of transport activities that maintains that gradient, which in turn sets the resting membrane potential, drives secondary transport of nutrients and other ions, and supports cell volume control. The core machinery here is the Na+/K+-ATPase, built from catalytic alpha subunits and beta subunits with tissue-specific distribution, pumping potassium inward against sodium efflux; related gastric and non-gastric H+/K+-ATPases couple potassium uptake to acid secretion. Small FXYD proteins act as regulatory subunits that tune pump kinetics, phosphorylation by cAMP-dependent protein kinase adjusts activity, and the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter provides a parallel entry route. Potassium exit through inwardly rectifying and calcium-activated channels completes the balance. Loss of this control underlies disorders of excitability, including familial hemiplegic migraine, alternating hemiplegia and dystonia-parkinsonism from alpha subunit mutations.

Almost no differentiated cell is isotropic: epithelia have an apical and a basal face, neurons have an axon and dendrites, a migrating cell has a front and a rear, and a dividing cell must orient its spindle. Establishment of cell polarity is the step that breaks symmetry and fixes those axes, and it underlies epithelial barrier formation, directed migration, ciliogenesis, and the asymmetric divisions that generate distinct daughter fates; its loss contributes to tissue disorganization and tumour invasion. Conserved modules do the work — the apical Par complex with atypical protein kinase C and PARD3, the basolateral Scribble–Lgl–Dlg-type module, Crumbs–PATJ at tight junctions — reading into Rho-family GTPases such as CDC42 and RHOA, their DOCK and cytohesin activators, and ROCK and PAK effectors. These reorganize actomyosin, microtubule anchoring and spindle orientation machinery, and direct polarized vesicle traffic through RAB10 and ARF6. Planar cues from WNT and PRICKLE align polarity across a tissue.

Once a cell has established an axis — an apical surface facing a lumen, a leading edge, a basolateral domain with its own transporters — that asymmetry has to be actively held in place against membrane turnover and cytoskeletal remodelling, and maintenance of cell polarity is that upkeep. It underlies epithelial barrier integrity, directed migration, and the correct sorting of channels and receptors to the surface where they work; its loss accompanies epithelial disorganisation and the invasive behaviour of carcinoma cells. Scaffolding and adaptor proteins anchor membrane proteins to the cortical cytoskeleton, with spectrin-based and PDZ-domain scaffolds tethering transporters and junctional components, while actin regulators and a crumbs-family apical determinant sustain the cortical architecture. Wnt ligands and GSK3B signalling orient and reinforce the axis, linking polarity maintenance to tissue patterning and to vesicle trafficking that continually replenishes each domain.

Manganese is needed as a cofactor by mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, arginase and glycosyltransferases, yet excess is a neurotoxin, so cells must hold internal manganese within a narrow band. The transporters that do this move manganese across the plasma membrane, into secretory compartments, and back out for biliary excretion. A divalent metal importer family brings manganese and iron into the cytosol from endosomes and from the gut lumen, a secretory-pathway calcium/manganese ATPase sequesters it into the Golgi where glycosylation enzymes use it, and a dedicated efflux transporter clears the surplus. Loss of efflux capacity causes inherited hypermanganesemia with dystonia, liver cirrhosis and polycythemia, while defective uptake through the zinc/manganese importer produces a congenital glycosylation disorder, showing how tightly protein glycosylation and neurological function depend on this balance.

Almost everything a cell does mechanically depends on actin filaments and the proteins that build, cap, sever, bundle and pull on them, and this actin filament-based process collects that biology: cell shape and polarity, migration, adhesion, endocytosis, cytokinesis, and muscle contraction. Nucleators such as the Arp2/3 complex with its WASP/WAVE activators, formins and spire proteins initiate filaments; profilin, thymosins, cofilin, gelsolin, capping proteins and tropomodulins set filament length and turnover; and Rho-family GTPases with their many GEFs, GAPs and kinase effectors such as ROCK, PAK and LIMK decide where assembly happens. Myosin motors generate force, while sarcomeric components including titin, nebulin, troponins and tropomyosins organize contraction in muscle. Linkage to membranes and junctions runs through spectrins, ezrin/radixin/moesin, talin, filamin and integrin-associated adaptors. Mutations across these families cause cardiomyopathies, myopathies, deafness, nephrotic syndrome and immunodeficiency, and their dysregulation underlies tumour cell invasion.

Cells build and maintain protrusions that extend beyond the cell body, and this programme covers the assembly, shaping and disassembly of those structures. It encompasses neuronal axons, dendrites and growth cones, motile and primary cilia, sperm flagella, microvilli and stereocilia, and the lamellipodia and filopodia of migrating cells. Its outputs include wiring of the nervous system by guidance cues and their receptors such as the semaphorins, slits, netrins, ephrins and Trk neurotrophin receptors; ciliary beating for mucociliary clearance and left-right patterning; and hearing, vision and sperm motility. Mechanistically it draws on actin nucleation and capping through Arp2/3, WAVE and profilin, Rho-family GTPases and their regulators, microtubule dynamics and severing, intraflagellar transport and dynein arm assembly, and membrane trafficking. Loss of components produces ciliopathies, primary ciliary dyskinesia, deafness, infertility and neurodevelopmental malformations.

Cells extend their surfaces into projections — cilia, flagella, microvilli, filopodia, lamellipodia, neuronal axons and dendrites — and this pathway covers the machinery that builds them. Such projections carry out motility, fluid propulsion, sensing and directed growth, so failures produce ciliopathies with retinal degeneration, cystic kidneys and situs defects, immotile sperm and airway clearance defects, and misrouted neurites. Two engines dominate: branched and bundled actin assembly driven by the Arp2/3 complex with WAVE regulatory subunits, profilins, cofilin, formins, Ena/VASP and myosins acting under Rho-family GTPase and GEF/GAP control; and microtubule-based axonemal construction, where centriole and transition-zone components, intraflagellar transport particles with kinesin-2 and cytoplasmic dynein-2, Bardet-Biedl coat proteins, dynein-arm assembly factors, radial spoke and tektin proteins build motile and sensory cilia. Rab GTPases and TBC-domain regulators supply membrane, while RFX and FOXJ1 transcription factors specify ciliated fates.

A migrating cell moves by pushing out a lamellipodium, the flat sheet of branched actin at its leading edge, and this pathway builds it. The output is directed motility: wound closure, immune cell chemotaxis, axon growth cone advance, and, when misregulated, tumour cell invasion. The core machinery is the Arp2/3 complex with its ARPC and actin-related subunits, activated by WAVE-family nucleation-promoting factors held in a regulatory complex with CYFIP1, ABI and NCKAP1, and by WAS protein in hematopoietic cells. Rho-family GTPases RAC1, RAC2 and CDC42, switched on by GEFs such as VAV2/3 and ARHGEF6/7, decide where protrusion happens, while cofilin, capping protein, twinfilin and fascin set filament length and bundling. Integrin and receptor tyrosine kinase inputs, PI3K signalling, and adhesion proteins including vinculin couple protrusion to substrate attachment so that the edge advances rather than ruffling in place.

Microvillus assembly builds the finger-like actin protrusions that give absorptive epithelia their brush border, expanding the apical surface of intestinal and kidney tubule cells for nutrient and solute uptake and anchoring digestive enzymes and transporters at the membrane. Loss of this program flattens the apical surface and produces malabsorptive diarrhoea, as in microvillus inclusion disease. The genes describe how a parallel actin bundle is made and tethered: espin and fascin crosslink the core filaments, ezrin and radixin with the scaffold NHERF1 link that core to the overlying membrane, and the unconventional motor MYO1A slides membrane along the bundle. Upstream, a Rap GTPase module and the STE20 kinases MST4 and TNIK set apical polarity and license brush border formation, tying protrusion growth to epithelial differentiation and apical membrane identity.

Microvillus assembly builds the dense apical projections that expand the absorptive surface of epithelial cells, most conspicuously the intestinal brush border and the kidney proximal tubule. Without it, enterocytes fail to present digestive and transport machinery at the correct density, and inherited defects in apical trafficking and brush border organisation cause congenital diarrhoeal disease and cholestasis. The projections are cored by actin bundles: espin and fascin crosslink the filaments, while ezrin and its relative radixin tether the bundle to the overlying plasma membrane, with the scaffold NHERF1 anchoring transporters and receptors at that interface, and myosin-1a moving membrane along the core. A Rap GTPase module with its exchange factors and a GTPase-activating protein, together with the STE20-family kinase MST4, sets apical polarity and licenses ezrin activation, linking apical membrane identity to surface architecture and nutrient uptake.

Cell shape, movement and division all depend on the controlled growth of actin filaments, and actin filament polymerization is the step in which monomers are added to a filament end. Its regulation determines whether a cell extends a lamellipodium, builds a phagocytic cup, forms a contractile ring, or holds a stable cortex; loss of control underlies immunodeficiency, deafness, kidney filtration defects and defective wound healing. Nucleation is driven by the branching Arp2/3 complex with its WASP/WAVE activators and Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42 effectors, and by formins that elongate unbranched filaments; profilins feed monomers in, while capping protein, gelsolin, tropomodulins and cofilin, itself reactivated by slingshot phosphatases, set filament length and turnover. Spectrins, adducins and villin-family proteins link the resulting filaments to membranes, tying polymerization to cortical architecture, adhesion and motility.

Actin filaments must be taken apart as readily as they are built, and this pathway covers the removal of monomers from filaments and the capping and severing steps that control it. Turnover of the actin pool is what allows cells to crawl, remodel their cortex, retract protrusions, divide and rebuild specialized structures such as stereocilia and the erythrocyte membrane skeleton; without it filaments persist inappropriately and cells lose motility and shape control. Cofilin and destrin sever and depolymerize aged ADP-actin, aided by WDR1, while gelsolin, scinderin, villin and advillin sever in a calcium-dependent manner. Capping protein subunits, twinfilins and tropomodulins block subunit exchange at filament ends, and spectrins, adducins and dematin organize short filaments into membrane skeletal networks. MICAL oxidoreductases destabilize filaments by oxidizing actin itself, linking depolymerization to semaphorin-directed cytoskeletal collapse.

Parallel actin filament bundle assembly builds the tightly packed, uniformly polarized filament arrays that stiffen cellular protrusions — filopodia, microvilli, and the stereocilia of inner ear hair cells. These bundles give such structures the rigidity to probe the environment, to project into a lumen for absorption, or to deflect as a unit in response to sound, and their disruption causes hearing loss and impaired cell motility. Cross-linking proteins such as fascin and espin hold neighbouring filaments at a spacing of roughly 10–20 nm with their barbed ends aligned, while formin and Spire family nucleators seed and elongate the filaments that are gathered in. Espin and harmonin operate within the stereocilium and its associated Usher syndrome protein network, linking bundle architecture to mechanotransduction. The process sits alongside branched network formation as one of the main ways cells organize the actin cytoskeleton for shape and mechanics.

actin filament-based movement covers the force-generating and cargo-hauling work that myosin motors perform on actin, spanning muscle contraction, cytoplasmic organelle transport, and the shape changes of migrating and polarized cells. It matters because it produces the heartbeat, moves melanosomes and vesicles, builds and maintains the hair-cell stereocilium and the intestinal brush border, and drives cytokinesis and cell crawling. Sarcomeric myosins with troponin, tropomyosin and titin convert calcium transients into shortening, while unconventional myosins such as MYO5A, MYO6 and MYO7A carry cargo and anchor membranes; nucleation promoting factors of the WASP family supply the tracks. A large cardiac contingent here reflects excitation-contraction coupling: sodium, potassium and calcium channels, ryanodine receptor and phospholamban set the electrical and calcium signal that the contractile apparatus reads. Mutations across these components cause cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, deafness and pigmentation disorders.

Actin filament-based movement covers the two ways cells use actin tracks to generate motion: myosin motors walking cargo along filaments, and myosin-driven sliding of filaments past one another to shorten a sarcomere. It underlies muscle contraction, cell migration and shape change, and the short-range transport of vesicles, melanosomes and mitochondria at the cell periphery. Conventional myosin heavy and light chains together with the troponin-tropomyosin regulatory system, titin, myosin-binding protein C and cardiac actins represent the contractile arm here, while unconventional single-headed myosins and MYO5A, MYO6, MYO7A and MYO19 handle cargo hauling, endocytic traffic, stereocilia and mitochondrial positioning. Actin nucleation regulators such as WAS and WIPF1 supply the tracks. A large complement of sodium, potassium and calcium channels, ryanodine receptor, calsequestrin and phospholamban links excitation and calcium release to force, and mutations in these components cause cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia, myopathy and deafness.

Short-range cargo movement inside cells depends on actin-based motors as well as microtubules, and vesicle transport along actin filaments is how membrane-bound cargo is delivered through the cortical actin meshwork to the cell periphery. This step matters for handing off organelles from long-distance microtubule tracks to their final destinations: melanosome positioning in pigment cells, delivery of secretory granules and recycling endosomes to the plasma membrane, and insertion of transporters into the cell surface. Unconventional myosins provide the mechanochemistry, with processive class V motors such as MYO5A and MYO5C walking cargo along filaments and MYO1C tethering membranes to cortical actin; accessory factors including an actin-crosslinking alpha-actinin and nucleation-promoting proteins shape the tracks themselves. Loss of the class V motor route disrupts pigment distribution and regulated secretion, linking this transport to hypopigmentation and neurological disease.

Insulin processing converts the inert precursor preproinsulin into the mature two-chain hormone that pancreatic beta cells secrete to control blood glucose. Everything downstream of it — hepatic glucose output, muscle and adipose glucose uptake, lipid storage — depends on correctly cleaved, properly folded insulin, and defects here cause hyperproinsulinemia, beta cell ER stress, and diabetes. After signal peptide removal in the endoplasmic reticulum, protein disulfide isomerase and the beta cell oxidase ERO1B install the interchain disulfide bonds, and cargo export requires YIPF5. In immature secretory granules the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 excise the C peptide and carboxypeptidase E trims the resulting basic residues, while zinc transported by SLC30A8 lets the hormone crystallize into storage granules. HID1 helps sort cargo toward the regulated secretory route, linking maturation to stimulus-coupled release.

Pancreatic beta cells store insulin in a ready-to-release form, and insulin processing is the maturation route that converts the newly translated precursor into the active hormone. Preproinsulin loses its signal peptide on entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, folds with help from the disulfide machinery — protein disulfide isomerase P4HB and the beta-cell oxidase ERO1B install the interchain bonds — and traffics through the secretory pathway to immature granules. There the endoproteases PCSK1 and PCSK2 excise the C-peptide and carboxypeptidase E trims the resulting ends, leaving A and B chains joined by disulfides. Zinc supplied by transporters including SLC30A8 lets the product crystallize as hexamers for storage. Output is controlled largely at the level of synthase expression and trafficking, with growth factors and inflammatory mediators such as TGFB1, EGF, PDGFB and IL1B acting through NF-kB-dependent transcription to raise production, and endocytic and transporter components influencing synthase turnover and precursor handling. Excess or misregulated hyaluronan accompanies fibrosis, inflammation and tumour stroma remodelling, while loss of HAS2 disrupts cardiac and skeletal morphogenesis.

Hyaluronan is the bulk space-filling glycosaminoglycan of skin, cartilage and other connective tissue, and its catabolic breakdown sets how much of it persists, how large the remaining fragments are, and therefore how tissue hydration, matrix stiffness and cell migration are tuned. Turnover begins at the cell surface, where receptors such as CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the liver clearance receptor STAB2 bind and internalise the polymer; hyaluronidases including HYAL1, HYAL2 and the CEMIP proteins cleave it into oligosaccharides, and lysosomal exoglycosidases such as beta-glucuronidase and the hexosaminidase subunits strip the terminal sugars to monosaccharides, with acidification and sodium-proton exchange shaping the local pH these enzymes need. Because short hyaluronan fragments signal quite differently from the intact polymer, this degradation feeds into inflammation, wound repair, TGF-beta and FGF2-driven responses, tumour invasion, and sperm penetration of the cumulus matrix.

Keratinocyte differentiation converts a dividing basal cell of a stratified epithelium into a flattened, cross-linked corneocyte, building the barrier that keeps water in and microbes and allergens out. Skin, oral mucosa, cornea and hair follicle all depend on it, and its failure produces ichthyosis, palmoplantar keratoderma, atopic barrier defects and impaired wound repair. Progression through the layers is marked by switching keratin pairs, from basal KRT5/KRT14 to suprabasal KRT1/KRT10 and stress-induced KRT6/KRT16/KRT17. Late stages assemble a cornified envelope from involucrin, loricrin, filaggrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins, cross-linked by transglutaminases, while ceramide synthesis and lipid transport by ABCA12 supply the extracellular lamellae. Desmosomal and plakin proteins anchor the layers mechanically; proteases, protease inhibitors and a dedicated caspase drive terminal breakdown. Grainyhead, OVOL, IRF6, p63-associated and Notch inputs specify the programme, with Hippo kinases and YAP restraining proliferation.

T cell differentiation is the developmental program that turns a bone marrow-derived lymphoid progenitor into a mature T cell bearing a rearranged, MHC-restricted T cell receptor, and then into one of the effector or regulatory subsets that direct adaptive immunity. Its failure produces severe combined immunodeficiency and thymic aplasia at one extreme and autoimmunity or T cell leukaemia at the other. In the thymus, Notch ligands and IL-7 support progenitor commitment, RAG1/RAG2 and non-homologous end joining assemble the receptor, and pre-TCR and TCR signalling through LCK, ZAP70 and CARD11 drive positive and negative selection against peptide-MHC displayed by cortical and medullary epithelium, with thymoproteasome subunits, AIRE and FOXN1 shaping self-tolerance. Lineage identity is fixed by transcription factors including BCL11B, TCF7, GATA3, RUNX3, ZBTB7B and FOXP3, while cytokine-STAT circuits and SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling specify helper, cytotoxic, regulatory and innate-like fates.

T cell differentiation covers the whole route from a bone marrow-derived precursor to a functional T lymphocyte defined by its rearranged T cell receptor, and then the further specialisation of mature cells into helper, cytotoxic and regulatory subsets. It underwrites cell-mediated immunity and self-tolerance; its failure produces severe combined immunodeficiency when receptor gene rearrangement or downstream signalling is broken, and autoimmunity when selection and regulatory commitment go wrong. Thymocytes rearrange receptor loci through RAG1/RAG2 and non-homologous end joining, express a pre-TCR chain, and are tested against peptide-MHC, with AIRE-dependent presentation and thymoproteasome subunits shaping the surviving repertoire. Notch ligands, WNT and cytokine receptors drive proliferation and stage transitions, while proximal kinases LCK and ZAP70 relay receptor engagement. Lineage identity is fixed by transcription factors including BCL11B, GATA3, TBX21, RORC and FOXP3, acting with chromatin remodelling complexes and STAT-dependent cytokine programmes.

Megakaryocyte differentiation is the route by which a myeloid progenitor becomes the large, polyploid marrow cell that sheds platelets into the circulation, so it sets the supply line for haemostasis; its failure produces thrombocytopenia and bleeding, while its dysregulation contributes to myeloproliferative disease and megakaryoblastic leukaemia. Thrombopoietin acting through its receptor, together with KIT and IL-6-family signalling via IL11RA and IL6ST, drives progenitor expansion, with PTPN11 relaying and PTPN6 and SH2B3 restraining the response. Commitment is imposed transcriptionally by GATA1 with its cofactor ZFPM1, GATA2, TAL1, FLI1, MYB and MEIS1, assisted by coactivators and chromatin regulators such as EP300, MED1, PRMT1 and RCOR1. Maturation brings endomitosis, histone-rich chromatin amplification, cytoskeletal remodelling through FLNA and WASF2, and expression of the platelet identity programme, including the GP1BA–GP1BB–GP9–GP5 adhesion complex and alpha-granule PF4.

Eosinophil differentiation is the route by which a myeloid progenitor commits to and matures into the granulocyte that populates mucosal tissues, defends against helminths, and drives tissue damage in asthma, eosinophilic esophagitis and hypereosinophilic syndromes. Lineage identity is set transcriptionally: GATA1 and GATA2 act through eosinophil-specific enhancers to impose the granule and surface programme on an uncommitted precursor, while TRIB1 shapes myeloid lineage output. Amplification comes from cytokine signalling, with IL5 as the eosinophilopoietin that expands and sustains the lineage, acting through receptor-associated kinases including LYN and the transcription factor STAT5A to drive proliferation and survival. IL25 links epithelial type 2 alarmin signals to this expansion. Because eosinophil numbers track so closely with IL5 availability, this axis is the target of anti-IL5 biologics used in severe eosinophilic asthma.

Neutrophils are the short-lived frontline phagocytes of innate immunity, and their differentiation is the step in which a granulocyte-monocyte precursor in the bone marrow acquires segmented nuclear morphology, granule content and microbicidal capacity. Failure of this maturation produces neutropenia and recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, as seen with loss of JAGN1, an endoplasmic reticulum protein required for granulocyte survival and glycosylation, or of the lamin B receptor, whose absence alters nuclear envelope shape in Pelger-Huet anomaly. Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor provides the extrinsic drive, while transcriptional and chromatin regulators including FOSL2, LEF1, TRIB1 and the deubiquitinase BAP1 set lineage output and restrain alternative myeloid fates. The inositol phosphatase INPP5D tempers phosphoinositide signalling during expansion, linking progenitor proliferation to terminal maturation, and fatty acid synthesis supports the membrane and granule biogenesis this programme demands.

Monocyte differentiation is the route by which an unspecialized myeloid precursor acquires the phenotype of a circulating monocyte, the progenitor pool that supplies tissue macrophages and inflammatory dendritic cells. Without it, innate immune surveillance, clearance of dying cells and antigen presentation via class II MHC all fail, while excessive or skewed output feeds chronic inflammatory and atherosclerotic disease. The decision is driven chiefly by colony-stimulating factor signalling: CSF1 and the related ligand IL34 act through the receptor CSF1R, with CSF2 pushing toward alternative myeloid fates, and downstream kinases and phosphatases such as FES and INPP5D setting the strength of the response. Transcriptional control combines proliferative and lineage regulators, including MYC, JUN, FOXP1 and the nuclear receptor pair PPARG-RXRA, and is tuned by a microRNA locus; inflammatory cytokines of the IL1 family and interferon-driven factors then shape the maturing cell's effector character.

Monocytes and their progenitors become macrophages, the tissue-resident phagocytes that clear pathogens and dying cells, remodel matrix, and set the tone of local inflammation; the same programme also gives rise to specialized populations such as microglia and osteoclast-related lineages. Growth factor signalling drives the transition, with CSF1 and IL34 acting through the receptor CSF1R, supported by GM-CSF and LIF, while transcription factors including SPI1, CEBPA, GATA2 and TRIB1 commit cells to the myeloid fate and microRNAs such as miR-223 tune the decision. Innate receptors TLR2 and TLR4 with the adaptor MYD88, interferon-gamma, TGFB1 and SOCS1 then shape activation state and restrain excessive responses. Death-machinery components including CASP8, FADD, RIPK1 and CFLAR couple differentiation to survival. Disturbances contribute to defective host defence, chronic inflammation, atherosclerosis and tumour-associated macrophage phenotypes.

Male sex determination is the decision point at which a bipotential gonad commits to becoming a testis rather than an ovary, and everything downstream — Sertoli and Leydig cell differentiation, androgen production, regression of the Müllerian ducts and masculinisation of the body — follows from it. The Y-linked SRY acts with NR5A1 to switch on SOX9, which is reinforced by an FGF9 feed-forward loop and by DMRT1 to lock the testicular fate and suppress the ovarian alternative; desert hedgehog signalling and prostaglandin D2 reception help organise the resulting somatic cell types, while the androgen receptor transduces the testosterone signal to target tissues. Dosage-sensitive NR0B1 and the insulin receptor family contribute to the timing and robustness of the switch. Disruption of these steps produces gonadal dysgenesis, sex reversal and disorders of sex development.

myofibril assembly builds the contractile apparatus of striated muscle: the ordered arrays of sarcomeres that let cardiac and skeletal muscle generate force along a defined axis. It is the process that turns a differentiating myoblast or cardiomyocyte into a contractile cell, and its disruption underlies congenital myopathies, nemaline myopathy and both hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy. Assembly begins with actin thin filaments whose length is set by tropomodulins, leiomodins and nebulin, capped and remodelled with the help of cofilin-2 and WDR1, while formins such as FHOD3 nucleate new filaments. Titin and obscurin act as molecular rulers spanning the sarcomere, alpha-actinin and telethonin organise the Z-disc, myomesins the M-band, and myosin-binding proteins register the thick filaments. Transcription factors including NKX2-5, SRF and SIX4 drive the sarcomeric gene programme, linking myofibrillogenesis to muscle differentiation, mechanical load sensing and hypertrophic growth.

Striated muscle contracts only because its actin and myosin filaments are built into precisely registered sarcomeres, and myofibril assembly is the process that constructs those repeating units and links them end to end and to the cell membrane. It defines cardiac and skeletal myocytes, and its disruption underlies dilated and hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies such as nemaline myopathy, and failure of heart tube maturation. Actin isoforms are nucleated and capped at defined lengths by leiomodins and tropomodulins, with cofilin and WDR1 trimming filaments; titin, nebulin, obscurin and myomesins act as molecular rulers spanning the sarcomere; alpha-actinin, telethonin, myopalladin and CSRP3 anchor thin filaments at the Z-disc, while myosin-binding proteins and troponin-tropomyosin tune contraction. Transcriptional inputs including NKX2-5, SRF and SIX4, plus integrin and growth factor signalling, coordinate assembly with myogenic differentiation and mechanical load.

Skeletal muscle thin filament assembly builds the actin-based half of the sarcomere, the filament that myosin pulls against to generate force. Getting thin filaments to a uniform, correct length is what allows a myofibril to contract efficiently, and failure of this process produces congenital myopathies with nemaline rods, muscle weakness and hypotonia from birth. Skeletal and cardiac actins polymerise into the filament, while leiomodin-3 nucleates and elongates actin at the thin filament ends within the sarcomere; loss of LMOD3 causes severe nemaline myopathy. Titin spans the sarcomere as a molecular ruler and, with its Z-disc partner telethonin, anchors filaments and sets sarcomeric dimensions. Transcriptional input from PROX1 links assembly to the myogenic differentiation programme, so that filament construction is coordinated with fibre-type specification and myofibrillogenesis during muscle development and repair.

Skeletal muscle contracts only if its actin-based thin filaments are built to a defined length and anchored correctly within each sarcomere, and this assembly programme is what produces them. Skeletal alpha-actin polymerises into the filament core, with cardiac actin contributing in developing and regenerating fibres; leiomodin-3 nucleates new actin filaments and sets thin filament length, and its loss causes nemaline myopathy with disorganised, rod-containing fibres and severe congenital weakness. Titin spans the sarcomere as a molecular ruler and elastic element, and telethonin binds its Z-disc end to help anchor the filament lattice. The transcription factor PROX1 contributes to the myogenic gene programme that establishes fibre-type-appropriate sarcomeric components. Together these activities link myofibrillogenesis during muscle development and repair to the force-generating geometry that thick-thin filament sliding requires.

Peroxisomes are made and destroyed according to demand, and pexophagy is the selective autophagic route that removes them when nutrient conditions change or when they become damaged or superfluous. Controlling peroxisome number in this way sets the cell's capacity for beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids, ether lipid synthesis and hydrogen peroxide handling, and its failure leaves aged or oxidatively damaged organelles in place. Recognition begins on the peroxisomal membrane, where the import receptor PEX5 and the ubiquitin ligase component PEX2 mark the organelle and the receptor SQSTM1 links that ubiquitin signal to the forming autophagosome; the deubiquitinase USP30 opposes this tagging and so restrains turnover. Downstream, the class III PI3-kinase complex with PIK3C3 and PIK3R4 generates PI3P, which recruits WIPI and ATG2 proteins to expand the engulfing membrane before delivery to the lysosome.

Growth hormone secretion is the regulated release of somatotroph secretory granules into the circulation, and it sets the pace of postnatal longitudinal bone growth, lean mass accretion, and hepatic IGF-1 production; too little causes short stature and too much causes acromegaly. Hypothalamic GHRH acting through its pituitary receptor drives cAMP-dependent release, while ghrelin from the stomach acts through its own receptor to amplify secretion and couple feeding state to growth; dopamine D2 and GABA-B receptors provide inhibitory input, and PACAP adds further stimulatory tone. Downstream of these receptors the pathway requires intact secretory pathway machinery for granule biogenesis and trafficking, along with regulators such as PTPN11 and transcriptional and chromatin factors that specify and maintain the somatotroph itself. Loss of these components underlies congenital growth hormone deficiency and pituitary developmental syndromes.

Fatty acyl chains are not fixed features of a lipid; they are shortened, oxygenated, hydroxylated, transferred and phosphorylated, and each such lipid modification changes how the molecule behaves as a fuel, a membrane component or a signal. Much of the gene content here is beta-oxidation in mitochondria and peroxisomes — acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, enoyl-CoA hydratases, thiolases, the carnitine shuttle, the peroxisomal import machinery and its PPAR-driven transcriptional control — which supplies ATP during fasting and, when defective, produces hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy or leukodystrophy. A second arm remodels signalling lipids: lipoxygenases and cytochromes P450 oxygenate arachidonate into eicosanoids, acyltransferases of the MBOAT family swap acyl chains into phospholipids and acylate ghrelin, and diacylglycerol kinases, phosphatidate phosphatases, inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases and myotubularins add or remove phosphates to set the levels of second messengers at membranes.

Before a cell divides, its long interphase chromatin must be folded into discrete, mechanically robust threads that can be pulled apart without breaking; chromosome condensation is that compaction step, and its failure produces anaphase bridges, chromosome breakage and aneuploidy. The core machinery is the condensin complexes built on the SMC2-SMC4 ATPase pair with distinct kleisin and HEAT-repeat subunits (NCAPH, NCAPD2, NCAPG and their condensin II counterparts), working alongside topoisomerase II to resolve catenated sister DNAs. Mitotic entry kinases CDK1-cyclin B and PLK1 license and time the process, while linker histones, HP1 and histone-modifying enzymes such as KMT5A and EHMT2 set the underlying chromatin state. Related compaction occurs elsewhere: nucleases drive apoptotic chromatin collapse, and protamines replace histones to condense the sperm genome. Loss of regulators such as MCPH1 causes premature condensation and microcephaly.

Cells dying by apoptosis dismantle their nuclei in an orderly way, and chromatin compaction is one of the visible hallmarks of that process, seen as the dense, marginated chromosome masses that precede nuclear fragmentation and packaging into apoptotic bodies. The condensation step is coupled to, but separable from, internucleosomal DNA cleavage: caspase-activated nuclease activity attacks chromatin, while the acinus protein drives compaction after its own caspase-3 processing, and topoisomerase II activity determines how chromatin strand topology is resolved as the fibre collapses. Ordered condensation and degradation keep genomic DNA from leaking into the extracellular space, limiting inflammatory and autoimmune responses to self nucleic acids, and it makes the dying cell recognizable to phagocytes. The pathway sits at the terminal, executioner end of programmed cell death, downstream of caspase activation, and its failure leaves incompletely degraded nuclear remnants.

The lining of the gut must renew and defend itself while bathed in acid, digestive proteases and a dense microbiota, and this pathway covers the protective and regenerative programme that keeps that barrier intact. Secreted gel-forming mucins such as MUC2 in the intestine and MUC6 in the stomach, together with membrane-tethered MUC4 and MUC13, build the mucus layer, while trefoil factors TFF1-TFF3 stabilise it and promote restitution after injury. Innate sensors including TLR4, TLR9 and NOD2 gauge microbial contact, and IL10 receptor signalling restrains the resulting inflammation; IL17A drives antimicrobial and repair responses. Transcription factors SOX9 and NEUROD1 specify secretory and enteroendocrine fates in the crypt, linking barrier upkeep to epithelial differentiation. Loss of these functions underlies ulceration, inflammatory bowel disease -- notably the NOD2 and IL10RA forms -- and susceptibility to gastrointestinal malignancy.

Bone is built, remodelled and sometimes formed in the wrong place, and this collection of regulators sets how fast and how far ossification proceeds — both the endochondral conversion of cartilage to bone and direct mineral deposition by osteoblasts. Its output determines skeletal mass and shape, fracture healing, and whether soft tissue or vasculature calcifies pathologically. BMP and TGF-beta ligands acting through activin and BMP type I/II receptors and SMAD effectors drive osteoblast commitment via RUNX2, while WNT signalling is tuned by the secreted antagonists SOST, DKK1, SFRP1 and GREM1, and NOTCH and SOX9 restrain premature differentiation. A parallel arm governs mineral chemistry: PTH, vitamin D activation through CYP27B1 and VDR, FGF23 with its coreceptor klotho, and inhibitors of hydroxyapatite growth such as ENPP1, ANKH and MGP. Mutations here cause heterotopic ossification, craniosynostosis, osteopetrosis and high-bone-mass syndromes.

Bone formation has to be held in check as much as driven, and this braking arm of ossification keeps mineral deposition confined to the right places and the right rate. Without it, ligaments, vessels and soft tissue calcify, sutures fuse prematurely, and skeletal mass climbs abnormally. Much of the restraint is exerted on two morphogen systems: secreted antagonists such as gremlin, sclerostin, DKK1 and SFRP1, together with the Kremen co-receptors, block BMP and Wnt reception at the osteoblast surface, while inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 shut down signalling inside the cell. A second arm controls the mineral itself, with ENPP1 generating pyrophosphate, fetuin-A binding calcium phosphate in serum, and FGF23 and parathyroid hormone tuning phosphate handling. Transcriptional regulators including SOX9 and BCOR steer progenitors toward cartilage or away from the osteoblast fate, linking this biology to skeletal patterning, ectopic ossification and osteosclerotic disease.

Bone mineralization is the step that turns a collagen-rich osteoid matrix into hard tissue, by nucleating and growing hydroxyapatite crystals within and around the fibrils. It gives the skeleton its stiffness and load-bearing strength and makes bone the body's calcium and phosphate reservoir; when it fails, the result is rickets, osteomalacia, brittle or hypomineralized bone. Local phosphate supply and inhibitor balance set the pace: tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase and PHOSPHO1 generate inorganic phosphate, while pyrophosphate handling by ENPP1 and ANKH, together with matrix Gla protein and fetuin-A, restrains crystal growth where it is not wanted. Endocrine control runs through parathyroid hormone and its receptor, vitamin D signalling, and FGF23-klotho regulation of renal phosphate. Osteoblast differentiation and matrix output are driven by BMP, WNT and ATF4-dependent transcription, with osteocalcin, bone sialoprotein and type I collagen as characteristic products.

Dietary and biliary cholesterol enters the body across the enterocyte brush border of the small intestine, and the efficiency of that step sets how much sterol reaches the circulation in chylomicrons. The pathway matters for whole-body sterol balance: raising uptake raises plasma LDL cholesterol and atherosclerotic risk, while loss of the sterol export pumps ABCG5 and ABCG8 causes sitosterolemia, in which plant sterols are absorbed and retained. Uptake is mediated by NPC1L1, the target of ezetimibe, assisted by CD36 and by LIMA1, which anchors the transport complex; ABCG5/ABCG8 pump excess and non-cholesterol sterols back into the lumen. Absorbed cholesterol is esterified by SOAT2 and packaged with APOA1, APOA4 and other apolipoproteins for lymphatic export. Luminal lipases and bile acid synthesis via CYP8B1 set the micellar conditions on which absorption depends.

regulation of intestinal cholesterol absorption controls how much dietary and biliary cholesterol enters the body across the enterocyte brush border, and equally how rigorously plant sterols are kept out. It sets whole-body sterol balance and plasma LDL levels, and its failure is clinically visible: loss of the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer, which pumps sterols back into the gut lumen, causes sitosterolemia with xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis. Absorption efficiency is tuned at several steps -- bile acid composition set by CYP8B1 determines micellar solubilization, sphingomyelin hydrolysis by ENPP7 and membrane phospholipid remodeling by LPCAT3 alter lipid uptake, SOAT2 esterifies cholesterol for packaging, and the apolipoproteins APOA1, APOA4 and APOA2 assemble it into chylomicrons for lymphatic export. Leptin signaling links this to nutritional state, connecting the pathway to lipoprotein metabolism and cardiovascular risk.

How much dietary and biliary cholesterol actually enters the bloodstream is set in the enterocyte, and this control point determines whole-body sterol balance and plasma cholesterol levels. Equally important is selectivity: plant sterols taken up along with cholesterol must be pumped back into the gut lumen, a job done by the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer on the apical membrane, whose loss causes sitosterolemia with xanthomas and premature atherosclerosis. Cholesterol that is retained is esterified by SOAT2 and packaged with apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV into chylomicrons for export into lymph. Bile acid composition, shaped by CYP8B1, alters micellar solubilization efficiency, while membrane phospholipid remodelling by LPCAT3 and sphingomyelin hydrolysis by intestinal alkaline sphingomyelinase modulate uptake. Leptin signalling links nutritional status to absorptive capacity, tying this step to dietary responses in hypercholesterolemia.

Cells increase in size and mass when nutrient and growth-factor signals license biosynthesis, and this collection covers the processes that push that balance toward growth. It matters for organ size, for cardiac and muscle hypertrophy, and for the axonal and dendritic outgrowth that builds neural circuits; unchecked, the same signalling supports tumour growth. The mTOR complexes are represented in full, with MTOR, RPTOR, RICTOR, MLST8 and MAPKAP1 integrating amino acid and insulin/IGF1 cues through AKT1 and ribosomal S6 kinases onto translation initiation factors. Receptor tyrosine kinase ligands such as EGF-family factors, NRG1, VEGFA and neurotrophins feed in, alongside TGF-beta/BMP receptors, Wnt ligands, and YAP1-TEAD1 transcriptional output. A large neuronal contingent, including L1CAM, MAPT, MAP1B, LIMK1, semaphorins and netrin, links growth control to axon extension and guidance.

negative regulation of cell growth covers the brakes cells put on their own increase in size and mass, keeping tissues at the right dimensions and blocking the unchecked expansion that underlies tumour formation. It brings together several distinct restraint systems: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors of the CDKN family acting with RB1 and TP53 to impose arrest and senescence; TGF-β and BMP receptor signalling through SMAD3/SMAD4 to suppress proliferation; Hippo components such as NF2, LATS2 and STK3 that limit organ size; and the STK11-ULK1/2 and sestrin arm that shuts down anabolic growth when nutrients or energy are scarce. A large repellent-cue contingent — semaphorins, slits, netrin receptors including DCC, and RTN4 with its receptor — restricts neurite and axon extension. Loss of these constraints is a defining feature of cancer, and several members are classical tumour suppressors.

Cells must be told when to stop enlarging and dividing, and this collection covers the brakes: processes that halt, slow or reverse cell growth. Loss of these restraints is the permissive step in tumour formation, and many of the genes here are classical tumour suppressors — TP53, RB1, BRCA1, the CDKN2A/CDKN1A family of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors, NF2, STK11 and the Hippo kinases LATS2 and STK3. Growth suppression is imposed both from outside and inside: TGF-beta and BMP ligands signalling through activin and BMP receptors to SMAD3/SMAD4, secreted Wnt antagonists such as SFRP1 and FRZB, and contact-dependent cues including cadherin-mediated adhesion. A large axon-guidance component — semaphorins, netrins, slits and their plexin, DCC and neuropilin receptors — restricts neurite outgrowth, the neuronal form of growth inhibition. Energy stress sensors including sestrins and ULK kinases couple nutrient limitation to arrest.

Poly-N-acetyllactosamine is the repeating Gal-beta-1,4-GlcNAc-beta-1,3 backbone that extends N- and O-glycans on cell surface and secreted proteins, and its synthesis and modification determine how long and how branched those chains become. Length matters because these extended chains carry the terminal decorations that selectins, galectins and other lectins read, so the pathway shapes leukocyte trafficking, cell adhesion, mucin barrier properties and the display of blood group and tumour-associated carbohydrate antigens. Alternating beta-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases and beta-1,4-galactosyltransferases add the two sugars in turn, each enzyme differing in acceptor preference and tissue distribution; B3GNT6 works on O-linked core structures, while B4GAT1 builds the glucuronyl-linked priming unit for matriglycan on alpha-dystroglycan. Sulfotransferase capping terminates or retunes the chain, generating ligands such as those recognised in lymphocyte homing. Defects in this chemistry disturb glycan-dependent recognition rather than any single metabolic route.

Bone is continually renewed, and osteoclast differentiation supplies the only cell able to dissolve mineralized matrix: monocyte-macrophage lineage precursors fuse into large multinucleated cells that acidify a sealed resorption zone and degrade collagen. Too little of this programme gives osteopetrosis and failure of tooth eruption and marrow cavity formation; too much gives postmenopausal osteoporosis, inflammatory bone erosion in arthritis, and osteolytic metastasis. Commitment depends on the RANKL-RANK-TRAF6 axis opposed by the decoy receptor osteoprotegerin, together with CSF1 acting through CSF1R, immunoreceptor adaptors such as TYROBP and FCER1G that feed calcium-calcineurin signalling, and transcription factors including SPI1, MITF, MAFB, FOS and CEBPB. Fusion proteins DCSTAMP and OCSTAMP, the acid-secreting V-ATPase subunit TCIRG1 and the chloride-bicarbonate exchanger SLC4A2 build the resorbing apparatus, while cytokines such as TNF, IL17A and IFNG tune it, linking immune activation to skeletal loss.

Melanocyte differentiation is the route by which neural crest-derived precursors become the pigment-producing cells of skin, hair follicles, eye and inner ear, and it determines pigmentation, protection against ultraviolet damage, and cochlear function.
