Lineage identity is set by the transcription factors SOX10 and MITF, with ZEB2 and MEF2C acting upstream or alongside them, while KIT and its ligand KITLG, together with endothelin 3 signalling through EDNRB, drive survival and migration of precursors to their target tissues; BCL2 keeps the differentiating cells alive. Downstream, the cells build melanosomes and load them with pigment, requiring OCA2, TYRP1, the biogenesis and transport factors BLOC1S6, HPS4, RAB27A and MREG. Loss of these steps produces hypopigmentation syndromes with deafness and megacolon, albinism and platelet or lysosomal storage defects, and the same programme is subverted in melanoma.

Moving chloride across an epithelial sheet, rather than simply into or out of a single cell, is how tissues set the volume and salt content of the fluids they secrete or reabsorb. Transepithelial chloride transport of this kind drives airway and intestinal surface hydration, urinary salt handling in the kidney, and acid secretion, and its failure produces salt-wasting and fluid-transport disease. The genes involved span the two halves of the job: basolateral uptake by the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter SLC12A2, an anion exchanger that swaps chloride for bicarbonate or oxalate, and chloride channels of the CLC family, including the kidney-specific CLCNKA and CLCNKB whose loss causes Bartter syndrome, plus CLCN7 with its partner OSTM1 in acidified compartments. Nucleotide receptors P2RY4 and P2RY6 place the whole process under purinergic control, so that secretion can be tuned by extracellular ATP and UTP signals.

Formation of the adrenal gland produces two functionally distinct tissues from a common urogenital primordium: steroidogenic cortex that makes glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and androgens, and neural crest-derived chromaffin cells of the medulla that release catecholamines. The programme matters because its failure gives adrenal hypoplasia or aplasia with neonatal salt wasting and adrenal crisis, while its dysregulation underlies adrenocortical hyperplasia and tumours. Nuclear receptors specify and maintain the steroidogenic lineage, with NR5A1 driving adrenal and gonadal fate and NR0B1 required for cortical organisation; WT1 and PBX1 act in the early adrenogonadal primordium. Proneural factors including ASCL1 and INSM1 direct chromaffin differentiation. Growth-factor and WNT inputs, TGF-beta/SMAD signalling, imprinted growth regulators such as CDKN1C and HMGA2, and hypothalamic CRH acting through its receptor to drive corticotropin-dependent growth coordinate proliferation with the gland's zonal architecture and retinoid and cholesterol handling for steroid output.

When a cell detects broken or stalled DNA, the p53 transcription factor converts that damage signal into a decision: pause and repair, enter senescence, or die. This is the core tumour-suppressive checkpoint of human cells, and its loss through TP53 mutation or through amplification of its negative regulators is among the most common events in cancer. Upstream kinases ATM, ATR and CHEK2 phosphorylate p53 and relieve its degradation by the ubiquitin ligase MDM2, which together with MDM4 and the phosphatase PPM1D keeps the protein low in unstressed cells. Stabilised p53 then drives CDKN1A to arrest the cell cycle, PMAIP1 and caspase-2 machinery to commit to apoptosis, and SESN2 for oxidative stress control, while acetyltransferases, methyltransferases, SIRT1 and PML bodies tune which of these outputs predominates.

Mature sperm carry their mitochondria in a distinctive arrangement: flattened, elongated organelles wound circumferentially into a tight helix around the outer dense fibres of the flagellar midpiece. Building this midpiece sheath is what sperm mitochondrion organization accomplishes, and it determines whether the tail has the local ATP supply and structural integrity needed for progressive motility. Loss of the genes involved gives sperm with disorganized or detached midpiece mitochondria, poor motility and reduced fertilizing ability, a recognized cause of male infertility in mouse models. The contributing proteins act during spermiogenesis, when the round spermatid is remodelled into a polarized cell: a sperm-specific mitochondrial protein such as SPATA19 anchors the organelles, an adhesion molecule of the nectin family supports germ cell-Sertoli cell contacts, and lipid-transfer and transporter proteins shape the membranes that must be apposed and compacted.

Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate sits at the committed step of glycolysis and the branch point with gluconeogenesis, so the reactions that make and consume it set how fast a cell burns glucose. Phosphofructokinase isoforms of liver, muscle and platelet type phosphorylate fructose 6-phosphate to form it, an irreversible and allosterically controlled step that responds to ATP, AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; aldolases then cleave it into the two triose phosphates that feed the ATP-generating lower half of the pathway. Tissue-specific isoforms matter clinically: the liver aldolase supports fructose handling and its loss causes hereditary fructose intolerance, while muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency produces exercise intolerance and myopathy. The molecule also acts as a signalling metabolite, feeding back on pyruvate kinase and on inflammatory and immune metabolic reprogramming, consistent with interferon-gamma appearing as a regulator of glycolytic flux.

Membrane disassembly is the regulated breakdown of a cellular membrane as part of a normal programme rather than as damage, and its clearest example is the dissolution of the nuclear envelope at the start of mitosis, which lets spindle microtubules reach the chromosomes. Without it chromosome segregation cannot proceed, and the same chemistry is used when membranes must be remodelled during autophagy. Mitotic kinases drive the step: CDK1 with PLK1 and NEK6 phosphorylate envelope and lamina components, and VRK1 phosphorylates the barrier-to-autointegration factor that tethers chromatin to the inner membrane. Lipid enzymes contribute the other half, as the phosphatidate phosphatase LPIN1 and its regulator CTDNEP1 alter lipid composition to permit envelope collapse and later reassembly, while a phospholipase of the PLAAT family remodels membranes directly. Dynein-based components and ATR-dependent controls couple the process to spindle attachment and genome surveillance.

Small interfering RNAs are the guide molecules of RNA interference, and siRNA processing is the step that converts long double-stranded RNA into the 21-23 nucleotide duplexes that programme silencing complexes. It matters because it lets cells suppress transposons, viral replication intermediates and specific transcripts, and because it is the route by which experimental and therapeutic RNAi reagents are made functional. The RNase III enzyme DICER1 performs the measuring cut, working with double-stranded RNA-binding partners TARBP2 and PRKRA that help select substrates and hand products to Argonaute for loading. HENMT1 contributes 2'-O-methylation that stabilises small RNA 3' ends, while the translin-TRAX complex formed by TSN and TSNAX provides an additional endonuclease activity linked to guide-strand maturation. Downstream, the loaded complex cleaves or represses complementary mRNAs, tying this processing step to post-transcriptional gene regulation and genome defence.

Sleep is the recurring, reversible state of reduced arousal and lowered metabolic rate that restores brain and body function, and the genes here span the signals that promote it, the ones that oppose it, and the circadian timing that positions it in the day. Adenosine accumulating with wakefulness acts through its A1 and A2A receptors to build sleep pressure, and adenosine deaminase variation alters how deep that sleep becomes; prostaglandin D2 synthase and its receptor form a parallel somnogenic route, while melatonin receptor signalling reads the darkness cue. Opposing this, orexin/hypocretin from the hypothalamus stabilises wakefulness, and its loss causes narcolepsy with cataplexy. Additional contributions come from inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmission, dopaminergic and cholinergic modulation, potassium and calcium channels that shape thalamocortical oscillations, cytokines linking immune activation to sleepiness, and neuroendocrine peptides such as growth hormone-releasing hormone, CRH and ghrelin that tie sleep to feeding and stress.

Peristalsis is the travelling wave of smooth muscle contraction and relaxation that moves luminal contents along tubular organs such as the gut, ureter and oesophagus, and it is what converts swallowing, digestion and urine transport into directed flow rather than static filling. Its failure produces obstruction-like syndromes without an obstruction: intestinal pseudo-obstruction, megacolon, reflux and impaired bladder emptying. The genes here point to the neural control of the wave rather than the muscle itself. GDNF signalling and the proneural factor NEUROG1 govern development of the enteric and sensory neurons that build the intrinsic reflex circuits, while purinergic receptors P2RX2 and P2RX3 transduce ATP released by distension into sensory firing that initiates the reflex. Dopamine receptors DRD1 and DRD2 modulate gut motility, and the scaffolding protein DLG1 organises junctional and receptor complexes in the tissues involved.

Complement is a fast, self-amplifying proteolytic cascade, and regulation of complement activation is what keeps it aimed at pathogens and immune complexes rather than at host tissue. Most members here are brakes: factor H and C4b-binding protein accelerate decay of the alternative and classical pathway convertases, factor I cleaves the deposited C3b and C4b they present, and membrane-anchored CD46, CD55 and CD59 protect cell surfaces, the last by blocking assembly of the membrane attack complex. C1 inhibitor restrains the initiating proteases, while properdin works the other way, stabilising the alternative pathway convertase to amplify the response. Receptors such as CR1, CR2 and VSIG4 couple opsonised targets to phagocytosis and B cell activation, and clusterin and A2M limit lytic damage. Loss of this restraint underlies paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, age-related macular degeneration and hereditary angioedema.

The classical complement pathway is powerful enough to lyse cells and opsonise them for destruction, so it is held in check by a set of regulators that decide how far activation proceeds and where it is allowed. Control is exerted mainly on the C3 and C5 convertases: C4b-binding protein, formed from the C4BPA and C4BPB chains, sequesters C4b, while membrane cofactor protein (CD46) and complement receptor 1 act as cofactors for factor I-mediated cleavage of C4b and C3b and accelerate decay of assembled convertases. CR2 links complement-tagged antigen to B cell responses, and SUSD4 and TREM2 add further restraint on host surfaces. Loss of this regulation drives self-directed attack: mutations in these genes underlie atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and complement-mediated kidney disease, and weakened restraint contributes to age-related macular degeneration and autoimmunity.

The alternative complement pathway is continuously active at low level, so control of its amplification loop is what keeps innate immune attack directed at microbes rather than at host tissue. C3 provides the central convertase substrate whose spontaneous hydrolysis seeds the loop; factor H and complement receptor 1 act as negative regulators by promoting decay of the C3 convertase and serving as cofactors for factor I, the protease that cleaves C3b into inactive fragments. Properdin works in the opposite direction, stabilising the convertase and sustaining amplification. VSIG4 on tissue macrophages and the membrane protein SUSD4 add further restraint, and microRNA-mediated tuning of C3 contributes at the transcript level. Loss of this regulation drives complement-mediated damage to self surfaces, seen in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, C3 glomerulopathy and age-related macular degeneration.

Moving the nucleus to the right place inside a cell requires gripping it from outside the nuclear envelope and pulling on the cytoskeleton, and directed nuclear migration along microtubules is how that pull is transmitted. It positions nuclei during neuronal migration in the developing brain, in myotube maturation, and in polarized migrating cells, and its loss leaves nuclei mispositioned with consequences for cell shape and differentiation. Mechanically, inner nuclear membrane SUN proteins pair with outer-membrane nesprin family members such as SYNE2 to form a bridge across the perinuclear space that couples the nucleoskeleton to microtubule motors; the nuclear envelope protein encoded by TMEM201 contributes to this envelope-cytoskeleton link. TRIM58 acts on dynein, tying motor abundance to nuclear movement, as in erythroblast enucleation. The pathway sits at the interface of nuclear envelope architecture and microtubule-based transport.

Transfer RNAs leave transcription as bare chains and are only made functional by chemical decoration, and methylation is the most common of those modifications. Methyl groups placed on specific bases and riboses stabilise tRNA folding, protect it from degradation by surveillance nucleases, and tune the anticodon so that codons are read accurately and at the right speed; wobble-position chemistry in particular prevents frameshifting and misreading. The enzymes involved include methyltransferases acting at N1 of adenosine and guanosine, cytosine-5 methyltransferases such as NSUN2 and NSUN3, ribose 2'-O-methyltransferases, and the shared activating subunit TRMT112, with separate mitochondrial members serving mitochondrially encoded tRNAs. Because translation depends on these marks, loss of individual enzymes causes intellectual disability and microcephaly syndromes, mitochondrial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis, and altered stress and tumour phenotypes through changes in ribosome output.

Every ribosome begins as a single long precursor transcript that must be cut, chemically modified and folded before its small subunit RNA can decode mRNA. Maturation of SSU-rRNA is that processing route: nucleolar assembly factors build the large U3 snoRNP-containing processome around the 5' end of the pre-rRNA, direct endonucleolytic cleavages that release the 18S precursor, and escort the resulting pre-40S particle to the cytoplasm, where final cleavage by the endonuclease NOB1 with PNO1 and RIO kinase-dependent quality control yields a translation-competent subunit. Fibrillarin-containing methylation complexes, the pseudouridine and base-modification enzymes such as EMG1 and NAT10, and small subunit ribosomal proteins act along the way. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on cell growth, defects here trigger nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation, and underlie ribosomopathies including Diamond-Blackfan anaemia and craniofacial disorders.

Cells extend fatty acids two carbons at a time, and this elongation cycle is what converts dietary and de novo synthesized chains into the long and very-long-chain species that membranes, sphingolipids and signalling lipids require. Each round runs through four steps on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane: an ELOVL condensing enzyme adds malonyl-CoA-derived carbon, a ketoacyl reductase and a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratase of the HACD family process the intermediate, and trans-2-enoyl-CoA reductase completes the cycle. The ELOVL enzymes differ in chain-length and saturation preference, so the mix expressed by a tissue sets its lipid composition; ELOVL2 and ELOVL5 feed polyunsaturated precursors toward arachidonic and docosahexaenoic acid. Substrate supply depends on peroxisomal import of very-long-chain acyl-CoAs via ABCD1, whose loss causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, while ELOVL4 mutations produce retinal degeneration and skin barrier disease.

Bone acquires its stiffness when osteoblasts deposit hydroxyapatite into collagenous matrix, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast and how much mineral is laid down. Getting the balance right distinguishes normal skeletal growth from rickets and osteomalacia on one side and pathological calcification of cartilage, vessels and soft tissue on the other. Much of the control is hormonal and phosphate-centred: parathyroid hormone, vitamin D activation by CYP27B1 acting through the vitamin D receptor, and FGF23 with its co-receptor klotho tuning phosphate availability, while ENPP1, ANKH and PHOSPHO1 govern the local pyrophosphate-to-phosphate ratio that permits or blocks crystal growth. Bone morphogenetic proteins and their receptors, WNT ligands and SMAD3 drive the osteogenic transcriptional programme, and matrix proteins such as osteocalcin, MGP and matrilin act as mineralization inhibitors or nucleators within the extracellular matrix itself.

Bone acquires its stiffness when osteoblasts deposit hydroxyapatite into the collagen matrix they secrete, and the processes gathered here push that mineralization harder or faster. The output is skeletal strength and a mineral reservoir; when these inputs are weak, bone stays under-mineralized as in rickets and osteomalacia, while excessive drive produces ectopic ossification and fused joints. BMP ligands acting through type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors and SMAD3 supply the dominant osteogenic signal, with Wnt ligands, frizzled receptors and transcription factors such as MEF2C and the OSR pair reinforcing osteoblast commitment. Endocrine control enters via parathyroid hormone, the vitamin D receptor with its retinoid X receptor partners, and klotho, coupling mineral deposition to systemic calcium and phosphate handling. Phosphate and calcium transporters plus the secretory kinase FAM20C, which phosphorylates matrix proteins, act at the mineralizing surface itself.

Negative regulation of bone mineralization is the braking system that keeps hydroxyapatite deposition confined to bone and prevents it from occurring too fast, too much, or in the wrong tissue. Its failure produces ectopic calcification of arteries and soft tissue, while excessive braking underlies rickets and osteomalacia. Circulating and matrix inhibitors do much of the work: fetuin-A binds nascent calcium-phosphate mineral in serum, ENPP1 generates pyrophosphate that poisons crystal growth, and salivary statherin blocks precipitation at mineralized surfaces. Endocrine control runs through parathyroid hormone and the bone-derived phosphaturic hormone FGF23, which lowers phosphate availability. Other members act on the osteoblast itself, with BMP antagonism by gremlin, SOX9-driven chondrogenic commitment, and hypoxic and inflammatory signals through HIF1A and chemokine receptors restraining matrix maturation. Together these set the balance between skeletal mineral accrual and vascular calcification.

Bone is not allowed to mineralize wherever calcium and phosphate happen to be available, and this negative regulation of bone mineralization is the restraint that sets where and how much mineral is deposited. Losing it produces ectopic calcification of arteries and soft tissue or over-dense bone; too much of it gives rickets-like undermineralization. Several distinct brakes converge here. Circulating and matrix inhibitors such as fetuin-A, ECM1 and salivary statherin bind mineral surfaces and block hydroxyapatite nucleation, while ENPP1 generates pyrophosphate, the principal chemical inhibitor of crystal growth. Endocrine control comes from parathyroid hormone and the osteocyte hormone FGF23, which lowers phosphate availability. Others act on the cells: gremlin-1 antagonizes BMP signalling, SOX9 and BCOR shape skeletal cell fate, and chemokine signalling through CCL3 and its receptor promotes the osteoclast side of remodelling.

Bone morphogenetic protein signalling instructs skeletal patterning, cartilage and bone formation, vascular development and iron homeostasis, and the set collected here is the machinery that sets how strongly and how long that signal runs. Control begins outside the cell, where secreted antagonists such as noggin, chordin, gremlins, follistatin-related proteins and sclerostin sequester BMP ligands, and pseudoreceptors like BAMBI blunt receptor engagement, while co-receptors including endoglin and RGM family proteins tune responsiveness. At the membrane and inside, inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2 and a cullin-RING complex to degrade receptors and effectors, phosphatases reverse SMAD phosphorylation, and SKI/SKIL repressors silence target transcription; several microRNAs add another damping layer. Loss of this restraint produces heterotopic ossification, high bone mass, pulmonary arterial hypertension, cardiac malformation and disordered hepcidin-driven iron control.

TGF-beta family signalling must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this collection of brakes sets how much of a signal reaches the nucleus and for how long. Restraining it limits fibrosis, excess extracellular matrix deposition, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and immune suppression by TGF-beta, while loss of individual components causes connective tissue and vascular disease. The mechanisms are layered: pseudoreceptors and decoy receptors such as BAMBI and betaglycan intercept ligand or receptor engagement; inhibitory SMADs SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2 to degrade receptors and effectors; a phosphatase, PPM1A, dephosphorylates activated SMADs; SKI and SKIL together with a SIN3A-HDAC corepressor complex silence SMAD target genes. Latent binding proteins and fibrillins sequester ligand in the matrix, and numerous microRNAs, including let-7 and miR-17-92 members, damp transcript levels of pathway components.

Bone morphogenetic protein signalling instructs skeletal and cartilage formation, vascular patterning, cardiac development and tissue homeostasis, and this collection covers the processes that turn its output up rather than down. Ligands such as BMP4 and GDF2, the latter circulating as the endothelial ligand for the ACVRL1 receptor and its co-receptor endoglin, initiate receptor-mediated SMAD phosphorylation; loss of that endothelial arm causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension. Enhancement also comes from extracellular modulators including glypican-3, SCUBE3, the sulfatase SULF1 and the twisted gastrulation protein, which shape ligand availability in the matrix, and from intracellular facilitators and transcriptional partners such as ZNF423 and GATA4 that amplify SMAD-dependent gene expression. Notch components appearing here reflect cross-talk that reinforces BMP responses during vessel and heart valve morphogenesis and bone formation.

negative regulation of BMP signaling pathway restrains bone morphogenetic protein signalling, the morphogen system that patterns the embryonic dorsoventral axis, drives bone and cartilage formation, and sets iron balance through hepcidin. Restraint is as informative as the signal itself: loss of the secreted antagonist noggin or of sclerostin alters skeletal mass, gremlin and chordin family antagonists shape limb and kidney patterning, and mutations affecting hemojuvelin-directed BMP input to the liver cause iron overload. Inhibition operates at every tier. Extracellular ligand traps such as chordin, noggin, cerberus and twisted gastrulation sequester BMPs before receptor contact; the pseudoreceptor BAMBI and inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 block receptor and R-SMAD activation; SMURF ubiquitin ligases and the phosphatase PPM1A degrade or dephosphorylate signalling SMADs; and SKI, SKIL and TRIM33 with a large set of microRNAs damp transcriptional output. The result is graded, spatially bounded signalling rather than an on-off switch.

Bone morphogenetic protein signals instruct skeletal patterning, joint formation, vascular development and iron homeostasis, and the cell must be able to switch them off with precision; negative regulation of the BMP signaling pathway is the collection of brakes that sets how much ligand reaches a receptor and how long the response lasts. Secreted antagonists such as noggin, chordin, gremlins, twisted gastrulation and sclerostin sequester ligands extracellularly, while a pseudoreceptor and BMPER tune receptor availability at the cell surface. Inside the cell, inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruit the SMURF ubiquitin ligases to degrade receptors and effectors, phosphatases reverse SMAD activation, and SKI/SKIL and TOB1 silence SMAD-driven transcription; numerous microRNAs damp component expression. Loss of these restraints produces heterotopic ossification and sclerosing bone disease, and the hepcidin-regulating arm involving hemojuvelin, erythroferrone and TMPRSS6 links the same brakes to systemic iron loading.

Regulation of axon extension controls how fast and how far a growing axon advances, setting the pace of wiring during nervous system development and limiting regrowth after injury in the adult. Neurons depend on it to reach appropriate targets at the right time; when the balance of promoting and inhibiting cues is disturbed, axon tracts are misrouted or truncated, and myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG and Nogo acting through NGR block regeneration after spinal cord damage. The genes span the whole chain from cue to cytoskeleton: attractive and repulsive guidance ligands and receptors including semaphorins with their plexin and neuropilin partners, netrin, slit, Wnts and chemokines; adhesion molecules of the L1 family and cadherins; and downstream kinases and cytoskeletal regulators such as CDK5, GSK3B, PAK1, LIMK1, shootin-1 and microtubule-associated MAP1B and tau that lengthen or stall the growth cone.

Neurons wire the brain by extending a single long axon toward its target, and this is the control layer that sets how fast, how far and in which direction that extension proceeds. It underlies axon guidance and tract formation during development and limits regrowth after injury in the adult, where myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG and RTN4 (Nogo) acting through the Nogo receptor collapse growth cones and block repair. Attractive and repulsive cues / netrin-1, slits, semaphorins with their plexin and neuropilin receptors, Wnts, CXCL12 and NGF / converge on Rho-family effectors including PAK1, LIMK1 and ABL1, and on kinases such as CDK5 and GSK3B that phosphorylate microtubule-associated proteins including MAPT, MAP1B and CLASP2 to remodel the cytoskeleton. Adhesion molecules L1CAM, NRCAM and DSCAM couple the growing tip to its substrate. Mutations in several members, including CDKL5 and PAFAH1B1, cause neurodevelopmental disease.

Growing axons must be told where not to go, and the negative regulation of axon extension supplies that instruction: repulsive and inhibitory cues that slow, stall or collapse a growth cone so that tracts stay in their corridors, cross the midline only once, and stop at their targets. Semaphorins acting through plexin and neuropilin receptors, slits, netrin-related draxin, and Wnt ligands signalling via Ryk provide the extracellular signals, while myelin-associated inhibitors such as MAG and Nogo acting on the Nogo receptor, together with the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan tenascin-R, enforce the same restraint in mature CNS tissue. Cytoplasmic effectors including Cdk5, a Rho-family GAP and the receptor phosphatase PTPRS convert these cues into cytoskeletal disassembly. The same inhibitory environment that stabilises adult circuits is what blocks regrowth after spinal cord injury, making these molecules targets for regeneration strategies.

Estrogens act largely by binding intracellular receptors that work as ligand-dependent transcription factors, and this pathway covers how that binding is converted into changes in gene expression. It sets up the hormone responsiveness of breast, uterine, bone, and neural tissue, underlies female reproductive physiology, and when deregulated drives the growth of hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer that endocrine therapy targets. The receptors ESR1 and ESR2, with the related androgen receptor, recruit coactivators such as NCOA1, MED1 and the arginine methyltransferase CARM1, or corepressor complexes containing the deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, to switch target promoters on or off. Chromatin and pioneer factors including FOXA1 and KMT2D determine which sites are accessible, while RNA helicases DDX5 and DDX17, the CCR4-NOT complex, and UFM1 conjugation components add post-transcriptional and post-translational layers of control over receptor output and turnover.

Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone act largely through a single intracellular receptor, and androgen receptor signalling is the route by which that hormonal cue becomes a change in gene transcription. It builds and maintains male reproductive tissues and secondary sex characteristics, drives prostate epithelial identity through targets such as NKX3-1, and is the therapeutic axis in prostate cancer, where receptor reactivation underlies castration resistance; loss-of-function causes androgen insensitivity. Ligand binding releases the receptor from chaperone control, with the immunophilin FKBP4 assisting maturation, and allows nuclear translocation and binding at hormone response elements. Output is then set by coregulators: the acetyltransferase EP300 and the remodeller SMARCA4 favour activation, NCOR1/NCOR2 with HDAC1 and SIRT1 repress, and lysine demethylases including KDM1A and KDM3A tune chromatin, while ubiquitin ligases, SUMO and palmitoylation enzymes control receptor stability and localisation.

Signalling that begins inside the cell rather than at its surface, where ligands that cross the membrane engage receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus and convert them directly into transcriptional or inflammatory outputs. One arm is the nuclear receptor superfamily — steroid and thyroid hormone receptors, retinoic acid and vitamin D receptors, PPARs, liver X and farnesoid receptors, ROR and REV-ERB clock receptors — which bind lipophilic hormones, sterols, bile acids and retinoids, exchange corepressor complexes for coactivators such as the NCOA proteins, MED1 and p300, and thereby set metabolic, reproductive, developmental and circadian gene programmes. A second arm comprises intracellular immune sensors: cGAS–STING and RIG-I/MDA5–MAVS for cytosolic nucleic acids, endosomal TLRs, NOD proteins and inflammasome scaffolds, driving interferon and NF-κB responses. Ligand availability is shaped by cytochrome P450 hydroxylases, and misregulation underlies hormone-driven cancers, metabolic disease and autoinflammation.

Adult behavior covers the coordinated actions of a mature organism – feeding, locomotion, grooming, social interaction, learning, anxiety and reward-seeking – and the genes grouped here are those whose disruption changes such behaviors rather than gross body plan. The collection spans the neural substrates on which behavior rests: neurotransmitter receptors and transporters for dopamine, serotonin, glutamate, glycine, GABA, acetylcholine and opioid peptides; hypothalamic appetite signals such as leptin, ghrelin and its receptor, orexin, NPY and AGRP that set feeding and energy balance; and synaptic organizers including neurexins, neuroligins and SHANK scaffolds that build and tune excitatory and inhibitory contacts. Also present are genes for neuronal survival and cytoskeletal or lysosomal maintenance, whose loss produces degenerative and storage diseases with behavioral onset. Mutations across these groups underlie autism spectrum conditions, obsessive grooming, addiction vulnerability, epilepsy, obesity and parkinsonism.

Male genitalia development covers the outgrowth and patterning of the external genitalia and associated ducts, from the indifferent genital tubercle through masculinization to mature structures. It depends on androgen action layered onto a limb-like outgrowth programme: luteinizing hormone signalling through its gonadal receptor drives testicular steroidogenesis, HSD17B3 completes testosterone synthesis, and 5-alpha-reductase converts it to the more potent dihydrotestosterone that the androgen receptor uses to masculinize the urogenital sinus and tubercle. Morphogenesis itself runs on SHH, FGF8 and FGF10, BMP, WNT/beta-catenin and posterior HOX13 factors, with WT1 and WNT9B shaping the gonad and nephric duct territory from which these structures derive. Loss of any step produces the recognizable spectrum of disorders of sex development typical undervirilization, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, or genital agenesis and the same androgen dependence is later exploited pharmacologically in prostate disease.

Formation of the female external and internal genitalia converts an indifferent embryonic primordium into mature structures, a programme whose failure produces ambiguous genitalia, vaginal or uterine agenesis, and infertility. The genes here span the two things this development requires: patterning signals and hormonal context. Transcription factors and morphogens including LHX1, TBX3, WNT5A and FGF10 shape the Müllerian ducts and genital tubercle, with CHD7 linking the process to broader developmental syndromes. Steroid signalling sets the female course, with aromatase generating oestrogen, the oestrogen receptor transducing it, and 5-alpha-reductase activity determining local androgen potency; retinoid supply through RBP4, STRA6 and LRP2 supports the same epithelial differentiation. Apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK1 and the TAM receptor kinases AXL, MERTK and TYRO3 contribute the tissue remodelling and clearance that accompany duct regression and growth.

Collagen is the most abundant protein of the extracellular matrix, and its controlled breakdown lets tissues remodel during wound healing, bone turnover, involution and immune cell migration; unchecked, the same proteolysis drives tumour invasion, arthritic cartilage loss and osteoporotic bone resorption. Secreted and membrane-anchored matrix metalloproteinases do the bulk of the cutting, with interstitial collagenases such as MMP1, MMP8 and MMP13 cleaving the triple helix and MMP2, MMP9 and membrane-type enzymes degrading the fragments and activating other proteases. Lysosomal cysteine cathepsins, notably CTSK in osteoclasts, degrade collagen intracellularly after receptor-mediated uptake, and prolidase completes the recycling of proline-containing dipeptides. Counterweights and modifiers appear as well: cystatin C restrains cathepsins, procollagen N-proteinases and furin act on maturation, and reticulophagy regulators handle degradation of collagen inside the secretory pathway.

Nuclear body organization covers the assembly, maintenance and dissolution of the membraneless compartments that punctuate the nucleoplasm outside the nucleolus — PML bodies, Cajal bodies, paraspeckles and splicing speckles. These condensates concentrate factors for small nuclear RNP maturation, telomerase trafficking, SUMO-dependent protein modification, and stress and DNA damage responses, so their formation determines where such reactions happen rather than whether the components exist. The architectural long noncoding RNA NEAT1 nucleates paraspeckles, PML scaffolds bodies where SUMO1 conjugation and partners such as HIPK2 and CDKN2A converge on p53 activation and senescence, and WRAP53 directs Cajal body components to their destination. Kinases including SRPK2, DYRK3 and VRK1 phosphorylate condensate constituents to drive disassembly, notably at mitotic entry. Disrupted body formation is linked to spinal muscular atrophy, viral antagonism of intrinsic immunity and failure of growth arrest.

PML bodies are dot-like nuclear structures that concentrate regulatory proteins for apoptosis, senescence, DNA damage responses and antiviral defence, and their organization — the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of these compartments — determines whether those responses can be staged. The scaffold is built by PML itself, whose oligomerization and SUMO modification, with SUMO1 supplied here, creates the shell and the binding surfaces that recruit client proteins through SUMO-interaction motifs. Recruited kinases such as HIPK2 use the body as a platform to phosphorylate p53 and drive cell death after genotoxic stress, while transcriptional and RNA-binding partners including ETS1, HABP4 and SERBP1 link the structure to gene expression control. Loss of this organization is characteristic of acute promyelocytic leukaemia, where a fusion protein disperses the bodies; therapeutic arsenic restores them, tying nuclear body integrity directly to growth suppression.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to arrive at infected or injured tissue, and neutrophil chemotaxis is the guidance system that gets them there: directed crawling up gradients of host- and pathogen-derived signals. Without it, bacterial and fungal infections go uncontained; with it unrestrained, the same cells drive tissue damage in sepsis, acute lung injury and chronic inflammation. Gradients are read by G protein-coupled receptors for interleukin-8 and related CXC chemokines (CXCR1, CXCR2), complement fragments (C3AR1, C5AR1) and alarmins such as S100A8/A9. Their signals converge on phosphoinositide 3-kinase gamma and delta, Rac GTPases with their VAV and PREX exchange factors, and the actin regulator NCKAP1L to polarize the cell and build a leading edge. Beta-2 integrins and junctional adhesion molecules then anchor adhesion and transendothelial migration, while SLIT2 and repressors of migration provide stop signals.

Directed migration of white blood cells toward a chemical cue is how the immune system concentrates defence at a site of infection or injury, and how leukocytes home to lymph nodes and tissues in the steady state. The gene set is built around chemokines and their G protein-coupled receptors — CXCL8 and CXCR1/CXCR2 for neutrophils, CCL2/CCR2 for monocytes, CCL19 and CCL21 with CCR7 for lymph node entry, CXCL12–CXCR4 for progenitor and lymphocyte positioning — together with complement fragment receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1, formyl peptide and lipid mediator receptors, and alarmins such as S100A8/A9 and HMGB1 released by damaged tissue. Downstream, PI3Kγ, SYK, LYN, Rac GTPases and their exchange factors convert a shallow gradient into polarised actin protrusion, while β2 integrins and ADAM proteases handle adhesion and shedding during transmigration. Too little of this causes recurrent infection; too much sustains chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and tumour-promoting myeloid infiltration.

Polyketides are acetate-derived natural products, and in human tissues the chemistry that concerns them is mostly catabolic: reducing and conjugating polyketide-derived compounds taken in from the environment or given as drugs. The aldo-keto reductase family dominates here, with members of the AKR1A, AKR1B, AKR1C and AKR7 groups using NADPH to reduce carbonyl groups on such substrates, alongside a carbonyl reductase subunit and a cytosolic sulfotransferase that adds a sulfate group to phenolic hydroxyls. The clinical stake is chiefly pharmacological: anthracycline anticancer agents are polyketides, and their carbonyl reduction yields alcohol metabolites that are less cytotoxic to tumour cells but implicated in cardiac toxicity, so the level of these enzymes shapes both drug response and resistance. The same reductases also handle steroid, prostaglandin and xenobiotic carbonyls, placing this activity within general phase I and phase II detoxification of small molecules.

Cells must hold internal phosphate within a narrow range, since phosphate is the currency of nucleotide synthesis, ATP, phospholipids and protein phosphorylation, yet excess drives calcification. Intracellular phosphate homeostasis is maintained by balancing uptake against export and by hormonal control of both. Sodium-dependent transporters of the SLC34 family import phosphate across apical membranes of renal proximal tubule and lung alveolar epithelium, while XPR1 provides the principal route for phosphate efflux. FGF23, whose parathyroid context is reflected by GCM2, acts as the phosphaturic hormone that suppresses renal reabsorption, and the scaffold NHERF1 positions transporters in the brush border. ENPP1 and ABCC6 govern extracellular pyrophosphate, the antagonist of mineral deposition. Loss of these controls produces hypophosphatemic rickets, nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis, pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, or ectopic arterial and soft-tissue calcification.

Vitamins must be taken up, activated and interconverted at rates matched to demand, and this pathway covers the control layer sitting over those reactions rather than the reactions themselves. Its outputs matter for retinoid and cobalamin supply in particular: RDH10 oxidises retinol to retinaldehyde as the committed step toward retinoic acid, AKR1C3 acts on retinoid and prostaglandin substrates, and CD320 is the receptor that delivers transcobalamin-bound vitamin B12 into cells, with loss of function causing methylmalonic acidaemia. Transcriptional regulators including GFI1, SNAI1 and SNAI2 and the NF-κB subunit NFKB1 tune expression of these enzymes and transporters, and inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IFNG feed into the same control, linking immune activation to altered vitamin handling. The consequences run through retinoic acid-dependent differentiation, one-carbon metabolism and tissue responses to nutritional status.

Cells are too large for diffusion alone to place organelles, vesicles and mRNAs where they are needed, and cytoskeleton-dependent intracellular transport is the machinery that moves cargo along microtubules and actin filaments to specific destinations. It sustains long neuronal axons, positions mitochondria and lysosomes according to local demand, delivers pigment and lytic granules, and builds the cilium. Kinesins such as KIF5 and KIF1A drive anterograde movement, cytoplasmic dynein with its dynactin subunit DCTN1 drives retrograde movement, and myosins including MYO5A handle short-range actin-based delivery, while adaptor families - HOOK proteins, BICD proteins, TRAK1/TRAK2 with the mitochondrial Rho GTPases RHOT1/RHOT2, BORC and BLOC-1 subunits - decide which cargo is coupled to which motor. Intraflagellar transport components carry cargo within cilia. Loss of these functions produces motor neuron disease, spastic paraplegia, hereditary neuropathy, ciliopathies and pigmentation disorders.

Fertility over a lifetime depends on keeping a reserve of germ-line stem cells undifferentiated and self-renewing rather than letting them all commit to gametogenesis at once; this maintenance programme preserves that reserve. Loss of it empties the germ line, causing infertility, while failure to restrain the germ cell state contributes to germ cell tumours. The genes here act at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels: NANOS2 represses meiotic entry by binding target mRNAs and keeping male germ cells in a stem-like state, PIWIL2 works in the piRNA pathway to silence transposons and protect germline genome integrity, and PRDM14, TFAP2C and ZIC3 belong to the regulatory network that specifies and sustains pluripotent and germ cell identity, including epigenetic resetting. The pathway therefore links stem cell self-renewal, germ cell specification and reproductive tissue homeostasis.

Ovulation is the release of a mature oocyte from the ovarian follicle, the single event that makes fertilization possible and that sets the timing of the menstrual and estrous cycle. Its failure produces anovulatory infertility, as seen when progesterone receptor signalling or its coregulators are lost. The LH surge triggers a coordinated remodelling programme in the preovulatory follicle: EGF-like factors such as epiregulin relay the surge to cumulus cells and drive their expansion, while proteases including ADAMTS1, MMP2 and MMP19 digest the follicular wall and extracellular matrix so the oocyte-cumulus complex can escape. Prostaglandin availability, controlled in part by degradative enzymes, and nitric oxide from endothelial NOS support the accompanying vascular and inflammatory changes. Activin subunits, FOXO3 and SIRT1 link the process to follicle recruitment, oocyte reserve and systemic metabolic and nutritional status signalled through leptin.

Triglyceride storage is the sequestration of neutral fat into cytoplasmic lipid droplets so that fatty acids are held in an inert form until the cell needs fuel or membrane lipid. It lets adipocytes act as the body's energy reserve and protects other tissues from lipotoxic free fatty acids and ceramides; when it fails, fat accumulates ectopically in liver and muscle and drives steatosis and insulin resistance. The genes here cover droplet formation and its regulation: a fat-storage-inducing transmembrane protein shapes droplet budding from the endoplasmic reticulum, while perilipins coat the droplet surface and control access to it, PLIN5 tethering droplets to mitochondria for regulated fatty acid oxidation. The same coat proteins gate ATGL-driven lipolysis, so storage and mobilisation are two settings of one system, extended in lipid-laden macrophages by TREM2 signalling.

Cells that take in more fatty acid than they immediately oxidise must sequester it as triglyceride inside lipid droplets, and triglyceride storage is the process that packages and confines these neutral lipid esters away from the rest of the cytoplasm. This buffering protects membranes and mitochondria from free fatty acid toxicity and provides a fuel reserve that can be mobilised during fasting or exercise. Droplet biogenesis machinery shapes nascent droplets at the endoplasmic reticulum, while perilipin family proteins coat the droplet surface and control access to it: PLIN5 is prominent in oxidative tissues such as heart and muscle, and PLIN2 accumulates in steatotic liver. The lipase ATGL, encoded by PNPLA2, initiates hydrolysis of stored triglyceride, so storage and release are set by competition at the droplet coat. TREM2 links this lipid handling to lipid-laden macrophage and microglial states in obesity and neurodegeneration.

Control over how fast cells make nucleotides, covering both the purine and pyrimidine building blocks used for nucleic acid synthesis and the cyclic and energy-carrying nucleotides ATP, cAMP and cGMP. Because these molecules serve simultaneously as genetic precursors, energy currency and second messengers, their rate of formation ties growth and proliferation to metabolic state. The regulators here are heterogeneous: ATP5IF1 restrains the mitochondrial ATP synthase and methyltransferases and assembly factors such as DNAJC30 and TAFAZZIN tune oxidative phosphorylation capacity, PINK1 and PRKN police mitochondrial quality, GUCA1A and RD3 set cGMP production by retinal guanylate cyclase for photoreceptor light adaptation, ADCY10 generates bicarbonate-responsive cAMP, and PARP1 consumes NAD+ during DNA damage responses. Transcriptional and signalling inputs from PPARA, STAT3, MAP2K1 and IL4 link the process to nutrient sensing and immune activation; its failure contributes to mitochondrial disease and retinal degeneration.

negative regulation of nucleotide biosynthetic process covers the brakes cells place on the synthesis of nucleotides and the cyclic nucleotides used as second messengers, keeping energy currency and signalling molecules from being made when they are not needed. Restraint here matters because uncontrolled nucleotide production wastes carbon, nitrogen and ATP, and because sustained cyclic nucleotide signalling is itself toxic in some tissues. The genes act at several levels: ATP5IF1 clamps the mitochondrial ATP synthase to prevent futile ATP hydrolysis and resynthesis when the proton gradient collapses during ischaemia, PARP1 consumes NAD+ while modifying chromatin, and RD3 suppresses retinal guanylate cyclase activity, a control whose loss causes photoreceptor degeneration and childhood blindness. Together they link nucleotide supply to mitochondrial energy state, DNA damage responses, and sensory neuron survival.

Nucleotide pools have to be held in check as well as replenished, and this is the restraining side of nucleotide biosynthesis " processes that slow or block the formation of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides and cyclic nucleotide second messengers. Damping such synthesis conserves phosphate and energy, keeps cyclic nucleotide signals transient, and limits the deoxynucleotide supply available for replication. The genes involved act through quite different routes: an inhibitory factor that blocks the mitochondrial ATP synthase from running in reverse and consuming ATP, a DNA damage sensor whose poly(ADP-ribose) synthesis draws heavily on NAD+, a regulator of retinal guanylate cyclase activity that restrains cGMP production in photoreceptors, and an insulin-signalling modulator. Loss of such restraint contributes to photoreceptor degeneration, where excess cGMP is toxic, and to the metabolic imbalance seen when nucleotide turnover outpaces demand.

Positive regulation of nucleotide biosynthetic process covers the signals that push cells to make more nucleotides, including the cyclic nucleotide second messengers cAMP and cGMP as well as the purine and pyrimidine precursors needed for nucleic acid synthesis and energy metabolism. Raising nucleotide output supports proliferation, mitochondrial ATP production, and sensory and hormonal signalling; guanylate cyclase activators such as GUCA1A set the cGMP levels that govern photoreceptor recovery after light, while soluble adenylate cyclase ADCY10 couples bicarbonate and calcium to cAMP generation. Other members act indirectly, through growth factor and cytokine signalling via MAP2K1 and STAT3, lipid-sensing transcription by PPARA, and mitochondrial quality control by PINK1 and PRKN, which sustains the respiratory capacity on which nucleotide synthesis depends. The grouping therefore links metabolic demand and stress status to nucleotide supply.

Nucleotides are needed for energy currency, nucleic acid synthesis and second-messenger signalling, and this grouping covers the regulatory inputs that raise the rate at which cells make them. Much of it concerns cyclic nucleotide production: a soluble bicarbonate- and calcium-sensitive adenylate cyclase generates cAMP, while guanylate cyclase activating protein tunes retinal guanylate cyclase to restore cGMP after photoreceptor excitation, a step whose failure causes inherited cone dystrophy. Other members act indirectly, by controlling mitochondrial capacity and the nucleotide pools that depend on it — PINK1 and parkin direct damaged mitochondria to mitophagy, tafazzin remodels cardiolipin for inner-membrane function, and a respiratory complex I subunit contributes to oxidative phosphorylation. Transcriptional and kinase regulators such as PPARA, STAT3 and MAP2K1 couple growth-factor, cytokine and lipid signals to biosynthetic demand, linking nucleotide supply to proliferation and metabolic state.

Nucleotides are both the currency of energy transfer and the substrates of nucleic acid synthesis, so restraining their breakdown is a way of conserving the ATP and nucleoside pool when demand or supply changes. The negative regulation of nucleotide catabolism collected here sits at the interface of energy sensing and metabolic gene control: transcriptional regulators such as PPARA, STAT3, NCOR1 and the deacetylases SIRT6 and HDAC4 set the expression of catabolic enzymes, while DDIT4 and FLCN feed into nutrient-responsive mTOR signalling, and PRKACA and PPP2CA impose kinase and phosphatase control on the same machinery. Glycolytic and gluconeogenic control points including FBP1, PFKFB1 and TIGAR link the fate of nucleotides to carbon flux and NADPH supply. Loss of such restraint contributes to ATP depletion, purine degradation to urate, and the metabolic stress responses seen in ischaemia, muscle wasting and tumour cells.

Cells raise the rate at which nucleotides are broken down when energy demand, oxygen supply or hormonal signals change, and this positive regulation of nucleotide catabolism links fuel sensing to the turnover of ATP and related nucleotides. Much of the control is transcriptional and hormonal: the hypoxia-inducible factor subunits HIF1A and ARNT reprogramme glycolytic and nucleotide-handling enzymes when oxygen is scarce, MLXIPL drives carbohydrate-responsive gene expression, and insulin acting through INSR, together with IGF1, couples nutrient availability to catabolic flux. Opposing energy sensors appear on both sides, with the AMP-activated kinase catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 responding to falling adenylate charge while mTOR with RPTOR, MLST8 signals sufficiency. Purinergic signalling through the ATP-gated channel P2RX7 ties extracellular nucleotide release to inflammation, and APP and PSEN1 connect the same control to neuronal metabolism.

How long an actin filament grows, and when it stops, determines whether a cell can crawl, form a lamellipodium, hold a sarcomere register, or maintain a membrane skeleton. Regulation of actin filament length covers the capping, severing, nucleation and monomer-supply activities that set filament size. Capping protein subunits and their CARMIL regulators block barbed-end growth, tropomodulins and adducins cap pointed ends and spectrin-associated junctions, gelsolin, scinderin and the cofilin/destrin family sever filaments, while profilins and thymosin manage the polymerizable monomer pool and the Arp2/3 complex with WAVE/WASP nucleation promoting factors initiates new branches. Rho-family GTPases, their GAPs, slingshot phosphatases and LIM-kinase-linked control place this machinery downstream of chemokine and guidance cues such as CXCL12, SLIT2 and semaphorins. Defects surface as immunodeficiency, deafness, nephrotic syndrome and myopathy, reflecting how many tissues depend on filament length control.

Cells build and dismantle actin filaments constantly, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how fast and how far filaments grow. It determines cell shape, migration, phagocytosis, membrane protrusion, cell-cell junction strength and specialized structures such as the podocyte foot process and the erythrocyte membrane skeleton. Nucleation is driven by the branched-filament Arp2/3 complex and its activating nucleation-promoting factors, while profilins charge monomers for elongation and formin- and Ena/VASP-type elongators extend barbed ends. Opposing activities cap, sever and depolymerize: capping protein subunits and their CARMIL regulators, gelsolin-family severing proteins, cofilin and its slingshot phosphatase activators, twinfilin, and tropomodulins that block thin-filament ends. Rho-family GTPases, notably RAC1 and CDC42 effectors together with GAPs and adaptors such as NCK and GRB2, couple receptor signalling to these choices; spectrins and adducins anchor the result to the membrane.

Actin filaments are constantly turning over, and the processes that block their disassembly determine which structures persist: stress fibres, the erythrocyte membrane skeleton, sarcomeric thin filaments of defined length, and the brush border of the intestinal epithelium. Negative regulation of actin filament depolymerization works largely by capping filament ends so that subunits can neither be added nor lost. Capping protein subunits (CAPZA1/2, CAPZB) with their CARMIL regulators cap barbed ends, while tropomodulins and leiomodins cap and stabilise pointed ends, setting thin filament length in striated muscle. Adducins and spectrins tie capped short filaments into the junctional complexes that give red cells and neurons their mechanical resilience. Gelsolin-family members such as gelsolin, scinderin and villin cap as well as sever, so their contribution depends on calcium and lipid context. Loss of these activities destabilises muscle, membrane skeleton and stereocilia architecture, causing nemaline myopathy, haemolytic anaemia and deafness.

Actin filaments must be taken apart as fast as they are built, and this is the regulatory arm that accelerates filament depolymerization to recycle subunits back into the polymerizable pool. Without it, cells cannot retract a lamellipodium, turn over adhesions, or remodel the cortex, so migration, cytokinesis and neuronal process dynamics stall. The core activity comes from the ADF/cofilin family — cofilin-1, cofilin-2 and destrin — which sever and disassemble aged, ADP-bound filaments, with WDR1 (AIP1) enhancing their severing and CARMIL proteins relieving capping protein so that ends remain available for turnover. The phosphatase PDXP dephosphorylates cofilin at the inhibitory serine, switching it on, while lipid- and receptor-linked inputs couple disassembly to extracellular cues. Villin adds calcium-dependent severing in the intestinal brush border, linking this control to specialized microvillar architecture as well as general motility.

Actin filaments must be stopped as well as started, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that cap, sever, sequester or otherwise limit filament elongation so that networks reach a defined length and cells do not run away with unproductive protrusion. It sets the architecture of the erythrocyte and neuronal membrane skeleton, the brush border, the sarcomere thin filament, and the leading edge of migrating cells. Barbed ends are blocked by the capping protein heterodimer and its CARMIL regulators, pointed ends by tropomodulins and leiomodins; gelsolin, scintillin and villin sever filaments in a calcium-dependent way, cofilin and twinfilin turn over ADP-actin, thymosin beta-4 sequesters monomers, and slingshot phosphatases reactivate cofilin. Spectrins and adducins cross-link and cap short filaments into the membrane lattice. Loss of this restraint destabilises red cell shape, muscle thin-filament length and directed migration.

Cells extend lamellipodia, form podosomes and lift membrane protrusions by driving new actin filament growth, and positive regulation of actin filament polymerization covers the activators that raise the rate and extent of that growth. It underlies cell migration, phagocytosis and immune cell chemotaxis, endocytic and membrane-remodelling events, and the maintenance of specialized structures such as the podocyte foot process, where nephrin-associated components link the slit diaphragm to the cytoskeleton. Rho-family GTPase signalling through RAC1 and CDC42 effectors converges on nucleation-promoting factors: the WAVE regulatory complex subunits, the branching activity of the Arp2/3 complex, BAR-domain and SH3 adaptors, and elongation factors including profilins and Ena/VASP proteins. Chemokine receptor engagement, tyrosine kinases such as FER and HCK, and mTOR complex components feed into the same output, coupling external cues to protrusion and shape change.

The prostate arises from the urogenital sinus as androgen-dependent epithelial buds that invade surrounding mesenchyme and branch into a secretory gland producing the alkaline fluid of semen. Prostate gland development depends on androgen receptor signalling in the mesenchyme, relayed to epithelium through diffusible factors: FGF10 acting via FGFR2 and its adaptor FRS2, sonic hedgehog through PTCH1 and GLI1, BMP4 and BMP7 restrained by noggin, and WNT5A with beta-catenin shaping ductal branching. Posterior HOX genes, including HOXB13 and HOXA13, provide positional identity, while FOXA1 and NKX3-1 specify luminal secretory differentiation and, with CDKN1B, hold proliferation in check. Oestrogen and prolactin receptors, aromatase and retinoid receptors modulate the hormonal environment. Because the same androgen and transcriptional circuitry is reactivated in adult disease, these genes are recurrently altered in benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostate cancer, where NKX3-1 loss is an early event.

Granulocyte differentiation converts a myeloid precursor into a neutrophil, eosinophil or basophil, cells defined by their cytoplasmic granules and deployed in antimicrobial defence, allergic inflammation and tissue injury responses. Without it, patients develop severe congenital neutropenia and cannot control bacterial and fungal infection; misdirected, the same programme underlies acute myeloid leukaemia, where differentiation arrests at the promyelocyte stage. Lineage identity is set by a transcription factor network in which SPI1, CEBPA and CEBPE drive granulocytic commitment while GATA1, GATA2 and TAL1 with its cofactor ZFPM1 bias toward eosinophil, mast and erythroid alternatives, and RUNX1 and RARA gate maturation. Cytokine input through CSF3 and CSF2 receptors, relayed by LYN and STAT5A, supplies proliferation and survival signals. Genes such as HAX1, JAGN1, CLPB, SRP54 and LBR link granule formation and secretory and nuclear architecture to the neutropenia syndromes.

Granulocytes — neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils — are produced continuously from myeloid progenitors, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast and how far that differentiation proceeds. Getting the balance wrong has direct clinical consequences: loss of HAX1 causes severe congenital neutropenia, RUNX1 and RARA are recurrently disrupted in acute myeloid leukaemia, where blocked granulocytic maturation is the defining lesion, and retinoic acid receptor signalling is the basis of differentiation therapy. Control is exerted at several levels — transcription factors such as RUNX1, LEF1, PRDM16 and ZBTB46 specify and restrain lineage output, cytokine signalling through IL5 drives eosinophil production, and inhibitory phosphatase and adaptor components including INPP5D and CEACAM1 damp progenitor responses. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of haematopoietic stem cell commitment and innate immune defence, determining the supply of short-lived phagocytes available to fight infection.

Granulocyte production from myeloid progenitors must be held in check as well as driven, and this set covers the braking side: processes that slow or block commitment of progenitors to the neutrophil and eosinophil lineages. Restraint matters because unchecked granulopoiesis distorts the balance between granulocytes, monocytes and dendritic cells, and loss of these controls contributes to myeloid leukaemias and to inflammatory tissue damage. The transcriptional arm includes RUNX1 and the retinoic acid receptor RARA, whose fusion in acute promyelocytic leukaemia freezes cells at the promyelocyte stage, alongside PRDM16 and ZBTB46, the latter marking classical dendritic cells rather than granulocytes. Signalling and degradation components contribute too: the inositol phosphatase INPP5D dampens phosphoinositide-dependent growth factor responses, TRIB1 directs turnover of myeloid transcription factors, and CUL4A supplies ubiquitin ligase activity. Together they set lineage output and the pace of emergency granulopoiesis.

Granulocytes — neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils — are the short-lived phagocytic and inflammatory effectors of innate immunity, and this pathway covers the signals that push progenitors toward that fate and raise the output of granulopoiesis. Its importance is clearest when it fails: loss of HAX1 causes severe congenital neutropenia with recurrent bacterial infection, and RUNX1, the transcription factor at the core of definitive haematopoiesis, is a recurrent target of leukaemic translocation and of familial platelet disorder with myeloid predisposition. The genes here act at several levels — cytokine input, with IL5 driving eosinophil production; transcriptional control through RUNX1 and LEF1; and cytoplasmic signalling and survival components such as HCLS1, TRIB1 and TESC that couple growth factor receptors to lineage commitment. Together they set how many granulocytes emerge from the marrow and how readily that output expands during infection.

epithelial cell differentiation describes how an unspecialized progenitor acquires the features of an epithelial cell: apical-basal polarity, junctional adhesion to its neighbours, a keratin cytoskeleton, and a tissue-specific secretory or barrier function. It builds the linings of skin, gut, airway, kidney, mammary gland, lens and inner ear, and its failure underlies ichthyoses and barrier defects, ciliopathies, deafness, nephrotic syndrome, and the loss of differentiation that accompanies carcinoma and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Lineage decisions are set by developmental signalling through WNT, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog and FGF and executed by transcription factors such as GRHL2, KLF4, TP63-family and OVOL, SOX and FOX regulators, together with GATA and HOX codes that give each epithelium its regional identity. Downstream come the structural outputs: claudins and tight junction scaffolds, desmosomes and plectin links, cornified envelope proteins crosslinked by transglutaminases, and ciliogenesis programmes for multiciliated cells.

Epithelia line every body surface and duct, and this pathway covers how an unspecialized progenitor takes on epithelial identity: apical-basal polarity, junctional sealing, and the terminal specializations of skin, gut, kidney, airway, lens, hair and inner ear. Its outputs are the barrier that keeps water in and microbes out, the absorptive and secretory surfaces of the viscera, and the ciliated and sensory epithelia; failure produces ichthyosis and other cornification disorders, ciliopathies, deafness, cataract and loss of the differentiation controls whose collapse underlies carcinoma and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Lineage transcription factors such as GRHL2, KLF4, FOXA1, CDX2 and OVOL family members act downstream of Wnt, BMP/TGF-beta, Notch, Hedgehog and Hippo cues, driving keratin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope genes, transglutaminase crosslinking, claudin and tight-junction assembly, and cell-cycle exit through CDKN1A and CDKN1B.

Epithelia line every surface and duct in the body, and their differentiation must be tuned rather than simply switched on: the balance between proliferating progenitors and specialised daughters sets barrier integrity, secretory capacity and ciliation, and its loss underlies hyperkeratotic skin disease, metaplasia and carcinoma. The regulators here modulate the rate and extent of that commitment. Developmental signalling inputs dominate — Notch ligands and receptors with their HES/HEY targets, Hedgehog through PTCH1/PTCH2 and SMO, WNT/beta-catenin with LEF1, and BMP/Nodal family ligands — read out through lineage transcription factors such as ATOH1, FOXJ1, GRHL1, OVOL2, SOX9 and GATA3. Superimposed are Hippo effectors YAP1 and WWTR1, cell-cycle brakes CDKN1B and CDKN1C, EMT drivers ZEB1/ZEB2 opposed by ESRP1, FGF pathway dampeners of the SPRY and SPRED families, junctional and cornification components, inflammatory cytokines, and numerous microRNAs including the miR-200 family.

Epithelia only keep renewing if some cells are held back from differentiating, and this is the braking side of that decision: processes that block, delay or reduce epithelial cell differentiation so that progenitors stay proliferative and undifferentiated. It keeps stem and basal compartments stocked in skin, airway, gut and lens, and its inappropriate persistence underlies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, tumour dedifferentiation and fibrosis, while premature loss of the brake exhausts progenitors. Notch signalling is a recurring theme, with ligands such as DLL1 and JAG1 acting through NOTCH1 and the HES repressors to impose lateral inhibition, alongside WNT/beta-catenin, Hedgehog through SMO, NODAL and BMP-related TGF-beta arms. Sprouty and SPRED proteins damp receptor tyrosine kinase output, YAP1 and ZEB1 favour the progenitor or mesenchymal state, EZH2 provides polycomb repression of differentiation genes, and several microRNAs and cytokines tune the same targets.

Epithelia acquire their specialised identities — keratinocytes that form a barrier, ciliated airway cells, secretory intestinal lineages, kidney tubule and thymic epithelium — through programmes that drive progenitors out of a proliferative state and into a differentiated one, and this collection covers the inputs that push that transition forward. Loss of such positive regulation leaves epithelia unstratified, unciliated or trapped in a stem-like state, a hallmark of carcinoma and of ciliopathies. The drivers span secreted morphogens and their receptors (BMP ligands, WNT10B acting through CTNNB1 and LEF1, Hedgehog receptors PTCH1/PTCH2, FGF2, GDNF), lineage transcription factors including ATOH1 for secretory intestinal fate, FOXJ1 and RFX3 for motile ciliogenesis, FOXN1 for thymic epithelium, and PAX2/PAX8 for renal tubules, plus nuclear receptor signalling through VDR. Several microRNAs, notably the miR-200 family and miR-34a, reinforce the epithelial state by restraining mesenchymal regulators such as ZEB2.

Epithelial sheets only work if their cells know which way is up: a nascent epithelial cell must build an apical surface, a basolateral surface, junctions that seal neighbours together, and a cytoskeleton aligned to that axis. Acquiring this polarized epithelial character is what allows epithelia to act as selective barriers, to secrete and absorb directionally, and to form tubes and lumens during organ development; its loss accompanies the disorganization seen in epithelial tumours. The genes here span the machinery involved: Rho-family GTPases CDC42 and RHOA with the GAP SH3BP1 set apical-basolateral asymmetry, scaffolds such as SCRIB and DLG5 define basolateral membrane identity, ezrin, moesin and NHERF1 organize the apical actin cortex and anchor membrane proteins, CAMSAP3 orients non-centrosomal microtubules, and WNT5A with PTK7 links planar polarity cues to this architecture. YAP1 couples junctional and mechanical state to growth control.

The layer of actin and associated proteins lying immediately under the plasma membrane gives a cell its shape, stiffness and ability to change both, and organizing this cortical cytoskeleton is what allows cells to divide, polarize, migrate and resist mechanical stress. Rho-family GTPases including RAC1, RHOG and RHOQ, together with their regulators such as ECT2 and RACGAP1 and the ROCK1/ROCK2 kinases, set where filaments are nucleated and how contractile they become; formins of the FMNL group and the WAVE component NCKAP1 build the filaments themselves, while spectrin-band 4.1 proteins, ezrin, talin and plectin tether them to membrane and adhesion receptors. IQGAPs and the LLGL/DLG1 polarity proteins link cortical actin to junctions and apical-basal asymmetry, and anillin-based assembly at the equatorial cortex drives cytokinesis. Loss of this organization compromises epithelial integrity, immune cell motility and faithful cell division.

The thin actin meshwork lying just beneath the plasma membrane gives a cell its shape, stiffness and surface mechanics, and building, rearranging and dismantling that layer is what cortical actin cytoskeleton organization does. It sets cell polarity, anchors membrane proteins, drives the cleavage furrow at cytokinesis, and lets epithelia form brush borders and adherent junctions; when it fails, cells round up, lose apicobasal identity and divide incorrectly. Membrane-cytoskeleton crosslinkers such as ezrin, plectin and the protein 4.1 family tether filaments to the bilayer, while formins and the WAVE complex subunit NCKAP1 nucleate and elongate new filaments. Rho-family signalling through ROCK1/2, IQGAP scaffolds and the ECT2-RACGAP1 pair couples GTPase activity to contractility and furrow positioning, and polarity proteins including DLG1 and LLGL1/2 direct where cortical assembly occurs. Bundlers such as plastins and villin organize the filaments into functional arrays.

Thyroid gland development builds the endodermal gland that makes thyroid hormone, tracing it from a midline thickening of the pharyngeal floor through migration, bilobation and differentiation into hormone-secreting follicles. Its failure causes thyroid dysgenesis — agenesis, ectopy or hypoplasia — the commonest cause of congenital hypothyroidism, with consequences for skeletal growth and brain maturation because fetal and neonatal development depends on maternal and thyroidal hormone supply. A small set of transcription factors specifies and maintains the lineage: NKX2-1, PAX8, FOXE1 and HHEX-type regulators act combinatorially to switch on thyroglobulin and the machinery of iodide organification. Pharyngeal patterning inputs from HOX genes, TBX1, SIX family factors and sonic hedgehog position the primordium, while FGF8/FGF10 and RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling drive precursor proliferation and survival. The same MAPK components, when mutated somatically, later transform thyroid follicular cells.

The thyroid arises from a patch of pharyngeal endoderm that buds, migrates down the neck, and differentiates into follicles capable of iodinating thyroglobulin, and this developmental programme determines whether an infant can make thyroid hormone at all. Its failure produces congenital hypothyroidism from an absent, ectopic, or hypoplastic gland, with consequences for growth and brain maturation. A combinatorial transcription factor code of NKX2-1, PAX8, FOXE1 and HHEX-like partners specifies the anlage and later drives thyroglobulin and hormone-synthesis genes, while HOX, SIX and TBX1 factors set pharyngeal arch and pouch identity around it. Sonic hedgehog, FGF8 and FGF10, endothelin signalling through EDNRA, and RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK kinases supply the mesenchymal and vascular cues guiding budding and descent. The same factors are reused in the mature gland, linking organogenesis to thyroid hormone output and thyroid tumour biology.

Mammary gland development traces the organ from an embryonic mammary line through ductal branching at puberty to the alveolar structures that secrete milk during lactation and regress at weaning. It is the biology that makes lactation possible, and the same growth and survival circuits, when deregulated, underlie much of breast cancer. Hormonal control is central: estrogen, progesterone and prolactin receptors, together with the androgen, glucocorticoid and vitamin D receptors, convert systemic endocrine signals into local proliferation, with prolactin acting through JAK2 and STAT5 to switch on milk protein genes such as the caseins. Reciprocal epithelial-stromal signalling by WNTs, FGF10/FGFR2, EGF-family ligands, TGF-beta, hedgehog and RANK ligand drives branching morphogenesis, while GATA3, ELF5, SOX9 and TBX3 specify luminal identity. Apoptotic effectors and IGFBP5 mediate post-lactational involution.

Myeloid dendritic cells bridge innate detection and T cell priming, and the strength of their activation sets whether an encounter with antigen produces immunity or tolerance. Tuning that step matters because excessive dendritic cell activation drives autoimmunity and inflammatory tissue damage, while insufficient activation leaves tumours and pathogens unchallenged. Both directions are represented here: a C-type lectin receptor senses microbial and damage-associated ligands to promote maturation, whereas interleukin-10 acts as a dominant brake that limits co-stimulation and pro-inflammatory cytokine output, and the checkpoint receptor encoded by HAVCR2 delivers further inhibitory input. Tetraspanins such as CD37 organise membrane microdomains and modulate receptor signalling thresholds, and CD2-family adhesion contributes to contacts with lymphocytes. Together these regulators position the pathway within antigen presentation, innate immune sensing and the control of adaptive immune responses.

How many B cells a response generates is set by the balance of signals described here, which tunes clonal expansion after antigen encounter and so determines antibody output, germinal centre size and the size of the memory pool. Positive input comes from antigen receptor signalling through BTK, LYN, CARD11 and VAV3, from CD40 and BAFF-family receptors such as TNFRSF13B and TNFRSF13C engaged by TNFSF13B, from Toll-like receptors sensing microbial DNA and LPS, and from T cell cytokines including IL-4, IL-21 and IL-2. Restraint is imposed by inhibitory receptors CD22, FCGR2B, BTLA and CD300A acting largely through the phosphatase INPP5D, and by cell cycle brakes such as CDKN1A and CDKN2A alongside the transcriptional repressors BCL6 and BMI1. Loss of the inhibitory arm favours autoantibody production and lymphoproliferation, while loss of the activating arm gives immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses.

B cell expansion has to be capped, or antigen-driven clones accumulate and self-reactive ones escape tolerance; this collection of brakes stops or slows B cell proliferation. Several of the components are inhibitory receptors and the machinery that reads them: FCGR2B senses immune-complex IgG and, with the Src-family kinase LYN and the inositol phosphatase INPP5D (SHIP-1), damps signalling downstream of the B cell receptor, while CD300A and CTLA4 add further inhibitory input. Other arms act on the cell cycle and survival directly, through the CDKN2A tumour suppressor locus, ATM-dependent damage checkpoints and caspase-mediated apoptosis, and IL10 supplies a cytokine-level restraint. Post-transcriptional control by the RNA-binding protein RC3H1 (Roquin) limits messages that drive lymphocyte activation. Loss of these restraints contributes to autoantibody production, systemic autoimmunity and B cell lymphomagenesis.

Clonal expansion of antigen-engaged B cells is what turns a rare specific lymphocyte into a population able to make antibody, and the signals that positively regulate B cell proliferation set the size and duration of that burst. Three input classes converge: antigen receptor signalling relayed through BTK, CARD11, VAV3 and NFATC2; help from T cells and stromal cells via CD40 and the BAFF/APRIL receptor axis; and cytokines including IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-7 and IL-21 that drive cycling and survival. Innate sensing through TLR4, TLR9 and their adaptors lowers the threshold for division, while BCL2 and CDKN1A tune survival against cell cycle arrest and transcription factors such as TCF3, BCL6 and MEF2C couple activation to the germinal centre programme. Too little of this output gives antibody deficiency; unchecked signalling contributes to autoantibody production and to B cell lymphoma.

Forebrain development covers the making of the anterior brain — cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, thalamus and hypothalamus — from the rostral neural tube to a layered, wired structure that handles sensory integration, voluntary movement, cognition and neuroendocrine control. Patterning signals (SHH with its receptors and GLI effectors, WNTs, BMPs and their antagonists, FGF8) set regional identity, which transcription factors such as FOXG1, SIX3, EMX2, PAX6, LHX2 and the DLX/GSX genes then maintain in telencephalic progenitors. Notch-HES signalling and neurogenic factors including NEUROG2, ASCL1, EOMES and TBR1 time the switch from progenitor amplification to neuron production, while spindle and centrosome proteins such as WDR62 and ASPM govern progenitor divisions. Reelin, DAB1, LIS1 and tubulins drive radial migration, and SLIT-ROBO, semaphorin and ephrin cues guide axons. Disruption causes holoprosencephaly, microcephaly, lissencephaly and hypothalamic-pituitary deficiency.
