It matters most in the nervous system, where growth cone advance, axon guidance and dendritic branching wire circuits, and in epithelial and sensory cells that depend on ciliary or brush border structures; loss of these activities underlies neurodevelopmental disability, intellectual disability and failed nerve regeneration. Mechanistically, guidance and growth factor receptors such as the neurotrophin receptors, Eph receptors, plexins and Robo family feed into Rho-family GTPases including CDC42 and RAC1, which in turn drive Arp2/3- and WAVE-dependent actin nucleation, cofilin- and profilin-mediated filament turnover, and microtubule regulators like MAPT and MAP1B. Wnt, BMP and reelin inputs, ciliary transport components, and cytoskeletal kinases such as LIMK1 and PAK1 complete the positive control of projection formation and remodelling.

Host defense has to be tuned as well as triggered, and this collection covers the machinery that sets the frequency, intensity and duration of immune and inflammatory responses to microbes and tissue damage. It spans the sensing arms — Toll-like receptors with their MyD88/TIRAP adaptors, cytosolic nucleic acid sensors such as cGAS-STING and RIG-I/MAVS, and NOD- and NLR-family inflammasome components acting through caspase-1 and gasdermin D — together with the NF-κB, MAPK and JAK-STAT circuits they feed. Equally represented are the brakes: IRAK3, SIGIRR, IL1RN, IL10, TNFAIP3, OTULIN and CYLD-type deubiquitinases, SOCS proteins, inhibitory receptors including PD-1, TIGIT and CD200R, complement regulators, and many microRNAs that damp transcript output. Balance here determines whether infection is cleared without collateral injury; loss of restraint underlies periodic fever syndromes, interferonopathies, septic shock and autoimmunity, while excess restraint permits chronic infection and tumour immune evasion.

Immune and inflammatory responses must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and negative regulation of defense response covers the brakes that limit their frequency, intensity and duration. Without these restraints, antimicrobial defence becomes autoinflammation, tissue damage and autoimmunity; with them too strong, infections and tumours go unchecked. The genes involved span most known braking mechanisms: anti-inflammatory cytokines and decoy or antagonist receptors such as IL10, IL1RN, IL1R2 and IL13RA2; inhibitory surface receptors that raise the threshold for lymphocyte and myeloid activation, including PDCD1, HAVCR2, TIGIT, SIRPA, CD200R1 and FCGR2B; phosphatases and deubiquitinases such as PTPN6, INPP5D, TNFAIP3, CYLD, OTULIN and USP18 that dismantle signalling from Toll-like, interferon and TNF receptors; negative regulators of inflammasomes including NLRC3, NLRP6 and NLRX1; the FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell programme; and numerous microRNAs, notably MIR146A and MIR21, that damp innate signalling post-transcriptionally.

Host defence against microbes and damaged self must be switched on quickly and amplified, and this collection covers the positive regulators that raise the magnitude, speed and duration of a defence response. It underlies innate immune activation in macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils and lymphocytes, and its dysregulation produces autoinflammatory fever syndromes, septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease, while its loss leaves hosts vulnerable to infection. Pattern recognition by Toll-like receptors, cytosolic nucleic acid sensors such as cGAS-STING and RIG-I/MAVS, and NOD- and NLR-family proteins feeds through adaptors MYD88, TICAM1 and the IRAK-TRAF6 axis into NF-kB, MAPK and interferon regulatory factor transcription, yielding interferons, IL-1 family cytokines, TNF and chemokines. Inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and caspase-1 drive gasdermin-dependent pyroptotic release, and ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, kinases and microRNAs tune signal output.

Proteins are rarely left with a bare N-terminus: modification of the N-terminal amino acid residue determines how long a protein lives, where in the cell it goes, and which partners it can bind. Acetyltransferases acting on nascent chains as they emerge from the ribosome, including the catalytic and auxiliary subunits of the major N-terminal acetylation complexes and the actin-specific enzyme NAA80, neutralise the free amine and so influence folding, complex assembly and degradation signals. Myristoyltransferases NMT1 and NMT2 attach a fatty acyl chain to N-terminal glycine to tether signalling proteins to membranes, while HHAT palmitoylates Hedgehog ligands to make them secretable and active. Methyltransferases NTMT1 and NTMT2 trimethylate exposed N-termini, affecting chromatin-associated and DNA repair proteins. Loss of these activities disturbs protein stability, membrane targeting and developmental signalling, with N-terminal acetylation defects causing severe inherited syndromes.

Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators that drive inflammation, pain, fever, vascular tone and labour, so restraining their synthesis matters as much as making them. This is the braking side of that system: processes that damp the rate or extent of prostaglandin formation, largely by limiting expression or activity of the cyclooxygenase step and its upstream phospholipase supply of arachidonic acid. Several microRNAs act post-transcriptionally on the relevant transcripts, while the NAD-dependent deacetylase SIRT1 suppresses inflammatory transcription, linking metabolic state to eicosanoid output. Progesterone-induced blocking factor contributes an immunomodulatory arm relevant to pregnancy maintenance, where premature prostaglandin production promotes uterine contraction. Loss of such negative control favours persistent inflammation and pain sensitisation, and this restraint is the endogenous counterpart of pharmacological cyclooxygenase inhibition by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.</description>}

positive regulation of prostaglandin biosynthetic process covers the signals that drive cells to make more prostaglandins, the short-lived lipid mediators that produce fever, pain sensitisation, vasodilation, platelet responses and uterine contraction. Its output is the substrate and enzyme supply for the cyclooxygenase route: phospholipase A2 activity liberates arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, and inducible COX-2 converts it to prostaglandin H2 for downstream synthases. Upstream inputs here are inflammatory and vasoactive: interleukin-1 beta, the endothelins, vasopressin acting through its V1A receptor, and the macrophage migration inhibitory factor receptor component CD74, each coupling receptor engagement to increased eicosanoid output. Because this amplification underlies inflammatory pain and inflammation-associated tumour promotion, it is the step blocked by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and selective COX-2 inhibitors, and it links hormonal and cytokine signalling to lipid mediator production.

Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators that drive inflammation, pain, fever, vascular tone and smooth muscle contraction, and the signals that increase their output determine how strongly those responses are mounted. This pathway covers the inputs that raise prostaglandin synthesis: inflammatory and vasoactive ligands such as interleukin-1 beta and the endothelins, and vasopressin acting through its V1A receptor, converge on cells to boost release of arachidonic acid by phospholipase A2 activity and to induce the inducible cyclooxygenase PTGS2, the rate-limiting step that non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs block. The migration inhibitory factor receptor component CD74 links cytokine sensing to the same output. Amplification here underlies inflammatory pain and fever, renal water and salt handling, and the prostaglandin surge in labour, while chronic overactivity contributes to arthritis and to tumour-promoting inflammation.

Attaching ubiquitin to a substrate decides whether that protein is degraded, relocated, or switched on, so the machinery controlling how fast and how far ubiquitination proceeds sets the lifetime of most regulatory proteins. This regulation determines the timing of cell cycle transitions, the strength and duration of inflammatory signalling, and the disposal of damaged proteins and mitochondria; its loss underlies tumour suppressor stabilisation failures, autoinflammation, and neurodegeneration. Contributors include E2 conjugating enzymes and cullin-RING components, substrate adaptors such as F-box and BTB proteins, anaphase-promoting complex regulators including CDC20 and FZR1 that license mitotic exit, and inhibitor-of-apoptosis proteins acting on death and NF-kB pathways. Chaperones and co-chaperones triage misfolded clients toward ubiquitin ligases, PINK1 and parkin mark depolarised mitochondria, deubiquitinases and the editing enzyme TNFAIP3 oppose chain assembly, and kinases and acetylation-regulating enzymes tune ligase-substrate recognition.

Ubiquitin tagging commits proteins to degradation, relocalization, or altered signalling, so the machinery that blocks or dampens ubiquitin conjugation sets how long a protein persists and how strongly a pathway fires. Negative regulation of protein ubiquitination works through several routes represented here: direct inhibition or sequestration of E3 ligases, competition for substrate lysines by other modifications, chaperone-mediated substrate protection, and deubiquitinating or protease activity that reverses the mark. Chaperones and co-chaperones such as HSPA1A and the BAG proteins steer clients away from ligase recognition, TNFAIP3 restrains ubiquitin-dependent NF-κB signalling, and mitotic checkpoint components including MAD2L1 and FBXO5 hold the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until chromosomes are attached. Loss of this restraint accelerates turnover of tumour suppressors and receptors, deregulates inflammatory signalling, and permits premature mitotic exit.

Attaching ubiquitin to a substrate marks it for degradation, relocalisation, or altered signalling, and this collection covers the factors that push that reaction forward — activators, adaptors and accessory subunits that increase the rate or extent of protein ubiquitination rather than the ligases' catalytic cores alone. The output determines how quickly damaged and misfolded proteins are cleared, how cell cycle transitions are timed, and how immune and stress signals are amplified. Conjugating enzymes such as UBE2C, UBE2N and UBE2S work with cullin-RING components including CUL3 and RBX1; substrate receptors like FBXW7 and SKP2 and the anaphase-promoting complex activators CDC20 and FZR1 drive mitotic and growth-regulatory turnover. Others act in innate immunity through TRAF6, RIPK2 and NOD2, in mitochondrial quality control through PINK1 and PRKN, and in chaperone-linked triage through STUB1. Loss of such control underlies cancers, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease.

regulation of protein modification process covers the control layer above post-translational modification itself: the kinases, ubiquitin ligases, acetyltransferases and their inhibitors, adaptors and receptors that decide when a residue on a target protein gets phosphorylated, ubiquitylated, SUMOylated, acetylated or neddylated. Because modification state sets protein activity, localisation and lifetime, this regulation is how cells convert extracellular cues into decisions about growth, division and death. The genes span growth factor and cytokine receptors feeding MAPK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and JAK-STAT cascades; cyclin-CDK and anaphase-promoting complex control of mitotic entry and exit; the COP9 signalosome and cullin-RING adaptors governing degradative ubiquitylation; TNF and Toll-like receptor modules that build ubiquitin chains to activate NF-kB; chaperone-linked quality control; and autophagy initiation by ULK1. Tumour suppressors such as PTEN, RB1, STK11 and FBXW7 sit here, and their loss deregulates these modification circuits in cancer.

Most signalling and most protein turnover run through covalent marks added to and removed from existing proteins, and this collection captures the upstream control of that chemistry control over how much phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acetylation or SUMOylation a substrate receives, rather than the marking reactions themselves. Regulation at this level sets the gain of growth factor and cytokine cascades, decides whether a protein is degraded or stabilised, and times cell cycle transitions. The membership spans receptor tyrosine kinases and their inhibitors, protein tyrosine phosphatases that reverse activating phosphorylations, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A and CDKN1B, the COP9 signalosome and neddylation factors that license cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, E2 conjugating enzymes and deubiquitinases, chaperones including HSP90 and CDC37, sirtuin and histone deacetylase activity, PIAS SUMO ligases, and adaptors of innate immune and autophagy signalling. Loss of such restraint underlies oncogenic kinase activation and failed protein quality control.

Post-translational modifications only convey information if they can be removed or blocked, and this collection covers the braking side of that chemistry: processes that stop, slow or limit phosphorylation, acetylation, ubiquitination and related covalent marks on proteins. Such restraint sets signalling thresholds, terminates responses after a stimulus passes, and keeps growth and survival pathways from firing constitutively. The genes span the enzymatic erasers and blockers themselves — protein tyrosine phosphatases such as PTEN, PTPN1, PTPN2 and PTPRC, sirtuin deacetylases, deubiquitinases including USP4, and kinase inhibitors of the CDKN1A/CDKN2A type — alongside adaptors, pseudosubstrates and scaffolds that sequester kinases or occlude substrate sites. Also present are negative regulators of cytokine and antigen receptor signalling, Hippo kinases, and ubiquitin-pathway components that redirect rather than add marks. Loss of this counterbalance underlies unchecked proliferation, autoimmunity and inflammatory signalling.

Most signalling inside a cell is carried by covalent marks added to proteins, and this collection brings together the factors that increase such modification — phosphorylation, ubiquitination, neddylation, SUMOylation, acetylation and methylation — rather than the enzymes that remove them. The output determines whether a receptor stays active, whether a substrate is destroyed, and whether a transcription factor enters the nucleus, so the same machinery sets growth, inflammatory and death decisions. Growth factors and cytokines with their receptors (EGF/EGFR, KIT, FLT3, VEGFA/KDR, IL4R, JAK2) feed into kinase cascades through RAF, MAP2K and MTOR; TNF and Toll-like receptor adaptors such as TRAF2, TRAF6, RIPK1 and MALT1 drive ubiquitin-dependent NF-κB activation; cullin-RING components with E2 conjugating enzymes and DCUN1D neddylation factors mark substrates for proteasomal turnover. Loss or hyperactivation of these positive regulators underlies oncogenic proliferation, chronic inflammation and neurodegeneration.

Keratinization is the terminal differentiation programme that converts living keratinocytes into the flattened, protein-crosslinked corneocytes of the stratum corneum, and the equivalent process that builds hair, nails and claws. It creates the body's outermost barrier against water loss, microbes and mechanical injury, and its failure produces ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, peeling skin and hair shaft defects, as well as the barrier leakiness that predisposes to atopic dermatitis. Keratin intermediate filaments such as KRT1/KRT10 in suprabasal epidermis and the hair keratins with their associated proteins provide the mechanical scaffold; transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins into the rigid cornified envelope. Filaggrin and hornerin aggregate filaments, ceramide synthesis and lipid transport by ABCA12 supply the intercellular lipid seal, and kallikrein and caspase-14 activity govern desquamation and filaggrin processing.

Keratinization is the terminal differentiation programme by which the outermost epidermal cells lose their cytoplasm and organelles and become flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes, producing the stratum corneum as well as hair, nails and other hard appendages. The result is the body's barrier against water loss, microbes and mechanical injury; its failure underlies ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas and the barrier defects that predispose to atopic dermatitis. Keratin intermediate filaments such as KRT1, KRT5 and KRT10, together with hair keratins and keratin-associated proteins, are bundled by filaggrin and trichohyalin, while transglutaminases crosslink involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins into an insoluble cornified envelope. Lipid handling by a ceramide synthase and a lipid transporter builds the extracellular permeability seal, and proteases including kallikrein 5 and caspase-14 drive desquamation and filaggrin processing into natural moisturizing factor.

Every mRNA must be cleaved at a defined site and given a poly(A) tail before it can be exported and translated, and the regulation of mRNA 3'-end processing is what sets where and how efficiently that happens. Choice of cleavage site determines which 3' untranslated region a transcript carries, and therefore which microRNA and RNA-binding-protein elements control its stability and localisation; shifts in this choice accompany proliferation, differentiation and tumour cell states. The cleavage stimulation factor subunits recognise downstream sequence elements, PCF11 and CLP1 act in cleavage and in transcriptional termination, and CDK9 couples the decision to the phosphorylation state of elongating RNA polymerase II. Contributions from the nuclear cap-binding complex, the polymerase-associated factor component CDC73 and the cytoplasmic polyadenylation factor CPEB1 place this control within a continuum linking transcription, capping and tail-length regulation to translational output.

positive regulation of mRNA 3'-end processing describes factors that stimulate the cleavage and polyadenylation reactions that finish a messenger RNA, the step that sets transcript stability, export competence and translational output. Efficient 3'-end formation is also what terminates transcription, so its enhancement couples the fate of an mRNA to the release of RNA polymerase II. The nuclear cap-binding complex, NCBP1 with NCBP2, ties events at the 5' cap to distal processing, illustrating how the two ends of a nascent transcript are communicated; CDC73, a component of the polymerase-associated PAF complex, links elongation to poly(A) site cleavage; the G-quadruplex-resolving helicase DHX36 acts on structured 3' untranslated regions; and CCNB1 brings cell-cycle control to bear on transcript maturation. Together these activities determine 3' untranslated region length and thus which regulatory elements a message retains.

Nearly every mRNA must be cleaved and polyadenylated at its 3' end before it can be exported and translated, and this pathway covers the inputs that stimulate that step. Enhancing 3'-end processing links transcription termination to the production of stable, translatable transcripts, and helps set which polyadenylation site is used, a choice that alters mRNA stability and untranslated-region content. The nuclear cap-binding complex, formed by NCBP1 and NCBP2 on the 5' cap, communicates across the transcript to promote efficient cleavage and polyadenylation as well as splicing and export. CDC73, a component of the PAF1 complex, couples RNA polymerase II elongation to 3'-end formation, while the helicase DHX36 acts on structured RNA that can otherwise impede processing. Coordination of these steps ties mRNA maturation to cell-cycle-regulated gene expression.

At the end of mitosis each daughter cell must rebuild a sealed nuclear envelope around its decondensing chromosomes, and nuclear membrane reassembly is the step that accomplishes this. Without it the nucleus remains leaky, chromatin fragments can be left outside, and micronuclei and DNA damage follow. The genes here describe two cooperating activities: an ESCRT-III based sealing machine in which CHMP7 recruits CHMP4B and partner subunits to the reforming envelope and the VPS4A/VPS4B ATPases recycle them once holes are closed, and a membrane-clearing arm in which reticulon-like REEP3 and REEP4 keep endoplasmic reticulum tubules away from chromatin while the spastin severing enzyme cuts residual spindle microtubules that would otherwise obstruct the gap. In parallel, BANF1 with the ANKLE2 regulator tethers membranes to chromatin, and RCC1 restores the Ran gradient that makes nucleocytoplasmic transport possible in the new nucleus.

Multi-subunit assemblies only work where they are put, and this pathway covers the targeting, delivery and retention of protein-containing complexes at defined cellular sites. Much of the gene content concerns neuronal synapses: scaffolds such as DLG4 and GRIP1, auxiliary subunits including CACNG2 and NETO1/2, and motor and vesicle components such as KIF17, RAB8A, RAB11A and the retromer subunits VPS35/VPS26B together control how many glutamate receptors and voltage-gated channels reach and stay in the postsynaptic membrane, which sets synaptic strength and plasticity. Related machinery clusters acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction through RAPSN and dystroglycan, positions nuclear pore and lamina components, and organizes centrosomal satellites. Failures produce synaptic and neurodevelopmental disease, congenital myasthenic and muscular dystrophy phenotypes, and mislocalized nuclear envelope structure, illustrating that assembling a complex and placing it correctly are separable requirements.

Chromosome ends are flanked by regions that must be kept silent and structurally stable, and subtelomeric heterochromatin formation is the compaction that achieves it. Packaging these regions suppresses transcription of nearby genes, limits recombination between repetitive end sequences, and contributes to how telomere length is sensed and maintained; when it fails, subtelomeric transcripts are derepressed, telomeres become fragile, and the cell drifts toward genome instability and premature senescence. The activities represented here act on histones in opposing directions: methyltransferases including EZH2 and DOT1L write repressive or elongation-associated marks, HAT1 acetylates newly synthesised histones, and the NAD-dependent deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT6 remove acetyl groups to favour a closed state. ATRX contributes chromatin remodelling and histone deposition at repeats, while RIF1 links this silencing to telomere protection and replication timing.

Ruffle organization covers the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of the sheet-like membrane protrusions that form at the leading edge of a crawling cell. These structures set the direction of migration, drive macropinocytic uptake of fluid and particles, and are how macrophages, dendritic cells and metastatic tumour cells move through tissue; without them chemotactic responses and wound closure fail. The genes here trace the route from receptor to actin: chemokine and growth factor receptors such as CCR7 and CSF1R feed into Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and RHOG, whose activity is set by exchange factors and GAPs including ARHGAP24 and SH3BP1. Downstream, WAVE-complex subunits CYFIP1 and ABI3, profilins, EPS8 family capping regulators, coronins and CARMIL proteins control filament nucleation, capping and turnover, while ARF6 and PIP5K1A couple phosphoinositide signalling and membrane traffic to the protruding edge.

Brain-derived neurotrophic factor acting on its receptor is the main trophic signal that keeps central neurons alive, shapes dendritic and axonal growth, and sustains activity-dependent changes in synaptic strength underlying learning and memory. Ligand binding to the TrkB receptor tyrosine kinase, encoded by NTRK2, triggers autophosphorylation and recruitment of downstream cascades, including guanine nucleotide exchange for Ras-family GTPases via RAPGEF2 and calcium-dependent transcriptional output through NFATC4, so that activity at the synapse is converted into lasting changes in gene expression. Regulated secretion of the neurotrophin itself is part of the pathway, with CAPS2 required for its release from dense-core vesicles. The same signalling operates outside the brain in energy balance and feeding, and loss or haploinsufficiency of the ligand or receptor produces hyperphagic obesity, developmental delay and impaired nociception, while reduced signalling is a recurring feature of depression and neurodegeneration.

Transcription does not simply stop; the decision of where RNA polymerase II releases its template is actively regulated, and this control sets which polyadenylation site is used, whether a gene's full-length message is made, and whether polymerase clears the DNA before it collides with replication or neighbouring genes. The regulators here work at the polymerase's phosphorylated C-terminal domain and elongation machinery: a phosphatase holoenzyme in which the catalytic PP1 subunit is targeted by PPP1R10 (PNUTS) reverses elongation-factor phosphorylation and slows polymerase for release, while the CTD-binding SR-like proteins SCAF4 and SCAF8 suppress premature termination and use of early poly(A) sites. Senataxin resolves the RNA-DNA hybrids left behind at termination regions, and its loss causes R-loop-driven genome instability and inherited neurodegeneration.

Cells must not divide with broken or incompletely copied chromosomes, and DNA integrity checkpoint signaling is the surveillance system that enforces this. It senses lesions, stalled replication forks and aberrant DNA structures, then halts or slows cell cycle progression until repair is complete, or directs irreparably damaged cells to senescence or apoptosis. Sensor kinases ATM and ATR, recruited through partners such as ATRIP, TOPBP1, ETAA1 and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, phosphorylate histone H2AX and adaptors including MDC1 and TP53BP1, and relay the signal to CHEK1 and CHEK2, which restrain CDK activity via TP53 and the inhibitor CDKN1A while licensing and origin-firing factors are held in check. The same network organises repair by homologous recombination through BRCA1, BARD1 and RAD51 and couples repair choice to chromatin ubiquitination. Loss of these controls produces genomic instability, chromosome rearrangements and cancer predisposition, and underlies radiosensitive breakage syndromes.

When DNA damage is encountered during S phase, cells must slow replication rather than copy a broken template. The intra-S DNA damage checkpoint of the mitotic cell cycle does exactly that: it suppresses firing of late replication origins and stabilizes forks that have slowed or stalled, buying time for repair and preventing fork collapse into double-strand breaks. Damage is sensed by the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp loaded by RAD17, by the MRE11 nuclease complex, and by lesion recognition proteins such as MSH2 and XPC, with MDC1 concentrating signalling at damaged chromatin. CHEK2 and NEK11 transmit the signal, while the CDC7-DBF4 kinase that licenses origin firing is a key target of restraint. TIMELESS and TIPIN travel with the fork to maintain its integrity, and MUS81-EME1/EME2 resolves persistent stalled structures. Loss of this control produces replication stress, chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition.

Cell membranes are not uniform: cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich nanodomains concentrate selected receptors and signalling proteins while excluding others, and membrane raft organization is the set of activities that builds, sizes and disperses these platforms. Their arrangement determines where immune receptor signalling is licensed to occur, how caveolae form at the cell surface for endocytosis and mechanosensing, and how lipids are trafficked and turned over. Caveolins and cavin-associated proteins such as PACSIN2 shape caveolar invaginations; flotillin and raftlin define non-caveolar domains; LAT and CD45 illustrate how lymphocyte signalling depends on partitioning into or out of ordered lipid environments. Cholesterol handling and lysosomal lipid catabolism genes, including NPC1, PPT1 and CLN3, link raft composition to storage and neurodegenerative disease, while cytoskeletal and scaffold proteins tether domains to underlying actin.

Hemidesmosome assembly builds the anchoring junctions that rivet basal epithelial cells to the underlying basement membrane, so that skin and mucosal epithelia resist shearing and mechanical stress. The complex couples the keratin intermediate filament network inside the cell to laminin-332 outside it: an integrin alpha6beta4 receptor and the transmembrane collagen XVII engage laminin subunits in the basal lamina, while plectin and the plakin family member dystonin/BPAG1 link the receptor tails to keratin filaments. Loss or autoimmune targeting of these components separates epidermis from dermis, producing the blistering diseases junctional and other forms of epidermolysis bullosa and bullous pemphigoid. Beyond adhesion, the junction is dynamically disassembled during keratinocyte migration and wound healing, and its integrin arm also feeds signals that influence epithelial proliferation and carcinoma invasion.

Anchoring a cell to the extracellular matrix beneath it determines whether the cell survives, where it sits in a tissue, and in which direction it migrates. Loss of this attachment triggers anoikis, while its inappropriate persistence or remodelling underlies fibrosis, wound-healing defects, blistering skin disease and tumour invasion. Integrin heterodimers formed from alpha and beta subunits bind matrix ligands such as fibronectin, laminins, collagens and vitronectin, and their cytoplasmic tails recruit talin, kindlins, paxillin, vinculin, zyxin, alpha-actinins and the ILK-PINCH-parvin complex to build focal adhesions that couple to the actin cytoskeleton. Adhesion signalling runs through FAK, Src, CRK adaptors and Rho-family GTPases with their ROCK effectors to control contractility, spreading and adhesion turnover. Matrix-modifying enzymes, proteoglycans and growth factor cues feed back on the same contacts, linking substrate attachment to angiogenesis, leukocyte arrest, epithelial sheet integrity and developmental morphogenesis.

Phenylalanine tRNA carries a bulky tricyclic modification next to the anticodon, and wybutosine biosynthesis is the multi-step route that builds it. The modified base at position 37 stacks against the codon-anticodon helix and stabilises the reading frame; without it, ribosomes slip into -1 frameshifts on phenylalanine codons, which is exploited by viruses such as HIV and degrades the fidelity of translation generally. The pathway begins with methylation of guanosine 37 by TRMT12 and proceeds through TYW1, a radical SAM flavoprotein that forms the imidazoline ring from pyruvate, followed by TYW3 methylation, LCMT2-dependent addition of the aminocarboxypropyl and methoxycarbonyl groups, and TYW5 hydroxylation to give hydroxywybutosine. It is one of the most elaborate tRNA modifications known, linking S-adenosylmethionine and iron-sulfur cluster chemistry to accurate protein synthesis.

Fever is a regulated rise in the body's temperature set point, and this pathway covers the signals that turn it up or damp it down. It matters because fever is the systemic hallmark of infection and inflammation, and because the same chemistry is the target of antipyretic drugs. Peripheral and central immune activation by cytokines such as IL1B and TNF induces cyclooxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E synthase, generating PGE2 that acts on EP receptors, including the EP3 receptor, in hypothalamic thermoregulatory neurons to drive heat conservation and thermogenesis. RANKL signalling through its receptor provides an additional central input, linking a bone-remodelling ligand pair to temperature control, and endothelin receptor signalling contributes vascular tone. Failure or excess of this regulation produces inadequate host response or dangerous hyperthermia.

Fever is a coordinated rise in the hypothalamic temperature set point during infection or injury, and this is the arm of that response that drives the set point upward. Pyrogenic cytokines released by activated macrophages and other innate immune cells, chiefly interleukin-1 beta and TNF, signal to the vascular and glial interface of the preoptic hypothalamus, where cyclooxygenase-2 is induced and prostaglandin E2 is synthesised. Acting on the EP3 receptor on preoptic neurons, PGE2 disinhibits downstream circuits that trigger brown fat thermogenesis, cutaneous vasoconstriction and shivering. RANKL and its receptor RANK provide an additional, cytokine-independent route to the same hypothalamic response. This axis explains why cyclooxygenase inhibitors are antipyretic, and its unrestrained activation contributes to the high fever of sepsis and inflammatory disease.

Cells set how strongly they respond to a hormone, growth factor or neurotransmitter by pulling the receptor off the surface, and receptor internalization is that removal step. It terminates signalling after ligand binding, clears ligand-receptor complexes, and decides whether a receptor is destroyed in the lysosome or returned to the plasma membrane, so it governs desensitization, resensitization and long-term receptor abundance. Activated receptors are marked by ubiquitin ligases such as NEDD4 and ITCH, captured by clathrin adaptors including the AP-2 subunits, EPS15 and PICALM, pinched off by dynamin, and sorted through RAB5-positive early endosomes toward degradative or recycling routes. Arrestins and GRK kinases perform the equivalent step for G protein-coupled receptors. The same machinery controls synaptic AMPA receptor number during plasticity, insulin and growth hormone receptor signalling, transferrin and LDL receptor uptake, and integrin turnover during migration.

Neurotransmitter release requires that a docked synaptic vesicle fuse with the presynaptic membrane at the active zone within a fraction of a millisecond of calcium entry, and this pathway covers the proteins that promote and accelerate that fusion step. It sets how much transmitter a nerve terminal releases per action potential and therefore the strength and timing of synaptic transmission, including short-term facilitation and asynchronous release. Calcium-binding C2-domain sensors of the synaptotagmin family, together with the double C2-domain proteins DOC2A and DOC2B, couple calcium influx to SNARE-mediated membrane merger, with different isoforms tuned to fast synchronous or slower spontaneous release. Rabphilin and the active zone scaffold protein ERC2 position vesicles and sensors near calcium channels, while PRRT2 modulates the release machinery; its loss causes paroxysmal dyskinesia and infantile epilepsy, illustrating how dysregulated release destabilises neuronal circuits.

Many proteases and protease-like enzymes are synthesized as inactive precursors and only become active when a limited cleavage removes a propeptide or splits a single-chain precursor into its working form; zymogen activation is that irreversible switch. It is how the body restricts destructive catalysis to the right place and moment, and it underlies blood clotting, fibrinolysis, complement activation and tissue remodelling. The genes here trace cascades in which one activated protease cleaves the next: coagulation factors converging on thrombin and fibrinogen conversion, plasminogen activators with their receptor and urokinase surface partners, complement C1r/C1s and the mannose-binding lectin-associated serine proteases, kallikreins, cathepsins and the propeptide-cleaving convertase furin. Serpin inhibitors and thrombomodulin appear alongside them, because an activating cascade is only safe if it is simultaneously restrained. Dysregulation produces thrombosis or bleeding, uncontrolled complement damage, and invasive tumour behaviour.

Conversion of circulating plasminogen into the broad-spectrum protease plasmin is the committed step of fibrinolysis, the arm of haemostasis that dissolves clots once a wound is sealed, and the same reaction supplies pericellular proteolysis for cell migration, tissue remodelling and tumour invasion. Tissue-type and urokinase-type activators cleave the zymogen at an internal Arg-Val bond to yield disulfide-linked A and B chains; urokinase acts while bound to its receptor, concentrating activity at the cell surface. Cell-surface receptors including the annexin A2-S100A10 complex, enolase-1 and PLGRKT dock plasminogen and accelerate its activation, while serpins such as PAI-1 and alpha-2-antiplasmin restrain activators and free plasmin. Contact-phase factors and fibrinogen chains link the reaction to coagulation, since fibrin itself is both a cofactor and the principal substrate. Imbalance produces thrombosis or bleeding, and unchecked activity aids metastasis.

Myelination is tuned, not simply switched on: this pathway covers the signals that set how much myelin oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells make, when they make it, and how thick the resulting sheath becomes around an axon. Getting the amount right determines saltatory conduction speed, axonal metabolic support, and the integrity of the node and paranode; too little or badly timed myelin underlies dysmyelinating neuropathies and hampers remyelination after demyelinating injury. Transcriptional control runs through SOX10, EGR2, MYRF, NKX6-2 and ZNF488, with HES5 and QKI restraining or timing differentiation, while IGF1 acting through AKT1 and MTOR scales membrane growth. Axoglial adhesion and polarity components such as MAG, DAG1 and PARD3 couple sheath formation to axonal contact, and inflammatory input via TNF and its receptors, together with lipid and phosphoinositide enzymes including LPIN1, FIG4 and MTMR2, modulates the process.

Myelination has to be held in check as well as driven: axons are only wrapped at the right time, in the right place, and to the right thickness, and the brake on sheath formation is as much a part of the programme as the stimulus. Genes acting here restrain oligodendrocyte and Schwann cell differentiation and limit sheath growth, through inflammatory signalling by TNF and its relatives, membrane and adhesion cues such as JAM2 and TMEM98, phosphoinositide turnover by MTMR2 and FIG4, lipid handling by LPIN1, and stress signalling from the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response. Loss of this restraint, or its excessive engagement, is reflected in dysmyelinating and demyelinating neuropathies and in the failure of remyelination after inflammatory injury, so the same machinery bears on peripheral nerve conduction and on repair in central white matter.

Myelin is the lipid-rich sheath that glial cells wrap around axons to speed conduction and support axonal integrity, and this pathway covers the signals that drive its formation forward. Increasing the rate or extent of myelination is what converts newly generated oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells into productive wrapping cells; when the programme is weak or lost, conduction slows, axons degenerate, and remyelination after demyelinating injury fails. Transcriptional control is central here: SOX10 with EGR2 and MYRF drives expression of structural myelin genes, and ZNF488 acts with them in oligodendrocyte differentiation. Post-transcriptional control is added by the RNA-binding protein QKI and by DICER1-dependent microRNA processing. Growth factor input through IGF1, axon-glia adhesion via MAG and dystroglycan, and PARD3-dependent polarity organise where and how much membrane is deposited, linking glial differentiation to cytoskeletal and membrane remodelling at the axonal contact.

Nervous system processes don't run at fixed gain: synaptic strength, neuronal excitability, nociceptive sensitivity, feeding and arousal drives are all tuned up or down, and this regulatory layer is what sets that gain. Its failure shows up as epilepsy, chronic pain, intellectual disability and autism spectrum phenotypes, and as demyelinating neuropathy. The genes span the main control points: NMDA and AMPA receptor subunits and metabotropic glutamate receptors that determine postsynaptic responsiveness; postsynaptic scaffolds such as DLG4, SHANK1 and SHANK3 with neurexin/neuroligin adhesion pairs that organise and calibrate synapses; presynaptic release machinery including syntaxins, RIMS1/2 and UNC13B; sodium leak channel components NALCN, UNC79 and UNC80 that set resting excitability; neuropeptides such as orexin, CRH, vasopressin and ghrelin acting on their receptors; and myelination regulators including SOX10 and MYRF that shape conduction.

Neural signalling must be damped as well as driven, and negative regulation of nervous system process covers the braking influences that reduce the rate or extent of neurophysiological events — synaptic transmission, sensory transmission, nerve impulse propagation and the myelination that supports it. The genes span several such brakes: an inhibitory glycine receptor subunit whose loss causes startle disease and exaggerated reflexes, a presynaptic neuropeptide Y receptor that suppresses transmitter release, a melatonin receptor that tunes circadian and insulin-related signalling, and itch-associated sensory receptors on primary afferents. Neuropeptides such as vasopressin, orexin and gastrin-releasing peptide act through their receptors to raise or lower excitability in defined circuits. Others constrain glial and axonal biology, including phosphoinositide phosphatases whose mutation produces demyelinating neuropathy, alongside inflammatory and stress-response mediators that depress neuronal function. Loss of such restraint yields hyperexcitability, pain and sleep disturbance.

Grouped here are gene products that raise the rate or extent of neurophysiological activity, whether by strengthening synaptic output, promoting myelination, or driving neuropeptide signalling that changes the behaviour of a circuit. The set spans several routes to the same end. Active-zone proteins such as RIMS1, RIMS2 and UNC13B prime synaptic vesicles for release and set the probability that an action potential produces transmitter, while NLGN2 organises the postsynaptic side of inhibitory contacts and GRM5 couples glutamate to intracellular signalling. A second arm promotes oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelin formation, with SOX10, MYRF, ZNF488, QKI and MAG among the drivers of conduction velocity in central axons. Neuropeptides including orexin, substance P and CART act as diffuse modulators of arousal, feeding and nociception. Loss of these activating influences appears as impaired transmission, demyelinating disease and disordered sleep or appetite control.

How long a protein survives inside a cell is set actively, and this regulation of protein stability collects the machinery that decides it: chaperones that keep nascent and stressed proteins folded, ubiquitin ligases that mark them for destruction, and deubiquitinases that reverse the mark. Chaperonin subunits, prefoldin, and the HSP90/HSP70 systems with their cochaperones hold clients in a foldable state, while HSP90 delivery to kinases depends on CDC37 and the R2TP complex. Opposing arms are represented by cullin-RING and HECT ligases such as FBXW7, MDM2, VHL and NEDD4L, the chaperone-linked ligase STUB1, and a large family of USP deubiquitinases that rescue substrates. Also here are ER-associated degradation components, autophagy and lysosomal routes, and N-terminal acetylation, which influences degron recognition. Loss of this balance drives protein aggregation in neurodegeneration and stabilizes oncoproteins or destroys tumour suppressors in cancer.

Proteins are not uniformly long-lived, and protein destabilization covers the processes that shorten a protein's half-life or push it toward aggregation, setting the rate at which regulatory proteins are cleared and damaged ones removed. This determines how quickly cells can reverse a signalling decision, and its failure leaves oncoproteins and misfolded species to accumulate. Much of the activity is ubiquitin-directed: cullin-RING modules with F-box substrate receptors such as BTRC, FBXW11, FBXL3 and FBXO4 mark targets including β-catenin, cryptochromes and cyclin D1, while MDM2 destabilizes p53 and PRKN, MUL1, RNF5 and TRIM21 act on mitochondrial, ER-associated and cytosolic substrates. Deacetylases and prolyl isomerization by PIN1 alter substrate stability without ubiquitin, and HDAC6-dependent clearance handles aggregation-prone proteins like α-synuclein, huntingtin and prion protein, linking this biology to neurodegeneration and amyloid formation.

Maintaining core body temperature against cold or during infection requires active heat production, and this thermogenic programme is how the body raises it. Adrenergic receptors on brown and beige adipocytes receive sympathetic noradrenaline and drive lipolysis and uncoupled fuel oxidation, with fatty acid uptake supplying substrate; an arrestin-domain protein tunes receptor availability and so sets the gain of that response. A second arm is febrile: pyrogenic cytokines such as IL1B and TNF act on the hypothalamic preoptic area, where cyclooxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E synthase generate PGE2 that signals through EP3 receptors to withdraw inhibition of sympathetic outflow, resetting the thermal set point. Neuropeptide, serotonergic, endothelin and RANK/RANKL inputs modulate the same circuitry, and TRPV1 reports thermal and chemical stimuli. Failure at these steps underlies impaired cold tolerance, disordered fever, and the metabolic consequences of inactive brown fat.

Body temperature is defended by modulating how much heat cells and tissues produce, and this regulatory layer sets the gain on that output. It spans both physiological thermogenesis — brown and beige adipose fuel oxidation, with a fatty acid transporter supplying substrate — and the pyrogenic response to infection, in which interleukin-1 beta and TNF act on hypothalamic circuits to raise the set point. Prostaglandin synthesis by cyclooxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E synthase produces the PGE2 that acts through its EP3 receptor on preoptic neurons, the step blocked by antipyretic drugs; serotonergic, endothelin, neuromedin U and RANK/RANKL signalling provide further modulatory input, and GABA transaminase links neurotransmitter turnover to the same circuitry. Loss of control here manifests as fever, hypothermia, or altered energy expenditure and susceptibility to obesity.

Mammals defend core body temperature by raising heat output, and this pathway covers the signals that turn that production up — both the fever response to infection and inflammation and the neural and hormonal control of thermogenesis in brown fat and muscle. Inflammatory mediators such as interleukin-1 beta and TNF act as endogenous pyrogens, and cyclooxygenase-2 generates the prostaglandin E2 that acts through the EP3 receptor on hypothalamic preoptic neurons to release the brake on sympathetic thermogenic drive; RANKL and its receptor contribute to the same central circuitry. Neuromedin U and serotonergic 5-HT2A signalling add further central input, while SLC27A1 supplies the fatty acid import that fuels oxidation in thermogenic tissue, and GABA aminotransferase shapes inhibitory tone. Loss of control here underlies failure to maintain temperature in the cold, and excessive activation produces fever and hypermetabolic energy expenditure.

Detection of lipopolysaccharide, the outer-membrane hallmark of Gram-negative bacteria, lets macrophages and other innate immune cells recognise infection and mount an inflammatory response; the same signalling, run at full strength, drives the cytokine storm and vascular collapse of septic shock. LBP and CD14 deliver LPS to a TLR4-MD2 complex at the cell surface, which recruits MYD88 and the IRAK kinases or the TRIF-family adaptors TICAM1 and TICAM2, converging on TRAF6, IKK-dependent release of NF-κB from NFKBIA, MAP kinase cascades and IRF3-driven interferon transcription. Negative regulators set the threshold and terminate the response: IRAK3 and SIGIRR restrain receptor complex assembly while TNFAIP3 removes activating ubiquitin chains, and their loss favours autoinflammation. The output reprogrammes the cell metabolically and transcriptionally, with ACOD1 marking the shift, and includes antimicrobial effectors such as BPI and lactoferrin.

Detection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide by the innate immune system triggers a powerful inflammatory response, and this pathway covers the tuning of that response — setting how strongly and how long cells react to endotoxin. The balance matters clinically: too little signalling leaves Gram-negative infection unchecked, too much drives septic shock and tissue injury. Positive components include the LPS-binding accessory proteins CD14 and the MD-2/MD-1 family members LY96 and LY86, the adaptor SCIMP, and TRAF6, which relays receptor engagement toward NF-κB-dependent cytokine transcription. Restraint is imposed by decoy and inhibitory receptors such as SIGIRR and CD180, the ubiquitin-editing enzyme TNFAIP3, inhibitory phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPN11, IL37, and TRIB1, alongside antimicrobial and LPS-sequestering proteins like lactoferrin and defensins. Immunometabolic feedback through ACOD1 and redox control by PRDX2 further shape the strength of macrophage activation.

Negative regulation of lipopolysaccharide-mediated signaling pathway is the braking system on innate immune recognition of bacterial endotoxin, limiting how strongly and how long a cell responds after TLR4 detects LPS. It matters because unchecked LPS signalling drives the cytokine storm of sepsis and sustains chronic inflammation, so these restraints set the threshold between protective host defence and tissue-damaging immunopathology. The genes act at several levels: decoy and inhibitory receptors such as SIGIRR, SIRPA and LILRA2 dampen receptor engagement; the phosphatase PTPN6 and adaptors including TRIB1 and CACTIN interrupt intracellular relay; TNFAIP3 and NFKBIL1 curb NF-κB output; and CARD8 and IL37 restrain inflammasome and IL-1 family amplification. Metabolic and secreted components contribute too, with ACOD1-derived itaconate imposing a tolerant state and lactoferrin sequestering LPS extracellularly. Together they enforce endotoxin tolerance and resolution of inflammation.

Bacterial lipopolysaccharide is one of the strongest triggers of innate immune activation, and the brakes on that response are what keep an antibacterial reaction from becoming septic shock or chronic inflammatory tissue damage. Negative regulation of lipopolysaccharide-mediated signalling covers the molecules that stop or dampen transmission from endotoxin sensing to inflammatory gene expression. Several act at the receptor itself, including a decoy-like member of the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor family, SIGIRR, and inhibitory surface receptors of the SIRP and leukocyte immunoglobulin-like families that recruit the phosphatase PTPN6. Others intervene downstream: TNFAIP3 restricts NF-kB activation through its ubiquitin-editing activity, TRIB1 and NFKBIL1 modulate the same output, and CARD-containing decoys constrain caspase-1 and interleukin-1 maturation, with IL37 acting as an anti-inflammatory cytokine. Antimicrobial and secreted factors such as lactoferrin and beta-defensins can also sequester or neutralise the ligand, while ACOD1-derived itaconate reprogrammes macrophage metabolism toward tolerance.

Detection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide by innate immune cells triggers inflammatory gene expression, and this pathway covers the processes that amplify that response, raising the sensitivity or magnitude of signalling downstream of endotoxin. It matters because the strength of this amplification sets the balance between clearing Gram-negative infection and driving septic shock and tissue damage. Much of the effect is at the receptor itself: CD14 captures LPS and delivers it to the receptor complex, LY96 (MD-2) provides the lipid A binding site that makes the complex responsive, and CD180 with its partner LY86 forms a related accessory module. Adaptor and scaffold proteins such as SCIMP, SASH1 and TRAF6 propagate and sustain the signal toward NF- tB-driven cytokine production, while kinase and phosphatase components including PRKCA and PTPN11 tune its output. The cytokine MIF reinforces the response in macrophages.

Cells and whole organisms constantly adjust metabolism, growth and behaviour to the supply of amino acids, glucose, lipids, vitamins and minerals, and this response to nutrient levels is the machinery that senses that supply and acts on it. When nutrients are plentiful, mTOR complex 1 on the lysosome — with its Rag GTPases, Ragulator, GATOR components and sestrin and CASTOR sensors — licenses protein synthesis and blocks autophagy; when they are scarce, AMPK subunits, the ULK1 kinases, the ATG conjugation machinery and TFEB turn on autophagic recycling, while amino acid deprivation activates GCN2–ATF4 and the integrated stress response. Nuclear receptors and SREBP/ChREBP-type factors retune lipid and glucose handling, and gluconeogenic and ketogenic enzymes supply fuel. Systemic arms include leptin, ghrelin, insulin-secretory and melanocortin signalling for appetite, plus vitamin D, calcium and phosphate regulation. Dysregulation underlies obesity, diabetes, fatty liver and tumour growth.

Cells constantly measure the supply of amino acids, glucose, lipids, and minerals and adjust growth, metabolism and gene expression to match it; this nutrient-sensing response is what allows tissues to survive fasting and prevents wasteful anabolism when building blocks are scarce. Two opposing kinase hubs dominate: mTOR complexes with their Rag GTPase, GATOR, Ragulator and TSC regulators promote protein synthesis when amino acids and growth signals are present, while AMPK subunits sense low energy charge and switch cells toward catabolism. When nutrients fall, ULK1, beclin-1, ATG proteins and the LC3/GABARAP conjugation machinery drive autophagy to recycle cytoplasmic material, and TFEB, ATF4 and the eIF2α kinase arm of the integrated stress response reprogram lysosomal and amino-acid biosynthetic transcription. Additional branches handle calcium, phosphate and vitamin D homeostasis, insulin and glucagon secretion, and lipogenic transcription. Persistent mis-signalling here underlies diabetes, obesity and tumour growth.

Cells continuously adjust growth, secretion and gene expression to the availability of nutrients, and this response links sensing of amino acids, lipids, vitamins and minerals to the programmes that consume them. The amino acid arm runs through mTOR and its partner SAMTOR, which reports S-adenosylmethionine levels supplied by MAT2A, with ribosomal S6 kinase downstream driving protein synthesis; O-GlcNAc transferase and the carbohydrate-responsive factor MLXIPL couple sugar and lipid status to transcription. A large part of the set is mineral and vitamin homeostasis: the calcium-sensing receptor, the vitamin D receptor with its retinoid X receptor heterodimer partners and coactivators, the activating and inactivating hydroxylases CYP27B1 and CYP24A1, and phosphate regulators FGF23 and PHEX, feeding into bone matrix output such as osteocalcin and collagen I. Folate receptors handle vitamin uptake, while leptin and lipoprotein lipase tie the response to whole-body energy balance. Failure produces rickets, phosphate-wasting bone disease and deranged growth control.

Chromosome ends resemble double-strand breaks, and the cell must stop its repair machinery from ligating them together. Protection from non-homologous end joining at telomeres is what keeps this from happening: without it, telomere fusions generate dicentric chromosomes, which break during mitosis and drive the translocations, aneuploidy and genome rearrangements characteristic of crisis and early tumorigenesis. Shelterin components TERF2 and its partner TERF2IP bind duplex telomeric repeats and suppress ligase-mediated end joining while also repressing an ATM-dependent damage response at the end; ACD (TPP1) contributes through the single-strand binding arm of the same complex. Associated nucleases handle the G-overhang and any intermediates generated during replication of the end, with DCLRE1B (Apollo) and the ERCC1-ERCC4 structure-specific endonuclease processing telomeric ends so they remain capped rather than repaired. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of telomere maintenance and double-strand break repair choice.</description>

Synapses are not fixed: their strength, sensitivity and number change with experience, and this pathway covers the events that push that capacity upward. Such enhancement underlies learning, memory formation and the refinement of circuits during development, and its loss contributes to cognitive impairment. Several routes converge here. A calcium/calmodulin-stimulated adenylate cyclase raises cAMP to couple activity to lasting potentiation, while actin regulators including cofilin, its slingshot phosphatase and drebrin remodel the spine cytoskeleton that determines synaptic size and stability. Microtubule-associated MAP1B and the EphB2 receptor link adhesion and structural signals to receptor localisation, complexin modulates vesicle fusion at the presynaptic side, and a neuronal transcription factor plus anaphase-promoting complex subunits show that transcriptional and ubiquitin-dependent proteolytic control also gate plasticity, connecting synaptic change to cell cycle machinery repurposed in neurons.

TOR signaling is the cell's central decision system for growth: it reads nutrient supply, amino acid levels, energy charge and growth factor input, and sets the rate of protein synthesis, lipid production, ribosome biogenesis and autophagy accordingly. When it is deregulated cells grow and divide inappropriately, which is why it is one of the most frequently activated axes in cancer, and why loss of its brakes causes tuberous sclerosis and related overgrowth and epilepsy syndromes. The mechanism converges on two kinase complexes built around mTOR with either RPTOR or RICTOR, activated at the lysosome by Rag GTPases, the Ragulator scaffold and RHEB, and restrained by the TSC1/TSC2 complex, GATOR, folliculin and amino-acid sensors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR. Outputs include S6 kinases, RPS6 and the eIF4E-binding proteins, with AMPK, sestrins and DDIT4 relaying stress and starvation signals inward.

TOR signaling is the cell's master decision point on whether conditions favour growth: the mTOR kinase integrates amino acid supply, glucose and energy status, oxygen and growth factor input, and converts a favourable verdict into protein synthesis, lipid and nucleotide production, and suppression of autophagy. Two complexes carry the output, one built on RPTOR that phosphorylates S6 kinases and the 4E-BP translation repressors, the other on RICTOR. Amino acids are sensed at the lysosome, where the Ragulator scaffold and Rag GTPases position the kinase, with GATOR components, FLCN and sensors such as CASTOR1 and SAMTOR tuning the response; the TSC1/TSC2 complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein toward RHEB, and AMPK and LKB1 impose energy restraint. Loss of these brakes causes tuberous sclerosis and related hamartoma syndromes, and pathway hyperactivation is common in cancer, epilepsy and metabolic disease.

Glucocorticoid output from the adrenal cortex is tuned rather than fixed, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the rate at which cortisol and related steroids are made and interconverted. It matters because circulating glucocorticoid levels set stress responses, gluconeogenesis, immune tone and blood pressure; too little causes adrenal insufficiency and too much causes Cushing's features. Control operates at several levels: POMC-derived ACTH acting on its adrenocortical receptor MC2R drives steroidogenesis, transcriptional regulators including NR5A2 and REST shape the expression of the biosynthetic machinery, and the glucocorticoid receptor itself feeds back on the axis. H6PD supplies NADPH in the endoplasmic reticulum for regeneration of active cortisol from cortisone, while BMP and WNT ligands together with DKK3 contribute paracrine signals that pattern and maintain the steroid-producing adrenal cortex.

negative regulation of glucocorticoid biosynthetic process describes the braking inputs that restrain cortisol and corticosterone synthesis in the adrenal cortex, setting the ceiling of the stress hormone axis. Restraint matters because sustained glucocorticoid excess drives hypertension, insulin resistance, muscle wasting, bone loss and immune suppression, while loss of these brakes contributes to adrenal hyperplasia and steroid-producing tumours. The genes point to paracrine and transcriptional control rather than to the steroidogenic enzymes themselves: BMP2 and BMP5 signal through SMAD pathways to suppress steroidogenic gene expression in adrenocortical cells, DKK3 modulates Wnt signalling that governs cortical zonation and progenitor identity, REST silences neuroendocrine transcriptional programmes, and ATP1A1 sets membrane potential and ion gradients that couple to steroidogenic output. Together they act as a counterweight to ACTH-driven stimulation, tuning adrenal hormone production to physiological demand.

Cortisol output from the adrenal cortex has to be held in check as well as driven, and this is the restraining side of that balance: processes that damp the rate and extent of glucocorticoid synthesis. Because glucocorticoids shape stress responses, gluconeogenesis, immune suppression and blood pressure, losing this brake permits hypercortisolism with its metabolic and immunological consequences, while excessive restraint limits the adrenal response to stress. The genes involved point to several routes of suppression: bone morphogenetic protein ligands acting as paracrine inhibitors of steroidogenic gene expression in adrenocortical cells, a secreted modulator of Wnt signalling that influences adrenal zonation and growth, a transcriptional repressor that silences neuronal and steroidogenic programmes, and the sodium pump alpha subunit, linking membrane ion gradients and cell excitability to steroid hormone production.

Many kinases switch themselves on by phosphorylating their own residues, and this trans- or cis-autophosphorylation step is what converts a ligand-binding or clustering event into sustained catalytic activity. Controlling it sets the threshold and duration of signalling, so the regulators here act as brakes and accelerators on kinase self-activation. Growth factors such as VEGFA and the EGF-family ligand NRG1 promote receptor dimerisation and thus autophosphorylation of their cognate receptor tyrosine kinases, driving angiogenesis and neuregulin-dependent development, while ERRFI1 restrains EGF receptor activation and RASSF2 and TOM1L1 modulate signalling output downstream. MOB1B is a coactivator subunit for the Hippo pathway kinases, where autophosphorylation controls growth suppression, and EPHA7 and NEK10 are themselves autophosphorylating kinases. Loss of such restraint underlies unchecked proliferative signalling in cancer.

Many kinases and kinase-linked receptors switch themselves on by phosphorylating their own residues, and this grouping covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of that autophosphorylation. Because autophosphorylation is the committing step that converts a ligand-binding or activation event into sustained catalytic output, controlling it sets the threshold and duration of downstream signalling. The members act at several levels: secreted growth factors such as neuregulin and VEGFA engage receptor tyrosine kinases whose dimerisation triggers trans-autophosphorylation of their cytoplasmic tails, while scaffolding and adaptor proteins including TOM1L1 and the RASSF-family member RASSF2 position kinases and their regulators to favour that self-modification. NEK10 is itself a NIMA-related kinase subject to autoactivation. The processes fed by this control include angiogenesis, epithelial and neural development, and proliferative signalling that is amplified in cancer.

Corticosteroids such as cortisol and aldosterone act by entering cells and binding intracellular receptors of the nuclear receptor family, which then move to the nucleus and reprogramme transcription; this is how the stress axis, glucose mobilisation, salt and water balance, and the damping of inflammation are enacted at the level of gene expression. The glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 is the central node here, and its output is tuned rather than simply switched on: chaperone and scaffold proteins including calreticulin, prohibitin and a 14-3-3 subunit govern its folding, nuclear traffic and DNA binding, PPP5C and ubiquitin ligase activity set its phosphorylation and turnover, and CREBRF restrains its transcriptional response. Circadian components CLOCK, BMAL1, the period and cryptochrome proteins both gate receptor activity and are themselves corticosteroid targets, coupling daily rhythm to hormone action. Dysregulation underlies steroid resistance, metabolic syndrome and disorders of the adrenal axis.

Adrenal steroid hormones reach nearly every tissue, and this is the set of cellular responses they provoke: the changes in gene expression, metabolism, transport and inflammatory tone that follow glucocorticoid or mineralocorticoid stimulation. It underlies the stress response, the anti-inflammatory action of steroid drugs, sodium and water handling in the kidney, and the catabolic shift that mobilises glucose during fasting. The glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 acts as a ligand-activated transcription factor, inducing gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and TAT, the anti-inflammatory mediators ANXA1, DUSP1 and IL1RN, and the muscle atrophy ubiquitin ligases FBXO32 and TRIM63, while suppressing TNF and IL6. Mineralocorticoid effects converge on epithelial sodium channel subunits and SGK1, with HSD11B2 protecting the receptor from cortisol. Hypothalamic CRH and urocortins close the feedback loop, and chronic excess produces the muscle wasting, bone loss and immune suppression of Cushing syndrome.

locomotion involved in locomotory behavior covers the neural control of self-propelled movement — the machinery that translates motivational state, dopaminergic tone and synaptic signalling into how much and how fast an animal moves. It matters because this output is the readout of basal ganglia function: its disruption produces hypokinesia, ataxia and the hyperactivity or catalepsy seen in Parkinsonian and psychostimulant models. Dopamine D2 receptors acting through G protein beta subunits set locomotor drive, while AMPA receptor subunit GRIA1 and calcineurin with its RCAN regulators tune the striatal synapses that gate movement initiation. Appetite- and arousal-related peptide signalling via CARTPT, the ghrelin receptor and prepronociceptin links feeding state to activity levels. Neurodegeneration genes including VPS35, CLN6 and the mitochondrial dynamics factor SLC25A46 show how loss of neuronal maintenance surfaces first as impaired gait and reduced locomotion.

Whole-body movement from place to place, as the motor output of behaviour, depends on intact motor circuitry and on the neuromodulatory signals that set how much an animal moves. The genes here point to dopaminergic and peptidergic control of activity and gait: the D2 dopamine receptor restrains movement initiation through striatal output, the ghrelin receptor and the CART neuropeptide link energy state to activity, and prepronociceptin supplies an opioid-related peptide that dampens locomotor drive. Downstream, G protein subunits, AMPA-type glutamate receptor signalling, and calcineurin with its RCAN regulators translate these inputs into excitability changes in motor pathways. Other members act on neuronal maintenance rather than signalling; loss of retromer or mitochondrial and lysosomal components such as VPS35, SLC25A46 and CLN6 produces ataxia, spasticity and neurodegenerative movement disorders, showing that locomotor behaviour reports on neuronal health as well as circuit tone.

Fatty acid beta-oxidation supplies ATP when glucose is scarce, and this pathway sets how fast that breakdown runs so that lipid fuel use matches demand during fasting, exercise and between feeding cycles. Control acts at several points: PPARA drives transcription of the oxidative programme, acetyl-CoA carboxylase ACACB and the malonyl-CoA decarboxylase MLYCD set malonyl-CoA levels that gate the rate-limiting carnitine palmitoyltransferase CPT1A, and insulin signalling through IRS1/IRS2 and AKT suppresses lipid catabolism in the fed state. PLIN5 governs release of substrate from lipid droplets, while ABCD1, ABCD2 and peroxisomal proteases and proteases-like factors direct very-long-chain substrates into peroxisomal oxidation. Loss of this regulation contributes to hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiac and skeletal muscle energy failure, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance, and defective peroxisomal import underlies adrenoleukodystrophy.

Cells that are taking up glucose or storing lipid must restrain the mitochondrial breakdown of fatty acids, and this set of inhibitory inputs is how that restraint is imposed. Suppressing beta-oxidation spares fatty acids for membrane synthesis and triglyceride storage and prevents futile cycling between lipid synthesis and lipid burning; in heart and muscle, too little restraint shifts substrate use toward fat and alters energy efficiency. The mechanisms are varied: ACACB generates malonyl-CoA at the outer mitochondrial membrane, which blocks carnitine-dependent entry of long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria; AKT1 relays insulin and growth-factor signalling that favours storage over oxidation; PLIN5 coats lipid droplets and limits release of stored fatty acids to mitochondria; and ETFBKMT methylates the electron transfer flavoprotein that conveys electrons out of the beta-oxidation cycle. Together they place lipid catabolism under nutritional and hormonal control.

Cells switch to burning fatty acids when glucose is scarce, and this pathway covers the signals and transporters that raise the rate of fatty acid beta-oxidation rather than the chain-shortening chemistry itself. It matters for fasting tolerance, hepatic ketogenesis, cardiac and muscle fuel selection, and for clearing lipid that would otherwise accumulate as steatosis or lipotoxic intermediates. The nuclear receptor PPARA acts as the transcriptional hub, inducing the enzymes and the carnitine palmitoyltransferase CPT1A that commits long-chain acyl groups to mitochondrial import; TWIST1 opposes this programme. Peroxisomal ABCD1 and ABCD2 deliver very-long-chain fatty acids for oxidation, and loss of ABCD1 causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. PLIN5 governs release of substrate from lipid droplets to mitochondria, while insulin signalling through IRS1, IRS2 and AKT2 sets how strongly the whole route runs with nutritional state.

Growth signalling through the TOR kinase must be switched off when cells lack nutrients, energy or oxygen, and this collection of brakes on TOR signaling is how that happens. Restraining it shifts cells from biosynthesis toward autophagy and catabolism; losing the restraint drives unchecked cell growth, and mutations in several of these genes cause tuberous sclerosis, Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome, focal cortical dysplasia and hereditary tumour predisposition. Mechanistically, the TSC1-TSC2-TBC1D7 complex inactivates the small GTPase RHEB, while GATOR1 subunits (DEPDC5, NPRL2, NPRL3) and its KICSTOR anchor block amino-acid-driven activation at the lysosome; CASTOR and SESN proteins sense arginine and leucine scarcity. Energy stress acts through the AMPK subunits PRKAA1/2 and their upstream kinase STK11, hypoxia through DDIT4, and DEPTOR and PRAS40 inhibit the kinase complex directly. Ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases tune component stability, linking nutrient sensing to protein synthesis, autophagy and cell size control.

Cells commit to growth only when nutrients, energy and growth factors are all available, and the processes that switch on TOR signalling are how that decision is made positively. Activation drives protein synthesis, ribosome biogenesis and lipid production while shutting off autophagy, so chronic overactivation underlies tumour growth, overgrowth syndromes and metabolic disease. Amino acid sufficiency is read by sensors such as SLC38A9, CASTOR1 and SAMTOR and relayed through the Rag GTPases and their GATOR/folliculin-related regulators, while the pentameric Ragulator complex (LAMTOR1-5) tethers the kinase to lysosomes. Insulin and growth factor input arrives via PI3K and AKT, which relieve inhibition of the small GTPase RHEB, the direct activator of the complex containing RPTOR and MLST8; RICTOR marks the second, distinct complex. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and other modifying enzymes tune the strength of the output, whose canonical readout includes RPS6KB1.

ARF-family small GTPases cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states to control where membranes bud, where coats assemble and where cargo goes, and ARF protein signal transduction is the relay by which that switch passes information onward. The output is Golgi and endosomal traffic, secretion, cell adhesion and spreading, and — in neurons — the surface delivery of receptors that sets synaptic strength; mutations in the brain-enriched exchange factor IQSEC2 cause intellectual disability and epilepsy. Most members here are regulators rather than the GTPases themselves: large Sec7-domain exchange factors such as GBF1, ARFGEF1 and ARFGEF2 load GTP onto ARFs at Golgi and trans-Golgi membranes, cytohesins and the PSD/EFA6 proteins act on ARF6 at the plasma membrane, and ARFGAP1 terminates the signal by stimulating hydrolysis. GIT1 and GIT2 couple the cycle to focal adhesion and cytoskeletal remodelling.

ISGylation is the interferon-induced tagging of proteins with ISG15, a ubiquitin-like modifier, and it is one of the main effector arms of the type I interferon antiviral response. Unlike ubiquitination, the modification generally does not mark proteins for degradation; instead it is attached broadly to newly synthesised proteins during infection, disrupting viral assembly and stabilising or altering the activity of host innate immune factors. The chemistry follows the ubiquitin template: UBA7 activates ISG15 in an ATP-dependent step, the conjugating enzymes UBE2L6, UBE2E1 and UBE2E2 carry it, and the HECT-domain ligase HERC5, tethered to polysomes, transfers it to substrate lysines. All of these components are themselves interferon-stimulated, so the system is largely dormant until infection. Loss of ISG15 in humans causes interferonopathy and mycobacterial susceptibility, reflecting roles beyond direct viral restriction, including regulation of interferon signalling itself.

Pancreatic beta cells release insulin in proportion to nutrient load, and this pathway covers the inputs that amplify that release, setting how quickly blood glucose is cleared after a meal. Glucose entry through the GLUT2 transporter and phosphorylation by glucokinase couple metabolism to closure of the KATP channel subunit SUR1, depolarisation and calcium entry, while mitochondrial handling of pyruvate and calcium uptake supplies amplifying signals. Incretin and fatty acid receptors such as GIPR and FFAR1 raise cAMP, acting through protein kinase A and the Epac exchange factors to prime granules for exocytosis with SNARE and Rab-effector machinery. Transcription factors including PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1 and RFX6 maintain the secretory identity of the cell. Weakening of these steps underlies type 2 diabetes and monogenic forms of hyperglycaemia, and their overactivity causes hypoglycaemia.

Cobalt ions are both a trace nutrient, as the metal center of vitamin B12, and a toxicant, and this pathway covers the cellular changes triggered when cells encounter Co2+. Because cobalt inhibits the oxygen-sensing prolyl hydroxylases, it stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor and is widely used as a chemical mimic of low oxygen; the response therefore overlaps with hypoxic gene expression, including induction of BNIP3, a BH3-only protein that drives mitophagy and cell death, and TIGAR, which shifts glucose flux toward the pentose phosphate pathway and limits reactive oxygen species. Heme biosynthesis is also affected, with cobalt altering the activity and expression of the early enzymes ALAS1 and ALAD. When the insult exceeds adaptive capacity, the extrinsic and intrinsic caspase cascades converge on CASP3 and kill the cell, linking metal exposure to apoptosis, redox balance and metabolic reprogramming.

Cells sense and react to changes in extracellular and intracellular magnesium, and this magnesium-responsive programme covers the transport, signalling and gene expression changes that follow. It matters because magnesium is the counter-ion for ATP and a competitive brake on calcium entry, so magnesium status sets nerve and muscle excitability, and because magnesium and phosphate handling are coupled in the kidney and bone: FGF23 and the sodium-phosphate cotransporter SLC34A1 tie this stimulus to mineral homeostasis, while SLC41A1 moves magnesium across membranes. Other members show the downstream reach of the signal, from potassium channels and ryanodine receptor calcium release that govern excitability, to enzymes of carbohydrate and sphingolipid metabolism, to matrix regulators such as ABCC6 and BMP6 that influence ectopic calcification. Loss of magnesium control manifests as seizures, arrhythmia, tetany and abnormal mineral deposition.

Each mitochondrion carries its own small circular genome, and this set covers the replication, repair and turnover reactions that keep that genome intact and present in adequate copy number. The dedicated machinery is distinct from the nuclear equivalent: a two-subunit polymerase gamma with its accessory subunit, the Twinkle helicase, a single-stranded DNA binding protein, a mitochondrial primase-polymerase, the mitochondrial RNA polymerase that also lays down replication primers, and a topoisomerase that resolves entangled daughter circles. Nucleases and ligases handle degradation of damaged molecules and end joining, while RRM2B supplies the deoxyribonucleotide pool that replication consumes. Because mitochondrial DNA encodes core respiratory chain subunits, defects here produce depletion or multiple deletions of the genome and the resulting mitochondrial diseases, including progressive external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia-neuropathy and hepatocerebral syndromes, with tissues of high energy demand affected first.

Cardiolipin is the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, and the reactions that make, remodel and degrade it determine whether that membrane can hold cristae shape, keep respiratory chain complexes assembled into supercomplexes, and support protein import and mitophagy.
