Synthesis proceeds from phosphatidic acid through CDP-diacylglycerol and phosphatidylglycerol phosphate, with TAMM41, PGS1, PTPMT1 and cardiolipin synthase acting in sequence; the nascent lipid is then remodelled to its mature, largely tetralinoleoyl acyl composition by deacylation through calcium-independent phospholipases and reacylation by TAFAZZIN and LCLAT1. Prohibitin and the import-motor partner DNAJC19 organise this remodelling at the membrane, while HADHA contributes acyltransferase activity. Loss of tazafferin-dependent remodelling causes Barth syndrome, with cardiomyopathy, neutropenia and skeletal myopathy, and altered cardiolipin also governs cytochrome c release during apoptosis, linking this lipid metabolism to bioenergetics and cell death.

Every cilium grows from a basal body, a modified centriole docked at the cell surface, and organizing that structure determines whether a cell can build a cilium at all. The genes here act at the transition from centriole to ciliary base: CCP110 caps the distal centriole and must be removed to license axoneme extension, CROCC (rootletin) forms the ciliary rootlet that anchors the basal body and gives it mechanical stability, DZIP1 supports recruitment of ciliogenesis machinery, and RTTN is needed for centriole integrity and duplication. FOXJ1 is the transcriptional master regulator that drives motile ciliogenesis in airway, ependymal and oviduct epithelia. Because basal body assembly, positioning and anchoring underlie both signalling cilia and motile ciliary beating, defects here produce ciliopathies with laterality defects, hydrocephalus, retinal degeneration and impaired mucociliary clearance, and RTTN mutation causes microcephaly with brain malformation.

When cells encounter stress, one of the fastest protective responses is to stop making new protein, and this is the pathway that shuts translation down. Halting bulk protein synthesis conserves energy and amino acids, prevents the accumulation of misfolded product in an already overloaded endoplasmic reticulum, and buys time for repair or for an orderly death decision. Much of the control converges on the initiation factor eIF2alpha: the ER-resident kinase PERK phosphorylates it when unfolded proteins accumulate, repressing cap-dependent initiation while permitting selective stress-response messages through, and a co-chaperone partner tunes that kinase's output. Other members act at different levels — angiogenin cleaves tRNA to generate fragments that block initiation, RBM4 redirects specific mRNAs, and SESN2 links the response to mTOR-dependent growth signalling. This translational arrest is a core arm of the integrated stress response and the unfolded protein response.

Stress normally shuts protein synthesis down, but cells also selectively raise translation of stress-response messages, and this regulatory arm is what keeps adaptive proteins being made when global initiation is suppressed. It matters for surviving amino acid deprivation, oxidative insult and endoplasmic reticulum overload, and for restarting growth once the insult passes. The genes involved act largely at initiation: a scaffolding initiation factor of the cap-binding complex, an RNA helicase that resolves structured 5' leaders, adaptor proteins that couple stress signals to the eIF2 pathway, and an ER-resident co-chaperone that restrains the eIF2-alpha kinase branch. The amino acid-sensing kinase GCN2 is included because its activity ultimately drives stress-specific translational output through altered start codon selection. Together these activities determine which mRNAs are read during stress, linking nutrient and folding surveillance to the integrated stress response and cell fate.

When cells meet stress, one of the fastest protective responses is to stop making most proteins, and this pathway is that shutdown at the level of translation initiation. Stress-activated kinases such as PERK, responding to misfolded protein load in the endoplasmic reticulum, and GCN2, responding to amino acid scarcity and uncharged tRNAs, phosphorylate the alpha subunit of eIF2. Phosphorylated eIF2 sequesters its guanine nucleotide exchange factor, so initiator tRNA delivery to ribosomes falls and global protein synthesis drops, conserving energy and reducing the folding burden. Selected transcripts escape the block: ATF4 is translated preferentially and drives the transcriptional arm of the integrated stress response, promoting adaptation or, if stress persists, apoptosis. PML contributes through nuclear body-based stress regulation. Loss of this brake underlies secretory cell failure, as in PERK-deficient diabetes, and the same axis is exploited by tumours surviving hypoxia and nutrient limitation.

Blebs are rounded, organelle-poor protrusions that balloon out where the plasma membrane locally detaches from the underlying actin cortex and is pushed outward by intracellular pressure. Their assembly matters for amoeboid cell migration through tissue, for shape changes during cytokinesis, and for the membrane dynamics of dying cells, where blebbing is a hallmark of apoptosis. The genes here supply the contractile drive and the membrane properties that permit it: ROCK1 and the myosin light chain kinase MYLK raise actomyosin tension in the cortex, anillin links actin, myosin and septins at the cleavage furrow, and lysophosphatidic acid receptors couple extracellular cues to Rho-dependent contractility. Membrane-level contributors include the purinergic channel P2RX7 and the scramblase ANO6, which alter lipid asymmetry and membrane mechanics, alongside small tetraspan-like proteins of the peripheral myelin protein family.

negative regulation of NF-kappaB transcription factor activity covers the brakes on inflammatory gene expression, restraining how much and how long NF-kappaB drives transcription of cytokines, chemokines and survival genes. This restraint keeps innate immune responses proportionate and self-limiting; its loss underlies chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and inflammation-driven tumour growth, while some of these genes act as tumour suppressors in their own right. The mechanisms are varied: deubiquitinases such as CYLD and OTULIN strip the ubiquitin chains that license IKK and upstream adaptors, TRAF3 and NLRC3-type sensors dampen receptor-proximal signalling, and nuclear factors including BCL3, SETD6 and SIRT1 modify or occupy RelA to silence promoters directly. Others act as decoys, notably the pyrin-only proteins that blunt inflammasome-linked activation, or as metabolic and G-protein-coupled inputs feeding back onto the pathway. Together they define the resolution phase of immune signalling and the tolerance imposed by regulatory T cells.

NF-kappaB drives inflammatory, antimicrobial and survival gene expression, and the brakes on it are what keep that output transient rather than chronic. Negative regulation of NF-kappaB transcription factor activity collects the inhibitors that limit how strongly and how long the factor occupies target promoters; when they fail, persistent inflammation, autoimmunity and inflammation-associated tumour growth follow. The mechanisms are varied: deubiquitinases such as CYLD and OTULIN strip activating and linear ubiquitin chains from upstream signalling components, TRAF3 restrains the non-canonical arm, BCL3 and NFKBIL1 act at the level of the DNA-bound complex, and SETD6 methylates RelA to hold it in a repressed state while SIRT1 deacetylates it. Pyrin-domain proteins and NLRC3 additionally damp inflammasome-linked and innate receptor input. Several members also explain how regulatory T cells and arrestin-coupled receptor signalling suppress inflammatory transcription.

Protein interactions are as often blocked as they are made, and negative regulation of protein binding covers the decoy proteins, competitive adaptors and modification events that keep a partner from engaging its target. Such interference sets thresholds in signalling, prevents premature assembly of complexes, and limits inflammatory and cytotoxic responses that would otherwise run unchecked. The genes here act through several distinct strategies: catalytically dead pseudo-enzymes such as STYX occupy substrate sites without turnover; CARD16 and CARD18 are caspase-recruitment decoys that obstruct inflammatory caspase assembly; complement factor H-related proteins compete for regulatory surfaces on complement components; and SLPI restrains protease and immune interactions at mucosal surfaces. Others, including RACK1, ITGB1BP1 and GOLGA2, sequester kinases, integrin tails or tethering partners. Loss of such restraint contributes to inappropriate complement activation, excess inflammation and deregulated mitotic and apoptotic signalling.

Protein-protein interactions are not fixed properties; they are set up and dismantled by other proteins, and this grouping collects factors that raise the rate or extent of protein binding by their partners. The effect matters because assembly of signalling complexes, scaffolds and immune effector platforms depends on such promotion rather than on the intrinsic affinity of the partners alone. The members act through diverse routes: GSK3B phosphorylates substrates in ways that create or expose docking surfaces, ubiquitin-pathway components such as DTX3L, TRIM21 and the deubiquitinase USP9X remodel modification states that govern partner recruitment, RAPGEF2 couples receptor input to Rap GTPase activation, and BMP4 acts extracellularly to engage its receptor complex. Collectively they illustrate how post-translational modification, chaperone-like adaptors and ligand engagement are used to stabilise interactions that drive development, signal relay and protein quality control.

Eating is a stimulus that the body must sense and respond to, and this pathway covers the cellular and organismal reactions triggered by food intake — from gut hormone release to shifts in metabolic gene expression and appetite signalling. It matters because it sets meal size, satiety, and the postprandial switch between fuel storage and mobilisation; its failure underlies hyperphagia, obesity, and syndromic forms such as Bardet–Biedl syndrome, represented here by BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS. Orexigenic ghrelin acting through GHSR and NPY opposes leptin and melanocortin signalling via MC4R, while GDF15 with its receptor GFRAL conveys aversive, appetite-suppressing signals. Downstream, SREBF1 and PPARA reprogram lipid and glucose handling, and G6PC1 supports hepatic glucose output. Gastrin, oxytocin, CART and urocortin contribute gut–brain communication, linking nutrient detection to digestion, endocrine output and feeding behaviour.

Feeding is not a reflex but a regulated behaviour, and this collection covers the signals that raise or lower an animal's response to food. Peripheral hormones report energy state to the brain: leptin from adipose tissue signals repletion and suppresses intake, ghrelin acting through its receptor GHSR signals fasting and stimulates appetite, and GDF15 acting on the brainstem receptor GFRAL drives aversive appetite loss of the kind seen in cachexia and chemotherapy. Within the hypothalamus, orexigenic NPY and anorexigenic CART peptide, together with neuropeptides such as spexin and NPFF and the stress peptide urocortin, set the balance. Ciliary proteins including BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS are required for these neurons to sense hormonal input, which is why Bardet-Biedl syndrome features hyperphagia and obesity. Loss of restraint at this level produces overeating, obesity and metabolic disease; excess restraint produces wasting.

Appetite regulation is the set of signals that raise or suppress the drive to eat, matching food intake to energy stores and to the body's tolerance for illness. It works through hypothalamic neurons that read peripheral hormones: leptin from adipose tissue reports fat reserves and suppresses feeding, ghrelin acting on its receptor GHSR reports an empty stomach and stimulates it, and GDF15 signalling through GFRAL in the hindbrain drives the anorexia and nausea of infection, cancer and cellular stress. Arcuate neuropeptides set the balance, with NPY and AgRP-type orexigenic tone opposed by POMC-derived melanocortins and CART. Serotonergic and nicotinic receptor inputs modulate the same circuits, which is why serotonin agonists and nicotine blunt hunger. Failure produces obesity, including the hyperphagia of leptin deficiency and of ciliopathies involving BBS proteins, or, at the other extreme, cachexia and anorexia.

Cells and tissues must set the gain on their reactions to things coming from outside — microbes, injury, wounding cues, chemotactic gradients — and this regulation of response to external stimulus covers the modulating layer rather than the response itself. It matters because both under- and over-shooting are pathological: too little permits infection, too much drives septic shock, chronic inflammation and autoimmunity. The membership is dominated by innate immune tuning: Toll-like receptors with their adaptors MYD88 and TICAM1, inflammasome sensors of the NLRP family with caspase-1 and PYCARD, cytosolic nucleic-acid sensing through RIGI/STING1/IRF3, and brakes such as IRAK3, TNFAIP3, SIGIRR and interleukin-1 receptor antagonists. Also present are chemokine and cytokine receptors, complement and coagulation components, wound and angiogenic growth factors, axon-guidance cues, and many ubiquitin ligases, phosphatases and microRNAs that dampen or amplify these circuits.

Responses to the outside world — infection, injury, bleeding, chemical and guidance cues — must be turned off as reliably as they are turned on, and this collection of negative regulators of response to external stimulus is the brake. It spans anti-inflammatory cytokines and their receptors such as IL10, IL1RN and IL37, decoy and inhibitory receptors including IL1R2 and FCGR2B, immune checkpoints like PDCD1, TIGIT, HAVCR2 and CD200, deubiquitinases and adaptors that terminate NF-kB signalling such as TNFAIP3, OTULIN and CYLD, phosphatases including PTPN6 and INPP5D, negative regulators of nucleic acid sensing such as USP18 and TREX1, serpins and anticoagulant factors that limit clotting and fibrinolysis, and Slit–Robo and semaphorin cues that repel migrating cells and axons. Many microRNAs tune the same circuits. Loss of this restraint underlies autoinflammatory syndromes, autoimmunity, thrombotic disease and failure of tumour immune evasion control.

positive regulation of response to external stimulus collects the amplifying arms of how cells detect and react to things outside themselves — microbes, tissue damage, chemotactic and wound signals — and it determines how vigorously inflammation, innate immunity, coagulation and wound repair are mounted. Its failure leaves hosts unable to clear infection, while unchecked activity drives sepsis, autoinflammatory syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease. The genes trace the sensing steps and their positive feedback: Toll-like receptors with MYD88, TIRAP and IRAK kinases; cytosolic nucleic-acid sensors such as cGAS–STING1, RIGI and MAVS; NOD-like receptors and inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1; and the NF-κB, MAPK and IRF modules they converge on. Downstream effectors are the cytokines, chemokines and their receptors that recruit leukocytes, alongside complement, ficolins, defensins and S100 alarmins, plus angiogenic and clotting factors that couple immunity to tissue response, with ubiquitin ligases and microRNAs tuning the output.

Cells that meet a microbe, an injury or a chemotactic gradient must not only detect it but amplify the reaction, and this collection of positive regulators of the response to external stimuli is what raises the gain. It underpins innate immune defence, inflammation, wound healing and leukocyte recruitment, and its over-activity produces septic shock, autoinflammatory fever syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like and RIG-I-like families feed through adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1, MAVS and STING1 into IRAK and TBK1 kinases, NF-kB and interferon-regulatory factors, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 mature IL-1B and IL-18 and drive gasdermin-mediated lytic death. Complement factors, ficolins, chemokines and their receptors, growth factors, coagulation proteins and many ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and microRNAs tune the strength and duration of the response.

Organisms must sense whether nutrients are abundant or scarce and then tune how strongly they react, and this pathway covers the regulatory layer that sets the gain of that response. It matters for appetite, body weight and energy balance: leptin, ghrelin with its receptor GHSR, NPY, CARTPT, spexin and urocortin act on hypothalamic circuits that decide feeding versus satiety, while GDF15 signalling through GFRAL drives nausea and anorexia during metabolic stress. Growth hormone receptor signalling links nutrient status to somatic growth. A second arm is nuclear receptor transcription: PPARA responds to fatty acid availability during fasting, the bile acid receptor NR1H4 and the vitamin D receptor with RXR partners and coactivators such as MED1 and TRIM24 set metabolic gene programmes. Ciliary Bardet-Biedl components and BCL2-family survival regulators modulate how cells and neurons respond to nutrient deprivation, and dysregulation here produces obesity, cachexia and metabolic syndrome.

Organisms sense nutrient availability and mount responses such as feeding, foraging and fuel mobilisation; this pathway covers the braking signals that damp those responses, and it is largely the biology of satiety and appetite suppression. Leptin from adipose tissue reports energy stores to hypothalamic circuits, GDF15 acting through its brainstem receptor GFRAL produces aversion and reduced food intake, and neuropeptides including CART, spexin and urocortin restrain feeding centrally; the ghrelin receptor GHSR is the counterpart orexigenic node whose signalling is opposed. Several Bardet-Biedl syndrome proteins, BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS, support ciliary trafficking of these receptors in hypothalamic neurons, which is why their loss causes hyperphagia and obesity. PPARA adds a transcriptional arm linking fatty acid oxidation to the fasting response. Failure of this restraint underlies obesity, while its overactivation contributes to cancer anorexia and cachexia.

Animals must sense whether nutrients are abundant or scarce and convert that reading into feeding behaviour, hormone release and metabolic adjustment; this pathway covers the steps that amplify such responses. Ghrelin, the stomach-derived hunger hormone, signals through its receptor GHSR to stimulate appetite and growth hormone secretion, and its downstream effector neuropeptide Y acts in hypothalamic circuits to drive food intake and lower energy expenditure. The bile acid receptor NR1H4 reports on post-prandial bile acid flux and adjusts bile acid, lipid and glucose handling in liver and intestine accordingly. Fibrillin-1 contributes through the asprosin peptide encoded within its C-terminus, released during fasting. Together these components enhance the organism's reaction to changing nutrient supply, and their dysregulation contributes to obesity, cachexia and disordered glucose metabolism.

Kinases are held inactive until a signal releases them, and this collection covers the switching-on step itself "the events that convert a dormant protein kinase into a catalytically active one. It matters because almost every growth, inflammatory and stress response depends on a kinase being turned on at the right moment and not before. Several distinct switching mechanisms appear together: regulatory subunits of cAMP-dependent protein kinase that keep the catalytic subunit restrained until cyclic AMP binds; pseudokinase adaptors that partner the LKB1 kinase to activate AMPK-family signalling under energy stress; death receptors and TNF-family receptors that nucleate complexes in which RIPK1 and RIPK3 become active and drive necroptosis or NF- cB signalling; growth factor and cytokine receptors acting through JAK2 and focal adhesion-type kinases; and mitotic activators such as TPX2, which switches on Aurora A at the spindle.

Protein kinase B, or AKT, sits at the hub of growth factor signalling, and the events described here are those that switch it from an inactive to an active kinase, committing cells to survival, growth, glucose uptake and migration rather than apoptosis. Most of the triggers are extracellular ligands acting through receptor tyrosine kinases: insulin-like growth factor 1, fibroblast growth factor 1 and the neuregulin ligands of ERBB receptors, together with GAS6, which engages the TAM receptor AXL. Their common route is receptor-proximal PI3K activity generating membrane phosphoinositides that recruit AKT for phosphorylation. Additional modulators act intracellularly, including an integrin beta-1 binding partner and a small membrane-associated activator. Because this step licenses anabolic metabolism and blocks cell death, its inappropriate activation is one of the most frequent features of human cancers, while insufficient signalling contributes to insulin resistance and impaired tissue repair.

Septins are GTP-binding proteins that polymerize into filaments and rings at the cell cortex, and septin cytoskeleton organization covers the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of those structures together with the proteins that recruit and stabilize them. Their best-known job is to mark the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis, where anillin links septins to actin and myosin so the contractile ring is positioned and the intercellular bridge resolved; failure produces multinucleate cells. Septin scaffolds also act as diffusion barriers that keep membrane domains distinct, contributing to ciliogenesis and planar-polarized epithelial architecture, consistent with the presence of a ciliogenesis and planar polarity effector and a cadherin-family adhesion protein here. Additional members contribute Rho-family regulation and membrane-cytoskeleton coupling. Mutations in the septin component cause hereditary neuralgic amyotrophy, tying this organization to peripheral nerve integrity.</description>

Transposition is the movement of DNA segments to new, nonhomologous sites in the genome, either by copy-and-paste through an RNA intermediate, as for LINE-1 and endogenous retroviruses, or by cut-and-paste excision and reintegration. Because unchecked mobilisation causes insertional mutation, chromosomal rearrangement and sterility, most of this biology is devoted to suppression: piwi-family proteins with their Tudor-domain partners and RNA helicases enforce piRNA-guided silencing in the germline; SETDB1 with the HUSH complex (TASOR, MPHOSPH8, PPHLN1) and the co-repressor SPOCD1 deposit repressive chromatin and direct de novo DNA methylation through DNMT3A and DNMT3L; APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases mutate retroelement cDNA, TREX1 degrades it, and rapidly evolving KRAB zinc fingers such as ZNF91 and ZNF93 recognise specific element families. Loss of these restraints leads to retroelement activation, interferon-driven inflammation and germ cell failure, and a few genes here retain genuine transposase activity.}

Chromosome ends must be distinguished from broken DNA and kept long enough to survive repeated division, and telomere organization is the assembly and remodelling of the nucleoprotein caps that achieve this. Without it, ends fuse or trigger a permanent DNA damage response, driving senescence, bone marrow failure and premature ageing syndromes; inappropriate reactivation instead grants tumour cells unlimited replicative capacity. A six-subunit shelterin complex built around TRF1, TRF2, POT1, TPP1, TIN2 and RAP1 binds the duplex repeats and the single-stranded overhang, while the telomerase enzyme with its RNA template, dyskerin and associated H/ACA proteins adds new repeats and is itself trafficked and assembled by chaperones. Replication of these repeats requires specialised helicases and nucleases, and homologous recombination, non-homologous end joining and shieldin components are actively restrained here, alongside chromatin remodellers, histones and SIRT6 that set the heterochromatic state of the ends.

Chromosome ends are replicated by the same fork machinery that copies the rest of the genome, and telomere maintenance via semi-conservative replication is that process together with the accessory factors needed to get through repetitive, G-rich, secondary-structure-prone sequence. Without it forks stall at telomeres, ends are lost or fuse, and cells enter premature senescence — the basis of the telomere defects seen in Bloom and Werner syndromes. Lagging-strand maturation is carried out by the sliding clamp PCNA with flap endonuclease FEN1, the nuclease-helicase DNA2 and ligase LIG1, while the helicases BLM, WRN and RTEL1 unwind G-quadruplexes and displace telomeric loops so replication can proceed. Shelterin components TERF1 and TERF2 recruit and license this activity at the duplex telomere, tying end protection directly to S-phase DNA replication and genome stability.

Chromosome ends must be kept long enough to avoid being read as broken DNA, yet short enough that cells retain a replicative limit; this is the control layer that sets telomere length and telomeric protein activity. Its outputs are cellular lifespan, stem cell renewal and tumour suppression: loss of control gives telomere shortening syndromes such as dyskeratosis congenita and bone marrow failure, while inappropriate maintenance licenses the unlimited division of cancer cells. Regulation operates at several levels. The shelterin proteins TRF1, TRF2, TIN2, TPP1 and POT1 cap the telomere and restrain telomerase access, the CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 limits G-overhang extension, and dyskerin with WRAP53 and PARN governs the stability and trafficking of telomerase RNA. Damage kinases ATM and ATR, p53, chromatin remodellers such as ATRX and the INO80 complex, SMC5/6-mediated recombination and helicases including RTEL1 and PIF1 tune elongation, resolve telomeric replication intermediates and support recombination-based lengthening.

Telomeres must be kept long enough to protect chromosome ends but short enough to limit unchecked proliferation, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that restrain telomerase recruitment, trim over-elongated ends and degrade the machinery's RNA and protein components. Shelterin proteins such as TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD cap the end and count its length, with POT1-ACD blocking telomerase access, while PINX1 directly inhibits the enzyme and the CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 terminates telomeric extension. Helicases including RTEL1 and PIF1, structure-specific nucleases acting with SLX4 and ERCC1-ERCC4, and damage signalling through ATM, the MRN components and TP53 resolve or remove aberrant telomeric structures. Loss of this restraint permits telomere lengthening that supports tumour cell immortalisation, whereas excessive braking drives premature senescence and telomere shortening syndromes.

Chromosome ends shorten with every division unless actively renewed, and the processes grouped here push telomere maintenance upward — extending telomeric DNA, promoting telomerase assembly and recruitment, and stabilising the protective proteins at the end. Sustained activity of this kind is what allows stem cells, germline and proliferating progenitors to divide indefinitely, and its inappropriate activation is a near-universal feature of cancer, while insufficient activity produces telomere biology disorders with bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis. Members include the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD that cap the end, the H/ACA components DKC1 and NAF1 and the chaperone WRAP53 that build and traffic telomerase RNA, damage-response kinases ATM and ATR with the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex, the INO80 and RUVBL-containing chromatin remodelling machinery, ATRX, SIRT6, and the transcription factors MYC and KLF4 that drive telomerase expression.

Telomerase adds telomeric repeats to chromosome ends, and this is the control layer that decides how much it adds, where, and when — the difference between replicative senescence in normal somatic cells and the unlimited division of most cancers. Shelterin subunits POT1, TERF1, TERF2, TINF2 and ACD cap the telomere and restrain enzyme access, with the CST complex (CTC1, STN1, TEN1) terminating extension and handing off to lagging-strand synthesis. A second arm governs the enzyme itself: DKC1 and WRAP53 stabilise and traffic the RNA subunit, while PARN, EXOSC10 and decay factors such as XRN1 and DCP2 trim or degrade it, setting the amount available. Chaperones including the CCT/TRiC ring and HSP90 assist assembly, and PINX1, tankyrases and the ATM/ATR–TP53 damage axis tune activity further. Loss of these controls produces telomere shortening syndromes such as dyskeratosis congenita, bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis.

Telomerase must be restrained as well as recruited, and this is the braking side of telomere length control: processes that block or limit the addition of telomeric repeats so that chromosome ends are capped at a set length rather than extended indefinitely. The restraint matters because unchecked elongation supports the unlimited division of tumour cells, while excessive repression drives replicative senescence and the short-telomere syndromes. Shelterin components including TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD count repeats and occlude the enzyme from the 3' overhang; the CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 terminates telomerase action and hands the end to conventional replication. PINX1 inhibits the catalytic enzyme directly, PIF1 displaces it from the DNA, and RNA-binding and exonucleolytic factors limit the abundance of the telomerase RNA itself. TP53 links this control to damage-responsive growth arrest.

Riboflavin transport moves vitamin B2 across membranes, supplying the cell with the precursor of FMN and FAD, the flavin cofactors that redox enzymes of the respiratory chain, fatty acid beta-oxidation, and folate and amino acid metabolism cannot work without. Because humans cannot synthesise riboflavin, uptake from the diet and its delivery to tissues depend entirely on dedicated carriers: SLC52A1 in placenta, and SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 in intestine and neurons. Loss-of-function mutations in the latter two cause Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, a childhood motor neuron disease with deafness and bulbar palsy that responds to high-dose riboflavin, showing how directly neuronal survival tracks flavin supply. Efflux and tissue-specific handling add another layer, with ABCG2 exporting riboflavin and retbindin retaining it in the retina to support photoreceptor metabolism.

Humans cannot synthesise riboflavin, so vitamin B2 must be absorbed from the diet and delivered to every tissue that makes FMN and FAD, the cofactors of flavoproteins in fatty acid beta-oxidation, the respiratory chain, and folate and amino acid metabolism. Riboflavin transport carries out that delivery: the SLC52 family encodes the plasma membrane riboflavin transporters that mediate intestinal uptake, placental transfer to the fetus, and entry into neurons and other cells, while ABCG2 effluxes riboflavin, contributing to its secretion into milk. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 cause Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, a childhood motor neuron disease with deafness and bulbar palsy that responds to high-dose riboflavin supplementation, showing how directly neuronal survival depends on flavin supply. Retbindin associates with riboflavin handling in photoreceptors, linking this transport to retinal energy metabolism.

Cholinergic synaptic transmission is tuned in strength and duration by the processes gathered here, which set how much acetylcholine reaches receptors and for how long — at neuromuscular junctions as well as in autonomic ganglia and brain circuits where acetylcholine shapes arousal, attention and motor output. Loading of the transmitter into synaptic vesicles by the vesicular acetylcholine transporter determines quantal content, while acetylcholinesterase terminates signalling; its anchoring at the synaptic basal lamina depends on the collagen-like tail subunit ColQ together with perlecan and laminin, and loss of this anchoring causes congenital myasthenic syndrome with prolonged endplate currents. Modulation also arrives from outside the cholinergic synapse: adenosine A2A receptors, substance P acting through neurokinin receptors, and amyloid precursor protein influence release probability, and nicotinic subunits and a sodium leak channel set the excitability on which release depends.

positive regulation of synaptic transmission, cholinergic covers the mechanisms that strengthen or sustain acetylcholine signalling between neurons, the transmitter system that drives neuromuscular activation, autonomic output, and the attentional and memory circuits of the basal forebrain. Its failure is felt directly: loss of cholinergic tone accompanies the cognitive decline of Alzheimer's disease, and drugs that boost it remain a mainstay of symptomatic treatment. The genes act at several levels of the same amplification problem. SLC18A3 loads acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles and so sets how much transmitter each release event delivers, while NALCN provides the sodium leak conductance that keeps cholinergic neurons depolarised and firing. Neuromodulatory input arrives through adenosine A2A receptors and through substance P acting on tachykinin receptors, and APP and the basement membrane component LAMA2 shape synapse assembly and stability at cholinergic contacts.

Acetylcholine-using synapses drive skeletal muscle contraction, autonomic output, and cortical and hippocampal circuits that support attention and memory, and this pathway covers the influences that turn that transmission up rather than down. The regulators act at several points: a vesicular acetylcholine transporter loads the neurotransmitter into synaptic vesicles and so sets quantal content, a sodium leak channel maintains the resting excitability that determines whether cholinergic neurons fire, and substance P acting through its receptors provides neuropeptide modulation that enhances release. An extracellular matrix laminin subunit contributes to the synaptic scaffolding required at neuromuscular junctions, while adenosine A2A receptor signalling and amyloid precursor protein link cholinergic gain to purinergic tone and to synaptic maintenance. Loss of cholinergic drive underlies the cognitive decline targeted by cholinesterase inhibitors and the weakness seen in neuromuscular transmission disorders.

Dopamine signalling sets the gain on movement, motivation and reward learning, and the processes that tune it determine how much dopamine reaches receptors and for how long. Modulation of dopaminergic synaptic transmission covers presynaptic control of release, receptor desensitisation and trafficking, and the membrane environment in which transporters and receptors operate. Arrestin beta-2 uncouples activated dopamine receptors from G proteins and routes them into internalisation and alternative signalling; nicotinic receptors containing the beta-2 subunit on dopaminergic terminals drive acetylcholine-evoked release, the entry point for nicotine reinforcement; flotillin-1 organises membrane microdomains supporting transporter function. PINK1 links mitochondrial quality control to the vulnerability of nigrostriatal neurons, and its loss causes early-onset parkinsonism. Failures here underlie movement disorders, paroxysmal dyskinesia, and susceptibility to addiction, and the same machinery is targeted by antipsychotics and psychostimulants.

Inhibitory tone in the brain depends on how strongly GABAergic synapses are driven, and this collection of modulators sets that strength. Tuning GABA release and postsynaptic responsiveness determines the excitation-inhibition balance that keeps cortical and hippocampal circuits from running away; its failure underlies epilepsy, and several members are mutated in human seizure and neurodevelopmental disorders. Control acts at several levels: GABA-A receptor subunits such as GABRB3 and GABRG2 form the postsynaptic chloride channels themselves, while palmitoyltransferases and scaffolding and trafficking proteins govern how many receptors reach and stay at the synapse. Trans-synaptic adhesion through neurexin and neuroligin partners, notably NLGN2, specifies and maintains inhibitory contacts. Presynaptically, release machinery including STXBP1 and synapsin, glutamine supply for transmitter synthesis, and G protein-coupled receptors for adenosine, dopamine, cannabinoids and neuropeptides adjust output, with activity-dependent transcription via NPAS4 feeding back onto inhibitory input.

GABA is the brain's main inhibitory transmitter, and this pathway covers the processes that damp it down — reducing the frequency or strength of transmission at GABAergic synapses. Because inhibition sets the gain of cortical and hippocampal circuits, weakening it shifts networks toward excitation, and the genes involved are closely tied to epilepsy and to disorders of sleep, anxiety and development. Presynaptic G protein–coupled receptors, including the adenosine A1 receptor, the CB2 cannabinoid receptor and a neuropeptide Y receptor, act as autoregulatory or heterosynaptic brakes that suppress GABA release. On the postsynaptic side, subunits of the ionotropic GABA-A receptor (alpha, beta and gamma types) determine how much chloride current a released quantum produces, so changes in their composition or surface expression scale inhibition down. STXBP1 ties the pathway to the vesicle fusion machinery that release depends on.

GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the mammalian brain, and this pathway covers the processes that strengthen or increase transmission at GABAergic synapses, tuning the balance between excitation and inhibition that keeps circuits from running away into seizure or hyperexcitability. Several routes converge on that outcome. Trans-synaptic adhesion by neurexins and neuroligins, with NLGN2 particularly associated with inhibitory contacts, specifies and stabilises the postsynaptic side; palmitoyl transferases such as ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC12 modify receptor and scaffold proteins to control their synaptic anchoring; and motor- and adaptor-dependent transport involving kinesin and HAP1 delivers receptors to the membrane. Superimposed on this are neuromodulatory inputs — adenosine and adrenergic receptors, substance P acting through TACR1, neuropeptide S, and protein kinase C signalling — that raise inhibitory drive in response to arousal, pain and stress states. Loss of such control contributes to epilepsy, anxiety and neurodevelopmental disorders.

regulation of actin filament bundle assembly controls how cells build stress fibres, filopodia and other bundled actin arrays, and thereby sets cell shape, adhesion strength, contractility and migration speed. It matters for wound healing, endothelial and epithelial barrier integrity, neuronal process outgrowth and the mechanical properties of muscle and podocytes; its misregulation contributes to invasive tumour behaviour and vascular leak. The core logic is Rho-family GTPase signalling: RhoA/RAC1/CDC42 are switched by an array of GEFs and GAPs, and downstream ROCK1/2, PAK and LIMK phosphorylate cofilin and TESK targets to stabilise filaments, while profilins, formins such as FHOD1/3, filamin A and tropomyosin nucleate, cap and crosslink them into bundles. Junctional and adhesion proteins including paxillin, ZO-1, kindlin-2 and syndecan-4 couple bundle assembly to integrin and cell-cell contact cues, with additional input from TGF-beta, Wnt, ephrin and lysophospholipid receptors and several microRNAs.

Actin filaments are cross-linked into parallel or antiparallel bundles to build stress fibres, filopodia and the contractile arrays that let cells adhere, stiffen, migrate and pull on their surroundings; this pathway covers the inputs that set how much bundling occurs and where. Control runs largely through Rho-family GTPases and their regulators — RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 with numerous GEFs and GAPs such as ARHGEF18 and DLC1 — converging on ROCK1/ROCK2 and LIMK1, which suppress the severing and depolymerising activity of cofilin, while profilins feed monomers to formins including FHOD1 and FHOD3. Adhesion and junction proteins (paxillin, filamin A, FERMT2, ZO-1), receptor signals from sphingosine-1-phosphate, TGF-β and ephrin systems, and several microRNAs tune the output. The balance determines endothelial and epithelial barrier tone, cytokinesis, neuronal and podocyte morphology, and smooth muscle contractility.

Actin stress fibres and other contractile bundles must be dismantled or held in check as often as they are built, and this pathway covers the restraint side of that balance. Limiting bundle assembly keeps cells able to change shape, migrate, form junctions and remodel their cortex rather than locking into a rigid contractile state. Much of the negative control runs through Rho family GTPase signalling: several GAPs, including DLC1 and ARHGAP6, switch RhoA off and so reduce ROCK-driven bundling, while cofilin severs and depolymerises filaments and profilin channels monomers toward other outcomes. Junctional and scaffolding proteins such as ZO-1, JAM-A and cingulin-like protein couple cell-cell contact to reduced bundle formation, and rhophilins, SHANK scaffolds and phosphoinositide phosphatases add further brakes. Loss of this restraint stiffens cells and distorts migration, neurite outgrowth and epithelial and endothelial barrier remodelling.

Bundled actin filaments give cells their stress fibres, filopodia, microvilli and contractile belts, and this pathway covers the signals and effectors that drive more of that bundling. It determines cell shape, adhesion strength, traction on the matrix, and the migration and contractility of fibroblasts, smooth muscle and endothelium; excessive activity stiffens tissue and contributes to fibrosis, while loss compromises wound closure and barrier integrity. The core is Rho-family GTPase signalling: RhoA and RhoC, activated by an array of guanine nucleotide exchange factors, act through ROCK2, while CDC42 and RAC1 work via PAK1; LIMK1 and TESK1 in turn phosphorylate cofilin to stabilise filaments, opposed by the phosphatases PPM1E and PPM1F. Formins such as FHOD1 and FHOD3, profilins, EVL, tropomyosin and synaptopodins elongate and crosslink the filaments, with integrin-associated adaptors including paxillin, filamin A and kindlin-2 coupling bundles to adhesions downstream of TGF-beta, Wnt and lysophosphatidic acid cues.

When intracellular calcium stores in the endoplasmic reticulum are depleted, cells must refill them by opening calcium channels in the plasma membrane, and this pathway describes how that opening is triggered. Store-operated calcium entry sustains the prolonged calcium signals that drive lymphocyte activation and cytokine gene expression, muscle function, and secretion; loss of it causes severe combined immunodeficiency with myopathy, while excessive entry contributes to inflammatory and thrombotic disease. The sensing step belongs to the ER membrane proteins STIM1 and STIM2, whose luminal EF-hand domains release calcium, oligomerize, and migrate to ER-plasma membrane junctions where they directly gate Orai channels. Accessory factors including CRACR2A and an ER membrane regulator promote and stabilize the STIM-Orai interaction, tuning the amplitude and duration of entry rather than initiating it, which makes this activation step a control point for calcium-dependent transcription.

Adenosine crosses membranes only with help, and these nucleoside carriers provide it, setting how much extracellular adenosine reaches its receptors and how much enters cells for salvage into nucleotides. The equilibrative transporters move adenosine and other nucleosides down their concentration gradient, terminating purinergic signalling at the cell surface and thereby shaping vasodilation, cardiac conduction, sleep pressure and inflammatory tone; a sodium-coupled concentrative carrier instead drives uptake against gradient in absorptive epithelia such as intestine and kidney. Because nucleoside analogue drugs use the same routes, adenosine transport largely determines cellular entry of cytarabine, gemcitabine and related agents, and the equilibrative pathway is the target of dipyridamole and the mechanism behind adenosine-sparing therapy. Loss of the lysosomal member of this family causes a histiocytosis-lymphadenopathy syndrome, tying nucleoside efflux from lysosomes to macrophage function.

regulation of nucleobase-containing compound transport controls how much nucleic acid and nucleotide traffic crosses membranes and the nuclear envelope, setting the rate at which mRNA reaches the cytoplasm and at which nucleosides are taken up by cells. It matters because gene expression is limited not only by transcription but by export: transcripts retained in the nucleus are never translated, and viral and oncogenic programs exploit this control point. The genes describe the export side in detail — the cap-binding and cleavage factors that mark a transcript as ready, the TREX component THOC2 and helicases DDX39A and DHX9 that drive mRNP release, and nucleoporins TPR and NUP153 that gate the pore and enforce retention of unspliced RNA. Chromatin and RNA modification enzymes such as SETD2, ALKBH5 and NSUN2 tune export through co-transcriptional marks, while transporter regulators including RSC1A1 and WNK1 adjust nucleoside uptake at the plasma membrane.

Nucleobases, nucleotides and RNA molecules must be moved across membranes and out of the nucleus at controlled rates, and this pathway covers the factors that tune those transport events up or down. Most of the genes act on messenger RNA export: nuclear pore and basket components such as NUP153 and TPR, the TREX-associated THOC2, the export adaptors DDX39A and CPSF6, and the cap-binding subunit NCBP2 together determine which transcripts leave the nucleus and how quickly. Chromatin and co-transcriptional regulators including SETD2 and IWS1 couple transcription to export competence, while the demethylase ALKBH5 and the methyltransferase NSUN2 add RNA modification marks that alter export and localisation. Other members regulate nucleoside handling at the cell surface, notably the adenosine receptor ADORA1 and the transporter regulator RSC1A1. The balance set here shapes gene expression output, and its disruption drives nucleocytoplasmic transport defects seen in cancer and neurodegeneration.

Increased movement of nucleic acids and nucleotide-containing molecules across membranes and between nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments, this regulatory activity mainly enhances the export of mRNA from the nucleus so that transcripts made in the nucleus can be translated. Most of the contributing proteins act at the interface between RNA processing and transport: a cap-binding component and a cleavage factor subunit couple capping and 3' end formation to export competence, while an RNA helicase and an RNA-binding adaptor promote loading of transcripts onto export machinery. Efficient coupling of this kind keeps gene expression responsive, prevents retention of incompletely processed transcripts, and governs how quickly newly induced mRNAs reach ribosomes. An adenosine receptor in the group links extracellular purine signalling to nucleoside handling, extending the theme beyond nucleic acids to small nucleobase-containing metabolites.

Cells that release hormones, neuropeptides or cytotoxic contents on demand must first move their secretory granules to the right place and hold them there, and secretory granule localization is that positioning step. Where it fails, vesicles never reach release sites, and neurotransmission, insulin and catecholamine secretion, and granule discharge by immune cells all falter. Kinesin motors of the KIF1 and KIF5 families haul granules along microtubules, with cytoskeletal and scaffold proteins such as MAP2 and TRIM46 shaping the tracks and defining where cargo is delivered. On arrival, tethering and priming factors including CADPS, the UNC13 proteins, RAB3A and STXBP1 dock granules and render them fusion-competent, coupling localization directly to the SNAP25-dependent fusion machinery. Loss-of-function in several of these genes causes severe epileptic encephalopathies, hereditary neuropathies and familial hemophagocytic syndromes, underscoring how much regulated exocytosis depends on where granules are kept.

Methylation covers the transfer of a methyl group, almost always from S-adenosylmethionine, onto DNA, RNA, proteins, lipids and small molecules, and it is the chemistry through which cells encode heritable gene silencing, tune protein activity and dispose of neurotransmitters and xenobiotics. Its failure is felt everywhere: loss of DNA methyltransferases derails imprinting and differentiation, histone methyltransferases such as the KMT2, EZH, SETD, SUV39 and PRMT families are recurrently mutated in developmental syndromes and cancer, and defects in tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes cause intellectual disability and mitochondrial disease. The genes span writers of the epigenome, cap and internal mRNA methylation that sets transcript stability and translation, ribosome and tRNA maturation, protein carboxyl and lysine methylation controlling translation factors and phosphatases, and catabolic transferases like COMT and NNMT. Methionine cycle enzymes regenerate the methyl donor, coupling all of this to one-carbon metabolism and nutrient sensing.

Transfer of a methyl group onto DNA, RNA, protein, lipid or small-molecule acceptors is one of the cell's most widely used covalent modifications, and this collection covers the enzymes that perform it. Nearly all draw the methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine, linking the reaction to one-carbon and folate metabolism. The consequences are functionally diverse: DNA methyltransferases such as DNMT1 and DNMT3A set heritable gene silencing marks; histone lysine and arginine methyltransferases including the KMT2, SETD, SUV39, EZH and PRMT families write the chromatin code that specifies cell identity; tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes tune translational fidelity and ribosome biogenesis; METTL3/METTL14 with RBM15 deposit m6A to control mRNA fate; and catechol, nicotinamide, thiopurine and histamine methyltransferases inactivate neurotransmitters, hormones and drugs. Loss or misdirection of these activities underlies overgrowth and imprinting syndromes, leukemias, and altered drug tolerance.

Cells rarely build purine rings from scratch when they can recycle them, and purine nucleotide salvage recaptures free bases and nucleosides released by nucleic acid turnover, converting them back into nucleotides at a fraction of the energetic cost of de novo synthesis. Tissues with little de novo capacity, notably brain and erythrocytes, depend on it outright: loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and neurological disease, while adenosine deaminase deficiency destroys lymphocytes and causes severe combined immunodeficiency. Phosphoribosyltransferases attach bases to PRPP, while kinases such as adenosine kinase and the deoxyribonucleoside kinases phosphorylate nucleosides, including the prodrug-activating steps that make these enzymes pharmacologically relevant. AMP deaminases and adenylosuccinate synthetase interconvert adenine and inosine nucleotides in the purine nucleotide cycle, and a parallel branch salvages nicotinamide and nicotinic acid into NAD, linking purine recycling to cellular redox and energy metabolism.

Cells can regenerate inosine monophosphate from breakdown products rather than paying the energetic cost of building the purine ring from scratch, and IMP salvage is that recycling route. It matters because purine turnover is continuous and the salvage arm dominates nucleotide supply in tissues such as brain, blood cells and muscle. Hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase condenses hypoxanthine with PRPP to give IMP directly; the AMP deaminase isoforms, expressed in muscle, ubiquitously, and in erythroid cells respectively, convert AMP back to IMP and so link adenylate energy charge to purine flux. A related phosphoribosyltransferase reclaims adenine as AMP, feeding the same pool. Loss of the hypoxanthine route causes hyperuricaemia with the neurological and self-injurious features of Lesch-Nyhan disease, while muscle AMP deaminase deficiency produces exercise intolerance, tying this recycling chemistry to both uric acid handling and energy metabolism.

Cells constantly build and dismantle filaments, and this regulatory layer sets how fast actin and tubulin subunits are added to or lost from polymers. Control of protein polymerization determines cell shape, motility, division and the mechanical integrity of specialized structures such as the erythrocyte membrane skeleton and the podocyte foot process. Nucleation and elongation are driven by the Arp2/3 complex with its WAVE-associated and IRSp53-type activators, profilins feed monomers in, while capping proteins, gelsolin-family severers, cofilin and its slingshot phosphatases, and thymosin promote disassembly. On the microtubule side, stathmins sequester tubulin, plus-end tracking proteins and CLASPs regulate growth, CAMSAPs stabilize minus ends, and the augmin complex nucleates branches within spindles. Spectrins, adducins and tropomodulins cap and cross-link the resulting networks. Loss of such control disrupts cytokinesis, immune cell migration, neuronal process outgrowth and hereditary spherocytic anemias.

Cytoskeletal filaments must be stopped as well as started, and this is the braking side of that balance: the negative regulation of protein polymerization, principally capping, severing and sequestration of actin and microtubule ends. It sets how long filaments grow, keeps monomer pools available for new assembly, and thereby determines cell shape, motility, membrane mechanics and the stability of specialised structures such as the erythrocyte membrane skeleton and sarcomeric thin filaments. Capping protein subunits and tropomodulins block barbed and pointed ends; gelsolin, scinderin, cofilin and twinfilins sever or depolymerize filaments, with slingshot phosphatases dephosphorylating cofilin to license that activity; stathmins sequester tubulin dimers. Spectrins and adducins cross-link and cap short filaments into a two-dimensional lattice. Cells build and extend filamentous polymers on demand, and this pathway covers the signals and factors that push assembly forward rather than restrain it. Actin nucleation and elongation are promoted by profilins, the WAVE regulatory complex subunits, cortactin, VASP/EVL, and the Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 with their effector-binding partners, driving lamellipodia, filopodia, phagocytic cups, podosomes and cell migration. In parallel, microtubule growth is favoured by plus-end tracking and stabilising proteins such as CLASP1, CLIP1, MAPRE1, CKAP5, SLAIN1/2, TPPP family members and the neuronal MAPT and MAP1B, with centrosomal and spindle scaffolds including CDK5RAP2, AKAP9 and NUMA1 organising where polymers form. The same machinery supports mitotic spindle assembly, neurite outgrowth, immune cell motility and podocyte and epithelial junction architecture, so its misregulation contributes to defective wound healing, neurodegeneration and tumour invasion.

Gonadotropin secretion is the controlled release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone from pituitary gonadotropes, the step that links the brain to the gonads and sets the timing of puberty, ovulation, spermatogenesis and fertility. Loss of this control produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed puberty or anovulatory infertility. Upstream, kisspeptin acting with neurokinin B and its receptor and with dynorphin signalling through the kappa opioid receptor generates pulsatile GnRH output, while RFRP/NPVF restrains it and leptin reports metabolic sufficiency; the pituitary responds through the GnRH receptor. Feedback comes from gonadal inhibins and activins, which oppose each other on FSH synthesis via SMAD-dependent transcription, alongside the shared glycoprotein alpha subunit and gonadotrope transcription factors such as FOXL2. Gap junction coupling and stress-related corticotropin-releasing hormone further tune secretory output, placing this pathway at the centre of neuroendocrine reproductive regulation.

Gonadotropin secretion is the regulated release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone from pituitary gonadotropes, the step that drives ovarian follicle maturation, ovulation, spermatogenesis and gonadal steroid output; its failure produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, delayed or absent puberty and infertility. Hypothalamic input dominates the control: kisspeptin and neurokinin B acting through their receptors, together with opioid and RFamide-related signals, shape pulsatile GnRH release, which the gonadotrope reads through its GnRH receptor. Feedback from the gonads arrives as activin and inhibin subunits signalling through SMAD-dependent transcription, selectively tuning FSH beta relative to the shared glycoprotein alpha subunit. Metabolic and stress cues enter through leptin and corticotropin-releasing hormone, linking reproductive competence to energy stores. Transcription factors including FOXL2 and TBX3 establish and maintain the gonadotrope and hypothalamic cell identities on which this endocrine axis depends.

Luteinizing hormone secretion is the pulsatile release of the gonadotropin from anterior pituitary gonadotropes, the signal that triggers ovulation in women and drives testosterone production by Leydig cells in men. Its control links reproductive capacity to nutritional and stress status: kisspeptin and neurokinin B signalling through its receptor set the frequency of hypothalamic GnRH pulses that reach the pituitary, leptin reports energy stores, opioid and corticotropin-releasing hormone inputs suppress the axis, and activin/TGF-beta signals acting through SMAD4 tune gonadotropin subunit gene expression together with the transcription factor FOXL2. The shared glycoprotein alpha subunit encoded by CGA is part of the mature hormone itself. Loss of components of this circuit produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, absent puberty and infertility, while dysregulated pulse frequency contributes to polycystic ovary syndrome and to amenorrhoea during undernutrition or chronic stress.

Reproduction depends on pituitary gonadotrophs releasing LH and FSH in pulses of the right frequency and amplitude, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune that release. Hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons, acting with neurokinin B through its receptor TACR3, drive pulsatile GnRH output, while RFamide-related peptide and opioid signalling through the kappa receptor restrain it; loss-of-function in the kisspeptin-neurokinin arm causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and failure of puberty. Gonadal feedback arrives as inhibins and activins, which act on gonadotrophs through SMAD4-dependent transcription to suppress or stimulate FSH selectively, with FOXL2 required for that response in the pituitary and the ovary. Metabolic and stress status are integrated too: leptin reports adequate energy stores as a permissive signal, and corticotropin-releasing hormone suppresses the axis during stress. The result links nutrition, stress and gonadal state to fertility.

Reproductive output depends on how much luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone the anterior pituitary releases, and this pathway covers the brakes on that release. Restraining gonadotropin secretion sets the timing of puberty, spaces the ovarian cycle, and suppresses fertility during stress, lactation and energy deficit; loss of such restraint underlies precocious activation of the reproductive axis, while excessive inhibition produces hypogonadotropic infertility. Several distinct signals converge on the gonadotrope and on the hypothalamic neurons that drive it: gonadal inhibins, assembled from an alpha subunit with a beta partner, feed back to selectively damp FSH; the RFamide peptide precursor NPVF gives rise to gonadotropin-inhibitory hormone acting on GnRH neurons; corticotropin-releasing hormone links stress responses to reproductive suppression; and opioid and tachykinin receptor signalling contributes further inhibitory tone, with gap junction coupling shaping pituitary cell communication.

Pituitary release of luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone paces puberty, ovulation and spermatogenesis, and the processes that raise that release are what open the reproductive axis. Kisspeptin acting through hypothalamic neurons is the central trigger, with neurokinin B signalling through its receptor TACR3 sustaining the pulsatile firing that drives gonadotropin-releasing hormone output; loss of either causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and absent puberty. Leptin ties the same circuit to energy stores, which is why gonadotropin secretion fails in starvation and low body fat. At the pituitary itself, activin subunits signal through SMAD4-dependent transcription to promote follicle-stimulating hormone synthesis, opposed by inhibin, while FOXL2 is required for gonadotrope and granulosa cell gene expression. The pathway therefore links nutritional status, gonadal feedback and hypothalamic pulse generation to fertility.

Myelin in the brain and spinal cord is not built once and left alone; it must be continuously renewed to keep axons insulated, conduction fast, and the underlying fibres metabolically supported. Maintenance of mature central nervous system myelin covers the lipid supply, membrane turnover and transcriptional upkeep that oligodendrocytes perform long after wrapping is complete, and its failure produces late-onset demyelination, axonal degeneration and leukodystrophy-like disease rather than a defect of initial development. The genes here reflect that division of labour: a fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies hydroxylated sphingolipids characteristic of the myelin membrane, a myelin-specific transcription factor sustains expression of the structural myelin programme in differentiated oligodendrocytes, and a lipid phosphatase restraining PI3K–AKT–mTOR signalling sets sheath thickness. Clusterin adds a secreted chaperone and lipid-handling component to the extracellular environment surrounding these sheaths.

Myelin in peripheral nerves must be actively maintained long after it is first wrapped, and this upkeep of mature Schwann cell myelin keeps internodes intact, compacted and able to support fast saltatory conduction. When it fails, the result is demyelinating neuropathy with slowed conduction, distal weakness and sensory loss, the clinical picture of several inherited Charcot-Marie-Tooth and related forms. The genes involved act largely in the Schwann cell rather than the axon: periaxin anchors the abaxonal membrane to the basal lamina through its dystroglycan complex, SH3TC2 and NDRG1 handle membrane trafficking and turnover in the myelinating cell, plectin provides cytoskeletal linkage, and fatty acid 2-hydroxylase supplies hydroxylated sphingolipids that stabilise the lipid-rich sheath. Akt signalling sustains the trophic and metabolic state needed for continual renewal, linking myelin maintenance to growth factor input and to axonal survival.

Myelin assembly is the wrapping of oligodendrocyte or Schwann cell membrane into compact spiral sheaths around axons, the step that gives vertebrate nerves saltatory conduction and high-speed signalling with low energetic cost. Failure produces dysmyelinating and demyelinating neuropathy: duplication or mutation of PMP22 and loss of MTMR2 or FIG4 underlie inherited Charcot-Marie-Tooth forms, while myelin basic protein is required for compaction of the cytoplasmic face. The genes here span the layers of the process — axo-glial recognition and paranodal junction formation by contactin with CNTNAP1 and the adhesion molecule MAG, lipid supply through galactosylceramide synthesis by UGT8 and ether-lipid production by GNPAT, tetraspanin and proteolipid components of the sheath, phosphoinositide turnover controlling membrane trafficking, and polarity and cytoskeletal regulators that orient wrapping. It connects glial differentiation to axonal support and long-term neuronal survival.

central nervous system myelin formation is the wrapping of oligodendrocyte plasma membrane into compacted multilamellar sheaths around CNS axons, the step that makes fast saltatory conduction and metabolic support of long axons possible. Where it fails or is undone, conduction slows and axons degenerate, as in multiple sclerosis and hypomyelinating leukodystrophies. The genes point to the axon-glia interface and to lipid handling: MAG in the periaxonal membrane and CNTN1 mediate recognition and adhesion between the sheath and the axon it ensheathes, TENM4 controls oligodendrocyte differentiation and small-diameter axon myelination, and ABCA2 supports the sphingolipid and cholesterol traffic that a membrane of this size demands. The process therefore couples cell-surface signalling from the axon to a program of lipid synthesis, membrane growth and compaction during postnatal white matter development and remyelination.

Oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord extend processes that spiral around axons and compact their membrane into myelin, the insulating sheath that permits fast saltatory conduction and supports long-term axonal integrity. Central nervous system myelin formation sets conduction velocity in white matter tracts, and its failure or breakdown underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease such as multiple sclerosis. The genes here act at several stages: recognition and adhesion between the glial membrane and the axon surface through myelin-associated glycoprotein and contactin, lipid handling and intracellular trafficking needed to build a membrane of unusual composition, and regulators that control oligodendrocyte differentiation and process outgrowth. The pathway therefore links glial cell fate and membrane biogenesis to axon-glia communication, and connects to broader programmes of neural development and white matter maintenance.

Axon ensheathment in central nervous system is the wrapping of CNS axons by oligodendrocyte membrane, the step that produces myelin and with it the fast saltatory conduction and metabolic support that central axons depend on. Loss of this process underlies leukodystrophies and demyelinating disease, and mutations in the major myelin proteins cause spastic paraplegia and Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease. The genes span the whole sequence: SOX10, MYRF, NKX6-2 and the HES5/ID4 pair specify and time oligodendrocyte differentiation; PLP1 and MAG build and compact the sheath; FA2H, B4GALT5/6 and ABCA2 supply the galactosphingolipids and cholesterol traffic that give myelin its lipid character; and CNTN1, CNTN2 and CNTNAP1 organise the paranodal junction and node so that channels such as KCNJ10 are positioned correctly. PTEN restrains the growth signalling that sets sheath thickness, linking ensheathment to axon-glia size matching.

Oligodendrocytes wrap central axons in layers of membrane, and this ensheathment programme covers both myelinating and non-myelinating glial contact with the axon in the brain and spinal cord. The resulting sheath permits saltatory conduction, supplies metabolic support to the axon, and its loss underlies demyelinating disease and leukodystrophy. Lineage transcription factors including SOX10, MYRF, NKX6-2 and the Notch effector HES5, opposed by ID4, drive oligodendrocyte specification and the switch to sheath formation. Structural output includes the major membrane proteins PLP1 and MAG, glycosphingolipid and hydroxylated fatty acid synthesis through B4GALT5/6 and FA2H, and axoglial junction components such as CNTN1, CNTN2 and CNTNAP1 that organise paranodes. PTEN restrains the PI3K signalling that sets sheath thickness, while KCNJ10 handles potassium buffering at the glial interface.

Peripheral nerves conduct impulses rapidly because Schwann cells wrap their membranes around axons, either spiralling into compact myelin or cradling small-calibre axons in Remak bundles. This ensheathment sets conduction velocity, supports axonal metabolism and long-term survival, and its disruption produces the demyelinating and axonal neuropathies typified by Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Axon-derived and matrix cues drive the programme: the adhesion GPCR ADGRG6 and neuregulin-responsive kinase signalling through AKT license myelination, laminin receptors such as dystroglycan and integrin-linked kinase couple the basal lamina to the Schwann cell cytoskeleton, and transcriptional regulators including POU3F1 time the switch to a myelinating state. Polarity proteins PARD3 and PALS1 orient the wrapping membrane, while periaxin, SH3TC2 and NDRG1 maintain the myelin sheath, its incisures and paranodal junctions once formed. Lipid modification by FA2H supplies galactolipids for stable compaction.

Eicosanoids — prostaglandins, leukotrienes and related oxygenated fatty acid mediators — act close to where they are made, so the point at which a cell is licensed to release them sets the intensity of inflammation, fever, pain sensitisation, vascular tone and renal salt handling. Control of eicosanoid secretion operates mostly at substrate supply: secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2, including the calcium-dependent PLA2G4A, liberate arachidonate from membrane phospholipids, ACSL4 recycles it back into lipids, and downstream prostaglandin E synthase and CYP4A/CYP4F hydroxylases determine which mediator leaves the cell. Upstream cues are diverse: cytokines such as IL1B and MIF, endothelin, neuropeptide and vasopressin receptors, RANKL–RANK signalling in bone, ATP acting on P2X4 and P2X7 channels, and SYK-dependent immune receptor signalling. Excessive output drives chronic inflammatory and pain states and underlies the therapeutic interest in blocking these steps.

Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators made on demand rather than stored, so their output is set by how fast arachidonic acid is liberated and converted, and by the signals that license release. Control of prostaglandin secretion shapes inflammation and pain, vascular tone, uterine contraction at labour, and bone remodelling, and its excess is the target of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Cytosolic and secreted phospholipases A2 cleave arachidonate from membrane phospholipids, an acyl-CoA synthetase feeds the competing re-esterification route, and prostaglandin E synthase completes synthesis of PGE2. Upstream, inflammatory cytokines such as IL1B, endothelin, oxytocin, the RANKL-RANK pair, and extracellular ATP acting through P2X4 and P2X7 purinergic channels raise or restrain output. The result couples immune, hormonal and nucleotide danger signals to local lipid signalling in fever, tissue injury and osteoclast biology.

Eicosanoids are C20 fatty acid mediators — prostaglandins, leukotrienes, thromboxanes and related oxygenated lipids — and this pathway covers their controlled release from cells into the surrounding tissue, where they act locally on inflammation, pain, fever, vascular tone and bone remodelling. Because eicosanoids are not stored, secretion is governed by substrate liberation: a large family of secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2, together with PNPLA8 and the arachidonate-preferring ligase ACSL4, frees arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids for conversion by cyclooxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E synthase, with ABCC4 exporting the finished prostanoid. Upstream triggers are diverse — interleukin-1β, bradykinin and purinergic P2X7 signalling, RANK/RANKL, and neuroendocrine and dopaminergic receptors — while annexin A1 restrains the phospholipase step and underlies glucocorticoid suppression of this output. Excessive release drives inflammatory pain and arthritis; blocking it is the mechanism of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Prostaglandins are lipid mediators that act locally on neighbouring cells, and prostaglandin secretion covers the regulated steps by which a cell makes and exports them into the extracellular space. This output drives inflammatory pain, fever, vasodilation, uterine contraction and bone remodelling, and it is the process blocked by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Secretory and cytosolic phospholipases liberate arachidonate from membrane phospholipids, cyclooxygenase-2 and prostaglandin E synthase convert it to PGE2, and the ABCC4 transporter carries the finished prostaglandin across the plasma membrane. Upstream, inflammatory and hormonal cues — interleukin-1β, MIF, endothelin-1, leptin, oxytocin and RANKL signalling through its receptor — induce the synthetic enzymes, while ATP-gated P2X4 and P2X7 channels couple extracellular nucleotide sensing to release. The same axis links macrophage activation and nitric oxide production to inflammatory lipid output, and its excess sustains chronic inflammation and osteoclast-driven bone loss.

Alanine transport moves this small neutral amino acid across membranes, and because alanine is the main carrier of nitrogen and carbon from muscle to liver for gluconeogenesis, the carriers that handle it sit at the junction of amino acid nutrition and whole-body fuel metabolism. The genes here are plasma membrane and organellar solute carriers with overlapping specificity for alanine, serine, glutamine and other small neutral amino acids: sodium-coupled system A and N carriers of the SLC38 family, proton-driven amino acid transporters of the SLC36 family that also serve lysosomal efflux, ASCT1 (SLC1A4), and heteromeric exchangers built on the SLC3A2 heavy chain with light chains such as SLC7A5, SLC7A8 and SLC7A10. SFXN1 contributes mitochondrial serine and alanine import. Collectively they support epithelial absorption, neurotransmitter precursor supply, hepatic nitrogen handling and the amino acid influx that sustains mTORC1 signalling and cell growth.

Serine transport moves L-serine across cell and organelle membranes, linking where the amino acid is made to where it is consumed. This matters because serine feeds one-carbon metabolism, glutathione and phospholipid synthesis, and sphingolipid production, and because in the brain serine shuttled between astrocytes and neurons supplies D-serine, the co-agonist required for NMDA receptor activation. The sideroflexins are mitochondrial inner-membrane carriers that import serine into the matrix, where it is cleaved to feed folate-dependent one-carbon units; loss of SFXN1 starves this route and forces cells onto glycine and formate. At the plasma membrane, ASCT1 and ASCT2 exchange small neutral amino acids including serine, threonine and alanine, SNAT-family carriers couple uptake to sodium gradients, and asc-1 mediates D-serine flux at synapses. Defects in these carriers disturb amino acid homeostasis, neuronal development and glutamatergic signalling, and tumour cells often upregulate them to sustain biosynthesis.

Cartilage forms when mesenchymal progenitors commit to the chondrocyte fate, and the pace at which they do so — and whether they stop at resting cartilage or proceed to hypertrophy and ossification — is what this regulatory programme controls. It sets limb and skeletal proportion through the growth plate, so its disturbance produces chondrodysplasias, short stature, joint malformation and, in adults, osteoarthritic cartilage loss. Control converges on the SOX9–SOX5–SOX6 trio that drives the cartilage matrix gene programme, opposed by RUNX2 in the switch toward hypertrophic differentiation. Bone morphogenetic proteins and their receptors, growth differentiation factors such as GDF5, TGF-beta/SMAD signalling with SMAD7 as a brake, WNT/beta-catenin with AXIN2 feedback, FGF18, and the PTHLH–PTH receptor loop that keeps proliferating chondrocytes from maturing prematurely all feed in. Secreted modulators including GREM1, LTBP3 and ADAMTS proteases tune these signals in the matrix.

Cartilage forms only where and when it is permitted, and restraint of chondrocyte differentiation is what keeps mesenchymal cells from committing to cartilage prematurely or in the wrong place. This braking function shapes the growth plate: parathyroid hormone-related peptide signalling holds proliferating chondrocytes back from hypertrophy, while BMP antagonism by gremlin and latent TGF-beta binding proteins limits how much inductive signal reaches the cell. Wnt/beta-catenin input, retinoic acid receptors, the phosphatase SHP2, and transcriptional repressors such as SNAI2 and NKX3-2 tune the same decision, alongside secreted proteoglycan and ADAMTS-family matrix regulators that modify the pericellular environment. Loss of this restraint produces skeletal dysplasias, abnormal endochondral bone length and joint patterning defects, and inappropriate cartilage formation in soft tissue; the same controls are relevant to osteoarthritic chondrocyte behaviour.

positive regulation of chondrocyte differentiation covers the signals and transcription factors that push mesenchymal progenitors to become cartilage-producing chondrocytes, the cell type that builds the fetal skeleton, the growth plate, and articular surfaces. Because most long bones form by endochondral ossification, this control determines limb and joint shape and adult stature; its failure produces chondrodysplasias, joint fusion, and degenerative cartilage loss. BMP and GDF ligands acting through BMPR1B and SMAD3, together with FGF18, converge on the SOX9-SOX5-SOX6 trio that switches on collagen II and aggrecan expression, while GLI3, HOX factors, and RUNX2 position chondrogenesis in space and set when cells progress to hypertrophy. Additional modifiers, including a cGMP-dependent kinase and matrix cross-linking and modifying enzymes, tune proliferation and matrix maturation, linking this program to skeletal patterning, growth plate output, and cartilage repair.

Cartilage forms when mesenchymal progenitors condense and commit to the chondrocyte fate, and the signals gathered here push that commitment forward. Because nearly every long bone is first laid down as a cartilage template, positively regulating chondrocyte differentiation sets limb and joint proportions, growth plate output, and ultimately adult stature; its disruption produces chondrodysplasias, brachydactyly and joint malformation, and its reactivation is a feature of osteoarthritic cartilage. BMP-family ligands and receptors such as BMP6, GDF5, GDF6 and BMPR1B, together with FGF18, feed into SMAD-dependent transcription, where SMAD3 promotes and SMAD7 restrains the response. The output converges on SOX9 with its partners SOX5 and SOX6, the master activators of collagen and aggrecan expression, while RUNX2 and GLI3 tilt cells toward hypertrophy and the transition to bone. Matrix-modifying and kinase components, including LOXL2 and PRKG2, tune growth plate maturation.
