Aldosterone from the adrenal zona glomerulosa sets sodium retention, potassium excretion and blood pressure, so processes that modulate how much of it is synthesised and turned over have direct cardiovascular consequences; excessive output underlies primary aldosteronism with hypertension and hypokalaemia. The genes here point to two sources of that control. Secreted BMP ligands and Wnt pathway components, including WNT4 and the Wnt modulator DKK3, act as paracrine signals that specify and maintain the glomerulosa steroidogenic phenotype and tune aldosterone synthase expression. The chloride channel CLCN2 shapes glomerulosa membrane potential and calcium entry, the proximate trigger for steroidogenesis, and its gain-of-function mutations cause early-onset aldosteronism. The transcriptional repressor REST and the endocytic adaptor DAB2 add nuclear and receptor-trafficking layers, placing this regulation at the intersection of developmental signalling, electrical excitability and mineralocorticoid endocrinology.

Hormone levels are set as much by how fast hormones are made, activated and cleared as by how much is secreted, and this pathway covers the controls placed on those reactions. It matters because it keeps circulating thyroid hormone, steroids and peptide hormones within the narrow ranges that growth, metabolic rate and reproduction depend on; loss of control produces congenital hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency or disordered steroid output. Several distinct arms appear together: thyroid follicular machinery generating the hydrogen peroxide needed for thyroperoxidase-mediated iodination, with a transporter delivering thyroid hormone across the blood-brain barrier; gonadotropin and corticotropin receptors with their precursor POMC driving gonadal and adrenal steroidogenesis; and the electron donor POR plus reductases and dehydrogenases that tune local steroid activation. Transcription factors including PAX8, GATA3, NR5A2 and HIF1A set the capacity of the tissues doing this work.

Hormone output is set not only by how fast hormones are made but by brakes on their synthesis and turnover, and this pathway collects the signals that damp hormone metabolism. Such restraint keeps steroid and thyroid hormone levels within range; its loss contributes to hyperandrogenism, adrenal and gonadal steroid excess, and thyroid dysfunction. The genes span several layers: secreted morphogens of the BMP and WNT families, together with the WNT antagonist DKK3, act on gonadal and adrenal steroidogenic cells to suppress steroidogenic gene expression; a cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase lowers cAMP and so dampens the second messenger that drives steroid hormone production downstream of trophic receptors; and a transcriptional repressor plus an arginine methyltransferase adjust the chromatin and transcriptional output of hormone-metabolising enzymes. The result is negative control over endocrine tissue responsiveness rather than hormone action at target cells.

Hormone output is set not only by how much of a signal a gland receives but by how fast the hormone itself is made, activated or cleared, and this pathway covers the inputs that push those reactions upward. Raising steroid, thyroid or peptide hormone metabolism drives adrenal cortisol production, thyroid hormone availability to tissues, and retinoid signalling during development. Concrete examples run through the list: POMC provides the ACTH precursor, MC2R receives that signal on adrenocortical cells, POR supplies electrons to the steroidogenic cytochrome P450 enzymes, RDH10 makes retinaldehyde for retinoic acid synthesis, and SLCO1C1 transports thyroxine across the blood-brain barrier. Transcriptional regulators including NR5A2, PAX8, GATA3 and the hypoxia-responsive HIF1A/ARNT pair specify and sustain endocrine tissue identity. Loss of such stimulation produces adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroid states and impaired developmental patterning.

Hormone output is set not only by how much synthetic capacity a gland has but by brakes that hold it down, and this pathway covers the signals that stop or slow hormone biosynthesis. Such restraint keeps steroid and peptide hormone levels within range, prevents autonomous overproduction, and allows endocrine tissue to respond to feedback rather than secrete continuously. The genes point to secreted morphogen systems acting on endocrine tissue: bone morphogenetic proteins and a WNT ligand, together with a WNT antagonist of the dickkopf family, modulate adrenal and gonadal steroidogenic differentiation and output. Cyclic nucleotide control also appears, as a phosphodiesterase limits cAMP downstream of trophic hormone receptors, so that loss of it de-represses steroid synthesis; a transcriptional repressor and an ion-transporting ATPase subunit add further negative input. Disruption of these brakes underlies endocrine hyperfunction and adrenal nodular disease.

Follicle-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary drives ovarian follicle growth and Sertoli cell support of spermatogenesis, and this pathway covers the cellular changes that follow once the hormone is sensed i granulosa, Sertoli and neighbouring cells. Detection begins at the G protein-coupled receptor FSHR, whose loss causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and anovulatory infertility, and whose signalling raises cAMP to reprogramme steroidogenic and growth-factor gene expression. Downstream responses represented here include endothelin signalling through EDN1 and EDNRA, activin/TGF-beta family communication via INHBA and the co-receptor TGFBR3 that tunes follicular maturation and feedback on pituitary FSH output, Notch-dependent cell fate decisions, and androgen metabolism by the steroid 5-alpha-reductases and the electron donor POR. Glutathione synthesis enzymes GCLC and GCLM point to accompanying redox demands. The programme links endocrine input to gonadal cell proliferation, differentiation and fertility.

Estradiol is the principal circulating estrogen, and this collection describes the cellular and organismal responses it triggers — changes in gene expression, proliferation, secretion, apoptosis and neuroendocrine output. These responses build the female reproductive tract and mammary gland, regulate the hypothalamic–pituitary axis and bone turnover, and when they run unchecked drive hormone-dependent breast and uterine cancers, which is why blocking them is the basis of endocrine therapy. Signalling begins with the nuclear receptors ESR1 and ESR2, which recruit coactivators such as NCOA1 and NCOA3 or the corepressors NCOR2 and NRIP1, together with pioneer factor FOXA1 that sets which enhancers are accessible; a membrane receptor, GPER1, adds rapid kinase-mediated responses. Downstream effects include cyclin D1-driven cell cycle entry, growth factor crosstalk through EGFR and AREG, modulated caspase-dependent apoptosis, oxidative stress defence, and altered neuropeptide and monoamine systems. CYP19A1 supplies the hormone itself by aromatization.

Cells must sense how much oxygen they have and adjust their metabolism and gene expression to match it, and this oxygen homeostasis programme is what keeps that internal level steady. It matters for erythropoiesis, vascular growth and the switch between oxidative and glycolytic ATP production; when it is deranged, tissues respond to normoxia as though hypoxic, a state central to tumour adaptation, pulmonary hypertension and inherited erythrocytosis. The hypoxia-inducible transcription factors HIF1A and EPAS1 drive the adaptive response, with HIF3A acting as a modulating family member, while the prolyl hydroxylase EGLN1 marks these subunits for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, making oxygen itself the substrate of the sensing reaction. Mitochondrial superoxide dismutase SOD2 limits the reactive oxygen species that accompany respiration, and ALAS2 ties the pathway to heme synthesis in erythroid cells.

Lipids are made in one membrane and used in another, and intracellular lipid transport is how cells move cholesterol, sphingolipids, fatty acids and their derivatives between compartments rather than letting them diffuse. It sets the cholesterol content of the plasma membrane, feeds fatty acids into mitochondria for oxidation, delivers ceramide for sphingomyelin synthesis, and supplies substrate for steroid hormone production. Soluble and membrane-contact-site carriers such as OSBP, the GRAMD1 sterol transporters, CERT1, STARD4 and STAR ferry lipids between the ER, Golgi, endosomes and mitochondria, while NPC1 and NPC2 release cholesterol from the lysosome and ABC transporters including ABCA1 and ABCG1 efflux it to acceptors. Carnitine shuttle components move acyl groups across the mitochondrial inner membrane. Loss of these routes causes lysosomal cholesterol storage disease, adrenoleukodystrophy, Tangier disease and defects in fatty acid oxidation.

Cholesterol and related sterols are poorly soluble in water, so cells cannot let them diffuse freely; intracellular sterol transport is the set of carriers and membrane contact sites that move them between organelles and out to the plasma membrane. It determines how much cholesterol reaches the endoplasmic reticulum where sterol sensing and esterification occur, supplies mitochondria with the substrate for steroid hormone synthesis, and feeds excess sterol to efflux pumps for disposal into HDL. Lysosomal handoff by NPC1 and NPC2 releases cholesterol derived from internalised LDL, receptor uptake through LDLR with its adaptor and the secreted regulator PCSK9 sets how much enters, GRAMD1 and oxysterol-binding proteins ferry sterol across organelle junctions, and ABCA1 and ABCG1 export it. Failure produces lysosomal cholesterol storage disease, hypercholesterolaemia and impaired steroidogenesis, and connects this traffic to atherosclerosis and endocrine function.</description>

Lipid movement between compartments and between cells is actively restrained, and this braking arm of lipid transport sets how much cholesterol leaves a cell, how much lipoprotein-borne lipid is cleared, and how much fatty acid enters tissues. Its failure tips the balance toward foam cell formation, hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. Several mechanisms converge here: PCSK9 directs the LDL receptor to lysosomal degradation and so limits hepatic LDL uptake; apolipoprotein C family members inhibit lipoprotein lipase-mediated triglyceride hydrolysis and receptor-mediated remnant clearance; the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 and the sterol-responsive factor SREBF2 tune efflux transporter expression; and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the miR-33 pair and miR-758, post-transcriptionally suppress ABC transporters. Insulin-responsive kinases, the circadian repressors CRY1 and CRY2, and adipokine signalling link this restraint to feeding and daily metabolic rhythm.

Lipids must be moved across membranes and between cells, and this grouping collects the agents that turn that movement up — transporters, lipid acceptors and the signals that induce them. It underlies reverse cholesterol transport from macrophages to HDL, surfactant secretion in the lung, bile phospholipid output and skin barrier lipid delivery, so its failure produces Tangier disease, respiratory distress, cholestasis and foam-cell-laden atherosclerotic plaque. Much of the output is transcriptional: the oxysterol-activated nuclear receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 with their RXRA partner, and PPARG, raise expression of ABCA1 and ABCG1, whose efflux of cholesterol and phospholipid is captured by APOA1 and APOE. Other members act as floppases and scramblases, phospholipases liberating fatty acids, acyl-CoA synthetases and transfer proteins such as CETP and PLTP, while inflammatory and endocrine cues feed in to link lipid handling to immune and metabolic state.

Cells must move cholesterol and related sterols across membranes and between tissues rather than synthesise and store them locally, and this pathway covers the controls placed on that traffic. Its output determines how much cholesterol is effluxed to nascent HDL, how lipoproteins are remodelled in plasma, and how much LDL receptor survives at the hepatocyte surface, so its dysregulation drives atherosclerosis, xanthoma and lipid-storage disease. Sterol-sensing nuclear receptors and their partners, acting with the sterol-responsive transcription factor SREBF2, set transporter levels, while a large family of microRNAs led by MIR33A/B restrains efflux transporters and apolipoprotein handling post-transcriptionally. ABCA1 and ABCG1 carry out efflux itself, apolipoproteins and transfer proteins accept and redistribute the lipid, and PCSK9 lowers receptor-mediated uptake. Macrophage foam cell formation, biliary lipid secretion and surfactant lipid handling all depend on how tightly this regulation is tuned.

Cells must limit as well as promote the movement of cholesterol and other sterols, and this pathway collects the brakes on that traffic — the factors that reduce sterol efflux, uptake or intercellular transfer. It matters for the balance of reverse cholesterol transport: too much restraint leaves macrophages and vessel walls loaded with cholesterol, a step in atherosclerotic plaque formation, while apolipoprotein-mediated control shapes plasma lipoprotein levels. Several exchangeable apolipoproteins (APOC1, APOC2, APOC3, APOA2, alongside APOE) modulate lipoprotein remodelling and receptor-mediated sterol delivery, and PCSK9 lowers hepatic LDL receptor abundance by directing it to degradation, curbing LDL cholesterol uptake. A large complement of microRNAs, notably the SREBP-embedded miR-33 family, post-transcriptionally represses efflux transporters and other lipid-handling genes, tying sterol transport restraint to the transcriptional network that senses cellular cholesterol.</description>}, {

Cells must be able to unload excess cholesterol, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate of sterol movement out of cells and between lipoproteins. It is the engine of reverse cholesterol transport: macrophages and hepatocytes efflux free cholesterol and phospholipid onto lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I and mature HDL through ABCA1 and ABCG1, with APOE, PLTP and CETP shaping the acceptor particles and their return to the liver. Oxysterol-activated liver X receptors partnering RXRA, together with PPARG and SIRT1, drive transcription of the transporters, so that sterol excess itself licenses its own removal. Caveolin-1, LRP1 and TREM2 contribute at the membrane and in lipid-laden myeloid cells. When efflux capacity falls, cholesterol accumulates in arterial macrophages as foam cells; loss of ABCA1 causes Tangier disease with near-absent HDL and premature atherosclerosis.

Lipids made or taken up by a cell must be delivered to the membranes and organelles that need them, and this pathway covers the control of that internal traffic rather than the transport steps themselves. Its outputs matter for cholesterol balance, for the lipid lamellae that make the skin an effective water barrier, and for how much low-density lipoprotein receptor a cell keeps at its surface. The members act at several levels: lipid-translocating ABC transporters, a sterol carrier that moves substrates toward peroxisomal beta-oxidation, adaptors and chaperones such as LDLRAP1 and the sigma-2 receptor TMEM97, the secreted protease PCSK9 that lowers LDL receptor availability, and microRNAs that tune the whole programme post-transcriptionally. Loss of regulation here underlies hypercholesterolaemia and, for ABCA12, the severe barrier defect of harlequin ichthyosis, tying intracellular lipid distribution to both plasma lipid levels and epidermal function.

Cells must move cholesterol and other lipids between membranes and organelles at a controlled pace, and this pathway covers the brakes on that traffic — processes that damp or block intracellular lipid movement. Restraining these routes helps set how much free cholesterol reaches the endoplasmic reticulum and therefore how strongly the sterol-sensing machinery calls for new synthesis or uptake, linking the biology to lipoprotein handling and atherosclerosis risk. The members act at different levels: a lysosomal ABC transporter of the A subfamily influences sterol and sphingolipid distribution in neurons and other cells, PCSK9 lowers cellular uptake capacity by directing the LDL receptor to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, and several microRNAs tune transporter and receptor transcripts post-transcriptionally. Together they illustrate negative control over lipid distribution as a counterweight to sterol acquisition, with PCSK9 a validated target of cholesterol-lowering therapy.

Cells constantly move cargo between compartments, and this pathway covers the control layer on that traffic — how fast, how far, and in which direction vesicles, organelles, proteins and RNAs travel inside a cell. It matters because polarity, secretion, receptor turnover and neuronal cargo delivery all depend on transport being tuned rather than merely possible; loss of that tuning underlies lysosomal and neurodegenerative disease, as mutations in LRRK2, VPS35 and ATP13A2 illustrate. Represented here are the cytoplasmic dynein motor and its light and intermediate chains moving cargo toward the minus end of microtubules, COPII coat components with SAR1 GTPases budding cargo from the ER, RAB11-dependent recycling endosomes and retromer-mediated retrograde sorting, nucleocytoplasmic shuttling through nucleoporins with RAN and exportins, and ER-associated degradation and glycoprotein quality-control factors. Kinases, phosphatases, ubiquitin ligases and small-GTPase regulators impose the regulation itself.

negative regulation of intracellular transport collects the braking mechanisms that limit how fast and how far cargo, ions and signalling proteins move inside a cell, keeping traffic proportionate to demand rather than continuous. Such restraint matters because unchecked movement of transcription factors into the nucleus, of receptors to the plasma membrane, or of calcium across the sarcoplasmic reticulum would decouple signalling from stimulus; loss of these controls contributes to neurodegeneration and dysregulated cholesterol handling. Several distinct arms appear: nucleocytoplasmic gatekeeping through nucleoporins and the Ran system with SUMO1 and RANGAP1; retention of NF- tkB by its inhibitor; sequestration of substrates by 14-3-3 proteins; ER-associated degradation components that divert misfolded proteins from export; sarcolipin, myoregulin and phospholamban inhibiting SERCA-mediated calcium uptake; and INSIG1 and PCSK9 curbing sterol sensor and receptor trafficking. Retromer and sorting nexins, LRRK2 and CDK5 tune endosomal and cytoskeletal transport.

Cells move cargo constantly — proteins into and out of the nucleus, calcium into stores, lipids and receptors along the endosomal route — and this grouping covers the braking side of that traffic, the processes that dampen or block directed intracellular movement. Restraint of this kind sets how much signal reaches a destination: sequestering a transcription factor in the cytoplasm, limiting calcium re-uptake, or diverting a misfolded protein away from export. The genes reflect several such brakes. Sarcolipin and myoregulin inhibit the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, controlling muscle relaxation; NFKBIA holds NF-κB out of the nucleus; RANGAP1, NUP153 and TPR govern the nucleocytoplasmic gradient; and OS9, ERLEC1, DERL2/3 with UBE2J1 retain glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum for degradation rather than forward transport. VPS35, SNX3 and LRRK2 tune endosomal sorting, a route whose failure is tied to parkinsonism.

Cells constantly move cargo along their interior — vesicles from ER to Golgi, endosomes and lysosomes along microtubules, mRNA and proteins in and out of the nucleus — and this pathway collects the regulators that raise the rate or extent of that traffic. Upregulated transport supports secretion, receptor turnover, organelle positioning, neuronal cargo delivery and signalling responses, and its loss leaves cargo stranded, with consequences ranging from ciliopathy to neurodegeneration. The membership spans the cytoplasmic dynein motor and its light, intermediate and light-intermediate chains for minus-end-directed movement; COPII coat components including the SAR1 GTPases, SEC24 paralogues and SEC13/SEC31 cage for ER export; nucleocytoplasmic carriers such as RAN, importin and exportin family members and the nucleoporin-associated TPR; plus kinases, adaptors and scaffolds (PRKACA, GSK3B, MAPK14, YWHAE, BAG3) that tune motor recruitment and cargo loading.

DNA does not simply sit as an inert duplex: bending, twisting and local unwinding of the double helix are actively imposed on it so that replication, repair, transcription and packaging machinery can reach the bases. This geometric remodelling changes twist and writhe without altering linking number, and it is the step that opens a duplex ahead of polymerases or exposes a lesion for excision. Two arms are represented here. The RecQ-family helicases BLM and WRN, working with the DNA2 nuclease-helicase, unwind and process duplex and branched structures during replication restart, end resection and telomere maintenance; loss of either helicase causes the genome-instability and cancer-predisposition syndromes Bloom and Werner. The HMGB proteins instead bend and distort DNA on binding, acting as architectural factors that bias nucleosome and repair-complex assembly. A mitochondrial transcription terminator extends the same principle to the mitochondrial genome.</br>

Transporters and channels are switched off as deliberately as they are switched on, and this pathway covers the proteins that stop or damp their activity. Its outputs set the duration of electrical signals and the size of ion gradients: calmodulin isoforms mediate calcium-dependent inactivation of voltage-gated calcium channels, phospholamban and sarcolipin restrain the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump SERCA and thereby govern cardiac and skeletal muscle relaxation, and the small KCNE subunits modulate KCNQ1 and related potassium channels so that repolarisation occurs on the right timescale. Scaffolding and trafficking proteins such as ankyrin-G and GOPC act indirectly, by controlling where channels sit or by diverting them from the surface. Loss of this braking produces excess calcium loading, arrhythmia such as long QT syndrome, and disordered excitability, making negative regulation of transporter activity a core part of ion homeostasis and membrane excitability control.

Transporters and channels are rarely left at a fixed activity; this pathway covers the accessory proteins and signals that turn them up, increasing ion or solute flux through an existing carrier or pore. It matters wherever flux must be matched to demand: calcium entry after store depletion, excitation-contraction coupling in muscle, salt handling in the kidney, and the gating of potassium and sodium currents in excitable cells. STIM1 and STIM2 sense endoplasmic reticulum calcium loss and activate plasma membrane Orai channels, with CRACR2A and STIMATE shaping that coupling; STAC3 is required for functional coupling of the skeletal muscle dihydropyridine receptor, and its loss causes congenital myopathy. LRRC26 and related leucine-rich subunits modify large-conductance potassium channel gating, SCN1B and CACNB3 act as sodium and calcium channel subunits, and WNK kinases together with SGK1 raise transport activity in epithelia, linking this regulation to blood pressure control.

Whether a ubiquitinated protein is actually destroyed, and how fast, is a decision point that cells use to set the lifetime of regulators such as p53, cyclins, beta-catenin and NRF2. Modulating proteasomal ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolism therefore controls cell cycle transitions, stress responses and developmental signalling, and its derangement underlies tumour growth, neurodegeneration and protein aggregate disease. Control is exerted at several steps: E3 ligases and their adaptors (MDM2, the CHIP chaperone-ligase, SCF and cullin-RING components including RBX1, KEAP1, AXIN scaffolds, the anaphase-promoting complex activators CDC20 and FZR1) select substrates; deubiquitinases such as USP7, USP5 and UCHL5 reverse or edit the mark; kinases including GSK3B, CSNK1 and CSNK2 create phosphodegrons; and shuttle factors, ubiquilins, VCP and co-chaperones deliver or extract substrates at the proteasome. SUMO and UFM1 machinery plus sirtuin deacetylases add further layers, coupling degradation rates to metabolic and proteotoxic stress.

Ubiquitin-tagged proteins are normally destroyed by the proteasome, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that spare them, setting how long a substrate survives rather than whether it can be marked at all. Stabilising short-lived regulators such as p53, HIF and cell-cycle and chromatin factors depends on it, and loss of that restraint shifts protein levels in ways that matter for tumour suppression, neuronal survival and muscle protein balance. Deubiquitinases including USP7, USP5, USP9X and UCHL5 remove or trim chains before commitment to degradation; UBXN1 and BAG-family cochaperones intercept substrates at the ubiquitin-proteasome interface; and casein kinase 2 subunits, OGT and other modifying enzymes alter substrate recognition by E3 ligases. Ribosomal and nucleolar proteins such as RPL11 and NOP53 contribute by sequestering ligases, linking proteostasis to stress sensing and growth control.

Targeted destruction of proteins by the ubiquitin-proteasome system is how cells terminate signals, clear damaged polypeptides and enforce cell cycle transitions, and the genes here act to accelerate or enhance that turnover rather than to perform the proteolysis itself. They include substrate-recognition subunits and adaptors of cullin-RING and other E3 ligases, the anaphase-promoting complex activators CDC20 and FZR1 that license mitotic exit, kinases such as GSK3B and casein kinase 1 isoforms that phosphorylate substrates to create phosphodegrons, the scaffold proteins AXIN1 and AXIN2 that drive beta-catenin degradation, and chaperone-linked triage factors including STUB1, BAG2 and VCP that commit misfolded clients to the proteasome. MDM2-mediated control of p53 and KEAP1-mediated control of NRF2 illustrate how such positive regulation sets the abundance of tumour suppressors and stress-response transcription factors; loss of it underlies tumorigenesis and neurodegenerative protein accumulation.

Cells tag proteins with small protein modifiers to decide how long they last, where they go, and whom they bind. This machinery for protein modification by small protein conjugation covers ubiquitin and the ubiquitin-like modifiers SUMO, NEDD8, ISG15, UFM1 and ATG8, each attached through an activating enzyme, a conjugating enzyme and a ligase that chooses the substrate. Cullin-RING assemblies with their F-box, BTB/KLHL, DCAF, SOCS and ASB adaptors, HECT and RBR ligases such as NEDD4 and PRKN, TRIM and MARCH families, and the anaphase-promoting complex together funnel targets to the proteasome or to lysosomal degradation, while non-degradative chains recruit DNA repair factors and activate NF-kB signalling. Deubiquitinases and SUMO proteases reverse the marks. The same logic drives cell cycle transitions, hypoxic and oxidative stress responses, mitophagy and antigen presentation, and its failure underlies parkinsonism, Fanconi anaemia and many cancers.

Internalised receptors, transporters and adhesion molecules are not all destined for degradation; endocytic recycling returns them from endosomes to the cell surface, setting how many of each remain available for signalling, nutrient uptake and cell adhesion. This retrieval sustains processes as varied as glucose transporter delivery, synaptic receptor turnover, cytokinesis and epithelial polarity, and its loss diverts cargo to the lysosome, degrading the surface proteome. Cargo selection is carried out by sorting nexin-containing coats — retromer with VPS35, VPS29 and VPS26, and the related commander/retriever assembly built from COMMD proteins and CCDC22\/CCDC93 — working with the WASH complex to generate actin on endosomes. RAB11, RAB8, RAB35 and ARF6, their DENND activators and EHD tubulating ATPases then drive tubule formation and fusion at the plasma membrane. Mutations in these components cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease.

Many proteins only work once they assemble into dimers or larger complexes, and this pathway covers the control points that determine whether, how fast, and to what extent that assembly happens. Setting oligomerization thresholds matters because the same chemistry that builds functional complexes also produces pathological aggregates, as in the misfolded protein deposits that accumulate when clearance and chaperone routes fail. The genes here act through varied routes: acetylation and deacetylation of substrates by a transcriptional coactivator acetyltransferase and by a cytoplasmic deacetylase that also handles aggregate clearance via the aggresome; oxygenase-mediated modification; ubiquitin-like ISG15 conjugation and a tripartite-motif ubiquitin ligase; and retromer-dependent endosomal sorting through VPS35, which determines the fate of membrane cargo. Together they link post-translational modification, trafficking and protein quality control to the assembly state of client proteins.

The final step of cell division, in which the cytoplasm is partitioned and two daughter cells are physically separated, is tuned by the activities collected here. Getting it right determines ploidy: failed or mistimed cytoplasmic division produces binucleate, tetraploid cells and centrosome amplification, a route toward chromosomal instability and tumour formation, while in the germline incomplete division is used deliberately to keep spermatocytes connected. Control operates at several levels — the chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin positions the cleavage plane; RhoA activated by ECT2 and restrained by the centralspindlin GAP component drives contractile ring assembly; kinesins and PRC1 organise the central spindle; Rab11 vesicle traffic and ESCRT components with VPS4A execute abscission; and a checkpoint acting through CHMP4C delays scission when chromatin is trapped in the bridge. Cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases and phosphatases reset the machinery afterwards.

Cells must not complete cytoplasmic division until chromosomes are fully cleared from the cleavage plane and the intercellular bridge is ready to be severed, and negative regulation of cytokinesis supplies that restraint. Braking abscission prevents the daughter cells from being cut apart across lagging chromatin, which would otherwise generate DNA damage, aneuploidy and tetraploid or multinucleate progeny. The aurora kinase AURKB acts at the midbody as the sensor arm of an abscission checkpoint, signalling to CHMP4C so that ESCRT-III assembly and the VPS4A ATPase that drives membrane constriction are held off until the bridge is clear. Other members impose delay for developmental reasons: TEX14 blocks abscission in germ cells so that spermatogenic clones remain connected by stable intercellular bridges, while the atypical E2F repressors E2F7 and E2F8 promote polyploidy in hepatocytes and megakaryocytes by uncoupling division from genome duplication.

Cytokinesis divides one mitotic cell into two, and this grouping covers the activators that drive and accelerate that final step, ensuring each daughter receives a complete genome and a sealed plasma membrane; failure produces binucleate cells, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability that seeds tumours. The chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin — positions the cleavage plane and delays abscission until chromatin clears the midzone. Small GTPase control is central: ECT2 and RACGAP1 with the centralspindlin kinesin MKLF1/KIF23 activate RhoA locally to assemble the actomyosin contractile ring, citron kinase and supervillin reinforce it, while ARF6 and RAB11 with its FIP3 effector plus exocyst and ESCRT components deliver membrane to the intercellular bridge and spastin severs residual microtubules. CDC14 phosphatases and CDC25B reverse mitotic phosphorylation to license exit. Several G protein-coupled and sensory receptors appear as peripheral, signalling-level inputs.

The endoplasmic reticulum is the cell's main calcium store, and keeping that store filled while allowing controlled release is what this homeostatic system does. The set point matters because ER calcium drives protein folding by chaperones, sets the amplitude of cytosolic calcium signals, and determines how much calcium reaches mitochondria at contact sites. SERCA pumps (ATP2A1, ATP2A2) load the lumen against a steep gradient, inositol trisphosphate receptors such as ITPR1 release it, and leak or counter-ion channels including TMCO1 and TMBIM6 prevent overfilling. BCL2 family members BAX, BAK1 and BCL2 tune store content, which is how ER calinsufficiency or overload is converted into apoptotic commitment; PACS2 and PML organise the ER-mitochondria interface. Chronic disturbance triggers the unfolded protein response, and loss of WFS1 causes Wolfram syndrome with diabetes and neurodegeneration.

The endoplasmic reticulum is the cell's main internal calcium store, and processes that lower the calcium concentration inside it shift the balance between calcium signalling, protein folding capacity and cell death. Depletion of the ER store can arise from reduced pumping, from leak across the ER membrane, or from regulated permeabilisation, and the consequence is a rise in cytosolic and mitochondrial calcium that can trigger apoptosis or, if chronic, an unfolded protein response driven by loss of calcium-dependent chaperone function. The pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family members BAX and BAK1 act at the ER as well as at mitochondria, promoting store loss that sensitises cells to death signals; ATP2A1, the fast-twitch skeletal muscle SERCA pump, ties the same store to excitation-contraction coupling and relaxation, where its dysfunction produces myopathy with impaired muscle relaxation.

Otoliths are the dense biomineral bodies of the inner ear vestibular organs, and their generation and shaping determines whether an animal can sense gravity and linear acceleration. Defective otolith morphogenesis produces balance and postural deficits without necessarily affecting hearing, the classic signature being head-tilt and vestibular ataxia phenotypes. The process requires seeding and growth of calcium carbonate crystals on a proteinaceous matrix within the endolymph, and depends on precise control of endolymph ion and pH composition as well as on tethering of the otoconial mass to the sensory macula. OTOP1 acts in the endolymphatic epithelium as a proton-conducting channel that regulates local pH and calcium handling during mineral deposition, while LRIG1 and LRIG3, leucine-rich repeat membrane proteins that dampen receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, contribute to patterning of the surrounding otic tissue. A membrane trafficking component also participates, linking vesicular delivery to matrix secretion.

Type I interferons are potent antiviral cytokines, and their production must be switched off as soon as an infection is controlled; sustained output drives interferonopathies, lupus-like autoimmunity and immunopathology, so this braking programme is as much a part of innate immunity as the sensing that triggers it. The genes here act at many levels of the nucleic-acid sensing cascades that converge on RIG-I-like receptors, STING and IRF3. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD and OTUD5 and E3 ligases including ITCH, RNF125, TRIM27 and cullin-RING components strip or mark signalling intermediates for turnover; NLRX1, NLRC3 and DHX58 restrain the sensors themselves; autophagy proteins ATG5-ATG12 and IRGM limit signalling platform assembly. Inhibitory receptors, IL10, transcriptional repressors and microRNAs add cell-extrinsic and transcriptional damping, tuning how strongly and how long a cell commits to the antiviral state.

Type I interferons are the cell's first broadcast alarm against viral infection, and this pathway covers the events that switch their production on and amplify it. Cytosolic and endosomal sensors detect foreign nucleic acid: RIG-I and MDA5 signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, cGAS makes cyclic GMP-AMP that activates STING at the ER, and Toll-like receptors recruit MyD88 or TICAM1. These arms converge on the kinases TBK1 and IKBKE, which phosphorylate IRF3 and IRF7 so they enter the nucleus and drive interferon-alpha and -beta transcription. RNA helicases, TRIM ubiquitin ligases and chaperones tune sensor activity, while an RNA polymerase III module converts cytosolic DNA into RIG-I ligands. Too little of this output leaves severe susceptibility to herpesviruses and other infections; too much underlies interferonopathies and contributes to lupus-like autoimmunity.

Rab GTPases act as molecular switches that time and direct membrane traffic, and this signalling cassette covers the cycle by which they are turned on, read out, and reset. Each Rab marks a particular compartment "— early and recycling endosomes, late endosomes, the Golgi — and when GTP-bound recruits effectors that tether, dock, and fuse vesicles or move them along the cytoskeleton. DENN-domain proteins such as DENND1A, MADD and the DENND4 family serve as guanine nucleotide exchange factors that load GTP onto specific Rabs, while GDI1 extracts prenylated inactive Rabs from membranes for redelivery, and SGSM3 contributes GTPase-activating activity that ends the signal. The output is control of receptor recycling, autophagosome maturation, secretion and synaptic vesicle supply; mutations in RAB39B and in components of this machinery cause intellectual disability and parkinsonism.

Rab GTPases direct which membrane goes where, and their activity is switched on and off by regulators such as the DENN-domain proteins collected here. Control over Rab protein signal transduction determines the timing of vesicle budding, transport and fusion, and thereby the delivery of cargo to the cell surface, endosomes and secretory granules. Most members of this group act as guanine nucleotide exchange factors that load GTP onto specific Rabs: DENND1A works on Rab35 in clathrin-mediated endocytic recycling, the DENND4 proteins on Rab10 in transport including insulin-responsive glucose transporter traffic, and MADD on Rab3 family GTPases governing regulated exocytosis in neurons and endocrine cells, where its loss causes severe neurodevelopmental and neuroendocrine disease. SGSM3 instead binds Rabs as a modulator rather than an activator. Together they set the spatial and temporal pattern of Rab activation underlying membrane trafficking.

Ral GTPases relay signals from Ras-family activation toward vesicle trafficking, exocytosis and cytoskeletal remodelling, and this cassette controls whether those switches are on or off. Its output matters for secretion, cell migration and anchorage-independent growth, and in Ras-driven cancers the Ral arm contributes to transformation alongside the better known MAP kinase and PI3K routes. Activation is handled by guanine nucleotide exchange factors of two kinds: RGL2 is recruited by active Ras, whereas RALGPS1 and RALGPS2 act independently of Ras through their PH domains. Shutdown is the job of the RalGAP heterodimer, in which RALGAPA2 supplies the catalytic subunit and RALGAPB the regulatory one, stimulating GTP hydrolysis and returning Ral to its inactive state. Also represented are the atypical Ras-like proteins NKIRAS1 and NKIRAS2, which restrain NF-κB signalling by stabilising its inhibitor.

Rap protein signal transduction is the relay step in which small GTPases of the Rap branch of the Ras family, switched on at membranes, convert upstream cues into changes in cell adhesion and shape. Its main output is integrin activation and cadherin-based junction stability, so it governs how leukocytes stick and crawl, how platelets aggregate, and how endothelial and epithelial barriers stay sealed; loss of control produces leaky vessels and defective immune cell arrest. RAP1A, RAP1B and the RAP2 isoforms cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states under the control of a large family of exchange factors, including the cAMP-responsive RAPGEF3 and RAPGEF4 and the tyrosine-kinase-coupled RAPGEF1, which links the cassette to growth factor and second-messenger inputs. GTPase-activating proteins and ubiquitin ligase activity terminate or limit the signal. Downstream effects extend to cytoskeletal remodelling, cell polarity and cytokinesis.

Cdc42 is a small Rho-family GTPase that translates upstream cues into local actin remodelling, and the cassette described here covers the exchange factors, effectors and receptors that switch it on and read its output. Its main consequence is cell shape and directed movement: filopodia formation, axon specification and growth-cone steering, immune cell polarity and chemotaxis toward lymphoid tissue, where a chemokine receptor and its ligand guide dendritic cells and T cells. Loss of the effector WAS, which couples active Cdc42 to Arp2/3-driven actin nucleation, causes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome with defective immune cell motility and platelet formation. Guidance receptors and netrin signalling feed into the same cassette during neuronal wiring, while lipid-handling apolipoproteins and a cholesterol transporter link membrane composition to Cdc42-dependent cytoskeletal responses.

Cdc42 is the Rho-family GTPase that sets cell polarity and drives actin-based protrusion, so anything that modulates Cdc42 signal transduction determines when a cell forms filopodia, polarizes its cytoskeleton, and migrates. The regulators gathered here act at several levels: a guanine nucleotide exchange factor promotes GTP loading, a GTPase-activating protein terminates signalling, and the kinase ABL1 couples upstream cues to cytoskeletal output. Chemokine input through CCR7 and its ligand CCL19 links this control to dendritic cell and lymphocyte homing toward lymph nodes, while neuropilin-1 ties it to guidance and vascular responses. The presence of apolipoprotein and cholesterol-efflux components points to lipid-dependent tuning of the pathway, since Cdc42 activity depends on membrane composition and on plasma-membrane cholesterol handling. Loss of balanced regulation leaves cells unable to migrate directionally or to maintain polarized architecture.

detection of molecule of bacterial origin is the front line of innate immune surveillance: the sensing of conserved microbial structures such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, peptidoglycan fragments and unmethylated CpG DNA, and their conversion into an inflammatory signal. Without it, tissue macrophages, dendritic cells and epithelia fail to register invading bacteria and infection proceeds unopposed; with it set too high, the same receptors drive sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors, acting as TLR2 heterodimers with TLR1 or TLR6 or as TLR4 paired with the co-receptor MD-2, work alongside lipid-transfer and scavenger proteins that capture and present the ligand. Cytosolic NOD2 covers bacteria that reach the intracellular compartment, and loss-of-function variants predispose to Crohn's disease. Downstream output is NF-κB- and interferon-driven cytokine transcription, phagocyte activation and instruction of the later adaptive response.

Innate immunity begins with recognizing that bacteria are present, and this is the sensing step: conserved microbial molecules such as lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, peptidoglycan fragments and bacterial DNA are bound and converted into an intracellular signal that triggers inflammatory gene expression. Without it, infection proceeds unopposed; with it dysregulated, the same receptors drive septic shock and chronic inflammatory disease. Surface Toll-like receptors act as heterodimeric pairs (TLR1, TLR2 and TLR6) for lipopeptides, while TLR4 with the co-receptor encoded by LY96 responds to LPS delivered by lipopolysaccharide-binding protein and scavenger-type receptors; TLR9 senses unmethylated CpG DNA in endosomes, and cytosolic NOD2 detects muramyl dipeptide, a link underlying Crohn's disease risk. TREM2 and complement components modulate the resulting macrophage and microglial response, tuning phagocytosis and cytokine output rather than initiating detection.

Bacterial lipoproteins and lipopeptides are among the first molecules the innate immune system reads as evidence of infection, and the response to them converts that recognition into inflammatory cytokine output, phagocyte activation and eventual instruction of adaptive immunity. Detection is centred on TLR2, which pairs with TLR1 or TLR6 to discriminate triacylated from diacylated lipopeptides, while CD14 and the scavenger receptor CD36 act as accessory binders that concentrate ligand at the cell surface; TLR10 modulates the same axis, and the scavenger receptor SSC5D also engages bacterial surface ligands. Signalling passes through the adaptor TIRAP to MyD88-dependent kinases and NF-κB, and several microRNAs, including the miR-19 family, tune the strength of the resulting transcriptional programme. Too little of this response leaves recurrent pyogenic infection; too much contributes to septic inflammation and tissue injury.

Peptidoglycan is the sugar-peptide scaffold of the bacterial cell wall, and its fragments are one of the clearest signatures of bacterial presence that host cells can read. Responding to peptidoglycan lets epithelia, macrophages and monocytes mount inflammation and antimicrobial defence against invading bacteria, and shapes tolerance of the commensal gut flora; loss-of-function variants in this circuitry, notably NOD2, predispose to Crohn's disease and granulomatous inflammation. Intracellular muropeptides are sensed by the NOD2 receptor, which recruits the kinase RIPK2 and, together with the MYD88-IRAK adaptor route used by surface receptors, converges on NF-kB (RELA) and IRF5 to drive IL6 and other cytokines. CARD9 links the signal onward, while cathelicidin and a beta-defensin provide direct bactericidal output. IRAK3 and INAVA temper the response, keeping antibacterial signalling proportionate at mucosal surfaces.

Muramyl dipeptide is a fragment of bacterial peptidoglycan, and the cellular response to it is how cytosolic innate immunity detects bacteria that have breached the membrane or been degraded inside the cell. NOD2 is the sensor, with the related NOD1 responding to a distinct peptidoglycan motif; ligand binding recruits the kinase RIPK2 and CARD9, driving NF-kB activation through RELA and p38 signalling to produce inflammatory cytokines, antimicrobial peptides and autophagic clearance of invading bacteria. The output is tuned by brakes and scaffolds: NFKBIA and the ubiquitin-editing enzyme TNFAIP3 restrain the response, ERBIN and INAVA modulate sensor signalling, and NAGK contributes to generating the ligand itself. This circuit shapes intestinal tolerance of the microbiota, and loss-of-function NOD2 variants are a well-known risk factor for Crohn's disease, while gain-of-function alleles cause granulomatous inflammatory syndromes.

Detection of lipopolysaccharide is how host cells recognise the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria and convert that encounter into an inflammatory response. It is the first step in innate antibacterial defence, arming macrophages and other sentinel cells to release cytokines and recruit neutrophils; when it overshoots, the same recognition drives endotoxic shock and sepsis, and when it is blunted, Gram-negative infection goes unchecked. Recognition centres on TLR4, which cannot bind endotoxin alone and depends on the secreted co-receptor MD-2 encoded by LY96 to form a competent lipid A binding surface. Lipid transfer and scavenger receptor activity, including SCARB1, helps deliver and clear the ligand, while TREM2 on myeloid cells tunes the magnitude of the resulting response. The immediate-early factor NR4A1 is induced downstream and feeds back on inflammatory gene expression, linking pathogen sensing to transcriptional control of macrophage activation.

Cytokinesis physically splits one cell into two, and the cytokinetic process covers everything from positioning the division plane to severing the last cytoplasmic bridge. Getting it wrong produces binucleate or aneuploid daughters, a route to genome instability and tumourigenesis, and in tissues such as germline or blood it changes how cells stay connected. RhoA activation by ECT2, restrained by the centralspindlin GAP RACGAP1, drives assembly of the actomyosin contractile ring with anillin, myosin heavy chain and IQGAP scaffolds. Aurora B and PLK1 time these events against chromosome segregation and impose the abscission checkpoint through CHMP4C. Final cutting is membrane work: CEP55 recruits ALIX and the ESCRT-III subunits, VPS4 ATPases remodel the filaments, spastin severs residual midbody microtubules, and Rab11 recycling endosomes deliver membrane to the intercellular bridge.

Membrane proteins marked for destruction are delivered to the lysosome by being packaged into the internal vesicles of multivesicular bodies, and this endosome-to-lysosome route is how the cell terminates signalling from activated surface receptors and disposes of damaged or ubiquitinated cargo. Most of the genes here are CHMP subunits of the ESCRT-III complex, which polymerises on the endosomal membrane to deform and sever the neck of an inward-budding vesicle; the AAA-ATPases VPS4A and VPS4B, assisted by VCP, then disassemble the filaments so the machinery can be reused, while MVB12A contributes to upstream cargo-recognition steps and sorting nexins shape the tubular endosome. The same membrane-scission chemistry is reused in cytokinetic abscission and nuclear envelope resealing. Loss of cargo delivery leaves receptors signalling from an internal compartment, and mutations in LYST, which affects lysosome-related organelle size, cause Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

Membrane proteins marked for destruction are not simply delivered to the lysosome; they must first be pulled into vesicles that bud into the endosome lumen, so that both their cytoplasmic and extracellular faces are exposed to hydrolases. This sorting route from late endosomes into multivesicular bodies and on to the degradative compartment terminates signalling by activated receptors, and its failure leaves growth factor and cytokine receptors active, contributing to oncogenic signalling and to defects in neuronal protein turnover. Ubiquitinated cargo is captured by HGS and STAM, passed through the ESCRT-I subunits TSG101 and VPS28 with their VPS37 and MVB12 partners, then via the VPS25/SNF8/VPS36 complex to CHMP proteins that polymerise and sever the neck of the inward bud. The same machinery is co-opted for cytokinetic abscission and for enveloped virus budding.

Each somite is polarised into rostral and caudal halves before any morphological boundary appears, and this patterning is what later dictates where sclerotome cells condense, where vertebrae segment relative to muscle, and along which corridor migrating neural crest cells and motor axons may travel. Loss of the polarity produces fused and malformed vertebrae and disordered spinal nerve segmentation, as seen in congenital spine disorders. The bHLH factors MESP1 and MESP2 are induced in the rostral presomitic mesoderm as segmentation clock and Notch signals converge, with TBX6 licensing their expression and NRARP tuning Notch output; RIPPLY1 and RIPPLY2 then feed back to extinguish TBX6 and MESP activity, sharpening the boundary. LHX1 and nodal-type signalling through GDF3 and SMAD4 contribute upstream, while EPB41L5 links the resulting polarity to epithelialisation of the forming somite.

Retinoic acid, the active vitamin A derivative, acts as a diffusible morphogen and differentiation signal, and this pathway covers how cells sense it and remodel their behaviour in response. It underlies anterior-posterior patterning of the embryo, neural and limb development, spermatogenic entry into meiosis, epithelial and skin differentiation, and the maturation of myeloid cells exploited therapeutically in acute promyelocytic leukaemia; excess or deficiency of the ligand is teratogenic. Signalling runs through nuclear retinoic acid receptors (RARA, RARG) heterodimerised with retinoid X receptors, which recruit coactivators such as NCOA1 or corepressor-associated HDAC2 to switch target genes on or off. Ligand supply and clearance are themselves encoded here, with ALDH1A2 synthesising retinoic acid, RBP4 and LRAT handling retinol, and CYP26A1/CYP26B1 degrading it to set graded fields. Downstream outputs converge on WNT ligands and receptors, HOX and other lineage transcription factors, and growth factor receptor signalling.

Proteins that have folded correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum must leave it, and those that have not must also leave — in the opposite direction, for destruction. Both routes of protein exit from the ER are represented here. Forward traffic runs through COPII: SAR1A/B GTPases, SEC13–SEC31 cage components, SEC16 scaffolds at ER exit sites, and the four SEC24 paralogues that select cargo, aided by receptors such as LMAN1, SURF4 and TMED9 that concentrate soluble and lipid-linked clients into budding vesicles. The opposing arm is ER-associated degradation, where mannosidase-like lectins (EDEM1/2, OS9, ERLEC1) mark terminally misfolded glycoproteins, derlins and SEL1L–SYVN1 or TMEM129 ubiquitin ligases with UBE2J1/UBE2G2 tag them, and the VCP–UFD1–NPLOC4 ATPase extracts them to the cytosol for proteasomal disposal. Together these steps set secretory output, enforce protein quality control, and tune sterol synthesis through INSIG1-dependent degradation.

Absorptive epithelia in the gut and kidney multiply their surface area by packing the apical membrane with microvilli, and microvillus organization is the process that builds these actin-cored protrusions, spaces them evenly, and takes them apart. The brush border it produces is where nutrient uptake and digestive enzymes reside; its loss underlies microvillus inclusion disease and the malabsorption seen when apical structure fails. Bundled actin is cross-linked by espin, villin, plastin and fascin, anchored to membrane by ezrin and radixin working with the scaffold NHERF1, and tensioned by the unconventional motor MYO1A. Adhesion between neighbouring tips through the protocadherins CDHR2 and CDHR5 sorts protrusions into an ordered array, while sialomucins such as podocalyxin and the prominins shape membrane curvature. Rap GTPase regulators and kinases including STK26 and TNIK tune apical polarity and assembly.</description>

Absorptive epithelia of the gut and kidney present a dense brush border of microvilli, and control over how those protrusions are built, packed and taken apart sets the surface area available for nutrient uptake. The genes here span the layers of that regulation: an intermicrovillar adhesion link formed by the protocadherins CDHR2 and CDHR5 with the scaffold harmonin (USH1C) tethers adjacent tips into ordered arrays, while ezrin couples the actin core to the plasma membrane and villin, plastin-1, fascin and twinfilin bundle or cap the core filaments. Podocalyxin contributes an anti-adhesive glycocalyx, the flippase ATP8B1 maintains apical lipid asymmetry, and Rap GTPase signalling through RAPGEF2/6, RAP2A and the kinases STK26 and TNIK relays apical polarity cues onto the cytoskeleton. Disruption gives flattened or disorganised brush borders, as in microvillus inclusion disease and congenital malabsorption, and in the inner ear underlies hearing loss.

Absorptive cells of the gut and kidney display a brush border of packed actin-bundled microvilli, and controlling how long those protrusions grow sets the surface area available for nutrient uptake and digestive enzyme display. Regulating microvillus length depends on coordinating actin filament elongation with membrane attachment and tip-to-tip adhesion: villin and plastin-1 crosslink the parallel actin core, ezrin tethers that core to the overlying plasma membrane, and twinfilin-2 acts on filament ends to limit elongation. At the tips, the protocadherins CDHR2 and CDHR5 form adhesion links between neighbouring microvilli, with the harmonin scaffold USH1C anchoring them to the core bundle so that protrusions become uniform in height and tightly packed. Loss of these adhesion and bundling components yields short, disordered microvilli and impaired absorption, and related defects underlie brush border disease and Usher syndrome-associated sensory hair cell dysfunction.

regulation of microvillus assembly controls how cells build the dense arrays of actin-cored surface protrusions that create absorptive brush borders in the intestine and kidney, and it determines whether that apical surface forms in the right place at all. Loss of this control underlies microvillus inclusion disease and cholestatic intestinal failure, where enterocytes internalise their brush border and cannot absorb nutrients. The genes describe a Rap GTPase module — activating exchange factors and a GAP that sets Rap1/Rap2 output — feeding into the STE20 kinases STK26 and TNIK, which phosphorylate the ezrin-based apical scaffold and specify where microvilli grow. Alongside these are effectors acting directly on the actin core and glycocalyx, including the bundling protein fascin and the apical marker podocalyxin, plus the aminophospholipid flippase ATP8B1 that maintains apical membrane lipid asymmetry. The pathway thus links polarity signalling to actin cytoskeletal architecture and epithelial transport function.

Microvilli are the dense actin-cored protrusions that expand the apical surface of absorptive epithelia, and the genes here tune whether and where that brush border is built. Control of microvillus assembly determines the absorptive capacity of intestinal and renal epithelium; its loss underlies severe congenital diarrhoea and cholestatic liver disease. Much of the regulation runs through Rap GTPase signalling, with Rap2A and its activating exchange factors acting upstream of the Ste20-family kinases STK26 and TNIK to shape apical actin and junctional organisation. Local membrane composition contributes too: the aminophospholipid flippase ATP8B1 maintains apical bilayer asymmetry needed for stable microvilli, podocalyxin provides an anti-adhesive apical glycoprotein that promotes protrusion, and fascin bundles actin filaments. Together these link apical polarity cues to cytoskeletal remodelling during epithelial differentiation.

Cells actively set the dimensions of their parts — how long an axon or dendrite grows, how far a microvillus or filopodium projects, how big a lysosome, peroxisome or vesicle becomes, and how much water and salt a cell holds. This regulation of cellular component size determines neuronal wiring and connectivity, the absorptive brush border of the gut, red cell shape and deformability, and cell volume homeostasis. Much of the machinery is actin-based: capping and severing proteins, profilins, cofilin with its slingshot phosphatases, tropomodulins and leiomodins, the Arp2/3 complex with WAVE regulatory subunits, and Rho-family GTPases with their guanine nucleotide exchange factors and GAPs. Spectrins, adducins and ERM proteins anchor the membrane skeleton, while guidance cues such as semaphorins, netrins, slits and Wnts, together with mTOR complexes, scale growth to external signals. Cation-chloride cotransporters and WNK-OXSR1 kinases tune osmotic volume; failure produces neurodevelopmental and hemolytic disease.

Cell projections such as microvilli, axons and dendrites must be built to a defined length, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets and modulates that dimension. Its output determines how much absorptive surface an epithelial brush border presents and how far a neurite extends, so its failure shows up as malabsorption, hearing loss or disordered axon and dendrite geometry. Much of the work is done at the membrane cytoskeleton interface: ezrin tethers actin bundles to the plasma membrane, villin, plastin and twinfilin organise and cap the filaments themselves, and the protocadherin pair CDHR2 and CDHR5 forms adhesion links that tie neighbouring microvilli into ordered arrays, with harmonin anchoring the complex. Secreted WNT7 ligands contribute the extrinsic signalling arm, influencing neurite and dendritic growth, while contactin-2 acts through neuronal surface adhesion.

Mitochondrial translation is the protein synthesis machinery that operates inside mitochondria, using its own ribosomes, tRNAs and a slightly divergent genetic code to make the thirteen hydrophobic subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Those subunits form the catalytic cores of the respiratory chain complexes and ATP synthase, so this pathway sets the ceiling on oxidative phosphorylation; its failure causes combined respiratory chain deficiency, encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy and Perrault syndrome. The genes cover the whole cycle: the small and large subunit mitoribosomal proteins, mitochondria-specific aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases such as AARS2 and LARS2, tRNA modification and processing enzymes, initiation, elongation and release factors including MTIF2, TUFM and TSFM, ribosome assembly GTPases, and the OXA1L insertase that threads nascent chains into the inner membrane. Translation is coupled to mRNA stability and to co-translational assembly of the complexes themselves.

The thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA are all made inside the organelle, and mitochondrial translation is the machinery that makes them. Those products are core subunits of the respiratory chain complexes and ATP synthase, so this process sets the ceiling on oxidative phosphorylation; mutations in its components cause infantile lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy, deafness and other mitochondrial disease. The bulk of the genes encode the small and large subunits of the mitoribosome, a structurally distinct particle with its own initiation, elongation and release factors and a genetic code differing from the nuclear one. Dedicated mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge the organellar tRNAs, with glutaminyl-tRNA generated indirectly by transamidation, and several enzymes install tRNA and rRNA modifications required for accurate decoding. Membrane insertion of the hydrophobic nascent chains is handled by an insertase acting co-translationally, coupling synthesis to complex assembly.

Progesterone acts on the uterus, breast, ovary, brain and sperm, and this pathway covers the cellular changes that follow that hormonal cue: altered gene expression, secretion, proliferation and contractility. In the reproductive tract it supports endometrial receptivity and the quiescence of pregnancy, while in the mammary gland it drives secretory differentiation, reflected here by milk protein and junctional components such as CSN1S1 and CLDN4. Most of the transcriptional output runs through the nuclear receptor with its steroid receptor coactivators NCOA1 and NCOA2 and the coregulator WBP2, producing immediate-early factors like FOS and FOSB and TGF-beta family ligands. Non-genomic arms also appear: SRC kinase signalling, CAV1-associated membrane events, the mitochondrial cholesterol translocator TSPO, and ABHD2, the sperm lipid hydrolase through which progesterone from the cumulus activates CatSper and enables fertilization. Disordered progesterone responsiveness contributes to infertility, endometriosis and preterm birth.

Vitamin K is the cofactor that allows glutamate residues in certain secreted proteins to be gamma-carboxylated, and the response to vitamin K describes how cells and tissues change when that vitamin is available or withheld. The clearest consequence is in blood clotting: coagulation factors such as factor VII and factor V function in the clotting cascade, and vitamin K antagonism is the basis of oral anticoagulant therapy, while deficiency causes bleeding. The same chemistry serves bone and matrix biology through osteocalcin, whose carboxylated form binds calcium and hydroxyapatite, and through periostin, a matrix protein of bone and connective tissue. Growth arrest-specific 6 extends the theme to receptor signalling, acting as a ligand for TAM-family receptor tyrosine kinases in cell survival and clearance of dying cells. Together these genes place vitamin K upstream of hemostasis, skeletal mineralization and extracellular matrix maturation.

Membrane proteins are not fixed where they are inserted; this pathway covers their directed movement within the plane of a lipid bilayer, redistributing them between membrane domains and subcompartments so that receptors, pumps and channels end up where their function requires. Such lateral sorting builds and maintains polarized surfaces: concentration of cargo at the base of the cilium, partitioning into detergent-resistant raft domains, and delivery of proteins to the apical membrane of epithelia. ARL6 and the RILPL proteins act at the ciliary compartment, controlling entry and retention of signalling proteins behind the diffusion barrier at the ciliary base, and loss of ARL6 causes Bardet-Biedl syndrome. RFTN1 organizes raft domains that support receptor signalling, while ATP1B1 and UMOD illustrate targeted positioning of transport machinery and secreted apical proteins in kidney and other polarized tissues.

protein transport into membrane raft describes the targeted delivery of proteins into cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains of the plasma membrane, where receptors, transporters and signalling molecules are concentrated so that they can act together. Raft residence sets the efficiency of many surface events: it clusters immune receptor complexes for productive signalling, positions ion pumps and channels for polarised transport, and provides platforms for membrane trafficking and shedding. The genes here span these roles, from raftlin, which organises raft-dependent receptor signalling in lymphocytes and innate immune cells, to the sialoglycoprotein CD24 and the Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunit ATP1B1, which depends on raft localisation for correct apical or basolateral placement in epithelia. Uromodulin, secreted from raft domains of the thick ascending limb, illustrates the physiological stakes, since mislocalisation of raft cargo underlies kidney disease and defective epithelial ion handling.

Membrane rafts are cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains that concentrate selected proteins into small, dynamic platforms, and protein transport into these domains determines which signalling and transport complexes get assembled where. Targeting a receptor or pump into a raft raises its local partner density and changes its activity and turnover, so this sorting step underlies processes from immune receptor triggering to ion handling in epithelia. The genes here illustrate the range of cargo and machinery involved: raftlin is a defining raft-resident scaffold that helps recruit signalling components, the Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunit couples pump assembly and localisation to these domains, the small GPI-anchored glycoprotein CD24 partitions into rafts on immune and tumour cells, and uromodulin is sorted through raft domains in kidney tubule cells before apical secretion. Disrupted raft partitioning alters signal strength and can mislocalise transporters, a route to epithelial and immune dysfunction.

Chemokine production is the induced synthesis and release of small secreted chemoattractants that tell leukocytes where to go, and it sets both the intensity of inflammation at a site of infection and the routine trafficking of cells through healthy tissue. The genes here are largely the stimulus side of that output: Toll-like receptors and their adaptors MYD88, TICAM1 and TIRAP, cytosolic sensors and inflammasome components such as PYCARD, MEFV and RIPK2, the C-type lectin CLEC7A with SYK and CARD9, and RNA sensors including MAVS and OAS enzymes. Cytokines such as IL1B, TNF, IL6, IL17A, IL18, IL33 and IFNG amplify the response, while IL10, TGFB1, SIGIRR, SOCS5 and a set of microRNAs including MIR146A restrain it. Products such as CXCL8 and CXCL6 then recruit neutrophils. Excessive or persistent output drives chronic inflammatory and autoimmune tissue damage; failure leaves infections uncontained.

Granulocyte macrophage colony-stimulating factor production is the regulated output of GM-CSF, the cytokine that drives myeloid expansion and licenses inflammatory monocytes, dendritic cells and alveolar macrophages. It sets the size and activation state of the granulocyte-macrophage compartment during infection, and its excess sustains autoimmune tissue damage while its loss impairs surfactant clearance and antifungal defence. The genes here are the upstream stimuli and relays rather than the cytokine itself: pattern recognition through nucleic acid and fungal sensors feeding the SYK-CARD9 axis, and an IL-1/IL-18 and IL-23-IL-17 cytokine circuit that instructs T cells and innate lymphocytes to release GM-CSF. Costimulatory and inhibitory surface receptors tune the magnitude of the response. Functionally this sits at the interface of innate sensing, myeloid haematopoiesis and the IL-17-associated inflammatory programmes targeted in neuroinflammation and arthritis.

GM-CSF is the cytokine that drives emergency production and activation of granulocytes and macrophages, and its output is a measure of how strongly the innate immune system has been alerted. Controlled release supports antimicrobial defence and alveolar macrophage function; excess sustains the inflammatory loops behind arthritis and autoimmune neuroinflammation. Here, pattern recognition upstream of GM-CSF is well represented: a nucleic acid sensing receptor and an endosomal DNA-sensing Toll-like receptor, together with a spleen tyrosine kinase and its CARD9 adaptor relaying C-type lectin signals from fungal cell walls. The cytokine environment that licenses GM-CSF-producing lymphocytes appears as IL-1 family members, IL-18 and the IL-23 subunit with its receptor, with IL-17 family cytokines as the accompanying effector output. Costimulatory and myeloid receptor components place this in antigen-presenting-cell-to-T-cell crosstalk rather than in one lineage.

type I interferon production is the innate immune cell's decision to make interferon-alpha and interferon-beta, the cytokines that put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state. It is the front line of defence against viruses and intracellular bacteria, and its miscalibration is equally consequential: constitutive activation by self nucleic acids produces the interferonopathies and contributes to lupus, while loss of components leaves severe viral susceptibility. Detection happens on several sensor arms — endosomal Toll-like receptors, cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, and cGAS-STING reading double-stranded DNA — which converge on the TBK1/IKKε kinases and the IRF3 and IRF7 transcription factors that drive interferon gene transcription. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, TRIM proteins and nucleases such as TREX1 set the threshold and terminate the response, coupling this pathway to autophagy, nucleic acid turnover and NF-κB-dependent inflammation.

Type I interferon production is the cell's first broadcast alarm on detecting a virus, and its output of interferon-alpha/beta primes neighbouring cells into an antiviral state while shaping the ensuing adaptive response. Sensing is compartmentalised: endosomal Toll-like receptors read viral nucleic acids through MyD88 and TRIF adaptors, cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 signal via MAVS on mitochondria, and cGAS detects DNA and activates STING. These routes converge on the TBK1/IKKe kinases and the IRF3/IRF7 transcription factors, with TRAF3, ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and phosphatases setting the threshold. Restraint matters as much as activation: loss of nucleases such as TREX1 or of negative regulators causes chronic interferon signalling and interferonopathy or lupus-like autoimmunity, while failure of the sensors leaves severe susceptibility to viral infection. Autophagy components, Siglec and SIRP-family receptors and paracrine amplification through STAT1 tune the magnitude and duration of the response.

Interferon-alpha is the front-line antiviral cytokine, and this pathway covers the sensing and signalling events that lead to its synthesis and release. Cells detect viral nucleic acids through cytosolic RNA helicases such as RIG-I and IFIH1, which signal via the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, and through endosomal Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 that recognise double-stranded RNA, single-stranded RNA and unmethylated DNA. These converge on the kinase TBK1 and on interferon regulatory factors, with IRF7 the principal driver of type I interferon transcription; plasmacytoid dendritic cells, marked here by LILRA4, are the specialist high-output producers. Damage-associated signals including HMGB1 and DExH helicases feed in as well, while NLRC3, IL10 and PTPRS restrain the response. Too little output leaves the host vulnerable to viral infection; unrestrained production underlies interferon signature autoimmunity such as lupus.

Interferon-beta production is the front line of antiviral defence: infected cells detect foreign nucleic acid and release a cytokine that alarms neighbouring cells, inducing hundreds of restriction factors before adaptive immunity engages. Too little leaves hosts vulnerable to severe viral disease, while unrestrained output drives interferonopathies and lupus-like autoimmunity. Detection runs through cytosolic RNA helicases such as RIG-I and IFIH1 signalling via MAVS on mitochondria, DNA sensing through STING1, and endosomal Toll-like receptors using the adaptor TICAM1; RNA polymerase III can convert cytosolic DNA into an RNA ligand. These routes converge on TBK1-dependent phosphorylation of IRF3 and IRF7, which with NF-kB subunits assemble the enhanceosome at the IFNB1 promoter. Ubiquitin ligases, TRIM proteins, phosphatases and negative regulators including NLRC3 and NLRX1 set the threshold and terminate the response.

Interferon-gamma is the defining cytokine of type 1 cellular immunity, and this pathway covers the stimuli and regulators that determine how much of it T cells, NK cells and innate lymphocytes make and release. Its output activates macrophages for killing intracellular bacteria and protozoa, drives MHC class I and class II presentation, and shapes tumour surveillance; too little permits mycobacterial and salmonella disease, while unrestrained production feeds autoimmunity, haemophagocytic syndromes and cytokine-driven tissue damage. Induction runs largely through IL-12, IL-18, IL-23 and IL-27 acting on their receptors, through Toll-like receptor and inflammasome sensing of microbial products by myeloid cells, and through activating receptors such as KLRK1, CD226 and SLAM-family molecules. Checkpoint and inhibitory receptors including PD-L1, TIM-3, VSIR and LILRBs, together with IL-10 and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells, restrain it. Antigen processing components and immunoproteasome subunits both support and respond to this circuit.

Interleukin-1 alpha is an alarmin cytokine that alerts tissue to injury and infection, and this pathway covers how much of it a cell makes and releases. Unlike most cytokines it is stored as a pre-formed, already active precursor and appears largely when cells are damaged or die, so its output sets the intensity of sterile inflammation, fever and the recruitment of neutrophils and monocytes; runaway production drives autoinflammatory disease, while a controlled pulse supports wound repair. Regulation here is both transcriptional and secretory: a decoy receptor and the accessory chain IL1RAP shape downstream signalling strength, purinergic P2RX7 and the pannexin channel PANX1 couple extracellular ATP sensing to release, S100A13 contributes to non-classical, leaderless export, and microRNAs of the miR-181 and miR-142 families restrain transcript levels. The result places IL-1 alpha output at the interface of cell damage sensing and innate immune activation.

Interleukin-1 production is the process by which cells, mainly monocytes and macrophages, make and release the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1α and IL-1β, driving fever, neutrophil recruitment and the acute-phase response; when it runs unchecked it underlies the periodic fever syndromes and much of sterile inflammation, and blocking it is the basis of anti-IL-1 therapy. Two tiers of control are represented here. Pattern and damage receptors such as TLR4, NOD1/NOD2, CLEC7A and RAGE, acting through MYD88, RIPK2 and NF-κB, induce transcription of the inactive precursor. Inflammasome sensors — NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRC4 with NAIP, AIM2, IFI16 and pyrin — then recruit ASC and caspase-1 to cleave pro-IL-1β, with gasdermin D and pannexin channels providing the release route. Negative regulators, decoy pyrin-only proteins, CARD-family antagonists, IL-10 and numerous microRNAs restrain the output.</description>

Interleukin-10 is the principal brake on inflammation, and this pathway covers the stimuli and signalling that drive its synthesis and release by macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells and regulatory and effector T cells. Without it, immune responses to infection or commensal microbes fail to resolve, a loss reflected in the colitis seen when IL-10 signalling is defective; too much of it blunts pathogen clearance and supports tumour immune evasion. Innate sensors such as TLR4, TLR9, the dectin-1/SYK axis and NOD2 initiate production, while cytokine inputs including IL-6, IL-27, IL-21 and IL-23 converge on STAT3 and IRF4 to sustain it. Co-stimulatory and inhibitory surface molecules — CD28, CD40 ligand, PD-L1, PD-L2, TIGIT, LILRB family receptors — tune the output, and FOXP3 links it to regulatory T cell function, with several microRNAs imposing post-transcriptional control.

Interleukin-12 is the cytokine by which dendritic cells and macrophages instruct naive T cells to become interferon-gamma-producing Th1 effectors, so its production sets the strength of cell-mediated defence against intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi; too little permits disseminated infection, too much drives autoimmune and inflammatory tissue damage. The genes here cover how that output is switched on and off: pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2, TLR4, TLR9 and the dectin-1 lectin CLEC7A, together with their adaptors TIRAP, TRAF6, SYK and RIPK2, signal through NF-kB subunits and p38 kinases to induce the shared IL12B subunit; interferon-gamma and CD40-CD40L contact from T cells amplify it, while IL10, IDO1, IRAK3, HLA-G and inhibitory receptors restrain it. Interferon regulatory factors, notably IRF8, provide the transcriptional requirement, and the related IL23A subunit links this control to Th17 responses.

Interleukin-13 production describes the stimuli and regulators that make cells synthesise and release IL-13, the type 2 cytokine that drives airway hyperresponsiveness, goblet cell mucus production, IgE class switching and tissue fibrosis, and whose blockade underlies modern asthma and atopic dermatitis therapy.
