The main producers are Th2 lymphocytes, group 2 innate lymphoid cells, mast cells and basophils, and the genes here trace how they are instructed: epithelial alarmins such as IL-33 and TSLP, together with IL-4 itself and costimulation through OX40 ligand, converge on the transcription factors GATA3 and IRF4 that license the type 2 programme. IL-17 family receptors, IL-18 and interferons appear as modulating inputs that can amplify or restrain output, while club cell secretoglobin marks the airway epithelial context. Excessive activity produces allergic inflammation; too little weakens antihelminth defence and wound repair.

Interleukin-17 production describes the induction and release of IL-17 family cytokines, chiefly by Th17 cells and innate lymphocytes, to recruit neutrophils and drive antimicrobial defence at mucosal surfaces and skin. Too little leaves the host prone to chronic candidiasis and staphylococcal infection; too much fuels psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune inflammation, which is why IL-17 blockade is therapeutically useful. The genes here span the signals that license this output: IL6 with TGFB1 for lineage commitment, IL23A acting through IL23R, and IL1-family and IL21 amplification, opposed by IL12/IFNG-driven Th1 polarisation and by FOXP3-dependent regulatory restraint. Innate sensing via TLR4, MYD88, NOD2 and CARD9 feeds into it, particularly after fungal exposure. Downstream, RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators such as ARID5A and ZBTB7B, kinases including BTK, PRKCQ and SPHK1, and several microRNAs tune how much cytokine is actually made.

Interleukin-18 production covers the steps by which cells make and release this IL-1 family cytokine, a driver of interferon-gamma output by T and NK cells and a key amplifier of inflammation in the gut, skin and liver. Because IL-18 is synthesised as an inactive precursor, its appearance outside the cell depends less on transcription than on inflammasome activation: microbial and nucleic acid sensing through Toll-like receptors primes the response, NLR sensors and the accessory factor GBP5 nucleate a caspase-1-activating platform, and caspase-1 cleaves the pro-cytokine while gasdermin D pores in the plasma membrane provide the exit route during pyroptosis. Negative regulators such as NLRP12 and IL-10, together with microRNA-mediated tuning, restrain the output. Excess IL-18 underlies macrophage activation syndrome and hemophagocytic states, while loss of control of this axis contributes to autoinflammatory and inflammatory bowel disease.

Interleukin-2 production is the induced synthesis and release of the T cell growth factor that drives clonal expansion of activated lymphocytes and sustains regulatory T cells; too little cripples adaptive responses and tolerance, while unrestrained output feeds autoimmune and inflammatory disease. The genes here trace the route from antigen recognition to cytokine output: the T cell receptor complex and CD4 with costimulation through CD28 and its ligands CD80/CD86, proximal signalling via PRKCQ, PLCG2 and the CARD11-MALT1 scaffold, and NF-kB activation requiring TRAF6 and MAP3K7. Proteasome subunits degrade IkB and process antigen, STAT5A/STAT5B relay the cytokine's own receptor signal, and lineage factors including IRF4, RUNX1, TBX21 and GATA3 shape transcription. Restraint is equally represented: FOXP3, the inhibitory receptors LAG3 and HAVCR2, TNFAIP3, cAMP-degrading phosphodiesterases, and the mRNA-destabilising protein ZFP36.

Interleukin-21 production describes the control of how much IL-21 a cell makes and releases, a cytokine produced chiefly by follicular helper T cells and NKT cells that drives germinal centre reactions, B cell differentiation into plasma cells, and the cytotoxic programmes of CD8 T and NK cells. Too little of it cripples high-affinity antibody responses; too much feeds autoantibody-driven autoimmunity and sustains some lymphoid malignancies. The regulators here act upstream of the cytokine rather than on its receptor: IL-6 signalling through STAT3 promotes the follicular helper programme that turns IL-21 transcription on, the transcription factor FOXP1 restrains that programme, and several microRNAs, including miR-21 and the miR-221/222 pair, tune the output post-transcriptionally. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of T cell helper fate choice and humoral immunity.

Interleukin-21 production describes the making and release of IL-21, the cytokine by which follicular helper T cells drive germinal centre reactions, B cell differentiation into plasma cells and antibody affinity maturation; too much of it is linked to autoimmunity and lupus-like pathology, while too little blunts humoral responses and antiviral T cell help. The genes here concern the upstream control of that output rather than the cytokine itself: IL-6 signalling promotes the T follicular helper programme that licenses IL-21 expression, the transcription factor FOXP1 restrains that programme, and several microRNAs tune the transcripts involved. This places the pathway at the intersection of cytokine-driven T helper cell fate decisions and post-transcriptional regulation, determining how much IL-21 reaches responding lymphocytes during an immune response.

Interleukin-23 production is the output of myeloid cells — dendritic cells and macrophages — that sustains and amplifies IL-17-driven inflammation, and it matters because this cytokine licenses Th17 cells to expand and persist. Without it, mucosal defence against fungi and extracellular bacteria falters; in excess it drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and spondyloarthritis, which is why IL-23 is a successful antibody drug target. The genes here mark the inputs: pattern recognition through TLR4 and the β-glucan receptor CLEC7A signalling via MYD88, PLCG2 and RAC1 to induce transcription of the p19 and p40 subunits, with feedback from T cell-derived IFNG, IL17A acting through IL17RA, and GM-CSF raising output, while TGFB1 restrains it. The pathway therefore sits at the junction between innate sensing of microbes and the decision to commit adaptive immunity to a Th17 response.

Interleukin-4 is the defining cytokine of type 2 immunity, and this pathway covers the stimuli and regulators that cause cells to make and release it. Its output drives B cell class switching to IgE, alternative macrophage activation, and mucosal responses to helminths, while excessive production underlies allergic asthma, atopic dermatitis and anaphylaxis. Naive CD4 T cells are pushed toward the IL-4-producing Th2 fate by antigen presentation through MHC class II together with costimulation via CD28, CD86 and OX40 ligand, relayed by T cell receptor-proximal kinases such as PRKCQ and SYK and locked in by the transcription factors GATA3 and IRF4 with its cofactor ZFPM1. Epithelial alarmins, notably IL-33, and innate signalling through the NLRP3 inflammasome amplify the response, whereas FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells and inhibitory receptors including HAVCR2 with its ligand galectin-9 restrain it.

Interleukin-5 production is the type 2 cytokine output that drives eosinophil growth, recruitment and survival; when it is sustained, eosinophils accumulate in the airway and gut, and the result is allergic asthma, eosinophilic esophagitis and helminth-directed inflammation. The genes here mark the upstream triggers and the transcriptional decision that licenses IL-5 release. Epithelial alarmins IL-33 and TSLP, acting through ST2 (IL1RL1) with the IL1RAP accessory chain and through the TSLP receptor CRLF2, activate group 2 innate lymphoid cells and Th2 cells, while GATA3 and LEF1 impose the Th2 programme and FOXP3 restrains it. IL-25 signalling via IL17RB and the adaptor TRAF3IP2, IL-9, and retinoic acid receptor input add further tuning, and interferons oppose the response. Eosinophil peroxidase and secretoglobin reflect the effector and airway epithelial context in which this cytokine acts.

Interleukin-6 production is the induced synthesis and release of a cytokine that drives fever, the hepatic acute-phase response, and the differentiation of Th17 and antibody-secreting cells; chronic overproduction underlies rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and inflammation-associated cachexia, which is why its receptor is a drug target. Most of the inputs are innate immune sensors: Toll-like receptors reading bacterial and viral ligands through MYD88, TIRAP and TICAM1, cytosolic RIG-I-like and NOD-like receptors signalling via MAVS and RIPK2, and inflammasome adaptors, all converging on NF-kB with RELA and on C/EBPbeta and STAT3 to switch on transcription. Amplifying signals come from IL-1, TNF and IL-17 family ligands and their receptors. Restraint is equally represented: TNFAIP3, ZC3H12A which degrades IL6 mRNA, phosphatases such as PTPN6 and INPP5D, IL-10, TGF-beta and a large set of microRNAs tuning transcript stability.

Interleukin-8 is the principal chemoattractant that recruits neutrophils out of the blood and into infected or injured tissue, so its production sets the speed and size of acute inflammation; excessive output drives chronic inflammatory disease, tumour angiogenesis and acute lung injury, while too little leaves bacterial infection unchecked. The genes here describe how the signal is triggered and tuned: surface and cytosolic pattern receptors including the Toll-like receptor family, NOD1/NOD2 and RNA sensors, with the CD14/LBP complex presenting lipopolysaccharide, feeding through MYD88, TIRAP, RIPK1 and inflammasome adaptors to NF-kB subunit RELA and STAT3. Proteinase-activated receptors, complement and formate/fatty-acid receptors add danger and metabolic input, cytokines such as IL1B, IL6 and TNF amplify, IL10 restrains, and numerous microRNAs including MIR146A impose post-transcriptional damping on the same circuit.

Chemokines recruit leukocytes to tissue, so damping their synthesis is how an inflammatory response is kept proportionate and how it is resolved once a stimulus clears. Negative regulation of chemokine production draws on secreted anti-inflammatory signals such as IL10, decoy and inhibitory receptors that blunt Toll-like receptor and inflammasome output including SIGIRR, MEFV and the myeloid inhibitory receptors LILRB4 and SIRPA, intracellular brakes on cytokine signalling such as SOCS5, and transcription factors including KLF4 and the bile-acid receptor NR1H4 that repress inflammatory gene programmes. Several microRNAs, notably MIR146A and MIR34A, add post-transcriptional restraint by targeting adaptors and signalling intermediates of innate immune pathways. Loss of this restraint favours persistent neutrophil and monocyte infiltration, and contributes to chronic inflammatory disease, atherosclerosis, autoinflammatory syndromes and tissue injury following infection.

Type I interferon is potent but dangerous, and interferon-alpha output must be shut down once a viral threat is cleared or autoimmunity and tissue damage follow. Negative regulation of interferon-alpha production covers the brakes applied to the cells that make it, chiefly plasmacytoid dendritic cells responding to nucleic acid sensing through Toll-like receptors. Inhibitory surface receptors such as HAVCR2 and the plasmacytoid dendritic cell-restricted LILRA4 dampen sensing-induced interferon transcription, IL10 acts as an anti-inflammatory cytokine restraining the response, and intracellular regulators including NLRC3 and NMI limit innate immune signalling to the interferon genes. Loss of this restraint sustains an interferon signature of the kind seen in lupus and other interferonopathies, while excessive suppression aids viral persistence and blunts antitumour immunity. The pathway therefore sets the amplitude and duration of an antiviral alarm rather than whether it is raised.

negative regulation of interferon-beta production is the set of brakes that limit type I interferon output after innate immune sensors detect nucleic acids, keeping antiviral responses proportionate and self-limited. Restraint matters because sustained interferon-beta drives interferonopathies, autoimmunity such as lupus, and immunopathology during infection, while excessive shutdown permits viral replication. The genes act at several points along the sensing-to-transcription axis: NLRC3, NLRX1 and CACTIN dampen STING- and MAVS-dependent signalling, PPM1B and other phosphatases reverse the kinase steps that activate IRF3 and NF- inB, ATG9A links autophagy machinery to attenuation of STING trafficking, and NMI, YY1, REL and RELB adjust transcription at the IFNB1 promoter. Inhibitory surface receptors including LILRB1 and SIRPA impose cell-extrinsic restraint. Together they set the threshold, amplitude and duration of interferon signalling in innate immune cells.

Interferon-beta is the front-line antiviral cytokine induced when cytosolic sensors detect viral nucleic acid, and because sustained type I interferon is toxic — driving inflammatory tissue damage and autoimmune interferonopathies — cells maintain brakes that shut the response down. This pathway collects those brakes: negative regulation of interferon-beta production. Several members restrain the STING and RIG-I/MAVS arms from inside the cell, including the mitochondrial protein NLRX1 and the NOD-like receptor NLRC3, while ATG9A links autophagy membranes to dampening of DNA-sensing signal output. Others act on the transcriptional and phosphorylation steps that drive the interferon promoter, with a phosphatase and NF-kB family members among them, and inhibitory surface receptors such as LILRB1 and SIRPA set thresholds in myeloid cells. The net effect is resolution of antiviral signalling and tolerance of self nucleic acid, at the cost of blunted early defence when overactive.

Negative regulation of type II interferon production is the set of brakes that limit how much interferon-gamma T cells and NK cells release, keeping antimicrobial and antitumour immunity from tipping into tissue damage, autoimmunity or cytokine-driven pathology. It matters because unrestrained interferon-gamma drives macrophage hyperactivation, as seen in haemophagocytic syndromes and chronic inflammatory disease, while too much restraint permits tumour escape and persistent infection. The genes describe several converging mechanisms: inhibitory checkpoint receptors and their ligands, including PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3 with its galectin-9 ligand, VISTA and LILR family receptors; suppressive cytokines such as IL-10 and the IL-33 axis; regulatory T cell and Th2 transcriptional programmes driven by FOXP3 and GATA3; and post-transcriptional decay of cytokine mRNA by ZC3H12A. Together they set the threshold and duration of Th1 effector output, and they are the substrate on which checkpoint blockade therapy acts.

Interferon-gamma drives macrophage activation and Th1 immunity, so limiting how much of it is made is how tissues avoid immunopathology once an infection is controlled. This braking programme keeps T cell and NK cell output of the cytokine in check, and its loss underlies autoimmune and inflammatory tissue damage, while its excess is exploited by tumours to escape immune attack. The genes act through several converging routes: inhibitory receptor-ligand pairs such as PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3 with galectin-9, and VISTA deliver co-inhibitory signals to T cells; IL-10 and the IL-20 family cytokines act as suppressive cytokines; FOXP3 and GATA3 impose regulatory and Th2 transcriptional programmes that oppose Th1 commitment; and ZC3H12A degrades cytokine transcripts post-transcriptionally. Together they set the threshold and duration of type II interferon production rather than blocking it outright.

Interleukin-1 alpha is a potent alarmin released by epithelial and myeloid cells that drives fever, neutrophil recruitment and sterile inflammation, so restraining how much of it is made protects tissue from self-inflicted damage. This dampening arm of IL-1 biology limits the frequency and amount of IL-1 alpha produced, keeping innate immune activation proportionate to the insult and preventing chronic inflammatory and autoinflammatory states. Control operates at several levels: IL1R2 acts as a decoy receptor that binds IL-1 without transducing a signal, sequestering the accessory protein IL1RAP away from productive signalling complexes and so cutting the feed-forward loop by which IL-1 induces its own expression. Several microRNAs, including members of the miR-181 family and miR-142, repress transcripts in this circuit post-transcriptionally, while the chemokine CX3CL1 contributes signals that temper myeloid cytokine output.

Interleukin-1 beta is one of the most potent pyrogenic and pro-inflammatory cytokines, and because mature IL-1β release drives fever, neutrophil recruitment and tissue damage, cells invest heavily in braking its production. The genes here represent that brake at several levels: pseudo-caspase and pyrin-domain-only decoys such as CARD16, CARD18, PYDC1 and MEFV interfere with inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 activation; CARD8 and NLRP7 restrain sensor oligomerisation; TNFAIP3 limits NF-κB-driven transcription of the IL1B gene; ZC3H12A degrades inflammatory transcripts; and a large group of microRNAs suppresses IL-1β and NLRP3 messages directly. Extracellular and receptor-level damping is also included, through the decoy receptor IL1R2, immunoreceptors such as TREM2, CD33 and LILRB4, fatty-acid and ghrelin receptor signalling, and the protease inhibitor SERPINB1. Loss of this negative regulation underlies periodic fever syndromes and other autoinflammatory disease, and sustained IL-1β output contributes to metabolic and neuroinflammatory pathology.

Interleukin-1 is among the most potent pyrogenic and pro-inflammatory cytokines, so its output must be actively damped; the processes that stop or reduce interleukin-1 production keep innate immune activation self-limiting and prevent tissue damage, fever and autoinflammatory disease. Restraint acts at several levels. Caspase recruitment domain-only and pyrin-domain-only proteins, along with pyrin itself and NLRP12, interfere with inflammasome assembly and caspase-1 maturation, so that pro-IL-1β is never cleaved; a decoy receptor sequesters the mature cytokine's signal. Anti-inflammatory cues from IL-10, apolipoprotein A-I, ghrelin acting through its receptor, free fatty acid sensors and the bile acid receptor FXR suppress transcription, while TNFAIP3 and ZC3H12A terminate NF-κB signalling and degrade cytokine mRNA respectively. Inhibitory receptors on myeloid cells such as TREM2, CD33 and LILRB4 add a surface brake, and numerous microRNAs trim transcript levels. Loss of these controls underlies periodic fever syndromes and chronic inflammation.

Negative regulation of interleukin-10 production restrains output of the principal anti-inflammatory cytokine, and so sets how strongly an immune response is allowed to proceed before it is damped. Because IL-10 suppresses macrophage and dendritic cell activation and antigen presentation, holding it down favours inflammatory and Th1/Th17-type immunity, pathogen clearance and antitumour responses; excessive restraint contributes to tissue-damaging inflammation and autoimmunity, while failure to restrain IL-10 underlies chronic infection and tumour immune escape. The genes act at several levels: IL-12/IL-23 subunits and their receptor drive programmes antagonistic to IL-10, inhibitory receptors such as FCGR2B, LILRB family members and VSIR together with TYROBP-coupled signalling and BTK/JAK3 kinases tune the threshold in myeloid and B cells, FOXP3 and IDO1 link the process to regulatory T cell biology, and several microRNAs including let-7 family members impose post-transcriptional limits on IL-10 messenger RNA.

Interleukin-10 is the principal brake on inflammation, so processes that restrain its production keep immune responses from being damped prematurely and allow effective clearance of pathogens and tumours. Curbing IL-10 output shifts myeloid cells and T cells toward inflammatory programmes, and excessive restraint contributes to autoimmunity and immunopathology while insufficient restraint favours chronic infection and tumour tolerance. The genes here act through several routes: the IL-12/IL-23 axis, including the p40 subunit shared by both cytokines and the IL-23 receptor, promotes inflammatory differentiation at IL-10's expense; kinases such as BTK and JAK3 couple receptor engagement to cytokine transcription; inhibitory receptors including FCGR2B, LILRB family members and their TYROBP adaptor, and checkpoint ligands like CD274 and PDCD1LG2 tune the output; and several microRNAs, among them let-7 family members, repress it post-transcriptionally. FOXP3 links the process to regulatory T cell identity.

Interleukin-12 from dendritic cells and macrophages drives Th1 differentiation and interferon-gamma output, so damping its production is one of the main brakes on cell-mediated inflammation; without such restraint, innate activation escalates toward tissue damage and autoimmunity, while excessive restraint blunts antitumour and antimicrobial responses. Negative regulation of IL-12 production operates at several levels: IL-10 acts as the classical suppressive cytokine, inhibitory surface receptors such as TIGIT, LILRB1 and SLAMF1 deliver dampening signals to antigen-presenting cells, and intracellular components including IRAK3 and beta-arrestin 2 limit Toll-like receptor and NF-kB-driven transcription of the IL-12 subunits. A microRNA arm adds post-transcriptional silencing, and MEFV links this control to inflammasome-associated regulation, mutations in which cause familial Mediterranean fever. The pathway matters for tolerance at mucosal surfaces, in pregnancy, and in tumour immune evasion.

Interleukin-13 is the type 2 cytokine that drives mucus secretion, goblet cell hyperplasia, IgE class switching and airway hyperresponsiveness, so restraining its output keeps allergic and asthmatic inflammation in check. The genes here act as brakes on IL-13 production rather than on the cytokine itself: interferons, including a type I and a type III species, suppress type 2 differentiation of helper T cells and skew responses away from the IL-13/IL-4 programme; secretoglobin 1A1, the uteroglobin secreted by airway club cells, dampens allergic inflammation in the lung; a leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor family member and a TNF receptor superfamily member modulate immune cell activation thresholds; and arginase 2 alters arginine availability in type 2 inflamed tissue. Loss of such negative control tips the balance toward chronic eosinophilic airway disease and atopic dermatitis, which is why this arm of type 2 immune regulation is a therapeutic focus.

IL-17 drives neutrophil recruitment and antimicrobial defence at mucosal surfaces, but sustained production causes the tissue damage seen in psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmune arthritis, so the cytokine's output is actively restrained. This braking programme reduces the frequency and extent of IL-17 family cytokine production by suppressing differentiation and effector function of Th17 cells and other IL-17 sources. Regulatory T cells acting through FOXP3, the cross-inhibitory cytokines IFNG and IL-27, and TGFB1-dependent signals shift helper T cell fate away from the IL-17 programme, while the receptor antagonist IL36RN blunts IL-36 driven amplification and the checkpoint ligand VSIR dampens T cell activation. Several microRNAs, including a miR-146 and a let-7 family member, add post-transcriptional control, and metabolic and stress components such as ARG2 and DDIT3 modulate the threshold. Loss of this restraint favours chronic neutrophilic inflammation and autoimmunity.

Interleukin-2 drives clonal expansion of activated T cells, so restraining its output is one of the main brakes on T cell responses and a safeguard against autoimmunity and immunopathology. Genes here act at several levels to damp IL-2 production: inhibitory surface receptors such as LAG3 and HAVCR2 raise the threshold for activation downstream of the T cell receptor, FOXP3 in regulatory T cells directly represses the IL2 locus, lineage transcription factors including GATA3 and TBX21 bias cells toward alternative cytokine programmes, TNFAIP3 limits NF-κB signalling, and the RNA-binding protein ZFP36 destabilises cytokine transcripts. Chromatin regulators, protein kinase A signalling and a microRNA add further negative input. Loss of this restraint produces excessive T cell proliferation and inflammation, while its reinforcement underlies immune tolerance and the suppressive function of regulatory T cells.

Interleukin-21 is a T cell-derived cytokine that drives follicular helper T cell function, germinal centre reactions, B cell differentiation into antibody-secreting plasma cells, and the activity of NK and cytotoxic T cells; when its output goes unchecked it contributes to autoantibody production and autoimmune pathology. Damping IL-21 production is therefore part of how adaptive immune responses are kept proportionate. Here that restraint is imposed post-transcriptionally by microRNAs, including miR-21 and the miR-221/222 pair along with the miR-192/215 family, which bind target transcripts to repress translation and destabilise mRNA and so lower the amount of cytokine a helper T cell can make. This places the pathway within small RNA-mediated control of immune gene expression, a layer of negative feedback that tunes cytokine dosage rather than switching lineages on or off.

Interleukin-4 is the defining cytokine of type 2 immunity, driving IgE class switching, eosinophil recruitment and alternative macrophage activation, so limiting how much of it is made sets the ceiling on allergic and anti-helminth responses. Negative regulation of IL-4 production operates mainly in T cells, through transcriptional restraint of the Th2 programme and through degradation of the factors that sustain it: FOXP3 enforces regulatory T cell identity and represses effector cytokine genes, ZFPM1 acts as a cofactor limiting GATA-driven Th2 differentiation, LEF1 contributes to lineage-specific transcriptional control, and NDFIP1 activates Nedd4-family ubiquitin ligases that target JUNB and curb Th2 cytokine output. Contributions also come from the airway, where club cell secretoglobin dampens local inflammation, and from stress-responsive and antigen-presenting components. Loss of this restraint favours asthma, atopic dermatitis and other allergic inflammation.

Interleukin-5 drives eosinophil growth, recruitment and survival, so restraining its production is how the immune system keeps type 2 responses from becoming allergic disease. Processes that reduce IL-5 output limit eosinophilic inflammation in asthma, atopic dermatitis and helminth-directed responses, and their loss leaves airway tissue exposed to eosinophil granule products. Several distinct brakes converge here: regulatory T cell identity imposed by FOXP3 suppresses cytokine transcription in helper T cells, type I and type III interferons bias differentiation away from the IL-5-producing Th2 state, an inhibitory leukocyte receptor of the LILRB family dampens myeloid and antigen-presenting cell activation, and airway club cell secretoglobin SCGB1A1 provides a local anti-inflammatory signal from the epithelium. Transcriptional control by LEF1 links this restraint to lymphocyte developmental programmes rather than to acute signalling alone.

Interleukin-6 is a pyrogenic, acute-phase-inducing cytokine, and the braking systems that restrain its production keep innate immune activation proportionate and self-limiting; their loss underlies chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and cytokine storm. The genes here act at every level of that restraint. Anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL10 and IL37, and receptor antagonists like IL36RN, signal cells to stand down, while inhibitory surface receptors including CD200R1, SIRPA, HAVCR2 and LILRB4 raise the threshold for myeloid activation. Intracellular phosphatases and adaptors — PTPN6, PTPN22, INPP5D, CSK, the arrestins, IRAK3 and the deubiquitinase TNFAIP3 — damp Toll-like receptor and antigen receptor signalling upstream of NF-κB, and NLRC3, NLRP12 and NLRX1 act as negative regulators within the NOD-like receptor family. ZC3H12A degrades IL6 mRNA directly, and numerous microRNAs, notably MIR146A, provide post-transcriptional feedback. FOXP3 links the programme to regulatory T cell suppression.

negative regulation of interleukin-8 production restrains output of the chemokine CXCL8, the principal signal that recruits neutrophils to infected or injured tissue. Because IL-8 release is fast, self-amplifying and highly destructive when unchecked, dampening it sets the ceiling on acute inflammation and protects against tissue damage in sepsis, colitis, asthma and chronic airway disease. The brakes act at several levels: anti-inflammatory mediators such as annexin A1 and IL-10, inhibitory receptors including CD33 and the phosphatase PTPN22, and intracellular checks on NF- inkappaB signalling by BCL3, CACTIN and the deubiquitinase OTUD7B. A large complement of microRNAs, notably miR-146a and let-7 family members, adds post-transcriptional damping of Toll-like receptor and cytokine-driven transcription. Together these mechanisms tune innate immune signalling toward resolution rather than persistent neutrophilic recruitment.

Interleukin-8 is a potent neutrophil chemoattractant, and restraining its output is how tissues keep an inflammatory response proportionate and self-limiting. Negative regulation of interleukin-8 production prevents runaway neutrophil recruitment of the kind seen in sepsis, chronic airway inflammation, inflammatory bowel disease and atherosclerosis, and it also limits the tumour-promoting angiogenic effects of sustained chemokine release. Much of the control converges on NF-kB: the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL10 dampens transcription, BCL3 and the deubiquitinase OTUD7B tune NF-kB activity, and CACTIN acts as a repressor downstream of Toll-like receptor input. The glucocorticoid-inducible annexins ANXA1 and ANXA4 suppress inflammatory signalling, KLF4 acts transcriptionally, PTPN22 modulates immune receptor phosphorylation, and inhibitory receptors such as CD33 contribute. A large complement of microRNAs, notably MIR146A and let-7 family members, adds post-transcriptional braking on the same circuits.

Chemokines are the guidance cues that bring neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes out of the blood and into tissue, and this collection describes the signals that turn their production up. It is the amplification step of acute inflammation and of the mucosal and antifungal defence programmes; sustained activation underlies chronic inflammatory disease, while loss leaves infections uncontained. Pattern recognition is the dominant input: Toll-like receptors for bacterial lipopeptide, double-stranded RNA and CpG DNA feed through MYD88, TIRAP and TICAM adaptors, the C-type lectin receptor for fungal beta-glucan signals via SYK and CARD9, and cytosolic RNA sensing runs through MAVS. Inflammasome and cytokine loops reinforce it, with IL1B, IL18, TNF, IL6 and IL-17 family ligands acting on their receptors, while alarmins such as HMGB1 and IL33 report tissue damage and HIF1A couples the response to hypoxic, inflamed microenvironments.

Type I interferon-alpha is the cytokine that puts cells into an antiviral state, and this pathway covers the events that raise its output once an infection is sensed. Detection happens in two compartments: cytosolic RNA helicases such as RIG-I and IFIH1 signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, while endosomal Toll-like receptors recognising double-stranded RNA, single-stranded RNA and CpG DNA feed in from the other side. Both arms converge on kinases including TBK1 and IKK activity that license the interferon regulatory factors IRF3 and IRF7, the transcription factors that drive interferon-alpha genes, with STAT1 sustaining the response downstream. Accessory RNA helicases, HMGB1 and other cofactors amplify sensing. Too little of this activity leaves severe viral disease; too much underlies interferonopathies and the interferon signature of lupus, so the magnitude of induction is itself tightly policed.

Interferon-beta is the first-line antiviral cytokine, and this pathway covers the sensing and signalling events that switch its transcription on. Cells detect foreign nucleic acid through cytosolic RNA helicases such as RIG-I and MDA5, DNA-triggered STING, and endosomal Toll-like receptors recognising double-stranded RNA, single-stranded RNA and CpG DNA; a nuclear-DNA-sensing RNA polymerase III converts AT-rich DNA into an RIG-I ligand. These sensors converge on the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS or the TRIF adaptor, then on the kinase TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 and IRF7 so they enter the nucleus and drive interferon-beta expression. Ubiquitin ligases and ISG15 conjugation tune sensor activity, while OAS enzymes and HMGB proteins amplify the response. Output determines resistance to viral infection; excessive signalling underlies interferonopathies and contributes to autoimmune disease such as lupus.

positive regulation of type II interferon production describes the signals that drive T cells and natural killer cells to make interferon-gamma, the cytokine that arms macrophages for intracellular killing, boosts antigen presentation, and defines Th1-type immunity. Loss of these inputs leaves patients vulnerable to mycobacteria and other intracellular pathogens, while excess drives autoimmunity and macrophage activation syndromes. The genes trace the whole induction circuit: innate sensing through Toll-like receptors, CD14 and inflammasome components that release IL-1beta and IL-18; the IL-12/IL-23/IL-27 cytokine family and their receptors, which with IL-18 synergise to switch on IFNG transcription; NK and T cell activating receptors such as NKG2D, CD2 and SLAM family members alongside inhibitory counterweights like TIM-3 and galectin-9; and proteasome and MHC class I components that supply the peptides triggering cytotoxic recognition in the first place.

Interferon-gamma is the signature cytokine of type 1 cellular immunity, and this pathway covers the inputs that drive T cells and NK cells to make it. The output licenses macrophage activation, MHC upregulation and control of intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses; too little permits disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection, while too much fuels autoimmunity and hemophagocytic inflammation. The strongest drivers here are the IL-12 family cytokines and their receptors acting with IL-18 and its receptor chains, plus IL-2, IL-21 and IL-23 signalling. Innate sensing feeds in through several Toll-like receptors, CD14, the beta-glucan receptor CLEC7A and inflammasome adaptors, while NK and T cell surface receptors such as KLRK1, CD226, SLAM family members and antigen-presenting MHC molecules provide contact-dependent triggers. Antigen processing by the immunoproteasome, negative regulators including HAVCR2 and PTPN22, and cyclic-nucleotide phosphodiesterases set the threshold.

positive regulation of interleukin-1 alpha production covers the signals that drive cells to make and release IL-1 alpha, an alarmin cytokine that initiates sterile inflammation when epithelial or myeloid cells are damaged. Unlike its relative IL-1 beta, IL-1 alpha is preformed and can act from dying cells, so control over its output determines how strongly tissue injury converts into neutrophil recruitment, fever and downstream cytokine cascades. The genes point to danger sensing at the cell surface and its coupling to unconventional secretion: extracellular ATP acting through the P2X7 receptor, pannexin channels that amplify nucleotide release and potassium efflux, and S100A13 as a partner in the non-classical export route used by IL-1 alpha and FGF1. NLRP10 and neuropeptide and transcription factor components add inflammasome-adjacent and neuroimmune regulation, linking this arm of innate immunity to chronic inflammatory disease.

Interleukin-1 alpha is an early alarm cytokine released by damaged or stressed epithelium and myeloid cells, and this pathway covers the signals that increase its production. Because IL-1 alpha is already made as an active precursor stored in the cytoplasm, its output depends heavily on danger sensing and on unconventional release rather than on classical secretion: extracellular ATP acting through the P2X7 receptor together with the pannexin-1 channel links nucleotide leakage from injured cells to cytokine output, while an inflammasome-related NLR protein and an S100 family partner contribute to activation and to non-vesicular export. Amplified IL-1 alpha drives fever, neutrophil recruitment, and sterile inflammation after necrosis, and sustained overproduction contributes to chronic inflammatory and autoinflammatory disease. Neuroendocrine and transcriptional regulators in the same programme connect the response to peptide signalling and to cell-type-specific control of cytokine gene expression.

Interleukin-1 is the prototypic fever-inducing, neutrophil-recruiting cytokine of innate immunity, and this pathway covers the signals that raise its output. Two tiers are represented: pattern- and damage-recognition receptors such as TLR4, CLEC7A, NOD1/NOD2 and RAGE that, via MYD88, RIPK2 and NF-κB subunit RELA, drive transcription of pro-IL-1β; and inflammasome sensors including NLRP3, NLRP1, AIM2, IFI16 and NLRC4 that nucleate PYCARD specks to activate caspase-1, which matures the cytokine while gasdermin D forms the pore that releases it. Purinergic P2RX7 and pannexin channels, extracellular ATP and HMGB1, and cytokines such as TNF, IFN-γ and IL-17A amplify the response. Excessive activity underlies gout, atherosclerosis and the hereditary periodic fever syndromes caused by MEFV and NLRP3 mutations, making these steps the target of IL-1 blockade.

Interleukin-10 is the immune system's main brake on inflammation, and this pathway covers the signals that drive its output. Boosting IL-10 limits collateral tissue damage during infection, sustains tolerance at mucosal surfaces and in pregnancy, and — when co-opted by tumours or chronic pathogens — permits immune escape; too little IL-10 predisposes to colitis and runaway inflammatory responses. The inputs are diverse: pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4, TLR9, the fungal lectin CLEC7A and the bacterial sensor NOD2 acting through SYK and PLCG2; T-cell costimulatory and checkpoint molecules including CD28, CD40LG, TNFSF4 and TIGIT; and cytokines of the IL-6 and IL-12 families, with IL-27 and IL-21 signalling through STAT3 and IRF4 to license IL-10 transcription in macrophages, dendritic cells and regulatory T cells. It represents a negative-feedback arm layered onto innate and adaptive activation rather than a linear cascade.

Interleukin-12 is the cytokine by which dendritic cells and macrophages tell naive T cells to become Th1 effectors, and the signals that raise its output set the strength of cell-mediated defence against intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and some viruses. Too little leaves the host prone to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection; too much drives Th1-skewed autoimmunity and septic inflammation. The genes here trace how that increase is achieved: pattern recognition through Toll-like receptors and the beta-glucan receptor CLEC7A, with UNC93B1 trafficking nucleic-acid sensors and TIRAP, TRAF6, SYK, RIPK2 and the p38 kinases MAPK14 and MAPK11 relaying the signal to NF-kB and to IRF1, IRF5 and IRF8, which transactivate the IL12B subunit shared with IL-23. CD40-CD40L contact with activated T cells and IFN-gamma priming amplify the response, while galectin-9, HLA-G and IDO1 mark the counter-regulatory context in which it operates.

Interleukin-13 is a type 2 cytokine that drives airway hyperresponsiveness, mucus hypersecretion, goblet cell metaplasia, IgE class switching and tissue fibrosis, and the processes gathered here increase its output. Epithelial alarmins such as IL-33 and TSLP, acting on innate lymphoid cells and T cells, together with IL-25 signalling through its receptor pair IL17RA/IL17RB and the adaptor TRAF3IP2, initiate the response; IL-4 amplifies it, and the transcription factors GATA3 and IRF4 lock in the Th2 programme that makes IL-13 transcription possible. Costimulation through OX40 ligand and antigen-presenting cell surface molecules provides additional licence, while kinase and nuclear receptor components tune the magnitude. Sustained upregulation of this axis underlies allergic asthma, atopic dermatitis and helminth-associated inflammation, and it is also the arm of immunity that expels intestinal worms and supports wound repair.

Interleukin-17 is the signature cytokine of Th17 cells and related innate lymphocytes, driving neutrophil recruitment and antimicrobial defence at mucosal barriers; too much of it underlies psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis and other autoimmune inflammation, which is why IL-17 blockade is now a therapy. This pathway collects the signals that turn IL-17 output up. Cytokine inputs dominate: IL-6 plus TGF-beta initiate the Th17 programme, IL-23 acting through IL23R and the shared IL12B subunit stabilises it, and IL-1 family and IL-21 signals amplify it, with MYD88 carrying receptor signals inward. Innate pattern recognition through NOD2 and CARD9 links microbial sensing to IL-17 induction, while T cell receptor-proximal kinases such as PRKCQ and BTK and SLAM-family contacts set the threshold. Post-transcriptional stabilisation of Il17 mRNA by ARID5A and amino acid supply via SLC7A5 add further layers of control.

positive regulation of interleukin-18 production describes the signals that drive cells to make and release IL-18, a cytokine that pushes T cells and NK cells toward interferon-gamma output and shapes mucosal barrier defence. It matters because IL-18 links detection of microbes and cell damage to type 1 immunity, and its unchecked release contributes to macrophage activation syndrome and inflammatory bowel disease, while its loss leaves epithelial surfaces poorly defended against enteric viruses. Mechanistically the genes converge on the inflammasome: pattern recognition through Toll-like receptors and nucleic acid sensors, together with TNF-driven priming, raises pro-IL-18 availability, while NLRP9 and GBP5 promote assembly of caspase-1-activating platforms. Caspase-1 cleaves the precursor and gasdermin D pores permit its export, coupling cytokine maturation to pyroptotic cell death rather than conventional secretion.

Interleukin-18 is made as an inactive precursor and only becomes an active cytokine after inflammasome-driven cleavage, so upregulating its production is a step in mounting inflammatory and antiviral responses. The mature cytokine drives interferon-gamma output from T and NK cells, links innate sensing to type 1 immunity, and contributes to mucosal defence; excessive output underlies macrophage activation syndromes and inflammatory bowel pathology. Here, pattern recognition through Toll-like receptors for bacterial lipoproteins and CpG DNA, together with nucleic acid sensing and NLR-family inflammasome scaffolds, converges on caspase-1, which processes the pro-cytokine. Gasdermin D pores and guanylate-binding protein support of inflammasome assembly provide the release route and amplification, while tumour necrosis factor contributes to the surrounding inflammatory milieu. The result couples microbial detection to cytokine maturation rather than to transcription alone.

Interleukin-2 is the growth factor that lets antigen-activated T cells clonally expand and that sustains regulatory T cells, so processes that raise its production set the size and quality of an immune response. The genes here describe how that output is increased: T cell receptor engagement through CD3 and the CD4 coreceptor, costimulation by CD28 meeting CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, and phosphatase and kinase steps involving CD45 and protein kinase C theta that feed the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 complex and TRAF-dependent kinases toward NF-kB. Transcription factors such as IRF4, RUNX1 and STAT5 act at the IL2 locus, while innate signals through IL-1 and dectin-1-RIPK2 amplify it; proteasome subunits contribute by degrading inhibitory NF-kB restraint. Too little of this signalling causes immunodeficiency and poor T cell expansion, too much drives autoimmune and inflammatory disease, which is why costimulation blockade targets it.

Interleukin-23 is the dendritic cell and macrophage cytokine that sustains Th17 cells and maintains IL-17 output, and the processes that raise its production set the strength of mucosal antifungal and antibacterial defence while also driving psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and spondyloarthritis — the reason IL-23 itself is a major antibody drug target. Upregulation is triggered largely by innate pattern recognition: the fungal beta-glucan receptor CLEC7A signals through a spleen tyrosine kinase route that requires PLCG2, while Toll-like and IL-1 family receptors converge on the adaptor MYD88 to activate NF-kB-dependent transcription of the IL-23 subunits. Feed-forward input from T cells and myeloid growth factors reinforces this: IFNG, GM-CSF and IL-17A acting through IL17RA all increase IL-23 output, creating a self-amplifying loop between antigen-presenting cells and the Th17 compartment they instruct.

Interleukin-4 is the defining cytokine of type 2 immunity, driving IgE class switching, alternative macrophage activation and the allergic response, and this pathway covers the signals that turn its production up. Antigen receptor engagement plus costimulation through CD28 and OX40 ligand, relayed by PKC-theta and adaptors such as SASH3 and FCER1G-coupled SYK signalling, licenses naive T cells to commit to a Th2 programme; GATA3 and IRF4 then act as the transcriptional core of that commitment. Innate alarmins, notably IL-33 released from damaged epithelium, prime mast cells, basophils and eosinophils to release IL-4 without prior sensitisation. Excessive activity of this circuit underlies asthma, atopic dermatitis and helminth-type inflammation, while its outputs also restrain Th1 and Th17 responses, so the pathway sits at the balance point of helper T cell polarisation.

Interleukin-5 is the cytokine that drives eosinophil production, recruitment and survival, so processes that increase its output shape allergic inflammation and the tissue eosinophilia of asthma and helminth defence. The genes here mark the upstream inputs that push lymphocytes toward this output: epithelial alarmins such as IL33 and TSLP acting through their receptors IL1RL1 with the IL1RAP co-receptor and CRLF2, and IL17B signalling through IL17RB, together with the autocrine amplifier IL9. GATA3 is the transcription factor that licenses type 2 cytokine genes, including IL5, in Th2 cells and group 2 innate lymphoid cells, while adaptor and second-messenger components including TRAF3IP2, PRKCZ and PDE4D set signal strength. Retinoic acid receptor signalling adds a nuclear hormone input. Blocking this axis is the rationale for anti-IL5 and anti-alarmin therapy in eosinophilic disease.

Interleukin-6 is the cytokine that converts local innate immune recognition into a systemic response — fever, acute-phase protein synthesis in liver, Th17 differentiation, plasma cell antibody output — and this pathway covers the upstream events that turn its production up. Most of the machinery here is pattern and damage recognition: Toll-like receptors for bacterial and viral ligands with their adaptors MYD88, TIRAP and TICAM1 feeding TRAF6 and the NF-κB subunit RELA; cytosolic sensors NOD1, NOD2, RIGI, IFIH1 and MAVS; C-type lectin signalling through SYK and CARD9; and inflammasome components with IL-1 and IL-17 family cytokines amplifying the output. Endogenous alarmins such as HMGB1 and AGER ligands, metabolic signals like leptin, and transcriptional regulators including STAT3, ARID5A and XBP1 also feed in. Sustained excess drives chronic inflammatory disease, autoimmunity and cytokine storm, which is why IL-6 receptor blockade is therapeutically useful.

Interleukin-8 is the principal chemokine that recruits neutrophils to infected or injured tissue, and this pathway covers the signals that turn its production up. Pattern recognition receptors dominate: the full Toll-like receptor family with the adaptors MyD88 and TIRAP, the cytosolic sensors NOD1, NOD2 and RIG-I with MAVS, and the C-type lectin dectin-1 signalling through SYK, all converging on NF-kB subunit RELA to drive transcription. Accessory recognition components such as CD14 and LBP present bacterial lipopolysaccharide, while inflammasome and death-domain proteins including PYCARD, RIPK1 and FADD couple cell stress to the same output. Cytokines TNF, IL1B and IL6, alarmins such as HMGB1, thrombin receptors and adipokines including leptin and adiponectin feed in as amplifying inputs. Sustained activation underlies neutrophil-rich chronic inflammation, sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease and tumour-promoting inflammation.

Mast cell cytokine production is the tissue mast cell's capacity to release TNF, IL-6, IL-13 and other mediators after activation, an output distinct from the immediate degranulation of histamine and proteases. It sustains the late phase of allergic inflammation, recruits eosinophils and neutrophils to mucosal and connective tissue, and contributes to asthma, chronic urticaria and helminth defence; unchecked, it drives persistent airway and skin inflammation. IgE crosslinking through the high-affinity receptor gamma chain initiates the signal, which requires the CARMA-BCL10-MALT1 complex to reach NF-kB and switch on cytokine transcription, while KIT signalling from stem cell factor sets mast cell survival and tunes the strength of the response. Transcriptional regulators including BCL6 and the immediate-early receptor NR4A3 shape which cytokines are made and for how long, linking receptor engagement to gene expression rather than to preformed granule release.

Mast cells do more than release preformed histamine and proteases; hours after activation they transcribe and secrete cytokines that sustain allergic inflammation, recruit eosinophils and neutrophils, and shape tissue remodelling in asthma and chronic urticaria. Cytokine output by mast cells is the slower, transcription-dependent arm of this response, and it is set by how strongly the cell is stimulated and by which transcriptional brakes are in place. Signalling through the IgE receptor gamma chain couples antigen crosslinking to the kinase cascades that engage an adaptor scaffold feeding NF-kB activation, while the KIT receptor for stem cell factor supplies the survival and priming input that mast cells depend on for maturation and tissue residence. Transcriptional regulators of the BCL6 and NR4A families then restrain or tune the resulting cytokine gene programme, determining whether mast cell activation resolves or drives persistent inflammation.

Machines that burn ATP — ion pumps, motors, translocases, chaperones — need brakes as much as fuel, and this grouping collects the proteins that damp their activity. The clearest examples are in muscle: phospholamban and sarcolipin inhibit the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump SERCA, setting how quickly cytosolic calcium is cleared and therefore the rate of relaxation and the strength of the next beat, while the troponin complex of cardiac muscle gates actomyosin ATPase in response to calcium. Elsewhere the theme recurs in mitochondria, where a component of the presequence translocase-associated motor restrains the import ATPase, and in the regulation of Na,K-ATPase activity. Loss of such restraint shows up as cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia, and more broadly as unchecked energy expenditure — sarcolipin-mediated futile SERCA cycling is itself a thermogenic mechanism.

Enzymes and motors that hydrolyse ATP are frequently held below their maximum rate until a partner protein stimulates them, and this pathway covers the positive regulation of such ATP-dependent activities. The effect matters wherever work must be coupled to ATP on demand: chaperone-mediated protein folding, calcium pumping, and muscle contraction. J-domain proteins such as DNAJB2, DNAJB11 and DNAJC9 deliver substrates to HSP70 and stimulate its ATPase cycle, while AHSA1 activates the ATPase of HSP90; TOR1AIP1 and TOR1AIP2 are the nuclear envelope and ER cofactors that switch on the AAA+ ATPase torsinA, whose loss causes dystonia. In striated muscle, troponin T subunits and the SERCA pump of the sarcoplasmic reticulum link ATP consumption to contraction and relaxation. Also represented are nucleic-acid-stimulated helicase and single-stranded DNA-binding activities, and regulators tied to autophagosome formation.

Hepatocytes must move bile acids from their cytoplasm across the canalicular membrane into bile, and this regulated secretion drives bile flow, biliary lipid excretion and the intestinal delivery of detergents needed for fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption. The bile salt export pump ABCB11 performs the ATP-dependent canalicular step, ABCB4 supplies phosphatidylcholine that buffers bile acid detergency, and the heterodimeric transporter subunits SLC51A and SLC51B provide a basolateral exit route into portal blood. Cytosolic binding and modifying proteins such as FABP1 and UGT1A3 handle and conjugate the acids en route, while a scaffold adaptor positions transporters apically, claudin-2 shapes paracellular permeability, calcium sensing and TNF-linked inflammatory signals tune output, and a microRNA constrains the programme transcriptionally. Loss of export function causes cholestasis, pruritus and progressive liver injury from retained bile acids.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it pauses, and whether it resumes and how fast it travels along a gene is decided by the factors collected here, which regulate transcription elongation. This control sets the timing and amount of mRNA made from inducible and developmental genes, and it determines co-transcriptional splicing and termination outcomes, so its misregulation drives cancers dependent on sustained oncogene output. NELF subunits together with the DSIF pair SUPT4H1/SUPT5H hold polymerase in a paused state; CDK9 with cyclin T, sequestered as an inactive complex by HEXIM1, LARP7 and the 7SK RNA, phosphorylates these factors to release it, while BRD4 helps recruit the kinase to chromatin. Mediator subunits couple enhancer-bound activators to the polymerase, the Integrator complex can prematurely terminate paused transcripts, ELL and PAF components stimulate processivity, and FACT plus chromatin readers let elongation proceed through nucleosomes.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it does not simply run to the end of the gene; it is held, paused and sometimes terminated early, and the negative control of transcription elongation is what imposes those brakes. Restraining elongation keeps genes poised for rapid induction, prevents collisions with replication and DNA repair, and limits transcription of damaged or heterochromatic templates. The NELF complex together with the DSIF subunits SUPT4H1 and SUPT5H halts polymerase just downstream of the start site, while the 7SK small nuclear RNA with LARP7 and HEXIM1 sequesters the kinase that would otherwise release it. Other members act through chromatin and damage signalling: EZH2 in Polycomb repression, SIRT6 and PARP1 at chromatin, and the RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin cascade silencing transcription near double-strand breaks. Loss of such restraint yields unscheduled, uncoordinated gene expression and genome instability.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it typically stalls, and the processes gathered here release it and keep it moving, making elongation rather than initiation the decisive step in expression of many inducible and developmental genes. Positive regulation of transcription elongation is carried out by P-TEFb, in which CDK9 pairs with cyclin T1 or T2 to phosphorylate the polymerase C-terminal domain and the DSIF subunits SPT4 and SPT5, converting a pausing factor into an elongation-promoting one; BRD4 recruits this kinase to acetylated chromatin, while a phosphatase-regulatory module containing PNUTS and PP1 opposes it. Related CDK12 and CDK13 cyclin K complexes sustain elongation on long genes. The Mediator complex couples activator binding to polymerase release, the PAF1 complex components CDC73 and LEO1 and the FACT histone chaperone allow transit through nucleosomes, and ELL family proteins limit transient pausing. Loss of these activities truncates long transcripts and disrupts lineage-specific gene programmes.

Monocarboxylic acids — fatty acids, lactate, pyruvate, ketone bodies, bile acids, retinoic acid and eicosanoids — are the currency of cellular fuel handling and of much lipid signalling, and this collection covers their synthesis, activation, breakdown, oxidation, conjugation and transport. Together these reactions determine whether a cell burns glucose or fat, how the liver exports ketones and bile acids during fasting, and how inflammatory lipid mediators are produced and cleared; their failure underlies fatty acid oxidation disorders, peroxisomal disease, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. Acyl-CoA synthetases prime fatty acids for use, carnitine palmitoyltransferases commit them to mitochondrial beta-oxidation, peroxisomal oxidases handle very-long-chain and branched substrates, cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases convert arachidonate to prostanoids and leukotrienes, and cytochrome P450s and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases oxidise and conjugate the products. Nuclear receptors, AMPK, mTOR and insulin signalling tune the whole programme to nutrient supply.

Ribosome disassembly separates a ribosome into its subunits so they can be reused, and it is how cells clear stalled or collided ribosomes from damaged or aberrant mRNAs. Normal termination recycling depends on the ABC-family factor ABCE1 splitting post-termination complexes, while the PELO–HBS1L pair with ABCE1 rescues ribosomes stalled without a complete codon–tRNA pairing. When ribosomes collide, sensors including ZNF598 and the GCN1/ASCC machinery mark the event and trigger ubiquitin-dependent quality control: NEMF and the ligase LTN1 tag the nascent chain for degradation, and VCP with its UFD1–NPLOC4 cofactors extracts it, with SKI-complex components and the UFMylation system acting on the associated mRNA and on ER-bound ribosomes. Mitochondrial recycling and initiation factors extend the same logic to organellar translation. Loss of these steps causes accumulation of toxic partial proteins and underlies neurodegenerative phenotypes.

positive regulation of CREB transcription factor activity describes the signalling inputs that switch on CREB, the transcription factor through which cyclic AMP and calcium signals are converted into lasting changes in gene expression. This step underlies long-term synaptic plasticity and memory consolidation, hepatic gluconeogenic gene programmes, and hormone-driven transcription in endocrine tissue; its loss blunts activity-dependent transcription of targets such as BDNF and PGC-1α. Calcium-stimulated adenylate cyclases generate the cAMP that activates protein kinase A, while calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and the MSK family kinases phosphorylate CREB at Ser133 to recruit the CBP/p300 coactivators. In parallel, the CRTC coactivators are dephosphorylated and enter the nucleus to engage CREB directly, providing a second, kinase-independent route to target-gene induction and integrating nutrient and neuronal stimuli at the same promoters.

CREB is the transcription factor that converts transient rises in cyclic AMP and calcium into lasting changes in gene expression, and this pathway covers the upstream events that switch it on. The output matters for memory consolidation and synaptic plasticity, for hepatic gluconeogenesis and gluconeogenic gene induction during fasting, and for hormone-responsive programmes generally. Calcium-stimulated adenylate cyclases ADCY1 and ADCY8 raise cAMP in neurons, a calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase and the MSK-family kinases RPS6KA4 and RPS6KA5 phosphorylate CREB at its regulatory serine, and the CREB-regulated transcription coactivators CRTC1 and CRTC2 are dephosphorylated and move to the nucleus to engage CREB at target promoters. Convergence of these inputs sets the threshold above which stimulation becomes transcription, linking neuronal activity and metabolic hormones to durable transcriptional responses.

Hepatic clearance of circulating LDL cholesterol depends on how many LDL receptors sit on the cell surface, and this metabolic process covers the reactions that set that number. Because receptor abundance determines plasma LDL levels, the pathway sits at the centre of cholesterol homeostasis and of atherosclerosis risk: gain-of-function changes in PCSK9, a secreted protease that binds the receptor and routes it to lysosomal degradation, cause familial hypercholesterolaemia, while loss of function lowers LDL and inspired the PCSK9-blocking therapies now in use. PCSK9 itself must be matured by proprotein convertase activity, and furin cleaves it into a less active form. In parallel, the E3 ubiquitin ligase MYLIP (IDOL) ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail to trigger its degradation under sterol-replete conditions. Apolipoprotein E supplies the ligand side, targeting remnant particles for receptor-mediated uptake.

Receptor catabolic process is the controlled destruction of signalling receptors, the step that sets how long and how strongly a cell can respond to a hormone, growth factor, morphogen or neurotransmitter. Because a receptor that is not degraded keeps signalling, this pathway is a brake on proliferation and metabolic signalling: loss of the ubiquitin ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3 leaves Frizzled receptors on the surface and drives Wnt-dependent tumours, while PCSK9 and MYLIP direct the LDL receptor to lysosomal or ubiquitin-dependent turnover and thereby set plasma cholesterol. Mechanistically, HECT and RING ligases such as NEDD4, ITCH and SMURF1 mark activated receptors with ubiquitin; sorting adaptors, ESCRT components and KIF16B route them into multivesicular bodies; and lysosomal proteases including legumain and calpain, together with the autophagy regulators BECN1, UVRAG and PIK3R4, complete degradation. Hepcidin-driven ferroportin removal and furin-family processing extend the same logic to iron and receptor maturation.

Signalling receptors are not permanent fixtures; their degradation sets how long and how strongly a cell can respond to a hormone, growth factor or ligand. This receptor catabolic process covers the routes by which receptors are marked, internalised and destroyed, chiefly ubiquitin-dependent sorting into lysosomes. HECT-domain and RING ligases such as NEDD4, NEDD4L, ITCH, SMURF1 and the Wnt-receptor ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3 tag receptors for downregulation, while MYLIP targets the LDL receptor and secreted PCSK9 drives its lysosomal disposal, a link that underlies cholesterol handling and lipid-lowering therapy. Endosomal and autophagy machinery -- BECN1, UVRAG, PIK3R4, KIF16B and ESCRT-associated MVB12A -- delivers cargo onward, and lysosomal proteases including legumain complete breakdown. Loss of this turnover leaves receptors signalling unchecked, a route to hyperproliferation, and also governs iron control through hepcidin-driven ferroportin loss.

Lacrimal gland development builds the tear-producing gland that lubricates and protects the cornea, from its first budding off the ocular surface ectoderm through branching to a mature secretory structure. Without it the eye lacks an aqueous tear film, giving dry eye, corneal keratinization and ulceration, and the vision loss that follows. The process is a classic case of epithelial branching morphogenesis driven by reciprocal signalling with surrounding mesenchyme: FGF10 from the mesenchyme acts on epithelial FGFR2 to induce and elongate the bud, and loss of either arrests gland formation, as in the lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital syndrome. PAX6 supplies the ocular surface identity that permits gland induction, FOXC1 patterns the periocular mesenchyme, and SOX9 with SOX10 direct acinar and secretory differentiation of the mature epithelium. The pathway therefore links organ induction, branching, and secretory cell specification.

Adrenal chromaffin cells and adrenergic neurons release epinephrine during stress, and this braking arm limits how much is released and for how long. Restraint matters because unopposed catecholamine output raises blood pressure and heart rate, and loss of feedback contributes to hypertension and exaggerated stress responses. The dominant mechanism is autoinhibition through alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, which sense released epinephrine and norepinephrine, couple to inhibitory G proteins, lower cyclic AMP and suppress calcium entry so that fewer secretory granules fuse; these are the receptors targeted by clonidine and dexmedetomidine. A metabotropic GABA-B receptor supplies parallel inhibitory input, while corticotropin-releasing hormone appears here as part of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal circuitry that sets the gain of adrenal output. Together these inputs make epinephrine secretion self-limiting rather than all-or-none.

regulation of natural killer cell activation sets the threshold at which NK cells commit to killing a target or releasing interferon-gamma, tuning innate surveillance against virus-infected and tumour cells while sparing healthy tissue. Too little restraint drives immunopathology and hyperinflammation; too much allows tumours to escape. Activation is balanced between inhibitory and activating receptor pairs "" the CD94/KLRD1 complex with KLRC1 or KLRC2 reading HLA-E, NKG2D ligands such as MICA, and FCGR3A with the TYROBP adaptor for antibody-dependent killing "" feeding into proximal signalling through FGR, RASGRP1 and the phosphatase PTPN22. Cytokine input from IL-15, IL-12, IL-18 and IL-21 acting via STAT5 sets responsiveness and survival, while checkpoint receptors like TIM-3 and AXL/GAS6 signalling dampen it. Transcriptional regulators including TOX, PRDM1, ZBTB1 and ZNF683 govern NK development and the acquired, memory-like state, and a CRL4-DCAF15 ubiquitin ligase module degrades activation substrates.

Natural killer cells must be licensed and tuned before they kill, and this collection of regulators sets how readily that activation occurs. The balance matters for clearing virus-infected and tumour cells while sparing healthy tissue; too little leaves malignancies and herpesvirus infections unchecked, too much drives haemophagocytic and autoimmune pathology. Activating and inhibitory receptor pairs read surface ligands — CD94/NKG2 family members with HLA-E, NKG2D ligands such as MICA, and the Fc receptor FCGR3A with its TYROBP adaptor — and feed into proximal signalling through kinases and RASGRP1, restrained by the phosphatase PTPN22 and checkpoint receptor HAVCR2. Cytokines set responsiveness from outside: IL-15 with its receptor alpha chain supports survival and priming, while IL-12, IL-18 and IL-21 promote interferon-gamma output via STAT5 and transcriptional regulators including PRDM1, TOX and ZNF683. A cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase module adds degradative control.

Negative regulation of natural killer cell activation is the set of brakes that keep NK cells from firing at healthy tissue, setting the threshold a target must cross before it is killed. This restraint matters for self-tolerance, for maternal acceptance of the fetus, and for limiting the collateral damage of antiviral and antitumour responses; conversely, tumours exploit the same brakes to escape immune surveillance. Inhibition acts at several levels: HLA-E displayed on normal cells engages inhibitory receptors and reports intact MHC expression, checkpoint receptors such as HAVCR2 and the inhibitory lectin CLEC12A dampen cytotoxic signalling, shed MICA blunts activating receptor engagement, and intracellular components including the kinase FGR, the adaptor CLNK and the ubiquitin-pathway regulator RHBDD3 tune signal strength downstream. Progesterone-induced blocking factor extends the same logic to pregnancy, linking innate cytotoxicity to reproductive immunology.

Natural killer cells kill without prior sensitization, so their activation has to be actively restrained to keep cytotoxicity off healthy tissue and to limit inflammatory damage during infection. This inhibitory arm sets the threshold: HLA-E signals intact self to the CD94/NKG2A receptor and licenses tolerance of normal cells, HAVCR2 (TIM-3) acts as a checkpoint receptor that dampens effector responses and marks exhausted lymphocytes, CLEC12A is an inhibitory C-type lectin receptor, and the kinase FGR and adaptor CLNK act inside the cell to tune receptor-proximal signalling. Shed ligands such as MICA can blunt activating receptor engagement, a route tumours exploit to escape NK surveillance. Pregnancy-associated and peptidoglycan-recognition factors contribute further suppression. Loss of this restraint favours autoimmunity and graft rejection; excess of it permits tumour and viral persistence, which is why several of these receptors are immunotherapy targets.

Natural killer cells kill virus-infected and tumour cells without prior sensitisation, and their readiness to do so is set by signals from myeloid and stromal cells; this is the arm of that control that raises NK activation. Cytokines dominate the set: IL15 with its presenting receptor chain drives NK development and survival, IL12 and IL18 act together to license interferon-gamma output and cytotoxicity, and IL21 and IL23 shape the response further, largely through JAK-STAT signalling in which STAT5A and STAT5B transduce IL15 and IL2-family input. Receptor-proximal components include the FcγRIII-TYROBP pair that couples antibody-coated targets to degranulation, HLA-E as ligand for inhibitory and activating receptor engagement, and RASGRP1 downstream of activating receptors, while TOX and ZBTB1 support lineage development. Loss of these inputs manifests as impaired antiviral and antitumour surveillance and susceptibility to mycobacterial and herpesvirus disease.

Natural killer cell numbers are tuned by cytokine and receptor signals, and this regulation sets how much innate cytotoxic capacity is available during viral infection and tumour surveillance. IL-15 is the dominant survival and proliferation signal for NK cells, acting through JAK-STAT output in which STAT5B transduces the growth program; loss of that axis leaves few functional NK cells. IL-12, acting through its IL12RB1/IL12RB2 receptor pair, together with IL-18 and the related IL-23 system, drives expansion and licenses interferon-gamma production during type 1 immune responses. Additional inputs come from the low-affinity Fc receptor FCGR3A, which links antibody-coated targets to NK activation, from HLA-E engagement by inhibitory and activating NKG2 receptors, from FLT3 ligand acting on progenitors, and from the metabolic hormone leptin. PTPN22 restrains the responses, tying this control to autoimmune risk.

Natural killer cells arise from lymphoid progenitors, and the pace and extent of that maturation is set by the cytokines and transcription factors collected here. Control over natural killer cell differentiation determines how much innate cytotoxic capacity is available for killing virus-infected and tumour cells, and its loss leaves patients with NK deficiency and susceptibility to herpesvirus infection. Interleukin-15 presented with its high-affinity receptor alpha chain is the dominant survival and developmental signal, acting through STAT5A and STAT5B, with IL-21 tuning later maturation and effector output. Nuclear factors including TOX, ZBTB1 and PRDM1 license or restrain progression along the lineage, ZNF683 marks tissue-resident and memory-like subsets, and RASGRP1 couples receptor engagement to Ras signalling. AXL with its ligand GAS6 provides an additional receptor tyrosine kinase input modulating NK development.

Natural killer cells arise from lymphoid progenitors, and this is the set of signals that push that developmental programme forward, increasing the rate and extent of NK cell differentiation. Without it the innate lymphoid compartment is depleted, leaving tumour surveillance and early antiviral control impaired; the same axis is exploited therapeutically to expand NK cells for cancer immunotherapy. The dominant input is interleukin-15 presented in trans by its high-affinity receptor alpha chain on accessory cells, which drives JAK-STAT signalling through STAT5A and STAT5B to support survival, proliferation and maturation, with IL-21 shaping the later stages. The receptor tyrosine kinase AXL and its ligand GAS6 provide an additional growth-promoting input, while transcriptional regulators such as TOX and ZBTB1 commit progenitors to the lineage. RASGRP1 couples receptor engagement to Ras-ERK signalling in developing lymphocytes.

Regulatory T cells hold peripheral immune responses in check, and this biology covers the signals that raise or lower how many of them are made from CD4 precursors. Without adequate output, self-reactive and anti-commensal responses go unopposed, producing autoimmunity and inflammatory bowel disease; excessive output blunts anti-tumour and antiviral immunity. FOXP3 is the lineage-defining transcription factor whose expression must be induced and then sustained for suppressive identity, and signalling through the shared cytokine receptor gamma chain feeds the interleukin-2 responsiveness on which these cells depend. Antigen presentation by MHC class II molecules sets the strength and duration of the T cell receptor input that biases a precursor toward the regulatory fate, while interferon gamma and galectin-9 act as opposing environmental cues linking inflammatory tone and cell surface glycan recognition to how much suppression is generated.

The filtering unit of the nephron is built when a capillary tuft is invested by podocytes and supported by mesangial cells inside Bowman's capsule, and glomerulus development is the sequence that takes this structure from an S-shaped body to a working filter. Its output is the glomerular filtration barrier, and disruption produces congenital nephrotic syndrome, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and Alport-type basement membrane disease. Transcription factors including WT1, PAX2, FOXC2 and TCF21 specify podocyte and stromal fates; slit diaphragm and foot process components such as NPHS1, NPHS2, PODXL, CD2AP and MAGI2 create the size-selective barrier; and COL4A3/COL4A4 with LAMB2 and NID1 assemble the basement membrane beneath it. Endothelial ingrowth and mesangial recruitment depend on angiopoietin-TEK and PDGFB-PDGFRB signalling, with Notch and BMP inputs patterning the segments of the developing nephron.

The glomerular basement membrane is the sheet of specialised extracellular matrix that sits between podocytes and the capillary endothelium and performs the actual sieving of plasma in the kidney. Its development, from an immature laminin- and collagen-rich lamina to the mature filter, sets the size and charge selectivity of the barrier; failure produces proteinuria, haematuria and progressive nephropathy. Maturation involves switching to the collagen IV alpha3/alpha4/alpha5 network and to laminin beta2-containing trimers, with nidogen bridging collagen and laminin lattices and heparan sulfate chains, edited by extracellular sulfatases and built on EXT1-dependent chain elongation, contributing anionic charge. Podocyte contributions are equally part of the process: WT1 drives the podocyte transcriptional programme, nephrin builds the slit diaphragm, and MYO1E supports foot-process actin. Mutations in these collagen and laminin genes underlie Alport syndrome and congenital nephrotic syndrome.

regulation of cellular pH reduction covers the control of processes that acidify the cell interior, a variable that sets enzyme activity, vesicle trafficking, and the balance between survival and death. Cytoplasmic and organellar pH must be held within narrow limits: sodium-hydrogen exchangers such as SLC9A7 and SLC9A8 extrude protons in exchange for sodium across Golgi and endosomal membranes, tuning the luminal acidity on which glycosylation and cargo sorting depend, while BCL2 opposes the intracellular acidification that accompanies mitochondrial apoptotic signalling. Hormonal input enters through vasopressin acting on its V1A receptor, linking systemic fluid and electrolyte handling to proton flux in target cells, and the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A adds post-translational control. Loss of these exchangers causes intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental disease, reflecting how tightly neuronal function is tied to organellar pH.

Cells hold their internal pH within a narrow band, and control over the processes that acidify the cytosol or intracellular compartments is part of how that band is maintained. Regulation of cellular pH reduction covers the modulation of acidifying activity, which matters because proton gradients set enzyme activity, vesicle trafficking, apoptotic sensitivity and, in the kidney, water and acid handling. The genes here point to two routes: hormonal signalling through vasopressin and its V1A receptor, which acts on renal and vascular target cells, and sodium/hydrogen exchangers of the intracellular Golgi and endosomal membranes, which trade sodium for protons and thereby limit compartmental acidification. BCL2 links pH control to mitochondrial apoptotic decisions, while the ubiquitin ligase UBE3A implies proteolytic turnover of the regulators themselves.

Insulin released after a meal tells liver, muscle and fat to take up glucose, store fuel and grow, and the cellular response to insulin stimulus is the sum of those instructions. Loss of responsiveness is insulin resistance, the core lesion of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Ligand binding to the insulin receptor or its close relative IGF1R recruits IRS adaptors and phosphoinositide 3-kinase, and AKT then drives GLUT4-containing vesicles to the plasma membrane via RAB and TBC1D4 traffic, inhibits GSK3, and activates mTOR-S6K signalling for protein synthesis. In parallel, FOXO1 and SREBF1 are reset so gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and G6PC1 are switched off while lipogenesis is switched on. Feedback through SOCS proteins, GRB10/GRB14, PTPN1 and adipokines including leptin, adiponectin and resistin tunes sensitivity, linking the pathway to appetite control and whole-body energy balance.

Insulin released after a meal tells liver, muscle and fat to take up glucose, store fuel and grow, and this pathway covers what a target cell does once the hormone binds. Loss of responsiveness is insulin resistance, the core lesion of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome. The receptor and its close relative the IGF1 receptor phosphorylate IRS adaptors, which recruit PI3K and activate AKT; AKT in turn inhibits GSK3 to permit glycogen synthesis, phosphorylates FOXO1 to shut off gluconeogenic genes such as PCK1 and G6PC1, relieves TSC2 restraint on mTOR for protein synthesis, and drives TBC1D4 to allow RAB-dependent trafficking of GLUT4 to the plasma membrane. A parallel RAS-MAPK arm supports mitogenic and transcriptional output.
