Negative regulators including PTPN1, SOCS proteins, GRB10, GRB14 and TRIB3 set the gain, and adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin modulate sensitivity.

Hormones act at a distance, and this collection covers what a target cell actually does when one arrives: the cellular response to hormone stimulus, spanning receptor engagement, intracellular signalling, and the transcriptional and metabolic changes that follow. It is the basis of endocrine control of metabolism, growth, reproduction, salt and water balance and circadian timing, and its disruption underlies insulin resistance and diabetes, hormone-dependent cancers of breast and prostate, and thyroid, adrenal and bone mineral disorders. Two broad mechanisms are represented. Peptide hormones such as insulin, growth hormone, leptin and glucagon act through cell-surface receptors feeding into adenylate cyclase and protein kinase A, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, MAPK and JAK-STAT cascades, with SOCS proteins and phosphatases restraining them. Steroid, thyroid and retinoid hormones act through nuclear receptors that recruit coactivators, corepressors and chromatin modifiers to reprogramme gene expression, alongside the enzymes that synthesise and inactivate the ligands themselves.

Cells are not internally symmetric: they place a front and a back, an apical and a basal face, and this control over the establishment or maintenance of cell polarity sets the rate and extent to which that asymmetry is specified and held. It underlies directed migration of leukocytes and endothelial cells, lumen formation in vessels, axon specification in neurons, and oriented divisions in epithelia; when it fails, junctions leak, migration loses direction, and tissue architecture degrades, as in cerebral cavernous malformations linked to KRIT1. The genes converge on the actin cytoskeleton and its regulators, with ROCK1 and ROCK2 driving actomyosin contractility, cofilin and gelsolin remodelling filaments, and LLGL1/LLGL2 acting in the conserved apicobasal polarity module. Others tune polarity through Rho and Rap GTPase signalling, membrane traffic, microtubule-cortex coupling and growth factor input, placing this regulation at the interface of cytoskeletal dynamics and cell shape.

Where a protein ends up inside a cell is as regulated as whether it is made at all, and this collection covers the control layer that sets those destinations: targeting proteins to the plasma membrane, sorting them through endosomes, retaining or releasing them from the ER, importing and exporting cargo across the nuclear envelope, and anchoring them at the centrosome, cilium, synapse or cell junction. The machinery is broad but recognisable: COPII coat and ER export components, Rab GTPases and their regulators with retromer and ESCRT sorting factors, clathrin adaptors for endocytosis, SNAREs for fusion, importins, exportins and the Ran system, 14-3-3 proteins, chaperones, and palmitoyltransferases and ubiquitin ligases that add the modifications acting as trafficking signals. Kinases and receptor pathways feed in so that localisation responds to signalling, as when insulin secretion, Wnt or Hedgehog output depends on relocating a key effector.

Cells store glucose as glycogen and mobilise it on demand, and this regulatory layer sets how fast that store is built or broken down — the difference between stable blood glucose and hyperglycaemia. Insulin and IGF ligands acting through the insulin receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT are the dominant input: AKT inhibits GSK3, relieving its restraint on glycogen synthase, while glucagon and parathyroid hormone receptor signalling and cyclases push the opposite way. A family of PPP1R3 targeting subunits directs protein phosphatase 1 onto glycogen particles to dephosphorylate synthase and phosphorylase, and phosphorylase kinase subunits together with AMPK's PRKAG3 tune breakdown in muscle and liver. Glucokinase and laforin-associated partners link flux to substrate availability and to glycogen quality control. Failure of these controls underlies insulin resistance, glycogen storage disease and progressive myoclonic epilepsy, and the same logic extends to hyaluronan synthesis.

Cells store glucose as glycogen and secrete polysaccharides such as hyaluronan, and this regulatory layer sets how fast those polymers are made. Its dominant theme is hormonal control of glycogen synthesis in liver and muscle: insulin and IGF ligands act through the insulin receptor and IRS adaptors to activate AKT, which inactivates the glycogen synthase kinases GSK3A and GSK3B and thereby relieves inhibition of glycogen synthase. A family of PPP1R3 subunits targets protein phosphatase 1 to glycogen particles, coupling dephosphorylation to glucose storage, while glucokinase, the AMPK subunit PRKAG3 and PASK tie synthesis to nutrient and energy status; several microRNAs tune the output. Growth factors including PDGFB and TGFB1 instead drive HAS2-dependent hyaluronan production in the extracellular matrix. Failure of this control contributes to insulin resistance, glycogen storage disease and disordered hepatic glucose handling.

Microtubules build the mitotic spindle, the axonal transport tracks and the axoneme of cilia and flagella, and this regulatory layer sets how fast they grow, how long they persist and where they are nucleated. Control here decides whether chromosomes segregate correctly, whether neurons extend and maintain processes, and whether motile and sensory cilia assemble at all; its failure underlies microcephaly, ciliopathies, sperm motility defects and tauopathy-like neurodegeneration. The regulators act through several routes: plus-end tracking and stabilising factors such as the EB proteins, CLASPs and CKAP5, minus-end capping by the CAMSAP family, destabilisation by stathmins and katanin-type severing, tubulin modification by acetyltransferases, HDAC6 and tubulin tyrosine ligase-like enzymes, and mitotic kinases including Aurora A and B, PLK1 and PLK4 with TPX2 and the augmin complex. Centriole duplication factors and basal body components tie the same control to ciliogenesis.

Cells must adjust how fast organic acids — amino acids, fatty acids, bile acids, neurotransmitter acids — cross their membranes, and this regulatory layer sets that rate rather than performing the transport itself. It matters for nutrient sensing and growth signalling, for bile acid secretion by the liver, for fatty acid handling in muscle and adipose tissue, and for controlling how much glutamate or GABA is loaded into synaptic vesicles and cleared from the synapse. Control is exerted through receptor and kinase signalling (AKT, IRS2, purinergic and adenosine receptors, metabotropic glutamate receptors), transcriptional regulators such as PPARA, neuropeptides including vasopressin, oxytocin and leptin, and inflammatory mediators like TNF and IL1B, all converging on carriers of the SLC amino acid and neurotransmitter transporter families and on ABCB11-dependent bile salt export. Dysregulation contributes to cholestasis, excitotoxicity and disordered lipid and energy metabolism.

Cells and tissues must be able to throttle the movement of organic acids — amino acids, neurotransmitter acids such as GABA and glutamate, fatty acids and their derivatives — across membranes, and this is the braking arm of that traffic. Restraint matters because unchecked transport alters synaptic neurotransmitter clearance, lipid loading of cells, and the availability of amino acids for growth signalling. The mechanisms here are heterogeneous: G protein-coupled receptors and their regulators, including GABA-B and metabotropic glutamate receptors, adenosine A1 receptors, and RGS proteins, dampen release and uptake presynaptically; insulin/leptin-responsive kinases AKT1 and AKT2 with IRS2 tune fatty acid and amino acid handling; a microRNA and inflammatory mediators such as TNF and thrombospondin act as transcriptional or paracrine suppressors. Loss of such negative control contributes to excitotoxicity, disordered lipid metabolism and metabolic disease.

Cells must move carboxylate-bearing molecules actoss membranes on demand, and this pathway covers the signals and accessory proteins that raise the rate of organic acid transport — amino acids and neurotransmitters such as glutamate and GABA, fatty acids, bile acids, and eicosanoid precursors. Increasing such flux matters for synaptic transmission, renal and hepatic handling of solutes, nutrient supply to proliferating cells, and the release of inflammatory lipid mediators. The members act at several levels: transporters and channels themselves, including a bile salt export pump, a vesicular glutamate transporter, a glutamine carrier, a large neutral amino acid carrier and purinergic channels; vesicle-fusion and trafficking machinery that positions them; phospholipases that liberate arachidonic acid for prostaglandin synthesis; and upstream hormonal and cytokine cues such as vasopressin, oxytocin, endothelin and interleukin-1 that switch the transport on.

Suppressing transcription of an integrated or nuclear viral genome is one way cells limit infection without killing the infected cell, and it underlies both innate antiviral defence and the transcriptional latency that keeps retroviruses such as HIV-1 silent. Two distinct mechanisms are represented. A 7SK small nuclear RNA complex, built around HEXIM1 and the RNA-binding chaperone LARP7, sequesters and inactivates the positive transcription elongation factor P-TEFb, denying viral promoters the CDK9 activity they need for productive elongation; the HIV-1 Tat protein works by capturing P-TEFb from this reservoir. Separately, a large family of TRIM ubiquitin ligases together with the nuclear body protein SP100 restricts viral gene expression through chromatin-based silencing, interferon-stimulated effector functions, and degradation of viral and host factors. The post-transcriptional regulator ZFP36 and the transcription factor UBP1 add further repressive input, linking this activity to inflammatory gene control.

neurotrophin production covers the synthesis, processing and release of the growth factors that keep developing and mature neurons alive. Target tissues make neurotrophins such as NGF and BDNF in limiting amounts, so the supply set by this pathway determines which innervating neurons survive, how far their axons grow, and how synapses are strengthened during learning; reduced availability contributes to neurodegeneration, neuropathic pain and depression. The genes point to two control points. Proprotein convertases including FURIN and PCSK6 cleave pro-neurotrophins into mature ligands, a step that switches the product from a death-promoting to a survival-promoting signal at TrkA/TrkB versus p75. Trafficking and neuromodulatory inputs, via the huntingtin-associated protein HAP1, adenosine A1 receptors and neuropeptide Y, tune how much factor is packaged and secreted, linking neuronal activity and metabolic state to trophic support.

Neurons survive and extend axons only if their target fields supply trophic support, and neurotrophin production is the synthesis, processing and release of those factors — NGF, BDNF and relatives — that suppress neuronal apoptosis and drive process outgrowth. Loss of this supply during development eliminates neurons that fail to secure enough of it, and in the adult it contributes to degeneration, impaired regeneration after injury, and altered pain and mood signalling. Much of the control is post-translational: proneurotrophins must be cleaved by proprotein convertases such as furin and PCSK6 to yield the mature, TrkA/TrkB-activating ligand, since the unprocessed precursors act through p75 to favour cell death instead. Vesicular trafficking and activity-dependent secretion set how much is actually delivered, with HAP1 implicated in BDNF transport, and neuromodulators including adenosine and neuropeptide Y tuning release.

TGF-beta1 is the dominant driver of tissue fibrosis and of immune tolerance, and this pathway covers the events that raise its levels, whether by inducing transcription of the cytokine or by processing and liberating it from latent stores. Output matters because too much sustains scarring in kidney, lung and liver, while too little unleashes autoimmunity; the presence of FOXP3 here reflects the regulatory T cell arm, where TGF-beta1 enforces peripheral tolerance and is itself part of the suppressive output. Control operates at several levels: AP-1 family transcription factors such as JUN and FOSL2 and lineage factors like GATA6 act on the gene, the proprotein convertase FURIN cleaves the precursor, and matrix and surface proteins including THBS1, COL3A1 and LUM influence activation of the latent complex. IL13 signalling and macrophage adaptors such as TYROBP link inflammatory cues to increased production.

This is the control of how much TGF-beta2 a cell makes and releases, a step that sets the local dose of a cytokine governing extracellular matrix deposition, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, immune suppression and tissue remodelling. Output of TGFB2 matters most in development: it shapes cardiac outflow tract and valve formation, palate and eye morphogenesis, and its dysregulation contributes to fibrosis, to glaucoma through aqueous humour composition, and to the immune evasion of tumours. Production is transcriptionally driven rather than stored, so the regulators here are largely nuclear or upstream of the nucleus: the stress-responsive factor ATF2, the hypoxia sensor HIF1A, and the lineage factor GATA6 act on the gene, while SMAD3 and SMAD4 relay TGF-beta family signals back onto it as feed-forward amplification. BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A and non-canonical WNT11 input link this ligand's synthesis to broader morphogen fields.

TGF-beta1 is a cytokine that drives extracellular matrix deposition, restrains inflammation and supports regulatory T cell function, so how much of it a cell makes and how much is released in active form is tightly controlled. This regulatory layer sets the balance between tissue repair and fibrosis: too much sustained output underlies kidney and lung fibrosis, cardiac remodelling and tumour immune evasion, while too little permits autoimmunity. Control operates at several levels. Transcriptional and immune inputs come from a lineage-defining regulatory T cell transcription factor, a developmental GATA factor and IL-13 signalling through its receptors. Proprotein processing by furin generates the mature growth factor, and the secreted matrix protein thrombospondin-1 liberates TGF-beta1 from its latent complex. Additional membrane and matrix components, including a renin receptor subunit and podocyte and myeloid adaptors, tune production in kidney, vascular and immune settings.

TGF-beta1 is a potent driver of fibrosis, immune suppression and extracellular matrix deposition, so the amount a cell releases must be held in check; this pathway covers the processes that reduce TGF-beta1 production. Restraining output matters in kidney podocytes, lung and liver, where unchecked TGF-beta1 promotes scarring, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and progressive organ failure, and in immune cells where it dampens effector responses. The contributing genes act at several levels: transcriptional control by a GATA-family factor, proprotein convertase-dependent handling of the latent precursor, adaptor and lysosomal membrane proteins that shape trafficking and receptor-proximal signalling, and an immunoreceptor signalling adaptor used by myeloid cells. Together they set the ceiling on latent TGF-beta1 available for activation, linking this regulation to fibrotic disease, wound healing and the control of inflammatory tone.

TGF-beta1 is made as a latent complex and its availability is set as much by how much is produced as by how it is unleashed, so processes that raise TGF-beta1 output shape tissue repair, fibrosis and immune tolerance. Increased production drives fibroblast activation and extracellular matrix deposition in kidney, heart and lung, and supports the suppressive function of regulatory T cells, where FOXP3 defines the lineage that relies on this cytokine to restrain other effector cells. Thrombospondin-1 is the best-characterised member here, binding latent TGF-beta1 and converting it to its active form; the (pro)renin receptor ATP6AP2 couples renin-angiotensin signalling to profibrotic TGF-beta1 induction, and the chemokine CX3CL1 links recruited monocytes and macrophages to the same output. Sustained upregulation underlies progressive organ fibrosis and immunosuppressive tumour microenvironments.

Nearly every tissue runs a self-sustaining 24-hour transcriptional cycle that aligns metabolism, sleep-wake behaviour and hormone release with the day, and this is the machinery that generates it. A heterodimer of CLOCK or NPAS2 with BMAL1 drives transcription of its own repressors, PER1-3 and CRY1/2, which feed back to shut the activator off; casein kinases CSNK1D/E and ubiquitin ligases set the delay that fixes the period near a day. Nuclear receptors including NR1D1, RORA and PPARA relay the clock onto lipid and glucose genes, while chromatin regulators such as HDAC1-3, SIRT1, KDM5A and OGT couple oscillation to NAD+ and nutrient state. Disruption of this circadian control of gene expression produces sleep-phase disorders, metabolic syndrome and the shift-work phenotypes of impaired glucose handling and tumour predisposition.

Activins, nodal and related TGF-beta superfamily ligands act through this receptor pathway to set body axes in the embryo and to tune reproductive and endocrine output in the adult. Ligand binding brings type II receptors such as ACVR2A and ACVR2B together with type I kinases including ACVR1B and ACVR1C, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3; these partner with SMAD4 and transcription factors like FOXH1 to drive target genes, with TGIF1, SKI and inhibitory SMAD6/SMAD7 damping the response. Availability of ligand is controlled extracellularly by follistatin, inhibin alpha, cerberus and DAND5, and by EGF-CFC coreceptors required for nodal signalling. The pathway specifies mesendoderm and left-right asymmetry, regulates FSH secretion and gonadal function, and contributes to iron sensing through hemojuvelin; disrupted signalling underlies laterality defects, heterotopic ossification and vascular malformation syndromes.

Activins signal through type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors to SMAD2/3, controlling follicle-stimulating hormone output from the pituitary, gonadal development, mesoderm patterning in the early embryo and tissue growth in adults; how strongly that pathway fires is set by the regulators collected here. Extracellular antagonists bind ligand directly or block receptor access — follistatin and its relative FSTL3, the inhibin alpha subunit that forms a decoy dimer with an activin beta subunit, and cerberus- and DAND5-type Nodal/activin inhibitors that shape left-right and head-trunk axes. Inside the cell, FKBP1A restrains the unliganded receptor, the inhibitory SMADs 6 and 7 recruit SMURF1 to degrade receptors, and SKI and DACT proteins damp transcriptional output. Loss of this restraint distorts embryonic patterning, gonadal differentiation and pituitary hormone control; the same receptors carry bone morphogenetic protein signals whose overactivity ossifies soft tissue.

negative regulation of activin receptor signaling pathway restrains signalling through activin type I and II receptors and the SMAD2/3 branch of the TGF-beta superfamily, setting how much activin output a cell receives. This braking is what allows graded mesoderm patterning in the embryo, controls pituitary FSH synthesis, and limits activin-driven growth suppression and fibrosis in adult tissues. Restraint acts at every level: secreted follistatin and FSTL3 sequester activin dimers, inhibin alpha pairs with beta subunits to form antagonistic inhibin and competes for receptors with betaglycan, and cerberus and DAND5 block ligand in the node. At the membrane FKBP1A guards the type I receptor from premature phosphorylation, while inhibitory SMAD6/7 recruit SMURF1 to ubiquitinate receptors and SMADs, and nuclear SKI and LEMD3 silence SMAD-dependent transcription. Loss of these controls skews reproductive endocrine output and developmental axis formation.

Activin signalling drives mesoderm patterning, gonadal function and pituitary FSH output, and the brakes on it set how much of that signal a cell actually receives. Negative regulation of activin receptor signalling operates at every level: secreted follistatin and follistatin-like 3 sequester activin ligands, Cerberus and the DAN-family antagonists Dand5 block ligand access during early embryonic patterning, and inhibin alpha pairs with a beta subunit to form inhibin, a competitive antagonist that restrains pituitary gonadotropin release. At the receptor, FKBP1A binds the unphosphorylated type I receptor to prevent leaky activation, while inhibitory Smads 6 and 7 recruit the ubiquitin ligase SMURF1 to degrade receptors and SKI represses Smad-driven transcription. Loss of these restraints gives excess Smad2/3 output, and mutations in several components cause skeletal overgrowth, heterotopic ossification and central hypothyroidism, illustrating how tightly this arm of TGF-beta family signalling must be dosed.

positive regulation of activin receptor signaling pathway covers the events that turn up transmission through activin receptors, the TGF-beta family route that controls follicle-stimulating hormone output, gonadal and reproductive development, erythroid maturation, pancreatic islet and mesodermal patterning, and the balance between cell proliferation and growth arrest in epithelia. Activins bind type II receptors ACVR2A and ACVR2B, which recruit and activate the type I kinase ACVR1B; that kinase phosphorylates SMAD2 and SMAD3, which enter the nucleus with SMAD4 to reprogram transcription. Enhancement can come from increased receptor availability and complex formation, from kinases such as casein kinase 2 that modify receptor or SMAD activity, from cooperating growth factor input including FGF9, and from RNA-binding regulators of the pathway's transcripts. Because activin signaling restrains growth in many tissues, its amplification shapes tumor suppression, wound healing, and the fibrotic and inflammatory response.

Activin signalling, a branch of the TGF-beta superfamily, controls reproductive endocrine function, mesoderm patterning and the follicle-stimulating hormone axis, and this grouping covers the influences that raise its output. Activin binds a type II receptor, ACVR2A or ACVR2B, which recruits and activates the type I kinase ACVR1B to phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3 and drive transcription of growth-inhibitory and differentiation genes. Casein kinase 2 activity and modulatory factors such as FGF9 and the zinc-finger protein ZC3H3 act as positive inputs that increase receptor complex activity or reinforce downstream transduction. Because activin signalling restrains proliferation in many epithelia and governs gonadal and pituitary hormone production, strengthening this route affects fertility, pancreatic and hepatic differentiation, and tumour cell growth arrest; loss of the same receptors is recurrent in several cancers.

Superoxide is made deliberately, chiefly by the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, and its generation is tuned rather than left free-running; this pathway covers the inputs that raise or damp that output. It matters most in innate immunity, where the oxidative burst kills ingested microbes, and in vascular and neural tissue, where excess superoxide drives oxidative injury and endothelial dysfunction. Receptors sensing microbial and inflammatory cues — a fungal β-glucan lectin, a formyl peptide receptor, a protease-activated receptor, and the integrin CD11b/CD18 pair — feed through Syk and its adaptor TYROBP and through protein kinase C isoforms onto the oxidase, whose p22phox subunit is encoded by CYBA. Countervailing components limit the burst: SOD1 dismutates superoxide to peroxide, TGFB1 suppresses activation, and glutathione transferase and paraoxonase activities buffer the resulting oxidative load.

Glands and epithelia release fluid, mucus and protein products in a regulated way, and this pathway collects the machinery by which whole tissues do so. It underlies salivary and tear secretion, airway and intestinal mucus output, pancreatic enzyme release and the water and electrolyte transport that keeps mucosal surfaces hydrated. Muscarinic, purinergic and other G protein-coupled receptors on secretory cells raise intracellular calcium, which opens the calcium-activated chloride channel ANO1 and the potassium channel KCNN4 to drive anion efflux, while aquaporins AQP1 and AQP5 allow water to follow. Bicarbonate transporters and the WNK/STK39 kinase network set the ionic composition of the secreted fluid, and VAMP-family SNAREs execute granule fusion. Goblet cell products such as MUC2, with AGR2 required for mucin folding, and salivary proteins including statherin and lacritin are the cargo; loss of this control produces dry mouth and eye, and mucus abnormalities in airway and gut disease.

Cytokinesis has to be timed and positioned precisely, and this small group of regulators tunes how fast and how completely the final split of a dividing cell proceeds. Failure gives binucleate cells, unresolved intercellular bridges and the aneuploidy that follows, so control here feeds directly into genome stability. The genes act at two connected points: signalling that specifies where the cleavage furrow forms and ingresses, with ECT2 serving as the RhoA-directed exchange factor at the central spindle, and membrane delivery to the intercellular bridge, where RAB11A with its effector RAB11FIP3, ARF6 and the exocyst component EXOC7 route recycling-endosome vesicles to the site of abscission. KIF20B contributes at the midbody to bridge organisation and timely severing, placing this biology at the interface of cytoskeletal contractility and polarised trafficking during the last stage of mitosis.

Inositol trisphosphate sits at the centre of calcium signalling: IP3 released into the cytosol opens endoplasmic reticulum calcium channels, and its rate of production and onward conversion sets how strongly and how long a cell responds to a stimulus. Metabolism of this second messenger therefore governs secretion, smooth muscle tone, platelet activation and lymphocyte responses. Phospholipase C enzymes, both the G protein-coupled beta form and the tyrosine kinase-coupled gamma form, generate IP3 by cleaving membrane phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate, acting downstream of receptors for nucleotides, neurotensin, platelet-activating factor, gonadotropin and estrogen. Kinases including IPMK, ITPK1 and the B-type inositol trisphosphate 3-kinase then phosphorylate IP3 further, terminating the calcium-releasing signal while feeding higher inositol polyphosphates that regulate transcription, chromatin and nuclear export. Disruption skews calcium transients and the receptor signalling that depends on them.

Inositol phosphates are the cell's soluble second-messenger and signalling-currency family, and this biosynthetic route builds them by stepwise phosphorylation of the inositol ring. Its immediate product, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate generated by phospholipase C downstream of G protein-coupled receptors such as those for vasopressin, parathyroid hormone, neurotensin and ADP, releases calcium from internal stores and so drives secretion, contraction and immune activation. Beyond that, dedicated kinases elaborate the higher species: ITPK enzymes add phosphates to InsP3, IPMK and IPPK complete the route to inositol hexakisphosphate, IP6K family members generate pyrophosphorylated InsP7, and PPIP5K enzymes extend this to InsP8. These highly phosphorylated forms regulate phosphate sensing, insulin secretion, mRNA export, vesicle trafficking and chromatin-associated processes. Loss of flux through the pathway blunts calcium signalling and disturbs metabolic and phosphate homeostasis, linking receptor activation to durable changes in cell behaviour.

Formation of inositol trisphosphate is the step that converts receptor occupancy at the cell surface into a rise in cytosolic calcium. IP3 generated from membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate diffuses to its receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum and releases stored calcium, while the co-product diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C; together these drive secretion, contraction, platelet activation and lymphocyte responses. The genes here represent both ends of that step: G protein-coupled receptors for nucleotides, neurotensin, luteinizing hormone/chorionic gonadotropin, platelet-activating factor and estrogen that couple to phospholipase C, and PLCG2, the phospholipase C isoform used by immune receptors and regulated by tyrosine kinases. Loss or gain of signalling through this route disturbs calcium-dependent hormone responses, haemostasis and B cell function, and activating PLCG2 variants cause inherited immune dysregulation.</description

Control over how much inositol trisphosphate a cell makes sets the pace of calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum, and with it contraction, secretion, and calcium-dependent gene expression. The receptors here are the upstream switches for that decision: purinergic receptors for extracellular ATP/ADP and UDP, the neurotensin receptor, the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor, and a membrane estrogen receptor. Each is a G protein-coupled receptor that, largely through Gq, engages phospholipase C to cleave PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, so ligand availability and receptor abundance directly tune second messenger output. The physiological consequences are tissue-specific: gonadal steroidogenesis and ovulation, platelet activation and vascular tone, smooth muscle and inflammatory responses to nucleotides released from damaged cells. Loss or gain of signalling at these receptors produces endocrine and hemostatic disease, illustrating that calcium mobilisation is regulated chiefly at the receptor step.

Collagen is the load-bearing protein of skin, bone, tendon and basement membranes, and this pathway covers its whole life cycle: synthesis and post-translational maturation, secretion and fibril assembly, then turnover and degradation. Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases together with the collagen-specific chaperone HSP47 and the mRNA-binding regulator LARP6 make procollagen foldable and secretable; procollagen N-propeptidases of the ADAMTS2/3/14 group and the enhancer PCOLCE trim propeptides so triple helices can pack into fibres. Breakdown is handled by matrix metalloproteinases, including the interstitial collagenases MMP1, MMP8 and MMP13, and by lysosomal cathepsins such as cathepsin K in bone resorption, with uptake via the endocytic receptor MRC2. TGF-beta, IL-6, HIF1A, WNT4 and several microRNAs set the balance. Loss of hydroxylation or propeptide processing causes osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, while unrestrained deposition underlies fibrosis and tumour stroma remodelling.

Collagen biosynthesis produces the triple-helical fibrous proteins that give tendon, bone, skin and vessel walls their tensile strength, and its output defines the extracellular matrix on which tissue architecture and wound healing depend. Because collagen chains are glycine- and proline-rich and must be chemically modified before they can fold, the pathway is as much about post-translational processing as about transcription: prolyl 3-hydroxylases and lysyl hydroxylases such as PLOD1-3 modify the nascent chains, the collagen-specific chaperone SERPINH1 (HSP47) assists helix assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum, and procollagen peptidases including PCOLCE and ADAMTS3 cleave propeptides so fibrils can form. Transcriptional and signalling inputs from TGFB1, BMP4, SCX and RUNX1, together with translational control by LARP6 and repression by miR-29 family members, set how much collagen a cell makes. Excess drives fibrosis and scarring; deficient or mismodified collagen underlies osteogenesis imperfecta and Ehlers-Danlos-type connective tissue fragility.

Control over how actin filaments are nucleated, elongated, capped, bundled, severed and contracted determines cell shape, motility, adhesion, division and muscle function, and this regulatory layer is what tunes those outcomes to external cues. Rho-family GTPases (RHOA, RAC1, CDC42) with their many exchange factors and GAPs sit at the centre, relaying signals from growth factor and chemokine receptors, integrins and cell-cell junctions to effectors such as ROCK kinases, PAK kinases, formins and the Arp2/3 complex with its WAVE and WASP activators. Filament turnover is set by cofilin and its regulators LIM kinases and slingshot phosphatases, by profilin, gelsolin, thymosin, capping proteins and tropomodulins, while spectrins, ezrin-radixin-moesin proteins and tropomyosins organise cortical and sarcomeric arrays. Disturbance of this regulation impairs wound healing, immune cell migration, podocyte and epithelial barrier integrity, and cardiac and smooth muscle contraction, and contributes to tumour invasion.

Some mitochondrial inner membrane proteins reach the bilayer not from the cytosol but from inside, and this route handles their insertion from the matrix side. It serves two classes of client: hydrophobic subunits translated on mitochondrial ribosomes, such as the core subunits of cytochrome c oxidase, and nuclear-encoded proteins that are first imported into the matrix and then integrated. Without it the respiratory chain and ATP synthase cannot be built, so the pathway sits upstream of oxidative phosphorylation itself. OXA1L is the central insertase, COX18 a related translocase dedicated to oxidase assembly, and BCS1L an AAA-ATPase that delivers the Rieske iron-sulfur subunit of complex III. Mutations produce mitochondrial disease, including the tubulopathy-encephalopathy-liver failure syndrome caused by BCS1L defects and optic atrophy from loss of TMEM126A.

Macromolecular assemblies must be taken apart as well as built, and this collection covers the machinery that drives protein-containing complex disassembly across many cellular settings. Cytoskeletal turnover dominates: cofilin and destrin sever actin filaments, gelsolin and villin cap and cut them, capping-protein and tropomodulin subunits terminate filament ends, while stathmins, katanin regulators and kinesin-13 family depolymerases such as KIF2A and KIF2C strip tubulin from microtubule ends. Spastin and the AAA-ATPase VCP use mechanical unfolding to disassemble filaments and ubiquitinated substrates. SNARE complexes are recycled after fusion by NSF with its SNAP adaptors, and ESCRT-III subunits are recycled from membranes by VPS4. Ribosome recycling factors release stalled subunits, chromatin remodellers evict nucleosomes, and autophagy components dismantle aggregates. Without such disassembly, cells cannot remodel their shape, divide, recycle vesicle fusion machinery, or clear damaged protein assemblies.

Taking protein-DNA complexes apart is as necessary as building them: nucleosomes and other DNA-bound assemblies must be loosened or dismantled before polymerases, repair enzymes and transcription factors can reach the underlying sequence. This disassembly activity underlies transcriptional activation, replication fork progression, DNA repair access and the wholesale replacement of histones by protamines during spermatid maturation, marked here by transition protein TNP1. Much of the work is ATP-dependent: the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling complex, represented by its SMARCA4 catalytic subunit together with SMARCB1, SMARCC1/2, ARID1A and ARID2, uses ATP hydrolysis to slide and evict nucleosomes, while the FACT heterodimer of SSRP1 and SUPT16H destabilises nucleosomes ahead of elongating polymerase and reassembles them behind. Histone chaperones such as SET and architectural factors like HMGA1 contribute by binding histones or bending DNA. Loss of SWI/SNF subunits is a common event in cancer.

Ribonucleoprotein assemblies have to be taken apart as well as built, and this pathway covers the disassembly of protein-RNA complexes back into free protein and RNA. It matters most for the clearance of stress granules and related condensates once stress subsides, and for recycling spliceosomal components after splicing: persistent, unresolved RNP aggregates are a feature of neurodegenerative disease. The AAA-ATPase VCP provides much of the mechanical force, recruited to granules through cofactors including ZFAND1 and the membrane-anchored adaptor FAF2, while ubiquitin signalling via TRIM21 marks substrates for removal. The kinase DYRK3 acts as a solubility switch that promotes dissolution of condensates, TFIP11 works on the intron lariat spliceosome, and kinesin-1 subunits link granule remodelling to microtubule transport. Together these activities restore free mRNA and protein to the translational and splicing pools.

Muscle cell proliferation covers the mitotic expansion of muscle cell populations — skeletal myoblasts and satellite cells, cardiomyocytes, and vascular smooth muscle cells — and the controls that decide when such cells divide rather than differentiate or remain quiescent. It underlies muscle growth and regeneration after injury, cardiac development and hypertrophic remodelling, and pathologically the neointimal thickening of atherosclerosis, restenosis and pulmonary hypertension. Growth factor and cytokine inputs (PDGF, FGF, IGF1, TGF-beta/BMP, neuregulin, interleukins and TNF) converge on PI3K-AKT, MAPK and JAK-STAT signalling and on cell cycle regulators such as CCNB1, CDK1 and the inhibitors CDKN1A and CDKN1B. Myogenic and cardiac transcription factors including MYOG, MEF2, SIX1, MYOCD and NKX2-5, Notch and Hippo-YAP signalling, and an extensive set of microRNAs including miR-1, miR-133 and miR-143/145 set the balance between proliferation and terminal differentiation.

Muscle cell populations expand by division during development, growth and repair, and this programme covers the signals that drive or restrain that expansion in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. It matters for heart chamber growth and cardiomyocyte cell-cycle exit after birth, for satellite-cell amplification during regeneration, and for the vascular smooth muscle proliferation that thickens vessel walls in atherosclerosis, hypertension and restenosis. Growth factor inputs such as PDGF-BB acting through PDGFRB, IGF1, FGF2 and neuregulin converge on PI3K-AKT and MAPK signalling, while TGF-beta and BMP ligands, Notch, Wnt/beta-catenin, Hippo effectors YAP1 and VGLL4, and myostatin set limits. Cyclin B1-CDK1 and the inhibitors CDKN1A and CDKN1B gate the division itself, and myogenic regulators including MYOG, MYOCD, MEF2 factors and SIX1 couple proliferation to differentiation. Inflammatory cytokines and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the muscle-enriched miR-1 and miR-133 family, tune the response.

Mast cells release histamine, proteases and lipid mediators within seconds of IgE crosslinking, so the tuning of mast cell activation sets the threshold between useful antiparasitic and barrier responses and the wheal, bronchoconstriction and anaphylaxis of allergic disease. Most of the genes here dampen rather than trigger that response: inhibitory surface receptors such as CD300A, CD300LF and the mast-cell-restricted allergin MILR1 recruit the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN6 to blunt signalling from the high-affinity IgE receptor, while PTPRE and the RAB5 exchange factor RABGEF1 restrain downstream kinase and trafficking events. LYN and FER act as Src-family and cytoplasmic kinases that can both propagate and negatively feed back on receptor signalling. Other members supply extrinsic context, including TSLP acting through its receptor chain CRLF2 and cannabinoid receptor CNR2, linking epithelial alarmins and neuroimmune input to how readily a mast cell degranulates.

Mast cells release histamine, proteases and lipid mediators within seconds of IgE crosslinking, so restraining that release is what keeps immune surveillance from becoming allergy or anaphylaxis. Negative regulation of mast cell activation is the braking arm of this system: inhibitory surface receptors bearing ITIM motifs, including CD300A, CD300LF, CD84 and the mast cell–specific allergin MILR1, recruit the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 encoded by PTPN6, which dephosphorylates components of the high-affinity IgE receptor signalling cascade and damps calcium mobilisation and degranulation. Other brakes act differently: the cannabinoid receptor CNR2 couples to inhibitory G protein signalling, the ectoenzyme ENPP3 limits responses by hydrolysing extracellular nucleotides, and RABGEF1 restrains downstream trafficking and signalling. Loss of these controls leaves mast cells hyperresponsive, a state associated with atopic dermatitis, chronic urticaria and exaggerated anaphylactic reactions, and makes these receptors attractive targets for allergy therapy.

Mast cells sit in tissues at barrier surfaces and release histamine, proteases, prostaglandins and cytokines when triggered, driving immediate hypersensitivity, allergic inflammation and antiparasite defence. Positive regulation of mast cell activation covers the signals that lower the threshold for, or amplify, that degranulation and mediator output. Epithelial-derived TSLP acting through its receptor chain CRLF2 is a central example, conditioning mast cells in allergic airway and skin disease and linking damaged or irritated epithelium to type 2 inflammation. Adhesion-receptor engagement between CD226 and its ligand NECTIN2 provides costimulatory input, HAVCR1 contributes a surface sensing arm, and intracellular components such as sphingosine kinase generating sphingosine-1-phosphate and the nuclear receptor NR4A3 shape the transcriptional and lipid-mediator response. Excessive activity here underlies asthma, atopic dermatitis and anaphylaxis, making these steps therapeutic targets.

Mast cells release histamine, proteases and lipid mediators within seconds of IgE cross-linking, so the strength of that response has to be held in check; this is the regulatory layer that sets how readily and how strongly mast cells fire during an immune response. Its output determines whether degranulation stays proportionate to a parasite or allergen challenge or tips into allergic inflammation, anaphylaxis and chronic urticaria. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CD300A raise the threshold for activation, while the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1, encoded by PTPN6, dampens signalling downstream of the IgE receptor by removing activating phosphorylations; the kinase FER and sphingosine kinase 2, which generates sphingosine-1-phosphate, tune the same signalling network. The ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase ENPP3 is induced on activated mast cells and feeds back on nucleotide-driven stimulation, linking purinergic cues to mediator release.

Tetrapyrroles are the four-ring pigments that let cells carry oxygen, run respiration and perform methyl transfer, so the reactions that build, transport and dismantle them determine whether a cell can make haem, cobalamin cofactors and bile pigments. The biosynthetic arm runs from glycine and succinyl-CoA through ALAS1 or the erythroid-specific ALAS2, the cytosolic steps of ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD and CPOX, and back into mitochondria for PPOX and ferrochelatase, which inserts iron; blocks at individual enzymes cause the porphyrias, with photosensitivity or neurovisceral attacks from accumulated intermediates, while defects in the mitochondrial glycine and iron supply lines such as SLC25A38 give sideroblastic anaemia. Degradation by HMOX1 and HMOX2 yields biliverdin, reduced by biliverdin reductase to bilirubin and conjugated by UGT1A1 for excretion. Membrane transporters, haem-binding proteins and cobalamin processing factors move these reactive pigments safely between compartments and tissues.

Tetrapyrrole biosynthesis builds the four-ring macrocycles that cells use as pigments and cofactors, principally heme, which carries oxygen in hemoglobin, holds the redox centres of cytochromes and catalase, and supports the cytochrome P450s. The route begins with condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA by ALAS1 in most tissues and the erythroid-specific ALAS2, proceeds through ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX, and ends with ferrochelatase inserting ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX. Because the pathway is split between mitochondrion and cytosol, transporters matter as much as enzymes: SLC25A38 supplies glycine to the matrix, ABCB10 and ABCB7 serve mitochondrial export steps, and FLVCR1 removes excess heme. Iron availability and IREB2-mediated sensing tie flux to iron status. Enzyme defects cause the porphyrias, with photosensitivity and neurovisceral attacks, or sideroblastic anaemia when erythroid supply fails.

Tetrapyrrole catabolism is the route by which the cell dismantles heme and related four-ring pigments, and in humans it is dominated by the daily turnover of hemoglobin heme from senescent red cells. Heme oxygenases open the porphyrin ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and yielding biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases reduce to bilirubin; the inducible isoform HMOX1 also serves as a stress-response and cytoprotective enzyme. Bilirubin is then glucuronidated by UGT1A1 and exported across membranes by ABCC transporters, while organic anion transporters of the SLCO family take it up into hepatocytes for biliary excretion. Loss of conjugating capacity produces the unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemias, from Gilbert syndrome to Crigler-Najjar, and neonatal jaundice with risk of kernicterus. The pathway thus links iron recycling, antioxidant defence and bile pigment clearance.

Programmed death of cells in the monocyte, granulocyte, mast cell, megakaryocyte and erythroid lineages sets the lifespan of the innate immune and blood-forming compartments. Because neutrophils and monocytes are produced in enormous numbers and carry destructive cargo, their timely apoptotic clearance is how inflammation resolves; too much of it produces neutropenia and failed erythropoiesis, too little sustains tissue damage and contributes to chronic inflammatory disease and myeloid leukaemia. Survival signals dominate the regulation here: erythropoietin acting through STAT5A keeps erythroid precursors alive, BCL2 restrains mitochondrial permeabilisation, and PI3K catalytic subunits relay growth factor and receptor input, while ANXA1, MIF and IL6 shape whether inflammatory myeloid cells persist or die. Transcriptional and epigenetic regulators including MEF2C, SIRT1 and CDKN2A tie the decision to differentiation state, and efferocytosis of the dying cells completes the process.</br>

Neutrophils are short-lived by design, and their programmed death is how acute inflammation is brought to an end; promoting neutrophil apoptosis allows macrophages to clear spent cells before they release proteases and oxidants into tissue. Failure to accelerate this death prolongs neutrophil survival at inflamed sites and contributes to tissue injury in conditions such as acute lung injury, arthritis and chronic airway disease, whereas the same process is exploited pharmacologically to resolve inflammation. Annexin A1, the glucocorticoid-inducible mediator of inflammatory resolution, acts on neutrophils to drive their apoptosis and subsequent efferocytosis. Receptor inputs including the IgA receptor and the hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor engaged by niacin and ketone bodies feed into this outcome, while class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic subunits set the balance between survival signalling and death, linking receptor engagement at the neutrophil surface to the timing of inflammatory resolution.

regulation of myeloid cell apoptotic process sets how long neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages and erythroid progenitors survive, and thereby determines both the size of the innate immune pool and how quickly inflammation resolves. Granulocytes are constitutively short-lived, so tuning their death is the main lever controlling their numbers: survival signals such as erythropoietin acting through STAT5A, growth-factor and immune-receptor input via PI3K catalytic subunits and Fc receptor adaptors, and BCL2-family control of the mitochondrial death step all raise the apoptotic threshold, while anti-inflammatory mediators including annexin A1 and adiponectin, and stress arbiters such as CDKN2A and cystine transport through SLC7A11, push cells toward death or ferroptotic vulnerability. Failure in either direction matters clinically: excessive myeloid apoptosis produces neutropenia and anemia, while blocked apoptosis sustains chronic inflammatory tissue damage and permits myeloid leukemic expansion. The pathway also covers macrophage clearance and erythroblast maturation decisions.

Neutrophils, monocytes and erythroid precursors are short-lived by design, and this pathway sets how fast they die. Organelles are not static structures: they are built, positioned, remodelled and taken apart on cue, and this broad regulatory programme sets how fast and how far those events go. It underlies mitotic fidelity, mitochondrial quality control, cytoskeletal remodelling and membrane traffic, so its outputs touch cell division, neuronal morphology, muscle architecture and autophagic clearance. Loss of such control produces aneuploidy, ciliopathies, neurodegeneration and defective organelle turnover.

Chromosomes must be compacted, held together, capped at their ends and then segregated accurately, and this set covers the controls that set how far and how fast those rearrangements go. Its outputs are genome stability and faithful mitosis: when the regulation fails, cells missegregate chromosomes, become aneuploid, or lose telomere protection and fuse chromosome ends, routes that underlie tumorigenesis and developmental and ageing syndromes. Cells that lose it missegregate chromosomes and become aneuploid, a route to tumourigenesis and to miscarriage when it fails in meiosis. Pigment cells make colour by building a specialized lysosome-related organelle, filling it with melanin, and moving it to where the pigment is needed, and this cellular pigmentation programme is what these genes serve. Its output is skin, hair and eye colour, photoprotection of the epidermis, and the pigmented support of the retina; loss of it produces albinism and the hypopigmentation seen alongside bleeding and immune defects in Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes. T cell differentiation in the thymus is the route by which bone marrow-derived progenitors become mature CD4 and CD8 T cells, supplying the adaptive immune system with a repertoire that recognizes foreign antigen while sparing self. Thymic epithelium sets the stage through FOXN1-driven niche programmes and Wnt, Notch ligand, hedgehog and BMP cues; committed thymocytes rearrange their antigen receptor genes using RAG1/RAG2 and non-homologous end joining factors such as PRKDC and LIG4, then survive or die according to the strength of receptor signalling through CD3 chains, ZAP70 and RASGRP1, with IL-7 receptor and STAT5 sustaining survival and proliferation. Most T cells acquire their identity in the thymus, but some mature or are reshaped outside it, and this extrathymic differentiation route is what the genes here describe. Butyrophilin-like molecules displayed by intestinal epithelium engage particular T cell receptor Vgamma chains and shape the local repertoire; interleukin-15 presented by epithelial and myeloid cells sustains survival and cytotoxic arming. Transcriptional regulators including Hobit and Blimp-1 then impose the tissue-residency programme, suppressing egress and driving effector gene expression. Disturbance of this axis features in coeliac disease and in the lymphomas that arise from intraepithelial T cells.

Before T cells acquire a functional receptor and leave the thymus, immature thymocyte populations must expand enormously, and proliferation of immature T cells describes the division that generates this pool. The output determines how broad the T cell repertoire will be, so defects constrain thymic cellularity and peripheral immune competence, while unchecked division of the same precursors underlies T-lineage leukaemia. Inflammatory cytokines such as IL1A and IL1B, adhesion and lectin receptors, and FOXP3 link this expansion to thymic selection and regulatory T cell output.

Thymocytes that have not yet completed selection must expand in number before they can generate a diverse T cell repertoire, and this proliferative burst in the thymus sets the size of the peripheral T cell pool. Output depends on signals from the thymic stromal niche: hedgehog ligands, WNT4 and BMP4 act on developing thymocytes to set the pace of division and the progression between developmental stages, while inflammatory cytokines such as IL1A and IL1B modulate the environment. Restraint is equally part of the programme, with the CDKN2A locus imposing cell-cycle arrest and BMI1 repressing it to permit self-renewal; TMEM131L tempers surface receptor signalling in early thymocytes. Too little expansion yields lymphopenia and poor immune coverage; unchecked division in this compartment is the origin of T cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

Thymocytes only become functional T cells if their maturation is paced correctly, and this is the set of influences that tune how fast and how far T cell differentiation proceeds in the thymus. It sets the size and diversity of the peripheral T cell repertoire; when it fails, the result is immunodeficiency on one side and autoimmunity or thymic lymphoma on the other. Epithelial-derived cues act on the developing cells from outside: FOXN1 programmes the thymic epithelial niche, while Hedgehog ligands and GLI2 together with BMP4 set thresholds for progression through the beta-selection and positive-selection checkpoints. Inside the thymocyte, RAG2 rearranges the antigen receptor, IL7R and IL2RG sustain survival and proliferation, and RASGRP1 with SOS1/SOS2 converts receptor engagement into Ras signalling whose strength is read out by EGR3 and restrained by PTPN2. ADA deficiency blocks the whole sequence, producing severe combined immunodeficiency.

Thymocyte expansion has to be controlled in amount as well as in timing, and this pathway covers the signals that raise or lower how much immature T cells divide before they are selected. The output sets thymus cellularity and the size of the naive T cell pool that leaves it, so both excessive and insufficient proliferation distort later immune competence and can favour lymphoid malignancy. The genes span opposing arms: hedgehog ligands and BMP4 act as stromal cues from the thymic microenvironment, cytokines of the interleukin-1 family and the signalling kinase RIPK2 relay inflammatory input, while BMI1 and the CDKN2A locus set the balance between polycomb-mediated repression and cell cycle arrest in dividing progenitors. FOXP3 links the same regulation to regulatory T cell identity, connecting proliferative control in the thymus with peripheral tolerance.

Thymocyte development has to be held in check as well as driven, and this is the braking side of it: processes that slow, limit or block T cell differentiation in the thymus, setting how many cells pass each developmental checkpoint and how strictly self-reactive clones are filtered out. Restraint comes from several directions. Morphogen signals from thymic stroma, including BMP4 and the hedgehog ligand IHH, dampen progression through the early double-negative and double-positive transitions. The phosphatase PTPN2 removes activating phosphates from JAK/STAT and receptor signalling components, tempering cytokine and TCR input, while CDKN2A limits proliferative expansion of thymocytes. Loss of such restraint biases the thymus toward excess or inappropriately selected T cells, a route to autoimmunity and to lymphoid malignancy, whereas excessive braking starves the periphery of naive T cells.

Thymocyte expansion has to be limited as well as driven, and this pathway covers the signals that restrain proliferation of immature T cells in the thymus. Holding developing thymocytes in check allows selection steps to proceed on a controlled cell number, prevents accumulation of cells that have not yet passed receptor checkpoints, and contributes to the age-related involution of thymic output; loss of such brakes is a route to lymphoid overgrowth and leukaemia. Neuroendocrine and growth factor receptor inputs link systemic hormonal state to thymic cellularity, connecting T cell development to whole-organism physiology.

Thymocyte expansion must be curbed as well as driven, and this pathway covers the signals that dampen proliferation of immature T cells in the thymus. Restraining the progenitor pool sets the size and timing of successive developmental stages, allowing selection to operate on a controlled number of cells; loss of such brakes contributes to thymocyte hyperplasia and lymphoid malignancy. The overall purpose is lineage commitment and repertoire generation for adaptive immunity.

Thymocytes must expand in number before selection can test their receptors, and this pathway covers the signals that push immature T cells to divide. The size and diversity of the peripheral T cell repertoire depend on it, so loss of these inputs yields a small thymus and poor T cell output. Together these inputs tie thymic output to the establishment of self-tolerance and to lymphocyte development generally.

Oxidative phosphorylation depends on multisubunit enzymes built from both nuclear- and mitochondrially-encoded subunits, and this pathway covers their stepwise construction in the inner membrane, including the further association of complexes into supercomplexes. Loss of individual factors produces isolated respiratory chain deficiencies presenting as Leigh syndrome, cardiomyopathy, encephalopathy and lactic acidosis in infancy.

Splicing is not simply switched on; many factors act to block or dampen use of particular splice sites, and that repression is what makes alternative splicing informative rather than random. Silencing of exons broadens the protein output of a single gene and gives tissues their distinct isoform repertoires — the polypyrimidine tract binding proteins PTBP1, PTBP2 and PTBP3 repress neuronal exons and hand over to one another during neural differentiation, while RBM20 restricts titin splicing in heart muscle, and its loss causes dilated cardiomyopathy. Repression operates through intronic and exonic silencer elements, through hnRNP-type and SR-family proteins that compete with activators, and through core spliceosomal components such as PRPF8, SNRNP200 and the Sm proteins whose activity can be constrained at specific sites. Kinase input, including DYRK1A, adjusts these decisions, coupling signalling to isoform choice.

Splicing removes introns and joins exons, and this collection covers the factors that push that reaction forward, raising the rate or extent with which transcripts are spliced. Enhancing splicing efficiency matters because most human genes are intron-containing, and the choice of which sites are used sets protein isoform identity in muscle, neurons and immune cells. Core components include the U1 snRNP protein SNRNP70, the 3' splice site recognition factor U2AF2, SR and SR-like activators such as SRSF5 and TRA2B, and the spliceosomal proteins PRPF19 and RBM22, coupled to transcription through RNA polymerase II and the cap-binding complex. Tissue-restricted regulators such as RBM20 in heart and CELF proteins in brain direct specific alternative events; loss of RBM20 splicing control causes dilated cardiomyopathy. Arginine methylation by PRMT5 with WDR77 modifies Sm proteins and supports snRNP assembly, linking this activity to snRNP biogenesis and surveillance of aberrant mRNA.

Serine phosphorylation is the most common switch in intracellular signalling, and this pathway covers the upstream inputs that raise or lower how much of it occurs on target proteins. Control at this level sets the gain of growth factor and cytokine responses, and its loss underlies unchecked proliferation and inflammatory signalling. The members include the kinases that do the work and the regulators that constrain them: the RAF family relays receptor activation from EGFR through the MAP kinase cascade, AKT1 phosphorylates serine residues on survival and metabolic effectors, and PTEN opposes this by removing the lipid signal that recruits AKT to the membrane. Scaffolds and negative regulators such as SPRY2, RASSF2 and PAQR3 tune cascade output, while secreted factors of the IL-6 family, including OSM and LIF, and interferon-gamma feed in from outside the cell. The balance determines whether signalling drives division, differentiation or apoptosis.

Serine phosphorylation on target proteins is set by the balance between kinases and the brakes applied to them, and this pathway covers the restraining side: factors that reduce the rate or extent of peptidyl-serine phosphorylation and so damp the signalling cascades that depend on it. The consequences are felt in growth control and stress responses, because unchecked serine kinase activity drives proliferation and survival signalling. PTEN is the clearest example, lowering PIP3 and thereby curbing AKT activation and its downstream serine phosphorylation of substrates; GADD45A couples genotoxic stress to stress-kinase signalling; PAQR3 tethers and sequesters upstream components of the RAF-MEK-ERK module at the Golgi. Scaffolds and adaptors such as CNKSR3 and RASSF2 place inhibitory constraints on RAS-family and kinase output. Loss of such negative regulation is a recurring route to tumorigenesis.

Serine phosphorylation is the commonest switch cells use to change protein activity, and this pathway covers the upstream events that increase it — the ligands, receptors, kinases and scaffolds that drive substrate serines to become phosphorylated. Its output determines whether a cell proliferates, survives stress, or differentiates, and mis-set thresholds contribute to tumour growth and to inflammatory disease. The kinases here span the RAF family (ARAF, BRAF, RAF1) feeding the MAPK cascade, the survival kinase AKT1, and the STE20 kinase STK4 acting in Hippo-related apoptotic control, with EGFR supplying receptor-level input and SPRY2 damping it. A second arm is cytokine-driven: IL6, IL11, LIF and OSM signal through shared gp130 receptors, while IFNG engages its own receptor, each converging on serine phosphorylation of transcription factors and adaptors that reprogramme gene expression.

Because receptor output is dose- and context-dependent, its misregulation underlies hormone-driven cancers of the prostate and breast and endocrine resistance to therapy.
