Vitamin A and its derivative retinoic acid act as dietary signals that reprogramme gene expression, and this is the cellular and organismal response to that stimulus: changes in transcription, enzyme production and metabolism triggered when retinoids are sensed. The response matters for embryonic patterning, epithelial differentiation, vision and immune function, and its failure through deficiency or excess causes birth defects and blindness. Nuclear receptors such as RARA and PPARD translate retinoid binding into transcriptional output, acting on targets including GATA4-dependent cardiac and gonadal programmes, erythropoietin production and the DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A. Equally prominent is feedback control of ligand concentration: ALDH1A2 generates retinoic acid from retinal, CYP26A1 and CYP26B1 degrade it, and LRAT esterifies retinol for storage. Additional members link the response to xenobiotic metabolism, lipid hydrolysis, phosphate transport and cytoskeletal remodelling.

Cells encounter hydroperoxides both as products of their own oxidative metabolism and as lipid peroxidation intermediates in membranes, and the response to hydroperoxide stimulus covers how they detect these oxidants and adjust to them. The adjustment matters because unchecked hydroperoxides propagate lipid radical chains, damage DNA, and drive the oxidative injury seen in atherosclerosis, ischaemia and neurodegeneration. Detoxification is handled by glutathione peroxidases, which reduce hydrogen peroxide and organic hydroperoxides at the expense of glutathione, alongside a microsomal glutathione S-transferase. Beyond removal, the genes here link oxidant exposure to signalling and transcription: kinases such as JAK2 and protein kinase C delta relay redox signals, a calcium-permeable TRPM2 channel is gated by oxidative stress, and transcriptional regulators including SP1, SIN3A and the p53-induced TP53INP1 reset gene expression. Base excision repair and scavenger receptor components tie the response to DNA damage and oxidised lipid uptake.

Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects membrane phospholipids from peroxidation, and cells respond to it by adjusting their antioxidant defences, growth signalling and metabolic gene expression. This response matters because tocopherol status influences oxidative damage to membranes and DNA, erythrocyte fragility, and the progression of atherosclerotic and neurodegenerative injury. The genes involved span several arms of that reaction: catalase and glutathione peroxidase handle hydrogen peroxide and lipid hydroperoxides directly, beclin-1 links the stimulus to autophagic turnover of damaged components, cyclin D1 and collagen I expression register effects on proliferation and extracellular matrix deposition, and leptin ties the response to adipose signalling and energy balance. Delta-aminolevulinate dehydratase, a thiol-sensitive heme biosynthetic enzyme, is a classic readout of redox status. Together these represent the transcriptional and enzymatic consequences of tocopherol exposure rather than its transport or metabolism.

Extracellular ATP is a danger and neurotransmitter signal, and this pathway covers how cells detect it and what they do in response. Released from damaged, stressed or stimulated cells, ATP acts on ionotropic P2X channels and G protein-coupled P2Y receptors to trigger calcium entry and mobilisation, platelet aggregation, smooth muscle and sensory responses, and inflammatory activation — P2X7 engagement drives inflammasome-dependent maturation and release of interleukin-1β, while P2Y12 on platelets is the target of widely used antithrombotic drugs. Pannexin channels provide a conduit for ATP release, and ectoenzymes such as ENPP1 and CD73 hydrolyse nucleotides, terminating the signal and generating adenosine with largely opposing effects. Downstream and parallel effectors include TRP channels, ryanodine receptor calcium release and ATP-sensitive potassium channels that couple nucleotide and metabolic state to membrane excitability, insulin secretion and vascular tone. Nociception, purinergic neurotransmission and sterile inflammation all depend on this signalling.

Meiotic cytokinesis is the physical division of the cytoplasm that follows each meiotic nuclear division, converting one germ cell into daughter cells with halved chromosome complements. In oocytes it is markedly asymmetric: a tiny polar body is extruded while the egg retains nearly all cytoplasm and maternal stores, so failure here yields eggs that lose essential reserves or retain extra chromosomes, a route to aneuploid embryos and infertility. The genes point to actin-based force generation rather than generic contractile ring assembly: the Arp2/3 complex with its WASH-family regulator nucleates branched filaments, while formin FMN2 and the Spire proteins cooperate to build the actin networks that position the spindle near the cortex and drive polar body abscission. Additional components link spindle midzone and chromatin cues to the division plane, coupling chromosome segregation to correctly placed cytoplasmic cleavage in gametogenesis.

Division of the cytoplasm following a meiotic nuclear division separates the products of meiosis into distinct daughter cells, and in the female germ line it is what makes an asymmetric division possible: one large oocyte plus a small polar body, preserving maternal stores for the embryo. The gene membership points to actin-based mechanics rather than generic contractile ring biology, with the Arp2/3 subunits ACTR2 and ACTR3 nucleating branched filaments, the formin FMN2 and the Spir actin nucleators SPIRE1 and SPIRE2 cooperating to build filament networks that position the spindle and the division plane, and a WASH complex component linking membrane traffic to actin assembly. CENPV and SHCBP1L act at the centromere and midzone. Failure produces binucleate or aneuploid gametes and oocyte maturation defects, with consequences for fertility and early embryonic viability.

tumor necrosis factor-mediated signaling pathway is the cell's response to TNF and related cytokines, the axis that drives inflammation, fever, and immune cell recruitment while simultaneously deciding whether a cell survives or dies. It is the target of anti-TNF biologics in rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, and its unchecked activation underlies septic shock and chronic inflammatory tissue damage. Ligand binding to TNFRSF1A or related receptors nucleates a membrane complex of TRADD, RIPK1 and TRAF adaptors that, when ubiquitinated by BIRC2/3, XIAP and the LUBAC component SHARPIN, activates IKK and releases NF- inkappaB subunits RELA and NFKB1 to transcribe survival and inflammatory genes. Deubiquitinases CYLD, OTULIN and TNFAIP3 restrain this output; when the survival arm fails, the same complex recruits CASP8 to trigger apoptosis. Related receptors here also govern osteoclast differentiation via RANKL and B cell survival via BAFF, and inflammasome components link the pathway to caspase-1-dependent inflammation.

Tumor necrosis factor binding to its receptors sets a cell's choice between inflammatory gene expression and death, and this signalling underlies fever, acute inflammation, lymphoid organ development and bone remodelling; its chronic overactivation drives rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, which is why TNF blockade is a mainstay of immunotherapy. Ligand is released from the membrane by the metalloprotease ADAM17 and engages TNFRSF1A or TNFRSF1B, recruiting TRADD, RIPK1 and TRAF adaptors that assemble ubiquitin scaffolds supporting IKK activation, degradation of the inhibitor NFKBIA and nuclear entry of NFKB1/RELA, alongside p38 and stress kinase arms. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD, OTULIN and TNFAIP3, together with cIAP proteins and XIAP, restrain the output, while failure of that restraint tips signalling toward caspase-8-dependent apoptosis. Related receptor-ligand pairs here extend the same logic to osteoclast differentiation and B cell survival.

Leptin is secreted by white adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, and the signalling it triggers tells the brain how much energy is stored. Leptin-mediated signalling therefore sets appetite, energy expenditure, and the neuroendocrine response to starvation; loss of the hormone or of its receptor causes severe early-onset obesity and hypogonadism, while obesity more commonly involves resistance to a signal that is already high. Circulating leptin binds LEPR on hypothalamic neurons and activates JAK-associated phosphorylation of STAT3, which enters the nucleus and drives transcription of the melanocortin and neuropeptide genes that suppress feeding. Receptor delivery to the neuronal surface depends on ciliary trafficking proteins including BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS, explaining the obesity of Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and SIRT1 modulates responsiveness, linking the pathway to nutrient-sensing metabolic control more broadly.

Adiponectin is a hormone secreted by fat cells that tells muscle, liver and other tissues to burn fatty acids and take up glucose, and its signalling is the route by which that message is read. Circulating levels fall with obesity, so weak output from this pathway accompanies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver and atherosclerotic inflammation. The hormone binds two seven-transmembrane receptors, ADIPOR1 and ADIPOR2, which unlike classical GPCRs work through the adaptor APPL1; APPL2 opposes it by sequestering the adaptor. Downstream come AMP-activated kinase and PPAR-alpha activation, raising fatty acid oxidation and suppressing gluconeogenesis, with long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase and a fatty acid transport protein linking the signal to actual lipid handling. The pathway therefore connects adipose tissue mass to whole-body energy balance and insulin sensitivity.

Iron import into cell is how cells acquire the iron they need for haem, iron-sulfur clusters, and the many enzymes of respiration and DNA synthesis, moving iron ions from the extracellular space into the cytoplasm either directly across the plasma membrane or through receptor-mediated endocytosis of iron carriers. Duodenal enterocytes depend on it for dietary iron absorption, and hepatocytes and macrophages use it to set systemic iron balance; loss of these transporters causes anaemia, while excess uptake drives tissue iron overload and oxidative damage. Ferric iron is first reduced by surface ferrireductases such as CYBRD1 and the STEAP proteins, then carried inward by divalent metal transporters including SLC11A2 and the SLC39 zinc-iron permeases. Transferrin receptor 2 links uptake to hepcidin-based hormonal control, and siderophore-binding lipocalin-2 and hypoxia-induced miR-210 tune it to inflammation and low oxygen.

Cells acquire iron from their surroundings either by pumping it across the plasma membrane or by internalising iron-loaded carriers, and this import step sets how much iron is available for haem synthesis, iron-sulfur cluster assembly and oxidative metabolism. It matters most in the duodenal enterocyte, where dietary iron enters the body, and in hepatocytes and macrophages that buffer systemic iron; too little causes anaemia, too much drives tissue iron overload. Because only ferrous iron is transported, surface ferrireductases such as CYBRD1 and the STEAP proteins reduce Fe(III) before the divalent metal transporter SLC11A2 carries it into the cytoplasm, with SLC39A8 and SLC39A14 providing additional routes shared with manganese and zinc. A transferrin receptor family member reports iron status to hepatic signalling, secreted lipocalin-2 scavenges siderophore-bound iron, and inflammatory and hypoxic inputs adjust the whole process to demand.

SUMO attachment changes where a protein sits, what it binds and how stable it is, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower how much of it happens. Because SUMO marks concentrate on transcription factors, chromatin regulators and nuclear body components, tuning the modification alters gene expression programmes, DNA damage responses and protein quality control rather than any single enzymatic step. The activating enzyme subunits SAE1 and UBA2 charge SUMO for transfer, PIAS family ligases direct it onto substrates such as NF-κB RelA and so restrain inflammatory transcription, and accessory factors including RWDD3, GNL3L and MAGEA2 either promote conjugation or shield targets from it. CDKN2A and β-catenin link the output to growth control, while mitochondrial MUL1 and PARK7 tie it to organelle and oxidative stress handling. Imbalance contributes to tumour progression and neurodegeneration.

SUMO attachment changes where a protein goes, what it binds and how long it lasts, so restraining that modification is a way of tuning target activity rather than abolishing it. Negative regulation of protein sumoylation covers the processes that block or reverse SUMO conjugation, keeping substrates such as transcription factors and chromatin regulators in their unmodified, often more active state. The genes involved act in several ways: some sequester or occlude E3-like SUMO ligase activity, others compete for substrate lysines or interfere with the conjugating machinery, and some, like the MAGE-A proteins expressed in tumours, suppress sumoylation of transcriptional regulators to alter gene expression. Because desumoylation of factors such as beta-catenin and NF-kB components shifts their stability and target-gene output, this control feeds into Wnt and inflammatory signalling, chromatin repression through LSD1-associated complexes, and stress responses linked to PARK7.

SUMO conjugation tags proteins with a small ubiquitin-like modifier, changing where they go, what they bind, and how long they last, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that reaction faster or more often. Much of the substrate pool is nuclear — transcription factors, chromatin regulators, DNA repair and PML body components — so raising SUMO flux is a way to reshape gene expression and nuclear body assembly without altering protein levels. The SAE1–UBA2 heterodimer activates SUMO in the first, ATP-dependent step of the cascade, while PIAS family proteins act as SUMO E3 ligases that select substrates and accelerate transfer; MUL1 is a mitochondrial ligase with SUMO activity toward fission machinery. Tumour suppressor and nucleolar factors such as CDKN2A and GNL3 feed in as regulators. Because sumoylation restrains transcriptional and stress responses, its enhancement shapes senescence, DNA damage tolerance, and mitochondrial dynamics.

Amines in cells range from neurotransmitters such as dopamine, serotonin and GABA to polyamines, and this pathway covers the controls that set how fast they are made, interconverted and broken down. Tuning amine turnover determines synaptic signalling strength, catecholamine availability and protection against the reactive aldehydes that amine oxidation generates. Several members define dopaminergic neuron biology and its failure in Parkinson disease: the dopamine transporter that clears released transmitter, alpha-synuclein, parkin, DJ-1 and a retromer subunit whose mutations disturb dopamine handling and neuronal survival, together with the transcription factor NR4A2 that specifies the dopaminergic phenotype. Degradative and detoxifying enzymes including GABA transaminase, aldehyde dehydrogenase and a polyamine oxidase act on the catabolic side, while receptors for dopamine, serotonin, neuropeptide Y and tachykinin feed back onto amine synthesis and release, linking this regulation to motor control, mood and neurodegeneration.

Amines encompass polyamines, catecholamines and other biogenic amines whose levels must be held in check, and this is the braking side of that control: processes that slow or shut down the reactions producing and interconverting them. Restraint matters because unchecked polyamine synthesis supports proliferative and tumour growth programmes, while excess catecholamine or dopamine turnover generates reactive intermediates toxic to neurons. The genes here act through several routes rather than one enzyme cascade: alpha-synuclein constrains dopamine synthesis and handling in presynaptic terminals, a calcium-extruding plasma membrane ATPase links calcium signalling to amine-metabolising enzyme activity, integrin subunits of the CD11b/CD18 leukocyte receptor connect immune cell adhesion to amine handling, and a microRNA imposes post-transcriptional repression. The theme is downregulation of amine metabolic flux, relevant to neurotransmitter homeostasis, inflammation and growth control.

Amines here span neurotransmitters, polyamines and related nitrogenous metabolites, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of their synthesis and turnover. Because amine levels set synaptic signalling strength and cell growth capacity, upward regulation of this chemistry matters for neurotransmission, mood and feeding behaviour, and for the polyamine supply that proliferating cells need. The genes point mainly to neural contexts: ABAT degrades GABA and so controls inhibitory transmitter pools, PAOX oxidises acetylated polyamines as part of the polyamine back-conversion route, and NPY acts as a neuropeptide modulating transmitter release. Others are better known for neuronal maintenance, including PARK7 and VPS35, both linked to Parkinson disease and to dopaminergic neuron survival, connecting amine handling to degeneration when it fails. HPRT1 ties the theme to purine salvage, whose loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with its neurological and behavioural features.

Nuclear DNA replication during the cell cycle must fire each origin once and only once, and this regulatory layer sets how often, how fast and how extensively that replication proceeds. Loss of the control causes re-replication, amplified DNA content and the replication stress that drives genome instability and tumorigenesis. The core of it is licensing and firing: CDT1 loads the replicative helicase onto origins, geminin sequesters CDT1 to prevent a second round in the same cycle, and the CDC7 kinase with its activating subunits DBF4 and DBF4B triggers origin activation at the G1/S transition. Chromatin context contributes through the ATRX helicase and the INO80 remodelling complex, which keep replication moving through difficult templates, while TIPIN supports fork stability and the replication checkpoint. Transcriptional regulators such as BCL6 and growth factor input link proliferative signals to the decision to replicate.

Vitamins act as signals as well as nutrients, and this collection captures how cells and tissues change state when exposed to them — altering gene expression, enzyme output, secretion and differentiation. Two arms dominate. Retinoid responses run through nuclear receptors RARA and RXRA/RXRB with coactivators such as NCOA3, MED1 and TRIM24, feedback catabolism by CYP26A1/B1, and retinaldehyde synthesis via ALDH1A2, driving patterning and cell fate decisions. Vitamin D responses centre on VDR together with the activating hydroxylase CYP27B1 and the inactivating CYP24A1, coupling to PTH, FGF23, KL, CASR, phosphate transport by SLC34A1 and bone matrix products including BGLAP, COL1A1 and SPP1. Folate and one-carbon genes MTHFR, SHMT2, FOLR1/2 and DNMT3A link vitamin supply to methylation, while antioxidant enzymes reflect vitamin-dependent redox handling. Disruption produces rickets, mineralisation disorders, neural tube defects and impaired immune and epithelial function.

Actin-myosin filament sliding is the contractile event itself: myosin thick filaments pulling calcium-activated actin thin filaments past one another to shorten a sarcomere. It is what makes a heartbeat and a skeletal muscle twitch, and its regulation sets force, speed and relaxation kinetics. The genes are the sarcomere's parts list cardiac and skeletal myosin heavy chains with their essential and regulatory light chains, sarcomeric actin, tropomyosin and the troponin complex that translates a calcium transient into thin-filament activation, plus myosin light chain kinase which tunes crossbridge sensitivity. Titin and telethonin provide the elastic backbone and Z-disc anchoring against which the sliding does work, while myosin-binding protein C brakes and paces crossbridge cycling. Mutations in these components underlie hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies and congenital skeletal myopathies such as distal arthrogryposis.

Muscle shortens because myosin thick filaments pull actin thin filaments past one another, and this sliding is the contractile event underlying heartbeat, breathing and voluntary movement. The genes here build the sarcomere itself: cardiac and skeletal actin, sarcomeric myosin heavy chains of embryonic, perinatal, fast and cardiac types, essential and regulatory light chains, and the giant elastic scaffold titin with its Z-disc partner telethonin. Calcium control is imposed through the troponin complex and tropomyosin, which occlude myosin binding sites on actin until cytosolic calcium rises; myosin binding protein C and a myosin light chain kinase tune the force and kinetics of the stroke. Mutations in these components are the classic causes of hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy, distal arthrogryposis and congenital myopathy, so the pathway links sarcomere mechanics directly to cardiac and skeletal muscle disease.

Expansion of progenitor populations in the developing midbrain sets how many neurons, in particular dopaminergic neurons of the ventral midbrain, will ultimately be made, and the genes here are almost entirely Wnt pathway components acting on that proliferative step. Secreted ligands including WNT1, WNT3A and WNT5A signal through Frizzled receptors FZD3 and FZD6 and the atypical receptor tyrosine kinase RYK, coupling extracellular cues to progenitor cell cycle progression and to the patterning of the midbrain–hindbrain region. PITX3 marks the dopaminergic neurons that arise from these progenitors and is required for their later differentiation and survival. Because midbrain dopaminergic neurons are the cells lost in Parkinson's disease, this proliferative programme is of interest both for understanding how the substantia nigra is built and for directing stem cells toward dopaminergic fates in vitro.

Vitamin D acts as a hormone, and this is the cellular and organismal response to that stimulus: hydroxylated vitamin D binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor, which partners with retinoid X receptors and recruits coactivators and mediator components such as NCOA3, MED1, SNW1 and TRIM24 to reprogramme transcription. The output is control of calcium and phosphate handling and bone turnover, alongside effects on innate and adaptive immunity, keratinocyte and epithelial differentiation, and cell cycle exit. Feedback is built in, with CYP27B1 producing the active hormone and CYP24A1 degrading it, while parathyroid hormone, the calcium-sensing receptor, FGF23 with its cofactor klotho, and PHEX set the endocrine context. Loss of receptor function or of activating hydroxylation causes rickets and osteomalacia with secondary hyperparathyroidism; osteocalcin, alkaline phosphatase and osteopontin are among the bone matrix genes it drives.

Striated muscle cells fire and contract in synchrony because the surface membrane dives inward as transverse tubules that carry depolarization deep to every sarcomere. Building and maintaining this network — T-tubule organization — is what allows excitation at the cell surface to be converted uniformly into calcium release and force; when the tubules fragment or detach, as in heart failure and several myopathies, calcium release becomes slow and spatially uneven and contraction weakens. The membrane-sculpting BAR-domain protein BIN1 generates and stabilizes tubular invaginations, caveolin-3 supplies muscle-specific caveolae at the surface and tubule openings, and ankyrin-B targets ion transporters and channels to the correct membrane domain. SERCA2 and the tubular membrane protein mitsugumin-29 tie the structure to calcium handling, while the LIM protein CSRP3 links it to the sarcomeric and mechanosensing apparatus. The result is reliable excitation–contraction coupling in cardiac and skeletal muscle.

Lysosomal hydrolases are normally retained inside the cell, and this pathway covers the regulated export of those enzymes to the cell surface or extracellular space, where they remodel matrix, contribute to bone resorption and to the release of granule contents by secretory lysosomes in immune cells and melanocytes. Sorting is decided by the mannose-6-phosphate tag: the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase subunits encoded by GNPTAB add the recognition mark, an uncovering enzyme completes it, and the mannose-6-phosphate receptor captures tagged hydrolases for delivery rather than secretion, so loss of tagging diverts enzymes out of the cell and causes mucolipidosis. Biogenesis-of-lysosome-related-organelle subunits direct cargo into secretory lysosome compartments, while the liver X receptors link this trafficking to sterol and lipid sensing, connecting lysosomal enzyme release to cholesterol handling in macrophages.</description>

Meiosis must not proceed until chromosomes have been replicated, paired, recombined and correctly attached to the spindle, and meiotic cell cycle checkpoint signaling is the surveillance that enforces that order. Its outputs are the delays that give cells time to repair double-strand breaks and to correct faulty kinetochore attachments; when the surveillance fails, gametes carry unrepaired breaks or the wrong chromosome number, a route to infertility, oocyte loss and aneuploid conceptions. Two arms are represented here. HORMAD1 and HORMAD2, with the AAA+ ATPase TRIP13 that removes them from synapsed axes, monitor synapsis and unrepaired recombination intermediates along meiotic chromosomes, while HUS1 and RAD1 contribute to the clamp that senses damaged or stalled DNA. Kinetochore components including KNL1, ZWINT and the MPS1-family kinase encoded by TTK support attachment error correction and spindle checkpoint signaling before anaphase.

Cells that begin mitosis with unfinished replication fragment their chromosomes, and the mitotic DNA replication checkpoint is the surveillance that prevents this by delaying mitotic entry until forks have completed. Stalled or slowed replication forks are sensed at the fork and at ssDNA-RPA structures, where the clamp loader RAD17 and the 9-1-1 subunit HUS1 load onto primer-template junctions and TOPBP1 together with the mediator claspin activates the apical kinase that in turn restrains CDK activity. Replication initiation factors in the same group dash ORC1 and CDC6 in origin licensing, the CDC7–DBF4 kinase, TICRR and DONSON in helicase activation dash tie the signal directly to origin firing and fork integrity. Loss of this coupling produces premature chromosome condensation, genome instability and the developmental microcephaly and dwarfism phenotypes seen with replication-checkpoint gene mutations.

Leydig cells are the testosterone-producing cells that sit in the interstitial space between seminiferous tubules, and this pathway covers how unspecialized interstitial progenitors acquire that identity. Their output drives masculinization of the fetus, descent of the testes, pubertal virilization and the androgenic support of spermatogenesis, so failure of the programme presents as disorders of sex development, hypogonadism and infertility. Signals from the adjacent tubules instruct the progenitors: Sertoli-derived desert hedgehog acts on interstitial precursors, platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha reads mesenchymal growth factor cues, and anti-Mullerian hormone and androgen receptor signalling feed back on how many steroidogenic cells form and how they mature. Nuclear receptor and transcription factor components including NR0B1 set the competence of the gonadal interstitium, while cyclin D1 links these cues to progenitor proliferation before differentiation.

Cells cannot catabolise cholesterol, so unloading it onto extracellular acceptors is the only way to avoid toxic accumulation. Cholesterol efflux is the first step of reverse cholesterol transport, moving sterol from macrophages and other peripheral cells onto apolipoprotein A-I and HDL particles for delivery to the liver; when it fails, macrophages become lipid-laden foam cells and atherosclerotic plaques grow. Membrane transporters of the ABCA and ABCG families, notably ABCA1 and ABCG1, pump cholesterol and phospholipid to nascent and mature acceptors, while scavenger receptor SR-BI and lipid transfer proteins such as CETP and PLTP remodel the particles. Lysosomal handling by NPC1, NPC2 and acid lipase supplies the exportable pool, and esterification by SOAT enzymes competes with it. The liver X receptors and their RXR partner induce the transporters transcriptionally, and a large set of microRNAs including the miR-33 pair restrains them post-transcriptionally, tying efflux to whole-body sterol and HDL metabolism.

Secretory granule organization covers the building, loading and maturation of membrane-bounded stores of concentrated cargo that a cell holds until a stimulus triggers release. It matters wherever regulated secretion defines a cell: platelet dense and alpha granules for haemostasis, mast cell and endocrine granules, and the sperm acrosome, whose enzymes are released at fertilization. Much of the machinery is cargo-sorting and vesicle-budding apparatus emanating from the Golgi — clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3, the BLOC-1 subunits and Hermansky-Pudlak proteins, RAB38 and VPS33B — whose loss produces bleeding diathesis and pigment dilution because lysosome-related granules never form properly. A second arm comprises acrosome biogenesis factors such as ZPBP, SPACA1 and ACRBP, and mutations here cause globozoospermia and male infertility. Granule proteins including serglycin and PTPRN contribute to cargo condensation and membrane identity.

Newly made proteins are useless in the wrong compartment, and this pathway covers the sorting steps that put them where they work: import into organelles and retention there. It spans nuclear import and export through the nuclear pore, with karyopherin and transportin carriers, RanGAP and RanBP2 setting directionality; mitochondrial entry through the outer-membrane translocase and the inner-membrane TIM machinery with matrix chaperones; peroxisome biogenesis via the peroxin receptors and membrane assembly factors; insertion of membrane proteins at the endoplasmic reticulum by the EMC and tail-anchored targeting components; and delivery to lysosomes, endosomes and cilia through ESCRT, retromer, Rab GTPases and intraflagellar transport. Because each route has its own recognition signal, mutations produce distinct diseases—peroxisome biogenesis disorders, mitochondrial import defects, and ciliopathies such as nephronophthisis and Bardet-Biedl syndrome—linking compartment identity to organ function.

geranylgeranyl diphosphate metabolic process produces and turns over the 20-carbon isoprenoid geranylgeranyl diphosphate, the lipid donor that anchors Rho, Rab and Rap GTPases to membranes and a branch point for other terpenoid products. Cells depend on it for cytoskeletal signalling, vesicle traffic and the prenylation-dependent activity of small GTPases; blocking its supply is much of how statins and bisphosphonates alter osteoclast function, muscle and vascular biology, and mutations in the upstream kinase steps cause periodic fever and mevalonate kinase deficiency. The genes trace the mevalonate route in order, from HMG-CoA synthase and reductase through mevalonate kinase, phosphomevalonate kinase and the decarboxylase to isopentenyl diphosphate, then chain elongation by farnesyl and geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthases. A polyprenol phosphatase provides the degradative arm, tuning how much prenyl donor accumulates. The pathway therefore links cholesterol biosynthesis to protein lipidation.

Geranylgeranyl diphosphate is a twenty-carbon isoprenoid built at the end of the mevalonate pathway, and its metabolism sets the supply of the lipid anchor used to prenylate Rho, Rab and Rac family GTPases so they can attach to membranes and signal. The route runs from acetyl-CoA through HMG-CoA synthase and the rate-limiting reductase HMGCR, then mevalonate kinase, phosphomevalonate kinase and mevalonate diphosphate decarboxylase to isopentenyl diphosphate, which IDI1 isomerises and FDPS condenses to farnesyl diphosphate; GGPS1 adds a final isoprene unit, while a phosphatase step can return prenyl diphosphates toward the alcohol pool. Because this branch competes with cholesterol synthesis for the same precursors, statin treatment and bisphosphonates lower prenylation as well as sterols, and inherited defects in the kinase steps cause periodic fever syndromes and severe mevalonate metabolism disorders.

cholesterol biosynthetic process via desmosterol is the branch of endogenous sterol synthesis that runs from acetyl-CoA through mevalonate and squalene to lanosterol, and then completes the sterol nucleus along the Bloch route, in which the side-chain double bond is reduced last so that desmosterol is the immediate precursor of cholesterol. Cells depend on this output for membrane fluidity and raft organisation, bile acid and steroid hormone production, and the covalent modification of Hedgehog ligands. The committed steps include HMG-CoA reductase, the target of statins, squalene epoxidase and lanosterol synthase, followed by C4 demethylation, C14 reduction and the sterol isomerase and reductase reactions carried out by EBP, SC5D and DHCR7, with DHCR24 performing the final desmosterol reduction. Loss of individual enzymes causes malformation syndromes such as Smith-Lemli-Opitz, desmosterolosis and chondrodysplasia punctata, reflecting how tightly embryonic patterning is tied to sterol supply.

Cholesterol synthesis via desmosterol is one of the two post-squalene routes, the Bloch pathway, in which the side-chain double bond is retained until the last step and desmosterol serves as the immediate precursor of cholesterol. The route supplies membrane sterol for growth, myelination, lipoprotein assembly and steroid hormone and bile acid production, beginning with acetyl-CoA condensation and mevalonate formation by HMGCS1 and the rate-limiting, statin-sensitive HMGCR, then isoprenoid condensation to squalene by FDPS and FDFT1, epoxidation by SQLE and cyclization by lanosterol synthase. Successive demethylation, reduction and isomerization steps by MSMO1, NSDHL, EBP, SC5D and others yield desmosterol, which DHCR24 reduces to cholesterol. Loss of individual enzymes causes malformation syndromes of skeletal, skin and brain development, including desmosterolosis from DHCR24 deficiency and Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome from DHCR7 deficiency, illustrating how sterol intermediates themselves shape embryonic patterning.

Dietary galactose, released mainly from lactose in milk, is converted into glucose-1-phosphate and fed into glycolysis and glycogen metabolism by the Leloir route. It matters most in infancy, when milk sugar is a principal energy source, and its failure causes galactosemia: loss of the transferase step leads to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate with liver damage, cataracts, and developmental injury, while defects at the kinase step cause cataracts alone. Mechanistically, a mutarotase first converts the beta anomer of galactose to the alpha form, a kinase phosphorylates it, and a uridylyltransferase exchanges it onto UDP, releasing glucose-1-phosphate that phosphoglucomutase isomerises to glucose-6-phosphate. An epimerase regenerates UDP-galactose from UDP-glucose, so the same chemistry also supplies the activated galactose donor used for glycoprotein and glycolipid glycosylation, linking sugar catabolism to biosynthesis of glycan chains.

carbohydrate homeostasis is the set of controls that hold blood glucose and intracellular sugar supply within a narrow range despite feeding, fasting and exercise. Its failure is diabetes: loss of beta cell identity or insulin secretion, or peripheral insulin resistance, with consequences for every tissue that depends on glucose. The genes span the whole regulatory circuit — the transcription factors that specify and maintain pancreatic beta cells (PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1, HNF1A, HNF4A, RFX6), the glucose-sensing and secretion apparatus (GCK, ABCC8, SLC30A8, insulin granule exocytosis), the counter-regulatory hormones glucagon, leptin, adiponectin, ghrelin and POMC-derived peptides, and the insulin receptor signalling chain through IRS1/2, PI3K, AKT and FOXO1 that drives GLUT4 trafficking. Downstream effectors control glycogen turnover, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, integrated with AMPK, mTOR, SIRT1 and circadian clock components so that hepatic glucose output matches demand.

Blood and cellular sugar levels are held within narrow limits, and carbohydrate homeostasis is the coordinated set of hormonal, transcriptional and transport events that does it. Its failure produces diabetes: pancreatic beta cells fail to secrete insulin, liver and muscle stop responding, and glucose rises unchecked. Glucose entry and phosphorylation by transporters and hexokinases, including the beta-cell sensor glucokinase, sets the rate at which insulin is released, a step requiring ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits, zinc handling and exocytic machinery. Secreted insulin and the opposing glucagon act through receptor tyrosine kinase and G-protein-coupled routes, converging on PI3K-AKT, FOXO1 and AMPK to switch between glycogen synthesis, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis via PCK1 and glucose-6-phosphatase. Lineage factors such as PDX1, NEUROD1 and NKX6-1 build and maintain the islet, while adipokines including leptin and adiponectin, circadian regulators and nutrient-stress signalling tie glucose control to whole-body energy balance and feeding.

The floor plate is a narrow strip of specialized cells at the ventral midline of the neural tube, and its formation over time is what gives the developing spinal cord and brain a ventral organizing centre. Once mature it secretes Sonic hedgehog and guidance cues that pattern motor neuron and interneuron progenitors along the dorsoventral axis and steer commissural axons across the midline; without it, ventral neural identities fail and midline crossing is disrupted, outcomes seen in holoprosencephaly-like and neural tube defects. The genes here reflect its dependence on midline signalling and on cilia: Nodal and the BMP antagonist chordin act in early node and axial mesoderm specification, GLI2 transduces hedgehog output, and ciliary and centriolar factors including CLUAP1, CBY1, CDK20, DZIP1L and STIL are required for the transduction machinery and progenitor divisions that build the plate.

fatty acid beta-oxidation using acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is the mitochondrial route by which fatty acids are broken down two carbons at a time to fuel ATP production and ketogenesis, and it is what sustains heart, muscle and liver during fasting or sustained exercise. Chain-length-specific flavoenzymes — very-long-, long-, medium- and short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenases — introduce the trans-2 double bond that starts each cycle, and the electrons they strip are handed to electron transfer flavoprotein and its ubiquinone oxidoreductase, feeding the respiratory chain rather than NADH directly. Related dehydrogenases such as IVD and GCDH act on branched-chain and lysine catabolic intermediates, linking this machinery to amino acid breakdown. Inherited loss of MCAD, VLCAD or the electron transfer components causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and metabolic crisis on fasting, and is screened for in newborns.

Mitochondria extract energy from fatty acids by shortening them two carbons at a time, and the flavin-dependent acyl-CoA dehydrogenases catalyse the first, committed oxidation of each round, converting acyl-CoA to trans-2-enoyl-CoA. This route supplies acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle and hepatic ketone bodies during fasting and sustained exercise, so heart, skeletal muscle and liver depend on it when glucose is scarce. Chain-length-specialised enzymes divide the work between very long, long, medium and short substrates, and related dehydrogenases handle branched amino acid intermediates such as isovaleryl-CoA and glutaryl-CoA. Electrons removed at this step are not passed directly to the respiratory chain but through electron transfer flavoprotein and its iron-sulfur dehydrogenase to ubiquinone, ending as water. Loss of individual dehydrogenases causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis, while electron transfer flavoprotein defects produce multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency.

Peroxisomes shorten fatty acids that mitochondria handle poorly — very-long-chain species, branched-chain acids such as pristanic acid, and bile acid intermediates — and this oxidase-initiated route is how they do it. The committed first step is performed by acyl-CoA oxidases rather than a dehydrogenase, so electrons go straight to oxygen and generate hydrogen peroxide that peroxisomal catalase disposes of, making the organelle both a lipid-catabolising and a redox-managing compartment. Downstream, a bifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase and a thiolase complete each cycle, with racemase and carnitine acyltransferase activities handling stereochemistry and export of chain-shortened acyl groups for mitochondrial completion; an acyl-CoA synthetase activates substrates on entry. Loss of individual steps causes peroxisomal disorders with accumulated very-long-chain or branched fatty acids, adrenoleukodystrophy-like demyelination, and defective bile acid maturation.

cellular response to stress is the broad umbrella covering how cells detect damaging conditions — DNA lesions, misfolded proteins, oxidants, hypoxia, nutrient shortage, heat, inflammatory and mechanical insults — and reprogram themselves to survive or die. It determines whether an injured cell repairs itself, arrests, senesces, or is eliminated, so it underlies tumour suppression, ageing, neurodegeneration, and the response to radiation and chemotherapy. The genes span the major arms: ATM/ATR–CHEK–TP53 damage signalling with excision, mismatch, Fanconi and double-strand break repair machinery; the unfolded protein response through ERN1, ATF6 and XBP1 with ER-associated degradation and chaperones; heat shock factors and HSP70/HSP90 proteostasis; NFE2L2–KEAP1 and peroxidase/superoxide dismutase antioxidant defence; HIF1A-driven hypoxia adaptation; mTOR and AMPK nutrient sensing with autophagy and mitophagy; and stress-activated MAPK, integrated stress response translational control, and BCL2-family apoptotic execution.

Cells continuously encounter insults — DNA damage, heat, oxidants, nutrient shortage, hypoxia, misfolded protein burden — and this broad response programme is how they detect the damage, pause growth, repair what can be repaired, and die when it cannot. Its coverage here spans the DNA damage checkpoints and repair routes (ATM/ATR, p53, mismatch, nucleotide- and base-excision, homologous recombination and end joining), the heat shock chaperones and HSF1, endoplasmic reticulum stress sensors with ERAD and the integrated stress response through eIF2α kinases and ATF4, antioxidant defence via NRF2, KEAP1, superoxide dismutases and peroxiredoxins, hypoxia sensing by HIF prolyl hydroxylases, nutrient sensing through mTORC1 and AMPK, autophagy and mitophagy, and apoptotic execution. Outcomes include cell cycle arrest, senescence, or death. Deficits give genome instability and cancer predisposition, neurodegeneration, and premature ageing syndromes.

Whole-animal responses to stressful stimuli are coordinated here: an organism under threat, injury, heat, or aversive challenge alters its behaviour, hormone output and gene expression rather than responding cell by cell. Two arms dominate. One is neuroendocrine: corticotropin-releasing hormone with its receptor, urocortin, vasopressin and the catecholamine enzymes DBH and COMT drive the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal and sympathetic limbs that set arousal, blood pressure and glucocorticoid release. The other is nociception and stress-induced analgesia, carried by sensory channels such as TRPV1, TRPA1, acid-sensing channels and the sodium channels SCN9A and SCN11A, with substance P, enkephalin and prepronociceptin peptides and their receptors modulating pain thresholds. Monoamine and glutamate receptors, neurotrophic signalling through RET and NTRK1, and MECP2-dependent transcription tune how strongly these circuits react. Dysregulation underlies anxiety and depressive states, chronic pain, and maladaptive responses to prolonged stress.

Unsaturated fatty acid metabolism covers the making, remodelling and breakdown of fatty acids carrying carbon-carbon double bonds, and it supplies both the fluid lipids of membranes and the precursors of nearly all lipid signalling molecules. Desaturases and elongases such as SCD, FADS1/FADS2 and the ELOVL family build monounsaturated and long-chain polyunsaturated chains including arachidonic acid, while peroxisomal beta-oxidation enzymes and the transporters ABCD1/ABCD2 degrade very long-chain species. Released from phospholipids by phospholipases, arachidonate is converted by cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases into prostaglandins, thromboxane, leukotrienes and epoxy- and hydroxy-eicosanoids, with prostaglandin synthases, reductases and glutathione transferases shaping the final mediator mix; parallel enzymes such as FAAH, MGLL and the diacylglycerol lipases control endocannabinoid tone. The output governs inflammation, platelet aggregation, vascular tone, pain, fever and skin barrier formation, and defects cause peroxisomal disease and ichthyosis.

Growing axons must choose whether to extend toward the head or the tail, and this anterior/posterior guidance step commits a growth cone to one direction along the body axis by reading attractive and repulsive cues laid down in gradients. The outcome determines how longitudinal tracts in the spinal cord and brainstem are wired, and errors in it leave projections running the wrong way or failing to reach their targets. Netrin-1 is the diffusible cue here, read by DCC as an attractant and by the UNC5 family of receptors, which convert the same ligand into repulsion; combinatorial receptor expression on a given neuron therefore sets its preferred direction. LIM-homeodomain transcription factors LHX1 and LHX9 act upstream, specifying neuronal identity and the receptor complement that identity implies, linking axon pathfinding to earlier neuronal fate decisions.

Cells acquire nearly all of their iron by capturing transferrin at the surface and recycling it, and transferrin transport is that itinerary: receptor-mediated uptake through clathrin-coated pits, delivery to acidified endosomes where iron is released, and return of the receptor and apo-transferrin to the plasma membrane. Erythroid precursors depend on this flux to make haemoglobin, and every dividing cell needs it for iron-requiring enzymes. The transferrin receptor TFRC is the entry point, with clathrin heavy chain and the fission GTPase dynamin-2 driving internalisation, Rab11-dependent traffic handling the recycling arm, and endolysosomal channel MCOLN1 contributing to cation handling in that compartment. HFE and TFR2, which partner with the receptor and with the beta-2-microglobulin-associated MHC class I fold, couple this uptake to systemic iron sensing; their loss causes hereditary haemochromatosis and iron overload.

Cells and tissues change their behaviour when exposed to testosterone, and the genes gathered here trace that response from hormone metabolism through receptor action to downstream targets. The androgen receptor is the central transducer, a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that binds testosterone or the more potent dihydrotestosterone generated by the 5-alpha reductases SRD5A1 and SRD5A2, then drives transcription of prostate and bone programmes including NKX3-1 and osteocalcin. Coregulators and modifiers such as NCOA4, SIRT1 and the ubiquitin ligase CBL tune the strength and duration of the signal. The consequences are broad: skeletal muscle growth restrained by myostatin, bone formation, erythropoiesis, HOX-dependent patterning of the reproductive tract, and feedback onto gonadotropin-releasing hormone. Loss or distortion of this responsiveness underlies androgen insensitivity, hypogonadal phenotypes, and the receptor dependence of prostate cancer that antiandrogen therapy exploits.

response to L-ascorbic acid covers the cellular changes triggered when cells encounter vitamin C, a dietary antioxidant and enzyme cofactor whose absence causes scurvy through failed collagen hydroxylation and whose availability shapes redox balance in tissues. The genes here point to the redox arm of that response: catalase and mitochondrial superoxide dismutase dispose of hydrogen peroxide and superoxide, while glutathione S-transferase P1 handles conjugation of electrophilic products, together determining whether ascorbate acts as an antioxidant or, at high local iron and concentration, as a pro-oxidant. Alongside these sit an adhesion receptor for collagen and the adipokine leptin, linking vitamin C exposure to matrix interaction and metabolic signalling. The pathway thus connects micronutrient status to oxidative stress defence, connective tissue behaviour, and endocrine control of energy balance.

Cells adjust their behaviour when vitamin C is available, and this response captures the transcriptional and enzymatic changes that follow an L-ascorbic acid stimulus. Because ascorbate is both a reducing agent and, at high concentration or in the presence of transition metals, a source of hydrogen peroxide, much of the response is redox handling: catalase disposes of peroxide, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to peroxide, and a glutathione S-transferase conjugates electrophilic products of oxidative damage. Alongside this antioxidant arm, changes in a collagen-binding integrin subunit and in leptin expression link ascorbate to cell-matrix adhesion and to endocrine control of energy balance. The pathway matters for how tissues use dietary vitamin C in collagen-rich matrix, adipose signalling, and defence against oxidative stress, and it frames ascorbate as a signal cells interpret rather than simply a cofactor they consume.

Response to genistein covers the cellular changes triggered by genistein, a soy isoflavone that acts both as a weak estrogen-receptor agonist and as a xenobiotic requiring detoxification. It matters because dietary isoflavone exposure alters hormone-responsive gene expression in reproductive, vascular and hepatic tissues, which is why soy phytoestrogens are studied for effects on breast tissue, coagulation and menopausal physiology. The genes trace two arms of that response: xenobiotic handling, through induction of the cytochrome P450 CYP1A1 and a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that conjugates the compound for excretion, and estrogen-like transcriptional output, including oxytocin, coagulation factor VII and the membrane metalloproteinase MMP14 involved in extracellular matrix remodelling. Together they place genistein at the intersection of nutrient sensing, drug metabolism and nuclear receptor signalling, with downstream consequences for hemostasis and tissue architecture.

Genistein is a soy-derived isoflavone that acts as a phytoestrogen and tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and this pathway covers the cellular changes that follow exposure to it — shifts in gene expression, enzyme induction, secretion and matrix turnover. It matters because dietary isoflavones reach concentrations that alter hormone-responsive tissues and drug metabolism, which is why genistein is studied both as a chemopreventive agent and as an endocrine disruptor. The responses represented span xenobiotic handling, with a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase and a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase that conjugates substrates for excretion; haemostasis, through coagulation factor VII; neuroendocrine peptide output via oxytocin; and pericellular proteolysis through a membrane-anchored matrix metalloproteinase. Together they illustrate how an oestrogen receptor-active plant compound reshapes metabolic, vascular and tissue-remodelling programmes rather than acting through a single receptor output.}
