Delivery and positioning of the receptor depend on UNC93B1, and the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 together with its adaptor TASL couples the activated receptor to interferon regulatory factor 5, providing a branch distinct from the NF-kB arm supported by PIK3AP1 and SCIMP. Inhibitory receptors such as HAVCR2 and LILRA4 restrain the response, and the induced effector RSAD2 acts directly against viral replication, illustrating how sensing, tuning and antiviral output are joined in one endolysosomal circuit.

Toll-like receptor 7 detects single-stranded RNA in endosomes and drives type I interferon production, above all in plasmacytoid dendritic cells; setting the gain of that response determines whether viral RNA is answered appropriately or self RNA is mistaken for infection. The genes here tune rather than transmit the core signal. A lysosomal peptide/histidine transporter and its partner adaptor recruit downstream kinase machinery to the endolysosome, coupling receptor engagement to interferon regulatory factor activation; an immunoglobulin-like receptor expressed on plasmacytoid dendritic cells restrains interferon output, while an interferon-inducible antiviral protein and a TREM-family surface receptor provide feedback on the strength of the response. Loss of restraint at this step feeds the nucleic-acid-sensing autoimmunity seen in lupus, whereas insufficient signalling blunts antiviral interferon defence.

Toll-like receptor 7 senses single-stranded RNA inside endosomes, and this set covers the factors that raise the output of that sensing, tuning how strongly a cell responds to viral RNA with type I interferon and inflammatory cytokines. The tone matters clinically: excessive TLR7 signalling in plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells drives lupus-like autoimmunity, while too little blunts antiviral defence. Amplification works partly through the endolysosomal transporter SLC15A4 and its adaptor TASL, which couple the receptor to IRF5 activation, and through the helicase DDX3X, which participates in interferon induction downstream of nucleic acid sensing. RSAD2 is itself an interferon-induced antiviral effector that feeds back on the response, and TREML4 is a myeloid immunoglobulin-superfamily receptor that potentiates it. The pathway sits at the junction of innate nucleic acid recognition, interferon production, and autoimmune risk.

TLR8 is an endolysosomal sensor of single-stranded RNA and its degradation products, and the signalling it initiates lets myeloid cells detect RNA viruses and bacteria that have been taken up and degraded in acidified compartments. Ligand binding drives recruitment of the adaptor MYD88 and a kinase cascade that turns on NF-κB-driven inflammatory cytokine production, while the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 together with its partner TASL provides a docking platform that routes the response toward interferon regulatory factor 5 and type I interferon. DDX3X participates in this RNA-sensing arm as an RNA helicase supporting interferon induction. The closely related TLR7 shares the same machinery. Because the pathway reads self-derived RNA when tolerance fails, overactivity is linked to lupus and other interferon-driven autoimmunity, making these components targets for immunomodulatory drugs and vaccine adjuvants.

Toll-like receptor 9 is the sensor that lets cells recognise unmethylated CpG DNA from bacteria and viruses, and from damaged self, inside the endolysosome rather than at the cell surface. The signalling it initiates drives inflammatory cytokine production and, in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the type I interferon burst that shapes early antiviral defence; the same pathway underlies nucleic-acid-driven autoimmunity when self DNA is mistaken for pathogen. Compartment control is much of the biology here: UNC93B1 chaperones the receptor out of the ER, SLC15A4 and lysosomal enzymes maintain the acidic environment needed for ligand recognition and cleavage, and trafficking and palmitoylation steps determine where signalling occurs. Downstream, MyD88-associated kinases IRAK1 and IRAK4 relay to NF-kB and interferon regulatory factors, with HMGB1 acting as a DNA-binding cofactor and TNIP2 restraining the response.

Toll-like receptor 9 detects unmethylated CpG DNA from bacteria and viruses within endolysosomes, and driving it too hard or too little decides whether an innate response clears infection or turns against self DNA. Regulating the strength and duration of TLR9 signalling therefore sets the output of type I interferon and inflammatory cytokines, particularly in plasmacytoid dendritic cells, where receptors such as LILRA4 dampen the interferon burst; loss of restraint contributes to lupus-like autoimmunity driven by nucleic acid-containing immune complexes. Control is exerted at several levels: HMGB1 binds DNA and promotes its delivery to the receptor, the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 and the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC3 govern receptor trafficking and membrane targeting, RAB7B routes the receptor through endosomal compartments, and phosphatase and cyclase activities tune downstream signalling. The pathway links nucleic acid sensing to compartmentalised trafficking rather than to surface receptor engagement.

Toll-like receptor 9 detects unmethylated CpG DNA inside endosomes and drives type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine output, particularly from plasmacytoid dendritic cells; braking that response keeps recognition of self DNA from tipping into autoimmunity. Negative regulation of TLR9 signalling gathers the mechanisms that limit how strongly and how long the receptor fires, and its loss is associated with interferon-driven disease such as lupus. The genes here act at distinct points: a plasmacytoid dendritic cell surface immunoreceptor delivers an inhibitory signal that dampens interferon production, a small GTPase controls endosomal and lysosomal trafficking of the receptor and so limits its residence in the signalling compartment, and a receptor phosphatase and a lysosomal thioesterase further restrain downstream activation. Together they set the threshold for innate sensing of DNA and enforce tolerance to host nucleic acids.

Toll-like receptor 9 detects unmethylated CpG DNA from bacteria, viruses and damaged host cells inside endosomes, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the strength of that response. It matters for early antiviral and antibacterial defence, particularly the type I interferon output of plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and for autoimmunity: excessive signalling on self DNA drives lupus-like disease, while its loss blunts responses to CpG-containing nucleic acid. Amplification happens at several levels. HMGB1 binds DNA and delivers it to the receptor, increasing ligand availability. The lysosomal peptide/histidine transporter SLC15A4 supports the endolysosomal environment and trafficking that TLR9 requires for cleavage and activation. Palmitoylation by ZDHHC3 and interaction with RTN4 act on receptor trafficking through the endoplasmic reticulum and endosomes, while the interferon-inducible RSAD2 and adenylate cyclase ADCY7 shape downstream cytokine and interferon production.

Acylglycerol transport moves mono-, di- and triacylglycerols across membranes and between tissues, the step that lets dietary and stored fat reach cells that burn or store it. It underlies intestinal fat absorption and the packaging of triglyceride into lipoproteins for export from enterocytes and hepatocytes; when it fails, as in loss of the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein subunit MTTP, chylomicrons cannot be assembled and fat and fat-soluble vitamins are malabsorbed. The genes span the whole route: a scavenger receptor that binds long-chain fatty acids and lipoproteins at the cell surface, an acyltransferase that remodels phospholipid to permit lipoprotein secretion, a lipid transfer protein that shuttles neutral lipid between circulating particles, and a microRNA that tunes the output. This places the pathway at the centre of whole-body lipid distribution, dyslipidaemia and hepatic steatosis.

Fats absorbed from the diet or mobilised from stores must be moved between compartments and between tissues, and acylglycerol transport covers that directed movement of mono-, di- and triacylglycerols by transporters, lipid transfer proteins and lipoprotein assembly. It sits at the centre of intestinal fat absorption and hepatic lipoprotein output: microsomal triglyceride transfer protein loads triglyceride onto apolipoprotein B to build chylomicrons and VLDL, and its loss causes abetalipoproteinaemia with fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. A scavenger receptor at the plasma membrane takes up long-chain fatty acids and lipoproteins, cholesteryl ester transfer protein exchanges neutral lipids between circulating particles, and an acyltransferase remodels membrane phospholipids to permit efficient particle secretion, with a microRNA and vesicle-trafficking components tuning the output. The pathway determines plasma triglyceride levels and contributes to steatosis and atherogenic dyslipidaemia when deranged.

Protein kinase A is the main effector of cyclic AMP, and activating it converts hormonal and neuromodulatory signals at the cell surface into phosphorylation of metabolic enzymes, ion channels and transcriptional regulators such as CREB. In the resting state the kinase is a tetramer in which two regulatory subunits clamp and inhibit two catalytic subunits; cAMP binding to the regulatory subunits releases that inhibition, so the regulatory proteins represented here are the switch rather than the catalyst. An adenylate cyclase supplies the cAMP that throws it, and the RI and RII isoforms differ in their anchoring and thresholds, which localises the response to particular subcellular sites. This step controls glycogen and lipid mobilisation, synaptic plasticity and learning, steroidogenesis and cell proliferation; loss of a regulatory subunit removes restraint on the kinase and underlies Carney complex and adrenal hyperplasia with hypercortisolism.

Lipid translocation moves lipids between the two leaflets of a membrane bilayer, and in doing so builds and breaks the asymmetry that cells use as information. Keeping phosphatidylserine on the inner face of the plasma membrane marks a cell as healthy; exposing it marks a cell as dying or a platelet as ready to clot, so this activity underlies apoptotic corpse clearance, coagulation, and bile and surfactant secretion. Three machineries are represented: ATP-dependent P4-ATPase flippases with their CDC50 subunits pulling lipids inward, ABC transporter floppases pushing cholesterol, phospholipid and bile lipid outward, and calcium- or caspase-activated scramblases of the anoctamin and XKR families that collapse asymmetry rapidly. Related lipid-mobilising proteins support autophagosome membrane expansion and restrict enveloped viruses. Mutations cause cholestasis, harlequin ichthyosis, retinal degeneration and Tangier disease.

Membrane bilayers are built asymmetrically, and lipid translocation is the set of activities that move phospholipids and sterols across a bilayer from one leaflet to the other. Maintaining that asymmetry defines the outward face of the plasma membrane; breaking it deliberately is how a cell signals that it is dying or that clotting should begin. Three kinds of machinery appear here: ATP-driven P4-ATPase flippases such as ATP8A2, ATP11A and ATP11C, which act with their CDC50 subunits (TMEM30A/B) to pull aminophospholipids inward; ABC transporters including ABCA1 and ABCA12, which export cholesterol, phospholipid and ceramide outward; and calcium- or caspase-activated scramblases of the anoctamin, XKR and phospholipid scramblase families that randomise the bilayer. Loss of individual components causes cholestasis, retinal degeneration, harlequin ichthyosis, Tangier disease and defective clearance of apoptotic cells, and the same lipid movements support autophagosome membrane expansion.

Amyloid-beta peptide is produced when the amyloid precursor protein is cut sequentially by BACE1 and the gamma-secretase complex, and its accumulation into plaques is the defining lesion of Alzheimer's disease. The genes here cover both the proteolytic machinery itself include presenilins PSEN1 and PSEN2, nicastrin, APH1 subunits and PSENEN, which together form gamma-secretase and the trafficking and regulatory layer that decides how much peptide is made. Sorting receptors and endocytic adaptors such as SORL1, PICALM and BIN1 route the precursor between the cell surface, endosomes and Golgi, determining its access to the secretases, while reticulon proteins restrain BACE1 and GSAP promotes cleavage. Lipid and lipoprotein handling through APOE, clusterin and ABC transporters influences peptide clearance and aggregation, and a large panel of microRNAs tunes expression of the enzymes. Inflammatory and kinase inputs modulate output further, linking neuronal stress to amyloid burden.

Many proteins only work once six copies come together, and this grouping covers the assembly of such hexameric complexes from identical or differing subunits held together noncovalently. The oligomeric state is what creates the functional unit: the volume-regulated anion channel formed from LRRC8A with LRRC8C or LRRC8D is a hexameric pore that releases chloride and organic osmolytes during cell swelling; nucleoside diphosphate kinases such as NME1 and NME3 are active only as hexamers that balance nucleotide pools; UGDH and MAT2A build hexamers to supply UDP-glucuronate and S-adenosylmethionine. Others are ring-shaped AAA+ ATPases for which the hexamer forms the working machine f spastin severing microtubules, YME1L1 degrading misfolded inner-membrane proteins, and the Twinkle helicase unwinding mitochondrial DNA. Loss of correct hexamer formation therefore disrupts osmotic balance, mitochondrial genome maintenance, and axonal transport, with hereditary spastic paraplegia among the consequences.

Movement of single-atom ions such as sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, protons, zinc, copper, iron and magnesium across membranes underlies nearly every excitable and secretory function in the body: the resting potential and action potential, muscle contraction, synaptic transmission, renal salt handling, gastric acidification, lysosomal and mitochondrial physiology, and cell volume control. Voltage-gated and ligand-gated channels, transient receptor potential and store-operated entry channels, chloride and anoctamin channels, and large families of solute carriers and exchangers set ionic gradients, while P-type pumps such as the sodium/potassium ATPase and sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase and the vacuolar proton ATPase spend ATP to build them; mitochondrial respiratory complexes and the calcium uniporter couple ion flux to bioenergetics. Accessory subunits, calmodulin, kinases and scaffolds tune gating. Mutations in these transporters cause channelopathies including epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia, cystic fibrosis, myotonia, deafness and renal tubular disorders.

Zinc is required as a cofactor by hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, so cells monitor its availability and remodel transport and gene expression when it runs short. This response to zinc ion starvation adjusts uptake at the cell surface and rewires transcription to preserve the most zinc-dependent functions. Intestinal zinc acquisition depends on SLC39A4, whose loss-of-function causes acrodermatitis enteropathica with dermatitis, diarrhoea and impaired growth, while SLC39A5 contributes to serosal zinc handling and has been linked to myopia and to systemic zinc balance. Downstream, the zinc-finger transcription factor SP1 and the immediate-early factor FOS alter target gene output, including osteoblast products such as osteocalcin and the osteoclast receptor RANK, connecting zinc supply to bone formation and remodelling as well as to epithelial integrity and immune competence.

Sulfur atoms added to specific tRNA nucleotides tune how accurately and efficiently the ribosome reads the genetic code. The best-characterised product is 2-thiouridine at the wobble position 34 of tRNAs reading lysine, glutamate and glutamine codons, a modification that stabilises codon-anticodon pairing and supports efficient translation elongation. Two parallel routes are represented: a cytoplasmic 2-thiouridylase formed by CTU1 with CTU2, and the mitochondrial enzyme TRMU acting on mitochondrially encoded tRNAs. Sulfur is mobilised by persulfide-transferring enzymes including MPST and delivered through the ubiquitin-like carrier URM1, which is adenylylated and thiocarboxylated by MOCS3, chemistry shared with molybdenum cofactor synthesis. Loss of TRMU activity impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis and is associated with infantile liver failure and with worsening of inherited deafness, tying this thio-modification to oxidative phosphorylation capacity and to stress-responsive control of translation.

Macrophages can fuse with one another to form multinucleated cells, and this pathway covers the recognition, adhesion and membrane merger steps that make that happen. The products matter physiologically: osteoclasts, which resorb bone, and the foreign-body and Langhans giant cells that wall off material too large for a single phagocyte, as in granulomas around implants or mycobacteria. Dedicated seven-transmembrane fusion regulators encoded by DCSTAMP and OCSTAMP are required for fusion competence, while TREM2 signalling through its adaptor TYROBP licenses the cytoskeletal and differentiation programme downstream of RANKL and cytokine cues. The tetraspanin CD81 organizes the membrane microdomains where fusion partners meet, and the metalloprotease-disintegrin ADAM9 contributes adhesive and proteolytic activity at the cell surface. Loss of these components leads to osteopetrosis-like bone phenotypes, and TREM2/TYROBP mutations also cause Nasu-Hakola disease.

Regulation of macrophage fusion controls whether monocyte-derived macrophages remain mononuclear or merge into multinucleated cells, the step that creates bone-resorbing osteoclasts and the giant cells of granulomas and foreign-body reactions. Its output determines skeletal remodelling capacity: too little fusion gives osteopetrosis and failed tooth eruption, too much gives the excessive resorption seen in osteoporosis and inflammatory bone loss. The genes point to two arms of the process. Dedicated transmembrane fusion regulators induced during osteoclast differentiation, together with a membrane metalloproteinase-disintegrin, act at the cell surface to license membrane merger; the TREM2-DAP12 receptor pair signals through an ITAM adaptor to tune it, and loss of either causes the Nasu-Hakola syndrome phenotype of bone cysts with presenile dementia. The pathway thus links innate immune receptor signalling to macrophage terminal differentiation and tissue remodelling.

Macrophages can merge with one another to form multinucleated cells, and this pathway controls how readily that happens. The fused products are functionally distinct: osteoclasts, which resorb bone and are needed for skeletal remodelling and tooth eruption, and the multinucleated giant cells that wall off persistent foreign material and infection in granulomas. Dedicated transmembrane proteins DCSTAMP and OCSTAMP are required for the membrane merger step itself, and loss of either yields mononuclear osteoclasts that resorb bone poorly, causing osteopetrosis. TREM2 signalling through its adaptor TYROBP tunes the fusion response alongside the metalloproteinase ADAM9, linking immune receptor input to cytoskeletal and adhesive remodelling at the fusion site. Mutations in the TREM2/TYROBP pair cause Nasu-Hakola disease, and the same receptor complex governs microglial activation, placing this fusion control at the intersection of bone homeostasis and macrophage inflammatory responses.

Cell-cell fusion that produces multinucleated syncytia must be held in check, and this pathway covers the restraints that limit how often and how far plasma membranes merge. Such control matters in muscle, where myoblast fusion has to be bounded so that myofibres form with the right size and nuclear number, and in placental trophoblast, where fusion into syncytiotrophoblast is tightly timed. The gene membership is dominated by large ribosomal subunit proteins together with the ubiquitin-ribosomal fusion product UBA52, pointing to translational output as a brake on fusion competence, while TMEM182 acts as a membrane restraint on myoblast fusion and CFLAR limits caspase-dependent signalling that accompanies fusion. Inflammatory and cAMP-linked inputs, represented by CXCL10 and the cAMP sensor RAPGEF3, further modulate the decision. Loss of this restraint yields inappropriate multinucleation, as seen in aberrant myogenesis and virus-induced syncytia.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it does not simply run to the end of a gene; its progress is actively restrained, and negative regulation of transcription elongation is how cells hold paused polymerase in reserve, time gene induction, and keep transcription from colliding with replication or damaged DNA. The NELF complex, working just downstream of promoters, is the core pausing factor here, while HEXIM1 together with the 7SK small nuclear RNA and LARP7 sequesters the P-TEFb kinase that would otherwise release paused polymerase. Other components act by different routes: RECQL5 physically limits polymerase movement along the template, SIRT6 and EZH2 impose repressive chromatin, PPP1R10 directs a phosphatase toward elongation factors, and RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin signalling silences transcription around double-strand breaks. Loss of such restraint yields untimely gene expression, transcription-replication conflict and genome instability.

Amides span a surprisingly broad chemical territory in cells — peptide bonds, ceramides, and other acylamino compounds — and this grouping collects the regulators that set how fast such compounds are made and broken down. Two themes dominate. One is control of amyloid-beta peptide levels, where secretase-associated and trafficking proteins such as GSAP, TMED10, SORL1, PICALM and BIN1, together with lipoprotein and chaperone factors APOE and clusterin, govern precursor processing and peptide clearance; failure here underlies Alzheimer disease pathology. The other is ceramide and sphingolipid amide homeostasis, with ORMDL proteins restraining serine palmitoyltransferase and sphingosine kinases diverting flux toward sphingosine-1-phosphate, shaping apoptosis and stress signalling. Overlying both are nutrient and stress hubs — mTOR complex components, AMPK, TP53, NFE2L2 and NF-κB — plus numerous microRNAs that tune the same targets post-transcriptionally, linking amide turnover to growth, inflammation and neuronal survival.

Amides in this context are peptides and sphingolipid amide bonds, and the genes collected here act to hold their production down — chiefly by limiting amyloid-beta generation from the amyloid precursor protein and by restraining ceramide synthesis. The theme is dominated by Alzheimer's disease risk biology: APOE, CLU, ABCA7, BIN1 and SORL1 influence how much amyloid-beta is made, trafficked and cleared, while reticulon family members bind BACE1 and reduce its access to substrate, and numerous microRNAs suppress APP or secretase expression post-transcriptionally. ORMDL proteins inhibit serine palmitoyltransferase, capping the first step of sphingolipid and ceramide production. Together these represent brakes rather than a biosynthetic route, and their weakening shifts the balance toward peptide aggregation and lipid-mediated stress, linking endosomal trafficking, lipid homeostasis and neurodegeneration.

Positive regulation of amide metabolic process covers the upregulation of reactions that make and break amide bonds, which in practice means peptides, and the genes gathered here point specifically at increased production of amyloid-beta from its precursor. That output matters because amyloid peptide load is the initiating lesion of Alzheimer's disease, and several members are among the strongest genetic risk factors for it: the lipid-handling and clearance proteins APOE and clusterin, the endocytic adaptor PICALM, and cholesterol transporters ABCA2 and ABCG1. Others act on the proteolytic machinery directly, including the gamma-secretase activating protein GSAP, or feed in through inflammatory and stress signalling via TNF, interferon-gamma with its receptor, NF-kB RELA, kinases such as GSK3A, PRKCD and ROCK2, and transcriptional regulators SP1 and NFE2L2. The theme is how lipid trafficking, neuroinflammation and kinase signalling converge to raise peptide generation in the brain.

negative regulation of GTPase activity describes the braking side of small GTPase switching: proteins that slow or block GTP hydrolysis so that a GTPase stays in its active, signal-transmitting conformation longer. Because Ras, Rho, Arf and Rab family switches are timed by hydrolysis, holding hydrolysis back changes the duration of signals that direct cytoskeletal remodelling, vesicle budding and membrane traffic, cell migration and mitotic progression. The members act by several routes — guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibition, occlusion of GAP binding, or sequestration of the GTPase, as with GPSM1 on heterotrimeric Gα subunits, ARL2 with its effectors, SH3BP4 restraining Rag-dependent mTORC1 activation, and LRCH1 acting on Rho signalling in lymphocytes. Plexin and NK receptor components link the same logic to axon guidance repulsion and immune recognition, while LRRK2 ties prolonged Rab signalling to Parkinson disease.

Small GTPases act as timers: they signal while bound to GTP and stop when it is hydrolysed, so anything that slows hydrolysis prolongs the active state. Negative regulation of GTPase activity covers the guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors, sequestering partners and GAP-blocking proteins that keep Ras-, Rho-, Arf- and Rab-family switches loaded with GTP, extending signals for cytoskeletal remodelling, vesicle budding and growth control. The genes here work by varied means: ARL2 and TMED2 bind and restrain partner GTPases, GPSM1 holds heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunits in an inactive-yet-undissociated state during asymmetric division, SH3BP4 and LRCH1 sequester Rab and Rho proteins, and LRRK2 links the theme to Rab-dependent membrane traffic and Parkinson disease. The balance matters because persistently active GTPases drive aberrant proliferation, migration and defective intracellular transport.

Cells and tissues must sense the arrival of sugars such as glucose or fructose and respond by changing secretion, metabolic flux and gene expression, and this response to monosaccharide stimulus is the coordinated programme that does so. Its clearest physiological output is nutrient homeostasis: pancreatic beta cells take up glucose through a transporter and phosphorylate it with glucokinase, raising ATP so that the KATP channel subunit encoded by ABCC8 closes and insulin granules fuse with the membrane, while incretin and counter-regulatory hormone signals tune the threshold. In parallel, transcriptional regulators including HNF4A, PDX1, MLXIPL and SREBF1 rewire glycolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipogenesis, and AMP-activated kinase subunits report energy status. Chronic excess sugar drives oxidative and endoplasmic reticulum stress responses here, and failure of these circuits underlies type 2 diabetes and monogenic forms of hyperglycaemia.

Cells and tissues adjust their behaviour when disaccharides such as sucrose, lactose or trehalose are present, and the response to disaccharide covers those changes in gene expression, secretion and signalling. In whole-organism terms this is largely the physiology of dietary sugar: sucrose feeding alters adipose endocrine output through adiponectin, drives lipogenic remodelling in liver where the lipid-droplet enzyme PNPLA3 acts, and modulates hypothalamic and neuroendocrine circuits that include oxytocin signalling and receptor components such as CALCRL. Glutamatergic signalling via the AMPA receptor subunit GRIA1 links sugar exposure to reward and feeding behaviour, while the lysosomal glycosidase NAGLU places carbohydrate catabolism alongside these responses. Together the biology connects sugar intake to appetite control, insulin sensitivity and hepatic fat accumulation, the axis that fails in fructose- and sucrose-driven metabolic disease.

Primary alcohols, from ethanol to retinol and long-chain fatty alcohols, are handled by an interconnected set of oxidoreductases and conjugating enzymes that convert them to aldehydes, acids or excretable esters. This metabolism determines how much alcohol and how many alcohol-derived aldehydes a tissue is exposed to, and it also sets retinoic acid levels that pattern developing tissues and maintain epithelia. Class I alcohol dehydrogenases oxidise ethanol and retinol, aldo-keto reductases and short-chain dehydrogenases such as RDH5, RDH10 and DHRS3 run the reverse and related reductions, and aldehyde dehydrogenases including ALDH2 and the ALDH1A enzymes commit the aldehyde onward to acetate or retinoic acid. Cytochrome P450s, sulfotransferases and esterases provide alternative oxidation and conjugation routes, while lipases and acyltransferases release or re-esterify retinyl and glycerol-derived alcohols. Variation here underlies differences in alcohol tolerance, acetaldehyde toxicity and vitamin A homeostasis, including retinoid-dependent visual cycle function.

Formation of primary alcohols here is essentially adrenal steroidogenesis, since 21-hydroxylation of steroid precursors installs the primary hydroxyl that defines cortisol, corticosterone and aldosterone. The enzymes named are the adrenal cortex cytochrome P450s: 17alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase, 21-hydroxylase and the 11beta-hydroxylase/aldosterone synthase pair, with a hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase supplying the reduced cofactor pool that sustains glucocorticoid metabolism. Their output governs blood pressure and sodium balance, the stress response, and gluconeogenesis; loss of 21-hydroxylase causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia with cortisol deficiency and androgen excess, and altered aldosterone synthase activity underlies forms of hyperaldosteronism. The accompanying bone morphogenetic proteins, WNT4 and DKK3 reflect the developmental signalling that patterns adrenal cortex zonation and specifies the steroidogenic cell types, while calcium and chloride channels couple angiotensin and potassium stimulation to hormone output.

Primary alcohols — ethanol and longer-chain or hydroxylated relatives such as retinol and sphingoid-derived alcohols — are catabolised by oxidation to the corresponding aldehyde and then to a carboxylic acid, or else conjugated and excreted. This is the body's main route for clearing ingested ethanol and for disposing of reactive aldehydes generated by lipid peroxidation, and its efficiency shapes individual tolerance to alcohol and susceptibility to alcohol-related tissue damage. Mitochondrial ALDH2 and ALDH1B1 carry the acetaldehyde-oxidising step, with the common ALDH2 deficiency producing the flushing response and elevated oesophageal cancer risk; ALDH3B family members handle longer aliphatic aldehydes. Acetate released from ethanol is re-activated to acetyl-CoA by ACSS1 and ACSS2, feeding oxidative metabolism and lipogenesis. Aldo-keto reductases interconvert alcohols and carbonyls, while cytosolic sulfotransferases add sulfate to hydroxyl groups, making the alcohols more water-soluble for elimination. The pathway is thus xenobiotic detoxification joined to intermediary metabolism.

Compounds bearing two hydroxyl groups sit at the centre of two otherwise separate metabolic routes, and this grouping covers both. One is the sphingoid base arm of sphingolipid metabolism: serine palmitoyltransferase subunits initiate de novo synthesis, ceramidases and acid ceramidase liberate sphingosine from ceramide, sphingosine kinases phosphorylate it, and phosphatases together with lipid phosphate phosphatases reverse that step, setting the balance between pro-apoptotic ceramide and pro-survival, migration-promoting sphingosine-1-phosphate. The other is tetrahydrobiopterin metabolism, where GCH1, PTS and sepiapterin reductase build the cofactor and QDPR with the pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratases regenerate it; BH4 supply governs aromatic amino acid hydroxylation and keeps nitric oxide synthase coupled. Loss of function in these routes produces lysosomal sphingolipid storage disease, hereditary sensory neuropathy, dopa-responsive dystonia and hyperphenylalaninaemia, and, via uncoupled NOS, endothelial dysfunction.

Formation of compounds bearing two hydroxyl groups on saturated carbons brings together two otherwise separate metabolic routes, and the diol biosynthetic process here is dominated by sphingoid bases and tetrahydrobiopterin. Serine palmitoyltransferase subunits initiate de novo sphingolipid synthesis, while ceramidases and glucocerebrosidase liberate sphingosine from ceramide and glucosylceramide; sphingosine kinases then phosphorylate it to the signalling lipid that governs vascular integrity, lymphocyte egress and cell survival, so defects in this arm produce lysosomal storage disease and sensory neuropathy. In parallel, GTP cyclohydrolase, pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase and sepiapterin reductase build tetrahydrobiopterin, the cofactor regenerated by pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase, dihydropteridine reductase and dihydrofolate reductase. That cofactor is required by phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases and by nitric oxide synthases, linking these reactions to catecholamine and serotonin production and to hyperphenylalaninaemia when they fail.

Branched actin networks are built by the Arp2/3 complex, which binds the side of an existing filament and nucleates a new one at roughly 70 degrees, generating the dendritic arrays that push out lamellipodia, drive endocytic vesicle internalisation, and propel intracellular pathogens. Cell migration, phagocytosis, membrane trafficking and dendritic spine morphology all depend on this activity. The seven-subunit complex itself is intrinsically weak and must be switched on by nucleation-promoting factors: the WAVE regulatory complex, assembled from WAVE proteins with CYFIP, NCKAP, ABI and BRK1, acts downstream of Rac at the leading edge, while the WASH complex directs branching on endosomes to support cargo sorting and tubule scission, and WHAMM and JMY couple it to Golgi membranes and the nuclear response to DNA damage. Capping-protein regulators and glia maturation factors set filament length and promote debranching, keeping network turnover balanced.

Branched actin networks are built when the Arp2/3 complex nucleates a new filament off the side of an existing one, and this pathway covers the proteins that decide when and where that happens. The output is the pushing force behind lamellipodial protrusion, cell migration, endocytic vesicle scission and tubular sorting out of endosomes, so its misregulation shows up as defective motility, immune cell function and membrane traffic. Most control is exerted through nucleation-promoting factors: the WAVE regulatory complex, assembled from CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2, BRK1 and a WASF subunit, relays Rac signals to Arp2/3 at the leading edge, while the WASH complex directs the same machinery onto endosomal membranes for cargo retrieval. Opposing activities restrain or disassemble branches — GMFB and GMFG promote debranching, CARMIL proteins tune capping protein, and coronin and HIP1R link nucleation to filament turnover and clathrin-coated pits.

Branched actin networks built by the Arp2/3 complex drive lamellipodial protrusion, endocytic vesicle formation and intracellular motility, and they must be switched off and dismantled as well as built. This pathway covers the restraint and disassembly side of that balance, limiting how often and how extensively Arp2/3 creates new branches on existing filaments. Glia maturation factors GMFB and GMFG bind the complex and promote debranching, while coronin CORO1B works with cofilin-driven turnover to recycle filament networks; HIP1R and PICK1 restrict nucleation at membranes, coupling the brake to clathrin-mediated endocytosis and receptor trafficking. The net effect is control over cell shape, migration speed and directional persistence, and over the lifetime of actin structures at endocytic sites and synapses. Without such negative regulation, branched networks persist inappropriately and protrusion, vesicle scission and membrane traffic lose their timing.

Cells hold together and talk to one another through junctions, and this pathway covers their assembly "— the recruitment, arrangement and bonding of adhesion receptors, scaffolds and cytoskeletal anchors into tight junctions, adherens junctions, desmosomes, gap junctions and synapses. Without it epithelia cannot form a sealed barrier, endothelium leaks, and neurons fail to build functional contacts. Cadherins and nectins engage catenins and afadin to nucleate adherens junctions; claudins, occludin and junctional adhesion molecules assemble with zonula occludens and polarity scaffolds such as PAR3, PAR6 and CRB3 to seal paracellular space; connexins build channels for direct intercellular coupling. In the nervous system neurexins, neuroligins, LRRTMs, SynCAM-like receptors and PSD scaffolds specify and organise synaptic contacts. Rho-family GTPases, their regulators and actin-binding proteins supply the force and remodelling; failures underlie barrier disease, epithelial–mesenchymal transition in cancer, cardiomyopathy and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Cell junction organization covers the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of the specialized contacts that hold cells to one another and to the extracellular matrix. It is what allows epithelia to form sealed, polarized sheets, endothelium to control vascular permeability, muscle to transmit force, and neurons to build synapses; its failure underlies loss of barrier function, blistering skin disease, and impaired synaptic wiring. The genes span the major junction types: cadherin-catenin adherens junctions, claudin and occludin tight junctions with their ZO-1 scaffolds, desmosomal cadherins and plakins, connexin gap junctions, and integrin-talin-vinculin adhesions to laminin and collagen. Neuronal contacts are heavily represented through neurexin-neuroligin, SynCAM-like and leucine-rich repeat adhesion molecules, synaptic scaffolds such as PSD-95 and Shank, and active-zone proteins. Rho-family GTPases, actin nucleators, Par polarity complexes, ephrin and semaphorin cues, and tyrosine kinase and phosphatase signalling coordinate where and when junctions form.

Cells stick to each other and to matrix through specialized contact sites, and cell junction organization covers the assembly, remodeling and dismantling of those contacts. It builds the epithelial barrier, the endothelial seal of blood vessels, the mechanical continuity of desmosomes and adherens junctions, the neuromuscular junction, and the synapse, and its failure produces leaky epithelia, blistering skin disease, vascular malformation and neurodevelopmental disorders. Cadherins, claudins, occludin and nectins provide the adhesive interfaces; catenins, tight-junction scaffolds such as TJP1 and PATJ, plakophilins, plectin and desmoplakin couple them to actin and intermediate filaments; integrins and laminins anchor cells to basement membrane; and connexins form communicating channels. Rho-family GTPases, Src- and Eph-family kinases, PAR polarity complexes and neurexin–neuroligin pairs control where junctions form, how strongly they adhere, and when they are released during migration and synaptic remodeling.

Once cells have contacted one another, the contact must be held: this pathway covers the maintenance of cell junctions, keeping adhesive and signalling contacts between neighbouring cells, and between cells and matrix, in a stable functional state rather than building them anew. Two contexts dominate. At epithelial contacts, tight and adherens junction components such as claudins, ZO-1, PLEKHA7 and polarity regulators including PARD6A and DLG1 preserve barrier integrity and apicobasal organization, with desmosomal plakophilin and desmocollin adding mechanical strength; loss of this upkeep causes barrier leak and tissue disorganization. At synapses, active-zone scaffolds such as bassoon, piccolo, RIMs and ERCs, together with cerebellin and C1QL trans-synaptic organizers, neuroligin and SHANK1, hold pre- and postsynaptic membranes aligned so that release sites face receptors. Small GTPase regulators, integrin-linked adaptors and cytoskeletal linkers supply the turnover control that keeps these structures stable under load.

Adherens junction organization builds, remodels and dismantles the cadherin-based contacts that hold epithelial and endothelial cells to their neighbours and couple that adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton. It sets tissue cohesion and apical-basal polarity, seals the vascular endothelium, and permits the coordinated cell rearrangements of morphogenesis and wound repair; its loss underlies the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas. Classical cadherins engage in calcium-dependent homophilic pairs whose cytoplasmic tails recruit beta-catenin and, through vinculin and alpha-catenin-linked adaptors, anchor actin filaments so that tension is shared across a sheet. Junction strength is tuned rather than fixed: Rho-family GTPases such as CDC42, tyrosine kinases and phosphatases, ADAM10-mediated cadherin shedding, and endocytic adaptors including NUMB control turnover. Scaffolds such as PLEKHA7 and CAMSAP3 tie the junction to microtubules and position it apically.

Epithelial and endothelial sheets hold together through adherens junctions, belt-like contacts where cadherin ectodomains engage partners on the neighbouring cell and the cytoplasmic face couples to the actin cytoskeleton. Building, remodelling and dismantling these contacts sets tissue cohesion, apical-basal polarity and the ability of cells to rearrange during morphogenesis and wound repair; loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) or its catenin link is a route to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and invasive carcinoma, while the endothelial cadherin CDH5 governs vascular permeability. The many classical and atypical cadherins here supply adhesive specificity across neurons, muscle, gut and skin, and beta-catenin, vinculin, plectin and the tight-junction scaffold ZO-1 anchor them to filaments. Junction turnover is regulated by CDC42 and PAK2 signalling, ADAM10-mediated cadherin ectodomain shedding, phosphorylation by FER and CSK, and endocytic control through NUMB, linking adhesion to growth-factor and BMP cues.

Epithelial sheets hold together through adherens junctions, and their assembly is the step that converts cadherin-mediated cell-cell recognition into a mechanically coupled tissue. Without it, epithelia lose apical-basal organisation and barrier integrity, cells detach and become motile, and the resulting loss of contact restraint is a recurring feature of tumour invasion and metastasis. The junction is built by clustering cadherin family adhesion receptors at the contact site and linking their cytoplasmic tails through beta-catenin and vinculin to the underlying actin cytoskeleton, so actin dynamics, lipid kinase activity and Rho-family effectors such as PAK2 shape where and how firmly junctions form. Scaffolding and polarity proteins including DLG5 help deliver and position the complex, while kinase signalling tunes junctional strength. Because beta-catenin also acts as a transcriptional coactivator, junction assembly sequesters it and couples adhesion status to growth control.}
}

Epithelial sheets stay sealed and mechanically coherent because cadherin-catenin contacts, once formed, are actively held in place; adherens junction maintenance is the upkeep of those belt-like contacts and their anchorage to the actin cytoskeleton. Loss of this upkeep loosens epithelial cohesion, disturbs apical-basal polarity and barrier function, and contributes to the junctional breakdown seen in intestinal inflammation and in tumour invasion. The genes here act at the cytoplasmic face of the junction rather than as adhesion receptors themselves: scaffolding proteins such as PLEKHA7 and TJP1 link the cadherin complex to the apical zonula, CAMSAP3 stabilises non-centrosomal microtubule minus ends beneath the apical membrane, KIFC3 delivers material along microtubules to the contact, FERMT2 couples integrin and actin machinery, and MTSS1 shapes the membrane. Together they sustain junctional architecture in polarised epithelia.

RNA molecules only work once folded, and this pathway covers the chaperoning of single or multimeric RNAs into their correct three-dimensional shape, including the noncovalent contacts and assembly steps that stabilize it. Much of the activity described here sits in mitochondria, where GTP-binding and RNA-binding factors such as ERAL1 and NOA1 act as assembly chaperones for the small subunit ribosomal RNA and support mitoribosome biogenesis, and MTERF4 helps deliver a methyltransferase partner to the large subunit RNA; loss of these steps blunts mitochondrial translation and oxidative phosphorylation, a recognized cause of infantile mitochondrial disease. WRAP53 instead guides the telomerase RNA component to nuclear Cajal bodies, linking correct RNA structure and trafficking to telomere maintenance, with mutations causing dyskeratosis congenita. Together the set connects RNA conformation to ribonucleoprotein assembly and to the enzymes that depend on it.

Type I interferons are the cytokines cells release when they detect viral nucleic acid, and this pathway covers both their production and the antiviral state they induce in responding cells. Sensors such as IFIH1, MAVS, STING1 and ZBP1 converge on the TBK1/IKBKE kinases and the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7 to drive interferon-alpha and -beta expression; secreted interferon then engages the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor, activating JAK1 and TYK2 and the STAT1-STAT2 complex to switch on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes. Effectors including MX1, the OAS enzymes, IFIT1, the IFITM proteins and the ISG15 conjugation system block viral entry, replication and translation, while the proteasome supports antigen presentation. Negative regulators such as USP18, the phosphatases PTPN1, PTPN2 and PTPN6, TREX1 and ADAR restrain the response; their loss causes interferonopathies and autoimmunity, and deficient signalling leaves patients vulnerable to severe viral infection.

Interferon-gamma, the sole type II interferon, is the cytokine by which activated T cells and NK cells license macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens and raise antigen presentation, and the cellular response to it underlies granuloma formation, control of mycobacteria and Salmonella, and much of the tissue damage in autoimmunity. Ligand binding to the IFNGR1/IFNGR2 receptor pair activates JAK1 and JAK2, which phosphorylate STAT1; STAT1 with IRF1 and IRF8 then drives transcription of guanylate-binding proteins, immunity-related GTPases, inducible nitric oxide synthase, arginase and tryptophan- and tetrahydrobiopterin-related enzymes that reshape macrophage metabolism. Parallel outputs include CIITA- and NLRC5-dependent MHC class II and class I expression, swapping of constitutive proteasome subunits for the immunoproteasome, and vesicle trafficking and autophagy machinery that deliver effectors onto pathogen-containing vacuoles. PTPN2 and other brakes limit the response; loss of receptor or STAT1 function causes susceptibility to mycobacterial disease.

response to type III interferon covers how cells react to interferon lambda, the antiviral cytokine family that guards epithelial surfaces. Because its receptor chain IFNLR1, paired with the shared IL10RB subunit, is largely restricted to epithelium of the gut, airway and liver, lambda interferons provide mucosal antiviral defence with far less inflammatory cost than type I interferons; variants in the IFNL3/IFNL4 locus are among the strongest determinants of spontaneous hepatitis C clearance and treatment response. Ligand binding drives JAK-STAT signalling and induction of interferon-stimulated genes, including antiviral effectors such as the shiftless translation inhibitor SHFL, converging on the same transcriptional programme as other interferons. The set also links to interferon-gamma and its receptor, reflecting overlap in downstream output, and to autophagy machinery through EPG5, tying interferon signalling to lysosomal degradation and immune homeostasis.

Type III interferons — the lambda family, IFNL1 through IFNL4 — are antiviral cytokines that act mainly at epithelial barriers, and the cellular response to them defines mucosal antiviral defence in gut, airway and liver without the systemic inflammation that type I interferon provokes. Responsiveness is set by the receptor: a dedicated IFNLR1 chain paired with the shared IL10RB subunit, a restricted distribution that explains why epithelium and some myeloid cells answer lambda while most tissues do not. Engagement drives JAK-STAT signalling and an interferon-stimulated gene programme overlapping that of type I interferon, including translational restriction factors such as SHFL that block viral replication. Genetic variation in this axis, notably at IFNL3/IFNL4, predicts spontaneous clearance of hepatitis C. Receptor components for interferon gamma appear alongside, reflecting how the interferon classes are compared and cross-regulated in antiviral and antimicrobial responses.

Type III interferon production is the induced synthesis and release of interferon lambda, the antiviral cytokine family whose receptor is largely confined to epithelial surfaces of the airway, gut and liver. Because of that receptor distribution, it provides antiviral protection at mucosal barriers with less of the systemic inflammation caused by type I interferons, and it shapes outcomes in respiratory and enteric viral infection as well as hepatitis. Induction begins with detection of viral nucleic acid: the endosomal double-stranded RNA sensor TLR3 and the cytosolic RNA helicases RIG-I and MDA5 (IFIH1) signal through adaptor-dependent routes to activate interferon regulatory factors and NF-κB, which drive transcription of the lambda genes. Additional regulators tune the response, including a microRNA and interferon-inducible guanylate-binding protein activity, linking sensing of infection to barrier-restricted antiviral defence.

Programmed death of glial cells shapes the nervous system twice over: during development, when oligodendrocyte and astrocyte precursors are produced in excess and trimmed to match the axons they must support, and in disease, when injured or inflamed glia are eliminated. This glial cell apoptotic process runs through the canonical intrinsic route, with p53 and RB1 setting the decision upstream and caspase-9 and caspase-3 executing it, alongside death receptor input via TNFRSF21 and the TRAF2 adaptor. Survival signals oppose it: GAS6 acting through receptor tyrosine kinase signalling keeps oligodendrocytes alive, TREM2 supports microglial viability, and several protein kinase C isoforms tune the threshold. Chemokine signalling through CCL2 links glial death to recruitment of inflammatory cells. Too much of this pathway contributes to demyelination and white matter injury; too little leaves supernumerary glia.

Glia vastly outnumber neurons, and how many of them survive is set partly by controlling when they die: this pathway modulates the rate and extent of apoptosis in astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and Schwann cells. It matters for myelin maintenance, for the pruning of surplus glia during development, and for whether glial loss or glial survival dominates after injury and in neurodegeneration. Survival inputs arrive as secreted ligands and their receptors — the growth-arrest-specific factor GAS6 acting through TAM receptor tyrosine kinases, the chemokine CCL2, and Notch ligand DLL1 — while the microglial receptor TREM2 sustains microglial viability and is a risk locus for Alzheimer disease. Downstream, several protein kinase C isoforms and the scaffolding protein AKAP12 shape the intracellular response, and TRAF2 couples tumour necrosis factor receptor engagement to either survival signalling or death.

Cells can build the redox coenzyme NAD+ from scratch, and in humans the only route that does so starts from dietary tryptophan rather than from a vitamin. This de novo branch, running through the kynurenine pathway, supplies the liver with enough NAD+ to spare niacin from the diet; when it fails or when tryptophan is scarce, the deficiency state pellagra follows. Tryptophan is opened by the dioxygenases IDO1 and IDO2 and processed by formamidase, kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, kynureninase and HAAO to an unstable intermediate that cyclises non-enzymatically to quinolinate; QPRT then couples quinolinate to a phosphoribosyl group, and NMNAT and NAD synthetase complete the dinucleotide. ACMSD diverts flux away from quinolinate toward complete oxidation, setting how much NAD+ the pathway actually yields. The same route generates neuroactive kynurenines and is engaged during immune activation and inflammation.

Lipoproteins are not fixed particles; they are continually rebuilt in plasma as lipids and apolipoproteins are exchanged, hydrolysed and modified, and this protein-containing complex remodeling is what converts nascent discs into mature HDL and triglyceride-rich particles into LDL. The process sets circulating cholesterol and triglyceride levels, so its failure produces hyperlipidaemia, atherosclerosis and, in extreme cases, chylomicronaemia. Lipases such as LPL, LIPC and LIPG strip triglyceride from particles, with ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 restraining them and GPIHBP1 anchoring LPL at the endothelium; LCAT esterifies cholesterol to expand the HDL core, while CETP and PLTP shuttle lipids between particles. Apolipoproteins including APOA1, APOB, APOE and APOC3 act as structural scaffolds and cofactors, and transporters such as ABCG1 load cellular cholesterol onto acceptors. Secreted phospholipases and PON1 further alter particle composition and oxidative state.

Triglyceride-rich lipoprotein particle remodeling is the set of extracellular reactions that convert newly secreted chylomicrons and VLDL into smaller, cholesterol-enriched remnants, delivering fatty acids to muscle and adipose tissue along the way. It sets circulating triglyceride levels, and its failure produces hypertriglyceridemia, chylomicronemia with pancreatitis, and accelerated atherosclerosis from persistent remnant particles. The core event is hydrolysis of core triglyceride by lipoprotein lipase, which must be anchored at the capillary endothelial surface by GPIHBP1 and is switched on or off by apolipoprotein cofactors and inhibitors: APOC2 and APOA5 activate, APOC3 and the angiopoietin-like proteins restrain. Particles simultaneously exchange surface and core lipids, with CETP swapping cholesteryl esters for triglyceride, LCAT esterifying cholesterol, and hepatic lipase trimming remnants before APOE-mediated receptor uptake. Bile acid signalling through NR1H4 links the process to hepatic lipid and lipoprotein output.

Chylomicrons and VLDL deliver dietary and hepatic fat to tissues, and their remodeling in plasma converts these triglyceride-rich particles into smaller remnants while releasing fatty acids for muscle to burn and adipose to store. The central reaction is hydrolysis of core triglyceride by lipoprotein lipase, which must be transported to the capillary endothelial surface by GPIHBP1 and is switched on by apolipoprotein C-II while APOC3, ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 restrain it; hepatic lipase acts on partially depleted particles. In parallel, cholesteryl ester transfer protein exchanges cholesteryl esters and triglyceride between particle classes, and lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase esterifies cholesterol, so remodeling couples triglyceride clearance to HDL metabolism and reverse cholesterol transport. Apolipoprotein E marks remnants for hepatic uptake, and bile acid-activated FXR signalling sets the transcriptional tone. Defects in these steps cause severe hypertriglyceridaemia, pancreatitis, and remnant-driven atherosclerosis.

Chylomicron remodeling is the process by which the large triglyceride-rich particles that carry dietary fat out of the intestine are stripped of their cargo in peripheral tissues and converted into remnants for hepatic clearance. It is how ingested fat is delivered to muscle for oxidation and to adipose tissue for storage, and its failure produces severe hypertriglyceridemia with pancreatitis. The reaction is carried out by lipoprotein lipase acting at the capillary endothelium, where GPIHBP1 binds the enzyme and shuttles it to the luminal surface to meet circulating chylomicrons. Activity is tuned by exchangeable apolipoproteins on the particle surface: APOC2 is the obligatory activator, while ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4 inhibit the lipase in response to feeding and fasting, partitioning fatty acids between tissues. Loss of triglyceride is accompanied by transfer of surface lipid and apolipoproteins, remodeling the particle itself.

Dietary fat leaves the intestine packaged in chylomicrons, and chylomicron remodeling is the series of protein and lipid exchanges that converts these triglyceride-rich particles into smaller remnants while delivering fatty acids to tissues. It is how muscle obtains fuel and adipose tissue obtains storage lipid after a meal, and its failure produces severe hypertriglyceridaemia with pancreatitis. The central event is hydrolysis of core triglyceride by lipoprotein lipase, which is anchored on the capillary endothelial surface by GPIHBP1 and requires APOC2 as an activating cofactor; the liberated free fatty acids are taken up locally and the particle shrinks. Activity is titrated by inhibitors of the lipase, ANGPTL3 and ANGPTL4, which restrain delivery according to feeding and fasting state, while exchangeable surface proteins such as APOA4 and APOH accompany the changing particle composition. This makes the pathway the regulated gateway of postprandial lipid distribution.

Low-density lipoprotein particles are not static once secreted: their lipid core and surface proteins are continuously reworked in plasma, and that remodeling sets how long LDL circulates, how readily it enters the arterial wall, and how atherogenic it becomes. Cholesteryl ester transfer protein swaps cholesteryl esters out of LDL for triglyceride from triglyceride-rich particles, hepatic lipase then hydrolyses that triglyceride, and the result is the small dense LDL associated with coronary risk. Secreted phospholipases act on the particle surface, while myeloperoxidase-derived oxidants modify apolipoprotein B, generating oxidized LDL that macrophage scavenger receptors take up to form foam cells. Apolipoproteins A-II and E, the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein and ABCG1-mediated sterol efflux link this remodeling to hepatic lipoprotein assembly and reverse cholesterol transport, and its dysregulation underlies dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis.

High-density lipoprotein particle remodeling is the continuous reshaping of HDL in plasma that lets it collect cholesterol from peripheral tissues and deliver it to the liver, the core of reverse cholesterol transport and a major determinant of atherosclerosis risk. Nascent discoidal particles built on apolipoprotein A-I mature as LCAT esterifies cholesterol to form a hydrophobic core, while phospholipid transfer protein fuses and redistributes surface lipids and CETP swaps cholesteryl ester for triglyceride with apoB-containing lipoproteins. Hepatic and endothelial lipases then hydrolyse HDL lipids, shrinking particles and releasing lipid-poor apoA-I for another cycle; SR-BI mediates selective uptake of the cholesteryl ester cargo by liver and steroidogenic tissue, and ABCG1 loads cholesterol from macrophages. Exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA2, APOC3 and APOE tune which enzymes act, linking this remodeling to triglyceride metabolism and clearance receptors.

High-density lipoprotein particles are not static cargo containers; they are continuously rebuilt as they circulate, and this remodeling sets how much cholesterol they can carry back from tissues to the liver. It underlies reverse cholesterol transport and is the biology behind HDL cholesterol as a cardiovascular risk marker. Nascent discoidal particles built on apolipoprotein A-I acquire cell-derived cholesterol via ABCG1, and LCAT esterifies it to form a hydrophobic core and a mature spherical particle. CETP then exchanges cholesteryl ester for triglyceride with apoB-containing lipoproteins, hepatic and endothelial lipases hydrolyse core and surface lipids to shrink particles, phospholipid transfer protein shuffles surface phospholipid, and SCARB1 delivers cholesteryl ester to hepatocytes and steroidogenic cells. Exchangeable apolipoproteins such as APOA2, APOC3, APOE and APOM determine particle composition and enzyme access; their imbalance produces dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis.

Chylomicron assembly is the step in fat absorption where enterocytes of the small intestine package dietary triglyceride and cholesterol with apolipoproteins into large lipoprotein particles for export into lymph and blood. Without it, absorbed lipid and fat-soluble vitamins cannot leave the intestinal epithelium, producing fat-laden enterocytes, steatorrhoea and deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K, as seen in abetalipoproteinaemia. Fatty acid uptake at the brush border via CD36 and cytosolic trafficking by FABP1 feed lipid to the endoplasmic reticulum, where LPCAT3 shapes membrane phospholipid composition permissive for particle formation and the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein MTTP lipidates apolipoprotein B; APOA4 is induced by lipid loading and stabilises the growing particle. PLAGL2 contributes transcriptional control of the lipid handling program. The pathway links intestinal lipid absorption to whole-body triglyceride delivery and postprandial lipaemia.

Dietary fat absorbed by the small intestine leaves the enterocyte packaged into chylomicrons, and this assembly step is where triglyceride, phospholipid and apolipoproteins are brought together non-covalently into that particle. Without it, fat and fat-soluble vitamins cannot be delivered to lymph and blood, producing steatorrhoea, failure to thrive and the lipid malabsorption seen in abetalipoproteinaemia. Fatty acid uptake and intracellular trafficking depend on a scavenger-type transporter and a cytosolic fatty acid binding protein, while an acyltransferase remodels membrane phospholipids to supply the particle surface. The microsomal triglyceride transfer protein lipidates apolipoprotein B in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, the committing event of particle formation, and apolipoprotein A-IV associates with the expanding surface. A transcription factor contributes to the enterocyte lipid-handling programme, linking this biology to postprandial lipid transport and whole-body energy supply.

very-low-density lipoprotein particle assembly is how the liver packages triglycerides and cholesteryl esters for export to peripheral tissues, converting stored and newly synthesised lipid into circulating fuel. Without it fat accumulates in hepatocytes and plasma lipids collapse, the basis of abetalipoproteinaemia and hypobetalipoproteinaemia; excessive output instead drives the atherogenic dyslipidaemia of insulin resistance. Assembly begins co-translationally, as microsomal triglyceride transfer protein lipidates nascent apolipoprotein B in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen and rescues it from degradation. Neutral lipid substrate is supplied by acyl-CoA synthetases and the diacylglycerol and cholesterol acyltransferases, while phospholipid remodelling and lysophospholipid transport set membrane and surface-monolayer composition. CIDEB governs maturation and fusion of the growing particle before secretion. Exchangeable apolipoproteins loaded during assembly, notably APOC3, later dictate how quickly the secreted particle is cleared from plasma.

Hepatocytes export lipid to the rest of the body by packaging triglyceride, cholesteryl ester and phospholipid around apolipoprotein B, and very-low-density lipoprotein particle assembly is the set of steps that builds that carrier before secretion. It sets the supply of fatty acids to muscle and adipose tissue between meals and determines circulating triglyceride and LDL levels, so its failure is consequential in both directions: loss of microsomal triglyceride transfer protein activity or of APOB itself blocks secretion and traps fat in the liver, producing steatosis and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, while excess output drives atherogenic dyslipidaemia. Mechanistically, acyl-CoA synthetase and diacylglycerol and cholesterol acyltransferases generate the neutral lipid cargo, lysophospholipid acyltransferase activity shapes the phospholipid surface, lipid transfer lipidates nascent apoB in the endoplasmic reticulum, and exchangeable apolipoproteins including APOC3 ride on the particle to govern its later lipolysis and clearance.

High-density lipoprotein particle assembly builds the HDL particles that carry excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver, the first step of reverse cholesterol transport and the basis of HDL's protection against atherosclerosis. Lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I, secreted largely by liver and intestine, docks on ABCA1 at the plasma membrane and accepts phospholipid and free cholesterol to form discoidal nascent HDL; LCAT then esterifies the cholesterol, driving maturation into spherical particles, while APOA2, APOE and APOM diversify particle composition and function. Output is tuned transcriptionally by the sterol-sensing nuclear receptor LXRb and post-translationally by protein kinase A phosphorylation of the transporter, with microRNA input restraining ABCA1 levels. Loss of ABCA1 function abolishes particle formation and causes Tangier disease, with near-absent plasma HDL, tissue cholesterol deposition and premature coronary disease.

High-density lipoprotein particles are built when lipid-poor apolipoproteins acquire phospholipid and cholesterol from cell membranes, and this assembly step is the start of reverse cholesterol transport, by which peripheral tissues and macrophages unload excess sterol for delivery to the liver. ABCA1 effluxes phospholipid and free cholesterol onto APOA1, generating discoidal nascent HDL that LCAT then matures by esterifying cholesterol and driving it into a spherical core; APOA2, APOE and APOM ride on the resulting particles and shape their fate. Transcriptional control through the oxysterol-sensing nuclear receptor NR1H2 tunes transporter expression, protein kinase A catalytic subunits contribute phosphorylation-dependent regulation of efflux, and a microRNA provides negative post-transcriptional input. Loss of ABCA1 or APOA1 function abolishes circulating HDL, as in Tangier disease, and low HDL accompanies atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk more generally.

Cholesterol and triglyceride carried in the blood must eventually be taken back out of circulation, and plasma lipoprotein particle clearance is the receptor-mediated removal and lysosomal breakdown of those particles by the liver and other tissues. It sets steady-state LDL levels, and when it fails cholesterol accumulates in plasma and in arterial macrophages, the basis of familial hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. Apolipoproteins such as APOB and APOE serve as ligands, while LDLR, VLDLR, SCARB1, CD36 and MSR1 act as the uptake receptors and LIPA degrades the delivered cholesteryl esters inside lysosomes. Receptor abundance is itself controlled: PCSK9 directs LDLR to degradation, MYLIP ubiquitinates it, LDLRAP1 couples it to endocytosis, and several microRNAs including the MIR33 pair tune the lipid programme. Upstream lipolysis by LPL with its cofactors APOC2 and GPIHBP1 generates the remnants that are cleared.

Circulating LDL is taken out of the blood mainly by hepatic receptor-mediated endocytosis, and the efficiency of this clearance sets plasma cholesterol concentration. When it fails, cholesterol accumulates in plasma and drives atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease: loss-of-function mutations in the LDL receptor or in its endocytic adaptor LDLRAP1, or in apolipoprotein B itself, cause familial hypercholesterolaemia, while PCSK9 lowers clearance by directing the receptor to lysosomal degradation and is the target of cholesterol-lowering antibodies. The receptor is further controlled by the E3 ligase MYLIP/IDOL, by vesicular trafficking and recycling factors, and by microRNAs and RNA-binding proteins acting post-transcriptionally. After uptake, lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters, which ACAT enzymes can re-esterify for storage. Related scavenger and fatty-acid receptors such as SCARB1 and CD36 handle other lipoprotein species and macrophage lipid loading, linking this route to foam cell formation.

Reverse cholesterol transport ends when high-density lipoprotein particles are taken out of the circulation and broken down, and high-density lipoprotein particle clearance is the step that sets how long HDL and its cholesterol cargo persist in plasma. Its rate helps determine steady-state HDL levels and the efficiency with which peripheral and macrophage-derived cholesterol reaches the liver for biliary excretion; imbalance contributes to dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis. Uptake is receptor-mediated, with the scavenger receptor SCARB1 mediating selective lipid uptake and holoparticle removal and LDLR contributing to apoE-containing particle clearance, after which apolipoproteins such as APOA1, APOA2 and APOM are degraded. Endothelial lipase and phospholipase activity remodel particles into forms cleared more rapidly, while several microRNAs, including the sterol-responsive miR-33 family, tune expression of the transporters and receptors involved, linking clearance to wider control of lipid homeostasis.

Cells store neutral lipid in droplets that bud from the endoplasmic reticulum, and lipid droplet organization covers how those droplets are formed, sized, positioned, coated and eventually broken down. This determines whether fatty acids are safely sequestered as triglyceride or released to damage membranes and drive lipotoxicity, and it defines the adipocyte as well as lipid handling in liver, muscle and macrophages. Seipin with its partner LDAF1 marks the ER sites where droplets emerge, FIT proteins and diacylglycerol/CDP-DAG enzymes shape the glycerolipid supply, perilipins coat the droplet surface and control access by lipases such as ATGL, and CIDE proteins mediate droplet fusion into the single large store of white fat. RAB18 and its GEF subunits tether droplets to the ER, while AMPK subunits couple droplet turnover to energy status. Loss of seipin causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy; perilipin and CIDEC defects give partial lipodystrophy with insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis.

Programmed death of smooth muscle cells shapes the vessel wall, the airway and the gut over a lifetime: it prunes cells during vascular remodelling and involution, but when it runs unchecked in atherosclerotic plaque it thins the fibrous cap, promotes medial degeneration and aneurysm, and destabilises lesions. The genes here cover both the executioners and the brakes. Stress-responsive kinase signalling through MAP2K4 and the MEK5-ERK5 arm, ATF4-dependent integrated stress responses, and mitochondrial control by MFN2 and the superoxide scavenger SOD2 set the threshold for death, while IGF1, BAG1, SIRT1 and PPARG signalling favour survival or quiescence and CDKN2A, FOXO1, E2F3 and PDCD4 push toward growth arrest and apoptosis. Inflammatory cues such as interferon-gamma, IL-12 and endothelin-1 act from outside, and numerous microRNAs, notably miR-21 and miR-210, tune the balance post-transcriptionally.

Smooth muscle cells in blood vessel walls and airways must survive mechanical stress, inflammation and metabolic insult, and this pathway covers the signals that hold their apoptotic machinery in check. Keeping them alive maintains vessel wall integrity and contractile tone; losing that restraint thins the media, destabilises atherosclerotic plaque caps and contributes to aneurysm formation, while excessive survival signalling drives the neointimal thickening seen after angioplasty and in pulmonary hypertension. Growth factor and hormonal inputs such as IGF1, endothelin-1 and oestrogen receptor signalling feed into survival kinases including the MEK5-ERK5 module, with Wnt co-receptor LRP6 and the chaperone-associated ubiquitin ligase STUB1 shaping the response. Several microRNAs, notably miR-21, miR-17/92 family members and the hypoxia-induced miR-210, suppress pro-apoptotic transcripts, linking cell survival here to oxygen availability and vascular remodelling.

Smooth muscle cells in vessel walls and hollow organs are normally long-lived, and signals that push them into programmed cell death set the balance between wall thickening and wall thinning. Enhanced smooth muscle cell apoptosis limits neointimal growth after injury but also destabilises atherosclerotic plaques and weakens aortic media, contributing to aneurysm and plaque rupture. The genes here converge on that outcome from several directions: stress-responsive transcriptional control through ATF4 and FOXO1, cell cycle and tumour suppressor input via CDKN2A and E2F3, mitochondrial handling of fusion and superoxide through MFN2 and SOD2, and chaperone-linked quality control by BAG1 and the ubiquitin ligase STUB1. Inflammatory cytokines including interferon gamma and the IL-12 subunits impose death signals from infiltrating immune cells, while PPARG, PDCD4 and several microRNAs tune the threshold at which a smooth muscle cell commits to apoptosis.

Getting a newly made receptor, channel or transporter to the outer face of the plasma membrane, and keeping it there, determines what a cell can sense and how strongly it responds. This trafficking step sets surface density for ion channels, adhesion receptors and immune recognition molecules, so its failure produces arrhythmia, impaired synaptic transmission, faulty lipid export and blunted receptor signalling. The genes here span the routes involved: recycling endosome machinery built around RAB11 and its effectors, adaptor and coat proteins such as PICALM and the GGA family, ARF6 and GBF1 acting on membrane budding, plasma membrane SNAREs STX3 and STX4 for the final fusion event, and cytoskeletal anchors including filamin A and vinculin that retain cargo at the cortex. Ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases oppose one another to decide whether surface protein is retrieved and degraded or stabilised, together with chaperones that license export from earlier compartments.

Positioning telomeres in a defined place in the nucleus, rather than letting chromosome ends drift, is what this localization process accomplishes, and in meiosis it is the basis of homologue pairing. During prophase I, telomeres are captured at the inner nuclear membrane by a cap built from TERB1, TERB2 and MAJIN working with the telomere-binding protein TERF1, and are handed to a LINC complex of SUN1 and KASH5 that couples them through the envelope to cytoplasmic motors. The resulting chromosome movements allow homologues to find each other, align and complete recombination, with SPO11 generating the initiating double-strand breaks and ATM and MLH1 acting in the damage response and crossover resolution that follow. Loss of the tethering components leaves chromosomes unpaired, blocks meiotic progression and causes infertility, making nuclear geography a prerequisite for producing viable gametes.

Anchoring telomeres to the nuclear periphery converts chromosome ends into handles that the cytoskeleton can pull, and in meiotic prophase this is how homologous chromosomes find each other. The TERB1-TERB2-MAJIN complex is recruited to telomeric chromatin through TRF1-bound TERB1 and caps the DNA end onto the inner nuclear membrane, where it couples to SUN1 and, through the intervening lumenal bridge, to cytoplasmic motors. The resulting rapid chromosome movements promote homologue pairing, synapsis and recombination, and a meiosis-specific CDK2 partner encoded by SPDYA is required at these attachment sites. Loss of these attachments leaves telomeres detached from the envelope, blocks synapsis and causes infertility with arrest in prophase I. Nucleoporin involvement links the same peripheral zone to nuclear pore territories, a chromatin environment that also shapes telomeric silencing and end protection.

Blood flow exerts a frictional drag on the endothelium, and cells read that drag as a signal. The response to fluid shear stress keeps vessels quiescent and anti-thrombotic where flow is laminar, and its failure at branch points and curvatures, where flow is disturbed, is what makes those sites the preferred locations for atherosclerotic plaque. Mechanosensors at the luminal surface and at junctions — polycystin channels, the ATP-gated P2RX4 and P2RX7 receptors, a proton-sensing GPCR, integrin-linked focal adhesion kinases and SRC — convert force into calcium flux, cyclic AMP production through adenylate cyclases and protein kinase A, and MAP2K5–MAPK7 signalling to MEF2C. The transcription factors KLF2 and KLF4 then drive endothelial nitric oxide synthase and suppress inflammatory output, while cyclooxygenase-2, TGFB1 with its inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 brakes, matrix remodelling and cholesterol handling tune vascular tone, permeability and remodelling.

Fatty acids are the densest fuel a cell can burn, and lipid oxidation is the set of reactions that strips electrons and hydrogens from them to feed respiration and ketogenesis. It sustains heart, liver and muscle during fasting and exercise; inherited defects in its enzymes cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis, while peroxisomal failures such as loss of the very-long-chain fatty acid transporter ABCD1 produce adrenoleukodystrophy. Carnitine shuttle components deliver acyl groups into mitochondria, where acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of distinct chain-length specificity pass electrons through the electron transfer flavoprotein system, and a trifunctional hydratase/dehydrogenase/thiolase machinery completes each round of beta-oxidation. Peroxisomes handle very-long-chain, branched and 2-hydroxy substrates, and lipoxygenases oxygenate polyunsaturated fatty acids toward signalling lipids. Transcriptional control by PPARs, PGC-1alpha and AMPK, with adipokine input from leptin and adiponectin, matches flux to nutritional state.

When a cell contacts extracellular matrix it does not simply stick; it flattens and extends over the surface, and this substrate adhesion-dependent spreading is the step that converts attachment into a polarised, migration-competent, mechanically anchored cell. It underlies wound healing, tissue morphogenesis, platelet plug formation and the anchorage dependence whose loss permits tumour cells to survive detached.
