Integrins such as ITGB1BP1-associated beta chains and ITGAV/ITGB3 engage fibronectin, laminins and fibrinogen, then recruit a focal adhesion platform of talin- and kindlin-family proteins, ILK with parvins, paxillin, FAK and Src, which transmits force and signals inward. Rho-family GTPases RAC1, CDC42 and RHOA, their exchange factors and Arp2/3-based actin nucleation drive lamellipodial protrusion and spread of the membrane, while actin crosslinkers like filamin and alpha-actinin stabilise the flattened shape. Receptor tyrosine kinases of the TAM and Eph families and phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling tune the response.

Very-low-density lipoprotein particles carry triglyceride from the liver to peripheral tissues, and their clearance from plasma is how that lipid is delivered and the remnant particle disposed of. When it fails, triglyceride-rich lipoproteins accumulate, producing hypertriglyceridaemia, pancreatitis risk and atherogenic remnant lipoproteins. Clearance begins with lipolysis: lipoprotein lipase hydrolyses the triglyceride core, with apolipoprotein C-II as its required activator, apolipoprotein C-III as an inhibitor of both lipolysis and uptake, and apolipoprotein A-V modulating the reaction at the endothelial surface. The shrunken remnant, enriched in apolipoprotein E, is then bound by hepatic receptors including the VLDL receptor and internalised by endocytosis for lysosomal degradation, with a receptor-associated chaperone needed for proper receptor folding. Upstream, microsomal triglyceride transfer protein assembles the particle in the first place, tying clearance to hepatic lipid export and whole-body energy distribution.

Microtubule anchoring keeps microtubules tethered where the cell needs them, holding minus ends at the centrosome, Golgi or cortex so that the array has a stable geometry rather than a transient one. This positioning determines where cargo is delivered, how the Golgi ribbon and cilium are organised, and which way a cell divides or migrates; losing it scatters organelles and disrupts ciliogenesis. Anchoring proteins such as ninein, its relative NINL and CEP350 dock minus ends at subdistal appendages and pericentriolar material, while CAMSAP3 caps and stabilises free minus ends at non-centrosomal sites and CLASP1/CLASP2 link plus ends to the Golgi and cortex. Dynactin, HOOK3 and the BICD adaptors couple anchored microtubules to dynein-driven transport, and PCM1, CEP19, CEP43 and BBS4 connect the same machinery to centriolar satellite traffic and cilium assembly, a route whose failure underlies ciliopathies.

Spliceosomal snRNAs are transcribed by RNA polymerase II as extended precursors, and snRNA 3'-end processing is what trims them to the defined length needed for snRNP assembly and splicing. Without it, snRNAs are misprocessed or degraded, spliceosome assembly falters, and splicing of every intron-containing mRNA is affected. The Integrator complex does the primary cut: a cleavage module built around the INTS11 endonuclease with INTS9 and INTS4, docked on a large INTS1/INTS2/INTS5/INTS8 scaffold, which also terminates promoter-proximal polymerase II transcription more broadly. Further trimming and quality control come from the nuclear exosome ribonuclease barrel, the deadenylase TOE1, and the U6-specific enzymes TUT1, which adds the 3' oligo-uridine tail, and USB1, which processes it. Mutations in TOE1 cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia, and USB1 loss causes poikiloderma with neutropenia, linking snRNA end maturation to human developmental disease.

Spliceosomal snRNAs are transcribed with extra 3' nucleotides that must be trimmed before the RNA can be assembled into a functional particle, and 3'-end processing of U4 snRNA is one such maturation step. Without it, the U4/U6 di-snRNP that primes the spliceosome cannot be built correctly, so pre-mRNA splicing fidelity depends on this trimming. The genes here constitute the nine-subunit core barrel of the RNA exosome, a 3'-to-5' exoribonucleolytic machine whose ring of RNase PH-like and S1/KH cap subunits threads substrate RNA through a central channel to associated catalytic nucleases. The same complex degrades and shapes many other transcripts, including rRNA precursors and aberrant or unstable RNAs, making snRNA end maturation one output of a general RNA surveillance and turnover system. Mutations in individual core subunits cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia and related neurodegenerative syndromes.

Moving solutes across the membrane of the vacuole or lysosome is what lets the organelle acidify, store ions and metabolites, and return the products of degradation to the cytosol. The transporters here span several substrate classes: zinc importers of the SLC30 family load zinc into vesicles and lysosome-related compartments, including the secretory granules that deliver zinc into milk, a nucleotide transporter packages ATP for vesicular release, a peptide/histidine transporter supports lysosomal peptide efflux and nucleic acid sensing in immune cells, and a heme transporter moves heme out of the lysosome for reuse of its iron. A vesicle-coat subunit is included because correct delivery of these proteins to the limiting membrane requires targeted trafficking. Failure of individual carriers produces transient neonatal zinc deficiency, lysosomal storage phenotypes and altered innate immune signalling, tying this transport to nutrient handling, organelle homeostasis and immunity.

Autophagosomes are built at a single dedicated location, and protein localization to the phagophore assembly site is how the machinery that builds them is delivered and held there. Without it a cell cannot initiate bulk autophagy, so damaged mitochondria, protein aggregates and surplus cytoplasm are not cleared — a failure that underlies neurodegeneration and defective control of intracellular bacteria. Membrane arrives on ATG9A-containing vesicles, whose trafficking depends on factors including RAB33B, STX17 and ER–mitochondria contact proteins such as MFN2 and PACS2. The class III PI3K complex generates PI3P on the nascent phagophore, which the WIPI/WDR45 beta-propeller proteins read to recruit the ATG16L1 conjugation machinery and the ATG4 proteases that process lipidated ATG8 family members. Mutations in WDR45 cause a childhood neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and ATG16L1 variants alter intestinal autophagy in Crohn's disease.

Retrograde traffic from early endosomes back to the Golgi recovers receptors, enzymes and membrane that would otherwise be degraded in lysosomes, sustaining repeated rounds of secretion and sorting. Mannose-6-phosphate receptors, TGN SNAREs and cargo adaptors are returned by this route, and it is also the path hijacked by Shiga and cholera toxins to reach the ER. Sorting nexins with membrane-bending BAR domains select tubular carriers from the endosomal surface, Rab GTPases such as RAB6A, RAB14 and RAB4B and their effectors including RUFY1 and rabenosyn specify carrier identity and movement, and syntaxins STX5 and STX10 provide the fusion machinery at the Golgi with TRAPP tethering support. Cargo receptors of the early secretory pathway, among them LMAN1, SURF4 and TMED9, link this recycling arm to anterograde ER-Golgi transport, keeping compartment composition and glycosylation capacity stable.

Retrieval of cargo from late endosomes back to the Golgi keeps receptors and enzymes from being lost to lysosomal degradation, and so sustains repeated rounds of hydrolase sorting and receptor reuse. Without this retrograde limb, mannose 6-phosphate receptors and similar sorting receptors are consumed in one pass and lysosome biogenesis suffers. The step depends on membrane-deforming sorting nexins such as SNX3 and SNX12, which read phosphoinositides on the endosomal surface and help select cargo into tubules, on Rab7B and the Rab GTPase regulator SGSM2 for identity and directionality of the carrier, and on the golgin GCC2 to capture arriving vesicles at the trans-Golgi. AP5Z1, an adaptor-related subunit whose loss causes hereditary spastic paraplegia, links this traffic to endosomal homeostasis in long neurons, where defective retrieval produces axonal degeneration.

Chromosomes are not passive DNA; specific proteins must be delivered to and held at defined chromosomal addresses, and protein localization to chromosome covers that targeting. It determines where centromeres form, where telomeres are capped, where cohesin holds sister chromatids together, and where repair factors accumulate after a break, so its failure produces missegregated chromosomes, eroded telomeres and unrepaired damage. Centromere identity is set by loading of the histone variant CENPA with its assembly factors, while kinetochore and checkpoint components such as BUB1B, BUB3, KNL1 and the dynein-recruiting ZW10/ZWILCH module are recruited only to that site. Shelterin proteins TERF2, TINF2 and ACD occupy chromosome ends, cohesin loading and WAPL-dependent release govern chromatid linkage, and damage signalling through ATR, TOPBP1, MDC1, NBN and TP53BP1 builds repair foci on chromatin marked by phosphorylated H2AX.

Getting a protein into the nucleus is an active, regulated step, and this pathway covers the machinery and the regulators that place cargo there or hold it there once arrived. It underlies essentially every inducible transcriptional response: signal-dependent import of transcription factors such as STAT3, SMAD3, NF-κB subunits and the Hippo effectors YAP1 and WWTR1 converts a cytoplasmic signal into a change in gene expression, while nuclear delivery of ribosome assembly factors, DNA repair proteins and replication components supports routine nuclear function. Mechanistically, importin-α/β adaptors and transportins recognise localisation signals and cross nucleoporin-lined pores, with the RAN GTPase gradient, RANGAP1 and RANBP2 setting directionality against XPO1-mediated export; kinases, SUMO conjugation and 14-3-3 proteins gate individual cargoes by masking or exposing their signals. Lamins and inner nuclear membrane proteins anchor retained proteins. Mislocalisation of such cargo, as with TARDBP, is a feature of neurodegeneration and of tumours with deregulated Hippo or Wnt signalling.

Teeth are hardened by the controlled deposition of calcium phosphate into enamel, dentin and cementum, and this mineralization programme determines whether the finished crown resists wear and decay. Ameloblasts secrete a protein matrix built from amelogenin, enamelin and amelotin that templates crystal growth, then proteases such as MMP20 degrade it so mineral can fill the space; ion handling by transporters and channels including SLC24A4, SLC4A2 and CFTR supplies calcium and buffers the protons released as crystals form. Alkaline phosphatase lowers pyrophosphate to permit mineral nucleation, while FAM20A and FAM20C phosphorylate secreted matrix proteins such as DMP1. Odontoblast collagen and transcription factors including SP7 and MSX2 set the differentiation context. Loss of these functions produces amelogenesis imperfecta, hypomineralized or hypoplastic enamel, and syndromic dental defects, and overlaps mechanistically with bone mineralization.

Cells adjust their behaviour when vitamin B6 becomes available, and this response links the vitamin's supply to the enzymes that depend on it. Pyridoxal 5'-phosphate is the cofactor for well over a hundred reactions, including transamination, decarboxylation and one-carbon transfer, so its availability sets the pace of amino acid catabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis. Two of the responding genes are classic PLP enzymes: kynureninase, which cleaves kynurenine along the tryptophan route toward NAD, and mitochondrial serine hydroxymethyltransferase, which feeds one-carbon units into folate metabolism. Tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase dephosphorylates circulating pyridoxal phosphate so the vitamin can cross membranes, and its loss in hypophosphatasia produces B6-responsive seizures. The remaining members form the BRISC deubiquitinating complex, connecting this stimulus to ubiquitin-dependent signalling and DNA damage response regulation.

Germ cells silence transposons with a dedicated small RNA system, and piRNA processing is how those guide RNAs are made. Precursor transcripts from repeat-rich clusters are unwound by an RNA helicase, cleaved by a mitochondrial surface nuclease, loaded onto PIWI proteins, trimmed at the 3' end by an exonuclease and then 2'-O-methylated for stability, all without Dicer. Tudor-domain proteins and germ granule components such as MAEL and DDX4 organise the machinery in nuage and intermitochondrial cement, and PIWI-bound piRNAs then direct target cleavage and DNA methylation of transposon loci. Because the pathway protects the germline genome, loss of its components causes transposon derepression, meiotic arrest and male infertility, and it also shapes the epigenetic reprogramming that accompanies spermatogenesis.

Aerobic metabolism constantly generates superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and hydroxyl radicals, and this is the programme by which a cell senses that burden and adjusts to it. Its outputs keep lipids, proteins and DNA from accumulating irreversible oxidative damage; chronic failure drives neurodegeneration, atherosclerosis, ageing phenotypes and tumour promotion, while deliberate loss of redox buffering is the basis of ferroptotic death. Detoxifying enzymes - superoxide dismutases, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin with their reductases - do the chemistry, supported by NADPH from glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and cystine import through SLC7A11. Transcriptional control runs largely through NFE2L2 released from KEAP1, with FOXO factors, TP53, HIF1A and sirtuins adding further arms. Stress-activated kinase cascades, mitophagy via PINK1 and PRKN, base excision repair of oxidised guanine, peroxisomal import and an ER stress limb complete the response, coupling redox state to survival, metabolism and cell death decisions.

When temperature rises above a cell's optimum, proteins begin to unfold and aggregate, and this response is how cells detect that insult and survive it. Its core is the heat shock transcriptional programme: HSF1 is released from chaperone restraint, trimerizes and induces inducible HSP70 family members, HSP90 isoforms and a large complement of DNAJ co-chaperones, which refold clients or route them to degradation via the CHIP ubiquitin ligase, VCP and HDAC6-dependent aggregate clearance. Nuclear import of HSP70 under stress depends on HIKESHI, and translation is throttled through eIF2alpha phosphorylation while stress granules assemble. Thermosensation proper is contributed by TRPV1, TRPV4 and TRPA1 channels in sensory neurons, linking cellular heat sensing to pain and body-temperature behaviour. Loss of chaperone capacity underlies protein aggregation disease and limits thermotolerance; the same machinery is co-opted by tumours and exploited in hyperthermia therapy.

Tumour necrosis factor is the cytokine cells use to announce infection and tissue damage, and the response to it decides whether a cell mounts an inflammatory programme or dies. Receptor engagement at TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF1B recruits TRADD, RIPK1 and TRAF adaptors, which either drive NF-kB and stress-activated MAP kinase signalling to switch on adhesion molecules, chemokines and its own transcription, or, if that survival arm fails, assemble a caspase-8 death complex. Ubiquitin editing sets the balance: CYLD, OTULIN, TNFAIP3 and the inhibitor-of-apoptosis proteins restrain signalling, and their loss causes autoinflammation. Sphingomyelinases and ADAM17-mediated shedding of receptors and ligands tune the strength of the signal, while ZFP36 family proteins and microRNAs terminate it by destabilising inflammatory transcripts. The output shapes endothelial activation, bone remodelling through RANK-RANKL, insulin sensitivity in adipose tissue, and the chronic inflammation targeted by anti-TNF therapy.

Cells continuously encounter superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants generated by respiration, oxidases and inflammation, and this pathway covers what they do about it: sense the oxidant load, neutralise it, repair the damage, and decide whether to adapt or die. Superoxide dismutases, catalase, peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin dispose of the species themselves, while NFE2L2 drives transcription of detoxifying and NADPH-generating enzymes such as NQO1. Redox-sensitive kinases including MAP3K5 and the stress-activated MAPKs, together with ATM, FOXO3 and SIRT1, couple oxidant exposure to growth arrest, autophagy and mitophagy through PINK1 and BNIP3, or to programmed necrosis via RIPK1 and RIPK3. Oxidised bases are excised by OGG1. Loss of this response underlies oxidative damage in neurodegeneration, ischaemia-reperfusion injury, ageing and atherosclerosis, whereas its persistent activation supports tumour cell survival.

Response to laminar fluid shear stress is how endothelial cells read the steady, unidirectional drag of flowing blood and convert it into an anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic phenotype. It defines the healthy arterial lining: regions of smooth laminar flow stay quiescent, while branch points and curvatures with disturbed flow lose this program and become the sites where atherosclerotic plaque forms. Mechanotransduction converges on MEK5-ERK5 signalling and cyclic AMP production through adenylyl cyclases and protein kinase A, inducing the transcription factors KLF2 and KLF4 that drive nitric oxide synthesis, suppress adhesion molecules, and restrain coagulation. Parallel arms include NRF2-dependent antioxidant defence, SMAD6/SMAD7 inhibition of TGF-beta signalling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR-mediated survival and alignment, and miR-126 support of vascular integrity. The output is cytoskeletal remodelling, cell elongation along the flow axis, and altered lipid handling via ABCA1 and SREBF2.

Endothelial cells lining arteries continuously read the drag of blood flowing over them, and steady unidirectional flow instructs them to adopt a quiescent, anti-inflammatory, anti-thrombotic state. This response to laminar fluid shear stress keeps vessels patent and explains the regional distribution of atherosclerosis: plaques form preferentially where flow is disturbed and this protective programme is absent. Mechanical force is converted into transcription through the MEK5-ERK5 module and the transcription factors KLF2 and KLF4, which drive nitric oxide synthesis and suppress adhesion molecule expression, with NFE2L2 adding antioxidant defence and ABCA1 contributing to cholesterol efflux. Adenylate cyclases and protein kinase A subunits supply cyclic AMP signalling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling supports survival and alignment with the flow axis, SMAD6 and SMAD7 restrain TGF-beta input, and miR-126 acts non-cell-autonomously on vascular repair.

Accumulation of unfolded or misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum forces a cell to change what it makes and whether it survives, and this response is how that decision is executed. It restores folding capacity in secretory cells such as plasma cells and pancreatic beta cells, and its failure underlies ER-stress-driven degeneration and diabetes syndromes, including the neurodegeneration seen with loss of WFS1 or VAPB. Three sensors report the problem: IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA, PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to throttle translation and induce ATF4 and CHOP, and ATF6 is cleaved by site-1 and site-2 proteases to release a transcription factor. Downstream outputs raise chaperone levels through BiP, HSPA1A and DNAJB9, expand ER-associated degradation via derlins, EDEM mannosidases and VCP, and, if stress persists, engage BAX, BAK and PUMA to commit the cell to apoptosis.

Glutathione is the cell's main thiol antioxidant and the conjugating partner for detoxification, but it is synthesised only in the cytosol, so its movement across membranes determines where redox buffering and drug conjugate disposal can happen. This transport activity covers efflux of reduced glutathione and of glutathione S-conjugates from cells by ATP-driven pumps such as ABCC1, ABCC2 and ABCC4, uptake of cystine for resynthesis by the SLC7A11 antiporter, and delivery of glutathione into mitochondria by the inner-membrane carriers SLC25A39 and SLC25A40, which supplies the matrix pool used for peroxide removal and iron-sulfur cluster handling. Connexin channels and a sodium-dicarboxylate cotransporter add intercellular and renal routes. Because the same pumps export chemotherapeutic conjugates, this traffic contributes to multidrug resistance, while loss of mitochondrial import drives oxidative damage and ferroptotic vulnerability.

Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in membranes and lipoproteins, and its catabolism both dismantles that pool and releases the signalling lipids hidden inside it. Hydrolysis at the sn-2 position by secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2 liberates arachidonic acid, the precursor of prostaglandins and leukotrienes, so this breakdown sets the pace of eicosanoid-driven inflammation; the lysophosphatidylcholine left behind is itself bioactive and is converted by autotaxin (ENPP2) to lysophosphatidic acid, driving cell migration and vascular development. Other members act in the lysosome, on membrane and lipid-droplet surfaces, or in the intestinal and plasma compartments, where hepatic lipase and receptors such as LDLR and SCARB1 couple phospholipid hydrolysis to lipoprotein remodelling and HDL metabolism. Loss or excess of these activities shows up as inflammatory disease, atherogenic dyslipidaemia, and, for PLA2G6, neurodegeneration with iron accumulation.

Mitochondria must be delivered to where ATP demand and calcium buffering are highest — growth cones, presynaptic terminals, nodes of Ranvier — and microtubule-mediated establishment of mitochondrial localization is how they get there. This is most consequential in neurons, whose axons are too long for diffusion to supply organelles, and disrupted mitochondrial transport is a recurring theme in axonal neuropathy, hereditary spastic paraplegia and tauopathy. Kinesin motors such as KIF5B and KIF1B carry the organelle along microtubules, coupled to the outer membrane through the Miro GTPases RHOT1 and RHOT2 and TRAK-family adaptors; ARMCX proteins and syntabulin contribute further membrane-side linkage. Microtubule-associated proteins including tau, MAP1B and spastin shape the tracks themselves, and tubulin modification by HDAC6 and the deglutamylase AGTPBP1 tunes motor engagement, so cargo attachment, track state and anchoring together set where mitochondria come to rest.

Ultraviolet light damages DNA and oxidises cellular components, and this response is how a cell detects that insult and decides between repair, arrest, and death. It underlies skin photobiology, sunburn, photoageing and the mutational route to skin cancer, and its failure in nucleotide excision repair produces the extreme UV sensitivity of xeroderma pigmentosum. Damage recognition by XPC and the DDB1-DDB2 complex, coupled to a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, initiates excision by XPA and the ERCC1-ERCC4 nuclease, while translesion polymerases such as POLH allow replication past unrepaired photoproducts. In parallel, ATR signalling and p53 with CDKN1A impose cell cycle arrest, and BAX, BAK1 and caspase-9 commit irreparably damaged keratinocytes to apoptosis. Stress kinases, integrated stress response components, chromatin remodellers, and matrix metalloproteinases that degrade dermal collagen extend the response to gene expression and tissue remodelling.

Cortisol metabolism covers both the building of the principal human glucocorticoid from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex and the local control of how much active hormone reaches its receptor. The hormone sets carbohydrate, lipid and protein handling during fasting and stress, restrains inflammation, and supports blood pressure, so disturbances here produce congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing or Addison phenotypes, and mineralocorticoid-excess hypertension. Side-chain cleavage of cholesterol by CYP11A1 begins the route, followed by hydroxylations from CYP17A1 and CYP21A2 and final 11-beta-hydroxylation by CYP11B1; the related CYP11B2 diverts flux toward aldosterone in the zona glomerulosa. Tissue-level tone is set separately, as HSD11B2 inactivates cortisol to cortisone and protects the mineralocorticoid receptor, while H6PD supplies the NADPH that favours reactivation in the endoplasmic reticulum. Developmental signals including BMP and WNT family members shape adrenal zonation and steroidogenic capacity.

Breaking down nucleobase-containing compounds covers everything from turnover of whole nucleic acids to the salvage and disposal of individual nucleotides and bases, and it sets the lifetime of a transcript as well as the size and purity of the nucleotide pools. Much of the membership is RNA decay machinery: decapping and deadenylase complexes, the multisubunit exosome with its helicase partners, cytoplasmic and nuclear 5'-3' exonucleases, nonsense-mediated decay factors, and the microRNA/Argonaute and RNA-binding protein systems that select which messages are destroyed. Alongside these sit deoxyribonucleases and repair glycosylases that degrade DNA during apoptosis and base excision, and catabolic enzymes such as adenosine and AMP deaminases, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, xanthine dehydrogenase, cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases and Nudix hydrolases that sanitise damaged nucleotides. Loss of individual components causes immunodeficiency, interferon-driven autoinflammation, or uric acid and pyrimidine metabolic disease.</description>ic disease.

Nucleosides and nucleotides that are no longer needed are dismantled rather than stored, and this catabolism of nucleobase-containing small molecules both disposes of them and recycles the ribose and base for salvage. Adenosine and methylthioadenosine are deaminated or phosphorolysed, purine nucleosides are cleaved by phosphorylase to free bases, and xanthine dehydrogenase carries hypoxanthine through to urate for excretion; on the pyrimidine side uridine phosphorylases and the dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase route degrade uracil and thymine to beta-amino acids. The flux matters clinically: loss of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic deoxyadenosine accumulation, deficiency of the pyrimidine route underlies fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxicity, and excess urate production drives gout. Hydrolases acting on nucleotides and a sanitising step that removes oxidised nucleotides feed substrate into the same pathway, linking it to nucleotide pool quality control and purinergic signalling.

Prostaglandins are short-lived lipid mediators released at sites of inflammation, injury, and in reproductive and vascular tissue, and this pathway covers how cells detect them and change their behaviour in response. The receiving end is a family of G protein-coupled receptors for prostaglandin D2, E2 and F2alpha, coupled through Gs, Gi and Gq subunits and heterotrimer components to adenylate cyclase, cAMP and protein kinase C, so that a single lipid signal can either raise or lower cyclic nucleotide tone depending on which receptor a cell carries. Downstream consequences span sensory neuron excitability and pain sensitisation, smooth muscle and vascular tone through endothelin, dendritic cell and lymphocyte migration via chemokine receptor signalling, neuroendocrine peptide release, and metabolic reprogramming through AMP-activated kinase and lipogenic enzymes. Aldo-keto reductases in the list both generate and inactivate prostaglandin species, tying ligand supply to the response itself.

Prostaglandin E2 is a lipid mediator released during inflammation, injury and normal tissue remodelling, and this pathway covers how cells register and act on that signal. Detection occurs through the EP receptor family, represented here by PTGER1, PTGER2 and PTGER4, which couple through heterotrimeric G proteins to raise cyclic AMP via adenylate cyclase or to mobilise calcium through Gq, with GNAS and GNAI1 setting opposite directions on the same adenylate cyclase step. The downstream consequences are diverse and physiologically concrete: fever and pain sensitisation, involving sodium channel excitability in sensory neurons; smooth muscle tone and hormone release including oxytocin and GnRH; metabolic reprogramming through AMP-activated kinase subunits and acetyl-CoA carboxylase; and immune cell positioning through chemokine and co-stimulatory genes. This responsiveness explains much of the anti-inflammatory and analgesic action of cyclooxygenase inhibitors, which remove the ligand rather than block the receptors.

Gonadotropins from the pituitary, FSH and LH, act on the gonads to drive follicle growth, ovulation, luteinization and steroidogenesis, and this describes the cellular responses that follow such a stimulus. The receptors FSHR and LHCGR set which cells can answer, coupling hormone binding to cAMP signalling that reprogrammes gene expression in granulosa, theca and Leydig cells; downstream consequences include cell cycle entry, activin and inhibin subunit production that feeds back on pituitary FSH output, steroid-modifying enzyme activity such as 5-alpha-reductase, and electron supply for cytochrome P450 steroid hydroxylases through P450 oxidoreductase. Vasoactive and matrix-remodelling changes, including endothelin signalling, accompany follicle rupture and corpus luteum formation. Loss or mutation of the gonadotropin receptors causes hypogonadism, amenorrhoea and infertility, while dysregulated responsiveness contributes to polycystic ovary syndrome and ovarian hyperstimulation.

Luteinizing hormone surges drive ovulation, luteinization of the ruptured follicle, and steroid output from ovarian theca and granulosa cells and testicular Leydig cells, so the cellular responses to this pituitary gonadotropin sit at the heart of reproductive competence and fertility. Signalling begins at the LH/choriogonadotropin receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP and reprograms transcription in the target cell; inactivating mutations cause hypogonadism and disorders of sex development, while activating ones produce precocious puberty. Downstream effects captured here include endothelin production and its receptor-mediated actions on follicular smooth muscle and vascular tone during follicle rupture, natriuretic peptide receptor signalling that governs oocyte meiotic arrest and its release, TGF-beta co-receptor modulation of local growth factor tone, and cell cycle and DNA topology changes accompanying proliferation and differentiation of the responding cells.

Piecemeal microautophagy of the nucleus is the selective turnover of small portions of the nuclear envelope and nucleoplasm, in which the lysosomal or vacuolar membrane engulfs a bleb of nucleus directly rather than wrapping it in a separate autophagosome. It lets cells trim nuclear content — damaged envelope, excess nucleolar or nucleoplasmic material — without destroying the whole organelle, contributing to nuclear quality control, genome maintenance and adaptation to starvation. The machinery is the core autophagy apparatus: the ULK1/ULK2–ATG13–RB1CC1 initiation complex that senses nutrient and energy status, the ATG7–ATG5–ATG12 conjugation system and ATG4 proteases that process and recycle LC3-family proteins, and the lipid-transfer and membrane proteins ATG2A/B and ATG9A/B, with sorting nexins shaping the membrane contacts involved. Its failure links defective nuclear housekeeping to senescence, aging and degenerative disease.

Piecemeal microautophagy of the nucleus is a selective form of nucleophagy in which small portions of the nuclear envelope and nucleoplasm are pinched off and degraded rather than the whole organelle, allowing a cell to trim damaged chromatin, excess nuclear membrane or defective nuclear envelope proteins without dying. It matters for nuclear quality control and for remodelling the nucleus during stress, starvation and differentiation, and impaired nuclear turnover is linked to laminopathies, senescence and neurodegeneration. The genes here supply the core autophagy machinery that makes such sequestration possible: the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinase complex with ATG13 and RB1CC1, the ATG9A/ATG9B vesicle and ATG2 lipid-transfer proteins that deliver membrane, the ATG5-ATG12-ATG7 conjugation system for lipidating ATG8 proteins, and ATG4 cysteine proteases that process and recycle them. Sorting nexins contribute membrane-binding and trafficking functions that shape the engulfing structure.

Nucleosome organization covers how DNA is packaged onto histone octamers, how those particles are spaced along the fibre, and how they are taken apart and rebuilt so that replication, transcription and repair can reach the underlying sequence. It determines which genes are accessible, keeps chromatin intact behind a passing polymerase or fork, and its failure produces genome instability and misregulated gene expression. Core and linker histones supply the building blocks, including variants such as H2AX, macroH2A and H3.3 that mark damaged, silenced or actively transcribed chromatin. Histone chaperones including ASF1A/B, NAP1 family proteins, nucleoplasmin, CAF-1 subunits, HIRA-UBN1 and the FACT heterodimer escort histones to and from DNA, while ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF and ISWI families slide and evict nucleosomes. HAT1 acetylates new histones before deposition, coupling assembly to replication and to chromatin maturation.

Iron must cross membranes to be used, and this pathway covers the carriers, channels and regulators that move iron ion by iron ion across the plasma membrane, endosomal and lysosomal membranes, and into mitochondria. It underpins dietary iron absorption in the gut, iron release from macrophages, and delivery of iron to the mitochondrial matrix where haem and iron-sulfur clusters are built. Divalent metal transporters such as SLC11A2 import ferrous iron after ferrireductase action, mitoferrins SLC25A37 and SLC25A28 carry it into mitochondria, and ferroportin SLC40A1 is the sole cellular exporter, restrained by the hepatic hormone hepcidin so that systemic iron is tuned to need. Endolysosomal release depends on mucolipin channels and on heme transport out of the compartment. Disruption causes anaemias, iron overload, and manganese-iron transport disorders, while iron restriction also serves innate defence against intracellular microbes.

Iron is indispensable but toxic in excess, so cells and organisms tightly control how much enters the bloodstream and how it is distributed. Regulation of iron ion transport covers the signals that raise or lower flux through iron transporters, setting systemic iron balance and keeping iron away from invading microbes. The hepatic peptide hepcidin is the central regulatory output, acting on the exporter ferroportin to restrict iron release from enterocytes and macrophages; HFE, together with beta-2 microglobulin as its partner for surface expression, senses transferrin saturation and tunes hepcidin production, and mutation of either causes hereditary hemochromatosis with progressive tissue iron overload. Hephaestin oxidizes exported ferrous iron for loading onto transferrin, lipocalin-2 sequesters siderophore-bound iron during infection, and interferon-gamma links inflammation to iron withholding, the basis of anemia of chronic disease. Hypoxia-responsive input arrives through a microRNA targeting iron-sulfur cluster assembly.

Iron entering or leaving a cell must be matched to the body's needs, and this regulatory layer sets how much iron actually crosses membranes. It links systemic iron status to the transporters and ferroxidases that move and load the metal: hepcidin, the liver-derived peptide hormone, restrains iron egress by driving degradation of the exporter ferroportin, while hephaestin oxidises exported ferrous iron so it can be handed to transferrin in the intestine. Other inputs are inflammatory and metabolic — interferon-gamma reshapes macrophage iron handling during infection, lipocalin 2 sequesters siderophore-bound iron as an antibacterial and signalling molecule, and a hypoxia-induced microRNA tunes iron-sulfur assembly machinery. When this control fails, iron either accumulates in tissues, as in hemochromatosis, or is withheld, producing the anemia of inflammation and iron-refractory anemia.

Cells constantly tune how fast ions and solutes cross their membranes, and this regulatory layer sets excitability, secretion, volume and nutrient uptake rather than performing transport itself. The genes here are the modulators: auxiliary subunits that reshape channel gating and trafficking (KCNE and KCNAB families, calcium channel beta and gamma subunits, FXYD peptides that tune the sodium pump, DPP6 and KCNIP proteins for A-type currents), scaffolds and anchors such as ankyrins, junctophilins, AKAPs and caveolins that place transporters at dyads and membrane domains, and kinases and phosphatases including PKA, PKC, CaMKII, calcineurin and the WNK-OXSR1/STK39 cascade that switch flux on and off. Calmodulin and STIM proteins couple transport to calcium sensing, while ubiquitin ligases, the proteasome and numerous microRNAs control channel abundance. Disruption produces arrhythmia, epilepsy, salt-handling and blood pressure disorders, and defective muscle excitation-contraction coupling.

Cells continually damp the traffic of ions and solutes across their membranes, and this collection covers the mechanisms that stop, slow or limit such transport. Restraint matters as much as transport itself: it sets resting membrane potential, protects against calcium overload, tunes renal salt handling and blood pressure, and keeps iron, zinc and glucose uptake within safe limits. Several routes converge here. Accessory subunits inhibit their partner channels, as KCNE proteins do for KCNQ1 and as sarcolipin and phospholamban do for the cardiac calcium pump. Ubiquitin ligases such as NEDD4L, acting with the WNK-activated kinases OXSR1 and STK39, remove or reduce transporters at the surface. Calmodulin, calcineurin subunits, kinases of the AKT and protein kinase C families, and many microRNAs provide feedback inhibition. Loss of this negative control produces arrhythmia, hypertension and disordered mineral homeostasis.

Solute movement across membranes is rarely left at a constant rate; this collection covers the regulatory inputs that switch transporters and channels on or raise their throughput, tuning ion gradients, nutrient uptake and electrical excitability to demand. Its outputs matter for cardiac repolarisation, muscle contraction, renal salt and phosphate handling, insulin-stimulated glucose entry and calcium signalling in immune and neural cells. Mechanistically it spans several layers: auxiliary and accessory subunits that modify pore behaviour, such as the FXYD family acting on the sodium pump, KCNE and KCNIP partners of potassium channels, and LRRC proteins that sensitise calcium-activated conductances; scaffolds and anchoring proteins that place kinases near their channel targets; store-operated calcium entry through STIM proteins acting on plasma membrane channels; and hormone, chemokine and growth factor receptors signalling through PI3K-AKT, phospholipase C, calcineurin and WNK kinases. Loss of such control produces arrhythmia, myopathy and disordered electrolyte balance.

Cells hold their membrane potential and internal ion concentrations within narrow limits, and this pathway covers the accessory proteins, kinases and signals that tune how fast ions cross membranes rather than forming the pores themselves. Its output is excitability: cardiac action potential duration, neuronal firing, skeletal muscle calcium release, and epithelial salt handling all depend on it, and its failure produces arrhythmia, epilepsy, deafness and hypertension. Channel behaviour is set by auxiliary subunits such as the potassium channel beta and KCNE proteins and calcium channel beta and alpha2delta subunits, by scaffolds and anchoring proteins that place kinases like PKA, PKC and CaMKII next to their substrates, by calmodulin and calcineurin acting as calcium sensors, by WNK kinases with the SPAK/OSR1 pair controlling cation-chloride flux, by junctophilins and triadin organising store-release sites, by STIM proteins reporting store depletion, and by ubiquitin ligases and microRNAs adjusting channel abundance.

negative regulation of monoatomic ion transmembrane transport covers the braking mechanisms that shut down or damp the flow of ions across membranes, setting the limits on excitability, contraction and ionic homeostasis. Because channel activity determines membrane potential, its restraint governs cardiac repolarization, neuronal firing thresholds, calcium handling in muscle and epithelial salt and water balance; loss of these brakes underlies long QT syndromes, arrhythmia and hypertension. Several distinct strategies appear together: accessory subunits such as the KCNE proteins that modify KCNQ1 and KCNH2 gating, inhibitory peptides like phospholamban and sarcolipin that clamp the SERCA calcium pump, calcium-sensing feedback through calmodulin and calcineurin, kinase cascades of the WNK-OXSR1-STK39 type acting on transporters, and ubiquitin ligases NEDD4/NEDD4L/WWP2 that remove channels from the surface. Numerous microRNAs tune channel and pump abundance transcriptionally, linking ion flux control to cardiac and neuronal remodelling.

Ion fluxes across membranes must be damped as well as driven, and this collection covers the braking mechanisms: processes that reduce the rate or extent of ion movement through channels, pumps and exchangers. Such restraint sets the duration of action potentials, limits calcium loading, and protects cells from the energetic and osmotic cost of unchecked flux. Several routes are represented. Accessory subunits such as the KCNE proteins modify the gating of partners including KCNQ1 and KCNH2, setting cardiac repolarisation; sarcolipin and phospholamban inhibit the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump to tune contractility; calmodulin with calcineurin subunits provides calcium-dependent feedback; NEDD4 and NEDD4L ubiquitin ligases remove transporters from the surface; MCUB blunts mitochondrial calcium uptake. Numerous microRNAs add post-transcriptional suppression of channel expression. Ion fluxes across membranes have to be turned up as well as turned down, and this pathway collects the processes that increase the activity of channels, pumps and exchangers. Enhanced conductance underlies excitability in neurons and cardiomyocytes, calcium signalling in immune cells, epithelial salt and fluid secretion, and muscle contraction; loss of such potentiation contributes to arrhythmia, impaired lymphocyte activation and secretory disease. The mechanisms are varied: auxiliary and accessory subunits such as the FXYD family, KCNE proteins and calcium channel beta subunits modify the gating and surface delivery of their partner pores; anchoring proteins of the AKAP family position kinases beside channels; STIM1 and STIM2 sense endoplasmic reticulum calcium depletion and open store-operated entry; WNK kinases acting through STK39 stimulate cation-chloride cotransport; calcineurin subunits, G protein-coupled receptors, purinergic P2X channels and chemokine signals feed activating inputs into these transport systems.

Glutathione is made in the cytosol but needed elsewhere, so its movement across membranes sets the redox and detoxification capacity of individual compartments and of the extracellular space. Glutathione transmembrane transport covers that traffic: ABCC-family pumps export reduced glutathione and glutathione conjugates of drugs, metals and electrophiles out of cells, an ATP-dependent step that completes phase III of xenobiotic detoxification and contributes to multidrug resistance in tumours. Mitochondria cannot synthesise glutathione and depend on carriers of the inner membrane, SLC25A39 and its paralogue, to import it and protect the respiratory chain and iron-sulfur enzymes from oxidative damage. The cystine/glutamate antiporter SLC7A11 supplies the limiting cysteine for synthesis and thereby couples uptake to production; its loss leaves cells glutathione-poor and prone to ferroptosis. A connexin and a dicarboxylate transporter provide additional release and uptake routes.

Histamine released from mast cells, enterochromaffin-like cells and neurons acts locally to provoke vasodilation, endothelial leak, itch and bronchoconstriction, drives gastric acid secretion, and in the brain modulates arousal and wakefulness; the cellular responses it evokes are what antihistamines are designed to block. Here the response is anchored by the H1 receptor, a Gq-coupled receptor whose signalling raises intracellular calcium and reshapes the endothelial and smooth muscle cytoskeleton, with a calcium-release-activated channel regulator and a formin-family actin nucleator linking receptor engagement to store-operated calcium entry and barrier change. Dopamine receptor subtypes and GABA-A receptor subunits place the response in a neuromodulatory context, where histaminergic input is integrated with inhibitory and dopaminergic transmission. Failure or excess of this signalling underlies allergic inflammation, urticaria and anaphylaxis, and shapes sleep-wake regulation.

Proteins destined for secretion, the plasma membrane or other organelles acquire their native structure in the endoplasmic reticulum, and this folding step decides whether they proceed through the secretory pathway or are degraded. The compartment provides what the cytosol cannot: high calcium, an oxidizing environment permitting disulfide bond formation, and a dedicated chaperone set. BiP (HSPA5) and its J-domain partners bind nascent chains in an ATP-dependent cycle, the lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin monitor N-glycans on glycoproteins, and GRP94 handles selected clients. Disulfide chemistry is carried out by protein disulfide isomerases such as P4HB and PDIA3, with ERO1 oxidases regenerating them and DNAJC10 reducing incorrect bonds. Insufficient folding capacity leaves misfolded protein accumulating, triggering the unfolded protein response and, in diseases from cystic fibrosis to antitrypsin deficiency, loss of a protein that was made but never matured.

Secretory and membrane proteins fold in the endoplasmic reticulum, and when that capacity is outstripped the cell mounts a coordinated response to ER stress that either restores proteostasis or commits the cell to death. It sustains professional secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells and plasma cells, and its failure underlies diabetes, Wolfram syndrome, neurodegeneration and tissue damage in ischaemia. Three sensors define the core: a kinase that phosphorylates eIF2α to attenuate translation and induce ATF4 and CHOP, an endonuclease that splices XBP1 mRNA, and a membrane-bound transcription factor liberated by proteolysis to expand chaperone and lipid synthesis capacity. Lumenal chaperones and oxidoreductases such as BiP, calnexin, calreticulin and protein disulfide isomerases assist folding, while mannosidases, lectins and ubiquitin ligase complexes retrotranslocate terminally misfolded substrates through VCP for proteasomal degradation. Persistent signalling tips the balance toward BCL-2 family-dependent apoptosis.

Most mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol with an N-terminal targeting signal that must be cut off after import, and other mitochondrial proteins are matured or turned over by resident proteases; mitochondrial protein processing covers this proteolytic maturation. It determines whether imported precursors become stable, functional proteins, and its failure underlies hereditary spastic paraplegia, spinocerebellar ataxia and cardiomyopathy. The matrix processing peptidase, built from a catalytic and a non-catalytic subunit, removes presequences, and an intermediate peptidase trims a second cleavage site; inner-membrane peptidase subunits process proteins sorted into the intermembrane space. Membrane-embedded AAA proteases such as AFG3L2, SPG7 and YME1L1, together with OMA1, both mature substrates and degrade damaged ones, and their cleavage of the fusion factor OPA1 links proteolysis to mitochondrial fusion and fission. Quality control, respiratory chain assembly and cristae organisation all depend on these steps.

Tissues that renew themselves — intestinal crypts, skin, kidney nephron progenitors, blood — depend on holding back a reservoir of undifferentiated somatic stem cells that divide without exhausting themselves, and this maintenance programme is what keeps that reservoir intact. Lose it and a tissue either differentiates entirely and fails to regenerate, or, when the same circuits are held on inappropriately, generates tumours. The genes converge on a handful of instructive signals and the transcription factors that read them: Wnt input through LRP5 and the BCL9 co-activators, Notch output via RBPJ and HES1, BMP7 balanced by its antagonist noggin, KIT and FGF10 receptor signalling into RAF/BRAF, and pluripotency or lineage regulators such as POU5F1, NANOG, SOX2, SOX9, CDX2, SIX2 and TP63. Chromatin and co-activator components including TAF5L, TAF6L and CUL4A, together with YAP1 and HMGA2, tune self-renewal against commitment.

Rac GTPases switch between GTP- and GDP-bound states to drive actin remodelling, lamellipodial protrusion, cell migration and neuronal process outgrowth, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly and how long that switch stays on. Control comes from both directions: activators such as SOS1, RASGRF1 and the adaptors GRB2, CRK/CRKL couple receptor and Src-family tyrosine kinase signals to Rac loading, while GAPs including ARHGAP17, ARHGAP24, ARHGAP44 and SH3BP1 accelerate GTP hydrolysis to terminate it. Additional modulation arrives through PI3K catalytic subunits, ARF6 traffic, Wnt5a-directed polarity cues, and the neuromuscular LRP4–DOK7 and dystroglycan axes that shape synapse and cytoskeletal architecture. Because balanced Rac output governs dendritic spine formation, immune cell chemotaxis toward CCL19 via CCR7, and invasive behaviour, its dysregulation contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders, motor neuron degeneration and tumour cell motility.

Rac GTPases drive actin branching at the cell periphery, so shutting their signalling off is what keeps lamellipodia, membrane ruffling and cell migration from running continuously. This negative arm of Rac signal transduction sets the timing and spatial limits of protrusion, contributing to endothelial and podocyte shape, neuronal process outgrowth, and restraint of invasive motility in tumours. The main mechanism is GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP24 and ARHGAP44, which accelerate hydrolysis of bound GTP and return Rac to its inactive state; NF1, best known as a Ras GAP and a tumour suppressor lost in neurofibromatosis, also acts to dampen Rho-family output. Additional control comes from microRNAs that lower the abundance of Rac pathway components post-transcriptionally, and from cytoskeletal regulators acting on microtubule dynamics that feed back onto actin remodelling.

Rac GTPases control actin remodelling, lamellipodial protrusion and cell polarity, and this pathway covers the inputs that switch them on — the guanine nucleotide exchange activity, adaptors and receptors that raise Rac-GTP levels and so increase signalling through Rac. Its output is directed cell movement: chemokine-guided lymphocyte migration via CCR7 and its ligand CCL19, endothelial responses downstream of the TEK receptor, growth-factor signals relayed by GRB2, SOS1, CRK and CRKL to Src and PI3K catalytic subunits, and neuronal process outgrowth and spine morphogenesis involving ALS2, AUTS2, CDKL5 and RASGRF1. A second theme is the neuromuscular junction, where LRP4, DOK7, dystroglycan and its glycosyltransferase LARGE1 organise postsynaptic architecture. Loss of individual activators produces motor neuron degeneration, epileptic encephalopathy, congenital myasthenia and muscular dystrophy, tying Rac activation to synapse assembly, immune trafficking and cytoskeletal integrity.

Rho-family GTPases switch between GTP- and GDP-bound states to control the actin cytoskeleton, cell shape, adhesion, migration and cytokinesis, and this collection covers the regulators that set how strongly and where that switching occurs. Guanine nucleotide exchange factors of the Dbl and DOCK families load GTP and activate Rho, Rac and Cdc42; GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP35, DLC1 and myosin IXb accelerate GTP hydrolysis and shut signalling off; and guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors hold inactive GTPases in the cytosol. Upstream cues feed in from integrins, semaphorin and plexin receptors, Robo and neuropilin guidance receptors, lysophosphatidic acid and thrombin-activated protease receptors, and chemokine signalling through CCR7, while ubiquitin adaptors of the cullin-3 system limit GTPase levels. Balanced output governs axon guidance, leukocyte trafficking, endothelial junction integrity and angiogenesis; loss of restraint contributes to tumour invasion and vascular malformation.

Rho-family GTPases drive actomyosin contractility, cell shape and adhesion, and this collection of brakes shuts that signalling down so that cells can spread, migrate directionally, form stable junctions and stop when they should. Negative regulation of Rho protein signal transduction works through several distinct devices: GTPase-activating proteins such as DLC1, ARHGAP35 and ARHGAP42 accelerate GTP hydrolysis and return RhoA to its inactive state; RIPOR1 and RIPOR2 bind active RhoA directly to sequester it, a step that restrains leukocyte adhesion and motility; and a cullin-3 ubiquitin ligase with BTB adaptors including KCTD10, KCTD13 and TNFAIP1 targets RhoA-pathway components for degradation. Additional input comes from integrin-linked adhesion proteins, the endothelial junctional factors HEG1 and RASIP1 that keep vascular lumens open, and transcriptional and microRNA-level repression. Loss of these constraints yields excessive contractility, invasive behaviour and tumour suppressor failure, as seen with DLC1 silencing in carcinoma.

Rho-family GTPases control the actin cytoskeleton, and this pathway covers the inputs that switch them on, raising the rate and extent of Rho signal transduction. It is how cells convert surface cues into shape change: stress fibre and focal adhesion assembly, cell contraction, migration, neurite retraction and axon guidance, endothelial barrier tone and platelet responses. Activation typically runs through guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as ARHGEF3, ARHGEF10, MCF2L, NET1 and the scaffold AKAP13, which load GTP onto Rho downstream of G protein-coupled receptors for thrombin and lysophosphatidic acid, receptor tyrosine kinases, and guidance receptors including plexin-B1 with its ligand SEMA4D, ROBO1 and the Nogo receptor RTN4R. Integrin-linked adaptors and the actin-associated proteins add mechanical input. Excessive or misdirected activation contributes to tumour cell invasion, vascular leak and inhibition of axon regeneration after injury.

Fertilization begins when a capacitated sperm first touches the outer coat of the egg, and sperm-egg recognition is the step that makes that contact species-specific and productive. It decides whether a gamete pair can fuse at all, so defects here cause unexplained infertility in otherwise normal-looking sperm and are an obvious target for contraception. Egg-side zona pellucida glycoproteins (ZP1-ZP4, with the astacin-family protease ovastacin hardening the coat after entry) provide the binding substrate, while sperm contribute zona-binding and acrosomal proteins such as ZPBP, ZAN, acrosin and hyaluronidase, ADAM-family heterodimers, and tetraspanin-associated surface factors. A distinct module handles adhesion to the oolemma itself: IZUMO1 with its egg receptor, together with SPACA6, TMEM81 and DCST1/DCST2, licenses membrane fusion. Chaperones, calnexin-like calmegin and proprotein convertases act earlier, folding and processing these proteins during spermatogenesis and epididymal maturation.

The first recognizable heart is a midline tube, and this programme covers its emergence from cardiac mesoderm through the looping and remodelling that convert it into a chambered organ. It is the developmental step on which septation, valve formation and normal cardiac output all depend; disruption produces congenital heart disease, including outflow tract and chamber defects and abnormal cardiac situs. Cardiac fate is specified by mesodermal and transcriptional regulators such as MESP1, NKX2-5, GATA4, MEF2C, HAND1/2 and TBX20, while Nodal, Shh, Wnt/planar-cell-polarity, Notch and BMP/TGF-beta signals position the rudiment and break its left-right symmetry, with PITX2 and ZIC3 acting on laterality. The prominent intraflagellar transport, ciliopathy and Hedgehog-transduction components underline that cilia-dependent signalling in node and cardiac progenitors sets the axis along which the tube loops.

Cardiocyte differentiation is the route by which mesodermal progenitors become beating heart muscle cells, acquiring sarcomeres, calcium-handling machinery and the electrical properties that let the heart contract as a unit. It underlies chamber formation and conduction-system specification in the embryo, and its disruption produces congenital heart malformations such as septal and outflow tract defects, while the same regulators are reactivated in hypertrophy and failure. A core transcriptional network of NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5, HAND2, MEF2C and MESP1 acts downstream of BMP, Wnt, Notch and TGF-beta signals from neighbouring tissue to commit progenitors and then drive expression of contractile genes including cardiac actin, myosin heavy and light chains, titin and telethonin. Muscle-enriched microRNAs and chromatin regulators tune the timing and dose of this programme, and distinct combinations, such as those involving TBX3, SHOX2 and HEY2, distinguish pacemaker from working myocardium.

Axoneme assembly builds the microtubule core of cilia and flagella, the structure that makes these organelles motile. It is what allows airway epithelium to clear mucus, ependymal cells to drive cerebrospinal fluid flow, embryonic node cilia to establish left-right body asymmetry, and sperm to swim; its failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, situs inversus, hydrocephalus and male infertility. The genes cover each substructure added to the nine-plus-two lattice: outer and inner dynein arm heavy, intermediate and light chains, the cytoplasmic pre-assembly factors and chaperones that fold dynein complexes before import, docking complex subunits that attach arms to the doublet, nexin-dynein regulatory complex and radial spoke head components, and ruler proteins that set 96-nanometre periodicity. Tubulin tyrosine ligase-like enzymes supply polyglutamylation marks, intraflagellar transport and centriolar satellite proteins deliver cargo, and FOXJ1 drives the motile ciliary program transcriptionally.

Motile cilia and sperm flagella beat because their core, the axoneme, is built to a precise plan, and this pathway covers that construction. Nine outer doublet microtubules and a central pair are decorated with dynein motors, radial spokes and nexin-dynein regulatory complexes, each assembled in a defined order and position. Cytoplasmic dynein assembly factors and their chaperone partners preassemble the axonemal dynein arms before intraflagellar transport delivers them; ruler proteins such as CCDC39 and CCDC40 set the 96-nm repeat that positions those cargoes, and tubulin polyglutamylases tune motor engagement. A master transcription factor drives the whole programme in multiciliated epithelia. Loss of these components produces primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic airway infection, situs inversus and hydrocephalus, male infertility from immotile or malformed sperm tails, and, for the photoreceptor-specific members, retinal degeneration.

Epithelial cells are structurally two-faced: an apical surface facing a lumen or the outside world and a basolateral surface contacting neighbours and the basement membrane. Once that axis is established, it must be actively held, and maintenance of apical/basal polarity is the ongoing work of keeping membrane domains, junctions and the underlying cytoskeleton in register. Loss of this asymmetry flattens the distinction between surfaces, disrupts barrier function and directional transport, and is a recurring feature of epithelial tumour progression and of kidney and retinal disease. The genes here span the layers involved: a Crumbs-family apical determinant whose mutation causes retinal degeneration and nephrotic syndrome, scaffolds that tether transporters and receptors beneath the apical membrane, actin-remodelling and membrane-trafficking components, and a Wnt ligand supplying extracellular positional cues, alongside transcriptional input that sustains epithelial identity.

During the final stages of spermatogenesis, the haploid spermatid nucleus is repackaged into a volume a fraction of its former size, and sperm DNA condensation is the programme that achieves it. The resulting chromatin is transcriptionally and replicatively silent, protecting the paternal genome during transit and shaping the sperm head; failure produces DNA fragmentation, abnormal morphology and male infertility. Histones are first hyperacetylated and read by the testis-specific bromodomain protein BRDT, then largely replaced by transition proteins TNP1 and TNP2 and finally by protamine PRM1, whose arginine-rich packaging is regulated by SRPK1-dependent phosphorylation. Chromatin remodellers and the acetyltransferase KAT5 prepare the substrate, RNF8-mediated ubiquitin signalling licenses histone eviction, and proteasomal removal clears displaced proteins. Meiotic and small-RNA components link this remodelling to the preceding synaptonemal and piRNA-dependent steps of germ cell differentiation.

Response to nicotine covers the cellular and systemic changes triggered when nicotine binds neuronal acetylcholine receptors, the events that underlie tobacco dependence and much of smoking's damage to the nervous, vascular and respiratory systems. Its core is the family of nicotinic receptor subunits, whose particular combinations set sensitivity to the drug; variants in the alpha5-alpha3-beta4 cluster are among the strongest known genetic influences on smoking behaviour and lung cancer risk. Receptor activation depolarises neurons and raises calcium, driving dopamine release through the transporter and D2 receptor in reward circuitry, engaging opioid and neuropeptide signalling, and inducing CREB-dependent transcription with lasting FOSB accumulation that marks addiction. In parallel, nicotine exposure shifts apoptotic balance through BCL2, BAD and caspase-3, activates NF-kB-driven inflammatory and adhesion responses, and provokes oxidative stress countered by heme oxygenase and glutathione peroxidase.

Nicotine acts on cells through ligand-gated cation channels, and the response to nicotine covers everything that follows: altered excitability, neurotransmitter release, gene induction, and the adaptations that underlie tobacco dependence. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunits dominate the set, spanning the neuronal alpha4/beta2 and alpha7 receptors that mediate reward and the alpha3/beta4 combinations of autonomic ganglia, alongside the muscle-type subunits of the neuromuscular junction. Downstream, dopaminergic components including the D2 receptor and the dopamine transporter, opioid and nociceptin receptors, and enkephalin link receptor activation to mesolimbic reinforcement, while CREB1 and FOSB record it as lasting transcriptional change. Other members report inflammatory, vascular and apoptotic consequences of smoke exposure through NF-kappaB subunits, TNF, adhesion and oxidative stress proteins, with caspase-3 and BCL2 setting whether exposed cells survive.

Nicotine changes behaviour because it hijacks the neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that normally tune dopamine and other transmitter release in reward circuitry; the behavioural response to nicotine is the locomotor, reinforcing and aversive output of that action, and it underlies tolerance, self-administration and dependence in smokers. The receptor subunits here assemble into pentamers with distinct pharmacology: alpha4-beta2 combinations mediate high-affinity nicotine binding and reward in the ventral tegmental area, alpha6-containing receptors act on striatal dopamine terminals, and the alpha5/alpha3/beta4 cluster in the medial habenula sets the aversive, intake-limiting arm, with human variants in that cluster among the strongest genetic risks for heavy smoking. Modulation beyond the receptors comes from presynaptic metabotropic glutamate and neuropeptide Y signalling and from PPARA-dependent lipid mediators, which shape how strongly nicotine reinforces behaviour.</br>

Operant conditioning is the form of associative learning in which an animal changes its behaviour according to the rewarding or aversive consequences that followed it before, and so learns to anticipate outcomes and act to obtain or avoid them. It underlies goal-directed action, habit formation and the motivational drive exploited by drugs of abuse, and its disruption contributes to addiction and to apathy or compulsive behaviour. The genes involved point to reward circuitry of the striatum and midbrain: dopamine D1 receptor signalling that raises cyclic AMP in medium spiny neurons, a phosphodiesterase that limits that second messenger, metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 coupling corticostriatal input to synaptic plasticity, and neuropeptide transmission through the CART peptide precursor and tachykinin receptors. Together they tie synaptic plasticity to the encoding of behavioural consequence.

Limbs and other appendages arise from small buds of lateral plate mesoderm that must be patterned along three axes while growing, and this morphogenetic programme builds them. Its failure produces the recognisable human limb malformations: polydactyly, syndactyly, split-hand/foot, phocomelia and the skeletal features of many multi-organ syndromes. A signalling loop between FGF8 in the apical ectodermal ridge and SHH in the posterior mesenchyme drives outgrowth, with GLI3, HAND2 and 5' HOX genes translating position into digit identity, BMPs and their antagonists NOG and GREM1 setting interdigital sculpting, and WNT/beta-catenin plus retinoic acid enzymes such as ALDH1A2 and CYP26B1 shaping proximodistal domains. Because hedgehog output depends on primary cilia, intraflagellar transport components and TULP3 belong here too. TBX5 and TBX4 distinguish forelimb from hindlimb, while SOX9, RUNX2 and COL2A1 commit condensing mesenchyme to cartilage and bone, and apoptotic regulators remove cells between digits.

Genitalia morphogenesis is the shaping of the external and internal reproductive organs during embryonic and fetal development, the step that translates gonadal sex determination into the anatomy used for reproduction. Its disruption produces hypospadias, micropenis, ambiguous genitalia and other disorders of sex development, and it is the process androgen-disrupting exposures interfere with. Androgen receptor signalling is the central input, masculinising the urogenital sinus, tubercle and swellings in response to testicular testosterone; loss of receptor function yields feminised external anatomy despite a male karyotype. Epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk supplies the growth and patterning signals, with FGF10 acting on urethral and tubercle epithelium and canonical WNT signalling through beta-catenin sustaining outgrowth. Retinoid delivery, natriuretic peptide receptor signalling and cohesin-associated regulation contribute to the wider developmental context in which these tissues are built.

Limbs, and other appendages that bud from the embryonic trunk, are patterned along three axes by a small set of signalling centres, and this morphogenetic programme is what turns a mesenchymal bud into a proximodistally ordered skeleton with a defined digit number and identity. Its failure produces the human limb malformations: polydactyly, syndactyly, split-hand/foot, phocomelia and radial ray defects, often as part of ciliopathy or cohesinopathy syndromes. Sonic hedgehog from the posterior margin, FGF8 and FGF4 from the apical ectodermal ridge, and WNT and BMP inputs form the feedback loops that sustain outgrowth, while GLI3, HAND2, and nested HOX and TBX factors read position into identity. Retinoic acid synthesis and degradation set proximal boundaries, and intraflagellar transport components are required because hedgehog output depends on the primary cilium. Selective apoptosis sculpts the interdigital spaces.

Embryonic forelimb morphogenesis is the process that turns a bud of lateral plate mesoderm into a patterned arm, with shoulder, forearm and digits laid out along three axes. It sets the body plan of the upper limb, and its disruption produces the human limb malformations seen in Holt-Oram syndrome, cleidocranial and craniofacial-limb disorders, and Cornelia de Lange syndrome. TBX5 initiates forelimb identity and drives WNT-dependent outgrowth signalling from the apical ectodermal ridge, while SHH in the posterior mesenchyme establishes anteroposterior polarity and WNT7A with EN1 fixes dorsoventral character. Retinoid supply through RDH10 and ALDH1A2 and 5' HOX gene expression assign position along the proximodistal axis, and cilium-associated proteins tune hedgehog output. Downstream, MSX, ALX, TWIST1 and RUNX2 couple this patterning to skeletal condensation and ossification, linking axis specification to the cartilage and bone that follow.

The hindlimb bud is patterned in the embryo into a leg with the right proportions along its length, its front-to-back axis and its top-to-bottom axis, and this programme is what distinguishes a hindlimb from a forelimb. Failures produce limb reduction, polydactyly and syndactyly, and the same genes underlie human limb malformation syndromes. Hindlimb identity is set by PITX1 and TBX4, after which a self-sustaining loop between apical ectodermal ridge fibroblast growth factors FGF4 and FGF8 and posterior SHH drives outgrowth and digit patterning, with WNT3 and WNT7A acting through beta-catenin on ridge maintenance and dorsoventral polarity and BMP4 shaping interdigital cell death. MSX, ALX and OSR transcription factors, retinoic acid receptors, Notch signalling and ciliary transduction of hedgehog by RPGRIP1L convert these gradients into skeletal pattern.

Building an arm from a bud of lateral plate mesoderm requires that position be specified along three axes at once, and forelimb morphogenesis is the programme that does it. Its failure produces the limb reduction and digit malformations seen in human skeletal syndromes — TBX5 mutation in Holt–Oram syndrome, HOXA13 in hand-foot-genital syndrome, cohesin-loader NIPBL loss in Cornelia de Lange. Limb initiation and forelimb identity are set by T-box and homeodomain transcription factors, then sustained by reciprocal signalling between the apical ectodermal ridge and underlying mesenchyme: WNT3 and WNT7A from ectoderm, SHH from the posterior zone of polarizing activity, with retinoic acid made by RDH10 and ALDH1A2 feeding proximal patterning. Ciliary proteins such as RPGRIP1L and IFT122 transduce hedgehog signals, while RUNX2, MSX and GDF5 carry the pattern into cartilage condensation and joint formation.

Hindlimb morphogenesis is the embryonic programme that turns a patch of lateral plate mesoderm into a patterned leg, with the correct proximal-distal segments, anterior-posterior digit order, and dorsal-ventral surfaces. It matters because failure of these steps produces the recognizable congenital limb malformations — polydactyly, syndactyly, limb reduction, patellar and hip defects — seen in syndromes such as those involving TBX4, PITX1 or GDF5. Identity of the posterior limb is set by TBX4 and PITX1, which distinguish leg from wing-level forelimb, while the three classical signalling centres operate through SHH from the posterior margin, FGF8 and FGF4 from the apical ectodermal ridge, and WNT7A from dorsal ectoderm, integrated with BMP4, RSPO2 and beta-catenin. HOXD genes, MSX and ALX homeobox factors, TWIST1 and retinoic acid receptors read these signals into skeletal element specification, condensation and joint formation.

Hollow organs only work if their epithelium encloses a continuous lumen, and tube formation is the morphogenetic step that creates that central space through which air, urine, blood or secretions can flow. It underlies neural tube closure, branching of the lung and kidney collecting system, and vascular and gut tube patterning; its failure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida, renal agenesis or dysplasia, and ciliopathy syndromes. The genes reflect the machinery involved: planar cell polarity components such as VANGL2, CELSR1, PRICKLE1 and SCRIB orient cells for convergent extension, intraflagellar transport and centriolar proteins including IFT172, CEP290 and MKS1 build the cilia through which Hedgehog signalling is read, and morphogen inputs from SHH, WNT, BMP, FGF and NOTCH set regional identity. Actin regulators, Rho GTPase control and apoptosis effectors then execute the cell shape changes, adhesion and cavitation that open and seal the tube.

Tubes in the body—principally blood vessels, but also airways and renal tubules—must hold a defined diameter and length, and regulation of tube size is how that calibre is set during development and adjusted moment to moment afterwards. In the vasculature this is the basis of blood pressure control and regional perfusion: loss of it produces hypertension, pulmonary arterial hypertension, or failure of tissue oxygen delivery. Vasoconstrictor and vasodilator ligands such as angiotensin, endothelin, adrenomedullin, natriuretic peptides and vasopressin act through G protein-coupled receptors on smooth muscle, converging on calcium handling, potassium and TRP channels, and the RhoA–ROCK pathway that sets myosin light chain phosphatase activity. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase and soluble guanylate cyclase drive the opposing cGMP–PRKG1 relaxation arm. Adrenergic, purinergic, serotonergic and prostanoid receptors tune the response, while integrins, caveolin and matrix components link wall mechanics to lumen geometry.

Blood formation in the embryo begins before the bone marrow exists, first in the yolk sac and then in the aorta-gonad-mesonephros and fetal liver, where hemogenic endothelium gives rise to the hematopoietic stem cells that will supply blood for life. Without it there are no erythrocytes to carry oxygen to a growing embryo, and failure is lethal in utero. The genes involved mark two linked problems: specifying mesoderm and endothelium toward a blood fate, through the VEGF receptor KDR, the transcription factors TAL1, LMO2 and GATA2 with its cofactor ZFPM1, and then expanding and differentiating the resulting progenitors under cytokine control by KIT and its ligand, FLT3 ligand, IL3 and thrombopoietin. GATA1 drives erythroid and megakaryocytic maturation specifically, while hypoxia sensing through HIF1A ties output to oxygen availability. Many of these regulators are recurrently rearranged or mutated in leukemia, where an embryonic programme is reactivated out of context.

Blood cell production does not stop at birth: post-embryonic hemopoiesis is the continuing generation of erythroid, myeloid and lymphoid cells from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells in fetal liver and bone marrow, sustaining oxygen transport, immune defence and clotting throughout life. Its maintenance depends on cytokine signalling, chromatin regulation and genome protection acting together on the stem cell pool. JAK2 relays receptor signals for erythropoietin and thrombopoietin, and its constitutive activation drives myeloproliferative disease; KAT8 acetylates histone H4 lysine 16 to keep progenitor transcription programmes open; KLF4 shapes monocyte and macrophage differentiation; and the nucleotide excision repair endonuclease partner ERCC1 limits the DNA damage that otherwise exhausts stem cells with age. Loss of these functions produces marrow failure, cytopenias or clonal expansion rather than a defect in embryonic blood formation.

miRNA processing builds the small RNAs that set the tone of gene expression across development, differentiation and stress responses, converting long primary transcripts into ~22-nucleotide guides that silence target mRNAs. Loss of this machinery is embryonic lethal and its dysregulation is a recurrent feature of cancer and developmental syndromes. Nuclear cropping by DROSHA with its RNA-binding partner DGCR8 releases a hairpin, which is exported and cleaved by DICER1 before loading onto an Argonaute protein and its TNRC6 scaffolds to form the effector silencing complex. The genes also capture the extensive regulation layered on these steps: LIN28 proteins and the terminal uridylyl transferases TUT4/TUT7 mark precursors for decay, m6A writers METTL3/METTL14 and helicases such as DDX5 mark substrates for processing, and SMAD proteins downstream of TGF- inity/BMP signalling, together with STAT3 and IL6, direct maturation of selected miRNAs.

microRNAs shut down gene expression after transcription, and this pathway covers how they are made: long primary hairpin transcripts are cropped in the nucleus, exported, and trimmed again in the cytoplasm to give the short duplexes that load into Argonaute. Because a single miRNA can tune hundreds of messages, the maturation machinery sets the tone of developmental timing, stem cell self-renewal and differentiation, and its loss is embryonic lethal while partial failure is common in cancer. DROSHA with its partner DGCR8 makes the nuclear cut, DICER1 the cytoplasmic one, and AGO proteins with TNRC6 scaffolds assemble the silencing complex that represses translation or destabilises targets. Processing is itself heavily regulated: SMAD transducers of TGF-beta and BMP signals promote maturation of specific precursors, LIN28 proteins recruit terminal uridylyl transferases to block let-7 production, and methylation and editing of precursors redirect their fate.

Germ cells migrate from their site of origin to the gonad, and those that stray off the route or settle outside it are eliminated rather than allowed to persist. This clearance of ectopic germ cells by programmed cell death shapes the final size of the germ line pool in the embryo and removes cells whose survival in somatic tissue can seed extragonadal germ cell tumours and teratomas. Survival depends on the local environment: KIT signalling from the correct niche sustains migrating germ cells, so cells lacking that support engage the intrinsic apoptotic route, with BAX permeabilizing mitochondria and caspase activity dismantling the cell. Inflammatory cytokines of the interleukin-1 family and the DNA-damage-responsive kinase encoded by PRKDC contribute further death-promoting input, linking positional control of germ cell survival to broader apoptotic and genome-surveillance machinery.</description>
