Most organs are built from tubes, and tube morphogenesis is the developmental programme that shapes epithelial and endothelial sheets into lumenized, branched conduits for blood, air, urine, milk and gut contents. It determines vascular patterning, kidney nephron and ureteric branching, lung airway arborization and heart outflow tract formation; its failure produces cystic kidney disease, cardiovascular malformation, lymphatic dysplasia and lethal defects in lumen continuity. Positional cues come from morphogen families — Wnt, Hedgehog, BMP/TGF-beta, FGF and Notch ligands such as DLL4 and JAG1 — read out by lineage transcription factors including GATA, SOX, HOX, PAX and TBX proteins. VEGF, angiopoietin and ephrin signalling through KDR, TEK and EPHB4 drives sprouting and arteriovenous identity, while junctional and polarity machinery (CDH5, TJP1, PODXL, SCRIB, VANGL2), Rho-ROCK actomyosin contractility, integrin–extracellular matrix adhesion and primary cilia set apical–basal polarity, lumen opening and tube diameter. Numerous microRNAs tune these outputs.

synaptic transmission, glutamatergic is excitatory neurotransmission in the brain: vesicular glutamate is released from a presynaptic terminal and activates receptors on the target cell, depolarising it and admitting cations. It carries most fast excitatory signalling in the CNS, sets the threshold for synaptic plasticity and learning, and when dysregulated produces excitotoxic neuronal death, epilepsy, and the synaptic deficits seen in schizophrenia, autism and neurodegeneration. Vesicular transporters load glutamate, and the release machinery — Munc13 priming factors, Munc18, synaptotagmin calcium sensing and SNARE recycling — couples action potential arrival to exocytosis. Postsynaptically, AMPA, NMDA and kainate receptors with their TARP and cornichon auxiliary subunits, metabotropic receptors, and scaffolds such as Homer and SHANK organise the response and its strength. Adhesion molecules including neurexins and neuroligins align the two sides, while dopaminergic, adenosine and neuromodulatory receptors tune release.

Glutamatergic synaptic transmission is the principal excitatory signalling route of the vertebrate nervous system, underlying fast point-to-point communication, learning and memory, and the activity-dependent strengthening and weakening of synapses. Glutamate is loaded into synaptic vesicles by the vesicular transporters VGLUT1-3 and released on arrival of an action potential through a calcium-triggered exocytic step requiring the sensor synaptotagmin, priming factors of the UNC13 family, and the SNARE-regulating proteins STXBP1 and the SNAP proteins. Released transmitter acts on ionotropic AMPA, NMDA and kainate receptors, whose auxiliary subunits (TARPs, CNIH proteins, FRRS1L) govern trafficking and gating, and on metabotropic receptors that feed back on release and postsynaptic excitability through scaffolds such as HOMER and SHANK. Adhesion molecules including neurexins and neuroligins align the two sides. Excessive glutamate signalling drives excitotoxic neuronal death, while disruption of these components underlies epilepsy, intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia.

multicellular organism growth covers the control of body size and mass at the level of the whole animal rather than the individual cell, integrating endocrine signals, nutrient sensing and skeletal patterning to determine adult stature and lean-versus-fat composition. Its centre is the growth hormone axis: hypothalamic GHRH and ghrelin acting through their receptors drive pituitary GH1, which signals via GHR to STAT5A/STAT5B and SOCS2 feedback to induce IGF1 and IGF2, with mTOR and PI3K relaying nutrient availability. Chondrocyte growth-plate signalling through IHH, PTCH1, SMO, NPPC-NPR2 and GDF5 converts these cues into long-bone elongation, while imprinted and chromatin regulators such as CDKN1C, HMGA2, PLAG1, NIPBL and EP300 set growth set-points. Loss of function produces dwarfism, overgrowth and progeroid or DNA-repair-deficient short-stature syndromes, and gain of signalling produces gigantism and acromegaly, linking the pathway to metabolism, adipose development and lifespan.

Body size is set by processes that act on the whole organism rather than on any single cell, and this pathway collects the machinery that determines how large an animal becomes and how fast it gets there. Its core is the somatotropic axis: hypothalamic releasing hormone and ghrelin signalling through their receptors drive pituitary growth hormone, whose receptor activates STAT5 to induce IGF1, with SOCS2 and STC2 restraining the output. Around it sit skeletal growth regulators such as natriuretic peptide signalling through NPR2, hedgehog and Indian hedgehog signalling in the growth plate, and imprinted growth genes including IGF2, CDKN1C and PLAG1/HMGA2. Genome maintenance and DNA repair factors appear because their loss produces growth failure and dwarfing syndromes. Disruption gives short stature, gigantism, overgrowth syndromes, or failure to thrive, linking endocrine signalling, nutrient sensing and bone elongation to final body mass.

Organ growth is the controlled increase in size and mass of a tissue once its identity is set, and it determines final body proportions, whether a heart can meet its workload, and whether a limb, kidney or mammary gland reaches functional size. The genes here converge on a small number of growth-setting circuits: Hippo kinases and their scaffolds (STK3/STK4, LATS1/2, SAV1, WWC family) restrain the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 and so cap organ size; insulin-like growth factors with PI3K-AKT and PTEN set cell-autonomous growth capacity; fibroblast growth factors with their receptors, hedgehog-GLI, Notch, Wnt and TGF-beta/BMP signals coordinate proliferation with surrounding tissue. Cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, GATA4 and TBX5, natriuretic peptides, and a large complement of microRNAs point to heart chamber growth and hypertrophy as a prominent instance. Loss of restraint produces overgrowth syndromes and tumours; insufficiency produces hypoplasia and dwarfism.

O-mannosylation attaches mannose directly to serine and threonine side chains and then extends it, and in humans its best-understood product is the matriglycan chain on alpha-dystroglycan that lets muscle and brain cells grip laminin and other basement membrane ligands. Loss of this modification uncouples the cytoskeleton from the extracellular matrix and causes congenital muscular dystrophies with brain and eye malformations, the dystroglycanopathies. A protein O-mannosyltransferase complex initiates the transfer in the endoplasmic reticulum using dolichol-phosphate-mannose supplied by the DPM synthase subunits, after which glycosyltransferases build the core, a ribitol-phosphate tandem is added from CDP-ribitol, and LARGE enzymes polymerise the glucuronic acid-xylose repeat that actually binds ligand. Related transmembrane O-mannosyltransferases modify cadherins and other substrates, linking this chemistry to adhesion more broadly than to muscle alone.

Hormone-secreting glands arise during embryogenesis from specified patches of endoderm, ectoderm and mesoderm that must be induced, committed and then organised into secretory tissue, and this developmental programme is what makes endocrine system development the origin of lifelong control over growth, metabolism, stress responses and reproduction. Its failure produces congenital hypopituitarism, thyroid dysgenesis, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal hypoplasia and neonatal diabetes. Gradients of Hedgehog, BMP, WNT and FGF signals position each primordium, feeding into lineage-restricted transcription factors that fix identity: POU1F1, PROP1, HESX1 and LHX3 for anterior pituitary cell types, NKX2-1, PAX8 and FOXE1 for thyroid follicular cells, GCM2 for parathyroid, NR5A1 and NR0B1 for adrenal and gonadal steroidogenic tissue, and PDX1 with NEUROD1, PAX4 and NKX6-1 for pancreatic islet endocrine cells. Hormones and receptors such as GHRH, CRH and their receptors appear as the maturing glands begin hypothalamic-pituitary-target axis signalling.

Exocrine system development covers the formation and maturation of glands that secrete through ducts rather than into blood "" salivary and lacrimal glands, sweat glands, mammary and prostate epithelium, and the pancreas and its acinar tissue. The programme yields the secretory epithelia responsible for saliva, sweat, digestive enzymes and milk, so its failure produces dry mouth and eyes, anhidrosis, and pancreatic insufficiency; ectodysplasin signalling defects of this kind underlie hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. Most of the biology is reciprocal epithelial tmesenchymal crosstalk driving branching morphogenesis: fibroblast growth factors acting through FGFR1 and FGFR2, hedgehog, BMP and TGF-beta family ligands, EGFR and hepatocyte growth factor, alongside laminins and basement-membrane cues that cleft the growing epithelial bud. Transcription factors including SOX9, SOX10, PTF1A and PDX1 specify duct and acinar identity, while XBP1 supports the secretory capacity of the differentiated cells.

Most human mRNAs are tuned rather than switched off, and this is the arm of microRNA action that does the tuning at the level of protein output: a mature miRNA loaded into Argonaute guides the silencing complex to partially complementary sites in a 3' untranslated region and blocks translation of the message without necessarily destroying it. The effect sets the quantitative level of proteins controlling proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis and stress responses, so altered miRNA dosage contributes to cancer, cardiac and neurological disease. Mechanistically, Argonaute proteins work with TNRC6 scaffolds and recruit factors that interfere with cap recognition and initiation, including the alternative cap-binding protein EIF4E2, the eIF4E transporter EIF4ENIF1, and the DDX6 helicase that shunts repressed mRNAs toward storage granules; LIMD1 and partners contribute to assembly. The many individual miRNAs here supply target specificity.

miRNA-mediated gene silencing by mRNA destabilization is the branch of microRNA regulation in which a targeted transcript is not merely blocked from translation but degraded, shortening its half-life and permanently lowering protein output. This is how animal cells set quantitative dosage for large programs of genes at once, tuning proliferation, differentiation, stress responses and lineage identity; loss or amplification of individual microRNAs of this kind is a common feature of cancer. Mature microRNAs load into an Argonaute-containing silencing complex, base-pair with sites usually in the 3' UTR, and recruit deadenylase activity through the CCR4-NOT complex, whose CNOT6, CNOT7 and CNOT8 subunits trim the poly(A) tail and commit the mRNA to decapping and decay. The RNA helicase MOV10 assists by unwinding structured targets. Represented microRNAs include the let-7 family, miR-17~92 members, and miR-34 and miR-200 family regulators of epithelial state.

Small non-coding RNAs tune how much protein a gene makes by shortening the lives of its transcripts, and this destabilization arm of microRNA-mediated silencing is how most animal microRNAs act. A mature miRNA loaded into an Argonaute-containing silencing complex pairs with sequences usually in the 3' untranslated region of a target mRNA; imperfect pairing recruits deadenylation machinery, and the CCR4-NOT catalytic subunits represented here trim the poly(A) tail, committing the message to decapping and decay. The helicase MOV10 associates with Argonaute proteins to help resolve structured target RNAs. Dozens of individual miRNA loci are included, among them the let-7 family, miR-17~92 members and miR-34, which collectively set thresholds for proliferation, differentiation, stress responses and stem cell identity. Loss or amplification of particular miRNAs contributes to cancer and developmental disorders, since their targets include oncogenes and tumour suppressors.

Vertebrate embryos build the vertebral column, ribs and axial muscle by carving the presomitic mesoderm into a repeating series of somites, and segmentation is the regionalization programme that sets the number, size and rostrocaudal identity of those blocks along the body axis. Failure produces fused or missing vertebrae and rib malformations, the basis of spondylocostal dysostosis. Timing comes from an oscillator built on Notch components and their negative feedback — DLL1 and DLL3 ligands, the RBPJ-dependent transcriptional response, and cyclic repressors such as HES7 — tuned by glycosyltransferases including LFNG and POFUT1 that modify Notch receptors. Wnt and FGF gradients from the tail bud, with TBXT, TBX6 and MSGN1, maintain the unsegmented progenitor pool, while MESP2 and the RIPPLY factors fix the boundary and rostrocaudal polarity of each somite. Hox and Cdx genes then assign regional identity to the resulting segments.

Tube development covers the making of the branched and hollow structures that organs are built from -- airways, nephrons, gut, mammary ducts, and the blood and lymphatic vasculature -- from the first budding of an epithelium or endothelium to a patent, functional lumen. Without it there is no gas exchange, filtration, secretion or perfusion, and its failure underlies renal agenesis and cystic kidney disease, pulmonary hypoplasia, congenital heart and outflow tract defects, and vascular malformations. The genes trace the recurring logic: inductive signalling by FGF, WNT, SHH, BMP/TGF-beta, NOTCH and VEGF/angiopoietin ligands read out through receptor tyrosine kinases and SMADs; lineage transcription factors such as PAX2, HNF1B, NKX2-1, SOX17 and GATA family members that assign regional identity; planar cell polarity, junctional and cilium components that orient cell rearrangement and lumen formation; and matrix remodelling that lets tubes elongate and branch.

Most organs are built from tubes, and tube development covers their whole history from the first epithelial or endothelial bud to a patent, functional conduit. Blood and lymphatic vessels, airways, nephrons and collecting ducts, gut and genitourinary tracts, and mammary ducts all depend on it; failure produces cystic kidney disease, pulmonary hypoplasia, vascular malformations and obstructive urinary defects. The genes converge on a small number of instructive inputs used repeatedly: VEGF, FGF, angiopoietin and PDGF ligands with their receptors, Notch lateral inhibition, Wnt/planar cell polarity, hedgehog, and BMP/TGF-beta signalling through SMADs, read out by lineage transcription factors such as SOX17, PROX1, HNF1B, PAX2 and NKX2-1. Downstream, junctional and polarity complexes, Rho-family GTPase control of the cytoskeleton, matrix and matrix-remodelling proteases, ciliary and intraflagellar transport components, and microRNA regulation set lumen formation, branching, diameter and directional sprouting.

Phosphatases need controlling as much as kinases do, and this pathway covers the processes that set how fast and where phosphate groups are removed from proteins and lipids. Because dephosphorylation terminates or reverses signalling, its regulation determines the duration of kinase output, the recycling of signalling intermediates, and the timing of events such as mRNA surveillance and cytoskeletal remodelling. The members act through several routes: regulatory and inhibitory subunits that gate protein phosphatase 1 and 2A holoenzymes, including IGBP1 and PPP1R17; myotubularin-family and inositol polyphosphate phosphatases that act on phosphoinositides rather than proteins, with MTMR2 loss causing demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy; the SMG5-SMG6-SMG7 module that directs dephosphorylation of UPF1 during nonsense-mediated decay; and receptors such as DRD2 and ADORA1 that tune phosphatase activity downstream of extracellular signals. Glycogen-associated EPM2A links the same logic to Lafora disease.

Phosphorylation states are set by the balance between kinases and phosphatases, and this grouping covers the braking side of that balance: processes that block or slow the removal of phosphate groups, thereby prolonging signals that would otherwise be reset. Suppressing phosphatase action is how a cell keeps a substrate phosphorylated long enough for it to act, and loss of such restraint flattens signalling dynamics in calcium handling, dopaminergic neurotransmission, glycogen metabolism and cytoskeletal organisation. The members act mainly through inhibitory binding rather than catalysis: CHP1 restrains calcineurin, URI1 is part of a prefoldin-like complex that holds protein phosphatase 1 activity in check, and IQGAP1 scaffolds signalling components at the membrane and cortex. Related activities include phosphoinositide turnover by INPP5K and the carbohydrate-binding phosphatase laforin, mutation of which causes Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

positive regulation of dephosphorylation covers the control layer that turns phosphatase activity up, shortening the lifetime of phosphate marks on proteins and lipids and thereby setting how long a signal persists. Because phosphorylation is the main switch in growth factor, adhesion and hormone signalling, processes that accelerate its removal determine signal duration, adaptation and reversibility rather than initiation. The genes point to several routes to that outcome: an adenosine receptor coupling extracellular purine levels to intracellular phosphatase output, a calcineurin B homologue subunit that activates its catalytic partner, a myotubularin-related regulatory subunit that promotes turnover of phosphoinositide signals on endosomes, and a bone morphogenetic protein ligand whose signalling feeds back on phosphatase expression. Src appears as a kinase that, through phosphorylation of phosphatases and their substrates, enhances subsequent dephosphorylation, linking kinase and phosphatase arms of the same circuit.

Phosphorylation is reversible, and the enzymes that remove phosphate groups are themselves regulated; this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of dephosphorylation. Because phosphatase activity sets how quickly kinase signalling is terminated, boosting it shortens the lifetime of phosphorylated intermediates and resets signalling systems for the next stimulus. The genes involved act through distinct routes: a G protein-coupled adenosine receptor that lowers cyclic AMP and thereby the balance of kinase to phosphatase output, a secreted bone morphogenetic protein ligand acting on receptor-regulated signalling, a calcineurin-interacting regulatory subunit, a pseudophosphatase of the myotubularin family that partners with catalytically active members to control phosphoinositide turnover, and the tyrosine kinase SRC, which can promote phosphatase activation. The net effect is tuning of signal duration in growth factor, calcium and lipid-based pathways.

wound healing, spreading of epidermal cells is the re-epithelialisation step of skin repair: keratinocytes at the wound edge flatten, loosen their adhesions and crawl across the denuded surface until a continuous epidermis is restored. Without it wounds remain open and chronic, as in diabetic ulcers, and excessive or misdirected migration contributes to fibrotic and hypertrophic scarring. Movement depends on integrin-based traction against the provisional matrix, with fibronectin and vitronectin receptors and their kindlin activators FERMT1 and FERMT2 coupling adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton; loss of FERMT1 causes Kindler syndrome with fragile, blistering skin. Directional persistence requires microtubule capture at the leading edge through CLASP proteins and Rho-GAP control of protrusion. Migration is driven by EGFR ligands released by ADAM17 shedding, by WNT and BMP-responsive transcriptional programmes, and by PTEN-restrained PI3K-mTOR signalling, while matrix metalloproteinases clear the path ahead.

Re-epithelialization after injury depends on keratinocytes at the wound edge losing their static adhesions and spreading across the denuded gap until a continuous epidermis is restored; failure of this epidermal cell spreading underlies chronic non-healing wounds, while its dysregulation contributes to hypertrophic scarring and keratinocyte invasion. Migration here is integrin-driven: fibronectin- and vitronectin-binding receptors pairing ITGB1, ITGB3 or ITGB5 with ITGA5 or ITGAV engage a provisional matrix, and the kindlin adaptors FERMT1 and FERMT2 activate and link them to the cytoskeleton, with loss of FERMT1 causing fragile, blistering skin. Microtubule-associated CLASP1 and CLASP2 and Rho regulation through ARHGAP24 orient the advancing lamellipodium, while PTEN and MTOR set the growth-factor input from shed ligands such as HB-EGF released by ADAM17. Matrix remodelling and WNT signalling coordinate the migrating sheet with the underlying dermis.

Mechanosensory hair cells of the inner ear are the cells that convert sound and head movement into neural signals, and hair cell differentiation is the programme by which an unspecialized epithelial progenitor acquires that identity. Loss or failure of these cells is the usual cause of sensorineural deafness and vestibular dysfunction, and because mammals cannot regenerate them the damage is permanent. Commitment is driven by the transcription factor ATOH1 with POU4F3 acting downstream, while Notch signalling through JAG1/JAG2, DLL1, RBPJ and the HES/HEY repressors restricts the fate to scattered cells surrounded by supporting cells. Differentiation then builds the apparatus itself: the graded stereocilia bundle and its tip links (CDH23, MYO7A, USH1C, WHRN, STRC), the transduction channel components TMC1 and LHFPL5, and planar polarity machinery orienting each bundle. Many of these genes are mutated in syndromic and nonsyndromic hearing loss.</description>

Hippo signalling sets organ size by deciding whether cells are permitted to keep growing. When the pathway is on, the MST1/MST2 kinases with their scaffold SAV1 activate LATS1/2 together with MOB1 cofactors, and LATS phosphorylates the co-activators YAP1 and WWTR1 (TAZ) so they are held in the cytoplasm or degraded; when it is off, YAP/TAZ enter the nucleus and drive TEAD-dependent transcription of proliferation and survival genes, opposed by the repressor VGLL4. Upstream input comes from cell-cell adhesion and polarity: the FAT4-DCHS1 pair, the NF2/merlin-WWC-KIBRA module, junctional angiomotins, FRMD6 and AJUBA-family LIM proteins, with striatin-containing STRIPAK phosphatase complexes and PP2A subunits tuning kinase output. The pathway restrains tissue overgrowth and regeneration, and its inactivation, which uncouples YAP/TAZ from contact and mechanical cues, is a recurrent route to tumour formation including NF2-mutant mesothelioma.

regulation of hippo signaling tunes the kinase cascade that decides whether cells keep proliferating or stop, and so sets organ size, contact inhibition and epithelial architecture. When its restraint is lost, the transcriptional coactivators YAP and TAZ escape into the nucleus and drive growth programs typical of tumours and regenerating tissue; when it is overactive, growth and repair stall. The genes span both the activating and the inhibitory sides: the upstream MST kinases and their scaffolds, the FERM-domain and junctional sensors NF2, FRMD6 and the WWC/KIBRA proteins that read cell density and cortical tension, LIM-domain adaptors such as AJUBA, LIMD1 and WTIP that sequester kinases at adherens junctions, the STRIPAK-associated striatin complex and PP2A subunits that dephosphorylate the cascade, and phosphatases and cofactors like PTPN14 and VGLL4 acting on the effectors. Mechanical, metabolic and stress inputs converge here to gate contact-dependent growth arrest.

Hippo signalling reads cell density, adhesion and mechanical tension and decides whether cells keep dividing, and this collection covers the inputs that tune its frequency and strength. When the pathway is held on, the kinases STK4 and STK3 phosphorylate downstream transcriptional coactivators so they are sequestered and degraded, restraining growth; when regulation fails, uncontrolled coactivator activity drives organ overgrowth and contributes to tumours such as mesothelioma, where the upstream inhibitor NF2 is lost. Activators here include the WWC/KIBRA family, FRMD6 and the FERM-domain scaffolds at the apical junction, while Ajuba-family LIM proteins and PTPN14 act as tension-sensitive brakes. Striatin-containing STRIPAK phosphatase modules together with PP2A subunits dephosphorylate the core kinases, providing the counterweight, and VGLL4 competes at the transcriptional output. The result is a tunable set point for contact inhibition, tissue size and regenerative proliferation.

negative regulation of hippo signaling describes the braking of the Hippo kinase cascade, and because that cascade restrains growth, damping it releases YAP/TAZ into the nucleus to drive proliferation, progenitor expansion and organ growth. Tissues use this arm to permit regeneration and to respond to low cell density or mechanical slack, while its chronic engagement is a common route to tumour growth and resistance to contact inhibition. Mechanistically the genes converge on suppression of MST/LATS activity: the Ajuba family proteins AJUBA, LIMD1 and WTIP sequester LATS at tension-bearing adherens junctions, and the striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase complex, built from STRN3/STRN4, STRIP1/2, MOB4, SLMAP and the PP2A subunits PPP2CA and PPP2R1A, dephosphorylates and inactivates the upstream kinases. Scaffolds and junctional regulators such as DLG5, MARK3 and the WWC proteins, plus SRC and p38 signalling, tune the set point.

The Hippo kinase cascade restrains growth by keeping YAP/TAZ out of the nucleus, so processes that damp it down permit proliferation, organ growth and regeneration; persistent suppression is a route to tissue overgrowth and to the YAP activation seen in many carcinomas. Genes here act as brakes on that cascade. Ajuba-family LIM proteins, including AJUBA, LIMD1 and WTIP, bind and sequester LATS kinases at junctions in a tension-dependent manner, coupling cell density and cytoskeletal mechanics to growth control. A striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase complex built from PP2A catalytic and scaffolding subunits with striatins and STRIP proteins dephosphorylates and inactivates MST kinases. Src and stress-activated MAPK14 signalling provide further inhibitory input. Notably, WWC scaffolds and VGLL4 normally support pathway output, indicating that these regulators sit in both directions of a feedback network rather than acting only as suppressors.

positive regulation of hippo signaling describes the inputs that switch on the Hippo kinase cascade, the growth-restraining circuit that keeps organ size, cell density and epithelial architecture in check. When it is strengthened, the transcriptional coactivators YAP and TAZ are phosphorylated, retained in the cytoplasm by 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAE, and degraded, so proliferative and stem-like gene programmes are shut down; loss of this restraint underlies tissue overgrowth and is a common feature of carcinomas. The genes here act at several tiers: the core kinases STK3 and STK4 (MST1/2) and the STE20 relative MAP4K4, FERM and scaffolding proteins such as FRMD6, DLG5 and SCHIP1 that read junctional and cortical cues, and phosphatases PTPN14 and PTPN21 that sequester YAP directly. Arrestin-domain ARRDC3 links receptor trafficking to the same output, tying mechanical and polarity signals to contact inhibition of growth.

Hippo signalling restrains organ growth by shutting down the transcriptional coactivators YAP and TAZ, and the genes here push that switch toward the off state for growth. Turning the pathway up keeps proliferation in check, maintains contact inhibition and epithelial architecture, and limits the regenerative or tumour-promoting output of YAP/TAZ-TEAD target genes; loss of this restraint contributes to tissue overgrowth and to cancers with constitutive YAP activity. Mechanistically the set centres on the core kinases STK3 and STK4, whose activating phosphorylation is promoted by MAP4K4-family input, and on upstream membrane- and junction-associated regulators such as FRMD6, DLG5 and the adaptor ARRDC3 that relay cell density and polarity cues. PTPN14 reinforces the output by binding YAP and helping hold it out of the nucleus, while a 14-3-3 protein sequesters phosphorylated coactivator in the cytoplasm.

Tyrosine phosphorylation is a reversible switch, and peptidyl-tyrosine dephosphorylation is the step that resets it, setting how long growth factor, cytokine and immune receptor signals last and how strongly they are read. Without it, kinase output goes unopposed: insulin and leptin signalling, ERK activation, and lymphocyte receptor thresholds all drift, which is why individual members here are studied as targets in diabetes, obesity and cancer. The enzymes fall into several classes — receptor-type phosphatases with extracellular domains such as PTPRF, PTPRJ and PTPRZ1 that couple cell contact and matrix cues to intracellular signalling; cytoplasmic phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPN2, PTPN6 and PTPN12 that act on receptor tails and adaptors; and dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP3, DUSP5 and DUSP6 that inactivate MAP kinases. PTPN11 is unusual in promoting rather than damping RAS–ERK signalling, and its mutation causes developmental and leukaemic disease.

Long-chain fatty acids are useless to a cell until they are activated as coenzyme A thioesters, and this metabolic route both makes those thioesters and decides what becomes of them. Acyl-CoA synthetases of the ACSL and ACSBG families charge C13-C22 fatty acids with CoA, committing them to oxidation, phospholipid and triglyceride synthesis, or protein acylation; thioesterases such as ACOT7 run the reverse step and release free fatty acid, setting the balance between activated and unesterified pools. Elongases of the ELOVL family, working with the condensation, reduction and dehydratase steps supplied by HACD1/2, HSD17B12 and TECR, lengthen the chains two carbons at a time, while fatty acyl-CoA reductases feed ether lipid and wax ester synthesis and DGAT1/2 direct acyl-CoA into stored triacylglycerol. The output determines membrane lipid composition, lipid droplet formation and the balance between fat storage and energy release, with defects causing retinal degeneration, ichthyosis and myopathy.

Fatty acids are chemically inert until they are activated as thioesters with coenzyme A, and fatty-acyl-CoA metabolism covers the making, elongating, trafficking and breaking of those activated intermediates. This is the gateway to essentially everything cells do with lipid: triglyceride and phospholipid synthesis, membrane remodelling, protein acylation, and β-oxidation for energy. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL1 and ACSL4 charge free fatty acids with CoA, after which ELOVL enzymes with the reductase and dehydratase steps of the microsomal elongation cycle extend chains, FASN builds them de novo from malonyl-CoA supplied by ACACA, and DGAT enzymes esterify them into triacylglycerol. Acyl-CoA thioesterases and Nudix hydrolases reverse activation to set free fatty acid and CoA pools. A peroxisomal arm handles very-long-chain species; loss of the ABCD1 transporter causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

Fatty acids taken up or newly made are metabolically inert until they are esterified to coenzyme A, and long-chain fatty-acyl-CoA biosynthesis is the activation step that commits them to oxidation, phospholipid and triglyceride synthesis, or protein acylation. The ACSL family, together with the bubblegum-type ligases ACSBG1 and ACSBG2, performs the ATP-dependent thioesterification, with individual isoforms localized to different membranes and tissues so that the same fatty acid can be routed to storage in adipocytes or to β-oxidation in muscle and liver. The ELOVL condensing enzymes, acting with the reductase and dehydratase steps supplied by HSD17B12, HACD1/2 and TECR, extend acyl-CoAs two carbons at a time in the endoplasmic reticulum, generating the very-long-chain and polyunsaturated species needed for sphingolipids, retinal membranes and skin barrier lipids. Defects cause ichthyosis, retinal degeneration and myopathy.

NAD is made mainly in the cytosol and nucleus, yet mitochondria consume it continuously for the TCA cycle, fatty acid oxidation and sirtuin-dependent deacetylation, so the dinucleotide must cross membranes that it cannot pass unaided. Transmembrane transport of NAD, in oxidized or reduced form, supplies these compartments and sets the size of their separate redox pools. The carriers here all belong to the mitochondrial solute carrier family: SLC25A51 and its paralogue SLC25A52 import NAD+ into the mitochondrial matrix, and loss of SLC25A51 collapses matrix NAD+, impairing oxidative phosphorylation and shifting cells toward glycolysis. SLC25A17 instead serves peroxisomes, moving cofactors including FAD, CoA and NAD into that organelle for β-oxidation. Because NAD availability governs both energy metabolism and NAD-consuming signalling enzymes, this transport step links cofactor biosynthesis to compartmentalized metabolic capacity.

Cells must hold neutral lipid at a workable level: enough triglyceride stored to buffer fatty acid flux and fuel demand, but not so much that droplets crowd the cytoplasm and lipotoxic intermediates accumulate. Intracellular triglyceride homeostasis is the balance between esterification and mobilisation that sets that level, and it is the point of failure in hepatic steatosis, obesity-associated insulin resistance and neutral lipid storage disease. Synthesis runs through DGAT2, which performs the final acylation step of triglyceride formation at the endoplasmic reticulum, while PNPLA2 initiates hydrolysis of stored triacylglycerol to release fatty acids. Droplet biogenesis and morphology depend on proteins such as FITM2 and LDAH, and the set point is adjusted transcriptionally by the bile acid receptor NR1H4, the deacetylase SIRT1 and the stress-responsive factor XBP1, linking storage to nutrient state and secretory load.

Peroxisome proliferator activated receptor signalling lets cells read their own lipid content and set metabolic gene expression accordingly. Fatty acids and eicosanoid-derived ligands bind PPARα, PPARβ/δ or PPARγ, which act as heterodimers with RXRA on DNA response elements; PPARα drives fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis in liver and muscle, while PPARγ commits preadipocytes to adipocytes and governs insulin sensitivity, making it the target of thiazolidinedione drugs. Ligand supply comes partly from lipoxygenases and prostacyclin synthase, and lipid-binding proteins such as FABP5 shuttle ligands to the receptor. Output depends on coregulator exchange: NCOA1, NCOA2 and the Mediator subunit MED1 are recruited on activation, whereas GPS2 participates in corepressor complexes, and SIRT1 and ubiquitin ligases including STUB1 and HUWE1 tune receptor activity and turnover. Disrupted signalling contributes to dyslipidaemia, hepatic steatosis, lipodystrophy and type 2 diabetes.

PPAR nuclear receptors sense fatty acids and their derivatives and turn that information into transcriptional programmes for lipid storage, fatty acid oxidation, adipocyte differentiation and inflammatory tone; this pathway covers the inputs that raise or damp that receptor output. Control is exerted at several levels: lipoxygenases and prostacyclin synthase generate oxidized lipid ligands, a fatty acid binding protein delivers ligands to the nucleus and a lipid droplet protein sequesters them, coregulators and chromatin-associated factors such as GPS2, ASXL1/2 and the deacetylase SIRT1 set the transcriptional response, and ubiquitin ligases including HUWE1 and STUB1 limit receptor abundance. Adipokine and developmental signals, notably leptin, BMP2 and TWIST1, plus microRNAs, tune the same axis. Because the balance determines adipose expansion and insulin sensitivity, its disturbance contributes to obesity, fatty liver and metabolic syndrome, and PPAR agonist drugs act through this tuning.

PPAR nuclear receptors sense fatty acids and their derivatives and turn on programmes for lipid oxidation, lipid storage and adipocyte differentiation; restraining that output keeps adipogenesis and lipid handling proportionate to need. The genes here damp PPAR signalling by several independent routes. HUWE1 and STUB1 are ubiquitin ligases that target receptor or coactivator proteins for degradation, ASXL1 acts through chromatin-associated corepression, and TWIST1 opposes the transcriptional programme that drives fat cell maturation and thermogenic gene expression. PLIN5 coats lipid droplets and limits release of the fatty acid ligands that would otherwise activate the receptor, while microRNAs including miR-27b and miR-34a suppress receptor transcript levels. PAQR3 contributes further negative input. Loss of this brake favours excess adipose expansion, hepatic steatosis and altered insulin sensitivity, and the same restraint shapes macrophage and tumour cell metabolism.

PPARs are lipid-activated nuclear receptors that couple fatty acid and eicosanoid availability to transcription of genes for fatty acid oxidation, lipid storage, adipocyte differentiation and resolution of inflammation; the processes collected here raise the output of that receptor signalling. They act at several levels: generation or delivery of the ligand, as with a lipoxygenase and a prostacyclin synthase that produce oxidized lipid agonists and a fatty acid binding protein that shuttles ligands to the nuclear receptor, and modulation of the receptor complex itself through cofactors and corepressor-associated subunits such as ASXL2, CITED2 and GPS2. Others act as upstream cues, including leptin and BMP2 signals that drive adipogenic commitment. Because this axis governs insulin sensitivity, adipose tissue expansion and macrophage lipid handling, its enhancement is the mechanism exploited by fibrate and thiazolidinedione drugs.

Many regulatory proteins only work once they are delivered to and held on the microtubule lattice, and protein localization to microtubules is the targeting step that puts them there. It determines where spindle and cytoskeletal activities occur: kinetochore attachment to spindle microtubules, midbody and cytokinetic organization, neuronal process outgrowth, and the coupling of microtubule ends to actin. End-binding proteins of the MAPRE family mark growing plus ends and act as a docking platform that recruits other factors, with tau-tubulin kinase 2 and the GAS2-like crosslinkers among the proteins whose position depends on such tracking. Depalmitoylating hydrolases of the ABHD17 family control membrane anchoring and thereby the availability of substrates for cytoskeletal association. Loss of correct targeting shows up as chromosome missegregation, failed cytokinesis, and defective neuronal and developmental morphogenesis, as seen with MID1 mutation.

Epithelia that line the gut, kidney tubule, airway and secretory glands move water across themselves in a directed way, and this transport sets the volume and consistency of urine, intestinal contents, bile and airway surface liquid. Water itself follows osmotic gradients rather than being pumped, so the pathway couples solute handling to water channels: AQP1 and AQP8 provide the high-capacity transmembrane route for water, the sodium-glucose cotransporter SLC5A1 drives absorption by bringing Na+ and glucose in together, and the CFTR chloride channel supports the anion secretion that pulls water in the opposite direction. Cell-cell junction components such as the desmosomal plakophilin PKP1 maintain the tight epithelial barrier that makes vectorial flux possible. Failure of this balance produces the thick secretions of cystic fibrosis, secretory or osmotic diarrhoea, and defects in urinary concentration.

Carbon dioxide produced by respiring tissues must cross cell membranes to reach the blood and eventually the lungs, and although it is small and lipophilic, its flux across some membranes is accelerated by dedicated channel proteins. This transmembrane movement of CO2 supports systemic acid-base balance and the red cell's role in carrying metabolic waste gas from tissues to the alveoli. Aquaporin-1, abundant in the erythrocyte membrane and in renal tubules, provides a pore that conducts water and dissolved gases, and the Rh-family glycoproteins RHAG, RHBG and RHCG act as gas channels closely related to ammonium transporters, with RHAG a component of the red cell Rh antigen complex and RHBG and RHCG placed in kidney and other epithelia. By coupling gas permeation to the bicarbonate buffering system, this transport contributes to pH regulation and renal nitrogen handling.

Roundabout signaling pathway is the guidance system that tells a migrating cell or a growing axon where not to go. Secreted SLIT ligands bind ROBO receptors on the responding cell and trigger repulsion, steering commissural axons across or away from the midline, setting nerve and vascular tract boundaries, and constraining the migration of neural precursors and, later, of tumour cells. The output converges on the actin cytoskeleton: ROBO1 activation engages RhoA and the unconventional myosin MYO9B, a Rho GAP, to remodel the leading edge and collapse growth cones, with parallel input to transcriptional programmes. SLIT2 and SLIT3 also act outside the nervous system in angiogenesis, kidney and lung branching morphogenesis, and leukocyte chemotaxis. Loss of this repulsive cue produces midline crossing defects and organ patterning abnormalities, and its silencing accompanies invasive growth in cancer.

Growing axons and migrating cells need to be told where not to go, and SLIT ligands binding Roundabout receptors provide that instruction. This is the canonical repulsive guidance cue of the developing nervous system: it steers commissural axons away from the midline after they cross, prevents recrossing, and shapes axon branching and neuronal migration; the same signals guide vascular sprouting, leukocyte movement and epithelial morphogenesis outside the brain. Secreted SLIT2 and SLIT3 engage ROBO1 on the responding cell, and the signal is read out largely as a change in the actin cytoskeleton, with RhoA and the unconventional myosin MYO9B, which carries a Rho GTPase-activating domain, tuning Rho activity and growth cone collapse. Loss or mutation of these components produces axon pathfinding defects such as horizontal gaze abnormalities, and altered SLIT-ROBO signalling contributes to tumour invasion and angiogenesis.

Synapses work only if the right proteins arrive at the right side of the cleft and stay there, and this pathway covers the delivery, capture and retention of proteins at synaptic sites. It builds the receptive apparatus of excitatory and inhibitory synapses and the neuromuscular junction, so its failure produces receptor mislocalization, weakened transmission, and phenotypes ranging from intellectual disability and epilepsy to congenital myasthenia. Kinesins and recycling and retromer components move cargo along axons and dendrites; scaffolds of the PSD-95 family, SHANK1, GRIP adaptors and the presynaptic proteins bassoon and piccolo anchor it once delivered. Trans-synaptic adhesion through neurexins, neuroligins and LRRTMs specifies where accumulation occurs, RAPSN and COLQ perform the equivalent job for acetylcholine receptors at muscle, and palmitoylating ZDHHC enzymes with the depalmitoylase ABHD17B tune membrane residence dynamically.

Autocrine signaling describes the case where a cell responds to a factor it has itself released, binding a receptor on its own surface or on neighbouring cells of the same type. This short feedback loop lets a cell amplify or sustain its own activation state without waiting for input from another tissue, and it is a common feature of inflammatory and tumour cell behaviour. Here the logic is illustrated by ligand-receptor pairs expressed together in the same cells: interleukin-6 with its receptor and the shared gp130 signal transducer, and fractalkine with its own chemokine receptor, alongside myeloid alarmins and a macrophage marker. Persistent autocrine loops of this kind drive chronic inflammation, monocyte and macrophage recruitment, and self-sustaining growth and survival signalling in cancer, where interleukin-6 autocrine circuits are a recognised therapeutic target.

Cells read their surroundings as well as diffusible signals, and extracellular matrix-cell signaling covers the transfer of information from matrix components across the plasma membrane into intracellular responses that guide adhesion, migration, and tissue patterning. The genes here converge on retinal and vascular development: Norrin, a secreted matrix-associated ligand, binds the Frizzled-4 receptor together with the LRP5 co-receptor to activate beta-catenin-dependent transcription, a route required for retinal capillary growth and for the blood-retina barrier. Mutations in these components cause familial exudative vitreoretinopathy and Norrie disease, with retinal hypovascularisation and blindness, while LRP5 loss also lowers bone mass. Netrin-4 is a basement-membrane laminin-related guidance cue acting on neurite outgrowth and vessel branching, and the tyrosine kinase FER transduces adhesion signals at cell-matrix contacts, linking matrix engagement to cytoskeletal remodelling.

Copper is needed as a cofactor by cytochrome c oxidase, superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase and ceruloplasmin, yet free copper catalyses damaging redox chemistry, so cells move it across membranes in a tightly chaperoned way rather than letting it diffuse. Copper ion transmembrane transport covers that movement: high-affinity uptake at the plasma membrane by SLC31A1 and its relative, reduction of Cu(II) to the transportable Cu(I) state by a metalloreductase, and export or compartmental loading by the ATP-driven pumps ATP7A and ATP7B, which also deliver copper to cuproenzymes in the secretory pathway. The soluble chaperone ATOX1 hands copper to those pumps, and additional carriers contribute lysosomal and endosomal handling. Loss of the pumps causes Menkes disease, with failed intestinal absorption and connective tissue defects, or Wilson disease, in which biliary copper excretion fails and copper accumulates in liver and brain.

Inorganic phosphate cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells rely on dedicated carriers to take it up, move it between compartments, and export it again. This transmembrane phosphate transport underpins bone and tooth mineralisation, renal phosphate reabsorption, ATP synthesis, and nucleotide and phospholipid biosynthesis. Sodium-dependent carriers of the SLC34 and SLC20 families import phosphate at the kidney brush border and in most cells; a mitochondrial carrier delivers phosphate to the matrix for oxidative phosphorylation, while SLC37 members exchange phosphate across the endoplasmic reticulum membrane in coordination with glucose-6-phosphatase activity during gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. XPR1 provides the main route for phosphate efflux, and the vitamin D receptor links hormonal control of calcium and phosphate balance to transporter expression. Loss of these activities produces hypophosphataemic rickets, nephrolithiasis, glycogen storage disease, and ectopic calcification of vessels and brain.

Resident proteins of the endoplasmic reticulum must stay there, and maintenance of protein localization in the ER is how the cell enforces that boundary — by holding proteins in place, stabilising them against packaging into transport vesicles, and retrieving those that leak forward into the Golgi. The KDEL receptors are the retrieval arm, binding C-terminal KDEL-type signals on escaped luminal chaperones such as BiP and returning them to the ER, while RER1 retains unassembled membrane subunits and OS9 works with the lectin-based quality control system that keeps misfolded glycoproteins in the lumen until they are degraded. The INSIG proteins illustrate the regulatory use of retention: they anchor SREBP cleavage-activating protein and HMG-CoA reductase in the ER when sterols are plentiful, blocking export and thereby switching off cholesterol synthesis. Loss of such retention scatters chaperones and biosynthetic enzymes, degrading secretory quality control and lipid homeostasis.

Dipeptide transmembrane transport moves intact two-amino-acid peptides across membranes rather than breaking them down first, which is how the small intestine and kidney recover most dietary and filtered protein-derived nitrogen. The proton-coupled oligopeptide transporters of the SLC15 family carry this traffic: PEPT1 handles high-capacity absorption at the intestinal brush border, PEPT2 reclaims peptides in renal tubules and choroid plexus, and PHT1 and PHT2 operate on lysosomal and endosomal membranes, where their delivery of bacterial peptidoglycan fragments feeds NOD-like receptor and TLR sensing in immune cells. Transport depends on an inward proton gradient, sustained by carbonic anhydrase and anion exchange, and the same carriers absorb beta-lactam antibiotics and peptidomimetic drugs, making them determinants of oral drug bioavailability. Loss of this route impairs nitrogen assimilation and blunts innate detection of intracellular bacteria.

Dipeptide transmembrane transport moves intact two-amino-acid peptides across membranes rather than breaking them down first, which is how the small intestine absorbs much of dietary protein and how the kidney reclaims filtered peptides. The proton-coupled peptide transporters SLC15A1 and SLC15A2 do this work at the apical brush border, using an inward proton gradient to drive uptake; because they are promiscuous, they also determine the oral bioavailability of beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors and peptidomimetic prodrugs. Their relatives SLC15A3 and SLC15A4 act instead on endosomal and lysosomal membranes, exporting bacterial peptide fragments into the cytosol and shaping innate immune sensing through nucleic acid and peptidoglycan receptors. Associated carbonic anhydrase and anion exchange activity supplies and recycles the protons and counter-ions that make coupled transport possible, linking peptide absorption to epithelial acid-base handling.

Tripeptide transmembrane transport moves three-residue peptides across membranes, and in human cells this largely means two things: absorbing dietary peptides and distributing glutathione. Intestinal and renal brush-border proton-coupled peptide transporters PEPT1 and PEPT2 take up di- and tripeptides released by digestion, and are the route by which many beta-lactam antibiotics and peptidomimetic drugs enter the body. The remaining machinery handles glutathione, the cysteine-containing tripeptide that buffers oxidative stress: ABCC-family pumps export reduced and oxidised glutathione and its conjugates from the cytosol, connexin 43 hemichannels release it to the extracellular space, and mitochondrial carriers SLC25A39 and SLC25A40 import it into the matrix, where the organelle cannot synthesise its own. Loss of these steps leaves compartments unable to maintain thiol redox balance, impairs detoxification of electrophiles, and shapes cellular sensitivity to ferroptosis.

Interferon-alpha is the front-line type I interferon released by virus-infected cells, and the response to it converts a bystander cell into one that resists infection. Ligand binding to the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 heterodimer triggers JAK-STAT signalling and a transcriptional programme of antiviral effectors, which is why this arm of innate immunity underlies recovery from viral infection and is exploited therapeutically, while its chronic overactivity drives interferonopathies and contributes to lupus. The effectors named here act at distinct steps: the IFITM proteins block viral entry and membrane fusion, BST2 tethers budding virions at the plasma membrane, MX2 restricts nuclear import of retroviral cores, and OAS1 and the kinase PKR shut down translation in response to double-stranded RNA. ADAR edits cellular RNA and so limits self-RNA sensing, restraining the same response it belongs to.

Cells exposed to interferon-beta switch into an antiviral state, and this response describes what they do about it: engagement of the type I interferon receptor pair IFNAR1/IFNAR2, JAK-STAT signalling through STAT1, and induction of a transcriptional programme that restricts viral entry, replication and spread. Effectors here act at distinct steps: the IFITM proteins block fusion of incoming virions, BST2 tethers budding particles at the membrane, OAS1 senses double-stranded RNA to trigger RNA decay, and PLSCR1 and SHFL add further restriction. Upstream sensors and adaptors, including cGAS-STING signalling components, IFI16, AIM2, MAVS and IKBKE, drive IFNB1 transcription itself, so the pathway is both stimulus and feedback loop. Loss of control causes interferonopathy: TREX1 mutations produce chronic type I interferon signalling and Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, while a blunted response leaves severe viral susceptibility.

Interferon-alpha is a type I interferon released chiefly during viral infection, and the cellular response to it converts that alarm into an antiviral and immunomodulatory state: transcription of restriction factors, restrained protein synthesis and cell growth, altered differentiation of responding lymphocytes. Signalling begins at the shared type I interferon receptor, of which IFNAR1 is one chain, and culminates in induced effectors such as the oligoadenylate synthetase OAS1, which makes 2'-5'-linked oligoadenylates to switch on RNase L and degrade viral and host RNA; PDE12 trims these second messengers and so damps the response. Other members tune sensitivity, including the AXL receptor tyrosine kinase with its ligand GAS6, which feeds negative regulation of interferon output, and transcriptional regulators such as GATA3 and MYC that shape the downstream program. Excessive or chronic signalling through this axis underlies interferon signatures in lupus and related autoimmunity, where RO60 is a classic autoantigen.

cellular response to interferon-beta is the set of changes a cell makes after sensing type I interferon, the cytokine arm of antiviral defence. Its output is the interferon-stimulated state: restriction of viral entry and replication, degradation of viral RNA, heightened antigen presentation, and priming for inflammatory or apoptotic death. Loss of the response leaves cells permissive to viral infection, while chronic engagement drives interferonopathies and autoimmunity. Signalling runs from IFNB1 through the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor to STAT1 and IRF1, which induce effectors such as OAS1 and IFITM2. Much of the gene content is the upstream sensing machinery that generates interferon-beta in the first place — cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors including IFI16, STING1 and MAVS, with TREX1 removing self-DNA that would otherwise trigger it — placing this pathway at the junction of innate nucleic acid surveillance and inflammasome-linked signalling.

Type I interferon-beta, released by virally infected or nucleic-acid-sensing cells, reprogrammes neighbouring cells into an antiviral state, and this pathway covers what a cell does once that signal arrives. Engagement of the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor pair drives STAT1-dependent transcription through factors such as IRF1, inducing effectors including the oligoadenylate synthetase OAS1, interferon-induced membrane proteins, and autophagy-related IRGM. Several members act upstream as well: the DNA sensors IFI16 and AIM2, the STING adaptor, and the mitochondrial RNA-sensing adaptor MAVS trigger IFNB1 transcription, so induction and response are coupled in a feed-forward loop. Negative regulators matter here too, since loss of the exonuclease TREX1 allows self-DNA to accumulate and produces chronic interferon signalling, the basis of type I interferonopathies such as Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome. Beyond antiviral defence, this response shapes inflammatory gene expression, metabolic shifts and cell survival decisions.

Transport vesicles are only useful if they carry the right molecules, and vesicle cargo loading is the step where coat proteins capture specific membrane and soluble cargo and concentrate it into a forming bud. This selectivity determines which proteins reach the cell surface, the lysosome or the bloodstream, and its failure causes recognizable disease: defective AP-3 adaptor subunits misroute lysosomal and melanosomal membrane proteins, producing pigmentation and platelet granule defects, while mutations in COPII machinery impair collagen and lipoprotein secretion. Two systems dominate the gene set. At the endoplasmic reticulum, SAR1 GTPases with SEC23/SEC24 inner-coat and SEC13/SEC31 outer-coat subunits, aided by cargo receptors such as SURF4, TMED proteins and the TANGO1-related family, select secretory cargo for export. On endosomal membranes, the heterotetrameric AP-3 complex and clathrin adaptors like PICALM recognize sorting signals and, with kinesin motors, direct carriers onward.

Vitamins cannot be synthesised by human cells, so they must be moved across membranes by dedicated carriers and receptors at every step from intestinal absorption to delivery inside the cell. This transmembrane transport of vitamins sets how much thiamine, folate, biotin, pantothenate, ascorbate, retinol and cobalamin reach the enzymes that depend on them, and its failure produces defined deficiency syndromes rather than general malnutrition. Proton-coupled and sodium-coupled solute carriers handle folate and thiamine uptake at the gut and blood-brain barrier, a mitochondrial carrier imports thiamine pyrophosphate for matrix enzymes, and sodium-dependent transporters bring in ascorbate. Fat-soluble vitamins travel bound to carrier proteins such as retinol-binding protein and vitamin D-binding protein and are taken up through receptors including STRA6 and the endocytic receptor LRP2. Loss-of-function mutations cause thiamine-responsive anaemia, biotin-responsive encephalopathy and cerebral folate deficiency.

The pancreas is not a midline organ: its head, body and tail adopt a fixed left-right orientation during gut rotation, and that placement is set by the same embryonic laterality cues that position the heart, spleen and liver. Determination of pancreatic left/right asymmetry depends on motile cilia at the embryonic node, which generate the directional fluid flow that breaks symmetry, and on the transcriptional response to that flow. Several members here are cilia assembly and motility factors — CCDC39 and CCDC40 organise the axonemal ruler and dynein regulatory complex, DNAAF1 acts in cytoplasmic preassembly of dynein arms — while NPHP3 links ciliary function to nephronophthisis and situs defects and the zinc-finger factor ZIC3 acts upstream in the nodal pathway. Loss of these functions produces situs inversus or heterotaxy, in which pancreatic and splenic arrangement is randomised or duplicated, often with congenital heart malformation.

When a blood vessel is injured, repair requires not just clot formation but regrowth of endothelium from surviving vessels, and positive regulation of vascular wound healing covers the signals that accelerate that sprouting and restore a sealed, perfused conduit. The genes here act at different levels of the same outcome: VEGFB engages endothelial VEGF receptor signalling to support endothelial survival and growth, the matricellular protein SMOC2 promotes endothelial proliferation and matrix remodelling at the wound edge, the transcription factor FOXC2 shapes arterial, venous and lymphatic vessel identity and mural cell recruitment, and XBP1, an effector of the unfolded protein response, couples secretory stress to endothelial proliferation. A histatin peptide and a microRNA regulator contribute further, showing that both extracellular cues and post-transcriptional control tune repair. Insufficient drive through this biology leaves chronic non-healing wounds and poor recovery after ischaemic vascular damage.

Gastric motility is the rhythmic peristaltic activity that mixes a meal with acid and enzymes and propels it through the pyloric sphincter into the duodenum, setting the rate at which nutrients reach the intestine and, with it, satiety and glucose excursions after eating. Delay or disorganisation of these contractions underlies gastroparesis and functional dyspepsia, with nausea, early satiety and bloating. The genes here represent the peptide signals that tune the smooth muscle and enteric neurons rather than the contraction itself: ghrelin, released from gastric endocrine cells during fasting, acts through its receptor GHSR to stimulate emptying and appetite, while neuromedin U signals through the enteric nervous system to alter contractile patterns. C-type natriuretic peptide acting on the guanylyl cyclase receptor NPR2 raises cyclic GMP in smooth muscle, a relaxing arm that balances excitatory drive and permits gastric accommodation.

Every intracellular membrane fusion event — a synaptic vesicle releasing neurotransmitter, a lysosome fusing with an autophagosome, a transport vesicle delivering cargo to the plasma membrane — is executed by a four-helix bundle zippering together from apposed membranes, and SNARE complex assembly is the step that builds it. Vesicle R-SNAREs such as VAMP1, VAMP2, VAMP3 and VAMP8 pair with target-membrane partners including STX1A and STX4, while SM proteins and tethering complexes decide where and when pairing is allowed: STXBP1 templates the syntaxin-VAMP interaction at the presynaptic active zone, and HOPS/CORVET subunits (VPS11, VPS16, VPS18, VPS33A, VPS39, VPS41) tether endosomes and lysosomes before fusion. Regulators like STXBP6 and PRRT2 tune release probability. Loss of this chemistry causes epileptic encephalopathy and movement disorders, and synuclein and LRRK2 link it to Parkinson disease.

The permanent mammalian kidney arises when the ureteric bud invades metanephric mesenchyme and branches repeatedly; this pathway covers development of the portion of that bud which builds the metanephros, giving rise to the collecting duct system, renal pelvis and ureter. Getting it right sets nephron number for life, and failure produces renal agenesis, hypoplasia, duplex or obstructed collecting systems. Reciprocal signalling between bud epithelium and surrounding mesenchyme drives branching and elongation, with transcriptional regulators such as WT1 and LHX1 specifying nephric duct and early tubular epithelial identity and FOXJ1 marking ciliated epithelial differentiation. PKD2 links the pathway to ciliary calcium signalling that constrains tubule diameter, connecting these events to cystic kidney disease when disrupted. Calcium-handling and cytoskeletal regulators reflect the epithelial polarity and morphogenetic movements that shape the growing duct.

Ubiquitin chains can be joined through several lysines, and linkage through lysine 29 of ubiquitin marks substrates for proteasomal destruction, adding to the repertoire of signals that set protein lifetime and quality control. Because chain topology determines whether a tagged protein is degraded, sorted or merely re-localised, building K29 linkages is one way cells commit a client to turnover rather than to a non-degradative fate. The step depends on E2 conjugating enzymes together with E3 ligases of varied architecture: HECT-type enzymes such as ITCH, UBE3C and the large ligase UBR5, RING-type membrane and endosome-associated ligases including RNF126, RNF167 and RNF186, and the Parkinson disease-linked ligase parkin. Through these enzymes the pathway feeds into receptor and membrane protein downregulation, ribosome- and translation-associated quality control, damaged mitochondrial protein clearance, and the removal of misfolded proteins whose accumulation drives neurodegeneration.

Monoubiquitination is a signalling mark rather than a degradation tag, and removing it from a monoubiquitinated protein reverses that signal, restoring the substrate to its unmodified state and setting how long the instruction lasts. The deubiquitinases here act on distinct arms of this control: BAP1 and USP16 strip monoubiquitin from histone H2A to regulate chromatin state and transcription, USP1 removes the monoubiquitin from FANCD2 and PCNA to terminate Fanconi anaemia crosslink repair and translesion synthesis, and USP7 and USP10 deubiquitinate substrates including p53 and its regulators to tune the DNA damage response. ATXN3 and USP9X act more broadly on protein quality control and receptor and kinase stability. Because these enzymes govern DNA repair exit, histone marks and tumour suppressor abundance, their loss or mutation is a recurrent feature of cancer and neurodegeneration, notably the polyglutamine disease caused by expanded ATXN3.

Proline transmembrane transport moves proline across cell membranes, supplying this imino acid for protein synthesis, collagen production, redox balance and osmotic adjustment, and recovering it from the intestinal lumen and the kidney filtrate. Its failure is seen directly in iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria, where renal reabsorption of proline and glycine is lost. Transport is carried out by proton-coupled amino acid carriers of the SLC36 family, sodium- and chloride-dependent carriers such as SLC6A20 and the neuronal proline transporter SLC6A7, and broader neutral amino acid systems including SLC1A4, SLC38A2 and SLC7A8. Several of these require the chaperones ACE2 or collectrin for correct surface delivery in intestine and kidney, linking this pathway to epithelial nutrient absorption. Lysosomal SLC36 members instead return proline from protein degradation to the cytosol, connecting the pathway to autophagy and mTOR-sensed amino acid supply.

Proline is taken up from the gut lumen, reabsorbed from the kidney filtrate, and moved into neurons and lysosomes by a set of carriers that together define proline transmembrane transport. The activity matters for whole-body amino acid economy and for collagen synthesis, which consumes proline in bulk; its failure in the kidney produces iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria, the classic disorders of proline and glycine reabsorption. Transport is largely secondary-active, using proton or sodium gradients: the SLC36 proton-coupled amino acid transporters handle proline and small neutral amino acids at the apical and lysosomal membranes, SLC6A20 carries imino acids across the intestinal and renal brush border, and SLC6A7 loads proline into synaptic terminals of glutamatergic neurons. ACE2 and its relative CLTRN act as brush-border chaperones required for correct surface expression of these carriers, coupling the transport step to membrane trafficking.

Membrane fusion requires SNARE proteins on two bilayers to zipper into a four-helix bundle, and this pathway covers the factors that promote or restrain that assembly step, setting where and when fusion happens. It matters most in neurons, where the rate of SNARE pairing governs synaptic vesicle priming and neurotransmitter release: STXBP1 chaperones syntaxin-1 into a fusion-ready conformation and its loss causes severe infantile epilepsy, while PRRT2 mutations produce paroxysmal dyskinesia and alpha-synuclein can both nucleate and, in excess, derange SNARE complex formation. A second arm is endolysosomal, with the HOPS and CORVET tethering subunits (VPS11, VPS16, VPS18, VPS33A, VPS39, VPS41, VPS8) coupling Rab-dependent tethering to SNARE engagement for late endosome and lysosome fusion. Other members, including LRRK2 and STXBP6, act as modulators that tune assembly rather than catalyse it, linking this control point to both neurotransmission and lysosomal delivery.

This is a regulatory category covering events that increase the ability of proteins to associate with chromatin, raising the frequency or extent with which factors dock onto DNA-protein fiber during interphase. Enhancing such binding is how cells license repair machinery, transcriptional coactivators and histone-modifying enzymes to reach their nuclear targets at the right moment. The members act at several such points: a DNA helicase involved in sister chromatid cohesion and fork progression, a histone demethylase that erases methyl marks on H3K9 and so alters the landscape other readers engage, a Mediator complex subunit that bridges activators to the transcription apparatus, and an interacting ubiquitin ligase and ADP-ribosyltransferase-related pair that promote recruitment of factors to damaged chromatin. Loss of this kind of positive control leaves chromatin-acting proteins poorly recruited, with consequences for transcriptional output, genome stability and DNA damage response.

Kidney size is set during development by the balance of nephron number, branching of the ureteric bud, and survival of progenitor cells, and processes that modulate it determine whether an organ ends up hypoplastic, dysplastic, cystic or compensatorily enlarged. The genes involved here span transcriptional control of nephric lineage specification and tubule differentiation, with PAX2 required for intermediate mesoderm to form the nephric duct and HNF1B acting with HNF1A on tubular and collecting duct gene programmes. Angiotensin receptor signalling contributes hormonal input to growth of the developing kidney, while chromatin regulation adds a further layer of control. Disruption at this level underlies congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, renal hypoplasia with early-onset diabetes, and reduced nephron endowment, which predisposes to hypertension and chronic kidney disease later in life.

Wnt ligands can steer cell behaviour without altering beta-catenin-dependent transcription, and this branch of Wnt signalling is what orients cells within a tissue and moves them. It governs planar cell polarity and convergent extension during gastrulation and neural tube closure, cochlear hair cell orientation, kidney tubule elongation and limb outgrowth; its failure produces neural tube defects, cystic kidney disease and disordered tissue architecture, and its reactivation drives invasive behaviour in tumours. Ligands such as WNT5A and WNT11 engage Frizzled receptors and alternative co-receptors including RYK, with Dishevelled proteins routing the signal to DAAM1 and the small GTPases RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 to remodel the cytoskeleton. Asymmetric membrane complexes built from VANGL1/2, PRICKLE and the cadherins CELSR1-3 set polarity axes across a cell sheet, while secreted SFRPs, DKK1 and FRZB restrain ligand availability.

Signalling by secreted growth factors can be switched off before it starts by trapping the ligand itself, and sequestering extracellular ligand away from its receptor is how morphogen gradients are shaped and how latent factors are held in reserve. Most members here are antagonists of the BMP/TGF-beta family: cerberus- and DAN-family proteins such as CER1, DAND5, GREM1, GREM2 and NBL1 bind BMPs directly and prevent receptor engagement, setting left-right asymmetry, limb and kidney patterning and neural induction. Fibrillins and latent TGF-beta binding proteins tether TGF-beta precursors in the extracellular matrix so that activation requires proteolysis or mechanical force, while NRROS restrains TGF-beta availability in microglia and macrophages. Loss of such buffering produces excess or mistimed signalling, with consequences ranging from skeletal and connective tissue disease to fibrosis and altered immune tone.

BMP signalling is positional information, and one way cells control it is to trap the ligand before it reaches a receptor. Sequestering BMP in the extracellular matrix confines secreted BMP homodimers to matrix proteins and to soluble antagonists, keeping them away from the cell surface and thereby setting how far and how strongly a BMP gradient acts. The result is patterning: left-right asymmetry, node and axis specification in the early embryo, and restraint of bone and cartilage formation where matrix rather than signalling is wanted. Cerberus and DAND5 are secreted DAN-family antagonists that bind BMP, Nodal and related ligands; NBL1 acts similarly; fibrillin-1 provides the matrix scaffold that holds BMP and TGF-beta family prodomains in reserve, which is why fibrillin mutation deregulates growth factor availability in connective tissue disease.

Extracellular nucleotides and nucleosides act as signals of tissue stress, injury and metabolic demand, and G protein-coupled purinergic receptor signalling is how cells read them. Adenosine receptors and nucleotide-sensing P2Y receptors couple ligand binding to heterotrimeric G proteins and to adenylate cyclase, raising or lowering cAMP depending on which receptor subtype dominates: the inhibitory ADORA1 and ADORA3 and the platelet ADP receptor P2RY12 restrain cyclase through Gi, while ADORA2A and ADORA2B stimulate it. The consequences are physiological and therapeutic — adenosine slows cardiac conduction and dampens inflammation, ADORA2A tunes striatal output and is the target of caffeine, and P2RY12 blockade is the basis of antiplatelet therapy. Availability of the ligands themselves is controlled upstream by ectonucleotidase and deaminase activity, including adenosine deaminase, linking purine catabolism directly to receptor tone.

Extracellular nucleotides such as ATP, ADP, UTP and UDP are released by damaged, stressed or activated cells, and the P2Y family of G protein-coupled receptors reads them as signals of injury, bleeding and inflammation. Signalling through these purinergic nucleotide receptors couples to Gq-driven phospholipase C activation with calcium mobilisation, or to Gi-mediated suppression of cyclic AMP, and so regulates platelet aggregation, vascular tone, epithelial chloride and fluid secretion, and the migration and activation of microglia and other immune cells. P2RY12 on platelets is the target of the antithrombotic thienopyridines, and P2RY1 acts alongside it in ADP-induced aggregation; P2RY2 and P2RY4 respond to pyrimidine nucleotides at mucosal surfaces. Related orphan and lipid-sensing receptors of the same branch, together with the adenosine receptor ADORA1, extend the response to nucleotide breakdown products and to lysophospholipid mediators of inflammation.

Extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP and UDP act as signals of tissue damage, secretion and cell activation, and purinergic nucleotide receptor signalling is how cells read them. It governs platelet aggregation, nociception and itch, smooth muscle and bladder contraction, and the inflammatory responses of microglia and macrophages, which is why its receptors are drug targets in antiplatelet therapy and chronic cough. Two receptor families do the work: P2X subunits assemble into ATP-gated cation channels that admit calcium and sodium directly, while P2Y receptors couple through G proteins such as GNAI2 to adenylyl cyclase and phospholipase C, raising or lowering cAMP and mobilising internal calcium. Sustained P2RX7 activation drives inflammasome output and lytic death. Nucleotide signals are terminated by ectoenzymatic breakdown to adenosine, which acts on the ADORA receptors here to impose a largely opposing, anti-inflammatory tone.

Acyl groups added to lysine side chains and to cysteines change how proteins behave, and protein deacylation is the erasing step that makes those marks reversible and therefore informative. Removing acetyl, succinyl, malonyl or long-chain acyl groups from histones, metabolic enzymes, tubulin and transcription factors sets the tempo of gene expression, mitochondrial fuel use and cytoskeletal dynamics; its loss is tied to ageing phenotypes, metabolic disease and tumour progression. Classical zinc-dependent deacetylases such as HDAC3, HDAC6 and HDAC7 work within corepressor and cytoplasmic complexes, while the NAD+-dependent sirtuins couple deacylation directly to cellular energy state, with SIRT3, SIRT4 and SIRT5 acting in mitochondria and SIRT6 and SIRT7 on chromatin. A separate branch removes thioester-linked lipids: ABHD17 enzymes and LYPLA1 depalmitoylate membrane-anchored signalling proteins, and PPT1 performs the lysosomal equivalent. Several acetyltransferase-complex subunits appear here as the opposing writers.

Tubulin and a handful of other proteins carry glutamate side chains added to their C-terminal tails, and protein deglutamylation is the reaction that takes them off, trimming glutamate residues to reset the code that microtubules use to recruit motors and regulatory proteins. The reaction is carried out by a family of cytosolic carboxypeptidases, among them AGTPBP1 and AGBL1 through AGBL5, which differ in whether they shorten a glutamate chain or clip the branch point where it attaches. Balance matters more than direction here: when deglutamylation fails, hyperglutamylated microtubules accumulate and neurons degenerate, as in the Purkinje cell loss and retinal degeneration linked to loss of AGTPBP1 and AGBL5. The same chemistry shapes cilia and flagella, where glutamylation state governs axonemal beating, and it also removes gene-encoded C-terminal glutamates from tubulin itself.

cytoplasmic stress granule disassembly clears the RNA-protein condensates that form when translation halts under stress, returning sequestered mRNAs to ribosomes once conditions improve. Timely dissolution matters because granules that persist mature into insoluble aggregates; failure of this clearance is a route to the RNA-binding protein pathology seen in ALS, frontotemporal dementia and inclusion body myopathy. Several mechanisms converge here. The kinase DYRK3 acts as a solubility switch that dissolves condensates on stress relief; VCP with its cofactors FAF2 and ZFAND1 extracts ubiquitinated and defective proteins from granules and routes them to the proteasome or to autophagic degradation; TRIM21 provides ubiquitin ligase activity directed at granule components. Kinesin-1 with its light chain contributes motor-dependent transport and mechanical dispersal along microtubules. The pathway thus links protein quality control, condensate biophysics and recovery of translation after stress.

Stress granules are transient cytoplasmic condensates of mRNA and RNA-binding proteins that form when translation stalls, and they must be taken apart once stress passes; the disassembly programme returns their constituent messages and proteins to normal use. Persistent, poorly cleared granules are a recognised route to the pathological protein aggregates seen in ALS and frontotemporal dementia, so the pace of clearance matters for neuronal proteostasis. Several routes converge here: the kinase DYRK3 dissolves condensates in a phosphorylation-dependent manner, the AAA+ ATPase VCP with its cofactors FAF2 and ZFAND1 extracts proteins and channels damaged granules toward degradation, TRIM21 ubiquitinates granule components, and kinesin-1 with its light chain moves granules along microtubules. The pathway therefore links phase separation, ubiquitin-dependent extraction, autophagic clearance and motor-driven transport to recovery from cellular stress.

Ceramides are made in the endoplasmic reticulum but consumed elsewhere, so cells need carriers that move them between membranes rather than relying on diffusion.
