Hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone acting through its receptor drives pituitary cleavage of proopiomelanocortin to ACTH, which in turn stimulates adrenal steroidogenesis; cholesterol delivery into mitochondria, aided by outer-membrane proteins such as TSPO, is the rate-limiting step. Secretion is not constant but pulsatile and diurnal, and the circadian repressors CRY1 and CRY2 help impose that daily rhythm, while neuropeptides including galanin, substance P and ghrelin modulate drive on the axis. Too little output produces adrenal insufficiency with hypoglycaemia and vascular collapse; chronic excess yields the muscle wasting, central adiposity, bone loss and immunosuppression of Cushing syndrome.

Corticosterone secretion is the controlled release of a glucocorticoid made in the adrenal cortex into the bloodstream, the output step of the stress axis that mobilises glucose, restrains inflammation and adapts an animal to physical and psychological challenge. Control comes from above: hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone acts through its receptor CRHR1 on pituitary corticotrophs, where the POMC precursor is cleaved to ACTH, which then drives steroidogenesis in the cortex. TSPO sits in the outer mitochondrial membrane at the point where cholesterol is delivered for conversion to steroid, linking mitochondrial cholesterol handling to hormone output. Additional modulators here include the neuropeptide precursor TAC1, the secreted factors ECRG4 and SELENOM, and the potassium channel KCNQ1, reflecting how electrical excitability and local peptide signalling tune release. Excess output produces Cushing-like features; insufficiency leaves the organism unable to withstand stress.

Interleukin-13 is the type 2 cytokine that drives allergic inflammation at mucosal barriers, and the cellular response to it converts that signal into the changes that define asthmatic airway disease: mucus hypersecretion, goblet cell metaplasia, eosinophil recruitment, smooth muscle hyperresponsiveness and tissue remodelling. Signalling runs through a shared type II receptor in which IL13RA1 pairs with the IL-4 receptor alpha chain, while IL13RA2 acts as a high-affinity decoy that sequesters the cytokine and limits the response. Downstream consequences visible here include transcription factor activation, induction of eotaxin to attract eosinophils, and the lipid-modifying enzyme ALOX15, a hallmark of alternatively activated macrophages and IL-13-exposed epithelium. The same programme shapes macrophage polarisation and antiparasitic responses, and it is the target of biologic therapies for asthma and atopic dermatitis.

Interleukin-13 is the type 2 cytokine that drives the tissue side of allergic inflammation, and this is the response a cell mounts when it encounters it. Binding of IL-13 to a receptor formed by IL13RA1 together with the shared IL-4 receptor alpha chain triggers JAK-STAT6 signalling, redirecting gene expression in epithelium, smooth muscle and macrophages: mucus hypersecretion, goblet cell metaplasia, airway hyperresponsiveness and subepithelial fibrosis in asthma, and alternative (M2) macrophage polarisation with induction of ALOX15 and the sedoheptulose kinase SHPK as part of that programme. IL13RA2 lacks signalling capacity and acts as a high-affinity decoy that dampens the response, while CD300LF is among the surface receptors upregulated on IL-13-exposed myeloid cells. The same signalling underlies helminth expulsion and wound repair, making this pathway a therapeutic target in atopic disease.

Retrograde traffic from the Golgi back to the endoplasmic reticulum depends on COPI-coated vesicle budding, the step in which a Golgi cisternal membrane deforms and pinches off a coated carrier. This is how escaped ER residents and recycling machinery are retrieved, how Golgi enzymes are redistributed between cisternae, and therefore how compartment identity in the early secretory pathway is maintained; its loss disorganises the Golgi and impairs secretion. The cycle begins when a large guanine nucleotide exchange factor, GBF1, loads GTP onto ARF1 so the coat can be recruited to the membrane, while ARFGAP2 and ARFGAP3 stimulate GTP hydrolysis to time coat release. p24-family cargo receptors such as TMED2, TMED9 and TMED10 link the coat to transmembrane cargo and help nucleate assembly.

Misfolded proteins are toxic, and cells detect them and respond by slowing translation, boosting folding capacity, and destroying what cannot be repaired. This response to topologically incorrect protein spans the cytosolic heat-shock programme and the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response, and its failure underlies proteinopathies, secretory cell stress, and the apoptotic death of cells that cannot restore folding balance. Three ER sensors initiate distinct arms: IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to expand the secretory machinery, PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to attenuate protein synthesis while inducing ATF4 and CHOP, and ATF6 is cleaved by Golgi proteases to release a transcription factor. Chaperones of the HSP70, HSP90, HSP60, small heat-shock and DNAJ families rebind clients, while glycan trimming by EDEM enzymes, lectins such as OS9, and retrotranslocation through derlins to VCP and ubiquitin ligases route terminally misfolded substrates to the proteasome. Sustained stress tips the output toward BAX/BAK-dependent apoptosis.

cellular response to topologically incorrect protein is the set of reactions a cell mounts when proteins fail to reach their native fold, and it determines whether that cell adapts or dies. It protects secretory tissues under heavy folding load — pancreatic beta cells, plasma cells, hepatocytes — and its failure underlies Wolfram syndrome, neurodegenerative aggregate diseases, and the vulnerability of tumours to proteotoxic stress. Three endoplasmic reticulum sensors dominate: PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to arrest translation and induce ATF4 and CHOP, IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to expand folding and lipid capacity, and ATF6 is cleaved by site-1 and site-2 proteases to a transcription factor. Terminally misfolded substrates are recognised by lectins and mannosidases, retrotranslocated through derlin channels, and degraded by VCP-dependent ubiquitin-proteasome routes, while cytosolic chaperones, HSF1 and autophagy receptors handle aggregates. Persistent stress switches the output to apoptosis through BAX, BAK and PUMA.

Misfolded proteins are toxic if left to accumulate, and the cellular response to topologically incorrect protein is the surveillance and corrective programme that detects them, restores folding capacity, and kills the cell if the burden cannot be cleared. It is what allows secretory tissues such as plasma cells and pancreatic beta cells to sustain heavy client loads, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, diabetes and inherited misfolding diseases. Three endoplasmic reticulum sensors dominate: IRE1 splices XBP1 mRNA to expand chaperone and lipid capacity, PERK phosphorylates eIF2 alpha to throttle translation while inducing ATF4 and CHOP, and ATF6 is cleaved by site proteases to release a transcription factor. In parallel, mannosidase-like lectins and derlins select terminally misfolded glycoproteins for retrotranslocation, ubiquitination and VCP-driven degradation, while cytosolic chaperones, HSF1 and aggresome routing handle misfolding outside the ER. Sustained stress tips output toward BH3-only proteins and apoptosis.

Phosphorylation on threonine residues is a reversible switch, and peptidyl-threonine dephosphorylation is the reaction that resets it, hydrolysing the phosphate from phosphothreonine to return the protein to its unmodified state. Because kinase cascades depend on being switched off as much as on being switched on, these phosphatases set signal duration and amplitude rather than merely terminating signals. The members shown act in distinct arenas: dual-specificity enzymes such as DUSP1 and DUSP5 inactivate MAP kinases by removing the phosphates from their activation loop threonine and tyrosine; magnesium-dependent PPM family enzymes including PPM1D dampen stress and DNA damage checkpoint responses; PDP1 dephosphorylates the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and thereby licenses entry of pyruvate into oxidative metabolism; and the PP2A catalytic subunit serves mitotic and growth signalling. Loss of this counterbalance produces sustained kinase output, seen in tumour growth and metabolic inflexibility.

Aggrephagy is the route by which cells clear protein aggregates that are too large for the proteasome, packaging them into autophagosomes for lysosomal destruction. It is the main defence against the inclusion bodies that accumulate in neurodegenerative disease, and its decline with age underlies the toxicity of aggregated huntingtin, tau and other misfolded species in neurons, which cannot dilute damage by division. Cargo is first concentrated: ubiquitin-binding receptors such as SQSTM1 and UBQLN1, the scaffold WDFY3, and the BAG3-HSPB8 chaperone module recognise misfolded protein and, with HDAC6-dependent transport along microtubules, deliver it to a perinuclear site where an autophagosome forms. ATG4 proteases and lipidated LC3 supply the membrane conjugation machinery, while casein kinase 2 phosphorylation of the receptor tunes cargo capture. The pathway sits within selective macroautophagy alongside mitophagy, coupling chaperone-based quality control to bulk membrane degradation.

Misfolded proteins that escape refolding and cannot be threaded into the proteasome are collected into inclusions and cleared by aggrephagy, the selective routing of protein aggregates into autophagosomes for lysosomal degradation. This is the main defence against proteotoxicity in long-lived cells such as neurons and muscle fibres, and its decline accompanies Huntington disease and other aggregate-associated neurodegeneration; huntingtin itself is both a substrate and a scaffold here. Ubiquitinated aggregates are recognised by receptors including p62 and ubiquilin, concentrated with the help of a chaperone-based sorting module built on BAG3, HSPB8 and the tubulin deacetylase HDAC6, which moves cargo along microtubules to the perinuclear aggresome. Large scaffolds such as WDFY3 and WDR81 organise cargo delivery, while ATG4 family cysteine proteases process and recycle LC3 proteins for autophagosome membrane formation, linking aggregate clearance to general macroautophagy and proteostasis.

endodermal cell differentiation is the specification of the innermost germ layer during gastrulation, the step that commits pluripotent epiblast cells to the lineage that will build gut, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid. Without it no endoderm-derived organ forms, and its regulators are the same signals used to direct stem cells toward hepatocytes or beta cells in vitro. Nodal/activin signalling acting through EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA6 and HNF1B drives the transcriptional switch, while pluripotency factors POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 must be dismantled and DKK1 tunes Wnt/beta-catenin input. Chromatin and elongation machinery, including the PAF1 complex, SETD2 and macroH2A, make the new programme heritable. The prominent collagens, laminins, fibronectin, integrins and matrix metalloproteinases reflect the cell-shape changes, basement membrane remodelling and migration by which nascent endoderm ingresses and forms an epithelial sheet.

Endodermal cell differentiation is the step by which pluripotent epiblast cells commit to the innermost germ layer, the source of gut epithelium, liver, pancreas, lung and thyroid; failure or misdirection of this choice leaves the embryo without an endoderm-derived organ programme, and its recapitulation in culture is how stem cells are steered toward hepatocytes and beta cells. Nodal and activin signalling acting through beta-catenin and DKK1-modulated Wnt input induces the definitive endoderm transcription factors EOMES, MIXL1, SOX17, GATA6 and HNF1B while pluripotency factors POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 are extinguished. The PAF1 transcription elongation complex with CDC73, LEO1, CTR9 and RTF1, together with SETD2-dependent chromatin methylation, licenses these lineage genes. Extensive collagen, laminin, fibronectin, integrin and matrix metalloproteinase components indicate that commitment is accompanied by matrix remodelling and cell migration during gastrulation.

Cartilage grows by expanding its chondrocyte population, and the controlled multiplication of these matrix-secreting cells sets the pace of endochondral bone growth in the fetal skeleton and the postnatal growth plate. Rates of division in the proliferative zone determine limb length and stature, so disturbance of this control produces skeletal dysplasias, chondrodysplasia and premature growth arrest, while its reactivation accompanies fracture repair and osteoarthritic cartilage remodelling. Growth factor input converges here: BMP receptors and SOX9 drive chondrogenic commitment and cycling, Indian hedgehog relays a feedback loop that couples proliferation to hypertrophic differentiation, and FGFR3 signalling restrains division, with gain-of-function alleles causing achondroplasia. Natriuretic peptide receptor NPR2 stimulates growth-plate expansion, SMAD7 dampens TGF-beta/BMP input, and matrix and matrix-remodelling components such as COMP, MMP14 and the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 tie the surrounding extracellular matrix to the proliferative response.

Tendons transmit the force of muscle contraction to bone, and their development builds a tissue that must withstand repeated tension without rupturing. The programme specifies tendon progenitors from limb and axial mesenchyme and then drives their maturation into aligned, collagen-rich fibres; failure of it leaves joints unable to convert muscle shortening into movement, and weakened matrix underlies tendinopathy and tendon rupture. The transcription factor scleraxis marks and directs the tendon lineage, while BMP-family signals including BMP4 and GDF7 pattern progenitors and influence tendon versus cartilage and bone fate at the insertion site. Much of the output is structural: fibrillar collagen V and collagen XI regulate the assembly and diameter of collagen I fibrils, and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein organises the surrounding extracellular matrix, linking this developmental route to musculoskeletal connective tissue biology generally.

Muscle cells sense when they are stretched beyond the sarcomere's slack length and convert that mechanical signal into changes in gene expression, calcium handling and secretion. In the heart this is the basis of load-induced hypertrophy and of the stretch-dependent release of natriuretic peptide from atrial myocytes, which links chamber filling to blood pressure and volume control; in skeletal muscle it tunes growth to mechanical demand. Detection occurs at the sarcomeric Z-disc and the costamere, where titin, telethonin and the muscle LIM protein CSRP3 sit alongside dystrophin and caveolin-3 and pass tension to signalling. Downstream, focal adhesion kinase, MAP kinase and PI3K routes activate immediate-early transcription by FOS and JUN and NF-kB-dependent programmes, while sodium-proton and sodium-calcium exchange with ryanodine receptor calcium release adjusts contractility. Loss of these components causes cardiomyopathy and muscular dystrophy.

Muscle fibres must sense how far they have been stretched in order to adjust their size, stiffness and gene expression to mechanical load, and detection of muscle stretch is the step that turns that physical deformation into a biochemical signal. The genes involved sit at the structures built to bear force: titin spans the sarcomere and, with telethonin at the Z-disc, acts as a length sensor; the muscle LIM protein CSRP3 shuttles from the Z-disc in response to strain; caveolin-3 organises sarcolemmal caveolae, while N-cadherin, beta-catenin and focal adhesion kinase couple membrane adhesion sites to downstream signalling and transcription. Through these routes stretch drives load-induced hypertrophy and adaptive remodelling. Mutations in several of these proteins cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy or muscular dystrophy, indicating that mechanical sensing, not just force generation, sustains cardiac and skeletal muscle integrity.

One-carbon units carried on tetrahydrofolate exist in several oxidation states, and their interconversion is what lets a cell direct the same pool of carbons toward nucleotide synthesis or toward methylation. This folate cycle supports thymidylate and purine production for DNA replication and supplies the methyl groups that regenerate methionine and S-adenosylmethionine, so its failure shows up as impaired proliferation, uracil misincorporation, and megaloblastic anemia. Serine is the main donor: cytosolic and mitochondrial serine hydroxymethyltransferases transfer its beta-carbon to tetrahydrofolate, and the trifunctional dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase/synthetase enzymes shuttle the resulting methylene form between methenyl, formyl, and formate. Methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase commits carbons irreversibly to the methylation arm, while thymidylate synthase consumes the methylene form and oxidizes the cofactor to dihydrofolate. A common reductase variant raises homocysteine, and these enzymes are classic antifolate and fluoropyrimidine targets in cancer.

Cells of the mononuclear phagocyte lineage depend on macrophage colony-stimulating factor for their production, survival and differentiation, and this pathway covers what a cell does once that cue arrives. CSF1 and the alternative ligand IL34 both engage the receptor tyrosine kinase CSF1R, triggering kinase and adaptor responses through effectors such as FER and DOK1, with the phosphatase PTPN2 restraining the output. The consequences are developmental as much as immunological: monocytes mature into tissue macrophages and microglia, and precursors fuse into multinucleated osteoclasts, a step marked by DCSTAMP and supported by TREM2 signalling, linking this axis to bone remodelling alongside markers of the osteoblast side such as ALPL and osteocalcin. Responding cells also become primed for inflammatory output through TLR2, TLR4, TNF and osteopontin. Loss or excess of this signalling produces osteopetrosis, microglial disease and tumour-associated macrophage accumulation.

Macrophage colony-stimulating factor instructs monocytes and their progenitors to survive, proliferate and differentiate into macrophages and osteoclasts, and the cellular response to that stimulus is what sets tissue macrophage numbers and bone resorption capacity. Two ligands, CSF1 and the alternative cytokine IL34, engage the receptor tyrosine kinase CSF1R; autophosphorylation recruits adaptors and kinases such as DOK1, FER and STAP1, while the phosphatase PTPN2 restrains the output. Downstream events include cytoskeletal remodelling for spreading and chemotaxis, cyclic nucleotide turnover by phosphodiesterases, and induction of fusion and phagocytic machinery including DCSTAMP for osteoclast multinucleation and TREM2 for microglial maturation. Innate receptors TLR2 and TLR4 intersect this programme, coupling growth factor input to inflammatory polarisation. Loss of receptor signalling produces osteopetrosis and microglial deficits; excess drives tumour-associated macrophage accumulation, making CSF1R a drug target.

Endosomes act as the cell's sorting station, and delivering or holding proteins there determines whether a receptor is recycled to the surface, handed on to lysosomes for degradation, or retrieved to the Golgi. The genes here cover several arms of that traffic: Rab GTPases such as RAB5A and RAB35 with ARF6 define endosomal identity and recycling routes, the retromer subunit VPS35 with WASH complex components drives retrieval and actin-dependent tubule scission, and ezrin/radixin/moesin proteins with NF2 couple endosomal membranes to the cortical cytoskeleton. Depalmitoylating ABHD17 enzymes and the lipid flippase subunit TMEM30A shape which cargo stays membrane-anchored on these compartments, while ligands and receptors like EGF, VEGFA, NRP1 and SORL1 are themselves the cargo. The outcome is control over signalling duration, nutrient receptor reuse and amyloid precursor processing; failures here contribute to neurodegeneration and aberrant growth factor signalling.

Interleukin-3 is a haematopoietic growth factor that keeps early progenitors, mast cells, basophils and myeloid precursors alive and dividing, and this pathway covers the cellular changes a cell makes when it senses that cue. The receptor is a two-part assembly: a ligand-binding alpha chain paired with the common beta chain also shared by GM-CSF and IL-5 receptors, so the response is intertwined with wider myeloid cytokine signalling. Because neither chain has catalytic activity, signalling depends on an associated Janus kinase that phosphorylates the receptor and launches STAT and PI3K-AKT output, with glycogen synthase kinase-3 acting downstream on survival and proliferation decisions and an SH2-domain adaptor imposing negative feedback on kinase activity. Dysregulated signalling through this axis, particularly constitutive JAK2 activity, drives myeloproliferative disease and leukaemic progenitor expansion.

response to erythropoietin is what a cell does when it encounters the kidney-derived hormone that governs red blood cell production. Erythroid progenitors depend on this response for survival, proliferation and terminal maturation; without it they die by apoptosis and anaemia follows, which is why recombinant erythropoietin treats the anaemia of renal failure, and why activating changes in the same axis drive erythrocytosis. Binding of the hormone to its receptor dimerises it and activates the associated kinase JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT5 for transport to the nucleus and, with CREB1, drives transcription of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle genes. The stem cell factor receptor KIT cooperates in expanding the progenitor pool, and induced metallothioneins reflect an accompanying shift in metal handling and oxidative stress tolerance as haemoglobin synthesis ramps up. The erythroid-specific adaptor RHEX marks the receptor-proximal branch of this signalling in human progenitors.

Erythropoietin is the kidney-derived hormone that tells red cell progenitors to survive, divide and mature, and the cellular reactions to it set the rate of erythropoiesis and thus blood oxygen-carrying capacity. Loss of the response causes anaemia, as in renal failure, while constitutive activation of its signalling drives polycythaemia and myeloproliferative disease. The hormone binds a dedicated receptor whose dimerisation activates the receptor-associated kinase JAK2; phosphorylated STAT5 then enters the nucleus to switch on anti-apoptotic and differentiation genes, with CREB1 contributing further transcriptional output. An erythroid-specific JAK2 substrate, RHEX, and cooperation with stem cell factor signalling through KIT amplify progenitor expansion. Induction of metallothioneins reflects the accompanying handling of metal and oxidative stress in maturing erythroblasts, linking this hormonal axis to iron and redox physiology.

Limb joint morphogenesis is the patterning step that interrupts a continuous cartilage condensation to create the flexible interzones separating the rigid segments of an arm or leg. Without it, the skeleton forms as fused rods and the joint cavity, articular cartilage and surrounding capsule never appear, the developmental basis of synostosis and congenital joint fusion. Wnt/beta-catenin signalling through CTNNB1 specifies and maintains interzone cells rather than letting them differentiate into growth-plate chondrocytes, while the zinc-finger factors OSR1 and OSR2 sustain that interzone identity. Heparan sulfate chain elongation by EXT1 shapes the diffusion of morphogens across the developing joint, and ERRFI1 restrains EGF receptor output. Fibrillar and microfibrillar collagens supply the matrix of the capsule and articular surfaces, linking joint patterning to the mechanics of controlled limb movement.</response>

Cytotoxic CD8 T cells are the arm of adaptive immunity that kills virus-infected and tumour cells, and their activation is the switch from a resting naive cell to a proliferating, granule-loaded effector. The response begins when a T cell receptor engages peptide presented on class I MHC, represented here by HLA-A and the non-classical HLA-E, with antigen supplied by proteasomal degradation ""the many PSMA and PSMB subunits, including the interferon-inducible immunoproteasome components PSMB9 and PSMB10 and the thymus-specific PSMB11 that shapes the selecting repertoire. Transcription factors decide lineage and fate: RUNX3 and ZBTB7B set the CD8 versus CD4 choice, EOMES drives cytotoxic effector programmes, and TOX accompanies chronic stimulation and exhaustion. Inhibitory receptors and ligands such as CD274, VSIR and LILRB family members restrain the response, while SOCS1 damps cytokine signalling; loss of these brakes underlies autoimmunity, and their exploitation by tumours is the target of checkpoint blockade.

O-fucosylation attaches a single fucose directly to serine or threonine hydroxyls within folded protein modules, and the resulting glycans tune how those modules work. Two protein O-fucosyltransferases carry out the reaction on distinct substrates: one modifies EGF-like repeats, most consequentially on Notch receptors, where the fucose and its subsequent elongation set the balance between Delta- and Jagged-type ligand responses; the other modifies thrombospondin type-1 repeats on secreted and matrix proteins, acting alongside quality control of their folding in the endoplasmic reticulum. Elongation follows, with a beta-1,3-glucosyltransferase capping the TSR-linked fucose; loss of that step causes Peters plus syndrome, a developmental disorder of eye, skeleton and growth. A nucleotide-sugar transporter-related membrane protein supports delivery of GDP-fucose to these compartments, while other family members shown here fucosylate N-glycans and glycolipids rather than protein hydroxyls.

Direct, or intramembranous, ossification builds bone straight from mesenchymal condensations without first laying down and then replacing a cartilage template, and it is the route by which the flat bones of the skull, the clavicle and much of the facial skeleton form. Its pace and extent set the timing of cranial suture closure: too much activity fuses sutures prematurely, as in craniosynostosis, while too little leaves calvarial defects and unmineralised gaps. Condensed mesenchyme differentiates directly into osteoblasts that secrete a type I collagen matrix, here represented by COL1A1, and then mineralise it; FGF18 signalling and Wnt pathway feedback through AXIN2 govern how quickly progenitors commit, MN1 supports calvarial osteoblast expansion, and MMP2 remodels the surrounding matrix. The pathway sits alongside endochondral bone formation as one of the two ways the vertebrate skeleton is made.

Most of the skeleton is not laid down directly as bone but replaces an earlier template, and replacement ossification covers that conversion — principally endochondral bone formation, in which a cartilage anlage is hypertrophied, vascularised, resorbed and substituted by mineralised matrix. It sets limb length, growth plate behaviour and fracture healing, and its disturbance produces skeletal dysplasias, short stature and defective mineralisation. Chondrocyte and osteoblast identity is imposed by transcription factors such as RUNX2, DLX5 and MEF2C, with FGF18–FGFR3 and BMP signalling and natriuretic peptide receptor NPR2 setting the pace of proliferation and hypertrophy. Matrix components including collagens I and II and proteoglycan-modifying enzymes build the template, while membrane-type and secreted matrix metalloproteinases degrade it. Mineral deposition depends on phosphatases ALPL and PHOSPHO1, whose loss underlies hypophosphatasia-like defective bone mineralisation.

At the end of mitosis the dividing cell must pinch itself in two at exactly the right place, and cleavage furrow formation is the step that marks that place: a shallow groove appears in the cortex over the position of the old metaphase plate, and the contractile ring assembles there. Getting the site wrong, or failing to ingress, yields binucleate cells and the aneuploidy that follows a failed division. Positional information comes from the central spindle and the midzone kinases Aurora B and PLK1, which drive localized activation of RhoA and hence actin nucleation and myosin engagement at the equatorial cortex; the SPIRE actin nucleators and the sorting nexins SNX9, SNX18 and SNX33 couple membrane remodelling and vesicle delivery to the deforming cortex. The pathway sits at the interface of cytoskeletal contractility, membrane traffic and mitotic exit control.

Phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate is the defining lipid mark of early endosomes and forming autophagosomes, and its synthesis is how a membrane is labelled for traffic, sorting and degradation. Effectors bearing FYVE and PX domains read the mark, so making it determines where endosomal maturation and autophagy actually happen; loss of this chemistry blocks autophagosome formation and misroutes endocytic cargo. The core producer is the class III enzyme VPS34 with its regulatory partner VPS15, directed by Beclin-1 in complexes specified by ATG14 for autophagy or UVRAG for endosomal function. Class II enzymes generate the lipid at distinct sites, while class I enzymes feed the broader 3-phosphoinositide pool. Counterbalancing phosphatases — including inositol polyphosphate 4- and 5-phosphatases, synaptojanins, OCRL and FIG4 — set steady-state levels, and mutations in several of them cause ciliopathies, Lowe syndrome and neuropathies.

Germ cell proliferation is the expansion of the reproductive cell population, the mitotic multiplication of spermatogonia or oogonia that builds and sustains the pool from which gametes are later made. Without adequate proliferation, and without the survival signals that keep dividing germ cells alive, the germline is depleted and infertility follows. The genes here point to two themes: transcriptional control of gonadal fate, with DMRT1 acting in Sertoli cells and germ cells to maintain male identity and prevent germ cell tumour-like transformation, and prostaglandin D2 signalling, where the synthases PTGDS and HPGDS generate a lipid mediator read by the receptor PTGDR2 to influence testis development. Additional components link germ cell survival to redox balance in the secretory pathway and to regulated proteolysis, with RHBDD1 acting in apoptotic control of male germ cells.

Leukotrienes are potent lipid mediators of inflammation that drive bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and neutrophil recruitment, so their inactivation sets how long and how strongly an inflammatory episode lasts. Two chemistries do most of that work here. Cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4A and CYP4F families carry out omega-hydroxylation of the terminal carbon of leukotriene B4 and related eicosanoids, converting them to 20-hydroxy metabolites with much reduced activity that are then oxidised further and cleared; the neutrophil-expressed CYP4F3 is the classic LTB4 omega-hydroxylase. The dipeptidases act on the cysteinyl arm, hydrolysing the glycine residue of leukotriene D4 to give leukotriene E4, the urinary end product used to gauge cysteinyl leukotriene output in asthma. Loss of this catabolic capacity prolongs receptor signalling and sustains leukocyte chemotaxis, linking the pathway to asthma, inflammatory bowel disease and the resolution phase of inflammation generally.

Leukotriene B4 is one of the strongest chemoattractants known for neutrophils, and how long it persists at a site of inflammation depends on the enzymes that dispose of it. This metabolic route is therefore a brake on inflammation: without it, LTB4 accumulates and drives sustained leukocyte recruitment, adhesion and degranulation, contributing to asthma, inflammatory bowel disease and atherosclerotic vessel wall injury. Inactivation begins with omega-hydroxylation at C20 by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4 family, notably the leukocyte-expressed CYP4F3 together with CYP4F2, CYP4F12 and the related fatty acid omega-hydroxylase CYP4A11; the 20-hydroxy product is far less active at the BLT receptors. Further oxidation and reduction steps, including the prostaglandin/leukotriene reductase PTGR1, complete degradation. The pathway sits within arachidonic acid eicosanoid metabolism and links lipid mediator turnover to resolution of innate immune responses.

alpha-linolenic acid metabolic process is the conversion of a dietary essential fatty acid into the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids that cells cannot make from scratch, above all EPA and DHA. It matters because humans depend on this route for the docosahexaenoic acid enriched in retinal photoreceptors, synaptic membranes and sperm, and for the substrates of anti-inflammatory lipid mediators; low conversion efficiency, worsened by variants in the desaturase locus, constrains omega-3 status on plant-based diets. Alternating desaturation by FADS1 and FADS2 and two-carbon elongation by the ELOVL family, notably ELOVL2 and ELOVL5, build progressively longer and more unsaturated chains in the endoplasmic reticulum; the final step requires a round of peroxisomal beta-oxidation, which explains the presence of ABCD1, ACAA1 and SCP2. The pathway thus links dietary lipid intake to membrane composition and eicosanoid signalling.

Alpha-linolenic acid is a dietary essential fatty acid that humans cannot synthesise, and its metabolism converts it into the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids that cells actually use. The route matters for brain and retinal membrane composition and for the supply of precursors to lipid signalling mediators; poor flux through it leaves tissues dependent on preformed dietary long-chain omega-3 fats. Alternating desaturation and elongation steps drive the conversion: FADS1 and FADS2 introduce double bonds, while ELOVL2 and ELOVL5, with related elongases, add two carbons at a time to the growing acyl chain. The final shortening step that yields docosahexaenoic acid occurs in peroxisomes, which is why peroxisomal components including the acyl-CoA transporter ABCD1, the thiolase ACAA1, SCP2 and an acyl-CoA thioesterase belong here, linking this biosynthetic route to peroxisomal beta-oxidation and its disorders.

Fatty acids of six to twelve carbons must be thioesterified to coenzyme A before they can be oxidised, and the medium-chain fatty-acyl-CoA metabolic process covers both their activation and the reversal of it. The balance matters because acyl-CoA esters are not merely substrates: they sequester the cell's free CoA pool, act as signalling and allosteric molecules, and must be kept in proportion to demand. Mitochondrial acyl-CoA synthetase activity charges the free acid with CoA, while thioesterase and CoA-diphosphatase activities work in the opposite direction, hydrolysing the thioester or cleaving the nucleotide to release free fatty acid and regenerate CoA. Several members act in peroxisomes, where chain shortening by beta-oxidation generates medium-chain intermediates that are exported rather than fully degraded, linking this chemistry to peroxisomal lipid catabolism and to energy supply during fasting.</description>}Rationale: ACSM2A is a mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetase; ACOT7 a cytosolic acyl-CoA thioesterase; NUDT7/NUDT8/NUDT19 are CoA diphosphatases (NUDT7 peroxisomal, NUDT19 peroxisomal, NUDT8 mitochondrial); HSD17B4 (DBP) is a peroxisomal beta-oxidation bifunctional enzyme.{

Fatty acyl-CoA esters are the activated form in which fatty acids are transported, oxidised and built into lipids, and their catabolism sets how much of that activated pool persists. Cleaving the thioester bond or the CoA moiety itself releases free fatty acid and either coenzyme A or a phosphopantetheine fragment, which regulates the ratio of acyl-CoA to free CoA in cytosol, mitochondria and peroxisomes and thereby the flux into beta-oxidation versus glycerolipid synthesis. Acyl-CoA thioesterase activity dominates in the brain and other tissues, while Nudix-family hydrolases degrade CoA esters largely in peroxisomes, the compartment that handles very-long-chain and branched substrates. Import of very-long-chain acyl-CoA into peroxisomes by the ABCD1 transporter feeds this route; loss of that transporter causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, with accumulated very-long-chain fatty acids damaging myelin and adrenal cortex.

Platelet-derived growth factor is the principal mitogen for mesenchymal cells, and this pathway covers what a cell does once it senses it: enter the cell cycle, migrate, remodel its matrix, and change transcription. It drives wound healing, pericyte and vascular smooth muscle recruitment to vessels, and fibroblast expansion, and when persistently engaged it contributes to fibrosis, intimal hyperplasia and tumour stroma; activating receptor mutations cause fibroblastic tumours. Ligands such as PDGFB and PDGFD act through the receptor tyrosine kinase PDGFRB, which recruits Src-family kinases including SRC, FYN and YES1 and is restrained by the ubiquitin ligase CBL, the phosphatase PTPN1 and the feedback inhibitor ERRFI1. Downstream outputs include CREB1- and SMAD3-dependent transcription, cyclin A accumulation, hyaluronan synthesis by HAS1 and HAS2, and cytoskeletal reorganisation via IQGAP1 and coronin, with crosstalk to TGF-beta signalling.

Phosphatidylglycerol is a minor but consequential glycerophospholipid: it is the immediate precursor of cardiolipin in mitochondria and, in the lung, the second most abundant lipid of pulmonary surfactant. Acyl-chain remodeling of phosphatidylglycerol determines which fatty acids it carries, and therefore how well it serves those roles. The cycle is a deacylation-reacylation loop: phospholipases of the A2 family cleave an acyl chain to yield lyso-phosphatidylglycerol, and acyltransferases such as LPGAT1, LPCAT1 and LPCAT4 re-esterify the position with a different fatty acid, favouring saturated species in surfactant and specific chains destined for cardiolipin once cardiolipin synthase condenses phosphatidylglycerol with CDP-diacylglycerol. Loss of SERAC1, which acts on phosphatidylglycerol remodeling, causes MEGDEL syndrome, with deafness, dystonia and mitochondrial dysfunction, illustrating how acyl-chain identity rather than lipid class alone shapes membrane function.

Phosphatidylinositol made by de novo synthesis does not carry the acyl chains found in the mature lipid, and acyl-chain remodeling of phosphatidylinositol is how that composition is corrected. Newly formed species are deacylated by phospholipases to lysophosphatidylinositol and then re-acylated by acyltransferases with a preferred fatty acid, so that the bulk of cellular phosphatidylinositol ends up bearing stearoyl and arachidonoyl chains. This matters because phosphatidylinositol is the precursor of the phosphoinositides that mark membranes for signalling and traffic, and because the arachidonate stored at the sn-2 position is a reservoir for eicosanoid production. Acyltransferases such as MBOAT7, LCLAT1 and LPGAT1 provide the re-acylation step, with MBOAT7 variants strongly linked to fatty liver disease and fibrosis progression. The pathway sits within broader glycerophospholipid metabolism and membrane lipid quality control, tuning bilayer physical properties as well as signalling output.

Phosphatidylserine is made with a generic acyl composition and then edited, and acyl-chain remodeling of phosphatidylserine is the editing step that sets which fatty acids it carries. This matters because phosphatidylserine is the inner-leaflet anionic lipid that recruits protein kinase C and other C2- and polybasic-domain proteins, and, when exposed on the cell surface, marks apoptotic cells for phagocytosis and provides the surface for coagulation complexes; the acyl chains determine membrane order and how well those functions work. A phospholipase removes one acyl chain to give lysophosphatidylserine, and membrane-bound O-acyltransferases such as MBOAT1, MBOAT2 and the LPCAT enzymes re-esterify the position with a preferred donor, oleoyl or arachidonoyl species among them. Oxysterol-binding-related proteins in the set place this chemistry in the context of lipid transfer between organelle membranes, where phosphatidylserine is moved out of the endoplasmic reticulum.

Phosphatidylcholine made de novo carries a fairly generic pair of acyl chains; acyl-chain remodeling replaces them, tuning membrane fluidity, curvature and the supply of signalling lipids. A phospholipase A2 step removes the sn-2 chain to give lysophosphatidylcholine and a free fatty acid — often arachidonate, which feeds eicosanoid production — and lysophospholipid acyltransferases of the LPCAT and MBOAT families then re-esterify a chosen chain, MBOAT7 and LPCAT3 favouring polyunsaturates and LPCAT1 generating the dipalmitoyl species that makes pulmonary surfactant work. Liver X receptors provide transcriptional control linking this remodeling to sterol and fatty acid status. The consequences are concrete: surfactant failure in the lung, altered susceptibility to fatty liver disease when polyunsaturated remodeling is reduced, and control over how much arachidonate is available for inflammatory mediator synthesis.

Phosphatidylethanolamine made by the de novo pathway carries a limited set of acyl chains, and acyl-chain remodeling is how cells edit it after synthesis to give membranes their final fatty acid composition. This tuning sets bilayer curvature and fluidity, supplies arachidonate for eicosanoid production, and determines how much polyunsaturated lipid is available for peroxidation, linking the pathway to inflammatory signalling and to susceptibility to ferroptotic cell death. The chemistry is a two-step cycle: phospholipases and related hydrolases of the PLA2 and PLAAT families remove one acyl chain to leave a lysophosphatidylethanolamine, and membrane-bound acyltransferases including LPCAT3, LPCAT4, MBOAT1 and MBOAT2 re-esterify it with a different fatty acid drawn from the acyl-CoA pool. ABHD4 also releases N-acylethanolamine precursors, tying this remodeling to bioactive lipid production in the endoplasmic reticulum.

Motile cilia and sperm flagella beat because outer dynein arms, the motor complexes docked at regular intervals along the outer doublet microtubules, generate most of the force that bends the axoneme. Building them is the job of this assembly pathway: heavy, intermediate and light chains such as DNAH5, DNAI1, DNAI2 and DNAL1 are folded and pre-assembled in the cytoplasm with the help of a large family of dynein assembly factors, including DNAAF1-DNAAF6 and the chaperone-associated ZMYND10, then transported into the cilium and anchored by the ODAD1-ODAD4 docking complex. Sperm-specific heavy chains such as DNAH8 and DNAH17 serve the flagellum. Loss of any step gives immotile or dyskinetic cilia, producing primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic airway infection, situs inversus, hydrocephalus and male infertility, and illustrates how cytoplasmic pre-assembly precedes ciliary transport.

Motile cilia and sperm flagella beat because dynein motors, anchored along the outer doublet microtubules of the axoneme, generate sliding forces; inner dynein arm assembly builds and installs that inner row of motors. Its failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, with impaired mucociliary clearance in the airways, chronic sinopulmonary disease, situs abnormalities from disrupted nodal cilia, and male infertility from immotile sperm. Assembly is largely cytoplasmic: dedicated dynein assembly factors act as a preassembly chaperone system, several working with HSP70/HSP90 machinery, to fold and combine heavy chains such as DNAH1, DNAH2, DNAH3 and DNAH7 with associated subunits before intraflagellar transport carries complete motors into the axoneme. The ruler proteins CCDC39 and CCDC40 set the 96-nanometre periodicity that spaces inner arms and nexin-dynein regulatory complexes correctly, linking motor placement to coordinated waveform generation.

Some differentiated cells can reversibly change identity without mutating, and phenotypic switching describes that adaptive reprogramming of state. In vertebrate vessels it is best characterised in smooth muscle cells, which move between a contractile phenotype maintained by myocardin-driven expression of contractile genes and a synthetic, proliferative, migratory phenotype that deposits matrix; the same plasticity underlies vascular repair and, when sustained, atherosclerotic plaque formation, restenosis and neointimal thickening. Growth factors such as PDGFB and FGF9 push cells away from the contractile programme, while epigenetic writers including the DNA methyltransferase DNMT1 and the histone methyltransferase EHMT2 lock expression patterns in place. A large set of microRNAs, notably the miR-143/145 pair together with miR-21 and miR-221, acts as the tuning layer, coupling external cues and redox state to the choice of phenotype.

Zymosterol is a late intermediate on the route from acetyl-CoA to cholesterol, and its metabolism covers both the mevalonate steps that build the isoprene backbone and the sterol-modifying reactions that convert lanosterol onward toward cholesterol. The output supplies membrane sterol for fluidity and raft organisation, plus precursors for steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D. HMG-CoA synthase and the rate-limiting reductase HMGCR generate mevalonate, which kinases and a decarboxylase convert to isopentenyl units; these are condensed by FDPS and FDFT1 to squalene, epoxidised by SQLE and cyclised by lanosterol synthase. Removal of the C4 methyl groups by MSMO1, NSDHL and HSD17B7, together with sterol reductase activity of the lamin B receptor, yields and consumes zymosterol. Defects in these demethylation steps cause CHILD syndrome and related skin and skeletal disorders, and the upstream reductase is the target of statins.

Most proteins acquire their working identity only after synthesis, through covalent chemistry added to and removed from particular amino acids, and this protein modification process is the collective machinery that performs it. Such marks set protein stability, localisation, activity and partner choice, so they underlie signal relay, cell cycle progression, DNA damage responses, immune activation and protein quality control; their misregulation is pervasive in cancer and neurodegeneration. The genes span kinases and their opposing phosphatases, ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades (E1, E2 and cullin-RING, HECT, TRIM and F-box ligases) together with deubiquitinases and SUMO proteases, acetyltransferases and sirtuin deacetylases, methyltransferases and demethylases, ADP-ribosyltransferases, palmitoyl- and myristoyl-transferases, prenylation and glycosylation enzymes, tubulin tyrosine ligases, transglutaminases and proline hydroxylases. Writers, erasers and the adaptors that select substrates are represented together, making reversibility and substrate targeting as central here as catalysis.

Granulocyte activation is the shift a neutrophil, eosinophil or basophil makes from a resting circulating cell to an armed effector after it meets a chemokine, cytokine, immune complex or microbial signal, and it is the step that converts innate immune recognition into killing, degranulation and tissue inflammation. Too little of it leaves recurrent bacterial and fungal infection; too much drives the collateral damage of sepsis, vasculitis and chronic inflammatory disease. Chemokine receptors such as CXCR1, CXCR2 and CCR2 direct recruitment, while integrins CD11b/CD18 mediate firm adhesion and Fc and lectin-like receptors sense opsonised targets through ITAM adaptors and Syk, with inhibitory receptors and the phosphatase PTPN6 setting the threshold. Signals converge on PKCδ, Src and Rac exchange activity to trigger fusion of granules at the membrane via SNARE and Munc18 proteins, releasing cathepsin G, cathelicidin, granulins and phospholipase A2 alongside TNF and CXCL8.

Multivesicular body organization is how a late endosome converts itself into a sorting station: patches of the limiting membrane bud inward, capturing ubiquitinated membrane proteins into intralumenal vesicles that are then delivered to lysosomes for degradation or released as exosomes. This is the route by which activated growth factor and cytokine receptors are permanently switched off, so its failure leaves signalling receptors recycling at the surface and contributes to tumour growth and to neurodegeneration. The machinery is the ESCRT series acting in order: a ubiquitin-recognizing complex built on HGS and STAM, TSG101 with VPS28 and VPS37 subunits, the VPS25/VPS36/SNF8 module, and CHMP proteins that polymerize to constrict and sever the bud neck. The AAA-ATPase VPS4, with VTA1, disassembles these filaments for reuse. The same membrane-scission chemistry serves cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope resealing and viral budding.

Every RNA polymerase II transcript acquires a modified 5' end within seconds of emerging from the polymerase, and RNA capping is the enzymatic sequence that builds it. The cap protects nascent RNA from 5' exonucleases, marks it as self rather than foreign, and serves as the binding site that licenses splicing, 3' end processing, export and translation initiation. A triphosphatase-guanylyltransferase adds the inverted guanosine, a methyltransferase converts it to 7-methylguanosine with an activating subunit, and cap-adjacent ribose methylation of the first and second transcribed nucleotides further distinguishes host mRNA from viral RNA sensed by innate immune receptors. Nuclear cap-binding proteins then hold the structure for downstream steps. Related chemistry hypermethylates the cap of small nuclear RNAs, which assemble with Sm and Lsm proteins into the spliceosomal and histone pre-mRNA processing particles represented here.

Small nuclear and small nucleolar RNAs are distinguished from messenger RNAs by an unusual 5' end, and hypermethylation of the 7-methylguanosine cap is the step that creates it. Converting the ordinary monomethylated cap into a 2,2,7-trimethylguanosine cap requires that N7 methylation has already occurred, and it marks the RNA as a mature snRNA rather than an mRNA. The trimethyl guanosine synthase TGS1 adds the extra methyl groups, but it acts only after the Sm core has assembled on the RNA in the cytoplasm — the canonical Sm proteins SNRPB, SNRPD1-3, SNRPE/F/G, and the U7-specific variants LSM10 and LSM11, are all represented here. The hypermethylated cap and the Sm ring together license nuclear reimport of the snRNP, so this modification feeds directly into spliceosome assembly, pre-mRNA splicing, histone mRNA 3' end processing and rRNA maturation.

RNA (guanine-N7)-methylation installs a methyl group on the N7 position of guanine in RNA, a modification that marks messenger RNA caps and stabilises the folds of transfer and ribosomal RNAs. It determines whether a transcript is recognised as translatable and whether tRNAs survive to deliver amino acids, so its loss degrades protein synthesis globally. Distinct enzymes serve distinct substrates: RNMT with its activating partner RAM caps nascent mRNA co-transcriptionally, licensing export and ribosome recruitment; METTL1 with WDR4 modifies G46 in tRNA variable loops; BUD23 acts on 18S rRNA during small subunit maturation. TRMT112 serves as a shared obligate subunit that stabilises several of these methyltransferases. Hypomorphic WDR4 and METTL1 mutations cause microcephalic primordial dwarfism through tRNA fragmentation and ribosome stalling, and cap methylation is exploited by proliferating cells to sustain translation of growth-promoting transcripts.

Methylation of guanine at the N7 position marks RNA for recognition and stability, and these enzymes carry it out on three different RNA classes. RNMT, with its activating subunit RAMAC, caps messenger RNAs by methylating the guanosine added at the 5' end, the modification that licenses nuclear export, efficient translation initiation and protection from decapping-dependent decay. METTL1 with WDR4 installs m7G at position 46 of tRNA variable loops, stabilising the fold and tuning translation elongation; loss-of-function mutations in WDR4 cause microcephalic primordial dwarfism. BUD23 methylates a guanine in 18S ribosomal RNA during small subunit maturation, coupling the modification to ribosome biogenesis. TRMT112 serves as the shared obligate partner that stabilises and activates several of these methyltransferases. Collectively the pathway sits upstream of protein synthesis capacity, and its disruption is linked to developmental disorders and to tumour growth driven by altered tRNA methylation.

Swimming behavior describes stimulus-driven locomotion through water, a whole-organism readout used to score how nervous system function translates into coordinated movement, and one of the standard behavioral endpoints by which neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental damage is detected in animal models. The genes here connect that output to amyloid biology and neuronal signalling: the amyloid precursor protein and the beta-secretase that cleaves it, an executioner caspase that carries out apoptotic pruning and neuronal death, a receptor tyrosine kinase that shapes neuronal differentiation and monoaminergic tone, and the tryptophan-degrading enzyme that feeds kynurenine metabolites acting on glutamatergic transmission. Together they place motor performance downstream of amyloid processing, programmed cell death and neuroactive metabolite production, so that loss of these functions registers as impaired swimming, altered escape responses, and reduced motor endurance.

Swimming behaviour is a whole-organism locomotor response to sensory or internal cues, and it is used experimentally as a readout of neural circuit integrity, motivation and stress coping. The genes grouped here are better known for neuronal maturation and degeneration than for movement itself: a receptor tyrosine kinase with roles in neurodevelopment and monoaminergic signalling, the amyloid precursor protein together with the beta-secretase that cleaves it to generate amyloid-beta, an executioner caspase that drives apoptosis and prunes synapses, and the tryptophan-degrading enzyme that initiates the kynurenine pathway and links inflammation to neuroactive metabolites. Their shared appearance in this context reflects how amyloid processing, programmed cell death and immune-driven tryptophan metabolism alter motor output and behavioural performance, the basis for using swimming assays in models of neurodegeneration and depression-like states.

Many kinases set their own activity level by phosphorylating serine residues on themselves, either in cis or on an identical partner molecule within a dimer, and this autophosphorylation on peptidyl-serine is what converts a latent enzyme into an active one or marks it as committed to signalling. The consequence is that pathway output does not depend only on upstream input: the kinase encodes part of its own switch and its own memory of activation. The proteins here span quite different circuits, including the DNA damage-responsive kinase ATM, which autophosphorylates as it is recruited to double-strand breaks, a MAP kinase cascade component, the lipid kinase PIKFYVE that phosphorylates endosomal phosphoinositides, and RIPK1, whose autophosphorylation status governs whether cells proceed to survival, apoptosis or necroptosis. Such self-modification also creates docking sites and stabilises the active conformation.

cellular response to increased oxygen levels is how cells sense and adapt to hyperoxia, the condition of oxygen tension above normal, which is both a therapeutic exposure in ventilated patients and neonates and a source of oxidative injury. Excess oxygen drives reactive species production, and cells must either detoxify, remodel damaged components, or die; failure of this balance underlies bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, and hyperoxic lung injury. The genes point to three linked responses: NADPH oxidase-derived superoxide generation as the proximal signal, autophagy and lysosomal acidification through ATG7 and the vacuolar ATPase subunits to clear oxidized cargo, and apoptotic and transcriptional arms through FAS and FOXO1 that commit damaged cells to death or to antioxidant and stress gene expression. Caveolin-1 and lipocalin-2 tie the response to membrane signalling platforms and iron handling.

Cells detect not only oxygen scarcity but oxygen excess, and this response covers what a cell does when oxygen levels rise above its accustomed set point. Hyperoxia raises the flux of reactive oxygen species, and the adaptive programme decides whether a cell clears damaged material and survives or commits to death, which matters in the lung and retina of oxygen-treated newborns and in reperfused tissue. Several components point to autophagy and lysosomal acidification: ATG7 drives autophagosome formation, while a set of vacuolar-type ATPase subunits together with assembly factors acidifies the lysosome so that autophagic cargo is degraded. FOXO1 provides the transcriptional arm, tuning antioxidant and autophagy gene expression, and FAS-driven death signalling offers an alternative outcome. Caveolin-1, a NADPH oxidase and the iron-sequestering protein lipocalin-2 link the response to membrane signalling and oxidative stress control.

response to increased oxygen levels is the cellular reaction to hyperoxia — the adjustments a cell or tissue makes when oxygen tension rises above what it is adapted to. It matters because oxygen excess is chemically dangerous: more oxygen means more superoxide and peroxide leaking from respiration, so lipid, protein and DNA damage follow unless detoxification keeps pace. This underlies retinopathy of prematurity and ventilator-associated lung injury, and it is the mirror image of the hypoxic response, with erythropoietin production and pulmonary vascular tone (via KCNA5) turning down as oxygen returns. The genes cover antioxidant defence (catalase, mitochondrial SOD2, thioredoxin reductase), base excision repair, NADPH oxidase as a deliberate source of signalling oxidants, and BNIP3- and ATG7-dependent autophagy and mitophagy that clear damaged mitochondria. Lysosomal V-ATPase subunits link the response to acidification and degradative turnover, alongside FOXO1-driven transcriptional adaptation, matrix remodelling and apoptotic commitment when damage cannot be contained.

Cells monitor oxygen tension in both directions, and this programme covers the adjustments made when oxygen rises — hyperoxia, reoxygenation after ischaemia, or the transition to air breathing at birth. Rising oxygen means more reactive oxygen species, so a large part of the response is antioxidant defence: catalase, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and thioredoxin reductase limit oxidative damage, while base excision repair handles the lesions that escape. At the same time oxygen-sensitive gene expression is reversed, with erythropoietin transcription falling and the hypoxia-induced mitophagy receptor BNIP3 no longer needed, and autophagic and lysosomal acidification machinery adjusts mitochondrial content. In the pulmonary vasculature, oxygen-sensitive potassium channels and caveolar signalling couple oxygen levels to vascular tone. Failure to buffer this transition underlies reperfusion injury, bronchopulmonary dysplasia and oxygen toxicity in ventilated patients.

Interstrand cross-link repair resolves lesions that covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together, which would otherwise block the strand separation required for replication and transcription. It is the pathway lost in Fanconi anemia, where its failure produces bone marrow failure, developmental defects, chromosome breakage and cancer predisposition, and it determines cellular sensitivity to crosslinking chemotherapies such as cisplatin and mitomycin C. Stalled replication forks are sensed by the ATR checkpoint and by FANCM, which recruits the core Fanconi complex to monoubiquitinate FANCD2-FANCI; ubiquitin signalling through RNF8/RNF168 and RFWD3 then organises downstream nucleases including ERCC1-ERCC4, FAN1, SLX-type activities and NEIL3-mediated unhooking. The unhooked crosslink is bypassed by translesion or template-switch synthesis, and the resulting double-strand break is repaired by RAD51-dependent homologous recombination, with MCM8-MCM9 and protein extraction by VCP and SPRTN clearing adducts.

Interstrand cross-links covalently tether the two strands of the double helix, so they block the strand separation required for replication and transcription and must be excised before a fork can proceed. This repair route keeps replication going in the face of aldehydes, platinum drugs and other cross-linking agents, and its loss causes Fanconi anaemia, with bone marrow failure, developmental defects and cancer predisposition; the same defect underlies the clinical sensitivity of tumours to mitomycin C and cisplatin. A stalled fork recruits the core Fanconi complex, which monoubiquitinates the FANCD2-FANCI pair to license nucleolytic unhooking by structure-specific endonucleases such as the ERCC1-ERCC4 and FAN1 activities, or in some contexts glycosylase-mediated cross-link cleavage. Translesion and gap-filling synthesis follow, and the resulting double-strand break is resolved by RAD51-dependent homologous recombination under ATR-coordinated checkpoint control, with ubiquitin signalling and replisome remodelling organising factor exchange at the lesion.

Macrophage colony-stimulating factor (M-CSF/CSF1) is the cytokine that drives monocyte, macrophage and osteoclast production from myeloid progenitors, and the biology described here concerns the stimuli and regulators that raise its synthesis and release. Because M-CSF availability sets tissue macrophage numbers and bone-resorbing osteoclast differentiation, control of its output links inflammation to both innate immune surveillance and bone remodelling, and sustained overproduction contributes to inflammatory tissue damage and tumour-associated macrophage accumulation. Contributors here include stromal and epithelial signals such as the IL-7-family cytokine TSLP, immune receptors on myeloid cells including the checkpoint molecule HAVCR2 (TIM-3) and a leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor, a transcription factor of the forkhead family, and a microRNA that tunes transcript levels post-transcriptionally. The presence of a haematopoietic progenitor marker points to the progenitor-rich niches where this cytokine acts.

The atrioventricular canal is the narrow segment joining atrium to ventricle in the developing heart, and its development produces the cushions and conduction tissue that become the mitral and tricuspid valves, the septal junction, and the slow-conducting region that delays impulse transfer between chambers. Failure here underlies atrioventricular septal defects, valve malformation and conduction abnormalities, and several of these genes are mutated in human congenital heart disease and syndromes such as CHARGE, Noonan and Holt-Oram-like presentations. Regionalisation depends on bone morphogenetic protein signalling through SMAD4 acting with GATA4 and GATA6, and on T-box repressors TBX2 and TBX3 that suppress chamber-specific gene programmes so canal myocardium stays distinct from working myocardium. Notch signalling via RBPJ and hyaluronan synthesis by HAS2 drive endocardial cells to transform into mesenchyme and expand the cushions.</description>

Lymphatic vessels drain interstitial fluid, absorb dietary lipid and carry immune cells to lymph nodes, and lymph vessel morphogenesis is how that network is built and patterned from venous endothelium. Failure produces lymphoedema, chylous effusions and lymphatic malformations, and the same programme is exploited by tumours for lymphatic metastasis. Specification depends on transcriptional identity: PROX1 commits endothelial cells to the lymphatic fate, with SOX18 and FOXC2 driving lineage entry and later valve formation, while PDPN marks the differentiated cells. Sprouting and migration run through VEGFC acting on the VEGFR3 receptor FLT4, with CCBE1 required for growth factor processing, alongside TIE1 and EPHA2 guidance input and TGF-beta/BMP receptor signalling that tunes vessel calibre. Extracellular matrix and adhesion components such as SVEP1 and calcineurin-dependent signalling shape valve and capillary architecture, linking this biology to vascular development and tissue fluid balance.

response to sterol covers how cells sense and react to cholesterol, oxysterols and related lipids, adjusting gene expression, transport and enzyme activity to keep membrane sterol content within tolerable limits. It matters because sterol excess is both toxic and atherogenic: cells that cannot register it fail to export cholesterol or to shut off its synthesis, the situation underlying foam cell formation and hypercholesterolaemia. The genes span the main sensing and effector arms — INSIG1 and INSIG2 restraining sterol synthesis through the SREBP–reductase axis, the GRAMD1/Aster proteins moving accessible cholesterol from the plasma membrane, ABCA1 effluxing it to acceptors, and CYP7A1 with CYP8B1 disposing of it as bile acids. Sterols also act as signals here, via Smoothened and Patched in Hedgehog reception and the RORA/RORC nuclear receptors, linking lipid status to developmental patterning, immune tone and TGF-beta signalling.

Cells sense sterols and adjust their metabolism, membrane composition and gene expression accordingly, and this response to sterol stimulus links cholesterol abundance to transport, catabolism and signalling decisions. When cholesterol is plentiful, INSIG1 and INSIG2 hold the sterol-sensing machinery of the endoplasmic reticulum in check to shut down sterol synthesis, while ABCA1 exports excess cholesterol to nascent HDL and CYP7A1 with CYP8B1 commit it to bile acid synthesis in the liver. GRAMD1 (Aster) proteins move accessible cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER, and oxysterol-binding proteins provide further intracellular transfer. Sterols also act as ligands and cofactors for signalling: cholesterol and oxysterols modulate Smoothened and Patched in the Hedgehog pathway, and oxysterol-responsive RORA and RORC couple sterol status to transcription. Loss of this regulation drives cholesterol overload, foam cell formation and atherosclerosis, with additional inflammatory and TGF-beta-linked outputs represented here.

Cells constantly sense how much sterol they hold and adjust transport, storage and disposal accordingly, and this is the response arm of that surveillance. It sets whether cholesterol is exported to acceptors, converted to bile acids, esterified or used to shut off its own synthesis, and its failure underlies foam cell formation and the lipid overload of atherosclerosis. Sterol binding at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane retains the sterol-sensing machinery through INSIG1 and INSIG2, blocking the proteolytic release of the transcription factors that drive lipogenic genes, while GRAMD1 family proteins move accessible cholesterol from the plasma membrane to the ER and ABCA1 effluxes it to apolipoprotein acceptors. CYP7A1 commits cholesterol to bile acid synthesis. Sterols also act as ligands in their own right, with oxysterols controlling RORA and RORC transcription and sterol modification governing Hedgehog reception through PTCH1 and SMO.

Signalling through vascular endothelial growth factor receptor-2 is the main route by which endothelial cells are told to proliferate, migrate, survive and increase vascular permeability, and it is the pathway that drives new blood vessel growth in development, wound healing, ischaemia and tumours. VEGFA binding to the KDR receptor tyrosine kinase triggers autophosphorylation and downstream kinase cascades that reach transcriptional and cytoskeletal outputs; the same axis is the target of anti-angiogenic antibodies and kinase inhibitors used in cancer and retinal disease. Regulation is built in: DAB2IP acts as a GTPase-activating protein that restrains Ras-dependent output downstream of the receptor, while the endothelial transmembrane lectin CLEC14A and the calcium-binding protein PDCD6 modulate receptor-driven migration and tube formation. A copper transporter in the set links receptor signalling to copper availability, which endothelial angiogenic responses require.

Intestinal stem cell homeostasis keeps the crypt stem cell pool at a constant size, balancing self-renewal against differentiation so that the intestinal epithelium can be replaced every few days without exhausting its progenitors or overgrowing. Loss of this balance underlies impaired regeneration after injury, defective barrier function, and the crypt hyperplasia that precedes colorectal tumorigenesis. The genes point to several inputs converging on the crypt niche: LGR4 receives R-spondin and amplifies Wnt signalling in the stem cell compartment; NOD2 senses bacterial peptidoglycan and links the microbiota to stem cell survival, a connection relevant to Crohn's disease; membrane lipid remodelling by LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases tunes stem cell proliferation through lipid availability and Paneth cell antimicrobial output; and chromatin regulation by ZNHIT1 restrains the stem cell programme. Together they couple nutrient, microbial and mechanical cues to epithelial renewal.

The intestinal epithelium is renewed every few days from stem cells in the crypt base, and intestinal stem cell homeostasis is the balance that keeps their numbers steady — enough proliferation to replace shed enterocytes, not so much that crypts hyperplase or transform. Loss of that balance underlies impaired mucosal repair, chronic inflammation and colorectal tumour initiation. The genes here touch several inputs to that balance: LGR4 potentiates Wnt signalling from Paneth and mesenchymal niche cells, the dominant driver of crypt stem cell self-renewal; NOD2 senses bacterial muramyl dipeptide and links microbial cues to stem cell survival, with variants predisposing to Crohn's disease; membrane lipid handling through LPCAT3 and secreted phospholipases shapes crypt lipid composition and antimicrobial defence; and ZNHIT1 acts in chromatin remodelling that constrains the stem cell state. Together they place niche signalling, microbial sensing and lipid metabolism upstream of epithelial renewal.

Dendritic cells only work as antigen-presenting cells if they can leave peripheral tissue, enter lymphatics and reach the T cell zones of draining lymph nodes, and this migratory programme is what connects innate antigen capture to adaptive immunity. Loss of it leaves antigen stranded in skin and mucosa, blunting T cell priming; unrestrained migration contributes to chronic inflammation and autoimmunity. Chemokine receptors set the itinerary, with CCR1, CCR2, CCR5 and CCR6 drawing immature cells toward inflamed tissue and CCR7 responding to lymph-node CCL19 and CCL21 after maturation, while CXCR4 and the oxysterol receptor GPR183 refine positioning within lymphoid organs. Downstream, CDC42, DOCK8 and PI3K-gamma remodel the actin cytoskeleton for the fast, adhesion-light crawling these cells use, and TRPM channels and damage signals such as HMGB1 tune responsiveness. Chemotaxis here is inseparable from maturation state.

Fas signalling is the death-receptor route by which one cell instructs another to die: Fas ligand engages the death-domain receptor FAS, a member of the tumour necrosis factor receptor superfamily, which recruits adaptors and initiator caspases to trigger apoptosis. This is how cytotoxic lymphocytes kill targets, how activated T cells are deleted after an immune response, and how self-reactive clones are removed; loss of the receptor or its ligand causes autoimmune lymphoproliferative disease, and tumours evade it to survive. The output is not solely cell death, since the same receptor can feed into transcriptional and inflammatory responses. Regulation enters at several levels here: FAF1 and CASP8AP2 act on receptor-proximal signalling, palmitoylation by ZDHHC7 influences receptor clustering, TMBIM1 restrains death signalling, and IL7/IL7R with the shared gamma chain supply survival cues that set the threshold for apoptosis in lymphocytes.

Vertebrate embryos extend a muscular tail behind the anus, and post-anal tail morphogenesis is the set of events that builds and patterns that posterior structure from the tail bud. It depends on continued axis elongation, orderly segmentation of paraxial mesoderm into somites, and coordinated cell movement, so its failure yields truncated or kinked tails, fused or malformed vertebrae and the caudal defects seen in human segmentation disorders. Much of the activity here is Wnt-based: WNT3A and WNT5A drive progenitor expansion and posterior growth, AXIN1 and SFRP2 restrain the pathway, SP5 acts as a transcriptional output, and FZD3, VANGL2 and PRICKLE1 provide planar cell polarity signals that give tissues directional elongation. A segmentation clock component and the somite boundary regulators HES7, RIPPLY2 and TCF15 time and delimit each new segment, while SCRIB and DCHS1 contribute apicobasal polarity and adhesion to the growing tissue.

Psychomotor behavior refers to actions that yoke cognition to movement erentially — coordinated, goal-directed performance such as driving, throwing, or playing an instrument — and the genes grouped here shape the neural excitability and signalling on which that coupling depends. They act mainly in the brain: a GABA-A receptor subunit mediates fast inhibitory neurotransmission and is implicated in developmental and epileptic disorders of the chromosome 15 region, while a voltage-gated potassium channel subunit sets the M-current that dampens repetitive neuronal firing, with loss of function causing seizures and developmental delay. Gastrin-releasing peptide and its receptor act as a neuropeptide pair influencing arousal, fear memory and locomotor responses, and dipeptidyl peptidase 4 can terminate such peptide signals by cleavage. Disruption of these components tends to appear clinically as altered activity level, impaired motor learning, or intellectual disability with abnormal movement.

Platelet morphogenesis is the process by which megakaryocytes build and release anucleate platelets, the cell fragments that seal vascular injury and initiate coagulation. Its failure produces thrombocytopenia and bleeding disorders, or conversely platelets of abnormal size and granule content, as in gray platelet syndrome caused by loss of NBEAL2. The pathway couples transcriptional specification of the megakaryocyte lineage — GATA1 with its cofactor ZFPM1, TAL1, MEF2C, SRF and the acetyltransferase EP300 — to thrombopoietin receptor signalling through MPL and the phosphatases PTPN11, PTPN6 and PTPRJ that set its gain. Execution depends on cytoskeletal remodelling: the β1-tubulin marginal band, non-muscle myosin MYH9, actinin, tropomyosin and WDR1 drive proplatelet extension and fragmentation, while granule biogenesis and apoptotic caspases contribute to final platelet maturation and shedding into the marrow sinusoids.

Platelets are anucleate fragments shed from megakaryocytes, and platelet morphogenesis covers the steps by which those giant marrow cells build and release them: cytoskeletal remodelling, proplatelet extension, granule loading, and final sizing of the circulating disc. Without it, bleeding follows from too few or structurally abnormal platelets, as in the macrothrombocytopenias caused by mutations in the actin-binding protein ACTN1, the nonmuscle myosin MYH9, or the platelet-specific tubulin TUBB1, and in the granule-deficient gray platelet syndrome caused by loss of NBEAL2. Thrombopoietin acting through its receptor MPL drives megakaryocyte expansion, with the transcription factors GATA1, TAL1, ZFPM1, MEF2C and SRF specifying the lineage and its cytoskeletal gene programme, while PTPN11, PTPN6 and PTPRJ tune the phosphotyrosine signalling that sets output. Caspase activity and membrane receptors such as CLEC1B and MPIG6B contribute to terminal platelet formation and marrow niche behaviour.

Sodium ion export across plasma membrane is the pumping of sodium out of the cell that sets up the electrochemical gradient nearly all other transport depends on. Because the sodium gradient powers secondary transport of glucose, amino acids, calcium and protons, and because it underlies the resting potential and the recovery of excitable cells after an action potential, its loss halts nerve conduction, cardiac rhythm and epithelial fluid handling. The core machinery is the Na+/K+-ATPase, built from catalytic alpha subunits with tissue-specific distribution in neurons, muscle and kidney, obligatory beta subunits, and FXYD proteins that tune pump kinetics locally. Related P-type pumps handle gastric acid secretion, while sodium-calcium and sodium-proton exchangers and a bicarbonate cotransporter couple sodium movement to calcium extrusion and pH control. Digitalis glycosides act here, and natriuretic peptide signalling regulates the same sodium balance systemically.

Pumping sodium out of the cell is what keeps the plasma membrane electrochemical gradient charged, and almost every secondary transport event — glucose and amino acid uptake, calcium and proton extrusion, neurotransmitter reuptake — runs on that gradient. Sodium ion export across the plasma membrane is dominated here by the Na+/K+-ATPase, built from catalytic alpha subunits (ATP1A1-ATP1A4, plus the related gastric and non-gastric proton pumps ATP4A and ATP12A) with obligatory beta subunits and a family of small FXYD regulators that tune pump kinetics in a tissue-specific way. Exchangers contribute too: SLC9A1 trades extracellular sodium for protons, while SLC8A1 uses the inward sodium gradient to expel calcium from cardiomyocytes. The alpha isoforms underlie neuronal and muscle excitability, and their mutation causes familial hemiplegic migraine, alternating hemiplegia and rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism; renal handling of sodium here also sets extracellular volume and blood pressure, with atrial natriuretic peptide as an endocrine input.

Vitamin D reaches the body as cholecalciferol, which has little hormonal activity until two hydroxylations convert it to calcitriol, the ligand that drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation and mineral homeostasis. The first step occurs in the liver, where 25-hydroxylases including CYP2R1 and CYP27A1, with a contribution from the broad-specificity CYP3A4, produce circulating calcidiol. The kidney then performs the rate-limiting 1-alpha-hydroxylation through CYP27B1, a step tuned by parathyroid hormone, phosphate and FGF23. CYP24A1 opposes the pathway by 24-hydroxylating both calcidiol and calcitriol toward inactivation, so it sets hormone duration. Loss of the renal hydroxylase causes vitamin D-dependent rickets, while loss of the catabolic enzyme produces infantile hypercalcaemia, placing this microsomal and mitochondrial cytochrome P450 chemistry at the centre of endocrine calcium control.
