The eye lens must stay clear and highly refractive for light to be focused sharply on the retina, and maintenance of lens transparency is the homeostatic upkeep that keeps it that way over a lifetime. Lens fibre cells are long-lived, have shed their nuclei and organelles, and depend on tightly ordered packing, controlled water and ion content, and protection of crystallins from oxidative and osmotic damage; when this fails, light scatters and cataract results. Contributors here span several of those requirements: MIP is the fibre-cell aquaporin that governs water permeability and cell-to-cell adhesion, CHMP4B acts in membrane remodelling through ESCRT-III, FOXC1 is a transcription factor of anterior segment development, and ALDH1A1 defends against reactive aldehydes. Mutations in these genes produce congenital or juvenile cataract and related anterior eye malformations.

Mitochondria take up calcium from the cytosol so that matrix Ca2+ can tune the pace of oxidative metabolism, and this import route links cytosolic signalling to ATP supply. Ca2+ crosses the outer membrane through VDAC1 at contacts with the endoplasmic reticulum, where ITPR1 releases store calcium in high local pulses, then passes the inner membrane through the uniporter: MCU as the pore, SMDT1 as an obligatory partner, MICU1, MICU2 and MICU3 setting the threshold so uptake begins only above a resting concentration, with MCUB and MCUR1 shaping conductance and assembly. Matrix proteases and chaperones including AFG3L2, SPG7 and HSPA9 control maturation and turnover of the machinery. Matrix calcium stimulates dehydrogenases of the TCA cycle; excessive loading opens the permeability transition pore and drives cell death, which is why this transport step matters in ischaemia, neurodegeneration and muscle disease.

Myofibroblast differentiation converts fibroblasts, pericytes and other undifferentiated mesenchymal cells into contractile, matrix-secreting cells that close wounds and remodel injured tissue. It is the cellular basis of scar formation, and when it persists rather than resolving it drives fibrosis of lung, liver, kidney and heart, as well as the stiff stroma that supports tumour growth. TGF-beta1 signalling through its type I receptor is the principal inducer, feeding into transcriptional effectors such as FOSL2 and the EMT-associated repressor ZEB2 to switch on smooth muscle actin and contractile machinery. A layer of microRNAs, including miR-145 and miR-21, sets the threshold for this conversion by tuning translational repressors such as PDCD4, while RB1, PARP1 and TP53INP1 couple the transition to proliferative and stress-response control. The balance between activation and reversal determines whether repair ends in restored tissue or permanent fibrotic remodelling.

TRAIL-activated apoptotic signalling is one branch of extrinsic, receptor-initiated cell death: the ligand TNFSF10 engages the death receptors TNFRSF10A and TNFRSF10B on the cell surface, which recruit the adaptor FADD and the initiator protease caspase-8 into a death-inducing complex that cleaves downstream caspases and commits the cell to apoptosis. Immune effector cells use this route to kill virally infected and transformed targets, and because many tumour cells are selectively sensitive to it while normal cells are not, the receptors are long-standing drug targets. Sensitivity is tuned rather than fixed: the decoy receptor TNFRSF10C binds ligand without signalling, palmitoylation and receptor trafficking affect clustering, stress-responsive transcription factors such as ATF3 and lineage factors such as SPI1 alter component levels, and microRNAs of the miR-221/222 pair further set the apoptotic threshold. Resistance at these steps contributes to tumour survival.

Synaptic vesicle recycling is how a presynaptic terminal reuses its vesicles: after fusion and neurotransmitter release, membrane and vesicle proteins are retrieved and reformed into release-competent vesicles. Because a bouton holds only a small vesicle pool, this retrieval sets how long a synapse can fire without fatiguing, and its failure underlies epilepsies, movement disorders and parkinsonism linked to synuclein, LRRK2, parkin, synaptojanin and auxilin. Mechanistically the genes trace clathrin-mediated endocytosis and its alternatives: AP-2 and AP-3 adaptors and cargo-specific stonins select synaptotagmin and VAMP2, BAR-domain proteins such as amphiphysin, endophilin and BIN1 bend the membrane, dynamins sever the neck, and phosphoinositide phosphatases plus Hsc70 co-chaperones uncoat the product. Actin, Rho-family GTPases and calcium-calmodulin/calcineurin signalling couple retrieval rate to activity, while Rab GTPases and SNAREs return vesicles to docking and priming.

Fast, sustained neurotransmission depends on presynaptic terminals rebuilding their vesicle supply locally, and synaptic vesicle recycling is how a fused vesicle is retrieved, refilled and returned to the releasable pool. Without it, terminals fatigue during repetitive firing and the presynaptic membrane cannot maintain its area or composition. After exocytosis, clathrin and its adaptor complexes with accessory proteins such as amphiphysin, endophilin, stonins and SGIP1 select vesicle cargo including synaptotagmin and VAMP2; dynamins sever the neck, and synaptojanin phosphoinositide phosphatases together with the uncoating chaperone auxilin strip the coat so vesicles can be re-acidified, reloaded by transporters, and docked via Rab3 and syntaxin-dependent priming. Actin and Rho-family GTPase regulators shape the endocytic membrane. Several members, notably LRRK2, synuclein, parkin, DNAJC6 and DJ-1, are Parkinson disease genes, linking failure of this cycle to dopaminergic neurodegeneration, while other mutations cause epileptic encephalopathies.

Synaptic vesicle recycling via endosome is the slower arm of vesicle reuse at the presynaptic terminal, in which membrane retrieved by clathrin-coated endocytosis is routed through an endosomal compartment before being reformed into vesicles that re-acidify and reload with neurotransmitter. This route sustains transmission during prolonged or high-frequency firing, when the local vesicle pool would otherwise be exhausted, and it also serves as a sorting station that keeps vesicle proteins and lipids correctly composed. The genes point to the machinery involved: intersectins couple endocytic coat assembly to actin and small GTPase signalling, an AP-3 adaptor subunit directs cargo sorting from endosomes into newly budded vesicles, RAB7A marks late endosomal identity and maturation, and a GRIP-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factor links the pathway to receptor trafficking. Defects impair synaptic endurance and neurotransmitter release fidelity.

Sustained neurotransmission depends on the local reuse of synaptic vesicle membrane, and one route to regeneration passes through an endosomal intermediate rather than returning directly to the releasable pool. After clathrin-mediated retrieval at the periactive zone, vesicle membrane fuses with a sorting endosome, where cargo composition is corrected before budding, re-acidification and refilling with neurotransmitter. Adaptor and small GTPase machinery gives the route its identity: an AP-3 subunit selects cargo for budding from endosomes, Rab7 marks the late endosomal compartment, intersectins couple endocytic sites to actin and GTPase regulators, and a GRIP-associated guanine nucleotide exchange factor links receptor and vesicle traffic to endosomal recycling. This slower pathway maintains vesicle protein quality and pool size during prolonged activity; its disruption is associated with impaired transmitter loading, presynaptic depression and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Neurons are long-lived, metabolically demanding and largely irreplaceable, so the decision to die when reactive oxygen species overwhelm antioxidant defences is tightly controlled; this intrinsic apoptotic route converts oxidative damage into commitment to the execution phase of neuronal death. Its failure at either extreme matters: excessive signalling contributes to neurodegeneration after ischaemia and in Parkinson and Alzheimer disease, while blunted clearance leaves damaged cells behind. Redox-sensitive kinase signalling through MAP3K5 and the adaptor DAXX, integrated stress responses via ATF4, and hypoxia sensing by HIF1A push toward death, while survival input from AKT1, WNT/frizzled and β-catenin, the anti-apoptotic MCL1, and the mitochondrial quality-control proteins PINK1, PRKN and PARK7 oppose it. PARP1 overactivation after oxidative DNA damage links genome injury to energetic collapse, tying this pathway to mitochondrial health, proline metabolism and microglial support.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a signalling molecule and a toxin, and when it accumulates beyond what a cell's antioxidant systems can handle, mitochondria commit that cell to death. This intrinsic apoptotic route converts peroxide-driven oxidative stress into mitochondrial permeabilization and caspase activation, setting the threshold at which redox damage becomes irreversible — a decision that matters in ischemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration and the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons. Several members restrain it: PARK7/DJ-1 and PINK1 protect mitochondria against oxidative insult, and the chaperone TRAP1 and the kinase AKT1 promote survival, while stress-activated kinase signalling through MAP2K4 pushes in the opposite direction. Scaffolding and adaptor proteins such as RACK1 and PDCD10 tune which outcome prevails, and microRNA-mediated control adds a further layer of regulation over the apoptotic response to peroxide.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells reduce the load on the folding machinery by throttling protein synthesis, and this translational arm of the unfolded protein response is what makes that possible. PERK, the ER-resident kinase, phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2, blocking the guanine nucleotide exchange needed for new initiation and so damping global translation while permitting selective synthesis of stress-response factors. The brake is transient: GADD34 (PPP1R15A) recruits protein phosphatase 1 to reverse the modification, and an ER co-chaperone together with NCK adaptors further tune kinase output, so cells resume synthesis once folding capacity recovers. Sustained signalling instead drives apoptosis. This control links secretory pathway homeostasis to cell survival decisions in secretory tissues, and its failure contributes to beta cell loss in diabetes and to neurodegenerative disease.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the usual response is to shut protein synthesis down; this pathway covers the opposite arm, in which translation is sustained or restored while the stress persists so that chaperones and recovery factors can still be made. Keeping selective translation running lets a stressed cell adapt rather than commit to apoptosis, and the balance between suppression and restoration decides whether secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells and plasma cells survive a heavy folding load. The genes involved act on the initiation machinery and its regulation: a scaffolding initiation factor for cap-dependent ribosome recruitment, an RNA helicase that promotes initiation on structured messages, adaptors that limit stress-induced inhibition of initiation, and an ER-resident co-chaperone that restrains the kinase arm responsible for translational shutdown.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the transmembrane sensor IRE1 oligomerizes and switches on the most ancient arm of the unfolded protein response, deciding whether a stressed cell expands its folding capacity or dies. IRE1's kinase activity triggers an unconventional splicing reaction on XBP1 mRNA, excising an intron that is then ligated by RTCB so that the resulting transcription factor can drive chaperones, ERAD components and lipid synthesis genes needed to enlarge the secretory pathway. The chaperone BiP and regulators such as TMBIM6, PTPN1 and the AMPylase FICD tune sensor activation, while sustained signalling engages JNK and the apoptotic machinery represented here by BAX, BAK1, PUMA and BIM. This output supports professional secretory cells such as plasma cells and pancreatic beta cells, and its dysregulation contributes to diabetes, neurodegeneration and tumour survival under stress.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the PERK branch of the unfolded protein response buys the cell time by shutting down most new protein synthesis. The kinase EIF2AK3 (PERK), held in check by the ER chaperone BiP/HSPA5, oligomerizes and phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2alpha (EIF2S1), which blocks general initiation while favouring translation of ATF4. ATF4 then drives a transcriptional programme covering amino acid supply, redox defence alongside NFE2L2, chaperone capacity, and — through CHOP/DDIT3 — genes that commit an irreparably stressed cell to apoptosis. Recovery depends on the GADD34-type phosphatase regulators PPP1R15A and PPP1R15B, which dephosphorylate eIF2alpha and restore translation. This decision between adaptation and death matters in secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells, where loss of PERK causes diabetes and skeletal dysplasia, and in neurodegeneration and tumour survival under hypoxia.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, one of the three arms of the unfolded protein response is launched by the ER membrane sensor ATF6, which restores folding capacity by expanding the chaperone and quality-control machinery. This branch keeps secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells, plasma cells and hepatocytes able to sustain heavy protein loads; its failure contributes to beta cell loss and, through WFS1, to the diabetes and neurodegeneration of Wolfram syndrome. On stress, ATF6 leaves the ER for the Golgi, where the site-1 and site-2 proteases encoded by MBTPS1 and MBTPS2 cleave it sequentially to liberate a cytosolic transcription factor fragment. That fragment, together with XBP1, drives expression of BiP/HSPA5, the ER stress protein MANF and the stress-responsive factor DDIT3/CHOP, linking adaptive folding capacity to apoptotic decisions if stress persists.

ERAD pathway is the quality-control system that clears misfolded and surplus proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, sending them across the ER membrane to the cytosolic proteasome. It keeps the secretory pathway from shipping defective glycoproteins and prevents accumulation of aggregation-prone material, and its overload triggers the unfolded protein response through ATF6 and XBP1; loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration, diabetes-like syndromes and immune dysfunction. Substrates are recognised by lectins and mannosidases such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the EDEM proteins that read trimmed N-glycans as a folding-failure signal, then delivered to membrane ubiquitin ligase complexes built around SYVN1-SEL1L, AMFR, MARCHF6 or RNF185. Derlins and the retrotranslocation channel pass the chain outward, and the VCP-UFD1-NPLOC4 ATPase, with UBX adaptors, deubiquitinases and ubiquilin shuttles, extracts and hands it off for degradation. The same machinery also regulates sterol metabolism and ER membrane protein abundance.

Proteins that fail to fold correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum are not simply retained there; ER-associated degradation recognises them, extracts them, and feeds them to the cytosolic proteasome. This quality-control route keeps the secretory pathway from shipping defective cargo and relieves ER stress, and its failure underlies conditions from alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency to neurodegeneration, while several viruses and toxins exploit it. Lectins and mannosidases such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the EDEM proteins read trimmed N-glycans as a signal that folding attempts have failed, with chaperones including BiP, calnexin and calreticulin upstream. Membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases -- SYVN1 with SEL1L, AMFR, MARCHF6, RNF5 and relatives -- together with E2 enzymes ubiquitinate substrates at the membrane, and the VCP/p97 ATPase with UFD1, NPLOC4 and UBX cofactors pulls them into the cytosol, where deubiquitinases tune the outcome. Transcriptional arms via XBP1 and ATF6 expand the machinery when demand rises.

Trimming mannose residues from N-linked glycans is how the endoplasmic reticulum times protein quality control: the glycan acts as a clock, and each mannose removed moves a glycoprotein further from the folding cycle and closer to disposal. Protein demannosylation therefore sets the deadline for folding, and its failure allows misfolded secretory and membrane proteins to linger or be degraded prematurely, with consequences for secretion capacity and ER stress. Class I mannosidases and the EDEM family generate the trimmed signal, while the UGGT glucosyltransferases oppose them by re-glucosylating incompletely folded substrates to give them another pass through the lectin chaperone cycle. Terminally marked substrates are handed to ER-associated degradation, where membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases such as SYVN1, RNF5, MARCHF6 and AMFR ubiquitinate them for retrotranslocation and proteasomal destruction, linking glycan editing directly to protein turnover.

Dopaminergic neuron axon guidance is the steering of growth cones from midbrain dopamine neurons toward their forebrain targets, the step that builds the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic projections underlying movement control, motivation and reward. If these axons fail to reach the striatum or misroute along the way, the circuitry for motor initiation and reinforcement learning is never properly wired, a defect relevant to both parkinsonian motor phenotypes and neurodevelopmental disorders of reward processing. Guidance here is dominated by Wnt cues read through non-canonical, planar cell polarity-type machinery: WNT5A and WNT7B act as attractive and repulsive gradients along the anterior-posterior axis, sensed by the Frizzled receptor FZD3 and the atypical receptor tyrosine kinase RYK, with CELSR3 and VANGL2 organising polarity within the growth cone. The output is directional cytoskeletal remodelling rather than transcription, linking this pathway to axon tract formation generally.

Midbrain dopaminergic neurons must send axons along stereotyped routes to the striatum and prefrontal cortex, and dopaminergic neuron axon guidance is the steering process that gets them there. The accuracy of this wiring sets the anatomy of the nigrostriatal and mesolimbic systems that control voluntary movement, motivation and reward; mistargeting leaves dopamine release in the wrong place and is a plausible developmental contributor to motor and psychiatric dysfunction. The cues here are Wnt ligands acting through non-canonical, planar-cell-polarity-type receiving machinery: a Frizzled receptor together with the atypical cadherin CELSR3, the core polarity protein VANGL2, and the atypical tyrosine kinase receptor RYK, which reads Wnt gradients as attractive or repulsive instructions at the growth cone. Signalling converges on cytoskeletal remodelling and oriented outgrowth, linking this pathway to the broader use of polarity proteins in axon tract formation.

Serotonergic neurons of the raphe nuclei send axons the length of the neuraxis, and the steering of their growth cones toward forebrain and spinal targets is what establishes the diffuse serotonin supply that modulates mood, sleep, appetite and pain. The guidance decisions here are dominated by planar cell polarity signalling: a Wnt ligand acts as a directional cue, Frizzled and Vangl transduce it across the growth cone membrane, and the atypical cadherin CELSR3 works with Frizzled3 to route ascending and descending tracts through the correct longitudinal pathways. A clustered protocadherin contributes the surface recognition that lets serotonergic axons tile their terminal fields rather than clump. Loss of these components misroutes major serotonergic and other long axon tracts during embryonic brain wiring, linking the pathway to circuit formation underlying affective and autonomic regulation.</description

Paracrine signalling is short-range cell-to-cell communication in which a secreted factor diffuses through interstitial fluid to receptors on neighbouring cells, coordinating the behaviour of tissue neighbourhoods rather than distant organs. It underlies wound repair, angiogenesis, inflammation and the stromal support of stem cell niches, and its distortion drives fibrosis, chronic inflammatory disease and tumour-promoting microenvironments. The genes here illustrate the principle: FGF2 and PDGFB act on nearby endothelium, fibroblasts and pericytes to drive proliferation and vessel maturation; IL6 signals through IL6R together with the shared receptor subunit IL6ST to trigger JAK-STAT responses in adjacent cells; and RANKL (TNFSF11), produced by osteoblastic and stromal cells under hormonal control that includes progesterone receptor signalling, instructs local osteoclast differentiation. Cytosolic DNA sensing by CGAS links cell-intrinsic damage to secreted signals that alert the surrounding tissue.

Opioid peptides such as the enkephalin precursor PENK act on cell-surface receptors to damp neuronal excitability, and this G protein-coupled opioid receptor signalling is the route by which analgesia, reward, mood and gut motility are modulated. The mu, delta, kappa and nociceptin receptors (OPRM1, OPRD1, OPRK1, OPRL1) couple through inhibitory G proteins to lower adenylate cyclase output, here represented by ADCY8, and to reduce neurotransmitter release at presynaptic terminals, with synaptophysin marking that vesicular compartment. Related peptide receptors for neuropeptides B and W sit alongside them, and SIGMAR1 and scaffolding through PPP1R9B tune downstream responses. Because the same receptors mediate both pain relief and respiratory depression, tolerance and dependence, this pathway defines the pharmacology of clinical opioids; its dysregulation underlies addiction, and receptor variants shift individual sensitivity to both endogenous and administered ligands.

Netrin-activated signalling tells a growing axon or migrating cell which way to go. Netrins are secreted guidance cues that attract some growth cones and repel others, and the response depends on which receptor is displayed: DCC-family receptors such as DSCAM support attraction, while the UNC5 receptors (UNC5A-D) mediate repulsion and turning away from the netrin source. Engagement is transduced to the cytoskeleton through focal adhesion kinase and the actin-polymerisation regulator shootin1, with tubulin remodelling in the growth cone converting a chemical gradient into directed movement. The same receptors also govern cell survival: unliganded UNC5 and DCC receptors trigger apoptosis, making netrin availability a check on which neurons and vascular cells persist. Beyond wiring the commissures and other axon tracts of the developing nervous system, this signalling shapes blood vessel branching and is co-opted in tumour growth and metastasis.

Reelin-mediated signalling tells migrating neurons where to stop, and it is what gives the cerebral cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum their layered architecture. Reelin is secreted by Cajal-Retzius cells and other early neurons and binds the lipoprotein receptors VLDLR and ApoER2 (LRP8), which cluster and recruit the intracellular adaptor DAB1. Src-family kinases such as FYN phosphorylate DAB1, creating docking sites for CRK and CRKL that feed into small GTPase and cytoskeletal control; the same phosphorylation marks DAB1 for a cullin-5 based ubiquitin ligase, giving the pathway built-in negative feedback. Downstream effects reach microtubule regulators including LIS1 (PAFAH1B1) and influence dendrite growth and synaptic plasticity in the mature brain. Loss of reelin or of DAB1 produces inverted cortical layers and cerebellar hypoplasia, and human mutations cause lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia; reduced reelin has also been linked to psychiatric disease.</description>}</parameter>|</invoke>ma</function_calls> Wait — output must be JSON only.</thinking>{

Apolipoprotein A-I is the main protein of HDL, and its engagement of cell-surface receptors does more than accept cholesterol: it initiates signalling that feeds back on lipid efflux, cytoskeletal organisation and gene expression. The signalling matters because it tunes reverse cholesterol transport, the route by which peripheral cells and macrophages unload excess cholesterol to the liver, and because its failure underlies foam cell formation and atherosclerosis. The lipid transporters ABCA1 and ABCA7 both bind apoA-I and mediate phospholipid and cholesterol transfer, with ABCA1 the principal exporter whose loss causes Tangier disease. An integrin pair, ITGAV and ITGB3, provides a receptor route into intracellular signalling, and RHOA links the response to actin remodelling and membrane dynamics. Regulation runs the other way too, with a microRNA encoded within a sterol-responsive locus restraining ABCA1 levels and so the capacity for efflux.

Cells that depend on trophic support die when that support is withdrawn, and this pathway covers the signalling that begins precisely when a receptor is unoccupied. Dependence receptors such as UNC5B and RET switch from promoting survival when bound by netrin or GDNF to actively triggering death when ligand is absent, a mechanism that prunes neurons lacking target-derived neurotrophin and restrains tumour cells that stray from their supportive niche. Growth factor and cytokine inputs (NGF, IGF1, IL7, FGF10) normally sustain AKT signalling, which keeps FOXO3 and BAD inactive; loss of that input flips the balance toward BAX, BAK1 and BCL2L11 over MCL1, BCL2 and BCL2L1, permeabilising mitochondria and engaging caspases. Adaptors including FADD and RIPK1 link the same logic to receptor-driven death. The outcome is apoptosis as a default state that survival signalling continuously suppresses.

Interleukin-5 is the cytokine that governs eosinophils, and signalling through its receptor drives their development in the marrow, their release into blood, their survival in tissue and their activation at sites of allergic inflammation; it also supports B cell responses in some settings. Because of this, the pathway is the target of anti-IL5 and anti-receptor antibodies used to control severe eosinophilic asthma and related hypereosinophilic disease. The cytokine engages a specific alpha chain, IL5RA, which pairs with the shared beta subunit CSF2RB also used by GM-CSF and IL-3 receptors. Neither chain has catalytic activity, so receptor assembly instead brings in associated tyrosine kinases — JAK1, JAK2, TYK2 and the Src-family kinase LYN — whose phosphorylation of STAT5A produces a transcription factor that enters the nucleus and switches on survival and lineage genes, tying receptor occupancy directly to eosinophil gene expression.

Nitric oxide made by one cell diffuses into a neighbour and is read there as a second messenger, and this cassette is how that message is converted into a cellular response — most visibly relaxation of vascular smooth muscle, but also platelet restraint, neuronal signalling and insulin-related metabolic tone. NO binds the haem of soluble guanylyl cyclase, assembled from alpha and beta subunits such as GUCY1A1 and GUCY1B1, which raises cGMP; cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG1 then phosphorylates targets that lower calcium, including the plasma membrane calcium pump ATP2B4, alongside effects on potassium channels. Inputs come from receptors that stimulate or oppose NO production, among them the VEGF receptor KDR and angiotensin signalling, while thrombospondin-1 acting through CD36 suppresses the pathway. Loss of this axis produces endothelial dysfunction, hypertension and impaired tissue perfusion.

Non-canonical NF-kappaB signalling is the slower, second route to NF-kappaB activation, and it is what lets lymphoid tissue organise itself: germinal centres, lymph node and Peyer's patch development, B cell survival, osteoclast formation and skin appendage patterning all depend on it. Ligands of the TNF receptor superfamily — lymphotoxin acting through LTBR, BAFF, CD40, RANKL via TNFRSF11A, TNFSF14 and ectodysplasin through EDAR — stabilise the kinase NIK (MAP3K14), which otherwise is continuously degraded by a TRAF-BIRC2/BIRC3 ubiquitin ligase complex. NIK phosphorylates IKKalpha (CHUK), which marks the NFKB2 p100 precursor for partial proteasomal processing, releasing p52 to enter the nucleus with RELB and drive transcription of chemokines such as CCL19 and costimulatory molecules. Deubiquitinases including CYLD, phosphatases and numerous TRIM and microRNA regulators tune the output; loss causes immunodeficiency and anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, while constitutive NIK activity underlies multiple myeloma and lymphoma.

collagen-activated tyrosine kinase receptor signaling pathway is how cells read the collagen scaffold around them as an instruction rather than a passive support, using receptor tyrosine kinases that are switched on by triple-helical collagen itself. It sets epithelial adhesion and basement membrane responsiveness, controls cell migration and matrix remodelling in fibrosis and tumour invasion, and in platelets converts exposed subendothelial collagen at a vascular injury into aggregation and thrombus formation. The discoidin domain receptors DDR1 and DDR2 bind fibrillar and network collagens, including the type IV collagens of the basement membrane, and autophosphorylate slowly and persistently to reshape transcription and protease output. The platelet arm works through GP6 with the tetraspanin TSPAN9 and the kinase SYK, whose signalling is damped by the phosphatase UBASH3B. Loss or mutation of these receptors causes bleeding disorders, skeletal and renal defects, and altered fibrotic responses.

Cells read the collagen in their surroundings partly through receptor tyrosine kinases, and this collagen-activated signalling converts that contact into changes in adhesion, migration, matrix remodelling and gene expression. The discoidin domain receptors DDR1 and DDR2 bind triple-helical collagens, including fibrillar type I and the basement membrane type IV chains, and autophosphorylate slowly to control epithelial adhesion, branching morphogenesis, cartilage and bone growth, and fibrotic and invasive responses in tumours; DDR1 loss disrupts kidney and mammary development, and DDR2 mutation causes a short-limbed skeletal dysplasia. A parallel arm operates in platelets, where the immune-type collagen receptor GP6 signals through the tyrosine kinase SYK to trigger activation and aggregation at sites of vessel injury, with TSPAN9 supporting receptor function and UBASH3B acting as a phosphatase that restrains the response. Together these routes link extracellular matrix composition to cytoskeletal and transcriptional output.

Collagen is not only a structural scaffold but a ligand that cells read directly, and collagen-activated signalling is how contact with the matrix is converted into changes in adhesion, migration, proliferation and gene expression. It matters for tissue remodelling and wound repair, for platelet responses at sites of vascular injury, and for osteoclast biology; persistent signalling of this kind accompanies fibrosis and tumour invasion. Fibrillar and basement-membrane collagens engage several receptor classes: the discoidin domain receptors DDR1 and DDR2 are receptor tyrosine kinases whose unusually slow activation follows collagen binding, the integrins ITGA2 and ITGA11 pair with beta1 for adhesive and mechanical coupling, and the immunoreceptor-like GP6 on platelets signals through SYK with JAK2 and the phosphatase UBASH3B tuning the output. OSCAR provides a parallel collagen-sensing route in the osteoclast lineage. Loss-of-function in the collagen IV chains themselves underlies basement-membrane disease.

Stress-activated signalling through the p38MAPK cascade lets cells respond to osmotic shock, oxidative and genotoxic stress, inflammatory cytokines and growth factors by altering transcription, mRNA stability and cell fate. It underlies innate immune and inflammatory output, senescence and stress-induced apoptosis, and its sustained activation drives chronic inflammatory disease, making p38 a long-standing anti-inflammatory drug target. Signal flows in tiers: MAP3Ks such as MAP3K5 (ASK1), MAP3K7 and MAP3K4, often engaged by GADD45 proteins, phosphorylate the dedicated kinases MAP2K3 and MAP2K6, which in turn activate p38alpha (MAPK14) and p38beta (MAPK11). Substrates include the transcription factor ATF2 and MAPKAPK2, whose downstream targets ZFP36 and ZC3H12A control decay of cytokine transcripts such as IL1B. DUSP1 and DUSP10 phosphatases and PHLPP1 restrain the cascade, and the pathway also feeds autophagy regulators including BECN1 and ULK-family components.

Receptor tyrosine kinases report the presence of a ligand by phosphorylating tyrosines on themselves, and peptidyl-tyrosine autophosphorylation is that self-modification step. It matters because the newly added phosphotyrosines both switch the kinase into a fully active conformation and create docking sites that recruit adaptors and downstream effectors, converting an extracellular cue into growth, survival, differentiation or migration. The kinases here span several families — the insulin-like growth factor receptor, the platelet-derived growth factor receptor, the neurotrophin receptor NTRK1, the collagen-binding receptor DDR1, and the anaplastic lymphoma kinase and its relative LTK — together with cytoplasmic kinases such as PTK2B and SRMS and ligands including neuregulin and a PDGF chain. Because autophosphorylation is the gate on activity, mutations, fusions or ligand excess that trigger it without ligand drive constitutive signalling in cancer, which is why these receptors are heavily targeted by kinase inhibitors.

vascular endothelial growth factor signaling pathway is the growth factor circuit that tells endothelial cells to sprout, migrate, survive and form new blood and lymphatic vessels. It drives developmental angiogenesis, wound healing and tissue responses to hypoxia, and its overactivation feeds tumour vascularisation and retinal neovascularisation, which is why VEGF and its receptors are among the most heavily drugged targets in oncology and ophthalmology. Secreted ligands VEGFA, VEGFB, PGF and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC/VEGFD, the latter activated by proteolytic processing involving ADAMTS3 and CCBE1, engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 together with neuropilin co-receptors and integrins, recruiting GAB1 and PI3K catalytic subunits to control motility and permeability. Transcriptional partners such as FOXC1, PROX1 and NR2F2 set arterial versus lymphatic identity, while decoy receptors, SPRY2, DAB2IP and several microRNAs restrain the output.

Endothelial cells decide whether to sprout, migrate and form new vessels largely on the basis of vascular endothelial growth factor signaling, which drives angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour growth, and lymphangiogenesis in the lymphatic bed. Ligands of the VEGF family, including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphatic ligands VEGFC and VEGFD, engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 together with the neuropilin co-receptors NRP1 and NRP2, activating PI3K catalytic subunits and adaptors such as GAB1 to change endothelial survival, permeability, cytoskeletal behaviour and transcription. Extracellular processing matters too: ADAMTS3 and CCBE1 mature VEGFC before it can act, while decorin, gremlin and integrins tune signalling from the matrix. Downstream, PROX1, FOXC1 and NR2F2 specify lymphatic identity. Excess signalling underlies tumour vascularisation and retinal neovascular disease, making these receptors the targets of anti-angiogenic therapy; loss causes lymphoedema and vascular malformation.

Nodal is a TGF-beta family ligand that patterns the early embryo, and the signalling route it triggers sets the body's axes: it induces mesoderm and endoderm, positions the primitive streak, and breaks left-right symmetry so that heart, gut and lungs acquire their normal asymmetric arrangement. Failure of this pathway underlies holoprosencephaly and laterality defects such as heterotaxy and transposition of the great vessels. Nodal binds type I receptors ACVR1B and ACVR1C together with EGF-CFC co-receptors of the Cripto/Cryptic family, driving phosphorylation of SMAD2 and SMAD3, which partner with the forkhead factor FOXH1 to activate target transcription. Output is tightly bounded: DAND5 and NOG antagonise ligand extracellularly, DACT1 and DACT2 restrain intracellular transduction, and TGIF1/TGIF2 repress SMAD-dependent transcription, while SHH input coordinates midline patterning alongside it.

Fc receptor signaling pathway is how immune cells read antibody that has already bound its target, converting immunoglobulin coating of a pathogen or immune complex into phagocytosis, degranulation, cytokine release and antibody-dependent cell killing. It is the effector arm that gives antibodies their power, underlies mast cell allergic responses through IgE receptors, and its inhibitory branch sets the threshold that prevents autoimmune tissue damage; therapeutic antibodies depend on it for activity. Receptor engagement clusters ITAM-bearing chains such as FCER1G and CD247, which are phosphorylated by Src-family kinases including LYN, FYN and HCK, recruiting SYK and BTK and assembling a signalosome with PLCG1/2, VAV guanine-nucleotide exchange factors and PI3K adaptors. Downstream output runs through protein kinase C isoforms, JNK-directed MAP kinase cascades and NF-kB activation, driving cytoskeletal remodelling for particle engulfment and transcription of inflammatory mediators. ITIM-containing receptors like FCGR2B and CD33 oppose this.

Antibodies do more than bind antigen: their constant regions are read by Fc receptors on myeloid, mast and lymphoid cells, converting humoral recognition into cellular action. This pathway couples immunoglobulin-loaded receptors to phagocytosis, antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, degranulation and inflammatory gene expression, and it is the basis of IgE-driven allergic responses as well as much of the efficacy of therapeutic antibodies. Receptor engagement clusters ITAM-bearing chains such as FCER1G and CD247, which are phosphorylated by Src-family kinases including LYN, FGR and HCK and recruit SYK; BTK, PLCG1/PLCG2, protein kinase C isoforms and VAV-family exchange factors then drive calcium flux, JNK cascade activation and cytoskeletal remodelling for particle internalisation. Inhibitory receptors, notably FCGR2B and CD33-family lectins, impose ITIM-based restraint, and loss of that balance contributes to autoantibody-mediated tissue damage and immune complex disease.

Antibody-coated targets are recognised by myeloid and lymphoid cells through Fc-gamma receptors, and the signalling that follows converts IgG binding into phagocytosis, degranulation, respiratory burst, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and cytokine production. This is how humoral immunity is translated into cellular effector action, and it underlies the clearance of opsonised microbes and the mechanism of many therapeutic antibodies; inappropriate engagement by immune complexes drives tissue damage in autoimmune disease. Activating receptors such as FCGR1A, FCGR2A and FCGR3A signal through ITAM-bearing chains including FCER1G and CD247, recruiting Src-family kinases (LYN, HCK, FGR, FYN, SRC) and SYK, which in turn engage VAV guanine nucleotide exchange factors, PAK1 and LIMK1 to remodel actin for particle engulfment, alongside phospholipase and protein kinase C arms. The inhibitory receptor FCGR2B sets the threshold, opposing activation and restraining B cell and myeloid responses.

Fc-epsilon receptor signaling pathway is the route by which IgE bound to mast cells and basophils triggers their activation, and it is the proximate cause of immediate hypersensitivity: allergic rhinitis, urticaria, asthma and anaphylaxis all begin here, while the same receptors mediate protective responses to parasites. Antigen crosslinking of IgE held on the high-affinity receptor clusters its alpha and gamma chains, whose ITAM motifs recruit the Src-family kinase LYN and then SYK. SYK activates BTK and phospholipase C-gamma to raise calcium and diacylglycerol, driving granule exocytosis of histamine and proteases, while VAV-family exchange factors, SOS1 and a MAP3K-MAP2K cascade feed JNK and NF-kappaB for transcription of cytokines and eicosanoid enzymes. The low-affinity receptor CD23 provides feedback control of IgE production, tying this signalling to the regulation of allergic sensitisation itself.

Mast cells and basophils sense antigen indirectly, through IgE already bound to their surface, and this is the signalling route that converts that recognition into an allergic response. Crosslinking of IgE-loaded high-affinity receptor complexes triggers degranulation, histamine and lipid mediator release, and cytokine transcription, producing the immediate hypersensitivity of asthma, urticaria, food allergy and anaphylaxis; the low-affinity IgE receptor instead tunes IgE production and antigen capture on B cells and other cells. Receptor subunits recruit the Src-family kinase LYN and the tyrosine kinase SYK, which engage BTK and phospholipase C-gamma isoforms to mobilise calcium and activate protein kinase C, while VAV family exchange factors and SOS1 feed into a JNK cascade through MAP3K and MAP2K tiers, and TRAF6 with IKK-beta drives NF-kappaB-dependent gene expression. Blocking receptor occupancy with anti-IgE antibody is an established treatment for severe allergic disease.

Interleukin-2 is the cytokine that turns an activated T cell into a proliferating clone and that sustains regulatory T cells, so signalling from its receptor sets the balance between immune expansion and tolerance. The receptor is built from a high-affinity alpha chain together with the beta chain and the shared common gamma chain; loss of the gamma chain or of JAK3 causes severe combined immunodeficiency, while defects in the alpha chain produce autoimmunity through failure of regulatory T cell support. Ligand binding juxtaposes the chains so that JAK1 and JAK3 phosphorylate each other and the receptor tails, recruiting STAT5A and STAT3 for dimerisation and nuclear entry, where they drive transcription of survival, cell cycle and lineage genes. PTPN2 dephosphorylates JAKs and STATs to damp the response, and ezrin links the receptor complex to the cortical actin cytoskeleton. The axis is the target of IL-2-based immunotherapy.

Interleukin-7 signalling is the survival and proliferation cue that lymphoid progenitors and naive T cells depend on, and it sets the size of the peripheral T cell pool. IL-7 binds a receptor made of its own alpha chain together with the shared gamma chain, bringing JAK1 and JAK3 into apposition so they phosphorylate the receptor and activate STAT5A and STAT1, which in turn drive transcription of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle genes and support rearrangement of antigen receptor loci. Loss of the receptor alpha chain, the gamma chain, or JAK3 causes severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T cells, while gain-of-function receptor mutations occur in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The same alpha chain pairs with a different partner to receive thymic stromal lymphopoietin, linking this module to epithelial-driven allergic inflammation as well as to lymphopoiesis.

Signalling through the ERBB family of receptor tyrosine kinases translates extracellular growth factor cues into decisions about proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation, and it governs epithelial development, wound repair and cardiac and neural morphogenesis. Ligands of the EGF and neuregulin families, several released from membrane precursors by ADAM17-mediated shedding, bind EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3 or ERBB4 and drive receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation. Adaptors such as GRB2, SHC1 and GAB1 with the phosphatase PTPN11 recruit SOS1 to activate RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK, while PIK3CA and AKT1 support survival and PLCG1 couples to lipid second messengers. Output is limited by CBL-family ubiquitin ligases and ESCRT-dependent receptor sorting into the endosomal system, by SPRY and ERRFI1 feedback inhibitors, and by multiple protein tyrosine phosphatases. Mutation or amplification of these receptors sustains growth signalling in lung, breast and colorectal cancers, making the pathway a major therapeutic target.

ERBB2 has no ligand of its own; it works by pairing with EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4 and amplifying the tyrosine kinase signal those receptors generate when they bind EGF-family growth factors such as EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin, HB-EGF or the neuregulins. The output drives proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation in epithelia, and also supports cardiac and neuromuscular development through neuregulin-ERBB pairs. Downstream, receptor autophosphorylation recruits SRC and feeds the RAF1-MEK1/2-ERK1/2 cascade to reprogramme transcription. Counterweights are built in: a receptor phosphatase dampens ERK, and the ubiquitin ligase machinery including CUL5 and the co-chaperone-associated CHIP directs receptor turnover. Because signal strength depends on dimer composition rather than ligand affinity, ERBB2 amplification converts normal growth-factor responsiveness into ligand-independent drive, the basis of HER2-positive breast and gastric cancer and of the therapies aimed at this receptor.

ERBB3 is the pseudokinase member of the EGF receptor family: it binds neuregulin ligands such as NRG1 but cannot phosphorylate on its own, so it must heterodimerise with a partner, typically ERBB2, to be transphosphorylated and transmit signal. Signalling through this receptor pair drives proliferation and survival programmes, and it matters physiologically for Schwann cell and peripheral nerve development, neuromuscular synapse formation and heart and mammary development, while its overactivation is a well-known route to breast and other epithelial cancers and a common escape mechanism from ERBB2-directed therapy. The phosphorylated tail recruits adaptors that feed the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade represented here by RAF1, MAP2K1/2 and the ERK kinases MAPK1 and MAPK3, ending in changes to transcription. Additional membrane and secreted partners, including reticulon RTN4 and myocilin, modulate receptor availability and output.

ERBB4 is a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by neuregulins and by EGF-family ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin and heparin-binding EGF, and the signalling it initiates shapes nervous system wiring, cardiac trabeculation and mammary gland differentiation. Ligand binding drives receptor dimerisation, either with itself or with ERBB2, and autophosphorylation that recruits adaptors to activate growth and survival routes; a distinctive feature is that certain ERBB4 isoforms are cleaved to release an intracellular fragment that travels to the nucleus and acts on transcription directly, so the output regulates gene expression as well as cytoplasmic kinase cascades. Neuregulin-to-ERBB4 communication supports Schwann cell myelination, interneuron migration and synapse formation, and variants in NRG1, NRG3 and the receptor have been linked to schizophrenia risk. The same axis, chiefly through ERBB2 partnership, is co-opted in breast cancer, where receptor levels influence proliferation and differentiation.

ERBB2-EGFR signaling pathway describes growth factor signalling through a mixed receptor pair, in which a ligand-bound EGFR partners with ERBB2 to drive epithelial proliferation, migration and survival. It matters because ERBB2 has no ligand of its own: it acquires signalling competence only by heterodimerising with an activated family member, and this partnership is the setting in which ERBB2 amplification becomes oncogenic in breast and gastric cancer. The upstream inputs are a family of related EGF-domain ligands — EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and HBEGF — several of which are made as membrane-anchored precursors and released by proteolytic shedding, so ligand availability is itself regulated. Dimer formation triggers tyrosine autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors feeding the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT routes, coupling extracellular cues to cell cycle entry, tissue repair and epithelial development.

Epidermal growth factor family ligands drive epithelial proliferation, wound repair and developmental morphogenesis, and this branch of that system routes the signal through a mixed receptor pair rather than EGFR alone. EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and heparin-binding EGF each engage EGFR with distinct affinity and duration; the activated receptor then partners with ERBB2, which binds no ligand of its own and depends on heterodimerisation to be switched on. The resulting complex is a more potent and less rapidly downregulated signalling unit than the EGFR homodimer, feeding into RAS-MAPK and PI3K outputs that control cell cycle entry, survival and migration. Because ERBB2 amplification supplies an excess of dimerisation partner, this receptor combination is a central driver in breast and gastric carcinoma and a direct target of antibody and kinase-inhibitor therapy, with ligand availability shaping the response.

Neuregulins and EGF-family ligands such as epiregulin and heparin-binding EGF act on ERBB4, and the activated receptor pairs with ERBB2 to transmit the signal inward. ERBB2 itself binds no known ligand, so this heterodimer is one of the routes by which it is switched on; signalling through ERBB2-ERBB4 supports cardiac trabeculation and ventricular development, Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte differentiation, neuromuscular junction formation, and mammary epithelial growth. Downstream of receptor tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation the output feeds the usual growth and survival machinery, while a cleaved ERBB4 intracellular fragment can act in the nucleus as a transcriptional partner. Loss of NRG1-ERBB signalling is embryonically lethal from heart and nerve defects, and excessive ERBB2 activity drives breast and gastric cancers, which makes this dimer pair both a developmental and an oncogenic axis.

Signalling through ERBB4 homodimers is one arm of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, activated when a neuregulin or an EGF-family ligand such as betacellulin or epiregulin binds two ERBB4 molecules and drives them together. Unlike its relatives, ERBB4 can signal both as a kinase at the membrane and, after cleavage, as a fragment that reaches the nucleus to influence transcription, so the output includes direct changes in gene expression alongside conventional growth and survival cascades. The receptor and its neuregulin ligands shape neural development, cardiac trabeculation and Schwann cell behaviour, and support differentiation of mammary epithelium and brown adipose tissue. Loss of ERBB4-neuregulin signalling is embryonically lethal through cardiac failure in mice, and variation in these genes has been linked to schizophrenia risk and to altered tumour behaviour in breast cancer, where ERBB4 output can oppose that of other family members.

Macrophage colony-stimulating factor signalling is the axis that tells myeloid progenitors to become and remain macrophages, and it sustains tissue-resident populations such as microglia, osteoclasts and Kupffer cells throughout life. Two ligands, CSF1 and the independently encoded IL34, bind the same receptor tyrosine kinase, CSF1R, whose dimerisation and autophosphorylation recruit adaptors and drive survival, proliferation, chemotaxis and differentiation programmes ending in transcriptional change. Output is tuned by negative regulators: the adaptor DOK1 dampens downstream kinase signalling and the phosphatase PTPN2 removes activating phosphotyrosines, while TREM2 cooperates with the receptor in microglial survival. Loss-of-function in the receptor or its ligands causes osteopetrosis and leukoencephalopathy, and excess signalling recruits tumour-associated macrophages, which is why CSF1R blockade is pursued therapeutically. The related receptor MST1R marks a neighbouring branch of macrophage-activating kinase signalling.

CXCL12 signalling is the axis that tells cells where to go and where to stay: stromal cells secrete the chemokine, and cells bearing its receptor CXCR4 follow the gradient. It retains haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow niches, guides B lymphocyte and neuronal precursor migration, directs germ cell and vascular patterning in development, and is co-opted by tumours for metastatic homing and by HIV strains that use CXCR4 as an entry coreceptor. Receptor engagement acts through heterotrimeric G proteins to reorganise the actin cytoskeleton and polarise the cell, with the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39 linking the signal to ion transport and volume regulation during movement. Receptor output is limited by trafficking: ENTREP1 and WBP1L route CXCR4 toward internalisation and degradation, and loss of this control produces the persistent signalling seen in WHIM syndrome.

interleukin-11-mediated signaling pathway is the arm of gp130 cytokine signalling driven by IL-11, a member of the IL-6 family that supports megakaryocyte maturation and platelet production, bone remodelling, mucosal repair after injury, and trophoblast and decidual function in early pregnancy. IL-11 binds its non-signalling alpha receptor, IL11RA, and the complex recruits the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), whose associated JAK1 phosphorylates the receptor tail and activates STAT3, which enters the nucleus and drives programmes of proliferation, survival and matrix production. Because the receptor chain is shared with IL-6 and CNTF, output depends on which alpha receptor a cell expresses, and pathway components overlap with those cytokines. Loss-of-function mutations in IL11RA cause craniosynostosis with dental and skeletal anomalies, while sustained IL-11 signalling promotes fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion and fibrosis in heart, lung, kidney and liver, and supports gastrointestinal tumour growth.

Interleukin-11 is a gp130-family cytokine that acts on stromal and epithelial cells to drive tissue remodelling, and interleukin-11-mediated signalling is the route by which that message is read. It supports megakaryocyte and platelet production, bone turnover and mucosal repair, and when persistently active it drives fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion and scarring in heart, lung, liver and kidney, making it a target of anti-fibrotic drug development. Signalling begins when the cytokine engages its specific alpha receptor IL11RA and recruits the shared signal-transducing subunit IL6ST (gp130); the associated kinase JAK1 then phosphorylates STAT3, which enters the nucleus and changes transcription of proliferation, survival and matrix genes. Because gp130 and JAK1/STAT3 are held in common with interleukin-6 and ciliary neurotrophic factor receptor complexes, specificity rests on the alpha chain, and loss-of-function mutations in it cause craniosynostosis with skeletal defects.

Interleukin-23 signalling sustains the Th17 arm of immunity, keeping IL-17- and IL-22-producing T cells and innate lymphoid cells in an effector state at mucosal barriers where they defend against fungi and extracellular bacteria. The cytokine is a heterodimer of a unique p19 subunit with the p40 subunit shared with IL-12, and it acts through a receptor pairing IL23R with IL12RB1; the associated kinases JAK2 and TYK2 phosphorylate STAT3, which drives transcription of the genes that stabilise the Th17 programme. Disulfide isomerase activity contributes to correct assembly and secretion of the subunit pair. Variants in the receptor and downstream kinase are among the strongest genetic associations with psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis and inflammatory bowel disease, and antibodies against p19 or p40 are established treatments, making this axis a link between cytokine-driven transcription and chronic inflammation.

Interleukin-3 is a haematopoietic growth factor that keeps multipotent progenitors and, in particular, mast cell, basophil and eosinophil lineages proliferating and alive; the signalling it initiates translates cytokine availability into survival and lineage output in the bone marrow. IL3 binds a private alpha chain, IL3RA, which pairs with the shared beta chain CSF2RB used also by GM-CSF and IL-5 receptors, so these cytokines converge on overlapping outputs. Receptor dimerisation activates the associated tyrosine kinase JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT5A for transport to the nucleus and transcription of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle genes; SYK and the immunoreceptor adaptor FCER1G link the pathway to kinase cascades shared with Fc receptor signalling in allergic effector cells. Constitutive activation of this axis, including through the beta chain and JAK2, contributes to myeloid leukaemias, and IL3RA is a surface target on leukaemic stem cells.

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor signalling is the route by which an extracellular cytokine instructs marrow progenitors to expand along the neutrophil lineage, survive, and mature into functional granulocytes. It is the axis exploited therapeutically to restore neutrophil counts after chemotherapy, and its failure produces severe congenital neutropenia with recurrent bacterial infection. The ligand CSF3 engages its receptor on myeloid cells, triggering kinase and transcriptional responses that drive proliferation and differentiation; a co-receptor-like adhesion molecule, CEACAM1, feeds inhibitory input back onto the receptor to limit granulopoiesis. Several members act downstream or in parallel inside the developing neutrophil: HAX1 preserves mitochondrial integrity and protects against apoptosis, JAGN1 operates in the secretory pathway and glycosylation, and HCLS1 links signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling. Together they connect cytokine perception to the size and competence of the circulating neutrophil pool.

CXCR4 is the receptor that keeps cells oriented toward gradients of its ligand CXCL12, and signalling through this axis is how haematopoietic stem cells are retained in bone marrow niches, how lymphocytes and neural and germ cell precursors home to their destinations, and how many tumour cells are guided to metastatic sites. Ligand binding activates a G protein-coupled cascade that reorganises the actin cytoskeleton for directed migration and feeds into survival and transcriptional responses; the Src-family kinase LYN couples receptor engagement to downstream phosphorylation in haematopoietic cells. Receptor output is set largely by how much CXCR4 remains at the surface, and endosomal adaptors including ENTREP1 and WBP1L direct its trafficking and degradation. Loss of this control produces the retained, hyperfunctional receptor of WHIM syndrome, with neutrophils trapped in marrow and severe immunodeficiency; the same receptor is an HIV-1 entry coreceptor.

CXCL12 binding to the receptor CXCR4 tells a cell where to go and when to stay, and this axis directs haematopoietic stem cell retention in bone marrow niches, lymphocyte trafficking, germ cell and neuronal migration, and vascular patterning during development. Receptor engagement acts through a G protein-coupled receptor that couples to Gi, lowering cAMP and driving calcium flux, PI3K and MAPK signalling, cytoskeletal remodelling and changes in transcription that translate a chemokine gradient into directed movement and survival. Signal output depends heavily on how much receptor reaches the surface: regulators in this set control CXCR4 endosomal sorting, recycling and degradation, setting the duration of the response. Loss of receptor downregulation causes the immunodeficiency of WHIM syndrome, while tumour cells exploit the same axis to home to CXCL12-rich tissues during metastasis.

Prolactin is a pituitary peptide hormone best known for driving mammary gland development and milk production, and it also acts on the ovary, prostate, liver and immune cells. Signalling begins when prolactin binds its single-chain cytokine-family receptor, which dimerizes and, through associated Janus kinases, activates STAT transcription factors as well as Ras-MAPK and PI3K routes, ending in changes to transcription of milk protein, proliferation and survival genes. Receptor loss blocks lactation, while sustained prolactin excess causes galactorrhoea, infertility and hypogonadism and has been linked to breast and prostate tumour growth. Crosstalk with inflammatory transcription control is represented here by the NF-kB subunit RELA, and with a cytokine receptor of the IL-12/IL-23 family, consistent with prolactin's immunomodulatory actions; CREBRF points to transcriptional regulators that shape the hormonal response.

Red blood cell output is set by a hormone made in the kidney in response to low oxygen, and this is the signalling route through which it acts. Erythropoietin binding to its receptor on erythroid progenitors licenses their survival, proliferation and terminal maturation; without it progenitors die by apoptosis and anaemia follows, which is why recombinant forms of the hormone are used to treat the anaemia of renal failure. The receptor has no catalytic activity of its own and works through an associated tyrosine kinase, JAK2, which phosphorylates the receptor tail and activates STAT5 for transport to the nucleus and transcription of anti-apoptotic and erythroid genes. Stem cell factor signalling through KIT cooperates at the progenitor stage. Constitutive activation of the same kinase drives polycythaemia and other myeloproliferative disease.

Platelet production depends on thrombopoietin, the liver-derived cytokine that drives megakaryocyte expansion and maturation and also sustains hematopoietic stem cells. Signalling begins when thrombopoietin binds its receptor MPL, which has no catalytic activity of its own and instead relies on the associated kinase JAK2; receptor dimerization brings JAK2 molecules together, and their phosphorylation of the receptor tail recruits STAT5A, which enters the nucleus to switch on survival and proliferation genes. The output is tuned by negative regulation, notably the adaptor SH2B3, a brake on JAK2 signalling whose loss raises blood counts. The pathway's clinical weight is substantial: activating MPL or JAK2 changes cause myeloproliferative neoplasms with excess platelets, while loss-of-function mutations in MPL or thrombopoietin produce congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia progressing to marrow failure, and recombinant agonists of this receptor are used to treat thrombocytopenia.

angiotensin-activated signaling pathway is the cellular response to angiotensin II, the effector hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, and it sets systemic blood pressure, vascular tone, and renal sodium and water handling. Chronic overactivity drives hypertension, cardiac and vascular hypertrophy, and fibrotic remodelling, which is why ACE inhibitors and receptor blockers are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensinogen is cleaved and converted by ACE to angiotensin II, which acts mainly through the AT1 receptor to mobilise calcium and engage protein kinase C, calcium/calmodulin kinase and calcineurin, while Rho-associated kinases and Rac1 reorganise the actin cytoskeleton for smooth muscle contraction. Src links the receptor to growth-factor-like transcriptional programmes and hypertrophic gene expression. AT2 and the MAS receptor for angiotensin-(1-7) oppose these effects, and caveolin scaffolding, receptor-associated adaptors and microRNAs tune signal strength in vascular smooth muscle and renal epithelium, where transporter regulation adjusts acid-base and solute transport.

Angiotensin II is the effector hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, and this pathway covers what happens once it engages its receptors on a target cell: vasoconstriction, sodium and fluid retention, aldosterone release, and longer-term changes in gene expression that drive cardiac and vascular remodelling. Sustained signalling through it underlies hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, which is why converting enzyme and receptor blockade are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensinogen is cleaved and processed by ACE to the active peptide, which acts on the type 1 receptor to mobilise calcium and activate protein kinase C, calcineurin, CaMKII, Src, Rac1 and the ROCK kinases, while the type 2 receptor and the MAS1 receptor oppose these effects. Receptor-associated and scaffolding proteins such as AGTRAP and caveolin tune output, and transporter coupling links the pathway to renal acid-base and sodium handling.

Somatostatin is the body's general inhibitory peptide hormone, and this receptor pathway is how it shuts things down: growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone release from the pituitary, insulin and glucagon from pancreatic islets, gastric acid and gut motility, and the proliferation of the cells that secrete these products. The peptide encoded by SST is processed to somatostatin-14 and -28 and acts on five related G protein-coupled receptors, SSTR1 through SSTR5, which couple through inhibitory G proteins to lower adenylyl cyclase activity and cAMP, open potassium channels, and suppress voltage-gated calcium entry, so hormone-containing vesicles are not released. Receptor subtypes differ in tissue distribution and ligand preference, a distinction exploited clinically: SSTR2- and SSTR5-preferring analogues treat acromegaly and neuroendocrine tumours, and the same receptors serve as targets for tumour imaging and radionuclide therapy.

Cannabinoid signalling is how endocannabinoids such as anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol, along with plant-derived cannabinoids, act through cell-surface G protein-coupled receptors to tune cellular output. Its best-known consequence is retrograde suppression of neurotransmitter release: CB1 on presynaptic terminals lowers cAMP and calcium entry, dampening excitatory and inhibitory transmission and shaping appetite, pain perception, mood and memory, while CB2 acts mainly on immune cells to restrain inflammatory responses. A related lysophospholipid-sensitive receptor broadens the pharmacology beyond the classical pair. Signal duration is set by ligand handling rather than receptor kinetics alone: monoacylglycerol lipase and a serine hydrolase both degrade 2-AG, lipid-binding and sterol carrier proteins ferry these lipophilic messengers, and an oxygenase diverts them to oxidised products. Downstream, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase signalling links receptor activation to synaptic plasticity and transcriptional change.

interleukin-33-mediated signaling pathway is the alarmin arm of innate immunity: IL-33 stored in epithelial and endothelial nuclei is released on tissue damage and alerts nearby cells to barrier injury. It drives type 2 inflammation, activating group 2 innate lymphoid cells, mast cells, eosinophils and Th2 cells to produce IL-5 and IL-13, and variation in this axis is among the strongest genetic risks for asthma and allergic disease; it also contributes to tissue repair and regulatory T cell maintenance. Signalling runs through the ST2 receptor with its shared accessory chain, recruiting MyD88 and the IRAK4-IRAK1 kinase module, then TRAF6 and TAK1, converging on NF-κB and MAP kinase activation and transcription of inflammatory cytokines. Because the receptor exists as a soluble decoy form, the pathway is tuned by ligand sequestration as well as by receptor expression on responding cell types.

Interleukin-33 is an alarmin released from the nucleus of damaged epithelial and endothelial cells, and the signalling it triggers alerts the immune system to barrier injury. Acting through the receptor ST2 (IL1RL1) together with the shared accessory chain IL1RAP, it drives type 2 inflammation: activation of mast cells, group 2 innate lymphoid cells and Th2 cells, with release of IL-5 and IL-13. This makes the pathway a major contributor to asthma, allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis, and a target of biologic therapy, while also supporting tissue repair and regulatory T cell maintenance. Mechanistically it follows the canonical interleukin-1 receptor family route, recruiting MYD88 and the kinases IRAK4 and IRAK1, then TRAF6 and TAK1 (MAP3K7), to converge on NF-κB and MAP kinase-dependent transcription of inflammatory genes.

Interleukin-17A is the signature cytokine of Th17 cells, and this is the route by which it instructs epithelial cells, fibroblasts and keratinocytes to mount antimicrobial defence. Engagement of a heterodimeric receptor built from IL17RA and IL17RC recruits the adaptor ACT1, encoded by TRAF3IP2, which acts with TRAF6 and the kinase TAK1 to switch on NF- interestingly, NF- canonical NF- canonical NF-kappaB and MAPK transcriptional programmes. The output is production of neutrophil-recruiting chemokines, G-CSF, defensins and matrix metalloproteinases, so the pathway governs mucosal and cutaneous protection against fungi such as Candida and against extracellular bacteria. Loss-of-function in the receptor or in the adaptor causes chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, while excessive signalling drives the neutrophilic inflammation of psoriasis and related autoimmune disease, which is why the cytokine and its receptor are targets of approved biologic therapies.

Secreted neurotrophins tell neurons whether to survive, grow and wire correctly, and this signalling cascade is how that instruction is read. NGF, BDNF, NT-3 and NT-4 bind the Trk receptor tyrosine kinases NTRK1, NTRK2 and NTRK3, whose activation recruits adaptors and phosphatases such as PTPN11, KIDINS220 and RAPGEF1 to drive Ras/Raf and Rap1 signalling toward transcriptional programmes for differentiation, axon and dendrite growth, and protection from apoptosis; Sprouty proteins damp the output. Sortilin and the same ligands in their pro-forms can instead promote death, so the balance of receptor engagement decides neuronal fate, with caspase-3 as an executioner. Actin regulators of the WAVE complex and DOCK3 link the cascade to growth cone motility and synaptic remodelling. Loss of NTRK1 signalling causes congenital insensitivity to pain, and reduced BDNF signalling is tied to neurodegeneration and mood disorders.

Nerve growth factor signalling tells sympathetic and sensory neurons to survive, grow axons, and specify pain- and temperature-sensing identity, and it keeps mature neurons dependent on target-derived trophic supply. NGF binding to the TrkA receptor tyrosine kinase triggers autophosphorylation and assembly of a signalling complex on adaptors and scaffolds, including the transmembrane scaffold KIDINS220 and the membrane-associated guanylate kinase MAGI2, which couple the activated receptor to Rap1 through exchange factors such as RAPGEF1 and RAPGEF2 and to sustained ERK output via SHOC2. Signalling endosomes carry the message retrogradely from axon terminals to the soma, where transcriptional programmes for survival and differentiation are set. Related neurotrophins BDNF, NTF3 and NTF4 act through the same receptor family, while sortilin partners with p75 to convert unprocessed proneurotrophins into a death signal. Loss of TrkA function causes congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis.

bile acid signaling pathway treats bile acids not merely as detergents for fat absorption but as hormones, sensed by dedicated receptors that feed back on the synthesis, transport and disposal of bile acids themselves. This is how the liver and intestine keep bile acid pools within a narrow range; loss of the sensing arm leads to cholestatic liver injury, bile acid diarrhoea, and disordered lipid and glucose handling. Two routes are represented. The nuclear receptor FXR, with vitamin D receptor as an additional bile acid-responsive transcription factor, reprograms gene expression to suppress CYP7A1 and induce transporters and FGF19. The membrane receptor GPBAR1 (TGR5), coupled through Gs to cAMP, acts on enterocytes, immune cells and enteroendocrine cells to release GLP-1 and modulate inflammation. Pruritogenic G protein-coupled receptors such as MRGPRX4 link bile acid accumulation to the itch of cholestasis.

Bile acids are not only detergents for fat absorption but hormones, and this signalling route is how cells read their concentration and respond by changing transcription and second-messenger tone. It closes the feedback loop on bile acid synthesis and export in liver and intestine, and contributes to lipid and glucose handling, gut motility, and the itch that accompanies cholestasis. Sensing is split between a nuclear and a membrane arm: the farnesoid X receptor NR1H4 binds bile acids to drive gene programmes that restrain their own production, the vitamin D receptor responds to secondary bile acids such as lithocholic acid, and the G protein-coupled receptor GPBAR1 raises cyclic AMP through Gs signalling. Mas-related receptors including MRGPRX4 link bile acids to sensory neurons and pruritus. Loss of this feedback underlies progressive cholestatic liver disease and bile acid toxicity.

Cells only commit to growth when nutrients, energy and growth factors are all available, and TORC1 signaling is the checkpoint that integrates those inputs. The complex of MTOR with RPTOR and MLST8 sits on the lysosomal surface, where the Ragulator scaffold and Rag GTPases recruit it and RHEB switches it on; when active it phosphorylates S6 kinases and translational regulators such as LARP1 to drive ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis while shutting down autophagy. Upstream, the TSC complex and the GATOR1 subunits relay growth-factor and stress signals, while leucine-, arginine- and methionine-sensing proteins including SESN2, CASTOR1, SAMTOR and SLC38A9 report amino acid supply, and AMPK with LKB1 reports energy deficit. Loss of the restraining arms underlies tuberous sclerosis, Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome and familial focal epilepsy, and chronic hyperactivation is a common feature of cancer.

Cells decide whether to survive, migrate and take up nutrients partly through the rapamycin-insensitive mTOR complex, and TORC2 signaling is that branch of mTOR output. Its defining function is phosphorylation of AKT1 at the hydrophobic motif, which licenses full AKT activity and thereby suppresses GSK3B and pro-apoptotic targets, supports glucose uptake, and shapes actin-dependent cell shape and motility. The complex is built from the mTOR kinase together with RICTOR, MLST8, MAPKAP1 (SIN1) and the mutually exclusive subunits PRR5 and PRR5L, with DEPTOR acting as an inhibitory partner; deubiquitinases such as USP9X and OTUD7B and kinases including TBK1 modulate its assembly and activity. Upstream input comes largely from PI3K, placing this arm downstream of growth factor and insulin receptors. Persistent activation is a feature of many cancers, where RICTOR amplification drives AKT-dependent growth and survival.

Cells detect viral replication by sensing RNA in the cytoplasm, and RIG-I signalling is the arm of that surveillance that converts detection of short double-stranded or 5'-triphosphate RNA into an interferon and cytokine response. Without it, RNA virus infections such as influenza and flaviviruses go unchecked at the earliest stage; with it left on too long, interferon-driven autoinflammation follows, so much of this biology is about tuning the sensor rather than firing it. The receptor encoded by RIGI is licensed by ubiquitin ligases including TRIM25 and RNF135 and by the co-sensor ZCCHC3, then relayed through mitochondrial adaptors to activate interferon regulatory factors and NF-kB. Counterbalancing components dampen the output: RNF125 and NLRX1 restrain signalling and deubiquitinases such as USP15 reverse activating marks. Interferon-induced effectors here, including OAS3, OASL and ZC3HAV1, degrade or block viral RNA directly.

Cells detect viral replication in their own cytoplasm by sensing double-stranded RNA, and MDA-5 signaling is the branch of that surveillance that responds to long dsRNA duplexes, particularly from picornaviruses. Recognition by the helicase IFIH1 drives assembly of a mitochondrial adaptor platform and activation of the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7, which induce type I interferon and downstream antiviral effectors such as the oligoadenylate synthetases. The output is an interferon-primed state in infected and neighbouring cells; loss of the receptor leaves hosts susceptible to enterovirus and rhinovirus disease, while gain-of-function variants cause interferonopathies including Singleton-Merten and Aicardi-Goutieres syndromes, illustrating how tightly the sensor must discriminate viral RNA from host RNA. Accessory factors tune the response: DHX58 and RIOK3 restrain or modulate signalling, DDX60 assists RNA sensing, and deubiquitinating and phosphorylation steps set the threshold for interferon induction.

Cells sense viral nucleic acids and bacterial products inside their own cytosol, and the sensors that do this must be tuned tightly: too little response permits infection, too much causes interferonopathy and autoinflammatory disease. This regulatory layer sets how strongly and how long cytoplasmic pattern recognition receptor signalling runs, acting on DNA sensing through cGAS and IFI16 with STING, RNA sensing through RIG-I-like helicases and MAVS at mitochondria, and inflammasome assembly around NLR and pyrin components. The control mechanisms are largely post-translational — ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases such as TRIM family members, TNFAIP3, ITCH, BIRC2/3 and BRCC3, palmitoylation by ZDHHC enzymes opposed by ABHD17 thioesterases, phosphatases, and negative regulators including NLRC3, NLRX1 and TREX1. Endolysosomal transporters of the SLC15 family and TASL position nucleotide and peptide ligands for sensing, linking trafficking to interferon and interleukin-1 output.

Cytosolic sensors such as RIG-I-like receptors, the DNA sensor cGAS-STING axis and NOD-like receptor inflammasomes must be switched off once an infection is cleared, and this braking programme is what prevents sustained type I interferon output and IL-1 family cytokine release from turning into autoinflammation. Loss of restraint underlies interferonopathies and gain-of-function inflammasome disease; TREX1, which degrades cytosolic DNA before it can be sensed, and pyrin-domain-only decoys such as PYDC1 illustrate the two commonest tactics, substrate removal and adaptor sequestration. Much of the rest is post-translational: E3 ligases and the deubiquitinase-adaptor TNFAIP3 mark signalling intermediates for degradation or edit their ubiquitin chains, palmitoyl transferases and thioesterases tune membrane targeting, and negative-regulatory NLRs including NLRC3 and NLRX1 dampen downstream kinase activation. The net effect is to set the threshold and duration of innate antiviral and inflammatory responses.

MDA-5 is a cytoplasmic sensor that detects long double-stranded viral RNA and triggers MAVS-dependent induction of type I interferon; tuning how strongly and how long it signals is the subject of this regulation.
