The balance matters in both directions: too little response permits picornavirus and other RNA virus replication, while unrestrained signalling drives interferonopathies and autoimmune inflammation. The genes here act as positive and negative modulators rather than as the sensor itself. A helicase-like partner and an RNA helicase can amplify or restrain ligand recognition, a mitochondrial protein influences signalling at the MAVS platform, a kinase-like protein and a metabolic enzyme dampen downstream interferon induction, and a deubiquitinase acts on the ubiquitin marks that gate activation. Together they set the threshold and duration of antiviral innate immune output.

RIG-I detects cytosolic double-stranded RNA bearing the signatures of viral replication and triggers interferon production, and the genes here set how strongly and how long that alarm sounds. Tuning matters in both directions: too little output leaves RNA viruses unchecked, while unrestrained signalling drives interferonopathy and autoimmune inflammation. Positive regulators include RNA-binding cofactors that help load ligand onto the sensor, such as ZCCHC3 and the helicase DHX58, alongside OASL and ZC3HAV1, which amplify detection of viral RNA. Restraint comes largely through ubiquitin: the ligase RNF125 marks RIG-I for degradation, the deubiquitinase USP15 and the BIRC2/BIRC3 pair act on signalling intermediates, and the NPLOC4-UFD1 complex feeds substrates to extraction and proteasomal turnover. Mitochondrial NLRX1 and C1QBP dampen adaptor engagement at MAVS, placing this control at the junction of innate immune sensing and protein quality control.

Detection of cytoplasmic viral RNA by RIG-I triggers interferon production, and this braking machinery keeps that alarm proportionate and self-limiting, preventing sustained type I interferon output and the autoinflammatory or interferonopathy-like damage that follows unchecked sensing. The regulators act at several points: a RIG-I-like helicase relative, LGP2 (DHX58), competes with and modulates recognition of duplex RNA; mitochondrial proteins such as NLRX1 and C1QBP restrain the adaptor MAVS at the outer membrane; RNF125 ubiquitinates RIG-I to drive its degradation; and the NPLOC4-UFD1 partners of the p97 segregase feed sensor and adaptor components into proteasomal turnover. Together they set the threshold and duration of antiviral innate signalling, so that interferon-stimulated gene expression resolves once infection is cleared. Loss of this negative control tips the balance toward chronic inflammation, while viruses exploit the same nodes to blunt host defence.

Retroviruses such as HIV-1 copy their single-stranded RNA genome into double-stranded DNA by reverse transcription, integrate that DNA into a host chromosome, and then rely on host RNA polymerase II to transcribe progeny genomes. Because the whole cycle runs on borrowed cellular machinery, it is shaped as much by host factors as by viral ones, and the genes here are largely those that oppose or modulate it. The APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases, with their relative AICDA, edit cytosine to uracil in nascent minus-strand viral DNA and hypermutate the provirus, a defence countered by the viral Vif protein. Chromatin and topology factors including TRIM28, SMARCB1 and the type II topoisomerases influence integration site selection and proviral silencing, determining whether an integrated genome is expressed or held latent. That latency is the barrier to curing retroviral infection, and the inflammatory output includes CXCL8 induction.

Replication of an RNA virus genome depends almost entirely on host proteins, and the genes here mark both sides of that dependency: factors the virus exploits and defences that restrict it. On the restriction side, the APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases edit viral nucleic acid to introduce hypermutation, crippling retroviral and hepatitis B replication, and are countered by viral antagonists such as HIV Vif. On the proviral side, membrane proteins including TMEM41B and VAPB, together with autophagy components ATG5 and ATG16L1, supply the lipid-derived membranes on which flavivirus and picornavirus replication complexes assemble, while poly(C)-binding proteins PCBP1 and PCBP2 bind viral 5' untranslated regions to support genome translation and synthesis. The balance between these activities sets whether infection is productive, and determines host range, interferon-driven control, and inflammatory output such as CXCL8 release.

Establishment of mitotic spindle localization positions the mitotic spindle within the dividing cell, thereby setting where the cleavage furrow forms and whether the two daughters inherit equal or distinct fates. It decides symmetric versus asymmetric division, keeps divisions planar in epithelia, and governs the balance between proliferative and differentiative divisions in neural progenitors; its failure underlies microcephaly, disordered epithelial architecture and cystic kidney disease. Cortical force generators anchored by LGN and NuMA recruit dynein-dynactin, which pulls on astral microtubules whose plus ends are stabilised and captured through EB1, CLASP proteins and the LIS1-NDEL1 module. Centrosomal and kinetochore components such as CDK5RAP2, MCPH1, NDC80 and the spindle checkpoint proteins ZW10 and SPDL1 couple orientation to spindle assembly and chromosome attachment, while cell adhesion through integrin signalling communicates tissue geometry to the cortex.

Where a cell divides is determined by where its mitotic spindle sits, and establishment of mitotic spindle localization is the process that moves and anchors the spindle to a chosen position within the cell. This positioning sets the cleavage plane and therefore whether division is symmetric or asymmetric, which governs stem cell self-renewal, the stratification of epithelia and the expansion of neural progenitors; its failure underlies microcephaly and disorganised tissue architecture. Cortical cues captured by GPSM1/GPSM2 and NuMA recruit dynein-dynactin, with LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1 licensing the motor to pull on astral microtubules, while CLASP1/2 and EB1 regulate microtubule plus-end behaviour at the cortex. Kinetochore and checkpoint components such as NDC80, ZW10 and SPDL1 couple positioning to faithful chromosome attachment, and centrosomal CDK5RAP2 and MCPH1 link spindle orientation to brain development.

Growth — the increase in size or mass of a cell, a tissue, or a whole organism — is the outcome of coordinated nutrient sensing, mitogenic signalling, and controlled restraint of cell size and number, and its dysregulation produces dwarfism and overgrowth syndromes at the organismal scale and tumours at the cellular one. Endocrine control runs through growth hormone and its receptor, growth hormone releasing hormone, insulin-like growth factors with their binding proteins, and the insulin receptor, converging on the mTOR complexes with raptor, rictor and LAMTOR subunits to license anabolic biosynthesis. Growth factor families (FGFs, EGF-family ligands, WNTs, TGF-beta/BMPs, Hedgehog, Notch) pattern how much tissue forms and where, while Hippo components including LATS kinases, NF2, SAV1 and the YAP/TAZ effectors, together with p53, RB1, PTEN and the CDK inhibitors, set upper limits. Also represented are neurite and axon outgrowth guidance cues and muscle hypertrophy regulators such as myostatin.

Cells, tissues and whole organisms must grow at the right speed and stop at the right size, and this collection of regulators sets that pace during development and in adult tissue homeostasis. It spans the endocrine axis that dictates body size — growth hormone and its releasing hormone and receptor, insulin-like growth factors with their binding proteins, insulin and leptin — together with the nutrient-sensing mTOR complexes, whose scaffolds and partners such as RPTOR, RICTOR, MLST8 and the sestrins couple amino acid and energy status to biosynthesis. Cell-intrinsic brakes are prominent: p53, RB1, the CDKN inhibitors, PTEN and STK11, and the Hippo kinases with LATS1/2, SAV1 and the YAP1/TEAD output that limits organ size. Also represented are TGF-beta, BMP and myostatin control of muscle and skeletal growth, Wnt, Hedgehog and Notch patterning cues, and semaphorin, slit, netrin and ephrin signals that govern axon and neurite outgrowth. Loss of these constraints underlies overgrowth syndromes, cardiac hypertrophy and cancer.

regulation of growth rate covers the controls that set how fast cells, tissues, or a whole organism increase in mass, tuning growth to nutrient supply, hormonal cues, and the limits imposed by genome maintenance. Its importance is visible at both extremes: too little growth signalling produces short stature and wasting, too much drives hyperplasia and tumour growth, and premature loss of these controls accompanies accelerated ageing. The genes point to several arms of that regulation. Ghrelin is the gut-derived hormone that stimulates growth hormone release and appetite, linking energy intake to somatic growth. ARMC10 acts at mitochondria to couple metabolic capacity to growth, while BNIPL and RFTN1 modulate proliferative and membrane-associated signalling. The WRN helicase ties growth rate to replication fidelity, since its loss causes a segmental premature ageing syndrome with growth failure and cancer predisposition.

Growth rate regulation covers the processes that set how fast a cell, tissue or whole organism enlarges, tuning mass accumulation to nutrient supply, hormonal cues and the limits imposed by genome integrity. The genes here act at very different levels of that control. Ghrelin is the stomach-derived peptide hormone that stimulates appetite and drives pituitary growth hormone release, linking energy intake to somatic growth. WRN encodes a RecQ family helicase-exonuclease whose loss causes Werner syndrome, in which growth arrest at adolescence and premature ageing follow from unrepaired replication and telomere damage. Others modulate growth indirectly through mitochondrial dynamics, membrane raft-dependent signalling, apoptotic regulation, or cell surface proteolysis affecting proliferation. Taken together they illustrate that growth rate is not one pathway but a convergence of endocrine signalling, metabolic capacity and damage surveillance, with failure producing dwarfism, overgrowth or tumour-like expansion.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and organisms from place to place, the capacity that lets leukocytes reach infected tissue, endothelial tips sprout new vessels, neurons extend axons to their targets, and sperm and ciliated cells generate motion. Its failure underlies immunodeficiency, defective wound healing and malformed nervous and vascular systems, while its inappropriate reactivation drives tumour invasion and metastasis. Mechanistically it joins directional cues to cytoskeletal output: chemokines and their receptors, growth factors such as VEGF, HGF and PDGF, and guidance ligands including semaphorins, slits, netrins and ephrins converge on Rho-family GTPases, PAK, ROCK and actin regulators like cofilin, profilin and WASP. Integrins, cadherins and matrix proteases anchor and remodel the substratum so traction can be produced, and transcriptional programmes of epithelial-mesenchymal transition, together with numerous microRNAs, tune how readily a cell becomes motile.

Locomotion covers the self-propelled movement of cells and whole organisms from one place to another, and in humans it is mostly cell migration: leukocytes crossing vessel walls to reach infection, endothelial tips sprouting new vessels, neural crest and axonal growth cones navigating the embryo, keratinocytes closing a wound, and sperm swimming. Its failure leaves immunodeficiency, defective vascular and neural patterning and poor healing, while its inappropriate reactivation underlies tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes span the layers this requires: chemokines and their receptors, growth factor and semaphorin/slit/ephrin guidance cues, integrins, cadherins and matrix components that provide traction, metalloproteinases that clear a path, and Rho-family GTPases with their regulators, actin nucleators, cofilin, profilin and myosin light-chain kinase that build and retract the leading edge. Ciliary and flagellar components add motile cilia and sperm propulsion, and numerous microRNAs and transcription factors tune the whole programme.

Cells and organisms move, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast, how often and how far. It gathers the control layer above motility itself: chemokines and their receptors that direct leukocyte trafficking, growth factors such as HGF, VEGFs, FGFs and PDGFs that drive endothelial and fibroblast migration, guidance systems including semaphorins with plexins, slits with Robos, netrins and ephrins that steer axons and vessels, and adhesion and matrix components — integrins, laminins, cadherins, metalloproteinases — that provide traction and clear a path. These converge on Rho-family GTPases, focal adhesion kinase, PI3K/AKT and actin regulators such as cofilin, profilin and cortactin, with numerous microRNAs and transcriptional repressors tuning output. Positive and negative regulation both appear, since inhibitory signals restrain movement as much as attractants promote it. The biology underlies wound healing, immune surveillance, neural wiring and angiogenesis, and its dysregulation supports tumour invasion and metastasis.

Cell movement has to be restrained as well as driven, and this collection covers the processes that stop, slow or limit locomotion of cells and of the whole organism. Such braking keeps epithelia sessile, confines leukocytes to the right tissue, stops growing axons at their targets, and holds endothelial sprouts in check; its loss underlies invasive and metastatic behaviour in cancer, excessive inflammatory infiltration and misrouted axons. Mechanisms include repulsive guidance through Slit ligands acting on Robo receptors and semaphorin-plexin signalling, Rho-family control via GAPs such as DLC1, SRGAPs and ARHGDIB, adhesive stabilisation by cadherin-catenin and tight-junction proteins, receptor tyrosine phosphatases and DUSPs that damp promigratory kinase signalling, TGF-beta/BMP and Wnt inputs, secreted inhibitors including THBS1, TIMP1 and SFRPs, and a large set of microRNAs that suppress motility transcripts post-transcriptionally.

Body size is not a passive outcome of feeding but an actively regulated trait, and this pathway covers the processes that set the rate and extent of whole-organism growth until adult stature is reached. Its core is the somatotropic axis: hypothalamic releasing hormone and ghrelin acting through their receptors drive pituitary growth hormone, which signals via its receptor through STAT5A/STAT5B and is damped by SOCS2, with IGF2 and stanniocalcin-like factors modulating growth-factor availability. Around this sit endocrine and neural inputs (beta-adrenergic receptors, dopamine and neuropeptide Y signalling, thyroid hormone inactivation by DIO3), chromatin regulators such as CHD7, NIPBL, HDAC3 and SUV39H1, and cartilage-growth mediators including GDF5 and NPPC. Loss of these controls produces dwarfism, gigantism, skeletal dysplasia, failure to thrive, or the growth retardation characteristic of many developmental syndromes.

negative regulation of multicellular organism growth covers the brakes on body size — the signals that limit how large an animal grows and when growth stops, setting adult stature rather than the growth of any single tissue. It matters because the same restraints, when lost, produce overgrowth syndromes, and when excessive produce growth failure and short stature. Several of the genes act on the growth hormone/IGF axis: SOCS2 terminates growth hormone receptor signalling and its loss causes gigantism, while stanniocalcin STC2 sequesters the proteases that liberate IGF from its binding proteins. Others impose systemic restraint through appetite and energy expenditure, including GDF15 as an anorexigenic stress signal and β-adrenergic receptors coupling to GNAS for catabolic tone. Developmental repressors such as PTCH1, and factors mutated in Bardet–Biedl and Smith–Magenis syndromes, link body-size control to hedgehog signalling, ciliary function and neuroendocrine regulation of feeding.

Body size is set not only by growth-promoting signals but by brakes on them, and this is the set of processes that limit how large an organism becomes. Its members restrain the growth hormone/IGF axis and systemic energy balance: SOCS2 dampens growth hormone receptor signalling, and its loss produces gigantism in mice, while stanniocalcin-2 inhibits the IGF-releasing protease PAPP-A, and GDF15 acts on hindbrain circuits to suppress appetite and lower body weight. Beta-adrenergic receptors and their coupling through the stimulatory G protein Gs link sympathetic tone to lipolysis and metabolic rate, and PTCH1 acts as the inhibitory receptor of Hedgehog signalling that restrains proliferative growth. Mutations here shift stature and body mass in both directions, as seen in overgrowth syndromes, Smith-Magenis syndrome from RAI1 haploinsufficiency, and the obesity of Bardet-Biedl syndrome, placing this biology at the junction of endocrine growth control and appetite regulation.

Embryonic cleavage is the run of rapid, specialized divisions that converts a fertilized egg into a multicellular early embryo, and it is unlike ordinary mitosis: cells divide without growing, rely on maternally stored proteins and RNAs, and progressively partition cytoplasmic material between blastomeres. Failure here ends development before implantation, and defects in the maternal-effect components produce early embryonic arrest and infertility rather than later malformation. The genes here reflect several requirements of these divisions at once: an oocyte cytoplasmic lattice protein that stores maternal material for use after fertilization, topoisomerases and a repair helicase that manage DNA topology and integrity during extremely fast replication cycles, and a cullin-based ubiquitin ligase scaffold that drives the timed protein degradation on which cleavage cycling and spindle behaviour depend.

Cells move during wound healing, immune surveillance, angiogenesis and development, and this collection covers the signals and machinery that switch motility on or increase it. Its reach is broad: chemokines and their receptors that recruit leukocytes to inflamed tissue, growth factor systems such as VEGF/KDR, HGF/MET, PDGF and EGF that drive endothelial sprouting and fibroblast or epithelial migration, and guidance ligands including semaphorins, netrin, SLIT2 and ephrin receptors that steer growth cones and vessels. Downstream, Rho-family GTPases RAC1, CDC42 and RHOA, focal adhesion components PTK2, BCAR1 and integrins, and actin regulators such as cofilin, profilin and cortactin remodel the cytoskeleton and adhesions so a cell can polarise and translocate, while matrix proteases and plasminogen activators clear a path. Transcription factors and microRNAs tune the output. Excessive activation underlies tumour invasion and metastasis, fibrosis and chronic inflammation.

Body size is set by endocrine and developmental signals that push tissues to grow until a species-typical size is reached, and this pathway covers the processes that drive growth upward. Its core is the somatotropic axis: hypothalamic releasing hormone acting through its pituitary receptor, ghrelin and its receptor as a second secretagogue input, growth hormone itself, the growth hormone receptor, and the STAT5A/STAT5B transcription factors that transduce receptor signalling into transcription of growth-promoting genes including insulin-like growth factor. Loss of these components produces proportionate short stature and pituitary dwarfism, while excess drives overgrowth. Also represented are chromatin and developmental regulators such as HMGA2, CHD7 and NIPBL, whose mutation causes syndromic growth retardation, along with ciliary and basal body proteins linked to Bardet-Biedl syndrome, and thyroid hormone and dopaminergic modulators of pituitary output.

Genes that push embryonic development forward, sustaining the transition from fertilised egg through gastrulation and early organ patterning. Two kinds of activity dominate. One is the maternal contribution stored in the oocyte: a subcortical complex built from NLRP5, OOEP, TLE6, PADI6 and KHDC3L supports the first cleavage divisions, and its loss in women causes hydatidiform mole, recurrent pregnancy loss and early embryonic arrest. The other is inductive signalling and transcriptional patterning, with WNT1, WNT3A and WNT4 ligands acting through beta-catenin-dependent routes alongside transcription factors such as FOXA2, LHX1, OTX2 and OSR1 that specify endoderm, forebrain and intermediate mesoderm. Cytoskeletal and scaffolding components including CFL1, PAFAH1B1, AMOT and RACK1 couple these cues to cell division, migration and polarity, so that growth signals translate into correctly shaped tissue.

regulation of meiotic nuclear division controls when germ cells enter meiosis, how far they proceed, and when they arrest, so that oocytes and sperm emerge with a single haploid genome set. Its failure produces infertility, premature ovarian insufficiency, or aneuploid gametes and miscarriage. The genes cover several regulatory layers: STRA8 and MEIOSIN license meiotic entry downstream of retinoic acid, PRDM9 designates recombination hotspots while HORMAD1/2 and TRIP13 police synapsis and crossover checkpoints, and a spindle assembly checkpoint module with CDC20, KNL1 and ZWINT guards chromosome segregation. Oocyte arrest and reawakening depend on cAMP tone through GPR3 and PDE3A, on EMI1/EMI2-type APC/C inhibitors with FZR1, and on MOS and WEE2 kinase activity. RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, NANOS2 and PIWIL2 impose translational and transposon control, linking germline gene expression to the meiotic cell cycle.

Meiosis must be started at the right moment and then stopped and restarted at defined arrest points, and this regulatory layer sets that timing so that a diploid germ cell yields haploid gametes. It matters for fertility: loss of control produces oocytes that fail to arrest or resume, aneuploid eggs, and spermatogenic failure. Retinoic acid-responsive entry factors such as STRA8 and its partner MEIOSIN license meiotic initiation, while DMRT1, NANOS2 and DAZL govern whether germ cells enter meiosis or stay mitotic. Prophase surveillance runs through HORMAD proteins, TRIP13 and the recombination hotspot determinant PRDM9. Oocyte arrest is maintained by cAMP signalling through GPR3 and PDE3A, and release depends on MOS kinase, WEE2, and control of the anaphase-promoting complex by CDC20, FZR1 and its inhibitors FBXO5 and FBXO43, with spindle checkpoint components monitoring kinetochore attachment.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is the layer of control that decides which genes a cell can read, using marks on DNA and histones rather than changes in sequence, and it is what allows one genome to specify many stable cell identities through repeated divisions. Its failure underlies imprinting disorders, loss of X inactivation, transposon reactivation in the germline, and a large fraction of cancers. The machinery here writes, reads and erases those marks: DNMT1 with UHRF1 propagates cytosine methylation at the replication fork while TET enzymes reverse it; Polycomb complexes built on EZH2, SUZ12 and RING1B compact developmental loci; SETDB1, SUV39H and the HUSH complex with TRIM28 silence repeats and retroelements; histone acetyltransferases, deacetylases and demethylases tune accessibility, and ATP-dependent remodellers reposition nucleosomes. Piwi proteins and Tudor partners extend the same logic to small RNA-guided silencing in gametes, and CTCF organizes the resulting domains.

Cells with identical genomes maintain different expression programmes because chromatin itself carries heritable information, and this is the machinery that writes, reads, erases and propagates it. Such epigenetic regulation of gene expression establishes lineage identity, silences repetitive and parasitic DNA, imprints maternal and paternal alleles, inactivates one X chromosome, and keeps the settings stable through rounds of DNA replication even after the initiating signal is gone. The components span DNA methylation writers and the TET dioxygenases that initiate demethylation, methyl-CpG readers such as MECP2 and UHRF1, histone acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC and sirtuin deacetylases, H3K9 and H3K27 methyltransferases with Polycomb and HP1 silencing complexes, ATP-dependent nucleosome remodellers, histone variants and linker histones, and a piRNA-guided arm that silences transposons in germ cells. Misdirection of these activities underlies imprinting disorders, Rett syndrome, and widespread silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer.

snRNA modification is the chemical decoration of spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs after they are transcribed, converting raw transcripts into stable, correctly folded components of the splicing machinery. Pseudouridines and 2'-O-methyl groups placed in and around the snRNA regions that base-pair with pre-mRNA branch points and splice sites tune the fidelity and efficiency of intron removal, while cap modification and 3' end binding determine whether an snRNA is protected or degraded. The genes cover both arms: the H/ACA pseudouridine synthase core of dyskerin with NHP2 and NOP10, the methyltransferases that install N6-methyladenosine and N6,2'-O-dimethyladenosine marks, and the MePCE-LARP7 pair that caps and stabilises 7SK. Loss of these activities destabilises snRNPs and disrupts splicing, and dyskerin mutations cause dyskeratosis congenita with failure of telomere maintenance and bone marrow function.

Spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs are not functional as bare transcripts; they carry pseudouridines, methylated bases and modified caps that stabilize them and tune how they pair with pre-mRNA. Modification of snRNA supplies these marks and so underwrites accurate splice-site recognition and the stability of the snRNPs themselves. Pseudouridine synthase activity is contributed by the dyskerin complex together with NHP2 and NOP10, the same H/ACA machinery used on ribosomal RNA and telomerase RNA, which is why its loss produces the multisystem failure of dyskeratosis congenita. MEPCE adds the gamma-monomethyl phosphate cap to 7SK, with LARP7 binding and protecting that transcript in the complex restraining transcription elongation, while METTL16 and METTL4 introduce adenine methylation, linking U6 snRNA maturation to broader RNA methylation regulating splicing and gene expression.

Developmental events must not only happen but happen on schedule, and heterochronic regulation is the control of that schedule — when a progenitor stops dividing and differentiates, and how fast a tissue advances from one stage to the next. Mistiming rather than misspecification underlies many malformations: precocious differentiation exhausts progenitor pools, while delay leaves tissues immature. The genes here act largely in the developing nervous system and at early patterning steps, where Notch signalling through RBPJ and the repressor HES1 holds neural progenitors undifferentiated and opposes the proneural driver ASCL1, and PAX6 and NR2E1 set the tempo of neurogenesis and progenitor self-renewal. Secreted cues such as FGF9 and NODAL, together with MSX1, couple this timing to axis formation and inductive signalling between tissues, linking the clock of differentiation to spatial pattern.

Fibroblast growth factor receptors drive proliferation, migration and patterning decisions in development, skeletal growth, wound repair and angiogenesis, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and how long those receptors signal. Tuning matters because unchecked FGF input causes skeletal dysplasias and craniosynostosis and contributes to tumour growth and resistance, while insufficient signalling disrupts limb, palate and neural patterning. Control operates at several levels: Sprouty proteins act as intracellular feedback brakes on the RAS-ERK output, secreted binding proteins such as FGFBP1 and FGFBP3 mobilise ligand from matrix stores, glypican and the sulfatases SULF1 and SULF2 alter heparan sulfate so that ligand-receptor-cofactor complexes form or fail to, and thrombospondin, integrin and WNT components integrate FGF activity with adhesion and other morphogen cues. Transcription factors including RUNX2, GATA3 and OTX2, plus several microRNAs, adjust pathway components themselves, linking receptor output to differentiation programmes in bone, ectoderm and stem cells.

Fibroblast growth factor receptors drive proliferation, patterning and branching morphogenesis, and the strength and duration of that output has to be held in check; this set covers the brakes on FGFR signalling. Negative regulation keeps limb, skeletal, lung and kidney development within bounds, restrains angiogenesis, and limits the growth-factor drive that becomes oncogenic when FGFR pathways are amplified or mutated. Several mechanisms are represented. Sprouty proteins are induced by FGF stimulation and feed back to dampen RAS-ERK output, forming a classic negative loop. Extracellular control comes from heparan sulfate handling: glypican and the sulfatases SULF1 and SULF2, which remove 6-O-sulfates and so alter ligand-receptor-heparan complex formation. SHISA2 retains receptors in the endoplasmic reticulum, ciliary and transcriptional regulators such as OFD1, GATA3 and PRDM14 act indirectly, and a group of microRNAs tunes pathway components post-transcriptionally.

Female meiosis divides the oocyte's chromosomes without dividing its cytoplasm evenly: at each of the two divisions a small polar body is pinched off and discarded, so that a single egg retains nearly all maternal stores while shedding surplus chromosome sets. Polar body extrusion is what makes this asymmetry possible, and its failure leaves oocytes aneuploid or blocked in maturation, a common source of infertility and early embryonic loss. The process depends on actin rather than on the spindle alone: the formin FMN2 and the nucleation-promoting factors SPIRE1 and SPIRE2 cooperate to build actin networks that move the meiotic spindle to the cortex and drive off-centre cleavage, with WASHC5-associated actin regulation and centromere-associated CENPV linking chromosome positioning to cortical remodelling. It couples cytoskeletal mechanics to meiotic cell cycle progression during oocyte maturation.

Some cells increase their DNA content without dividing, re-replicating the genome within a single cycle so that ploidy rises. Endoreduplication of this kind produces the polyploid cells of mammalian liver, the giant trophoblast cells of the placenta, and megakaryocytes, whose high DNA content supports the biosynthetic output needed for platelet production; where it is not controlled, uncontrolled re-replication instead causes genome instability. The genes here mark the switch that uncouples S phase from mitosis: the atypical repressors E2F7 and E2F8 shut down the classical E2F transcriptional programme and are required for hepatocyte polyploidisation, while FBXO5 (Emi1) restrains the anaphase-promoting complex so that mitotic cyclins and licensing factors escape destruction and origins can fire again. SUMO protease activity and other regulators tune the same transition, placing this biology at the interface of cell cycle control and terminal differentiation.

Protein refolding is the cell's repair arm for damaged proteins: when heat, oxidation, or mutation unfolds a polypeptide, chaperones bind the exposed hydrophobic surfaces, prevent aggregation, and drive ATP-dependent cycles that return the protein to its native, active shape. This is what allows cells to survive proteotoxic stress instead of accumulating inclusions, and its decline underlies aggregation diseases of neurons, muscle, and the lens. The machinery here spans compartments and families: cytosolic and stress-inducible HSP70s with their DNAJ co-chaperones and nucleotide-exchange regulators such as BAG5, HSP90, the mitochondrial HSP60 chaperonin and mortalin, the endoplasmic reticulum BiP with its SDF2L1 partner, and ATP-independent small heat shock proteins including HSPB1 and the lens alpha-crystallins that hold unfolded clients in a refoldable state. Refolding competes with degradation, so these factors also triage substrates toward proteasomal disposal when repair fails.

When heat, oxidative stress or mutation leaves a protein unfolded or misfolded, chaperones can restore it to its active shape rather than let it aggregate or be degraded, and this refolding capacity is what allows cells to survive proteotoxic stress. The gene complement is dominated by the HSP70 family (HSPA1A/B, HSPA8, the endoplasmic reticulum BiP HSPA5, mitochondrial HSPA9) together with their J-domain co-chaperones DNAJA2, DNAJA4 and DNAJB2, which deliver substrates and stimulate ATP-driven cycles of binding and release; HSP90 and the mitochondrial HSP60 chaperonin provide additional folding routes, while small heat shock proteins such as HSPB1 and the lens alpha-crystallins hold partly unfolded clients soluble in an ATP-independent manner. Nucleotide exchange factors like BAG5 tune the cycle. The same activity operates in cytosol, ER and mitochondria, and its decline underlies cataract, myopathy and protein aggregation disease.

Movement of water and the solutes that drag it across epithelial barriers is what allows kidneys to concentrate urine, airways to keep surface liquid thin, glands to secrete saliva and sweat, and the eye lens and brain to hold their water content steady. Aquaporin channels dominate this fluid transport programme, providing the selective water pores of collecting duct, lens fibre, glia and gut, while urea and glucose carriers and anion exchangers set the osmotic gradients that pull water through. Vasopressin acting on its renal receptor triggers trafficking of aquaporin-2 to the apical membrane, linking systemic osmolarity to reabsorption, and epithelial sodium channel and CFTR activity govern surface hydration. Calcium release and scaffolding adaptors tune channel placement. Loss of these components causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, cataract, corneal dystrophy and the dehydrated secretions of cystic fibrosis.

Epithelia move water across themselves by first moving salt, and this directed fluid transport sets the volume and composition of airway surface liquid, intestinal contents, pancreatic and biliary secretions, and lung alveolar fluid. Anion secretion through the CFTR chloride channel, coupled to bicarbonate exchange by SLC26A6, drives osmotic water flow through aquaporin water channels, while the epithelial sodium channel subunit SCNN1B and the glucose-coupled sodium transporter SLC5A1 mediate absorption in the opposite direction. Tight junction and desmosomal proteins such as claudin-18 and plakophilin-1 set paracellular permeability so that transcellular gradients are not short-circuited. Calcium release through ITPR1, the regulator AHCYL1, and endothelin acting on EDNRB tune secretion rates. Loss of balance here produces cystic fibrosis airway and pancreatic disease, secretory diarrhoea, or failure to clear alveolar oedema.

Olfactory behavior covers the responses an animal makes to odors — approach, avoidance, feeding, mating and social recognition — and therefore the whole chain from odorant detection to a motor decision. It matters because anosmia and hyposmia disrupt appetite, hazard avoidance and social interaction, and appear early in neurodegenerative and developmental syndromes. The genes point mainly to the olfactory sensory neuron and its cilium, where adenylyl cyclase ADCY3 generates the cAMP signal that opens transduction channels, and where ciliary and trafficking factors such as BBS1 and CFAP69 maintain the sensory compartment; loss of these produces ciliopathy-associated smell defects. Others act on circuit assembly and central processing, including CHD7, mutated in CHARGE syndrome with olfactory bulb hypoplasia, the transcription factor LMX1A, and the postsynaptic scaffold SHANK1. The pathway thus links chemosensory transduction to behavior.

Behavioural responses to odours depend on the machinery that lets olfactory sensory neurons detect volatile cues and relay them to the brain, and on the developmental programmes that build that circuitry. Loss of these functions produces anosmia or hyposmia, which in humans blunts appetite and flavour perception and removes a warning system for spoiled food and smoke. Odorant receptor signalling converges on adenylate cyclase 3 to raise cAMP in the cilia of sensory neurons, so ciliary assembly and maintenance genes such as BBS1 and CFAP69 are required for smell as much as the transduction enzymes are. Transcriptional regulators including CHD7 and LMX1A shape formation of the olfactory epithelium and bulb, and CHD7 mutation underlies the anosmia seen with CHARGE syndrome. Synaptic scaffolding contributes at the downstream relay, tying sensory input to behavioural output.

Restoring integrity to injured tissue runs as an ordered programme, and this collection spans all of its phases. Bleeding is stopped first: platelet adhesion and activation through von Willebrand factor, the GPIb-IX-V complex and GPVI, granule release, and the coagulation cascade from tissue factor through thrombin to cross-linked fibrin, balanced by anticoagulant and fibrinolytic regulators such as antithrombin, protein C, thrombomodulin and plasminogen activators. Inflammatory mediators including TNF, IL6, HMGB1 and lipoxygenase products then recruit leukocytes, after which growth factors and their receptors drive granulation tissue: fibroblast proliferation and collagen and fibronectin deposition under TGF-beta, angiogenesis via VEGFA, KDR and the angiopoietins, and keratinocyte migration and re-epithelialisation supported by integrins, focal adhesion and actomyosin machinery, matrix proteases and tight junction reassembly. Defects produce bleeding disorders, chronic non-healing ulcers, or excessive fibrosis and scarring.

Glia outnumber neurons in much of the nervous system, and gliogenesis is the programme by which neural progenitors are diverted away from neuronal fate to produce astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, Schwann cells and microglia, then driven to maturity. Its output supplies myelin, potassium and glutamate buffering, blood-brain barrier support and immune surveillance; its failure or misregulation underlies leukodystrophies, dysmyelinating neuropathies, impaired remyelination and glioma. Lineage identity is set by transcription factors including OLIG1/OLIG2, SOX9, SOX10, NKX2-2, NFIA/NFIB and MYRF, with Notch effectors HES1/HES5 and polycomb components EZH2 and SUZ12 timing the switch from neurogenesis. Extrinsic cues run through Sonic hedgehog, BMP, neuregulin-ERBB2/ERBB3, PDGF-responsive OPC markers such as CSPG4 and PTPRZ1, and cytokine-STAT3 signalling via CNTF, LIF and IL6ST. Microglial specification and maintenance depend on CSF1R, IL34, TREM2 and fractalkine signalling.

Catecholamine metabolism — the synthesis, packaging, reuptake and breakdown of dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline — is tuned rather than run at a fixed rate, and this regulatory layer sets how much transmitter a neuron makes and how long it persists. It matters most in midbrain dopaminergic neurons, where the balance between cytosolic dopamine and its safe storage or catabolism determines vulnerability to oxidative damage; several genes here, including PARK7, PRKN, SNCA and VPS35, are Parkinson's disease loci, and their failure links disturbed dopamine handling to nigral degeneration. Control acts at multiple points: presynaptic and postsynaptic receptors such as DRD1 and DRD4 feed back on transmitter output, SLC6A3 clears released dopamine back into the terminal, aldehyde-metabolising enzymes dispose of reactive breakdown products, and the transcription factor NR4A2 maintains the dopaminergic phenotype itself. Neuromodulatory peptides and other transmitter receptors adjust the same output.

Cilia have no ribosomes, so every protein inside them must be carried in from the cell body and spent components carried back out; intraciliary transport is that shuttle service along the axonemal microtubules. It builds and maintains the axoneme and loads the membrane receptors that make cilia into sensory antennae, so its failure produces the ciliopathies — retinal degeneration, polycystic kidney disease, skeletal dysplasias, situs defects and Bardet-Biedl syndrome. Cargo is packaged into IFT-A and IFT-B particle complexes (IFT88, IFT172, IFT52, WDR19, IFT43 and partners), moved outward by a kinesin-2 motor and returned by cytoplasmic dynein-2 with its light and intermediate chains. Small GTPases such as ARL3, IFT27 and RABL2B control cargo loading and release, while kinases including CILK1 set train turnaround and ciliary length. Hedgehog signalling depends on this traffic to concentrate its components in the organelle.

Gastrulation converts a single-layered embryo into a three-layered body plan, and it depends on cells physically leaving the epithelial surface and moving to new positions in the interior. The migratory component of this process sets where mesoderm and endoderm form, and therefore where the heart, gut and axial structures will later arise; its failure produces early lethality or laterality and axis defects. Nodal signalling with its inhibitor CER1 and the ligand-like APELA patterns the region where cells ingress, FGF8 provides the chemotactic cue that moves them away from the primitive streak, and transcriptional outputs such as MIXL1 and SOX17 commit the migrating cells to mesendodermal fates. Apical-basal and polarity proteins including CRB2, EPB41L5 and AMOT, together with actin regulators, remodel junctions and the cytoskeleton so that epithelial cells can detach and crawl.</description>

T-helper 1 type immune response is the arm of adaptive immunity that clears pathogens living inside host cells — intracellular bacteria, fungi and protozoa — by arming macrophages and cytotoxic effectors with interferon-gamma. Its overactivity underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease including arthritis, while loss of the IL-12/IL-23 receptor axis leaves patients susceptible to mycobacteria and salmonella. Commitment runs from dendritic cell IL-12 and IL-18 production through IL12RB1/IL12RB2 to STAT4 and the master transcription factor TBX21, with HLX and LEF1 reinforcing the program and IL-10, SOCS5, IL18BP and STAT6 restraining or diverting it. Innate priming via TLR4, HMGB1, IL-1 family cytokines, RIPK2 and TRAF6-dependent NF-kB feeds the same circuit. Immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8/PSMB9 and MHC class II reflect the antigen processing and presentation on which Th1 differentiation depends, alongside costimulation through CD80 and TNFSF4.

Clearance of pathogens that hide inside cells depends on the T-helper 1 arm of CD4 T cell differentiation, which commits naive T cells to making interferon-gamma and so licenses macrophages to kill intracellular bacteria, fungi and protozoa. The same programme, run too hard, drives inflammatory arthritis and other autoimmune tissue damage, while its loss leaves people vulnerable to mycobacteria and salmonella. Commitment is instructed by IL-12 and IL-18 from activated dendritic cells and macrophages acting through their receptor chains, and is read out by STAT4 and the lineage-defining transcription factor TBX21, with IL-27, IL-23 and IL-33 shaping the balance and STAT6, IL-10 and IL18BP restraining it. Innate sensing through TLR4 and RIPK2, costimulation by CD80 and peptide display on MHC class II together with proteasome subunits that generate those peptides supply the priming context.</description>}</invoke></function_calls></response>}</invoke>ilmiş</invoke>

Defence against helminths and other extracellular parasites, and the immunopathology of allergy and asthma, both run through the type 2 immune response. It is defined by production of IL-4, IL-5, IL-10 and IL-13 by T helper 2 cells, innate lymphoid cells, eosinophils, basophils and mast cells, which drives IgE class switching, mast cell arming through the high-affinity IgE receptor, mucus secretion and tissue remodelling and repair. Epithelial alarmins such as IL-33 initiate the response; IL-4 signalling through STAT6 with GATA3 commits and stabilises the T helper 2 programme, while TBX21 and BCL6 represent the competing type 1 and follicular fates that must be suppressed. Arginase expression marks the alternatively activated macrophages recruited downstream. Too little leaves parasite burdens unchecked; too much produces atopy, and the interferon and inflammasome components here mark the regulatory checks on that balance.

After an antigen-specific T cell is activated, it must undergo clonal expansion to generate enough effector cells to clear an infection; this proliferative burst is what turns a rare precursor into a functional response, and its miscalibration produces either immunodeficiency or autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation. Antigen recognition through the CD3 complex with CD4 and the kinases ZAP70, FYN and PRKCQ is integrated with costimulation from CD28 engaging CD80/CD86, while CTLA4, PD-L1, BTLA, TIM-3 and other coinhibitory ligands set the ceiling — the basis of checkpoint blockade in tumours. Growth is sustained by IL-2 acting through IL2RA and STAT5, together with IL-12, IL-15, IL-21 and IL-23 signals, and by MYC- and cyclin-driven entry into cycle. Opposing arms include TGF-beta, IL-10, FOXP3 regulatory T cells, arginine and tryptophan catabolism by ARG1/ARG2 and IDO1, and ubiquitin ligases such as CBLB and ITCH that enforce anergy.

After an antigen engages the B cell receptor, the responding clone must expand before it can supply useful quantities of antibody, and B cell proliferation is that expansion step. It sets the size of a germinal centre reaction and thus the magnitude of humoral immunity; too little gives immunodeficiency and poor vaccine responses, too much underlies lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity and B cell lymphoma. Antigen receptor components and their proximal kinases and adaptors, notably BTK, LYN, CD19 and CARD11, drive entry into cycle, while co-stimulation through CD40 and BAFF-family receptors and cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21 and IL-2 sustain it. Inhibitory receptors including CD22, FCGR2B, CTLA4 and BTLA, together with the phosphatase-linked brake INPP5D, restrain the response, and checkpoint and apoptotic regulators such as ATM, CDKN1A, BCL2 and BAX determine which dividing cells survive.

positive regulation of T cell proliferation covers the signals that drive antigen-experienced T cells to expand into clones large enough to clear an infection, and that sustain the lymphocyte pools underlying adaptive immunity, vaccine responses and transplant rejection. Three inputs converge: peptide-MHC engagement of the T cell receptor complex, relayed through CD3, ZAP70, PRKCQ, CARD11 and calcineurin; costimulation by CD28, ICOS, OX40 and 4-1BB ligands presented on dendritic cells; and growth-promoting cytokines, chiefly IL-2 acting via IL2RA and STAT5, with IL-12, IL-15, IL-21 and IL-23 shaping the expanding subset. Adhesion, chemokine and actin-regulatory components such as VCAM1, CCL19 and CORO1A position cells for productive contacts. Several members are inhibitory checkpoints whose loss increases proliferation, so the same wiring sets the threshold: too little yields immunodeficiency, too much autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation.

Clonal expansion of antigen-specific T cells is what turns a handful of naive lymphocytes into an effective response, and the processes gathered here are those that drive or amplify that expansion. Antigen presentation on MHC class I and class II molecules, engagement of the TCR complex and CD4, and costimulation through CD28 with its ligands CD80 and CD86 or the TNF-family ligands OX40L and 4-1BBL set the threshold for division. Proximal signalling by ZAP70, LCK-associated adaptors, PRKCQ, CARD11 and calcineurin feeds into IL-2 production, while IL-2, IL-15, IL-12, IL-21 and IL-23 act through their receptors and STAT5 to sustain cycling. Several members are better known as brakes -- PD-L1, PD-L2, TIM-3, B7-H4, FOXP3 -- reflecting how tightly proliferative drive is balanced. Excessive output underlies autoimmunity and transplant rejection; failure leaves immunodeficiency and poor tumour control.

Once a T cell has seen antigen, its clonal expansion must be driven and sustained, and this is the biology that raises the rate and extent of proliferation in already-activated T cells. It determines the size of an effector response, and so the strength of antiviral and antitumour immunity; excessive signalling contributes to autoimmunity, while blockade of it is how several immunosuppressive drugs work. Interleukin-2 acting through its high-affinity receptor chain drives the core growth signal via STAT5A and STAT5B, with calcineurin (PPP3CA) linking receptor engagement to the transcription of these cytokines. Costimulatory ligands such as ICOSLG, TNFSF9 and SLAMF1 lower the threshold for division, IL-12, IL-18 and IL-23 with their receptors push polarised effector expansion, and alarmins including HMGB1 signalling through AGER couple tissue damage to lymphocyte growth. Insulin-like growth factors and microRNA control add further tuning.

T cell activation is the transition by which a resting T lymphocyte, on encountering antigen presented by MHC together with costimulatory and cytokine signals, changes shape, proliferates, and acquires effector function. It is the decision point of adaptive cellular immunity: too little produces immunodeficiency and failed tumour and pathogen control, too much drives autoimmunity, and its deliberate manipulation underlies checkpoint blockade and transplant immunosuppression. Antigen recognition by the T cell receptor complex is relayed through LCK, ZAP70, LAT and PLC-coupled adaptors into calcineurin-NFAT, NF-kB via the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 module, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, while CD28 and TNF-receptor family costimulators amplify and CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3 and TIGIT restrain the response. Cytokine receptors feeding JAK-STAT signalling, together with TBX21, GATA3, RORC and FOXP3, assign helper and regulatory fates, and ubiquitin ligases such as CBLB and ITCH enforce anergy and tolerance.

B cells respond to antigen, cytokines and helper-cell contact by changing shape, dividing, and differentiating into antibody-secreting or memory cells, and this activation programme is the basis of humoral immunity and of vaccine responses. Antigen engagement of the receptor complex signals through Src and Syk-family kinases, BTK, BLNK, PLCG2 and PI3K into NF-kB and calcium-dependent transcription, while co-stimulation through CD40 and cytokine receptors for IL-4, IL-21 and IL-6 shapes the outcome. Inhibitory receptors and phosphatases such as CD22, FCGR2B, PTPN6 and INPP5D set the threshold, and negative regulators including TNFAIP3 and CYLD restrain the response. Later steps recruit AICDA, uracil processing and double-strand break repair for class switching, together with BCL6, PAX5, XBP1 and MZB1 governing germinal centre and plasma cell fates. Defects cause immunodeficiency, autoantibody-driven autoimmunity, or lymphoma.

macrophage activation is the switch by which a resting tissue macrophage becomes an effector cell, changing shape, metabolism and secretory output in response to microbial products, cytokines or damaged host material. It sets the tone of innate immunity: too little leaves mycobacterial and other intracellular infections uncontrolled, too much drives the cytokine storms, granulomas and neuroinflammation seen in sepsis and neurodegeneration. Recognition runs through Toll-like receptors, Fc and complement receptors, formyl-peptide and purinergic sensors, and the TREM2-TYROBP-SYK axis of microglia, converging on JAK2, PLCG2 and AP-1 factors to induce TNF, IL1B, IL6 and CCL3. Opposing inputs polarise the response, with IFNG driving classical activation and IL4, IL13, IL10 and the nuclear receptors NR1H3 and RORA promoting alternative, resolving states. Brakes such as CD200, HAVCR2, ZC3H12A and VSIG4 keep activation self-limiting.

Macrophage activation is the shift in shape, gene expression and behaviour that turns a resting tissue macrophage into an effector cell, triggered by cytokines, microbial ligands or host-derived damage signals. It sets the tone of innate immunity: classical activation by interferon-gamma and Toll-like receptor agonists such as LPS drives TNF, IL-1B and IL-6 production and microbial killing, while IL-4 and IL-13 acting through IL4R and JAK2 promote the alternative, tissue-repair state, and IL-10 restrains both. Receptor sensing runs through TLR1/4/6/9 with the TICAM1 adaptor, complement and Fc receptors, and ITAM-coupled TREM2-TYROBP signalling to SYK and PLCG2, with nuclear receptors and transcription factors including NR1H3 and JUN fixing the resulting programme. Excessive or mistimed activation underlies septic inflammation and chronic inflammatory disease, while hypofunction, notably of TREM2 or GRN in microglia, contributes to neurodegeneration and failed clearance of debris.

Monocytes circulate in blood as sentinels that, on encountering cytokines, chemokines, or ligands displayed by damaged tissue or pathogens, change shape, adhere, and switch on inflammatory and phagocytic programmes before differentiating into macrophages or dendritic cells. This activation step determines how much inflammation a tissue experiences, and its dysregulation contributes to atherosclerosis, sepsis, and chronic inflammatory disease. Genes here span the stimuli and the machinery that responds: colony-stimulating factor signalling that drives monocyte survival and maturation, membrane sheddases of the ADAM family that release surface receptors and adhesion molecules, and fibronectin and hyaluronidase activity that couple cells to remodelled matrix. Inhibitory receptors such as CD33 and LILRB4 set thresholds that restrain the response, while NFKBIZ tunes NF-κB-dependent cytokine output and FOXP1 acts transcriptionally on myeloid differentiation.

Endothelial cell activation is the shift in shape and behaviour that lines of blood vessels undergo when they meet cytokines, chemokines, matrix cues or soluble mediators, converting a quiescent barrier into a surface that recruits leukocytes, remodels, and sprouts. It underlies inflammation and its resolution, wound healing, angiogenesis and the early steps of atherosclerosis, where persistent activation gives a leaky, adhesive, thrombogenic endothelium. The genes here span the inputs and the interpreters: a TGF-beta family receptor with SMAD4 transmits signals that endothelium uses to set quiescence versus growth, BMPER modulates BMP availability in the vessel wall, CXCL10 is an interferon-induced chemokine the activated cell secretes to draw in T cells, and P2RX4 lets ATP and shear-linked purinergic signals raise calcium. Transcriptional and epigenetic regulators including FOXP1, HOXA9 and PRMT5, together with microRNA control, determine how strongly and how long the activated state persists.

Whether a cell divides, pauses, or exits the cycle altogether is set by this broad regulatory layer, which modulates the rate and extent of cell proliferation across essentially every tissue. It underlies embryonic growth, wound healing, immune expansion after antigen encounter, and tissue renewal, and its loss of balance produces either atrophy and immunodeficiency or the unrestrained growth of cancer. Mitogenic inputs arrive as growth factors and their receptor tyrosine kinases, cytokines and interleukin receptors acting through JAK-STAT, and morphogen systems including Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, BMP and TGF-beta. These converge on cyclins, cyclin-dependent kinases and their CDKN-family inhibitors, on transcriptional hubs such as MYC, E2F and the retinoblastoma protein, and on tumour suppressors including TP53, PTEN and the Hippo kinases feeding YAP/TAZ. Chromatin remodellers, many microRNAs, and antiproliferative BTG/TOB factors tune the output further, while immune checkpoint ligands restrain lymphocyte division specifically.

T cell clonal expansion has to be actively restrained, and this collection of brakes on T cell proliferation sets the threshold for self-tolerance and for the resolution of an immune response. Inhibitory receptors and their ligands dominate: CTLA4, PD-1 ligands CD274 and PDCD1LG2, BTLA with TNFRSF14, TIM-3 (HAVCR2) engaging galectin-9, and LILRB family receptors reading HLA-G and HLA-E. Regulatory T cells contribute through FOXP3, high-affinity IL2RA that sequesters IL-2, latent TGF-β anchored by LRRC32, and IL-10. Myeloid and stromal cells starve T cells of amino acids via arginases, IDO1 and IL4I1. Intracellularly, the E3 ligases CBLB, ITCH and RC3H1 and the phosphatase PTPN6 dampen receptor signalling and enforce anergy. Loss of these controls produces autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while tumours exploit them to escape immunity — the basis of checkpoint blockade therapy.

Meiotic recombination begins with deliberate damage: during meiosis I, the cell cuts its own chromosomes at defined hotspots so that homologues can find each other and exchange material. These programmed double-strand breaks are what generate crossovers, allowing accurate homologue pairing and segregation as well as the genetic diversity of gametes; too few breaks leave chromosomes unpaired and cause aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility, and germ cell loss. The cut is made by a topoisomerase-like transesterase, SPO11, acting with its partner TOP6BL, while REC114, MEI4 and IHO1 form a pre-break complex tethered to the chromosome axis. Axis proteins such as HORMAD1 and the regulator ANKRD31 control where and how many breaks form, including on the sex chromosome pairing region, and MRE11 participates in processing the ends toward strand invasion and repair.

Receptors and enzymes that deliver cargo to endosomes must be returned to the trans-Golgi network to work again, and retrograde endosome-to-Golgi transport is the route that recovers them. It keeps mannose-6-phosphate receptors, sortilin-family sorting receptors such as SORL1, and SNARE and glycosylation machinery in circulation, so lysosomal hydrolase delivery and Golgi homeostasis both depend on it. Retromer (VPS35 with VPS26 and VPS29) and the associated WASH complex select cargo and drive actin-dependent tubule formation on endosomes, GARP and EARP complexes with their Rab and TBC regulators, Rab6, Rab7, Rab9 and Arl1 control budding and targeting, and syntaxin-6, syntaxin-16 and VTI1A-type SNAREs execute fusion at the Golgi. Disruption of these steps underlies lysosomal storage disease, and retromer and LRRK2-Rab29 defects link this trafficking arm to Parkinson's disease and neurodegeneration.

Strand invasion is the committed step of homologous recombination: a single-stranded DNA end coated by a recombinase searches the genome for a matching sequence, invades the intact duplex, displaces one strand and pairs with its complement to create the joint molecule from which repair synthesis proceeds. This is how cells repair double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks accurately, using the sister chromatid or homolog as a template, and how meiotic crossovers are made so that chromosomes segregate correctly. RAD51 performs the search and exchange in somatic cells while DMC1, with its activator PSMC3IP, does so during meiosis; RAD51D and XRCC2 belong to the paralog complexes that help load and stabilise the filament, and the WRN helicase processes the resulting intermediates. Loss of these activities gives chromosome instability, infertility, and cancer predisposition.

When glucose runs low, cells must switch from growth and biosynthesis to conservation and self-digestion, and this starvation response is what makes that switch. It preserves ATP levels and viability during ischaemia, exercise and nutrient-poor tumour microenvironments, and its failure leaves cells unable to survive metabolic stress. Falling energy charge activates the AMP-activated kinase complex through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, which restrains anabolic signalling and licenses autophagy via the class III PI3-kinase complex containing beclin 1, VPS34 and ATG14. In parallel, the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response drives ATF4 to induce amino-acid supply enzymes such as asparagine synthetase, while sestrins, FOXO3, p53 and SIRT1 reinforce catabolic and antioxidant programmes. Glucose and amino acid transporters, GATOR/KICSTOR components and lipid droplet perilipins tie nutrient sensing to mTORC1 control and to mobilisation of internal fuel stores.

Lipoprotein metabolism covers two related kinds of protein-lipid conjugate: the circulating particles that carry cholesterol and triglyceride through plasma, and individual proteins that acquire a covalently attached lipid. The first arm determines plasma lipid levels and atherosclerosis risk - apolipoproteins such as APOA1, APOB and APOE build the particles, MTTP loads lipid onto nascent apoB, LCAT esterifies cholesterol within HDL, and clearance depends on LDLR, whose availability is set by PCSK9-directed degradation; ABCA1 exports cholesterol to acceptors, and lipases and transfer steps remodel particles in transit. The second arm is protein lipidation itself: N-myristoylation by NMT1/NMT2, S-palmitoylation by the ZDHHC acyltransferase family reversed by ABHD17 and LYPLA thioesterases, and palmitoleoylation of Wnt and Hedgehog ligands by PORCN and HHAT, which controls membrane anchoring, trafficking and morphogen signalling. Lysosomal and autophagy components link both arms to lipid turnover.

Lipoprotein biosynthesis covers the covalent attachment of lipids to proteins and the assembly of lipid-carrying particles, two routes that both make proteins able to associate with membranes or travel through blood. One arm is protein lipidation: palmitoyl transferases of the ZDHHC family S-acylate cysteines to anchor and traffic signalling proteins, N-myristoyltransferases add myristate to nascent N-termini, and dedicated acyltransferases lipid-modify secreted ligands, Wnt proteins by PORCN, Hedgehog by HHAT, and ghrelin by MBOAT4, which is required for their receptor activity. A related activity conjugates phosphatidylethanolamine to ATG8 proteins during autophagosome formation, hence the ULK1-ATG13 and ATG7-ATG16L1 machinery here. The other arm is plasma lipoprotein assembly and remodelling, where APOB, APOA1 and APOE, the ABCA1 lipid exporter and LCAT build HDL and apoB-containing particles; defects cause abetalipoproteinaemia, Tangier disease and dyslipidaemia.

Lipoprotein catabolic process covers the breakdown of lipid-modified proteins and lipid-carrying particles, spanning both the clearance of circulating lipoproteins and the enzymatic removal of lipid anchors from proteins. It determines how much cholesterol and triglyceride is taken out of plasma, and failure of its receptor and lysosomal arms produces familial hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis, and lysosomal acid lipase deficiency. Particle clearance runs through apolipoprotein ligands such as APOB and APOE binding LDLR, followed by endocytosis and hydrolysis of cholesteryl esters by LIPA and cathepsin D in the lysosome; APOC2 tunes upstream lipolysis. A parallel set of thioesterases and hydrolases, including PPT1, LYPLA1 and the ABHD17 depalmitoylases, strips palmitate from cysteine residues, reversing S-acylation and controlling the membrane localisation and turnover of signalling proteins. NOTUM removes palmitoleate from Wnt ligands, extinguishing Wnt signalling in the extracellular space.

Lipoproteins carry cholesterol and triglyceride through plasma, and their catabolism determines how much lipid is delivered to cells and how much remains in circulation — the step whose failure produces hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. Receptor-mediated uptake via the LDL receptor, guided by apolipoprotein B and apolipoprotein E ligands, routes particles to lysosomes, where cathepsin D degrades the protein moiety and lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters and triglycerides to free cholesterol and fatty acids; loss of that lipase causes Wolman disease and cholesteryl ester storage disease. Apolipoprotein C-II acts instead as the cofactor that lets lipoprotein lipase strip triglyceride from circulating particles. Also represented is breakdown of protein-attached lipid itself: depalmitoylating thioesterases and serine hydrolases remove S-acyl groups from cysteines, with palmitoyl-protein thioesterase deficiency causing infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and NOTUM removing the palmitoleate required for Wnt activity.

Cells constantly decide which proteins to destroy and how fast, and this regulation of protein catabolism sets that tempo. Tuning it determines how quickly cell cycle inhibitors, transcription factors and damaged or misfolded proteins disappear, so it underlies cell cycle progression, quality control of the secretory pathway, and clearance of aggregation-prone species; when it fails, substrates either accumulate toxically, as in neurodegeneration, or are destroyed prematurely, as when tumour suppressors are lost. The machinery spans the whole 26S proteasome with its activators and inhibitors, ubiquitin ligases and adaptors such as MDM2, FBXW7, ITCH, NEDD4 and cullin-RING components, deubiquitinases that reverse the mark, chaperones and shuttling factors including VCP, STUB1 and the ubiquilins, and sorting proteins that route cargo to lysosomes. Protease inhibitors of the TIMP and serpin families and antizymes controlling ornithine decarboxylase add non-ubiquitin modes of control.

Protein turnover has to be restrained as well as driven, and this is the braking side of it: processes that slow or block the destruction of proteins by the proteasome, by lysosomal and autophagic routes, and by extracellular proteases. Restraint sets how long a regulatory protein persists, so it governs the stability of tumour suppressors, cell cycle and signalling components, and it limits tissue damage from unchecked proteolysis. Several mechanisms converge here. Deubiquitinases such as USP7, USP14 and UCHL5 remove ubiquitin chains before degradation commits, with USP14 acting at the proteasome itself; PSMF1 inhibits proteasome activity directly; TIMP family members and serpin-type inhibitors block metalloproteinases and serine proteases outside the cell. Antizyme inhibitors protect ornithine decarboxylase from degradation, coupling this control to polyamine synthesis. Loss of such restraint leads to premature loss of stabilising substrates, excessive matrix breakdown and defective proteostasis.

Cells break down foreign chemicals — drugs, plant alkaloids, industrial compounds, combustion products — and this xenobiotic catabolic activity determines how long such compounds persist and whether they are cleared or converted into something more toxic. Much of the work is hepatic and proceeds in phases: cytochrome P450 monooxygenases such as CYP1A1, CYP2D6 and CYP3A4 oxidise the parent compound, flavin-containing and other oxidoreductases contribute, then glutathione S-transferases and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases conjugate the products for excretion. The nuclear receptor PXR senses xenobiotic load and induces many of these enzymes, coupling exposure to capacity. Thiopurine methyltransferase, DPYD and NUDT15 handle nucleotide-analogue drugs, and inherited variation in them causes severe toxicity from standard doses. Polymorphism across this group is the main source of interindividual differences in drug response, drug interactions and susceptibility to chemical carcinogens activated rather than inactivated by metabolism.

Ketone metabolism covers the making, interconversion and disposal of carbonyl-bearing compounds, and in mammals it links fasting fuel supply to steroid hormone production and detoxification. When glucose is scarce, fatty acid oxidation in liver mitochondria yields ketone bodies that the brain, heart and muscle burn instead; the transferase OXCT1 activates acetoacetate for use in those extrahepatic tissues, while CPT1A, ACADVL and ACADL feed the substrate in and PPARA, PPARGC1A and SIRT1 set the transcriptional tone of the switch. Insulin signalling through IRS1/IRS2 and the PDK/PDP control of pyruvate dehydrogenase decide when this programme runs, and its failure underlies ketoacidosis and hypoketotic hypoglycaemia. Overlapping enzymology handles other ketones: cytochrome P450s and hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases build and modify steroid ketones, aldo-keto reductases and carbonyl reductases reduce reactive carbonyls, and UGT conjugation clears them. Quinone-related genes extend the same carbonyl chemistry to ubiquinone and vitamin K.

Grouped here are the reactions that generate carbonyl-bearing (ketone) compounds, which in human cells means two dominant chemistries: steroid hormone synthesis and the assembly of the ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) quinone ring. The steroidogenic arm converts cholesterol-derived precursors into cortisol, aldosterone, androgens and oestrogens through mitochondrial and microsomal cytochromes P450 such as CYP11B1, CYP11B2, CYP17A1, CYP19A1 and CYP21A2, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, and electron supply from ferredoxin and its reductase; loss of these steps causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia and disorders of sex development, and their output is tuned by pituitary gonadotropins LHB and FSHB. The COQ and PDSS enzymes build and prenylate the benzoquinone head group, supplying the lipid electron carrier of the respiratory chain, and their failure produces coenzyme Q deficiency with encephalomyopathy and nephropathy. Accompanying BMP, WNT and transcriptional regulators place this output under developmental and endocrine control.

Ketone catabolism covers the enzymatic breakdown of carbonyl-bearing compounds, from ketone bodies used as fuel during fasting to reactive ketoaldehydes that must be disposed of before they damage proteins. Its clearest physiological arm is extrahepatic use of acetoacetate: the mitochondrial CoA transferase OXCT1 activates acetoacetate so that heart, muscle and brain can oxidise it, and loss of this step causes ketoacidotic crises in infancy. A second arm is detoxification, where glyoxalase-family and reductase activities such as HAGH, PARK7 and carbonyl reductase convert methylglyoxal and related electrophilic ketones to harmless hydroxyacids or alcohols. Other members handle side chains and ring systems of steroids, kynurenine intermediates and eicosanoid-like lipids, including omega-hydroxylating cytochromes P450 of the CYP4F family. Together these reactions link energy supply during carbohydrate scarcity with protection from carbonyl stress.

Modified amino acid catabolic process is the disposal arm for amino acid derivatives — conjugates, methylated and hydroxylated forms, thyroid hormones and glutathione-linked adducts — returning their carbon, nitrogen and sulfur to usable pools. It matters because these modified compounds are not simply recycled through standard amino acid routes: they require dedicated hydrolases and dehydrogenases, and their accumulation is toxic. Gamma-glutamyl transferases and cyclotransferases dismantle glutathione and its conjugates at the cell surface and in the cytosol, supplying cysteine for resynthesis; betaine, dimethylglycine and sarcosine dehydrogenases feed the one-carbon and methionine cycles; proline and hydroxyproline oxidation converges on glutamate and, via HOGA1, on glyoxylate handling, where failure causes primary hyperoxaluria. Iodothyronine deiodinases activate and inactivate thyroid hormone, coupling this catabolic chemistry to systemic metabolic rate.

Amino acids are extensively modified in the body — methylated, conjugated to glutamate or glutathione, iodinated, hydroxylated — and this catabolic route disposes of those derivatives so their carbon, sulfur and nitrogen return to general metabolism. It matters because accumulated derivatives are toxic or signalling-active: failure of proline oxidation causes hyperprolinaemia with neuropsychiatric features, and defects in hydroxyproline and glutamate semialdehyde handling produce oxalate overload and kidney stones. The gene complement spans several chemistries: gamma-glutamyl transferases and related hydrolases strip glutamate from glutathione conjugates and other gamma-glutamyl amides, sarcosine, dimethylglycine and betaine dehydrogenases with formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases feed one-carbon units into folate metabolism, iodothyronine deiodinases remove iodine from thyroid hormone to set local hormone activity, and prenylcysteine oxidases degrade products of protein prenylation. The pathway therefore links amino acid turnover to glutathione salvage, methyl group supply and hormone inactivation.

response to cocaine covers the cellular and behavioural changes triggered when cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake, the biology that underlies psychostimulant reward, sensitisation and addiction. Cocaine's immediate targets are here as the dopamine and serotonin transporters, and the consequences run through dopamine receptors D1-D5 and the striatal signalling hub DARPP-32, with CDK5, FOSB and CREB1 converting acute stimulation into lasting transcriptional change. Chromatin and DNA methylation enzymes such as HDAC5, EHMT2 and DNMT3A make that change persistent, which is why drug-associated plasticity outlives the drug. Glutamatergic components including GRIA1, HOMER1/2 and the astrocytic glutamate transporters remodel synapses in reward circuitry, while CRH, oxytocin, prodynorphin-related and kappa-opioid signalling link drug exposure to stress and aversive withdrawal states. COMT and MAO-adjacent metabolic genes set individual sensitivity, tying this pathway to relapse risk and to dopaminergic neuron identity.

Cocaine blocks monoamine reuptake, and the cellular and behavioural response to cocaine describes how neurons in the reward circuitry adapt to the resulting surge in dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline. These adaptations underlie sensitization, craving and relapse, so the pathway is the molecular substrate of psychostimulant addiction. The direct targets appear as the dopamine and serotonin transporters, alongside the full set of D1-D5 dopamine receptors, a serotonin receptor and glutamate receptors and Homer scaffolds that shape striatal synaptic plasticity. Downstream, dopamine signalling converges on DARPP-32 and CREB-dependent transcription, with FOSB accumulation and chromatin modifiers such as DNMT3A, HDAC5 and EHMT2 imposing longer-lasting changes in gene expression. Stress and neuropeptide components -- corticotropin-releasing hormone and its binding protein, oxytocin, CART, prochineurin/nociceptin and kappa-opioid receptor -- link drug exposure to stress axis activity and negative affect during withdrawal. Astrocytic glutamate transporters contribute to altered synaptic glutamate clearance.

Tissue regeneration is the regrowth of tissue lost to injury, and in mammals it depends on resident stem or progenitor cells re-entering the cell cycle, expanding, and then differentiating to restore the original architecture. The genes here point most strongly at skeletal muscle repair: PAX7 marks satellite cells, MYOD1 and MYF6 drive their myogenic commitment, and MYMK and MYMX execute the membrane fusion that builds multinucleated fibres, while myostatin restrains the expansion. Growth factor and morphogen inputs including IGF1, FGF10, midkine and pleiotrophin, WNT7A/WNT10B with FZD receptors, NOTCH1 and YAP1 set the balance between self-renewal and differentiation, and CDKN1A/CDKN1B enforce cell cycle exit. Other members cover nerve and cardiac repair, extracellular matrix and dystroglycan glycosylation, and inflammation resolution. Failure of this programme underlies poor wound healing, fibrotic scarring in place of functional tissue, and the progressive weakness of muscular dystrophies.

Embryonic epithelia must decide not only which side faces the lumen but also which direction is forward within the plane of the sheet, and establishing that planar polarity gives whole fields of cells a shared orientation. The alignment drives convergent extension during gastrulation and neural tube closure, oriented cell division and intercalation, and the uniform tilt of structures such as inner ear hair cell bundles; its loss produces craniorachischisis and other neural tube defects. Core to the process are the atypical cadherin CELSR1 and the transmembrane protein VANGL2, which segregate to opposite cell faces and propagate orientation from neighbour to neighbour, with SEC24B providing the cargo adaptor that delivers VANGL2 to the surface. A secreted Wnt-modulating factor and a transcription factor of the forkhead family, together with a dynein-associated regulator of cytoskeletal organization, tie the axis to cell movement and gene expression.</description>

Making ribosomes is the largest biosynthetic commitment a growing cell makes, and this pathway covers the whole route: transcription of ribosomal RNA, its chemical modification and stepwise trimming, assembly with ribosomal proteins, and export of pre-subunits to the cytoplasm for final maturation. Growth rate, protein synthesis capacity and cell proliferation all scale with it, which is why nucleolar stress from failed assembly stabilises p53 through ribosomal protein sequestration of MDM2, and why inherited defects in individual factors cause ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome and Treacher Collins syndrome. Small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins built around fibrillarin or dyskerin guide 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation; DEAD-box and DEAH helicases remodel folding intermediates; exosome subunits and exonucleases process and discard spacer RNA; AAA-ATPases and GTPases drive irreversible maturation steps. Parallel factors serve mitochondrial ribosome assembly, supporting respiratory chain translation.

Making a ribosome requires more than its RNA and proteins: assembly is the staged process that folds rRNA, loads ribosomal proteins onto pre-particles, and joins the small and large subunits into a translation-competent monosome. Cells scale this output to growth demand, and defects produce ribosomopathies — impaired erythropoiesis, skeletal and pancreatic disease, and bone marrow failure, as in Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, where SBDS with the GTPase EFL1 releases eIF6 from the large subunit so that joining can occur. Assembly factors here include RNA helicases, AAA-ATPases and GTPases, rRNA methyltransferases, and nucleolar chaperones such as nucleophosmin that act on pre-rRNA processing intermediates. A substantial arm of the set operates in mitochondria, where dedicated maturation factors and rRNA modification enzymes build mitoribosomes for synthesis of respiratory chain subunits, linking this biology to both cell growth control and oxidative phosphorylation.
