Making a working cytosolic ribosome is more than transcribing rRNA: the large and small subunits are built and matured in the nucleolus and nucleus, exported, and then given final licensing in the cytoplasm before they can join into a translation-competent 80S particle. This late assembly step sets how much protein synthesis capacity a cell has, and it is the point at which ribosome biogenesis is quality-controlled. A key cytoplasmic event is removal of the anti-association factor eIF6 from the large subunit, carried out by SBDS together with the GTPase EFL1; loss of SBDS function causes Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, with bone marrow failure and pancreatic insufficiency, illustrating how tissue-specific the consequences of a general translation defect can be. Contributing factors include RNA helicase activity, nucleolar chaperone-like proteins, and structural subunits such as RPL38 whose loss alters translation of particular developmental mRNAs rather than all of them.

Genomes are damaged not only by radiation and chemicals but by the cell's own oxidised nucleotide pool, and DNA protection covers the activities that intercept such threats before they are fixed into the sequence. Sanitising enzymes hydrolyse aberrant triphosphates so they are never used by polymerases: NUDT1 removes oxidised guanine nucleotides such as 8-oxo-dGTP, while NUDT15 and DCTPP1 clear other non-canonical or modified nucleotides, a function that also shapes the toxicity of thiopurine drugs. Redox buffering by a mitochondrial glutaredoxin and by cystathionine beta-synthase, which channels homocysteine into cysteine and hydrogen sulfide production, limits the oxidative burden reaching DNA. ERCC6 couples transcription to repair of lesions that stall RNA polymerase. Loss of these safeguards raises mutation rates and underlies premature ageing and neurodegenerative phenotypes.

Natural killer cells kill any cell that fails to display the right self markers, so healthy cells must actively signal their own legitimacy; protection from natural killer cell mediated cytotoxicity is that self-preservation function. Classical class I molecules such as HLA-A and HLA-B, together with the non-classical HLA-E and HLA-G, engage inhibitory receptors on NK cells and veto the lytic programme, which is why loss of surface class I during viral infection or tumour progression licenses killing. HLA-G is prominent at the maternal-fetal interface, where trophoblast expression shields semi-allogeneic fetal tissue from maternal NK attack. A second layer works inside the target cell: serpin family inhibitors, notably the granzyme B inhibitor SERPINB9, neutralise cytotoxic proteases delivered by the attacking lymphocyte. Tumours exploit both arms to escape immune surveillance, making this biology a barrier to NK-based immunotherapy.

Every translating ribosome needs a large subunit, and large ribosomal subunit biogenesis is the assembly line that builds it: processing of the pre-rRNA that becomes 28S and 5.8S, loading of 5S rRNA and the large-subunit proteins, and stepwise maturation through the nucleolus and nucleoplasm to a cytoplasmic particle competent for translation. The pathway sets the ceiling on a cell's protein synthesis capacity, which is why it is tightly coupled to growth signalling and to nucleolar stress responses; defective ribosome assembly releases free proteins such as RPL5 and RPL11 to stabilise p53, and mutations in subunit proteins underlie ribosomopathies with bone marrow failure and developmental defects. AAA-ATPases and GTPases including MDN1, NVL and GTPBP4 drive irreversible remodelling steps, PELP1-TEX10-WDR18 and the RPF2-RRS1 pair act as assembly factors, and EIF6 blocks premature joining with the small subunit. Several members act instead on the mitochondrial large subunit.

Every round of translation initiation requires a 40S subunit, and small ribosomal subunit biogenesis is the nucleolar assembly line that builds one: transcription of the rRNA precursor, its modification and cleavage, loading of the small-subunit proteins, and export of a pre-40S particle to the cytoplasm for final maturation. The small subunit selects mRNA and reads the codon, so the pathway sets a cell's capacity for growth and proliferation. Large multiprotein processome modules built around WD40 proteins such as WDR3, WDR36 and WDR43, together with UTP components, fold the 5' region of pre-rRNA; snoRNP-associated factors including fibrillarin and NOP56 direct methylation and pseudouridylation; and cytoplasmic kinases RIOK1/RIOK2 with TSR1 and LTV1 license the last processing steps. Defects cause ribosomopathies with anaemia and developmental anomalies, and nucleolar stress here stabilises p53 through NPM1 and ribosomal protein sequestration of MDM2.

When a replication fork meets a lesion it cannot copy, the cell can either stall or push through with a polymerase that tolerates damaged templates. Error-prone translesion synthesis takes the second option: specialized low-fidelity polymerases insert nucleotides opposite the lesion so replication can resume, leaving the damage in place and raising the mutation rate. This trade of accuracy for completion preserves fork integrity and cell survival after UV and chemical damage, and it is a major source of the mutation signatures seen in tumours and of resistance to DNA-damaging chemotherapy. Y-family enzymes such as pol eta, iota and kappa perform the insertion step, while REV1 together with the REV3L catalytic subunit and its MAD2L2 partner extends past the lesion; accessory replicative polymerase subunits and PRIMPOL contribute, and deubiquitination by USP1 of PCNA restrains polymerase recruitment.

Purine nucleoside metabolism handles the interconversion, salvage and breakdown of adenosine, inosine, guanosine and their deoxy counterparts, deciding whether a purine is recycled into nucleotides or degraded to uric acid and excreted. This balance supports nucleic acid synthesis at low energetic cost and keeps signalling nucleosides in check, so its failure is unusually visible in medicine: loss of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic deoxyadenosine accumulation, HPRT1 deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with urate overproduction, and xanthine oxidase activity is the step blocked in gout therapy. Kinases such as ADK and DGUOK phosphorylate nucleosides for reuse, phosphoribosyltransferases reattach bases to ribose phosphate, 5'-nucleotidases and the ectoenzyme NT5E run the opposite direction to release nucleosides, and phosphorylase and deaminase steps feed degradation. The extracellular arm generates adenosine that damps immune and vascular responses.

Hair follicles and other keratinized appendages are not static structures: they cycle, destroying and rebuilding their lower portion so that the shaft can be shed and replaced. This molting cycle is what makes hair growth periodic, and its disruption underlies alopecias, hypotrichosis and ectodermal dysplasias in which hair, teeth and sweat glands are all affected. Stem cells in the bulge and their niche are held quiescent or released by competing signals: Wnt ligands and beta-catenin drive anagen entry while secreted inhibitors such as DKK1, DKK4 and SOSTDC1 restrain it, with Hedgehog, Notch, ectodysplasin-EDAR, FGF and BMP/TGF-beta inputs setting the timing and the follicle's regional identity. Transcription factors including HOXC13, LHX2, FOXN1 and DLX3 then specify differentiation of the hair keratins and keratin-associated proteins that form the shaft, while circadian components modulate the pace of cycling.

Cells must match the rate at which they make fatty acids to the supply of carbon and the demand for membranes and stored energy, and this is the control layer that sets that rate. Its outputs determine hepatic lipogenesis, triglyceride export in lipoproteins, and whether excess nutrients become fat; chronic misregulation underlies fatty liver disease, hypertriglyceridaemia and insulin resistance. Sterol-sensing machinery at the endoplasmic reticulum, where SCAP escorts SREBP precursors and the INSIG proteins retain them when lipids are plentiful, works alongside the carbohydrate-responsive factor MLXIPL and the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 to gate transcription of lipogenic enzymes. ERLIN proteins and ubiquitin ligase components add degradative control, SIRT1 and KAT2B impose acetylation-dependent tuning, and several microRNAs including the SREBP-embedded MIR33A trim the output. Apolipoproteins, ANGPTL4 and GPIHBP1 link the programme to circulating lipid handling.

Whether a transcription factor or signalling protein reaches chromatin is itself a regulated decision, and this pathway covers the controls that speed, slow or gate protein import into the nucleus. It is how cells convert events at the membrane into changes in gene expression: NF-kB is held in the cytoplasm by its inhibitor IkBa until degradation frees it, SMAD3 translocates only after TGF-beta receptor phosphorylation, GLI factors are retained by SUFU until Hedgehog signalling through SMO releases them, and 14-3-3 proteins sequester cargo in the cytoplasm through phosphorylation-dependent binding. Core transport machinery -- the RAN GTPase, importins, nucleoporins and the basket protein TPR -- provides the route, while kinases, acetyltransferases and SUMO or ubiquitin marks tune access to it. Mislocalisation of such cargo, as with TDP-43 in neurodegeneration, disconnects signalling from the transcriptional response it should produce.

Many signalling pathways end at the nuclear pore: a transcription factor or kinase sits latent in the cytoplasm until a stimulus licenses its entry, and stimulating that entry is how a cell converts a surface event into a change in gene expression. Positive regulation of protein import into the nucleus covers the events that raise the rate or extent of such translocation, from cargo modification to the transport machinery itself. The RAN GTPase, importin-5 and the nucleoporin TPR provide the shuttling apparatus, while HSP90 and BAG3 chaperone cargoes toward it. Specific arms are recognisable here: TGFB1 driving SMAD3 accumulation in the nucleus, hedgehog ligand and SMO controlling GLI3 entry, and stress kinases such as MAPK14 and PRKCD relaying signals inward. Loss of control over this step blunts transcriptional responses to growth factors, cytokines and innate immune stimuli, and mislocalisation of TARDBP is a hallmark of neurodegeneration.

Many transcription factors and signalling kinases are held inactive simply by being kept out of the nucleus, and this pathway covers the mechanisms that block or slow their nuclear entry. It is a major way cells keep inflammatory, developmental and metabolic programmes silent until a stimulus arrives, and loss of such restraint produces constitutive gene activation. The strategies represented here are varied: NFKBIA masks the nuclear localisation signal of NF-κB and retains it in the cytoplasm until degraded; PKIA and PKIG inhibit protein kinase A catalytic subunits that would otherwise enter the nucleus to phosphorylate CREB; SUFU sequesters GLI transcription factors downstream of Hedgehog reception; and the 14-3-3 proteins YWHAB and YWHAE anchor phosphorylated cargoes in the cytosol. Covalent modifiers such as SUMO1 and UFM1 add a further layer by altering cargo trafficking and localisation.

Narrowing of arteries and arterioles by contraction of their smooth muscle sets vascular resistance and therefore arterial blood pressure and regional blood flow; chronic excess of this response underlies hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, vasospasm and ischaemia, and its acute failure contributes to shock. The genes cover the full arc from agonist to force: circulating and local constrictors such as angiotensin, endothelin, vasopressin, noradrenaline, serotonin and thromboxane, together with their G protein-coupled receptors including AGTR1, EDNRA, the alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenoceptors and TBXA2R; the enzymes that generate or clear them, ACE, ACE2, DBH, ECE1 and TBXAS1; and the downstream calcium handling and cytoskeletal machinery, ATP2B1, SLC8A1, potassium and TRPM4 channels, RHOA with its regulator ARHGAP42, and smooth muscle actin. Endothelial and mechanosensory components such as CAV1 and BMPR2 tune the response, coupling wall tone to systemic haemodynamics.

Widening of arterioles and small vessels by relaxation of their smooth muscle sets local perfusion and systemic blood pressure, matching blood flow to tissue oxygen demand; its failure underlies hypertension, vasospasm, and the endothelial dysfunction of diabetes and atherosclerosis. Much of the signalling converges on nitric oxide made by endothelial and neuronal synthases, which stimulates soluble guanylate cyclase to raise cGMP and activate protein kinase G, lowering smooth muscle calcium sensitivity. Parallel routes act through G protein-coupled receptors for adenosine, bradykinin, beta-adrenergic agonists, angiotensin II via its type 2 receptor, and estrogen, and through natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP. Hyperpolarising potassium channels, including large-conductance calcium-activated and ATP-sensitive channels with their sulfonylurea subunit, relax the vessel directly, while shear-responsive endothelial factors such as KLF2 and gap junction coupling spread the response along the vessel wall.

REM sleep is the phase of the sleep cycle marked by desynchronized cortical activity, vivid dreaming and muscle atonia, and its amount and timing are actively set by neuropeptide and cholinergic signals rather than emerging passively from sleep itself. The genes here act on hypothalamic and brainstem circuits that gate transitions between waking, non-REM and REM states, tuning how often REM bouts occur and how long they last. Growth hormone-releasing hormone promotes sleep alongside its endocrine role, corticotropin-releasing hormone couples stress axis activity to arousal and sleep fragmentation, ghrelin links feeding state to sleep architecture, and the beta-2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit carries cholinergic drive; mutations in this subunit cause a form of sleep-related frontal lobe epilepsy. Disturbance of this control appears as insomnia, REM behaviour disorder and narcolepsy, and connects sleep regulation to neuroendocrine and metabolic rhythms.

regulation of phosphorylation covers the control layer above protein kinases and phosphatases: the ligands, receptors, adaptors, scaffolds, inhibitors and pseudokinases that set how much phosphate is added to a substrate and when. Because phosphorylation gates cell cycle entry, growth, survival, migration and immune activation, this regulation determines whether a cell divides or arrests, and its loss is a route into cancer and inflammatory disease. The genes span growth factor and cytokine inputs such as EGF, FGFs, VEGFA and the interleukins with their receptors, the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR relays, CDK partners and CDK inhibitors like CDKN1A that time mitotic entry, and innate immune kinase modules built on MYD88, IRAK and TRAF adaptors. Counterweights are equally represented: PTEN and PTP-family phosphatases, DUSPs, SOCS proteins, tribbles pseudokinases and PKA regulatory subunits that restrain or redirect kinase output.

Protein phosphorylation is the main switch cells use to relay information, and this collection concerns the upstream control of that switch s- any process that raises or lowers the rate and extent of phosphate addition to substrates. It matters because the amplitude and duration of kinase output determine whether a cell divides, differentiates, survives or dies, and its misregulation underlies cancer and inflammatory disease. Control is exerted at many levels: growth factors and cytokines (EGF, VEGFA, FGFs, IL6, TNF) engage receptor kinases and cytokine receptors; adaptors and scaffolds such as KSR1, CDC37, MYD88 and TRAF6 assemble signalling complexes; cyclin s-CDK partners with CDC25 phosphatases and CDKN1A/CDKN1B inhibitors gate the cell cycle; and counter-regulators including PTEN, PTPN family phosphatases, SOCS proteins, SPRY2 and DUSP7 damp signalling. Also represented are mTOR, MAPK, Hippo kinase and PKA regulatory subunits coordinating growth with nutrient and stress cues.

Phosphorylation is the main currency of intracellular signalling, and the brakes on it are as much a part of signal transduction as the kinases themselves. Negative regulation of phosphorylation covers the many ways cells damp kinase output so that growth factor, cytokine, stress and cell-cycle signals are transient and graded rather than runaway. Several mechanisms are represented: protein tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN1, PTPN2, PTPN22, PTPRC and PTPRJ remove phosphate from receptors and their substrates; DUSP7 acts on MAP kinases; PKIA blocks protein kinase A catalytic activity; DEPTOR and AKT1S1 restrain mTOR complexes; SOCS proteins and ERRFI1 curb cytokine and ErbB receptor signalling; and PTEN reverses PI3K lipid phosphorylation upstream of AKT. Tumour suppressors including RB1, CDKN2A, LATS1/2, APC and MEN1 sit here as well, which is why loss of this restraint underlies much of oncogenic signalling and inflammatory disease.

Phosphorylation is how cells convert an external cue into a rapid change in protein activity, and this grouping collects the ligands, receptors and adaptors that drive kinase activity upward rather than the kinases' housekeeping roles. Positive regulation of phosphorylation covers growth factor and cytokine input at one end and the mitogenic and inflammatory responses at the other: EGF, FGF and VEGF family ligands with their receptor tyrosine kinases, PDGFRB, KIT and FLT3, interleukins and interferon-gamma feeding JAK2, and TNF superfamily receptors working through TRAF and RIPK adaptors. Downstream, RAF-MEK-ERK components, PI3K subunits with AKT1 and MTOR, and MAP3K/MAP2K relays propagate the signal, while Rho-family GTPases and exchange factors couple it to the cytoskeleton. The output is proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, immune activation and cell migration; persistent overactivation of these same relays is a common route to tumour growth.

Taxis is directed cell movement along a gradient of an external cue, and it is how immune cells reach infected tissue, how growth cones find their targets, and how endothelial sprouts follow angiogenic signals. Loss or misdirection of these cues underlies failed host defence, immunodeficiency, malformed neural wiring, and the invasive spread of tumour cells. The genes span the full chemokine ligand and receptor families with their decoy receptors, complement and formyl-peptide receptors that sense bacterial and damage signals, guidance systems built on semaphorins and plexins, slits and their Robo receptors, netrin, ephrins and neuropilins, plus growth factor gradients from VEGF, PDGF and FGF. These inputs converge on Rho-family GTPases, PI3K isoforms, focal adhesion and integrin signalling, and actin regulators such as cortactin and coronins, which polarise the cell and steer protrusion toward or away from the source.

Keratan sulfate proteoglycans are the glycoproteins that keep the corneal stroma transparent and hydrated and that cushion cartilage and intervertebral disc, and this pathway covers both their construction and their breakdown. Chains are elongated by alternating addition of N-acetylglucosamine and galactose, carried out by B3GNT and B4GALT family glycosyltransferases, then sulfated on either sugar by carbohydrate sulfotransferases; sialyltransferases of the ST3GAL family cap and terminate the growing chain. Sulfation determines charge density and therefore water binding and collagen fibril spacing, which is why loss of the corneal-specific GlcNAc 6-O-sulfotransferase CHST6 causes macular corneal dystrophy with progressive clouding of vision. Degradation runs through lysosomal hydrolases including GNS and beta-galactosidase, linking this biology to mucopolysaccharide storage disease when catabolism fails and glycosaminoglycan fragments accumulate.

Vitamin D metabolism converts dietary and skin-derived cholecalciferol into the hormone that governs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation, then disposes of it when enough has acted. Loss of these steps causes rickets and osteomalacia, while excess signalling produces hypercalcaemia. Hepatic 25-hydroxylases such as CYP2R1 and CYP27A1 make the circulating precursor, which travels bound to vitamin D binding protein and is reclaimed in kidney by megalin-mediated endocytosis; renal CYP27B1 performs the activating 1alpha-hydroxylation, and CYP24A1 initiates catabolism by 24-hydroxylation. Glucuronidation and other cytochrome P450 activities provide additional clearance routes. The bone-derived hormone FGF23, acting through FGFR1, suppresses activation and promotes degradation, linking the pathway to phosphate homeostasis, and inflammatory mediators including interferon-gamma and TNF modulate it in macrophages, where local hormone production supports antimicrobial responses.

Vitamin E metabolism governs how the body takes up, distributes and disposes of tocopherols, the lipid-soluble antioxidants that protect membrane polyunsaturated fatty acids from peroxidation. The pathway sets circulating alpha-tocopherol levels and explains why humans retain that form preferentially: a cytosolic transfer protein selects alpha-tocopherol in the liver for secretion into lipoproteins, while a phospholipid transfer protein redistributes it among lipoprotein particles, and an intestinal sterol transporter contributes to its absorption from the gut. Cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4F family initiate omega-hydroxylation of the side chain, committing the less-favoured tocopherols and excess vitamin to catabolism and excretion, and a quinone reductase participates in redox recycling of tocopheryl intermediates. Loss of the hepatic transfer protein causes ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency, linking this handling system to neuronal and erythrocyte membrane integrity.

Vitamin K2, or menaquinone, is supplied largely by intestinal bacteria and acts as the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors and bone matrix proteins; its catabolism sets how much of the vitamin is available to do that work. The route begins with omega-hydroxylation of the polyprenyl side chain by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4F family, which converts the lipid-soluble quinone into a form that can undergo further oxidation and conjugation for excretion. CYP4F2 is the principal vitamin K oxidase, and common variants that lower its activity raise hepatic vitamin K stores and shift the warfarin dose needed for anticoagulation, making this degradation step a pharmacogenetic determinant of anticoagulant response. Related CYP4F members act on overlapping lipid substrates, placing menaquinone breakdown within broader microsomal fat-soluble vitamin and eicosanoid inactivation.

Formation of the fat-soluble vitamins covers two arms represented here: retinoid production and the successive hydroxylations that turn vitamin D into a hormone. BCO1 cleaves dietary beta-carotene to retinal, the precursor of retinol and retinoic acid used in vision and epithelial differentiation, while UBIAD1 synthesises menaquinone-4, the vitamin K form needed for gamma-carboxylation and for protecting membranes from oxidation. The cytochrome P450 enzymes carry the vitamin D route: 25-hydroxylation in liver by CYP2R1 and CYP27A1, activating 1-alpha-hydroxylation by CYP27B1 in kidney and macrophages, and inactivating 24-hydroxylation by CYP24A1, which together set circulating calcitriol and thereby calcium and phosphate handling and bone mineralisation. Inflammatory mediators such as TNF and interferon-gamma, acting through NF-kB, and transcriptional repressors including SNAI1/2 and GFI1 modulate this capacity, linking immune activation to vitamin status. Loss of activating steps causes rickets; loss of catabolism causes hypercalcaemia.

Fat-soluble vitamin catabolic process is the enzymatic destruction of vitamins A, D, E and K, the step that sets how long these lipid-soluble signalling molecules persist in tissues. Because retinoic acid and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D act as hormones on nuclear receptors, their degradation is as much a part of endocrine control as their synthesis: without it, retinoid gradients that pattern the embryonic hindbrain and limb collapse, and unchecked vitamin D signalling drives hypercalcaemia. Cytochrome P450 enzymes do most of the work, with CYP26 family members hydroxylating retinoic acid, CYP24A1 inactivating active vitamin D under FGF23 and phosphate control, and CYP4F2 setting vitamin K tocopherol turnover and thereby warfarin dose requirements. The pathway sits in liver and target-tissue microsomes and links dietary lipid intake to hormone action, mineral homeostasis and xenobiotic metabolism.

Vitamins A, D, E and K are stored rather than excreted, so their levels must be set by controlled destruction as well as by intake. This catabolic arm inactivates fat-soluble vitamins and their hormonally active derivatives, protecting tissues from the teratogenicity of excess retinoic acid and from the hypercalcaemia that follows unchecked vitamin D signalling. Cytochrome P450 enzymes do most of the work: the CYP26 family hydroxylates retinoic acid to set morphogen gradients in the developing embryo, CYP24A1 degrades calcitriol and its precursor, and CYP4F enzymes omega-hydroxylate tocopherol and vitamin K side chains to route them for elimination. The programme is hormonally regulated rather than constitutive, with FGF23 from bone suppressing CYP27B1 and inducing CYP24A1 to lower circulating active vitamin D. Loss of CYP24A1 causes infantile hypercalcaemia; broad-specificity CYP3A4 links this chemistry to drug metabolism.

Water-soluble vitamins arrive from the diet as inactive precursors, and this biosynthetic and activation route converts them into the coenzymes that central metabolism runs on. The genes here cover two branches. One handles vitamin B6: a kinase phosphorylates pyridoxal and related forms, an oxidase converts pyridoxine and pyridoxamine phosphates to pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, and a transaminase-linked step ties the vitamer pool to serine synthesis. The other handles thiamine: dedicated plasma membrane carriers take up thiamine, a mitochondrial carrier delivers the pyrophosphate form to the matrix, and thiamine pyrophosphokinase generates the cofactor used by pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, with further phosphorylation states interconverted. Riboflavin kinase feeds the flavin cofactor pool. Loss of these steps causes thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia, biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease and vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, disorders treatable by supplying the vitamin or its active form.

Vitamin D biosynthesis converts a sterol precursor made in skin into the hormone that governs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation; without it, children develop rickets and adults osteomalacia. The route is a two-step hydroxylation: hepatic 25-hydroxylases, chiefly CYP2R1 with contributions from CYP27A1 and CYP3A4, generate 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and the renal mitochondrial 1-alpha-hydroxylase CYP27B1 produces the active 1,25-dihydroxy form. Flux is bounded by CYP24A1, the 24-hydroxylase that initiates catabolism and inactivation, so loss-of-function on either side yields deficiency states or hypercalcaemia. Production is not purely endocrine: inflammatory mediators such as interferon-gamma and TNF, acting partly through NF-kappaB, induce the activating hydroxylase in macrophages, and transcriptional repressors including GFI1 and the SNAI factors tune expression of these enzymes, linking the pathway to immune regulation as well as mineral homeostasis.

Vitamin K metabolism supplies and recycles the quinone cofactor that allows gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues, the modification that makes prothrombin and the other clotting factors, as well as osteocalcin and matrix Gla protein, able to bind calcium. Without it, coagulation fails and vascular and bone mineralization go unchecked; with it deliberately blocked, anticoagulant therapy works. The carboxylase GGCX consumes reduced vitamin K hydroquinone and generates the epoxide, which VKORC1 reduces to regenerate the active form — the step warfarin inhibits, with VKORC1L1 providing a related activity that supports protection against oxidative damage. Other members handle synthesis and turnover: UBIAD1 converts menadione to menaquinone-4, CYP4F2 and related omega-hydroxylases initiate side-chain degradation to limit vitamin K levels, and quinone reductases including NQO1 and FSP1 offer warfarin-insensitive routes to the hydroquinone.

Vitamin K is the quinone cofactor that lets gamma-carboxylase activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X along with bone and vascular Gla proteins, so the rate at which the body degrades it sets how much is available for that chemistry. Catabolism of vitamin K begins with omega-hydroxylation of the phytyl or prenyl side chain by cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4F family, principally CYP4F2, generating hydroxylated metabolites that are further oxidised and conjugated for biliary and urinary excretion; a carbonyl reductase contributes reduction steps on quinone-derived intermediates. Because this route competes with vitamin K recycling, its activity shapes dietary vitamin K requirements and individual sensitivity to coumarin anticoagulants, with common CYP4F2 variants altering warfarin dose requirements. The same enzymes act on related lipid substrates, placing vitamin K disposal within broader microsomal fat-soluble vitamin and eicosanoid metabolism.

Cells hold an electrical gradient across their membranes, and the machinery gathered here sets and adjusts that voltage, whether across the plasma membrane of an excitable cell or the inner mitochondrial membrane. This control underlies the resting potential, action potential firing and repolarization in neurons, cardiomyocytes and muscle, hormone and neurotransmitter release, and the proton-motive force that drives ATP synthesis. Voltage-gated sodium, potassium and calcium channels act alongside inward rectifier and two-pore potassium channels, HCN pacemaker channels, ligand-gated receptors for glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine and ATP, and electrogenic pumps and exchangers such as Na+/K+-ATPase subunits and sodium-calcium exchangers. Auxiliary subunits, anchoring and scaffolding proteins, kinases and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling tune channel availability. Disruption produces epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia and long QT syndrome, myotonia, deafness and pain disorders, and mitochondrial depolarization that commits a cell to apoptosis or mitophagy.

Amino acids are not only building blocks for protein; cells convert them into dedicated small-molecule cofactors, antioxidants and energy buffers, and this modified amino acid biosynthetic programme covers those conversions. Three themes dominate. Creatine synthesis from arginine and glycine, via GATM and GAMT, feeds the creatine kinase isoenzymes that buffer ATP in muscle, brain and mitochondria. Glutathione production from glutamate, cysteine and glycine by GCLC/GCLM and GSS, supported by cystine and glutamate transporters and by NFE2L2-driven induction, sets the cell's capacity to handle oxidative and electrophilic stress, with gamma-glutamyl transferases recycling the tripeptide. Folate uptake and polyglutamylation, together with one-carbon enzymes such as SHMT1 and MTHFD1, supply methyl and formyl groups for nucleotide and methionine metabolism. Also included are carnitine synthesis from trimethyllysine and the prolyl/lysyl hydroxylation that stabilises collagen, linking these routes to fatty acid oxidation and connective tissue integrity.

Thyroid hormone metabolic processes cover the making, activating, inactivating and clearing of thyroxine and triiodothyronine, the hormones that set basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, and brain and skeletal development. Synthesis requires iodide capture by the sodium-iodide symporter, its organification onto thyroglobulin by thyroid peroxidase using hydrogen peroxide generated by the dual oxidases and their maturation factors, iodotyrosine recycling by the deiodinase-like dehalogenase IYD, and lysosomal cathepsin proteolysis to release hormone; transcription factors such as PAX8 and FOXE1 give the follicular cell its identity. Potency is then tuned peripherally: DIO1 and DIO2 convert thyroxine to active T3 while DIO3 inactivates it, sulfotransferases mark hormone for disposal, and carriers including MCT8 and OATP1C1 move hormone across cell and blood-brain barriers. Failure produces congenital hypothyroidism, goitre, and the severe psychomotor retardation of impaired hormone transport into neurons.

Cristae formation builds and maintains the folded inner membrane compartment where oxidative phosphorylation actually happens. Cristae surface area sets a cell's respiratory capacity, and the narrow cristae junctions sequester cytochrome c so that its release during apoptosis is a controlled event; loss of this architecture produces optic atrophy, cardiomyopathy and mitochondrial encephalopathy. The core work is done by a membrane-shaping scaffold at cristae junctions built around mitofilin and its CHCHD partners, tethered to the outer membrane sorting machinery through SAMM50 so that the two membranes stay in register. Long and short forms of OPA1 govern junction width and inner membrane fusion, with the proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2 cleaving OPA1 in response to stress or loss of membrane potential. Cardiolipin remodelling by tafazzin supplies the lipid curvature the scaffold requires, linking cristae shape to phospholipid metabolism, calcium uptake and mitochondrial quality control.

Cristae are the folded invaginations of the inner mitochondrial membrane where the respiratory chain and ATP synthase are concentrated, and their formation determines how much oxidative phosphorylation capacity a cell has and how readily it can release cytochrome c during apoptosis. The shaping machinery centres on a large inner-membrane complex built around mitofilin (IMMT) with CHCHD3, CHCHD6, APOO and APOOL, which stabilises cristae junctions and, through SAMM50, bridges to the outer membrane to keep the two membranes in register. OPA1 controls junction width and inner-membrane fusion, and is cleaved by the proteases OMA1 and AFG3L2 in response to stress or loss of membrane potential, collapsing cristae structure. Cardiolipin remodelling by tafazzin supplies the lipid environment these curved membranes require. Disruption causes dominant optic atrophy, Barth syndrome, spastic ataxia and broader mitochondrial disease, and links cristae architecture to mitochondrial dynamics and quality control.

Epinephrine is the fight-or-flight hormone of the adrenal medulla, raising heart rate and contractility, dilating airways and mobilising glucose and fatty acids for sudden effort; the reactions that make and dispose of it are what this pathway covers. Synthesis begins with tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step that converts tyrosine to L-DOPA and commits cells to catecholamine production, and ends with phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, which methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine and thereby defines the adrenal chromaffin phenotype as distinct from sympathetic neurons. A copper-transporting ATPase supplies the cofactor needed by dopamine beta-hydroxylase, linking catecholamine output to copper handling. Cytosolic sulfotransferases sulfonate circulating catecholamines, inactivating them and limiting the duration of adrenergic signalling. Disturbed flux through these steps underlies catecholamine-secreting tumours and disorders of autonomic cardiovascular control.

Norepinephrine is the transmitter of sympathetic nerves and of brainstem noradrenergic neurons, and is also released as a hormone from the adrenal medulla; the reactions that make, modify and dispose of it set sympathetic tone, blood pressure, arousal and attention. Synthesis proceeds from tyrosine through the rate-limiting hydroxylase TH and then dopamine β-hydroxylase, a copper enzyme that depends on copper delivery by the ATP7A transporter, while inactivation runs through O-methylation by COMT and sulfonation by SULT1A3/1A4. Transcription factors including GATA3, HAND2, PHOX2-type partners and INSM1 specify the catecholaminergic phenotype, linking this metabolism to sympathoadrenal and neural crest development and to neuroblastoma. Hypoxia signalling through EPAS1 tunes output, and loss of parkin-dependent quality control is tied to degeneration of noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurons. Deficiency of the pathway causes orthostatic hypotension and autonomic failure.

Dopamine biosynthesis supplies the neurotransmitter used by midbrain neurons to shape movement, motivation and reward, and also provides the precursor from which noradrenaline and adrenaline are made. Loss of these neurons and their dopamine output produces the rigidity and bradykinesia of Parkinson's disease, while inherited defects in the synthetic steps cause dopa-responsive dystonia treatable with L-DOPA. Tyrosine hydroxylase performs the rate-limiting hydroxylation and requires tetrahydrobiopterin, whose supply depends on GCH1; aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase then removes the carboxyl group to yield dopamine. Transcriptional control by NR4A2 establishes and maintains the dopaminergic phenotype, and reuptake through the transporter SLC6A3 recycles released transmitter. Several members tie synthesis to neuronal proteostasis and vesicle trafficking, including SNCA, PARK7 and VPS35, all mutated in familial parkinsonism, linking transmitter production to the vulnerability of these cells.</description>

Dopamine metabolism covers the making, packaging, recycling and breakdown of a catecholamine that governs voluntary movement, motivation, reward learning and prolactin release, and that serves as the precursor from which noradrenaline and adrenaline are built. Tyrosine hydroxylase performs the rate-limiting hydroxylation, supported by the tetrahydrobiopterin supply from GCH1, and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase produces dopamine itself; dopamine beta-hydroxylase, a copper enzyme dependent on ATP7A for metal loading, converts it onward to noradrenaline. Signalling through D1- to D4-class receptors transmits the message, while the transporter SLC6A3 clears dopamine from the synapse and monoamine oxidases, COMT and sulfotransferases degrade or conjugate it. Handling this chemistry safely matters because its oxidation products are reactive: several genes here, including PRKN, PARK7, SNCA and VPS35, are mutated in Parkinson disease, where nigrostriatal dopamine neurons are lost and movement fails.

Norepinephrine biosynthesis supplies the transmitter of sympathetic nerves and one of the catecholamines released from the adrenal medulla, driving vasoconstriction, heart rate, arousal and the response to stress; it is also the immediate precursor pool from which epinephrine is made. Two enzymes define the route: tyrosine hydroxylase makes L-DOPA in the rate-limiting step, and dopamine beta-hydroxylase, a copper-dependent monooxygenase, converts dopamine to norepinephrine inside secretory vesicles. That copper must be delivered by the ATP7A transporter, which links catecholamine output to cellular copper handling and explains the neurochemical abnormalities of Menkes disease. Transcription factors including GATA3, HAND2 and INSM1 specify noradrenergic identity during sympathoadrenal development, so this pathway is as much a cell-fate programme as a metabolic one; failure produces orthostatic hypotension and defects in autonomic neuron differentiation.

Serotonin biosynthesis produces 5-hydroxytryptamine, the monoamine that signals as a neurotransmitter in raphe neurons of the brain and as a locally released hormone from gut enterochromaffin cells, where it shapes mood, sleep, appetite, vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation and intestinal motility. The route is short and rate-limited at its first step: tryptophan hydroxylases convert tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan, with the neuronal and peripheral isoforms TPH2 and TPH1 dividing the two pools, and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (DDC) then yields serotonin. DDC and the associated aldehyde-metabolising and catecholamine-synthesising enzymes tie this chemistry to monoamine metabolism more broadly, since the same decarboxylase serves dopamine formation. Loss of tryptophan hydroxylase or decarboxylase activity depletes serotonin and causes movement and autonomic disorders, and the pathway is the upstream source for melatonin synthesis in the pineal gland.

Serotonin metabolic process covers the synthesis, turnover and disposal of 5-hydroxytryptamine, the monoamine that sets mood, sleep, appetite, nociception and gut motility, and that also acts as a circulating hormone shaping platelet function and vascular tone. Tryptophan hydroxylase, in its neuronal and peripheral forms, performs the rate-limiting hydroxylation, and aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase completes synthesis; monoamine oxidases A and B, working with aldehyde dehydrogenases, degrade released serotonin to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, while sulfotransferases conjugate it for excretion. The balance of these steps determines how much transmitter is available at receptors such as the inhibitory autoreceptor HTR1A, linking the pathway to serotonergic tone rather than to any single synapse. Loss of monoamine oxidase A produces excess serotonin with aggressive behaviour, and disturbed turnover is implicated in depression, anxiety and restless legs syndrome.

Serotonin acts as a neurotransmitter in the brain and as a local hormone in gut, platelets and vasculature, and this pathway covers how it is made, inactivated and cleared. Tryptophan hydroxylases carry out the rate-limiting hydroxylation step, with distinct neuronal and peripheral isoforms, and the product is decarboxylated by the aromatic amino acid decarboxylase shared with catecholamine synthesis. Breakdown runs through monoamine oxidases A and B to an aldehyde that aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidise to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, while sulfotransferase conjugation provides an alternative route to excretable metabolites. Levels are further shaped by autoreceptor feedback through the 5-HT1A receptor and by downstream second-messenger turnover. Because serotonergic tone governs mood, sleep, appetite, aggression and gut motility, disruption of these enzymes is tied to depression, anxiety, impulsive behaviour and restless legs syndrome, and the oxidative arm is the target of monoamine oxidase inhibitors.

Compounds built on an indole skeleton — tryptophan and its descendants serotonin, melatonin and the kynurenines — are handled by this branch of amino acid metabolism, which links diet to neurotransmission, circadian physiology, immune tolerance and de novo NAD+ synthesis. One route hydroxylates tryptophan (TPH1, TPH2) and decarboxylates it to serotonin, which is then either degraded by monoamine oxidases, sulfated, or acetylated and O-methylated by AANAT and ASMT to give the pineal hormone melatonin. The larger flux runs through indoleamine and tryptophan dioxygenases (IDO1, IDO2, TDO2) into kynurenine, where KMO, KYNU, HAAO and QPRT generate quinolinic acid and feed nicotinamide nucleotide synthesis, with ACMSD diverting intermediates away. Neuroactive kynurenines act on glutamate receptors, so shifts in this balance are tied to depression, neurodegeneration and tumour immune evasion, and loss of individual enzymes produces inherited metabolic disease.

Formation of indole-containing compounds in humans centres on the tryptophan-derived neurotransmitter serotonin and its conversion to the pineal hormone melatonin. This chemistry sets the tone of mood, appetite, gut motility and vascular constriction, and, through nocturnal melatonin output, entrains circadian and seasonal physiology; loss or pharmacological blockade of its steps underlies both antidepressant action and disorders of sleep timing. Tryptophan hydroxylases, in neuronal and peripheral forms, carry out the rate-limiting ring hydroxylation, and an aromatic amino acid decarboxylase removes the carboxyl group to give serotonin. In the pineal gland an acetyltransferase, whose activity rises at night, and a subsequent O-methyltransferase complete melatonin synthesis. Aldehyde dehydrogenase links to oxidative disposal of the aldehyde intermediates generated when these amines are degraded, while tyrosine hydroxylase reflects the shared monoamine biosynthetic context.

Breakdown of indole-containing compounds is, in human cells, largely the degradation of tryptophan and its amine derivatives, and it serves two ends at once: disposal of surplus amino acid carbon and production of signalling metabolites. The dominant route is the kynurenine pathway, opened by the dioxygenases TDO2, IDO1 and IDO2 that cleave the indole ring, followed by formamidase, kynureninase and kynurenine 3-monooxygenase steps that generate 3-hydroxykynurenine and anthranilate derivatives; HAAO and ACMSD then determine how much flux is diverted toward quinolinate and de novo NAD+ synthesis rather than complete oxidation. Monoamine oxidase and aldehyde dehydrogenase activity handle the indoleamines serotonin and tryptamine. Because tryptophan depletion and kynurenine accumulation suppress T cell responses, this catabolism underlies immune tolerance at tumours and the placenta, while its intermediates are neuroactive and implicated in neurodegeneration and mood disorders.

Pigment metabolism covers the synthesis, transport and breakdown of the colored molecules of the body tdash melanin in skin, hair and eye, heme in red cells and respiratory enzymes, and the bile pigments heme is degraded into. Its outputs determine skin and hair color, ultraviolet protection, oxygen carriage and iron handling. One arm runs melanogenesis inside melanosomes, where tyrosinase and its related enzymes, the transporters OCA2 and SLC45A2 and the structural fibril protein PMEL build eumelanin under melanocortin receptor control; loss of these steps causes oculocutaneous albinism. A second arm is the eight-step tetrapyrrole route from ALAS through porphobilinogen deaminase, uroporphyrinogen and coproporphyrinogen oxidases to ferrochelatase, whose partial failures cause the porphyrias and sideroblastic anemia. Heme oxygenases then open the ring to biliverdin, biliverdin reductases give bilirubin, and glucuronidation plus hepatic uptake transporters clear it, the step that fails in jaundice.

Hormones only act if they are made, activated, and cleared on schedule, and this hormone metabolic programme covers the whole chemical lifetime of steroid, thyroid, retinoid, and peptide signals. It sets circulating levels of cortisol, aldosterone, androgens, oestrogens, thyroxine and angiotensin, so its failure produces congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and hormone-dependent cancers. Steroidogenesis begins with cholesterol delivery by STAR to the mitochondrial side-chain cleavage enzyme, then proceeds through cytochrome P450s, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and reductases to finished ligands for nuclear receptors. Thyroid hormone is built on thyroglobulin by peroxidase and dual oxidases, taken up by iodide and hormone transporters, then activated or inactivated by the deiodinases. Peptide hormones such as proopiomelanocortin are matured by proprotein convertases and carboxypeptidases and degraded by peptidases including ACE, neprilysin and insulin-degrading enzyme. Sulfotransferases and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases terminate signalling by conjugation for excretion.

Hormone biosynthesis covers the enzymatic routes by which specialized endocrine cells manufacture the signalling molecules that regulate metabolism, reproduction, stress responses and growth in distant tissues. Much of this set concerns steroidogenesis: cholesterol is delivered to mitochondria by STAR and cleaved by CYP11A1 with its electron donors FDX1 and POR, after which CYP17A1, CYP21A2, CYP11B1/B2, CYP19A1 and a family of hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and 5-alpha-reductases generate cortisol, aldosterone, androgens and oestrogens. A second arm builds thyroid hormone, where thyroglobulin, thyroperoxidase and dual oxidases support iodination and deiodinases set local T3 levels. Pituitary precursors including POMC, LHB and FSHB, pineal melatonin synthesis via AANAT and ASMT, and transcriptional regulators such as NR5A2 and HIF1A place the chemistry under hierarchical control. Loss of individual steps produces congenital adrenal hyperplasia, disorders of sex development, and congenital hypothyroidism.

Hormone signals must be terminated as well as produced, and this hormone catabolic process covers the enzymatic inactivation and clearance of circulating hormones so that target tissues see a pulse rather than a permanent signal. Its reach spans thyroid, steroid and peptide hormones: the iodothyronine deiodinases convert thyroxine to active T3 or to inactive reverse T3, setting local thyroid hormone tone in brain, placenta and liver independently of the gland itself; sulfotransferase-mediated conjugation of estrogens and steroid oxidoreductase steps limit androgen and estrogen availability in peripheral tissue. Peptide hormone turnover runs through zinc metallopeptidases including neprilysin and insulin-degrading enzyme, which degrade natriuretic peptides, insulin and amyloid-beta, and through endothelin- and angiotensin-converting activities that also generate vasoactive products. Loss of this catabolic capacity produces hormone excess locally, and these enzymes are drug targets in heart failure, prostate disease and hormone-dependent cancer.

Progesterone metabolism covers the making, interconversion and disposal of the steroid that prepares the endometrium for implantation and sustains pregnancy, and the same chemistry feeds the precursor pool for androgens, glucocorticoids and neurosteroids. Synthesis begins with cholesterol delivery and side-chain handling in steroidogenic mitochondria, with lipid transfer and sterol carrier proteins supplying substrate, and 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converting pregnenolone to progesterone. Its fate is then decided by competing enzymes: 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase diverts it toward androgen synthesis, 5-alpha-reductase and the aldo-keto reductases of the AKR1C family reduce it to allopregnanolone-type and other inactive or neuroactive metabolites, setting how much active hormone reaches receptors. Gonadotropins LH and FSH drive the ovarian arm, placing this metabolism under hypothalamic-pituitary control. Disordered flux contributes to luteal insufficiency, infertility, congenital adrenal hyperplasia and hormone-responsive cancers.

Cells obtain most of their purine nucleosides and nucleotides by recycling rather than building them from scratch, and this biosynthetic and salvage biology is what keeps adenosine, inosine and guanosine pools balanced against the demands of nucleic acid synthesis and energy metabolism. Extracellular AMP is dephosphorylated to adenosine by the ecto-5'-nucleotidase CD73, adenosine is either rephosphorylated by adenosine kinase or deaminated by adenosine deaminase to inosine, and phosphorylases release free bases from nucleosides, including the methylthioadenosine salvage step that feeds back into polyamine and methionine metabolism. Phosphoribosyltransferases such as HPRT1 and APRT then return hypoxanthine, guanine and adenine to the nucleotide pool. Loss of these activities is consequential: ADA deficiency destroys developing lymphocytes and causes severe combined immunodeficiency, HPRT1 loss produces hyperuricaemia with neurological disease, and altered adenosine output reshapes purinergic signalling and immune suppression in tissues and tumours.

Ribonucleoside catabolism is the salvage-or-dispose arm of nucleotide metabolism, dismantling adenosine, inosine, guanosine and uridine into bases, ribose phosphate and ultimately urate. It keeps nucleoside pools from accumulating to toxic levels and feeds ribose-1-phosphate and free bases back toward salvage or excretion. Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine to inosine, purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves inosine and guanosine to hypoxanthine and guanine, and xanthine dehydrogenase carries out the final oxidations to urate; uridine phosphorylases handle the pyrimidine side. The consequences of failure are clinically stark: loss of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through accumulation of deoxyadenosine metabolites toxic to lymphocytes, ADA2 deficiency produces a vasculitic inflammatory syndrome, and purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency likewise impairs T cell immunity. Because adenosine is itself an immunosuppressive signalling molecule, these enzymes also set extracellular adenosine tone and thereby shape immune and vascular responses.

Rod and cone photoreceptors are the retinal neurons that convert light into electrical signals, and their development builds the most elaborate specialisation in the eye: a stacked outer segment packed with phototransduction machinery, connected to the cell body by a modified cilium. The genes here cover the two halves of that programme. Transcription factors including NRL, NR2E3, RORB, PRDM1 and PAX6 commit progenitors to photoreceptor fate and choose between rod and cone identity, while ciliary transport and outer-segment structural components — CEP290, RPGR and its interactor RPGRIP1, intraflagellar transport subunits, PRPH2 and ROM1, TULP1, RP1 — deliver and organise opsins and the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel and phosphodiesterase subunits that carry out phototransduction. Disruption of these steps causes retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, cone dystrophies and the retinal degeneration of syndromic ciliopathies such as Bardet-Biedl and Usher syndrome.

Eye photoreceptor cell development builds the rod and cone cells of the retina, the sensory neurons that convert light into neural signals and make vision possible. Its failure is the origin of inherited blindness: retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Usher syndrome and cone dystrophies all trace to genes acting here. The pathway combines transcriptional fate specification, in which NRL, NR2E3, RORB and PRDM1 act downstream of PAX6 to choose rod over cone identity, with the structural elaboration that follows. Ciliary and transport proteins including CEP290, RPGR, RPGRIP1, BBS4 and TULP1 assemble the connecting cilium and traffic opsins into the outer segment, while CRB1 and MYO7A organise apical polarity and photoreceptor-Muller glia adhesion. Phototransduction components such as GNAT1, GNAT2 and PDE6C mark the terminal differentiated state, linking morphogenesis directly to sensory function and outer segment maintenance.

Rods and cones are the light-detecting neurons of the retina, and this programme covers their specification, polarisation and the construction of the outer segment where phototransduction occurs. Its output is vision itself: when it fails, photoreceptors are born but cannot build or maintain their light-sensing compartment, and the result is retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, cone dystrophy or Usher syndrome with combined deafness and blindness. Transcription factors including PAX6, NRL, NR2E3, RORB and PRDM1 commit progenitors and then decide between rod and cone identity, while ciliary and connecting-cilium proteins such as CEP290, RPGR, RPGRIP1, BBS4 and TULP1 traffic opsins and other cargo into the outer segment. Apical junction components CRB1 and CRB2 organise the outer limiting membrane, MYO7A and USH1C serve the photoreceptor–pigment epithelium interface, and transducin subunits with PDE6C carry the light signal onward.

Building the ear means shaping three linked structures: the pinna and external canal, the middle ear ossicles and cavity, and the inner ear labyrinth that houses the organs of hearing and balance. Ear morphogenesis converts otic placode induction and pharyngeal arch patterning into that final anatomy, and its disruption produces microtia, ossicular malformation, vestibular dysfunction and congenital deafness, often as part of syndromes such as branchio-oto-renal or CHARGE. Transcription factors including EYA1, SIX1, PAX2, GATA3 and DLX5/6 specify otic and arch territories, while FGF, WNT and endothelin signalling position and elaborate them. Planar cell polarity components such as VANGL2 and SCRIB orient hair cell stereocilia, ATOH1 drives hair cell fate, and structural and mechanotransduction proteins including MYO7A, CDH23, USH1C and TECTA assemble the hair bundle and tectorial membrane that make sound detection possible.

Hearing and balance depend on an elaborate fluid-filled labyrinth being carved out of a simple ectodermal placode, and inner ear morphogenesis is the programme that builds it. It patterns the otic vesicle into cochlea, vestibule and semicircular canals, specifies sensory patches, and positions the hair cells and supporting cells of each organ; when it fails the result is congenital deafness, vestibular dysfunction and malformed canals, as in syndromic forms involving CHD7 or EYA1 and SIX1. Regional identity comes from transcription factors such as PAX2, GATA3, DLX5/6 and TBX1, acting with FGF and WNT signals, while ATOH1 and POU4F3 commit and mature hair cells. Planar cell polarity components including VANGL2 and SCRIB orient stereociliary bundles, and structural and mechanotransduction proteins — cadherin-23, myosin VII, harmonin, whirlin, tectorin — assemble the bundle and its extracellular matrix. Ion-transport genes establish the endolymph needed for transduction.

Shaping of the outer ear — the pinna and the external auditory canal that funnel sound to the eardrum — depends on this morphogenetic programme, which patterns the first and second pharyngeal arches and the neural crest–derived mesenchyme that fills them. Because the same signals build the jaw, middle ear ossicles and facial skeleton, its disruption produces the recognisable craniofacial syndromes of microtia, preauricular pits and conductive hearing loss, often alongside cardiac outflow and branchial defects. Transcriptional regulators set arch identity and boundaries: TBX1 and HOXA1 specify pharyngeal territory, EYA1 acts in otic and branchial development, and TWIST1 governs cranial neural crest and mesenchymal condensation. FGFR1 signalling through the ERK kinases MAPK1 and MAPK3 relays epithelial growth cues into the underlying mesenchyme, coupling outgrowth and survival to the positional information that determines final ear form.

Hearing depends on a lever system of three tiny bones that carries tympanic membrane vibration to the fluid of the inner ear, and middle ear morphogenesis is the embryonic programme that builds them along with the tympanic cavity and Eustachian tube. The ossicles and their supporting structures derive from neural crest and mesoderm of the first and second pharyngeal arches, so this biology is patterning of the proximal arch skeleton: endothelin signalling through its receptor establishes ventral arch identity, homeodomain and transcription factor codes including HOXA2, GSC, NKX3-2, MSX1, PRRX1 and the EYA1/SIX network assign each element its shape and position, and BMP antagonism by noggin and FGF receptor signalling shape cartilage condensation. Failure produces conductive hearing loss and the ear anomalies seen in craniofacial syndromes such as branchio-oto-renal and 22q11 deletion, linking middle ear defects to broader pharyngeal arch malformation.

Tooth development builds an organ of dentin capped by enamel from an epithelial thickening in the jaw, and this programme covers the whole trajectory from placode induction through cusp patterning to terminal mineralization. Reciprocal signalling between oral epithelium and neural crest-derived mesenchyme drives it: hedgehog, BMP, FGF, WNT and ectodysplasin cues are read out by transcription factors such as MSX1, DLX, RUNX2 and PAX-family partners that specify tooth number, position and shape. Later stages depend on secreted matrix proteins and their processing enzymes, including amelogenin, enamelin, ameloblastin, dentin sialophosphoprotein, the kallikrein and MMP20 proteases, and FAM20 kinases, together with ion transporters that supply calcium and control pH for crystal growth. Loss of individual components causes tooth agenesis, hypodontia in ectodermal dysplasia syndromes, amelogenesis or dentinogenesis imperfecta, and enamel that is thin, soft or discoloured.

Tooth development turns a patch of oral epithelium and underlying neural crest mesenchyme into an enamel-capped, root-anchored organ, and the same genes explain why teeth fail to form, erupt, or mineralise. Reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signalling drives it: sonic hedgehog, BMPs, FGFs, Wnt/beta-catenin with LEF1 and AXIN2, and ectodysplasin through EDAR set tooth number, position and cusp shape, read out by transcription factors such as MSX1, PAX9, PITX2, DLX family members and RUNX2 with SP7. Later stages build matrix and mineral, with amelogenin, ambn and enamelin secreted by ameloblasts and processed by MMP20 and KLK4, dentine sialophosphoprotein and DMP1 laid down by odontoblasts, and alkaline phosphatase, PHEX and FAM20C controlling phosphate handling. Osteoclast genes including RANKL and TCIRG1 permit eruption. Mutations here cause hypodontia, ectodermal dysplasia, amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta.

Teeth form from reciprocal signalling between oral epithelium and neural crest-derived mesenchyme, and this pathway covers the inputs that set where, when and how many teeth develop and how far each one progresses. Its outputs are tooth number, crown shape and the differentiation of enamel- and dentin-forming cells; disruption produces tooth agenesis, supernumerary teeth and enamel defects, and in humans mutations in PAX9, MSX1 and WNT10A are recognised causes of missing teeth. The regulators here span the main morphogen families that pattern the dental placode and enamel knot — hedgehog signalling through SHH, BMP2 and BMP4, FGF8, and WNT ligands with their modulators RSPO2 and APCDD1 — feeding into transcription factors such as RUNX2 and SP6 that drive odontoblast and ameloblast programmes. The same machinery links tooth development to wider craniofacial patterning and to bone and mineralised tissue formation.

Teeth form through a reciprocal dialogue between oral epithelium and neural crest-derived dental mesenchyme, and this grouping covers the signals that drive that programme forward — promoting tooth bud initiation, cusp patterning, and the differentiation of odontoblasts and ameloblasts that lay down dentin and enamel. Loss of these inputs produces tooth agenesis or malformed crowns; MSX1 mutations in particular cause familial hypodontia, and BMP2 signalling from the enamel knot is a classic inducer of dental mesenchyme. TGFB1 and EDN1 contribute growth-factor and peptide cues shaping craniofacial mesenchyme, while CSF1 supports the osteoclast and macrophage activity needed for alveolar bone remodelling and tooth eruption. NGFR marks dental pulp and periodontal progenitors, linking this developmental programme to the stem cell populations that support dentin repair after injury.

Teeth form from reciprocal signalling between oral epithelium and neural crest-derived mesenchyme, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how many teeth develop, where they are placed, and how far their mineralized dentin-bearing crowns and roots mature. Control here determines tooth number and shape: loss of WNT10A or of the WNT amplifier RSPO2 causes tooth agenesis and abnormal crown morphology, while APCDD1 acts as a negative feedback brake on WNT signalling. BMP2 and BMP4 together with FGF8 pattern the dental placode and enamel knot, and RUNX2 drives the differentiation of odontoblasts and the surrounding bone, its haploinsufficiency producing supernumerary and unerupted teeth. CSF1 and the osteoprotegerin gene TNFRSF11B tie the programme to osteoclast biology, which is what allows alveolar bone remodelling and tooth eruption to proceed on schedule.

Mechanoreceptor differentiation is the route by which an unspecialized progenitor becomes a cell that converts mechanical force into electrical signalling and passes it to the central nervous system; in humans this is dominated by the hair cells of the cochlea and vestibular organs, and its failure is a common cause of congenital deafness and balance disorder. A proneural transcription factor programme centred on ATOH1 and POU4F3 commits the cell, while Notch-mediated lateral inhibition through DLL1, JAG1/2, RBPJ and HES/HEY effectors sets the alternating pattern of sensory and supporting cells, with FGF, BMP and planar polarity signalling orienting them. Differentiation then builds the transducing apparatus itself: stereocilia tip links and rootlets from cadherin-23, the Usher syndrome proteins, MYO7A, TRIOBP and whirlin, tip-link-associated channel components such as TMC1 and LHFPL5, and ciliogenesis factors needed for the kinocilium. Neurotrophin receptors support the sensory neurons that innervate them.

Hearing depends on a small number of cochlear hair cells, and this is the programme by which unspecialized epithelial progenitors in the inner ear become auditory receptor cells. Its output is irreplaceable in mammals: hair cells lost to mutation, noise or age are not regenerated, and failure of the programme causes congenital and progressive sensorineural deafness. Commitment turns on the transcription factor ATOH1 acting with POU4F3, while Notch signalling through DLL1, JAG1/JAG2, RBPJ and the HES/HEY repressors enforces lateral inhibition so that hair cells alternate with supporting cells rather than forming in blocks. Differentiation then builds the mechanotransduction apparatus itself — tip-link cadherins CDH23 and PCDH-associated Usher proteins USH1C, MYO7A and WHRN, the stereocilia rootlet and crosslinking proteins TRIOBP and STRC, and the TMC1/LHFPL5 channel complex — alongside planar polarity and hair-bundle orientation cues. Many of these genes are individually mutated in syndromic and non-syndromic hearing loss.

Gamma-delta T cell differentiation is the branch of thymic development in which an uncommitted progenitor adopts the features of a T cell bearing a gamma-delta rather than an alpha-beta receptor. The cells produced are tissue-resident lymphocytes of skin, gut and lung epithelia that respond rapidly to stress ligands and microbial metabolites without classical MHC presentation, contributing an early layer of barrier immunity and wound surveillance; their loss or misdirection shifts the balance of thymic output and weakens epithelial defence. Receptor-proximal signalling through LCK, SYK and the CD45 phosphatase encoded by PTPRC sets the strength of selection that steers a precursor toward this fate, cytokine signalling via STAT5A and STAT5B sustains expansion, and transcriptional regulators including SOX13, SOX4, TCF7 and LEF1 specify the lineage and its effector subsets. Chemokine receptor and Notch-ligand components couple commitment to migration and thymic niche interactions.

STAT transcription factors only become active when a tyrosine near their C-terminus is phosphorylated, so controlling the frequency and extent of that modification is how cells set the gain on cytokine signalling. The pathway determines whether an immune cell responds to an interleukin or interferon by proliferating, differentiating into a particular helper subset, or shutting down inflammation, and it governs haematopoietic and neural trophic responses as well. Most members are ligands and receptors that recruit JAK kinases upon engagement — interferon gamma, IL-4 with its receptor, the IL-10 receptor pair, IL-7, IL-21, oncostatin M, ciliary neurotrophic factor — alongside receptor tyrosine kinases such as KIT, FLT3, CSF1R and FGFR3 that also feed into STAT activation. Negative regulation matters equally: the phosphatase PTPN2 removes the activating phosphate. Dysregulation here produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity and the constitutive STAT activation typical of myeloproliferative and leukaemic states.

Cytokine receptors signal by having JAK kinases phosphorylate a tyrosine on STAT transcription factors, and this grouping covers the braking mechanisms that limit that step. Damping STAT tyrosine phosphorylation sets how long and how strongly a cell responds to interleukins and interferons; without it, signalling runs unopposed, a state linked to lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, and its components are also exploited by tumours to blunt immune signalling. The mechanisms represented are heterogeneous: PTPN2 is a nonreceptor tyrosine phosphatase that dephosphorylates JAKs and STATs directly, while receptor and ligand components such as IL7, IL7R and the shared gamma chain IL2RG contribute to feedback and competition that reduce downstream STAT activation. PARP14 and PIBF1 act as modulators of STAT-dependent responses, placing this regulation within cytokine control of lymphocyte growth, differentiation and immune tolerance.

Handling of benzene rings and their derivatives draws together xenobiotic detoxification and the catabolism of aromatic amino acids. Cytochrome P450 enzymes, notably CYP2E1 and CYP1B1, oxidise benzene and related aromatics to epoxides and phenols; epoxide hydrolase opens the reactive intermediates and glutathione S-transferases of the mu class conjugate them for excretion. The same chemistry explains benzene's toxicity, since incomplete clearance leaves quinones and semiquinones that damage marrow DNA and cause aplastic anaemia and leukaemia, and why GSTM1 deletion alters individual susceptibility. In parallel, the kynurenine route degrades tryptophan through indoleamine and tryptophan dioxygenases, kynurenine monooxygenase, kynureninase and aminotransferases to quinolinic and anthranilic acids, feeding NAD synthesis and generating immunoregulatory and neuroactive metabolites; phenylalanine and tyrosine breakdown converges via fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, whose loss causes tyrosinaemia.

Cells exposed to rising external salt must defend their volume and protein stability or shrink, arrest and die, and the hyperosmotic salinity response is the sensing-and-adaptation programme that prevents that. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where the concentrating mechanism routinely subjects tubular cells to extreme NaCl and urea; the same logic applies to any epithelium facing a salty lumen. Adaptation is partly osmolyte accumulation, with aldose reductase converting glucose to sorbitol as a compatible solute, and partly mechanical, with the TRPV4 cation channel transducing osmotic and stretch cues into calcium entry. Calcium handling extends into mitochondria through the uniporter regulator MICU1, a carrier of the mitochondrial solute family, and LETM1, linking osmotic stress to organelle volume and metabolic output. Contributions from gluconeogenic and ion-transport components, and from DNA-damage-tolerant repair proteins, reflect the metabolic and genotoxic burden that hypertonicity imposes.

Hemoglobin biosynthesis is the coordinated production of globin chains and their heme cofactors in developing erythroid cells, the step that gives red blood cells their capacity to carry oxygen from lung to tissue. It matters because the two halves must be matched: unpaired globin or unliganded iron is toxic, and failures of the pathway produce sideroblastic anemia, porphyria and ineffective erythropoiesis. Erythroid-specific ALAS2 initiates heme synthesis from glycine and succinyl-CoA, ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX, and mitochondrial transporters including SLC25A37 and ABCB10 supply iron and support the pathway inside the mitochondrion. Erythropoietin and hypoxia-responsive signalling raise output when oxygen is scarce, while transcriptional regulators such as KLF4 and the LDB1-containing complex organise globin gene expression. EIF2AK1 provides the translational brake that suppresses globin synthesis when heme is limiting.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a damaging oxidant and a diffusible second messenger, and this pathway covers how cells sense and respond to it, determining whether they detoxify the insult, adapt, or die. It matters for ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation, neurodegeneration and ageing, where sustained peroxide exposure overwhelms the response. Catalase, glutathione and thioredoxin peroxidases, superoxide dismutases and peroxiredoxins remove the oxidant, while NFE2L2 drives an antioxidant transcriptional programme that includes heme oxygenase. Redox-sensitive kinases such as MAP3K5 and SRC-family members, along with NF-kB signalling through RELA, convert oxidation into changes in gene expression, and TRPM2 channels translate it into calcium entry. When damage persists, the same signals engage apoptosis via caspase-3 and mitochondrial permeability, necroptosis through RIPK1/RIPK3, or autophagy. Sirtuin and AMPK components tie the response to metabolic and stress-adaptive control.

Once a neuron has been born and has sent out its processes, it must still become functional: express the right ion channels, build synapses that work, refine connectivity, and settle into a stable transmitter phenotype. Neuron maturation covers that final acquisition of functional competence, distinct from the shape changes of morphogenesis, and it determines whether circuits fire and signal correctly rather than whether they merely exist. Contributors here span potassium channel subunits and their accessory proteins that set firing properties, adhesion and axon-glia molecules that organise nodal and juxtaparanodal domains, trophic signalling through NGF and RET, and transcriptional and chromatin regulators such as MECP2, KDM1A and ACTL6B that lock in mature gene expression. Complement components and neuron-microglia cues contribute to synaptic refinement. Disruption underlies intellectual disability and autism-spectrum syndromes, Rett syndrome and neurodegenerative vulnerability.

Cells deliberately make superoxide, the one-electron reduction product of oxygen, both as a weapon and as a signal. In neutrophils and macrophages this is the respiratory burst that kills ingested bacteria and fungi; loss of the phagocyte oxidase causes chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent infection and granuloma formation. The core machinery is a membrane flavocytochrome, CYBB with CYBA, activated by assembly of the cytosolic subunits NCF1, NCF2 and NCF4 together with a Rho-family GTPase, RAC1 or RAC2. Related catalytic subunits including NOX1, NOX4, NOX5 and the dual oxidases extend the same chemistry to epithelium, thyroid and vasculature, where the anion and its derivatives act as second messengers in growth factor, angiotensin and integrin responses. Upstream cues arrive through pattern-recognition and chemoattractant receptors and kinases such as SYK and protein kinase C; superoxide dismutases set the limit on how far the signal spreads.

Metabolism of pteridine-containing compounds covers two linked cofactor economies: folates, which carry one-carbon units, and tetrahydrobiopterin, which supplies reducing equivalents to aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthase. Both underpin nucleotide synthesis, methionine regeneration and neurotransmitter production, so loss of either causes megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects, hyperphenylalaninaemia or dopa-responsive dystonia. Dietary folate is taken up by a receptor and by proton- and reduced-folate transporters, trimmed or extended by glutamate carboxypeptidase and folylpolyglutamate synthase, reduced by dihydrofolate reductase, then interconverted among formyl, methylene and methyl forms by serine hydroxymethyltransferases, MTHFD enzymes and MTHFR before methionine synthase transfers the methyl group to homocysteine. A parallel branch built on GCH1, PTS and sepiapterin reductase makes biopterin de novo, with QDPR and the pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratases regenerating it after each hydroxylation cycle. Thymidylate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase are long-standing chemotherapy targets here.

Pteridines are the bicyclic cores of two cofactor families that cells cannot do without: tetrahydrofolate, which carries one-carbon units for purine and thymidylate synthesis and methionine regeneration, and tetrahydrobiopterin, the cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthases. Biosynthesis and salvage of pteridine-containing compounds therefore sits upstream of nucleotide supply, methylation capacity, and the production of dopamine, serotonin and nitric oxide. GTP cyclohydrolase I commits GTP to the pterin route, with pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase and sepiapterin reductase completing biopterin, while PCBD1 and QDPR regenerate the reduced cofactor after hydroxylase turnover. On the folate side, receptor- and transporter-mediated uptake feeds dihydrofolate reductase and polyglutamylation, which traps folates intracellularly for the one-carbon interconversions run by MTHFD1 and ATIC. Defects cause dopa-responsive dystonia, atypical hyperphenylalaninemia, and folate malabsorption; the same enzymes are targets of antifolate chemotherapy.

Folates and related pteridines must be turned over as well as used, and this catabolic route disposes of one-carbon-loaded and dead-end folate species so that the usable tetrahydrofolate pool stays productive. Its central activity is 10-formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase, present as cytosolic and mitochondrial forms, which oxidises the formyl group to CO2 and regenerates tetrahydrofolate, thereby setting how much formate-derived one-carbon unit is spent on purine and methionine synthesis versus simply discarded. The cytosolic enzyme is abundant in liver and is lost in many tumours, linking this pathway to proliferative one-carbon demand. A phosphopantetheinyl transferase supplies the carrier modification that the dehydrogenase's acyl-carrier-like domain requires for activity. Methenyltetrahydrofolate synthetase salvages 5-formyltetrahydrofolate, a metabolically inert reservoir, back into the active cycle, so breakdown and recovery of pteridine cofactors are handled together.

Vitamin A cannot be made by animals, so retinol metabolism is how dietary carotenoids and retinyl esters are converted into the forms cells actually use: 11-cis-retinal for vision and all-trans retinoic acid for transcriptional control of growth and patterning. Provitamin A is cleaved by BCO1, retinol is esterified for storage in hepatic stellate cells and retinal pigment epithelium by LRAT and acyltransferases, mobilised again by lipases and carboxylesterases, and carried in blood on RBP4. Short-chain dehydrogenases and alcohol dehydrogenases interconvert retinol and retinaldehyde, ALDH1A enzymes commit retinaldehyde irreversibly to retinoic acid, and cytochrome P450s degrade it to limit signalling. RPE65 regenerates the 11-cis chromophore of the visual cycle; its failure causes early-onset retinal dystrophy, while deficient retinoid supply impairs epithelial maintenance, immunity and embryonic development.
