Retinoic acid is the hormonally active derivative of vitamin A, and its metabolism sets the local concentration that patterns embryos and maintains epithelia. Retinol drawn from carotenoid cleavage and retinol-binding proteins is oxidised to retinaldehyde by alcohol and retinol dehydrogenases such as RDH10 and the ADH enzymes, then irreversibly oxidised to all-trans retinoic acid by the ALDH1A aldehyde dehydrogenases. Intracellular binding proteins including CRABP2 and RBP1 chaperone the ligand toward nuclear retinoic acid receptors, while the CYP26 family hydroxylates it for degradation and UGT glucuronidation completes disposal; several broad-specificity cytochromes P450 contribute additional oxidation. Because synthesis and catabolism are expressed in opposing domains, the balance creates the gradients that guide hindbrain segmentation, limb and germ cell development. Excess or deficiency is teratogenic, and this same chemistry governs the clearance of retinoid drugs used in acne and leukaemia.

Retinal is the aldehyde form of vitamin A, and its metabolism supplies both the chromophore that opsins need to detect light and the precursor for retinoic acid, the signal that patterns embryonic tissues. The genes here cover the whole route: carotenoid cleavage enzymes such as BCO1 generate retinal from dietary provitamin A, RBP4 carries retinoid in plasma, short-chain dehydrogenases and reductases including RDH10, RDH11 and DHRS4 interconvert retinal and retinol, and aldehyde dehydrogenases of the ALDH1A family oxidise retinal irreversibly to retinoic acid. In the eye, RPE65 isomerises retinyl esters to regenerate 11-cis-retinal for the visual cycle, while ABCA4 clears retinaldehyde adducts from photoreceptor discs; its loss causes Stargardt macular degeneration, and RPE65 mutations cause congenital blindness. Disturbed retinal handling also affects skin, immune and developmental retinoic acid signalling.

Cross-presentation lets an antigen-presenting cell display peptides taken up from outside the cell on MHC class I, so that CD8 T cells can be primed against viruses that never infected the presenting cell and against tumour antigens acquired from dying cells. Dendritic cells are defined in large part by this capacity, and vaccine and checkpoint strategies depend on it. Internalised protein reaches endosomal and phagosomal compartments where thiol reductase activity and controlled proteolysis limit degradation, and immunoproteasome subunits such as PSMB10 generate peptides suited to class I binding; an aminopeptidase then trims them before loading onto molecules such as HLA-A. Fc and C-type lectin receptors route immune complexes and glycosylated cargo into the appropriate compartments, linking antibody-mediated uptake to cytotoxic T cell priming rather than to antibody help alone.

Cells and whole organisms hold their internal conditions steady — ion and pH balance, water content, metal and lipid levels, redox state, temperature, glucose and energy supply, cell numbers — and this homeostatic programme is the collected machinery that does it. Its scope is visible in the gene membership: transporters and channels that set sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, zinc, copper and iron gradients, vacuolar ATPase subunits that acidify organelles, aquaporins for water, ferritins, hepcidin and transferrin receptors for iron, metallothioneins for metal buffering, peroxiredoxins and thioredoxin reductases for redox control, plus hormones and receptors such as insulin, leptin, parathyroid hormone, vasopressin and natriuretic peptides that coordinate whole-body set points. Sensing is coupled to correction through AMPK, mTOR, HIF and nuclear receptor signalling, feedback loops on transcription, and apoptotic or autophagic removal of excess cells. Failure produces diabetes, anaemia, hypertension, renal salt-wasting and neurodegenerative disease.

When nutrients run short, cells and tissues switch from growth to self-preservation, and this starvation response is the programme that makes the switch. Amino acid and energy sensing converge on mTORC1 through the Rag GTPases, GATOR/KICSTOR components, Sestrins, CASTOR1 and the TSC complex, while AMPK subunits report a falling energy charge; both arms release ULK1/ULK2 to initiate autophagy. Downstream, the class III PI3K complex with Beclin-1, the ATG conjugation machinery, LC3/GABARAP proteins, WIPI and SNARE factors build autophagosomes and fuse them with lysosomes, with TFEB driving lysosomal biogenesis. In parallel, GCN2 and PERK trigger eIF2α phosphorylation and an ATF4/CHOP transcriptional output, and PPARA, PGC-1α, FOXO and SIRT1 shift metabolism toward fatty acid oxidation, ketogenesis and gluconeogenesis. Failure of these responses underlies fasting intolerance, and their chronic activation supports tumour cell survival.

Fear responses let an animal detect threat and mount defensive behaviour — freezing, startle, avoidance, autonomic arousal — and then update that behaviour as danger passes. The genes here map onto the amygdala–hippocampal–prefrontal circuitry that acquires, stores and extinguishes aversive memories, and their disruption underlies anxiety disorders, panic, and post-traumatic stress. Monoamine machinery (dopamine beta-hydroxylase, COMT, adrenergic and serotonergic receptors including HTR1A) sets arousal tone, while corticotropin-releasing hormone with its receptor CRHR1 and urocortin couple threat perception to the stress axis. Fast synaptic components — kainate and metabotropic glutamate receptors, a GABA-A subunit, acid-sensing channels responsive to pH shifts in amygdala neurons — and translational control through eIF4E and S6 kinase support the plasticity that consolidates fear learning. Neuropeptide signalling via gastrin-releasing peptide and enkephalin, and transcriptional regulators such as MECP2 and MEF2C, shape circuit development and restraint of fear.

Hair follicles do not grow continuously; each one cycles through a growth phase, a regression phase, quiescence and shedding, and the timing of those transitions is what this regulatory programme sets. Control of the hair cycle determines coat density and renewal, and its disruption produces alopecia, hypotrichosis, abnormal hair shafts and, in the follicle stem cell compartment, loss of regenerative capacity. Wnt ligands and their DKK antagonists, Hedgehog signalling through SMO, and TGF-beta/SMAD4 input drive entry into and exit from anagen, while transcription factors such as FOXN1 and MSX2 specify differentiation of the shaft and inner root sheath. Circadian components including CLOCK, BMAL1 and PER1 gate the speed of these transitions, tying follicle cycling to the cell cycle clock. Additional keratin, cadherin and plakophilin genes anchor the growing shaft, and TNF-TRADD signalling contributes to catagen regression.

anagen is the active growth phase of the hair cycle, the period in which the follicle rebuilds its lower portion, matrix keratinocytes proliferate, and a new hair shaft is produced and extended; its duration sets how long scalp hair can grow before regression and shedding. Entry into and maintenance of this phase depends on Wnt/β-catenin signalling between the dermal papilla and follicular stem cells, with WNT10B and WNT5A acting as mesenchymal-epithelial cues and CTNNB1 transducing them into hair-follicle fate. Adhesion and epidermal barrier components such as the integrin-linked adaptor FERMT1 and the protease inhibitor SPINK5 tie follicle growth to the surrounding epithelium, and their loss produces poikiloderma with hair defects and Netherton syndrome. Disrupted anagen entry or premature exit underlies alopecia and chemotherapy-induced hair loss.

Hair grows only during anagen, the active phase of the hair cycle in which the follicle rebuilds its lower portion, the matrix proliferates, and a new shaft is produced and pushed outward; in human scalp hair this phase can last several years and so sets hair length. Entry into and maintenance of this phase depends on Wnt signalling to the follicular stem cell and dermal papilla compartments, with WNT10B and WNT5A acting as ligands and CTNNB1 as the transcriptional effector that drives hair placode and matrix fate. Adhesion and epidermal barrier components such as the focal adhesion protein FERMT1 and the protease inhibitor SPINK5 link follicle growth to the integrity of the surrounding epithelium. Failure of anagen entry, or premature exit into regression and rest, produces thinning and alopecia, while its dysregulation contributes to hair shaft and follicular malformations.

Regulation of cell fate specification controls the decisions by which an uncommitted embryonic or progenitor cell adopts one identity rather than another, setting the germ layers, body axes and organ primordia that all later development builds on. Its failure produces patterning defects and, in adult tissues, loss of the boundary between stem and differentiated states that underlies tumour formation. Two kinds of input converge here. Secreted signals and their receptors — WNT3A, FZD7 and the antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2, BMP receptor signalling, FGF2 through FGFR1 — provide positional information to which cells respond. Chromatin machinery then makes the response durable: the nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase complex, built from CHD3/CHD4, HDAC1/2, MTA and MBD3 subunits with RBBP4/7, silences alternative programmes so that lineage factors such as SOX17 and MESP1 can lock in mesodermal and endodermal fate.

Cell fate specification is the step at which a still-flexible progenitor commits to one identity rather than another, and its regulation sets how readily that commitment happens and which choice is made. The genes here act on two levels. Secreted cues and their receptors — WNT3A with FZD7, the inhibitors DKK1 and SFRP2, FGF2 signalling through FGFR1, and BMP reception via BMPR1A — grade the positional information that a progenitor reads. Inside the nucleus, a full complement of the NuRD chromatin remodelling and deacetylase complex (CHD3/CHD4, HDAC1/2, MBD3, MTA1-3, GATAD2A/B, RBBP4/7) closes off alternative programmes, while MESP1 and SOX17 drive mesoderm and endoderm identities respectively. The balance matters for gastrulation, germ layer allocation and cardiovascular lineage choice, and its disturbance underlies developmental malformation and the fate reversions exploited by tumours.

regulation of mesodermal cell fate specification controls how many cells in the early embryo are directed into the mesodermal lineage, and when. Mesoderm gives rise to heart, blood, skeletal muscle, bone and kidney, so tuning this decision sets the size and timing of every one of those tissues; excess or deficient specification distorts the body plan and causes gastrulation failure or cardiac malformation. The genes place the control in the crosstalk of three morphogen systems at the primitive streak: WNT3A signalling promotes mesodermal commitment while the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain it, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A patterns mesoderm along the dorsoventral axis, and FGFR1 sustains the migratory, proliferative state of nascent mesoderm. MESP1 acts downstream as the transcription factor that marks and commits cardiac mesoderm. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of gastrulation, axial patterning and organ progenitor allocation.

During gastrulation, epiblast cells must decide whether to become mesoderm, and this regulatory layer sets how many do so, where, and when. The outcome determines the heart, blood, skeleton and muscle that later derive from mesoderm, and misregulation produces axis duplication, failed primitive streak formation or absent cardiac progenitors. Control is exerted largely by extracellular signals and their tuning: WNT3A drives streak formation while the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain WNT signalling to limit the mesodermal domain, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A patterns posterior and extraembryonic mesoderm, and FGFR1 is required for cells to ingress through the streak and adopt mesodermal identity. Downstream, the transcription factor MESP1 marks and specifies nascent cardiovascular mesoderm. The same signalling logic is exploited to steer pluripotent stem cells toward mesodermal lineages in culture.

Cone photoreceptors provide daylight and colour vision and the high acuity of the central retina, and this pathway covers how an uncommitted retinal progenitor acquires that identity and its specialized phototransduction apparatus. Commitment depends on nuclear receptor transcription factors such as RORB acting with thyroid hormone signalling, where the deiodinase DIO3 degrades active hormone locally and so shapes which cone opsin subtype is chosen. The differentiating cell then builds an outer segment and its signalling cascade, including the cone transducin alpha subunit GNAT2 and the cone cyclic GMP phosphodiesterase PDE6C, plus ribbon synapse machinery such as the calcium-binding protein CABP4 and hyperpolarization-activated HCN1 channels that shape the light response. Structural and ciliary components governing outer segment formation are also represented. Disruption underlies achromatopsia, cone dystrophies and the photoreceptor degeneration seen in syndromic ciliopathies.

Muscle cell differentiation is the route by which an unspecialized progenitor takes on the machinery and identity of a skeletal, cardiac or smooth muscle cell, producing the contractile tissue that moves the body, pumps blood and sets vascular and gut tone. Lineage commitment runs through myogenic transcription factors such as MYF5, MYOD1 and MYOG together with MEF2 family partners, cardiac regulators including NKX2-5, GATA4 and TBX5, and serum response factor with myocardin and MRTF cofactors for smooth muscle; chromatin modifiers, class II histone deacetylases, Notch, Wnt, BMP and IGF signals, and muscle-enriched microRNAs set the timing of exit from proliferation. Differentiation then builds sarcomeres and excitation-contraction coupling from titin, nebulin, actins, myosins, troponins, tropomodulins and calcium handling proteins, and fuses myoblasts via myomaker and myomerger. Defects underlie congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophies, cardiomyopathy and impaired muscle regeneration.

Muscle cell fate commitment is the step at which a mesodermal progenitor stops being uncommitted and becomes a myoblast or cardiomyocyte precursor, fixing an identity that persists through differentiation into contractile tissue. Skeletal muscle mass, heart chamber formation and the availability of satellite cells for regeneration all follow from it, and its failure underlies congenital muscle deficits and cardiac outflow tract and septal malformations. Myogenic determination factors such as MYF5 and MYOD1 act as the lineage switch, with MYOG and MYF6 carrying cells onward into differentiation, while MEF2C cooperates with NKX2-5 and T-box factors including TBX1, TBX5 and TBX2/3 to specify cardiac and pharyngeal muscle territories. Signals from the surrounding tissue, notably WNT3A, FGF10 and BMP-type receptor activity through ACVR1, position commitment in the embryo, and MYL2 marks the contractile output of committed cells.

Thelarche is the onset of breast development at puberty, when ovarian estrogen drives the rudimentary ductal tree of the mammary gland to elongate and branch into the fat pad. It marks the first outward sign of female puberty and establishes the epithelial architecture that later supports lobuloalveolar differentiation and lactation; its premature or delayed appearance is a clinical signal of disordered gonadal or hypothalamic-pituitary function. Mechanistically, estrogen receptor signalling in a subset of luminal cells, dependent on the coactivator MED1 and modulated by the receptor chaperone PHB2, induces amphiregulin, which is shed at the cell surface to act as a paracrine EGF-family growth signal on the surrounding stroma. Stromal feedback through WNT5A and TGFB1 restrains ductal elongation and spacing, so that terminal end bud invasion is patterned rather than unlimited.

Thelarche is the onset of breast development in girls, the first visible sign of puberty in most, and it commits mammary epithelium to the ductal outgrowth that will later support lactation. Its timing is set by rising ovarian oestrogen, and shifts in that timing define precocious or delayed puberty; the same growth-factor and hormone-receptor circuitry is reused during pregnancy and is subverted in breast cancer. Mechanistically, oestrogen receptor signalling in the stroma and epithelium requires a nuclear receptor coactivator, MED1, and acts largely through a paracrine relay in which amphiregulin released from receptor-positive cells stimulates neighbouring epithelium to proliferate and invade the fat pad. WNT5A and TGFB1 restrain that expansion, limiting ductal branching and side-branch density, while PHB2 contributes to repression of receptor-driven transcription. Net ductal architecture reflects this balance of growth and restraint.

The recurring female reproductive cycle coordinates follicle growth, ovulation and preparation of the endometrium for implantation, and its failure underlies anovulatory infertility, premature ovarian insufficiency and polycystic ovary syndrome. Hypothalamic GnRH drives pituitary gonadotropin output, and FSH and LH act through their receptors FSHR and LHCGR on granulosa and theca cells to select a dominant follicle, induce steroidogenesis and trigger follicle rupture. Oocyte-derived GDF9 and the NPPC-NPR2 pair hold meiosis in check and shape cumulus expansion, while hyaluronan synthesis and the matrix proteins HAS2, PTX3, TNFAIP6 and ADAMTS1 build and then remodel the cumulus matrix and follicle wall. Steroid receptors ESR1 and PGR with coregulators such as NCOA1 and NRIP1 convert hormonal signals into cyclical transcription in ovary and uterus; caspase-dependent atresia removes non-selected follicles. Metabolic signals including leptin link nutritional status to cycle continuity.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) is useless to a cell until it is taken up, phosphorylated and delivered to the enzymes that depend on it, and this handling of thiamine and its derivatives is what the pathway covers. Its products support oxidative decarboxylation by pyruvate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenases and the transketolase step of the pentose phosphate pathway, so failure starves cells of ATP and of NADPH-linked reducing power, with neurons and pancreatic beta cells affected first. Plasma membrane carriers of the SLC19 family import the free vitamin, a mitochondrial carrier moves the pyrophosphate form across the inner membrane, and thiamine pyrophosphokinase generates the active cofactor; phosphatase activity reverses these modifications, and a separate enzyme handles the triphosphate form. Mutations in the transporters and kinase cause thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia, biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease and Amish microcephaly.

Riboflavin taken in from the diet has to be transported into cells and converted into the cofactors that redox enzymes actually use, and this flavin-containing compound metabolism is that route. Membrane carriers of the SLC52 family absorb riboflavin across the intestine and deliver it to tissues, riboflavin kinase phosphorylates it to FMN, and FLAD1 adenylylates FMN to FAD, the cofactor of the respiratory chain complexes, fatty acid acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, and numerous oxidases and reductases. Because flavoproteins dominate mitochondrial fatty acid and amino acid oxidation, loss of these steps produces severe neurometabolic disease: SLC52 transporter mutations cause Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome with bulbar palsy and motor neuron degeneration, and FLAD1 defects give a multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency phenotype, both of which can respond to riboflavin supplementation. The pathway thus links a vitamin to cellular energy production.

Clots must be removed once a vessel wall is repaired, and fibrinolysis is the proteolytic clearance of fibrin that accomplishes this, keeping thrombi from outgrowing their purpose and occluding flow. Plasminogen circulates as an inactive precursor and is converted to the active protease plasmin by tissue-type and urokinase-type activators, the latter working at the cell surface through its receptor to couple proteolysis to cell migration and matrix remodelling as well as clot dissolution. The fibrin substrate itself is supplied by the three fibrinogen chains. Activity is held in check by serpin inhibitors of the activators and of plasmin, by a carboxypeptidase that trims lysine residues needed for plasminogen binding, and by histidine-rich glycoprotein; contact-system proteases and thrombin-thrombomodulin link the pathway to coagulation. Too little activity favours thrombosis and impaired stroke recovery, too much causes bleeding, and these proteins are the targets of thrombolytic and antifibrinolytic therapy.

Fingers and toes are carved out of a paddle-shaped limb bud during embryogenesis, and embryonic digit morphogenesis is the programme that sets their number, identity and spacing. Sonic hedgehog from the posterior limb bud, read out through GLI3 and requiring intact primary cilia and intraflagellar transport, patterns digits along the anterior-posterior axis, while BMP4 signalling through BMPR1A and SMAD4, opposed by the antagonist noggin, drives the interdigital apoptosis that separates individual digits; BAX and BCL2L11 execute that cell death. WNT and planar cell polarity components, posterior HOX genes such as HOXD13, and limb transcription factors including HAND2, ALX4, MSX1/2 and TWIST1 refine skeletal element identity and outgrowth. Disruption of these steps produces the human limb malformations polydactyly, syndactyly, brachydactyly and synpolydactyly, and cilia-gene failures give skeletal ciliopathies in which extra digits accompany multi-organ disease.</description>

Host protection against bacteria combines direct killing of microbes at epithelial and mucosal surfaces with inflammatory signalling that recruits and arms leukocytes. This defense response to bacterium underlies the sterility of airway, gut, skin, urinary and reproductive tract secretions; its failure produces recurrent infection, while its overactivity drives sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis-like inflammation. A large arsenal of secreted antimicrobials acts on bacterial envelopes and nutrient supply: alpha- and beta-defensins, lysozyme, cathelicidin, lactoferrin, lipocalin-2, peptidoglycan recognition proteins, phospholipases, secretory RNases and protease inhibitors of the WFDC family, plus hepcidin-mediated iron withholding. Recognition runs through Toll-like receptors, NOD1/NOD2 with RIPK2, and CARD9, converging on MyD88, TAK1 and NF-kB to induce IL-1beta, IL-6, TNF and IL-17/IL-23 axis cytokines. Inflammasomes built on NLRC4, NLRP1 and PYCARD activate caspase-1 and gasdermin-D pyroptosis, while guanylate-binding proteins, IRGM and nitric oxide destroy intracellular bacteria. Neutrophil granule enzymes and opsonins including complement, fibrinogen, collectins and immunoglobulins complete clearance.

Hydrogen peroxide is both an unavoidable byproduct of aerobic metabolism, capable of oxidizing DNA, lipids and protein thiols, and a diffusible signalling molecule, and this pathway covers the enzymes that make it and those that dispose of it. Superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to peroxide, NADPH oxidases and dual oxidases with their maturation factors and cytosolic regulators generate it deliberately at membranes, and peroxisomal oxidases release it during fatty acid breakdown. Removal falls to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and the peroxiredoxin family working with thioredoxin, while heme peroxidases such as myeloperoxidase, eosinophil peroxidase and lactoperoxidase consume it to produce antimicrobial oxidants, and thyroid peroxidase uses it to iodinate thyroglobulin. Balance here sets redox tone for kinase and transcription factor signalling; loss of control contributes to neurodegeneration, chronic granulomatous disease and thyroid hormone deficiency.

Hydrogen peroxide is generated continuously by aerobic metabolism and by dedicated oxidases, and its removal keeps a diffusible oxidant from damaging lipids, proteins and DNA while preserving its use as a signalling molecule. Catalase performs bulk disproportionation in peroxisomes, glutathione peroxidases reduce peroxide at the expense of glutathione in cytosol and plasma, and the peroxiredoxins cover distinct compartments — cytosolic, mitochondrial and secretory — using cysteine thiols recycled by thioredoxin, with their reversible oxidation acting as a redox relay. A second branch consumes peroxide productively: myeloperoxidase and eosinophil peroxidase turn it into hypohalous acids for microbial killing, thyroid peroxidase uses it to iodinate thyroglobulin for hormone synthesis, and peroxidasin cross-links collagen IV in basement membranes. Dual oxidases supply the substrate at epithelial surfaces. Loss of this capacity underlies oxidative-stress pathology, hypothyroidism and defective mucosal defence.

Sleep and wakefulness alternate on an approximately 24-hour schedule, passing through an ordered succession of non-REM and REM stages, and this circadian sleep/wake cycle is what keeps rest consolidated into a single daily bout rather than scattered across the day. Its disruption produces insomnia, narcolepsy-like fragmentation, delayed or advanced sleep phase, and the restless legs and periodic limb movements linked to variants in genes such as BTBD9. The genes here span the two interacting layers: a molecular clock and its output, including PER3 and the nuclear receptor NR1D1, and the neurochemical systems that set arousal level dash adenosine accumulation and its A1 and A2A receptors as a sleep-pressure signal, orexin and melatonin receptor signalling, dopaminergic and cholinergic tone, GABAergic inhibition, and prostaglandin D synthase. Hypothalamic peptides including CRH, GHRH and ghrelin tie sleep timing to feeding, growth hormone release and stress physiology.

circadian sleep/wake cycle, REM sleep covers the control of rapid eye movement sleep, the stage in which dreaming occurs and the body shows rapid eye movements, muscle atonia and loss of reflexes alongside heightened cortical activity and quickened pulse. Adequate REM sleep supports memory consolidation and emotional regulation, and its disruption is a feature of narcolepsy, REM behaviour disorder, depression and chronic stress. The genes point to the neuromodulatory and neuroendocrine inputs that set REM amount and timing: a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit acting in the cholinergic brainstem circuits that generate REM, GABA-A receptor signalling that gates arousal state transitions, and hypothalamic and gut-derived peptides including growth hormone-releasing hormone, ghrelin, CART and corticotropin-releasing hormone, which couple sleep architecture to feeding, growth hormone release and the stress axis.

Rapid eye movement sleep is the phase of the daily sleep/wake cycle in which dreaming occurs, muscle tone is lost, and eye movements, pulse rate and cortical activity rise toward waking levels; its timing and amount are set by brainstem and hypothalamic circuits under circadian control. Adequate REM sleep supports memory consolidation and emotional regulation, and its disruption is characteristic of narcolepsy, REM behaviour disorder and depression. The genes here point to the neuropeptide and neurotransmitter inputs that gate this state: growth hormone-releasing hormone and ghrelin promote sleep and link it to somatotropic and feeding signals, corticotropin-releasing hormone couples stress-axis activation to arousal and REM fragmentation, and cholinergic nicotinic and GABA-A receptor subunits mediate the fast synaptic transmission that switches brainstem REM-on and REM-off populations. Together they place REM sleep at the intersection of circadian timing, endocrine state and neuronal excitability.

Non-REM sleep is the deep, slow-wave portion of the daily sleep/wake cycle, during which cortical activity synchronises and slows, metabolic rate and body temperature fall, and growth hormone secretion peaks; it is the phase most strongly regulated by prior time awake and the phase whose loss produces daytime sleepiness and restorative deficits. The genes here act at the interface between sleep pressure and sleep depth: adenosine signalling through its A1 receptor converts accumulated metabolic activity during waking into sleep propensity, melatonin receptor signalling ties sleep timing to the circadian clock, and growth hormone-releasing hormone and ghrelin signalling promote slow-wave activity while coupling it to endocrine and feeding state. Potassium channel and neuropeptide components shape the thalamocortical firing patterns that generate slow waves. Variation in this circuitry contributes to insomnia, restless legs and other disorders of sleep depth and continuity.

Almost every tissue keeps a roughly 24-hour clock, and this is the set of processes that tunes its period, amplitude and phase so that sleep, feeding, hormone release and metabolism stay aligned with the day. The core is a transcriptional feedback loop in which CLOCK and BMAL1 drive expression of the PER and CRY repressors, which then shut their own activators off; nuclear receptors of the REV-ERB and ROR families add a second, opposing loop. Timing is set largely after transcription: casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and GSK3B phosphorylate clock proteins, SCF complexes containing FBXL3 or beta-TrCP target them for degradation, deubiquitinases and sirtuin- and HDAC3-containing corepressors adjust turnover and chromatin state. Light and arousal inputs enter through opsins, adenosine, dopamine and orexin receptors, while AMPK and mTOR couple the clock to nutrient state. Disruption produces sleep phase disorders and metabolic disease.

Daily rhythms in behaviour, hormone release and metabolism depend on a transcriptional clock whose amplitude and pace must be actively reinforced; this is the set of influences that strengthen or accelerate circadian output. At its core the BMAL1-CLOCK heterodimer, with the paralogue BMAL2, drives rhythmic transcription of clock-controlled genes, while ROR nuclear receptors (RORA, RORC) sustain BMAL1 expression and F-box proteins such as BTRC and FBXW11 time the degradation of repressors, setting period length. Peripheral and neuroendocrine inputs act on the same rhythm: melatonin acting through MTNR1B, adenosine signalling via ADORA2A, and hypothalamic peptides including CRH, GHRH and ghrelin couple sleep pressure, feeding and growth hormone pulses to the clock. Loss of this reinforcement flattens rhythm amplitude, producing sleep-wake disruption and metabolic disturbance.

Circadian clocks keep near-24-hour time by building in their own brakes, and this grouping covers the processes that damp or shut down clock output. The core of it is the negative limb of the transcriptional feedback loop: CRY1 and CRY2 together with PER2 accumulate and repress the CLOCK/BMAL1 activators that drove their own expression, while CIPC provides an additional inhibitory input on that activator complex and SIN3A contributes corepressor and histone-deacetylase activity at clock-controlled promoters. PASD1 can suppress clock transcription, and SFPQ links splicing and repressor assembly to rhythmic gene output. Neuromodulatory and hormonal signals act on the same endpoint from outside the oscillator, with adenosine through ADORA1, dopamine through DRD2, and the peptides CRH and ghrelin adjusting phase, arousal and feeding rhythms. Loss of this restraint flattens or desynchronises rhythms, disturbing sleep timing and metabolic scheduling.

eating behavior covers the neural and hormonal control of food intake — when an animal starts eating, how much it consumes, and when it stops — and it sets body weight and energy balance over a lifetime. Its failure produces obesity, hyperphagia and cachexia; mutations in the melanocortin receptor MC4R and in leptin signalling are among the commonest causes of severe early-onset human obesity. Peripheral signals of nutritional state, including leptin from fat, ghrelin from the stomach, cholecystokinin from the gut and the stress-induced factor GDF15 acting on GFRAL, converge on hypothalamic and brainstem circuits where orexigenic AGRP/NPY neurons oppose anorexigenic POMC and CART neurons through STAT3-dependent transcription. Orexin, oxytocin, CRH, neuromedin U and opioid receptors add arousal, stress and reward dimensions, and ciliary and Bardet-Biedl proteins are required for these neurons to sense satiety signals at all.

Eating behavior — the regulated drive to seek, initiate and terminate food intake — is how an animal matches energy consumption to energy need, and its miscalibration underlies obesity, cachexia and eating disorders. Peripheral signals of fuel status converge on the hypothalamus: leptin from adipose tissue reports long-term stores through STAT3 signalling, ghrelin acting at its receptor GHSR drives hunger before meals, cholecystokinin and GDF15 acting via GFRAL signal satiety and aversion. Arcuate neurons translate these inputs into opposing orexigenic NPY/AGRP and anorexigenic POMC tone, with melanocortin receptor MC4R as the principal output node whose loss causes severe hyperphagic obesity. Additional layers include orexin and CART peptides linking feeding to arousal, oxytocin and CRH restraining intake, opioid and endocannabinoid components supplying food reward, and ciliary and Bardet-Biedl proteins required for hypothalamic neurons to sense these cues at all.

Drinking behaviour is the motivated intake of fluid that keeps body water and plasma osmolality within narrow limits, and it links sensing of thirst to the reward and arousal circuits that make an animal seek and consume water. Without it, osmoregulation fails despite intact renal handling of salt and water. The genes here span both halves of that control: renin and angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 place the pathway downstream of the renin-angiotensin system, oxytocin and vasopressin-related hypothalamic peptides couple fluid status to neuroendocrine output, and orexin, galanin, neuropeptide Y with its Y2 receptor, CART, enkephalin and nociceptin act in hypothalamic and limbic circuits that also govern feeding, arousal and reward. Dopamine D2 receptor and tachykinin receptor signalling add appetitive and aversive modulation, while osmosensitive and mechanosensitive membrane proteins contribute to detecting the stimulus itself.

Long-chain fatty acids with tails of roughly 13 to 22 carbons are a dense fuel source, and their breakdown supplies acetyl-CoA for oxidative energy production while clearing lipid species that would otherwise accumulate to toxic levels. Degradation begins with transport and activation: a peroxisomal ABC transporter delivers very-long- and long-chain acyl-CoAs across the peroxisomal membrane, and long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase performs the first oxidation step of mitochondrial beta-oxidation. An alternative omega-oxidation route, carried out by CYP4A and CYP4F family monooxygenases, hydroxylates the terminal methyl carbon and is the main way leukotriene B4 and related eicosanoids are inactivated. Additional hydrolase and acyltransferase activities handle fatty acid esters and conjugates. Failure of this catabolism causes fatty acid oxidation disorders with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy, while loss of the peroxisomal transporter underlies X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

Long-chain fatty acid biosynthetic process covers the making and remodelling of fatty acids with 13-22 carbon tails, the building blocks of membrane phospholipids, energy stores, and the precursors of lipid signalling molecules. Cells depend on it to set membrane fluidity and to supply arachidonate and related substrates; when it is dysregulated the consequences appear as altered inflammatory tone and disturbed myelin or skin barrier lipids. Two arms are visible here. One elongates and desaturates saturated chains and activates them as CoA thioesters, with ELOVL6, FADS1 and acyl-CoA synthetases balanced by a thioesterase that releases free acid. The other oxygenates these chains: lipoxygenases and cyclooxygenase together with glutathione transferases and leukotriene C4 synthase generate eicosanoids, while cytochrome P450 monooxygenases add hydroxylated and epoxidised products. QKI links the output to oligodendrocyte lipid programmes.

Formation of long-chain fatty acids — aliphatic chains of roughly 13 to 22 carbons — supplies the cell with membrane phospholipid acyl groups, storage lipids, and the precursors of lipid signalling molecules. The genes here cover both the elongation and desaturation steps that build and tailor these chains, exemplified by ELOVL6 adding two carbons to saturated and monounsaturated substrates and FADS1 introducing a double bond during polyunsaturated fatty acid synthesis, and the downstream oxygenation routes that convert arachidonate and related acids into eicosanoids: lipoxygenases of several positional specificities, prostaglandin endoperoxide synthase 2, leukotriene C4 synthase, and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases. Acyl-CoA synthetases and a thioesterase set the balance of activated acyl pools, while glutathione transferases and GPX4 handle conjugation and peroxide reduction. The output shapes inflammation, skin barrier lipid formation, myelin composition, and hepatic lipid handling.

very long-chain fatty acid catabolic process shortens fatty acids too long for mitochondria to handle, and it does so in the peroxisome. It matters because these substrates are toxic when they accumulate: failure of the transport step causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, with demyelination of the central nervous system and adrenal insufficiency, while loss of the first oxidative enzyme produces a related peroxisomal leukodystrophy. The genes trace the route substrates take. ABCD half-transporters import very long-chain acyl-CoAs across the peroxisomal membrane, acyl-CoA synthetases of the SLC27 family activate free fatty acids to their CoA thioesters so they can enter, and acyl-CoA oxidase performs the committed desaturation that begins each round of peroxisomal beta-oxidation. Chain-shortened products are then passed to mitochondria for complete oxidation, linking this route to cellular lipid homeostasis and myelin membrane integrity.

Fatty acids longer than 22 carbons cannot be handled by mitochondria and must instead be shortened in peroxisomes, and this catabolic route is how cells dispose of them. It begins with activation to a CoA thioester by acyl-CoA synthetases such as SLC27A2 and SLC27A4, followed by ATP-dependent import across the peroxisomal membrane by ABCD-family transporters and then the first, rate-setting oxidation step catalysed by acyl-CoA oxidase 1. The chain is trimmed by successive beta-oxidation cycles until the product can be exported for mitochondrial completion. Loss of ABCD1 causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, in which accumulating saturated very long-chain fatty acids damage myelin and adrenal cortex, while acyl-CoA oxidase deficiency produces a similar leukodystrophy. The pathway therefore links peroxisomal lipid handling to myelin maintenance, membrane lipid composition and overall fatty acid homeostasis.

Fatty acids longer than 22 carbons are made by extending pre-existing chains two carbons at a time on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum, and this elongation supplies the lipids that skin, retina, brain myelin and sperm membranes depend on. Each cycle uses a condensing enzyme of the ELOVL family, which sets substrate length and saturation preference, followed by reduction, dehydration by a HACD hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratase, and a final trans-2-enoyl-CoA reduction by TECR. ELOVL4 builds the ultra-long species required for the epidermal water barrier and photoreceptor function, and its loss causes ichthyosis and macular degeneration, while ELOVL2 and ELOVL5 extend polyunsaturated precursors toward DHA and arachidonate. The pathway feeds sphingolipid, glycerophospholipid and wax ester synthesis, and defects in it also underlie peroxisomal disorders in which very long-chain fatty acids accumulate.

Sulfur in cells is mostly locked up in cysteine, glutathione and the thiol- or thioester-bearing cofactors thiamine and lipoamide, and this pathway covers the control points that set how fast those species are made and used. Its output determines antioxidant capacity and the flux of pyruvate into the mitochondrion. One arm is redox-driven transcription: NFE2L2, with SP1, induces SLC7A11, the cystine/glutamate antiporter that supplies the cysteine limiting glutathione synthesis, and loss of this arm sensitises cells to oxidative and ferroptotic death. A second arm regulates lipoamide-dependent dehydrogenases, where the PDK kinases phosphorylate and inhibit pyruvate dehydrogenase, PDP1 reverses it, BCKDK acts on branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and SIRT4 adds a deacylation-based brake. TPK1 activates thiamine to its diphosphate form, coupling vitamin supply to the same decarboxylation steps.

When a cell detects broken or improperly replicated DNA, it converts that detection into a decision: pause the cell cycle, repair the lesion, or die. This damage-response signalling cascade is the basis of the DNA damage checkpoint, and its loss underlies genomic instability, cancer predisposition and sensitivity or resistance to radiation and chemotherapy. Sensor and scaffold components at the lesion — the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex, RPA-coated single-stranded DNA with ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp — activate the apical kinases ATM and ATR, which phosphorylate H2AX and recruit MDC1, RNF8 and TP53BP1 to amplify the signal through chromatin. CHEK1 and CHEK2 then restrain CDK activity, while stabilised TP53, opposed by MDM2 and PPM1D, drives CDKN1A-mediated arrest or apoptosis via PMAIP1 and BID. Repair factors, ubiquitin ligases, chromatin modifiers and cell-cycle regulators are coordinated by the same network.

When DNA damage is too severe to repair, p53 decides between arrest and death, and this is the branch that commits the cell to die. It is the route by which genotoxic chemotherapy and radiation kill tumour cells, and its loss through TP53 mutation is one of the commonest events in cancer, allowing damaged genomes to persist. Damage sensing kinases such as CHEK2 and HIPK2 phosphorylate p53, while acetylation by EP300 and deacetylation by SIRT1 tune its activity and USP28 stabilises it; the stabilised tetramer then transactivates targets including the BH3-only gene PUMA (BBC3), the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, PHLDA3 and RPS27L. BH3 proteins overwhelm BCL2 to permeabilise mitochondria and release cytochrome c, triggering caspase execution. The p53 relatives TP63 and TP73 contribute overlapping transcriptional output, linking genome surveillance to cell cycle control and mitochondrial apoptosis.

Aerobic ATP production depends on passing electrons from NADH and succinate along a chain of carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane, and this is the pathway that performs that transfer and couples it to proton pumping. Most of the cell's ATP comes from the proton gradient it builds; when it fails, tissues with high energy demand degenerate, producing the encephalomyopathies, optic neuropathies and lactic acidosis of mitochondrial disease, and electron leak becomes a source of reactive oxygen species. The genes encode the subunits of complex I, succinate dehydrogenase, the cytochrome bc1 complex and cytochrome c oxidase, drawn from both nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, together with cytochrome c, assembly factors and coenzyme Q biosynthesis. Regulators such as PINK1 and DJ-1 link respiratory integrity to mitochondrial quality control, a connection central to Parkinson's disease.

Before a tRNA can be charged with an amino acid it must be trimmed to its exact mature length, and 3'-end processing is the step that does it. An endonuclease of the ELAC family cleaves the precursor immediately after the acceptor stem, removing the trailer sequence, and a nucleotidyltransferase then adds the universal CCA end that the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and the ribosome recognise. In mitochondria this cleavage is carried out by a complex that also houses a methyltransferase and a short-chain dehydrogenase subunit, coupling tRNA maturation to the excision of tRNAs from the long polycistronic mitochondrial transcript and thus to the supply of mitochondrially encoded respiratory chain proteins. La protein binds nascent 3' oligouridylate tails to protect precursors. Loss of these activities causes anaemia with mitochondrial dysfunction and inherited neurological disease.

Ribosome production begins in the nucleolus with transcription of the large rRNA precursor by RNA polymerase I, the single most active transcription event in a growing cell and the step that sets how many ribosomes it can build. Because output scales with nutrient and growth-factor status, this process is the point at which growth signalling, including mTOR, is converted into biosynthetic capacity; its suppression accompanies quiescence, stress and nucleolar disruption. The polymerase itself is assembled from dedicated subunits together with those shared with the other nuclear polymerases, and is recruited to ribosomal DNA promoters through basal factors such as TAF1B and the rDNA-associated proteins treacle and UBF-like regulators. Chromatin remodellers, the deacetylase SIRT7, nucleolin and processing-linked factors including NOL11 and NOP53 tune output further. Loss of treacle function causes Treacher Collins syndrome, a craniofacial disorder attributed to insufficient rRNA synthesis in neural crest cells.

5S class rRNA transcription by RNA polymerase III produces the 5S rRNA that is built into the large ribosomal subunit, so its output sets a hard ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can assemble and therefore on growth and protein synthesis capacity. Transcription of 5S genes begins at a type 1 internal promoter, an unusual arrangement in which the control elements lie within the transcribed sequence rather than upstream. The six-subunit TFIIIC complex recognises those internal boxes and acts as the assembly platform that positions TFIIIB upstream, which in turn recruits RNA polymerase III to the start site. Because ribosome production is tuned to nutrient and growth-factor status, this step is a control point downstream of mTOR and MYC signalling, and its deregulated activation is a common feature of transformed, rapidly proliferating cells.

Every ribosome needs one copy of 5S rRNA, and this is the transcription route that supplies it. Unlike the other rRNAs, which are made as a single precursor by RNA polymerase I, 5S rRNA is transcribed separately by RNA polymerase III from a type 1 promoter, then imported into the nucleolus and built into the large ribosomal subunit; its supply therefore sets a limit on ribosome production and on cell growth. The genes here encode the six subunits of the general transcription factor IIIC complex, which binds internal promoter elements, recognises the assembled upstream factor on the 5S gene, and recruits TFIIIB and polymerase III to position the start site. Because ribosome output is tuned to nutrient and growth signals, this machinery is a control point for anabolic capacity and is upregulated in transformed cells.

The spliceosomal snRNAs U1, U2, U4 and U5 are made by RNA polymerase II from promoters quite unlike those of protein-coding genes, and this specialised transcription programme supplies the RNA components of the splicing machinery on which nearly all pre-mRNA processing depends. Recognition of the proximal sequence element by the multi-subunit SNAPc complex, built from SNAPC1 through SNAPC5, directs polymerase to these genes, while CDK7 within the general transcription apparatus phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license initiation and downstream 3' end formation. Elongation and termination require the little elongation complex, in which ELL family proteins partner with ICE1 and ICE2. LARP7 and MEPCE, known as the stabilising cap of the 7SK small nuclear RNA, link this activity to control of polymerase pause release. Disruption compromises snRNA supply and therefore global splicing fidelity.

A handful of small nuclear RNAs, notably U6 and its relatives that form the catalytic core of the spliceosome, are made not by the polymerase that transcribes mRNA but by RNA polymerase III from a distinct class of promoter. This pathway covers that specialised transcription, and it matters because splicing capacity depends on a continuous supply of these non-coding RNAs. Recognition of the proximal sequence element is handled by the multisubunit SNAP complex, whose SNAPC subunits bind the promoter and recruit polymerase III; the catalytic machinery is represented here by POLR3B. Elongation and snRNA-specific control involve the little elongation complex, in which ELL partners with ICE1 and ICE2 at snRNA gene loci. Loss of these components reduces snRNA output and perturbs pre-mRNA processing, linking gene-specific transcriptional control to the fidelity of splicing across the transcriptome.

vitamin B6 metabolic process converts dietary pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine into pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, the cofactor that transaminases, decarboxylases and racemases depend on. Because that cofactor supplies amino acid metabolism, heme synthesis, one-carbon and sphingolipid pathways, and the decarboxylation steps that make GABA, serotonin and dopamine, its supply sets the tone of neurotransmitter balance; loss of the oxidase PNPO or of the homeostatic carrier protein PLPBP causes neonatal vitamin B6-dependent epilepsy, treatable by supplying the vitamer directly. Extracellular phosphatase activity by ALPL dephosphorylates circulating pyridoxal phosphate so the free vitamer can cross membranes, after which the salvage kinase PDXK rephosphorylates it inside the cell and PDXP reverses that step, giving a futile-cycle control point. PSAT1 illustrates the demand side, using the cofactor for serine biosynthesis.

Vitamin B6 metabolism converts dietary pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine into pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, the cofactor that scores of enzymes require for transamination, decarboxylation and amino acid interconversion, including the synthesis of GABA, serotonin, dopamine, heme and sphingolipids. Interconversion runs through a small set of steps: a kinase phosphorylates the free vitamers, an oxidase converts the phosphorylated pyridoxine and pyridoxamine forms to the active aldehyde, a phosphatase reverses phosphorylation to set intracellular cofactor levels, and an alkaline phosphatase acts extracellularly so that the vitamer can cross membranes before being re-trapped inside cells. A carrier protein buffers free pyridoxal phosphate, whose reactive aldehyde is otherwise toxic. Loss of the oxidase or of this buffering causes neonatal epileptic encephalopathy that responds to pyridoxal phosphate supplementation, reflecting how sharply neurotransmitter synthesis depends on cofactor supply.

Pyruvate sits at the junction of glycolysis, mitochondrial oxidation, amino acid catabolism and gluconeogenesis, and the reactions that generate it determine how much carbon and reducing equivalent flux is available to those routes. Several distinct chemistries converge on it: the terminal glycolytic step, in which the liver and erythrocyte pyruvate kinase PKLR commits phosphoenolpyruvate to pyruvate and ATP, the oxidative decarboxylation of malate by the NADP-dependent malic enzyme ME3, and the deamination of serine by serine dehydratase, which links amino acid disposal to energy metabolism. Regulation enters through bifunctional PFKFB2, which sets fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels and thus glycolytic rate, and through the outer-membrane channel VDAC1, which governs metabolite exchange with mitochondria. Loss of PKLR activity causes hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia, illustrating how directly red cell survival depends on glycolytic pyruvate and ATP output.

Pyruvate sits at the junction of glycolysis and oxidative metabolism, and its catabolism decides whether a cell burns sugar completely or ferments it. Two fates are represented here: oxidative decarboxylation to acetyl-CoA, carried by the dihydrolipoamide acetyltransferase core of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, which feeds the citric acid cycle; and reduction to lactate by the lactate dehydrogenase isoenzymes, which regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen. Monocarboxylate transporters then move lactate and pyruvate across the plasma membrane, letting tissues export or import fuel and underpinning the lactate shuttle between muscle, liver and brain. This branch point is central to anaerobic exercise, to the fermentative metabolism of proliferating tumour cells, and to lactic acidosis when oxidative capacity fails. Deficiency of the dehydrogenase arm causes congenital lactate accumulation and neurological disease.

Amide transport covers the movement of amide-containing compounds "" urea, di- and tripeptides, amidated peptide hormones and related nitrogenous solutes "" across membranes and out of cells, and the genes gathered here span both the carriers themselves and the secretory machinery that releases peptide cargo. Proton-coupled oligopeptide carriers of the SLC15 family absorb dietary and lysosomal peptides, SLC14 urea transporters and several aquaporins (including the glycerol- and urea-permeable AQP3, AQP7 and AQP9) support renal concentrating ability and osmotic balance, while ABC transporters such as TAP1 and TAP2 deliver peptides for antigen loading. A large second component is regulated exocytosis of peptide hormones: insulin, glucagon, ghrelin, CRH, VIP and chromogranin cargo, packaged through CPE and released by SNARE and Rab-dependent granule fusion under nutrient and circadian control. Failure affects glucose homeostasis, nitrogen handling and neuroendocrine signalling.

Cells must move drugs, toxins and other foreign compounds across membranes, and this transport determines how such chemicals are absorbed, distributed and eliminated. The activity sits behind oral drug bioavailability, hepatobiliary and renal excretion, the blood-brain and placental barriers, and the multidrug resistance that limits chemotherapy. Two families do most of the work: ATP-binding cassette pumps such as ABCB1, ABCG2 and the ABCC multidrug resistance-associated proteins export substrates out of cells against a gradient, while solute carriers including the organic cation and anion transporters of the SLC22 family, nucleoside carriers and the MATE proteins SLC47A1 and SLC47A2 mediate uptake and coupled efflux. Expression is tuned by the xenobiotic-sensing nuclear receptor PXR and by numerous microRNAs, and scaffolds and lipid-handling proteins support transporter localisation in polarised epithelia. Loss or variation in individual carriers produces cholestasis, altered drug response and toxic accumulation.

Movement of alkanesulfonates across membranes is, in practice, mostly the handling of taurine, the abundant free sulfonic amino acid that cells use as an organic osmolyte and that the liver conjugates to bile acids. Two directions are represented. Sodium- and chloride-coupled carriers of the SLC6 family, chiefly the taurine transporter SLC6A6 together with the betaine/GABA-preferring SLC6A11 and SLC6A13, accumulate taurine against a steep gradient and thereby set intracellular osmolyte content in retina, kidney, brain and heart; loss of SLC6A6 causes retinal degeneration and cardiomyopathy. Release runs through volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8A with LRRC8C or LRRC8D, which open on cell swelling and let taurine and other osmolytes escape, shrinking the cell back toward its set point. Proton-coupled SLC36A1 and SLC16A6 add lysosomal and efflux routes, linking this transport to osmotic homeostasis and bile salt supply.

Tripeptide transport moves three-residue peptides across membranes, and in human cells the tripeptide that matters most is glutathione, so this biology largely governs where reducing power and detoxification capacity are distributed. Proton-coupled peptide transporters of the SLC15 family absorb di- and tripeptides from the intestinal lumen and reclaim them from the kidney filtrate, a route also exploited for oral delivery of beta-lactams and peptidomimetic drugs. ABCC-family export pumps efflux glutathione and its conjugates from the cytosol, coupling phase II conjugation to elimination and contributing to multidrug resistance, while SLC25A39 and SLC25A40 import glutathione into mitochondria to protect the respiratory chain from oxidative damage. Cystine uptake through SLC7A11 supplies the cysteine that limits glutathione synthesis, linking this transport network to redox homeostasis, xenobiotic clearance and susceptibility to ferroptosis.

D-amino acids, chiefly D-serine, act as signalling molecules rather than protein building blocks in mammals, and moving them across membranes sets how much co-agonist is available at NMDA-type glutamate receptors. The transport step therefore shapes synaptic plasticity, learning and excitotoxic risk, and is a point of vulnerability in schizophrenia, stroke and motor neuron disease. Astrocytes dominate the process: the neutral amino acid exchanger SLC7A10 (Asc-1) moves D-serine in and out of cells, while the excitatory amino acid transporters SLC1A1, SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 clear glutamate and also handle D-aspartate. The presence of GFAP marks this as astroglial biology, placing D-amino acid handling within the tripartite synapse, where glia supply and retrieve the small molecules that tune neuronal excitability. Neurotensin receptor signalling links the pathway to neuromodulatory control of glutamate release.

Amyloid precursor protein metabolism covers everything that happens to APP after it is made: its trafficking through the secretory and endosomal system, its cleavage, and the clearance of the fragments released. It matters because one cleavage route yields amyloid-beta, whose aggregation defines Alzheimer's disease, while the alternative route does not. Alpha-secretase activity by ADAM10 and ADAM17 cuts within the amyloid-beta sequence and precludes its formation, whereas BACE1 cleaves at the beta site and hands the stub to gamma-secretase, the intramembrane protease built from presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN. Sorting and lipid-handling proteins such as SORL1, PICALM, BIN1, APOE and clusterin set how much APP meets each enzyme and how efficiently the peptide is removed, and many of them are Alzheimer's risk loci. A large complement of microRNAs tunes the abundance of these components post-transcriptionally.

This is the set of factors that determine how much amyloid precursor protein a cell makes, the membrane glycoprotein whose proteolytic fragment amyloid-beta accumulates in Alzheimer's disease. Because plaque burden depends on substrate supply as much as on cleavage, controlling APP synthesis sets the ceiling on amyloid production and is a point of therapeutic interest. Much of the control is post-transcriptional: numerous microRNAs, acting through the Argonaute effector machinery, repress APP mRNA translation, while transcriptional regulators such as AATF influence its expression. Other members modulate APP maturation and processing, including the BRICHOS-domain ITM2 family proteins that bind APP and restrain amyloid-beta generation, nicastrin as part of the gamma-secretase complex, the aspartyl protease BACE2, and lipid and cholesterol handling proteins including SOAT1 and ABCA transporters that couple membrane sterol content to APP metabolism.

Amyloid precursor protein is the source of the amyloid-beta peptide that accumulates in Alzheimer's disease, so limiting how much of it is made is one way cells set the ceiling on amyloidogenic load. This is the restraining arm of APP production: a cluster of microRNAs, acting with the Argonaute machinery, binds the APP transcript and lowers its translation, while transcriptional repressors and lipid-handling regulators reduce APP expression and processing. Several BRICHOS-domain membrane proteins of the ITM2 family also bind APP and interfere with its maturation and cleavage, and a related aspartyl protease of the BACE family can cut APP at sites that do not yield amyloid-beta. Loss of this braking influence raises APP dosage, the same situation created by APP triplication in Down syndrome, and shifts the balance toward plaque formation and neurodegeneration.

Amyloid precursor protein is a transmembrane glycoprotein that is continually cleaved, and the route its catabolism takes decides whether a cell releases harmless fragments or amyloid-beta peptide that aggregates into the plaques of Alzheimer's disease. Two competing proteolytic branches are represented: alpha-secretase activity by ADAM10 and ADAM17 cuts within the amyloid-beta region and forestalls its production, while BACE1 followed by the gamma-secretase complex of presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN liberates the peptide. Trafficking and sorting determine which enzymes meet the substrate, with SORL1, PICALM and BIN1 governing endosomal itineraries, and lipid and cholesterol handling proteins such as APOE, CLU and the ABC transporters modulating processing and clearance. Numerous microRNAs tune expression of the secretases and the precursor itself, and kinases including GSK3A and DYRK1A feed in regulatory input. Variants across these steps underlie both familial and late-onset Alzheimer's risk.

regulation of Golgi to plasma membrane protein transport controls how much cargo leaves the trans-Golgi network and how quickly it reaches the cell surface, setting the abundance of receptors, transporters and channels available for signalling, nutrient uptake and secretion. It acts on the final, post-Golgi leg of the secretory route, where carriers are budded, sorted toward apical or basolateral domains in polarized epithelia, and tethered for fusion. The genes point to several control points: a SNARE directing trans-Golgi vesicle traffic, an annexin implicated in apical delivery, a Golgi calcium/manganese pump and a lysosomal-Golgi membrane protein that maintain the lumenal environment needed for sorting, acyl-protein thioesterases that reverse S-palmitoylation and thereby retarget membrane proteins, and a scaffold that restrains surface delivery of glucose transporters. Failure distorts cell polarity, surface receptor density and the secretory output of specialized cells.

Newly synthesized membrane and secreted proteins leave the Golgi in carriers destined for the cell surface, and this pathway covers the control of that final delivery step rather than the transport machinery itself. Setting the rate and extent of Golgi-to-plasma-membrane traffic determines how much of a receptor, transporter or channel actually reaches the surface, so it shapes nutrient uptake, secretion and polarized epithelial delivery. The contributing activities are varied: a Golgi-localized calcium/manganese pump maintains the luminal ion environment that cargo sorting depends on, a lysosomal membrane protein linked to neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis influences trafficking itineraries, and acyl-protein thioesterases remove palmitate from cargo and regulatory proteins to alter their membrane attachment and routing. Vesicle SNARE and scaffolding components couple these inputs to carrier fusion at the cell surface, making surface protein abundance a regulated rather than constitutive output.

Delivery of newly made proteins from the Golgi to the cell surface sets how many transporters, receptors and channels a cell displays, and the traffic must be damped as well as driven. This is the braking side of that route: processes that slow or block the final secretory step, keeping cargo in intracellular compartments and lowering surface abundance. Such restraint tunes nutrient uptake and receptor signalling, and matters most in polarized epithelia, where apical and basolateral deliveries are separately controlled. Among the participants, RSC1A1 suppresses the exocytotic insertion of the sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1, annexin A13 acts in apical membrane trafficking, and the acyl-protein thioesterases LYPLA1 and LYPLAL1 remove palmitate from substrate proteins, altering their membrane association and itineraries. CSK, the inhibitory kinase for Src-family kinases, links this control to the signalling state of the cell.

Newly made membrane and secreted proteins leave the Golgi in vesicles destined for the cell surface, and this pathway covers the influences that increase the rate and extent of that Golgi-to-plasma-membrane delivery. Getting it right determines how much of a transporter, receptor or adhesion protein actually reaches the surface, and so sets the cell's capacity for secretion, surface signalling and, in epithelia, apical membrane identity. The genes involved act at different points rather than as one complex: a secretory-pathway calcium/manganese pump maintains the luminal ion environment on which Golgi enzymes and cargo sorting depend, an annexin associated with apical trafficking in intestinal epithelium participates in carrier formation, a lysosomal-endosomal membrane protein links surface delivery to later endomembrane traffic, and a scaffolding subunit couples signalling kinases to the trafficking machinery. Loss of individual components produces disorders ranging from acantholytic skin disease to neuronal degeneration.

Golgi to plasma membrane protein transport is the final leg of the secretory route: cargo sorted at the trans-Golgi network is packaged into vesicles, carried outward, and delivered to the cell surface before exocytosis. It determines which receptors, transporters and channels reach the plasma membrane, and so sets surface composition, polarity and secretory capacity in cells as different as neurons, epithelia and endocrine cells. Coats and adaptors of the GGA family act with ARF-family and Rab GTPases such as ARFRP1, RAB10 and RAB11A to select cargo and generate carriers; golgins and GOLPH3 link membranes to the cytoskeleton, kinesin motors and spectrin-ankyrin networks move them, and VAMP SNAREs with NSF drive fusion at the target membrane. Loss of components disrupts ciliary and apical delivery, and underlies disorders including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Hailey-Hailey disease and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

Newly made membrane and secreted proteins reach the cell surface by budding from the trans-Golgi network and travelling to the plasma membrane, the step that immediately precedes exocytosis. This route delivers receptors, transporters and channels to the surface, sets the composition and polarity of the plasma membrane, and supplies cargo for regulated secretion; when it falters, surface proteins are mistargeted or retained internally. Carrier formation involves Golgi scaffolds and adaptors such as GOLGA4, the GGA clathrin adaptors and GOLPH3, with ARFRP1 and SYS1 organising the exit face. Rab GTPases including RAB10, RAB11A and RAB8-related machinery specify carrier identity and, with kinesin motors and spectrin-ankyrin cytoskeletal links, direct movement outward. Fusion is executed by v-SNAREs of the VAMP family together with NSF-dependent SNARE recycling. Related components also support ciliary and polarised delivery.

Myeloid dendritic cell differentiation converts monocytic and common dendritic progenitors into the antigen-presenting cells that sample tissues and prime naive T cells, and it sets the identity of the conventional dendritic cell subsets on which vaccine responses, tolerance to self, and antitumour immunity depend. Transcription factors do the committing: SPI1 establishes myeloid potential, IRF4 pairs with BATF-family partners to specify one branch, and BATF3 is required for the cross-presenting lineage. Extrinsic cues feed in through GM-CSF and IL-4 for monocyte-derived cells, Notch2 signalling via RBPJ and presenilin for splenic and intestinal subsets, TGF-beta acting with the integrins that activate it for Langerhans cells, and lymphotoxin-beta receptor signalling through RELB and TRAF6. Loss of individual factors deletes specific dendritic cell populations rather than all of them, leaving selective gaps in antigen presentation.

The T cell pool is kept at a stable size over time by balancing proliferation, survival and deletion, so that lymphocyte numbers recover after infection without drifting into lymphopenia or lymphoproliferation. Survival signals come largely from interleukin-2 acting through its high-affinity receptor and the JAK3-STAT5 axis, with AKT1 and BCL2 opposing the pro-apoptotic arm of BAX, BIM and NOXA; death receptor signalling through FAS and FADD to caspase-3 removes activated and autoreactive cells, and failure here causes lymphoaccumulation and autoimmunity. Regulatory T cells specified by FOXP3, together with TGF-beta, restrain expansion, while thymic components including FOXN1, RAG1 and the thymoproteasome subunit PSMB11 set the selection and output of new cells. Phosphatase modules, RNA-binding repressors of the Roquin family and sphingosine-1-phosphate transport add further control over activation thresholds and tissue distribution.

Macrophages can be pushed toward inflammatory killing or toward tissue repair and tolerance, and this set governs how strongly and in which direction that switch is thrown. Tuning it matters because unchecked activation drives septic shock, chronic inflammatory and neurodegenerative damage, while excessive restraint leaves bacteria and debris uncleared. Positive input comes from pattern recognition at the cell surface, notably TLR4 with its lipopolysaccharide-delivering partner LBP, from IL-33 acting through IL1RL1, and from cytokines such as IL-6, MIF and CCL3. Restraint is imposed by IL-10, the CD200 receptor axis, the inhibitory Fc receptor FCGR2B, VSIG4, TREM2 and the RNase ZC3H12A, which degrades inflammatory transcripts. Nuclear receptors including NR1H3, RORA and the clock-linked NR1D1 add transcriptional and circadian control, and several microRNAs set response thresholds. IL-4 receptor signalling and WNT5A steer alternative, repair-associated activation states.

Macrophages must be restrained as well as switched on, and this pathway covers the braking signals that stop, limit or reverse macrophage activation so that inflammation resolves rather than damaging host tissue. Loss of such restraint contributes to chronic inflammatory disease, autoimmunity and neurodegeneration, where persistently activated macrophages and microglia sustain tissue injury. The brakes act at several levels: neuronal and epithelial ligands such as CD200 and fractalkine engage inhibitory receptors on macrophages to keep them quiescent; FCGR2B provides the inhibitory arm of immune-complex sensing; VSIG4 is a complement receptor that dampens responses; progranulin and the lysosomal protein network limit microglial reactivity. Transcriptional and post-transcriptional controls contribute too, with the nuclear receptors NR1H3 and NR1D1 coupling lipid handling and circadian timing to inflammatory output, and ZC3H12A degrading cytokine mRNAs.

Macrophages sit idle until signalled, and this collection of inputs raises the rate at which they switch into an activated, effector state — phagocytosing, secreting cytokines, remodelling tissue and instructing surrounding lymphocytes. The output matters for clearing bacteria, resolving wounds and, when overdriven, for the tissue damage of sepsis, atherosclerosis and chronic inflammatory disease. Pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4 with its lipopolysaccharide-delivering partner LBP and TLR6 sense microbial surfaces; the alarmin IL33 acting through its receptor IL1RL1 and the IL4 receptor chain drive the alternative, tissue-repair mode of activation; chemokine, protease and lipid mediators including CCL3, MMP8 and a cytosolic phospholipase amplify the response. Autophagy and lipid-handling regulators such as IRGM, LRRK2 and TREM2 tune it, and immunomodulatory members including IL10, CD200 and HAVCR2 mark where the same circuitry is restrained, since positive regulation is defined against that brake.

Before an amino acid can be added to a growing polypeptide it must be chemically activated and joined to its matching tRNA, and this is the step that sets the accuracy of the genetic code. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases carry it out in two stages, adenylating the amino acid with ATP and then transferring it to the 3' end of the cognate tRNA; proofreading by editing domains removes near-cognate products. Separate cytosolic and mitochondrial enzyme sets serve the two translation systems, and several cytosolic enzymes assemble with scaffolding factors such as AIMP1, AIMP2 and EEF1E1 into a multisynthetase complex that also supplies signalling and angiogenic activities outside translation. An indirect route generates glutaminyl- and asparaginyl-tRNA by amidotransferase action. Mutations in individual synthetases cause peripheral neuropathies, leukoencephalopathies and mitochondrial disease affecting tissues with high protein synthetic demand.

Peptide biosynthetic process covers the making of short amino acid chains, either by non-ribosomal enzymatic ligation or by translating a larger precursor and cutting it into active fragments. Two themes dominate here. One is glutathione: the ligase and synthetase steps (GCLC, GCLM, GSS), the cystine and glutamate transporters that feed them, the gamma-glutamyl transferases that recycle the tripeptide, and NFE2L2, the transcription factor that raises the whole program during oxidative stress. The other is proprotein convertase processing, in which FURIN, PCSK1 and PCSK5 cleave prohormones and proproteins at basic residues to release mature peptide hormones and neuropeptides, while epidermal proteases such as KLK5 and KLK7, restrained by SPINK5, process substrates during skin desquamation. Loss of these activities produces glutathione deficiency and haemolysis, endocrine failure from unprocessed prohormones, or ichthyosis-like barrier disease.

Peptide biosynthesis covers the routes by which cells build short amino acid chains, either enzymatically from free amino acids or by cutting a larger precursor protein into active fragments. The gene membership highlights two such routes. One is glutathione synthesis and turnover: a glutamate-cysteine ligase pair and glutathione synthetase assemble the tripeptide, gamma-glutamyl transferases and hydrolases break it down and recycle its constituents, cystine and glutamate transporters supply substrate, and NFE2L2 drives the whole programme as the core of antioxidant defence. The other is proprotein convertase processing, where furin and related endoproteases cleave inactive precursors at basic residues to release mature hormones and neuropeptides, a step that determines endocrine output. Kallikrein proteases and their inhibitor SPINK5 add a regulated proteolysis arm in skin. Loss of glutathione capacity leaves cells vulnerable to oxidative and electrophilic damage.

Epigenetic programming of gene expression sets, during early embryonic development, the chromatin states that determine how genes can be expressed much later in life, including adulthood. Its most familiar output is genomic imprinting: parent-of-origin marks laid down in the germline and maintained through cleavage divisions, which is why imprinted loci such as IGF2 and CDKN1C and the machinery that protects them appear here. DNA methyltransferases and their cofactors write cytosine methylation, TET3 and KDM1B remove or restrict marks, and a ZFP57-TRIM28 complex with ZNF445 recruits repressive activity to methylated imprinting control regions, while CTCF and its testis paralogue organise boundaries and histone methyltransferases add repressive marks. Maternal-effect factors contribute to the oocyte-to-embryo transition. Loss of these controls causes imprinting disorders, growth syndromes, and, when reprogramming fails, developmental arrest.

Dolichyl monophosphate is the lipid carrier on which the endoplasmic reticulum builds sugars for glycosylation, so its biosynthesis sets the ceiling on N-linked glycosylation, O-mannosylation, GPI anchoring and C-mannosylation. Cells lacking it accumulate unglycosylated proteins and trigger ER stress; in humans, defects in these steps cause congenital disorders of glycosylation with developmental delay, epilepsy, retinal degeneration and, for some genes, muscular dystrophy from failed alpha-dystroglycan modification. The route begins with a cis-prenyltransferase, in which DHDDS is the catalytic subunit and NUS1 its partner, elongating an isoprenoid chain; SRD5A3 reduces polyprenol to dolichol, and DOLK phosphorylates dolichol to the monophosphate. DOLPP1 recycles the carrier by dephosphorylating dolichyl pyrophosphate. The DPM1-DPM2-DPM3 complex then consumes dolichyl phosphate to make dolichol-phosphate-mannose, linking this lipid supply to isoprenoid metabolism and secretory pathway quality control.

Cells that are damaged, infected, superfluous or misplaced are removed by genetically encoded suicide programmes, and this pathway covers everything that raises or lowers how readily that happens. Such control sets tissue size during development, clears virus-infected and DNA-damaged cells, sculpts the immune repertoire, and when it drifts produces cancer, neurodegeneration or autoimmunity. The regulators span the BCL2 family, which decides mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation and cytochrome c release, initiator and executioner caspases with their adaptors such as FADD, APAF1 and CRADD, death receptors of the TNF and TRAIL families, IAP proteins and their antagonist SMAC/DIABLO, and the p53 network with targets including PUMA, NOXA and CDKN1A. Also included are the inflammasome and necroptosis arms built on RIPK1, RIPK3, PYCARD and gasdermin E, survival signalling through PI3K-AKT, NF-kB, JAK-STAT and growth factor receptors, ferroptosis-linked GPX4 and SLC7A11, and numerous microRNAs that tune these outputs.

This grouping collects the drivers that push a cell over the threshold into programmed death, raising the rate or likelihood of apoptosis, pyroptosis and necroptosis rather than restraining them. Controlled cell killing shapes tissues during development, removes damaged or infected cells, and enforces the DNA-damage checkpoint; its failure permits tumour survival and resistance to chemotherapy, while excessive firing contributes to neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury. Represented here are death receptors and their ligands such as FAS/FASLG and TNFSF10 with TRADD, FADD and RIPK1; pro-apoptotic BCL2 family members including BAX, BAK1, BID, BBC3 and PMAIP1 that permeabilise mitochondria and release cytochrome c toward APAF1 and the caspase cascade; inflammasome and pyroptotic components PYCARD, CASP1 and GSDME; and p53 with its transcriptional targets. Numerous microRNAs, kinases such as MAP3K5 and DAPK1, and stress-response factors including DDIT3 and ATF4 tune the decision.
