In the thymic cortex, immature thymocytes whose newly assembled T cell receptors engage self-peptide-MHC with low affinity are rescued from death by neglect and allowed to mature; this positive selection step builds a peripheral T cell repertoire that is MHC-restricted yet self-tolerant, and sets the CD4 versus CD8 lineage choice. Signals begin at the receptor complex through CD3 chains, ZAP70 and THEMIS, are tuned by the phosphatases PTPN2 and PTPRC and by inositol kinase ITPKB, and are integrated with survival signalling via BCL2, mTOR-dependent metabolism and JAK-STAT cytokine input. Transcriptional enforcers such as BCL11B, TOX and IRF4 fix the lineage programme, while thymic epithelial FOXN1 and the invariant chain CD74 with cathepsin L supply the selecting peptide-MHC surface. Defects yield immunodeficiency, restricted repertoires, or escape of autoreactive clones.

In the thymus, a double-positive thymocyte must choose between the helper and cytotoxic fates, and this lineage commitment step is what makes a T cell either CD4-positive or CD8-positive within the alpha-beta lineage. The choice sets the composition of the peripheral T cell repertoire: without it there are no helper cells to license antibody responses and no cytotoxic cells to clear infected or transformed targets. Commitment reads out the strength and duration of T cell receptor and co-receptor signalling and converts it into a stable transcriptional program, with TOX, ZFPM1, GATA-associated and STAT-dependent inputs, chromatin readers and acetyltransferase activity such as EP300 fixing the decision. Cytokine receptors signalling through JAK1, JAK3 and STAT3, STAT5A or STAT6, together with IRF4, BATF, TBX21 and FOXP3, link the same machinery to the later effector and regulatory differentiation of mature T cells, and survival factors including BCL2 determine which thymocytes persist.

Naive CD4 T cells leaving the thymus adopt distinct helper fates, and this pathway covers the signals that set how strongly and in which direction that choice is made. The outcome determines whether an immune response is skewed toward intracellular pathogen clearance, mucosal and antifungal defence, follicular help for antibody production, or suppression, and miscalibration underlies autoimmunity, allergy and failure to control infection. Antigen presentation on class II MHC together with costimulatory ligands such as CD80, CD86 and OX40L provides the initiating input, while cytokines including IL-2, IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 act through shared receptor chains and JAK3 to activate STATs. Lineage-defining transcription factors — TBX21, GATA3, BCL6, RORgt-associated partners and FOXP3 — then lock in identity, with IRF4, BATF and RUNX cofactors shaping the choice. SOCS proteins, SMAD7, the roquin RNA-binding proteins and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A restrain the process.

negative regulation of CD4-positive, alpha-beta T cell differentiation collects the brakes that limit how many helper T cells are made and which helper fates they adopt. Restraint here keeps antigen-driven CD4 responses proportionate: loss of it permits autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while excessive suppression blunts protective immunity. Several distinct mechanisms converge on this outcome. Lineage-determining transcription factors act reciprocally, so that RUNX3, TBX21, ZBTB7B, BCL6 and FOXP3 each repress alternative helper programmes and enforce mutually exclusive identities, including the choice between CD4 and CD8 lineages during thymic development. Cytokine signalling is throttled by SOCS5 and by feedback on the IL-2–JAK3–STAT5 axis, and mRNA-level control by roquin proteins and the endoribonuclease ZC3H12A degrades transcripts encoding costimulatory and inflammatory mediators. Surface and secreted regulators such as galectin-1, annexin A1 and TNF-family ligands tune activation thresholds, linking this control to peripheral tolerance and regulatory T cell dominance.

Helper T cell fate is as much a matter of restraint as of instruction, and this pathway covers the brakes applied to CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell differentiation. Limiting how readily naive CD4 cells commit, and blocking entry into the wrong effector programme, keeps the balance between Th1, Th2, Th17 and regulatory outputs appropriate to an infection and prevents autoimmune or allergic pathology. The machinery is largely transcriptional and post-transcriptional: RUNX1 and RUNX3 with their CBFB partner, BCL6, the CD4/CD8 lineage factor ZBTB7B, and FOXP3, which enforces a regulatory rather than conventional effector identity; TBX21 commits toward Th1 while excluding alternatives. Cytokine signalling is dampened by SOCS5 and by SMAD7 acting on TGF-beta responses, while the RNA-binding proteins RC3H1, RC3H2 and ZC3H12A degrade transcripts encoding costimulatory and cytokine drivers, and galectin-1 and annexin A1 impose extrinsic limits.

Naive CD4 T cells acquire helper identities only when antigen presentation and cytokine cues push them along a particular route, and this pathway covers the signals that promote and amplify CD4-positive alpha-beta T cell differentiation. What results determines the character of an adaptive immune response: interferon-gamma-producing Th1 cells that control intracellular pathogens, IL-17-lineage cells driven by IL-23 and inflammasome-derived IL-18, and FOXP3-expressing regulatory cells that restrain the rest. Class II MHC molecules present peptide while costimulatory ligands such as CD80, CD86 and OX40L set the activation threshold; downstream, NF-kappaB regulators, MALT1, PKC-zeta and TCR-proximal adaptors transmit the signal, transcriptional coactivators and bromodomain proteins remodel lineage gene loci, and ZBTB7B enforces the CD4 rather than CD8 fate. SOCS proteins provide negative feedback, and unbalanced output underlies autoimmunity, chronic inflammation, and failure to clear infection.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes arise when a thymocyte commits to the CD8 lineage rather than the helper fate, and this differentiation programme supplies the killer cells that eliminate virus-infected and tumour cells through MHC class I-restricted recognition. Lineage choice is decided by competing transcription factors: RUNX3, with its RUNX1 and CBFB partners, drives CD8 commitment and silences CD4, while ZBTB7B promotes the alternative helper fate; TOX and EOMES shape thymocyte selection and the acquisition of cytotoxic effector features. Proteasome subunits are prominent because peptide supply for MHC class I determines which thymocytes survive positive selection, and the thymoproteasome subunit PSMB11 tailors that peptide repertoire in cortical epithelium. Survival and signal-strength control come from BCL2, IRF1 and the negative regulator SOCS1. Defects in this route leave antiviral and antitumour cytotoxicity impaired.

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes arise from thymocytes that commit to the CD8 lineage rather than the CD4 helper fate, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how readily and how far that commitment proceeds. The outcome determines the supply of killer cells for antiviral and antitumour immunity, and its balance against the helper programme shapes the whole peripheral T cell repertoire. RUNX3 with its obligate partner CBFB drives CD8 lineage genes and silences CD4, while ZBTB7B acts as the opposing helper-fate determinant, so their relative activity is the switch point. Cytokine sensitivity is tuned by SOCS1, which restrains JAK-STAT signalling downstream of interleukin receptors, and adaptor and immunoreceptor components adjust the strength of signals cells receive during selection. Loss of this control skews thymic output and disturbs cell-mediated immune responses.

positive regulation of CD8-positive, alpha-beta T cell differentiation covers the signals and transcriptional inputs that drive thymocytes toward the cytotoxic CD8 lineage rather than the CD4 helper fate. Cytotoxic T cells are the arm of adaptive immunity that kills virus-infected and tumour cells, so the strength of this regulation shapes antiviral and antitumour capacity. Its core is the RUNX family acting with their obligate partner CBFB: RUNX3, induced during positive selection, silences the CD4 gene and enforces CD8 identity together with RUNX1, while loss of this activity redirects cells to the helper program. Efficient differentiation also requires proper T cell receptor signal transmission and cytoskeletal reorganisation at the immunological synapse, contributed by the hematopoietic adaptor NCKAP1L, and is tuned by inhibitory receptor input. The pathway therefore links thymic selection to effector lineage commitment.

Cytotoxic T cells arise from thymocytes that commit to the CD8 lineage rather than the CD4 helper fate, and this regulatory input drives that commitment forward, increasing the rate and extent of CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell differentiation. Without it the repertoire of killer cells available for antiviral and antitumour surveillance is depleted. RUNX3 acting with its obligate partner CBFB is the decisive transcriptional effector, silencing the CD4 gene and reinforcing the cytotoxic programme, with RUNX1 contributing at earlier thymocyte stages. Signalling into this decision requires intact T cell receptor coupling to the actin cytoskeleton, supplied by the haematopoietic adaptor NCKAP1L, whose loss causes immunodeficiency with skewed T cell subsets. An immunoreceptor of the inhibitory leukocyte receptor family is also represented, indicating that the strength of the signal a thymocyte receives shapes the outcome.

Memory T cells are the reason a second encounter with a pathogen is handled faster and more effectively than the first, and this pathway covers the signals that push activated T cells toward that long-lived fate rather than terminal effector differentiation or death. Positive regulation of memory T cell differentiation here runs through antigen presentation on MHC class II, costimulation by OX40 ligand, and cytokine input from the IL-12 and IL-23 families acting through their shared receptor subunit IL12RB1. CD46 engagement on T cells contributes a complement-derived signal that shapes effector-to-regulatory transitions and metabolic state, and the presence of the gluconeogenic enzyme PCK1 points to the metabolic rewiring toward oxidative, glucose-sparing metabolism that memory cells adopt. Defects here weaken durable immunity and vaccine responses, while excess drives persistent inflammatory T cell populations in autoimmunity.

Developing thymocytes that recognise self too strongly are deleted rather than allowed to mature, and this negative selection is what keeps the T cell repertoire from attacking host tissue. Its failure produces autoimmunity: loss of the thymic transcriptional regulator AIRE, which drives promiscuous expression of peripheral tissue antigens in medullary epithelium, causes a multi-organ autoimmune syndrome. The decision depends on how strongly the T cell receptor engages self-peptide-MHC, read out through the CD3 complex, the kinase ZAP70 and the thymocyte-specific adaptor THEMIS, with CD28 costimulation and the phosphatase CD45 tuning the threshold that separates deletion from positive selection. Chemokine-guided migration into the medulla brings thymocytes to antigen-presenting cells, while autophagy in epithelial cells supports self-antigen loading onto MHC class II. The outcome is central tolerance, established before T cells ever reach the periphery.

Mycotoxin metabolism describes how the body handles poisons made by fungi, with aflatoxin B1 from contaminated grains and nuts the best-studied example, and it determines whether a dietary exposure is cleared harmlessly or converted into a carcinogen. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, chiefly CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 in liver with CYP2A13 contributing in airway tissue, oxidise the parent toxin to a reactive epoxide that attacks guanine in DNA; the resulting mutational signature underlies much hepatocellular carcinoma in regions with high dietary exposure, especially alongside hepatitis B infection. Detoxification depends on downstream reduction and conjugation, including the aflatoxin aldehyde reductase AKR7A3, and these protective enzymes are induced through the NRF2 antioxidant response, encoded by NFE2L2. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of xenobiotic phase I bioactivation, phase II conjugation, and chemoprevention, and individual variation in these enzymes shapes susceptibility to toxin-driven liver cancer.

positive regulation of DNA binding covers the mechanisms that make a protein bind DNA more readily, and so sets how strongly transcriptional programs can be switched on. Because a transcription factor is only as active as its access to chromatin, control at this step determines cell fate decisions, growth-factor responses and stress adaptation rather than merely fine-tuning them. The genes act through several routes: chromatin architecture and nucleosome accessibility via HMGB1 and linker histone H1-0; redox and post-translational control, with thioredoxin reducing critical cysteines to license factor binding and SUMO and sirtuin-mediated modifications altering affinity; core promoter recognition through GTF2B; and lineage factors such as GATA3, FOXC1 and the POU4F proteins that recruit partners to their own sites. Growth-factor inputs including EGF and IGF1 feed into the same control, coupling extracellular signals to transcriptional output.

Grouped here are gene products that increase the ability of other factors to engage DNA, a layer of control that sits above transcription itself and determines whether a promoter is read at all. Because a transcription factor is only as active as its access to chromatin, these positive regulators of DNA binding set the gain on developmental and stress-responsive gene programmes. The mechanisms represented are varied: HMGB1 bends and distorts DNA to help partner factors load, thioredoxin keeps redox-sensitive cysteines in DNA-binding domains reduced, general factor GTF2B stabilises polymerase II preinitiation assembly, and SUMO and coactivator-like proteins modify or bridge factors to change their affinity. Lineage regulators such as GATA3, FOXC1 and the POU4F factors, together with RB1 and HES1, connect this control to immune cell specification, eye and neuronal development, and proliferative restraint, so loss of it distorts differentiation rather than any single metabolic step.

Transcription is controlled not only by recruiting DNA-binding proteins but by preventing them from engaging their sites, and negative regulation of DNA binding covers the steps that block or weaken that protein-DNA contact. It sets the off state of gene expression programmes, allowing cells to terminate a transcriptional response, keep lineage regulators silent in the wrong context, and restrain proliferative signals. The mechanisms represented here are varied: architectural chromatin proteins such as HMGA2 and the chromatin remodelling subunit RSF1 alter access to DNA; ZNF593 interferes with the DNA binding of homeodomain factors; SUMO conjugation modifies transcription factor behaviour; and sequence-specific regulators including E2F1, JUN, LEF1, SOX11, NFIB and TFAP4 act within networks where one factor's occupancy excludes another's. Loss of such restraint contributes to unchecked cell cycle entry and developmental misregulation, linking this control to growth, differentiation and innate immune signalling.

Protein-protein interactions are not fixed: they are switched on and off by modifications, competing binders, decoy subunits and scaffolds, and the regulation of protein binding covers the processes that raise or lower how readily two proteins associate. Controlling interaction strength is how cells set the output of signalling complexes, restrict enzyme activity to the right partner, and dismantle assemblies when a signal ends. The genes here act through several such devices: kinases including GSK3B, ROCK1 and MAPK8 that mark partners for altered affinity; scaffolds and adaptors such as RACK1 and LDLRAP1 that bring proteins together; catalytically dead pseudo-phosphatases and truncated decoy proteins that occupy binding sites without acting on them; secreted antagonists such as GREM2 that sequester BMP ligands; and ubiquitin-pathway components including TRIM21 and USP9X. Cytokine receptor sharing via IL6ST and complement-regulatory factor H-related proteins illustrate the same logic extracellularly.

Cortisol secretion is the regulated release of the principal glucocorticoid of the human adrenal cortex, the hormone that mobilises glucose, restrains inflammation and coordinates the body's response to stress, fasting and injury. Output is set by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis: hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone drives pituitary ACTH release, which in turn stimulates steroidogenesis in the adrenal cortex, with negative feedback from circulating cortisol closing the loop. Neuropeptide modulators shape this drive, including galanin acting through its receptor and the stomach-derived hormone ghrelin, which links nutritional state and appetite signalling to adrenal activation. Intracellular relay is supported by the phosphatase encoded by PTPN11 downstream of receptor signalling. Too little cortisol produces adrenal insufficiency with hypoglycaemia and circulatory collapse; chronic excess produces the metabolic, immune and cognitive features of Cushing syndrome.

Steroid hormones circulate freely and act by binding intracellular receptors that then work directly as transcription factors, and this pathway covers the signals set in motion by that binding. It is how androgens, oestrogens, progesterone, glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids shape sexual development, reproductive tissue growth, stress and salt handling, and it is the axis exploited therapeutically in breast and prostate cancer, where the androgen receptor and oestrogen receptors remain the principal drug targets. Ligand binding displaces chaperone and co-chaperone complexes, licences nuclear entry and DNA binding at hormone response elements, and recruits coactivators and corepressors such as NCOA1, MED1, EP300, NCOR1/2 and the HDAC1/2 and KDM1A machinery to switch target genes on or off. Lineage factors including FOXA1 and NKX3-1 direct receptors to tissue-specific sites, while ubiquitin, UFM1 and phosphorylation-dependent steps tune receptor stability and output. Membrane progesterone and oestrogen receptors add faster, non-genomic responses, and circadian clock components link hormone action to daily timing.

After injury, skeletal muscle rebuilds itself from resident satellite cells, and this postnatal regenerative programme is what restores contractile fibres rather than scar. It sustains muscle mass through life, and its decline or genetic disruption underlies poor repair in ageing, cachexia and the progressive weakness of muscular dystrophies. Quiescent PAX7-positive progenitors are activated, proliferate, and commit through myogenic transcription factors such as MYOD1 and MYF6, while WNT ligands acting on FZD7 and IGF1 signalling drive expansion and growth; MSTN restrains it. Nascent myoblasts then fuse, a step requiring the muscle-specific fusogens MYMK and MYMX together with tetraspanins such as CD9 and CD81. Repair also depends on rebuilding the link between fibre and basement membrane, involving dystroglycan and its glycosylating enzymes LARGE1 and FKRP, alongside membrane resealing proteins including CAPN3 and annexin A1.

regulation of MAP kinase activity sets how strongly and how long cells respond to growth factors, cytokines and stress through the ERK, JNK and p38 cascades, which in turn dictate proliferation, differentiation, inflammatory gene expression and apoptosis. Because these kinases are shared by many stimuli, output specificity depends on this tier of control, and its loss underlies oncogenic growth signalling and chronic inflammation. Receptor tyrosine kinases such as FGFR1, ERBB2, PDGFRB and FLT3 feed in from the plasma membrane, while innate immune adaptors MYD88, IRAK1/4 and TRAF6 route TLR and TNF signals through MAP3K7 to stress kinases. Amplitude is tuned by scaffolds and pseudokinases including KSR1, MAPK8IP1 and the Tribbles proteins, by phosphatases such as DUSP7, PTPN1 and PTPRJ, and by ESCRT-dependent receptor sorting through HGS and TSG101, which terminates signalling by degrading activated receptors.

MAP kinase cascades convert signals at the cell surface into changes in proliferation, differentiation, stress responses and inflammatory gene expression, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and how long those cascades fire. Positive input comes from growth factor receptors and their ligands (FGFR1, PDGFRB, ERBB2, FGF2), from innate immune receptor adaptors (MYD88, IRAK1/4, TRAF6, TRAF2) feeding into MAP3K7, and from scaffolds such as KSR1 and MAPK8IP1 that assemble tiers of the cascade into productive modules. Braking is supplied by the phosphatase DUSP7, receptor-proximal tyrosine phosphatases including PTPN1 and PTPN22, pseudokinase tribbles proteins, and small GTPases of the DIRAS family. Balanced control matters because persistent MAP kinase output drives oncogenic growth and chronic inflammatory cytokine production, while inadequate signalling blunts wound repair and immune activation.

MAP kinase cascades convert signals at the cell surface into changes in proliferation, differentiation, stress responses and inflammatory gene expression, and this grouping collects the inputs and upstream kinases that turn those cascades on. Growth factors and their receptor tyrosine kinases feature prominently — FGF1, FGF2 and FGF18 with FGFR1, PDGFB with PDGFRB, ERBB2, FLT1 and FLT3 — linking mitogenic and angiogenic stimulation to ERK and JNK activation. A second arm is immune and stress signalling, where TNF acting through TRAF2 and Toll-like receptor engagement through TRAF6 feed into MAP3K7 and related MAP3K/MAP4K/TAOK kinases that phosphorylate the intervening MAP2K tier. Small GTPases and exchange factors such as RASGRP1 and ARHGEF5 couple receptor occupancy to this relay. Sustained or unrestrained activation of these steps drives oncogenic growth, while loss blunts inflammatory and wound-healing responses.

MAP kinase cascades must be switched off as well as on, and this collection of brakes on MAP kinase activity sets how long and how strongly ERK, JNK and p38 signals persist after a growth factor, stress or immune stimulus. Without such damping, proliferative and inflammatory signalling runs unopposed, a route to tumour growth and to exaggerated immune responses. The inhibitors act at several levels: a dual-specificity phosphatase removes the activating phosphates from ERK, protein tyrosine phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPN22 and PTPRJ blunt receptor and kinase-level tyrosine phosphorylation upstream, scaffolds such as MAPK8IP1 and PAQR3 sequester or mislocalise cascade components, and inhibitory immune receptors like CD300A recruit phosphatase activity to the membrane. Hormonal signals, among them adiponectin, angiotensinogen and natriuretic peptide, feed into the same restraint in metabolic and cardiovascular tissue.

Signalling through MAP kinase cascades must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and the negative regulation of these cascades sets how long and how strongly cells respond to growth factors, cytokines and stress. Without it, ERK, JNK and p38 outputs run unchecked, driving inappropriate proliferation, inflammation and, in the case of germline lesions, tumour-prone developmental syndromes. Several mechanisms converge here: dual-specificity MAP kinase phosphatases such as DUSP1 and DUSP6 dephosphorylate the activation loop of the kinases; Sprouty and SPRED proteins and the RasGAP neurofibromin restrain signal flow at the level of Ras and Raf; tyrosine phosphatases including PTPN6 and PTPN22 and the kinase CSK damp receptor- and Src-family-initiated input; RKIP sequesters Raf. Ubiquitin ligases, scaffolds, transcriptional repressors and a set of microRNAs add feedback layers, tying pathway shutdown to immune tolerance, metabolic control and tissue homeostasis.

positive regulation of MAPK cascade collects the many ways cells turn on the ERK, JNK and p38 kinase relays that convert surface signals into changes in proliferation, differentiation, migration, stress adaptation and inflammatory gene expression. Growth factor and cytokine receptors dominate it — the FGF, PDGF, EGF/ERBB, insulin/IGF, NTRK, KIT and VEGF receptor families — together with G protein-coupled receptors for catecholamines, lipids and neuropeptides, integrins and innate immune receptors such as the Toll-like receptors and MYD88. Their signals converge through adaptors and exchange factors (SHC1, FRS2, PTPN11, RASGRP1, GRB2-type scaffolds), small GTPases including HRAS and RAP1, scaffolds such as KSR1/2 and JIP proteins, and tiers of MAP3Ks and MAP2Ks feeding RAF–MEK–ERK or stress kinase output. Because this circuitry sets growth and survival decisions, its inappropriate activation underlies much of oncogenic transformation, fibrosis and chronic inflammation.

Growth factors, cytokines, hormones and immune stimuli converge on mitogen-activated protein kinase cascades, and this is the collection of activators that turn those cascades up. Positive regulation of MAPK signalling determines whether a cell proliferates, differentiates, migrates, survives stress or mounts an inflammatory response, and its excess drives much of cancer and chronic inflammation. Receptor tyrosine kinases for FGF, EGF, PDGF, insulin/IGF, NGF and VEGF families feed through adaptors such as SHC1, FRS2, GRB2-associated proteins and the phosphatase PTPN11 to RAS proteins and the RAF-MEK-ERK module; parallel input from Toll-like receptors, MYD88, TRAF6 and MAP3K7 activates the stress-responsive JNK and p38 arms via MAP2K3, MAP2K6 and MAP2K7, with scaffolds including KSR1 and MAPK8IP proteins organising the tiers. G protein-coupled receptors, integrins, Wnt and TGF-beta ligands, and regulatory microRNAs also raise cascade output.

Methylation is one of the most widespread covalent modifications in the cell, and this pathway covers its transfer onto proteins, RNA and other macromolecules using S-adenosylmethionine as donor. The consequences are broad: methylated histone lysines set chromatin states, arginine methylation by the PRMT family tunes RNA-binding proteins and spliceosomal Sm proteins, ribosomal RNA and tRNA methylations by the NSUN, TRMT and METTL enzymes license ribosome assembly and accurate, efficient translation, and N6-methyladenosine deposited by the METTL3-METTL14 complex with its cofactors controls mRNA fate. Specialized writers modify translation factors, protein N-termini and C-termini, and mitochondrial rRNA and tRNA, linking the pathway to oxidative phosphorylation. Loss of individual methyltransferases causes intellectual disability, mitochondrial disease and cancer, and the shared dependence on SAM ties these modifications to one-carbon and methionine metabolism.

Skeletal muscle repairs itself after injury by activating resident satellite cells, which proliferate, fuse and rebuild damaged fibres; this pathway covers the inputs that drive that repair harder or faster, positively regulating skeletal muscle tissue regeneration. Its output determines how well muscle recovers from exercise damage, trauma or disease, and its failure contributes to the progressive wasting and fibrotic replacement seen in muscular dystrophies and in age-related sarcopenia. The myogenic transcription factor MYOD1 commits activated satellite cells to differentiation, with SOX15 and the homeodomain protein HOPX acting as transcriptional modulators of the progenitor state, while the nuclear receptor PPARD links regeneration to oxidative and lipid metabolic programmes in muscle. CAPN3, a muscle-specific calpain protease of the sarcomere, is required for normal repair and remodelling, and its loss causes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

Skeletal muscle repairs itself after injury by activating satellite cells, which proliferate, fuse and rebuild damaged fibres; this pathway covers the inputs that set how readily and how far that regeneration proceeds. Its tuning matters because too little repair leaves progressive weakness and fibrosis, as seen in muscular dystrophies and in the blunted regenerative capacity of aged muscle, while unchecked activation exhausts the satellite cell pool. The myogenic transcription factor MYOD1 drives commitment of activated progenitors to differentiation, with SOX15 and HOPX acting on progenitor state, and the nuclear receptor PPARD links regeneration to oxidative fuel use and fibre-type character. Structural and sarcomeric components such as the calpain CAPN3 and the Z-disc protein MYOZ1 tie the integrity of the mature fibre back to repair signalling, connecting this biology to exercise adaptation, muscle growth and myopathy.

Transcription factors are held in check as well as switched on, and this collection covers the processes that stop, prevent or reduce the activity of DNA-binding transcription factors. Much of the content concerns restraint of NF- inkB: IkB-family and IkB-like inhibitors, the deubiquitinases CYLD and OTULIN that strip activating ubiquitin chains from signalling intermediates, COMMD proteins that promote clearance of chromatin-bound subunits, and SETD6, which methylates an NF-kB subunit to keep target genes silent. Inflammasome-associated pyrin-domain proteins and NLR regulators such as NLRC3 damp innate immune transcriptional output, while ID proteins sequester E-box factors as dominant-negative partners and SIRT1 deacetylates factors to reduce their activity. The theme matters because loss of such brakes gives persistent inflammatory gene expression, autoimmunity and unchecked proliferation; FOXP3 and MEN1 link the same logic to regulatory T cell function and tumour suppression.

Peptide hormones circulating in the blood — insulin, glucagon, growth hormone, leptin, angiotensin, oxytocin, ghrelin and the POMC-derived peptides among them — instruct cells to change metabolism, gene expression, secretion and growth, and the response to peptide hormone stimulus covers the receptors and downstream machinery that carry out those instructions. This is the basis of systemic glucose and lipid homeostasis, appetite and energy balance, blood pressure control, growth and reproduction; its derangement underlies type 2 diabetes, obesity and hypertension. Mechanistically it spans receptor tyrosine kinases signalling through IRS adaptors, PI3K, AKT and mTOR to GLUT4 trafficking and FOXO-dependent gluconeogenic genes; G protein-coupled receptors acting via adenylate cyclases, PKA and phospholipase C; and cytokine-like receptors using JAK kinases and STAT transcription factors, with SOCS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN1 providing negative feedback.

Corticotropin-releasing hormone is the hypothalamic trigger of the stress axis, and this pathway covers what a cell does once that signal arrives: how it changes secretion, gene expression and excitability in response. It is the entry point of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal cascade, where CRH acting on pituitary corticotropes drives ACTH release and ultimately glucocorticoid output, while the same ligand family also shapes anxiety, arousal, appetite and autonomic tone in the brain and periphery. Two G protein-coupled receptors, CRHR1 and CRHR2, transduce the signal largely through cAMP, with CRHR1 dominating pituitary and anxiety-related responses and CRHR2 favouring peripheral and modulatory roles. Downstream, the immediate-early nuclear receptors NR4A1, NR4A2 and NR4A3 are rapidly induced and rewire transcription, including steroidogenic and neuropeptide genes; the anorectic peptide precursor CARTPT is among the neuropeptide outputs. Dysregulation contributes to depression, anxiety disorders and maladaptive stress responses.

Control over the rate and extent of secondary metabolism here resolves, in humans, into regulation of melanin synthesis — a pigment not needed for cell growth but decisive for skin, hair and eye colour and for protection of keratinocytes and melanocytes against ultraviolet damage. The core switch is hormonal: POMC-derived melanocortin peptides act on MC1R to raise cyclic AMP and drive eumelanin production, while agouti signalling protein antagonises that receptor and shifts output toward pheomelanin. Downstream, melanosome identity and maturation depend on PMEL fibril formation, RAB38-directed trafficking, and transporters including ATP7A, SLC24A5, MFSD12 and the cystine machinery that sets substrate supply for TYRP1. Loss or variation in these components produces albinism, pigmentary dilution and the common human variation in complexion, and links pigmentation to melanosome biogenesis and lysosome-related organelle traffic.

Control over flux through the pentose phosphate shunt determines how much glucose a cell diverts away from glycolysis toward NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate rather than ATP. That balance sets a cell's capacity to regenerate reduced glutathione and thioredoxin against oxidative stress and to supply sugar phosphates for nucleotide synthesis during growth, which is why proliferating and tumour cells lean on it heavily. Regulation here operates on two levels: the p53-inducible phosphatase TIGAR lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, restraining glycolysis and pushing carbon into the oxidative branch with an antioxidant, apoptosis-limiting effect, while mTOR in complex with raptor and mLST8 couples nutrient and growth-factor status to biosynthetic demand for reducing equivalents. Aldolase links the shunt back to the glycolytic pool. Loss of this coordination leaves cells vulnerable to reactive oxygen species and redox-driven damage.

Regulation of cellular respiration controls how fast mitochondria oxidise fuels and make ATP, tuning energy output to oxygen availability, nutrient supply and stress. It matters because respiratory rate sets the balance between ATP yield and reactive oxygen species production, and because its misregulation underlies the metabolic shift of hypoxic and inflammatory tissue, neurodegeneration, and cardiomyopathy. Control is exerted at several levels: transcription and replication of the mitochondrial genome (TEFM, PNPT1, PRDM16), assembly and remodelling of respiratory complexes (UQCC2, NDUFA4L2, DNAJC15), deacetylation of matrix enzymes by SIRT3, chaperone-mediated restraint of complex activity by TRAP1, and calcium and permeability transition gating through SLC25A23 and PPIF. Hypoxia acting via MIR210 and cytokine signals including interferon-gamma, TNF and IL-4 suppress oxidative phosphorylation, while PINK1 and PARK7 protect it, linking respiratory tone to immune activation and mitochondrial quality control.

Cells tune how much of their fuel is burned oxidatively, and this regulatory layer sets the rate and extent of cellular respiration rather than carrying out the reactions themselves. The tuning matters because oxidative phosphorylation must be matched to oxygen availability, biosynthetic demand and redox safety: too much flux generates damaging reactive oxygen species, too little starves the cell of ATP. Inputs are diverse. SIRT3 deacetylates mitochondrial enzymes to raise oxidative capacity, PINK1 and PARK7 protect respiratory function and are mutated in Parkinson disease, PPIF governs the permeability transition pore, and a hypoxia-induced microRNA together with NDUFA4L2 dampens electron transport when oxygen is scarce. Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, IFNG and IL4 remodel respiration during immune activation, while brown-fat and lipogenic transcription factors couple it to thermogenesis and nutrient state. Calcium and phosphate carriers, iron-sulfur and assembly factors provide further control points.

This grouping collects proteins that tune the rate at which ATP-hydrolysing machines work, rather than performing the hydrolysis themselves. Two themes dominate. One is control of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium pump: the small transmembrane regulators phospholamban, sarcolipin and related micropeptides bind SERCA and restrain its calcium uptake, setting the speed of cardiac and skeletal muscle relaxation, while troponin and tropomyosin subunits govern the actin-activated ATPase of myosin during contraction. The other is regulation of chaperone ATPases, where J-domain cochaperones such as DNAJB11, DNAJB2 and DNAJC9 stimulate Hsp70 ATP turnover and AHSA1 accelerates the Hsp90 cycle, coupling nucleotide hydrolysis to productive client folding. Further members modulate AAA-ATPases and membrane translocases at the nuclear envelope and mitochondria. Loss of such restraint shows up as impaired calcium cycling in heart failure and as defective protein quality control.

Cells must match their production of energy and of the carbon skeletons that feed biosynthesis to what the organism actually needs, and this collection covers the control layer imposed on those routes rather than the enzymes that carry them out. It matters because the same regulators set fasting versus fed metabolism, aerobic versus glycolytic ATP supply, and mitochondrial content and quality. Insulin and its receptor acting through IRS proteins, PI3K and AKT, the AMP-activated kinase subunits, mTOR with its partners RPTOR and MLST8, and cAMP-dependent protein kinase together tune glucose uptake, glycolysis and glycogen handling, the latter via the PPP1R3 family of glycogen-targeting phosphatase subunits and phosphorylase kinase. Transcriptional and hypoxic arms add HIF1A with ARNT, PPARA, PRDM16, TP53 and the sirtuins SIRT3 and SIRT6, while PINK1, PARK7 and PPIF link the same control to mitochondrial integrity. Dysregulation here underlies insulin resistance, glycogen storage disease and tumour metabolic reprogramming.

Control over how fast cells break down sugars and glycogen lets tissues match ATP supply to demand and keeps blood glucose within range. The genes here are the regulators rather than the glycolytic enzymes themselves: insulin and its receptor, glucokinase setting hepatic and beta-cell glucose sensing, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and TIGAR opposing flux, and phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-bisphosphatase and phosphorylase kinase subunits gating glycogen mobilisation. Nutrient- and energy-sensing hubs dominate — AMPK subunits, the mTOR complex with RPTOR and MLST8, FLCN — alongside transcriptional control by HIF1A with ARNT, which shifts cells toward glycolysis under hypoxia, plus PPARA, MLXIPL, TP53 and chromatin regulators such as EP300, NCOR1, HDAC4 and SIRT6. Protein phosphatases and O-GlcNAc transferase add post-translational tuning. Loss of this regulation underlies hypoglycaemia and diabetes, glycogen storage disease, and the glycolytic reprogramming of tumours.

pigmentation covers how melanin and related pigments are made, packaged and delivered to the tissues that display them, giving skin, hair and eye their colour and shielding skin from ultraviolet damage. Its failure produces albinism, piebaldism and Waardenburg syndrome, and the same signalling axis is co-opted in melanoma. The genes trace the whole route: MITF and SOX10 with KIT and EDNRB specify and expand the neural crest-derived melanocyte lineage; TYR, TYRP1, DCT, PMEL, OCA2 and SLC45A2 build and acidify the melanosome interior; and the BLOC/HPS complexes, AP-3 and AP-1 adaptors, and RAB27A-MYO5A-MLPH machinery sort cargo into this lysosome-related organelle and haul it along the cytoskeleton for transfer to keratinocytes. Hormonal tuning through POMC, MC1R and ASIP sets the balance between eumelanin and pheomelanin, linking pigmentation to endocrine and stress responses.

Pigmentation covers how melanin and related pigments accumulate in skin, hair, eyes and inner ear, whether by making more pigment per cell or by generating more pigment cells. It determines visible colour, shields keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage, and supports retinal and cochlear function; its failure gives albinism, Waardenburg and Hermansky-Pudlak syndromes, piebaldism and hearing loss, while dysregulated melanocyte growth underlies melanoma. Melanoblasts arise from neural crest under MITF, SOX10 and KIT signalling, then build melanosomes as lysosome-related organelles: tyrosinase and TYRP1 catalyse melanin synthesis, PMEL forms the internal matrix, and OCA2 and SLC45A2 set organelle pH and ion balance. Adaptor and biogenesis complexes together with Rab GTPases deliver cargo to maturing melanosomes, and myosin Va with RAB27A and melanophilin captures them for transfer to neighbouring cells. Melanocortin receptor signalling opposed by agouti protein tunes the pigment type produced.

Pigment accumulation is the concentration of coloring matter at a defined site in a cell or tissue, typically in response to an external cue such as ultraviolet light, and in humans it accounts for skin, hair and eye color as well as retinal pigment epithelium function. The genes here point to how melanin is confined to lysosome-related organelles: adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3 sort melanogenic enzymes and transporters into forming melanosomes, BLOC-1 subunits drive tubular cargo transport out of endosomes, the Rab32/Rab38 pair with its effector machinery directs vesicle delivery, and CD63 marks the organelle membrane. SHROOM proteins shape the apical cytoskeleton of pigmented epithelia, while glucuronidation and ABC-family transport handle conjugation and efflux of pigment-related metabolites. Loss of these trafficking steps produces hypopigmentation syndromes combining albinism with bleeding and immune defects.

Most human genes produce more than one mRNA, and the choice of which exons survive is made by the regulators collected here. Control over RNA splicing determines cell-type-specific protein isoforms as neurons, muscle and epithelia each impose their own splicing programme and its disruption underlies myotonic dystrophy, spinal muscular atrophy-like phenotypes, cardiomyopathy and many cancers. Sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins such as the SR family, hnRNPs, NOVA, RBFOX, PTBP, CELF, MBNL, QKI and ESRP bind enhancer and silencer elements to promote or repress spliceosome recruitment at competing sites, while core snRNP and spliceosomal components provide the catalytic machinery being tuned. Kinases of the CLK and SRPK families, arginine methylation by PRMT5, and m6A writers and readers add post-transcriptional control, and coupling to transcription and to nonsense-mediated decay links splice-site choice to overall gene output.

Malate-aspartate shuttle moves the reducing power of cytosolic NADH into mitochondria, since the inner membrane is impermeable to NADH itself. This is what allows glycolysis to keep running while its electrons are oxidized on the respiratory chain, and it sets the cytosolic NAD+/NADH ratio that governs whether pyruvate is burned or converted to lactate. It works as a cycle of two paired enzymes and two carriers: cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters via the oxoglutarate carrier and is re-oxidized inside, while transaminases and the aspartate-glutamate carriers return carbon to the cytosol. The neuronal and hepatic aspartate-glutamate carrier isoforms link the shuttle to glutamate handling and urea cycle nitrogen; their loss causes citrin deficiency and epileptic encephalopathy, illustrating how tightly energy metabolism, amino acid flux and redox balance are coupled here.

The inner mitochondrial membrane is impermeable to NADH, so cytosolic reducing equivalents generated by glycolysis must be moved indirectly; the malate-aspartate shuttle does this by carrying the electrons as malate. Without it, glycolytic NAD+ cannot be regenerated by oxidative means and cells fall back on lactate production, so the cycle underpins the coupling of glycolysis to oxidative phosphorylation and is especially relied upon in heart, liver, brain and pancreatic beta cells, where it contributes to glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Paired cytosolic and mitochondrial isoforms of aspartate aminotransferase (GOT1, GOT2) and malate dehydrogenase (MDH1, MDH2) interconvert malate, oxaloacetate, aspartate and glutamate on either side of the membrane, while the dicarboxylate, aspartate-glutamate and glutamate carriers of the SLC25 family move the intermediates across. Loss of the liver aspartate-glutamate carrier SLC25A13 causes citrin deficiency, with impaired ureagenesis and hyperammonemia.

phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/protein kinase B signal transduction is the core growth and survival cassette that converts signals from surface receptors into lipid second messengers and Akt activity, coupling nutrient and mitogen availability to cell growth, metabolism, motility and resistance to apoptosis. Its outputs govern insulin action on glucose uptake, angiogenesis, immune cell activation and neuronal survival, and its constitutive activation through PIK3CA mutation or PTEN loss is among the commonest events in human cancer. Ligand-engaged receptor tyrosine kinases, cytokine, integrin and G protein-coupled receptors recruit class I PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits via adaptors such as IRS1/2 and GAB1; the resulting phosphoinositides bring PDPK1 and AKT1 to the membrane, feeding into TSC2/mTOR complexes and autophagy regulators. Phosphatases including PTEN, INPPL1 and PHLPP1, plus inhibitory microRNAs, set signal duration and amplitude.

A signalling cassette that converts stimulation of surface receptors into cell growth, survival and metabolic commitment. Growth factor, cytokine, integrin and hormone receptors — insulin and IGF receptors, EGFR family members, PDGFR, KIT, FLT3, RET and the neurotrophin receptors — recruit class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic and regulatory subunits through adaptors such as IRS1/2, GAB1 and PTPN11. The resulting phosphoinositide pool docks PDPK1 and Akt at the membrane, and phosphorylated Akt then suppresses apoptosis, drives glucose uptake, and releases mTOR complex activity by inactivating TSC2, linking this route to nutrient sensing and autophagy control. Opposing activities set the tone: PTEN and other inositol phosphatases degrade the lipid signal, PHLPP1 and PP2A dephosphorylate the kinase, and numerous microRNAs tune the components. Persistent activation through PIK3CA mutation or PTEN loss is among the commonest oncogenic events, while impaired signalling underlies insulin resistance.

Muscle is a plastic tissue: its fibre size, contractile protein composition and metabolic capacity are continually reset by use, load, hormones and nutrient supply, and this adaptive remodelling is what produces endurance versus strength phenotypes, cardiac hypertrophy in response to pressure overload, and the wasting that follows disuse, denervation or chronic illness. Contractile activity raises calcium, engaging calmodulin-dependent kinases and calcineurin to drive MEF2- and myogenin-directed transcription and switches between slow and fast myosin and troponin isoforms. Growth signals through IGF1 act against myostatin and the FOXO-driven atrophy programme, in which the muscle-specific ubiquitin ligases encoded by FBXO32 and TRIM63 target sarcomeric proteins for degradation. Sarcolemmal and sarcoplasmic reticulum components, PPAR-family metabolic regulators, and a large complement of muscle-enriched microRNAs including the miR-1, miR-133 and miR-208/499 families tune the response. Satellite-cell-based repair and fusion contribute to the structural side of adaptation.

Skeletal muscle adapts its size, fibre-type composition and contractile properties to the demands placed on it, and this remodelling programme is what converts training, disuse, denervation or hormonal change into lasting alterations in muscle phenotype. It matters for endurance versus power performance, for recovery after immobilisation, and for the atrophy seen in ageing, cachexia and heart failure. Calcium released through the excitation-contraction machinery is read out by calmodulin-dependent kinases and the phosphatase calcineurin, whose catalytic subunit PPP3CA drives slow, oxidative gene expression; the resulting shift is visible in slow-fibre contractile proteins such as MYH7, TNNI1, TNNT1 and TNNC1, with myomiRs encoded within myosin genes reinforcing the switch. Opposing arms set mass: myostatin restrains growth, the ubiquitin ligase TRIM63 marks sarcomeric proteins for degradation during atrophy, while MYOD1 and fusion machinery support regeneration and myonuclear addition.

Muscle remodels itself in response to load, hormones and activity, and this collection governs how far and how fast that adaptation proceeds yen in cardiac hypertrophy, skeletal fibre-type switching, and atrophy during disuse or disease. Calcium-dependent signalling is central: calcineurin and CaMKII isoforms, working with MEF2 transcription factors and the repressor HDAC4, translate contractile activity into changes in gene expression, while sarcoplasmic reticulum and sarcolemmal calcium handling proteins such as ATP2A2 and calsequestrin set the signal itself. Growth input through IGF1 opposes FOXO1/FOXO3, which drive the atrophy-associated ubiquitin ligases TRIM63 and FBXO32 and autophagic protein breakdown, so the balance of these arms determines whether muscle mass is gained or lost. A large complement of microRNAs, including the muscle-enriched miR-1, miR-133 and miR-208 families, tunes the same programme. Slow and fast troponin and myosin isoforms mark the resulting phenotypes, and dysregulation underlies pathological cardiac hypertrophy, cachexia and sarcopenia.

mitochondrial DNA repair keeps the mitochondrial genome intact so that the handful of genes it encodes for the respiratory chain and mitochondrial translation remain readable. Mitochondrial DNA sits close to the site of oxidative phosphorylation and accumulates oxidative lesions, strand breaks and deletions; without repair and tolerance mechanisms these accumulate into the large deletions and depletion seen in mitochondrial myopathies, neurodegeneration and ageing tissue. The genes here cover the main routes available in the organelle: base excision repair completed by a mitochondrial ligase and PARP1-mediated break sensing, nuclease and helicase activities that trim flaps and degrade damaged linear ends, and a primase-polymerase that permits replication restart past lesions rather than repairing them outright. The pathway therefore links genome maintenance to mitochondrial replication and turnover, and its failure is registered as loss of oxidative capacity rather than as nuclear mutation.

Mitochondria carry their own small genome close to the respiratory chain, where reactive oxygen species and replication stress leave it heavily damaged, and repairing that DNA keeps oxidative phosphorylation genes intact. Loss of this capacity leads to mitochondrial DNA deletions, depletion and point mutations, and underlies mitochondrial myopathies and progressive multi-organ disease as mutant genomes accumulate with age. The proteins here cover the main routes available in the organelle: base excision repair completed by a ligase that seals nicks, nuclease and exonuclease activities that trim flaps and degrade damaged or linear mitochondrial DNA, a primase-polymerase able to reprime replication past lesions, and a poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase that senses strand breaks. Because the organelle lacks nucleotide excision repair, tolerance and degradation of damaged genomes, rather than repair of every lesion, substantially shapes mitochondrial genome maintenance and copy number.

JNK, the stress-activated arm of the MAP kinase family, converts inflammatory and stress signals into changes in transcription that determine whether a cell proliferates, differentiates or dies, and the genes here set how strongly and how long that kinase is switched on. Upstream MAP kinase kinase kinases such as MAP3K7, MAP3K4 and the mixed-lineage kinases MAP3K10 and MAP3K11 feed the cascade, while the adaptors TRAF2 and TRAF6 couple it to tumour necrosis factor and Toll-like receptor engagement, placing this control immediately downstream of innate immune and cytokine sensing. Scaffolding by MAPK8IP1 assembles the kinase module and focuses signalling, and negative regulators including AIDA and PDCD4 restrain output. Because sustained JNK activity drives apoptosis and inflammatory gene expression, the balance struck here matters in chronic inflammation, autoimmunity, insulin resistance and tumour cell survival.

Stress, inflammatory cytokines and innate immune stimuli converge on the c-Jun N-terminal kinase branch of MAP kinase signalling, and this pathway covers the upstream events that switch it on. The output shapes whether a cell mounts an inflammatory transcriptional response, arrests, differentiates or dies by apoptosis, and sustained activation contributes to chronic inflammation, insulin resistance and neuronal injury. Ligand-engaged receptors such as the TLR2/TLR6 heterodimer and TNF receptors recruit the adaptors TRAF6 and TRAF2, which nucleate ubiquitin-dependent assembly of MAP3K7 (TAK1) and related kinases. Mixed-lineage kinases MAP3K10 and MAP3K11, together with MAP3K4, TAOK3 and the germinal-centre kinase MAP4K2, act as the tier that phosphorylates JNK-activating MAP2Ks, while a Rho-family exchange factor links cytoskeletal and adhesion cues into the same cascade, ultimately driving AP-1-dependent transcription.

JNK signalling drives stress-activated transcription through phosphorylation of JUN, and pushing it too hard or for too long tips cells toward apoptosis, inflammatory cytokine output and insulin resistance; negative regulation of JUN kinase activity is the brake that keeps the cascade proportionate and self-limiting. The restraint is applied at several levels. Scaffold-type proteins such as MAPK8IP1 and AIDA govern whether the upstream kinases assemble productively with JNK or are held apart, so the same binding surfaces that enable signalling can also suppress it. Phosphatase activity, exemplified by PTPN22 in immune cells, removes activating marks, while chaperone and kinase components including DNAJA1 and HIPK3 tune stability and pathway crosstalk. Loss of this damping contributes to excessive stress-induced cell death and to chronic inflammatory and metabolic disease, and the pathway operates alongside dual-specificity phosphatase feedback on other MAP kinase arms.

When DNA is damaged, p53 converts that signal into arrest, repair or death, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly and how long that response runs. Tuning matters in both directions: too little and damaged cells divide and accumulate mutations, too much and tissues lose stem and progenitor cells to unnecessary apoptosis, which is why tumours so often disable the restraints. The apical kinases ATM and ATR initiate the cascade, while MDM2 caps it by targeting p53 for degradation and CDKN2A/ARF relieves that brake. A further layer works on p53 itself through covalent marks, including deacetylation by SIRT1 and methylation by SMYD2 and KMT5A, alongside chromatin and nucleolar factors such as KDM1A, ING4 and NPM1. Output is biased toward particular fates by cofactors, with PMAIP1 and ZNF385A favouring apoptotic versus arrest-associated target genes.

When DNA is broken or replication stalls, p53 must be switched on quickly and kept on long enough to impose a cell cycle arrest or trigger death, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that decision forward. Amplifying p53 signalling is how cells with damaged genomes are prevented from dividing, which is why loss of these components favours tumour formation and why their activity sets sensitivity to radiation and chemotherapy. The apical kinases ATM and ATR sense double-strand breaks and replication stress and phosphorylate p53 and its regulators; CDKN2A acts through the ARF arm to stabilise p53 by opposing its ubiquitin-mediated turnover; RPL26 binds p53 mRNA to raise its translation; ZNF385A biases the response toward apoptotic targets such as PMAIP1. Together they determine whether a damaged cell pauses, repairs, senesces or dies.

negative regulation of DNA damage response, signal transduction by p53 class mediator is the braking system on p53 signalling, setting how much arrest, senescence or apoptosis a cell commits to after its DNA is damaged. It matters because unrestrained p53 output kills or permanently arrests cells that could be repaired, while excessive braking allows damaged cells to keep dividing — the route by which many tumours inactivate p53 without mutating it. The dominant mechanism is ubiquitin-dependent turnover through MDM2, reinforced by gankyrin (PSMD10) and other ubiquitin ligase components; deacetylation by SIRT1 and demethylation by KDM1A strip p53 of activating modifications, and DYRK kinases and the cytokine MIF, acting via CD74, damp the response from outside the nucleus. Notably, the EMT transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 suppress p53 output, linking checkpoint attenuation to invasive and stem-like cell states.

Damage-induced p53 signalling must be switched off once repair is complete, and damping of this DNA damage response by p53-class mediators sets how readily a cell commits to arrest, senescence or apoptosis. The brake matters in both directions: too much restraint lets damaged cells proliferate and is a route to tumour formation, while too little causes excessive cell death and loss of stem and progenitor pools. MDM2 is the central ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for degradation and holds its level low in unstressed cells; SIRT1 deacetylates p53 to blunt its transcriptional output, and the demethylase KDM1A removes methyl marks that otherwise stabilise activated p53. DYRK-family kinases, the gankyrin proteasome regulator PSMD10, and the mesenchymal transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 add further repression, linking p53 suppression to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and to signals from MIF and CD74.

regulation of neuron apoptotic process sets the threshold at which a neuron either survives or dies, and because most neurons are never replaced, where this threshold sits determines the size of the mature nervous system and the pace of neurodegeneration. During development, excess neurons are eliminated unless they receive trophic support, and the pathway is built around that competition: neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF and NT-3 acting through TRK receptors and PI3K-AKT survival signalling, opposed by JNK-cascade kinases, CDK5, and the BCL-2 family gatekeepers BAX, BCL2L11 and MCL1 that license mitochondrial permeabilisation and caspase-3/9 activation. Stress inputs converge here too, including DNA damage sensing by ATM and p53 targets, the integrated stress response through ATF4 and CHOP, hypoxia, and glial cytokines. Many familial neurodegeneration genes, among them PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, PSEN1, APP, GRN and SOD1, act as modulators, linking this control point to Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

Neurons are largely post-mitotic and irreplaceable, so whether one lives or dies is tightly controlled, and this regulation of neuronal apoptosis sets both the sculpting of the developing nervous system and the survival of mature circuits under stress. During development, excess neurons die unless they capture target-derived trophic support; neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF, NT-3 and GDNF acting through TRKA, TRKB and related receptors engage PI3K-AKT and STAT3 signalling to suppress the intrinsic death machinery, while withdrawal activates JNK-pathway kinases, FOXO3 and BH3-only proteins including BIM, PUMA and HRK to permit BAX-dependent mitochondrial permeabilization and caspase-9/caspase-3 activation. BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 oppose this, and DNA damage, ER stress effectors ATF4 and CHOP, hypoxia sensing, and neuroinflammatory signals from microglia feed in. Many familial neurodegeneration genes, among them PARK7, PINK1, PRKN, SNCA, APP, PSEN1, GRN and SOD1, act here, linking dysregulated neuronal death to Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and motor neuron disease.

Neurons are largely post-mitotic and irreplaceable, so the machinery that holds their death programme in check determines how many survive development and how long they persist in the adult brain. Suppression of neuronal apoptosis is driven chiefly by trophic factor signalling: neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF, NTF3 and GDNF act through TRK receptors and co-receptors, engaging PI3K-AKT and RAS-ERK cascades, while cytokines acting via gp130, JAK2 and STAT3 provide a parallel survival input. Downstream, anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members oppose BAX and BOK at the mitochondrion, and antioxidant and mitochondrial quality control proteins including SOD1, SOD2, PARK7, PINK1 and PRKN remove the stresses that would otherwise trigger release of cytochrome c. Transcriptional regulators and stress-response factors such as ATF4, JUN, MEF2C and SIRT1 set the threshold. Loss of these safeguards underlies neurodegeneration, from Parkinson and motor neuron disease to neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

Neurons are largely post-mitotic and irreplaceable, so the machinery that pushes them into programmed death sets the limits of both developmental pruning and neurodegeneration. Positive regulation of the neuron apoptotic process covers the signals and effectors that raise the rate of this death: trophic-factor withdrawal and stress kinase routes, death receptor ligands such as FASLG and TNF, and the BH3-only proteins PUMA, BIM and HRK that neutralise MCL1 and license BAX-dependent mitochondrial permeabilisation, releasing cytochrome c and AIF to activate the caspase cascade through CASP9, CASP3 and CASP7. Transcriptional stress arms contribute through ATF4 and CHOP, while CDK5 with its activator p35, GSK3 isoforms, ATM and FOXO3 relay DNA damage and excitotoxic input. Amyloid precursor protein, BACE1, prion protein and progranulin tie the same effectors to Alzheimer and related neurodegenerative disease, and excessive activity during development causes neuronal loss.

New blood vessels form when endothelial cells detach from the vessel wall and move directionally into surrounding extracellular matrix, and this migratory programme is the step that converts an angiogenic signal into an actual sprout. It underlies wound healing, ischaemic collateral growth and the vascularisation of tumours, and its misregulation contributes to retinopathy, vascular malformation and tumour progression. Growth factor input through VEGFA and its receptor KDR, together with FGF2/FGFR1, angiopoietin–TIE signalling and TGF-beta family ligands acting via ACVRL1, is relayed by PI3K–AKT, PLCG1 and MAPK cascades onto RHOA, RHOJ and integrin-linked adhesion to remodel the actin cytoskeleton and focal contacts. Notch–DLL4 and ephrin/EPHB4 cues assign tip versus stalk behaviour and arterial–venous identity, NOS3-derived nitric oxide and HIF1A couple migration to hypoxia and flow, thrombospondin and vasohibin restrain it, and numerous microRNAs tune the whole response.

New blood vessels form when endothelial cells detach from the vessel wall and move toward a pro-angiogenic cue, and this pathway covers the inputs that increase the rate and extent of that movement. It underlies wound healing, collateral growth after ischaemia and the embryonic patterning of the vasculature, and when driven excessively it supplies tumours with blood and contributes to retinopathy. Growth factor ligands and their receptors, chiefly VEGFA and VEGFC acting through KDR with neuropilin-1 as coreceptor, plus FGF2 signalling via FGFR1, converge on PI3K-AKT and p38 modules, with GAB1 and PDPK1 relaying the signal and endothelial nitric oxide synthase, RHOJ and thymosin beta-4 reshaping the cytoskeleton. Hypoxia acts through HIF1A, while class IIa histone deacetylases, GATA2, ETS1 and a large complement of microRNAs including miR-126 and miR-210 set how strongly cells respond.

Angiogenesis requires endothelial cells to move, and equally requires them to stop; the braking arm of that control is what restrains blood vessel endothelial cell migration and keeps sprouting vessels from overgrowing. Loss of this restraint contributes to tumour neovascularisation, retinopathy and vascular malformation, while excess restraint impairs wound healing and collateral vessel formation. The effectors are diverse: Notch signalling through DLL4 and NOTCH1 specifies stalk cells that trail rather than lead, thrombospondin-1 and vasohibin act as secreted anti-angiogenic cues, TGF-beta family members signalling through ACVRL1 and GDF2 stabilise the endothelium, and multimerin-2 and cerebral cavernous malformation protein PDCD10 maintain junctional and cytoskeletal quiescence through RHOA-directed regulation. A large complement of microRNAs, including members of the let-7, miR-15/16 and miR-200 families, tunes these messages post-transcriptionally, linking vessel patterning to inflammatory and metabolic input from TNF, PPARG and KLF4.

Endothelial cells must crawl out into the extracellular matrix and organise into new tubes whenever a tissue needs fresh blood or lymphatic vessels, and this migratory programme is the motile core of angiogenesis, vascular repair after injury, and the vascularisation of tumours. Growth factor receptors such as KDR, FGFR1, TEK and FLT4 read VEGF, angiopoietin and FGF gradients and feed into PI3K-AKT, PLCG1, RAC1/RHOA and focal adhesion signalling through PTK2, paxillin and BCAR1, converting integrin-matrix attachment into directed movement. Guidance cues from Slit-Robo, ephrins, semaphorins and DLL4-NOTCH sort tip from stalk cells, while junctional proteins including CDH5 and PECAM1 keep the advancing sheet coherent. Transcription factors such as SOX18, PROX1 and GATA2 and a large complement of microRNAs tune the response. Defective control underlies hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, cavernous malformations, and pathological neovascularisation in retinopathy and cancer.

Proteins acquire acyl groups on specific amino acids, and this covalent tagging decides where a protein sits in the cell, how long it lasts, and whether it can act as a transcriptional switch. The genes here cover the main chemistries: lysine acetyltransferases such as CREBBP/EP300, KAT2A/2B, KAT5 and the HAT1 and KAT6A/KAT7 enzymes that mark histones and nonhistone substrates to open chromatin, opposed by the NAD-dependent deacetylase SIRT1; N-terminal acetyltransferases of the NAA family that modify nascent chains during translation; N-myristoyltransferases NMT1/2; and the large ZDHHC family of palmitoyl acyltransferases that anchor signalling proteins to membranes and to synaptic sites. Specialised members lipidate secreted ligands — PORCN for Wnts, HHAT for Hedgehog, MBOAT4 for ghrelin — while AANAT acetylates serotonin for melatonin synthesis alongside the CLOCK–BMAL1 circadian machinery. Loss of individual enzymes causes developmental syndromes, cohesinopathies and intellectual disability.

GTP-binding proteins act as timed switches, and this pathway covers the accelerators that turn them off or hand them on — processes that increase GTPase activity and so set how long a signal lasts. Because hydrolysis terminates the active state, these regulators determine the duration of Rho, Ras, Rab, Ran and heterotrimeric G protein signalling, and with it cytoskeletal remodelling, cell migration and adhesion, vesicle traffic, nucleocytoplasmic transport and growth control. Members include GTPase-activating proteins for Rho family switches, TBC-domain proteins acting on Rab GTPases, RGS proteins that accelerate hydrolysis on Gα subunits, and the Ras and Ral GAPs; guanine nucleotide exchange factors and receptors such as plexins and semaphorin partners appear as upstream activators of the same cycles. Loss of individual brakes is tumour-promoting or neurodegenerative, as with neurofibromin and the TSC1 complex.
