Kinases are only useful if they fire at the right moment, and this collection covers the machinery that sets their activity up or down. Positive and negative control appear together: cyclins and CDK-activating phosphatases such as CDC25A and CDC25C oppose the CIP/KIP inhibitors CDKN1A and CDKN1B and the WEE1-family kinase PKMYT1 at cell cycle transitions; regulatory subunits of protein kinase A and the PKA inhibitor PKIA tune cAMP responses; SOCS proteins and phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPRC and PTPRJ damp receptor tyrosine and JAK signalling; Tribbles pseudokinases and KSR1 act as scaffolds or brakes on MAP kinase cascades; and DEPTOR with STK11-STRADA modulates mTOR and AMPK-directed growth control. Adaptors of innate immune receptors, MYD88, IRAK family members and TRAFs, illustrate how ligand binding is converted into kinase output. Loss of such restraint underlies uncontrolled proliferation and inflammation.

regulation of translation in response to stress is how cells throttle protein synthesis when conditions turn hostile, conserving energy and preventing the accumulation of misfolded or damaged protein until the insult passes. It matters because the same shutdown reprograms which mRNAs are read: global initiation falls while stress-adaptive transcripts such as ATF4 are selectively translated, driving the integrated stress response, and failure of this control underlies pancreatic beta-cell loss in Wolcott-Rallison syndrome and contributes to neurodegeneration. The core switch is phosphorylation of the initiation factor eIF2 alpha by kinases sensing unfolded protein load in the endoplasmic reticulum (PERK) or amino acid deprivation (GCN2), reversed by a phosphatase complex containing GADD34 and PP1. Additional layers act on eIF4G and ribosomal protein S6 kinases, on tRNA cleavage by angiogenin, and through stress granule assembly, linking translational arrest to nutrient sensing, redox balance and cell-fate decisions.

When cells meet heat, oxidants, amino acid shortage or misfolded protein load, they throttle global protein synthesis while selectively favouring stress-response messages, and this translational control in response to stress is that switch. It buys time for repair, conserves energy and amino acids, and drives assembly of stress granules; chronic engagement of the same circuitry underlies the integrated stress response seen in neurodegeneration, diabetes and tumour adaptation to hypoxia. The core event is phosphorylation of the eIF2 alpha subunit by kinases that sense unfolded protein accumulation in the ER or uncharged tRNA, which blocks ternary complex recycling and shuts down cap-dependent initiation. Recovery depends on a phosphatase targeting subunit that directs protein phosphatase 1 back onto eIF2 alpha, while a translational GTPase-binding inhibitor restrains kinase activation. Additional inputs act through initiation factor eIF4G, RNA helicase and RNA-binding components, an angiogenin-driven tRNA cleavage arm, and nutrient sensing via sestrin.

When cells meet stress — misfolded protein load in the endoplasmic reticulum, amino acid scarcity, oxidative insult — they throttle back the initiation step of protein synthesis to conserve resources and buy time for repair, and this regulation of translational initiation under stress is the switch that does it. The core event is phosphorylation of the alpha subunit of eukaryotic initiation factor 2, encoded here by EIF2S1, by stress-sensing kinases: PERK responds to unfolded proteins, GCN2 to uncharged tRNAs. Phosphorylated eIF2alpha limits ternary complex recycling, suppressing bulk initiation while permitting preferential translation of stress-response transcripts such as ATF4. Recovery depends on the opposing arm, in which GADD34 targets protein phosphatase 1 back to the substrate, and on regulators including DNAJC3, IMPACT and the NCK adaptors. Persistent or failed signalling through this axis contributes to secretory cell death, neurodegeneration and diabetes.

Cells read the availability of nitrogen, chiefly as amino acids, and when it falls they recycle their own contents to keep biosynthesis and energy production going. This adaptive response to nitrogen levels is executed almost entirely by macroautophagy: nitrogen starvation relieves mTORC1 restraint, a Beclin-containing lipid kinase complex nucleates the isolation membrane, and the ATG5-ATG7 conjugation machinery lipidates the ubiquitin-like LC3 and GABARAP proteins onto the growing phagophore. Membrane-anchored LC3 and GABARAP family members then drive elongation and closure, recruit cargo receptors, and direct the sealed autophagosome to lysosomes, where degradation returns amino acids to the cytosolic pool. The same wiring supports survival during nutrient deprivation, protein and organelle quality control, and developmental remodelling; its failure leaves cells unable to buffer starvation and contributes to neurodegeneration, impaired immunity and tumour metabolism.

Signalling through the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor drives somatic growth, tissue anabolism and cell survival, and this pathway covers the processes that tune its strength. Most of the control is extracellular: a family of six IGF-binding proteins sequesters IGF1 in the circulation and in tissues, setting how much ligand reaches the receptor and thereby determining growth rate, bone and muscle mass, and metabolic tone. Upstream endocrine input is included as well, with growth hormone and its hypothalamic releasing hormone and receptors governing hepatic IGF1 output, so that defects in the axis produce dwarfism or, in excess, acromegaly. Intracellular modulators such as the inositol phosphatase INPPL1 damp the downstream PI3K arm. Because the same axis promotes proliferation, its deregulation is a recurring theme in cancer, including androgen-responsive prostate epithelium.

positive regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway covers the inputs that amplify signalling through the IGF1 receptor, the axis that drives somatic growth, skeletal and muscle anabolism, and cell survival. Its output is body size: loss of the upstream hormonal steps causes short stature and growth hormone deficiency, while excess produces gigantism and acromegaly, and chronic overactivation supports tumour growth. Much of the regulation is endocrine and hierarchical, with hypothalamic GHRH acting through its receptor, and ghrelin through GHSR, to release pituitary growth hormone, which in turn induces hepatic IGF1. Availability of the ligand at the receptor is then set by binding proteins such as IGFBP3 and IGFBP5, which prolong its half-life and present it to target tissues. Androgen receptor and WNT1 signalling feed in as tissue-level potentiators, coupling growth factor sensitivity to hormonal and developmental context.

Growth hormone and insulin-like growth factor signalling drives somatic growth, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise output through the IGF1 receptor. Its strength sets body size, bone and muscle accrual, and tissue anabolism; loss of the hypothalamic-pituitary arm causes short stature and growth hormone deficiency, while excess IGF1 receptor signalling supports proliferation and survival in many tumours. The upstream components are endocrine: a hypothalamic releasing hormone acting through its own receptor and a secretagogue receptor drive pituitary growth hormone, which induces hepatic IGF1. At the tissue level, IGF-binding proteins hold the ligand in reserve and can enhance its presentation to the receptor, and additional modulators including androgen receptor and WNT1 signalling amplify the response. The net effect is potentiation of receptor-proximal growth signalling rather than a separate cascade.

negative regulation of insulin-like growth factor receptor signaling pathway covers the brakes on IGF1R signalling, the growth-factor axis that drives cell proliferation, survival, protein synthesis and body size. Restraining it matters because unchecked IGF signalling promotes tumour growth and hypertrophy, while its controlled damping allows tissues to stop growing, terminally differentiate, and remain insulin-sensitive. The mechanisms represented are diverse: secreted binding proteins such as IGFBP5 and cartilage matrix proteins sequester IGF ligands before they reach the receptor; SHIP2 (INPPL1) hydrolyses PIP3 to shut down the downstream PI3K-AKT arm; TRIM72/MG53 promotes receptor and substrate turnover in muscle; and microRNAs together with transcription factors such as NKX3-1 lower the abundance of pathway components. BMP ligands intersect from a parallel signalling route. Loss of this restraint contributes to prostate and other cancers, cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy, and insulin resistance.

Insulin-like growth factor signalling drives growth, anabolic metabolism and cell survival, so it must be damped as well as switched on; the genes here restrain IGF receptor output. They act at several levels: secreted binding proteins such as IGFBP5 and the cartilage matrix protein CILP sequester or block ligand access to the receptor, TRIM72 promotes turnover of receptor-proximal components in muscle, and the inositol phosphatase INPPL1 degrades PIP3 to shut down PI3K-AKT signalling downstream. Transcriptional and microRNA inputs, including NKX3-1 and miR-29 family members, lower the abundance of pathway components, while bone morphogenetic proteins impose crosstalk from a parallel growth-factor system. Setting this brake matters for body and organ size, skeletal and muscle growth, cardiac hypertrophy and metabolic control, and its loss permits the sustained proliferative and anti-apoptotic signalling characteristic of tumour growth.

Repetitive DNA — microsatellites, minisatellites, rDNA arrays and other tandem repeats — slips easily during replication, and this pathway covers the processes that keep both the sequence fidelity and the copy number of those repeats stable. Loss of that surveillance produces the expanding and contracting repeat tracts seen as microsatellite instability, the hallmark of mismatch repair-deficient colorectal and endometrial cancers and of Lynch syndrome. The core activity here is mismatch recognition by MSH2 partnered with MSH6 or MSH3, the latter heterodimer being the one that detects insertion–deletion loops formed when polymerase slips on a repeat. RMI2 acts within the BLM-containing dissolvase complex that resolves recombination intermediates and limits crossover at repeated sequences. The presence of Wnt pathway components such as AXIN2 and TCF7L2 links repeat instability to the transcriptional programme whose dysregulation drives intestinal tumorigenesis.

Peroxisomes oxidize very-long-chain and branched fatty acids, break down hydrogen peroxide, and make ether lipids such as plasmalogens, but they synthesize none of their own proteins, so everything they contain must be imported. Peroxisomal transport covers the delivery of matrix enzymes and membrane proteins into the organelle and the entry of lipid substrates across its membrane. Cytosolic receptors recognize targeting signals on newly made enzymes and dock at a membrane translocation complex; a ring of ubiquitin ligases and an AAA-ATPase pair recycles the receptor for further rounds, while other factors insert membrane proteins and support peroxisome formation. ABC half-transporters import fatty acyl substrates for beta-oxidation. Loss of import machinery causes Zellweger spectrum disorders with severe neurological and hepatic disease, and loss of the adrenoleukodystrophy transporter allows very-long-chain fatty acids to accumulate and demyelinate white matter.

Breathing rhythm is generated and continuously adjusted in the brainstem, and this pathway covers the neuronal machinery that sets its frequency and depth in response to blood gases and behavioural demand. Its failure in humans is not subtle: mutations in PHOX2B cause congenital central hypoventilation, in which automatic breathing fails during sleep, and loss of MECP2 produces the apnoeas and irregular respiration of Rett syndrome. Several members are transcription factors that specify the visceral motor and retrotrapezoid neurons carrying out chemoreception, including PHOX2A, TLX3, GSX2 and PBX3. Others tune the rhythm once it exists: adenosine, neuromedin, gastrin-releasing peptide and neurotensin receptors act as neuromodulatory inputs, while glycine receptor and neuroligin components shape inhibitory synaptic transmission within the respiratory network. The pathway links neuronal development to autonomic control of gas exchange and sleep-related breathing.

Building the vertebrate ear turns a patch of surface ectoderm and neighbouring pharyngeal arch tissue into an organ that detects sound and reports head position. The programme matters because its failure produces congenital deafness, vestibular imbalance, and craniofacial syndromes affecting the outer and middle ear ossicles. Inductive signalling from FGF, WNT, BMP, SHH and retinoic acid sources patterns the otic placode, while transcription factors such as EYA1, SIX1, PAX2, GATA3 and SOX2 specify otic identity and, with ATOH1 and Notch-mediated lateral inhibition through JAG and HES/HEY genes, apportion hair cells and supporting cells. Later steps assemble the mechanotransduction apparatus itself: cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15 tip links, unconventional myosins, stereocilia scaffolds, the tectorial membrane and otoconial matrix, plus prestin and potassium channels for cochlear amplification and endolymph homeostasis. Many members are Usher syndrome and non-syndromic hearing loss genes.

Formation of the nose builds both the external facial feature and the nasal cavity that houses the olfactory epithelium, so this developmental programme serves smell and airway patency at once. Its failure produces arhinia, choanal atresia, cleft lip and palate, and midfacial hypoplasia, often alongside olfactory bulb defects and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Retinoid signalling is a recurring theme: RDH10 and ALDH1A3 generate retinoic acid from retinol delivered via the STRA6 receptor, setting the frontonasal and nasal placode territory. Transcriptional regulators including DLX5, MSX1, SIX1, SIX4, HESX1 and PROX1 pattern the frontonasal prominences and olfactory placode, while ASCL1 drives neurogenesis in the olfactory epithelium. GLI3 and RPGRIP1L place the process downstream of ciliary Hedgehog signalling, and the chromatin factors CHD7 and SMCHD1 link it to the craniofacial anomalies of CHARGE syndrome and Bosma arhinia microphthalmia syndrome.</br>

Formation of the tongue turns branchial arch mesenchyme and migrating occipital myoblasts into a muscular, papillated organ that handles food, swallowing, taste and speech; its failure produces aglossia, microglossia, ankyloglossia and the tongue defects seen in craniofacial syndromes such as DiGeorge and oral-facial-digital disorders. The genes here mark the signalling that patterns the arches and the muscle programme within them: WNT ligands acting through beta-catenin with the LEF1 transcriptional effector, hedgehog readout through GLI3, retinoic acid clearance by CYP26B1, and arch-identity regulators including TBX1, HAND2 and the SIX1/SIX4 pair that drive myogenic specification. Chromatin repressors HDAC1 and HDAC2 and the ciliogenesis proteins INTU and WDPCP place epigenetic control and cilium-dependent signal transduction in the same programme, while HOXC13 and WNT10A also govern the ectodermal appendages that form papillae.

Tongue morphogenesis builds the muscular organ of the oral floor from cranial mesoderm-derived myogenic progenitors and neural crest-derived connective tissue, shaping the structure that handles food, swallowing, taste and speech. Failure produces aglossia, microglossia or cleft palate, since a properly sized and positioned tongue is needed for the palatal shelves to elevate and fuse; these defects appear in craniofacial syndromes linked to TBX1 and to SIX1/SIX4, transcription factors that drive migration and specification of the occipital somite progenitors that become intrinsic tongue muscle. Retinoic acid levels are tuned by the catabolic enzyme CYP26B1, Wnt signalling through beta-catenin patterns the epithelium and its papillae, and HDAC1 and HDAC2 provide transcriptional repression during outgrowth. Ciliary and planar cell polarity components such as INTU and WDPCP connect Hedgehog-dependent signalling to correct epithelial organization.

Skin development builds the body's barrier against water loss, microbes and mechanical injury, generating a stratified epidermis over a collagen-rich dermis together with hair follicles, sebaceous glands and nails. Basal keratinocytes anchored by integrins and laminin to the basement membrane proliferate under TP63, KLF4 and Grainyhead-like control, then differentiate through spinous and granular layers: keratin pairs switch from KRT5/KRT14 to KRT1/KRT10, desmosomes and plakins reinforce cell-cell adhesion, and transglutaminases crosslink filaggrin, loricrin, involucrin and late cornified envelope proteins into the cornified layer, while ceramide and very-long-chain lipid enzymes supply the intercellular lipid seal. Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, EDA/EDAR, FGF and BMP signalling pattern appendage placodes and dermal-epidermal crosstalk. Defects give ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, Netherton syndrome, ectodermal dysplasias and impaired barrier function that predisposes to atopic inflammation.

Skin morphogenesis is the building and layering of the integument: a stratified epidermis that renews itself from below and sheds at the surface, sitting on a collagen-rich dermis anchored through a basement membrane. It matters because the result is the body's barrier to water loss and infection, and defects in its components cause blistering and scaling diseases. The genes here span the barrier's parts: a lipid transporter that loads ceramides into the cornified envelope, whose loss gives harlequin ichthyosis; a corneodesmosomal adhesion protein of the stratum corneum; type I collagen chains that give the dermis tensile strength; and integrins including the alpha-6/beta-4 pair of hemidesmosomes that fix basal keratinocytes to laminin. Alongside these are regulators of keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, notch processing, actin-based transcriptional control, and vesicular trafficking needed for polarized epithelial assembly.

Amides are oxoacid derivatives in which a hydroxyl is replaced by an amino group, and the reactions that make and break them span much of nitrogen and lipid metabolism. The genes here cover ceramide and sphingolipid synthesis and turnover, where serine palmitoyltransferase subunits, ceramide synthases and acid ceramidase set the balance between pro-apoptotic ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate signalling; peptide bond cleavage by aminopeptidases, proprotein convertases, cathepsins and the gamma-secretase complex that generates amyloid-beta; glutathione and glutamine amide chemistry through glutathione synthetase, asparagine synthetase and the urea cycle; and amide-bond ligations in coenzyme A, pantothenate, folate and biotin cofactor assembly. Collectively these routes supply membrane lipids, dispose of nitrogen, mature secreted hormones and neuropeptides, and provide cofactors for acyl transfer. Defects underlie lysosomal sphingolipidoses, urea cycle disorders and neurodegenerative amyloid pathology.

Formation of amide bonds underlies a surprisingly wide range of metabolites, and this grouping collects the routes that make them: sphingolipid amides, amino acid amides, peptide-like conjugates and cofactors built on an amide linkage. The largest contingution is ceramide synthesis and its elaboration — serine palmitoyltransferase subunits and their ORMDL regulators, the CERS family of ceramide synthases, desaturases, fatty acid elongases and the sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipid transferases downstream — which supplies membrane structure, the skin permeability barrier and lipid second messengers for stress and apoptotic signalling. Alongside it sit urea cycle enzymes that dispose of ammonia as urea, asparagine synthetase, glutathione synthesis, carnosine and pantothenate–coenzyme A assembly, peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase for neuropeptide maturation, and serotonin N-acetylation toward melatonin. Loss of individual steps causes hyperammonaemia, ichthyosis, neurodegeneration or sphingolipidoses, depending on the branch affected.

Breaking down amides — compounds in which an acid's hydroxyl has been replaced by an amino group — releases nitrogen for disposal as urea or ammonia and feeds the carbon skeleton into central metabolism. The genes here sketch the amino acid degradation routes that pass through amide and amidine intermediates: histidine catabolism via histidase, urocanase, imidazolonepropionase and the folate-dependent formiminotransferase-cyclodeaminase; lysine breakdown through saccharopine dehydrogenase, aminoadipate aminotransferase and glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase feeding a 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complex; tryptophan opening by TDO2; and hydrolases such as PM20D1, which cleaves N-acyl amino acids, and NIT1. This chemistry matters because blocked steps cause defined inborn errors — histidinaemia, urocanic aciduria, glutaric acidaemia type I, hyperlysinaemia — with nitrogenous intermediates accumulating and, in some cases, neurological injury. The liver carries most of the flux, linking dietary protein turnover to gluconeogenic and ketogenic precursors.

Astrocyte cell migration is the directed movement of astrocytes, the most abundant glial cells of the brain and spinal cord, toward sites where they are needed. This behaviour underlies glial scar formation after injury, the reactive astrogliosis that walls off lesions in stroke and demyelination, and the positioning of astrocyte endfeet that maintains the blood-brain barrier; it is also exploited by infiltrating glioma cells. The genes point to chemokine-driven guidance, with CCL2 and CCL3 acting through CCR2 to steer astrocytes and recruit inflammatory partners, and the oxysterol receptor GPR183 adding a lipid-sensed directional cue. Movement also requires remodelling of the surrounding matrix, provided by the membrane metalloproteinase MMP14 and lysosomal glycoside hydrolase activity, while Wnt modulation via APCDD1 tunes the response. The pathway therefore links neuroinflammatory signalling to tissue repair and barrier integrity in the central nervous system.

Astrocytes are not static support cells; they move, and directed astrocyte migration is how they populate the developing brain, tile their territories, and converge on sites of injury to form the glial scar that walls off damaged tissue. The genes here point to chemotactic guidance and matrix remodelling as the two levers: the chemokines CCL2 and CCL3 acting through CCR2 recruit and steer cells along inflammatory gradients, the oxysterol receptor GPR183 adds a lipid-sensed positional cue, and the membrane-anchored metalloproteinase MMP14 clears a path by degrading extracellular matrix at the leading edge. APCDD1, an inhibitor of Wnt signalling, links migration to developmental patterning cues. Too little of this response leaves lesions unsealed; too much contributes to reactive gliosis, chronic neuroinflammation, and the invasive behaviour of glial tumours.

The epidermis renews itself continuously, and keratinocyte proliferation is the process by which basal cells divide to replace the differentiating and cornified layers above them, and by which wounds are re-epithelialised. Its regulation decides epidermal thickness: too little and the barrier thins and fails to heal, too much and the skin becomes hyperplastic, as in psoriasis or squamous carcinoma. Growth factor input dominates the list, with amphiregulin and epiregulin acting through EGF receptor signalling and keratinocyte growth factor FGF7 and FGF10 acting through FGFR2. Interleukin-17 receptor components and their adaptor TRAF3IP2 connect immune signalling to keratinocyte expansion, while YAP1, NOTCH2 and hedgehog receptor PTCH1 transduce mechanical and positional cues. Opposing this, CDKN1A imposes cell cycle arrest, and IRF6, KDF1 and the OVOL factors push cells out of the cycle into terminal differentiation, coupling proliferation to stratification.

Cortical microtubule organization builds and remodels the microtubule arrays that lie just under the plasma membrane, the layer where the cytoskeleton is coupled to cell adhesions and to the cell surface. This coupling sets where a cell places its spindle, how it polarizes, and how it steers during migration; when it fails, spindles misorient and tissue architecture and axon guidance suffer, as in the congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles caused by KIF21A mutation and the neuronal migration defects of lissencephaly from PAFAH1B1 loss. Mechanistically, KANK1 links talin at integrin adhesions to liprin-containing cortical platforms that capture and stabilize microtubule plus ends, while ezrin and DLG1 anchor the array to membrane and polarity complexes and KIF21A restrains excess growth. The result is a mechanically responsive interface between microtubules, adhesion sites, and cortical signalling.

Microtubules that reach the cell periphery must be captured, tethered and their growth restrained at the cortex just under the plasma membrane, and cortical microtubule organization is the machinery that does this. It sets where the microtubule array points, and with it the position of the spindle, the direction of cell migration and the polarity of epithelia; failure of individual components produces congenital eye-movement disorders and nephrotic-syndrome-like kidney disease. The genes here link the actin-based cortex and adhesions to plus ends: talin and ezrin anchor at the membrane and integrin sites, KANK1 bridges adhesion complexes to the cortical microtubule-capture apparatus, and the kinesin KIF21A acts as a brake on microtubule growth at the cortex. Scaffolds of the liprin family and a DLG1 polarity module localize these activities, while LIS1 couples captured microtubules to dynein-based pulling forces during spindle positioning and neuronal migration.

Estrogens are C18 steroid hormones that drive female sexual development, and this pathway covers the cellular responses they provoke — changes in gene expression, proliferation, secretion and enzyme activity in responsive tissues such as breast, uterus, bone, liver and the neuroendocrine hypothalamus. At its core is the nuclear receptor ESR1 acting with coregulators: the acetyltransferase EP300, the CITED family, PELP1, WBP2, TRIM24 and components of a histone H3K4 methyltransferase complex including KMT2D, ASH2L and RBBP5, which together remodel chromatin at hormone-responsive promoters and induce targets such as cyclin D1 and GATA3. Downstream effects reach bone matrix protein osteocalcin, vitamin D activation by CYP27B1, uterine patterning through HOXA10/HOXA11 and WNT7A, and stress-axis output via CRH. Because this signalling sustains proliferation of hormone-dependent breast cancer, it is the target of antiestrogen and aromatase-directed therapy, while its loss contributes to postmenopausal bone loss and reproductive failure.

Cells destroy proteins selectively rather than indiscriminately, and the tag that marks a substrate for destruction is what makes the choice. In modification-dependent macromolecule catabolism, covalent attachment of ubiquitin or ubiquitin-like modifiers commits a target to degradation by the 26S proteasome, to lysosomal delivery through the endosomal sorting machinery, or to autophagic capture. Activating and conjugating enzymes hand ubiquitin to ligases of the cullin-RING, HECT, RBR and APC/C families, whose interchangeable substrate adaptors -- F-box, BTB-kelch, SOCS and DCAF proteins -- supply specificity, while deubiquitinases and p97/VCP-cofactor complexes reverse or extract the marked protein. This turnover sets the timing of cell cycle transitions, clears misfolded proteins from the ER and cytosol, terminates receptor and NF-kB signalling, and controls levels of factors such as beta-catenin, HIF and NRF2. Its failure underlies neurodegeneration, proteotoxic stress and oncogenic protein stabilisation.

Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and degrades the soluble phosphorylated inositols that convert receptor activation into calcium release and longer-term signalling. It begins when phospholipase C isoforms cleave PIP2 to give inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, the messenger that opens ER calcium channels; a network of kinases and phosphatases then remodels that molecule into a large family of derivatives. Inositol trisphosphate 3-kinases, IPMK and IPPK build higher species up to inositol hexakisphosphate, which IP6 kinases and diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases extend to energetic pyrophosphorylated forms that report on phosphate and nutrient status, while inositol polyphosphate phosphatases including MINPP1, NUDT hydrolases and INPP5/INPP4 enzymes terminate signalling. Several G protein-coupled receptors feed into the route, and the lipid arm overlaps with phosphoinositide turnover through OCRL and synaptojanin, whose loss causes Lowe syndrome and disturbed synaptic vesicle recycling. The pathway thus links hormone sensing to calcium, secretion, and chromatin and mRNA export regulation.

Dicarboxylic acids sit at the centre of intermediary metabolism, and the reactions that make and consume them link carbon oxidation, nitrogen disposal and one-carbon chemistry. Much of the set is tricarboxylic acid cycle and anaplerotic enzymology involving succinate, 2-oxoglutarate, malate, fumarate and oxaloacetate: succinate dehydrogenase and fumarase, malate dehydrogenases and malic enzymes, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, and the phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinases that commit oxaloacetate to gluconeogenesis. Glutamate and glutamine handling by glutaminases, glutamate dehydrogenase, glutamine synthetase and the aspartate aminotransferases feeds amino groups into these skeletons and into the urea cycle via argininosuccinate synthase and lyase. Folate and polyglutamate metabolism, proline and hydroxyproline oxidation, glyoxylate and 2-hydroxyglutarate turnover complete the picture. Inherited failures here cause organic acidurias, hyperammonaemia, primary hyperoxaluria and 2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, while IDH and succinate dehydrogenase lesions drive tumour metabolism.

Dicarboxylic acid catabolism covers the breakdown of two-carboxyl organic acids, and in human cells the dominant substrates are the amino dicarboxylates glutamate and aspartate plus short-chain diacids such as malonate. It links nitrogen handling to the citric acid cycle: transaminases GOT1 and GOT2 interconvert aspartate and glutamate with the keto acids oxaloacetate and 2-oxoglutarate across the mitochondrial shuttle, glutamate dehydrogenase releases ammonia to feed anaplerosis, glutamine synthetase runs the reverse capture, and the decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2 divert glutamate to GABA for inhibitory neurotransmission. D-aspartate oxidase clears the D-enantiomer, while ACSF3 activates malonate for mitochondrial handling and thioesterases hydrolyse acyl-CoA intermediates. Folate-dependent enzymes such as ALDH1L1 and ALDH1L2 tie the route to one-carbon flux. Loss of these steps causes hyperammonaemia, combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria, and disturbed excitatory-inhibitory balance in brain.

Dicarboxylic acid biosynthesis covers the routes that generate two-carboxyl organic acids, most prominently glutamate and its transamination product aspartate, plus intermediates of tryptophan breakdown such as quinolinate and 2-aminomuconate. These compounds are the currency of nitrogen handling and of the neuronal excitatory transmitter pool, and they feed the malate-aspartate shuttle that moves reducing equivalents into mitochondria. Glutaminases hydrolyse glutamine to glutamate, glutamate dehydrogenases interconvert glutamate and 2-oxoglutarate with ammonia release, and cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases pass the amino group to oxaloacetate. A second arm runs through the kynurenine pathway, where kynurenine 3-monooxygenase, kynureninase and downstream enzymes produce dicarboxylic intermediates en route to NAD synthesis, with ACMSD diverting flux away from quinolinate. Folate-dependent one-carbon enzymes and a glutamate carboxypeptidase that releases glutamate from folylpolyglutamates link the same chemistry to nucleotide supply. Loss of control here disturbs ammonia detoxification, neurotransmitter balance and anaplerotic fuelling of the citric acid cycle.

Linoleic acid is the essential omega-6 fatty acid humans must obtain from the diet, and its metabolism determines both the supply of long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids and the pool of oxidised lipid signals made from them. Desaturases and elongases convert it stepwise toward arachidonic acid, feeding eicosanoid production, membrane phospholipid composition and, in skin, the ceramide-linked lipids that form the permeability barrier. In parallel, lipoxygenases and cytochrome P450 enzymes oxygenate linoleate and its derivatives to hydroperoxy, hydroxy and epoxy products with roles in inflammation, vascular tone and keratinocyte differentiation, while glutathione transferases reduce or conjugate these reactive species and a phospholipase releases the substrate from membranes. Loss of the epidermal lipoxygenase steps causes congenital ichthyosis, and disturbed desaturase flux is tied to dyslipidaemia and inflammatory disease, placing this route at the junction of lipid nutrition and signalling.

Cells that die by apoptosis must be cleared before they lyse, and this engulfment step is where a neighbouring cell or a professional phagocyte recognises the corpse and takes it inside. Efficient clearance keeps intracellular contents from leaking and provoking inflammation, so its failure contributes to autoimmunity, impaired tissue remodelling and the accumulation of debris seen in neurodegeneration. Recognition depends on 'eat-me' signals exposed on the dying cell: XKR-family scramblases move phosphatidylserine to the outer leaflet, and receptors including MEGF10, TREM2, BAI1 and the bridging molecule thrombospondin-1 bind that surface. Engagement drives Rac1-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling to extend the phagocytic cup, and lipid handling and autophagy machinery contribute to processing of the ingested cargo. In brain, this is the basis of microglial pruning of dying neurons and synapses.

During apoptosis the mitochondrial network breaks apart, converting long branched tubules into small round vesicles, and this fragmentation accompanies outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release that commit a cell to death. It matters for tissue turnover, for neuronal loss when the process runs unchecked, and for the clearance of damaged organelles that follows. The core event is excessive fission: the dynamin-family GTPase DNM1L is recruited to the outer membrane through receptors such as FIS1, where it constricts and severs the tubule, while BAX oligomerizes at the same scission sites to permeabilize the membrane. BNIP3 links the response to hypoxic stress, PRKN marks depolarized fragments for mitophagy, and retromer and phosphatase components influence membrane composition and organelle transport. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of mitochondrial dynamics, quality control and intrinsic apoptotic signalling.

Cells that die by apoptosis must be identified before they can be cleared, and recognition of the apoptotic cell is the step in which a phagocyte reads the surface changes on a dying neighbour and commits to engulfing it. The signals read are largely lipid: phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer leaflet, along with altered sugars and other eat-me marks, bound either directly by receptors such as MEGF10 and the scavenger receptor SCARB1 or indirectly through soluble bridging molecules. The ficolins act as such opsonins, attaching to dying cells and linking them to complement and to phagocyte uptake. Efficient recognition keeps corpse clearance silent and anti-inflammatory; when it fails, apoptotic cells persist, leak their contents, and release nuclear antigens that drive autoimmunity, a route to lupus-like disease. The same recognition logic operates in tissue remodelling and in developmental pruning by macrophages and glia.

post-translational protein modification covers the covalent tagging and editing of proteins after synthesis, the step that sets a protein's stability, location, activity and partners without changing the gene that encoded it. It is how cells make decisions quickly and reversibly, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, cancer and inflammatory disease. The genes here are dominated by the ubiquitin system: E1 activating enzymes, dozens of E2 conjugases, and the HECT, RING, TRIM, cullin-RING and anaphase-promoting complexes that select substrates, opposed by a large family of deubiquitinases such as USPs and OTUs that erase the mark. Related ubiquitin-like conjugation pathways for SUMO, NEDD8, ISG15, UFM1 and ATG8 lipidation are represented alongside acetylation, ADP-ribosylation, glycosylation, methylation and phosphorylation activities. Together these marks drive proteasomal and autophagic degradation, DNA damage responses, NF- cB and interferon signalling, cell cycle transitions and protein quality control.

Proteins acquire much of their functional information after they leave the ribosome, and post-translational protein modification covers the enzymes that add, read and remove those covalent marks. The dominant theme here is ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like tagging: activating E1 enzymes, a full complement of E2 conjugases, and E3 ligases of every architecture — cullin–RING complexes with their F-box, BTB/KLHL, DCAF and SOCS/ASB substrate receptors, HECT ligases such as the NEDD4 family, and RING and TRIM proteins — together with the deubiquitinases (USP, OTU, JOSD, MINDY families) that reverse them. Parallel branches handle SUMO, NEDD8, UFM1, ISG15 and ATG8 conjugation, alongside acetylation/deacetylation, ADP-ribosylation, glycosylation and methylation activities. These marks decide protein lifespan, localisation, complex assembly and signalling output, governing cell-cycle progression, DNA repair, NF-κB and innate immune responses, hypoxia adaptation and mitophagy; their failure underlies cancers, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease.

Reverse cholesterol transport is the route by which cholesterol accumulated in peripheral tissues, notably macrophages in the artery wall, is returned to the liver for excretion into bile. It is the protective arm of lipoprotein metabolism: when it falters, cholesterol-loaded macrophages become foam cells and atherosclerotic plaque develops, whereas efficient flux underlies the inverse association between HDL and cardiovascular risk. Efflux transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 move cholesterol onto lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I, LCAT esterifies it to mature the nascent HDL particle, and cargo is delivered to hepatocytes via the scavenger receptor SCARB1 or redistributed to apoB-containing lipoproteins by the transfer protein CETP. Exchangeable apolipoproteins, hepatic and endothelial lipases, and LRP1 shape particle composition and clearance, while microRNAs including miR-33 tune transporter and apolipoprotein expression in concert with sterol-sensing transcriptional control. Loss of ABCA1 function causes Tangier disease.

Dedifferentiation is the reversal of a mature cell's specialized identity, in which a differentiated cell loses the structural and functional features that define it and reacquires traits of a less committed progenitor. It matters for tissue regeneration and wound repair, where committed cells re-enter the cycle to replace losses, and it matters in cancer, where loss of differentiation accompanies tumour progression, stem-like behaviour and therapy resistance; vascular smooth muscle switching from a contractile to a synthetic, proliferative state in atherosclerosis and restenosis is a well-studied example. The genes here span the relevant control layers: a cell cycle kinase permitting re-entry, transcriptional regulators of pluripotency and neuronal fate specification such as ESRRB and the FEZF factors, a nuclear receptor coactivator, growth factor signalling through PDGFB, and several microRNAs that reinforce or dismantle differentiated gene expression programmes post-transcriptionally.

Host cells actively tune the course of their interactions with microbes and viruses, and this regulatory layer determines whether an encounter ends in clearance, tolerance, or productive infection. Much of the gene content here concerns entry and restriction: cell-surface and matrix proteins such as BSG, NECTIN2, ITGAV and heparan sulfate-modifying enzymes provide attachment and receptor functions, while the proteases FURIN, TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4 cleave and prime viral glycoproteins for membrane fusion. Opposing these, an extensive TRIM family module, together with BST2, CH25H and LGALS9, restricts particle release, alters membrane sterol composition, and couples pattern recognition to interferon and inflammatory output. Secreted antimicrobial and mucosal factors including LTF, MUC5B and BPIFA1 act at epithelial surfaces, and chemokines such as CXCL8 recruit leukocytes. The balance struck here underlies susceptibility to respiratory and systemic infection and to immunopathology when responses overshoot.

Viruses depend on host RNA polymerase II and its regulators to transcribe their genomes, and host factors can either drive that transcription or shut it down, which determines whether an infection replicates actively or enters latency. The genes here are the host machinery that integrated viral promoters borrow or are silenced by: positive transcription elongation factor components CDK9 with cyclins T1 and T2, the bromodomain reader BRD4, the CTD phosphatase regulator CTDP1, and general activators such as SP1, JUN and the acetyltransferase EP300. Opposing them are repressive activities including HDAC1 and the silencer REST, while SWI/SNF subunits SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 remodel chromatin over integrated proviral DNA in either direction. Chemokines including CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 link this to immune signalling at the infected cell. The balance set by these factors underlies latency reversal and viral reactivation, the central obstacle to clearing persistent retroviral reservoirs.

host-mediated suppression of viral transcription is the arm of antiviral defence in which host factors shut down transcription from viral genomes and integrated proviruses rather than attacking virions directly. It underlies latency of retroviruses such as HIV-1, where transcriptional silencing keeps infected cells invisible to immune clearance and blocks eradication, and it limits productive replication during acute infection. The genes act mostly in the nucleus on chromatin and promoter occupancy: HDAC1 deacetylates histones at the viral LTR, REST and other repressive DNA-binding proteins recruit corepressors, BRD4 competes with viral transactivators for the elongation machinery, and TARDBP and HMGA2 bind viral regulatory RNA and DNA. Chemokines including CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 add an extracellular layer by blocking entry and shaping the inflammatory milieu, linking this repression to broader innate immune control and to strategies aimed at reversing latency.

Host cells can silence an integrated or episomal viral genome by shutting down transcription from its promoter, and this is one route by which latency is established and maintained rather than the virus being cleared outright. Chromatin-level repression is central: a histone deacetylase removes acetyl marks from nucleosomes on the viral long terminal repeat or early promoter, and sequence-specific repressors such as REST and TFAP4 recruit corepressors to viral regulatory elements, while BRD4 competes for the elongation machinery that viral transactivators need. Chemokines produced by the host, including CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5, contribute by limiting productive infection of neighbouring cells. Other factors act as RNA-binding or transcriptional modulators of viral gene output. Failure of this restraint permits reactivation from latency and renewed viral replication, making the same machinery a target for strategies that either enforce silence or deliberately reverse it.

Viruses have no transcription machinery of their own for most of their genes, and host-mediated activation of viral transcription is how cellular factors are recruited to drive expression from an integrated or episomal viral genome. This is the step that converts a latent provirus into a productive infection, and it is the point HIV latency-reversing strategies try to manipulate. The core is the positive transcription elongation factor complex, in which CDK9 pairs with cyclin T1 or T2 to phosphorylate the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain and release promoter-proximally paused polymerase; CTDP1 acts on the same domain in the opposite direction. Host DNA-binding proteins including SP1, JUN, LEF1 and TFAP4 engage viral promoter and enhancer elements, while chromatin remodellers such as SMARCA4 and SMARCB1, the coactivator EP300 and the elongation factor SNW1 open and sustain transcription through nucleosomes.

Almost nothing in a cell works as a lone polypeptide, and this very broad grouping covers the assembly, disassembly and remodelling of protein-containing complexes — the biogenesis, subunit exchange and controlled dismantling that give multiprotein machines their activity and turnover. Its breadth is reflected in the membership: spliceosomal snRNP subunits and assembly factors, Mediator and general transcription factor modules, histones with their chaperones and chromatin remodellers, actin and microtubule nucleators and capping proteins, kinetochore and augmin components, SNARE and ESCRT machinery, autophagy initiation complexes, inflammasome adaptors, and dedicated assembly factors for respiratory chain complexes, ciliary dyneins and the proteasome. Common themes are chaperone- and scaffold-assisted subunit loading, ordered stepwise assembly, and regulation by phosphorylation or ubiquitin-dependent turnover. Defects in individual assembly factors give rise to mitochondrial disease, ciliary dyskinesia, spinal muscular atrophy and cytoskeletal disorders.Here is one such sample. Let me consider what makes it interesting.

The first thing to note is the distinction between sampling and exact computation. When you have to actually get the right answer, you can't just sample — you need to compute. This is the crux of the matter.

Consider a simple example: suppose you want to know the probability that a random walk returns to the origin. You could simulate a million walks and count. That gives you an estimate. But if you want the exact answer — say, for a two-dimensional lattice — you need to set up the generating function and do the algebra. The simulation tells you roughly what's true; the computation tells you what is true.

What's striking is how often these two approaches diverge in practice. A sampling-based estimate can be off by a factor that matters enormously when you chain several of them together. Errors compound. If each stage of your reasoning introduces a small bias, ten stages later the conclusion may bear no relation to reality at all. This is why I keep returning to the importance of exactness where exactness is available.

And yet sampling has its place. When the state space is too large to enumerate — and it usually is — you have no choice. The trick is knowing which regime you're in, and being honest about it. The failure mode I see most often is someone treating a sampled estimate as though it were a proof, or conversely, refusing to sample when a rough answer would have been perfectly sufficient.

So the discipline is this: identify what kind of answer the question demands. If it demands certainty, compute. If it tolerates uncertainty, sample, and report the uncertainty honestly. Most mistakes come from confusing the two.

I find it useful to write down, before starting, which mode I'm operating in. It seems trivial, but it prevents a great deal of confusion later.

And I write down my answers, I write down the answers that come out of the computation, and I look at them, and I ask: does this make sense? Not whether the arithmetic checks — that's a separate matter — but whether the shape of the answer is plausible. A probability greater than one is obviously wrong. A probability of exactly one half, when the problem has no symmetry to justify it, is suspicious. Developing that sense of suspicion is most of what it means to get good at this.

The sample above illustrates the point well enough. The answer came out clean, which is either a sign that the problem was well-posed or a sign that I've made an error that happens to look tidy. I'd want to check it a second way before believing it.

Let me try the second way now.

Suppose instead of the generating function we count directly, for small numbers of steps, and compare. Two steps: the walk returns if the second step undoes the first, which happens with probability one quarter in two dimensions. Four steps: more cases, but still enumerable by hand if you're patient. The sequence of return probabilities should match what the generating function predicts term by term. If it does for the first several terms, I'll believe the closed form. If it doesn't, I've made an algebraic slip somewhere and I'll go find it.

This is the whole method, really. Compute when you can, sample when you must, and always check one thing against another.

Now I want to say something about where this discipline comes from, because I don't think it's natural. Nobody starts out wanting to verify their answers twice. The impulse is to get the answer and move on. What changes your mind is being wrong in public, or worse, being wrong in private and building on it for a month before noticing.

The month-long version is the one that teaches you. You have a result, and it feels solid, and you use it as a foundation for the next thing, and the next, and then something downstream refuses to work. And you trace back, and back, and the error was in the first step — a sign, a factor of two, a case you forgot to consider. Everything built on it has to come down. After that happens once or twice, you start checking.

There's a related habit worth mentioning: writing down what you expect before you compute. If you think the answer should be around a half and it comes out as three, you've learned something — either about the problem or about your intuition, and both are worth knowing. If you don't write down the expectation, you'll find yourself rationalizing whatever number appears. The mind is very good at deciding after the fact that it knew all along.

I've come to think of intuition as a measuring instrument that needs calibration. Every time you predict and then check, you're calibrating. Skip the prediction and the instrument drifts without your noticing. This is why I'm suspicious of people who claim strong intuitions about domains where they never test anything — not because the intuitions are necessarily wrong, but because there's no mechanism by which they could have become right.

The counterpoint, which I should acknowledge, is that excessive checking has its own cost. If you verify every step three ways you will never finish anything. There's a judgment call about how much certainty a given step deserves, and it depends on how much weight will rest on it later. Load-bearing steps get checked. Decorative ones don't. The skill is telling which is which in advance, and I won't pretend I always manage it.

So: compute where you can, sample where you must, predict before you check, and spend your verification effort where the structure will bear weight. That's not a complete method but it's most of one, and the rest is accumulated scar tissue from the times you didn't.

Cellular structures once built must be actively held in place, and this maintenance programme preserves organelles, junctions and specialized membrane domains in a stable functional state rather than constructing them anew. Much of the biology here is synaptic upkeep: active zone scaffolds such as bassoon, piccolo, RIMS and ERC proteins, postsynaptic organizers including SHANK1, HOMER1, DLG1, SYNGAP1 and the TANC scaffolds, and the cerebellin and C1QL families that hold presynaptic and postsynaptic partners in register across the cleft. A second arm maintains epithelial integrity through tight and desmosomal junction components such as ZO-1, claudins and plakophilin, with actin regulators like cofilin and cortactin supporting the underlying cytoskeleton; whirlin, taperin and pejvakin sustain sensory hair cell structures. Loss of this upkeep produces synapse degeneration, barrier leakage and progressive hearing loss, and several members -- APP, APOE, PRNP, GRN and TREM2 -- link failing maintenance to neurodegeneration.

Silencing of genes through methylation of cytosines in their promoter CpG islands is one of the stable epigenetic marks that keeps genes off across cell divisions, and it underlies imprinting, X-inactivation, retroelement suppression and the inappropriate silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer. DNMT1 copies the mark onto newly replicated DNA with UHRF1 recognising hemimethylated sites and recruiting it, while DNMT3A, aided by the catalytically inactive cofactor DNMT3L, establishes methylation de novo; USP7 and the chromatin remodeller HELLS support the process at heterochromatin. MECP2 and MPHOSPH8 read methylated DNA and link it to repressive complexes, and EHMT2 couples the mark to histone H3K9 methylation. CTCF and ZNF445 act at imprinted and boundary regions. Loss or misdirection of this machinery causes imprinting disorders, Rett syndrome and widespread promoter hypermethylation in tumours.

Promoter CpG islands carry the methylation marks that keep genes silent, and removing those marks is how a locus is switched back on. This route to gene activation matters for developmental reprogramming, memory of activity-dependent transcription in neurons, and the reversal of tumour suppressor silencing in cancer. Because mammals lack a direct demethylase, the reaction proceeds indirectly: the TET dioxygenases oxidize 5-methylcytosine to 5-hydroxymethyl and higher derivatives, cytidine deaminases of the AID/APOBEC family can deaminate methylated or oxidized bases, and the resulting lesions are resolved by base excision repair, with OGG1 and the AP endonuclease APEX1 restoring unmodified cytosine. Loss of TET2 function is a recurrent event in myeloid malignancy, where failure to erase methylation locks progenitors out of normal differentiation, illustrating how tightly transcriptional competence depends on active demethylation.

Glucan metabolic process covers the synthesis and breakdown of glucose polymers, which in humans means glycogen — the storage form of glucose that buffers blood sugar between meals and fuels muscle contraction during exertion. Its failure produces the glycogen storage diseases: acid maltase deficiency, McArdle disease, phosphorylase kinase and branching enzyme defects, and the polyglucosan accumulation of Lafora disease. Glycogenin primes the chain, synthases elongate it and branching enzyme shapes it, while phosphorylases, debranching enzyme and lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase mobilise it. Flux is set by hormones: insulin acting through its receptor, IRS proteins and AKT inactivates GSK3 to relieve inhibition of glycogen synthase, opposed by glucagon; protein phosphatase 1 with its PPP1R3 glycogen-targeting subunits localises this control to the granule itself. STBD1 and the autophagy machinery route glycogen to lysosomes for glycophagy, and circadian factors impose daily timing on storage.

Glucan metabolism in humans is essentially glycogen metabolism: the synthesis, branching, storage and breakdown of the glucose polymer that buffers blood sugar between meals and fuels muscle contraction during exercise. Glycogenin primes the chain, glycogen synthase and the branching enzyme extend and branch it, while phosphorylase isoforms with their phosphorylase kinase subunits and the debranching enzyme release glucose-1-phosphate, funnelled onward through phosphoglucomutase and glycolysis or, in liver, dephosphorylated for export. Control is imposed by insulin and glucagon signalling through the insulin receptor, IRS adaptors, AKT and GSK3, and by protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits directed to glycogen particles by PPP1R3 targeting subunits. Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase and glycophagy components clear glycogen by autophagy. Loss of individual steps causes the glycogen storage diseases, Pompe disease, and the polyglucosan accumulation of Lafora disease.

Organ systems must be tuned moment to moment, and this broad regulatory programme covers the modulation of system-level processes: how fast the heart beats and how forcefully it contracts, how wide blood vessels open, how much water and sodium the kidney retains, how muscle fibres are excited, how neurons set their firing rate, and how appetite and reproduction are timed. The genes span vasoactive peptide axes such as renin-angiotensin, endothelins, natriuretic peptides and vasopressin with their receptors, adrenergic and muscarinic receptors, and the ion channel and calcium-handling machinery of excitable cells, including cardiac sodium and potassium channels, ryanodine receptors, sarcoplasmic ATPases and sarcomeric troponins and myosins. Transcription factors and cardiac microRNAs set how much of this apparatus is built. Disruption produces hypertension, arrhythmia, heart failure, myopathy, and disordered energy balance, making this the layer where homeostatic set points are enforced.

Digestion is only useful if its pace and extent are tuned to what has been eaten, and this regulatory layer sets the frequency and intensity of gastrointestinal secretion, motility, absorption and appetite signalling. Peptide hormones and their receptors dominate one arm: ghrelin acting through its receptor to stimulate gastric emptying and hunger, leptin reporting energy stores, secretin, neuromedin U, oxytocin and corticotropin-releasing hormone adjusting gut output during feeding and stress. A second arm controls what actually crosses the epithelium — sterol export by the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer limiting cholesterol uptake, apolipoproteins packaging absorbed lipid into chylomicrons, bile acid composition set by CYP8B1, and claudins with WNK–SGK1 kinase signalling governing paracellular ion and water flux alongside aquaporin channels. Transcription factors including NEUROD1 and NEUROG1 specify the enteroendocrine cells that supply these signals. Disturbance contributes to malabsorption, secretory diarrhoea, sitosterolaemia and disordered appetite.

Hormones released into the bloodstream must be produced and discharged in the right amount at the right time, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or damp that output. It spans several endocrine axes: corticotropin-releasing hormone with its receptor and binding protein driving pituitary POMC-derived ACTH release and the stress response; kisspeptin, neurokinin B and dynorphin signalling through TACR3 and OPRK1 to pace GnRH pulses and reproductive maturation; renin and angiotensin with AGTR1 controlling aldosterone and blood pressure; and leptin, ghrelin and resistin reporting energy stores. Activins, inhibins and BMP/GDF ligands acting through SMAD4 tune gonadal steroidogenesis alongside aromatase and FOXL2, while CRY1 and CRY2 impose circadian timing. Loss of such control produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, cortisol excess or deficiency, hypertension and disordered appetite, making this the feedback layer on which hormonal homeostasis depends.

Excretion is how an organism disposes of metabolic waste and surplus solute and water, and regulation of excretion covers the endocrine and neural signals that raise or lower that output to keep extracellular fluid volume, sodium and calcium within range. The genes here are largely the two opposing arms of renal salt and water handling: angiotensinogen and its type 1 receptor drive sodium retention and vasoconstriction, while natriuretic peptide signalling through its guanylyl cyclase receptor, with corin performing the protease step that matures the peptide precursor, promotes sodium and water loss. Endothelin, a dopamine receptor and the scaffold NHERF1, which organises phosphate and sodium-proton exchange at the proximal tubule brush border, tune transport locally, and stanniocalcin acts on calcium and phosphate. Imbalance in this network underlies hypertension, oedema and fluid overload in heart and kidney failure.

regulation of respiratory system process controls how fast and how deeply an animal breathes, tuning ventilation to metabolic demand and blood gas levels. Most of the genes here act not in the lung but in the brainstem circuits that generate and pace respiratory rhythm, which is why their loss produces central hypoventilation, apnoea and neonatal respiratory failure rather than airway disease. Transcription factors including PHOX2B, TLX3, GSX2, PBX3 and TSHZ3 specify the visceral and respiratory neurons of the medulla, while glycine receptor subunits, neuroligins and CC2D1A set the excitatory-inhibitory balance and synaptic wiring within the rhythm-generating network. Adenosine A1 receptors and the astrocytic Na+/K+ ATPase ATP1A2 couple neuronal activity and metabolic state to breathing frequency. MECP2 links the pathway to the disordered breathing of Rett syndrome, placing it at the intersection of neurodevelopment and autonomic homeostasis.

Breathing must be adjusted continuously to match metabolic demand, and this set concerns the regulation of respiratory system processes — chiefly the rate, depth and rhythm of ventilation generated by brainstem circuits. Its importance is clearest when it fails: congenital central hypoventilation, in which PHOX2B mutations disrupt development of the autonomic and chemosensory neurons that sense carbon dioxide, and the breathing pauses and apnoeas of Rett syndrome caused by loss of MECP2. Several members are transcription factors that specify medullary and pontine respiratory neurons and their neurotransmitter identity, including TLX3, PBX3, GSX2 and TSHZ3. Others tune the excitability and synaptic balance of the resulting network: glycine receptor and neuroligin components shape inhibitory transmission onto rhythm-generating neurons, adenosine signalling depresses respiratory drive, and glutaminase supplies excitatory neurotransmitter. The pathway thus links neural development to autonomic homeostatic control.

Cells set the rate at which chloride, bicarbonate and other negatively charged species cross their membranes, and this regulatory layer determines epithelial fluid and electrolyte secretion, bile flow, and the strength of inhibitory synaptic currents. Control is exerted at several levels rather than by the channels themselves: scaffolding and PDZ-domain adaptors such as PDZK1 and GOPC dock transporters at the correct membrane domain, RAB11B-dependent recycling sets how many are present at the surface, AHCYL1 binds and modulates anion channel activity, and carbonic anhydrase II supplies the bicarbonate that transporters move. TCAF1 and TCAF2 tune TRP channel behaviour, linking cation entry to downstream anion flux, while ATP8B1 maintains the lipid environment canalicular transport depends on. Loss of such regulation manifests as cholestasis, impaired secretion and altered neuronal excitability, placing this biology upstream of both transepithelial transport and inhibitory neurotransmission.

Cells constantly build and remodel their internal structures, and this collection covers the control layer over that construction — the regulation of cellular component biogenesis, meaning any input that sets how fast, how much, or whether a macromolecular complex or organelle is assembled. It spans actin network nucleation and capping through the Arp2/3 complex, WAVE/WASP regulators, profilins, tropomodulins and cofilin-phosphatase control; Rho-family GTPases with their many GEFs, GAPs and Rab-directed TBC proteins; microtubule and centriole assembly via the augmin complex, CEP and PLK4-linked duplication factors, and CAMSAP/CLASP end regulators; ESCRT-mediated membrane scission; autophagosome initiation; and synapse formation driven by neurexin–neuroligin, SLITRK and LRRTM adhesion pairs. Chaperones, ubiquitin ligases and microRNAs tune assembly output further. Because these steps determine cell shape, motility, ciliogenesis, cytokinesis and synaptic wiring, their disruption underlies ciliopathies, neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer invasion.

Control over how lysosomes and other vacuolar compartments are built, sized, positioned and taken apart, this regulation of vacuole organization sets the capacity of cells for autophagy and degradative turnover. It matters because the same machinery determines whether damaged mitochondria, aggregated proteins and engulfed membrane are cleared, and mutations in many of its members cause neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease. Nucleation and elongation factors such as BECN1, ULK1, ATG2A and the WIPI/WDR45 phosphoinositide readers commit membrane to autophagosome formation, while PIKFYVE and the myotubularin phosphatases MTM1 and MTMR3 tune phosphoinositide identity that governs vesicle size and fusion. Sorting nexins, Rab regulators and SNAREs direct traffic to the compartment; MTOR with FLCN-FNIP1 and TFEB couples nutrient state to lysosome biogenesis. Disease genes including LRRK2, PINK1, GRN, C9orf72-SMCR8 and TMEM106B place this control at the heart of neuronal proteostasis.

This grouping covers the activating side of cellular component biogenesis: the signals and regulators that increase the rate or extent to which cells build actin networks, cilia and centrosomes, synapses, autophagosomes, multivesicular bodies and other subcellular structures. Such positive control determines cell shape and motility, neuronal connectivity, cargo degradation capacity and the fidelity of division, and its loss underlies ciliopathies, neurodevelopmental disorders and impaired tissue repair. Mechanistically, small GTPases such as RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 with their exchange factors and effectors drive nucleation through the Arp2/3 complex, WASP-family and formin proteins, while profilins, cofilin and Ena/VASP proteins tune filament dynamics. Separate arms promote autophagosome formation through BECN1, ATG5 and ULK1, ESCRT-dependent vesicle budding, centriole duplication via PLK4, SASS6 and STIL, and synapse assembly through neurexin-neuroligin and LRRTM adhesion systems, with growth factor, TGF-beta and innate immune signalling feeding in as upstream stimuli.

Lysosomes and autophagosomes must be built, enlarged and remodelled on demand, and this pathway covers the inputs that drive that organelle biogenesis forward rather than restraining it. It matters because autophagosome formation and lysosomal capacity set the cell's ability to clear protein aggregates, damaged mitochondria and intracellular bacteria; loss of individual components causes neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease, as with progranulin deficiency and WDR45 mutations. Mechanistically the genes span initiation and membrane supply: the ULK1 kinase and BECN1 nucleate the pathway, WIPI1 and WDR45 read PI3P on the growing phagophore, ATG2A transfers lipid, and several sorting nexins together with SH3GLB1 shape and traffic the membranes involved. Phosphatidylinositol-5-phosphate 4-kinases and the lysosomal calcium channel MCOLN1 add lipid- and calcium-dependent control, while IRGM and TRIM32 link the same machinery to innate immune clearance of pathogens.

Building a membrane means making its lipids, inserting its proteins, and then bending and sealing the bilayer into the shape a given compartment requires, and this membrane biogenesis programme covers all three. Cells depend on it to rebuild the nuclear envelope after mitosis, to generate peroxisomes, to form surface invaginations, and to organize specialized membrane domains at cell-cell contacts. ESCRT-III subunits with the VPS4 ATPases carry out the constriction and scission steps used for both nuclear envelope resealing, directed by CHMP7 with the BAF and LEM-domain proteins, and for endosomal and cytokinetic membrane remodelling. Peroxins PEX16 and PEX19 deliver tail-anchored proteins into nascent peroxisomal membranes, caveolins and flotillin shape caveolae, and lipid enzymes such as UGCG supply glycosphingolipids. Spectrin and ankyrin link the finished bilayer to the cytoskeleton, while neurexin-neuroligin pairs specify synaptic membrane identity.

Cells rely as much on shutting activities off as on turning them on, and this collection represents the inhibitory side of molecular activity: proteins that block catalysis, occlude binding surfaces, sequester partners, or hold enzymes in an inactive state. The theme spans many systems rather than one route. Endogenous protease inhibitors such as the serpins, TIMP1 and TIMP2 restrain proteolysis of extracellular matrix and of inflammatory enzymes; PKIA blocks protein kinase A, while DEPTOR and TSC1 damp mTOR signalling and GSK3-interacting and dual-specificity phosphatase-related proteins limit kinase output. Inhibitory receptors and adaptors including HAVCR2, CD300A and PTPN22 raise the threshold for immune activation, pyrin-domain decoys and NLRC3 restrain inflammasome assembly, and KCNE subunits and phospholamban tune ion channel and calcium pump activity. Tumour suppressors such as RB1, TP53 and CDKN2A act here by constraining the machinery of proliferation, so loss of such brakes underlies cancer, autoimmunity and arrhythmia.

This is a broad regulatory grouping for processes that switch on or amplify the activity of another molecule — enzyme catalysis, binding affinity, channel conductance or nucleotide exchange — rather than a single coherent route. It captures the activator side of cellular control: guanine nucleotide exchange factors and GTPase-activating proteins that set Rho, Ras and Rab timing; kinase activators and scaffolds feeding MAP kinase, PI3K–AKT–mTOR and protein kinase A/C cascades; adaptors such as MYD88, IRAK1 and the TRAF and CARD families that license NF-κB signalling downstream of Toll-like and tumour necrosis factor receptors; inflammasome components including NLRP3, NLRC4 and PYCARD that trigger caspase activation; STIM and ORAI partners that open store-operated calcium entry; and chaperones, ubiquitin ligases and anaphase-promoting complex cofactors that stimulate folding, degradation and mitotic exit. Because activation steps are where signals gain amplitude and directionality, members here are recurrent drivers of growth factor signalling, immune activation and oncogenic transformation.

Cells can regenerate UMP from pyrimidine breakdown products rather than building the ring from scratch, and UMP salvage is that recycling route. It conserves the energy and glutamine that de novo pyrimidine synthesis would consume, keeps uridine and cytidine nucleotides available for RNA synthesis, glycogen and glycolipid metabolism, and phospholipid head-group activation, and matters most in tissues with limited de novo capacity such as bone marrow, gut epithelium and brain. Uridine-cytidine kinases phosphorylate uridine and cytidine directly to their monophosphates, cytidine deaminase converts cytidine to uridine, and uridine phosphorylases run the reversible cleavage of uridine to uracil and ribose-1-phosphate that feeds the pool. The same enzymes determine the fate of pyrimidine analogue drugs: capecitabine and gemcitabine activation or inactivation runs through these steps, so salvage activity shapes chemotherapy response and toxicity.

Adenine nucleotides must be made from scratch in proliferating cells, and this is the route that builds AMP de novo, ending with the two-step conversion of inosine monophosphate into adenylate. Adenylosuccinate synthetase adds aspartate to IMP to form adenylosuccinate, and adenylosuccinate lyase then releases fumarate to yield AMP, linking purine supply to the aspartate pool and to fumarate returning to the citric acid cycle. The upstream multifunctional enzymes that assemble the purine ring on phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate feed the pathway, beginning with the glutamine-dependent amidophosphoribosyltransferase step that sets overall flux. Output supports DNA and RNA synthesis, ATP regeneration and signalling nucleotides, so demand rises sharply in dividing tissue and in tumours. Loss of adenylosuccinate lyase causes a neurometabolic disorder with seizures and developmental delay, and the pathway's enzymes are targets of antifolate and antipurine chemotherapy.

Dietary fat arrives as triglyceride, cholesteryl ester and phospholipid droplets that cannot cross a membrane, and lipid digestion is the sequence of emulsification, hydrolysis and uptake that converts them into absorbable fatty acids, monoglycerides and sterols. It sets how many calories and how much cholesterol the body actually extracts from a meal, and its manipulation underlies lipase-inhibitor and cholesterol-absorption-inhibitor drugs. Pancreatic lipase and its related proteins, carboxyl ester lipase and intestinal sphingomyelinase and ceramidase strip the substrates apart in the gut lumen; bile acids, whose composition depends on CYP8B1, keep the products in solution. At the enterocyte brush border NPC1L1 takes up cholesterol while the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer pumps sterols back out, setting net absorption. CD36 assists fatty acid uptake, and re-esterification with apolipoprotein assembly of A-I, A-II and A-IV loads the products onto chylomicrons for delivery to the lymph.

Sulfur-containing metabolites are built here: the transsulfuration route from methionine to cysteine, glutathione synthesis, taurine and hypotaurine production, coenzyme A, lipoic acid, thiamine cofactors and the activated sulfate donor PAPS. Together these supply the cell's main antioxidant buffer, the acyl carrier chemistry of fatty acid and pyruvate metabolism, and the sulfate used to modify proteins and xenobiotics. Methionine adenosyltransferases generate S-adenosylmethionine for methylation, while CBS and CTH commit homocysteine to cysteine, and GCLC with GCLM catalyse the rate-limiting step of glutathione formation under NFE2L2 control; SLC7A11 imports the cystine that feeds it, linking this biology to ferroptosis resistance. Pantothenate kinases and downstream enzymes construct coenzyme A, and lipoate synthase installs the lipoyl group on pyruvate and ketoglutarate dehydrogenase subunits. Defects cause homocystinuria, neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and cofactor-responsive metabolic disease.

Sulfur-containing metabolites must be dismantled as well as made, and this catabolic branch handles the breakdown of cysteine, methionine, glutathione and coenzyme A-derived thioesters. It matters for detoxifying sulfide and cyanide, for generating taurine and hypotaurine as osmolytes and bile acid conjugates, and for recycling the cysteine held in glutathione during oxidative stress. Cysteine dioxygenase and sulfinoalanine decarboxylase commit cysteine to the taurine route, while cystathionine beta-synthase directs homocysteine into transsulfuration; loss of CBS causes homocystinuria. Gamma-glutamyl transferases and dipeptidases cleave glutathione and its conjugates extracellularly, and intracellular ChaC-family glutathione-specific hydrolases degrade it in the cytosol. Rhodanese-family sulfurtransferases transfer sulfane sulfur for cyanide clearance and cofactor sulfuration, and nudix hydrolases plus succinyl-CoA ligases turn over CoA thioesters, linking sulfur disposal to amino acid and acyl-CoA metabolism.

Small molecule metabolism encompasses the reactions that build, break down and interconvert low-molecular-weight compounds — sugars, amino acids, fatty acids, nucleotides, sterols, vitamins and their cofactors — and it supplies the energy, precursors and redox equivalents on which every cell depends. The genes here cover glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, the citric acid cycle, the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, fatty acid activation and beta-oxidation in mitochondria and peroxisomes, cholesterol and bile acid synthesis, purine and pyrimidine salvage, one-carbon and folate metabolism, amino acid catabolism and urea cycle chemistry. Also represented are cytochrome P450 and conjugating enzymes that handle xenobiotics and steroid hormones, transporters and lipoproteins that move metabolites between compartments and tissues, and the nutrient-sensing regulators — insulin signalling, AMP-activated kinase, SREBP and PPAR transcription factors — that match flux to demand. Inherited defects in individual steps produce the classical inborn errors of metabolism, while coordinated dysregulation underlies diabetes, dyslipidaemia and fatty liver disease.

Cells continuously dismantle low-molecular-weight metabolites — amino acids, fatty acids, sugars, nucleotides, bile acids and xenobiotics — and this small molecule catabolic process is the collected chemistry by which they do it, releasing carbon into the citric acid cycle and reducing equivalents into respiration while clearing compounds that become toxic if they accumulate. Branched-chain and aromatic amino acid breakdown, glycine cleavage, the kynurenine route through tryptophan, glycolysis, peroxisomal and mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, ketone body handling and sulfotransferase- or cytochrome P450-mediated inactivation all belong here, supported by carnitine shuttles, peroxisomal import machinery and transcriptional control through PPAR receptors that matches catabolic capacity to nutrient supply. Loss of single steps produces much of classical inherited metabolic disease — phenylketonuria, maple syrup urine disease, medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, tyrosinaemia, hyperoxaluria — where the missing reaction matters less than the substrate that builds up behind it.

This is the anabolic side of metabolism: the reactions by which cells build low-molecular-weight, non-polymeric molecules rather than degrade them. The gene collection spans the major biosynthetic routes a human cell runs — fatty acid and complex lipid synthesis through acetyl-CoA carboxylase, fatty acid synthase and the elongase/desaturase series; cholesterol and isoprenoid production via the mevalonate route under HMG-CoA reductase and SREBP/SCAP control; sphingolipid and ceramide formation; steroid, bile acid and retinoid generation by cytochrome P450 enzymes; prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis; ubiquinone assembly; purine, pyrimidine and folate one-carbon metabolism; amino acid, polyamine, creatine and urea-cycle chemistry; and gluconeogenesis and inositol phosphate synthesis. Because these outputs supply membranes, signalling mediators, hormones, cofactors and nucleotides, the whole programme is held under nutrient- and energy-sensing control by AMPK, nuclear receptors, sirtuins and transcription factors such as ATF4 and ChREBP, and its dysregulation underlies dyslipidaemia, fatty liver and inborn errors of metabolism.
