Ubiquitin can be joined through any of its seven lysines, and chains built through lysine 27 mark a comparatively rare signal used for DNA damage responses, mitochondrial quality control and degradation of misfolded membrane proteins rather than for routine proteasomal turnover. Because K27 chains are compact and poorly recognised by conventional shuttle factors, they tend to recruit specialised readers and to modify substrates in place, including damaged mitochondria and stalled ER clients. The enzymes here span both halves of the transfer reaction: E2 conjugating enzymes such as UBE2S, UBE2T and UBE2D4 charge and position ubiquitin, while RING-type E3 ligases including the ER-associated AMFR, RNF185 and RNF126, the mitochondrial MARCHF5, the Parkinson disease ligase PRKN, the antibody-binding TRIM21 and the cullin component RBX1 select substrates. Loss of this linkage impairs mitophagy, protein quality control and innate immune signalling.

cellular response to leptin stimulus describes how cells read the adipose-derived hormone leptin, the signal that reports how much fat the body is carrying. Hypothalamic neurons use this input to suppress appetite and raise energy expenditure, while peripheral tissues adjust glucose handling and lipid storage; loss of leptin or its receptor produces severe early-onset obesity and hyperphagia, and obesity itself is characterised by resistance to the signal. Binding to the long-form receptor activates JAK-STAT signalling, with STAT3 carrying transcriptional output to targets governing feeding and metabolism, and SIRT1 and nuclear receptors such as NR4A3 shaping the response. Ciliary and BBSome components including BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS are required to traffic the receptor and sustain sensitivity, linking this hormone axis to cilium biology, and downstream effects extend to glucokinase-dependent glucose sensing.

Leptin is secreted by white adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, and the cellular response to it is how tissues read that signal and adjust appetite, energy expenditure and metabolic gene expression. Hypothalamic neurons are the best-known responders, where leptin binding to its receptor drives STAT3-dependent transcription that suppresses food intake; loss of either the hormone or its receptor causes severe early-onset obesity and hypogonadism. Trafficking of the receptor to the cell surface and its signalling competence depend on the BBS/chaperonin-like proteins represented here by BBS2, BBS4 and MKKS, explaining the leptin resistance and obesity of ciliopathy syndromes. Downstream and cooperating factors include SIRT1, nuclear receptor NR4A3 and glucokinase, linking the response to insulin sensitivity, glucose handling and lipid signalling rather than to appetite alone.

Leptin is secreted by white adipocytes in proportion to fat mass, and the cellular responses to it are how the body reports its energy stores to the brain and periphery. Binding of leptin to its receptor engages STAT3-dependent transcription that suppresses appetite and raises energy expenditure; loss of either the hormone or the receptor causes hyperphagia and severe early-onset obesity, and the more common obese state is marked by resistance to the signal rather than its absence. Several members here are ciliary and trafficking proteins of the BBSome, whose disruption blunts leptin receptor signalling and produces obesity as part of a syndromic disorder. Downstream and modulatory components link the stimulus to glucose handling through glucokinase, to circadian and metabolic transcription via NR1D1 and SIRT1, and to proliferative and vascular responses, placing this hormone response at the junction of adiposity sensing, feeding behaviour and insulin action.

Cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion is how cells of the same type recognise and hold onto one another, and it is the basis of epithelial sheets, endothelial barriers and the sorting of tissues during development. Classical cadherins such as E-cadherin, N-cadherin and VE-cadherin bind homophilically through calcium-dependent extracellular repeats and couple through their cytoplasmic tails to beta-catenin and p120-catenin, which in turn link to the actin cytoskeleton via afadin, ZO-1 and PLEKHA7 at adherens junctions. Loss of E-cadherin releases beta-catenin toward transcription and converts epithelia to a migratory phenotype, a step central to epithelial-mesenchymal transition and to tumour invasion and metastasis. Atypical members including the FAT and CELSR proteins instead relay planar polarity and growth-control signals, and adhesion here is modulated by TGF-beta, WNT and Notch inputs as well as by sheddases that cleave cadherin ectodomains.

Phosphate is charged and cannot cross membranes unaided, so cells import it against its gradient using the inward sodium gradient as the driving force. This sodium-coupled phosphate transport sets whole-body phosphate balance and the supply of phosphate for ATP, nucleotides, phospholipids and bone mineral. The type II carriers SLC34A1 and SLC34A3 sit in the renal proximal tubule brush border and determine how much filtered phosphate is reclaimed; their loss causes phosphate wasting, hypophosphatemic rickets and nephrolithiasis, while SLC34A2 handles phosphate uptake in alveolar type II cells for surfactant synthesis and, when mutated, produces pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis. Related type I and vesicular members of the SLC17 family move phosphate and organic anions, with VGLUT isoforms loading glutamate into synaptic vesicles. Transcriptional and secreted regulators including ATF4, CEBPB and SFRP4 adjust transporter abundance, linking phosphate handling to stress responses, circadian timing and endocrine control.

type B pancreatic cell proliferation describes the expansion of insulin-secreting beta cells within pancreatic islets, the process that sets and maintains functional beta cell mass. It matters because beta cell number determines how much insulin can be released on demand: mass expands during pregnancy, obesity and insulin resistance, and its failure to keep pace underlies the transition to type 2 diabetes, while autoimmune destruction of the same population causes type 1. The genes span growth-factor and hormonal inputs to the cell cycle, including insulin-like growth factor binding proteins, secreted regulators such as ANGPTL8 and CCN3, and the hepatic-islet protease inhibitor SERPINB1 that drives compensatory replication. Alongside these sit immediate-early and circadian transcription factors, the beta cell identity factor NKX6-1, and survival regulators such as BAD, linking nutrient sensing and metabolic demand to proliferation, differentiation state and apoptosis.

Insulin-secreting beta cells of the pancreatic islets are normally quiescent, but their number can expand during growth, pregnancy, obesity and insulin resistance; this proliferative capacity sets how much insulin a person can secrete and its loss underlies the beta cell deficit of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. The genes here act as drivers and brakes on beta cell replication rather than on insulin release itself: hepatokine and secreted growth-regulatory signals, IGF-binding proteins that sequester and modulate IGF availability, a hepatocyte-derived protease inhibitor that stimulates beta cell mitosis, and apoptotic and stress regulators such as BAD that couple nutrient sensing and survival to cycle entry. Nuclear receptors of the NR4A family and a circadian factor place proliferative decisions under transcriptional and daily metabolic control, while NKX6-1 maintains the mature beta cell identity that expanding cells must retain.

Fibroblasts build and remodel the collagen-rich extracellular matrix of connective tissue, and their programmed death is how a healing wound resolves: granulation-tissue fibroblasts are cleared once repair is complete, and failure to remove them underlies fibrotic scarring in lung, skin, liver and kidney. Apoptosis in these cells runs through the mitochondrial route, with BAK1 permeabilizing the outer membrane after activation by the BH3-only proteins BIM and BID, while API5 and survival signalling through PI3K catalytic subunits raise the threshold for commitment. Growth-factor and Wnt-modulating cues such as GAS6 and SFRP1 set that threshold from outside the cell, and transcriptional regulators including MYC and TP63 couple proliferative and differentiation state to death sensitivity. Serine/threonine kinases of the DRAK family and ubiquitin ligase activity provide additional control, linking matrix production, growth arrest and genome integrity to fibroblast survival.

Macropinocytosis is the bulk, non-selective drinking of extracellular fluid, in which the plasma membrane throws up actin-driven ruffles that close back on themselves to trap a large droplet in a macropinosome up to several micrometres across. It lets cells sample soluble antigen, scavenge extracellular protein and amino acids as a nutrient source, and internalise surface receptors in bulk; dendritic cells and macrophages depend on it for immune surveillance, and tumour cells with activated Ras exploit it to feed on serum protein. It is also the route many viruses and bacteria use to enter cells. The genes point to the actin and Rho-GTPase machinery that builds the ruffle, notably a Rac exchange factor and a capping-protein regulator, together with endosomal adaptors and sorting nexins that shape and mature the resulting vesicle, plus kinase and ion-channel inputs that control ruffling and inflammasome-linked responses.

Macropinocytosis is the bulk, non-selective drinking of extracellular fluid: the plasma membrane throws up actin-driven ruffles that close back on themselves, trapping a droplet of medium in a large, irregular macropinosome up to several micrometres across. Cells use it to sample soluble antigen, to scavenge extracellular protein and amino acids as a nutrient source, and as an entry route exploited by viruses and bacteria; in macrophages and dendritic cells it is a major contributor to immune surveillance, and in RAS-driven tumour cells it supports growth under nutrient limitation. The process depends on regulated actin remodelling at the cortex, with capping-protein regulators and a Rac-directed guanine nucleotide exchange factor shaping the ruffle, kinases downstream of stress signalling tuning cytoskeletal dynamics, and endosomal adaptors and sorting nexins together with Rab and SNARE proteins directing macropinosome closure, maturation and traffic toward lysosomal degradation.

Protein localization to cytoskeleton covers the targeting and retention of proteins on microtubules, actin filaments and the centrosome, which is how a cell decides where its machinery acts rather than merely whether it is present. Correct positioning underlies mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation, centriole duplication and ciliogenesis, cell polarity and directed migration; its failure produces multipolar divisions, aneuploidy, microcephaly and ciliopathies. The genes describe the docking platforms and their cargo adaptors: centrosomal and pericentriolar scaffolds such as PCM1, CEP131 and CEP192 that recruit satellite and appendage components, microtubule plus-end tracking proteins of the MAPRE/EB family and GAS2L cross-linkers, dynactin and BICD/HOOK adaptors that load dynein cargo, and kinases including AURKA, GSK3B, CSNK1D and MARK4 that switch attachment on and off. Depalmitoylating ABHD17 enzymes and ubiquitin-pathway members add reversible membrane and turnover control to the same targeting decisions.

Getting a protein to the right place on the cytoskeleton is what gives microtubules and actin filaments their functional identity, and this pathway covers the targeting and retention steps that put cargo, regulators and scaffolds onto those filaments. It underlies centrosome and centriole composition, cilium assembly, spindle organization and directed transport, so its failure shows up as mitotic errors, microcephaly and ciliopathy. Much of the machinery here is centrosomal or satellite-associated, including several CEP proteins, PCM1 and STIL, which recruit components to the centriole and distal appendages; the end-binding proteins encoded by MAPRE1-3 mark growing microtubule plus ends and load partners such as GAS2L1 and APC there. Kinases including AURKA, GSK3B, CSNK1D and MARK4 set these interactions dynamically, while dynactin and HOOK3 link the network to motor-driven traffic and Golgi positioning.

glucose import in response to insulin stimulus is the step that lets muscle and adipose tissue clear glucose from the blood after a meal, and its impairment is the defining lesion of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Insulin signalling causes storage vesicles holding the transporter GLUT4 (SLC2A4) to translocate to the plasma membrane, raising glucose uptake many-fold without new transporter synthesis. The genes point to the machinery that builds and traffics these vesicles: TRARG1 marks GLUT4 storage compartments and promotes their insulin-responsive delivery, and the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC7 modifies substrates that tune this trafficking, linking protein lipidation to transporter targeting. Fatty acid transport proteins couple the same stimulus to lipid uptake, and a sarcoglycan component ties the response to the muscle membrane cytoskeleton. The pathway sits downstream of the insulin receptor and PI3K-AKT cascade and upstream of glycogen and triglyceride storage.

After a meal, insulin tells muscle and fat cells to take up glucose from the blood, and this pathway is the transport step that carries out that instruction. It sets whole-body glucose tolerance: when the response is blunted, glucose stays in the circulation and insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes follow. The central effector is the GLUT4 transporter, held in intracellular storage vesicles under basal conditions and translocated to the plasma membrane when insulin signalling reaches the cell surface. TRARG1 is a component of those GLUT4 storage vesicles and supports their trafficking, while ZDHHC7 palmitoylates GLUT4 and influences its sorting. Fatty acid transport proteins of the SLC27 family link this uptake to lipid handling in the same insulin-responsive tissues, and the sarcoglycan component ties it to the muscle membrane environment in which much postprandial glucose disposal occurs.

negative regulation of protein kinase activity by regulation of protein phosphorylation describes how cells switch kinases off by controlling whether the kinase itself is phosphorylated, rather than by blocking its substrate or degrading it. This form of restraint sets the duration of signalling bursts and prevents runaway kinase output in stress responses, cell cycle progression and innate immune activation. The genes point to two convergent themes: the adenosine deaminases that edit double-stranded RNA and thereby limit activation of the RNA-sensing kinase PKR, keeping translational shutdown and interferon-driven inflammation in check; and nucleolar and cytoskeletal regulators including NPM1, CDK5RAP3 and CORO1C that damp CDK and stress-kinase activity through phosphorylation-dependent interactions. Loss of such braking permits sustained kinase signalling, and the RNA-editing arm in particular guards against autoinflammatory disease driven by misread endogenous transcripts.

Kinases are switched off as well as on, and one route to shutting them down is to alter their own phosphorylation state rather than block their catalytic site directly. This form of negative regulation of protein kinase activity keeps signalling transient, sets thresholds for stress responses, and prevents the sustained kinase output that drives inappropriate proliferation or cell death. The genes here act indirectly on kinase phosphorylation: the RNA-editing enzymes ADAR and ADARB1 limit activation of the double-stranded RNA-sensing kinase PKR by marking cellular RNA as self, thereby restraining translational shutdown and interferon-driven signalling; CDK5RAP3 and the nucleolar chaperone NPM1 modulate kinase and cyclin-dependent kinase signalling in growth and stress pathways. Loss of such restraint contributes to autoinflammatory disease and to dysregulated cell-cycle and stress kinase output in cancer.

Host proteins that mediate intimate association with another organism are collected here, and in practice the genes describe the interface between human cells and microbes — overwhelmingly viruses and bacteria. The set matters because it defines how pathogens gain entry, how they exploit membrane trafficking to replicate and exit, and how innate defences push back. Receptors and attachment factors such as ACE2, CD4 with CCR5 and CXCR4, DPP4, TFRC, NPC1, nectins and claudins determine tropism, while proteases including TMPRSS2, furin and cathepsin L prime surface glycoproteins for fusion. The full ESCRT machinery, with TSG101, CHMP subunits and VPS4 ATPases, is co-opted for budding and for late endosomal sorting alongside RAB7A, LAMP1 and PIKFYVE. Opposing these are antimicrobial peptides and proteins — defensins, cathelicidin, lactoferrin, peptidoglycan recognition proteins — complement regulators, tetherin and TRIM restriction factors. The balance struck determines whether infection, commensal tolerance, or clearance follows.

Attachment of a symbiont to its host surface is the first committed step of infection, and the same molecules that permit it also define which tissues a microbe can colonize. The genes here are largely host-side entry and docking factors exploited by viruses and bacteria: ACE2 and DPP4 serve as coronavirus receptors, TMPRSS2 primes the viral spike by proteolysis to allow membrane fusion, the lectins CD209 and CLEC4M capture glycosylated envelopes on dendritic cells and liver endothelium, and NECTIN2 and SCARB1 act as receptors for herpesviruses and hepatitis C virus respectively. Set against these are secreted airway defences such as lactoferrin, MUC5B and BPIFA1 that trap and aggregate organisms before they can bind. ICAM1 and GAS6 bridge adhesion to leukocyte recruitment and phagocytic clearance, so this biology sits at the interface of mucosal barrier function, tropism and innate immune recognition.

Viruses and other intracellular microbes reach the cytoplasm only by exploiting host surface proteins, and this pathway collects the host molecules that permit a symbiont or pathogen to attach to and enter cells and tissues. It matters because these entry factors set tissue tropism and species susceptibility, and they are the targets of blocking antibodies and entry inhibitors. Receptors range widely: ACE2 and DPP4 for coronaviruses, CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4 for HIV, nectins and heparan sulfate modification for herpesviruses, NPC1 for filoviruses, transferrin and LDL receptors, integrins, tetraspanins, claudins, and lectins such as CD209 that capture glycosylated envelopes. Entry also requires proteolytic priming by TMPRSS2, furin, or endosomal cathepsins, caveolin- and clathrin-dependent uptake, endolysosomal trafficking and membrane fusion. Several TRIM proteins and cholesterol 25-hydroxylase act against these steps, so restriction and invasion are described together.

Living alongside microbes, viruses and parasites requires a dedicated set of host functions, and this very broad grouping collects the processes by which human cells sense, resist, tolerate or are exploited by organisms of another species. It underpins barrier defence, innate and adaptive immunity, and the outcome of infection: without it, commensal containment fails and pathogens replicate unchecked. The genes span pattern recognition by Toll-like, NOD-like, RIG-I-like and lectin receptors; signalling through MyD88, TBK1 and NF-kB to interferon and cytokine output; interferon-stimulated effectors such as MX1, OAS enzymes, IFITMs and APOBEC3 deaminases; complement and antimicrobial peptides including defensins, lysozyme and cathelicidin; phagosome maturation, xenophagy and inflammasome-driven pyroptosis; and antigen presentation by MHC molecules to T and NK cells. Also present are receptors and proteases that viruses hijack for entry, notably ACE2 and TMPRSS2, reflecting interactions that favour the microbe rather than the host.

Motile cilia and sperm flagella are built by this assembly programme, which converts a centriole-derived basal body into an axoneme capable of generating beat. Its output clears mucus from the airways, circulates cerebrospinal fluid, moves the ovum through the fallopian tube and propels sperm; when it fails the result is primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic sinopulmonary disease, situs abnormalities, hydrocephalus and male infertility. Transcriptional control by FOXJ1 and MCIDAS commits a cell to the multiciliated or spermatogenic fate, intraflagellar transport components deliver axonemal cargo, and cytoplasmic dynein assembly factors such as DNAAF1, DNAAF3 and ZMYND10 preassemble dynein arms before import. Ruler and nexin-dynein regulatory complex proteins including CCDC39, CCDC40 and DRC1 set the 96-nanometre repeat, while radial spoke and central apparatus subunits impose waveform. Tubulin polyglutamylation tunes motility of the finished organelle.

Mitochondria transcribe their genome as long polycistronic RNAs that must be cut, tailed and either protected or destroyed, and the control of mitochondrial mRNA stability sets how much of each message survives to be translated. Because the thirteen mitochondrially encoded proteins are core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, the balance between stabilization and decay directly tunes oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and its loss produces respiratory deficiency and mitochondrial disease. The FASTK family of RNA-binding proteins, including FASTKD2 and the TBRG4 product FASTKD4, associates with RNA granules in the matrix and acts on individual transcripts, some members promoting processing and accumulation of specific mRNAs while others accelerate their turnover. PDE12 trims the poly(A) tails added to these transcripts, linking tail length to message half-life and to the fidelity of mitochondrial gene expression.</br>

Fibrinogen is the soluble plasma precursor that thrombin converts into the fibrin mesh of a clot, and its circulating concentration sets both clotting capacity and plasma viscosity; persistently high levels track with thrombotic and cardiovascular risk, while deficiency causes bleeding. Control of that concentration is exerted here at two levels: glycosylation and post-transcriptional repression. The galactosyltransferase B4GALT1 builds galactose-terminated N-glycans on hepatocyte secretory proteins, and altering this modification changes fibrinogen output and clearance from the blood. The miR-29 family members, together with miR-409, act as microRNA regulators that dampen hepatic expression of target transcripts feeding into fibrinogen production; miR-29 is better known for restraining extracellular matrix and collagen genes, placing this regulation at the intersection of liver secretory function, coagulation balance and matrix remodelling.

Cells that burn or store fat must first bring long-chain fatty acids across the plasma membrane, and this uptake route supplies muscle and heart with oxidative fuel, adipose tissue with triglyceride substrate, and liver and intestine with lipid for packaging and export. Uptake is not simple diffusion: the scavenger receptor CD36 and the SLC27 family of fatty acid transport proteins capture and translocate the ligand, while long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases esterify it to acyl-CoA on arrival, trapping it inside and keeping the inward gradient steep. Cytosolic fatty acid binding proteins then buffer and shuttle the load. Insulin signalling through IRS2, AKT and S6 kinase tunes transporter availability at the surface, linking import to nutritional state. Excessive or misdirected uptake contributes to lipotoxicity, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance, whereas deficient uptake starves the heart of its preferred substrate.

Formation of compounds not required for basic growth and maintenance, the secondary metabolite biosynthetic process in human cells is dominated by pigment chemistry: the synthesis of eumelanin and pheomelanin inside melanosomes of melanocytes and retinal pigment epithelium. The output determines skin, hair and eye colour, shields keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage, and its loss underlies albinism and hypopigmentation syndromes, while its dysregulation accompanies melanoma. Tyrosinase and the related TYRP1 and DCT oxidize tyrosine along the melanin route; a copper transporter and melanosomal solute carriers such as OCA2, SLC45A2 and SLC24A5 set the cofactor supply and internal pH that these enzymes require, and PMEL forms the amyloid fibrils on which pigment is deposited. Upstream, POMC-derived melanocortin acting through MC1R, antagonized by agouti signalling protein, switches synthesis between the dark and light pigment types.

Smooth muscle relaxation reverses contraction in the walls of blood vessels, airways, gut and bladder, and it sets vascular tone, blood pressure and regional perfusion; its loss underlies hypertension, vasospasm, bronchoconstriction and erectile dysfunction. The genes here trace the two classical relaxant routes. Nitric oxide and natriuretic peptide signals raise cyclic GMP through soluble guanylate cyclase, and cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG1 acts on the IRAG1-IP3 receptor complex to curb calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, while NPR3 clears natriuretic peptides to limit the signal. In parallel, adenosine acting at A2B receptors elevates cyclic AMP, with RGS2 and GRK2 damping opposing Gq- and Gi-coupled contractile input. Calcium is lowered further by sodium-calcium exchange, and ATP-sensitive potassium channels hyperpolarise the membrane to close voltage-gated calcium entry, so relaxation is ultimately a coordinated fall in cytosolic calcium and myosin light chain phosphorylation.

Many enzymes work only with an iron-sulfur cofactor, and [2Fe-2S] cluster assembly is the step that builds the simplest of these clusters and hands it on. The reaction occurs on the mitochondrial scaffold protein ISCU, where the cysteine desulfurase NFS1 with its partner LYRM4 donates sulfur from cysteine, frataxin stimulates the reaction and helps deliver iron, and the ferredoxin FDX2 provides reducing equivalents; an acyl carrier protein subunit ties the complex to mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis. A dedicated co-chaperone system then releases the nascent cluster, and monothiol glutaredoxins together with BOLA partners carry [2Fe-2S] units onward to recipient apoproteins or to cytosolic assembly. The products supply respiratory complexes, aconitase and other metabolic and DNA repair enzymes, and also report cellular iron status. Loss of individual steps causes mitochondrial myopathy, sideroblastic anemia and, for frataxin, Friedreich ataxia.

Building a [4Fe-4S] cofactor requires four iron and four sulfur atoms to be assembled on a scaffold before delivery to an apoprotein, and the core mitochondrial machinery that does this work is what this pathway describes. The products are cofactors for respiratory complexes I, II and III, aconitase, lipoate synthase and several DNA repair enzymes, so the process sits upstream of oxidative energy metabolism, TCA cycle flux and genome maintenance. A cysteine desulfurase mobilises sulfide from cysteine, its accessory subunit stabilises the enzyme, frataxin stimulates the reaction and helps supply iron, a ferredoxin provides reducing equivalents, and the scaffold ISCU holds the nascent cluster. Loss of frataxin causes Friedreich ataxia, and mutations in the scaffold or its partners produce myopathy and multisystem mitochondrial disease, often with disturbed cellular iron sensing and mitochondrial iron overload.

Attachment of a symbiont to a host cell is the first committed step of infection, and the molecules listed here are the host surface receptors and cofactors that pathogens exploit to make that contact. Several are entry receptors for enveloped viruses: ACE2 for SARS-related coronaviruses, DPP4 for MERS coronavirus, and the C-type lectins CD209 and CLEC4M, which capture high-mannose glycoproteins on virions and hand them to permissive cells. TMPRSS2 is a serine protease that primes coronavirus spike after binding, coupling adhesion to membrane fusion, while GAS6 bridges phosphatidylserine on virions to receptor tyrosine kinases in apoptotic mimicry. NECTIN2 and ICAM1 are adhesion receptors subverted by herpesviruses and rhinoviruses respectively. Tropism, transmissibility and the targets of entry-blocking antibodies and protease inhibitors are all set at this step.

Tooth eruption is the final stage of odontogenesis, in which a formed tooth moves through alveolar bone and gingiva to appear in the mouth and meet its opposing partner. It depends less on the tooth than on the bone around it: eruption requires coordinated osteoclastic resorption to open a pathway, so genes that build the osteoclast ruffled border and its acid-secreting machinery are central here. RANKL signalling drives osteoclast formation, while the vacuolar ATPase a3 subunit and a sorting nexin required for its trafficking allow bone dissolution; loss of these causes osteopetrosis with failure of teeth to emerge. Ciliary transport and the enamel-related secretory regulator FAM20A link eruption to dental follicle and enamel matrix integrity, and mutations produce enamel renal syndrome with unerupted teeth. Clinically the pathway explains primary retention, delayed eruption and impacted dentition.

Some physiological processes cannot be completed by one body alone: they require a second organism, whether a mate, a fetus, a nursing infant, or an infecting microbe. This collection of multi-organism processes is dominated by mammalian reproduction and pregnancy — sperm maturation and fertilization proteins such as acrosin, transition protein and oviductal glycoprotein; hypothalamic and pituitary hormones including GnRH, oxytocin, prolactin and CRH; steroid receptors for androgen, oestrogen and progesterone; and a large pregnancy-specific glycoprotein family expressed by trophoblast. Placental function is represented by nutrient transporters, hypoxia and angiogenic factors such as VEGFA and EPO, relaxin signalling, and cortisol-inactivating HSD11B2, which shields the fetus from maternal glucocorticoid. Parturition depends on prostaglandin synthesis and oxytocin receptor signalling in myometrium. Failure across these axes produces infertility, implantation loss, pre-eclampsia and preterm birth; a smaller host-defence component, including ACE2, IDO1 and IL1B, covers interaction with other species.

Peroxisomal matrix enzymes are made on cytosolic ribosomes and imported fully folded, and this step is the end of that journey: the cargo is let go inside the organelle so the receptor can be recycled for another round. Release matters because it is what actually delivers catalase, beta-oxidation enzymes and plasmalogen-synthesis enzymes into the compartment where they work; when it fails, peroxisomes remain empty membrane ghosts and the result is the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders. The shuttling receptor PEX5 carries PTS1-bearing cargo to the docking complex at the membrane, where PEX14 participates in translocation and cargo discharge, and the RING-finger ubiquitin ligases PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 mark the receptor for extraction back to the cytosol. Cargo release and receptor recycling are thus coupled arms of the same import cycle.

Epigenetic programming in the zygotic pronuclei is the wholesale rewriting of DNA methylation and chromatin marks that happens in the hours after fertilization, before the one-cell embryo divides. It converts two highly specialized gametic genomes into a totipotent one, and its failure produces developmental arrest, imprinting disorders and recurrent hydatidiform mole. The paternal pronucleus is actively demethylated by TET3-driven oxidation of 5-methylcytosine, while the maternal pronucleus, marked by DPPA3 binding to H3K9me2 laid down by KDM1B and the SUV39H methyltransferases, is shielded from the same enzymes. Imprinted loci in both genomes escape erasure through ZNF445 and the maternal-effect machinery, with DNMT3L supporting the oocyte methylation that must be preserved. Subcortical maternal complex proteins such as PADI6 and TLE6 supply the oocyte-derived scaffold on which this asymmetric reprogramming depends.

Immediately after fertilization the two parental genomes sit in separate pronuclei in the same cytoplasm and are treated very differently, and this asymmetric epigenetic reprogramming is what converts two terminally differentiated gametes into a totipotent embryo. The paternal chromatin, stripped of protamines, undergoes active demethylation driven by the dioxygenase TET3, while the maternal genome is shielded: DPPA3 (Stella) binds H3K9me2-marked maternal chromatin and blocks TET3 access, with SUV39H enzymes supplying the heterochromatic methylation that defines it. Against this global erasure, imprinted loci must keep their gamete-of-origin marks, which requires DNMT3L and the zinc-finger protein ZNF445, while KDM1B removes H3K4 methylation during oocyte imprint establishment. Subcortical maternal complex components such as PADI6 and TLE6 supply the oocyte-derived scaffold. Failure produces imprinting disorders, early embryonic arrest and recurrent hydatidiform mole.

Proteins destined for an organelle must be recognised in the cytosol and moved bodily across its bounding membrane, and this pathway covers that import step for peroxisomes. Because peroxisomes have no internal ribosomes, every matrix enzyme of beta-oxidation, ether lipid synthesis and hydrogen peroxide detoxification arrives this way; failure of import produces the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, with neuronal migration defects, liver disease and accumulated very long chain fatty acids. Soluble receptors PEX5 and PEX7 bind matrix targeting signals and dock at a membrane complex built around PEX13 and PEX14, cargo is released into the lumen, and the ubiquitin ligase components PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12 together with the ATPases PEX1 and PEX6 and their anchor PEX26 recycle the receptor back to the cytosol. Deubiquitination and peroxisomal proteolysis modulate receptor turnover and matrix protein quality.

Progression through the cell cycle is not continuous but punctuated by decision points, and this collection covers the machinery that commits a cell to the next phase — G1/S entry, the G2/M transition, and the metaphase-to-anaphase switch. Cyclin–CDK pairs with their CDK inhibitors, the retinoblastoma protein and E2F transcription factors set the restriction point for DNA replication; WEE1 and PKMYT1 hold CDK1 inhibited until CDC25 phosphatases reverse that block; the anaphase-promoting complex with CDC20 or FZR1 destroys securin and mitotic cyclins once the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD2L1, BUB1B, kinetochore NDC80 components) is satisfied. Damage and replication-stress sensing through ATM, ATR, CHEK1/2 and p53 imposes delay so that lesions are repaired before commitment. These transitions determine proliferation rate, differentiation timing and genome stability, and their deregulation — loss of RB1, CDKN2A or TP53, amplified cyclins — is a recurring route to tumorigenesis and aneuploidy.

Meiosis proceeds through ordered phase transitions, and this is the switch biology that commits a germ cell to the next one: entry into and exit from meiotic M phase, the metaphase-to-anaphase step, and the arrest points that hold an oocyte or spermatocyte until fertilization or hormonal cues release it. Getting these commitments right determines gamete ploidy; failure produces aneuploid eggs and sperm, miscarriage and infertility. The machinery is the mitotic engine repurposed: cyclin B partners with CDK1, CDC25 phosphatases remove the inhibitory phosphates that PKMYT1 places on it, and the kinase MOS drives MAP kinase signalling that sustains metaphase arrest. Kinetochore components including NDC80, KNL1 and ZWINT report attachment status, and CDC20 activates the anaphase-promoting complex only once that status is satisfied, coupling chromosome segregation to spindle checkpoint control.

Progression through mitosis is not continuous but punctuated by commitment points, and this collection covers the switches that carry a cell from G1 into S phase, from G2 into mitosis, and from metaphase into anaphase. Getting these transitions right determines whether chromosomes are replicated once and segregated evenly; getting them wrong yields aneuploidy, genome instability and the unchecked proliferation typical of tumours. The core machinery pairs cyclins with cyclin-dependent kinases, whose activity is tuned by CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27, by inhibitory phosphorylation from WEE1 and PKMYT1 and its removal by CDC25 phosphatases, and by PP2A antagonism controlled through MASTL and ENSA. Irreversibility comes from ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis via the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF ligases feeding the proteasome. Overlaid are the DNA damage and spindle assembly checkpoints, ATM/ATR-CHEK signalling, p53 and the RB-E2F switch, which delay transitions until replication and kinetochore attachment are complete.

Cells entering or passing through mitosis must not divide with broken or incompletely replicated chromosomes, and mitotic DNA integrity checkpoint signaling is the surveillance that enforces this. Damage sensing arrests or delays cell cycle progression so that repair can occur; loss of the response produces chromosome missegregation, genomic instability and the mutational burden underlying cancer predisposition, which is why several components are familiar tumour suppressors. Lesions and stalled forks are recognised by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, replication protein A-coated single strands, the RAD9A-HUS1-RAD17 clamp and TOPBP1, activating the ATM and ATR kinases; MDC1 and BRCA1-associated ubiquitin machinery amplify the signal at chromatin. CHEK1 and CHEK2 then restrain CDK1 and CDK2 activity and PLK1, while TP53 and CDKN1A impose longer-term arrest. Structure-specific nucleases such as MUS81-EME1 resolve the branched intermediates that trigger the alarm.

Cilium organization covers the building, arrangement and disassembly of the microtubule-based projections that cells extend from a basal body derived from a centriole. It underlies two broad functions: motile cilia and sperm flagella that clear airway mucus, circulate cerebrospinal fluid, break left-right symmetry and drive sperm swimming, and the solitary primary cilium that acts as a signalling antenna for Hedgehog, polycystin-mediated flow sensing and photoreceptor outer segment function. Basal body and distal appendage proteins dock the axoneme to the membrane, transition zone modules such as the MKS and NPHP components gate protein entry, and intraflagellar transport trains moving on kinesin-2 and cytoplasmic dynein-2 carry cargo along the axoneme, with BBSome and small GTPase traffic delivering membrane proteins. Dynein arm assembly factors, radial spoke and tektin components confer motility, while RFX and FOXJ1 transcription factors specify the programme. Loss produces the ciliopathies: polycystic kidney disease, retinal degeneration, situs inversus, hydrocephalus and infertility.

Progression from metaphase to anaphase during meiosis is the irreversible commitment step in which paired chromosomes or sister chromatids are released to opposite poles, and getting its timing right determines whether an egg or sperm carries the correct chromosome number. Errors here produce aneuploid gametes, the leading cause of miscarriage and of trisomies. The genes involved couple kinetochore surveillance to the ubiquitin ligase that triggers separation: KNL1 and ZWINT build the outer kinetochore platform that recruits checkpoint components, the kinase TTK (Mps1) is required to generate the wait signal at unattached kinetochores, and CDC20 acts as the substrate-specifying activator of the anaphase-promoting complex once attachments are satisfied. MOS-driven MAP kinase signalling imposes the oocyte-specific arrest and meiosis I/II control, while CHFR contributes mitotic-stress checkpoint regulation. Together they enforce the order of chromosome segregation against premature anaphase onset.

Once per division, a cell must copy its genome exactly once, and this is the replication programme that runs inside the cell cycle. It sets the number of chromosome copies a daughter cell inherits; when it misfires, cells re-replicate segments of DNA, stall at damaged templates and accumulate the rearrangements that drive cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Origins are licensed by loading of the MCM2-7 helicase with CDT1, restrained from reuse by geminin, and fired after phosphorylation by the CDC7-DBF4 kinase, which recruits CDC45 and the GINS subunits to build an active replisome. Polymerase alpha primes, PCNA clamps the elongating polymerases, and FEN1 with LIG1 finishes lagging-strand maturation. Helicases and nucleases such as BLM, WRN, DNA2 and RTEL1 handle difficult templates, stalled forks and telomeric ends, linking fork progression to homologous recombination repair through RAD51 and BRCA2.

Infected cells do not merely host a virus; they actively interfere with its replication cycle, and this host-mediated perturbation of viral processes covers the ways cellular factors block, silence, or redirect steps the virus depends on. It matters because the outcome of infection — latency, clearance, or productive spread — is set largely by which of these restrictions hold. The genes span several arms: cytidine deaminase-mediated mutagenesis of viral genomes by an APOBEC3 family member; chemokines such as CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 that occupy entry coreceptors and recruit immune cells; transcriptional silencing through chromatin remodellers, HDAC1, REST and the positive transcription elongation factor components CDK9, cyclin T and BRD4 that gate viral promoter elongation; an SMC5/6 complex that represses episomal viral DNA; plus endosomal trafficking, lipid and membrane factors that constrain replication compartments. Failure of these controls permits reactivation and unchecked viral gene expression.

Newly assembled virions must bud from the host cell to spread, and this is the step at which infected cells fight back, restricting egress so that infection remains contained rather than propagating to neighbouring cells. Much of the activity comes from the TRIM family of RING-domain ubiquitin ligases, which tag viral structural proteins and capsids for degradation or sequestration; TRIM5 targets incoming retroviral capsids, TRIM21 acts as a cytosolic antibody receptor, and TRIM25 links ubiquitination to RIG-I-driven interferon induction, tying direct restriction to innate immune signalling. PML organizes nuclear bodies that silence incoming viral genomes, while a charged multivesicular body protein and a membrane-associated ligase intersect the ESCRT and secretory machinery that budding viruses hijack. Many of these factors are themselves interferon-inducible, so the blockade strengthens once infection is sensed, and viral antagonists of these proteins are a recurring determinant of host range and pathogenicity.

host-mediated suppression of viral proces covers the ways an infected cell or organism actively blocks steps of the viral life cycle rather than merely detecting the pathogen, and it determines whether an incoming virus establishes productive replication or is silenced. The genes span several distinct blocking strategies: soluble innate effectors such as lactoferrin and the pentraxins that neutralise particles before entry, chemokines of the CCL3/CCL4/CCL5 family that occupy the CCR5 coreceptor and shut out HIV while recruiting leukocytes, and a large nuclear arm that represses viral promoters. There, chromatin and transcription regulators including HDAC1, BRD4, REST, JUN and TARDBP act on integrated proviruses and viral enhancers to enforce transcriptional latency or restrict genome expression. Loss of this restriction favours viral reactivation and spread, and its manipulation underlies both latency-reversal and silencing approaches to antiviral therapy.

Infected cells push back against the virus that occupies them, and this collection captures host activities that interfere with viral processes rather than simply detecting the pathogen. Some members act by shutting down viral gene expression: chromatin and transcriptional regulators such as HDAC1, BRD4, REST and the repressive activity of host factors on viral promoters keep integrated or episomal viral templates silent, which is how latency is imposed and maintained. Others act extracellularly — lactoferrin and the pentraxins bind and neutralise particles or block attachment, while the CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 chemokines occupy the coreceptor used by HIV and recruit leukocytes to the site of infection. Transcription factors including JUN and TFAP4 tie this restriction to inflammatory and stress signalling. When these defences fail, viral replication proceeds unchecked or latent reservoirs reactivate.

Viruses cannot replicate on their own, and this grouping collects the host activities that a virus co-opts so that its own replication cycle proceeds efficiently — host-mediated activation of viral processes. Much of it is transcriptional: the positive transcription elongation factor complex of CDK9 with cyclin T1 or T2 is recruited to viral promoters to release paused RNA polymerase II, while EP300, SP1, JUN, LEF1, SNW1 and the SWI/SNF subunits SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 remodel chromatin and drive integrated proviral gene expression. Other members serve entry, trafficking and assembly: caveolin-2 and IGF2R at the cell surface, VAPA and VAPB as membrane tethers that viruses recruit to build replication organelles, PIK3C3 and TBC1D20 in vesicular traffic, and palmitoyltransferases of the ZDHHC family that lipid-modify viral glycoproteins. Because these are host proteins, they are attractive targets for antivirals that the virus cannot easily mutate around.

Nucleophagy is the selective autophagic turnover of nuclear material — damaged chromatin, lamina fragments, nucleolar components, or in extreme cases a whole nucleus — delivered to the lysosome for degradation. It matters as a quality-control route for the genome compartment: clearing micronuclei and damaged nuclear envelope limits genome instability and inflammatory DNA sensing, and it contributes to nuclear remodelling during differentiation and to phenotypes of premature ageing and laminopathy. The machinery here is the core autophagy apparatus rather than a nucleus-specific set: the ULK1/ULK2–ATG13–RB1CC1 initiation complex nucleates autophagosome formation, ATG7 and ATG3 conjugate ATG8-family proteins with the ATG12–ATG5 complex acting as E3-like ligase, ATG4 proteases prime and recycle them, ATG9A-containing vesicles and the lipid transfer proteins ATG2A/ATG2B supply membrane, and PI3P-binding WIPI and WDR45 proteins mark the growing phagophore. Mutations in WDR45 cause neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.

Before a cell commits to mitosis it must confirm that its DNA is intact and fully replicated, and the G2/M transition checkpoint is the surveillance step that holds it back when it is not. Delay here gives time for repair; loss of the restraint lets cells enter mitosis with broken or unreplicated chromosomes, producing missegregation, genome instability and the mutator phenotype typical of cancer. Damage is sensed by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and the RAD17-loaded clamp, which activate the ATM and ATR kinases; ATR signals through TOPBP1, ETAA1 and claspin to CHEK1, while p21 and inhibitory control of CDK1 and PLK1 block mitotic entry. BRCA1 with BARD1 and the BRCC36-containing deubiquitinase module couples ubiquitin signalling at damage sites to the same arrest. Checkpoint recovery requires reversing these marks, linking the pathway to DNA repair and replication origin licensing.

mitotic G1/S transition checkpoint signaling is the surveillance step that decides whether a cell in G1 is fit to begin copying its DNA, and blocks entry into S phase when it is not. It is the main guard against replicating a damaged genome, and its loss is one of the commonest routes to unchecked proliferation in cancer. The core logic runs through p53 induction of the CDK inhibitor p21, which restrains cyclin E/CDK2 and holds the retinoblastoma pathway in its repressive state; parallel inputs degrade cyclin D1 through the ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor FBXO31 and signal damage via PLK3, DNA-PK and the RPA-associated sensor RFWD3. Cytoplasmic nuclease activity such as TREX1 limits self-DNA accumulation that would otherwise trigger the response. Arrest here allows repair, or commits the cell to senescence or apoptosis rather than division.

Before a cell commits to replicating its genome it must confirm that conditions are suitable, and the G1/S transition checkpoint is the brake that holds it in G1 when they are not. Loss of this restraint allows damaged or under-resourced cells to enter S phase, propagating mutations and driving transformation, which is why several of its components are tumour suppressors and its bypass is a hallmark of cancer. The core logic couples DNA damage sensing to cyclin-dependent kinase inhibition: p53 induces the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, which blocks cyclin D1-CDK and CDK2 activity and prevents origin firing, while replication protein A subunits and RFWD3 report single-stranded DNA and help route the response. Additional regulators direct destruction of cyclin D1 and modulate apoptotic commitment, so the checkpoint decides not only whether to pause but whether to die.

Host cells do not passively host viral replication; they actively interfere with it, and this pathway covers the host-side activities that alter or subvert replication of an incoming viral genome. It matters because the outcome determines whether an infection is contained or proceeds to productive replication, and because many of the same host factors are hijacked by viruses rather than merely opposing them. The genes point to membrane and lipid biology at replication sites: VAPA and VAPB tether ER membranes to other organelles, ZFYVE1 and PIK3C3 read and generate phosphoinositides that shape autophagic and endosomal membranes, and TBC1D20 regulates Rab1-dependent ER traffic. Others act on the viral template and its proteins, including the RNA helicase YTHDC2, the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase PPIB, the translation factor EEF1A1, and the interferon-inducible IFI27. Together they place antiviral restriction within membrane remodelling, protein folding and RNA metabolism.

Cells carry an intrinsic arsenal aimed at stopping an invading virus from copying its genome, and this host-mediated suppression of viral replication is what limits infection before, and alongside, the adaptive immune response. Its members act by distinct chemistries rather than one shared cascade: a cytidine deaminase of the APOBEC3 family mutates viral single-stranded DNA during reverse transcription; the SMC5/6 complex recognises and silences episomal viral DNA such as hepatitis B covalently closed circular DNA; a kinase that senses amino acid scarcity shuts down translation initiation to starve viral protein synthesis; a ribonuclease degrades viral and inflammatory transcripts; microRNAs and ER-associated VAP proteins constrain replication-organelle formation and viral RNA synthesis. Loss or viral antagonism of these factors, as when HBx degrades the SMC5/6 complex, permits persistent infection, and the same restriction machinery shapes which viruses can cross between hosts.

Viruses with RNA genomes replicate inside host membranes and depend on host proteins for almost every step, so the host cell is never a passive substrate: it can obstruct, redirect or inadvertently enable genome copying. This collection of host-mediated interference with viral RNA genome replication brings together factors that act at the membrane compartments where replication complexes are built and at the RNA itself. TMEM41B and VAPB shape endoplasmic reticulum membranes and lipid transfer at contact sites, the setting in which flavivirus and coronavirus replication organelles form; DDX56 is an RNA helicase, FMR1 an RNA-binding protein, and PHB1 a mitochondrial and membrane scaffold, while FBXL2 supplies substrate recognition to a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase that can direct viral or host proteins for degradation. The outcome determines viral yield and shapes which cells are permissive to infection, making these proteins candidate points of antiviral intervention.

When a dividing cell pinches itself in two, it does so with a transient belt of actin filaments and myosin beneath the equatorial membrane; organization of this actomyosin contractile ring covers its assembly, positioning, constriction and eventual disassembly. Without it cytokinesis fails, producing binucleate and aneuploid progeny, and the same machinery is repurposed for cell shape change and wound closure. Positional information comes from central spindle signalling: a RhoGEF and a Rho-family GAP act as a centralspindlin-associated module that concentrates active RhoA at the equator, while anillin and IQGAP scaffolds crosslink actin, myosin and septins to the plasma membrane and rhotekin reads out Rho activity. Late steps overlap with membrane remodelling and abscission, where ESCRT-associated components including ALIX and a VPS4 ATPase resolve the intercellular bridge. Plectin links the contractile apparatus to the wider cytoskeleton.

Entry into mitosis from G2 is a switch-like commitment step, and this pathway covers both the machinery that throws the switch and the surveillance that holds it shut. Its core is cyclin B-CDK1, kept inactive by the inhibitory kinases WEE1 and PKMYT1 and activated when CDC25 phosphatases remove those phosphates; a counteracting arm in which MASTL phosphorylates ARPP19/ENSA to restrain PP2A locks the transition in once begun, with AURKA and PLK1 driving centrosome maturation and mitotic entry. Much of the remainder is the G2/M DNA damage checkpoint: ATM and ATR, activated at breaks and stalled forks through MRE11-RAD50-NBN, TOPBP1 and claspin, signal via CHEK1/CHEK2 and p53-p21 to delay division until repair is complete. Losing this restraint lets cells divide with broken or unreplicated chromosomes, generating aneuploidy and genomic instability characteristic of cancer, which is why WEE1 and CHK1 inhibitors are pursued therapeutically.

The G1/S transition is the point at which a cell stops responding to growth signals and commits irreversibly to duplicating its genome, and it is the decision most often subverted in cancer. Cyclin D partners with CDK4 and CDK6 to phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein, releasing E2F transcription factors with their DP partners so that replication genes including CDC6, CDC7-DBF4, POLE and the ribonucleotide reductase subunits are switched on; cyclin E-CDK2 then completes the switch. Restraint comes from the INK4 and CIP/KIP inhibitors, from p53-driven induction of p21 after DNA damage, and from SCF-type cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases with the proteasome that time the destruction of inhibitors and regulators. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, MYC, mTORC1-linked translational control, Hippo kinases and numerous microRNAs tune where the threshold sits. Loss of this control produces unscheduled proliferation and genomic instability.

biological phase covers the timed stages that cyclical developmental programs pass through, and here the genes point to the hair follicle cycle and the epidermal appendage patterning that depends on it. Follicles alternate between growth, regression and rest, and the switch between those stages determines hair density, wound-associated regeneration and the barrier properties of skin; mutations in these components cause hair loss, palmoplantar keratoderma and skin fragility syndromes. WNT ligands with beta-catenin drive the growth phase and specify placode fate, TGFB2 signals the transition into regression, and MSX2 acts in the transcriptional program of the follicle matrix. Adhesion and cytoskeletal linkage through P-cadherin and kindlin-1 hold the specialised epithelium together, while SPINK5 restrains protease activity in the differentiating layers. Together they illustrate how phase transitions in a tissue are enforced by coupling signalling to adhesion.

Many developmental programmes run as discrete stages rather than continuously, and this set captures the regulators that define and time such a biological phase — most recognisably the cyclical phases of the hair follicle, whose growth, regression and rest periods repeat throughout life. Wnt ligands such as WNT10B and WNT5A acting through beta-catenin drive the growth phase and follicular induction, while TGFB2 signalling pushes follicles into regression, and the transcription factor MSX2 sets the timing of hair shaft differentiation. Adhesion and structural components, including P-cadherin and the focal adhesion protein encoded by FERMT1, hold the epithelial compartments together during these transitions; the protease inhibitor SPINK5 restrains proteolysis in overlying epidermis. Mutations in these genes cause hair loss and hypotrichosis, skin fragility syndromes, and Netherton syndrome, showing how stage boundaries, once mistimed, disrupt whole tissues.

The estrous cycle is the recurring ovulation cycle of most therian mammals, in which the uterine lining is reabsorbed rather than shed when fertilisation fails, coordinating follicle maturation, receptivity and mating behaviour with ovarian steroid output. Genes here span the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and its downstream tissue remodelling: GnRH drives gonadotropin release that times follicular development and ovulation, while nuclear receptor coregulators such as NCOA1 and NCOR2 set how strongly estrogen and progesterone receptors activate or repress target transcription in uterus, ovary and brain. Immediate-early transcription factors, PCNA-marked proliferation, and hyaluronan synthesis by HAS2 reflect the cyclical waves of endometrial and cumulus matrix growth, and opioid signalling contributes to behavioural and neuroendocrine feedback. Disruption of this timing produces acyclicity, failed ovulation and infertility, and underlies models of reproductive ageing and endocrine disruption.

Plasma membrane rafts are cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains that concentrate receptors, channels and signalling enzymes into discrete platforms, and this pathway covers how such domains are built and held together. Their assembly determines where signals are initiated at the cell surface, supports caveola formation and clathrin-independent endocytosis, and contributes to mechanosensing in endothelium and muscle; loss of the caveolin scaffolds causes muscular dystrophy and cardiomyopathy and disturbs nitric oxide and lipid handling. The caveolins oligomerize in the membrane to drive invagination, flotillin marks a separate raft population, and PACSIN2 provides membrane-bending and cytoskeletal coupling. Integrin-linked kinase, IQGAP1 and extracellular matrix contacts tie raft organization to the actin cytoskeleton and adhesion, so domain formation is coordinated with cell shape rather than being a purely lipid-driven event.

Cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains in the plasma membrane concentrate receptors and signalling molecules into discrete platforms, and this pathway covers their assembly, arrangement and disassembly. Raft and caveolar organization determines where growth factor, integrin and immune receptors can cluster, sets the sites of caveola-mediated endocytosis and cholesterol efflux, and shapes membrane mechanics in muscle and endothelium. The caveolin family provides the scaffold that invaginates raft membrane, flotillin and the membrane-sculpting protein PACSIN2 contribute to domain curvature and trafficking, and EMP2 and ILK link domains to integrin-based adhesion and the underlying cytoskeleton alongside IQGAP1. Lipid supply matters too: FA2H hydroxylates sphingolipid fatty acids and ABCA7 moves cholesterol and phospholipid, altering domain composition. Loss of caveolin function causes muscular dystrophy, cardiomyopathy and lipodystrophy, illustrating how much cell signalling depends on membrane sub-compartmentalization.

Cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains in the plasma membrane concentrate particular proteins into signalling and transport platforms, and this pathway covers the delivery of proteins to those rafts and their retention there. Where a receptor or pump sits laterally in the membrane determines which partners it meets, so raft targeting shapes signal output, ion transport and membrane organisation rather than merely protein abundance. The genes involved include the principal scaffolds of such domains: caveolin-1, which builds caveolae, and flotillin-2, a marker of non-caveolar rafts, alongside MYADM, which influences membrane domain organisation and cell polarity, the Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunit ATP1B1, the GPI-anchored kidney protein uromodulin and the IgLON adhesion molecule NEGR1. Loss of raft partitioning disrupts caveola-dependent endocytosis, mechanosensing and the localised assembly of adhesion and signalling complexes.

Lipoprotein localization covers the routing of lipoproteins from the cells that build them to the tissues that consume them, the step that turns dietary and hepatic lipid into circulating cholesterol and triglyceride. It sets plasma lipid levels, and its failure produces abetalipoproteinemia, chylomicron retention disease and, at the receptor end, defective clearance and atherosclerosis. Assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum requires apolipoprotein B, the lipid transfer activity of MTTP, and cargo receptors such as SURF4 that load particles into COPII vesicles budded by SAR1A/SAR1B and the large-cargo TANGO1 machinery. On the receiving side, LRP1, CD36, CUBN and the scavenger receptor MSR1 capture particles for endocytosis, while PPARG and RXRA set the transcriptional tone and several microRNAs tune apolipoprotein output. Palmitoyltransferases and lipid-binding proteins support trafficking through membranes, linking secretory vesicle transport to whole-body lipid distribution.

Lipoprotein localization covers the steps that put lipoproteins where they must be: assembled and loaded in the endoplasmic reticulum, packaged into secretory carriers for export from liver and intestine, and captured at the surface of target cells for uptake. This traffic is how dietary and hepatic lipid is distributed to peripheral tissues, and its failure produces abetalipoproteinaemia and chylomicron retention disease, fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, or conversely the retention of atherogenic particles in the artery wall. Apolipoprotein B is edited by a cytidine deaminase to generate the intestinal isoform, lipidated by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, and loaded into large COPII carriers requiring SAR1B, TANGO1 and the cargo receptor SURF4. At the receiving end, LRP1, CD36, cubilin and a scavenger receptor mediate binding and endocytosis, with nuclear receptors and microRNAs setting the expression of the machinery.

When a double-strand break falls between two direct repeats, cells can rejoin it by chewing back the 5' ends until the complementary repeat sequences are exposed, letting them pair, and trimming away the flaps. Single-strand annealing repairs the break at a price: the unique DNA between the repeats is deleted, so this route is inherently mutagenic and contributes to the repeat-mediated rearrangements and copy-number losses seen in tumours. RAD52 is the annealing factor that brings the resected complementary strands together, CtIP works with nuclease activity at the break ends to generate the 3' single-stranded tails, and the SLX4 scaffold with its SLX1 nuclease partners removes the resulting non-homologous 3' overhangs. The pathway operates alongside homologous recombination and end joining as one of the competing choices made at a resected break.

Synthesis-dependent strand annealing is the homologous recombination route that mends a double-strand break without swapping flanking sequence, so a somatic cell can copy information from an intact homologue and return to a normal chromosome rather than a crossover product. This bias toward non-crossover repair keeps mitotic genomes free of loss of heterozygosity and translocations, and its failure underlies chromosome instability, Fanconi-type phenotypes and cancer predisposition. A resected 3' end loaded with RAD51, assisted by the RAD51 paralogues RAD51C and XRCC3 and by the SWI5-SFR1 and RAD54L activities, invades homologous duplex DNA; the extended nascent strand is then unwound from the template and annealed to the other broken end, with RAD52 supporting annealing and helicase activities such as FANCM and HELQ promoting displacement. Related components also serve meiotic recombination.

Accurate copying of the genome depends not only on polymerase selectivity but on a large apparatus that protects replication forks when they stall or collide with damage. Maintaining fidelity during DNA-templated replication is what keeps mutation rates low and prevents the chromosome rearrangements, gross deletions and aneuploidy that drive cancer and premature ageing syndromes. The genes here cover replicative polymerases and their sliding clamp, the checkpoint kinase ATR with its activators, fork remodellers and translocases such as SMARCAL1, HLTF and ZRANB3, helicases of the RecQ family including BLM and WRN, and the homologous recombination machinery centred on BRCA1, BRCA2 and RAD51 that restarts broken forks. Nuclease complexes resolve stalled or reversed structures, while replisome protection factors prevent uncontrolled nucleolytic degradation of nascent strands. Loss of individual members underlies Bloom and Werner syndromes, Fanconi-like disorders and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.

Stripping the amino group from a cytosine in DNA converts it to uracil, and cells use this deliberate chemical lesion as a weapon and as a source of diversity. DNA deamination by the AID/APOBEC family underlies antibody maturation — AICDA acting on immunoglobulin loci to initiate somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination — and innate restriction of retroviruses and retroelements, where APOBEC3G and its paralogues hypermutate reverse-transcribed viral single-stranded DNA. The resulting uracils are read out by base excision repair and mismatch repair, so the mutagenic outcome depends on how the lesion is processed. Misdirected activity is a major endogenous mutation source in cancer, producing the characteristic APOBEC mutational signatures and contributing to lymphoma-associated translocations. RNA exosome subunits are included because the exosome helps expose transcribed single-stranded DNA substrates to the deaminase during switch recombination.

Depyrimidination is the first step of base excision repair acting on damaged or mispaired cytosine and thymine: a DNA glycosylase cleaves the N-glycosidic bond and releases the offending pyrimidine, leaving an abasic sugar for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps to restore. This removal is how cells cope with spontaneous cytosine deamination, oxidative pyrimidine lesions such as thymine glycol, and alkylation damage; failure raises mutation rates at CpG sites and contributes to cancer predisposition, as seen with germline defects in NTHL1 and MBD4. The genes are the pyrimidine-directed glycosylases: uracil-specific UNG and SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 acting on G:U and G:T mismatches at methylated CpGs, and NTHL1 with NEIL1 and NEIL2 handling ring-fragmented oxidation products. TDG additionally excises oxidised 5-methylcytosine derivatives, linking this repair chemistry to active DNA demethylation and epigenetic reprogramming.

Cytosine and thymine in DNA are chemically fragile: they deaminate, oxidise and pick up alkyl groups, and a mispaired or damaged pyrimidine left in place becomes a mutation at the next round of replication. Depyrimidination is the excision step that prevents this, cleaving the N-glycosidic bond between deoxyribose and a damaged or inappropriate C or T base and leaving an abasic sugar for downstream processing. The glycosylases here cover complementary substrate ranges — uracil arising from cytosine deamination or misincorporation, thymine mispaired with guanine at deaminated methylcytosine, and oxidised or ring-fragmented pyrimidines such as thymine glycol and hydantoins. The resulting abasic site is incised and repaired by the rest of the base excision repair route, so this chemistry is the entry point to that pathway. Loss of these activities raises spontaneous mutation rates; MBD4 and TDG additionally link repair to CpG methylation and epigenetic turnover.

actin nucleation is the rate-limiting birth of new actin filaments, the step that decides where and when a cell builds fresh cytoskeleton. Because filament elongation is fast but spontaneous seed formation is not, nucleators control lamellipodial protrusion, cell migration, endocytosis, phagocytosis, membrane tubule scission and sarcomere assembly; their loss produces immunodeficiency, nemaline myopathy and neurodevelopmental disease. The core machinery here is the seven-subunit Arp2/3 complex, whose actin-related subunits mimic a filament barbed end, together with the WAVE regulatory complex and WASH, WHAMM and JMY activators that recruit it to plasma membrane, endosomes and Golgi. Formins and Spire-family and leiomodin proteins nucleate unbranched filaments instead, while arpin, GMF, coronins, gelsolin and CARMIL proteins impose negative regulation and turnover, so that nucleation is spatially restricted and reversible rather than continuous.

Building a new actin filament from scratch is kinetically the hardest part of making one, and actin nucleation is the step that overcomes it: monomers are gathered into a stable seed from which rapid elongation follows. Cells depend on it for lamellipodial protrusion and migration, endocytosis, phagocytosis, junction assembly, sarcomere thin-filament length control and the fission of endosomal and Golgi membranes. The core machinery here is the Arp2/3 complex with its ARPC subunits, switched on by WAVE-family and WASH complex nucleation-promoting factors together with JMY and WHAMM, and restrained by ARPIN, coronins and GMF. Formins and the Spire proteins nucleate by a separate, profilin-linked route, while leiomodins seed thin filaments in muscle and gelsolin, scinderin and capping regulators such as the CARMILs set how many filament ends are available. Loss of these activities impairs immune cell motility, vesicle traffic and myofibril integrity, as in nemaline myopathy.

Glycerolipid biosynthesis builds every lipid that carries a glycerol backbone, from the triacylglycerols stored in adipose and liver droplets to the phospholipids that form all cellular membranes. It supplies the bilayer material needed for growth, division and organelle expansion, and its dysregulation produces hepatic steatosis, lipodystrophy and insulin resistance. Acyl-CoA synthetases and successive acyltransferases build phosphatidic acid from glycerol-3-phosphate; phosphatidate phosphatases of the lipin family and diacylglycerol kinases set the balance between diacylglycerol and phosphatidic acid, committing flux either to storage triglyceride via DGAT enzymes or to headgroup addition through the CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine routes, cardiolipin and phosphatidylserine synthesis. A large phosphoinositide arm — PI kinases, phosphatases such as PTEN, OCRL and the myotubularins, and the GPI-anchor assembly machinery — converts the same backbone into membrane signalling lipids and protein anchors, with transcriptional input from SREBP and liver X receptors.

Nitric oxide is a potent vasodilator and immune effector, and damping its synthesis keeps that signal brief and local; without restraint, sustained NO output drives hypotension, nitrosative stress and tissue injury during inflammation. This negative regulation of nitric oxide biosynthesis acts at several levels. Caveolin-1 sequesters and inhibits endothelial NO synthase at the plasma membrane, and calcium handling by ATP2B4 limits the calcium rise that activates the constitutive synthases. Transcriptional and post-transcriptional brakes operate on inducible NOS in macrophages: interleukin-10 suppresses its induction, while RNA-binding and ribonuclease activities of KHSRP and ZC3H12A, together with microRNAs, destabilise the transcript. Receptor-level input from opioid, sigma-1 and SIRPA signalling, and substrate availability, provide further tuning. The result is control over vascular tone, platelet behaviour and the balance between microbial killing and collateral damage in innate immunity.

Quiescent cells are not simply resting: re-entry into the cell cycle from G0 into G1 is a controlled decision that underlies wound healing, lymphocyte activation, liver regeneration and stem cell mobilisation, and its deregulation permits tumour cells to proliferate without appropriate stimulation. The transition demands a wholesale change in gene expression, and much of the gene list is the SWI/SNF ATP-dependent chromatin remodelling machinery — the SMARCA2/SMARCA4 ATPases with SMARCB1, ARID1A/ARID1B or PBRM1, and accessory BCL7 and DPF subunits — which repositions nucleosomes to open growth-responsive promoters. Alongside it sit cyclin C with CDK3, a kinase pair implicated specifically in exit from quiescence, the CDK inhibitor CDKN2B and the DREAM-associated repressor LIN37 that hold cells back, and ribonucleotide reductase subunits that prepare nucleotide pools for the DNA synthesis to come.

Two cells become one only rarely in development, and this pathway covers those events: the merging of plasma membranes between separate cells. Most of the machinery here serves fertilization, where a capacitated sperm binds and fuses with the oocyte. Sperm-surface factors including IZUMO1, SPACA6, TMEM95 and DCST1/DCST2 act with the egg receptor JUNO (IZUMO1R) and the tetraspanin CD9 on the oolemma; loss of any of the core sperm components blocks fusion and causes male infertility despite normal binding. A second arm governs muscle formation, where myomaker (MYMK) and myomerger (MYMX) drive myoblasts to fuse into multinucleated myofibres, and MYMK mutations underlie a congenital myopathy with facial weakness. Accessory acrosomal hydrolases, sperm-coating proteins and trafficking factors support the membrane remodelling and adhesion steps that precede bilayer merger.

Nearly every protein of the mitochondrial inner membrane is made elsewhere, so respiration depends on machinery that delivers hydrophobic carriers and subunits into the lipid bilayer and threads them to the correct topology. Insertion into the inner membrane happens by several routes: small chaperones of the intermembrane space escort hydrophobic precursors to the carrier translocase TIMM22, while OXA1L and its relative COX18 insert proteins from the matrix side, including mitochondrially encoded respiratory chain subunits. Assembly factors such as BCS1L and NDUFA13 link the process to building of the respiratory complexes themselves. Failure here causes mitochondrial disease: mutations in the TIMM8A escort gene cause deafness-dystonia syndrome, AGK deficiency underlies Sengers syndrome, and TMEM126A loss causes optic atrophy, reflecting how heavily neurons and muscle depend on correctly populated inner membranes for oxidative phosphorylation.

Peroxisomes are built rather than inherited fully formed, and inserting proteins into the peroxisomal membrane is the step that creates the organelle's boundary and the import machinery embedded in it. This route is distinct from matrix protein import: membrane proteins carry their own targeting signals, are captured in the cytosol by the soluble receptor and chaperone PEX19, and are delivered to the membrane anchor PEX3, with PEX16 required for insertion and for generating peroxisomes from the endoplasmic reticulum. PEX26 tethers the AAA-ATPase complex that recycles the matrix receptor PEX5, linking membrane assembly to cargo import. Without functional membrane biogenesis, cells lack peroxisomes altogether, and mutations in these genes cause Zellweger spectrum disorders, in which failure of fatty acid beta-oxidation and ether lipid synthesis produces severe neurological and hepatic disease.

Membrane proteins only work if they end up in the bilayer with the right number of spans facing the right way, and this is the machinery that inserts them into the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and sets that topology. Topogenic signals in the substrate are read by distinct routes: the Sec61 translocon channel handles co-translational insertion of signal-anchored and multipass proteins, the EMC complex inserts marginally hydrophobic and reversed-topology helices and acts as an insertase for tail-anchored clients, and a post-translational route built around GET3 with its GET1/CAMLG receptor and the BAG6-SGTA-UBL4A-GET4 targeting complex delivers tail-anchored proteins while triaging failures for degradation. Accessory factors including CCDC47, TMCO1, the nicalin-NOMO-TMEM147 assembly and TRAM proteins assist multipass folding and assembly. Loss of these components causes misfolded, mislocalised receptors and channels, and underlies congenital disorders affecting brain, heart and eye development.

Membrane proteins that are translocated into the endoplasmic reticulum must stop partway and leave a hydrophobic segment behind in the lipid bilayer; this is how a stop-transfer membrane-anchor sequence becomes a stable ER membrane-spanning helix. The pathway explains how type I and multipass membrane proteins acquire their correct topology as they are made, and failure of it leaves marginally hydrophobic anchors unable to partition into the bilayer, so nascent clients are degraded rather than folded. Almost all the components here are subunits of the ER membrane protein complex, a multi-subunit insertase that works alongside the main translocon, providing a hydrophilic vestibule that lowers the energetic cost of inserting weak transmembrane segments and acting as a chaperone for their assembly. Loss of these subunits reduces the levels of many receptors, transporters and channels, linking co-translational insertion to secretory pathway capacity and ER protein quality control.

Golgi-resident enzymes and membrane proteins must be held in the stack rather than swept forward to the cell surface, and protein retention in the Golgi apparatus is the set of activities that keeps them there. Glycosylation depends on it: the carbohydrate-modifying enzymes of the Golgi have a short cytosolic tail, one transmembrane helix, and a luminal catalytic domain, and if they escape to the plasma membrane the ordered sequence of sugar additions along the cis-to-trans axis breaks down.
