Its main consequence is pathway choice: by blocking resection and homologous recombination, the shieldin complex with 53BP1, RIF1 and MAD2L2 channels double-strand breaks into end joining, which preserves genome stability in some contexts and causes mutagenic repair in others. Related mechanisms include anti-recombinase helicase activity from RECQL5, FBH1, HELB and RADX that strips or displaces RAD51 from single-stranded DNA, ubiquitin- and chromatin-based signalling through RNF169, OTUB1 and KMT5A that curtails repair factor accumulation at damage sites, and cGAS, which also dampens repair. The same restraint explains why BRCA-mutant tumours regain recombination and resistance to PARP inhibitors when shieldin components are lost.

Damage-response factors that raise the efficiency of DNA repair rather than carrying out the chemistry themselves are grouped here, and they determine whether a break is repaired accurately, repaired badly, or left to kill the cell. Much of the activity is chromatin work: SWI/SNF and INO80 remodelling complexes, the NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase module with RUVBL1/RUVBL2, and histone methyltransferases open damaged sites so that repair enzymes can load. A parallel arm is signalling and ubiquitin marking, with ATM and DNA-PK kinases, H2AX phosphorylation, RNF8 and RNF168 ligases, and the BRCA1-A complex concentrating repair factors at breaks. Additional members bias pathway choice, including shieldin subunits and RIF1 that favour end joining over homologous recombination, plus MRE11-RAD50-NBN end processing. Loss of these amplifying steps produces genome instability, cancer predisposition and hypersensitivity to radiation and crosslinking agents.

Cells only duplicate their genome when licensed to do so, and this collection covers the activating inputs that raise the rate and extent of DNA replication. It spans the origin-licensing and firing machinery — CDT1 loading, the CDC7–DBF4 kinase pair, CDK2 and CDK1 with the phosphatase CDC25A that removes inhibitory phosphates — together with chromatin remodellers and histone acetyltransferase components such as SMARCA5, INO80 and KAT7 that make origins accessible. Mitogenic receptor signalling through EGFR and FGFR1, and developmental cues via GLI factors, feed into S-phase entry, while PCNA, DNA2 and ATAD5 act at the fork itself. Telomere-associated CTC1 and STN1 support replication of chromosome ends. Notably, CDKN1A, CDKN1B and WEE1 appear as restraints whose modulation tunes the same decision. Deregulated activation here drives the unscheduled proliferation and replication stress characteristic of tumours.

Fibroblast growth factors drive limb and skeletal patterning, branching morphogenesis, wound repair and angiogenesis, but only when their receptors are efficiently engaged; this set covers the processes that raise the frequency or strength of fibroblast growth factor receptor signalling. Several members act by increasing ligand availability rather than by transducing the signal: the FGF-binding proteins FGFBP1 and FGFBP3 release FGFs sequestered on heparan sulfate in the extracellular matrix so they can reach their receptors, and the matricellular protein SMOC2 potentiates receptor-driven mitogenic responses. Others couple receptor activity to adhesion and downstream kinases, including integrin beta-1, the kinase DSTYK and protein kinase D2, while beta-catenin ties the pathway into Wnt-dependent transcriptional output. Because dosage matters here, amplified signalling promotes tumour proliferation and neovascularisation, whereas insufficient signalling causes skeletal and renal developmental defects.

G protein-coupled receptors must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this collection of dampening mechanisms sets how long and how strongly a cell responds to hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines and light. Without it, receptors signal persistently, producing desensitization failure, runaway second messenger accumulation and loss of the sharp temporal responses that vision, cardiac output and chemotaxis depend on. Several strategies converge here: GRK kinases phosphorylate agonist-occupied receptors so that arrestins (including the visual arrestins) uncouple them from G proteins and route them to internalization; RGS proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis on G alpha subunits to shorten signalling bursts; phosphodiesterases degrade cAMP and cGMP downstream; and inverse agonists or antagonist peptides such as agouti-related protein block receptor occupancy itself. Accessory factors like MRAP2 and GPRASP1 further tune receptor trafficking and availability, linking this negative control to energy balance and neuronal signalling.

Cells read hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines and sensory stimuli through G protein-coupled receptors, and this grouping collects the influences that raise the gain of that signalling rather than transmit it. Enhancement can happen at any step: agonist supply and processing, as with proopiomelanocortin-derived peptides, gastrin-releasing peptide, endothelin-1 and complement- or kallikrein-generated ligands; receptor trafficking and accessory proteins, including the melanocortin receptor accessory proteins that license MC2R responsiveness and caveolar and retromer components that position receptors; and downstream amplification through phosphodiesterase subunits, protein kinase C and regulators of G protein signalling. Positive regulation of this kind sets tissue sensitivity to dopamine, estrogen-like and prostanoid signals, adrenal stress hormone output, platelet and vascular reactivity, and neuronal excitability. Because receptor sensitivity is the main pharmacological handle on these pathways, its dysregulation contributes to hypertension, inflammatory disease and neurodegeneration, the latter reflected by LRRK2, APP and TREM2 here.

Notch signalling decides cell fates by direct contact, and it must be damped as often as it is fired; this collection covers the processes that stop or reduce Notch output. Restraint matters because persistent Notch activity keeps progenitors undifferentiated and is oncogenic in T-cell leukaemia, while insufficient signalling disrupts somite patterning, arterial specification and neurogenesis. The brakes act at several levels: cis-inhibitory and non-canonical ligands such as DLL3 and DLK1 block receptor activation, glycosylation and trafficking steps set ligand and receptor competence, the ubiquitin ligase FBXW7 targets activated Notch for proteasomal degradation, and HEY1, HEY2 and NRARP act as transcriptional feedback repressors of the target-gene programme. Additional layers include microRNAs of the miR-200 family, m6A readers and writers, and nuclear corepressors that limit CSL-dependent transcription, together tuning how long and how strongly a cell responds to a neighbour's Notch ligand.

Notch signalling decides cell fates between neighbours, and this collection covers the inputs that turn its output up rather than down. Amplified Notch activity keeps progenitors undifferentiated in the nervous system and gut, specifies arterial versus venous identity in endothelium, and patterns tip and stalk cells during sprouting angiogenesis; too much or too little produces vascular malformations, skeletal and cardiac defects, and lineage-inappropriate differentiation. Enhancement acts at several levels: ligands such as DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 and JAG2 engage the receptor; fringe glycosyltransferases and the O-glucosyltransferase POGLUT1 modify receptor EGF repeats to bias ligand preference; tetraspanins TSPAN5 and TSPAN14 promote ADAM10-dependent cleavage; and endocytic kinases and epsins provide the pulling force ligands need. Downstream, HES1 and HES5 execute repression, while ZMIZ1 and YAP1 reinforce transcription. Human-specific NOTCH2NL paralogues extend the same amplification to cortical progenitor expansion.

Excitable cells must be restrained as well as excited, and negative regulation of action potential covers the processes that damp firing rate, block propagation, or raise the threshold for spike generation. It matters because unchecked excitability produces seizures, arrhythmia and pain sensitisation, so this braking arm sets the operating range of neurons and cardiomyocytes. Most of the control acts on voltage-gated and related channels: HCN1 carries the hyperpolarization-activated pacemaker current that shapes rhythmic firing and dendritic integration, SUMO1-dependent modification alters channel gating and surface availability, and BIN1 organises membrane microdomains and channel trafficking in cardiac and muscle T-tubules. Receptor-level input also contributes, with presynaptic nicotinic and cannabinoid CB2 signalling tuning transmitter release and excitability. Together these mechanisms represent inhibitory and modulatory limits on electrical signalling rather than the depolarizing machinery itself.

Excitable cells fire action potentials, and this grouping covers the influences that make them fire more readily, more often, or for longer. Such tuning sets heart rate and conduction, pain sensitivity, and the excitability of neurons and muscle; when it runs unchecked it produces arrhythmia, hyperalgesia and seizure-like hyperexcitability. Most of the effect is exerted on voltage-gated and other cation channels: the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A carries the depolarizing upstroke in working myocardium, while the calcium-activated cation channel TRPM4 and the sodium-proton exchanger SLC9A1 shape resting potential and intracellular pH and sodium load. Upstream of these, neuropeptide and adrenergic signalling acts through receptors such as TACR1, the substance P receptor, and the alpha-1A adrenoceptor, and inflammatory mediators including TNF sensitize nociceptors, linking tissue injury and autonomic drive to increased firing.

regulation of adenylate cyclase activity governs how much cyclic AMP a cell makes, and therefore how strongly it responds to hormones and neurotransmitters that work through this second messenger. cAMP output sets heart rate and contractility, water reabsorption in the kidney, insulin release from beta cells, and the strength of synaptic signalling, so its tuning is the point at which many drugs act. The genes describe both directions of control: stimulatory receptors for peptide hormones and neuropeptides such as the vasopressin, GLP-1, GIP and CRH receptors acting through Gs, opposed by adenosine, chemokine, GABA-B, metabotropic glutamate and galanin receptors coupling through inhibitory Gi subunits. Additional layers come from calcium, supplied by voltage-gated channels and by STIM1-ORAI1 store-operated entry, from cyclase-associated proteins, and from AKAP scaffolds that place the enzyme next to its targets.

Adenylate cyclase sets the intracellular level of cyclic AMP, the second messenger that drives protein kinase A and thereby hormone responses, neuronal excitability, secretion and metabolic switching, so control over the enzyme's activity is control over how strongly a cell answers an extracellular signal. Much of this regulation is exerted by G protein-coupled receptors and their transducers: stimulatory and inhibitory G protein alpha subunits such as GNAS versus GNAI2 and GNAI3 push cyclase output in opposite directions, while receptors for adenosine, vasopressin, dopamine, endothelin, GABA, incretins including GLP1R and GIPR, and neuropeptides like ADCYAP1 and CALCA feed into them. Calcium provides a second input, through voltage-gated channels and the STIM1-ORAI1 store-operated route, and scaffolding by AKAP5 localises the resulting signal. Loss of balanced regulation underlies endocrine resistance syndromes and altered vascular and neuronal tone.

Growing axons must elongate over long distances to reach their targets, and this is the set of influences that push that elongation forward, increasing the rate and extent of axon extension. It underlies the wiring of the nervous system during development and the regrowth of injured nerves; when it fails, tracts are short or mistargeted, and several members are mutated in intellectual disability and epileptic encephalopathy, as with CDKL5. Diffusible and substrate cues act through receptors and guidance molecules such as netrin-1, NGF acting on Trk receptors, NRP1, L1CAM and semaphorins, converging on Rho-family effectors including PAK1 and LIMK1 to reorganise the growth cone cytoskeleton. Microtubule-associated proteins such as MAP1B, MAPT and MACF1, together with polarity and membrane-trafficking factors like shootin-1 and RUFY3, supply the structural elongation and forward delivery of membrane that sustain neurite outgrowth.

Arterial pressure is held within a narrow range by opposing sets of signals, and this is the depressor arm: the processes that lower vascular tone, promote natriuresis and diuresis, and blunt sympathetic drive. Its failure underlies hypertension and its sequelae, while excessive activity contributes to hypotension and shock. Vasodilator capacity is supplied largely by nitric oxide synthases acting on vascular smooth muscle, by natriuretic peptides ANP and BNP released from stretched cardiac atria, and by peptides such as adrenomedullin-related ligands, apelin, CGRP, bradykinin and substance P acting on their G protein-coupled receptors. Adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors, adenosine and neuropeptidergic inputs tune the balance centrally and in the kidney, potassium channels and gap junction connexins set smooth muscle excitability and conducted dilation, and Rho-GAP regulation of contractility links these signals to the cytoskeleton. Adipokines and PPARA connect metabolic state to vascular resistance.

Blood pressure is held within a narrow range by opposing regulatory arms, and this is the pressor side: the processes that raise vascular tone, cardiac output and extracellular fluid volume. It matters for standing up without fainting and for defending perfusion during haemorrhage, while chronic overactivity of the same machinery produces hypertension and its cardiac and renal sequelae. Vasoconstriction is driven through G protein-coupled receptors for catecholamines, vasopressin, oxytocin, tachykinins and thromboxane, converging on RhoA-dependent contraction of vascular smooth muscle. Angiotensin-converting enzyme and aldosterone synthase supply the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone limb, with renal sodium and water retention reinforced by vasopressin receptors and by WNK1 signalling to tubular ion transport; HSD11B2 protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol, and its loss causes severe salt-sensitive hypertension. Central neuropeptides and NADPH oxidase-derived oxidant signalling modulate the set point.

Bone is deposited when mesenchymal progenitors are pushed toward the osteoblast fate and existing matrix is mineralised, and this collection represents the signals that drive that process forward. Positive regulation of ossification governs skeletal growth, fracture healing and the maintenance of bone mass, and its inappropriate activation produces heterotopic bone in soft tissue and vascular calcification, as seen with gain-of-function ACVR1 mutations. Much of the drive comes from bone morphogenetic protein ligands acting through type I and type II serine/threonine kinase receptors and SMAD transcriptional effectors, reinforced by WNT ligands, FZD receptors and osteogenic transcription factors such as MEF2C, RUNX-associated cofactors and ZBTB16. Endocrine and mineral-handling inputs are represented too: parathyroid hormone, the vitamin D receptor, klotho, phosphate transport and calcium pumps, plus FAM20C-dependent phosphorylation of secreted matrix proteins that sets where crystal growth occurs.

Bone is continually broken down by osteoclasts, and this pathway covers the signals that drive that breakdown harder or faster. Positive regulation of bone resorption sets the balance against osteoblast bone formation; too much of it thins the skeleton, as in postmenopausal osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis and tumour-induced bone loss, while too little yields the dense, brittle bone of osteopetrosis. The central input is the RANKL ligand acting on its receptor RANK on osteoclast precursors, which licenses differentiation and, with integrin αvβ3 and the tyrosine kinase SYK, couples attachment of the cell to bone to formation of the sealing zone and ruffled border. Fusion factors such as DC-STAMP make the cells multinucleate, PLEKHM1 directs lysosomal trafficking of acid and protease cargo, and osteopontin supports matrix attachment. Endocrine and systemic modifiers, including FSH and melanocortin signalling, tie resorption to whole-body physiology.

Cells attach to each other and to extracellular matrix in a regulated way, and this collection covers the signals and effectors that increase such adhesion. Strengthening adhesion is what lets leukocytes arrest on inflamed endothelium and form stable contacts with antigen-presenting cells, what holds epithelial sheets and endothelial junctions intact, and what anchors migrating and differentiating cells to matrix during development, wound repair and tumour invasion. Mechanistically the genes span adhesion receptors and their ligands — integrins with talin- and kindlin-type activators, selectins, cadherin- and desmosome-associated proteins, junctional and immunoglobulin-family molecules — together with fibronectin, laminins and fibrinogen as substrates. Upstream, chemokines, cytokines, growth factors, MHC and costimulatory molecules feed through Src- and Syk-family kinases, PI3K, Rho/Rac/Cdc42 GTPases and their regulators to remodel actin and raise receptor affinity, while transcriptional and chromatin regulators set adhesive competence.

Cells divide only when conditions permit, and the braking machinery gathered here is what stops, delays or slows progression through the cell cycle. It underlies quiescence, differentiation, senescence and the tumour suppression that fails in cancer, and it protects genome integrity by halting division when DNA is damaged or chromosomes are unattached. Cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A, CDKN1B and CDKN2A restrain CDK-cyclin complexes, while RB1 and its relatives hold E2F-driven transcription in check until commitment to S phase. Damage sensing through ATM, ATR, CHEK1/CHEK2 and TP53 imposes checkpoint arrest and recruits repair factors including BRCA1, MRE11-RAD50-NBN and FANCD2. Spindle assembly checkpoint components including MAD2L1, BUB1B, BUB3 and the kinetochore NDC80 complex block anaphase-promoting complex activity until attachment is correct. Growth-inhibitory cues, Hippo kinases LATS1/LATS2, and numerous microRNAs add further restraint.

Cells divide only when growth signals, nutrient supply and checkpoint clearance all point the same way, and this collection covers the processes that push the cell cycle forward rather than restrain it. It matters for tissue growth, wound repair, lymphocyte expansion and germ cell production, and its inappropriate activation is a route to tumour growth. Mitogenic inputs through receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFR and the insulin/IGF receptors feed into AKT-mTOR translational control and into D- and E-type cyclins with CDK4 and CDK1, while CDC25 phosphatases remove inhibitory phosphorylation to license mitotic entry. The anaphase-promoting complex with CDC20 destroys cyclins and securin to trigger sister chromatid separation, and aurora kinases, PLK1, condensin subunits and kinetochore and dynein components execute spindle assembly and cytokinesis. Also present are drivers of meiotic entry and replication licensing, plus microRNAs and transcription factors that raise proliferative gene expression.

negative regulation of cell size covers the braking mechanisms that keep cells from growing too large, setting the balance between anabolic growth and restraint that determines organ size and cell mass. Its failure produces hypertrophy: enlarged cardiomyocytes and muscle fibres, overgrown neurons, and the tumour-prone tissue overgrowth seen when growth suppression is lost. Most of the genes converge on mTOR complex 1, the central sensor of nutrients and growth factor input. PTEN limits the PI3K signal that activates it, TSC1 restrains the small GTPase that switches it on, and PRAS40 and DEPTOR bind the complex directly as inhibitory subunits, damping ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis. Alongside these, cytoskeletal regulators such as RhoA and cofilin shape cell volume and geometry, while caveolin-3 restrains hypertrophic signalling at the muscle membrane. The pathway thus links metabolic sensing to cell growth control and tumour suppression.

Cells hold their size within limits, and the processes that push size back down are as much a part of growth control as the anabolic signals they oppose. Negative regulation of cell size is largely the restraint arm of nutrient and growth-factor signalling: the TSC1 complex and the lipid phosphatase PTEN act upstream of mTOR to limit ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis, while PRAS40 and DEPTOR bind and dampen mTOR complex 1 directly. Loss of these brakes produces overgrowth and hypertrophy, and underlies tuberous sclerosis and PTEN-related overgrowth syndromes as well as pathological cardiac and skeletal muscle enlargement. Cytoskeletal and membrane components contribute too: cofilin severs actin filaments, RhoA shapes cortical tension, and caveolin-3 organises muscle membrane domains that set myocyte growth, with urocortin signalling providing hormonal input to cardiomyocyte size.

Cells enlarge when growth signalling outpaces division, and this is the set of activities that push cell size upward. Such control determines organ mass in tissues where cells hypertrophy rather than proliferate — cardiac and skeletal muscle, kidney podocytes, neurons — and its loss or excess shows up as atrophy on one side and pathological hypertrophy on the other. The genes here span the inputs and the machinery: AKT3 relays phosphoinositide signalling toward anabolic growth, RET and the peptide endothelin-1 act as extracellular growth cues, MAP3K7 and PRKD1 carry stress- and diacylglycerol-linked kinase signals, and RB1CC1 links the programme to autophagy and ribosome biogenesis, where the balance of protein synthesis against degradation is actually set. AMOT ties in Hippo-pathway control of cell and tissue dimensions, placing cell size regulation alongside proliferation control in the sizing of organs.

Cells that swell must be able to shrink again, and the negative regulation of cell volume describes the processes that reduce cell volume by driving osmotically active solutes out across the plasma membrane. Water follows the loss of chloride and potassium, so volume-sensitive anion channels and calcium-activated potassium channels of the large-conductance type work together to restore size after osmotic or mechanical challenge. Calcium entry through ATP-gated P2X7 channels links extracellular nucleotide release to this response, while ANO6 contributes anion and scramblase activity at the same membrane and SHANK3 provides a scaffold that organises the participating channels. Controlled shrinkage matters for epithelial fluid handling, for the shape changes of migrating and dividing cells, and for apoptosis, where loss of cell volume is one of the defining early events. Persistent swelling instead contributes to cytotoxic oedema and lytic cell death.

Cells constantly internalise membrane, receptors and extracellular material, and this pathway covers the brakes on that traffic — the processes that slow or block endocytic uptake so that surface receptors persist, phagocytosis is restrained, or cargo is diverted from internalisation. Such restraint sets receptor residence time at the plasma membrane and therefore the duration of signalling, and it underlies the "don't eat me" logic by which healthy cells escape clearance: CD47 engaging SIRPA, and inhibitory immune receptors such as FCGR2B, LILRB1 and the CD300 family, all damp uptake by phagocytes. Other members act on the machinery itself, including caveolin-1 and PICALM at coated and caveolar structures, PACSIN/syndapin proteins, ANKRD13 ubiquitin-binding adaptors, small GTPases and their regulators, and several microRNAs. Sterol-sensing nuclear receptors and PCSK9 link the same control to lipoprotein receptor availability and cholesterol handling.

Cells take up membrane, receptors and extracellular material by internalising patches of plasma membrane, and the processes gathered here are those that raise the rate or extent of that uptake. Enhanced endocytosis matters for clearing pathogens and dying cells, for terminating signalling by removing activated receptors, and for delivering nutrients such as iron, lipoproteins and cholesterol into the cell. Several distinct routes are represented: clathrin-coated pit assembly through the AP-2 adaptor subunits with accessory factors such as DAB2, HIP1 and SGIP1; receptor downregulation driven by arrestins, CBL-mediated ubiquitination and ESCRT components; and opsonin-triggered phagocytosis, in which complement proteins, collectins and ficolins tag particles for Fc receptors and SYK-dependent signalling. Also present are apolipoprotein and transferrin-receptor ligands directing lipid and iron internalisation, and bridging molecules such as GAS6 with MERTK and AXL that drive engulfment of apoptotic cells.

Cells keep large parts of their genome off without changing its sequence, and epigenetic negative regulation of gene expression is that silencing programme: heritable, chromatin-based repression of specific loci. It defines which genes a differentiated cell may use, keeps imprinted alleles monoallelic, inactivates one X chromosome in females, silences transposons and retroviral elements in germ cells and early embryos, and holds developmental regulators in check until needed; its collapse drives derepression of repeats, loss of lineage identity and the promoter hypermethylation and Polycomb misregulation typical of cancer. Mechanistically it converges on histone-modifying and reader complexes — Polycomb PRC1 and PRC2 with EZH2, SUZ12, RNF2 and the chromobox proteins, H3K9 methyltransferases SETDB1 and SUV39H1 with HP1, histone deacetylases and sirtuins — together with DNA methylation by DNMT1, DNMT3A and UHRF1, piRNA-guided targeting, ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling and anchoring of repressed chromatin at the nuclear lamina.

Innate immune activation must be damped as well as triggered, and the negative regulation of innate immune response covers the brakes that keep antiviral and inflammatory signalling proportionate and self-limited. Without them, interferon and inflammasome output persists after a threat is cleared, producing interferonopathies, autoinflammation and tissue damage; excessive braking instead permits infection or tumour escape. The mechanisms are varied: deubiquitinases and ubiquitin-editing enzymes such as TNFAIP3, USP18 and TRIM21 dismantle activating signalling complexes; nucleic acid-handling enzymes including TREX1, ADAR and SAMHD1 limit the endogenous ligands that would otherwise engage cytosolic sensors; NLRC3, NLRX1 and NLRP4 restrain pattern-recognition and inflammasome pathways from within the cell. Inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands — TIGIT, HAVCR2, LILRB1, CEACAM1 and the HLA class I molecules read by NK cells — enforce self-tolerance, while phosphatases, complement regulators, TGFB1 and RNA-binding and microRNA factors tune the magnitude and duration of the response.

Antibody isotype switching lets an activated B cell change the constant region of its immunoglobulin from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE while keeping antigen specificity, tailoring effector function to the type of infection; the genes here act to promote that switch. Positive regulation comes from two directions. Extracellular cues — CD40 ligation, co-stimulation through CD28 and OX40 ligand, and cytokines such as IL-4 acting via STAT6, TGF-beta, IL-2 and APRIL — open particular switch regions and bias which isotype is chosen, with T-bet directing others. Inside the nucleus, activation-induced lesions are converted into productive recombination by mismatch repair components MLH1, MSH2 and PMS2 and by the 53BP1–RIF1–shieldin axis, which protects DNA ends from resection and channels them into non-homologous end joining. Loss of these steps produces hyper-IgM immunodeficiency and poor class-specific antibody responses.

Lipid synthesis and breakdown are held in check as tightly as they are driven, and this collection covers the braking mechanisms: the processes that stop or slow reactions involving fatty acids, triglycerides, cholesterol, sphingolipids and their derivatives. Restraint of this kind sets how much fat a cell stores, keeps membrane lipid composition stable, and limits cholesterol and bile acid accumulation; losing it contributes to obesity, fatty liver, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. Mechanisms are varied. INSIG1 and INSIG2 retain SCAP-SREBP in the endoplasmic reticulum so that sterol synthesis genes stay off, ORMDL proteins damp serine palmitoyltransferase and thus sphingolipid output, and ANGPTL4 inhibits lipoprotein lipase to spare circulating triglycerides from hydrolysis. Nuclear receptors and corepressors, AMPK and sirtuins, perilipins coating the lipid droplet surface, and a set of microRNAs including the cholesterol-tuned miR-33 add transcriptional and post-transcriptional layers of suppression.

positive regulation of lipid metabolic process covers the signals and transcriptional programs that turn up the synthesis, transport, storage and breakdown of lipids according to nutritional state. It sets how much cholesterol a cell makes and takes up, how fatty acids are mobilised from triglyceride stores and burned, and it underlies whole-body energy balance; its dysregulation produces dyslipidaemia, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance. The core is a set of lipid-sensing nuclear receptors and bHLH factors — PPARs with RXRA, the liver X receptors, the bile acid receptor, and SREBP1/2 with SCAP — acting alongside coactivators such as PPARGC1A and sirtuins. Upstream, insulin signalling through IRS1/2, AKT and mTOR complexes, AMPK, PKA and cytokines including TNF and IL1B relay hormonal and inflammatory input. Downstream effectors span lipases and their activators, apolipoproteins and lipoprotein receptors, acyl-CoA synthetases and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation entry via CPT1A.

This grouping collects the genes that push lipid metabolism upward — raising the rate of fatty acid oxidation, triglyceride synthesis, cholesterol handling and lipoprotein turnover rather than restraining them. Such positive regulation of lipid metabolic process matters because it lets tissues switch fuels with feeding and fasting, mobilise stored fat, secrete steroid hormones and clear circulating lipids; when it is miscalibrated the results are hepatic steatosis, dyslipidaemia, insulin resistance and atherosclerosis. Much of the control is transcriptional, through nuclear receptors and their partners such as PPARA, PPARG, RXRA, the liver X receptors and the bile-acid receptor NR1H4, together with the SREBP branch and its sterol sensor SCAP. Layered on top are nutrient and hormone signals — insulin acting via IRS proteins and AKT, mTOR complex components, AMPK and PKA — plus lipases, acyl-CoA synthetases, transporters and apolipoproteins that execute the flux itself.

Germ cells must not enter or complete meiosis at the wrong time, and the restraining influences grouped here as negative regulation of meiotic nuclear division are what hold them back. The consequences of losing that brake are concrete: premature meiotic entry in fetal male germ cells, loss of the spermatogonial stem cell pool, aneuploid gametes and infertility. Sex-specific factors such as DMRT1 and NANOS2 suppress the meiotic programme in male germ cells to preserve mitotic self-renewal, while LIF supports undifferentiated germ cell states. Other members act inside meiosis itself: FBXO43 and FBXO5 inhibit the anaphase-promoting complex to arrest oocytes, kinetochore and checkpoint components including KNL1 and ZWINT delay division until attachments are correct, and HORMAD proteins with TRIP13 police recombination and synapsis before chromosomes are allowed to segregate.

Germ cells must switch from mitotic proliferation to the reductional divisions of meiosis at the right moment, and this positive regulation of meiotic nuclear division covers the signals and factors that license and accelerate that entry. It matters because the timing of meiotic initiation sets fertility: premature entry exhausts the spermatogonial pool, delayed or failed entry leaves oocytes and spermatocytes arrested, and errors here produce aneuploid gametes. Retinoic acid-responsive STRA8 together with its partner MEIOSIN drives the transcriptional commitment to meiosis, DMRT1 governs whether spermatogonia remain mitotic or proceed, and DAZL supplies the germ-cell competence needed for the response. Downstream, PRDM9 specifies recombination hotspots and RAD51AP1 supports strand invasion during homologous recombination. Oocyte-restricted factors, WNT ligands and natriuretic peptide signalling through NPR2 link the surrounding somatic environment and follicular arrest to meiotic progression.</description": "

negative regulation of membrane potential covers the processes that dissipate or oppose the charge separation held across a membrane, most conspicuously the inner mitochondrial membrane. Loss of that potential is not merely a metabolic inconvenience: it is the commitment step of intrinsic apoptosis and the signal that marks a mitochondrion for mitophagy, so this biology sits at the interface of cell death, quality control and energy balance. The genes reflect that emphasis, with BAX and the BH3-only proteins PMAIP1 and BNIP3 permeabilising or depolarising mitochondria, MTCH2 and PRELID1 acting at the outer and inner membranes to shape lipid transfer and apoptotic sensitivity, and the uncoupling-related carrier SLC25A27 leaking protons to lower the gradient. Others act on plasma membrane excitability and calcium handling. Failure of restraint here contributes to neurodegeneration and to the apoptotic resistance of tumour cells.

Membrane potentials are built by asymmetric charge distribution across a membrane, and processes that lower or prevent them — negative regulation of membrane potential — determine whether a mitochondrion keeps its proton-motive force or a cell keeps its resting excitability. Much of the biology here is mitochondrial depolarization tied to cell death: BAX permeabilizes the outer membrane, the BH3-only proteins NOXA and BNIP3 promote loss of potential and mitophagy, and MTCH2 acts at the outer membrane to support recruitment of apoptotic effectors. An uncoupling-type mitochondrial carrier dissipates the gradient as heat rather than ATP, linking this activity to metabolic flexibility and protection from oxidative stress. Other members act at the plasma membrane or through bicarbonate-sensitive signalling. Because sustained potential is what licenses oxidative phosphorylation, its controlled collapse commits cells to apoptosis, organelle clearance, or altered energy output.

Cells spend energy to hold charge across their membranes, and this pathway covers processes that build up or strengthen that potential difference, whether across the plasma membrane of an excitable cell or the inner mitochondrial membrane that drives ATP synthesis. Both readings are represented here: a scaffolding protein that clusters sodium channels at axon initial segments and nodes, a glutamate receptor subunit that depolarises postsynaptic membranes, a phosphate transporter, and a set of mitochondrial factors including a respiratory complex I subunit, a mitofusin, and regulators of mitochondrial quality control that determine whether the proton-motive force is sustained or collapses. Loss of proton-motive force marks mitochondria for elimination and triggers apoptotic release of cytochrome c, linking this regulation to neuronal excitability, energy supply, and cell death.

This is the set of activities that push cells through mitosis faster or more often, spanning both the intracellular machinery that executes nuclear division and the extracellular cues that license it. Its core is the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator CDC20 and the E2 enzyme UBE2C, which ubiquitinates securin and cyclin B so that separase can cleave cohesin and sister chromatids can part; Aurora A and PLK1 drive spindle assembly and mitotic entry, while the SKA complex and NUSAP1 stabilise kinetochore-microtubule attachments. Silencing of the spindle checkpoint, via MAD2L1BP acting on MAD1L1-dependent signalling, releases the brake on anaphase. Layered on top are growth factor and cytokine inputs — EGF-family ligands, insulin and IGFs through their receptors, PDGF, and inflammatory mediators such as TNF and IL1 — that overcome RB1-imposed restraint. Deregulation here underlies proliferative disease and chromosome missegregation in cancer.

Acidification of a compartment or body fluid — pH reduction, in effect pumping protons to raise hydrogen ion concentration — underlies gastric digestion, urinary acid excretion, bone resorption and the acidic interior of lysosomes. The gastric H+/K+-ATPase subunits ATP4A and ATP4B carry out parietal cell acid secretion, driven by gastrin acting through its receptor CCKBR, while anion exchange by SLC4A3 supports the bicarbonate movement that sustains continued proton export. Vacuolar ATPase subunits, including ATP6V1B1 and TCIRG1, acidify intracellular organelles and are secreted onto the ruffled border of osteoclasts and the apical membrane of renal intercalated cells. Loss of these components causes distal renal tubular acidosis with deafness, or osteopetrosis when osteoclasts cannot acidify the resorption lacuna and dissolve mineral. The pathway therefore links ion transport to digestion, systemic acid-base balance and skeletal remodelling.

Proteolysis is irreversible, so cells and tissues invest heavily in restraining it, and this collection of brakes on peptide bond hydrolysis keeps protease activity confined in space, time and target. Its arms are distinct but convergent: secreted inhibitors of serine proteases and of the coagulation and plasminogen-activation cascades, cystatins that block lysosomal cysteine cathepsins, tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases that limit extracellular matrix turnover, and SPINK-family inhibitors whose loss in skin causes barrier failure and severe atopic disease. Inside the cell, deubiquitinating enzymes, proteasome-associated regulators and chaperone-like factors rescue substrates from degradation, tuning the half-life of tumour suppressors, ribosomal proteins and signalling intermediates. Losing this restraint produces unchecked clotting or bleeding, matrix destruction and invasion in cancer, emphysema-like tissue damage, and inflammatory injury, while excessive restraint stabilises proteins that should be cleared.

Regulated destruction of proteins lets cells terminate signals, clear damaged polypeptides, and switch cell-cycle states irreversibly; this collection covers the factors that promote peptide bond hydrolysis rather than perform it. Much of it converges on the ubiquitin-proteasome system: cullin-RING and F-box substrate adaptors such as FBXW7, BTRC and FBXW11, the E3s MDM2, STUB1 and PRKN, proteasome ATPase subunits, and the chaperone-like escorts VCP, UBQLN1/2 and BAG6 that extract and deliver misfolded or ER-derived substrates for degradation. Other members promote extracellular and membrane proteolysis — ADAM sheddases, MMP14, the proprotein convertase FURIN, contact-activation factors of the plasma kinin system — or drive caspase activation through FADD, CASP8 and inflammasome components, or gamma-secretase cleavage via PSEN1 and PSENEN. Loss of this control underlies protein aggregation in neurodegeneration, stabilization of oncogenic substrates, and failure of inflammatory and coagulation cascades that depend on timed activating cleavage.

Retroviruses and retroelements copy their single-stranded RNA genomes into double-stranded DNA before integrating, and this restriction programme blocks that step, limiting replication of HIV-1 and related agents and curbing mobilization of endogenous retroelements that would otherwise mutate the genome. Most of the members are cytidine deaminases of the APOBEC3 family, packaged into virions and acting on minus-strand reverse transcripts to convert cytosine to uracil, producing hypermutated, degraded or non-functional proviral DNA; HIV-1 Vif counters them by driving their degradation, and their off-target activity on cellular DNA contributes to mutational signatures in cancer. The related AICDA deaminase links this defence to antibody diversification. TRIM28 adds a transcriptional arm, silencing integrated proviral and retroelement sequences through heterochromatin formation, so both nucleic-acid editing and epigenetic repression contribute to innate antiviral immunity and genome stability.

Sister chromatids must be held together from replication until anaphase, and then released on cue; this is the counter-force that limits and dissolves that cohesion. Without it chromosomes cannot separate, and cells arrest or missegregate their genomes; too much of it loosens cohesion prematurely, with the same aneuploid result. Separase is the protease that cleaves the cohesin subunit holding the ring shut once the spindle checkpoint is satisfied, while WAPL opens cohesin in a non-proteolytic way to allow turnover along chromosome arms during interphase. Tankyrase-dependent poly(ADP-ribosyl)ation acts at telomeres, where resolution of sister telomere cohesion is required before mitotic exit, and chromatin factors such as ATRX influence cohesion at heterochromatic and telomeric regions. The balance set here determines faithful chromosome segregation and, when broken, chromosomal instability in cancer and cohesinopathy-like phenotypes.

Sister chromatids must stay physically linked from replication until anaphase so that the spindle can attach to both and split them evenly; this is the set of activities that promote and reinforce that cohesion. Loss of it produces premature chromatid separation, missegregation and aneuploidy, and underlies cohesinopathy-like chromosome instability. Several routes converge here: the cohesin subunit RAD21 forms the ring itself, the kinase BUB1 phosphorylates histone H2A at centromeres to concentrate the shugoshin-based protection of centromeric cohesion, and the helicase DDX11 works with the replication fork and flap endonuclease FEN1 so that cohesion is established correctly behind the fork. An SMC5/6 arm, with the SUMO ligase NSMCE2 and the SLF1-SLF2 recruitment module, supports cohesion during repair of damaged or stalled forks. Chromatin context contributes through macroH2A and the RNA-binding protein SFPQ, linking cohesion to genome maintenance and accurate mitosis.

negative regulation of smoothened signaling pathway is the collection of brakes on Hedgehog signalling, keeping the pathway off in the absence of ligand and limiting its output once it is on. This restraint sets morphogen thresholds during limb, neural tube and skeletal patterning, and its loss underlies basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma and overgrowth syndromes. Repression acts at several levels: the receptor PTCH1 holds Smoothened inactive, HHIP and GPC3 sequester the ligand extracellularly, and MEGF8 with MGRN1 and MOSMO promote receptor turnover. Inside the cilium, GPR161 and PKA catalytic subunits drive phosphorylation of GLI proteins, while SUFU sequesters them and KCTD11-containing cullin complexes and BTRC direct their proteasomal degradation or partial processing into the GLI3 repressor. Intraflagellar transport components and KIF7 organise the ciliary compartment where this repression is executed, tying pathway silencing to ciliary integrity.

Hedgehog signalling must be kept off in most cells and most of the time, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that restrain the Smoothened-dependent branch of that cascade. Without them, pathway output runs unopposed, producing the digit, skeletal and craniofacial patterning defects of ciliopathies and the constitutive activation seen in basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. The receptor PTCH1 and its relative PTCH2 suppress Smoothened until ligand arrives, secreted HHIP and glypican-3 sequester Hedgehog ligands, and an orphan receptor at the cilium keeps protein kinase A active so that GLI proteins are phosphorylated and processed. SUFU sequesters GLI, GLI3 is cleaved into a transcriptional repressor, and cullin-3 adaptors of the KCTD family together with a beta-TrCP-containing ubiquitin ligase target activator GLI for degradation. Intraflagellar transport components and TULP3 set the ciliary trafficking on which all of this depends.

Hedgehog ligands instruct pattern and growth in developing tissues, and this pathway covers the inputs that turn Smoothened signalling up rather than damping it. Its output sets neural tube and limb polarity, skeletal and craniofacial morphogenesis, and cerebellar granule cell expansion; too little gives holoprosencephaly and limb and rib defects, while inappropriate activation drives medulloblastoma and basal cell carcinoma. Positive regulators here act at several levels: the ligands themselves (SHH, IHH, DHH) and modifiers of their release and reach, sulfation and glycosaminoglycan enzymes and the glypican GPC3 that shape ligand distribution, and the ciliary machinery central to transduction inside the organelle involving intraflagellar transport, basal body and centriole components, and the kinesin KIF7, which together permit Smoothened accumulation and GLI1 activation. Transcription factors and kinases downstream extend the response into cell-type-specific programmes.

regulation of RNA polymerase II transcription preinitiation complex assembly controls the step at which general transcription factors, TFIID and polymerase II are loaded onto a promoter, setting whether a gene is transcribed at all and how often. Because preinitiation complex formation is the commitment point of gene expression, factors acting here determine responsiveness to hormones, stress and developmental cues. The genes span both directions of control: the DR1-DRAP1 (NC2) heterodimer binds TBP and represses promoter assembly, HMGB1 bends DNA and facilitates factor loading, while CREB1, p53 and the thyroid hormone receptor recruit coactivators and stabilise the complex at specific response elements. Proteasomal and cullin-associated components link initiation to regulated turnover of activators. Loss of this tuning underlies failures of stress-induced and hormone-dependent transcription, and contributes to the transcriptional deregulation seen in tumours with p53 pathway defects.

Before a protein-coding gene can be transcribed, general factors and RNA polymerase II must be loaded onto the promoter in an ordered assembly, and this pathway covers the inputs that speed up, slow down or block that step. It is where gene-specific control converges on the basal machinery, so it sets how readily a promoter fires rather than what the polymerase does afterwards. The negative cofactor heterodimer DR1 and DRAP1 binds TBP and prevents productive complex formation, while HMGB1 bends promoter DNA to favour factor binding. Sequence-specific regulators including CREB1, the thyroid hormone receptor THRA and the tumour suppressor TP53 act on the same step to recruit or withhold the polymerase, linking hormonal signals, cAMP responses and DNA damage to transcriptional output. Loss of such control underlies deregulated gene expression in cancer and endocrine disease.

Before RNA polymerase II can begin synthesising a transcript, general factors and the polymerase must be recruited onto a promoter as a preinitiation complex, and this grouping covers the influences that push that assembly step forward, raising how often and how readily transcription starts. Activators bound at promoters and enhancers can stabilise the arriving general machinery, so the rate-limiting nucleation of initiation becomes a controllable point for gene regulation. The genes here span the routes that converge on that step: the cAMP-responsive activator CREB1 and the stress-responsive activator TP53 work as DNA-binding transcription factors, a proteasomal ATPase subunit and a cullin-associated regulator connect ubiquitin-proteasome activity to initiation, and a Wnt family ligand indicates control by extracellular signalling. Through this step, hormonal, developmental and damage signals are translated into altered transcriptional output.

Slowing or halting the elongation phase of protein synthesis is a way for cells to control how much protein a given mRNA yields after the ribosome has already engaged it, and to arrest ribosomes that are damaged, mistargeted, or hijacked. The negative regulation of translational elongation described here brings together sequence-specific mRNA binding proteins of the CPEB family, which repress elongation on their target transcripts and contribute to synaptic plasticity and memory-related local translation in neurons, with the ribosome-associated scaffold RACK1, which sits on the 40S subunit and couples signalling to ribosome behaviour. Other members act during co-translational events: signal recognition particle protein SRP9 participates in the elongation arrest that holds nascent secretory chains until the ribosome docks at the endoplasmic reticulum, while SHFL restrains programmed ribosomal frameshifting used by viruses, linking elongation control to antiviral defence.

Ribosomes stall on difficult sequences, and this biology speeds the elongation phase of protein synthesis so that translation continues through them. Its core is eIF5A, which despite its name acts during elongation rather than initiation: it binds between the ribosomal subunits and resolves stalling at polyproline stretches and other awkward motifs, and it also assists termination. eIF5A is the only protein carrying hypusine, a polyamine-derived modification required for its activity, which links polyamine metabolism to translational output. A paralogue and a related gene copy extend the same function, and the set also includes chromatin and ubiquitin-pathway enzymes that modulate elongation capacity. Increasing elongation rate supports proliferation and cell growth, and eIF5A overexpression is associated with tumour progression, while loss of hypusination impairs synthesis of proline-rich proteins.</description

Blood vessel tone is set by the balance between constricting and relaxing influences on smooth muscle, and this pathway covers the braking side: signals and regulators that limit or reverse vasoconstriction to keep perfusion pressure within range. Its output matters for systemic and pulmonary blood pressure, and loss of these restraints contributes to hypertension and to pulmonary arterial hypertension, where BMPR2 mutations remove a vasodilatory and antiproliferative input to the pulmonary vasculature. Adrenomedullin is a secreted peptide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and lowers pressure; ARHGAP42 restrains RhoA-dependent contractile signalling in smooth muscle, a locus linked to blood pressure variation in humans. Integrin subunits and matrix remodelling by MMP2 tie tone to adhesion and the mechanical state of the vessel wall, while leptin and melatonin receptor signalling connect vascular resistance to metabolic and circadian control.

Blood pressure and regional perfusion depend on how strongly arterial smooth muscle is told to contract, and this pathway covers the signals that push that balance toward narrowing of the vessel lumen. It matters for acute responses such as haemostasis and defence of pressure during blood loss, and its persistent overactivity contributes to hypertension, vasospasm and vascular remodelling. Much of the input arrives through G protein-coupled receptors on smooth muscle: alpha-1 adrenergic receptors responding to noradrenaline supplied by dopamine beta-hydroxylase, vasopressin receptors, receptors for histamine, serotonin, substance P and thrombin, and the thromboxane receptor acting downstream of thromboxane synthase. These converge on calcium entry and on RhoA-dependent sensitisation of the contractile apparatus to calcium, with caveolin-1 organising the membrane platforms involved. Extracellular calcium sensing and a calcium-activated cation channel add further tone-setting control.

Homologous recombination is powerful but dangerous: used at the wrong time, on the wrong template, or between repeats, it produces translocations, deletions and loss of heterozygosity. Negative regulation of DNA recombination is the braking system that keeps exchange events rare and channels breaks toward safer outcomes. Anti-recombinases and helicases such as BLM, RECQL5, FBH1, HELB and RTEL1 dismantle RAD51 filaments or dissolve joint molecules, while mismatch repair proteins including MSH2 and MLH1 reject recombination between diverged sequences. At double-strand breaks, 53BP1 with RIF1, shieldin subunits and MAD2L2 blocks end resection and favours non-homologous joining, a choice that governs class switch recombination and underlies the sensitivity of BRCA1-mutant tumours to PARP inhibition. Linker histones compact chromatin against illegitimate exchange, and TERF2 with TRF2-interacting partners suppresses recombination at telomeres. Loss of these restraints yields genome rearrangement, cancer predisposition and premature ageing syndromes.

Recombination between DNA molecules is promoted rather than merely permitted, and this pathway covers the factors that raise its frequency and extent — in meiosis, in homologous repair of broken chromosomes, and in the programmed rearrangements that diversify antibodies. Chromatin is a major control point: the NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase module with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, actin-related subunits and MRGBP/MORF4L partners opens damaged loci, while PRDM9 methylates histones to designate meiotic recombination hotspots. Damage signalling through RNF8-dependent ubiquitination, 53BP1, RIF1 and the shieldin subunits channels breaks toward end-joining versus resection, and mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2 and PMS2 act in both correction and crossover resolution. Cytokine and costimulatory genes including CD40, IL4 and STAT6 reflect the B-cell signals that license class switch recombination. Loss of these activities reduces immunoglobulin diversity, impairs crossover formation and destabilises the genome.

Carbohydrate flux must be turned down as well as up, and this collection covers the braking side: processes that slow or block glycolysis, glycogen synthesis and breakdown, and gluconeogenesis so that fuel use matches supply. Such restraint underlies fasting adaptation, insulin action and hepatic glucose output, and its loss contributes to hyperglycaemia, insulin resistance and inappropriate glycogen storage. Mechanisms are heterogeneous: glycogen synthase kinase-3 isoforms phosphorylate and inhibit glycogen synthase, TIGAR degrades fructose-2,6-bisphosphate to damp glycolytic flux, and fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-bisphosphatase enzymes set the gluconeogenic-glycolytic balance. Hormonal and transcriptional inputs act alongside them, including insulin and leptin receptor signalling, adiponectin and related C1q-TNF ligands, PPARA, STAT3, and the corepressor and acetyltransferase machinery that tunes metabolic gene expression. Circadian and nutrient-sensing components such as CRY1, SIRT6, DDIT4 and FLCN link the restraint to daily and growth-factor cues.

This is the set of signals that push carbohydrate handling upward coordinated stimulation of glycolysis, glycogen synthesis and breakdown, and glucose uptake in response to hormones, nutrient status and oxygen availability. It matters because blood glucose homeostasis depends on these inputs being dialled up at the right time; their derangement underlies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and the glycolytic shift of hypoxic and tumour tissue. Insulin and IGF signal through their receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT to mTOR complex components, opposing FOXO1-driven gluconeogenic transcription, while glucagon acts through cAMP and protein kinase A to mobilise glycogen via phosphorylase kinase subunits. Energy stress recruits AMPK subunits, and PPARGC1A with SIRT1 reprogrammes oxidative and gluconeogenic gene expression. Hypoxia-inducible factor with ARNT, the lipogenic factor MLXIPL, glucokinase and PP1 glycogen-targeting subunits set flux at specific steps, with circadian and microRNA inputs layered on top.

Complement is a rapidly amplifying proteolytic cascade, and restraining it is what keeps that amplification aimed at pathogens rather than at host tissue. Negative regulation of complement activation is carried out by soluble and membrane-bound inhibitors that block cascade initiation, dismantle the C3 and C5 convertases, and prevent assembly of the lytic membrane attack complex. C1 inhibitor holds the classical and lectin initiation proteases in check; C4b-binding protein and CD46 act as cofactors for factor I-mediated cleavage of C4b and C3b; CD55 accelerates convertase decay, and CD59 stops terminal pore formation on self membranes. Loss of these brakes produces recognisable disease — hereditary angioedema when C1 inhibitor is deficient, and complement-mediated haemolysis when erythrocytes lack CD55 and CD59. The same regulators mark host cells as off-limits, shaping immune tolerance, clearance of apoptotic debris and inflammation in kidney, eye and blood.

Complement is the humoral arm of innate immunity that opsonizes microbes and damaged cells, recruits phagocytes, and punches lytic pores into targets; this pathway covers the influences that push that cascade harder or faster. Enhanced complement activation speeds clearance of pathogens and of dying cells and immune complexes, but unchecked it drives tissue injury in glomerulonephritis, haemolytic disease and inflammatory conditions of the eye and brain. Central components here include C3, whose cleavage seeds all downstream amplification, and C6 as part of the terminal membrane attack complex; properdin stabilizes the alternative-pathway C3 convertase and so sustains amplification. Cell-surface receptors such as CR1 and the microglial receptor TREM2 couple complement opsonins to phagocytic recognition, while IL1B links inflammatory signalling to increased complement output. The genes also include microRNAs acting as post-transcriptional modulators of this output.

Secretion has to be restrained as well as triggered, and this is the braking side of regulated exocytosis: processes that reduce the rate or extent of vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane. It sets the tone of neurotransmitter and hormone release at synapses and endocrine cells, and it limits degranulation by mast cells, neutrophils and platelets, where inhibitory immune receptors such as FCGR2B, CD300A and CEACAM1 damp granule discharge after activation. Mechanisms represented here include presynaptic autoreceptor signalling through ADRA2A and inhibitory G proteins, sequestration of SNARE partners by STXBP6 and other Munc18-related proteins, calcium-sensor and kinase control via SYT4 and CDK5, and Rab-dependent trafficking steps that divert vesicles from fusion. Loss of such restraint produces excess release: alpha-synuclein and C9orf72-SMCR8-WDR41 links tie failure of this control to neurodegeneration, while immune-receptor loss drives inflammatory tissue damage.

Cells release neurotransmitters, hormones, granule contents and extracellular vesicles by fusing vesicles with the plasma membrane, and this collection covers the inputs that raise the rate and extent of that release. Upregulated exocytosis underlies synaptic transmission and its potentiation, degranulation of neutrophils, mast cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes, and peptide hormone secretion. Calcium sensing is central: synaptotagmins, DOC2 proteins and CADPS couple calcium entry, partly through voltage-gated channels, to SNARE-mediated fusion involving syntaxins, VAMP7/VAMP8 and the priming factor STXBP1. Rab GTPases such as RAB27A and RAB3A direct granule trafficking and docking, UNC13D licenses cytotoxic granule release, and kinases including CDK5, PRKCA and SYK transmit receptor signals to the fusion machinery. ESCRT components add the multivesicular route to exosome release. Loss of these steps causes immunodeficiency with impaired killing, bleeding disorders and defective neurosecretion.

Fatty acid synthesis, oxidation and storage are all costly, and cells restrain them as tightly as they drive them; this is the braking side of lipid metabolism, tuning flux to nutritional state. Its failure contributes to hepatic steatosis, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. Several distinct brakes converge here: insulin signalling through AKT1 and feedback regulators, the ER-resident INSIG proteins and ERLIN paralogues that hold SREBP processing and HMG-CoA reductase in check, lipase inhibitors such as ANGPTL4 and the apolipoproteins APOC1 and APOC3 that limit lipoprotein lipase action, and transcriptional repression via NCOR1 and the NAD-dependent deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT4, the latter damping fatty acid oxidation in mitochondria. A set of microRNAs, notably MIR33A, adds post-transcriptional suppression of lipid and cholesterol genes, while UGT glucuronosyltransferases and flavin monooxygenases divert lipophilic substrates toward conjugation and disposal.

Fatty acid metabolism is switched up or down according to nutritional state, and this collection describes the inputs that push it upward — toward greater oxidation, elongation, desaturation, or release of fatty acids from stored and circulating lipid. It matters because it sets how much fat a tissue burns versus stores, and its derangement underlies hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance and dyslipidaemia. Nuclear receptors of the PPAR family together with the coactivator PPARGC1A and the oxysterol-sensing liver X receptors drive transcription of oxidative and lipogenic enzymes; CPT1A commits long-chain acyl-CoA to mitochondrial beta-oxidation while MLYCD removes the malonyl-CoA that inhibits it, and the peroxisomal transporters ABCD1 and ABCD2 handle very-long-chain substrates. Hormonal and inflammatory signals — adiponectin, endothelins, IL1B, GDF15, insulin signalling through IRS1 and IRS2 — feed in, and lipoprotein lipase cofactors APOC2 and GPIHBP1 increase substrate delivery.

Growth must be actively restrained as well as driven, and this collection covers the processes that stop, slow or cap increases in cell size, cell number and tissue mass. Losing that restraint underlies tumour formation, cardiac hypertrophy, organ overgrowth and excessive muscle or axon growth. Several distinct brakes converge here: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A, CDKN1B and CDKN2A act with TP53 and RB1 to halt cell cycle progression; the Hippo kinases STK3, STK4, LATS2 and SAV1 with their WWC scaffolds limit organ size; TGF-beta family ligands including TGFB1 and myostatin signal through SMAD3 and SMAD4 to suppress proliferation and muscle growth; PTEN and STK11 curb anabolic signalling. Secreted guidance cues -- semaphorins, slits, netrins and the Nogo receptor system -- restrict neurite outgrowth, while metallothioneins and sestrins buffer growth under metal and oxidative stress.

Growth in size and mass, whether of a whole organism, an organ, or a single process such as an axon, is actively driven rather than passive, and this collection covers the signals that push it upward. It matters for body size and stature, organ scaling, muscle hypertrophy and neurite extension, and its dysregulation underlies overgrowth syndromes, dwarfism and the proliferative drive of tumours. Endocrine control appears as the growth hormone axis with its releasing hormone, receptor and downstream STAT5 transcription factors, feeding into insulin and IGF signalling through the insulin receptor and AKT1. Nutrient and mitogenic inputs converge on mTOR with both its complex partners RPTOR and RICTOR, raising protein synthesis via ribosomal S6 kinases and translation initiation factors. Developmental morphogens — WNTs, BMPs, FGFs, Notch and Hedgehog components — plus neurotrophins and cytoskeletal regulators extend the same theme to axon and dendrite growth.

Cells that divide when damaged or unprepared propagate mutations, so the machinery that brakes the mitotic cell cycle is as much a part of proliferation control as the machinery that drives it. This is the collected restraint: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A, CDKN1B and CDKN2B, the retinoblastoma protein and its relatives holding back E2F-dependent transcription, and TP53 acting on damage signals relayed by ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and CHEK2 from sensors including the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and BRCA1-BARD1. A second arm is the spindle assembly checkpoint, where MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1, BUB3 and the kinetochore NDC80 complex keep the anaphase-promoting complex activator CDC20 inert until chromosomes are correctly attached. WEE1 and PKMYT1 phosphorylate CDK1 to delay mitotic entry, and several microRNAs add post-transcriptional damping. Loss of these controls underlies aneuploidy and tumour formation, and the same brakes enforce quiescence, differentiation and senescence.

Cells only divide when growth signals, cyclin availability and checkpoint clearance all permit it, and this collection of drivers describes the positive regulation of mitotic cell cycle progression — the inputs that push a cell from quiescence into S phase and through mitosis. It underlies tissue growth and regeneration, and its inappropriate activation is one of the commonest routes to cancer, which is why many of these genes are oncogenes or drug targets. Mitogenic receptor and kinase signalling through EGFR, AKT1 and mTOR-associated translation regulators induces D- and E-type cyclins that activate CDK4 and CDK2 to inactivate RB1; CDC25 phosphatases dephosphorylate and switch on CDK1 for mitotic entry; and the anaphase-promoting complex with CDC20 destroys cyclin B and securin partner ESPL1's inhibitor to allow chromosome segregation. Aurora A, PLK1, centriole factors and ribonucleotide reductase subunits supply the spindle and nucleotide capacity division requires, alongside regulatory microRNAs.

Muscle relaxation is an active process, and negative regulation of muscle contraction covers the signals and transporters that damp contractile force in smooth, cardiac and skeletal muscle. It sets vascular tone and airway calibre, allows chambers and vessels to refill, and prevents the sustained contracture that follows unopposed calcium signalling. Much of it runs through cyclic nucleotides: beta-adrenergic and adenosine receptors raise cAMP, soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase act on an IP3 receptor-associated substrate to limit calcium release, and RGS2 and GRK2 restrain the G protein-coupled receptors that drive contraction instead. Calcium removal and sequestration by a sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, sorcin and the sodium/potassium ATPase lower cytosolic calcium, while Rho-pathway regulators such as ARHGAP42 reduce myosin light chain phosphorylation. Loss of this restraint contributes to hypertension, bronchoconstriction and impaired cardiac relaxation.

Contraction can be dialled up as well as switched off, and this pathway covers the signals that increase the force, rate or frequency of contraction in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. It matters for vascular tone and blood pressure, gut and uterine motility, airway constriction and cardiac output, and its overactivity underlies hypertension, bronchospasm and preterm labour. Much of the input arrives through G protein-coupled receptors for vasoconstrictors and neuropeptides — endothelins, tachykinins, thromboxane, thrombin, oxytocin, muscarinic and adrenergic agonists — which raise intracellular calcium and engage RhoA-dependent sensitisation of the contractile apparatus. Voltage-gated calcium channels, including their accessory alpha-2/delta, beta and gamma subunits, and SERCA-type calcium pumps set the excitation-contraction coupling that translates these signals into cross-bridge cycling, while myocardin and serum response factor maintain the smooth muscle contractile gene programme itself.

This is the collected machinery by which cells damp down the metabolism of nucleic acids and their building blocks, overwhelmingly by shutting off gene expression. Most members are repressive transcription factors and corepressors — zinc-finger and KRAB proteins, homeodomain and forkhead repressors, HES/ID/SNAI antagonists, Polycomb and NuRD/Sin3/CoREST complexes, histone deacetylases, DNA methyltransferases and methyl-CpG binding proteins — that close chromatin and block promoter firing. Others act after transcription: transcription elongation brakes, splicing and deadenylation factors, RNA-binding proteins and decay enzymes that destabilise transcripts, and APOBEC deaminases that edit nucleic acids. A further arm restrains replication and repair, including p53, RB–E2F components, CDK inhibitors and telomere-capping proteins. Negative regulation of this kind sets cell-type identity during development, enforces circadian and hormonal timing, limits proliferation, and guards genome stability; its loss underlies many cancers and developmental malformations.

Sleep is actively promoted, not merely permitted, and this pathway covers the signals that increase how long and how deeply an animal sleeps within the daily sleep/wake cycle. It matters because sleep pressure must be translated into behavioural shutdown for memory consolidation, growth hormone release and metabolic recovery; weakened drive here contributes to insomnia and fragmented rest. Adenosine acting through the A2A receptor links accumulated metabolic activity during waking to the induction of slow-wave sleep in basal forebrain and hypothalamic circuits. Growth hormone-releasing hormone and its receptor couple non-REM sleep to the somatotropic axis, while ghrelin and neuropeptide Y signalling tie feeding state to sleep. Melatonin acting at its receptors conveys the circadian, light-entrained timing signal that positions sleep at night.

Steroid synthesis is expensive and its products are potent, so cells maintain brakes on it; this is the dampening arm of steroid metabolism, reducing the rate at which sterols and steroid hormones are made or activated. Much of it converges on cholesterol feedback: INSIG1 and INSIG2 hold the SCAP–SREBP complex in the endoplasmic reticulum when sterols are plentiful, while ERLIN1/ERLIN2 and the membrane ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 direct degradation of HMG-CoA reductase and related targets. Oxysterol production by CH25H generates the ligands that signal sterol sufficiency, APOE removes cholesterol from cells, and several microRNAs including the miR-33 and miR-27 families repress lipid and sterol gene programmes post-transcriptionally. Other members restrain gonadal and adrenal steroidogenesis through transcriptional repression, notably NR0B1, or accelerate hormone clearance by glucuronidation. Loss of this restraint underlies hypercholesterolaemia and inappropriate steroid hormone excess.

Steroid output — cholesterol, bile acids, and the steroid hormones — is tuned up in response to hormonal, nutritional and inflammatory cues, and this is the collection of activities that drives that increase. It matters for adrenal and gonadal hormone production, for clearing cholesterol from cells, and for converting cholesterol into bile acids for excretion; loss of control at these steps underlies hypercholesterolaemia, adrenal insufficiency and disordered reproductive endocrinology. The mechanisms are varied: pituitary tropic hormones such as POMC-derived ACTH and FSHB act through receptors including MC2R to raise cAMP and PKA activity, which mobilises STAR-dependent cholesterol import into mitochondria for side-chain cleavage supported by the electron donor POR. In parallel, the SREBP transcription factors with SCAP and site-2 protease raise lipogenic and sterol-synthetic gene expression, while apolipoproteins, sterol transfer proteins and ABCG-family transporters move sterols between compartments. CYP7A1 commits cholesterol to bile acid synthesis, and cytokines, angiotensin and circadian regulators impose additional positive input.

Ribosome production begins with rRNA synthesis in the nucleolus, and this is the set of activities that raises RNA polymerase I output to match a cell's demand for ribosomes. Because ribosome biogenesis consumes a large share of a growing cell's resources, upregulating it commits the cell to growth; tumours exploit this, and inherited defects in the machinery cause ribosomopathies and progeroid syndromes. Activation works through the polymerase I transcription factor UBTF binding rDNA promoters, chromatin remodellers such as SMARCA4, SMARCA5 and BAZ1B opening the repeats, and nucleolar helicases and assembly factors including DDX21, DHX33, NCL and the UTP-like WDR43 and WDR75 coupling synthesis to pre-rRNA processing. Nutrient and stress signals feed in directly, notably via mTOR and the ATF4/PERK axis, while SIRT7 and CARM1 tune the response, linking growth-factor and amino-acid availability to nucleolar activity.</description>}

positive regulation of transcription by RNA polymerase II is the broad set of activities that switch on or increase the output of protein-coding genes, and it underlies essentially every cell-fate decision, differentiation program and stimulus response in the body. The genes span the whole activating apparatus: sequence-specific activators from most major families (homeodomain, forkhead, SOX, GATA, bHLH, nuclear receptor, STAT, NF- u03baB, AP-1), the general machinery they recruit (TBP and TAF subunits, TFIIA/TFIIF, the full Mediator complex), coactivators and chromatin modifiers such as CREBBP/EP300, KAT and KMT2 enzymes, and elongation regulators including CDK9, the PAF1 complex and NELF that release paused polymerase. Also present are the upstream signals u2014 WNT, BMP/TGF- u03b2, Notch, Hedgehog, cytokines and Toll-like receptors u2014 that converge on these factors, so tissue patterning, immune activation and metabolic adaptation all read out through this step; its dysregulation is a common route to cancer and developmental syndromes.

Gene expression in eukaryotes is set largely by how often RNA polymerase II is recruited to and released from a promoter, and this collection covers the machinery that raises that rate. It spans the events by which sequence-specific activators, coactivators and chromatin modifiers converge on core promoter assembly: general transcription factors and TBP-associated factors build the preinitiation complex, the Mediator subunits relay activator signals to the polymerase, CDK7 and CDK9 phosphorylate the enzyme and its negative elongation partners to license promoter escape, and elongation factors together with histone acetyltransferases, methyltransferases and demethylases keep the template accessible. Developmental regulators of nearly every lineage act here, including HOX, SOX, GATA, PAX, MYOD1 and NEUROG proteins, alongside inducible responses such as NF-kB, STAT, SMAD, nuclear receptor and heat-shock signalling. Because it converts developmental and environmental cues into transcriptional output, its misregulation underlies congenital malformation syndromes and oncogenic overexpression.

RNA polymerase III makes the small, abundant, untranslated RNAs that set the ceiling on a cell's biosynthetic capacity — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others — so increasing its output is how growing cells license protein synthesis. Positive regulation of this transcription couples nutrient and growth signalling to ribosome and tRNA supply: the mTOR complex, through its partner RPTOR, relieves repression of polymerase III promoters, while hormone receptor signalling and chromatin remodellers such as SMARCA5 and CHD8 act on the same templates. The core activating machinery includes TBP and the polymerase III-specific factors BDP1, BRF1 and BRF2, which distinguish type 1–3 promoters, with BRF2 dedicated to U6 snRNA. Additional components support U6 biogenesis and nucleolar RNA processing. Because tRNA output tracks proliferation, sustained activation of this arm is a feature of transformed cells, and loss of restraint links it to oncogenic growth.

Cells throttle protein synthesis at its slowest, most regulated step, and this negative control of translational initiation is how they conserve energy under stress, silence specific mRNAs, and keep growth matched to nutrient supply. Two main brakes appear here: stress-activated kinases such as the heme-regulated, ER-resident and amino-acid-sensing eIF2α kinases phosphorylate eIF2α to block initiator tRNA delivery, triggering the integrated stress response and ATF4 induction; and 4E-BP proteins sequester cap-binding eIF4E downstream of mTOR to limit cap-dependent initiation. Additional repression is mRNA-specific, through poly(A)-binding protein inhibitors, LARP1 acting on 5' TOP messages, the GIGYF–4EHP module, microRNA-directed silencing via AGO2, and RNA-binding repressors including FMR1 and RBM4. ZNF598 links stalled ribosomes to quality control. Loss of this restraint drives unchecked anabolic translation, a common feature of tumour growth, while excessive repression underlies stress-induced translational shutdown and neurodevelopmental defects such as those from FMR1 loss.

Cells decide how much protein to make largely at the step where a ribosome is recruited to an mRNA, and this collection covers the events that push that step faster. Raising initiation rates supports growth, proliferation and the translation of stored messages in oocytes and sperm precursors, while the same controls are hijacked in cancer and blunted during stress. Growth-factor input through AKT and mTOR, with its downstream S6 kinases and the mRNA-binding protein LARP1, licenses cap-dependent initiation; the eIF2B complex regenerates active initiator tRNA-carrying eIF2 and so sets the global ceiling on initiation, with GADD34 reversing stress-induced eIF2 phosphorylation. Helicases such as DDX3X and DHX29 unwind structured 5' leaders, m6A writer and reader proteins including METTL3 and the YTHDF family couple methylation marks to ribosome loading, and DAZ-family and related RNA-binding proteins activate specific messages in germ cells.

Natural killer cells kill virus-infected and transformed cells without prior sensitization, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate and extent of that killing. It matters for early antiviral defence and tumour surveillance, and its outputs are the granule-release events that destroy a target cell. Activating receptors such as NKG2D with its DAP10/CD94 partners, the nectin-binding receptor CD226, and natural cytotoxicity receptors read stress ligands including MICA-like RAET1 proteins and PVR/nectin-2 on the target surface, while HLA-E engagement by the NKG2A/NKG2C family sets the balance between inhibition and activation. Downstream, VAV1, RASGRP1 and PI3K-linked signalling drive cytoskeletal polarization and degranulation, marked by surface LAMP1.
