Cytokines act in parallel: IL-12, IL-18 responsiveness and IL-21 signal through STAT5 to license effector function, and SLAM-family adaptor SH2D1A tunes target recognition.

Regulated secretion triggered by a rise in intracellular calcium must be damped as well as driven, and this pathway covers the brakes: processes that reduce the rate or extent of calcium-dependent exocytosis at synapses, neuroendocrine cells and other secretory tissues. Restraining vesicle fusion sets how much neurotransmitter, hormone or catecholamine is released per stimulus, which shapes synaptic strength, short-term plasticity and endocrine tone. Mechanisms represented here act at several levels: presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors coupled through inhibitory G proteins lower cyclic AMP and suppress release, CBARP dampens voltage-gated calcium channel activity to limit calcium entry, CDK5-dependent phosphorylation modifies release machinery, and synaptotagmin 4 acts as a non-calcium-binding isoform that interferes with productive fusion. Transcriptional repression by REST keeps neurosecretory genes off in non-neuronal cells. Loss of such inhibition produces excessive or poorly timed secretion.

Neurotransmitters and hormones are released when a rise in cytosolic calcium triggers fusion of secretory vesicles with the plasma membrane, and this pathway covers the factors that enhance that calcium-dependent exocytosis. Its output sets synaptic strength, neuropeptide and insulin secretion, and the acrosome reaction in fertilization. Calcium sensors of the synaptotagmin family and the double C2-domain proteins DOC2A and DOC2B couple the ion signal to the SNARE fusion machinery, with syntaxin-1A and its chaperone STXBP1 (Munc18-1) forming the core assembly; rabphilin and SCAMP5 act on vesicle priming and recycling. Upstream, the N-type channel CACNA1B supplies the local calcium transient, while CDK5 with its activator and the phosphatase calcineurin tune release probability. Loss of these components produces severe synaptic and epileptic encephalopathy phenotypes and impaired hormone secretion.

Nucleotide pools, and ATP above all, must be held within bounds, and this collection covers the braking side of nucleotide metabolism: processes that lower the rate or extent of nucleotide synthesis, turnover and ATP generation. The restraint matters because unchecked glycolytic and oxidative flux wastes substrate, generates reactive oxygen species and removes the metabolic checkpoint that couples growth to nutrient supply. Several routes converge here. ATP5IF1 clamps the mitochondrial ATP synthase to prevent futile ATP hydrolysis when the proton gradient collapses; TIGAR, induced by TP53, drains fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and diverts glucose away from glycolysis toward NADPH production; DDIT4 and FLCN restrain mTORC1-driven anabolism; gluconeogenic FBP1 and ALDOB oppose glycolytic flow. Transcriptional and post-translational regulators including PPARA, NCOR1, STAT3, SIRT6 and PARP1 set these limits over longer timescales, linking the pathway to stress responses, fasting metabolism and tumour metabolic reprogramming.

This grouping collects the signals and enzymes that push nucleotide metabolism upward covering both nucleotide biosynthesis and the generation of the cyclic nucleotide and adenylate pools that report a cell's energy state. It matters because ATP supply, cAMP/cGMP second messengers and the AMP:ATP ratio couple nutrient availability to growth decisions. Insulin and IGF1 signalling through their receptor and the mTOR complexes (with RPTOR and MLST8) drives anabolic nucleotide production, while the AMP-activated kinase catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 sense adenylate depletion and redirect metabolism toward ATP regeneration. Hypoxia-responsive HIF1A with ARNT and glycolytic enzymes such as ENO1 shift flux that feeds nucleotide pools, and TIGAR diverts carbon toward the pentose phosphate route. Soluble adenylyl cyclase ADCY10 and guanylate cyclase activator GUCA1A raise cyclic nucleotides, and mitochondrial quality-control proteins PINK1 and PRKN tie the pathway to oxidative ATP output and neurodegeneration.

Negative regulation of smooth muscle contraction covers the signals that relax smooth muscle, setting vascular tone, blood pressure, airway calibre and the motility of gut, bladder and uterus. Loss of these brakes produces hypertension, vasospasm, bronchoconstriction and hypercontractile hollow organs, which is why several members are drug targets. The dominant mechanism here is nitric oxide acting through soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP-dependent protein kinase, which phosphorylates the IP3 receptor-associated substrate IRAG1 to suppress calcium release from internal stores; GPCRs including β2- and β3-adrenoceptors, adenosine A2B and the CGRP receptor system add cAMP-driven relaxation. In parallel, RhoA signalling toward myosin light chain phosphatase inhibition is dampened by ARHGAP42 and by RGS2, which curtails Gq-coupled contractile input. The net effect is reduced myosin light chain phosphorylation and calcium desensitisation of the contractile apparatus.

Smooth muscle tone in blood vessels, airways and gut must be actively dialled down as well as raised, and this relaxation programme is what opposes contraction. It sets vascular resistance and blood pressure, keeps bronchi patent, and permits gastrointestinal and urogenital filling; loss of it contributes to hypertension, vasospasm and bronchoconstriction. Two arms dominate. Nitric oxide activates soluble guanylate cyclase to make cGMP, which acts through protein kinase G and an IP3 receptor-associated regulator to lower cytosolic calcium and desensitise the contractile apparatus. In parallel, Gs-coupled beta-adrenergic and adenosine receptors raise cAMP, while alpha-2 adrenergic receptors and an RGS protein restrain Gq signalling, and a RhoA GAP together with DOCK-family exchange factors tunes cytoskeletal tone. Calcitonin gene-related peptide contributes as a circulating vasodilator neuropeptide, linking sensory nerves to this relaxation.

Smooth muscle in blood vessels, gut, airways, bladder and uterus sets vascular tone, peristalsis and organ emptying, and this pathway covers the signals that turn that contraction up. Agonists acting through G protein-coupled receptors dominate: endothelins, thromboxane A2, thrombin via its protease-activated receptor, muscarinic M3 and alpha-adrenergic receptors, tachykinin receptors for substance P and neurokinins, oxytocin, neuromedin U and ghrelin acting on its receptor. These converge on calcium release and on RhoA-dependent sensitisation of the contractile apparatus, with sphingosine kinase supplying lipid mediators; myocardin and serum response factor maintain the differentiated contractile phenotype that makes the response possible. Excessive drive here contributes to hypertension, vasospasm, bronchoconstriction and preterm labour, which is why several of these receptors are drug targets, while loss of tone underlies intestinal dysmotility and atonic bladder.

negative regulation of striated muscle contraction covers the braking mechanisms that limit how forcefully and how often skeletal and cardiac muscle contract. Relaxation is as much an active process as contraction: without it, cardiac output falls because chambers cannot refill, and skeletal muscle stiffens or fatigues. The genes point to the main routes of restraint. Calcium is cleared from the cytosol by the sarcoplasmic reticulum pump ATP2A1 with sorcin modulating release, while ATP1A2 maintains the ion gradients that set excitability. Signalling arms dampen contractile drive through beta-adrenergic receptor desensitisation by GRK2 and through phosphoinositide 3-kinase gamma acting on cyclic nucleotide compartments. Membrane organisation by BIN1 shapes the T-tubules where excitation-contraction coupling occurs. Loss of these controls contributes to diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmia and myopathy.

Striated muscle must relax as reliably as it contracts, and this collection represents the braking side of that cycle u2014 processes that damp the rate, force or frequency of contraction in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Relaxation depends heavily on removing calcium from the cytosol: the fast-twitch sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump ATP2A1 sequesters calcium back into the SR, sorcin modulates calcium release channels, and the Na+/K+-ATPase subunit ATP1A2 maintains the ionic gradients that set excitability. Signalling inputs tune this negatively as well, with u03b2-adrenergic receptor and G protein-coupled receptor kinase activity, phosphoinositide 3-kinase u03b3 and adenylate cyclase shaping cyclic nucleotide tone, while BIN1 organises the membrane architecture of transverse tubules that couples excitation to calcium handling. Loss of this restraint produces incomplete relaxation, contracture and diastolic dysfunction, and mutations in several of these genes cause myopathy or cardiomyopathy.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle must be able to contract harder or faster on demand, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the force and frequency of striated muscle contraction. It matters for cardiac output during exercise or stress and for skeletal muscle power, and its dysregulation contributes to arrhythmia, hypertrophy and heart failure. The genes span the routes by which contraction is enhanced: adrenergic receptor signalling and its modulators, calcium handling by the sarcoplasmic reticulum pump and calcium-permeable channels, sodium-potassium pumping and potassium channel control of the action potential that sets excitation, and structural components of the sarcomeric Z-disc that influence how much force a fibre generates. Neuroendocrine and peptide factors, including natriuretic and corticotropin-releasing family peptides, act as circulating or local signals that reset contractile performance, linking muscle output to systemic cardiovascular regulation.

Carbon catabolite regulation of transcription is the logic by which the availability of one carbon source, typically glucose, sets the transcription of genes handling alternative fuels, so that a cell burns the most favourable substrate first and represses the machinery for the rest. In mammals this is the transcriptional arm of nutrient sensing that couples feeding and fasting to lipogenic and glycolytic gene programmes; its failure contributes to hepatic steatosis, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. Glucose-derived metabolites act through carbohydrate-response element binding factor MLXIPL together with USF1 and SRF at sugar-responsive promoters, while the coactivator NCOA1 and the acetyltransferase KAT2B supply chromatin-modifying activity. O-GlcNAc transferase adds a direct metabolic input, glycosylating transcription factors in proportion to hexosamine flux and thereby reporting carbohydrate abundance onto the transcriptional apparatus itself.

Cells and tissues meet their energy needs from whichever carbon source is most abundant, and carbon catabolite regulation of transcription is the gene-expression arm of that choice: the presence of one fuel, characteristically glucose, tunes transcription of genes that handle alternative substrates. In mammals this is the logic behind nutrient-responsive metabolic gene programmes in liver and adipose tissue, where carbohydrate intake drives lipogenic and glycolytic gene expression and its failure contributes to dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. The carbohydrate-responsive transcription factor encoded by MLXIPL, together with the sterol- and glucose-sensitive factor USF1, binds carbohydrate and E-box elements at such promoters, while a histone acetyltransferase and the coactivator NCOA1 supply chromatin-modifying and bridging activity. Glucose flux is also read directly through O-GlcNAc modification of transcriptional regulators by OGT, linking hexose availability to promoter output.

Cells adjust which metabolic genes they transcribe according to the sugar available, and carbon catabolite activation of transcription is the arm of that control in which one carbon source, typically glucose, raises the transcription of genes handling other fuels. In mammals this is how a carbohydrate load is translated into a genomic programme for lipogenesis and glucose disposal, and its dysregulation underlies hepatic steatosis and the metabolic consequences of chronic overnutrition. The glucose-responsive transcription factor ChREBP, encoded by MLXIPL, partners with MLX and is licensed by glycolytic intermediates to occupy carbohydrate response elements. Nutrient status is further read out by O-GlcNAc transferase, which glycosylates transcriptional machinery in proportion to hexosamine flux, while coactivators including NCOA1 and the acetyltransferase KAT2B remodel chromatin at target promoters. The pathway links intermediary metabolism directly to nuclear gene expression rather than to acute enzyme regulation.

Embryonic development is regulated in rate and extent by control layers that sit above the individual lineage programmes, setting how fast cells divide, when they commit, and where axes and germ layers form. The genes here cluster into a few recognisable machines: the INO80 chromatin remodelling complex with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, SAGA-type histone acetyltransferase modules built around KAT2A/KAT2B with TADA2A and WDR5, and HDAC1/HDAC2-containing corepressor assemblies, all of which reshape nucleosomes and histone marks as the zygotic genome is activated. Alongside them sit WNT ligands and beta-catenin, the NODAL arm of TGF-beta with its TGIF repressors, and transcription factors such as OTX2, LHX1, SOX17, FOXA2 and HNF4A that specify endoderm and anterior structures. A distinct subset -- NLRP5, NLRP7, PADI6, OOEP, TLE6, KHDC3L -- forms the oocyte subcortical maternal complex, whose loss causes early embryonic arrest and hydatidiform mole. Laminins supply the basement membrane on which these events are organised.

Once T cells are activated they must be reined in, and this braking of activated T cell proliferation is what keeps an immune response proportionate and prevents autoimmunity and immunopathology after the threat is cleared. The genes here act through several distinct brakes: surface ligands such as CD274 and PDCD1LG2 engage inhibitory receptors on the responding T cell, galectin-9 and butyrophilin-family and LILRB4 molecules deliver further co-inhibitory signals, arginase depletes the arginine that proliferating lymphocytes require, and LRRC32 tethers latent TGF-beta at the cell surface. FOXP3 defines the regulatory T cell lineage that enforces much of this suppression, while RC3H1 degrades mRNAs encoding costimulatory molecules and caspase-3 contributes to deletion of expanded clones. Tumours and chronic infections exploit these same checkpoints to blunt effector responses, which is why they are the targets of checkpoint blockade.

Glucose availability is itself a transcriptional signal, and this is the machinery that converts nutrient status into changes in gene expression, tuning lipogenic, glycolytic and stress-response programmes to how much sugar a cell is handling. In the fed state, sugar-sensing transcription factors such as MLXIPL and USF1 turn on lipogenic and carbohydrate-response genes in liver and adipose tissue; the same circuitry, run in reverse during fasting, depends on the NAD+-dependent deacetylase SIRT1 to repress them. Glucose flux is also read chemically: O-GlcNAc transferase modifies transcription factors and chromatin proteins in proportion to hexosamine supply, while acetyltransferase and histone methyltransferase activities set the chromatin context. Persistent misreading of this signal contributes to hepatic steatosis, hypertriglyceridaemia and the transcriptional component of insulin resistance, linking metabolism directly to gene regulation.

AMP sits at the hub of adenine nucleotide economy, and the reactions that make, interconvert and dispose of it set the cell's energy charge and its supply of adenine nucleotides for RNA, cofactors and signalling. Synthesis runs two ways: the multistep de novo purine route building IMP from ribose-5-phosphate through PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS and ATIC, then adenylosuccinate synthetase and lyase converting IMP to AMP; and salvage, where APRT and HPRT1 recapture free bases and adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine. Adenylate kinases equilibrate AMP, ADP and ATP across cytosol and mitochondria, an exchange that generates the AMP signal read by energy-sensing kinases. Catabolism proceeds through AMP deaminase and 5'-nucleotidases toward inosine, hypoxanthine and ultimately urate via xanthine dehydrogenase. Defects here cause gout, myoadenylate deaminase deficiency, and immunodeficiency from loss of adenosine deaminase; extracellular NT5E generates immunosuppressive adenosine.

Cells spend and remake their ATP continuously, and this pathway covers the reactions that generate and consume it, together with the regulators that match supply to demand. Two routes dominate: glycolysis, from hexokinases and phosphofructokinases through aldolase, GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, represented here by the complex I subunits, succinate dehydrogenase, and the F1Fo ATP synthase with its inhibitory factor. Adenylate kinases interconvert adenine nucleotides to buffer the energy charge, while AMP-activated protein kinase and mTOR complex components sense it and reset anabolic and catabolic programmes, and HIF1A shifts flux toward glycolysis in hypoxia. Also included are ATP-consuming ion pumps, insulin and insulin-receptor signalling that drives glucose uptake, and mitochondrial quality control through PINK1 and parkin. Defects here cause mitochondrial myopathies, glycolytic enzymopathies with haemolysis, and the metabolic rewiring typical of tumours.

Cells obtain pyrimidine nucleotides either by building them from scratch or by recycling cytidine and uridine released from degraded RNA and taken up from the diet, and CMP metabolism sits at the heart of that salvage route. Uridine-cytidine kinases phosphorylate cytidine and uridine directly to CMP and UMP, deoxycytidine kinase handles the deoxyribose forms, and cytidine deaminase converts cytidine to uridine, shunting carbon toward uracil. What is not salvaged is broken down: phosphorylases release the free base, and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase open the ring toward beta-alanine. These enzymes determine the fate of nucleoside analogue drugs such as gemcitabine, cytarabine and 5-fluorouracil, so variation in them drives both chemotherapy resistance and severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity, while inherited deficiency causes neurological and metabolic disease.

Guanosine monophosphate sits at the branch point of purine supply, feeding GTP for RNA synthesis, translation, G-protein signalling and DNA replication, so GMP metabolism sets how fast a cell can proliferate. The pathway combines de novo synthesis of the purine ring from phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate through the multistep route carried by PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS, ADSL and ATIC, conversion of inosine monophosphate to GMP by IMPDH1/2 and GMPS, salvage of guanine and hypoxanthine by HPRT1, phosphorylation by guanylate kinase, and catabolism through guanine deaminase and xanthine oxidase to urate. Loss of HPRT1 salvage causes Lyme-Nyhan syndrome, and IMPDH inhibition is the basis of mycophenolate immunosuppression, while nucleotidases and AMP deaminases tune the balance between adenine and guanine pools. Several membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffold proteins, including DLG family and MAGI3 members, are included by domain homology rather than catalytic activity.

GTP metabolic process covers the reactions that make, interconvert and consume GTP, the nucleotide that fuels protein synthesis, microtubule dynamics and the entire family of regulatory GTP-binding switches. Because GTP pools are set separately from ATP pools, this chemistry determines whether translation, ribosome assembly and small-GTPase signalling can proceed at all; its failure is felt in proliferating cells first, and inhibiting the committed step is the basis of immunosuppressive therapy. Two arms are represented: de novo and salvage supply, where IMPDH1/2 control the rate-limiting oxidation of inosine monophosphate and nucleoside diphosphate kinases (NME family) transfer phosphate to GDP, and consumption by hydrolytic GTPases -- Ran in nucleocytoplasmic transport, Rab and Rho proteins in membrane traffic, and mitofusin and OPA1 in mitochondrial fusion and inner-membrane remodelling. LRRK2 links the same nucleotide chemistry to Parkinson disease.

GTP is both the nucleotide substrate for RNA synthesis and the switch that powers most molecular motors and signalling GTPases, so the reactions that make, interconvert and hydrolyse it set the pace for growth and intracellular traffic. Synthesis here runs through IMP dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting step of de novo guanine nucleotide production and the target of immunosuppressive drugs, while nucleoside diphosphate kinases of the NME family and adenylate kinase relatives phosphorylate GDP and balance nucleotide pools across cytosol and mitochondria. The consuming side is represented by hydrolases that use GTP to do work: RAN for nucleocytoplasmic transport, RAB and RHO family members for vesicle and cytoskeletal control, heterotrimeric G protein subunits for receptor signalling, and the mitochondrial dynamin-like proteins OPA1 and MFN1 for inner- and outer-membrane fusion. Depletion of guanine nucleotides therefore stalls proliferation, protein synthesis and organelle remodelling simultaneously.

Inosine monophosphate sits at the branch point of purine nucleotide supply, and the reactions that make, consume and recycle it determine whether a cell has adequate ATP and GTP for replication, translation and signalling. The de novo arm builds IMP stepwise from ribose-5-phosphate and glutamine through multifunctional enzymes such as PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS and ATIC, while salvage routes let HPRT1 and APRT rebuild nucleotides from hypoxanthine and adenine rather than paying the full biosynthetic cost. From IMP, adenylosuccinate synthetase and adenylosuccinate lyase route flux to AMP, and AMP deaminases return AMP to IMP, a cycle that buffers adenylate charge in exercising muscle. Catabolic steps through nucleotidases, purine nucleoside phosphorylase and xanthine oxidase end in urate. Defects here cause immunodeficiency, myopathy with exercise intolerance, gout and, in the case of HPRT1 loss, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.

UDP sits at the hub of pyrimidine nucleotide traffic, and the reactions that make and consume it keep cells supplied with the uridine nucleotides needed for RNA synthesis, glycogen and glycoprotein assembly, and phospholipid head-group activation. De novo synthesis contributes here through the multienzyme CAD protein, the mitochondrial dehydrogenase DHODH that couples orotate oxidation to the respiratory chain, and UMPS, which decarboxylates orotidine monophosphate to UMP; a nucleoside monophosphate kinase then phosphorylates UMP to UDP. Working in the opposite direction, ENTPD-family nucleotidases hydrolyse UTP and UDP, several of them inside the secretory pathway where they recycle the UDP released by glycosyltransferases and so sustain glycosylation. Blocking this route is the basis of antiproliferative and immunosuppressive drugs, since dividing lymphocytes and tumour cells depend on continuous pyrimidine supply, and inherited defects cause orotic aciduria.

Uridine monophosphate is not only recycled but also disposed of, and this degradative route is how cells clear excess pyrimidine nucleotides and convert them to beta-alanine and ammonia. It sets the size of the uridine and uracil pools available for salvage, and it is the route that detoxifies fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy: patients with reduced dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity suffer severe, sometimes fatal 5-fluorouracil toxicity, while loss of the downstream ring-opening step causes dihydropyrimidinuria with neurological disease. Mechanistically, a cytosolic 5'-nucleotidase removes the phosphate to give uridine, uridine phosphorylases cleave the ribosidic bond to release uracil and ribose-1-phosphate, and DPYD then reduces uracil to dihydrouracil in the committed, rate-limiting step before DPYS hydrolyses the ring. The pathway links nucleotide turnover to amino acid and central carbon metabolism, and to drug clearance in the liver.

UTP is the uridine nucleotide that powers RNA synthesis, sugar activation for glycosylation and glycogen, and lipid head-group assembly, so the reactions that make and consume it set the supply of a currency used well beyond transcription. Production runs largely through nucleoside diphosphate kinases, which transfer a phosphate from ATP to UDP; the NME family members here act in the cytosol, mitochondria and on ciliary or flagellar structures, and NME1 has additional roles in metastasis suppression. CAD carries the first committed steps of de novo pyrimidine synthesis that feed the pool, while ENTPD7 hydrolyses nucleoside triphosphates in intracellular vesicles and AK3 handles GTP-dependent phosphoryl transfer in mitochondria. Balancing synthesis against hydrolysis keeps pyrimidine pools matched to demand, and imbalance distorts nucleotide ratios, glycosylation and proliferative capacity.

Deoxyadenosine monophosphate sits at the junction between DNA precursor supply and purine breakdown, and the reactions that make and consume it set the size of the deoxyadenine nucleotide pool available for replication and repair. Salvage kinases phosphorylate deoxyadenosine to dAMP in the cytosol and in mitochondria, while a 5'-nucleotidase dephosphorylates it back, so the two activities form a substrate cycle that buffers pool size; the released deoxynucleoside can instead be deaminated and cleaved to hypoxanthine and oxidised toward urate for disposal. Because mitochondria depend on salvage rather than on de novo synthesis for their dNTPs, loss of the mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase causes mitochondrial DNA depletion and hepatocerebral disease, while failure to clear deoxyadenosine allows dATP to accumulate to lymphotoxic levels, the basis of adenosine deaminase deficiency and severe combined immunodeficiency.

dGMP metabolic process governs the turnover of deoxyguanosine monophosphate, the nucleotide that must be supplied in balanced amounts for DNA replication and repair and cleared when it is in excess or damaged. Guanylate kinase phosphorylates dGMP onward toward dGTP, while cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases such as NT5C, NT5C1A and NT5C2 dephosphorylate it back to deoxyguanosine, setting up a substrate cycle that tunes the size of the deoxynucleotide pool; downstream, guanine deaminase and xanthine oxidoreductase feed the freed base into purine catabolism and urate production. DNPH1 hydrolyses the modified nucleotide 5-hydroxymethyl-dCMP-like species and sanitises the pool against genotoxic incorporation. Imbalance here distorts replication fidelity, and these same enzymes determine the activation and clearance of nucleoside analogue drugs used in leukaemia and antiviral therapy.

Cells must keep the deoxyribonucleotide pool balanced, and dGMP metabolism is the set of reactions that make, phosphorylate and dispose of deoxyguanosine monophosphate on the way to and from DNA precursors. The balance matters because excess or depleted dGTP pools distort replication fidelity, and because guanine breakdown feeds urate production. Guanylate kinase phosphorylates GMP and dGMP toward the diphosphate needed for DNA synthesis, while several 5'-nucleotidases dephosphorylate the monophosphate back to deoxyguanosine, setting the direction of a substrate cycle. Salvage and catabolism continue through guanine deaminase to xanthine and xanthine dehydrogenase to urate, linking this chemistry to purine turnover and to hyperuricaemia when catabolism runs high. A related hydrolase clears modified deoxyribonucleotides, a step exploited therapeutically to sensitise tumour cells to nucleoside analogues.

Breakdown of dGMP disposes of deoxyguanosine monophosphate arising from DNA turnover and from the deoxynucleotide pool, keeping precursor supply balanced and preventing the nucleotide imbalances that distort replication fidelity. Cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases remove the phosphate to give deoxyguanosine, which guanine deaminase converts toward xanthine, and xanthine dehydrogenase completes oxidation to urate for excretion; a nucleotide N-glycosidase offers an alternative route that cleaves the base directly from the sugar phosphate. The same enzymes govern how much of a purine is salvaged versus degraded, so their activity sets intracellular deoxynucleotide levels and influences the activation of nucleoside-analogue drugs. Excess flux through the terminal oxidation step contributes to hyperuricaemia and gout, while nucleotidase activity in this route affects sensitivity to thiopurine and cytarabine-type chemotherapeutics, linking deoxypurine catabolism to both purine homeostasis and pharmacology.

cAMP is the second messenger that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at the cell surface into changes in protein kinase A activity, and its metabolism — the balance between synthesis and hydrolysis — sets how strong and how brief that signal is. This balance underlies pacemaker activity in the heart, water and calcium handling in kidney and bone, learning-related plasticity in neurons, and the resolution of inflammation. Membrane adenylate cyclases coupled to G proteins generate cAMP from ATP, with the soluble, bicarbonate- and calcium-sensitive ADCY10 acting independently of receptors and serving sperm capacitation. Opposing them, cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases of several families degrade cAMP to AMP and confine it to subcellular microdomains; PDE4 inhibition is exploited therapeutically in airway and skin inflammation. Upstream inputs here include parathyroid hormone and its related peptide, PACAP and neurotensin receptors, which raise or lower cyclase output.

Deoxycytidine monophosphate sits at the junction between DNA precursor supply and pyrimidine breakdown, and the reactions grouped here govern how the cell disposes of it and recycles its parts. Dephosphorylation by cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases releases deoxycytidine, cytidine deaminase converts cytidine and deoxycytidine to uridine and deoxyuridine, uridine phosphorylases cleave the nucleoside to uracil and a sugar phosphate, and dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase followed by dihydropyrimidinase opens the ring for terminal catabolism. Together these steps set the balance between salvage and degradation, and so shape the size and symmetry of the deoxynucleotide pools that replication and repair draw on. The same enzymes determine the fate of cytidine and fluoropyrimidine analogue drugs: deaminase activity inactivates cytarabine and gemcitabine, while loss of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase causes severe fluorouracil toxicity, and defects further down the route produce inherited pyrimidine degradation disorders with neurological features.

Cyclic GMP is a second messenger that relaxes smooth muscle, tunes natriuresis, and carries the light signal in photoreceptors, and this pathway covers both its synthesis and its destruction. Guanylate cyclases make it: the soluble heterodimeric enzyme built from GUCY1A and GUCY1B subunits responds to nitric oxide in vascular smooth muscle, while membrane-bound receptor cyclases are activated by the natriuretic peptides ANP, BNP and CNP acting through NPR1 and NPR2, or by retinal guanylate cyclases that restore cGMP after phototransduction. Phosphodiesterases including PDE5A, PDE2A, PDE9A and PDE10A hydrolyse it, setting the duration of the signal and making them drug targets in erectile dysfunction, pulmonary hypertension and heart failure. Loss of tone in this system contributes to hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy, skeletal dysplasia through CNP signalling, and inherited retinal degeneration.

Thymidylate (dTMP) is the one deoxynucleotide DNA synthesis cannot borrow from RNA precursors, so the reactions that make and degrade it set the pace of replication and repair. Thymidylate synthase builds dTMP from dUMP using a methylene group carried by folate, which is regenerated in part through serine hydroxymethyltransferase; dUTPase keeps the competing dUTP pool low so that uracil is not misincorporated into DNA, a failure that triggers futile excision repair and strand breaks. Salvage and catabolic steps run alongside, with deoxycytidylate deaminase feeding dUMP into the pool, thymidine phosphorylase and uridine phosphorylases releasing bases from nucleosides, and 5'-nucleotidases dephosphorylating pyrimidine monophosphates. Because tumour cells depend heavily on this supply, the route is the target of fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy, and inherited defects in its components cause nucleotide imbalance and mitochondrial DNA instability.

Breakdown of dTMP, the immediate precursor of the DNA building block dTTP, is how cells dispose of surplus thymidine nucleotides and recycle the sugar and base for other uses. Cytosolic 5'-nucleotidases remove the phosphate to give thymidine, and phosphorylases then cleave the nucleoside into thymine and deoxyribose-1-phosphate, which can feed back into pentose metabolism. Because this route sets the size of the thymidine pool available for salvage into DNA, it matters for genome replication and for the balance of deoxynucleotide pools; loss of thymidine phosphorylase activity allows thymidine to accumulate, unbalancing mitochondrial dNTP supply and producing mitochondrial DNA depletion and the multisystem disease MNGIE. The same enzymes govern the activation and inactivation of pyrimidine analogue chemotherapeutics, making this catabolic arm of nucleotide turnover a determinant of drug response.

dUMP sits at the junction between pyrimidine salvage and DNA synthesis: it is the substrate thymidylate synthase converts to dTMP, and it is also the sink into which excess dUTP must be diverted to keep uracil out of DNA. Handling it correctly matters because dUTP that escapes into replication is incorporated opposite adenine, triggering repair cycles and strand breaks; a dUTP-hydrolysing pyrophosphatase guards against this, while deoxycytidylate deamination supplies dUMP from the cytosine branch. Nucleotidases of the 5'-nucleotidase family dephosphorylate dUMP to deoxyuridine, which uridine phosphorylases and the dihydropyrimidine degradation enzymes can shunt toward catabolism. The balance set here determines thymidylate supply and, clinically, sensitivity to fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy and toxicity when dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase activity is deficient.

Breakdown of dUMP disposes of a deoxynucleotide that, if allowed to accumulate, distorts thymidylate metabolism and promotes uracil misincorporation into DNA. The route begins with dephosphorylation by 5'-nucleotidases, including cytosolic NT5C and NT5C3A and the mitochondrial NT5M, releasing deoxyuridine; uridine phosphorylases UPP1 and UPP2 then cleave the nucleoside to uracil and deoxyribose-1-phosphate. Uracil enters reductive pyrimidine degradation, where dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPYD) reduces it and dihydropyrimidinase (DPYS) opens the ring toward β-ureidopropionate and ultimately β-alanine. This catabolic arm balances salvage and de novo synthesis, sets deoxyribonucleotide pool sizes for DNA replication and repair, and governs the clearance of pyrimidine analogue drugs: reduced DPYD activity causes severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity, while DPYD or DPYS deficiency produces neurological disease with accumulation of uracil and thymine.

Adenosine sits at the junction between nucleotide turnover and extracellular signalling, and the reactions that make and destroy it set how much of it is available to act on adenosine receptors. Production comes from dephosphorylation of AMP by cytosolic and ecto-5'-nucleotidases, including the cell-surface enzyme that, with CD39, converts released ATP into an anti-inflammatory adenosine signal in tissues and tumours. Removal is by deamination to inosine, which is then handed to purine catabolism through xanthine oxidoreductase toward urate. Loss of adenosine deaminase causes accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine nucleotides and severe combined immunodeficiency, while deficiency of the secreted ADA2 produces a vasculitis and immune dysregulation syndrome. The same chemistry governs purine salvage economy, cardiac and vascular tone, sleep pressure, and the immunosuppressive adenosine tone that limits T cell responses.

Guanine sits at a junction between recycling nucleic acid bases and disposing of them, and this metabolic process covers both fates. Salvage returns free guanine to the nucleotide pool: hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase transfers a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP to make GMP, sparing cells the energetic cost of building purine rings from scratch, and PRTFDC1 is a closely related phosphoribosyltransferase homologue. Degradation runs the other way, with guanine deaminase converting guanine to xanthine and xanthine dehydrogenase oxidising xanthine to uric acid, the terminal purine excretion product in humans. The balance matters clinically: loss of the salvage transferase causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease, while excess flux through the oxidative arm underlies gout and generates reactive oxygen species. Adequate guanine nucleotide supply also sustains GTP-dependent signalling, translation and RNA synthesis.

Inosine sits at the junction between purine salvage and purine breakdown, and the reactions that make and consume it determine how much adenosine a tissue sees and how much urate it excretes. Adenosine deaminases convert adenosine to inosine, purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves inosine to hypoxanthine and ribose-1-phosphate, and xanthine dehydrogenase oxidises hypoxanthine onward to xanthine and uric acid, the terminal product of human purine catabolism. The stakes are clinical: loss of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through accumulation of toxic deoxyadenosine nucleotides in lymphocytes, deficiency of the phosphorylase produces its own T cell immunodeficiency, and altered flux through the oxidase underlies hyperuricaemia and gout. Because adenosine is itself a signalling nucleoside acting on cell-surface receptors, its deamination also tunes vascular tone, inflammation and immune suppression rather than merely disposing of a metabolite.

Making the purine and pyrimidine bases that nucleic acids are built from, this biosynthetic route supplies the nucleotide pools needed for DNA replication, transcription and the deoxynucleotide demands of dividing cells. Both arms are represented: a glutamine-dependent phosphoribosyltransferase and the multifunctional GART and PAICS steps build the purine ring on a ribose phosphate donated by PRPS1, while CAD, dihydroorotate dehydrogenase and UMPS generate UMP for conversion to CTP by the CTP synthases. Salvage enzymes such as HPRT1 and APRT recycle preformed bases, and folate-dependent one-carbon transfer through DHFR, SHMT1 and thymidylate synthase supplies methyl groups for thymidine. Growth signalling via mTOR raises flux to match proliferation. These enzymes are classic chemotherapy and immunosuppressant targets, and inherited defects cause gout, immunodeficiency from ADA loss, and urea cycle disease.

Breakdown of the nitrogenous bases released from nucleic acid turnover feeds their carbon and nitrogen back into general metabolism and disposes of bases that would otherwise accumulate. Pyrimidine degradation proceeds through dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, which reduces uracil and thymine, then a hydantoinase ring-opening step, with ALDH6A1 handling the methylmalonate semialdehyde generated downstream of thymine; this route also clears the chemotherapeutic fluoropyrimidines, so DPYD deficiency causes severe 5-fluorouracil toxicity, and defects in these steps produce inherited aminoaciduria with neurological disease. On the purine side, guanine deaminase yields xanthine and xanthine dehydrogenase completes oxidation to urate, the endpoint of purine disposal in humans and the substance that precipitates in gout. Several dihydropyrimidinase-related proteins are included by homology; in practice they act as collapsin response mediator proteins guiding axon growth and cytoskeletal remodelling rather than catabolising bases.

Breakdown of 2'-deoxyribonucleosides releases the base from deoxyribose and feeds both units into salvage or disposal, keeping deoxynucleoside pools balanced and preventing toxic accumulation of intermediates. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves deoxyinosine and deoxyguanosine to their bases plus deoxyribose-1-phosphate, adenosine deaminase converts deoxyadenosine to deoxyinosine, and guanine deaminase and xanthine oxidoreductase carry the freed bases onward to urate for excretion; deoxyribose-phosphate aldolase splits the sugar into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and acetaldehyde, linking the route to central carbon metabolism. On the pyrimidine side, dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase initiates thymine and uracil degradation and also determines clearance of fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics. Loss of these steps is clinically stark: adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, because accumulating deoxynucleotides are especially lethal to lymphocytes.

purine deoxyribonucleoside metabolic process governs the turnover of deoxyadenosine and deoxyguanosine, the deoxyribose-linked purine nucleosides that sit between DNA breakdown and either salvage into nucleotide pools or catabolism to uric acid. Keeping these metabolites low matters most in lymphocytes: loss of adenosine deaminase allows deoxyadenosine and its phosphorylated derivatives to accumulate and kill developing T and B cells, producing severe combined immunodeficiency, while purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency causes a related immune failure with neurological disease. The genes trace the route itself — deaminases and a guanine deaminase strip amino groups, phosphorylase cleaves the glycosidic bond to free the base, and xanthine dehydrogenase completes oxidation to urate. Opposing this, mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase phosphorylates the same nucleosides to feed mitochondrial DNA replication, and its mutation causes hepatocerebral mtDNA depletion. The pathway thus balances nucleotide supply against nucleoside toxicity.

Purine deoxyribonucleoside metabolism handles the turnover and salvage of deoxyadenosine and deoxyguanosine, the nucleosides released when DNA is degraded, and it keeps their concentrations low enough that deoxynucleotide pools stay balanced. Adenosine deaminase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase strip and cleave these nucleosides toward hypoxanthine and guanine, guanine deaminase feeds xanthine into the final oxidation by xanthine dehydrogenase, and a mitochondrial deoxyguanosine kinase pulls salvaged nucleosides back into the phosphorylated pool used for mitochondrial DNA replication. The consequences of failure are well defined in humans: loss of adenosine deaminase or nucleoside phosphorylase allows toxic deoxynucleotide accumulation that kills developing lymphocytes and causes severe combined immunodeficiency, while deoxyguanosine kinase deficiency depletes mitochondrial DNA and produces hepatocerebral disease. The route also sets urate production, linking it to gout and to purine catabolism generally.

Pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside metabolism handles the interconversion and turnover of thymidine, deoxycytidine and deoxyuridine, the sugar-linked bases that feed DNA replication and repair. It matters because dividing cells and mitochondria must keep balanced dTTP pools: too little stalls replication, too much causes mutagenic misincorporation. The salvage arm recovers preformed deoxyribonucleosides by phosphorylation, with a cytosolic thymidine kinase that rises sharply in S phase and a mitochondrial counterpart that supplies the separate nucleotide pool used for mitochondrial DNA; loss of the latter causes mitochondrial DNA depletion with myopathy. A thymidylate kinase then completes the route to the triphosphate, while dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase initiates catabolic breakdown of uracil and thymine. These same enzymes determine the activation and clearance of pyrimidine analogue drugs, so variation in them shapes toxicity from fluoropyrimidine and antifolate chemotherapy.

Purine ribonucleoside catabolic process dismantles adenosine, inosine and guanosine, converting spent nucleosides into free bases, ribose-1-phosphate and ultimately uric acid for excretion. It sets the size of the cellular purine pool, disposes of nucleotides released by RNA turnover and cell death, and terminates the signalling actions of extracellular adenosine at its receptors. Adenosine deaminase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase perform the successive deamination and phosphorolysis steps, with xanthine dehydrogenase completing oxidation to urate; ENPP4 releases nucleoside from dinucleotide substrates upstream. The clinical stakes are high: loss of adenosine deaminase causes severe combined immunodeficiency because deoxyadenosine metabolites are toxic to lymphocytes, ADA2 deficiency produces a vasculitis and immune dysregulation syndrome, and excess flux through xanthine dehydrogenase underlies hyperuricaemia and gout. The pathway also feeds ribose-1-phosphate back into central carbon metabolism and supports purine salvage.

Purine ribonucleoside catabolism dismantles adenosine, inosine and guanosine, recovering ribose and funnelling the purine ring toward uric acid or back into salvage. It sets the ambient concentration of nucleosides that act as signalling molecules and immune modulators, so its failure is felt most sharply in lymphocytes: loss of adenosine deaminase allows deoxyadenosine and its nucleotides to accumulate and kill developing T and B cells, producing severe combined immunodeficiency, while deficiency of the related secreted deaminase causes a vasculitic and inflammatory syndrome. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase cleaves inosine and guanosine to their bases plus ribose-1-phosphate, and xanthine dehydrogenase performs the terminal oxidations to urate, the step whose overactivity underlies hyperuricaemia and gout. Additional phosphodiesterase and deaminase activities feed nucleosides in from extracellular nucleotides, linking this route to nucleotide turnover, purine salvage and adenosine receptor signalling.

Cells need a steady supply of pyrimidine nucleosides and their phosphorylated forms to copy DNA and make RNA, and this branch of pyrimidine nucleoside biosynthesis supplies them largely by recycling preformed bases and nucleosides rather than building rings from scratch. Thymidine kinases phosphorylate thymidine as the entry step, with a cytosolic enzyme that rises sharply in S phase and a mitochondrial counterpart that keeps the organelle's own deoxynucleotide pool filled; loss of the mitochondrial activity causes mitochondrial DNA depletion with myopathy and encephalopathy. A thymidylate kinase then converts dTMP onward toward dTTP, while dihydrofolate reductase activity regenerates the reduced folate needed for thymidylate synthesis, and a uridine-cytidine kinase relative feeds pyrimidine ribonucleosides into the same pools. Because the same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs, this chemistry also sets sensitivity to antiviral and chemotherapeutic prodrugs.

Vitamin supply must be matched to need, and this grouping covers the braking side of that balance: processes that slow or shut down the reactions by which vitamins are made, activated or turned over. Restraint matters because vitamin-derived cofactors and hormones drive transcription, one-carbon chemistry and redox reactions, and unchecked production is as disruptive as deficiency. The members act largely through transcriptional repression and enzymatic inactivation. GFI1 and the SNAI1/SNAI2 zinc-finger repressors recruit corepressor complexes to silence target promoters, NFKB1 contributes to inflammation-linked reprogramming of metabolic gene expression, and PRMT3 acts as an arginine methyltransferase modifying substrates that influence metabolic output. AKR1C3, an aldo-keto reductase, carries out reductive conversions of retinoid and prostaglandin substrates that lower the pool of active vitamin A derivatives, linking this control to differentiation and hormone signalling.

Tetrahydrobiopterin is the redox cofactor that lets aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthases run, so its synthesis and recycling set the supply of tyrosine, dopamine, serotonin and nitric oxide. Loss of it causes hyperphenylalaninaemia that phenylalanine restriction alone cannot fix, because the same cofactor deficit starves monoamine neurotransmitter production and produces dystonia and developmental delay. De novo synthesis runs from GTP through GTP cyclohydrolase I, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase and sepiapterin reductase, while regeneration after each hydroxylation step proceeds via pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase and dihydropteridine reductase, with dihydrofolate reductase providing a salvage route from dihydrobiopterin. Because endothelial nitric oxide synthase depends on this cofactor to couple electron flow to NO rather than superoxide, cofactor availability also governs vascular tone and oxidative stress in the endothelium.

Coloring matter in animals comes mainly from two chemistries, and pigment biosynthesis covers both: melanin made in melanosomes and the tetrapyrrole heme made in mitochondria and cytosol. Melanin production determines skin, hair and eye color and shields keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage; tyrosinase and its related enzymes TYRP1 and DCT act inside an organelle whose pH and metal supply are set by transporters such as OCA2, SLC45A2 and SLC24A5, with melanocyte output tuned by the melanocortin receptor MC1R responding to POMC-derived peptides and antagonized by agouti signaling protein. Loss of these steps produces albinism and pigmentary dilution. In parallel, ALAS-initiated porphyrin synthesis through HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX ends with ferrochelatase inserting iron, supplying hemoglobin and respiratory cytochromes; defects here cause porphyrias and sideroblastic anemia. Mitochondrial iron handling and melanosome trafficking link the two branches.

alcohol catabolic process covers the routes by which cells dispose of hydroxyl-bearing metabolites, converting them into aldehydes, acids, sulfate conjugates or glycolytic intermediates that can be oxidised or excreted. It matters because several of these substrates are toxic if allowed to accumulate: ethanol and its aldehyde, glycerol released from triglyceride, sorbitol and inositol from polyol metabolism, and cholesterol, whose only bulk disposal route is conversion to bile acids. Alcohol dehydrogenase and the aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH2 and ALDH1B1 handle the ethanol arm, and ALDH2 variants explain much of the population variation in alcohol tolerance and flushing. Glycerol kinase, triokinase and glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase channel small alcohols into glycolysis, while CYP7A1, CYP27A1 and CYP46A1 hydroxylate sterols for bile acid synthesis and brain cholesterol turnover. Sulfotransferases cap the process by making phenolic and steroid alcohols water-soluble for elimination.

Alcohols reach cells from diet, gut microbes and endogenous metabolism, and alcohol catabolism is how their hydroxyl groups are oxidised, reduced, conjugated or phosphorylated so the carbon can enter central metabolism or leave the body. The clearest route is ethanol disposal: an alcohol dehydrogenase generates acetaldehyde, mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidise it to acetate, and acetyl-CoA synthetases activate that acetate for lipogenesis or oxidation; loss of ALDH2 activity causes acetaldehyde accumulation and flushing. Related chemistry handles other hydroxylated substrates — glycerol kinases and glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase feed glycolysis, sorbitol and aldo-keto reductases interconvert sugar alcohols, and cytochrome P450 hydroxylases such as CYP7A1 and CYP46A1 commit cholesterol to bile acid synthesis and brain sterol turnover. Sulfotransferases cap the process by conjugating sterols, phenols and hormones for excretion, linking this catabolism to detoxification, redox balance and lipid homeostasis.

Grouped here are the routes by which cells make hydroxyl-bearing metabolites, dominated by cholesterol synthesis and its regulation but extending to steroid hormones, vitamin D, bile acids, sphingoid bases and inositol phosphates. The output supplies membrane sterol for fluidity and raft formation, precursors for adrenal and gonadal steroids, and signalling lipids, so the pathway sits at the centre of lipid homeostasis and endocrine function. The mevalonate arm runs from HMGCS1 and HMGCR through squalene epoxidation by SQLE to the post-lanosterol demethylation and reduction steps, with SREBF2, SCAP and INSIG proteins sensing sterol levels in the endoplasmic reticulum to set flux, and AMP-activated kinase subunits linking it to energy status. Cytochrome P450 enzymes such as CYP7A1, CYP27B1 and CYP17A1 divert sterol into oxygenated products, while serine palmitoyltransferase subunits and ceramidases generate sphingosine. Defects cause hypercholesterolaemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, rickets and sterol-synthesis malformation syndromes.

Formation of polyols — alcohols bearing three or more hydroxyls on saturated carbons — groups together several otherwise unrelated biosynthetic routes that supply small hydroxylated metabolites used as signals, cofactors and osmolytes. One arm makes myo-inositol and its phosphorylated derivatives, with inositol-3-phosphate synthase and inositol monophosphatases generating free inositol and kinase families (ITPK, IPMK, IP6K, PPIP5K) elaborating inositol phosphates and pyrophosphates that govern calcium release, phosphate sensing and vesicle traffic. A second arm generates tetrahydrobiopterin through GCH1, PTS and sepiapterin reductase with QDPR-mediated regeneration, the cofactor required for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and nitric oxide synthase; its deficiency causes hyperphenylalaninaemia and neurotransmitter failure. Sphingoid bases arise from serine palmitoyltransferase subunits and ceramidases, while cytochrome P450 hydroxylases build the vitamin D hormone. Glycerol-related output links to gluconeogenic PCK enzymes and osmotic balance.

Sugar alcohols such as glycerol, sorbitol, myo-inositol and other polyols enter central metabolism only after being broken down, and polyol catabolism is the set of reactions that does it, feeding carbon into glycolysis, gluconeogenesis and lipid synthesis. This matters most in liver, kidney and adipose tissue, where glycerol released by lipolysis is recovered as an energy substrate, and in tissues that must dispose of osmotically active polyols. Glycerol kinase phosphorylates glycerol, mitochondrial glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase links the resulting triose to the respiratory chain as part of the glycerophosphate shuttle, and triosephosphate isomerase channels the product into glycolysis. Sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidises sorbitol to fructose, completing the polyol pathway whose flux is implicated in diabetic cataract and neuropathy, while myo-inositol oxygenase opens the inositol ring toward glucuronate. Triokinase/FMN cyclase handles related short-chain phosphorylation steps.

Grouped here are the routes that produce compounds bearing an aldehyde group, a chemical class broader than any single metabolic route. Much of the content is adrenal: the steroid 11-beta-hydroxylases CYP11B1 and CYP11B2 generate cortisol and aldosterone, the latter carrying the C18 aldehyde that gives it its name, and mineralocorticoid output sets sodium retention and blood pressure. Accordingly the set includes regulators of zona glomerulosa identity and excitability — the T-type calcium channel CACNA1H, the chloride channel CLCN2, WNT4 and BMP ligands, DAB2 and the transcriptional repressor REST — whose mutation causes familial hyperaldosteronism. A second strand is vitamin B6 activation by PDXK and PNPO, which yields the aldehyde cofactor pyridoxal 5'-phosphate, while TKT, TPI1 and PCK1 handle aldehyde-bearing sugar phosphates in central carbon metabolism.

Aldehydes are reactive carbonyl compounds generated by alcohol oxidation, lipid peroxidation, sugar metabolism and amino acid turnover, and they crosslink proteins and DNA if allowed to persist; aldehyde catabolism is the set of reactions that converts them into harmless carboxylic acids, alcohols or downstream metabolites. Its failure underlies alcohol intolerance and elevated cancer risk in people carrying the low-activity ALDH2 variant, and contributes to carbonyl stress in diabetes and neurodegeneration. Oxidative routes use NAD-dependent aldehyde dehydrogenases, while reductive routes run through aldo-keto reductases such as AKR1A1 and alcohol dehydrogenases including the formaldehyde-handling ADH5. Related thiolester and glyoxal detoxification enzymes, among them hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase and the deglycase-active PARK7, clear methylglyoxal adducts, and transaminases such as AGXT convert glyoxylate to glycine, a step whose loss causes primary hyperoxaluria with kidney stone disease.

Formation of phenolic compounds in humans converges on tyrosine and tryptophan chemistry, and the genes here trace two of its major outputs: catecholamine neurotransmitters and melanin pigment. Tyrosine hydroxylase, aromatic amino acid decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase and PNMT build dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline in dopaminergic neurons and chromaffin cells, supported by tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis through GCH1 and by phenylalanine hydroxylase; loss of these steps underlies dopa-responsive dystonia, phenylketonuria and the vulnerability of nigral neurons in Parkinson's disease. In melanocytes, tyrosinase, TYRP1 and DCT within melanosomes generate eumelanin and pheomelanin, with transporters such as OCA2, SLC45A2 and SLC24A5 setting melanosomal conditions and MC1R signalling determining pigment type; mutations cause albinism and account for much normal variation in skin and hair colour. Transcription factors including GATA3, HAND2 and ZEB2 specify the cells that carry out this synthesis.

Cells switch between burning fat and burning glucose depending on nutrient supply, and the regulation of fatty acid oxidation is the control layer that sets how fast fatty acids are delivered into mitochondria and peroxisomes and broken down. It matters most during fasting, exercise and cold, when hepatic and muscle tissue must mobilise lipid for ATP and ketone production; when the controls fail, lipid accumulates, insulin sensitivity falls and cardiac and hepatic steatosis follow. The nuclear receptors PPARA and PPARD with the coactivator PPARGC1A drive the transcriptional arm, inducing uptake and beta-oxidation enzymes. Flux is gated metabolically at the carnitine shuttle, where CPT1A activity is restrained by malonyl-CoA, itself set by the balance of ACACB and the decarboxylase MLYCD. Insulin signalling through IRS proteins and AKT, PDK4 induction, lipid droplet protein PLIN5 and peroxisomal transporters add further tiers of restraint or permission.

Cells switch to burning fatty acids when glucose is scarce, and this is the set of controls that turns that flux up — driving mitochondrial and peroxisomal β-oxidation in liver, muscle, heart and brown fat during fasting, exercise and cold. It matters because failure to raise fat oxidation leaves lipid accumulating in tissue, contributing to steatosis, insulin resistance and impaired endurance. The nuclear receptors PPARA and PPARD, with the coactivator PPARGC1A, drive transcription of the oxidative enzyme programme, while TWIST1 acts as a brake on it. Entry of long-chain acyl groups into mitochondria is set by CPT1A, and MLYCD lowers malonyl-CoA to relieve inhibition of that step; ABCD1 and ABCD2 import very-long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes. Insulin signalling through IRS1, IRS2 and AKT2, the stress cytokine GDF15, and lipid droplet-associated PLIN5 link substrate supply and whole-body energy demand to this output.

Cells that are well fed, or that need to build lipid rather than burn it, must actively switch off fat oxidation, and this is the braking arm of fatty acid catabolism. Restraining beta-oxidation spares fatty acids for triglyceride and membrane synthesis, protects against excess acetyl-CoA and ketone production, and helps set the fuel choice between glucose and lipid in liver, heart and muscle; loss of the brake contributes to insulin resistance and lipotoxic cardiac and hepatic disease. Mechanistically it works at several levels: ACACB generates malonyl-CoA at the outer mitochondrial membrane to block carnitine-dependent entry of long-chain acyl groups, DGAT2 diverts fatty acids into stored triacylglycerol, PLIN5 coats lipid droplets and limits lipolytic release to mitochondria, the mitochondrial sirtuin SIRT4 dampens acyl-CoA dehydrogenase flux, and insulin-activated AKT1 signalling reinforces the anabolic state.

Glucose cannot cross membranes unaided, and this pathway covers its import into cells together with the signalling that sets how much gets in. It underlies whole-body glucose homeostasis: muscle and fat take up glucose after a meal under insulin control, while brain, red cells and other tissues rely on constitutive uptake, and failure of the insulin-responsive arm is the core lesion of type 2 diabetes. Facilitative carriers of the SLC2A/GLUT family do the transport itself, with GLUT4 held in intracellular vesicles until insulin triggers its trafficking to the plasma membrane. That trigger runs from the insulin receptor through IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT to vesicle tethering and fusion machinery, with RHOQ, ASPSCR1 and sorting factors acting at the vesicle step. Adipokines and hepatokines such as leptin, adiponectin and FGF21, and negative regulators including GRB10 and ENPP1, tune sensitivity of the system.

Cells tune how much glucose they take up from the blood, and this regulation of D-glucose import across the plasma membrane is the control layer that sets that rate. In muscle and adipose tissue it is dominated by insulin: the receptor autophosphorylates, recruits IRS1 and IRS2 with the PI3K regulatory subunit, and activates AKT1/AKT2, which releases GLUT4-containing vesicles from intracellular storage for docking and fusion at the cell surface via TBC1D-like and Rho-family components such as RHOQ, with ASPSCR1 and SORBS1 acting on the trafficking step. Adipokines and hepatic hormones including adiponectin, leptin, FGF21 and IGF1 modulate sensitivity, while TNF, ENPP1, GRB10, PTPN11 and specific microRNAs dampen the signal. Loss of this control produces insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes; excess uptake supports the glycolytic shift of proliferating cells, with hexokinase 2 trapping incoming glucose.

Cells restrain how much glucose they take up, and this braking arm of glucose transport keeps uptake matched to demand rather than maximal. The genes here act mostly by damping insulin signalling and the trafficking of glucose transporters to the plasma membrane: GRB10 and PEA15 restrict insulin receptor and downstream kinase output, ENPP1 and APPL2 blunt receptor-proximal signalling, GSK3A opposes the anabolic arm, and STXBP3 participates in the vesicle fusion steps that deliver transporters to the surface. Hormonal and inflammatory inputs feed in through leptin, CART and TNF, while the microRNAs of the miR-103/107 and miR-143 families tune the same axis post-transcriptionally, and SIRT6 and SELENOS act through transcriptional and ER-stress-linked control. Loss of this restraint produces unchecked uptake; excessive restraint is the molecular substance of insulin resistance in muscle and adipose tissue.

positive regulation of D-glucose import across plasma membrane covers the signals that push cells to take up glucose from blood or extracellular fluid, the step that sets postprandial glucose disposal in muscle and fat and keeps circulating glucose within range. Its centrepiece is insulin action: insulin binding its receptor recruits IRS1 and IRS2, activates PI3K and the AKT1/AKT2 kinases, and drives GLUT4-containing vesicles to the cell surface, with RHOQ, CLTCL1 and SORBS1 acting on the trafficking and cytoskeletal steps. Adipokines and hepatokines including adiponectin, FGF21 and CTRP12 sensitise this axis, while IGF1, PTH and stress-responsive regulators such as MAPK14 and NFE2L2 modulate uptake capacity. Transcriptional inputs from KLF15 and MEF2A set transporter expression. Blunting of this regulation is the defining lesion of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

Muscle and fat cells take up glucose from blood only when told to, and this pathway covers the signals that switch that uptake on, raising the rate of glucose import across the plasma membrane. It is the basis of postprandial glucose clearance: insulin binds its receptor, IRS1 and IRS2 relay to PI3K and the AKT1/AKT2 kinases, and downstream effectors including the Rho-family GTPase RHOQ (TC10) and clathrin-related trafficking machinery drive glucose transporter vesicles to the cell surface. Adipose-derived and hepatic hormones such as adiponectin, IGF1 and FGF21 feed into the same output, as do transcriptional regulators and a microRNA that tune transporter abundance. Loss of this positive regulation produces insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, while excessive signalling underlies hypoglycaemia; the components are also the standard readout for metabolic action of insulin-sensitising drugs.

The JNK cascade is a stress-activated MAP kinase route that converts inflammatory, cytokine, oxidative and developmental cues into changes in transcription, apoptosis and cytoskeletal behaviour, and the genes here set how strongly and how long that cascade fires. Tuning matters because sustained JNK output drives cell death, insulin resistance and inflammatory tissue damage, while too little impairs wound responses, planar polarity and neuronal morphogenesis. Upstream kinases such as MAP3K5, MAP4K4, the TAOK and mixed-lineage kinases feed MAP2K7; scaffolds of the MAPK8IP family and SH3RF1 assemble productive modules, and dual-specificity phosphatases including DUSP10 and DUSP19 shut signalling off. Input arrives from Toll-like and interleukin-1 receptors through MYD88 and TRAF6, from TNF receptor family members via TRAF2 with RIPK1, from non-canonical WNT and Dishevelled, and from ER stress sensors, with ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases such as ITCH, XIAP and CYLD setting the threshold.

The JNK cascade drives stress-activated transcription, inflammatory gene expression and apoptosis, and it must be actively shut off for cells to survive transient stress without committing to death or chronic inflammation. Negative regulation of this cascade is carried out at every tier: dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP10, DUSP19 and DUSP3 dephosphorylate JNK and upstream MAP kinases, the deubiquitinase CYLD and the E3 ligase ITCH restrain the ubiquitin-dependent signals that feed MAP3K activation, and scaffold-binding proteins including AIDA and MAPK8IP1 partners can disrupt productive kinase assembly. Transcriptional corepressor components such as NCOR1, GPS2 and HDAC3 limit the output of JNK-driven AP-1 targets, while PINK1 and PRKN link mitochondrial quality control to reduced stress-kinase tone. Loss of such braking contributes to excessive apoptosis, insulin resistance, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease.

positive regulation of JNK cascade gathers the receptors, adaptors and kinases that switch on stress-activated JNK signalling, the arm of MAP kinase signalling that converts inflammatory, cytokine and stress cues into changes in gene expression, apoptosis and cytoskeletal remodelling. Its output determines whether a cell dies, differentiates or mounts an inflammatory response, and its inappropriate activation contributes to insulin resistance, neurodegeneration and chronic inflammation. Upstream triggers are diverse: Toll-like receptors and NOD-like sensors acting through MYD88, TIRAP and TRAF6; TNF and TNF-family receptors such as EDAR, LTBR and RANK working with RIPK1 and TRAF adaptors; non-canonical WNT ligands through Frizzled and Dishevelled; and ER stress sensed by IRE1. These converge on MAP3Ks including ASK1, MLK2/3 and TAOKs, and on MAP2K7, with scaffolds such as JIP1/JIP3 and SH3RF1 assembling the module and GADD45 proteins amplifying it during genotoxic and developmental stress.

The JNK cascade is a stress-activated MAP kinase route that converts inflammatory, cytokine, developmental and cell-stress inputs into changes in gene expression governing apoptosis, cell migration, differentiation and cytokine production; the genes here are those that switch it on or amplify it. Upstream receptors span innate immune sensing (Toll-like receptors with MYD88 and TIRAP, NOD1/NOD2, RIPK2), TNF-family receptors and their adaptors such as TRAF6 and RIPK1, non-canonical Wnt signalling through Frizzled and Dishevelled, and receptor tyrosine kinases. These converge on MAP3K-level kinases including MAP3K5, MAP3K10/11 and the TAOK and MINK1 kinases, on the dedicated activator MAP2K7, and on scaffolds such as MAPK8IP1 and SH3RF1 that assemble the module. GADD45 proteins couple genotoxic stress to the same output. Excessive flux contributes to inflammatory tissue damage, neuronal death and insulin resistance, while its activation underlies osteoclast differentiation and wound responses.

Phosphatidylethanolamine is the second most abundant phospholipid in animal cells and is concentrated on the cytosolic faces of internal membranes, where its cone shape favours membrane curvature, vesicle fusion, and mitochondrial cristae integrity; it is also the lipid anchor donor for autophagosome-conjugated ATG8 proteins and for GPI anchors. Its synthesis and turnover run through two routes: ethanolamine kinases and the cytidylyltransferase PCYT2 feed the Kennedy pathway, with CEPT1 and SELENOI transferring phosphoethanolamine onto diacylglycerol, while PISD decarboxylates phosphatidylserine to make PE inside mitochondria. Degradative and remodelling steps dominate the rest: multiple secreted and intracellular phospholipases A2 release fatty acids and lysophospholipids, and NAPEPLD with ABHD4 and NAAA route N-acylated PE toward endocannabinoid and N-acylethanolamine signalling. Loss of flux through these steps impairs mitochondrial function, autophagy, and lipid droplet and membrane biogenesis.

Diacylglycerol sits at the junction of fat storage and signalling, and the reactions that make and consume it decide whether a cell stores energy as triglyceride or transmits a lipid second messenger. Acyltransferases build it from monoacylglycerol and lysophosphatidate precursors and then esterify it to triacylglycerol via DGAT1 and DGAT2, the committed step of fat deposition in adipose tissue, liver and intestine, while lipases such as PNPLA2 and hormone-sensitive lipase run the route in reverse to mobilise stored lipid. On the signalling side, diacylglycerol generated by phospholipase C activates protein kinase C and related effectors, and the diacylglycerol kinase family terminates that signal by phosphorylating it to phosphatidic acid; DAGLA and DAGLB instead release the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol. Disordered flux through these steps contributes to hepatic steatosis, insulin resistance and altered lipid-mediated neurotransmission.

Diacylglycerol sits at a junction between lipid storage and signalling, and its catabolism determines how quickly that signal is terminated and what products are released. Two routes dominate here: diacylglycerol lipases DAGLA and DAGLB hydrolyse the sn-1 position of arachidonoyl-containing diacylglycerol to generate 2-arachidonoylglycerol, the principal endocannabinoid acting on presynaptic CB1 receptors to dampen neurotransmitter release, while diacylglycerol kinase DGKD instead phosphorylates diacylglycerol to phosphatidic acid, ending protein kinase C activation and feeding glycerophospholipid synthesis. Hormone-sensitive lipase contributes to the stepwise breakdown of stored glycerides during lipolysis, and phospholipase B activity provides further acyl hydrolysis. Because the same molecule both activates kinases and serves as an endocannabinoid precursor, the balance among these enzymes shapes synaptic plasticity, appetite and pain signalling, adipocyte fat mobilisation, and insulin sensitivity, with excess diacylglycerol accumulation implicated in lipid-induced metabolic disease.

CDP-diacylglycerol is the activated lipid intermediate through which cells commit phosphatidic acid to the anionic phospholipids, and its metabolism sets the supply of phosphatidylinositol in the endoplasmic reticulum and of phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin inside mitochondria. Membrane biogenesis, mitochondrial cristae structure and the whole inositol lipid signalling system depend on this step. Glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases and the AGPAT family build phosphatidic acid by sequential acylation, CDS1 and CDS2 then activate it with CTP to form CDP-diacylglycerol, TAMM41 performs the equivalent activation on the mitochondrial inner membrane, and CDIPT condenses the intermediate with inositol to give phosphatidylinositol. Related acyltransferase activity such as LCLAT1 remodels the acyl chains of the resulting lipids. Defects in this route disturb lipid droplet and adipose biology, as loss of AGPAT2 causes congenital generalised lipodystrophy, and impair cardiolipin-dependent mitochondrial function.

Amino sugar catabolic process breaks down hexosamines such as glucosamine, N-acetylglucosamine and sialic acid so their carbon and nitrogen can re-enter glycolysis and general metabolism rather than being lost. It closes the loop on glycan turnover: material released from degraded glycoproteins, glycosaminoglycans and dietary or microbial chitin is either recycled into UDP-GlcNAc for new glycosylation or dismantled to fructose-6-phosphate and ammonia. Chitinases and chitobiase cleave chitin and the chitobiose core of N-glycans, kinases and deacetylases such as NAGK and AMDHD2 process the released monosaccharides, GNPDA1/2 deaminate glucosamine-6-phosphate, and NPL cleaves sialic acid. Several members, notably the chitinase-like proteins CHI3L1 and CHIT1, have been repurposed as macrophage secretory products and serve as markers of inflammation, asthma and lysosomal storage disease. Loss of chitobiase activity impairs lysosomal glycoprotein degradation.

Amino sugars entering from glycan turnover, dietary chitin and cell surface sialic acid must be degraded before their carbon can be reused, and this catabolic route performs that dismantling. It feeds glucosamine and N-acetylglucosamine into glycolysis and converts sialic acid to pyruvate and N-acetylmannosamine, linking glycoconjugate breakdown to central energy metabolism and to the supply of precursors for renewed glycosylation. Chitinases and chitobiase cleave chitin and chito-oligosaccharides, a kinase phosphorylates N-acetylglucosamine, a deacetylase and glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminases strip the amine and acetyl groups, and an epimerase interconverts the acetylated hexosamines. Several members are chitinase-like lectins secreted by macrophages and epithelia that have lost catalytic activity and instead act in innate immunity and tissue remodelling, so this chemistry also shapes airway inflammation and asthma; loss of chitobiase causes a lysosomal storage disorder.

Amino sugar biosynthesis supplies the activated sugar donors that cells use to glycosylate proteins and lipids, build glycosaminoglycans and cap glycans with sialic acid. Its flagship route is the hexosamine pathway, in which glutamine:fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferases GFPT1 and GFPT2 commit fructose-6-phosphate to glucosamine-6-phosphate, followed by acetylation, phosphomutase conversion by PGM3 and pyrophosphorylase activity of UAP1 to yield UDP-GlcNAc. That nucleotide sugar feeds N- and O-linked glycosylation and O-GlcNAc modification, making the pathway a nutrient sensor that couples glucose, glutamine and acetyl-CoA availability to signalling and transcription. A downstream branch through GNE, NANS and NANP generates sialic acid for terminal glycan decoration. Catabolic deaminases and AMDHD2 return amino sugars to glycolysis, balancing the flux. Defects cause congenital myasthenic syndromes, immunodeficiency and hereditary inclusion body myopathy, and chronically elevated flux is linked to insulin resistance.

Dietary sugars arrive as disaccharides that no transporter will carry, so they must be split at the intestinal brush border before absorption; this disaccharide catabolic process is that final step of carbohydrate digestion. The enzymes named here are membrane-anchored hydrolases of the enterocyte apical surface: lactase releases glucose and galactose from milk lactose, sucrase-isomaltase handles sucrose and the branched limit dextrins left by amylase, maltase-glucoamylase trims maltose and linear oligosaccharides, and trehalase acts on trehalose from fungal foods. Their products feed into glycolysis and hepatic glucose handling. Loss or developmental decline of any one activity leaves unabsorbed sugar in the lumen, drawing water osmotically and feeding colonic fermentation, which produces the bloating, gas and diarrhoea of lactose intolerance and congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency.

Making sugar rather than burning it: this monosaccharide biosynthetic programme covers gluconeogenesis and related hexose- and polyol-forming routes that keep blood glucose available to brain and red cells during fasting. Its core enzymes run the carboxylation and dephosphorylation steps unique to glucose synthesis — pyruvate carboxylase, the cytosolic and mitochondrial PEPCK isoforms, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase with its ER transporter — alongside reversible glycolytic steps, aldolase, enolase and phosphoglycerate enzymes, plus pentose phosphate and sorbitol branches. Because output must match nutritional state, much of the set is regulatory: insulin, glucagon and leptin signalling converge on FOXO1, CRTC2, PPARGC1A and the glucocorticoid receptor, with AMPK subunits, sirtuins, acetyltransferases and circadian factors setting transcription and enzyme activity. Dysregulation here underlies fasting hypoglycaemia and glycogen storage disease on one side and the excessive hepatic glucose output of type 2 diabetes on the other.

Breaking down simple sugars for energy and biosynthetic precursors is the job of monosaccharide catabolism, and glycolysis is its central route: hexokinases and glucokinase trap glucose as glucose-6-phosphate, phosphofructokinases commit it, and the aldolase, triose phosphate isomerase, GAPDH, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase and pyruvate kinase steps deliver pyruvate plus ATP and NADH, with lactate dehydrogenase regenerating NAD+ when oxygen is limiting.
