Alongside this core, dedicated entry routes handle other sugars — galactose through galactokinase, the transferase and the epimerase, mannose through phosphomannose isomerase, fructose and ribose through triokinase and ribokinase, and pentose recycling through transketolase. Control is exerted by the fructose-2,6-bisphosphate cycle and by TIGAR, which lowers glycolytic flux and shifts carbon toward NADPH production. Defects in these enzymes cause galactosemia, hereditary fructose intolerance and haemolytic anaemias, and their upregulation supports the fermentative metabolism of proliferating and hypoxic cells.

Fucose must be activated to GDP-L-fucose before it can be attached to glycans, and this metabolic route is how cells make and supply that donor sugar. It matters because fucosylated glycans carry the ABO and Lewis blood group structures, direct leukocyte rolling on selectins, and tune Notch signalling; the core fucose added to antibody N-glycans by FUT8 also sets IgG effector potency. Two routes converge: de novo conversion of GDP-mannose by GMDS and the bifunctional reductase-epimerase GFUS, and a salvage arm in which FCSK phosphorylates free L-fucose and FPGT couples it to GTP, with FUOM handling fucose anomer interconversion. A dedicated transporter, SLC35C1, moves the finished donor into the Golgi lumen, and its loss causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency II with immunodeficiency and developmental delay, showing how directly glycan fucosylation depends on this supply line.

Sialic acids cap the glycans on most cell surface proteins and lipids, and before they can be attached they must be activated as CMP-N-acetylneuraminate, the sole donor used by sialyltransferases. Metabolism of this nucleotide sugar therefore sets the ceiling on sialylation, which governs cell-cell recognition, complement and Siglec-mediated self/non-self discrimination, serum protein half-life and neural adhesion. The route begins with an epimerase/kinase that converts UDP-GlcNAc to N-acetylmannosamine 6-phosphate, condensation with phosphoenolpyruvate to the sialic acid 9-phosphate, dephosphorylation, and finally nuclear activation with CTP by CMP-sialic acid synthetase; the product is then imported into the Golgi. Loss-of-function in the epimerase step causes hereditary inclusion body myopathy and sialuria, and defects in the synthase arm underlie a congenital disorder with skeletal dysplasia and developmental delay. The hydroxylase that would convert the CMP sugar to its N-glycolyl form is inactivated in humans, a species-specific loss relevant to xenoantigen responses.

Ribose phosphate biosynthesis supplies the phosphorylated sugar backbone from which all nucleotides are built, so this activity sits upstream of DNA and RNA synthesis, energy currency, and nucleotide-based second messengers. PRPP synthetases convert ribose-5-phosphate from the pentose phosphate branch into activated PRPP, which feeds de novo purine assembly (PPAT, GART, PFAS, PAICS, ATIC, ADSL) and pyrimidine synthesis through CAD, DHODH and UMPS, as well as salvage routes using HPRT1, APRT, ADK and uridine/cytidine kinases. Kinase families including adenylate kinases and NME nucleoside-diphosphate kinases interconvert mono-, di- and triphosphates, while mitochondrial respiratory complexes and ATP synthase regenerate the ATP these reactions consume. Adenylyl and guanylyl cyclases divert nucleotides into cAMP and cGMP signalling. Defects produce hyperuricaemia, gout, immunodeficiency and neurological disease, and the enzymes are longstanding targets of antiproliferative and immunosuppressive drugs.

PRPP, or 5-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate, is the activated ribose donor that every purine, pyrimidine, pyridine nucleotide and histidine/tryptophan-related salvage reaction draws on, and this pathway covers its production and control. Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetases transfer the pyrophosphoryl group of ATP onto ribose-5-phosphate coming out of the pentose phosphate pathway, setting the rate at which nucleotides can be made de novo or salvaged from free bases. Two associated proteins act as non-catalytic regulatory subunits of the synthetase complex, tuning activity alongside allosteric feedback from ADP and purine nucleotides. Because flux here dictates nucleotide supply, loss-of-function mutations in PRPS1 cause X-linked deafness, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and Arts syndrome, while gain-of-function superactivity floods the purine pathway and produces uric acid overproduction with gout and kidney stones.

Urate is the end product of purine breakdown in humans, and its metabolic handling sets the circulating level that determines whether crystals form in joints and kidneys. The genes here span both halves of that balance: production and transport. Purine nucleoside phosphorylase and PRPS1 feed the salvage and de novo arms of purine turnover, while G6PC1 and GCKR link urate output to hepatic carbohydrate flux, explaining why sugar and glycogen storage disorders raise uric acid. Most of the set, however, is renal and intestinal transport: SLC2A9 and SLC22A12 mediate urate reabsorption from the filtrate, whereas ABCG2, SLC17A1 and SLC17A3 secrete it, and common variants in these carriers are among the strongest determinants of serum urate and gout risk. Failure of excretion produces hyperuricemia, gouty arthritis and urate nephrolithiasis.

regulation of receptor signaling pathway via JAK-STAT governs how strongly and how long cytokine and growth factor receptors signal through Janus kinases to STAT transcription factors, setting the amplitude of immune responses, growth hormone and prolactin action, and haematopoiesis. Tight control matters because unrestrained JAK-STAT output drives inflammatory disease and myeloproliferative and lymphoid malignancy, while insufficient signalling causes immunodeficiency and growth failure. Positive input comes from ligands and their receptors -- interferons, IL-6, IL-7, IL-10, IL-12/IL-23, leptin, growth hormone and prolactin -- coupling through JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2. Restraint is imposed by feedback inhibitors of the SOCS/CISH family, phosphatases such as PTPN2, PTPRC and SH2B3, receptor trafficking and degradation, and microRNAs. Additional modulation arises from scaffolds and cofactors including caveolin-1, EP300 and Notch-pathway components, integrating JAK-STAT strength with cell adhesion, transcriptional coactivation and differentiation decisions.

Cytokine and hormone receptors signal to the nucleus through Janus kinases and STAT transcription factors, and this collection covers the processes that set how strongly and how long that signalling runs. Tuning matters because the same route carries interferon antiviral responses, interleukin-driven T helper differentiation, growth hormone, prolactin and leptin action, and erythroid and myeloid growth factor signals; unchecked output drives inflammation and myeloproliferative disease, while loss of input causes immunodeficiency and growth failure. Ligands and receptor chains such as IFNG, IL6, IL12/IL23 subunits, GHR, PRLR and the shared IL2RG chain provide the activating input through JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2. Negative control is prominent: SOCS1, SOCS2, SOCS3 and CISH form inducible feedback brakes, the phosphatases PTPN2 and PTPRC dephosphorylate receptor complexes, and SH2B3 restrains kinase activity. Acetyltransferase, ubiquitin and microRNA components add further layers.

Cytokine receptors signalling through JAK kinases and STAT transcription factors must be switched off promptly, and this is the braking system that does it. Without it, cytokine responses become chronic: unrestrained JAK-STAT output drives inflammation, lymphoproliferation and myeloid malignancy, and loss of individual brakes causes fulminant inflammatory disease in infancy. Several mechanisms converge here. SOCS proteins, including SOCS1 and SOCS3 plus the cytokine-inducible CISH, are STAT-induced feedback inhibitors that bind activated receptors and JAKs and direct them to degradation. Phosphatases such as PTPN2, PTPRC and SH2B3 strip activating phosphates from receptors and kinases, while receptor trafficking and endosomal sorting components, leptin receptor overlapping transcript and HGS among them, limit how long receptors persist at the surface. MicroRNAs including miR-146a add a transcriptional layer, tuning the strength of interleukin and interferon responses in immune cells.

Phosphate esters are the common currency of metabolism, and this catabolic branch covers their degradation: the breakdown of sugar phosphates, nucleotides, cyclic nucleotides, phospholipids and phosphoanhydrides back to simpler products. It supplies ATP and carbon skeletons, terminates second-messenger signals, and clears damaged or non-canonical building blocks before they poison the genome. The largest contingent is glycolytic — hexokinases, phosphofructokinases, enolases, pyruvate kinase and their PFKFB regulators — feeding glucose carbon toward pyruvate under insulin, HIF1A and mTOR/AMPK control. Nucleotide turnover is handled by 5'-nucleotidases, ecto-nucleotidases and NUDT hydrolases together with purine and pyrimidine salvage enzymes, while phosphodiesterases degrade cAMP and cGMP and phospholipases and sphingomyelinases release lipid-derived messengers. Loss of individual steps produces haemolytic anaemia, glycogen and lysosomal storage disease, immune dysregulation from nucleotide accumulation, and inherited neurodegeneration.

Eicosanoid biosynthesis converts twenty-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acids, chiefly arachidonic acid, into the prostaglandins, thromboxanes, prostacyclin and leukotrienes that drive inflammation, fever, pain, platelet aggregation, vascular tone and bronchoconstriction. It begins with phospholipases such as PLA2G4A liberating arachidonate from membrane phospholipids, after which two branches diverge: cyclooxygenases PTGS1 and PTGS2 generate the endoperoxide that terminal synthases convert to PGE2, PGD2, PGI2 or thromboxane A2, while ALOX5 with its activating protein ALOX5AP makes leukotriene A4, hydrolysed to LTB4 or conjugated to glutathione by LTC4S to yield the cysteinyl leukotrienes. Cytochrome P450 enzymes add hydroxy- and epoxy-eicosanoid routes. Inflammasome components and cytokines here link eicosanoid output to innate immune activation. This chemistry is the target of aspirin, other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and anti-leukotriene asthma therapy, and its dysregulation sustains chronic inflammation, thrombosis and allergic airway disease.

Prostanoid biosynthesis converts membrane arachidonic acid into prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane, the short-range lipid mediators that drive fever, pain sensitisation, inflammatory vasodilation, platelet aggregation and vascular tone, and that regulate gastric mucosal protection, renal perfusion and parturition. Phospholipases such as PLA2G4A release the fatty acid substrate; the cyclooxygenases PTGS1 and PTGS2 form the unstable endoperoxide PGH2; and a set of terminal synthases then decides which mediator is made — PTGES for PGE2, PTGDS and HPGDS for PGD2, PTGIS for prostacyclin, TBXAS1 for thromboxane — so that the same precursor yields opposing physiological outputs depending on cell type. Inflammatory cytokines including IL1B induce the inducible arm, which is the target of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and COX-2 inhibitors, while additional regulators here include microRNAs, SIRT1 and fatty-acid-binding proteins that shape flux and substrate delivery.

Short-chain fatty acids — acetate, propionate, butyrate and their relatives, with tails under six carbons — arrive largely from gut microbial fermentation and from the breakdown of branched amino acids and odd-chain lipids, and the reactions that handle them decide whether that carbon is burned for energy, converted to acetyl-CoA for lipid synthesis, or funnelled into the citric acid cycle. Activation to CoA thioesters is the committing step, carried out by cytosolic and mitochondrial acetyl-CoA synthetases and medium/short-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, while thioesterases release free acid to balance CoA pools. Propionyl-CoA is carboxylated by the two-subunit propionyl-CoA carboxylase and then epimerised and isomerised by a cobalamin-dependent mutase to succinyl-CoA; loss of these steps causes propionic and methylmalonic acidaemia. A short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase performs the corresponding beta-oxidation step, and its deficiency is a recognised inborn error of fatty acid oxidation.

Neutral lipid biosynthesis builds triacylglycerols, wax and sterol esters — the uncharged, solvent-soluble lipids that cells use to store energy and sequester excess fatty acids away from membranes. It is the basis of adipocyte lipid droplets, hepatic and intestinal fat handling, and sebum production, and its imbalance produces fatty liver, hypertriglyceridaemia and lipodystrophy. Fatty acids are activated by acyl-CoA synthetases and esterified stepwise onto a glycerol backbone by glycerol-3-phosphate and lysophosphatidate acyltransferases, dephosphorylated by lipin-family phosphatidate phosphatases, and finished by diacylglycerol acyltransferases; monoacylglycerol acyltransferases provide the resynthesis route used after intestinal fat absorption. Transcriptional control runs through SREBP1, liver X receptors and thyroid-hormone-responsive regulators, with SIRT1 and microRNAs tuning output, while lipases such as PNPLA2 and droplet proteins including PLIN5 set the balance between storage and mobilisation.

Neutral lipid catabolism releases fatty acids and glycerol from triacylglycerol, diacylglycerol and related nonpolar esters, supplying fuel between meals and clearing dietary and circulating fat. It underlies adipose lipolysis, intestinal fat digestion and lipoprotein turnover, and its failure produces hypertriglyceridaemia, pancreatitis, fatty liver and neutral lipid storage disease. Within adipocytes, hormone-sensitive lipase and the triglyceride lipase ATGL act sequentially on stored droplets, with ABHD5 as ATGL's coactivator, perilipins gating access to the droplet surface, monoacylglycerol lipase finishing the cascade, and protein kinase A relaying catecholamine signals to the droplet. In plasma, lipoprotein lipase tethered by GPIHBP1 hydrolyses triglyceride in chylomicrons and VLDL, assisted by apolipoprotein C2 and restrained by APOC3, while pancreatic lipases digest dietary fat in the gut lumen. Related serine hydrolases degrade endocannabinoids, linking this chemistry to appetite and neural signalling.

Monoacylglycerol metabolic process covers the making and breaking of single-fatty-acid glycerol esters, the small lipids that sit at the junction between fat storage, dietary fat absorption, and endocannabinoid signalling. Its most consequential product is 2-arachidonoylglycerol, the main agonist at cannabinoid receptors, so the hydrolases here set the tone of retrograde synaptic signalling, pain perception, appetite and inflammatory lipid output; loss of ABHD12 causes a neurodegenerative disease with ataxia and retinal degeneration. Monoacylglycerol lipase and the related serine hydrolases ABHD6 and FAAH terminate that signal and release free fatty acid, while the acyltransferases MOGAT2/MOGAT3 and DGAT1/DGAT2 run the opposite direction, re-esterifying absorbed monoacylglycerol into diacyl- and triacylglycerol in enterocytes and adipocytes. Phospholipase and fatty-acid-binding activities feed substrate into and out of the cycle, linking it to triglyceride homeostasis and eicosanoid production.

Monoacylglycerols sit at a junction between fat storage and lipid signalling, and the reactions that make and break them determine both how efficiently dietary fat is re-esterified and how long endocannabinoid signals last. In the small intestine, monoacylglycerol acyltransferases condense absorbed monoacylglycerol with acyl-CoA to diacylglycerol, which diacylglycerol acyltransferases DGAT1 and DGAT2 convert to triacylglycerol for chylomicron assembly and lipid droplet deposition. On the degradative side, monoacylglycerol lipase and the serine hydrolases ABHD6 and ABHD12 hydrolyse 2-arachidonoylglycerol to arachidonic acid and glycerol, terminating cannabinoid receptor signalling and feeding substrate to eicosanoid synthesis; FAAH acts on the related fatty acid amides. Loss of ABHD12 causes a neurodegenerative disorder with lysophosphatidylserine accumulation, and blocking these hydrolases is pursued for pain and inflammation, while the acyltransferase arm is a target in obesity and hypertriglyceridaemia.

Membranes are not permanent structures, and their lipids must be broken down for turnover, for recycling of building blocks, and to release the bioactive fragments that act as signals. This catabolic route is dominated by sphingolipid degradation: sphingomyelinases such as SMPD1 and the neutral SMPD3 cleave sphingomyelin to ceramide, ceramidases including ASAH1 and the alkaline ACER enzymes release sphingosine, and kinases and phosphatases of the SPHK/SGPP pair together with the lyase SGPL1 set the balance of sphingosine-1-phosphate. A large set of lysosomal glycosidases — GBA1, GALC, GLA, HEXA/HEXB with their GM2 activator, NEU1, GLB1 — strips sugars from glycosphingolipids, assisted by sulfatase maturation and lysosomal trafficking receptors. Loss of individual steps causes the sphingolipidoses, including Gaucher, Fabry, Krabbe and Tay-Sachs disease, in which undegraded lipid accumulates and neurons degenerate; the same chemistry governs ceramide-driven apoptosis and stress signalling.

Membranes are built from more than phospholipid, and this collection covers the synthesis of the sphingolipid and glycolipid components that give bilayers their ordered domains, their outward-facing sugar code, and their ability to anchor proteins. Serine palmitoyltransferase subunits with their ORMDL regulators set the entry rate into sphingolipid synthesis; a family of ceramide synthases and very-long-chain fatty acid elongases then define acyl chain length, after which ceramide is converted to sphingomyelin, glucosyl- or galactosylceramide and elaborated by glycosyltransferases and sialyltransferases into the ganglioside series. A parallel arm assembles glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors and remodels them for surface protein attachment. Degradative enzymes such as acid ceramidase, sphingomyelinase and glucocerebrosidase balance the flux, and their loss produces lysosomal storage diseases. The products also serve as signals: ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate control apoptosis, vascular tone and lymphocyte trafficking, while specialized ultra-long-chain lipids build the skin permeability barrier.

Platelet-activating factor is an ether phospholipid released by leukocytes, endothelium and platelets that acts through its own G protein-coupled receptor to trigger platelet aggregation, neutrophil recruitment, vascular leak and bronchoconstriction; the metabolic processes that make and destroy it set how much of this mediator is available and for how long. Synthesis proceeds by remodelling an alkyl-ether lysophospholipid, with phospholipases such as the cytosolic and secreted forms of phospholipase A2 liberating the lyso intermediate and an acetyltransferase activity capping the sn-2 position, while choline phosphotransferase contributes the de novo branch. Termination depends on acetylhydrolases: the plasma, lipoprotein-associated enzyme encoded by PLA2G7 and the intracellular hydrolase subunits, one of which also functions in neuronal migration. Overproduction or defective degradation drives anaphylaxis, asthma, sepsis and atherosclerotic inflammation, linking this chemistry to both innate immune signalling and lipid turnover.

Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in mammalian membranes, and this metabolic network builds it, remodels its fatty acyl chains, and breaks it down. Synthesis runs from choline uptake by SLC44 transporters through choline kinases (CHKA, CHKB), the rate-limiting cytidylyltransferases PCYT1A/PCYT1B, and final transfer by CHPT1 or CEPT1, with PEMT providing a liver-specific route from phosphatidylethanolamine. Turnover is handled by a large family of phospholipases A2 that release arachidonate for eicosanoid signalling and generate lysophosphatidylcholine, which LPCAT and MBOAT acyltransferases re-acylate to tune membrane composition. The products also serve beyond membranes: surfactant secretion via ABCA3, lipoprotein surface lipid and reverse cholesterol transport through LCAT, CETP and apolipoproteins, and omega-3 lysolipid delivery across the blood-brain barrier by MFSD2A. Defects cause surfactant deficiency, fatty liver, and neurodegenerative disease.

Phosphatidylglycerol is the anionic phospholipid made on the inner mitochondrial membrane as the obligatory precursor of cardiolipin, and it is also a major surfactant lipid in the lung. The pathway covers its synthesis, remodelling and breakdown: CDP-diacylglycerol is generated by CDS2 and TAMM41, condensed with glycerol-3-phosphate by PGS1, dephosphorylated by PTPMT1, and converted to cardiolipin by CRLS1, after which acyl chains are exchanged by tafazzin and lysophospholipid acyltransferases such as LCLAT1, LPGAT1 and LPCAT1. Secreted and intracellular phospholipases of the PLA2 family, together with PNPLA8 and the transacylase SERAC1, release fatty acids and reshape the acyl composition. Correct acyl remodelling determines cristae architecture, respiratory supercomplex stability and mitochondrial protein import; ABCA3 exports these lipids into pulmonary surfactant. Loss of tafazzin causes Barth syndrome, and SERAC1 mutations cause MEGDEL syndrome, while defective ABCA3 produces neonatal respiratory failure.

Phosphatidic acid sits at the junction of membrane lipid synthesis and lipid signalling, and the reactions that make and consume it set how much of it is available for either purpose. It is the common precursor from which cells build triglycerides and all the glycerophospholipids, so the enzymes here determine fat storage in adipose tissue and liver as well as membrane biogenesis; it is also a signalling lipid that recruits and activates effector proteins and influences membrane curvature and fusion. Glycerol-3-phosphate and lysophospholipid acyltransferases build it acyl chain by acyl chain, phospholipases D release it from phosphatidylcholine, diacylglycerol kinases regenerate it from diacylglycerol, and lipin-family phosphatases dephosphorylate it back to diacylglycerol. Loss of the lipin step causes lipodystrophy and rhabdomyolysis, illustrating how tightly these fluxes are tied to triglyceride handling and muscle integrity.

Glycerophospholipid biosynthesis builds the lipids that make up most of every cellular membrane, setting bilayer composition, curvature and charge, and supplying the precursors for lipid second messengers. Glycerol-3-phosphate is acylated in sequence by mitochondrial and ER acyltransferases, dephosphorylated by lipins to diacylglycerol, and coupled to head groups through the Kennedy route: choline and ethanolamine kinases, the cytidylyltransferases PCYT1A and PCYT2, and the final choline/ethanolamine phosphotransferases yield phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while CDP-diacylglycerol synthases feed phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylserine and cardiolipin synthesis. Downstream, a large phosphoinositide kinase and phosphatase network including PI3Ks, PIP5Ks, PTEN, myotubularins and inositol polyphosphate phosphatases generates the phosphoinositide codes that mark organelle identity and drive membrane traffic, autophagy and growth signalling, and a PIG/PGAP arm uses phosphatidylinositol to make GPI anchors. Remodelling enzymes such as LPCAT and MBOAT7 tailor acyl chains. Defects cause inherited neuropathies, myopathies, lipodystrophy, GPI-anchor deficiencies and cancer.

Membrane glycerophospholipids are continually degraded as well as built, and this catabolic arm releases the fatty acids, lysolipids and glycerophosphodiester intermediates that serve as signalling molecules, fuel and precursors for resynthesis. Its outputs matter directly: cytosolic phospholipase A2 liberates arachidonic acid for eicosanoid production in inflammation, platelet-activating factor hydrolases terminate that lipid mediator, and lysophospholipase D activity generates lysophosphatidic acid for receptor-driven growth and motility. Downstream glycerophosphodiesterases and a glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase complete the route to free glycerophosphate and choline. Serine hydrolases of the ABHD and PNPLA families set the tone of bioactive lipid pools, and loss of individual members causes neurodegenerative and neuropathic disease, including ABHD12-related PHARC and PNPLA6-associated spastic paraplegia, illustrating how dependent neural membrane homeostasis is on ordered lipid turnover. Lipoprotein-associated components link the same chemistry to plasma lipid handling and vascular inflammation.

Glycosylceramides are ceramides carrying a single sugar, and their catabolism is the step that returns those lipids to free ceramide and sugar for recycling or further degradation. This turnover keeps membrane and lysosomal lipid pools balanced, and when it stalls the stored substrate is itself pathogenic: loss of glucocerebrosidase activity causes Gaucher disease and predisposes to Parkinson disease, while galactosylceramidase deficiency produces the demyelinating Krabbe disease, reflecting how heavily myelinating glia depend on this chemistry. The enzymes split between an acid lysosomal glucosidase, a non-lysosomal membrane-associated activity, and a related galactosidase, so hydrolysis occurs in more than one compartment; the lysosomal enzyme requires a dedicated receptor, encoded by SCARB2, for delivery from the endoplasmic reticulum to the lysosome. Additional regulatory inputs include a protein kinase and several microRNAs that tune the level of these hydrolases.

Ether lipids carry an alkyl or alkenyl chain joined to glycerol by an ether rather than an ester bond, and their synthesis and turnover supply the plasmalogens that make up a large share of membrane phospholipid in brain, heart and myelin, as well as the potent inflammatory mediator platelet-activating factor. The committed early steps are peroxisomal: a dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase and an alkyl-DHAP synthase, aided by fatty acyl-CoA reductase and the peroxisomal import receptor PEX7, create the ether bond, after which desaturation and headgroup transfer complete plasmalogen assembly in the endoplasmic reticulum. Degradation runs through an alkylglycerol monooxygenase that cleaves the ether linkage and through phospholipases that release or inactivate platelet-activating factor. Because plasmalogens buffer oxidative stress and shape membrane fusion, defects in the peroxisomal steps cause rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with cataracts, skeletal shortening and neurological impairment.

Glycerolipid metabolism covers the making and breaking of every lipid built on a glycerol backbone "" triacylglycerols stored in fat droplets, the diacylglycerol and phosphatidate intermediates that feed membrane synthesis, and the glycerophospholipids that form the bilayer itself. It sets how much fat a cell stores versus burns, supplies the phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylinositol and cardiolipin that membranes and mitochondria require, and generates second messengers. Acyltransferases and phosphatidate phosphatases (lipins, AGPATs, DGATs) build the backbone stepwise; lipases and phospholipases (LPL, PNPLA2, MGLL, the secreted and cytosolic PLA2 families) release fatty acids and lysolipids; lipid kinases and phosphatases including the PI3Ks, PIP5Ks, PTEN and the myotubularins interconvert phosphoinositides that mark organelle identity. Apolipoproteins and lipases handle transport between tissues. Defects cause lipodystrophy, hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver, neuropathy, and "" through the GPI-anchor arm "" inherited multisystem disease.

Glyoxylate is a small, reactive two-carbon aldehyde acid generated during hydroxyproline and glycolate turnover, and the reactions that consume it determine whether it is safely converted to glycine or oxidized to oxalate. Handling it matters because oxalate cannot be degraded in humans and precipitates with calcium: loss of the peroxisomal alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase, of glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase, or of the mitochondrial hydroxyproline pathway enzyme HOGA1 causes the primary hyperoxalurias, with recurrent kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis and renal failure. The transaminases move an amino group onto glyoxylate to regenerate glycine, while the reductase diverts it to glycolate, both routes competing with lactate dehydrogenase for the same substrate. Related carboxylic acid handling is represented by the isocitrate dehydrogenases, linking this chemistry to peroxisomal, mitochondrial and cytosolic organic acid metabolism and to the dietary and endogenous sources of oxalate load.

Phosphatidylinositol and its phosphorylated derivatives are the lipid address labels of membranes, and this metabolic process covers their synthesis, phosphorylation, dephosphorylation and hydrolysis. Which phosphoinositide sits in a given membrane determines where endosomes fuse, where autophagosomes nucleate, how vesicles bud, and whether growth factor receptors can recruit AKT; the soluble inositol phosphates released by phospholipase C cleavage carry calcium and nuclear signals of their own. Kinases such as the PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits, PI4K enzymes and PIP5K/PIP4K families install phosphates, while PTEN, the myotubularins, OCRL, INPP4 and INPP5 phosphatases and synaptojanins remove them, and a large PIG/PGAP branch commits phosphatidylinositol to GPI anchors for cell-surface proteins. Loss of individual enzymes produces centronuclear and X-linked myopathy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy, Lowe syndrome, GPI-deficiency disorders and, through PTEN or PIK3CA, cancer and overgrowth syndromes.

S-adenosylmethionine is the universal methyl donor, and the reactions that make, consume and regenerate it set the methylation capacity of the cell for DNA, histones, RNA, phospholipids, creatine and neurotransmitters. Methionine adenosyltransferases build it from methionine and ATP, with a liver-specific isoform and a widely expressed catalytic-regulatory pair; glycine N-methyltransferase disposes of excess by methylating glycine, while S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase clears the product inhibitor and feeds homocysteine back toward methionine through betaine-dependent transfer and folate-dependent remethylation. An RNA methyltransferase in the group doubles as the sensor that tunes methionine adenosyltransferase expression to methyl donor supply. Disturbance of this cycle raises homocysteine, alters genome-wide methylation, and underlies hypermethioninemia, fatty liver and neural tube defect risk, tying one-carbon metabolism to epigenetic regulation and to folate and vitamin B12 status.

Protoporphyrinogen IX sits at the penultimate stage of heme biosynthesis, and the reactions that produce and consume it determine whether a cell can make the iron-containing cofactor needed for hemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes and catalase. The route runs from succinyl-CoA and glycine through aminolevulinic acid synthase, which in erythroid cells is the iron-responsive ALAS2 isoform, then through the porphobilinogen and uroporphyrinogen intermediates, with coproporphyrinogen oxidase generating protoporphyrinogen IX, PPOX oxidising it to protoporphyrin IX, and ferrochelatase inserting ferrous iron to complete protoheme. Iron supply and heme demand are coordinated by iron-regulatory protein activity and by a heme-regulated kinase that restrains globin translation when heme is scarce. Partial loss of individual enzymes causes the porphyrias, with photosensitivity or neurovisceral attacks depending on which intermediate accumulates, while defective erythroid flux produces sideroblastic anaemia.

Breaking down lipids built on a glycerol backbone releases fatty acids and glycerol for energy, remodels membranes, and generates lipid signals. This catabolism supplies fuel during fasting, clears dietary fat from the circulation, and maintains the skin barrier; its failure underlies hypertriglyceridaemia, lipodystrophy, neutral lipid storage disease and inherited ichthyosis. Pancreatic and lipoprotein lipases hydrolyse triacylglycerol in the gut lumen and on capillary endothelium, with apolipoproteins and GPIHBP1 controlling access to substrate and receptors such as LDLR and SCARB1 handling the remnants. Inside cells, adipose triglyceride lipase with its activator ABHD5, hormone-sensitive lipase under protein kinase A control, and perilipins on the lipid droplet surface mobilise stored fat, while monoacylglycerol lipase and diacylglycerol lipases terminate or produce endocannabinoid signals. Phospholipases of several families release arachidonate and degrade glycerophosphodiesters, linking membrane turnover to eicosanoid production.

Ceramides are the hub of sphingolipid metabolism and the structural backbone of the skin's permeability barrier, and their synthesis also generates a lipid second messenger that drives stress signalling, growth arrest and apoptosis. Production begins at the endoplasmic reticulum, where serine palmitoyltransferase subunits condense serine with palmitoyl-CoA under negative regulation by ORMDL proteins, KDSR reduces the ketodihydrosphingosine intermediate, and a family of six ceramide synthases N-acylates the sphingoid base with distinct fatty acid chain lengths before DEGS desaturases introduce the 4,5-trans double bond. A salvage route regenerates ceramide from sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids through sphingomyelinases and glucocerebrosidase, while sphingomyelin synthases, glucosylceramide synthase and downstream galactosyl- and sialyltransferases consume it. Loss of individual steps causes ichthyosis and epidermal barrier failure, hereditary sensory neuropathy, and lysosomal sphingolipid storage disease.

Ceramide sits at the hub of sphingolipid metabolism, and its catabolism determines how much of it accumulates in a cell. Because ceramide drives apoptosis, growth arrest and stress signalling while its breakdown product sphingosine is phosphorylated into a pro-survival mediator, the ceramidases that hydrolyse it into sphingosine and free fatty acid set the balance between those opposing signals. Acid, neutral and alkaline ceramidases act in lysosomes, at the plasma membrane and in the endoplasmic reticulum respectively, and upstream glycosidases and sialidases strip sugars from complex glycosphingolipids to release the ceramide backbone. Failure of individual steps causes lysosomal storage disease: acid ceramidase loss gives Farber disease, while defects in the hexosaminidases, galactosylceramidase, glucocerebrosidase and its trafficking receptor cause Tay-Sachs, Krabbe and Gaucher disease. Skin barrier lipid turnover and neuronal membrane homeostasis both depend on this route.

Sphingoid metabolism builds and dismantles the long-chain amino alcohol backbones s sphinganine, sphingosine and their phosphorylated forms s that sit at the centre of sphingolipid biology. The pathway matters because these molecules are both structural precursors of ceramides and membrane sphingolipids and potent signals in their own right: sphingosine-1-phosphate drives lymphocyte egress, endothelial barrier integrity and cell survival, while accumulated ceramide and sphingosine push cells toward growth arrest and death. Serine palmitoyltransferase subunits with their small activating partners commit serine and palmitoyl-CoA to the de novo route, a reductase and desaturase steps complete the backbone, and ceramidases together with acid glucosidase release free sphingoid base from complex lipids. Kinases phosphorylate sphingosine, and dedicated phosphatases and lipid phosphate phosphatases reverse that step, setting the balance that determines cell fate. Mutations in the committing enzymes cause hereditary sensory neuropathy, and lysosomal failure of this catabolism underlies Gaucher and Farber disease.

Sphingoid bases are the backbone of every sphingolipid, and their biosynthesis sets how much ceramide, sphingomyelin and sphingosine-1-phosphate a cell can make. The committed first step is condensation of serine with palmitoyl-CoA by serine palmitoyltransferase, whose catalytic subunits SPTLC1-3 pair with the small regulatory subunits SPTSSA and SPTSSB to fix chain-length preference; mutations in SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 cause hereditary sensory neuropathy through production of aberrant deoxysphingoid bases. Sphingoid bases are also regenerated by hydrolysis of complex lipids, by acid, neutral and alkaline ceramidases and by glucocerebrosidase, whose loss underlies Gaucher disease. Sphingosine kinases SPHK1 and SPHK2 phosphorylate the free base to generate a signalling lipid that drives cell survival, lymphocyte trafficking and vascular integrity, so this route feeds both membrane structure and bioactive lipid signalling.

Rods and cones acquire their identity and their light-sensing architecture through photoreceptor cell differentiation, the programme that converts a retinal progenitor into a cell with an outer segment packed with phototransduction machinery. Without it there is no vision, and partial failure of its components is the dominant cause of inherited retinal degeneration — retinitis pigmentosa, cone dystrophy, Leber congenital amaurosis and the retinal disease of ciliopathy syndromes. Transcription factors including PAX6, NRL, NR2E3 and PRDM1 specify rod versus cone fate and enforce it, while structural and trafficking proteins build the connecting cilium and outer segment: intraflagellar transport subunits, ciliary and centrosomal components such as CEP290 and RPGR, and disc rim proteins PRPH2 and ROM1. Phototransduction genes encoding transducin subunits, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and cone phosphodiesterase mark the differentiated endpoint, tying cell fate choice to photoreceptor ciliary biology and outer segment maintenance.

Rod and cone photoreceptors are the light-sensing neurons of the retina, and their production must be timed and limited so that the correct proportion of progenitors becomes photoreceptors rather than bipolar, amacrine or glial cells. This pathway covers the signals that modulate the rate and extent of photoreceptor cell differentiation, acting mostly as a brake on progenitor commitment. Notch signalling keeps retinal progenitors proliferative and suppresses premature photoreceptor fate; the SOX group factors and DLX homeodomain proteins bias progenitors toward alternative retinal and glial identities, while CNTF acts as a secreted cytokine that alters photoreceptor maturation and survival through gp130-family receptors. Too little restraint depletes the progenitor pool, and too much leaves the outer retina underpopulated, so this regulation determines the cellular composition on which visual transduction and, ultimately, photoreceptor degeneration outcomes depend.

Salivary glands produce a fluid that lubricates the mouth, buffers acid, begins starch digestion and protects the teeth, and this pathway covers the regulated secretion of that fluid by the parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands. Loss of the process gives dry mouth, with the dental caries, dysphagia and taste disturbance that accompany it, as in Sjögren syndrome or after irradiation of the head and neck. Secretion is driven by parasympathetic muscarinic receptors, chiefly CHRM3, which raise intracellular calcium; calcium-activated potassium channels and anion transport then set up the osmotic gradient, and aquaporin water channels, notably acinar AQP5, allow water to follow. Other members concern gland development and branching morphogenesis, while statherin is a secreted product that keeps saliva supersaturated with calcium phosphate without mineral precipitating on enamel.

Female secondary sexual characteristics — breast growth, body hair distribution, cyclical endometrial shedding — appear at puberty as target tissues respond to ovarian steroid output, and this pathway covers the hormone-driven maturation of those structures. Its central axis is estrogen and prolactin signalling converted into local growth: a nuclear receptor coactivator relays estrogen receptor activity to transcription, the transcription factors STAT5A and STAT5B carry prolactin and growth hormone signals in mammary epithelium, and amphiregulin acts as the paracrine EGF-family mediator that spreads the proliferative cue from receptor-positive cells to their neighbours. WNT5A and TGFB1 impose restraint on ductal outgrowth and branching, so the tissue elaborates a patterned duct tree rather than an expanding mass. Loss or disruption of this signalling underlies delayed or absent puberty and failure of lactational competence, while its inappropriate reactivation contributes to hormone-dependent breast cancer.

This is the programme that builds the ovary, the primary female sex organ, from the indifferent gonad and then matures it into a follicle-bearing, hormone-secreting tissue. Its output is female fertility: a finite oocyte reserve, cyclic follicle growth and ovulation, and the oestrogen supply on which the rest of the reproductive tract depends. Lineage factors such as WT1, NR5A1, LHX9, FOXL2 and WNT4 specify somatic gonadal cells and sustain granulosa identity, while AMH and its receptor suppress the alternative male duct programme. Gonadotrophin signalling through FSHR and LHCGR, aromatase-driven oestrogen synthesis, KITLG-KIT and GDF9 exchanges between oocyte and granulosa cells, and inhibin/activin feedback then drive folliculogenesis. Meiotic recombination genes including SPO11, DMC1 and MSH4, together with apoptotic and DNA repair components, set oocyte quality and number; their failure produces gonadal dysgenesis, premature ovarian insufficiency and infertility.

Retinal rod cell development is the differentiation program that turns a postmitotic photoreceptor precursor into a rod, the highly light-sensitive cell that carries vision in dim conditions. It matters because rods vastly outnumber cones in the human retina and their loss produces night blindness and the progressive peripheral field loss of retinitis pigmentosa, often followed by secondary cone degeneration. The transcription factors NRL and RORB commit precursors to rod rather than cone identity and drive expression of rhodopsin and the phototransduction cascade, with SAMD7 and SAMD11 acting as photoreceptor-specific repressors that tune that output. A second group builds and maintains the cell's architecture: RP1 organizes the outer segment axoneme, while RPGRIP1, RPGRIP1L and BBS4 operate at the connecting cilium to traffic opsin into the stacked discs, linking rod development to ciliary biology and syndromic ciliopathies.

Rod photoreceptors carry dim-light vision, and their development is the process by which a retinal progenitor commits to the rod fate, builds a light-sensitive outer segment packed with rhodopsin, and maintains it for life. The identity step is transcriptional: a leucine-zipper factor together with a nuclear receptor drives rod-specific gene expression and suppresses the alternative cone programme, with additional SAM-domain regulators tuning the photoreceptor gene battery. Structural and ciliary components act later, at the connecting cilium and outer-segment axoneme, where they organise the stacked membrane discs and the trafficking of opsin into them; a basal body/ciliary protein of the type mutated in Bardet-Biedl syndrome links the same process to broader ciliopathy. Loss of these functions produces retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, night blindness and syndromic retinal degeneration, in which rods die first and cones follow.

Retinal cone cell development builds the photoreceptors responsible for daylight and colour vision, the cells that give the fovea its acuity and whose loss produces achromatopsia, cone dystrophy and central vision failure. It covers the specification of cone identity by nuclear receptors such as RORB acting with thyroid hormone signalling, where the deiodinase DIO3 locally controls hormone availability and thereby which opsin subtype a cone adopts. It also covers the maturation of the machinery that makes a cone functional: the outer segment axoneme scaffold, the transducin and phosphodiesterase components of the phototransduction cascade, hyperpolarisation-activated channels that shape the light response, and the calcium-binding protein and scaffolding proteins that organise the ribbon synapse for transmission to bipolar cells. Photoreceptor polarity and outer limiting membrane adhesion complete the structural program.

Cone photoreceptors provide daylight and colour vision and the high acuity of the central retina, and this programme covers their specification, outer segment construction and maturation into functioning sensory cells. Loss of it produces achromatopsia, cone dystrophy and progressive loss of photopic vision while rod-driven night vision can persist. The genes span the steps involved: nuclear receptor control of photoreceptor subtype identity by RORB, thyroid hormone availability set by the deiodinase DIO3 which inactivates T3 and thereby shapes regional opsin choice, axoneme and outer segment scaffolding through RP1 and the Usher protein harmonin, apical polarity and adhesion at the outer limiting membrane via CRB2, and the phototransduction machinery itself, with cone transducin and the cone phosphodiesterase PDE6C hydrolysing cGMP. CABP4 and HCN1 shape calcium handling and the response kinetics of the synaptic terminal.

Ras proteins act as nucleotide-dependent switches that convert growth factor binding at the cell surface into proliferation, differentiation and survival decisions, and the regulation of Ras protein signal transduction sets how strongly and how long that switch stays on. Control comes from both directions: guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as RASGRF1 and RASGRP1 load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, while GTPase-activating proteins including NF1, SYNGAP1 and several RASA family members accelerate hydrolysis and shut signalling off. Sprouty proteins and DAB2IP damp the response at the level of receptor-proximal events, SHOC2 and MAP2K1 relay it onward through the MAP kinase cascade, and LZTR1 limits Ras abundance itself. Ligands such as NGF, IGF1 and FGF10 feed in through receptor tyrosine kinases. Loss of the braking components underlies neurofibromatosis and the RASopathies, and inappropriate pathway output is a common route to cancer.

Ras GTPases sit at the hub that converts receptor occupancy into proliferation, differentiation and survival decisions, and this collection describes the inputs that push that switch toward the active, GTP-bound state. Growth factors and cytokines such as NGF, IGF1, FGF10, CSF1 and erythropoietin, acting through receptors including the NGF receptor TrkA, recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors of the RasGRF and RasGRP families to load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS, NRAS or MRAS; the scaffold SHOC2 with protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits sustains signalling into MAP2K1 and the downstream kinase cascade. Positive regulation of Ras signalling underlies lineage choices in haematopoiesis and neuronal outgrowth, and is modulated by Notch receptor input. Because gain of flux through this route drives transformation, the same components are the mutated oncogenes of human cancer, while germline hyperactivation produces developmental RASopathies.

Ras GTPases switch on proliferation and differentiation programmes, and the damping of Ras protein signal transduction is what keeps that output brief and proportionate rather than continuous. The main mechanism is acceleration of GTP hydrolysis by GTPase-activating proteins — neurofibromin, the RASA and RASAL family members, SYNGAP1 at excitatory synapses, DAB2IP — which return Ras to its inactive GDP-bound state. Other brakes act differently: LZTR1 promotes ubiquitin-dependent turnover of RAS itself, Sprouty proteins interpose between receptor tyrosine kinases and Ras-ERK activation, and phosphatase subunits reduce downstream kinase phosphorylation. Because these restraints limit growth signalling, their loss causes disease: neurofibromatosis and Noonan-spectrum RASopathies, sporadic cancers, and, through the synaptic GAPs, altered dendritic signalling and intellectual disability. The pathway therefore sits at the heart of tumour suppression and of activity-dependent neuronal plasticity.

Regulation of viral entry into host cell covers the host factors that make the first step of infection easier or harder — the proteolytic activation, membrane and receptor events that let an enveloped virus attach and fuse, and the countermeasures that block them. It sets susceptibility to infection at the level of individual tissues, which is why the same virus enters airway epithelium and not other cells, and why several of these proteins are antiviral drug targets. Surface proteases such as TMPRSS2, TMPRSS4 and FURIN cleave viral glycoproteins to prime fusion, while receptors and attachment factors including BSG, NECTIN2 and heparan sulfate modification supply the docking site; sphingomyelinase, P4HB and cholesterol-25-hydroxylase alter membrane lipid and redox conditions for fusion. Opposing them, TRIM family ligases and secreted galectins restrict capsid entry and trafficking, coupling entry control to innate immune sensing.

Whether a virus particle actually gets inside a cell is not settled by the virus alone; host factors set the efficiency of that step, and this regulation of viral entry into host cell determines susceptibility to infection and the tissue tropism that follows. Some members promote entry: surface proteases such as TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4 and the proprotein convertase FURIN cleave viral glycoproteins to prime membrane fusion, receptors and attachment factors including BSG, NECTIN2 and heparan sulfate modification supply docking sites, and lysosomal sphingomyelinase and the thiol isomerase P4HB alter membrane and disulfide states needed for fusion. Others restrict it: cholesterol 25-hydroxylase generates an oxysterol that blocks fusion, galectins bind glycans on virions, and TRIM family ubiquitin ligases including TRIM5 impose early post-entry blocks. The balance shapes innate antiviral defence and is a target for entry-inhibiting drugs.

Blocking a pathogen before it ever reaches the cytoplasm is the cheapest form of defence, and host-mediated suppression of symbiont invasion covers the machinery that stops viruses and other microbes at the point of cell entry. It underlies innate resistance to influenza, HIV, flaviviruses and other enveloped viruses, and its loss leaves cells permissive to infection that adaptive immunity must then clear at greater cost. Interferon-induced transmembrane proteins rigidify endosomal membranes and prevent viral fusion, LY6E similarly modulates entry, while TRIM family E3 ubiquitin ligases act as restriction factors and as regulators of antiviral signalling; TRIM5 recognises incoming retroviral capsids and TRIM25 supports RIG-I-dependent interferon induction. Soluble recognition molecules including ficolins and pentraxins opsonise microbes for clearance, and CD74 with the transcriptional coactivator CIITA link this front line to antigen presentation. Type I interferon drives much of the programme.

Cells must build exactly one new centriole per existing one per cell cycle, and the control of centriole replication is what enforces that count. Getting it wrong produces extra centrosomes, multipolar spindles and chromosome missegregation, a route to aneuploidy and a common feature of tumours; too few centrioles compromises cilium assembly, and mutations in several of these components cause microcephaly, dwarfism and ciliopathies. The master kinase PLK4 licenses assembly by recruiting STIL and the cartwheel protein SASS6, while CPAP, CEP120 and SPICE1 govern procentriole elongation and CEP295 drives conversion of the daughter into a mother competent for the next round. Counterbalancing activities limit copy number: TRIM37 suppresses ectopic centriolar structures, and further regulators including BRCA1, NPM1, RBM14 and PLK2 restrain or time duplication, linking centrosome biogenesis to genome stability.

Cells must build exactly one new centriole per existing one per cycle, and the restraints that block extra rounds of centriole replication are what keep centrosome number at two. Losing them produces supernumerary centrioles, multipolar spindles, chromosome missegregation and the aneuploidy typical of tumours, which is why several of these genes behave as tumour suppressors. The brakes act at different points: BRCA1 restrains centrosome amplification through ubiquitin ligase activity, TRIM37 degrades pericentriolar assembly factors and suppresses ectopic centriolar structures, CDK5RAP2 organises pericentriolar material and couples centrosome integrity to mitotic fidelity, while MDM1 and RBM14 block inappropriate elongation or de novo assembly of centriolar cartwheels. The acetyltransferases KAT2A and KAT2B contribute through chromatin and non-histone acetylation that limits duplication licensing. Mutations in this circuitry underlie microcephalic dwarfism syndromes and predispose to cancer.

Centrioles duplicate exactly once per cell cycle, and the factors here push that event forward, setting how many centrioles a cell builds and therefore whether it forms a bipolar spindle or a functional cilium. The master trigger is the kinase PLK4, which together with STIL recruits SASS6 to nucleate the ninefold cartwheel that templates a new procentriole; CEP295, CPAP and CEP120 then support elongation and conversion of the nascent centriole into a mother capable of further rounds. Too much activity here yields centriole amplification, multipolar divisions and chromosome missegregation, a route to aneuploidy in tumours, while loss of the same components underlies microcephaly and dwarfism syndromes in which progenitor divisions fail. The pathway sits within centrosome biogenesis and cell cycle control, upstream of spindle assembly and ciliogenesis.

Before a cell divides, its two duplicated centrosomes must split apart and move to opposite sides of the nucleus so that a bipolar spindle can form; this pathway tunes when and how far that separation goes. Getting the timing wrong produces monopolar or misoriented spindles, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, which is why the step is watched by cell cycle checkpoints. Mechanistically, the linker holding the two centrosomes together must be dissolved, and the kinase NEK2 phosphorylates linker components to do so, with CEP85 acting as a NEK2-binding regulator and CHEK1 imposing checkpoint control. Motor proteins then supply force: the kinesin KIF11 generates outward sliding within the forming spindle, while KIF25 restrains premature splitting. The p97 cofactors NSFL1C and UBXN2B link centrosome behaviour to AAA-ATPase-dependent protein remodelling at spindle poles.

Each cell cycle a cell must duplicate its centrosome exactly once and then separate the two copies to build a bipolar spindle; the controls that set the timing and extent of that duplication and separation constitute the regulation of the centrosome cycle. Losing this restraint gives centrosome amplification, multipolar or error-prone mitoses and chromosome missegregation, and mutations in these genes cause primary microcephaly, ciliopathies and skeletal dysplasias, reflecting the centriole's second job as the basal body of cilia. Licensing runs through PLK4 and its cartwheel substrates SASS6 and STIL, with CEP120, CEP295 and PPP1R35 extending and maturing the daughter centriole, while SCF ubiquitin ligase components including SKP1, CUL1, RBX1 and FBXW5 limit reduplication. AURKA and MARK4 act at maturation and separation, and ESCRT subunits couple centrosomal and abscission events at the end of division.

Cells protect themselves from foreign chemicals by pumping them back out, and xenobiotic export from the cell is the transport step that does it. It sets the pharmacokinetics of most orally administered drugs, governs biliary and renal elimination, and is a major cause of multidrug resistance when tumour cells overexpress its components. ATP-binding cassette pumps such as ABCB1, ABCC2 and the bile salt export pump ABCB11 use ATP hydrolysis to drive substrates across the plasma membrane, while multidrug and toxin extrusion carriers SLC47A1 and SLC47A2 and other solute carriers move drugs down electrochemical or proton gradients at hepatocyte and proximal tubule surfaces. Scaffolding by PDZK1 positions transporters in apical membranes, and a substantial complement of microRNAs tunes their expression, linking efflux capacity to drug response and cholestatic or metal-handling disease when it fails.

Organs must reach a species-typical size and then stop, and this collection of regulators sets that endpoint by tuning proliferation, cell survival and hypertrophic growth during development and tissue repair. Much of it is Hippo signalling: the STK3/STK4 and LATS1/LATS2 kinases with their SAV1 and WWC scaffolds restrain the transcriptional coactivator YAP1, whose release drives progenitor expansion, while VGLL4 competes for the same transcriptional output. Growth-factor inputs through IGF1/IGF2, FGF ligands and their receptors, neuregulin-ERBB4 and TGF-beta/BMP receptors converge on AKT1 and PTEN to set anabolic tone, and cardiac transcription factors such as NKX2-5, TBX5, TBX20, GATA6 and MEF2C, together with several microRNAs, scale heart chamber growth in particular. Loss of these brakes underlies overgrowth syndromes, cardiac hypertrophy and tumorigenesis; excessive restraint produces organ hypoplasia and congenital heart defects.

Organs stop growing at the right size because brakes are applied to cell proliferation and cell enlargement, and this set collects those restraining influences. Loss of such negative control over organ growth produces overgrowth, hamartomas and tumour predisposition, and in the heart drives pathological hypertrophy rather than adaptive growth. A prominent module here is the Hippo kinase cassette and its scaffolds — STK3 and STK4 with SAV1 and the WWC/KIBRA family, plus the VGLL4 co-repressor — which limits the transcriptional output that would otherwise promote proliferation and survival. PTEN opposes phosphoinositide signalling to growth, NOG sequesters bone morphogenetic proteins, and several microRNAs together with transcriptional regulators such as FOXP1, TBX5 and YY1 tune cardiomyocyte and muscle growth. Cardiac-restricted components including CAV3 and PPARA link the pathway to load-induced hypertrophy and metabolic status.

Organs reach and keep their proper size because growth-promoting signals are actively switched on during development and, in some tissues, reactivated in adulthood. This positive regulation of organ growth determines heart size, limb and gut proportions, and organ regenerative capacity, and its inappropriate persistence underlies pathological overgrowth such as cardiac hypertrophy. The genes here converge on the classic growth-instructing pathways: insulin-like growth factors IGF1 and IGF2 acting through AKT1, fibroblast growth factors with their receptors FGFR1 and FGFR2, BMP and TGF-beta family ligands, Hedgehog through SMO and GLI1, Notch with its transcriptional partner RBPJ, WNT2, and the Hippo effector YAP1 that couples mechanical cues to proliferation. Cardiac transcription factors including TBX5, TBX20, MEF2C and GATA6, together with neuregulin-ERBB4 signalling, direct much of this toward myocardial expansion, while cell cycle drivers CDK1 and cyclin B1 and several microRNAs tune the proliferative output.

Insulin acts through a receptor tyrosine kinase, and the strength and duration of that signal is tuned by a large set of positive and negative modulators; this regulatory layer sets whole-body insulin sensitivity and its failure produces insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Adaptors such as IRS1 couple the activated receptor to PI3K-AKT and onward to mTOR complex signalling and S6 kinases, while GRB10 and GRB14 bind the receptor and dampen it. Tyrosine phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPN2 and PTPN11 reverse receptor and substrate phosphorylation, SOCS proteins and TRIB3 impose feedback inhibition, and serine kinases such as GSK3A and several protein kinase C isoforms attenuate substrate signalling. Circulating factors including insulin itself, IGF2, leptin, myostatin and inflammatory IL1B feed in, as do microRNAs and nutrient sensors like SIRT1, AMPK and O-GlcNAc transferase, linking receptor output to energy status.

gamma-delta T cell activation describes how an unconventional T cell lineage responds to stress ligands and antigens by changing shape, proliferating and acquiring effector function. Gamma-delta T cells patrol epithelial barriers in skin, gut and lung, respond rapidly without classical MHC restriction, and provide early cytotoxic and IL-17 or interferon-gamma responses to infection and transformed cells; loss of this arm weakens barrier immunosurveillance and tumour control. Signalling runs from the gamma-delta receptor and its CD3 chains through LCK, ITK and SYK, with CD45 setting the activation threshold, while stress-induced NKG2D ligands MICA and MICB and receptors such as KLRC1 and LILRB1 tune the response. Transcription factors including SOX13, SOX4, TCF7, LEF1 and EGR3, together with STAT5-dependent cytokine signals, commit thymic progenitors to this lineage and drive their effector programming and tissue homing.

Gamma-delta T cells are an unconventional T lineage that patrols epithelial barriers and responds rapidly to stressed or infected cells without classical MHC-restricted antigen presentation, and this pathway covers their shift from resting to effector state on encountering antigen, cytokine or cellular ligand. Activation produces cytokine output and cytotoxicity that bridges innate and adaptive immunity in skin, gut and reproductive tract, and shapes antitumour surveillance. Signalling runs through a gamma-delta T cell receptor whose constant regions are encoded here, coupled via CD3 subunits and the CD247 chain to the kinases LCK, ITK and SYK, with CD45 setting the activation threshold. Stress-induced ligands MICA and MICB mark target cells for recognition, STAT5 transduces cytokine support for survival and expansion, and transcription factors including SOX13, TCF7, LEF1 and EGR3 specify the lineage and its effector programmes.

Alpha-beta T cell activation is the transition of a resting T cell into a proliferating, cytokine-secreting effector after its receptor engages peptide displayed on MHC, and it is the step that converts antigen recognition into adaptive immunity. Without it there is no help for antibody responses and no cytotoxic clearance of infected cells; when it proceeds without restraint the result is autoimmunity, and when it is deliberately blocked, transplants survive. Receptor chains with CD3 subunits recruit LCK, ZAP70 and ITK to trigger calcium, NF-kB and mTOR signalling, while CD28 and ICOS supply costimulation and inhibitory receptors such as CD274 and VSIR, together with ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH, set the threshold. Cytokines acting through JAK/STAT modules and transcription factors including TBX21, GATA3, RORC and FOXP3 then assign helper, regulatory or memory fates, with proteasome subunits supporting antigen processing and display.

Most circulating T cells carry an alpha-beta antigen receptor, and this is the programme by which thymic precursors acquire that identity and the helper or cytotoxic fate that follows it. Without it there is no adaptive cellular immunity: loss of components such as ZAP70, IL2RG, JAK3 or adenosine deaminase produces severe combined or selective T cell immunodeficiency. Pre-T cell receptor signalling through PTCRA, ZAP70, ITK and SYK drives beta-selection, while the thymoproteasome subunit PSMB11 and MHC class II on stromal cells shape the peptides used for positive and negative selection. Lineage-defining transcription factors then partition outcomes: BCL11B and TOX for commitment, ZBTB7B versus RUNX3 for CD4 or CD8 choice, and TBX21, GATA3, RORC, FOXP3 and PRDM1 for effector and regulatory subsets, each reinforced by cytokine receptor and STAT signalling with SOCS proteins limiting the response.

When an alpha-beta T cell recognises antigen it must divide many times to build a clone large enough to clear the pathogen, and this clonal expansion is what the pathway describes. Its magnitude sets the strength of adaptive cellular immunity; too little leaves infections uncontrolled, too much drives autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation. Receptor engagement through the CD3 complex and proximal kinases ZAP70 and SYK, reinforced by CD28 costimulation, converges on MYC-driven metabolic and cell cycle entry. Cytokines of the IL-12 family together with IL-15 and IL-23 receptor signalling amplify and shape the response, while brakes are equally represented: the E3 ligases CBLB and ITCH raise the activation threshold, and PD-L1, VSIR, galectin-9 and TGF-beta receptor signalling restrain expansion. ZBTB7B contributes lineage identity, linking proliferative capacity to CD4 versus CD8 commitment and to peripheral tolerance.

Alpha-beta T cells must be switched on strongly enough to clear a pathogen but not so strongly that they attack host tissue, and this regulatory layer sets where that threshold lies. It determines whether a naive cell proliferates, differentiates toward a helper or cytotoxic fate, or is held in tolerance, and its failure produces autoimmunity at one extreme and tumour or chronic-infection exhaustion at the other. Antigen presented on MHC class I and II engages the CD3 u-ZAP70-PRKCQ-SYK cascade, while costimulatory and coinhibitory receptors such as CD28, CD80/CD86, PD-L1 and TNFRSF14 tune the strength of that signal. Cytokines of the IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 family act through JAK-STAT to bias lineage choice, transcription factors including TBX21, GATA3, RORC-associated ZBTB16, FOXP3 and BCL6 fix the outcome, and negative regulators such as CBLB, SOCS1, ITCH, ZC3H12A and the roquin RNA-binding proteins restrain it.

Alpha-beta T cells only respond when antigen presentation is reinforced by costimulation and cytokines, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the frequency and strength of that activation. It underlies protective adaptive immunity and vaccine responses, and when it runs unchecked it drives autoimmunity, graft rejection and inflammatory tissue damage. Peptide-MHC engagement of the T cell receptor complex is transduced through CD3 chains, the phosphatase CD45, ZAP70 and protein kinase C-theta into NF-kB activation via MALT1 and related adaptors, while CD28 ligation by CD80 and CD86 on dendritic cells supplies the second signal. Cytokines of the IL-12 family, together with IL-18 and IL-23 and their receptors, then bias effector differentiation toward interferon-gamma-producing and IL-17-producing fates. Transcriptional regulators including RUNX1, RUNX3, ZBTB7B and FOXP3 set lineage choice and impose limits, as do the SOCS proteins acting as feedback brakes.

Alpha-beta T cells must be restrained as well as switched on, and this collection of brakes sets the threshold for their activation, limits the size of a response, and enforces tolerance to self. Without such negative regulation, T cells respond to weak or self antigen and drive autoimmunity and immunopathology; tumours exploit the same brakes to escape immune attack. Inhibitory surface receptors and ligands such as PD-L1, VISTA and the galectins deliver suppressive signals at the immune synapse, while E3 ubiquitin ligases including CBLB and ITCH and the RNA-binding proteins RC3H1/2 and ZC3H12A degrade signalling components and cytokine transcripts. Cytokine signalling is dampened by SOCS proteins, and FOXP3 with RUNX and ZBTB7B transcription factors programme regulatory and lineage decisions. This is the counterweight to costimulation, and the pharmacological target of checkpoint blockade.

Alpha-beta T cells acquire their identity and effector character through a tightly controlled developmental programme, and this pathway covers the signals and factors that raise or lower the rate and extent of that differentiation. It governs thymic lineage decisions, including the CD4 versus CD8 choice directed by ZBTB7B and RUNX3, and the later commitment of peripheral naive cells to helper and regulatory fates specified by GATA3, TBX21, BCL6 and FOXP3. Cytokines and their receptors, antigen-presenting costimulation, and proximal receptor kinases such as ZAP70, SYK and JAK3 feed into these transcriptional programmes, while SOCS1, SMAD7 and the roquin RNA-binding proteins RC3H1 and RC3H2 restrain them. Loss of control here produces immunodeficiency when differentiation fails, as in adenosine deaminase deficiency, and autoimmunity or unchecked inflammation when effector skewing escapes regulation.

positive regulation of alpha-beta T cell differentiation covers the signals that drive thymocytes and peripheral T cells to commit to alpha-beta lineages and their effector fates, from CD4 versus CD8 choice in the thymus to Th1, Th17 and regulatory T cell programmes in the periphery. It is what gives an organism a functional, self-tolerant T cell repertoire; its loss produces immunodeficiency, as in adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency, or autoimmunity when regulatory output fails. Antigen receptor signalling through ZAP70 and SYK, costimulation by CD80/CD86 and OX40 ligand, peptide-MHC class II presentation, and cytokines including IL-12, IL-18, IL-23 and TGF-beta feed into lineage-determining transcription factors such as RUNX1, RUNX3, ZBTB7B, ZBTB16 and FOXP3, with hedgehog signalling and chromatin readers tuning thymic development.

Thymocytes bearing an alpha-beta T cell receptor must be pushed through lineage commitment and, once mature, directed toward particular helper or regulatory fates; this set collects the signals and factors that promote that differentiation. It underwrites adaptive cellular immunity, and its loss produces immunodeficiency — mutations in ADA or the shared cytokine receptor chain IL2RG block T cell development outright, while defective FOXP3 removes the regulatory subset and causes systemic autoimmunity. Antigen receptor signalling through ZAP70 and SYK is coupled to NF-kB activation via MALT1, and lineage decisions are enforced by transcriptional regulators including RUNX1, RUNX3, CBFB, ZBTB7B and ZBTB16 together with the acetyltransferase EP300. Antigen-presenting surfaces (MHC class II, CD80, CD86, CD83) and polarising cytokines such as IL-12, IL-18 and IL-23 supply the extrinsic instruction, with SOCS1 and TGF-beta receptor signalling setting limits on the response.

Alpha-beta T cells acquire distinct fates — CD4 helper versus CD8 cytotoxic, and among helpers Th1, Th2, Th17 or regulatory — and this arm of the programme applies the brakes, restraining how often and how far those differentiation steps proceed. Damping it permits runaway effector commitment, loss of tolerance and autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disease, so the same genes that limit differentiation also enforce self-restraint in the periphery. Transcriptional repressors and lineage arbiters such as BCL6, ZBTB7B, RUNX1/RUNX3 with their CBFB partner, and FOXP3 suppress alternative or excessive fate choices; SOCS1 and SOCS5 blunt cytokine receptor signalling through JAK3 and STAT5A; and the RNA-binding proteins RC3H1, RC3H2 and ZC3H12A degrade transcripts encoding costimulatory and inflammatory mediators. Hedgehog ligands, annexin A1 and galectin-1 add extrinsic thymic and peripheral signals that curb maturation and effector expansion.

positive regulation of alpha-beta T cell proliferation covers the signals that drive conventional T cells to expand clonally after they recognise antigen, converting a handful of specific cells into the effector population that clears an infection. Without it immunity is blunted; unchecked, it feeds autoimmunity and chronic inflammation. Three input layers are represented: the T cell receptor complex itself with its proximal kinases and phosphatase (CD3E, ZAP70, SYK, PTPRC) reading peptide presented on MHC class I; costimulation through CD28 and OX40 ligand that licenses full activation rather than anergy; and cytokines of the IL-12 family, including IL-12, IL-23 and IL-27 subunits with their receptors, plus IL-18, which sustain division and bias differentiation toward Th1 and Th17 fates. Chemokine and adhesion components position cells for these encounters, while TGF-beta receptor signalling sets the counterweight.

Clonal expansion of conventional alpha-beta T cells after antigen encounter is what converts a rare precursor into an effector population large enough to clear an infection, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that expansion up. Antigen recognition through the T cell receptor complex is relayed by ZAP70 and SYK-family kinases and by the phosphatase CD45, while CD28 and the TNF-family ligand OX40L supply costimulation that licenses division rather than tolerance. Cytokine signals reinforce it: IL-12 and IL-23 subunits with their shared receptor chains, IL-27's EBI3 subunit, and IL-18 drive proliferation alongside helper-cell polarisation. Peptide presentation by class I molecules and chemokine cues such as XCL1 and CCR2 position cells for these encounters. Excessive output underlies autoimmune and inflammatory tissue damage; too little leaves adaptive responses undersized.

Alpha-beta T cell responses must be damped as well as triggered, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that limit how much conventional T cells divide after antigen encounter. Without such restraint, clonal expansion continues unchecked, favouring autoimmunity and chronic inflammation; with it engaged too strongly, tumours and chronic infections escape immune control. Several distinct brakes converge here. Inhibitory surface ligands including PD-L1 and VISTA engage receptors on activated T cells to shut down proliferative signalling, while TNFRSF14 provides a co-inhibitory arm through its own receptor partners. Galectin-9 binds glycosylated receptors to curb effector T cells. Intracellularly, the E3 ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH degrade proximal signalling components and enforce anergy. ARG2 depletes arginine needed for T cell growth, and ZBTB7B acts at the level of lineage and thymic development.

Gamma-delta T cells are an unconventional lymphocyte population that patrols epithelia and responds rapidly to stress ligands and microbial products without classical MHC presentation, and this pathway sets how readily they are switched on. Tuning their activation matters for mucosal barrier defence, early antitumour surveillance and IL-17-driven inflammation; loss of restraint contributes to inflammatory pathology, while weak responses leave tissue surfaces poorly guarded. The genes cover proximal receptor signalling, where the kinases LCK and SYK and the phosphatase CD45 encoded by PTPRC set signalling thresholds at the T cell receptor, and the cytoskeletal adaptor NCKAP1L supports immune synapse formation. Downstream, STAT5A and STAT5B relay cytokine signals for survival and expansion, EGR3 acts as an immediate-early transcriptional response, and TCF7, LEF1, SOX4 and SOX13 bias lineage commitment between gamma-delta and alpha-beta fates. NOD2 links innate bacterial sensing to this control.

Gamma-delta T cells are an unconventional lymphocyte population that responds rapidly at epithelial surfaces without the MHC-peptide restriction used by conventional T cells, and this pathway covers the signals that push them toward activation. Proximal receptor signalling is carried by the kinases LCK and SYK together with the phosphatase CD45 (PTPRC) and the hematopoietic adaptor NCKAP1L, which couple antigen receptor engagement to downstream effector programmes. Transcriptional input comes from LEF1 and the SOX factors SOX4 and SOX13, the latter being a determinant of gamma-delta rather than alpha-beta lineage choice, while STAT5A and STAT5B transmit cytokine signals that support expansion and survival. Innate sensing through NOD2 links bacterial products to this response. The output matters for early antibacterial defence, mucosal surveillance and tumour immunity, and dysregulated activation contributes to inflammatory tissue damage.

Lymphocyte activation is the change in shape, metabolism and behaviour that a T, B or NK cell undergoes when it meets antigen, a cytokine, or a ligand on another cell, and it is the step that converts a resting surveillance cell into a proliferating effector. Adaptive immunity, antibody production, cytotoxic killing and immunological memory all depend on it, while its failure produces immunodeficiency and its miscontrol produces autoimmunity or lymphoma. Antigen receptor complexes and their coreceptors feed through proximal kinases such as LCK, SYK and ZAP70 and adaptors like LAT and BLNK into calcium/calcineurin, PI3K and NF-kB signalling, integrated with costimulation through CD28 and ICOS and restrained by checkpoint receptors including CTLA4, PDCD1 and phosphatases such as PTPN22. Peptide-MHC display, cytokine and JAK-STAT circuits, receptor gene rearrangement and repair, and lineage transcription factors set the resulting effector programme.

Tetrahydrofolate is the carrier that moves single carbon units around the cell, and the reactions that make, recycle and interconvert it supply the methyl and formyl groups needed for thymidylate synthesis, purine ring assembly, and regeneration of methionine from homocysteine. Without adequate flux, DNA replication stalls for want of dTMP, methylation reactions falter, and homocysteine accumulates — the basis of megaloblastic anaemia, neural tube defects, and the antifolate sensitivity exploited by methotrexate and 5-fluorouracil. Dietary folate enters through a receptor and a proton-coupled intestinal transporter, is reduced by dihydrofolate reductase, and is loaded with carbon by serine hydroxymethyltransferases in cytosol and mitochondria. Cyclohydrolase-dehydrogenase and synthetase activities shuttle between formyl, methylene and methyl oxidation states, with methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase committing carbon to methionine synthase and formyl-tetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases returning it as CO2. Related pterin synthesis is represented by GCH1.

Tetrahydrofolate is the carrier that ferries one-carbon units into thymidylate, purine and methionine synthesis, and its biosynthesis keeps that pool charged. Cells acquire folate from the diet, using a high-affinity receptor and an intestinal proton-coupled transporter, and then reduce it: dihydrofolate reductase converts dihydrofolate to the tetrahydro form, a step repeated every time thymidylate synthesis oxidises the cofactor, which is why this enzyme is the target of methotrexate and related antifolates. GTP cyclohydrolase I opens the parallel route to pterin ring formation, linking this chemistry to biopterin and nitric oxide synthase function.
