Multifunctional formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase/dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase activities and a formyltransferase step in purine synthesis interconvert and regenerate the substituted forms. Disruption impairs nucleotide supply and methylation capacity, underlying megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects.

Folic acid metabolism supplies the one-carbon units that cells need to make purines, thymidylate and methionine, so it sits upstream of DNA replication, repair and methylation. Dietary folate must first be taken up and retained: a high-affinity receptor and the reduced folate and proton-coupled intestinal transporters bring it into cells, a mitochondrial carrier moves it across the inner membrane, and polyglutamylation traps it intracellularly. Dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate, the carrier onto which serine hydroxymethyltransferase and the methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase enzymes load and interconvert formyl, methylene and methenyl one-carbon groups in cytosol and mitochondria; methionine synthase reductase keeps the methyl-transfer step active. Deficiency or blockade causes megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects, and this route is the target of antifolate chemotherapy such as methotrexate.

Female sex differentiation is the route by which an undifferentiated gonad and reproductive tract acquire ovarian and female identity, establishing the follicle reserve, the uterus and oviduct, and the hormonal axis that later supports ovulation and pregnancy. Its disruption produces gonadal dysgenesis, sex reversal, premature ovarian insufficiency and infertility. Transcriptional regulators such as FOXL2, WNT4, NR5A1 and WT1 specify granulosa and somatic gonadal fates and suppress the testicular alternative, while AMH signalling through AMHR2 governs regression or retention of the Müllerian ducts. Germ cell entry into meiosis relies on recombination machinery including SPO11, DMC1 and MSH4, and germ cell survival on KIT–KITLG and apoptotic balance among BAX, BAK1 and BCL2. Gonadotropins and their receptors, with aromatase-driven oestrogen synthesis acting through ESR1, drive folliculogenesis, oocyte growth factors such as GDF9, and steroid-dependent maturation of female tissues.

Male sex differentiation is the developmental program that converts a bipotential gonad and indifferent reproductive tract into testes, male ducts and male external genitalia. It determines fertility and the hormonal setting of the whole male body, and its disruption produces disorders of sex development, hypospadias, cryptorchidism and infertility. The genes trace the canonical cascade: SRY acting with SOX9, NR5A1, WT1, GATA4 and ZFPM2 to commit supporting cells to the Sertoli fate while suppressing the ovarian WNT4/RSPO branch; anti-Müllerian hormone and its receptor regressing the Müllerian ducts; and androgen synthesis through HSD17B3 and 5α-reductase acting on the androgen receptor to virilise the urogenital sinus and genital tubercle. Gonadotropin signalling through LHCGR and FSHR, KITLG-KIT support of germ cells, INSL3-RXFP2 control of testicular descent, and HOX-patterned tract morphogenesis complete the program.

Male sex differentiation is the programme that turns a bipotential embryo into a male one: the gonadal ridge is committed to testis fate, the resulting hormones remodel the internal ducts, and the external genitalia and reproductive tract acquire male form. The genes here trace that sequence from its switch to its endocrine output. SRY acting with SOX9, NR5A1, WT1, GATA4 and ZFPM2 drives Sertoli cell specification while WNT4 and RSPO-type signalling for the ovarian alternative is suppressed; DMRT1 then maintains the decision. Downstream, anti-Müllerian hormone signalling through AMHR2 regresses the Müllerian ducts, while androgen synthesis by HSD17B3 and SRD5A2 acts on the androgen receptor to masculinise the Wolffian derivatives, urogenital sinus and genital tubercle, with RXFP2 required for testicular descent. Additional factors support germ cell survival, meiosis and sperm function. Lesions in these steps cause disorders of sex development, hypospadias, cryptorchidism and infertility.

The developing retina produces more neurons than it retains, and programmed cell death in retinal cells removes the excess, prunes cells whose axons fail to reach or hold targets in the brain, and matches photoreceptor, bipolar and ganglion cell numbers to the circuits that need them. Survival here is a balance: the pro-apoptotic BAX commits cells to mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation and caspase activation, while BCL2 opposes it, so the ratio of the two effectively sets the death threshold. Trophic factors including ciliary neurotrophic factor and FGF2 act as the extrinsic side of that decision, sparing cells that receive adequate support. The same machinery is re-engaged pathologically in retinal degeneration, glaucoma and ischaemic injury, where photoreceptor or ganglion cell loss produces irreversible visual deficit, which is why apoptotic regulation in the retina is studied as both a developmental and a neuroprotective problem.

Cells exposed to antibiotics alter their behaviour, and this grouping collects the mammalian responses to such compounds — changes in gene expression, enzyme activity, transport and secretion triggered when an antibiotic acts as a chemical stimulus. Because many antibiotics and related natural products are also used experimentally or therapeutically in human cells, these responses underlie both drug side effects and the pharmacology of agents that reach intracellular targets. The members span stress and damage signalling through TP53 and its regulator MDM2, cell cycle restraint via CDKN1B, inflammatory output through TNF and phospholipase A2 enzymes, and cytokine relay by JAK1 and JAK2. A large chromatin component, including the demethylases KDM1A, KDM5B and KDM6B and the methyltransferase EZH2, indicates that much of the reaction is transcriptional reprogramming, alongside solute carriers that govern drug and ion handling at the membrane.

response to organophosphorus covers how cells and tissues react to phosphorus-containing organic compounds, a category that spans physiological nucleotide messengers such as ATP and cyclic AMP as well as toxic agents like organophosphate insecticides and nerve agents, which inhibit cholinesterase and cause cholinergic crisis. The genes trace the receptive and effector arms of that response: purinergic P2X ion channels and P2Y G protein-coupled receptors together with pannexin release channels detect extracellular nucleotides, while phosphodiesterases, A-kinase anchoring proteins, Rap guanine nucleotide exchange factors and CREB coactivators shape the resulting cyclic nucleotide signals. Downstream come immediate-early transcription factors, calcium-permeable TRP and ryanodine channels, ATP-sensitive potassium channels, and monoamine transporters, linking the stimulus to secretion, excitability, inflammatory cytokine output, and metabolic and circadian gene expression. It is the framework through which nucleotide signalling and xenobiotic stress converge on cell physiology.

Organophosphorus compounds range from insecticides that inhibit cholinesterase to the cell's own phosphorylated nucleotides, and this grouping collects the cellular and organismal reactions they provoke: altered secretion, channel gating, gene induction and enzyme output. Much of it is purinergic, since extracellular ATP and related nucleotides act through the full family of ionotropic P2X receptors and G protein-coupled P2Y receptors, with pannexin and ectonucleotidases such as NT5E and ENPP1 shaping the signal. Downstream lie cyclic nucleotide relays -- phosphodiesterases, PKA-anchoring proteins, Rap guanine-nucleotide exchange factors and CREB-regulated coactivators -- plus calcium release channels and potassium, HCN and TRP conductances that translate the stimulus into excitability and fluid or ion transport changes. Immediate-early genes including FOS and DUSP1 and inflammatory mediators mark the transcriptional arm, which matters for neurotoxicity, secretory control and how tissues register nucleotide release from damaged cells.

Arsenic exposure forces cells into a coordinated defensive response, and this pathway covers how they sense arsenite and arsenate, dispose of them, and survive the oxidative and proteotoxic damage they cause. It matters because arsenic in drinking water is a widespread cause of skin, bladder and lung cancer, and because arsenic trioxide is used therapeutically in leukaemia, where the same responses limit or mediate its effect. Uptake occurs partly through aquaglyceroporin channels, while GSTO1 and GSTO2 catalyse arsenate reduction steps and glutathione supply from GCLC feeds conjugation and export. NFE2L2 drives antioxidant genes including HMOX1, HSF1 and associated zinc-finger AN1 proteins mount a heat-shock and stress-granule response, and VCP with RNF4 handles arsenic-damaged, aggregated protein. ATR-dependent checkpoint signalling and heme biosynthesis enzymes reflect the genotoxic and metabolic consequences of exposure.

Cadmium is a non-essential heavy metal that enters cells through transporters meant for zinc, manganese and iron, then poisons them by binding thiols, displacing zinc from proteins and driving oxidative stress; the cellular response to cadmium ion is the defensive programme that limits this damage, and its capacity underlies susceptibility to cadmium nephrotoxicity, bone disease and carcinogenesis. Its core is metal-responsive transcription: MTF1 senses free metal and induces the metallothionein family, small cysteine-rich proteins that sequester cadmium and zinc, alongside heat shock factor-driven proteostasis. Efflux and compartmentalization by zinc transporters such as SLC30A1, and uptake routes including SLC39A8, set intracellular load. Antioxidant and glutathione arms, including catalase, superoxide dismutases, heme oxygenase-1 and the glutamate-cysteine ligase and glutathione synthetase steps, neutralize reactive oxygen species, while stress kinase and cell cycle components couple exposure to arrest or death.

Copper is needed as an enzyme cofactor yet is toxic in excess, so cells mount a coordinated response to a copper ion stimulus that buffers the metal, redistributes it, and adapts gene expression to the load. The bulk of the capacity here is metallothionein: the many MT1 isoforms plus MT2A, MT3 and MT4 are cysteine-rich thiolate cages induced on demand to sequester copper and zinc, with HSF1 and NFE2L2 driving the stress and antioxidant arms of that induction. Export and delivery depend on the copper-transporting ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B, whose loss causes Menkes and Wilson disease respectively. Downstream consequences touch superoxide dismutase activity, mitochondrial respiratory subunits, autophagy, and the copper-binding amyloid and prion proteins APP, PRNP and SNCA, linking copper handling to oxidative stress and neurodegeneration.

Mercury is a thiol-avid heavy metal that poisons cells by binding cysteine residues, and the response to mercury ion covers the cellular and organismal changes that follow such exposure inhibition of susceptible enzymes, altered transport, and the handling and disposal of the metal. Kidney and nervous tissue bear the brunt of mercury toxicity, which is reflected here in the aquaporin water channels, the renal phosphate carrier SLC34A1, the glutamate/cysteine transporter SLC1A1 and the metal-ion transporter SLC39A8; conjugated mercury is exported across membranes by the ABCC2 efflux pump. Sulfhydryl-dependent enzymes such as ALAD, a step in heme synthesis, and the metabolic enzymes TAT and PGAM2 are among the classic targets whose inhibition underlies poisoning, while PARK7 and the transcription factor JUND link exposure to oxidative stress defence and stress-responsive gene expression.

Decidualization is the transformation of the uterine endometrium into decidua at the start of pregnancy, converting fibroblast-like stromal cells into large secretory, often polyploid decidual cells that build the maternal side of the placenta. Without it a blastocyst cannot implant or be sustained, and defective decidual responses underlie infertility, recurrent miscarriage and preeclampsia. The genes trace the signals that drive it: LIF as the classic implantation cytokine, prostaglandin synthesis through PTGS2 and PTGIS coupling inflammation to vascular remodelling, vitamin D activation via CYP27B1 and VDR, and stanniocalcins, osteopontin and pleiotrophin acting on stromal adhesion and angiogenesis. Transcriptional and chromatin regulators such as JUNB, CITED2 and ASH1L, together with PARP1/PARP2, reprogramme the stromal genome, while receptors for ghrelin and erythropoietin tie the response to maternal metabolic and hypoxic status.

Decidualization converts the fibroblast-like stromal cells of the endometrium into secretory, polyploid decidual cells after a blastocyst implants, creating the maternal tissue that supports trophoblast invasion, remodels uterine vessels and becomes the maternal side of the placenta. Without it implantation fails or is shallow, a route to infertility, recurrent pregnancy loss and defective placentation. The transition is driven by progesterone and cyclic AMP signalling together with locally acting cues: leukaemia inhibitory factor is required for uterine receptivity, prostaglandin synthesis through cyclooxygenase-2 and prostacyclin synthase with the nuclear receptor PPARD supports implantation-site vascular change, and vitamin D activation by CYP27B1 acting on its receptor modulates the stromal response. Transcriptional and chromatin regulators such as JUNB, CITED2 and the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases, alongside matrix and secreted factors like osteopontin, cathepsin B and the stanniocalcins, shape stromal proliferation, differentiation and tissue remodelling.

Guanosine 5'-diphosphate sits between GMP and GTP, and the reactions that interconvert them set the size of the guanine nucleotide pool that fuels transcription, translation, glycosylation and every GTPase switch in the cell. Guanylate kinase is the committed step here, phosphorylating GMP to GDP, and its activity also determines how efficiently guanine-analogue prodrugs are converted to their active forms. A nucleotide diphosphatase and a nudix hydrolase counterbalance this by degrading nucleotide substrates, while a nucleoside diphosphatase acting in the secretory compartments recycles the GDP released by glycosyltransferase reactions. Several members are membrane-associated scaffolds of the PSD95/DLG family and related junctional proteins, whose guanylate kinase-like domains descend from this enzyme but serve protein-interaction roles at synapses, tight junctions and immune signalling platforms rather than nucleotide catalysis.

muscle cell cellular homeostasis covers the maintenance programs that keep a differentiated muscle fiber structurally and metabolically stable through repeated cycles of contraction. It matters because muscle is post-mitotic and mechanically stressed: fibers must continuously repair membrane damage, turn over damaged sarcomeric proteins, and match fuel supply to workload, and failure of any of these produces the muscular dystrophies and myopathies. The genes span the load-bearing links between cytoskeleton and matrix, including dystrophin, sarcoglycan and the glycosyltransferases that decorate dystroglycan; the quality-control arms that clear damaged proteins and organelles through chaperone-assisted autophagy, lysosomal glycogen breakdown and ubiquitin ligase activity; the calcium-dependent protease and actin-severing proteins that remodel sarcomeres; and glycolytic enzymes with hypoxia and growth signaling that set fiber size, with myostatin and TGF-beta restraining mass and SRF driving the contractile gene program.

Muscle fibres are long-lived, mechanically stressed cells that must keep their sarcomeres, membranes and energy supply in a steady working state, and this homeostatic programme is what maintains them. Its components span the pathways whose failure causes muscular dystrophy and myopathy: dystrophin and sarcoglycan linkage of the cytoskeleton to the basal lamina, glycosyltransferases that build the matrix-binding sugars on dystroglycan, calpain-3 and TRIM32-mediated turnover of sarcomeric proteins, and BAG3-dependent chaperone quality control of the Z-disc. Lysosomal function contributes through acid maltase and LAMP2, whose loss produces glycogen storage myopathy, while glycolytic enzymes and HIF1A match ATP supply to contractile demand. Growth and repair are set by myostatin and TGF-beta signalling and by serum response factor-driven actin gene expression, and actin dynamics are trimmed by cofilin-2. Together these keep fibre size, membrane integrity and contractile performance stable.

Controlled release of acid by cells and tissues, exemplified by the gastric parietal cell, which acidifies the stomach lumen to activate pepsin, sterilize ingested food and permit iron and B12 absorption. Loss of control at either extreme matters clinically: too much acid produces peptic ulceration and reflux oesophagitis, too little produces hypochlorhydria and bacterial overgrowth. Secretion is set by hormonal and neural input converging on the secreting cell, with gastrin and histamine receptors (CCKBR, HRH2) and muscarinic, prostaglandin, somatostatin-related and calcium-sensing inputs raising or damping the response, and ghrelin, secretin and neuromedin U acting as gut peptide modulators. Downstream, potassium and chloride channels, sodium-proton and anion exchangers (SLC9A4, SLC26A7) supply the counter-ion flux that lets the proton pump work, while trafficking proteins remodel the apical membrane. Bile acid transporters and hepatic metabolic enzymes place related acid handling in liver and bile.

Viruses do not simply make protein; they tune how much of each viral protein accumulates in the infected cell, and this control over viral protein levels shapes replication timing, particle assembly and how visible the infection is to innate immunity. The host factors co-opted here span several steps: an adaptor of a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase that viral proteins hijack to redirect degradation, a double-stranded RNA-binding protein and dynein light chain that influence viral RNA transport and translation, and endoplasmic reticulum membrane and trafficking proteins such as VAPB and the Rab GTPase-activating protein TBC1D20 that support replication organelle formation. Interferon-induced components, including STAT1 and the translation-inhibiting IFIT1, mark the opposing host restriction that the virus must balance against. The net effect sets the stoichiometry of structural and non-structural proteins, determining whether infection proceeds to productive burst or persists at low output.

Many enveloped viruses leave an infected cell without killing it, budding through the plasma membrane or exiting in vesicles so that the producer cell survives and continues to release progeny. This non-lytic route of viral egress matters because it permits persistent, low-level shedding and helps virions escape immune detection, and it is the step targeted by inhibitors of budding. The genes here are the ESCRT-III subunits and their AAA-ATPase disassembly machinery, the module that normally deforms and severs membrane necks during multivesicular body formation, cytokinetic abscission and membrane repair. Retroviral and other viral late domains recruit these CHMP proteins so that the same constriction-and-scission chemistry closes the neck of a budding particle. VPS4A and VPS4B then recycle the polymer for reuse, making the host's own membrane remodelling apparatus the direct means of particle release.

Enveloped viruses leave a cell by wrapping themselves in host membrane and cutting it free, and viral budding is the final step in which the particle is pinched off and released. The host machinery co-opted for this is the ESCRT system, normally used to sort ubiquitinated cargo into multivesicular bodies and to sever membranes during cytokinesis and nuclear envelope resealing. Viral late domains recruit TSG101 with the ESCRT-I subunits VPS28 and VPS37, or ALIX, which in turn nucleate CHMP polymers that constrict the bud neck; the AAA-ATPase VPS4A/VPS4B then disassembles those filaments to complete scission, with NEDD4-family ubiquitin ligases marking cargo for engagement. Retroviruses including HIV-1, filoviruses and hepatitis viruses all depend on this route, so blocking it traps immature particles tethered at the membrane and limits spread of infection.

Protein autophosphorylation is the self-activating step of kinase signalling: a kinase phosphorylates residues on itself, or on an identical partner molecule, to switch itself on, stabilise an active conformation, or create docking sites for downstream effectors. It is how receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR-family ERBB4, FGFRs, INSR, IGF1R, KIT, FLT3 and the VEGF and PDGF receptors convert ligand-induced dimerisation into an intracellular signal, and how checkpoint and stress kinases including ATM, CHEK2, the eIF2-alpha kinases and ULK1/2 commit to a response once a threshold is crossed. Trans-autophosphorylation within dimers makes the switch cooperative and effectively irreversible until phosphatases intervene, so it sets the sensitivity of growth factor, metabolic, DNA damage, autophagy and cytoskeletal signalling. Mutations that permit ligand-independent autophosphorylation in ALK, FLT3, KIT or LRRK2 drive cancers and neurodegeneration, making these activation loops the principal targets of kinase inhibitor drugs.

Kinases commonly switch themselves on, and protein autophosphorylation covers the self-directed transfer of phosphate onto a kinase's own residues or onto identical partner molecules in a dimer. This is how an inactive enzyme becomes competent after a ligand binds or a stress is sensed: receptor tyrosine kinases such as the insulin, FGF, PDGF, VEGF and KIT receptors trans-autophosphorylate across ligand-induced dimers to create docking sites for adaptors, while soluble kinases including ATM, CHEK2, JAK2, AURKA, LRRK2 and the ULK autophagy initiators use it to license catalytic activity or mark their own activation loops. Because the modification is both a switch and a signalling handle, it sets the threshold and duration of growth factor responses, DNA damage checkpoints, translational stress control and mitotic entry. Mutations that make autophosphorylation constitutive are a recurring route to oncogenic kinase activation and a reason these enzymes dominate targeted drug development.

Viral genomes depend on host transcription machinery, and host cells in turn have ways to tune how much viral RNA gets made. Regulation of viral transcription covers both sides of that contest: cellular factors that promote transcription from integrated or episomal viral templates, and restriction factors that silence them. Several components act through the positive transcription elongation factor P-TEFb, with HEXIM1 and LARP7 holding it in an inactive small nuclear RNP so that it cannot be recruited to viral promoters, a mechanism central to HIV latency and reactivation. A large family of tripartite-motif ubiquitin ligases contributes restriction and interferon-linked antiviral activity, while SP100 participates in nuclear body-mediated repression of incoming herpesvirus genomes, and chromatin remodelling and RNA-binding proteins such as RSF1, DHX9 and ZFP36 alter template accessibility and transcript fate. The balance set here determines whether an infection remains latent or enters productive replication.

Microtubules grow by adding tubulin heterodimers to their ends, and this polymerization is what lets a cell build a mitotic spindle, extend an axon, position organelles and run intracellular transport. The genes here cover the whole chain of events: alpha, beta and gamma tubulins as the subunits, the gamma-tubulin ring complex with its associated MZT and NEDD1 components as the nucleation template, centrosomal and pericentriolar scaffolds such as pericentrin, CDK5RAP2 and CEP192, the augmin complex that nucleates new microtubules off existing ones, and plus-end tracking proteins including EB family members, CKAP5/ch-TOG, CLASPs and CLIP1 that sustain growth. Opposing them are destabilizers such as stathmins, while CAMSAPs and ninein organize minus ends. Tubulin chaperones and folding cofactors supply polymerization-competent dimers. Mutations in tubulins and their regulators cause cortical malformations and neuropathies, and the polymer itself is the target of taxanes and vinca alkaloids.

Viruses cannot move themselves, so they borrow the host's trafficking machinery to get from the cell surface to the site of replication and back out again, and this directed transport of viral particles and components into, within and out of the cell determines whether an infection succeeds. Attachment lectins such as CD209 and CLEC4M capture enveloped virions and hand them to endocytic routes; dynein light chain DYNLT1 links cargo to microtubule motors for inward movement; importins of the KPNA family and the nucleoporin NUP153 deliver viral genomes and proteins through the nuclear pore. Host restriction acts on the same steps, with BST2 tethering budding virions at the plasma membrane and TRIM family proteins intercepting incoming capsids. The balance between these hijacked transport steps and their antiviral counterparts sets cell tropism, the efficiency of nuclear entry, and the amount of infectious virus released.

Infection begins with attachment, and this is the step in which a virion engages a specific receptor on the surface of a host cell and so determines which tissues a virus can enter. The receptors here are ordinary host membrane proteins with day jobs unrelated to infection: ACE2, a peptidase of the renin-angiotensin system, and DPP4 are both entry receptors for coronaviruses; CLEC4M is a lectin that captures glycosylated envelope proteins; ICAM1 and LRRC15 act as adhesion-type attachment factors, and secreted GAS6 can bridge virions to host phosphatidylserine receptors. Binding is usually followed by proteolytic priming of the viral glycoprotein, which TMPRSS2 provides at the cell surface, committing the particle to membrane fusion and genome delivery. Because tropism and species barriers are set at this point, attachment receptors are the principal targets of neutralising antibodies and entry inhibitors.

Whether a transcription factor, mRNA or signalling kinase sits in the nucleus or the cytoplasm is itself a regulated decision, and this pathway covers the machinery and signals that set it. Controlling traffic across the nuclear envelope is how cells convert a cytoplasmic stimulus into a change in gene expression, sequester factors until they are needed, and restrict viral access to the nucleus. Nucleoporins such as NUP153, NUP214 and TPR, the RAN GTPase with its GAP, and exportins including XPO1 provide the transport apparatus, while kinases, phosphatases, 14-3-3 proteins and SUMO modification determine which cargoes are recognised and when. Familiar clients illustrate the logic: NFKBIA holds NF-κB out of the nucleus, SUFU restrains GLI in hedgehog signalling, and GSK3B-directed phosphorylation relocalises substrates. Disrupted shuttling of RNA-binding proteins such as TARDBP is a hallmark of neurodegeneration, and export dependence makes this route a cancer drug target.

Whether a transcription factor or signalling protein reaches the nucleus is itself a regulated decision, and this pathway covers the mechanisms that restrain such traffic: holding cargo in the cytoplasm, blocking import receptors, or limiting export through the pore. It matters because signal-responsive factors such as NF-κB, GLI and the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A must be kept out of the nucleus until the right cue arrives, and loss of this restraint produces constitutive transcriptional output, as in inflammatory and oncogenic states. Anchoring proteins act directly: NFKBIA masks the NF-κB nuclear localisation signal, SUFU sequesters GLI factors, PKIA and PKIG bind and exclude PKA catalytic subunits, and 14-3-3 proteins retain phosphorylated clients in the cytosol. Nucleoporin and basket components including NUP153 and TPR, together with RANGAP1 and SUMO1, set the permeability and directionality of the pore itself.

Whether a transcription factor, mRNA or signalling protein reaches its destination depends on traffic through the nuclear pore, and this collection captures the events that increase that traffic. Enhanced nucleocytoplasmic transport is how cells convert an extracellular cue into a change in gene expression: growth factor and cytokine signalling through kinases such as JAK2, MAPK14, GSK3B and PRKACA promotes nuclear entry of effectors, SMAD3 shuttles in response to TGFB1, and hedgehog signalling through SMO and GLI3 depends on regulated nuclear access. Core machinery is represented by the RAN GTPase, importin and exportin carriers, the nucleoporin TPR and the cap-binding and cleavage factor subunits that license mRNA export. Because nuclear import of stress- and immune-responsive factors is rate-limiting, the same regulation underlies interferon and inflammatory responses, and its breakdown contributes to the cytoplasmic mislocalisation of TARDBP seen in neurodegeneration.

Whether a transcription factor, kinase or tumour suppressor acts in the nucleus or is held in the cytoplasm is often decided not by its synthesis but by how fast it is exported, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune that rate. Control of protein export from the nucleus sets the duration of transcriptional responses, restrains proliferation when checkpoint proteins are retained on chromatin, and is exploited by tumours that expel p53-class regulators to the cytoplasm — the rationale for blocking the exportin XPO1. Mechanistically it combines the carriers themselves (XPO1, XPO4) and the RanGTP gradient maintained by RANGAP1, nuclear pore and basket components such as TPR and EMD, kinases including GSK3B, CDK5 and PRKACA that phosphorylate cargo near its export signal, and 14-3-3 proteins (SFN, YWHAE) that bind phosphorylated cargo and sequester it outside the nucleus.

Negative regulation of protein export from nucleus is the control layer that keeps selected proteins from leaving the nucleus, thereby holding transcription factors, tumour suppressors and repair proteins where they act. Retention is a decision point: BRCA1 kept nuclear by its BARD1 partner can support DNA damage repair and checkpoint arrest, whereas premature export shifts the same protein toward cytoplasmic, apoptotic roles, and forced nuclear accumulation of stress-responsive factors such as PARK7 alters oxidative stress protection. Mechanistically these regulators act by masking nuclear export signals, modifying cargo or interfering with the RanGTP gradient and exportin loading that drive translocation through the pore, with RANGAP1 setting the nucleotide state that gives transport its directionality. Chromatin- and body-associated components including HDAC3 and SP100 tie retention to nuclear organisation, making compartmentalisation itself a mode of signalling control.

Where a protein sits relative to the nuclear envelope often determines whether it can act, so blocking nuclear export is a way of retaining transcription factors, repair proteins and signalling molecules in the nucleus where their targets are. Negative regulation of protein export from the nucleus covers the events that hold cargo back, whether by masking a nuclear export signal, modifying the cargo, or altering the Ran GTPase gradient that gives transport its directionality; RANGAP1 stimulates GTP hydrolysis on Ran in the cytoplasm and thereby sets that gradient. Other contributors act through protein modification and complex formation, including the deacetylase HDAC3, the kinase CDK5, the tumour suppressor BARD1 in complex with BRCA1, and PARK7. Retention of this kind matters for DNA damage responses, for apoptotic decisions, and for keeping antiviral and interferon-responsive factors such as SP100 in nuclear bodies.

Whether a protein sits in the nucleus or the cytoplasm often decides whether a signal is transmitted at all, and this pathway covers the events that push proteins out through the nuclear pore. Enhanced nuclear export switches off transcription factors, releases cytoplasmic enzymes to act on their local substrates, and enforces cell cycle checkpoints by sequestering regulators away from chromatin. Several routes are represented: kinases such as GSK3B, PRKACA and PRKD1 phosphorylate cargo to expose export signals or mask import signals, 14-3-3 proteins including SFN and YWHAE bind phosphorylated cargo and retain it outside the nucleus, and a dedicated exportin together with nucleoporin TPR handles passage through the pore. Phosphatases like PPM1A act in the opposite direction on the same switches. Loss of this control leaves transcriptional and checkpoint regulators inappropriately nuclear, a recurring feature of tumour cells.

Messenger RNAs are only useful once they reach the cytoplasm, and this pathway covers the factors that promote and accelerate the export of RNA from the nucleus. It sits at the junction between transcript maturation and translation: efficient export depends on correct 3' end formation, splicing and cap recognition, so the proteins that stimulate it are typically the same ones that license a transcript as finished. A nuclear cap-binding subunit marks the 5' end for the export machinery, a cleavage and polyadenylation factor couples 3' end processing to release, and an RNA helicase resolves the duplex and R-loop structures that would otherwise trap transcripts on chromatin; RNA-binding adaptors of the KH-domain type shuttle bound mRNAs across the pore. Loss of this stimulatory input strands transcripts in the nucleus, reducing protein output and provoking nuclear RNA surveillance and degradation.

Attaching a phosphate to a lipid converts it from a structural molecule into a signal, and lipid phosphorylation by this family of kinases is how cells terminate one lipid second messenger while creating another. The diacylglycerol kinases consume diacylglycerol generated by phospholipase C downstream of receptor activation, producing phosphatidic acid; this both switches off protein kinase C recruitment and supplies a lipid that recruits its own effectors and feeds glycerophospholipid synthesis. The individual isoforms differ in domain organisation, calcium and lipid regulation, and tissue distribution, giving distinct control over T cell activation and anergy, neuronal and synaptic signalling, cardiac and vascular responses, and insulin action. A mitochondrial member of the group phosphorylates monoacylglycerol and sphingosine, and its loss causes Sengers syndrome with cataract and cardiomyopathy, tying this chemistry to membrane lipid remodelling as well as signalling.

Carbohydrate phosphorylation is the committing step of sugar metabolism: attaching a phosphate to a sugar traps it inside the cell and activates it for glycolysis, glycogen synthesis, or nucleotide-sugar and glycan pathways. Hexokinases and glucokinase phosphorylate glucose at entry, with glucokinase acting as the glucose sensor of pancreatic beta cells and hepatocytes, so that its mutation causes monogenic diabetes. Parallel kinases handle other sugars — galactose, fructose, ketohexoses, ribose, xylulose, fucose and N-acetylglucosamine — feeding them into central carbon flux; defects here underlie galactosemia and hereditary fructose intolerance. The bifunctional PFKFB enzymes set fructose-2,6-bisphosphate levels and thereby the glycolytic rate, while GnT-phosphotransferase subunits and POMK phosphorylate sugars on glycoproteins to direct lysosomal targeting and dystroglycan function. Together these reactions link nutrient uptake, energy production, and glycan-dependent trafficking and muscle integrity.

Phosphorylating a sugar is usually the first committed step in using it: the charge traps the sugar inside the cell and readies it for further metabolism. This is the entry point for glucose, galactose, fructose, mannose, ribose, xylulose and fucose into glycolysis and into nucleotide-sugar and glycan synthesis, so its capacity sets how quickly tissues can consume dietary carbohydrate. Hexokinases and the glucose-sensing glucokinase commit glucose to glycolysis, while ketohexokinase initiates rapid hepatic fructose handling, and galactokinases feed the Leloir route; GNE and NAGK supply amino-sugar precursors for sialylation. Bifunctional PFKFB enzymes make and degrade fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, the allosteric signal that governs glycolytic versus gluconeogenic flux. Other members phosphorylate sugars already attached to macromolecules, including a kinase acting on O-mannosyl glycans of dystroglycan and the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase that tags lysosomal enzymes. Deficiencies cause galactosemia, MODY, muscular dystrophy and mucolipidosis.

Glycolipids made in one membrane must reach another, and glycolipid transport is the set of carriers and lipid-binding proteins that move glycosylated lipids between membranes and compartments rather than letting them diffuse. This traffic sets the glycosphingolipid composition of the plasma membrane, feeds lysosomal degradation, and supplies substrates for glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum. Soluble transfer proteins such as GLTP and its ceramide-1-phosphate-selective relative CPTP shuttle lipids in the cytosol, while PLEKHA8 delivers glucosylceramide from the Golgi for further glycosylation. In the lysosome, saposins derived from prosaposin and the cholesterol-binding NPC2 extract membrane lipids and present them to degradative enzymes; loss of prosaposin function causes sphingolipid storage disease, and CLN3 mutation underlies juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. RFT1 acts on the flipping of an oligosaccharide-lipid intermediate needed for N-linked glycosylation, linking this transport to glycan biosynthesis.

Removing phosphate groups from phosphorylated lipids sets the code that tells a membrane where it is and what it should do. Phosphoinositide phosphatases acting at the 3-, 4- and 5-positions, together with lipid phosphate phosphatases, reverse the work of lipid kinases and thereby terminate signalling, drive vesicle maturation along the endocytic route, and control the recruitment of proteins that read specific phosphoinositide species. PTEN degrades PIP3 to restrain PI3K-AKT growth signalling and is among the most frequently lost tumour suppressors; myotubularins and OCRL shape endosomal and lysosomal identity, with mutations causing centronuclear myopathy, demyelinating neuropathy and Lowe syndrome; synaptojanins recycle synaptic vesicles after clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Related enzymes dephosphorylate sphingosine-1-phosphate and phosphatidic acid, linking this chemistry to lipid mediator turnover and membrane biosynthesis.

Filopodia are the thin, finger-like actin bundles that a migrating fibroblast, an immune cell or an axonal growth cone pushes ahead of itself to sample the surroundings, and their assembly is how a cell decides where to go and what to touch. The process underlies cell migration, axon pathfinding and dendritic spine formation, so its misregulation shows up in neurodevelopmental disorders and in invasive tumour behaviour. Mechanistically it centres on Cdc42 and related small GTPases, activated by FGD-family and other exchange factors and restrained by GAPs such as the SRGAP proteins; these converge on the I-BAR protein BAIAP2, N-WASP and formins to nucleate parallel actin filaments, which fascin cross-links into stiff bundles. Myosin X walks cargo out to filopodial tips, while VASP elongates filaments there. Guidance receptors including EphB2, neuropilin and neurexin-neuroligin adhesion pairs couple external cues to this protrusive machinery.

Adult bone is continuously turned over, with osteoclasts resorbing mineralized matrix at discrete foci and osteoblasts refilling the cavity, and this remodeling both maintains the mechanical integrity of the skeleton and provides a reservoir for calcium homeostasis. Loss of balance between the two arms produces osteoporosis, osteopetrosis and other metabolic bone disease. The RANKL-RANK-TRAF6 axis, together with CSF1R signalling, drives osteoclast differentiation and fusion, while tyrosine kinases such as SRC, SYK and PTK2B organise the sealing zone; acid delivery through the vacuolar ATPase subunit TCIRG1 and the anion exchanger SLC4A2, plus secretion of cathepsin K and tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase, dissolves mineral and collagen. Osteoblast output is set by WNT-β-catenin signalling through LRP5 and LGR4 with SFRP1 and sclerostin-like antagonism, and by Indian hedgehog and BMP-family cues. Systemic control comes from parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, leptin and hypothalamic circuits, IL-6 and sympathetic β-adrenergic input.

Skeletal mass is maintained by continuous cycles in which osteoclasts resorb mineralised matrix and osteoblasts replace it, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast and how extensively that turnover proceeds. Tipping the balance toward resorption produces osteoporosis and erosive joint disease, while excessive suppression yields osteopetrosis and brittle, poorly remodelled bone. The RANKL/RANK axis drives osteoclast differentiation from myeloid precursors, supported by CSF1R signalling, cell fusion via DC-STAMP, and a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase module of SRC, SYK and the ITGB3-containing integrin that organises the sealing zone and acidified resorption lacuna, where SLC4A2 handles anion exchange. Osteoblast output is tuned by Wnt and BMP antagonists such as SFRP1 and GREM1 and reported by osteocalcin. Systemic endocrine inputs, including leptin and its receptor, calcitonin-related peptides, and central melanocortin and kisspeptin signalling, link bone turnover to energy balance and reproductive state, with IL6 and TNFAIP3 coupling it to inflammation.

negative regulation of bone remodeling covers the brakes on skeletal turnover — the signals that restrain osteoclast-driven resorption and the coupled bone formation that follows it, keeping bone mass stable in the adult and preventing the excess remodeling seen in osteoporosis, hyperparathyroid states and inflammatory bone loss. Several arms converge here. Calcitonin and amylin, products of the CALCA and IAPP genes, act on osteoclasts as endocrine suppressors of resorption, while KISS1/KISS1R and FSHR link gonadal and pituitary axes to skeletal output. Intracellular restraint comes from negative regulators of immune-receptor and cytokine signalling in the osteoclast lineage — the inositol phosphatase INPP5D, the kinase CSK, the ubiquitin-editing protein TNFAIP3 and the phosphatase UBASH3B — while secreted Wnt and BMP antagonists SFRP1 and GREM1 damp osteoblast activity. Purinergic signalling through P2RX7 and CD38-dependent calcium messengers tune mechanically and inflammation-driven remodeling.

Bone mass is maintained by balancing osteoclast resorption against osteoblast formation, and this pathway covers the braking signals that hold remodeling in check. Restraint matters because unopposed resorption produces osteoporosis and pathological bone loss, while excessive suppression yields overly dense, brittle bone. Several distinct kinds of brake appear here: calcitonin, encoded by CALCA, and the related peptide amylin directly quiet osteoclasts; secreted antagonists such as gremlin-1 and SFRP1 dampen bone-anabolic BMP and Wnt signalling; and intracellular negative regulators including the inositol phosphatase SHIP1, the Src-family inhibitor CSK, the phosphatase UBASH3B and the NF-kB brake TNFAIP3 limit signalling downstream of osteoclast receptors. Endocrine and neuropeptide inputs, among them FSH and kisspeptin receptors and CART, tie skeletal turnover to reproductive and central metabolic state, linking bone remodeling to whole-body hormonal control and to inflammatory mediators such as IL-6 and P2RX7.

Phosphoinositides are low-abundance membrane lipids that mark organelle identity and recruit effector proteins, and this pathway covers their synthesis interconversion by lipid kinases together with the phosphatases and inositol-phosphate enzymes that set their levels. The products define where a membrane is and what it can do: PI4P at the Golgi and plasma membrane, PI(4,5)P2 driving endocytosis and actin attachment, PI(3)P on early endosomes and forming autophagosomes, and PI(3,4,5)P3 recruiting AKT to drive growth and survival signalling. Class I PI3Ks with their regulatory subunits act downstream of growth factor and immune receptors, while a class III complex with beclin-1, ATG14 and VPS15 initiates autophagy; PI4K isoforms work with palmitoylated scaffolds and TTC7 partners at the plasma membrane. Loss of the phosphatases causes Lowe syndrome, ciliopathies and demyelinating neuropathy, and activating PIK3CA mutation is among the commonest events in cancer.

Phosphatidylinositol dephosphorylation is the removal of phosphate groups from phosphoinositide lipids, the step that terminates lipid second-messenger signalling and gives each membrane its distinctive phosphoinositide identity. Because the position and number of phosphates on the inositol ring specify where vesicles bud, where proteins dock, and how strongly growth-factor signalling runs, these phosphatases control endosomal traffic, autophagy, cilium function and cell growth. The genes span the major families: 5-phosphatases such as OCRL, SYNJ1 and the SHIP proteins, the myotubularin 3-phosphatases acting on PI3P and PI(3,5)P2, the Sac-domain enzymes including SACM1L and FIG4, and PTEN, which reverses PI3K signalling and is among the most frequently lost tumour suppressors. Loss of individual members causes Lowe syndrome, X-linked myotubular myopathy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and Joubert syndrome, illustrating how tightly neurons, muscle and kidney depend on correct phosphoinositide turnover.

Phosphoinositides mark membranes with a positional code that recruits trafficking and signalling proteins, and the phosphatases that strip phosphates from the inositol ring erase and rewrite that code. Removing the 5-phosphate from PIP3 by PTEN terminates growth and survival signalling downstream of PI3K, making this chemistry a tumour suppressive brake; loss of other members causes disease in its own right, including Lowe syndrome from OCRL, X-linked myotubular myopathy from MTM1, and demyelinating neuropathy from MTMR2. The set spans 5-phosphatases acting on PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P3, the myotubularin family of 3-phosphatases specific for PI3P and PI(3,5)P2, and 4-phosphatases including SACM1L, which keeps PI4P low in the endoplasmic reticulum. Their combined output governs endosome maturation, autophagy, synaptic vesicle recycling by synaptojanins, cytoskeletal remodelling, and insulin and immune receptor signalling.

Quinolinate sits at the junction where tryptophan degradation becomes NAD+ synthesis, and the handling of this pyridine dicarboxylate determines both how much NAD the liver and other tissues can make de novo and how much accumulates as a neurotoxin. Kynurenine 3-monooxygenase and kynureninase convert kynurenine to 3-hydroxyanthranilate, which HAAO oxidises to an unstable intermediate that cyclises spontaneously to quinolinate; QPRT then condenses it with phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate to give nicotinate mononucleotide, committing carbon to the NAD pool. ACMSD diverts the same intermediate toward complete oxidation instead, and its activity sets the balance between NAD production and catabolism. Because quinolinate is an NMDA receptor agonist, excess produced by activated microglia and macrophages during inflammation contributes to excitotoxic damage, linking this branch of tryptophan catabolism to neurodegeneration, immune tolerance and niacin nutrition.

regulation of saliva secretion controls how much fluid and protein the salivary glands release, the process that keeps the oral cavity lubricated, buffers acid, initiates starch digestion, and protects teeth and mucosa from microbial damage. Loss of this control produces xerostomia, with difficulty swallowing and speaking and accelerated dental decay. The genes point to several layers of that control: water permeability of acinar and ductal membranes through the aquaporin channel that carries transcellular fluid flux, calcium-calmodulin-dependent phosphatase signalling downstream of muscarinic and adrenergic stimulation by autonomic nerves, opioid receptor input that dampens secretory drive, and developmental regulators such as FGF10 and NEUROG1 that build the branched gland epithelium and its innervation in the first place. The pathway therefore links secretory physiology to glandular morphogenesis and neural tone.

Saliva output is set by neural and hormonal input to acinar and ductal cells of the salivary glands, and modulating that output matters for lubrication of food, taste perception, oral antimicrobial defence and dental health; loss of control produces xerostomia and its downstream caries and swallowing difficulty. Regulation of saliva secretion acts at several levels represented here: water movement through an aquaporin channel, which sets the fluid volume once ions are secreted; calcium-dependent signalling through the phosphatase calcineurin, whose catalytic subunit couples stimulation to transcriptional and secretory responses; opioid receptor signalling, which dampens secretomotor drive; and developmental factors including FGF10 and neurogenin family transcriptional regulators that build the glandular epithelium and the sensory and autonomic innervation on which secretion depends. The pathway therefore links exocrine fluid transport to autonomic control and gland morphogenesis.

Pituitary gonadotropes release follicle-stimulating hormone to drive ovarian follicle growth and spermatogenesis, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise that release. Activin subunits encoded by INHBA and INHBB dimerise into ligands that act on gonadotropes, signalling through receptor-activated SMADs with SMAD4 as the shared partner to the FSH beta-subunit promoter; the forkhead factor FOXL2 cooperates with these SMADs on that promoter and is required for normal gonadotrope output as well as for ovarian granulosa cell identity. Leptin adds a metabolic permissive signal, coupling adequate energy stores to reproductive endocrine drive, which is why undernutrition suppresses gonadotropin secretion. INHA contributes the alpha subunit that pairs with beta subunits to form inhibins, tying this stimulatory arm to the feedback loop that opposes it. Disruption shifts follicular recruitment and fertility.

regulation of hormone secretion covers the control layer that sets how much of a hormone an endocrine cell releases, and when. It underlies glucose homeostasis, growth, reproduction, stress responses and calcium balance, and its failure produces diabetes, hypogonadism, growth deficiency and endocrine tumours. The genes trace the full arc from stimulus to release: nutrient sensing and glycolytic coupling through glucokinase, GLUD1 and monocarboxylate transport; membrane excitability set by the KATP channel subunits ABCC8 and KCNJ11 together with voltage-gated and TRP channels; cyclic AMP and calcium amplification via adenylate cyclases, PKA, EPAC and MCU; and the SNARE and synaptotagmin machinery that docks and fuses secretory granules. Layered on top are hypothalamic and paracrine ligands with their receptors, adipokines and cytokines, circadian clock components, and the islet transcription factors PDX1, NKX6-1 and NEUROD1 that maintain secretory competence.

Endocrine cells store hormones in secretory granules and release them only when instructed, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how much is released and when. It underlies glucose homeostasis, the hypothalamic-pituitary axes, calcium balance and appetite control, and its derangement produces diabetes, hyperinsulinism and disorders of growth and reproduction. Nutrient and metabolic sensors such as glucokinase, fatty acid receptors and mitochondrial transporters are coupled through ATP-sensitive potassium channels and their sulfonylurea receptor subunit, voltage-gated and TRP channels, and calcium entry to the exocytic machinery of syntaxins, VAMPs, SNAP25 and synaptotagmins. Overlaid on this are G protein-coupled receptors for somatostatin, dopamine, ghrelin, GIP and kisspeptin acting through cyclic AMP, PKA and PKC, transcription factors including PDX1, NKX6-1 and NEUROD1 that maintain secretory competence, and circadian components that time release across the day.

Follicle-stimulating hormone secretion is the controlled release of FSH from gonadotrope cells of the anterior pituitary, the hormone that drives ovarian follicle maturation and spermatogenesis. Its output sets fertility: too little gives hypogonadism and absent gametogenesis, while loss of feedback restraint disrupts cyclicity. The genes describe how that release is tuned. Activin subunits signal through SMAD4 to promote transcription of the gonadotropin subunit genes, while inhibin, assembled from the shared alpha chain with a beta subunit, antagonises this input as an endocrine brake from the gonad. FOXL2 and TBX3 act in the pituitary and gonad as transcriptional regulators that shape gonadotrope identity and activin responsiveness, and leptin links nutritional and adipose status to reproductive competence. Together they place FSH output at the junction of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis and metabolic state.

Release of follicle-stimulating hormone from gonadotropes of the anterior pituitary sets the pace of ovarian follicle growth and spermatogenesis, so its regulation determines fertility and the timing of the menstrual cycle. Secretion is tuned by feedback from the gonads: activin subunits drive FSH beta transcription through SMAD signalling, while inhibin, whose alpha subunit pairs with the same beta chains, opposes that drive, and the SMAD4 co-factor together with the gonadotrope and granulosa transcription factor FOXL2 shapes the transcriptional response. The shared glycoprotein hormone alpha subunit contributes the common chain of the assembled dimer, and TBX3 acts in pituitary development. Leptin links nutritional and adipose status to gonadotropin output, which is why energy deficit suppresses reproduction. Loss of this control produces hypogonadotropic infertility, while dysregulated activin–inhibin balance alters follicle recruitment.

Hormone output has to be tuned, not just enabled, and this pathway covers the upstream controls that set how fast steroid, peptide and other hormones are made. It matters for stress responses, reproduction and salt and water balance: too little cortisol or gonadal steroid causes adrenal insufficiency and infertility, too much drives Cushing-type disease and virilisation. Control is exerted at several levels. Trophic receptors such as the ACTH receptor MC2R and the LH/choriogonadotropin receptor transduce pituitary signals into steroidogenic gene expression, with cyclic nucleotide turnover by phosphodiesterases setting signal duration. Nuclear receptors including the glucocorticoid receptor and NR5A2 provide transcriptional drive and feedback, while POMC supplies the precursor for corticotropin itself. Secreted BMP and WNT ligands, DKK3 and stanniocalcin modulate gland responsiveness, and hypoxia sensing through HIF1A and ARNT links hormone synthesis to oxygen availability. POR and H6PD support the redox cofactor supply that steroidogenic enzymes require.

Hormone output is adjusted not only by releasing stored product but by turning up the enzymes and precursors that make it, and this is the regulatory arm that increases hormone biosynthesis. It matters for adrenal and gonadal steroid production, where trophic signals set how much cortisol, aldosterone or sex steroid an endocrine cell can synthesise, and for iron and salt homeostasis through hepcidin and hormonal control of blood pressure. Several routes converge here: melanocortin receptor signalling driven by pituitary POMC-derived ACTH, transcriptional control by nuclear receptors and early-response factors such as NR5A2 and EGR1, hypoxia sensing through HIF1A with its partner ARNT, and BMP and WNT ligands acting on gland development and steroidogenic capacity. The cytochrome P450 electron donor POR supplies reducing equivalents for the hydroxylations involved. Loss of such upregulation gives endocrine insufficiency; unchecked activity gives hormone excess.

Endocrine cells release hormones on demand, and this collection describes the inputs that push that release upward — the positive arm of regulated hormone secretion. It matters because glucose homeostasis, growth, reproduction and the stress response all depend on secretion being amplified at the right moment; blunted amplification underlies type 2 diabetes, while unrestrained output drives hypoglycaemia and endocrine excess. Much of the content is pancreatic beta cell stimulus–secretion coupling: glucokinase and GLUT2 set the metabolic threshold, the sulfonylurea receptor subunit couples ATP to membrane depolarisation, and calcium then drives exocytosis through syntaxin, VAMP and Doc2/rabphilin-family effectors, with cAMP acting via protein kinase A and Epac proteins. Incretin, free fatty acid, calcium-sensing and aminergic receptors feed in from outside, and hypothalamic–pituitary releasing factors such as GHRH, CRH, kisspeptin and urocortins extend the same logic to other axes. Transcription factors including PDX1, NKX6-1 and NEUROD1 maintain the secretory phenotype.

Hormone output has to be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this set gathers the brakes: the processes that stop, slow or reduce regulated hormone release from endocrine cells. Loss of such restraint produces hyperinsulinism, uncontrolled stress-axis drive, or inappropriate feeding signals, so the same machinery that tunes glucose homeostasis also sets appetite and neuroendocrine tone. Much of it acts at the exocytosis trigger itself: the ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits SUR1 and Kir6.2 hold beta cells hyperpolarised, other potassium channels and inhibitory G proteins downstream of dopamine D2, alpha-2 adrenergic, adenosine and opioid receptors suppress calcium entry, and granule-associated regulators such as synaptotagmin-like and Rab11-interacting proteins limit granule availability. Circulating and paracrine factors — leptin, adiponectin, ghrelin, inhibins, urocortin and CRH-binding protein — impose feedback, while circadian and metabolic sensors including CRY1/CRY2, SIRT4 and UCP2 gate secretion to time of day and fuel status.

positive regulation of lipid biosynthetic process covers the signals and transcriptional switches that turn up synthesis of fatty acids, triglycerides, cholesterol, phospholipids and steroids when a cell or tissue needs membrane, fuel storage or hormone precursors. It sets the anabolic side of lipid homeostasis, and its overactivation underlies hepatic steatosis, hyperlipidaemia and atherosclerotic risk, while its loss impairs membrane expansion and steroidogenesis. The core is sterol-sensing control of the SREBP transcription factors through SCAP and site-2 protease, working alongside carbohydrate-responsive MLXIPL and the nuclear receptors PPARA, LXR and FXR that couple oxysterol and bile acid levels to lipogenic gene expression. Insulin acts through AKT and mTORC1, and cAMP-PKA and cytokine inputs such as TNF and IL1B feed in as well. Lipoprotein handling genes, StAR-mediated cholesterol delivery for steroid synthesis, and microRNA repression of lipogenesis complete the regulatory circuit.

Cells and tissues must ramp up lipid production on demand — to build membranes during growth, to store energy in adipose and liver, to make steroid hormones, and to package lipids into lipoproteins — and this collection captures the inputs that drive that increase. Positive regulation of lipid biosynthetic processes is exerted largely through transcriptional master switches: the sterol-sensing SREBP factors with their escort protein SCAP and site-2 protease, the carbohydrate-responsive factor MLXIPL, and nuclear receptors including PPARA, the liver X receptors and the bile acid receptor NR1H4, which couple sterol, fatty acid and oxysterol levels to synthetic output. Hormonal and nutrient signals feed in through insulin, AKT1 and the mTOR complex, cAMP-dependent kinase, and adrenal stimulation via ACTH and STAR-dependent cholesterol delivery, while inflammatory cytokines, lipases, acyltransferases and specific microRNAs tune the response. Excessive drive here underlies hepatic steatosis, hyperlipidaemia and atherosclerotic lipid loading.

Cells must match lipid production to demand, and this collection of regulators sets how fast cholesterol, fatty acids, triglycerides and sphingolipids are made. The core is the sterol-sensing switch in the endoplasmic reticulum, where SCAP and the INSIG proteins retain SREBF1 and SREBF2 until sterols fall, whereupon site-1 and site-2 proteases release the transcription factors that drive LDLR and lipogenic enzyme expression. Nuclear receptors add hormonal and metabolic input: PPARA for fatty acid oxidation, the liver X receptors NR1H2/NR1H3 for cholesterol efflux, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 with FGF19 feedback onto CYP7A1. Nutrient and hormone signalling through mTOR complex components, AMPK, insulin, leptin and sirtuins, plus microRNAs such as the SREBF-embedded miR-33, tune the same outputs. Loss of this control produces hypercholesterolaemia, fatty liver and dyslipidaemia, and shapes membrane composition and steroid hormone supply.

Whether a mitochondrion keeps its contents inside determines whether a cell lives or dies, and regulation of mitochondrial membrane permeability is the control layer over that decision. Two distinct events are governed: outer membrane permeabilization, which releases cytochrome c and commits a cell to apoptosis, and inner membrane permeability transition, which collapses the proton gradient and kills by energetic failure and swelling. BAX, BAK1 and BOK form the pores; BCL2, BCL2L1 and other guardians restrain them; BH3-only proteins such as BID, BCL2L11, PMAIP1 and BAD tip the balance in response to stress, growth factor withdrawal and DNA damage. Adenine nucleotide translocases, VDAC2 and the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase PPIF modulate transition pore behaviour, while BNIP3 and BNIP3L link permeability to mitophagy. Too much promotes neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury; too little allows tumour cells to escape apoptosis.

Secretion covers the controlled release of substances from cells, spanning neurotransmitter release at synapses, hormone output from endocrine tissues, granule discharge by immune cells, and fluid and enzyme secretion by epithelia. Regulated exocytosis dominates the machinery here: SNAREs such as syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMPs drive membrane fusion, Munc18 and Munc13 proteins prime vesicles, synaptotagmins act as the calcium sensors that trigger release, and complexins clamp fusion until a stimulus arrives. Rab GTPases, exocyst subunits and coat and Golgi components deliver and tether the vesicles, while prohormone convertases and granule proteins such as chromogranin A build the cargo. Insulin release supplies a clear example, with glucokinase, the KATP channel subunits and the transcription factors PDX1 and NKX6-1 all represented. Upstream, G protein-coupled receptors, ion channels, kinases and cytokines set when and how much is released; failure produces diabetes, endocrine deficiency and synaptic disease.

Intracellular transport is the whole logistics system of the cell: the directed movement of proteins, lipids, RNAs, organelles and metabolites from where they are made to where they act. Nearly every compartment depends on it, and its failure produces lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration with axonal cargo stalling, and secretory and pigmentation disorders. The genes span coat complexes and cargo adaptors that bud vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and plasma membrane, Rab and Arf GTPases with their effectors that assign identity to each membrane, SNAREs and tethers that execute fusion, ESCRT and retromer machinery that sort cargo toward degradation or recycling, and kinesin, dynein and myosin motors that haul cargo along cytoskeletal tracks. Also included are nuclear pore components with karyopherin-mediated import and export, mitochondrial and peroxisomal import translocases, and mRNA export and localisation factors, making this the union of all trafficking routes rather than a single itinerary.

Cells are compartmentalized, so almost every protein, lipid and RNA must be actively routed to the place it works. Intracellular transport covers that directed movement: secretory traffic from the endoplasmic reticulum through the Golgi via COPI, COPII and TRAPP components, SNARE- and Rab-dependent vesicle docking and fusion, clathrin and adaptor-protein-mediated endocytosis, endosomal sorting and recycling by retromer, retriever, WASH and ESCRT complexes, delivery to lysosomes, peroxisomal and mitochondrial protein import, and nucleocytoplasmic exchange through the nuclear pore using karyopherins, exportins and the Ran system. Long-range movement rides on microtubules and actin through kinesins, dynein with its adaptors, and myosin V motors. Because this machinery also positions receptors, degrades cargo and delivers mRNAs, its failure underlies lysosomal storage disease, hypopigmentation and immunodeficiency syndromes, hypercholesterolaemia, peroxisome biogenesis disorders, and neurodegeneration from failed axonal transport.

Neurons communicate by releasing transmitter from vesicles at the active zone, and this pathway covers the controls that set how much is released and when. Tuning release strength is the substrate of short-term plasticity and of presynaptic drug action, and its disruption produces epilepsy, movement disorders and intellectual disability. Calcium entry through voltage-gated channels such as CACNA1B is sensed by synaptotagmins, which trigger fusion driven by the SNARE proteins STX1A/1B with STXBP1 and complexins acting as regulatory clamps; RIMS proteins and their partners organise channels and vesicles at the release site, while RAB3A and SV2 isoforms govern vesicle priming and recycling. Overlaid on this core are kinases and phosphatases, presynaptic G protein-coupled receptors including adenosine and purinergic receptors, neuropeptide and neurotrophin signals, and synucleins and LRRK2, whose failure links release control to Parkinson disease.

Negative regulation of neurotransmitter secretion covers the braking mechanisms that limit how much transmitter a synapse releases per stimulus, setting the gain of synaptic transmission and protecting circuits from runaway excitation. Restraint is exerted at the vesicle fusion step itself: synaptotagmin isoforms act as calcium sensors that can clamp as well as trigger release, and synaptotagmin-11 in particular suppresses dopamine exocytosis, while parkin regulates its abundance — a link that ties this control to dopaminergic vulnerability in Parkinson disease. Other components tune release presynaptically through ion flux and metal handling, including proton-gated ASIC1 channels and zinc export by SLC30A1, or through neuromodulatory signalling as with neurofibromin. Loss of such restraint produces paroxysmal movement disorders, as mutations in PNKD illustrate, and more broadly shifts the balance between excitation and inhibition that underlies stable neural coding.

Synapses must be able to hold back transmitter release as well as trigger it, and negative regulation of neurotransmitter secretion covers the braking mechanisms that limit how often and how much a vesicle pool discharges. Restraint of this kind sets the tone of excitatory and inhibitory circuits; when it fails, transmission becomes excessive or paroxysmal, as in the involuntary movement attacks linked to PNKD mutations and the dopaminergic dysfunction of parkin-related parkinsonism. The genes involved act at several levels: synaptotagmin family members serve as calcium sensors for fusion, with SYT11 acting as a clamp rather than a trigger, PRKN ubiquitinates synaptic substrates, and zinc and proton handling by SLC30A1 and ASIC1 modulate the presynaptic environment. NF1 links Ras signalling to release probability, connecting synaptic gain control to broader neuronal growth signalling.

Building openings that let material cross a membrane, this grouping spans two distinct kinds of pore: the nuclear pore complex and the lytic pores that open in the plasma membrane. Nucleoporin scaffolds such as NUP107, NUP93, NUP205, NUP153, NUP98 together with the membrane-anchored NDC1, the basket protein TPR and the chromatin-tethering factor ELYS assemble the channels that mediate all nucleocytoplasmic transport and reform around chromosomes after mitosis, a step requiring endoplasmic reticulum shaping proteins such as reticulon 4. The second arm covers regulated membrane permeabilization: gasdermin D oligomerizes into pores that execute pyroptosis and release IL-1 family cytokines downstream of inflammasome activation, with the ATP-gated channel P2RX7 and the scramblase-channel ANO6 contributing to the associated ion flux, phospholipid exposure and ADAM10-dependent ectodomain shedding. Failures produce nuclear transport defects or unrestrained inflammatory cell death.

Cells hold nucleotides in a usable balance by adding phosphates to nucleoside monophosphates, converting them to the diphosphate and ultimately triphosphate forms that fuel synthesis, signalling and energy transfer. This phosphorylation step supplies the immediate precursors for DNA replication and RNA transcription and buffers the adenylate pool, so that ATP consumption is sensed and replenished rather than allowed to collapse. Adenylate kinases interconvert ATP, ADP and AMP across distinct compartments — cytosol, mitochondrial intermembrane space, nucleus and the axonemes of motile cilia, where AK7 loss causes ciliary dyskinesia — while cytidylate kinases phosphorylate pyrimidine monophosphates and also activate nucleoside analogue drugs. Mitochondrial AK2 deficiency causes reticular dysgenesis, a severe immunodeficiency, and CMPK2 supports mitochondrial DNA synthesis in inflammatory responses. The chemistry sits between salvage or de novo nucleotide synthesis and every process that spends nucleotides.

Fatty acids are only metabolically usable once they carry coenzyme A, and fatty-acyl-CoA biosynthesis is how cells generate these thioesters, both by activating free fatty acids and by building longer chains de novo. The products feed membrane phospholipid and triglyceride synthesis, protein acylation, beta-oxidation and signalling, so the pathway sits at the junction of lipid storage and lipid consumption. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL1 and ACSL4, together with the bubblegum-family enzymes and the peroxisomal transporter SLC27A2, perform ATP-dependent activation in distinct compartments and with distinct chain-length preferences. Cytosolic fatty acid synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase supply nascent chains, which the ELOVL elongases extend through a condensation, reduction, dehydration and reduction cycle involving HACD hydratases and TECR. Mutations in individual elongases and in the palmitoyl-protein thioesterases cause retinal degeneration, ichthyosis and neuronal storage disease.

During fasting, prolonged exercise or carbohydrate restriction, the liver converts fatty acid-derived acetyl-CoA into ketone bodies that circulate as an alternative fuel for brain, heart and skeletal muscle. This ketogenic route condenses acetyl-CoA units into hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA through the mitochondrial synthase HMGCS2, the rate-setting and hormonally regulated step, and HMGCL then cleaves that intermediate to release acetoacetate, which is reduced to beta-hydroxybutyrate or spontaneously decarboxylated to acetone. Related activating enzymes, including the acetoacetyl-CoA synthetase AACS and short-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, link ketone bodies back into cytosolic lipid and sterol synthesis, so the pathway sits at the junction of fat oxidation and energy distribution between organs. Loss of the synthase or the lyase causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with metabolic crises during fasting, while unrestrained flux in uncontrolled diabetes produces ketoacidosis.

Nonassociative learning is the simplest way a nervous system adjusts to experience: repeated exposure to a single stimulus makes the response to it weaker or stronger, as in habituation and sensitization, without any pairing of one cue with another. It underlies sensory filtering and startle modulation, and its disruption contributes to the sensorimotor gating deficits seen in schizophrenia and to hyperexcitable, seizure-prone states. The genes here point to two levels of control. Monoaminergic tone sets the gain: dopamine acting through D1-class receptors, serotonergic signalling through the 5-HT2A receptor, and catechol-O-methyltransferase degrading released catecholamines. Postsynaptic scaffolds and signalling adaptors such as SHANK1 and the JNK-interacting protein MAPK8IP2 organise glutamate receptors and kinase cascades at excitatory synapses, where the plasticity itself is expressed. The glycogen-metabolism gene EPM2A links this behavioural plasticity to neuronal excitability more broadly.

Moving solutes from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen against a gradient requires dedicated ATP-driven pumps, and this pathway covers that directed import. Two of its jobs are physiologically distinct. The sarco/endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases ATP2A2 and ATP2A3 pump cytosolic Ca2+ back into the ER and sarcoplasmic reticulum, terminating calcium signals, refilling the store that supports muscle relaxation and secretory signalling, and maintaining the high-calcium environment that ER chaperones need; loss of ATP2A2 function causes Darier disease and its depletion triggers ER stress. The transporters TAP1 and TAP2 form a heterodimeric ABC pump that translocates proteasome-generated peptides into the ER for loading onto MHC class I, so cytotoxic T cell surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells depends on it. Together these activities link store loading, ER homeostasis and antigen presentation to import across the ER membrane.

Erythroid cells devote almost their entire biosynthetic output to hemoglobin, and the controls gathered here set how much of it is made and keep globin chains matched to available heme and iron. The stoichiometry matters: unpaired globin or free heme is toxic, and imbalance underlies the ineffective erythropoiesis of thalassemia and sideroblastic anemias. Mitochondrial transporters deliver the raw materials, with a ferrous iron importer feeding ferrochelatase, the terminal enzyme that inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX, while an accessory ABC transporter supports the same step. Heme availability is sensed translationally by a kinase that phosphorylates eIF2α to restrain globin synthesis when heme is scarce. Transcriptional input comes from a Krüppel-like factor and from a LIM-domain binding adaptor that organizes long-range enhancer contacts at globin loci, with arginine methylation tuning erythroid transcription factor activity.

Erythroid cells devote most of their protein synthesis to haemoglobin, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate and extent of haemoglobin production during red cell maturation. Adequate output determines oxygen-carrying capacity; failure leaves cells hypochromic and anaemic, and defects in the same machinery underlie sideroblastic and iron-loading anaemias. Two mitochondrial inner membrane transporters supply the raw materials: a mitoferrin imports ferrous iron for heme synthesis, and a partner transporter supports heme biosynthesis and protects against porphyrin intermediate accumulation, while a glycine transporter feeds the first, rate-setting step of the porphyrin route. On the globin side, a transcriptional adaptor tethers erythroid factors into looping complexes at globin loci, an arginine methyltransferase modifies erythroid regulators, and KLF4 acts in the transcriptional network governing globin gene expression. Together they couple heme availability to globin transcription.

Cells must sense and act on changes in external solute concentration, and this pathway covers the upstream control of how strongly and how quickly that osmotic stress response is mounted. It matters for maintaining cell volume and hydration in tissues exposed to swings in tonicity — kidney medulla, brain astrocytes and glia, airway and vascular epithelium — where failure produces cell swelling, lysis or apoptotic loss. Regulation operates at several levels: TRPV4 provides an osmosensitive cation channel that converts mechanical and hypotonic cues into calcium entry; MICU1, LETM1 and the mitochondrial carrier SLC25A23 tune mitochondrial calcium handling and ion balance during the response; MLC1 and CLN3 act on astrocytic volume regulation and lysosomal osmotic homeostasis. Other members modulate transcriptional and survival output, linking osmotic challenge to inflammatory gene expression through PTGS2 and to apoptotic decisions through BAD. Loss of this control contributes to leukodystrophy and neurodegeneration.

Membrane cargo does not diffuse to where it is needed; it is carried, and this pathway covers the motor-driven movement of vesicles along microtubule tracks from attachment through delivery. It sustains long-range traffic in polarised cells above all neurons, where synaptic vesicle precursors, lysosomes, autophagosomes and mitochondria must travel metres of axon, and its failure produces hereditary spastic paraplegia, distal neuropathies and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. Kinesins such as KIF1A, KIF5A/B and KIF3A/B drive anterograde transport while dynein intermediate chains with LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1 pull cargo retrogradely; adaptors including TRAK1/2, HAP1 with huntingtin, FYCO1 and BICD-like proteins couple specific organelles to the right motor. The AP-3 adaptor and BLOC-1 subunits link cargo sorting at endosomes to this transport step, connecting lysosome-related organelle biogenesis with directed delivery along the cytoskeleton.

T cells only see antigen as short peptides displayed on MHC molecules, and this pathway is the machinery that generates those peptides and loads them. It defines how infected or transformed cells are recognised by cytotoxic T cells and how dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells instruct helper T cells; its subversion by viruses and tumours permits immune escape, and its HLA variation underlies transplant rejection and much autoimmune risk. Proteasome subunits and cathepsins plus legumain and IFI30 perform proteolysis in cytosol and endolysosome; TAP1/TAP2 pump peptides into the ER where tapasin, calreticulin, PDIA3 and beta-2-microglobulin assemble class I, while aminopeptidases such as ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim peptides to length. For class II, the invariant chain CD74 blocks the groove until HLA-DM catalyses peptide exchange, with MARCH ubiquitin ligases controlling surface turnover.
