Related nonclassical molecules present lipid-like metabolites or mark stressed cells for NK surveillance.

Antigen processing and presentation of lipid antigen via MHC class Ib is how cells display lipids and glycolipids, rather than peptides, to T lymphocytes. It gives the immune system a way to recognise mycobacterial cell wall components and self lipids, and it defines the ligand for invariant natural killer T cells, whose rapid cytokine output shapes early antibacterial and antitumour responses. The CD1 family members do the presenting, each trafficking through a distinct endosomal itinerary so that different lipid pools are sampled; CD1e acts in the lysosome as an accessory lipid transfer protein that edits glycolipids for loading rather than reaching the surface. Adaptor protein-3 subunits direct CD1b and CD1d into late endosomal compartments where acidic pH and lipid transfer proteins permit exchange, while transporter activity contributes to lipid handling. Loss of this route blinds T cells to lipid-based microbial signatures.

Not all T cells recognise peptides; some respond to lipids and glycolipids displayed by CD1 molecules, the non-classical class Ib presentation route captured here. This pathway gives the immune system a way to detect mycobacterial cell wall lipids, self lipids altered by disease, and microbial glycolipids that peptide-based presentation would miss, and it is the basis for activating invariant natural killer T cells through CD1d. Dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells take up lipids, route them through endosomal and lysosomal compartments, and load them onto CD1a, CD1b, CD1c or CD1d, with CD1e acting inside the lysosome as a lipid transfer protein that edits antigens rather than presenting them. Adaptor protein 3 subunits direct CD1 trafficking to the right compartment, and a transporter contributes to lipid handling. Loss of this route blunts lipid-specific T cell responses and antimycobacterial immunity.

Lipids can be antigens, and the CD1 family is how a cell shows them to T cells. This route of antigen processing and presentation handles endogenous lipid antigen loaded onto non-classical MHC class Ib molecules, giving the immune system a way to survey self and microbial lipids, glycolipids and lipopeptides that conventional peptide-presenting class I and class II molecules cannot display. Dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells route CD1 proteins through endosomal and lysosomal compartments, where lipid transfer proteins and the non-surface member CD1E assist in exchanging and editing bound lipids before display. CD1D presentation of glycolipids is what selects and activates invariant natural killer T cells, linking this pathway to rapid innate-like cytokine responses, antimicrobial defence, tumour surveillance and lipid-driven autoimmune and inflammatory disease.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptor signalling drives the proliferation, survival and migration of mesenchymal cells — fibroblasts, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle, glia and their precursors — and so governs wound repair, vessel stabilisation and connective tissue formation, while its overactivity underlies fibrosis, atherosclerotic intimal thickening and tumours driven by receptor fusions or mutation. Four dimeric ligands, PDGFA through PDGFD, engage the receptor tyrosine kinases PDGFRA and PDGFRB, whose autophosphorylated tails recruit SRC-family and ABL kinases, the adaptor and phosphatase PTPN11, PI3K components and scaffolds such as BCAR1 and IQGAP1 to reach transcription and the cytoskeleton. Output is limited at several points: protein tyrosine phosphatases including PTPRJ, PTPN1 and PTPN2 dephosphorylate the receptor, CBL-family ubiquitin ligases with endosomal sorting proteins route it for degradation, and microRNAs and co-receptors like NRP1 and LRP1 tune ligand availability and response.

Insulin-like growth factor receptor signalling converts circulating IGF1 and IGF2 into instructions for cells to grow, survive, and differentiate, and it is the route through which growth hormone produces most of its effects on body size. Ligand binding to IGF1R recruits the adaptors IRS1/IRS2, SHC1 and GRB2, which branch into PI3K-AKT signalling for anabolic metabolism and anti-apoptotic survival, and into the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade for proliferative gene expression. Availability of ligand is set outside the cell by a family of IGF binding proteins that sequester or present IGF, while GRB10 and INPPL1 damp the intracellular response. The axis drives skeletal growth, muscle hypertrophy and regeneration, and neural development; loss-of-function causes growth failure and short stature, while excess activity supports the proliferation and survival of many tumours, including prostate and breast cancer. Related growth hormone releasing and receptor components place this pathway at the endocrine end of growth control.

Blood and lymphatic vessels grow where VEGF ligands are released, and vascular endothelial growth factor receptor signaling is how endothelial cells read that cue and respond with migration, survival, permeability and tube formation. The pathway drives developmental angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis, wound healing and the vessel supply that solid tumours depend on, which is why its receptors are major drug targets; loss of components causes embryonic vascular failure, and dysregulation contributes to diabetic retinopathy and retinal disease. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, VEGFC and placental growth factor engage KDR, FLT1 and FLT4 with neuropilin and glycocalyx co-receptors, triggering Src-family and focal adhesion kinases, VAV and PAK-linked cytoskeletal remodelling, PKC and PKD arms, and p38 signalling through MAPKAPK2. Hypoxia-inducible factors and their asparaginyl hydroxylase set ligand availability, while integrins, ubiquitin ligases, endosomal sorting and microRNAs tune receptor output.

Neurotrophins such as NGF act on TRK receptor tyrosine kinases to tell neurons to survive, grow axons and dendrites, and differentiate; the same signalling sustains sensory and sympathetic neurons throughout life. Loss-of-function mutations in the NGF receptor NTRK1 cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis, and rearrangements that leave the kinase constitutively active drive tumours. Ligand binding dimerises the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation, recruiting adaptors and the phosphatase PTPN11 to launch RAS-RAF-ERK signalling through SOS1 and RAF1, with PI3K-AKT and mTOR-linked components tuning growth and survival; SPRY1 and SPRY2 feed back to restrain the kinase cascade. Output converges on transcription, translational control and cytoskeletal remodelling, the latter through WAVE-complex members and their regulators, which shape growth cone motility. Receptor trafficking matters too: sortilin partners with p75 to divert immature neurotrophin signals toward apoptosis rather than growth.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to its receptor MET triggers a signalling programme that drives epithelial cells to survive, scatter, migrate and rebuild tissue; it is the main mitogenic and morphogenic cue in liver and kidney regeneration and in wound repair, and its persistent activation through MET amplification or mutation makes it one of the recurrent oncogenic drivers in gastric, lung and kidney cancers. Ligand engagement of the receptor tyrosine kinase recruits scaffolds and adaptors such as BCAR1, feeding into Rho-family GTPase RAC1 and its effector kinase PAK1 to remodel actin and focal adhesions, with STMN1 acting on microtubule dynamics during motility. The phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN2 dampen receptor phosphorylation, while NRP1, MUC20 and CDCP1 modulate receptor availability and output, setting the balance between controlled regeneration and invasive behaviour.</br>

Ephrin receptor signaling pathway is contact-dependent communication between neighbouring cells: membrane-tethered ephrins engage Eph receptor tyrosine kinases on the apposed cell, converting cell-cell touch into cytoskeletal decisions. It tells growth cones where not to go, keeps arterial and venous endothelium segregated, sets boundaries between tissue compartments, and shapes dendritic spines during synaptic plasticity; its misregulation contributes to tumour invasion and aberrant angiogenesis. Signalling is bidirectional, forward through the clustered receptor and reverse through the ephrin-bearing cell. Src-family kinases, ABL1 and the phosphatase PTPN11 tune receptor phosphorylation, while NCK and CRK adaptors, GIT1/ARHGEF7 and Rho-family exchange factors such as TIAM1 and KALRN feed onto PAK kinases and RASA1 to remodel actin, usually producing repulsion and adhesion loss. Matrix metalloproteinases and ADAM-type cleavage terminate contact, and CDK5 activity couples the pathway to neuronal migration.

Ephrin receptor signalling lets cells read the identity of the cells they touch and decide whether to adhere, repel, or turn away. It builds the wiring of the nervous system — axon guidance, topographic retinotectal maps, dendritic spine and synapse formation — and draws tissue boundaries, patterns the vasculature into arterial and venous territories, and positions cells in intestinal crypts; the same receptors are frequently misexpressed in tumours, where they alter invasion and angiogenesis. Because both the membrane-tethered ephrin ligands and their Eph receptors sit on cell surfaces, engagement is bidirectional at the contact site. Clustered receptors recruit Src-family kinases, the phosphatase PTPN11 and adaptors such as NCK and CRK, and act largely through Rho and Rac regulators — exchange factors including TIAM1 and ephexin, the Rac GAP CHN1, and PAK kinases — to remodel actin and retract or stabilise protrusions, with matrix metalloproteinases shedding contacts and some output reaching transcription.</description>

Angiopoietin ligands acting on the endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase TEK (Tie2) control whether blood vessels stay quiescent and sealed or become plastic and responsive. Signalling through this route maintains endothelial junctions, restrains leak and leukocyte entry, and supports pericyte coverage during vascular remodelling; loss of it produces unstable, permeable vessels, and the axis is central to the vascular leak of sepsis, to tumour angiogenesis, and to lymphatic and ocular vascular disease. ANGPT1 acts as a clustering agonist that promotes receptor autophosphorylation and downstream survival and barrier-stabilising signals, while ANGPT2 behaves context-dependently and can oppose that stabilisation; SVEP1 is a further ligand supporting Tie2 activity in lymphatic vessels. Downstream kinase cascades feed into transcriptional programmes governing endothelial quiescence, migration and sprouting, placing the Tie pathway alongside VEGF signalling in vessel formation and maturation.

Phosphatidylinositol-mediated signaling is the use of membrane inositol lipids as second messengers, converting receptor activation at the cell surface into growth, survival, secretion and calcium responses inside the cell. It underlies insulin action, immune receptor signalling and neuronal excitability, and its deregulation — most notably activating PIK3CA mutations — is among the commonest events in human cancer and in overgrowth syndromes. Two arms dominate: phosphoinositide 3-kinases and PI4-kinases phosphorylate the inositol headgroup to create docking sites that recruit AKT and other effectors, feeding into mTORC1 and its substrate S6 kinase; phospholipase C isoforms instead cleave PIP2 into diacylglycerol and IP3, releasing stored calcium and activating protein kinase C. Class II and III enzymes serve membrane trafficking and autophagy rather than mitogenesis, so the same lipid currency also organises vesicle identity and organelle turnover.

Membrane inositol lipids act as both second messengers and docking sites, and phosphatidylinositol-mediated signaling is how receptor activation at the plasma membrane is converted into intracellular responses through these lipids. Two branches dominate. Class I, II and III phosphoinositide 3-kinases together with PI4KA and PI4KB phosphorylate the inositol headgroup, generating PIP3 and other phosphoinositides that recruit AKT and downstream growth effectors such as the S6 kinase RPS6KB1, while PIK3C3 output serves autophagy and endosomal traffic. In parallel, phospholipase C isoforms of the beta, gamma, epsilon and eta families cleave PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C. Receptor tyrosine kinases like FGFR1 and G protein-coupled receptors feed into these arms, coupling them to proliferation, survival, motility, secretion and immune cell activation. Gain-of-function mutation of PIK3CA is among the most common oncogenic events in human cancer.

Most human genes yield several mRNAs, and this is the layer of control that decides which exons are kept when the spliceosome acts on a pre-mRNA. It sets tissue- and stage-specific isoform choices — RBFOX and NOVA proteins shaping neuronal transcripts, RBM20 governing titin isoforms in heart muscle, CELF and QKI proteins timing developmental switches — so its failure produces cardiomyopathy, neurodevelopmental disorders and widespread mis-splicing in cancer. Mechanistically, SR proteins such as SRSF1 and hnRNPs including PTBP1 and HNRNPA1 compete at splice sites and silencer or enhancer elements, while core small nuclear ribonucleoproteins, PRPF8 and SNRNP200 carry out catalysis. Kinases and arginine methyltransferases (SRPK1/2, DYRK1A, PRMT5–WDR77) tune splicing factor localisation and activity, and m6A readers and writers add a further input. Coupling to nonsense-mediated decay through UPF1 links isoform selection to transcript stability.

Splicing of pre-mRNA is not run at a fixed rate; it is actively promoted by factors that recruit or stabilise spliceosomal components at particular introns, and this positive regulation of spliceosome-mediated mRNA splicing sets how efficiently and in which isoform a transcript is processed. It matters because the same gene can yield alternative products in different tissues, and splicing-enhancing factors are what tip that choice toward the tissue-appropriate form. The genes here act at several levels: sequence-specific RNA-binding enhancers such as TRA2B, DAZAP1, RBMX and the neural CELF proteins bind exonic and intronic elements to favour exon inclusion; SNRNP70 is a core U1 snRNP subunit; PRPF19 and SNW1 function within the spliceosome itself; PRMT5 with its partner WDR77 methylates Sm proteins to support snRNP assembly; and cap-binding and surveillance proteins including NCBP1 and the UPF factors couple splicing to downstream mRNA fate.

Cells grip the extracellular matrix through focal adhesions, and their assembly is how a spreading or migrating cell converts an integrin engagement into a mechanically loaded, signalling-competent attachment. Without it cells cannot spread, sense substrate stiffness, or move directionally, which matters for wound healing, angiogenesis and tissue architecture, and is subverted during tumour invasion. Clustered integrins recruit talin, kindlin, vinculin and alpha-actinin to link receptor tails to actin filaments, while FAK and Src initiate phosphorylation cascades that mature the contact and later license its turnover. Rho-family GTPases with their exchange factors and GAPs, together with ROCK-driven actomyosin contractility, tune adhesion size and tension, and phosphatases such as PTEN and PTPRA set the signalling threshold. The result couples cytoskeletal mechanics to growth, survival and motility decisions.

Embryonic eye morphogenesis builds the optic vesicle, optic cup, lens and anterior segment from neuroepithelium, surface ectoderm and periocular mesenchyme, setting up the tissue geometry that vision later depends on. Failure produces anophthalmia, microphthalmia, coloboma and cataract, and the same programme underlies anterior segment dysgenesis and optic fissure closure defects. Master transcription factors including PAX6, SIX3, VAX2, PAX2 and PROX1 specify retinal, optic stalk and lens fates and impose dorsoventral pattern, while retinoid signalling through STRA6, ALDH1A3 and the retinoic acid receptors supplies the positional cue that periocular tissue reads. WNT, BMP and hedgehog ligands coordinate invagination and closure, and extracellular matrix components such as the fibrillins, microfibril-associated proteins and EFEMP1 give the developing eye and its lens zonule mechanical form. Lens crystallin expression marks terminal differentiation of the fibre cells.

Shaping of the eye continues after embryonic development, and this post-embryonic phase of eye morphogenesis refines the structures that keep the optics stable: the lens and its suspensory apparatus, the vitreous and retinal vasculature, and the anterior segment. The genes involved point to two kinds of work. One is extracellular matrix construction and remodelling, with fibrillin and microfibril-associated proteins building the elastic fibre systems that anchor the lens zonule, and fibulin-3 contributing to Bruch's membrane; mutations in these components produce lens dislocation and macular degeneration. The other is controlled cell removal and vessel regression, in which the pro-apoptotic effectors BAK1 and BAX eliminate cells no longer needed as the eye matures, alongside VEGF receptor signalling through KDR that patterns ocular blood vessels. Failure of either arm leaves the eye malformed and vision impaired.

Developmental pigmentation is the program that builds pigment-producing cells and gives skin, hair, eyes and inner ear their colour. It matters because the same cells are needed for retinal and cochlear function, so its failure produces albinism, piebaldism, Waardenburg syndrome and deafness, and its dysregulation underlies melanoma. The genes trace the whole arc: SOX10, MITF and ZEB2 specify neural crest-derived melanoblasts; KIT and KITLG, together with endothelin ligand and receptor signalling, drive their survival and migration to the skin; and TYR, TYRP1, DCT, OCA2 and SLC45A2 carry out melanin synthesis inside a specialised lysosome-related organelle. Biogenesis and trafficking of that organelle depend on BLOC-1 subunits, HPS proteins and adaptor complexes, while RAB27A, RAB32/38 and melanoregulin control melanosome transport and transfer to keratinocytes, linking pigmentation to general endosomal sorting biology.

Pigmentation during development depends on melanocytes being specified from the neural crest, migrating to skin, hair follicle, eye and inner ear, and then building melanin-filled organelles. Loss of the programme produces albinism, piebald and Waardenburg-type depigmentation with deafness, while its transcriptional core is redeployed in melanoma. Lineage identity is set by SOX10, MITF and PAX-family partners acting with the KIT receptor and its ligand KITLG, and with endothelin signalling through EDNRB, to drive survival and migration; ZEB2 and GLI3 shape the crest environment. Melanin itself is made by tyrosinase with DCT and TYRP1 inside melanosomes, whose biogenesis requires the BLOC-1 and HPS subunits, adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3, and transport by RAB27A, RAB32 and RAB38, with OCA2 and SLC45A2 controlling the ionic conditions that permit pigment synthesis and transfer to keratinocytes.

eye pigmentation is the developmental programme that lays down melanin in the eye, giving the iris its colour and, more consequentially, supplying the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid with the pigment that absorbs stray light and guides the wiring of the visual pathway. When it fails, the result is ocular or oculocutaneous albinism, with foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, misrouted optic nerve fibres and poor acuity. Tyrosinase performs the committed step of melanin synthesis, while GPR143 and the Hermansky-Pudlak factor HPS4 govern the biogenesis, sizing and trafficking of melanosomes as lysosome-related organelles. Hedgehog signalling and the accessory proteins that acidify and sort within the endolysosomal system set the patterning and pH context in which pigment is deposited. The pathway therefore links organelle biogenesis and secretory trafficking to eye morphogenesis and visual function.

Eye pigmentation refers to the establishment of pigment patterning in the eye, chiefly the melanin deposited in the retinal pigment epithelium, iris and choroid, which shields photoreceptors from stray light and guides the wiring of retinal projections during development. Its failure produces albinism of the eye, with iris transillumination, foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus and misrouted optic fibres. The core chemistry is melanin synthesis by tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme oxidising tyrosine toward eumelanin, acting inside melanosomes. Other members govern how those organelles are made and used: a biogenesis complex subunit associated with Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, and an intracellular G protein-coupled receptor mutated in ocular albinism that controls melanosome size and number. Hedgehog signalling and a lysosomal-type proton pump accessory subunit link the process to eye morphogenesis and organelle acidification, since pigment production depends on tightly set melanosomal pH.

Pigmentation of skin, hair and eyes depends on melanocytes surviving their migration from the neural crest and on melanosomes being built and filled with pigment once they arrive. This grouping covers the influences that push that developmental programme forward, raising the amount of pigment ultimately deposited. KITLG acts as the ligand that sustains melanoblast survival and dispersal, and ZEB2 contributes to neural crest specification and melanocyte fate, with its loss underlying the pigmentary and craniofacial features of Mowat-Wilson syndrome. Survival is set by the BAX/BCL2 balance, determining how many melanoblasts persist to populate the skin. Pigment organelle biogenesis requires BLOC-1 subunits and HPS4, whose failure produces the hypopigmentation and bleeding of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome. Secreted ADAMTS proteases remodel the extracellular matrix through which melanoblasts travel, linking pigmentation to cell migration and organelle trafficking more broadly.

Autophagic cell death is a programmed self-destruction route in which the cell digests itself: autophagosomes accumulate and the cytoplasm becomes massively vacuolated, without the chromatin condensation or phagocytic clearance typical of apoptosis. It matters where cells must be eliminated during tissue remodelling, in neurons and glia under metabolic or lysosomal stress, and in tumour cells responding to nutrient deprivation or chemotherapy, where the same machinery can either protect or kill depending on how far it is driven. The genes here connect the core autophagy apparatus to death decisions: ATG5 is required for autophagosome formation, BNIP3 links mitochondrial stress and hypoxia to mitophagy, DAPK1 is a death-associated kinase promoting autophagic death, SH3GLB1 shapes membranes during autophagosome biogenesis, and p27-type cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors and p53-induced stress genes tie growth arrest to the outcome. Lysosomal and immune components such as LAPTM5 and TREM2 place the process alongside phagocytic and degradative pathways.

Tissues that turn over throughout life depend on somatic stem cell division, the self-renewing divisions by which a non-germline stem cell replaces itself while also producing daughters that differentiate. Getting the balance right determines whether an epithelium, the blood system or a muscle can be maintained and repaired; too little self-renewal exhausts the pool and drives ageing phenotypes, too much underlies tumour-initiating cell behaviour. The genes here converge on the main levers. BMI1 represses the CDKN2A locus, keeping p16INK4a-driven senescence and ARF-p53 arrest off so that divisions can continue, while HOXB4 promotes expansion of haematopoietic progenitors. Wnt ligands acting through Frizzled receptors, Notch signalling and TGF-beta supply niche instructions, and planar cell polarity components such as VANGL2 orient the division axis, linking spindle placement to whether a daughter stays a stem cell. Post-transcriptional regulators and glycosyltransferases tune the resulting programme.

Astrocytes switch from quiet metabolic and synaptic support to a reactive state when they sense injury, infection, or protein aggregates, and this activation is what converts a local insult into sustained neuroinflammation. The change in astrocyte shape and behaviour follows exposure to cytokines and soluble cues, and it determines whether reactive glia limit damage or drive it: reactive astrocytes remodel their processes, form glial scar, release inflammatory mediators, and alter lipid and cholesterol handling for neighbouring neurons. Inputs here include interferon-gamma acting through its receptor, IL1B, IL6 and TNF, complement components and their receptors, and damage sensors such as RAGE and TREM2, alongside neurodegeneration-associated proteins including APP, PSEN1, MAPT and progranulin. Microglia-derived signals and microRNA-level and transcriptional control tune the response, which is central to Alzheimer's disease, lysosomal storage disease, and injury repair.

Fibroblast proliferation is the expansion of the connective-tissue cell population that builds and remodels extracellular matrix, and it sets the pace of wound healing, scar formation and organ fibrosis. Growth factors dominate the input side: the PDGF ligand family with its receptor PDGFRA, EGFR ligands such as epiregulin, FGF10, IGF1 and TGFB1 drive fibroblasts out of quiescence, while WNT ligands and beta-catenin, together with the antagonist SFRP1, tune how strongly they respond. The output is cell cycle entry through CDK4, CDK6, cyclins A and B, E2F1 and MYC, opposed by p53, CDKN1A and PML, so the same gene collection covers both mitogenic drive and the senescence and apoptotic brakes that limit it. Matrix and adhesion components including collagen III, fibronectin and fibulin provide the substrate context. Excessive proliferation underlies fibrotic disease; insufficient proliferation leaves wounds unclosed.

Fibroblasts are the connective-tissue cells that build and remodel extracellular matrix, and driving them to divide is how tissues repair wounds, thicken scars and, when unchecked, become fibrotic. Positive regulation of fibroblast proliferation gathers the growth factors and receptors that deliver the mitogenic signal — PDGF ligands acting through PDGFRA, EGFR ligands such as epiregulin, IGF1, FGF10 and TGFB1 — together with the matrix and integrin contacts (fibronectin, DDR2, ITGB3) that license a response, and the nuclear machinery that executes it, including MYC, JUN, E2F1 and the cyclin–CDK4/CDK6 module opposed by the p21 inhibitor. Wnt ligands, sphingosine kinase, angiotensinogen and immune mediators such as MIF and IL13 feed in from inflammation and hormonal signalling. Sustained activity underlies pulmonary and cardiac fibrosis, keloid formation and tumour stroma expansion, while loss of drive leaves wounds poorly closed.

Fibroblasts must be held in check once tissue repair is complete, and this set represents the restraint side of that balance: processes that stop or slow fibroblast multiplication. Without such brakes, persistent fibroblast expansion drives scarring and fibrosis, and loss of the same controls permits fibroblast-derived tumours. The restraint is imposed at several levels. Tumour suppressors including TP53 and its target TP53INP1 arrest the cycle or commit cells to death through effectors such as BAX, while NF1 limits Ras-dependent growth signalling. Secreted and receptor-level modulators such as SFRP1 dampen Wnt input, and transcriptional repressors and cofactors, among them SKI, DACH1 and Mediator subunits, reset proliferative gene expression. Redox and stress regulators like SOD2, GSTP1 and NUPR1 couple oxidative and metabolic state to growth arrest, linking this control to senescence, wound resolution and connective tissue homeostasis.

Cocaine acts by blocking monoamine transporters, and the behavioral response to cocaine is the set of neural changes that convert that raised synaptic dopamine into locomotor activation, sensitization and drug seeking. It matters because these adaptations in striatal circuits underlie addiction, relapse and withdrawal-associated dysphoria. Dopamine receptors of both D1- and D2-like families, together with the striatal signalling hub DARPP-32 encoded by PPP1R1B and the kinase CDK5, tune the phosphorylation state that determines how strongly medium spiny neurons respond to repeated exposure. Persistent induction of the transcription factor FosB and chromatin modification by the histone methyltransferase EHMT2 give the response its long-lasting character, while Homer scaffolds reorganize glutamatergic synapses. Serotonergic components, including the serotonin transporter and the 5-HT2A receptor, and the kappa opioid receptor with the neuropeptide CART, modulate the affective and reinforcing dimensions of the drug response.</description>}“ 期待

behavioral response to ethanol covers the neural circuitry that converts alcohol exposure into changes in movement, sedation, reward seeking and withdrawal-associated distress, and it is the biology underlying individual differences in alcohol sensitivity and risk of alcohol use disorder. The genes name the neuromodulatory systems involved: dopaminergic reward signalling through D2 and D4 receptors and noradrenaline synthesis by dopamine beta-hydroxylase; opioid peptide tone through the mu receptor with its enkephalin and nociceptin ligands; and stress signalling through corticotropin-releasing hormone, its receptor and binding protein, which drives negative affect during withdrawal. Hypocretin and galanin link intake to arousal and feeding state, while chromatin regulation by HDAC2 and deubiquitination by USP46 alter the persistence of these responses. Together they describe how a single drug engages reward, stress and arousal circuits to shape voluntary consumption and tolerance.

Alcohol changes behaviour — sedation, locomotor activation, loss of righting reflex, and the drive to drink again — and this pathway covers the neural signalling that turns an ethanol stimulus into those responses. It matters because these circuits set individual sensitivity to alcohol and susceptibility to alcohol use disorder. Dopamine receptors and the noradrenaline-synthesising enzyme dopamine beta-hydroxylase place the response in catecholamine reward and arousal circuitry; the mu-opioid receptor with its peptide ligands proenkephalin and prepronociceptin mediates the reinforcing and analgesic components and is the target of naltrexone therapy. Corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor 1 and its binding protein link drinking to stress responsivity and withdrawal-associated negative affect, while orexin and galanin tie intake to arousal and feeding state. Cytoskeletal and chromatin regulators such as EPS8 and HDAC2 contribute to the synaptic and transcriptional plasticity underlying tolerance.

Late in follicle growth, the small fluid-filled cavities within an antral follicle merge into one, producing the fused antrum stage: a single antral space with the oocyte held on a stalk of cumulus cells, poised for ovulation. This configuration matters because it sets the final steps of oocyte competence, meiotic arrest and its release, and the formation of the cumulus-oocyte complex that the oviduct can capture. C-type natriuretic peptide acting on its guanylyl cyclase receptor NPR2 in mural granulosa cells sustains cyclic GMP levels that keep the oocyte meiotically arrested until the ovulatory surge; epiregulin relays that surge signal outward through EGF receptor family signalling, while BMPR1B transmits oocyte-derived growth factor input that shapes granulosa differentiation. PTX3 and TNFAIP6 then cross-link the hyaluronan-rich cumulus matrix during expansion. Failure of these steps causes anovulation and infertility.

Synapses change strength with experience, and this collection governs how that change is induced, scaled and consolidated — the cellular substrate of learning, memory and the refinement of circuits during development. Glutamate receptor subunits and their auxiliary and scaffolding partners set how much current a synapse passes and how many receptors it holds, while calcium entry through NMDA receptors is decoded by calmodulin, CaMKII isoforms and calcineurin to drive potentiation or depression. Neuromodulatory input from dopamine, adenosine and neurotrophin receptors biases the outcome, and transcription-dependent consolidation follows through CREB, MEF2C, NPAS4 and immediate-early products such as Arc, with local translational control by FMRP and its relatives. Vesicle release machinery and postsynaptic actin remodelling execute the structural side. Disruption underlies intellectual disability and autism syndromes, Rett syndrome, and the synapse loss of Alzheimer disease.

Synapses adjust their strength and number with experience, and this is the regulatory layer that sets how far and in which direction those changes go. It underlies learning, memory formation and the refinement of circuits during development, and its disruption is a recurring theme in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration — FMR1 loss, SHANK3 and SYNGAP1 mutations, and the APP and APOE contributions to Alzheimer pathology all act here. Mechanistically it centres on the postsynaptic density: NMDA and metabotropic glutamate receptors admit and sense calcium, CaMKII isoforms and Ras-family regulators such as SYNGAP1, NF1 and RASGRF1 convert that signal into changes in receptor trafficking, and scaffolds including DLG4 and SHANK3 anchor the apparatus. Rab GTPases and Arc control receptor insertion and removal, while actin regulators reshape spine morphology to consolidate the new synaptic state.

Long-lasting changes in synaptic strength and in the number of synapses themselves underlie learning, memory and the refinement of circuits during development, and this pathway covers the molecules that set how readily those changes occur. It acts on the postsynaptic side: scaffolds such as PSD-95 and SHANK3 organise glutamate receptors, metabotropic and kainate receptors (GRM5, GRIK2) and the calcium/calmodulin kinase CAMK2B translate activity into signalling, and SYNGAP1 and neurofibromin restrain Ras-family output so that potentiation is graded rather than saturating. Local translational control by the fragile X proteins FMR1, FXR1 and FXR2, together with Rab-dependent receptor trafficking and recycling, supplies the protein synthesis and membrane delivery that make a change persist. Loss of this regulation produces intellectual disability and autism spectrum phenotypes, and altered plasticity accompanies the neurodegenerative roles of APP and alpha-synuclein.

positive regulation of long-term neuronal synaptic plasticity covers the signals that push synapses toward lasting change, strengthening or adding connections in a way that outlives the stimulus that triggered them. This is the cellular substrate of learning and long-term memory, and of the experience-dependent refinement of circuits during development; when it is disrupted, the result is intellectual disability and autism, as loss of FMR1 or SHANK3 demonstrates. The genes act at the postsynaptic side of glutamatergic contacts: metabotropic glutamate receptor signalling through GRM5 drives local dendritic translation controlled by the fragile X family of RNA-binding proteins, while SHANK3 scaffolds the postsynaptic density and EPHB2 and neuroplastin transduce adhesive contact into receptor recruitment. Ubiquitin ligase activity from NEURL1 tunes the process, coupling protein turnover at the spine to durable changes in synapse number and strength.

Lasting changes in synaptic strength and number are how experience is written into circuits, and this pathway covers the influences that push long-term synaptic plasticity upward — favouring synapse formation, stabilisation and enduring potentiation rather than their reversal. It supports learning, memory consolidation and the refinement of cortical and hippocampal connections during development. Mechanistically it spans surface receptors that read extracellular cues, including the EphB2 receptor tyrosine kinase at excitatory contacts, the metabotropic glutamate receptor GRM5 that couples glutamate to dendritic signalling, and the adhesion molecule neuroplastin; postsynaptic scaffolding by SHANK3 organises receptors and the actin cytoskeleton beneath the density; and FMR1 with its relatives FXR1 and FXR2 regulates local translation of synaptic mRNAs. Loss of FMR1 or SHANK3 produces fragile X syndrome and autism spectrum phenotypes, tying dysregulated plasticity to intellectual disability.

Synapses adjust their strength over milliseconds to minutes, and the regulation of short-term neuronal synaptic plasticity covers the molecules that set how much a synapse facilitates or depresses during a train of activity. This tuning underlies working memory, sensory adaptation and the temporal filtering that lets circuits respond to patterns of firing rather than single spikes. On the presynaptic side, RAB3A and its regulator RAB3GAP1 control vesicle priming and release probability, while synaptophysin, synaptogyrin and the calcium-sensing synaptotagmin SYT4 shape vesicle cycling and retrograde signalling. Postsynaptically, the Shisa-family proteins SHISA6, SHISA9 and GSG1L together with GRIK2 act as AMPA- and kainate-receptor auxiliary subunits that govern desensitization and resensitization kinetics. Ion transporters such as SLC8A2 and SLC4A10 set the calcium and pH environment in which these steps occur. Disruption of these components produces altered synaptic gain, seizure susceptibility and intellectual disability.

Secreted and membrane proteins reach their destinations by a series of vesicle-mediated steps into, through and out of the Golgi apparatus, and this traffic is what sustains secretion, surface receptor delivery, lysosome biogenesis and cell wall or matrix export. Cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated carriers built at exit sites by SAR1, SEC23/24 and SEC13/31, is captured by receptors such as LMAN1 and KDEL receptors, and is returned by COPI; clathrin adaptors and GGA proteins sort cargo at the trans-Golgi toward endosomes and lysosomes. ARF and RAB GTPases with their activators, tethers including the conserved oligomeric Golgi and TRAPP complexes, golgins, and SNARE-NSF fusion machinery give each step its direction and specificity, with motors and cytoskeletal adaptors moving the carriers. Defects cause congenital glycosylation disorders, skeletal dysplasias, hypercholesterolaemia-related sorting failures and neurodegeneration.

Golgi vesicle budding is the step that pinches transport carriers off Golgi membranes, and it sets the rate at which secretory and membrane proteins move through and out of the stack. Without it cargo cannot be sorted forward to the plasma membrane or retrieved back to the endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi ribbon architecture collapses. Coat assembly begins when the guanine nucleotide exchange factor GBF1 activates ARF GTPases on the membrane, recruiting COPI; ARFGAP2 and ARFGAP3 time the hydrolysis that permits coat release and cargo selection. p24 family proteins such as TMED2, TMED9 and TMED10 act as transmembrane cargo receptors that concentrate clients into nascent buds. GOLPH3 and GOLPH3L, reading phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate, link the membrane to MYO18A and actin so that tensile force helps extrude the vesicle, a step regulated by atypical protein kinase C and responsive to DNA damage signalling.

Vesicle budding from Golgi membranes is the step that turns a flat cisterna into a discrete carrier, and it sets how secretory cargo and resident enzymes are sorted as they move through and back out of the Golgi stack. Without it, secretion stalls, Golgi architecture collapses, and glycosylation enzymes end up in the wrong cisternae. A guanine nucleotide exchange factor activates Arf GTPases on the membrane to recruit coat components, while Arf GAPs time the nucleotide hydrolysis that allows coats to be shed and the bud to release. p24-family transmembrane proteins act as cargo receptors and coat-binding adaptors that select which proteins enter a forming vesicle. A separate arm couples the trans-Golgi to the actin cytoskeleton through GOLPH3 and an unconventional myosin, providing the tensile force that extends a bud, with atypical protein kinase C contributing regulatory phosphorylation.

Secretory cargo leaving the endoplasmic reticulum must be packaged into coated vesicles and delivered to the right face of the Golgi, and this pathway covers the targeting steps that make that traffic directional. It supports collagen and other bulky cargo export, ciliogenesis, and the general capacity of cells to secrete and to build their surface; loss of components causes skeletal dysplasias and neurodevelopmental disease. Mechanistically, SAR1A/SAR1B GTPases and SEC16A organise ER exit sites where COPII carriers bud, TMED/p24 proteins act as cargo receptors and coat adaptors, ARFGAP2/3 and the Arf guanine nucleotide exchange factor GBF1 control COPI budding for retrograde and intra-Golgi transport, and the multisubunit TRAPP complex tethers arriving vesicles and activates Rab GTPases at the acceptor membrane. Ubiquitin ligase activity involving CUL3 with KLHL12, along with calcium-binding PDCD6 and PEF1, tunes carrier size and exit-site behaviour.

Newly made secretory and membrane proteins leave the rough endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles, and this step governs how those carriers are aimed at and delivered to the cis-Golgi. Without correct targeting, collagen, lipoproteins and other bulky cargo never reach the Golgi for processing, and the resulting defects appear in humans as skeletal dysplasias, neurodegeneration and hypercholesterolaemia. Coat assembly begins with the small GTPases SAR1A and SAR1B acting at ER exit sites organised by SEC16A and TFG, with TMED2 and TMED10 contributing cargo selection and coat interactions. The multisubunit TRAPP complex then acts at the receiving end as a tethering factor and Rab activator that licenses fusion with the Golgi. Regulation is layered on top: a CUL3–KLHL12 ubiquitin ligase module and kinase and phosphatase activities adjust carrier size and coat dynamics to accommodate oversized cargo, linking early secretion to extracellular matrix output.

Plasma membrane to endosome transport covers the first leg of endocytic traffic: vesicles budded from the cell surface are delivered to and fused with early endosomes, the sorting station that decides whether a receptor is degraded, retained, or returned. This step sets how long growth factor, nutrient and adhesion receptors remain signalling-competent, and how quickly membrane and lipid are recycled during processes such as cytokinesis and neurite outgrowth. The pathway is built around Rab GTPase switching: RAB5A/B/C mark and mature nascent endocytic vesicles, RAB11A and RAB35 govern the recycling arm back to the surface, and regulators including the TBC-domain proteins USP6NL, TBC1D21 and SGSM3 time GTP hydrolysis. Cargo adaptors such as SORT1 and the copper-handling protein COMMD1 link the route to lysosomal delivery and to metal homeostasis, illustrating how surface uptake feeds broader cellular sorting decisions.

Material taken up at the cell surface has to reach an endosome before it can be sorted, and plasma membrane to endosome transport is the vesicle traffic step that delivers it. This is how cells internalise nutrient and signalling receptors, terminate or sustain their signalling, and retrieve membrane after exocytosis; blocking it strands cargo at the surface and dysregulates receptor turnover. The route is organised by small GTPases of the Rab family: the three RAB5 isoforms define and mature the early endosome and recruit its tethering and phosphoinositide machinery, while RAB35 and RAB11A govern fast recycling back to the plasma membrane. Their activity is timed by regulators including a GTPase-activating protein and a Rab GDP/GTP exchange modulator, and cargo receptors such as sortilin couple selected ligands to the incoming vesicles, linking endocytosis to downstream lysosomal and recycling decisions.

Male gamete generation is the developmental programme that turns spermatogonial stem cells into motile sperm, and its failure is a leading cause of male infertility, from azoospermia to immotile or morphologically abnormal sperm. Entry into meiosis is licensed by retinoic acid-responsive factors such as STRA8 and MEIOSIN, after which synaptonemal complex proteins (SYCP1-3), recombination initiation by SPO11 and hotspot selection by PRDM9 pair homologues and resolve crossovers. Haploid spermatids then remodel almost completely: histones are replaced by transition proteins and protamines to compact the genome, an acrosome is assembled, and axonemal, outer dense fibre and intraflagellar transport components build the flagellum. Distinctive features include piRNA-pathway silencing of transposons by PIWI proteins and Tudor-domain partners, translational storage of mRNAs, a testis-specific proteasome subunit, and CatSper channels that later confer hyperactivated motility and capacitation. Hormonal control through androgen receptor, FSH and Sertoli cell junction proteins sustains the niche.

Ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize an egg until they have spent time in the female tract undergoing capacitation, the maturation programme that licenses hyperactivated motility and the acrosome reaction. Bicarbonate and cholesterol efflux raise cyclic AMP, and the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A drives the tyrosine phosphorylation of flagellar and fibrous sheath proteins such as CABYR and the ROPN1 family of A-kinase anchoring partners. The decisive event is calcium entry through the sperm-specific CatSper channel complex, built from pore-forming CATSPER1-4 with auxiliary beta, delta, epsilon, gamma and zeta subunits plus EFCAB9; progesterone opens it indirectly when the lipid hydrolase ABHD2 clears inhibitory endocannabinoid. Anion transporters including CFTR and SLC26 exchangers set internal pH, while seminal plasma and epididymal proteins modulate the timing. Defects here are a recognized cause of male infertility with otherwise normal sperm counts.

Epinephrine transport covers the carrier-mediated movement of adrenaline across membranes and its regulated release from cells, the step that determines how much catecholamine reaches its receptors and how quickly the signal is terminated. Organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and the plasma membrane monoamine transporter SLC29A4 clear epinephrine and related monoamines from extracellular fluid in liver, kidney and brain, and they are the same routes that handle many cationic drugs. Presynaptic alpha-2 adrenoceptors (ADRA2A, ADRA2B, ADRA2C) close the loop as autoreceptors, damping further catecholamine release and thereby lowering sympathetic outflow and blood pressure. Neuropeptide modulators such as CRH, VIP and the CART prepropeptide act on the same secretory output from adrenal chromaffin cells and central noradrenergic neurons, linking this biology to stress responses, cardiovascular tone and appetite control.

Epinephrine secretion is the regulated release of adrenaline from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla and from adrenergic neurons, and it underlies the acute stress response: raising heart rate and blood pressure, mobilising glucose and free fatty acids, and dilating airways within seconds of a threat. The genes here are largely the controls rather than the synthetic enzymes. Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors act as inhibitory autoreceptors that feed back on catecholamine-releasing cells and neurons to damp further output, which is why alpha-2 agonists lower sympathetic tone clinically. Corticotropin-releasing hormone links hypothalamic stress signalling to medullary and pituitary activation, while GABA-B receptor signalling and neuropeptides such as vasoactive intestinal peptide and the CART peptide provide inhibitory and stimulatory modulation. Together they set how much hormone reaches the circulation, with consequences for blood pressure regulation and stress adaptation.

Norepinephrine secretion is the regulated release of this catecholamine from sympathetic nerve terminals and adrenal chromaffin cells, where it acts as both neurotransmitter and circulating hormone to set heart rate, vascular tone, blood pressure and arousal. Because output must be tuned moment to moment, much of the machinery here is inhibitory feedback: the alpha-2 adrenoceptors ADRA2A, ADRA2B and ADRA2C act as presynaptic autoreceptors that suppress further release, and adenosine receptors and the purinergic receptor P2RY1 add further presynaptic restraint. Peptide and metabolite signals including CRH, oxytocin, ghrelin's receptor GHSR and the short-chain fatty acid receptor FFAR3 link stress, feeding and gut-derived cues to sympathetic drive. Exocytosis itself requires the SNARE protein STX1A, with KCNB1 shaping the excitability that triggers it, while COMT degrades the released transmitter. Dysregulation contributes to hypertension, orthostatic intolerance and stress-related cardiovascular disease.

Eosinophils are recruited out of the blood into tissue by soluble chemoattractant gradients, and this directed migration is what places them at sites of allergic inflammation, parasite infection and mucosal injury. The pathway matters because it underlies the eosinophilic infiltrate of asthma, atopic dermatitis, eosinophilic esophagitis and rhinitis; blocking the eotaxin arm reduces tissue eosinophilia. Most members are secreted CC chemokines, including the eotaxins CCL11, CCL24 and CCL26 that act through the eosinophil receptor CCR3, together with CCL5, CCL7 and CCL2 and the membrane-anchored chemokine CX3CL1. Epithelium, endothelium and resident leukocytes release these ligands under type 2 cytokine control, establishing gradients that drive adhesion, cytoskeletal polarisation and transendothelial crawling. Non-chemokine contributors such as galectin-3 and secretogranin II-derived peptide add further chemoattractant and kinase-dependent motility control.

Macrophage chemotaxis is the directed migration of macrophages and their monocyte precursors toward sites of infection, tissue injury or remodelling, and it determines where innate immune cells accumulate in inflammation, wound healing and tumours. Chemoattractants acting here include the complement fragment receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1, chemokines such as CCL2, CCL3 and CCL5, the membrane-anchored CX3CL1, chemerin sensed through CMKLR1, and the cytokine MIF; CSF1 and IL34 signalling through the shared receptor CSF1R couples recruitment to macrophage survival and differentiation. Downstream, focal adhesion kinases PTK2 and PTK2B and the ERK kinases MAPK1 and MAPK3 convert receptor engagement into cytoskeletal remodelling and adhesion turnover, with coronin and matrix proteases supporting movement through tissue. Too little recruitment leaves infection uncleared; excessive or persistent recruitment drives atherosclerosis, fibrosis and tumour-associated macrophage infiltration.

Lymphocyte chemotaxis is the directed migration of T, B and NK cells along chemical gradients, and it is what allows lymphocytes to leave the blood, home to lymph nodes and mucosal tissues, and concentrate at sites of infection or tumour growth. Without it, secondary lymphoid organs are poorly populated, antigen encounter becomes a matter of chance, and immune surveillance fails. Most of the signal is carried by secreted chemokines acting on G protein-coupled receptors — CXCL12, CXCL13 and CCL21 for homeostatic positioning, CXCL10 and CXCL11 through CXCR3 for inflammatory recruitment — with PI3Kγ and PI3Kδ and the focal adhesion kinase PTK2B relaying receptor engagement to cytoskeletal polarisation and adhesion. Oxysterol synthesis by CH25H and CYP7B1 generates the ligand read by GPR183 for follicular positioning, while WNK1–OXSR1–STK39 signalling to SLC12A2 links cell volume regulation to motility.

Elastic fiber assembly builds the resilient extracellular matrix elements that let arteries, lung parenchyma, skin and elastic ligaments stretch and spring back without deforming permanently. Tropoelastin deposited onto a fibrillin microfibril template is organised by scaffolding and chaperone proteins — fibulin-5, EFEMP2/fibulin-4, EMILIN1, MFAP4 and the microfibril-associated ADAMTSL2-related protein THSD4 — while lysyl oxidase covalently cross-links lysine residues to make the polymer durable, using copper delivered by the ATP7A transporter. Latent TGF-beta binding protein 4 ties the process to growth factor sequestration, and collagen III and tenascin-XB place the fibers within the surrounding matrix; smooth muscle myosin marks the vascular cells that produce them. Loss of these steps underlies cutis laxa, aortic aneurysm and tortuosity, emphysema and connective tissue fragility, since mature elastin is laid down mainly in development and is poorly replaced thereafter.

Small nucleolar RNAs guide the methylation and pseudouridylation of ribosomal RNA, but they only work once they have been assembled into ribonucleoprotein particles and delivered to the nucleolus. This pathway covers that trafficking and retention step, which determines whether newly made snoRNAs reach the site of ribosome biogenesis or are degraded. The proteins involved are core box C/D particle components and their assembly chaperones: a 2'-O-methyltransferase and its partner core protein form the catalytic particle, while additional factors act as a chaperone platform and a loading factor that places core proteins onto the RNA. One member also functions in spliceosomal snRNP biology, and its mutation causes autosomal dominant retinitis pigmentosa, linking defective small RNP assembly to photoreceptor degeneration. Failures here limit ribosome production and cell growth.

Cells decide which surface receptors to internalise, how fast, and what happens to them afterwards, and this regulatory layer sets those rates for receptor-mediated endocytosis. It governs how long a growth factor or hormone signal persists, how much cholesterol and iron a cell takes up, and how many neurotransmitter receptors sit at a synapse. Clathrin adaptors and accessory factors such as AP2 subunits, PICALM, DAB2, epsin- and endophilin-family proteins, HIP1/HIP1R and the kinases AAK1 and BMP2K nucleate and shape coated pits, while arrestins and the ubiquitin ligases CBL and CBLB mark activated receptors for uptake and degradation. Rab regulators and ARF GTPases direct the resulting vesicles onward to sorting or recycling. Ligands and receptors including PCSK9, transferrin, HFE, insulin receptor and EGF illustrate the cargo involved; disturbed control contributes to hypercholesterolaemia, iron overload, altered synaptic plasticity and oncogenic signalling.

Cells tune how fast they internalize ligand-bound surface receptors, and this collection covers the signals and adaptors that raise the rate and extent of receptor-mediated endocytosis. Turning uptake up removes receptors from the surface to dampen signalling, and it also drives nutrient and lipid acquisition therefore shaping cholesterol handling, iron loading and hormone responsiveness. Clathrin-coat adaptors (AP2A1, AP2M1, DAB2, LDLRAP1, HIP1, SGIP1) recruit cargo into forming pits, while cargo-specific accelerators act on particular receptors: PCSK9 promotes LDL receptor internalization and degradation, HFE and hepcidin govern transferrin- and ferroportin-linked iron uptake, and CBL ubiquitinates activated growth factor receptors such as EGF and insulin receptors. Arrestins (ARRB1, ARRB2) couple agonist-occupied G protein-coupled receptors, including chemokine receptor CCR7 and dopamine D2, to internalization, and Rab and TBC1D5 activity feeds the endosomal sorting that follows. Excessive or deficient uptake distorts lipoprotein clearance, immune cell trafficking and synaptic receptor turnover.

Receptor-mediated endocytosis is how cells selectively internalise lipoproteins, growth factors and neurotransmitter receptors, and this collection describes the brakes on it — the processes that slow or block uptake and so set how long a receptor stays at the surface. Restraint matters most for cholesterol handling and for synaptic signalling: PCSK9 diverts the LDL receptor to degradation rather than recycling, and gain-of-function mutations cause hypercholesterolaemia, while apolipoprotein C family members on lipoprotein particles impede their receptor-mediated clearance. Other components act on the trafficking machinery itself, including ankyrin-repeat proteins that promote ubiquitin-dependent sorting of activated receptors, ARF6 and RAC1 as small GTPases shaping membrane dynamics, and the clathrin assembly protein PICALM. Several microRNAs contribute post-transcriptional damping. Loss of such control alters receptor density, lipid uptake, and the tuning of glutamatergic synapses.

Setting up the dorsal-ventral axis is one of the first decisions an embryo makes, and it fixes where the nervous system, notochord and ventral mesoderm will form; failure produces axis duplication or loss and gross malformation of the body plan. The genes here act at the level of the two signalling systems that pattern this asymmetry: BMP/activin signalling through the type I receptor ACVR1, and Wnt signalling through beta-catenin with the ligand WNT8B. Much of the control is inhibitory and extracellular, with the secreted BMP antagonists CER1, GREM1, GREM2, NBL1 and SOSTDC1 restricting BMP activity to create a graded field, while the cytoplasmic regulator AIDA counteracts axis-dorsalising signals. Graded antagonism, rather than ligand expression alone, is what makes one side of the embryo dorsal and the other ventral.

Nociception is how the body detects tissue-damaging heat, pressure and irritant chemicals and converts them into the sensation of pain and the reflexes, stress responses and behaviours that follow. The response to pain begins at peripheral sensory endings, where transducing channels such as TRPV1 and TRPA1 and ATP-gated P2X receptors depolarize nociceptors, and voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A set their excitability; loss-of-function mutations in SCN9A or in the NGF receptor NTRK1 cause congenital insensitivity to pain, while gain-of-function variants produce severe inherited pain syndromes. Downstream, substance P encoded by TAC1 acting through its receptor TACR1, glutamate receptors, protein kinase C gamma and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling drive central sensitization and chronic pain. Noradrenergic and corticotropin-releasing hormone components link the stimulus to descending modulation and systemic stress responses, and these molecules are the main targets of analgesic drug development.

Pain is useful only if it changes what an animal does, and the behavioral response to pain covers the chain from nociceptor activation to withdrawal, guarding, vocalization and avoidance learning. These genes define the sensory end of that chain: voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A, SCN11A and SCN3A set nociceptor excitability and firing threshold, TRPV1 with its modulator PIRT transduces noxious heat and capsaicin, ATP-gated P2X2, P2X3 and P2X4 channels carry chemical and injury signals, and NTRK1 responds to nerve growth factor to support nociceptor survival and sensitization. Substance P signalling through TACR1, glutamatergic AMPA transmission via GRIA1, and AKT1-mTOR translational control contribute to central amplification and persistent hypersensitivity. Loss-of-function in this machinery produces congenital insensitivity to pain, while its excessive activity underlies inflammatory and neuropathic chronic pain, making it a principal target space for analgesics.

Clathrin coat assembly is the step that turns a flat patch of membrane into a cargo-loaded vesicle, and it underlies receptor-mediated endocytosis, synaptic vesicle recycling, and trafficking between the Golgi and endosomes. Triskelia of heavy and light chains (CLTC with CLTA) polymerise into a curved cage, but only where adaptors say they should: the AP-2 subunits here bind cargo motifs and membrane lipids, FCHO1/2 and EPS15 nucleate sites, and sorting adaptors such as DAB2 and PICALM select specific receptors. HIP1 and HIP1R couple the growing coat to actin, dynamin pinches the neck, and the auxilin-family cochaperone DNAJC6 with GAK recruits Hsc70 to uncoat the vesicle so clathrin can be reused. Loss of the neuronal components impairs synaptic vesicle regeneration, and variants in these genes are linked to parkinsonism and to Alzheimer's disease risk through altered receptor and lipid handling.

Before a transport vesicle can fuse, it must first be captured and held against the correct target membrane, and vesicle docking is that initial tethering and attachment step. It determines where cargo is delivered: neurotransmitter release at the active zone, insertion of receptors and channels into the plasma membrane, and traffic through endosomes, Golgi and lysosomes. Multisubunit tethers such as the exocyst and the HOPS-related VPS components, together with the Rab GTPase RAB8A and the golgin-binding tether USO1, bring membranes into proximity; syntaxins and their SNARE partners, held in check by Munc18 proteins and primed by UNC13 family priming factors, then form the complexes that commit to fusion. Calcium sensing by synaptotagmin and regulation by complexins and RIM proteins couple docking to stimulus, so defects here produce synaptic transmission failure, epilepsy and secretion disorders such as familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

Membrane traffic arriving at the Golgi only delivers its cargo when the transport vesicle's bilayer merges with the target cisterna, and this fusion step is what sustains secretion, glycosylation and the flow of newly made proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell surface. Tethering precedes fusion: a long coiled-coil tether captures incoming vesicles at a distance and holds them against the Golgi membrane, after which SNARE proteins on the two bilayers zipper into a four-helix bundle that forces lipid mixing. Members of the SNARE machinery here serve distinct arrival routes, with some pairing at the cis-Golgi for ER-derived vesicles and others at the trans-Golgi for endosomal traffic. Yip-family multipass membrane proteins contribute to Golgi organization and ER exit site function. Loss of these steps collapses Golgi structure and blocks the secretory pathway.

Organelle fusion is the set of events by which two membrane-bounded compartments merge into one, the step that lets material move between organelles rather than simply between vesicles and the cytosol. It supports neurotransmitter release, endosome and lysosome maturation, autophagosome clearance, lipid droplet growth, and the continual remodelling of the mitochondrial network. Most of the machinery is SNARE-based: syntaxins, VAMPs and SNAP proteins pair across apposed bilayers, tethering complexes such as HOPS and its VPS subunits confer specificity, Rab GTPases and their effectors mark the target membrane, and synaptotagmins with complexins impose calcium control at the synapse. A separate arm uses dynamin-family GTPases, with mitofusins and OPA1 joining outer and inner mitochondrial membranes and PLD6 supplying the lipid signal. Loss of these activities produces neurodegeneration, optic atrophy, hereditary spastic paraplegia, and failures of lysosomal degradation.

Organelle fusion merges two membrane-bound compartments into one, and it underlies much of how cells deliver, degrade and remodel material. Endosomes ripen and converge on lysosomes, autophagosomes discharge their cargo, secretory and synaptic vesicles empty at the plasma membrane, lipid droplets coalesce, and mitochondria join into a connected network. The machinery here is largely SNARE-based: syntaxins, VAMPs and SNAP partners pair across apposed bilayers, with Munc18/complexin and synaptotagmin sensors timing calcium-triggered release, Rab GTPases and tethering complexes such as HOPS and its VPS subunits conferring specificity, and ESCRT CHMP proteins remodelling membranes. Mitochondrial fusion runs through the dynamin-family GTPases MFN1, MFN2 and OPA1 with their proteases, balancing fission and quality control by mitophagy. Loss of these steps causes lysosomal storage, failed autophagy, optic atrophy and neuropathy, and links this biology to Parkinson's disease genes including PRKN and LRRK2.

Organelle fission covers the division of a single organelle into two, and the genes here span both meanings of that: the division of the nucleus during mitosis and meiosis, and the scission of mitochondria and peroxisomes. Nuclear division dominates, with condensins, cohesins and their release by separase, kinetochore and spindle-checkpoint components, Aurora and Polo kinases, the anaphase-promoting complex, and the meiosis-specific synaptonemal complex and recombination machinery that partition homologues in germ cells. Membrane organelle fission runs through the dynamin-related GTPase DNM1L and its outer-membrane receptors MFF, FIS1 and MIEF1/2, with OPA1 and peroxisomal PEX11 proteins shaping the balance between division and fusion. Dividing these compartments is what lets daughter cells inherit a complete genome and a working complement of mitochondria; failure produces aneuploidy, infertility, and neuropathies tied to disturbed mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy.

Alveolar development turns the smooth terminal airways of the fetal lung into millions of thin-walled air sacs, creating the enormous surface area and short diffusion distance that gas exchange requires. Its completion underlies the transition to air breathing at birth, and its arrest produces the simplified, under-septated lungs of bronchopulmonary dysplasia in preterm infants, while later disruption of the same signals contributes to emphysema and fibrosis. Reciprocal epithelial/mesenchymal signalling drives the process: FGF10 acting through FGFR2 patterns distal outgrowth, BMP4, TGF-beta ligands and PDGFA direct septation and myofibroblast behaviour, and VEGF receptors KDR and FLT4 couple alveolar growth to capillary formation. Transcription factors including NKX2-1, GATA6, FOXA1, FOXF1, TCF21 and HOPX specify alveolar epithelial and mesenchymal identities, with surfactant, claudin-based junctions and extracellular matrix remodelling completing a functional gas-exchange barrier.

isotype switching to IgA isotypes is the step in which an activated B cell abandons IgM production and commits to making IgA, the antibody class that dominates mucosal secretions in the gut, airway and breast milk. It gives rise to the plasma cells that coat epithelial surfaces with secretory antibody and keeps commensal bacteria in check; its failure leaves selective IgA deficiency and heightened mucosal and respiratory infection. Commitment is driven by mucosal cues — TGF-beta is the decisive instructive signal, with APRIL from stromal and dendritic cells and CCR6-guided homing to gut lymphoid tissue supplying the context. The rearrangement itself deletes the DNA between the IgM and IgA switch regions, and mismatch repair proteins MSH2, MLH1 and PMS2 process the deaminated switch-region lesions into double-strand breaks, while NSD2-dependent chromatin marking targets the reaction. It is thus recombination-based class switching harnessed to mucosal immunity.

Mucosal immunity depends on B cells abandoning IgM and rewriting their heavy chain locus to produce IgA, the antibody secreted across gut, airway and mammary epithelium to neutralise microbes without provoking inflammation. Isotype switching to IgA isotypes is the recombination event that makes this possible: an intrachromosomal deletion joins the switch region upstream of IgM to an IgA switch region, permanently replacing the constant region while leaving antigen specificity intact. TGFB1 is the principal cytokine directing B cells toward this choice, with APRIL (TNFSF13) supplying additional class-switch and survival signals, and CCR6 positioning responding cells in gut-associated lymphoid tissue. Mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2 and PMS2 process the staggered breaks so that switch regions resolve correctly, and chromatin modification by NSD2 helps make the target region accessible. Defects impair secretory antibody defence at mucosal surfaces.

Activated B cells that have already made IgM can rewrite their heavy chain constant region to produce IgG instead, and this class switch is what gives antibody responses their opsonising, complement-fixing and placentally transferred arm. Vaccine responses and protection against encapsulated bacteria depend on it; its failure produces hyper-IgM syndromes in which IgM is abundant but IgG is absent. Switching is a targeted deletional recombination between repetitive switch regions upstream of the constant gene segments, and repair of the resulting lesions draws on mismatch repair proteins such as MLH1, MSH2 and PMS2, with PAXIP1 supporting the DNA damage response at the locus. The decision to switch is imposed from outside the B cell: CD40 engagement by helper T cells, costimulation through CD28, and cytokine cues including IL-4 and IL-2 determine which isotype is chosen, while FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells restrain the response.

Whether a B cell rewrites its heavy chain locus to produce IgE rather than another antibody class determines the capacity for allergic responses, and this regulatory layer sets how often that happens. IgE arms mast cells and basophils, so excessive switching underlies atopy, asthma and anaphylaxis, while its restraint keeps humoral immunity directed toward other isotypes. The dominant positive input is interleukin-4 acting through STAT6 to license germline transcription at the epsilon locus, with costimulatory signals such as OX40 ligand from antigen-presenting cells supporting the helper T cell responses that supply it. Opposing that, BCL6 limits the transcriptional programme, FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells suppress the helper T cell output that drives switching, and the ubiquitin ligase adaptor NDFIP1 dampens type 2 cytokine production. The net balance defines how strongly a T helper 2 response translates into IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.

Antibody responses only become effective against many pathogens once a B cell switches from IgM to IgG, and this is the set of inputs that pushes that switch forward. Enhancing class switch recombination toward IgG isotypes determines whether high-affinity opsonising and neutralising antibodies are produced, and how vaccines and infections generate lasting serum protection; too little yields hyper-IgM-like immunodeficiency, too much contributes to autoantibody-driven disease. Cognate T cell help supplies the trigger through CD40 engagement together with CD28 costimulation and the cytokines IL-2 and IL-4, with TBX21 biasing the choice of IgG subclass. The recombination itself requires mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2 and PMS2 to process deaminated switch-region DNA, while PAXIP1 licenses switch-region accessibility, linking lymphocyte activation signals directly to programmed DNA breakage and repair at the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus.

Organelle inheritance is the problem of making sure each daughter cell receives a working set of organelles when a mother cell divides. Membrane compartments such as the Golgi are single copy and continuous, so they must be disassembled, partitioned, and rebuilt on a schedule locked to mitosis; failure leaves daughters with defective secretory capacity or blocks mitotic entry outright. The genes describe that mitotic Golgi checkpoint: CDK1 and the Polo-like kinases phosphorylate the golgin GRASP65/GM130 module to unlink cisternal stacks, ERK cascade components contribute to cisternal unstacking, and GBF1, STX5 and the deubiquitinase VCPIP1 drive vesicle tethering and post-mitotic reassembly. STK25 and PDCD10 link Golgi positioning to cell polarity. This couples organelle biogenesis to cell cycle control, and connects to lysosomal and endosomal partitioning through VPS13B.

When a cell divides it must not only split its chromosomes but also hand each daughter a working set of membrane organelles, and organelle inheritance is the partitioning step that accomplishes this. The genes here point mainly at the Golgi, which in mammalian cells is disassembled into dispersed elements before mitosis and reassembled afterwards in each daughter; failure to do so blocks entry into mitosis and leaves daughters with defective secretory capacity. Mitotic kinases including CDK1 and polo-like kinases phosphorylate Golgi structural proteins such as GM130, while GBF1, the SNARE STX5 and the deubiquitinase VCPIP1 act in vesicle tethering and post-mitotic membrane fusion, and a GCKIII-striatin module contributes to ribbon organisation. The pathway thus links cell cycle control to membrane traffic, coupling organelle architecture to division timing.

Mitochondria must be placed where energy demand and calcium buffering are needed, and this pathway governs how they are distributed within a cell and partitioned between daughter cells. Position matters most in polarized cells: neurons deliver mitochondria along axons to synapses, and failure to do so leaves distal compartments energetically starved, a defect linked to neurodegeneration and to congenital myopathy. Transport runs on microtubules through kinesin motors such as KIF5B coupled to organelle adaptors of the TRAK family, with myosin-based movement on actin contributing via MYO19; DNM1L-driven fission generates the smaller units that can be trafficked and inherited. Regulators include the microtubule-binding protein MAPT, the kinase LRRK2, and CLUH, which binds mRNAs encoding nuclear-coded mitochondrial proteins. The pathway therefore ties cytoskeletal motor logic to mitochondrial dynamics, cell polarity, and inheritance during division.

Mitochondria must be positioned where energy demand and calcium buffering are needed for example at synapses, at the immunological synapse, or apically in secretory cells and this pathway covers the processes that set their spatial arrangement inside a cell. Distribution depends on transport along cytoskeletal tracks, on anchoring, and on fission and fusion that determine how divisible and mobile the network is: DNM1L drives the scission events that generate transportable mitochondria, MAPT binds microtubules and influences trafficking along them, and LRRK2 mutations that disturb mitochondrial positioning and dynamics cause familial Parkinson disease. CLUH binds mRNAs encoding nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins and shapes where the organelles cluster, while BHLHA15 links the arrangement to secretory cell maturation. Mispositioning starves distal compartments such as axons of ATP and contributes to neurodegeneration.

Axial mesoderm development tracks the midline mesoderm of the early embryo from its specification in the organizer through to the prechordal plate and notochord. These are the structures that set the body's midline and anterior-posterior axis: the notochord patterns the neural tube and somites by secreting signals that establish ventral neural fates and induce the sclerotome, and its remnants persist in the intervertebral disc. Failure of this programme produces midline defects, left-right patterning errors and laterality disorders such as heterotaxy, and disturbed vertebral segmentation. The genes here span the signalling and transcriptional inputs that establish midline identity: Nodal signalling and its BMP-antagonist and forkhead partners, a zinc-finger regulator whose loss causes X-linked laterality defects, Wnt pathway scaffolding through Axin1, and cell-shape and adhesion components that drive the convergent movements gathering mesoderm at the midline.</description>

Mesoderm morphogenesis is the shaping of the middle germ layer after gastrulation, turning a sheet of newly ingressed cells into the somites, heart, blood, kidney, limb skeleton and connective tissues on which the rest of the body plan depends. Its failure is embryonic lethal or produces axial, cardiac and renal malformations. Nodal, BMP and WNT ligands with their receptors and SMAD effectors, tuned by secreted antagonists such as NOG, DKK1 and TWSG1, set up the primitive streak, while TBXT, EOMES, MESP1/2, MSGN1 and TBX6 specify nascent and presomitic mesoderm and ETV2, TAL1 and HAND1 divert subsets into endothelium, blood and heart. SNAI1-driven loss of epithelial character, integrin-dependent adhesion to extracellular matrix, and FGF signalling supply the cell movement and rearrangement that accompany specification, with FOX, PAX, EYA and SIX factors patterning derivative organ fields.

Mesodermal cell differentiation is the step at which an uncommitted early embryonic cell takes on the identity of mesoderm, the germ layer that gives rise to blood, heart and skeletal muscle, bone, kidney and connective tissue. Without it there is no cardiovascular system, no haematopoiesis and no metanephric kidney, and the embryo fails at gastrulation. The genes here trace how that commitment is imposed and stabilised: Nodal, WNT3A and BMP4 acting through its receptor BMPR1A and SMAD1 provide the inducing signals, with DKK1 and SFRP2 restraining Wnt; FGFR1 and FGFR2 relay fibroblast growth factor input; and MESP1, TAL1, PAX2, SIX2, FOXC2, FOXF1 and the EYA factors specify cardiac, blood-forming, nephron and mesenchymal fates downstream. Integrin-mediated adhesion to extracellular matrix, chromatin regulators such as KDM6B, and microRNAs including the miR-200 family couple the transcriptional programme to the cell shape changes and epithelial-mesenchymal transitions that accompany it.

Paraxial mesoderm is the band of tissue flanking the notochord and neural tube that gives rise to somites and from them to the axial skeleton, skeletal muscle and dermis. Its development covers the whole progression from specification of mesodermal progenitors in the primitive streak and tailbud, through their anterior-posterior patterning, to segmentation into epithelial somites. WNT ligands acting through LEF1, BMP receptor and SMAD2/SMAD3-mediated TGF-beta signalling, and FGFR1 set up and maintain the progenitor pool, while Notch signalling through the ligand DLL3 provides the oscillatory clock that times somite boundary formation; FOXC1, FOXC2, TCF15 and ZIC3 act as transcriptional determinants of somite identity and epithelialization, with YAP1 and TEAD2 coupling tissue mechanics to the process. Failure of segmentation produces congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis and broader axial skeletal defects.

Paraxial mesoderm morphogenesis shapes the block of mesoderm flanking the neural tube into the segmented tissue that gives rise to somites, and from them the vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis of the trunk. Failure here produces axial skeletal malformations, fused or missing vertebrae, and defective body wall closure.
