Much of the set is inhibitory feedback and heteroreceptor modulation at the terminal, including alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors, D2 and D3 dopamine receptors, adenosine, opioid, GABA-B and metabotropic glutamate receptors, nicotinic receptors driving chromaffin cell excitation, and potassium channels that shape terminal excitability; COMT terminates signalling by degrading released amine. Alpha-synuclein, PINK1 and parkin place this biology at the heart of dopaminergic neuron vulnerability in Parkinson's disease, where loss of striatal dopamine release produces motor impairment.

Amyloid-beta metabolic process covers the production, trafficking, clearance and degradation of amyloid-beta peptide and its parent amyloid precursor protein, the balance that determines whether the peptide accumulates into the plaques of Alzheimer's disease. Generation depends on sequential cleavage by the beta-secretase BACE1 and the gamma-secretase complex of presenilins with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2, with reticulons and GSAP modulating those cleavages. Opposing this, extracellular peptidases such as insulin-degrading enzyme, neprilysin and ACE degrade the peptide, while apolipoprotein E, clusterin, LRP1, SORL1 and phagocytic receptors including TREM2 and CD36 govern lipoprotein-associated clearance and microglial uptake. Endocytic adaptors PICALM and BIN1, kinases GSK3 and DYRK1A, inflammatory signalling through TNF and interferon-gamma, and a large set of microRNAs tune precursor expression and processing. Most late-onset Alzheimer's risk loci act somewhere in this balance.

Amyloid-beta metabolism covers the making, trafficking, clearing and degrading of the peptide whose accumulation defines Alzheimer's disease plaques. Its balance determines whether a neuron keeps a low steady-state burden or accumulates aggregation-prone species, and most inherited early-onset dementia mutations act here. Amyloid precursor protein is cut by the beta-secretase BACE1 and then by the gamma-secretase complex, whose catalytic presenilins act with nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN; reticulon proteins and GSAP modulate these cleavages, while endocytic and sorting factors such as SORL1, PICALM, BIN1 and LRP1 route the precursor between compartments. Clearance runs through proteases including insulin-degrading enzyme and neprilysin, lipoprotein-based carriers such as APOE and clusterin, microglial uptake via TREM2 and CD36, and autophagy. Cholesterol and lipid transporters, inflammatory cytokine signalling, kinases and a large set of microRNAs tune precursor expression and processing, linking lipid handling and immune activation to plaque formation.

Arachidonic acid is the precursor for prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, and its controlled release from membrane phospholipids sets the pace of eicosanoid production in inflammation, pain, fever, platelet aggregation and vascular tone. The release step is catalysed by phospholipases A2, which hydrolyse the sn-2 position of glycerophospholipids; the secreted group II, V and X enzymes act extracellularly while cytosolic PLA2G4A liberates arachidonate for downstream cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase pathways, and PNPLA8 acts on mitochondrial membranes. Upstream control is largely receptor-driven: G protein-coupled receptors for bradykinin, vasopressin, neurotensin, neuromedins and dopamine couple to calcium and kinase signals that mobilise these lipases, with SYK contributing in immune cells and annexin A1 and MIF imposing glucocorticoid-linked restraint. Excess flux through this route drives inflammatory and allergic disease, and it is the point at which anti-inflammatory drugs intervene.

Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans are the space-filling, water-binding components of cartilage and other extracellular matrices, and they also form the inhibitory scars that block axon regrowth after central nervous system injury. Their biosynthesis begins with xylose transfer to serine residues of a core protein by xylosyltransferases, extension of the tetrasaccharide linker by galactosyl- and glucuronyltransferases, and polymerisation of alternating glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine by the chondroitin synthase and polymerising-factor complexes. Sulfotransferases acting at the 4-O, 6-O and uronyl positions then generate the charge patterns that dictate growth-factor binding, while nucleotide-sugar supply and Golgi transporters for UDP-sugars and the sulfate donor PAPS set the ceiling on output. A phosphatase removes a transient xylose phosphate to license chain elongation. Loss of linker-region enzymes causes skeletal dysplasias and connective tissue fragility, including forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

Dermatan sulfate proteoglycans give skin, tendon, blood vessels and cornea much of their tensile strength and water-binding capacity, and they organise collagen fibril spacing and sequester growth factors in the matrix. Their biosynthesis begins in the Golgi with xylose transfer onto serine residues of a core protein by xylosyltransferases, followed by two galactoses and a glucuronic acid to complete the tetrasaccharide linker; chain polymerisation then adds alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and hexuronic acid. What distinguishes dermatan from chondroitin sulfate is epimerisation of glucuronate to iduronate by the dermatan sulfate epimerases, which adds conformational flexibility, together with sulfotransferases acting at the 4-O, 6-O and 2-O positions to set the charge pattern that ligands read. Loss of linker-region or epimerase/sulfotransferase enzymes causes connective tissue fragility, notably the musculocontractural and spondylodysplastic forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with skeletal and skin involvement.

Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan metabolic process builds and breaks down the sulfated sugar chains that give cartilage, bone and the extracellular matrix their compressive strength, and that pattern cell surfaces in the nervous system. Its products control growth factor availability, matrix hydration and axon guidance, and perineuronal nets built from these proteoglycans close critical periods of plasticity and block regeneration after injury. Synthesis begins with xylose transfer to a core protein serine and extension of the common linker tetrasaccharide, followed by alternating GalNAc and glucuronic acid addition by chondroitin synthases and sulfation at the 4-, 6- and 2-positions by dedicated sulfotransferases using PAPS imported into the Golgi. Epimerases divert chains toward dermatan sulfate. Lysosomal hyaluronidases, sulfatases and exoglycosidases complete turnover, and their loss causes mucopolysaccharidoses, while defects in linker assembly produce skeletal dysplasias and connective tissue fragility.

Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans are the main space-filling, water-binding components of cartilage and other extracellular matrix, and they also form the inhibitory scars that block axon regrowth in the injured central nervous system. Their metabolism covers the whole life cycle of the chain: xylosyltransferases and galactosyl/glucuronyltransferases build the tetrasaccharide linker on a core protein serine, polymerising glycosyltransferases extend the glucuronic acid-N-acetylgalactosamine repeat, epimerases convert it toward dermatan, and a family of sulfotransferases places sulfate at specific positions to create the binding codes read by growth factors and guidance receptors. Nucleotide-sugar supply and Golgi sulfate transport feed the reactions, while hyaluronidases, sulfatases and exoglycosidases carry out lysosomal turnover. Loss of the linker enzymes causes skeletal dysplasias and connective tissue disorders, and defective degradation underlies mucopolysaccharidoses with progressive storage in bone, cartilage and brain.

Dermatan sulfate proteoglycans are core proteins carrying long sulfated sugar chains that fill the extracellular matrix of skin, tendon, blood vessels and cornea, where they organise collagen fibrils, retain water and bind growth factors. Their turnover comprises both synthesis and lysosomal breakdown. Chain assembly begins with a shared linker tetrasaccharide built by xylosyltransferases and galactosyl/glucuronyltransferases on a serine of the core protein, then polymerised by GalNAc transferases; epimerases such as DSE convert glucuronic acid to iduronic acid, the feature that distinguishes dermatan from chondroitin sulfate, and sulfotransferases including CHST14 and UST decorate the chain. Degradation returns the polymer to monosaccharides via iduronidase, iduronate-2-sulfatase and hexosaminidase. Loss of the biosynthetic enzymes causes connective tissue fragility of the Ehlers-Danlos and skeletal dysplasia type, while failure of the catabolic steps produces mucopolysaccharide storage disease.

Hydrogen peroxide is made deliberately as well as accidentally, and this biosynthetic route covers the enzymes that generate it. Its products serve host defence, hormone synthesis and redox signalling, but the same molecule oxidises DNA, lipids and protein thiols when it escapes control. The NADPH oxidase subunits CYBA, CYBB and NCF1 produce superoxide at phagosomal and plasma membranes, which the superoxide dismutases SOD1 and SOD2 convert to peroxide in cytosol and mitochondria; the dual oxidases DUOX1 and DUOX2, with their maturation partners DUOXA1 and DUOXA2, release peroxide directly at epithelial surfaces, supplying thyroid peroxidase for thyroid hormone synthesis and antimicrobial activity in airway and gut. Peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation by ACOX1, monoamine breakdown by MAOB and cytochrome P450 turnover add further flux. Loss of DUOX function causes congenital hypothyroidism, and oxidase defects impair microbial killing.

Homocysteine sits at the junction of methionine recycling and sulfur amino acid disposal, and how a cell handles it determines both its capacity for methylation and its supply of cysteine and glutathione. Remethylation returns homocysteine to methionine using a folate-derived methyl group and vitamin B12, with methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase generating the donor, methionine synthase transferring it, and a reductase keeping the cobalamin cofactor active. The alternative route commits homocysteine irreversibly to transsulfuration, where cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase produce cysteine and hydrogen sulfide. Blockage at either branch raises plasma homocysteine, and inherited defects cause homocystinuria with lens dislocation, skeletal changes, thrombosis and vascular disease; milder elevations are linked to endothelial dysfunction and oxidative stress. Related sulfur- and amidohydrolase-handling enzymes and the urea cycle entry step place this chemistry within broader nitrogen and sulfur amino acid metabolism.

Epithelia line every surface and duct of the body and must renew themselves continuously, so the controlled multiplication of epithelial cells underlies wound healing, gut and airway turnover, mammary and prostate development, and the branching morphogenesis of glands and kidney. The same controls, when released, permit carcinoma growth, which is why many of these genes are oncogenes and tumour suppressors. Growth factor input dominates: EGF-family ligands such as AREG, TGFA and EREG acting through EGFR and its ERBB partners, fibroblast growth factors with FGFR1/2, HGF, and IGF1 with its binding proteins, feeding into RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and mTOR complexes. Developmental signalling by WNT, Hedgehog, Notch and TGF-beta/BMP ligands and receptors sets regional competence, while CDKN1A, CDKN1B, RB1, STK11, FBXW7 and a large complement of microRNAs restrain cycle entry. Cytokines, hypoxia and stromal matrix cues modulate the response during inflammation and repair.

Epithelia must renew themselves continuously yet stop dividing once a sheet is complete, and this is the control layer that sets how fast and how often epithelial cells proliferate. It governs branching morphogenesis in lung, kidney and mammary gland, wound repair and gut and skin turnover; when the brakes fail, hyperplasia and carcinoma follow, which is why so many of its members are oncogenes and tumour suppressors. Growth factor input runs through EGF-family ligands such as amphiregulin, epiregulin and TGFA acting on EGFR and its ERBB partners, alongside FGF, IGF1, VEGF and WNT ligands, developmental Hedgehog, Notch and BMP/TGF-beta arms, and nuclear receptors including AR and PGR. Restraint comes from CDK inhibitors CDKN1B and CDKN1C, RB1, STK11, FBXW7, the Hippo component SAV1 opposing YAP1, and a large complement of microRNAs that tune the same receptors and cyclins post-transcriptionally.

positive regulation of epithelial cell proliferation covers the signals that drive epithelial sheets to expand, the process behind organ growth and branching morphogenesis in development, wound re-epithelialisation, and the regenerative turnover of gut, lung, skin, mammary and kidney linings. Its deregulation is a route to hyperplasia and carcinoma, which is why many of these components are oncogenes and drug targets. The genes describe growth factor input from EGF-family ligands and their ERBB receptors, FGF, IGF1, PDGF and VEGF ligand-receptor pairs, converging on RAS-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR (with both RPTOR and RICTOR present), STAT3 and cyclin D1-driven G1 entry. Developmental morphogens, WNT/beta-catenin, Hedgehog, Notch, BMP/TGF-beta and YAP1, set the proliferative competence of the epithelium, while inflammatory mediators such as TNF and TGFB1 couple injury to repair. Numerous microRNAs tune the same circuits post-transcriptionally.

Epithelia renew themselves throughout life, and this collection captures the signals that drive that division upward — the inputs that push epithelial cells, including the endothelium of blood and lymphatic vessels, into cycle during development, wound repair, glandular branching and regeneration of gut and skin surfaces. The same circuitry, sustained rather than transient, underlies hyperplasia, fibrosis and carcinoma, which is why so many of its members are oncogenes and drug targets. Growth factors acting through receptor tyrosine kinases (EGF and its relatives via EGFR and ERBB2-4, FGFs, IGF1, VEGFs via KDR and FLT4) converge on RAS-PI3K-AKT and mTOR complexes, while WNT/beta-catenin, hedgehog through SMO, NOTCH, BMP and TGF-beta arms supply positional and developmental context. Transcriptional outputs such as MYC, CCND1, STAT3 and YAP1 execute the decision, and numerous microRNAs tune it.

Epithelia must stop dividing once a sheet is complete, and negative regulation of epithelial cell proliferation covers the brakes that enforce that limit. It underlies tissue size control, terminal differentiation of skin, breast, prostate, lung and gut linings, and the maintenance of epithelial barriers; loss of these restraints is a step toward hyperplasia and carcinoma, which is why many members are tumour suppressors. The brakes act at several levels: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1B, CDKN1C and CDKN2B together with RB1, FBXW7 and STK11 halt cell cycle progression; TGF-beta and BMP ligands with their receptors, along with Hippo-associated SAV1 and secreted WNT antagonists, deliver antiproliferative cues from outside; and a large complement of microRNAs damps growth-promoting transcripts. Lineage transcription factors, cilium-associated components and cell-junction and polarity proteins contribute contact-dependent restraint.

Regulation of mRNA processing covers the controls that decide how a primary transcript is spliced, cleaved and polyadenylated, and therefore which protein isoform a gene actually makes. It is how one genome generates tissue-specific proteomes: neuronal splicing regulators such as NOVA1/2, RBFOX proteins and SRRM4 build neuron-specific exon patterns, RBM20 and RBM24 shape sarcomere transcripts in heart and muscle, and QKI acts in glial differentiation. Mechanistically it combines the core spliceosome and its Sm proteins, U2AF2, PRPF8 and SNRNP200, with SR proteins and hnRNPs that compete at exonic and intronic elements, SRPK and CDK9 kinases and arginine methyltransferases that set their activity, cleavage and polyadenylation factors including the CSTF subunits and PCF11, exon junction complex and surveillance components, and m6A writers and readers such as METTL16, WTAP and YTHDC1. Misregulation here produces aberrant isoforms in myopathy, neurodevelopmental disease and cancer.

Newly transcribed pre-mRNA must be capped, spliced, cleaved and polyadenylated before it can be exported and translated, and this grouping covers factors that increase the rate or extent of those maturation steps. Enhancing mRNA processing sets how much functional message a gene produces and which isoform predominates, so it feeds directly into tissue-specific splicing programmes, transcription-coupled RNA handling, and quality control of aberrant transcripts. The cap-binding complex subunits NCBP1 and NCBP2 mark the 5' end for splicing and export; SNRNP70 is a core U1 snRNP protein and PRPF19 and SNW1 act within the spliceosome; PRMT5 with its partner WDR77 methylates Sm proteins to license snRNP assembly. Tissue-biased RNA-binding proteins such as CELF3, CELF4, TRA2B and DAZAP1 promote particular splice choices, while UPF1 and UPF3B couple processing to nonsense-mediated decay of transcripts carrying premature stop codons.

Not every splice site or polyadenylation site in a pre-mRNA should be used, and the negative regulation of mRNA processing covers the factors that suppress them, sharpening which isoforms a cell actually makes. Repression of this kind sets tissue-specific splicing patterns: PTBP1 silences neuronal exons in non-neuronal cells, RBM20 restrains inclusion in cardiac transcripts such as titin, and CELF4 and RBMX act in similar exon-skipping roles. The machinery includes core spliceosomal components — the Sm proteins, the U5 factors PRPF8 and SNRNP200, EFTUD2 and its assembly partner AAR2 — alongside SR proteins and exon junction–associated factors like ACIN1, RNPS1 and SAP18, which can inhibit as well as promote site selection. Phosphorylation by DYRK1A tunes SR protein behaviour. Loss of this restraint produces aberrant isoforms, and mutations in several members cause cardiomyopathy, craniofacial and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Antiviral responses have to be switched off as well as on, and this set covers the brakes: processes that dampen or terminate defense responses to virus, limiting interferon output and inflammatory damage at the cost of permitting viral replication. Most of the components act on the RIG-I/MAVS and STING sensing axis or on downstream kinases and transcription factors. The ATG5-ATG12 conjugate and IRGM restrain RNA-sensing signalling at mitochondrial and autophagic membranes; MUL1 and RNF26 are ubiquitin ligases acting on innate signalling adaptors, ITCH and TRIM38 promote degradation of signalling intermediates, PPM1B removes activating phosphorylation, and PCBP2 and C1QBP negatively modulate MAVS-dependent induction. FOXP3 and FGL2 contribute immunosuppressive, regulatory-T-cell-associated control, while MICB engages NK cell recognition. Too little of this restraint produces interferonopathy and autoimmunity; too much favours chronic or persistent infection.

Antiviral defence must be strong enough to clear infection but restrained enough to avoid immunopathology, and this pathway covers the processes that tune the magnitude and duration of that response. Its members sit largely on the nucleic-acid sensing arms of innate immunity: cytosolic DNA is detected by cGAS feeding into STING, RNA by RIG-I signalling through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, with TRAF3 and downstream STAT1 driving interferon output, while inflammasome components such as AIM2 and PYCARD couple sensing to IL-1β maturation. Much of the set is regulatory rather than effector — ubiquitin ligases and TRIM proteins, deubiquitinases, the negative regulators TNFAIP3 and ZC3H12A, autophagy factors, and FOXP3-dependent restraint — alongside direct restriction factors of the APOBEC3 family. Loss of this control produces either uncontrolled viral replication or sterile interferon-driven autoinflammation.

Host cells must tune their own antiviral responses: strong enough to clear infection, restrained enough to avoid immunopathology. This regulatory layer sets the amplitude and duration of innate antiviral defence, and its members act at every stage of the response. Cytosolic sensors including cGAS with its adaptor STING, RIG-I signalling through MAVS, and the inflammasome components AIM2 and PYCARD detect viral nucleic acids and trigger interferon and interleukin-1 output; interleukin-12, -23 and -27 subunits with their receptors direct the downstream lymphocyte response, while STAT1 transduces interferon signals. Positive and negative modifiers include ubiquitin ligases and TRIM proteins, the deubiquitinase-like brake TNFAIP3, the ribonuclease ZC3H12A that degrades inflammatory transcripts, and APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases that hypermutate retroviral genomes directly. Loss of restraint here produces interferonopathy and autoinflammation; loss of activation leaves cells permissive to viral replication.

Cells that make their living by releasing proteins must decide when to do so, and this collection covers the control layer over regulated protein secretion — how the frequency and extent of cargo release from secretory granules and vesicles is tuned to stimuli. Much of it reads as the machinery of glucose-stimulated insulin release from pancreatic beta cells: glucokinase and GLUT2 sense nutrient load, ATP-sensitive potassium channels built from KCNJ11 and ABCC8 couple metabolism to membrane depolarisation, and calcium entry then drives SNARE-dependent granule fusion through syntaxin-1A, SNAP25 and synaptotagmins, with PDX1, NKX6-1 and NEUROD1 maintaining the identity of the cell that does this. Alongside are incretin, adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors that modulate the same event, cyclic-AMP and protein kinase C amplification, Rab11 effectors and trafficking components, and inflammatory cytokine release. Loss of this control produces diabetes and hormone-secretion disorders.

Cells that release hormones, cytokines and other cargo must also be able to hold back, and negative regulation of protein secretion covers the brakes on that controlled release. It sets the tone of endocrine and immune output: too little restraint on insulin release causes hypoglycaemia, too much contributes to diabetes, and unchecked cytokine release drives inflammatory damage. Much of the machinery here is pancreatic beta cell biology, where the KATP channel subunits SUR1 and Kir6.2 hold the membrane hyperpolarised and suppress exocytosis, UCP2 and SIRT4 damp the metabolic signal that couples glucose to secretion, and granule proteins such as synaptotagmin-like and Rab11 effector components restrain vesicle trafficking. Inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors for catecholamines, dopamine, opioids, melatonin and ghrelin feed in through Gi/Go, while several microRNAs and transcriptional regulators lower secretory capacity over longer timescales.

Cells that signal at a distance must not only make a protein but release it on cue, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of regulated protein secretion. Much of the gene content describes pancreatic beta cell insulin release: glucose sensing through a glucokinase and GLUT2 step, closure of the KATP channel subunit SUR1, calcium entry, and exocytic machinery including syntaxin-4, Munc13, synaptotagmin-like and rabphilin proteins, all under transcription factors such as PDX1, NEUROD1, NKX6-1 and RFX6 that define the cell type. Parallel arms enhance secretion of glucagon, ghrelin, CRH and urocortin, cytokines such as IL1A and TGF-beta, and inflammatory mediators released by TLR- and P2RX7-stimulated myeloid cells. Cyclic AMP acting via protein kinase A and EPAC proteins, protein kinase C, and ER-to-Golgi trafficking components tune the response. Loss of this control underlies diabetes and defective immune mediator release.

Inflammation must be strong enough to clear infection or repair injury and then be shut off, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets its amplitude and duration. Loss of control at either end produces disease: uncontrolled amplification underlies sepsis, autoinflammatory fevers and chronic tissue damage, while excessive restraint leaves infection unchecked. Pattern-recognition receptors such as the Toll-like receptors, NOD2 and cytosolic DNA sensors feed through MYD88 and NF-kB subunits to cytokine output, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and caspase-1 mature IL-1 beta and IL-18 and drive gasdermin-dependent pyroptosis. Braking is equally represented: IL-10 and its receptor, the IL-1 receptor antagonist, decoy receptors, SOCS3, TNFAIP3 and phosphatases such as PTPN6 damp signalling, and numerous microRNAs tune transcript levels. Eicosanoid enzymes, chemokines, acute-phase proteins and nuclear receptors including PPARs link the response to lipid metabolism and leukocyte recruitment.

Inflammation has to be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this collection covers the brakes: the signals, receptors, enzymes and microRNAs that damp, terminate or restrain an inflammatory response once host defence or tissue repair no longer requires it. Loss of these controls underlies autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, chronic tissue damage and metabolic inflammation. Anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and IL-37 act through their receptors to suppress myeloid activation; decoy and antagonist molecules including IL-1RN, IL-1R2 and SIGIRR block IL-1 family signalling; deubiquitinases such as TNFAIP3, CYLD and OTULIN limit NF-kB output downstream of TNF and Toll-like receptors; phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPN2 and inhibitory receptors such as CD200R1 and SIRPA raise activation thresholds. Nuclear receptors, resolvin-type lipid sensing, regulatory T cell programmes driven by FOXP3, and inflammasome-restraining NLRs contribute further layers of resolution.

Inflammation must be actively amplified once a threat is detected, and this collection covers the processes that raise the intensity, speed and duration of the inflammatory response. It underlies effective defence against pathogens and tissue injury, and its overactivity drives fever, septic shock, autoinflammatory syndromes such as familial Mediterranean fever, and chronic conditions from atherosclerosis to arthritis. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like family sense microbial and endogenous ligands and relieve inhibition of NF- uB, while inflammasome components including NLRP3, NLRC4, AIM2 and the adaptor PYCARD activate caspase-1 to mature IL-1 u and IL-18 and to cleave gasdermin D for pyroptotic release. Downstream amplification runs through TNF, IL-6 and its receptor subunit IL6ST into STAT3 signalling, chemokines that recruit neutrophils and monocytes, prostaglandin synthesis via COX-2, alarmins such as S100A8/A9, and interferon- u-induced guanylate-binding proteins. Several microRNAs and NFKBIA provide counterbalancing restraint.

Tyrosine phosphorylation is the switch that receptor kinases use to convert an extracellular cue into an intracellular decision, and this pathway covers the inputs and brakes that set how much of it occurs. Its members are largely ligands and receptors that trigger tyrosine kinase activity combined with the machinery that limits it: growth factor and angiogenic cues such as VEGFA, FGF7/FGF10, NRG1 and angiopoietins acting through EGFR, ERBB4, FGFR3, KIT, CSF1R and FLT3; and cytokines including IL4, IL6, IL7, IL21, LIF, OSM and interferon-gamma signalling via shared receptor chains and JAK2. Restraint comes from SOCS proteins, the phosphatase PTPN2, the EGFR feedback inhibitor ERRFI1, and receptor sorting by endosomal components such as TSG101 and VPS25. The balance determines proliferation, angiogenesis, haematopoiesis and lymphocyte differentiation, and its loss of control is a recurring route to cancer and inflammatory disease.

Tyrosine phosphorylation is the switch that turns extracellular cues into intracellular signalling, and this pathway covers the ligands, receptors and kinases that increase it. Growth factors and their receptor tyrosine kinases are well represented colon stem cell factor with KIT, CSF1R, FLT3, FGF ligands with FGFR3, neuregulin with ERBB4, angiopoietins and VEGF family members driving vascular and haematopoietic responses. A second arm is cytokine-driven: interleukins such as IL4, IL6, IL21 and the IL10 receptor subunits, plus LIF, OSM and CNTF, signal through shared receptor chains and JAK2 to phosphorylate STAT proteins. Non-receptor kinases and adaptors including TNK2, NEDD9, ABI1 and BANK1 propagate or amplify the signal. Collectively this determines proliferation, differentiation, immune activation and angiogenesis, and its unchecked elevation through mutated receptor kinases is a common route to leukaemia and solid tumours.

Tyrosine phosphorylation is the switch that turns growth factor and cytokine receptors on, so damping it is how cells set the duration and amplitude of those signals rather than letting them run. This braking function — negative regulation of peptidyl-tyrosine phosphorylation — keeps receptor tyrosine kinase and JAK-STAT output transient, and its loss underlies unchecked proliferative signalling in cancer. Several distinct mechanisms converge here: the phosphatase PTPN2 removes phosphate from receptor and JAK substrates directly; SOCS4 and SOCS5 are inducible feedback adaptors that target activated receptors for degradation; ERRFI1 restrains EGFR catalytic activity; SFRP1 and SFRP2 sequester Wnt ligands upstream. A prominent endosomal contingent, including TSG101, VPS25, CHMP6 and sorting nexins, terminates signalling by sorting activated receptors into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal disposal, making receptor trafficking as much a part of this control as enzymatic dephosphorylation.

Circulating lipoproteins carry triglyceride and cholesterol between gut, liver and peripheral tissues, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast they are assembled, remodelled and cleared. Tuning that rate determines plasma lipid levels, so its dysregulation underlies hypertriglyceridaemia, dyslipidaemia and atherosclerotic risk. Several members act on lipolytic processing: ANGPTL8 restrains lipoprotein lipase to spare triglyceride for storage, endothelial lipase (LIPG) hydrolyses HDL phospholipid, and DGAT2 supplies triglyceride for particle loading, while APOD associates with HDL as a lipid-binding carrier and leptin signals whole-body energy status back onto hepatic lipid handling. Others link lipoprotein flux to autophagic and vesicular machinery — the ULK1–ATG13–RB1CC1 initiation complex with PIK3C3, plus Rab regulatory subunits — reflecting lipophagy and secretory control of lipid droplet mobilisation, with integrin αvβ3 contributing receptor-mediated cell-surface interactions.

Phagocytes must decide what to eat, how fast, and when to stop, and this set of modulators of phagocytosis sets that threshold. It governs clearance of microbes by neutrophils and macrophages and the silent removal of apoptotic cells and debris, so its tuning determines whether infection is contained, whether dying cells provoke autoimmunity, and whether microglia prune synapses or leave plaque material uncleared. Opsonins mark targets — complement components, collectin and ficolin lectins with their MASP proteases, pentraxins, surfactant protein D — while Fc and scavenger receptors, TREM2, MERTK and CLEC7A read them out through SYK, BTK, PLCG2 and Rac-directed cytoskeletal machinery. Countervailing signals impose restraint: CD47 engaging SIRPA marks a cell as self, FCGR2B and the phosphatases CSK, PTPRJ and PTPRC damp activating signals, and cytokines such as IFNG or TGFB1 shift capacity up or down. Failures here appear in Alzheimer risk, lysosomal and granule disorders, and defective bacterial killing.

Phagocytes must be restrained as well as armed, and this collection covers the braking mechanisms that stop, slow or limit engulfment of targets. Its best-understood arm is self-recognition: CD47 displayed on healthy cells engages the myeloid receptor SIRPA, which recruits phosphatase signalling and blocks cytoskeletal cup formation, so that erythrocytes, platelets and other host cells are spared. Tumours exploit the same axis to evade macrophages, which is why blocking it is an immunotherapeutic strategy. Additional inhibitory receptors, including CD300A and CD300LF and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, damp activating signals from opsonised particles, while Csk-mediated suppression of Src-family kinases and actin-associated regulators such as calponin-2 act inside the cell. Cytokine and damage-signal inputs such as TGFB1 and HMGB1 set the overall threshold, tuning clearance of apoptotic cells and microbes so that inflammation and autoimmunity are avoided.

Phagocytes engulf microbes, dying cells and debris, and this collection captures the signals that raise the rate and extent of that engulfment. It matters for bacterial clearance, for silent removal of apoptotic cells that prevents autoimmune inflammation, and for microglial clearance of amyloid and damaged synapses in the brain. Opsonisation is the dominant theme: complement components and their activating lectins and proteases, along with collectins, ficolins and pentraxins, coat targets, while Fc gamma receptors and their signalling chain relay engagement inward through spleen-family kinases, BTK and PLCG2 to actin remodelling via Rac-activating adaptors. Bridging receptors such as MERTK with its ligand GAS6, CD36, TREM2 and the scavenger transporter ABCA7 recognise exposed phosphatidylserine on dying cells. Countering these, CD47 read by SIRPA delivers a "don't eat me" restraint that tumours exploit, making this axis a target for antibody-based cancer therapy.

Generating the right number of neurons and glia at the right time requires that proliferation, fate choice, differentiation and process outgrowth all be held under control, and this pathway covers the modulators that set the pace and extent of neurogenesis. It underlies cortical layering and brain size during development and the continued production of neurons in the adult hippocampus; when it is perturbed the results are microcephaly, cortical malformation, intellectual disability and autism. Notch signalling through DLL ligands and HES/HEY repressors keeps progenitors undifferentiated while proneural factors such as ASCL1, ATOH1 and NEUROG-type bHLH proteins and the patterning factors PAX6, FOXG1, OLIG2 and GLI3 drive commitment. Wnt, BMP, SHH, neurotrophin and cytokine inputs, guidance receptors of the Robo, Plexin, Eph and Reelin systems, chromatin regulators including EZH2, HDAC1/2 and REST, and a set of microRNAs tune these decisions, linking migration, polarity and growth to progenitor output.

Grouped here are the activators of neurogenesis factors and signals that increase the production, differentiation and maturation of neurons and glia from neural progenitors, both in the developing nervous system and in adult neurogenic niches. Their output determines cortical size and layering, the balance between progenitor self-renewal and differentiation, and the capacity for circuit repair; loss of individual members produces microcephaly, intellectual disability and epilepsy. Morphogen and growth factor inputs f Shh acting through Smo and Gli3, Wnt ligands feeding -catenin, BMP and TGF-, and neurotrophins signalling via NTRK2 and NTRK3 f converge on transcriptional programmes run by PAX6, ASCL1, FOXG1, SOX11 and the oligodendroglial factor OLIG2, with Notch and HES1 restraining premature commitment. Guidance and adhesion molecules such as Slits, Robos, semaphorins, ephrins, reelin and L1CAM direct migration and neurite outgrowth, while cytokines including IL6, LIF and CXCL12 couple inflammation and niche signalling to neuron generation.

Neurons acquire their single long output process through axonogenesis, and this collection covers the influences that promote or restrain it — setting how many axons form, how fast they extend, and how far they go. The outcome is the wiring of the nervous system: without proper control, tracts fail to cross the midline or reach their targets, and regeneration after injury stalls. Guidance ligand–receptor pairs dominate, including netrin acting through DCC, slits through ROBO receptors, semaphorins through plexins and neuropilin, and ephrins through Eph kinases, alongside growth factors such as BDNF and NGF signalling via TRKB and TRKC. These converge on Rho-family regulators, PAK and LIM kinases, GSK3B and CDK5, and on microtubule and neurofilament proteins including MAPT, MAP1B and MAP2. Inhibitory cues such as myelin-associated glycoprotein and the NOGO receptor limit outgrowth in the mature CNS.

Wiring the nervous system requires not only growing axons but restraining them: negative regulation of axonogenesis suppresses the initiation, extension and branching of axons so that only appropriate neurons project, only one axon forms per neuron, and growth stops where it should. Repulsive guidance dominates the mechanism — semaphorins acting through neuropilin and plexin co-receptors, slits, ephrins and Eph receptors, and the netrin receptor DCC together with the antagonist DRAXIN — converging on Rho-family GTPase regulators and cytoskeletal effectors to collapse growth cones. Myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG and RTN4 (Nogo) signalling through RTN4R impose the block on regrowth that limits recovery after spinal cord and brain injury. Intracellular brakes including PTEN, CDK5 and the ULK kinases restrict neurite outgrowth and polarity, while disruption of these controls contributes to aberrant connectivity and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Neurons acquire their shape by extending a single long axon, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that promote that outgrowth. It underlies wiring of the nervous system during development and regrowth after injury, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, malformations of cortical development and failed axon regeneration. Neurotrophins acting through TrkB and TrkC receptors, netrin, Slit-Robo, semaphorin-plexin and Wnt cues converge on Rho-family GTPase regulators such as TIAM1 and PAK1 and on the MAP kinase cascade through BRAF and MEK1/2. These signals are executed on the growth cone cytoskeleton: microtubule-associated proteins including MAP1B, MAPT and MAP6, the LIS1-dynein machinery, and actin regulators such as LIMK1 and shootin. Adhesion molecules like L1CAM and DSCAM, together with transcription factors including SRF and POU4F2, set the competence to elongate.

Dendrites are the receptive surface of a neuron, and how far they grow, how much they branch and where they arborize sets how many synapses a cell can receive. Regulation of dendrite development covers the signals that tune this growth, and its disturbance produces the simplified or over-exuberant dendritic trees seen in intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism. Extracellular cues act through guidance and adhesion receptors such as DCC, EPHA4/EPHB2, PTPRD and the reelin receptors VLDLR and LRP8, converging on Rho- and Rap-family GTPase regulators, actin and microtubule effectors including DBN1, COBL, BAIAP2 and CAMSAP2, and kinases such as GSK3B, CDKL5, MARK1 and CAMK2B. Bone morphogenetic protein ligands and receptors, transcription factors of the CUX and NR2E1 type, ubiquitin ligases including NEDD4 and HECW2, and RNA-binding proteins such as STAU2 add transcriptional and local translational control, linking dendrite shape to activity and to cortical circuit assembly.

Dendrites must stop growing and branching as well as start, and this is the restraining side of dendrite morphogenesis: signals that dampen outgrowth, limit arbor expansion, and hold branching within the pattern a neuron needs to sample its inputs correctly. Without such braking, arbors overgrow and receptive fields and circuit wiring are distorted, a defect seen in several neurodevelopmental disorders. The genes point to calcium as the main brake: a store- and stretch-sensitive cation channel of the TRPC family raises local calcium, the calcineurin catalytic subunit PPP3CA dephosphorylates the transcription factor NFATC4 to alter growth-related gene expression, and Rap-directed nucleotide exchange plus a 14-3-3 adaptor and the CRMP-family protein DPYSL5 feed into cytoskeletal and microtubule control at the growing tip. A homeobox factor contributes transcriptional limits on neuronal differentiation.

Immune responses must be tuned as well as triggered, and this broad regulatory programme sets how strongly, how long and in which direction an organism reacts to an immunogenic stimulus. It spans antigen presentation by classical and non-classical MHC molecules and CD1, antigen receptor signalling through T and B cell receptor chains, ZAP70, LCK, SYK and BTK, innate sensing by Toll-like receptors, NOD proteins, inflammasome components and cytosolic nucleic acid sensors feeding NF-kB and interferon induction, and complement activation and its regulators. Balancing this are inhibitory checkpoints such as CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3, TIGIT and killer-cell receptors, phosphatases like PTPN6 and PTPN22, ubiquitin editors including TNFAIP3 and CYLD, and suppressive cytokines. Loss of restraint yields autoimmunity and chronic inflammation; loss of activation yields immunodeficiency and tumour escape.

Immune responses must be restrained as well as launched, and negative regulation of the immune response covers the brakes that limit the magnitude and duration of reactions to antigen, infection and damaged tissue. Without them, cells that should quiet down instead drive autoimmunity, chronic inflammation or cytokine-driven tissue injury; with them overused, tumours and chronic infections escape clearance. The genes here span the main braking strategies: inhibitory surface receptors on T and NK cells such as PDCD1, CTLA-family ligands CD274 and CD80, LAG3, TIGIT, HAVCR2 and BTLA; phosphatases and adaptors including PTPN6, PTPN2 and INPP5D that dampen antigen-receptor and Fc-receptor signalling; complement regulators such as CD46, CD55 and CD59 that protect host cells from lysis; suppressive cytokines IL10 and TGFB1 with FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cells; and ubiquitin-editing and RNA-binding restraints on innate sensing, notably TNFAIP3, ZC3H12A, USP18, ADAR and TREX1.

This is the collection of processes that switch immunity on and amplify it once a threat is detected, spanning innate sensing, complement activation, antigen presentation and lymphocyte activation. Pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like and cytosolic nucleic acid sensing families feed through adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1, MAVS and STING1 into NF-kB and interferon regulatory factor programmes, producing inflammatory cytokines and type I and III interferons; inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 mature IL-1 family cytokines. In parallel, MHC class I and II molecules and CD1 lipid-presenting proteins display antigen to T cells, while receptor-proximal kinases and adaptors (LCK, ZAP70, SYK, BTK, LAT, LCP2, CARD11) and costimulatory pairs such as CD28-CD80/CD86 and CD40 drive clonal expansion and antibody responses. The complement cascade and Fc receptors link these arms to pathogen clearance. Excessive or misdirected activation underlies autoimmunity and autoinflammatory disease, while deficiency causes immunodeficiency and impaired tumour surveillance.

Enzymes are rarely left to run at a constant rate; this collection covers the regulation of catalytic activity, the modulation of enzyme output by activators, inhibitors, cofactors and accessory subunits. It is how cells convert signals into changes in metabolic flux, cytoskeletal remodelling, proliferation and cell death, and its failure underlies cancers driven by unrestrained kinases and by loss of the brakes that normally restrain them. Represented mechanisms include cyclins and CDK inhibitors such as CDKN1A and CDKN1B setting cell cycle kinase activity, regulatory subunits of protein kinase A holding the catalytic core inactive until cAMP rises, GTPase-activating proteins and exchange factors that switch Ras-, Rho- and Rab-family GTPases between states, RGS proteins accelerating G protein deactivation, serpins and TIMPs restraining proteases, and phosphatases, scaffolds and chaperones that position enzymes with their substrates.

Host cells do not merely serve as passive substrates for viruses; they actively raise or lower the rate of viral entry, replication, assembly and release, and this regulation of the viral process determines whether an infection is aborted or productive. Much of the set comprises intrinsic restriction factors and interferon-stimulated effectors: APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases that hypermutate retroviral cDNA, tetherin (BST2) retaining budded virions at the membrane, MX1, OAS-RNase L and PKR shutting down translation, IFITM proteins blocking fusion, and a large family of TRIM ubiquitin ligases including TRIM5 and TRIM25. Countering these are host factors viruses depend on, such as the proteases FURIN and TMPRSS2 for glycoprotein cleavage, entry receptors, cyclophilins, karyopherins, and ESCRT components used for budding. Sensors like IFIH1, IFI16 and MAVS feed into interferon induction, linking innate detection to the balance between restriction and permissiveness that shapes viral tropism and pathogenesis.

Behaviour is modulated rather than fixed, and this pathway collects the signals that set its frequency and intensity — how much an animal eats, sleeps, explores, or reacts to threat. Much of the gene content is neuroendocrine appetite control: leptin receptor, ghrelin and its receptor, AGRP, POMC-derived melanocortins acting through MC3R and MC4R, NPY and CARTPT, whose loss in humans causes hyperphagia and obesity. A second arm is neuromodulatory signalling — dopamine D2, serotonin 1A/1B/1D and kappa-opioid receptors, adenosine receptors, orexin and neuropeptide S receptors — which tunes reward, anxiety, arousal and locomotor drive. Clock components including PER3, NPAS2, NR1D1 and melatonin receptor signalling impose circadian timing on these outputs, while synaptic scaffolds such as DLG4 and NLGN1 and the GRIA1 glutamate receptor subunit provide the plasticity through which experience changes behaviour. Disruption maps onto feeding disorders, sleep disturbance, addiction and autism-related social deficits.

regulation of insulin secretion controls how much insulin pancreatic beta cells release, and thereby sets systemic glucose tolerance; its failure is the proximate cause of type 2 diabetes and of monogenic forms of hyper- and hypoglycaemia. The genes trace the canonical stimulus-secretion coupling chain: glucose entry and phosphorylation by glucokinase, glycolytic and mitochondrial metabolism, closure of the KATP channel formed by ABCC8 and KCNJ11, voltage-gated potassium and TRP channel shaping of electrical activity, calcium influx, and SNARE-dependent granule fusion via SNAP25, STX1A and synaptotagmins. Layered on top are incretin and adrenergic receptors acting through cyclic AMP, adenylate cyclases, PKA and RAPGEF4, cytokine and adipokine inputs, circadian clock components, and the beta cell transcription factors PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1 and RFX6 that maintain secretory identity and granule zinc handling.

Pancreatic beta cells release insulin in proportion to blood glucose, and the tuning of that release sets whole-body glucose tolerance; its failure is the proximate defect in type 2 diabetes and, in monogenic forms, in neonatal diabetes and congenital hyperinsulinism. Glucose entry through GLUT2 and phosphorylation by glucokinase drive mitochondrial metabolism, which closes the KATP channel formed by KCNJ11 and the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8, depolarizes the cell and triggers calcium-dependent fusion of granules via SNAP25, syntaxin and synaptotagmin machinery. Layered on this core are incretin and adrenergic inputs acting through cyclic AMP, protein kinase A and Epac proteins, somatostatin and dopamine receptors that brake secretion, leptin, cytokine and inflammatory signals, circadian components, and transcription factors such as PDX1, NKX6-1, NEUROD1 and HNF4A that maintain the secretory identity of the beta cell.

After a T cell recognises antigen, it must undergo clonal expansion to generate enough effector cells to clear an infection, and this proliferative burst is what turns a rare precursor into a functional response. The programme is controlled as much by brakes as by accelerators: interleukin-2 acting through its high-affinity receptor and STAT5A/STAT5B drives cycling, calcineurin and Src-family kinase signalling downstream of the T cell receptor set the activation threshold, and IL-12/IL-23 family cytokines shape the accompanying differentiation. Opposing it are inhibitory ligands such as PD-L1 and PD-L2, tryptophan catabolism by IDO1, arginine depletion by ARG1, galectin-9, and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell suppression, alongside apoptotic clearance through FADD and caspase-3. Too little expansion leaves immunodeficiency; unchecked expansion underlies autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while tumours exploit the inhibitory arms to escape immune attack.

Cells and whole organisms must hold the concentrations of simple ions — calcium, sodium, potassium, protons, chloride, iron, copper, zinc, magnesium and manganese — within narrow limits, and monoatomic ion homeostasis is the collective machinery that does so. It sets membrane potential and excitability, drives secretion and absorption in kidney, gut and stomach, acidifies lysosomes, supplies metal cofactors to enzymes, and keeps free metal low enough to avoid oxidative damage. Pumps and exchangers such as the Na+/K+-ATPases, SERCA and plasma membrane calcium ATPases, sodium-proton and sodium-calcium exchangers, and the vacuolar proton ATPase establish gradients; release channels, store-operated entry via STIM proteins, and the mitochondrial calcium uniporter shape calcium signals; ferritin, metallothioneins, transferrin receptor, hepcidin and dedicated zinc and copper transporters buffer and distribute metals. Failure produces cardiac arrhythmia, renal salt-wasting and stone disease, deafness, iron overload or anaemia, copper toxicosis and neurodegeneration.

Sleep is the behavioural state that occupies one phase of the circadian sleep/wake cycle, and the genes here govern how it is initiated, sustained and timed. It matters because sleep supports memory consolidation, metabolic and immune recovery, and growth hormone release; its disruption produces insomnia, restless legs, narcolepsy-like fragmentation and the metabolic and cognitive costs of sleep loss. Adenosine signalling provides the homeostatic sleep drive, with adenosine deaminase setting nucleoside levels and A1 and A2A receptors mediating sedation, the latter the target of caffeine. Prostaglandin D synthase generates a sleep-promoting lipid mediator, melatonin receptor signalling and a period gene tie sleep timing to the clock, and GABA-A, cholinergic and dopaminergic receptors plus potassium channels shape arousal-state switching. Neuropeptides including CRH, ghrelin, growth hormone-releasing hormone and its receptor, CART and neuromedin U couple sleep to endocrine and feeding control.

Synapses are not fixed structures: their size, number, receptor content and strength are continuously adjusted, and this regulation of synapse structure or activity is what allows circuits to be wired during development and remodelled by experience. It underlies learning and memory, and its disruption is a recurring theme in autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia and neurodegeneration. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs such as neurexins with neuroligins and LRRTMs, together with SLITRKs, PTPRD/PTPRS, cadherins and cerebellins, specify and stabilise contacts, while secreted cues including reelin, netrins, Slits, semaphorins, ephrins, Wnts and BDNF acting through Trk receptors instruct where and whether synapses form. Inside the spine, scaffolds such as SHANK3 and HOMER1 organise receptors, and Rho-family GTPases with their regulators, cofilin and WAVE-complex components reshape the actin cytoskeleton. Palmitoylation, ubiquitin ligases, local translation control and calcium-dependent kinases tune the outcome, including at the neuromuscular junction via agrin, LRP4 and MuSK.

Synapses must be turned down as well as up, and this collection covers the processes that stop or dampen communication from a neuron to its target cell. Such braking sets the dynamic range of circuits, terminates transmitter action, and protects against runaway excitation; its loss contributes to epilepsy, autism spectrum conditions and fragile X syndrome. Inhibitory tone comes partly from GABA-A receptor subunits and the metabotropic GABA-B receptor, partly from presynaptic autoreceptors and Gi-coupled receptors for adenosine, dopamine, neuropeptide Y and endocannabinoids, whose signals lower cyclic AMP and reduce release probability. Acetylcholinesterase and its collagenous anchor clear transmitter at the neuromuscular junction, while serotonin reuptake ends serotonergic signalling. Other members act intracellularly: ARC and PLK2 drive homeostatic removal of AMPA receptors, and scaffold and RNA-binding proteins such as SHANK3 and FMR1 restrain synaptic strength during plasticity.

Neurons strengthen and sustain their output to partner cells, and this collection of enhancing influences on synaptic transmission covers the machinery that raises the probability, frequency or amplitude of that signalling. It underlies learning-related plasticity such as long-term potentiation, and its disturbance features in intellectual disability, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Presynaptic release is boosted through the SNARE apparatus and its regulators, including SNAP25, VAMP2, syntaxins, STXBP1 and synaptotagmins, together with voltage-gated calcium entry. Postsynaptically, NMDA and AMPA receptor subunits, TARP auxiliary subunits, PSD-95 and Shank scaffolds, and calcium-dependent kinases and phosphatases such as CaMKII and calcineurin convert calcium influx into lasting potentiation. Trans-synaptic adhesion via neurexin, neuroligins, LRRTMs and calsyntenins aligns and stabilises the contact, while neuromodulators, neuropeptides, glial transporters and inflammatory mediators tune the gain from outside the synapse.

Synapse organization covers the building, shaping, and dismantling of the junctions through which neurons contact other neurons, muscle fibers, or secretory cells, and it determines how many synapses form, where, and of what type. This is the cellular basis of circuit wiring, learning-related structural plasticity, and neuromuscular transmission; its disruption underlies autism, intellectual disability, schizophrenia risk, myasthenic syndromes, and synapse loss in neurodegeneration. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs such as neurexins with neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and cerebellins specify and align pre- and postsynaptic membranes, while agrin signalling through LRP4, MuSK and rapsyn clusters acetylcholine receptors at the motor endplate. Scaffolds including PSD-95, SHANKs, gephyrin, bassoon and piccolo organize receptor and release-site architecture, Rho-family GTPases with actin regulators remodel spines, and complement components with microglial receptors prune unwanted connections.

Steroid output — cholesterol and the hormones made from it — is held under tight control, and this regulatory layer sets how fast those synthetic routes run. It matters because cholesterol levels determine membrane composition and atherosclerotic risk, while gonadal and adrenal steroid production governs reproduction, stress responses and electrolyte balance. One arm is the sterol-sensing SREBP system: SCAP and the INSIG proteins retain the precursor in the ER until sterols fall, whereupon site-1 and site-2 proteases release the transcription factor to induce lipogenic and cholesterogenic genes, with ABCG1 and ABCA2 handling efflux and microRNAs such as the miR-33 family tuning the same circuit. Another arm is trophic hormone signalling — ACTH and gonadotropin receptors acting through PKA and StAR-mediated cholesterol delivery to mitochondria, with NR5A1 and NR0B1 specifying steroidogenic tissue identity. Nuclear receptors and bile acid feedback close the loop; failure produces dyslipidaemia or adrenal insufficiency.

Control over how much acetyl-CoA and related acyl-CoAs a cell makes sets the entry point into the TCA cycle and determines whether carbohydrate or fat is burned. The regulation centres on phosphorylation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex: a family of kinases (PDK1-4) switches the complex off, while the phosphatase PDP1 with its regulatory subunit PDPR switches it back on, so that pyruvate oxidation is suppressed during fasting and restored after feeding. A related kinase, BCKDK, applies the same logic to branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and thus to acyl-CoAs derived from leucine, isoleucine and valine. Cofactor supply matters too, since TPK1 generates the thiamine pyrophosphate these dehydrogenases require, and SIRT4 adds mitochondrial NAD-dependent regulation. Loss of this control produces lactic acidosis and neurological disease, and inappropriate PDK activity contributes to the glycolytic shift of tumours and to insulin resistance.

Blood must clot at a wound and nowhere else, and the balance is set by processes that modulate the rate and extent of coagulation. Procoagulant drive comes from tissue factor and the contact and intrinsic factors (F12, F11, prekallikrein, kininogen) converging on thrombin, which cleaves fibrinogen into fibrin and signals through its own protease-activated receptors on platelets and endothelium. Opposing arms restrain it: antithrombin and other serpins inhibit active proteases, thrombomodulin with its endothelial receptor switches thrombin to activating protein C and its cofactor protein S, tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks initiation, and plasminogen with its activators dissolves formed clot. Endothelial nitric oxide and prostanoid–thromboxane signalling tune platelet reactivity. Loss of control produces thrombosis, bleeding disorders, or consumptive coagulopathy; vitamin K epoxide reductase recycling makes this circuitry the target of oral anticoagulants.

Blood must clot at a wound and nowhere else, and the restraining arm of haemostasis — negative regulation of coagulation — is what keeps thrombin generation local, self-limiting and reversible. Loss of this braking causes thrombosis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and pregnancy loss, while excess bleeds. Several mechanisms act together: tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks the initiating protease complex; thrombomodulin and the endothelial protein C receptor convert thrombin into an activator of protein C, which with protein S degrades the cofactors driving its own production; serpins and heparin-binding inhibitors neutralise contact-phase and downstream proteases. In parallel, plasminogen and its activators dissolve fibrin already formed, with plasminogen activator inhibitors and a carboxypeptidase setting the pace of lysis. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase and platelet-surface proteins such as CD9 and GP1BA link these controls to suppression of platelet activation.

Blood loss is stopped by converting a soluble plasma cascade into an insoluble fibrin plug, and this grouping covers the influences that push that conversion faster and further. Tissue factor initiates the extrinsic route with factor VII, factor XII seeds contact activation, and prothrombin yields thrombin, which cleaves fibrinogen and also signals to platelets and endothelium through protease-activated receptors; thromboxane receptor engagement amplifies platelet recruitment. A phospholipid scramblase exposes phosphatidylserine so that coagulation complexes can assemble on the membrane surface, while VKORC1 regenerates the vitamin K required for gamma-carboxylation of the procoagulant factors and is the target of warfarin. Clot persistence is favoured by plasminogen activator inhibitor and alpha-2-antiplasmin restraining fibrinolysis, and by adhesive matrix proteins such as thrombospondin and vitronectin. Excessive drive here underlies thrombosis, disseminated intravascular coagulation and thromboinflammatory vascular injury.

Proteins only work while they are folded, soluble and not yet degraded, and protein stabilization covers the activities that keep them that way. It matters because the stability of individual regulators sets their effective dose: tumour suppressors, kinases and transcription factors are switched on and off as much by how long they survive as by how much is made. The chaperone machinery dominates here, with HSP90 and its co-chaperones CDC37 and PTGES3, the small heat-shock protein CRYAB, the HSP70 nucleotide-exchange BAG family, the CCT/TRiC folding chamber and the prefoldin subunits that deliver nascent actin and tubulin to it. Opposing the ubiquitin route, deubiquitinases such as USP7 and USP9X rescue substrates from proteasomal destruction, while ligase-associated factors including STUB1, CBL and FBXW7 mark the balance point. Loss of this buffering produces aggregation, misfolding disease and unrestrained turnover of signalling proteins.

Host defence against Gram-negative bacteria covers the recognition of these organisms and the killing and containment that follows, at mucosal surfaces, in the urinary tract, on skin and within phagocytes. Its failure leaves epithelial barriers colonised and permits endotoxin-driven sepsis, while its components define neutrophil and monocyte antimicrobial capacity. Lipopolysaccharide is captured by LBP and signalled through TLR4, and bacterial peptidoglycan fragments through cytosolic NOD1, converging on NF-κB-dependent cytokine output including IL6, IL23A and the IL17 axis that recruits and licenses neutrophils. Effector arms are largely direct: alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, lysozyme, lactoferrin, BPI and neutrophil granule proteases such as elastase and cathepsin G permeabilise or starve bacteria, hepcidin and SLC11A1 withhold iron and other metals, and inflammasome adaptor PYCARD with gasdermin D drives pyroptotic lysis of infected cells. Autophagy regulators IRGM, OPTN and TFEB support intracellular clearance.

Host recognition and killing of Gram-positive bacteria such as staphylococci, streptococci and listeria depends on this arm of innate immunity, which operates at epithelial surfaces, in phagocytes and in the bloodstream. Its core output is a battery of secreted antimicrobials: alpha- and beta-defensins, lysozyme, cathelicidin, lactoferrin, hepcidin, RNase family peptides, phospholipase A2 and the regenerating-islet lectin REG3G, which permeabilise thick peptidoglycan cell walls or starve bacteria of iron. Sensing is largely through TLR2 with MYD88 and TIRAP, peptidoglycan recognition proteins, NOD1 with RIPK2, and CARD9, converging on inflammasome components PYCARD and GSDMD to release IL-1beta and IL-18, and on TNF, IL-6 and IL-17 for neutrophil recruitment. Acute-phase proteins, lectins and complement receptor signalling promote opsonisation and phagocytosis. Weakness here predisposes to skin, gut and invasive pyogenic infection, while excessive output drives inflammatory skin and bowel disease.

Progesterone acts through an intracellular nuclear receptor to reprogramme gene expression in the uterus, mammary gland, ovary and brain, making this pathway the basis of endometrial receptivity, pregnancy maintenance, mammary branching and the suppression of uterine contractility; its dysregulation underlies endometriosis, infertility and hormone-driven breast and endometrial cancer, and it is the target of progestins and antiprogestins. Ligand-bound PGR dimerises and binds progesterone response elements, where transcriptional output depends on the coactivators recruited -- NCOA1 and WBP2 favour activation while HDAC2 supports repression through chromatin deacetylation. The receptor's level and activity are themselves tightly controlled: ubiquitin ligases including NEDD4, UBE3A and UBR5 direct turnover and coregulation, ZDHHC7-mediated palmitoylation supports membrane-proximal receptor pools, and SRC kinase links ligand binding to rapid non-genomic signalling that converges with growth factor pathways.

Regulation of calcium-mediated signaling sets the gain on one of the most widely used intracellular messages: how strongly, how often, and for how long a cell responds when cytosolic calcium rises. Because calcium transients drive muscle contraction, immune activation, secretion, and activity-dependent gene expression in neurons, the regulators here determine whether those responses are appropriately scaled or become pathological, as in cardiac hypertrophy, excitotoxic neurodegeneration, and defective lymphocyte activation. Mechanistically the genes cover calcium sensors and buffers (calmodulins, CIB1, PCP4), release and clearance machinery (ITPR1, ATP2B4, sodium-calcium exchangers, P2X receptors), scaffolds that localise signalling to receptors and channels (AKAP5, HOMER2/3, FKBP1B), and the calcineurin holoenzyme with its inhibitor RCAN1, which converts sustained calcium into NFAT-dependent transcription. Antigen receptor components and the SYK/ZAP70 module tie the same logic to immune cell decisions.

Calcium is the cell's most widely used second messenger, and this collection of modulators sets how strongly and how long a calcium signal is allowed to run after a receptor fires. Tuning matters because the same ion drives muscle contraction, lymphocyte activation, synaptic plasticity and gene induction, and unrestrained calcium is cytotoxic. Calmodulin and the calcineurin catalytic and regulatory subunits form the core decoder that relays elevated calcium to transcription factor activation, with RCAN1 acting as a brake on calcineurin. Release and clearance are shaped by the ITPR1 channel, plasma membrane and sodium-coupled extrusion systems, and buffering or scaffolding proteins such as HOMER and AKAP family members. Immune receptor arms feeding in through SYK, ZAP70 and PLCG2 illustrate the link to antigen-receptor signalling, while neuronal components including APP, MAPT, HTT and LRRK2 tie calcium dysregulation to neurodegeneration.

Calcium spikes must be terminated as reliably as they are initiated, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that damp calcium-mediated signalling once a cell has responded. It sets the duration and amplitude of calcium transients in excitable and immune cells, and its loss leaves signals that run too long, driving pathological hypertrophy, arrhythmia and overactive lymphocyte responses. Several routes converge on the same aim: plasma membrane calcium pumps and sodium-calcium exchange remove cytosolic calcium, an inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase degrades the messenger that opens the inositol trisphosphate receptor, and Homer and calcineurin-inhibitory proteins such as RCAN1 restrain downstream calcium-dependent transcription. Calsarcin family myozenins act at the sarcomeric Z-disc to hold calcineurin away from its targets in muscle, while CD22 and adaptor proteins dampen calcium flux after antigen receptor engagement in B and T cells.

positive regulation of calcium-mediated signaling covers the mechanisms that amplify intracellular calcium as a second messenger, raising the frequency or amplitude of calcium transients so that cells convert an external stimulus into contraction, secretion, gene transcription or activation. It matters because calcium signalling sets the threshold for lymphocyte activation, neuronal plasticity and vascular tone, and its dysregulation contributes to autoimmunity, immunodeficiency and neurodegeneration. The genes span the layers that boost the signal: receptors and channels that admit or release calcium, including purinergic P2X channels, metabotropic glutamate and serotonin receptors, and endothelin and neuromedin receptors; proximal immune receptor kinases and adaptors such as ZAP70, SYK and PLCG2 acting downstream of the T cell receptor and pattern-recognition receptors; scaffolds that position kinases near calcium sources; and the calcineurin holoenzyme subunits that decode sustained calcium into NFAT-driven transcription. Amyloid precursor protein, prion protein, huntingtin and TREM2 tie the same machinery to neuronal and microglial calcium handling.

Calcium is the cell's most widely used second messenger, and this collection describes the machinery that raises or prolongs calcium signalling rather than terminating it. Amplifying these signals drives lymphocyte activation, neurotransmitter-evoked plasticity, smooth muscle tone and hormone secretion; failure or excess contributes to immunodeficiency, neurodegeneration and vascular disease. Receptors that initiate the rise include metabotropic glutamate and serotonin receptors, ATP-gated P2X channels, endothelin and neuromedin U receptors, and growth factor receptors such as PDGFRA/B. In immune cells the antigen receptor chain CD3E with the kinases ZAP70 and SYK and phospholipase PLCG2 couples engagement to sustained calcium flux. Downstream, the calcineurin phosphatase catalytic and regulatory subunits decode the signal for transcription factor activation, while scaffolds of the AKAP family and calcium-binding proteins such as CIB1 and PCP4 tune amplitude and localisation. Amyloid precursor protein, prion protein, huntingtin and TREM2 link this amplification to neuronal and microglial calcium handling.

Lymphocytes commit to responding only when their clonally rearranged receptor engages antigen, and this is the signalling cascade that converts that binding event into activation, proliferation, differentiation or, when the signal is inappropriate, deletion and anergy. It defines adaptive immunity: its thresholds set the boundary between protective responses and autoimmunity, and its components are the targets of checkpoint blockade and lymphoma therapy. Ligated T cell receptor and B cell receptor complexes signal through ITAM-bearing chains such as CD3 subunits and CD79A/B, Src-family and Syk-family kinases including LCK, LYN, SYK and ZAP70, then adaptors LAT, BLNK and LCP2 that nucleate PLC-gamma, PI3K and Ras-MAPK outputs, with CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 driving NF-kB and calcineurin driving NFAT. Co-receptors and inhibitory modules -- CD28, CTLA4, PD-1 and its ligands, FCGR2B, and phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN22 and CD45 -- tune the strength and duration of the response.

Antigen recognition by T cells begins when peptide-MHC cross-links the T cell receptor, and this pathway covers everything from that binding event to the transcriptional response that commits a T cell to activate, tolerate, or die. It underlies adaptive cellular immunity and self-tolerance; too little signal leaves immunodeficiency, too much or misdirected signal produces autoimmunity, and its molecules are the targets of checkpoint blockade. Clonotypic receptor chains pair with the invariant CD3 subunits and zeta chain, whose ITAMs are phosphorylated by LCK and read by ZAP70, which builds a LAT-SLP76 scaffold feeding phospholipase C-gamma, calcium flux, RAS-ERK, and CARD11-BCL10-MALT1-driven NF-kB. Coreceptors CD4 and CD8 focus the kinase, CD28 and ICOS ligands costimulate, and CTLA4, PD-1, LAG3, phosphatases such as PTPN22 and CBL-family ubiquitin ligases impose thresholds and terminate signalling. Thymic selection factors like THEMIS and the regulatory lineage factor FOXP3 tie the same machinery to repertoire and tolerance.

When antigen cross-links surface immunoglobulin on a B cell, the receptor complex converts that binding event into decisions about proliferation, survival, anergy or antibody production, and this is the pathway that carries the message. It sets the threshold for humoral immunity: too little signal and B cells fail to mature or respond, too much and autoreactive clones escape tolerance, a route to autoimmunity and to lymphomas and leukaemias that depend on tonic receptor signalling. The immunoglobulin heavy and light chains pair with the CD79A/CD79B signalling module, whose phosphorylation by LYN and related Src kinases recruits SYK and BTK onto the BLNK scaffold, driving PLCG2, protein kinase C beta, calcium-dependent NFAT activation and NF-kB. Coreceptors tune the output in opposite directions, CD19 and CD81 amplifying it while CD22, FCGR2B and the phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPN22 restrain it.

Lymphocytes must scale their response to antigen, and this regulatory layer sets how strongly and how long signalling from the B cell or T cell antigen receptor proceeds once the receptor is cross-linked. Tuning it decides the difference between productive immunity, anergy and autoimmunity: loss of restraint produces lymphoproliferation and self-reactivity, while excessive damping leaves cells unresponsive to infection or tumour antigen. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1 with its ligands, CD22 and FCGR2B raise the threshold for activation, and phosphatases including PTPN6, PTPN22 and PTPRC together with the kinase CSK reverse or prevent the tyrosine phosphorylation laid down by LCK, FYN and LYN. Positive components feed the same circuit — CD28 costimulation, the CARD11–BCL10–MALT1 complex driving NF-κB, and CBL/CBLB ubiquitin ligases that terminate it. Diacylglycerol kinase and several microRNAs add metabolic and post-transcriptional control, and these checkpoint molecules are the targets of cancer immunotherapy.

When antigen cross-links the B cell receptor, the strength and duration of the resulting signal decide whether the cell proliferates, is tolerized, or dies, and this regulatory layer sets that threshold. Tuning it correctly is what separates protective antibody responses from autoimmunity: loss of restraint permits autoreactive clones to survive, and a variant of the phosphatase PTPN22 is among the most reproducible genetic risks for autoimmune disease. Positive input comes from coreceptor and adaptor components such as CD19 and CD81 and the kinase LYN, which also delivers inhibitory signals through immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibition motifs on CD22, CD72 and FCGR2B that recruit the phosphatases PTPN6 and SHP-family activity. Transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulators, including FOXP1 and several microRNAs, shift the set point, while germinal-centre-associated molecules adapt it during affinity maturation and plasma cell differentiation.

When a T cell engages antigen through its receptor, the strength and duration of the resulting signal decide between activation, tolerance and exhaustion, and regulation of T cell receptor signaling is the tuning layer that makes that decision. It sets the threshold for self versus foreign, and its failure produces autoimmunity when restraint is lost or unresponsive tumour-infiltrating cells when restraint dominates. Positive input comes from the CD28 costimulatory axis and proximal kinases LCK and FYN; brakes include CTLA4 and PD-1 with their ligands CD80, CD86 and CD274, the inhibitory phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN22 and PTPN2, CSK, and the E3 ligases CBL and CBLB that degrade receptor components. Downstream, the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 complex routes signals to NF-kB while CYLD and diacylglycerol kinase zeta damp it. These molecules are the targets of checkpoint blockade and the loci of inherited immune dysregulation.

Lymphocytes only respond when antigen receptor engagement is amplified above a threshold, and this is the set of activities that raise the strength, duration or likelihood of signalling downstream of a cross-linked B or T cell receptor. Such positive regulation determines whether a naive cell proliferates and differentiates or remains quiescent, and it underlies the costimulatory requirement that keeps responses antigen-specific; too little produces immunodeficiency, too much predisposes to autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation. Mechanistically it spans costimulatory surface pairs such as CD28 with CD80 and CD86, proximal kinases and phosphatases including LCK and CD45, and the CARD11–BCL10 scaffold that couples receptor engagement to NF-κB activation through the IKK complex. Calcium- and potassium-flux components, protein kinase C and D family members, and adaptors that stabilise receptor microclusters tune the response, placing this biology at the interface of immune activation and tolerance.

Lymphocytes must damp signalling from their antigen receptors as well as start it, and negative regulation of antigen receptor-mediated signaling is what sets the threshold for activation, terminates responses once antigen is cleared, and enforces tolerance to self. Losing it produces autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; exaggerating it produces the exhausted, unresponsive T cells that tumours exploit. The brakes act at several levels: inhibitory surface receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1 and CD22 and their ligands CD80, CD86 and PDCD1LG2 recruit phosphatases including PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN22 to dephosphorylate receptor-proximal substrates; CSK holds Src-family kinases such as LYN and FYN in a repressed state; and the ubiquitin ligases CBL and CBLB drive degradation of activated signalling components. Diacylglycerol kinase and dual-specificity phosphatases further curtail second messengers and MAPK output. These molecules are the basis of immune checkpoint blockade.

Antigen binding to the B cell receptor must be damped as well as transmitted, and this braking arm sets the threshold at which a B cell responds, limiting reactions to self antigen and terminating responses once antibody has been made. Inhibitory surface receptors carrying ITIM motifs — CD22, CD72, CD300A and the low-affinity IgG receptor FcGR2B — are phosphorylated by the Src-family kinase LYN and then recruit the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 (PTPN6), which dephosphorylates receptor-proximal kinases and adaptors and blunts calcium flux; FcGR2B engagement by immune complexes provides feedback from secreted antibody. Additional restraint comes from the adaptor LPXN, the catalytically inactive phospholipase-like PLCL2, the corepressor component GPS2 and microRNA-mediated control. Loss of this restraint lowers the activation threshold and favours autoantibody production and autoimmunity, placing the pathway at the heart of peripheral B cell tolerance.

T cells that respond to antigen must also be told when to stop, and negative regulation of T cell receptor signaling is the set of brakes that sets activation thresholds, enforces peripheral tolerance, and ends responses once antigen is cleared. Losing these brakes drives autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; keeping them engaged inside tumours is how cancers escape immunity, which is why several members are the targets of checkpoint blockade. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CTLA-4, PD-1 and LAG-3 and their ligands, including CD80/CD86 and PD-L1/PD-L2, recruit phosphatases: SHP-1, SHP-2, PTPN22 and PTPN2 strip activating phosphorylations, while CSK restrains Lck by phosphorylating its inhibitory tyrosine.
