In parallel, the E3 ligases CBL and CBL-B ubiquitinate receptor-proximal components for degradation, diacylglycerol kinase zeta damps the DAG arm, and dual-specificity phosphatases limit downstream MAP kinase output.

When antigen cross-links the B cell receptor, the strength and duration of the resulting signal decides whether a B cell proliferates, survives, or is silenced; this pathway covers the inputs that amplify that signal. Tuning it upward lowers the threshold for antigen responsiveness and supports survival of developing and activated B cells, while excessive amplification is a route to autoreactivity and lymphoid transformation. The contributing genes act at several levels: membrane and tetraspanin-associated proteins that organise receptor complexes and co-receptor coupling, an adaptor and an immune receptor-family protein that feed into proximal kinase and calcium signalling, a protein kinase C isoform acting downstream of receptor engagement, a zinc transporter influencing signalling metal availability, and transcriptional and microRNA regulators that set the expression of signalling components. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of antigen recognition, B cell development and humoral immune activation.

When a T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC, the strength of the resulting signal decides whether the cell proliferates, differentiates or is ignored, and this pathway comprises the inputs that amplify that signal. Costimulation through CD28 binding CD80 or CD86, together with adhesion and nectin-family ligands, lowers the activation threshold so that antigen recognition in the presence of a licensed antigen-presenting cell produces a full response; without it, engagement tends toward anergy rather than effector differentiation. Downstream, the kinase LCK initiates proximal phosphorylation, while CARD11 and BCL10 assemble a scaffold that routes the signal to NF-kB activation via the IKK complex. A calcium-activated potassium channel sustains the membrane potential needed for continued calcium influx. The same amplifying steps underlie autoimmune reactivity when unchecked, and are the substrate on which checkpoint-directed immunotherapy acts.

Whether a T cell responds to antigen, how strongly, and for how long is set by the machinery gathered here as regulation of T cell activation. It determines the balance between protective immunity and tolerance: too little and infection or tumours go unchecked, too much and autoimmunity, chronic inflammation or cytokine-driven pathology follow. Antigen is presented on MHC class I and class II molecules and read by the CD3/TCR complex, which signals through LCK, ZAP70, LAT, VAV1 and PRKCQ into the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 module and calcineurin. Costimulatory and coinhibitory receptors tune the outcome, with CD28 and ICOS amplifying and CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3, HAVCR2, TIGIT and BTLA dampening it. Phosphatases such as PTPN22 and PTPN6, ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH, SOCS proteins, and the FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell programme impose negative control, while cytokines including IL2, IL12, IL23 and TGFB1 bias differentiation toward particular helper lineages. Checkpoint blockade therapy targets this biology directly.

B cells must be switched on strongly enough to mount antibody responses but not so freely that they attack self, and this is the tuning machinery that sets that threshold. Positive input comes through the antigen receptor and its proximal kinases SYK, LYN and BTK with the CARD11 scaffold, reinforced by CD19, CD40, BAFF receptors and cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21 and IL-6 acting via STAT5 and STAT6. Restraint is imposed by inhibitory receptors and phosphatases including CD22, FCGR2B, PTPN6 and INPP5D, by ubiquitin-pathway brakes such as TNFAIP3 and CYLD, by RNA-destabilising factors, and by regulatory T cell products including IL-10 and TGFB1. Also represented are class switch recombination and mismatch-repair components that couple activation to genome editing of immunoglobulin loci. Loss of the negative arm produces autoantibodies and lymphoproliferation; loss of the positive arm gives immunodeficiency with poor antibody output.

regulation of cell activation governs how strongly and how long a cell responds after it meets an activating ligand, and in practice this is largely the control of immune cell activation u2014 lymphocyte, myeloid, mast cell and platelet responses that must be switched on to clear infection and switched off to avoid autoimmunity and chronic inflammation. The genes cover both directions of that balance: antigen receptor proximal kinases and adaptors such as LCK, ZAP70, SYK, BTK, LAT and VAV1; costimulatory receptor u2013ligand pairs including CD28, CD40/CD40LG, ICOS and the TNF superfamily; inhibitory checkpoints such as CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3, TIGIT and BTLA; phosphatases and ubiquitin ligases (PTPN22, PTPN6, INPP5D, CBLB, TNFAIP3) that raise the activation threshold; MHC class II and antigen presentation components; and cytokines with their JAK u2013STAT outputs that set lineage bias. Transcriptional and chromatin regulators, including FOXP3, TBX21, GATA3 and SWI/SNF subunits, fix the resulting activation state.

Immune cells sit quiescent until a ligand tells them to change shape, proliferate and secrete, and this collection covers the machinery that sets how readily and how strongly that switch is thrown. Tuning it determines whether an infection is cleared, whether tolerance holds, and whether autoimmunity, allergy or chronic inflammation follows. Antigen receptor proximal kinases such as LCK, SYK, ZAP70 and BTK with adaptors LAT and VAV1 drive activation, while phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN22 and INPP5D, the ubiquitin ligases CBLB and ITCH, and coinhibitory receptors CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3, HAVCR2 and TIGIT restrain it against costimulation through CD28, CD40 and ICOS. MHC class II presentation, cytokines and their receptors, and lineage transcription factors including FOXP3, TBX21, GATA3 and BCL6 set the context and outcome, extending the same logic to platelet and mast cell triggering.

Immune cells must be restrained as well as switched on, and this collection of brakes — negative regulation of cell activation — sets the threshold at which lymphocytes, myeloid cells and mast cells respond, then shuts them down once a response is no longer needed. Loss of these controls produces autoimmunity, allergy and chronic inflammation; their exploitation by tumours and by the placenta produces immune evasion and tolerance. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3, HAVCR2, TIGIT, BTLA and the LILRB and FCGR2B families recruit phosphatases including PTPN6, PTPN22 and INPP5D to dampen antigen-receptor signalling, while CBL and CBLB, ITCH, TNFAIP3 and the RC3H proteins degrade activating components and transcripts. Suppressive cytokines led by IL10 and TGFB1, tryptophan and arginine catabolism by IDO1 and the arginases, FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell programmes, SOCS-mediated feedback and proteasomal turnover complete the braking system.

positive regulation of cell activation covers the signals that push resting immune cells -- chiefly lymphocytes, but also myeloid cells and platelets -- out of quiescence into proliferation, cytokine secretion and effector function. It is what turns antigen encounter into a productive immune response, and its miscalibration underlies autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and the immune evasion exploited by tumours. The genes trace the full arc: MHC class I and II presentation to the T cell receptor, proximal kinases and adaptors such as LCK, ZAP70, SYK, BTK and the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 complex, costimulatory and checkpoint receptor pairs including CD28-CD80/CD86, ICOS, CD40-CD40LG and PD-L1, and a large cytokine and receptor component driving JAK-STAT outputs. Downstream, lineage transcription factors such as TBX21, GATA3, FOXP3 and RUNX3, together with SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, fix the activated state as a differentiation programme rather than a transient response.

Immune responses begin when a resting lymphocyte, myeloid cell or platelet is pushed into an activated state, and this collection covers the inputs that raise the rate and extent of that switch. It is what allows antigen encounter to be converted into clonal expansion, cytokine output and effector differentiation; too little leaves immunodeficiency and poor vaccine responses, too much drives autoimmunity and inflammatory disease. The components span antigen presentation by class I and class II MHC together with CD4, CD74 and the peptide-loading accessory chains, costimulatory ligand-receptor pairs such as CD28, CD40/CD40LG, ICOS and the TNF superfamily members, and proximal receptor signalling through LCK, ZAP70, SYK, BTK, VAV1, CARD11/BCL10/MALT1 and PI3K-AKT-mTOR. Cytokines and their receptors, chemokine-driven encounter of cells in lymphoid tissue, pattern-recognition receptors, and lineage transcription factors including TBX21, GATA3, FOXP3 and RUNX3 set the magnitude and flavour of the resulting response.

Restraining B cell activation is what keeps antibody responses proportionate and self-tolerant; when it fails, autoreactive B cells expand and drive autoimmune disease such as lupus, while excessive germinal centre activity favours lymphomagenesis. The negative regulators assembled here act at several levels. Inhibitory surface receptors including the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B and the ITIM-bearing CD300A recruit the phosphatase SHIP-1 (INPP5D), which hydrolyses PIP3 and blunts signalling downstream of the B cell receptor; the kinase LYN and the adaptors BANK1 and SAMSN1 dampen the same cascade. TNFAIP3 terminates NF- inkappaB signalling, RC3H1 degrades mRNAs encoding costimulatory molecules, and BCL6 and ID2 impose transcriptional brakes on differentiation. Extrinsic control comes from regulatory T cells through CTLA4, FOXP3 and IL10, with apoptotic and checkpoint components removing cells that are activated inappropriately.

Antigen encounter alone does not commit a B cell to proliferate and secrete antibody; a set of amplifying inputs must push it over the threshold, and this is the biology that raises the rate and extent of B cell activation. It underlies antibody responses to infection and vaccination, germinal centre formation and class switching, and when it runs unchecked it feeds autoantibody production and lymphoid malignancy. Receptor-proximal signalling through SYK, BTK, CARD11 and VAV3 is reinforced by co-stimulation via CD40, CD28 and BAFF receptor, by innate sensing through TLR4 and TLR9, and by cytokines such as IL-4, IL-21 and IL-6 acting through STAT5 and STAT6. Transcriptional controllers including PAX5-partner TCF3, SPI1, BCL6 and MEF2C set the response, while the shieldin components and mismatch repair factors here support the DNA double-strand break handling that immunoglobulin diversification requires.

White adipocytes are the body's long-term energy store, holding triglyceride in a single large lipid droplet and secreting hormones that report nutritional status to the brain, liver and muscle. The differentiation of precursors into these cells determines fat mass and insulin sensitivity, and its deficiency underlies lipodystrophy while its excess accompanies obesity. A transcriptional cascade drives the switch: PPARG acts as the master regulator with CEBPA in a mutually reinforcing loop, TLE3 and corepressors of the CtBP family steer commitment toward the white rather than brown program, and PRDM16 antagonizes that choice by favouring thermogenic identity. PDGFRA marks the mesenchymal progenitors that supply new adipocytes. Lipid handling and signalling genes such as FABP4, PNPLA3 and the fatty acid receptor FFAR4 mark the mature phenotype, while SIRT1 and the clock protein PER2 tie adipogenesis to nutrient and circadian cues.

Brown fat cell differentiation converts mesenchymal precursors into thermogenic adipocytes, the cell type that burns lipid to produce heat rather than store it. This programme sustains adaptive thermogenesis in cold-exposed newborns and adults, and its loss or inactivity contributes to obesity and insulin resistance, which is why recruiting brown and brown-like fat is pursued as a metabolic therapy. The commitment step is transcriptional: PRDM16, EBF2 and ZBTB7B act with PPARG and the C/EBP factors to specify the lineage, while PPARGC1A drives mitochondrial biogenesis and the uncoupling protein UCP1 dissipates the proton gradient as heat. Beta-adrenergic receptors relay sympathetic noradrenaline to switch the differentiated cell on, and BMP7 and secreted factors such as FNDC5 and METRNL promote browning. Mature markers including ADIPOQ, FABP4 and the glucose transporter SLC2A4 tie the cell into whole-body lipid and glucose handling.

This is the broad set of physiological functions performed by neural tissue: detecting stimuli, transmitting and integrating signals, and driving behaviour and homeostatic control. It spans the sensory modalities — a very large family of odorant receptors plus vomeronasal and taste receptors for smell and chemosensation, opsins with the phototransduction cascade of transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels for vision, and hair-cell machinery such as myosins, cadherin-23, protocadherin-15 and mechanotransduction channels for hearing and balance — alongside nociception through TRP and acid-sensing channels and sensory sodium channels. Central signalling is represented by glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine, dopamine and neuropeptide receptors, synaptic release and scaffolding proteins, voltage-gated channels, and neuromuscular junction components. Failure of individual members produces retinal degeneration, congenital deafness, anosmia, pain insensitivity, epilepsy, movement disorders and neurodegeneration, linking this biology to perception, reflexes, muscle control and cognition.

Regulation of body fluid levels covers the processes that hold the volume, tonicity and containment of extracellular fluids within narrow limits, spanning renal water and salt handling, secretion by exocrine and mammary tissue, vascular tone and permeability, and the haemostatic responses that keep blood inside vessels. Its failure produces diabetes insipidus, hypertension, oedema, cystic fibrosis-type secretory defects, or bleeding and thrombotic disease. Vasopressin acting through AVPR2 and cAMP mobilises aquaporin-2 while ENaC subunits, WNK kinases and STK39 set sodium reabsorption; oxytocin, adrenomedullin, apelin, endothelin, natriuretic peptides and nitric oxide synthase tune vessel calibre and fluid flux. In parallel, the coagulation cascade, platelet glycoprotein receptors, von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen and their serpin and fibrinolytic counterweights, together with platelet granule biogenesis, restore vascular integrity after injury. Chloride channels such as CFTR and anoctamins drive epithelial fluid secretion.

Body fluid homeostasis covers the processes that set the volume and composition of blood, urine, and secreted fluids, and this broad programme unites three of them. One arm is renal water and salt handling: vasopressin acting through its V2 receptor and aquaporins controls water reabsorption, while epithelial sodium channel subunits, WNK kinases, mineralocorticoid signalling and 11β-HSD2 set sodium balance and thereby blood pressure. A second arm is hemostasis, where fibrinogen chains, clotting factors, von Willebrand factor, platelet glycoprotein receptors and their anticoagulant and fibrinolytic counterweights (antithrombin, protein C, plasminogen activators) keep blood fluid yet able to seal a breach. A third arm is exocrine and endocrine secretion, including CFTR- and chloride-channel-driven fluid transport in airway, salivary and lacrimal epithelia, and prolactin-dependent milk protein output. Failure produces hypertension, diabetes insipidus, edema, bleeding disorders or thrombosis.

Body movement in a multicellular organism depends on nerve impulses being converted into coordinated muscle contraction, and the genes here cover that chain from synapse to sarcomere. Acetylcholine receptor subunits at the neuromuscular junction and the skeletal sodium channel SCN4A set off the action potential; STAC3 and its relatives couple depolarisation to calcium release through the ryanodine pathway, the SERCA pump ATP2A1 and calsequestrin CASQ1 handle calcium storage and reuptake, and troponin and myosin isoforms together with titin and dystrophin generate and transmit force. Because so many of these steps are non-redundant, mutations produce congenital myasthenic syndromes, periodic paralysis, malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, core and nemaline myopathies, muscular dystrophy and cardiomyopathy. Locomotion, posture, breathing and cardiac output all rest on this excitation-contraction machinery working in register.

Willed movement of the body depends on a chain that runs from sensory feedback through the nervous system to striated muscle acting on the skeleton, and voluntary musculoskeletal movement names the controllable output of that chain. Loss of it produces ataxia, tremor, paralysis or the progressive motor decline of neurodegenerative disease rather than any single metabolic defect. The genes here point to neuronal contributions to motor control: an intracellular calcium release channel whose mutation causes cerebellar ataxia, a microtubule-associated protein of axons and dendrites, a kinase implicated in motor neuron survival, and retromer and SNARE-associated components that direct endosomal sorting and membrane traffic in neurons. Together they place cerebellar and motor neuron integrity, calcium signalling and intracellular trafficking upstream of coordinated, deliberate movement, connecting this behaviour to neuronal maintenance more than to muscle contraction itself.

Holding the body upright and aligned requires continuous neural adjustment of muscle tone, and the neuromuscular control of posture is the set of activities by which an organism sets and corrects that alignment. It draws on spinal inhibitory circuits, proprioceptive feedback, and cerebellar and basal ganglia output; when it fails the result is ataxia, spasticity, rigidity, dystonia or paroxysmal loss of postural control. Genes here span those levels: glycine receptor subunits and GABA-A receptor subunits mediate the inhibition that keeps tone in check, voltage-gated sodium channels and PRRT2 govern neuronal excitability and underlie paroxysmal movement disorders, GCH1 supplies the cofactor for dopamine synthesis in dystonia, and frataxin loss produces sensory and cerebellar ataxia. Lysosomal enzymes such as HEXA and GAA, and glycosyltransferase-dependent muscle integrity, connect posture to storage disease and myopathy. MECP2 and developmental transcription factors place the circuit's wiring upstream of its function.

Maintaining balance — keeping the body and head correctly oriented with respect to gravity — depends on integrating vestibular input from the inner ear labyrinth with vision, proprioception and skin pressure cues, and on the motor output that corrects posture and gait. Genes here span that whole arc: Usher-type hair cell and stereocilia proteins such as MYO7A, CDH23, PCDH15, USH1C and CLRN1 build the mechanosensory apparatus, POU4F3, NEUROG1, HMX3 and REST specify and maintain inner ear and neuronal identity, while synaptic and cerebellar components including SHANK3, NLGN2, NRXN1, DLG4, GRIN2C, JPH3/JPH4 and the glial glutamate transporter SLC1A3 shape the circuits that compute corrective movement. Lysosomal enzymes such as HEXA, HEXB, GAA and TPP1 appear because their deficiency produces progressive ataxia. Failure anywhere along this path gives unsteady gait, head tilt, circling or deafness with vestibular dysfunction.

Hormones released into the bloodstream coordinate organs that never touch each other, and this endocrine biology covers both their secretion and the receptors that read them. Much of the gene content is the renin-angiotensin system — renin, angiotensinogen, the converting enzymes ACE and ACE2, and the AT1 and AT2 receptors — which sets blood pressure, sodium handling and aldosterone output through CYP11B2, with endothelins, vasopressin receptors and NOS3 acting on the same vascular tone problem. A second strand is hypothalamic-pituitary control: CRH and its receptor and binding protein, POMC, GnRH receptor, kisspeptin and the glycoprotein hormone alpha subunit drive stress and reproductive axes, while inhibins, activins and GDF9 tune gonadal feedback. Adipose signals such as leptin, adiponectin and resistin link energy stores to this network. Failures produce hypertension, adrenal and reproductive disorders, and metabolic disease.

Cognition covers the mental operations by which an animal perceives, learns and remembers, and the molecules gathered here are those whose loss changes learning, memory or intellectual ability. The set is dominated by the machinery of excitatory synaptic plasticity: NMDA and AMPA receptor subunits such as GRIN1, GRIN2A/B and GRIA1, the scaffolds DLG4 and SHANK1-3, presynaptic adhesion neurexins and neuroligins, and the calcium-dependent kinases, phosphatases and cAMP effectors that convert activity into lasting synaptic change. Activity-regulated transcription through CREB1, FOS, EGR1, NPAS4 and ARC consolidates those changes into long-term memory. Neuromodulatory tone is represented by dopaminergic, serotonergic, cholinergic and neuropeptide receptors and their biosynthetic enzymes. Disruption of these components underlies intellectual disability, autism spectrum conditions and schizophrenia, while APP, PSEN1, MAPT, APOE, TREM2 and PICALM tie the same circuitry to age-related dementia and neurodegeneration.

Whole-body water balance keeps the volume and osmolality of blood and other extracellular fluids within narrow limits, and most of the work is done by the kidney concentrating or diluting urine. Vasopressin released in response to rising plasma osmolality acts on its V2 receptor in collecting duct cells, raising cAMP through adenylate cyclases and Gs, and activating protein kinase A holoenzymes; the phosphorylated aquaporin-2 water channel is then trafficked to the apical membrane so water can follow the osmotic gradient. Sodium entry through the epithelial sodium channel subunits, chloride movement via CFTR, and the corticosteroid pathway that makes aldosterone set that gradient, while uromodulin and osmosensitive TRPV4 tune it. Loss of receptor or channel function causes diabetes insipidus with massive dilute urine output, and failure elsewhere gives hyponatraemia, hypertension or the dehydration of Wolfram syndrome.

Intestinal absorption is the uptake of digested nutrients from the gut lumen into enterocytes and onward into blood and lymph, the step that converts food into usable substrate for the rest of the body. Its failure produces malabsorption, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, iron or folate deficiency anaemia, and failure to thrive. The genes describe the specialised absorptive enterocyte and its brush border: transporters for glucose and fructose (SLC5A1, SLC2A5), folate and anion carriers, sterol uptake and efflux machinery (NPC1L1 opposed by the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer), lipases and acyltransferases that re-esterify fatty acids, and apolipoproteins that package them into chylomicrons. Iron handling by hephaestin and hepcidin, tight junction and claudin proteins that set paracellular permeability, and villin and ezrin that build the microvillar cytoskeleton complete the picture, with vitamin D receptor signalling tuning capacity to demand.

Intestinal absorption is the step at which dietary nutrients cross the gut epithelium and enter the body, and it sets what fraction of ingested fat, sugar, iron, sterols and vitamins is actually available to the organism. The genes here cover the main routes: luminal digestion by pancreatic lipase and bile salt-dependent lipase, brush-border transport of glucose and galactose by SLC5A1 and fructose by SLC2A5, folate uptake by SLC46A1, and cholesterol entry via NPC1L1 with efflux back to the lumen by the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer. Absorbed lipids are re-esterified and packaged with apolipoproteins into chylomicrons, while hepcidin, hephaestin and iron-responsive proteins tune iron handling. Microvillar and tight-junction proteins such as villin, ezrin and the claudins build the absorptive surface and control paracellular flux. Loss of these functions produces malabsorption, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, sitosterolemia or disordered iron balance.

Leukocyte migration is the traffic control system of the immune system: it moves neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes out of blood and through tissue to sites of infection or injury, and routes them between lymphoid organs during immune surveillance. Without it, wounds are not cleared of pathogens and adaptive responses are never initiated; when it is excessive, the result is chronic inflammatory and autoimmune tissue damage. The genes trace the classic adhesion cascade — selectins and their fucosylated ligands mediating rolling, chemokines and their G protein-coupled receptors triggering integrin activation, and junctional proteins such as PECAM1, JAM family members and CD99 permitting diapedesis across endothelium. Downstream, Rho-family GTPases, Src and Syk kinases, PI3K isoforms and actin regulators drive polarised motility. Cytokines including TNF, IL1B and TGFB set the endothelial and chemotactic context, linking migration to inflammation, lymphocyte homing and haematopoietic cell positioning.

Immune surveillance depends on white blood cells leaving the circulation and travelling to the right tissue, and leukocyte migration is the programme that directs that movement. It underlies neutrophil recruitment to infected or injured sites, lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes and gut, and monocyte entry into tissues; when it is excessive it drives the leukocyte infiltrates of asthma, atherosclerosis and autoimmune inflammation, while loss of its adhesion components causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency with recurrent infection. Chemokines and their receptors, along with formyl-peptide and complement receptors, set the directional cue; selectins and their fucosylated ligands capture cells on activated endothelium; integrins with ICAM, VCAM and MADCAM partners firm up attachment; and junctional proteins such as PECAM1 and JAM family members permit passage between endothelial cells. Inside the cell, Rho-family GTPases, Src- and Syk-family kinases and actin regulators convert these signals into polarised crawling and diapedesis.and matrix proteases clear a path.

The first contact between a circulating leukocyte and an inflamed or specialized vessel wall is a catch-and-release interaction that slows the cell from bloodstream velocity to a slow roll, and without it leukocytes cannot leave the circulation to reach infected or damaged tissue. Selectins on endothelium and on the leukocyte itself bind sialylated, fucosylated glycans built by fucosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and sialyltransferases on scaffolds such as PSGL-1, CD43 and podocalyxin-like proteins; the bonds form and break repeatedly so the cell tumbles along the endothelium. Integrin pairs including α4β1 and α4β7 with VCAM-1 and MAdCAM-1 contribute slower rolling and the transition to firm arrest, while chemokines displayed on the surface deliver the activating signal. TNF-driven induction of E- and P-selectin links this step to inflammation; defects in the glycan machinery cause leukocyte adhesion deficiency with recurrent infection. The same interactions guide lymphocyte homing to lymph node and gut.

Diapedesis is the final step by which a leukocyte already adherent to and crawling on the vessel wall squeezes through the endothelial barrier to reach inflamed tissue. Without it, immune cells remain confined to the bloodstream and cannot mount defence at sites of infection or injury; with too much of it, neutrophil and lymphocyte influx drives tissue damage in conditions such as atherosclerosis, arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. The step depends on junctional adhesion molecules that engage counter-receptors on the leukocyte, notably PECAM1 and the CD99-family protein CD99L2, together with the integrin alpha-4 chain binding endothelial VCAM-1. Adaptor proteins CRK and CRKL and the tyrosine kinase FER couple these engagements to cytoskeletal remodelling and junction loosening, allowing transient opening of endothelial contacts and resealing behind the migrating cell.

Movement depends on nerve and muscle working as one system, and this neuromuscular process collects the machinery that links motor command to contraction and posture. Its components define the neuromuscular junction itself — the muscle acetylcholine receptor subunits CHRNA1, CHRNB1, CHRND, CHRNE and CHRNG — together with excitation–contraction coupling in the sarcomere and sarcoplasmic reticulum, where voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, ryanodine-receptor partners such as STAC3, JPH3/JPH4, the calcium pump ATP2A1, calsequestrin and troponin, titin, dystrophin and myosin heavy chains set force and relaxation. Central elements contribute too: glycine and NMDA receptor subunits for spinal and cortical motor control, dopaminergic signalling, and axonal transport and glycosylation factors. Loss of individual members produces congenital myasthenic syndromes, muscular dystrophies and myopathies, periodic paralysis, dystonia and paroxysmal dyskinesia, motor neuropathy and spasticity, tying this biology to both movement disorders and muscle disease.

Sensory perception begins with detection: a chemical, photon, mechanical force, or noxious stimulus is captured by a receptor cell and converted into a molecular and electrical signal. This collection spans all of the major modalities. Hundreds of odorant receptors, together with their accessory trafficking factors, give the nose its combinatorial discrimination of volatile chemicals, while sweet and umami receptor subunits and the bitter receptor family, coupled through gustducin and phospholipase C, define taste cell responses. Phototransduction contributes rhodopsin, cone and rod transducins, cyclic nucleotide-gated channel subunits and the visual cycle isomerase RPE65. Hair-cell mechanotransduction is represented by TMC1, LHFPL5, stereociliary adhesion and scaffold proteins mutated in Usher syndrome and deafness. Somatosensation and nociception rely on TRPV1, TRPA1, ASIC channels, PIEZO2 and voltage-gated sodium channels whose loss abolishes pain sensing. Failure of individual components causes anosmia, retinal degeneration, hearing loss, or pain insensitivity.

Sensory perception of taste is how the tongue reads the chemical composition of food and turns it into a neural signal, allowing an animal to seek out nutrients and reject toxins and spoiled or bitter material before swallowing. Taste receptor cells in the taste buds express dedicated detectors: TAS1R heterodimers for sweet and umami, a large TAS2R family for the chemically diverse bitter compounds, epithelial sodium channels for salt, and acid-sensing channels including PKD2L1 for sour. Sweet, umami and bitter receptors converge on the gustducin-PLCB2-ITPR3 cascade, which raises calcium and opens CALHM1/CALHM3 channels to release ATP onto purinergic P2RX2/P2RX3 receptors on gustatory afferents. Salivary proteins such as carbonic anhydrase VI and cystatins shape the stimulus, while Wnt signalling and RGS21 support taste bud renewal and signal tuning. Variation here, notably at TAS2R38, sets individual bitter sensitivity and dietary preference.

Taste lets an animal judge food before swallowing it, distinguishing nutritious sugars, amino acids and salt from bitter or sour compounds that signal toxins or spoilage; loss of this sense blunts appetite and dietary choice, and common variation in bitter receptors explains why individuals differ in their response to foods such as brassicas. Sweet and umami detection uses dimeric TAS1R receptors, bitter a large TAS2R family, both coupling through gustducin, phospholipase C-beta 2 and IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release to ATP secretion via CALHM1/CALHM3 channels onto purinergic P2X receptors on afferent fibres. Sour and salt detection instead use ion channels, including PKD2L1 and epithelial sodium channel subunits, while acid-sensing channels and TRPV1 add chemesthetic and thermal input. Salivary proteins such as carbonic anhydrase 6, lipocalin and cystatins shape the oral environment in which these stimuli are presented, and Wnt signalling components support renewal of taste bud cells.

Hearing begins when sound-driven vibration deflects the hair bundles of cochlear hair cells and opens mechanically gated channels, converting movement into an electrical signal; this is the mechanotransduction step of sound perception, and its failure produces congenital and progressive sensorineural deafness. The genes here build and tune that apparatus: TMC1 and TMC2 form the pore of the hair-cell transduction channel with LHFPL5 as an obligatory partner, while stereocilin (STRC) and PTPRQ shape the links and surface coat between stereocilia, and whirlin, PDZD7 and the very large adhesion receptor ADGRV1 assemble the scaffolds and transient ankle-link complexes that organize the bundle during development. Efferent olivocochlear feedback onto outer hair cells acts through the CHRNA9/CHRNA10 nicotinic receptor, adjusting cochlear gain. Associated defects cause Usher syndrome, nonsyndromic hearing loss and auditory neuropathy.

Taste begins when a soluble chemical in the mouth is bound by a receptor on a gustatory cell and converted into an electrical signal, and this detection step is what allows animals to accept nutritious food and reject bitter or toxic material. Two receptor families dominate: the T1R proteins, which pair up to sense sweet compounds and L-amino acids including umami, and a large panel of T2R bitter receptors whose sequence variation explains why people differ in their sensitivity to compounds such as phenylthiocarbamide. Both funnel through a shared transduction cassette involving phospholipase C-beta 2 and gustducin-type G protein subunits to raise intracellular calcium. Sour sensing is attributed to PKD2L1 with PKD1L3, a fatty-acid receptor contributes to fat taste, and saliva-derived proteins including carbonic anhydrase 6 and cystatins shape the chemical environment at the taste bud.

Bitter taste perception warns an animal away from plant alkaloids, spoiled food and other potential toxins, and it accounts for much of the individual variation in what people find palatable — the classic example being TAS2R38 variants that determine whether phenylthiocarbamide tastes bitter. Detection begins with a large family of TAS2R G protein-coupled receptors on type II taste cells, which are broadly tuned so that a few dozen receptors can cover thousands of bitter compounds. Ligand binding activates gustducin (GNAT3) and phospholipase C-β2, releasing calcium through the IP3 receptor ITPR3; the resulting depolarization drives ATP release through the CALHM1 channel to excite gustatory afferents. RGS21 damps the cascade, RTP chaperones support receptor trafficking, and accompanying salivary proteins such as carbonic anhydrase 6 and cystatins shape the oral environment in which tastants are presented.

Sensory perception of sour taste is the detection of acids on the tongue and the conversion of that chemical signal into neural activity, one of the five basic taste modalities. It warns against spoiled or unripe food and shapes dietary acid intake, and its loss flattens the perception of anything vinegary or citric. Sour transduction occurs in a distinct subset of taste bud cells that respond to intracellular acidification rather than to receptor binding. The genes encode the ion channels proposed to carry this response: the PKD2L1/PKD1L3 polycystin pair that marks sour-responsive taste cells, acid-sensing ion channels of the ASIC family, and subunits of the epithelial sodium channel that also underlie salt taste. Depolarization of these cells drives transmitter release onto gustatory afferents, linking chemosensation at the epithelial surface to taste coding in the brainstem.

Sour taste detection lets an animal recognize acids, warning it away from spoiled or unripe food while contributing to the appreciation of fermented and citrus flavours. The genes here encode acid- and ion-sensitive channels of the taste bud: a candidate sour receptor formed by the polycystin-family subunits PKD2L1 and PKD1L3, which marks a distinct population of type III taste cells, together with acid-sensing ion channels of the ASIC family and the subunits of the epithelial sodium channel, ENaC, which is better established as the amiloride-sensitive salt-taste sensor. Protons entering or acting on these channels depolarize the receptor cell, triggering transmitter release onto gustatory afferents that carry the signal to the brainstem and cortex. This sensory transduction step is the entry point for reflexive rejection of acidic foods and for behavioural regulation of acid and electrolyte intake.

Sweet taste perception begins when sugars and other sweeteners bind a G protein-coupled receptor on the apical surface of type II taste cells, and it drives the innate attraction to calorie-dense food that shapes diet and energy intake. The heterodimer of TAS1R2 and TAS1R3 is the sweet receptor proper, while TAS1R3 paired with TAS1R1 detects amino acids, linking sweet and umami detection to a shared subunit. Receptor activation engages the taste-specific G protein transducin subunit gustducin, releasing calcium from stores through the IP3 receptor ITPR3; the resulting calcium rise opens CALHM1 channels that release ATP as the transmitter onto gustatory afferents. RGS21 damps the G protein signal and REEP2 supports receptor delivery to the membrane. Loss of these components blunts sweet responsiveness and alters feeding preference.

Umami is the savoury taste of glutamate-rich foods, and its perception tells an animal that a food contains protein or amino acids, driving appetitive feeding behaviour. Detection begins at the apical surface of type II taste receptor cells, where the heterodimeric receptor formed by TAS1R1 and TAS1R3 binds L-glutamate and related amino acids, with purine nucleotides acting as potentiators. Receptor occupancy activates the taste-specific G protein transducin subunit encoded by GNAT3 (gustducin) and a phospholipase C cascade, releasing calcium through the IP3 receptor ITPR3; the resulting depolarisation opens the CALHM1 channel, which releases ATP to excite afferent gustatory fibres. RGS21 dampens the G protein signal and sets response magnitude. The same cascade serves sweet and bitter detection, so receptor identity rather than downstream machinery specifies umami quality; variation in these genes shifts taste sensitivity and food preference.

positive chemotaxis is the attraction arm of directed cell migration: cells sense a gradient of a soluble cue and crawl toward its source. It organises immune surveillance, wound healing, new blood vessel growth and the guidance of axons and neural crest, and its misuse lets tumour cells recruit vasculature and invade. The genes fall into ligands and their receptors on the migrating cell: chemokines such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL8 and CXCL12 that draw leukocytes and stem cells; VEGFA-D with KDR and NRP1, plus angiopoietins and FGFs, that pull endothelial tip cells into avascular tissue; HGF-MET and PDGFB for epithelial and mesenchymal movement; and neurotrophic factors GDNF, ARTN and NTF3 with semaphorin and WNT guidance cues. Antimicrobial defensins and damage signals such as HMGB1 and azurocidin act as alarmins summoning phagocytes to injury. Downstream, polarity proteins and cytoskeletal regulators convert the gradient into persistent, oriented protrusion.

Positive chemotaxis is the steering of a motile cell up a chemical gradient, and it underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, immune surveillance and axon guidance. Without accurate attraction, leukocytes fail to reach infected or injured tissue, new vessels do not sprout toward hypoxic regions, and growing axons miss their targets; the same cues are co-opted by tumour cells to invade and by leukocytes to sustain chronic inflammation. The attractants here span several families: chemokines such as CCL2, CCL5, CXCL12, CXCL8 and CX3CL1 acting on G protein-coupled receptors; VEGF family ligands with KDR and the co-receptor NRP1 drawing endothelial tip cells; HGF through MET and neurotrophic factors such as GDNF, ARTN and NTF3 guiding epithelial and neuronal migration; plus defensins, alarmins including HMGB1 and MIF, and formyl peptide sensing via FPR2. Downstream, cytoskeletal and polarity regulators including CORO1A and SCRIB convert the gradient into directed protrusion.

Negative chemotaxis is movement away from a chemical cue rather than toward it, and in humans it is largely the business of repellent guidance: growth cones, migrating neurons, endothelial tip cells and immune cells steering clear of territory they must not enter. It builds the nervous system's wiring diagram, keeping commissural axons from recrossing the midline and confining motor and sensory projections to their proper tracts, and it also patterns vasculature and bone. The core logic is ligand-receptor repulsion: secreted and transmembrane semaphorins acting through plexins with neuropilin co-receptors, Slits read by Robo receptors, netrin converted into a repellent by UNC5C, and ephrin-Eph pairs, all converging on RhoA and cytoskeletal collapse so that filopodia retract on the cue-rich side. Loss of these signals produces axon misrouting and midline crossing defects, and semaphorin-plexin signalling is reused to restrain angiogenesis and tumour cell invasion.

Cells navigate by reading chemical gradients, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly and in which direction they move. It governs leukocyte recruitment to infected or injured tissue, endothelial sprouting during angiogenesis, and axon pathfinding in the developing nervous system, so its dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, tumour invasion and defective wiring. The bulk of the machinery is ligand-receptor: CC and CXC chemokines acting through receptors such as CCR2, CCR7, CXCR2 and CX3CR1, complement fragments signalling via C5AR1 and C3AR1, and growth factor systems including VEGF-KDR, PDGF, CSF1-CSF1R and HGF-MET. Guidance cues of the slit-robo, semaphorin-plexin and netrin-related families set repulsion and attraction in neurons and vessels alike. Downstream, Rac GTPases, focal adhesion kinases, ERK signalling and actin regulators convert receptor occupancy into polarised protrusion, while phosphatases, DUSP1 and several microRNAs damp the response.

Cells crawl toward chemical cues, and this collection covers the signals and machinery that switch that directed migration on or make it stronger. It is the basis of leukocyte recruitment to infection and injury, of vascular and neuronal wiring, and of tumour cell dissemination; blocking it underlies anti-inflammatory strategies, while excessive activity sustains chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Much of the content is ligand-receptor pairing: CC and CXC chemokines with receptors such as CCR2, CCR7 and CXCR3 guide monocytes, dendritic cells and lymphocytes, complement fragments and formyl peptides act through C3AR1, C5AR1 and FPR2 on neutrophils, and growth factor axes including VEGF-KDR, PDGF-PDGFRB and CSF1-CSF1R steer endothelium, pericytes and macrophages. Downstream, Rac GTPases, focal adhesion kinases, protein kinase D isoforms and ERK signalling convert gradient sensing into polarised actin remodelling, adhesion turnover and ion flux at the leading edge.

Directed cell migration must be stopped as well as started, and this is the braking side of chemotaxis: the signals and enzymes that damp or terminate movement up a chemical gradient. It matters for resolving inflammation, for keeping leukocyte infiltration proportionate to injury, and for steering growth cones and migrating neurons away from inappropriate territory. Repulsive guidance cues dominate the mechanism — SLIT ligands acting through ROBO receptors, semaphorins signalling via plexins and neuropilin — alongside decoy and scavenging receptors such as C5AR2 that blunt complement-driven recruitment. Phosphatases including DUSP1 and PTPN2 shut down the kinase cascades that convert receptor occupancy into cytoskeletal polarization, several microRNAs tune chemokine output, and matricellular proteins such as THBS1 restrain endothelial and monocyte movement. Loss of this restraint contributes to chronic inflammatory infiltration, aberrant angiogenesis and axon misrouting.

Moving away from a chemical cue is as directed a behaviour as moving toward one, and this pathway controls how strongly and how often a cell or growth cone turns down a gradient. It is the logic behind axon repulsion in the developing nervous system: Slit ligands secreted by the midline are read by Robo receptors on crossing axons, and plexin signalling reads semaphorin cues, together steering commissural projections, setting whether an axon crosses the midline once and never again, and shaping longitudinal tract position. Tuning this repulsive output determines the precision of wiring rather than whether growth occurs at all. Loss of Robo3 function in humans causes horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, a direct consequence of commissural axons failing to cross. The same repulsive guidance is reused outside neurons in branching morphogenesis and in the migration of leukocytes and other motile cells.

regulation of positive chemotaxis controls how strongly cells are drawn up a chemical gradient, tuning the attractant cues that guide endothelial cells during blood vessel growth, leukocytes to sites of injury, and axons toward their targets. Its output determines whether a wound revascularises and heals, whether a tumour recruits its own blood supply, and how quickly neutrophils arrive at an infection. The genes are dominated by the VEGF family and their receptor KDR, together with angiopoietin, placental growth factor and FGF10, which set endothelial migratory drive; CXCL12 and CXCL8 provide the chemokine arm for immune and progenitor cell recruitment; neurotrophins acting through NTRK3 orient neurites. Coagulation and protease-activated signalling through tissue factor, F7 and F2RL1 links injury to attraction, while S1PR1, integrin α2 and SMAD3 modulate responsiveness to the gradient itself.

Cells that migrate up a chemical gradient do so because secreted cues and their receptors are switched on, amplified or damped, and this control over positive chemotaxis is what directs endothelial sprouting, leukocyte recruitment and axon guidance to the right place. Much of the content here is angiogenic: VEGFA and its relatives acting through KDR, placental growth factor, angiopoietin-2 and FGF10 steer endothelial cells toward hypoxic or wounded tissue, while sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor signalling and cadherin-13 tune how strongly they respond. Chemokines such as CXCL12 and CXCL8 pull immune cells into inflamed sites, coagulation-linked receptors and tissue factor couple haemostasis to cell movement, and neurotrophins with NTRK3 guide neurite extension. Transcriptional input from SMAD3 and CREB3 sets the output level. Deregulation feeds tumour vascularisation, chronic inflammation and defective wound repair.

Cells find their way to a target by reading a chemical gradient, and induction of positive chemotaxis covers the signals that start that attraction — the ligands and regulators that tell a motile cell to move up a concentration gradient. The genes here are largely secreted attractants: VEGFA and its relatives, including the lymphangiogenic VEGFC, guide endothelial cells during blood and lymphatic vessel growth; placental growth factor and FGF10 act on vascular and epithelial targets; CXCL12 and CXCL8 recruit leukocytes and stem cells; neurotrophic factors such as artemin and NTF3 draw axons and neural crest derivatives toward their destinations. Neutrophil azurocidin and secretogranin II contribute chemoattractant activity in inflammation, while AGER and the transcription factor CREB3 modulate the response. This biology underlies wound healing, immune cell recruitment, neuronal wiring and tumour angiogenesis and metastasis.

Pigment cell differentiation is the route by which neural crest-derived precursors become melanocytes, the cells that make melanin for skin, hair and eye colour and shield keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage. Its failure produces depigmentation and deafness syndromes such as Waardenburg and piebaldism, while its transcriptional core is reactivated in melanoma. Lineage specification runs through SOX10 and MITF, which switch on pigment enzymes including TYRP1, with ZEB2, MEF2C and GLI3 shaping the decision; survival and migration of precursors depend on KIT signalling from its ligand KITLG and on endothelin 3 acting through EDNRB. A second arm builds the organelle itself: BLOC-1 subunits, adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3, and HPS4 sort cargo into maturing melanosomes, OCA2 controls their lumenal environment, and RAB27A with melanophilin-related transport machinery moves them to the cell periphery for transfer.

Melanocytes arise from the neural crest, migrate into skin, hair follicles, eye and inner ear, and only then switch on the machinery of melanin synthesis; the control of pigment cell differentiation sets how many of them commit, survive and mature. Its failure produces the depigmentation and deafness phenotypes seen when melanocyte development is disturbed, and its deregulation contributes to melanoma. KITLG is the ligand that drives melanoblast survival and expansion through its receptor kinase, BCL2 keeps differentiating melanocytes alive, and ZEB2 acts transcriptionally in neural crest-derived lineage decisions. Secreted metalloproteases of the ADAMTS family shape the extracellular matrix through which melanoblasts migrate, while BLOC1S5 and BLOC1S6 belong to the complex that routes cargo into melanosomes, linking lineage commitment to biogenesis of the pigment granule itself.

Thermosensation is how an organism detects heat and cold and turns that physical stimulus into a neural signal it can act on, driving withdrawal reflexes, thermoregulatory behaviour and the burning or freezing quality of pain. Transduction begins in peripheral sensory neuron endings, where temperature-gated ion channels open: TRPV1 responds to noxious heat and capsaicin, TRPM8 to cool and menthol, and TRPA1 to irritants and cold, while TRPV1 sensitisation by nerve growth factor acting through its receptor TRKA underlies inflammatory heat hyperalgesia. Voltage-gated sodium channels SCN9A and SCN11A convert the resulting depolarisation into action potentials, and loss-of-function mutations in either, or in the developmental factor PRDM12, cause congenital inability to feel pain. Neuropeptides such as substance P, opioid and monoamine receptors, and glutamate and GABA receptors then shape and modulate transmission of thermal and nociceptive information centrally.

sensory perception of light stimulus is vision at its molecular root: the capture of photons in the retina, their conversion into an electrical signal, and the transmission of that signal to the inner retina and brain. It defines the photoreceptor as a cell type and accounts for a large share of inherited blindness, from retinitis pigmentosa and Leber congenital amaurosis to achromatopsia, congenital stationary night blindness and Usher syndrome. The genes trace the whole phototransduction cascade — opsins, transducin, PDE6 subunits, cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels and the recoverin/GRK1/RGS9 machinery that shuts it off — together with the visual cycle enzymes (RPE65, LRAT, RDH12) that regenerate retinal, the outer-segment and connecting-cilium proteins that build the photoreceptor, and ON-bipolar synaptic components such as TRPM1 and GRM6. Also included are lens crystallins and transcription factors like PAX6 and CRX that shape the eye and specify photoreceptor identity.

Vision begins when photons are captured in the retina and converted into a neural signal, and this is the machinery that accomplishes it. Opsins in rods and cones initiate a cascade through transducin, cGMP phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels that hyperpolarizes the photoreceptor; arrestin, rhodopsin kinase and RGS proteins shut the response off, while guanylate cyclases and their calcium-sensing activators restore sensitivity for the next stimulus. Retinoid recycling enzymes such as RPE65 and LRAT regenerate chromophore in the pigment epithelium, and lens crystallins keep the light path clear. Transcription factors including CRX and NRL specify photoreceptor subtypes, and ciliary and adhesion components maintain the outer segment. Hearing, balance and touch all begin with the conversion of a mechanical force into an electrical signal, and this collection covers that mechanotransduction from hair cells of the inner ear to somatosensory neurons of the skin. Hair-cell stereocilia are built and tuned by unconventional myosins, espin and the cadherin-23/protocadherin-15 tip links, while TMC1, TMIE and LHFPL5 form the transduction channel complex; PIEZO2 and several TRP and ASIC channels serve touch, stretch and nociception. Potassium recycling through connexins, KCNQ4 and the pendrin transporter maintains the endolymphatic driving force, and prestin confers outer hair cell electromotility. Transcription factors such as POU4F3, SIX1 and EYA1 specify the sensory epithelium, and tectorial and otolithic matrix proteins couple sound to the bundle. Loss of these components produces syndromic and non-syndromic deafness, Usher syndrome, vestibular dysfunction and altered pain and touch sensitivity.

Thermoception is how an organism senses temperature: converting heat or cold into electrical and chemical signals that sensory neurons can report to the brain, allowing avoidance of tissue-damaging extremes and behavioural thermoregulation. In mammals the primary detectors are thermosensitive ion channels in skin-innervating sensory afferents, with TRPV1 opening to noxious heat and capsaicin, TRPM8 to cooling and menthol, and TRPA1 to irritants and cold-evoked stimuli; opening these channels depolarises the nerve ending and triggers firing. Downstream and modulatory components tune that sensitivity, including glutamatergic signalling through GRIK2 and GRM5 and adrenergic input via ADRA2A, which shapes pain thresholds. Opsins such as OPN4 and RHO link the same sensory machinery to light-driven detection. Sensitisation of these pathways during inflammation or nerve injury underlies thermal hyperalgesia and cold allodynia, making them targets for analgesic development.

Equilibrioception is the sense of balance and orientation with respect to gravity, built from vestibular input in the inner ear labyrinth together with visual, pressure and proprioceptive cues about which parts of the body are moving or touching the ground. The genes here point to the mechanosensory hair cells that convert head motion into neural signals: cadherin 23 and protocadherin 15 form the tip-link that gates the transduction channel, while harmonin, SANS and myosin VIIa anchor and organize the stereociliary bundle, and clarin-1 supports hair cell synapses. Mutations in these components cause Usher syndrome, combining congenital deafness with retinal degeneration and, in the type 1 forms, vestibular areflexia with delayed motor milestones and unsteady gait. POU4F1 contributes to the sensory neuron identity that relays this information centrally.

Thermoception begins with sensory cells converting heat or cold into an electrical signal, and this step is the transduction event itself: a temperature change opening or gating a receptor to produce a molecular and then neural signal. It underlies the ability to sense ambient warmth, to feel noxious heat as pain, and to drive behavioural and autonomic thermoregulation such as withdrawal and sweating. The best-characterised element here is the heat- and capsaicin-sensitive cation channel TRPV1, which opens at noxious temperatures in nociceptor endings and feeds into pain signalling; its blockade lowers heat sensitivity and alters body temperature set point. Opsins, normally thought of as light sensors, also contribute temperature-dependent responses, and glutamate receptor signalling carries the information onward to central circuits. Loss of this detection leaves an animal unable to avoid damaging heat or to defend core temperature.

Vision begins when photons are captured in retinal photoreceptors and converted into a change in membrane potential, the step described here as detection of light stimulus during sensory perception. The genes involved cover the phototransduction cascade itself — rod and cone transducin subunits that couple activated opsin to cGMP hydrolysis, a cyclase and a cyclic nucleotide-gated channel subunit that reset and read out cGMP levels, and a GAP anchoring protein that times cascade shutoff — together with the visual cycle enzyme RPE65 and retinol-binding protein that regenerate chromophore. Others build the structural platform on which this chemistry occurs: outer-segment disc rim proteins PRPH2 and ROM1, a lipid flippase, and ciliary and outer limiting membrane components. Synaptic transfer to bipolar cells requires the photoreceptor calcium channel and the metabotropic glutamate receptor GRM6. Loss of these functions causes retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness, and macular dystrophy.

Noxious heat and cold are detected by specialized nociceptor endings, and this pathway covers the conversion of a painful temperature stimulus into electrical and chemical signals that reach the central nervous system. It defines thermal nociception, the protective reflex that withdraws a limb from a hot surface, and its loss in humans produces congenital insensitivity to pain with unnoticed burns and injuries, while its sensitization underlies the thermal hyperalgesia of inflammation. Heat-gated TRPV1 and the acid-sensing channel ASIC3 act as transducers, the sodium channels encoded by SCN9A and SCN11A set nociceptor excitability and carry the resulting action potentials, and NTRK1 signalling with the transcriptional regulator PRDM12 is required for these neurons to develop at all. Peptides such as substance P and CART, together with adenosine, serotonin and neurotensin receptors, tune the gain of the response.

Mechanical nociception begins when noxious pressure, pinch or stretch deforms a sensory ending and is converted into electrical activity, and this transduction step sets the threshold at which touch becomes pain. It underlies protective withdrawal from injury, and its sensitization produces the mechanical hyperalgesia and allodynia of inflammatory and neuropathic pain states. Mechanically and chemically gated channels at the peripheral terminal, including the acid-sensing channel ASIC3 and the irritant receptor TRPA1, depolarize the ending, while voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN11A and SCN1A convert that depolarization into propagated action potentials and potassium channels oppose firing. Inflammatory mediators, among them TNF and CXCL12, together with NTRK1 signalling through Fyn kinase, lower the threshold of these endings, linking tissue damage and nerve growth factor availability to heightened mechanical pain sensitivity in small-diameter afferents.

detection of mechanical stimulus involved in sensory perception is the front end of touch, hearing, balance and mechanical pain: the conversion of physical force into electrical signals in specialized sensory cells. It defines cochlear hair cells and cutaneous mechanoreceptors, and its failure produces congenital deafness, vestibular dysfunction, loss of proprioception and altered pain thresholds. Force opens mechanically gated ion channels — PIEZO2 in light touch and proprioceptive endings, TMC1/TMC2 with LHFPL5 and TMIE-like partners at hair cell stereocilia tips, along with acid-sensing channels and TRPA1 — while stereocilia tip links and the ankle-link adhesion GPCR ADGRV1, whirlin, PDZD7 and stereocilin build and tension the structures that deliver force to the gate. Depolarization is then shaped by voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN9A and SCN11A and by potassium channels including KCNQ1 and two-pore leak channels, tuning sensitivity and adaptation.

Touch, hearing, balance and mechanical pain all begin with a cell converting force into an electrical signal, and this is the transduction step of that sensory perception. Hair cells of the inner ear and mechanoreceptive and nociceptive neurons of the dorsal root ganglia depend on it; when it fails the result is deafness, vestibular dysfunction, loss of discriminative touch, or altered pain thresholds. Force-gated channels sit at the centre: PIEZO2 in light-touch and proprioceptive endings, TMC1 and TMC2 with the accessory subunits LHFPL5 and the tip-link and stereocilia proteins whorlin, stereocilin, PTPRQ and the very large adhesion GPCR ADGRV1 in cochlear hair bundles, alongside acid-sensing channels and TRPA1 in irritant and mechanical nociception. Voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A and potassium channels such as KCNQ1 and KCNK2 then shape the resulting receptor potential into propagated firing, with neurotrophin and transcriptional regulators supporting the sensory cells themselves.

Touch perception begins when mechanoreceptors in skin and mucous membranes convert mechanical deformation into electrical signals that the nervous system reads as light contact, pressure, or vibration. The genes here point to the ion channels that set the sensitivity and firing properties of sensory neurons: two-pore potassium channels such as TRAAK and TREK-1 are mechanosensitive and regulate mechanical and thermal thresholds, a voltage-gated potassium channel shapes action potential repolarisation in afferent fibres, an ATP-gated purinergic channel contributes to nociceptive and mechanical signalling, and a GABA-A receptor subunit supports inhibitory modulation of the sensory circuit. Vesicle trafficking and transcriptional regulators, including MECP2, influence how these circuits develop and are maintained, which is one reason tactile hypersensitivity or blunted touch is a feature of Rett syndrome and related neurodevelopmental disorders. Loss of this signalling degrades discriminative touch and proprioceptive feedback needed for movement and social contact.

Cells convert physical force into electrical and biochemical signals, and this mechanosensory capacity underlies hearing, balance, touch, proprioception, blood flow sensing and the perception of noxious pressure. The core of the pathway is mechanically gated ion channels: PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 open in response to membrane tension in endothelium and sensory neurons, TMC1 and TMC2 with LHFPL5 form the hair-cell transduction apparatus, and polycystin subunits including PKD1 and PKD2 report flow and stretch in kidney and other epithelia. Acid- and stretch-sensitive channels, two-pore potassium channels and voltage-gated sodium channels shape the resulting receptor potential and its propagation. Structural partners such as stereocilin, whirlin, PDZD7, cadherins and titin-associated proteins couple force to the channel gate or tether it to the cytoskeleton. Loss of these components causes hereditary deafness, vestibular dysfunction, altered pain sensitivity and polycystic kidney disease.

Whether stored fat is burned or retained depends on regulation of lipid catabolic processes, the control layer sitting above lipolysis, fatty acid oxidation and lipoprotein triglyceride hydrolysis. It sets how quickly adipocytes release fatty acids between meals, how much substrate reaches mitochondria and peroxisomes for oxidation, and how plasma triglyceride is cleared; loss of control produces obesity, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridaemia and hepatic steatosis. Hormonal input converges on cyclic AMP and protein kinase A versus insulin-driven PDE3B and AKT signalling, which toggle the lipid droplet surface where perilipins, CIDE proteins and the ABHD5 coactivator gate access of ATGL to stored triacylglycerol. Nuclear receptors such as PPARA and thyroid hormone receptor set oxidative gene capacity, CPT1A controls mitochondrial fatty acid entry, and apolipoprotein modulators including APOC3 and ANGPTL3 tune lipoprotein lipase activity in the circulation. Inflammatory cytokines and energy-sensing AMPK feed into the same decision.

Restraining lipid breakdown is how cells and tissues hold onto stored fuel when it is not needed, and the negative regulation of lipid catabolism is the collection of brakes that do it. In adipocytes this is largely the anti-lipolytic arm of insulin action: insulin signalling through AKT1 activates the cyclic-nucleotide phosphodiesterase PDE3B, lowering cAMP and shutting down protein kinase A-driven lipolysis, while Gi-coupled receptors for adenosine, catecholamines and lactate or ketone bodies (ADORA1, ADRA2A, HCAR1-3) suppress cAMP from the cell surface. Lipid droplet proteins such as PLIN1, PLIN5, CIDEA, CIDEC and seipin shield triglyceride from lipase access and promote droplet growth, and apolipoprotein C3 and related apolipoproteins inhibit lipoprotein lipase in plasma. ACACB restrains fatty acid entry into mitochondria for oxidation by generating malonyl-CoA. Loss of these controls gives unchecked lipolysis, ectopic lipid and dyslipidaemia; several members are also engaged by inflammatory signals such as TNF and IL1B.

Stored and circulating lipids are released and oxidized on demand, and this collection of activators drives that breakdown faster. It matters for fasting and cold adaptation, when adipose triglyceride must be mobilized and fatty acids delivered to mitochondria for energy; loss of such activation favours lipid accumulation, hypertriglyceridaemia and insulin resistance. Adipocyte lipolysis is set by an adrenergic-to-cyclic-AMP route through protein kinase A and by the lipase ATGL together with its coactivator ABHD5 and the lipid droplet scaffold PLIN5. Plasma triglyceride hydrolysis depends on apolipoprotein cofactors such as APOC2 and APOA5 acting on lipoprotein lipase, opposed by ANGPTL3. Downstream, PPARA induces the oxidative programme and CPT1A commits long-chain acyl groups to mitochondrial beta-oxidation, while peroxisomal transporters handle very long-chain substrates. Insulin receptor substrates and inflammatory signals tune the whole output.

Nitric oxide is a short-lived signalling gas that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, tunes neurotransmission and contributes to innate immune killing, so the amount made at any moment is set by control over nitric-oxide synthase rather than by the enzyme alone. This regulation determines endothelial function and blood pressure, and its loss underlies the impaired vasodilation of diabetes, obesity and inflammatory disease. Control acts at several levels: GCH1 sets the supply of tetrahydrobiopterin, the cofactor without which the synthase uncouples and generates superoxide instead of NO; NOSIP binds the enzyme and alters its subcellular localisation and output; hormonal and metabolic inputs including estrogen acting through ESR1, insulin and leptin raise endothelial NO production, while the inflammatory cytokine IL1B drives the inducible form. The result links endocrine, metabolic and immune status to vascular tone.

Microtubule severing cuts filaments internally rather than at their ends, generating new plus and minus ends that can be released, regrown, or amplified. It lets cells remodel a cytoskeleton that would otherwise be too stable to rearrange: releasing microtubules from the centrosome, amplifying arrays in the mitotic spindle, pruning and branching neuronal processes, and clearing filaments during cytokinesis and ciliary turnover. The work is done by AAA ATPases that thread tubulin subunits out of the lattice — katanin, built from a catalytic subunit and its p80 targeting partner, spastin, and fidgetin family enzymes — with tubulin tyrosine ligase‑like glutamylases marking the lattice to tune where and how strongly they cut. Loss of spastin causes hereditary spastic paraplegia, reflecting how dependent long axons are on continual microtubule turnover and transport.

Actin networks have to be taken apart as fast as they are built, and actin filament severing is the step that cuts existing filaments into shorter pieces, creating new ends for depolymerisation or fresh elongation. This turnover sets how quickly a cell can remodel its cortex, extend and retract protrusions, migrate, divide, and rebuild specialised structures such as intestinal microvilli and the sarcomere. Cofilin and its relative destrin bind ADP-actin and sever filaments, while gelsolin-family proteins including gelsolin, scinderin, adseverin-like villin and advillin sever in a calcium-dependent manner and cap the resulting barbed ends; GMFB and GMFG act instead on branched networks by dismantling Arp2/3 junctions. Loss of this disassembly capacity stalls filament recycling, and the pathway's members feature in platelet and immune cell function, epithelial brush border integrity and cardiomyopathy.

Actin filaments grow mainly at their barbed (plus) ends, and capping that end is how a cell decides where and how fast filament elongation stops. Blocking subunit addition and loss keeps networks short and densely branched rather than long and sparse, which is what gives lamellipodia their pushing force, stabilises the erythrocyte membrane skeleton, and builds the brush-border and stereocilia bundles of epithelial and sensory cells. The heterodimeric capping protein formed by CAPZA subunits with CAPZB is the central capper, itself regulated by CARMIL proteins that lower its affinity and allow uncapping; gelsolin-family members such as GSN, CAPG and SCIN sever filaments and cap the new ends in a calcium-dependent manner, while adducins and twinfilins cap and link filaments to spectrin or tune monomer handling. Loss of this control disorganises cell motility, platelet and red cell morphology, and hearing.

Chiasma assembly is the step in meiosis at which a subset of recombination intermediates between homologous chromosomes is designated to mature into a genuine crossover, creating the physical link that holds homologues together until anaphase I. These connections both shuffle parental alleles and provide the tension needed for correct segregation, so failure produces achiasmatic chromosomes, aneuploid gametes, infertility and miscarriage. The genes here act at the interface between the synaptonemal complex and crossover designation: a transverse filament protein of the synaptonemal complex provides the track along paired homologues, a meiosis-specific MutS-family protein stabilises recombination intermediates, and SUMO/ubiquitin ligase activities together with a ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme mark selected sites for crossover maturation. Related factors license double-strand break repair by homologous recombination, tying chiasma formation to DNA repair chemistry operating under meiotic control.

Messenger RNAs are made in the nucleus but used in the cytoplasm, and mRNA transport is the machinery that licenses and carries them across that boundary and then to the places in the cytoplasm where their proteins are needed. Only properly capped, spliced and packaged transcripts are exported, so this step doubles as a quality filter; defective transcripts are instead handed to surveillance factors such as UPF1 and the SMG proteins for degradation. Export runs through the nuclear pore, built here from the many nucleoporins and the Ran-dependent carriers that dock cargo, with the TREX complex and the NXF1-NXT1 receptor loading mRNA and a DEAD-box helicase at the cytoplasmic face releasing it. Downstream, RNA-binding proteins including FMR1, IGF2BPs and ZFP36 direct localisation, translational silencing and turnover, which matters for neuronal dendritic mRNA delivery and for stress responses.

Spliceosomal snRNAs are transcribed in the nucleus but must visit the cytoplasm before they can work, and snRNA transport is the shuttling that makes this possible. Newly made U snRNAs acquire a monomethyl cap that is bound by the nuclear cap-binding complex, whose subunits appear here together with the adaptor PHAX; phosphorylated PHAX links the capped transcript to export machinery and the Ran GTPase gradient provides directionality, delivering the RNA to the cytoplasm. There the Sm protein core is added and the cap is hypermethylated, creating the signal read by snurportin for return to the nucleus, where the assembled snRNPs enter splicing. Because every round of pre-mRNA splicing depends on snRNPs built along this route, defects in the cycle compromise gene expression broadly, and disruption of snRNP biogenesis underlies motor neuron disease.

Transfer RNAs are made in the nucleus but used in the cytoplasm and in mitochondria, so their directed movement across membranes is what links tRNA maturation to protein synthesis. Export from the nucleus depends on a dedicated karyopherin, XPOT, which recognises correctly processed and end-matured tRNA and delivers it to the cytoplasm in a RAN-dependent cycle, giving the cell a quality-control step in which incompletely modified transcripts are retained. La protein (SSB) binds nascent pre-tRNA 3' trailers and protects and chaperones them through processing before release to the export machinery, while YBX1 binds RNA and contributes to cytoplasmic RNA handling and packaging. Import at the mitochondrial surface involves the outer-membrane translocase component TOMM20. Together these steps set the supply of charged tRNA available for translation, and mutations affecting tRNA trafficking constrain the rate and fidelity of protein synthesis.

Endosomes must be kept at a workable size as they receive incoming endocytic cargo, and regulation of endosome size determines whether internalised receptors and membrane are sorted efficiently or pile up in swollen compartments. The pathway sits at the junction of membrane fusion, cargo sorting and organelle positioning: RAB5A is the master switch for early endosome identity and homotypic fusion, ALS2 acts as its activator on endosomal membranes, and CHMP3 contributes to the ESCRT machinery that deforms membrane during intralumenal vesicle formation and scission. Most of the remaining components form the BORC complex together with shared BLOC-1 subunits and snapin, which couples endosomes and lysosomes to microtubule motors so that compartments are dispersed rather than clustered. Loss of this control produces enlarged, mispositioned endosomes and impaired degradative traffic; ALS2 mutation causes juvenile motor neuron disease, linking endosome morphology to neuronal survival.

Many transmembrane proteins are switched off, switched on, or converted into soluble signals by having their extracellular domain clipped away at the cell surface, and this pathway covers the controls placed on that shedding. Its output determines how much soluble TNF, growth factor and cytokine receptor ectodomain reaches the extracellular space, so it sets the strength of inflammatory signalling and, through cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein, the balance of amyloidogenic versus non-amyloidogenic processing. Regulation acts at several levels: TIMP family inhibitors restrain the metalloproteinases directly, tetraspanins such as TSPAN5, TSPAN15 and TSPAN17 chaperone and position sheddases in the membrane, sorting nexins and PACSIN3 couple shedding to membrane trafficking, and cytokines including IFNG, IL1B and IL10 adjust the whole system according to immune context. Dysregulation feeds into chronic inflammation, tissue remodelling and neurodegeneration.

Many receptors, cytokines and adhesion molecules are switched on or off by having their extracellular domain clipped from the membrane, and this pathway covers the inputs that increase the rate of such ectodomain shedding. Its output is soluble signalling: release of TNF and TNF receptors, growth factor ligands and cleaved adhesion proteins, which converts a cell-surface state into a diffusible one and terminates or propagates inflammatory signalling. Sheddase activity itself resides in membrane metalloproteinases such as ADAM8 and ADAM9, while proprotein convertase processing by FURIN licenses those enzymes, and inflammatory mediators including TNF, IL1B and IFNG stimulate the process. Scaffolding and endocytic proteins of the SH3-domain and sorting nexin families position sheddases at the membrane and control their trafficking. The same cleavage chemistry acts on APP, linking regulated shedding to amyloid generation, and unrestrained shedding drives chronic inflammation.</br>

Many membrane proteins are activated or switched off by shedding: a protease clips the extracellular domain and releases it as a soluble ligand or decoy. Restraining that shedding keeps receptors, adhesion molecules and cytokine precursors anchored at the surface, and its loss contributes to inflammatory tissue damage, matrix turnover and tumour invasion. The dominant brake here is the TIMP family of endogenous inhibitors, which bind metalloproteinases and ADAM-type sheddases stoichiometrically; TIMP3 in particular curbs TNF-alpha converting activity and is tethered to the extracellular matrix. Other routes act on the cell itself — an anti-inflammatory cytokine lowers sheddase activity transcriptionally, a tyrosine phosphatase and a LRIG-family transmembrane protein modulate receptor availability, and Rho-associated kinase links cytoskeletal contractility to cleavage. Together these set how much ectodomain release a tissue permits.

Cells release hormones, neurotransmitters, digestive enzymes, cytokines and mucus on demand rather than continuously, and this pathway covers the controls that set how much is released and when. It spans the machinery of regulated exocytosis — SNAREs such as SNAP25, VAMP2 and syntaxins, the priming factors STXBP1 and UNC13 proteins, calcium sensors of the synaptotagmin and complexin families, and Rab GTPases that dock and tether secretory granules — together with the upstream inputs that tune them: G protein-coupled receptors for monoamines, opioids and peptides, ATP-sensitive and voltage-gated potassium and calcium channels, cyclic AMP and protein kinase C cascades, and transcription factors and circadian components that set secretory capacity over longer timescales. Glucose-stimulated insulin release from beta cells, neuropeptide and pituitary hormone output, and inflammatory mediator degranulation all depend on it, and its dysregulation contributes to diabetes, endocrine disorders and neurotransmission defects.

Cells export hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines, enzymes and mucosal factors on demand, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that turn that release up. It underlies glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, hypothalamic and pituitary hormone release, neurotransmitter output at synapses, degranulation by mast cells, platelets and neutrophils, and cytokine release during inflammation.
