Upstream, G protein-coupled receptors for adenosine, purines, tachykinins, fatty acids and neuropeptides feed into cAMP-dependent kinases, protein kinase C, calcineurin and calcium entry through channels and transporters. Downstream, calcium sensors such as synaptotagmins and DOC2 proteins, priming factors of the UNC13 and CADPS families, Rab GTPases and SNARE complexes with STXBP1 drive vesicle tethering, priming and fusion; exosome release via ESCRT components is also represented. Transcription factors including PDX1, NKX6-1 and NEUROD1 set secretory competence, and their loss causes diabetes and endocrine failure.

negative regulation of secretion collects the brakes on regulated release of hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and fluid, ensuring that exocytosis is switched off as well as on. Restraint of this kind sets the tone of endocrine and synaptic output: without it, insulin release becomes unrestrained hypoglycaemia, immune cells over-release inflammatory mediators, and neurotransmission loses its presynaptic gain control. The genes represent several layers of inhibition. Inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors coupled through GNAI2/GNAO1 -- adrenergic alpha-2, dopamine D2-like, opioid, somatostatin-like and GABA-B receptors -- lower cyclic AMP and calcium entry; ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits KCNJ11 and ABCC8 hyperpolarise beta cells to close off granule fusion; synaptotagmins, syntaxin-binding proteins and RAB11 effectors act on the vesicle machinery itself. Adipokines, inhibins, and inhibitory immune receptors add endocrine and paracrine feedback, and several microRNAs damp secretory gene expression transcriptionally.

Secretion is as tightly restrained as it is triggered, and this collection covers the braking mechanisms that stop, slow or limit the controlled release of hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and other substances from cells and tissues. Such restraint sets basal tone: it keeps insulin release matched to glucose, damps neurotransmitter output at presynaptic terminals, and holds inflammatory mediator release in check so that immune activation resolves. Much of the work runs through inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors, including adrenergic alpha-2, dopamine D2-class, opioid, GABA-B and somatostatin-like receptors, which act via Gi/Go subunits to lower cyclic AMP and calcium entry. Potassium channels and the sulfonylurea receptor subunit of the ATP-sensitive channel hyperpolarize secretory cells, while synaptotagmins, VAMPs and Rab11 effectors constrain vesicle fusion and recycling. Additional layers come from peptide hormones such as leptin and inhibins, binding proteins, and microRNAs. Loss of these controls underlies hyperinsulinism, endocrine excess and unchecked cytokine release.

Cells constantly tune how fast and how much material moves across membranes, along the cytoskeleton, and between compartments, and this regulatory layer sits on top of the transporters, channels, pumps and vesicle machinery themselves. It determines how a neuron sets its excitability and releases neurotransmitter, how a beta cell couples glucose sensing to insulin exocytosis, how cholesterol and lipoproteins are loaded and cleared, and how ions and water are handled in kidney, heart and epithelia. Control is exerted through kinases and phosphatases, calcium and cyclic nucleotide second messengers, auxiliary and beta subunits that modify channel gating, G protein-coupled receptors and their arrestins, Rab and SNARE regulators that direct vesicle docking and fusion, endocytic adaptors that set surface transporter density, ubiquitin ligases that trigger internalisation and degradation, and transcriptional and microRNA programmes. Dysregulation underlies arrhythmia, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and neurological channelopathies.

This is a broad regulatory grouping: gene products that increase the rate or extent of substance movement across membranes, through the cytoplasm, or between cells. It covers the positive control arms of ion homeostasis, hormone and neurotransmitter release, vesicle traffic and nutrient uptake, and so underlies excitability, endocrine responses and secretory output. Mechanistically it spans calcium signalling components such as STIM1 and ORAI1 that drive store-operated entry, synaptotagmins, syntaxins and VAMPs that execute calcium-triggered exocytosis, dynein subunits and Rab GTPases that direct motor-based and endosomal transport, COPII coat subunits and SEC-family proteins that raise ER export capacity, and many receptors, kinases and transcription factors (insulin, adrenergic, purinergic and peptide receptors; PKA and PKC subunits) that act upstream to stimulate transporters and channels. Also included are lipid transfer and ABC transporter activators governing cholesterol efflux and iron handling, processes whose failure produces metabolic, neurological and secretory disease.

negative regulation of transport collects the braking mechanisms that limit how much material moves across membranes, along secretory routes, or between cells. Restraint of this kind sets resting membrane potential, caps hormone and neurotransmitter release, terminates signalling after a stimulus, and keeps lipid and ion loads within physiological range; its loss underlies arrhythmia, hyperinsulinism, hypertension and excitotoxic neuronal damage. The genes span several distinct brakes: inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors and their Gi/Go transducers that suppress calcium channel opening and exocytosis, small regulatory peptides such as phospholamban and sarcolipin that inhibit SERCA calcium pumping, KCNE subunits and WNK-OSR1/SPAK kinases that damp potassium and chloride flux, ubiquitin ligases including NEDD4L that remove transporters from the surface, ERAD and sorting nexin components that divert cargo from delivery, and numerous microRNAs that lower transporter expression. Sterol sensors such as INSIG1 and SREBF add feedback control over lipid uptake.

Transport across membranes and between compartments is not simply switched on; it is actively damped, and this collection of brakes on transport covers the mechanisms that stop, slow or restrict the movement of ions, lipids, sugars, neurotransmitters and cargo vesicles. Such restraint sets excitability and secretory tone: potassium channel subunits and their modulators limit repolarizing current, calcium-handling inhibitors such as phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin hold back sarcoplasmic reticulum pumping, and G protein-coupled receptors for catecholamines, opioids and neuropeptides suppress presynaptic release. Other arms work by disposal and retrieval — ubiquitin ligases including NEDD4 and NEDD4L mark surface transporters for removal, sorting nexins and retromer redirect them, and WNK–OXSR1/STK39 kinases reset ion cotransport. Sterol sensors, insulin-signalling adaptors and many microRNAs impose transcriptional and post-transcriptional limits. Loss of this restraint produces arrhythmia, hyperexcitability, salt-handling defects and metabolic dysregulation.

Cells must control how fast and how faithfully their DNA is copied, repaired, recombined and packaged, and this regulatory layer sets the rate and extent of those DNA metabolic reactions. It determines whether replication origins fire on schedule, whether a damaged fork is protected or collapses, which repair pathway is chosen at a double-strand break, and how long telomeres remain. Loss of this control produces genome instability, the mutational burden behind cancer, and premature ageing syndromes. The machinery spans damage sensors and checkpoint kinases such as ATM, ATR and CHEK1 acting through p53 and CDK inhibitors; ubiquitin and SUMO ligases that mark chromatin around breaks; chromatin remodellers and histone-modifying complexes including INO80, SWI/SNF-type and NuA4-type assemblies that open templates; replication licensing factors; telomere-capping proteins; and mismatch, base-excision and nucleotide-excision repair components whose activity is tuned rather than simply switched on.

negative regulation of DNA metabolic process collects the brakes on DNA transactions — the mechanisms that limit replication, recombination, repair and telomere elongation so that genome maintenance does not itself become a source of instability. It matters because unrestrained activity is as dangerous as too little: re-replication, illegitimate recombination, or runaway telomerase all produce chromosomal rearrangements and cancer. The genes describe several distinct restraints. Licensing inhibitors such as geminin and CDT1 antagonists prevent origins from firing twice per cycle, while p53 and CDKN1A halt replication after damage. Shelterin components and the CST complex cap chromosome ends and block nuclease and telomerase access. The shieldin–RIF1–53BP1 module suppresses resection to steer double-strand breaks away from homologous recombination, and helicases and structure-specific nucleases dissolve or restrain recombination intermediates. Linker histones and chromatin modifiers add a further layer by limiting access to DNA itself.

DNA transactions are as tightly restrained as they are promoted, and this collection captures the braking side: processes that limit or block DNA replication, recombination, repair and telomere extension. Restraint matters because unchecked activity is mutagenic — re-replication, illegitimate recombination between repeats, unscheduled resection of broken ends, or runaway telomerase all destabilise the genome and drive cancer and premature ageing. Licensing inhibitors such as geminin and the CDT1/CDC6-directed degradation machinery ensure origins fire once per cycle; the shelterin complex with POT1, TERF1/2 and the CST components caps chromosome ends and prevents their recognition as damage; 53BP1 with the shieldin subunits and RIF1 blocks end resection to channel breaks away from homologous recombination; helicases including BLM, RECQL5 and FBH1 dismantle recombination intermediates. p53, CDKN1A, ATM and ATR impose the checkpoint arrest that halts replication until repair is complete.

This grouping collects the activators that raise the rate or extent of DNA transactions — replication, recombination, repair, telomere maintenance and chromatin-templated access to the genome. Its output is a genome that can be copied on schedule and mended after damage; loss of these stimulatory inputs produces replication stress, unrepaired breaks, telomere attrition and the mutability that underlies cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Much of the work is chromatin remodelling and histone modification that opens damaged or replicating DNA: SWI/SNF subunits such as SMARCA4 and ARID1A, the INO80 and TIP60/EP400 complexes with their RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases, and acetyltransferase KAT5. Damage sensing and signalling run through ATM, ATR and PRKDC with the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex, RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin marks and 53BP1–shieldin control of end resection. Replication licensing and clamp loading factors, shelterin components including POT1 and TERF2, and growth-factor and cytokine signals that drive cells into S phase also feed in.

negative regulation of lipid biosynthetic process is the braking system on fat, sterol and sphingolipid production, holding synthesis in check when supply is sufficient so that cells do not accumulate toxic lipid loads. Its failure underlies hypercholesterolaemia, hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance. The core sterol-sensing arm works through INSIG1/INSIG2 retaining SCAP-SREBP in the ER and through MARCHF6- and ERLIN-mediated degradation of HMG-CoA reductase, while bile acid feedback via FGF19 and CYP7A1 limits sterol turnover. Energy sensing by AMPK and SIRT1, ubiquitin ligases such as FBXW7 and COP1 acting on lipogenic transcription factors, and ORMDL proteins restraining sphingolipid synthesis add parallel restraints. Secreted apolipoproteins and ANGPTL4 feed back on lipid handling, and a large set of microRNAs, notably miR-33a paired with SREBF, tunes lipogenic transcripts post-transcriptionally, linking this control to whole-body energy balance.

Lipid synthesis is expensive and potentially toxic, so cells maintain brakes on it; this is the collected set of processes that stop or slow the formation of sterols, fatty acids, triglycerides and sphingolipids. Restraint here keeps membrane cholesterol within range, limits hepatic lipogenesis and VLDL output, and prevents the steatosis, hyperlipidaemia and lipotoxic stress that follow when lipogenic drive goes unchecked. Mechanisms are varied: INSIG1 and INSIG2 retain SCAP-SREBP in the endoplasmic reticulum so sterol synthesis genes are not induced, while MARCHF6 and the ERLIN proteins direct degradation of HMG-CoA reductase; ORMDL proteins damp serine palmitoyltransferase and hence ceramide production. Energy and nutrient sensors such as PRKAA1 and SIRT1, secreted regulators including ANGPTL4, APOE and FGF19, transcriptional repressors, and lipogenesis-targeting microRNAs such as MIR33A add hormonal and feedback layers, tying the pathway to whole-body energy balance and bile acid control.

Small GTPases of the Ras, Rho, Arf, Rab and Ral families cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and this pathway covers the regulators that set how fast and how strongly they signal. Because these switches control cell shape and motility, adhesion, cytokinesis, membrane traffic and growth-factor-driven proliferation, their regulators determine whether a cell migrates, divides or differentiates. Guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as the Vav, Trio, DOCK and cytohesin proteins load GTP; GTPase-activating proteins including the many ARHGAP members, NF1, TSC2 and RASA family proteins accelerate hydrolysis and switch signalling off; guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors like ARHGDIA sequester inactive Rho proteins in the cytosol. Upstream receptors, integrins and adaptors feed into these regulators, and loss of GAP function underlies neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis and widespread oncogenic Ras and Rho activation.

positive regulation of small GTPase mediated signal transduction covers the inputs that switch Ras- and Rho-family GTPases into their active, GTP-bound state, converting receptor engagement at the cell surface into cytoskeletal remodelling, growth and migration. Because these GTPases sit at the head of the MAPK and PI3K cascades, this activating layer determines how strongly cells respond to growth factors and guidance cues, and its hyperactivation through mutant HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, or through amplified ERBB2, underlies much of human cancer. The genes span receptor tyrosine kinases and their adaptors GRB2, CRK and SOS1, guanine nucleotide exchange factors of the Dbl and RasGRP families, and G protein-coupled receptors for lysophosphatidic acid, thrombin and chemokines. Prominent among the outputs are axon guidance and neuronal morphogenesis, via semaphorin, Robo, reelin and Nogo receptor signalling onto RAC1, along with integrin-dependent adhesion and immune cell trafficking.

Small GTPases of the Ras and Rho families act as switches that cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and the processes gathered here push that switch toward the active form, amplifying small GTPase mediated signal transduction. The output shapes cell proliferation, cytoskeletal remodelling, adhesion, migration and axon guidance, which is why the same components recur in developmental patterning and in cancer, where mutant HRAS, KRAS and NRAS lock the switch on. Activation is largely the work of guanine nucleotide exchange factors — SOS1, RASGRF1, RASGRP1 and Rho-directed exchange factors such as ARHGEF3 and MCF2L — recruited to receptors by adaptors including GRB2, CRK and SRC. Upstream triggers are diverse: growth factor and neurotrophin receptors, integrins and laminin contacts, chemokine and protease-activated receptors, and guidance cues acting through plexin, ROBO1 and reelin signalling.</br>

Small GTPases of the Ras and Rho families act as switches that are on only while bound to GTP, so shutting them off is as much a part of their signalling as turning them on. This collection of negative regulators sets the duration and spatial limits of that signalling, and its loss produces unrestrained growth signalling, disordered actin remodelling and defective cell migration. The bulk of the work is done by GTPase-activating proteins that accelerate GTP hydrolysis – numerous Rho-directed ARHGAPs, DLC1 and SH3BP1 among them, alongside Ras-directed RASA family members, SYNGAP1 and neurofibromin. Others act indirectly: Sprouty proteins dampen receptor input to Ras, LZTR1 with CUL3 targets RAS proteins for ubiquitin-dependent turnover, and RIPOR proteins sequester active RHOA. Failure at these nodes underlies neurofibromatosis, Noonan syndrome and intellectual disability, and contributes broadly to tumour progression.

Transcription factors are rarely constitutively active; their output is set by upstream kinases, ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, cofactors and inhibitory binding partners, and this pathway collects the processes that modulate DNA-binding transcription factor activity. It matters because it is the step at which extracellular signals become changes in gene expression, and because its dysregulation drives chronic inflammation and tumour growth. Much of the content is NF-κB control: Toll-like and IL-18 receptors acting through MYD88 and IRAK1, the IKK subunits IKBKB and IKBKG, TRAF adaptors, and restraining deubiquitinases such as CYLD and OTULIN, alongside inflammasome components including NLRP3, NOD2 and PYCARD that couple danger sensing to cytokine induction. Other members set activity in different registers — nuclear receptors ESR1 and ESR2, CREB coactivators CRTC1/2, clock and heat-shock proteins, acetyltransferase EP300, the deacetylase SIRT1, and ID proteins that sequester bHLH factors such as NEUROD1 and NEUROG2 during neuronal differentiation.

This grouping covers the upstream events that switch transcription factors on, converting receptor engagement and stress signals into new gene expression. The dominant theme is NF- inkappaB activation: Toll-like and IL-18 receptors feed through MYD88, IRAK1 and TRAF adaptors to the IKK complex (CHUK, IKBKB, IKBKG), with CARD-domain scaffolds, RIPK kinases and linear ubiquitin ligases (RBCK1, RNF31) plus the UBE2N conjugating enzyme shaping the signal, and inflammasome sensors such as NLRP3, NLRC4 and AIM2 acting alongside via PYCARD. Other arms activate CREB through adenylate cyclases and CRTC coactivators, MEF/SRF-type and ATF2 responses through MAP kinase-activated kinases, and nuclear receptors ESR1 and ESR2. Basic helix-loop-helix factors including NEUROG1/2 and NEUROD1/2 tie the same logic to neuronal differentiation. These steps determine inflammatory output, cell survival and developmental commitment, and their deregulation underlies chronic inflammation and tumourigenesis.

NF-kappaB is the transcriptional switch that converts danger signals into inflammatory, survival and immune gene expression, and this grouping covers the inputs and relays that turn it on. Pattern recognition receptors and cytokine receptors at the top of the cascade — Toll-like receptors, intracellular NOD sensors, and the IL-18 receptor chains — recruit MYD88 and IRAK1, while antigen receptor signalling in lymphocytes passes through protein kinase C isoforms into the CARD11–BCL10 module. These converge on TRAF adaptors and non-degradative ubiquitin chains built by UBE2N and the LUBAC components RNF31 and RBCK1, which activate the IKK complex of CHUK, IKBKB and IKBKG to free NF-kappaB from its inhibitor. Inflammasome components such as NLRP3, AIM2 and PYCARD tie the same circuitry to IL-18 and TNF output. Persistent activation sustains chronic inflammation and tumour cell survival.

Development requires brakes as much as drivers, and this collection gathers the activities that stop, delay or limit developmental progression — holding progenitors undifferentiated, restricting how far a tissue grows, and shutting a programme off once a structure is complete. Without such negative regulation, differentiation happens in the wrong place or at the wrong time, organs overgrow, and the same restraints lost in embryos are lost again in tumours. The mechanisms are broad: secreted antagonists of morphogen signalling such as noggin, chordin, follistatin, DKK and SFRP family members; inhibitory HES, ID and SNAI transcriptional repressors; chromatin repressors including Polycomb, histone deacetylases and Sin3/NuRD components; Hippo kinases and SPRED/SPRY dampeners of growth factor kinase cascades; cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors; guidance cues such as semaphorins and ephrins that halt axon and cell migration; and many microRNAs that clamp differentiation transcripts post-transcriptionally.

Grouped here are the gene products that push development forward — that initiate, accelerate or extend the programmes turning a zygote into a patterned embryo and progenitors into differentiated tissue. Their collective output is organogenesis and lineage commitment: neurons, muscle, bone, blood, vasculature and immune cells all depend on such positive regulation, and its misfiring underlies congenital malformation syndromes and the re-activation of growth programmes in cancer. The membership spans the classic inductive signalling families — Wnt, Hedgehog, Notch, BMP/TGF-beta with their SMAD transducers, FGF and receptor tyrosine kinases, ephrins and semaphorins — together with lineage transcription factors such as MYOD1, NEUROD1, RUNX2, GATA and SOX proteins, chromatin remodellers of the SWI/SNF class, and many microRNAs that set the timing and amplitude of these decisions. Also present are cytokines, growth factors and extracellular matrix components through which one cell population promotes the differentiation, growth or morphogenesis of its neighbours.

Molecular interactions are not left to chance: cells actively tune how readily one molecule engages a specific site on another, and this regulation of binding is the layer that decides whether a transcription factor reaches its response element, whether a receptor engages its ligand, and whether a protein complex assembles at all. The genes here act at many such interfaces. Transcriptional regulators including E2F1, RB1, JUN, GATA3, LEF1 and RARA are controlled at the level of DNA and cofactor occupancy, with general initiation factors and chromatin modifiers such as DOT1L, NSD1, KDM4D and HMGB1 altering the accessibility of the template. Others govern adhesion and cytoskeletal engagement, ubiquitin and SUMO conjugation, or protease and complement inhibition. Because binding affinity sets the threshold for signalling output, its modulation shapes proliferation control, differentiation decisions and inflammatory responses, and its loss produces inappropriate pathway activation.

Molecular interactions are not left to chance: cells actively promote the binding of one macromolecule to another, and this collection covers factors that increase the rate or extent of such selective interactions. Much of the activity is nuclear and transcriptional, where coactivators and general factors such as MED25, GTF2B and EDF1 help transcription factors engage promoters, while chromatin and DNA-binding proteins including HMGB1, histone H1-0 and the demethylase KDM4D alter how readily regulators reach their sites. Lineage regulators such as GATA3, FOXC1, RARA and HES1 depend on these enhanced contacts to specify cell identity, and RB1 and GSK3B link the same principle to cell cycle arrest and kinase signalling. Other members act outside the nucleus, promoting ligand-receptor and adhesion interactions, as with EGF, IGF1, BMP4, MMP9 and the urokinase receptor PLAUR, connecting facilitated binding to growth control, immunity and tissue remodelling.

Molecular interactions are as often controlled by being blocked as by being made, and this grouping collects the proteins that stop or reduce the binding of one molecule to another. The tactics are varied: decoy and pseudo-substrate proteins such as the caspase-1-inhibiting CARD16 and CARD18 occupy interaction surfaces without productive output; complement factor H-related proteins compete for the regulatory sites on C3b and so tune how strongly the complement cascade attacks a surface; STYX is a catalytically dead phosphatase fold that sequesters partners rather than dephosphorylating them; WAPL releases cohesin's hold on DNA. Others limit transcription factor occupancy of promoters or displace cofactors, as in the E2F1, JUN, LEF1 and HMGA2 arms, or restrict receptor-ligand engagement in interleukin-6 family and integrin signalling. Collectively these steps set thresholds, terminate responses, and prevent inappropriate complex assembly in signalling, chromosome dynamics and immune regulation.

Regulation of DNA binding covers the controls that determine whether a DNA-binding protein actually engages chromatin, and how strongly and for how long. This is the layer that lets a cell change transcriptional output without changing its transcription factor repertoire, and it sets the timing of proliferation, differentiation and stress responses; its failure contributes to unchecked cell cycle entry and to tumour-associated gene expression programmes. The mechanisms represented include redox control of factor binding by thioredoxin, cofactor sequestration such as RB1 restraining E2F1, IkB-like modulation of NF-kB activity by BCL3, chromatin remodelling and histone methylation by RSF1, DOT1L and NSD1, linker histone and HMG-box proteins that alter DNA accessibility and bending, and covalent marks including sumoylation and deacetylation. Also present are lineage factors such as GATA3, LEF1, SOX11 and POU-domain proteins whose own binding is the regulated output.

This grouping covers the control layer that sets how readily proteins engage DNA, tuning transcription factor occupancy rather than carrying out transcription itself. Because a factor's affinity for chromatin determines which genes are heard, this regulation shapes lineage decisions, proliferation control and stress responses, and its loss contributes to developmental malformation and cancer. Several routes are represented: redox and cofactor modulation of factor binding, as by thioredoxin acting on AP-1 components such as JUN; architectural and chromatin proteins including HMGB1, HMGA2, linker histone H1-0 and the remodelling subunit RSF1 that alter DNA accessibility; histone methyltransferases DOT1L and NSD1 that mark the template; and inhibitory partners such as RB1, which restrains E2F1, and the co-repressor SKI. Also present are lineage factors GATA3, LEF1, SOX11, FOXC1 and POU4F1/2 whose own binding is subject to this control, together with the general initiation factor GTF2B.

Hepoxilins are epoxy-hydroxy fatty acid signals derived from arachidonic acid that act on ion transport, insulin secretion, inflammatory cell recruitment and vascular tone, and their synthesis also feeds the lipid processing that builds the skin's permeability barrier. Their biosynthesis begins with lipoxygenase oxygenation of arachidonate to a hydroperoxy intermediate, which is then converted by hydroperoxide isomerase activity into the epoxy alcohol; the 12- and 15-lipoxygenases in this route and the epidermis-restricted lipoxygenase-3 provide these successive steps, the latter acting mainly as an isomerase on the product of its partner enzyme. Glutathione transferases of the mu and pi classes attach glutathione to the epoxide, generating hepoxilin conjugates and terminating or redirecting signalling. Loss of the epidermal arm of this pathway causes congenital ichthyosis, tying these eicosanoids directly to keratinocyte differentiation and barrier formation.

Every protein-coding gene must be read by RNA polymerase II, and assembly of the preinitiation complex is the step that decides where and when that reading starts. Promoter recognition begins with TBP and its associated factors in TFIID, joined by TFIIA, TFIIB and TFIIE, which together position the polymerase on the template strand, open a DNA bubble and license synthesis of the first nucleotides before promoter escape. The Mediator complex, represented here by its head, middle, tail and kinase-associated subunits, bridges promoter-bound activators to this machinery and converts regulatory input into initiation rate; the NC2 heterodimer of DR1 and DRAP1 restrains TBP to damp basal transcription. Sequence-specific factors such as p53, CREB1 and nuclear receptors act through these surfaces, so the complex is the common endpoint of signalling that changes gene expression, and mutations in its subunits cause developmental and intellectual disability syndromes.

The neuromuscular junction is the synapse through which motor neurons command skeletal muscle, and its assembly is what aligns presynaptic transmitter release sites with acetylcholine receptor clusters on the muscle fibre. Without it, nerve and muscle fail to couple, producing fetal akinesia, arthrogryposis, and congenital myasthenic weakness. Motor-neuron-derived agrin binds the muscle surface receptor LRP4, which activates the kinase MUSK to nucleate receptor clustering; dystroglycan and its glycosyltransferase LARGE1 anchor the synaptic basal lamina, where COLQ tethers acetylcholinesterase to terminate transmission. A ubiquitin arm built around MYCBP2, FBXO45 and SKP1 restrains and refines synapse formation and axon terminal growth, while LIN7 scaffolds with PDZD11 organise membrane protein complexes at the postsynaptic specialisation and SIX1/SIX4 supply the myogenic transcriptional context. The pathway sits at the intersection of synaptogenesis, muscle differentiation and extracellular matrix organisation.

New actin filaments do not appear spontaneously; cells decide where and when branched networks are born, and the regulation of actin nucleation is how that decision is enforced. It sets the pace of lamellipodial protrusion, cell migration, endosomal sorting tubule formation and membrane remodelling, and its misregulation distorts cell shape, adhesion and neuronal morphogenesis. Most of the machinery here converges on the Arp2/3 complex through its nucleation-promoting factors: WAVE family members with their regulatory partners CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2 and BRK1, the endosomal WASH complex with its WASHC subunits, and WHAMM at Golgi and autophagic membranes. Opposing them are inhibitors and disassembly factors, including ARPIN, the glia maturation factor debranching proteins GMFB and GMFG, and coronins, while gelsolin and scinderin sever filaments and CARMIL proteins control capping protein availability. Small GTPase and Arf-associated components link nucleation to membrane traffic.

negative regulation of actin nucleation is the braking system on new actin filament formation, restraining the Arp2/3 complex and related nucleators so that branched filament networks are built only where and when they are needed. This restraint sets the limits of lamellipodial protrusion, keeps cell migration directional rather than uncontrolled, and allows existing networks to be disassembled and their subunits recycled. ARPIN binds and inhibits Arp2/3 directly, opposing WAVE-driven activation at the leading edge, while coronins and the GMF proteins displace or debranch Arp2/3 from filament junctions and promote turnover. Others act locally at membranes and junctions: HIP1R links the network to clathrin-coated pits, PICK1 dampens nucleation in trafficking compartments, and alpha-catenin restrains branching at cadherin contacts. Loss of this braking activity produces excess protrusion, impaired chemotaxis, and defective endocytosis and immune cell motility.

Cells build actin filaments to move, divide and shape membranes, and they need brakes on that process just as much as accelerators; this is the negative arm of actin nucleation control, damping the birth of new filaments and branches. Most of the genes here converge on the Arp2/3 complex, which nucleates branched networks at the leading edge: ARPIN and PICK1 bind and inhibit it directly, the coronins CORO1A and CORO1B restrain branch formation and promote debranching, and the GMFB/GMFG glia maturation factors dissociate existing branch junctions. HIP1R links actin to clathrin-coated pits, where restraining nucleation shapes endocytic geometry. Without such inhibition, lamellipodial protrusion becomes unpolarised and cells lose directional migration — relevant to immune cell chemotaxis, where coronin loss causes T cell immunodeficiency, and to the invasive motility of tumour cells.

New actin filaments do not form spontaneously at useful rates, so cells rely on activators that seed them where and when they are needed; positive regulation of actin nucleation is the step that sets the pace of lamellipodial protrusion, membrane remodelling and cell migration. Most of the genes here build or activate the WAVE regulatory complex — the WASF proteins with CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2 and BRK1 — which relays Rac and phospholipid signals to the Arp2/3 complex to generate branched networks at the leading edge. WHAMM couples nucleation to membrane tubulation in the early secretory and autophagic pathways, while gelsolin and scinderin sever and cap filaments, creating free ends that serve as nucleation sites. Loss of this control blunts chemotaxis, wound closure, phagocytosis and neuronal process outgrowth, and CYFIP1 and MAGEL2 link the same machinery to neurodevelopmental disorders.

Cells build and dismantle structures constantly, and this collection covers the braking side of that activity: processes that block, slow or limit the assembly, arrangement or disassembly of cellular structures. The restraint is what gives structural change direction and timing. Several themes are visible. Actin filaments are capped and severed by capping protein subunits, gelsolin, cofilin, twinfilin and tropomodulins, while Rho-family GAPs and inhibitory regulators of the Arp2/3 machinery suppress branched network growth. Microtubules are destabilized by stathmins and regulated by dynein subunits and katanin-associated factors. Axon growth is held back by the repulsive cues of the semaphorin, ephrin, slit and Nogo receptor families, which collapse growth cones and limit regeneration after injury. Spindle assembly checkpoint components restrain chromosome segregation, and autophagy and telomere regulators impose further limits. Loss of such constraint underlies uncontrolled migration, aneuploidy and disordered neuronal wiring.

Cells constantly build, remodel and take apart internal structures, and this grouping collects the regulators that push those events forward — the positive arm of control over cellular component organization. Its reach is broad: actin nucleation and branching through the Arp2/3 complex with WASP-family activators and Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1, RHOA and CDC42; microtubule and centrosome behaviour via plus-end trackers, katanin regulators and polo-like kinases; spindle assembly, chromosome condensation and cytokinesis; endosomal sorting, autophagosome formation and mitochondrial fission through dynamin-related machinery; and synapse assembly driven by neurexin–neuroligin and leucine-rich repeat adhesion molecules. Many members are receptors and ligands — ephrin receptors, neurotrophin receptors, Wnts, BMPs and TGF-beta — that translate extracellular cues into structural change, so the biology sits at the junction of signalling and morphogenesis. It underlies cell migration, neurite outgrowth, immune cell shape change, and tissue remodelling in development, wound repair and tumour invasion.

Many multi-subunit machines cannot self-assemble at useful rates in the crowded cytosol, and chaperone-mediated protein complex assembly is the set of activities that bring their subunits together and then step away, leaving no chaperone in the finished product. It underlies the biogenesis of the proteasome, the BBSome that traffics cargo in cilia, respiratory chain complexes, and the folding of newly made cytoskeletal and signalling proteins. Dedicated assembly chaperones such as PSMG1-PSMG3 template proteasome core particle formation, while BBS10, BBS12 and MKKS form a chaperonin-like module whose mutation causes Bardet-Biedl syndrome and obesity. HSP90 paralogues with their co-chaperone p23, HSPA1A, the HSPD1 mitochondrial chaperonin and the CCT/prefoldin system handle general client folding, and the ubiquitin ligase STUB1 diverts terminally misfolded clients to degradation instead of assembly.

Natural killer T cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity, responding rapidly to lipid antigen and to cytokine cues with a burst of interferon-gamma and IL-4 that shapes downstream antibody, antitumour and antimicrobial responses. Activation here is the switch from a resting cell to a cytotoxic, cytokine-secreting one, and it depends on two convergent inputs: antigen receptor engagement relayed by the kinase LCK and adaptors, and inflammatory cytokine signalling through IL-12, IL-18, IL-15 and IL-23 with their cognate receptor chains. Surface receptors of the NKR-P1/CLEC2 and NCR3 families read stress-induced ligands such as CLEC2D and NCR3LG1 on target cells, while CD300A and RASAL3 restrain the response. ZBTB7B and ELF4 act transcriptionally to specify and sustain the lineage, and MYC supports the proliferative expansion. Defects skew tumour surveillance and tip the balance toward autoimmune or allergic inflammation.

Natural killer T cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity, responding within minutes to lipid antigens presented on CD1d and releasing large bursts of IFN-γ and IL-4 that set the tone of a subsequent immune response. The processes gathered here tune how readily those cells are switched on, and hence how strongly downstream inflammation, tumour surveillance and antimicrobial defence proceed. Much of the control is cytokine-driven: IL-12, composed of the p35 and p40 subunits, acts through the IL12RB1/IL12RB2 receptor pair, with IL-18 and IL-23 providing additional co-stimulatory input toward IFN-γ production. Counter-regulation comes from inhibitory surface receptors such as CD300A, while ZBTB7B shapes the lineage and effector character of the cells themselves and RASAL3 restrains Ras signalling downstream of antigen receptor engagement. Excessive activation contributes to inflammatory tissue injury; blunted activation weakens early tumour and pathogen control.

Natural killer T cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity, responding within hours to lipid antigens presented on CD1d and releasing large bursts of interferon-gamma and other cytokines that shape downstream T cell and macrophage responses. Signals that raise the frequency or extent of NK T cell activation therefore set the tone of early antitumour and antimicrobial immunity, and unchecked they contribute to autoimmune and inflammatory tissue damage. The dominant input here is heterodimeric cytokine signalling: IL-12 acting through its receptor chains IL12RB1 and IL12RB2, the related IL-23 with its own receptor, and IL-18 acting cooperatively to drive interferon-gamma output. RASAL3, a Ras GTPase-activating protein expressed in lymphocytes, links the pathway to antigen-receptor-proximal Ras signalling, while HSPH1 chaperone activity supports the response. Together these define how accessory cytokines from dendritic cells and macrophages license NK T effector function.

Natural killer T cells are an unconventional lineage that recognises lipid antigens presented on CD1d and responds rapidly with cytokines that shape downstream innate and adaptive immunity. Control over how many of these cells are made, and how far their maturation proceeds, is exerted at several levels. Transcriptional regulators set the programme: ZBTB16 drives acquisition of the innate-like effector phenotype, PRDM1 restrains effector differentiation and cytokine output, and ZNF683 contributes to the tissue-resident and cytotoxic character of these cells. Signalling input from transforming growth factor beta, received through TGFBR2, tunes thymic development and survival of the lineage. The adaptor protein 3 complex subunits act earlier in the process, in lysosomal trafficking needed for lipid antigen loading onto CD1d, so that thymocytes receive the selecting signal at all. Loss of these controls reduces or skews the NK T compartment and blunts early antitumour and antimicrobial responses.

Natural killer T cells bridge innate and adaptive immunity, responding rapidly to lipid antigens presented on CD1d and releasing large bursts of IFN-γ and IL-4; controlling how many of them expand determines how strong that early response is. The genes here set that limit from two directions. Secreted IL-12 (a heterodimer of IL12A and IL12B), IL-18 and IL-23 act through their receptor chains IL12RB1, IL12RB2 and IL23R to drive STAT-dependent activation and outgrowth of NKT populations, linking myeloid cytokine output to lymphocyte number. ZBTB7B is a transcription factor governing thymic agonist-selection decisions that generate the invariant NKT lineage, while RASAL3 is a Ras GTPase-activating protein whose loss disturbs NKT development and homeostasis. Too little proliferative control weakens antitumour and antimicrobial surveillance; excess contributes to cytokine-driven inflammatory and autoimmune pathology.

Smooth muscle cell differentiation is how mesenchymal, neural crest or progenitor cells acquire the contractile, non-striated phenotype that lines blood vessels, gut, airway and bladder and gives these organs their tone and peristalsis. Without it vessels fail to muscularize and remain fragile, and in adults the same programme is reversed when mature cells de-differentiate into proliferative, matrix-secreting states that drive atherosclerosis, restenosis and aneurysm. The core transcriptional output runs through serum response factor with myocardin and the related MRTF coactivators, which switch on contractile genes and are reinforced by MEF2C, GATA6 and FOXF1. Instructive signals arrive as TGF-beta and BMP4 ligands, Notch ligand-receptor pairs with HEY targets, PDGF-B, sonic hedgehog and Wnt/beta-catenin input, while endothelin and apelin receptors tie specification to vascular tone. Numerous microRNAs, notably miR-145 and miR-21, together with chromatin regulators such as DNMT1 and PRDM6, set the balance between contractile and synthetic phenotypes.

Striated muscle cell differentiation is the route by which mesodermal progenitors become the contracting cells of skeletal muscle and heart, acquiring the sarcomeric striations that give the tissue its name. It underlies limb and trunk muscle formation, cardiac chamber development, and the regenerative response of satellite cells after injury; its disruption produces congenital myopathies, muscular dystrophy and cardiac malformation. Lineage-determining transcription factors act in two programmes, MYF5, MYOD1 and MYOG with MEF2C for skeletal myogenesis, and NKX2-5, GATA4, TBX5 and ISL1 for cardiac, integrating BMP, WNT, Notch and hedgehog signals from surrounding tissue. Chromatin regulators and class II histone deacetylases gate these factors, while muscle-restricted microRNAs reinforce commitment. Downstream, cells exit the cell cycle, fuse through MYMK and MYMX, and build sarcomeres from titin, actins, tropomodulins, troponins and myosins anchored at Z-discs, coupling excitation to contraction via calcium release machinery.

Muscle cell differentiation must be switched on at the right time and held off until then, and this regulatory layer sets how fast and how far progenitors convert into skeletal, cardiac or smooth muscle cells. It governs skeletal muscle development and regeneration from satellite cells, cardiomyocyte maturation, and smooth muscle identity in vessels and gut; misregulation underlies rhabdomyosarcoma, congenital myopathies and cardiac hypertrophic remodelling. At its core are myogenic transcription factors such as MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG and MEF2C, opposed and tuned by chromatin modifiers including class II histone deacetylases, EZH2 and EHMT1, and by Notch, BMP, TGF-beta, Wnt and Hedgehog inputs that keep progenitors proliferative. Calcineurin-NFAT signalling, MAP kinase cascades, IGF and mTOR growth signalling, and myogenic microRNAs add post-transcriptional control, while MYOCD and SRF drive the smooth muscle and cardiac branches of the same decision.

Muscle progenitors must be held in an undifferentiated, proliferative state until the right time and place, and negative regulation of muscle cell differentiation is the set of brakes that does this across skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. Losing these brakes depletes the satellite cell and progenitor pool, while excessive braking blocks regeneration after injury and contributes to rhabdomyosarcoma, where differentiation arrest is the defining defect. The repression works at several levels: Notch signalling through DLL1, NOTCH1 and the HEY factors together with ID2 and BHLHE41 antagonises myogenic bHLH factors; chromatin repressors including HDAC1-5, EZH2, DNMT1, EHMT1 and MECP2 keep muscle structural genes silent; secreted cues such as BMP2, SHH, DKK1, FGF9 and PDGFB signal from surrounding tissue; and a large complement of microRNAs plus RNA-binding proteins like PTBP1 and PDCD4 impose post-transcriptional control. Calcineurin-NFAT signalling and its regulators RCAN1 and RGS proteins tune the same decision.

positive regulation of muscle cell differentiation covers the signals and regulators that drive precursor cells to commit to and mature into skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle, the step that builds contractile tissue during development and regenerates it after injury. Failure or misdirection of these inputs underlies muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies, cardiac outflow and chamber defects, and the loss of satellite cell-driven repair in ageing muscle. The core drivers are the myogenic transcription factors MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG and MYF6 together with MEF2C, MYOCD and chromatin modifiers such as SMARCD3 and SMYD1, which are switched on downstream of IGF1, BMP, WNT, Notch, SHH and TGF-beta cues, mechanical sensing through PIEZO1, and p38 MAPK signalling. A large complement of muscle-enriched microRNAs, including miR-1, miR-133 and miR-206, reinforces commitment by silencing proliferative and non-muscle programmes, while laminin-rich basement membrane supports the niche.

Muscle cells are made, not inherited: progenitors must exit the cell cycle, switch on contractile gene programmes and fuse or mature into skeletal myofibres, cardiomyocytes or smooth muscle. This collection of activators pushes that decision forward, and its output determines muscle mass, regenerative capacity after injury, and the formation of the heart and vascular wall. The core drivers are the myogenic basic helix-loop-helix factors MYOD1, MYF5, MYF6 and MYOG acting with MEF2C, alongside MYOCD for smooth muscle and MESP1 for cardiac mesoderm, while chromatin regulators such as SMARCD3, SMYD1 and SIRT1 set the permissive state. Extracellular cues feed in through Notch, BMP, Wnt, Shh, TGF-beta, neuregulin and IGF1-mTOR signalling, with laminin-rich basement membrane and p38 MAPK relaying mechanical and adhesive context. Numerous microRNAs, including the muscle-specific miR-1, miR-133 and miR-206 families, reinforce commitment post-transcriptionally. Failure contributes to myopathy, impaired regeneration and cardiac malformation.

Smooth muscle cells switch reversibly between a contractile, differentiated state and a proliferative, synthetic one, and this control layer sets where a cell sits on that spectrum. It matters for building the vessel wall, gut and airway musculature, and for what happens afterwards: loss of the contractile programme underlies neointima formation in atherosclerosis and restenosis, while excess drives fibrotic stiffening. The core output is myocardin acting with serum response factor to switch on contractile genes; Notch receptors with their HEY targets, TGF-beta and BMP4 ligands, PDGFB, SHH and FGF signals push cells toward or away from that state, and NFAT family factors and the calcineurin modulator RCAN1 couple calcium to the decision. Epigenetic regulators including DNMT1, MECP2, SIRT1 and PRDM6 and a large complement of microRNAs, notably miR-145 and miR-21, tune the balance post-transcriptionally.

negative regulation of smooth muscle cell differentiation holds vascular and visceral smooth muscle cells away from the contractile, differentiated state, keeping them proliferative, migratory and synthetically active. This restraint is needed during vessel development and wound repair, but its persistence drives the phenotypic switching that underlies atherosclerotic plaque growth, restenosis after angioplasty, and pulmonary hypertension. The genes act at several levels: growth factors such as PDGFB, EREG and FGF9 and morphogens including Hedgehog signal from outside; Notch effectors HEY1 and HEY2, calcineurin-NFAT components, and the methyltransferase PRDM6 repress contractile gene programmes; DNMT1 and MECP2 impose epigenetic silencing; and a set of microRNAs, notably miR-21, miR-221 and miR-143/145-related regulators, tune the balance post-transcriptionally alongside RBPMS2 and PDCD4. Together they form the counterweight to myocardin- and serum response factor-driven maturation.

Smooth muscle cells are not terminally fixed: they switch between a contractile state and a proliferative, synthetic state, and this control arm holds differentiation back so that vessels and visceral muscle can grow, remodel and repair. Loss of the brake contributes to vascular disease, since the balance between contractile marker expression and dedifferentiation governs neointima formation after injury and the fate of cells in atherosclerotic plaques. Growth factors such as PDGFB and FGF9 and Notch effectors HEY1 and HEY2 suppress the contractile programme, calcineurin-NFAT signalling with its regulator RCAN1 feeds into the same decision, and epigenetic repressors including DNMT1, MECP2 and the methyltransferase PRDM6 silence differentiation genes. Several microRNAs act here as post-transcriptional switches, tuning how strongly progenitors and existing smooth muscle commit to the contractile phenotype during development and vascular remodelling.

Smooth muscle cells give blood vessels, airways and gut their contractile tone, and this pathway covers the signals that push precursors toward that contractile fate and reinforce it. It matters for vascular development and for the stability of the adult vessel wall: when the programme is lost, smooth muscle cells de-differentiate into proliferative, synthetic states that drive atherosclerotic plaque growth, neointima formation after injury, and aneurysm. The core driver is myocardin, a coactivator that partners with serum response factor to switch on smooth muscle actin and myosin genes, assisted by chromatin components such as SMARCD3. Upstream inputs include TGF-beta, Notch receptors, hedgehog signalling and the endothelial TGF-beta coreceptor endoglin, while a large set of microRNAs, notably miR-145, tunes the switch between contractile and proliferative phenotypes. Extracellular matrix and redox factors provide additional context.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle cells acquire their contractile identity through a transcriptional programme that must be switched on at the right time and held off until then, and this set captures the inputs that tune how fast and how far that differentiation proceeds. The core myogenic factors MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG and MYF6 act with MEF2C and cofactors such as SMYD1 and MYOCD to drive sarcomeric gene expression, while class IIa histone deacetylases including HDAC4, HDAC5 and HDAC9, along with HDAC1, HDAC3 and the methyltransferase EZH2, restrain them until differentiation cues arrive. Secreted signals from the BMP, WNT, Notch, hedgehog, TGF-beta and IGF1 families, plus muscle-enriched microRNAs such as miR-1, miR-133 and miR-206, set the balance between proliferating progenitors and fused myotubes. Its regulation governs muscle growth, regeneration after injury, cardiac chamber formation, and the failure of repair seen in muscular dystrophies.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle cells differentiate only when the transcriptional programme driven by myogenic regulators is released from restraint, and this pathway is that restraint: the set of processes that block, delay or damp striated muscle cell differentiation. It keeps progenitors and satellite cells proliferative and undifferentiated, prevents premature fusion, and allows growth and repair to be timed; its loss or excess contributes to failure of muscle regeneration and to pathological remodelling of the heart. Mechanistically it works through repressive chromatin and transcription factors, including class I and class II histone deacetylases that silence MyoD- and MEF2-dependent targets, the Polycomb methyltransferase EZH2, and YY1; through Notch signalling via NOTCH1 and DLL1 that maintains the progenitor state; through BMP2/SMAD4 and Wnt modulators such as DKK1 and FZD7; and through microRNAs that tune the same targets post-transcriptionally.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle cells arise from progenitors that exit the cell cycle and switch on contractile gene programmes, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that decision forward. Its output is the muscle fibre itself: sarcomere assembly, myoblast fusion, and the cardiomyocyte identity on which heart contraction depends, with failures underlying congenital myopathies and cardiac malformation. Myogenic transcription factors such as MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG and MYF6 act with MEF2C, MYOCD and chromatin-modifying partners including SMYD1 to drive differentiation, while secreted cues from BMP, WNT, SHH, TGFB1, NRG1 and IGF1 set where and when the programme runs. Muscle-enriched microRNAs, among them miR-1, miR-133 and miR-206, reinforce commitment by silencing proliferative targets. Mechanical and metabolic signals through PIEZO1 and mTOR feed into the same decision, linking growth and load to muscle gene expression.

Glucose 6-phosphate sits at the branch point of carbohydrate metabolism, and the reactions that make and consume it decide whether a sugar is burned for ATP, stored, or diverted to biosynthesis. Hexokinases and the higher-Km glucokinase trap incoming glucose as glucose 6-phosphate, while glucose-6-phosphatase subunits release free glucose in liver, kidney and neutrophils, the step that sustains blood sugar between meals; loss of these activities causes glycogen storage disease and, for the beta-cell enzyme, altered insulin secretion. Isomerization by GPI feeds glycolysis, whereas G6PD, PGLS and PGD commit the same metabolite to the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH for antioxidant defence and ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotides through transketolase, transaldolase and the ribose-phosphate interconverting enzymes. Flux between these routes is tuned by p53 and its target TIGAR, and by mTOR complex components, linking sugar handling to growth signalling and redox stress.

Xylulose 5-phosphate sits at the junction between the non-oxidative pentose phosphate pathway and the glucuronate/uronic acid route of sugar catabolism, and its metabolism lets cells interconvert five-carbon sugars with glycolytic intermediates while also serving as a signal of carbohydrate abundance that drives lipogenic gene expression. Transketolase uses the ketopentose as a donor in transfers that generate ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis and return carbon to fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. The remaining enzymes handle the glucuronate arm: aldo-keto and sorbitol dehydrogenase activities together with the dicarbonyl/L-xylulose reductase convert xylulose to xylitol and back, and a xylulokinase phosphorylates the free sugar. Loss of the reductase step causes essential pentosuria, a benign inborn error in which L-xylulose is excreted in urine, illustrating how this small branch of pentose handling connects to NADPH-dependent redox balance and polyol metabolism.

nuclear export covers the directed movement of macromolecules from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, the step that couples gene expression in the nucleus to protein synthesis and signalling outside it. Nothing made in the nucleus is useful until it is exported: mRNAs, tRNAs, ribosomal subunits, snRNAs and regulatory proteins all leave through nuclear pore complexes, and blocking that traffic shuts down translation and traps tumour suppressors and transcription factors in the wrong compartment. Directionality comes from the RAN GTPase gradient, set by RANGAP1 and RANBP1 in the cytoplasm, which loads and unloads karyopherin-family carriers such as XPO1, XPOT and CSE1L. Bulk mRNA takes a separate route, packaged by the TREX complex and ALYREF and handed to NXF1-NXT1, with the exon junction complex and helicases DDX19A/B and GLE1 driving release at the pore. Export is also a quality checkpoint, feeding surveillance by UPF1-dependent nonsense-mediated decay.

Everything made in the nucleus that works in the cytoplasm must cross the nuclear envelope, and nuclear export is the directed traffic that moves it: mature mRNAs, ribosomal subunits, tRNAs, small RNAs and a large set of regulatory proteins. Selective export sets where a transcription factor or cell cycle inhibitor acts, licenses translation only of properly processed transcripts, and is the step tumour cells subvert when they mislocalise tumour suppressors. Nucleoporins of the pore channel provide the conduit, while the RAN GTPase gradient maintained by its exchange and activating factors gives directionality to karyopherin carriers such as XPO1 and the tRNA exporter XPOT. Messenger RNA takes a separate route, packaged by the TREX complex and cap-binding and exon junction components and handed to the NXF1-NXT1 receptor, coupling export to splicing, 3' end formation and surveillance of aberrant transcripts.

Separating the genome from the cytoplasm only works if there is a controlled way across the envelope, and nuclear transport is that system: the traffic of proteins, RNAs and ribosomal subunits into and out of the nucleus. It sets where transcription factors act, when cell cycle regulators are sequestered, and how mature mRNA reaches the ribosome, so its failure shows up as misregulated signalling and as cytoplasmic mislocalisation of RNA-binding proteins in neurodegeneration. Nucleoporins build the pore channel and its scaffold; karyopherins of the importin and exportin families, together with transportins, recognise localisation and export signals; and directionality comes from the RAN GTPase gradient maintained by its GAP and nucleotide exchange partners. A separate branch handles bulk mRNA export through the TREX complex and the NXF1-NXT1 receptor, linking splicing, the exon junction complex and nonsense-mediated decay to nucleocytoplasmic movement.

Nearly every nuclear protein is made in the cytoplasm, so directed import into the nucleus is what gives the nucleus its protein content and lets signalling events in the cytoplasm change gene expression. The machinery here is the nuclear pore and its transport receptors: nucleoporins including the NUP62 and NUP93 complexes, POM121 and TPR build the channel, karyopherin alpha adaptors recognise classical localisation signals, importin beta and transportins carry cargo through, and the RAN GTPase with RANBP2 and NUTF2 sets the directionality that makes accumulation against a gradient possible. Cargoes in this group show what depends on it: STAT3, SMAD3, NFKBIA-regulated NF-kB components, glioma-associated GLI factors and cell cycle regulators are all held out of the nucleus until a signal permits entry. Dedicated routes also exist for histone chaperones, ribosomal proteins and heat-shock proteins. Defective import or mislocalisation of cargo such as TARDBP contributes to neurodegeneration.

Phosphorus-containing compounds are the cell's currency of information and energy, and this grouping collects the regulators that set the rate and extent of their chemical transformation — chiefly protein phosphorylation and dephosphorylation, but also nucleotide, phosphoinositide and phosphate-ester handling. Its reach explains why so much of growth control passes through it: receptor tyrosine kinases and their ligands (EGF/EGFR, FGFs and FGFR1, KIT, VEGFA with KDR and FLT1), the RAF–MEK–ERK relay, PI3K subunits opposed by the PTEN phosphatase, and the mTOR complex with RPTOR, MLST8 and DEPTOR. Counter-regulation comes from AMPK subunits, protein phosphatases, SOCS and dual-specificity phosphatases, cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A and CDKN1B, and tumour suppressors including TP53, RB1, STK11 and the LATS/MST Hippo kinases. Cytokine, Toll-like receptor and TNF receptor signalling feed in, and mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases link the same logic to fuel choice. Imbalance here underlies cancer, insulin resistance and inflammatory disease.

During meiosis, sister chromatids must stay physically joined from replication until anaphase II, and the specialised cohesion programme described here is what holds them. Meiotic cohesin rings built with REC8 or RAD21L in place of the mitotic kleisin, together with the meiosis-specific subunits SMC1B and STAG3, encircle the chromatids and also support the axes along which homologues pair and recombine. Protection is regional and staged: shugoshin proteins recruit a PP2A phosphatase complex to pericentromeric cohesin so that arm cohesion is released at anaphase I while centromeric cohesion persists to orient sisters together at meiosis II, with MEIKIN and BUB1 kinases acting at the kinetochore. Loss of this stepwise protection produces premature sister separation, aneuploid gametes, miscarriage and infertility, and underlies the maternal age effect on chromosome missegregation.

Vitamins cannot be synthesised by human cells, so every tissue depends on dedicated carriers and receptors to absorb them from the gut, move them through blood, and deliver them across membranes into the compartments where they are converted to cofactors. Vitamin transport covers that whole relay: intrinsic factor and cubilin-amnionless-CD320 receptor uptake of cobalamin with its transcobalamin carriers, folate receptors and reduced folate and proton-coupled folate carriers, riboflavin transporters of the SLC52 family, thiamine carriers including the mitochondrial SLC25A19, sodium-dependent ascorbate and biotin/pantothenate uptake, retinol handling by RBP4, STRA6 and LRP2, vitamin D binding protein, and alpha-tocopherol transfer protein for vitamin E. Loss of single components produces recognisable deficiency diseases — megaloblastic anaemia, thiamine-responsive encephalopathy, Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, ataxia with vitamin E deficiency — which places this transport machinery upstream of one-carbon metabolism, redox balance, and energy production.

Prosthetic group metabolism covers the making and handling of the non-protein cofactors that many enzymes need to work at all, and the genes here centre on one of them: the molybdenum cofactor. Its synthesis begins with conversion of a guanine nucleotide to cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate, followed by sulfur transfer to build the dithiolene of molybdopterin and finally metal insertion, the last steps carried out by the multidomain scaffolding protein gephyrin. Sulfur is mobilised from cysteine by a desulfurase and relayed through sulfurtransferases, and a dedicated cofactor sulfurase further modifies the enzymes that require a terminal sulfido ligand. The cofactor is what allows sulfite oxidase, xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase to function, so loss of these steps causes molybdenum cofactor deficiency, with toxic sulfite accumulation, severe neonatal seizures and early neurodegeneration, or the milder isolated xanthinuria.

Membrane proteins only work once their hydrophobic segments are threaded into a lipid bilayer in the right orientation, and this insertion machinery is what puts them there. It supplies the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with their transporters, receptors, channels and respiratory chain subunits; when it fails, unassembled hydrophobic proteins are degraded or aggregate, and cells lose oxidative phosphorylation capacity and secretory competence. Several distinct routes converge on the same outcome: the Sec61 translocon with TRAM and the EMC and PAT-like complexes handle co-translational and marginally hydrophobic substrates, while a cytosolic targeting factor delivers tail-anchored proteins to a dedicated ER insertase. In mitochondria, the outer membrane TOM complex and SAM/metaxin components, the small TIM chaperones with the TIM22 carrier insertase, and OXA1L in the inner membrane perform the equivalent tasks. Receptor transport proteins act as chaperones for olfactory-type receptors reaching the plasma membrane.

Cells keep cytosolic calcium extremely low by confining it inside stores, and this sequestering of calcium ion covers the buffering and store loading that make calcium usable as a signal at all. Luminal buffers of the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum such as calsequestrins, calreticulin, HRC and sarcalumenin hold large amounts of calcium in a releasable form, while phospholamban tunes the pump that refills the store and junctophilins and triadin organise the junctions where release channels sit. Ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors, fed by phospholipase C isoforms, discharge that store for muscle contraction, secretion and lymphocyte activation; mitochondrial transporters and sodium-calcium exchangers provide additional uptake and clearance. Loss of store capacity or leaky release underlies malignant hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmia, myopathy and calcium-dependent cell death.

Cartilage development covers the whole life of a skeletal cartilage element, from mesenchymal condensation and chondrocyte commitment through matrix deposition, proliferation in growth plate columns, hypertrophy and eventual replacement by bone. It sets the length and shape of the limbs, ribs, vertebrae and craniofacial skeleton, and provides the articular surfaces of joints; its failure produces chondrodysplasias, short stature and, in the adult, osteoarthritic cartilage breakdown. SOX9 with SOX5 and SOX6 drives transcription of the defining matrix genes, chief among them collagen II along with collagen XI, aggregan-associated proteoglycans and cartilage oligomeric matrix protein, while sulfotransferases and sulfate transport supply chondroitin sulfate chains. Pace and timing are set by opposing signals: Indian hedgehog with parathyroid hormone-related peptide acting through its receptor, FGF signalling via FGFR3, and BMP, TGF-beta and WNT inputs, with RUNX2 and MMP13 marking the transition to hypertrophy and matrix remodelling.

Grouped here are the regulators that increase the rate or extent of protein movement into, out of and within cells — secretion, vesicle trafficking, nuclear import and export, and delivery of cargo to the plasma membrane. Cells depend on this positive control to release hormones and cytokines on cue, to place transporters and receptors at the surface, and to move transcription factors into the nucleus once a signal arrives. Much of the set is regulatory rather than structural: kinases such as PRKACA, PRKCA and GSK3B, adaptors and scaffolds, and transcriptional regulators that raise trafficking capacity. Machinery is represented too, notably COPII coat components (SEC13, SEC23/24 paralogues, SEC31A, SAR1A/B) and SNARE and synaptotagmin-like proteins driving exocytosis. A strong pancreatic beta-cell flavour — INS, PDX1, NKX6-1, GCK, SLC2A2, SLC30A8 — reflects regulated insulin granule release, whose failure contributes to diabetes.

regulation of protein transport covers the control layer over where proteins go — their export from the ER, transit through the Golgi, delivery to the surface, secretion, and import into the nucleus — rather than the transport machinery alone. Setting the rate and destination of protein movement is how cells time hormone release, present receptors at the membrane, and clear misfolded cargo, and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and lipid storage disease. The genes span COPII budding and cargo selection, Rab11-dependent recycling endosomes, SNARE-mediated fusion, ERAD-linked retrotranslocation and quality control, nucleocytoplasmic shuttling via importins and exportins, and ESCRT sorting. A large regulatory contingent — kinases such as PKA, PKC and GSK3B, 14-3-3 adaptors, nuclear receptors, and microRNAs — tunes these steps to metabolic and inflammatory cues, with insulin granule exocytosis from pancreatic beta cells and neuronal vesicle release as prominent outputs.

This is a broad control layer over where proteins go: the regulated movement of proteins into, out of and within cells, including secretion, nuclear import and export, vesicle budding and the retrieval of misfolded cargo from the secretory pathway. The genes span COPII coat and cargo-selection machinery (SAR1A/B, SEC13, SEC23/24 paralogues, SEC31), ER quality control and retrotranslocation factors (EDEM1/2, OS9, DERL2/3, UBE2J1), nucleocytoplasmic carriers such as RAN, RANGAP1, XPO1 and IPO5, and Rab11-based recycling endosome effectors. A large part of the set concerns regulated exocytosis of hormones, with insulin granule release in pancreatic beta cells prominently represented through glucose sensing, ATP-sensitive potassium channels, SNARE and synaptotagmin-family fusion proteins, and transcription factors that specify islet identity. Kinases, phosphatases and cytokines tune the rate of these steps, linking nutrient state, circadian timing and inflammation to protein delivery, and their dysregulation contributes to diabetes and to disorders of impaired secretory flux.

Before a cell can divide it must build the bipolar microtubule array that pulls sister chromatids to opposite poles, and spindle assembly is the process that constructs it. Accurate construction is what keeps chromosome numbers stable; errors produce lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the mitotic defects underlying microcephaly and tumour progression. Microtubules are nucleated from centrosomes by the gamma-tubulin complex and amplified along existing microtubules by the augmin complex, while motors such as the kinesin KIF11 slide antiparallel microtubules apart to separate the poles. Aurora kinases with INCENP and survivin, PLK1 and the RAN-GTP gradient set by RCC1 position spindle components in space, TPX2 and NUMA1 organise poles, and NDC80 and the SKA complex couple kinetochores to microtubule ends. Later members act in central spindle formation and midbody abscission, linking spindle organisation to cytokinesis.

Spindle elongation is the step in mitosis where the two spindle poles are pushed further apart, separating the segregated chromosome sets far enough that a cleavage furrow can divide them into distinct daughter cells. It matters because pole separation sets the geometry of cytokinesis; when it fails, chromosomes end up too close to the division plane and cells become aneuploid or tetraploid. Motor proteins do the mechanical work: a bipolar kinesin slides antiparallel microtubules apart, while other kinesins act with the microtubule bundler PRC1 to organise the central spindle. The chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin — phosphorylates these midzone components and positions them, and a Rho GAP-containing centralspindlin module links the array to furrow signalling. NUMA1 anchors microtubule minus ends at the poles, coupling elongation to cortical pulling forces.

Cells must not only move things but also hold them still, and maintenance of location covers the processes that keep an ion, protein or organelle where it belongs rather than letting it disperse. Much of the gene list reflects calcium retention: ryanodine receptors, inositol trisphosphate receptors, calsequestrins, junctophilins, triadin and the sarcoplasmic reticulum pump and its regulator phospholamban confine calcium stores within the ER/SR, while sodium-calcium exchangers and mitochondrial carriers limit its spread in the cytosol. Other members retain protein cargo in compartments, including KDEL receptors and ER chaperones such as HSPA5 and CALR that prevent escape of resident proteins, and nuclear envelope SUN proteins that anchor the nucleus to the cytoskeleton. Chemokines and their receptors keep leukocytes positioned in tissues. Loss of such tethering produces store leak, excitation-contraction failure in muscle, and mislocalised organelles and proteins.

Getting RNA to the right place is what makes gene expression spatially meaningful, and establishment of RNA localization covers both export of transcripts from the nucleus and their targeted delivery within the cytoplasm. Nuclear pore components, the Ran GTPase system and its import/export carriers provide the conduit, while the TREX complex, the cap-binding complex and the NXF1-NXT1 export receptor load mRNA for passage and DDX19 helicases release it on the cytoplasmic face; separate carriers handle tRNA, snRNA and microRNA precursors. Once exported, RNA-binding proteins such as IGF2BP family members, FMR1, QKI and STAU-like adaptors couple transcripts to motors including kinesins and dynein-adaptor BICD2, so that messages are translated at dendrites, at the leading edge, or at other destinations. Exon junction and surveillance factors link correct localization to nonsense-mediated decay, and defects in these steps underlie fragile X syndrome, motor neuron disease and stress-granule pathology.

This is a very broad collection of genes whose activity increases the rate or extent of processes carried out by tissues and organs rather than single cells. It spans the signalling systems by which cells in a multicellular body instruct one another: cytokines and their receptors driving inflammation and lymphocyte activation, Toll-like receptors and inflammasome components raising innate immune output, developmental morphogens of the Wnt, BMP/TGF-beta, Hedgehog and Notch families, neurotrophins and axon guidance receptors shaping neural circuits, angiogenic factors such as VEGF and angiopoietins, and peptide hormones including insulin, leptin, oxytocin and growth hormone that set metabolic and reproductive state. Lineage transcription factors, chromatin remodelling subunits and many microRNAs appear as upstream amplifiers of these programmes. Collectively the members promote organ development, immune defence, vascular growth, neural signalling, muscle and adipose differentiation, and systemic homeostasis; their misregulation underlies inflammatory, metabolic, neurodevelopmental and malignant disease.

This is the braking side of organism-level physiology: the collected processes that stop, slow or restrain functions carried out by tissues and organs rather than by single cells. Restraint of this kind sets the ceiling on immune responses, blood clotting, bone and vessel remodelling, feeding and metabolic tone, and axon and epithelial patterning, and its loss is recognisable as autoimmunity, chronic inflammation, thrombosis, fibrosis or uncontrolled growth. The members reflect that breadth: inhibitory immune checkpoint receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1 and their ligands; negative feedback regulators including SOCS proteins, TNFAIP3, NFKBIA and SMAD6/SMAD7; secreted antagonists of morphogen signalling such as NOG, DKK1, GREM1 and SFRP family proteins; serpin and TFPI-type inhibitors of proteolysis and coagulation; guidance repellents including semaphorins and SLIT/ROBO components; and a large complement of microRNAs that damp the transcripts encoding these programmes. Together they enforce limits, resolution and timing on multicellular processes.

Cells continuously adjust how much of each protein they make, how it is modified, and how long it survives, and the regulation of protein metabolic process gathers the controls that set those rates. It determines whether a growth signal is translated into new protein mass, whether a damaged or no-longer-needed protein is cleared, and whether stress halts biosynthesis until conditions improve. The components span translational control through initiation factors, their 4E-binding inhibitors and mTOR-linked kinases; eIF2alpha kinases and the integrated stress response; mRNA-binding repressors, deadenylase complexes and microRNA effectors that limit output before translation begins; and ubiquitin conjugation, cullin-RING and proteasome machinery with opposing deubiquitinases that govern degradation. Chaperones, protein kinases and phosphatases, acetyltransferases and methyltransferases, and secreted protease inhibitors add further layers. Loss of this balance underlies oncogenic growth, protein-aggregation neurodegeneration and failures of stress tolerance.

This grouping collects the machinery that drives protein metabolism upward from synthesis through modification to destruction f wherever a cell needs more protein flux rather than less. It spans translation initiation and its control (eIF4G, eIF2B subunits, eIF5A, LARP and PABP family mRNA-binding proteins, mTOR with the S6 kinases), chaperone and folding support (HSP90, HSPA5/BiP, XBP1-linked ER stress output), and a very large ubiquitin f-proteasome component: E2 conjugating enzymes, cullin f-RING scaffolds with substrate adaptors such as FBXW7, BTRC and SKP2, HECT ligases including NEDD4 and HUWE1, deubiquitinases, and the SUMO conjugation pair SAE1/UBA2. Growth-factor, cytokine and innate-immune receptors feed into it, illustrating how extracellular signals raise proteolytic turnover and translational output together. Coordinated increases of this kind underlie cell growth, cell-cycle progression, inflammatory responses and clearance of damaged proteins; loss of control contributes to tumour growth and to neurodegenerative protein accumulation.

Cells constrain how much protein they make, modify and destroy, and this collection of brakes on protein metabolic processes is how that restraint is imposed. It sets the ceiling on translation, limits kinase and protease activity, and blocks unwanted degradation, so that growth signals, stress and nutrient supply are matched by protein output; loss of these brakes underlies oncogenic growth, neurodegenerative protein aggregation and inflammatory overactivation. Translation is dampened by eIF4E-binding proteins, PDCD4, eIF2alpha kinases and a large complement of microRNAs acting with Argonaute and TNRC6 proteins, together with CCR4-NOT deadenylation and RNA-binding repressors such as ZFP36 and CPEBs. Enzyme activity is curbed by phosphatase and deubiquitinase modules, serpin and cystatin family inhibitors of proteases, and negative regulators of mTOR, PI3K-AKT and receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, including PTEN, DEPTOR and TSC-adjacent factors.

Whether a T or B cell responds to antigen or stays quiet is decided by a large set of positive and negative modulators, and the regulation of lymphocyte activation covers all of them. Tuning this balance sets the threshold between protective immunity and autoimmunity, and its manipulation underlies checkpoint blockade and transplant tolerance.
