Antigen receptor signalling through Lck, ZAP70, Syk, Btk, LAT and the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 module is amplified by costimulatory receptors such as CD28, ICOS and CD40, and damped by CTLA4, PD-1, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA and phosphatases including PTPN22, PTPN6 and PTPN2, plus ubiquitin ligases CBLB, ITCH and TNFAIP3. Cytokines and their JAK-STAT and SOCS circuits, MHC class II-restricted antigen presentation, chromatin remodelling complexes, and lineage factors such as FOXP3, TBX21, GATA3 and BCL6 direct how strongly and toward which fate an activated lymphocyte differentiates.

Immune responses must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and negative regulation of lymphocyte activation covers the brakes that keep T and B cell responses proportionate and self-tolerant. Loss of these controls produces autoimmunity, lymphoproliferation and chronic inflammation, while their exploitation by tumours and chronic infections drives lymphocyte exhaustion. Inhibitory surface receptors such as CTLA4, PDCD1, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA and HAVCR2, together with ligands including CD274 and the galectins, raise the threshold for antigen receptor signalling, and phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN22 and INPP5D dephosphorylate proximal signalling components downstream of kinases like LYN and CSK. Ubiquitin ligases including CBLB, ITCH and TNFAIP3, RNA-binding repressors of the roquin family, SOCS proteins, and suppressive cytokines IL10 and TGFB1 add further layers, with FOXP3 marking regulatory T cells. These checkpoints are the targets of cancer immunotherapy.

positive regulation of RNA metabolic process collects the machinery that increases the production, processing, or turnover of RNA, and it is effectively the activating side of gene expression control: how cells decide which transcripts are made and how long they persist. Nearly every developmental decision, stress response, and immune activation runs through it, and its dysregulation is a common route to cancer and congenital malformation. The bulk of the members are sequence-specific activators — homeobox, forkhead, SOX, GATA, ETS, nuclear receptor, STAT and NF- inB families — together with the general transcription factors, TBP-associated factors, Mediator subunits, and CDK7/CDK9 kinases that build and release elongating RNA polymerase II. Chromatin remodellers and histone-modifying complexes such as SWI/SNF, INO80, NuA4/TIP60 and MLL provide the permissive template, while microRNAs, Argonaute proteins, deadenylases, decapping factors and m6A readers set transcript stability. Upstream, WNT, BMP/TGF-β, Notch, Hedgehog and Toll-like receptor signalling feed into these outputs.

This is the broad collection of factors that raise the rate or extent of RNA synthesis, processing and turnover, and it underlies essentially every inducible change in gene expression — developmental patterning, immune activation, hormone response, stress adaptation and cell cycle entry. Most members are sequence-specific transcription factors and their coactivators: homeodomain, HOX, SOX, FOX, GATA, bHLH and nuclear receptor families, together with NF-κB, STAT, SMAD and Wnt/Notch effectors that deliver signals to promoters. Acting with them are the general machinery and Mediator complex, chromatin remodellers and histone-modifying enzymes such as SWI/SNF, INO80, NuA4-type acetyltransferases and KMT2 methyltransferases, elongation factors, and RNA-binding proteins, m6A writers and readers, microRNAs and deadenylation and decapping components that set transcript stability. Mutation of individual members causes congenital malformation syndromes, immunodeficiency and cancer, reflecting how tightly cell identity depends on correctly tuned RNA output.

As a cell exits metaphase, antiparallel microtubules from the two poles must be cross-linked and organised into a stable overlap zone at the spindle equator; assembly of this spindle midzone marks where the cleavage furrow will form and where chromosome segregation is monitored. Without it, anaphase spindles fail to elongate properly and cytokinesis is mispositioned or abortive, producing binucleate and aneuploid cells. The chromosomal passenger complex contributes Aurora B kinase with INCENP, survivin and borealin, relocating from centromeres to the midzone to phosphorylate substrates there. Cross-linking and length control come from PRC1 together with the kinesins KIF4A and KIF23, while the centralspindlin partner RACGAP1 links the midzone to Rho-dependent furrow assembly. CCDC69 and LZTS2 act as scaffolding contributors, tying midzone organisation to the timing and placement of division.

Cells build much of their internal architecture by stringing monomers into filaments, and this polymerization biology covers the nucleation, elongation, capping and severing steps that determine how much filament exists and where. Actin and tubulin dominate: profilins charge monomers for addition, the Arp2/3 complex with its WAVE/WASP nucleation-promoting factors and formins such as DIAPH1 generate branched and linear networks, capping protein and gelsolin terminate growth, and cofilin with the slingshot phosphatases recycles subunits. On the microtubule side, gamma-tubulin ring components, the augmin complex and TPX2 template new polymer, while stathmins and plus-end tracking proteins tune dynamics. Spectrins, adducins, tropomodulins and fibrinogen chains add other polymer systems, from the erythrocyte membrane skeleton to fibrin clots. The outputs are cell shape, motility, phagocytosis, junction integrity, spindle assembly and cytokinesis, and mutations here cause nephrotic syndrome, immunodeficiency, myopathy and neurodegeneration.

Many proteins only work once several copies come together, and this pathway covers the self-association steps that build such oligomers — dimers, trimers, tetramers and higher assemblies — as well as their disassembly back to monomers. The consequences are concrete: voltage-gated potassium channels formed from four alpha subunits, with KCTD adaptors tuning their turnover and signalling; tetrameric aquaporin water channels; TRP, ryanodine and IP3 receptor channels that gate calcium; inflammasome scaffolds such as NLRP3, PYCARD and CARD adaptors that polymerize into filaments to activate caspases; and gasdermin, MLKL and NINJ1, whose oligomerization punches holes in membranes during pyroptotic and necroptotic death. Antiviral sensing by MAVS and STING and mitochondrial fission and fusion by DNM1L and OPA1 likewise depend on it. Aberrant self-assembly underlies amyloid and prion pathology, as with APP, SNCA, PRNP and IAPP.

protein homooligomerization is the self-assembly of identical protein subunits into dimers, trimers, tetramers and higher-order complexes, the step that converts many inactive monomers into functional machines. It matters because oligomeric state is itself a regulatory switch: voltage-gated potassium channels only conduct as tetramers, aquaporins as tetrameric water pores, and inflammasome sensors such as NLRP3, NLRC4 and PYCARD only signal after nucleating filamentous platforms that recruit caspases. The same principle drives pore-forming executioners of cell death, GSDMD, MLKL, NINJ1 and perforin, and the oligomeric ryanodine and IP3 receptors that gate calcium release. Metabolic enzymes including aldolase, SOD2, glutaminase and the serine hydroxymethyltransferases are obligate oligomers, while KCTD adaptors assemble pentameric substrate-recognition modules for ubiquitin ligases. Aberrant self-association underlies prion propagation, amyloid formation by APP, IAPP and tau, and stress-granule pathology of FUS, linking this process to neurodegeneration.

Many proteins only work once several copies of themselves come together, and this pathway covers the self-association of identical subunits into dimers, trimers, tetramers and larger assemblies. The genes show how broadly that principle applies: voltage-gated potassium channel subunits and their KCTD-family assembly partners build tetrameric pores, aquaporins form water-conducting tetramers, and TRP, ryanodine receptor, inositol-trisphosphate receptor and purinergic channels likewise depend on symmetric multimers to gate ion flux. Innate immune sensors such as NLRP3, PYCARD, CARD9 and caspase-recruitment adaptors oligomerize to nucleate inflammasomes, while GSDMD, MLKL and NINJ1 oligomerize in membranes to execute pyroptosis and lytic cell death. Metabolic enzymes, transglutaminase and prion or amyloid-forming proteins including PRNP, APP, MAPT, FUS and IAPP are here too, where uncontrolled self-assembly produces the aggregates of neurodegenerative disease rather than functional complexes.

Cytoskeletal filaments are only useful if they can be taken apart again, and this pathway covers the controlled disassembly of protein polymers "" chiefly actin filaments and microtubules "" back into their subunits. Turnover of this kind supplies the free monomer pool that lets cells crawl, divide, remodel spines and rebuild membrane skeletons; when it stalls, filament networks become static and mitosis, endocytosis and cell motility fail. Severing and monomer removal are carried out by cofilin and destrin, gelsolin and scinderin, and the MICAL oxidoreductases that oxidise actin to weaken filaments, while capping and pointed-end proteins such as the CapZ subunits, tropomodulins and twinfilin set where disassembly can occur. On microtubules, kinesin-13 depolymerases, katanin and spastin, and the stathmin family sequestering tubulin dimers perform the equivalent job. Spectrins, adducins and clathrin-uncoating chaperones extend the same logic to membrane skeletons and coated vesicles.

Protein tetramerization is the assembly of four subunits into a single functional unit, a quaternary arrangement that many proteins require before they can work at all. Its importance is clearest in ion channels: voltage-gated potassium channels, TRP channels, ryanodine and IP3 receptors, aquaporin water pores and glutamate receptors are all built from four subunits surrounding a central conduction pathway, so tetramer formation is what creates the pore itself. The same principle governs metabolic enzymes such as aldolase, glutaminase, serine hydroxymethyltransferase, ribonucleotide reductase and manganese superoxide dismutase, where the interface between subunits completes the active site or allows allosteric control. Tetramerization also licenses transcription factor activity, most notably for p53 and its relatives, whose DNA binding and tumour suppression depend on an intact oligomerization domain. Mutations that disrupt these interfaces cause channelopathies, polycystic kidney disease and cancer predisposition.

Many proteins only work once four subunits come together, and this set collects proteins whose function depends on assembling into a tetramer. The arrangement is the functional unit in several unrelated areas of biology: voltage-gated and inwardly rectifying potassium channels, TRP and ryanodine channels, IP3 receptors and ionotropic glutamate receptors all form four-fold symmetric pores, so tetramerization is what creates the ion conduction pathway itself, while aquaporins assemble as four independent water channels. Enzymes such as acetyl-CoA carboxylase, aldolase, glutaminase, serine hydroxymethyltransferase, superoxide dismutase 2 and ribonucleotide reductase subunits likewise depend on oligomeric interfaces for catalysis or allosteric control, and the p53 family requires a tetramerization domain to bind DNA and activate transcription. Mutations that disrupt these interfaces behave as dominant negatives, since one bad subunit can poison the whole complex.

Chromosome organization covers everything cells do to build, shape, arrange and take apart chromosomes, from covalent histone marks to the large-scale geometry of centromeres, telomeres and chromosome arms. It is what allows a genome to be replicated once, segregated accurately, recombined in meiosis and repaired without loss of sequence; its failure produces aneuploidy, chromosome fusions, telomere attrition and the genome instability typical of cancer and progeroid syndromes. The members span core histones and chromatin remodellers such as the SWI/SNF and INO80 complexes, cohesin and condensin rings with their loaders and releasing factors, kinetochore and spindle-checkpoint machinery, topoisomerases, the telomerase holoenzyme with shelterin and CST, double-strand break repair and crossover factors, and the synaptonemal complex proteins that pair homologues during gametogenesis. Together these define chromatin state, sister chromatid cohesion, chromosome end protection and faithful inheritance.

Cells store calcium in the endoplasmic and sarcoplasmic reticulum and release it in bursts to drive contraction, secretion and transcriptional responses; this pathway covers the machinery that sets how readily and how often that release occurs. Tuning it matters most in heart and skeletal muscle, where ryanodine receptor gating determines beat-to-beat contractility and where mutations in the receptor, its accessory subunits or the luminal calcium buffers calsequestrin and triadin cause arrhythmia and myopathy. Regulation comes from several directions: junctophilins and triadin organise the junctional membrane, FKBP proteins and phospholamban clamp channel and pump activity, calmodulin and calcium/calmodulin-dependent and cAMP-dependent kinases relay activation state, and sodium-calcium exchange and store-operated entry reset the load. Receptor inputs including thrombin, chemokine and purinergic receptors couple external signals to the same stores in non-muscle cells.

Cytosolic calcium signals must be terminated and kept from firing spontaneously, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that limit calcium release from internal stores such as the endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum. It matters most in excitable and contractile cells, where leaky release channels produce arrhythmia, wasted energy and inappropriate activation of calcium-dependent proteases and transcription factors. Calmodulin, encoded by more than one gene here, binds calcium and feeds back onto ryanodine and inositol trisphosphate receptors to close them, while FKBP1B (FKBP12.6) associates with cardiac ryanodine receptor RyR2 and stabilises its closed state, suppressing diastolic calcium leak. Other members act more indirectly, through redox modification of release channels or through receptor and growth factor signalling that reshapes store content and channel sensitivity. The net effect is to set the amplitude, frequency and spatial confinement of calcium transients rather than to abolish them.

Cytosolic calcium spikes that drive contraction, secretion, and gene expression mostly come from internal stores rather than from outside the cell, and this pathway covers the inputs that enhance that release from the endoplasmic reticulum or mitochondria. Many of the genes are cell-surface receptors coupled to phospholipase C, including thrombin and protease-activated receptors, a purinergic receptor, neurotensin and neuropeptide S receptors, a dopamine receptor, bradykinin B1, and the chemokine receptor CXCR3 with its ligands, all converging on inositol trisphosphate generation and store depletion. Others act at the store itself: calsequestrin and sorcin tune ryanodine receptor behaviour in muscle, TRPC1 contributes to refilling, and calpain-3 and AKAP6 organise local signalling. BAX links store release to mitochondrial apoptosis. Excessive or poorly controlled release promotes calcium overload, contractile dysfunction, and cell death, as in alpha-synuclein toxicity.

positive regulation of sequestering of calcium ion describes control over the removal of free calcium from the cytosol into stores such as the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum, the step that terminates a calcium signal and resets a cell for the next one. In cardiac and skeletal muscle this determines relaxation between contractions and protects against the calcium overload that drives arrhythmia and hypertrophy; more broadly it shapes the amplitude and frequency of calcium transients that gate secretion, gene expression and metabolism. The genes point to regulation at the ryanodine receptor, where calmodulin and the FK506-binding protein FKBP1B stabilise the closed channel and limit store leak, alongside mitochondrial and redox modifiers such as mitoregulin and GSTO1 that tune uptake and release. Receptor and cytokine inputs including neurotensin and TGF-beta signalling adjust this balance in response to extracellular cues.

Cytosolic calcium must be pulled back into stores after each signalling event, and this pathway covers the influences that increase that sequestration, chiefly uptake and retention of calcium within the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum. In heart and smooth muscle it sets the pace of relaxation and determines how much calcium is available for the next contraction; failure to restore store calcium promotes leak, arrhythmia and contractile dysfunction. Calmodulin acts as the sensor that couples calcium levels to downstream effectors, while FKBP1B binds the cardiac ryanodine receptor RYR2 and stabilises it in the closed state so that released calcium can be recaptured rather than leaking back out. Receptor and cytokine inputs such as neurotensin receptor signalling and TGFB1 modulate the process, linking store calcium handling to hormonal and remodelling cues in excitable and secretory cells.

Many proteins only work once four identical subunits come together, and this set collects human proteins whose functional form is a homotetramer. The arrangement is the structural basis of whole classes of activity: ion channels built from four subunits around a central pore, including voltage- and ligand-gated potassium channels, TRP channels, ryanodine and inositol trisphosphate receptors, polycystin-2 and aquaporin water channels assembled as tetramers of independently conducting monomers. Tetramerization also underlies metabolic enzymes such as aldolase, serine hydroxymethyltransferase, glutaminase, methionine adenosyltransferase and mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, where the interface completes active sites shared between subunits. Because oligomeric state dictates gating, allostery and cooperativity, mutations that disrupt these interfaces typically cause loss of function even when catalytic residues are intact, and are found behind channelopathies, polycystic kidney disease and inherited metabolic disorders.

Many proteins only work once four subunits of more than one kind come together, and protein heterotetramerization describes that assembly step. The genes involved show how varied its consequences are: ionotropic glutamate receptors combine obligatory NMDA-type subunits with regulatory ones to set the calcium permeability and kinetics of excitatory synapses; ribonucleotide reductase pairs a large catalytic subunit with a small radical-generating one to supply deoxynucleotides for DNA replication; phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase joins alpha and beta chains for translation; and a cleavage factor built from CPSF6 or CPSF7 with NUDT21 selects poly(A) sites during mRNA 3' end processing. Keratin 1 and 10 pair to build epidermal filaments, while PKD1 and PKD2 form a ciliary channel complex whose loss causes polycystic kidney disease. Subunit composition, not merely expression level, determines activity, localization and stability in each case.

protein heterooligomerization is the assembly of small complexes from non-identical subunits, the step that converts individual polypeptides into the mixed obligate units that actually carry out their function. It matters because for many proteins the heteromer, not the monomer, is the functional species: NMDA receptors require GRIN1 paired with GRIN2B subunits to gate calcium at excitatory synapses, PKD1 and PKD2 must associate to form the polycystin channel complex whose loss causes polycystic kidney disease, peripherin and ROM1 co-assemble in photoreceptor outer segment discs, and keratins 1 and 10 pair as obligate heterodimers to build epidermal filaments. Similar logic governs the CALHM channels, ribonucleotide reductase, the CPSF6/CPSF7-NUDT21 cleavage factor of mRNA 3' end processing, and heterodimeric phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase. Partner-specific recognition therefore sets channel conductance, filament mechanics, enzyme activity and substrate choice, and mismatched or absent partners typically destabilise the whole complex.

Many proteins only work once they have joined with a different partner subunit, and protein heterooligomerization covers the assembly of such mixed complexes from non-identical monomers. The consequences are concrete: NMDA receptors need an obligatory GRIN1 subunit paired with GRIN2B to form a functional glutamate-gated channel; ribonucleotide reductase requires the RRM1-RRM2 pair to supply deoxynucleotides for DNA replication; the phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase alpha and beta chains must combine to charge tRNA; keratins 1 and 10 pair as obligate heterodimers that build the suprabasal keratin filaments of epidermis. Other members form calcium-permeable or potassium channels, polycystin complexes of the renal cilium, photoreceptor outer-segment tetraspanins, and the cleavage factor that selects mRNA polyadenylation sites. Because each partner is non-functional alone, loss of one subunit disables the whole complex, as in polycystic kidney disease and retinal degeneration.

Nuclear pore complex assembly builds the channels that pierce the nuclear envelope and control all traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm. New pores must be made both as the envelope reforms at the end of mitosis and as the nucleus grows during interphase, so this process sets how much transport capacity a cell has and how tightly it separates transcription from translation. Members of the Y-complex scaffold such as NUP107, inner-ring components NUP93 and NUP205, and the transmembrane anchor NDC1 are placed into the double membrane, while NUP98 and NUP153 contribute phenylalanine-glycine-rich regions that create the permeability barrier and TPR extends the nuclear basket. Reticulon-family and other membrane-shaping proteins supply the curvature required to fuse inner and outer membranes. Defects disrupt nucleocytoplasmic transport, mitotic progression and nuclear envelope integrity.

Where a cell places its mitotic spindle determines where the cleavage furrow falls and whether the two daughters inherit the same fate, so establishing spindle orientation is what converts a division into either a symmetric expansion or an asymmetric, fate-diversifying one. It governs epithelial architecture, stratification of skin and neuroepithelium, and the balance between neural progenitor self-renewal and differentiation; its failure depletes progenitor pools and underlies forms of primary microcephaly, as mutations in CDK5RAP2 and MCPH1 show. Mechanistically, cortical polarity cues acting through GPSM1/GPSM2 and the Lethal giant larvae homologues recruit NUMA1 and cytoplasmic dynein with its regulators LIS1 (PAFAH1B1), NDE1 and NDEL1, generating pulling forces on astral microtubules. Centrosomal and plus-end factors such as CLASP1 and MAPRE1, together with kinetochore and checkpoint components, couple attachment status to the final rotational position of the spindle.

Oocytes divide asymmetrically, keeping nearly all cytoplasm for the egg and discarding chromosomes into a tiny polar body, and that outcome depends on moving the meiotic spindle from the centre of the cell to the cortex and holding it there. Establishing meiotic spindle localization is therefore what makes a fertilizable egg with adequate maternal stores; failure yields symmetric division, aneuploidy and oocyte loss. The formin FMN2 acting with the actin nucleators SPIRE1 and SPIRE2 builds a cytoplasmic actin meshwork that drives spindle translocation, while non-muscle myosin IIA contributes contractile force at the cortex. The MOS kinase, an upstream activator of the MAPK cascade in oocytes, couples meiotic cell cycle progression to spindle positioning, and the SKA1/SKA2/SKA3 complex stabilizes kinetochore attachments to dynamic microtubule ends so the spindle can be moved without losing chromosome connections.

Once per cell cycle, each centriole templates a single daughter, so that a dividing cell enters mitosis with exactly two centrosomes and builds a bipolar spindle. Getting the count wrong produces multipolar divisions, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and mutations in these components cause primary microcephaly, dwarfism, ciliopathies and polycystic kidney disease, reflecting the centriole's second job as the basal body of a cilium. Procentriole assembly is driven by the kinase PLK4 recruited to the mother centriole by CEP152 and CEP192, which triggers cartwheel formation by SASS6 and STIL and elongation involving CPAP, CEP120 and CEP135, with CP110 capping growth. Copy number is restrained by ubiquitin ligase activity, including SCF complexes with FBXW5 and by TRIM37, while CDK2 licenses duplication in step with DNA replication. ESCRT components and centrin-containing distal machinery contribute to centriole maturation and disengagement.

Before a cell can divide, its two duplicated centrosomes must be pulled apart and converted into the opposing poles of the mitotic spindle, and centrosome separation is that step. It sets spindle bipolarity, and when it fails cells build monopolar or multipolar spindles, missegregate chromosomes and become aneuploid — a route to the chromosomal instability seen in tumours. Mechanistically, the intercentrosomal linker holding the pair together is dissolved by NEK2 kinase, acting on linker components and regulated in part by CEP85 and by AURKA-dependent centrosome maturation; plus-end-directed kinesins, notably the bipolar KIF11 with KIF15, then generate the outward force that drives the asters to opposite faces of the nucleus. Dynein regulators NDE1 and NDEL1 tie centrosomes to the nuclear envelope and cortex, while CHEK1 links separation timing to cell cycle and damage checkpoints.

cell division is the machinery that duplicates a cell and partitions its contents into daughters, the basis of tissue growth, renewal, germ cell production and, when deregulated, of tumour formation and aneuploidy syndromes. The genes span the whole sequence: cyclin-CDK pairs and their phosphatases and inhibitors that time entry and exit from mitosis, the anaphase-promoting complex and cohesin that couple chromosome segregation to ordered proteolysis, kinetochore and spindle-checkpoint components such as NDC80, MAD2L1 and BUB1 that refuse anaphase until attachments are correct, condensins and topoisomerases that shape mitotic chromosomes, and augmin, kinesins and centriolar proteins that build the bipolar spindle. Completion requires RhoA-directed actomyosin constriction, septins, anillin and centralspindlin, then ESCRT-mediated abscission at the midbody. Meiotic synaptonemal proteins and asymmetric-division polarity modules extend the same core to germline and developmental contexts, where spindle orientation determines daughter cell fate.

Cell division is how one cell becomes two, duplicating and then partitioning chromosomes, centrosomes and cytoplasm so that each daughter receives a complete complement; tissue growth, renewal and gamete production all depend on it, and its miscarriage produces aneuploidy, tumours and developmental failure. The genes here span the whole sequence: cyclin–CDK pairs and their phosphatase and kinase regulators drive entry into mitosis, cohesin and condensin organise sister chromatids, kinetochore and spindle-checkpoint components couple chromosomes to microtubules and delay anaphase until attachment is correct, and the anaphase-promoting complex triggers separase-dependent cohesion cleavage. Aurora and Polo kinases, the augmin complex and septins position the spindle, while RhoA-driven actomyosin and ESCRT machinery build and sever the intercellular bridge. Meiotic synaptonemal proteins extend the same logic to germ cells.</description>

Cell division must be timed, positioned and completed correctly, and this regulatory programme sets how often cells divide and how faithfully one cell is physically partitioned into two. It matters for tissue growth and renewal, stem cell self-renewal and oriented divisions in development; loss of control produces aneuploidy, binucleate cells and tumour growth. Two layers are represented. One drives the mechanics of late mitosis: the chromosomal passenger complex with Aurora B, INCENP and survivin, the centralspindlin components RACGAP1 and KIF23, PRC1, PLK1, citron kinase, RhoA and ECT2 at the cleavage furrow, and ESCRT proteins with VPS4A for abscission. The other is mitogenic and transcriptional input deciding whether division happens at all — FGF, PDGF, VEGF, TGF-beta and Hedgehog ligands, MYC and E2F7/E2F8, CDC14 phosphatases and cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases that reverse or destroy mitotic regulators.

chromosome separation is the step of mitosis in which duplicated sister chromatids are pulled apart, so that each daughter cell inherits exactly one copy of every chromosome; errors here produce aneuploidy, the hallmark of tumour cells and of many developmental disorders. Cohesin holds the sisters together until separase, released when the anaphase-promoting complex destroys securin and mitotic cyclin, cleaves the RAD21 subunit. Timing is enforced by the spindle assembly checkpoint, in which unattached kinetochores generate a MAD2/BUB3/BUBR1 inhibitor of CDC20 until every chromosome is bioriented. Kinetochore-microtubule attachments are built by the NDC80 and SKA complexes, corrected by Aurora B within the chromosomal passenger complex, and monitored via dynein-dependent stripping of checkpoint proteins. Condensins shape chromatid axes and topoisomerase III/GEN1-type activities resolve the remaining DNA links, coupling chromatid disjunction to genome stability.

Chromosome separation is the step at anaphase where the two copies of each duplicated chromosome are finally pulled apart, so that each daughter cell inherits one complete genome. It is the point at which mis-segregation produces aneuploidy, a hallmark of tumours and of chromosomal disorders arising from meiotic error. Sister chromatids are held together by cohesin, whose kleisin subunit RAD21 is cleaved by the protease separase once the anaphase-promoting complex, activated by CDC20, destroys securin and mitotic cyclin. Release is licensed only after the spindle assembly checkpoint — MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUB3 and the outer kinetochore NDC80 complex — reports that every kinetochore is attached. Condensin subunits shape the chromatid axes, the chromosomal passenger complex with Aurora B corrects faulty attachments, and topoisomerase activity resolves residual interlinks before the chromatids move poleward.

This is the anaphase A step of mitosis: once sister chromatids separate, each is hauled from the spindle midzone to its pole as the kinetochore microtubules attached to it shorten, so that the two daughter nuclei receive complete and equal chromosome complements. Errors here produce lasting aneuploidy and micronuclei, a route to chromosomal instability in tumours. The genes involved span the activities the movement requires: a kinetochore-associated kinesin that couples chromosomes to microtubule ends, a microtubule-severing regulatory subunit that helps control polymer length and pole organisation, actin-nucleating machinery, and a nuclear transport receptor that also governs spindle assembly factors after nuclear envelope breakdown. The process is thus embedded in broader spindle assembly and cytoskeletal control rather than being a purely kinetochore-local event, and in oocytes actin-based mechanisms contribute to chromosome transport as well.

Mitotic sister chromatid separation is the irreversible step of mitosis in which duplicated chromosomes are pulled apart, giving each daughter cell one complete genome. If it happens too early, or on chromosomes that are not properly attached to the spindle, the result is aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind that characterises tumours. The genes describe the licensing machinery for that step: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator CDC20 destroys securin and cyclin B so that separase can cleave the cohesin subunit RAD21 holding sisters together. Until every kinetochore is occupied, the spindle assembly checkpoint - MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1 and the RZZ and NDC80 kinetochore modules - keeps that activator sequestered, while Aurora B and the chromosomal passenger complex correct faulty attachments and dynein strips checkpoint proteins once attachment succeeds.

Equal division of the genome requires that paired sister chromatids, held together from S phase onward, be released simultaneously and only after every chromosome is correctly attached to the spindle. Mitotic sister chromatid separation is that irreversible step, and errors in it produce aneuploid daughter cells, the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. Cohesin subunits such as RAD21 hold the pairs until separase (ESPL1) cleaves them, an event licensed by the anaphase-promoting complex and its activator CDC20 once securin/FBXO5 and cyclin B are destroyed. Until then, unattached kinetochores signal through the spindle assembly checkpoint / MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUB3, BUBR1 and the RZZ and dynein-dependent machinery / to sequester CDC20 and delay cleavage. The chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B, INCENP and survivin, with Haspin and PLK1, corrects faulty attachments so that separation occurs only when biorientation is achieved.

Meiotic chromosome separation is the physical detachment of homologues and then sister chromatids that allows a diploid germ cell to produce haploid gametes; when it fails, eggs and sperm carry the wrong chromosome number and the result is aneuploid embryos, miscarriage or infertility. Separase cleaves the cohesin ring that holds chromatids together, while WAPL removes cohesin from chromosome arms by a non-proteolytic route, and condensin subunits compact the chromosomes so they can be resolved and pulled apart. Timing is enforced by the spindle assembly checkpoint, with a kinetochore scaffold and the kinase TTK recruiting checkpoint components until every kinetochore is properly attached, and MOS-driven MAP kinase signalling holds the oocyte at metaphase arrest. Several members are testis-enriched, linking this machinery directly to spermatogenic failure.

Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be captured by microtubules from both spindle poles and brought to the spindle equator; metaphase chromosome alignment is that positioning step, and it is what makes equal partitioning of the genome possible. Failure produces lagging chromosomes, micronuclei and aneuploidy, a hallmark of tumours and of miscarriage-causing errors in meiosis. Kinetochores built on centromeric chromatin marked by the histone variant CENPA and its constitutive partners connect to spindle microtubules through the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes and the SKA complex, while plus-end motors and depolymerases such as CENPE, KIF18A and KIF2C tune attachment and congression. The chromosomal passenger complex, with Aurora B kinase, INCENP and survivin, destabilises erroneous attachments, and checkpoint proteins including BUB3, MAD1L1, TTK and the RZZ components delay anaphase until alignment is achieved. Cohesion regulators and spindle pole organisers complete the process.

Before a meiotic division can proceed, chromosomes must be brought into ordered position at the spindle equator, oriented so that each is pulled toward the correct pole. This alignment step is what guarantees balanced chromosome numbers in gametes; when it fails, eggs and sperm carry extra or missing chromosomes, the main source of aneuploid conceptions and of miscarriage and trisomy. The genes here act mostly at the kinetochore, the interface between centromeric chromatin and spindle microtubules: inner centromere proteins such as CENPC and CENPV build the platform, while KNL1 and ZWINT are part of the outer kinetochore network that captures microtubules and feeds the surveillance machinery that delays anaphase until attachments are correct. MLH1 links the process to the crossovers formed earlier in meiosis, which hold homologues together so that they can align as bivalents.

Chromosomes can only be segregated correctly if each kinetochore captures microtubules from the mitotic spindle, and this pathway covers the formation and correction of those attachments during mitosis. Its output is biorientation of sister chromatids: without it cells missegregate chromosomes, become aneuploid, and either arrest at the spindle checkpoint or propagate karyotype instability of the kind seen in tumours. Core microtubule-binding activity comes from the NDC80 complex with NUF2, stabilised by the SKA complex, while MIS12 and CENPC link these receptors to centromeric chromatin and CENPE contributes motor-driven capture. The chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B kinase with INCENP, survivin and borealin — destabilises attachments that are not under tension, and the depolymerase KIF2C helps release erroneous ones, so error correction and checkpoint signalling through MAD1 are inseparable from attachment itself.

Meiosis halves the genome to make eggs and sperm, and this programme covers progression through its two specialized divisions, from commitment to meiotic entry through recombination, chromosome segregation and oocyte maturation arrest. Its fidelity determines fertility and the aneuploidy rate of human conceptions; failures give azoospermia, premature ovarian insufficiency, or trisomic embryos. Programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11 with REC114, MEI4 and IHO1 at PRDM9-designated hotspots are repaired by DMC1 and RAD51 with MEIOB and BRCA2, and resolved as crossovers by MSH4/MSH5, MLH1/MLH3 and RNF212. Synaptonemal complex and meiosis-specific cohesin components such as SYCP1-3, SYCE proteins, REC8, STAG3 and SMC1B pair homologues, while telomere-LINC bridges of TERB1/2, MAJIN, SUN1 and KASH5 move chromosome ends. Anaphase-promoting complex, separase, shugoshin, kinetochore and spindle factors execute segregation, with CDK1-cyclin B, MOS, WEE2 and piRNA/RNA-binding regulators timing germ cell progression.

Enzymes that cleave bonds by adding water are held under tight control, and this set collects the regulators that raise or lower hydrolase activity across many cellular settings. The largest theme is control of the GTPase switches that time cytoskeletal remodelling, vesicle traffic and growth signalling: GTPase-activating proteins for Rho, Ras, Ral, Rab and Ran families accelerate GTP hydrolysis and switch these proteins off, while nucleotide exchange factors of the DOCK, FGD and RAPGEF groups and regulators of G protein signalling act on the same cycles from the other side. A second theme is restraint of secreted and lysosomal peptidases and lipases by serpins, TIMP metalloproteinase inhibitors and related inhibitory proteins, which protects tissue matrix during inflammation and wound repair. Loss of such braking underlies uncontrolled proteolysis, aberrant cell migration and tumour growth, and mutations in components including NF1, TSC1 and LRRK2 cause inherited disease.

Enzymes that transfer chemical groups — phosphate, methyl, acetyl, ubiquitin, glycosyl — are rarely left running at a constant rate; this collection covers the regulatory inputs that raise or lower transferase activity so that growth, division and stress responses are coupled to conditions. Most of the content concerns protein kinases and the machinery that gates them: cyclin-dependent kinase partners and inhibitors such as CDKN1A, CDKN1B and CDC25 phosphatases set cell cycle transitions, PKA regulatory subunits tune catalytic output to cyclic AMP, and receptor kinases with growth factor ligands, adaptors and phosphatases like PTPN1 and PTPRC establish signalling thresholds. Also represented are activators of ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes through anaphase-promoting complex cofactors, methyltransferase control via EZH2 and MEN1, and nutrient control of mTOR by DEPTOR and the STK11 pathway. Loss of such restraint underlies unchecked proliferation and tumour formation, while excessive inhibition blocks immune and metabolic signalling.

Redox enzymes are controlled rather than left to run freely, and this collection covers the upstream inputs that raise or lower oxidoreductase catalysis. The consequences are physiological: how much nitric oxide a vessel makes, how much superoxide leaks from respiring mitochondria, and how efficiently fuel is oxidised. Control operates at several levels. Cofactor supply is one, with GTP cyclohydrolase I committing the first step of tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis needed to keep nitric oxide synthase coupled, and riboflavin kinase generating FMN for flavoenzymes. Protein interaction and localisation are another, as NOSIP influences where nitric oxide synthase sits, while ECSIT and OXA1L act on respiratory complex assembly. Post-translational regulation appears through the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3, and hormonal and inflammatory signals such as insulin, leptin, oestrogen receptor signalling and IL-1β set the tone. Loss of such control shifts cells toward oxidative stress and vascular dysfunction.

Hydrolase-catalysed reactions are switched on rather than left to run at basal rate, and the positive regulation of hydrolase activity collects the activators that do this. The dominant theme here is control of GTP hydrolysis on small GTPases and heterotrimeric G proteins: RhoGAPs such as ARHGAP11A and SRGAP2, Ras and Ral GAPs including NF1, RAP1GAP and the RALGAP subunits, TBC-domain Rab GAPs, RANGAP1 for nuclear transport, and RGS proteins that accelerate Gα inactivation to terminate receptor signalling. By forcing GTPases back to their inactive state these regulators set the duration of signals governing cytoskeletal remodelling, cell migration, adhesion, vesicle traffic and growth control, which is why loss of NF1 or TSC1 drives tumour predisposition. Also represented are activators of lipases and proteases, including cofactors and adaptors that stimulate phospholipase and peptidase turnover, linking the same regulatory logic to lipid and protein catabolism.

Hydrolases break bonds, and cells restrain them constantly; this collection covers processes that stop or slow that catalysis, spanning enzyme classes from proteases to GTPases and ATPases. Restraint matters because unchecked hydrolysis destroys tissue and wastes energy: tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases such as TIMP1 and TIMP2 limit matrix degradation during remodelling and wound repair, serpin-family inhibitors block neutrophil and epidermal serine proteases, and fetuin-like and extracellular matrix proteins add further protease buffering in plasma and connective tissue. Inside the cell, an inhibitory factor dampens reverse hydrolysis by the mitochondrial ATP synthase to preserve the proton gradient when respiration falters, while GDP-dissociation inhibitor-like and G-protein regulatory proteins hold small GTPases and heterotrimeric G alpha subunits in states that slow nucleotide hydrolysis, prolonging signalling. Loss of such braking contributes to emphysema, fibrosis and tumour invasion.

Lyases that make second messengers are switched on rather than left constitutively active, and this collection of activators shows how that control is exerted. Most of the members converge on adenylyl cyclase: Gs-coupled receptors for pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating peptide, vasopressin, endothelin, CRH, adenosine, dopamine and the incretins GIP and GLP-1, together with the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit GNAS, raise cAMP and thereby drive protein kinase A signalling in endocrine, cardiac and neuronal cells. A second arm stimulates guanylyl cyclase, with guanylate cyclase activator proteins conferring calcium-dependent restoration of cGMP in photoreceptors during light adaptation. Calcium entry through L-type channels and through store-operated STIM1-ORAI1 coupling supplies the ion signal that several of these cyclases read. Loss or gain of function here produces hormone resistance, endocrine tumours and retinal dystrophy, underscoring how second-messenger tone is set.

Redox enzymes rarely work at a fixed rate; their activity is tuned by cofactor supply, post-translational modification and hormonal signals, and this pathway covers the processes that raise oxidoreductase output. Two of the members act by providing cofactors: GCH1 catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis, the cofactor without which nitric oxide synthase and the aromatic amino acid hydroxylases become uncoupled or inactive, while RFK phosphorylates riboflavin to FMN, the precursor of the flavin cofactors used across dehydrogenases and reductases. SIRT3, the major mitochondrial deacetylase, relieves inhibitory acetylation on matrix enzymes including superoxide dismutase and respiratory chain components. Insulin and estrogen receptor signalling add hormonal control. Collectively this tuning sets vascular nitric oxide availability, mitochondrial antioxidant capacity and fuel oxidation, and its loss favours oxidative stress and endothelial dysfunction.

Redox enzymes are tightly held in check, and this grouping covers the mechanisms that damp down oxidoreductase catalysis rather than promote it. Restraint of this kind matters because unchecked oxidoreductase output generates reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, so limiting enzyme activity protects cells from oxidative injury and keeps signalling molecules such as nitric oxide within a usable range. The routes are varied: a dedicated interacting protein sequesters nitric oxide synthase and reduces its output, a metallothionein-family metal-binding protein buffers zinc and copper and thereby the metal supply on which many redox enzymes depend, and a peroxiredoxin consumes peroxide substrates. Mitochondrial and lysosomal members point to control exerted in several compartments, including the assembly environment of respiratory chain subunits. Loss of such negative control shifts cells toward oxidative stress and inappropriate nitric oxide production.

Chromosomes are pulled apart in mitosis by microtubules that grip a protein platform built on centromeric chromatin, and kinetochore organization is the assembly, arrangement and disassembly of that platform. Without it chromosomes attach improperly or not at all, the spindle checkpoint cannot be satisfied, and cells missegregate chromosomes to become aneuploid — a route to developmental failure and to the karyotypic instability of tumours. The foundation is epigenetic: the histone H3 variant CENPA, deposited by its chaperone HJURP with help from the MIS18 complex and NASP, marks centromeres independently of DNA sequence. On that mark the constitutive centromere-associated network, including CENPC, CENPT/W/X and CENPN, recruits the MIS12 complex and the NDC80–NUF2 microtubule-binding module. Condensin subunits, the cochaperone SUGT1 and SUMO turnover by SENP6 and RNF4 keep the structure correctly composed through the cell cycle.

Aldosterone and related C21 steroids tell epithelia to retain sodium and excrete potassium, and this pathway covers the cellular responses that follow such a mineralocorticoid stimulus. It sets blood volume and pressure, and its overdrive in primary aldosteronism or its loss in pseudohypoaldosteronism produces hypertension or salt wasting with hyperkalaemia. The transport end point is explicit here: all four epithelial sodium channel subunits together with the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter, controlled by the aldosterone-induced kinase SGK1 and the WNK-responsive kinase STK39, which alter channel abundance and activity at the apical membrane of distal nephron and colon. Beyond salt handling, immediate-early transcription factors, endothelin-1, NADPH oxidase subunits and a membrane oestrogen receptor link the same stimulus to vascular tone, oxidative stress and cardiac remodelling, alongside neuroendocrine components such as CRH and urocortin that tie the response to stress signalling.

Neurotrophins such as NGF and BDNF act through TRK receptor tyrosine kinases to drive neuronal survival, axon and dendrite growth, and synaptic plasticity, and the strength and duration of that signal is itself controlled. Tuning of TRK receptor signalling sets how much downstream Ras-ERK and PI3K output a neuron receives from a given amount of neurotrophin, which shapes neurite outgrowth, target innervation and activity-dependent synapse remodelling. Sprouty proteins damp the Ras-ERK arm downstream of receptor activation, a phosphatase regulatory subunit contributes dephosphorylation, and adaptors such as DOK5 couple the receptor to effectors. Other members link the pathway to actin and membrane biology: CYFIP proteins with WASF1 form the WAVE regulatory complex that builds branched actin in growth cones, while ZDHHC17 palmitoylates neuronal substrates. Angiotensin components indicate crosstalk from a G protein-coupled receptor. Misregulation here contributes to disordered neuronal wiring and neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric phenotypes.

Neurotrophins such as NGF, BDNF and NT-3 act through TRK receptor tyrosine kinases to keep neurons alive, drive axon and dendrite growth, and strengthen synapses; the genes here raise the output of that signalling rather than initiate it. Their effect is felt in neuronal differentiation and activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, processes whose disruption contributes to neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disease. Two of the components are cytoplasmic FMR1-interacting proteins that, with a WASP-family nucleation-promoting factor, link receptor activation to Arp2/3-dependent actin branching and to translational control at the synapse, coupling neurotrophin input to growth cone and spine remodelling. A protein phosphatase 2A regulatory subunit tunes the phosphorylation state of downstream kinase cascades, and a transmembrane protein of this group promotes BDNF-TrkB trafficking and signalling in developing neurons, particularly in the hippocampus.

Neurons are largely post-mitotic and irreplaceable, so whether one lives or dies by apoptosis shapes both the wiring of the developing nervous system and the course of neurodegeneration. During development, excess neurons that fail to secure trophic support are eliminated, matching neuron number to target size; in the adult brain, inappropriate activation of the same machinery contributes to Alzheimer's, Parkinson's and motor neuron disease. Survival is enforced by neurotrophin signalling through receptor tyrosine kinases such as NTRK1 and NTRK2 and their PI3K/AKT and Ras-ERK outputs, opposed by the death receptor FAS and the p75 receptor NGFR. Commitment runs through BCL2-family control of mitochondrial permeabilisation, cytochrome c-dependent APAF1 caspase activation, and executioner caspases, with XIAP and cFLIP restraining them. Stress inputs include DNA damage sensing, the integrated stress response through ATF4 and DDIT3, oxidative stress, JNK-pathway kinases, CDK5 activity, and mitochondrial quality control via PINK1 and PRKN.

Nitric oxide and the peroxynitrite formed when it meets superoxide modify protein thiols and damage DNA and lipids, and cells mount a defined response to this nitrosative stress to limit and reverse that damage. The capacity matters wherever NO is produced in bulk, as in activated macrophages and inflamed or ischaemic tissue, and its loss contributes to neurodegeneration and cytotoxic protein S-nitrosylation. The genes here cover the main arms: ADH5 acts as the S-nitrosoglutathione reductase that clears the principal nitrosothiol reservoir, GCLC and GCLM form the rate-limiting enzyme of glutathione synthesis to keep thiol buffering supplied, and PARK7 guards against oxidative and nitrosative insult. Downstream, ATM signals DNA damage, DDIT3 couples persistent stress to the integrated stress response and apoptosis, ATG5 enables autophagic removal of damaged material, and chaperone and phosphatase components temper the resulting signalling.

Nitrogen-containing xenobiotics and metabolites "" aromatic amines, N-hydroxylated bases, hydroxylamines, nitrosamines and reactive nitrogen electrophiles "" can damage DNA and protein unless they are neutralised, and detoxification of nitrogen compounds covers the reactions that make them harmless. Two chemistries are represented. Mu-class glutathione S-transferases conjugate reduced glutathione onto electrophilic centres, raising water solubility and committing the adduct to mercapturic acid excretion; the common deletion polymorphism of GSTM1 leaves many people without one of these activities and is studied as a modifier of carcinogen susceptibility. The mitochondrial amidoxime-reducing components are molybdenum cofactor enzymes of the outer mitochondrial membrane that, with a partnering electron supply, reduce N-hydroxylated amidines and hydroxylamines back to the parent amine, limiting mutagenic N-hydroxy species and also activating amidoxime prodrugs. Together they sit within phase II drug metabolism and cellular defence against chemical stress.

Corticosterone is the main glucocorticoid released from the adrenal cortex during stress in many species, and the cellular response to it re-tunes fuel metabolism, immune reactivity and neuronal excitability to match the demands of the stressor. The genes here trace that response largely in the brain, where glucocorticoid feedback acts on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis: corticotropin-releasing hormone and the related peptide urocortin 3 are themselves regulated targets, while vasopressin receptor signalling and calcium- and kinase-dependent effectors such as calmodulin and protein kinase C relay the stimulus. Immediate-early and activity-dependent transcription factors including FOS, FOSB and NPAS4 mark the transcriptional arm, and neurotrophin receptor, glutamate receptor and cytoskeletal components link it to synaptic remodelling. Sustained or dysregulated signalling through this axis underlies stress-related mood disorders, metabolic syndrome and immune suppression.

Cortisol is the main human glucocorticoid, released from the adrenal cortex under stress and circadian control, and the cellular responses to it reset metabolism, immune tone and growth. This is the receiving end of that signal: the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 binds cortisol, moves to the nucleus and reprogrammes transcription, with KLF9 acting as an early glucocorticoid-induced transcription factor that relays the hormone into secondary gene expression changes. Characteristic outputs include induction of hepatic amino acid catabolism, with tyrosine aminotransferase and tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase feeding tyrosine and tryptophan degradation, alongside changes in growth-factor availability and guidance cues such as IGFBP7 and the SLIT ligands. Loss or excess of this response underlies glucocorticoid resistance, Cushing's and adrenal insufficiency, and explains the metabolic and immunosuppressive effects of steroid therapy.

Cells build their microtubule arrays from defined sites rather than letting tubulin polymerize at random, and nucleation at a microtubule organizing center is the step that starts each new filament there. This spatial control sets up the mitotic spindle, the interphase array that positions organelles, and the templates for cilia and axonemes; when it fails, spindles form with the wrong number of poles and chromosomes missegregate. The genes here act at centrosomes and associated structures: a scaffolding protein that recruits nucleation machinery to centrosomes, an anchoring component of the subdistal appendages and Golgi-associated sites, a small subunit that helps assemble and target the gamma-tubulin ring template, and a regulator of tubulin polymerization that also influences microtubule bundling. Together they explain why microtubule minus ends are clustered and stably anchored rather than dispersed.

Ubiquitin ligases decide which proteins are destroyed and when, so their own activity must be switched on and off with precision; this is the set of controls that modulate ubiquitin-protein transferase activity. Much of the biology here converges on the anaphase-promoting complex, the ligase that drives mitotic exit: CDC20 and FZR1 act as substrate-recruiting activators, MAD2L1 restrains it as part of the spindle assembly checkpoint, FBXO5 inhibits it directly, UBE2C and UBE2S serve as its chain-building E2 enzymes, and USP44 opposes ubiquitination to hold the checkpoint. Other members tune ligase output elsewhere: arrestin-domain adaptors recruit substrates to NEDD4-family ligases, CDKN2A blocks MDM2-directed degradation of p53, and MAGE proteins redirect ligase specificity in cancer. Loss of this regulation produces premature chromosome segregation, aneuploidy, and failure of tumour suppressor turnover control.

Ubiquitin ligases are switched on at particular moments rather than running continuously, and this pathway covers the events that raise the rate at which ubiquitin is transferred onto substrates. Much of the content is cell cycle control: CDC20 and FZR1 act as substrate-recruiting activators of the anaphase-promoting complex, while UBE2C and UBE2S are the ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes that build and elongate the degradative chains on securin, cyclin B and other mitotic regulators, so that sister chromatids separate and cells exit mitosis on schedule. CDC14B contributes phosphatase-dependent timing to that activation. Other members point to different ligases: arrestin-domain adaptors ARRDC3 and ARRDC4 deliver cargo to NEDD4-family enzymes for receptor downregulation, BMI1 supports Polycomb-directed histone H2A ubiquitination, and MAGE proteins stimulate associated ligases in a way that is exploited in tumours. Loss of such control leads to failed substrate turnover and chromosome missegregation.

Ubiquitin ligases commit proteins to proteasomal destruction, so dampening their activity is how cells keep substrates alive until the right moment. This negative regulation of ubiquitin-protein transferase activity matters most in mitosis, where inhibitors of the anaphase-promoting complex hold sister chromatids together until the spindle checkpoint is satisfied. FBXO5 (Emi1) binds and inhibits that ligase to prevent premature cyclin and securin degradation, while MAD2L1 acts through the checkpoint complex that restrains its activating subunit; USP44 reinforces the arrest by opposing ubiquitination of a checkpoint component rather than by acting as a ligase itself. Loss of such restraint produces premature anaphase, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, linking the process to genome stability and tumorigenesis. Other members connect ligase inhibition to kinase signalling and DNA damage tolerance, indicating that ligase output is tuned rather than simply switched on.

Meiosis must be entered at the right time, paused at defined stages, and resumed only on cue, and this regulatory layer sets that timing in germ cells of both sexes. It determines when a spermatogonium or oocyte leaves mitotic proliferation for the meiotic programme, how long an oocyte arrests before ovulation, and when the metaphase-to-anaphase transition is allowed; errors produce aneuploid gametes, infertility and miscarriage. Control converges on cyclin-dependent kinase activity through CDC25 phosphatases and the inhibitory kinases WEE2 and PKMYT1, and on the anaphase-promoting complex with its activators CDC20 and FZR1, whose premature action is restrained by EMI-type inhibitors and spindle checkpoint components. Overlaid on this are germline-specific inputs: retinoic acid-responsive STRA8 with MEIOSIN for meiotic initiation, RNA-binding regulators such as DAZL, NANOS2, MEIOC and YTHDC2, and cGMP signalling from the follicle through NPPC and its receptor that holds the oocyte arrested.

Germ cells only make haploid gametes if they are pushed into and through meiosis at the right moment, and this positive regulatory programme is what drives that entry and progression. It matters for fertility in both sexes: loss of its components leaves spermatogonia or oocytes stalled in a mitotic-like state or arrested mid-prophase, producing azoospermia and premature ovarian failure. Retinoic acid-responsive initiators such as STRA8 and MEIOSIN switch on the meiotic transcriptional programme, while MEIOC and the RNA helicase YTHDC2 act with RNA-binding factors including DAZL and RBM46 to remodel the germ cell transcriptome away from the mitotic cycle. CDC25 phosphatases dephosphorylate and thereby activate cyclin-dependent kinases to license divisions, PRDM9 specifies recombination hotspots, and signals from WNT ligands and natriuretic peptide receptor NPR2 time meiotic resumption within the gonadal environment.

Gametes are made by meiosis, but the divisions must be held back until the cell is ready: negative regulation of the meiotic cell cycle is the set of brakes that arrests oocytes and spermatogonia at defined stages and blocks premature progression. Oocytes stay arrested at prophase I under a follicle-derived signal acting through a natriuretic peptide receptor, and again at metaphase II under cytostatic factor, where a MAP kinase kinase kinase and the anaphase-promoting complex inhibitors EMI1 and EMI2 keep cyclin B from being destroyed; an inhibitory kinase phosphorylates CDK1 to reinforce the block. Other members enforce checkpoints rather than arrest: kinetochore and spindle-assembly components delay anaphase until attachments are correct, while HORMA-domain proteins and their AAA+ regulator couple progression to completion of recombination. Loss of these controls produces aneuploid eggs, precocious germ cell differentiation, and infertility.

Myoblast proliferation is the expansion of the mononucleate muscle precursor pool that must occur before those cells fuse into myotubes and mature into skeletal muscle fibres. It sets the size of the muscle formed in the embryo and the regenerative capacity of adult muscle, where satellite cells marked by PAX7 re-enter the cycle after injury; when it fails, muscle grows poorly and repairs badly, and when it is not switched off, differentiation never begins. The genes describe the balance between the two states: growth factor and kinase inputs such as HGF, IGF1, KRAS and ABL1 drive cycling, myostatin restrains it, and the myogenic transcription factors MYOD1 and SOX15 with cofactors like PAXBP1 couple exit from the cycle to differentiation. Muscle-specific microRNAs including miR-1 and miR-133 tune the switch. The pathway sits at the junction of cell cycle control and myogenic lineage commitment.

Skeletal muscle is built and repaired by mononucleate myoblasts that must first expand in number before they stop dividing and fuse into myotubes, and myoblast proliferation is the phase that sets how many nuclei a muscle can acquire. Growth of this pool supports fetal muscle formation and, in the adult, regeneration from satellite cells; its collapse leaves muscle unable to repair after injury, while failure to exit the cycle blocks differentiation. Mitogens such as HGF and IGF1 drive expansion through Ras and downstream kinase cascades feeding immediate-early transcription, while myostatin restrains it. Lineage regulators including PAX7, MYOD1, SOX15 and MEIS2 set the balance between staying proliferative and committing to fusion, and a large muscle-enriched microRNA contingent, notably the miR-1 and miR-133 families, tunes that switch. MEGF10 and KLHL41 link the same population to fusion and sarcomere assembly, and their mutation causes congenital myopathy.

Skeletal muscle is built by myoblasts that must travel to the right place before they fuse, and myoblast migration is the movement step that positions them for myotube formation and, later, for repair of injured fibre. Without it, muscle masses form in the wrong locations or regenerate poorly, since satellite-cell-derived myoblasts have to reach a wound before they can differentiate. The genes here combine cytoskeletal and adhesion control with extrinsic cues: a Rho-dependent kinase and a RhoA exchange factor drive actomyosin contractility, an integrin-binding adaptor couples cells to matrix, and thrombospondin provides matricellular signal. Transcription factors of the sine oculis family specify the myogenic programme in which migration occurs, while myostatin restrains myoblast proliferation and motility and hedgehog signalling through its receptor supplies a developmental patterning input. Engulfment receptor MEGF10 links the same cells to subsequent fusion and regeneration.

Acidification of intracellular compartments, and of the cytosol itself, is what makes lysosomes and secretory organelles work: hydrolases need a low-pH lumen, and the proton gradient drives secondary transport of amino acids, metals and other solutes. The dominant machinery here is the vacuolar H+-ATPase, with its membrane-embedded V0 ring and cytosolic V1 catalytic sector plus accessory and assembly factors, which pumps protons into endosomes, lysosomes, phagosomes and the osteoclast ruffled border; chloride and cation-proton exchangers provide the counter-ion flux and set the final pH. Rab GTPases and lysosomal membrane proteins deliver and mature the compartments being acidified. Loss of these components causes osteopetrosis, distal renal tubular acidosis and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and failure of phagosomal acidification impairs killing of ingested microbes.

intracellular pH elevation covers the transport processes that raise cytosolic or organellar pH by removing protons or importing base equivalents. Setting pH upward matters because enzyme activity, pigment synthesis, lysosomal hydrolase function and epithelial fluid secretion each depend on a defined proton concentration, and cells that cannot alkalinise a compartment lose those functions. The genes are largely channels and anion exchangers: CFTR conducts chloride and bicarbonate at secretory epithelial surfaces, SLC26A3 and SLC26A6 exchange chloride for bicarbonate in intestine and pancreas, and SLC7A11 imports cystine in exchange for glutamate to support glutathione synthesis. Others act on organelles, where TMEM175 provides lysosomal proton and potassium conductance and CLN3 supports lysosomal homeostasis, while OCA2 and SLC45A2 raise melanosomal pH to permit tyrosinase activity. Their loss produces cystic fibrosis, chloride diarrhoea, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis and albinism.

Cells must hold their internal pH within a narrow band, and this is the set of activities that push it upward by removing protons or importing base equivalents. The effect matters both for whole-cell cytosolic homeostasis and for tuning the pH of organelles: melanosomes, for example, must be de-acidified for tyrosinase to work, and the pigmentation transporters OCA2 and SLC45A2 raise melanosomal pH, with loss-of-function causing oculocutaneous albinism. Other members act at epithelial and endolysosomal membranes, including the chloride channel CFTR and the anion exchangers SLC26A3 and SLC26A6, which couple chloride movement to bicarbonate secretion in gut and pancreatic ducts, and the lysosomal potassium channel TMEM175, whose loss acidifies and impairs lysosomes. Alkalinization of this kind supports enzyme activity, vesicle trafficking, fluid secretion and cystine transport by SLC7A11.

Getting a protein into the nucleus is only half the problem; keeping it there determines whether transcription factors, repair proteins and signalling molecules act where they are meant to. Maintenance of protein location in the nucleus covers the retention side of nucleocytoplasmic partitioning: sequestration into subnuclear compartments, stabilisation of the resident form, and recapture of proteins that leak out. Several members act by building the compartments that hold cargo, notably PML and SP100 in nuclear bodies, while SUN1 and SUN2 anchor the inner nuclear membrane to the nucleoskeleton and cytoskeletal linkers. RANGAP1 sets the directionality of the Ran gradient on which import and export depend, and CIZ1 retains replication factors at nuclear matrix sites. Loss of retention mislocalises tumour suppressors such as BARD1 and nuclear receptors including PGR and NR5A1, uncoupling hormone and damage signals from their gene targets.

Corticotropin secretion is the pituitary step of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis: anterior pituitary corticotropes release ACTH into the circulation, which drives adrenal cortical glucocorticoid output and so sets the body's response to stress, inflammation, and daily metabolic demand. Hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone and the related peptide urocortin act on the CRHR1 receptor to trigger release, while a secreted binding protein sequesters free CRH and limits how much reaches the receptor, providing a tier of control outside negative feedback by cortisol. Additional modulators tune the set point, including the gastric hormone ghrelin, which links nutritional state to the axis, and a secreted regulatory peptide of hypothalamic tissue; vesicular trafficking components contribute to the exocytic release itself. Loss of control here underlies Cushing's disease and adrenal insufficiency, and chronic overactivity accompanies depression and stress-related illness.

Control of corticotropin release from pituitary corticotropes sets the pace of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and thus the body's glucocorticoid output during stress, fasting and inflammation. Hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone is the principal drive, reaching the anterior pituitary through the portal circulation, with urocortin acting on related receptors as an additional stimulus; a dedicated binding protein sequesters circulating CRH and tempers how much reaches its receptors. Ghrelin links nutritional and gut-derived signals to the same output, while an augurin-type secreted factor and a Rab GTPase involved in vesicle traffic point to local paracrine and secretory-machinery contributions at the pituitary. Because the resulting corticotropin governs adrenal cortisol synthesis, disturbed regulation here underlies stress-related endocrine dysfunction, and negative feedback by glucocorticoids normally restrains the loop.

positive regulation of corticotropin secretion describes the signals that drive pituitary corticotrope cells to release ACTH, the step that sets adrenal glucocorticoid output and therefore the body's cortisol response to stress. Hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing hormone is the principal stimulus, acting through its receptor on corticotropes to raise cAMP and trigger secretory granule exocytosis; urocortin acts on the same receptor family, and the gastric peptide ghrelin and the secreted factor ECRG4 provide additional stimulatory input, linking energy status and local tissue signals to the axis. A Rab GTPase contributes to granule trafficking and membrane fusion during release. This is the activating arm of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, normally restrained by glucocorticoid negative feedback; its persistent overactivity underlies hypercortisolism, and its failure blunts the metabolic, immune and behavioural adaptations to stress.

Corticotropin release from pituitary corticotropes is the middle step of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and processes that increase its frequency or amount set how strongly the body mounts a glucocorticoid response to stress. The hypothalamic releasing factor corticotropin-releasing hormone is the principal driver, acting on corticotropes to trigger ACTH secretion; urocortin is a related peptide acting through the same receptor family, and the stomach-derived peptide ghrelin also stimulates the axis, linking energy status and feeding to stress hormone output. ECRG4 is a secreted peptide of the hypothalamic and choroid plexus region implicated in neuroendocrine signalling, and RAB8B contributes trafficking machinery for regulated secretory vesicles. Excessive or sustained activation of this arm drives hypercortisolism, while loss of drive causes adrenal insufficiency, so the pathway sits at the interface of neuroendocrine stress responses, metabolism and immune suppression.

Cytosolic free calcium is held far below its extracellular and store concentrations so that brief rises can act as a signal, and this pathway covers the transporters, channels, buffers and receptors that set and restore that resting level. It underlies muscle contraction and relaxation, neurotransmitter release, hormone secretion and fertilisation, and its failure produces arrhythmia, excitotoxic neuronal death and malignant hyperthermia. Calcium enters through store-operated and receptor-operated TRPC channels and voltage-gated channel subunits, and is released from the endoplasmic and sarcoplasmic reticulum by inositol trisphosphate receptors and the ryanodine receptors RYR1 and RYR2. Removal falls to plasma membrane calcium ATPases and sodium/calcium exchangers, while calbindins and phospholamban-regulated store uptake shape the amplitude and decay of each transient. G protein-coupled receptors for glutamate, purines, cannabinoids and orexin feed into the same cytosolic calcium pool.</description>}“””</br>}

Cytosolic calcium must be returned to resting nanomolar levels after every signalling event, and the processes that lower it set the duration of contraction, secretion and synaptic transmission and protect cells from calcium-triggered death. Extrusion across the plasma membrane is the core activity here: a calcium-pumping ATPase (ATP2B1) drives Ca2+ out at the expense of ATP, while a sodium/calcium exchanger (SLC8A1) uses the sodium gradient maintained by Na+/K+-ATPase to do the same at higher capacity. Potassium channels such as KCNA5 and KCNK3 hyperpolarise the membrane and thereby reduce voltage-gated calcium entry, and inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors including dopamine D2/D3, mu-opioid and melatonin receptors suppress calcium influx downstream of ligand binding. Anti-apoptotic and ER-resident proteins such as BCL2 and TMBIM6 shape store content and leak. Loss of this restraint produces calcium overload, excitotoxicity and arrhythmia.

Filopodia are thin, finger-like actin bundles that motile cells and growth cones push ahead of themselves to sample the environment, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how many form, how fast, and how long they persist. Tuning filopodium assembly determines whether an axon finds its target, whether a dendritic spine forms a synapse, and whether a fibroblast or leukocyte migrates directionally; misregulation shows up in neurodevelopmental disorders and in invasive cell behaviour. The core actin machinery here works through the Rho-family GTPase CDC42 and related small GTPases, with formins and the WASP-family nucleator WASL driving barbed-end polymerisation, fascin cross-linking the resulting bundles, and the unconventional motor MYO10 trafficking cargo to filopodial tips. Upstream, guidance and adhesion receptors such as EPHB2, neuropilin, neurexin/neuroligin and teneurins, plus chemokine and TGF-beta signalling, feed positional cues into this protrusive response.

negative regulation of filopodium assembly restrains the formation of the thin, actin-bundled protrusions that cells extend to explore their surroundings, keeping membrane protrusion in check so that motility, adhesion and neurite outgrowth remain spatially and temporally controlled. Limiting filopodia matters most in the nervous system, where the density of growth cone and dendritic protrusions sets how many synapses a neuron can sample and form; too much protrusive activity yields excess immature spines and mislocalised contacts. The genes act at the membrane–cytoskeleton interface: Rho-family GAP and F-BAR proteins such as ARHGAP44 and the human-specific SRGAP2 paralogue dampen Rac/Cdc42-driven actin bundling and slow spine maturation, a kinase arm adds phosphorylation control, and a synaptic adhesion molecule couples cell contact to protrusion shutdown. Together they oppose filopodium initiation downstream of small GTPase signalling and thereby shape neuronal morphology and migration.

Filopodia are the thin, finger-like actin bundles that motile cells and axonal growth cones push out to sample their surroundings, and their assembly must be restrained as well as driven; this pathway covers the braking side, limiting how many protrusions form and how fast. Restraint shapes neuronal morphology in particular: by slowing filopodial emergence, it sets the pace of dendritic spine maturation and the timing of synapse formation, and the human-specific paralogue SRGAP2C acts by antagonising ancestral SRGAP2 function, a change linked to the protracted spine development characteristic of human cortex. Other members contribute Rho-family GTPase regulation through a GAP domain, membrane deformation and small GTPase-dependent membrane traffic, and kinase signalling, while presynaptic adhesion molecule neurexin-1 ties the process to synaptic contact. Loss of such control yields excess protrusions and miswired connectivity.

Filopodia are the thin, finger-like actin bundles that a motile cell or a growth cone pushes ahead of itself to sample the environment, and this pathway covers the signals that increase their formation. It matters for directed cell migration, axon pathfinding and synapse formation, where filopodia become the first contacts that mature into dendritic spines and synaptic junctions. Upstream cues include chemokine signalling through CCR7, neuropilin and teneurin adhesion systems, and TGF-beta receptor engagement; these converge on Rho-family GTPases such as CDC42 and RHOQ, their exchange factor DOCK11 and the ARAP1 GAP domain module, which in turn recruit WASL and the F-BAR protein FNBP1L to nucleate and elongate actin. Fascin (FSCN1) cross-links the resulting filaments into stiff parallel bundles, while SRF-dependent transcription sustains the actin cytoskeletal programme. Loss of such regulation, as in FMR1 deficiency, distorts spine and neurite morphology.

Cells change shape, crawl, divide and hold their junctions by continuously rebuilding actin filaments and microtubules, and this pathway covers the control layer that decides when and where those polymers are assembled, bundled or taken apart. It underpins cell migration, neurite and dendritic spine growth, spindle assembly and cytokinesis, epithelial and endothelial barrier integrity, and muscle sarcomere organization; its failure contributes to tumour invasion, immunodeficiency and neurodevelopmental disease. Rho-family GTPases with their many exchange factors and GAPs relay signals from growth factor receptors, integrins and chemokine receptors to effectors such as ROCK, PAK and LIMK, which in turn control cofilin severing, profilin- and formin-driven elongation, Arp2/3 branching via WAVE and WASP complexes, and capping by CapZ and tropomodulins. In parallel, plus-end tracking proteins, stathmins, katanin, CAMSAPs and augmin-dependent nucleation tune microtubule dynamics and centrosome behaviour.

Cytoskeletal structures must be dismantled and restrained as well as built, and negative regulation of cytoskeleton organization covers the activities that stop, slow or reverse filament assembly.
