This braking is what allows cells to change shape, retract protrusions, turn over adhesions, and keep actin and microtubule networks from overgrowing during migration, division and neuronal remodelling. Capping proteins of the CapZ family and tropomodulins block filament ends, gelsolin, scinderin and cofilin sever or depolymerize actin, while profilin, thymosin beta-4 and twinfilins sequester monomers; stathmins destabilize microtubules and slingshot phosphatases feed back onto cofilin. Rho-family GAPs and spectrin/adducin lattices impose further constraint, and CLASPs, KANKs and CAMSAP2 govern microtubule ends at cortical sites. Loss of such restraint distorts cell polarity, dendritic spine architecture, erythrocyte membrane stability and ciliary function, and several components act as tumour suppressors.

Cells change shape, move, divide and form protrusions by actively driving the assembly and rearrangement of their cytoskeleton, and this collection represents the activating side of that control: signals and effectors that increase actin polymerisation, filament bundling, microtubule dynamics and centrosome duplication. It underlies lamellipodial and filopodial protrusion in migrating and immune cells, sarcomere and podocyte architecture, neuronal growth-cone extension, and spindle and cilium formation, so its misregulation contributes to defective wound healing, tumour invasion and microcephaly-type developmental disorders. Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1, CDC42 and RHOA act through WAVE-complex and Arp2/3 components, formins, profilins and Ena/VASP proteins to nucleate and elongate filaments, while LIMK1 and TESK1 phosphorylate cofilin to stabilise existing networks. Parallel members regulate microtubule plus ends, dynein-based transport, katanin severing and centriole biogenesis, linking upstream receptor and chemokine cues to cytoskeletal output.

Stress fibers are contractile bundles of actin filaments, myosin and crosslinkers that let adherent cells such as fibroblasts pull on their substrate, mature focal adhesions, and sense matrix stiffness; upregulating their assembly is how cells stiffen, migrate directionally, close wounds and differentiate into myofibroblasts, and persistent activation of this route contributes to tissue fibrosis and to the contractility of trabecular meshwork cells in glaucoma. The positive arm of this control runs largely through Rho-family GTPases and their activators: several Rho-specific exchange factors feed RHOA, RHOC, RAC1 and CDC42, ROCK2 and LIMK1 with the TESK kinase restrain cofilin-mediated filament severing, and formins such as FHOD1 nucleate and bundle filaments. Upstream cues include TGF-beta receptor and SMAD3 signalling, lysophosphatidic acid and neuropeptide receptors, syndecan-4 and integrin-associated adaptors, linking extracellular mechanical and soluble signals to adhesion proteins like paxillin and kindlin.

Elastin gives lung, skin, and large arteries their recoil, and its turnover is the balance between depositing crosslinked elastic fibres and degrading them. Because mature elastin is made once and expected to last a lifetime, net degradation is largely irreversible, and excess proteolysis produces emphysema, arterial stiffening, aneurysm, and the loss of dermal elasticity seen with ageing and smoking. The genes here sit on both sides of that balance: macrophage elastase and a pancreatic-type elastase cleave the polymer, cathepsin L adds lysosomal cysteine-protease activity, and cystatin C restrains cysteine proteases to limit fibre breakdown. Regulatory inputs include the hypoxia-responsive transcription factor HIF1A and leptin signalling, linking elastin handling to oxygen availability and metabolic state. Released elastin peptides are themselves chemotactic, so degradation can feed back on the inflammatory cells that drive it.</description>

Keratinocyte migration is the directed crawling of epidermal cells across a wound bed, the step that re-epithelialises broken skin and restores its barrier. When it stalls, wounds become chronic; when it is driven too hard, it contributes to hyperproliferative epidermis and to the invasive behaviour of squamous carcinoma. The genes describe how migration is licensed and steered: keratinocyte growth factors FGF7 and FGF10 and the EGFR ligand HB-EGF signal from the wound margin, PTEN and mTOR set the balance of PI3K output that governs polarity and protrusion, and ARF6 with its exchange factor IQSEC1 recycles integrins and adhesion receptors at the leading edge. Kindlin-1 and epiplakin couple the cytoskeleton to adhesions, wound-induced keratin 16 remodels the intermediate filament network for compliance, and ADAM9, MMP9 and hyaluronan synthesis clear a path through matrix.

When the epidermis is wounded, keratinocytes at the wound edge loosen their attachments and crawl across the defect to restore the barrier, and this migratory programme is what closes skin wounds. Its failure underlies chronic ulceration, while its dysregulation contributes to invasive behaviour in squamous carcinoma. The genes here span the layers such motility requires: integrin-linked adhesion and cytoskeletal coupling through kindlin-1, plectin-family and keratin components, with FERMT1 loss causing Kindler syndrome; secreted cues such as keratinocyte growth factor, FGF10 and heparin-binding EGF that drive re-epithelialization; matrix remodelling by ADAM9, MMP9 and hyaluronan synthesis; and ARF6- and IQSEC1-dependent membrane trafficking that recycles adhesion receptors at the leading edge. Growth-factor signalling converges on mTOR, opposed by PTEN, linking nutrient and lipid sensing to how fast the sheet advances.

Skin repair depends on keratinocytes crawling from the wound edge across the denuded surface, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast and how far they go. Too little and wounds fail to re-epithelialise, as in chronic ulcers; too much unrestrained motility accompanies invasive behaviour in squamous carcinoma. Growth factors released after injury provide the promigratory cues, including keratinocyte growth factor and related fibroblast growth factor signals plus heparin-binding EGF, which act through receptor tyrosine kinases onto PI3K signalling that PTEN opposes and mTOR relays into protein synthesis and cytoskeletal output. Adhesion turnover and matrix remodelling are handled by a metalloproteinase and a sheddase, hyaluronan synthesis alters the pericellular environment, and ARF6 with its exchange factor controls integrin and receptor trafficking at the leading edge. Cytolinker and microtubule-associated components tie polarity to the keratin network.

Flavones and related flavonoids enter the body only through the diet, and this pathway describes how the human gut and liver handle them. It matters because these plant polyphenols are absorbed poorly and cleared fast: the same enzymes that dispose of them set how much reaches the circulation, and they are a common route of food–drug interaction. Most dietary flavones arrive as glycosides, and the brush-border enzyme lactase-phlorizin hydrolase cleaves the sugar so the aglycone can cross the enterocyte membrane. Inside, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the UGT1A family attach glucuronic acid to phenolic hydroxyls, converting the compounds into water-soluble conjugates for biliary and urinary excretion. The intestinal and hepatic members of that family differ in substrate preference, so flavone metabolism is a first-pass phenomenon shared with bilirubin, drugs and other xenobiotic glucuronidation.

Mitochondria take up calcium from the cytosol and release it again, and how much they hold sets the pace of oxidative metabolism, shapes cytosolic calcium signals, and decides whether a stressed cell survives or dies. The uptake side is the inner-membrane uniporter complex: a pore formed by MCU with its dominant-negative paralogue MCUB, the regulatory subunit EMRE, and the MICU gatekeepers that keep the channel shut at resting calcium and open it once a threshold is crossed, with MCUR1 and SLC25A23 tuning the response. Efflux runs largely through the mitochondrial sodium/calcium exchanger encoded by SLC8B1, and LETM1 contributes to ion balance across the same membrane. Contact sites with the endoplasmic reticulum, supported by tethers such as PDZD8 and cristae organisers, deliver calcium locally. Overload opens the permeability transition and drives excitotoxic and ischaemic cell death; chronic imbalance features in neurodegeneration.

Mitochondria take up calcium from the cytosol to match ATP output to demand, and the processes that raise mitochondrial calcium set that link between signalling and oxidative metabolism. Calcium entering the matrix stimulates dehydrogenases of the TCA cycle and the respiratory chain, but excess loading opens the permeability transition pore and commits the cell to death, so this is also a node in ischemic injury and neurodegeneration. Uptake occurs through the inner-membrane uniporter channel formed by MCU with its regulators MICU1 and MICU2, which set a threshold so that the channel stays shut at resting cytosolic calcium, alongside MCUR1 and the matrix carrier SLC25A23. Endoplasmic reticulum calcium handling by SERCA pumps and the mitochondrial contacts maintained by BNIP3 shape how much calcium reaches the organelle.

regulation of neurotransmitter uptake controls how quickly released transmitter is cleared from the synapse, and therefore how long and how strongly a signal is felt by the postsynaptic cell. Clearance sets the duration of dopaminergic, glutamatergic and monoaminergic transmission, and its misregulation underlies both drug responses and neurodegeneration. The genes act at several levels: dopamine autoreceptors D2/D3 feed back on transporter activity and surface expression, integrins and flotillin organise the membrane microdomains and trafficking that place transporters at the plasma membrane, and the astrocytic sodium pump subunit ATP1A2 with GFAP marks glial uptake as a major contributor. Presynaptic proteins including alpha-synuclein, synaptogyrin-3, parkin and torsinA modulate transporter function, linking this regulation directly to Parkinson's disease and dystonia. Nitric oxide signalling, GDNF trophic support and circadian input through PER2 provide additional layers of control.

Synaptic signalling is terminated largely by clearing transmitter from the extracellular space, and this pathway covers the control of that clearance step by neurons and surrounding glia. Setting how fast dopamine, glutamate or GABA is recaptured determines the amplitude and duration of transmission, the size of refillable vesicular stores, and how much transmitter is left exposed to oxidation. Regulation acts on transporter abundance, surface delivery and trafficking, and on the ion gradients that power uptake, with the sodium pump subunit ATP1A2 in astrocytes supplying the driving force and membrane and vesicle proteins such as flotillin, synaptogyrin and RAB3B influencing transporter localisation. Dopamine receptors and presynaptic proteins including alpha-synuclein, parkin and GDNF tune dopamine reuptake, linking this control to striatal function, addiction-related plasticity and the vulnerability of dopaminergic neurons in Parkinson's disease.

Synaptic signalling is terminated largely by clearing transmitter back into neurons and surrounding glia, and this pathway covers the influences that raise the rate or extent of that reuptake. Stronger uptake shortens the lifetime of transmitter in the cleft, sharpens signalling, and replenishes vesicular stores; weak or dysregulated uptake leaves transmitter to act too long and exposes cells to oxidative breakdown products, a concern in dopaminergic neurons in particular. The dopamine receptors DRD2 and DRD4 act as autoreceptors whose activation increases dopamine clearance capacity, and the parkinsonism-associated ubiquitin ligase PRKN influences transporter levels. Vesicular and trafficking components such as RAB3B and the vesicular glutamate transporter SLC17A8 tie plasma-membrane uptake to refilling of secretory vesicles, while integrin-mediated adhesion contributes to positioning transporters at the membrane.

Chemical signalling between neurons depends not just on releasing transmitter but on tuning how much is released and when, and this regulation of neurotransmitter transport covers the processes that set that level. It determines synaptic strength and plasticity, and its disturbance underlies movement disorders, epilepsy and psychiatric disease. Much of the control converges on the release machinery itself: syntaxins, SNAP-binding and Munc18-type proteins, synaptotagmin calcium sensors, complexins, RAB3 and RIM active-zone scaffolds, and synaptic vesicle proteins such as SV2 and synapsin, with vesicular carriers loading glutamate and acetylcholine. Upstream, presynaptic calcium channels, calmodulin, CaMKII, protein kinase C and calcineurin couple activity to secretion, while dopamine, adenosine, purinergic and nicotinic receptors provide autocrine and neuromodulatory feedback. Alpha-synuclein, parkin, LRRK2, FMR1 and neuroligin link the same machinery to neurodegeneration and synaptic pathology.

negative regulation of neurotransmitter transport is the braking side of chemical neurotransmission: the set of processes that dampen how much neurotransmitter is loaded, released, or taken back up at a synapse. Restraint of this kind sets the gain of synaptic signalling, protects against excitotoxic glutamate spillover, and keeps dopamine release episodic rather than continuous; its loss contributes to paroxysmal movement disorders and to the synaptic dysfunction seen early in Parkinson disease. The genes act at several points. Alpha-synuclein and synaptotagmin-11 clamp vesicle fusion and limit exocytosis, parkin ubiquitinates synaptic substrates and maintains presynaptic quality control, nitric oxide synthase and an acid-sensing channel provide diffusible and ionic feedback onto release, and PNKD suppresses release through interaction with the exocytic machinery. Together they place negative feedback and vesicle-cycle control at the heart of presynaptic homeostasis.

Synaptic signalling is tuned as much by restraint as by release, and this grouping covers the processes that dampen neurotransmitter movement — both vesicular release at the terminal and carrier-mediated uptake or efflux. Such brakes set how much transmitter reaches receptors per stimulus and protect against excitotoxicity and runaway excitation; their loss is linked to movement disorders and neurodegeneration. Several members act directly at the release machinery: synaptotagmin-1 is the calcium sensor that triggers fusion, while synaptotagmin-11 and alpha-synuclein constrain exocytosis, and parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase mutated in recessive parkinsonism, regulates their abundance. Others impose modulatory control — nitric oxide produced by neuronal NOS acts as a diffusible retrograde signal, acid-sensing channels couple extracellular pH to terminal excitability, and PNKD variants cause paroxysmal dyskinesia. Together they place presynaptic gain control within broader regulation of neuronal communication and dopaminergic vulnerability.

positive regulation of neurotransmitter transport covers the signals and machinery that increase how much neurotransmitter is loaded into vesicles and released at synapses, setting the gain of chemical communication between neurons. Its output determines synaptic strength, and its dysregulation underlies parkinsonian dopamine loss, schizophrenia-associated signalling defects, and epilepsy caused by mutations in the release apparatus. The genes span the layers involved: vesicular loading by transporters such as the vesicular glutamate and acetylcholine carriers, the calcium sensor and SNARE core (SYT1, STX1A/B, STXBP1) that executes exocytosis, RAB3 GTPases and their regulators that govern vesicle trafficking, and presynaptic receptors including dopamine D2 and adenosine A2A that tune release from outside. Calcium handling by mitochondrial uptake and calcineurin, plus synaptic adhesion through neuroligin, link activity and contact to release probability.

Chemical signalling between neurons depends on loading neurotransmitter into vesicles and releasing it on cue, and this pathway covers the influences that increase that movement. Upregulating release sets synaptic strength and underlies learning, motor control and neuroendocrine output; loss of the machinery causes epileptic encephalopathy and movement disorders, and its dysregulation figures in Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia. The genes span the steps involved: vesicular transporters that fill vesicles with glutamate or acetylcholine, calcium entry through a presynaptic N-type channel, and the SNARE and regulatory proteins syntaxin-1, synaptotagmin-1 and STXBP1 that execute calcium-triggered fusion, with Rab3 proteins and their regulators controlling vesicle trafficking. Receptor-level modulation by adenosine A2A and dopamine D2/D4 receptors, calcineurin signalling and adhesion molecules such as neuroligin-1 tune how much transmitter a terminal delivers and where release sites form.

Cyclic AMP is the second messenger that converts hormone and neurotransmitter binding at G protein-coupled receptors into cellular action, and this pathway covers what cells actually do once cAMP rises. The outputs are diverse but concrete: immediate-early transcription through FOS/FOSB and the CRTC coactivators that license CREB-dependent gene expression, gating of ion channels and transporters such as the CFTR chloride channel, HCN pacemaker channels and KCNQ1/KCNE1, activation of Rap GTPases via exchange factors including the cAMP sensor RAPGEF3, and induction of gluconeogenic and ureagenic enzymes in liver. Scaffolding AKAPs restrict kinase activity to particular compartments while phosphodiesterases such as PDE4D and PDE2A terminate the signal, so both the amplitude and the address of the response are controlled. This logic underlies hormone-driven secretion, epithelial fluid transport, cardiac rhythm, melatonin and pigment synthesis, and circadian gene expression.

Calcium is the cell's most versatile second messenger, and this collection covers what cells actually do once intracellular calcium rises: contract, secrete, change excitability, and rewire transcription. The response depends on sensors and buffers that read the signal — calmodulin and its kinase targets, calcineurin acting on NFAT, penta-EF-hand and copine proteins, synaptotagmin for vesicle fusion — together with the channels and transporters that shape the transient itself, including ryanodine receptors and store-operated entry through STIM1 and TRPC channels, mitochondrial uptake gated by the MICU regulators, and calcium-activated potassium channels that feed the signal back into membrane potential. Immediate-early transcription factors such as FOS and JUN family members translate transients into lasting gene expression. Excitation-contraction coupling in heart and skeletal muscle, synaptic transmission, lymphocyte activation and keratinocyte differentiation all rest on this decoding, and its failure underlies arrhythmia, myopathy and disordered secretion.

Folate is a dietary vitamin that cells sense as well as consume, and this response pathway covers the changes in gene expression, enzyme activity and metabolism that follow a folic acid stimulus. It matters most in early development and in vascular health: inadequate folate intake or impaired handling raises homocysteine and underlies neural tube defects, the basis for periconceptional supplementation and flour fortification. Uptake is mediated by high-affinity folate receptors, while MTHFR generates the methyl donor form of the vitamin and CBS disposes of homocysteine through transsulfuration, tying the response to one-carbon and methionine metabolism. Downstream effects reach neuronal differentiation factors such as ASCL1, inflammatory regulators, and antioxidant and cholinesterase activity, indicating that folate status feeds into redox balance, neurogenesis and transcriptional programmes rather than acting only as a cofactor supply.

Methylglyoxal is a reactive dicarbonyl formed as an unavoidable side product of glycolysis; it glycates arginine and lysine residues and nucleic acids, so cells must sense and dispose of it to keep proteins and the genome functional. The response to methylglyoxal covers the detoxification and transcriptional adjustments triggered by this stimulus, and its failure contributes to the advanced glycation seen in diabetic complications, aging tissue and neurodegeneration. HAGH carries out the second step of the glutathione-dependent glyoxalase route, hydrolysing S-D-lactoylglutathione to D-lactate and regenerating glutathione. PARK7/DJ-1 acts as a protein deglycase and oxidative stress sensor whose loss causes early-onset parkinsonism. PNKD and GATD1 belong to related glyoxalase-domain families, and the corepressor SIN3A links dicarbonyl stress to chromatin-level control of gene expression.

response to hydrostatic pressure covers how cells sense and react to the static load imposed by surrounding fluid, a stimulus that matters wherever tissues sit under sustained pressure: kidney tubules, vascular walls, cartilage and intraocular chambers. Reading that load lets cells adjust calcium handling, gene expression, secretion and cytoskeletal stiffness to match the mechanical environment; failure to read it correctly contributes to cystic kidney disease and to pressure-driven remodelling of vessels and joints. The genes point to the sensing apparatus and its downstream arms: the polycystin channel PKD2 as a mechanically gated calcium conduit, the plasma membrane calcium pump ATP2B4 restoring resting calcium, plectin linking intermediate filaments into a load-bearing network, basement membrane collagen XVIII, and PI3K and NTRK1 signalling converting the mechanical cue into growth and survival responses. It is one branch of mechanotransduction, distinct from shear stress sensing by flowing fluid.

Cells sense the standing weight of surrounding fluid and adjust their behaviour accordingly, a response to hydrostatic pressure that matters wherever tissues hold fluid under load: kidney tubules, cartilage and intervertebral disc, vascular walls, and the eye. The mechanism blends mechanosensitive ion flux with mechanically anchored structure and growth-factor signalling. PKD2 forms a cation channel implicated in transducing mechanical and flow cues in tubular epithelium, and its loss underlies polycystic kidney disease; ATP2B4 is a plasma membrane calcium pump that clears the resulting calcium rise; plectin cross-links intermediate filaments to junctions and so distributes force across the cytoskeleton. COL18A1 contributes to basement membrane architecture, while NTRK1 and the PI3K catalytic subunit PIK3CA couple pressure to survival and proliferative signalling, changing gene expression, secretion and matrix turnover in loaded tissue.

Secretory vesicles do not fuse with the plasma membrane at random; they are delivered to sites marked by the octameric exocyst, and getting that complex to the right patch of membrane is what this pathway accomplishes. Correct exocyst placement underlies polarized secretion, insulin granule release, ciliogenesis, and the directed membrane addition that lets a cell extend a front edge during migration or expand a new junction. Positioning is controlled by the small GTPase RalB, whose active form recruits exocyst subunits and thereby switches vesicle tethering between secretory and innate-immune signalling outputs; RalGAP components restrain that GTPase by stimulating GTP hydrolysis. The EXOC3 subunit and its paralogues provide the binding surface for these regulators, linking upstream Ras-family signalling to the spatial decision of where docking and fusion will occur.

Cells that can sense voltage change their behaviour when current passes through them, and this pathway collects the machinery by which an electrical stimulus is converted into altered signalling, secretion and gene expression. Excitable tissues depend on it: neurons adjust synaptic strength and transcription after stimulation, neuroendocrine cells release vasopressin and oxytocin in response to depolarisation, and muscle translates activity into growth or atrophy through myogenin and the ubiquitin ligase TRIM63. Mechanisms represented include glutamate receptors and ionotropic purinergic channels that admit cation flux, the G protein-gated potassium channel KCNJ3 that shunts excitability, calcium sensors such as hippocalcin, vesicle trafficking through RAB3A, and activity-dependent transcriptional regulators including BTG2 and the repressor REST. Phototransduction components are also present, reflecting light-evoked changes in membrane potential. Disordered coupling of this kind contributes to epilepsy, arrhythmia and disuse-related muscle wasting.

proteolysis involved in protein catabolic process covers the regulated destruction of intracellular proteins, the arm of proteostasis that removes damaged, misfolded, short-lived and no-longer-needed proteins so that cells can control the abundance of their own regulators. It sets the timing of cell cycle transitions, terminates signalling, clears aggregates in neurons, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration and the accumulation of oncogenic drivers. Most of the machinery here is ubiquitin-dependent: E1 and E2 enzymes charge ubiquitin, hundreds of RING, HECT and cullin-RING ligases with F-box, BTB-KELCH and DCAF substrate receptors select targets, deubiquitinases and p97/VCP with its UBX cofactors edit and extract them, and the 26S proteasome degrades them. Parallel routes are included: ER-associated degradation through SEL1L-HRD1 and derlins, ESCRT-driven sorting of membrane cargo to the lysosome, cathepsin and legumain proteolysis, and mitochondrial LONP1, CLPP and AFG3L2 quality control.

Cells continually destroy proteins that are damaged, misfolded, or no longer needed, and this pathway covers the peptide-bond cleavage steps that carry out that turnover. It sets protein half-lives and thereby controls cell cycle transitions, signalling output, transcription factor abundance, and the clearance of aggregation-prone species; its failure underlies neurodegeneration, cancer, and disorders of endoplasmic reticulum stress. Most substrates are first marked by ubiquitin through E1, E2 and E3 enzymes, including cullin-RING complexes with their F-box, KLHL and DCAF substrate adaptors, the anaphase-promoting complex, and HECT and RING ligases, then unfolded by VCP and degraded by the 26S proteasome, whose subunits are represented throughout. Complementary routes appear too: ER-associated degradation via SEL1L-HRD1 and derlins, lysosomal cathepsins and legumain, ESCRT-driven sorting of membrane receptors, and mitochondrial proteases such as LONP1, CLPP and AFG3L2. Deubiquitinases and shuttle factors tune the flux.

Newly synthesized polypeptides are rarely functional as made; protein maturation covers everything done to them afterwards so that they reach full activity. Chaperones of the HSP70, HSP90, chaperonin/TRiC and small heat-shock families, together with DNAJ co-chaperones, prefoldin and tubulin-folding cofactors, guide folding and prevent aggregation, while ER oxidoreductases and protein disulfide isomerases, calnexin/calreticulin, peptidyl-prolyl isomerases and glycosylation and GPI-anchor machinery install the modifications that stabilize secretory proteins. Proteolytic activation is the other half: signal peptidase and mitochondrial processing peptidases remove targeting sequences, proprotein convertases such as FURIN and PCSK1/2 cut prohormones, caspases and granzymes are themselves activated by cleavage, and coagulation factors, kallikreins and TMPRSS proteases circulate as zymogens. Failures produce misfolding disease, bleeding disorders, hormone deficiency and lysosomal or glycosylation defects.

Detection of stimulus covers the first step of all sensation: the conversion of a physical or chemical cue outside a cell into an intracellular signal it can act on. It underlies vision, smell, taste, hearing, balance, touch, pain and temperature sensing, as well as the innate immune recognition of microbes, and its failure produces retinal degeneration, deafness, anosmia and congenital insensitivity to pain. The largest contingent is the odorant receptor repertoire, joined by sweet, umami and bitter taste receptors and their gustducin transducers. Phototransduction appears in full, from opsins through transducin, phosphodiesterase and cyclic-nucleotide channels to arrestin-mediated shutoff. Mechanotransduction and nociception are carried by PIEZO, TRP, ASIC and hair-cell tip-link components such as TMC1 and STRC, while Toll-like and NOD-like receptors detect pathogen-associated molecules. Most routes converge on G-protein cascades or directly gated ion channels that change membrane potential.

Sensing the outside world begins with converting a physical or chemical stimulus into an intracellular signal, and this collection of receptors and transduction machinery covers that first step across essentially every sensory modality. Light detection is represented by rhodopsin and the cone opsins with their transducin subunits, phosphodiesterase, guanylate cyclases, arrestin and the retinoid cycle enzymes whose mutation causes retinitis pigmentosa and Leber congenital amaurosis. A very large olfactory receptor repertoire, together with sweet/umami and bitter taste receptors and their phospholipase and gustducin coupling, handles chemosensation. Mechanotransduction and hearing appear through hair-cell channel and stereocilia components such as TMC1, STRC, LHFPL5 and whirlin, alongside PIEZO1/2 and polycystins. Nociception and thermosensation run through TRPV1, TRPA1 and voltage-gated sodium channels, while Toll-like receptors, NOD proteins and inflammasome sensors detect microbial and danger cues. Loss of individual members produces blindness, deafness, anosmia or altered pain thresholds.

Antiviral defense encompasses everything a cell and organism do once viral material is detected, from raising the alarm to destroying infected cells. It underlies recovery from infection, and its loss produces overwhelming viral disease, while its inappropriate activation drives interferonopathies and autoimmune inflammation. Cytosolic sensors for foreign nucleic acid — RIG-I and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, cGAS with STING, AIM2 and IFI16, and endosomal Toll-like receptors — converge on TBK1 and the IRF3/IRF7 and NF-κB transcription factors to induce type I, II and III interferons. Interferon receptors then act through STAT1/STAT2 and IRF9 to switch on effectors that block translation, degrade viral RNA, restrict entry or replication, and tag viral proteins for destruction, including PKR, the OAS–RNase L system, MX proteins, IFIT and IFITM families, APOBEC3 deaminases, tetherin and numerous TRIM ubiquitin ligases. Autophagy components, inflammasomes and regulated necrosis eliminate compromised cells, while deubiquitinases and negative regulators restrain the response.

Histamine acts on target tissues only after it has been moved across membranes, and histamine transport covers both its packaging into secretory granules and its passage across plasma membranes. It underlies the wheal-and-flare of allergic responses, gastric acid secretion, and histaminergic neurotransmission, and its failure or blockade changes how much amine reaches receptors and how quickly it is cleared. The vesicular monoamine transporter SLC18A2 loads histamine into granules using a proton gradient, while the organic cation transporters SLC22A2 and SLC22A3 and the plasma membrane monoamine transporter SLC29A4 carry it into cells for degradation or reuptake. Release itself depends on regulated exocytosis: several v-SNAREs together with SNAP23 drive granule fusion in mast cells and basophils, downstream of the tyrosine kinases LYN and BTK that couple IgE receptor engagement to degranulation. Sorting nexins and RAB44 contribute to granule traffic and maturation.

Serotonin uptake is the transport of the monoamine 5-hydroxytryptamine out of the extracellular space and into cells, the step that terminates serotonergic signalling at the synapse and replenishes releasable stores. It sets the duration and intensity of serotonin action on mood, appetite, sleep, gastrointestinal motility and platelet function, and it is the direct target of SSRI antidepressants and of amphetamine-type psychostimulants. High-affinity reuptake at the presynaptic membrane is carried out by the sodium-dependent transporter SLC6A4, whose surface expression and kinetics are tuned by partners including integrin beta-3, alpha-synuclein and nitric oxide signalling. Lower-affinity organic cation and plasma membrane monoamine transporters provide uptake-2 clearance in glia, liver, gut and kidney, while vesicular monoamine transporters load the internalised amine into secretory vesicles, linking clearance to storage and re-release.

Serotonin signalling is terminated not by degradation at the synapse but by transport of the transmitter back into cells, and this uptake sets how long and how strongly 5-hydroxytryptamine acts on its receptors in brain, gut and platelets. The high-affinity plasma membrane serotonin transporter SLC6A4 is the principal route and the target of SSRI antidepressants; lower-affinity organic cation transporters and a plasma membrane monoamine transporter provide uptake-2 clearance in peripheral tissues. Once inside, vesicular monoamine transporters load serotonin into secretory vesicles for regulated release and protect it from cytosolic oxidation. Accessory proteins including integrin beta-3, neuronal nitric oxide synthase and alpha-synuclein modulate transporter surface expression and activity. Altered serotonin clearance is linked to depression and anxiety, platelet serotonin storage defects, and gastrointestinal motility disorders.

Noradrenergic signalling is terminated largely by clearing the transmitter from the synapse rather than degrading it, and norepinephrine uptake is that clearance step. It sets the amplitude and duration of sympathetic and central adrenergic tone, recycles transmitter for repackaging, and is the target of antidepressants, stimulants and cocaine. High-affinity plasma membrane carriers dominate at the presynaptic terminal, with SLC6A2 the noradrenaline transporter and the closely related dopamine transporter contributing where their selectivities overlap; lower-affinity organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family and the plasma membrane monoamine transporter SLC29A4 provide uptake-2 capacity in non-neuronal and peripheral tissues. Once inside, a vesicular monoamine transporter sequesters the amine into secretory vesicles, protecting it from oxidation. Alpha-synuclein and cytoskeletal actin influence transporter trafficking and vesicle handling, linking this transport system to catecholaminergic neuron vulnerability.

Cells build branched, crosslinked meshes of actin rather than single filaments wherever they must resist deformation, spread on a substrate, or push a membrane forward, and actin filament network formation is the assembly of exactly that mesh: filaments of mixed orientation bundled and tied together into a continuous network. The result supports cell shape, adhesion to extracellular matrix, lamellipodial protrusion and migration, and in immune cells the formation of a rigid cortical scaffold. Crosslinking is contributed by alpha-actinin and the plastin/fimbrin family, which bridge filaments on different axes; nucleation and elongation control come from Spire proteins and Cobl, while CARMIL proteins regulate capping protein to keep filament ends available for growth. An integrin-linked kinase complex with PINCH and parvin adaptors couples the network to adhesion sites, linking matrix engagement to cytoskeletal architecture.

Cells are spatially organized, and organelle localization is the set of processes that move organelles to defined positions and hold them there: mitochondria delivered along axons to synapses, lysosomes repositioned between the perinuclear cluster and the periphery, melanosomes handed to the actin cortex for transfer to keratinocytes, secretory vesicles docked at release sites, and chromosomes and spindle poles placed for accurate division. Movement is powered by kinesins, dynein with its dynactin and Lis1/NDE1 regulators, and myosin V, with adaptors such as the TRAK/Miro pair for mitochondria and Rab27/melanophilin for melanosomes specifying cargo. Tethering complexes, SNAREs, exocyst, BORC and HOPS finish the job by docking organelles at target membranes, while nuclear envelope LINC bridges anchor the nucleus itself. Loss of this positioning underlies neurodegeneration and axonal neuropathy, pigmentation and immune granule disorders, ciliopathies, and chromosome missegregation.

Positioning the endoplasmic reticulum within the cell determines where lipids are exchanged, where calcium is released, and which organelles the ER can communicate with, since the network must be held against the plasma membrane and other compartments rather than drifting freely. The extended synaptotagmins tether cortical ER to the plasma membrane in a calcium- and lipid-regulated manner and transfer glycerolipids across the narrow gap, while GRAMD2A marks a separate class of ER-plasma membrane contacts. VAPA and VAPB act as general ER-resident receptors that capture FFAT-motif proteins from other organelles, building contacts used for sterol and phosphoinositide transfer and for refilling ER calcium stores. Loss of this organization disturbs store-operated calcium entry and lipid homeostasis, and VAPB mutation causes a familial motor neuron disease, linking ER placement to neuronal survival.

Cells position the Golgi apparatus deliberately rather than letting it drift, and this positioning determines where secretory cargo and new membrane are delivered — toward the leading edge of a migrating cell, the immune synapse, or the growing axon. Golgi localization also underlies apicobasal polarity in epithelia and the compact perinuclear ribbon that distinguishes mammalian Golgi architecture; when it fails, directed secretion and directional motility are lost. The machinery combines coat subunits such as ARCN1 and COPG1, which sustain membrane identity and traffic, with cytoskeletal and motor adaptors including HOOK3, which links Golgi membranes to dynein along microtubules. Small GTPase control through CDC42 and its regulator ARHGAP21 couples Golgi placement to cell polarity signalling, while kinases such as STK11 and STK25 and the scaffolding protein PDCD10 tie organelle position to polarity establishment and lumen formation.

mitochondrion localization is the set of processes that move mitochondria along the cytoskeleton and anchor them where energy demand and calcium buffering are highest. It matters most in neurons, where mitochondria must be delivered along axons to synapses and growth cones; failure of this transport underlies axonal degeneration, hereditary spastic paraplegia and features of Parkinson and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Mechanistically, outer-membrane Miro GTPases (RHOT1/RHOT2) couple mitochondria through TRAK1/TRAK2 adaptors to kinesin and dynein motors on microtubules, with MYO19 supporting actin-based movement and syntabulin, FEZ1 and MAP/tau proteins tuning track engagement. Calcium and hypoxic signals arrest motility so that organelles are captured locally, while Miro degradation by PINK1-Parkin and MUL1 immobilises damaged mitochondria for mitophagy. Fission and fusion factors including DNM1L, MFN1/2 and OPA1 link positioning to organelle morphology, and ARMCX family proteins regulate trafficking during neuronal regeneration.

Mitochondria must be delivered to where energy demand and calcium buffering are needed, and this positioning machinery moves them along the cytoskeleton and anchors them in place. In neurons the need is acute: axons and synapses depend on transported mitochondria, and failure of the system contributes to axonal degeneration and neuropathy, with mutations in KIF1B, MFN2 and OPA1 causing inherited neurological disease. Kinesin motors work through the TRAK adaptors and the outer-membrane GTPases RHOT1 and RHOT2, which couple calcium and metabolic cues to whether a mitochondrion keeps moving or stops; dynein-associated and myosin components including MYO19 handle other routes and actin-based tethering. Microtubule-binding proteins such as MAPT, MAP1B and SPAST shape the tracks, while fission, fusion and mitophagy factors like DNM1L, MFN1 and PRKN tie placement to organelle quality control and inheritance during division.

Where a cell puts its nucleus is an actively controlled property, and this pathway covers the machinery that moves the nucleus to a defined position and holds it there. It matters for neuronal migration in the developing cortex, for the peripheral placement of nuclei in mature skeletal muscle fibres, and for the polarity of migrating and differentiating cells; its failure underlies lissencephaly and centronuclear myopathy. Mechanically, LINC complexes formed by inner-membrane SUN proteins paired with outer-membrane nesprins couple the nuclear lamina to actin, intermediate filaments and microtubule motors, so that dynein with its dynactin and LIS1-NUDC regulators, kinesins and myosin-driven actin flow can exert force on the envelope. Rho-family and DOCK-type regulators, centrosomal and microtubule-anchoring proteins, and lamins that give the envelope its stiffness together determine whether that force translates into movement or stable anchorage.

Membrane traffic only works if vesicles end up in the right place, and vesicle localization covers the transport and positional maintenance that puts them there: moving carriers along cytoskeletal tracks, tethering them at target membranes, and clustering them at sites of use such as the presynaptic active zone or the apical surface of an epithelial cell. Kinesins, cytoplasmic dynein subunits and myosin V motors with their Rab adaptors drive the movement; exocyst, TRAPP and coat-adaptor complexes (AP-3, BLOC-1) specify destinations; synaptic proteins including synapsins, Munc13s, Munc18 and synaptotagmins hold and position neurotransmitter vesicles for release. The same machinery delivers pigment granules in melanocytes, glucose transporter stores in muscle and fat, and cargo to the ciliary base. Defects give Hermansky-Pudlak and Griscelli syndromes, Bardet-Biedl syndrome, deafness, and neurodegeneration linked to LRRK2, PINK1 and alpha-synuclein.

Cells constantly move molecules to where they are needed, and the establishment of localization within a cell covers the whole of that work: vesicle budding and fusion, motor-driven transport along cytoskeletal tracks, translocation across organelle membranes, and nucleocytoplasmic exchange. Without it, secretion, synaptic transmission, receptor turnover and organelle biogenesis all fail. Coat complexes and adaptors select cargo at the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi and plasma membrane; Rab GTPases with their exchange factors and effectors, tethering complexes and SNARE pairs specify where a carrier docks and fuses; kinesins, dyneins and myosins carry cargo along microtubules and actin; ESCRT components sort ubiquitinated proteins into multivesicular bodies; retromer and related sorting complexes recycle receptors from endosomes. Import machineries at the mitochondrion, peroxisome and nuclear pore, plus transporters and channels, complete the movement of proteins, lipids, ions and RNA. Failures underlie lysosomal storage, neurodegenerative and ciliopathy disorders.

Where a cell places its mitotic spindle determines where the cleavage furrow falls and therefore whether division is symmetric or hands different fates to the two daughters. Spindle localization is the machinery that positions and anchors the spindle within the cell, coupling it to cortical cues and to the cell's long axis. Cortical anchors such as NuMA and the LGN-family partners GPSM1/GPSM2 recruit dynein and dynactin, which pull on astral microtubules; the actin nucleators and regulators present, including the Arp2/3 subunits ACTR2 and ACTR3, cofilin and formins, provide the cortical mechanics, while LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1 tune dynein force. Kinetochore and microtubule-binding components (the Ska complex, NDC80, CLASP1/2, MAPRE1, ASPM, CDK5RAP2) link chromosome attachment to spindle geometry. The same processes drive asymmetric spindle placement in oocyte meiosis and orient divisions in neuroepithelium, where defects cause microcephaly and disrupted epithelial architecture.

Mitochondria must be delivered to where ATP demand and calcium buffering are needed, and establishing their localization is the transport step that puts them there. In neurons this determines whether axon terminals, growth cones and nodes are energetically supplied; failed positioning contributes to axonal degeneration and is a recurring theme in hereditary spastic paraplegia and optic atrophy. Mitochondrial Rho GTPases RHOT1 and RHOT2 anchor the organelle to adaptors such as TRAK2 and syntabulin, which couple it to kinesin motors including KIF5B and KIF1B for microtubule-based movement, while MYO19 supports actin-based positioning. Tubulin-binding and microtubule-regulating proteins such as tau, MAP1B and spastin shape the tracks, and fission and fusion mediators DNM1L and OPA1 tie organelle shape to transportability. Calcium and hypoxia signals halt motile mitochondria, docking them at sites of sustained demand.

establishment of organelle localization is the process by which a cell puts its organelles where they need to be — mitochondria along axons and beneath the plasma membrane, lysosomes at the periphery or clustered at the centre, secretory granules docked for release, the spindle and nucleus positioned relative to the cell axis. Correct placement determines where energy, degradation and secretion happen, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, pigmentation and granule-release disorders, and defects in asymmetric division. The genes describe motors and their cargo adaptors — kinesins, dynein with dynactin, myosin V — the microtubule and actin tracks they run on, Rab GTPases and tethering complexes that specify destinations, and mitochondrial adaptors such as the Miro/TRAK module. Also represented are nuclear envelope LINC bridges that anchor the nucleus to the cytoskeleton, spindle-pole and kinetochore components, and BLOC/BORC and AP-3 complexes directing lysosome-related organelle biogenesis and positioning.

Cells position their organelles rather than letting them drift, and the establishment of organelle localization covers the directed movement of mitochondria, lysosomes, melanosomes, secretory granules, Golgi elements, the nucleus and the spindle pole to defined sites. Position determines function: mitochondria must reach axonal regions of high energy demand, lysosomes must be delivered to the periphery or clustered perinuclearly, lytic and secretory granules must dock beneath the plasma membrane before release, and the nucleus must be anchored in muscle and migrating cells. Kinesins, dynein with its dynactin and adaptor partners, myosin V with Rab27, mitochondrial Miro/TRAK adaptors, BLOC-1 and BORC complexes, LINC-complex nesprins and SUN proteins, and tethers such as the TRAPP and exocyst complexes carry out the transport, capture and docking steps. Failures produce pigmentation and immunodeficiency syndromes, neurodegeneration, ciliopathies, muscular dystrophy and defective chromosome segregation.

Once an organelle has reached its proper place in the cell, it has to be held there, and maintenance of organelle location covers the anchoring and tethering processes that resist displacement. This matters for asymmetric division and for polarized cells: keeping the centrosome and spindle poles at a defined position sets the orientation of the division plane, and keeping the Golgi and endomembrane compartments at their sites preserves directional secretion. Several of the genes act at the centrosome, spindle pole or Golgi — a scaffolding protein of pericentriolar material, a spindle-associated protein required for mitotic spindle positioning, a Rho-family GAP that links Golgi membranes to the actin cortex, and a receptor-independent G protein regulator that couples cortical cues to astral microtubules. Loss of such positioning disturbs progenitor division in the developing brain and underlies microcephaly and neuronal migration defects.

Establishment of centrosome localization describes the directed positioning of the centrosome within a cell, an event that sets where the microtubule array is anchored and therefore where the cell points its spindle, its cilium, or its migratory front. Correct placement determines the plane of division in epithelia, the apical docking of the basal body that permits ciliogenesis, and the polarity of neuronal precursors during migration; when it fails, mitotic spindles misorient, cilia are lost, and tissue architecture degenerates, as in cystic kidney disease. The genes link the centrosome to cortical and cytoskeletal cues: an actin-bundling cortical protein and a formin generate force, ezrin and a scaffolding protein of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase family tie it to the apical membrane, LIS1 couples it to dynein-driven nuclear-centrosome movement, and CEP83 anchors the distal appendages to the plasma membrane.

Where a cell places its centrosome determines where its microtubules radiate from, and therefore the orientation of the spindle, the direction of migration, and the site of cilium formation. Establishment of centrosome localization is the directed movement and anchoring of the centrosome to a defined position within the cell, and it underlies asymmetric division, epithelial apical-basal organization and ciliogenesis at the apical surface. The genes here link the centrosome to the cortex and the actin cytoskeleton: an actin-binding membrane crosslinker and a formin-family protein, a cortical actin-associated protein that helps orient the spindle in mitosis, a scaffolding protein of epithelial polarity, a distal appendage component that docks the basal body for ciliary axoneme growth, and a dynein-pathway regulator required for nuclear and centrosomal movement in migrating neurons. Failure of such positioning disturbs cortical neuronal migration, ciliary assembly and renal tubule architecture.

Where the centrosome sits determines where the spindle forms and therefore how a dividing cell splits its contents, so holding it at a fixed position is a prerequisite for oriented division rather than a passive consequence of it. Maintenance of centrosome location keeps the organelle anchored against the pulling forces of the cytoskeleton, which matters for asymmetric divisions in neural progenitors, for the plane of division in epithelia, and for centrosome positioning relative to nucleus and cilium. The proteins involved link the centrosome to microtubule minus ends and to cortical machinery: a large scaffolding anchor for kinase and microtubule regulators, a spindle-pole protein associated with brain size control, a dynein-pathway regulator, and a cortical adaptor that orients spindle pulling. Loss of such anchoring produces mispositioned spindles and is reflected in microcephaly and cortical malformation syndromes.

Nuclear pore complexes must be distributed across the nuclear envelope and held in place, and this pathway covers the positioning and maintenance of pores at their sites in the membrane. Even spacing of pores matters because every exchange of mRNA, ribosomal subunits and transcription factors between nucleus and cytoplasm passes through them, and clustered or displaced pores compromise that traffic. The nuclear lamins A/C, B1 and B2 form the filamentous meshwork underlying the inner nuclear membrane that anchors pores and sets envelope shape and mechanical stiffness, while NDC1 is a transmembrane nucleoporin that embeds the pore scaffold in the double membrane. Loss of lamin function produces laminopathies with abnormal nuclear morphology and mislocalized pores, linking this positioning activity to nuclear architecture, chromatin organization at the periphery, and mechanotransduction.

Cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains act as staging platforms that concentrate receptors and signalling enzymes, and membrane raft localization covers the processes that deliver these domains to a particular region of the cell surface and hold them there. The most concrete setting suggested here is the T lymphocyte: the adaptor LAT, the transmembrane proteolipid MAL, the adhesion receptor CD2 and the phosphatase CD45 all depend on raft partitioning for productive antigen receptor signalling, and MAL-dependent vesicular transport carries raft components to the immune synapse. Cytoskeletal and small GTPase contributions from gelsolin, the hematopoietic guanine nucleotide exchange factor DOCK2 and RALA link raft positioning to actin remodelling and polarized membrane traffic. Where such clustering fails, receptor signalling is poorly amplified and cells polarize and migrate ineffectively, so this compartmentalization underlies lymphocyte activation as much as general membrane organization.

Membranes are not uniform sheets: receptors, channels, transporters and adhesion molecules must be delivered to the right bilayer and then held in the right domain of it, and this collection of processes covers that targeting and retention. It determines where a cell senses and secretes, keeps epithelia polarized, clusters neurotransmitter receptors at synapses, and positions ion channels in excitable membranes; misdelivery underlies ciliopathies, pigment and lysosome disorders, and many channelopathies. Mechanistically it spans co-translational insertion by signal recognition particle and the translocon, tail-anchored and multipass insertion by the GET and EMC machineries, protein import into mitochondria and peroxisomes, vesicle budding, tethering and SNARE-mediated fusion, and endosomal sorting by retromer, retriever and the WASH complex. Lipid anchoring by palmitoyltransferases and myristoyltransferases, scaffolds such as PDZ proteins and the spectrin-ankyrin lattice, and small GTPases with their exchange factors fix proteins in place once delivered.

Cell localization covers the processes that move a cell to a particular place and hold it there, a requirement for tissue architecture wherever cells must reach and stay at a defined position. The genes here point to two routes. Three of them — POMGNT1, FKRP and LARGE1 — build the O-mannosyl glycan on alpha-dystroglycan that lets it bind laminin and other basement membrane ligands; when this glycosylation fails, muscle fibres and migrating neurons lose their anchorage to extracellular matrix, producing congenital muscular dystrophy with brain malformation from disordered neuronal positioning. CD2AP links membrane receptors to the actin cytoskeleton at adhesive junctions, including the podocyte slit diaphragm, where its loss causes glomerular disease. BHLHA15 contributes transcriptional control of secretory cell identity and apical organization. Together they tie cell positioning to matrix adhesion and cytoskeletal attachment rather than to motility alone.

Positioning the Golgi apparatus at a particular place in the cell is what this pathway accomplishes, and it matters because the Golgi's location sets the direction in which newly made membrane and secretory cargo are delivered. Cells use this to orient secretion toward a leading edge during migration, toward a nascent cilium, or toward a junction during epithelial polarization; when it fails, the ribbon fragments or scatters and directional trafficking is lost. Mechanistically the genes point to Rho-family control at Golgi membranes: a GTPase-activating protein acting on CDC42 at the Golgi, with CDC42 itself governing local actin dynamics, alongside a coatomer subunit for vesicle formation, a scaffolding adaptor, and a kinase-scaffold module built around STK25 and PDCD10 that links polarity signalling to Golgi orientation and cell migration.

Pointed-end actin filament capping fixes the length of actin filaments by blocking their slow-growing minus end, so that subunits can neither be added nor lost there. This is what allows sarcomeric thin filaments in skeletal and cardiac muscle to hold a uniform length, and it stabilises the spectrin-actin network of erythrocytes and the cortical actin of other cells. The tropomodulins bind the pointed end together with tropomyosin and seal it, while the related leiomodins, which share the capping architecture but extend it, instead nucleate new filaments and elongate them. The balance between the two sets thin filament number and length during myofibril assembly and turnover; loss of the muscle-specific members causes nemaline myopathy and dilated cardiomyopathy. The pathway is thus one arm of actin cytoskeleton dynamics, complementary to barbed-end capping and severing, and central to contractile architecture.

Actin filaments grow and shrink at both ends, and capping the pointed (minus) end fixes filament length by blocking subunit addition or loss there. This is how sarcomeric thin filaments acquire and keep their uniform length: tropomodulins sit at the minus end of each actin filament, working together with tropomyosin, while the leiomodins are related proteins that instead nucleate new filaments and can compete for the same site. The balance between them sets thin filament length in cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle, and also stabilises the short actin filaments of the erythrocyte membrane skeleton and neuronal cytoskeleton. Loss of the skeletal muscle isoform LMOD3 causes nemaline myopathy with disorganised, poorly formed thin filaments, and TMOD1 loss disrupts myofibril assembly, tying pointed-end capping directly to contractile function and cell shape.

Lipid anchors attached to proteins are not permanent, and protein delipidation is the reverse reaction: hydrolysis of the covalent bond that ties a lipid group to a polypeptide, releasing the protein from the membrane it was tethered to. The clearest example is the recycling of autophagy machinery, where a family of cysteine proteases cleaves the phosphatidylethanolamine conjugated to ATG8-family proteins such as LC3 and GABARAP, freeing them from the autophagosomal membrane so they can be reused and allowing mature vesicles to fuse with lysosomes; the same enzymes prime those proteins by exposing the glycine used for conjugation. A sirtuin family member contributes a distinct activity, removing long-chain fatty acyl groups from lysine residues and thereby controlling the secretion of substrates such as TNF. Together these reactions make lipidation a reversible switch governing membrane association, autophagic flux and cytokine release.

Host-microbe interaction biology covers the molecular contacts that let a pathogen or symbiont engage the larger partner it lives on or in, and here the genes read overwhelmingly as the host side of viral entry, trafficking and restriction. Surface receptors and attachment factors define which cells a given virus can infect: ACE2, DPP4, CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4, NPC1, TFRC, nectins, integrins and lectins such as CD209 and SIGLEC1. Proteases including TMPRSS2, FURIN, cathepsins B and L prime envelope glycoproteins for fusion, while endolysosomal components, Rab7, NPC1 and two-pore channels govern delivery of the genome to the cytoplasm. The ESCRT machinery and VPS4 ATPases are appropriated for budding, and TRIM ubiquitin ligases plus PLSCR1 push back as restriction factors. Complement regulators, peptidoglycan recognition proteins and airway mucins add the secreted and innate defence arm. Together these determine tropism, susceptibility and the therapeutic entry blockade targets.

Host cells interact with organisms living on or inside them, and this collection of processes covers the molecular contact between a host and a resident or invading symbiont, whether parasitic, commensal or mutualistic. Most of the activity here is host defence and microbial containment: defensins, cathelicidin, lactoferrin and dermcidin permeabilise or starve microbes, neutrophil granule proteases such as elastase, cathepsin G and azurocidin kill ingested organisms, and arginase and superoxide-generating machinery shape the antimicrobial environment. Recognition and signalling arms include mannose-binding lectin, TREM1 and the MYD88 adaptor feeding Toll-like receptor output, alongside NLRP6 and gasdermin-linked inflammasome activity in mucosal epithelium. Complement factor H-related proteins and coagulation components tune the humoral response and are themselves targets of microbial evasion. Together these activities set which microbes colonise a surface, and their failure allows commensals to become pathogens.

biological process involved in intraspecies interaction between organisms covers the ways one animal acts on another of its own kind — social approach and recognition, pair bonding, aggression, mating and parental care, vocal communication — and the neural substrate that makes such behaviour possible. Its failure is the core of autism spectrum and related neurodevelopmental disorders, where social interaction and communication are selectively impaired. The genes point to two convergent levels: neuropeptide signalling through oxytocin, vasopressin and their receptors, which tunes affiliation and territoriality, and the trans-synaptic adhesion and scaffolding machinery of excitatory synapses — neurexins, neuroligins, SHANK proteins and DLG4 — together with chromatin and translational regulators such as MECP2, CHD8 and PTEN that set synaptic gene expression. Also represented are dopamine and GABA receptor subunits shaping reward and inhibitory tone, and microglial TREM2 and CX3CR1, linking synaptic pruning to later social competence.
