Control over how strongly an organism kills the cells of another organism — the tuning of antimicrobial and cytotoxic attack rather than the attack itself. This matters because host defence must be strong enough to clear bacteria, fungi and infected or transformed cells, yet restrained enough to spare host tissue; failure in either direction produces uncontrolled infection or immunopathology. The genes involved span several arms of that defence: perforin, the pore-forming effector that cytotoxic lymphocytes and NK cells use to deliver granzymes into a target cell, sits alongside antimicrobial peptide sources such as the proopiomelanocortin precursor and the chemokine CXCL6, which both recruits neutrophils and has direct bactericidal activity. Arginase-1 acts as a brake, depleting arginine and limiting nitric oxide–dependent killing by myeloid cells, while protease-activated receptor signalling links coagulation and inflammation to the strength of the response.

Host defence sometimes ends with the target cell simply bursting, and this is the arm of innate immunity that kills a cell in another organism by rupturing its membranes so that its cytoplasm is lost. The genes here act against microbes rather than host tissue: guanylate-binding proteins are interferon-induced GTPases that coat intracellular bacteria and parasitophorous vacuoles, stripping the protective membrane and exposing the pathogen to lytic and inflammasome-activating machinery, while RNASE7 and the chemokine CCL28 double as cationic antimicrobial peptides that permeabilise bacterial and fungal envelopes at epithelial and mucosal surfaces. The result is direct microbial killing at barrier sites and inside infected cells, complementing phagocytosis and complement. Loss of this capacity leaves epithelia colonised and vacuolar bacteria able to replicate unchecked; its interferon dependence links it to cell-autonomous immunity downstream of pathogen sensing.

ADP-ribosylation is a reversible modification, and the hydrolases gathered here are the erasers that remove it, terminating signals set down by ARTD/PARP enzymes and by bacterial toxins. Reversal matters most in the DNA damage response, where poly- and mono-ADP-ribose marks recruit repair factors to breaks but must be cleared for repair to finish and for chromatin to return to its resting state; persistent marks trap repair proteins and deplete cellular NAD+. Different family members handle different linkages: macrodomain hydrolases such as MACROD1, MACROD2 and OARD1 strip terminal mono-ADP-ribose from glutamate or acidic residues, while ADPRH-type enzymes act on arginine-linked ADP-ribose and ADPRS resolves ribose-linked remnants. Loss of these activities has been linked to genome instability and, for MACROD2, to recurrent deletions in colorectal and other cancers.

Cell division must be licensed, timed, and halted when conditions are wrong, and this is the regulatory layer that sets the rate and extent of progression through the cell cycle. It determines whether a cell proliferates, pauses, differentiates, or dies, and its loss underlies tumour growth, developmental microcephaly and infertility. Cyclins acting with cyclin-dependent kinases drive the transitions, opposed by inhibitors such as p21, p27 and p16 and by the retinoblastoma protein restraining E2F-dependent transcription. Ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF impose irreversibility by timed degradation, while phosphatases of the CDC25 family and WEE1/MYT1 kinases set mitotic entry. DNA damage and spindle assembly checkpoints, built around ATM/ATR, CHEK1/2, p53 and the MAD/BUB proteins, delay progression until lesions are repaired and chromosomes are correctly attached; growth-factor, Wnt, TGF-beta and mTOR inputs, microRNAs and chromatin remodellers tune the decision.

Meiosis halves chromosome number by releasing sister chromatid cohesion in two steps, and protecting cohesion at the centromere during the first division is what makes that possible. Arm cohesion is cleaved in meiosis I so homologues can separate, while centromeric cohesion must survive until meiosis II, when sisters finally part; losing this protection produces premature sister separation and aneuploid eggs and sperm, a major source of miscarriage and trisomy. Kinetochore kinases of the spindle checkpoint family, BUB1 and BUB1B, phosphorylate histone H2A to recruit shugoshin to inner centromeres, where the PP2A scaffolding subunits PPP2R1A and PPP2R1B bring a phosphatase that keeps cohesin dephosphorylated and therefore uncleavable. The meiosis-specific factor MEIKIN acts with this machinery to enforce mono-orientation of sister kinetochores, coupling cohesion protection to the unique chromosome segregation geometry of the first meiotic division.

Actin filaments do little on their own; their mechanical usefulness comes from being tied to one another into bundles and networks, and actin crosslink formation is the step that makes those higher-order arrays. Crosslinked bundles stiffen filopodia and microvilli, brace the cortex beneath the plasma membrane, and give migrating and phagocytosing cells the scaffolding to push membrane forward. The proteins here work in different geometries: filamin A joins filaments at wide angles into orthogonal gels, plastin and the small allograft inflammatory factor bundle them tightly in leukocytes and in protrusions, and the I-BAR proteins of the BAIAP2 family couple membrane curvature to bundled actin at the tips of filopodia. Others, including EPS8 and the GAS2-family proteins, cap or bundle filaments and link them to microtubules. Loss of filamin A causes periventricular nodular heterotopia, reflecting how much neuronal migration depends on a properly crosslinked cytoskeleton.

Cells continually monitor the balance of oxidized and reduced electron carriers — glutathione GSH/GSSG, NAD+/NADH and NADP+/NADPH — and this response to redox state is how that balance is converted into changes in gene expression, enzyme activity and secretion. It matters because redox poise reports on metabolic flux and oxidative burden, so reading it lets a cell adjust antioxidant supply, calcium handling and timing of daily physiology before damage accumulates. Several of the components make the link concrete: the cystine/glutamate antiporter subunit SLC7A11 imports cystine for glutathione synthesis, glutaredoxin GLRX2 and ADH5 handle thiol and S-nitrosothiol chemistry, and the NAD+-dependent deacetylase SIRT2 couples nucleotide redox status to protein acetylation. The clock proteins CLOCK, BMAL1 and NPAS2 bind DNA in a manner sensitive to NAD(P)H, tying redox sensing to circadian transcription, while cardiac RYR2 and FKBP1B connect thiol oxidation to calcium release.

Cells are pushed into and through division both by extracellular growth signals and by the machinery that physically completes it, and this collection of positive regulators of cell division spans both. Mitogens dominate one half: fibroblast growth factors and a receptor, the PDGF and VEGF families, TGF-alpha, betacellulin and epiregulin, midkine, IGF2, sonic hedgehog and inflammatory cytokines such as IL1 and oncostatin M, all acting through receptor kinases and G protein-coupled receptors to license S-phase entry. The other half executes the final step: the chromosomal passenger complex of aurora B with survivin, INCENP and borealin, the centralspindlin components ECT2, RACGAP1 and KIF23, citron kinase, and RHOA and CDC42 with RAB11-dependent membrane delivery to the cleavage furrow. Unrestrained mitogenic input here underlies tumour growth and angiogenesis, while failure of the abscission machinery leaves binucleate, aneuploid progeny.

Cells that divide when they should not become tumours, so restraining division is as much a part of proliferation control as driving it. Negative regulation of cell division covers the brakes applied at several points: transcriptional repression of the S-phase programme by the atypical E2F factors E2F7 and E2F8, growth suppression through the Hedgehog receptor PTCH1, and metabolic restraint via TXNIP, which limits glucose uptake and proliferative signalling. A distinct arm acts at the very end of mitosis, where the abscission checkpoint — CHMP4C and the ESCRT-associated machinery working with Aurora B — delays the final severing of the intercellular bridge until chromatin has cleared, preventing tetraploidy and DNA damage. Genome-stability factors such as the BLM helicase and a microRNA that represses MYC output contribute further inhibitory input. Loss of these constraints underlies unchecked growth, aneuploidy and cancer predisposition.

Control over how often and how accurately a nucleus divides determines whether daughter cells inherit a complete, undamaged genome, and the regulation of nuclear division gathers the brakes and accelerators that act on mitotic and meiotic chromosome partitioning. Its failure produces aneuploidy, tetraploidy and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours, or arrested gametogenesis and infertility. Much of the machinery here is the spindle assembly checkpoint and its target: kinetochore and checkpoint proteins such as BUB1, MAD1L1, MAD2L1, NDC80 and the ZW10–ZWILCH–ZWINT module restrain the anaphase-promoting complex through CDC20 until attachments are correct, after which separase releases cohesin. Mitotic kinases including AURKA, AURKB, PLK1 and NEK2 with the chromosomal passenger subunits INCENP and survivin direct spindle and centrosome behaviour, while ATM and CHEK1 couple damage detection to entry. Meiosis-specific factors such as STRA8, PRDM9, HORMAD1 and MOS adapt the same controls to oocyte and spermatocyte divisions, and growth-factor and cytokine inputs set proliferation rate.

Cells delay splitting their nucleus until chromosomes are correctly attached and damage is repaired, and this braking of nuclear division is what keeps daughter cells euploid. The bulk of the genes form the spindle assembly checkpoint: kinetochore sensors and the outer-kinetochore attachment machinery recruit checkpoint kinases and MAD/BUB proteins, which sequester CDC20 into a mitotic checkpoint complex and so hold the anaphase-promoting complex inactive, preserving cyclin B and securin until the last chromosome is bioriented. Dynein subunits strip checkpoint proteins from attached kinetochores to silence the signal, TRIP13 and USP44 tune its reversal, and ATM and CHEK1 impose a parallel damage-dependent delay. Meiotic regulators such as HORMAD1/2 and FBXO43 arrest oocyte and spermatocyte divisions. Loss of this restraint produces chromosome missegregation, aneuploidy and tumour-prone genome instability.

Positive regulation of nuclear division covers the inputs that push a cell through the partitioning of its nucleus and genome, whether in mitosis or in meiosis, and it sets how often and how fast cells divide in growing tissues and in the germ line. One arm is the core mitotic machinery: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator CDC20 and the ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2C drive the degradation that triggers sister chromatid separation by separase, while Aurora A and PLK1 license spindle assembly and the SKA components and NUSAP1 stabilise kinetochore-microtubule attachments. Another arm is extrinsic: growth factors and cytokines acting through their receptors, insulin and IGF signalling, and WNT ligands raise proliferative drive. Meiotic entry factors such as STRA8, MEIOSIN, PRDM9 and DAZL commit germ cells to reductional division. Loss of restraint here, as with RB1, permits unscheduled division and tumour growth.

Cells detect proteins that have failed to fold correctly and respond by refolding, sequestering or destroying them, and this response to misfolded protein is what keeps aggregation-prone species from accumulating into inclusions. It matters because its decline underlies neurodegenerative proteinopathies and because secretory and membrane proteins that misfold must be cleared before they poison the endoplasmic reticulum. Chaperones of the DNAJ family and the clusterin chaperone recognise exposed hydrophobic surfaces; the CHIP ubiquitin ligase with UBE2W, and other ligases including RNF126 and cullin-RING complexes, mark substrates with ubiquitin; and the VCP ATPase with its UFD1 cofactor and the derlin channel extracts misfolded proteins from the ER membrane for proteasomal degradation. Deubiquitination by ataxin-3 and HDAC6-dependent transport toward aggresomes provide alternative routes when degradation capacity is exceeded, linking this surveillance to autophagy and proteasome control.

Fatty acids with six to twelve carbons are handled differently from long-chain species: they enter mitochondria without carnitine shuttling and are oxidised quickly for energy, making medium-chain fatty acid metabolism the route that turns dietary and milk-derived lipids into rapidly available fuel. Its best-known component is the medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase that begins mitochondrial beta-oxidation; loss of this enzyme is a common inherited disorder of fatty acid oxidation, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic crisis during fasting or illness. Other members set chain length and fate rather than degrade: a thioesterase releases free medium-chain acids from their CoA esters, carnitine acyl-transferases move short and medium acyl groups between compartments, hydrolases and carboxylesterases cleave lipid esters, and cytochrome P450 enzymes omega-hydroxylate fatty acids as an alternative disposal route. The pathway connects lipid catabolism to ketogenesis, energy homeostasis and secreted milk fat composition.

Medium-chain fatty acid biosynthesis produces fatty acids with six to twelve carbon tails, species that are handled differently from long-chain lipids: they are more water-soluble, enter mitochondria without carnitine shuttling, and serve as rapidly oxidised fuel as well as substrates for milk lipid and lipid mediator formation. Chain length is set largely by when a growing acyl chain is released from its synthase, and the enzymes here act at that decision point. Oleoyl-ACP hydrolase releases medium-chain acyl groups from the fatty acid synthase machinery, giving mammary and other tissues a route to shorter fatty acids, while a mitochondrial ketoacyl synthase contributes to the separate intramitochondrial route that supplies octanoyl groups for lipoic acid synthesis. Acyl-CoA thioesterase and the ABHD hydrolases trim thioester and lipid intermediates, balancing free fatty acid against activated pools and thereby influencing membrane remodelling and energy metabolism.

Fatty acids of intermediate length, six to twelve carbons, are broken down for energy by a route distinct from that used for long-chain species, because they enter mitochondria without carnitine-dependent transport and are handled by chain-length-specific enzymes. Medium-chain fatty acid catabolism matters most during fasting, when the liver switches to fat oxidation and ketogenesis; loss of medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, the first step of the mitochondrial beta-oxidation spiral for these substrates, causes one of the commonest inherited disorders of fatty acid oxidation, presenting as hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic crisis after intercurrent illness. Upstream of oxidation, alpha/beta hydrolase-domain lipases release medium-chain acyl chains from lipid esters, and glycine N-acyltransferase-like activity offers a conjugation route that detoxifies and excretes acyl groups when oxidative flux is exceeded. The pathway links dietary and stored lipid to hepatic energy supply.

Hair follicles form through repeated dialogue between epidermal placodes and underlying mesenchyme, and the processes that tune the pace and extent of hair follicle development determine follicle spacing, hair shaft shape, and the timing of cyclical regrowth. WNT ligands such as WNT10B and WNT5A drive placode initiation, while the secreted inhibitor DKK4 restrains neighbouring cells so follicles are spaced rather than fused; hedgehog signalling through SMO and TGF-beta/SMAD4 input push the follicle into downgrowth, and follistatin and TGFB2 modulate activin-family signalling in the same field. Transcriptional regulators including FOXN1 and MSX2 specify the differentiating hair shaft and inner root sheath, with structural components such as CDH3, PKP3, KRT17 and FERMT1 holding follicle cells together. Mutation of these factors produces hypotrichosis, ectodermal dysplasia, and woolly or fragile hair, and the same signals are reused when follicles regenerate in adult skin.

Hair follicles form and cycle through phases of growth, regression and rest, and this grouping covers the signals that push that programme forward controlling when follicles are induced, how fast they grow, and whether keratinocytes commit to hair shaft and inner root sheath fates. Its output is visible in skin biology: loss of the transcription factor FOXN1 produces the hairless, athymic nude phenotype, while MSX2 shapes hair shaft differentiation. WNT10B and WNT5A supply the canonical and non-canonical Wnt input that initiates placode formation and reactivates resting follicles, follistatin tunes activin and BMP availability, and TGFB2 acts as a dermal papilla-derived inducer. TNF signalling through TRADD and structural keratins such as KRT17 link inflammatory and mechanical context to follicle behaviour, connecting this biology to epithelial appendage morphogenesis, stem cell activation in the bulge, and alopecias that follow its disruption.

Hair follicles form from reciprocal signalling between epidermis and underlying dermis, and the placement, spacing and number of follicles depend as much on restraining that signalling as on driving it. Negative regulation of hair follicle development covers the inhibitory inputs that limit how many follicles form and how far morphogenesis proceeds, keeping follicle density patterned rather than continuous. A secreted Wnt antagonist of the Dickkopf family dampens the Wnt/beta-catenin activity that specifies placodes, while Smoothened-dependent hedgehog transduction and the p75 neurotrophin receptor, an inducer of apoptosis and a regulator of follicle regression, act on downgrowth and cycling. Adhesion and adhesion-linked components including P-cadherin and the kindlin family member FERMT1 tie epithelial cell contacts to this control; loss of these genes in humans causes hypotrichosis and ectodermal dysplasia phenotypes affecting skin, hair and nails.

Synapses do not merely change strength, they change shape, and the control of synapse structural plasticity sets how readily dendritic spines are formed, enlarged or stabilised in response to activity. This remodelling of the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton is what converts patterns of firing into lasting changes in connectivity, and it underlies learning, memory consolidation and the refinement of circuits during development. Calcium entry during strong stimulation is read out by calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases such as CAMK2B and CAMK1, which couple activity to cytoskeletal and receptor trafficking changes; scaffolding proteins of the postsynaptic density including SHANK3 and FRMPD4 organise glutamate receptors and their signalling partners within the spine, while adhesion and neuromodulatory inputs, including dopamine acting through DRD2, bias the outcome. Loss of these regulators produces spine dysmorphology and is associated with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorders.

Hosts kill invading microbes outright by breaching their membranes, and this set captures cytolysis directed by a host against the cells of a smaller symbiont or pathogen. It is the destructive arm of innate immunity at mucosal surfaces and in blood, acting where phagocytosis is too slow or the target too numerous. Cationic antimicrobial peptides such as cathelicidin and epididymal beta-defensin-like proteins insert into and permeabilise bacterial envelopes; lactoferrin sequesters iron and destabilises the outer membrane; complement factor H-related proteins govern where lytic complement attack is permitted on a surface. Coagulation-associated proteins including prothrombin and histidine-rich glycoprotein contribute peptides that trap and damage microbes, while apolipoprotein L1 lyses trypanosomes and defines human resistance to them. Loss or variation in these effectors shifts susceptibility to infection and, for some, to kidney disease.

Ubiquitin ligases commonly modify themselves, and protein autoubiquitination is that self-directed reaction, in which an E3 attaches ubiquitin to lysines on its own chain or on an identical partner subunit through an isopeptide bond. It matters as a self-limiting control device: autoubiquitination with lysine-48 chains marks a ligase for proteasomal destruction and terminates its activity, while non-degradative chains can instead switch on scaffolding and recruitment functions, as seen in the signalling roles of TRAF2 and TRAF6. The genes here span RING, HECT, RBR and cullin-based enzymes together with the E2 conjugating partners such as UBE2D2 and UBE2D3 that charge them. Consequences reach across DNA damage responses and chromatin ubiquitination, ER-associated and mitochondrial quality control, p53 turnover by MDM2, chaperone-linked degradation via STUB1, and innate immune signalling. Loss-of-function in PRKON-family ligases including PRKN and LRRK2 links this chemistry to parkinsonism.

The general adaptation syndrome is the body's stereotyped, multi-organ response to strong physiological or psychological stressors, unfolding as an initial alarm reaction, a period of adaptation in which defences are mobilised, and eventual exhaustion when those defences are depleted. Its core axis is neuroendocrine: corticotropin-releasing hormone acting through its receptor CRHR1 in the pituitary and brain drives glucocorticoid output and coordinates behavioural arousal, autonomic tone and metabolic mobilisation. Opioid peptides derived from proenkephalin modulate the accompanying pain and anxiety responses, the transcription factor NR4A2 links stress signalling to changes in gene expression in catecholaminergic and limbic neurons, and HCN1 channels set the excitability of neurons that sustain these circuits. Chronic or unresolved activation of this programme contributes to depression, anxiety disorders, hypertension and immune suppression, making it a bridge between perceived stress and systemic disease.

Behavioural responses to stress are part of the general adaptation syndrome, the coordinated reaction of the body to a strong or sustained threat, and this arm covers the changes in arousal, anxiety-like behaviour, feeding and coping that accompany hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal activation. It matters because the same circuitry that lets an animal mobilise appropriately under acute threat becomes maladaptive when chronically engaged, contributing to anxiety disorders, depression and stress-related changes in pain sensitivity. Central to the response is the corticotropin-releasing hormone receptor CRHR1, which transduces hypothalamic and limbic CRH signals into neuroendocrine and behavioural output, while the opioid precursor proenkephalin supplies enkephalin peptides that dampen stress and nociceptive signalling. The hyperpolarisation-activated channel HCN1 sets excitability and rhythmic firing in the cortical and hippocampal neurons through which these stress signals are integrated, linking neuronal biophysics to emotional behaviour.

Pigment granule localization is the positioning of melanosomes within a cell — dispersed, clustered around the nucleus, or delivered to the cell periphery for transfer to neighbouring keratinocytes — and it determines skin, hair and eye pigmentation as well as the shielding of retinal photoreceptors. Long-range movement runs along microtubules using dynactin components, after which a tripartite actin-based system of myosin Va, melanophilin and the GTPase RAB27A captures granules in the peripheral actin cortex; loss of any of the three causes the pigment-dilution and immune defects of Griscelli syndrome. Additional RAB GTPases and the biogenesis-of-lysosome-related-organelles subunits, together with VPS33A/VPS33B tethering factors, couple granule transport to the trafficking routes that build the organelle, and ciliary BBSome proteins and GPR143 link melanosome placement to signalling control. Failure produces albinism, Hermansky–Pudlak-type pigment dilution, and disturbed retinal pigment epithelium function.

The charge gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane is the currency that drives ATP synthesis, protein import, calcium uptake and metabolite exchange, and processes that set or modulate mitochondrial membrane potential therefore determine whether a mitochondrion works or is marked for destruction. Loss of potential is also the decision point of intrinsic apoptosis: BCL-2 family members, including BAX, BAK1, BID and their antagonists BCL2 and BCL2L1, act at the outer membrane, while cyclophilin D (PPIF) governs permeability transition pore opening. Uncoupling proteins and an ATP synthase inhibitory factor tune proton leak and reverse-mode hydrolysis, respiratory complex I subunits and antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and PRDX3 preserve the electron flow that generates it, and PINK1 with parkin reads depolarization as the signal to clear damaged organelles by mitophagy. Failures here link to neurodegeneration and defective cell-death control.

Mitochondrial depolarization is the collapse of the electrochemical gradient that the respiratory chain maintains across the inner membrane, and it marks the point at which a mitochondrion stops making ATP and starts deciding whether the cell should die. Loss of membrane potential drives cytochrome c release and caspase activation, flags damaged organelles for mitophagy, and is a common endpoint of oxidative and calcium stress in neurons, cardiomyocytes and immune cells. The genes here converge on that transition from several directions: BCL2 and BOK set the threshold for outer membrane permeabilization, PPIF encodes the cyclophilin D regulator of the permeability transition pore, ATP5IF1 restrains reverse-mode ATP synthase activity when potential falls, and P2RX7 and PARP1 link extracellular ATP sensing and DNA damage to energetic failure. Glutathione synthesis enzymes GCLC and GCLM oppose the process by limiting oxidant load, while LRRK2 ties it to Parkinson disease pathology.

Cardioblast differentiation is the step at which mesodermal cells commit to a cardiac fate while still retaining the capacity to divide, and the controls over how fast and how completely that commitment proceeds set the size and patterning of the forming heart. Too little or badly timed commitment leaves septal, valve and conduction defects, which is why the regulators here are classic congenital heart disease genes: the homeodomain factor NKX2-5 and the T-box factor TBX5 act together on cardiac structural and conduction gene programmes, and mutations in either cause septal defects with atrioventricular block or Holt-Oram syndrome. TGFB2 supplies extracellular signalling from surrounding tissue, PRICKLE1 links the process to planar cell polarity and the oriented cell behaviours of the cardiac crescent, and DHX36 acts post-transcriptionally on target mRNAs. Together they tune progenitor expansion against terminal cardiomyocyte maturation during early cardiogenesis.

Focal adhesions are the integrin-based contacts through which a cell grips extracellular matrix, transmits force, and senses substrate stiffness; pushing their assembly forward makes cells adhere more firmly, spread, and migrate directionally, as endothelial cells must during angiogenesis and fibroblasts must during wound repair. The genes here act as accelerators of that process: kindlin-2 (FERMT2) and ITGB1BP1 engage integrin beta tails to control activation and adhesion turnover, RAC1 and ROCK1 couple cytoskeletal contractility and actin remodelling to adhesion maturation, and CFL1 supplies actin filament severing. Growth factor input arrives through VEGFA acting on KDR and NRP1, and through TEK, linking vascular signalling to adhesion strengthening, while SDC4 and collagen XVI provide matrix-side cues and SMAD3 and WNT4 tie transcriptional programmes in. Excessive signalling of this kind contributes to fibrosis and to tumour cell invasion.

Growth factors, cytokines and adhesion cues converge on class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase and the kinase AKT to tell a cell to grow, take up glucose, migrate and resist apoptosis; this pathway collects the inputs and regulators that turn that signalling up. Receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, INSR/IGF1R, KIT, FLT3, RET, the PDGF and VEGF receptors and the TAM family (AXL, MERTK, TYRO3) recruit adaptors including IRS1/IRS2, GAB1 and PIK3AP1, while PTPN11 and Src-family kinases amplify the signal and PDPK1 together with the mTORC2 components RICTOR and PRR5 completes AKT activation. Chemokine and G protein-coupled receptor inputs feed the gamma isoform. Output sustains cell survival, insulin-responsive metabolism, angiogenesis and immune cell activation; persistent activation, as through PIK3CA mutation or loss of negative control, is a common route to tumour growth and resistance to therapy.

Growth factor signalling through PI3K and AKT drives cell growth, survival, glucose uptake and protein synthesis, and the brakes on it are what keep those responses transient and proportionate. Negative regulation of PI3K/protein kinase B signal transduction covers the lipid phosphatases, protein phosphatases, scaffold restraints and microRNAs that terminate the pathway; when they are lost, cells acquire growth-factor-independent survival, and several of the genes here are among the most frequently inactivated tumour suppressors. PTEN and the inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases degrade the PIP3 second messenger that recruits AKT to the membrane, PHLPP1 dephosphorylates AKT's hydrophobic motif, protein phosphatase 2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylations, PIK3IP1 restrains the catalytic kinase directly, and TSC2 blocks the downstream mTORC1 arm. A large complement of microRNAs, including the miR-34 and miR-29 families, suppresses pathway components transcript by transcript, linking this restraint to differentiation, senescence and metabolic control.</description>

Excitable cells signal by letting their membrane potential swing positive, and membrane depolarization is that rising phase: inward cation current overwhelms the resting potassium conductance and drives the potential from negative toward zero and beyond. It initiates action potentials in neurons, cardiac myocytes and skeletal muscle, triggers calcium entry and hence contraction and transmitter release, and sets the pace of the heartbeat. The genes here are the currents and their accessory subunits — voltage-gated sodium channels with their beta subunits, L-type and T-type calcium channels with their alpha2delta and beta partners, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and other ligand-gated cation channels, HCN pacemaker channels, and the sodium-calcium exchanger — together with cytoskeletal anchors such as ankyrins that position them, and regulators including CAMK2D and SRC. Mutations in these channels cause long QT and Brugada syndromes, epilepsies, pain disorders and myasthenic syndromes.

Mitochondria hold a negative inner-membrane potential that drives ATP synthesis, protein import and calcium uptake; controlling when that potential collapses is effectively controlling whether a cell lives or dies. Depolarization accompanies permeability transition pore opening, cytochrome c release and the commitment step of intrinsic apoptosis, and it also marks damaged organelles for mitophagy. The regulators here act from several directions: BCL2 and BOK set the threshold for outer-membrane permeabilization, TSPO and P2RX7 influence pore behaviour and calcium loading, GCLC and GCLM supply glutathione synthesis that buffers oxidative stress, and PARP1 overactivation drains NAD+ and precipitates collapse. LRRK2 links the process to dopaminergic neuron loss in Parkinson disease, while ABCD1 ties it to peroxisomal fatty acid handling. Failure of this restraint underlies neurodegeneration, ischemic injury and the apoptosis resistance of tumour cells.

Mitochondria normally hold a strongly negative inner membrane potential, and processes that promote its collapse push cells toward permeability transition, loss of ATP synthesis and death. Positive regulation of mitochondrial depolarization covers the signals that increase the rate or extent of this potential loss, linking it to apoptosis, necrosis and the clearance of damaged mitochondria. The genes involved are heterogeneous rather than a single complex: a purinergic channel that opens during extracellular ATP-driven inflammatory death, a translocator protein of the outer membrane associated with the permeability transition, a DNA damage-activated ADP-ribosyltransferase whose overactivation depletes NAD+ and energy stores, a soluble bicarbonate-sensitive adenylate cyclase, and secreted and receptor proteins including a VEGF receptor and proteoglycan. Together they illustrate how growth factor, nucleotide and genotoxic stress inputs converge on mitochondrial energetics and cell fate.

establishment of pigment granule localization is the directed transport and anchoring of melanosomes within pigment cells, the step that determines whether pigment is delivered to keratinocytes and retinal epithelium or left stranded in the cell body. It gives skin, hair and eye their colour and supports the light-absorbing screen the retina needs for normal visual acuity; its failure produces the hypopigmentation and ocular defects of Griscelli and Hermansky-Pudlak type syndromes. Granules first travel long distances on microtubules using dynactin-linked motors, then transfer to actin filaments, where a tripartite complex of RAB27A, melanophilin and myosin Va captures and tethers them at the periphery. Melanoregulin, RAB11 and RAB17 route cargo through recycling endosomes, BLOC-1 subunits build the organelle itself, and the BBSome components tie melanosome positioning to ciliary trafficking machinery.

Pigment granules must be put in the right place to work: melanosomes are hauled outward along microtubules and then captured on cortical actin so they can be transferred to keratinocytes, and in the retinal pigment epithelium they are repositioned to shield photoreceptors. Establishing that localization depends on a tripartite actin-based tether in which RAB27A on the granule surface recruits melanophilin, which links to the actin motor MYO5A; loss of any of the three produces the diluted, silvery pigmentation and immune defects of Griscelli syndrome. Dynactin subunits and RAB11 isoforms support the microtubule-based and recycling-endosome legs of the journey, while BBSome components and MKKS connect the process to ciliary and intracellular trafficking, and BLOC-1 subunits to lysosome-related organelle biogenesis. GPR143 and MYO7A mutations cause ocular albinism and Usher syndrome respectively, underscoring how positioning defects translate into visual impairment.

Blood clots must be dissolved once a vessel has healed, and the control of fibrinolysis sets how quickly and how completely fibrin is cleared. Too little activity leaves thrombi in place and predisposes to thrombosis and vascular occlusion; too much causes bleeding, since clots are broken down before they can serve. The core reaction is conversion of plasminogen to plasmin by tissue-type and urokinase-type activators, the latter focused at the cell surface by its receptor, with plasmin then cleaving fibrin. Opposing this, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and alpha-2-antiplasmin restrain activator and protease respectively, while vitronectin, thrombospondin-1 and histidine-rich glycoprotein tune where activity is localised. Contact-phase proteins and thrombomodulin link the process to coagulation itself, so clot formation and clot removal are regulated as one balance in haemostasis, wound healing and tissue remodelling.

Clots must be dissolved on schedule, and this pathway is the brake on that dissolution, restraining fibrinolysis so that a fibrin plug persists long enough for a wound to seal. When the brake is too strong, thrombi resist breakdown and the risk of venous thrombosis, myocardial infarction and fibrotic tissue remodelling rises; when it fails, clots lyse prematurely and bleeding recurs. The central actors are inhibitors of the plasminogen activation cascade: SERPINE1 neutralises tissue-type and urokinase plasminogen activators, SERPINF2 inactivates plasmin itself, and histidine-rich glycoprotein together with vitronectin and thrombospondin modulates plasminogen and activator availability on surfaces. Thrombin and thrombomodulin link the process to coagulation, generating an activated inhibitor of fibrin lysis, so control of clot turnover is coupled to control of clot formation, with endothelium and platelets as the main sites of regulation.

Sulfation transfers an activated sulfate group from PAPS onto small molecules, carbohydrates or protein tyrosines, changing a substrate's charge, solubility and binding properties. In liver and gut the cytosolic sulfotransferases of the SULT1, SULT2 and SULT6 families are a major phase II conjugation route, inactivating and clearing drugs, phenols, catecholamines, bile acids and steroids – SULT1E1 sulfonates estrogens and SULT2A1 acts on DHEA, so this chemistry sets how much free hormone reaches receptors, and it can also bioactivate certain procarcinogens. Golgi-resident members work on macromolecules instead: the tyrosylprotein sulfotransferases TPST1 and TPST2 modify secreted and receptor proteins to strengthen ligand binding, while carbohydrate sulfotransferases together with the heparan and chondroitin chain-building enzymes EXT1, EXT2 and CHSY1 generate the sulfated glycan patterns that guide leukocyte homing and growth factor presentation.

Calcium is a signal, and its usefulness depends on being kept low at rest and raised only briefly and locally; the regulation of calcium ion transport is the layer of control that sets when channels open, how fast pumps clear the ion, and how much store is available to release. It governs cardiac and skeletal muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, immune cell activation, and hormone secretion, and its failure produces arrhythmia, myopathy, and excitotoxic or apoptotic cell death. Voltage-gated channel subunits and their accessory proteins, ryanodine receptor partners such as triadin, calsequestrin and junctophilins, and small pump regulators including phospholamban and sarcolipin tune release and reuptake at the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Store depletion is sensed by STIM proteins that gate ORAI-mediated entry, while calmodulin, calcineurin and CaMK isoforms feed the signal back onto transport itself; G protein-coupled receptors, purinergic P2X channels, chemokines, and mitochondrial and exchanger components broaden the control to whole-cell calcium balance.

Calcium entry and release must be damped as well as triggered, and this collection covers the braking processes that reduce calcium movement across the plasma membrane, the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the mitochondrial inner membrane. Such negative regulation of calcium ion transport sets the relaxation phase of muscle contraction, limits excitotoxic and arrhythmogenic calcium overload, and keeps mitochondrial uptake below the threshold that opens the permeability transition pore. Small sarcoplasmic reticulum peptides — phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin — inhibit the SERCA calcium pump, while calmodulin and calcineurin subunits transduce and feed back on calcium signals; MCUB acts as a dominant-negative subunit of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter, and accessory proteins including CBARP and caveolin-3 restrain voltage-gated channels. Nitric oxide synthases, growth factors and several microRNAs impose slower, transcriptional and second-messenger layers of restraint, linking this control to cardiac contractility and neuronal excitability.

Calcium is the cell's most widely used second messenger, and this collection describes the processes that raise its movement across membranes — increasing influx from outside the cell, release from internal stores, or the rate of its clearance and reuptake. Upregulating calcium entry couples receptor stimulation to muscle contraction, secretion of hormones and neurotransmitters, immune cell activation, and gene expression through calcineurin and calmodulin-dependent kinases. Mechanisms represented include store-operated entry via STIM and ORAI with its regulator CRACR2A, ATP-gated P2X channels, TRP channels, voltage-gated L-type channels with their beta subunits, and store handling by sarcoplasmic reticulum pumps and calsequestrin. Many entries are upstream agonists — chemokines, thrombin and its receptors, peptide hormones and G protein-coupled receptors signalling through phospholipase C — while scaffolds such as AKAPs and HOMER1 position the machinery. Excessive or mistimed calcium loading drives excitotoxicity and apoptosis.

Sensory systems do not simply report stimuli; their gain is set by modulators that raise or lower the threshold at which a stimulus is felt. This collection of gain-setting influences on sensory perception is dominated by pain and itch: neuropeptides such as substance P and its relatives, the metabotropic glutamate receptors GRM1 and GRM5, adenosine A1 receptor signalling, endocannabinoid turnover by monoacylglycerol lipase, and PIRT, an accessory subunit that tunes TRP channel responsiveness in sensory neurons. MRGPRX1 marks the itch-selective afferents, while ZFHX2 mutation causes congenital insensitivity to pain, showing how far perception can be shifted by single regulators. Salivary proline-rich and related secreted proteins contribute instead to taste sensitivity. Together these elements explain analgesia, hyperalgesia and sensitization, and they are where inflammatory mediators such as CCL3 act to make normal stimuli painful.
