The genes here converge on that output from several directions: cytoskeletal and transport machinery such as TUBA1A, WDR47 and the dynein-dynactin subunit DCTN1 builds and maintains long axons; lysosomal and glycosphingolipid enzymes including GBA1, NAGLU, SGSH and MFSD8 keep neurons free of storage material; and ion channels, transporters and receptors such as KCNQ3, GABRB3, SLC1A1 and ATP1B2 set excitability and synaptic drive. Loss of individual members produces recognisable movement disorders — spastic paraplegia, chorea-acanthocytosis, motor neuron degeneration, ataxia, tubulin-related malformations of the brain — so this grouping marks the shared vulnerability of locomotion, posture and gait to neuronal transport, degradative and excitability defects.

Selective autophagy only works if the right cargo is brought to the forming autophagosome, and substrate localization to autophagosome is the step that accomplishes that recruitment. The genes here act largely as cargo receptors that tether a particular substrate to the growing phagophore, typically by binding ATG8-family proteins on the nascent membrane through LIR motifs while holding the cargo on the other side. Each covers a different substrate class: BNIP3 marks damaged or surplus mitochondria for mitophagy, the reticulophagy regulator family fragments and delivers endoplasmic reticulum sheets and tubules, and STBD1 targets glycogen for degradation in lysosomes. SMURF1, a ubiquitin ligase, and the adaptor TOM1 contribute to targeting and membrane trafficking around this step. Loss of such receptors leaves organelle quality control incomplete, with consequences ranging from sensory neuropathy to failed clearance of mitochondria during development.

Leukocytes leaving the blood must first stick to the vessel wall, and this adhesion step to vascular endothelium sets where inflammation and immune surveillance occur. It underlies wound healing and pathogen clearance, and its failure produces recurrent infection with poor pus formation, as in defects of the shared beta-2 integrin subunit; its excess drives atherosclerosis and chronic inflammatory tissue damage. Selectins and their sialylated, fucosylated ligands, built by fucosyltransferases and sulfotransferases, capture flowing cells and support rolling; chemokines and their receptors then trigger integrin activation, so that alpha-4 and beta-2 integrins bind endothelial ICAM1, VCAM1, MADCAM1 and junctional adhesion molecules for firm arrest. Endothelial adhesion molecule expression is induced by TNF and IL6 signalling through TRAF6, IRAK1 and NF-kB, restrained by KLF4 and by several microRNAs, while RHOA-ROCK1 shapes the cytoskeletal changes on both sides.</description>}Fondly Fondly Fondly

Leukocyte adhesion to arterial endothelium is the committing step of vascular inflammation: circulating monocytes and neutrophils are captured on the luminal surface of an artery through adhesion molecules before they transmigrate into the wall. Because this capture is where atherosclerotic lesions begin, the process links haemodynamic and metabolic stress to plaque initiation, and its inappropriate activation drives chronic arterial disease. Endothelial adhesiveness is set by opposing regulators. TNF signalling and leukotriene-generating 5-lipoxygenase activity promote an adhesive, pro-inflammatory endothelial phenotype, whereas the shear-responsive transcription factor KLF4 suppresses adhesion molecule expression and maintains a quiescent surface; a microRNA sensitive to flow patterns tunes the same balance. Ephrin-B2 and its Eph receptor partners contribute arterial identity and contact-dependent guidance cues, while zinc transport and protein palmitoylation modify the trafficking and activity of the adhesion machinery itself.

Fungi are recognized before any antibody exists, and this antifungal arm of innate immunity is how myeloid cells detect fungal cell wall carbohydrates and mount an immediate response. It matters clinically because people who lose its central adaptor suffer chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and invasive fungal disease despite otherwise intact immunity. C-type lectin receptors such as Dectin-1 and Dectin-2, together with Mincle and related CLEC4 family members, bind beta-glucans and mannose-rich structures on yeast and hyphae; signalling through phospholipase C-gamma2 converges on CARD9, which with BCL10 assembles a complex that drives NF-kB-dependent cytokine production and Th17 polarization, with TRIM62 and USP15 tuning that step. Defensin peptides contribute direct microbicidal killing at epithelial surfaces, and chemerin and CX3CR1 recruit phagocytes to infected tissue. The output is fungal clearance by neutrophils and macrophages.

Rising intracellular calcium can switch on the cell's energy-sensing kinase without any change in nucleotide levels, and the CAMKK-AMPK cascade is that route. Calcium-loaded calmodulin activates CAMKK2, which phosphorylates the catalytic subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase (PRKAA1) on its activation loop, shifting metabolism toward catabolism: glucose uptake and fatty acid oxidation are favoured, biosynthesis and mTORC1 signalling are restrained, and autophagy and mitochondrial turnover are promoted. This gives excitable and immune cells a way to couple calcium signalling directly to fuel management. The branch matters in hypothalamic appetite control and insulin secretion, in microglial metabolic reprogramming downstream of TREM2, and in autophagy regulation involving IRGM and LRRK2. Loss or dampening of this arm contributes to obesity, insulin resistance, and neurodegenerative phenotypes in which damaged organelles are not cleared efficiently.

multivesicular body-lysosome fusion is the final delivery step of the endolysosomal route, in which a late endosome loaded with intraluminal vesicles merges with a lysosome so that internalised receptors, ubiquitinated membrane cargo and engulfed material are exposed to acid hydrolases and degraded. It sets how long activated growth factor and immune receptors keep signalling, and it clears autophagic and phagocytic cargo; when it stalls, undigested material accumulates and cells acquire the storage phenotypes seen in lysosomal and neurodegenerative disease. The CHMP proteins here are the ESCRT-III subunits that polymerise into spiral filaments on the endosome, driving the membrane deformation and scission that both generates intraluminal vesicles and remodels membranes for fusion, with accessory subunits governing filament turnover. RUFY4 links this machinery to Rab-directed trafficking and autophagosome maturation, coupling cargo sorting to lysosomal consumption.

Endocytosed cargo destined for destruction is packaged into intraluminal vesicles within multivesicular bodies, and fusion of those bodies with lysosomes is the delivery step that commits the cargo to degradation. This route terminates signalling from internalised receptors, clears damaged membrane proteins, and supplies amino acids and lipids from recycled material; when it stalls, undegraded cargo accumulates in swollen endosomes, a phenotype linked to neurodegeneration. The bulk of the machinery here is the ESCRT-III family of CHMP subunits, which polymerise into filaments on the cytosolic face of endosomal membranes and drive constriction and scission with a topology opposite to that of conventional vesicle budding, together with the accessory subunits that cap and recycle those filaments. RUFY4 acts as an effector linking these late endosomal compartments to lysosomal fusion and autophagic flux.

When food energy intake falls short, cells and tissues shift from storing fuel to mobilising and sparing it, and this response to caloric restriction is the set of transcriptional and enzymatic adjustments that make the switch. It matters for whole-body glucose supply during fasting, for the lipid remodelling that follows weight loss, and for the stress tolerance and longevity effects attributed to dietary restriction. Lipogenic enzymes such as fatty acid synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase are suppressed while hepatic glucose output through glucose-6-phosphatase rises; cholesterol handling adjusts through the LDL receptor and apolipoprotein E. Amino acid and integrated stress signalling appears via the transcription factor CHOP and its target CHAC1, oxidative defence via NRF2 and its target NQO1, and nutrient-sensitive deacetylation via a sirtuin, alongside adipokine signalling from chemerin.

The Golgi lumen is kept mildly acidic, and that pH gradient is what allows glycosyltransferases and processing proteases to work, cargo to sort correctly, and glycans to be built in the right order along the stack. Acidification is driven by the vacuolar H+-ATPase, whose membrane-embedded V0 subunits form the proton pore while the cytosolic V1 subunits hydrolyse ATP, with accessory factors such as ATP6AP1 and ATP6AP2 needed for assembly of the pump. Counteracting cation/proton exchangers, including the organellar antiporters SLC9A7 and SLC9A8, leak protons back and set the steady-state pH rather than simply lowering it. Loss of this control has visible consequences: mutations in the a2 subunit of the pump cause a congenital glycosylation disorder with cutis laxa, reflecting how dependent secretory-pathway glycan processing and connective tissue matrix assembly are on correct Golgi pH.

The endoplasmic reticulum does not float free: it is held within nanometres of the plasma membrane at dedicated contact sites, and this tethering creates the narrow cytosolic gap where lipids and calcium signals are exchanged between the two compartments without vesicles. Such junctions support store-operated calcium entry, replenishment of plasma membrane phosphoinositides after receptor stimulation, and non-vesicular transfer of glycerolipids and sterols. The extended synaptotagmins bridge the gap in a calcium- and PIP2-dependent manner through their membrane-binding and lipid-transfer modules, a GRAM-domain protein provides a constitutive phosphoinositide-dependent tether, and the VAP proteins anchor in the ER membrane to recruit FFAT-motif lipid transfer and regulatory proteins. Loss or distortion of these attachments blunts lipid resupply and calcium handling, and VAPB mutation is linked to motor neuron degeneration.

Telomeres protect chromosome ends partly by folding back on themselves: the single-stranded TTAGGG overhang invades the adjacent duplex to form a three-stranded displacement loop within a larger t-loop. These structures must be taken apart in a controlled way so that replication forks can pass and the end can be processed, and the disassembly of telomeric D-loops is that resolution step. It couples shelterin proteins, which coat and organise the telomere, to enzymes that unwind or cut branched DNA: the RecQ-family helicases BLM, WRN and RECQL4 unwind the invaded strand, while the SLX4 scaffold with its SLX1 nuclease partner provides structure-specific cleavage. Loss of control here produces telomere-length heterogeneity, fragile telomeres and catastrophic loop excision, and the helicases involved are mutated in Bloom, Werner and Rothmund-Thomson syndromes, linking this chemistry to premature ageing and cancer predisposition.

Most cilia are built inside a membrane-bound compartment, but in cytosolic ciliogenesis the axoneme is assembled or extended while exposed directly to the cytoplasm, a route used most conspicuously by the sperm flagellum and by some insect sensory cilia. Because tubulin and axonemal cargo are recruited without an intraciliary transport barrier, this mode of assembly depends on membrane traffic and centriolar satellite components rather than on classical gating: a small GTPase of the Rab family contributes to ciliary vesicle and membrane delivery, a WD-repeat effector links Rab activity to ciliogenic membrane supply, and a satellite scaffold together with a nephrocystin-family protein organises factors at the basal body. A deubiquitinating enzyme adds a protein-stability layer to this control. Failure of the underlying machinery produces ciliopathy phenotypes, including retinal and renal disease and defective sperm motility.

Microtubule organizing center localization is the set of processes that put the centrosome, and its associated spindle poles or basal bodies, in the right place inside a cell. Position matters because the microtubule array radiating from it sets the axis of cell division, the direction of migration, the apical-basal orientation of epithelia, and the docking site for cilium assembly. The genes describe how this is achieved: dynein and its regulators LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1 pull on astral microtubules, kinesin and BICD2 provide cargo transport, and a LINC complex of SUN proteins and nesprins tethers the centrosome to the nuclear envelope so nucleus and MTOC move together. Cortical cues via GPSM2 and DLG1 orient the spindle during asymmetric division. Failure produces mispositioned spindles, defective neuronal migration and microcephaly, and impaired ciliogenesis.

Where a cell puts its microtubule organizing center determines the axis along which it divides, migrates, or builds a cilium, and this pathway covers the positioning and anchoring of that center. Positioning the centrosome or nucleus-associated MTOC underlies spindle orientation in dividing epithelium and neural progenitors, centrosome migration to the apical surface during ciliogenesis, and nuclear movement in migrating and differentiating cells. Dynein and kinesin motors with their adaptors and regulators — including LIS1, NDE1 and NDEL1, BICD2 and KIF5B — pull on astral microtubules, while LINC complex components SUN1, SUN2 and the nesprins SYNE1/SYNE2 couple the cytoskeleton across the nuclear envelope. Scaffolds and cortical cues such as AKAP9, ninein, GPSM2, DLG1 and ezrin fix the attachment site. Loss of these functions produces microcephaly, lissencephaly and other neurodevelopmental and ciliopathy phenotypes.

antimicrobial humoral immune response mediated by antimicrobial peptide is the chemical arm of innate defence at wet surfaces: small secreted peptides in mucus, saliva, sweat, tears, gut fluid and blood that kill or disable bacteria, fungi and viruses within minutes of contact, long before lymphocytes respond. It keeps epithelial barriers of the skin, airway, gut and urogenital tract colonised by commensals rather than pathogens, and its failure underlies recurrent skin and mucosal infection, while dysregulated output drives psoriasis, Crohn's disease and other inflammatory conditions. Effectors include alpha- and beta-defensins from neutrophils and Paneth cells, cathelicidin, lactoferrin, histatins, RegIII lectins, S100 proteins, peptidoglycan recognition proteins and RNases, which permeabilise membranes or sequester nutrient metals; hepcidin additionally links this response to systemic iron withholding. Many chemokines act dually as direct microbicides and as recruiters of phagocytes, and IL-17 signalling induces the epithelial peptide programme.

Epithelial surfaces, secretions and blood plasma are defended by small secreted peptides that kill or disable microbes directly, and this antimicrobial humoral response is the arm of innate immunity that operates outside cells in body fluids. It shapes skin, gut, airway and oral barrier function, restrains commensal overgrowth, and its failure underlies recurrent infection, while overproduction contributes to psoriasis and other inflammatory skin disease. Alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, lactoferrin, dermcidin, histatins, granulysin and the peptidoglycan-recognition proteins act by permeabilising membranes or sequestering nutrients; hepcidin instead withholds iron systemically. Many chemokines and neuropeptides included here have intrinsic microbicidal activity alongside their signalling roles, and regenerating islet-derived proteins and S100 members link epithelial repair to bacterial killing. Neutrophil granule proteases and kallikreins process precursors into active peptides, coupling release from leukocytes and keratinocytes to local antimicrobial capacity.

Astrocytes switch from homeostatic support of synapses and the blood-brain barrier into a reactive, inflammatory state after injury, infection or protein aggregation, and this pathway covers the signals that set how readily and how strongly that switch is thrown. Tuning it matters because reactive astrogliosis walls off damage and clears debris, yet sustained activation drives neurotoxic phenotypes seen in Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis and chronic neuroinflammation. Control is exerted at several levels: the cytokine IL6 amplifies reactive responses, the microglial receptor TREM2 shapes the crosstalk that licenses astrocyte activation, the nuclear receptor NR1D1 links circadian timing to repression of glial inflammatory genes, and LDLR ties lipoprotein and cholesterol handling to the response. Several microRNAs impose post-transcriptional restraint, while the kinase TTBK1 connects tau pathology to glial reactivity.

Astrocytes shift into a reactive state after injury, infection or aging, and restraining that shift is what keeps glial responses proportionate rather than chronically inflammatory. Dampening astrocyte activation limits the release of cytokines and the neurotoxic reactive phenotypes implicated in neurodegeneration, demyelination and post-ischemic injury, where sustained astrogliosis impedes repair and damages neurons. The contributing molecules act through distinct routes: lipoprotein receptor-mediated cholesterol uptake constrains sterol-driven inflammatory tone, a circadian nuclear receptor represses inflammatory transcription in glia on a daily cycle, and a microglial immune receptor of the TREM family shapes the signals that would otherwise drive neighbouring astrocytes reactive. Small regulatory RNAs of the miR-181 family add post-transcriptional braking on inflammatory targets. Together these define an inhibitory layer over neuroinflammation, linking lipid handling, circadian timing and microglia-astrocyte crosstalk to control of central nervous system glial reactivity.

Microglia and astrocytes shift from surveillance to a reactive state when they meet cytokines, chemokines, damage signals or misfolded protein, and this glial activation is what converts an insult in the brain into inflammation, debris clearance and, if sustained, neuronal injury. It underlies the neuroinflammatory component of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, demyelination and responses to infection. Pattern and damage receptors such as TLR1/6/9, AGER, C5AR1 and formyl peptide receptors sense ligands including aggregated amyloid precursor protein products, tau and alpha-synuclein; TREM2 with its adaptor TYROBP, complement C1QA and the fractalkine ligand-receptor pair CX3CL1-CX3CR1 set the threshold and tone of the response. Downstream IL1B, IL6, TNF, interferon-gamma receptor signalling and JAK2-JUN transcription drive the morphological and secretory change, while progranulin, clusterin and neurotrophic CNTF restrain or redirect it.

Autophagy only degrades anything once the sealed autophagosome merges with the lysosome, and this fusion step delivers the acidic lumen and hydrolases that break down engulfed cytoplasm, protein aggregates and damaged organelles. Blocking it causes autophagosomes to pile up undigested, a lesion seen in neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease; mutations in ATP13A2, CLN3 and C9orf72 among these genes cause parkinsonism, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis and ALS/frontotemporal dementia respectively. Mechanistically, the autophagosomal SNARE STX17 pairs with lysosomal partners under the control of the HOPS tethering complex (VPS11, VPS16, VPS18, VPS33A, VPS39, VPS41), while PLEKHM1 and RUBCNL act as adaptors and small GTPases including ARL8B, RAB2A and RAB39A position lysosomes and license tethering. Phosphoinositide kinases and ubiquitin ligases in the group tune the reaction, linking vesicle trafficking and lysosomal positioning to cellular quality control and nutrient recycling.

Autophagy is the route by which cells wrap portions of their own cytoplasm in a double membrane and deliver it to lysosomes for breakdown, recycling amino acids during starvation and clearing damage that no other system can remove. It sustains cells through nutrient deprivation, disposes of protein aggregates, damaged mitochondria, excess peroxisomes, ER fragments and intracellular bacteria, and its decline underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and defective host defence. Nutrient and energy status converge on mTORC1 and AMPK, which control the ULK1 initiation complex; a class III PI3K complex built on BECN1 and VPS34 nucleates the phagophore, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades through ATG7, ATG3 and the ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 complex lipidate LC3 and GABARAP proteins on the growing membrane. Cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1, OPTN and CALCOCO2 read ubiquitin marks for selective capture, while SNAREs, HOPS and Rab GTPases complete lysosomal fusion and TFEB drives lysosomal gene expression.

Chains of ubiquitin joined through lysine 48 are the canonical signal that sends a protein to the proteasome, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower how readily such chains are built on a substrate. Because degradation rate sets the abundance and half-life of signalling proteins, transcription factors and damaged or misfolded polypeptides, tuning K48-linked ubiquitination determines protein quality control, cell cycle timing and the strength of inflammatory and death signalling. The genes here act at different points: an inhibitor-of-apoptosis E3 ligase directs degradative ubiquitination of kinases and death-pathway components, a small-molecule kinase and a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase modulate ligase activity or substrate presentation, and TRIM44 and TCF25 influence chain formation on their partners. Loss of this control leads to inappropriate accumulation or premature destruction of regulatory proteins, a feature of cancer and neurodegeneration.

Delivering a newly made or recycled protein to the cell surface, and keeping it there, is what establishment of protein localization to the plasma membrane accomplishes. It sets the density of receptors, transporters and adhesion molecules available to a cell, and so determines nutrient uptake, synaptic strength, epithelial polarity and ciliary signalling. Cargo leaving the Golgi is sorted by GGA adaptors, golgins and GOLPH3, carried on Rab-marked vesicles including RAB8A, RAB10 and RAB11A with their effectors, moved by kinesin and along spectrin-ankyrin and radixin-supported cortical scaffolds, and fused at the surface through VAMP SNAREs and NSF. Palmitoylation by ZDHHC2 and removal by acyl-protein thioesterases tunes membrane anchoring, while retromer and BBSome components route recycling and ciliary targeting. Loss of these steps causes mistargeted transporters, polarity defects and ciliopathies such as Bardet-Biedl syndrome.

The last physical step of cell division is the cutting of the intercellular bridge that still joins two daughter cells, and midbody abscission is that severing event. Until it happens, division is incomplete; failure leaves cells connected or drives regression of the furrow, producing binucleate and aneuploid progeny. The machinery is the ESCRT-III system: CEP55 recruits ALIX and ESCRT-I to the midbody, CHMP4 and related subunits polymerise into spiral filaments that constrict the bridge from within, and the AAA-ATPase VPS4A/VPS4B remodels and disassembles them. Timing is policed by an Aurora B-dependent checkpoint that delays cutting while chromatin remains trapped in the bridge, with CHMP4C as the responsive subunit. Accessory factors including IST1, MITD1, spartin and midbody-localised kinesin contribute to bridge organisation and membrane handling, linking this biology to the same membrane-scission chemistry used in endosomal sorting and viral budding.

Vertebrate embryos look symmetric from the outside but place the heart, stomach, liver and spleen consistently on one side, and establishment of left/right asymmetry is how that choice is made and then imposed on the body plan. The decision is taken at the embryonic node, where motile monocilia generate a leftward fluid flow that is sensed and converted into asymmetric gene expression, so most of the genes here concern cilium assembly, axonemal structure and ciliary beating: a cytoplasmic dynein assembly factor, coiled-coil and cilia- and flagella-associated components of the axoneme, and a calmodulin-binding ciliary protein. When the process fails, organ position is randomized or mirrored, producing situs inversus and heterotaxy with complex congenital heart malformations, frequently alongside the airway and sperm motility defects of primary ciliary dyskinesia.

Articular cartilage is the smooth, load-bearing tissue capping the ends of long bones in synovial joints, and its formation from the interzone into a permanent, non-calcifying layer determines whether a joint can glide under decades of mechanical loading. Loss of this tissue underlies osteoarthritis, in which the matrix is degraded faster than chondrocytes can rebuild it. The genes here point to two themes: construction and turnover of the proteoglycan-rich extracellular matrix, through small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as biglycan, epiphycan, osteoglycin and opticin that organise collagen fibrils and tune growth factor availability, and lysosomal glycosaminoglycan catabolism via beta-glucuronidase, whose deficiency produces skeletal dysplasia. Intraflagellar transport machinery is also required, tying chondrocyte differentiation to primary cilium-dependent signalling during skeletal patterning and joint morphogenesis.

The first meiotic division separates homologous chromosome pairs rather than sister chromatids, halving chromosome number and creating the genetic diversity that recombination provides; failure produces aneuploid gametes, infertility and miscarriage. The genes here cover the whole reductive division: programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11 with REC114, MEI4 and ANKRD31 at hotspots specified by PRDM9; strand invasion and homology search by DMC1, RAD51 and the MEIOB-SPATA22 complex; synaptonemal complex assembly from SYCP1-3 and the central-element SYCE proteins; crossover designation and resolution through MSH4/MSH5, CNTD1, RNF212 and MLH1-MLH3. Meiosis-specific cohesin subunits REC8 and STAG3 with shugoshin protect centromeric cohesion so that only arm cohesion is lost, while telomere-LINC components attach chromosome ends to the nuclear envelope for pairing. ATM-dependent checkpoint control and cyclin-CDK-APC regulation time the division, and piRNA factors silence transposons in the same germ cells.

The roof of the mouth forms when paired palatal shelves grow out from the maxillary prominences, elevate above the tongue, meet at the midline and fuse; failure at any of these steps leaves a cleft palate, one of the commonest human birth defects. The genes here trace the signalling that drives shelf outgrowth and fusion: TGF-beta ligands TGFB2 and TGFB3 acting through TGFBR2 and the SMAD2/SMAD4 effectors, which are required for medial edge epithelial breakdown and seam removal; WNT ligands with FZD receptors and LEF1 for mesenchymal proliferation and patterning; JAG2-Notch signalling that keeps palatal epithelium from adhering to the tongue; and integrins ITGB6 and ITGB8 that activate latent TGF-beta. Transcriptional regulators such as CHD7, TBX1, FOXE1, SOX11 and TSHZ1 link this programme to craniofacial syndromes, while COL11A2 supplies extracellular matrix for the fusing shelves.

Cells and whole organisms must match the flux of fuels, lipids and cofactors to changing supply and demand, and this collection captures the control layer that sets those rates rather than the enzymes doing the chemistry. Regulation of small molecule metabolic processes spans hormonal inputs such as insulin, leptin, glucagon and adiponectin acting through their receptors and IRS/AKT/mTOR and AMPK kinase modules, nuclear receptors and transcription factors including PPARs, SREBPs, LXRs, FXR, HNF4A and the PGC-1 coactivator, sirtuin deacetylases, and microRNAs that tune metabolic transcripts. Downstream targets include fatty acid oxidation and synthesis, cholesterol and bile acid handling by LDLR, CYP7A1 and apolipoproteins, glycogen and glycolytic control via PDK isoforms and phosphatase subunits, and UGT- and FMO-mediated conjugation of small molecules. Loss of this coordination produces insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia, fatty liver and disturbed energy balance, linking it to circadian and stress signalling.

This grouping collects the regulators that push small molecule metabolism upward — the hormones, sensors and transcription factors that raise the rate of glucose, lipid, sterol, amino acid and nucleotide handling when a cell or tissue needs fuel mobilised or stored. It is the control layer of whole-body energy balance: insulin and its receptor acting through IRS1/IRS2 and AKT, glucagon and adrenergic input through PKA, and the AMP-activated kinase subunits that report low energy charge. Nuclear receptors and their coactivators (PPARA, PPARD, PPARG with PPARGC1A, the liver X and farnesoid receptors) and the SREBP–SCAP axis drive cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis genes, while sirtuins, mTOR complex components and circadian factors such as CRY1 and NR1D1 time these outputs. Inflammatory and stress signals (TNF, IL1B, HIF1A) feed in, linking failure of this regulation to insulin resistance, dyslipidaemia and metabolic disease.

Metabolism is as much about restraint as about flux, and this collection covers the brakes: processes that slow or shut down the turnover of small molecules such as fatty acids, cholesterol, bile acids, glucose and xenobiotics. Such damping sets the switch between fed and fasted states, prevents futile cycling, and protects tissues from lipid overload and toxic intermediates; its loss contributes to fatty liver, dyslipidaemia and insulin resistance. Mechanisms represented include feedback inhibition of sterol synthesis by the INSIG proteins acting on SCAP, transcriptional repression through NCOR1, REST and the sirtuins, hormonal and nutrient signals from insulin, leptin receptor, adiponectin and PPARA, stress-induced inhibitors such as DDIT4 and TRIB3, and p53-linked suppression of glycolysis via TIGAR. Numerous microRNAs, including the cholesterol-associated MIR33A, add post-transcriptional dampening, while UGT1A glucuronosyltransferases terminate the activity of lipophilic substrates.

SCF complexes — built from Skp1, Cul1 and an interchangeable F-box substrate receptor — mark selected proteins with ubiquitin so the proteasome can destroy them, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower how fast that destruction proceeds. Because SCF targets include cell cycle regulators, signalling intermediates and structural proteins of muscle, tuning its output determines whether a cell divides, adapts its metabolism, or loses mass. The muscle-enriched F-box protein FBXO32 (atrogin-1) illustrates the stakes: its induction during denervation, fasting and cachexia drives the protein loss of skeletal muscle atrophy, and it is held in check by growth signalling through mTOR. Other regulators act by acetylating or dephosphorylating components of the pathway, or by sequestering substrate receptors, so that ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis is set by nutrient and growth-factor context rather than running constitutively.

When cells meet oxidative, heat or nutrient stress, stalled translation initiation complexes and their mRNAs condense into cytoplasmic stress granules, and this regulatory layer sets how readily those granules form and how large they grow. The decision matters because granule assembly sequesters mRNA away from ribosomes, buys time for repair, and tunes signalling and survival; persistent or aberrant condensation is the entry point to pathological aggregation in neurodegeneration. Scaffolding RNA-binding proteins such as UBAP2L, CAPRIN1 and IGF2BP1 promote condensation, while USP10 acts with G3BP-family scaffolds to restrain it, and the catalytic subunits of AMP-activated protein kinase couple granule dynamics to energy stress. Autophagy components ATG5 and BECN1 tie granule turnover to bulk degradative clearance, linking this process to the broader stress response and to mRNA storage and triage.

Accurate partitioning of duplicated chromosomes to the two daughter cells depends on processes that promote and accelerate mitotic sister chromatid segregation; when they fail, cells missegregate chromosomes and become aneuploid, a hallmark of tumours and of miscarriage-causing embryonic errors. The genes here act at the kinetochore-microtubule interface and at the spindle itself. Aurora B kinase corrects improperly attached kinetochores so that only bi-oriented pairs are stabilised, CDK1 drives entry into and progression through mitosis, and the SKA complex components strengthen kinetochore attachment to depolymerising microtubule ends, enabling chromatids to be pulled apart. NUMA1 focuses spindle poles and anchors the spindle to the cortex, while MAD1L1 and a MAD2-binding partner tie this activity to the spindle assembly checkpoint, which must be extinguished before anaphase can begin. Chromatin modification by the acetyltransferase KAT5 contributes a further regulatory layer.

Heart valves and septa are built from cells that begin as endocardial epithelium and must be released from it: control over cardiac epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition sets how many of these cells delaminate, when, and where. Cells losing apical-basal polarity, breaking cell-cell junctions and invading the underlying matrix populate the cushions that become valve leaflets, so too little or too much of this transition produces valve malformation and septal defects, and the same programme is reactivated in fibrotic remodelling of the adult heart. The regulators here are largely TGF-beta family ligands and their receptors, with the type I receptor ACVR1 and the accessory receptor endoglin tuning signal strength and the BMP antagonist noggin restraining it. Notch1 and its ligand JAG1 act with TWIST1 to drive the transcriptional switch, while microRNAs of the miR-19 family and the membrane protein EMP2 modulate the response.

Heart valves and septa are built by cells that begin as endocardial epithelium and then leave it: they dismantle apical-basal polarity, break intercellular junctions, break through basement membrane and migrate into the underlying cushion matrix as mesenchyme. This set covers the inputs that initiate or accelerate that cardiac epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. TGF-beta family ligand and receptor components, including TGFB2 with the type I and type II receptors, along with the BMP receptor ACVR1 and its partner ENG, drive the transition, while JAG1-NOTCH1 signalling primes endocardial cells to respond and TWIST1 acts as the transcriptional executor of the migratory, invasive state. Insufficient signalling leaves valve cushions hypoplastic and produces septal and outflow tract malformations; inappropriate reactivation in the adult heart contributes to valve disease and fibrotic remodelling after injury.

Stomach development traces the foregut from a simple tube into a compartmentalised organ with glands that store food, secrete acid and begin protein digestion, and it sets up the epithelial and neural cell types the adult stomach depends on. Patterning and cell-fate decisions dominate: Notch-dependent transcriptional repression through HES1 restrains the endocrine programme so that proliferative progenitors and mucus- or acid-secreting lineages form in the right proportions, while ASCL1 drives neurogenesis in the enteric innervation that controls gastric motility. Heparan sulfate chain elongation by EXT1 shapes the growth factor gradients guiding regional specification, and KCNQ1 channel activity is required for parietal cell acid secretion and normal glandular architecture. Failures produce gastric hypoplasia, glandular metaplasia or hyperplasia, and impaired secretory function, linking this developmental programme to digestive physiology and to stomach tumour predisposition.

Necrosis can be a programmed outcome rather than an accident, and this pathway covers the controls that set how readily cells take that route. It matters because regulated necrosis releases intracellular contents and drives inflammation, so its tuning shapes antiviral defence, ischaemic tissue damage and inflammatory disease. Much of the control sits at the death-receptor complex, where caspase-8 with FADD and the caspase-like inhibitor CFLAR normally restrains RIPK1-RIPK3 signalling, while ubiquitin editing by CYLD, the linear ubiquitin ligase components RNF31 and RBCK1, and the IAP proteins BIRC2 and BIRC3 determine whether RIPK1 promotes survival or death. A parallel arm runs through PARP1 overactivation and AIFM1, a mitochondrial flavoprotein that relocates to the nucleus. Nucleic-acid sensing by ZBP1, lymphotoxin receptor signalling, p53, and several microRNAs feed into the same decision.

Necroptosis and related programmed necrotic death are lytic, inflammatory ways for a cell to die, and this pathway covers the brakes that hold them off so that tissue turnover proceeds quietly by apoptosis instead. Restraint matters because unchecked necroptosis drives inflammatory pathology in skin, gut and liver, while its loss of restraint in tumours can be exploited therapeutically. The core of the control is the death receptor platform: caspase-8 with its adaptor FADD cleaves RIPK1 and prevents necrosome assembly, while the inhibitor-of-apoptosis proteins BIRC2 and BIRC3 and the linear ubiquitin ligase components RNF31 and RBCK1 ubiquitinate RIPK1 to keep it signalling for survival rather than death. Additional inputs come from a caspase-inhibitory ARC-family protein, mitochondrial and PARP-linked metabolic factors, and several microRNAs that tune the abundance of necroptotic machinery.

Cells can die by a regulated form of necrosis that ruptures the membrane and spills contents, provoking inflammation rather than the silent clearance typical of apoptosis; this pathway covers the inputs that push cells toward that fate. It matters in ischemic injury, neurodegeneration and antiviral defence, where necroptotic death both limits pathogen replication and drives tissue damage. The core machinery is the RIPK1–RIPK3 kinase axis, activated downstream of death receptors or of ZBP1 sensing nucleic acid, while parallel routes operate through PARP1 hyperactivation and energy collapse with AIFM1 translocating from mitochondria to the nucleus to fragment DNA. TP53 and caspase-6 contribute additional death-promoting signals, and several microRNAs tune the amplitude of the response. Suppressing these steps preserves tissue in infarction models, making the pathway a target for cytoprotection.

Cells keep free cytosolic zinc vanishingly low while still supplying it to secretory granules, vesicles and the Golgi, and this is the transport step that moves zinc out of the cytosol across an organelle membrane into the lumen. The ZnT-family exchangers involved run zinc inward against its gradient, typically coupled to proton counterflow, loading compartments where zinc is stored, secreted or used to metalloate client proteins. Specific members define particular organelles and cell types: one loads insulin granules in pancreatic beta cells, another supplies synaptic vesicles in glutamatergic neurons, others charge Golgi enzymes such as alkaline phosphatase, and one builds zinc into milk-secreting mammary vesicles. Adaptor protein complex 3 subunits place these transporters on the correct vesicles. Loss of individual components causes zinc-deficiency dermatitis, impaired insulin storage and altered diabetes risk, and disturbed neuronal zinc signalling.

regulation of mitochondrial gene expression controls how much protein the mitochondrial genome makes, tuning the supply of the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded there to the cell's demand for oxidative phosphorylation. Because those subunits must be stoichiometrically matched with nuclear-encoded partners, this regulation sets respiratory capacity, and its failure causes combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, lactic acidosis and encephalomyopathy. The genes act at every step downstream of the mitochondrial promoter: transcription elongation and termination via TEFM and MTERF3, processing and stabilisation of polycistronic transcripts by LRPPRC and the RNase P subunit TRMT10C, and chemical modification of mitochondrial tRNAs and rRNAs by pseudouridine synthases, methyltransferases and NSUN3, whose tRNA marks license accurate decoding. Others assemble and license the mitoribosome, including MALSU1, MTG1 and MTG2, or act as translational activators such as TACO1 for COX1. Nuclear factors and AMPK link the programme to cellular energy state.

The mitochondrial genome encodes core subunits of the respiratory chain, and its own dedicated transcription and translation machinery must be tuned to demand — this pathway covers the factors that set how much mitochondrial RNA and protein is made. Because output feeds directly into oxidative phosphorylation, loss of these regulators causes combined respiratory chain deficiency, lactic acidosis and infantile encephalomyopathy. Members act at several steps: TEFM and MTERF3 control transcription elongation and its termination, LRPPRC and FASTKD3 govern processing and stability of mitochondrial mRNAs, and a large group of modification enzymes — TRMT10C, NSUN3, CDK5RAP1, RPUSD3/4, TRUB2 — install methyl, pseudouridine and thiolation marks that make mitochondrial tRNAs and rRNAs functional. Others assist ribosome assembly and subunit joining, including MALSU1 and the GTPases MTG1 and MTG2, while TACO1 licenses translation of COX1 specifically. Nuclear-encoded inputs such as the AMPK subunit PRKAA1 link this output to cellular energy status.

detection of stimulus involved in sensory perception of pain is nociception at its first step: the conversion of noxious heat, acid, mechanical force or inflammatory chemicals into electrical signals by primary sensory neurons. It defines the nociceptor as a cell type and sets the threshold at which tissue damage becomes conscious pain; loss of its components produces congenital insensitivity to pain, while sensitisation of the same machinery underlies chronic inflammatory and neuropathic pain. Transduction runs through cation channels such as TRPV1, TRPA1 and the acid-sensing channel ASIC3, whose depolarisation is converted to action potentials by the dorsal root ganglion sodium channels NaV1.7, NaV1.9 and NaV1.1. NGF signalling through TRKA and the transcription factor PRDM12 specify and maintain these neurons, while TNF, chemokine and neuropeptide signalling (substance P, CGRP-related tachykinins) amplify their output during injury and inflammation.

Nociception begins when a noxious stimulus — heat, acid, mechanical force, or an inflammatory mediator — is converted into electrical activity in a sensory neuron, and this pathway covers that detection and transduction step. It defines the nociceptor as a cell type and explains both congenital insensitivity to pain and the hypersensitivity that follows injury. Transducing channels such as TRPV1 and TRPA1 open in response to heat and irritant chemicals, acid-sensing channels report tissue acidosis, and voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN9A and SCN11A set the threshold for firing and propagate the resulting action potentials; loss-of-function mutations in these genes, or in the transcription factor PRDM12 needed for nociceptor development, abolish pain sensation. Neuropeptides of the tachykinin family, NGF signalling through NTRK1, and inflammatory mediators such as TNF sensitize these endings, linking peripheral detection to inflammatory and chronic pain states.

R-loops form when nascent transcripts reanneal with template DNA, displacing the non-template strand; the resulting RNA:DNA hybrids stall transcription elongation, expose single-stranded DNA and drive replication-transcription collisions unless they are taken apart. R-loop processing is the set of activities that disassemble these structures and so protects genome stability, limits double-strand break formation and prevents the DNA damage signalling and rearrangements seen in cancers and in neurodegenerative repeat disorders. RNA helicases such as DDX21 and DDX23 unwind the hybrid, coupling their action to transcription and ribosome biogenesis; the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex senses and processes breaks that arise when hybrids are encountered by replication forks, while PRIMPOL repriming allows synthesis to restart past a blocked fork. Chromatin and kinase components including SIRT7 and SRPK2 link hybrid resolution to histone modification and splicing-factor control, tying RNA processing to replication fidelity.

Lysosomes must be kept at an appropriate size and distribution for degradation, nutrient signalling and membrane repair to work, and regulation of lysosome size is the process that sets that dimension. Most of the components here form the BORC complex, a multisubunit assembly built from shared BLOC-1 subunits such as BLOC1S1, BLOC1S2, SNAPIN and KXD1 together with the dedicated BORCS subunits, which docks on the lysosomal membrane and recruits small GTPase and kinesin machinery to drive lysosomes outward along microtubules. Because positioning, fusion and fission are coupled, loss of these subunits leads to clustered perinuclear lysosomes with altered size and impaired autophagosome-lysosome turnover. A two-pore potassium channel contributes to the ionic and osmotic balance across the lysosomal membrane that influences organelle volume, linking ion flux to organelle morphology and to mTORC1-dependent nutrient responses.

cellular response to chemical stress is the broad set of programs a cell runs when its internal chemistry is perturbed — by oxidants, electrophiles, heavy metals, osmotic shifts or drugs — deciding whether the cell detoxifies and adapts or commits to death. It underlies tissue tolerance of inflammation and ischaemia, drug metabolism, and the neuronal vulnerability seen in Parkinson's disease, where PINK1, PRKN, PARK7 and LRRK2 act. Sensing is largely thiol-based: KEAP1 releases NFE2L2 to drive an antioxidant transcriptional program of NQO1, glutathione and thioredoxin enzymes, superoxide dismutases, peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases, while cystine import through SLC7A11 sustains it. In parallel, the integrated stress response through EIF2AK3, ATF4 and DDIT3, ER stress via ERN1 and XBP1, FOXO and TP53 outputs, mTOR and AMPK metabolic rebalancing, autophagy and mitophagy, osmotic WNK signalling, and inflammasome or RIPK-dependent death pathways set the outcome.

Cells constantly meet chemical insults — reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, electrophiles, heavy metals, osmotic and redox imbalance — and this programme is the coordinated response that lets them survive or die cleanly. It underlies ageing, neurodegeneration, ischaemia–reperfusion injury and the resistance of tumour cells to oxidative and drug-induced killing. Antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutases, catalase, glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins, thioredoxin and its reductase) detoxify oxidants, while KEAP1–NFE2L2 sensing of electrophiles drives transcription of NQO1, G6PD and the cystine importer SLC7A11 to rebuild glutathione and NADPH. Parallel arms include the endoplasmic reticulum stress branch through EIF2AK3, ERN1, ATF4 and DDIT3, FOXO and TP53-dependent transcription, mitophagy via PINK1 and PRKN, AMPK–mTOR metabolic adjustment, and osmotic signalling by WNK and STK39 kinases. Where damage exceeds repair, inflammasome activation, caspase-dependent apoptosis or RIPK3 necroptosis removes the cell.

Innate immune cells detect microbes and damaged self through pattern recognition receptors, and this collection covers the tuning of those detection pathways rather than detection itself. Setting the threshold matters in both directions: too little signalling leaves infection unchecked, too much drives septic shock, sterile inflammation and autoimmune interferonopathies. The receptors represented include Toll-like receptors at the surface and in endosomes, cytosolic DNA and RNA sensors such as cGAS, IFI16 and RIG-I-like helicases, and inflammasome-forming NLRs, with adaptors MYD88, TIRAP, MAVS and TASL relaying to NF-kB and IRF-driven transcription. Modulation runs through ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases, TNFAIP3 and TRIM proteins among them, palmitoylation by ZDHHC enzymes and its reversal, phosphatases, lysosomal transporters that deliver nucleic acid ligands, decoy pyrin-domain proteins, and a large set of microRNAs including MIR146A that damp the response after activation.

Innate immune cells detect microbes through pattern recognition receptors, and this pathway groups the factors that amplify those receptors' output, raising the strength of the inflammatory and interferon response to a given amount of microbial ligand. Enhancement acts at every layer: co-receptors and lipid-binding proteins such as CD14, LBP and CD36 load ligands onto Toll-like receptors including TLR4 and TLR9; MYD88 with the adaptors TIRAP and TICAM2 and the kinase MAP3K7 with TAB1 drive downstream signalling to MAPK8 and NF-kB; MAVS and the helicase DHX58 relay cytosolic nucleic acid sensing; SLC15A4 with TASL and the palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC3 and ZDHHC5 position sensors in the right endolysosomal membrane; NEK7 licenses inflammasome assembly. Tuning this amplification upward improves pathogen clearance but, unchecked, underlies septic shock, sterile inflammation driven by HMGB1, and autoimmune interferon signatures.

Synaptic strength depends on how many receptors and scaffolds are held on the receiving side of the synapse, and protein localization to the postsynapse is the trafficking and anchoring machinery that puts them there and keeps them there. It sets the composition of the postsynaptic density, underlies long-term potentiation and depression, and when it fails produces intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism-spectrum phenotypes. Membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffolds such as DLG4 (PSD-95) and DLG1 tether glutamate receptor subunits including GRIN2A, while GRIP1/GRIP2 and the transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory proteins encoded by CACNG2 and related genes escort AMPA receptors to the surface. Recycling endosome GTPases RAB11A and RAB8A and the retromer components VPS35 and VPS26B govern delivery and retrieval, palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC2/ZDHHC15 anchor cargo to membrane, and GPHN and RAPSN perform the equivalent clustering job at inhibitory and cholinergic synapses. Secreted cues such as C1QL2/C1QL3, LGI1 and glypicans align this apparatus with the presynaptic terminal.

Proteins destined for organelle interiors must cross a lipid bilayer after they are made, and this transmembrane import machinery is what moves them. Two routes dominate here: translocation into the endoplasmic reticulum through the Sec61 channel, aided by the signal recognition particle, the Sec62/Sec63 and TRAM components, the translocon-associated subunits and the lumenal chaperone BiP, which drives secretory and membrane protein biogenesis; and peroxisomal matrix import, in which PEX5 and PEX7 recognise targeting signals on folded cargo and dock at the PEX13/PEX14 membrane complex, with RING ligases and the PEX1/PEX6 AAA-ATPase recycling the receptor. Loss of peroxin function causes Zellweger spectrum disorders with severe neurological and hepatic disease, while defects in ER translocation components underlie secretory deficiencies and polycystic kidney and liver disease. Both arms couple cargo recognition to channel gating and energy-dependent release.

Lipids are insoluble in plasma, so they travel packaged with dedicated proteins, and this pathway covers the assembly of those protein-lipid complexes. Its products are the lipoproteins that move cholesterol and triglyceride between gut, liver and peripheral tissues: apolipoprotein A-I and A-II accepting phospholipid and cholesterol effluxed by the ABCA1 transporter to nucleate nascent HDL, and apolipoprotein B being loaded with neutral lipid by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein to form chylomicrons and VLDL. Supporting enzymes esterify cholesterol and acylate lysophospholipid, and liver X receptor signalling tunes transporter expression. Loss of function here produces recognisable lipid disorders — Tangier disease, abetalipoproteinaemia, familial HDL deficiency — while apolipoprotein E variants shape both atherosclerosis and Alzheimer risk. Membrane remodelling and scaffolding proteins connect the process to vesicle budding and lipid droplet biology.

This is a broad regulatory category covering any process that raises or lowers the activity of a molecular function — enzyme catalysis, binding affinity, channel conductance, or transcription factor output. Rather than a single route, it gathers the cell's tuning machinery: kinase and phosphatase modules (AKT1, MTOR, MAP2K1, PTPN1, GSK3B) that set signalling thresholds; GTPase switches with their activating and exchange proteins (RAP1GAP, RALGAP and DOCK, FGD and RAPGEF families) that time cytoskeletal and vesicular events; cyclin–CDK inhibitors such as CDKN1A and CDKN1B that gate cell cycle progression; proteasome regulatory subunits and ubiquitin ligases that control protein turnover; calcium sensors and channel accessory subunits (CALM1, STIM1, ORAI1, CACNG and KCNE proteins) that shape excitability; and inflammasome and TLR adaptors that license innate immune responses. Because activity modulation underlies proliferation control, immunity and neuronal signalling, its failure appears across cancer, autoinflammatory and neurodegenerative disease.

Neurons are long-lived, non-dividing cells that must hold their differentiated structure and excitability steady for decades, and neuron cellular homeostasis is the set of processes that maintains that stable state. Much of the work here is ionic and degradative: calcium buffers such as calbindin and calretinin, plasma-membrane and sodium/calcium exchange pumps, and potassium and chloride channels keep intracellular calcium and membrane potential within tolerable limits, while a near-complete vacuolar ATPase, the lysosomal potassium channel TMEM175, parkin, and a chaperone that clears misfolded protein support acidification, autophagy and mitochondrial quality control. Neuromodulatory and inflammatory inputs — adenosine and cannabinoid receptors, purinergic signalling, fractalkine, interleukin-6 — tune this set point through glial crosstalk. Loss of these buffering and clearance capacities underlies the selective vulnerability of neurons in Parkinson's disease, motor neuron degeneration and excitotoxic injury, linking the pathway to neuronal survival and ageing.

When misfolded protein accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum beyond what the unfolded protein response can resolve, the cell switches from adaptation to self-destruction, and this is the route it takes. It sets the threshold for survival in secretory cells under folding load — pancreatic beta cells, plasma cells, neurons — and its chronic activation contributes to diabetes, neurodegeneration and disorders such as Wolfram syndrome, while its blockade lets damaged cells persist. The ER stress sensors PERK and IRE1 (EIF2AK3, ERN1) signal through ATF4 and the transcription factor CHOP (DDIT3), with TRIB3 and GADD34 shaping the output, and IRE1 recruits TRAF2 to activate ASK1-JNK signalling. Death is executed mitochondrially: BH3-only proteins including PUMA, NOXA and BIM overcome BCL2 and BCL2L1 to permit BAX/BAK pore formation, cytochrome c release and apoptosome assembly. Calcium transfer through ITPR1 and SERCA pumps couples ER stress to mitochondrial commitment.

Vacuolar-type ATPases pump protons into endosomes, lysosomes and secretory compartments and, in specialized cells, across the plasma membrane; before any of that can happen, the multi-subunit pump must be built and delivered. This assembly step matters because acidification drives lysosomal degradation, receptor recycling, autophagic clearance and urinary acid excretion by kidney intercalated cells. Dedicated endoplasmic reticulum chaperones assist folding and assembly of the membrane-embedded proton-conducting sector and its escort to downstream compartments, while accessory membrane proteins of the TMEM9/TM9SF family promote engagement of the cytosolic catalytic sector with the membrane rotor. Loss of individual assembly factors causes disease with an organelle-acidification signature: X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy from defective escort of the pump, and distal renal tubular acidosis when the intercalated-cell B1 subunit is mutated.

Proton-transporting two-sector ATPase complex assembly builds the rotary proton pumps that convert an electrochemical gradient into ATP, or ATP hydrolysis into acidification of a compartment. Two related machines depend on it: the mitochondrial F1Fo ATP synthase that produces most cellular ATP, and the vacuolar V-ATPase that acidifies lysosomes, endosomes and the kidney intercalated-cell membrane. Neither assembles spontaneously; dedicated chaperones such as ATPAF1/ATPAF2 mature the F1 catalytic head, TMEM70 and TMEM242 act on membrane subunits, OXA1L inserts them into the inner membrane, and an ER-resident group including VMA21 and VMA12 assembles the V-ATPase V0 sector before delivery. Loss of these factors produces mitochondrial encephalocardiomyopathy with lactic acidosis, X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy, or distal renal tubular acidosis, illustrating that pump biogenesis limits both oxidative phosphorylation and organelle acidification.

Rotary proton-pumping ATPases — the mitochondrial ATP synthase and the vacuolar-type ATPase — must be built from many subunits and embedded correctly in a membrane before they can couple proton movement to ATP synthesis or hydrolysis, and this pathway covers that assembly. It matters because the finished machines supply most cellular ATP and acidify lysosomes and other organelles; defective assembly causes mitochondrial encephalomyopathy and, for the V-ATPase, distal renal tubular acidosis and X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy. Dedicated chaperones such as ATPAF1 and ATPAF2 escort the F1 catalytic subunits, TMEM70 and FMC1 assist assembly and stability of the complex, and OXA1L inserts membrane subunits from the matrix side. Endoplasmic reticulum factors including VMA21 and VMA12 perform the equivalent role for V-ATPase V0 subunits, linking organelle acidification to autophagic turnover.

Acidification of lysosomes, endosomes and other vacuolar compartments depends on a multi-subunit proton pump that must be built correctly before it can work, and the assembly of the vacuolar proton-transporting V-type ATPase is that construction step. The pump couples ATP hydrolysis in its cytosolic V1 sector to proton translocation through the membrane-embedded V0 sector, setting the low pH needed for lysosomal hydrolase activity, receptor-mediated endocytic sorting, autophagic degradation and, in specialised cells, acid secretion by kidney intercalated cells and bone-resorbing osteoclasts. Dedicated endoplasmic reticulum chaperones oversee V0 subunit folding and rotor assembly; loss of the VMA21 assembly factor reduces pump output and causes X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagy, while mutations in the B1 subunit gene cause distal renal tubular acidosis. Assembly is therefore the point at which organelle acidification capacity is set.}

Cells switch off signalling from the plasma membrane by tagging receptors with ubiquitin and pulling them inside, and ubiquitin-dependent endocytosis is that route: an internalized cargo is sorted into endosomes and ultimately degraded in the lysosome rather than recycled back to the surface. This is how growth factor and cytokine receptor output is limited in time, and why loss of the machinery leaves receptors on the surface signalling persistently, a common feature of oncogenic transformation. CBL is the E3 ligase that marks activated receptor tyrosine kinases, LRSAM1 and the neuralized-family ligases add ubiquitin to other membrane substrates, and EPS15 is a ubiquitin-binding adaptor at clathrin-coated pits. TSG101 and VPS28, subunits of an ESCRT complex, recognize the ubiquitin mark on endosomes and drive cargo into intralumenal vesicles, committing it to destruction.

Glucagon from pancreatic alpha cells raises blood glucose by driving hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so control over how much is released, and when, sets the counter-regulatory arm of glucose homeostasis. This regulation matters clinically at both extremes: blunted glucagon release leaves diabetic patients without defence against hypoglycaemia, while inappropriate secretion contributes to fasting hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes. The genes here act at several levels. Nutrient and hormonal signals reach the islet through a free fatty acid receptor sensing long-chain lipids, adipose-derived leptin, and the cytokine interleukin-6; hypothalamic and neuropeptide inputs, including corticotropin-releasing hormone and the CART peptide, link stress and feeding state to islet output. Within the alpha cell, a calcium-sensing synaptotagmin couples stimulation to granule fusion, and a metabolic kinase contributes to nutrient sensing, placing this pathway at the junction of neuroendocrine signalling and regulated exocytosis.

Chemokine signalling tells leukocytes where to go, and the tuning of that signalling sets how strongly and how long a cell responds to a gradient. Modulating chemokine-mediated pathways determines the size of an inflammatory infiltrate, the speed of wound repair and the extent of tissue damage when recruitment runs unchecked. The genes here act at several levels: a chemokine ligand itself, CCL5, feeds the pathway forward; SLIT2 and SLIT3 acting through ROBO1 dampen chemotactic responsiveness and hold migrating cells in check; HIF1A links hypoxic tissue to receptor and ligand output; TREM2 and SH2B3 adjust signalling downstream in myeloid and haematopoietic cells; microRNAs and PADI2-mediated citrullination of chemokines alter ligand availability and potency. Together they explain why identical chemokine levels produce different amounts of leukocyte trafficking in different tissues and inflammatory states.

Chemokines guide leukocyte migration and positioning, and damping that signalling sets when a cell stops responding to a gradient — a brake that limits inflammatory infiltration and keeps migrating cells from overshooting their targets. Negative regulation of chemokine-mediated signalling operates at several levels: secreted SLIT ligands acting through the ROBO1 receptor blunt chemokine-driven chemotaxis in leukocytes, neurons and tumour cells; the adaptor SH2B3 restrains downstream kinase signalling; post-transcriptional control by small regulatory RNAs lowers the output of chemokine and receptor transcripts. Post-translational modification, including citrullination by the deiminase PADI2, can alter chemokine ligands so that receptor engagement is weakened. Loss of this restraint favours persistent inflammatory cell recruitment, while the SLIT–ROBO arm also links the same biology to axon guidance and vascular patterning, where repulsive cues counterbalance attractive ones.

Interleukin-6 is the cytokine that drives the acute phase response, fever, and the shift of B cells toward antibody secretion, and it sustains the chronic inflammation behind rheumatoid arthritis, Castleman disease and cytokine release syndromes. Signalling begins when IL6 engages its specific receptor IL6R and recruits the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), whether as membrane-bound classic signalling or trans-signalling on cells lacking IL6R. Receptor-associated JAK1 and JAK2 phosphorylate gp130 tails, recruiting STAT3, which dimerises and enters the nucleus to drive transcription of acute phase and survival genes; SRC and FER add further tyrosine kinase input. The output is tuned rather than switched: SOCS3 imposes negative feedback at gp130, the phosphatase PTPN2 dephosphorylates JAK/STAT components, and several let-7 and miR-125 family microRNAs, along with miR-146a, restrain the circuit. Transcription factors such as CEBPA, SPI1 and GFI1 link this input to myeloid differentiation.

Interleukin-6 drives acute-phase responses, fever, hepatocyte protein production and the differentiation of Th17 and antibody-secreting cells, and its signalling must be damped as sharply as it is switched on; chronic excess underlies rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and inflammation-associated cancers, which is why IL-6 receptor blockade is clinically useful. Setting the rate and duration of this pathway operates at several levels. The shared receptor subunit IL6ST (gp130) determines whether IL-6 signals classically or through soluble receptor trans-signalling, and the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN2 removes activating phosphates from JAK-STAT components to terminate output. A large contingent of microRNAs, including the let-7 and miR-125 families and miR-146a, tunes transcript levels of pathway components and of the upstream innate signalling that induces IL-6, while transcriptional repression and death-domain kinase signalling provide further input. The net effect is calibration of inflammatory amplitude and resolution.

Interleukin-6 drives acute-phase responses, fever, and the differentiation of Th17 and antibody-secreting cells, so the signal must be damped once it has done its work; unchecked IL-6 signalling sustains chronic inflammation and contributes to rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm, and inflammation-associated cancer. This braking arm acts at several levels of the receptor-to-JAK-STAT3 axis. A tyrosine phosphatase, PTPN2, dephosphorylates JAK kinases and STAT3 to shorten signalling bouts, while the shared signal-transducing subunit gp130 is itself subject to regulation that limits how much receptor engagement is converted into transcription. A large share of the control is post-transcriptional: let-7 family members and miR-125, miR-26, miR-98, miR-99 and miR-146 microRNAs repress transcripts encoding IL-6 itself and pathway components, tuning the magnitude and duration of the response. The result is a negative feedback layer that resolves inflammation rather than blocking it outright.

Interleukin-27 is a heterodimeric cytokine of the IL-6/IL-12 family, made by activated antigen-presenting cells, that shapes how strongly and in which direction a T cell response develops. Signalling through it restrains Th17 and Th2 differentiation, promotes IL-10-producing regulatory T cells, and so limits immunopathology during infection and autoimmunity, while also giving cells an antiviral state. The cytokine pairs a p28 subunit with EBI3 and engages a receptor composed of IL27RA together with the shared gp130 chain encoded by IL6ST, activating JAK-associated phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT3. STAT1-driven transcription accounts for the interferon-like output seen here: induction of MX1 and the oligoadenylate synthetase genes OAS1, OAS2, OAS3 and OASL, which sense double-stranded RNA and trigger RNA degradation. Loss or excess of this axis tips the balance between effective pathogen control and inflammatory tissue damage.

Ciliary neurotrophic factor signalling keeps motor neurons and glia alive and supports their response to injury, and loss of the receptor is lethal at birth with motor neuron deficits, while ligand deficiency in humans is tolerated but modifies neuromuscular disease. CNTF binds a GPI-anchored alpha receptor that itself has no signalling capacity; the complex then recruits gp130 and the LIF receptor beta chain to form a tripartite signalling receptor shared with the wider interleukin-6 cytokine family. Assembly juxtaposes receptor-associated JAK kinases, which phosphorylate the cytoplasmic tails and recruit STAT3, driving transcription of survival and gliogenic programmes alongside MAPK and PI3K output. The soluble IL-6 receptor can substitute in trans-signalling on cells lacking the alpha chain. Beyond neurons, this axis influences energy balance and hypothalamic control of feeding, and regulates astrocyte differentiation and muscle trophic responses.

Mitochondria run their own protein synthesis machinery to make the thirteen hydrophobic subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, and elongation is the step where those nascent chains are actually built residue by residue on mitoribosomes. The cycle depends on a small set of dedicated GTPases and their recycling factors: an elongation factor Tu that delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosomal A site, its nucleotide exchange partner EFTs, and translocases that advance the mitoribosome along the transcript after peptide bond formation. A large mitoribosomal subunit protein anchors the process to the ribosome itself. Because the respiratory chain is built from both nuclear- and mitochondrially-encoded subunits, a stall here starves complexes I, III, IV and ATP synthase of their core components. Mutations in these factors cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, typically presenting as infantile encephalopathy, cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis.

Mitochondria run their own translation system to make the thirteen hydrophobic subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, and mitochondrial translational termination is the step that releases each finished polypeptide from the mitoribosome when a stop codon enters the A site. Release factors recognise the termination codons of the mitochondrial genetic code, which differs from the cytosolic code, and hydrolyse the ester bond linking the nascent chain to tRNA; a ribosome recycling factor and the GTPase-dependent machinery that follows then separate the subunits so they can initiate again. Because supply of these subunits limits oxidative phosphorylation, loss of this step stalls ribosomes on their messages and causes combined respiratory chain deficiency — mutations in the recycling factor produce a severe encephalopathy with early-onset mitochondrial disease. The process couples mitochondrial gene expression to cellular energy production and to the quality control that clears obstructed mitoribosomes.

tRNA aminoacylation for mitochondrial protein translation charges mitochondrial tRNAs with their cognate amino acids so that the organelle's own ribosomes can synthesise the thirteen subunits of the respiratory chain encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Each enzyme joins an amino acid to the 3'-hydroxyl of the terminal adenosine of its tRNA in an ATP-dependent two-step reaction, with proofreading that keeps mistranslation low in a compartment already burdened by oxidative stress. Most of these synthetases are nuclear-encoded and imported, and several, such as GARS1, are shared with the cytosolic translation apparatus. Because oxidative phosphorylation depends entirely on this step, loss-of-function mutations produce a recognisable family of mitochondrial diseases — leukoencephalopathy with brainstem involvement, sideroblastic anaemia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ovarian failure and hearing loss — with tissue specificity that reflects each tissue's reliance on mitochondrial energy production.

Mitochondria translate their own thirteen respiratory chain subunits on a dedicated ribosome, and that translation can only begin once each mitochondrial tRNA has been charged with its matching amino acid. The enzymes here are the mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which attach alanine, aspartate, glutamate, glycine, serine, threonine, tryptophan or tyrosine to the 3' end of the corresponding tRNA inside the organelle, supplying the substrates for mitochondrial protein synthesis. Because most of these genes are nuclear-encoded and imported, the pathway is a point where nuclear and mitochondrial gene expression must stay matched. Loss-of-function mutations cause a recognizable group of recessive mitochondrial diseases with combined respiratory chain deficiency and strikingly tissue-specific presentations u2014 leukoencephalopathy, cardiomyopathy, sideroblastic anemia, ovarian failure, hearing loss u2014 placing this charging step upstream of oxidative phosphorylation capacity in every tissue that depends on it.

Regulation of mitochondrial translation controls how much protein the mitochondrion makes from its own genome, tuning the supply of the thirteen core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase to the rest of the organelle's assembly needs. Because those subunits must be produced in step with nuclear-encoded partners, defects here cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, with infantile lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy. The regulators act at several levels: mitochondrial tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes, including methyltransferases and pseudouridine synthases together with the RNase P subunit TRMT10C, determine decoding fidelity; ribosome assembly GTPases and an anti-association factor govern monosome and subunit maturation; LRPPRC stabilises and polyadenylates transcripts; and translational activators such as TACO1 select individual mRNAs. Others couple synthesis directly to complex assembly, delivering newly made subunits into cytochrome c oxidase and complex III. Folate one-carbon metabolism feeds in through formylmethionine and tRNA taurinomethylation.

Mitochondria translate their own handful of mRNAs, all encoding subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, and control over that translation sets how much respiratory chain a cell can build. The genes here modulate the rate and fidelity of mitoribosomal protein synthesis rather than performing peptide bond formation themselves: mitoribosome assembly GTPases and assembly factors such as MTG1, MTG2 and MALSU1 mature the large subunit, tRNA and rRNA modifying enzymes including TRMT10C, NSUN3, RPUSD3/4, TRUB2 and CDK5RAP1 tune decoding, LRPPRC stabilises and polyadenylates mitochondrial transcripts, and TACO1 acts as a translational activator for COX1. Others couple synthesis to co-translational insertion and complex assembly, as COA3 and UQCC2 do for cytochrome c oxidase and complex III. Loss of these regulators causes combined respiratory chain deficiency, lactic acidosis, encephalomyopathy and cardiomyopathy, and connects mitochondrial gene expression to cellular energy supply and one-carbon metabolism through SHMT2.

Positive regulation of mitochondrial translation describes the factors that raise the output of the mitochondrial ribosome, which synthesises the thirteen core subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Because those subunits must be made in stoichiometry with imported nuclear-encoded partners, boosting and coordinating this translation is what allows respiratory chain assembly to proceed, and loss of individual components causes infantile mitochondrial disease with combined complex deficiencies, lactic acidosis and encephalomyopathy. Mechanistically the group spans several layers: mitochondrial tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes such as TRMT10C, CDK5RAP1, METTL8 and the pseudouridine synthases, mitoribosome assembly factors including NGRN, MPV17L2 and RMND1, and mRNA-specific translational activators, notably TACO1, which is required for COX1 synthesis. Others, such as COA3 and UQCC2, couple nascent chain production directly to assembly of complexes IV and III, linking translation rate to respiratory demand.

Mitochondria translate their own handful of mRNAs into core subunits of the respiratory chain, and this pathway covers the factors that raise the rate and efficiency of that process. Because every one of the thirteen mitochondrially encoded proteins sits in complexes I, III, IV or the ATP synthase, boosting or sustaining mitoribosome output is directly tied to oxidative phosphorylation capacity, and loss of these activators produces combined respiratory chain deficiency, lactic acidosis and infantile encephalomyopathy. The genes act at several steps: tRNA and rRNA modification enzymes such as TRMT10C, CDK5RAP1 and the pseudouridine synthases RPUSD3, RPUSD4 and TRUB2 mature the RNA substrates, RNA-binding proteins including C1QBP, NGRN and FASTKD3 work within RNA granules and mitoribosome assembly, and translational activators such as TACO1 promote synthesis of specific messages, with COA3 and UQCC2 coupling output to assembly of complexes IV and III.

Long-wave ultraviolet light between 315 and 400 nm penetrates deep into skin and reaches the lens and retina, and the response to UV-A is the set of cellular reactions that follow that exposure. It matters because repeated UV-A dosing drives photoaging, dermal matrix breakdown and photocarcinogenesis, and contributes to lens damage. Much of the output here is proteolytic: several matrix metalloproteinases degrade collagen and other extracellular matrix components, held in check by the inhibitor TIMP1, so the balance between them sets how much irreversible dermal remodelling occurs. Upstream, EGFR and AKT1 signalling and cyclin D1 induction couple the irradiation to proliferation and survival decisions, while ceramide synthesis contributes a stress-lipid arm. The presence of opsins, including the non-visual OPN3 and OPN5 alongside a cone pigment and a lens crystallin, points to genuine photoreception as one route by which cells sense this waveband rather than only oxidative damage.

Recycling of synaptic vesicles at the presynaptic terminal depends on pinching new vesicles off a donor membrane, and this budding step sets how quickly a neuron can refill its releasable pool and sustain transmission during repeated firing. Two activities dominate the gene list: an adaptor complex of the AP-3 type, including the neuron-enriched AP3B2 subunit together with AP3D1 and small sigma and mu chains, which selects cargo and deforms the membrane into a coated bud; and the dynamin GTPases DNM1, DNM2 and DNM3, which oligomerise around the bud neck and sever it. Related large GTPases of the MX family share that mechanochemical fission chemistry. Loss of AP-3 or of the neuronal dynamin causes vesicle depletion, pigment and lysosome-related organelle defects, and epileptic encephalopathy, placing this step within the broader logic of clathrin- and adaptor-dependent vesicle traffic.

Adiponectin is an adipocyte-derived hormone that sensitises liver and muscle to insulin and restrains vascular inflammation, so control over how much of it is released sets systemic metabolic tone; low circulating levels accompany obesity, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. The genes here act at two levels. Transcriptional and signalling inputs tune adipocyte output, with PPARG driving the mature adipocyte programme that supports adiponectin expression, a nicotinic acid-responsive receptor coupling lipolytic signalling to secretion, and the inflammatory cytokine IL1B suppressing it as adipose tissue becomes inflamed. The remainder are Rab11 family interacting proteins, which direct recycling-endosome traffic and the delivery of secretory vesicles to the plasma membrane, placing the final release step under vesicle-tethering control.
