Modulating this secretory arm therefore alters whole-body glucose and lipid handling rather than adipocyte behaviour alone.

Enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and its mineralization is the stage at which ameloblasts convert a soft protein matrix into densely packed carbonated hydroxyapatite crystallites. Ameloblasts first secrete a scaffold of amelogenin, enamelin and amelotin that guides crystal orientation, then degrade it with the matrix metalloproteinase MMP20 as mineral replaces protein. Because apatite deposition releases protons, ions must be moved with precision: bicarbonate and chloride transport, calcium entry through store-operated channels and a potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchanger all shape the mineralizing front, while FAM20A and FAM20C control secretory-pathway phosphorylation of matrix proteins. Transcription factors and adhesion molecules maintain the ameloblast layer itself. Loss of these functions produces amelogenesis imperfecta, with hypoplastic or hypomineralized enamel prone to attrition and caries, sometimes as part of syndromes affecting other mineralized tissues.

Bone, teeth and cartilage acquire their hardness through controlled deposition of calcium phosphate mineral, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast and how far that mineralization proceeds. Its balance determines skeletal strength and enamel integrity, and its failure produces rickets and osteomalacia, osteopetrosis or osteoporosis, ectopic calcification of vessels and soft tissue, and enamel and dentin defects. BMP and TGF-beta ligands acting through their type I and II receptors and SMAD3, together with Wnt ligands, Notch effectors and transcription factors such as ATF4, SOX9 and TWIST1, drive osteoblast and chondrocyte differentiation. Superimposed on this is mineral chemistry: PTH, FGF23 with its coreceptor klotho, and vitamin D activation via CYP27B1 and the vitamin D receptor set systemic phosphate and calcium, while pyrophosphate handling by ENPP1 and ANKH, matrix Gla protein and osteopontin-like phosphoproteins, and enamel matrix proteins including amelogenin and enamelin act locally as promoters or inhibitors of crystal growth.

Hard tissues must form only where they belong, and negative regulation of biomineral tissue development is the set of brakes that keeps mineral out of soft tissue and limits how much is laid down in bone and tooth. Its failure shows up as vascular and valve calcification, ectopic ossification, and mineralization disorders. Circulating and matrix inhibitors act directly on crystal growth: fetuin-A binds calcium phosphate in serum, ENPP1 generates pyrophosphate that blocks hydroxyapatite nucleation, salivary statherin restrains mineral deposition on enamel, and matrix proteins such as asporin and ECM1 sequester or oppose pro-mineralizing signals. Hormonal control sets the ionic supply, with FGF23 and parathyroid hormone lowering phosphate availability and remodelling calcium handling. Transcriptional and signalling inputs, including Notch effectors HEY1 and HEY2, SOX9, HIF1A, TGFB1 and the BMP antagonist gremlin, hold osteoblast differentiation in check, linking this restraint to skeletal patterning and cartilage maintenance.</description>

Hard tissues such as bone, dentine and enamel form by depositing mineral onto an organic matrix, and this pathway covers the signals and effectors that drive that process forward. Its output is skeletal mass, tooth structure and fracture repair; too little gives rickets-like undermineralization, brittle bone or defective enamel, while inappropriate activation produces heterotopic ossification and vascular calcification. Bone morphogenetic proteins acting through type I and type II receptors and SMAD3 provide the dominant osteoinductive input, with Wnt ligands, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D acting via its nuclear receptor, and the transcription factors ATF4, MEF2C and CEBPB reinforcing osteoblast differentiation and matrix gene expression. Mineral supply depends on phosphate and calcium transport, and matrix proteins such as amelogenin, enamelin and amelotin, phosphorylated by the kinase FAM20C, template crystal growth. Klotho and phosphatonin signalling tie local mineralization to systemic phosphate balance.

regulation of tooth mineralization controls how much calcium phosphate is deposited into enamel and dentin, and how well ordered the resulting crystal is. It is what gives teeth their hardness and wear resistance; when it fails the result is amelogenesis imperfecta, hypomineralized or hypoplastic enamel, and dentin defects seen in hereditary rickets and syndromic craniofacial disease. Ameloblasts secrete a provisional matrix of amelogenin, enamelin and amelotin that templates crystal growth, and proteinases such as MMP20 then degrade that matrix so mineral can expand to fill the space. Ion handling supports the same end: anion exchange and CFTR-dependent transport buffer the protons released as apatite forms, while DMP1 nucleates mineral in dentin. Transcriptional and signalling inputs including TFAP2A, BCOR and WNT6 set ameloblast and odontoblast identity upstream of secretion, tying this process to tooth morphogenesis and biomineralization generally.

Enamel and dentine become the hardest tissues in the body only if calcium phosphate deposition is timed and shaped by the matrix laid down before it, and this regulatory control over tooth mineralization sets how much mineral forms and where. When it fails the result is amelogenesis imperfecta, hypomineralized or hypoplastic enamel, and teeth that chip and decay. Secreted matrix proteins including amelogenin, enamelin, amelotin and the dentine phosphoprotein DMP1 template crystal growth, while the protease MMP20 degrades that matrix so crystals can expand and mature. Ion handling matters as much as protein: the anion exchanger SLC4A2 and the chloride channel CFTR support the pH buffering that ameloblasts need to neutralize protons released during mineral deposition. Transcriptional and signalling inputs such as TFAP2A, BCOR and WNT6 position and differentiate the enamel- and dentine-forming cells themselves.

Enamel and dentine become hard because ameloblasts and odontoblasts secrete a protein matrix and then drive calcium phosphate deposition into it, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote that mineral gain during tooth mineralization. It matters because failure yields hypoplastic or hypomineralized enamel: mutations in amelogenin, enamelin, amelotin and the odontogenesis-associated ODAPH cause inherited amelogenesis imperfecta, with soft, thin, discoloured enamel prone to wear and caries. The secreted matrix proteins template and nucleate crystal growth at the mineralizing front, while the anion transporters CFTR and SLC4A2 move chloride and bicarbonate to buffer the protons released as hydroxyapatite forms, keeping the local pH permissive for continued deposition. Transcriptional and signalling regulators such as TFAP2A and WNT6 act earlier, specifying and maintaining the secretory dental epithelium on which the whole process depends, linking tooth mineralization to craniofacial development.

Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and its formation depends on ameloblasts secreting a protein matrix, then removing it as hydroxyapatite crystals grow to full thickness and hardness. This regulatory programme tunes how fast and how completely calcium phosphate is deposited during that maturation. Enamelin and amelotin are matrix and basal-lamina proteins that guide crystal nucleation and the attachment of maturation-stage ameloblasts, while MMP20 proteolytically processes the enamel matrix so that crystallites can expand. Mineral deposition consumes protons, so pH must be buffered: the anion exchanger SLC4A2 and the chloride channel CFTR support bicarbonate movement into the enamel space, and DMP1 contributes to mineralized matrix regulation more broadly. Loss of these functions produces amelogenesis imperfecta, with hypoplastic or hypomineralized enamel prone to wear, sensitivity and caries.

Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and it reaches that state only when ameloblasts drive the ordered deposition of calcium phosphate into a protein scaffold; this pathway covers the processes that promote enamel mineralization. Enamelin and the amelotin and ODAPH proteins of the ameloblast secretory and maturation stages organize crystal growth and the attachment of cells to the mineralizing front, while ion transport across the ameloblast membrane keeps the extracellular environment permissive: the anion channel CFTR and the anion exchanger SLC4A2 handle chloride and bicarbonate movement that buffers the protons released as hydroxyapatite forms. Loss of these functions produces hypoplastic or hypomineralized amelogenesis imperfecta, with soft, discolored, chip-prone enamel, and explains the enamel defects seen in cystic fibrosis. The biology links epithelial ion homeostasis and pH control to biomineralization.

Most dietary tryptophan is not used for protein or serotonin but is degraded along the kynurenine route, and these enzymes carry out that conversion. The pathway supplies the cell with NAD precursors via quinolinic acid, generates neuroactive intermediates, and is a major brake on immune responses: interferon-induced IDO1 depletion of local tryptophan and accumulation of kynurenine suppress effector T cells and favour regulatory ones, a mechanism tumours exploit to evade immunity. TDO2 handles the same first oxidation in liver under substrate and hormonal control. Downstream, formamidase opens the ring product, a monooxygenase and hydrolase generate 3-hydroxykynurenine and 3-hydroxyanthranilate, and transaminases divert kynurenine to kynurenic acid, an antagonist at glutamate receptors. Imbalance between the neurotoxic and neuroprotective branches is implicated in neurodegeneration, depression and schizophrenia, linking amino acid catabolism to immune tolerance and brain function.

Meiosis demands a chromosome architecture found nowhere else, and this programme builds it: sister chromatids are held by a meiosis-specific cohesin (REC8, STAG3), axial elements form, and homologues are zipped together by the synaptonemal complex of SYCP1-3 and the SYCE/TEX12 central element. Its purpose is to produce haploid gametes with correctly recombined, correctly segregated chromosomes; failure causes infertility, azoospermia, oocyte loss and aneuploid eggs. Programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11 at PRDM9-marked hotspots are resected and loaded with RAD51 and DMC1 for homologue-directed strand invasion, while MSH4/MSH5, RNF212 and MLH1/MLH3 designate and resolve the subset of intermediates that become crossovers. Telomeres attach to the nuclear envelope through TERB1/TERB2 with SUN1 and KASH5 to drive chromosome movement and pairing, and condensins plus checkpoint kinase ATM enforce structure and quality control.

During meiotic prophase I, homologous chromosomes are zipped together along their lengths by a proteinaceous ladder, and the assembly, arrangement and later disassembly of this synaptonemal complex is what makes accurate homolog pairing and crossover formation possible. Without it, chromosomes fail to synapse, recombination intermediates go unresolved, and gametes are lost to apoptotic checkpoints or carry aneuploidy — a route to infertility and pregnancy loss in both sexes. Transverse filament and central element proteins such as SYCP1, SYCE1-3 and TEX12 polymerise between the lateral elements built on meiosis-specific cohesin subunits including REC8 and STAG3, while HORMA-domain proteins and the AAA+ ATPase TRIP13 monitor synapsis and couple it to double-strand breaks initiated by SPO11. Crossover maturation and telomere attachment to the nuclear envelope are coordinated with the same scaffold, linking chromosome structure to recombination control.

Meiotic attachment of telomere to nuclear envelope tethers chromosome ends to the inner nuclear membrane during meiotic prophase so that homologous chromosomes can find each other and pair. Without it, telomeres fail to cluster into the transient bouquet, homolog synapsis and recombination are incomplete, and gametogenesis arrests — a route to infertility in both sexes. The mechanism is a dedicated cap built on the shelterin-bound telomere: TERB1 and TERB2 recruit MAJIN, which inserts into the inner nuclear membrane, and the complex couples through SUN1 to KASH partners and cytoskeletal motors that drag telomeres across the envelope to drive chromosome movement. SPDYA-CDK2 activity licenses and regulates this attachment. The pathway thus links nuclear envelope architecture, telomere biology and the chromosome dynamics that make meiotic recombination possible.

During meiotic prophase, chromosome ends must be tethered to the inner nuclear membrane so that cytoskeletal forces can move chromosomes and bring homologues into register for pairing and recombination. This telomere-to-nuclear-envelope attachment gathers telomeres into the bouquet configuration; without it, homologue pairing and synapsis fail, crossovers are not formed, and germ cells arrest, producing infertility in both sexes. A dedicated telomere adaptor complex built from TERB1, TERB2 and MAJIN caps the chromosome end, replacing shelterin contacts and anchoring the DNA directly in the membrane, where it couples to SUN1 and thence across the nuclear envelope to cytoplasmic dynein and the microtubule network. Cyclin-dependent kinase activity, acting with the meiotic activator SPDYA, times and licenses these attachments, linking envelope tethering to progression through the meiotic cell cycle.

Chromosome ends must be coated with the right proteins or they look like broken DNA. Recruiting and retaining proteins at the telomeric region is what keeps chromosome termini capped, controls whether telomerase gains access, and determines telomere length homeostasis; loss of this control produces end-to-end fusions, senescence, or the unchecked elongation seen in cancer. Shelterin subunits such as TERF2, its partner TERF2IP, TINF2 and ACD/TPP1 form the platform, with poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases TNKS and TNKS2 modifying that platform to release binding and PINX1 acting as a telomerase inhibitor. The chromatin remodeller ATRX and the histone variant macroH2A shape the underlying nucleosomes, PML bodies provide a site for recombination-based lengthening, ATR signals replication stress at these fragile sequences, and Ku contributes to end protection. The pathway sits at the intersection of genome stability, replicative ageing and tumour suppression.

Chromosomes are not passively decorated; specific proteins must be delivered to defined chromosomal addresses, and establishment of protein localization to chromosome covers that targeted recruitment. It matters because telomere protection, origin licensing, cohesin loading and repair-factor assembly all depend on the right factor arriving at the right locus. A large part of the activity here is telomeric: shelterin components such as TRF1, POT1 and TPP1 are brought to chromosome ends, while WRAP53 traffics telomerase to them, so loss of this delivery step produces telomere attrition and the marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis of telomere biology disorders. Other members recruit repair and recombination machinery to damaged or single-stranded DNA, load the cohesin complex via NIPBL, deposit histone variants including macroH2A into repressive chromatin, and mark replication origins. Chaperone and deubiquitinase activities stabilise the escorted cargo, linking this biology to genome maintenance and chromatin organisation.

Establishment of protein localization to telomere is the targeted delivery and loading of protective and enzymatic factors onto chromosome ends, the step that decides whether a telomere is capped or read as a broken chromosome. It sustains replicative capacity in stem and germ cells and, when hijacked, sustains cancer cell immortality; when it fails, telomeres shorten or fuse and cells enter senescence or crisis, as in telomere biology disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita. Shelterin components including TRF1, POT1 and TPP1 must be recruited to single- and double-stranded telomeric DNA, and telomerase itself must be trafficked there — TCAB1 directs the RNA component through Cajal bodies, while chaperonin subunits assist folding and USP7 controls the stability of loaded factors. Related activities bring homologous recombination and single-strand binding proteins to ends during replication and alternative telomere lengthening.

Telomeres are only protected if the right proteins are delivered to them, and establishment of protein localization to telomere covers the targeting and loading steps that put capping and elongation factors onto chromosome ends. Without it, chromosome termini are read as double-strand breaks, triggering fusions, senescence or crisis, while insufficient telomerase recruitment shortens telomeres and causes bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis syndromes. The shelterin components TERF1, POT1 and its partner ACD bind duplex and single-stranded telomeric DNA, and ACD also delivers the TERT catalytic subunit to the 3' overhang; WRAP53 traffics telomerase from nuclear bodies to chromosome ends, and USP7 acts through deubiquitination to stabilise telomere-associated factors. Chaperonin subunits assist folding of clients en route, and BRCA2 and single-stranded DNA-binding activity link the process to recombination-based telomere maintenance and replication of these fragile regions.

Proteins only work where they are put, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how fast and how far proteins are moved to their destinations "" secretory export, membrane insertion, nuclear import and export, vesicle delivery to the cell surface, and mitochondrial or degradative targeting. Regulation here determines whether a hormone is released on cue, whether a transporter or channel reaches the plasma membrane, and whether a misfolded protein is retained and cleared instead of trafficked. Components include COPII coat and cargo-selection machinery for ER exit, Rab GTPases and their effectors for recycling and exocytosis, karyopherins and nucleoporin-associated factors for nucleocytoplasmic shuttling, SNAREs and synaptotagmins for regulated fusion, and ER-associated degradation and ubiquitin enzymes that divert cargo. Kinases, phosphatases, chaperones and transcriptional regulators tune these steps, linking the pathway to insulin granule secretion, glucose and lipid handling, neuronal signalling and immune mediator release.

Getting a protein to the right place on a chromosome is regulated, not incidental, and this pathway covers the control of that targeting "— most clearly the delivery of telomerase and its partners to chromosome ends. Telomere-binding proteins such as TERF1 and the shelterin subunit ACD (TPP1) set how much telomerase is recruited and how far it extends the repeat tract, while WRAP53 (TCAB1) directs the telomerase RNP through nuclear bodies to telomeres; loss of that trafficking step underlies short-telomere disease. Chaperonin subunits TCP1 and CCT6A supply the folding capacity that such assemblies depend on, USP7 acts as a deubiquitinase controlling the stability of chromatin-associated factors, and SPIDR scaffolds recombination proteins at damaged DNA. Together the set links telomere length homeostasis and DNA repair factor loading to proliferative lifespan and genome stability.

Trimerization is the assembly step by which three subunits, identical or not, associate noncovalently into a functional unit, and for many proteins it is the state in which they actually work. The genes here span unrelated functions but share that quaternary requirement: purinergic P2X receptors gate cation currents only as trimers, glutamate and neutral amino acid transporters of the SLC1 family operate as trimeric carriers at synapses and in nutrient uptake, and collagen chains wind into triple helices that give extracellular matrix its tensile strength. MIF, CD74, HLA-G and the arachidonate-activating protein ALOX5AP contribute to immune and inflammatory signalling in oligomeric form, while MLKL acts in the pore-forming execution step of necroptosis. Because subunit stoichiometry determines conductance, ligand selectivity and stability, defective oligomerization converts otherwise intact proteins into nonfunctional ones, a route to matrix disease, excitotoxicity and misregulated cell death.</description>

Many proteins only work once three identical subunits come together, and homotrimerization describes that self-assembly step. The trimer is the functional unit for each of these products, so the assembly is inseparable from the activity: ATP-gated P2X receptor channels open as trimers of P2RX3 or P2RX7 subunits, the glutamate transporter SLC1A2 and the neutral amino acid transporter SLC1A5 carry substrate as trimeric bowl-shaped carriers, and the cytokine MIF and the leukotriene-synthesis accessory protein ALOX5AP likewise present three-fold symmetric surfaces. MLKL oligomerization at the plasma membrane executes necroptotic lysis. Because subunit composition sets ligand sensitivity, conductance and turnover, trimer formation is a point of regulation for purinergic signalling, synaptic glutamate clearance, inflammatory mediator release and programmed necrosis, and mutations that block assembly typically leave a stable but inert monomer.

Attaching chains of ADP-ribose to proteins, using NAD as the donor, creates a bulky negatively charged mark that recruits repair and signalling factors within seconds of a stimulus. Protein poly-ADP-ribosylation is best known at DNA breaks, where PARP1 and PARP2 sense damaged DNA, modify themselves and histones, and assemble the single-strand break and base excision repair machinery; this dependence is what makes PARP inhibitors lethal to tumours lacking homologous recombination. Other members act elsewhere: the tankyrases TNKS and TNKS2 modify axin to release beta-catenin for Wnt signalling and regulate telomere-binding proteins, while PARP9, PARP14 and ZC3HAV1 operate in interferon-driven antiviral and macrophage responses. Because each chain consumes NAD, excessive activation can deplete cellular NAD pools and drive a distinct form of cell death. Chains are reversible, and their turnover sets the duration of the resulting signal.

protein auto-ADP-ribosylation is the self-modification step by which ADP-ribosyltransferases attach ADP-ribose units from NAD+ onto their own residues, a reaction that both switches the enzyme's activity on or off and creates a docking platform for reader proteins. It matters because it sets the amplitude and duration of ADP-ribose signalling in DNA damage response, Wnt signalling and stress adaptation. PARP1 and PARP2 automodify heavily on detecting DNA strand breaks, and the resulting poly(ADP-ribose) chains recruit repair factors and then trigger the enzymes' own release from chromatin; unchecked automodification drains cellular NAD+ and drives cell death. The tankyrases automodify to promote their turnover and control axin stability, while mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases such as PARP10, PARP12, TIPARP and the membrane-anchored PARP16 use automodification in interferon-linked antiviral responses, translational stress control and unfolded protein signalling. This self-marking underlies the sensitivity of these enzymes to clinical PARP inhibitors.

Several ADP-ribosyltransferases modify themselves, transferring ADP-ribose from NAD+ onto their own residues or onto an identical subunit, and this auto-modification is how the family sets its own activity and recruits partners. The clearest case is PARP1, which on binding damaged DNA builds poly(ADP-ribose) chains largely on itself; the resulting negatively charged polymer recruits repair factors, relaxes chromatin, and then drives the enzyme off DNA, so that failure to auto-modify traps PARP1 on the lesion. PARP2 and PARP3 act similarly at breaks, while the tankyrases automodify in the course of controlling telomere protection and Wnt signalling through axin turnover. Mono-ADP-ribosylating members, including TIPARP and the PARP7-related and membrane-associated enzymes, use the same self-modification in interferon-linked and aryl hydrocarbon receptor responses. Because the reaction consumes NAD+, its scale couples DNA damage signalling to cellular energy state and underlies the sensitivity of repair-deficient tumours to PARP inhibitors.

Programmed death of lymphocytes is how the immune system sets the size of its T and B cell pools, removes self-reactive clones during development, and shuts down a response once antigen is cleared. Failure at either extreme is pathological: too little leaves autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy, too much produces immunodeficiency and lymphopenia. Both routes to death appear here. Extrinsic signalling runs through FAS and FASLG to FADD and RIPK1, engaging caspase activation and DNA fragmentation, while intrinsic control rests on the BCL2 family balance in which BAX, BAK1, BBC3 and BCL2L11 commit mitochondria to permeabilisation under TP53 control. Survival inputs oppose them, notably IL7R and IL2/IL2RA with JAK3 and AKT1 signalling, so that cytokine withdrawal itself becomes a death signal. Thymocyte selection, negative regulation by galectins, and glucocorticoid-induced death of T cells are all part of the same control problem.

Lymphocyte numbers are set as much by controlled death as by division, and this pathway covers the signals that raise or lower the rate at which T and B cells die by apoptosis. It governs thymic and bone marrow selection, the contraction of clonal expansions after an infection is cleared, and the deletion of autoreactive cells; too little killing permits autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy, too much produces immunodeficiency and lymphopenia. Pro-apoptotic effectors such as BAX, PUMA and FADD act with TP53, while survival inputs from the IL-7 receptor, IL-2, JAK3 and antigen-receptor kinases including BTK and LYN oppose them. Transcriptional regulators such as BCL6, MYC, FOXP1 and RORC, the glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3, and immunoregulatory signals including PD-L1, IDO1, IL-10, TGFB2 and galectins tune the threshold, linking lymphocyte lifespan to tolerance and to the resolution of immune responses.

Lymphocytes are produced in excess and most die by apoptosis unless actively rescued, so negative regulation of lymphocyte apoptotic process is what determines which cells survive selection in the thymus and bone marrow and which persist as memory after an immune response. Survival signals come from cytokine receptors and their kinases, notably IL-7 receptor signalling through JAK3, from costimulatory receptors such as CD27, and from antigen receptor-proximal machinery including PRKCQ and the BCL10 adaptor feeding NF-kB activation; transcriptional regulators such as BCL6, FOXP1 and RORC set the survival programme in developing and effector subsets. Metabolic and stress inputs, including HIF1A and amino acid-catabolising enzymes like ARG2 and IDO1, tune the threshold. Loss of these inputs produces lymphopenia and immunodeficiency, as in adenosine deaminase deficiency or DOCK8 and JAK3 defects, while excessive survival signalling favours autoimmunity and lymphoma.

Clonal deletion keeps the lymphocyte compartment in check, and the processes that raise the rate of lymphocyte apoptosis are how autoreactive clones are removed during development, how expanded effector populations contract after an infection is cleared, and how tissues enforce immune privilege. Two broad routes converge here: an intrinsic, mitochondrial arm in which p53 induces the BH3-only protein PUMA and the pore-forming effector BAX to commit thymocytes and activated T cells to death after DNA damage or growth-factor withdrawal; and extrinsic cues delivered by other cells, including PD-L1 engagement of exhausted T cells, galectin-9 binding to TIM-3, tryptophan depletion by IDO1, TGF-beta and IL-10, and ATP-driven P2RX7 signalling. MYC-driven activation sensitises lymphocytes to the same machinery. Too little of this deletion permits autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy; too much, driven by tumours exploiting these ligands, leaves T cell responses blunted.

Programmed death of T lymphocytes is how the immune system deletes cells with useless or self-reactive receptors during thymic development and how it shuts down an expanded effector population after an infection clears. Without it, autoreactive clones persist and lymphoproliferative and autoimmune disease follows; excessive death instead produces immunodeficiency and lymphopenia. Both major routes are represented: death receptor signalling through Fas and its ligand, recruiting FADD and RIPK1, and the mitochondrial arm in which BAX and BAK1 are engaged by BH3-only proteins such as BIM and PUMA under TP53 control. Withdrawal of survival input via IL7R and JAK3 sensitises cells, while glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3, galectins, IDO1-driven tryptophan depletion and PD-L1 impose death or anergy from the environment. The same machinery underlies negative selection in the thymus and peripheral tolerance to tumours.

Whether a T cell lives or dies by apoptosis is decided repeatedly: during thymic selection, at the peak of an immune response, and whenever tolerance to self must be enforced. Controlling the rate of T cell apoptotic death shapes the repertoire, terminates expansion once antigen is cleared, and prevents both autoimmunity and lymphopenia. The genes here act on both sides of that balance. Survival inputs include IL7R signalling through JAK3 and costimulation via CD27, while death is promoted by the FADD adaptor, the BH3-only protein PUMA encoded by BBC3, and p53-dependent transcription. Environmental and immunosuppressive cues feed in too: PD-L1 engagement, tryptophan depletion by IDO1, arginine consumption by ARG2, galectin binding to surface glycans, TGF-beta, and glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3. Defects cause immunodeficiency, as with ADA or DOCK8 loss, or failure of peripheral tolerance.

T lymphocytes are produced in excess and most die by apoptosis during thymic selection or after an immune response, so the processes that hold that death in check determine which cells survive to form the mature and memory repertoire. Negative regulation of T cell apoptosis supports thymocyte survival through development and maintains peripheral T cell numbers; its loss contributes to lymphopenia and immunodeficiency, while excessive survival signalling favours autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy. Survival input comes largely from cytokine and costimulatory receptors / IL7R signalling through JAK3, CD27 engagement, and T cell receptor-proximal kinases such as PRKCQ / together with pre-TCR components and RAG1 acting during selection. Metabolic and environmental modifiers including HIF1A, IDO1 and arginine handling tune the threshold, and TSC22D3 links glucocorticoid exposure to thymocyte survival decisions.

Deleting T cells on purpose is how the immune system ends a response, removes self-reactive clones, and keeps tissues from being destroyed by their own defenders; this pathway covers the signals that raise the rate of T cell apoptosis. It spans death signals delivered from outside the cell and the intrinsic machinery that executes them: PD-L1 engaging its inhibitory receptor on activated T cells, galectin-9 binding TIM-3, tryptophan depletion by IDO1 starving proliferating lymphocytes, and TGF-beta acting as a suppressive cue. Inside the target cell, p53 and its target PUMA tip the mitochondrial balance toward caspase activation. The same logic is exploited by tumours and by the placenta to enforce local immune tolerance, so gain of these signals produces immune evasion while their loss contributes to autoimmunity and failure of peripheral tolerance.

regulation of activation-induced cell death of T cells tunes how readily an activated T cell is deleted after it has responded to antigen, the brake that ends an immune response and enforces peripheral tolerance. Without it, activated clones persist and accumulate, favouring autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation; with it set too high, effector and memory populations are lost prematurely and immunity is blunted. The genes point to two converging arms: death receptor signalling through the adaptor FADD and the kinase RIPK3, which route Fas and related TNF-family engagement toward apoptosis or programmed necrosis, and extrinsic suppressive cues, with TGF-beta and the glucocorticoid-induced regulator TSC22D3 damping activation and altering susceptibility to deletion. This places the pathway at the interface of antigen receptor signalling, glucocorticoid and cytokine control of lymphocyte homeostasis, and the contraction phase that follows clonal expansion.

Once a T cell has been activated and repeated antigen stimulation is no longer useful, it is deleted, and regulation of activation-induced cell death of T cells sets how readily that deletion happens. Tuning this threshold keeps immune responses self-limiting and helps purge autoreactive clones as an expansion resolves; too little restraint wastes effector cells prematurely, while too much allows activated lymphocytes to persist and drive autoimmunity or lymphoproliferation. The regulators here act on death receptor signalling and on transcriptional programmes that determine sensitivity to it: an adaptor coupling Fas-family receptors to caspase activation, a kinase associated with regulated necrotic death, a glucocorticoid-induced factor that mediates steroid effects on lymphocyte survival, and a TGF-beta family ligand that dampens T cell activation. The pathway sits at the contraction phase of adaptive immune responses and underlies steroid-induced lymphocyte killing.

Most developing thymocytes die rather than mature, and apoptosis of thymocytes is how the T cell repertoire is edited: cells whose rearranged receptors fail to signal are discarded, and those reacting too strongly against self are deleted, so that autoimmunity is avoided and only useful specificities leave the thymus. Death is executed through the mitochondrial arm, with the BH3-only proteins PUMA and BIM tipping the balance toward BAX and BAK pore formation and downstream caspase-activated DNA fragmentation; p53 links damage and failed receptor rearrangement to the same outcome. Selection is set up by receptor assembly and pre-TCR components such as RAG1 and PTCRA, while ADA deficiency and defective JAK3 signalling cause excess thymocyte loss and immunodeficiency. RORC-dependent survival, hypoxic and morphogen cues from the thymic microenvironment tune how many cells survive each round.

Most developing thymocytes die in the thymus, and control over thymocyte apoptosis is what decides which ones survive. Tuning the rate of this death sets the size and specificity of the T cell repertoire: too much killing depletes the periphery of T cells, too little allows self-reactive clones through, so this regulation sits upstream of both immunodeficiency and autoimmunity. Pro-apoptotic and survival inputs converge on the mitochondrial pathway, with p53 and its target PUMA promoting death after DNA damage, while cytokine receptor signalling through JAK3 and the nuclear receptor RORC favour survival of immature cells. Pre-T cell receptor components and RAG1 tie survival to successful receptor gene rearrangement, and adenosine deaminase loss illustrates the consequence of failure, with toxic metabolites triggering thymocyte death and severe combined immunodeficiency. Morphogens such as BMP4 and WNT5A modulate these thresholds from the thymic stroma.

Most developing thymocytes die in the thymus, and survival signals decide which ones live long enough to complete selection. Suppressing thymocyte apoptosis is what allows double-positive cells to persist while their rearranged receptors are tested, and it sets the size and diversity of the mature T cell pool. The genes here span the checks that grant that reprieve: RAG1-mediated receptor gene rearrangement and the pre-T cell receptor chain PTCRA signal that a functional receptor has been assembled, JAK3 relays cytokine receptor survival signals, and the nuclear receptor RORC sustains anti-apoptotic gene expression in immature thymocytes. Metabolic and microenvironmental inputs also contribute, including adenosine deaminase, whose loss causes accumulation of toxic nucleosides and profound lymphocyte depletion, hypoxia sensing through HIF1A, and stromal BMP and ephrin cues. Failure at this level produces immunodeficiency; excessive survival permits escape of autoreactive cells.

Developing T cells in the thymus are selected by death: thymocytes whose receptors bind self-antigen too strongly, or fail to bind at all, are removed by apoptosis, and this pathway comprises the influences that raise the rate of that killing. Increasing thymocyte apoptosis shapes the repertoire that leaves the thymus and enforces central tolerance, so its loss permits autoreactive clones to escape while excessive signalling depletes the thymus, as happens with glucocorticoid or stress-induced involution. The genes act at different levels: p53 and its transcriptional target PUMA, a BH3-only protein, tip the mitochondrial apoptotic balance toward BAX/BAK activation after damage or strong signalling, while WNT5A signalling and the surface metalloprotease ADAM8 modulate death sensitivity from outside the cell. The process links apoptotic commitment to thymic selection and T cell repertoire formation.

Cell shortening driven by myosin pulling on actin filaments underlies the heartbeat, skeletal muscle movement and the tone of smooth muscle, and this actin-mediated cell contraction programme covers both the force-generating machinery and the electrical events that time it. Sarcomeric myosin heavy and light chains, actins, titin, tropomyosin and the troponin complex convert ATP hydrolysis into sliding filaments, while calcium release through the ryanodine receptor and reuptake by SERCA pumps, tuned by phospholamban and calsequestrin, set each contraction's amplitude and duration. A large complement of voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels, L-type calcium channels, gap junction connexins and desmosomal proteins propagates and couples excitation between cardiomyocytes. Mutations here cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia syndromes such as long QT and Brugada, and skeletal myopathies, placing this biology at the centre of excitation-contraction coupling.

Mucus secretion is the regulated release of the gel layer that coats the airways, gut and other mucosal surfaces, providing lubrication and a physical and antimicrobial barrier between epithelium and the outside world. Loss of it leaves epithelia exposed to pathogens and mechanical damage, while excessive or poorly hydrated mucus underlies airway obstruction in asthma and cystic fibrosis and disrupts colonic barrier integrity in colitis. The genes cover the whole arc: the gel-forming mucin MUC2 and the disulfide isomerase AGR2 needed to fold and package it, inflammasome and autophagy components in goblet cells that license granule exocytosis, purinergic, adenosine and serotonin receptors with PKC signalling that trigger release, and VAMP2/3/8 SNAREs that fuse granules with the apical membrane. Chloride and sodium channels including ANO1 and SCNN1B set the fluid and salt content that determines mucus viscosity.

Goblet cells and other mucosal epithelia release a viscous gel of mucins, salts and water that lubricates airways and gut and forms the first barrier between the body and its lumenal contents. Losing this output leaves the epithelium exposed to pathogens, abrasion and desiccation; oversecretion or dehydration of the gel obstructs airways in asthma and cystic fibrosis. The programme couples extracellular cues to granule exocytosis: purinergic and adenosine receptors, a serotonin receptor and protein kinase C signalling trigger release, VAMP2, VAMP3 and VAMP8 drive fusion of mucin granules with the apical membrane, and the calcium-activated chloride channel ANO1 with the epithelial sodium channel subunit SCNN1B set the ion and fluid flux that hydrates secreted mucin. AGR2 is required for MUC2 folding in the ER, while NLRP6 and autophagy machinery govern granule exocytosis in intestinal goblet cells.

Mucus is the protective gel layer over airway, gut and ocular surfaces, and this pathway covers the signals that dial its release up or down. Too little leaves epithelium exposed to pathogens and injury; too much obstructs airways and underlies the plugging seen in asthma and chronic bronchitis. Control is exerted through purinergic input at the cell surface, where extracellular nucleotides acting on P2RY2 and adenosine acting on ADORA1 stimulate goblet cell granule release, with ADA setting local adenosine levels and PRKCE transducing signals to the secretory machinery. In the intestine, NLRP6 inflammasome signalling together with autophagy machinery including ATG5 is required for goblet cells to exocytose mucin granules, linking innate immune sensing of the microbiota to barrier maintenance. Lipoxygenase and NADPH oxidase components tie mucus output to lipid mediators and redox signalling.

Mucus is the protective gel that lines airways and gut, trapping particles and pathogens and keeping epithelial surfaces hydrated; upregulating its release is part of how epithelia respond to irritation and infection. Increased mucus secretion clears inhaled debris, but sustained overproduction underlies the plugging seen in asthma, chronic bronchitis and cystic fibrosis. The genes here point to several routes that raise secretory output: extracellular nucleotides acting through the P2Y2 purinergic receptor couple ATP released from stressed or injured cells to goblet cell granule release, protein kinase C epsilon transduces such stimuli toward exocytosis, and the NADPH oxidase subunit encoded by CYBA links reactive oxygen production to the same response. Involvement of the autophagy protein ATG5 reflects the contribution of autophagic membrane traffic to granule handling, placing this control at the intersection of epithelial defence, purinergic signalling and regulated secretion.

Necroptosis is a regulated form of cell death that proceeds without caspase activity and ruptures the cell, releasing its contents as inflammatory danger signals; it matters as a backup death route when apoptosis is blocked, notably during viral infection, and as a driver of inflammatory tissue injury in ischaemia, neurodegeneration and gut disease. Death receptor, Toll-like receptor and nucleic-acid sensor inputs (FAS/FASLG, TNF, TLR3, ZBP1) converge on RIPK1 and RIPK3, which phosphorylate MLKL so that it oligomerises and permeabilises the plasma membrane. Whether a cell takes this route is decided by a ubiquitin- and caspase-based switch: CASP8 with FADD and CFLAR suppresses it, the inhibitor-of-apoptosis proteins BIRC2/3 and the linear ubiquitin ligase components restrain RIPK1, and CYLD with SPATA2 removes that restraint. Mitochondrial permeability and PARP1-driven energy collapse contribute to the necrotic execution phase.

Cornification is the terminal differentiation programme by which epidermal keratinocytes die in a controlled way and become corneocytes, the flattened, protein- and lipid-filled cells that form the skin's outermost barrier. It gives skin its mechanical resistance, elasticity and water impermeability, and its failure underlies ichthyoses, atopic dermatitis and related barrier diseases. Keratins such as KRT1, KRT2 and KRT10 build the internal cytoskeletal scaffold, while transglutaminase 1 cross-links small proline-rich proteins and other precursors into the cornified envelope; filaggrin aggregates keratin filaments and is later degraded into natural moisturising factor. Ceramide synthase 3 and epidermis-specific lipases generate the lipid lamellae sealing the corneocyte layer. Controlled proteolysis by kallikrein 5, restrained by protease inhibitors, and loss of corneodesmosomal adhesion govern desquamation, so that barrier formation and orderly shedding are two halves of the same process.

Pyroptotic inflammatory response is the lytic, gasdermin-driven form of cell death and cytokine release that macrophages and epithelial cells use to expose intracellular bacteria and to broadcast alarm. Sensors such as NLRP3, NLRP1, NLRC4 with NAIP, and the DNA sensor AIM2 nucleate inflammasomes through the adaptor PYCARD/ASC, activating caspase-1 to mature IL-1beta and IL-18; CASP4 responds directly to cytosolic LPS, and granzymes delivered by cytotoxic lymphocytes cleave gasdermins independently. Cleaved GSDMD and GSDME form plasma membrane pores, guanylate-binding proteins liberate bacterial ligands, and NINJ1 completes membrane rupture so that cell contents escape. The output is pyrogenic, neutrophil-recruiting inflammation that clears pathogens but damages tissue when unrestrained: mutations in MEFV cause familial Mediterranean fever, and NLRP3 gain of function produces periodic fever syndromes treated by IL-1 blockade.

Extracellular matrix constituent secretion covers the regulated export of collagens, proteoglycans and matrix glycoproteins from the cells that build tissue scaffolds, chiefly osteoblasts, fibroblasts and endothelium. Without it bone fails to mineralise and connective tissue loses tensile strength: loss of CREB3L1, the transcription factor that drives the collagen secretory program, or of TMEM38B, an ER cation channel needed for procollagen handling, causes recessive osteogenesis imperfecta. The genes span the whole route from instruction to release — BMP2 and NOTCH1 specify the matrix-secreting fate, TNF receptors couple inflammatory signals to matrix turnover, and RIC1, part of the RAB6 guanine nucleotide exchange complex, together with IER3IP1 supports the enlarged ER-to-Golgi carriers that bulky matrix cargo requires. The pathway therefore links secretory trafficking capacity to skeletal development, vascular remodelling and wound repair.

Matrix-producing cells such as osteoblasts, chondrocytes and fibroblasts must not only synthesise collagens, proteoglycans and matrix glycoproteins but also route them through the secretory pathway to the outside of the cell, and this regulated secretion of extracellular matrix constituents is the step that converts biosynthetic capacity into actual tissue architecture. When it fails, bone and connective tissue form poorly: loss of the transcription factor CREB3L1, which drives collagen secretory machinery, and of the ER cation channel TMEM38B each cause osteogenesis imperfecta with brittle bones. Contributing activities include ER and Golgi trafficking components, calcium and ion handling that supports procollagen folding and transport, and signals that instruct cells to secrete at all — BMP2 and Notch signalling in skeletal differentiation, TNF receptor signalling during inflammatory matrix remodelling. The pathway therefore links vesicular transport to skeletal development, wound healing and fibrosis.

Motile cilia and sperm flagella beat because rows of dynein motors along the axoneme walk on adjacent microtubules, and this pathway builds and installs those motors. The heavy, intermediate and light chains are folded and pre-assembled in the cytoplasm with the help of dedicated assembly factors such as DNAAF1-DNAAF11, ZMYND10 and SPAG1, then trafficked into the cilium and docked at defined positions: an outer row anchored by the ODAD docking complex, and inner arms positioned by the nexin-dynein regulatory complex and by the ruler proteins CCDC39 and CCDC40 that set the 96-nm repeat. Loss of any step leaves cilia present but immotile or dyskinetic, producing primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic airway infection, situs inversus, hydrocephalus and male infertility. It is a cytoplasmic pre-assembly programme feeding a compartment that has no protein synthesis of its own.</description>

N-acylethanolamine metabolic process governs the production and breakdown of a family of lipid signalling molecules that includes the endocannabinoid anandamide, the anti-inflammatory mediator palmitoylethanolamide, and the satiety factor oleoylethanolamide. Through these products the pathway tunes pain perception, feeding behaviour, energy balance, and the resolution of inflammation. Synthesis proceeds from membrane N-acyl-phosphatidylethanolamine precursors, cleaved directly by a phospholipase D-type enzyme or routed through glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine intermediates that glycerophosphodiesterases such as GDE1, GDPD1 and GDPD3 hydrolyse to release the free acylethanolamine. Termination is equally part of the pathway: acid ceramidase-related amidase activity degrades these lipids to fatty acid and ethanolamine, setting their local concentration and therefore how strongly they engage cannabinoid receptors, PPAR-alpha and TRP channels. Because signalling here is controlled by on-demand synthesis and rapid hydrolysis rather than storage, the degradative enzymes are pursued as analgesic and anti-inflammatory drug targets.

N-acylethanolamines are lipid signalling molecules — among them anandamide, the endocannabinoid, and the anti-inflammatory mediators palmitoylethanolamide and oleoylethanolamide — and this pathway covers how they are made and destroyed. Their turnover sets the tone of cannabinoid receptor and PPAR-alpha signalling, and thereby influences pain thresholds, appetite and feeding behaviour, neuronal excitability and the resolution of inflammation. Synthesis begins with membrane N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines, which a dedicated phospholipase D releases directly as N-acylethanolamines; a parallel route proceeds through glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine intermediates hydrolysed by glycerophosphodiesterases such as GDE1, GDPD1 and GDPD3. Degradation limits signalling duration, with the lysosomal amidase NAAA preferentially hydrolysing palmitoylethanolamide in macrophages and other immune cells. Because these lipids are produced on demand rather than stored, the balance between the synthetic and hydrolytic arms determines local signal strength, and NAAA blockade is pursued as a non-opioid analgesic strategy.

N-acylphosphatidylethanolamines are minor membrane phospholipids that serve as the storage precursors for the fatty acid ethanolamides, including the endocannabinoid anandamide and the anti-inflammatory mediator palmitoylethanolamide. Their metabolism therefore sets how much signalling lipid a tissue can release on demand, with consequences for pain perception, appetite, inflammatory tone and neuronal protection. Formation depends on transfer of an acyl chain onto the ethanolamine nitrogen of phosphatidylethanolamine, a reaction carried out by the phospholipase A/acyltransferase family (PLAAT1-5) and by a cytosolic phospholipase of the PLA2G4 group. Release of the free ethanolamide is then achieved either directly by the N-acylphosphatidylethanolamine-hydrolysing phospholipase D, NAPEPLD, or through a stepwise route via glycerophospho-N-acylethanolamine involving the serine hydrolase ABHD4. NAAA degrades the resulting acylethanolamides in lysosomes, terminating their action, and is pursued as an anti-inflammatory drug target.

Renal absorption is the recovery of filtered water, electrolytes, glucose, amino acids and proteins from the nephron lumen back into the blood, and it is what allows the kidney to filter the entire plasma volume many times a day without losing its contents. Failure of individual components causes recognisable tubular diseases: salt-wasting and hypomagnesaemia, glucosuria, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, or vitamin B12 malabsorption. Segment-specific transporters do the work — sodium-glucose cotransporters in the proximal tubule, the tight-junction magnesium pathway built from claudin 16 and 19 in the thick ascending limb, the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter distally — and are tuned by vasopressin acting through its V2 receptor on aquaporin water channels and by the WNK–OXSR1/STK39 kinase cascade with its KLHL3 ubiquitin ligase adaptor. Endothelin and aldosterone-responsive SGK1 signalling adjust reabsorptive load, linking tubular transport to blood pressure control.

Concentrating urine depends on renal water absorption, the recovery of water from tubular fluid across the proximal tubule, descending limb and collecting duct back into the blood. It is how the body defends plasma osmolality and blood volume during dehydration, and its failure produces diabetes insipidus, with large volumes of dilute urine and unquenchable thirst. Vasopressin released from the hypothalamus acts on the V2 receptor on principal cells, raising cAMP and driving aquaporin water channels into the apical membrane, while constitutive basolateral channels such as AQP3 and the AQP1 of the proximal tubule and descending limb complete the transcellular route. Hyaluronan turnover in the medullary interstitium, through synthase and hyaluronidase activity, modulates the osmotic gradient that makes this absorption possible, linking water handling to interstitial matrix composition.

Sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ion transport is the calcium cycling that turns an action potential into a contraction and then relaxes the muscle again. It sets the strength and timing of each heartbeat and each skeletal muscle twitch, and its failure produces heart failure, arrhythmia and myopathy. Voltage-gated L-type channels and junctophilins organise the junction where the dihydropyridine receptor meets the ryanodine receptor, so that depolarisation triggers release of stored calcium into the cytosol; calsequestrin, triadin and histidine-rich calcium protein buffer and regulate the luminal side. Reuptake by SERCA pumps, tuned by the small inhibitory peptides phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin and by PKA and CaMKII phosphorylation, plus sodium-calcium exchange at the surface membrane, restores the resting state. The same machinery links beta-adrenergic stimulation to inotropy, and mutations in the ryanodine receptors cause malignant hyperthermia and catecholaminergic arrhythmias.

Every heartbeat and every skeletal muscle twitch depends on calcium being released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and then pumped back in, and this transport cycle sets both the strength and the speed of contraction and relaxation. Voltage-gated L-type channels at the plasma membrane signal across the junctional gap, through junctophilins and triadin-calsequestrin complexes, to ryanodine receptors that release stored calcium; SERCA pumps encoded by ATP2A1 and ATP2A2 return it to the lumen, with phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin tuning pump activity and the sodium-calcium exchanger handling extrusion. Calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA place this machinery under beta-adrenergic and calcium-dependent control. Loss of fidelity here produces malignant hyperthermia and central core myopathy through ryanodine receptor mutation, catecholaminergic arrhythmias, and the impaired calcium handling that characterises heart failure, linking store loading directly to excitation-contraction coupling.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a by-product of aerobic metabolism and a deliberate second messenger, and this pathway covers how a cell senses it and reshapes its behaviour in response. The outcome ranges from restored redox balance to inflammation, growth arrest and regulated death, so it sits at the heart of oxidative stress biology in ageing, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration. Detoxification and thiol buffering by catalase, thioredoxin and PARK7 limit the signal, while NFE2L2 drives the antioxidant transcriptional programme and SIRT1 and histone-modifying enzymes tune the longer-term response. Peroxide-sensitive kinases including SRC, ABL1, PRKCD and MAP3K5 relay the stimulus, RELA links it to cytokine output such as IL6, and TRPM2 and TRPA1 convert it into calcium and sensory signals. When damage exceeds repair, autophagy, mitochondrial permeability transition and RIPK1/RIPK3 necroptosis are engaged instead.

Cells respond to osmotic shock, oxidative damage, inflammatory cytokines and microbial products by routing those inputs into JNK and p38 cascades, and this pathway covers the positive and negative control of how strongly and how long that stress-activated protein kinase signaling runs. The balance determines whether a stressed cell adapts, arrests, or commits to apoptosis, and it shapes inflammatory output in innate immunity and tissue injury. Upstream activation comes from pattern-recognition and death receptors such as TLR4, NOD1/NOD2 with their adaptors RIPK2 and CARD9, and from FAS; TAOK1-3 act as MAP kinase kinase kinases feeding the cascade. Restraint is imposed by phosphatases such as DUSP10, which dephosphorylates stress-activated kinases, and by redox buffering proteins including PRDX1 and GSTP1. Scaffolds and transcription factors like FOXO1 and MYC couple the output to survival and proliferation decisions.

Stress-activated protein kinase cascades, chiefly the JNK and p38 routes, convert oxidative, inflammatory and genotoxic stress into decisions about growth arrest, cytokine production and apoptosis, and they must be switched off once the stress passes. This negative regulatory arm restrains that signalling so that transient insults do not commit a cell to death or chronic inflammatory output. It works at several levels: a dual-specificity phosphatase removes the activating phosphates from p38 and JNK, a glutathione transferase sequesters the upstream kinase ASK1 in a redox-sensitive complex, and a phosphatase-regulatory subunit and peptidyl-prolyl isomerase act on upstream kinase modules, while transcription factors including FOXO1, FOXM1 and MYC set the expression of pathway components. Loss of this braking contributes to excessive apoptosis and inflammatory injury, whereas its overuse in tumours helps cancer cells tolerate stress.

Cells respond to stress, damage and microbial cues by turning on the JNK and p38 kinase cascades, and this pathway covers the inputs that switch those cascades on or push them harder. The output is a stress transcriptional programme controlling inflammatory cytokine production, apoptosis and adaptation to osmotic, oxidative and ER insults. Upstream activation arrives from several directions: innate immune sensing through TLR4, the cytosolic peptidoglycan receptors NOD1 and NOD2 with their kinase adaptor RIPK2 and the CARD9 adaptor, growth factor and TGF-beta family ligands, and double-stranded RNA sensing by the kinase EIF2AK2. The TAOK1/2/3 kinases and the germinal centre kinase STK25 act as upstream MAP kinase kinase kinases, while scaffolds such as MAPK8IP2 organise JNK modules. Excessive signalling through this route drives chronic inflammation, and NOD2 variants link it to inflammatory bowel disease.

Cyclic GMP is the second messenger generated downstream of nitric oxide and natriuretic peptides, and this pathway covers what cells do once it accumulates: relax smooth muscle, alter ion flux, change secretion, and adjust gene expression. The consequences are cardiovascular above all, which is why cGMP-directed drugs are used in pulmonary hypertension, heart failure and erectile dysfunction. Effectors here span several classes. Hyperpolarization-activated channels HCN2 and HCN4 are directly modulated by cyclic nucleotide binding and set pacemaker rhythm in sinoatrial cells and neurons. Phosphodiesterases PDE2A and PDE3A both respond to cGMP while hydrolysing cAMP, so cGMP can raise or lower cAMP depending on which enzyme dominates, a key node of crosstalk between the two messengers. NPR2 is itself a guanylate cyclase receptor for C-type natriuretic peptide, and renin release, serotonin transport and Rap signalling are among the downstream responses.

Lens fiber cell differentiation builds the transparent bulk of the ocular lens, converting proliferating anterior epithelial cells into elongated, organelle-free fibers packed with crystallins. Transparency and refractive power depend on it, and disruption of these genes produces congenital cataract, microphthalmia and lens degeneration. Cells first exit the cell cycle under CDKN1B and CDKN1C control, then execute a transcriptional program driven by MAF, PROX1, PITX3, FOXE3, SIX3 and HSF4 that switches on alpha- and gamma-crystallins. Elongation requires cytoskeletal remodelling through the beaded filament proteins BFSP1 and BFSP2, vimentin and tropomodulin, with cell-cell adhesion and membrane organization maintained by NF2 and ephrin-EPHA2 signalling. FGF, TGF-beta and WNT inputs pattern the differentiation gradient across the lens and are tuned by SPRY and SPRED feedback inhibitors, while programmed organelle and nuclear breakdown clears light-scattering structures from mature fibers.

The transparency and refractive power of the vertebrate lens depend on this differentiation programme, in which epithelial cells at the lens equator exit the cell cycle, elongate enormously, degrade their nuclei and other organelles, and fill with crystallins. Loss of any step gives cataract or microphthalmia, and several of the genes here are classic congenital cataract loci. Cell cycle withdrawal is enforced by CDK inhibitors such as CDKN1B and CDKN1C; transcription factors including MAF, PITX3, FOXE3, PROX1, HSF4 and SIX3 drive crystallin expression and fibre elongation. FGF and TGF-beta/SMAD inputs are tuned by Sprouty and SPRED antagonists, while EPHA2-ephrin signalling and the beaded filament proteins BFSP1/BFSP2 with vimentin and tropomodulin build the specialised cytoskeleton that packs fibres together. Organelle clearance and RNA granule functions, as for TDRD7, complete the conversion to an optically clear cell.

Lens fiber cell development describes how the elongated, tightly packed cells that fill the ocular lens mature after their fate is set, producing the transparent, refractive tissue on which vision depends. Failure of this program gives cataract: loss of clarity through disordered cell packing, cytoskeletal collapse, or crystallin aggregation. Maturation involves extreme cell elongation, formation of the beaded filament cytoskeleton from BFSP1, BFSP2, vimentin and tropomodulin, massive accumulation of crystallins such as CRYAA that act as both refractive proteins and chaperones, and eventual organelle degradation to create an organelle-free zone. Ephrin-EphA2 signalling and Wnt ligands direct the precise hexagonal packing and apical-basal alignment of fibers, while PROX1 and ATF4 sustain the transcriptional program of differentiation. The pathway links cell shape control, cytoskeletal organization and protein homeostasis to an optical function.

The transparency of the eye's lens depends on fiber cells that elongate enormously, pack together with almost no extracellular space, and degrade their nuclei and organelles to eliminate light scattering. Lens fiber cell development covers that maturation programme after fate commitment, and its disruption produces cataract and lens opacities. Structural output dominates: crystallins such as CRYAA and CRYGB accumulate to extreme concentrations and act as chaperones holding the cytoplasm in a clear, refractive state, while the beaded filament proteins BFSP1 and BFSP2 together with vimentin and tropomodulin build the specialised cytoskeleton that shapes the elongating cell. Positional cues organise the process, with EPHA2 and ephrin-A5 governing fiber alignment and hexagonal packing, Wnt ligands and FRS2-linked growth factor signalling driving elongation, and PROX1 directing exit from the cell cycle and differentiation at the lens equator.

The transparency of the vertebrate lens depends on epithelial cells at the lens equator elongating into long, tightly packed fiber cells that lose their organelles and fill with crystallins. This morphogenetic programme builds the refractive bulk of the eye, and its disruption produces cataract and lens opacity: mutations in the alpha-crystallin chaperone CRYAA and in gamma-crystallins cause inherited cataract, as do defects in the receptor tyrosine kinase EPHA2 and its ligand ephrin-A5, which guide fiber cell adhesion and the hexagonal packing of cells at the sutures. The transcription factor PROX1 drives withdrawal from the cell cycle and crystallin gene expression as fibers differentiate, while actin regulators such as ABI2 shape the elongating cytoskeleton. ATF4 links the process to stress-responsive translational control, and membrane trafficking contributes to the organelle clearance that leaves the mature fiber cell optically clear.

Cells that are not committed to divide leave the cycle in G1 and settle into quiescence, and this exit is what keeps stem and progenitor pools intact, prevents exhaustion of renewing tissues, and denies a proliferative signal to cells carrying damage. The G1 to G0 transition is enforced by tumour suppressor signalling, with p53 blocking passage through the restriction point after stress and the LKB1 kinase acting with its pseudokinase partner STRADA to couple energy status to growth arrest. Chromatin and nucleolar regulators including the histone methyltransferase EZH2, MYBBP1A and the ribosome biogenesis factor RRP8 dampen the transcriptional and translational output that a cycling cell requires, while ZBTB17 and GATA6 tune cyclin-dependent kinase activity and lineage-specific quiescence. Loss of this control underlies unrestrained proliferation in cancer; conversely, failure to re-enter the cycle limits tissue regeneration.

Terminal differentiation usually requires a cell to stop dividing permanently, and this is the exit from the G1 phase of the cycle into the quiescent G0 state as part of a differentiation programme rather than as a response to damage or starvation. The arrest lets progenitors in muscle, neural and endodermal lineages commit to a specialised fate, since proliferation and the expression of mature contractile, synaptic or secretory programmes are largely incompatible. Transcriptional regulators such as GATA6 and ZNF503 link lineage specification to withdrawal from the cycle, while CDK5R1 supplies the neuronal activator of a kinase that acts outside cycle progression, and CAPN3 marks skeletal muscle maturation. Loss of control at this step leaves differentiating cells cycling, a state associated with failed tissue maturation and with tumours that retain progenitor character.

Quiescent cells sit in G0, and re-entry into G1 must be licensed rather than automatic; negative regulation of the G0-to-G1 transition is the set of brakes that holds cells out of cycle. This restraint maintains stem and progenitor pools, keeps differentiated and senescent cells from dividing, and, when lost, permits the unscheduled proliferation characteristic of tumours. The brakes act at several levels: a checkpoint kinase couples replication stress and DNA damage surveillance to delayed entry, a forkhead transcription factor drives expression of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors and antioxidant genes downstream of growth-factor withdrawal, a Ras GTPase-activating protein dampens mitogenic signalling, and a protein phosphatase 2A regulatory subunit redirects dephosphorylation of cycle substrates. Microluster miRNAs add post-transcriptional repression of cyclin-pathway messages, while an immune ligand contributes to contact- and environment-dependent growth arrest.

Quiescent cells are not permanently withdrawn from division, and positive regulation of the G0 to G1 transition covers the inputs that push a resting cell back into the cycle. Re-entry underlies tissue regeneration, wound healing and the reactivation of stem and progenitor pools, and its inappropriate stimulation contributes to unchecked proliferation. The genes here point to two requirements for leaving quiescence: transcriptional competence, with a Mediator complex subunit coupling nuclear-receptor and other activators to RNA polymerase II and a SOX-family factor acting in muscle progenitor activation; and provision of deoxyribonucleotides, since ribonucleotide reductase subunits must supply the dNTP pools that a cell entering G1 will need for replication and repair. A RAD9-HUS1-RAD1-associated genome stability factor links re-entry to replication-stress signalling, so that cells resume cycling without accumulating DNA damage.

Thyroid hormones act on nuclear receptors inside cells, so they must first be carried across plasma membranes by dedicated transporters; this transport step sets how much T4 and T3 any given tissue actually sees. The membrane carriers include the monocarboxylate transporters SLC16A2 and SLC16A10, heterodimeric amino acid transporters built from SLC3A2 with SLC7A5 or SLC7A8, and organic anion transporting polypeptides such as SLCO1C1, which delivers hormone across the blood-brain barrier, and the hepatic uptake carrier SLCO1B1. Extracellular distribution depends on thyroxine-binding globulin encoded by SERPINA7, while CRYM binds T3 intracellularly and buffers its availability. Because brain development requires timely hormone entry into neural cells, loss of SLC16A2 causes Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome, with severe psychomotor retardation despite abnormal circulating hormone levels. The pathway thus links systemic endocrine signalling to tissue-specific hormone action, growth and metabolic rate.

Adipose tissue can grow either by enlarging existing fat cells or by adding new ones, and this pathway covers the latter: division of preadipocytes and adipocytes to expand the fat cell population. How much of tissue growth proceeds this way shapes whether obesity is metabolically tolerated, since hyperplastic expansion with many small, insulin-sensitive cells is less harmful than hypertrophy of a fixed number. The gene complement joins cell cycle control through E2F transcription factors and their DP partner with adipogenic and lipid-handling machinery such as CEBPA, FABP4, the insulin-responsive glucose transporter encoded by SLC2A4, and the lysosomal acid lipase LIPA. Interleukin-6 acting through its receptor and the shared signalling subunit IL6ST links the process to inflammatory and endocrine cues, alongside circadian input from PER2, thyroid hormone inactivation by DIO3, and the obesity-associated FTO locus.

White fat cell proliferation is the division of adipocytes and their precursors to expand the white adipose population, one of the two ways fat mass grows alongside enlargement of existing cells. How much of each occurs shapes metabolic health: hyperplastic expansion with many small adipocytes preserves insulin sensitivity, whereas failure to recruit new cells drives hypertrophy, lipid spillover and insulin resistance. The genes here span the signals that recruit preadipocytes and the transcriptional programme that commits them, including a master adipogenic transcription factor, a fibroblast growth factor acting on adipose precursors, and secreted and transcriptional modulators of early commitment. Markers of the differentiated state, such as the adipocyte fatty acid binding protein and the insulin-responsive glucose transporter, link the expanded cell population to lipid handling and glucose uptake. Variation at the obesity-associated locus containing FTO ties this biology to adiposity in humans.

Adipose tissue expands both by enlarging existing adipocytes and by multiplying preadipocytes, and the control of fat cell proliferation sets how many fat cells a depot can hold. This matters for whether excess energy is stored safely in new small adipocytes or unsafely in overloaded large ones, a distinction that separates metabolically tolerable obesity from insulin resistance and lipodystrophy. Cell cycle entry of preadipocytes is driven through E2F transcription factors with their DP partner, while FGF10 and VSTM2A act as paracrine signals promoting precursor expansion and commitment. Interleukin-6 acting through its receptor and the shared gp130 subunit links inflammatory and endocrine input to proliferative capacity, and TREM2 marks lipid-associated macrophages that accompany remodelling depots. Circadian input via PER2 and the obesity-associated FTO locus tie depot growth to systemic timing and energy balance.</description>

Adipose tissue mass depends not only on how large fat cells become but on how many are made, and this pathway covers the brakes on preadipocyte proliferation. Restraining that expansion limits hyperplastic growth of fat depots and shapes how tissue responds to overnutrition; loss of restraint contributes to obesity and its metabolic consequences, while excessive restraint pushes lipid into hypertrophic cells and ectopic sites. The components act through several routes: E2F transcription factors with their dimerization partner TFDP1 gate the G1/S transition of adipocyte precursors, IL6 signalling through its receptor and the shared gp130 subunit imposes cytokine-driven inhibition, the circadian repressor PER2 ties proliferative timing to the clock, and TREM2 marks lipid-associated macrophages that sense and regulate the expanding depot. This sits at the intersection of cell cycle control, inflammatory signalling and energy balance.

Some intracellular bacteria move through the host cytoplasm without any motor of their own, propelled by a comet tail of actin that they nucleate continuously at one pole. This actin polymerization-dependent motility lets pathogens such as Listeria and Shigella cross the cytosol and push into neighbouring cells, spreading infection while staying hidden from antibodies and extracellular immune surveillance. The machinery involved is entirely borrowed from the host's own leading-edge apparatus: the Arp2/3 complex, represented here by ACTR3 and the ARPC subunits, nucleates branched filaments against the bacterial surface, while nucleation-promoting and elongation factors including JMY, ENAH and EPS8 control filament branching, capping and tail length. The same components drive lamellipodial protrusion in motile eukaryotic cells, so this describes pathogen subversion of normal cytoskeletal force generation rather than a dedicated bacterial system.

Hepatocyte differentiation is the route by which an unspecialized endodermal or progenitor cell acquires the identity of the liver's principal epithelial cell, the hepatocyte, which is arranged into plates and lobules and carries out most of the organ's metabolic work. Acquiring this fate means switching on the enzymatic repertoire that defines liver function: urea cycle entry via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, gluconeogenic control through the phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinases, and xenobiotic oxidation by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases. The transcriptional side involves homeodomain regulators of the PROX family that drive hepatoblast delamination and growth, atypical E2F factors that govern hepatocyte polyploidization and endoreduplication, and Wnt ligands with secreted Frizzled-related antagonists that position and pattern the hepatic bud. Failure of this programme compromises liver formation and regenerative repopulation, and its partial reversal accompanies dedifferentiation in chronic liver injury and hepatocellular carcinoma.

The ERK1 and ERK2 cascade is the core mitogenic relay that converts signals from growth factor receptors, integrins, cytokine receptors and G protein-coupled receptors into decisions about proliferation, differentiation, survival and migration. Ligands such as EGF, FGFs, PDGFs, VEGFA and NGF engage receptor tyrosine kinases including EGFR, FGFRs, PDGFRA/B, KDR and NTRK1, which recruit adaptors and phosphatases such as FRS2, CRKL and PTPN11 to load RAS proteins, activating BRAF, then MAP2K1/2, then MAPK3 and MAPK1 themselves; the activated kinases phosphorylate nuclear targets including JUN and MYC. Output is tightly bounded by negative regulators present here in force a family of DUSP phosphatases that dephosphorylate ERK, SPRY and SPRED proteins, NF1 and ERRFI1 and a set of microRNAs. Persistent activation through RAS or RAF mutation drives tumour growth, while germline lesions in the same components cause developmental RASopathies.

Growth factor and mitogen signalling through the ERK1/ERK2 MAP kinase cascade must be switched off as well as on, and negative regulation of this cascade is what sets its duration and amplitude — determining whether a cell proliferates transiently or continuously, and whether it differentiates. Loss of these brakes underlies much of the growth advantage seen in RAS/RAF-driven cancers, while germline disruption of Sprouty- and SPRED-family inhibitors produces developmental overgrowth syndromes. Several mechanisms converge here: dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP1 and DUSP6 dephosphorylate the activating threonine and tyrosine of ERK; protein tyrosine phosphatases and the kinase CSK restrain upstream receptor and Src-family activity; Sprouty and SPRED proteins block signal relay between receptors and RAF; ERRFI1 curbs EGF receptor output; and microRNAs including miR-21 and miR-200c tune component levels. Scaffolds and adaptors add spatial control over where active ERK can act.

Cells decide whether to divide, differentiate, survive or migrate largely through the ERK1/ERK2 cascade, and this grouping collects the ligands, receptors and adaptors that turn that cascade on or raise its output. Growth factors and their receptor tyrosine kinases — FGFs with FGFR2-4, PDGFs with PDGFRA/B, VEGFA with KDR, IGF1, NGF with NTRK1, EGFR — feed through RAS (HRAS), BRAF and MAP2K1 to MAPK3, while G protein-coupled receptors for chemokines, monoamines, purines and peptides, arrestins, SRC-family and PTK2B kinases, and the phosphatase PTPN11 provide parallel entry points. Innate immune sensors such as TLR4, NOD1/2 and TREM2 couple inflammation to the same output. Sustained or inappropriate activation drives tumour growth, fibrosis, angiogenesis and pathological bone remodelling through TNFSF11–TNFRSF11A, which is why this arm of mitogenic signalling is a major drug target.

The ERK5 cascade is one of the mitogen-activated protein kinase relays, running from a MAP3K through MAP2K5 to the ERK5 kinase, and it converts growth factor, stress and G protein-coupled receptor input into programmes of proliferation, differentiation and development. It is best understood in endothelial biology, where it supports vessel integrity under shear stress and cardiovascular development, and it also contributes to neuronal survival and muscle differentiation; sustained activity is implicated in tumour cell growth and survival. MAP2K5 is the dedicated kinase immediately upstream of ERK5 and phosphorylates no other MAPK, which gives the route its specificity. Small GTPase input arrives through RAC1 and its regulators, while the ALKAL ligands activate ALK-family receptor tyrosine kinases that feed into MAPK signalling, illustrating how receptor-level stimuli are relayed to nuclear transcriptional responses.

Deaminating cytosine in DNA converts it to uracil, a base that does not belong there, and the cell's response to that mismatch is what makes the chemistry useful. In activated B cells, AID targets immunoglobulin loci and the resulting uracils are processed by uracil excision and mismatch repair into the point mutations of somatic hypermutation and the double-strand breaks that drive class switch recombination, so antibody affinity maturation and isotype switching depend on it; loss of AID causes hyper-IgM immunodeficiency.
