The APOBEC3 enzymes apply the same reaction to single-stranded viral and retroelement DNA, hypermutating reverse transcripts of HIV and other retroviruses as an innate restriction mechanism. Because the enzymes are mutagenic by design, off-target activity leaves characteristic cytosine-to-thymine and clustered kataegis signatures in tumour genomes, linking this deaminase family to cancer mutagenesis as well as to immunity.

Lipoteichoic acid is a surface polymer of Gram-positive bacteria, and the cellular response to it is how innate immune cells recognize staphylococci, streptococci and related organisms and mount inflammation against them. Detection depends on TLR2, assisted by the lipid-binding accessory proteins CD14, LBP and the scavenger receptor CD36, which capture and deliver the amphipathic ligand to the receptor; the adaptor TIRAP relays the signal inward, converging on p38 MAP kinase and NF-kB (RELA) to drive cytokine transcription and antimicrobial peptide production. TREM2 and RIPK2 contribute modulatory and cooperative input, the latter linking to cytosolic peptidoglycan sensing. Because this arm sets the magnitude of cytokine release, it shapes both protective clearance of Gram-positive infection and the excessive inflammation of sepsis, and it informs how macrophages and microglia respond to bacterial cell wall debris.

Cells exposed to temperatures below their optimum mount a defensive and adaptive response, and this cold-response programme covers both the sensing of chill and the metabolic switch that answers it. Its clearest physiological output is non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, where uncoupling protein UCP1 dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient as heat, lipid droplet proteins such as PLIN1 and CIDEA govern the release and oxidation of stored triglyceride, and PKA catalytic activity downstream of adrenergic stimulation drives lipolysis and thermogenic gene expression. Sensory neurons contribute the detection arm: the TRPA1 channel and the sodium channel SCN11A transduce cold and noxious cold into electrical signals. Alongside these, translational control kinases of the integrated stress response, chaperone cofactors and stress-responsive transcription factors adjust protein synthesis, redox and survival signalling while the cell is cold. Failure of this adaptation impairs thermal tolerance and energy expenditure, linking it to obesity and cold pain.

regulation of nucleotide-binding domain, leucine rich repeat containing receptor signaling pathway sets the gain on cytosolic innate immune sensing, determining how strongly NOD- and NLR-family receptors respond to bacterial peptidoglycan fragments and other intracellular danger signals. Because these receptors drive NF-κB- and inflammasome-dependent cytokine output, their tuning decides whether an infection is cleared or turns into damaging inflammation; loss of restraint here underlies Crohn's disease, Blau syndrome and other autoinflammatory conditions. Regulation acts at several levels: peptide transporters of the SLC15 family deliver muramyl peptide ligands from endosomes to the cytosol, NAGK generates the phosphorylated sugar ligand, and TLR4 signalling primes receptor expression. Downstream, the ubiquitin ligases XIAP, BIRC2 and BIRC3 assemble activating signalling complexes while the deubiquitinase TNFAIP3 and the scaffold ERBIN dampen them, with chaperones and PTPN22 modulating receptor stability and output.

Cytosolic NOD-like receptors sense bacterial cell-wall fragments and other danger signals, and the tuning of NLR signalling sets how strongly a cell mounts inflammatory NF- cB and cytokine responses to intracellular bacteria. Too little output leaves mucosal defence weak; too much drives Crohn's disease, Blau syndrome and other autoinflammatory states, which is why this arm of innate immunity is heavily regulated. Control acts at several levels. Peptide transporters of the SLC15 family, including SLC15A3 and SLC15A4, deliver muramyl peptide ligands from endosomes into the cytosol where receptors can engage them, and NAGK contributes to generating the activating sugar-peptide ligand. Ubiquitin machinery then decides signal duration: BIRC2, BIRC3 and XIAP support productive complex assembly, while TNFAIP3 restrains it. Chaperones, ERBIN, PTPN22 and TLR4 add further positive and negative input, coupling NLR output to broader pattern-recognition signalling.

Intracellular NLR sensors detect bacterial cell-wall fragments and other cytosolic danger signals, and the genes here act to switch that sensing on rather than to carry it out, giving positive regulation of NLR receptor signalling. Their output is inflammatory: NF- u03baB-driven cytokine production, inflammasome priming and antimicrobial defence against intracellular pathogens, with excessive activity contributing to autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease. Much of the control is about substrate delivery and ligand supply. The lysosomal peptide/histidine transporters SLC15A3, SLC15A4 and the related SLC46A2 move bacterial muropeptides out of endolysosomes into the cytosol where NOD-type receptors can bind them, while NAGK phosphorylates N-acetylglucosamine to generate the activating ligand for NOD2. TLR4 sensing of lipopolysaccharide raises sensor expression and cooperates with this arm, and HSPA1A/HSPA1B chaperone activity supports receptor folding and complex assembly.

nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain containing 1 signaling pathway is the cytosolic arm of bacterial sensing: NOD1 detects peptidoglycan fragments that reach the cytoplasm of epithelial and immune cells, signalling that a bacterium has breached the membrane rather than merely touched its surface. This drives NF-kB-dependent transcription of chemokines and antimicrobial peptides, shaping mucosal defence against invasive enteric pathogens and influencing susceptibility to inflammatory bowel disease and asthma-associated inflammation. Ligand binding triggers NOD1 oligomerization and recruitment of the kinase RIPK2, which together with the ubiquitin ligase XIAP builds the scaffold that activates the IKK complex; peptide transporters such as SLC15A4 and SLC46A2 deliver muropeptides to the cytosol, while IkBa and the deubiquitinase A20 restrain the output. The pathway cooperates with surface Toll-like receptor sensing, notably TLR4, to set the magnitude of the innate inflammatory response.

NOD1 is a cytosolic sensor that detects peptidoglycan fragments from bacteria that have reached the cell interior, and signalling from it lets epithelial cells and phagocytes mount an inflammatory response to invasive or intracellular microbes without any surface receptor engagement. Activation drives NF-κB-dependent transcription of chemokines and antimicrobial genes, contributing to neutrophil recruitment, mucosal defence and shaping of adaptive responses; dysregulated output contributes to inflammatory bowel disease and asthma-associated inflammation. Ligand binding promotes oligomerization and recruitment of the kinase RIPK2, whose ubiquitination by XIAP licenses downstream IKK activation; the inhibitor NFKBIA restrains NF-κB until it is degraded, and TNFAIP3 acts as a brake by removing ubiquitin marks. Peptide transporters of the SLC15 and SLC46 families deliver peptidoglycan fragments into the cytosol, and the pathway operates alongside surface sensing by TLR4.

NOD2 is a cytoplasmic sensor that detects muramyl dipeptide, a fragment of bacterial peptidoglycan, and its signalling lets epithelial cells, macrophages and Paneth cells recognise bacteria that have reached the cytosol rather than the cell surface. The output is NF-κB-driven inflammatory transcription plus autophagic clearance and antimicrobial peptide release, so this arm of innate immunity shapes tolerance of the intestinal microbiota; loss-of-function NOD2 variants are the strongest known genetic risk for Crohn's disease, and other alleles cause granulomatous inflammation. Ligand binding recruits the kinase RIPK2, whose ubiquitination by XIAP nucleates a signalling complex that frees RELA from IkB inhibition. Counter-regulators keep the response transient: TNFAIP3 and the deubiquitinase OTULIN strip ubiquitin marks, ERBIN restrains receptor output, and peptide transporters such as SLC15A3 and SLC15A4 deliver the ligand from endolysosomes to the sensor.

NOD2 is an intracellular sensor of bacterial peptidoglycan fragments, and this pathway covers the machinery that tunes how strongly and how long it signals to NF-kB and inflammatory gene expression. The balance matters clinically: excessive or deficient NOD2 output is linked to Crohn's disease and to granulomatous inflammation, and the same signalling shapes antimicrobial defence in intestinal epithelium and myeloid cells. Regulation acts at several levels. Peptide transporters of the SLC15 family deliver muramyl peptide ligands from endosomes to the cytosolic sensor, and a sugar kinase contributes to generating the activating ligand. Chaperones of the HSP70 family and the scaffold ERBIN set receptor stability and restrain activation, while TNFAIP3 removes ubiquitin marks to terminate downstream signalling and ZNRF4 promotes receptor turnover. A phosphatase and crosstalk with TLR4 integrate this sensing with surface innate immune input.

Myelination of central nervous system axons depends on a pool of oligodendrocyte progenitors being expanded before it differentiates, and the proliferation of these progenitors sets how many myelinating oligodendrocytes a region of brain or spinal cord can eventually make. The same capacity is drawn on in remyelination after demyelinating injury, so its failure contributes to persistent conduction deficits in diseases such as multiple sclerosis. The genes here act on progenitor mitogenic signalling and cell-surface context rather than on myelin itself: a receptor-type phosphatase and a cadherin link the progenitor to its extracellular environment and to neighbouring cells, a Src-family kinase carries growth factor signals inward, an endocytic receptor takes up ligands and morphogens from cerebrospinal fluid, and a deacetylase and a nutrient-sensing complex component tune the balance between continued division and exit into differentiation.

Prolactin is the anterior pituitary hormone that drives mammary development and milk production, and its release from lactotroph secretory granules is gated by a balance of hypothalamic inhibitory and stimulatory inputs. Dopamine tonically suppresses secretion, so the pathway is most visible when that brake is lifted during suckling, pregnancy or stress; loss of control produces hyperprolactinaemia with infertility, amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. The genes here represent the stimulatory side and its neurochemical context: vasoactive intestinal peptide and neuromedin U act as releasing factors on pituitary cells, a tachykinin receptor couples neuropeptide signalling to intracellular calcium, and GABA transaminase degrades GABA, an inhibitory transmitter of the hypothalamic circuits that set lactotroph tone. The output links neuroendocrine signalling to reproductive physiology, lactation and maternal behaviour.

Contraction of the myometrium, the smooth muscle wall of the uterus, drives labour and delivery and also shapes menstrual cramping and implantation-phase uterine activity. Force is produced by actin-myosin cross-bridge cycling fuelled by ATP hydrolysis, and the genes here mostly govern how that machinery is switched on. Oxytocin is the archetypal uterotonic signal at term, while tachykinin receptors for substance P and neurokinins, alpha-2 adrenoceptors, and the G protein-coupled oestrogen receptor tune contractile tone in response to neural, hormonal and steroid cues. SETD3 acts differently: it is the histidine methyltransferase that modifies actin itself, and its loss impairs uterine contraction and delivery. Failure or misregulation of this programme underlies preterm labour, uterine atony and postpartum haemorrhage, making these receptors long-standing targets for tocolytic and labour-inducing drugs.

Labour depends on turning the quiescent pregnant myometrium into a coordinated, forceful contractile organ, and this is the signalling that pushes uterine smooth muscle contraction up in frequency and strength. Oxytocin is the classic driver, acting on myometrial receptors to raise intracellular calcium and trigger the contractions of parturition and the post-partum tone that limits bleeding; tachykinin receptors responsive to substance P and neurokinins provide a parallel neuropeptide route, and adrenergic input through an alpha-2 receptor adds sympathetic control. Estrogen acting at a membrane G protein-coupled receptor tunes myometrial responsiveness, while GABA catabolism links the inhibitory transmitter tone that this pathway works against. Failure to engage these inputs contributes to prolonged or dysfunctional labour and uterine atony, and inappropriate activation is associated with preterm contractions; the same receptors are pharmacological targets for inducing or suppressing labour.

Ribosomes carry a defined set of chemically modified nucleotides, and rRNA base methylation installs the methyl marks on adenine, cytosine and guanine bases within the maturing subunits. These modifications cluster at functional centres such as the decoding site and the peptidyl transferase region, where they tune folding of pre-rRNA, licence processing steps, and set translational fidelity and the efficiency of start codon selection. The enzymes involved span distinct catalytic families: m7G and m5C methyltransferases such as BUD23, NOP2 and NSUN5 act on cytoplasmic rRNA, often needing the activator TRMT112 as an obligate partner, while METTL15 modifies mitochondrial 12S rRNA and so feeds into assembly of the mitoribosome and oxidative phosphorylation. Loss of individual writers stalls ribosome biogenesis and causes developmental and neurological disease, linking this chemistry to growth control and protein synthesis capacity.</answer>

Cells and tissues continuously sense how much oxygen is available and adjust metabolism, blood supply and survival decisions accordingly; this is the collective response to oxygen levels, spanning hypoxia, hyperoxia and reoxygenation. Its outputs keep ATP production matched to supply, drive new vessel growth into ischaemic tissue, and stimulate red cell production, while chronic distortion of the same programme sustains tumour growth, pulmonary hypertension and ischaemia-reperfusion injury. The core switch is the HIF system: prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1-3 tag HIF1A and EPAS1 for VHL-mediated degradation when oxygen is plentiful, and their stabilisation with ARNT and the p300/CBP coactivators turns on erythropoietin, VEGF family angiogenic factors, glucose transporters and glycolytic enzymes. Parallel arms shift mitochondrial respiration and remove damaged mitochondria through BNIP3, BNIP3L, FUNDC1 and PINK1-dependent mitophagy, mount antioxidant and p53-dependent apoptotic responses, and gate oxygen-sensitive potassium and calcium channels in chemoreceptor and vascular cells.

Leukocyte aggregation is the sticking together of white blood cells through surface adhesion molecules, a step that concentrates immune cells at sites of infection or injury and lets them act as a cohesive mass rather than as isolated migrants. It contributes to inflammatory recruitment, transendothelial passage and the clustering seen in granulomas and thrombo-inflammatory lesions; excessive aggregation contributes to vascular occlusion and tissue damage. Adhesion is mediated by hyaluronan-binding CD44 together with the hyaluronan synthase that supplies its ligand, junctional adhesion molecule JAM2 at endothelial and leukocyte contacts, and semaphorin SEMA4D signalling between immune cells. Cytoskeletal reorganisation behind the adhesive contact requires moesin and the hematopoietic Rho-family GTPase RAC2, while IL1B and the S100A8/S100A9 calprotectin pair provide the inflammatory context, and ZAP70 links antigen receptor engagement in lymphocytes to adhesive responses.

Monocytes stick to each other during inflammatory recruitment, and this clustering of monocyte to monocyte through surface adhesion molecules helps concentrate them at sites of tissue injury before and during extravasation. The hyaluronan axis carries much of the work here: a synthase generates the hyaluronan matrix that CD44 on the monocyte surface binds, so adhesion depends on the cell making its own ligand as well as its receptor. Inflammatory input from interleukin-1 beta drives the process, while a BMP family ligand and an immediate-early nuclear receptor place it under developmental and transcriptional control. The result matters for monocyte trafficking, macrophage accumulation in inflamed tissue, and the aggregation seen in atherosclerotic lesions and other chronic inflammatory disease, where excessive monocyte retention promotes tissue damage rather than repair.

Thrombin-activated receptor signaling pathway is how cells sense the central protease of the coagulation cascade and convert that signal into shape change, secretion and gene expression. It is what makes platelets aggregate at a wound, and what lets endothelium and inflammatory cells register vascular injury, so it sits at the junction of haemostasis, thrombosis and inflammation. Thrombin does not bind and release like a hormone: it cleaves the extracellular tail of protease-activated receptors (F2R, F2RL1, F2RL2, F2RL3), unmasking a tethered ligand that activates the receptor irreversibly through Gq, G12/13 and Gi, driving calcium release, Rho-dependent cytoskeletal contraction and granule release, with GP1BA on the platelet surface helping localise thrombin. Downstream output includes PAI-1 induction, which feeds back to restrain fibrinolysis. Overactivity promotes thrombosis and vascular inflammation, making these receptors antiplatelet drug targets.

Thrombin does more than cleave fibrinogen: it acts as a protease that signals, cutting the N-terminus of protease-activated receptors on platelets, endothelium and smooth muscle to convert a coagulation event into a cellular response. Signalling through this route drives platelet shape change, granule secretion and aggregation, endothelial permeability and inflammatory gene expression, linking haemostasis to vascular tone, wound repair and thrombosis. Thrombin (F2) is generated at sites of injury and engages PAR1 (F2R) and the related PAR2, PAR3 and PAR4 receptors, with the platelet glycoprotein Ib complex subunit GP1BA serving as a cofactor that localises thrombin at the platelet surface. The receptors couple to heterotrimeric G proteins and downstream Rho, phospholipase C and diacylglycerol kinase-dependent effectors; PAI-1 (SERPINE1) induction ties the output back to fibrinolytic control. Excessive signalling promotes arterial thrombosis, and PAR1 is a validated antiplatelet drug target.

Interleukin-1 is the archetypal alarm cytokine of innate immunity, and the signalling it triggers converts tissue damage or infection into fever, acute-phase responses, and recruitment of leukocytes. The two agonists IL1A and IL1B engage the IL1R1/IL1RAP receptor complex, which recruits MYD88 and the IRAK kinases, and through TRAF6 and MAP3K7 activates the IKK complex to degrade NFKBIA and release RELA-containing NF-kB, alongside MAP kinase and downstream kinase arms that drive immediate-early transcription of targets such as EGR1 and IL6. Because unchecked output is destructive, the pathway is heavily braked: the secreted antagonist IL1RN and decoy receptor IL1R2 block ligand engagement, SIGIRR and TOLLIP dampen receptor complex assembly, kinase-dead IRAK3 restrains activation, and microRNAs including MIR146A impose feedback. Failure of this restraint underlies autoinflammatory fevers and chronic inflammatory disease, and IL-1 blockade is used therapeutically.

Microtubules must be nucleated, elongated, stabilised, severed and reoriented on demand, and the regulation of microtubule cytoskeleton organization is the control layer that sets how much polymer exists and where it points. It governs mitotic spindle assembly and chromosome segregation, centrosome and cilium function, neuronal axon outgrowth and intracellular transport, so its failure produces aneuploidy, microcephaly and neurodegeneration. Plus-end tracking and stabilising factors such as the EB proteins, CLASPs, CKAP5 and TACC3 build and cap growing ends, while CAMSAPs mark minus ends; stathmins sequester tubulin dimers and spastin and katanin subunits sever existing polymer. Post-translational marks written and erased by an acetyltransferase and HDAC6 tune filament mechanics and motor traffic. Mitotic kinases including PLK1 and AURKB, the augmin complex, and GSK3 and Rho-ROCK signalling couple cell cycle and adhesion cues to this remodelling, with MAPT and MAP2 acting in neurons.

Cells that cannot make enough cholesterol themselves take it up from the outside, and this pathway covers the directed movement of cholesterol into cells and between organelles. It supplies membrane sterol for growth, substrate for steroid hormone and bile acid synthesis, and is the route by which circulating lipoprotein cholesterol is cleared; its failure is the basis of familial hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerotic risk. The low-density lipoprotein receptor internalises apoB-containing particles by endocytosis, while the scavenger receptors SCARB1 and CD36 mediate selective uptake of cholesteryl ester from high-density lipoprotein and of modified lipoproteins by macrophages. Apolipoproteins such as APOA1 and APOA2 define the donor particles, STARD4 and STARD5 shuttle sterol between membranes in the cytosol, and endosomal and lysosomal regulators including COMMD1 and LAMTOR1 tie uptake to receptor trafficking and nutrient signalling.

Calcium is the cell's most widely used signalling ion, and calcium ion import — its directed movement across the plasma membrane or into organelles — is what sets the amplitude and timing of every calcium-dependent response, from muscle contraction and neurotransmitter release to gene transcription and hormone secretion. Voltage-gated channels of the CACNA1 family with their accessory subunits admit calcium when a cell depolarises; TRP channels including the heat- and vanilloid-sensitive TRPV1 and the epithelial uptake channels TRPV5 and TRPV6 respond to sensory and hormonal cues; ORAI1 carries store-operated entry after depletion of internal stores; sodium/calcium and sodium/potassium/calcium exchangers plus SERCA pumps and their regulators phospholamban and sarcolipin move calcium into stores or out again, while MICU1 gates mitochondrial uptake. Downstream, the calcineurin subunits illustrate what the influx is for: decoding calcium into transcriptional programmes. Defects cause channelopathies of epilepsy, ataxia, arrhythmia, and disordered renal and intestinal calcium absorption.

tRNA threonylcarbamoyladenosine metabolic process covers the synthesis of t6A, a bulky modification placed at position 37 of tRNAs that read ANN codons, together with the wider set of anticodon-loop and mitochondrial tRNA modifications that keep translation in frame and accurate. t6A stabilises codon-anticodon pairing, and its loss causes ribosomal frameshifting, mistranslation and stress; in humans, defects in the KEOPS complex components OSGEP, TP53RK, TPRKB, LAGE3 and GON7 cause Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with nephrotic-range kidney disease and microcephaly. YRDC supplies the threonylcarbamoyl donor from threonine, ATP and bicarbonate, while OSGEPL1 serves the mitochondrial tRNAs. The accompanying activities — pseudouridine synthases, methyltransferases, the GTPBP3/MTO1 taurinomethyluridine pair, CDK5RAP1 and the RNase P subunits TRMT10C and HSD17B10 — place this chemistry at the heart of mitochondrial tRNA maturation and oxidative-phosphorylation capacity.

Transfer RNAs that read ANN codons carry a bulky modification at position 37, adjacent to the anticodon, and the making of threonylcarbamoyladenosine is how that mark is installed. It matters because the modification enforces correct codon-anticodon pairing: without it ribosomes slip frames and misread, protein synthesis becomes error-prone, and cells show growth and stress phenotypes. A small nuclear complex built from OSGEP, LAGE3, TP53RK, TPRKB and GON7 performs the cytoplasmic transfer, with YRDC generating the threonylcarbamoyl donor from threonine and bicarbonate, while OSGEPL1 handles the mitochondrial tRNA pool. Alongside these sit other anticodon-loop and mitochondrial tRNA modifying enzymes such as GTPBP3, MTO1, TRIT1, PUS1 and TRMT5, placing this chemistry within the broader tRNA maturation programme that supports translational fidelity. Loss of complex subunits causes Galloway-Mowat syndrome, with nephrotic disease and microcephaly.

Platelet aggregation is the step that turns individual activated platelets into a plug that stops bleeding at a site of vessel injury, and the same reaction driven inappropriately produces the arterial thrombi behind heart attack and stroke. Agonists such as collagen acting through GP6 and SYK, thrombin acting through F2RL3, and ADP acting through P2RY12 converge on inside-out activation of the integrin ITGB3, which requires talin and kindlin binding to the integrin tail; fibrinogen chains then bridge adjacent platelets. Cytoskeletal and contractile machinery including filamin A, actinin, vinculin, myosin heavy and light chains and the platelet tubulin support shape change, spreading and clot retraction, while granule release depends on Munc18 proteins and VPS33B. Negative regulators such as PTPN6, UBASH3B and cyclic GMP signalling restrain the response, and defects in these components cause bleeding disorders or thrombotic risk.

Protein kinase C signaling converts receptor-generated second messengers into serine/threonine phosphorylation of downstream targets, shaping proliferation, secretion, cytoskeletal remodelling and stress responses. Diacylglycerol produced at the membrane, together with calcium for the conventional isoforms, recruits and activates kinases such as PRKCA, PRKCB and the novel isoform PRKCD, which then phosphorylate substrates including the small heat shock protein HSPB1 and transporters like the anion exchanger SLC26A6. Scaffolding by AKAP12 positions the kinase near its substrates, while diacylglycerol kinase activity terminates the signal by converting the lipid messenger to phosphatidic acid. Upstream triggers include growth factor input through EGFR and immune costimulation through CD40, so the same kinase family serves epithelial growth control and lymphocyte activation. Because these isoforms are the receptors for tumour-promoting phorbol esters, their dysregulated activity is tied to oncogenic signalling and to altered apoptotic thresholds.

Attaching ubiquitin chains linked through lysine 63 marks a protein for a change in behaviour rather than for destruction by the proteasome. These chains build binding platforms that recruit kinase complexes and repair factors, so the modification is how cells convert receptor engagement into inflammatory gene expression and how they license error-free bypass of replication-blocking DNA lesions. The dedicated conjugating machinery is a heterodimer of UBE2N with UBE2V1 or UBE2V2, working with RING and TRIM-family ligases: TRAF6 and the interleukin-17 receptor adaptor arm drive NF-kB and MAP kinase output, RNF8 and RNF168 chains assemble repair factors at double-strand breaks, HLTF supports replication fork remodelling, and TRIM proteins couple innate immune sensing of pathogens to antiviral signalling. Loss or deregulation of these linkages impairs damage tolerance, mitophagy and antimicrobial responses, and contributes to autoimmunity and cancer.

Lysine-63-linked polyubiquitin chains are non-degradative signals that assemble scaffolds rather than mark proteins for the proteasome, and their removal is how cells switch off inflammatory signalling, terminate DNA damage responses, and sort membrane cargo. K63-linked deubiquitination is carried out by hydrolases from several families — JAMM/MPN metalloproteases such as BRCC3, STAMBP and the proteasomal subunit PSMD14, and cysteine proteases including CYLD, TNFAIP3, ZRANB1 and multiple OTU and USP enzymes — many of which show marked preference for this linkage. Several act within defined complexes: BRCC3 with ABRAXAS2 and BABAM2 in the BRISC assembly, CYLD with its partner SPATA2, and the cofactor VCP driving extraction of ubiquitylated substrates. Loss of this editing activity leaves NF-κB signalling constitutively on and endosomal receptor trafficking deranged, and CYLD and TNFAIP3 mutations underlie tumour syndromes and autoimmune and inflammatory disease.

Fatty acids are not only fuel but signals, and the response to fatty acid covers how cells sense them and reset metabolism, gene expression and secretion accordingly. This sensing determines whether a cell oxidises lipid or stores it, and its derangement underlies insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis and lipotoxic beta-cell failure. Free fatty acids act at the cell surface through the FFAR1-3 receptors and the scavenger receptor CD36, which imports them, and through channels including the TREK/TRAAK potassium subunits. Internalised ligands engage nuclear receptors and lipogenic transcription factors such as PPARA, SREBF1 and the bile acid receptor NR1H4, driving uptake and oxidation machinery (ACSL1, CPT1A, LPL, HMGCS2) or triglyceride synthesis. Downstream, insulin receptor substrate signalling, FOXO factors and PDK isoforms shift substrate preference, while adiponectin and the uncoupling proteins tie the response to whole-body energy balance and thermogenesis.

Interleukin-1 is a front-line alarm cytokine of innate immunity, and this pathway covers how cells sense and answer it: fever, acute-phase protein production, leukocyte recruitment, cartilage and matrix turnover, and the amplification loops that sustain inflammation. Ligands IL1A and IL1B engage IL1R1 with the accessory chain IL1RAP, recruiting MYD88 and the IRAK kinases to TRAF6 and the TAK1 complex, which activates NF-kB through IkB degradation and the p38 and ERK arms of MAP kinase signalling. Output includes IL6, CXCL8, CCL2 and adhesion molecules such as E-selectin. Restraint is built in: a decoy receptor, the secreted antagonist IL1RN, SIGIRR, TOLLIP, IRAK3, the RNase ZC3H12A and microRNAs including miR-146a limit duration. Excess signalling drives autoinflammatory syndromes, rheumatoid joint destruction and atherosclerosis, and is the target of IL-1 blockade.

The hormonal form of vitamin D acts as a ligand for a nuclear receptor, and this signaling route is how that hormone is converted into changes in gene transcription that govern calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralization, epithelial differentiation and immune cell behaviour. Loss of receptor function causes hereditary vitamin D-resistant rickets, while the same axis underlies the antiproliferative effects of vitamin D analogues. Ligand-bound VDR heterodimerizes with retinoid X receptors on response elements and recruits coactivator and mediator components such as NCOA3, MED1, SNW1 and TRIM24, with corepressors and factors like SNAI2 restraining output. Hormone supply and termination are set enzymatically: CYP27B1 performs the activating 1α-hydroxylation, and its target gene CYP24A1 catabolizes the active hormone, forming a negative feedback loop that keeps signalling self-limiting.

regulation of vitamin D receptor signaling pathway controls how strongly cells respond to vitamin D, tuning the transcriptional output that governs calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, epithelial differentiation and innate immune defence. Loss of appropriate control produces rickets and osteomalacia at one extreme and hypercalcaemia at the other, and blunted responsiveness is a feature of many cancers. Regulation acts at two levels. Ligand supply is set by the renal and macrophage hydroxylase CYP27B1, which makes the active hormone. Receptor output is then set at the promoter: VDR heterodimerises with RXRA or RXRB and recruits coactivators such as MED1 and SNW1, while TRIM24, KANK2, SNAI2 and MN1 act as corepressors or competing cofactors that restrain or redirect target gene induction. This makes the pathway a case study in nuclear receptor coregulator balance rather than simple hormone availability.

Vitamin D acts as a hormone, and its effects on calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, epithelial differentiation and immune tone all depend on how strongly its nuclear receptor drives transcription. Regulation of vitamin D receptor signalling sets that gain. Ligand supply is one control point: the renal 1alpha-hydroxylase CYP27B1 converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxy form that binds the receptor. Downstream, VDR partners with retinoid X receptors and recruits coactivators such as MED1, SNW1 and TRIM24 to target promoters, while corepressor-associated factors including KANK2, MN1 and the transcription factor SNAI2 restrain or redirect the response. Tuning this axis determines intestinal calcium absorption and parathyroid feedback; loss of ligand production or receptor responsiveness produces rickets and osteomalacia, and altered coregulator balance shifts vitamin D-dependent growth control in epithelia.

Vitamin D acts as a hormone, and this is the biology that raises the gain on its receptor, increasing how strongly target genes respond to the sterol signal. The output governs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralization, and immune and epithelial differentiation programmes, so stronger receptor output means better calcium handling while failure of the axis produces rickets and osteomalacia. Activation occurs at two levels: CYP27B1 performs the renal 1α-hydroxylation that converts circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D into the active ligand, and at the promoter the liganded receptor VDR pairs with a retinoid X receptor partner, RXRA or RXRB, on response elements. Coactivator recruitment amplifies transcription, with SNW1 serving as a nuclear receptor coactivator that couples the complex to the transcriptional machinery, and MN1 acting as a further transcriptional enhancer of receptor activity.

Whether a damaged axon regrows is decided largely by regulatory brakes and accelerators acting on the injured neuron, and this pathway covers the processes that set the rate and extent of neuron projection regeneration. It matters because regrowth failure after spinal cord or central nervous system injury leaves deficits permanent, while peripheral nerves regenerate far better. Growth-promoting input comes from neurotrophic and cytokine signalling through receptors such as NTRK3 and CNTF acting via the BRAF-MEK1/MEK2 kinase cascade, together with pleiotrophin and osteopontin. Opposing it are myelin-associated inhibitory receptors RTN4R and RTN4RL1, the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan receptors PTPRS and PTPRF, EPHA4 repulsion, and the transcriptional brake KLF4, whose loss enhances outgrowth. Post-transcriptional control by microRNAs and the RNA-binding protein PUM2, plus RNA repair activity of RTCA, adds a further regulatory layer.

After injury, axons in the adult central nervous system usually fail to regrow, and this pathway covers the molecular brakes that enforce that failure. The restraint matters clinically: it is why spinal cord and optic nerve damage is largely permanent, and why blocking these signals is a long-standing strategy for repair. Growth cones are held back by receptors for myelin-associated and extracellular matrix inhibitors, including the Nogo receptor family RTN4R and RTN4RL1, the chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan receptor PTPRS, and the matrix glycoprotein tenascin-R; repulsive guidance signalling through EPHA4 and NEO1 adds further stop cues, while THY1 and SPP1 modulate neuronal growth capacity. Converging intracellular signalling suppresses cytoskeletal remodelling and the injury-induced growth programme. The same machinery restrains inappropriate sprouting in the intact nervous system, stabilising established circuitry against remodelling.

After axotomy or crush injury, a neuron must rebuild its process, and this pathway covers the signals that push that regrowth forward rather than merely permit it. It matters for functional recovery after peripheral nerve damage and for the failure of regeneration in the injured central nervous system. Secreted factors dominate: ciliary neurotrophic factor acting through gp130-type receptor signalling on injured motor and sensory neurons, pleiotrophin as a growth-promoting matrix-associated cytokine, and progranulin, whose loss in humans causes frontotemporal dementia and which supports neurite outgrowth and lysosomal health. Intracellular relays include the neurotrophin receptor TrkC and the kinase BRAF feeding the MAPK cascade toward a growth-competent transcriptional state. Post-transcriptional control is represented too, with microRNAs and the RNA-binding protein PUM2 tuning local message stability in regenerating processes.

Cadmium has no biological function, yet it enters cells because it resembles the essential metals that transporters are built to carry. This pathway describes that movement of cadmium ions across membranes, and it explains much of the metal's toxicity: kidney tubule damage, bone loss and hepatic injury follow from uptake by carriers meant for iron, zinc and manganese. The divalent metal transporters SLC11A1 and SLC11A2 move cadmium inward along with their proper substrates at the plasma membrane and endosomes, while zinc transporters of the ZIP family including SLC39A8 and SLC39A14 provide a second route that is prominent in liver and kidney. SLC30A1 works in the opposite direction, effluxing metal from the cytosol and limiting accumulation. Transport capacity therefore sets tissue cadmium burden, and competition with nutritional iron or zinc status modifies exposure risk.

Almost all mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol, so getting them to the right sub-mitochondrial location is what allows the organelle to respire, oxidize fats and buffer calcium at all. Targeting sequences are recognized at the outer membrane by a receptor-and-pore assembly built around TOMM20, TOMM22, TOMM70 and the TOMM40 channel; small TIMM chaperones ferry hydrophobic carriers across the intermembrane space to the TIMM22 insertase, while TIMM23 with TIMM44 and the PAM16/DNAJC19 motor, powered by matrix HSPA9-type chaperones, GRPEL nucleotide exchange factors and HSPD1 folding, pulls presequence-bearing proteins into the matrix. Parallel routes handle disulfide relay import via GFER and CHCHD4, beta-barrel assembly through SAMM50 and metaxins, and OXA1L-mediated insertion from the matrix side. Import failure depolarizes mitochondria, stabilizes PINK1 to recruit Parkin for mitophagy, and underlies deafness-dystonia, optic atrophy and neurodegeneration.

Gastrulation converts a simple epithelial sheet into the three germ layers, and the cell-cell attachments that hold migrating cells together are what make that rearrangement orderly rather than dispersive; when adhesion fails, germ layer organisation and the body axis are lost. The genes here point to endothelial and epithelial adhesion control rather than adhesion molecules themselves: the MEK5-ERK5 kinase pair (MAP2K5, MAPK7) acting through KLF4 sets a flow- and stress-responsive transcriptional programme that tunes junctional and anti-inflammatory gene expression, RIC8A is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor for heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunits required for cortical polarity and gastrulation movements, and WNK1 links ion and volume regulation to junction behaviour. Alongside them sit secreted modifiers of inflammatory adhesion such as IL10 and IL1RN, connecting embryonic morphogenesis to the same adhesion signalling used by vascular endothelium.

Calcium is the cell's most widely used signalling ion, and everything it does depends on proteins that move it across membranes: into the cytosol to trigger a response, and back out or into stores to end it. This transmembrane transport machinery sets muscle contraction, neurotransmitter and hormone release, fertilisation, immune activation and cell death thresholds, and its failure underlies arrhythmias, malignant hyperthermia, myopathies, immunodeficiency and neurodegeneration. Entry routes include voltage-gated channels with their auxiliary subunits, ligand-gated receptors, TRP and store-operated ORAI channels; release from the endoplasmic and sarcoplasmic reticulum runs through inositol trisphosphate receptors and ryanodine receptors with their accessory partners. Removal is handled by SERCA and plasma membrane ATPases and by sodium/calcium exchangers, while the mitochondrial uniporter complex and its MICU gatekeepers couple cytosolic transients to oxidative metabolism and apoptotic signalling. Calmodulin and calcineurin read the resulting signals.

A neuron's dendritic arbor covers its receptive territory efficiently only if branches from the same cell repel one another rather than overlapping, and dendrite self-avoidance is the recognition system that enforces this. The result is the evenly spread, non-redundant arbor that determines how much of a sensory or synaptic field a single neuron samples; when it fails, sister branches cross and bundle, tiling breaks down, and wiring specificity in retina and spinal cord is degraded. Recognition depends on homophilic immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion molecules, notably DSCAM and DSCAML1 together with contactins and IGSF9, which convert self-contact into a local repulsive signal. Roundabout receptors contribute guidance and repulsion cues, a heparan sulfate polymerase shapes the ligand environment, and actin-associated proteins such as palladin, myopalladin and nexilin link surface recognition to cytoskeletal retraction of the contacting branch.

Centromeric sister chromatid cohesion keeps replicated sister chromatids physically joined at their centromeres until the moment of anaphase, so that spindle attachments can be tested and the two copies of each chromosome are pulled to opposite poles. Loss of this protection produces premature sister separation, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and in meiosis underlies the errors that generate trisomic conceptions. The core activity is protection of centromeric cohesin from cleavage: shugoshin proteins recruit a PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme to dephosphorylate cohesin locally, while BUB1 kinase marks the inner centromere to license that recruitment and links cohesion to spindle assembly checkpoint signalling. N-terminal acetyltransferase subunits and BOD1 modulate the same protective step, MEIKIN adapts it to the reductional division of meiosis I, and CTCF ties centromeric cohesin to chromatin architecture.

Sister chromatids must stay glued together at their centromeres from replication until anaphase, and centromeric sister chromatid cohesion is the process that keeps them so. It matters because premature loss of centromeric cohesion produces unequal chromosome segregation, aneuploid daughter cells and, in oocytes, the chromosome missegregation behind trisomy and age-related infertility. The shugoshin proteins SGO1 and SGO2 mark the inner centromere and recruit a PP2A phosphatase holoenzyme, whose scaffolding subunits PPP2R1A and PPP2R1B appear here, to keep the cohesin ring dephosphorylated and protected from cleavage. The kinase BUB1 phosphorylates centromeric histone H2A to place shugoshin there, linking cohesion protection to the spindle assembly checkpoint and kinetochore geometry; MEIKIN adapts the system for the stepwise, two-division cohesion loss of meiosis. N-terminal acetylation by NAA10/NAA50 and the accessory factor BOD1 tune the same centromeric machinery.

Sister chromatids must stay glued together at their centromeres until every kinetochore is correctly attached to the spindle; controlling how tightly and how long that centromeric cohesion is maintained determines whether chromosomes segregate evenly or a daughter cell inherits the wrong number. The regulation of centromeric sister chromatid cohesion protects cohesin in the pericentromere while cohesin elsewhere along the arms is removed in prophase, and its failure produces premature chromatid separation and aneuploidy. The kinetochore kinase BUB1 is the canonical input, phosphorylating histone H2A at the centromere to recruit shugoshin-type protectors, and it also feeds the spindle assembly checkpoint. The remaining components link this control to chromatin architecture and to Wnt/β-catenin signalling, where CTCF organises cohesin-bound chromatin boundaries and AXIN2, CTNNB1 and the N-terminal acetyltransferase catalytic subunit NAA10 connect proliferative signalling to chromosome segregation fidelity and tumour-associated genome instability.

Epithelia that line the gut, kidney tubules, airways and biliary tree do not merely form barriers; they move salt, water, nutrients and xenobiotics vectorially from one compartment to another, and transepithelial transport is that directed movement across the cell layer. It depends on apical and basolateral membranes being furnished with different transporters and on tight-junction claudins setting the paracellular permeability that determines whether transport is absorptive or secretory. Sodium entry through epithelial sodium channels and Na-coupled cotransporters such as SLC5A1 and the loop-diuretic-sensitive SLC12A1 drives nutrient uptake and urinary concentration; CFTR and anion exchangers supply chloride and bicarbonate secretion; ABC pumps including ABCB1 and ABCC2 export drugs and conjugates into bile and lumen; aquaporins allow the osmotically obliged water to follow. Calcium and purinergic signalling tune secretion. Loss of these steps produces cystic fibrosis, Bartter-type salt wasting, hypomagnesaemia and secretory diarrhoea.

Excretion of acid by the kidney depends largely on shuttling ammonium across the tubular epithelium, and transepithelial ammonium transport is the coordinated set of entry and exit steps that accomplishes it. Ammonium generated from glutamine in the proximal tubule is reabsorbed in the loop of Henle and then secreted into the collecting duct lumen, where it traps protons as NH4+ and allows net acid loss without lowering urine pH to damaging levels. Rhesus-family glycoproteins RHBG and RHCG provide basolateral and apical channels for NH3/NH4+ movement in collecting duct cells, while the cation-chloride cotransporters SLC12A1 and SLC12A2 carry ammonium in place of potassium, coupling it to salt reabsorption; an NHE-family exchanger contributes apical cation flux. Loss of this capacity impairs the renal response to metabolic acidosis and contributes to distal renal tubular acidosis.

Vitamin D3 acquired from skin synthesis or diet is biologically inert until it is hydroxylated, and this metabolic route performs both the activation and the disposal that set circulating hormone levels. It governs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation and immune modulation; loss of the activating step causes vitamin D-dependent rickets, while loss of the catabolic step leads to hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis. Cytochrome P450 enzymes carry out the chemistry: hepatic 25-hydroxylases such as CYP2R1 and CYP27A1 generate the major circulating form, the renal 1alpha-hydroxylase CYP27B1 produces the active hormone, and CYP24A1 initiates inactivation by 24-hydroxylation. Glucuronidation provides a further route to excretion. Endocrine control ties the pathway to mineral homeostasis, with fibroblast growth factor signalling through FGFR1 suppressing activation and promoting catabolism in response to phosphate load.

Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like tags are reversible, and the enzymes that strip them make protein modification by small protein removal the counterweight to ligase activity. By editing or erasing these marks, the pathway decides whether a substrate is destroyed by the proteasome, rerouted through endosomes, or simply resignalled, and it also recycles free ubiquitin so the pool is not exhausted. The bulk of the activity comes from cysteine protease families — the USP, OTU, Josephin, MINDY and UCH deubiquitinases — together with SUMO- and NEDD8-specific proteases and a metalloenzyme class that includes the proteasome-associated PSMD14 and the COP9 signalosome subunit that removes NEDD8 from cullins. Specific effects are wide-ranging: restraint of NF-κB signalling by CYLD, TNFAIP3 and OTULIN, DNA repair control via BAP1, USP1 and BRCC3, and mitophagy through USP30 acting against PRKN. Loss of individual enzymes causes neurodegeneration, inflammatory disease and cancer.

Immune responses depend on the ability of white blood cells to expand clonally once they detect antigen or inflammatory cues, and leukocyte proliferation is that expansion by cell division. It sets the size of a lymphocyte clone, the output of myeloid progenitors, and therefore the strength of an immune response; too little produces immunodeficiency and poor vaccine responses, too much drives autoimmunity, lymphoproliferative disease and leukaemia. Antigen receptors and their proximal kinases such as ZAP70, SYK, LYN and BTK, with adaptors CARD11 and RASGRP1, couple recognition to calcium, MAPK and NF-kB signalling and to cyclin and MYC-driven cell cycle entry. Growth is licensed by cytokines including IL2, IL7, IL15, IL21, CSF1, CSF2 and FLT3LG acting through shared receptor chains and STAT5, and by costimulation via CD28 and CD40. Counterweights are equally represented: CTLA4, PD-L1, PTPN22, CBLB, TNFAIP3 and FOXP3-dependent regulatory restraint impose tolerance and limit expansion.

Immune responses depend on clonal expansion of white blood cells, and this is the control layer that sets how far and how fast that expansion goes. Positive and negative inputs are both represented: growth-promoting cytokines and their receptors (IL2 with its receptor chains, IL7, IL15, IL21, CSF2 and CSF1 with CSF1R) signalling through JAK2, TYK2 and STAT5, antigen receptor proximal kinases such as SYK, ZAP70, LYN and BTK, and costimulatory ligands of the CD28 and TNF superfamilies. Opposing them are checkpoint receptors including CTLA4, PD-1 ligands, BTLA and HAVCR2, phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN22 and INPP5D, ubiquitin ligases, and immunosuppressive enzymes like IDO1 and arginases, alongside FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell activity. Balanced output gives effective clearance of pathogens; loss of restraint underlies autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while excess restraint permits chronic infection and tumour escape.

Immune responses must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this is the braking side of lymphocyte expansion: the set of signals that stop, slow or limit leukocyte proliferation so that clonal bursts resolve, self-tissue is spared and chronic inflammation does not follow. Its failure underlies autoimmunity and lymphoproliferation, while tumours exploit it to evade attack. Much of the work is done by inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands inclu... coinhibitory pairs such as CTLA4 with CD80 and CD86, PD-L1 and PD-L2, BTLA, TIM-3 with galectin-9, and LILRB family receptors, which recruit the phosphatases PTPN6 and PTPN11 and the inositol phosphatase INPP5D to blunt antigen-receptor signalling. Regulatory T cells acting through FOXP3, IL2RA and TGFB1, suppressive metabolism via arginases and IDO1, E3 ligases such as CBLB and ITCH, and IL-10 add further layers of restraint.

Immune responses depend on clonal expansion: after a lymphocyte or myeloid progenitor detects antigen or an inflammatory cue, it must divide many times to generate enough effector cells. Positive regulation of leukocyte proliferation covers the signals that drive or amplify that expansion, and its strength sets the scale of infection control, vaccine responses, and also autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy when it is unrestrained. Growth-promoting cytokines and their receptor chains act through Janus kinases and STAT5 to license cell cycle entry, with interleukin-2 signalling through a shared gamma chain as the prototype. Antigen receptor engagement is transduced by kinases such as ZAP70, SYK and BTK, adaptors including CARD11 and calcineurin-NFAT, while costimulatory ligands of the CD28 and TNF superfamilies, MHC-dependent antigen presentation, and innate Toll-like receptor input through MYD88 and TRAF6 raise the response further.

Interleukin-2 is the growth and survival signal that expands antigen-activated T cells and sustains regulatory T cells, and this pathway covers what a cell does once it encounters that cytokine. The response begins at a receptor built from the high-affinity alpha chain together with shared beta and common gamma chains, which recruit the tyrosine kinases JAK1 and JAK3; these phosphorylate STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT3, driving transcription of proliferation, differentiation and FOXP3-linked tolerance programmes. The phosphatase PTPN2 dampens the same kinases, setting signal duration, while ezrin links receptor engagement to the cortical cytoskeleton. Loss of the gamma chain or JAK3 causes severe combined immunodeficiency, and loss of alpha-chain signalling produces lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity because regulatory T cells fail; pharmacologically, the axis is exploited both to boost and to suppress immunity.

Interleukin-4 is the cytokine that steers immunity toward type 2 responses, and the cellular response to it defines helper T cell polarization, B cell class switching to IgE, and the alternatively activated macrophage. It is the reason allergic asthma and atopic dermatitis are treated by blocking this axis, and the reason anti-helminth defence depends on it. Signalling runs through the IL4 receptor chain paired with the shared gamma chain or IL13RA1, engaging JAK1 and JAK3 to phosphorylate STAT6, with STAT5 contributing; STAT6 then drives GATA3 and a transcriptional programme including the mannose receptor MRC1, eotaxin CCL11, CD40 and NFIL3, while PTPN2 restrains the kinases. Downstream consequences reach beyond transcription to lipogenesis through fatty acid synthase, secretory expansion via XBP1 and HSPA5, and proliferative entry involving CDK4 and MCM2, so target cells change metabolism and division state as well as identity.

Interleukin-12 is the cytokine by which activated dendritic cells and macrophages instruct T cells and NK cells to become interferon-gamma producers, and the cellular response to it is what commits a helper T cell to the Th1 program. Without it, control of intracellular bacteria and mycobacteria fails: loss-of-function in the shared receptor chain IL12RB1 underlies susceptibility to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella disease, while excessive responsiveness contributes to psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, the rationale for antibodies against the shared p40 subunit. The heterodimeric cytokine formed by IL12A and IL12B engages a receptor pair whose associated kinases JAK2 and TYK2 phosphorylate STAT4, driving transcription of interferon-gamma and other Th1 genes. Additional members place this response alongside innate signalling through RIPK2 and modulation by the CD47-SIRPA axis, linking myeloid recognition to cytokine output.

Interleukin-15 is the cytokine that keeps natural killer cells and memory CD8 T cells alive, and the cellular response to it defines how those populations are generated and maintained. Unlike most cytokines, IL-15 is presented on the surface of neighbouring cells bound to its private high-affinity receptor chain, so the signal is delivered by cell contact; the shared beta and gamma chains then recruit JAK1 and JAK3 to phosphorylate STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT3, driving survival, proliferation and cytolytic gene expression. Loss of the gamma chain or JAK3 abolishes this and other related cytokine responses, producing severe combined immunodeficiency with absent NK cells, while excessive IL-15 signalling sustains the intraepithelial lymphocytes that destroy gut mucosa in coeliac disease and feeds large granular lymphocytic leukaemia. The same axis is exploited therapeutically to expand antitumour lymphocytes.

Interleukin-18 is an inflammasome-derived cytokine, cleaved from an inactive precursor by caspase activity, and the cellular response to it drives interferon-gamma production by T and NK cells, neutrophil recruitment, and epithelial barrier defence in the gut and skin. Signalling begins at a heterodimeric receptor formed by IL18R1 and the accessory chain IL18RAP, which recruits adaptor and kinase components shared with Toll-like receptor pathways, including RIPK2 and TICAM2, and converges on NF-kB with the atypical regulator NFKBIZ shaping the transcriptional output; AKT1 and the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1 provide a parallel survival and proliferation arm, while CYLD restrains the response through deubiquitination. Inclusion of NLRP6 and CASP4 links the response back to the inflammasome that generates the ligand, and claudin-1 marks the tight-junction remodelling that follows. Excess signalling contributes to autoinflammation, macrophage activation syndrome and colitis; loss compromises antimicrobial immunity.

Cyclic nucleotide transport moves cAMP, cGMP and related cyclic dinucleotides across membranes, which sets how far and how long a second messenger signal reaches and provides an alternative to phosphodiesterase degradation for terminating it. Export also matters immunologically: the same carriers release cyclic di-nucleotides and take up bacterial or tumour-derived cGAMP, feeding the STING surveillance pathway that triggers interferon responses. The ABC transporters ABCC4 and ABCC5 act as ATP-driven efflux pumps for cAMP and cGMP, shaping intracellular signalling tone in platelets, vascular smooth muscle and secretory epithelia, and their activity contributes to resistance against nucleotide analogue drugs. Volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits provide a separate, swelling-activated conduit for cGAMP between cells, while SLC19A1 and SLC46A2 import it. Together these routes make cyclic nucleotide signalling intercellular rather than strictly cell-autonomous.

Cyclic nucleotides act as second messengers inside cells and as immune signals between them, and cyclic nucleotide transport is how they cross membranes rather than being degraded in place. Efflux pumps of the ABCC family export cAMP and cGMP from the cytosol, providing a route to terminate or tune signalling alongside phosphodiesterase hydrolysis, and ABCC4 also handles nucleotide analogue drugs. A second arm moves cyclic dinucleotides: volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits pass 2'3'-cGAMP between cells, while the reduced folate carrier SLC19A1 and SLC46A2 import it, allowing cGAS-derived messenger to activate STING in neighbouring and bystander cells. This transfer shapes interferon responses to cytosolic DNA, antitumour immunity and the efficacy of STING agonists, linking nucleotide metabolism to innate immune communication.

response to interleukin-6 is the set of cellular changes triggered when a cell encounters IL-6, the cytokine that drives the acute phase response, fever, emergency granulopoiesis and the switch from innate inflammation to antibody-producing plasma cell differentiation. Its chronic activation underlies rheumatoid arthritis, Castleman disease, cachexia and inflammation-associated cancer, which is why the receptor is a major therapeutic target. IL-6 binds IL6R and signals through the shared gp130 subunit, activating JAK1 and JAK2 to phosphorylate STAT3, which enters the nucleus and induces acute phase and survival genes together with NF- involvedB subunits RELA and NFKB1. Feedback restraint is built in: SOCS3 and phosphatases such as PTPN2 terminate JAK activity, and several microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-125 families tune the output. Downstream effects include hepatic and myeloid gene programmes, neutrophil antimicrobial products such as LCN2 and CAMP, and FGF23-linked mineral regulation.

Interleukin-6 is the cytokine that converts local inflammation into a systemic response, and this is the cellular reaction to it: the acute phase response in liver, fever and hepcidin-driven iron sequestration, plasma cell differentiation, and the emergency granulopoiesis that raises neutrophil output. Persistent signalling of this kind drives rheumatoid arthritis, Castleman disease and cytokine storm, which is why the receptor is a drug target. Ligand engages IL6R with the shared signalling subunit IL6ST (gp130), activating JAK1 and JAK2 to phosphorylate STAT3, with parallel input through SRC, RIPK1 and NF-κB subunits. Negative feedback is built in: SOCS3 and the phosphatase PTPN2 restrain the kinases, and several microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-125 families tune the output. Downstream transcription factors including CEBPA, SPI1, GFI1 and MYB translate the signal into myeloid and hepatic gene programmes.

D-aspartate is an endogenous amino acid that acts at NMDA receptors and accumulates in brain and neuroendocrine tissue, and its movement across membranes is handled by the same high-affinity excitatory amino acid carriers that clear L-glutamate. SLC1A1, SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 are sodium-dependent transporters that take up dicarboxylic amino acids, including the D-enantiomer, and their action keeps extracellular excitatory signalling molecules low enough to prevent tonic receptor activation and excitotoxic neuronal death. Most of this uptake capacity sits in astrocytes, consistent with the presence of the astrocytic intermediate filament GFAP here, so glial cells set the concentration of D-aspartate that neurons experience. Because transport is driven by sodium and potassium gradients, it couples amino acid clearance to ion homeostasis, and its loss is associated with seizure susceptibility and neurodegeneration.

Aspartate is both an excitatory amino acid in the brain and a node in nitrogen and redox metabolism, and moving it across membranes is what keeps those two roles separated and supplied. Plasma-membrane carriers of the excitatory amino acid transporter family clear aspartate and glutamate from the synaptic cleft into astrocytes and neurons, terminating excitatory signalling and preventing excitotoxic damage; related sodium-dependent neutral amino acid exchangers handle overlapping substrates. On the inner mitochondrial membrane, calcium-binding aspartate/glutamate carriers run the malate-aspartate shuttle, exporting aspartate to the cytosol in exchange for glutamate and a proton so that cytosolic NADH reducing equivalents reach the respiratory chain; loss of the liver-type carrier causes citrin deficiency with hyperammonaemia. Mitochondrial glutamate carriers and a related uncoupling-protein family member complete the transport capacity that links neurotransmitter cycling, ureagenesis and aspartate supply for nucleotide synthesis.

A dying cell must advertise itself, and exposure of phosphatidylserine on the apoptotic cell surface is that advertisement. Normally phosphatidylserine is held in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane; when apoptosis begins, lipid asymmetry collapses and the anionic lipid flips outward, where macrophages and neighbouring cells read it through bridging molecules and receptors as an 'eat-me' signal. Prompt recognition matters because corpses that are not cleared leak their contents and provoke autoimmunity and inflammation. The scrambling activity is carried by XKR-family proteins, of which XKR8 is activated by caspase cleavage during apoptosis, alongside phospholipid scramblases; calcium entry through channels can drive comparable exposure in non-apoptotic settings. The process links death receptor signalling, as initiated by FAS ligand, to the phagocytic disposal step that ends apoptosis, and also contributes to platelet procoagulant surfaces.

Hydrogen sulfide is both a toxic gas and an endogenous signalling molecule, and its metabolism keeps the two roles in balance by generating it from sulfur amino acids and oxidizing it away before it accumulates. Production runs through the transsulfuration route, where cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase act on homocysteine and cysteine, with a sulfurtransferase supplying an additional mitochondrial source from persulfide intermediates. Disposal depends on mitochondrial sulfide oxidation; loss of the persulfide dioxygenase ETHE1 causes ethylmalonic encephalopathy, in which sulfide poisons cytochrome c oxidase. The signalling output relaxes vascular smooth muscle, tunes mitochondrial respiration and protects against oxidative stress, and transcriptional control by SP1 together with microRNA-mediated regulation sets how much enzyme is available. The same reactions link this chemistry to cysteine and glutathione supply and to homocysteine clearance.

Large stretches of the genome are kept compact, late-replicating and transcriptionally silent, and heterochromatin organization is how that state is specified, built and propagated through division. It keeps repetitive DNA, transposons, pericentromeric satellites and the inactive X quiet, provides the rigid platform centromeres need for kinetochore assembly, and anchors silent domains to the nuclear lamina. Histone H3K9 methyltransferases such as SUV39H1 and SETDB1 create the mark that HP1 proteins read and spread; Polycomb complexes deposit and interpret H3K27 methylation for developmental gene repression; DNA methyltransferases with UHRF1, methyl-CpG readers, histone deacetylases, ATP-dependent remodellers and linker histones consolidate compaction. A piRNA-guided arm silences retrotransposons in germ cells. Loss of this control derepresses repeats, destabilises centromeres and drives developmental syndromes, immunodeficiency with chromosomal instability, and cancer-associated epigenetic reprogramming.

Epithelial and endothelial sheets only work as barriers because each cell is sealed to its neighbours by a belt of tight junctions at the apical margin, and this is the assembly programme that builds them. Without it, solutes and pathogens leak across the paracellular space, apical-basal polarity is lost, and the blood-brain and gut barriers fail. Claudins such as CLDN1, CLDN3 and CLDN5 polymerise into sealing strands whose composition sets ion selectivity, occludin and the tricellulin-related MARVEL proteins join them, and junctional adhesion molecule F11R links the strands to the cytoplasm. Scaffolds including ZO-1, afadin and PARD3 anchor the belt to actin, while Rho-family signalling through RAC1, ROCK1/2 and PAK2, vesicle delivery via RAB13, and transcriptional input from GRHL2 and the SNAI factors determine whether junctions are built or dismantled during wound healing, inflammation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition.

Epithelia, endothelia, muscle and nerve all sit on a basement membrane, a thin sheet of dense extracellular matrix that separates cells from the underlying connective tissue, anchors them, filters what passes and presents growth factor cues. Its assembly is a matter of secreting the right components and then cross-linking them into a coherent sheet: a lysyl hydroxylase acting on collagen lysines to license glycosylation and stable triple helices, a peroxidase that forms sulfilimine bonds within collagen IV networks, netrin-4 binding laminin lattices to modulate their density, and collagen VIII chains contributed by endothelium and corneal Descemet's membrane. Failure of these steps produces fragile or malformed membranes, seen clinically as anterior segment eye malformations, corneal dystrophy and connective tissue disease, and it alters vascular and epithelial barrier behaviour during development, angiogenesis and tumour invasion.

Vitamin C circulates in two forms, and cells can take up the oxidized one, dehydroascorbate, as well as ascorbate itself. This route matters because dehydroascorbate resembles glucose closely enough to enter through facilitative hexose carriers, so tissues rich in these transporters can recover vitamin C from its oxidized form and regenerate ascorbate intracellularly by glutathione-dependent reduction. Erythrocytes, endothelium and the brain rely on this recycling to sustain antioxidant capacity and the ascorbate-dependent hydroxylases of collagen synthesis and catecholamine production without continuous dietary resupply. The GLUT family members listed span the ubiquitous glucose carrier of erythrocytes and the blood-brain barrier, the insulin-responsive muscle and adipose transporter, intestinal and hepatic isoforms, and a urate carrier, alongside a sodium-dependent ascorbate transporter that handles the reduced vitamin. Competition with glucose for these carriers links hyperglycaemia to impaired vitamin C uptake.

When misfolded or aggregation-prone proteins exceed a cell's capacity to refold or degrade them, they are collected into discrete deposits; inclusion body assembly is the regulated aggregation, arrangement and bonding of such components into those structures. Far from being passive debris, sequestration into a single site is protective, concentrating toxic oligomers where autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system can act on them, and its products are the diagnostic hallmarks of neurodegeneration — tau tangles, synuclein-containing bodies, ubiquitinated inclusions in myopathy and motor neuron disease. The machinery is largely chaperone-based: HSPA1A/HSPB-partner J-domain cochaperones such as DNAJB1, DNAJB2 and DNAJB6 suppress or remodel amyloid assembly, BAG3 couples HSP70 clients to selective autophagy, HDAC6 and VCP route ubiquitinated cargo toward aggresome formation, and parkin marks substrates for disposal. Extracellular chaperones including clusterin and apolipoprotein E influence deposition outside the cell.\n

When misfolded protein overwhelms the proteasome, cells sweep the excess into a single perinuclear inclusion rather than let it accumulate diffusely, and aggresome assembly is that sweeping step. It buys time for degradation by autophagy, protects against proteotoxic stress in neurons and muscle, and its failure is linked to neurodegeneration and myofibrillar myopathy. Ubiquitinated cargo is recognised and hauled along microtubules to the centrosomal region by dynein, with HDAC6 acting as the adaptor that reads polyubiquitin and couples it to the motor, and BAG3 routing chaperone-bound clients into the same destination as part of chaperone-assisted selective autophagy. The AAA-ATPase VCP extracts and remodels ubiquitinated substrates, while the E3 ligase parkin contributes the ubiquitin marks that specify cargo. The process sits at the junction of the ubiquitin-proteasome system, autophagy and cytoskeletal transport.

Cells read secreted growth factors as instructions to divide, differentiate, migrate, survive or remodel their surroundings, and the response to growth factor stimulus collects the receptors, adaptors and transcriptional machinery that convert those cues into altered gene expression and behaviour. Several ligand families appear together: FGFs with their FGFR receptors, VEGFs with FLT1/KDR, PDGFs, HGF, neurotrophins acting through TRK receptors, and the TGF-beta/BMP/activin superfamily signalling via type I and type II serine-threonine kinase receptors to SMAD complexes. Downstream, GRB2-SOS-RAS-ERK, PI3K-AKT-mTOR and SRC-focal adhesion routes are represented, along with dedicated brakes such as SPRY and SPRED proteins, SMAD6/7, SMURF ubiquitin ligases, extracellular BMP antagonists including noggin and gremlins, and many microRNAs. This signalling shapes skeletal, vascular, neural and epithelial development, wound healing and fibrosis, and its deregulation drives tumour growth and angiogenesis.

Cells detect epidermal growth factor through receptor tyrosine kinases of the EGFR/ERBB family and convert that cue into proliferation, survival, migration and changes in gene expression. This response underlies epithelial wound repair and developmental growth, and its constitutive activation by receptor mutation or amplification drives carcinomas, making the same components the targets of anti-EGFR antibodies and kinase inhibitors. Ligand binding triggers receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, recruiting adaptors and the phosphatase PTPN11 to launch the ERK cascade through MAPK1 and MAPK3, and the PI3K-PDPK1-AKT1 arm, alongside PLCG1 signalling; immediate-early transcription via FOS follows. Negative regulation is built in, with ERRFI1 restraining the receptor, DUSP phosphatases reversing MAPK phosphorylation, DAB2 directing receptor endocytosis, and ZFP36 family proteins destabilising induced transcripts. Cytoskeletal effectors such as CFL1, BAIAP2 and IQGAP1 link the signal to motility and shape change.

Bile acids emulsify dietary fat and act as hormones, so their synthesis from cholesterol must be matched to demand; regulation of bile acid biosynthesis is the feedback system that sets that rate and prevents the detergent toxicity and cholestatic liver injury that follow overproduction. The controlled step is hepatic CYP7A1, the rate-limiting cholesterol 7alpha-hydroxylase. Bile acids returning from the gut activate the nuclear receptor FXR (NR1H4), which in the ileum induces FGF19; that hormone travels to the liver and signals through FGFR4 to shut down CYP7A1 transcription, with MALRD1 supporting the intestinal arm. Additional inputs tie the pathway to cholesterol handling and metabolic timing: SIRT1 and the clock repressor NR1D1 impose circadian and nutrient-sensitive control, PROX1 acts as a transcriptional corepressor, and STAR/STARD4 govern sterol delivery for side-chain oxidation. The system links lipid absorption to whole-body cholesterol disposal.

Proteins that fold correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum must be packaged and sent onward, while those that fail must be held back and destroyed; this regulation of protein exit from the ER controls the balance between the two fates and so sets the quality of everything delivered to the secretory pathway and cell surface. Export is executed by COPII: the SAR1 GTPases initiate budding, SEC24 paralogues select cargo, and SEC13-SEC31 forms the outer coat cage, with SEC16 organising exit sites. Opposing this, misfolded substrates are recognised by mannose-trimming and lectin factors such as EDEM1/2 and OS9, retrotranslocated via derlins, and ubiquitinated by ER-associated degradation enzymes including UBE2J1 and UBE2G2. Chaperone-like escorts and lipid flippase subunits govern exit of specific clients, linking this step to cholesterol sensing, membrane protein biogenesis, and diseases of protein misfolding.

Proteins that fail to fold correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum must be prevented from continuing along the secretory route, and this set describes the machinery that restrains protein exit from the ER by committing terminally misfolded or regulated substrates to degradation instead of forward transport. The lectins OS9 and ERLEC1 recognise trimmed N-glycans on unfolded clients and deliver them to membrane-embedded Derlin channels for retrotranslocation to the cytosol, where the ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes UBE2J1 and UBE2G2 work with ER-resident ligase complexes to mark substrates for proteasomal destruction; YOD1 is a deubiquitinase that trims chains to permit extraction, and SVIP acts as a brake on this degradation machinery. INSIG1 applies the same logic to sterol homeostasis, retaining SREBP cleavage-activating protein in the ER when cholesterol is abundant. Loss of this quality control allows aberrant proteins to reach the secretory pathway and underlies ER stress-associated disease.

Newly folded secretory and membrane proteins leave the endoplasmic reticulum only after being selected, concentrated and packaged, and this pathway covers the events that increase the rate and extent of that export. It sustains secretion, plasma membrane delivery and organelle biogenesis; when export stalls, cargo accumulates in the ER and triggers stress and degradation responses. The core machinery is the COPII system: the SAR1 GTPases initiate budding at ER exit sites organised by SEC16, SEC24 paralogues read cargo sorting signals, and SEC13-SEC31 forms the outer cage that shapes the vesicle. Accessory factors act as cargo receptors or chaperone-like escorts, including BCAP31 for membrane proteins, SORL1 for sorting itinerant cargo, and the TMEM30 subunits required for P4-ATPase flippases to exit. Mannosidase-like EDEM proteins work alongside, diverting misfolded glycoproteins toward degradation rather than export.

Glycogen is the body's rapidly mobilisable glucose store, and this pathway covers the controls that decide whether it is built up or broken down. In liver it buffers blood glucose between meals; in muscle it fuels contraction, and loss of control underlies insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes and glycogen storage disorders. Insulin acting through its receptor, IRS adaptors and AKT suppresses GSK3, relieving inhibition of glycogen synthase, while glucagon receptor signalling pushes the opposite way. A family of regulatory subunits targets protein phosphatase 1 to glycogen particles so that synthase and phosphorylase are dephosphorylated where the polymer is stored, and phosphorylase kinase subunits together with the AMPK gamma subunit couple breakdown to energy demand and calcium. Glucokinase, hexokinase-independent fructose entry and several microRNAs add further tiers of regulation at the level of substrate supply and transcript abundance.

Glycogen stores buffer blood glucose and fuel muscle contraction, and this pathway covers the braking signals that restrain glycogen synthesis and turnover so that carbon is not committed to storage when it is not wanted. Its best-characterised effectors are the glycogen synthase kinase 3 isoforms, which phosphorylate and inactivate glycogen synthase, an inhibition that insulin relieves; losing this restraint contributes to the dysregulated hepatic and muscle glucose handling seen in insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Negative input also arrives through dampening of insulin receptor signalling itself, by the adaptor GRB10 and the ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase ENPP1, through phosphoinositide turnover, through AMP-activated kinase regulatory subunits that sense energy charge, through the glycogen-targeting phosphatase subunit PPP1R3B, and through microRNAs that lower the levels of the enzymes involved. The net theme is suppression of storage in favour of glucose availability.

Glycogen is the cell's rapidly mobilizable glucose store, and this pathway covers the signals and enzymes that push glycogen turnover upward — both its synthesis after a meal and its breakdown when glucose is needed. The dominant input is insulin: hormone binding to its receptor recruits IRS adaptors and activates AKT1 and AKT2, which relieve inhibition of glycogen synthase, while related growth factors IGF1 and IGF2 feed the same axis. Targeting subunits such as PPP1R3B, PPP1R3E and PPP1R3G direct protein phosphatase 1 catalytic activity onto glycogen particles, dephosphorylating the synthetic and degradative enzymes; phosphorylase kinase subunits PHKA1 and PHKG2 instead drive mobilization, and glucokinase commits incoming glucose to storage in liver.
