Coordinated control of these steps sets hepatic and muscle glucose output; its failure underlies insulin resistance and glycogen storage disease.

Before a gene can be transcribed, a large protein assembly must be built at its promoter to position RNA polymerase on the template and license synthesis of the first nucleotides. Preinitiation complex assembly is that step, and it is where most regulation of gene expression converges: activators, repressors and chromatin state all act by promoting or blocking it. TBP and the TAF subunits of TFIID recognise promoter DNA, TFIIA, TFIIB and TFIIE join in ordered fashion, and the multisubunit Mediator complex bridges DNA-bound transcription factors such as CREB1, TP53, ESR1 and thyroid hormone receptor to the polymerase. Related factor sets serve the other polymerases, with UBTF and SL1 components acting at ribosomal RNA promoters and BRF1/BRF2 with BDP1 at polymerase III genes. Chromatin remodelling subunits and the NC2 repressor pair tune how readily the complex forms.

The 22 tRNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA must be chemically decorated after transcription before they can decode messages accurately on the mitoribosome, and mitochondrial tRNA modification supplies those covalent marks. Because the mitochondrial genome encodes only subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, defects here are read out as combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, with cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis, encephalopathy and sideroblastic anaemia among the presentations. The enzymes act on distinct positions: methyltransferases and a methylthiotransferase modify anticodon-loop and other bases, pseudouridine synthases isomerise uridines, a GTP-dependent pair installs taurinomethyl groups at the wobble position to set codon reading, and a threonylcarbamoyl-transferring module modifies A37 adjacent to the anticodon. TRMT10C works within the RNase P complex that also cleaves mitochondrial transcripts, tying base modification to maturation of the primary polycistronic RNA and, through it, to mitochondrial translation capacity.

Sunlight crosslinks adjacent pyrimidines into cyclobutane dimers and 6-4 photoproducts that block transcription and replication, and UV-damage excision repair is the route by which these lesions are cut out of the genome and the gap resynthesised. Its loss underlies xeroderma pigmentosum and extreme sensitivity to sunlight, with massive skin cancer risk, so this chemistry is what keeps keratinocytes and melanocytes mutation-free under daily UV exposure. Damage is recognised at the helix distortion by XPC and by DDB2 acting within a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase built on DDB1 and CUL4B, which ubiquitinates histones and repair factors to open chromatin; XPA verifies the lesion, the ERCC1-containing nuclease incises the damaged strand, and replicative polymerases fill in. Chromatin remodelling by INO80 and its subunit ACTR5, together with SIRT1-dependent regulation, tunes access to lesions, while MC1R signalling links pigmentation status to repair capacity.

Regulatory non-coding RNAs are not made in their final form; they are cut, trimmed, modified and loaded onto effector proteins, and regulatory ncRNA processing is the set of steps that turns a primary transcript into a functional silencing guide. Its output sets post-transcriptional gene expression across development, stem cell self-renewal and germ cell biology. Two arms are visible here: microRNA maturation, where Drosha with its partner DGCR8 crops the hairpin in the nucleus and Dicer completes the cut before an Argonaute and a GW182-family scaffold assemble a silencing complex, and the piRNA arm, in which PIWI proteins, Tudor-domain partners, the helicase MOV10L1, mitochondrial PLD6 and the trimmer PNLDC1 build guides that keep transposons silent in the germline. Terminal nucleotidyltransferases, deaminases, methyltransferases and RNA-binding proteins such as LIN28A tune which precursors survive. Loss of these steps causes infertility, developmental failure and widespread miRNA dysregulation in cancer.

Small regulatory RNAs such as microRNAs only become functional after precursor transcripts are cleaved and trimmed, and the regulation of regulatory ncRNA processing is how cells set how much mature product emerges from that route. Because a single microRNA family can tune hundreds of transcripts, changing processing efficiency shifts whole programmes of differentiation, stemness and inflammation; loss of control here contributes to tumour progression and to failures of developmental timing. Control acts at several levels: DGCR8 confers precursor recognition on the nuclear cleavage step, TARBP2 and PRKRA partner the cytoplasmic dicing machinery, LIN28A and LIN28B bind let-7 precursors and block their maturation, and BCDIN3D methylates pre-microRNA ends to impair processing. Signalling inputs feed in as well, with TGFB1 and BMP4 ligands and IL6-STAT3 activity altering the maturation of particular species in response to extracellular cues.

Small RNAs only silence genes once they are loaded into an Argonaute protein, and this loading step is what RISC complex assembly accomplishes. A precursor duplex is cut to size by Dicer acting with its double-stranded RNA-binding partners, the duplex is handed to one of the four Argonaute proteins, and the passenger strand is discarded so that the guide strand remains base-paired to the protein and free to find complementary mRNAs. The result is the effector that carries out microRNA-mediated repression and RNA interference, setting translational output and transcript stability across development, differentiation and antiviral defence; only one Argonaute here has slicer activity, so most targets are repressed rather than cleaved. Editing and helicase activities acting on the same double-stranded substrates influence which duplexes enter the pathway, and loss of the machinery destabilises miRNA populations and broad gene-expression programmes.

Cells build discrete internal structures, and this broad organelle assembly programme covers the construction of those compartments and machines from their parts: centrioles and centrosomes, cilia and flagella, autophagosomes, lysosome-related organelles, ribosomes, the mitotic spindle and kinetochore, sarcomeres, and stress granules and P-bodies. Its breadth reflects how much physiology depends on getting these structures made correctly, from sperm motility and airway mucociliary clearance to chromosome segregation and muscle contraction. Recurring themes include centriole duplication factors such as PLK4, SASS6 and STIL, intraflagellar transport and transition-zone modules that build and gate the cilium, axonemal dynein assembly factors, core autophagy machinery from ULK1 and BECN1 through the ATG conjugation systems, ESCRT components for membrane scission, Rab GTPases and their TBC-domain regulators for trafficking, and nucleolar factors for ribosome biogenesis. Defects produce ciliopathies, primary ciliary dyskinesia, microcephaly, pigmentation and bleeding disorders, and cardiomyopathy.

How long an mRNA survives in the cytoplasm sets how much protein it makes, and this pathway describes the protective arm of that decision: RNA-binding proteins dock onto a coding region instability determinant within the open reading frame and shield the transcript from endonucleolytic attack and deadenylation-dependent decay. The classic client is MYC mRNA, whose half-life is raised when IGF2BP1 and its paralogues coat the determinant, linking message stability directly to proliferative output. Partners include hnRNP D, hnRNP U, SYNCRIP, YBX1 and the DHX9 helicase, alongside PABPC1 and its interactor PAIP1 acting at the poly(A) tail, so stabilization is coordinated with translational efficiency rather than separate from it. Because IGF2BP proteins are oncofetal and re-expressed in tumours, this determinant-based protection contributes to sustained oncogene expression, and it also governs localized messages in migrating and developing cells.

How long a messenger RNA survives in the cytoplasm is set largely by proteins that dock onto its 3' untranslated region, and this pathway covers the binding events that prolong rather than shorten transcript half-life. It determines how much protein is made from an existing pool of mRNA, which matters most for transcripts whose levels must change quickly: cytokine and inflammatory messages, cell cycle regulators, and germ-cell and muscle differentiation programmes. HuR family proteins such as ELAVL1 bind AU-rich elements and protect the message, opposing destabilizing factors like ZFP36 that target the same sequences; p38 signalling through MAPK14 and MAPKAPK2 shifts this balance during inflammatory and stress responses. Other members act in specialized contexts, including QKI and RBM24 in myelination and muscle, DAZ family proteins in spermatogenesis, and non-canonical poly(A) polymerases that extend tails. Failure of this control underlies chronic inflammation and contributes to tumour growth.

protein K48-linked ubiquitination is the tagging step that commits a protein to destruction by the 26S proteasome, building ubiquitin chains linked through lysine 48 on substrates that must be removed on schedule. It sets the half-life of cell cycle regulators, misfolded secretory proteins, transcription factors and damaged mitochondrial proteins, so its failure produces aberrant proliferation, proteotoxic stress and neurodegeneration. The genes span the enzymatic cascade: E2 conjugating enzymes such as UBE2R2, UBE2G1/2 and UBE2D family members that dictate chain linkage, cullin-RING ligases assembled from CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and F-box receptors like BTRC and SKP2, the anaphase-promoting complex that drives mitotic exit, and ER membrane ligases including SYVN1 and AMFR that execute ER-associated degradation. TRIM and HECT ligases add substrate specificity in antiviral and inflammatory signalling, where degradation of adaptors terminates the response.

Attaching a ubiquitin chain linked through lysine 48 is the canonical way a cell marks a protein for destruction by the 26S proteasome, and it underlies the timed removal of cell cycle regulators, misfolded proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, and signalling intermediates that must be switched off. E2 conjugating enzymes of the UBE2D, UBE2G, UBE2R and UBE2A/B families build the chain while cullin-RING and multisubunit E3 ligases select the substrate: SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 complexes with F-box receptors such as SKP2 and BTRC, CUL3 with BTB/kelch adaptors, the anaphase-promoting complex with its many ANAPC and CDC subunits, and RING or HECT enzymes including HUWE1, ITCH, PRKN and the ER-resident SYVN1 and AMFR that drive retrotranslocation-coupled degradation. Degradative ubiquitination of this kind governs mitotic progression, protein quality control, antiviral and inflammatory signalling, and its failure contributes to tumorigenesis and neurodegeneration.

Neutrophils kill targeted cells and microbes directly, and the machinery collected here is what makes that killing possible: granule proteases, oxidant generation, antimicrobial peptides and the extracellular DNA traps that trap and expose pathogens. This is a front-line arm of innate immunity, and when it is weak, bacterial and fungal infection follows, while when it is excessive the same proteases and oxidants damage host tissue, as in acute lung injury, vasculitis and chronic inflammatory disease. Serine proteases such as elastase, cathepsin G and azurocidin degrade microbial and host substrates after release from azurophilic granules; the NADPH oxidase subunit NCF1 supports the respiratory burst; DNASE1 and DNASE1L3 govern the turnover of extracellular DNA, including trap remnants whose persistence drives autoimmunity. Receptor and adaptor components including TREM1 and MYD88 amplify activation, and arginase-1 release additionally restrains surrounding lymphocytes.

Neutrophils are the first phagocytes recruited to bacterial infection, and their capacity to kill ingested or extracellular organisms is what limits pyogenic infection before adaptive immunity engages. Killing draws on two arsenals: the oxidative burst, in which the NADPH oxidase subunit NCF1 supports superoxide generation in the phagosome, and the granule proteases, with neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G and azurocidin degrading bacterial envelope components and contributing to extracellular trap-associated antimicrobial activity. D-amino acid oxidase adds hydrogen peroxide from bacterial D-amino acid substrates. Upstream, Toll-like receptor signalling through MYD88, the thrombin receptor F2RL1 and the triggering receptor TREM1 license and amplify the response, while chemokine signalling brings cells to the site. Loss of oxidase function produces chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent bacterial and fungal abscesses; unrestrained protease release instead drives tissue injury in inflammatory lung disease.

Neutrophil-mediated killing of gram-negative bacterium is the effector step of innate antibacterial defence in which a recruited neutrophil destroys an ingested or surface-bound gram-negative organism. It underlies clearance of enteric and respiratory pathogens, and its failure leaves patients with recurrent pyogenic infection and endotoxaemia, while its excess drives tissue injury in sepsis and acute lung inflammation. The genes span chemotactic recruitment, activation and armament: a chemokine that brings granulocytes to infected tissue, thrombin and its receptor linking coagulation to leukocyte activation, and a myeloid immunoglobulin-family receptor that amplifies inflammatory responses to bacterial contact. Killing itself depends on granule contents such as neutrophil elastase, which degrades outer membrane proteins of gram-negative bacteria, alongside oxidative mechanisms generating hydrogen peroxide from amino acid substrates. The pathway thus connects chemotaxis, phagocytosis, degranulation and oxidative burst into a single microbicidal program.

Neutrophils are the first responders that clear gram-negative bacteria from infected tissue, and this pathway covers the killing step itself: recognition of the microbe followed by deployment of proteolytic and oxidative weapons within phagosomes and at the site of infection. Loss of this capacity leaves patients with recurrent pyogenic infection, while excessive or misdirected activity damages host tissue, as in the lung injury attributed to unrestrained neutrophil elastase. The genes involved span several arms of the response: the serine protease ELANE degrades bacterial outer membrane proteins and virulence factors, a chemokine recruits further neutrophils, TREM1 amplifies inflammatory activation on myeloid cells, and thrombin with its receptor PAR2 links coagulation to inflammatory signalling. D-amino acid oxidase contributes oxidative antimicrobial chemistry by generating hydrogen peroxide from bacterial D-amino acids, connecting innate defence to peroxide-dependent killing.

Neutrophils kill targets with oxidants, granule proteases and extruded DNA traps, and this pathway covers the signals that dial that killing up or down. Tuning matters because unrestrained neutrophil cytotoxicity damages host tissue in sepsis, vasculitis and autoimmune disease, while too little leaves bacterial and fungal infection unchecked. The members act at different points: a chemokine of the interleukin-8 family recruits and primes neutrophils, a protease-activated receptor couples extracellular serine proteases such as trypsin and tryptase to neutrophil activation, and the proopiomelanocortin-derived peptides provide melanocortin and opioid restraint on inflammatory effector function. Arginase depletes extracellular arginine, limiting nitric oxide production and suppressing effector activity, and the secreted nucleases degrade extracellular chromatin, dismantling neutrophil extracellular traps. Loss of that nuclease-mediated clearance leaves DNA-protein complexes that drive lupus-like autoimmunity, linking this regulation to self-tolerance as well as host defence.

When a ribosome stalls in the middle of elongation — on a stable RNA structure, a damaged base, or a hard-to-decode stretch — the transcript is cleaved and destroyed rather than translated, and no-go decay is the surveillance route that carries this out. It protects cells from accumulating truncated and potentially toxic polypeptides and keeps ribosomes from being sequestered on defective messages, working alongside the rescue machinery that splits and recycles the stalled subunits. The central activity is a ribosome-dissociation module in which PELO, a release-factor-like protein, partners with the GTPases HBS1L and GTPBP2 to recognise an empty A site and free the subunits, after which exonucleolytic activity associated with the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex and RNA-binding regulators such as CSDE1 shape degradation of the transcript body. Loss of this quality control causes neurodegeneration in model organisms, linking translational fidelity to neuronal survival.

Getting proteins to the endoplasmic reticulum and keeping them there is the first step of the secretory pathway and of ER-based quality control. Newly made polypeptides are captured at the ribosome by nascent-chain associated factors such as BTF3 and NACA and delivered to the ER membrane, where chaperones including the Hsp70 BiP (HSPA5) and protein disulfide isomerases assist folding. Residents are retained or retrieved rather than lost to the secretory flow: KDEL receptors return escaped soluble ER proteins from the Golgi, and RER1 and BCAP29/BCAP31 retain or sort membrane cargo, while OS9 diverts terminally misfolded glycoproteins to degradation. SEC16A/B and MIA2/MIA3 organize ER exit sites for onward transport, and INSIG1/2 exemplify regulated ER residence that couples sterol sensing to cholesterol synthesis. Failure produces protein mislocalization, ER stress and impaired secretion.

Newly folded secretory and membrane proteins do not leave the endoplasmic reticulum at random; they are concentrated at discrete exit sites where COPII carriers form, and this pathway covers the delivery and retention of cargo and machinery at those sites. It determines which proteins enter the secretory route and how fast, and it matters most for bulky cargo such as procollagen, whose export depends on TANGO1-family proteins encoded by MIA3 and MIA2 acting at the exit site to build large carriers. Scaffolding proteins SEC16A and SEC16B define exit site organization on the ER membrane, the Arf-activating factor GBF1 supports coat recruitment, and BCAP31 with its relative BCAP29 chaperone specific membrane cargo toward export. Failure impairs collagen secretion and connective tissue formation, and disturbs the general capacity of cells to deliver proteins to the Golgi and cell surface.

Bone maturation covers the steps that turn a formed skeletal element into a fully functional, mineralized, load-bearing bone, separate from the shaping events that gave it its outline. It sets adult stature and bone strength, and its disturbance produces skeletal dysplasias, rickets-like mineralization defects, dwarfism and osteopetrosis. Endocrine input dominates: growth hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1, parathyroid hormone and leptin set the pace of growth plate activity, while FGFR3 signalling restrains chondrocyte proliferation and BMP2 with its antagonist gremlin balances osteogenic commitment. Matrix maturation depends on proteoglycan glycosylation and heparan sulfate synthesis, on ADAMTS proteinases and thrombospondin, and on PHOSPHO1-dependent generation of phosphate for hydroxyapatite deposition. Ciliary transport, semaphorin-plexin cues, RhoA cytoskeletal signalling and osteoclast vesicle trafficking through SNX10 couple mechanical and cellular remodelling to final bone quality.

Ubiquitin chains built through lysine 11 of the ubiquitin moiety are a degradation signal, and this pathway covers the enzymes that assemble them. Its best-understood use is in mitosis: the anaphase-promoting complex, represented here by its full subunit roster including the cullin-like scaffold, the RING subunit and the substrate-recognition adaptors, together with its activator FZR1, cooperates with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S to tag cyclins and securin for proteasomal destruction so that sister chromatids separate and cells exit mitosis on schedule. Loss of this timing causes chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy. Beyond the cell cycle, other RING and HECT ligases listed here, among them PRKN, RNF4 and RNF115, use K11 or mixed K11/K48 linkages in protein quality control, mitophagy and endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation, making the linkage a general instruction for turnover rather than a signalling mark.

Vertebrate embryos look outwardly symmetric but place the heart, stomach, spleen and lung lobes asymmetrically, and left/right axis specification is the process that assigns those sides relative to the anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral axes. It matters because its failure produces situs inversus, heterotaxy and the complex congenital heart malformations that accompany them. The genes here cover the two halves of the problem: motile and sensory cilia at the embryonic node, where intraflagellar transport components, the small GTPase ARL13B, the axonemal protein MNS1 and the polycystin-family channel PKD1L1 generate and detect directional leftward flow, and the transcriptional response that follows, in which Notch receptors and the ligand DLL1 set up nodal signalling and PITX2 and ZIC3 impose left-sided identity on lateral plate mesoderm. Hedgehog signalling through SMO and chromatin and cofactor regulators tune the output, linking cilium biology to organ situs.

Replication forks stall at bulky DNA lesions such as UV-induced thymine dimers, and rather than removing the damage, error-free translesion synthesis allows a specialized polymerase to copy accurately past it so that post-replicative gaps are converted into full-length daughter strands. This branch of damage tolerance preserves genome integrity without raising mutation load, in contrast to the mutagenic bypass polymerases that share the same access route. DNA polymerase eta inserts the correct nucleotides opposite cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers, with REV1 acting as a scaffold at the lesion, POLDIP2 and the replicative polymerase delta catalytic subunit supporting polymerase exchange and extension, and RCHY1 contributing ubiquitin-dependent regulation of polymerase availability. Loss of accurate bypass capacity underlies extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition, as seen in xeroderma pigmentosum variant patients lacking functional polymerase eta.

Demethylation covers the enzymatic removal of methyl groups from DNA, histones, other proteins and small molecules, and it matters because methylation is used throughout biology as a reversible mark: chromatin states, protein activity and drug structures all depend on being able to strip it away again. Two broad chemistries appear here. Dioxygenases of the AlkB and JmjC families, including nucleic acid repair demethylases and the histone demethylases PHF2 and JMJD6, use iron and 2-oxoglutarate to hydroxylate a methyl group so it falls off, reversing epigenetic marks and repairing alkylation damage to DNA and RNA. Separately, cytochrome P450 monooxygenases with their NADPH-dependent reductase partner POR carry out oxidative N- and O-demethylation of drugs and xenobiotics in the liver, a step that governs clearance and pharmacogenetic variation in drug response. MMACHC dealkylates cobalamin during its cytosolic processing for cofactor use.</description>,

Methyl groups are stripped from substrates by iron- and oxygen-dependent oxidation, and this chemistry underlies both the reversal of nucleic acid methylation and the clearance of methylated xenobiotics. Two enzyme families carry it out here. Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate dioxygenases such as ALKBH1, ALKBH7 and JMJD6 hydroxylate methyl groups on DNA, RNA or protein so that the carbon leaves as formaldehyde, repairing alkylation damage and editing epigenetic and RNA marks that control gene expression. In parallel, hepatic cytochrome P450 monooxygenases including CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 use heme, molecular oxygen and NADPH-derived electrons to O- and N-demethylate drugs, caffeine, steroids and other lipophilic compounds, converting them to more polar metabolites for excretion. Loss or variation in these activities shows up as sensitivity to alkylating agents, altered methylation landscapes, and the pharmacogenetic differences that make drug dosing unpredictable between individuals.

Cells constantly produce RNAs that are truncated, misprocessed, mistranslated or simply no longer needed, and RNA surveillance is the set of activities that recognises these molecules and destroys them before they poison gene expression. Its failure leaves the transcriptome cluttered with aberrant species and stalls ribosomes on defective messages, and mutations in several components cause neurological and skeletal disease. The core here is the exosome, a multisubunit 3'-to-5' ribonuclease barrel with the catalytic subunits DIS3 and EXOSC10, fed substrates by adaptors and acting on rRNA precursors, promoter-associated transcripts and unstable non-coding RNA. Complementary routes include 5'-to-3' decay by XRN1, decapping-related quality control by DXO, premature transcription termination through the Integrator complex, mitochondrial RNA turnover, and ribosome rescue by PELO. tRNA end maturation by TRNT1 also feeds into which RNAs are judged acceptable.

Transcription generates a large fraction of RNA that is misprocessed, improperly capped, or never properly packaged for export, and nuclear mRNA surveillance is the quality-control system that recognises these species and destroys them before they reach the cytoplasm. It keeps aberrant transcripts from being translated into truncated or toxic proteins and sets the steady-state level of many normal mRNAs and non-coding RNAs as well. The core machinery is the nuclear RNA exosome, a barrel of structural subunits that channels substrates to associated ribonucleases: DIS3 and EXOSC10 provide 3'-to-5' exonucleolytic activity, while DXO removes defective cap structures and commits the transcript to decay. Adaptor and cofactor proteins such as ZCCHC7 recruit particular classes of RNA to the exosome, coupling surveillance to transcription termination, polyadenylation and export. Loss of exosome components disturbs nuclear RNA homeostasis and causes neurological and haematological disease.

Pervasive transcription generates large numbers of non-productive, cryptic unstable transcripts, and their catabolism keeps these species from accumulating in the nucleus and interfering with gene expression. The work is done by the nuclear RNA exosome: a barrel of structural subunits including EXOSC2 and EXOSC3 channels RNA to processive 3'-to-5' exoribonucleases, with DIS3 acting in the nucleoplasm and EXOSC10 providing a distributive hydrolytic activity at the cap of the complex. Substrates are marked for destruction by an adaptor module in which the zinc-knuckle protein ZCCHC7 helps recruit non-coding and aberrant transcripts to the exosome, typically after untemplated adenylation. The same machinery trims and matures stable RNAs, so this degradative surveillance sits at the interface of RNA quality control, ribosome and snoRNA biogenesis, and suppression of spurious transcriptional noise; loss of exosome subunits causes neurodegenerative and hematopoietic disease.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are made only while DNA is being copied, and they must disappear within minutes once replication stops or is blocked, so that free histones do not accumulate and disrupt chromatin assembly. This decay route gives histone transcripts their unusually short life. Instead of a poly(A) tail, these mRNAs end in a stem-loop processed by a U7 snRNP-containing complex built on Lsm10 and Lsm11 together with core Sm proteins and cleavage and polyadenylation factors such as CPSF2, CPSF3 and symplekin. When replication halts, the 3' end is oligo-uridylylated by terminal uridylyl transferases, marking it for degradation by the Lsm1-containing decapping route with Xrn1 and Dcp2, by 3'-to-5' trimming through the exosome and Eri1, and with help from Upf1. Loss of this coupling produces histone imbalance, replication stress, and genome instability, consistent with ATM involvement in the damage-triggered response.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are made only while DNA is being copied, and they must be destroyed promptly when replication stops or when cells are arrested, so that histone supply stays matched to the amount of DNA to be packaged; excess free histones are toxic and cause genome instability. Nuclear turnover of these transcripts is intimately tied to how their unusual 3' ends are made: instead of being polyadenylated, histone pre-mRNAs are cleaved after a conserved stem-loop by the U7 snRNP, whose Sm-like core includes LSM10 and LSM11 alongside canonical Sm proteins, working with cleavage and polyadenylation factors such as CPSF3, CPSF2, symplekin and CSTF2. The same 3' end machinery and the La protein SSB direct degradation of unprocessed or no-longer-needed histone transcripts, linking RNA surveillance to cell cycle control of chromatin assembly.

Small nucleolar RNAs guide the modification and folding of ribosomal RNA, and they only work once their precursors have been trimmed to precise mature ends. In poly(A)-dependent snoRNA 3'-end processing, a short poly(A) tail added to the precursor acts as a signal and a handle for exonucleolytic trimming rather than as a stabilising element. A non-canonical poly(A) polymerase provides the tail, the deadenylase PARN removes it, and the multisubunit RNA exosome, built from a barrel of core subunits together with the processive 3'-to-5' exonuclease EXOSC10, resects the residual extension until the mature end is reached. This coupling of tailing to degradation lets the nucleolus discriminate correctly folded snoRNPs from aberrant precursors, which are destroyed outright. Loss of PARN activity depletes certain snoRNAs and the telomerase RNA, linking this quality-control step to ribosome biogenesis and to bone marrow failure syndromes.

Membrane lipid supply has to be matched to demand, and this set covers the controls that set how fast phospholipids are made. Output determines whether a cell can expand its membranes during growth and secretion, build pulmonary surfactant, or store and export lipid, and unchecked or deficient synthesis contributes to fatty liver, surfactant deficiency and lipotoxic stress. Regulation acts at several levels: transcriptional, through the stress-activated factor XBP1 that expands endoplasmic reticulum membrane during the unfolded protein response and the bile acid receptor NR1H4, which restrains hepatic lipogenesis; and enzymatically, through phosphatidate phosphatase LPIN1 and the acyltransferase LPCAT1, which remodels phosphatidylcholine toward the disaturated species of surfactant. Acyl-CoA synthetase and lipid-binding and transfer proteins feed substrate in, while serotonin receptors and platelet-derived growth factor ligands couple extracellular signals to lipid synthetic rate.

Positive regulation of phospholipid biosynthetic process covers the signals that push cells to make more membrane lipid, matching phospholipid supply to demand during membrane expansion, secretion, and surfactant production. It matters wherever a cell must build membrane fast: the endoplasmic reticulum expanding under secretory load, alveolar type II cells generating pulmonary surfactant, and tissues remodelling lipid stores. The transcription factor XBP1, produced by the unfolded protein response, drives ER membrane biogenesis by upregulating phospholipid synthesis enzymes, while the bile acid receptor NR1H4 links lipid synthesis to nutrient and enterohepatic signalling. Serotonin receptors of the 5-HT2 family act through phospholipase C to stimulate phosphoinositide turnover and resynthesis, and ACSL3 activates fatty acids for incorporation into glycerolipids. ADGRF5 and RAB38 tie the process to surfactant homeostasis and lamellar body trafficking in lung epithelium.

Membrane expansion, lipid droplet formation and surfactant production all require phospholipid synthesis to be turned up on demand, and this is the regulatory arm that increases the flux through those biosynthetic routes rather than catalysing them directly. Upregulation matters when a cell must build membrane quickly: secretory cells expanding the endoplasmic reticulum during the unfolded protein response, where the transcription factor XBP1 drives lipid biosynthetic gene expression, and alveolar type II cells, where ADGRF5 and RAB38 support surfactant phospholipid production and lamellar body trafficking. Other inputs are hormonal and neurotransmitter-driven: serotonin 5-HT2 receptors couple through phospholipase C to stimulate lipid turnover, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 links sterol sensing to lipid gene programmes. Fatty acid handling proteins such as ACSL3 and FABP3 feed activated acyl chains into the pathway. Loss of this control compromises surfactant function and membrane biogenesis.

Whenever DNA is replicated, transcribed, repaired or packaged, its double helix must be bent, unwound, or have its supercoiling and linking number reset, and this collection of activities carries out those changes in DNA conformation. Without them, torsional stress accumulates ahead of polymerases, strands become catenated or knotted, and replication forks stall and break. Type I and type II topoisomerases, including a mitochondrial-specific enzyme and TOP3A acting with the BLM helicase, cut and religate the backbone to relieve supercoiling and resolve tangled intermediates; HMGB proteins bend and distort the helix to make it accessible to other factors; WRN and DNA2 process aberrant structures at forks and resected ends. The topology of DNA thus sits upstream of transcription, chromosome segregation and genome stability, and defects in these helicases cause premature ageing and cancer predisposition syndromes. Topoisomerase II is the target of widely used chemotherapeutics.

Interleukin-9 is a T cell-derived cytokine that supports mast cell growth, mucous cell hyperplasia and type 2 immunity, and this pathway covers the changes a cell makes when it encounters it. The response matters most in allergic airway disease and asthma, where IL-9 amplifies mast cell accumulation and mucus production, and in supporting the survival of certain T and innate lymphoid populations. Signalling runs through a receptor complex of the IL-9-specific chain paired with the shared gamma chain, which recruits the JAK1 and JAK3 kinases; these phosphorylate STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5, which then move to the nucleus and drive transcription of survival and proliferation genes. The shared gamma chain ties this cytokine to the wider interleukin family that depends on it, so loss of that chain removes IL-9 responsiveness along with much of lymphocyte development.

Parathyroid hormone is the body's main minute-to-minute regulator of blood calcium and phosphate, and this pathway covers what target cells do once they sense it. In bone, PTH acting through its Gs-coupled receptor raises cAMP via GNAS and activates protein kinase A, which drives immediate-early transcription through FOS and CREB-dependent programmes and remodels chromatin with coactivators and deacetylases such as KAT2B and HDAC3; osteocytic output shifts, with SOST suppressed and Wnt signalling permitted, favouring bone formation under intermittent exposure and resorption under continuous exposure. In kidney, the response retrieves calcium while promoting phosphate excretion by downregulating the sodium-phosphate cotransporter SLC34A1, and it intersects with the FGF23-PHEX axis that sets systemic phosphate tone. Loss or distortion of these responses produces hypoparathyroid and pseudohypoparathyroid states, renal osteodystrophy, and the skeletal consequences of chronic hyperparathyroidism.

Lysine-48-linked polyubiquitin chains are the canonical signal for proteasomal destruction, and the enzymes that strip them decide whether a tagged protein is degraded or spared. This editing step sets the half-life of cell cycle regulators, signalling intermediates and misfolded proteins, so it governs how quickly cells respond to stress and how much substrate flux reaches the proteasome. Most members are cysteine-protease deubiquitinases of the USP, OTU, MINDY and Josephin families, with OTUB1 notable for also blocking ubiquitin transfer non-catalytically and USP14 acting at the proteasome itself to trim chains and slow degradation. Others work in retrotranslocation and quality control alongside the p97/VCP machinery, or restrain inflammatory signalling, as TNFAIP3 does downstream of receptors that activate NF-κB. Loss or expansion of individual members contributes to neurodegeneration, autoimmunity and tumour suppressor failure.

Homologous recombination leaves DNA molecules physically linked — Holliday junctions and other branched joint molecules — and these must be taken apart before chromosomes can segregate. Resolution of DNA recombination intermediates does exactly that, either cutting the junction symmetrically or unwinding it, yielding two intact duplexes that may have exchanged genetic material. Two routes are represented: a dissolution route in which the BLM helicase works with topoisomerase III alpha and the RMI1–RMI2 subunits to unlink joint molecules without crossing over, and nucleolytic resolution by structure-selective endonucleases, MUS81 paired with EME1 or EME2 and the junction resolvase GEN1, which can generate crossovers. RAD51 paralogue XRCC3 contributes to the recombination steps that create these substrates. Loss of the dissolution route causes the excessive sister chromatid exchange and genome instability of Bloom syndrome, with cancer predisposition; failure of resolution altogether leaves anaphase bridges and chromosome missegregation.

When homologous recombination repairs a broken or stalled replication fork in a dividing somatic cell, it leaves behind joint molecules — Holliday junctions, nicked junctions and D-loops — that physically tether the two duplexes together. Resolution of mitotic recombination intermediates is the nucleolytic step that cuts and rejoins these structures so that two intact, separable chromosomes emerge, with genetic material exchanged between them. Without it, entangled sister or homologous duplexes persist into anaphase and produce bridges, breaks and gross chromosomal rearrangements. The structure-selective endonuclease MUS81 paired with its partners EME1 or EME2 cleaves branched substrates, while GEN1 acts as a junction resolvase that can work independently in the cytoplasmic phase after nuclear envelope breakdown; XRCC3 contributes to the upstream strand-exchange steps that create the joints. This late-acting machinery safeguards chromosome segregation and genome stability, and its loss sensitises cells to replication stress and crosslinking damage.

Ribonucleoprotein complex localization covers the transport of RNA-protein assemblies to, and their retention in, defined cellular sites — nuclear speckles and paraspeckles, sites of ribosome subunit maturation, and the cytoplasm reached through nuclear pores. Getting these complexes to the right place determines whether an mRNA is exported and translated or held back, and is how cells build the nuclear bodies that sequester RNA-binding proteins. The genes here act at several of those steps: a nuclear pore basket component and a subunit of the export-linked THO/TREX complex move messages out of the nucleus, a splicing factor and a transcription elongation-coupled histone methyltransferase couple processing to export competence, an m6A demethylase and a cytosine methyltransferase mark RNAs to change their fate, and a long noncoding RNA nucleates paraspeckle formation. Mutations in these components cause retinal degeneration and neurodevelopmental disease.

Chromatin is not a passive substrate: repair factors, cohesins, transcriptional regulators and histone variants must be actively recruited to and retained at specific chromosomal sites, and this targeting step determines where DNA repair, replication and gene silencing actually happen. Loading of the centromeric histone variant CENPA defines kinetochore position for the next mitosis, cohesin subunits RAD21 and WAPL govern sister chromatid pairing and its release, and damage sensors such as PARP1 and the TONSL-MMS22L module mark and license repair at stalled forks and breaks. Reader modules recognise existing marks -- bromodomains in BRD2 and BRD3, the chromodomain of CBX5 binding methylated H3, UHRF1 coupling hemimethylated DNA to maintenance methylation -- while writers and erasers including EZH2, SETD2 and SIRT6 rewrite the landscape they are recruited to. Extraction by the VCP segregase removes factors when their job is done, so mislocalisation here produces genome instability and aberrant lineage transcription programmes.

establishment of protein localization to chromatin covers the targeted delivery and loading of regulatory proteins onto chromatin, the step that converts a diffusible nuclear factor into a positioned occupant of a specific chromosomal site. This is how epigenetic states are written and maintained: without correct loading, histone variants fail to mark repressed domains, cohesin fails to encircle chromosome arms, and chromatin readers never reach their target marks. The genes span several such loading events — NIPBL as the cohesin loader that establishes sister chromatid cohesion and looping, the macroH2A variants that build transcriptionally silent chromatin including the inactive X, linker histone H1-5 that compacts nucleosome arrays, and LRWD1 which recognises repressive methylation to anchor origin recognition complex components. RUVBL2 and SGF29 contribute chaperone-like ATPase and methyl-mark reading activities within chromatin-modifying complexes, linking this process to replication licensing, transcriptional silencing and genome stability.

Chromatin is not a passive substrate: factors that read, remodel or organise it must first be delivered to defined genomic positions, and the establishment of protein localization to chromatin covers the loading and targeted deposition steps that put them there. This determines which regions are silenced, which loops form, and which promoters recruit coactivators, so it sits upstream of transcriptional control, replication licensing and chromosome architecture. The genes here span several of those routes: NIPBL loads cohesin onto DNA to build topological domains, LRWD1 recognises methylated histones at heterochromatin and origin regions, macroH2A variants are incorporated into nucleosomes to enforce repression, a linker histone compacts the fibre, and SGF29 and RUVBL2 tether acetyltransferase and remodelling complexes to chromatin. Failure of such targeting misroutes epigenetic marks and disrupts genome stability and developmental gene expression.

Autophagy ends by delivering cargo into the lytic compartment, and this pathway covers the recognition and routing steps that send selected proteins to the vacuole or lysosome for digestion during autophagy. It matters because it lets cells clear aggregated proteins, damaged organelles and intracellular pathogens rather than simply degrading bulk cytoplasm, and its failure underlies aggregate accumulation in neurodegeneration and defective control of infection. Cargo is marked and gathered by ubiquitin-binding receptors such as SQSTM1, which links tagged substrates to the forming autophagosome; chaperone activity from HSPA8 and the chaperone-like CLU helps keep misfolded cargo competent for delivery, and LAMP2 works at the lysosomal membrane where substrates are translocated or fused in. IRGM contributes the immunity-related arm, coupling this degradative route to defence against intracellular bacteria, while SMURF1 provides ubiquitin ligase input to targeting.

Cells constantly register non-living features of their surroundings — light, temperature, mechanical force, osmolarity, pH, radiation and oxidative or chemical insult — and this pathway covers the cellular responses to abiotic stimulus that follow. It determines whether a stressed cell adapts, arrests, or dies, and underlies vision, touch and pressure sensing, osmotic balance and the protection of the genome. Sensory arms include the opsins and phototransduction machinery of photoreceptors, mechanosensitive PIEZO and TRP channels, acid-sensing channels and proton-sensing receptors. Osmotic and ionic challenge engages WNK–OXSR1/STK39 kinases, aquaporins, epithelial sodium channels and volume-regulated anion channels, while DNA damage from UV or ionising radiation activates ATM/ATR–CHEK1/2 and p53, nucleotide excision and recombinational repair, cell cycle arrest via CDKN1A, and apoptosis through BAX, PUMA and caspases. Heat shock factors, stress-activated MAP kinases, integrated stress response through ATF4, mTOR signalling and inflammasome activation complete the adaptive repertoire; its failure yields photoreceptor degeneration, impaired repair and cancer predisposition.

Cells detect molecules made by other organisms infectious or otherwise and rewire themselves in response, and this cellular response to biotic stimulus is the front line of innate immune defence at barrier surfaces and in myeloid cells. Recognition runs largely through Toll-like receptors and the LPS-sensing accessory proteins CD14, LBP and LY96, through the dectin-1 lectin receptor, and through cytosolic sensors such as NOD2 and NLRP3, converging on MyD88-IRAK-TRAF6 and TRIF adaptors to activate NF- tkB and the stress-activated MAP kinases. The output is inflammatory cytokine and chemokine production IL1B, IL6, TNF, CXCL8 together with inflammasome-dependent caspase-1 processing, antimicrobial peptides and proteins including defensins, cathelicidin, lactoferrin and lipocalin-2, and nitric oxide synthesis. Negative regulators such as A20, TNIP proteins, IRAK3, SIGIRR and several microRNAs restrain the response; their failure drives sepsis, chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

Innate immune cells detect conserved bacterial products — lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, peptidoglycan fragments, flagellin, CpG DNA — and the cellular response to molecules of bacterial origin is the programme that converts that detection into inflammation, microbial killing and instruction of adaptive immunity. Surface and endosomal Toll-like receptors with their co-receptors CD14, LBP and the LY96/MD-2 partner signal through MYD88, TIRAP and TICAM adaptors to the IRAK–TRAF6 module, activating NF-κB and MAP kinases and the IRF arm, while cytosolic sensing by NOD2–RIPK2 and the NLRP3–PYCARD–caspase-1 inflammasome matures IL-1β and IL-18. Outputs include chemokines that recruit neutrophils and monocytes, TNF and IL-6, inducible nitric oxide synthase, antimicrobial peptides and lipocalin, and costimulatory molecules on antigen-presenting cells. Negative regulators such as TNFAIP3, IRAK3, SIGIRR, ZC3H12A and miR-146a restrain the response; their loss favours sepsis, whereas defective signalling permits uncontrolled bacterial infection.

Peptidoglycan is the bacterial cell wall polymer that alerts host cells to infection, and the cellular response to peptidoglycan converts its detection into an inflammatory and antimicrobial programme. Fragments released by dividing or lysing bacteria are sensed intracellularly, and the adaptor kinase RIPK2 couples that sensing to NF-kB activation through RELA, with IRF5 driving a parallel arm of inflammatory gene transcription. The output includes secreted antimicrobial peptides — cathelicidin and a beta-defensin — that permeabilise bacterial membranes at epithelial and phagocyte surfaces, while TREM2 tunes the magnitude of the myeloid response. This axis shapes mucosal defence and macrophage behaviour, and its dysregulation contributes to chronic inflammatory disease, most clearly in the gut, where inherited variation in peptidoglycan sensing predisposes to granulomatous inflammation.

Muramyl dipeptide is a fragment of bacterial peptidoglycan, and the cellular response to it is how cells detect bacteria that have reached the cytosol rather than remaining outside the plasma membrane. This intracellular surveillance shapes innate immunity at mucosal surfaces, drives the cytokine burst that recruits phagocytes, and is genetically tied to Crohn's disease and other inflammatory disorders when it misfires. Sensing runs through NOD2, a cytosolic nucleotide-binding receptor that engages the kinase RIPK2 to nucleate a signalling complex and switch on NF-kB and interferon-regulatory-factor-driven transcription, with IRF5 among the outputs; the related sensor NOD1 recognizes a distinct peptidoglycan motif. Cytoskeletal and scaffolding components including vimentin and the RhoA exchange factor ARHGEF2 position the machinery at membranes, while PTPN22 and TRIM41 temper the response, illustrating how tightly this arm of antibacterial defence must be restrained.

Cells adjust growth, gene expression and secretion when they detect particular acid anions in their surroundings, and this cellular response to acid chemical groups those adjustments together. Much of the content is nutrient sensing: amino acid availability is read out at the lysosome by SLC38A9 and the Ragulator subunits, transmitted through the Rag GTPases to mTORC1 and its partner RPTOR, with Sestrins, CASTOR and SAMTOR acting as inhibitory sensors of leucine, arginine and methionine metabolites so that protein synthesis and autophagy track supply. Other arms cover responses to retinoic acid and fatty acids, including collagen and matrix remodelling genes, growth factor receptors, and redox and stress regulators such as NFE2L2, GCLC and XBP1. Loss of this coupling underlies unchecked mTORC1 signalling in cancer, and mismatched growth during starvation or acid-base and oxidative stress.

Cells gauge amino acid sufficiency before committing to growth, and the cellular response to L-leucine is the branch of that surveillance that reports on this particular branched-chain amino acid. When leucine is plentiful the signal permits mTORC1 activity, licensing protein synthesis, ribosome biogenesis and suppression of autophagy; when it is scarce the same machinery restrains anabolism so the cell conserves resources, which links this sensing to muscle protein balance, insulin action and lysosomal catabolism. Leucine binds the sestrins, relieving their inhibition of the Rag GTPase machinery that recruits mTOR and its partner RPTOR to the lysosomal surface, with RRAGD among the GTPases involved; a leucyl-tRNA synthetase provides a second read-out of leucine availability. Ubiquitin ligases and a deubiquitinase tune the stability of these components, and EP300 couples the pathway to transcriptional output.

Cells exposed to antibiotics mount a response that alters growth, gene expression and membrane signalling, and this cellular response to antibiotic captures the changes a mammalian cell makes when such a compound is present. It matters clinically because many antibiotics have effects on host cells as well as on microbes, contributing to cytotoxicity, altered proliferation and side effects during therapy. The genes here span several arms of that reaction: a cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor and the p53 tumour suppressor arrest the cell cycle and decide whether damage is repaired or the cell dies; a chromatin methyltransferase and a MADS-box transcription factor remodel gene expression programmes; phospholipases release arachidonic acid for lipid mediator signalling; and a sodium-hydrogen exchanger adjusts intracellular pH and volume. Together they link drug exposure to growth control, transcriptional reprogramming and ion homeostasis.

Ammonia is a constant by-product of amino acid and nucleotide turnover and is toxic to the brain, so cells must sense rising ammonium and respond by disposing of it or by adjusting excitability. This cellular response to ammonium ion couples nitrogen detoxification to neural signalling: CPS1 commits ammonia to carbamoyl phosphate as the first, rate-setting step of hepatic urea synthesis, and ASS1 carries the cycle forward by condensing citrulline with aspartate, while loss of either causes hyperammonaemia with encephalopathy. On the neural side, the glutamate transporter SLC1A1 clears extracellular glutamate, an AMPA receptor subunit mediates excitatory transmission, and a Kv3-family potassium channel shapes repolarisation, together reflecting how ammonium loading perturbs glutamatergic signalling, astrocyte glutamine handling and membrane excitability. The grouping links hepatic nitrogen disposal to the neurological consequences of its failure.

Arsenic compounds — arsenite, arsenate and organoarsenicals — poison cells by binding protein thiols, generating oxidative stress and stalling translation, and this response is how a cell detects that insult and adapts to it. It matters both for toxicology of contaminated drinking water and for therapy, since arsenic trioxide cures acute promyelocytic leukaemia by triggering degradation of the PML-RARA fusion at nuclear bodies, where DAXX resides. The programme combines heat-shock transcription through HSF1 with antioxidant output such as heme oxygenase, detoxifying arsenate reductase activity from the omega-class glutathione transferases GSTO1 and GSTO2, and disposal of damaged proteins via the VCP segregase and zinc-finger AN1-type cofactors. RNA helicases and hnRNP components reflect the arrest of translation into stress granules, while p38-family MAPK13 signalling and the mitochondrial permeability regulator PPIF set the balance between adaptation and cell death.

Metal ions are both signals and threats, and the cellular response to metal ion stimulus covers how cells sense changing zinc, copper, calcium, iron and cadmium levels and adjust transport, gene expression and survival accordingly. Its outputs protect against metal toxicity and oxidative damage while keeping trace elements available for enzymes that need them. A core detoxification arm runs through the metal-responsive transcription factor MTF1 and the metallothionein family, whose cysteine-rich proteins buffer zinc and sequester heavy metals; iron handling appears via transferrin, its receptor TFR2, HFE and heme oxygenase, and stress responses via NRF2 and heat shock factor. Calcium-triggered effectors are prominent too, including copines, ryanodine receptors, mitochondrial uptake regulators and NFAT signalling. Because metal mishandling drives ferroptotic and oxidative injury, several members here, among them SOD1, SNCA, APP, PRNP, PARP1, LRRK2 and ATP13A2, tie this biology to neurodegeneration.

Excitable cells translate changes in membrane voltage and applied electric fields into lasting changes in their behaviour, and the cellular response to an electrical stimulus covers that conversion: altered gene expression, secretion, cytoskeletal remodelling and enzyme activity following depolarisation or field exposure. This is how activity shapes neurons over minutes to days rather than milliseconds, underlying activity-dependent transcription, synaptic and dendritic remodelling, and the responses exploited by electrical stimulation therapies. Calcium is the usual intermediary: the neuronal sensor hippocalcin and the metabotropic glutamate receptor GRM1 couple stimulation to downstream cascades, while calreticulin buffers calcium in the endoplasmic reticulum. Transcriptional control appears through the repressor REST, which silences neuronal genes outside neurons, and the differentiation factor NEUROD2; NSMF links synaptic activity to nuclear signalling, and the exchanger SLC9A1 adjusts intracellular pH as activity proceeds.

Cadmium is a non-essential heavy metal that enters cells through transporters meant for zinc, manganese and iron, then poisons thiol-containing proteins and provokes oxidative damage; the cellular response to cadmium ion is how cells detect that burden and limit it. The dominant arm is the metallothionein family, a set of small cysteine-rich proteins induced strongly on exposure that chelate the metal and buffer physiological zinc and copper at the same time. Alongside them, heme oxygenase-1 and superoxide dismutase handle the accompanying oxidative stress, heat shock factor 1 drives a broader stress transcriptional programme, and transporters such as SLC39A8 and SLC11A1 govern entry while ABCB6 contributes to efflux and sequestration. Failure to mount this response underlies cadmium toxicity in the kidney proximal tubule, lung and liver, and the metal's links to renal dysfunction and carcinogenesis.

Calcium is the cell's most widely used second messenger, and the cellular response to calcium ion covers what happens after its concentration rises: neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction, changes in membrane excitability, enzyme activation and a wave of new gene expression. Calcium sensors and effectors dominate here — the copine family of phospholipid-binding proteins, the neuronal sensor hypocalcin, synaptotagmin for vesicle fusion, and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase signalling that feeds into transcription factors including the immediate-early FOS and JUN families, MEF2 factors and NFATC2. Release and uptake components set the signal itself: ryanodine receptors liberate store calcium, while MICU1–3 gate the mitochondrial uniporter and buffer the rise. Calcium-activated and calcium-modulated channels, inositol-trisphosphate kinases and phospholipase C shape the decay. Mishandling of these steps underlies excitotoxic neuronal death, arrhythmia and malignant hyperthermia.

Copper is needed as an enzyme cofactor but is redox-active and toxic in excess, so cells detect changes in copper availability and respond by buffering the metal, adjusting gene expression, and disposing of damaged components. This cellular response to copper ion is dominated by the metallothionein family, small cysteine-rich proteins that chelate copper and zinc and are transcriptionally induced on metal exposure, together with stress-responsive transcription factors including HSF1 and the NRF2/NFE2L1 arm of antioxidant defence that couples metal load to oxidative stress protection. Autophagy components such as BECN1 and an LC3 protein contribute to clearance, while copper-binding proteins of the nervous system, notably the prion protein, amyloid precursor protein and alpha-synuclein, link this biology to neurodegeneration. Failure to hold copper in a bound, non-reactive form produces free-radical damage, protein aggregation and the tissue injury seen in disorders of copper overload.

Cells must sense how much iron is available and adjust uptake, storage and export accordingly, because both scarcity and excess are damaging — too little starves haem synthesis and iron-sulfur cluster assembly, too much drives oxidative damage and ferroptosis. This cellular response to iron converts the level of the ion into changes in gene expression and receptor behaviour. Transferrin delivers ferric iron to the surface, where the transferrin receptor family member TFR2 acts less as a bulk importer than as a sensor of saturation, working with HFE and its partner B2M to set the tone of hepatic iron signalling. BMP6, induced when liver iron rises, drives SMAD-dependent transcription of the hormone hepcidin and so restrains dietary absorption. SLC25A39 handles mitochondrial delivery of metabolites feeding this system. Failure of these sensors underlies hereditary haemochromatosis and iron-loading anaemias.

Lithium is both a trace environmental cation and the mainstay mood stabiliser, and cells respond to it by remodelling signalling and transcription. The clearest molecular entry point here is glycogen synthase kinase 3, whose inhibition by Li+ releases downstream substrates and feeds into Wnt-type and hedgehog signalling, adhesion, and cell cycle exit; the presence of GSK3A alongside CDH1, CDKN1B and SHH reflects that axis. Other members place the response in transcriptional programmes of differentiation, including adipogenic and myogenic regulators such as CEBPA, FABP4 and MYOG, and calcium-dependent control through NFATC4, while adenylate cyclase links lithium to cyclic AMP output. Sodium-dependent dicarboxylate and citrate transporters connect the stimulus to ion and metabolite handling. This biology explains lithium's effects on neuronal and progenitor cell fate, and underlies both its therapeutic action and its narrow toxic margin.

Magnesium is the most abundant divalent cation inside cells, and the cellular response to a magnesium ion stimulus covers how cells sense changing Mg2+ levels and adjust transport, excitability and enzyme activity accordingly. This matters because Mg2+ availability sets the tone of neuronal and muscle excitability, gates many ATP-dependent enzymes, and is defended by tight renal and intestinal handling; when handling fails, hypomagnesaemia presents as tetany, arrhythmia and seizures. The genes here span the arms of that response: a plasma membrane magnesium efflux exchanger that helps set intracellular Mg2+, a voltage-gated potassium channel and a ryanodine-family intracellular calcium release channel whose behaviour is magnesium-sensitive, an ankyrin scaffold that positions channels at specialised membrane domains, a gluconeogenic phosphatase requiring divalent metal, and a magnesium-dependent sphingomyelinase generating ceramide. Together they link ion status to metabolism, membrane signalling and electrical activity.

cellular response to manganese ion is how cells sense and adapt to manganese, a required cofactor for mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and glycosyltransferases that becomes a neurotoxin in excess. The response matters because manganese overload produces a parkinsonian movement disorder, and several of the genes here are hereditary parkinsonism genes: the lysosomal manganese transporter ATP13A2, whose loss causes Kufor-Rakeb syndrome, together with PRKN and LRRK2, linking metal handling to mitophagy and lysosomal quality control. Excess manganese accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi and triggers the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response, with EIF2AK3 phosphorylating eIF2α to slow translation and induce ATF4, while chaperones such as HSP90B1 buffer misfolded secretory protein load. Manganese also shifts amyloid precursor protein processing through BACE1, tying the response to neurodegenerative proteostasis more broadly.

Manganese is required as a cofactor for enzymes such as mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and glutamine synthetase, but in excess it is a neurotoxin, and the cellular response to manganese ion describes how cells sense and adapt to that stimulus. Chronic overexposure produces a parkinsonian syndrome, which explains why several of the genes here are Parkinson's disease loci: the lysosomal polyamine/cation transporter ATP13A2 sequesters and detoxifies manganese, while parkin and LRRK2 shape mitochondrial and endolysosomal handling of the metal. Much of the adaptive output runs through the integrated stress response, where the ER kinase PERK phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α to dampen protein synthesis and induce ATF4, alongside ER chaperone induction. Manganese also alters amyloid precursor protein processing via BACE1, linking metal overload to neurodegenerative proteostasis and to the vulnerability of basal ganglia neurons.

Zinc is required as a catalytic and structural cofactor yet is toxic in excess, so cells detect changes in free zinc and respond by buffering it, sequestering it, and adjusting gene expression. The cellular response to zinc ion is built around the metal-responsive transcription factor MTF1, which senses rising cytosolic zinc and drives transcription of the metallothionein family — the cysteine-rich MT1 isoforms, MT2A, brain-enriched MT3 and MT4 — whose thiolate clusters bind the metal with high affinity and release it when demand rises. Other members show how zinc acts as a signal rather than just a nutrient: it modulates ligand-gated channels such as glycine and GABA-A receptors and the P2RX4 purinoceptor, gates the proton channel HVCN1, and influences PARP1 and CREB1-dependent transcription. Loss of zinc handling, as with ATP13A2 mutation, contributes to neurodegeneration, and the same machinery shapes tolerance to cadmium and other heavy metals.

Cells adjust their behaviour when a vitamin is present, and this response programme covers how that stimulus is sensed and converted into changes in gene expression, secretion and differentiation. Much of it is vitamin D biology: the receptor VDR partners with retinoid X receptors and recruits coactivators and mediator components such as NCOA3, MED1, SNW1 and TRIM24 to transcribe target genes, while CYP27B1 activates and CYP24A1 inactivates the hormone to set local ligand levels. The outputs are largely skeletal and mineral: osteocalcin, type I collagen and periostin from bone-forming cells, and FGF23, PHEX and the calcium-sensing receptor tuning phosphate and calcium handling. Folate receptors handle uptake of a second vitamin. Loss of signalling here produces rickets, osteomalacia and disordered phosphate metabolism, and the same receptors influence proliferation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition programmes.

Retinoic acid, the active vitamin A metabolite, acts as a diffusible positional and differentiation signal, and this pathway covers what a cell does once it perceives it: changes in transcription, growth arrest, lineage commitment and, in the germline, entry into meiosis. Ligand binds nuclear receptors such as RARA partnered with RXRB, which recruit coregulators including HDAC2 and SNW1 to activate target genes, while CYP26B1 degrades the ligand to sharpen its gradient and ALDH1A2 generates it locally. Downstream outputs include HOX and other developmental regulators (HOXA2, PAX2, SOX9, TBX1, HAND2), Hippo effector YAP1, and a broad WNT and Frizzled module that translates the signal into patterning of limb, craniofacial, kidney and neural tissue. STRA8 marks the retinoic acid-dependent switch into meiosis. Disrupted signalling underlies the teratogenic effects of excess or deficient vitamin A.

Vitamin D acts as a hormone, and this is the programme by which a cell registers that signal and changes what it transcribes. The response governs calcium and phosphate handling, bone mineralisation, and immune and epithelial differentiation; when it fails, rickets and osteomalacia follow, and inherited loss of receptor function causes hormone-resistant disease. The active metabolite is bound by the nuclear vitamin D receptor, which heterodimerises with retinoid X receptors and recruits coactivators and mediator subunits such as NCOA3, MED1, TRIM24 and SNW1 to target promoters. Feedback is built in: the activating hydroxylase CYP27B1 and the catabolic enzyme CYP24A1 set hormone levels, while FGF23 and PHEX tie the response to renal phosphate handling and the calcium-sensing receptor to parathyroid control. Osteocalcin induction marks the osteoblast output of this axis.

Plant-derived nitrogenous compounds such as nicotine, morphine, caffeine, capsaicin, ryanodine and colchicine act on animal cells through a small number of highly sensitive targets, and this pathway collects the cellular responses they provoke. Much of it is calcium handling: ryanodine receptors and their accessory subunits release calcium from sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum stores, with a voltage sensor, calsequestrin and a sodium/calcium exchanger shaping the signal in muscle. Sensory ion channels of the TRP family mediate the burning and irritant responses to capsaicin and related irritants, while opioid receptor signalling, glutamate transporters, adenylate cyclase and dopamine- and cAMP-regulated phosphoprotein signalling underlie neuromodulatory and reward effects. Alkaloid exposure can also trigger apoptosis through executioner caspases opposed by BCL2L1, engage recombinational DNA repair when spindle or topoisomerase poisons damage the genome, and drive detoxification and stress-hormone output.

Caffeine acts on cells largely by sensitizing intracellular calcium release channels, and the cellular response to caffeine is essentially the machinery of calcium handling in the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum. The ryanodine receptors RYR1, RYR2 and RYR3 are the direct targets: caffeine lowers their threshold for opening, so a caffeine challenge is used clinically and experimentally to test their excitability. Around them sit the proteins that shape the release event — the skeletal voltage sensor CACNA1S, the luminal calcium buffer calsequestrin CASQ2, the trimeric intracellular cation channels TMEM38A/B that provide counter-ion flux, SELENON and GSTM2 as channel modulators, and the sodium-calcium exchanger SLC8A1 for extrusion. TRPA1 adds a sensory nociceptor component. This biology underlies excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal and cardiac muscle, and its dysregulation produces malignant hyperthermia and catecholaminergic arrhythmias.

Cocaine acts on the brain by blocking monoamine reuptake, and the cellular response to cocaine covers the changes a cell makes after that exposure: altered gene expression, neurotransmitter handling, and stress hormone output that together underlie sensitization, reward learning and addiction. The genes here point to several arms of that response. Dopamine signalling in striatal neurons is integrated by DARPP-32, encoded by PPP1R1B, whose phosphorylation state switches protein phosphatase 1 inhibition on and off downstream of dopamine receptors, while COMT degrades released catecholamines. Glutamate homeostasis is remodelled through the excitatory amino acid transporters SLC1A1, SLC1A2 and SLC1A3, largely astrocytic, linking drug exposure to synaptic plasticity in reward circuits. Corticotropin-releasing hormone and its binding protein tie the response to hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal stress signalling, and the histone methyltransferase EHMT2 contributes chromatin-level transcriptional adaptation that persists after the drug is gone.

Nicotine acts on cells largely through neuronal nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and the cellular response to nicotine covers what happens downstream once those channels open: changes in gene expression, survival signalling, and inflammatory output. This is the biology that underlies nicotine addiction and the effects of tobacco smoke on neurons, immune cells and developing tissues. Here a nicotinic receptor subunit provides the sensing step, while NF-κB components NFKB1 and RELA carry the signal to transcription and drive TNF production, linking receptor activation to inflammatory and stress responses. Neurotrophin receptor signalling through NTRK1 and the pro-apoptotic BH3 protein BAD tie the same stimulus to the balance between neuronal survival and death, and MSX1 points to effects on craniofacial and palatal development, consistent with the developmental toxicity of prenatal nicotine exposure.

Extracellular ATP acts as a danger and neurotransmitter signal, and this pathway covers how a cell detects it and changes its behaviour in response. Released from damaged, stressed or stimulated cells, ATP drives pain sensation, platelet aggregation, microglial activation and inflammasome-driven cytokine release, so its receptors are drug targets in chronic pain, thrombosis and inflammation. Detection runs through two receptor families: ionotropic P2X channels such as P2RX3, P2RX4 and P2RX7, which open a cation conductance and admit calcium directly, and G protein-coupled P2Y receptors including P2RY1, P2RY2 and the platelet receptor P2RY12, which work through phospholipase C and cyclic AMP. Downstream, calcium release via ryanodine receptors, TRPV1 and TRPM4 channel activity, and actin regulators such as slingshot phosphatase translate the nucleotide signal into secretion, excitability changes, cytoskeletal remodelling and altered transcription.

cellular response to cAMP covers what a cell does once cyclic AMP rises, converting hormonal and neurotransmitter signals received at G protein-coupled receptors into changes in ion transport, secretion, metabolism and gene expression. It is the effector arm of adrenergic, glucagon and vasopressin signalling, and its failure is felt in disorders of epithelial salt and fluid movement, cardiac pacemaking and hepatic fuel output. AKAP scaffolds localise protein kinase A to particular substrates, while phosphodiesterases such as PDE4D and PDE2A terminate the signal and set its spatial limits. cAMP-gated HCN channels drive the cardiac and neuronal pacemaker current; CFTR and paired SLC26 anion exchangers drive chloride and bicarbonate secretion; CRTC coactivators enter the nucleus to switch on CREB target genes, including gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK-pathway partners FBP1, ASS1 and CPS1. Rap1 and its RAPGEF exchange factors provide a kinase-independent branch controlling adhesion.

cAMP is the second messenger through which hormones acting on G protein-coupled receptors change what a cell does, and this pathway covers the downstream responses: ion and water transport, secretion, gene expression, and electrical pacemaking. Scaffolding proteins of the AKAP family tether kinase activity to particular substrates and compartments so that a diffusible signal produces localised effects, while phosphodiesterases such as PDE4D and PDE2A terminate it. Nuclear output runs partly through CRTC coactivators, which relay cAMP to CREB-dependent transcription of metabolic genes, including gluconeogenic and urea cycle enzymes. Effectors also include cAMP-gated exchange factors that load Rap GTPases, HCN channels that set cardiac and neuronal rhythm, and the CFTR chloride channel with partnering anion exchangers, whose cAMP-driven activation governs epithelial fluid secretion and fails in cystic fibrosis and secretory diarrhoea.

Cyclic GMP is the second messenger made downstream of nitric oxide and natriuretic peptides, and this pathway covers what a cell does once cGMP rises: changes in ion flux, contractility, secretion and gene expression. The genes here represent the main classes of cGMP sensor other than protein kinase G. Hyperpolarization-activated cation channels HCN2 and HCN4 are directly gated by cyclic nucleotide binding and set the pacemaker current that determines heart rate and rhythmic firing in neurons. Phosphodiesterases PDE2A and PDE3A are the cross-talk node, with cGMP either stimulating or inhibiting cAMP breakdown and so redirecting the response. NPR2 is itself the guanylate cyclase receptor for C-type natriuretic peptide, required for chondrocyte growth-plate expansion and skeletal elongation. RAPGEF2 links cyclic nucleotide levels to small GTPase signalling, and SLC6A4 serotonin transport is modulated by this arm.

Cells must sense sugar availability and change their behaviour accordingly, and this pathway covers the responses triggered when glucose or other carbohydrates rise. The clearest example is the pancreatic beta cell: glucose entry through transporters such as SLC2A2, closure of the ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunit encoded by ABCC8, calcium entry and exocytosis of insulin granules, with identity maintained by PDX1, NKX6-1, FOXA2 and RFX6 and secretory competence supported by XBP1 and ERN1 arms of the unfolded protein response. Beyond the islet, sugar signals reprogramme metabolic gene expression through ChREBP, USF factors and PPARs, tune gluconeogenesis via PCK1 and FBP1, and act on energy sensors including the AMPK catalytic subunits and mTOR partner RPTOR, alongside O-GlcNAc transferase. Counter-regulatory hormones such as glucagon, ghrelin and leptin feed in. Failure of these responses underlies glucose intolerance, monogenic and type 2 diabetes.

A nerve-muscle synapse works only if acetylcholine receptors are packed densely in the postsynaptic membrane directly beneath the motor nerve terminal, and skeletal muscle acetylcholine-gated channel clustering is how that concentration is built and held in the narrow endplate band of each fiber. Without it, neuromuscular transmission fails and the result is congenital myasthenia with fatigable weakness and respiratory compromise. Nerve-derived agrin acts through the muscle receptor LRP4 and the kinase MUSK, whose activation drives the scaffold RAPSN to anchor receptors to the cytoskeleton; MESD chaperones LRP4 folding, and COLQ tethers acetylcholinesterase into the synaptic basal lamina. Laminin subunits, dystroglycan and its glycosyltransferase LARGE1 link the cluster to extracellular matrix, while Wnt components including DVL1 and Frizzled feed into MUSK signalling, tying synapse assembly to muscle differentiation and matrix adhesion.

Interferon gamma, the sole type II interferon, is the macrophage-activating cytokine, and this is the programme a cell runs in response to it: killing intracellular bacteria and parasites, raising antigen presentation, and shaping T helper 1 immunity. Ligand engagement of the IFNGR1/IFNGR2 receptor pair activates JAK1 and JAK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 to drive transcription of IRF1, IRF8 and downstream effectors, with CIITA and NLRC5 turning on MHC class II and class I genes respectively. Effector arms include guanylate-binding proteins and IRGM that target pathogen-containing vacuoles, inducible nitric oxide synthase and arginine-handling enzymes, inflammasome-linked caspase-1, and chemokines such as CCL2 and CCL5 that recruit further leukocytes; vesicle trafficking and cytoskeletal remodelling reposition membranes for phagosome maturation. PTPN2 and macrophage-polarising nuclear receptors restrain the response. Loss of receptor or JAK function causes susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, while excess drives granulomatous inflammation and macrophage activation syndromes.

Interleukin-1 is the archetypal alarm cytokine of innate immunity, and this pathway covers what a cell does once it senses it: switch on inflammatory gene expression, secrete chemokines, remodel matrix, and mount fever and acute-phase responses. Binding of IL-1A or IL-1B to IL1R1 with the accessory chain IL1RAP recruits MYD88 and the IRAK kinases, which act through TRAF6 and the MAP3K7 complex to activate IKK-dependent NF- cB (RELA, restrained by NFKBIA) and p38-family stress kinases, driving CCL2, CXCL8, IL6 and CD40. Because unchecked IL-1 signalling produces tissue destruction and autoinflammatory disease, the response is heavily damped b by the antagonist IL1RN, the decoy receptor IL1R2, SIGIRR, TOLLIP, the RNase ZC3H12A and microRNA-146a. Outputs also include cartilage and hyaluronan turnover, endothelin and prostacyclin production, and metabolic rewiring via ACOD1 and HIF1A.

Interleukin-12 is the cytokine by which activated dendritic cells and macrophages instruct T and NK cells to become interferon-gamma producers, and the cellular response to it is what commits a naive helper T cell to the Th1 program that controls intracellular bacteria and parasites.
