Loss of this response, as in inherited deficiency of the shared receptor chain IL12RB1, leaves people susceptible to mycobacterial and salmonella infection despite otherwise intact immunity; excessive signaling contributes to autoimmune inflammation and is the target of antibodies against the shared p40 subunit. The heterodimeric cytokine formed from IL12A and IL12B engages a two-chain receptor whose cytoplasmic tails carry JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT4 to drive transcription of interferon-gamma and related effector genes. Disulfide handling by P4HB, phospholipase signaling, and the CD47-SIRPA axis modulate this output.

Interferon lambda is the type III interferon, and this is the cellular programme it triggers: binding of IFNL1, IFNL2, IFNL3 or IFNL4 to a receptor made of the lambda-specific chain IFNLR1 paired with the shared IL10RB subunit, followed by JAK-STAT signalling that switches on antiviral effector genes. Because IFNLR1 is largely confined to epithelial surfaces, this arm provides antiviral defence at the gut, airway and liver barriers with less systemic inflammation than type I interferon, and genetic variation at the IFNL3/IFNL4 locus is a strong determinant of whether hepatitis C virus infection clears spontaneously or responds to therapy. The presence of IFNG with its IFNGR1 and IFNGR2 receptor chains reflects how closely the type II and type III responses converge on shared transcriptional output driving interferon-stimulated gene expression, antigen presentation and epithelial restriction of viral replication.

Double-stranded RNA is a signature of viral replication, and the cellular response to it is how a cell recognises that it has been infected and converts that recognition into antiviral defence. The pathway drives type I interferon induction and an antiviral transcriptional programme; when it fails, viruses replicate unchecked, and when it is triggered inappropriately by self RNA it produces interferonopathies and autoimmune inflammation. Cytosolic helicase sensors such as RIG-I and MDA5 signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, while endosomal TLR3 covers ingested dsRNA, and both routes converge on IRF3 and NF-kB to switch on interferon beta. Parallel effectors act directly: oligoadenylate synthetases trigger RNA degradation, and interferon-induced proteins block viral translation. Shared components with cytosolic DNA sensing, including cGAS and STING, place this within a broader innate immune surveillance of nucleic acids.

Double-stranded RNA is rarely made by healthy human cells, so its appearance is read as evidence of viral replication and triggers an antiviral state. The cellular response to exogenous dsRNA converts that detection into type I interferon production and an interferon-stimulated gene programme that blocks translation of viral messages and alerts neighbouring cells; loss of it leaves the host susceptible to viral encephalitis, while chronic activation drives interferonopathies and autoinflammation. Sensing is compartmentalised: endosomal TLR3 surveys ingested RNA, while cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, and OAS enzymes make second messengers that activate latent ribonuclease activity. Both routes converge on IRF3 phosphorylation and IFNB1 transcription. Shared adaptors such as STING1 and cofactors including DHX9, ZCCHC3 and PQBP1 tie this arm to cytosolic DNA sensing through cGAS, making the two nucleic-acid alarm systems partly interlocked.

Cells exposed to ethanol change their signalling, gene expression and metabolic state, and this response underlies both acute intoxication and the adaptations that lead to tolerance and dependence. Ethanol acts directly on ligand-gated ion channels, including glycine receptors, and shifts neuromodulatory tone through dopamine D2 receptors and the opioid-related peptide precursor prepronociceptin, linking drinking to reward and motor effects. Downstream, adenylate cyclase and protein kinase C epsilon alter cyclic nucleotide and phosphorylation signalling, inositol trisphosphate receptors release calcium stores, and AMPK-dependent sensing couples ethanol to energy balance. A second arm is stress and injury: superoxide production by the phagocyte oxidase, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase, ascorbate transport and p53-inducible targets reflect oxidative damage, while chemokine release and myeloid transcriptional control recruit inflammation. Epigenetic change through DNA methyltransferase activity gives the response persistence, relevant to alcoholic liver disease and fetal alcohol effects.

Cells exposed to ether compounds, including volatile anaesthetics and ether-linked lipids, alter their signalling, gene expression and secretory behaviour, and this cellular response to ether is one branch of the broader adaptation to small-molecule chemical stimuli. The genes involved point less to a dedicated receptor pathway than to a convergence on growth and survival signalling: a protein kinase B isoform and phospholipase C beta relay the stimulus, a cyclin-dependent kinase links it to cell cycle entry, and cofilin and caveolin place part of the response at the actin cytoskeleton and membrane microdomains. Others govern translational output and mRNA stability, so the response reaches both transcript turnover and protein synthesis. Such sensitivity matters for how anaesthetics perturb immune and muscle cells, and for interpreting off-target effects of lipophilic drugs on membrane-proximal signalling.

Cellular response to gonadotropin stimulus covers what a target cell does when it receives pituitary FSH or LH — the step that converts a hormonal pulse into ovulation, follicle maturation, corpus luteum formation and gonadal steroid output. It is the effector end of the hypothalamic–pituitary–gonadal axis, and its failure produces anovulatory infertility, hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, or, with activating receptor mutations, precocious puberty. The gonadotropin receptors FSHR and LHCGR are G protein-coupled and act through cyclic AMP to reprogram granulosa and theca cell transcription, driving cell cycle entry via cyclins, steroidogenic electron transfer through cytochrome P450 reductase, and paracrine signals such as inhibin/activin subunits, endothelin and Notch that coordinate follicular remodelling and vascular change. Antioxidant glutamate–cysteine ligase subunits buffer the oxidative load of steroid synthesis, while GATA and WT1 factors set the gonadal transcriptional context in which the hormone is read.

Gonadotropins from the pituitary — FSH and LH — instruct gonadal cells to grow, differentiate and make steroids, and this describes what a target cell does once that signal arrives. The response drives follicle maturation, ovulation, luteinization and Sertoli and Leydig cell function, so its failure produces hypogonadism, anovulatory infertility and disordered sex steroid output. Hormone recognition depends on the G protein-coupled receptors FSHR and LHCGR, whose cAMP output is translated into transcriptional change through factors such as WT1, GATA6 and NOTCH1, into cell cycle entry via cyclin A2, and into steroidogenic capacity through electron supply by the P450 reductase POR. Local mediators including endothelin-1 acting on EDNRA and the activin subunit INHBA feed back on the same cells, tying gonadotropin action to paracrine control of follicular and interstitial tissue.</description>

cellular response to follicle-stimulating hormone stimulus describes what happens inside a cell once pituitary FSH binds its receptor, the step that drives ovarian follicle growth and Sertoli cell support of spermatogenesis. It sets the pace of the reproductive cycle: loss of receptor signalling causes hypogonadism and infertility, while its manipulation is the basis of ovulation induction. FSHR is the entry point, a G protein-coupled receptor that raises cAMP in granulosa and Sertoli cells and reprogrammes transcription toward proliferation, aromatase expression and steroidogenic support, with POR supplying electrons to the cytochrome P450 enzymes involved. The remaining genes show the downstream consequences rather than the receptor itself: inhibin/activin subunits that feed back on pituitary FSH output, endothelin and ephrin signalling that shape follicular vasculature and cell contacts, Notch-dependent granulosa differentiation, and glutathione synthesis enzymes that protect the follicle from oxidative damage.

Follicle-stimulating hormone acts on gonadal somatic cells to drive ovarian follicle growth and Sertoli cell support of spermatogenesis, and this pathway covers what a target cell does once the hormone arrives. Binding to the FSH receptor, a G protein-coupled receptor coupled to cAMP production, changes gene expression, steroidogenic capacity and paracrine output; loss of receptor signalling causes hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, follicle arrest and infertility, while its regulation sets the ovarian response in assisted reproduction. Downstream effectors here include the inhibin/activin subunit INHBA, which feeds back on pituitary FSH secretion, endothelin-1 with its receptor EDNRA acting on follicular and vascular tone, Notch and ephrin components mediating cell-cell contacts within the follicle, cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase supporting steroid hydroxylation, and the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits that build glutathione against oxidative stress during follicular maturation.

Luteinizing hormone acts on gonadal cells to trigger ovulation, luteinization of the follicle, and steroid hormone output, and the cellular response described here is what those target cells do once the hormone arrives. Responsiveness depends on the G protein-coupled luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor, whose loss causes hypogonadism and disordered sexual development, while activating mutations drive precocious puberty. Receptor engagement raises cyclic AMP and reprogrammes gene expression in granulosa and theca cells, including induction of endothelin-1 and its receptor EDNRA, a locally acting vasoconstrictor arm implicated in follicle rupture and corpus luteum function. Changes in cell cycle regulators such as cyclin A2 accompany the switch from proliferating follicular cells to terminally differentiated, progesterone-secreting luteal cells. The pathway therefore links pituitary endocrine signalling to fertility, ovarian cycling, and testicular androgen production.

Parathyroid hormone is the body's main minute-to-minute regulator of calcium and phosphate, and this pathway covers what a target cell does once the hormone binds: bone and kidney cells rewrite their transcriptional programmes and change how they handle phosphate. Loss of these responses leaves calcium homeostasis uncontrolled, contributing to rickets, osteoporosis, renal phosphate wasting and the bone disease of chronic kidney failure. Hormone binding raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, whose catalytic subunit PRKACA drives immediate-early transcription through FOS and modulates chromatin via a histone acetyltransferase and a deacetylase acting with the myocyte enhancer factor MEF2C. Output includes FGF23 and SOST, secreted osteocyte hormones that feed back on phosphate handling and Wnt-dependent bone formation, alongside PHEX and the renal sodium-phosphate cotransporter SLC34A1, whose regulated removal from the brush border reduces phosphate reabsorption.

cellular response to peptide hormone stimulus covers how cells detect and act on hormones secreted into the blood as peptides — insulin, glucagon, growth hormone, leptin, angiotensin, GnRH and others — and convert that endocrine signal into altered metabolism, gene expression, growth and secretion. It is the machinery of whole-body homeostasis: blood glucose control, lipid and glycogen handling, body-weight and appetite regulation, blood pressure, growth and reproductive timing, and its derangement defines insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, obesity and hypertension. Mechanistically it spans receptor tyrosine kinase signalling through IRS adaptors to PI3K–AKT–mTOR and FOXO, cytokine-type receptors acting via JAK–STAT with SOCS feedback, and G protein-coupled receptors driving adenylate cyclase, PKA and PKC. Outputs converge on gluconeogenic and lipogenic enzymes, GLUT4 vesicle trafficking to the plasma membrane, and transcription factors such as CREB, PPARG, SREBF1 and the KLF family.

Peptide hormones such as insulin, IGFs, growth hormone, glucagon, leptin and angiotensin act at the cell surface, and this pathway covers how a target cell converts that endocrine signal into altered metabolism, gene expression and growth. It underlies whole-body glucose and lipid homeostasis, somatic growth, blood pressure and salt balance, and reproductive and stress axes; its blunting is the molecular definition of insulin and leptin resistance in type 2 diabetes and obesity. Receptor tyrosine kinases signal through IRS adaptors to PI3K, AKT, mTOR and FOXO transcription factors, driving GLUT4 vesicle translocation and suppressing gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and G6PC1, while G protein-coupled receptors for glucagon, GLP-1, TSH and angiotensin work via adenylate cyclases, PKA and PKC. Cytokine-type receptors engage JAK kinases and STATs. Negative regulators including SOCS proteins, PTPN1 and TRIB3 set signal duration and sensitivity.

Corticotropin-releasing hormone is the opening signal of the stress axis, and this pathway covers what a target cell does once it arrives. In anterior pituitary corticotropes the response drives proopiomelanocortin transcription and ACTH secretion, setting adrenal glucocorticoid output; in brain regions such as the amygdala and locus coeruleus the same ligand shapes anxiety, arousal and feeding behaviour. Two G protein-coupled receptors, CRHR1 and CRHR2, read the signal with different ligand preferences and largely opposing behavioural effects, coupling mainly through Gs to raise cyclic AMP and activate protein kinase A. A prompt transcriptional output follows, typified by the NR4A immediate-early orphan nuclear receptors NR4A1, NR4A2 and NR4A3, which convert the acute hormonal pulse into changes in gene expression. Dysregulated signalling here is tied to depression, anxiety disorders and the pathological cortisol excess of Cushing disease.

Glucagon released from pancreatic alpha cells during fasting tells the liver to raise blood glucose, and this describes how a target cell reacts to that hormone. The response defines the counter-regulatory arm of glucose homeostasis; its loss or excess underlies hypoglycaemia on one side and the inappropriate hepatic glucose output of diabetes on the other. Glucagon and the related incretin peptides act through class B G protein-coupled receptors, including the glucagon receptor and the GLP-1 and GLP-2 receptors, which couple via the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit to adenylyl cyclases. The resulting cAMP engages protein kinase A, built from catalytic and regulatory subunits, to phosphorylate metabolic enzymes and transcriptional regulators. Downstream output includes ureagenesis, with carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and argininosuccinate synthase linking amino acid catabolism to nitrogen disposal during gluconeogenesis.

Growth hormone released by the pituitary reaches target tissues and tells them to grow, and this is the set of events a cell runs in response. The hormone binds its receptor on hepatocytes, chondrocytes, muscle and adipose cells, triggering JAK2-dependent phosphorylation of STAT5A and STAT5B, which enter the nucleus and switch on IGF1 and other growth-promoting genes; IGF1 then carries much of the effect systemically, driving postnatal linear growth. Parallel branches through PI3K regulatory subunits, focal adhesion components paxillin and PTK2, and the Src-family kinase LYN link the receptor to metabolism and cytoskeletal responses. Negative regulators keep the output bounded: SOCS2 limits receptor signalling and the phosphatase PTPN1 dephosphorylates JAK2, while LEPROT-family proteins control receptor surface levels. Loss of receptor or signalling function causes growth hormone insensitivity and short stature; excess drives acromegaly and insulin resistance.

Prostaglandins are lipid mediators released at sites of inflammation, injury and in reproductive tissue, and this pathway covers what a target cell does when it senses them: changes in gene expression, secretion, contraction, metabolic tone and migration. Signalling runs mainly through G protein-coupled receptors for prostaglandin E2, D2 and F2alpha, including PTGER2 and PTGER4, PTGDR and PTGDR2, and PTGFR, which couple via heterotrimeric G proteins such as GNAS with beta and gamma subunits to adenylate cyclase and cAMP, or to phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Downstream, AKT1 and the AMP-activated kinase subunits PRKAA1/PRKAA2 link the stimulus to survival and lipid metabolism, with acetyl-CoA carboxylase as a metabolic output. Aldo-keto reductases interconvert prostaglandin species locally, and chemokine components tie the response to dendritic cell and lymphocyte trafficking. These receptors are the targets acted on indirectly by NSAIDs.

Cellular response to prostaglandin E stimulus describes how cells read the lipid mediator PGE2, the dominant prostanoid of inflammation, fever, pain sensitisation and mucosal protection, and convert it into changes in gene expression, secretion and motility. It matters because PGE2 is the product blocked by NSAIDs: its receptors set vascular tone, gastric mucosal defence, and the balance between immune activation and restraint. The receptors EPTGER2 and EP4 couple through GNAS and heterotrimeric G protein subunits to adenylate cyclase and cAMP, engaging PKA scaffolds, PKC and AKT, while AMPK subunits link the signal to acetyl-CoA carboxylase and lipid metabolism. In dendritic cells and lymphocytes the same signal drives CCR7 and its chemokines CCL19 and CCL21, directing migration to lymph nodes, and induces the costimulatory ligand OX40L, so PGE2 shapes adaptive immune priming as well as smooth muscle and metabolic responses.

Prostaglandin E2 is a lipid mediator released during inflammation, and this pathway covers what a cell does once it arrives: bind it, convert it into second-messenger signalling, and change migration, secretion and gene expression accordingly. The receptors EP2 and EP4 (PTGER2, PTGER4) couple through Gs heterotrimers (GNAS with beta and gamma subunits) to adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP and engaging PKA scaffolding, with additional input through PKC and AKT1 and metabolic branches via AMPK subunits and acetyl-CoA carboxylase. The immune output is prominent: CCR7 and its ligands CCL19 and CCL21 link prostaglandin exposure to dendritic cell and lymphocyte homing into lymph nodes, while OX40 ligand shapes T cell costimulation. Because PGE2 is the product of cyclooxygenase activity, these responses are what NSAIDs blunt, and they underlie inflammatory pain, fever, vasodilation and tumour-associated immune suppression.

Steroid hormones — glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, androgens, oestrogens and progestogens — reach nearly every tissue, and this pathway covers how a cell reads them and rewrites its behaviour in response. It underlies stress metabolism, salt and water balance, reproductive tissue growth and sexual differentiation, and its subversion drives hormone-dependent breast and prostate cancers as well as steroid resistance in inflammation. Most of the input converges on nuclear receptors such as NR3C1, NR3C2, AR, ESR1/ESR2 and PGR, which bind hormone, exchange chaperones such as FKBP4 and HSP-family proteins for coactivators or corepressors, and recruit chromatin modifiers — p300, MED1, HDAC1/2, KDM and KMT2D activities — to reprogramme transcription. Membrane receptors including GPER1 and progestin-binding PAQR proteins add rapid non-genomic signalling. Downstream outputs are concrete: epithelial sodium channel subunits and SGK1 for sodium reabsorption, PCK1 and gluconeogenic enzymes for glucose output, UGT glucuronosyltransferases for steroid clearance, and coupling to the circadian clock via PER, CRY and CLOCK.

Adrenal steroid hormones reach nearly every tissue, and this is the set of cellular responses they trigger once bound by their receptor. The glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 acts as a ligand-gated transcription factor, switching on gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and PCK2, the anti-inflammatory mediator annexin A1, and mRNA-destabilizing zinc-finger proteins of the ZFP36 family that shorten the half-life of cytokine transcripts. In muscle, the same signal drives atrophy through FBXO32, myostatin and FOXO3 while DDIT4 restrains mTOR-dependent growth. Mineralocorticoid responses appear as induction of SGK1 and the epithelial sodium channel subunits that set renal sodium reabsorption and blood pressure. Additional outputs include apoptotic priming via BCL2L11 and caspase-9, feedback on CRH in the stress axis, and glucuronidation enzymes that clear steroid ligands. Excess or deficiency produces the metabolic, immune and electrolyte disturbances of Cushing and Addison states.

Aldosterone and related mineralocorticoids tell a cell to conserve sodium, and this response programme is how that instruction is carried out. It governs sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron, colon and airway epithelia, and through them extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure; excessive signalling drives hypertension, hypokalaemia and cardiac and vascular fibrosis, while loss of it causes salt wasting. The core effector is the epithelial sodium channel, whose alpha, beta, gamma and delta subunits set the rate-limiting apical entry step, and the immediate transcriptional target SGK1, a kinase that stabilises the channel at the membrane by suppressing its ubiquitin-dependent removal. Additional responses include endothelin-mediated vascular tone, FOXO3-dependent stress and survival transcription, and membrane-initiated steroid signalling through GPER1, so the output spans ion transport, gene expression and remodelling.

Estrogens are C18 steroid hormones that drive development of female reproductive tissues, and this pathway covers how a cell changes its gene expression, growth and secretory behaviour once estrogen is sensed. The nuclear receptor ESR1 is the entry point: on binding hormone it acts as a ligand-dependent transcription factor at target promoters, working with coactivators and scaffolds such as PELP1, WBP2, NCOA4 and TRIM24 and cooperating with general factors like SP1 to select which genes respond. Related nuclear receptors including AR and RARA are represented, reflecting shared coregulator use across steroid and retinoid signalling, while CDK12 links transcriptional elongation to the response and SFRP1 ties it to Wnt modulation in the mammary gland. This axis governs uterine and breast epithelial proliferation, bone and cardiovascular homeostasis, and its deregulation underlies hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer and resistance to endocrine therapy.

Estradiol is the principal circulating estrogen, and this describes how a cell reorganises its behaviour when it arrives — altering gene expression, proliferation, secretion, adhesion and migration. The response underlies female reproductive tissue growth, bone and cardiovascular maintenance, and neural and muscle differentiation, and its subversion drives hormone-dependent breast and endometrial cancers, which is why receptor status guides endocrine therapy. Signalling runs through the nuclear receptors ESR1 and ESR2, which recruit coactivators such as NCOA3 and the corepressor NRIP1 to hormone-responsive promoters, and through the membrane receptor GPER1 for rapid, non-genomic effects that converge on EGFR and kinase cascades. Downstream targets seen here include cell cycle machinery, chromatin components, matrix remodelling by MMP2, myogenic factors, and neuropeptide and somatostatin receptor systems, together with SRD5A1 as a determinant of local steroid metabolism.

cellular response to progesterone stimulus covers the changes a cell makes in gene expression, secretion, and behaviour when it senses progesterone, the steroid that prepares the endometrium for implantation, sustains pregnancy by quieting uterine contraction, and shapes mammary and neural tissue. Loss of responsiveness underlies implantation failure and progesterone-resistant endometrial disease. The response runs through both classical and rapid arms: nuclear receptor-dependent transcription, aided by coregulators such as TRERF1 that remodel promoters of steroidogenic and target genes, and non-genomic signalling in which the SRC tyrosine kinase couples receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and proliferative outputs. Downstream effects reach differentiation programmes controlled by SOX10 and inflammatory metabolism through ACOD1, linking hormonal state to immune tone. This places progesterone sensing within steroid hormone signalling and reproductive tissue remodelling rather than in any single metabolic route.

Progesterone acts on target cells to reprogramme gene expression and behaviour, and this response underlies the secretory transformation of the endometrium, maintenance of pregnancy, mammary development and effects on neural and immune cells. The genes here represent the cell-side machinery engaged once the hormone is sensed: SRC links steroid receptor signalling to rapid, non-genomic kinase cascades that modulate proliferation and cytoskeletal responses, while TRERF1 acts as a transcriptional regulator that can influence steroidogenic gene expression, and SOX10 marks a lineage context in which the hormonal input is interpreted. Induction of ACOD1, which produces itaconate from cis-aconitate, points to progesterone's ability to shift inflammatory and metabolic output in responding cells. Loss or distortion of such responses contributes to progesterone resistance in endometriosis and endometrial disease, and to failures of implantation.

Testosterone reaching a target cell triggers a change in its transcriptional and signalling state, and this response underlies male sexual differentiation, muscle and bone mass, spermatogenesis, and hair and prostate growth. The classical route runs through the androgen receptor, a ligand-activated nuclear receptor that binds hormone, translocates to the nucleus and drives androgen-responsive genes such as the secreted phosphoprotein osteopontin; coactivators including NCOA4 and the deacetylase SIRT1 tune that output. Ligand potency is set locally by steroid 5-alpha-reductase, which converts testosterone to the more avid dihydrotestosterone. Rapid, non-genomic effects also occur, with a membrane-associated zinc transporter implicated in androgen binding and kinase cascades converging on ELK1 to alter immediate-early transcription, and NADPH oxidase activity linking androgen exposure to oxidant signalling. Loss or distortion of this response causes androgen insensitivity, while its reactivation sustains castration-resistant prostate cancer.

cellular response to lipid covers the ways cells sense lipids and lipid-derived molecules and change their behaviour accordingly, from switching on transcriptional programmes for cholesterol and fatty acid handling to mounting inflammatory responses against bacterial lipids. It is how metabolic state is translated into gene expression, and its dysregulation underlies atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, and chronic inflammatory disease. Two broad arms are represented. Lipophilic ligands -- oxysterols, bile acids, fatty acids, retinoids, steroid hormones, vitamin D -- act through nuclear receptors such as PPARs, LXR, FXR, VDR, RXR partners and RAR, together with coactivators and corepressors, to control transport (ABCA1, LDLR, SCARB1, NPC1), oxidation, and detoxifying UGT and AKR1C enzymes. In parallel, lipid A and oxidised lipids engage TLR2/TLR4 with CD14, LBP and MyD88 adaptors, driving NF-κB, MAPK and inflammasome output, while eicosanoid and lysophospholipid receptors couple through G proteins and adenylate cyclases to acute cellular responses.

Lipids are not only structural and metabolic molecules but signals, and the cellular response to lipid covers how a cell changes its gene expression, secretion, metabolism and behaviour when it encounters one. It spans two broad arms. Nuclear receptors and their coregulators — PPARs, LXR, FXR, RXR partners, VDR, retinoic acid receptors, together with NCOR/NCOA complexes, SREBF1 and INSIG proteins — read sterols, oxysterols, bile acids, fatty acids and retinoids and reset cholesterol efflux, lipogenesis and fatty acid oxidation, with LDLR, ABCA1, CPT1A and CD36 among the outputs. The second arm is innate immune sensing of lipid-bearing microbial products: TLR2/TLR4 with CD14, LBP, MYD88 and TRAF6 drive NF-κB and MAPK activation, inflammasome assembly and cytokine and chemokine release. Also included are receptors for eicosanoids, lysophospholipids and free fatty acids. Failure of this signalling underlies atherosclerosis, insulin resistance, fatty liver and chronic inflammation.

Cells sense how much cholesterol they contain and respond by adjusting efflux, storage, conversion to bile acids and gene expression, and this cellular response to cholesterol keeps membrane sterol content within the narrow range that membrane function and signalling require. Loss of control here underlies foam cell formation and atherosclerosis, and the failure of reverse cholesterol transport in Tangier disease, where ABCA1 can no longer export cholesterol and phospholipid to apolipoprotein A-I. Sterol-binding GRAM-domain proteins and oxysterol-binding-related proteins move cholesterol between the plasma membrane and the endoplasmic reticulum, where the signal is registered; CYP7A1 commits excess cholesterol to bile acid synthesis and CES1 handles cholesteryl ester hydrolysis. Cholesterol also acts informationally rather than structurally: PTCH1 and SMO couple sterol availability to Hedgehog signalling, and microRNAs tune the transcriptional output.

Fatty acids are not only fuel but signals, and this pathway covers how a cell senses them and changes its behaviour in response — switching fuel use, remodelling lipid handling, altering gene expression, and in immune cells tuning inflammation. Detection occurs through cell-surface receptors for short-chain fatty acids such as FFAR2 and FFAR3, through nuclear receptors including the bile acid receptor NR1H4, and through mechanosensitive potassium channels of the KCNK family that polyunsaturated fatty acids open. Downstream, transcriptional programmes controlled by SREBF1, CREB1 and E2F1 adjust lipogenesis, cholesterol uptake via LDLR, triglyceride synthesis and ketogenesis, while CPT1A, PDK4, UCP1 and HMGCS2 shift oxidation and thermogenesis. Insulin signalling through IRS1 is a major point of intersection, which is why lipid oversupply blunting this response contributes to insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis and metabolic inflammation.

cellular response to lipoprotein particle stimulus describes how cells sense circulating lipoprotein particles — LDL, oxidized LDL, and HDL — and remodel their lipid handling, gene expression and inflammatory output accordingly. It is the cell-level basis of cholesterol homeostasis and of atherosclerosis: macrophages that take up modified LDL through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and SCARB1 become foam cells, while HDL and apolipoprotein A-I acting on the ABCA1 and ABCG1 transporters drive cholesterol efflux back out. Uptake via the LDL receptor and intracellular trafficking through NPC1 feed sterol-sensing circuits that adjust SREBF2, PPARG and RXRA target genes, and oxidized lipids engage TLR4/TLR6 with MYD88 to trigger cytokine production. Microglial TREM2 and several microRNAs tune these responses. Persistent activation links dyslipidaemia to vascular inflammation, plaque formation, and lipid-associated changes in macrophage and microglial phenotype.

Cells monitor the lipoproteins around them and respond by rewiring cholesterol handling, gene expression and inflammatory output. This cellular response to lipoprotein particle stimulus is central to macrophage biology and to atherosclerosis: uptake of modified LDL through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and SCARB1 converts macrophages into foam cells, while HDL and its apolipoprotein A-I acceptor drives cholesterol efflux through the transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1. Sterol sensing feeds into the nuclear receptor pair PPARG and RXRA and into SREBP-driven transcription that tunes LDL receptor and lipase levels, and NPC1 moves sterol out of lysosomes. In parallel, lipoprotein-derived lipids engage innate immune receptors including TLR4 and TREM2 with MYD88 adaptors, coupling lipid load to cytokine production. Failure of the efflux arm produces cholesterol accumulation, plaque inflammation and cardiovascular disease.

Cells read extracellular purines such as ATP and ADP as signals, and the usual output is a rise in cytosolic calcium. This cellular response to purine-containing compound stimulus links nucleotide sensing to muscle contraction, platelet activation, secretion and nociception, and its components are the same ones that set excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Purinergic G protein-coupled receptors of the P2RY family trigger store release, while the ryanodine receptors RYR1, RYR2 and RYR3 form the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release channels themselves, gated in cardiac muscle by the luminal buffer calsequestrin CASQ2 and supported by trimeric intracellular cation channels and the ER redox protein SELENON. A sodium-calcium exchanger and a voltage-gated calcium channel subunit handle sarcolemmal flux, and the irritant sensor TRPA1 adds a sensory arm. Mutations here cause malignant hyperthermia, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and congenital myopathy.

Histamine released by mast cells, basophils and histaminergic neurons acts on target cells to produce the familiar features of allergy and inflammation — vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchoconstriction, itch — and also shapes gastric secretion and arousal in the brain. This cellular response to histamine centres on the H1 receptor, a Gq-coupled receptor whose activation raises intracellular calcium and drives cytoskeletal and contractile changes; the formin DIAPH1 links such receptor signalling to actin remodelling and endothelial barrier behaviour. Antihistamines that block this receptor are among the most widely used drugs for allergic rhinitis and urticaria. The inclusion of several GABA-A receptor subunits reflects histamine's modulatory action at these chloride channels, connecting the amine to inhibitory neurotransmission and to the sedation that accompanies centrally acting H1 antagonists.

Manganese is needed as a cofactor by glycosyltransferases, mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and other enzymes, yet is a neurotoxin in excess, so cells depend on dedicated carriers to move it across membranes and keep its concentration within a narrow window. Uptake transporters of the divalent metal carrier and ZIP families bring manganese in across the plasma membrane, secretory-pathway calcium/manganese pumps and a Golgi antiporter load it into the Golgi where glycosylation enzymes use it, and an efflux transporter clears surplus metal for biliary excretion. Loss of the efflux route or of the importer SLC39A8 causes inherited manganese overload with dystonia-parkinsonism and liver disease, or manganese deficiency with a congenital glycosylation disorder, respectively. The same proteins also handle iron, zinc and calcium, which links manganese handling to broader trace-metal homeostasis and to Golgi function.

Succinate is both a tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate and a signalling molecule, and moving it across membranes determines whether it is reclaimed, oxidised, or released to act on receptors. Transport across the plasma membrane is handled by sodium-dependent dicarboxylate carriers that reabsorb succinate and related di- and tricarboxylates from the renal and intestinal lumen and take up citrate and succinate into liver and neurons, while a monocarboxylate transporter provides an additional route coupled to lactate and pyruvate handling. At the inner mitochondrial membrane, a dicarboxylate carrier exchanges succinate and malate for inorganic phosphate, feeding substrate to succinate dehydrogenase and supporting gluconeogenesis and fatty acid synthesis. Because cytosolic citrate and succinate levels set lipogenic and metabolic tone, loss of these carriers alters energy balance; mutations in the neuronal citrate transporter cause an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy.

All blood and immune cells descend from a small pool of hematopoietic stem cells, and the proliferation of that pool sets how much output the marrow can sustain after bleeding, infection, chemotherapy or transplantation. Too little division exhausts the reserve and produces bone marrow failure and cytopenias; unchecked division, particularly with lesions in the transcription factors here, is a route to leukaemia. Thrombopoietin acting through its receptor is the dominant extrinsic cue driving stem cell self-renewal, alongside Wnt ligands and modulators such as SFRP2 that tune niche signalling. Inside the cell, RUNX1, MECOM and ETV6 govern the self-renewal programme, the kinase PIM1 supports survival and cycling, telomere maintenance factors permit repeated division, and the m6A reader YTHDF2 and microRNAs restrain expansion post-transcriptionally. CD34 marks the cells in which this occurs and is the basis of graft selection.

Hydroperoxides, the monosubstituted relatives of hydrogen peroxide, arise from lipid and membrane oxidation, and cells must sense them and respond by changing gene expression, redox enzyme output, survival signalling or growth arrest. The cellular response to hydroperoxide covers that adaptation, which sets the threshold between tolerated oxidative stress and oxidant-driven death, and is relevant to atherosclerosis, where oxidised lipoproteins taken up by scavenger receptors such as CD36 deliver the oxidant load. Detoxification capacity is supplied by glutathione transferase activity in membranes, while oxidation resistance factors and p53-induced stress genes bias the outcome toward antioxidant defence or apoptosis. Kinases including PRKCD and DAPK1 transduce the oxidant signal into death and cytoskeletal programmes, and chromatin corepressor activity links it to transcriptional reprogramming. Together these place peroxide handling at the junction of lipid metabolism, redox homeostasis and stress-induced cell fate decisions.

Superoxide and hydroxyl radicals damage lipids, protein thiols and DNA, and cells meet that stimulus with an ordered defensive and signalling response. This cellular response to oxygen radicals determines whether a stressed cell adapts or dies, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, vascular disease and inflammatory tissue injury. Dismutases in the cytosol, mitochondrial matrix and extracellular space convert superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, which peroxiredoxins then reduce, while a copper chaperone loads SOD1 and a copper transporter supplies the metal. Radical exposure also shifts gene expression through NFE2L2, which drives antioxidant and detoxifying genes such as NQO1. Other members link the response to nitric oxide and tetrahydrobiopterin availability, to myeloid oxidant production, and to heme-based oxygen handling, so the pathway sits at the junction of redox buffering, vascular tone and inflammatory signalling.

cellular response to oxygen levels is how cells sense oxygen availability and rewire their metabolism, growth and survival to match it. It underlies adaptation to hypoxia in ischaemia, wound healing and tumour growth, and its constitutive activation through VHL loss drives clear cell renal carcinoma and polycythaemia. The core is a hydroxylation-based oxygen sensor: prolyl hydroxylases (EGLN1-3) and VHL mark HIF1A and EPAS1 for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so that under hypoxia the HIF-ARNT heterodimer accumulates and induces glycolytic enzymes, PDK1, VEGFA and erythropoietic and angiogenic factors. Downstream branches shift ATP production away from oxidative phosphorylation, trigger BNIP3- and PINK1-dependent mitophagy and autophagy, restrain mTOR signalling and the cell cycle, and, if stress persists, engage p53-dependent apoptosis. Additional layers include microRNAs such as miR-210, sirtuins, oxidative-stress responses and pH regulation through vacuolar ATPases and NHE1.

Cells sense how much oxygen they have and reorganise their metabolism, growth and survival accordingly; this oxygen-responsive programme is what allows tissues to tolerate ischaemia, drives new blood vessel growth in wounds and tumours, and adapts muscle and brain to altitude or vascular occlusion. Its core is the hypoxia-inducible factor system: prolyl hydroxylases such as EGLN1-3 mark HIF1A and EPAS1 for VHL-dependent degradation when oxygen is plentiful, and stabilised HIF partnered with ARNT switches on glycolytic enzymes, PDK-mediated suppression of pyruvate oxidation, erythropoietic and angiogenic factors including VEGFA, and mitophagy receptors BNIP3 and BNIP3L. Overlapping arms couple low oxygen to mTOR and AMPK control of translation, to p53-dependent apoptosis, to redox defence through NFE2L2, and to oxygen-sensitive ion channels. Chronic activation supports tumour adaptation and pulmonary vascular remodelling, while failed adaptation gives infarction and cell death.

Oxygen above normal tension is toxic, and cells respond to hyperoxia with a defined programme of stress signalling, antioxidant and clearance responses, and, when damage exceeds repair, death. This matters most in the lung, where supplemental oxygen given to preterm infants and ventilated patients injures alveolar epithelium and endothelium, contributing to bronchopulmonary dysplasia and acute lung injury. Raised oxygen drives reactive species production, with NADPH oxidase activity adding superoxide to the burden, while the FOXO1 transcription factor redirects gene expression toward stress resistance and apoptosis. Death receptor signalling through FAS commits irreversibly damaged cells to apoptosis, and autophagy machinery requiring ATG7 clears oxidised proteins and damaged mitochondria, a response that can protect or contribute to cell loss. Caveolin-1 links the membrane compartment to these decisions. The balance between adaptation and death determines tissue outcome.

Faithful chromosome segregation depends on loading the right proteins onto the centromere at the right moment, and this pathway covers the targeting and retention of proteins at the centromeric region of chromosomes. Its outputs are the epigenetic mark that defines centromere identity, the kinetochore that grips microtubules, and the spindle assembly checkpoint that delays anaphase until attachments are correct; failure produces missegregation, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. The centromere-specific histone CENPA is deposited by a licensing step involving MIS18A, while replication-coupled histone genes supply the surrounding chromatin. Mitotic kinases act as the positional signal: Haspin phosphorylates histone H3 threonine 3 to recruit Aurora B and the chromosomal passenger complex to inner centromeres, and BUB1B, BUB3, TTK and KNL1 assemble checkpoint signalling, with ZW10, ZWILCH and SPDL1 supporting dynein-mediated checkpoint silencing once tension is achieved.

Cells monitor their water status and adjust transport, volume and gene expression accordingly, and the cellular response to a water stimulus covers those adjustments. In the kidney this is the basis of urine concentration: vasopressin acting through its receptors drives trafficking of the water channel aquaporin-2 to the apical membrane of collecting duct cells, so that water is reabsorbed rather than lost. Loss of this response produces diabetes insipidus, with polyuria and an inability to conserve water during dehydration. Downstream lipid kinase signalling, cytoskeletal linkage through plectin, and the polycystin-2 cation channel connect osmotic and mechanical cues to membrane trafficking and calcium signalling. More broadly this biology links systemic osmoregulation and fluid balance to epithelial transport and cell volume control.

Cells continually encounter foreign chemicals a drugs, plant toxins, pollutants, carcinogens a and this response programme detects them and converts them into products that can be excreted. It sets the pharmacokinetics of most medicines, determines individual susceptibility to chemical carcinogenesis and hepatotoxicity, and explains much clinically important drug-drug interaction. Ligand-activated transcription factors such as the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and the pregnane X receptor, together with the oxidative-stress sensor NFE2L2, induce the enzymes that do the work: cytochrome P450 and flavin monooxygenases, epoxide hydrolase and carbonyl reductases oxidise or hydrolyse the compound, then glutathione S-transferases, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and N-acetyltransferases conjugate it. Solute carrier uptake transporters and ATP-binding cassette efflux pumps move substrates and conjugates across membranes, chiefly in liver, intestine and kidney. Common variants in these enzymes and transporters underlie pharmacogenetic differences in drug response and toxicity.

Cellular response to pH is how cells sense protons and act on that information, keeping intracellular and extracellular acid-base conditions within the narrow range that enzymes, excitability and secretion require. It matters for sour taste, nociception during tissue acidosis, renal acid handling, immune cell function in acidic tumour and inflammatory environments, and defence against ingested acid. Detection runs through several device families: acid-sensing ion channels and the capsaicin receptor depolarise sensory neurons when protons accumulate; proton-sensing G protein-coupled receptors such as GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68 signal through Gq and Gs to change gene expression; acid-inhibited two-pore potassium channels set resting membrane potential; and PKD2L1-containing channels serve taste cells. Effector arms restore balance, with the sodium-proton exchanger SLC9A1 and its regulator CHP1 extruding acid, epithelial sodium channels adjusting transport, and the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1 supporting the respiratory burst.

Cells monitor extracellular and intracellular acidity and respond to it, and this proton-sensing capacity underlies sour taste, acid-evoked pain, immune cell function in inflamed or tumour tissue, and renal and systemic acid-base balance. Acid-gated ion channels convert a proton stimulus into electrical signalling: ASIC1 and ASIC2 open on extracellular acidification, TRPV1 is potentiated by low pH at nociceptor endings, PKD2L1 with PKD1L3 marks sour-sensing taste cells, and several two-pore potassium channels are inhibited by acid, depolarising the cell. A parallel arm uses proton-sensitive G protein-coupled receptors, GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68, signalling through Gq/11 and Gs to alter gene expression and secretion. Homeostatic effectors restore pH, chiefly the sodium-hydrogen exchanger SLC9A1 with its regulator CHP1 and the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1, which supports the respiratory burst in phagocytes. Dysregulation contributes to chronic pain, ischaemic injury and the acidic tumour microenvironment.

Cells detect extracellular acidification and convert it into electrical, secretory and transcriptional responses, which is how the body senses tissue ischaemia, inflammation, sour taste and the acid load that must be corrected to keep systemic pH stable. Proton-gated cation channels such as ASIC2 and the capsaicin receptor TRPV1 depolarize sensory neurons, giving acid its painful quality, while a PKD2L1-containing channel complex marks the sour-responsive taste cells. Acid-sensing G protein-coupled receptors including GPR4, GPR65 and GPR68 signal through Gq and Gs to shape immune cell behaviour and vascular tone in acidic microenvironments such as tumours and inflamed tissue. Background potassium channels of the two-pore domain family are inhibited by protons, setting resting excitability and contributing to central chemoreception, and the sodium-proton exchanger SLC9A1 together with its regulator CHP1 extrudes protons to restore intracellular pH. Epithelial sodium channel subunits and Rab11-dependent trafficking link acid exposure to transport regulation.

Cells must defend their volume when external solute concentration shifts, and this osmotic stress response is how they sense the change and correct it. Without it cells swell and lyse or shrink and lose enzyme function, which matters most in the kidney medulla, where urinary concentration exposes tubular cells to extreme tonicity, and in brain during hyponatremia. Sensing feeds into the WNK1/WNK3-OXSR1/STK39 kinase cascade that phosphorylates cation-chloride cotransporters to adjust ion flux, while volume-regulated anion channels built from LRRC8 subunits release chloride and organic osmolytes during swelling. Aquaporins provide the water route, and the transcription factor NFAT5 drives accumulation of compatible osmolytes, including sorbitol via aldose reductase. Hypertonicity also engages mTOR complexes and, when severe, inflammasome activation and caspase-dependent death, linking osmotic imbalance to inflammation and apoptosis.

Cells exposed to changing extracellular salt must defend their volume and internal ion balance or lose enzyme function and membrane integrity; the cellular response to salt stress is the set of adjustments that follow such a change. It matters most in tissues that routinely face osmotic swings, above all the kidney medulla, where interstitial sodium and urea reach concentrations that would kill most cells. The genes here span the main arms of that defence: aldose reductase generates sorbitol as a compatible osmolyte, aquaporin-1 provides regulated water flux, a potassium-chloride cotransporter and the sodium pump gamma subunit tune ion movement, and the mechanosensitive channel TRPV4 reports cell swelling. Mitochondrial calcium uptake components and LETM1 link osmotic and ionic stress to organelle homeostasis, while transcript-stability and DNA-repair factors handle the downstream consequences of hypertonic damage.

cellular hyperosmotic response is the set of adjustments a cell makes when the surrounding fluid becomes too concentrated and water is drawn out of it. It protects cells against shrinkage-induced damage, and it is the basis of how the kidney medulla, whose cells work in extreme salt and urea, survives concentrating urine. Sensing feeds through the WNK1/WNK3 kinases to the downstream kinases OXSR1 and STK39, which switch on sodium- and chloride-coupled cotransport to reclaim ions and water, while the transcription factor NFAT5 drives genes for compatible osmolyte accumulation, including the sorbitol-producing aldose reductase AKR1B1, and for aquaporin water channels. Glucose transport, gluconeogenic enzymes and mitochondrial calcium and ion carriers adjust metabolism to the stress. Failure of this response causes cytoskeletal disruption, DNA damage and apoptosis, and contributes to defective urinary concentration and to hypertonicity in diabetes and dehydration.

Cells exposed to a solute concentration higher than their own shrink as water leaves, and the cellular hyperosmotic response is how they sense that loss and restore volume and ionic balance. It matters most in the kidney medulla, where interstitial osmolality is extreme by design, and its failure leaves cells with concentrated intracellular salt, protein damage and DNA breaks. Two arms dominate the gene list. A kinase cascade in which WNK1 and WNK3 activate the related kinases OXSR1 and STK39 switches on electroneutral cation-chloride transport to reaccumulate ions, while the transcription factor NFAT5 drives expression of organic osmolyte machinery, including aldose reductase for sorbitol synthesis, so that volume can be regained without raising intracellular ionic strength. Aquaporin-mediated water flux, glucose uptake, mitochondrial calcium and magnesium handling, and cytoskeletal remodelling through ARHGEF2 accompany the adaptation.

Cells placed in a hypotonic environment take up water and swell, and the cellular hypotonic response is how they sense that swelling and restore volume before the membrane or cytoskeleton is damaged. It matters for epithelial fluid secretion, corneal and lens transparency, renal water handling and nociceptor mechanosensitivity; loss of its components causes corneal endothelial dystrophy, neuropathy and skeletal dysplasias. Mechanism begins with detection of membrane stretch and dilution, notably through the stretch-sensitive cation channel TRPV4 and water flux via aquaporin channels, and continues as solutes leave the cell through chloride and potassium-chloride cotransport pathways such as CLCN2 and SLC12A6, driving regulatory volume decrease. The WNK-activated kinases OXSR1 and STK39 with their scaffold CAB39 set cotransporter phosphorylation according to tonicity, while myosin light chain kinase links volume change to cytoskeletal tension.

Cells exposed to ionizing or ultraviolet radiation, or to visible light, must detect the insult and respond, and this collection of responses spans genome protection, cell fate decisions and photoreception. Ionizing radiation and UV damage DNA, and much of the machinery here is the damage response that follows: the ATM and ATR kinases and CHEK2 signal to p53, driving CDKN1A-dependent arrest or apoptosis through BAX, BAK1 and PUMA, while BRCA1, BRCA2 and RAD51 repair double-strand breaks, LIG4 and the Ku proteins rejoin them, and XPA, XPC, DDB2 and ERCC1 excise UV photoproducts, with translesion polymerases allowing replication past lesions. Failure of these steps underlies radiosensitivity syndromes and cancer predisposition. A separate arm handles light as information rather than injury, with opsins, transducin, guanylate cyclases and cryptochromes serving phototransduction, pigmentation and circadian entrainment.

Ionizing radiation breaks DNA on both strands and oxidizes cellular constituents, and this is the coordinated cellular reaction to that damage: sense the lesions, halt the cell cycle, repair what can be repaired, and kill the cell if it cannot. It determines the tolerance of normal tissue to radiotherapy and the sensitivity of tumours to it, and its failure underlies radiation-induced mutagenesis and cancer predisposition. The apical kinases ATM and ATR, with CHEK2 and the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp, relay damage signals to p53 and its transcriptional outputs CDKN1A, GADD45A and the pro-apoptotic BBC3, while MDM2 restrains p53 once signalling subsides. Repair proceeds through homologous recombination (BRCA1, BRCA2, RAD51, BLM, WRN) and non-homologous end joining (XRCC5, XRCC6, LIG4). Chromatin remodelling, stress kinases and cytokine responses such as TGFB1 and TNF extend the reaction beyond the damaged nucleus.

Gamma rays deposit enough energy to break both strands of DNA, and the cellular response to gamma radiation is the coordinated damage-response programme that decides whether an irradiated cell pauses, repairs, or dies. It underlies the therapeutic window of radiotherapy and the tissue toxicity that limits it, and its loss produces radiosensitivity, genomic instability and cancer predisposition. The apical kinases ATM and ATR sense broken and stalled DNA and signal through CHEK2 to p53, whose stabilisation depends on the balance with its negative regulator MDM2; the resulting induction of CDKN1A enforces cell cycle arrest while apoptotic decisions are tuned by survival factors such as BCL2L1. In parallel, repair proteins act on the lesions themselves: RAD51 for homologous recombination, the Ku subunits XRCC5 and XRCC6 for non-homologous end joining, alongside stress-responsive transcription factors and chaperone induction.

X-rays deposit energy that breaks DNA, and the cellular response to X-ray irradiation is how a cell registers that damage and decides whether to arrest, repair or die. This determines the tolerance of normal tissue to radiotherapy and diagnostic imaging, and its failure underlies radiosensitivity syndromes and radiation-induced cancer. The apical sensor here is the ATM kinase, which is activated by double-strand breaks and propagates signals to cell cycle regulators and repair factors; XRCC6 (Ku70) binds broken ends for non-homologous end joining, while NIPBL, a cohesin loading factor, and the chromatin-associated NUCKS1 link the response to chromosome organisation and transcriptional change. Downstream outputs include altered cyclin D2-dependent cycle progression, secreted modulators such as lipocalin-2 and the Wnt antagonists SFRP1 and SFRP2, and lineage transcription factors, so the response extends beyond repair into growth control and intercellular signalling.

Light is both a source of information and a source of damage, and cells respond to it along several routes represented here. In the retina, opsins including rhodopsin and the cone pigments, together with transducin, rhodopsin kinase, arrestin and the guanylate cyclases and their RGS regulator, convert photons into changes in cyclic GMP and membrane current, then shut the signal off so the cell can respond again; melanopsin and cryptochromes tie irradiance to circadian timing and pupillary reflexes. Ultraviolet exposure instead triggers a genotoxic arm: damage recognition by XPC and DDB2 with a cullin-RING ligase, excision by XPA and ERCC1-ERCC4, translesion synthesis by POLH and POLK, and p53-dependent arrest or apoptosis. Stress kinases, melanocortin signalling through MC1R and matrix metalloproteinase induction add pigmentary and dermal photoaging responses. Failure of these arms produces retinal dystrophy, xeroderma pigmentosum and skin cancer.

Photoreceptors must work across many orders of magnitude of ambient brightness, and the cellular response to light intensity is how they adjust gain so that neither dim nor bright conditions saturate the signal. Without such adaptation, vision would be limited to a narrow band of illumination and recovery after a bright flash would be slow. The genes here point to the shutoff and calcium-handling arms of phototransduction: an RGS protein acting with a G protein beta subunit accelerates deactivation of the transducin signal, terminating the response and setting temporal resolution, while sodium/potassium-calcium exchangers extrude calcium from the outer segment, and the resulting fall in internal calcium feeds back on cyclic nucleotide synthesis and channel sensitivity. A kinase component links these events to broader survival and metabolic signalling in the retina, tying light exposure to cellular state as well as to moment-to-moment sensitivity.

Long-wave ultraviolet light in the 315-400 nm band penetrates deep into the dermis, and the cellular response to UV-A is how skin and eye cells register that exposure and remodel themselves afterwards. Much of the output is degradative: interstitial and stromal collagenases and gelatinases, balanced by their inhibitor TIMP1, break down dermal collagen and elastin, which is the proximate cause of photoaging, wrinkling, and loss of tensile strength, and the same proteolytic burst contributes to tumour-permissive tissue remodelling. Detection itself appears to involve opsins expressed outside the classical visual pathway alongside a short-wavelength cone pigment, implying direct photoreception by keratinocytes and melanocytes rather than damage sensing alone. Sphingolipid synthesis and a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase provide additional stress and signalling arms, linking photon absorption to ceramide-dependent stress responses and altered secretion.

UV-B is the fraction of solar ultraviolet that penetrates the epidermis, damaging DNA and oxidising membrane lipids, and this response is how a cell registers that exposure and decides between repair, arrest, inflammation or death. It matters for skin: sunburn, photoageing of the dermal matrix, and the mutational burden that leads to keratinocyte carcinomas all follow from how well it is executed. Stress-activated kinase signalling through p38 family members and an upstream MAP3K relays the insult to transcriptional programmes, while CDKN1A imposes p53-dependent cell cycle arrest to allow repair before replication. An inflammasome sensor links UV-B to interleukin-1 processing and the inflammatory component of sunburn, and hyaluronidases together with matrix and cell-surface peptidases remodel the extracellular matrix that photodamage degrades. STK11 ties the response to energy-sensing and growth control.

cellular response to endogenous stimulus collects the ways cells detect and react to signals generated within the body itself — hormones, growth factors, cytokines, neurotrophins, metabolites and mechanical or metabolic cues — rather than to external insult. It is the basis of endocrine and paracrine coordination: insulin and IGF signalling through receptor tyrosine kinases, IRS adaptors, PI3K/AKT and mTOR; TGF-beta, BMP, activin and nodal ligands acting through SMAD transcription factors; steroid, retinoid and thyroid hormone receptors acting directly on chromatin; and FGF, VEGF, WNT and Notch cues that pattern developing tissues. Outputs range from altered gene expression, secretion and glucose or lipid metabolism to proliferation, differentiation and apoptosis, with feedback from SOCS, SPRY, SMAD7 and microRNAs setting signal duration. Disruption underlies diabetes, hormone-dependent cancers, skeletal and vascular malformations, and circadian and reproductive disorders.

Cells constantly adjust their behaviour to cues generated inside the organism itself — hormones, growth factors, cytokines, peptides and metabolites — rather than to external insults, and this broad response programme covers how those internal signals are received and converted into changes in gene expression, metabolism, secretion, growth and movement. It spans receptor families for insulin and IGF, leptin, glucocorticoids and other steroids acting through nuclear receptors, TGF-beta/BMP/activin ligands with their SMAD effectors, FGFs and VEGFs with their tyrosine kinase receptors, and neurotrophins, plus the shared downstream machinery of PI3K–AKT–mTOR, MAPK cascades, JAK–STAT with SOCS feedback, cAMP-dependent kinases and Wnt–beta-catenin. Extracellular modulators such as follistatin, noggin, gremlins and IGF-binding proteins tune ligand availability, while microRNAs and chromatin regulators shape the transcriptional output. Collectively this is the basis of endocrine homeostasis, growth control, tissue patterning and circadian timing; its derangement underlies diabetes, skeletal and cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Cells continuously read cues arriving from outside — microbial molecules, death ligands, mechanical load, osmotic and nutrient shifts — and the cellular response to external stimulus is the collected machinery that converts those cues into altered gene expression, secretion, survival or death. Much of it is receptor-initiated: Toll-like receptors with MYD88 detect pathogen-associated patterns and drive NF-κB-dependent inflammatory output including IL1B, while FAS, TNFRSF1A and the TRAIL receptors recruit FADD and caspase-8 to commit a cell to apoptosis. A mechanosensory arm built on PIEZO1 and PIEZO2 channels, integrins and junctional proteins lets endothelium and connective tissue sense stretch and shear. Stress kinases MAP3K1 and JNK, checkpoint signalling through CHEK1 and GADD45A, and transporters handling glucose, sodium and amino acids complete the adaptive response. Blunted or excessive signalling here underlies chronic inflammation, failed tissue remodelling and resistance to programmed cell death.

Blood flow over the endothelial surface is not just a mechanical fact but an instruction: the cellular response to fluid shear stress is how vessel-lining cells read flow and set their phenotype accordingly. Laminar flow maintains an anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic, vasodilatory endothelium, while disturbed or low flow at branch points and curvatures favours inflammation and is where atherosclerotic plaque preferentially forms. Mechanotransduction begins at junctions, focal adhesions and the primary cilium, with PKD2 as a mechanosensitive calcium channel and adhesion kinases PTK2 and SRC relaying force inward; an ERK5-MEK5 module then drives the transcription factors KLF2 and KLF4, with MEF2C and NFE2L2 supporting flow-protective and antioxidant gene programmes. Cyclic AMP generation through adenylate cyclases and PKA subunits, PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, and microRNA control tune the output, alongside matrix remodelling by MMP2 and glycocalyx synthesis. Loss of this flow sensing underlies endothelial dysfunction, aneurysm and vascular remodelling.

When nitric oxide or peroxynitrite accumulates, proteins become S-nitrosylated and tyrosine-nitrated and DNA is damaged; the cellular response to nitrosative stress is the set of adaptations that let a cell survive or die cleanly under those conditions. It matters most in inflamed tissue and in neurons, where sustained nitric oxide output from activated glia contributes to neurodegeneration, and it is one reason macrophage-derived NO is toxic to bystander cells. The genes here connect several arms of that defence: PARK7/DJ-1 acts as a redox-sensitive protector whose loss causes early-onset parkinsonism, DNAJA1 provides chaperone support for misfolded and modified proteins, autophagic turnover through ATG5 clears damaged cargo, ATM couples nitrosative DNA lesions to checkpoint signalling, and DDIT3/CHOP links persistent stress to apoptotic commitment. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of proteostasis, genome surveillance and inflammatory injury.

Heparin and related sulfated glycosaminoglycans are not just anticoagulants; cells read them as an extracellular cue, and this pathway covers the changes in gene expression, adhesion and secretion that follow such a stimulus. It matters because heparin binding governs how growth factors, guidance molecules and lipases are presented at the cell surface, and because therapeutic heparin perturbs these same interactions. The genes involved span the biosynthetic machinery that builds heparan sulfate chains, an immediate-early transcription factor induced rapidly on stimulation, and heparin-binding effectors: a guidance cue that steers axons and migrating cells, an adhesion molecule holding epithelia together, and an endothelial transporter that captures lipoprotein lipase for triglyceride clearance, the basis of post-heparin lipolytic activity. A developmental transcription factor links the response to cartilage and skeletal differentiation.

Genomic imprinting is the parent-of-origin memory in the mammalian genome: a small set of loci is marked during gametogenesis so that only the maternal or only the paternal copy is expressed, and that mark is maintained through every subsequent cell division. It sets the balance of fetal growth and placental function, and its loss produces Beckwith-Wiedemann, Silver-Russell, Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes as well as loss of imprinting in tumours. Establishment depends on de novo methylation by DNMT3A with its cofactor DNMT3L in the germ line, and on H3K4 demethylation by KDM1B to license those marks; maintenance runs through ZFP57 and TRIM28 recruiting silencing complexes to methylated imprinting control regions. CTCF binding at unmethylated regions builds the chromatin loops that route enhancers to one allele, controlling IGF2 and CDKN1C dosage, while MECP2 and Polycomb components read and reinforce the silent state.

A minority of mammalian genes are expressed from only one parental allele, and genomic imprinting is how that asymmetry is set up in the germline and maintained afterwards. It matters for fetal growth and placental function, for neurodevelopment, and for the parent-of-origin disease patterns seen in Prader-Willi, Angelman and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes, as well as for loss of imprinting in tumours. Imprints are laid down as DNA methylation at control regions during gametogenesis by de novo methyltransferase machinery with its non-catalytic partner DNMT3L, aided by the histone demethylase KDM1B; they are then read and protected through embryonic reprogramming by the ZFP57-TRIM28 complex, which recruits repressive chromatin activity. Downstream, methylation-sensitive CTCF binding partitions enhancers into allele-specific chromatin loops, so that growth regulators such as IGF2 and CDKN1C are dosed according to parental origin.

Semaphorins are guidance cues that tell a growing axon, a migrating cell or a sprouting vessel where not to go, and semaphorin-plexin signaling is how that instruction is read. Secreted class 3 semaphorins such as SEMA3A act through a holoreceptor in which neuropilin-1 or -2 binds the ligand and a plexin transduces it, while membrane-bound classes engage plexins directly; SEMA7A instead uses integrins. The output is cytoskeletal: plexins act on Rho-family GTPases including RAC1 and RHOA, with GAP and exchange-factor partners and collapsin response mediator proteins remodelling actin and microtubules to collapse growth cones and retract processes. Cross-talk with receptor tyrosine kinases such as MET, ERBB2 and VEGFR2 links the same cues to cell motility, angiogenesis and cardiac outflow tract and neural crest patterning. Loss of these signals produces axon misrouting, defective vascular and craniofacial development, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; the pathway is also co-opted in immune cell interactions and tumour invasion.

Cementum mineralization is the deposition of carbonated hydroxyapatite into the acellular cementum layer covering the tooth root, the mineralized tissue into which periodontal ligament fibres insert. Without it the tooth cannot be anchored to alveolar bone, and defective cementum underlies periodontal attachment loss and premature tooth loss, as seen in hypophosphatasia when tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase fails to clear pyrophosphate and permit crystal growth. The pathway couples secretion of an appropriate extracellular matrix by cementoblasts to control of local phosphate and inhibitor levels, with the osteoblast-lineage transcription factor SP7 driving differentiation of the mineralizing cell and FGF receptor and Wnt secretion signals patterning root formation. It is best understood as a tooth-specific arm of biomineralization, closely related to bone and dentin matrix mineralization and dependent on the same balance between promoters and inhibitors of apatite nucleation.

Cementum is the mineralized layer that coats the tooth root and anchors periodontal ligament fibers to it, so the deposition of carbonated hydroxyapatite into the initial acellular cementum determines whether a tooth stays attached to its socket. The gene complement points to the same machinery used elsewhere in skeletal mineralization: tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase hydrolyzes extracellular pyrophosphate, the inhibitor that otherwise blocks crystal growth, and its deficiency in hypophosphatasia causes cementum failure and premature loss of primary teeth. Osterix (SP7) drives the transcriptional programme of the mineralizing cell lineage, while FGF receptor signalling and Wnt ligand secretion through WLS supply the inductive cues that pattern root formation. The process links matrix chemistry to periodontal attachment, and its disruption presents clinically as periodontal breakdown rather than as a defect in enamel or dentin.

Dopaminergic neuron differentiation is the programme by which a neuroblast becomes a dopamine-secreting neuron, the cell type that supplies midbrain motor and reward circuits and whose loss in the substantia nigra produces the motor deficits of Parkinson's disease. Positional cues set the stage: sonic hedgehog and FGF8 mark the ventral midbrain, and the floor-plate factors FOXA1/FOXA2, LMX1A/LMX1B and OTX2 specify progenitors that are then locked into identity by NR4A2 (Nurr1), PITX3 and EN1, which drive expression of the dopamine synthesis and transport machinery. Canonical WNT signalling through several WNT ligands, FZD1, LRP6, beta-catenin and GSK3B, tuned by the secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP1/2, controls progenitor expansion and the timing of maturation. Trophic factors CDNF, MANF and VEGFs support survival of the differentiating neurons, while PHOX2A/PHOX2B relate the programme to neighbouring catecholaminergic fates. These steps underlie stem-cell protocols for generating replacement dopaminergic neurons.

Inositol pyrophosphates such as 5-IP7 and IP8 carry high-energy diphosphate groups on the inositol ring and act as metabolic messengers, reporting cellular phosphate and ATP status and tuning insulin secretion, vesicle trafficking, phosphate homeostasis and the response of proteins to pyrophosphorylation. Turnover of these molecules is as regulated as their synthesis, and the diphosphoinositol polyphosphate metabolic route described here is the catabolic side: a small family of Nudix hydrolases removes the beta-phosphate from the diphosphate group, converting the pyrophosphorylated species back to inositol hexakisphosphate and related lower forms. NUDT3, NUDT4 and the closely related NUDT10 and NUDT11 perform this hydrolysis, setting the steady-state concentration and therefore the signalling output of the pyrophosphates. The same enzymes also act on diadenosine polyphosphates and on mRNA decapping substrates, linking this chemistry to broader nucleotide turnover and to control of cell growth and energy balance.

Dexamethasone is a synthetic glucocorticoid, and the cellular response to it is essentially the pharmacological version of stress-hormone signalling through the glucocorticoid receptor encoded by NR3C1. Ligand-bound receptor enters the nucleus and reprograms transcription, which is why the drug suppresses inflammation, redistributes fuel, and causes the side effects of long-term steroid use: muscle wasting, hyperglycaemia and altered hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal tone. Several arms are visible here. Gluconeogenic and nitrogen-handling enzymes such as PCK1, PCK2, TAT, CPS1 and ASS1 shift the liver toward glucose and urea production. In muscle, induction of FBXO32 and myostatin together with FOXO3 and repression of growth signalling through DDIT4 on mTOR/S6 kinase drives atrophy. Feedback on CRH reflects adrenal axis suppression, while effects on apoptotic regulators including CASP9 and CFLAR underlie glucocorticoid-induced lymphocyte death exploited in leukaemia therapy.

Dexamethasone is a synthetic glucocorticoid, and this pathway covers how a cell reacts when it binds the glucocorticoid receptor: transcriptional reprogramming that suppresses inflammation, mobilises fuel, and, in muscle, drives atrophy. It explains both the therapeutic power and the side effects of steroid drugs. Ligand-bound NR3C1 acts as a transcription factor, inducing gluconeogenic enzymes such as PCK1 and PCK2 to raise glucose output, and switching on the atrophy programme through myostatin and the muscle-specific ubiquitin ligase FBXO32 while DDIT4 restrains mTORC1 signalling upstream of RPS6KB1 and cap-dependent translation. Glucocorticoid action also feeds back on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis through CRH, and modulates apoptotic set-point via CASP9 and the caspase-8 inhibitor CFLAR. The net result is catabolic, growth-suppressive, and immunosuppressive, which is why prolonged exposure produces muscle wasting and hyperglycaemia.

Cells change shape, secretion and gene expression when they detect transforming growth factor beta, and this response governs wound healing, immune restraint, extracellular matrix production and epithelial plasticity. Latent ligand released from matrix stores by integrins and proteases engages type I and II serine/threonine kinase receptors, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3; with SMAD4 these enter the nucleus and recruit coactivators such as CREBBP/EP300 or corepressors including SIN3A-HDAC and SKI/SKIL complexes to switch on collagens, fibronectin-associated matrix proteins and cell-cycle inhibitors. Inhibitory SMAD6/SMAD7, SMURF ubiquitin ligases, phosphatases and a large set of microRNAs tune the duration of signalling, while decoy and accessory receptors set ligand access. Sustained output drives fibrosis, smooth-muscle and myofibroblast differentiation and epithelial-mesenchymal transition; loss of pathway components underlies aortic aneurysm syndromes, skeletal and cardiac malformation, and tumour escape from growth arrest.

Ufmylation is the covalent tagging of substrate proteins with the ubiquitin-like modifier UFM1, a modification most closely tied to endoplasmic reticulum homeostasis and the response to ER stress. It matters for secretory-pathway quality control and for ribosome-associated quality control at the ER membrane, where stalled translocating ribosomes are marked for clearance; loss of the machinery impairs erythroid development and hematopoiesis and underlies neurodevelopmental and encephalopathic disease in humans. The chemistry follows the familiar three-enzyme logic: UBA5 activates UFM1, UFC1 carries it as a thioester, and the ligase UFL1, anchored at the ER by the membrane protein DDRGK1 and working with CDK5RAP3 as a substrate adaptor, transfers it to targets. The modification is reversible, with UFSP1 acting as a UFM1-specific protease that both matures the precursor and removes the mark, making ufmylation a dynamic signal rather than a degradation tag.

Zinc is required as a catalytic and structural cofactor by hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, but it is toxic when free in the cytosol, so cells control its entry at the plasma membrane. Uptake of zinc ions from the extracellular space into the cytosol is carried out largely by ZIP-family carriers: SLC39A4 mediates dietary zinc absorption in the intestine, and its loss causes acrodermatitis enteropathica, while SLC39A8 and SLC39A14 also carry manganese and iron and are linked to manganese-deficiency disorders and hepatic metal handling. SLC39A6 and SLC39A10 raise cytosolic zinc in contexts including epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and immune cell signalling. Balancing these importers, ZnT-family proteins such as SLC30A1 move zinc in the opposite direction, out of the cytosol, and SLC30A8 loads insulin granules in pancreatic beta cells, tying this transport network to secretion, growth and zinc homeostasis.

detoxification of cadmium ion is how cells limit damage from cadmium, a non-essential heavy metal that enters through transporters meant for zinc, manganese and iron, then binds thiols, displaces zinc from proteins, and drives oxidative stress. Chronic exposure through diet and tobacco smoke injures the kidney proximal tubule, bone and lung, so the capacity to bind and export cadmium sets individual susceptibility. Protection works on two fronts: cysteine-rich metallothionein sequesters the ion in a nearly inert complex, while membrane transporters move it out of the cytosol or into vesicular compartments, including a mitochondrial ABC transporter and the zinc efflux protein SLC30A1.
