Together they illustrate why oxygen handling sits at the junction of energy metabolism, redox signalling and oxidative stress, where excess reactive oxygen contributes to inflammation and tissue injury.

Reactive oxygen species metabolism covers both the deliberate production of superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants and the machinery that disposes of them, and cells depend on keeping the two in balance. Controlled bursts are how phagocytes kill ingested microbes, how thyroid and mucosal peroxidases perform oxidative chemistry, and how growth factor and cytokine signals are transduced through reversible cysteine oxidation; uncontrolled accumulation damages lipids, proteins and DNA and drives inflammation, neurodegeneration and ageing phenotypes. NADPH oxidases with their regulatory subunits and small GTPases generate oxidants at membranes, while leaky mitochondrial respiratory complexes contribute a constant background. Opposing them are superoxide dismutases, catalase, glutathione and thioredoxin peroxidases and the peroxiredoxins, with NFE2L2 inducing antioxidant genes and p53, FOXO and sirtuin programmes tuning the setpoint. Redox stress also feeds into apoptosis, mitophagy and hypoxia responses.

Most proteins are made in the cytosol but must end up somewhere else, and this pathway covers the targeting and delivery steps that put them there: import into the nucleus, mitochondria and peroxisomes, insertion into the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and sorting onward to lysosomes and endosomes. Each route has its own recognition machinery — signal recognition particle subunits and the Sec61 translocon with signal peptidase for the secretory pathway, importins, nucleoporins and the Ran system for nucleocytoplasmic transport, TOM and TIM complexes with matrix processing peptidases for mitochondria, and peroxins with the PEX5 receptor for peroxisomal matrix enzymes. Mannose-6-phosphate tagging and receptors such as M6PR and IGF2R route hydrolases to lysosomes, while ESCRT components and Rab GTPases handle cargo in multivesicular bodies. Because compartment identity depends on correct delivery, mistargeting underlies peroxisome biogenesis disorders, lysosomal storage disease, mitochondrial dysfunction and protein aggregation.

Once a protein has reached its correct compartment it must be held there, and this retention biology is what keeps resident proteins from drifting away with bulk traffic or diffusing out of the subdomain where they work. Its failure shows up as secretion of proteins that belong in the endoplasmic reticulum, loss of nuclear body integrity, and mislocalized metabolic enzymes. Several distinct retrieval and anchoring systems are represented: KDEL receptors and RER1 capture escaped ER residents from the Golgi and return them; INSIG proteins tether SREBP cleavage machinery and HMG-CoA reductase in the ER membrane according to sterol levels; SUN domain proteins and nesprins hold components at the nuclear envelope and link them to the cytoskeleton; PML and SP100 retain partners within nuclear bodies. Hexokinase docking at mitochondria and PINK1-dependent retention illustrate how localization control feeds into energy metabolism and mitochondrial quality surveillance.

Secreted and membrane proteins are made on cytosolic ribosomes but must be delivered into the endoplasmic reticulum, and establishment of protein localization to the endoplasmic reticulum is how that delivery is achieved and made accurate. Signal sequences are captured co-translationally by the signal recognition particle and its RNA scaffold, handed to the SRP receptor at the ER surface, and threaded through the Sec61 translocon with SEC62, SEC63 and the translocon-associated complex assisting insertion; signal peptidase subunits then remove the targeting sequence and TRAM proteins aid membrane integration. Tail-anchored proteins take a separate route, with BAG6, UBL4A, SGTA and GET factors shielding hydrophobic tails until insertion. Chaperones such as HSPA5 and quality-control components including EDEM1 and HERPUD1 handle proteins that fold poorly or mislocalize. Loss of translocon function causes secretory deficiency and ER stress, underlying immunodeficiency and polycystic kidney disease.

Almost all mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol and must be delivered across one or both mitochondrial membranes, and this pathway covers that delivery and the sorting decisions that follow. It sustains oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial gene expression and organelle biogenesis; when import stalls, precursors clog the translocases, quality-control proteases and ubiquitin machinery are recruited, and neurodegenerative and metabolic disease follows. Outer-membrane receptors and the TOM channel accept precursors, TIM22 and TIM23 complexes with their motor and chaperone partners drive insertion or matrix translocation, small intermembrane-space carriers and a disulfide relay handle hydrophobic and cysteine-rich substrates, and processing peptidases trim targeting sequences. The set also spans regulated targeting of cytosolic proteins to mitochondria — hexokinases, BAX and BID during apoptosis, and PINK1 with parkin in damage sensing and mitophagy — linking import competence to cell death and organelle turnover.

Keeping a protein where it belongs inside a mitochondrion is a regulated act, not a passive one, and this maintenance of protein location in mitochondria governs both cell survival decisions and mitochondrial quality control. The clearest stake is apoptosis: retaining cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins behind an intact outer membrane prevents caspase activation, so loss of retention commits a cell to death. Hexokinases 1 and 2 bind the outer membrane and, with AKT1 signalling that promotes and stabilises that association, couple glycolytic activity to membrane integrity and anti-apoptotic protection, a link exploited by tumour cells. PINK1 accumulates on depolarised mitochondria rather than being imported and cleaved, and its retention there marks damaged organelles for mitophagy. TSPO sits in the outer membrane as part of cholesterol and ligand-responsive regulation of these interactions.

Membranes only work if the right proteins arrive at the right face of the right compartment and stay there, and protein localization to membrane covers the delivery, insertion, anchoring and retention steps that make this happen. It sets up epithelial polarity, synaptic receptor density, ciliary composition and the surface display of transporters, adhesion molecules and signalling receptors; when it fails, receptors are mistargeted or trapped internally, and the consequences range from ciliopathies to neuromuscular junction failure. Mechanistically it draws on vesicle traffic and fusion (Rab GTPases, SNAREs such as VAMP2 and syntaxins, clathrin adaptors, exocyst and retromer), lipid modification that tethers proteins to bilayers (myristoyltransferases and ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases), scaffolds and PDZ adaptors such as DLG4 and NHERF proteins that hold cargo in place, tail-anchored and peroxisomal insertion via PEX machinery, and cytoskeletal links through ankyrins, spectrin and ezrin-radixin-moesin proteins.

The identity of a cell surface "" which transporters, channels, receptors and adhesion molecules face the outside world "" depends on protein localization to the plasma membrane, the sorting, delivery, insertion and retention of membrane proteins at the cell periphery. It determines ion transport capacity, hormone and growth factor responsiveness, epithelial polarity and synaptic receptor content, and its failure underlies channelopathies, defective glucose and water handling, and mislocalized receptor signalling in cancer. Cargo leaves the secretory pathway with help from COPII and Golgi adaptors, travels on Rab-, kinesin- and myosin-dependent vesicles, and fuses via SNAREs such as VAMP2 and syntaxins. Once there, scaffolds including ankyrins, spectrins, ezrin/radixin and PDZ adaptors like NHERF1 and SCRIB anchor proteins in polarized domains, while clathrin adaptors, EHD proteins and retromer control internalization and recycling. Palmitoylation by ZDHHC enzymes and chaperone-like accessory subunits set membrane targeting and residence time.

Peroxisomes have no genome of their own, so every enzyme inside them must be made in the cytosol and imported; establishing protein localization to the peroxisome is that delivery step, and it determines whether the organelle can carry out beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids, ether lipid synthesis and hydrogen peroxide detoxification at all. Cargo bearing a type 1 or type 2 targeting signal is captured by the receptors PEX5 or PEX7, docked at a membrane translocon built around PEX13 and PEX14, and released into the matrix, after which an AAA-ATPase pair, PEX1 and PEX6, anchored by PEX26, recycles the receptor by ubiquitin-dependent export. A separate branch, using PEX19, PEX3 and PEX16, inserts membrane proteins and supports organelle biogenesis. Loss of these steps leaves empty peroxisomal ghosts and causes Zellweger spectrum disorders, with severe neurological and hepatic disease.

Delivering proteins into the lysosome or vacuole is how cells dispose of membrane receptors, degrade damaged organelles, and stock the acidic compartment with hydrolases. Several routes converge here: mannose-6-phosphate tagging by the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase complex and its uncovering enzyme, with sorting receptors such as M6PR, IGF2R and SORT1 carrying enzymes from the Golgi; ESCRT machinery (HGS, STAM, TSG101, VPS37 subunits, SNF8, VPS4A) sorting ubiquitinated cargo into intraluminal vesicles of multivesicular bodies; and autophagic capture by BECN1, PIK3C3 and the cargo receptors SQSTM1 and NCOA4. Tethering and conversion steps involving RAB7A, MON1 proteins and HOPS component VPS41 complete fusion, while LAMTOR/Rag components couple the lysosomal surface to mTORC1 nutrient sensing. Loss of these routes produces lysosomal storage disease, defective receptor downregulation, and neurodegeneration, as seen with ATP13A2 and VPS13 mutations.

establishment of protein localization to vacuole is the set of sorting routes that deliver proteins into the lysosome (the animal cell's vacuole), either as resident hydrolases or as cargo destined for degradation. It supports lysosomal digestive capacity, receptor downregulation, antigen processing and autophagic turnover; its failure produces lysosomal storage disease, pigment and platelet granule defects, and neurodegeneration. Newly made acid hydrolases are tagged by the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase complex and captured by mannose 6-phosphate receptors, while sortilin, SORL1 and LIMP-2 route other cargo; AP-3 and the HOPS/GARP-associated factors direct carriers to the organelle. Ubiquitinated membrane proteins take a different path, packaged by ESCRT-0 through ESCRT-III and VPS4 into multivesicular bodies, with RAB7A and MON1 controlling maturation and fusion. Autophagic delivery through the class III PI3K complex and receptors such as SQSTM1 and NCOA4 converges on the same endpoint.

Delivery of proteins into the lysosome or vacuole is how cells dispose of membrane receptors, degrade damaged organelles, and stock the acidic compartment with the hydrolases that do the digesting. Establishment of protein localization to the vacuole covers the routes that accomplish this: mannose 6-phosphate tagging of newly made hydrolases by the GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase subunits and their carriage by the M6P receptors and sortilins; ubiquitin-dependent sorting of internalized receptors through the ESCRT complexes into multivesicular bodies; adaptor complexes and HOPS/GARP-associated tethers that direct cargo from Golgi and endosomes; and autophagic capture by beclin-1 and the class III PI3-kinase with receptors such as p62 and NCOA4 for ferritin. Rab7 and its MON1 activators govern the late endosome-lysosome fusion step. Loss of these components causes lysosomal storage disease, pigment and platelet granule defects in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, and neurodegeneration.

Neutrophils reach infected or injured tissue only by leaving the bloodstream, and neutrophil extravasation is the sequence of rolling, firm adhesion, crawling and squeezing between or through endothelial cells that gets them there. It sets the pace of acute inflammation: without it, bacterial and fungal infections go uncontained, as in leukocyte adhesion deficiencies, while excessive transmigration drives tissue damage in sepsis, reperfusion injury and vasculitis. The genes here span the stages. A fucosyltransferase builds the sialyl-Lewis-X selectin ligands needed for capture, junctional adhesion molecules such as PECAM1, CD99, CD99L2 and JAML guide passage across endothelial contacts, and CD177 pairs with the neutrophil serine protease PRTN3 at the surface. Class I PI3K catalytic subunits p110delta and p110gamma relay chemoattractant and integrin signals into polarised motility, with RIPOR2 restraining integrin activation and IL1R1 linking the process to inflammatory cytokine cues.</description

Lamellipodium morphogenesis builds and shapes the flat, branched actin sheet at the leading edge of a crawling cell, the structure that lets fibroblasts, immune cells and metastatic tumour cells advance in a chosen direction. Without it cells lose directional protrusion and wound healing, immune trafficking and developmental migration all stall. The core machinery is the WAVE regulatory complex, where WASF1/WASF2 and ABI1 activate Arp2/3-dependent actin branching downstream of Rac; ARHGEF7 supplies Rho-family GTPase activation, ARPIN provides an inhibitory brake that sets protrusion frequency, and coronins remodel and debranch the network as it matures. Surface receptors such as CD44 and podoplanin couple the extracellular matrix and membrane signals to this actin machine, with SRC kinase and sorting nexin-dependent membrane traffic positioning the response, making lamellipodium formation the point where migratory cues become mechanical movement.

Lamellipodium morphogenesis is the shaping of the flat, actin-rich sheet at the front of a crawling cell, and it determines whether a cell can migrate at all — the same protrusion that lets leukocytes chase chemoattractants, keratinocytes close a wound, and tumour cells invade surrounding tissue. Its core is branched actin nucleation: WAVE-complex members such as WASF1, WASF2 and the adaptor ABI1 activate the Arp2/3 machinery at the leading edge, while ARPIN opposes it and coronins remodel and debranch the resulting network, so protrusion depends on balancing assembly against turnover. Rho-family control enters through the exchange factor ARHGEF7 and the myosin-family GAP MYO9B, and adhesion and membrane cues arrive via CD44, podoplanin and the lysophospholipid-generating enzyme autotaxin. Coordinating these inputs sets protrusion direction and persistence, linking the pathway to wound healing, immune surveillance and metastasis.

Bone is continually resorbed by osteoclasts, and multinuclear osteoclast differentiation is the route by which monocyte-lineage precursors commit to that fate and then fuse into the large multinucleated cells capable of dissolving mineralized matrix. Without it, resorption fails and bone accumulates as osteopetrosis; with too much of it, the balance tips toward the bone loss seen in osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis and skeletal metastasis. RANK, encoded by TNFRSF11A, receives the RANKL signal from osteoblasts and stromal cells that licenses commitment and drives the downstream transcriptional programme, with SBNO2 acting as one of its induced regulators. Cell-cell fusion then requires dedicated membrane proteins, notably DC-STAMP and OC-STAMP, alongside the tetraspanin CD81. SH3PXD2A supplies the scaffold for podosomes and the sealing zone through which the mature cell secretes acid and proteases onto the bone surface.

Osteoclast fusion is the step that turns mononuclear macrophage-lineage precursors into the large multinucleated cells that resorb bone. Fusion is what gives the osteoclast the sealed resorption zone and the secretory capacity needed to dissolve mineral and degrade collagen, so bone remodelling, tooth eruption, and calcium release from the skeleton all depend on it; when fusion fails, cells remain small and mononuclear and bone accumulates, while excessive fusion accompanies the erosive lesions of osteoporosis, arthritis, and metastatic bone disease. The process runs downstream of RANKL and M-CSF signalling and requires dedicated membrane machinery: DCSTAMP acts as the master fusogenic receptor, tetraspanin CD81 organises the fusion-competent membrane microdomains, and SH3PXD2A links podosome and invadopodial actin structures to the cell-cell contacts where merger occurs, with SBNO2 acting as a transcriptional output of the same differentiation programme.

Bone resorption is carried out by large multinucleated cells, and this fusion step is how they are made: mononuclear osteoclast precursors of the monocyte/macrophage lineage merge their plasma membranes to form a single syncytium capable of sealing onto bone and dissolving mineral and matrix. Multinucleation gives the cell the size and cytoskeletal organisation needed for an effective resorptive apparatus, so blocking it reduces bone loss, while excessive fusion accompanies the osteolysis of osteoporosis, inflammatory arthritis and bone metastasis. Fusion is driven downstream of RANKL and inflammatory signalling by dedicated surface molecules, including a transmembrane protein required specifically for precursor fusion and a tetraspanin that organises membrane microdomains, together with a podosome-associated adaptor linking membrane contact to actin remodelling. Transcriptional modulators tune how readily precursors commit to fusing.

Lymphocytes are only useful where they are needed, and this pathway covers the movement that gets them there: exit from bone marrow and thymus, entry into lymph nodes and gut, patrolling of blood and tissue, and recruitment to inflamed sites. It underlies immune surveillance, germinal centre organisation and the tissue tropism that vaccines and lymphocyte-trafficking drugs exploit; when it fails, immunodeficiency, lymphopenia or misdirected inflammation follow. Chemokines and their receptors, including the CCL21/CCR7 axis for lymph node homing and CXCL13 and CXCL12 gradients, provide directional cues sensed through Gi-coupled receptors and PI3K isoforms. Integrins such as LFA-1 and the gut-homing α4β7 pair with endothelial ICAM1 and MADCAM1 for adhesion and diapedesis, while RHOA, moesin, WNK1 and actin regulators remodel the cell to squeeze through. Sphingosine-1-phosphate sensing via S1PR1, and oxysterol cues through GPR183, set egress and positioning within tissue.

Eosinophil migration is the recruitment and trafficking of eosinophils out of the bloodstream and through tissues, and it determines where allergic and antiparasitic inflammation is actually felt — in the airway wall in asthma, in the oesophageal mucosa in eosinophilic oesophagitis, and in the gut and skin in other eosinophil-driven disease. The dominant signals are chemokines acting on eosinophil receptors, above all the eotaxins CCL11, CCL24 and CCL26 that signal through CCR3, together with CCL5, CCL7 and related ligands and the membrane-anchored chemoattractant CX3CL1. Additional modulators tune the response: a prostaglandin E2 receptor, a surface immunoreceptor that restrains eosinophil activation, a galectin promoting adhesion, and a metalloprotease-disintegrin implicated in transmigration. Eosinophil peroxidase marks the granule contents these cells carry to the site, linking migration to the tissue damage and remodelling that follow.

T cell migration is how the adaptive immune system positions its effectors: thymocytes leave the thymus, naive cells recirculate through lymph nodes, and activated cells home to inflamed tissue, gut, or skin. Without it, antigen is never encountered and immunity fails at the level of geography rather than specificity. Chemokine receptors and their ligands set direction, with a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor and its transporter governing egress from lymphoid organs into circulation. Integrins such as LFA-1 and the gut-homing u03b14 u03b27 pair, together with ICAM1 and junctional proteins, mediate arrest on endothelium and diapedesis. Inside the cell, Rho GTPase signalling, PI3K isoforms, DOCK8, moesin and myosin remodel the actin cortex for amoeboid movement, while a WNK1-OXSR1-STK39-SLC12A2 module couples ion and volume regulation to motility. Defects impair immune surveillance and underlie immunodeficiency with poor lymphocyte trafficking.

Developing T cells do not mature in one place: they move through cortex and medulla in a set order, and each stop supplies the signals and the selecting cells they need. Thymocyte migration is what makes that itinerary happen, and it matters most for central tolerance, because thymocytes that never reach the medulla are never tested against the self-antigens displayed there and can escape as autoreactive clones. Chemokine receptors on the thymocyte read gradients laid down by stromal and epithelial cells, with XCL1 from medullary epithelium recruiting dendritic cells that present self-peptide and CCR6 responding to CCL20; the transcriptional regulator AIRE drives promiscuous self-antigen expression in that same medullary compartment. Loss of these cues underlies autoimmune disease arising from defective negative selection rather than from failed T cell production.

T cell extravasation is the exit of circulating T cells from the bloodstream into tissue, the step that converts a blood-borne lymphocyte pool into local immune surveillance and inflammatory infiltrate. Without it, pathogens in peripheral tissue go unchallenged; in excess, it drives the lymphocytic infiltration seen in autoimmune and chronic inflammatory disease and in allograft rejection. Chemokine signalling through CCL2 and its receptor CCR2 arrests and directs cells toward inflamed endothelium, while the integrin LFA-1 (ITGAL) engaging endothelial ICAM1 provides firm adhesion. Passage through the junction itself depends on junctional adhesion molecule A (F11R) and on CD99 and CD99L2, which act sequentially at the endothelial cell border, with CRK and CRKL adaptors relaying signals into cytoskeletal rearrangement. The process links leukocyte trafficking to endothelial barrier regulation and to the cytokine environment that licenses recruitment.

Targeting and retention of proteins at the cell cortex, the actin-rich layer beneath the plasma membrane, determines where a cell anchors its membrane to the cytoskeleton and where it positions its spindle. Two themes run through the genes involved. One is structural linkage: band 4.1 proteins, ezrin and the integrin-linked kinase complex tether membrane proteins and adhesion receptors to cortical actin, giving epithelial and blood cells their shape and mechanical resilience. The other is mitotic: a cortical force-generating module built on heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunits, the LGN scaffold and NuMA captures astral microtubules and orients the spindle, with PLK1 and SAPCD2 acting as timing and polarity inputs. Spindle orientation set at the cortex decides whether division is symmetric or asymmetric, shaping tissue architecture and the balance between progenitor self-renewal and differentiation.

Hydroxyurea depletes deoxyribonucleotides by blocking ribonucleotide reductase, so cells exposed to it must stabilise replication forks that have run out of substrate and restart them without breaking the chromosome. The response defines how cells tolerate replication stress, and its failure underlies the chromosome fragility and cancer predisposition seen in recombination and helicase disorders. Members act at the stalled fork: RAD51 coats resected single-stranded DNA and protects nascent strands, the BLM helicase and its partner SPIDR resolve recombination intermediates, DDX11 and TIMELESS support fork progression and sister chromatid cohesion, and an SMC5/6 subunit and chromatin factors such as ATRX and the acetyltransferase KAT7 maintain fork-associated chromatin. Nuclease and protease activities, including TREX1 and the DDI1/DDI2 pair, remove DNA and protein obstacles, the latter also driving proteasome gene expression to cope with damage.

Cisplatin kills cells by forming platinum-DNA crosslinks, and the cellular response to this drug determines whether a tumour cell dies or survives treatment. The genes here span the main arms of that response: homologous recombination repair of crosslink-induced breaks through RAD51, replication fork and fork-protection functions carried by the helicase DDX11 and the replisome component TIMELESS, and commitment to mitochondrial apoptosis through the BCL-2 family effector BOK. Drug handling and stress adaptation also feature, with the ABCC2 transporter effluxing platinum conjugates out of the cell and heme oxygenase-1 plus the NF-kB regulator NFKBIZ supporting oxidative-stress and inflammatory adaptation. Because these activities set the threshold for cisplatin-induced death, they underlie both chemotherapy resistance in ovarian, testicular and lung cancers and the nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity that limit dosing.</description

Pathogens do not enter cells unaided; they exploit host surface proteases, receptors and lipid-remodelling enzymes, and this pathway collects the host-encoded activities a symbiont or pathogen recruits to promote its own entry. It matters because these steps set tropism and infectivity, and several members are drug targets in respiratory viral infection. Cell-surface serine proteases such as TMPRSS2 and TMPRSS4, together with the proprotein convertase furin, cleave viral envelope glycoproteins to prime membrane fusion, while acid sphingomyelinase remodels sphingolipids to form the ceramide platforms that facilitate uptake. Basigin and the galectins LGALS1 and LGALS9 act as attachment or co-receptor surfaces, protein disulfide isomerase P4HB supports redox-dependent conformational changes in entry glycoproteins, and released HMGB1 modulates the inflammatory context. TRIM proteins bring ubiquitin-dependent regulation, linking entry to intrinsic antiviral defence and its subversion.

Many viruses do not fuse at the plasma membrane but are swallowed whole, and endocytic uptake during viral entry is the step that delivers them into endosomes where acidification and host proteases trigger escape into the cytoplasm. This route determines which cells a virus can infect and supplies several of the best drug targets in antiviral therapy. Receptors and attachment factors such as ACE2, DPP4, the lectins CLEC4M and SIGLEC1 concentrate particles at the surface; clathrin adaptors including EPS15 and the caveolar coat proteins CAV1 and CAV2 internalise them; and the endolysosomal protease cathepsin L cleaves viral glycoproteins to license fusion. Progression through the endosomal system depends on the lipid kinase PIKFYVE and on the two-pore channels TPCN1 and TPCN2, whose calcium release is required for trafficking of Ebola and coronavirus particles to the compartment where penetration occurs.

Picornaviruses and related viruses cannot rely on the cap-binding machinery their infected host often shuts down, so their messages carry an internal ribosome entry site in the 5' untranslated region that recruits the 43S preinitiation complex directly. This IRES-dependent route lets viral protein synthesis continue while cap-dependent initiation is suppressed by eIF4G cleavage or stress-induced eIF2 phosphorylation, and it is one of the main reasons infected cells are taken over so efficiently. Structured RNA elements are bound by host factors acting as IRES trans-acting proteins, including the poly(C)- and poly(pyrimidine)-binding proteins PCBP2 and PTBP1, the La antigen SSB, and the RNA-binding regulator CSDE1, which remodel the element into a ribosome-competent shape. Core eIF3 subunits provide the ribosome contact, while DENR, MCTS1 and EIF2D support non-canonical start-site selection and initiator tRNA delivery.

Some viruses encode two proteins in overlapping reading frames and rely on the ribosome slipping to a different frame partway through an mRNA, a recoding event known as programmed ribosomal frameshifting. Because the slip happens at a fixed efficiency set by an mRNA structure and a slippery sequence, viruses use it to fix the stoichiometry between structural and enzymatic products, as in the Gag-Pol polyproteins of retroviruses. The cellular counterparts here show that the mechanism is not exclusively viral: the antizyme genes use a +1 frameshift to couple their own synthesis to polyamine levels, and PEG10 is a domesticated retroelement whose expression still depends on frameshifting. SHFL is an interferon-induced antiviral protein that suppresses this recoding and thereby restricts viruses that require it, placing the process at the interface of translational control and innate immune defence.

viral translational termination-reinitiation is a translational strategy that lets a single viral mRNA express two proteins from separate open reading frames, giving segmented and dicistronic viral genomes a way to make structural and nonstructural proteins in fixed ratios without extra transcripts. Caliciviruses and influenza B use it to control capsid and accessory protein stoichiometry, so it determines viral particle output rather than merely adding protein diversity. Mechanistically, ribosomes translate the upstream ORF and terminate normally, but a short upstream element base-pairs with 18S rRNA and holds a fraction of 40S subunits on the message; retention of the eIF3 complex on those subunits, through core and peripheral subunits such as eIF3a, eIF3b and eIF3d, keeps them initiation-competent so they can recruit initiator tRNA at the downstream start codon. The pathway is thus a hijacking of canonical cap-dependent initiation factors for non-canonical reinitiation.

Some viruses pack two genes into one messenger RNA and get both translated by letting the ribosome restart rather than reload. In this termination-reinitiation strategy, ribosomes finish the upstream open reading frame, but instead of dissociating completely a fraction of 40S subunits stay tethered to the message and resume initiation at the downstream start codon, so a single dicistronic transcript yields two proteins in fixed proportion. The tethering depends on subunits of the eIF3 complex, the large multisubunit initiation factor that normally binds the 40S subunit and coordinates mRNA and initiator tRNA recruitment; a short upstream RNA element near the stop codon holds eIF3-bound ribosomes in place. This gives viruses such as caliciviruses and influenza B a way to control the stoichiometry of structural and accessory proteins without additional promoters or subgenomic RNAs, exploiting host initiation machinery for gene expression the cell would not otherwise permit.

Cells and tissues meet damage, infection, heat, nutrient shortage and oxidative insult with defined defensive programmes, and this pathway covers the regulatory layer that sets how strongly and how long those programmes run. Tuning matters as much as triggering: too little response leaves DNA breaks unrepaired or pathogens unchecked, while too much produces chronic inflammation, autoimmunity or unnecessary cell death. The membership spans the main stress arms and their brakes — DNA damage sensing and repair around ATM, ATR, BRCA1 and 53BP1; innate immune detection through Toll-like receptors, RIG-I-like sensors, cGAS–STING and inflammasome components, restrained by negative regulators such as TNFAIP3, IRAK3, CYLD and SIGIRR; the unfolded protein response via ATF6, XBP1, ERN1 and PERK; heat-shock chaperones under HSF1; antioxidant control through KEAP1–NRF2; plus apoptotic decision-making, ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, chromatin remodellers and microRNAs that dose each output.

regulation of cellular response to stress governs how strongly and for how long a cell reacts when its DNA, proteins, or metabolism are damaged, deciding between repair and adaptation on one hand and death on the other. This tuning determines whether irradiated or misfolded-protein-burdened cells survive intact, senesce, or apoptose, and its loss underlies genome instability, tumour progression and degenerative disease. The genes cover the DNA damage response and its control -- ATM, ATR, CHEK1, BRCA1/2, 53BP1 and shieldin, PARP1 and RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitin signalling -- together with chromatin remodelling and acetyltransferase complexes (SWI/SNF, INO80, NuA4/TIP60, SAGA) that make damaged chromatin accessible. Parallel arms set the threshold of the unfolded protein response through IRE1, PERK, ATF6 and ERAD, the heat shock response through HSF1 and DNAJ chaperones, oxidative and hypoxic signalling via NFE2L2 and VHL, and p53-MDM2 control of BAX, PUMA and NOXA at the apoptotic commitment point.

Cells constantly tune how strongly they react to damaging conditions, and this regulatory layer sets the frequency and extent of the cellular response to stress "— deciding whether a damaged cell pauses, repairs, adapts, or dies. It gathers the control points of several stress programmes at once: DNA damage sensing and checkpoint signalling through ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and the MRE11"–RAD50"–NBN complex with its downstream repair and end-protection factors; the unfolded protein response arms centred on ATF6, ERN1, XBP1, EIF2AK3, HSPA5 and CHOP; heat shock control via HSF1 and DNAJ/HSPA chaperones; and oxidative and redox defence through NFE2L2, peroxiredoxin and SLC7A11. Chromatin remodellers, acetyltransferases, deubiquitinases and ubiquitin ligases such as MDM2 and STUB1 act as the dials, while p53 targets including BAX, PMAIP1 and BBC3 set the apoptotic threshold. Miscalibration here underlies tumour survival under genotoxic therapy, neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury.

Cells must keep their internal pools of amino acids within a narrow range, because those pools feed protein synthesis, neurotransmitter production, glutathione supply and the nutrient signals that decide whether a cell grows. Maintenance of intracellular amino acid homeostasis combines transport across the plasma membrane and lysosomal membrane with enzymatic interconversion and protein turnover. Carriers such as the glutamate transporter SLC1A1, the glutamine carrier SLC38A3 and the cystine/glutamate exchanger SLC7A11 set influx and efflux, a lysosomal transporter returns amino acids from degraded protein to the cytosol, glutaminase converts glutamine to glutamate, and tripeptidyl peptidase II trims peptides released by proteasomal degradation. The balance matters most in neurons and in cells under oxidative stress, where cysteine supply limits glutathione; loss of KCTD7 causes progressive myoclonic epilepsy, and disturbed cystine uptake shifts cells toward ferroptotic death.

Fertilization is not a single event but a set of tightly controlled steps, and this pathway covers the processes that set how readily sperm and egg fuse and how the resulting zygote is protected. Its components act on both gametes: zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP1, ZP2 and ZP4 build the egg coat that binds sperm and, once ASTL (ovastacin) cleaves ZP2 after the first fusion event, hardens it to block additional sperm and prevent polyspermy. Sperm-side factors including PRSS37, RNASE10, CFAP69 and TPST2 govern epididymal maturation, motility and the capacity to bind and penetrate the coat, while WEE2 and PLCB1 control egg activation and release from meiotic arrest. Loss of these functions produces oocyte maturation arrest, fertilization failure or male infertility, and underlies several human forms of unexplained infertility and empty follicle syndrome.

Nitric oxide is a short-lived gas that dilates blood vessels, kills microbes inside macrophages and tunes neuronal signalling, so how much of it is made and when is tightly controlled; this pathway collects the inputs that raise or lower nitric oxide output. Endothelial production is set by shear-responsive transcription factors such as KLF2 and KLF4, by AKT1-dependent phosphorylation of the synthase, and by chaperone and scaffolding partners including HSP90 and caveolin-1, which sequesters the enzyme at the plasma membrane. Substrate and cofactor supply matter too: argininosuccinate synthase and lyase regenerate arginine, while DDAH1 and DDAH2 destroy the endogenous inhibitor ADMA and GCHFR feeds back on tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis. Inflammatory signals through TLR4, TNF, IL1B and IFNG drive the inducible high-output route, opposed by IL10. Loss of control underlies endothelial dysfunction, hypertension and nitrosative tissue damage.

Lytic vacuole organization covers the building, positioning, and remodelling of the cell's degradative compartment — in human cells, the lysosome and its relatives such as melanosomes and lytic granules. It matters because lysosomes are where macromolecules are broken down and recycled, where nutrient status is sensed, and where membrane traffic terminates; when their biogenesis fails the result is lysosomal storage disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, or neurodegeneration. Mechanistically the genes describe acidification by the vacuolar ATPase, delivery of mannose-6-phosphate-tagged hydrolases such as glucocerebrosidase and hexosaminidase, ESCRT-dependent membrane scission, tethering and fusion by RAB7A, HOPS and adaptor complexes, and movement along microtubules via ARL8B and HOOK proteins. Ionic homeostasis through MCOLN1, TPCN2 and TMEM175 and transcriptional control by TFEB and TFE3 tune lysosome number and capacity to demand, linking the compartment to mTORC1 signalling and autophagy.

Lysosomes and related lytic vacuoles must be built, acidified, loaded with hydrolases, positioned along microtubules, and eventually remodelled or reformed, and this pathway covers that whole organizational programme. It sustains the cell's capacity to degrade and recycle macromolecules, so its failure produces lysosomal storage disease, neurodegeneration and pigmentation or immune defects. The vacuolar H+-ATPase subunits establish the acidic lumen needed for acid hydrolases such as GBA1, HEXA/HEXB, GAA and TPP1, while GNPTAB-dependent mannose-6-phosphate tagging routes those enzymes there. Channels including MCOLN1, TMEM175 and TPCN2 set lumenal ion balance, ESCRT-III CHMP proteins and tethering complexes shape membranes and deliver cargo, and ARL8B, RAB7A, HOOK adaptors and BORC-linked factors control motor-driven placement. Nutrient signalling through mTORC1 on the lysosomal surface, opposed by TFEB and TFE3, adjusts lysosome number to demand, linking organelle biogenesis to autophagy and growth control.

Phenylpropanoids are plant-derived phenolics include flavonoids, coumarins, anthocyanins and small phenolic esters and mammalian cells respond to them by altering gene expression, detoxification capacity and redox state. This response covers those changes, and it matters mostly through diet and pharmacology: coumarin-type molecules act on vitamin K-dependent clotting, and flavonoids modulate xenobiotic handling in liver and other tissues. The genes involved span the two arms of that response. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor-driven induction of the cytochrome P450 CYP1A1 and conjugation by a UDP-glucuronosyltransferase mark the metabolic disposal of these compounds, while catalase links them to antioxidant defence. Coagulation factor VII reflects the anticoagulant activity of coumarins, and osteocalcin, oxytocin and a membrane metalloproteinase point to downstream effects on bone matrix and tissue remodelling. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of plant secondary metabolite sensing, drug metabolism and hormone-responsive physiology.

Ubiquitin chains can be built through any of seven lysines, and linkage through lysine 6 marks a minority chain type associated with the DNA damage response and with mitochondrial quality control. Attaching these atypical polymers changes how a substrate is read rather than simply condemning it to the proteasome, so the same tagging machinery can recruit repair factors to chromatin or flag damaged organelles for removal. The BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer is the best-characterised source of K6 linkages, acting at double-strand breaks alongside RNF8 and the E2 enzymes UBE2D3 and UBE2T that load ubiquitin onto them; PRKN generates similar chains on outer mitochondrial membrane proteins during mitophagy. Other RING enzymes here, including RNF4, RNF144A and TRIM21, broaden the substrate range. Loss of this activity compromises homologous recombination repair and predisposes to breast and ovarian cancer.

Extracellular matrix assembly is the step after secretion: collagens, elastin and their associated glycoproteins must be aligned, cross-linked and bonded into fibrils, elastic fibres and basement membranes before tissue can bear load. It gives skin, blood vessels, cartilage and bone their mechanical properties, and its failure produces vessel wall fragility, joint and skeletal dysplasia, and the stiffened fibrotic matrix of chronic organ disease. Fibrillar and network collagens supply the scaffold, while lysyl oxidase and peroxidasin form the covalent cross-links, prolyl hydroxylation and FKBP10 handle collagen maturation in the ER, and fibulin-5, EMILIN1, MFAP4 and LTBP4 organise elastic fibre deposition around microfibrils. Hyaluronan synthases add the space-filling polysaccharide. TGF-beta acting through its receptors and SMAD3/SMAD4, together with several microRNAs, sets how much matrix is made and how it is arranged.

The cardiac muscle cell action potential is the electrical event that triggers each heartbeat, and its shape and timing set heart rate, conduction velocity and the refractory period that protects against arrhythmia. Depolarisation is carried by voltage-gated sodium channels led by SCN5A with its beta subunits, the plateau by L-type calcium channels such as CACNA1C, and repolarisation by potassium currents including KCNQ1 with KCNE1, KCNH2, and the inward rectifier KCNJ2; HCN channels generate the pacemaker current in nodal cells. Calcium handling through RYR2, SERCA2 and the sodium-calcium exchanger couples excitation to contraction, while connexins, ankyrins, caveolins and desmosomal proteins position channels and propagate current between myocytes. Mutations in these components underlie long and short QT syndromes, Brugada syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, sick sinus syndrome and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, and the same channels are the targets of antiarrhythmic drugs.

Each heartbeat begins with an electrical event: the cardiac action potential that depolarizes a working myocyte and triggers the calcium release driving contraction. This pathway covers the ion channels, accessory subunits and anchoring proteins that shape that waveform, from the rapid sodium upstroke through L-type calcium influx during the plateau to repolarizing potassium currents. Sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits set conduction velocity, CACNA1C carries the depolarizing calcium current that loads RYR2-mediated release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and KCNQ1 with KCNE1, KCNH2 and KCNJ2 return the cell to rest and fix action potential duration. Gap junction connexins and desmosomal proteins propagate excitation between coupled myocytes, while scaffolds like ANK2 and caveolins position channels correctly. Mutations here underlie long QT and Brugada syndromes, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation.

Each heartbeat depends on cardiac muscle cell contraction, in which electrical excitation is converted into actin-myosin sliding and force generation. The genes here trace the whole excitation-contraction sequence: voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits depolarize the membrane, L-type calcium channels (CACNA1C) admit the calcium trigger, RYR2 releases stored calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum with CASQ2 as its luminal buffer, troponin C and myosin-binding protein C translate that calcium into sarcomere shortening, and SERCA2 with its inhibitor phospholamban pumps calcium back for relaxation. Potassium channels including KCNQ1 and KCNH2 set repolarization and refractoriness, gap junction connexins and desmosomal proteins propagate excitation between cells, and beta-adrenergic, adenosine and nitric oxide signalling tune contractile strength and rate. Mutations across these components cause long QT and Brugada syndromes, catecholaminergic arrhythmias, cardiomyopathy and sudden cardiac death.

The electrical impulse of a ventricular cardiac muscle cell is what times each beat: a rapid sodium-driven upstroke, a long calcium-dependent plateau, and repolarization by potassium efflux, all of which set the duration of contraction and the refractory period that prevents re-excitation. The genes here encode the channels that carry those currents — SCN5A with its beta subunits, the L-type calcium channel CACNA1C, and the potassium channels KCNQ1 and KCNH2 with their KCNE accessory subunits — together with RYR2 and CASQ2, which release stored calcium to link excitation to contraction. Also present are proteins that position and anchor channels at the membrane, including ankyrin-B, caveolins, and desmosomal and plaque components such as PKP2 and DSP. Loss of this tight control produces long QT and Brugada syndromes, catecholaminergic arrhythmia, and sudden cardiac death.

After an excitable cell fires, it must return its membrane potential toward rest before it can fire again, and membrane repolarization is the ion movement that accomplishes this. The timing of that return sets action potential duration and refractoriness, which in the heart determines the QT interval; delayed or accelerated repolarization underlies long and short QT syndromes, Brugada syndrome and catecholaminergic arrhythmias. The bulk of the work is done by voltage-gated potassium channels — the rapid and slow delayed rectifiers KCNH2 and KCNQ1 with their KCNE accessory subunits, transient outward KCND2/KCND3 with KCNIP subunits, and inward rectifiers such as KCNJ2 — alongside the Na+/K+-ATPase subunits that restore gradients and sodium channel beta subunits that shape inactivation. Anchoring and scaffolding proteins including ankyrin-B, caveolins, AKAPs and NOS1AP position these channels and tune them, and several microRNAs adjust their abundance.

The upstroke of an action potential is the rapid swing of membrane potential from a negative resting value toward its positive peak, and it is what allows neurons, skeletal and cardiac muscle to fire and conduct excitation over distance. Voltage-gated sodium channels carry most of the inward current, with pore-forming subunits such as SCN1A, SCN2A, SCN8A in brain, SCN4A in skeletal muscle and SCN5A in heart, modulated by beta subunits and by the ankyrins that anchor them at axon initial segments and intercalated discs. L-type and T-type calcium channels contribute inward current, particularly in cardiac pacemaker and nodal tissue alongside hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels, while sodium-calcium exchange, chloride and potassium conductances and the sodium pump set the threshold and repolarizing counterforce. Mutations in these channels underlie epilepsies, long QT and Brugada syndromes, periodic paralysis and inherited pain disorders.

After an action potential peaks, the membrane must return toward its negative resting potential before the cell can fire again, and this repolarization phase sets action potential duration, refractory period and firing frequency in excitable cells. In cardiac myocytes it determines the QT interval; when it is delayed or accelerated the result is long or short QT syndrome, torsades de pointes and sudden arrhythmic death. The work is done mainly by voltage-gated potassium channels carrying transient outward, rapid and slow delayed rectifier and inward rectifier currents — KCNH2, KCNQ1, KCND3 and KCNJ2 among them — shaped by KCNE accessory subunits and KCNIP2, with the sodium–potassium ATPase restoring gradients. Calcium channel subunits, calsequestrin and NOS1AP modulate the repolarizing drive, while scaffolding and trafficking proteins such as caveolin-1, filamin A and 14-3-3 control where channels sit and how much current reaches the surface.

Each heartbeat begins with a rapid upstroke of membrane potential in cardiac myocytes, and this depolarizing phase of the cardiac action potential sets both the timing of contraction and the speed at which excitation spreads through the myocardium. The fast inward current comes from the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A with its auxiliary beta subunits, while L-type calcium channels (CACNA1C with CACNB2 and CACNA2D1) sustain depolarization and trigger calcium-induced calcium release; T-type channels and the pacemaker channels HCN2 and HCN4 contribute to spontaneous diastolic depolarization in nodal tissue. Ankyrins, caveolin-3 and SLMAP target and organize these channels in the sarcolemma and T-tubules, and the sodium-calcium exchanger and Na/K-ATPase set the ionic gradients that make the current possible. Mutations in these components cause Brugada syndrome, long QT syndrome, conduction block and sinus node dysfunction, linking the pathway directly to arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death.

The heartbeat is coordinated by an electrical impulse that arises in the sinoatrial node and spreads cell to cell through the myocardium, and this is the signalling that carries it. Pacemaker depolarization depends on HCN channels and L- and T-type calcium channels, while SCN5A with its beta subunits drives the fast upstroke and potassium channels such as KCNQ1 and the acetylcholine-activated KCNJ3 set repolarization and vagal slowing of rate. Gap junction connexins GJA1 and GJA5 physically couple myocytes so that current passes between them, and RYR2 with calsequestrin links the action potential to sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release and contraction. Anchoring and trafficking proteins such as ANK2 place these channels correctly at the membrane. Mutations here produce long QT and Brugada syndromes, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and conduction block, with sudden cardiac death as the common endpoint.

Electrical impulses arriving from the atria must be relayed through the atrioventricular node into the bundle of His before they can reach the ventricles, and signalling between AV node cells and bundle of His cardiomyocytes is the step that makes that relay possible. It sets the delay between atrial and ventricular contraction that allows ventricular filling, and its failure produces heart block, bundle branch conduction disease and arrhythmia. Depolarisation depends on voltage-gated sodium channels including SCN5A with its beta subunit and on L-type and T-type calcium channel subunits such as CACNA1C and CACNA1G, while RYR2-mediated calcium release and the calcium-activated cation channel TRPM4 shape excitability. Cell-to-cell transfer requires gap junctions containing connexin 40 and intact intercalated disc contacts, with a muscle-specific microRNA tuning conduction gene expression.

Electrical impulses leaving the atrioventricular node must pass down the bundle of His and into the Purkinje network for the ventricles to contract as a coordinated unit, and this signalling step is that handoff between bundle of His cardiomyocytes and Purkinje myocytes. The genes involved describe how conduction tissue is wired and how fast it conducts: connexin 40 forms the low-resistance gap junctions that couple neighbouring conduction cells, the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A with SCN10A and the regulator RANGRF sets upstroke velocity, a voltage-gated potassium channel and an L-type calcium channel subunit shape repolarization and excitability, and TRPM4 contributes a calcium-activated cation current. Disruption here produces bundle branch block, progressive cardiac conduction disease, Brugada syndrome and arrhythmias, linking this specialised cell-to-cell communication to the timing of the normal QRS complex.

Cardiomyocytes must reset their membrane potential and ion gradients after every beat, and this regulatory biology sets how far and how fast that potential is established. It links excitation to contraction: sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium handling by the SERCA2 pump, its inhibitor phospholamban, and triadin at the junctional release complex determines how much calcium is cycled per beat, while sodium-proton exchange and mitochondrial sodium-calcium exchange manage cytosolic pH and calcium load, and the small FXYD1 protein modulates the sodium-potassium pump that maintains the resting gradient. EHD3 contributes by directing trafficking of transporters to the correct membrane domains. Disturbance of this balance shortens or prolongs repolarisation, produces calcium overload and arrhythmia, and underlies the impaired relaxation and contractile reserve seen in heart failure and inherited cardiomyopathy.

Working heart muscle depends on neighbouring cardiomyocytes being physically joined end to end, and this adhesion between cardiac muscle cells is what holds them together at the intercalated disc so that force generated in one cell is transmitted to the next and electrical coupling stays stable. The proteins involved build the desmosomal and adherens-type junctions of that structure: desmosomal cadherins such as desmoglein-2 and desmocollin-2 span the gap between cells, while plakoglobin, plakophilin-2, desmoplakin and the cardiac-enriched alpha-T-catenin anchor them to the intermediate filament and actin cytoskeleton, and the coxsackievirus and adenovirus receptor contributes junctional adhesion and conduction. Loss of these links underlies arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, in which junctions fail under mechanical load, myocytes detach and are replaced by fat and fibrous tissue, producing ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death. The same junctions also position gap-junction and sodium channel complexes.

The atrioventricular node passes electrical excitation from atria to ventricles, and the upstroke of its action potential is what sets the delay and the safety factor of that conduction. Unlike ventricular muscle, nodal cells depolarize largely through calcium current: the L-type channel pore CACNA1C with its CACNB2 subunit carries the main inward charge, with T-type CACNA1G contributing to the approach to threshold, while SCN5A sodium current and the calcium-activated cation channel TRPM4 shape the rise and the diastolic drift toward firing. Because the node is the only normal electrical bridge between chambers, weakening or slowing this depolarization produces AV block and bradycardia, whereas the node's intrinsic slowness is what protects ventricles during atrial fibrillation. A muscle-restricted microRNA in the set points to transcriptional tuning of conduction properties, linking cardiac gene regulation to impulse propagation and rhythm.

The heart's own pacemaker sets its rate in the sinoatrial node, where cells have no stable resting potential and depolarize spontaneously to fire the action potential that spreads through the atria. Membrane depolarization in these cells during the upstroke and the diastolic phase before it is what determines heart rate and, through autonomic modulation of the same currents, how rate responds to exercise, sleep and vagal tone. HCN4 carries the hyperpolarization-activated "funny" current that drives slow diastolic depolarization; L-type CACNA1D and T-type CACNA1G calcium channels contribute inward current and provide the calcium-dependent upstroke that dominates nodal cells, while ANK2 anchors channels and transporters to the correct membrane domains. Loss-of-function in these components produces sinus bradycardia, sick sinus syndrome and arrhythmia, and this current set is the pharmacological target of rate-lowering drugs.

Each heartbeat requires depolarization to spread from cell to cell through the working myocardium and conduction system, and electrical coupling at gap junctions is what makes the tissue behave as a functional syncytium. Connexins including GJA1 and GJA5 form the intercellular channels that pass current between adjacent cardiomyocytes, clustered at intercalated discs where the desmosomal protein PKP2 helps organize and stabilize them; loss of this organization slows conduction and produces reentrant arrhythmia and sudden death. Coupling operates alongside the excitation machinery represented here: L-type calcium entry through CACNA1C, ryanodine receptor RYR2 with its triadin and sorcin partners, sodium–calcium exchange by SLC8A1, and Na+/K+-ATPase subunits that restore ionic gradients. Calmodulin, CAMK2D and PKA-dependent phosphorylation tune the system, while transcription factors TBX5 and IRX3 pattern conduction tissue during development.

The heartbeat spreads as a wave, and this is the cell-to-cell communication that carries it: electrical coupling through gap junctions and the mechanical junctions that hold cardiomyocytes together so the wave passes reliably from one cell to the next. Connexins such as GJA1 and GJA5 form the low-resistance channels, while desmosomal and plaque proteins including PKP2, DSP, DSG2 and JUP anchor the intercalated disc; mutations in these are a recognised cause of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. The excitable machinery itself is here too, with sodium channels led by SCN5A and its beta subunits, L-type and T-type calcium channels, potassium channels including KCNQ1, HCN pacemaker channels of the sinoatrial node, and calcium handling via RYR2, CASQ2 and the sodium-calcium exchanger. Transcription factors TBX5 and TBX18 pattern the conduction system. Failure produces conduction block, long QT and sudden cardiac death.

atrial cardiac muscle cell to AV node cell communication is the electrical handoff by which a depolarising wave spreading through the atria reaches the atrioventricular node, the sole conduction bridge to the ventricles. It sets the timing of atrial-to-ventricular coupling, so that ventricular filling precedes contraction, and its disturbance underlies atrial fibrillation, AV block and inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Conduction depends on gap junctions built from connexins including GJA5 and GJA1 that pass current between neighbouring cells, and on the ion channels that shape the atrial action potential: SCN5A-based sodium channels for upstroke and propagation, L-type calcium channels, and a suite of potassium channels for repolarisation. Cytoskeletal and anchoring proteins such as ANK2 and FLNA localise these channels to the sarcolemma, while RYR2 links excitation to calcium release, tying propagation to contraction in the same cells.

Each heartbeat requires the atrial depolarisation wave to reach the atrioventricular node, and this pathway covers the cell-to-cell coupling and electrical signalling by which atrial cardiomyocytes hand the impulse on to nodal cells. It sets the timing of atrial-to-ventricular delay, and its disturbance underlies atrial fibrillation, conduction block and inherited arrhythmia syndromes. Gap junction connexins, including the atrial-selective GJA5, provide the low-resistance channels that pass current between coupled myocytes, while voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with its beta subunit drive rapid upstroke, L-type calcium channel subunits carry depolarising calcium entry, and potassium channels including KCNQ1, KCNJ3 and KCNA5 shape repolarisation and acetylcholine-sensitive responses. RYR2 links excitation to calcium release, and cytoskeletal and anchoring proteins such as ANK2 and FLNA position these channels at the membrane where propagation depends on them.

AV node cell to bundle of His cell communication is the handoff of the electrical impulse from the atrioventricular node into the His bundle, the single electrical bridge between atria and ventricles. It sets the PR interval and the delay that lets ventricles fill before they contract; its failure produces heart block, and its accelerated conduction underlies pre-excitation arrhythmias. The genes describe how one conduction cell excites the next: L-type and T-type calcium channels and ryanodine receptor-mediated calcium release drive nodal depolarization, sodium channels and their beta subunit propagate the impulse into faster-conducting tissue, and TRPM4 shapes the repolarizing phase. Coupling itself depends on connexins, notably GJA5 and GJC1, which form the gap junctions that pass current between adjacent cells, with CXADR supporting the junctional adhesion needed to hold them in register. A muscle-specific microRNA tunes conduction gene expression.

Electrical impulses arriving from the atria must be relayed through the atrioventricular node into the bundle of His before they can reach the ventricles, and this cell-to-cell communication step sets the AV delay that lets the ventricles fill before they contract. Its failure produces heart block and the need for pacing, while inappropriate coupling supports re-entrant arrhythmia. Coupling depends on gap junction channels, including connexins encoded by GJA5 and GJC1, held in register by junctional and adhesion components such as CXADR, together with the currents that generate and propagate the action potential: L-type and T-type calcium channels (CACNA1C, CACNA1G, CACNB2), the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A with its beta subunit, the calcium-activated cation channel TRPM4, and RYR2-mediated calcium release from internal stores. Muscle-specific microRNA input links the conduction programme to broader cardiac gene regulation.

The final handoff of the cardiac impulse, in which specialized Purkinje conduction fibres transmit excitation to ventricular working myocytes, sets the timing and sequence of ventricular contraction. Without faithful communication across this junction, activation becomes slow or fractionated, favouring bundle branch block, re-entry and ventricular arrhythmia. Electrical continuity depends on gap junction channels, with connexin 40 (GJA5) supporting rapid conduction through the specialized conduction system, while voltage-gated sodium channel alpha and beta subunits (SCN5A, SCN1B) generate the upstroke that propagates from cell to cell. Calcium handling contributes as well: the ryanodine receptor RYR2 and the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium buffer calsequestrin 2 shape release and, when mutated, cause catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. The calcium-activated cation channel TRPM4 modulates depolarization and is linked to conduction disease, tying this pathway to cardiac conduction and excitation-contraction coupling.

bundle of His cell to Purkinje myocyte communication describes how the electrical impulse is handed from the His bundle down into the Purkinje network, the step that lets both ventricles depolarise almost simultaneously and contract as a unit. Failure here produces bundle branch block, fascicular block and ventricular arrhythmia. Two kinds of machinery are represented. Fast conduction depends on the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A with its regulators SCN10A, RANGRF and TRPM4, on the calcium channel subunit CACNA2D1, and on connexin-40 gap junctions that couple neighbouring conduction cells. Mechanical and electrical continuity is provided by the desmosome and area composita — desmoplakin, plakophilin-2, desmoglein-2, plakoglobin and αT-catenin — whose mutation causes arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy by uncoupling cells. TBX5 specifies the conduction system itself, tying this transmission step to cardiac developmental patterning.

Each heartbeat depends on the impulse passing cleanly from the bundle of His into the Purkinje fibres, and this pathway covers the cell-to-cell coupling and signalling that let one conduction cell excite the next. Fast propagation requires low-resistance electrical continuity through connexin-40 gap junctions, mechanical anchoring at desmosomes and area composita junctions built from plakophilin-2, desmoplakin, desmoglein-2, desmocollin-2, plakoglobin and alpha-T-catenin, and rapid depolarisation carried by the cardiac sodium channel SCN5A with its regulators SCN10A and RANGRF. Calcium channel and potassium channel subunits shape the action potential, while TBX5 specifies the conduction system during development. Loss of these interactions produces bundle branch block, progressive cardiac conduction disease, Brugada syndrome and the arrhythmias of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, where junctional failure and electrical uncoupling occur together.

The heartbeat begins in the sinoatrial node, and this biology covers how pacemaker cells pass their depolarisation on to the surrounding atrial myocardium so that the atria contract in step with the node's rhythm. Without effective electrical coupling at this junction the node fires without driving the atria, producing sinoatrial exit block, bradycardia and sick sinus syndrome. Spontaneous diastolic depolarisation depends on the hyperpolarisation-activated funny current carried by HCN4 and its relatives, together with low-voltage T-type and L-type calcium channels and calcium release through RYR2; the resulting impulse spreads through gap junctions built from connexins such as GJA5 and GJC1 into atrial cells, where sodium channels including SCN5A and its accessory subunit take over propagation. ANK2 organises many of these channels at the membrane, and TBX18 marks the developmental origin of the node itself.

regulation of heart rate by cardiac conduction sets how fast the heart beats by controlling the electrical impulse that originates in the sinoatrial node and spreads through the myocardium. It is what makes the heartbeat regular and rate-responsive, and its failure produces sick sinus syndrome, atrioventricular block, long QT and other arrhythmias with risk of sudden death. The genes are the ion channels that shape the action potential and its pacemaker phase: HCN4 and related channels carry the depolarising "funny" current, L- and T-type calcium channels support nodal upstroke and conduction, SCN5A with its beta subunits drives rapid propagation, and repolarising potassium channels such as KCNQ1, KCNH2 and KCNJ2 with their KCNE partners set cycle length. Gap junctions, desmosomal proteins and anchoring scaffolds like ANK2 and AKAP9 position these channels so that excitation passes cell to cell, while calcium-calmodulin kinase and autonomic input tune the rate.

The pace of the heartbeat is set by how quickly electrical impulses are generated in pacemaker tissue and propagated through the myocardium, and this pathway covers the ion channels and junctional proteins that tune that rate. Hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels, notably HCN4, carry the pacemaker current in sinoatrial cells; L- and T-type calcium channels support depolarization; and repolarization is shaped by potassium channels such as KCNQ1, KCNH2 and KCNJ2 together with their KCNE accessory subunits, while inward-rectifier channels coupled to muscarinic signalling slow the rate under vagal input. Sodium channel SCN5A with its beta subunits, the anchoring proteins ANK2 and AKAP9, and desmosomal and gap-junction components including PKP2, DSP and GJA5 position and connect these channels between cells. Mutations here produce long QT and Brugada syndromes, sick sinus syndrome, atrial fibrillation and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

Endothelin peptides are among the most potent vasoconstrictors known, and the receptor signalling they initiate sets vascular tone, blood pressure and the growth responses of smooth muscle, while a parallel branch guides neural crest derivatives such as enteric neurons and melanocytes. Endothelin-1 and endothelin-2 act on two G protein-coupled receptors, EDNRA and EDNRB, which couple through Gq-family subunits including GNA11 to phospholipase C beta, raising inositol phosphates and calcium to drive contraction. Downstream, focal-adhesion and scaffold proteins such as PTK2B, BCAR1, BCAR3 and CRKL together with the Rho-family GTPase CDC42 link the receptors to cytoskeletal remodelling, adhesion and migration, and to transcriptional output involving factors such as SIX1. Loss of EDNRB signalling causes aganglionic megacolon and pigmentation defects, whereas excessive endothelin tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension, the rationale for receptor antagonist therapy.

Histidine must cross membranes to reach the cytosol, the mitochondrial matrix, or the lysosomal lumen, and the carriers grouped here perform that directed movement. The transport matters beyond protein synthesis: histidine is the precursor of histamine, a carnosine building block, and a nitrogen carrier, so its distribution shapes amino acid metabolism in liver and the secretory capacity of mast cells and neurons. The transporters involved are chemically diverse, including a sodium-coupled amino acid carrier that also handles glutamine, a cationic amino acid permease, a mitochondrial carrier for basic amino acids, and lysosomal proteins that move histidine out of the degradative compartment. Because those same proteins serve endolysosomal signalling and nutrient sensing, histidine flux is tied to immune receptor trafficking as well as to amino acid supply, and loss of individual carriers produces metabolic and inflammatory phenotypes rather than a single deficiency.

Cells cannot synthesise all of the amino acids they need, so they rely on carrier proteins that bring them in across the plasma membrane into the cytosol. This import supplies substrates for protein synthesis, neurotransmitter and glutathione production, nitrogen handling and mTOR-dependent growth signalling, and it sets how much dietary protein the intestine and kidney actually recover. Most of the work is done by solute carrier families with distinct selectivities and driving forces: sodium-dependent glutamate and aspartate transporters such as SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 clear synaptic glutamate in astrocytes, neutral amino acid and glutamine carriers of the SLC38 group feed metabolism, heterodimeric exchangers pair a light chain with the SLC3A2 heavy chain, and SLC7A11 imports cystine to support antioxidant defence. Accessory and regulatory proteins, including ACE2 and its homologue CLTRN, control surface delivery of intestinal and renal transporters; loss of individual carriers causes aminoacidurias, Hartnup disorder and neurological disease.

Gastrulation begins with the primitive streak, a transient midline ridge at the posterior of the embryo through which epiblast cells ingress to generate mesoderm and definitive endoderm. Its appearance fixes the anterior-posterior axis and sets the starting point for left-right and dorsal-ventral patterning, so defects here produce axis duplication, absent notochord, caudal truncation and heterotaxy rather than any single organ malformation. Nodal signalling from the posterior epiblast, reinforced by WNT input and the related ligand GDF3, induces streak fate; the T-box factor TBXT (brachyury) marks and maintains streak and nascent mesoderm, while FOXA2 and LHX1 specify endoderm and anterior mesendoderm and OTX2 restricts anterior identity. PRICKLE1 and WNT5A contribute planar polarity and directed cell movement during ingression, and ZIC3 mutation in humans causes X-linked laterality disturbance, tying streak formation to later asymmetry.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes recruited to infected or injured tissue, and this pathway covers the signals that tune how strongly and in which direction they move. Control matters in both directions: too little recruitment leaves bacterial and fungal infection unchecked, while excessive or misdirected influx drives the tissue damage of sepsis, acute lung injury, arthritis and reperfusion injury. Chemoattractant receptors sit at the core, including the interleukin-8 receptor axis and the complement-derived anaphylatoxin receptors C3AR1, C5AR1 and C5AR2, alongside chemokine ligands such as CCL19 and CCL21. Their signals converge on Rac1 and Rac2 GTPases and cytoskeletal regulators that build the leading edge, with adhesion and junctional molecules governing passage across endothelium. Negative regulators, among them SLIT2 and RIPOR2, restrain migration, and calcium handling and mitochondrial dynamics modulate directional persistence during the innate inflammatory response.

Monocytes leave the bloodstream and migrate into tissue along chemical gradients, and this pathway covers the signals that set how strongly and how fast they do so. The response supplies macrophages and dendritic cells to sites of infection and injury, and when it is sustained it drives the monocyte influx underlying atherosclerotic plaque growth, adipose inflammation and chronic inflammatory disease. Chemokines such as CCL2-type ligands, CCL5, CXCL12 and CXCL10 act through receptors including CCR1, CCR2 and CX3CR1, with the formyl peptide receptor FPR2 and the alarmin HMGB1 adding danger-sensing input. Intracellular adaptors and kinases such as the Src-family kinase LYN and the phosphatase DUSP1 tune the strength of the resulting motility signal, while SLIT2 and its guidance biology, along with matrix and secreted modulators, can restrain migration. The net output is the positioning of mononuclear phagocytes during innate immunity and wound repair.

Monocytes are recruited out of the blood into tissues wherever infection, injury or metabolic stress generates a chemoattractant gradient, and this pathway covers the signals and receptors that increase that recruitment. It underlies the monocyte influx of acute inflammation, wound repair and atherosclerotic plaque growth, and its persistent activation sustains the macrophage burden in chronic inflammatory and metabolic disease. Secreted chemokines such as CCL2-type ligands, CCL5, CXCL10 and CXCL12 act through the monocyte receptors CCR1, CCR2 and CX3CR1 to trigger directed migration, while damage-associated and host-defence molecules including HMGB1, defensins, S100 proteins and formyl-peptide receptor ligands broaden the range of cues that can attract monocytes. Additional components shape the response indirectly through membrane phospholipid scrambling, proteolytic processing of chemoattractants, or transcriptional induction of chemokine genes, coupling tissue damage sensing to myeloid cell traffic.

Monocytes are recruited out of the bloodstream toward chemokine gradients at sites of injury and infection, and this recruitment has to be damped as well as driven; damping it is what negative regulation of monocyte chemotaxis does. Restraining monocyte influx limits the tissue damage of prolonged inflammation and shapes how atherosclerotic lesions, fibrotic scars and healing wounds develop, since each depends on how many monocyte-derived macrophages arrive. The activities represented here work at different levels: secreted matricellular and BMP-antagonist proteins such as CCN3, NBL1 and GREM1 act in the extracellular milieu, the repulsive guidance cue SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to block directed migration of myeloid cells, DUSP1 dephosphorylates MAP kinases to cut short inflammatory signalling, and the immune receptor SLAMF8 tempers macrophage responses. Together they set a brake on innate immune cell trafficking rather than on chemokine production alone.

Steroid hormones — cortisol, aldosterone, androgens, oestrogens, progesterone — are made on demand, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast that synthesis runs. Control operates at several levels: pituitary POMC-derived ACTH acting through its adrenocortical receptor MC2R and luteinising hormone through LHCGR raise cyclic AMP to mobilise cholesterol, while a phosphodiesterase restrains that same signal; loss-of-function in PDE8B causes adrenal hyperactivity. Nuclear receptors including the glucocorticoid receptor and NR5A2 provide transcriptional feedback over steroidogenic gene expression, and electron supply through cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase together with hexose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase determines the reducing power available to the P450 and 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzymes. Secreted BMP and WNT ligands and their antagonists tune adrenal and gonadal zonation and differentiation. Failure of this regulation produces congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hyperaldosteronism and disorders of sexual development.

Steroid hormones "- cortisol, aldosterone, androgens, oestrogens and progesterone "- are made on demand rather than stored, so their output is set by signals that raise the rate of the biosynthetic route itself. This is the positive arm of that control, and it determines adrenal stress responses, salt and water balance, gonadal function and pregnancy maintenance; its loss produces adrenal insufficiency and disordered sex steroid production. Pituitary-derived corticotropin cleaved from proopiomelanocortin acts through its melanocortin type 2 receptor to drive cholesterol delivery and side-chain cleavage in adrenocortical cells, with an adaptor protein supporting receptor trafficking and lipoprotein-derived cholesterol uptake. A nuclear receptor transcription factor of the steroidogenic factor family activates the enzyme genes, and cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase supplies electrons to every microsomal P450 step. Secreted BMP and WNT ligands modulate the gonadal and adrenal cells in which this occurs.

Protein kinase C sits downstream of receptors that generate diacylglycerol and calcium, and it relays those second messengers into changes in cell shape, proliferation, secretion and inflammatory gene expression. Setting the strength and duration of that relay is what this regulatory biology does, and the genes involved act at several different levels. A diacylglycerol kinase consumes the lipid activator by converting it to phosphatidic acid, terminating the signal; a scaffold protein positions kinases and their substrates at the cell periphery so that activation is local rather than diffuse; receptors such as the epidermal growth factor receptor and the co-stimulatory molecule CD40 feed into the cascade from growth factor and immune contexts respectively; and a small heat shock protein serves as both substrate and modulator. Because unchecked protein kinase C activity drives proliferative and inflammatory responses, this tuning matters for tumour growth and immune activation.

Acetylation of lysine 40 on alpha-tubulin marks long-lived, mechanically stressed microtubules, and tubulin deacetylation is the reaction that strips this mark, tuning microtubule stability, motor traffic, ciliary length and cell motility. Two enzymes do the removing: the cytoplasmic deacetylase HDAC6, which also clears acetyl groups from cortactin and HSP90 and drives aggresome clearance, and the NAD-dependent sirtuin SIRT2. Their activity is set in opposition to acetyltransferase activity and to regulators that shield the polymer, including the microtubule-binding protein TPPP and the actin crosslinker FLNA, while BEX4 and FRY influence the balance in dividing and polarized cells. Several subunits of a multiprotein histone acetyltransferase module, among them KAT2A, KAT2B, WDR5, TADA2A and TADA3, appear here as the counterweight supplying acetylation. Loss of deacetylase control alters axonal transport and is pursued therapeutically in neurodegeneration and cancer.
