Acetylation of α-tubulin on lysine 40 marks long-lived, stable microtubule populations such as axonemes, axonal tracts and the mitotic spindle, and the balance between adding and removing that mark determines microtubule mechanics, motor traffic and resistance to breakage. This grouping covers the control of tubulin deacetylation — the limiting of acetyl group removal by cytoplasmic deacetylases — and so sets how much acetylated tubulin a cell retains. Much of it works by opposing the deacetylases directly: TPPP and BEX4 restrain deacetylase action on tubulin, while a large acetyltransferase module built around KAT2A/KAT2B with its ATAC-type subunits KAT14, TADA2A, TADA3, ZZZ3, YEATS2, MBIP and WDR5, plus the coactivator EP300, supplies acetylation activity. Shifting this balance alters ciliary stability, neuronal transport and spindle behaviour, and deacetylase inhibition is exploited therapeutically in cancer and neuropathy.

New capillaries form by sprouting, and this is the control layer that sets how fast and how far endothelial cells crawl out into the surrounding matrix to build them. It matters for wound healing, ischaemic tissue recovery and the menstrual cycle, and its overdrive supplies tumours with blood and drives proliferative retinopathy. VEGFA acting through KDR and the co-receptor NRP1 provides the promigratory cue, while Notch signalling with its ligand DLL4 restricts how many cells adopt the leading tip phenotype; Rho-family GTPases including RHOA and the endothelial-enriched RHOJ, integrin-associated adaptors and class IIa histone deacetylases translate these signals into directed motility and cytoskeletal remodelling. Transcription factors such as GATA2, KLF4 and FOXC2, secreted modulators including FGF2, THBS1 and GREM1, and a large complement of microRNAs tune the response up or down, making this as much a brake system as an accelerator.

New blood vessels form when endothelial cells at the tip of an existing vessel break through basement membrane and migrate into surrounding matrix, and this pathway covers the inputs that increase that migration during sprouting angiogenesis. It determines how quickly a tissue can be vascularised, and so governs wound healing, ischaemic collateral growth, retinal vessel disease and tumour blood supply. VEGFA acting through the receptor kinase KDR and its co-receptor NRP1 is the central promigratory cue, with FGF2, prostaglandin synthesis via PTGS2, heme oxygenase activity and PI3K-AKT signalling reinforcing it. Transcriptional control comes from GATA2, FOXC2 and class IIa deacetylases HDAC7 and HDAC9, while RHOJ shapes the cytoskeleton for directed movement. Numerous microRNAs, including the endothelial-enriched miR-126, tune the output, and secreted modulators such as GREM1 and TGFBR3 adjust BMP and TGF-beta input to sprouting.

New capillaries form when endothelial cells break from an existing vessel and migrate into surrounding matrix, and this pathway covers the brakes on that movement — the restraint that keeps sprouting angiogenesis orderly rather than producing tangled, leaky, over-branched networks. Tip-cell selection is limited laterally by Notch signalling, where DLL4 binding NOTCH1 suppresses migratory behaviour in neighbouring stalk cells; matrix-derived thrombospondin and the multimerin MMRN2 act as anti-angiogenic cues at the endothelial surface; SPRED1 dampens growth-factor input to the MAP kinase route, while RHOA, STARD13 and PDCD10 shape cytoskeletal and junctional stability. A large complement of microRNAs, including the miR-15/16 and miR-503/424 families and miR-221, tunes the migratory transcriptome post-transcriptionally. Loss of such restraint contributes to tumour vascularisation, retinopathy and vascular malformation, whereas excess restraint impairs wound healing and ischaemic revascularisation.

positive regulation of microtubule nucleation covers the inputs that raise the rate at which new microtubules are born from organizing centres, setting how many filaments a cell builds and where. This determines mitotic spindle assembly, centrosome and Golgi-based array organization, and the directed transport and shape changes that depend on a polarized cytoskeleton; too few nucleation events yield disorganized spindles and chromosome missegregation. The genes act at the nucleation site rather than on tubulin itself: the XMAP215-family polymerase CKAP5 works with gamma-tubulin ring complexes to template and elongate new filaments, the dynactin subunit DCTN1 and the Golgi-associated myomegalin PDE4DIP anchor nucleating activity at centrosomes and Golgi membranes, and PAK1 with its partner GIT1 supplies kinase signalling that licenses nucleation during cell motility. Stress-inducible HSP70 chaperones and the chromatin regulator MECP2 link nucleation capacity to proteostasis and neuronal cytoskeletal maturation.

New microtubules do not assemble spontaneously at useful rates; they are seeded at defined sites, and this pathway covers the influences that raise the frequency of that seeding. Boosting nucleation determines how many microtubules a cell builds and where, which shapes spindle assembly in mitosis, centrosomal and Golgi-associated arrays in interphase, and the axonal and dendritic arrays that neurons depend on for transport and growth. The members act at these sites rather than as tubulin itself: a large microtubule-associated polymerase that promotes growth from seeds, a dynactin subunit that anchors minus ends, a Golgi-localized scaffold that supports non-centrosomal nucleation, chaperones, and signalling components including a Rac/Cdc42-activated kinase and its interacting scaffold. A transcriptional regulator mutated in Rett syndrome links the programme to neuronal cytoskeletal maturation, and loss of such nucleation control disturbs cell division and neurite architecture.

Body parts, cells and subcellular compartments must reach and hold a defined size, and this broad regulatory programme sets those dimensions. It spans several distinct size-setting problems: vascular tone and lumen diameter, controlled by vasoconstrictor and vasodilator signalling through angiotensin, endothelin, adrenergic and natriuretic peptide receptors together with nitric oxide synthases and smooth muscle contractile machinery; cell volume homeostasis, maintained by aquaporins, cation-chloride cotransporters, volume-regulated anion channels and the WNK-OXSR1/STK39 kinase cascade; cell and organ growth, governed by mTOR complexes with their regulators TSC1 and PTEN; and neurite, axon and microvillus dimensions, shaped by actin capping, severing and elongation factors, spectrins, tropomodulins, Rho-family GTPases and their guidance cues such as semaphorins, slits and netrins. Loss of control here produces hypertension, cardiac and vascular hypertrophy, tissue overgrowth, oedema and defective neuronal wiring.

Cells advance through the cell cycle only when positive inputs push each step forward, and this collection captures the activators that raise the rate and extent of cycle progression: mitogenic ligands and receptors, cyclin–CDK pairs, and the machinery that executes S phase, mitosis and cytokinesis. Growth factors such as EGF, TGFA and IGF1 acting through their receptors converge on D- and E-type cyclins with CDK4 and CDK1 to drive commitment past the restriction point, while CDC25 phosphatases remove inhibitory phosphorylation to license mitotic entry. Downstream, the anaphase-promoting complex with CDC20, aurora kinases and the chromosomal passenger proteins, condensin subunits, kinetochore and spindle components, and centriole duplication factors such as PLK4 and STIL carry chromosomes apart and split the cell. Because these activators set proliferative output, their excess underlies tumour growth, and several are targets of cell cycle inhibitor drugs.

Making ribosomes is the largest biosynthetic commitment a growing cell undertakes, and the genes here modulate how fast and how extensively rRNA is processed and subunits are assembled, tuning output to growth signals and nutrient supply. Because ribosome production sets the ceiling on protein synthesis, its regulation feeds into cell growth, proliferation and stress responses, and defective assembly triggers nucleolar stress and p53-dependent arrest — the basis of ribosomopathies such as bone marrow failure and craniofacial malformation syndromes. The members act at several levels: AAA-ATPases of the AFG2 family drive release of assembly factors from pre-ribosomal particles, MALSU1 acts in mitochondrial large subunit assembly, METTL18 methylates a ribosomal protein histidine, NUDT16 turns over RNA cap and nucleotide metabolites, and chromatin and transcription-associated factors including KAT2B and USP16 influence rDNA and ribosomal protein gene expression.

Contraction must be actively terminated, and muscle relaxation is the set of processes that lowers cytoplasmic calcium and reverses the contractile state so that cardiac chambers refill, skeletal fibres reset between twitches, and smooth muscle in vessels and airways dilates. The core machinery is calcium removal: sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pumps (ATP2A1, ATP2A2) driven back into the lumen under the control of their inhibitory regulators phospholamban and sarcolipin, sodium-calcium exchange at the plasma membrane, and luminal buffering proteins such as HRC and sorcin. Cyclic nucleotide signalling tunes the process, with soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP-dependent kinase acting through IRAG1 to suppress calcium release, while phosphodiesterases, adenosine and purinergic receptors, and RGS2 set the tone. Impaired relaxation underlies diastolic heart failure, vasospasm and bronchoconstriction, and mutations here cause myopathy and arrhythmia.

Foam cell differentiation converts a macrophage into the lipid-engorged cell that fills atherosclerotic plaque, and is the step at which a lesion becomes inflammatory and irreversible. Its balance determines whether arterial macrophages clear modified lipoprotein harmlessly or accumulate cholesterol esters, die, and enlarge the necrotic core. Scavenger receptors such as CD36 and MSR1 take up oxidised and aggregated LDL, secretory phospholipases and lipoprotein lipase modify the particles beforehand, and ACAT enzymes esterify the incoming sterol for storage in cytoplasmic droplets. Opposing this, the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 drive ABCA1 and ABCG1 to efflux cholesterol to HDL acceptors, while PPARs tune the whole lipid-handling program. Inflammatory input from TNF, IL1B and NF-kB signalling, together with angiotensin and growth factor cues, biases the cell toward retention, linking lipid metabolism directly to vascular disease progression.

Foam cells are the lipid-engorged macrophages that form the fatty streak of an atherosclerotic plaque, and this pathway covers how a macrophage becomes one. Uptake of modified lipoprotein through scavenger receptors such as CD36 and MSR1, esterification of the incoming cholesterol by the acyl-CoA:cholesterol acyltransferases SOAT1 and SOAT2, and storage in cytoplasmic droplets are opposed by cholesterol efflux through the transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1 to apolipoprotein and HDL acceptors. Nuclear receptors including the liver X receptors and PPARs set the balance between loading and unloading, while inflammatory input from TNF, IL1B and NF-κB signalling, secreted phospholipases and lipoprotein lipase favour retention. When efflux fails, foam cells accumulate, die and enlarge the necrotic core, driving plaque growth and instability; the same programme appears in xanthomas and other lipid-storage lesions.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor signalling that raises the activity of the downstream MAPKKK cascade is the route by which endocrine FGFs reach the nucleus and change gene expression, and here it is represented by the hormone-like arm of the family. FGF23, made by osteocytes, and FGF21, made largely by liver, bind FGFR1 only when it is partnered with a co-receptor: alpha-Klotho for FGF23, beta-Klotho for FGF21. That obligatory partnership is what confines these hormones to kidney, adipose and other Klotho-expressing tissues despite the receptor being widespread. Receptor engagement triggers a phosphorylation relay through a MAP kinase kinase kinase to ERK, driving transcriptional responses that lower phosphate reabsorption and vitamin D activation in the case of FGF23, and reshape fatty acid and glucose handling in the case of FGF21. Excess FGF23 causes hypophosphatemic rickets; loss of Klotho or FGF23 produces hyperphosphatemia and ectopic calcification.

When misfolded proteins escape refolding and degradation they are swept into inclusion bodies, and this pathway governs how readily those deposits form and how large they grow. It matters because inclusion bodies are the defining lesion of neurodegeneration — Lewy bodies in Parkinson disease, polyglutamine aggregates in Huntington disease, amyloid and tau deposits in Alzheimer disease — and whether aggregation is suppressed, redirected or sequestered determines whether a neuron survives the burden. The machinery is largely chaperone-based: inducible HSP70s work with a panel of J-domain co-chaperones, several of which (notably DNAJB6 and DNAJB8) block amyloid nucleation directly, while BAG5 modulates HSP70 nucleotide cycling. Proteasomal ATPase subunits link deposits to degradation, extracellular chaperones such as clusterin and the lipid carrier APOE influence amyloid handling, and kinases including DYRK1A and MARK2 alter substrate phosphorylation and aggregation propensity.

Misfolded proteins that escape refolding tend to coalesce into inclusion bodies, and this pathway describes the chaperone activity that keeps that from happening, suppressing the rate and extent of inclusion body assembly. It matters most in neurons and muscle, where polyglutamine expansions, mutant superoxide dismutase and aggregation-prone myofibrillar proteins accumulate over a lifetime and cannot be diluted by division. The core machinery is the HSP70 system: inducible HSPA1A and HSPA1B provide ATP-driven binding and release of exposed hydrophobic segments, while J-domain cochaperones of the DNAJB family confer substrate selectivity, with DNAJB6 and DNAJB8 notably potent at blocking polyglutamine fibril formation and DNAJB2 linked to neuropathy when lost. SACS encodes sacsin, a large chaperone-like protein whose mutation causes an early-onset spastic ataxia, and SORL1 routes substrates through endosomal sorting. Failure of this suppression underlies the aggregate pathology of neurodegenerative and myopathic disease.

Ubiquitin marks on a protein are reversible, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how readily deubiquitinating enzymes strip those marks off. Because ubiquitin chains decide whether a substrate is degraded, trafficked, or licensed to signal, tuning their removal changes protein lifetime and the strength of signalling downstream of it. Much of the activity here converges on inflammatory signalling: ABIN1 and its partners restrain NF- inkB activation by shaping ubiquitin editing at receptor complexes, while TRIM21 and ITCH act on the ubiquitin side of the same balance. Other members link deubiquitination to protein quality control, with VCP extracting ubiquitinated substrates from membranes and complexes, UBXN1 and DNAJB2 acting as cofactors, and PARK7 tied to oxidative-stress protection of degradation pathways. Loss of this regulation produces unchecked inflammatory signalling or the accumulation of misprocessed proteins seen in neurodegeneration.

This is the control layer over how cells release and move peptides, and in practice it is dominated by the machinery that sets insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells against the hormones and nutrients that tune it. Glucose entry through GLUT2 and phosphorylation by glucokinase raise ATP, closing the KCNJ11/ABCC8 potassium channel and triggering calcium-dependent exocytosis through SNAP25, STX1A and synaptotagmin-family sensors. Incretin and neuropeptide receptors (GIPR, GHSR, GHRHR, SSTR5, DRD2) feed cyclic AMP and G protein signals into PKA and EPAC effectors to amplify or damp release, while transcription factors such as PDX1, NEUROD1, NKX6-1 and RFX6 maintain the secretory identity of the cell. Circadian, inflammatory and lipid-sensing inputs modulate the same output. Loss of this regulation produces diabetes, hyperinsulinism, and disordered growth hormone, glucagon and stress-peptide signalling.

Canonical Wnt signalling drives beta-catenin into the nucleus to switch on target genes, and its negative regulation sets how much of that signal a cell tolerates. Restraint is what keeps stem and progenitor compartments from expanding without limit; loss of the brake, most notoriously through mutation of the APC tumour suppressor, underlies colorectal cancer, while excess suppression impairs bone formation and patterning during development. Control is layered. Secreted antagonists such as the Dickkopf proteins, sclerostin and the frizzled-related proteins block ligand-receptor engagement, and a deacylase removes the lipid needed for Wnt activity. At the membrane, ubiquitin ligases including ZNRF3 remove frizzled receptors. Inside the cell, an axin-based destruction complex with GSK3 and casein kinase 1 phosphorylates beta-catenin for degradation, and repressive TLE/groucho partners of TCF7L2 silence target promoters. Hippo kinases, FOXO factors and several microRNAs feed additional inhibitory input.

Tissue remodelling requires that the matrix scaffold be taken apart as well as built, and this is the regulatory arm that raises the rate and extent of extracellular matrix disassembly. Increased matrix breakdown lets cells invade, migrate and rebuild during wound healing, angiogenesis and inflammation, and the same push toward degradation underlies tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes converge on several routes to that output: collagen sensing through the receptor tyrosine kinase DDR2, heparan sulfate cleavage by heparanase, cytokine signalling in which IL6 acts through STAT3, and TGFB2 as a secreted regulator of the stromal response. Cytoskeletal and microtubule-associated proteins such as FSCN1 and the CLASPs position the machinery at invadopodia and adhesion sites, while podoplanin marks the motile, remodelling cell surface. Net effect is a cell that clears its surrounding matrix rather than maintaining it.

Control over signalling by transmembrane serine/threonine kinase receptors is essentially control over the TGF-beta, activin and BMP system, which sets cell fate decisions, extracellular matrix production, growth arrest and patterning throughout development and adult tissue repair. The genes here span every tier of that control: ligands and their propeptide-binding latency factors, secreted antagonists such as noggin, gremlins, chordin, follistatins and sclerostin, co-receptors including endoglin and betaglycan, and accessory modulators like BAMBI and caveolins. Downstream, receptor-activated SMAD2/3 and SMAD4 complexes are tuned by inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7, by SMURF ubiquitin ligases, phosphatases, deubiquitinases, and by transcriptional co-activators and repressor complexes containing SKI, SnoN, and histone deacetylase-Sin3 assemblies. Numerous microRNAs add post-transcriptional damping. Loss of this restraint produces fibrosis, vascular malformations, skeletal overgrowth or heterotopic ossification, and tumour progression once growth-inhibitory output is subverted.

This is the set of activities that amplify signalling through transmembrane serine/threonine kinase receptors, essentially the TGF-beta, activin, nodal and BMP branches of the TGF-beta superfamily. Enhancing this output drives mesoderm patterning, skeletal and cardiac development, vascular wall integrity, epithelial growth arrest and fibrotic responses to injury; too much of it underlies tissue fibrosis and tumour-promoting TGF-beta signalling, while too little disturbs vessel formation, as loss of the endoglin and ALK1 arm does in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Positive regulators here act at several levels: ligands and growth-factor propeptides such as BMP2/4 and TGFB1-3, accessory receptors and co-receptors including ENG, TGFBR3 and NEO1, extracellular modulators like TWSG1 and thrombospondin that control ligand availability, and nuclear amplifiers acting on receptor-activated SMAD2/3 and SMAD4 complexes, notably the CREBBP/EP300 coactivators and the ubiquitin ligase that degrades inhibitory SMADs.

Signalling by TGF-beta, activin and BMP receptors must be limited in time and space, and this set collects the brakes on those serine/threonine kinase receptors. Without such restraint, sustained SMAD activity drives fibrosis, skeletal overgrowth or heterotopic ossification, and the same dampeners are lost or overexpressed in tumours where TGF-beta switches between suppressor and promoter. Inhibition acts at every tier: secreted ligand traps and antagonists such as noggin, follistatin, chordin, gremlins, sclerostin and DAN-family proteins; pseudoreceptors and co-receptors including BAMBI and betaglycan; inhibitory SMAD6 and SMAD7 recruiting the SMURF ubiquitin ligases to degrade receptors; phosphatases such as PPM1A that dephosphorylate activated SMADs; and nuclear repressors SKI, SKIL and TRIM33 working with HDAC1/2 and SIN3A complexes. Numerous microRNAs add post-transcriptional damping. Related mechanisms control iron homeostasis through hemojuvelin, erythroferrone and matriptase-2 acting on hepcidin.

The snail-shaped cochlea is the organ that turns airborne sound into neural signals, and this programme covers its emergence from the otic vesicle through to a functioning sensory epithelium. Its failure produces congenital deafness, and many of the genes here are recognised human deafness loci. Transcriptional regulators such as EYA1, SIX1, PAX2, GATA3 and NEUROG1 specify otic tissue, prosensory domains and spiral ganglion neurons, while Notch effectors like HES1 and HEY2 restrict how many cells become hair cells. Planar cell polarity components including VANGL2, PTK7, DVL1/2 and WNT5A orient stereociliary bundles along the duct, and ciliary trafficking proteins contribute to that orientation. Hair cell function genes follow: MYO7A and CDH23 build and link stereocilia, SLC26A5 drives outer hair cell electromotility, SLC17A8 loads glutamate at ribbon synapses, and KCNQ1 supports endolymph secretion for the endocochlear potential.

Cochlea morphogenesis shapes the spiral, tonotopically ordered organ of hearing from the ventral otic vesicle, and its failure produces congenital sensorineural deafness and malformations such as an incompletely coiled or truncated duct. Much of the work is done by planar cell polarity signalling: WNT5A, the Frizzled and Dishevelled components, VANGL2 and PTK7 orient hair cell stereociliary bundles and drive the convergent extension that elongates the cochlear duct, while RAC1 couples polarity cues to the cytoskeleton and NECTIN1/NECTIN3 adhesion enforces the checkerboard arrangement of hair cells and supporting cells. Transcriptional regulators including EYA1, SIX1, PAX2, SOX9, the T-box factors and NEUROG1 specify otic identity, prosensory domain formation and the neurons that innervate it, and POU3F4 acts in surrounding mesenchyme. Mutations in several of these underlie syndromic and non-syndromic hearing loss, linking inner ear patterning to craniofacial and branchio-oto-renal development.

Newly folded secretory and membrane proteins leave the endoplasmic reticulum only if they are captured into a forming vesicle, and cargo loading into COPII-coated vesicles is the selection step that decides what goes forward to the Golgi. It sets the throughput of the whole secretory route, so collagen, lipoproteins and cholesterol-regulatory sensors all depend on it; inherited defects in coat subunits cause craniolenticulodental anomalies, chylomicron retention disease and anaemia with abnormal red cell secretion. The small GTPase SAR1A/SAR1B, activated at the ER membrane, recruits the inner SEC23-SEC24 layer that contacts cargo and signal motifs directly, with SEC13-SEC31 forming the outer cage; the four SEC24 paralogues broaden the range of recognised sorting signals. Dedicated receptors add specificity, including SURF4 for soluble cargo and MIA3 for bulky procollagen, while SCAP and INSIG1 link loading to sterol sensing and RAB1A to downstream tethering.

Newly made secretory and membrane proteins leave the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles, and this budding step is the entry point for the entire secretory route to the Golgi and cell surface. It sets how much collagen, lipoprotein, or receptor a cell can export, and its failure causes human disease: defects in the SEC23A coat subunit and in cargo receptors such as MIA3 produce skeletal and connective tissue disorders, while SAR1B mutations block chylomicron secretion from enterocytes. Mechanistically, the GTPase SAR1 is activated at ER exit sites by the PREB exchange factor and recruits the inner SEC23/SEC24 adaptor layer, which selects cargo, and the outer SEC13/SEC31 cage; SEC16A and TFG organise the exit site, ubiquitin ligase activity with KLHL12 enlarges carriers for bulky cargo, and RAB1 with the TRAPP complex directs the vesicle onward to the Golgi.

Cells obtain most of their cholesterol not by making it but by capturing lipoprotein particles from the blood, and this receptor-mediated uptake route is how that cholesterol gets inside and into the endolysosomal system for distribution. The LDL receptor binds apoB-containing particles at the cell surface and is drawn into clathrin-coated pits by an adaptor, LDLRAP1, that links it to the endocytic machinery; loss of either causes familial hypercholesterolaemia and premature atherosclerosis. Receptor abundance is set post-translationally by PCSK9, which binds LDLR and directs it to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, and by microRNAs that tune the transcripts of this module; PCSK9 blockade is the basis of a major class of lipid-lowering drugs. Downstream handling of the internalised sterol involves annexin-mediated membrane traffic and ABCA2, an endolysosomal lipid transporter, linking uptake to intracellular cholesterol movement.

Cholesterol reaching cells in lipoprotein particles must be moved out of endosomes and lysosomes and delivered onward to other membranes, and one route for that traffic is packaging into membrane-bounded vesicles. Vesicle-mediated cholesterol transport therefore links lipoprotein uptake to the sterol supply of the plasma membrane and the endoplasmic reticulum, where esterification and feedback control of sterol synthesis occur; when it stalls, unesterified cholesterol accumulates in late endocytic compartments. The genes here point to the late endosome and lysosome as the staging ground: an Arf-family GTPase governing lysosome positioning and motor coupling, a two-pore channel that releases lysosomal calcium, a synaptotagmin calcium sensor for membrane fusion, a phosphatidylinositol-5-phosphate 4-kinase shaping endosomal lipid identity, and the four subunits of the GARP tethering complex that direct retrograde vesicles back to the Golgi. A carboxylesterase contributes by hydrolysing cholesteryl esters.

Newly formed synaptic contacts are weak and labile; converting them into stable, fully functional connections with the right complement of receptors and release sites is what regulation of synapse maturation controls. The tuning it provides sets the strength and number of synapses that survive early circuit development and underlies experience-dependent refinement, learning, and the balance of excitation and inhibition; its disruption is recurrently linked to intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia. Trans-synaptic adhesion and secreted organizers such as neurexin, calsyntenin, C1QL2 and FGF22 instruct differentiation of nascent contacts, while Reelin signalling through DAB1 and Rho-kinase activity shape the cytoskeleton beneath them. Activity is read out by CaMKII and calcineurin-NFAT transcription, and receptor content is adjusted by endosomal retrieval through the retromer subunit VPS35 with SNX27, by ubiquitin ligase activity and by microRNA-directed silencing.

Newly formed synapses are initially weak and labile; this pathway drives the transition to a stable, fully functional contact, with defined receptor composition, presynaptic release capacity and proper spine morphology. Promoting synapse maturation sets the pace of circuit refinement during development and constrains how much plasticity remains in adult networks, and disruption of these components is linked to autism, schizophrenia and intellectual disability. The genes act at several levels: trans-synaptic adhesion through neurexin-1 aligns pre- and postsynaptic specializations, reelin signalling from extracellular cues shapes dendritic and synaptic architecture, CaMK2B couples calcium influx to structural and receptor changes, and NEUROD2 provides transcriptional control of synaptic gene programmes. An anaphase-promoting complex module with its activator CDC20 contributes ubiquitin-dependent turnover of synaptic proteins, showing that cell-cycle ubiquitin ligase machinery is reused postmitotically to sculpt synapses.

Whole sheets and populations of cells move in a coordinated direction during tissue migration, the behaviour that closes wounds, shapes epithelial organs in development, and guides germ cells and primordia to their destinations. When it is misdirected the same machinery drives tumour invasion and metastasis; when it fails, epithelial barriers do not re-seal. The genes here span the steps needed for directed movement: actin and actin-binding regulators including profilins and coronin, formin- and Rho-kinase-dependent contractility, integrin adhesion and focal adhesion signalling through PTK2 and SRC, and Rab11/Rab25-dependent recycling that returns receptors to the leading edge. Growth factor and cytokine cues (FGF family members, HBEGF, KIT, TGFB2 acting through TGFBR2 and SMAD4) set direction, while transcriptional regulators such as GRHL2, ZEB2 and SOX9 license the epithelial state that migrates, and PTEN and phosphatases restrain it.

Mesenchyme migration is the directed movement of loosely organised, non-epithelial embryonic cells to the sites where they will build connective tissue, smooth muscle, vessel walls and the stroma of developing organs. Getting these cells to the right place on schedule is what allows the gut, lung and heart to acquire their muscular and supportive layers; failure leaves organs hypoplastic or malrotated and, in the lung, disrupts alveolar and vascular development. The actin isoforms here supply the contractile cytoskeleton that generates traction for movement and is later retained in differentiated muscle, linking migratory behaviour to the smooth and cardiac muscle fates these cells adopt. FOXF1 is a mesenchymal transcription factor that responds to epithelial hedgehog signalling and drives the migratory and differentiation programme, and its loss underlies alveolar capillary dysplasia with foregut malformations.

Epithelial sheets hold together because neighbouring cells bind each other directly, and this adhesion is what gives epithelia their barrier function, apical-basal polarity and resistance to mechanical stress. Loss of it underlies epidermal and cardiac fragility disorders and is a step in the epithelial-mesenchymal transition that accompanies tumour invasion. The genes here build and anchor the two principal junction types: alpha-catenin, vinculin and plakophilin-3 link cadherin-based adherens junctions and desmosomes to the cytoskeleton, while desmoplakin and junction plakoglobin couple desmosomal cadherins to intermediate filaments. Associated proteins such as PLEKHA7 and CAMSAP3 tether non-centrosomal microtubules to the apical junctional belt, tying adhesion to cytoskeletal organisation. Matricellular and signalling components, including thrombospondin-4, CCN3, Indian hedgehog and the transcription factor SRF, connect junction integrity to contractility and to signals that regulate epithelial differentiation and tissue remodelling.

Mitochondria continually divide, and how fast they do so sets their size, distribution and disposability. Control over mitochondrial fission determines whether damaged segments can be pinched off for mitophagy, whether the network fragments during apoptosis, and how mitochondria are partitioned to daughter cells or trafficked into axons and dendrites. The central event is recruitment of the dynamin-family GTPase DNM1L (Drp1) to the outer membrane by receptors including FIS1, MFF, MIEF1 and MIEF2, where it constricts and severs the organelle; actin regulators such as INF2, SPIRE1 and the myosin MYO19 supply force and positioning. Ubiquitin ligases MARCHF5 and MUL1, the phosphatase PGAM5, and mitochondrial calcium entry through MCU tune the rate, while PINK1 and PRKN link fission to quality control. Loss of balance produces excessively fragmented or elongated networks, a recurring feature of neurodegeneration, with LRRK2, MAPT and VPS35 implicated in Parkinson's and tauopathy.

Mitochondria divide as well as fuse, and the signals that push the balance toward division are what this pathway describes. Fission lets cells partition mitochondria at mitosis, distribute them along cytoskeletal tracks, and segregate damaged segments so they can be cleared by mitophagy; too little leaves elongated, interconnected networks, while excessive fragmentation accompanies stress and apoptotic commitment. The core event is recruitment of the dynamin-family GTPase DNM1L (Drp1) to the outer membrane by receptors including MFF, FIS1 and the MIEF proteins, where it constricts and severs. Positive regulators here work through Drp1 itself "" phosphatase and kinase activity, ubiquitin ligases such as MARCHF5 and MUL1, and actin- and ER-associated factors that mark the division site. PINK1 and PRKN link the process to damage sensing and mitochondrial quality control, connecting fission to neurodegeneration when it fails.

Membrane fission is the step that severs one continuous bilayer into two, and without it no vesicle can be released, no cargo internalised into a multivesicular body, and no dividing cell can separate from its sister. Two mechanochemical solutions dominate here. Dynamins, including DNM1 and DNM2 at endocytic necks and DNM1L at mitochondrial and peroxisomal constrictions, assemble as collars and constrict on GTP hydrolysis. The ESCRT machinery works from the opposite topology: HGS/STAM recognise ubiquitinated cargo, ESCRT-I and -II components such as TSG101 and the VPS25/VPS36 subunits nucleate CHMP filaments, and the VPS4 AAA-ATPases drive constriction and disassembly during intraluminal vesicle budding, cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope resealing and plasma membrane repair. Spastin couples this to microtubule severing, while exocyst subunits tether vesicles at the sites where scission occurs. Defects underlie hereditary spastic paraplegia and mitochondrial fragmentation disorders.

Roughly a third of the proteome works in or on a membrane, and establishment of protein localization to membrane covers the routes by which such proteins reach the correct bilayer and adopt the right topology. Without it, receptors, channels and transporters never reach the cell surface, mitochondria cannot import their carriers, and misinserted proteins are degraded or aggregate. Several insertion machineries are represented: signal recognition particle subunits with their receptor and the Sec61 translocon for co-translational entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, the ER membrane protein complex and TMCO1 for multipass substrates, a guided-entry pathway with cytosolic chaperones for tail-anchored proteins, TOM and TIM complexes for mitochondrial import, and PEX3/PEX19/PEX16 for peroxisomal membrane proteins. Downstream, Rab GTPases, SNAREs, retromer and ESCRT components direct vesicular delivery, while palmitoyltransferases and prenylation enzymes tether otherwise soluble proteins such as Ras to membranes.

Nearly all mitochondrial proteins are made in the cytosol, so getting them into the correct membrane is what allows mitochondria to be built at all. This pathway covers the delivery and insertion of proteins into the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes, supplying the respiratory chain, carrier proteins, and the apoptotic machinery that acts at these surfaces. Precursors are recognised by the outer membrane translocase, whose receptors TOMM20 and TOMM70 feed substrates through the TOMM40 channel; small TIM chaperones such as TIMM9, TIMM10 and TIMM8A escort hydrophobic carriers across the intermembrane space to the TIMM22 insertase, while OXA1L and COX18 insert proteins from the matrix side. SAMM50 and the metaxins fold β-barrel proteins into the outer membrane. BAX and MOAP1 illustrate the regulated side, where membrane targeting commits a cell to apoptosis. Defects cause deafness-dystonia and mitochondrial disease.

Sphingolipids are structural components of membranes and also potent signalling molecules, so cells must control how fast they are made rather than letting synthesis run freely. Regulation of sphingolipid biosynthesis sets the balance between ceramide, which promotes stress responses, growth arrest and apoptosis, and sphingosine-1-phosphate, which favours survival, proliferation and cell migration. Much of the control acts at the committed first step: the ORMDL proteins sit in the endoplasmic reticulum and restrain serine palmitoyltransferase in response to ceramide levels, a feedback loop whose disturbance is linked to asthma susceptibility. Other regulators act downstream or through metabolic signalling, including the sphingosine kinases that generate sphingosine-1-phosphate, a ceramidase-like and sphingomyelinase activity that redistributes flux, AMP-activated kinase, and protein kinase C. Loss of this tuning shifts membrane composition and skews cell fate decisions toward death or unchecked growth.

Sphingolipids are structural components of membranes and also signalling molecules that set the balance between cell survival and death, so increasing the flux into their synthesis changes both membrane composition and the ceramide/sphingosine-1-phosphate tone of a cell. This positive regulation of sphingolipid biosynthesis is exerted by a heterogeneous group of upstream activators rather than the biosynthetic enzymes themselves: a secreted matricellular protein, a phospholipase, a protein kinase C isoform that couples stress and receptor signalling to lipid metabolism, a mitochondrial deacetylase linking the pathway to nutrient state, and a sphingosine kinase that generates sphingosine-1-phosphate. An intestinal alkaline sphingomyelinase contributes by releasing ceramide from dietary sphingomyelin. Raising output from this route influences apoptosis, inflammatory responses, insulin sensitivity and myelin and skin barrier lipid supply, and sustained overproduction of ceramide species is associated with lipotoxicity and metabolic disease.

Sphingolipids are structural components of membranes and potent signalling molecules, so cells restrain their synthesis as tightly as they drive it; this braking arm keeps ceramide and its derivatives from accumulating. The ORMDL proteins sit in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and inhibit serine palmitoyltransferase, the committed first step of de novo sphingolipid production, providing feedback that senses ceramide levels and shuts the route down. Loss of this restraint raises ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate, altering membrane order, stress signalling and apoptotic thresholds; variants at one ORMDL locus are among the strongest inherited associations with childhood asthma. The AMP-activated kinase catalytic subunit links the pathway to energy status, so lipid synthesis is curbed when ATP is scarce, and a sphingosine kinase and a lipid-handling ABC transporter tie flux control to downstream metabolite disposal.

Sphingolipids are both membrane building blocks and potent signalling molecules, so cells hold their intracellular levels within a narrow range; this homeostatic control sets how much ceramide and sphingomyelin a cell makes and where it ends up. The ORMDL proteins sit in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and restrain serine palmitoyltransferase, the committed first step of de novo sphingolipid synthesis, acting as a feedback brake that responds to ceramide abundance. Loss of that brake allows sphingolipid overproduction, with consequences for membrane ordering, lipid raft behaviour and stress signalling; variation at ORMDL3 is among the strongest inherited associations with childhood asthma. A transporter of the ABC family contributes to lipid movement in endosomal and lysosomal compartments, and a reticulon shapes the endoplasmic reticulum tubules where this synthesis occurs, tying lipid balance to organelle architecture.

Endoplasmic reticulum membrane organization builds and maintains the shape of the ER: the flat sheets studded with ribosomes, the branching tubular network that reaches into the cell periphery, and the three-way junctions that keep it continuous. This geometry determines where protein synthesis, lipid production and calcium handling occur, and where the ER makes contact with mitochondria, endosomes and the plasma membrane. Reticulons and REEP proteins impose high membrane curvature to generate tubules, atlastin GTPases fuse tubule tips into junctions, and lysophospholipid acyltransferase activity tunes the lipid composition that permits such curvature; SNARE and vesicle-tethering components support homotypic ER fusion and reassembly after mitosis. Loss of these functions is a recurrent cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron degeneration, reflecting how much long axons depend on a properly extended ER network.

The endoplasmic reticulum is not a featureless bag but a continuous network of sheets and branching tubules, and this pathway builds and maintains that shape. Reticulon and REEP family proteins, together with ARL6IP1, insert wedge-like hydrophobic hairpins into the bilayer to generate and stabilize the high membrane curvature of ER tubules and sheet edges, while the atlastin GTPases catalyse homotypic fusion of tubule tips to keep the network interconnected. Membrane composition contributes too: LPCAT3 adjusts phospholipid acyl chains and so bilayer flexibility, and SNARE-associated components such as STX18, BNIP1 and VAPB support fusion and tethering at ER contact sites. Because ER geometry sets the platform for protein synthesis, lipid production, calcium handling and organelle contacts, defects here cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron degeneration, axons being especially dependent on an intact ER network.

Newly made lysosomal hydrolases and membrane proteins are sorted in the trans-Golgi network and delivered onward to endosomes and lysosomes, and this Golgi-to-lysosome transport route is what gives the lysosome its degradative enzyme content. Cargo is captured by sorting receptors such as sortilin and packaged into clathrin-coated carriers, with adaptor complexes selecting cargo, GAK and associated factors driving coat assembly and uncoating, and Rab effectors including ANKFY1 and rabenosyn directing tethering and fusion with the endosomal system. Resident lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP1 and CLN3 travel the same way. When the route fails, hydrolases are missecreted rather than delivered, lysosomes cannot degrade their substrates, and undigested material accumulates; loss of CLN3 causes a neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. The pathway therefore links secretory biosynthesis to cellular catabolism, autophagy and membrane turnover.

In mammalian cells the individual Golgi stacks are laterally linked into a single continuous ribbon positioned near the centrosome, and this pathway covers the tethering and cytoskeletal machinery that builds and maintains that arrangement. Ribbon organisation matters for orderly anterograde traffic, for uniform glycosylation of secreted and surface proteins, and for directing secretion toward one face of a migrating or polarised cell; the ribbon is also deliberately dismantled at mitosis so that Golgi membranes partition between daughters. Golgins and GRASP-family tethers such as GOLGA2, TRIP11, GCC2 and GORASP1 bridge adjacent cisternal rims, while GOLPH3 with the actin motor MYO18A applies tension that flattens and stretches membranes, and VAMP4 and TMED5 contribute membrane fusion and cargo-receptor functions. Ribbon fragmentation is a recurring feature of neurodegeneration and of cells under stress.

Epithelial sheets only work because each cell knows which surface faces the lumen and which faces the basement membrane, and establishing that apical-basal polarity is what this biology does. It underlies formation of tight junction belts, directional secretion and absorption, oriented cell division, and lumen formation in tubes and glands; its loss accompanies the disorganisation seen in epithelial tumours and in kindlin-1 deficiency of skin. Small GTPase signalling through CDC42 and RHOA, with ARF6 and its cytohesin exchange factors, positions the apical determinant PARD3 and remodels the cortical cytoskeleton. Ezrin, moesin and the scaffold NHERF1 link apical membrane proteins to actin, while CAMSAP3 anchors non-centrosomal microtubule minus ends to give the cell a longitudinal axis. Ciliary and trafficking components such as IFT20 and GOLPH3, together with WNT5A and Notch-responsive factors, couple polarity to tissue-level patterning.

Before a cell divides it must take apart its Golgi apparatus so that the stacks can be partitioned between daughters and rebuilt, and Golgi disassembly is that mitotic breakdown step, which underlies Golgi inheritance. Loss of the process blocks progression into mitosis in some settings, because Golgi fragmentation is itself monitored as a checkpoint, and it leaves membrane and secretory cargo unequally distributed at division. The mechanism is largely mitotic phosphorylation: cyclin-dependent kinase 1 together with polo-like and VRK kinases modify structural and trafficking components, notably the golgin GM130 encoded by GOLGA2, the SNARE syntaxin 5 and the Arf activator GBF1. Phosphorylation severs golgin-mediated tethering between cisternae and suspends vesicle fusion, converting stacked ribbon into dispersed tubules and vesicles. It links cell cycle control directly to secretory pathway organisation and organelle biogenesis.

When a cell divides, the Golgi ribbon fragments and is partitioned between daughters; Golgi reassembly is the reformation of stacked, functional cisternae from those fragments, and it is what allows each daughter cell to resume secretion, glycosylation and polarised membrane traffic without rebuilding the organelle from scratch. It is therefore part of organelle inheritance rather than of trafficking as such. Membrane fusion is the central step: a deubiquitinating enzyme acting on p97/VCP-associated substrates reverses the ubiquitin marks that keep mitotic membranes apart, while a 14-3-3 adaptor and the CCM3-STK25 kinase module link Golgi architecture to cell polarity and stress signalling. VPS13B, a lipid-transfer protein at the Golgi whose loss causes Cohen syndrome, ties defective Golgi organisation to developmental disease, neutropenia and intellectual disability.

Before a cell can divide, it must build a bipolar microtubule array capable of gripping and separating sister chromatids; the processes gathered here tune how fast and how completely that spindle is assembled. Getting this regulation wrong produces multipolar or misoriented spindles, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and it also determines the plane of division that governs whether a progenitor self-renews or differentiates. Contributors include centriole duplication and centrosome factors such as SASS6, STIL and CEP97, the mitotic kinase PLK1, the chromatin-bound Ran nucleotide exchange factor RCC1 that establishes the gradient licensing microtubule nucleation near chromosomes, and NUMA1 with GPSM2, which anchor dynein-dependent pulling forces at the cortex to orient the spindle. An ESCRT-III and VPS4 module links the same machinery to nuclear envelope and membrane remodelling around the dividing spindle, alongside SUMO-pathway and chaperone regulators.

Membrane-bound compartments constantly exchange material, and every such exchange ends with two lipid bilayers merging into one. Organelle membrane fusion is the final, committed step of vesicle traffic: endosome maturation, lysosome and autophagosome merger, phagosome degradation, Golgi and ER remodelling, and regulated exocytosis of neurotransmitter and hormone granules all depend on it. Cognate SNAREs on opposing membranes zipper into a four-helix bundle that pulls the bilayers together, with syntaxins, VAMPs, SNAP25-family proteins and YKT6 supplying the helices, Munc18 and complexins licensing or clamping assembly, and synaptotagmins acting as the calcium sensors that trigger release. Rab GTPases and multisubunit tethers such as the HOPS/CORVET core recognise the correct partner compartment beforehand, ESCRT-III subunits and VPS4A catalyse related reverse-topology scission and sealing events, and atlastins fuse ER tubules. Defects cause lysosomal storage disease, hereditary spastic paraplegia, parkinsonism and epileptic encephalopathy.

Epithelial sheets do more than cover surfaces: their cells share a common orientation within the plane of the tissue, and control over how strongly and where that planar polarity is established shapes hair cell alignment in the inner ear, directional ciliary beating, and the convergent extension movements that close the neural tube. The genes here tune rather than simply execute that coordination. VANGL2 is a core planar polarity transmembrane component whose asymmetric distribution defines cell-level axes, and SEC24B is the cargo adaptor that selects it for ER export, so secretory trafficking becomes a limiting step. SFRP1 and SFRP2 are secreted Wnt-binding modulators that shape the extracellular cues read across the tissue, while SAPCD2 restrains spindle orientation and PKHD1 and JHY link the process to ciliated epithelia. Failure produces neural tube defects, disordered sensory hair bundles, and cystic kidney phenotypes.

regulation of cholesterol metabolic process is the control layer over how much cholesterol a cell makes, imports, stores and disposes of, keeping membrane sterol content within narrow limits while supplying precursors for bile acids and steroid hormones. Its failure produces hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis, and several of its components are the targets of lipid-lowering therapy. The core sensing device is the sterol-responsive SCAP-INSIG1 complex in the endoplasmic reticulum, which permits site-1 and site-2 protease cleavage of SREBP transcription factors to switch on the LDL receptor and lipogenic genes when sterols fall; ERLIN proteins and the ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 add degradative control. Opposing arms handle efflux and catabolism through ABCG1 and ABCG4, apolipoprotein-mediated transport by APOA1, APOB and APOE, oxysterol production by CH25H, and bile acid synthesis via CYP7A1 under FXR restraint. Kinase signalling and a set of microRNAs tune the whole circuit.

Cells must hold cholesterol within narrow limits, since too little blocks membrane and steroid synthesis while too much is cytotoxic and drives atherosclerosis. This regulatory layer sets how fast cholesterol is made, taken up, esterified, converted to bile acids or exported. Its core is the sterol-sensing machinery of the endoplasmic reticulum: SCAP and INSIG1 retain the SREBF transcription factors until sterols fall, whereupon site-1 and site-2 proteases release the active factors to induce the LDL receptor and lipogenic genes, with MARCHF6 and the ERLIN proteins imposing degradative control. Opposing arms include oxysterol production by CH25H, bile acid feedback through the nuclear receptor NR1H4 and CYP7A1, efflux by ABCG1 and ABCG4, lipoprotein handling by APOA1, APOB and APOE, and a set of microRNAs that tune these transcripts. Failure produces hypercholesterolaemia, fatty liver and cardiovascular disease.

Kidney formation depends on a reciprocal conversation between the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme, and the genes here set the pace and extent of that process: how far the bud branches, how long nephron progenitors are retained, and when they differentiate. Glial-derived neurotrophic factor signalling through RET drives bud outgrowth, while BMP4 and the BMP antagonists gremlin and noggin tune where branching is permitted. Transcription factors including PAX2, PAX8, WT1, HNF1B, GATA3, LHX1, OSR1 and the SIX family specify progenitor identity and nephron patterning; FOXD1 marks the stromal compartment that constrains it, and WNT4 is required for mesenchymal-to-epithelial conversion. Angiotensin signalling and VEGFA link the programme to vascular and collecting-system maturation. Disruption causes renal agenesis, hypodysplasia and the congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract that underlie much childhood renal failure, and reduced nephron endowment predisposes to adult hypertension.

Formation of a functioning kidney requires that inductive signals be actively reinforced, and the genes here act as the accelerators: processes that positively regulate kidney development sustain ureteric bud outgrowth, branching morphogenesis and the conversion of metanephric mesenchyme into nephrons. Loss of this input produces renal hypoplasia, dysplasia or outright agenesis, and underlies congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract in humans. GDNF signalling through the RET receptor tyrosine kinase drives and patterns ureteric branching; PAX2 marks and maintains the nephric lineage; WNT4 is needed for mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition during nephron induction; FOXD1 identifies the stromal progenitors that support the nephron progenitor niche, while NOG relieves BMP antagonism and SOX9 contributes to collecting duct and tubule differentiation. The result is a branched, filtering organ whose nephron number is set before birth.

Kidney formation depends as much on restraint as on induction, and this pathway covers the inputs that damp the rate or extent of nephrogenesis. Branching of the ureteric bud and conversion of metanephric mesenchyme into nephrons must be limited in space and time, or the organ acquires too many or misplaced branches, cysts, or hypoplastic segments; the transcription factors here are themselves causes of human renal malformation syndromes when mutated. BMP4 secreted by mesenchyme around the nephric duct restricts ectopic budding, while HNF1B and OSR1 set boundaries on tubular and nephron progenitor fate, HNF1B loss producing renal cysts and malformed collecting systems. STAT1 links cytokine signalling to suppression of growth responses, and adiponectin connects metabolic state to renal tissue growth, placing kidney morphogenesis under both local patterning and systemic control.

The exocrine pancreas releases a bicarbonate-rich, enzyme-laden fluid into the duodenum, and this pathway sets how much of it is secreted and when. The output neutralises gastric acid and delivers the digestive enzymes needed for fat, starch and protein breakdown, so disturbed control contributes to maldigestion and to the ductal fluid defects seen when anion and water transport fail. Secretin, released by duodenal endocrine cells in response to acid, is the principal hormonal stimulus acting on duct cells to drive bicarbonate and fluid output. Intracellular control runs through the WNK kinases and their downstream SPAK kinase, a module that governs cation-chloride cotransporters and cellular chloride handling and thereby tunes ductal electrolyte secretion. The liver X receptors add a nuclear-receptor layer linking lipid and sterol status to secretory regulation.

Damping of pancreatic juice secretion sets a brake on the exocrine pancreas, limiting the volume and bicarbonate-rich fluid released by acinar and duct cells into the duodenum. Restraint matters because unchecked secretion loads the gut with digestive enzyme precursors and stresses the ductal epithelium; tuning output to the arrival of a meal keeps enzyme delivery matched to need. Most of the components here form a kinase cascade in which WNK family serine/threonine kinases (WNK1, WNK3, WNK4) phosphorylate the downstream kinase SPAK, encoded by STK39, thereby controlling cation-chloride cotransporters and the epithelial ion and water movements that drive ductal fluid flow. The nuclear receptor NR1H3 adds a transcriptional, lipid-sensing layer of control. The same WNK-SPAK signalling governs salt handling in kidney and other secretory epithelia, placing this regulation within general epithelial ion transport physiology.

The collecting system of the kidney is built by repeated branching of the ureteric bud into the surrounding metanephric mesenchyme, and the number of branches achieved sets the final number of nephrons. This pathway covers the signals that promote, restrain and pattern that branching. Mesenchyme-derived GDNF drives outgrowth at the bud tip, while BMP4 acts as a brake whose activity is locally neutralised by the antagonists gremlin and noggin, so that branch points form in the right places; hedgehog signalling through SMO, WNT and angiotensin inputs, and transcriptional regulators including SIX1, SIX2, LHX1, PAX8, SOX9 and HOXB7 maintain the tip progenitor state and the reciprocal epithelial/mesenchymal dialogue. Too little branching yields renal hypoplasia or agenesis and a reduced nephron endowment predisposing to hypertension and chronic kidney disease; ectopic budding produces duplex ureters and reflux.

regulation of glomerulus development tunes the pace and extent to which the kidney's filtering units are built, determining how many functional glomeruli a nephron endowment contains and how well each capillary tuft is invested with podocytes and mesangium. Because glomerular number is fixed early in life, disturbance here sets lifelong susceptibility to proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis and hypertension, and underlies congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract. The genes represent the signalling and transcriptional inputs that act during nephrogenesis: BMP4 and its extracellular antagonist noggin form an opposing pair that shapes ureteric branching and nephron induction, RET transduces GDNF signals driving ureteric bud outgrowth, PAX2 maintains nephric lineage identity, and calcineurin signalling through PPP3CA supports podocyte differentiation and survival. Angiotensin receptor signalling links the local renin-angiotensin system to glomerular maturation, coupling kidney development to blood pressure control.

The glomerulus is the filtering unit of the nephron, a capillary tuft enclosed by Bowman's capsule whose podocytes and endothelium together form the barrier that produces urine from blood plasma; regulation of glomerulus development sets how quickly and how completely that structure is built and matured. Too few or malformed glomeruli translate directly into reduced filtration reserve, congenital kidney hypoplasia and later hypertension and glomerulosclerosis. The control points here are largely those governing branching of the ureteric bud and induction of metanephric mesenchyme: RET signalling directs branch outgrowth, PAX2 specifies nephric lineage and drives the mesenchyme-to-epithelium transition, and BMP4 opposed by its extracellular antagonist noggin tunes how much branching occurs. Calcineurin signalling through PPP3CA and angiotensin receptor input link this morphogenesis to intracellular calcium and to the renin-angiotensin system that later regulates glomerular haemodynamics.

The glomerulus is the filtering unit of the nephron, a capillary tuft enclosed in Bowman's capsule where blood plasma is first separated from the forming urine; signals that promote its development set how many functional filters a kidney ends up with. Positive regulation of glomerulus development covers the inputs that increase the rate and extent of this maturation, and shortfalls in them produce hypoplastic kidneys, reduced nephron endowment and later hypertension or chronic kidney disease. The genes involved span several arms of nephrogenesis: PAX2 is a transcription factor that specifies intermediate mesoderm and nephric lineages, RET is the receptor tyrosine kinase driving ureteric bud outgrowth and branching in response to GDNF, NOG antagonises BMP signalling to shape inductive patterning, and calcineurin signalling through PPP3CA and angiotensin receptor input act on podocyte and capillary tuft maturation.

Commitment to apoptosis is decided at the mitochondrial outer membrane, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the chance that cytochrome c escapes the intermembrane space into the cytosol, where it nucleates the apoptosome and activates caspases. Setting that threshold determines whether damaged, infected or growth factor-deprived cells die or persist, and its miscalibration underlies both tumour survival and excessive neuronal loss. The effector pore proteins BAX and BAK1 are held in check by anti-apoptotic relatives such as BCL2L1 and unleashed by BH3-only sensors including BID, BAD, BBC3, PMAIP1, BCL2L11 and HRK, several of them induced by TP53. Survival signalling through AKT1 and growth factors opposes them. Cristae architecture set by OPA1 and PARL governs how much cytochrome c is available for release, while PPIF links permeability transition and calcium stress to the same outcome.

Committing a cell to apoptosis means opening its mitochondrial outer membrane, and this pathway covers the events that promote that opening so cytochrome c escapes into the cytosol. Once there, cytochrome c nucleates the apoptosome and activates caspase-9 and downstream effector caspases, making this the point of no return for the intrinsic death pathway; its failure permits survival of damaged or oncogene-bearing cells, while excess activity drives degenerative loss. The effectors are the pore-forming BCL-2 family members BAX and BAK1, licensed by BH3-only proteins — BID linking death receptor signalling, BAD and BIK sensing survival factor withdrawal, and PMAIP1 and BBC3 induced by p53 after genotoxic stress. Additional inputs come from BNIP3 and PINK1 in mitochondrial stress and quality control, granzyme- and TRAIL-mediated killing by immune cells, and inflammasome components that couple caspase-1 activity to mitochondrial permeabilization.

Cytochrome c escape from the mitochondrial intermembrane space commits a cell to caspase activation and apoptotic death, so holding that release in check is how cells survive stress, and this set covers the braking mechanisms. Anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family members such as BCL2L1 oppose pore formation in the outer membrane, while OPA1 and its processing protease PARL keep cristae junctions tight so that the bulk of cytochrome c stays sequestered where the respiratory chain can use it. Lipid transfer and intermembrane-space proteins including PRELID1 and TRIAP1 support cardiolipin remodelling that anchors the haem protein, and antioxidant and survival signalling inputs — GPX1, AKT1, IGF1, HGF — raise the threshold for permeabilisation. Loss of this restraint drives neurodegeneration and ischaemic tissue loss; its excess underlies apoptosis resistance and chemotherapy failure in tumours.

Cells must keep sterol levels within a narrow window, and this pathway covers the inputs that push cholesterol turnover upward — increasing its synthesis, uptake, mobilization, or conversion to bile acids and other products. It matters for whole-body lipid balance: too little flux starves membranes and steroidogenic tissues of sterol, while excessive drive contributes to hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. The sterol-sensing machinery of SCAP and the site-2 protease releases the SREBF transcription factors to switch on cholesterol-synthetic and LDL-receptor genes; CYP7A1 commits cholesterol to bile acid formation in liver; the ABCG1 and ABCG4 transporters together with APOA1 and APOE move cholesterol onto acceptor lipoproteins for efflux and reverse transport. Kinase signalling through PRKAA1, PRKACA and MAPK1, intracellular sterol carriers such as STARD4, and microRNA-mediated repression tune the magnitude of the response.

Cells hold cholesterol within narrow limits, and this is the restraining arm of that control: the processes that damp sterol synthesis, uptake and turnover once cholesterol is sufficient. Losing this brake leads to sterol overaccumulation, and the same feedback circuitry is the target of lipid-lowering strategies and a determinant of atherosclerosis risk. Mechanistically it centres on the endoplasmic reticulum sterol sensor: INSIG1 retains the SCAP-SREBP complex in the ER when sterols are abundant, blocking transcription of cholesterol synthesis genes, while ERLIN1 and ERLIN2 together with the membrane ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 direct sterol-accelerated degradation of rate-limiting biosynthetic enzymes. CH25H supplies 25-hydroxycholesterol, an oxysterol that strengthens this suppression, and APOE promotes lipoprotein-mediated cholesterol clearance. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional repression of the same lipid-handling programme, linking negative regulation of cholesterol metabolism to broader lipid homeostasis.

Triglycerides are the body's main energy store, and this regulatory layer sets how fast they are synthesized, packaged into lipoprotein cores, and hydrolysed back to fatty acids. Its outputs determine plasma triglyceride levels, hepatic fat content and the capacity of adipocytes to buffer nutrient excess, so imbalance produces hypertriglyceridaemia, fatty liver and insulin resistance. Control acts at several points: apolipoprotein cofactors such as APOC2 and APOA5 tune lipase activity on circulating particles, LMF1 licenses lipase maturation, and DGAT2 commits diacylglycerol to storage. At the lipid droplet, perilipins and the coactivator ABHD5 gate access of the lipase PNPLA2 to stored triacylglycerol, with PKA signalling and CIDE proteins shaping droplet turnover and size. Transcription factors including SREBF1, the liver X receptors and SIRT1, together with several microRNAs, adjust the programme to hormonal and nutritional state.

positive regulation of triglyceride metabolic process covers the signals and enzymes that drive triglyceride synthesis, storage and breakdown upward, setting how much fat a cell or tissue makes, deposits in lipid droplets, and releases as fatty acids for fuel. It matters for whole-body energy balance: too little flux through it causes lipodystrophy and hypertriglyceridaemia when lipoprotein handling fails, while excess drives hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance. Both directions of flux are represented. DGAT2 and the SREBP and liver X receptor transcription factors promote esterification and lipogenesis, while ATGL with its coactivator ABHD5, PLIN5 on the droplet surface and PKA-dependent phosphorylation mobilise stored triacylglycerol. Apolipoprotein C-II and A-V govern lipoprotein lipase activity in plasma, and receptors such as LDLR and SCARB1 with the fatty acid transporter SLC27A1 feed substrate back into cells.

Triglycerides are the body's main storage and transport form of fatty acids, and this pathway covers the inputs that push their synthesis, turnover and clearance upward. It matters for how fat is deposited in adipose tissue and liver, how circulating lipoprotein triglyceride is unloaded, and how failure of the balance produces hypertriglyceridaemia and fatty liver. On the lipolytic side, adipose triglyceride lipase and its coactivator ABHD5, together with perilipin-coated droplets and protein kinase A signalling, release stored fatty acids. On the storage side, DGAT2 performs the final esterification step and SREBF1 with the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3 drives lipogenic transcription. Secreted apolipoproteins including APOC2, the activator of lipoprotein lipase, and APOA5 govern plasma triglyceride hydrolysis, while LDLR and SCARB1 handle lipoprotein uptake and fatty acid transporters feed substrate back in.

Triglyceride stores must be built and broken down on demand, and this pathway covers the braking influences that hold that traffic down inhibition of triglyceride synthesis, lipolysis, secretion and clearance. Such restraint sets how much fat a cell or a plasma lipoprotein carries, and its loss shows up as hypertriglyceridaemia, hepatic steatosis and altered atherosclerotic risk. Several members act on lipoprotein handling: APOC3 restrains lipoprotein lipase-mediated hydrolysis of circulating triglyceride, while APOE, APOC1 and the sorting receptor SORL1 govern particle uptake and remodelling. Others work at the lipid droplet surface, where perilipins and CIDEC limit access of lipases to stored triacylglycerol. Transcriptional and metabolic regulators including SREBF1, SIRT1 and SIK1, together with microRNAs targeting lipogenic messages, tune the underlying synthetic capacity, linking this control to insulin signalling, energy balance and adipocyte and hepatocyte function.

The mitotic spindle has to be built to the right size, shape and position before chromosomes can be pulled apart, and this pathway covers the factors that tune spindle assembly, organization and disassembly rather than simply supplying its tubulin. Its output determines whether division is symmetric or oriented, which matters for tissue architecture and stem cell fate, and its failure produces multipolar or misoriented spindles, missegregated chromosomes and aneuploidy. Contributors include the Aurora A activators TPX2 and BORA acting with PLK1, the spindle-pole and centriole duplication factors STIL, SASS6 and CEP97, and TACC3 with clathrin heavy chain crosslinking kinetochore fibres. NUMA1 and GPSM2 anchor dynein-dynactin at the cortex to orient the spindle, while nucleoporins, RCC1-generated Ran gradients and ESCRT-III/VPS4 components link nuclear transport and membrane remodelling to spindle behaviour and mitotic exit.

Cells hold off anaphase until every chromosome is properly attached to the mitotic spindle, and this is the tuning of that surveillance system s s not the alarm itself but the machinery that sets how strongly and how long it fires. Too little restraint permits division on an incomplete spindle and yields aneuploid daughters; too much leaves cells arrested in mitosis. Unattached kinetochores recruit checkpoint proteins through scaffolds such as KNL1 and ZWINT, with MAD1L1 and MAD2L1 generating the inhibitory signal against the anaphase-promoting complex. Silencing is equally regulated: cytoplasmic dynein subunits strip checkpoint components from attached kinetochores, MAD2L1BP dismantles the active MAD2 conformer, and the deubiquitinase USP44 opposes that release. Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin corrects erroneous attachments, while NDC80 and SKA complex members stabilise the correct ones. This underlies chromosomal stability and the response of tumours to antimitotic drugs.

Cells must not separate their chromosomes until every one is properly attached to the mitotic spindle, and this is the machinery that strengthens that delay. Reinforcing the spindle checkpoint keeps the metaphase-to-anaphase transition on hold while unattached or improperly tensioned kinetochores persist, protecting against missegregation and the aneuploidy that follows its loss. Two modules dominate: the chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin, which senses lack of tension and destabilises erroneous attachments, and the outer kinetochore scaffold KNL1 and NDC80 that recruits the checkpoint proteins MAD1L1 and MAD2L1 to generate the inhibitory signal against anaphase onset. Cytoplasmic dynein subunits contribute by trafficking checkpoint components along spindle microtubules and stripping them from attached kinetochores, coupling attachment status to signal silencing. GEN1 and XRCC3 link the response to unresolved recombination intermediates.

Regulation of metaphase plate congression controls how quickly and completely duplicated chromosomes are gathered onto the spindle equator before anaphase, the step that guarantees each daughter cell receives one copy of every chromosome. Errors here produce lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. The genes centre on the chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora B with INCENP, survivin and borealin — which corrects improperly attached kinetochore–microtubule connections so that only bioriented attachments persist, together with CDK1 driving mitotic entry and the spindle checkpoint protein MAD1L1 delaying progression until alignment is achieved. Motor and spindle pole components such as cytoplasmic dynein, NuMA and astrin contribute the pulling and cross-linking forces that move chromosomes, while acetyltransferases and SIRT1 tune the process through post-translational modification, including tubulin tyrosination state.

Before a cell divides, every chromosome must be pulled to the spindle midzone and held there in a single plane; regulation of metaphase plate congression covers the inputs that tune how fast and how completely that alignment is achieved. Getting it right is what makes chromosome segregation accurate, and slippage produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. Much of the control resides in the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase together with INCENP, survivin and borealin corrects improperly attached kinetochores, while CDK1 sets mitotic timing and MAD1L1 links alignment status to the spindle assembly checkpoint. Dynein-based transport, the spindle pole organiser NuMA and the microtubule-binding protein astrin contribute the mechanical and positional side, and acetyltransferase and sirtuin activities modulate the process, connecting congression to chromatin and tubulin modification.

Arachidonic acid released from cell membranes is the substrate for prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, so the rate at which cells export it sets the tone of inflammatory and vascular signalling downstream. This regulatory pathway modulates how much arachidonate leaves a cell or tissue, acting largely through control of secreted and cytosolic phospholipase A2 activity and its receptor-mediated triggering. Included here are G protein-coupled receptors for vasopressin and neurotensin, which couple hormone and peptide stimulation to lipid release, a secreted group X phospholipase A2 together with a binding partner that captures it at the cell surface, and the cytokine MIF, a long-recognised amplifier of inflammatory eicosanoid production. The kinase SYK links immune receptor engagement to the same output. Excessive flux through this step sustains inflammatory pain, fever and bronchoconstriction, which is why phospholipase A2 and its regulators are drug targets.

Arachidonic acid released from cells is the raw material for prostaglandins, leukotrienes and other eicosanoids, so anything that raises the rate of its secretion sets the level of downstream inflammatory and vasoactive signalling. The genes here represent two routes to that outcome: secreted phospholipase A2 activity, which liberates arachidonate from membrane phospholipids and can act extracellularly on neighbouring cells, and receptor-driven stimulation, where G protein-coupled receptors for vasopressin and neurotensin couple calcium and kinase signalling to phospholipase activation. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor acts as an upstream inflammatory cue that promotes the same release. The net effect links hormonal and cytokine stimuli to eicosanoid production, relevant to fever, pain, smooth muscle tone, platelet function and the amplification of inflammation; excessive activation contributes to inflammatory tissue damage and asthma.

axis elongation involved in somitogenesis is the posterior growth of the embryonic body axis that supplies the presomitic mesoderm from which somites — the precursors of vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis — are budded off in sequence. Without it the axis is truncated and the posterior skeleton and musculature fail to form, the phenotype seen in caudal dysgenesis and short-tail mutants. The genes point to WNT3A signalling from the tailbud as the driver, maintaining progenitors in the node-streak border and coupling their proliferation to the segmentation clock. Its output is tuned rather than simply switched on: secreted SFRP1 buffers ligand availability, NKD1 provides intracellular negative feedback, a phosphatase regulatory subunit modulates transduction, and the Mediator subunit MED12 couples the pathway to transcription. Axis elongation therefore links growth control to periodic patterning along the rostral-caudal axis.

Vertebrate embryos build their trunk and tail progressively from a caudal progenitor zone, and axis elongation during somitogenesis is the growth that extends the head-to-tail axis so that successive somites can be laid down behind the advancing tail bud. Without it the axis is truncated, somite number is reduced, and the vertebrae, ribs and axial muscles derived from those segments are correspondingly incomplete. The genes here point to WNT signalling as the driver: WNT3A ligand from the posterior growth zone maintains presomitic mesoderm progenitors, SFRP1 sequesters Wnt ligands and NKD1 acts as an induced negative feedback regulator, tuning pathway output rather than simply switching it on. A Mediator complex subunit links the pathway to transcriptional output, and a protein phosphatase 2A regulatory subunit contributes phosphorylation-dependent control. The result couples posterior progenitor renewal to the segmentation clock that times somite formation.

Contraction of cardiac, skeletal and smooth muscle has to be tuned to demand, and this collection captures the modulation of muscle system processes inclusive of contractile force, relaxation rate, heart rhythm and vascular tone. Much of the control converges on calcium handling: release channels and their stabilising partners, the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pumps and their inhibitor phospholamban, calsequestrin and triadin in the junctional store, sodium-calcium exchangers, and the junctophilins that hold membranes in register. Adrenergic, muscarinic, endothelin, tachykinin and purinergic receptors feed into cyclic nucleotide and kinase cascades that shift myofilament calcium sensitivity through troponin and myosin light chain phosphorylation. Transcription factors and microRNAs set the contractile gene programme and muscle mass, while atrophy ubiquitin ligases and myostatin restrain growth. Disruption produces arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, hypertension, malignant hyperthermia and myopathy.

negative regulation of mitochondrial fission restrains the division of mitochondria, biasing the organelle network toward elongated, interconnected forms.
