Loss of the barrier causes germ cell loss, autoimmune orchitis and infertility, so its assembly is a precondition for spermatogenesis rather than an accessory feature. The genes here point to two requirements: chromatin regulators such as ARID4A and ARID4B that set the Sertoli transcriptional programme, and cytoskeletal and trafficking components including the actin crosslinker FLNA and the small GTPase RAB13, which delivers junctional cargo to cell contacts.

Interleukin-17 cytokines mobilise epithelial and stromal cells against extracellular bacteria and fungi, and the cellular response to them is what turns a T cell signal into neutrophil recruitment at a barrier surface. The same response, sustained, drives psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis and other autoimmune inflammation, which is why the ligands and their receptors are drug targets. IL17A and IL17F act through IL17RA paired with IL17RC, while IL25 signals through IL17RB; all converge on the adaptor TRAF3IP2, which recruits TRAF6 and related TRAFs to activate NF-kB and induce IL1B, CXCL10 and other chemokines and acute-phase products. NFKBIZ supplies a transcriptional coactivator arm, mRNA stability control adds a post-transcriptional layer, and SOCS3 together with deubiquitination by USP25 restrains the output. STAT3 links this axis back to the Th17 differentiation programme that generates the ligands.

Interleukin-17 family cytokines released by Th17 cells, innate lymphocytes and epithelium act on tissue cells to summon neutrophils and reinforce mucosal barrier defence, and the signalling they trigger is what turns that cytokine cue into changes in gene transcription. The output is antimicrobial peptides, chemokines and granulopoietic factors, which is why loss of the pathway produces chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and staphylococcal skin infection, while excess drives psoriasis, ankylosing spondylitis and other inflammatory disease now treated with IL-17 and receptor blockade. IL-17A and IL-17F engage a heterodimeric IL-17RA/IL-17RC receptor, and the related IL-25 signals through IL-17RA with IL-17RB toward type 2 responses. The adaptor ACT1, encoded by TRAF3IP2, couples the receptor to TRAF6 and NF-κB activation, with TRAF2 and TRAF5 stabilising target transcripts; ubiquitin editing by USP25 and TRIM32 tunes signal strength, and SRSF1 links the pathway to mRNA handling.

Neurotransmitter cannot be concentrated into synaptic vesicles unless the vesicle interior is first made acidic, and synaptic vesicle lumen acidification is the step that provides that driving force. A vacuolar-type proton ATPase, built from a membrane-embedded rotor sector and a cytoplasmic catalytic sector with accessory subunits, hydrolyses ATP to pump protons inward; the resulting pH and voltage gradients are then spent by vesicular transporters that exchange lumenal protons for glutamate, GABA, monoamines or acetylcholine. A chloride transporter contributes counterion flux so that charge does not oppose further pumping, and the glutamate transporter shown here defines excitatory terminals. Without adequate acidification, vesicles fill poorly and quantal size falls, weakening synaptic transmission; the same proton pump also acidifies endosomes and lysosomes, so its subunit mutations produce neurodevelopmental disease alongside renal tubular acidosis and deafness.

Cells detect falling oxygen and reprogramme their metabolism through HIF-1alpha, the oxygen-labile subunit that dimerises with ARNT and drives transcription of hypoxia-response genes. This is the master switch that shifts energy production from oxidative phosphorylation toward glycolysis, promotes erythropoiesis and angiogenesis, and adapts tissues to ischaemia; the same programme is hijacked by solid tumours to survive poorly perfused regions. Oxygen sensing is set by the prolyl hydroxylase encoded by EGLN1, which marks HIF1A for degradation when oxygen is plentiful, so that loss of hydroxylation stabilises the factor; RWDD3-mediated SUMOylation and COMMD1 binding further tune its transcriptional output. Among its outputs are pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases, which restrain entry of pyruvate into the TCA cycle, and the hypoxia-induced microRNA miR-210, extending the response into post-transcriptional control of mitochondrial function.

The liver is unusual among solid organs in being able to restore its mass after resection or toxic injury, and this regenerative response is what allows recovery from hepatectomy, viral hepatitis and acetaminophen damage; when it fails, acute liver failure follows, and when it runs unchecked it feeds fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Quiescent hepatocytes are first primed by inflammatory cytokines such as IL6 and TNF acting through CEBPB, then driven into cycle by cyclin D1 with PCNA and AURKA marking DNA replication and mitosis, while TGFB1 and IL10 restrain proliferation and terminate the response. Hedgehog components including IHH, PTCH1 and GLI1 contribute to progenitor and stromal responses, and chromatin regulators EZH2 and PRMT5 reset hepatocyte gene expression. Accompanying shifts in fatty acid oxidation, amino acid transport and tyrosine catabolism reflect the need to sustain metabolic duties while rebuilding tissue.

Cells build their shape, mechanics and internal transport on long polymers, and this pathway covers the assembly, bundling, arrangement and disassembly of those supramolecular fibers: actin filaments, microtubules, intermediate filaments such as keratins, vimentin, desmin and neurofilaments, and the sarcomeric and collagen-elastin fibers built from them. What depends on it is broad — cell migration and adhesion, cytokinesis and spindle formation, muscle contraction, epidermal and hair integrity, stereocilia and cilia, neuronal process outgrowth. Mechanism runs through nucleators and elongators (Arp2/3 with WASP-family and WAVE regulators, formins, spire proteins), capping, severing and depolymerizing factors (capping protein, gelsolin, cofilin, katanin, stathmins), crosslinkers and stabilizers (filamins, plectin, spectrins, tropomyosins, MAPs), and Rho-family GTPase signalling through ROCK, PAK and LIM kinases. Mutations here cause myopathies, cardiomyopathies, epidermolysis and keratin disorders, deafness and neurodegeneration.

Programmed cell death in response to reactive oxygen species is the decision a cell makes to kill itself when oxidative damage exceeds what its antioxidant defences can absorb. It sets the threshold between adaptive stress tolerance and elimination, and shapes outcomes in ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, noise-induced hair cell loss and the oxidative stress of tumour cells. The components span sensing, survival signalling and execution: PARK7 and PINK1 buffer mitochondrial oxidant load and are lost in parkinsonism, HGF-MET and AKT1 signalling suppresses death while FOXO3 and stress kinases such as MAP2K4 and STK25 promote it, and endonuclease G translocating from mitochondria fragments DNA once commitment occurs. Several microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-34a and let-7b, tune this balance in cardiomyocytes and other post-mitotic cells. The pathway therefore links redox metabolism to apoptosis rather than being a separate death programme.

Oxidative stress that exceeds a cell's antioxidant capacity does not simply damage it passively; beyond a threshold it triggers programmed cell death in response to reactive oxygen species, an active suicide programme that removes irreparably oxidised cells. This decision shapes ischaemia-reperfusion injury, cardiac and neuronal loss, and the survival of tumour cells under redox stress. Survival signalling opposes it, with hepatocyte growth factor acting through its receptor MET to engage AKT1, which restrains the pro-apoptotic transcription factor FOXO3; stress kinases such as MAP2K4 and the scaffold RACK1 push the balance the other way. Mitochondria are central: PINK1 and PARK7 protect against oxidant-induced degeneration, TRAP1 buffers the organelle, and endonuclease G relocates to fragment nuclear DNA. Several microRNAs, including miR-21 and miR-34a, tune the threshold at which commitment occurs.

Motor neurons must reach the correct position within the spinal cord and hindbrain before their axons can find target muscles, and the orderly migration of these efferent neurons from their birthplace to their final settling site is what establishes the columnar and pool organization underlying coordinated movement. Reelin secreted in the developing neural tube acts through the intracellular adaptor DAB1 to control how migrating somatic motor neurons stop and cluster, the same ligand-adaptor pairing that positions cortical and cerebellar neurons. Guidance cues overlap with vascular signalling: VEGFA and its receptor neuropilin-1 steer facial branchiomotor and other motor neuron somata as well as their processes. Transcriptional inputs including LHX1 and OLIG3 specify subtype identity in the dorsoventral progenitor domains from which these cells emerge. Misplacement of motor neuron cell bodies produces cranial nerve and congenital motility disorders.

Neurotransmitter release depends on synaptic vesicles being delivered to the presynaptic terminal and held in reserve near release sites, and this positioning and clustering of vesicles is what synaptic vesicle localization accomplishes. Kinesin motors such as KIF5A/B/C and KIF1B haul vesicle precursors down the axon along microtubules, while synapsins tether vesicles into the reserve pool and the active zone scaffolds bassoon and piccolo organize them at the membrane. Adaptor complex AP-3 subunits together with the BLOC-1 subunits and their partner snapin handle vesicle biogenesis and cargo sorting from endosomes, and dynamins with synaptojanin recycle membrane after fusion. Adhesion and organizing molecules including neurexin, neuroligins and cadherins align the pools with postsynaptic partners. Disruption is tied to neurodegeneration and movement disorders, as reflected by LRRK2, PINK1, parkin, alpha-synuclein and huntingtin, and to impaired synaptic strength and plasticity.

Dendrite extension is the long-distance outgrowth of a single dendritic process during neuronal development, the step that determines how far a neuron reaches and which inputs it can collect. Without it, arbors stay stunted, synaptic connectivity is sparse, and circuit wiring and cognition suffer; several members here are linked to intellectual disability and autism. Growth requires coordinated actin remodelling at the growing tip, where the WAVE regulatory complex components CYFIP1/2 and WASF1 drive branched filament assembly, together with membrane addition through calcium-sensitive trafficking proteins of the synaptotagmin and copine families and endocytic regulators such as SH3GL2 and ITSN2. Ubiquitin ligases including SMURF1, NEDD4L and PRKN set protein turnover that restricts or permits elongation, while STK11 polarity signalling and presynaptic-type scaffolds like RIMS1/2 and UNC13A tie extension to subsequent synapse formation and neuronal maturation.

Wiring the nervous system requires each growing axon or dendrite to find one target among many, and neuron projection guidance is the process that steers it there. Growth cones read attractive and repulsive cues laid out across developing tissue — netrins read by DCC and UNC5 receptors, slits read by ROBO receptors, semaphorins read by plexins and neuropilins, ephrins read by EPH kinases, plus morphogens such as SHH, WNTs and BMPs — and convert them into local cytoskeletal remodelling through Rho-family GTPases, actin regulators like ENAH and VASP, CDK5 with its activators, and microtubule and kinesin components. Adhesion molecules of the L1, contactin and DSCAM families provide substrate and fasciculation choices, while transcription factors including LHX, ISL and POU4F proteins set which receptors a neuron expresses. Errors produce commissural and midline crossing defects, cranial nerve misrouting, and malformed cortical and retinal projections.

Sympathetic neurons must send axons over long distances to reach targets such as blood vessels, sweat glands, heart and brown adipose tissue, and this pathway covers the long-range extension of a single sympathetic projection during development. Getting it right sets the density of sympathetic innervation, and with it the autonomic control of vascular tone, thermogenesis and cardiac rate; failure leaves target organs under- or misinnervated. Guidance here is largely repulsive and neuropilin-dependent: class 3 semaphorins acting through NRP1 and NRP2 sculpt the trajectory and branching of growing axons, while CLSTN3 promotes sympathetic innervation of adipose tissue and S100B is supplied by the surrounding glial environment. The biology therefore sits at the intersection of axon guidance, growth cone cytoskeletal remodelling and the matching of neuron number and arbor size to peripheral target demand.

Membrane-bound compartments are not fixed in dimension: endosomes, lysosomes and secretory vesicles are continually enlarged by fusion and trimmed by fission, and control over vesicle size determines how much cargo a compartment holds and how quickly it matures. The genes here bring together the machinery that sets that balance. Clathrin-coat adaptors and the fission GTPase dynamin pinch buds from the plasma membrane, so their loss yields fewer, aberrantly sized vesicles; Rab5 and its exchange-factor partners promote homotypic endosome fusion and thus growth; BLOC-1 and BORC subunits, with shared components such as snapin and KXD1, act with the WASH complex in tubulation and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis; an ESCRT-III subunit contributes to membrane scission during multivesicular body formation. Failures distort endolysosomal morphology and are linked to pigmentation and platelet granule defects, neurodegeneration and impaired synaptic vesicle recycling.

Non-motile cilia, including the photoreceptor outer segment, work only if the right proteins are delivered into a compartment that has no ribosomes of its own, so targeting and retention of cargo within the sensory cilium determines whether signalling and phototransduction machinery ever reaches its post. Failure produces ciliopathies: retinal degeneration, Bardet-Biedl syndrome features, and skeletal dysplasia. Small GTPases of the ARL family, notably ARL13B and ARL6, together with the BBSome components BBS4 and BBIP1, recognise cargo and couple it to intraflagellar transport, of which IFT80 and TTC21B are part; tubby-family proteins TUB and TULP1 hand membrane proteins to that machinery at the ciliary base. Photoreceptor-specific factors such as RPGR, SPATA7 and PCARE act at the connecting cilium, and ZDHHC3-mediated palmitoylation illustrates how lipid modification licenses ciliary membrane residence.

Non-motile primary cilia work as signalling antennae, and that role depends on delivering the right receptors into the ciliary membrane and holding them there. Receptor localization to the non-motile cilium is what concentrates Hedgehog pathway components, GPCRs and sensory receptors in a compartment separated from the rest of the plasma membrane, so that ligand binding produces a graded intracellular response. The genes here act at distinct steps: a small ARL-family GTPase pair on the ciliary membrane recruits trafficking effectors, an intraflagellar transport subunit carries cargo along the axoneme, and a BBSome-associated subunit contributes to the coat that sorts membrane proteins into and out of the organelle. When these steps fail, receptors never reach the cilium, and the resulting ciliopathies present with retinal degeneration, obesity, polydactyly, cystic kidneys and developmental patterning defects.

Sialylation caps glycoproteins and glycolipids with negatively charged sialic acid, the terminal sugar that determines how a cell surface is read by lectins, antibodies and pathogens. Because sialic acid is the outermost residue, its placement sets serum glycoprotein half-life, masks underlying galactose from clearance receptors, and builds the ligands used in leukocyte trafficking and complement regulation. The enzymes here are Golgi sialyltransferases that differ in linkage and acceptor: the ST3GAL family adds sialic acid in alpha2,3 linkage to galactose, ST6GAL1 and ST6GAL2 in alpha2,6 linkage, ST6GALNAC2 onto O-linked mucin-type cores, and the ST8SIA enzymes form alpha2,8 linkages, with ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 polymerising polysialic acid on NCAM to loosen cell adhesion during neural development and plasticity. Aberrant sialylation is a recurrent feature of tumour cells, altering immune recognition, adhesion and metastatic behaviour.

Necroptotic signalling is a regulated route to cell death that ruptures the cell rather than dismantling it quietly, so its execution spills intracellular contents and provokes inflammation. It matters as a backup when apoptosis is blocked, for example when caspase-8 is inhibited by viral proteins, and as a driver of tissue damage in ischaemic injury, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease. Death receptor ligation by TNF or FAS ligand, or sensing of double-stranded RNA through TLR3, assembles complexes in which RIPK1 and RIPK3 phosphorylate one another through their RIP homotypic interaction motifs. Active RIPK3 then phosphorylates the pseudokinase MLKL, which oligomerises and permeabilises the plasma membrane to commit the cell to lysis. FADD and caspase-8 normally restrain this branch, and the balance between them decides whether a receptor signal produces apoptosis, necroptosis or survival.

Neutrophils, monocytes, macrophages, eosinophils and mast cells reach sites of infection and injury by directed movement out of the blood and through tissue, and myeloid leukocyte migration is the programme that steers them. It sets the pace of acute inflammation: too little leaves bacterial infection uncontained, as in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, while excess drives tissue damage in sepsis, asthma and atherosclerosis. Chemokines and their receptors, complement fragments acting through C3AR1 and C5AR1, formyl-peptide and lipid mediators establish the gradients; beta-2 integrin ITGB2 with endothelial junctional proteins such as PECAM1 and JAM3 mediates firm adhesion and transendothelial squeezing; Rac GTPases, VAV exchange factors, SYK, LYN and PI3K isoforms convert receptor input into actin remodelling and polarity. Damage-associated alarmins including S100A8/A9 and HMGB1 amplify recruitment, and matrix proteases open a path through basement membrane.

Granulocyte migration is the directed movement of neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils out of the bone marrow, through blood, and across endothelium into tissues where they must reach an infection or injury. It is the first cellular arm of innate defence: without it, bacteria and fungi grow unchecked, as in leukocyte adhesion deficiency, while excess recruitment drives the tissue damage of acute lung injury, gout and chronic inflammation. Chemoattractants set the direction, including interleukin-8 acting through CXCR1 and CXCR2, complement fragments through C3AR1 and C5AR1, formyl and lipid mediators, and a broad set of CC chemokines for eosinophil influx. Adhesion and transendothelial crossing depend on beta-2 integrin, PECAM1 and junctional molecules, with selectin ligands built by fucosyltransferases. Inside the cell, SYK, VAV proteins, PI3K gamma and delta, and Rac GTPases remodel actin to generate motility, and S100A8/A9 and other alarmins amplify the response.

Mast cells are made in the bone marrow but do their work in skin, gut and airway mucosa, and this pathway covers the directed movement that gets them there and redistributes them during inflammation. It matters because local mast cell density sets the intensity of allergic and anaphylactic responses, contributes to fibrosis and tissue remodelling, and underlies the abnormal accumulation seen in mastocytosis. Chemotactic input comes from the eotaxin CCL11 and from vascular growth factors of the VEGF family together with placental growth factor, while the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT responding to stem cell factor is the dominant survival and migration cue; gain-of-function KIT mutations drive clonal mast cell disease. Inside the cell, a PI3K catalytic subunit, STAT5B, the Rho-family GTPase RAC2 and the actin regulator SWAP70 convert these signals into cytoskeletal remodelling, adhesion turnover and polarised crawling.</description>

Almost every rapid cellular decision — muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, secretion, lymphocyte activation, gene induction — begins with a rise in cytosolic calcium, and this pathway covers the routes by which that ion enters the cytosol across a membrane. Two sources feed it: influx from outside through voltage-gated channels, ligand-gated receptors such as NMDA receptors and purinergic P2X channels, and TRP channels; and release from internal stores through inositol trisphosphate receptors and ryanodine receptors, the latter organised at junctional membranes with triadin, calsequestrin, junctophilins and FKBP accessory subunits. Phospholipase C isoforms generate the second messenger that opens store channels downstream of chemokine and monoamine receptors, while sodium–calcium exchangers, a plasma-membrane pump and calmodulin–calcineurin decode and reset the signal. Sustained or mislocalised calcium entry drives excitotoxicity, arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia and apoptotic commitment at mitochondria.

Vacuolar and lysosomal compartments do not stay separate: they merge with one another and with incoming vesicles to form larger degradative organelles, and this fusion is how cargo delivered by endocytosis and autophagy reaches hydrolases. The genes here are dominated by the ESCRT-III subunits, the CHMP proteins that polymerise into spiral filaments on membrane necks and, with VPS4-type remodelling, drive the constriction and scission steps that also remodel endosomes into multivesicular bodies and reseal damaged lysosomal and nuclear membranes. Tethering is represented by VPS16 and VPS39, subunits of the HOPS-type complexes that capture Rab-marked membranes and license SNARE-mediated bilayer merger. Loss of these activities blocks cargo degradation and autophagic flux, and mutations in individual CHMP genes cause neurodegenerative disease, linking membrane fusion capacity to neuronal proteostasis.

Crawling cells push forward by extending a lamellipodium, the flat actin-filled sheet at the leading edge, and its organization covers the assembly, shaping and dismantling of that structure. This underlies fibroblast migration in wound healing, immune cell chasing of chemotactic cues, neuronal growth cone advance and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. The core engine is Rac- and CDC42-directed activation of the WAVE regulatory complex, whose subunits include CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI proteins and BRK1, which in turn switches on the ARP2/3 complex to nucleate branched actin networks. Filament length and turnover are tuned by cofilin, capping protein and its CARMIL regulators, twinfilin and coronins, while ARPIN provides negative control. Integrin and CD44 adhesion, Src and phosphoinositide 3-kinase signalling, and vinculin-linked attachments couple the protrusion to substrate so that membrane extension produces net translocation rather than futile ruffling.

Potassium efflux across the plasma membrane sets the resting membrane potential and repolarises excitable cells after each action potential, so this transport underlies cardiac rhythm, neuronal firing frequency and epithelial potassium secretion. Voltage-gated channels of several families carry the current: the delayed rectifiers KCNQ1 and KCNH2 that terminate the cardiac action potential, KCNA2 and KCNB1 in neurons, and the transient outward channel KCND3, together with two-pore leak channels such as KCNK5 and KCNK18 that conduct background potassium. Small KCNE subunits and KCNIP calcium-binding proteins reshape gating kinetics and voltage dependence, while scaffolding by DLG1 and ubiquitin ligases NEDD4, NEDD4L and WWP2 control channel surface density; WNK4 provides kinase input from ion-handling pathways. Loss-of-function mutations in these channels produce long QT syndrome, arrhythmia, epilepsy and migraine susceptibility.

Arginine cannot be made in sufficient quantity by most cells, so its uptake from the extracellular space sets the intracellular supply for protein synthesis, polyamine and creatine production, urea cycle intermediates, and nitric oxide generation by the NOS enzymes. Import across the plasma membrane is carried largely by cationic amino acid transporters of the SLC7 family: SLC7A1 is broadly expressed and supports proliferating cells and endothelium, SLC7A2 is induced during inflammation and in macrophages where arginine is partitioned between nitric oxide synthesis and arginase, and SLC7A3 is more restricted in distribution. Polyspecific organic cation transporters, including the renal basolateral carrier SLC22A2 and the efflux-capable SLC47A1, also handle organic cations at epithelial surfaces. Limiting arginine entry constrains endothelial vasodilation and immune effector function, and transport defects contribute to disturbed cationic amino acid handling in kidney and intestine.

calcitonin family receptor signaling pathway covers the peptide hormones calcitonin, CGRP, adrenomedullin and amylin and the receptors through which they act, controlling bone turnover and calcium handling, vascular tone and permeability, satiety and glucose homeostasis, and the sensitization of nociceptors that underlies migraine. Its defining mechanistic feature is combinatorial: two class B G protein-coupled receptors, the calcitonin receptor and the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, each associate with one of three receptor activity-modifying proteins, and the RAMP partner dictates which peptide is bound and trafficked to the surface, converting two receptors into a family of pharmacologically distinct ones. Signalling proceeds largely through Gs and cAMP, relaxing smooth muscle, restraining osteoclasts and modulating sensory neuron excitability alongside channels such as NaV1.9. Adrenomedullin signalling through RAMP2 is required for lymphatic and vascular development, and CGRP receptor blockade is now standard migraine therapy.

Signalling by the calcitonin family of peptides lets cells respond to a set of related ligands — calcitonin, the calcitonin gene-related peptides, amylin, adrenomedullin and intermedin — that control bone turnover and calcium handling, vascular tone and endothelial barrier integrity, appetite and glucose homeostasis, and the sensitisation of nociceptors. Two class B G protein-coupled receptors, the calcitonin receptor and the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, generate this diversity by pairing with receptor activity-modifying proteins: association with RAMP1, RAMP2 or RAMP3 reshapes ligand preference, converting one receptor into a CGRP or amylin receptor and the other into adrenomedullin receptors, with cAMP as a principal downstream output. Loss of adrenomedullin-RAMP2 signalling causes lethal vascular and lymphatic defects, islet amylin aggregates in type 2 diabetes, and blockade of CGRP transmission is now used to treat migraine.

Amylin, the peptide co-secreted with insulin from pancreatic beta cells, acts on the brainstem and hypothalamus to signal meal-related satiety, slow gastric emptying and restrain glucagon release, making this receptor pathway part of the hormonal control of food intake and postprandial glucose. The receptor is not a single gene product: the calcitonin receptor encoded by CALCR acquires amylin selectivity only when it associates with a receptor activity-modifying protein, and the RAMP1/RAMP2/RAMP3 subunits shift the same core receptor between calcitonin, amylin and calcitonin gene-related peptide pharmacology, which is why CALCA appears alongside IAPP as a related ligand. Downstream coupling is largely to Gs and cyclic AMP. The pathway is exploited therapeutically by amylin mimetics for diabetes and obesity, while aggregation of the ligand itself forms islet amyloid in type 2 diabetes.

Double-strand break repair via classical nonhomologous end joining is the fast, template-independent route for rejoining broken chromosomes, and the one that lymphocytes depend on to seal the coding ends generated during V(D)J recombination. It operates throughout the cell cycle, including G1 when no sister chromatid is available for homology-directed repair, and its loss produces radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and genome instability. Broken ends are captured by the KU70/80 heterodimer, held in a synaptic complex, minimally processed, and sealed by DNA ligase IV with its XRCC4 partner. Access to this route is decided upstream by chromatin ubiquitylation and reader proteins: RNF168-dependent marks recruit 53BP1, which shields ends from resection and thereby channels repair away from homologous recombination and away from the error-prone alternative end-joining that generates translocations. Additional factors such as ERCC6L2 and TOPBP1 tune end protection and checkpoint coupling.

Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous lesions a genome can carry, and classical nonhomologous end joining is the pathway that rejoins them directly, without needing a homologous template, throughout the cell cycle. It is the route used to seal the programmed breaks of V(D)J recombination, so its loss causes immunodeficiency alongside radiation sensitivity and genome instability. The Ku70 subunit encoded by XRCC6 binds broken ends and recruits the ligase IV complex that performs the final religation, while the chromatin ubiquitin ligase RNF168 and the reader 53BP1 mark damaged nucleosomes and bias repair away from homologous recombination and end resection. Additional factors here couple end joining to transcription-associated damage, checkpoint signalling through TOPBP1, and transcriptional control of repair capacity. Unlike alternative, microhomology-mediated end joining, this pathway rejoins the correct partners and does not generate chromosomal translocations.

When a chromosome breaks and neither homologous recombination nor the classical end-joining machinery seals it, cells fall back on alternative nonhomologous end joining, a mutagenic backup that anneals short stretches of microhomology exposed at resected ends and ligates across them. The repair is intrinsically lossy, leaving deletions, insertions and templated junctions at the scar, and it is a major source of the chromosomal rearrangements and translocations that accumulate during tumour development and after chemotherapy or radiation. The polymerase POLQ is the defining activity, capturing annealed ends and extending them, with LIG3 completing the seal; NBN contributes the end resection that exposes microhomology, while TOPBP1 and RHNO1 tie the process to damage checkpoint signalling. Because homologous recombination-deficient tumours depend on this route for survival, it is an actively pursued synthetic-lethal drug target.

cell surface receptor signaling pathway via STAT is the route by which cytokines, growth factors and hormones binding at the plasma membrane change gene transcription within minutes, without a second messenger relay. It is the backbone of immune communication and blood cell production: interferons, interleukins, erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, growth hormone, prolactin and leptin all act this way, and loss of its components causes severe combined immunodeficiency, mycobacterial susceptibility, and hyper-IgE syndrome, while constitutive activation drives leukemias and myeloproliferative disease. Receptor-associated JAK kinases phosphorylate STAT1 through STAT6, which dimerize, enter the nucleus and bind target promoters, with lineage outcome determined by which STAT is engaged. Negative regulation is built in and prominent here: SOCS and CIS proteins are themselves STAT targets, forming a feedback loop, while PIAS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN2 and PTPRC set signal duration. Coactivators and microRNAs tune the transcriptional output.

Many cytokines, hormones and growth factors act on cells by routing their signal through STAT transcription factors, and this cell surface receptor signalling via STAT is the route by which immune polarisation, haematopoiesis, growth and metabolic status are translated into changed gene expression. Ligands and their receptors here span the interleukins, interferons, growth hormone, prolactin, erythropoietin, thrombopoietin and leptin; receptor engagement activates associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2), which phosphorylate STAT1 through STAT6, driving dimerisation, nuclear import and target promoter binding with coactivators such as EP300. Feedback and restraint are built in: SOCS and CISH proteins, PIAS1, and phosphatases including PTPN2 and PTPRC terminate the response, and several microRNAs tune it. Loss of individual components produces immunodeficiency, growth hormone insensitivity or defective antiviral defence, while constitutive STAT activity, particularly STAT3 and STAT5, supports leukaemias and solid tumour inflammation.

vascular endothelial cell response to fluid shear stress describes how the cells lining blood vessels sense the drag of flowing blood and convert it into changes in shape, gene expression and vasodilator output. This mechanosensing keeps endothelium quiescent and anti-thrombotic in regions of steady laminar flow, while disturbed or oscillatory flow at branch points and curvatures produces the inflammatory, permeable phenotype where atherosclerotic plaque forms; the same responses guide vascular remodelling and arterial adaptation to changing hemodynamics. Mechanical load is transmitted through focal adhesions and the cytoskeleton, with focal adhesion kinase, ABL1 and calpain remodelling adhesive contacts, and relayed by adenylate cyclase-generated cAMP acting on protein kinase A holoenzymes, by PI3K-PDPK1-AKT and mTOR signalling toward survival and nitric oxide production, and by phosphatases and SOCS5 that restrain the response. MIR92A1 provides flow-sensitive post-transcriptional control of endothelial activation.

Blood flow is not just a delivery system but a signal: endothelial cells lining arteries continuously read the frictional drag of moving blood and adjust their shape, alignment, permeability and gene expression accordingly. Laminar shear keeps the endothelium quiescent, anti-thrombotic and vasodilatory, whereas disturbed flow at branch points and curvatures favours inflammatory activation and is where atherosclerotic plaque preferentially forms. Mechanical force at junctions and focal adhesions is converted into chemistry through focal adhesion kinase and ABL1, the PI3K-AKT-mTOR axis with PDPK1, and phosphatases such as PPP2CA and PTPN1 that set signal duration. A large complement of adenylate cyclases with GNAS and the regulatory and catalytic subunits of protein kinase A supplies cAMP-dependent control of barrier function and tone, while miR-92a acts as a flow-sensitive brake on the atheroprotective endothelial phenotype.

Endothelial cells lining arteries continuously sense the drag of flowing blood, and steady laminar shear stress is the signal that keeps them quiescent, aligned with flow, and anti-inflammatory. This mechanotransduction underlies the regional distribution of atherosclerosis: plaques form at branch points and curvatures where flow is disturbed and this protective response is absent, while regions of uniform laminar flow resist lesion formation. The genes here trace two arms of the resulting signalling. A stimulatory G protein and a full complement of adenylate cyclases raise cAMP, engaging protein kinase A catalytic and regulatory subunits to alter transcription and junctional behaviour. In parallel, PDPK1 and AKT1 with mTOR support endothelial survival, nitric oxide production and vascular tone, while calpain and PKN2 contribute to the cytoskeletal remodelling that elongates cells along the flow axis. Together these outputs maintain a healthy, non-thrombogenic vessel wall.

response to oscillatory fluid shear stress is how vascular endothelial cells sense and react to disturbed, back-and-forth blood flow of the kind found at arterial branch points and curvatures, as opposed to the steady laminar flow that keeps endothelium quiescent. This distinction matters because oscillatory flow drives endothelial dysfunction — loss of nitric oxide output, inflammatory activation and increased permeability — and explains why atherosclerotic plaques form at predictable, flow-defined sites rather than uniformly along the vessel. Mechanotransduction here runs through focal adhesions and the cytoskeleton: focal adhesion kinase and the ABL1 tyrosine kinase are activated at sites of integrin engagement, while the phosphatases PTPN1 and PP2A set the threshold and duration of that signalling, and calpain-mediated proteolysis remodels adhesion complexes. The output is altered cell shape, alignment, and gene expression, linking hemodynamics to vascular remodelling and disease susceptibility.

Blood does not flow smoothly everywhere: at arterial branch points and curves it becomes disturbed and reverses direction with each cycle, and endothelial cells read this oscillatory fluid shear stress differently from steady laminar flow. The response matters because it is where atherosclerosis begins — disturbed-flow regions lose endothelial quiescence and barrier integrity, turn on inflammatory adhesion, and become the sites where plaques form, while laminar regions remain protected. Mechanotransduction here converges on focal adhesions and the cytoskeleton, with focal adhesion kinase and the Abl kinase transmitting force-dependent signals, calpain-mediated proteolysis remodelling adhesion components, and a phosphatase pair opposing tyrosine and serine/threonine phosphorylation to set signal duration. The result links mechanical stimulus to changes in cell shape, alignment, and gene expression, making vascular geometry a determinant of regional disease susceptibility.

ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by runaway peroxidation of membrane phospholipids rather than by caspases, and it is the vulnerability exploited to kill therapy-resistant and mesenchymal tumour cells, as well as a contributor to neurodegeneration, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and kidney damage. The balance is set by cystine supply through SLC7A11, glutathione, and GPX4, which reduces lipid hydroperoxides; parallel defence comes from FSP1 (AIFM2) and NQO1 acting on ubiquinone, and from NRF2-driven antioxidant and iron-handling genes including HMOX1 and ferritin. On the pro-death side, ACSL4 loads polyunsaturated fatty acids into membrane lipids, making them oxidisable, while labile iron and cell-cycle- and stress-linked kinases push peroxidation forward. Serine and citrate metabolism, autophagic ferritin turnover via SQSTM1, and NINJ1-dependent membrane rupture link the process to nutrient state and to inflammatory release of cell contents.

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by runaway peroxidation of polyunsaturated membrane lipids rather than by caspases. It shapes tumour suppression, ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration and the vulnerability of therapy-resistant cancer cells, which is why drugs that trigger it are of interest. The balance is set by supply and defence: the cystine/glutamate antiporter light chain SLC7A11 feeds cysteine into glutathione synthesis so that GPX4 can reduce lipid hydroperoxides, while AIFM2/FSP1 provides a parallel, glutathione-independent radical-trapping route. On the other side, ACSL4 loads polyunsaturated fatty acids into phospholipids and makes membranes oxidizable, and labile iron released via heme oxygenase or held by ferritin determines how much radical chemistry follows. NFE2L2 and its targets, together with autophagic turnover of ferritin, tune sensitivity, and NINJ1-dependent membrane rupture links the death to release of intracellular contents and inflammation.

When tissue is destroyed and the cells lost cannot regenerate, or when a fibrinous exudate is never cleared, the defect is filled in with connective tissue instead — the scarring response that underlies fibrosis of the heart, lung, liver and kidney. It preserves structural integrity at the cost of function, so persistent activation stiffens organs and drives progressive failure. TGFB1 is the dominant driver, converting fibroblasts into contractile matrix-producing myofibroblasts; ROCK1 and ROCK2 transmit the cytoskeletal contractility that accompanies this switch, TIMP1 blocks metalloproteinases so deposited collagen is not degraded, and hypoxia signalling through HIF1A together with IL1A-driven inflammation sustains the process. PPARG activity opposes it. Several microRNA families, including the miR-34 and miR-15/16 groups and miR-21-related regulators, tune fibroblast proliferation and survival, placing this repair programme under post-transcriptional control as well as cytokine control.

Calcineurin-mediated signaling converts a sustained rise in intracellular calcium into changes in gene expression, and is the route by which T lymphocytes commit to activation after antigen receptor engagement — the step blocked by cyclosporine and tacrolimus in transplant immunosuppression. Calcium entry, largely through store-operated ORAI1 channels, loads calmodulin, which activates the phosphatase built from a catalytic subunit (PPP3CA/CB/CC) and a regulatory subunit (PPP3R1/R2). The phosphatase dephosphorylates NFAT family transcription factors, unmasking their nuclear localisation signals so they enter the nucleus and drive cytokine genes such as TNF. Opposing kinases including GSK3B and DYRK2 rephosphorylate and export NFAT, while RCAN1/RCAN2 and the myozenin and calsarcin-like anchors tune or localise phosphatase activity. Beyond immunity, the same module directs cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy and fibre-type specification, bone and neuronal differentiation, and organogenesis, with chronic activation contributing to pathological cardiac remodelling.

Sustained rises in intracellular calcium are converted into changes in gene expression through calcineurin-mediated signaling, the route that licenses T cell activation, cardiac and skeletal muscle remodelling, and numerous developmental commitment decisions. Calmodulin loaded with calcium activates the phosphatase built from a catalytic subunit (PPP3CA, PPP3CB, PPP3CC) and a regulatory subunit (PPP3R1/R2); the phosphatase then removes phosphates from NFATC1-NFATC4, exposing nuclear localisation and allowing these transcription factors to enter the nucleus and drive target genes such as TNF. Opposing kinases including GSK3B and DYRK2 rephosphorylate NFAT to terminate the signal, while RCAN1 and RCAN2 and the sarcomeric myozenins restrain the phosphatase directly, and store-operated entry through ORAI1 supplies the calcium. This is the step blocked by cyclosporine and tacrolimus in transplant immunosuppression, and its chronic overactivity contributes to pathological cardiac hypertrophy.

Most centrioles are copied from a pre-existing mother centriole, but some cells build them from scratch. De novo centriole assembly matters most in multiciliated epithelia of the airway, ependyma and oviduct, where a single cell must mass-produce hundreds of basal bodies to template motile cilia; failure yields too few or malformed cilia and impairs mucociliary clearance and cerebrospinal fluid flow. The genes here mark the deuterosome route: DEUP1, a paralogue of the canonical centriolar protein CEP63, nucleates deuterosomes that serve as amplification platforms, recruiting CEP152 and the master kinase PLK4 to seed many procentrioles simultaneously. CCDC78 and the microRNA-hosting locus CDC20B act in the same amplification programme downstream of multiciliogenesis transcription factors. The pathway thus links cell cycle-independent centriole biogenesis to terminal differentiation of ciliated cells.

Membranes are deformed into narrow tubes wherever cargo must be sorted away from a bulk compartment or an organelle must be remodelled, and membrane tubulation is the shaping step that makes this possible. Outwardly directed tubules carry receptors out of endosomes for recycling or retrograde delivery to the Golgi, preventing their degradation in lysosomes; inward tubular invaginations feed endocytic uptake. BAR and sorting nexin proteins such as SNX1, SNX2, SNX5, SNX6 and endophilin sense and impose curvature on the bilayer, actin and coronin provide the pulling and scaffolding force, and the dynamin GTPase DNM2 severs the resulting tubule to release a carrier. The same geometry problem recurs inside mitochondria, where OPA1 shapes cristae and inner-membrane fusion. Loss of these activities disrupts receptor recycling, cell migration and organelle architecture, and is linked to neuropathy and optic atrophy.

Cargo leaving an endosome must first be concentrated into a tubular extension that can be pinched off as a recycling carrier, and endosome membrane tubulation is the deformation step that makes those carriers possible. Without it, receptors and transporters that should return to the plasma membrane or the Golgi are instead delivered to lysosomes and degraded, so surface levels of nutrient receptors, adhesion molecules and signalling receptors fall. Sorting nexins with BAR domains provide the curvature-sensing scaffold, SNX1 and SNX2 pairing with SNX5 or SNX6 to form dimers that read the membrane shape and select cargo; TMCC1 acts at endoplasmic reticulum contacts where tubules are constricted and severed. Actin dynamics and Rab-directed traffic contribute through a coronin family actin regulator and a MICAL-family effector, tying tubule formation to the cytoskeleton and to polarised recycling routes.

Chromosomal DNA must be held intact through replication and repair, and regulation of DNA stability covers the processes that set how vulnerable DNA is to breakage and damage. When these controls fail, cells accumulate strand breaks and stalled replication forks, triggering damage checkpoints, apoptosis, or genome rearrangements that seed tumour formation. The genes here act at the interface of replication stress and proteolysis: the aspartic protease-like DDI1 and DDI2 family members participate in ubiquitin-dependent protein turnover linked to replication-associated damage and to activation of stress-response transcription, and RTF2 governs the removal of protein obstacles from replication forks so that forks can restart. DDIAS is induced by DNA damage and supports survival of cells under replication stress, while CASP2 connects unresolved genomic insult to apoptotic elimination, tying DNA integrity surveillance to cell fate decisions.

Deforming a flat lipid bilayer into a curved one is the physical step behind vesicle budding, tubule formation and organelle fission, and the proteins that impose or sense curvature make membrane bending possible. Lipid-binding modules insert into or scaffold one leaflet so the bilayer adopts a defined curvature: PICALM uses a phosphoinositide-binding ANTH domain to help nucleate clathrin-coated pits during endocytosis and cargo uptake, while the ICA1 and ICA1L arfaptin-like proteins bind membranes of the secretory and endosomal system. Spatacsin and spastizin, encoded by SPG11 and ZFYVE26, act together in autophagic lysosome reformation, where tubules are pulled and severed from autolysosomes to regenerate lysosomes; loss of either causes hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum, linking curvature generation to the maintenance of long axons and neuronal membrane turnover.</description>

Skeletal muscle fibre differentiation is the route by which unspecialised myogenic precursors become contractile muscle: myoblasts exit the cycle, fuse into multinucleate myotubes, switch on sarcomeric and structural genes, and mature into fibres that generate force. Failure at these steps underlies congenital myopathies and muscular dystrophies. Several of the genes here build or decorate the glycan on alpha-dystroglycan that links the fibre to laminin in its basement membrane, so that loss of the glycosyltransferases and their partners produces dystroglycanopathy with weakness and, in severe forms, brain and eye malformation; a collagen VI chain contributes the matrix side of the same connection. Others act earlier or inside the fibre: transcriptional and RNA-binding regulators drive the myogenic programme and stabilise muscle transcripts, retinoic acid catabolism shapes patterning cues, and a kelch-family sarcomeric protein is needed for thin-filament assembly and normal fibre strength.

Centriole assembly builds the barrel-shaped microtubule structures that form the core of centrosomes and the basal bodies of cilia and flagella, so it sets the number of spindle poles a dividing cell has and determines whether a cell can grow a cilium at all. Duplication is licensed once per cycle: PLK4 kinase is recruited by scaffolds such as CEP152 and CEP192, and with STIL and the cartwheel protein SASS6 nucleates a single daughter procentriole, which is then elongated and capped through CPAP/CENPJ, CEP120, CEP135, POC5 and CCP110. A separate deuterosome-dependent route driven by MCIDAS, CDC20B and DEUP1 mass-produces basal bodies in multiciliated epithelia. Loss or misregulation of these factors causes centriole amplification and chromosome missegregation in cancer, and underlies primary microcephaly, Seckel syndrome and oral-facial-digital and other ciliopathies.

de novo centriole assembly involved in multi-ciliated epithelial cell differentiation is how cells of the airway, ependyma, and oviduct mass-produce the hundreds of basal bodies each motile cilium requires. Ordinary cycling cells make two centrioles by duplicating existing ones; multiciliated cells instead build most of theirs on deuterosomes, electron-dense spherical platforms that nucleate many procentrioles at once, independently of the parental centriole. DEUP1, a paralogue of CEP63, forms the deuterosome core and recruits CEP152, which in turn docks the kinase PLK4 to seed cartwheel assembly, while CCDC78 marks and supports the structure. The amplified centrioles migrate apically, dock at the plasma membrane, and template ciliary axonemes. Failure of this program produces reduced generation of multiple motile cilia, with impaired mucociliary clearance, chronic airway infection, hydrocephalus, and infertility.

Multiciliated cells of the airway, ependyma and oviduct need hundreds of motile cilia, far more than the two centrioles a dividing cell inherits, so during their differentiation centrioles are built de novo rather than by duplication of an existing one. The nucleating platform is the deuterosome, an electron-dense cytoplasmic structure from which many procentrioles grow in parallel; DEUP1 is its defining scaffold, a paralogue of the centrosomal CEP63 that pairs instead with CEP152 to recruit the master procentriole kinase PLK4, while CCDC78 marks and supports the amplification machinery. The output is the basal body pool that anchors each cilium and sets coordinated beating, which clears mucus from the airway, circulates cerebrospinal fluid and moves the ovum. Loss of this amplification step gives too few cilia, producing mucociliary clearance defects, hydrocephalus and infertility.

Host defence against bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites is assembled here as a single programme: the detection of foreign organisms and the effector responses that kill or contain them. It underlies innate immunity at epithelial surfaces and in phagocytes, and its failure produces recurrent infection, while its overactivity drives autoinflammatory and interferon-driven disease. Pattern recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like, RIG-I-like and C-type lectin families, together with cytosolic DNA sensing through cGAS and STING, converge on NF-kB and interferon regulatory factor signalling to induce type I, II and III interferons, chemokines and cytokines. Effectors include the complement cascade, defensins and other antimicrobial peptides, lysozyme, lactoferrin, neutrophil granule proteases and NADPH oxidase, inflammasome assembly with caspase-1 and gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis, guanylate-binding proteins, APOBEC3 deaminases, TRIM ubiquitin ligases, xenophagy, and natural killer cell recognition of stressed cells.

Host cells must recognise that a microbe is present before any defence can be mounted, and the detection of other organisms is the sensing step that converts foreign molecular patterns into intracellular signals. The genes here span the major surface and cytosolic sensor families: Toll-like receptors that bind bacterial lipopeptides and lipopolysaccharide, the C-type lectins CLEC7A and CLEC6A that read fungal beta-glucan and mannose structures, and the cytosolic NOD proteins that detect peptidoglycan fragments, along with NAIP and NLRC4, which recognise bacterial flagellin and secretion-system proteins and assemble an inflammasome. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins bind and in some cases degrade bacterial cell wall, while MHC class I and II molecules and CD1D present peptide and lipid antigens to T cells. Loss or variation in these sensors shifts susceptibility to infection and, as with NOD2 in Crohn's disease, to chronic inflammation.

Host cells recognise that another organism is present, converting molecular signatures of microbes into intracellular signals that launch defence. This detection of external biotic stimulus is the first step of innate immunity: without it, bacteria and fungi are not sensed, inflammation is not initiated, and adaptive responses are never instructed. Surface Toll-like receptors, partnered with the LPS-binding accessory proteins LBP and LY96, respond to lipopeptides, endotoxin and microbial DNA, while the C-type lectins CLEC7A and CLEC6A read fungal glucans and mannans. Cytosolic NOD1 and NOD2 detect peptidoglycan fragments, and NAIP with NLRC4 recognises bacterial flagellin and secretion-system components to nucleate an inflammasome. Peptidoglycan recognition proteins act as secreted, directly bactericidal sensors, and antigen-presenting molecules including classical HLA class I, HLA-DRB1 and lipid-presenting CD1D carry microbial material to T cells. Mutations in these sensors underlie inflammatory bowel disease and susceptibility to chronic infection.

Infected cells detect viral nucleic acid and switch into an antiviral state, and this response is the first line of host defence before adaptive immunity arrives. Sensors including the RNA helicase IFIH1 and the endosomal receptors TLR3 and TLR7 signal through kinase and transcription factor modules such as IKBKE, IRF3 and NF-κB to induce type I, type II and type III interferons, which act back on IFNAR, IFNGR and IFNLR receptor complexes to drive interferon-stimulated effectors like OAS1, ADAR and IFI6. Chemokines CXCL10 and CCL5 recruit leukocytes, inflammasome components and gasdermin E can commit infected cells to inflammatory death, and several microRNAs tune the output so it resolves. Too little of this response permits uncontrolled viral replication; too much underlies interferonopathies and cytokine-driven tissue damage during severe infection.

Observational learning is the acquisition of behaviour by watching others rather than by direct trial and error, a capacity that underlies social imitation, vocal learning and the transmission of learned skills within groups. The genes associated with it converge on synapse formation and the excitatory-inhibitory balance of cortical and striatal circuits: neurexins and SHANK3 build and scaffold the presynaptic and postsynaptic sides of glutamatergic contacts, CNTNAP2 organises axonal domains and neuronal adhesion, and FOXP2 is a transcription factor governing corticostriatal circuits required for learned vocalisation. Others act more broadly on neuronal growth and signalling, including the RAS regulator neurofibromin and huntingtin. Disruption of these components produces autism spectrum disorders, specific language impairment, learning disability and neurodegenerative decline, in which imitation and social learning are among the first abilities lost, linking this behaviour to synaptic plasticity and cognition generally.

Learned vocalization is the capacity to acquire and refine vocal output by imitation and auditory feedback rather than producing it innately, the basis of human speech acquisition and of song learning in songbirds. It depends on cortico-striatal and cortico-cerebellar circuits that link auditory perception to motor sequencing of the larynx and articulators, and on the synaptic plasticity that lets those circuits be tuned during a sensitive developmental period. FOXP2 is the transcription factor whose disruption causes an inherited speech and language disorder with orofacial apraxia, and it regulates CNTNAP2, a neurexin-family membrane protein tied to language delay in autism. Other members encode synaptic organizers and scaffolds — neurexins and SHANK3 — whose loss produces autism spectrum and Phelan-McDermid phenotypes in which speech is absent or severely limited; huntingtin loss likewise degrades vocal motor control. The theme is transcriptional and synaptic specification of speech-capable circuitry.

cell-cell adhesion covers the molecules by which one cell physically binds another, and the intracellular machinery that turns those contacts into signals. It is what allows epithelia to form continuous sheets with sealed barriers, neurons to select and stabilise synaptic partners, and immune cells to recognise and engage each other; loss of it underlies tissue disorganisation, barrier failure, blistering skin disease, and the invasive spread of carcinoma cells. The genes span the principal adhesion families: classical and protocadherins, desmosomal cadherins and plakins, claudins and tight-junction scaffolds, integrins, nectins, selectins and their glycan ligands, and the immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors including MHC molecules and costimulatory pairs such as CD28-CD80/86. Cytoplasmic partners including catenins, talin, vinculin and actin link junctions to the cytoskeleton, while Src-family and receptor phosphatases, Rho GTPases and transcriptional regulators couple adhesion to proliferation, polarity, migration and lymphocyte activation.

Cell-cell adhesion covers the molecular attachments by which one cell binds another, holding tissues together and letting cells recognise their neighbours. It underlies epithelial sheet integrity, endothelial barrier function, synapse formation, and the transient contacts immune cells make when a lymphocyte scans an antigen-presenting cell. The machinery falls into recognisable families: classical and non-classical cadherins with their catenin and plakophilin adaptors at adherens junctions and desmosomes, claudins and junctional adhesion molecules with ZO scaffolds at tight junctions, clustered protocadherins and neurexin-neuroligin pairs giving neurons individual identity, and immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors, selectins, integrins and their ligands such as ICAM1, VCAM1 and nectins mediating leukocyte arrest and costimulation. Adhesive engagement is coupled through actin, talin, vinculin and Src-family kinases to signalling that tunes proliferation, polarity and migration. Loss of these contacts drives epithelial dedifferentiation, invasion, blistering skin disease and barrier failure.

Cells acquire nutrients, ions, signalling molecules and particulate cargo from their surroundings, and import into cell covers both routes by which that happens: carrier- and channel-mediated transport across the plasma membrane, and engulfment by endocytosis or phagocytosis. The transporter side is dominated by solute carrier families and pumps handling amino acids, sugars, metals, neurotransmitters, phosphate and drugs, together with potassium, calcium, sodium and chloride channels that set membrane potential and ion gradients. The vesicular side runs through clathrin coats and their adaptors, dynamins, caveolins, BAR-domain and actin regulators, and Rab GTPases such as RAB5A and RAB7A that direct cargo into early and late endosomes. Receptors including the transferrin receptor, LDL receptor family members, scavenger and lectin receptors, and Fc and complement receptors select what is taken up, supporting iron and lipoprotein handling, phagocytosis of pathogens and dead cells, synaptic vesicle recycling, and downregulation of activated signalling receptors.

Serotonin acts on the nervous system and periphery almost entirely through G protein-coupled receptors, and this is the signalling that converts receptor occupancy into changes in neuronal excitability, mood, appetite, sleep, vascular tone and gut motility. The receptor families here split by the G protein they recruit: HTR1 subtypes and HTR5A couple through inhibitory Gi/Go subunits such as GNAI1 and GNAO1 to lower cyclic AMP and dampen firing, including the autoreceptor feedback that HTR1A and HTR1B exert on raphe neurons; HTR4, HTR6 and HTR7 raise cyclic AMP through adenylate cyclase; and the HTR2 subtypes act via GNAQ and phospholipase C beta to mobilise calcium. These receptors are the targets of antidepressants, triptans, antipsychotics and prokinetic drugs, and mis-signalling through them underlies migraine, valvulopathy from HTR2B agonism, and hallucinogen action. DRD4 appears as a co-regulated aminergic receptor sharing the same Gi-coupled machinery.

Chemical neurotransmission depends on synaptic vesicles being filled, docked, fused and then recovered for reuse, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how fast and how strongly that cycle runs. Tuning it determines synaptic strength, short-term plasticity and the reliability of transmission during sustained firing; when it fails, neurons cannot sustain release, and several of the genes involved are tied to neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disease, including C9orf72 in ALS/frontotemporal dementia, PSEN1 in Alzheimer disease, and DNAJC5 in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. Regulation acts at multiple steps: active zone scaffolding by Bassoon organises release sites, synapsin tethers the reserve vesicle pool, Rab3B and the cAMP sensor RAPGEF4 govern exocytosis and priming, and calcineurin and protein kinase A subunits couple calcium and cAMP signals to release probability and endocytic retrieval. Lipid signalling and cytoskeletal regulators contribute to vesicle trafficking and membrane remodelling.}

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane, and this pathway controls the delivery, retention and removal of those receptors at the postsynaptic specialization. It underlies activity-dependent plasticity such as long-term potentiation and depression, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. Trans-synaptic organizers and adhesion molecules including glypicans, dystroglycan and olfactomedin position receptors opposite release sites, while auxiliary subunits of the NETO family shape kainate and NMDA receptor trafficking and kinetics. Small GTPase signalling through HRAS and RAP1A with the MAP2K1 kinase, the ARF guanine nucleotide exchange factor IQSEC2, and retromer-associated VPS26B govern endocytic and exocytic cycling of receptors, and GABARAP links receptors to the cytoskeletal and autophagic machinery. The ADAM10 metalloprotease remodels synaptic adhesion by shedding ectodomains, adjusting the scaffold that anchors receptors.

Postsynaptic specialization assembly builds the receptive apparatus on the receiving side of a synapse — the dense scaffold beneath the postsynaptic membrane that clusters neurotransmitter receptors opposite a presynaptic release site. Getting this assembly right determines synapse number, excitatory–inhibitory balance and the capacity for plasticity; disruption of its components underlies autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia, as mutations in SHANK3 and NRXN family members illustrate. The genes describe trans-synaptic adhesion complexes — neurexins pairing with neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and LRFNs, and receptor phosphatases such as PTPRD and PTPRS — that nucleate scaffolds and recruit glutamate or GABA receptors. Secreted organizers including cerebellins, C1QL proteins, neuronal pentraxins and reelin specify which contacts mature, while ARHGEF9 anchors inhibitory sites and kinases such as ABL1 and PTK2B, with PTEN, tune the cytoskeletal remodelling that stabilizes the new specialization.

Synapses work only if the receiving side builds a matching apparatus directly beneath the presynaptic terminal, and assembly of the postsynaptic specialization is how that scaffold, receptor and adhesion machinery is brought together and locked in place. It sets the strength and identity of each contact — excitatory versus inhibitory, glutamatergic versus GABAergic — and its disruption underlies intellectual disability, autism spectrum conditions and cerebellar ataxia. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs do much of the recognition work: neurexins engaging neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and leucine-rich partners, with C1QL and cerebellin proteins bridging to receptors such as the delta-2 glutamate receptor. Receptor-type phosphatases, kinases including ABL1 and PTK2B, Rho-family regulators, and SHANK3 and CASKIN scaffolds then organise the cytoplasmic density, anchoring receptors, cytoskeleton and downstream signalling. The same machinery supports activity-dependent remodelling of existing synapses, not only their initial formation.

Chemical neurotransmission requires that a transmitter be concentrated inside synaptic vesicles before release, and this loading step sets how much signal each vesicle carries when it fuses. The transporters here do that work, riding on the proton electrochemical gradient built by the vesicular ATPase: glutamate uptake by the SLC17 family members defines excitatory terminals, SLC32A1 loads GABA and glycine into inhibitory ones, and the SLC18 vesicular monoamine transporters package dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin and histamine. Because a neuron's transporter complement largely determines which transmitter it releases, these genes are used as markers of excitatory, inhibitory and monoaminergic identity. Loss of loading capacity silences transmission and leaves cytosolic transmitter vulnerable to degradation; monoamine transport is also the target of reserpine and the route by which amphetamines and some neurotoxins redistribute vesicular stores.

Cytosolic calcium is kept extremely low at rest, so opening a route for calcium entry across the plasma membrane is one of the fastest ways a cell converts an external stimulus into an internal signal. This import underlies action potential-triggered neurotransmitter and hormone release, muscle contraction, sensory transduction, and dietary calcium absorption. Voltage-gated channels built on CACNA1 pore subunits with auxiliary subunits such as CACNA2D1 carry depolarization-driven entry, while TRP channels, including the heat- and capsaicin-sensitive TRPV1 and the epithelial calcium-selective TRPV5 and TRPV6, respond to temperature, chemical and osmotic cues; ATP-gated P2X receptors add purinergic entry. Sodium/calcium and sodium/potassium-calcium exchangers and the plasma membrane calcium pump ATP2B4 set the opposing extrusion, and downstream calcineurin subunits decode the resulting transients. Scaffolds and kinases such as AKAP5 and FYN tune channel localization and gating, and mutations in these channels cause ataxias, epilepsies, arrhythmias and retinal or muscle disease.

Cells that burn sugar must first bring it in, and this pathway covers the carrier proteins that move glucose, fructose and related carbohydrates from the extracellular space across the plasma membrane into the cytosol. Two strategies are represented: facilitative carriers of the GLUT family, including the ubiquitous GLUT1 and the neuronal GLUT3, which let sugar flow down its concentration gradient, and sodium-coupled symporters such as SGLT1 and SGLT2, which use the inward sodium gradient to accumulate glucose against a gradient in intestinal absorption and renal reabsorption. GLUT5 is the main fructose entry route. The consequences of failure are specific and clinical: impaired glucose delivery across the blood-brain barrier causes an infantile epileptic encephalopathy, intestinal transporter defects cause glucose-galactose malabsorption, and pharmacological blockade of renal reabsorption is a mainstay of diabetes treatment. Import sets the ceiling on glycolysis and on whole-body glucose handling.

Cells acquire iron from the extracellular space through dedicated transport and reductase steps at the plasma membrane, and this uptake sets the intracellular iron supply used for haem synthesis, iron-sulfur cluster assembly and the many oxidoreductases that depend on them. Too little uptake starves mitochondrial respiration and erythropoiesis; too much leaves labile iron that drives Fenton chemistry and lipid peroxidation. The genes here span the steps that make import possible and the signals that tune it: a metal-ion transporter of the SLC39 family, a ferric reductase of the STEAP family that reduces Fe(III) so it can cross the membrane, and lipocalin-2, which captures siderophore-bound iron for delivery. Inflammatory and hypoxic cues, including interferon-gamma and a hypoxia-induced microRNA, adjust this uptake, linking cellular iron entry to host defence, where iron is withheld from pathogens, and to oxygen sensing.

Uptake of L-glutamate from the extracellular space into the cytosol keeps synaptic and interstitial glutamate low, which is what prevents the excitotoxic overstimulation of NMDA and other glutamate receptors seen in stroke, epilepsy and neurodegeneration, while also recycling transmitter and supplying carbon and nitrogen for metabolism. The work is done chiefly by high-affinity sodium-dependent excitatory amino acid transporters, with SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 carrying the bulk of astrocytic clearance and SLC1A1 and SLC1A6 acting in neurons; SLC7A11 instead exchanges extracellular cystine for intracellular glutamate and so links this transport to glutathione synthesis and oxidative stress defence. Efficient import depends on the sodium and potassium gradients set by Na+/K+-ATPase and on potassium channel-mediated buffering, and on trafficking and scaffolding partners that position transporters at the membrane. Inflammatory and receptor signalling inputs modulate transporter abundance and activity.

Sodium entry into the cytosol across the plasma membrane sets the electrochemical gradient that cells spend most of their ATP maintaining, and it powers secondary transport of glucose, phosphate, vitamins, neurotransmitters and protons while shaping excitability and body salt and water balance. The routes gathered here include epithelial sodium channels of the kidney collecting duct and airway, whose subunits are downregulated by the ubiquitin ligase NEDD4L and whose mutation causes Liddle syndrome and pseudohypoaldosteronism; sodium-coupled cotransporters for glucose, phosphate and biotin; the NKCC-type chloride cotransporter regulated by the kinase STK39; sodium/proton exchangers that govern intracellular pH and cell volume; the sodium/calcium exchanger; and hyperpolarization-activated HCN channels that generate pacemaker current in heart and neurons. Loss of individual members produces renal salt wasting, glucosuria, hypophosphatemia, arrhythmia and neurological disease, and these carriers are targets of diuretics and glucose-lowering drugs.

Tissues hold their size steady by balancing stem and progenitor self-renewal against differentiation and loss, and maintenance of cell number is the collective name for the programmes that keep a given pool at the right size. Where it fails, stem cell compartments are exhausted or overgrow, giving hypoplastic tissues, impaired regeneration, or tumour-initiating expansion. The genes here are dominated by pluripotency and self-renewal control: the core transcription factors POU5F1, SOX2, NANOG and PRDM14 with LIF-STAT3 and NODAL inputs; Wnt/beta-catenin, Notch-Delta-Jagged, BMP, Hippo-YAP and Hedgehog signalling that set the balance between renewal and commitment; chromatin machinery including SWI/SNF subunits, Polycomb EZH2, Sin3-HDAC complexes and PAF1; and post-transcriptional regulators such as LIN28A, METTL3/METTL14 m6A writers and CCR4-NOT that control how long renewal transcripts persist. Together they specify progenitor identity and license divisions that replace cells without depleting the pool.

Acyl groups added to proteins and other macromolecules are reversible marks, and this pathway covers the enzymes that take them off again — deacetylation of histones and of thousands of non-histone substrates, removal of palmitate and other thioester-linked lipids from membrane-anchored proteins, desuccinylation, demalonylation and depalmitoleoylation. Through it, chromatin can be re-compacted and transcription silenced, metabolic enzymes switched between states, and signalling proteins released from the membrane. Classical zinc-dependent deacetylases such as HDAC3, HDAC6 and HDAC7 act within larger corepressor and coactivator assemblies, while the NAD+-dependent sirtuins couple removal of acyl marks to cellular energy status, linking nutrient availability to gene expression, mitochondrial metabolism and genome stability. Serine hydrolases including the ABHD17 family, acyl-protein thioesterases and palmitoyl-protein thioesterases reverse S-acylation and control protein trafficking; loss of PPT1 causes neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis.

Palmitoylation is reversible, and depalmitoylation is the step that makes it a switch rather than a permanent modification. By hydrolysing thioester-linked palmitate from cysteine residues, these enzymes control how long a protein stays anchored in a membrane, how it partitions between the plasma membrane and internal compartments, and how quickly signalling complexes turn over; substrates include Ras family GTPases, synaptic scaffolds such as PSD-95, and many neuronal proteins. The serine hydrolases here act in distinct places: cytosolic and membrane-associated thioesterases including LYPLA1/LYPLA2 and the ABHD17 family work on the cytoplasmic face, while PPT1 and PPT2 degrade lipid-modified proteins inside the lysosome. Loss of that lysosomal activity causes infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, with storage material accumulation and neurodegeneration, and defects in related hydrolases give further neurological disease, tying this chemistry to protein turnover and neuronal membrane homeostasis.

Cardiac output can be raised by increasing how forcefully each ventricular beat contracts, and this positive inotropic control is how the heart matches its output to demand during exercise or sympathetic stimulation. The genes involved sit at the points where calcium delivery to the sarcomere is set: the ryanodine receptor releases stored calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to trigger contraction, the sodium-calcium exchanger and the sodium-proton exchanger shape the sodium and pH gradients that determine how much calcium is retained beat to beat, and the regulatory light chain MYL2 tunes the sensitivity of the myosin motor itself. Neuronal nitric oxide synthase provides local nitric oxide signalling that modulates this calcium handling. Loss of control in either direction matters clinically: impaired inotropy contributes to heart failure, while excess calcium release predisposes to arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy.

Cells depend on bringing nutrients, ions and metabolites in from outside, and this pathway covers the machinery that moves substances across the plasma membrane into the cytosol. It underlies glucose and amino acid uptake, epithelial absorption of sugars, peptides, phosphate and folate in gut and kidney, calcium and sodium entry that drives excitability, neurotransmitter clearance by glial and neuronal carriers, and uptake of zinc, iron and fatty acids. Members include facilitative and sodium-coupled solute carriers, ion channels such as voltage-gated calcium channels, inward-rectifier potassium channels and TRP channels, epithelial sodium channels, cation-chloride cotransporters, sodium/proton and sodium/calcium exchangers, and the sodium pump subunits whose electrochemical gradient powers secondary active transport, together with regulators including kinases, calcineurin subunits and PDZ scaffolds. Loss of individual transporters causes aminoacidurias, renal salt-wasting syndromes, epilepsy, deafness and metal overload disorders.

Cell aggregation is the step in which dispersed cells cluster and stick together to form a condensed mass, the starting point for tissue formation. In vertebrate development its clearest expression is mesenchymal condensation, where loosely packed cells pack tightly and commit to becoming cartilage; without it, skeletal elements fail to form at the right size, shape and position. The genes here reflect that bias: SOX9 with its partners SOX5 and SOX6 drives the chondrocyte programme and switches on collagen II and XI, while BMP and TGF-beta family signals, FGFs and WNT7A set where and when condensations appear, and matrix proteins such as MGP and CCN2 modulate the surrounding environment. Related adhesive clustering occurs among suspended cells, including blood and epithelial cells with secreted mucins and defence proteins. Disrupted condensation underlies chondrodysplasias and other skeletal malformations.

Bone cell development covers the maturation of committed progenitors into the functional cells that build and resorb the skeleton — osteoblasts that deposit mineralized matrix and multinucleated osteoclasts that dissolve it. Getting the balance right determines bone mass, tooth eruption, marrow cavity formation and the capacity to repair fracture; failure gives osteopetrosis when resorption is deficient or osteoporotic bone loss when it runs unchecked. The genes here span the osteoclast side heavily: RANKL (TNFSF11) drives commitment of myeloid precursors, TYROBP and SIGLEC15 supply immunoreceptor-based costimulatory signalling, SRC and LRRK1 are required for the sealing zone and ruffled border, and vacuolar ATPase-associated ATP6AP1 supports acidification of the resorption lacuna. Others act on matrix and patterning, including the kinase FAM20C that phosphorylates secreted matrix proteins, fibrillin-1, and NOTCH2. The pathway therefore links immune-type signalling machinery to skeletal remodelling and calcium homeostasis.

Cells constantly encounter reactive oxygen species, electrophiles, heavy metals and xenobiotics, and detoxification is the collective machinery that neutralises or exports them before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA. Without it, oxidative injury drives ageing, inflammation, haemolysis, drug toxicity and metal-overload disease. Three strategies are visible here. Antioxidant enzymes reduce peroxides and superoxide: catalase, the superoxide dismutases, glutathione peroxidases, peroxiredoxins and the thioredoxin and glutathione reductase systems that keep them recycled. Conjugating and reducing enzymes derivatise electrophiles for disposal, including glutathione S-transferases, UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, NQO1, aldo-keto and aldehyde dehydrogenases.
