Efflux pumps and solute carriers then expel the products, while metallothioneins and zinc, copper and manganese transporters sequester or extrude metals. NFE2L2 coordinates much of this response transcriptionally, and sestrins tie it to stress and nutrient signalling, making the programme inducible rather than merely constitutive.

Interleukin-7 is the survival cytokine of the lymphoid lineage, and the cellular responses it triggers determine whether T and B cell progenitors persist, proliferate and populate the periphery. Loss of the signal causes severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T cells, while chronic overactivity drives lymphoblastic leukaemia; the same receptor also sets the size of the naive and memory T cell pool. Ligand engages a receptor pair of the IL7 alpha chain with the shared common gamma chain, which brings JAK1 and JAK3 together to phosphorylate the receptor tail and recruit STAT5A, driving transcription of anti-apoptotic and cell cycle genes; STAT1, the adaptor CRKL and the kinase BTK contribute further branches. The related cytokine TSLP uses the same alpha chain with a distinct partner. Chaperone and redox proteins here reflect receptor folding and trafficking rather than signalling itself.

Inorganic ion homeostasis is the collective machinery that holds intracellular and systemic levels of calcium, iron, zinc, copper, sodium, potassium, magnesium and phosphate within narrow limits, so that membrane excitability, enzyme cofactor supply and mineral balance remain workable. Its failure produces hemochromatosis and anaemia, Wilson and Menkes disease, rickets and nephrolithiasis, cardiac arrhythmia and neurodegeneration. Mechanistically it spans pumps and exchangers (Na+/K+- and Ca2+-ATPases, NCX and NHE families), release and store-operated calcium channels (IP3 receptors, ryanodine receptors, STIM/Orai and TRP channels) with buffers such as calsequestrin and calreticulin, mitochondrial uptake through the MCU-MICU complex, and metal-specific transporters of the SLC11, SLC30, SLC31 and SLC39 families together with ferritin, transferrin receptors and metallothioneins. Hormonal control by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, FGF23-Klotho and the hepcidin-ferroportin axis links cellular handling to whole-body mineral and iron balance.

Cells and whole organisms hold the concentrations of calcium, iron, copper, zinc, sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium and phosphate within narrow limits, and inorganic ion homeostasis is the collection of transporters, channels, pumps, buffers and hormonal circuits that achieves it. Loss of this control underlies cardiac arrhythmia, seizures, hypertension, iron overload and anaemia, Wilson and Menkes disease, and defective bone mineralization. Plasma-membrane and organellar ATPases, exchangers and solute carriers move ions across membranes; ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors release calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum while sarcoplasmic pumps and a mitochondrial uniporter complex clear it; ferritin, metallothioneins and calsequestrin buffer stored metal. Systemic set-points are imposed by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D signalling, FGF23-klotho and hepcidin-ferroportin regulation of intestinal iron export.

skin epidermis development builds the stratified, keratinized barrier that separates the body from its environment, together with the hair follicles and other appendages that arise from it. Its output is a self-renewing epithelium in which basal progenitors, held in that state by TP63 and Notch-Wnt inputs, commit to terminal differentiation and produce the cornified envelope of filaggrin, keratins, transglutaminases and lipid-processing enzymes such as ABCA12 and the lipoxygenases ALOX12B and ALOXE3. Loss of these steps causes ichthyoses, Netherton syndrome and atopic barrier defects with water loss and inflammation. Appendage patterning depends on ectodysplasin-EDAR, hedgehog, FGF and WNT10A signalling, with SOX9 and LGR5 marking follicular stem cell compartments and HOXC13 and DLX3 driving hair keratin expression. The pathway therefore links epithelial stem cell fate, barrier lipid metabolism and mesenchymal-epithelial signalling during skin morphogenesis and repair.

Skin epidermis development covers the formation and maturation of the stratified, keratinized surface of the skin, together with the hair follicles and other appendages that arise from it. Its end product is the barrier that retains water, excludes microbes and withstands mechanical stress; when it fails, the result is ichthyosis, ectodermal dysplasia, defective hair, or atopic disease driven by barrier leak. Surface ectoderm is first committed and held in a basal progenitor state by TP63 and associated transcription factors, then instructed to stratify and differentiate through Notch, Wnt, hedgehog and TGF-beta/BMP signalling, with EDA-EDAR and FGF cues patterning appendage placodes. Terminal differentiation builds the cornified envelope from filaggrin and keratins cross-linked by transglutaminase, while lipid-processing and lipid-transport enzymes such as ABCA12, ALOX12B and ALOXE3 supply the intercellular lipid seal, and protease inhibitors like SPINK5 restrain desquamation.

Response to mitochondrial depolarisation is the cell's reaction to loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, the signal that an organelle has failed and must be cleared or compensated for. This surveillance keeps damaged mitochondria from leaking reactive oxygen species and pro-apoptotic factors, and its impairment underlies the accumulation of defective mitochondria seen in Parkinson's disease and in ageing tissues. Depolarisation recruits autophagy initiation machinery to the affected organelle: the Beclin-1 complex with ATG14 and the ATG13-containing initiation complex nucleate an isolation membrane, AMBRA1 links regulation of that complex to the mitochondrial surface, and the receptor SQSTM1 bridges ubiquitinated cargo to the forming autophagosome, delivering the organelle for lysosomal degradation. GPS2 adds a retrograde arm, relaying mitochondrial status to nuclear transcription. The pathway thus couples organelle quality control to autophagy and to mitochondrial biogenesis programmes.

When a mitochondrion loses its membrane potential, the cell must recognise the damaged organelle and either repair or dispose of it, and the response to mitochondrial depolarisation is that decision point. Its principal output is selective autophagy of mitochondria: loss of potential marks an organelle for engulfment, and the autophagy initiation machinery represented here — the class III PI3-kinase complex with BECN1, ATG14 and AMBRA1, the ULK1-associated subunit ATG13, and the ubiquitin-binding cargo receptor SQSTM1 — nucleates and targets the nascent autophagosome. GPS2 links the depolarisation signal to nuclear transcriptional adjustment, so the response is not purely degradative but also retrograde. Keeping this quality-control arm intact limits accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, reactive oxygen production and apoptotic priming; its failure is a recurring theme in neurodegeneration, particularly in dopaminergic neurons, and in age-related decline of mitochondrial fitness.

Xenophagy is the arm of selective autophagy that captures intracellular bacteria, viruses and their damaged vacuoles and delivers them to lysosomes for destruction, giving cells an innate defence against pathogens that escape phagocytic killing. It matters because failure of this route allows intracellular survival of organisms such as Salmonella and mycobacteria; variants in ATG16L1 and IRGM predispose to Crohn's disease, and OPTN and TBK1 mutations link the same ubiquitin-directed cargo recognition to neurodegeneration. Damaged pathogen-containing membranes expose host glycans that are read by galectins such as LGALS8, while ubiquitin ligases including LRSAM1, RNF213 and a cullin-RING complex built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1 coat the target. Autophagy receptors CALCOCO2 and OPTN, phosphorylated by TBK1, bridge that ubiquitin coat to nascent autophagosomes. Bacterial sensing through NOD1 and RIPK2 couples pattern recognition and inflammatory signalling to the same degradative response.

Kidney function is continuously tuned by hormones and local mediators that set glomerular filtration, renal blood flow and tubular handling of salt and water, and this regulatory layer is what keeps blood pressure and extracellular fluid volume within range. Its failure underlies hypertension, oedema and proteinuric kidney disease. The genes here span both arms of that control: angiotensinogen and its type 1 receptor drive vasoconstriction and sodium retention, while natriuretic peptide signalling through the B-type peptide and its guanylyl cyclase receptor, together with the protease that cleaves pro-peptide to active hormone, opposes them. Endothelin, adenosine and dopamine receptor signalling adjust afferent and efferent arteriolar tone and tubuloglomerular feedback, and podocyte and slit-diaphragm associated proteins such as PTPRO and the NHERF1 scaffold couple these signals to filtration barrier integrity and transporter positioning. Stanniocalcin and adiponectin add endocrine modulation of calcium-phosphate handling and podocyte metabolism.

Chemical synapses stop signalling largely by clearing transmitter from the extracellular space, and neurotransmitter reuptake is the transport step that pulls dopamine, serotonin, noradrenaline, GABA and glutamate back into neurons or surrounding glia. It sets the amplitude and duration of synaptic signals, replenishes releasable transmitter stores, and is the target of most antidepressants and psychostimulants. Sodium-dependent carriers of the SLC6 family handle monoamines and GABA, the astrocytic transporter SLC1A2 removes the bulk of synaptic glutamate, and vesicular transporters of the SLC18 group repackage the recovered amine for release, with organic cation carriers providing lower-affinity uptake. Astrocytic potassium channels and the sodium pump maintain the ionic gradients the transporters depend on, while dopamine receptors, alpha-synuclein, parkin and DJ-1 modulate transporter trafficking and activity. Loss of clearance produces excitotoxicity, and dysregulated dopamine handling links this biology to parkinsonism and addiction.

Faithful partitioning of nuclear chromosomes to daughter nuclei is what keeps ploidy constant across cell generations; when it fails, cells become aneuploid, a state underlying tumour progression, miscarriage and trisomy syndromes. The genes here cover the whole sequence: condensin and topoisomerase II compact and disentangle chromatids, cohesin rings with their regulators hold sisters together until separase cleaves them, and centromeric histone variants build the kinetochore platform onto which the NDC80, MIS12 and SKA complexes attach spindle microtubules. Aurora kinases, PLK1 and CDK1 phosphorylate these interfaces to correct erroneous attachments, while the spindle assembly checkpoint holds the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until every kinetochore is engaged. Kinesins and dynein generate the forces that move chromosomes poleward. A large meiotic component, including synaptonemal complex proteins, SPO11 and crossover machinery, handles the specialised reductional division that produces gametes.

Synapses leak transmitter even when no action potential arrives, and this spontaneous release produces the miniature postsynaptic currents that keep receptors engaged and postsynaptic cells trophically supported between bouts of evoked signalling. It sets a baseline that tunes local protein synthesis, synapse maintenance and homeostatic scaling, and its measurement is the standard readout of presynaptic function. The genes here span the release machinery itself: a SNARE component of the fusion complex, the principal fast calcium sensor synaptotagmin 1 and the double C2 proteins DOC2A and DOC2B that support calcium-dependent release at resting calcium levels, together with active-zone and vesicle-associated regulators such as RIMS2 and rabphilin. Also represented are modulators acting on synaptic ion handling and adhesion, along with amyloid precursor protein and parkin, linking tonic release rates to neurodegenerative disease.

Excitatory synaptic transmission is graded, and the processes that modulate the excitatory postsynaptic potential set how strongly a depolarizing input pushes a neuron toward threshold. This tuning underlies long-term potentiation, learning and memory, and the balance of excitation that keeps circuits from seizing; its disruption recurs in autism, intellectual disability and neurodegeneration. Control is exerted at several points: ionotropic glutamate receptors of the AMPA, NMDA and kainate families (GRIA1, GRIN1 with its GRIN2 subunits, GRIK2 with its NETO1 auxiliary subunit) carry the current itself, while metabotropic GRM5 and G protein-coupled receptors bias it. Scaffolds such as DLG4, SHANK1 and SHANK3 organize receptors in the postsynaptic density, and trans-synaptic neurexin-neuroligin and reelin signalling align the release site with the receptive apparatus. Kinases, sodium-calcium exchangers and presynaptic release machinery adjust the response further, making this a convergence point for synaptic plasticity.

Inhibitory synapses hyperpolarise the postsynaptic membrane and raise the threshold for firing; this pathway covers the processes that tune the size, timing and frequency of those inhibitory postsynaptic potentials. Such modulation sets the balance between excitation and inhibition in cortical and hippocampal circuits, controls network rhythms, and when it fails contributes to epilepsy, anxiety states and altered pain processing. The genes involved act at several levels: NLGN2 is an adhesion molecule that specifies and organises inhibitory postsynaptic sites, RIMS1, RIMS2 and UNC13B operate in the active zone to prime vesicles and govern release probability from interneuron terminals, and ABAT degrades GABA, linking transmitter supply to inhibitory strength. Neuromodulatory and peptidergic receptors, including nicotinic CHRNA2, neurotensin and prepronociceptin signalling, adjust interneuron output in response to behavioural state.

Cells move proteins and protein-bearing cargo over long distances by loading them onto motor proteins that walk along microtubule tracks, and this directed transport is what allows a neuron to supply a synapse metres from its cell body or a cell to position organelles and signalling complexes where they are needed. Kinesin-1 heavy chains carry cargo toward microtubule plus ends, while HOOK proteins together with FHIP subunits form adaptor complexes that link vesicles and endosomes to motors and help specify which cargo is carried in which direction. Scaffolds and adaptors such as MAPK8IP3 and CLIP3 couple particular cargoes to motors, and chaperone-associated components including HSPB1 and BAG3 connect the system to protein quality control. Loss of this transport underlies axonal degeneration, and KIF5A mutations cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron disease.

intestinal lipid absorption is the route by which dietary fat, cholesterol and fat-soluble nutrients cross the enterocyte and enter the circulation, and it sets how much of a meal's lipid load the body actually acquires. Its efficiency determines plasma lipid levels and body fat accumulation, and its failure produces fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins. Luminal digestion by pancreatic lipase and cholesterol esterase releases fatty acids and sterols, which enter through transporters such as CD36 and NPC1L1; ABCG5/ABCG8 pump excess and plant sterols back into the lumen, setting the net absorbed fraction. Inside the cell, FABP2 and LPCAT3 direct fatty acids toward triglyceride and phospholipid synthesis, and APOA1, APOA2 and APOA4 with LIMA1 support chylomicron assembly and secretion. Bile acid synthesis genes and leptin signalling tune the process, linking gut absorption to systemic lipid and energy balance.

Dietary fat and cholesterol enter the body across the small intestinal epithelium, and intestinal lipid absorption is the set of steps that captures them from the lumen and hands them on as lipoprotein cargo. It sets how much of a meal's fat and sterol reaches the circulation, so it underlies energy intake, fat-soluble nutrient uptake, and plasma cholesterol levels; loss of its sterol-limiting components causes sitosterolemia, while blocking cholesterol uptake at the brush border is the basis of ezetimibe therapy. Pancreatic lipase and carboxyl ester lipase release fatty acids and sterols from dietary lipid, NPC1L1 and CD36 mediate uptake at the apical membrane, ABCG5/ABCG8 pump plant sterols back into the lumen, and cytosolic FABP2 with LPCAT3 and SOAT2 direct re-esterification toward chylomicron assembly with apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV. Bile acid composition and epithelial tight junction claudins tune the process.

Bone growth is the increase in bone size and mass that gives each skeletal element its final shape and length, and it is the process that sets adult stature and limb proportion. Most of the action occurs at the growth plate, where SOX9-dependent chondrocytes proliferate, hypertrophy, and are replaced by bone; COL27A1, MATN1 and COMP build the cartilage matrix, MMP13 remodels it, and DDR2 reads collagen as a signal. Growth factor input is decisive: FGFR3 restrains chondrocyte proliferation, while the CNP ligand NPPC acting through its guanylyl cyclase receptor NPR2 and cGMP-dependent kinase signalling promotes elongation, and TGF-beta and retinoic acid receptors tune differentiation. Leptin signalling links nutritional status to skeletal growth, and ciliary components such as IFT80 and EVC transduce hedgehog cues. Mutations here produce achondroplasia, acromesomelic dysplasia and other skeletal dysplasias with disproportionate short stature.

Cellular oxidant detoxification is the set of enzymatic defences that dispose of superoxide and hydrogen peroxide before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the redox tone of the cell, permits aerobic metabolism and controlled oxidant signalling, and its failure drives oxidative stress in neurodegeneration, atherosclerosis, ischaemic injury and ageing. Superoxide dismutases in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space convert superoxide to peroxide, which catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins then reduce; thioredoxin, thioredoxin reductases, glutathione reductase and sulfiredoxin regenerate the oxidised catalysts, and glutathione S-transferases conjugate reactive electrophiles. Selenoproteins and stress-inducible sestrins extend this capacity, while NRF2 coordinates transcription of the whole antioxidant programme, including NQO1. Heme proteins such as haemoglobin, myoglobin and cytoglobin, plus scavengers like haptoglobin and ceruloplasmin, limit iron- and heme-driven radical chemistry, linking the pathway to oxygen transport and inflammation.

Aerobic metabolism constantly leaks superoxide and hydrogen peroxide, and cellular oxidant detoxification is the set of reactions that removes them before they oxidise lipids, proteins and DNA. It sets the redox tone in which signalling, proliferation and inflammation occur; its failure produces oxidative damage linked to neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury, ageing and tumour promotion. Superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to peroxide in cytosol, mitochondria and extracellular space, and catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins then reduce peroxides, with thioredoxin, thioredoxin reductases, glutathione reductase and sulfiredoxin regenerating the oxidised catalysts. Glutathione transferases conjugate reactive electrophiles, several selenoproteins support thiol chemistry, and NFE2L2 drives transcription of many of these defences. Haem and metal-binding proteins sequester the iron and copper that would otherwise catalyse radical formation, while peroxidases such as MPO and TPO use peroxide productively in host defence and hormone synthesis.

Once an excitable membrane fires, the depolarization spreads to neighbouring membrane and regenerates itself; action potential propagation is that self-sustaining spread along axons and muscle fibres, and it is what allows a signal generated at one point to reach a synapse or a contractile apparatus metres away. Voltage-gated sodium channels and their accessory subunits carry the regenerative inward current, chloride and calcium channels plus the sodium-potassium pump set resting potential and restore ionic gradients, and cell-adhesion and paranodal proteins such as CNTNAP1 and NRCAM organize the axon-glia junctions that cluster channels at nodes for rapid saltatory conduction. Neurotrophin receptors link this excitable machinery to trophic support of the neurons that use it. Mutations here produce epilepsies, pain and insensitivity syndromes, myotonia and hemiplegic migraine, reflecting conduction that is either too easily triggered or fails outright.

Delivering newly made and recycled cargo to the cell surface is how a cell controls what its plasma membrane displays: nutrient transporters, adhesion receptors, ion channels and secreted material. This vesicle-mediated transport to the plasma membrane sustains polarity in epithelia, insulin-responsive glucose transporter movement, neurotransmitter and hormone release, and cytokinesis, and its failure underlies ciliopathies, neurodegeneration and copper-handling and lysosomal storage disorders. Rab GTPases such as RAB8A, RAB10, RAB11A and RAB35, with their DENND-family activators and effectors, mark recycling and post-Golgi carriers; retromer and retriever with the WASH complex, sorting nexins and the CCC/COMMD machinery rescue receptors from endosomes rather than letting them degrade; EHD proteins and MICAL-like adaptors shape tubular intermediates. Tethering by the exocyst and GARP complexes then positions vesicles for SNARE-driven fusion via syntaxins, VAMPs and NSF, completing exocytosis.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane, and this pathway covers the vesicular delivery step that puts them there. Newly synthesized and recycled receptors are carried through recycling endosomes to the cell surface, so the process sets the gain of excitatory transmission and underlies the receptor insertion that accompanies long-term potentiation; when it fails, synapses cannot be strengthened and dendritic spine composition drifts. Small GTPases of the recycling and exocytic routes, RAB11A and RAB8A, direct the carriers, a syntaxin supplies the fusion machinery, and scaffolds such as GRIP1 and GRIP2 with their associated GRIPAP1 link AMPA-type glutamate receptors to motors and tethering complexes. Retromer, via VPS35, and the polarity scaffold SCRIB sort cargo away from degradation, tying receptor trafficking to endosomal sorting and neuronal polarity generally.

maintenance of postsynaptic specialization structure keeps the receptor-bearing side of a synapse assembled once it has formed, preserving the arrangement of scaffolds, adhesion molecules and receptor anchors that hold neurotransmitter receptors opposite the release site. Synapses are not static, so continuous maintenance determines whether a circuit retains its wiring and its capacity for stable plasticity; loss of these proteins produces spine and postsynaptic density abnormalities and is a recurring cause of intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. The genes span the layers of that structure: PDZ scaffolds such as SHANK1, DLG1 and TANC2 that organize glutamate receptor complexes, RAPSN which clusters acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, integrin-based adhesion to the synaptic cleft, and small GTPase regulators including ARF6, GIT1, OPHN1 and SYNGAP1 that restrain actin and membrane turnover beneath the membrane.

Synapses must not only be built but held in place, and this process keeps the postsynaptic specialization intact once it has formed, preserving the size, composition and protein arrangement of the postsynaptic density over time. Stable receptor anchoring underlies the persistence of synaptic strength that long-term memory depends on, and the genes involved are recurrently mutated in intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. Scaffolding proteins such as SHANK1, DLG1, TANC2 and the liprin PPFIA2 organize receptors and signalling enzymes beneath the membrane, while SYNGAP1 restrains Ras-family signalling that would otherwise drive premature spine maturation, and ARF6, GIT1 and OPHN1 link the specialization to membrane traffic and actin remodelling. At the neuromuscular junction the same requirement is met by RAPSN, which clusters acetylcholine receptors; its loss causes congenital myasthenia.

Developing and adult brains make more synapses than they keep, and synapse pruning is the controlled elimination of the excess so that circuits are refined to their mature wiring. Weak or inappropriate connections are tagged and removed, and when the process fails or runs too far the consequences are behavioural: excess pruning strips synapses in neurodegeneration, while insufficient pruning leaves immature, hyperconnected circuits implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. Much of the mechanism is borrowed immunity. Complement components C1q and C3 opsonise synapses for recognition by microglial receptors including complement receptor 3, while fractalkine signalling from neurons to CX3CR1 on microglia and TREM2-dependent recognition license engulfment. Neuronal cues contribute the selection step, with adhesion GPCRs, Eph and plexin receptors, planar polarity and Wnt modulators marking which contacts are retained, and axonal degeneration machinery such as SARM1 contributing local breakdown.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane, and internalization is the arm that removes them. Clathrin-mediated uptake at the endocytic zone beside the postsynaptic density withdraws AMPA-type glutamate receptors and other receptors into vesicles, driving long-term depression, homeostatic scaling and the forgetting or reversal of potentiated states; loss of this control leaves synapses unable to weaken, and several members are mutated in intellectual disability and autism. The AP-2 adaptor complex and accessory proteins such as EPS15, HIP1 and NUMB select cargo and bend membrane, while ARC couples neuronal activity to receptor removal, calcineurin's regulatory subunit links calcium influx to dephosphorylation-dependent endocytosis, and IQSEC/BRAG Arf guanine nucleotide exchange factors and OPHN1 shape the local trafficking machinery. Deubiquitinases and ubiquitin ligases set how long internalized receptors persist before recycling or degradation.

Dendritic spines are actin-rich compartments, and remodelling of the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton is how they change shape, size and number as synapses are made, strengthened or lost. This structural plasticity underlies learning and memory, and its disruption produces the spine abnormalities seen in intellectual disability, autism spectrum conditions and neurodegeneration. Branched filament nucleation is driven through WAVE complex components such as WASF1, CYFIP1 and ABI3 acting on the Arp2/3 machinery, with cortactin and its neuronal partner CTTNBP2 stabilising branches at the spine head. Profilins supply actin monomers, cofilin severs and depolymerises filaments to permit turnover, and RHOA signalling together with the membrane-deforming I-BAR protein BAIAP2 couples receptor activity to cytoskeletal output. Scaffolds and adhesion-linked proteins including ITSN1, CTNNA2 and spectrin anchor the network beneath the postsynaptic density, tying filament dynamics to glutamate receptor positioning.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane, and recycling of receptors from postsynaptic endosomes back to the surface is how that number is raised. This trafficking step supports long-term potentiation and the maintenance of dendritic spines; when it fails, receptors are retained internally or degraded and synapses weaken, a defect linked to cognitive and neurodevelopmental impairment. Receptors captured in recycling endosomes are loaded into transport vesicles and delivered to the membrane under the control of RAB11A and RAB8A, with retromer subunit VPS35 diverting cargo away from the degradative route. Scaffolds of the GRIP family and their associated guanine nucleotide exchange regulator link AMPA-type receptors to this itinerary, while densin-180 and the polarity protein scribble help organise the postsynaptic site at which delivery occurs.

Excitable cells fire only when their ion channels open and close on schedule, and this pathway covers the processes that set how often action potentials arise, how fast they propagate, and when they terminate. Much of the membership is cardiac: the sodium channel SCN5A, the L-type calcium channel CACNA1C with its auxiliary subunits, the inward rectifier KCNJ2, HCN channels that generate the pacemaker current, and the sarcoplasmic reticulum release and reuptake machinery of RYR2, ATP2A2 and CASQ2 that couples excitation to contraction. Anchoring and adhesion proteins including ANK2, AKAP9, the caveolins and the desmosomal plaque position channels and hold conduction stable, while calmodulin, CAMK2D and NOS1AP tune gating. Loss of this control produces long QT and Brugada syndromes, catecholaminergic arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy; neuronal members such as NALCN, KCNQ3 and KCNC2 set resting potential and firing frequency in neurons.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell action potential tunes the electrical impulse of heart muscle cells — how readily it fires, how fast it spreads, and how long each beat's depolarisation lasts. This control sets heart rate and the coordinated sequence of atrial and ventricular contraction; when it fails the result is long QT syndrome, sick sinus and conduction disease, catastrophic arrhythmia and sudden death. The genes span the machinery that shapes the waveform: L-type calcium entry through CACNA1C with calmodulin and CaMKII feedback, ryanodine receptor and SERCA-mediated calcium cycling, HCN channels generating the pacemaker current of the sinoatrial node, and TRPM4 background conductance. Others govern where channels sit and how excitation passes between cells — ankyrin-B and AKAP9 scaffolding, caveolins and BIN1 membrane organisation, connexin-40 gap junctions, and desmosomal proteins whose loss underlies arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy.

Every heartbeat begins with a cardiomyocyte action potential, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets its shape, duration and rate of firing rather than the depolarization itself. Its outputs are pacemaker automaticity and orderly conduction: HCN channels carry the funny current that drives sinoatrial diastolic depolarization, GJA5 forms the connexin channels through which excitation spreads, and L-type calcium entry through CACNA1C, coupled to RYR2 release and SERCA2 reuptake, links electrical activity to contraction. Calmodulin, CaMKII and NOS1AP tune channel behaviour, while anchoring and cytoskeletal proteins such as AKAP9, ANK2, BIN1 and CAV3 place channels at the membrane domains where they act. Desmosomal components including PKP2, DSP, DSG2 and JUP tie mechanical junctions to conduction. Mutations here underlie long QT and Brugada syndromes, sick sinus syndrome, and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with sudden cardiac death.

The upstroke of an action potential is set by how fast and how far the membrane depolarizes, and this regulatory layer tunes that phase rather than generating it. It matters most in excitable tissues where conduction velocity and rhythm depend on precise sodium channel behaviour: in heart muscle, altered control here produces conduction disease, Brugada-type arrhythmia and susceptibility to sudden cardiac death, while in neurons it shapes spike initiation and repetitive firing. The genes act largely by positioning and trafficking channels rather than conducting current themselves — ankyrin-G anchors sodium channels at the axon initial segment and cardiac intercalated discs, caveolin-3 and a sarcolemmal membrane-associated protein organise channel-containing membrane domains, and a chaperone-like regulator influences surface expression of the cardiac sodium channel. Gap junction and chloride channel components contribute by shaping the local electrical environment in which depolarization spreads.

After an excitable cell fires, it must return to resting potential before it can fire again, and control over the rate and extent of membrane repolarization during an action potential sets action potential duration and refractoriness. In heart muscle this determines the QT interval: delayed repolarization predisposes to long QT syndrome and torsades de pointes, while excessive shortening favours other arrhythmias. The genes here act largely as modulators rather than as the main repolarizing channels themselves — accessory subunits such as CACNA2D1 and CACNB3 shape L-type calcium current, KCNE3 modifies potassium channel gating, calsequestrin and caveolin link sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium handling and membrane microdomain organisation to the process, NOS1 with its adaptor NOS1AP couples nitric oxide signalling to repolarization timing, and microRNAs tune channel and adaptor levels post-transcriptionally. The result is an adjustable link between electrical excitability and calcium-dependent contraction.

The sinoatrial node sets the heart's rate, and this pathway covers the processes that tune the pacemaker action potential's frequency, shape and timing. Sinoatrial myocytes depolarize spontaneously rather than waiting for input, so modulating their firing is how autonomic tone, exercise and drugs change heart rate; loss of control produces sick sinus syndrome, bradycardia and arrhythmia. Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, principally HCN4 with contributions from HCN1 and HCN3, carry the funny current that drives diastolic depolarization and is directly responsive to cAMP. Rhythmic calcium release through the ryanodine receptor RYR2 provides the intracellular clock that works with these surface channels. Ankyrin-B organizes ion transporters in the membrane so that currents are correctly positioned, while TBX18 specifies pacemaker identity, linking transcriptional programming of the node to its electrical behaviour.

Neurons encode information in the timing and frequency of action potentials, and this regulatory biology sets how readily a neuron fires, how fast spikes propagate, and when firing stops. It works largely by tuning voltage-gated and leak channel behaviour rather than by carrying the spike itself. The sodium leak channel NALCN, together with its UNC79, UNC80 and FAM155/NALF1 partners, sets the resting sodium conductance that determines how close a neuron sits to threshold; loss of these components disrupts rhythmic motor output, breathing and sleep-wake patterning, and causes severe neurodevelopmental disease. Fibroblast growth factor homologous factor FGF12 binds sodium channel tails and shifts their inactivation, while FMR1 regulates channel availability and excitability in fragile X syndrome. TRPA1 and a melatonin receptor add sensory and neuromodulatory input. Failures here produce epilepsy, pain sensitisation and arrhythmic neural firing.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell action potential involved in regulation of contraction tunes the electrical signal that tells a cardiomyocyte when and how strongly to contract, setting heart rate and the timing of excitation-contraction coupling. Its failure produces arrhythmia: long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, sinus node dysfunction and impaired contractile reserve. The genes act at several points in this control. HCN4 carries the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous depolarisation in sinoatrial cells, while FGF13 and RANGRF modulate sodium channel availability and trafficking. AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to potassium channels so that adrenergic input shortens repolarisation, and CAMK2D phosphorylates channels and calcium-handling proteins in response to beat-to-beat calcium. Caveolins organise the sarcolemmal microdomains where these channels reside, and the SERCA2 pump links action potential duration to sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium load, coupling membrane excitability directly to force generation.

Each heartbeat begins with an electrical event, and this pathway covers the modulation of the cardiac myocyte action potential in ways that feed directly into how strongly and how often the cell contracts. Its components tune the ion currents that shape depolarization, plateau and repolarization, and thereby set excitation-contraction coupling: the SERCA2 pump encoded by ATP2A2 reloads the sarcoplasmic reticulum with calcium between beats, CAMK2D phosphorylates calcium-handling and channel proteins in response to sustained calcium signals, and HCN4 carries the pacemaker current that drives spontaneous firing in the sinoatrial node. Scaffolding and membrane-organizing proteins such as AKAP9 and the caveolins position kinases and channels together in the sarcolemma, while FGF13 and RANGRF act as accessory regulators of the cardiac sodium channel. Mutations here produce long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, sick sinus syndrome and arrhythmia-associated cardiomyopathy.

Each heartbeat begins with a ventricular myocyte depolarizing, and regulation of the ventricular cardiac muscle cell action potential sets how long that depolarization lasts, how it propagates cell to cell, and how reliably calcium release follows. The L-type calcium channel CACNA1C carries the depolarizing current that sustains the plateau phase, RYR2 releases sarcoplasmic calcium in response to it, and TRPM4 contributes a calcium-activated cation conductance affecting repolarization; BIN1 and CAV1 shape the membrane microdomains where these channels are positioned. Much of the remainder is desmosomal and adherens junction machinery — PKP2, DSP, DSG2, DSC2, JUP, CTNNA3 — together with the scaffold DLG1, which anchors channels at the intercalated disc so that electrical coupling matches mechanical coupling. Mutations in these genes cause arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and inherited arrhythmia syndromes, linking action potential control to sudden cardiac death.

Atrial cardiomyocytes end each action potential by letting potassium out, and the repolarizing currents that do this set atrial action potential duration, refractoriness, and therefore susceptibility to fibrillation. The channels involved are largely atrial-selective, which is why they attract drug development: KCNA5 carries the ultrarapid delayed rectifier current, KCNQ1 contributes the slow delayed rectifier, KCNJ3 and KCNJ5 form the acetylcholine-activated inward rectifier through which vagal input shortens the atrial action potential, and KCNN2 provides calcium-activated potassium conductance. FLNA links channel behaviour to the actin cytoskeleton and membrane organization, and a microRNA component points to post-transcriptional control of channel abundance. Loss- or gain-of-function changes in these currents shorten or prolong repolarization and underlie familial atrial fibrillation and long QT phenotypes, making this arm of cardiac electrophysiology distinct from its ventricular counterpart.

After a ventricular cardiomyocyte depolarizes and contracts, potassium efflux must return the membrane toward its negative resting potential, and the timing of that repolarization sets the QT interval and the refractory period that protects the heart from re-entrant arrhythmia. The genes here are the potassium channels and their accessory subunits that carry the repolarizing currents: KCNQ1 and KCNH2 pore-forming subunits with KCNE1-KCNE5 modulatory partners generating the slow and rapid delayed rectifier currents, KCND3 underlying transient outward current, and inward rectifier subunits including KCNJ3, KCNJ5 and the ATP-sensitive KCNJ8. Trafficking and scaffolding factors such as DLG1, NOS1AP and RNF207, together with nitric oxide signalling and microRNA regulation, tune channel surface density and current amplitude. Loss- or gain-of-function in these components produces long and short QT syndromes, drug-induced arrhythmia and susceptibility to sudden cardiac death.

Synapses are tuned not only by signals travelling forward from axon to dendrite but by messengers sent backwards, from the postsynaptic cell to the terminal that innervates it. This retrograde trans-synaptic signalling sets presynaptic release probability, shapes short- and long-term plasticity, and guides synapse formation and matching of partners during development. A prominent arm is endocannabinoid production in the postsynaptic compartment, where diacylglycerol lipase acting downstream of phospholipase C generates 2-arachidonoylglycerol that crosses the cleft to engage CB1 receptors and suppress transmitter release, with hydrolases such as ABHD6 limiting the signal. Other routes use nitric oxide acting on soluble guanylate cyclase, synaptotagmin-dependent release of retrograde messengers, and adhesion systems including dystroglycan and teneurins that align pre- and postsynaptic specializations. Loss of this feedback destabilizes excitatory-inhibitory balance and is linked to epilepsy and neurodevelopmental disorders.

At many synapses the receiving cell can turn down its own input, and one way it does so is by releasing a lipid messenger backwards across the cleft. This retrograde trans-synaptic signalling by a lipid ligand is the basis of endocannabinoid-mediated short- and long-term depression, which shapes synaptic gain, protects against runaway excitation, and underlies the effects of cannabis on memory, appetite and pain. Postsynaptic activity and Gq-coupled receptor stimulation drive phospholipase C beta to generate diacylglycerol, which diacylglycerol lipase alpha converts to 2-arachidonoylglycerol; a lipid-binding protein assists its movement, and the ligand engages presynaptic cannabinoid receptor CB1 to suppress neurotransmitter release. Serine hydrolase ABHD6 degrades 2-AG, limiting the duration of the signal. The same chemistry operates in interneuron circuits and in feedback control of both excitatory and inhibitory terminals.

Postsynaptic signal transduction covers the events that begin when a neurotransmitter binds a receptor on the receiving side of a synapse and convert that binding into changes in excitability, calcium levels and gene expression. It is what makes synaptic transmission adaptive rather than merely electrical, and it underlies neuromuscular contraction, autonomic control, nociception and learning-related plasticity. The genes here are dominated by cholinergic receptors: the pentameric nicotinic channels that gate cation flux, including the muscle endplate subunits, alongside the five muscarinic receptors that act through Gq and Gi heterotrimers, phospholipase C beta, IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release and protein kinase C. Acetylcholinesterase terminates the signal, agrin organizes endplate receptor clustering, and secreted GPI-anchored Ly6/LYNX-family modulators tune nicotinic responses. Downstream, kinase and transcription factor components carry synaptic activity into nuclear responses. Loss of these components produces myasthenic syndromes and altered synaptic plasticity.

Material internalized from the cell surface is not simply dumped into a single bag: vesicle-mediated transport between endosomal compartments moves cargo stepwise between early, sorting, recycling and late endosomes, and this sorting decides whether a receptor is returned to the plasma membrane or committed to lysosomal degradation. It therefore sets the duration of growth factor and adhesion signalling, nutrient uptake, and antigen handling, and its failure leaves undegraded cargo and mis-sorted receptors behind. Rab GTPases such as RAB5A, RAB7A, RAB11A and RAB21 mark successive compartments and recruit tethers and effectors including EEA1 and RILP; the FHF/HOOK adaptors, dynein light chain and kinesin KIF16B pull vesicles along microtubules; the class III PI3-kinase complex with BECN1 and PIK3R4 generates PI3P that sorting nexins read. ESCRT components contribute to cargo sorting into intraluminal vesicles, while ERM proteins and SRC couple sorting to cortical and signalling events.

Neurons build axons far longer than their cell bodies can reach by diffusion, so cargo must be walked along microtubules in both directions; this axonal transport supplies synapses with mitochondria, synaptic vesicle precursors, lysosomes and autophagosomes and returns aged organelles and signalling endosomes to the soma. Kinesins such as KIF1A, KIF5A and KIF5B drive anterograde movement while the dynein heavy chain DYNC1H1 with its dynactin adaptor DCTN1 drives retrograde traffic, and scaffolds and adaptors including HAP1, MAPK8IP3, FEZ1 and the BLOC-1 and AP-3 complexes select which cargo rides. Microtubule stability and polarity are set by MAPT, MAP2, TRIM46 and the severing enzyme spastin, and tubulin modifications tune motor engagement. Loss of these components underlies hereditary spastic paraplegia, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, ALS and other neurodegenerations in which distal axons die back first.

Neurons must deliver receptors, mitochondria and messenger RNAs from the cell body out into dendrites, often to individual synapses, and dendritic transport is the directed, microtubule-based movement that accomplishes it. Because dendrites can extend far from the soma, local supply of cargo sets which synapses can be built, maintained and strengthened, linking this traffic to synaptic plasticity, memory and dendritic arbor growth. Kinesin motors of several families, including KIF17, KIF5A/B/C and the heterotrimeric KIF3B complex with its associated subunit KIFAP3, provide the anterograde force, while adaptors such as TRAK2 couple motors to mitochondria and Rab-dependent steps route membrane cargo. RNA-binding proteins including Staufen homologues, SFPQ and PURA package transcripts into granules for transport and translation at distal sites. Disruption of these motors and adaptors produces axonal and dendritic degeneration, as seen in KIF5A-linked spastic paraplegia and motor neuron disease.

Neurons must supply their dendrites with receptors, mRNAs and organelles built in the cell body, and anterograde dendritic transport is the outward leg of that supply line, moving cargo along microtubules from the soma toward the postsynaptic compartment. It determines which glutamate receptors, ion channels and locally translatable messages reach a given spine, and so underlies dendritic growth, synapse maturation and the local protein synthesis that supports long-term plasticity and memory. Kinesin motors do the work: KIF17 carries NMDA receptor-containing cargo, the kinesin-1 heavy chains KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C move a broad set of vesicles and RNA granules, and a kinesin-2 heavy chain with its associated subunits contributes further. Staufen paralogues package dendritic mRNAs for the ride, while a Rab GTPase and a lipid raft scaffold direct membrane cargo. Motor mutations cause axonal and motor neuron degeneration.

Receptor diffusion trapping is the mechanism that fixes neurotransmitter receptors in place at synapses instead of letting them wander through the plasma membrane. Receptors such as AMPA-type glutamate receptors diffuse laterally at all times; synaptic strength depends on how many are captured and held opposite a release site, so this capture step sets the gain of excitatory transmission and underlies long-term potentiation and homeostatic scaling. The TARP family of calcium channel gamma subunits and SHISA6 act as auxiliary subunits that tether AMPA receptors to PSD-95 scaffolds, while palmitoylation by ZDHHC2 and links to the actin cortex through radixin stabilise the trap. Integrin adhesion and tetraspanin microdomains provide the extracellular and membrane-organising anchors, and KCC2 couples chloride homeostasis to the same submembrane cytoskeletal corral, tuning inhibitory receptor confinement in parallel.

Receptors do not need to be synthesized anew to change a synapse's strength; they can simply be caught and held where they are needed. Diffusion trapping describes the capture of laterally mobile plasma membrane receptors within a defined domain, typically by tethering to scaffold or matrix components beneath the membrane, and it underlies how many AMPA-type glutamate receptors accumulate at postsynaptic sites during synaptic plasticity. The transmembrane AMPA receptor regulatory proteins encoded by the CACNG family, of which stargazin is the prototype, bind receptor subunits and link them to postsynaptic density scaffolds, while SHISA6 restrains receptor desensitization and mobility. Palmitoylation by ZDHHC2 and adhesion through integrin beta-3 tune how firmly receptors are immobilized, and the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 ties this to inhibitory synapse organization. Loss of trapping weakens synaptic transmission and produces ataxia and epilepsy phenotypes.

Anterograde dendritic transport of neurotransmitter receptor complex delivers assembled glutamate and other neurotransmitter receptors outward along dendritic microtubules to the postsynaptic membrane, setting how many receptors a synapse can display and therefore its strength. Because synaptic plasticity, learning and memory depend on regulated receptor supply, disruption of this traffic weakens excitatory transmission and contributes to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease; mutations in the kinesin heavy chain KIF5A cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and motor neuron degeneration. The carriers are plus-end-directed kinesins: KIF17 with its scaffold adaptors moves NMDA receptor subunit cargo, while kinesin-1 heavy chains and the kinesin-2 components KIF3B and KIFAP3 carry receptor-containing vesicles and associated cargo. This is a specialised branch of microtubule-based intracellular transport, linked to dendritic polarity, vesicle sorting from the secretory pathway, and activity-dependent remodelling of postsynaptic receptor composition.

Excitatory synapses only work if glutamate receptors reach the postsynaptic membrane, and anterograde dendritic transport of neurotransmitter receptor complexes is how they get there: kinesin motors carry receptor-bearing cargo outward along dendritic microtubules toward the postsynapse. The capacity to deliver and replenish receptors sets synaptic strength, so this traffic underlies learning-related plasticity and, when it fails, contributes to cognitive and neurodegenerative disease. KIF17 is the motor most closely tied to NMDA receptor subunit delivery, working with a scaffold adaptor complex that includes KIFAP3 and the kinesin-2 subunit KIF3B, while the kinesin-1 heavy chains KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C move receptor and associated cargo through dendritic shafts. Directionality matters because dendritic microtubules are mixed in orientation, so motor choice and cargo adaptors together determine where receptors are deposited. Mutations in KIF5A cause motor neuron and spastic paraplegia phenotypes, underscoring the dependence of neurons on this transport machinery.

Postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton organization builds and remodels the actin scaffold inside dendritic spines, the structural basis of how excitatory synapses change strength during learning. Spine enlargement, stabilization, or collapse all follow from this actin turnover, and its dysregulation underlies intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorders and the synapse loss of neurodegeneration. Actin monomers themselves (ACTB, ACTG1) polymerize under the control of Rho-family GTPase signalling, with RAC3 and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor FARP1 relaying adhesion and receptor cues to the WAVE complex component WASF2, which activates branched filament nucleation. Membrane-shaping and linker proteins such as SH3GL2, EZR and DBNL couple the filament network to the postsynaptic membrane and endocytic machinery, while non-muscle myosin MYH10 provides contractility and SRCIN1 and NOS1AP tie the network to postsynaptic density scaffolds and glutamate receptor trafficking.

Dendritic spines are built on actin, and remodelling that actin at the postsynaptic side is how synapses change shape and strength. Organization of the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton underlies spine formation, enlargement and retraction, and therefore the structural component of long-term potentiation and depression; when it is dysregulated, spine density and cognitive function suffer, as seen in intellectual disability and neurodegenerative conditions. Actin monomers themselves are supplied by the cytoplasmic beta and gamma isoforms, while a Rho-family GTPase and a WASP-family nucleation-promoting factor drive branched filament assembly, and a non-muscle myosin II heavy chain provides contractile force. Adaptors and membrane-linking proteins including drebrin-like protein, ezrin, FARP1 and the endophilin SH3GL2 couple filaments to the postsynaptic membrane, receptor scaffolds and endocytic machinery, tying cytoskeletal geometry to receptor trafficking and synapse maturation.

Excitatory chemical synaptic transmission is the process by which a presynaptic neuron depolarises its partner, generating an excitatory postsynaptic potential that pushes the cell toward firing; it is the basic currency of information flow in the brain and the substrate on which learning-related plasticity is built. The genes here centre on the NMDA-type glutamate receptor, with the obligatory GRIN1 subunit combining with GRIN2A-D to form calcium-permeable channels whose subunit composition sets response kinetics and changes over development. Accessory and regulatory proteins such as SHISA6 shape receptor desensitisation and synaptic anchoring, while KCNQ3 contributes potassium conductance that opposes excitation, and parvalbumin marks the fast-spiking interneurons that keep excitation in check. Too much or too little signalling of this kind underlies epilepsy, excitotoxic neuronal death, and intellectual disability caused by GRIN2B mutation.

Glutamate acting on NMDA-type receptors converts synaptic activity into calcium entry, and calcium entry into lasting change in the synapse — the basis of long-term potentiation, dendritic spine remodelling and the activity-dependent transcription that consolidates learning. Because these receptors require both ligand binding and membrane depolarization, they act as coincidence detectors, and excessive activation drives the calcium overload and excitotoxic neuronal death seen in stroke and neurodegeneration. The genes here span the route from adhesion to nucleus: neurexin and neuroligin align pre- and postsynaptic membranes, PSD-95 scaffolds receptors within the postsynaptic density, calpain-1 provides calcium-activated proteolysis that remodels synaptic proteins, and MEF2C carries the signal into transcriptional programmes controlling synapse number. Amyloid precursor protein links this signalling to the synaptic dysfunction of Alzheimer disease, where NMDA receptor signalling is a therapeutic target.

AMPA selective glutamate receptor signaling pathway covers fast excitatory neurotransmission at glutamatergic synapses: glutamate binds AMPA-type ionotropic receptors, the channel opens to sodium and potassium flux, and the resulting depolarization drives synaptic integration and the downstream signalling and transcriptional changes that store information. This is the principal route of moment-to-moment excitation in the brain, and its regulated strengthening or weakening is the substrate of long-term potentiation, learning and memory; disturbed AMPA receptor signalling contributes to autism spectrum disorders, epilepsy and excitotoxic neuronal death. The genes here emphasize how the receptor is positioned and controlled rather than the pore itself: trans-synaptic neurexin-neuroligin adhesion aligns pre- and postsynaptic sites, SHANK1 scaffolds receptors within the postsynaptic density, MEF2C couples activity to a transcriptional program of synapse elimination, and a beta-adrenergic receptor links neuromodulatory input to receptor trafficking and phosphorylation.

Fast excitatory transmission at most central synapses runs through AMPA-type glutamate receptors, and this pathway covers what happens after glutamate binds them: cation flux depolarises the postsynaptic membrane and sets off events that reach as far as gene expression. The strength and number of these receptors at a synapse is the physical substrate of learning, and their trafficking underlies long-term potentiation and depression; too much flux contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death. The genes here emphasise the structural and regulatory context rather than the channel itself — a trans-synaptic neurexin–neuroligin adhesion pair aligns pre- and postsynaptic sides, SHANK1 scaffolds receptors within the postsynaptic density, and MEF2C links synaptic activity to transcriptional programmes that prune or stabilise connections. A β-adrenergic receptor component reflects neuromodulatory tuning of receptor phosphorylation and synaptic gain.

vesicle-mediated transport in synapse is the membrane trafficking that makes chemical neurotransmission possible: loading transmitter into vesicles, docking and fusing them at the active zone when calcium arrives, and retrieving membrane afterwards so the terminal can fire again. Without it synapses fatigue and fail, and mutations in its components cause epilepsies, movement disorders and intellectual disability. Vacuolar ATPase subunits acidify vesicles so that vesicular transporters for glutamate, GABA and monoamines can fill them; SNAREs such as SNAP25, syntaxin-1 and VAMP2, together with Munc18, Munc13, RIM and synaptotagmin calcium sensors, execute fast release, while complexins clamp it. Endocytic retrieval uses clathrin adaptors, dynamins, synaptojanin and endophilin. The same machinery governs postsynaptic receptor trafficking and dense-core vesicle release of neuropeptides, linking it to synaptic plasticity and to neurodegenerative proteins including alpha-synuclein, LRRK2 and parkin.

Chemical neurotransmission depends on a local membrane traffic cycle, and this is the pathway that runs it: synaptic vesicles are filled with transmitter, docked and primed at the active zone, fused with the plasma membrane on calcium influx, and retrieved by endocytosis for reuse. Its throughput sets synaptic strength and short-term plasticity, and receptor-containing vesicle traffic on the postsynaptic side underlies changes in synaptic efficacy. Vesicular transporters such as the glutamate and GABA carriers load transmitter using the proton gradient built by the vacuolar ATPase; synaptotagmins act as calcium sensors, SNAREs including SNAP25, syntaxin-1 and VAMP2 with Munc18 and Munc13 drive fusion, complexins clamp it, and clathrin adaptors, dynamins and synaptojanin recover membrane. Mutations here cause epileptic encephalopathies, movement disorders and intellectual disability, and alpha-synuclein and LRRK2 tie the cycle to Parkinson disease.

Excitatory synapses are not fixed structures; the postsynaptic side remodels its shape, size and spine number in response to activity, and this remodelling of postsynaptic structure is the physical substrate of learning and memory. The gene collection is dominated by actin biology, because dendritic spine morphology is set by the branched and bundled filament networks beneath the postsynaptic density: nucleation promoting factors such as WASF1, WASF3 and CYFIP1 with BAIAP2, filament severing and monomer handling by cofilin and the profilins, cortactin and its brain-enriched partner CTTNBP2, and upstream control by RhoA-family GTPases and their regulators. Scaffolds of the DLGAP family couple receptor complexes to this cytoskeleton, and cadherin-linked CTNNA2 ties spine shape to adhesion. Loss of control here yields immature or unstable spines, and such defects recur in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegenerative synapse loss.

Neurons release neuropeptides, neurotrophins and monoamine neuromodulators from dense core vesicles, and this calcium-triggered exocytosis is how they exert slow, diffuse modulation of circuits rather than fast point-to-point synaptic transmission. It shapes appetite, stress responses, mood and neuroendocrine output, and loss of its machinery produces severe early epileptic encephalopathies and movement disorders. Unlike synaptic vesicles, dense core granules fuse at sites away from the active zone and require priming before they become release-competent: Munc13 proteins open syntaxin for SNARE assembly, Munc18-family chaperones stabilise the syntaxin template and escort it into the fusion complex, SNAP25 completes the membrane-bridging SNARE, and a Rab3 GTPase governs vesicle tethering and pool maintenance. A synaptotagmin family member contributes calcium-dependent regulation of release. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of vesicle trafficking, calcium signalling and peptide-based intercellular communication.

Before a transport vesicle can fuse, it must first be caught and held close to its target membrane, and vesicle tethering is that initial capture step, carried out by multi-subunit complexes that bridge the two bilayers and precede SNARE-mediated fusion. It gives directionality to secretion and endosome-to-Golgi traffic: without it, cargo vesicles fail to be delivered to the right compartment and Golgi architecture collapses. The exocyst octamer, built from EXOC1 through EXOC8, docks secretory vesicles at defined sites on the plasma membrane and supports polarized growth, cell migration and ciliogenesis. The TRAPP complexes act at the Golgi and ER-Golgi interface, where they also serve as activators of Rab GTPases that recruit downstream effectors. Other members, including TBC1D23 and WDR11-FAM91A1, link endosome-derived vesicles to Golgi tethers. Mutations in TRAPP subunits cause skeletal dysplasia and neurodevelopmental disorders, illustrating how sensitive tissue growth is to membrane traffic fidelity.

Sphingolipids are made on one face of a membrane but must reach the other to build the asymmetric bilayer that cells depend on, and sphingolipid translocation is the ATP-driven flipping that accomplishes this. The transporters here are ABC-family pumps that move lipid substrates across the plasma membrane and organelle membranes, exporting sphingomyelin and glycosphingolipids to the exoplasmic leaflet. This matters for the lipid composition of the outer leaflet, which governs raft formation, receptor clustering and cholesterol efflux; ABCA1 links sphingolipid handling to HDL particle formation, while ABCB1 and ABCC1 also translocate a wide range of amphipathic drugs, and ABCB4 acts at the canalicular membrane in bile lipid secretion. Loss of these activities disturbs membrane asymmetry, sterol export and biliary lipid balance, with consequences ranging from lipid storage defects to cholestatic liver disease.

Transport vesicles arriving at the Golgi must first be captured and held close to the target membrane before SNAREs can drive fusion, and this tethering step gives vesicle traffic its specificity. The genes here support capture at the trans-Golgi: the golgin TRIP11 (GMAP-210) projects from Golgi membranes as a long coiled-coil that catches incoming carriers, while TBC1D23 bridges golgins to the FAM91A1-containing complex that recognises endosome-derived vesicles, linking the two membranes indirectly rather than fusing them. Correct tethering keeps cargo recycling between endosomes and the Golgi on track and maintains Golgi architecture and glycosylation capacity. Loss of these components disrupts retrograde transport and, for TBC1D23 and TRIP11, causes human developmental disease affecting the brain and the skeleton, underscoring how much membrane organisation depends on this pre-fusion recognition step.

Cells can attack the genetic material of an invader directly, and this branch of innate defense handles the clearance of foreign intracellular nucleic acids by chemically corrupting them. The APOBEC3 family of single-stranded DNA cytidine deaminases converts cytosine to uracil in reverse-transcribed viral cDNA, so that the resulting G-to-A hypermutation destroys coding capacity, and some members additionally block reverse transcription without deaminating. Their targets include retroviruses such as HIV-1, hepatitis B virus, and endogenous retroelements whose retrotransposition would otherwise destabilise the genome, which makes them part of the barrier that limits horizontal movement of genetic elements. The same activity, when it strays onto the host genome, generates the characteristic APOBEC mutational signatures found in breast, bladder and other cancers, so restriction and mutagenesis are two faces of one enzymology. Expression is induced by interferon in lymphoid and myeloid cells, and viral antagonists such as HIV Vif exist to degrade these enzymes.

Building the transmitter-releasing side of a synapse requires that an axon, on contact with a target cell, converts an adhesive interaction into an organized active zone with clustered vesicles and calcium channels. Presynapse assembly is how nascent contacts are selected, stabilized and matured, and it sets synapse number and specificity during circuit wiring; disruption of its components is recurrent in autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. Much of the work is done by trans-synaptic adhesion pairs, with presynaptic neurexins and PTPRD-type receptors read out by postsynaptic partners such as neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs, IL1RAPL family proteins and calsyntenins, which send a retrograde differentiation signal back across the cleft. Wnt ligands acting through Frizzled and Dishevelled, glypican and cerebellin cues, and membrane traffic via ARF6 and the retromer subunit VPS35 shape where assembly occurs, while the scaffolds bassoon and piccolo organize the resulting release site.

Building the receiving side of a synapse means clustering neurotransmitter receptors, scaffolds and cytoskeletal regulators opposite a presynaptic terminal, and postsynapse assembly is the process that organizes those components into a functional junction. It determines where dendritic spines form and how many, setting the substrate for synaptic transmission, plasticity and circuit wiring; disruption is a recurring theme in autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs such as neurexins with neuroligins or LRRTMs, together with leucine-rich repeat and receptor phosphatase partners, nucleate the site and recruit intracellular scaffolds like SHANK3 and CASKIN1. Rho-family GTPases and their exchange factors and GAPs, acting through actin nucleation-promoting machinery, shape the spine head, while guidance and growth-factor receptors, reelin signalling, Wnt ligands and palmitoylating enzymes tune where and when assembly proceeds. The same machinery is reused for synapse maturation and elimination.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane at any moment, and this pathway is the trafficking and anchoring machinery that sets that number. It underlies long-term potentiation and depression, homeostatic scaling, and learning-related plasticity; its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism spectrum conditions. Receptors reach and leave the surface through clathrin-mediated endocytosis via the AP-2 adaptor complex, recycling through Rab-dependent endosomes and the retromer complex, and degradation in lysosomes. At the membrane, scaffolds such as PSD-95 and other DLG family proteins, GRIP adaptors and gephyrin hold AMPA-, kainate-, NMDA- and GABA/glycine-type receptors in register with presynaptic release sites, while auxiliary subunits including stargazin-like TARPs, cornichon and GSG1L govern delivery and gating. Palmitoylation, ubiquitination and activity-driven ARC expression tune receptor removal, linking neuronal firing to lasting changes in synaptic efficacy.

Receiving neurons build a dense protein specialization beneath the postsynaptic membrane that anchors neurotransmitter receptors opposite the presynaptic release site, and its organization — assembly, remodelling and disassembly — sets synapse number, strength and identity. This is the substrate of learning-related plasticity: scaffolds such as SHANK1/SHANK3 and DLG1 cross-link receptors to the actin cytoskeleton, while Rho-family regulators including ARHGEF9, OPHN1 and GIT1 and the Ras/Rap regulator SYNGAP1 translate synaptic activity into cytoskeletal and signalling change. Trans-synaptic adhesion codes — neurexins with neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRK, LRFN and receptor phosphatases PTPRD/PTPRS, plus secreted cues such as cerebellins, C1QL proteins and reelin — specify which contacts mature and whether they become excitatory, inhibitory or, through rapsyn, neuromuscular. Mutations in many of these genes cause autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy, marking postsynaptic assembly as a core vulnerability of brain wiring.

Cells move cargo over long distances by walking it along microtubules, and this transport machinery is what positions organelles, vesicles and mRNAs where they are needed. It matters most in cells with extreme geometry: neurons depend on it to supply axons and dendrites with mitochondria, lysosomes and synaptic precursors, and its failure underlies motor neuron disease, hereditary spastic paraplegia and axonal neuropathies. Kinesins such as KIF5A and KIF1A carry cargo toward microtubule plus ends while the cytoplasmic dynein complex with its dynactin and adaptor proteins moves it back toward the centre; TRAK and RHOT proteins couple mitochondria to these motors, and BORC and BLOC-1 subunits govern lysosome positioning. A related dynein-2 and intraflagellar transport system shuttles components within cilia and flagella, linking this biology to ciliopathies, sperm motility and left-right patterning.

Every tRNA is transcribed with an extra leader at its 5' end, and removing that leader is the first cut in making a functional tRNA; without it no aminoacylation or ribosomal decoding can proceed. This endonucleolytic step is performed by RNase P, represented here by a large set of protein subunits including POP1, POP4, POP5, POP7 and the RPP proteins that support catalysis on nuclear pre-tRNA substrates. Mitochondria use a distinct protein-only enzyme, in which PRORP provides the nuclease activity while TRMT10C and HSD17B10 form the partner subcomplex that also acts in mitochondrial RNA methylation and tRNA maturation, linking 5'-end processing to the release of individual RNAs from polycistronic mitochondrial transcripts. Associated factors include the La protein SSB, which binds nascent polymerase III transcripts and protects their ends, and THG1L, which adds the guanosine required at position -1 of histidine tRNA. Defects in these mitochondrial components cause combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency and neurodegenerative disease.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane, and controlling the rate at which those receptors are pulled out by endocytosis is one of the main ways neurons set it. Regulating postsynaptic receptor internalization underlies long-term depression, homeostatic scaling and the reversal of potentiation, and its disruption is linked to intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. The machinery combines activity-induced effectors such as ARC, which drives AMPA receptor removal, with clathrin-associated and endosomal components including HIP1, RABEP1 and NUMB, calcium- and calcineurin-dependent signalling through the PPP3R1 regulatory subunit, and Arf guanine-nucleotide exchange factors of the IQSEC family that couple receptor complexes to membrane budding. Ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases add another layer by marking receptors and scaffolds for removal or rescue, while ATAD1 extracts receptor-bound proteins to reset the synapse.

The receiving side of a synapse must build a dense scaffold of receptors, adaptors and cytoskeletal anchors directly opposite a presynaptic release site, and this pathway covers the signals that tune how fast and how extensively that postsynaptic specialization is assembled. Setting the number, strength and molecular identity of excitatory and inhibitory synapses, it shapes circuit wiring during development and its remodelling during plasticity and learning; disturbed control here is a recurring theme in autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy. Much of the regulation is contact-mediated: leucine-rich repeat adhesion proteins such as LRRTM2, LRFN family members and LRRC4B engage presynaptic receptor phosphatases like PTPRD and PTPRS, while secreted cerebellin bridges to the delta-type glutamate receptor GRID2. Kinases including ABL1 and PTK2B, and the Rho-family exchange factor ARHGEF9 that clusters inhibitory scaffolds, relay these cues to the underlying actin and spectrin cytoskeleton.

The postsynaptic density is the protein-dense scaffold beneath an excitatory synapse that holds receptors, adhesion molecules and signalling enzymes in register with the presynaptic release site; controlling how fast and how extensively it is built sets synapse number and strength during circuit wiring and plasticity. Genes here largely act as trans-synaptic organizers and their intracellular partners: leucine-rich repeat adhesion proteins such as LRRTM2, LRFN1/4 and LRRC4B engage presynaptic partners, receptor phosphatases PTPRD and PTPRS serve as presynaptic-facing hubs, and the secreted cerebellin CBLN1 bridges to the delta-type glutamate receptor GRID2 at parallel fibre synapses. Scaffolds and kinases including CASKIN1, CRIPT and PTK2B tune assembly downstream. Because synapse assembly is dose-sensitive, variants in these organizers are recurrently linked to autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia, and to cerebellar ataxia when the cerebellin-GRID2 axis fails.</description>

Excitatory synapses are not fixed structures: the actin-rich spine head grows, shrinks and changes shape as synaptic activity dictates, and this regulatory layer sets how readily that remodelling occurs. It underlies the structural side of long-term potentiation and depression, and thus learning, memory consolidation and the pruning of circuits during development; genes here are recurrent candidates in intellectual disability and autism, with CYFIP1 in the 15q11.2 region a notable example. Control converges on the actin cytoskeleton beneath the postsynaptic density. RHOA and RHOB signal through their kinase effectors to constrain spine growth, BAIAP2 and CYFIP1 link receptor and Rac signalling to actin nucleation, CTTNBP2 targets cortactin to spines, and PDXP (chronophin) dephosphorylates cofilin to promote filament severing. Scaffolds and adaptors such as ITSN1 and AGAP1 couple membrane traffic and small GTPase cycling to the same structural output.

Synapses do not transmit at a fixed gain, and this pathway covers the processes acting on the receiving side of the synapse that raise or lower that gain. Such postsynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission underlies long-term potentiation and depression, and therefore learning, memory and the behavioural adaptations altered in addiction and schizophrenia. Metabotropic receptors for acetylcholine, dopamine and glutamate couple through G proteins and phospholipase C to second-messenger cascades, with protein kinase A, the calcium-dependent phosphatase calcineurin and Ras/ERK components converting calcium and cyclic AMP signals into changes in receptor number and sensitivity. Local translation initiation factors allow dendrites to make new protein on demand, while cytoskeletal regulators, a Rho-family exchange factor, adhesion and guidance molecules, sorting receptors and ubiquitin-pathway enzymes remodel spine structure and control receptor trafficking and degradation. Glutamate uptake and autophagy components shape the duration of the response.

Presynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission covers the machinery that tunes how much neurotransmitter a nerve terminal releases, rather than whether release occurs at all. This gain control sets the strength and short-term plasticity of synapses, underlies presynaptic inhibition and facilitation, and is the point of action of nicotine, caffeine, opioid-like adenosine signalling, and antipsychotics acting at dopamine and serotonin receptors. Autoreceptors and heteroreceptors on the terminal — muscarinic M2, dopamine D2, metabotropic glutamate mGluR2, adrenergic alpha-2A, adenosine and nicotinic receptors — converge on adenylate cyclase, kinases such as GSK3B, and the release apparatus itself through RAB3A, synaptotagmins and Munc18-interacting proteins. Trans-synaptic and translational regulators including neurexins and FMR1 with its paralogues adjust terminal properties over longer timescales, linking this modulation to learning, and its disruption to fragile X syndrome and addiction.

Neurotransmitter release is not fixed: receptors and regulatory proteins sitting on the presynaptic terminal raise or lower how much transmitter a given action potential releases, and this presynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission is the substrate of short-term plasticity, gain control and the dampening of excess excitation. Autoreceptors and heteroreceptors dominate the list — adenosine A1-family and A2 receptors, alpha-2 adrenergic, M2 muscarinic, dopamine D1 and D2, metabotropic glutamate mGluR2, serotonin 5-HT2A, and several nicotinic subunits that facilitate release at axon terminals — converging on cyclic AMP through adenylyl cyclase 1 and on the release machinery itself via RAB3A, synaptotagmin and Munc18-interacting proteins. Additional regulators include FMR1 and its paralogues, which couple local translation to synaptic strength; loss of that control contributes to fragile X syndrome and to the imbalance of excitation seen in epilepsy and addiction.

The presynaptic terminal has to be built in the right place, with its release sites aligned to a postsynaptic partner, and this is the programme that assembles, arranges and can dismantle it. It determines where neurotransmitter release occurs, how many vesicles are poised at the active zone, and therefore the strength of a nascent connection; its disruption underlies intellectual disability and autism, and several members are risk genes for those conditions. Trans-synaptic adhesion complexes do the organizing work — neurexins engaging neuroligins, leucine-rich repeat and SLITRK family receptors, protein tyrosine phosphatase receptors, calsyntenin and cerebellin bridging to glutamate receptor subunits — while bassoon and piccolo scaffold the cytomatrix at the active zone. Secreted Wnts, their frizzled receptors and Dishevelled, together with glypican and DKK1, act as positional cues, and actin regulators plus membrane trafficking components supply the structural response.

The receiving side of a synapse is a built structure, and postsynapse organization covers its assembly, remodelling and disassembly — the work that sets how strongly one neuron responds to another.
