Dendritic spine shape, receptor number and scaffold composition are all determined here, so this biology underlies learning, memory and activity-dependent circuit refinement, and its disruption features in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration. Trans-synaptic adhesion pairs such as neurexins with neuroligins and LRRTMs align the postsynaptic site with the presynaptic terminal, while PSD-95, SHANK and HOMER scaffolds tether glutamate receptors and signalling enzymes. Rho-family GTPases, their regulators, and actin nucleation and severing machinery reshape the spine cytoskeleton, and palmitoylating and depalmitoylating enzymes tune scaffold residency. Parallel components organize inhibitory synapses through gephyrin and the neuromuscular junction through agrin–LRP4–MuSK signalling to cluster acetylcholine receptors.

Synapses are built from two sides, and this pathway covers the signals that shape the presynaptic terminal itself — how large it grows, how many vesicles it clusters, and whether it matures into a functional release site. Most of the control is retrograde: postsynaptic adhesion molecules and secreted factors bind partners on the incoming axon and instruct terminal assembly. Neurexins are the central presynaptic receiving hub, engaged by neuroligins, LRRTM and SLITRK families, cerebellins acting with glutamate delta receptors, and glypican-4; Wnt ligands with Frizzled and the antagonist DKK1 provide a parallel instructive input, alongside calsyntenin, IL1RAP-family proteins and neurotrophin receptor signalling. Getting terminal size and number right sets synaptic strength and circuit wiring, and variants in these adhesion genes recur in autism, intellectual disability and Tourette syndrome, while APP and alpha-synuclein tie the same machinery to neurodegenerative synapse loss.

regulation of postsynapse organization controls the size, shape and molecular composition of the receiving side of a synapse, and with it the strength of synaptic transmission. Dendritic spine formation, maturation, pruning and collapse all depend on this regulation, which is the structural basis of learning and memory; disruption of these genes recurs in intellectual disability, autism, schizophrenia and neurodegeneration. The core machinery converges on actin: Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42, their GEFs and GAPs, and effectors including PAK3, cofilin and WAVE/WASP-associated regulators remodel the spine cytoskeleton. Scaffolds of the SHANK, HOMER and TANC families organize glutamate receptors and their signalling partners, while adhesion molecules such as neuroligins, LRRTMs and ephrin receptors instruct postsynaptic assembly from across the cleft. Local translation, palmitoylation cycling and ubiquitin-like modification tune this architecture in an activity-dependent manner.

Excitatory synapses are not fixed structures: the size, shape and receptor content of the postsynaptic compartment change with activity, and this remodelling is the physical substrate of learning, developmental circuit refinement and synapse elimination. Regulation of postsynapse organization covers the signals that drive those changes, converging on the dendritic spine actin cytoskeleton. Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42 with their many activators and GAPs (ARHGAP32, ARHGAP33, DOCK4) control actin through cofilin, drebrin and WAVE-complex components, while scaffolds including SHANK3, HOMER1, TANC1/2 and BAIAP2 organize the postsynaptic density around NMDA and metabotropic glutamate receptors. Trans-synaptic adhesion molecules — neuroligins, LRRTMs, EphB receptors, cadherins — instruct where and how large a postsynapse forms, and palmitoylation cycling by ZDHHC enzymes and ABHD17 thioesterases tunes scaffold anchoring. Disruption of these components recurs in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration, where spine loss tracks cognitive decline.

regulation of trans-synaptic signaling covers the control of how strongly and how reliably one neuron communicates with the next, setting synaptic gain across the nervous system. This tuning is the physical basis of learning, memory and circuit refinement, and its derangement underlies epilepsy, autism, intellectual disability, addiction and neurodegeneration. Regulation acts on both sides of the cleft: presynaptic release probability through the active zone and SNARE-associated machinery (RIMS, UNC13, synaptotagmins, complexins, STXBP1), and postsynaptic responsiveness through glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, dopamine and neuropeptide receptors held in place by scaffolds such as PSD-95, SHANK and HOMER. Trans-synaptic adhesion complexes -- neurexins with neuroligins, LRRTMs, cerebellins and teneurin-like partners -- align and specify these compartments, while calcium sensors, CaMKII, calcineurin and kinase cascades convert activity into lasting potentiation or depression. Neurotrophins, glia and neuromodulators supply additional slow, state-dependent adjustment.

Synapses do not transmit at a fixed gain; regulation of trans-synaptic signaling covers the processes that tune how much neurotransmitter is released and how strongly the postsynaptic cell responds, which is the substrate of learning, memory and circuit refinement. Presynaptic release machinery and its modulators, including syntaxins, SNAP25, synaptotagmins, complexins, RIM proteins, UNC13A and STXBP1, set vesicle priming and calcium sensitivity, while voltage-gated calcium channels and auxiliary subunits control the calcium trigger. On the receiving side, ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, dopamine and neuropeptide receptors feed into scaffolds such as PSD-95, SHANK and HOMER, with CaMKII, calcineurin and kinase cascades altering receptor number and gating. Adhesion systems -- neurexins, neuroligins, LRRTMs, cerebellins and ephrin receptors -- align the two sides and specify synapse identity. Disruption produces epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism, and this machinery is degraded in neurodegeneration.

BDNF released at synapses acts as a retrograde and anterograde messenger that tunes how strongly a synapse transmits, and it is the best-characterised neurotrophin link between activity and lasting synaptic change. This trans-synaptic signalling supports long-term potentiation, dendritic spine growth and experience-dependent plasticity in the hippocampus and cortex, and its disruption is tied to depression, anxiety-like behaviour and impaired learning. Pro-BDNF is packaged into dense-core vesicles and released in an activity-dependent manner; tissue plasminogen activator and plasminogen provide the extracellular proteolytic step that converts the proneurotrophin to mature BDNF, which then engages the TrkB receptor encoded by NTRK2 on the partner cell. Synaptotagmin-4 constrains postsynaptic BDNF secretion, while SLITRK5 shapes TrkB trafficking and responsiveness, making receptor availability as much a control point as ligand supply.

Neurotransmitter release depends on a structured actin and microtubule scaffold beneath the active zone, and presynaptic cytoskeleton organization is the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of that scaffold together with its associated proteins. It sets the size and position of the synaptic vesicle cluster, supports vesicle mobilisation and recycling during sustained firing, and anchors the terminal to its postsynaptic partner, so that changes in it accompany synapse formation, pruning and activity-dependent plasticity. The genes here cover the relevant filament chemistry: profilin and cyclase-associated protein handle actin monomer supply and turnover, a formin nucleates and elongates filaments under Rho control, plastin crosslinks them into bundles, a CLIP-associated protein regulates microtubule plus ends, and talin links integrin-based adhesion to actin. Piccolo, a very large active zone scaffold, ties this cytoskeletal remodelling to the vesicle release machinery itself.

The shape and strength of an excitatory synapse depend on the actin-based skeleton beneath the postsynaptic membrane, and organizing that postsynaptic cytoskeleton is how dendritic spines are built, enlarged, and retracted. This underlies structural plasticity: spine growth during long-term potentiation, spine shrinkage during depression, and the stable anchoring of receptor scaffolds that keeps neurotransmitter receptors apposed to release sites. Beta- and gamma-actin provide the filaments, while regulators such as the Rho-family GTPase RAC3, the nucleation-promoting factor WASF2, and actin-binding adaptors including DBNL, EZR and SRCIN1 control assembly, branching and membrane attachment; endophilin SH3GL2 links the process to endocytic membrane remodelling, and a non-muscle myosin heavy chain supplies contractile force. Neurofilament and internexin subunits, plus a kinesin, connect spine actin to the wider neuronal cytoskeleton. Disordered spine morphology of this kind recurs in intellectual disability and neurodegeneration.

The final step of regulated secretion is fusion of a vesicle with the plasma membrane, which releases neurotransmitters, hormones and granule contents into the extracellular space and delivers vesicle proteins to the cell surface. Fusion is driven by SNARE proteins — syntaxins with SNAP25 and related partners — whose zippering pulls the two bilayers together, while Munc18 (STXBP1) chaperones syntaxin and templates complex assembly. Calcium sensing by synaptotagmins and DOC2 proteins triggers release on demand, and complexins clamp primed vesicles so that fusion stays synchronous rather than spontaneous. Rab3A with rabphilin and active-zone scaffolds position vesicles for rapid reuse. Because this machinery sets the speed and fidelity of synaptic transmission, mutations cause epileptic encephalopathy and paroxysmal dyskinesia, while defects in the syntaxin-11 arm impair cytotoxic granule release and cause haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

Whether a nerve terminal releases transmitter depends on the voltage across its own membrane, and this pathway covers the receptors and channels that set that voltage at the presynaptic side rather than the postsynaptic one. It is the substrate of presynaptic inhibition and facilitation: by depolarizing or hyperpolarizing the terminal, and by shaping the width and amplitude of the invading action potential, it scales calcium entry and hence how much transmitter each spike releases. Ionotropic GABA, glycine, kainate, AMPA and NMDA receptors act as autoreceptors and heteroreceptors on terminals, metabotropic GABA-B receptors and G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels dampen excitability, while Kv1, Kv3, calcium-activated potassium and voltage-gated sodium channels determine spike shape and repolarization. This layer of control underlies short-term plasticity and gain setting in circuits, and mutations in these channels produce epilepsy and pain disorders.

Neurotransmitter release is triggered by a brief rise in calcium at the nerve terminal, and the processes that set presynaptic cytosolic calcium concentration determine how much transmitter a spike releases and how reliably a synapse follows repeated activity. Calcium enters through voltage-gated channels whose auxiliary beta subunits, CACNB2 and CACNB4, control channel trafficking and gating, and through ionotropic purinergic receptors; it is cleared by plasma membrane calcium ATPase pumps and buffered by the EF-hand proteins calbindin and calretinin, which shape the amplitude and time course of the transient. Presynaptic receptors for adenosine, ATP-derived nucleotides and endocannabinoids feed back on this calcium signal to depress release, while active zone scaffolds such as ERC2 and TSPOAP1 position channels near docked vesicles. Through these mechanisms the pathway underlies short-term plasticity, presynaptic inhibition and the excitability of synaptic terminals, with disruption linked to epilepsy and ataxia.

synaptic vesicle cytoskeletal transport moves synaptic vesicles and their precursors along microtubules and actin filaments so that presynaptic terminals, often far down an axon, are stocked with the vesicles needed for neurotransmitter release. Neurons depend on it because vesicle proteins are made in the soma but used at the synapse, and failures produce impaired transmission and neurodegenerative or neurodevelopmental phenotypes. The genes describe the machinery that links cargo to motors: the AP-3 adaptor complex, which sorts vesicle membrane proteins into transport carriers destined for the terminal; the BLOC-1 complex with dysbindin and snapin, which couples this sorting to vesicle biogenesis; a BORC subunit that recruits kinesins; the anterograde motor KIF1B; and microtubule-associated proteins including MAP2 and the axon-initial-segment organiser TRIM46 that define the tracks and their polarity. This connects membrane traffic, cytoskeletal organisation and synaptic function.

Neurons must deliver synaptic vesicles and their precursors from the cell body, where membrane proteins are packaged, out along the axon to distant presynaptic terminals, and this cytoskeletal transport of synaptic vesicles is how that delivery happens. Without it terminals are starved of releasable vesicles and neurotransmission fails, a defect linked to axonal neuropathy and to neuropsychiatric and pigmentation disorders. Two coat and sorting complexes dominate: the AP-3 adaptor, which routes cargo into vesicles destined for the terminal, and the BLOC-1 complex including dysbindin and snapin, which cooperates with it in cargo sorting and couples vesicles to motors. Kinesin KIF1B carries cargo anterograde along microtubules, while MAP2 and TRIM46 organise and bundle the axonal microtubule tracks that give the transport its direction. The pathway therefore ties membrane traffic to cytoskeletal polarity and to presynaptic vesicle supply.

Moving cargo along actin filaments gives cells a short-range transport system that complements microtubule-based trafficking, delivering organelles, vesicles and pigment granules into cortical regions and terminal processes where microtubules do not reach. Myosin motors do the work: MYO5A carries melanosomes and secretory vesicles toward the cell periphery and into neuronal dendrites, its loss causing pigmentary and neurological disease in Griscelli syndrome, while MYO1C links membranes to cortical actin and MYO19 positions mitochondria on actin tracks. Cargo attachment and track organisation are handled by partners such as the actin crosslinker ACTN4, the actin nucleation-promoting factor WASL and the F-BAR protein FNBP1L, which couples membrane curvature to actin assembly. SUN2 and SYNE2 tether the nucleus to the cytoskeleton, illustrating how the same machinery repositions the largest organelle during migration and tissue morphogenesis.

Vesicle cytoskeletal trafficking moves membrane cargo to the right place inside a cell by attaching it to motor proteins that walk along microtubules and actin filaments. It sets where organelles, lysosomes, synaptic vesicles and pigment granules sit, and is the reason neurons can supply distant axons and synapses at all; its failure produces hereditary spastic paraplegia, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome and the transport deficits seen in Huntington disease. Kinesins such as KIF1A, KIF5B and KIF13A drive anteriograde movement, myosin V hands cargo to actin at the cell periphery, and dynein with its regulators LIS1, NDEL1 and the BICD-like and TRAK adaptors pulls cargo back toward the centre. Adaptor and biogenesis complexes, including AP-3 and BLOC-1, select which cargo is loaded, coupling sorting at the endosome directly to long-range delivery and organelle positioning.

Membrane traffic inside a cell is not diffusion: vesicles and organelles are hauled along microtubules and actin filaments by motor proteins, and this directed transport is what places synaptic vesicles, endosomes, lysosomes and pigment granules where they are needed. Long-range movement depends on kinesins such as KIF1A, KIF5A and KIF13A for outward transport and on cytoplasmic dynein with its regulators NDE1, NDEL1 and PAFAH1B1 for retrograde delivery, while myosin V handles the final actin-based capture at the cell periphery. Adaptors link the motors to particular cargo: the AP-3 complex and the BLOC-1 subunits sort lysosome-related organelle proteins, TRAK1 and TRAK2 couple mitochondria, and huntingtin with HAP1 supports axonal transport. Because neurons have the longest routes, failure here produces hereditary spastic paraplegia, axonal neuropathies and neurodegeneration; defective AP-3 and BLOC-1 function instead causes albinism with bleeding diathesis.

Neurons release fast transmitters from small clear vesicles, but neuropeptides and neuromodulators such as serotonin and dopamine are packaged separately in dense core vesicles, and their calcium-triggered fusion at the presynaptic terminal is what this pathway describes. Because dense core vesicle cargo acts over longer distances and timescales than classical transmitter, this secretion sets the slow, modulatory tone of circuits, shaping mood, appetite, pain and neuroendocrine output rather than point-to-point signalling. Fusion uses the same core machinery as synaptic vesicle release: SNAP25 contributes to the SNARE complex, Munc18 proteins including STXBP1 chaperone syntaxin and prime vesicles for fusion, and the small GTPase RAB3A governs vesicle trafficking and docking near release sites. Loss of STXBP1 function causes severe early-onset epilepsy and developmental delay, underscoring how dependent neuronal signalling is on these shared exocytic steps.

Synaptic activity must be able to change gene expression if a transient stimulus is to become a lasting change in synaptic strength, and postsynapse-to-nucleus signalling is how that message travels. Rather than relying solely on diffusible second messengers, proteins resident at the postsynaptic density detach upon stimulation and are carried along the cytoskeleton into the nucleus, where they alter transcription, splicing or chromatin marks. The importin adaptor KPNA1 provides nuclear import competence for such cargoes, JAK2 and STAT3 couple receptor activation to transcription, RELA brings NF-kB-dependent programmes under synaptic control, and PRR7 and RNF10 are postsynaptic proteins with demonstrated nuclear roles. Wnt ligand signalling links extracellular cues at the synapse to the same output. This route underlies activity-dependent plasticity, learning and memory consolidation, and homeostatic scaling of synapses, and its disruption is relevant to intellectual disability and neurodegeneration.

After a synaptic vesicle has released its neurotransmitter and been retrieved from the presynaptic membrane, it can be routed through an endosomal intermediate rather than reused directly. Synaptic vesicle endosomal processing covers that detour: vesicles fuse with a presynaptic sorting endosome, vesicle proteins and lipids are separated from cargo destined for degradation or recycling, and fresh vesicles bud off competent for another round of release. This quality-control step keeps the releasable vesicle pool uniform in composition during sustained firing, so its failure degrades synaptic transmission and is linked to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease. The machinery is the general endomembrane toolkit adapted to the synapse: early and late endosomal Rab GTPases such as RAB11A and RAB7A with the tethering factor EEA1, a syntaxin for endosomal fusion, an adaptor complex subunit for cargo selection, and intersectins coupling endocytic events to the actin and vesicle cycle.

Synaptic signaling covers the transmission of chemical and electrical messages to, from and within synapses, the process that underlies all neural computation, learning and memory, and the control of muscle by motor neurons. Presynaptic machinery loads transmitter into vesicles and releases it in response to calcium entry through voltage-gated channels, using SNARE proteins such as SNAP25, syntaxin and VAMP2 together with synaptotagmin calcium sensors, Munc13 and Munc18 priming factors, and active zone scaffolds including bassoon, piccolo and RIM. Postsynaptically, ionotropic and metabotropic receptors for glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin and neuropeptides are organised by PSD-95, Homer and SHANK scaffolds and coupled to CaMKII, calcineurin and kinase cascades that adjust synaptic strength. Transporters clear and recycle transmitter, while neurexin, neuroligin and cadherin adhesion systems specify and maintain contacts. Disruption produces epilepsy, myasthenia, intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration.

Neurons communicate not only with fast transmitters but also with peptides released from dense-core vesicles, and synaptic signaling via neuropeptide covers that slower, modulatory layer of transmission. Peptides such as neuropeptide Y and proenkephalin act on G protein-coupled receptors, including the Y2 and Y5 receptors, to tune synaptic strength over seconds to minutes rather than milliseconds, shaping feeding behaviour, anxiety and stress responses, pain modulation and reward. Release depends on calcium-sensing machinery on secretory vesicles, with synaptotagmin family members coupling depolarisation to peptide exocytosis, while glutamate receptor components such as the delta-type receptors and a metabotropic glutamate receptor place this modulation alongside conventional excitatory signalling at the same synapses. Loss or dysregulation of peptidergic modulation contributes to appetite and mood disorders and to altered nociception.

Lipid messengers made in the postsynaptic cell can travel backwards across the synaptic cleft to tune transmitter release from the presynaptic terminal, and this trans-synaptic signalling by lipid is essentially the endocannabinoid arm of synaptic feedback. It provides short-term depression of excitatory and inhibitory transmission, protects circuits from over-excitation, and underlies the effects of cannabis on memory, appetite, pain and mood. Depolarization and Gq-coupled receptor activation drive phospholipase C beta, and diacylglycerol lipase alpha converts the resulting diacylglycerol into 2-arachidonoylglycerol, which acts on presynaptic cannabinoid receptors CNR1 and CNR2 with CNRIP1 as an interacting partner. Signalling is terminated by degradative enzymes: ABHD6 and FAAH hydrolyse the endocannabinoids, while FABP5 carries these hydrophobic ligands intracellularly. Loss of this restraint shifts the balance of excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Synapses are held together and instructed by protein bridges that span the cleft, and trans-synaptic signaling through these complexes is how a presynaptic terminal and its postsynaptic partner recognize each other, match their molecular contents, and decide whether a contact becomes a functioning synapse. Presynaptic neurexins and receptor phosphatases such as PTPRD engage postsynaptic partners, often through secreted intermediaries: cerebellins bridge neurexins to the delta-type glutamate receptors GRID1 and GRID2, while IL1RAPL1 and IL1RAP link back across the cleft to organize excitatory contacts, with FARP1 relaying adhesion into cytoskeletal and receptor clustering. Teneurin and ephrin-B3 contribute additional recognition codes, and dystroglycan anchors inhibitory inputs. This adhesive signalling specifies synapse identity, number and alignment of release sites with receptor fields, which is why mutations in NRXN1, IL1RAPL1 and PTPRD appear in autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia.

Synapses are not fixed connections; their strength and properties are continuously tuned by molecules released or displayed across the cleft, and this trans-synaptic modulation of synaptic transmission is how that tuning is achieved. It underlies learning-related plasticity, the wiring of specific circuits such as cerebellar parallel fibre inputs, and the structural maintenance of existing contacts; disruption is linked to autism, intellectual disability and obsessive-compulsive behaviour. Secreted C1q-domain proteins of the cerebellin and C1QL families bridge presynaptic neurexins to postsynaptic delta-type glutamate receptor subunits, forming a tripartite complex that specifies and stabilises excitatory synapses. Other members contribute retrograde and modulatory signals: endocannabinoid tone shaped by its degrading hydrolase and receptor, neurotrophin signalling through TrkB, ephrin and Slitrk adhesion cues, and proteases acting in the extracellular matrix surrounding the synapse.

Synapses are held together and tuned by protein bridges that span the cleft, and this trans-synaptic signalling adjusts how strongly and reliably a synapse transmits. The genes here form one of the best-defined of these bridges: secreted cerebellin adaptors bind presynaptic neurexins on one side and the delta-type glutamate receptors GRID1 and GRID2 on the other, physically linking the two halves of the synapse while setting postsynaptic receptor content and release properties. Ephrin-B3 contributes contact-dependent signalling at the same interface. The arrangement specifies where synapses form, which partners they choose, and how their strength is modulated during plasticity, with the cerebellin-neurexin-GluD2 axis governing parallel fibre to Purkinje cell connections and motor learning. Disruption of neurexins or GRID2 causes ataxia and is associated with autism and schizophrenia risk, placing this adhesion-based communication upstream of circuit refinement.

Synapses must hold their shape for years, and maintenance of synapse structure is the housekeeping that keeps presynaptic active zones aligned with postsynaptic scaffolds once a contact has formed. Loss of this upkeep produces synapse shrinkage, loss of spines and the cognitive and motor decline seen in neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disease; mutations in SYNGAP1 and TANC2 cause intellectual disability, and progranulin loss contributes to frontotemporal dementia. Large active-zone proteins such as Bassoon, Piccolo, ELKS/ERC and RIM family members organise vesicle release sites, while DLG1 and SHANK1 anchor receptors and cytoskeleton on the postsynaptic side. Secreted cerebellins and C1q-like proteins bridge the cleft as trans-synaptic adhesion complexes with adhesion GPCRs, and small GTPase regulators including ARF6, OPHN1 and GIT1 tune the underlying actin and membrane trafficking. Rapsyn performs the analogous clustering job at the neuromuscular junction.

Synapses hold together because the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes are physically clamped across the cleft by transmembrane adhesion molecules, and this attachment is what allows a contact to mature, specify whether it becomes excitatory or inhibitory, and persist as a stable circuit element. The genes here supply the trans-cellular pairs that do the clamping: cadherins and protocadherins for homophilic recognition, leucine-rich repeat proteins such as the SLITRK, LRRTM-like LRFN and NGL/LRRC4 families binding presynaptic receptor phosphatases PTPRD, PTPRS and PTPRF, netrin-G ligands, ephrin-A5, teneurin and FLRT3, with MDGA1 acting as a negative regulator of neuroligin-dependent adhesion and glypican-4 and SPARCL1 contributing secreted organizing cues. Through these codes adhesion sets synapse number, partner choice and receptor recruitment; disruption of several members is linked to autism, schizophrenia and obsessive-compulsive traits.

Excitatory synapses depend on a dense protein lattice beneath the postsynaptic membrane that anchors glutamate receptors and their signalling partners; maintaining postsynaptic density structure is what keeps that lattice organised once a synapse has formed. Without it, receptor content and spine morphology drift, synaptic strength becomes unstable, and the result is the kind of circuit dysfunction seen in autism spectrum and intellectual disability disorders, where several of these genes are recurrently mutated. The work is done largely by scaffolds: SHANK1 and DLG1 provide the multidomain platforms onto which receptors, adhesion molecules and cytoskeletal regulators are docked, TANC2 stabilises spines and dendritic arbors, and a liprin family member links the scaffold to presynaptic alignment. Membrane trafficking through ARF6 and planar-polarity signalling contribute, tying synaptic maintenance to receptor recycling and actin remodelling rather than to new synapse assembly.

Synapses are not fixed structures; dendritic spines and presynaptic terminals grow, shrink and change shape as circuits form and as experience modifies them, and this remodelling of synaptic structure is the physical substrate of learning and memory. The gene products here converge on the actin cytoskeleton beneath the postsynaptic membrane: cofilin and profilins control filament turnover, cortactin and the WAVE complex with CYFIP1 and BAIAP2 nucleate branched actin, and Rho-family GTPases such as RHOA together with GAPs and ABL1 kinase set the direction of change. Scaffolds of the DLGAP family and CTTNBP2 anchor this machinery to the postsynaptic density, while EPHA4 and dopamine receptor signalling supply extrinsic cues. Failure of spine remodelling is a recurring theme in intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia, and spine loss accompanies neurodegeneration, where SARM1-driven axon degeneration also acts.

Neurons communicate when transmitter released from one cell changes the membrane potential and internal ion composition of the next, and this describes the receiving half of that exchange: postsynaptic chemical synaptic transmission. It converts a brief chemical signal into depolarization, hyperpolarization, or calcium entry, setting whether a target neuron fires and how strongly its synapses are subsequently modified. Ligand-gated ion channels dominate — NMDA and AMPA-type glutamate receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors including the muscle endplate subunits, glycine and GABA-A subunits, serotonin type 3 channels and purinergic P2X channels — alongside G protein-coupled receptors for dopamine, adenosine and neuropeptides that tune responsiveness. Scaffolds and adhesion molecules such as PSD-95, SHANK proteins, neuroligins and neurexin organize receptors opposite release sites, while kinases and calcineurin link activity to plasticity. Disruption underlies myasthenic syndromes, hyperekplexia, epilepsy, and autism and schizophrenia risk.

Calcium entering the postsynaptic cytosol is the signal that converts synaptic activity into lasting change, and controlling how high it rises and how fast it falls sets the threshold for long-term potentiation and depression. The genes here span the routes that shape that transient: group I metabotropic glutamate receptors coupled to phospholipase C, the inositol trisphosphate receptor releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores, a plasma membrane calcium ATPase and neuronal sodium/calcium exchangers that clear it again, and calbindin buffering free ion in the cytosol. Several are enriched in cerebellar Purkinje cells, where this regulation underlies parallel fibre synaptic plasticity and motor learning; a scaffold linking delta2 glutamate receptors to the signalling machinery and Wnt5a-driven modulation tie the calcium response to synapse organisation. Loss of control here produces ataxia and disordered dendritic signalling.

Inorganic ion import across plasma membrane covers the channels, pumps and carriers that bring sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, protons, phosphate and trace metals such as zinc into the cytosol, setting the electrochemical gradients on which excitability, secretion and epithelial transport depend. Loss of these activities produces cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, renal salt-wasting and deafness, and several members are drug targets in diabetes and hypertension. The genes span voltage-gated calcium channels, inward-rectifier and KATP potassium channels with their sulfonylurea receptor subunits, epithelial sodium channels, TRP and purinergic cation channels, sodium-potassium ATPase subunits with FXYD modulators, and cation-chloride, sodium-proton, sodium-calcium and ZIP/ZnT solute carriers. Regulation is built in: calcineurin subunits, WNK-activated STK39, NEDD4L-mediated channel ubiquitination, scaffolds such as AKAP5 and ankyrin, and microRNAs tune transport capacity to hormonal and ischaemic demand.

Cells draw sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, protons, zinc and phosphate inward across the plasma membrane, and this inward transport sets resting membrane potential, drives electrical excitability, loads intracellular calcium stores, and supplies trace metals and nutrients. The machinery spans voltage-gated and ligand-gated channels, pacemaker and inwardly rectifying potassium channels, TRP channels acting as sensors of temperature and irritants, epithelial sodium channels, sodium-potassium pumps with their FXYD modulators, sodium-coupled cotransporters and exchangers of the chloride, proton and calcium families, plus zinc importers. Coupling is the theme: energy stored in a sodium or proton gradient pays for uptake of glucose, chloride or calcium extrusion. Regulation comes through kinases, calcineurin subunits, ubiquitin ligase-mediated channel retrieval and scaffolding proteins. Failures produce long QT and other arrhythmias, epilepsy, hypertension, renal salt-wasting syndromes, deafness and disorders of insulin secretion.

Synaptic strength depends not just on how many neurotransmitter receptors are present but on how they behave, and this regulatory layer tunes receptor gating, kinetics and ligand sensitivity at the postsynaptic membrane. Much of the set is the AMPA receptor auxiliary machinery: the TARP family of calcium channel gamma subunits, cornichon homologues, PRRT1 and SHISA7, which chaperone receptors to the surface and slow their deactivation and desensitization, shaping excitatory postsynaptic current amplitude and decay. A second theme is cholinergic modulation by secreted and GPI-anchored three-finger proteins such as LYNX1 and SLURP2, which act as endogenous brakes on nicotinic receptors and constrain cortical plasticity. Proteasome subunits contribute by degrading receptors and scaffolds during activity-dependent remodelling, while DAPK1 and opioid and CRH signalling components adjust receptor function during stress and injury. Disruption underlies epilepsy, ataxia and disordered synaptic plasticity.

Protein localization to axon is the sorting problem that makes a neuron polarized: proteins destined for the axon must be delivered there and held in place rather than diffusing back into the soma or dendrites. This positioning creates the functional domains of the axon, above all the axon initial segment and the nodes and juxtaparanodes of myelinated fibres, where clustered ion channels and adhesion molecules allow action potentials to initiate and propagate. TRIM46 organizes the parallel microtubule bundles that give the initial segment its identity, ankyrin-G anchors membrane proteins to that scaffold, and contactin and Caspr-family adhesion complexes fix components at axon-glia contact sites, with COPI coat subunits and myelin lipid enzymes supporting delivery. Loss of these anchoring and trafficking steps degrades conduction and is linked to epilepsy, neuropathy and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Neurons keep distinct protein compositions in the axon and the somatodendritic compartment, and protein localization to axon is the sorting, transport and anchoring activity that establishes and maintains that asymmetry. It underlies excitability itself: ion channels and adhesion molecules must be held at the axon initial segment, at nodes of Ranvier and along juxtaparanodes for action potentials to initiate and propagate saltatorily. Ankyrin-G provides the membrane-cytoskeletal scaffold that tethers channels at the initial segment and nodes, TRIM46 organizes the parallel microtubule bundles that define axonal identity and direct cargo entry, and contactin-family adhesion proteins with their associated CNTNAP partners position components at axon-glial contacts. Vesicular trafficking components and myelin-associated lipid and membrane proteins contribute to delivery and stabilization. Disruption affects nerve conduction and is linked to epilepsy, neurodevelopmental disorders and demyelinating neuropathy.

After a cardiac action potential fires, the ventricular or atrial myocyte must return its membrane to a negative resting potential before it can fire again, and cardiac muscle cell membrane repolarization is that recovery phase. Its timing sets action potential duration and the refractory period, so the pathway determines the QT interval on the electrocardiogram; delayed or accelerated repolarization causes long and short QT syndromes, Brugada syndrome and catecholaminergic arrhythmias, with risk of torsades de pointes and sudden death. Repolarizing current is carried largely by voltage-gated potassium channels and their accessory subunits — the rapid and slow delayed rectifiers KCNH2 and KCNQ1 with KCNE partners, transient outward KCND3 with KCNIP2, and inward rectifiers of the KCNJ family — balanced against depolarizing sodium and calcium channels such as SCN5A and CACNA1D. Anchoring and scaffolding proteins including ANK2, AKAP9, CAV3 and SNTA1 localize these channels, while nitric oxide signalling and calcium handling modulate the process.

regulation of cardiac muscle cell membrane repolarization controls how quickly a heart muscle cell returns to its resting potential after each action potential, and therefore sets the QT interval and the refractory period that keeps beats orderly. When it fails, repolarization is delayed or dispersed and the myocardium becomes vulnerable to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes, the basis of congenital and drug-induced long QT syndromes as well as short QT and Brugada phenotypes. The work is done largely by potassium channels carrying the delayed rectifier currents, KCNQ1 and KCNH2 tuned by their KCNE accessory subunits, balanced against depolarizing sodium and L-type calcium currents. Scaffolding and anchoring proteins such as ankyrin-B, AKAP9, caveolin-3 and syntrophin position these channels in the sarcolemma and couple them to kinase and nitric oxide signalling, while calcium handling and microRNA-mediated control adjust the balance beat to beat.

Each heartbeat ends with repolarization, the potassium-driven return of the cardiomyocyte membrane toward its resting potential, and the processes that tune this phase set the duration of the action potential and hence the QT interval. Control here determines refractoriness and the safety margin against arrhythmia: too little repolarizing current lengthens the plateau and invites torsade de pointes and sudden death, as in the long QT syndromes, while excess shortens it. The core effectors are the delayed rectifier channels KCNQ1 and KCNH2 together with their KCNE accessory subunits, whose gating and surface levels are modulated by the scaffold AKAP9, ankyrin-B-dependent targeting, caveolin-3 and syntrophin microdomains, and nitric oxide signalling via NOS1 and its adaptor NOS1AP. Sodium channel beta subunits, L-type calcium channel components and calsequestrin link repolarization to depolarizing and calcium-handling currents, and microRNAs add transcriptional-level tuning.</description>

Atrial myocytes must return their membrane potential to rest after each action potential, and how quickly they do so sets atrial refractoriness and the vulnerability of the atria to fibrillation. Repolarization here is carried by potassium currents with a distinctly atrial flavour: KCNA5 underlies the ultrarapid delayed rectifier largely confined to atrium, KCNQ1 with accessory subunits such as KCNE5 carries the slow delayed rectifier, KCNJ3 and KCNJ5 form the acetylcholine-activated inward rectifier through which vagal input shortens the atrial action potential, and KCNN2 provides calcium-activated potassium efflux. Opposing them, the sodium channel SCN5A and the L-type calcium channel CACNA1D shape upstroke and plateau, while FLNA anchors channels in the sarcolemma. Mutations in these channels cause inherited atrial fibrillation, short and long QT syndromes, and conduction disease, linking the process to electrical remodelling, natriuretic peptide signalling and arrhythmia risk.

Each ventricular beat ends with repolarization of the cardiac muscle cell membrane, the outward-current phase that terminates the action potential plateau and restores a negative resting potential so the chamber can relax and refill. Its timing sets the QT interval, and delay or shortening of it produces long QT and short QT syndromes, torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death. The repolarizing charge is carried mainly by potassium channels — the rapid and slow delayed rectifiers built from KCNH2 and KCNQ1 with their KCNE accessory subunits, plus transient outward and inward rectifier channels — while sodium channel subunits around SCN5A determine how much depolarizing current persists. Scaffolding and anchoring proteins including ANK2, AKAP9, CAV3, SNTA1 and NOS1AP place these channels in the sarcolemma and couple them to kinase and nitric oxide signalling, and calcium handling proteins such as CASQ2 link the process to excitation–contraction coupling.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane at any moment, and neurotransmitter receptor transport is the trafficking machinery that sets that number. Receptors are carried from the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi to dendrites, inserted at or near the synapse, endocytosed, and then either recycled back or sorted for degradation; this turnover is the physical substrate of long-term potentiation and depression, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, autism and neurodegenerative synapse loss. The genes here span the steps: GRIP1 and GRIP2 with GRIPAP1 tether AMPA receptor subunits to motors and endosomes, RAB8A and RAB11A direct recycling-endosome delivery into spines, the retromer subunit VPS35 sorts receptors away from the lysosomal route, HIP1 and AP3D1 act in clathrin- and vesicle-based internalization, and AKAP5 anchors kinases that control receptor insertion locally.

Proteins that reach the endosome are not necessarily destined for degradation; endosome-to-plasma-membrane transport returns them to the cell surface in vesicles, setting how many receptors, channels and transporters a cell displays at any moment. This recycling arm determines synaptic strength, since AMPA receptor delivery depends on the GRIP scaffolds, GRIPAP1 and the retromer subunit VPS35, and it controls metabolic responses such as insulin-stimulated glucose transporter appearance, where TRARG1 acts. Rab GTPases give the route its identity: RAB11A marks recycling endosomes, RAB8A drives exocytic delivery, and RAB7A marks the late endosomal compartment from which cargo may instead be retrieved. Polarity determinants like SCRIB and the retromer-associated sorting receptor SORL1 select cargo, linking this traffic to epithelial organisation and, through amyloid precursor protein handling, to Alzheimer's disease risk.

Neurons are extreme in scale: proteins made in the soma must travel far along axons and dendrites to reach synapses, and axo-dendritic protein transport is the microtubule-based delivery system that gets them there. Without it, synaptic receptors, scaffolds and organelles fail to reach their destinations, and the resulting traffic jams underlie motor neuron degeneration and hereditary spastic paraplegia. Kinesin-1 heavy chains KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C provide the anterograde motor force, with MAPK8IP3 (JIP3) acting as an adaptor linking cargo to motors and coupling transport to stress-activated kinase signalling. Microtubule-associated MAP1A stabilises the tracks, HSPB1 chaperones the cytoskeleton against proteotoxic stress, and cargoes include synaptic membrane proteins such as the postsynaptic scaffold DLG2 and the glutamate receptor auxiliary subunit NETO1. The pathway therefore sets how quickly and where synaptic composition can be remodelled.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors are held in the postsynaptic membrane facing the release site, and this pathway covers their delivery to, clustering at, and retention within the postsynaptic specialization. It underlies learning-related plasticity, since trafficking of AMPA-type glutamate receptors in and out of the density is the substrate of long-term potentiation and depression, and its failure produces intellectual disability, epilepsy and autism phenotypes. Scaffolds of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase family, notably PSD-95, tether receptors beneath the membrane, while gephyrin and rapsyn perform the analogous job for inhibitory glycine/GABA receptors and for acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Auxiliary subunits such as the TARPs, cornichon and NETO proteins chaperone receptors to the surface and tune their gating, and secreted organizers including C1QL and pentraxin proteins align receptor fields with presynaptic terminals across the cleft.

Expansion of the endothelial cell population lining blood vessels is the proliferative step that allows new vessels to sprout and grow, underlying wound healing, the menstrual cycle and placental development, and also tumour vascularisation and retinopathy when it runs unchecked. Growth factor input dominates: FGF2 acting through FGFR1, VEGF binding FLT1, and the apelin/APJ and ghrelin ligand-receptor pairs feed into PI3K-AKT signalling via PDPK1 and AKT3, phospholipase C-gamma, and STAT3-dependent transcription, with TGFBR1 and PPARG providing restraining or modulating input. Inflammatory cues such as CCL2 and extracellular HMGB1 couple vessel growth to tissue damage, while ADAM17 shedding and integrin-basement membrane contacts set the local context. A large complement of microRNAs, among them the endothelial-enriched miR-126, miR-21 and the miR-424/503 cluster, tunes how strongly these cues translate into cell division.

mitotic nuclear membrane organization covers the breakdown of the nuclear envelope as a cell enters mitosis and its rebuilding around the two daughter nuclei at exit. Getting this right determines whether chromosomes are correctly enclosed, whether nuclear transport and chromatin organisation are restored, and whether micronuclei or envelope ruptures arise that drive genome instability. Reassembly requires clearing endoplasmic reticulum membrane tubules from the chromatin surface, a job of the REEP proteins, followed by membrane recruitment and flattening onto chromatin through BAF and the ANKLE2-dependent dephosphorylation of BAF that reverses its mitotic inactivation. Closure of the reforming envelope uses the ESCRT machinery, with VPS4A and its regulators together with spastin-mediated severing of spindle microtubules trapped in the sealing gap. SIRT2 and RCC1 tie the process to mitotic timing and to Ran-based nuclear identity.

When a cell divides, the nuclear envelope must be taken apart and then rebuilt around each daughter genome, and this mitotic nuclear membrane organization covers both halves of that job. It matters because reforming a sealed envelope is what restores nuclear compartmentalization, allows chromatin decondensation and nucleocytoplasmic transport to resume, and prevents micronuclei and DNA damage from persisting membrane holes. Barrier-to-autointegration factor tethers chromatin to inner membrane proteins during reassembly and is regulated by phosphorylation, with ANKLE2 controlling that cycle; ESCRT-associated activities including VPS4A and BROX contribute to sealing the final gaps, while the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin clears spindle microtubules trapped in the closing envelope. Membrane-shaping reticulon-like REEP proteins clear endoplasmic reticulum from the metaphase chromatin region, and SUMO conjugation and RCC1-generated Ran-GTP gradients help position these events in space and time.

intestinal hexose absorption is the step by which dietary sugars released by carbohydrate digestion cross the small intestinal epithelium and enter the blood, supplying the body with its main circulating fuel. Loss of the machinery causes osmotic diarrhoea and malabsorption, as in glucose-galactose malabsorption from defects in the sodium-glucose cotransporter, while fructose handling depends separately on the facilitative carrier GLUT5. Uptake occurs across the brush border of absorptive enterocytes, whose microvillar structure is built and maintained by villin, ezrin and plastin, greatly expanding the surface available for transport. Sodium-coupled uptake requires a continuously replenished luminal sodium supply, which claudin-2 and claudin-15 provide by making the tight junctions of the small intestine cation-permeable. The pathway thus links epithelial architecture, paracellular ion flux and transcellular transport to whole-body glucose supply and postprandial nutrition.

Dietary carbohydrate is useless until its monosaccharide products cross the intestinal epithelium, and intestinal hexose absorption is the step that moves glucose, galactose and fructose from the gut lumen into the blood. It sets the postprandial rise in blood sugar and, when it fails, produces osmotic diarrhoea and carbohydrate intolerance: loss of the sodium-glucose cotransporter SLC5A1 causes glucose-galactose malabsorption, while the facilitative fructose transporter SLC2A5 handles fructose entry. Uptake is secondarily active, driven by the sodium gradient across the brush border, so it depends on the architecture of the absorptive enterocyte surface. Villin, ezrin and fimbrin build and anchor the microvillar actin bundles that provide that surface, and the claudins CLDN2 and CLDN15 make the tight junction cation-permeable, recycling luminal sodium to sustain transport.

Tissue injury triggers an inflammatory reaction that must be strong enough to clear debris and microbes yet contained enough to allow repair, and this pathway sets that balance by tuning the intensity and duration of the inflammatory response to wounding. Its failure shows up as chronic non-healing wounds, fibrosis, or excessive scarring, and in the gut and skin as persistent barrier inflammation. Alarmins and cytokines released from damaged epithelium, including IL33 and IL17A, recruit and activate leukocytes, while ALOX5 initiates leukotriene synthesis from arachidonate to amplify chemotaxis. Restraint comes from the phosphatase PTPN6, which dampens immunoreceptor signalling, from SIGLEC10 engagement of damage-associated ligands, and from progranulin, whose loss unleashes neuroinflammation. STAT3 couples these cytokine inputs to epithelial survival and proliferation, linking inflammatory control directly to wound closure and regeneration.

Wound healing depends on inflammation being switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this damping of the inflammatory response to wounding limits collateral tissue destruction, chronic ulceration and fibrosis once repair is underway. The genes involved act at several levels: the phosphatase PTPN6 restrains immunoreceptor signalling in myeloid cells, SIGLEC10 delivers inhibitory signals upon engagement of danger-associated ligands, and STAT3 mediates anti-inflammatory cytokine responses that curtail neutrophil-driven damage. Epithelial and matrix components such as DSG2 and REG3A contribute to barrier restoration and to shaping the local immune tone, while alarmins and growth factors including IL33 and MDK couple tissue injury to controlled resolution rather than sustained inflammation. Loss of this restraint favours persistent inflammatory infiltration, delayed re-epithelialisation and scarring, which is why the same machinery is relevant to inflammatory skin, gut and lung disease.

Neurons acquire their shape by building, arranging and dismantling axons and dendrites, and this organization of neuronal projections determines where a cell can receive input and where it can send output. It underlies circuit wiring during development and the structural plasticity that supports learning, and its disruption features in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration. Much of the work is cytoskeletal: Rho-family GTPase signalling through CDC42 and PAK3, actin regulators such as cofilin, cortactin and drebrin, and microtubule-based transport by kinesins and dynactin shape growth cones and spines. Guidance and adhesion receptors, including several Eph receptors, ephrins, neuroligin and reelin signalling through LRP8, position projections, while scaffolds of the postsynaptic density such as DLG4, SHANK and HOMER1 organize dendritic spines. Kinases including CDK5 with its activator p35, GSK3B and FYN couple these cues to the cytoskeleton, and APP, PSEN1, APOE and LRRK2 tie the process to disease.

Calcineurin is the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase that converts a sustained rise in cytosolic calcium into gene expression, chiefly by dephosphorylating NFAT transcription factors so they enter the nucleus. Tuning this relay sets the threshold for T cell activation, cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophy and fibre-type switching, and it is the axis blocked therapeutically by immunosuppressants. Regulation operates at several levels: the catalytic subunits PPP3CA/CB/CC pair with regulatory subunits, scaffolds such as AKAP5 and AKAP6 tether the enzyme near calcium channels and receptors, and inhibitory modules including RCAN1, the calcineurin B homologues CHP1/CHP2, and the sarcomeric myozenins restrain or localise its activity. Counteracting kinases like GSK3B re-export NFAT from the nucleus, while calcium extrusion and exchange proteins shape the signal itself. Excessive output drives pathological cardiac remodelling; too little compromises lymphocyte responses.

negative regulation of calcineurin-mediated signaling restrains the calcium-activated phosphatase that dephosphorylates NFAT transcription factors, setting limits on how strongly a rise in intracellular calcium is converted into changes in gene expression. This braking function matters in T cell activation, where unchecked calcineurin drives cytokine production, and in striated muscle and heart, where sustained NFAT activity remodels fibre type and produces pathological hypertrophy. The genes act through several devices: RCAN1 and TBC1D10C bind and inhibit the phosphatase directly, myozenins and HOMER proteins tether it to the sarcomeric Z-disc away from its substrates, calcium pumps and CHP1 lower the activating signal, and kinases including GSK3B and DYRK2 re-phosphorylate NFAT to export it from the nucleus. Loss of this restraint underlies cardiac remodelling and contributes to the immune overactivation that calcineurin inhibitor drugs are used to suppress.

Calcineurin is the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase that dephosphorylates NFAT transcription factors and lets them enter the nucleus, driving T cell activation, cardiac hypertrophic growth and slow-twitch muscle fibre programmes. The braking arm described here keeps that output transient and proportional to the calcium signal, so that lymphocytes are not chronically activated and the heart does not remodel inappropriately. Inhibition works at several levels: direct inhibitors such as RCAN1 and CHP1 bind the phosphatase, sarcomeric scaffolds including the myozenins and FHL2 sequester it at the Z-disc away from nuclear substrates, and kinases such as GSK3B and DYRK2 counter-phosphorylate NFAT to promote its nuclear export. Calcium clearance by the plasma membrane ATPase ATP2B4 removes the upstream trigger. Loss of this restraint contributes to pathological cardiac hypertrophy and to Down syndrome-associated phenotypes linked to RCAN1 dosage.

Calcineurin is the calcium- and calmodulin-activated phosphatase that translates sustained rises in intracellular calcium into changes in gene expression, most famously by dephosphorylating NFAT transcription factors so they enter the nucleus. Positive regulation of calcineurin-mediated signaling covers the inputs and scaffolds that raise the rate or extent of this relay, and it matters because the same axis drives T cell activation after antigen receptor engagement, cardiac and skeletal muscle hypertrophic growth, and activity-dependent plasticity in neurons; it is the step blocked therapeutically by cyclosporine and tacrolimus to prevent graft rejection. The catalytic and regulatory subunits themselves are present alongside anchoring proteins that position the phosphatase near calcium channels and receptors, calcium-binding modulators, and upstream stimuli including growth factor and innate immune receptor signalling and inflammatory cytokine exposure.
