Receptors that couple to Gs raise cAMP, and this pathway covers the controls that set how strongly and how long that signal runs. Tuning matters physiologically: melanocortin signalling in the hypothalamus and skin depends on it, so the same regulators shape appetite and energy balance as well as pigmentation. Control is exerted at several levels. Endogenous peptides derived from POMC act as agonists while AGRP and agouti signalling protein act as antagonists or inverse agonists at melanocortin receptors, and accessory proteins MRAP and MRAP2 determine receptor trafficking and responsiveness. Inhibitory Gα subunits oppose cyclase activation, and a large family of phosphodiesterases including PDE3B, PDE4B and PDE4D hydrolyses cAMP to terminate the response. Kinases, scaffolds such as RACK1, and the transcriptional coactivator CRTC3 feed the output back onto gene expression. Loss of these brakes contributes to obesity and metabolic disease.

Many hormones and neurotransmitters act by engaging receptors that couple through Gs to adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP; this pathway covers the inputs that turn that signalling up, increasing how often or how strongly the cyclase is engaged. Enhanced cAMP output matters for adrenal steroid production, energy balance and synaptic modulation, and losing it produces recognisable disease: the accessory proteins MRAP and MRAP2 are needed for melanocortin receptors to reach the surface and respond properly, with MRAP loss causing familial glucocorticoid deficiency and MRAP2 disruption causing obesity. POMC supplies the melanocortin peptide agonists themselves, so ligand availability is part of the regulation. Kinases such as PRKCA and GSK3A act on receptors and downstream components to bias signalling, while presynaptic adhesion and nitric oxide components link the same amplification to neuronal and synaptic contexts.

Receptors that raise cAMP through Gs and adenylate cyclase must be shut off as well as switched on, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that limit such signalling. Damping cAMP output sets the gain on hormone responses ranging from melanocortin control of appetite and pigmentation to catecholamine effects on heart and adipose tissue, and losing the brakes produces persistent signalling, obesity, or unchecked lipolysis. The genes act at several levels: endogenous antagonists and inverse agonists of melanocortin receptors such as agouti and agouti-related peptide, accessory proteins and an E3 ligase that control receptor trafficking and surface availability, the inhibitory G protein alpha subunit that opposes adenylate cyclase directly, and a set of phosphodiesterases that hydrolyse cAMP to terminate the second-messenger signal. Downstream, a CREB-regulated transcription coactivator provides feedback onto cAMP-driven gene expression.

Accurate protein synthesis depends on each tRNA carrying the amino acid its anticodon specifies, and this proofreading arm of aminoacyl-tRNA metabolism is what keeps translational fidelity high. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases for alanine, isoleucine, leucine, valine and threonine can misactivate near-isosteric amino acids, so they carry editing domains that hydrolyse mischarged products; separate trans-editing factors, including the D-aminoacyl-tRNA deacylases and free-standing synthetase-like domains, clear errors the synthetases themselves miss, notably D-amino acids wrongly attached to tRNA. Both cytosolic and mitochondrial enzyme pairs are represented, so the same quality control operates on the mitochondrial translation machinery. When editing fails, mistranslated proteins accumulate and misfold, and mutations in these enzymes cause neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy, hypomyelination and other mitochondrial disease phenotypes, placing this chemistry upstream of proteome integrity rather than within any one biosynthetic route.

Excitatory synapses work only if AMPA- and NMDA-type glutamate receptors are concentrated in the postsynaptic membrane opposite a release site, and regulation of glutamate receptor clustering sets how many receptors are held there. The strength of an individual synapse, and its capacity for long-term potentiation and depression, follows directly from this control, so disruption produces intellectual disability and movement disorders as well as blunted learning. The genes involved act at several points: auxiliary subunits such as FRRS1L, SHISA6 and SHISA7 bind AMPA receptors and govern their trafficking, gating and retention at the synapse; the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC2 lipid-modifies scaffold proteins to stabilise receptor anchoring; GIT1 links small GTPase signalling to spine architecture; and SSH1, a slingshot phosphatase, acts on cofilin to remodel the actin cytoskeleton that supports the postsynaptic density. The result connects synaptic adhesion and cytoskeletal dynamics to receptor number and synaptic plasticity.

Enzymes that act on DNA can become stuck to it, and topoisomerases, methyltransferases and abasic-site intermediates all leave bulky protein adducts that block replication forks and transcription. Repair of protein-DNA covalent cross-links clears these lesions so that replication can finish, and its failure produces replication stress, chromosome instability and premature-ageing phenotypes; loss of the protease SPRTN causes Ruijs-Aalfs syndrome with early hepatocellular carcinoma. The pathway works largely by proteolysis at the fork: SPRTN and the related FAM111 proteases and the germ-cell protease GCNA degrade the trapped protein, TEX264 and the ubiquitin-selective segregase VCP with its deubiquitinase partner VCPIP1 deliver and extract substrates, and TRAIP marks barriers encountered by the replisome. HMCES instead shields abasic sites in single-stranded DNA by forming a protective, reversible crosslink of its own, linking this repair to translesion synthesis and fork restart.

Newly made tRNAs that are misfolded, hypomodified or incorrectly processed are identified and destroyed rather than allowed to enter translation, and tRNA surveillance is the quality-control arm that makes this decision. Removing defective tRNAs protects the fidelity and efficiency of protein synthesis, since a mischarged or unstable tRNA would otherwise cause mistranslation or ribosome stalling. Much of the work is done by the multisubunit exosome, whose core and catalytic subunits provide the 3'-to-5' exonuclease activity that degrades rejected transcripts, aided by a zinc-knuckle cofactor that helps recruit substrates to the nuclear complex. The CCA-adding enzyme contributes by rebuilding or repeatedly appending 3' ends, so that a failure to mature properly marks a tRNA for turnover. Loss of these activities links nucleotide-level surveillance to human disease, including the anaemia and immunodeficiency syndromes caused by CCA-enzyme and exosome subunit mutations.

Cells rebuild purine nucleotides from bases and nucleosides recovered from nucleic acid turnover rather than paying the energetic cost of de novo synthesis, and purine ribonucleotide salvage is that recycling route. It keeps adenine and guanine nucleotide pools balanced in tissues that synthesise little purine of their own, notably brain and erythrocytes. Phosphoribosyltransferases reattach ribose phosphate to hypoxanthine, guanine and adenine, while adenosine kinase phosphorylates adenosine and so also limits how much adenosine escapes to act on extracellular receptors. Deaminases converting AMP to IMP and a synthetase returning IMP toward AMP complete an interconversion cycle that couples salvage to adenylate energy charge. Loss of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase causes urate overproduction with severe neurological and self-injurious disease, and muscle AMP deaminase deficiency produces exercise intolerance, showing how directly these steps support nucleotide homeostasis.

basolateral protein secretion is the arm of polarized trafficking that delivers proteins to the basal and lateral surfaces of an epithelial cell, the faces that contact neighbouring cells and the underlying basement membrane. Epithelia depend on it to keep transporters, adhesion receptors and growth factor receptors segregated away from the apical membrane, which is what allows vectorial transport across a sheet of cells in kidney, gut and liver. Sorting occurs largely at the trans-Golgi network and recycling endosomes through the AP-1 clathrin adaptor complex, whose subunits recognize cytoplasmic basolateral sorting signals; the epithelium-specific mu subunit AP1M2 confers this selectivity, and its loss causes cargo such as anion exchangers to be missorted apically. Failure of the pathway collapses epithelial polarity, disrupting ion and bicarbonate handling and contributing to congenital diarrhoeal and cholestatic disease.

Epithelial cells face two different worlds, and basolateral protein secretion is how they deliver cargo to the side and base of the cell, toward neighbouring cells and the underlying basement membrane, rather than to the apical surface. This polarized delivery establishes and maintains epithelial asymmetry, positioning transporters, adhesion receptors and growth factor receptors where they can act on the interstitial side; its loss scrambles polarity and compromises vectorial transport in kidney tubule and intestinal epithelium. Sorting depends on a clathrin adaptor complex built from large, medium and small subunits, in which an epithelium-enriched mu subunit recognizes tyrosine- and dileucine-based basolateral signals in cargo cytoplasmic tails at recycling and trans-Golgi compartments. Bicarbonate-transporting membrane proteins are among the cargoes whose basolateral placement makes transepithelial ion and acid-base handling possible.

Basement membranes are thin sheets of specialized extracellular matrix that underlie epithelia and surround muscle, nerve and endothelium, and their assembly has to be controlled in time and place for tissues to acquire polarity and mechanical integrity. The genes here govern that control: laminin heterotrimers built from alpha, beta and gamma subunits polymerize at the cell surface after engaging integrins and dystroglycan, and nidogen bridges the laminin network to type IV collagen, so their availability sets the rate and extent of membrane formation and remodelling. Consequences of failure are tissue-specific and severe — laminin alpha-2 loss causes congenital muscular dystrophy through detachment of muscle fibres from their sheath, while laminin beta-2 loss disrupts the glomerular filtration barrier and neuromuscular junction. The same regulation shapes epithelial branching, neurite guidance and vascular basement membrane maturation.

Contractile bundles built from actin filaments and myosin drive cell shape change, adhesion, migration, cytokinesis and the contractility of muscle and smooth-muscle-like cells, and this pathway covers the control of how such actomyosin structures are assembled, arranged and taken apart. Much of the regulation converges on Rho-family GTPases: RHOA, RHOC, RAC1 and CDC42 are switched by a large set of exchange factors and GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGEF18, DLC1 and ARHGAP28, and act through ROCK1/2, PAK kinases and LIMK1 to tune myosin light-chain phosphorylation and cofilin-dependent filament turnover. Formins including FHOD1 and FHOD3, profilins, tropomyosin, WAS-family nucleation promoters and focal-adhesion proteins such as paxillin and kindlin-2 supply the filaments and their anchorage, while upstream cues from TGF-beta, lysophospholipid, integrin and endothelin receptors set the level of tension. Proper regulation maintains endothelial and epithelial junction integrity, sarcomere organization in cardiac muscle, and orderly wound closure; loss of it produces cardiomyopathy and unrestrained invasive motility.

Cardiac muscle myoblast proliferation is the expansion of cells already committed to a heart muscle fate but still able to divide, and it determines how much myocardium is built during development and how much regenerative reserve remains afterwards. Because adult cardiomyocytes divide poorly, the size of this progenitor pool constrains repair after infarction, and its misregulation contributes to hypertrophic and congenital heart disease. Control here is transcriptional and post-transcriptional: GATA6 and the homeodomain factor MEIS2 act within the cardiac gene regulatory network that specifies and patterns progenitors, while ATF2 couples stress- and growth-factor-activated kinase signalling to CRE-dependent transcription of cell cycle genes. Several microRNAs tune the same decision by repressing proliferative or differentiation transcripts, setting the balance between continued division and exit into a contractile, terminally differentiated cardiomyocyte state.

When a replication fork stalls or reverses, the nascent DNA end must be trimmed back in a controlled way so that the fork can be restarted or repaired by homologous recombination, and this resection step at processed forks is that trimming. Too little leaves an unusable structure; too much degrades nascent DNA and causes the genome instability and chemosensitivity seen when BRCA1 function is lost. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex makes the initial nicks and provides the nuclease activity, CtIP (RBBP8) and the BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer license and direct end processing, and EXO1 extends resection to generate long 3' single-stranded tails for RAD51 loading. Counterweights limit the reaction: DYNLL1 restrains MRE11, and SAMHD1 also contributes to fork resection control. The balance struck here determines whether a stressed fork is rescued or collapses into a break.

Oocytes and spermatocytes arrest in G2 before entering the first meiotic division, and the controls that govern the G2-to-metaphase I transition decide when that arrest is released. This is the gate that licenses meiotic entry, so its timing determines oocyte maturation competence and orderly chromosome segregation; premature or delayed release contributes to aneuploid gametes and infertility. The switch is imposed on cyclin-dependent kinase activity by opposing enzymes: the CDC25 family of dual-specificity phosphatases removes the inhibitory phosphates that hold CDK1 inactive, while the membrane-associated kinase PKMYT1 places them, keeping the kinase silent until the balance tips. Additional kinases and a deubiquitinase modulate this set point, coupling upstream hormonal and checkpoint inputs to commitment. The logic is shared with the mitotic G2/M decision but is adapted to the prolonged arrest characteristic of germ cells.

Enzymes are not perfectly specific, and normal metabolism continuously generates side products that are useless or actively toxic. Metabolite repair is the housekeeping chemistry that intercepts these by-products and converts them back into usable intermediates or disposes of them, protecting enzymes and cofactor pools from poisoning. Two dedicated damage-repair activities illustrate the logic: NAXE and NAXD together handle hydrated, non-functional forms of NADH and NADPH, restoring redox cofactor supply and, when lost, causing a severe early-onset neurometabolic encephalopathy. Other members act in mitochondrial acyl-CoA and organic acid handling, with CLYBL cleaving citramalyl-CoA in a route that intersects itaconate and vitamin B12 metabolism, and AUH acting in leucine catabolism. Adenosine kinase salvages adenosine, while succinyl-CoA ligase subunits link the pathway to the citric acid cycle. Failures surface as accumulating abnormal metabolites and inborn errors of metabolism.

Primary metabolism generates side products that are chemically reactive or inhibitory, and toxic metabolite repair is the set of enzymatic steps that convert such by-products back into usable intermediates rather than letting them accumulate. This kind of metabolite damage control protects enzymes and cofactors from being poisoned or irreversibly inactivated, and its loss produces metabolic disease even though no canonical biosynthetic route is missing. Several members act in mitochondrial acyl-CoA and citric acid cycle metabolism: citramalyl-CoA lyase clears the itaconate-derived thioester that would otherwise inactivate vitamin B12-dependent chemistry, methylglutaconyl-CoA hydratase handles an intermediate of leucine breakdown, and the two subunits of succinyl-CoA ligase interconvert succinate and its CoA thioester. Others return modified or salvaged nucleotides to the adenylate pool through phosphorylation and deamination. Deficiencies in the succinyl-CoA ligase subunits cause encephalomyopathy with mitochondrial DNA depletion, linking this repair capacity to mitochondrial maintenance.

regulation of actin filament organization controls how actin filaments are nucleated, capped, severed, bundled and cross-linked, and therefore sets cell shape, motility, adhesion and division. It is the layer of control that lets a leukocyte crawl toward a chemokine, a podocyte maintain its foot processes, a platelet spread, and a growth cone steer. Rho-family GTPases and their many exchange factors and GAPs act as the master switches, feeding into effectors such as ROCK, PAK and LIMK, which in turn regulate cofilin and other severing and depolymerising factors. Nucleation and elongation are handled by Arp2/3 with its WAVE, WASH and WASP activators, formins, profilins and Ena/VASP proteins, while capping proteins, gelsolins, tropomodulins, spectrins and adducins define filament length and higher-order networks. Loss of components produces immunodeficiency, nephrotic syndrome, cardiomyopathy and neurodevelopmental disease, reflecting how broadly cytoskeletal remodelling is used.

Cells build, branch, bundle and dismantle actin filaments continuously, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how much of each happens and where. It determines cell shape and stiffness, lamellipodial and filopodial protrusion, migration, phagocytosis, junction and podocyte integrity, and sarcomeric and spectrin-based cortical architecture; loss of control produces defects in immune cell motility, wound healing, kidney filtration and neuronal morphology. Rho-family GTPases with their many activators and inactivators feed into effector kinases such as ROCK, PAK and LIMK, which in turn govern cofilin-mediated severing, counterbalanced by slingshot phosphatases. Nucleation and elongation are handled by Arp2/3 with WAVE, WASH and WASP regulators, formins and profilin, while capping proteins, gelsolin, tropomodulins, twinfilin and thymosin set filament ends and monomer pools. Adhesion, membrane phosphoinositide and growth factor inputs, including PI3K and mTOR complex components, couple external cues to this remodelling.

Negative regulation of ferroptosis is the set of defences that keep cells from dying by iron-dependent lipid peroxidation. Ferroptosis destroys membranes when polyunsaturated phospholipids oxidise unchecked, and suppressing it lets cells survive oxidative and nutrient stress; tumour cells exploit these same defences to resist therapy, while their failure contributes to neurodegeneration and ischaemic tissue injury. The core protection is glutathione-dependent: a cystine importer supplies cysteine and a selenoprotein peroxidase reduces lipid hydroperoxides, backed by a parallel CoQ/vitamin K route through FSP1. Iron is sequestered in ferritin and handled by heme oxygenase, while NRF2 with its adaptor SQSTM1 drives the transcriptional arm, inducing NQO1, glutathione transferases and cysteine-supplying serine metabolism. Citrate transport and ACLY link lipid synthesis to susceptibility, and AMPK signalling restrains fatty acid production under energy stress, tying survival decisions to metabolic state.

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent death triggered when lipid peroxides accumulate faster than a cell can detoxify them, and the defences collected here are what keep most cells from crossing that threshold. Their failure is exploited therapeutically in tumours and contributes to neurodegeneration and ischemic tissue injury. The core protection is enzymatic: a selenoprotein glutathione peroxidase reduces lipid hydroperoxides using glutathione, whose cysteine supply comes from the cystine/glutamate antiporter subunit SLC7A11, while a parallel oxidoreductase regenerates reduced coenzyme Q at the membrane. Iron is sequestered in ferritin, and a stress-responsive transcriptional programme driven by NFE2L2, with SQSTM1 releasing it from KEAP1 restraint, raises antioxidant and NAD(P)H quinone reductase capacity. Metabolic inputs including citrate export, lipid and serine biosynthesis and AMPK-dependent energy sensing tune susceptibility, linking redox balance to nutrient state.

Hippocampal neuron apoptotic process is programmed cell death of neurons in the hippocampus, the structure that supports spatial and declarative memory formation. Because hippocampal pyramidal and granule neurons are not replaced, their loss translates directly into memory impairment, and this route of death is a central event in Alzheimer's disease, epilepsy, and ischemic and inflammatory brain injury. The genes involved place neuron-microglia communication at the heart of the process: fractalkine released by neurons signals through its microglial receptor to restrain or license neurotoxic activation, TREM2 sets the microglial response to damage-associated lipids and debris, and lipocalin-2 acts as an acute-phase mediator of neuroinflammatory neuronal death. Amyloid precursor protein links the pathway to amyloidogenic processing, while ELK1 couples upstream stress kinase signalling to transcription of the death programme.

Programmed death of hippocampal neurons is a route to memory impairment, since the hippocampus is the structure on which spatial learning and episodic memory depend, and its pyramidal and dentate neurons are among the most vulnerable in ischaemia, epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. The genes here point to neuron-microglia crosstalk as the setting in which this cell death is decided: amyloid precursor protein and its processing products provide the insult and the amyloid link, fractalkine released from neurons signals through its microglial receptor to restrain inflammatory activation, and TREM2 tunes microglial phagocytic and survival responses. Lipocalin 2, induced in reactive glia, sensitises neurons to death, while the transcription factor ELK1 couples stress-activated kinase signalling to changes in gene expression. The balance of these signals determines whether stressed hippocampal neurons survive or are lost.

Aldehydes formed during alcohol metabolism, lipid peroxidation and sugar breakdown are electrophiles that crosslink proteins and DNA, so cells maintain a dedicated capacity for aldehyde detoxification that converts them to the corresponding acids or alcohols or otherwise neutralises them. The enzymes here work in two directions: dehydrogenases such as ALDH2 and ALDH1A1 oxidise aldehydes irreversibly, while aldo-keto reductases (AKR1A1, AKR1B10) and retinol dehydrogenases reduce them back to alcohols, with ADH5 handling formaldehyde adducts of glutathione. Glyoxalase-type activities represented by HAGH and PARK7 dispose of methylglyoxal and related reactive carbonyls before they glycate proteins. Loss of this buffering underlies alcohol flushing and raised cancer risk from the common ALDH2 variant, carbonyl stress in diabetes, and photoreceptor degeneration when retinaldehyde is not cleared; PARK7 mutations link the same chemistry to parkinsonism.

Aldehydes are reactive electrophiles generated by alcohol metabolism, lipid peroxidation, and sugar chemistry, and cells respond to them both by detoxifying the compound and by changing gene expression, ion transport, and matrix output. The detoxifying arm dominates here: alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidize substrates such as acetaldehyde and retinaldehyde, aldo-keto reductases and retinol dehydrogenases reduce carbonyls, and the glyoxalase route with hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase clears methylglyoxal, while PARK7 defends against glycation damage. Loss of this capacity leaves protein and DNA adducts behind, the basis of alcohol-flush physiology in ALDH2 deficiency and of aldehyde-driven genotoxicity. A second arm is the cellular consequence of exposure: epithelial sodium channel subunits with SGK1 link aldehyde stimulus to salt and fluid transport, and TGFB1, COL1A1, and TIMP1 tie it to fibrotic remodelling of injured tissue.

Mitochondria take up cytosolic calcium to match ATP production to demand, and tuning how much enters — regulation of calcium import into the mitochondrion — sets the balance between stimulating dehydrogenases of the Krebs cycle and overloading the organelle into permeability transition and cell death. The proteins here act at both membranes: a voltage-dependent anion channel provides the outer-membrane route for calcium reaching the intermembrane space, while MCUB incorporates into the inner-membrane uniporter pore as a dominant-negative subunit that lowers conductance. The m-AAA protease subunits AFG3L2 and SPG7 govern the maturation and turnover of uniporter components, linking mitochondrial protein quality control to calcium handling, and presenilin-2 shapes transfer at endoplasmic reticulum–mitochondria contacts. Loss of this control contributes to neurodegeneration, hereditary spastic paraplegia and ataxia, and to ischaemic injury, where calcium overload triggers irreversible mitochondrial damage.

Organs acquire their shape through iterative signalling between epithelium and mesenchyme, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote and amplify that shaping rather than restrain it. It matters because the same signals set kidney branching, limb and craniofacial outgrowth, gonad and mammary development, and heart field patterning; their loss produces renal agenesis, skeletal and palatal defects, and disorders of sex development. Secreted ligands of the FGF, BMP, WNT and GDNF families act through receptors such as FGFR1 and the adaptor FRS2, with CTNNB1 transducing canonical WNT input, while SPRY1 and DKK1 tune the amplitude of these cues. Transcription factors including SIX1, SOX9, GATA3, MSX1 and posterior HOX genes translate the signals into regional identity and cell fate, and guidance receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 position the responding progenitors. Hormonal and cytokine inputs such as AR, TGFB1 and CSF1 modulate the process.

RNA decapping removes the protective 5' cap from messenger RNA, the committing step that turns a translatable transcript into substrate for degradation. Because the cap is what recruits the translation initiation machinery and blocks 5'-to-3' exonucleases, decapping sets mRNA half-life and therefore how long a gene's output persists after transcription stops — the basis of rapid turnover for inflammatory and growth-factor messages. The core reaction is carried out by the DCP2 catalytic subunit with DCP1A/B and scaffolding activators EDC3 and EDC4, assisted by the LSM1-7 ring and PATL1, which recognise deadenylated 3' ends produced by the CCR4-NOT complex. The DEAD-box helicase DDX6 couples decapping to translational repression, and XRN1 degrades the exposed body of the transcript. Related Nudix hydrolases scavenge free cap dinucleotides and clear aberrant caps, and these activities concentrate in cytoplasmic processing bodies.

Removal of the 5' cap commits an mRNA to destruction, and this decapping step sets how long a transcript survives and therefore how much protein it makes. It is the decisive event in the major cytoplasmic decay route: after deadenylation, the LSM1-7 ring and its partner PATL1 mark the shortened 3' end, and the DCP2 catalytic subunit, held in an active configuration by DCP1 and the scaffold EDC4 with EDC3 and DDX6, cleaves the cap to expose the body of the message to 5'-to-3' degradation by XRN1. Related Nudix-family hydrolases and DCPS handle cap dinucleotides and non-canonical caps, while ZFP36 and CAPRIN1 link sequence-specific RNA binding to this machinery. The reactions concentrate in processing bodies and underlie rapid shutoff of cytokine and cell cycle transcripts, quality control of aberrant RNAs, and translational silencing in oocytes and neurons.

Removing the 5' methylguanosine cap commits an mRNA to destruction: the cap is what recruits the translation initiation machinery and what shields the transcript from 5'-to-3' exonucleolytic attack, so decapping simultaneously silences the message and opens it to degradation. This step sets mRNA half-lives and thus how long a transcriptional response persists, and it is the endpoint of deadenylation-triggered turnover and of decay directed by sequence elements in 3' untranslated regions. The DCP2 nuclease, held and stimulated by DCP1 proteins together with scaffolding and enhancer factors such as EDC3 and EDC4, acts on transcripts delivered by the LSM1-7 ring, the DDX6 helicase and PATL1 after poly(A) shortening by CCR4-NOT and PAN components; XRN1 then degrades the decapped body. Many of these proteins concentrate in cytoplasmic processing bodies, where translationally repressed mRNAs are stored or destroyed, and ZFP36 links the machinery to rapid clearance of cytokine mRNAs.

Lipids made in one membrane must reach others that cannot make them, and intermembrane lipid transfer is how individual lipid molecules cross the cytosol shielded from water, moving from the outer leaflet of a donor bilayer to that of an acceptor without consuming ATP. This non-vesicular route sets the distinct lipid composition of each organelle, supplies the growing autophagosome, and drives countertransport at membrane contact sites, where sterol-binding proteins such as OSBP and its relatives exchange cholesterol for phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate to couple lipid delivery to phosphoinositide turnover. Other carriers are specialised by cargo: phosphatidylinositol transfer proteins, ceramide and glycosphingolipid carriers, PRELI/TRIAP complexes handling mitochondrial phospholipids, and lipoprotein-associated transfer activities. Related proteins govern lipid droplet fusion and surfactant lipid handling. Loss of specific carriers causes vitamin E deficiency ataxia, lipodystrophy, and defects in surfactant and lipoprotein assembly.

Cells restrain the outgrowth of membrane protrusions as actively as they build them, and this braking arm of plasma membrane bounded cell projection assembly keeps filopodia, lamellipodia, neurites and cilia from forming at the wrong time or place. It matters for growth cone guidance, for cell shape and migration, and for coupling ciliogenesis to the cell cycle, since an unsuppressed axoneme would extend from an actively dividing cell. Two mechanistic themes dominate. Rho-family GTPase inactivation by GAPs such as ARHGAP24 and SRGAP2C, together with actin-binding and severing proteins including cofilin, profilin and LIM kinases, limits actin-driven protrusion, and repulsive guidance cues such as SLIT2 and plexin signalling feed into this. Separately, a centriolar module built around CP110 and CEP97 caps the distal centriole and blocks cilium extension. Loss of such restraint produces aberrant neuronal branching and inappropriate ciliary assembly.

Cells extend membrane-bounded projections — filopodia, lamellipodia, microvilli, neurites, cilia — and this pathway covers the inputs that promote their assembly. Such protrusions let neurons find targets, immune cells migrate toward chemokine gradients, epithelia build brush borders, and cilia sense the extracellular environment; when their formation fails the consequences range from ciliopathies with retinal and renal disease to defective axon outgrowth and impaired cell motility. Rho-family GTPases including CDC42, RAC1 and their effectors drive branched actin nucleation through the Arp2/3 complex and WAVE regulatory components such as WASF2, CYFIP1 and NCKAP1, while profilin, cofilin and EPS8 family proteins tune filament elongation and bundling. A parallel arm acts at the centriole and basal body, where CEP120, CEP135, TTBK2 and intraflagellar transport proteins license ciliogenesis. Upstream growth factor, Wnt, TGF-beta and chemokine receptor signalling feeds into these cytoskeletal outputs.

Tissue macrophages are maintained in large part by local self-renewal rather than continuous replacement from the bone marrow, and control over macrophage proliferation sets how many of these cells populate a tissue and how strongly they expand during inflammation or repair. The pathway centres on the colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase whose two ligands here, CSF1 and IL34, drive survival and division of macrophages and their specialised relatives such as microglia and osteoclast precursors. Receptor engagement feeds into the ERK cascade through MAPK1 and MAPK3, with focal adhesion kinase linking adhesive cues to the same growth response, while IL33 provides a tissue alarmin signal that amplifies local expansion and a microRNA imposes a dampening constraint. Loss of this control underlies microglial and bone disorders, and its excess supports tumour-associated macrophage accumulation.

regulation of peptidyl-lysine crotonylation controls how much of the histone mark lysine crotonylation accumulates on chromatin, a modification that marks active promoters and is especially prominent during spermatogenesis. The chromodomain Y-linked proteins here work by two linked activities: they read repressive histone methylation through their chromodomains and, as crotonyl-CoA hydratases, consume the acyl donor needed for crotonylation, so they lower the local substrate pool and dampen the mark. Through this they restrain transcription of genes in male germ cells and participate in the histone-to-protamine transition that reorganises the sperm nucleus. The Y-linked members map to the region deleted in azoospermia factor, tying loss of this regulation to defective spermatid maturation and male infertility, while the autosomal member also shapes neuronal gene expression. The pathway links acyl-CoA metabolism directly to epigenetic control.

Crotonylation marks lysine residues on histones and other proteins with a short unsaturated acyl group, and the balance of that mark shapes chromatin state and transcriptional output, particularly during spermatogenesis, where crotonylated histones accompany the shift from histone- to protamine-packaged DNA in maturing germ cells. The genes here control how much crotonylation accumulates: the chromodomain Y-linked family and their autosomal relative CDYL combine a chromodomain that reads methylated histone marks with a coenzyme A-binding catalytic region, allowing them to act as crotonyl-CoA hydratase activity that depletes the donor for crotonylation and thereby limits the mark, while also serving as transcriptional corepressors recruited to target chromatin. Loss or deletion of the Y-linked members is associated with male infertility, linking this regulation to sperm chromatin remodelling and epigenetic control of germline gene expression.

When ambient temperature falls, mammals defend core body temperature by burning fuel for heat rather than for ATP, and this pathway covers the signals and regulators that turn that response up. Its endpoint is brown and beige adipose tissue: sympathetic noradrenaline acting on beta-adrenergic receptors raises cAMP through Gs, liberating fatty acids that feed uncoupled respiration via UCP1 in the inner mitochondrial membrane, with thyroid hormone activation by the deiodinase DIO2 amplifying the response locally. Transcriptional drivers such as PRDM16, PPARGC1A and EBF2 specify the thermogenic phenotype, while leptin, FGF21, adiponectin and type 2 cytokine signalling through IL4/STAT6 tune it systemically, and cold-sensing channels including TRPM8 contribute afferent input. Beyond thermal homeostasis in newborns and cold-exposed adults, this capacity consumes glucose and lipid, so its activity influences body weight and insulin sensitivity.

Mammals defend body temperature in the cold by burning fat in brown and beige adipocytes, and this braking arm sets a limit on that response so heat production is not sustained wastefully. The genes here restrain browning and uncoupled respiration at several levels: transcriptional repressors and cofactors such as TLE3, ID1, ZNF423, RB1 and the Notch effector RBPJ oppose the thermogenic gene programme, circadian factors including BMAL1 and NR1D1 time it, nuclear receptors of the liver X family and lipid-handling enzymes such as ACOT11 and PCTP tune substrate supply, and inflammatory input through TLR4 and ADAM17 suppresses adipocyte function. Nutrient and growth signalling via STK11, RHEB, FLCN and TFE3, together with stress-response mediators ATF4 and DDIT3, couple energy status to heat output. Loss of this restraint shifts white fat toward a beige phenotype and raises energy expenditure, which is why these nodes are targets in obesity and insulin resistance.

Steroid hormones are made, not stored, and this biosynthetic programme converts cholesterol into the glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, androgens and oestrogens that set stress responses, salt and water balance, sexual development and fertility. It defines the steroidogenic cells of the adrenal cortex, gonad and placenta, and its failure is clinically stark: mutations in the 21-hydroxylase or 11β-hydroxylase enzymes cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia with cortisol deficiency and androgen excess, while loss of the cholesterol delivery protein STAR blocks the pathway at its first committed step. Mitochondrial side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1 begins the route, and cytochrome P450s together with hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and 5α-reductases then tailor the product to each tissue, with aromatase producing oestrogen. Upstream, hypothalamic CRH, pituitary ACTH from POMC, and the gonadotropins LHB and FSHB acting through receptors such as MC2R drive output, with nuclear receptors and coactivators tuning enzyme expression.

Cells that migrate must let go of the surface they are gripping, and cell-substrate junction disassembly is the controlled dismantling of focal adhesions into their component parts. Without it, adhesions mature into immobile anchors and cells cannot turn over attachments during wound healing, tissue remodelling or invasion; excess turnover instead gives unstable, poorly adherent cells. The genes here point to two routes: small GTPase-driven membrane traffic that internalises integrins, with ARF6 and its exchange factor IQSEC1 plus the atypical Rho family member RHOU, and post-translational control of adhesion proteins, including a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase module (CUL5 with RNF7) and a Rab40 subunit that couples GTPase function to ubiquitination. Kinases and a phosphatase, among them PAK4, MAP4K4 and DUSP3, set the phosphorylation state of adhesion components, linking the process to phosphoinositide signalling, microtubule targeting of adhesions, and planar cell polarity cues during directed movement.

regulation of focal adhesion disassembly controls how quickly cells release their integrin-based attachments to the extracellular matrix, the step that allows a stationary adherent cell to become a migrating one. Cells must break rear and central adhesions in a timed way to move at all, so this regulation shapes wound healing, immune cell trafficking, epithelial remodelling and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. The genes act through several convergent routes: an ARF6 GTPase module with its exchange factor IQSEC1 drives membrane traffic and integrin internalisation; Rho-family signalling via RHOU and the effector kinase PAK4 remodels the actin cytoskeleton anchored at the adhesion; a CUL5-RNF7 ubiquitin ligase and the RAB40A adaptor mark adhesion proteins for degradation; and the phosphatase DUSP3 with PI3K regulatory subunits tunes the phosphotyrosine signals that hold the plaque together. Microtubule contact, through MAPRE2, targets adhesions for turnover.

Cells move by making and breaking their attachments to the extracellular matrix, and control over focal adhesion disassembly sets how fast those attachments turn over. Regulating the rate at which an adhesion complex comes apart determines migration speed and directionality, and matters for wound healing, immune cell trafficking and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells; adhesions that will not release leave a cell stalled, while premature release leaves it unable to generate traction. The genes here act through several converging routes: small GTPase signalling and its guanine nucleotide exchange control of membrane traffic that retrieves integrins from the cell surface, a phosphatase acting on adhesion-associated tyrosine phosphorylation, kinase signalling downstream of phosphoinositide 3-kinase, and a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase module that targets adhesion components for degradation. Microtubule-associated regulation also contributes, linking microtubule contact with adhesion sites to their turnover.

Cells can only move if the integrin-based contacts anchoring them to the extracellular matrix are taken apart as fast as they are built, and this pathway covers the signals that accelerate focal adhesion turnover. Promoting disassembly releases the rear and flanks of a migrating cell, allowing lamellipodial protrusion to translate into net displacement; when it fails, cells remain over-adherent and poorly motile, with consequences for wound healing, angiogenesis and tumour cell invasion. The genes here act through small GTPase and kinase relays: ARF6 and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor IQSEC1 drive the membrane traffic that internalises adhesion components, Rho-family members and their effector kinases remodel the associated actin, a phosphatase acts on adhesion-linked phosphotyrosine signalling, and a regulatory subunit of PI3-kinase links receptor input to the same machinery. Microtubule-dependent targeting of adhesions also contributes.

Chromatin-bound proteins must be removed or kept away as well as recruited, and this negative arm of protein localization to chromatin covers the processes that stop or reduce a factor's loading onto DNA. It matters for resetting chromatin between cell cycle stages, terminating transcriptional and repair responses, and preventing proteins from lingering where they would block replication or mitosis. Several routes converge here: kinases such as AURKB, CDK2, CDK9, PRKACA and JAK2 phosphorylate substrates to release them from chromatin, while SUMO ligation by PIAS4 followed by the SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4 and extraction by the VCP segregase strip proteins from DNA. SIRT6 deacetylation and lineage factors including SPI1 further restrict access, and a long non-coding RNA contributes as a regulatory element. Loss of such eviction leaves persistent chromatin complexes, genome instability and mis-set transcriptional programmes.

regulation of bile acid secretion controls how much bile acid hepatocytes export into bile, setting the driving force for bile flow, biliary lipid excretion and intestinal fat absorption. Because bile acids are detergents, this control is also protective: too little export traps them in the hepatocyte and causes cholestatic liver injury, while their release feeds the enterohepatic circulation that signals systemic cholesterol and energy balance. The canalicular pump ABCB11 performs the rate-limiting transport step, and its expression and activity are tuned transcriptionally and post-transcriptionally, including by miR-33a acting alongside the sterol-regulatory network. Inflammatory signalling through TNF suppresses transporter output during sepsis and hepatitis, producing acquired cholestasis, while claudin-2 shapes the paracellular permeability of the tight junctions that retain secreted bile acid, and carboxylesterase activity contributes to hepatic lipid and bile acid handling.

Bile acid secretion into bile drives biliary flow, lipid emulsification in the intestine, and the disposal of cholesterol, and its rate is tuned rather than fixed. The regulation of this export sets how much bile acid leaves the hepatocyte and how much accumulates inside it, which matters because retained bile acids are detergent and cytotoxic. The canalicular pump ABCB11 is the rate-limiting exporter, and its loss or inhibition causes intrahepatic cholestasis; a claudin contributes to paracellular permeability at the tight junctions that seal the canaliculus. Inflammatory signalling through TNF suppresses transporter expression, linking sepsis and hepatitis to cholestatic injury, while a microRNA encoded within a sterol-regulatory gene ties bile acid handling to cholesterol and fatty acid homeostasis. Together these inputs connect hepatic lipid metabolism, enterohepatic circulation, and susceptibility to cholestatic liver disease.

Epithelia and endothelia only work as barriers if neighbouring cells are sealed to one another, and tight junction organization is the assembly, remodelling and disassembly of that seal. It sets how much water, ions and solutes can pass between cells rather than through them, and it defines apical versus basolateral membrane domains, so its loss produces leaky gut and airway epithelium, breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, renal magnesium wasting and the junction dissolution that accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Claudins and occludin, together with tricellulin and other MARVEL-domain proteins, form the paired strands that determine charge and size selectivity, while scaffolding proteins such as ZO-1, PARD3, PATJ and afadin link them to polarity complexes and to the actomyosin ring. Rho-family GTPases and their kinases, kinase signalling, and inflammatory cytokines including TNF and IL1B tune barrier tightness dynamically.

The airways defend themselves by trapping inhaled particles and microbes in a mucus layer and sweeping it upward toward the pharynx, a process termed mucociliary clearance that depends on coordinated beating of motile cilia on the respiratory epithelium. When it fails, mucus stagnates and produces chronic rhinosinusitis, recurrent airway infection and bronchiectasis, the clinical picture of primary ciliary dyskinesia. The genes here build and tune the axoneme rather than the mucus: an axonemal dynein heavy chain and an outer dynein arm docking component supply and position the motors, cilia- and flagella-associated proteins together with a radial-spoke-associated subunit set waveform and beat regularity, and a tubulin polyglutamylase modifies axonemal microtubules to stabilise motility. Planar cell polarity contributors orient the beating cilia in a common direction across the epithelial sheet, so that individual strokes sum into directional transport.

Motile cilia and sperm flagella beat only if their axonemal motors and accessory structures are delivered to the right place inside the organelle, and protein localization to the motile cilium is the targeting step that puts them there. Dynein arms assembled in the cytoplasm must be ferried into the axoneme and docked periodically along the outer doublets; failure leaves cilia immotile or dyskinetic, producing primary ciliary dyskinesia with chronic airway infection, situs abnormalities and infertility. The genes here span that chain: a cytoplasmic dynein assembly factor, an outer dynein arm heavy chain, a docking complex subunit that anchors the arms to the doublet, and cilia- and flagella-associated proteins contributing to axonemal architecture. The pathway therefore links intraciliary trafficking to mucociliary clearance, cerebrospinal fluid flow and left-right patterning rather than to signalling from primary cilia.

Hydrocarbons — molecules of carbon and hydrogen alone — reach cells both from the diet and from the environment, and this metabolic process covers the enzymes that transform them. Two branches dominate. Carotene oxygenases cleave dietary carotenoids: BCO1 splits beta-carotene at its central double bond to yield retinal, the entry point for vitamin A, retinoid signalling and visual pigment, while BCO2 performs eccentric cleavage of xanthophylls and other carotenoids. The second branch handles xenobiotic hydrocarbons, where inducible cytochrome P450 monooxygenases such as CYP1A1, CYP2E1 and CYP2F1 oxidise aromatics and small alkanes, and epoxide hydrolase EPHX1 converts the resulting arene oxides to diols for conjugation and excretion. Because these oxidations can generate reactive, DNA-binding intermediates, the same chemistry that clears polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and solvents also underlies their carcinogenicity and organ toxicity.

Compounds carrying carbon-carbon double bonds include retinoids, prostaglandins, steroid intermediates, unsaturated fatty acids and endocannabinoids, and their turnover is what this olefinic metabolism covers. The chemistry matters because these molecules are signalling ligands: retinoic acid patterns tissues and drives differentiation, prostanoids mediate inflammation, pain and platelet behaviour, steroid hormones set reproductive and adrenal physiology, and 11-cis-retinal is the chromophore that makes vision possible. Much of the work is oxidation and reduction of allylic alcohols and aldehydes by alcohol dehydrogenases, short-chain retinol dehydrogenases and aldehyde dehydrogenases, with cytochrome P450s and epoxide hydrolases handling oxygenation and epoxide turnover, cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases converting arachidonate into prostaglandins and leukotrienes, and lipases plus amide hydrolases releasing or terminating fatty acid and endocannabinoid signals. Desaturases and elongases introduce and extend double bonds in fatty acyl chains. Loss of individual steps causes retinal degeneration, adrenal hormone deficiency, or disordered inflammatory signalling.

Steroid hormones are the olefinic compounds at issue here: cholesterol-derived molecules whose ring systems carry carbon-carbon double bonds, and whose synthesis sets sexual development, reproductive cycling, salt balance and the stress response. The route runs through cytochrome P450 enzymes and hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases — side-chain cleavage and 17α-hydroxylation by CYP17A1, aromatization of androgens to estrogens by CYP19A1, 11β-hydroxylation and aldosterone synthesis by CYP11B1 and CYP11B2, 21-hydroxylation by CYP21A2, and interconversion of androgens and estrogens by HSD17B and HSD3B enzymes. Cholesterol delivery and intracellular trafficking steps, together with the pituitary gonadotropins LHB and FSHB, place the chemistry under endocrine control, while BMP, WNT, inhibin and transcription factor components modulate gonadal and adrenal steroidogenic output. Loss of individual enzymes produces congenital adrenal hyperplasia, disorders of sex development or aldosterone excess with hypertension.

Heterochromatin is the compacted, transcriptionally silent fraction of the genome that keeps repetitive DNA, pericentromeric satellites and inactive chromosome regions switched off, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how much of it forms and where. Control of heterochromatin organization matters for silencing of transposable elements, for centromere function during mitosis, and for locking in cell-type-specific gene expression; its loss produces inappropriate transcription of repeats and genome instability. The genes here act through several routes: a histone variant that promotes compaction and X-inactivation, JmjC-family demethylases such as PHF2 and PHF8 that erase repressive methyl marks, chromatin remodelling and methylation cofactors including BAZ1A and DNMT3L, and mitotic kinases CDK1 and CDK2 that couple chromatin state to cell-cycle progression. Nuclear pore-associated TPR links heterochromatin positioning to nuclear architecture, a spatial dimension of silencing as important as the marks themselves.

negative regulation of heterochromatin organization describes the counterforce to chromatin silencing: processes that limit how much of the genome is packaged into condensed, transcriptionally inert heterochromatin. Keeping heterochromatin in check preserves access to genes needed for differentiation and neural function, and losing that restraint contributes to intellectual disability syndromes and inappropriate gene silencing. The genes act at several levels. The JmjC demethylases PHF8 and PHF2 erase repressive histone methylation at promoters and rDNA, converting silent chromatin into a permissive state; mutations in PHF8 cause X-linked intellectual disability with cleft lip. DYRK1A phosphorylates chromatin substrates and is dosage-sensitive in Down syndrome. KMT2A deposits activating H3K4 methylation that antagonises spreading of repressive marks, DNMT3L modulates de novo DNA methylation, and the ERI exonucleases limit small-RNA-directed silencing. Together they set the balance between open and closed chromatin during development.

Heterochromatin has to be kept out of places where genes must stay accessible, and this is the counter-pressure that limits how much of it forms and how far it spreads. Restraining heterochromatin organization keeps developmental and housekeeping loci available for transcription, and its loss shifts chromatin toward silencing, with consequences for neuronal gene expression and for the intellectual disability syndromes linked to several of these factors. The activities involved are largely mark-editing and mark-opposing: JmjC-domain demethylases such as PHF8 and PHF2 strip repressive lysine methylation from histones, while a histone methyltransferase of the KMT2 family deposits the H3K4 methylation that is incompatible with compact chromatin. Additional regulators, including a kinase and RNA-degrading exonucleases, act on the signals and small RNAs that would otherwise nucleate silencing.

Pigmentation depends on melanocytes reaching the skin and hair follicles in the right numbers and on melanin being made and distributed within them, and this regulatory programme sets how much colour is deposited and where. It matters for coat and skin colour patterning, hair greying, and the pigmentary defects seen alongside deafness and bowel innervation problems. Several components act on melanocyte precursors migrating from the neural crest: KITLG signalling and endothelin-3 support their survival and expansion, ZEB2 and hedgehog signalling shape neural crest fate, and the balance of BAX, BCL2 and BCL2L11 determines whether melanoblasts persist or die. Others act inside the cell, where BLOC-1 subunits, HPS4 and VPS33A route cargo into maturing melanosomes and the TPCN2 channel modulates melanosomal lumen properties, linking pigment output to lysosome-related organelle biogenesis.

Sperm are motile only because a long flagellum is built during spermiogenesis, and this pathway covers the construction of its microtubule axoneme and the accessory structures wrapped around it. Loss of these components produces immotile or morphologically deformed sperm — short, coiled or headless tails, the multiple morphological abnormalities of the flagella phenotype — and male infertility, sometimes alongside broader ciliary disease. Intraflagellar transport and centriole/basal body proteins deliver and dock cargo at the growing tip; cilia- and flagella-associated proteins together with radial spoke, nexin–dynein regulatory complex and central apparatus components such as SPAG6 and SPEF2 impose the 9+2 architecture; axonemal dyneins and their assembly factors supply the motor force. Tubulin-modifying enzymes and a sperm-specific fibrous sheath protein, FSIP2, tie axoneme assembly to the outer dense fibres and mitochondrial sheath unique to the sperm tail.

Sperm motility depends on mitochondria being packed into a tight helical sheath around the midpiece of the flagellum rather than scattered through the cell, and this assembly programme is what puts them there and holds them in place. Formed during spermiogenesis, the sheath supplies ATP locally to the adjacent axoneme and gives the midpiece its characteristic architecture; when it fails, sperm show bent or short tails, disorganised midpieces and reduced motility, a recognised cause of male infertility and asthenozoospermia. The genes involved link mitochondria to the cytoskeleton and to the outer dense fibres: ARMC12 and TBC1D21 act in mitochondrial positioning and coiling, KLC3 is a kinesin light chain associated with the outer dense fibres, and several cilia- and flagella-associated proteins tie sheath organisation to axonemal and accessory structure assembly. The pathway sits at the intersection of organelle transport, mitochondrial biogenesis and flagellar morphogenesis.

L-aspartate import across plasma membrane is the sodium-dependent uptake of extracellular aspartate into the cytosol, carried out by the same excitatory amino acid transporter family that clears glutamate from synapses. Because aspartate is itself a candidate excitatory transmitter and a substrate for the malate-aspartate shuttle, nucleotide synthesis and the urea cycle, this uptake links neurotransmitter clearance to intermediary metabolism and to the supply of carbon and nitrogen for proliferating cells. The transporters cotransport sodium and protons while countertransporting potassium, using the ion gradients to concentrate substrate against a steep gradient; the astrocytic members handle the bulk of clearance around glutamatergic synapses, while ASCT1 and ASCT2 also serve neutral amino acid exchange in epithelia and tumours. Loss of this capacity allows extracellular excitatory amino acids to accumulate, driving excitotoxic neuronal death in ischaemia and neurodegeneration.

Uptake of L-aspartate across the plasma membrane supplies cells with a carbon and nitrogen source for nucleotide and amino acid synthesis and, in the nervous system, clears an excitatory dicarboxylic amino acid from the extracellular space. The transporters here belong to the excitatory amino acid carrier family, which co-transports acidic amino acids with sodium and protons in exchange for potassium, using the ion gradients to concentrate substrate against a steep gradient; SLC1A4 and SLC1A5 are the neutral amino acid exchangers of the same family that also accept aspartate. In brain, astrocytic SLC1A2 and SLC1A3 perform the bulk of glutamate and aspartate clearance, terminating synaptic signalling and preventing excitotoxic neuronal death, while SLC1A1 loss in kidney and intestine causes dicarboxylic aminoaciduria. The same uptake feeds tumour cell anabolism, since aspartate is otherwise poorly permeant.

Mitotic nuclear division is the step in which a cell's duplicated genome is condensed, aligned and partitioned into two nuclei with identical chromosome complements, and it is the event that makes accurate cell proliferation, tissue growth and renewal possible. Condensin and cohesin complexes compact chromosomes and hold sister chromatids together until separase cleaves the linkage; kinetochore assemblies including the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes, KNL1 and centromeric CENPA capture spindle microtubules, while kinesins, dynein and TPX2-dependent spindle organisation generate the pulling forces. Aurora kinases, PLK1 and CDK1-cyclin B time the transitions, the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD1, MAD2 and BUB1 delay anaphase until attachments are correct, and the anaphase-promoting complex then triggers degradation of securin and cyclin. Errors produce aneuploidy, micronuclei and chromosomal instability, linking this machinery to tumourigenesis and to developmental microcephaly syndromes.

Oxidative phosphorylation depends on a continuous supply of ADP to the matrix, and this transport step delivers it across the inner mitochondrial membrane in exchange for the ATP that is exported to the cytosol. Without it, ATP synthase runs out of substrate, the proton gradient cannot be discharged productively, and cells that rely heavily on aerobic metabolism cannot match energy supply to demand. The carriers named here are the adenine nucleotide translocase family, expressed in tissue-restricted patterns: heart and muscle, ubiquitous and proliferative, and testis-enriched forms, giving each tissue its own balance of exchange capacity. Beyond nucleotide exchange these carriers contribute to proton leak with uncoupling proteins and participate in permeability transition during cell death. Mutations cause mitochondrial myopathy and cardiomyopathy, linking this exchange directly to cellular energy charge.

Exocytosis is how cells deliver the contents of secretory vesicles to the outside world, and this collection covers the machinery that makes it happen: vesicle tethering, priming, calcium sensing and the final membrane fusion step. It is the basis of chemical neurotransmission, hormone and enzyme secretion, granule release by immune cells, and delivery of transporters and receptors to the cell surface. SNARE proteins such as SNAP25, VAMP2 and syntaxins form the fusion complex, with STXBP1/Munc18 and UNC13 family proteins priming vesicles, synaptotagmins and DOC2 acting as the calcium triggers, and complexins clamping fusion until a stimulus arrives; the multisubunit exocyst directs vesicles to defined sites on the plasma membrane. Mutations here cause epileptic encephalopathies, movement disorders and defects in cytotoxic granule release underlying haemophagocytic syndromes, while alpha-synuclein links the same machinery to Parkinson disease.

Lipid droplet formation is how cells package neutral lipids into discrete cytoplasmic organelles, giving them a way to store fatty acids and sterol esters safely and release them on demand. Without it, excess lipid remains free in membranes and cytosol, driving lipotoxicity, endoplasmic reticulum stress and insulin resistance; loss of seipin causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy, in which adipocytes fail to build functional droplets at all. Droplets bud from the ER bilayer, and the genes here mark that birthplace: seipin with its partner LDAF1 defines nucleation sites, FIT proteins promote droplet budding, and phospholipid-synthesizing enzymes such as CDS1/2 and PISD tune the monolayer surface that determines droplet size and fusion. Fatty acid binding proteins deliver substrate, perilipins coat the mature droplet and control lipase access, and AUP1 links droplets to ubiquitin-dependent protein quality control.

Cells store neutral lipid in droplets that bud from the endoplasmic reticulum, and lipid droplet formation is the set of steps that nucleates these organelles and gives them their phospholipid monolayer and protein coat. It matters because droplets buffer fatty acids that would otherwise be lipotoxic, supply substrate for beta-oxidation and membrane synthesis, and define the storage capacity of adipocytes and hepatocytes; loss of seipin, encoded by BSCL2, causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy with severe insulin resistance and fatty liver. Seipin acts with its partner LDAF1 at ER sites where triglyceride lenses form, fat-storage-inducing proteins FITM1 and FITM2 shape emerging droplets, CDS1 and CDS2 and PISD supply phospholipid precursors for the surface, and perilipin PLIN5 coats droplets and controls lipase access. Fatty acid binding proteins and ER-contact factors deliver and traffic the lipid cargo, linking droplet biogenesis to membrane contact sites and whole-body energy balance.

Oxidised LDL accumulating in the artery wall is read by cells as a danger signal, and the responses it triggers convert macrophages into lipid-laden foam cells and drive the inflammation that underlies atherosclerosis. Scavenger receptor CD36 binds the modified particle and cooperates with TLR4 and TLR6, which signal through MYD88 and TICAM1 to induce inflammatory gene expression, while TREM2 and CD68 mark the lipid-handling macrophage states that result. Downstream consequences include AKT1-dependent survival and metabolic signalling, sphingomyelinase-generated ceramide from SMPD3, and TXNIP-linked redox and inflammasome activation; microRNAs such as MIR146A provide negative feedback restraining the TLR arm. This cellular response to oxidised low-density lipoprotein thus couples lipid uptake to innate immune activation, foam cell formation and plaque progression, and is a point of intervention in cardiovascular disease.

Thirteen subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation machinery are encoded in mitochondrial DNA, and mitochondrial gene expression is the dedicated apparatus that transcribes, processes and translates that genome so those subunits can be made and inserted into the inner membrane. Without it cells cannot assemble functional respiratory complexes, and mutations across its components cause encephalomyopathies, deafness, cardiomyopathy and Leigh-like disease. A single-subunit RNA polymerase with TFAM and its accessory factors initiates transcription from the two strands, while endonucleases including the tRNA-processing RNase P subunits and ELAC2 cut the polycistronic transcripts, and methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases and TRNT1 mature the tRNAs. Mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge them, the large and small mitoribosomal subunits with their initiation, elongation and release factors then synthesise the proteins, and OXA1L delivers the hydrophobic products into the membrane. RNA-binding proteins such as LRPPRC and SLIRP control transcript stability and thereby output.

Neurons acquire their input and output fields by elaborating axons and dendrites into branched trees, and this arborization sets how many partners a cell can contact and where its synapses form. Too little or too much branching distorts cortical wiring and shows up in intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration. Guidance and growth cues drive the process: semaphorin signalling through neuropilin, netrin-G ligands, WNT5A acting via frizzled receptors and dishevelled proteins, and pleiotrophin all bias where new branches sprout or retract. Their signals converge on the cytoskeleton through ROCK1, PAK6, TAOK2 and the spectraplakin MACF1, which link microtubules and actin so a nascent branch can be stabilized. Synaptic scaffolds such as DLG4 and the adhesion molecule NLGN1 tie branch formation to synapse assembly, while local mRNA regulators contribute translational control in growing processes.

Dendrite arborization is the process by which a neuron elaborates and patterns its dendritic tree, setting the surface available for synaptic input and therefore how much and what kind of information the cell can integrate. Branch number, length and orientation are shaped by extracellular guidance cues and their receptors, including secreted semaphorin signalling through neuropilin, together with growth factors such as pleiotrophin, and by intracellular effectors that remodel the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton, among them an actin-regulatory phosphatase partner and a kinase acting at the membrane-cytoskeleton interface. RNA-binding and transcriptional regulators contribute by controlling local and nuclear gene expression during outgrowth, and cholinergic receptor activity links neuronal excitation to branch refinement. Because dendritic geometry determines circuit connectivity, disruption of these steps produces simplified or misoriented arbors and is associated with intellectual disability, autism and other neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

Crotonylation adds a bulky, rigid acyl group to lysine side chains, and peptidyl-lysine crotonylation of histones marks active promoters and enhancers in a way that is read and erased differently from acetylation. It links the cell's acyl-CoA pools to transcription, since crotonyl-CoA levels rise and fall with fatty acid and amino acid catabolism and thereby tune gene expression to metabolic state. The acetyltransferase p300 also transfers crotonyl groups to histone H3, stimulating transcription more strongly than acetylation at the same sites. Chromodomain Y proteins, encoded by a testis-expressed Y-chromosomal family and their autosomal relative CDYL, engage this chemistry through crotonyl-CoA hydratase activity and histone-binding chromodomains, and are tied to the histone-to-protamine transition in spermatogenesis. Loss of this regulation is associated with impaired male germ cell maturation and infertility.

Lipoprotein transport through plasma and into tissues has to be tuned to the body's cholesterol and fatty acid needs, and this regulatory pathway sets how much lipoprotein is delivered to and cleared by cells. Its main lever is the abundance and activity of lipoprotein receptors and the apolipoprotein ligands that engage them, with apolipoprotein E acting as the ligand that directs remnant and HDL particles to hepatic clearance; its variants are among the strongest genetic determinants of plasma lipid levels and late-onset Alzheimer's disease risk. The nuclear receptor pair PPARG and RXRA drives transcription of lipid handling genes, while microRNAs such as miR-148a repress receptor expression post-transcriptionally, and TMEM97 with PGRMC1 modulates cholesterol handling at the LDL receptor. When this control fails, cholesterol-rich particles accumulate and atherosclerosis follows.

Cholesterol and triglyceride carried in lipoproteins must be moved out of the circulation and into cells, and this pathway describes the inputs that raise the rate of that movement. It matters for clearance of atherogenic particles: reduced flux leaves lipoproteins in plasma, and the best-known member here, apolipoprotein E, is the ligand that targets remnant particles to hepatic receptors, with its isoforms shaping both cardiovascular and Alzheimer risk. A second arm is transcriptional: the nuclear receptor PPAR-gamma partnered with RXR-alpha drives expression of lipid-handling and uptake genes in macrophages and adipocytes, the basis of thiazolidinedione action. Membrane proteins including TMEM97 and PGRMC1 act with the LDL receptor at the cell surface to promote particle internalization, linking sterol sensing to uptake capacity.

Protein storage is the setting aside of protein reserves inside a cell for use at a later developmental stage, so that a cell can carry out programmes for which it cannot yet transcribe new material. The genes here define the subcortical maternal complex of the mammalian oocyte and early embryo, a cytoplasmic lattice-associated assembly in which KHDC3L, NLRP5, OOEP, PADI6 and TLE6 act together to organise maternal stores of protein and mRNA and position organelles before zygotic transcription begins. Loss of any component disturbs the maternal-to-zygotic transition and causes early embryonic arrest; in humans, mutations underlie recurrent hydatidiform mole, imprinting disturbance and female infertility. The pathway therefore links cytoplasmic maternal inheritance to the first cleavage divisions rather than to any metabolic route.

Interleukin-10 is the principal brake on inflammation, and the signalling it triggers is what keeps an immune response from destroying the tissue it is defending. The cytokine engages a two-chain receptor, IL10RA paired with the shared IL10RB, which recruits the kinases JAK1 and TYK2 to phosphorylate STAT3; activated STAT3 then drives a transcriptional programme that suppresses production of TNF, IL-1 and IL-12 by macrophages and dendritic cells and limits antigen presentation. Loss of this axis in humans causes very-early-onset inflammatory bowel disease, showing how much intestinal tolerance depends on it, while excessive signalling contributes to the immune suppression seen in chronic infection and tumours. Inhibitory leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptors of the LILRA and LILRB families are included here as parallel negative regulators of myeloid activation, converging on the same outcome of restrained inflammatory output.

extracellular vesicle biogenesis is how cells package proteins, lipids and RNA into membrane-bounded vesicles and release them, creating a channel of intercellular communication that operates at a distance from the donor cell. It underlies antigen transfer between immune cells, delivery of morphogens and miRNAs, disposal of unwanted membrane proteins, and the spread of tumour and prion-like material in disease. Two routes are represented: intraluminal budding into multivesicular endosomes, driven by ESCRT components such as TSG101, HGS, the CHMP proteins and the ALIX–syntenin–syndecan axis with VPS4 ATPases for membrane scission, and direct budding from the plasma membrane using arrestin-domain adaptors that recruit the same machinery. Rab GTPases including RAB27A and RAB11A direct multivesicular body trafficking and docking for exosome release, while neutral sphingomyelinase supplies the ceramide that favours inward budding. The pathway thus sits at the intersection of endosomal sorting, secretion and lysosomal quality control.

Cells release membrane-bounded vesicles into their surroundings, and extracellular vesicle biogenesis covers how those exosomes, microvesicles and related particles are formed, loaded and shed. The process underlies intercellular transfer of proteins, lipids and RNA, and is exploited in immune communication, tissue repair, and the spread of tumour and infectious material; the same vesicles are the basis of liquid-biopsy biomarkers. Mechanistically it centres on the ESCRT machinery, with TSG101, HGS and the charged multivesicular body proteins driving inward budding of endosomal membranes, ALIX bridging to a syndecan-syntenin route, and the AAA-ATPases VPS4A and VPS4B completing scission. Rab GTPases including RAB27A, RAB11A and RAB7A direct multivesicular body trafficking and fusion with the plasma membrane, while neutral sphingomyelinase generates ceramide for budding and arrestin-domain proteins recruit cargo for direct plasma-membrane vesicle release.

Cells must move ions, metabolites, drugs and lipids outward across the plasma membrane, and this export activity sets cytoplasmic composition, membrane potential and the disposal of xenobiotics. The genes span several export modes: ATP-binding cassette transporters that efflux drugs, bile constituents, cyclic nucleotides and cholesterol; P-type pumps that extrude sodium, calcium, protons and copper; secondary transporters including sodium/calcium exchangers, sodium/proton exchange, zinc and manganese efflux carriers, and ferroportin for iron release; and potassium channels with their accessory and auxiliary subunits that carry outward current during repolarization. Regulation is represented too, with calmodulin, ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family, scaffolds such as PDZK1 and DLG1, kinase control by WNK4, and hepcidin, which triggers ferroportin degradation to limit iron export. Losses here cause pharmacological resistance or hypersensitivity, cardiac arrhythmia, cholestasis, copper and iron overload, and disturbed systemic electrolyte handling.

Lymphocytes only work if they arrive where they are needed, and this pathway covers the signals that increase their directed migration toward chemical cues. It governs lymphocyte entry into lymph nodes and their recruitment into inflamed or infected tissue, so it underlies both normal immune surveillance and the leukocyte infiltration seen in autoimmunity, transplant rejection and tumours. Secreted chemokines including CCL3, CCL4, CCL5, CCL21, CXCL13 and XCL1 form the attractant gradients, acting through receptors such as CCR2 to trigger cytoskeletal remodelling and adhesion changes; CXCL13 and CCL21 in particular organise B and T cell positioning within lymphoid follicles and stroma. Kinases including PTK2B and the WNK1-OXSR1-STK39 module transduce and tune the response, controlling cell volume and motility, while the sheddases ADAM10 and ADAM17 release surface ligands that modify how strongly cells respond.}

Small peptides left over from protein digestion are not wasted: they are carried intact across the plasma membrane into the cytosol, where cytosolic peptidases release their amino acids. This import route is how the small intestine absorbs much of dietary nitrogen as di- and tripeptides rather than free amino acids, and how the kidney reclaims filtered peptides, and it doubles as the entry pathway for peptidomimetic drugs such as beta-lactam antibiotics and ACE inhibitors. Transport is driven by the inward proton gradient, coupling peptide uptake to pH rather than sodium. The family members differ in location and purpose: the intestinal high-capacity and renal high-affinity carriers handle nutrient absorption, while the lysosomal and endosomal members of the group deliver bacterial peptide fragments to innate immune sensors, linking peptide handling to inflammatory signalling. A cystine-glutamate exchanger is included, connecting this transport with cysteine supply for glutathione.

Cells that burn or store fat must first pull long-chain fatty acids across the plasma membrane, and this pathway covers the controls that set how fast that uptake occurs. It matters for how heart and skeletal muscle fuel contraction, how adipocytes load triglyceride, and how insulin redirects lipid traffic after a meal; dysregulated uptake contributes to lipid overload in muscle and liver and to insulin resistance. Two mechanisms recur among the genes. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases trap incoming fatty acids as CoA thioesters, and this metabolic trapping, together with cytosolic fatty acid binding protein, maintains the inward gradient that sustains further import. Separately, insulin signalling through IRS2 and the AKT kinases promotes transporter translocation to the surface, linking hormonal status to the rate at which a cell acquires its lipid fuel.

Most serotonin receptors act through G proteins, but the 5-HT3 family is an ion channel in its own right, and this pathway is the fast, ionotropic arm of serotonergic signalling. Serotonin binding opens an intrinsic cation-selective pore, depolarising the cell within milliseconds and admitting sodium and calcium to trigger firing, neurotransmitter release and downstream changes in gene expression. The five subunits listed assemble as pentamers of the Cys-loop receptor superfamily, with the A subunit able to form homomeric channels and the others tuning conductance and pharmacology in heteromers. These receptors are concentrated on enteric and vagal sensory neurons and in brainstem nuclei, where they drive the nausea and vomiting reflex and modulate gut motility; blocking them is the mechanism of antiemetic drugs used with chemotherapy, and variants in the subunit genes have been linked to emesis susceptibility and psychiatric traits.

Presynaptic endocytosis is the membrane retrieval arm of the synaptic vesicle cycle: after vesicles fuse and release neurotransmitter, this machinery recovers their lipids and proteins from the axon terminal surface so that release sites can be cleared and vesicle pools regenerated. Without it, sustained neurotransmission fails, terminals swell with unretrieved membrane, and synapses fatigue during high-frequency firing. Clathrin coats assembled through AP-2 adaptors, accessory factors such as AP180/CALM homologues, epsin- and intersectin-family scaffolds, and cargo-specific adaptors like stonins select vesicle proteins including synaptotagmin and VAMP2; BAR-domain proteins including amphiphysin, endophilin and BIN1 sculpt the neck, dynamins sever it, and synaptojanin with auxilin/GAK uncoats the product. Actin, Rho-family GTPases and phosphoinositide kinases shape the process, and calcium acting via calmodulin and calcineurin couples it to activity.
