Several components -- LRRK2, PRKN, PARK7, synucleins, SYNJ1 -- are Parkinson's disease genes, tying terminal membrane traffic to neurodegeneration.

Sustained neurotransmission depends on retrieving synaptic vesicle membrane and proteins after exocytosis, and presynaptic endocytosis is the recycling arm that keeps the vesicle pool and the active zone usable during repeated firing. Without it, terminals run down, the presynaptic membrane expands, and vesicle protein sorting fails — defects linked to epilepsy, intellectual disability and Parkinsonian degeneration. Clathrin and the AP-2 adaptor complex, with accessory factors such as amphiphysin, intersectins, endophilin and SGIP1, curve the membrane at the periactive zone; dynamins pinch off the bud; the phosphatase synaptojanin and the co-chaperone auxilin (DNAJC6) strip phosphoinositides and clathrin so vesicles can be reloaded. Calcium sensing through calmodulin and calcineurin couples retrieval rate to activity, while CDK5 phosphorylation sets the opposing tone. Actin, Rac1 and ROCK1 supply mechanical force, and LRRK2, parkin, DJ-1 and synucleins tie this step to synaptic maintenance in neurodegeneration.

Synapses make their own proteins on demand, and regulating translation locally is how a stimulated spine changes its protein content within minutes rather than waiting for the soma. This local control underlies long-lasting synaptic plasticity, learning and memory, and its loss is the clearest molecular route to intellectual disability and autism: FMR1 encodes the RNA-binding protein FMRP, whose absence causes fragile X syndrome and releases dendritic mRNAs from translational repression. FMRP acts with its paralogues FXR1 and FXR2 and with CYFIP1, which sequesters the cap-binding initiation factor eIF4E and so blocks assembly of an initiation complex until synaptic activity relieves the block. Elongation is separately tuned by the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase EEF2K, which phosphorylates elongation factor 2 to slow general elongation while permitting specific transcripts to be made. Together these steps couple neurotransmitter receptor signalling to the local proteome.

Synapses maintain their protein composition locally, and control over protein catabolic processes at the synapse sets how fast receptors, scaffolds and damaged organelles are cleared from the terminal. Tuning this turnover matters for synaptic strength and plasticity: too little degradation leaves damaged mitochondria and aggregated proteins in axon terminals, a route to dopaminergic neuron loss in parkinsonism, while excessive clearance strips the postsynaptic machinery needed for transmission. The genes here act on the two main disposal routes. Ubiquitin ligase activity, including a cullin-based complex and the E3 mutated in recessive Parkinson disease, marks substrates for proteasomal or autophagic destruction, an E3 of the Cbl family regulates receptor downregulation, and a deubiquitinase counteracts chain assembly to spare substrates. A small Rab GTPase directs synaptic vesicles toward autophagic degradation, and a prolyl hydroxylase links substrate stability to oxygen availability.

Aminophospholipid translocation is the ATP-driven flipping of phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine from the outer to the inner leaflet of a membrane bilayer, and it is what keeps these lipids hidden from the cell surface. The resulting asymmetry defines a healthy plasma membrane: exposed phosphatidylserine is the signal that marks apoptotic cells for engulfment and helps trigger blood coagulation, so continuous inward pumping suppresses both. The work is done by P4-type ATPases, including ATP8A1, ATP8A2, ATP11A, ATP11C and ATP8B1, each of which must pair with a CDC50 accessory subunit, TMEM30A or TMEM30B, to fold, leave the endoplasmic reticulum and reach its target membrane. Loss of individual flippases causes intrahepatic cholestasis, hearing and retinal degeneration, and defective B lymphocyte development, and the same activity shapes membrane curvature during vesicle budding and intracellular trafficking.

export from cell covers the many routes by which cells release material into their surroundings, from regulated secretion of hormones and neurotransmitters to constitutive vesicle trafficking and transport of ions, metabolites and drugs across the plasma membrane. It is the basis of endocrine and neuronal communication, immune signalling, and tissue homeostasis: without it synapses cannot transmit, insulin cannot reach the circulation, and cells cannot rid themselves of xenobiotics or excess ions. The machinery spans SNAREs, synaptotagmins and Munc13/Munc18 proteins that fuse dense-core and synaptic vesicles in a calcium-dependent way, Rab GTPases, exocyst subunits and coat adaptors that direct carriers to the surface, and large families of ABC transporters, solute carriers, channels and ATPases that pump substrates outward. Also here are the cargoes themselves - insulin, glucagon, oxytocin, cytokines, growth factors - and the transcriptional and circadian regulators that time their release. Defects underlie diabetes, neurodegeneration and secretory disorders.

Cells must move material out into the extracellular space, and this broad export programme covers both transport across the plasma membrane and release by exocytosis. It underlies hormone and neurotransmitter secretion, cytokine and chemokine release during inflammation, lipid and metal efflux, and delivery of matrix and signalling proteins, so its failure produces diabetes, neurological disease, immunodeficiency and cholestasis. Mechanistically it spans ABC transporters and solute carriers that pump drugs, bile acids, lipids, zinc and iron outward; ion channels and pumps that set the electrical and calcium signals triggering release; and the vesicle machinery itself, where SNAREs such as syntaxins, SNAP25 and VAMPs, Sec1/Munc18 and Munc13 proteins, synaptotagmin calcium sensors, complexins, Rab GTPases and the exocyst tether, dock and fuse secretory granules and synaptic vesicles. Prohormone convertases, granins and transcriptional regulators set the cargo and the secretory identity of the cell.

Lipids made inside a cell are of little use to its neighbours unless they are exported, and this pathway covers the directed release of lipids into the extracellular space together with the signals that drive it. Two arms are visible. One is eicosanoid output: secreted and cytosolic phospholipases liberate arachidonate, cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin E synthase convert it, and an ABC-family transporter carries prostaglandin out of the cell, so inflammation, fever, pain and vascular tone depend on this step. The other is bulk lipid secretion through the early secretory pathway, where COPII components required for chylomicron and lipoprotein budding from the endoplasmic reticulum determine dietary fat absorption; their loss causes lipid malabsorption. Much of the remainder is regulatory input from hormones and cytokines, including leptin, resistin, interleukin-1, endothelin and hypothalamic-pituitary peptides, linking lipid release to endocrine and immune state.

Cells that burn or store fat must first bring it across the plasma membrane, and lipid import into the cell is the set of transporters, receptors and trapping enzymes that accomplishes this. It supplies fatty acids to muscle and heart for oxidation, to adipocytes and liver for storage, and delivers retinol for vision and epithelial differentiation; its dysregulation underlies ectopic lipid accumulation, insulin resistance and fatty liver. The scavenger receptor CD36 and the SLC27 fatty acid transport proteins move long-chain fatty acids inward, long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL1 esterify them so they cannot diffuse back out, and cytosolic fatty acid binding proteins shuttle them to organelles. Retinol arrives bound to RBP4 and is taken up through the membrane receptor STRA6, while lysosomal acid lipase releases fatty acids and cholesterol from endocytosed lipoproteins. Insulin signalling through IRS2 and AKT tunes uptake capacity to nutritional state.

Cells can sense cGAMP made by their neighbours, and this depends on carrying the cyclic dinucleotide across the plasma membrane into the cytosol, where it activates STING and drives type I interferon responses. Such import spreads innate immune alarm from an infected or damaged cell to bystanders, matters for the anti-tumour immunity elicited by STING agonists, and determines which cell types respond to extracellular cGAMP at all. The volume-regulated anion channel formed by LRRC8A together with LRRC8B-E subunits provides one conduit, gated by low ionic strength and cell swelling, while the folate transporter SLC19A1 imports cGAMP and related cyclic dinucleotides and SLC46A2 serves this role in monocytes and keratinocytes. Because these same carriers move folates, chemotherapeutic antifolates and osmolytes, cGAMP uptake is coupled to nutrient transport and volume homeostasis rather than being a dedicated immune route.

Antibacterial innate immune defence is the germline-encoded first response to bacterial invasion, acting within minutes to hours of exposure and setting the tone for any later adaptive response; without it, commensal and pathogenic bacteria breach epithelial barriers and disseminate. Pattern recognition sits at its core: surface receptors such as TLR2 with its partner TLR6 detect bacterial lipopeptides, while the cytosolic sensor NOD2 responds to peptidoglycan fragments, both converging on NF-kB-driven transcription of cytokines and chemokines that recruit neutrophils. Effector arms include pore-forming and lytic proteins, defensin-type antimicrobial peptides, the alarmin IL33 released from damaged barrier cells, and lysosomal and autophagic degradation programmes coordinated by the transcription factor TFEB. Peptide transport and urinary tract protection by uromodulin extend the response to mucosal surfaces. Defective NOD2 signalling illustrates the cost of failure, predisposing to granulomatous intestinal inflammation.

Cells detect viruses before any antibody exists, using germline-encoded sensors that recognise viral nucleic acid and trigger interferon production and an antiviral state. This innate antiviral response limits replication in the first hours of infection and shapes the later adaptive response; its loss underlies severe viral disease, while its inappropriate activation drives interferonopathies and autoimmunity. Cytosolic RNA helicases such as RIG-I and MDA5 signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, DNA sensing converges on STING, and both routes activate TBK1 and IRF3 alongside NF-kB to induce interferon, CXCL10 and TNF. Interferon-stimulated effectors then act directly: the OAS enzymes and PKR shut down translation and degrade RNA, MX1 and the IFIT proteins block viral replication, and APOBEC3 cytidine deaminases mutate retroviral genomes. Ubiquitin ligases including TRIM25 and deubiquitinases such as USP18 tune the strength and duration of signalling.

Many cytokines are made as inactive precursors and only become signalling molecules when a protease cuts them, so cytokine precursor processing is the step that decides whether an inflammatory message is sent. The cleavages involved release mature ligands from membrane-anchored or intracellular pro-forms: a membrane sheddase liberates soluble TNF and related ectodomains from the cell surface, an inflammatory caspase converts pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into active cytokines downstream of inflammasome assembly, and proprotein convertases of the furin family mature growth factors and cytokine precursors such as TGF-β in the secretory pathway. A mast cell chymase provides an extracellular route to the same end. Because activation is post-translational, cells can store precursors and respond quickly; excessive processing drives chronic inflammation and autoinflammatory disease, and blocking these proteases is a therapeutic strategy.

Many hormones, growth factors and cytokines are made as inactive precursors and only become receptor-activating ligands after proteolytic cleavage; this maturation step is what converts stored proprotein into signal. It underlies insulin and glucagon production from proinsulin and proglucagon, blood pressure control through the renin–angiotensin axis, ghrelin acylation and appetite signalling, and the shedding of membrane-anchored TNF and EGF-family ligands. Subtilisin-like proprotein convertases such as FURIN, PCSK1 and PCSK2 cut at basic residues in the secretory pathway, assisted by chaperones including SCG5 and the granule zinc transporter SLC30A8, while carboxypeptidase E trims the products. At the cell surface, ADAM10 and ADAM17 release ectodomains, and peptidases including ACE, ACE2, ECE1, DPP4 and neprilysin generate or destroy active peptides. Mast cell proteases and caspase-1 supply parallel routes, the latter maturing interleukin-1 family cytokines. Loss of these steps causes endocrine and metabolic disease.

Gram-positive organisms such as staphylococci, streptococci and listeria present lipoteichoic acid, peptidoglycan and pore-forming toxins rather than the lipopolysaccharide of Gram-negative bacteria, and host cells mount a distinguishable response to them. This response determines whether colonisation stays superficial or becomes invasive disease, and it operates at two levels. At the epithelial barrier, junctional proteins including E-cadherin and claudin-3 both seal the tissue and serve as points of bacterial attachment and entry, so infection is accompanied by remodelling of cell-cell adhesion. In leukocytes, the integrin subunit encoded by ITGAM mediates complement-dependent adhesion and phagocytic uptake, while NFKBIZ and the AP-1 component FOSL2 shape the transcriptional output that follows receptor engagement, tuning cytokine production; IL27 contributes an immunoregulatory signal that restrains the ensuing T cell response. Together these link bacterial recognition to barrier integrity, engulfment and inflammatory gene expression.

Cells facing amino acid deprivation, heme limitation, viral RNA, or protein misfolding in the ER converge on a single adaptive circuit: the integrated stress response. Its purpose is to buy time — global translation is throttled so that folding capacity and nutrient demand fall, while a small set of stress mRNAs is selectively translated to rebuild homeostasis. The core event is phosphorylation of the eIF2 alpha subunit by one of the eIF2 alpha kinases, here represented by HRI, PERK and GCN2, with GCN1 and IMPACT tuning the amino acid-sensing arm and the mitochondrial OMA1–DELE1 axis relaying organelle damage. Output is transcriptional: ATF4 and CHOP, together with CEBP, AP-1 and NFE2L family partners, drive recovery genes, and PPP1R15A/B feed back by promoting eIF2 alpha dephosphorylation. If stress persists, the same wiring commits the cell to death, linking this response to neurodegeneration, ER stress disease and tumour cell survival.

HRI-mediated signaling is the arm of the integrated stress response that lets a cell report trouble in its mitochondria and in heme supply to the translational machinery. Erythroid cells depend on it to match globin synthesis to available heme, and in other tissues it converts mitochondrial damage into a protective transcriptional programme. The kinase EIF2AK1 phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eIF2 (EIF2S1), which throttles general cap-dependent translation while favouring ATF4, and thence CHOP (DDIT3), driving amino acid supply, redox defence and, when stress persists, apoptosis. Mitochondrial input arrives through the inner-membrane protease OMA1, which cleaves DELE1 so that a released fragment reaches the cytosol and activates the kinase; ATAD3A restrains this axis, and the ubiquitin ligase components KCMF1 and UBR4 set DELE1 stability. The result couples organelle quality control to protein synthesis rates.

Migrating cells leave behind vesicle-like structures at the tips and branch points of retraction fibres, and migracytosis is the process by which those migrasomes form, mature and burst to release their contents into the extracellular space. It gives a motile cell a way to deposit signals, membrane material and even damaged mitochondria along its path, so that chemokines and other cues are laid down as a spatial trail for neighbouring cells during processes such as organ patterning and tissue repair; discarding defective mitochondria through the same route also links it to mitochondrial quality control. Tetraspanin-enriched microdomains provide the membrane platform for migrasome assembly, integrin-based adhesion anchors the retraction fibres, and kinesin- and myosin-dependent transport moves cargo, including mitochondria, into the forming structures before release.

The spindle assembly checkpoint holds cells in mitosis until every kinetochore is properly attached to microtubules, and it must be switched off once that condition is met; damping checkpoint signalling is what allows anaphase onset and timely mitotic exit. Cells that cannot turn it down arrest in mitosis and may die or slip through with missegregated chromosomes, so this arm of checkpoint control sits at the interface of chromosome segregation fidelity and proliferation. p31comet, encoded by MAD2L1BP, binds closed-conformation MAD2 and antagonises its incorporation into the inhibitory complex that restrains the anaphase-promoting complex, while MAD1L1 provides the kinetochore platform whose occupancy determines signal strength. SKA1 and SKA3 belong to the Ska complex that stabilises kinetochore-microtubule attachments, removing the very defect that generates the signal.

Cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells kill virus-infected and tumour cells by delivering granzymes into them, and granzyme-mediated programmed cell death is the route from that delivery to the target cell's demise. It underlies antiviral defence and tumour immunosurveillance, and is the effector arm exploited by checkpoint-blockade and engineered T cell therapies. Granzymes are stored with perforin in cytotoxic granules, where serglycin serves as the proteoglycan matrix and proteins such as NKG7 and LAMP1 support granule maturation and exocytosis; perforin then permits granzyme entry across the target membrane. Once inside, granzyme B cleaves caspases and BID to commit mitochondria to apoptosis, while cleavage of gasdermin E redirects killing toward pyroptosis, a lytic and inflammatory outcome. Granzyme A acts through a caspase-independent path. Loss of this cytotoxic machinery produces immunodeficiency and hyperinflammatory syndromes.

Interphase chromosomes are folded into loops and domains, and this loop-extrusion process is how that architecture is built: a ring-shaped SMC complex is loaded onto chromatin and reels DNA through itself until it meets an anchor. The resulting loops bring distant enhancers into contact with promoters, insulate neighbouring regulatory landscapes from one another, and organise sister chromatid cohesion and DNA repair templates. Cohesin subunits such as RAD21 with the NIPBL-MAU2 loader drive extrusion, WAPL releases the complex to limit loop length, and CTCF together with ZNF143 marks the boundaries where extrusion halts. An SMC5/6 arm with its NSMCE partners and the SLF1-SLF2 recruitment module handles replication-associated lesions and topological stress. Loss of loader or boundary function rearranges gene expression and underlies cohesinopathies such as Cornelia de Lange syndrome, and boundary disruption can activate oncogenes.

Proteins can be marked for destruction by what lies at their very end: this C-degron pathway, also called DesCEND, recognises C-terminal residues as degradation signals and routes the bearer to the proteasome. It provides quality control over truncated and proteolytically cleaved proteins, whose newly exposed C-termini flag them as aberrant, and it also sets the half-life of intact regulatory proteins. Substrate receptors with distinct C-end preferences — KLHDC2 and KLHDC3 for diglycine ends, FEM1A/B/C for arginine ends, DCAF12 for acidic ends, plus APPBP2, TRPC4AP and PRAME — plug into Cullin-2 or Cullin-4 RING ligase scaffolds through elongin B and C and RBX1, which delivers ubiquitin. Through these receptors the pathway controls SELENOK and SELENOS readthrough products, redox and apoptotic regulators, and degradation-coupled protein maturation, complementing the better-known N-degron route.

Pyroptosis is a lytic, inflammatory form of cell death used to destroy infected cells and release interleukin-1 family cytokines, and the genes here act to raise its frequency and extent. Guanylate-binding proteins, induced by interferon, coat intracellular bacteria and pathogen-containing vacuoles, liberating ligands such as LPS to the cytosolic sensors that activate inflammatory caspases and gasdermin cleavage; their action links pathogen detection to commitment to death. Palmitoyltransferase activity contributes by S-acylating substrates required for membrane targeting of pore-forming and sensor components, showing that lipid modification is a control point rather than a housekeeping detail. Caspase-3 connects this route to apoptotic executioner biology, where gasdermin processing can switch the outcome between quiet apoptosis and inflammatory lysis. Amplification of this response drives antibacterial defence but also the tissue damage of sepsis and autoinflammatory disease.

RNA polymerase II cannot elongate through a nucleosome without disrupting it, and this transcription elongation-coupled chromatin remodeling activity puts the chromatin back together behind the advancing polymerase. Restoring nucleosomes over the body of a gene keeps promoter-like sequences buried, so that cryptic initiation inside coding regions is suppressed and only the proper start site is used; loss of this restoration produces spurious intragenic transcripts and antisense noise. The core of the process is a histone chaperone and elongation factor module in which SUPT6H binds histones and travels with the polymerase, partnered with IWS1, while SUPT4H1 forms part of the DSIF elongation complex and CDK9 phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and elongation factors to license productive elongation. Associated chromatin readers and a deubiquitinase tune histone modification state, linking elongation speed to the fidelity of transcript start sites.

Not every organelle is enclosed by a membrane; many are self-organizing assemblies of protein and RNA held together by multivalent interactions, and this pathway covers their construction. It spans stress granules and P-bodies that sequester mRNAs and stall translation during stress, nucleoli where ribosomes are built, centrosomes and centrioles that nucleate microtubules, kinetochores that grip spindle microtubules at centromeres, the midbody that completes cytokinesis, sarcomeres of striated muscle, and lipid droplets. RNA-binding scaffolds such as G3BP1/2, TIA1, FUS and LSM14A drive granule condensation, while centriolar factors including PLK4, SASS6, CEP152 and the augmin complex template new microtubule organizing centres, and CENP proteins with HJURP deposit centromeric histone H3 variants. Because these condensates concentrate reactions without compartmentalizing them, their mis-assembly underlies aberrant protein aggregation in neurodegeneration, microcephaly from centriole defects, chromosome missegregation, and myopathies from disordered sarcomere assembly.

Cells silence genes reversibly, and facultative heterochromatin is the compacted, transcriptionally refractory state that can be reopened when development, the cell cycle, or an external signal demands it. This underlies lineage commitment, monoallelic expression such as X inactivation and imprinting, and the silencing of rDNA and repeat elements; its loss lets inappropriate programmes fire, and the enzymes involved are recurrently mutated or overexpressed in cancer. The core is a Polycomb repressive complex in which EZH2 methylates histone H3K27, with EED, SUZ12 and JARID2 governing its recruitment and activity, complemented by H3K9 methyltransferases SUV39H1 and EHMT1. Consolidation involves linker histone H1, the histone variant macroH2A, sirtuin deacetylases, the nucleolar silencing factor BAZ2A with the remodeller SMARCA5, and demethylases such as PHF8 and KDM5A that set the balance between silenced and active chromatin.

Large tracts of the genome — pericentromeric repeats, transposons, satellite DNA — are kept permanently silent, and constitutive heterochromatin formation is how that silence is built and inherited. It protects genome stability by preventing retrotransposon mobilisation and aberrant recombination between repeats, and its loss is associated with derepression of repetitive elements, replication stress and features of cellular ageing. The core chemistry is methylation of histone H3 lysine 9 by SETDB1 and the EHMT1/EHMT2 complex, read by the HUSH components MPHOSPH8 and TASOR and reinforced by the corepressor TRIM28; DNA methyltransferases DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3L add and maintain cytosine methylation, which MBD-family proteins read back into repression. Chromatin remodellers such as ATRX, HELLS and SMARCA5 give the machinery access to nucleosomal repeats. A piRNA arm — PIWIL1/2/4, MOV10L1, Tudor-domain proteins and SPOCD1 — directs this silencing to transposons in the germline.

Long non-coding RNAs are transcripts over 200 nucleotides that are not translated yet regulate chromatin state, neighbouring gene expression and nuclear organisation, and their synthesis from DNA templates is the process captured here. Because pervasive transcription generates far more non-coding RNA than the cell needs, this biology is as much about where transcription stops as where it starts: WDR82 and ZC3H4 act together in restrictor and termination surveillance complexes that prematurely terminate unproductive non-coding transcription units and so limit interference with protein-coding genes. Other members contribute sequence-specific and tissue-restricted control, including the inducible transcription factor NFATC2 and the germline-associated TOPAZ1, which is required for meiotic gene expression in spermatocytes. Loss of such control leads to read-through transcription, misregulated enhancer and antisense RNAs, and developmental or gametogenic failure.

DNA lesions occur in packaged chromatin, and repair enzymes cannot reach them until nucleosomes and histone marks are locally rearranged; this remodeling around damage sites is what licenses access. Its output is accurate double-strand break repair and single-strand break sealing, and failure of individual components causes genome instability, radiosensitivity and predisposition to cancer. Sensing of breaks by PARP enzymes and their serine-ADP-ribosylation cofactor HPF1 recruits chromatin factors, while the RNF8-RNF168 ubiquitin ligase relay ubiquitylates histone H2A to build a platform for downstream repair proteins; deubiquitinases such as USP3 and BRCC3, within the BRCA1-A complex alongside BABAM1 and UIMC1, restrain and reverse that signal. Acetyltransferases including KAT5 and EP300, the deacetylases HDAC3 and the sirtuins, the demethylase KDM1A and the histone chaperone ASF1A together relax and then restore chromatin, coupling repair to transcriptional silencing and chromatin recovery afterwards.

Interferon-mediated signalling is how cells announce and respond to viral infection and intracellular pathogens, converting receptor engagement into a transcriptional programme that restricts pathogen replication and shapes immune activation. Type I, type II and type III interferons each bind their own receptor pairs, yet all converge on receptor-associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 kinases that phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2 to drive interferon-stimulated gene expression. The induced effectors act directly: oligoadenylate synthetases and ADAR act on RNA, IFITM proteins block membrane fusion during viral entry, SAMHD1 and TREX1 limit nucleic acid substrates, and ISG15 conjugation marks targets broadly. Upstream nucleic acid sensing through IFIH1, MAVS, STING1 and TBK1 induces interferon production itself, while phosphatases such as PTPN2 and the isopeptidase USP18 damp the response. Loss of control causes susceptibility to mycobacteria and viruses at one extreme and interferonopathy or autoimmunity at the other.

Endolysosomal toll-like receptor signaling pathway is how cells detect microbial nucleic acids after they have been internalised, sensing viral RNA and unmethylated CpG DNA from within acidified endosomes rather than at the cell surface. It drives type I interferon and inflammatory cytokine output from plasmacytoid dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells, and its loss leaves patients vulnerable to herpesvirus encephalitis, while its inappropriate activation against self nucleic acids underlies lupus and related autoimmunity. TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 must first be trafficked and proteolytically matured, a step requiring UNC93B1 and the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 with its adaptor TASL; ligand binding then assembles MYD88-IRAK4-IRAK1-TRAF6 or TICAM1 complexes that activate TAK1, IKK and NF-kB alongside interferon regulatory factors. Compartment identity is the control point, and negative regulators such as TNFAIP3 and PTPN22 keep the response self-limiting.

Nucleic acids from viruses and bacteria are sensed not at the cell surface but inside acidified endosomes and lysosomes, and this compartmentalised arm of Toll-like receptor signalling is how innate immune cells detect them. TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 recognise double-stranded RNA, single-stranded RNA and CpG DNA respectively, and depend on the trafficking chaperone UNC93B1 and the transporter SLC15A4 with its adaptor TASL to reach and function in these compartments. Ligand binding recruits MYD88 or TICAM1, and through IRAK4, IRAK1, TRAF6 and MAP3K7 drives NF-kB and IRF-dependent transcription of TNF and type I interferons, with TNFAIP3 and PTPN22 restraining the output. Because the receptors see self nucleic acids released from dying cells, loss of this restraint underlies lupus and other interferon-driven autoimmunity, while defects impair antiviral defence, notably herpes encephalitis.

Toll-like receptors on the plasma membrane are the innate immune system's front line for detecting bacteria and fungi, and signalling from them converts that detection into inflammation. TLR4 with its accessory proteins CD14, LBP and LY96 senses lipopolysaccharide, while TLR2 pairs with TLR1 or TLR6 for lipopeptides and TLR5 recognises flagellin; ligand binding recruits MYD88 and the TIRAP/TICAM2 adaptors, activating IRAK4 and IRAK1, TRAF6 and MAP3K7 to release NF-kB subunits from NFKBIA and drive cytokine transcription, with TBK1 and IRF3 adding an interferon arm. Because unrestrained output is damaging, the pathway is heavily braked by TNFAIP3, TNIP2, PELI1, receptor trafficking and a set of microRNAs including MIR146A. Too little signalling leaves patients vulnerable to pyogenic infection; too much contributes to septic shock, and to sterile inflammation driven by endogenous ligands such as HMGB1.

Cytosolic DNA is a danger signal: it means a virus, a bacterium, or the cell's own damaged genome has escaped its proper compartment. The cGAS/STING pathway is how cells detect it and mount a type I interferon response. The sensor cGAS binds double-stranded DNA and synthesizes the cyclic dinucleotide cGAMP, which activates the endoplasmic reticulum adaptor STING; STING traffics and recruits the kinase TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 to drive interferon transcription, with parallel NF-κB output through TAK1 and RELA. Output is held in check at multiple points, including cytosolic degradation of DNA by the exonuclease TREX1, cGAMP transport and hydrolysis, palmitoylation of STING, and ubiquitin-dependent turnover. Loss of restraint produces sterile interferon-driven autoinflammation and interferonopathies, while the same axis shapes antiviral defence, senescence, and antitumour immunity after DNA damage.

MicroRNAs are usually stable once loaded into Argonaute, but some targets turn the relationship around and destroy the miRNA that binds them; this target-directed miRNA degradation lets cells clear specific miRNAs rapidly during developmental transitions and neuronal maturation rather than waiting for dilution by division. A highly complementary RNA — a long non-coding RNA such as OIP5-AS1 or an mRNA site — pairs extensively with the guide inside the silencing complex, which displaces the miRNA 3' end from the Argonaute PAZ pocket and exposes it to tailing by a terminal nucleotidyltransferase and to trimming nucleases. Recognition of this altered conformation by the ZSWIM8 substrate receptor, working with the elongin B and C subunits of a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, instead commits Argonaute itself to proteasomal degradation, releasing and destabilising its guide. The outcome is directed, sequence-specific control over miRNA lifetime and hence over the repression of whole target networks.

Body fluids such as blood and urine must be held at steady composition, and this organism-level chemical homeostasis is what keeps water, salt, iron and airway surface liquid within tolerable limits across tissues rather than inside a single cell. Much of the set is renal: vasopressin acting through its V2 receptor and adenylate cyclase-protein kinase A signalling controls aquaporin-2 trafficking to the collecting duct membrane, while epithelial sodium channel subunits, uromodulin and a vacuolar ATPase subunit set sodium reabsorption and urinary acidification. A second arm is systemic iron balance, where hepcidin, ferroportin, transferrin and its receptors, HFE and the protease TMPRSS6 match absorption to demand; loss of this control produces haemochromatosis or anaemia. Surfactant lipid transport and CFTR-dependent fluid secretion extend the same logic to the lung, and failures here underlie diabetes insipidus and cystic fibrosis.

Germ cells silence transposable elements before they can mutate the genome that will be passed to the next generation, and piRNA-mediated heterochromatin formation is how that silencing is made durable. Small RNAs bound to PIWI proteins guide the machinery to nascent transposon transcripts, and the targeted loci acquire repressive chromatin marked by H3K9 methylation together with de novo DNA methylation, so the elements stay off through later development. The pathway depends on a helicase that feeds precursor transcripts into piRNA biogenesis, a set of Tudor-domain proteins that scaffold the processing and effector complexes in germ granules, and the SPOCD1 adaptor that couples nuclear PIWIL4 to the DNMT3A-DNMT3L methyltransferase. Loss of these components leads to transposon reactivation, meiotic failure and male infertility, placing this biology at the intersection of small RNA silencing, epigenetic imprinting of the germline and spermatogenesis.

Cytosolic double-stranded DNA, whether from a bacterium that has escaped its vacuole, a DNA virus, or damaged host chromatin, is read as a danger signal, and assembly of the AIM2 inflammasome is how that signal becomes an inflammatory response. AIM2 binds DNA through its HIN domain and oligomerises via its pyrin domain into a platform that recruits and autoactivates caspase-1, which then matures IL-1β and IL-18 and cleaves gasdermin D to drive pyroptotic death of the infected cell. Guanylate-binding proteins contribute by lysing pathogen-containing vacuoles and liberating microbial DNA for detection, while IFI16 provides a related DNA sensor. Because unrestrained assembly is damaging, it is held in check by regulators including a pyrin-domain-only decoy protein and TRIM11. Overactivity of this route contributes to autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, notably where self-DNA accumulates.

regulation of AIM2 inflammasome complex assembly sets the threshold for one of the cell's cytosolic DNA alarms. AIM2 binds double-stranded DNA released by intracellular bacteria, DNA viruses, or damaged host nuclei and mitochondria, then nucleates a caspase-1 platform that matures IL-1beta and IL-18 and drives gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis; because that outcome kills the cell and inflames the tissue, assembly must be licensed rather than automatic. The genes here act on both sides of that decision. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins promote it by rupturing pathogen-containing vacuoles and bacterial surfaces so ligand DNA reaches the sensor, linking the response to prior interferon priming. Countering them, a PYD-only protein competes for pyrin-domain interactions and a tripartite-motif ubiquitin ligase restrains the sensor, while IFI16 provides a related nuclear DNA-sensing arm. Imbalance contributes to autoinflammation and interferon-driven disease.

Cytosolic double-stranded DNA, whether from bacteria, viruses or damaged host nuclei, nucleates the AIM2 inflammasome, and this control layer sets how readily that complex forms. Because assembly commits a cell to caspase-1 activation, IL-1β and IL-18 maturation and pyroptotic death, tuning it decides whether an infected cell is sacrificed or spared, and mistuning contributes to autoinflammatory tissue damage. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins act upstream by helping lyse pathogen-containing vacuoles and bacteria so that DNA reaches the cytosol, raising the amount of ligand available. IFI16 is a related DNA sensor of the same family that can also engage nuclear and cytoplasmic DNA, while pyrin-domain-only proteins act as decoys that block productive PYD-PYD polymerisation, and TRIM11 contributes ubiquitin-dependent regulation. The net effect is threshold-setting for innate immune detection of misplaced DNA.

Alpha-defensins are small cationic peptides that kill microbes by attacking their surface structures, and this activity is how they contribute to innate immunity at the body's barriers. Neutrophil-derived members are packaged into azurophilic granules and released into the phagosome or the extracellular space, while the enteric forms are secreted by Paneth cells in the small intestinal crypt, where they shape the resident microbiota and protect stem cells from invading bacteria. Their mechanism is physical rather than enzymatic: the amphipathic, disulfide-constrained fold binds anionic bacterial membranes and lipid components of the envelope, permeabilizing them so that ion gradients and barrier integrity fail and the target cell dies. The same chemistry inactivates some enveloped viruses and fungi. Reduced Paneth cell defensin output is associated with ileal Crohn's disease, linking this antimicrobial disruption of another organism's structures to mucosal homeostasis.

Transposable elements make up much of the genome and their mobilization can disrupt genes and destroy genome integrity, so cells package them into heterochromatin that transcription cannot read. The set combines two arms of this defence. In the germ line, PIWI proteins loaded with piRNAs, assisted by the RNA helicase MOV10L1 and a series of Tudor-domain cofactors, recognize transposon transcripts and direct de novo DNA methylation through DNMT3A with its catalytically inactive partner DNMT3L and the recruiter SPOCD1; loss of this arm causes transposon activation, meiotic arrest and male infertility. In somatic cells, the HUSH complex components TASOR, MPHOSPH8 and PPHLN1 together with the methyltransferase SETDB1 deposit H3K9 trimethylation over young retroelements and integrated proviruses, with MORC2 compacting the resulting chromatin. Both routes convert sequence recognition into stable transcriptional repression rather than cleavage, and they also silence exogenous retroviruses and transgenes.

Germ cells must keep transposons quiescent to pass an intact genome to the next generation, and piRNA-guided heterochromatin formation is the branch of that defence that acts on DNA and chromatin rather than on transcripts. Small RNAs loaded onto PIWI proteins recognise nascent transposon transcripts in the nucleus and recruit repressive machinery, converting active transposon loci into transcriptionally silent chromatin; in mammals this includes directing de novo DNA methylation at young LINE-1 elements, with SPOCD1 linking the piRNA machinery to the methyltransferase complex and TDRD9 acting as an accessory helicase in nuclear silencing. DDX4 marks the germ granule compartment where piRNA biogenesis and PIWI function are organised. Loss of these components de-represses transposons in developing germ cells, causing meiotic failure, spermatogenic arrest and male infertility, and the established silent state is heritable through subsequent development.

Disruption of anatomical structure in another organism covers the host's offensive chemistry against microbes and infected cells: molecules that physically breach membranes, walls and cell envelopes rather than merely signalling alarm. It is the effector end of innate and cytotoxic immunity, and its loss leaves mucosal surfaces, skin and blood open to bacterial and fungal colonisation. Several distinct weapons converge here. Terminal complement components polymerise into the membrane attack complex; defensins, cathelicidin, histatins and RNASE7 permeabilise microbial membranes at epithelial and neutrophil sites; lysozyme and peptidoglycan recognition proteins digest the bacterial wall; lactoferrin and hepcidin starve invaders of metals. Perforin, granulysin and granzymes deliver the same principle from cytotoxic lymphocytes into target cells, while guanylate-binding proteins rupture intracellular pathogen vacuoles. Chemokines recruit the cells that release these agents, many doubling as direct antimicrobials themselves.

Host defence often works by physically breaking the invader, and this pathway collects the effectors that disrupt anatomical structures in another organism — chiefly the membranes and cell walls of bacteria, fungi and infected or transformed cells. It underpins innate antimicrobial immunity at epithelial surfaces, in neutrophil granules, and in cytotoxic lymphocytes, and its loss leaves recurrent infection and impaired tumour surveillance. Cationic peptides of the defensin, cathelicidin and histatin families permeabilise microbial membranes; lysozyme and peptidoglycan recognition proteins attack the cell wall; lactoferrin and hepcidin starve microbes of iron; complement components C5 through C9 polymerise into the lytic membrane attack complex; and perforin with granulysin and granzymes breaches target cells directly. Neutrophil serine proteases such as elastase and cathepsin G, guanylate-binding proteins, and gasdermin- and ninjurin-dependent membrane rupture extend the same destructive logic, with chemokines recruiting the cells that deliver it.

Cells must keep nitrogen-bearing metabolites such as ammonia, glutamine and arginine within a tolerable range, and intracellular nitrogen homeostasis is the balancing act that holds that steady state. It matters most in liver and brain, where failure lets ammonia accumulate and produces the encephalopathy seen in urea cycle defects. Argininosuccinate lyase performs the urea cycle step that releases arginine and fumarate, disposing of waste nitrogen while feeding arginine into nitric oxide and creatine synthesis; a glutamine synthetase-like enzyme contributes to ammonia fixation onto glutamate. Transport and regulatory components round out the picture, with a multidrug resistance-associated efflux pump handling glutathione conjugates and a bile acid-activated nuclear receptor coupling nitrogen and bile metabolism to transcription. The presence of opposing apoptotic regulators reflects how nitrogen and ammonia stress feed into cell survival decisions.

Genomic imprinting on autosomes makes a gene's expression depend on which parent it came from, so that a maternal and a paternal allele of the same locus behave differently. Imprints are laid down as DNA methylation marks at germline differentially methylated regions during gametogenesis, then maintained through the somatic divisions of the whole life of the organism, where they generate heterochromatin or alter chromatin looping at the affected cluster. The de novo methyltransferase DNMT3A with its catalytically inactive cofactor DNMT3L establishes the marks in germ cells, and the KRAB zinc finger protein ZFP57 recognizes methylated imprinted regions to keep them silenced in the embryo. Because imprinted loci govern fetal growth and placental function, loss or gain of these marks produces overgrowth and growth-restriction syndromes, neurodevelopmental disorders, and, when reactivated, contributes to tumour phenotypes.

Cells detect microbial invasion and damage in their own cytosol by assembling inflammasomes, and this route converts that detection into overt inflammation. Sensors such as NLRP1, NLRP3 and IFI16 oligomerize with the adaptor ASC (PYCARD) to activate caspase-1, which matures IL-1β and IL-18 and cleaves gasdermin to drive pyroptotic death, releasing alarmins and recruiting phagocytes. Upstream cues are diverse: Toll-like receptors and MyD88-IRAK signalling prime expression, potassium efflux through P2RX7 and KCNK channels and other stress signals license assembly, and NEK7 licenses the NLRP3 particle. A large regulatory layer keeps the response restrained — pyrin-only proteins, NLRC3 and NLRP6 as negative sensors, TRIM and FBXL2 ubiquitin ligases, BRCC3 deubiquitination, palmitoylation by ZDHHC enzymes and SIRT2 or OGT modification. Failure of this restraint underlies familial Mediterranean fever, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes, gout and metabolic inflammation.

Inflammasomes are cytosolic sensor platforms that assemble in response to infection or cellular damage, activating caspase-1 to mature IL-1β and IL-18 and to trigger pyroptotic cell death; the regulation of inflammasome-mediated signalling determines how far that response goes, and its failure underlies autoinflammatory fevers, gout, metabolic inflammation and sepsis-like pathology. Both positive and negative controls appear here: NEK7 licenses NLRP3 oligomerisation, BRCC3 deubiquitinates the sensor to prime it, and NLRC3 together with pyrin-domain-only proteins dampens assembly, while TRIM and F-box factors direct ubiquitin-dependent turnover of sensor components. Upstream inputs include Toll-like receptors and MyD88-dependent priming, P2RX7 and potassium-channel-driven ionic flux, lipid and calcium sensing through CD36 and CASR, and post-translational modification by palmitoylation, acetylation, O-GlcNAcylation and kinase signalling. Pyrin itself, mutated in familial Mediterranean fever, is part of the same regulated network.

Inflammasomes are cytosolic sensor complexes that activate caspase-1 to mature IL-1β and IL-18 and to drive pyroptosis, so the braking mechanisms that restrain them are what keep an innate immune alarm from becoming sterile inflammation. Negative regulation of inflammasome-mediated signalling covers several distinct strategies: decoy PYD-only proteins such as PYDC1 and PYDC2 and the CARD-containing CARD8 compete for the adaptor interfaces needed for complex assembly; NLRC3 and IFI16 act as non-activating sensors that dampen assembly; TRIM11, TRIM31 and FBXL2 route sensor subunits to ubiquitin-dependent degradation; and autophagy-related and lysosomal routes, including IRGM and LAMP2-dependent chaperone-mediated autophagy, clear assembled components. Post-translational modification contributes too, through palmitoylation and depalmitoylation, O-GlcNAcylation by OGT, casein kinase 1 phosphorylation and SIRT2 deacetylation. Loss of such restraint underlies autoinflammatory disease, and MEFV mutations causing familial Mediterranean fever illustrate the consequence in humans.

Inflammasomes are cytosolic sensor complexes that, once assembled, activate caspase-1 to mature IL-1β and IL-18 and drive gasdermin-mediated pyroptosis; the factors here push that assembly and signalling upward. This positive regulation sets the threshold at which infection, crystals, extracellular ATP or metabolic stress are converted into overt inflammation, and its excess underlies autoinflammatory fever syndromes, gout and gouty crystal responses, and sterile tissue injury. The genes act at several tiers: Toll-like receptors and MyD88 provide priming signals that raise sensor and pro-cytokine expression; the P2X7 channel and potassium flux report extracellular nucleotides and ionic perturbation; NEK7 licenses NLRP3 oligomerisation, while BRCC3 deubiquitination, palmitoylation by ZDHHC enzymes, and kinases such as BTK, PRKD1 and MARK4 modify the sensor or position it on microtubules and mitochondria. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins liberate bacterial ligands for caspase activation.

Cytosolic DNA is a danger signal, and the cGAS/STING axis is how cells read it, converting detection of mislocalised DNA into type I interferon and inflammatory gene expression against viruses, intracellular bacteria and damaged self. Positive regulation of this pathway sets the gain of that response: too little leaves cells permissive to infection and blunts antitumour immunity, too much drives interferonopathies and sterile inflammation. The regulators here act at several levels. STING is stabilised and activated by post-translational modification, including palmitoylation by a Golgi-resident acyltransferase and ubiquitin transfer by a mitochondrial E3, while a kinase adaptor module feeds into downstream NF-kB-directed inflammatory output. A folate transporter doubles as an importer of extracellular cyclic dinucleotides, allowing cells to respond to second messengers made elsewhere, and a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase contributes signal amplification.

Chromatin can be made permissive as well as repressive, and this is the activating side of epigenetic control: processes that raise transcription at defined loci by remodelling nucleosomes, marking histones, or erasing DNA methylation. It underlies developmental gene activation, lineage identity and the reprogramming of cell states, and its loss or hyperactivity is a recurrent theme in cancer, where remodeller and methylation-machinery genes are among the most frequently mutated. The TET dioxygenases oxidise 5-methylcytosine to intermediates that base-excision enzymes such as TDG and APEX1 replace with unmodified cytosine, completing active demethylation. Histone acetyltransferases including EP300, KAT7 and KAT8 deposit activating acetylation, a WDR5-RBBP5-ASH2L-DPY30 core supports KMT2A-directed H3K4 methylation, and SWI/SNF subunits such as SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and ARID1A slide nucleosomes to open promoters and enhancers for transcription factors.

cAMP/PKA signal transduction is the classic second-messenger cassette by which hormones and neuropeptides acting at G protein-coupled receptors change what a cell does within seconds and what genes it transcribes within hours. It underlies hormone responsiveness in endocrine tissue, cardiac contractility, memory-related synaptic plasticity, lipolysis and pigmentation, and its loss or constitutive activation produces endocrine tumours and syndromes such as Carney complex. Adenylate cyclase output raises cAMP, which binds regulatory subunits (PRKAR1A, PRKAR2B) to release catalytic PKA, while A-kinase anchoring proteins confine that activity to discrete subcellular microdomains and PKI restrains it. A large family of phosphodiesterases terminates the signal, giving each tissue its own kinetics and providing the drug targets exploited in inflammation, erectile dysfunction and heart failure. Downstream, CREB1, ATF1 and CREM with the coactivator CREBBP convert the transient signal into transcription. Upstream ligands here include VIP, CRH, GHRH, secretin and urocortin.

Hormones and neuropeptides that act through G protein-coupled receptors are largely translated into cellular action by the cAMP/PKA cassette, which converts adenylate cyclase-derived cyclic AMP into phosphorylation of cytoplasmic and nuclear targets. Ligands and receptors here include VIP, secretin, CRH, urocortin, GHRH with its receptor, calcitonin and melanocortin receptors, illustrating the breadth of endocrine and neural inputs that converge on one second messenger. Cyclic AMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A, freeing catalytic PRKACA to phosphorylate substrates and activate CREB1, ATF1 and CREM-family transcription factors together with the coactivator CREBBP, linking acute stimulation to changes in gene expression. Specificity and termination come from anchoring proteins, the inhibitor PKIA, and a large phosphodiesterase family that hydrolyses cyclic nucleotides in defined microdomains. Loss of control underlies endocrine tumour syndromes, as with PRKAR1A mutation, and makes phosphodiesterases widely used drug targets.

Cyclic AMP is the second messenger through which hormones and neurotransmitters reach protein kinase A, and this pathway covers the machinery that sets how strongly and how long that signal runs. Tuning it determines hormone responsiveness in metabolism, cardiac contractility, neuronal plasticity, pigmentation and smooth muscle tone, and its components are heavily drugged. Peptide ligands and their receptors, including VIP, secretin, CRH, GHRH, urocortin and the melanocortin receptor MC1R, raise cAMP through adenylate cyclase. A large family of phosphodiesterases hydrolyses cAMP and cGMP to terminate signalling, with distinct members dominating in heart, brain, immune cells and photoreceptors. Specificity is imposed by regulatory subunits that hold PKA inactive until cAMP binds, by A-kinase anchoring proteins that tether the kinase near its substrates, and by the inhibitor PKIA. Mutation of the regulatory subunit PRKAR1A causes Carney complex.

Cyclic AMP is a short-lived second messenger, and its usefulness depends on being switched off as decisively as it is made. Damping of cAMP/PKA signalling sets the amplitude, duration and spatial confinement of responses to hormones and neurotransmitters, so that a cell can distinguish one pulse from the next rather than sitting in a state of tonic kinase activity. Two mechanisms dominate here: a large family of cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases hydrolyses cAMP (and cGMP) to the inactive 5' monophosphate, while the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A bind cAMP and, in its absence, clamp the catalytic subunits in an inactive holoenzyme. A dedicated inhibitor peptide blocks free catalytic subunits directly, and inhibitory G protein-coupled receptors such as NPY2R lower cyclase output upstream. Loss of this restraint underlies endocrine tumour syndromes, and phosphodiesterases are drug targets in cardiac, inflammatory, retinal and cognitive disease.

Many hormones and neuropeptides act by raising intracellular cAMP and thereby switching on protein kinase A, and this set collects the ligands and accessory proteins that push that cascade upward — positive regulation of cAMP/PKA signal transduction. Because PKA phosphorylates metabolic enzymes, ion channels and transcriptional regulators such as CREB, strengthening this input shapes stress hormone output, vasodilation and smooth muscle relaxation, pigmentation, insulin and growth hormone secretion, and activity-dependent gene expression in neurons. The peptide members are classic Gs-coupled agonists: pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide, vasoactive intestinal peptide, secretin, corticotropin-releasing hormone and urocortin, growth hormone-releasing hormone, calcitonin acting through its receptor, and melanocortin signalling through MC1R in melanocytes, with RAMP3 modifying receptor pharmacology. Loss or blunting of such stimulation impairs hormone release and adaptive responses, while excess drives conditions of unrestrained cAMP tone.

Removing a methyl group from 5-methylcytosine is chemically hard, so cells erase DNA methylation indirectly: the methylated or deaminated base is converted into a lesion that base excision repair can recognise, and repair synthesis restores an unmodified cytosine. This route to chromosomal 5-methylcytosine demethylation matters because methylation patterns must be reset during germ cell and early embryonic reprogramming and adjusted at promoters and enhancers when gene expression programmes change. Here the emphasis falls on deaminase-mediated conversion: the cytidine deaminase APOBEC1 with its cofactor A1CF, plus related RNA-binding partners, can act on cytosine bases to generate a mismatch, and thymine DNA glycosylase excises the resulting thymine or uracil opposite guanine to hand the gap to repair polymerases and ligase. Loss of the glycosylase step leaves epigenetic marks unerased and causes developmental failure.

Every RNA and DNA molecule in a cell eventually has to be destroyed, and nucleic acid catabolism is how that happens in a controlled, selective way: it sets the half-life of each transcript, clears defective or foreign nucleic acids, and disposes of chromosomal DNA during apoptosis. mRNA turnover dominates here, through deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT and PAN2-PAN3 complexes, decapping by DCP2 with its LSM and DDX6 partners, 5'-to-3' degradation by XRN1, and 3'-to-5' degradation by the multisubunit RNA exosome with its helicase and SKI cofactors. Sequence-specific adaptors direct these enzymes to targets: microRNAs loaded onto Argonaute and TNRC6 proteins, AU-rich element binders such as ZFP36 and ELAVL1, and the UPF-SMG machinery that destroys transcripts bearing premature stop codons. Nucleases including DNASE1L3, TREX1, ENDOG and the RNase H enzymes clear DNA and RNA-DNA hybrids, and their loss provokes interferon-driven autoimmunity such as lupus and Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome.

Steroids, retinoids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D, fatty acids and bile acids act largely by binding receptors inside the cell that are themselves transcription factors, and nuclear receptor-mediated signaling is the route from ligand to altered gene expression. It sets sexual development and fertility, metabolic fuel choice, calcium handling, circadian timing and inflammatory tone, and its subversion drives breast and prostate cancers treated by blocking oestrogen and androgen receptors. Ligand-bound receptors such as ESR1, AR, NR3C1, PPARG, RARA, THRB, VDR and their RXR partners exchange corepressor complexes containing NCOR1/2 and histone deacetylases for coactivators including NCOA1-3, MED1, EP300 and CARM1, remodelling chromatin at hormone response elements. Ligand supply and clearance is built in through enzymes like CYP27B1, CYP24A1 and the CYP26 retinoic acid hydroxylases, while chaperones, ubiquitin ligases and lineage factors such as FOXA1 determine which genes each receptor can reach.

Ubiquitin chains are not always simple: a single ubiquitin can be modified at more than one lysine, producing branched polyubiquitin such as K11/K48- or K11/K63-linked chains that mark substrates for unusually efficient proteasomal destruction or, in other contexts, tune signalling output. This form of branched polyubiquitination matters most at cell cycle transitions, where the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome — represented here by its full subunit roster including the cullin-like ANAPC2, the RING subunit ANAPC11, and the substrate-recognition adaptor ANAPC10 — tags cyclins and securin for timely degradation so that mitotic exit is irreversible. HECT-family ligases such as HUWE1 and ITCH, and the large ligases UBR4 and UBR5, elaborate and diversify chain architecture, while TRAF6 links branched chains to inflammatory and innate immune signalling rather than proteolysis. Chain topology thus encodes which fate a substrate receives.

Pyroptotic cell death is a lytic, inflammatory way for a cell to die, used mainly by macrophages and epithelia to expose intracellular infection and alert neighbouring tissue. Unlike apoptosis it ends in rupture and release of interleukin-1 family cytokines and other alarmins, so it drives fever and neutrophil recruitment but also tissue damage in sepsis, inflammatory bowel disease and autoinflammatory syndromes. Execution depends on gasdermins, which are cleaved to liberate a pore-forming N-terminal fragment that oligomerises in the plasma membrane; GSDMD is the canonical inflammasome caspase substrate, GSDME is cut by caspase-3 to convert apoptotic signals into lytic death, and GSDMB can be processed by the cytotoxic lymphocyte protease granzyme A. Membrane rupture itself is not passive: NINJ1 oligomerises to break the swollen, permeabilised cell open and complete release of its inflammatory contents.

A short intracellular relay in which phospholipase C cleaves membrane phosphoinositides to generate inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from internal stores and together with DAG switching on protein kinase C, which then phosphorylates downstream effectors. This cassette converts receptor occupancy — typically by G protein-coupled receptors such as the chemokine receptor CCR7 responding to CCL19 and CCL21, or by endothelin — into changes in secretion, contraction, cytoskeletal remodelling, adhesion and gene expression, and it underlies lymphocyte and dendritic cell homing to lymph nodes as well as cardiac and vascular responses to mechanical and hormonal stress. Diacylglycerol kinases terminate the DAG signal by converting it to phosphatidic acid, setting how long PKC isoforms such as PRKCD and PRKCH stay active. Persistent or misdirected flux through this route contributes to cardiac hypertrophy and to inflammatory and neoplastic signalling.

positive regulation of phospholipase C/protein kinase C signal transduction covers the inputs that switch on the classical second-messenger arm of receptor signalling, in which phospholipase C cleaves membrane PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate to raise cytosolic calcium and activate protein kinase C. Amplifying this branch converts surface receptor occupancy into cytoskeletal remodelling, adhesion changes, transcriptional responses and directed cell movement. The chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 illustrate the physiology: this axis guides naive T cells and mature dendritic cells into lymph nodes across high endothelial venules, organising adaptive immune priming, and is co-opted by tumour cells for lymph node metastasis. Cytoplasmic regulators such as the ABL1 tyrosine kinase and the Rho GTPase-activating protein ARHGAP6 couple phospholipase C output to actin dynamics, linking calcium and kinase C signalling to shape and motility.

Upregulating phospholipase C/protein kinase C signalling amplifies the arm of receptor signalling in which PIP2 is cleaved into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, raising cytosolic calcium and recruiting protein kinase C to membranes to drive cytoskeletal remodelling, secretion and transcriptional responses. The genes here point to two settings. The chemokines CCL19 and CCL21 acting through CCR7 direct naive T cells and dendritic cells into lymph node stroma, and the phospholipase C/PKC output of that receptor supports the actin rearrangement and integrin activation needed for chemotaxis and immune surveillance; loss of this axis impairs lymphoid organ architecture and priming of adaptive responses. ABL1, a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, and the Rho GTPase-activating protein ARHGAP6 tie the same lipid-derived signalling to cytoskeletal and adhesion control, showing that enhancement of this cascade is typically exerted by upstream receptors and cytoskeletal regulators rather than by the lipase itself.

Synapses release neurotransmitter not only when an action potential arrives but also spontaneously, in miniature events that set the resting tone of a circuit and help maintain synaptic strength and postsynaptic health. Regulation of spontaneous synaptic transmission covers the processes that tune how often these events occur, and it matters because their frequency shapes dendritic protein synthesis, receptor stabilisation and the excitability of developing and mature networks. The genes here point to several control points: a presynaptic SNARE component governing vesicle fusion, a cation-chloride cotransporter setting intracellular chloride and hence the driving force for inhibitory currents, an adhesion receptor linking the synapse to its matrix, and an E3 ubiquitin ligase mutated in parkinsonism that limits presynaptic protein turnover. Amyloid precursor protein and a receptor for advanced glycation end products tie the same regulation to neurodegenerative synaptic dysfunction.

How far and how densely a neuron's axons and dendrites branch determines how many partners it can contact, so control of neuron projection arborization shapes circuit wiring, synapse number and the refinement of connectivity during development. Failure to tune branching contributes to malformed circuits and neurodevelopmental disease. The genes here converge on Wnt signalling through a Frizzled receptor and the Dishevelled adaptors, with WNT5A as a branching cue and a Sprouty-family antagonist restraining growth-factor input; cytoskeletal effectors including the spectraplakin MACF1 and an unconventional myosin couple these signals to actin and microtubule remodelling in the growth cone. Netrin-G ligands and their scaffolding partners position branches onto appropriate dendritic targets, while postsynaptic scaffolds such as DLG4 and GRIP1 tie branch stabilisation to synapse formation, linking guidance cues, RNA handling and lipid transport to the final shape of the arbor.

positive regulation of neuron projection arborization describes the signals that drive neurons to elaborate branched dendrites and axon arbors, setting how many synaptic partners a neuron can reach. Arbor complexity determines circuit wiring and receptive field size, and impoverished branching is a recurring feature of intellectual disability and neurodegenerative conditions. The genes centre on Wnt signalling: WNT5A acting through FZD4 and the Dishevelled proteins reorganizes the cytoskeleton at growing branch tips, largely via non-canonical, planar-polarity-like output rather than transcription. Scaffolds contribute the other half, with PSD-95 and GRIP1 anchoring glutamate receptors and trafficking cargo to nascent branches so that arbor growth is coupled to synaptic activity, while the kinase MAP3K13 relays stress and growth cues into branch initiation. Together they position dendrite morphogenesis downstream of extracellular guidance cues and synapse formation.

Neurons acquire their input and output capacity by branching, and processes that promote neuron projection arborization set how many dendritic or axonal branches a cell extends and where they go. The extent of branching determines how many synapses a neuron can host, so this regulation shapes circuit connectivity and, when it fails, contributes to intellectual disability and other neurodevelopmental disorders. Much of the activity here is Wnt-driven: a secreted ligand acting through Frizzled receptors and the Dishevelled adaptors reorganizes the cytoskeleton at growing branch tips, while a MAP kinase kinase kinase carries the signal into branch-promoting phosphorylation events. Scaffolding proteins of the postsynaptic density and glutamate receptor trafficking machinery link new branches to synapse assembly, coupling structural growth with the maturation of excitatory transmission.

Lysosomes only work as signalling and degradative hubs if the right proteins are delivered to and held at their membrane, and this pathway covers the control of how much protein gets targeted there. The genes point to the lysosomal surface as a platform for nutrient sensing: Ragulator, through its LAMTOR1 anchor, tethers Rag GTPases and mTORC1 to the limiting membrane, GPR137B is a lysosomal transmembrane protein that acts on Rag-dependent mTORC1 recruitment and lysosome positioning, and MEAK7 also associates with mTOR. Alongside them, kinases such as AKT1 and ROCK2 tune membrane trafficking and cytoskeletal steps that govern recruitment. Because mTORC1 activity depends on being brought to this compartment, modulating protein localization to lysosomes sets the balance between anabolic growth and autophagic degradation, and helps determine lysosomal biogenesis and cargo clearance capacity.

Excitatory and inhibitory synapses are built largely on the receiving side, where receptor scaffolds, actin and adhesion molecules are gathered into a functional postsynaptic specialization; this pathway covers the signals that tune how fast and how extensively that assembly proceeds. Its output is dendritic spine number and shape, and hence synaptic strength, learning and the balance of circuit excitability, with defects contributing to intellectual disability, autism and schizophrenia risk. Much of the control converges on Rho-family GTPase signalling: Rac1 and Rac3 with their DOCK-family activators and ARHGAP-family inactivators remodel the spine actin cytoskeleton, while RhoG and GNA13 feed in upstream cues. Trans-synaptic adhesion and guidance receptors including neurexin, nectin-3, LRP4 and the Nogo receptor position nascent contacts, and neddylation enzymes, retromer trafficking and translational repressors such as CPEB3 and PUM2 set the local supply of postsynaptic components.

Injury, infection or protein aggregation in the brain triggers a rapid defensive reaction by resident glia, and this neuroinflammatory response is how microglia and astrocytes detect the insult, amplify it into a cytokine signal, and clear debris. It is protective when brief and damaging when sustained: chronic activation of these same components accompanies Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and several members here are risk genes for them. Pattern and damage receptors including Toll-like receptors, the advanced glycation end-product receptor and complement receptors sense danger; TREM2 with its adaptor TYROBP and PLCG2 sets microglial phagocytic and metabolic activation; interleukin-1β, TNF, IL-6 and interferon-γ with their receptors propagate the response through JAK2 and MAP kinase cascades, while cyclooxygenase-2 and matrix metalloproteinases remodel tissue. Neuronal CX3CL1 and CD200 restrain microglia, and glucocorticoid receptor signalling and specific microRNAs damp the reaction.

Inflammation inside the central nervous system is tuned rather than simply switched on, and this pathway covers the signals that set how strongly and how long microglia and astrocytes react to injury, infection or protein aggregates. Getting the setting wrong matters clinically: sustained glial activation contributes to neurodegeneration, while too little response impairs debris clearance and repair. Neuron-to-microglia brake signals such as CD200 acting through CD200R1 and fractalkine restrain activation, whereas cytokines and chemokines including TNF, IL1B, IL6, IL18 and CCL3/CCL5 with their receptors amplify and recruit. Microglial sensors and effectors such as TREM2, PLCG2, GRN, LRRK2 and cathepsin-related genes shape the activated state, matrix metalloproteinases remodel tissue, and prostaglandin synthesis via PTGS2 plus MAPK1/MAPK3 signalling and several microRNAs provide additional layers of damping or reinforcement.

Inflammation inside the central nervous system is driven largely by microglia and infiltrating leukocytes, and this pathway covers the signals that turn that response up. Amplified neuroinflammation is protective when it clears pathogens and debris, but sustained activation contributes to neurodegeneration, chronic pain and the tissue damage that follows stroke or trauma. The genes here span the layers of that amplification: pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL1B, IL6, IL18, IL33 and TNF; chemokines CCL3 and CCL5 with the receptor CCR1 that recruits myeloid cells; the microglial receptor TREM2 and its downstream signalling partner PLCG2, both carrying Alzheimer's disease risk variants; LRRK2, a kinase linking Parkinson's disease to immune activation; and ERK-family kinases MAPK1 and MAPK3 that relay these inputs to inflammatory gene transcription. Regulatory microRNAs and a matrix metalloproteinase add post-transcriptional and extracellular control.

Negative regulation of neuroinflammatory response is the set of brakes that keep microglia and other CNS immune cells from sustained activation, limiting the collateral damage that inflammation inflicts on neurons and synapses. It matters because its failure underlies chronic neuroinflammation in neurodegeneration: loss-of-function in progranulin causes frontotemporal dementia with florid microgliosis, and TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's disease risk by disturbing the balance between microglial activation and restraint. Mechanistically, neurons signal their healthy presence to microglia through CD200 and fractalkine acting on CD200R1 and CX3CR1, delivering tonic inhibitory input; lysosomal and phagocytic proteins such as granulin and cystatin F, anti-inflammatory cytokines including IL4 and IGF1, decoy and regulatory receptors, and circadian control through NR1D1 further damp cytokine output. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional suppression of inflammatory transcripts, tuning the resolution phase of CNS immune responses.

Microglia and astrocytes must be able to switch off an inflammatory response once a threat has passed, and dampening the neuroinflammatory response is what keeps immune activity in the brain from damaging the tissue it protects. Neurons signal their health directly to microglia through ligand-receptor pairs such as CD200-CD200R1 and fractalkine, holding resident phagocytes in a quiescent state; loss of this restraint gives synapse loss, chronic gliosis and progressive neurodegeneration. Other components act inside the microglial cell, where progranulin, TREM2 and cystatin F set the threshold and duration of activation, and mutations in progranulin or TREM2 cause frontotemporal dementia and raise Alzheimer risk. Anti-inflammatory cytokine and growth factor input, a circadian transcriptional repressor, and several microRNAs add further layers of suppression, linking immune tone in the CNS to lipid handling, sleep-wake timing and repair.

Amyloid-beta produced in the brain must be exported to the blood to keep interstitial levels low, and transcytosis across the endothelium of the blood-brain barrier is one of the main routes by which that happens. When this clearance arm falters, the peptide accumulates in the parenchyma and around vessels, a step upstream of plaque deposition, cerebral amyloid angiopathy and Alzheimer disease risk. Uptake begins with receptor capture at the luminal or abluminal endothelial surface by LRP1, whose folding and trafficking depend on its chaperone LRPAP1, followed by clathrin-mediated internalization in which CLTC forms the coat and PICALM acts as an adaptor that also directs the resulting vesicle toward the far membrane rather than to degradation. Early endosomal sorting through RAB5A and recycling through the RAB11 GTPases determines whether the cargo is released on the other side, linking vesicle traffic directly to brain amyloid burden.

Amyloid-beta peptide is continuously produced in the brain, and whether it accumulates depends on how fast cells take it up and destroy it. Clearance by cellular catabolic processes is that disposal arm: surface receptors bind soluble or aggregated peptide, deliver it by endocytosis into the endolysosomal system, and proteases break it down, while insulin-degrading enzyme and neprilysin (MME) also cut the peptide extracellularly. Lipoprotein receptors such as LRP1 and LDLR handle receptor-mediated uptake, the scavenger receptor CD36 and the microglial receptor TREM2 couple recognition to phagocytic engulfment, and the lipid transporter ABCA7 shapes microglial clearance capacity. This is a major determinant of amyloid burden, linking lipid handling, microglial phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation; variants in several of these genes raise Alzheimer's disease risk, and impaired clearance rather than overproduction drives the common late-onset form.

Glia listen in on neuronal activity, and neuron-to-glial cell signaling is the route by which transmitters released at and around synapses inform astrocytes, oligodendrocyte lineage cells and microglia of what neurons are doing. This eavesdropping sets glial calcium responses, potassium and glutamate clearance, metabolic support, myelination of active axons and activity-dependent synapse remodelling, so its loss uncouples neuronal firing from the support functions that sustain it. The receptors here illustrate two arms of that conversation: alpha-1 adrenergic receptors couple through Gq to phospholipase C and inositol trisphosphate-mediated calcium release, letting noradrenaline from locus coeruleus projections trigger widespread astrocytic calcium elevations during arousal; the GABA-B receptor heterodimer, an obligate pairing of two subunits, signals through Gi/o to slow, sustained inhibitory responses. Similar signalling operates with glutamate, acetylcholine, dopamine and adenosine, placing this communication at the centre of neurovascular coupling and reactive gliosis.

Reactive gliosis is the coordinated reaction of astrocytes, microglia and NG2 glia to CNS injury, infection or neurodegeneration, spanning transient activation through to the dense glial scar that walls off damaged tissue. It shapes whether injury resolves or leaves a permanent barrier to axon regrowth, and so bears on outcomes after stroke, trauma, demyelination and glial tumours. The genes here point to the cell-surface and matrix side of that response: beta-1 integrin mediates glial adhesion to the injury-associated extracellular matrix, while glycosyltransferases including LARGE1, POMT2 and POMGNT1 build the O-mannosyl glycans of dystroglycan that let glial endfeet engage laminin at the basal lamina. Also represented are an inwardly rectifying potassium channel subunit associated with glial and mural potassium handling, linking reactive change to ion buffering and blood-brain barrier integrity at the lesion border.

Cell-cell junctions only hold tissue together if their components are delivered to the contact site and kept there, and this pathway covers the targeting and retention of proteins at adherens junctions, tight junctions and desmosomes. It underlies epithelial and endothelial barrier function, apical-basal polarity, and the mechanical cohesion of skin and heart; loss of it produces leaky vasculature, blistering skin disease and disorganised epithelia. Scaffolding proteins of the zonula occludens family, the polarity regulators Scribble and DLG5, and catenin-family CTNND1 anchor transmembrane partners such as VE-cadherin, desmogleins, JAM-A and PECAM-1, while the actin cytoskeleton, vinculin and filamin link junctions to contractile force. Rho-family control through ARHGEF18 and PAK2, and palmitoylation by ZDHHC7, tune where junctional proteins accumulate. Tricellular contacts depend on LSR and ILDR1, and desmoplakin couples desmosomes to intermediate filaments.

Cell-cell junctions only hold if their components are delivered to and retained at the contact site, and this pathway covers the control of that targeting. It matters for epithelial sheet integrity, cardiac and endothelial barrier function, and the mechanical coupling that lets tissues resist shear.
