The genes point to several junction types at once: p120 catenin stabilises E-cadherin at adherens junctions and limits its internalisation, vinculin links junctional and adhesion complexes to actin and transmits force, and desmogleins are desmosomal cadherins whose loss of surface localisation underlies blistering skin disease and contributes to arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. PECAM1 accumulates at endothelial contacts and participates in barrier maintenance and leukocyte transmigration, while a palmitoyltransferase illustrates how lipid modification can dictate whether a protein reaches the junctional membrane. Together they represent trafficking, anchoring and post-translational control converging on junction composition.

Cells anchor to the extracellular matrix through focal adhesions and, in epithelia, hemidesmosomes, and this pathway covers how those cell-substrate junctions are built, matured, rearranged and taken apart. Controlled turnover of these contacts is what allows cells to migrate during wound healing, angiogenesis and development, to sense matrix stiffness, and to survive at all, since loss of adhesion triggers apoptosis; unchecked remodelling contributes to tumour invasion and metastasis. Integrin heterodimers engaging fibronectin and laminin recruit talin, vinculin, kindlin, tensin and alpha-actinin to link clustered receptors to actin, while FAK and SRC signalling, Rho-family GTPases with ROCK and PAK effectors, and phosphatases such as PTEN and PTPRJ set assembly and disassembly. Plectin and dystonin instead tie integrin beta-4 to intermediate filaments, and MMP14 cleaves matrix beneath advancing edges.

regulation of cell-substrate junction organization controls how cells build, strengthen and disassemble the focal adhesions that anchor them to extracellular matrix. This tuning sets whether a cell stays put or migrates, and it underlies wound healing, angiogenesis, tissue morphogenesis and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells; adhesion turnover that is too slow or too fast stalls motility in either direction. Integrin engagement is transduced through a core adhesion plaque of talin, vinculin, kindlin and focal adhesion kinase, with SRC and ABL1 kinases and phosphatases such as PTEN, PTPRA and PPM1F setting phosphorylation state. Rho-family GTPases and their GAPs, together with ROCK kinases and cofilin, couple adhesions to actomyosin contractility and microtubule-based delivery via CLASP and MACF1 proteins. Growth factor and guidance cues, including VEGF, ephrin and syndecan signalling, feed into the same machinery to time adhesion assembly and release.

Cells grip the extracellular matrix through integrin-based focal adhesions, and this pathway covers the signals that build, strengthen and disassemble those contacts. Regulated turnover of cell-substrate junctions is what allows a cell to migrate, to sense matrix stiffness, and to hold an epithelium or endothelium in place; loss of control contributes to invasive tumour spread and to defective wound repair and angiogenesis. The core machinery is represented by talin, vinculin, kindlin and focal adhesion kinase linking clustered integrins to actin, with Src and ABL1 kinases, phosphatases such as PTPRJ and PTEN, and Rho-family switches RHOA, RAC1 and their ROCK and PAK effectors setting contractility and adhesion lifetime. Microtubule-associated CLASP proteins and MMP14-dependent matrix cleavage feed in, while cues from VEGF, ephrin and WNT ligands tune adhesion to the cell's environment.

Cells grip the extracellular matrix through integrin-based adhesions, and this pathway covers the signals that promote the assembly, maturation and turnover of those cell-substrate junctions. Strengthening focal adhesions is what lets cells migrate directionally, spread, sense matrix stiffness and remodel tissue during angiogenesis and wound repair; when the same machinery is misregulated, tumour cells invade and endothelial barriers fail. Small GTPases RAC1 and RHOU, the kinases ROCK1, PAK4 and ABL1, and actin regulators such as cofilin link adhesion receptors to the cytoskeletal tension that adhesions require. Integrin partners including FERMT2 and ITGB1BP1 act at the beta-1 tail to control activation and clustering, while syndecan-4 and collagen XVI contribute matrix engagement. Angiogenic receptor input from VEGFA-KDR, NRP1 and TEK, together with WNT4 and SMAD3, ties adhesion dynamics to growth factor and morphogen signalling.

Cells attach to extracellular matrix through focal adhesions, and this pathway covers the restraining arm of that system: processes that limit, disassemble or prevent the assembly of cell-substrate junctions. Turning adhesions over is what allows a cell to release its rear and move forward, so negative regulation here sets migration speed, matrix remodelling and the balance between anchored and motile states in wound healing, angiogenesis and tumour invasion. Mechanisms include Rho-family inactivation by GAPs such as DLC1 and ARHGAP6, phosphatase activity from PTEN acting against adhesion-linked survival signalling, Src-dependent phosphorylation that destabilises contacts, competition with integrin activation by ITGB1BP1, pericellular proteolysis of matrix by MMP14, and cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase components including CUL5 and RNF7 that degrade adhesion proteins. Thrombospondin adds a secreted, anti-adhesive input.

Cell junctions are not permanent: adherens contacts, tight junctions and synapses are actively taken apart when tissues remodel, cells migrate, or connections are pruned. The disassembly programme underlies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions, wound healing and inflammatory barrier breakdown, and in the nervous system it is how supernumerary synapses are eliminated during development. Much of the machinery here is small-GTPase-based: ARF6 and its exchange factor IQSEC1 drive endocytic internalization of junctional cadherins and integrins, while Rho-family signalling through PAK4, RHOU and NGEF reorganizes the actomyosin that holds contacts under tension. Complement components C1QA/B/C and C3 acting with microglial receptors such as CX3CR1, TREM2 and ITGAM tag and remove synapses, and SNAI2 downstream of TGF-beta receptor signalling transcriptionally represses junctional genes. Excessive activation of these routes contributes to tumour invasion, vascular leak and synapse loss in neurodegeneration.

Cell-cell junctions must be taken apart as well as built: their disassembly releases the adhesive contacts that hold an epithelium or endothelium together, allowing cells to migrate during wound healing, morphogenesis and inflammation, and permitting solutes and leukocytes to cross a barrier. The genes here point to several routes into that outcome. TGFB3 acting through the type I receptor TGFBR1 drives the transcription factor SNAI2, a repressor of junctional adhesion genes and a core effector of epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The tyrosine kinase FER phosphorylates junctional and adherens-junction components, and the inflammatory cytokine IL1B loosens barriers as part of the response to injury and infection, while myosin light chain kinase activity links junction opening to actomyosin contractility. Uncontrolled junction breakdown underlies vascular leak, tissue oedema and the invasive behaviour of carcinoma cells; failure to disassemble impedes repair and remodelling.

Phosphatidylcholine is the dominant phospholipid of cellular membranes and of pulmonary surfactant, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast it is made, remodelled and moved. Control points span fatty acid supply and activation, lysophospholipid reacylation, lipoprotein-mediated delivery of lipid precursors through receptor uptake, and transport steps that load phosphatidylcholine into secretory or specialised organelles. LPCAT1 and ACSL3 act directly on acyl chain composition, while ABCA3 and RAB38 govern lamellar body biogenesis in alveolar type II cells, linking this regulation to surfactant function and neonatal respiratory distress when it fails. MFSD2A imports lysophosphatidylcholine carrying docosahexaenoic acid across the blood-brain barrier, tying the same chemistry to brain lipid accretion. Together these activities determine membrane fluidity, lung compliance and the lipid composition available for signalling.

Not all GABA signalling happens at synapses. Ambient GABA that lingers in the extracellular fluid, escaping uptake, persistently activates receptors sitting outside the synaptic cleft, and the resulting tonic chloride conductance sets the baseline excitability and input-output gain of neurons rather than delivering discrete inhibitory events. The receptors involved are pentameric GABA-gated chloride channels built from alpha, beta, gamma and delta subunits; delta-containing assemblies partnered with alpha4 or alpha6, as in thalamic neurons, dentate granule cells and cerebellar granule cells, are characteristically extrasynaptic and high-affinity, desensitising little under sustained low agonist. This tonic inhibition shapes network oscillations and seizure threshold, and it is the substrate on which neurosteroids, general anaesthetics, ethanol and some antiepileptics act. Mutations in these subunits, notably beta3 and gamma2, cause epilepsy and developmental encephalopathy syndromes.

Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by uncontrolled peroxidation of membrane phospholipids, and the genes here push cells toward it rather than restraining it. Promoting this death pathway matters in two directions: it limits tumour cell survival and is being exploited therapeutically, while excessive ferroptosis contributes to ischemic injury and neurodegeneration. The most direct contributor is ACSL4, which charges polyunsaturated fatty acids such as arachidonate into the phospholipids that become the lethal peroxidation substrate; TMEM164 similarly directs polyunsaturated lipid supply into ether phospholipids. Other members act through transcriptional and post-translational control, protein kinase C signalling, chaperone and lysosomal handling of ferroptosis regulators, and metabolic rewiring that alters antioxidant capacity. Together they set how readily a cell commits to lipid peroxidation-driven membrane rupture, linking lipid composition, iron handling and redox buffering to cell fate.

After fertilisation the embryo initially runs on mRNA and protein deposited in the oocyte; the maternal-to-zygotic transition is the handover in which those maternal transcripts are cleared and the embryo's own genome begins to be read. Getting this switch right determines whether a cleavage-stage embryo can progress to blastocyst, and failure is a cause of early developmental arrest and infertility. Two arms are represented here. On the maternal side, an RNA-binding protein of cytoplasmic mRNA storage granules and an oocyte-specific poly(A)-binding protein govern the stability, translational silencing and timed degradation of stored transcripts. On the zygotic side, paired-like homeodomain factors act as activators of embryonic genome activation in human cleavage embryos, while a nuclear receptor contributes to opening the earliest zygotic transcriptional programme. Together they couple destruction of the oocyte legacy to initiation of embryonic transcription.

Itch is the sensation that provokes scratching, a protective reflex against irritants and parasites on the skin that becomes disabling when it runs unchecked in chronic urticaria, atopic dermatitis and cholestatic liver disease. The genes here mark the pruriceptor subset of dorsal root ganglion neurons: Mas-related G protein-coupled receptors that detect pruritogens including β-alanine and bile acids, the Gq alpha subunit that couples them to phospholipase C signalling, and the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.9, which sets the threshold for firing in these small-diameter afferents. Neuropeptides such as neuromedin B and proenkephalin-derived opioid peptides act as transmitters shaping itch and its modulation by analgesic circuits. Bile pigment and sulfotransferase enzymes point to the hepatic metabolites that make cholestatic itch a systemic rather than cutaneous problem, linking peripheral sensory coding to spinal transmission and behaviour.

Cytosolic DNA sensing by cGAS and its adaptor STING triggers type I interferon and inflammatory gene expression, and this pathway describes the brakes that keep that response proportionate and self-limiting. Restraint matters because unchecked activation by the cell's own DNA drives interferonopathies, lupus-like autoimmunity and sterile inflammation, while excessive signalling during infection is itself damaging. The brakes act at every step: nucleases such as TREX1 degrade cytosolic DNA before it is sensed, cGAS itself is held in check by kinase- and acyltransferase-mediated modification and by nuclear tethering to chromatin via BANF1, the second messenger cGAMP is hydrolysed extracellularly, and adaptor turnover through autophagy factors and ubiquitin-ligase adaptors such as SPSB3 limits signalling duration. Phosphatase activity and DNA-damage-response proteins including PARP1 and PRKDC further couple genome surveillance to dampened interferon output.

Proteins with many transmembrane helices — transporters, channels, GPCRs — must have each helix threaded into the endoplasmic reticulum bilayer in the correct orientation and with the correct topology, and this insertion route handles that job. It acts after the SEC61 channel has delivered the first one or two segments, with a dedicated multi-pass translocon taking over to integrate the remaining helices while holding them in a protected lipid environment until the nascent protein can fold and pack its helices together. The membrane components include the TMCO1–CCDC47 module and the nicalin–NOMO–TMEM147 arrangement together with associated small ER proteins. Because polytopic proteins dominate the secretory and ion-transport machinery of the cell, defects here cause misfolding, calcium-handling problems and ER stress; loss of TMCO1 in humans produces a developmental syndrome with skeletal and craniofacial anomalies.

Lipid droplets are not static stores; adjacent droplets can merge so that neutral lipid is transferred from one into the other, converting many small droplets into a single large one. This fusion determines droplet size and therefore how much surface is available to lipases and how efficiently a cell can bank triglyceride, and it is the step that gives white adipocytes their characteristic unilocular droplet. The CIDE family proteins act at contact sites between apposed droplets to permit directional lipid flux, with CIDEC required for large droplet formation in adipose tissue and CIDEB acting in liver. Loss of this capacity yields multilocular, small-droplet cells and is associated with partial lipodystrophy and insulin resistance, tying droplet morphology to systemic lipid handling. The lipase ATGL, encoded by PNPLA2, links the same droplet surface to mobilisation of stored fat.

CD27 is a tumour necrosis factor receptor family member on T, B and NK cells that, on engaging CD70 presented by activated antigen-presenting cells, delivers a costimulatory signal supporting clonal expansion, survival and memory formation. Signalling through this receptor-ligand pair sets the size and persistence of the effector pool that follows antigen encounter; loss-of-function mutations in either partner cause an immunodeficiency marked by failure to control Epstein-Barr virus, with lymphoproliferation and hypogammaglobulinaemia, while the axis is exploited therapeutically as an agonist target in tumour immunotherapy. Downstream, the receptor recruits TRAF2 to its cytoplasmic tail to trigger NF-κB and stress kinase activation and thereby anti-apoptotic transcription. The associated tyrosine kinase LCK and the phosphatase PTPN6, which dampens proximal signalling, place this costimulation alongside the antigen receptor signalling it reinforces rather than acting independently of it.

The size of the cytotoxic CD8 alpha-beta T cell pool is held steady over time by balancing proliferation against death, and the peptide supply that sustains it comes from proteasomal protein degradation. Members here are the core 20S alpha and beta subunits together with the interferon-inducible immunoproteasome subunits PSMB8, PSMB9 and PSMB10 and the thymus-specific subunit PSMB11 (beta5t). Cleaving cytosolic proteins into peptides for loading onto MHC class I is what allows CD8 T cells to be positively selected in the thymic cortex and then to receive the tonic self-peptide signals that maintain naive and memory cells in the periphery. Loss of the thymoproteasome distorts the selected CD8 repertoire, while defects in immunoproteasome subunits impair antigen presentation and are linked to autoinflammatory disease, placing this biology at the junction of protein turnover, T cell development and antiviral and antitumour immunity.

Epithelia leak on purpose: between adjacent cells, tight junctions form charge- and size-selective channels that allow water and small ions to cross a sheet without passing through the cells themselves. This paracellular route accounts for much of the bulk ion and fluid movement in kidney tubule and intestine, and the claudins listed here are the proteins that set its selectivity. Different family members build pores with different preferences — some favour cations such as sodium, magnesium and calcium, others restrict permeation or favour anions — so the mix of claudins expressed in a segment determines what that segment can reabsorb. Loss of the magnesium-handling claudins of the thick ascending limb causes familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis, illustrating that transepithelial salt balance depends as much on the junctional barrier as on transcellular pumps.

Dopamine receptors signal not only through G proteins but also through beta-arrestin, and this arm is what links dopamine to the AKT–GSK3 axis rather than to cyclic AMP. After dopamine binds the D2 receptor, beta-arrestin 2 is recruited to the activated receptor, where it both uncouples and internalises the receptor and serves as a scaffold that assembles AKT1 with a phosphatase, causing AKT to be dephosphorylated and inactivated; the consequence is loss of inhibitory phosphorylation on GSK3A and GSK3B, so these kinases become more active. The resulting change in GSK3 signalling shapes striatal neuron excitability, locomotor behaviour and responses to psychostimulants, and this branch is where lithium and many antipsychotics exert part of their effect. Selective engagement of arrestin- versus G protein-dependent output underlies efforts to design biased dopaminergic drugs with fewer motor side effects.

Some G protein-coupled receptors act not by changing cyclic nucleotide levels but by reshaping the actin cytoskeleton, and this Rho-activating branch of receptor signalling is how they do it. It governs cell shape, adhesion, migration and contractility — smooth muscle tone, platelet responses, neuronal and glial process outgrowth, and the confinement of germinal centre B cells to their niche. Ligand-bound receptors, including adhesion-type receptors such as ADGRG1 and ADGRL3, couple through the G12/G13 subfamily encoded by GNA12 and GNA13; the activated alpha subunits bind RhoGEFs of the regulator-of-G-protein-signalling-homology class, ARHGEF1 and ARHGEF12, which load GTP onto RhoA and its relatives. Downstream Rho effectors drive actomyosin assembly. Loss of ADGRG1 signalling disrupts cortical development, and P2RY8 coupling through this route is recurrently disrupted in B cell lymphoma.

Most human genes do not commit to full-length transcription the moment they initiate; instead RNA polymerase II halts 20-60 nucleotides past the start site and waits. This promoter-proximal pausing gives cells a rapid-response switch, keeping developmental and stimulus-responsive genes poised with polymerase already loaded so induction requires only release rather than new initiation, and it also provides a window for capping and other early RNA processing. Pausing follows Ser-5 phosphorylation of the polymerase C-terminal domain and is imposed by two complexes represented here: the four-subunit negative elongation factor, and the SPT4/SPT5 heterodimer that clamps the enzyme. Release into productive elongation requires P-TEFb-mediated phosphorylation, which evicts the negative factor and converts the clamp into an elongation aid. Misregulated release underlies oncogenic transcriptional addiction and is the target of CDK9 inhibitors.

Not every transcript a cell starts is worth finishing, and this quality-control step aborts Pol II transcription early when a nascent RNA is poorly configured for productive elongation, releasing the polymerase from DNA or targeting it for degradation. The result is a checkpoint just downstream of promoter-proximal pausing that sets how much of a gene's initiation converts into full-length mRNA, restrains enhancer and antisense transcription, and shapes rapid responses to growth and developmental cues. The Integrator complex supplies the activity: a core scaffold of INTS subunits positions an endonuclease module built around INTS11 and INTS9 to cleave the short nascent transcript, while an associated phosphatase module containing the PP2A catalytic and scaffolding subunits reverses elongation-promoting phosphorylation. ARMC5 with the cullin-ring component RBX1 links the pathway to ubiquitin-dependent turnover of polymerase and Integrator subunits; loss of these factors underlies adrenal hyperplasia and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Granzyme K, a serine protease released by cytotoxic T cells and NK cells, can engage the complement cascade directly, and this route links cell-mediated cytotoxicity to the lytic arm of innate immunity. The genes here span the cascade from the early convertase components C2, C3 and the C4 isoforms through C5 and the assembly of the membrane attack complex from C6, C7, the C8 subunits and polymerising C9, which perforates bacterial and cellular membranes. Beyond direct microbial killing, the cleavage fragments generated along the way act as chemoattractants and opsonins that recruit phagocytes and shape downstream inflammatory and adaptive responses. Deficiency of individual components predisposes to recurrent pyogenic and meningococcal infection, while unchecked activation drives tissue damage in inflammatory and autoimmune disease, so the amplification achieved here is tightly regulated in normal tissue.

Beige fat cell differentiation converts white adipocytes within white fat depots into inducible thermogenic cells that burn substrate to produce heat when animals are cold-exposed or stimulated by adrenergic and other cues. Because beige cells raise whole-body energy expenditure and improve glucose and lipid handling, this browning programme is a long-standing target for obesity and type 2 diabetes, and its loss accompanies age- and diet-associated depot whitening. The master adipogenic nuclear receptor PPARG partners with the transcriptional coregulator PRDM16 to redirect a white adipocyte toward the thermogenic gene programme, with the histone methyltransferase EHMT1 stabilising PRDM16 and contributing repressive methylation at muscle-related genes. A cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase built on CUL2 and RBX1 with its substrate adaptor sets PRDM16 abundance by proteasomal turnover, so ubiquitin-dependent protein stability, rather than transcription alone, gates how much beige character a fat cell acquires.

Amino acids are not only the building blocks of protein but also fuels, nitrogen carriers and precursors for neurotransmitters, nucleotides, glutathione, haem and pigment, and L-amino acid metabolism is the collected chemistry that makes, interconverts and degrades them. It supports nitrogen disposal through the urea cycle, gluconeogenic and ketogenic entry of carbon skeletons into the TCA cycle, and one-carbon transfer for methylation. Transaminases, dehydrogenases, oxidases and decarboxylases handle individual residues: phenylalanine hydroxylase and the downstream tyrosine route feed catecholamine and melanin synthesis, branched-chain and lysine catabolism converge on acyl-CoA intermediates, proline and serine biosynthesis supply proliferating cells, and tryptophan flows through kynurenine toward NAD and immune suppression. Inherited failures of single steps produce classic metabolic disease -- phenylketonuria, urea cycle defects, maple syrup urine disease, tyrosinaemia, hyperoxaluria -- with neurological damage from accumulated substrates.

Breaking down L-amino acids lets cells dispose of surplus protein-derived nitrogen and feed the carbon skeletons into the TCA cycle for energy or gluconeogenesis. The enzymes here cover the classical degradative routes: phenylalanine and tyrosine catabolism through PAH, TAT, HPD and FAH; branched-chain breakdown via BCAT2 and the dehydrogenase complex with IVD, MCCC1/2 and ECHS1; tryptophan flux down the kynurenine arm through IDO1, TDO2, KMO and KYNU toward NAD synthesis; plus histidine, proline, serine, glycine and lysine routes. Transaminases and glutamate dehydrogenase funnel amino groups into glutamate and onward to the urea cycle via OTC and ARG1, while decarboxylases such as GAD1/2 and HDC divert substrates into neurotransmitter and amine production. Loss of single steps causes inherited metabolic disease — phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria, tyrosinemia, maple syrup urine disease, hyperammonemia — typically through toxic accumulation of the blocked intermediate.

Mitochondria must acquire from the cytosol the metabolites that feed their internal chemistry, and import into the mitochondrion covers the carrier proteins that perform this transfer across the inner membrane. Two carrier families dominate here. The mitochondrial pyruvate carrier, a hetero-oligomer of MPC1 and MPC2, delivers glycolytic pyruvate to the matrix for oxidation by pyruvate dehydrogenase and for anaplerotic carboxylation, placing it at the junction between glycolysis and the TCA cycle and making it a control point in fuel selection, insulin secretion and tumour metabolism. The sideroflexins transport serine into the matrix to supply one-carbon units for folate metabolism, nucleotide synthesis and methylation, while SLC25A38 imports glycine for the first step of heme biosynthesis; its loss causes congenital sideroblastic anaemia. Together these transporters set the substrate supply for respiration, biosynthesis and erythroid heme production.

Human cells make only a subset of the amino acids they need, and this biosynthetic capacity supplies those non-essential residues for protein synthesis while linking nitrogen handling to central carbon metabolism. Serine is built from a glycolytic intermediate by PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH and converted to glycine by the serine hydroxymethyltransferases, feeding one-carbon folate metabolism; methionine is regenerated from homocysteine by methionine synthase with its reductase, by the betaine-dependent BHMT route, and through methylthioadenosine salvage. Glutamine synthetase and the glutaminases set glutamate-glutamine balance, transaminases such as GOT1 and GOT2 interconvert aspartate and glutamate, and proline arises via ALDH18A1 and the pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductases. Arginine synthesis shares enzymes with the urea cycle, and phenylalanine hydroxylase makes tyrosine. Loss of individual steps causes phenylketonuria, urea cycle defects, hyperoxaluria and serine-deficiency encephalopathy, and the serine-glycine arm is frequently amplified in proliferating tumours.

non-proteinogenic amino acid metabolic process covers the synthesis, interconversion and breakdown of amino acids that are never incorporated into protein but act as metabolic intermediates, neurotransmitters and signalling molecules — ornithine and citrulline of the urea cycle, GABA, D-serine, kynurenine, homocysteine, hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine. It supplies nitrogen disposal, inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmission, collagen stability and one-carbon flux, and its failure produces some of the best-known inborn errors of metabolism: hyperammonaemia from urea cycle defects in OTC or CPS1, homocystinuria from CBS or methionine-synthase deficiency, primary hyperoxaluria, and epilepsy from impaired glutamate decarboxylation. Mechanistically it links transaminases, dehydrogenases and aldehyde dehydrogenases to prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases and to mitochondrial carriers that move ornithine and glutamate across membranes. The tryptophan-kynurenine arm, driven by IDO1 and TDO2, additionally shapes immune tolerance and NAD supply.

Amino acids that never enter proteins nonetheless carry much of the body's nitrogen traffic, and this is the metabolism that makes and disposes of them. Ornithine and citrulline shuttle waste nitrogen through the urea cycle, where loss of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase or ornithine transcarbamylase produces hyperammonaemia; homocysteine sits between the methionine cycle and transsulfuration to cysteine, with cystathionine beta-synthase and methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase defects causing homocystinuria and vascular disease. Tryptophan degradation through kynurenine, driven by IDO1 and TDO2, yields neuroactive and immunosuppressive intermediates and feeds NAD synthesis. GABA is made by glutamate decarboxylases and cleared by transaminase and aldehyde dehydrogenase steps, D-serine by serine racemase for NMDA receptor co-agonism, while D-amino acid oxidases degrade these isomers. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine arise from collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, and asymmetric dimethylarginine, hydrolysed by DDAH1, tunes nitric oxide output.

non-proteinogenic amino acid biosynthetic process covers the making of amino acids that are never incorporated into protein but instead serve as neurotransmitters, metabolic intermediates, or structural modifications. Its products include GABA, the main inhibitory transmitter of the central nervous system, made by the glutamate decarboxylases and cleared by transamination; D-serine, generated by serine racemase as the co-agonist that gates NMDA receptor activation; ornithine and citrulline, made by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase and ornithine transcarbamylase as the nitrogen-carrying core of the urea cycle; and hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine, formed by collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases to stabilise the triple helix. Beta-alanine arises from pyrimidine catabolism. Failure in these routes produces hyperammonaemia, epilepsy, altered glutamatergic excitability, and connective-tissue fragility, so the pathway links neurotransmission, nitrogen disposal, and extracellular matrix maturation through a shared chemistry of amino acid modification.

Not every amino acid a cell makes is destined for protein; this route covers synthesis of amino acids that act as neurotransmitters, metabolic intermediates or structural modifications. Glutamate decarboxylases GAD1 and GAD2 generate GABA, the principal inhibitory transmitter, and serine racemase produces D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, tying this chemistry directly to synaptic excitability; loss of GABA synthesis provokes seizures. Other members feed ornithine and citrulline production for the urea cycle and carbamoyl phosphate synthesis, while procollagen lysyl hydroxylases create hydroxylysine residues needed for collagen crosslinking, and their deficiency causes a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Transporters and catabolic enzymes such as ABAT and DPYD set the surrounding flux, so the pathway sits at the junction of nitrogen disposal, neurotransmission and extracellular matrix maturation.

Amino acids that never enter proteins "" GABA, ornithine, homocysteine, sarcosine, hydroxyproline, kynurenine, D-amino acids "" still accumulate from neurotransmission, the urea cycle, collagen turnover and dietary intake, and this catabolic route disposes of them. It matters because the intermediates are toxic or neuroactive when they build up: failure of cystathionine beta-synthase causes homocystinuria, ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency produces hyperammonaemia, proline dehydrogenase loss underlies hyperprolinaemia, and defective glyoxylate handling by HOGA1 leads to oxalate stones. Chemically, the work is done by transaminases and by flavin- and NAD-dependent oxidases and dehydrogenases that convert amines to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids, with aldehyde dehydrogenases including ALDH5A1 committing succinic semialdehyde from GABA into the TCA cycle. Kynurenine-pathway enzymes feed tryptophan carbon toward NAD synthesis, tying nitrogen disposal to mitochondrial energy metabolism and to hepatic and neural amino acid homeostasis.

nutrient storage is how cells set aside energy and micronutrients in reserve depots that can be mobilised on demand, the process that lets an organism buffer feeding and fasting rather than depend on continuous intake. Most of the genes describe lipid storage in particular: triacylglycerol synthesis by DGAT1/2, the perilipins and CIDE proteins that coat and enlarge cytoplasmic lipid droplets, seipin and the droplet-assembly factors that nucleate them at the ER, and PNPLA2-driven lipolysis that releases the stores again. Around this sit the transcriptional controllers that decide how much to store, notably PPARs, liver X receptors and SIRT1, plus lipoprotein and scavenger-receptor routes (APOB, LPL, CD36, SCARB1) that import substrate, and lysosomal hydrolases that recycle it. The same machinery defines adipocytes, sets leptin-mediated energy signalling, and when overloaded or misdirected produces obesity, hepatic steatosis and foam-cell atherosclerosis.

Cells bank surplus energy and lipid-soluble material for later use, and this nutrient storage programme covers how those reserves are built, packaged and mobilised. Its main physical product is the cytoplasmic lipid droplet: acyltransferases such as DGAT1 and DGAT2 esterify fatty acids into triglyceride, perilipins and CIDE proteins coat and expand the droplet, and lipases including PNPLA2 and LIPA release the stores when demand rises. Uptake and delivery components such as CD36, LPL, the fatty acid binding proteins and apolipoproteins bring substrate in, while nuclear receptors of the PPAR and liver X families, SREBF2 and SIRT1 set the transcriptional balance between storage and oxidation. Cholesterol efflux via ABCA1 and ABCG1 and lysosomal handling by NPC1 and NPC2 prevent toxic accumulation. Adipocyte-derived leptin links the size of the reserve to appetite; failure of these steps yields lipodystrophy, obesity, fatty liver and foam-cell-driven atherosclerosis, and inflammatory mediators here tie storage to metabolic disease.

Nearly every mRNA ends not where transcription stops but where it is cut, and this cleavage-and-polyadenylation step defines the 3' end while transcription is still underway, coupling maturation of the transcript to termination by RNA polymerase II. The poly(A) tail it adds determines mRNA stability, export and translatability, and the choice among alternative cleavage sites shortens or lengthens 3' UTRs, changing which microRNA and protein binding sites a message retains. Recognition of the polyadenylation signal and the downstream sequence is divided between a cleavage factor bearing the CPSF3 endonuclease and a CSTF3-containing complex, with NUDT21 and CPSF6/CPSF7 forming the heterodimer that reads UGUA elements and biases site selection. PAPOLA then extends the tail, while PCF11 and the SSU72 phosphatase link processing to release of polymerase from the template. Disrupted site choice reshapes gene expression in proliferation and differentiation.

Nearly every protein-coding mRNA ends where it does because the polymerase II transcript is cut and given a poly(A) tail while transcription is still under way. This co-transcriptional 3'-end processing by cleavage and polyadenylation defines the mature mRNA end, sets transcript stability and export competence, and is coupled to termination, so its failure leaves polymerase reading through into downstream genes. Recognition of the polyadenylation signal is performed by a cleavage factor complex whose subunits here include CPSF1 and the endonuclease CPSF3, together with the CPSF6/CPSF7-NUDT21 module that biases which of several alternative poly(A) sites is chosen; PAPOLA then adds the tail. PCF11 links cleavage to release of the polymerase and SSU72 acts as a phosphatase on the polymerase C-terminal domain and associated termination factors. Alternative site choice shortens or lengthens 3' UTRs, remodelling microRNA and RNA-binding-protein control during proliferation and differentiation.

Mitochondria run their own translation machinery, and the small subunit of the mitoribosome must be built correctly before any of the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA can be made. Assembly of this subunit is therefore upstream of oxidative phosphorylation, and its failure produces combined respiratory chain deficiency, cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy. The factors here act on the 12S rRNA and its maturing particle: a GTPase chaperone binds the rRNA to nucleate assembly, additional GTPase and ribosome-binding factors license later steps, and methyltransferases modify the rRNA, including dimethylation of adjacent adenosines near the decoding site by TFB1M. Loss of that modification alters mitoribosome stability and has been linked to aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss. Related chaperone and acyl-carrier-associated components couple assembly to mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, tying ribosome biogenesis to the organelle's metabolic state.

Cells and tissues must notice when an essential metal runs short and adjust uptake, gene expression and metabolism accordingly; this is the response to metal ion starvation. Deprivation of zinc or iron limits hundreds of metalloenzymes, haemoglobin synthesis and bone turnover, so sensing it is a prerequisite for growth. The genes here span both ends of the process: intestinal and basolateral zinc importers of the SLC39 family adjust absorption when dietary zinc is low, HFE ties iron status to hepcidin-controlled iron supply, and the haem-regulated kinase EIF2AK1 (HRI), with its mitochondrial relay partner DELE1, shuts down translation initiation when haem or iron is scarce. Transcriptional output follows through factors such as SP1 and FOS, while osteocalcin and the RANK receptor connect mineral availability to bone remodelling. Failure gives anaemia, acrodermatitis enteropathica-like zinc deficiency, and disordered mineral homeostasis.

Protein O-linked glycosylation via glucose attaches glucose directly to serine residues in the folded EGF-like repeats of secreted and cell-surface proteins, then extends that glucose with xylose. Its best-known client is the Notch receptor, where O-glucosylation controls folding, trafficking out of the ER and the strength of ligand-induced signalling, so the pathway feeds into somite segmentation, vascular development and stem cell fate decisions; loss of the initiating transferase causes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and Dowling-Degos disease. Protein O-glucosyltransferases recognise a consensus within properly disulphide-bonded EGF domains, effectively acting as folding sensors, while glucoside xylosyltransferases add the first xylose and a further enzyme caps the trisaccharide. The chemistry is unusual among O-glycans in occurring on structured domains rather than mucin-like regions, and it operates alongside O-fucosylation as a tuning layer on the same receptor repeats.

Certain protein domains are decorated with a glucose attached directly to a serine side chain, and that sugar is then extended with xylose to build the O-glucose glycans characteristic of epidermal growth factor-like repeats. The best-understood target is the Notch receptor extracellular domain, where this modification tunes receptor folding, trafficking and ligand responsiveness, linking the pathway to cell fate decisions in somite, vascular and skeletal development; loss of the initiating glucosyltransferase disrupts Notch signalling, and mutations in the human enzyme cause Dowling-Degos disease. Mechanistically, protein O-glucosyltransferases in the endoplasmic reticulum transfer glucose from UDP-glucose to consensus sites within EGF repeats, after which glucoside xylosyltransferases add a first xylose and a second enzyme completes the trisaccharide. The sequence operates as a quality-control and modulatory layer on secreted and membrane proteins rather than as a bulk glycosylation route.

Proteoglycans are built by attaching a xylose to a serine of the core protein and extending it, and this xylose-initiated O-linked glycosylation is where that decision is made. The resulting heparan sulfate and chondroitin/dermatan sulfate chains fill the extracellular matrix, shape cartilage and bone, and control how growth factors and morphogens diffuse and bind their receptors; loss of the pathway causes connective tissue disorders of the Ehlers-Danlos and skeletal dysplasia type. Two xylosyltransferases prime the linker, which is completed by galactosyl- and glucuronyltransferases, after which polymerases such as the EXT enzymes or the chondroitin synthases commit the chain to one class. Sulfotransferases and an epimerase then write the sulfation and uronic acid patterns that create binding sites, supported by nucleotide-sugar transporters and UDP-glucose dehydrogenase supplying precursors in the Golgi.

Neurons collect synaptic input on dendrites, and the pathways that promote dendrite development set how large and how branched that receptive tree becomes, which in turn determines how many connections a neuron can receive. Growth-promoting cues here include bone morphogenetic proteins acting through a type I receptor and SMAD1 to drive dendritic arbor extension, the reelin pathway working through the lipoprotein receptors LRP8 and VLDLR to position and elaborate neurons in the developing cortex, and pleiotrophin and receptor tyrosine kinase signalling via ALK and the cytoplasmic kinase ABL1. Downstream, actin and membrane regulators such as COBL and PACSIN1 and the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC15 shape branch formation locally. Insufficient or excessive dendritic growth alters circuit wiring, and disturbance of these regulators is linked to intellectual disability, cortical malformation and neurodegenerative change.

Inflammation must be switched off as well as on, and this collection covers the brakes that limit how much pro-inflammatory cytokine an activated cell makes. Loss of such restraint underlies chronic inflammatory and autoinflammatory disease; MEFV mutations, for example, cause familial Mediterranean fever, and TREM2 variants impair the damping of microglial responses in neurodegeneration. The braking acts at several levels: decoy and inhibitory receptors such as IL1R2, LILRB4 and SIRPA blunt receptor engagement; NFKBIA sequesters NF-κB subunits to curb transcription; NLRC3 and other regulators restrain inflammasome signalling; and post-transcriptional controls dominate the output, with the RNase ZC3H12A and the AU-rich element binding protein ZFP36 degrading cytokine mRNAs while a large complement of microRNAs, notably MIR146A, targets the signalling adaptors themselves. Anti-inflammatory metabolic and stress mediators including HMOX1 and PPARA contribute resolution signals.

Inflammation is amplified when cells that have detected danger are pushed to make more cytokine, and this pathway collects the receptors, adaptors and transcription factors that raise cytokine output during an inflammatory response. It sets the magnitude of fever, leukocyte recruitment and acute-phase responses, and when it runs unchecked it drives septic shock, psoriasis and chronic autoimmune tissue damage. Pattern recognition upstream comes from Toll-like receptors sensing bacterial and viral ligands, the C-type lectin dectin-1 with its CARD9 adaptor sensing fungal glucans, and the intracellular sensor NOD2; signals converge through MYD88 and TICAM1 onto NF-kB subunit RELA, IRF3 and STAT3 to induce TNF, IL6 and other mediators. An IL-17 and IL-36 receptor module provides a self-reinforcing epithelial arm, while HIF1A and XBP1 tie output to hypoxia and ER stress, and several microRNAs tune the amplitude.

When a cell first contacts extracellular matrix it flattens and extends lamellipodia over the surface, and this pathway sets how fast and how far that spreading goes. The output governs adhesion strength, migration speed, wound closure, and the anchorage dependence whose loss accompanies metastasis. Integrin engagement, chiefly through beta1 and beta3 receptors and their cytoplasmic partners kindlin-2, ILK and filamin, nucleates focal adhesions where focal adhesion kinase and ABL1 phosphorylate docking proteins such as CRK, CRKL and NEDD9. These recruit exchange factors including DOCK1, DOCK5 and ARHGEF7 that load RAC1 and CDC42, driving Arp2/3-dependent branched actin assembly at the leading edge, while actinin, coronin and TESK1-regulated cofilin tune the resulting network. Matrix and secreted cues, among them fibrinogen chains, fibulin and midkine, feed into the same decision, and KANK1 opposes it by restraining adhesion maturation.

Cells that have attached to the extracellular matrix normally flatten and extend lamellipodia, and this pathway covers the braking signals that limit how far that spreading goes. Restraining spreading matters because adhesion strength and cell shape set migration speed, and unchecked spreading disturbs the cycles of protrusion and retraction that motile cells depend on; the same brakes influence invasive behaviour of tumour cells. Mechanistically, the members act at integrin tails and the adhesion-associated actin network: ITGB1BP1 competes with talin for the beta-1 integrin cytoplasmic tail and opposes activation, KANK1 engages talin to limit focal adhesion maturation, and RCC2 restrains Rac1- and Arf6-dependent protrusion. Actin crosslinkers and organisers such as ACTN4, CORO1C and dematin, together with matrix and guidance cues including fibulin-1 and ephrin-A5, feed into the same restraint of matrix-dependent flattening.

When a cell first touches extracellular matrix it must flatten and extend its membrane over the surface, and this pathway comprises the activities that promote that substrate adhesion-dependent spreading. Spreading is the step that converts a transient attachment into a stable focal adhesion, and it sets the stage for migration, wound closure, platelet aggregation on fibrinogen, and the survival signals cells draw from anchorage; cancer cells exploit the same machinery to invade. Integrin engagement, here represented by the beta-3 subunit with its activators kindlin-2 and ILK, recruits adaptors such as CRK, DOCK1 and ARHGEF7 that load the Rho-family GTPases CDC42 and RAC1, which in turn drive branched actin polymerization at the leading edge through the Arp2/3 complex. Kinases including ABL1, TESK1 and GSK3A tune actin and adhesion turnover, while filamin A links the network to the membrane.

Membrane ruffles are the transient sheet-like protrusions a cell throws forward when it migrates, engulfs material by macropinocytosis, or spreads on a surface, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower how readily they form. Control of ruffling determines how fast a fibroblast crawls, how a macrophage or microglial cell samples its surroundings, and how growth-factor and nucleotide signals are converted into shape change; misregulation contributes to invasive behaviour of tumour cells. The core switch is Rho-family GTPase activity, with RAC1 and RHOG promoting branched actin assembly at the leading edge and GAPs such as ARHGAP24 restraining it. Downstream, EPS8 family proteins and capping-protein regulators tune filament elongation, profilins supply polymerisation-competent actin monomer, and caveolin, adhesion receptors and purinergic receptors couple membrane and extracellular cues to the protrusive response.

Membrane ruffles are transient actin-rich folds that form when branched actin polymerisation pushes the plasma membrane forward; suppressing their assembly is how a cell limits spreading, lamellipodium formation and migration when it should stay put. The genes here act at several points in that restraint. ARHGAP24 is a GTPase-activating protein that lowers Rac signalling toward the actin nucleation machinery, KANK1 constrains talin-dependent adhesion and actin coupling at the cell edge, ABI3 participates in the WAVE regulatory complex without promoting ruffling, and EVL and PFN2 shape filament elongation and available actin monomer rather than allowing unchecked branching. The net effect is control of cell shape, adhesion turnover and motility, with relevance to how epithelial and immune cells balance movement against stable contact, and to invasive behaviour when negative regulation of ruffle assembly is lost.

positive regulation of ruffle assembly drives the formation of membrane ruffles, the sheet-like actin protrusions that a cell throws up at its leading edge to migrate, to sample its surroundings, and to internalise extracellular fluid by macropinocytosis. This behaviour underlies wound closure, immune cell chemotaxis, growth-factor-stimulated motility, and the nutrient uptake route exploited by transformed cells; its loss leaves cells poorly polarised and slow to move. The genes act mostly through Rac1 and its upstream activators, with HRAS relaying receptor input, profilin and the EPS8 family plus COBL tuning actin filament elongation and capping, and CARMIL2 controlling capping protein at the barbed end. mTOR and lysosome-associated PLEKHM1 tie ruffling to nutrient and membrane-traffic status, while microglial P2RY12 and NDEL1 illustrate how purinergic and cytoskeletal cues elicit ruffling in specific cell types.

Membrane ruffles are transient sheet-like protrusions built from branched actin at the cell edge, and this pathway covers the signals and actin regulators that promote their formation. Ruffling drives macropinocytosis, cell spreading and migration, and lets phagocytes and microglia sample their surroundings; the same machinery is exploited during growth-factor-stimulated fluid-phase uptake. The core input is Rac1 activation downstream of receptor and Ras signalling, with HRAS and mTOR-dependent growth cues feeding in, while EPS8 family proteins together with CARMIL2, COBL and profilin shape barbed-end elongation and capping to convert that signal into protrusive actin. Additional components link ruffling to microtubule and lysosome-associated regulation, and in microglia the purinergic receptor P2RY12 couples extracellular nucleotide sensing to protrusion. Loss of positive control leaves cells poorly motile and impairs macropinocytic nutrient scavenging and immune surveillance.</description>

Cells respond to a temperature rise by rapidly inducing chaperones that keep proteins folded, and this pathway governs how strongly and how long that response runs. Its centre is the transcription factor HSF1, which is held inactive by chaperone binding and by inhibitory phosphorylation, then released to drive heat shock gene transcription; GSK3B and MTOR-linked kinase signalling, MAPKAPK2, the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300, the deacetylase SIRT1 and the inducible regulator IER5 tune its activity and stability. Co-chaperones of the DNAJ family, together with CHORDC1, feed back on the same circuit. Because proteotoxic stress also reaches the DNA damage response, ATM and ATR connect thermal insult to genome surveillance. Set-point control here determines thermotolerance, and shapes how tumour cells survive proteotoxic stress and how aggregation-prone proteins such as tau are handled in neurons.

Cells that run short of oxygen mount a transcriptional response led by the HIF transcription factors, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly and how long that response runs. Tuning matters because the same programme drives adaptive angiogenesis and glycolytic switching in ischaemic tissue and, when left on, supports tumour growth and metastasis. The core brake is oxygen-dependent destruction of HIF-1alpha: a prolyl hydroxylase marks it for the VHL ubiquitin ligase complex and proteasomal degradation, with COMMD1 and deubiquitinating activity acting on the same axis. Layered onto this are kinase and signalling inputs through PI3K, MAP2K1, ROCK2 and STAT3, mitochondrial oxygen sensing via PINK1 and CHCHD2, oxidative-stress coupling through NFE2L2, and microRNAs including miR-210 that reinforce the hypoxic state. The output shapes cell survival, metabolism and apoptotic threshold under low oxygen.

Cells sense falling oxygen and mount a HIF-driven transcriptional response, and this pathway is the brake on it — the set of processes that damp, restrain or terminate the cellular response to hypoxia so that adaptation is proportionate and reversible. Without such restraint, HIF signalling persists into normoxia, driving inappropriate angiogenesis, glycolytic reprogramming and tumour-promoting growth. The prolyl hydroxylase EGLN1 provides the canonical oxygen-dependent step, tagging HIF-1α for degradation when oxygen is available, while COMMD1 interferes with HIF heterodimer assembly and transcriptional output. Other members set the surrounding context: NFE2L2 coordinates antioxidant defence against hypoxia- and reoxygenation-associated stress, PINK1 links mitochondrial quality control to oxygen handling, and NOL3 and TMBIM6 blunt the apoptotic and calcium-mediated consequences of ischaemic stress. The balance matters most in ischaemia, cardiac and neuronal survival, and tumour oxygen adaptation.

Cells sense falling oxygen and respond by remodelling metabolism, survival and gene expression; this pathway covers inputs that amplify that response, making the hypoxic programme stronger or longer-lasting than the oxygen signal alone would produce. Such positive regulation matters in ischaemic tissue, in the hypoxic cores of solid tumours, and in pulmonary and neuronal adaptation to low oxygen, where the size of the response determines whether a cell adapts or dies. The contributing genes are heterogeneous rather than a single complex: a de novo DNA methyltransferase links hypoxia to epigenetic reprogramming, a two-pore potassium channel and a metabotropic glutamate receptor connect membrane excitability and neurotransmitter signalling to oxygen stress, and two microRNAs tune the downstream transcript pool. Together they act as modifiers upstream of hypoxia-inducible transcription and its metabolic, angiogenic and apoptotic outputs.

Ubiquitin chains linked through lysine 63 do not mark proteins for destruction but act as scaffolds that recruit kinase complexes, so controlling how much K63-linked ubiquitination occurs sets the gain on inflammatory and DNA-damage signalling. The genes here sit on both sides of that balance: the UBE2N (Ubc13) catalytic enzyme with its UEV partners UBE2V1/UBE2V2 builds the chains, BIRC2 supplies E3 activity downstream of innate immune receptors, and NOD2 with its kinase RIPK2 uses such chains to assemble the platform that activates NF-kB after bacterial peptidoglycan sensing. Others restrain the output, including the phosphatase PTPN22 and the adaptor GPS2, while PLAA acts in ubiquitin-dependent protein sorting. Because the same chain type coordinates repair factor recruitment and centrosomal signalling, misregulation here tips cells toward chronic inflammation, as in Crohn disease, or toward genome instability.

Lysine-63-linked polyubiquitin chains are non-degradative signals that assemble scaffolds for NF-kB activation, DNA damage responses and endosomal sorting, and this pathway describes the braking mechanisms that limit their formation. Restraining K63 chain build-up keeps inflammatory signalling self-limiting and prevents inappropriate persistence of repair and trafficking complexes after the initiating stimulus has passed. The regulators act at several levels: GPS2 blocks the E2 enzyme UBC13 that is dedicated to K63 chain synthesis, PARP10 uses ADP-ribosylation to interfere with NEMO ubiquitination downstream of NF-kB activation, and a microRNA tunes the abundance of components of the machinery. PLAA works with p97/VCP in ubiquitin-dependent extraction and chain remodelling, while CEP63 links the control to centrosomal and DNA damage signalling. Loss of such negative control tips cells toward chronic inflammatory signalling and genome instability.

Ceramide sits at the hub of sphingolipid metabolism, and cells restrain how much of it they make because excess ceramide drives apoptosis, insulin resistance and inflammatory stress. This braking arm — negative regulation of ceramide biosynthesis — keeps sphingolipid output matched to membrane demand. The ORMDL proteins are ER membrane subunits of the serine palmitoyltransferase complex that sense sphingolipid levels and clamp down the first, committed step of de novo synthesis, forming a feedback loop; the asthma-associated ORMDL3 locus ties this control to airway inflammation and mast cell biology. The AMPK catalytic subunit PRKAA1 links the same restraint to energy status, so that lipid synthesis is curtailed when ATP is scarce. Sphingosine kinase 1 pulls flux the other way at the sphingosine node, phosphorylating sphingosine toward the pro-survival mediator sphingosine-1-phosphate rather than back into ceramide.

Insulin sensitivity is not fixed; it is set by a layer of regulators that tune how strongly a cell answers insulin, and this modulation of the cellular response to insulin stimulus determines whether glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis and lipogenesis proceed or stall. Loss of tuning in the direction of dampened signalling is the molecular basis of insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes, obesity and metabolic syndrome. Negative regulators dominate: SOCS1 and SOCS3 and the GRB10/GRB14 adaptors bind and restrain the receptor or IRS1, phosphatases such as PTPN1 and PTPN11 reverse receptor and substrate phosphorylation, and a cullin-RING ubiquitin module targets components for degradation. Downstream, mTOR with RPS6KB1 and TSC2 feeds back onto IRS1, while adipokines and hepatokines including leptin, adiponectin receptor signalling and ENPP1 impose systemic, tissue-crosstalk control on the same node.

Insulin signalling must be damped as well as switched on, and this collection of brakes sets how strongly a cell responds to the hormone. Their combined action determines insulin sensitivity in muscle, liver and fat; excessive braking, driven by inflammatory cytokines such as IL1B and by lipid and nutrient excess, produces the insulin resistance underlying type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Mechanisms are varied: phosphotyrosine phosphatases including PTPN1 dephosphorylate the receptor and its substrates, SOCS proteins and the CUL7/FBXW8/RBX1 ubiquitin ligase target IRS1 for silencing or degradation, GRB10 and GRB14 bind the receptor and block substrate access, and serine/threonine kinases such as GSK3A, several protein kinase C isoforms and mTORC1-driven S6 kinases feed back onto IRS1. Phosphoinositide phosphatases and PIP4K enzymes limit the lipid second messengers, while microRNAs tune receptor and adaptor levels.

Insulin sensitivity is set not only by how much insulin is secreted but by how strongly a target cell answers it, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise that responsiveness in liver, muscle and fat. Enhanced signalling through the insulin receptor and IRS adaptors drives glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid storage, and suppression of hepatic glucose output; blunting of these steps is the core lesion of type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome. Adipokine and hepatokine inputs such as leptin and adiponectin receptor signalling feed in from whole-body energy status, while intracellular components including atypical PKC, PAK1, SORBS1 and MYO1C act on GLUT4 vesicle trafficking to the plasma membrane. Phosphatases such as PTPN1 and PTPN2 normally damp receptor phosphorylation, so their regulation is part of tuning the response, alongside transcriptional and metabolic modulators like SIRT1 and NR1H4.

Cells commit irreversibly to division at the G1/S boundary, and positive regulation of this transition is what pushes them past the restriction point into DNA replication. It underlies proliferative responses to growth factors and is the step most often deregulated in cancer, where loss of restraint gives continuous cycling. The core drive comes from D-type cyclins with cyclin E partners activating cyclin-dependent kinases, inactivating retinoblastoma protein and releasing E2F/DP transcription factors such as TFDP1 to switch on replication genes; CDC6 licenses origins and RRM1/RRM2 supply the deoxynucleotides that replication consumes. Upstream inputs include receptor tyrosine kinase and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling through EGFR, AKT1 and RPTOR, ubiquitin ligase activity by CUL4 complexes and MDM2-mediated relief of p53 restraint, while numerous microRNAs tune the same switch. Centriole duplication factors and histone mRNA processing components couple the transition to organelle and chromatin duplication.

Plasma cells are the antibody factories of the immune system, and the decision to become one is tightly controlled because too little output leaves infections uncleared while too much fuels autoantibody disease and myeloma. This regulatory layer sets how often and how far activated B cells complete that terminal differentiation. Cytokines supply the external cues: interleukin-10 drives B cells toward antibody secretion, while interleukin-2 shapes the helper T cell context in which the decision is made, and complement receptor engagement tunes how strongly antigen is perceived. Inside the cell, XBP1 links commitment to secretory capacity, expanding the endoplasmic reticulum and the unfolded protein response machinery that a cell pouring out immunoglobulin cannot survive without, with DDRGK1 acting on ER-associated protein quality control. Together these inputs couple lineage choice to the biosynthetic burden it imposes.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount an unfolded protein response; this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly and how long that response runs. Tuning matters because a mild, well-damped response restores folding capacity and secretory output, while an unrestrained one commits the cell to apoptosis — a switch relevant to secretory tissues, pancreatic beta cells and neurodegeneration. The ER chaperone BiP (HSPA5) holds the sensors IRE1 (ERN1) and ATF6 inactive until unfolded protein load rises; IRE1 then splices XBP1 mRNA to drive chaperone and ERAD gene expression, with DNAJB9 and WFS1 acting as negative feedback. PPP1R15A and PPP1R15B direct phosphatase activity that reverses translational attenuation, while FICD adenylylates BiP to buffer its activity. Apoptotic effectors such as BAX, BAK1, PUMA and BIM define the terminal outcome when adaptation fails.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, sensors trigger an adaptive stress programme; this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that restrain and terminate that unfolded protein response once folding capacity is restored, so that a transient adaptive signal does not become chronic stress signalling or apoptosis. Tonic restraint matters because prolonged branch activity drives secretory cell death, and loss of components such as WFS1 causes Wolfram syndrome with diabetes and neurodegeneration through unchecked ER stress. Mechanistically, the ER chaperone BiP holds sensors inactive until it is titrated away by unfolded substrates; WFS1 and DNAJB9 promote turnover or inhibition of ATF6 and IRE1 arms; GADD34-family phosphatase regulatory subunits reverse eIF2α phosphorylation to resume translation; and AKT and other kinase and calcium-handling proteins tune the threshold. The result is negative feedback that limits response duration and shapes recovery versus commitment to death.

positive regulation of endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response covers the inputs that switch on and amplify the cell's reaction to misfolded protein accumulating in the endoplasmic reticulum. This response lets secretory cells expand their folding capacity under load, and when amplification is sustained it commits the cell to death instead, which is why the pathway sits at the junction between adaptation and apoptosis in diabetes, neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury. The genes include the proximal stress sensors IRE1 (ERN1) and ATF6, whose activation drives XBP1 splicing and chaperone transcription, together with modulators such as TMEM33 and the phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN2 that tune sensor output. The BCL-2 family members BAK1, BAX, BOK and the BH3-only proteins PUMA and BIM link the stressed ER membrane to mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, coupling failed folding to programmed cell death.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, sensors in the ER membrane trigger a transcriptional and translational programme that expands folding capacity, slows new protein entry and clears damaged clients; this set covers the events that switch that response on or amplify it. Tuning the setpoint matters because a prolonged or overshooting response commits the cell to death rather than recovery, a decision that shapes secretory cell survival, insulin-producing beta cells, and the outcome of ER stress in neurodegeneration and cancer. The ER stress sensor IRE1 (ERN1) and the membrane-bound transcription factor ATF6 are the activated arms here, with TMEM33 and scaffolding or phosphatase partners modulating sensor output. BAX, BAK1 and the BH3-only proteins PUMA and BIM link sustained signalling to mitochondrial apoptosis, marking the transition from adaptive stress response to programmed cell death.

Nodal is the TGF-beta family signal that establishes the vertebrate body plan, and control over its strength and duration is what turns a broad gradient into a mesendoderm, a primitive streak and a left-right asymmetric body. Regulation of nodal signalling here works largely by restraint: secreted antagonists of the Cerberus/DAN class block ligand binding to the activin-type receptors, DACT proteins act intracellularly on Dishevelled and Nodal-pathway components to dampen output, and a nicalin-NOMO endoplasmic reticulum complex limits Nodal activity during mesoderm patterning. Hedgehog input and a gonadal transcription factor tie the same circuitry to midline signalling and sexual differentiation. Too little restraint expands mesoderm and disrupts laterality, producing situs inversus and heterotaxy with associated cardiac malformation; too much blocks germ layer formation altogether.

Nodal, a TGF-beta family ligand, sets up the vertebrate body axes, and its signalling must be damped in space and time or left-right asymmetry and mesoderm patterning go wrong. Negative regulation of the nodal pathway covers the antagonists that limit how strongly and how long cells respond. DAND5 is a secreted Cerberus/DAN-family antagonist that binds Nodal extracellularly and is central to breaking left-right symmetry around the embryonic node; its loss causes laterality defects such as situs inversus and associated heart malformations. DACT2 acts intracellularly to promote turnover of Nodal receptor-pathway components, restraining signalling strength. Nicalin together with NOMO forms an endoplasmic reticulum membrane complex that also suppresses Nodal responsiveness, linking secretory-pathway quality control to mesoderm and endoderm specification. Together these constraints convert a diffusible cue into a sharply bounded patterning signal.

Signals that travel between cells can be tuned before they ever reach a receptor, and this extracellular regulation of signal transduction covers the secreted antagonists and matrix proteins that do it. Most of the members act on the TGF-beta/BMP family: cerberus-like and DAN-family antagonists such as CER1, DAND5, GREM1, GREM2 and NBL1 bind BMP ligands directly and block receptor engagement, while latent TGF-beta binding protein LTBP1 and the fibrillins FBN1 and FBN2 tether latent TGF-beta complexes to elastic fibres, making the extracellular matrix a reservoir that sets how much active ligand is available. NRROS restrains TGF-beta1 release from myeloid cells, and LRPAP1 chaperones the receptor that clears such ligands. This layer patterns the embryo along its axes, shapes limb and kidney development, and keeps growth factor activity local; its failure produces skeletal and connective tissue disease, as in fibrillin-related Marfan syndrome.

Once a cell has committed to apoptosis, the execution phase is the terminal stage in which effector caspases dismantle the cell and its DNA is fragmented; this pathway covers the inputs that speed, slow or restrain that endpoint. Tuning it determines whether a damaged or infected cell dies cleanly or persists, and loss of control contributes to tumour survival, autoimmunity and excess tissue loss after injury. Death receptor components such as TNFRSF1A with the adaptors FADD and RIPK1 feed into initiator caspases CASP8, CASP10 and CASP9, while BCL2L1 and BOK set the mitochondrial threshold and the DNA fragmentation factor subunit DFFA gates nuclease activity toward chromatin. TP53 and its binding partner promote commitment, and several microRNAs together with regulators including SIRT2 and the mitochondrial protease HTRA2 adjust how far the programme proceeds.

negative regulation of execution phase of apoptosis restrains the final, committed steps of programmed cell death — the point at which caspases are active and the cell is being dismantled by DNA fragmentation, chromatin condensation and membrane blebbing. Braking this stage lets cells survive sublethal stress and preserves post-mitotic and slowly renewing tissues such as neurons and pancreatic islets; loss of the brake contributes to degenerative cell loss, while excessive braking allows damaged cells to persist and supports tumour survival. Mechanistically it works at several levels: BCL2L1 holds mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation in check, the DFFA subunit sequesters and inhibits the apoptotic nuclease until caspase cleavage releases it, chaperone and trophic inputs including HSPD1 and glucagon-derived peptides promote survival signalling, and microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-30 families tune the abundance of death effectors post-transcriptionally.

Once a cell has committed to apoptosis, the execution phase carries out the visible demolition dash caspase activation, chromatin condensation and internucleosomal DNA fragmentation. Restraining that final step lets cells survive sublethal insults and limits unnecessary tissue loss; its failure contributes to degenerative cell loss, while excessive restraint supports tumour cell survival. The brake operates at several levels. BCL2L1 (Bcl-xL) preserves mitochondrial outer membrane integrity and blocks release of apoptogenic factors. DFFA (ICAD) binds and chaperones the apoptotic nuclease DFF40/CAD, holding it inactive until caspase cleavage frees it, so intact ICAD directly prevents DNA laddering. Chaperone and metabolic signals, including HSPD1 and glucagon-derived peptides, and microRNAs of the let-7 and miR-30 families tune survival thresholds post-transcriptionally. The net effect is control over whether a death signal is completed or aborted, linking this biology to tissue homeostasis and cancer cell persistence.

Once a cell has committed to apoptosis, the execution phase is the irreversible dismantling step, and the genes here push cells into and through it. This drive matters for clearing damaged, infected or superfluous cells: too little and cells with genomic damage persist, contributing to tumour growth and autoimmunity; too much contributes to degenerative and ischaemic tissue loss. Death receptor engagement through TNFRSF1A recruits FADD and RIPK1 to activate initiator caspases CASP8 and CASP10, while mitochondrial permeabilisation, promoted by BOK and sensed through p53 with its binding partner TP53BP2, routes through CASP9; the mitochondrial serine protease HTRA2 removes inhibitor-of-apoptosis restraint. Additional contributors act by amplifying these steps, including the deacetylase SIRT2 and the microRNA MIR15A, which lowers anti-apoptotic BCL2. The output is caspase-driven substrate cleavage, chromatin condensation and packaging of the cell for phagocytic removal.

Whether a secreted ligand actually reaches and engages its receptor is itself regulated, and this pathway covers the processes that raise or lower ligand-receptor binding. Such control sets the gain of cytokine and growth factor signalling, determining how strongly a cell responds to a fixed amount of ligand. Several routes appear here: a decoy-like receptor, CCRL2, presents chemerin (encoded by RARRES2) for engagement by its signalling receptor rather than transducing itself; GREM2 sequesters bone morphogenetic proteins and so prevents their receptors from being occupied; IL11 with IL11RA and the shared signal-transducing subunit IL6ST illustrates how co-receptor availability licenses complex formation. The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL10 and the receptor-type phosphatase PTPRF add further modulation at the cell surface. Together these mechanisms shape inflammatory tone, bone and tissue remodelling, and the fidelity of developmental morphogen gradients.

Ligand access to a receptor can be reduced as well as increased, and this pathway covers the processes that stop or dampen a ligand binding its receptor, setting a ceiling on how strongly a cell responds to a cytokine or growth factor. Such restraint matters because unopposed cytokine signalling drives chronic inflammation, fibrosis and tumour-promoting immune states. The genes here point to the interleukin-6 family: IL11 acts through IL11RA together with the shared signal-transducing subunit gp130 (IL6ST), and receptor subunits in soluble or competing form can sequester ligand rather than transmit its signal, while IL10 is the archetypal anti-inflammatory cytokine limiting responses of macrophages and other antigen-presenting cells. PTPRF, a receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatase, contributes by opposing receptor tyrosine phosphorylation and interfering with productive receptor engagement. Together they illustrate negative control exerted at the level of receptor occupancy itself.

Hyaluronan is the unsulfated glycosaminoglycan that hydrates the extracellular matrix, lubricates joints, and provides the loose, swollen scaffold cells crawl through during wound healing, ovulation and tumour invasion. Control over how much of it is made therefore sets tissue water content and matrix stiffness, and excess synthesis contributes to fibrosis, intimal thickening and inflammatory oedema. The regulation of hyaluronan biosynthesis converges on hyaluronan synthase enzymes at the plasma membrane, with HAS2 the principal inducible isoform; growth factors such as EGF, PDGFB and TGFB1 raise its transcription, and NFKB1 links inflammatory signalling to the same output. Clathrin and adaptor components point to endocytic control of synthase availability at the cell surface, while sphingomyelinase activity connects membrane lipid turnover to synthase behaviour. The pathway thus couples proliferative and inflammatory cues to remodelling of the pericellular matrix.

Fungal infection is met by phagocyte recruitment, oxidative killing and cytokine output, and this pathway covers the modulation of that antifungal defense response, setting how strongly and how long it runs. Too little permits invasive candidiasis or aspergillosis; too much drives the inflammatory tissue damage seen in chronic fungal disease. The genes act at several tiers: SPI1 is a myeloid transcription factor that specifies the macrophage and neutrophil lineages doing the killing, TRIM62 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes CARD9-dependent signalling downstream of fungal glycan recognition, and USP15 is a deubiquitinase that tunes such signalling in the opposite direction. ARG1 depletes arginine and restrains nitric oxide-based effector function, PLA2G5 liberates arachidonic acid for eicosanoid mediators, and POMC-derived peptides feed neuroendocrine modulation of inflammation, linking innate antifungal immunity to metabolic and hormonal control.

How long a cytoplasmic mRNA survives is set largely by how fast its poly(A) tail is removed, and this pathway covers the factors that speed up or restrain that deadenylation-dependent decay. It sets the half-lives of inflammatory cytokine, growth factor and cell cycle transcripts, so loss of control here produces persistent inflammation, autoimmunity and oncogenic overexpression. Sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins recognise AU-rich or constitutive decay elements — ZFP36 and its paralogues, HNRNPD, RC3H1 — and recruit the CCR4-NOT deadenylase, whose CNOT1 scaffold and CNOT7 catalytic subunit shorten the tail before decapping and exonucleolytic destruction. The same complex is the endpoint of microRNA silencing through AGO2 and TNRC6 proteins, and is activated by TOB1. Opposing activities stabilise transcripts: PABPC1 with PAIP1 protects the tail, and TENT4A/TENT4B add mixed poly(A) that slows trimming.

How long an mRNA survives in the cytoplasm is set largely by how fast its poly(A) tail is trimmed, and this pathway covers the protective side of that balance: restraining deadenylation-dependent decay of nuclear-transcribed messages so that transcripts persist long enough to be translated. Such stabilization lets cells hold onto specific mRNAs during growth signalling, development and stress, and its loss shortens transcript half-lives and flattens gene expression programmes that depend on post-transcriptional timing. The poly(A)-binding protein PABPC1 with its partner PAIP1 shields the tail and links it to the translation initiation machinery, while the non-canonical nucleotidyltransferases TENT4A and TENT4B extend tails with mixed guanosine residues that deadenylases handle poorly. Sequence-specific RNA-binding proteins including IGF2BP1, YBX1, CSDE1, SYNCRIP and hnRNP family members coat target transcripts and compete with decay machinery, making mRNA stability a regulated, message-by-message decision.

Most cytoplasmic mRNAs are destroyed by first shortening their poly(A) tail, and this pathway covers the factors that accelerate that step and the decay which follows. Speeding deadenylation is how cells impose short half-lives on transcripts that must not persist templates for cytokines, growth regulators and cell cycle proteins so that inflammatory and proliferative responses switch off as quickly as they switch on. The CCR4-NOT complex, represented here by its CNOT1 scaffold and the CNOT7 deadenylase subunit, is the catalytic core, and the specificity comes from adaptors recruited to it: AU-rich element binding proteins of the ZFP36 family, microRNA-directed silencing through AGO2 and the TNRC6 scaffolds, and antiproliferative TOB1. PABPC1 coats the tail being removed. Loss of this control stabilises cytokine messages and contributes to chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.
