Bone reaches its adult strength only when the osteoid matrix laid down by osteoblasts is mineralized at the right rate and to the right extent, and this control point tunes that deposition during skeletal maturation. Too little mineral gives rickets-like softening and fragility; unrestrained or ectopic mineralization stiffens tissue that should remain compliant. BMP2 drives osteoblast commitment and matrix production, while the secreted antagonist GREM1 binds BMPs and restrains that signal, so the balance between them sets mineralization output. Parathyroid hormone acts systemically on calcium and phosphate handling and, depending on whether exposure is intermittent or continuous, either favours bone formation or mobilizes mineral. Lactoferrin acts on osteoblast proliferation and survival, and the refilin proteins shape the actin cytoskeleton of skeletal cells. Together these link endocrine calcium control, growth factor signalling and cell architecture to skeletal mineral accrual.

Whether a signalling protein reaches the nucleus is often the decisive step in whether a gene programme is switched on, and this collection covers the processes that tune how much of a given protein gets there. Control points include import receptors and the RAN GTPase system, nucleoporins and the nuclear lamina, chaperone systems such as the CCT/TRiC complex, and post-translational marks — phosphorylation, SUMOylation, acetylation — that mask or expose localisation signals. Much of the biology is regulatory output: 14-3-3 proteins and LATS kinases retain YAP and TAZ in the cytoplasm as the Hippo pathway's brake on growth, NFKBIA sequesters NF-κB until stimulation, and SMAD3, GLI factors downstream of Hedgehog, STAT-activating JAKs and XBP1 all depend on regulated entry. Misrouting here contributes to cancer, and cytoplasmic mislocalisation of TARDBP is a hallmark of neurodegeneration.

Signalling decisions are often made by controlling whether a transcription factor or kinase is allowed into the nucleus at all, and this pathway covers the machinery that blocks or reduces such nuclear entry. Keeping latent regulators in the cytoplasm sets the threshold for inflammatory, growth and developmental responses, and its loss produces inappropriate constitutive signalling, as when NF-kB escapes its inhibitor. Several distinct restraint mechanisms converge here: NFKBIA masks the NF-kB nuclear localisation signal; 14-3-3 proteins encoded by YWHAB, YWHAE and YWHAZ sequester phosphorylated cargo in the cytosol; LATS1 and LATS2 phosphorylate Hippo pathway effectors to exclude them from the nucleus; SUFU holds GLI proteins back from Hedgehog target genes; and PKIA and PKIG inhibit the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A. Additional anchoring, ubiquitin-related and scaffolding components tune the same partitioning, making cytoplasmic retention a general layer of transcriptional control.

Many signalling decisions are executed not by changing a protein's abundance but by moving it into the nucleus, and this pathway covers the events that promote such import. Transcription factors and co-activators held in the cytoplasm — SMAD3 downstream of TGF-beta, YAP1 and WWTR1 in Hippo signalling, GLI3 and SMO in hedgehog output, STAT-activating kinases JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 — only reach their target genes when this control is engaged, so it converts receptor activation at the surface into changes in gene expression. Contributors include the nuclear transport machinery itself (importins, RAN, the nucleoporin TPR), chaperones such as HSP90AA1 and the CCT/TRiC folding complex that keep cargo import-competent, and kinases including AKT1, SRC and MAPK14 that unmask localisation signals. Misdirected nuclear traffic features in cancer, in stress responses such as the XBP1 arm of the unfolded protein response, and in TARDBP mislocalisation in neurodegeneration.

An oocyte arrested in meiotic prophase must be held there until ovulatory signals release it, and this regulatory layer sets when and how fast that maturation proceeds. Getting the timing wrong yields eggs that are immature or overripe, with consequences for fertilization, embryo viability and fertility; several of these genes are mutated in human oocyte maturation failure. Cumulus-derived natriuretic peptide acting through its guanylyl cyclase receptor sustains the cyclic GMP supply that keeps the oocyte's cell cycle brake engaged, while the oocyte kinase WEE2 inhibits the maturation-promoting kinase CDK1 to enforce arrest. Release involves Aurora kinase A activity at spindle poles for meiotic spindle assembly and polar body formation, with SIRT2 and signalling adaptors tuning chromosome segregation fidelity. The pathway thus links follicular somatic signals to the oocyte's own meiotic machinery.

Amyloid-beta peptide is continuously produced in the brain, and whether it accumulates into plaques depends on how fast it is removed; this pathway covers the inputs that set that removal rate. Its failure is central to Alzheimer's disease, where reduced uptake and degradation, rather than overproduction, drives deposition in most late-onset cases. Clearance routes represented here include receptor-mediated endocytosis and transport across the blood-brain barrier via LRP1 with its chaperone LRPAP1, lipoprotein-dependent handling through APOE and clusterin, and microglial phagocytosis governed by TREM2 and the lipid transporter ABCA7 cholesterol synthesis genes under SREBF2 control, such as HMGCR and CYP51A1, tune membrane lipid composition and thereby uptake efficiency. Inflammatory cytokines including TNF, IFNG and IL4 shift microglia between clearing and damaging states, and microRNAs add post-transcriptional control over these components.

Negative regulation of amyloid-beta clearance covers the processes that impede removal of amyloid-beta peptide from brain tissue, tipping the balance between production and disposal toward plaque accumulation. Because Alzheimer's disease pathology reflects failed clearance at least as much as excess generation, restraint of these routes matters for how quickly deposits build up in the parenchyma and cerebral vessels. Two themes appear. Inflammatory signalling through interferon-gamma and TNF acting on their receptors dampens microglial and astrocytic uptake and degradation of the peptide. Cholesterol and lipid handling supplies the second: the SREBF2 transcriptional programme with HMGCR and CYP51A1, together with a microRNA arm including miR-1908 and miR-34a, alters membrane lipid composition and the abundance of clearance receptors, while LRPAP1 modulates LRP-mediated transport across the blood-brain barrier. Myocardin and SRF contribute through vascular smooth muscle control of perivascular drainage.

Amyloid-beta is continuously produced in the brain and must be removed by microglial uptake, enzymatic degradation, and transport across the blood-brain barrier; this pathway covers the influences that suppress that removal and so allow the peptide to accumulate. Impaired clearance rather than overproduction is the dominant lesion in sporadic Alzheimer's disease, making these restraining inputs directly relevant to plaque formation. Two themes run through the genes: inflammatory signalling, where TNF and interferon-gamma acting through its receptor blunt microglial and receptor-mediated clearance, and cholesterol biosynthesis, where the SREBF2-driven programme including HMGCR and CYP51A1 alters membrane lipid composition and lipoprotein-receptor handling of the peptide. LRPAP1 constrains LRP1-mediated uptake and efflux, while microRNAs including miR-34a act post-transcriptionally on clearance machinery. The net effect links neuroinflammation and brain lipid metabolism to amyloid deposition.

Amyloid-beta peptide is continuously produced in the brain, and whether it accumulates into plaques depends on how efficiently it is taken up, degraded and exported. Enhancing amyloid-beta clearance is the arm of that balance that removes the peptide, and its failure underlies the plaque deposition of Alzheimer's disease; several of the genes here are among the strongest genetic risk factors for late-onset disease. Clearance runs largely through phagocytic and endocytic uptake by microglia and astrocytes: TREM2 licenses microglial activation and phagocytosis, LRP1 with its chaperone LRPAP1 binds amyloid-beta and lipoprotein complexes for internalisation, ABCA7 supports lipid transport and engulfment, and the APOE isoform carried strongly shapes how readily the peptide is bound and cleared. Cytokine input from IL4 pushes microglia toward a clearance-competent state, while ROCK1 activity modulates cytoskeletal remodelling during uptake.

The NLRP3 inflammasome converts danger signals into caspase-1 activation, IL-1β and IL-18 release, and pyroptotic death, so cells need brakes on its assembly to avoid self-damaging inflammation. Restraining that assembly is what keeps sterile injury, crystal deposition and infection from tipping into chronic inflammatory disease; loss of these brakes underlies periodic fever syndromes and contributes to gout, atherosclerosis and neuroinflammation. The restraint works at several levels: ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM31 and FBXL2 target NLRP3 for degradation, autophagy machinery including IRGM and LAMP2-dependent chaperone-mediated autophagy clears the sensor, pyrin-domain-only proteins PYDC1 and PYDC2 act as decoys that block adaptor recruitment, and depalmitoylases together with kinases and SIRT2 tune NLRP3 through reversible lipid and post-translational modification. Other NLR and pyrin-domain proteins, and the microglial receptor TREM2, provide additional inhibitory input, setting the threshold for innate immune activation.

regulation of phenotypic switching controls how readily a differentiated cell abandons its specialised program and adopts another state, most clearly in vascular smooth muscle cells that toggle between a contractile phenotype and a proliferative, migratory, matrix-secreting one. This plasticity allows vessels to remodel and repair, but its dysregulation drives neointima formation, restenosis, atherosclerotic plaque instability and pulmonary hypertension. The genes span the layers that set the switch point: myocardin acts with serum response factor to drive contractile gene expression, the miR-143/145 cluster reinforces that state by silencing repressors of smooth muscle identity, DNA methyltransferase activity locks or releases lineage promoters epigenetically, and FGF9 signalling from the surrounding tissue pushes cells toward dedifferentiation. Together they place transcriptional, microRNA and chromatin control of cell identity downstream of growth factor cues in the vessel wall.

Vascular smooth muscle cells are not terminally fixed: they can convert between a contractile, differentiated state and a proliferative, migratory, matrix-secreting one, and the regulation of this phenotypic switching sets how blood vessels respond to injury. Restraining the switch keeps vessels contractile and quiescent; permitting it drives neointima formation, atherosclerotic plaque remodelling and restenosis, and comparable state transitions underlie fibrotic and airway remodelling. The controls represented here span transcription, epigenetics and small RNAs: myocardin acts as the master coactivator driving smooth muscle contractile gene expression, DNA methyltransferase activity stabilises the chosen state through DNA methylation, a clustered pair of microRNAs reinforces the differentiated programme by damping pro-proliferative targets, and fibroblast growth factor signalling pushes cells toward dedifferentiation. Together they determine how readily a differentiated cell abandons its identity under stress.

Sustained neurotransmission depends on recovering vesicle membrane and proteins from the presynaptic terminal after fusion, and this pathway sets how fast and how much of that retrieval occurs. Tuning it matches vesicle supply to firing rate; when it fails, terminals deplete their releasable pool during heavy activity and synaptic transmission fatigues. Control is exerted on the clathrin-adaptor and actin machinery that deforms and pinches the membrane, with an AP-2 subunit, actin isoforms and an Arp2/3 component acting alongside Rho-family regulators such as RAC1, ROCK1 and the Rho-GAP oculocerebral protein OPHN1. Calcium provides the trigger signal, read out through calmodulin, calcineurin catalytic subunits and synaptotagmin-7, while LRRK2, PRKN and PARK7 link the process to Parkinson disease, where impaired vesicle recycling is an early feature of dopaminergic and glutamatergic terminals.

positive regulation of RIG-I signaling pathway comprises the factors that amplify cytosolic detection of viral RNA, raising the output of the RIG-I/MDA5 sensing arm of innate immunity toward type I interferon production. Because RIG-I signalling is held under tight restraint to avoid autoinflammation, these positive regulators set the threshold at which an infected cell commits to an antiviral transcriptional program; too little amplification permits RNA virus replication, too much drives interferonopathy. Mechanistically they act at several tiers: co-sensors and RNA-binding cofactors such as ZCCHC3, DDX60 and DHX58 improve ligand recognition and loading, ZC3HAV1 and OASL mimic or promote ubiquitin- and ISG15-like modification of the sensor, and deubiquitinases and TRIM-family ligases including USP15 and TRIM15 stabilise signalling intermediates en route to MAVS, TBK1 and IRF3. Several members are themselves interferon-inducible, creating a feed-forward loop that sustains the response.

Cytosolic RIG-I detects viral RNA and triggers interferon production; the genes here amplify that detection, raising the sensitivity and output of RIG-I signaling so that an antiviral state is established quickly after infection. This positive regulation matters because RIG-I sensing sets the threshold between rapid viral clearance and unchecked replication, and it must be tuned upward transiently without provoking interferon-driven autoinflammation. Several members act as cofactors that help load or stabilise RNA ligands on the sensor, including the helicases DDX60 and DHX58 and the zinc-finger protein ZCCHC3, while OASL mimics ubiquitin to enhance signalling and ZC3HAV1 engages viral RNA and downstream adaptors. Ubiquitin-pathway components such as USP15 and TRIM15 modulate the ubiquitination steps that license sensor oligomerisation and MAVS-dependent signalling, and RNA-binding regulators contribute post-transcriptional control. The output feeds into type I interferon induction and innate immune defence.

DNA polymerases are only weakly processive on their own, and this pathway covers the accessory factors that boost their activity at the replication fork. Most of the members form an alternative clamp loader in which the small replication factor C subunits RFC2-RFC5 pair with CHTF18, CHTF8 and DSCC1, an ATP-driven complex that loads the PCNA sliding clamp onto primed DNA so that replicative polymerases can be tethered and extended over long stretches. The same complex contributes to the replication checkpoint and to establishing sister chromatid cohesion, linking polymerase stimulation to accurate chromosome duplication and segregation. POLG2 acts in the mitochondrion, where as the accessory subunit of polymerase gamma it confers processive, high-affinity synthesis on the mitochondrial genome. Loss of these stimulatory functions causes replication stress, genome instability and, for the mitochondrial arm, mtDNA depletion disorders.

Long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of synapses that underlies learning and memory formation, and this pathway covers the molecules that set how readily it is induced and how long it endures. Tuning matters: too little potentiation impairs hippocampal memory, while unchecked strengthening destabilises circuits, and several members here link the process to Alzheimer disease and intellectual disability. Calcium-stimulated adenylyl cyclases and anchored PKA subunits couple synaptic activity to cAMP signalling and CREB-dependent transcription, while ARC and other activity-induced products remodel receptor content at the postsynaptic density, where scaffolds such as SHANK3 and auxiliary AMPA receptor subunits including SHISA7 organise glutamate receptors. Adenosine and dopamine receptors, reelin, ephrin receptors, APP and prion protein provide extracellular and neuromodulatory constraints, and translational regulators acting locally in dendrites gate the protein synthesis that makes potentiation persistent.

Long-term potentiation strengthens synapses and stores information, but unchecked strengthening saturates a circuit and leaves it unable to encode anything new, so brakes on potentiation are as much part of learning as potentiation itself. This pathway covers the processes that damp or block the persistent increase in synaptic strength, setting the threshold that a stimulus must exceed to leave a lasting trace and preserving dynamic range for later plasticity. The genes point to several routes: adenosine acting through an inhibitory receptor to suppress transmission, amyloid precursor protein and prion protein as membrane proteins whose misfolded or cleaved forms depress potentiation, apolipoprotein E and a microglial signalling adaptor linking glial and lipid handling to synaptic depression, and Eph receptor and kinase signalling shaping the postsynaptic response. The same machinery is implicated in the synaptic failure and memory loss of neurodegenerative disease.

Long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of synapses that underlies learning and memory formation, and the genes here act to promote or enhance it rather than simply carry it out. Positive regulation of long-term synaptic potentiation runs largely through calcium- and cAMP-dependent signalling: calcium-stimulated adenylyl cyclases ADCY1 and ADCY8 raise cAMP, PKA subunits and the scaffold AKAP5 position that signalling at the postsynaptic membrane, phosphodiesterase PDE9A shapes cyclic nucleotide decay, and CREB1 converts the signal into transcription needed for late-phase persistence. Postsynaptic scaffolding and adhesion components such as SHANK3, EPHB2, SHISA7 and IGSF11 stabilise glutamate receptors, while neuromodulatory inputs through dopamine D2, adenosine A2A and nicotinic alpha7 receptors, and extracellular cues such as reelin, tune the threshold. Loss of this regulation impairs hippocampal memory and features in autism-spectrum disorders and Alzheimer's disease, where APP processing enzymes also appear.

Melanin is a secondary metabolite, and this is the restraining arm of pigment production — the processes that lower the rate or extent of melanin biosynthesis in melanocytes and so set skin, hair and eye colour and the balance between eumelanin and the lighter pheomelanin. Agouti signalling protein acts as an antagonist of melanocortin receptor signalling, switching pigment synthesis away from eumelanin, while mahogunin, a ubiquitin ligase, and the melanosomal transporters and channels that control lumenal ion and amino acid content modulate how much pigment a melanosome can make. A light-sensitive opsin and WNT5A add further negative input, linking UV exposure and paracrine cues to pigment output. Variation here underlies normal pigmentation differences and hypopigmentation phenotypes, and the same tone-setting determines constitutive photoprotection against ultraviolet damage.

Upregulation of secondary metabolite biosynthesis here means increased melanin production, the pigment pathway that determines skin, hair and eye colour and shields keratinocyte DNA from ultraviolet damage. Melanocortin signalling sets the pace: POMC-derived α-MSH acts on the MC1R receptor to raise cyclic AMP and drive pigment gene expression, while the agouti signalling protein competes at the same receptor to switch output toward lighter pigment; APPL1 and GIPC1 act as trafficking and signalling adaptors in this cascade, and OPN3 provides light-responsive input. Downstream, TYRP1 works in melanin synthesis itself, PMEL forms the amyloid fibril matrix on which melanin is deposited, ATP7A supplies copper to tyrosinase, and RAB38 directs cargo to maturing melanosomes. ZEB2 supports melanocyte identity. Loss of this regulation produces pigmentation disorders and lighter phototypes with heightened melanoma risk.

Cells continually adjust how strongly they react to reactive oxygen species, and this regulatory layer sets the gain of that response, determining whether an oxidative insult is buffered or tips into lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial damage and death. NFE2L2 is the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, and SLC7A11, the cystine/glutamate exchanger it induces, supplies cysteine for glutathione; AIFM2 (FSP1) and the tetrahydrobiopterin-generating enzyme GCH1 provide lipid-radical defences that restrain ferroptosis. PINK1 and PRKN couple oxidative damage to selective clearance of dysfunctional mitochondria, while uncoupling-protein-family carriers and OXR1 modulate mitochondrial radical output and resistance. Lipid-handling components such as CD36, ALOX5, FADS2 and PNPLA8 shape the peroxidizable membrane pool that is the substrate of injury. Loss of this tuning contributes to neurodegeneration, peroxisomal disease and the redox adaptations that allow tumour cells to survive.

Cells mounting a response to oxidative stress must also be able to damp that response, and this dampening arm limits how strongly and how long the oxidative stress programme runs. Restraining the reaction matters because sustained stress signalling drives apoptosis and inflammatory damage even when the original insult is modest, so the balance set here influences neuronal survival in particular. The genes converge on the TLDc protein family, whose members share a domain implicated in protecting cells from reactive oxygen species; OXR1 and its relatives NCOA7, MEAK7 and TBC1D24 act at lysosomal and mitochondrial interfaces, with TBC1D24 mutations causing epilepsy and deafness syndromes. A microRNA contributes post-transcriptional tuning of the same axis. Together these components fix the threshold at which redox imbalance is translated into a full cellular stress response.

Antibacterial defence has to be tuned: strong enough to clear an infection, restrained enough to spare the host's own tissue, and the genes here set that level rather than performing the killing themselves. Their outputs shape epithelial and phagocyte responses at barrier surfaces and in the gut and airway, where chronic over-activation produces inflammatory disease and under-activation permits colonisation. Several act on the oxidative arm, with a dual oxidase generating hydrogen peroxide at mucosal surfaces and a cytochrome b subunit supporting the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, while arginase competes for the arginine used in nitric oxide production. Others work through receptors and checkpoints: a protease-activated receptor and an inflammasome-related NLR modulate signalling thresholds, a checkpoint receptor dampens activated lymphocytes, and a serine protease inhibitor limits proteolysis in skin. Transcriptional and secreted regulators complete the control layer over innate immune output.

Antibacterial defence has to be restrained as well as triggered, and this is the braking side of that balance: processes that damp the frequency or intensity of the host response to bacteria, limiting collateral tissue injury and preventing sustained inflammation once a threat is contained. The genes involved act through several routes. Arginase 2 consumes L-arginine, lowering the substrate available for nitric oxide production by macrophages. HAVCR2, an inhibitory receptor on T cells and myeloid cells, delivers negative signals that curb effector activity. SPINK5 inhibits epithelial serine proteases in skin and mucosa, and its loss causes Netherton syndrome with barrier breakdown and inflammation; a microRNA and a kinase-binding scaffold add post-transcriptional and signalling-level restraint. Excessive suppression favours bacterial persistence, while too little permits immunopathology, making this tuning central to mucosal and skin homeostasis.

Upregulation of antibacterial defence describes the processes that raise the strength or speed of a host's response to bacterial challenge, tuning how aggressively epithelia and phagocytes attack invading organisms. It matters at mucosal surfaces and in wounds, where too weak a response permits invasion and too strong a response damages tissue. The genes here act on several arms of that output: a component of the phagocyte NADPH oxidase and a dual oxidase generate reactive oxygen and hydrogen peroxide for microbial killing; a protease-activated receptor couples extracellular proteolysis to inflammatory signalling; progranulin, elastin microfibril interface proteins and multimerin operate in the extracellular matrix and modulate leukocyte behaviour; a NOD-like receptor family member and immune receptors such as HAVCR2 and a sialic-acid-binding lectin set thresholds for inflammasome and myeloid activation. Together they position innate antibacterial immunity as an adjustable rather than fixed response.

Excitatory transmission in the brain depends on how strongly glutamate receptors respond, and this control layer tunes that response rather than carrying the signal itself. It sets the gain of AMPA and NMDA receptor signalling at synapses, shaping learning-related plasticity, excitotoxic vulnerability, and the balance between excitation and inhibition whose disruption contributes to autism spectrum disorders, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Postsynaptic scaffolds and adhesion proteins such as SHANK3 and neuroligin-3 organise receptors opposite the presynaptic terminal, FRRS1L acts as an auxiliary subunit controlling AMPA receptor assembly and trafficking, and the kinase FYN phosphorylates NMDA receptor subunits to modulate their activity. Contributions also come from outside the neuron: chemokine signalling through CX3CL1 and the CCL2/CCR2 axis, and interferon-gamma receptor signalling, let microglia and inflammatory state feed back onto synaptic glutamate responsiveness.

Excitatory transmission in the brain depends on how strongly glutamate receptors respond to released transmitter, and this pathway covers the processes that raise that responsiveness. Enhancing ionotropic and metabotropic glutamate receptor signalling supports synaptic strengthening, learning and memory, while unchecked potentiation contributes to excitotoxic neuronal injury and to seizure susceptibility. The genes act at several levels: postsynaptic scaffolding and adhesion proteins such as SHANK3 and NLGN3 organise receptor complexes at the excitatory synapse, EPHB2 couples contact signalling to NMDA receptor recruitment, FOLH1 (glutamate carboxypeptidase II) liberates glutamate from the peptide NAAG, and the prion protein and calcium-binding NECAB2 modulate receptor activity locally. Immune and neuromodulatory inputs including CCL2 with its receptor CCR2, interferon-gamma signalling and beta-adrenergic stimulation sensitise synapses, linking inflammation and arousal state to glutamatergic tone. Disruption of these regulators is recurrent in autism spectrum disorders and neuropathic pain.

Long-term synaptic depression is the weakening arm of synaptic plasticity, and the processes that modulate its extent and rate set how readily a circuit discards or rescales previously strengthened connections dash a requirement for cerebellar motor learning, hippocampal memory updating and developmental pruning. Regulation acts at several levels: metabotropic glutamate receptor signalling through GRM5 initiates the protein-synthesis-dependent form, cerebellar delta2 glutamate receptors with their cerebellin ligand organise parallel fibre synapses where depression is expressed, and adenosine A1 receptors and opioid peptides tune the threshold presynaptically. Activity-induced ARC drives receptor internalisation, while FMR1 and STAU2 govern the local mRNA translation that supplies the necessary proteins; scaffolds and adaptors such as SHANK3 and IQSEC2 couple these signals to receptor trafficking. Loss of this control contributes to fragile X syndrome and autism, and excessive depression accompanies amyloid and tau pathology in Alzheimer's disease.

Long-term synaptic depression is the persistent weakening of synaptic strength that complements potentiation, and the genes here act to promote it — enhancing how readily, quickly or durably synapses are depressed. This form of plasticity underlies motor learning in the cerebellum, where a secreted cerebellin binds the delta-2 glutamate receptor GRID2 to build parallel fibre–Purkinje cell synapses whose depression is the cellular basis of adaptation, and where adenylyl cyclase ADCY8 links calcium rises to cAMP signalling. Other components regulate receptor trafficking and the postsynaptic scaffold: IQSEC2 is an ARF GTPase activator at excitatory synapses, STAU2 governs dendritic mRNA localisation for local translation, and amyloid precursor protein together with its receptor LILRB2 mediates the excessive depression and spine loss associated with Alzheimer's disease. Tilting the balance toward depression weakens circuits and impairs memory maintenance.

Many hormones, neurotransmitters and proteases act through receptors that couple to Gq and switch on phospholipase C, raising inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol and releasing calcium from intracellular stores. This gene set covers the tuning of that route rather than the core transduction itself, setting how strongly and how long a cell responds to agonists such as thrombin or gastrin-releasing peptide. Losing that brake contributes to fibrosis of the lung, liver, kidney and heart, and to the stiffened stroma that accompanies tumour progression. Much of the restraint here is post-transcriptional: several microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, suppress transcripts encoding collagens and other matrix components, while others act on TGF-beta pathway output. TGFBR3, the type III TGF-beta receptor, sequesters ligand and limits signalling through the pro-fibrotic type I/II receptor pair, and the nuclear receptor PPARG opposes fibroblast activation and myofibroblast differentiation. Together these define the negative side of matrix homeostasis, balancing deposition against turnover during wound healing and tissue remodelling.

Tissues gain their mechanical properties from an organised extracellular matrix, and this pathway covers the signals that push matrix assembly forward — increasing the rate and extent to which secreted collagens, fibrillins and associated glycoproteins are deposited and cross-linked into fibrils. The core driver here is transforming growth factor beta signalling: TGFB1 acting through its type I receptor TGFBR1 and the SMAD3–SMAD4 transcriptional complex to raise matrix gene expression, with SOX9 directing the cartilage-specific version of that programme. Angiotensinogen links the pathway to haemodynamic and fibrotic stimuli, EMILIN1 contributes an elastic-fibre scaffold component, and a microRNA and the regulator RGCC provide restraint and tuning. Sustained activation of this axis produces the fibrosis and scarring seen in kidney, lung, liver and heart disease, while too little compromises wound healing and skeletal matrix formation.

Alongside the classical route, cells run a second NF-kappaB arm in which NIK-dependent processing of p100 liberates RelB-containing dimers, and this pathway is the tuning of that cascade up or down. It is engaged by a distinct set of TNF-family receptors represented here — RANK and its ligand, CD27, LIGHT, the ectodysplasin receptor — and it governs lymphoid organ development, B cell survival, dendritic cell maturation, osteoclast differentiation and the formation of skin appendages. Control is exerted largely through the stability of the kinase that drives it: ubiquitin ligases and the deubiquitinase CYLD, together with IAP proteins, set its abundance, while phosphatases, TRIM proteins, RNA-binding repressors and numerous microRNAs add further restraint. Loss of restraint sustains RelB target gene expression and contributes to lymphoma, autoimmunity and pathological bone resorption; loss of signalling impairs immune tissue architecture and ectodermal development.

Non-canonical NF-kappaB signalling, driven by NIK-dependent processing of p100 to p52, sustains lymphoid organogenesis, B cell survival and osteoclast differentiation, and the restraining arm described here keeps that output brief and proportionate. Without such brakes, persistent NF-kappaB activity drives chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy, which is why several of these genes behave as tumour suppressors. The mechanisms are varied: the deubiquitinase CYLD and the phosphatases PPM1A and PPM1B strip activating modifications from pathway intermediates, TRIM-family ubiquitin ligases target signalling components for degradation, NLR proteins such as NLRP12 and NLRC3 act as intracellular negative regulators of inflammatory signalling, and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A degrades inflammatory transcripts. A large complement of microRNAs adds post-transcriptional damping, alongside transcriptional and adaptor-level control from FOXJ1, HDAC7 and LITAF, placing this biology within the broader feedback control of innate and adaptive immune activation.

positive regulation of non-canonical NF-kappaB signal transduction covers the inputs that switch on the slower, NIK-dependent arm of NF-kappaB, in which p100 is processed to p52 and pairs with RelB to drive gene expression distinct from the classical p65 response. This arm builds and maintains lymphoid tissue, germinal centres and B cell survival niches, and drives osteoclast differentiation; its loss underlies immunodeficiency and ectodermal dysplasia, while its overactivation supports lymphoid malignancy and bone erosion. The genes here are largely the receptors and ligands that feed it — RANK with RANKL, CD27, LIGHT, ectodysplasin and its receptor — together with adaptors and kinases such as RIPK1, MAP3K7 and RBCK1, ubiquitin-pathway TRIM proteins and VCP that govern NIK stability, and inflammasome and damage-sensing components including NLRP3, NOD1/2 and HMGB1 that couple innate immune recognition to this cascade.

Upregulation of the non-canonical NF-kappaB cascade drives the alternative arm of NF-kappaB activation, in which stabilised NIK directs IKK-alpha to process the p100 precursor into p52, releasing p52-RelB dimers into the nucleus. Sustained rather than transient, this branch builds and maintains lymphoid tissue: signalling through TNF receptor superfamily members such as CD27, RANK with its ligand RANKL, LIGHT, and the EDA-EDAR pair supports germinal centre and stromal organisation, dendritic cell maturation, osteoclast differentiation and the formation of skin appendages, while chemokine cues such as CCL19 recruit cells into those niches. Positive regulators here include upstream kinases and ubiquitin machinery, TRIM ligases, and inflammatory triggers ranging from IL-1beta and TNF to innate sensors like NOD1, NOD2 and NLRP3. Excessive output feeds lymphoproliferation, autoimmunity, bone loss and B-cell malignancy; loss compromises immune tissue architecture and ectodermal development.

Sugars and sugar-containing molecules rarely cross membranes unaided, and carbohydrate derivative transport covers the carriers, channels and pumps that move them between compartments and cells. The traffic supplies the raw material for glycosylation, nucleotide metabolism and glucose release into blood. A large family of nucleotide-sugar transporters loads the Golgi and ER lumen with CMP-sialic acid, UDP-galactose, UDP-GlcNAc and GDP-fucose so that glycosyltransferases can extend glycans; loss of the GDP-fucose carrier SLC35C1 causes a leukocyte adhesion deficiency because selectin ligands go unfucosylated. Glucose-6-phosphate translocation into the ER by SLC37A4 paired with glucose-6-phosphatase underlies hepatic glucose output, and defects produce glycogen storage disease. Other members carry nucleosides, adenine nucleotides across the inner mitochondrial membrane, sialic acid out of lysosomes, and glycolipids between membranes, while pannexin, CALHM and volume-regulated anion channels release nucleotides and osmolytes for extracellular signalling.

Succinyl-CoA sits at a junction of the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling, heme synthesis and the breakdown of odd-chain fatty acids and several amino acids, and its catabolism is how that thioester is consumed rather than allowed to accumulate. The main route is the succinyl-CoA ligase reaction, in which a shared alpha subunit pairs with either an ADP-forming or a GDP-forming beta subunit to cleave the thioester bond and capture the energy as ATP or GTP, yielding succinate for the rest of the cycle. Loss of the ADP-forming subunit causes encephalomyopathy with mitochondrial DNA depletion, linking this step to nucleotide supply inside the organelle. A second, hydrolytic route uses Nudix-family CoA diphosphatases, which cleave acyl-CoA esters to the corresponding phosphopantetheine derivative and AMP, contributing to CoA turnover and to housekeeping of acyl-CoA pools in mitochondria and peroxisomes.

Succinyl-CoA is the point where two quite different metabolic streams enter the citric acid cycle, and its biosynthesis supplies the cycle with carbon for energy production as well as the starting unit for heme synthesis. One route is oxidative decarboxylation of 2-oxoglutarate by the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, in which OGDH, the dihydrolipoyl succinyltransferase DLST and the shared flavoprotein dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase DLD act in sequence using thiamine and lipoate cofactors. The other is the anaplerotic disposal of propionyl-CoA generated from odd-chain fatty acids, branched-chain amino acids and cholesterol side chains: biotin-dependent propionyl-CoA carboxylase, an epimerase, and the cobalamin-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase convert it to succinyl-CoA. Loss of these steps causes propionic and methylmalonic acidemias or 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase deficiency, with acidosis and neurological damage.

Nucleoside phosphates are both the energy currency and the building blocks of nucleic acids, and their controlled breakdown sets intracellular ATP, cyclic nucleotide and nucleotide pool levels. This catabolic activity determines how much purine and pyrimidine salvage material is available, how quickly second messengers are terminated, and how much uric acid is produced; its failure underlies immunodeficiency from adenosine deaminase loss, gout, and autoinflammatory disease when cytosolic nucleotide and nucleic acid degradation is impaired. Ectonucleotidases and 5'-nucleotidases strip phosphates from extracellular and cytosolic nucleotides to generate adenosine, phosphodiesterases hydrolyse cAMP and cGMP, Nudix hydrolases clear damaged or modified nucleotides, and phosphorylases and deaminases feed bases back into salvage or on to xanthine oxidase. Overlapping glycolytic enzymes and AMPK and mTOR components tie this turnover to cellular energy sensing and biosynthetic demand.

Nucleoside phosphate biosynthesis supplies the phosphorylated nucleosides that serve as DNA and RNA precursors, energy currency, sugar and lipid donors, and signalling second messengers, so essentially every anabolic and proliferative process depends on it. Purine and pyrimidine rings are built de novo from amino acids, folate-derived one-carbon units and phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate, or recovered by salvage kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases such as HPRT1, APRT, ADK and thymidine kinase, whose loss causes disorders including Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and immunodeficiency. Ribonucleotide reductase and thymidylate synthase commit ribonucleotides to deoxynucleotides for replication and repair, making these steps the target of many antimetabolite and antiviral drugs. Nucleoside monophosphate and diphosphate kinases interconvert phosphorylation states, while mitochondrial respiratory complexes and ATP synthase regenerate ATP. The same chemistry yields NAD, coenzyme A, FAD, activated sugars, and the cyclic nucleotides made by adenylate and guanylate cyclases.

Hydrogen peroxide is both a signalling molecule and a killer, and this pathway covers the controls that set how readily a cell commits to death when peroxide accumulates. Tuning that threshold decides whether oxidative stress from ischaemia, inflammation or mitochondrial dysfunction is tolerated or triggers cell loss, which matters for cardiomyocyte and neuronal survival in particular. Survival input flows through the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET and AKT1, which suppresses the pro-apoptotic transcription factor FOXO3; mitochondrial quality-control and redox proteins including PINK1, PARK7/DJ-1 and the chaperone TRAP1 limit peroxide-driven damage, while ENDOG and the kinase-C-interacting protein PAWR act on the death side. Several microRNAs, among them miR-21 and miR-133a, adjust the balance post-transcriptionally. Loss of this restraint contributes to neurodegeneration and to oxidative injury of heart and vessel wall.

Hydrogen peroxide generated during oxidative stress can push cells past a threshold into programmed death, and this pathway describes the braking mechanisms that keep them alive. It matters wherever cells face chronic oxidant load: cardiomyocytes after ischaemia, dopaminergic neurons, and tissues undergoing regeneration, where premature death would mean irreplaceable loss. Survival signalling through the hepatocyte growth factor receptor MET converges on AKT1 to suppress apoptotic commitment, while the scaffold RACK1 and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrain death machinery at the organelle. PARK7 and PINK1, both mutated in recessive parkinsonism, protect mitochondria from oxidative damage and support removal of damaged ones, linking failure of this protection to neurodegeneration. Several microRNAs, including miR-21 and members of the miR-17/92 and let-7 families, tune the same survival programmes post-transcriptionally, and carbonic anhydrase 3 contributes antioxidant buffering in muscle.

Hydrogen peroxide accumulating inside a cell can either be detoxified or read as a death signal, and this pathway covers the inputs that push the balance toward death, increasing the rate and extent of peroxide-triggered programmed cell death. It matters wherever oxidative stress decides cell fate: ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration, cardiomyocyte loss, and the removal of cells whose redox damage exceeds repair. The regulators involved act at different levels. FOXO3 is a stress-responsive transcription factor that drives pro-apoptotic and redox target genes, PAWR acts as a pro-apoptotic effector partner, and the mitochondrial nuclease endonuclease G is released to fragment nuclear DNA in a caspase-independent branch of cell death. A microRNA and a forkhead-family transcriptional repressor add post-transcriptional and transcriptional tuning, so sensitivity to peroxide is set by gene expression as much as by the oxidant burden itself.

Sperm only become motile after they leave the testis, and this pathway covers the signals and structural components that set how vigorously and in what pattern the flagellum beats. It matters for fertility: sperm that cannot switch from progressive swimming to the hyperactivated beating needed to penetrate the cumulus and zona will not fertilize an oocyte, and defects here produce asthenozoospermia. Several members are epididymal or seminal plasma proteins that coat the sperm surface and restrain or license motility, including EPPIN and the semenogelins that bind it, alongside ADAM7 and secreted RNase- and defensin-family proteins. Others are axonemal and flagellar: cilia- and flagella-associated proteins, a kinesin, a calcium-binding calaxin-type sensor, and TPPP2, linking calcium signalling and glycolytic ATP supply to dynein-driven bending. Tachykinin peptides and their receptors provide additional neuropeptide-like modulation of sperm and tract motility.

regulation of odontoblast differentiation controls how dental papilla mesenchymal cells commit to becoming odontoblasts, the polarized cells that secrete and mineralize dentin. Tooth shape, dentin thickness and pulp integrity all depend on the timing and extent of this commitment, and its disruption underlies dentin dysplasias, hypoplastic tooth defects and failed reparative dentin formation after injury. The genes trace the inductive dialogue between dental epithelium and mesenchyme: BMP2 and BMP4 act as the differentiating signals, MSX1 transduces them as a transcription factor whose loss causes tooth agenesis, and canonical Wnt output through beta-catenin with LEF1 sets the pace of odontogenic gene expression. mTOR signalling via RPTOR couples nutrient and growth cues to secretory maturation, while DSPP encodes the dentin matrix phosphoprotein that marks the terminally differentiated state. The pathway sits within craniofacial development and biomineralization.

Odontoblasts are the dentin-secreting cells that line the pulp chamber of the tooth, and this pathway covers the signals that promote or restrain their differentiation from dental papilla mesenchyme. Its output determines how much dentin is laid down during tooth formation and whether reparative dentin can be made after injury or caries; disruption gives hypoplastic or malformed dentin, as seen with mutations in DSPP, the dentin sialophosphoprotein that is both the principal non-collagenous matrix product and a marker of the differentiated state. Control is largely transcriptional and instructive from the epithelium: BMP2 and BMP4 ligands, canonical WNT signalling through CTNNB1 with LEF1, and homeobox and bZIP factors such as MSX1 and CEBPB converge on the odontoblast gene programme, with mTOR-associated RPTOR linking nutrient and growth-factor status to secretory maturation.

Lactone metabolic process covers the handling of cyclic esters in human tissues, including their hydrolysis by serum and cellular lactonases and the redox chemistry of ascorbate, a lactone itself. It matters for detoxification of oxidised lipid species and xenobiotics, for quorum-sensing signal breakdown at host surfaces, and for maintaining vitamin C supply to collagen hydroxylases and antioxidant defence. The paraoxonase family provides the hydrolytic activity, PON1 riding on HDL where it limits lipoprotein oxidation and is linked to atherosclerosis risk, while PON2 acts intracellularly. Ascorbate transport by SLC23A1 and SLC23A2, dehydroascorbate uptake through glucose carriers, and recycling by glutathione-dependent omega-class transferases and glutamate-cysteine ligase connect this chemistry to thiol redox balance and to oxidative protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum.

Lactones are cyclic esters that arise from drugs, dietary plant compounds, bacterial signalling molecules and oxidative damage to lipids, and this pathway covers their handling — hydrolysis of the ring and the redox chemistry that accompanies it. The paraoxonase family provides the lactonase activity, with PON1 in plasma associated with HDL and linked to organophosphate detoxification and atherosclerosis risk, while PON2 acts intracellularly and can degrade bacterial quorum-sensing lactones. Glutathione supply and transfer enzymes, including the catalytic subunit of glutamate–cysteine ligase and omega-class glutathione transferases, support the thiol-dependent steps, and ascorbate handling appears through vitamin C transporters and the glucose carriers that import its oxidized lactone form, dehydroascorbate. Together these activities connect xenobiotic disposal to cellular antioxidant defence.

When endoplasmic reticulum calcium stores are depleted, cells refill them by opening plasma membrane channels, and this pathway tunes how strongly and how long that store-operated calcium entry runs. The output matters for sustained calcium signalling in lymphocyte activation, mast cell degranulation, muscle function and secretion; loss of control produces immunodeficiency or myopathy on one side and inappropriate calcium overload on the other. The ER sensors STIM1 and STIM2 detect falling luminal calcium through their EF-hand domains, oligomerise, and migrate to junctions with the plasma membrane to gate Orai channels, with STIM2 responding to smaller drops than STIM1. Accessory factors modulate this coupling: CRACR2A stabilises the STIM1-Orai1 complex in a calcium-dependent manner, STIMATE promotes STIM1 conformational activation, and luminal calcium-binding proteins such as calsequestrin and ASPH set the store content that is being sensed.

Blood and lymphatic vessels are built and remodelled under tight positive and negative control, and this set captures the regulators that set how much vasculature forms, where, and when. The balance matters for embryonic vessel patterning, wound healing, the menstrual cycle and placentation, and its loss underlies tumour angiogenesis, diabetic retinopathy, vascular malformations and ischaemic disease. Pro-angiogenic ligand-receptor pairs such as VEGFA with KDR and FLT1, angiopoietins with TEK and TIE1, and hypoxia sensing through HIF1A and EGLN1 drive endothelial sprouting, while thrombospondins, VASH1, SERPINF1 and RECK restrain it. TGF-beta and BMP9 signalling through ENG, ACVRL1 and SMAD1 controls vessel maturation, mutations in which cause hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and KRIT1, CCM2 and PDCD10 maintain junctional integrity. Inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, guidance cues and a large complement of microRNAs tune the output.

Blood vessel growth is held in check as actively as it is driven, and the brakes on vasculature development set when and where new capillaries are allowed to form. Their loss permits pathological neovascularisation in tumours, diabetic retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration, while excess suppression impairs wound healing and collateral formation after ischaemia. Secreted inhibitors such as thrombospondins, pigment epithelium-derived factor, decorin and endostatin-bearing basement membrane collagens act on endothelial cells to limit migration, proliferation and survival; angiopoietin-2 and the TIE receptors destabilise nascent vessels; brain-specific angiogenesis inhibitors and class 3-6 semaphorins deliver repulsive guidance cues. Interferon-inducible chemokines and cytokines contribute an immune arm, and shear-responsive factors including KLF2 and KLF4 favour quiescent, claudin-5-sealed endothelium. A large complement of microRNAs tunes these outputs post-transcriptionally, making antiangiogenic control as much a matter of transcript-level dosage as of ligand availability.

Rapamycin blocks the mTOR kinase, and the cellular response to that drug is the set of changes cells make when mTOR signalling is suppressed: translation of growth-related messages falls, autophagy and lysosomal catabolism rise, and proliferation slows. This is the basis for rapamycin's use as an immunosuppressant, a coronary stent coating, and an anti-tumour agent, and for its effects on lifespan in model organisms. Among the genes here, LARP1 binds the 5' cap region of mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins and translates mTOR activity into their selective repression, AKT1 lies upstream as an activator of mTOR-dependent growth signalling, and FOXP3 marks the regulatory T cells whose expansion rapamycin favours over conventional T cell proliferation. Others report on downstream membrane traffic and lysosomal lipid handling, the compartment through which mTOR senses nutrient supply.

Acetylcholine is an acetate ester, and its movement across membranes — into secretory vesicles, out of cells, and back through plasma membrane carriers — is what this transport activity describes. Cholinergic transmission at neuromuscular junctions, autonomic ganglia and in the brain depends on it: without vesicular loading there is no quantal release, and cholinergic neurons lose their defining secretory capacity. The vesicular acetylcholine transporter SLC18A3 uses the proton gradient to concentrate acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles, and is co-expressed with the vesicular glutamate transporter SLC17A8 in terminals that release both messengers. Polyspecific organic cation carriers of the SLC22 family and the choline transporter-like protein SLC44A4 handle acetylcholine and related cations at the plasma membrane in neurons and epithelia. Receptors including the nicotinic subunit CHRNA3, an adenosine receptor and a tachykinin receptor place the transport step in the context of presynaptic modulation and downstream signalling.

Potassium flux across the plasma membrane sets resting potential, shapes action potential repolarization and controls cell volume and secretion, so it is tuned rather than left to the channels alone. This regulatory layer works largely through accessory and scaffolding proteins: KCNE subunits and KCNAB beta subunits alter gating and kinetics of KCNQ1 and Kv channels, KCNIP calcium sensors modulate A-type currents, DPP6 and DPP10 modify surface expression, and KCNS and KCNG subunits act as electrically silent partners that suppress or shift Kv activity. Anchoring by ankyrins, filamin, caveolins and AKAPs localizes channels and couples them to kinase signalling, while NEDD4/NEDD4L and WWP2 ubiquitin ligases and WNK-OXSR1/STK39 kinases set channel abundance and are central to renal potassium handling. Miscalibration produces long QT and other arrhythmia syndromes, altered excitability and potassium-wasting or retaining phenotypes.

Potassium channels set resting potential and shape how quickly excitable cells repolarise, so processes that damp potassium flux across the membrane are a way of tuning electrical excitability rather than merely shutting a pore. Negative regulation of potassium ion transmembrane transport here operates at several levels: accessory KCNE subunits modify the gating and current amplitude of partner channels such as the cardiac KCNQ1 and KCNH2 conductances; ubiquitin ligases of the NEDD4 family and WWP2 target channel proteins for internalisation and degradation, reducing surface density; scaffolding and membrane-organising proteins including ANK3, BIN1 and caveolins control where channels sit and how much current a given microdomain carries; and kinases of the WNK-activated OXSR1/STK39 module with CAB39 impose inhibitory phosphorylation. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional dampening. Loss of this restraint distorts repolarisation, as seen in inherited long QT and other arrhythmia syndromes.

Potassium flow across the plasma membrane sets resting potential and shapes the repolarising phase of action potentials, and this collection covers the influences that increase that flow. Rather than the channels alone, much of it is accessory and scaffolding protein: KCNE1 and KCNE5 subunits that modify KCNQ1 gating, KCNIP2 which confers rapid transient currents, AKAP anchoring proteins that position kinases near their channel substrates, and ankyrin-B and filamin that place channels correctly in the membrane. The cardiac emphasis is strong, with KCNH2 and KCNQ1 carrying the delayed rectifier currents whose loss produces long QT syndrome and arrhythmia, alongside Na/K-ATPase beta subunits that maintain the gradient being used. Neuronal Kv3 channels supporting fast-spiking firing and calcium-activated KCNN4 broaden the reach to excitability and volume regulation more generally.

Voltage-gated calcium channels convert membrane depolarization into calcium entry, and the processes that tune their opening, inactivation and surface density set how much calcium a cell admits per electrical event. This regulation shapes neurotransmitter release, excitation contraction coupling in muscle, and hormone secretion, so its failure produces disorders of excitability and contractility. Auxiliary beta subunits such as CACNB3 bind the pore-forming alpha1 subunit to control trafficking and gating kinetics, while CBARP acts on beta subunit function; STAC adaptor proteins couple channels to downstream machinery, and STAC3 mutations cause a congenital myopathy by disrupting skeletal muscle coupling. Calmodulin and the neuronal calcium sensor hippocalcin provide calcium-dependent feedback onto channel activity, and receptors including CRHR1 and GPR35 modulate currents through G protein signalling. CACNA1F itself is the retinal L-type channel mutated in congenital stationary night blindness.

Voltage-gated calcium channels convert membrane depolarisation into calcium entry that drives neurotransmitter release, muscle contraction and activity-dependent gene expression, and this influx must be damped as well as triggered. Negative regulation of these channels sets how much calcium a cell admits per electrical event, protecting against excitotoxic overload and shaping synaptic strength and excitability. The mechanisms represented here are varied: calmodulin bound to the channel's carboxy terminus mediates calcium-dependent inactivation, a feedback loop in which the permeating ion terminates its own entry; CBARP acts on the auxiliary beta subunit to restrain channel availability; G protein-coupled receptors including CRHR1 and GPR35 signal to reduce channel opening; and the RNA-binding protein FMR1, lost in fragile X syndrome, limits channel abundance and presynaptic calcium influx. Loss of such braking contributes to neuronal hyperexcitability and, for CACNA1F mutations, to retinal signalling disease.

Voltage-gated calcium channels convert membrane depolarisation into a calcium signal, and this pathway covers the accessory proteins that increase their activity, trafficking and coupling to downstream events. The auxiliary beta subunit CACNB3 binds the pore-forming alpha1 subunit and promotes its delivery to the plasma membrane while shaping activation and inactivation gating. The STAC family adaptors bind the channel's cytoplasmic regions; STAC3 is required in skeletal muscle for excitation-contraction coupling, where the dihydropyridine receptor must trigger ryanodine receptor calcium release, and its mutation causes congenital myopathy with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. STAC and STAC2 act similarly on neuronal and muscle channels, slowing inactivation. Together these regulators set how much calcium enters in response to a given action potential, and so influence muscle contraction, neurotransmitter and hormone secretion, and calcium-dependent gene expression.

Tetrapyrroles "heme, and the intermediates leading to it" are made in a pathway that must be held in balance, because the porphyrin precursors are phototoxic and pro-oxidant when they accumulate and heme itself is damaging when free. This regulatory arm modulates the rate and extent of tetrapyrrole synthesis and turnover rather than catalysing the committed steps. Mitochondrial ABC transporters act at the compartment boundary: one supports export of iron-sulfur cluster intermediates needed for the cytosolic arm of iron handling, the other is required for normal erythroid heme production and protects against oxidative stress in maturing red cells. A glycine transporter supplies the amino acid substrate that condenses with succinyl-CoA at the first step. Loss of control here manifests as sideroblastic anaemia, porphyria-like precursor accumulation, and disturbed cellular iron sensing.

Lymphatic vessels drain interstitial fluid, absorb dietary lipid and carry immune cells to lymph nodes, and the growth of new lymphatics from existing ones is tuned by the factors collected here. Control of lymphangiogenesis determines whether tissue fluid balance is maintained: too little sprouting produces lymphoedema, while excess sprouting accompanies inflammation and provides a route for tumour cells to reach draining nodes. The central input is VEGFC acting on lymphatic endothelium, and CCBE1 is required for its proteolytic maturation into the fully active form, so loss of either causes generalised lymphatic dysplasia. VEGFA contributes an overlapping angiogenic signal, FOXC1 acts transcriptionally in lymphatic endothelial patterning and valve formation, EPHA2 provides guidance-receptor input, and vasohibin and a microRNA impose negative regulation. The set therefore spans growth factor availability, receptor signalling and transcriptional control of vessel morphogenesis.

ether catabolic process is the breakdown of ether-linked lipids, chiefly the potent signalling molecule platelet-activating factor and related oxidized phospholipids. Terminating platelet-activating factor signalling matters because this mediator drives platelet aggregation, neutrophil activation, vascular leak and bronchoconstriction; failure to degrade it sustains inflammation, and loss-of-function variants in the secreted plasma form are linked to asthma and cardiovascular risk. The catalytic step is hydrolysis of the sn-2 acetyl group to yield inactive lyso-PAF, performed by the intracellular acetylhydrolase catalytic subunits and by the lipoprotein-associated plasma enzyme, with a secreted group X phospholipase A2 acting on related substrates. The regulatory subunit of the intracellular complex doubles as LIS1, a dynein regulator required for neuronal migration, so this lipid-degrading machinery is also tied to cortical development and cytoskeletal transport.

Ether-linked lipids such as platelet-activating factor are potent signalling molecules, and their controlled breakdown is what limits how long and how widely they act. The ether catabolic process here is largely the destruction of PAF: acetylhydrolases remove the acetyl group at the sn-2 position to yield inactive lyso-PAF, terminating signalling through the PAF receptor and so damping platelet aggregation, neutrophil activation, vascular leak and bronchoconstriction. The secreted and plasma-associated phospholipases in this group circulate with lipoproteins and also hydrolyse oxidized phospholipids, linking the pathway to inflammation and atherosclerosis risk. The intracellular acetylhydrolase subunits have a second life in the cell: the regulatory subunit encoded by PAFAH1B1, better known as LIS1, governs dynein-dependent nuclear migration in the developing cortex, and its loss causes lissencephaly.

ether biosynthetic process builds the ether-linked lipids of membranes, chiefly plasmalogens, in which a fatty alcohol is attached to glycerol by an ether rather than an ester bond. These lipids are abundant in myelin, heart, and immune cells, contribute to membrane fluidity and antioxidant defence, and serve as precursors of platelet-activating factor; their loss underlies peroxisomal disorders such as rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with skeletal, ocular, and neurological damage. Synthesis begins in the peroxisome, where dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase form the ether bond using fatty alcohols supplied by FAR1, with PEX7 importing the enzymes; the ether lipid is then completed in the endoplasmic reticulum by desaturation and headgroup addition through PEDS1, SELENOI, and choline phosphotransferase. Phospholipase A2 activity releases the arachidonate and lyso-species that feed eicosanoid and PAF signalling.

Ether lipids carry an alkyl chain attached to glycerol by an ether rather than an ester bond, and their synthesis is what allows cells to make plasmalogens and platelet-activating factor. Plasmalogens are abundant in myelin, heart and sperm membranes, where they buffer oxidative stress and influence membrane fusion; loss of the peroxisomal steps causes rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with skeletal shortening, cataracts and severe neurological impairment. The committed reactions begin in peroxisomes, where GNPAT and the PEX7-imported AGPS build the ether bond onto a fatty alcohol supplied by FAR1, after which the intermediate moves to the endoplasmic reticulum for desaturation by PEDS1 and headgroup addition by enzymes such as SELENOI and CHPT1. The same backbone feeds inflammatory lipid signalling: phospholipase A2 release and LPCAT2 acetylation generate platelet-activating factor, linking this ether biosynthetic process to leukocyte activation.

Blood vessels form when endothelial cells align, hollow out and stabilise into patent tubes, and this pathway covers the signals that dial that tube-forming behaviour up or down. The balance matters for wound healing, placental and retinal vascular development, and the aberrant vessel growth of tumours and ischaemic tissue. Both positive and negative inputs appear here: fibroblast growth factor acts as a pro-angiogenic cue, the interferon-inducible chemokine CXCL10 opposes new vessel formation, a secreted metalloproteinase of the ADAMTS family remodels the surrounding matrix to permit or restrain sprouting, and a transcription factor of the forkhead family together with a microRNA sets the endothelial transcriptional state. Myeloid contributions are implied as well, consistent with infiltrating leukocytes and their secreted mediators shaping whether nascent endothelial cords mature into perfused lumens.

Eicosanoid signals such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes act locally and briefly, and their breakdown is what makes that brevity possible; icosanoid catabolism terminates the signal and limits inflammation, pain, fever, bronchoconstriction and vascular tone changes to the time and place they are needed. Several routes converge here. A prostaglandin dehydrogenase oxidises the 15-hydroxyl group of prostaglandins to inactive keto forms, setting tissue prostaglandin tone in gut, lung and placenta. Cytochrome P450 family 4 enzymes, including CYP4F2, CYP4F3 and CYP4A11, hydroxylate the omega terminus of leukotriene B4 and related fatty acid mediators, committing them to further degradation. Dipeptidases of the DPEP family cleave the cysteinyl-glycine bond of leukotriene D4 to yield leukotriene E4, while lysophospholipase and hydrolase activities act on related lipid esters. Loss of this catabolic capacity prolongs eicosanoid action and favours chronic inflammatory and proliferative states.

Blood formation depends on progenitors choosing whether to remain multipotent, expand, or commit to a lineage, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune the rate and extent of that commitment. It determines the output of the marrow across the erythroid, myeloid and lymphoid arms, so its disturbance produces cytopenias, lineage skewing or leukaemic transformation. Control is exerted at several levels: lineage transcription factors such as MYB and SPI1 set commitment, Notch signalling with its HES effectors and the KITLG and OSM cytokine axes relay niche cues, CDK6 links progenitor cycling to differentiation timing, and the m6A methyltransferases METTL3 and METTL14 with the reader YTHDF2 regulate the stability of transcripts that keep stem and progenitor identity. Chromatin and signalling components including SETD1A, KAT5, ABL1 and the SOS1/SOS2 exchange factors act as additional modifiers of progenitor fate.

Blood formation depends as much on holding progenitors back as on pushing them forward, and this pathway covers the brakes: processes that block or slow the differentiation of hematopoietic progenitor cells so that a self-renewing pool is preserved rather than exhausted in a single wave of output. Notch signalling and its Hes-family transcriptional repressors keep progenitors undifferentiated, while MYB sustains progenitor proliferation and immaturity; loss of such restraint drives premature differentiation and marrow failure, whereas excessive restraint contributes to leukemic blockade of maturation. Contributions come from chromatin-associated and RNA-level regulators as well, including a BAF complex subunit and the m6A methyltransferase component METTL14, alongside stress-responsive and mesodermal patterning factors. The biology sits at the interface of stem cell maintenance, lineage commitment timing, and the transcriptional control of definitive hematopoiesis.

Blood cell production depends on progenitors leaving their uncommitted state on cue, and this is the regulatory arm that drives them to do so, increasing the rate and extent of hematopoietic progenitor cell differentiation. Too little of this push leaves progenitors stalled or self-renewing, with cytopenias and failed lineage output; too much exhausts the stem cell pool. The genes here act at several levels: KITLG is the stem cell factor ligand for the KIT receptor and is the classic extrinsic signal supporting progenitor survival and expansion, while FOXC1 and ZBTB1 are transcriptional regulators, the latter required for lymphoid development. Others act on RNA and chromatin, including a DEAH-box helicase resolving G-quadruplex structures, a subunit of the cleavage factor that selects polyadenylation sites, and a component of chromatin-remodelling complexes. Together they link niche signalling to the transcriptional commitment of blood lineages.

Blood vessels are lined by a continuous endothelium whose maturation and barrier character must be tuned to the needs of the surrounding tissue, and this pathway covers the inputs that set the pace and extent of endothelial cell development. What emerges from it is a monolayer that controls permeability, leukocyte passage and vessel stability; when the controls fail, the result is leak, oedema and the endothelial dysfunction that accompanies sepsis and chronic inflammation. Junctional proteins such as VE-cadherin, claudin-5 and JAM-A build and seal cell-cell contacts, while vinculin, adducin and myosin phosphatase link them to the actin cytoskeleton whose tension ROCK1 and ROCK2 raise. VEGFA drives endothelial specification and growth, sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors and activated protein C favour barrier integrity, and TNF and IL-1B acting through their receptors and IKK-dependent NF- cappaB signalling push the endothelium toward an activated, permeable state.

Endothelial cells acquire their mature identity by building the cell-cell junctions that make a vessel wall a selective barrier, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote that maturation. It matters for vascular integrity: without it, vessels leak, oedema follows, and in the brain the blood-brain barrier fails. The genes converge on the junctional apparatus itself — VE-cadherin as the endothelium-specific adherens junction cadherin, claudin-5 as the tight junction protein that restricts paracellular passage in brain microvessels, and JAM-A contributing to junction assembly and polarity — with adducin linking membrane complexes to the spectrin-actin cytoskeleton. Extracellular cues feed in through sphingosine-1-phosphate signalling and through protein C, an anticoagulant zymogen whose activated form also signals to endothelium to stabilise barrier function, tying vessel maturation to the control of coagulation and inflammation.

Camptothecin traps topoisomerase I on DNA, converting normal replication into collapsed forks and single-ended double-strand breaks, so the cellular response to camptothecin is essentially a homologous recombination and fork-restart programme. It matters because it defines how proliferating cells survive this class of drug, and it underlies the clinical activity of topoisomerase I poisons such as irinotecan and topotecan. The genes here center on recombination control: the RAD51 recombinase performs strand invasion, the BLM helicase and its partner SPIDR act together on recombination intermediates and stalled forks, RECQL5 restrains inappropriate RAD51 filament activity and helps resolve transcription-replication conflicts, and neddylation contributes to the ubiquitin-like signalling that governs repair factor turnover at damage sites. Loss of these activities gives hypersensitivity to camptothecin, chromosomal instability and, for BLM, a cancer-predisposing genome instability syndrome.

fatty acid derivative metabolic process covers the enzymatic conversion of fatty acids into the activated, elongated, oxygenated and esterified forms that cells actually use, rather than the core beta-oxidation of fat for fuel. It supplies the very-long-chain and ether lipids of myelin and skin barrier, the wax and diacylglycerol esters of sebum, the ketone bodies that sustain brain and heart during fasting, and the eicosanoid mediators of inflammation. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and transporters activate substrates; ELOVL enzymes with the HACD/TECR reductase steps extend chains; lipoxygenases and CYP4 omega-hydroxylases oxidise them to leukotrienes and hydroxy acids; HMGCS2 and OXCT1 run ketogenesis and ketolysis; DGAT and AWAT enzymes complete esterification. Loss of individual steps causes peroxisomal disease such as X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, ichthyosis and retinal degeneration, linking this metabolism to membrane structure, barrier function and immune signalling.

Fatty acids are rarely used as they are taken up; this metabolic programme converts them into the activated, elongated, oxygenated and esterified derivatives that cells actually need, and it links lipid supply to membrane composition, energy balance and lipid signalling. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and thioesterases set the pool of activated fatty acids, an elongation cycle built on ELOVL enzymes with HSD17B12, HACD and TECR extends chains for sphingolipids and very-long-chain lipids, and fatty acyl-CoA reductases feed ether lipid and wax ester synthesis alongside DGAT-dependent triglyceride formation. Lipoxygenases and CYP4 omega-hydroxylases generate eicosanoid and leukotriene derivatives, with gamma-glutamyl transferases and dipeptidases processing cysteinyl leukotrienes. Ketone body enzymes such as HMGCS2, HMGCL and OXCT1 handle the oxidative fate. Defects produce peroxisomal and very-long-chain lipid disorders, ichthyosis and inflammatory signalling imbalance.

Fatty acid derivatives "— acyl-CoA thioesters, ketone bodies, eicosanoids, leukotrienes and acylated lipids — must be degraded or inactivated once they have served their purpose, and this catabolic programme does that work. It terminates lipid signalling, recycles coenzyme A, and lets peripheral tissues burn ketone bodies for fuel. Thioesterases and nudix hydrolases cleave acyl-CoA species to free fatty acid plus CoA or to 3'-phosphoadenosine derivatives, setting the size of cellular acyl-CoA pools. Cytochrome P450 enzymes of the CYP4A and CYP4F families omega-hydroxylate fatty acids and inactivate leukotriene B4, while a prostaglandin dehydrogenase oxidises prostaglandins to inert keto forms and dipeptidases process leukotriene conjugates. A peroxisomal ABC transporter delivers very-long-chain substrates for beta-oxidation, and its loss causes adrenoleukodystrophy; ketolytic enzymes return acetoacetate to acetyl-CoA for oxidation in heart, brain and muscle.

Fatty acids are rarely used as they are made; this pathway covers the reactions that convert them into the derivatives cells actually deploy — activated acyl-CoA thioesters, elongated and very-long-chain acids, fatty alcohols, wax esters, oxygenated eicosanoid mediators and ketone bodies. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and transporter-like activating enzymes prime free fatty acids for every downstream fate, while the cytosolic synthase and the microsomal elongation cycle (condensation by ELOVL enzymes followed by reduction, dehydration and final reduction by TECR) extend chain length for membrane lipids, sphingolipids and retinal and skin barrier lipids. Fatty acyl reductases generate alcohols for ether lipid and wax ester synthesis, lipoxygenases initiate leukotriene and hydroxy-fatty-acid signalling in inflammation, and HMG-CoA synthase and lyase support hepatic ketogenesis during fasting. Loss of individual steps produces retinal degeneration, ichthyosis, neurodegeneration and defective inflammatory signalling.

This is the broad set of reactions by which cells synthesize, interconvert and degrade alpha-amino acids, feeding their carbon skeletons into the citric acid cycle and gluconeogenesis while disposing of the nitrogen as urea. It supports dietary protein utilization in liver and kidney, supplies precursors for neurotransmitters, polyamines, glutathione, nitric oxide, creatine and pigment, and links one-carbon and folate metabolism to methylation. Transaminases, dehydrogenases and dedicated catabolic routes handle individual amino acids: phenylalanine hydroxylase and the tyrosine degradation enzymes, branched-chain ketoacid pathway components, the glycine cleavage system, proline and serine biosynthetic enzymes, and the kynurenine branch of tryptophan breakdown toward NAD. Urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1 clear ammonia. Inherited defects here produce a large fraction of classical inborn errors of metabolism, including phenylketonuria, hyperammonaemia, homocystinuria and maple syrup urine disease.

Cells must make many of their own amino acids, and this pathway covers the biosynthetic routes that generate alpha-amino acids for protein synthesis, nitrogen handling and one-carbon metabolism. It supplies serine and glycine from glycolytic intermediates through PHGDH, PSAT1 and PSPH with interconversion by the folate-linked serine hydroxymethyltransferases, builds proline via glutamate reduction by P5C reductases, generates glutamine and glutamate through glutamine synthetase, glutaminases and glutamate dehydrogenase, and regenerates methionine from homocysteine using methionine synthase, betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase and the methionine salvage cycle. Arginine and ornithine synthesis overlaps the urea cycle enzymes CPS1, OTC, ASS1 and ASL, whose loss causes hyperammonaemia, while transaminases shuttle amino groups between carbon skeletons. Related reactions make selenocysteine and hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen. Defects underlie phenylketonuria, homocystinuria, serine-deficiency encephalopathy and urea cycle disorders, and serine biosynthesis is frequently amplified in tumours.

Regulation of lymphocyte chemotaxis controls how strongly and how far T, B and NK cells migrate toward chemical cues, setting the pace of immune surveillance, lymph node homing and the recruitment of effector cells into inflamed or tumour tissue. Too little and lymphoid tissue fails to organise or infection goes uncleared; too much and tissue is damaged by persistent infiltration, as in autoimmunity and graft rejection. The genes span both the signals and the machinery that tunes them: inflammatory and homeostatic chemokines such as CCL5, CCL21, CXCL13 and CXCL10 with receptors including CCR2, sheddases ADAM10 and ADAM17 that release surface ligands and receptors, and intracellular regulators of adhesion and cytoskeletal polarity including PTK2B, NEDD9, and the WNK1-OXSR1-STK39 module that couples cell volume and ion transport to motility. NK-activating receptor KLRK1 and TNFSF14 link cytotoxic recognition to directed movement.

Lymphocytes reach the tissues and lymphoid compartments where they are needed by following chemokine gradients, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the strength of that directed migration. It determines how efficiently T, B and NK cells enter lymph nodes, home to inflamed sites, or accumulate in tumours and autoimmune lesions.
