Secreted attractants dominate the list — CCL2, CCL3/4/5 and CCL7 acting on CCR2-type receptors, CCL21 guiding entry into lymphoid tissue, CXCL13 organising B cell zones, CXCL10 recruiting activated T cells, and XCL1 attracting dendritic partners. Intracellular control comes from the WNK1–OXSR1/STK39 kinase module, which restrains migration while coupling it to ion transport and cell volume, and from PTK2B and NEDD9 acting on adhesion and cytoskeletal turnover. Surface proteases ADAM10 and ADAM17 tune receptor and ligand availability by shedding, and TNFSF14 and WNT5A modify the surrounding stroma.

Synaptic strength depends on how many neurotransmitter receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane and how they are anchored there, and regulation of postsynaptic membrane organization is the control layer over that arrangement. It matters for learning-related plasticity, for the fidelity of neuromuscular transmission, and for the receptor scaffolds whose loss causes myasthenic and cognitive phenotypes. The genes involved act through distinct handles on the same problem: clustering of acetylcholine receptors beneath the nerve terminal at the neuromuscular junction, palmitoylation-dependent cycling of scaffold proteins between intracellular membranes and the synapse, actin and phosphatase-cofilin control of the cytoskeleton that shapes the spine, and small GTPase signalling that positions receptor complexes. APOE additionally links lipid handling and glial support to synapse maintenance, connecting this biology to synapse loss in neurodegeneration.

Neurotransmitter release depends on synaptic vesicles fusing with the presynaptic membrane at the right moment and no sooner, and this pathway covers the proteins that set the rate and extent of that fusion. It sits upstream of synaptic transmission itself: too little control gives spontaneous, untimed release, too much blocks evoked release, and either way information transfer across the synapse degrades. Synaptotagmins act as the calcium sensors that trigger fusion once an action potential raises presynaptic calcium, complexins clamp and then help activate the assembled SNARE complex, and Munc18-1 (STXBP1) chaperones syntaxin into fusion-competent assemblies. Rab3A with rabphilin and active-zone scaffolds position vesicles for release, while DOC2 proteins support calcium-dependent spontaneous fusion. Mutations here cause epileptic encephalopathies and paroxysmal movement disorders, as seen with STXBP1 and PRRT2.

Cells that cannot make purines and pyrimidines from scratch rely on salvage, and salvage begins with carrying nucleosides across the plasma membrane. This transport activity sets the intracellular supply of adenosine, uridine and their relatives, and with it the tone of adenosine receptor signalling in heart, vasculature and brain. Two families do the work: concentrative sodium-coupled carriers that drive nucleosides inward against a gradient, with distinct preferences for purine and pyrimidine substrates, and equilibrative carriers that move them down their concentration gradient at the cell surface or in intracellular membranes. A mitochondrial carrier for S-adenosylmethionine links the same solute logic to organellar methylation. These proteins are also the route by which nucleoside analogue drugs enter cells, so their expression shapes antiviral and chemotherapy response; loss of the lysosomal equivalent causes a histiocytosis-pigmentation syndrome.

Cells constantly adjust their behaviour to peptide signals arriving from outside — hormones, cytokines, chemokines, growth factors and neuropeptides — and this broad response programme covers the receptors, transducers and transcriptional outputs that convert such a stimulus into altered gene expression, secretion, motility or survival. Much of the content is immune: interleukins and their receptor chains, chemokines with their G protein-coupled receptors, interferons of all three classes, and tumour necrosis factor superfamily ligands and receptors, feeding into JAK–STAT, NF-κB, MAPK and inflammasome signalling with negative regulators such as SOCS proteins, NFKBIA and TNFAIP3 setting the limits. Metabolic and endocrine peptides are represented too, including leptin and its receptor, adiponectin, insulin-pathway adaptors, growth hormone, prolactin and vasopressin signalling. The same machinery underlies host defence, inflammatory tissue damage, haematopoiesis, bone remodelling and energy balance, and its dysregulation drives autoimmunity and chronic inflammation.

Cells adjust their behaviour when they encounter peptide hormones and other short peptide signals, and this response covers the downstream changes in gene expression, secretion, enzyme activity and ion flux that follow. It links endocrine and paracrine cues to concrete cellular outcomes: insulin-type signals converging on AKT1 to drive growth and metabolic adjustment, natriuretic peptides acting through the guanylyl cyclase receptor NPR2 to regulate vascular tone and to pace chondrocyte growth in the long bones, and calcium-sensing by CASR tuning parathyroid hormone release and renal calcium handling. Other members contribute effector steps rather than reception, including a chloride channel, a sphingomyelinase generating ceramide, a scaffolding protein of the actin cytoskeleton, a mitochondrial fission factor and an inhibitor of matrix metalloproteinases. Loss of such responsiveness underlies hormone resistance, skeletal dysplasia and disordered mineral homeostasis.

response to ketone collects the cellular and physiological programmes triggered by ketone-bearing signalling molecules and metabolites — most prominently steroid hormones such as progesterone, corticosteroids and androgens, along with prostaglandins and ketone bodies themselves. It matters because these compounds coordinate stress adaptation, salt and water balance, reproduction and fuel switching during fasting. The genes trace several arms of that response: nuclear receptors and their coactivators (NR3C1, AR, NR1H3, NCOA1/2) driving transcriptional output; aldosterone-responsive sodium handling in the kidney through the epithelial sodium channel subunits, SGK1 and SLC12A3; prostanoid G-protein-coupled receptors feeding adenylate cyclase and PKC cascades; and ketogenic and gluconeogenic enzymes such as HMGCS2, PCK1 and FBP1 acting with AMPK subunits, SIRT1 and uncoupling proteins to reset energy metabolism. Immediate-early factors including FOS and DUSP1 provide the rapid transcriptional wave, linking hormonal exposure to lasting changes in cell behaviour.

Cells and tissues adjust their transcriptional and metabolic programmes when exposed to ketone-containing compounds, a category that spans ketone bodies generated during fasting as well as steroid and prostanoid ligands built on ketone groups. This adaptive response links nutrient scarcity and hormone exposure to gene expression, and it underlies how liver, muscle, kidney and adipose tissue survive starvation or glucocorticoid and androgen signalling. The genes involved include ketogenic and gluconeogenic enzymes such as HMGCS2, PCK1 and FBP1, the energy sensor subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2, uncoupling proteins that dissipate mitochondrial proton gradients, and nuclear receptors including the glucocorticoid and androgen receptors with their coactivators. Downstream effects reach immediate-early transcription factors, prostaglandin receptors, epithelial sodium channel subunits and salt-handling transporters, so the response touches fuel selection, inflammation, and renal electrolyte balance. Its dysregulation accompanies diabetic ketoacidosis, muscle wasting and steroid-driven disease.

Cellular response to ketone covers how cells detect and react to ketone-bearing signalling molecules — glucocorticoids and other steroid ketones, prostaglandins, ketone bodies and related metabolites — and convert that exposure into changes in metabolism, gene expression and transport. It matters because these are the messengers of fasting, stress and inflammation: they redirect fuel use toward gluconeogenesis and fatty acid handling, restrain protein synthesis, and adjust salt and water balance in epithelia. Mechanistically the genes span receptor-proximal signalling through prostanoid receptors, adenylate cyclases and G protein subunits to CREB, ELK1 and FOS; nuclear receptor arms via the glucocorticoid and androgen receptors with SGK1 and epithelial sodium channel subunits; and an energy-sensing arm through AMPK subunits, SIRT1, FOXO3 and the atrophy ligase FBXO32. Failure of these responses underlies steroid resistance, disordered gluconeogenesis, and muscle wasting during catabolic stress.

Cells adjust their metabolism and gene expression when exposed to ketone-containing compounds, a class that spans ketone bodies produced during fasting, steroid hormones and ketone-bearing prostaglandins. This cellular response to ketone links nutrient and hormone sensing to transcriptional output: glucocorticoid and androgen receptors together with coactivators and steroid-modifying reductases translate steroid exposure into changes in gluconeogenic and muscle-atrophy programmes, evident in the presence of PCK1 and PCK2, FBP1, FBXO32 and myostatin. A second arm is prostanoid receptor signalling through heterotrimeric G proteins and multiple adenylate cyclase isoforms to cAMP, CREB1 and immediate-early factors such as FOS and ELK1. Energy-status kinases including AMPK subunits, AKT1, RPS6KB1 and SIRT1 couple the same stimuli to catabolic versus anabolic decisions, while epithelial sodium channel subunits and SGK1 tie corticosteroid response to salt and fluid handling. Failure of these responses underlies dysregulated glucose production, muscle wasting and inflammatory imbalance.

Glycosides — sugars joined to another moiety — must cross membranes on carriers rather than diffusing, and this transport activity covers that movement into, out of and between cells. It matters most in the intestine and kidney, where sodium-coupled glucose carriers SLC5A1 and SLC5A2 harvest dietary sugar and reclaim filtered glucose from the tubule; blocking the latter lowers blood glucose and is the basis of a widely used diabetes therapy. SLC50A1 exports sugar down its gradient, providing the efflux step that complements uptake. The ABC transporters ABCC2 and ABCC3 handle glucuronide and glutathione conjugates, moving glucuronidated drugs and bilirubin out of hepatocytes into bile or back into blood, so the pathway also determines how conjugated metabolites are cleared. Loss of ABCC2 function causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, linking this transport to both nutrient absorption and detoxification.

Breakdown of glycosyl compounds covers two related jobs: stripping sugars from glycoconjugates and cleaving the glycosidic bond that joins a sugar to a nucleobase. Both feed salvage and recycling rather than energy production. Lysosomal and cytosolic glycosidases such as glucocerebrosidase, alpha-galactosidase A, alpha-N-acetylgalactosaminidase and the alpha-L-fucosidases degrade glycolipid and glycoprotein sugars, and their loss causes lysosomal storage diseases including Gaucher and Fabry disease. In parallel, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, methylthioadenosine phosphorylase and the uridine phosphorylases release ribose or deoxyribose phosphate from nucleosides, handing the base to adenosine deaminase, guanine deaminase or xanthine dehydrogenase for further catabolism toward urate, while pyrimidine ring opening by dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and beta-ureidopropionase completes that branch. The pathway therefore links glycoconjugate turnover, nucleotide salvage, methionine recycling and the handling of nucleoside-analogue drugs.

Glycosyl compound biosynthetic process covers the reactions that build and interconvert nucleosides and related sugar-linked compounds, supplying the ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides that feed nucleotide pools for DNA replication, RNA synthesis and methyl-group metabolism. It matters because cells recycle purine and pyrimidine bases rather than making them anew: salvage kinases and phosphoribosyltransferases such as TK1, TK2, ADK, HPRT1 and APRT re-attach sugars or phosphates to free bases, while phosphorylases and deaminases including PNP, ADA and MTAP run the reverse, degradative direction and set the balance. Loss of individual steps has clear consequences, from immunodeficiency when adenosine or purine nucleoside catabolism fails to disturbed thymidine supply and mitochondrial DNA depletion. A distinct branch, the TYW enzymes with TRMT12, constructs the hypermodified wybutosine nucleoside in tRNA-Phe, linking this sugar chemistry to translational accuracy.

Glycosyl compound biosynthesis here is largely nucleoside and nucleotide chemistry: the salvage and interconversion reactions that build purine and pyrimidine ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides from free bases, sugar phosphates and recycled precursors. Salvage spares cells the cost of de novo synthesis and supplies the dNTP pools that replication and repair consume, which is why thymidine kinase and thymidylate kinase activity tracks proliferation and why loss of adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase causes severe combined immunodeficiency through toxic metabolite accumulation in lymphocytes. Hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency underlies Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, and MTAP loss is a common collateral deletion in cancer. A second arm builds the hypermodified nucleoside wybutosine on tRNA-Phe, a set of ribose- and base-modifying steps that maintain reading-frame fidelity during translation.

Quinones serve as mobile electron carriers and redox-active metabolites, and this pathway covers both their synthesis and their handling once formed. Its best-characterised output is coenzyme Q, built by a mitochondrial complex in which prenyl diphosphate synthase subunits PDSS1 and PDSS2 make the polyprenyl tail, COQ2 attaches it to a benzoquinone ring, and COQ3-COQ9 with the COQ8 kinase-like proteins carry out ring modification and assembly; electrons for hydroxylation steps come from the ferredoxin system. The product feeds the respiratory chain, pyrimidine synthesis and lipid antioxidant defence, and loss of these enzymes causes primary coenzyme Q deficiency with nephrotic syndrome, encephalomyopathy and ataxia. Separately, UBIAD1 makes vitamin K2 for gamma-carboxylation, while the quinone oxidoreductases NQO1, NQO2 and AIFM2 perform two-electron reduction that detoxifies reactive quinones and regenerates reduced forms used in membrane protection.

Quinone biosynthesis in human cells is dominated by the making of coenzyme Q, the lipid electron carrier that shuttles electrons from respiratory complexes I and II to complex III and also serves as the cofactor for pyrimidine synthesis and as a membrane antioxidant. Cells build it at the inner mitochondrial membrane: PDSS1 and PDSS2 make the polyprenyl tail, COQ2 attaches it to a hydroxybenzoate ring, and the COQ3-COQ9 proteins with the COQ8 kinase-like subunits carry out ring hydroxylation and methylation within a multisubunit assembly, with a ferredoxin/ferredoxin reductase pair supplying electrons. Loss of these steps causes primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, presenting as encephalomyopathy, steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome or ataxia, and often responding to supplementation. UBIAD1 extends the theme to non-mitochondrial prenylquinones, generating menaquinone-4 for vitamin K-dependent carboxylation.

Before a cell can divide accurately it must build a bipolar microtubule array, and the processes that tune mitotic spindle assembly set how fast and how faithfully that array forms. Getting this wrong produces multipolar or misoriented spindles, lagging chromosomes and aneuploidy, which is why several members are studied as mitotic drug targets. The ESCRT-III machinery is prominent here — the CHMP proteins with the VPS4B ATPase and the ALIX adaptor — linking membrane remodelling activity at the nuclear envelope and midbody to spindle organisation. PLK1 provides the master mitotic kinase input, RCC1 generates the chromatin-associated RanGTP gradient that releases spindle assembly factors near chromosomes, and CEP97 restrains centriole and cilium behaviour so centrosomes act as poles. Additional microtubule- and RNA-binding components, including EML3 and HNRNPU, contribute to spindle microtubule stability and chromosome alignment.

Iron in cells is mostly not free ion but iron bound within a coordinating molecule — heme, or a siderophore — and this pathway covers the carriers that move such iron coordination entities across membranes and between cells. It matters because heme is toxic when it escapes its proteins and precious when a cell needs it: erythroid precursors must export or import heme intermediates, macrophages must clear heme released by hemolysis, and enterocytes must salvage dietary folate and heme. Members include exporters and importers of heme and its porphyrin precursors, a transporter that releases heme from endosomes into the cytosol, mitochondrial carriers that link the organelle to cytosolic iron‑sulfur and heme synthesis, and the plasma‑ and receptor‑side handling of heme‑ and siderophore‑binding proteins such as hemopexin and lipocalin‑2. Loss of individual carriers causes anemia, neurodegeneration and posterior column ataxia, and folate malabsorption.

Nucleotide transmembrane transport moves nucleotides and nucleotide-derived cofactors across membranes that they cannot cross unaided, keeping each compartment supplied with the currency it needs. Mitochondria depend on it most visibly: adenine nucleotide translocases exchange ADP for newly made ATP across the inner membrane so that oxidative phosphorylation can power the cytosol, while related carriers import NAD+, FAD, folates, pyrimidine nucleotides and ATP-Mg/phosphate, sustaining mitochondrial DNA replication and redox balance. Other members serve secretion and signalling, including vesicular loading of ATP for purinergic transmission, ABC-type efflux of cyclic nucleotides, volume-regulated anion channels that release nucleotides and second messengers during cell swelling, and Golgi transporters supplying PAPS for sulfation. Loss of individual carriers causes mitochondrial myopathy, cardiomyopathy and progressive external ophthalmoplegia, linking this transport layer directly to energy metabolism, nucleotide salvage and extracellular signalling.

Nucleotides are charged, membrane-impermeant molecules, so their movement across membranes requires dedicated carriers, and this transmembrane transport determines where in the cell the energy currency and nucleotide cofactors are available. The largest contribution comes from mitochondrial carriers: the ADP/ATP translocases exchange cytosolic ADP for matrix ATP to complete oxidative phosphorylation, while relatives import NAD+, FAD, folate-linked and pyrimidine nucleotides or handle ATP-Mg/phosphate exchange, supplying the matrix with cofactors it cannot synthesise. Other members move nucleotide-sugar donors and PAPS into the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum for glycosylation and sulfation, load ATP into secretory vesicles for release as an extracellular purinergic signal, or export cyclic nucleotides and nucleotide analogues across the plasma membrane. Volume-regulated anion channels provide a further conduit for ATP efflux. Loss of these routes causes mitochondrial myopathy, cardiomyopathy and defects in glycosylation and nucleotide salvage.

Cells constantly adjust their behaviour to nitrogen-containing molecules in their environment — neurotransmitters, peptide hormones, amino acids, nucleotides, nitric oxide, ammonia and drugs — and this broad response programme collects the receptors, transducers and effectors that make those adjustments. It spans acetylcholine, dopamine, serotonin, histamine, glutamate, GABA and purinergic receptor families with their G protein, adenylate cyclase, phospholipase and kinase relays; insulin, leptin, growth hormone and interferon receptors feeding PI3K–AKT, mTOR and JAK–STAT; amino acid sensing through the mTORC1 machinery and CASTOR/SAMTOR; urea cycle and one-carbon enzymes handling nitrogen load; and ER stress and ERAD components responding to misfolded protein and redox challenge. Outputs include ion flux, secretion, metabolic reprogramming, immediate-early gene induction and apoptosis. Because it underlies synaptic transmission, endocrine control of glucose and appetite, and innate immune recognition of nucleic acids, its perturbation appears in diabetes, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease.

Cells constantly adjust their behaviour to nitrogen-containing molecules in their surroundings — amino acids, neurotransmitters, peptide hormones, purines and nucleotide-based signals — and this broad response programme collects the receptors, transducers and transcriptional outputs through which that adjustment happens. It underlies how tissues sense nutritional and endocrine state and how neurons and muscle react to chemical transmission, so its components determine insulin sensitivity, glucose production, synaptic excitability and growth control. Acetylcholine receptor subunits and dopamine, serotonin, histamine and glutamate receptors feed into G protein, adenylate cyclase and kinase cascades; insulin and IGF receptors act through IRS adaptors, PI3K and AKT; and amino acid sufficiency is relayed to mTOR by Sestrins, CASTOR and Rag proteins to set protein synthesis and autophagy. Nucleic acid sensing through cGAS–STING and RIG‑I‑like receptors, urea cycle and gluconeogenic enzymes, and transcription factors such as FOXO, CREB and NFE2L2 carry the downstream consequences.

This is a very broad stimulus-response category: the cellular and organismal reactions triggered by oxygen-containing chemicals, a class that spans reactive oxygen species and peroxides, steroid and retinoid hormones, prostaglandins and other lipid mediators, glucose and other sugars, nitric oxide derivatives, drugs and xenobiotic metabolites. Because so many signalling molecules contain oxygen, the genes collected here cut across endocrine, metabolic, immune and neuronal physiology. Recurrent themes include antioxidant defence and redox buffering through superoxide dismutases, catalase, peroxiredoxins, thioredoxin and NRF2-driven glutathione synthesis; nuclear receptor signalling by glucocorticoid, estrogen, androgen, retinoic acid, vitamin D and PPAR receptors; insulin and growth factor cascades feeding PI3K-AKT and mTOR; inflammatory sensing via Toll-like receptors, inflammasome components and cytokines; and transcriptional and microRNA programmes that adjust metabolism, proliferation and survival. Failure of these adaptive responses underlies oxidative-stress pathology, insulin resistance, chronic inflammation and neurodegeneration.

Cells continually adjust their behaviour to chemically diverse oxygen-containing signals — hormones and steroids, retinoids and vitamin D, prostanoids and other lipid mediators, glucose and other sugars, nucleotides, peroxides and reactive oxygen species, drugs and xenobiotics — and this collective response programme is how such stimuli are converted into altered secretion, metabolism, gene expression and growth. Its breadth is the point: receptor families spanning G-protein-coupled receptors, receptor tyrosine kinases such as the insulin and IGF1 receptors, ligand-gated channels and nuclear receptors including VDR, PPARs, RARA and the glucocorticoid receptor feed into shared kinase cascades (PI3K–AKT–mTOR, MAPK, PKA, PKC) and into transcription factors like NFE2L2, HIF1A, FOXO and NF-κB. Downstream outputs include antioxidant defence, inflammatory cytokine production, insulin-stimulated glucose uptake and apoptotic decisions, so miscalibration underlies metabolic disease, chronic inflammation and oxidative tissue injury.

regulation of cell proliferation involved in kidney development controls how many cells the developing kidney makes, and where, setting nephron number and the final size and architecture of the organ. Getting this wrong produces renal hypoplasia or dysplasia, reduced nephron endowment with lifelong hypertension risk, or persistent nephrogenic blastema that can give rise to Wilms tumour. The genes span the signals and transcription factors that balance progenitor expansion against differentiation: BMP4 and BMP7 gradients acting on the ureteric bud and cap mesenchyme, PDGF ligands driving mesangial and stromal cell proliferation, and the nuclear regulators WT1, PAX-partner GATA3, MYC and the stem-cell RNA-binding factor LIN28A, whose overexpression sustains proliferation and drives tumourigenesis. FLCN, CFLAR and IL6R link the process to growth-factor, survival and inflammatory inputs on nephron progenitors.

Kidney formation depends on tight control of how many cells each lineage makes and when they stop dividing, and this is the tuning of cell proliferation during renal development. Getting it wrong produces hypoplastic or dysplastic kidneys, reduced nephron endowment, and, when growth control fails outright, embryonal kidney tumours such as Wilms tumour. Bone morphogenetic proteins BMP4 and BMP7 act on the branching ureteric epithelium and the nephrogenic mesenchyme to balance proliferation against differentiation, while PDGF ligands drive expansion of mesangial and stromal populations that build the glomerulus and vasculature. Transcriptional regulators including WT1, GATA3, EGR1 and MYC set proliferative output in nephron progenitors, and LIN28A with miR-125a links progenitor self-renewal to developmental timing. FLCN and apoptotic modulators such as CFLAR further limit inappropriate growth, connecting this biology to organ size control and renal tumour suppression.

Kidney formation depends as much on stopping cell division at the right moment as on driving it: nephron progenitors must be restrained so that they differentiate into tubules and glomeruli rather than expanding indefinitely. This brake on proliferation during kidney development shapes branching of the ureteric bud, the size of the progenitor pool, and the timing of nephron induction, and its loss underlies both congenital renal malformations and childhood kidney tumours. Bone morphogenetic proteins signalling from the surrounding mesenchyme and epithelium limit progenitor expansion and promote differentiation, while the transcription factors WT1 and GATA3 enforce the differentiation programme in glomerular and ductal lineages. WT1 mutation causes Wilms tumour and glomerulosclerosis, and FLCN links growth-factor and nutrient signalling to renal epithelial growth control, with its failure producing renal cysts and tumours.

Kidney formation requires nephron progenitors and stromal, endothelial and mesangial populations to expand in number before and while they differentiate, and this pathway covers the signals that drive up proliferation during that growth. Too little expansion leaves a hypoplastic kidney with a reduced nephron endowment, a predisposition to hypertension and chronic kidney disease; unchecked progenitor proliferation instead underlies embryonal kidney tumours such as Wilms tumour. The genes point to growth factor and cytokine input acting through mitogenic transcription: platelet-derived growth factor ligands signal to mesangial and stromal cells during glomerular assembly, interleukin-6 receptor conveys cytokine signals, and MYC and EGR1 provide the immediate-early and proliferative transcriptional output. LIN28A links the same programme to developmental timing and progenitor self-renewal, while integrin beta-3 ties proliferative signalling to the extracellular matrix of the developing organ.</description

Platelet aggregation is the clumping of platelets to one another that seals a breach in the vessel wall, and this pathway covers the signals that push that process harder and faster. Its output is a haemostatic plug, and its excess is arterial thrombosis, so the same activating inputs that prevent bleeding also drive myocardial infarction and stroke. The genes span several kinds of trigger: collagen sensing through the platelet-specific receptor GP6, the podoplanin–CLEC-2 axis, serotonin acting on HTR2A to amplify recruitment, cathepsin G released from neutrophils, and interleukin-6 signalling through its receptor and JAK2, linking inflammation to a more aggregation-prone platelet. Extracellular matrix elastin-associated EMILIN proteins and multimerin contribute adhesive context, and the junctional adhesion molecule F11R supports stable platelet–platelet contact. Together these illustrate how vascular injury, inflammatory mediators and matrix cues converge on platelet activation.

Skeletal muscle fibres are multinucleated because myoblasts fuse with one another, and this pathway covers the signals that push that fusion forward during development, growth and repair after injury. Without it, regenerating muscle fails to build myotubes of adequate size and nuclear number, contributing to poor recovery and muscle wasting. The genes act at several levels: MYOD1 drives the myogenic differentiation programme that makes a myoblast fusion-competent, NFATC2 promotes the later recruitment of cells to nascent myotubes, and the p38 kinase MAPK14 relays stress and differentiation signals to muscle transcription factors. Membrane remodelling proteins of the EHD family and the calcium-dependent protease calpain-2 act at the plasma membrane and cytoskeleton where fusion occurs, while secreted chemokines and TNF-family ligands supply the inflammatory and cytokine context in which regenerating muscle recruits and merges cells.

Leukotriene D4 is one of the cysteinyl leukotrienes, the lipid mediators that constrict airway smooth muscle, drive mucus secretion and increase vascular permeability in asthma and allergic inflammation; it is the most potent agonist at the CysLT1 receptor and the step described here is what generates it. The reaction is not a new oxygenation but a cleavage: gamma-glutamyl transferase activity removes the glutamate residue from the glutathione conjugate leukotriene C4, leaving the cysteinylglycine adduct LTD4, which is subsequently trimmed to LTE4 by dipeptidases. GGT1 and GGT5 carry this activity on the cell surface of endothelium, epithelium and myeloid cells, so conversion happens extracellularly after LTC4 export. The same enzyme family handles general glutathione turnover and cysteine salvage, placing eicosanoid maturation alongside thiol metabolism and making these enzymes determinants of how long a leukotriene signal persists.

The p53 tumour suppressor decides whether a damaged or stressed cell arrests, repairs itself, senesces or dies, and this collection covers the inputs that tune how strongly and how long that decision signal runs. Because the strength of the response sets the boundary between tolerable damage and elimination, its regulators are among the most frequently altered genes in cancer. DNA damage kinases such as ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and CHEK2, together with HIPK2 and casein kinase 2, mark p53 for stabilisation, while MDM2 and MDM4 restrain it through ubiquitin-dependent turnover, opposed by deubiquitinases including USP7. Acetyltransferase, methyltransferase and demethylase activities, among them EP300, SIRT1, SMYD2 and KDM1A, write and erase modifications that reset target selectivity. A distinct ribosomal arm, in which free RPL5, RPL11 and RPL23 sequester MDM2, links defective ribosome biogenesis to the same checkpoint, and outputs such as PMAIP1 drive apoptosis.

p53 activity must be kept low in unstressed cells and switched off again once damage is repaired, and this is the braking arm of the pathway: the processes that stop or dampen signal transduction by the p53 class mediator. Without it, basal p53 output drives inappropriate cell cycle arrest, senescence and apoptosis, while excessive braking allows damaged cells to survive and is a common route to tumour formation when p53 itself is intact. The dominant mechanism is ubiquitin-dependent turnover and direct occlusion of the transactivation domain, with MDM2 and its partner MDM4 acting as the principal negative regulators, supported by additional E3 ligases such as RFFL and RNF34. Other inputs work through modification and chromatin: casein kinase 2 and DYRK-family kinases, the deacetylase SIRT1, the demethylase KDM1A, and TAF subunits that shape promoter responsiveness. Anti-apoptotic BCL2 and the transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 blunt p53 outputs further downstream.

p53 acts as the hub that converts cellular damage and stress into cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis, and this pathway covers the inputs that turn that signalling up. Its output decides whether a damaged or oncogene-stressed cell is allowed to divide, which is why the same circuitry is disabled in most cancers. DNA damage is relayed by the checkpoint kinases ATM and ATR together with the mediator 53BP1, while ribosomal proteins such as RPL11, RPL5-family members and RPS7 titrate away the MDM2 ubiquitin ligase when ribosome biogenesis is disrupted, stabilising p53. Other members supply tumour suppressor input through the CDKN2A locus and PML nuclear bodies, chromatin cofactors including ING4 and SMARCA4 assist transactivation, and targets like the BH3 protein NOXA and GADD34 carry the response into apoptosis and translational control.

Proteins condemned to the proteasome can be rescued, and this collection of brakes on proteasomal protein catabolism sets how long a substrate survives after it has been ubiquitinated. The outcome matters for the stability of tumour suppressors and oncoproteins, for the clearance of misfolded chaperone clients, and for muscle protein balance, where escape from degradation preserves mass. Several routes converge: deubiquitinases such as USP7, USP14, USP5, USP9X and UCHL5 strip ubiquitin chains before commitment, with USP14 acting at the proteasome itself; the inhibitor PSMF1 blocks substrate entry at the 20S gate; UFMylation components and UBX-domain cofactors modulate delivery through p97-associated routes; and chaperone-linked factors like BAG6 and SGTA triage hydrophobic clients away from destruction. Kinases and the O-GlcNAc transferase OGT tune these decisions, linking degradation control to nutrient and stress signalling.

Proteins destined for destruction must be marked, escorted and unfolded before the 26S proteasome can degrade them, and this pathway covers the factors that push that flux upward. Enhanced proteasomal turnover sets the half-life of cell cycle regulators, transcription factors and signalling intermediates, clears misfolded and mislocalized proteins, and its loss underlies the aggregate accumulation seen in neurodegeneration. The genes here act at several steps: cullin-RING and other E3 ligases such as MDM2, FBXW7, RBX1, KEAP1 and parkin select substrates; the anaphase-promoting complex activators CDC20 and FZR1 time mitotic degradation; kinases including GSK3B and casein kinase 1 create phosphodegrons that license ubiquitination; chaperone-linked cofactors such as STUB1, BAG6, VCP and the ubiquilins deliver clients from the cytosol and the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. ATPase subunits of the proteasome base and shuttle receptors complete the handoff, linking this activity to protein quality control, ER-associated degradation and cell cycle progression.

Ribosome production begins with RNA polymerase I transcribing the large rRNA precursor in the nucleolus, and the rate of that transcription sets how many ribosomes a cell can build. Control over this step couples growth signalling to biosynthetic capacity: nutrient and growth-factor input through mTOR raises rRNA output when conditions permit, while stress and nucleolar damage shut it down, and persistently elevated polymerase I activity is a hallmark of proliferating tumour cells. The genes here act as modulators rather than as the polymerase itself — nucleolin and other nucleolar factors organise the rDNA template and processing machinery, the deacetylase SIRT7 supports polymerase I output, chromatin remodelling subunits such as SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 alter rDNA accessibility, and macroH2A histone variants contribute to repressive chromatin. Nucleolar stress signalling through factors including NOL11 and NOP53 links failure of this programme to p53 activation and arrest of growth.

Ribosome production begins with RNA polymerase I transcribing the nucleolar large rRNA precursor, and the genes here push that step upward — increasing the rate and extent of 47S/45S pre-rRNA synthesis to match ribosome supply to growth demand. Because rRNA output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis, this control point links nutrient and growth-factor status to cell size and proliferation: mTOR signalling stimulates polymerase I activity, nucleolin acts on rDNA chromatin and nascent pre-rRNA, and NOL11 and PWP1 support nucleolar transcription and processing. Chromatin remodelling subunits SMARCA4 and SMARCB1 contribute through rDNA promoter accessibility, while PIH1D1 functions in an assembly chaperone complex that scaffolds polymerase I regulators. Excessive activity enlarges nucleoli and is characteristic of tumour cells, whereas insufficient output constrains growth and underlies ribosomopathy-like phenotypes, making polymerase I activation a target of anticancer strategies.

Cardiac muscle contracts as a unit because current spreads from cell to cell through gap junctions, and this pathway covers the processes that tune how strongly and how fast that electrical coupling propagates impulses through the myocardium. Setting the gain on conduction determines whether the atria and ventricles activate in an orderly sequence; when it is disturbed, conduction slows or becomes heterogeneous and re-entrant arrhythmias, bundle branch block and sudden death follow. Much of the regulation is calcium- and cyclic-nucleotide-dependent: calmodulin and CaMKII translate local calcium signals into changes in junctional and channel behaviour, triadin, sorcin and histidine-rich calcium-binding protein shape sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release, and a phosphodiesterase limits local cAMP. Transcription factors such as TBX5 and IRX3 specify the conduction system itself and the connexin repertoire of its cells, including the GJD3 junction protein.</description>

Nicotinate metabolism supplies and recycles the precursors from which cells build NAD, the electron carrier that every dehydrogenase in glycolysis and the TCA cycle depends on and the substrate consumed by NAD-degrading signalling enzymes. Because NAD is spent as well as used, salvage is continuous: NAMPT performs the rate-limiting step of the salvage route, nicotinamide riboside kinases phosphorylate the riboside form, and a mitochondrial carrier imports NAD into the matrix so that oxidative metabolism has its own pool. Consumption is represented by CD38 and by ADP-ribosyltransferases acting in stress and immune signalling, while NNMT methylates nicotinamide toward excretion and diverts flux away from NAD synthesis. The balance set here determines sirtuin activity, DNA damage responses and redox capacity; its decline accompanies ageing, metabolic disease and pellagra-like niacin deficiency.

Cells do not always run their respiratory chain at full capacity, and this collection of brakes on cellular respiration lowers oxidative flux when oxygen is scarce, when substrate supply shifts, or when mitochondria must be protected from damage. Restraining electron transport limits reactive oxygen production and spares oxygen, but sustained suppression pushes metabolism toward glycolysis instead, a switch exploited by hypoxic and tumour tissue. A hypoxia-induced microRNA and the alternative complex I subunit NDUFA4L2 dampen electron entry into the chain, the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 and DNAJC15 tune complex activity and import, and cyclophilin D (PPIF) sensitises the permeability transition pore that collapses the proton gradient outright. Inflammatory signalling through TNF and accumulation of alpha-synuclein also depress respiration, linking this regulation to hypoxic adaptation, inflammatory metabolic reprogramming and neurodegenerative mitochondrial dysfunction.

Cells raise their oxidative metabolism when demand or signalling calls for it, and positive regulation of cellular respiration covers the inputs that push mitochondrial substrate oxidation and electron transport upward. This matters for matching ATP supply to workload, for the metabolic reprogramming that accompanies immune activation, and for keeping neurons supplied with energy. The contributors here are heterogeneous: cytokine receptor components and interferon signalling shift oxidative capacity in activated cells, an interleukin acting on macrophage polarisation does the same, and a mitochondrial deacetylase tunes the activity of respiratory chain and TCA enzymes directly. Other members maintain the machinery rather than stimulate it, including a factor for iron-sulfur cluster assembly and the mitochondrial quality-control kinase whose loss causes parkinsonism. Together they place respiratory output under both immune and stress-responsive control, with failure contributing to neurodegeneration and mitochondrial disease.

regulation of mitochondrial DNA metabolic process controls how the mitochondrial genome is copied, repaired and turned over, setting the copy number and integrity of the DNA that encodes core respiratory chain subunits. Because each cell carries many mitochondrial genomes, this regulation determines whether damaged or mutant molecules accumulate to the threshold at which oxidative phosphorylation fails, as happens in mitochondrial myopathies, depletion syndromes and age-related decline in tissue energetics. The activities represented span nicking and degradation of mitochondrial DNA by an endonuclease, sealing of nicks during base excision repair by DNA ligase III, stabilisation of the single-stranded template at the replication fork by mitochondrial single-stranded DNA binding protein, and adenine methylation that marks the genome. Together these steps couple mitochondrial genome maintenance to nuclear signals, cell death execution and metabolic demand.

Mitochondria carry their own small genome, and its copy number and integrity must be actively managed because every respiratory chain complex depends on genes encoded there. This regulatory layer tunes how fast mitochondrial DNA is replicated, repaired and degraded, and its failure leads to depletion or mutation of the mitochondrial genome and the energy deficits that follow. The proteins involved act directly on mitochondrial nucleic acid: a single-stranded DNA-binding protein stabilises unwound replication intermediates, a DNA ligase seals nicks during replication and base excision repair, an endonuclease cleaves mitochondrial DNA during cell death and turnover, and a methyltransferase marks adenine in DNA. Together they place mitochondrial genome maintenance under control that is separate from the nuclear replication and repair machinery, linking it to organelle biogenesis and oxidative metabolism.

Muscle forms only where and when it should, and part of that control is active suppression: signals and factors that hold progenitors in an undifferentiated, proliferative state and restrain myotube formation. This braking arm of muscle tissue development keeps somitic and limb myogenic precursors expanding before differentiation, prevents premature or ectopic muscle in surrounding tissue, and its loss or persistence skews the balance between muscle growth, regeneration and wasting. Secreted cues from the bone morphogenetic protein, fibroblast growth factor and transforming growth factor beta families act on progenitors, while TWIST1 and SOX15 oppose the myogenic transcription programme and LEF1 couples Wnt input to it. IGFBP5 sequesters insulin-like growth factors that would otherwise drive hypertrophy, and SIRT2 and USP19 add deacetylase- and ubiquitin-dependent restraint, linking this control to satellite cell quiescence and muscle atrophy.

Proteins are switched on, tagged for destruction, or relocated by chemical marks added after synthesis, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how much of that marking happens. It matters because the same substrate can be stabilised or degraded depending on whether a ligase, a kinase or an eraser wins, and the balance determines cell cycle timing, NF-kB inflammatory output, hypoxia responses and protein quality control. Much of the membership concerns ubiquitination: E2 conjugating enzymes, cullin-RING ligases with their substrate adaptors and the deneddylating COP9 signalosome, anaphase-promoting complex activators such as CDC20 and FZR1, and deubiquitinases that reverse the mark. Alongside these sit SUMO conjugation and PIAS ligases, chaperone-linked triage through STUB1 and HSP90, and kinases and acetylation regulators. Loss of restraint here drives oncogenic stabilisation, neurodegeneration linked to PRKN and PINK1, and failed apoptotic and immune signalling.

negative regulation of post-translational protein modification collects the brakes on protein modification: the deubiquitinases, desumoylases, deacetylases, competitive inhibitors and decoy substrates that stop, reverse or slow the addition of chemical marks to proteins. Because modification marks set protein stability, localisation and activity, restraining the enzymes that write them is how cells keep signalling from becoming self-sustaining. Examples span several mark types — TNFAIP3 and USP4 removing or editing ubiquitin chains, SENP2 stripping SUMO, PIAS3 blocking STAT modification, HDAC8 and SIRT7 erasing acylation, and the mitotic checkpoint proteins MAD2L1 and FBXO5 holding the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until chromosomes align. Chaperone and autophagy adaptors such as BAG2, DNAJB2 and SQSTM1 act by shielding substrates from ligases. Loss of these constraints drives inflammatory NF-κB activation, chromosome missegregation and oncogenic stabilisation of substrates like β-catenin.

Post-translational modifications are reversible or blockable, and this pathway gathers the brakes: factors that prevent, slow or reverse the addition of ubiquitin, SUMO, ADP-ribose, phosphate, acetyl and sugar groups onto other proteins. Restraining modification matters because ubiquitin marks commit proteins to degradation, and premature or excessive tagging destabilises substrates that a cell still needs. Deubiquitinases such as USP4 and USP44, the SUMO protease SENP2, and the ubiquitin-editing enzyme TNFAIP3, which dampens NF-κB signalling, remove or trim existing marks. Others act by occlusion or by sequestering ligases and kinases: BAG and DNAJ co-chaperones, UBXN1, MAD2L1 restraint of the anaphase-promoting complex, and FBXO5 inhibition of that same ubiquitin ligase during mitosis. The theme links protein quality control, mitotic timing, inflammatory signalling and circadian feedback through PER2 and CRY1.

Proteins are switched on, tagged for destruction, or relocated by covalent marks added after synthesis, and this pathway covers the regulators that increase the rate and extent of that marking. Most of the machinery here drives ubiquitination and the related SUMO and NEDD8 conjugations: E2 enzymes such as UBE2N, UBE2D1 and UBE2S, cullin-RING components including RBX1 and CUL3, substrate-selecting F-box and BTB proteins such as FBXW7 and SKP2, the anaphase-promoting complex activators CDC20 and FZR1, IAP family ligases, SUMO ligases of the PIAS family and the SAE1-UBA2 activating enzyme, plus DCUN1D neddylation cofactors. The outputs are timed proteolysis in mitosis, NF-kB activation downstream of innate immune receptors such as NOD2 and TRAF6, Wnt pathway control through AXIN1 and GSK3, protein quality control at the ER, and mitophagy via PINK1 and parkin. Misregulation feeds into tumourigenesis, inflammation and neurodegeneration.

Cytoskeletal filaments are only as useful as their turnover, and this pathway covers the control of protein depolymerization — how quickly actin filaments and microtubules lose subunits from their ends or are severed along their length. Setting that rate determines cell shape, motility, the stability of sarcomeres and erythrocyte membrane skeletons, spindle and axonal architecture, and how fast a cell can remodel in response to signals. The members act largely as end-capping and stabilizing factors: tropomodulins and leiomodins cap actin minus ends, capping protein heterodimers and its CARMIL regulators cap plus ends, spectrins and adducins build the membrane-associated network, while cofilin, destrin, gelsolin and twinfilin promote severing and subunit loss and are themselves held in check by phosphorylation. On microtubules, CAMSAP2, CLASP proteins and the severing enzymes spastin and katanin components tune minus-end and lattice stability.

Filaments are not permanent structures, and this is the regulatory arm that drives their disassembly faster, promoting the breakdown of actin and microtubule polymers back into subunits. Accelerated depolymerization matters because it recycles the subunit pool for new assembly, allows lamellipodia to turn over during migration, lets a dividing cell resolve its cytoskeleton, and permits neurons to prune and remodel processes. Cofilins and destrin sever and disassemble actin filaments, with WDR1 acting as a cofactor that speeds their action, while PDXP dephosphorylates cofilin to relieve its inhibition; stathmin sequesters tubulin dimers, and spastin and the katanin regulatory subunit sever microtubules outright. Additional inputs come from capping-protein regulators and from receptor and channel signalling that raises severing activity. Loss of such control underlies axonopathies including hereditary spastic paraplegia and impairs cell motility and cytokinesis.

Cells attach to one another through tight junctions, adherens junctions, synapses and neuromuscular contacts, and this collection covers the signals that set how fast and how extensively those contacts are built or dismantled. The balance matters for epithelial barrier integrity, endothelial permeability, synapse number in the developing brain, and the loss of adhesion that accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumour invasion. Much of the control converges on Rho-family GTPases and their exchange factors and GAPs, which remodel actin at the nascent junction, with cadherin-catenin and tight-junction components such as CTNNB1, TJP1, F11R and claudins as the structural endpoint. A large synaptic arm is represented by neurexin-neuroligin pairs, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and ephrin receptors that induce and specify pre- and postsynaptic assembly, while Wnt, semaphorin, netrin and integrin-linked inputs, kinases and phosphatases tune adhesion strength in response to extracellular cues.

Cell junctions must be dismantled or held in check as often as they are built, and this collection of restraining activities limits the assembly of adherens junctions, tight junctions and synaptic contacts. The brake matters for epithelial barrier turnover, for leukocyte passage across endothelium, for cell migration and invasion, and for pruning inappropriate synapses. Inflammatory mediators such as TNF and IL1B, together with Toll-like receptor and NF-kB signalling components, loosen barriers during infection; SRC phosphorylates junctional cadherin complexes to destabilise them; ROCK1 and ROCK2 act downstream of Rho to reorganise the actomyosin that junctions depend on, while DLC1 and ARHGAP6 oppose Rho activity. Secreted cues including WNT5A, DKK1, THBS1 and SLIT-ROBO repel contact formation, and MMP14 proteolytically clears adhesive substrate. Loss of such restraint yields rigid, non-motile epithelia; excess drives barrier failure, oedema and tumour cell dissemination.

This grouping collects the signals and adhesion molecules that drive cell junction assembly upward, increasing how readily and extensively cells build stable contacts with each other. Two contexts dominate. One is synaptogenesis: neurexin and neuroligin partners, leucine-rich repeat transmembrane proteins, SLITRKs, calsyntenins, cerebellins and PTPRD act as trans-synaptic bridges that nucleate and mature pre- and postsynaptic specialisations, with neurotrophins and their TRK receptors supplying the growth signals; loss of these interactions underlies intellectual disability and autism-spectrum phenotypes. The other is epithelial and endothelial barrier formation, where claudins, CRB3, DLG5 and EPB41L5 shape tight junctions and polarity while VEGF, angiopoietin and TGF-beta family inputs, including ACVRL1 and SMAD3, stabilise vascular contacts. Rho-family GTPase signalling through RAC1, ROCK1 and actin regulators executes the cytoskeletal remodelling that lets a nascent contact become an organised junction.

Calcium pumped back into the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum by SERCA sets how fast a muscle relaxes and how much calcium is available for the next contraction, and this pathway covers the proteins that tune that pump's activity. The regulators are small transmembrane peptides that dock into the pump: phospholamban and sarcolipin restrain SERCA1-type activity and lower its calcium affinity until phosphorylation by beta-adrenergic signalling relieves the block, while a related micropeptide acts in the opposite direction to enhance uptake. Setting this balance determines cardiac and skeletal muscle relaxation kinetics and contractile reserve, and disturbed phospholamban regulation contributes to heart failure and inherited cardiomyopathy. Other members link pump control to endoplasmic reticulum membrane remodelling and autophagy and to innate immune signalling, placing reticular calcium load within broader control of organelle homeostasis.

Between beats the heart must actively relax, and how quickly it does so sets diastolic filling and therefore stroke volume. Regulation of cardiac muscle relaxation operates largely on calcium removal from the cytosol by the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump: phospholamban restrains that pump until it is phosphorylated, whereupon reuptake accelerates and the myocyte relaxes faster. The genes here define the signalling microdomain that controls this switch — an anchoring protein tethering kinases and phosphodiesterases to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cAMP-hydrolysing PDE4 isoforms that limit local protein kinase A activity, and CaMKIIδ as a calcium-dependent kinase acting on the same targets. Histidine-rich calcium-binding protein and chromogranin A contribute to luminal calcium handling and release. Disturbance of this balance produces diastolic dysfunction, heart failure with impaired relaxation, and arrhythmias arising from calcium leak.

Dense core granule transport moves the vesicles that store neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines from the soma, where they are made, to the axon terminals and dendritic sites where they are released. Neurons depend on it because dense core granules cannot be replenished locally; without long-range delivery, peptidergic and neuromodulatory transmission fails, and mutations in the kinesins involved cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-motor neuropathies. Transport is driven by kinesin-3 and kinesin-1 motors walking along axonal microtubules, whose polarity and organisation are set by microtubule-associated proteins such as MAP2 and the axon initial segment factor TRIM46. Scaffolds including liprin-α and TANC2 couple cargo to motors and to postsynaptic architecture, while the granule protein synaptotagmin-4 links delivery to regulated exocytosis. The pathway thus connects intracellular trafficking to synapse formation, plasticity and neuroendocrine secretion.

Neurons and neuroendocrine cells package neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines into dense core granules at the Golgi, but release sites lie far away at axon terminals and dendritic sites, so the granules must be actively hauled there. Dense core granule transport is that directed delivery step, and it sets where and how much peptide signalling a cell can perform; when it fails, cargo such as BDNF never reaches synapses and axonal trafficking deficits follow. Kinesin motors of the KIF1 family together with kinesin-1 heavy chains provide plus-end-directed movement along microtubules, while MAP2 and TRIM46 organise and bundle the microtubule tracks that define axonal versus dendritic routing. Adaptor and scaffold proteins including PPFIA2, TANC2 and the granule-associated synaptotagmin SYT4 couple motors to cargo and to release sites. Mutations in these motors cause hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-autonomic neuropathies.

At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, paired sister chromatids must be released from one another simultaneously and only once every kinetochore is properly attached; this pathway comprises the activities that license and accelerate that release. It matters because premature or delayed separation produces aneuploid daughter cells, the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours. The core event is activation of the anaphase-promoting complex with its coactivator CDC20, which together with the E2 enzyme UBE2C ubiquitinates securin and cyclin B for destruction, freeing the separase ESPL1 to cleave cohesin. Aurora B kinase with INCENP and survivin corrects faulty attachments from the inner centromere, the SKA complex stabilises kinetochore-microtubule contacts, and PLK1 contributes phosphorylation-dependent timing. Silencing of the spindle assembly checkpoint, involving MAD1L1 and the MAD2 disassembly factor MAD2L1BP, is what allows the signal to proceed.

Checkpoints hold the cell cycle in place until chromosomes are repaired and correctly attached, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly and how long those brakes are applied. Two arms are represented. One is the spindle assembly checkpoint, where the kinetochore-associated MAD1L1-MAD2L1 module, NDC80/KNL1 attachment components, the chromosomal passenger complex of AURKB, INCENP, BIRC5 and CDCA8, and silencing factors such as MAD2L1BP and the deubiquitinase USP44 set the threshold for anaphase onset and the timing of ubiquitin-dependent degradation. The other is the DNA damage response, with BRCA1-BARD1, BRCA2, RAD51 and XRCC3 coupling homologous recombination to arrest, ETAA1 and RPA2 activating signalling at stressed replication forks, and TTI1-TTI2-TELO2 stabilising the checkpoint kinases themselves. Loosening these controls permits division with unrepaired breaks or missegregating chromosomes, producing the aneuploidy and genomic instability characteristic of tumours.

Checkpoints halt division until damage is repaired or chromosomes are correctly attached, and this pathway covers the opposing activity that switches them off so the cell cycle can resume. Silencing a checkpoint is as consequential as raising one: without it cells arrest indefinitely, while premature silencing allows division with unattached kinetochores or unrepaired DNA and yields aneuploidy. The genes here act mainly at the spindle assembly checkpoint, where MAD2L1BP (p31comet) extracts Mad2 from the mitotic checkpoint complex to dismantle the signal, and the SKA1-SKA3 complex stabilises kinetochore-microtubule attachment so the checkpoint is satisfied; MAD1L1 also contributes to the timing of its turn-off. PPP1R10 and BRD4 link the process to phosphatase regulation and chromatin-based control of the DNA damage response. Together these activities set how quickly a cell exits arrest and commits to anaphase.

Cell cycle checkpoints halt division when chromosomes are not properly attached or DNA is damaged, and this is the set of activities that switch those brakes on or make them stronger. Most of the members reinforce the spindle assembly checkpoint: the chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B, survivin, borealin and INCENP senses tension at centromeres, the kinetochore components KNL1 and NDC80 recruit checkpoint proteins, and MAD1L1 with MAD2L1 sustain inhibition of the anaphase-promoting complex until attachment is correct. Cytoplasmic dynein subunits contribute by stripping checkpoint proteins from attached kinetochores and by nuclear envelope and spindle positioning. A second arm supports DNA damage signalling, including the TELO2-TTI1-TTI2 chaperone module that stabilises ATM and ATR and the recombination and resolution factors XRCC3 and GEN1. Loss of this reinforcement permits premature anaphase, chromosome missegregation and the aneuploidy typical of tumours.

Acetylation of lysines on histones and other proteins is a reversible mark that tunes transcription, DNA repair and metabolic enzyme activity, and this pathway covers the upstream inputs that set how much of it happens. Control is exerted on both sides of the balance: the acetyltransferase KAT5 acts within chromatin remodelling and damage-response complexes, while the NAD+-dependent deacetylase SIRT1 removes acetyl groups and links the reaction to cellular energy status. Additional regulators tie acetylation to physiological programmes — the circadian transcription factor BMAL1 to daily cycles of chromatin state, XBP1 to the unfolded protein response, and KLF15 to metabolic gene expression, while MAGE family proteins can modulate acetyltransferase availability. Because acetylation levels govern gene accessibility and protein stability, misregulation here contributes to metabolic disease, ageing phenotypes and tumour cell behaviour.

Acetylation of lysine residues on histones and other proteins tunes gene expression, protein stability and complex assembly, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of that modification rather than performing it directly. Upregulated acetylation of chromatin opens promoters to transcription, so the regulators here sit upstream of transcriptional programmes: the circadian transcription factor BMAL1 links acetylation to daily rhythms of metabolic and clock gene output, XBP1 connects it to the unfolded protein response and secretory capacity, and the DIP2 proteins act as partners that promote acetyltransferase activity. KAT5 is the catalytic acetyltransferase whose activity these signals enhance, modifying histones and participating in DNA damage responses. Loss of such positive control blunts inducible transcription and shifts the balance between acetylation and deacetylation that governs chromatin state.

Cells only commit to replicating DNA or segregating chromosomes when conditions permit, and regulation of cell cycle phase transition is the collected machinery that licenses or blocks those commitments. It sets proliferation rate in development and tissue renewal, and its failure produces genomic instability and cancer, which is why so many of its components are tumour suppressors and oncogenes. Cyclin-CDK pairs drive the G1/S and G2/M switches while CDK inhibitors of the p21/p27 and INK4 families, the RB-E2F axis, and phosphatase-kinase antagonism between CDC25 enzymes and WEE1/PKMYT1 restrain them. Damage and replication-stress checkpoints signalled through ATM, ATR, CHEK1/CHEK2 and p53 impose delay; the spindle assembly checkpoint holds MAD2 and BUB proteins over the anaphase-promoting complex until kinetochores attach. Ubiquitin ligases, the proteasome, chromatin remodelling complexes and numerous microRNAs make these transitions irreversible and tune their timing.

Cells advance from one cell cycle phase to the next only when positive regulators push them past discrete restriction points, and this collection of activators drives those transitions forward. Their combined action sets proliferation rate in development, tissue renewal and wound repair, and their overexpression is one of the commonest routes to unchecked tumour growth. Mechanistically, D- and E-type cyclins with CDK4 relieve RB1-imposed restraint on E2F-dependent transcription, CDC25 phosphatases dephosphorylate and activate CDK1 to license mitotic entry, and CCNB1-CDK1 with PLK1 executes it. Progression is then made irreversible by the anaphase-promoting complex and its activator CDC20, which target mitotic regulators for ubiquitin-dependent destruction, with UBE2C supplying the conjugating activity. Growth-factor and kinase inputs such as EGFR and AKT1, replication factors including CDC6 and ribonucleotide reductase subunits, and several microRNAs feed into the same decision.

Cells commit to division only at defined transition points, and the regulation of mitotic cell cycle phase transition is the collected machinery that decides whether each of those gates opens, stalls, or reverses. It keeps replication, chromosome segregation and exit from mitosis in order; when it fails, cells enter mitosis with damaged or unreplicated DNA and acquire the aneuploidy and unchecked proliferation typical of cancer, which is why so many of its components are tumour suppressors and oncogenes. Cyclin/CDK pairs drive the transitions, CDK inhibitors of the p21 and INK4 families restrain them, and Wee1/Myt1 kinases oppose CDC25 phosphatases to set CDK1 activity at the G2/M boundary. Damage sensing through ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and p53 imposes delays, while the spindle assembly checkpoint holds CDC20 and the anaphase-promoting complex inactive until kinetochores are attached, coupling ubiquitin-proteasome degradation to irreversible progression.

Cells that divide with damaged DNA, unreplicated chromosomes or unattached kinetochores produce aneuploid or mutated progeny, and the braking mechanisms collected here are what hold a mitotic cell cycle phase transition until conditions are safe. Two arms dominate. DNA damage and replication stress checkpoints run through the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, ATM and ATR with TOPBP1 and CLSPN, CHEK1, and p53-driven induction of the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, reinforced by RB1 family repression of E2F-dependent entry and by WEE1 and PKMYT1 phosphorylating CDK1 to keep it inactive. The spindle assembly checkpoint arm, built on MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1, BUB3 and the kinetochore NDC80 complex, sequesters CDC20 to delay anaphase-promoting complex activation until all chromosomes are attached. Numerous microRNAs add post-transcriptional restraint on cyclins. Loss of these controls underlies genomic instability and tumorigenesis, and the same machinery mediates senescence and damage-induced arrest.

Cells advance through mitosis only when specific transitions are licensed, and this pathway collects the activities that push those transitions forward -- entry into S phase, commitment to mitosis, and the metaphase-to-anaphase switch. Its output is proliferative capacity: the same activators are the drivers amplified or deregulated in cancer, where checkpoints are overridden and division continues without proper growth or repair signals. Mechanistically, D- and E-type cyclins with CDK4 and CDK1 phosphorylate substrates including RB1 to release E2F-dependent transcription, while CDC25 phosphatases remove inhibitory phosphates from mitotic CDK and PLK1 promotes mitotic entry. The anaphase-promoting complex with its activator CDC20, together with separase and UBE2C, destroys cyclin B and securin to trigger chromosome segregation. Growth-factor and mTOR inputs, several cullin-based ubiquitin ligases, and a set of microRNAs tune how readily each transition is made.

Meiosis proceeds through two rounds of division punctuated by arrests, and this regulatory biology controls when a cell is allowed to move from one meiotic phase to the next. It matters most in gametogenesis: oocytes must hold at prophase I, resume maturation on hormonal cue, then arrest again at metaphase II until fertilisation, and errors in these transitions produce aneuploid eggs and sperm. The core switch is cyclin-dependent kinase activity, raised by CDC25 phosphatases that remove inhibitory phosphates and opposed by the kinase PKMYT1, which places them. The MOS kinase drives the MAP kinase arm that sustains metaphase arrest, while spindle assembly checkpoint components including TTK, KNL1 and ZWINT delay anaphase until chromosomes attach correctly. Additional kinases and a checkpoint ubiquitin ligase tune the timing, linking damage and stress signals to meiotic progression.

Meiosis must be halted at defined points if gametes are to be made correctly, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that block or delay progression from one meiotic phase to the next. Oocytes rely on such arrest to wait for hormonal cues and to hold metaphase II until fertilisation, while spermatocytes depend on checkpoint delay to avoid segregating chromosomes that are not properly attached to the spindle. The genes here act through distinct brakes: an inhibitory kinase that phosphorylates and restrains CDK1 keeps cells out of M phase, a MAP kinase kinase kinase sustains cytostatic arrest, and kinetochore components including a checkpoint kinase and the KNL1 scaffold with its ZWINT partner signal unattached chromosomes to stall the division. Loss of these restraints permits premature division, producing aneuploid eggs and sperm and consequent infertility or pregnancy loss.

Fatty acids are largely insoluble and cannot simply diffuse to where they are burned or stored, so dedicated carriers move them across the plasma membrane and across the membranes of mitochondria and peroxisomes. This transmembrane transport sets how much lipid fuel a muscle or heart cell can oxidise and how much a hepatocyte or adipocyte takes up, and its failure produces recognisable disease: peroxisomal import defects in ABCD1 cause X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy with very-long-chain fatty acid accumulation, while defects in the carnitine shuttle formed by CPT1, the carnitine/acylcarnitine translocase and CPT2 cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy during fasting. Uptake at the cell surface involves the scavenger receptor CD36 and SLC27 family transporters working with acyl-CoA synthetases that trap incoming fatty acids as CoA esters. Insulin signalling through IRS2 and AKT tunes the whole process to nutritional state.

Amyloid-beta is released from the amyloid precursor protein by sequential secretase cleavage, and this pathway covers the influences that push that processing harder, raising peptide output. It matters because amyloid-beta accumulation into plaques is the initiating lesion of Alzheimer's disease, so factors that increase its formation are effectively risk factors for dementia. The genes here act at several levels: a gamma-secretase activating protein and a membrane trafficking adaptor determine how much precursor reaches the cleavage machinery; lipid transporters and the lipoprotein carriers apolipoprotein E and clusterin link cholesterol handling and amyloid production; inflammatory signalling through interferon-gamma, TNF and the NF-kB subunit RELA, together with transcriptional input from SP1, couples glial activation to increased processing. Kinases and an Eph receptor with its ephrin ligand add neuronal signalling control, tying synaptic activity and injury responses to amyloid burden.

Cilia are built only at the right time and place, and this pathway covers the controls that set whether a cell grows one, how fast, and how long it becomes. Ciliogenesis is licensed at the mother centriole, so much of the regulation is centriolar: distal-end capping proteins such as CP110 and CEP97 with the kinase KIF24 suppress axoneme extension until TTBK2 triggers their removal, while CEP120, CEP135 and CPAP govern centriole elongation and basal body competence. A large contingent of RAB GTPase regulators and RAB11/RAB8 effectors direct vesicle traffic to the ciliary base, feeding membrane and intraflagellar transport cargo (IFT20, IFT88, IFT140) into the growing organelle, with autophagy components and kinases including LRRK2, GSK3B and AKT1 tuning the response to serum and cell cycle cues. Loss of this control produces ciliopathies: retinal degeneration, cystic kidney disease, skeletal and left-right patterning defects.

Most cells build a primary cilium only when they exit the cycle, and the suppression of cilium assembly is how a cell keeps that antenna from forming at the wrong time. The programme matters because ciliation is coupled to quiescence and to Hedgehog-dependent patterning: losing the brake causes cilia on proliferating cells, while excessive braking blocks signalling reception and contributes to ciliopathy-like defects. Capping proteins at the distal centriole, notably CP110 with CEP97 and the kinesin KIF24, prevent axoneme extension until they are removed, and kinases such as MAK and CDK10 reinforce length control. Rab regulators and TBC-domain GTPase-activating proteins restrain vesicle delivery to the ciliary base, actin and microtubule regulators including LIMK2, TESK1 and LUZP1 oppose docking, and growth-factor and mechanotransduction inputs through AKT1 and YAP1 tie ciliation to proliferative state.

Cells that swim for a living — above all the sperm cell — depend on the beat of a motile cilium or flagellum, and this is the regulatory layer that sets how fast and in what pattern that beating occurs. Its output is sperm motility and hyperactivation, and therefore fertilization; loss of components produces asthenozoospermia and male infertility, while the ciliopathy proteins here link the same machinery to the broader syndromic consequences of dysfunctional cilia. Control runs through several routes: calcium entry via a sperm-specific cation channel and calaxin-type sensors, axonemal and flagellar accessory proteins that tune waveform and stability, tubulin polyglutamylation that modifies the axoneme itself, ciliary trafficking by the Bardet-Biedl body, and epididymal and seminal plasma factors such as eppin and semenogelins that hold motility in check until ejaculation. Tachykinin peptides and their receptors provide neuropeptide-mediated stimulation.

Lysine is an essential amino acid that cells must import for protein synthesis, and this transport activity moves it across the plasma membrane, out of lysosomes, and into mitochondria. The cationic amino acid transporters SLC7A1, SLC7A2 and SLC7A3 carry lysine together with arginine and ornithine across the cell surface in a sodium-independent manner, supplying arginine for nitric oxide synthesis as well as lysine for growth; SLC7A6 works as a heteromeric exchanger partnered with a heavy chain. SLC66A1 exports cationic amino acids from the lysosome after proteolysis, returning them to the cytosolic pool. The mitochondrial carriers SLC25A15 and SLC25A2 exchange ornithine and lysine across the inner membrane, linking this transport to the urea cycle, and loss of SLC25A15 causes hyperornithinaemia-hyperammonaemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome with hyperammonaemia and neurological impairment.

NADPH is the cell's main reducing currency for fatty acid and nucleotide synthesis and for regenerating glutathione and thioredoxin, so controlling how much of it is made sets the balance between biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Regulation of NADP metabolism operates largely by directing carbon toward the enzymes that reduce NADP+: the malic enzymes ME1 and ME2 decarboxylate malate to pyruvate with NADPH output, while TIGAR lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate to divert glucose from glycolysis into the pentose phosphate pathway. TP53 induces TIGAR as part of its metabolic and redox arm, and the mTORC1 components MTOR, RPTOR and MLST8 couple nutrient and growth-factor status to anabolic demand for reducing equivalents. Loss of this control leaves cells vulnerable to oxidative stress, and its subversion supports the reductive biosynthesis that proliferating tumour cells require.

Blood production over a lifetime depends on hematopoietic stem cells dividing only as much as demand requires, and this regulatory layer sets that rate. Too little proliferation exhausts the pool and produces marrow failure and cytopenias; too much drives stem cells out of quiescence toward premature exhaustion or clonal expansion, a step in leukaemogenesis. The controls act at several levels: thrombopoietin acts through its receptor as the dominant extrinsic cue supporting stem cell self-renewal as well as platelet production, the kinase PIM1 transmits pro-proliferative signals downstream of cytokine receptors, and microRNAs of the miR-221/222 pair restrain progenitor expansion by silencing target transcripts. Chromatin regulators such as the histone acetyltransferase KAT7 and transcriptional modulators including ATXN1L and TSC22D1 tune how progenitors read these cues, linking niche signalling to the balance between quiescence, self-renewal and differentiation.

Blood formation depends on a pool of hematopoietic stem cells that must decide, cell by cell, whether to stay undifferentiated or commit to a lineage; this set concerns the inputs that tune how fast and how far that commitment proceeds. Getting the balance wrong exhausts the stem cell pool, causing marrow failure and cytopenias, or blocks maturation and permits leukemic expansion. The regulators act at several levels: cytokine and kinase signalling through oncostatin M, ABL1 and CDK6 couples niche cues to cell cycle entry; chromatin and transcriptional control via SETD1A, KAT5 and FOXC1 sets lineage-priming gene expression; and RNA-based control through the m6A writer METTL3 with the reader YTHDF2, plus the tRNA modifier PUS7, adjusts translation and transcript stability so that self-renewal transcripts are cleared at the right moment. Ubiquitin ligase and chaperone activities add further checks on differentiation output.

Blood formation depends on a reservoir of hematopoietic stem cells that remain undifferentiated; negative regulation of hematopoietic stem cell differentiation is the braking side of that balance, restraining commitment to progenitor and lineage fates so that the stem cell pool is not exhausted by a single burst of output. Loss of this restraint depletes long-term repopulating cells, causing marrow failure and poor recovery after transplantation or cytotoxic injury, while excessive braking contributes to cytopenias and to the quiescence that shelters leukemic stem cells. The contributing activities are heterogeneous: transcriptional control, including a bHLH factor and a stress-responsive antioxidant regulator, a transcriptional corepressor-associated protein implicated in erythroid and myeloid commitment, a mitochondrial chaperone linking protein homeostasis to erythropoiesis, and an actin-sequestering peptide acting on cytoskeletal and niche cues. Together they tie stem cell fate decisions to redox state, metabolism, and signals from the bone marrow microenvironment.

Death receptors such as Fas, TRAIL receptors and TNFR1 kill cells from the outside in, and this pathway covers the controls that decide whether such a signal proceeds to caspase activation or is damped. Setting that threshold matters for immune contraction after infection, for deletion of autoreactive and virus-infected cells, and for the sensitivity of tumours to death-ligand therapy; loss of restraint drives tissue damage while excess restraint permits cells to survive signals that should eliminate them. The genes here act mostly at the receptor-proximal complex: CFLAR competes with caspase-8 recruitment, FAIM and FAIM2 blunt Fas-induced death, TNFAIP3 and ubiquitin ligases such as RFFL and RNF34 modify signalling components, PEA15 and MADD shape adaptor assembly, and BCL2L1 with PMAIP1 tune the mitochondrial amplification step.
