Kinases including GSK3B, RAF1 and the Hippo-related STK3/STK4 add further input.

Death receptors such as Fas and the TNF and TRAIL receptors carry a death domain that nucleates caspase-8 activation, and cells restrain that signal constantly so that immune surveillance, inflammation and tissue turnover do not kill bystander cells. This is the braking side of extrinsic apoptotic signalling: FLIP (CFLAR) occupies the death-inducing complex as a catalytically dead caspase-8 mimic, FAIM and FAIM2 raise the threshold for Fas-induced death in neurons and lymphocytes, ubiquitin ligases RFFL and RNF34 and the deubiquitinase A20 (TNFAIP3) tune receptor complex composition, and PEA15 and BCL2L1 block downstream commitment. Survival inputs from growth factors and kinases such as HGF and RAF1, along with redox buffering by HMOX1, GPX1 and PARK7, feed into the same decision. Excessive braking allows tumour cells to escape cytotoxic lymphocyte killing; too little produces hepatocyte and immune cell loss.

Death receptors such as Fas and TNFR1 kill cells from the outside in, and this grouping covers the influences that push that extrinsic, death-domain-dependent route toward commitment rather than restraining it. Enhancing it matters for clearing virus-infected and damaged cells, for immune contraction after a response, and for tumour suppression, since resistance to ligand-induced death is a common feature of malignant and autoimmune-prone cells. The members act at different levels: FAF1 associates with Fas and favours signalling complex assembly, MAL contributes to receptor partitioning in membrane microdomains, and the kinases STK3 and STK4 of the Hippo pathway relay apoptotic and stress input downstream. Others act indirectly, including the secreted matrix protein THBS1, the Wnt antagonist SFRP1, and transcriptional regulators such as ATF3, while PMAIP1 links the outcome to mitochondrial amplification of the death signal.

Fas (CD95) engagement by its ligand assembles a death-inducing complex that activates caspase-8 and kills the cell, and the strength of that signal has to be tuned rather than left to run — this is the control layer that raises or lowers how readily a cell dies through Fas. It matters most in the immune system, where Fas-driven apoptosis deletes activated lymphocytes after an immune response and enforces peripheral tolerance; too little killing permits lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, too much depletes lymphocytes. Survival cytokine input through interleukin-7 and its receptor, sharing the common gamma chain, opposes death receptor sensitivity, while microRNAs of the miR-23a cluster, transcriptional regulators such as SMAD5 and SP100, and post-translational control including palmitoylation by ZDHHC7 adjust receptor abundance, clustering and downstream coupling. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of cytokine-dependent survival and receptor-initiated apoptosis.

negative regulation of Fas signaling pathway describes the mechanisms that damp death receptor signalling through Fas/CD95, setting the threshold at which a cell commits to extrinsic apoptosis. This restraint matters most in lymphocytes, where Fas ligation is used to delete activated or autoreactive clones: too little Fas signalling permits lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, while unchecked signalling wastes cells needed for immune memory and tissue homeostasis. Survival cytokine input is one arm of the control, with interleukin-7 acting through its receptor and the shared gamma chain to sustain anti-apoptotic programmes in developing and resting T cells that oppose Fas-induced caspase-8 activation. Additional brakes come from transmembrane BAX inhibitor motif proteins that buffer death receptor and calcium-linked apoptotic signals, and from SMAD-mediated transcriptional regulation, linking receptor-driven cell death to growth factor and cytokine context.

Fas engagement by its ligand normally commits a cell to caspase-8-dependent apoptosis, and this pathway describes the brakes that hold that decision back, damping the frequency or extent of death receptor signalling. Restraint of Fas matters most in the immune system, where activated lymphocytes carry abundant Fas and would be deleted prematurely without survival input; unchecked Fas killing depletes T cell pools, while too much restraint permits autoreactive cells to persist. Interleukin-7 acting through its receptor and the shared common gamma chain provides exactly this kind of cytokine survival signal to developing and memory T cells, opposing apoptotic commitment. Other members contribute intracellular anti-apoptotic buffering, including a transmembrane BAX inhibitor motif protein that limits death signalling and calcium-linked stress. The biology sits at the junction of cytokine-dependent survival and extrinsic apoptosis, setting lymphocyte homeostasis and immune tolerance.

Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter in the mammalian brain, and this is the set of cellular responses a neuron mounts when it encounters it e2 e80 e94 from ion flux and membrane excitability changes through to altered gene expression and, at high doses, death. The immediate effectors here are ionotropic receptors such as the AMPA subunit GRIA1 and the NMDA subunit GRIN2D, whose calcium entry is shaped by the calcium sensor hippocalcin and by potassium and HCN channels that set firing properties. Downstream, the kinase FYN and the transcription factor CREB1 couple receptor activity to synaptic strengthening and transcriptional programmes underlying learning and memory. The same signalling, when excessive, drives excitotoxic injury in stroke and neurodegeneration, and participants including parkin, AIFM1 and TNF link glutamate exposure to mitochondrial stress, inflammation and cell fate decisions.

Cells and tissues adjust to changes in salt availability, and this response to salt stimulus collects the sensing and adaptive machinery that follows, spanning both sodium chloride handling and responses to mineral salts such as calcium and phosphate. Physiologically it underlies blood pressure regulation and renal electrolyte balance: the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter SLC12A3 reabsorbs salt in the distal tubule and is lost in Gitelman syndrome, while endothelin-1 acting through its receptor, natriuretic peptide receptor signalling and renalase shape vascular tone and natriuresis. A second arm concerns phosphate and mineralization, where FGF23, its receptor, the phosphate-regulating endopeptidase PHEX, alkaline phosphatase and RUNX2 govern bone and prevent ectopic calcification. Stress-responsive regulators including HSF1 and NFE2L2 couple osmotic and oxidative load to transcription. Dysregulation produces salt-sensitive hypertension, rickets, and vascular calcification.

cellular response to salt is the set of adjustments a cell makes when the ionic strength of its surroundings changes, as happens in the kidney medulla, in secretory epithelia, and in any tissue facing dehydration or hypertonic shock. Getting this right preserves cell volume, protein folding and genome integrity; failing it causes osmotic stress, aggregation of macromolecules, and death. The genes point to several arms of that response: HSF1 drives the heat shock transcriptional program that supplies chaperones when high salt destabilises proteins, the stress-activated kinase MAPK13 relays the osmotic signal, and HNRNPA1 together with the nuclear export factor XPO1 links tonicity to altered RNA processing and nucleocytoplasmic trafficking. DAXX and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A tie the response to apoptotic signalling and to the turnover of inflammatory transcripts, connecting osmotic stress to inflammation and cell fate decisions.

Cells exposed to high salt face osmotic stress that shrinks them, concentrates intracellular ions, damages DNA and destabilises proteins, and the cellular response to salt is the adaptive programme that follows. It matters most in tissues that routinely encounter steep solute gradients, such as the renal medulla, and in inflamed tissue where sodium accumulates and shapes immune cell behaviour. The response spans stress-activated kinase signalling through p38 family members, transcriptional reprogramming by heat shock factor 1 to bolster chaperone capacity, altered nucleocytoplasmic trafficking by exportin 1, and changes in mRNA stability and hnRNP-dependent RNA handling as transcripts are redistributed between nucleus and cytoplasm. Regulators of transcription and of inflammatory transcript decay link salt sensing to survival decisions and to cytokine output, so the same stimulus can drive either adaptation or apoptosis depending on severity and duration.

Regulation of calcium ion import into sarcoplasmic reticulum tunes how quickly muscle relaxes after a contraction and how much calcium is stored for the next beat. Cardiac output, skeletal muscle endurance, and the pace of relaxation all depend on it, and its failure contributes to heart failure, where blunted calcium reuptake leaves the cytosol loaded and the store depleted. The pathway centres on the SERCA pump, which drives calcium back across the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane at the cost of ATP, and on a family of small transmembrane micropeptides — phospholamban, sarcolipin, myoregulin and related regulins — that dock into the pump and inhibit it, each with its own muscle-type distribution. Phosphorylation of phospholamban downstream of beta-adrenergic signalling relieves that brake, linking sympathetic drive to faster relaxation, while sarcolipin uncoupling of the pump generates heat in non-shivering thermogenesis.

After each contraction, muscle relaxes only because calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the rate of that uptake sets both relaxation speed and the size of the store available for the next beat. Regulation of calcium import into this store is largely exerted on the SERCA pump, represented here by the fast-twitch skeletal isoform ATP2A1, through a family of small transmembrane peptides — phospholamban, sarcolipin, myoregulin and a related micropeptide — that bind the pump and lower its apparent calcium affinity. Their inhibition is relieved by β-adrenergic signalling and phosphorylation, which is how catecholamines accelerate cardiac relaxation and increase contractile force. Sarcolipin-dependent uncoupling of the pump also contributes to muscle-based thermogenesis. Disturbed control at this step underlies impaired relaxation and contractile failure in heart disease, and mutations in phospholamban cause inherited cardiomyopathy.

Chromosomes separate only once, and only after every kinetochore is attached, so the switch from metaphase to anaphase is tightly held shut until it is deliberately opened. Promoting that transition means overriding the spindle assembly checkpoint and licensing the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, whose subunits and the activator CDC20 dominate this group, together with the E2 enzyme UBE2C that charges it for ubiquitin transfer. Once active, the complex targets securin and mitotic cyclins for destruction, freeing separase (ESPL1) to cleave cohesin and allowing sister chromatids to move apart. Checkpoint silencing is helped by the MAD2-binding protein MAD2L1BP and by kinetochore-microtubule couplers of the SKA complex, while PLK1 contributes mitotic phosphorylation. Premature activation gives aneuploidy and chromosome missegregation; failure to activate leaves cells arrested in mitosis, the outcome exploited by antimitotic chemotherapy.

Blood cell lineages are specified from progenitors by tuning how strongly and in which direction differentiation proceeds, and the regulation of leukocyte differentiation covers the signals, transcription factors and chromatin machinery that set those decisions. It determines how many T helper subsets of each flavour arise, whether regulatory T cells are induced, how monocytes become macrophages or osteoclasts, and how B and myeloid output is balanced; failure produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or leukaemia. Cytokine receptor signalling through JAK3 and STAT5, antigen receptor signalling via LCK, ZAP70 and SYK, and costimulatory or inhibitory surface receptors including CD28, CTLA4 and LAG3 feed into lineage-defining factors such as SPI1, GATA3, TBX21, FOXP3, BCL6, RUNX1 and PRDM1. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, proteasome components, microRNAs and m6A methyltransferases add layers of epigenetic and post-transcriptional control, while RAG1 and RAG2 couple maturation to receptor gene assembly.

Cells commit to apoptosis when the mitochondrial outer membrane becomes permeable and releases cytochrome c and other intermembrane proteins, and this pathway covers the controls that decide whether that happens. It is the point of no return in the intrinsic death programme, so its setting determines whether damaged, virus-infected or growth-factor-deprived cells are eliminated or persist, and its failure underlies both tumour survival and excessive neuronal loss. The core machinery is the BCL-2 family: BAX, BAK1 and BOK oligomerise to form the pore, BH3-only proteins such as BID and BCL2L11 promote their activation, while BCL2L1 restrains them. Additional regulators include VDAC2 and MTCH2 at the outer membrane, the mitophagy receptors BNIP3 and BNIP3L, the ATP synthase inhibitory factor ATP5IF1, kinases such as GSK3B and LRRK2, and microRNAs of the miR-29 family that tune apoptotic thresholds.

Cells build and dismantle subcellular structures on demand, and this collection covers the control layer that sets how fast and how far organelle assembly proceeds. Several distinct structures are represented. One large arm governs centriole duplication and cilium formation — PLK4, SASS6, STIL, CEP135 and CEP120 with the intraflagellar transport components IFT88 and IFT20 — whose failure produces microcephaly, ciliopathies and disordered left-right patterning. A second arm builds the autophagosome, with ULK1, BECN1, ATG5 and WIPI proteins deciding when a membrane nucleates. A third comprises the ESCRT machinery and its CHMP subunits, which shape and sever membranes during multivesicular body formation and abscission. Threaded through all of them are many TBC-domain RAB GTPase-activating proteins and RAB GTPases that time membrane traffic, plus kinases such as MTOR, AMPK subunits and LRRK2 that couple assembly decisions to nutrient state, stress and cargo load.

Organelles are not built continuously, and the restraining half of that control is what negative regulation of organelle assembly describes: the processes that block, delay or limit construction of a structure until the cell is in the right state. Two branches dominate here. One suppresses cilium formation, keeping the centriolar distal end capped and the axoneme unbuilt in cycling cells — CCP110 with CEP97, KIF24, MPHOSPH9, LUZP1, TCHP and CDK5RAP2 act at the centrosome, and their loss produces inappropriate or elongated cilia. The other limits autophagosome biogenesis and related membrane assembly, where AKT1 phosphorylation of BECN1, SMCR8, TMEM39A, USP10 and the SEC22B/SCFD1 trafficking machinery set how much autophagic membrane is made. Because ciliogenesis must be coupled to cell cycle exit and autophagy to nutrient supply, these brakes matter for ciliopathies, proliferative signalling through YAP1 and SMAD4, and neurodegeneration linked to LRRK2 and PINK1.

Cells build organelles on demand, and this grouping covers the signals and factors that promote, accelerate or extend that assembly rather than carrying it out passively. Two programmes dominate the membership. One is centriole and cilium biogenesis: PLK4, SASS6, STIL, CEP135, CEP120 and CEP295 drive procentriole formation, TTBK2 and the intraflagellar transport proteins IFT20 and IFT88 license and extend the axoneme, and loss of these steps produces ciliopathies and mitotic spindle errors. The other is autophagosome formation, where ULK1, BECN1, ATG5, ATG2A and the PI3P-binding WIPI1 and WDR45 nucleate and expand the isolation membrane that delivers cargo for lysosomal degradation. Around them sit Rho-family regulators, sorting nexins, septins and stress granule components that couple cytoskeletal and membrane-trafficking cues to organelle construction, linking nutrient state and cell cycle progression to how many organelles a cell makes.

regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to DNA damage by p53 class mediator sets the threshold at which a cell with damaged DNA decides to kill itself rather than repair and continue. This decision determines whether genotoxic stress ends in tumour suppression or in the survival of a mutated clone, and its tuning explains much of why cancer cells resist chemotherapy and radiation. The genes act on p53 itself and on the mitochondrial step it commands: acetylation-dependent control through SIRT1 and KDM1A, cofactor and coactivator input via TAF9 and ZNF385A, translational amplification of p53 by RPL26 and HNRNPK, and direct restraint of mitochondrial permeabilisation by BCL2 and TRIAP1. Others, including MIF, CD74, MUC1 and CD44, dampen the response in a way that favours survival. The pathway therefore sits where DNA damage checkpoints hand over to the mitochondrial apoptotic machinery.

When DNA damage is severe enough that repair fails, p53 commits the cell to death through the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis; the genes here tune how readily that commitment is made. Setting this threshold decides whether a damaged cell is eliminated or survives with mutations, so it sits at the heart of tumour suppression and also governs how tumours respond to genotoxic chemotherapy and radiation. Control is exerted at several levels: cofactors and chromatin regulators such as ING2, KDM1A, SIRT1 and the TAF9/TAF9B subunits shape p53 stability, modification and promoter selectivity, ZNF385A biases transcription toward apoptotic targets, and HNRNPK and RPL26 act on p53 mRNA. Downstream, BCL2 and TRIAP1 restrain mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and caspase-9 activation, while CD44, MIF and MUC1 provide survival input that dampens the death response.</description>

cellular response to reactive nitrogen species is how a cell registers and reacts to nitric oxide, peroxynitrite and related nitrogen radicals, molecules generated during inflammation and vascular signalling that both convey information and damage proteins, lipids and DNA. The response determines whether a cell adapts or dies: it governs redox-sensitive stress kinase signalling through ASK1 and TRAF2, apoptotic commitment via AIFM1 and the caspase modulator CFLAR, cell-cycle arrest through CDK2-cyclin A and FOXO1-dependent transcription, and remodelling of the extracellular matrix by MMP3. Nitric oxide is also read as a legitimate second messenger by soluble guanylate cyclase, linking this biology to vasodilation and smooth muscle tone, while methionine synthase and phosphatase targets such as PTPN1 illustrate the direct susceptibility of thiol and cobalamin centres to nitrosative modification. Persistent nitrosative stress of this kind accompanies chronic inflammation, ischaemia-reperfusion injury and neurodegeneration.

Nitric oxide, peroxynitrite and related reactive nitrogen species are both signalling molecules and sources of damage, and this is the cellular response that decides which outcome follows. It matters in inflammation, where macrophage-derived nitrogen species reach neighbouring cells, and in vascular tissue, where nitric oxide acts as a physiological messenger rather than a toxin. Part of the response is productive signalling: the soluble guanylate cyclase subunit encoded by GUCY1B1 converts nitric oxide into a cyclic GMP signal that relaxes smooth muscle. Part is stress handling, with the MAP3K5 kinase and TRAF2 relaying redox stress toward apoptosis while CFLAR restrains death receptor signalling and the mitochondrial flavoprotein AIFM1 provides a caspase-independent death route. Cysteine nitrosation and tyrosine nitration also alter enzymes such as the phosphatase PTPN1, and transcriptional output through FOXO1 shifts cell cycle and survival gene expression.

Reactive oxygen species can push mitochondria past the point of no return, and this regulatory layer sets how readily oxidative damage is converted into intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis. It matters wherever oxidant load is chronic: dopaminergic neurons, cardiomyocytes under ischaemia, and aging tissues generally, where too little restraint gives neurodegeneration and cell loss while too much permits damaged cells to survive. Antioxidant enzymes such as SOD1, SOD2 and GPX1 and the NFE2L2 stress-response programme lower the triggering signal itself, while PINK1, PRKN, PARK7, HTRA2 and TRAP1 act at mitochondria to preserve quality control and blunt commitment to death. Survival inputs from AKT1, HIF1A, SIRT1 and anti-apoptotic MCL1 and NOL3 oppose permeabilisation, and several microRNAs tune the balance post-transcriptionally. The outcome is a threshold, not a switch, coupling redox state to cell survival decisions.

Reactive oxygen species damage mitochondria and can trigger the intrinsic, mitochondrial route to apoptosis; this pathway describes the brakes that keep that from happening, letting cells survive transient oxidative insults instead of committing to death. It matters most in long-lived, metabolically active cells — neurons and cardiomyocytes especially — and its weakening underlies neurodegeneration and ischaemic injury, which is why several familial Parkinson's disease genes appear here: PINK1 and parkin clear damaged mitochondria by mitophagy, while DJ-1 (PARK7) and HTRA2 act at the mitochondrion to blunt death signalling. Antioxidant defence and transcriptional adaptation contribute through the NRF2 factor NFE2L2, superoxide dismutase SOD2, glutathione peroxidase GPX1 and the hypoxia factor HIF1A. Survival signalling via AKT1, Wnt/β-catenin and growth factors, chaperones such as HSPB1 and TRAP1, the deacetylase SIRT1 and a set of microRNAs converge on raising the threshold for cytochrome c release.

When reactive oxygen species overwhelm a cell's antioxidant defences, mitochondria permeabilize and caspases are activated; this grouping covers the influences that push that oxidative stress-induced intrinsic apoptotic route forward, raising the likelihood that a damaged cell is eliminated rather than persisting with oxidized proteins, lipids and DNA. The balance matters for neuronal survival and for tissue responses to ischaemia and inflammation, and loss of restraint on it contributes to neurodegeneration, while failure to engage it permits damaged cells to survive. Mechanistically the theme is redox sensing coupled to mitochondrial commitment: a soluble adenylyl cyclase responsive to bicarbonate and calcium, superoxide-handling and superoxide-generating enzymes such as SOD1 and NOX1, and the redox-sensitive protein deglycase PARK7, converge on the apoptotic machinery. Ubiquitin ligase-mediated turnover of the anti-apoptotic factor MCL1 provides one route by which the mitochondrial threshold is lowered.

When DNA damage or other stress activates p53, one outcome is mitochondrial permeabilisation and cell death; this pathway covers the brakes that restrain that decision, damping p53-driven intrinsic apoptosis so a stressed cell can pause, repair and survive instead of dying. Delayed rectifier potassium currents repolarize excitable cells after an action potential, and their regulation sets how long a cardiac myocyte stays depolarized and how quickly a neuron can fire again. Growing axons extend toward their targets under instruction from extracellular cues, and this is the growth that guidance signals steer: elongation of a neuron projection coupled to the decision about where it goes. It builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system — midline crossing, topographic mapping, peripheral nerve and vascular co-patterning — and its failure produces axon misrouting, commissural defects and malformed circuits. Ceramide 1-phosphate is made at the trans-Golgi but acts elsewhere, notably in activating cytosolic phospholipase A2 and driving eicosanoid production, so its movement between membranes is what converts a locally synthesised lipid into a signal with cell-wide reach. MTTP, a lipid-loading transfer protein of lipoprotein assembly, links the process to broader intracellular lipid distribution.

Cells that fail here arrest at the spindle assembly checkpoint or divide with aneuploid genomes, a route to chromosomal instability in tumours. Much of the activity comes from the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase together with INCENP, survivin and borealin concentrates at inner centromeres, phosphorylates outer kinetochore substrates to release incorrect attachments, and thereby biases the system toward bioriented, tension-bearing connections. Acetyltransferases such as KAT5 and KAT2B contribute through centromeric chromatin and passenger complex modification, and additional factors link the process to autophagy machinery and to RNA-binding proteins acting at the centromere.

Accurate chromosome segregation depends on each sister kinetochore capturing microtubules from the correct spindle pole, and this pathway covers the activities that promote and stabilise those attachments during mitosis. Without them, kinetochores remain unattached or wrongly attached, the spindle checkpoint holds cells in mitosis, and cells that escape become aneuploid cat- a route to chromosomal instability in cancer. Four of the genes form the chromosomal passenger complex, in which Aurora B kinase partners with INCENP, survivin and borealin to localise at inner centromeres, phosphorylate kinetochore substrates and destabilise incorrect attachments so that correct ones can form. The acetyltransferases KAT2B and KAT5 contribute through chromatin and non-histone acetylation, and Beclin 1 links this biology to its broader roles in membrane trafficking and autophagy, placing kinetochore-microtubule attachment within mitotic fidelity control rather than spindle assembly alone.

Stem cells must eventually stop renewing themselves, and this pathway covers the processes that curtail stem cell population maintenance so that progenitors exit self-renewal and commit to differentiation. Loss of such restraint keeps cells in an undifferentiated, proliferative state and is a route to tumour initiation and failure of organ patterning. Much of the activity here is chromatin-based: a large Sin3-histone deacetylase complex, built around SIN3A with HDAC1/HDAC2, the histone-binding subunits RBBP4 and RBBP7, SAP30, SUDS3 and the ARID4 proteins, removes acetyl marks from promoters of pluripotency and self-renewal genes to silence them. Tumour suppressors of the ING family and the metastasis suppressor BRMS1 associate with the same machinery, while TET1 and O-GlcNAc transferase link DNA demethylation and nutrient-responsive glycosylation to the decision. Developmental cues from BMP7, WNT9B and the PAX2/PAX8-HNF1B axis apply this control during nephron and epithelial differentiation.

Stem cells persist only if the programmes that keep them undifferentiated are actively reinforced, and this pathway covers the inputs that increase self-renewal and hold a stem cell population in place. It matters for embryonic and tissue stem cell pools, for reprogramming to pluripotency, and for the cancers that arise when self-renewal is sustained inappropriately. Most of the activity is chromatin-based: SWI/SNF-family remodellers built around SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 with SMARCB1 and the ARID, BCL7 and SMARCC subunits, the non-canonical BRD9-containing form, and the SIN3A-HDAC1/2 corepressor with RBBP4/7 and SAP30 all set which lineage genes stay accessible or silenced. Transcriptional regulators including PRDM14, ESRRB, REST and TP63 act with the TET1 DNA demethylase and the Hippo effectors YAP1 and TEAD4 to couple these chromatin states to pluripotency and progenitor identity.

Mesenchymal stem cells give rise to bone, cartilage, fat and connective tissue, and how fast that pool expands sets the size of the progenitor reservoir available for skeletal growth, fracture healing and tissue repair. Control of mesenchymal stem cell proliferation is exerted largely through TGF-beta: the ligand TGFB1, its type I receptor TGFBR1, and LTBP3, which stores latent ligand in the extracellular matrix and governs when it becomes available, together tune whether progenitors divide or commit to differentiation. CITED1 acts as a transcriptional coregulator in this context, FERMT2 links integrin-based matrix adhesion to the same decision, and VEGFC couples expansion to vascular and lymphatic cues. Several microRNAs impose post-transcriptional limits, with cell cycle entry through CCNE1 as a shared endpoint. Excessive or deficient output contributes to skeletal dysplasia, impaired healing and fibrotic overgrowth.

Mesenchymal stem cells supply the progenitor pool for bone, cartilage, fat and connective tissue, and signals that increase their proliferation determine how much of that pool is available for skeletal growth, tissue repair and the stromal support of haematopoiesis. The genes here converge on TGF-beta as the driving input: a latent TGF-beta binding protein sequesters and positions the ligand in the matrix, an integrin-linked adaptor helps release and transduce it, and the ligand acting through its type I receptor kinase drives SMAD-dependent transcription, with CITED1 acting as a transcriptional coregulator of that output. A VEGF family member links expansion to vascular and lymphatic cues from the niche, while cyclin E1 marks the G1-to-S commitment through which these signals are ultimately expressed. Too little of this activity limits regeneration and bone formation; unchecked activity contributes to fibrosis and tumour stroma expansion.

Migrating cells concentrate specific proteins at the leading edge, the membrane front where actin polymerizes and new adhesions form, and this targeting is what makes movement directional rather than random. Delivery and retention of cargo at that site depends on vesicular traffic and on actin regulators that define where the front is: a Rab GTPase directs recycling endosome traffic to the protruding membrane, coatomer subunits supply secretory transport, and cofilin together with coronin remodels filaments to keep the actin network dynamic. Junctional and receptor proteins carried to this compartment link the machinery to epithelial barrier remodeling and to chemotactic responses in leukocytes, where a RhoA-binding inhibitory protein restrains rear contractility. When front-directed targeting fails, cells lose polarity and cannot sustain wound healing, immune cell trafficking, or tissue morphogenesis.

Synapses work only if the right proteins are delivered to the right side of the contact and held there, and this pathway covers the processes that set how much of a given protein reaches a synapse. Its outputs determine receptor number at the postsynaptic membrane, and therefore synaptic strength, plasticity and the balance of excitation and inhibition; mis-set delivery contributes to intellectual disability, autism and neurodegeneration. Control is exerted at several levels: trans-synaptic adhesion and organizer molecules such as neuroligin, calsyntenin, dystroglycan and glypicans recruit partners across the cleft; auxiliary subunits including NETO1/2 and a calcium channel subunit escort glutamate receptors and channels to the surface; scaffolds and small GTPase regulators such as DLG1, GRIPAP1 and IQSEC2 sort receptors through endosomes; and Wnt ligands, depalmitoylation and O-GlcNAc modification tune the process. Microtubule-associated tau links the same logic to axonal transport.

Synapses work only if the right proteins are delivered to them, and this pathway covers the signals that increase recruitment and retention of proteins at synaptic sites. It underlies the maturation and strengthening of nascent contacts during development and the remodelling that supports learning, so its failure leaves synapses sparse or functionally incomplete. Secreted Wnt ligands such as WNT5A and WNT7A act on presynaptic and postsynaptic partners through Dishevelled to promote clustering of synaptic components; adhesion molecules including neuroligin-2 and calsyntenin-3 specify contacts and help concentrate scaffolding and receptor proteins at inhibitory and excitatory sites. The microtubule-associated protein tau, mutated or hyperphosphorylated in tauopathies, links these events to axonal transport, connecting failed synaptic protein delivery to the synapse loss that accompanies neurodegeneration and to disorders of neurodevelopment.

L-alpha-amino acid transmembrane transport moves amino acids across membranes, the step that lets cells acquire nitrogen and carbon skeletons, sense nutrient sufficiency, and clear neurotransmitters from the synapse. It sustains intestinal and renal absorption of dietary amino acids, supplies glutamine and leucine to growing cells, and loads vesicles with glutamate; its failure produces cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, Hartnup disorder and excitotoxic neuronal injury. Carriers of the SLC1, SLC7, SLC38 and SLC17 families, some as heterodimers with the heavy chains SLC3A1 and SLC3A2, work as ion-coupled symporters, obligatory exchangers or vesicular transporters, with mitochondrial SLC25 members shuttling glutamate, aspartate and ornithine for the malate-aspartate shuttle and the urea cycle. Associated proteins including PSEN1, CLN3 and accessory chaperones govern trafficking and surface delivery, and SLC38A9 links lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 activation, tying transport directly to growth control.

Amino acids cannot cross lipid bilayers unaided, so cells rely on a large family of carriers to move them into the cytoplasm, across epithelia, and in and out of mitochondria. This transmembrane transport of L-alpha-amino acids supplies substrates for protein synthesis and nitrogen metabolism, loads neurotransmitter pools, and feeds the nutrient sensing that governs growth. Members include the sodium-dependent glutamate and neutral amino acid carriers of the SLC1 family, the SLC38 system A and N transporters, heteromeric exchangers in which SLC3A2 or SLC3A1 chaperones an SLC7 light chain, vesicular glutamate transporters, and mitochondrial carriers for glutamate, aspartate and ornithine. The output is concrete: glutamate clearance at synapses, cystine import for glutathione, urea-cycle flux, renal and intestinal reabsorption. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, hyperornithinaemia and epileptic encephalopathy, and SLC38A9 links lysosomal arginine to mTORC1 activation.

Freshly ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize an egg; they must first undergo capacitation in the female tract, a maturation step involving membrane cholesterol loss, altered ion fluxes and protein tyrosine phosphorylation that licenses hyperactivated motility and the acrosome reaction. The genes here tune how fast and how completely that switch occurs, rather than executing it outright. Epididymal and seminal plasma factors act on the sperm surface as it transits the male tract, including a disintegrin-metalloprotease family member delivered by epididymosomes and a glycodelin from endometrial and seminal secretions that restrains premature capacitation and zona binding. A testis-expressed receptor family implicated in fertility-related signalling and a transmembrane serine protease contribute to sperm membrane remodelling and migration competence. Mistimed capacitation wastes fertilizing capacity and contributes to male infertility, and the same controls are of interest for contraception and assisted reproduction.

Many ubiquitin ligases modify themselves, and self-ubiquitination is one of the ways a ligase sets its own abundance and activity; controlling how fast that happens tunes how long the ligase persists and how much substrate it can mark for the proteasome. Regulation of protein autoubiquitination covers the inputs that raise or dampen this self-directed modification, which matters for the stability of ligase complexes and for the strength of the degradation signals they generate. The genes here span a RING component that nucleates cullin-based ligase complexes, a membrane-associated RING-CH ligase, a kinase mutated in Parkinson disease, and chromatin-associated regulators, pointing to control exerted both on the ligases themselves and through transcriptional and scaffolding partners. Because ligase self-turnover limits substrate ubiquitination, this regulation feeds into protein quality control, signalling shutoff and cell survival decisions.

regulation of organelle transport along microtubule tunes how far, how fast and in which direction membrane-bound cargoes such as lysosomes, endosomes and mitochondria are hauled along microtubule tracks by kinesin and dynein motors. This control is what allows a neuron to place lysosomes at growth cones, deliver mitochondria to distant synapses, and clear autophagosomes from long axons; its loss produces cargo stalling and the axonal transport deficits seen in neurodegeneration. The genes act at several levels: BORC subunits and LAMP1 mark lysosomes for kinesin coupling, adaptors such as FEZ1 and HAP1 link cargo to motors, TRIM46 organises parallel microtubule bundles in the proximal axon that set transport polarity, and microtubule-associated proteins including MAP2 and neurofilament heavy chain modify track availability. STK11 signalling ties this trafficking to axon specification and polarity, and TRIM58 restricts transport during erythroid maturation.

Organelles do not drift to their destinations; they are hauled along microtubules by kinesin and dynein motors, and this regulatory layer sets how far, how fast and in which direction that hauling goes. It matters most in neurons, where mitochondria, lysosomes and secretory cargo must be delivered over axonal distances and where stalled or misdirected transport contributes to neurodegeneration. The genes here act as adaptors and modulators rather than motors themselves: a BLOC-one-related complex subunit couples lysosomal membranes to kinesin for outward movement, scaffolds such as FEZ1 and the huntingtin-associated protein link cargo to motor complexes, and TRIM46 organises the parallel microtubule bundles of the axon initial segment that give transport its polarity. Microtubule-associated and cytoskeletal proteins including MAP2 and neurofilament heavy chain tune track availability, while the kinase STK11 contributes through neuronal polarity signalling.

Ubiquitin chains linked through lysine 63 do not mark proteins for destruction; they build scaffolds that recruit kinase complexes, and this pathway covers the events that raise the rate at which such chains are made. The output matters most in innate immune signalling and DNA damage tolerance, where K63 chains on receptors and adaptors assemble the platforms that switch on NF-kB and stress kinases. Here the bacterial peptidoglycan sensor NOD2 works with its adaptor kinase RIPK2 and the E3 ligase BIRC2 to drive chain formation, while UBE2N acts as the K63-specific E2 enzyme in partnership with the UEV cofactors UBE2V1 and UBE2V2. PTPN22 and DDX3X modulate the response, and variants in NOD2 and PTPN22 predispose to inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmunity, linking control of this chain type to the threshold for inflammation.

Attaching a single ubiquitin to a substrate, rather than a chain, changes where a protein goes or how it is read rather than marking it for destruction, and the control of protein monoubiquitination sets how much of that signal accumulates. It matters most in DNA damage tolerance and in receptor and repair-factor signalling: monoubiquitinated FANCD2-type and histone marks recruit repair machinery, and the level of the mark is set by opposing writing and erasing activity. Here ubiquitin itself is supplied by a polyubiquitin precursor gene, WDR48 acts as an activating partner for USP-family deubiquitinases that strip the single ubiquitin off substrates, and the FANCM component links the process to replication fork sensing in interstrand crosslink repair. BIRC2 contributes E3 ligase activity, while the penta-EF-hand calcium-binding proteins ALG-2 and peflin tie the process to calcium-dependent trafficking.

Attaching a single ubiquitin to a protein, rather than a polyubiquitin chain, changes where that protein goes and what it binds instead of marking it for destruction, and the processes described here raise the rate at which such monoubiquitination occurs. The output matters for DNA damage tolerance and for membrane trafficking: monoubiquitination of Fanconi anaemia pathway substrates licenses repair of interstrand crosslinks at stalled replication forks, and FANCM acts within that pathway as part of the complex that recognises the lesion and promotes the modification. BIRC2 contributes ubiquitin ligase activity associated with death receptor and NF-kB signalling, the penta-EF-hand calcium sensors PDCD6 and PEF1 couple calcium status to ESCRT-associated membrane repair and budding, and UBB supplies the ubiquitin itself. Loss of such control impairs crosslink repair and genome stability.

Signalling inside a cell must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this collection covers the brakes: the phosphatases, GAPs, decoy adaptors, ubiquitin ligases, degradative feedback inhibitors and microRNAs that terminate or damp intracellular cascades once a stimulus has been read. Their output sets signal duration and amplitude, and losing them produces constitutive growth signalling, autoimmunity or unchecked inflammation. Concrete examples run through the list: dual-specificity phosphatases dephosphorylate activated MAP kinases, PTEN reverses PI3K lipid signalling, the TSC1–TSC2 complex and the GATOR/sestrin components restrain mTORC1 in response to nutrient and energy status, RasGAPs such as NF1 and Sprouty/Spred proteins limit Ras–ERK flux, SMAD6/SMAD7 and SFRP/DKK proteins oppose TGF-β and Wnt inputs, and A20, NFKBIA and TNIP proteins curtail NF-κB after innate immune receptor engagement. Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases and NLR-family regulators of inflammasome activity extend the same logic to second messengers and cytokine maturation.

positive regulation of intracellular signal transduction collects the activating inputs that switch on and amplify signalling inside cells, converting receptor engagement at the surface into sustained cytoplasmic and nuclear responses that drive proliferation, survival, differentiation, immune activation and metabolic adaptation. Its breadth is the point: growth factor and cytokine ligands with their receptor tyrosine kinases (FGFs and FGFRs, EGFR, insulin/IGF, PDGF, TRK family), adaptors such as GRB2, SHC1, IRS1 and GAB1 feeding RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K-AKT, mTOR complexes with their Rag GTPase and LAMTOR amino-acid sensing machinery, TGF-beta/BMP and WNT arms, small GTPases of the Rho and RAS families, and innate immune relays through TLRs, MYD88, IRAK kinases, TRAFs and inflammasome components toward NF-kB. Kinase cascade scaffolds, ubiquitin ligases, and microRNAs set the gain. Aberrant amplification here underlies oncogenic transformation, chronic inflammation and fibrosis, which is why many of these nodes are drug targets.

This is the aggregate of activating inputs into intracellular signalling: processes and molecules that switch on, amplify or prolong the relay of information from receptors to the cytoplasmic and nuclear machinery that changes cell behaviour. It spans growth factor and cytokine receptor tyrosine kinases with their adaptors and exchange factors, feeding RAS-RAF-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and mTOR complexes together with their amino-acid-sensing Rag and lysosomal scaffolds; innate immune receptors signalling through MyD88, IRAKs and TRAFs to NF-kB; inflammasome and death-receptor modules; TGF-beta/BMP, WNT, Hippo and G-protein-coupled receptor arms; and stress-, DNA-damage- and unfolded-protein-response kinases. Positive control is exerted by kinases, ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases, small GTPases, scaffolds and secreted ligands. The output is decisions about proliferation, survival, differentiation, metabolism and inflammation, which is why persistent overactivation of these steps underlies cancer, autoinflammatory and fibrotic disease.

Endothelial cells read vascular endothelial growth factor as an instruction to sprout, migrate and form tubes, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or damp that response so vessel growth stays proportionate to demand. Tuning matters because unchecked VEGF signalling drives tumour angiogenesis, diabetic retinopathy and vascular leak, while too little leaves tissue ischaemic or lymphatics malformed. Control is exerted at several levels: extracellular matrix and secreted modulators such as decorin, gremlin-1, EMILIN1 and vitronectin alter ligand availability and receptor engagement; integrins including ITGA5, ITGB1 and ITGB3 couple matrix adhesion to receptor output; ANGPT1, DLL1, ROBO1 and semaphorin cues integrate competing guidance signals; SPRY2 and DAB2IP restrain downstream kinase cascades while PIK3CB transmits them. Several microRNAs add post-transcriptional damping, and PROX1 with CCBE1 and ADAMTS3 links the same growth factor axis to lymphatic endothelial specification.

VEGF drives endothelial cells to proliferate, migrate and sprout new vessels, and this braking programme limits how strongly they respond, keeping angiogenesis proportionate rather than runaway. Such restraint matters for vascular quiescence in adult tissues, for orderly wound and retinal vessel patterning, and its loss contributes to tumour vascularisation and proliferative retinopathy. Several mechanisms converge here: secreted matrix and plasma proteins such as decorin, EMILIN1, histidine-rich glycoprotein and an ADAMTS metalloproteinase dampen growth-factor availability and receptor engagement; angiopoietin-1 acting through endothelial TIE signalling stabilises vessels; Sprouty2 and DAB2IP attenuate receptor tyrosine kinase output toward ERK and PI3K; the transcription factor NR2F2 and guidance cues including SEMA6A and ADGRA2 shape endothelial responsiveness. Interleukin-12 subunits add an immune-derived antiangiogenic input, and a set of microRNAs, among them miR-424 and miR-16, tunes VEGF pathway transcripts post-transcriptionally.

Neutrophils are potent but indiscriminate effectors, and the control of their activation sets how readily they degranulate, produce oxidants and release inflammatory mediators once recruited to tissue. Tuning this threshold protects host tissue from collateral damage during infection; its failure underlies neutrophil-driven pathology in sepsis, arthritis and acute lung injury. Much of the restraint comes from inhibitory surface receptors bearing cytoplasmic tyrosine-based motifs, including CD300A, CLEC12A and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, which recruit the phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 to dampen activating kinase signalling; SRC-family activity acts on the opposite side of the same balance. Secreted modulators also contribute, with progranulin and interleukin-16 restraining responses while TNF primes neutrophils for enhanced degranulation and respiratory burst. Regulation therefore operates at receptor engagement, at proximal phosphorylation, and through soluble cues in the inflammatory environment.

Neutrophils are armed with proteases, oxidants and adhesion machinery that damage host tissue if deployed without restraint, and negative regulation of neutrophil activation is the braking system that keeps that arsenal in check. It sets the threshold for degranulation, oxidative burst and integrin-mediated adhesion, so that responses are proportionate to infection and resolve afterwards; loss of these brakes contributes to autoinflammatory and autoimmune tissue injury. Inhibitory surface receptors bearing cytoplasmic tyrosine-based inhibitory or lectin-type recognition motifs, including CD300A, CLEC12A and the low-affinity IgG receptor FCGR2B, recruit the tyrosine phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 to dephosphorylate and dampen activating kinase cascades, with SRC family signalling both feeding and being counter-regulated by this circuit. Secreted progranulin and microRNA-mediated control of activation transcripts add extracellular and post-transcriptional layers, linking this restraint to inflammation resolution and myeloid tolerance.

The nucleolus is a membraneless compartment assembled around ribosomal DNA, and proteins must be actively delivered to it and retained there for ribosome subunit production, telomerase maturation and nucleolar stress signalling to work. Targeting depends on nucleolar localization signals read against RNA polymerase I transcription and on chaperone-like hubs: nucleophosmin shuttles between nucleolus and nucleoplasm and escorts partners in, while the ARF tumour suppressor encoded at the CDKN2A locus is sequestered there and, when released, stabilises p53. Other members act in pre-rRNA processing and large subunit assembly and export, including the AAA-ATPase NVL, the NMD3 adaptor, and RRS1/RPF2, with RAN providing the nucleocytoplasmic gradient. Mislocalisation of these factors underlies ribosomopathies, drives the nucleolar stress response after ribosome biogenesis is blocked, and disturbs telomere maintenance through TERT and PINX1.

Moving protons across membranes is how cells store and spend energy and how they set the pH of every compartment, and this collection of transporters covers both. Respiratory chain complexes and the mitochondrial ATP synthase pump protons out across the inner membrane and let them back through to make ATP, while uncoupling proteins and other carriers dissipate or exploit the same gradient for heat production and metabolite exchange. Vacuolar-type ATPases acidify endosomes, lysosomes and secretory vesicles, supporting protein degradation, receptor recycling and the loading of neurotransmitters by vesicular transporters that run on the resulting proton gradient. At the plasma membrane, sodium-proton exchangers, gastric and Na+/K+ pumps, otopetrin channels and proton-coupled peptide, amino acid and drug carriers control cytosolic pH, gastric acid secretion, urinary acidification and nutrient uptake. Loss of individual components causes mitochondrial disease, distal renal tubular acidosis, deafness and osteopetrosis.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to reach infected or injured tissue, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast, how far and how many of them go. Tuning it matters in both directions: too little recruitment leaves bacterial and fungal infection unchecked, while too much drives the tissue damage of sepsis, acute lung injury and chronic inflammatory disease. Chemoattractant receptors read gradients of interleukin-8, complement fragments C3a and C5a, and chemokines, while endothelial junctional and adhesion molecules such as JAM3 and CD99 govern the diapedesis step. Inside the cell, Rac GTPases direct actin polymerization and polarity so that a cell can crawl directionally, and MyD88-dependent innate signalling amplifies output. Repellent and brake components, including SLIT2 and RIPOR2, restrain migration, and LBP-mediated sensing of lipopolysaccharide links microbial detection to the decision to leave the vasculature.

Neutrophils are the first cells recruited to infection or injury, and the braking mechanisms that damp their migration determine whether that response resolves or becomes tissue-destroying. Negative regulation of neutrophil migration covers signals that reduce the rate and extent of chemotactic movement out of the vasculature and through tissue, limiting collateral damage in conditions such as acute lung injury, ischemia-reperfusion and chronic inflammatory disease. The genes here act at several levels: SLIT2 signals through Robo receptors to repel chemotaxing neutrophils and stabilise their cytoskeleton, C5AR2 serves as a non-canonical receptor for the complement fragment C5a that tempers signalling through the classical C5a receptor, TNFAIP6 modifies hyaluronan-rich matrix to interfere with adhesion and extravasation, and the microRNA MIR223 restrains myeloid activation transcriptionally. Together they represent the resolution side of innate immune recruitment rather than its initiation.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes recruited to infected or damaged tissue, and enhancement of their migration determines how quickly and how strongly an inflammatory response is mounted. Genes here act at every step of recruitment: chemoattractant receptors for complement fragments and for interleukin-8 set the directional cue, fucosyltransferases build the selectin ligands that let cells tether and roll on activated endothelium, and CD99 family adhesion molecules support the final squeeze through the junction into tissue. Inside the cell, the Rac GTPases together with the hematopoietic adaptor NCKAP1L remodel actin for polarised crawling, and calcium and kinase signals tune chemotactic sensitivity. Too little of this activity leaves bacterial infection uncontrolled, as in leukocyte adhesion deficiency; too much drives the neutrophil-rich tissue injury of sepsis, acute lung injury and chronic inflammatory disease.

Hyperpolarization drives a cell's membrane potential more negative than its resting value, damping excitability and setting the interval before the next action potential; control over how often and how deeply it occurs tunes firing patterns in neurons, cardiac pacemaker cells and smooth muscle. Regulation of membrane hyperpolarization therefore shapes rhythmic activity, afterpotential duration and vascular tone, and its disturbance contributes to arrhythmia, altered pain signalling and epilepsy. The genes here act at several levels: HCN1 forms a hyperpolarization-activated cation channel whose current depolarizes the cell and limits how far hyperpolarization proceeds, TRPC5 provides a calcium-permeable cation conductance that feeds calcium-dependent potassium responses, angiotensinogen supplies the precursor for a peptide that modifies excitability and vessel behaviour, and mitochondrial superoxide dismutase links redox state to channel function. CRTC1 couples calcium and cAMP signals to transcription, allowing activity to reset excitability over longer timescales.

Tertiary alcohols — hydroxyl groups on fully substituted carbons — arise chiefly in steroid chemistry, and the handling of these compounds is essentially the chemistry of adrenal and gonadal steroid hormone synthesis and inactivation. The 17α-hydroxylations performed by CYP17A1 on pregnenolone and progesterone create exactly such centres, and the downstream cytochromes CYP11A1, CYP21A2 and CYP11B1/CYP11B2 carry the resulting intermediates on to cortisol and aldosterone, hormones that set blood pressure, electrolyte balance and the stress response; loss of CYP21A2 gives congenital adrenal hyperplasia. A broad family of aldo-keto reductases and carbonyl reductases interconverts ketone and hydroxyl forms of steroids and other carbonyl substrates, tuning receptor-active from inactive ligands, while HSD11B2 protects the mineralocorticoid receptor from cortisol and H6PD supplies luminal reducing power. Sulfotransferase activity adds a conjugation route to excretion. Developmental signals including WNT4 and BMP family members pattern the steroidogenic tissues themselves.

Growing axons are steered to their targets by attractive and repulsive cues, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly and how accurately that steering happens. Setting the gain on guidance determines whether commissural axons cross the midline, whether retinal ganglion cell projections reach the correct visual targets, and whether cortical neurons send axons along the right tracts; failures produce miswiring disorders such as congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles, horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, and cortical malformations. Control is exerted at several levels: transcription factors including ATOH7, POU4F2 and TBR1 specify which guidance receptors a neuron expresses, RNA-binding regulators such as NOVA2 and YTHDF1 govern splicing and translation of guidance machinery, SLIT2 and ROBO3 set midline repulsion, and MYCBP2, KIF21A and TUBB2B act on the cytoskeletal and degradative responses within the growth cone.

Transcription is as much a matter of restraint as of activation, and this collection covers the machinery that stops, slows or blocks RNA synthesis. It keeps lineage-inappropriate genes silent, terminates responses to hormones, stress and inflammation once they are no longer needed, and enforces the boundaries that let a single genome specify many cell types; its loss underlies developmental malformation and cancers driven by inappropriate gene expression. The mechanisms are varied: sequence-specific repressors such as the KRAB zinc finger, HES/HEY, SNAI and ID families; corepressor complexes built on NCOR/SMRT, SIN3, NuRD and CoREST that recruit histone deacetylases; Polycomb components including EZH2, SUZ12 and RING1 that deposit and read repressive chromatin marks; DNA methyltransferases and methyl-CpG readers; retinoblastoma-family and E2F repressors gating cell cycle genes; circadian repressors PER and CRY; and negative elongation factors that pause RNA polymerase II after initiation.

Regulation of receptor localization to synapse controls how many neurotransmitter receptors are delivered to, retained at, or removed from synaptic membranes, which is the physical basis of synaptic strength and its plasticity. Learning, memory consolidation and the maintenance of excitatory/inhibitory balance depend on it, and its disruption contributes to intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy. The genes span the steps involved: auxiliary and adhesion proteins such as NETO1/2, glypicans and dystroglycan that capture and stabilise AMPA, kainate and GABA receptors at the postsynaptic site; vesicular trafficking, endosomal sorting and exocytic machinery (GRIPAP1, VPS26B, STX7) that shuttle receptors to and from the surface; Rho and Ras/Rap GTPase modules with actin regulators like drebrin that remodel the spine cytoskeleton; and post-translational modifiers, including palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC2/3 and the sheddase ADAM10, that set receptor and scaffold residence times.

How many neurotransmitter receptors sit in a postsynaptic membrane, and which ones, sets the strength of a synapse, so the trafficking steps that put them there are the substrate of learning and memory. This pathway covers the controls on receptor delivery to, and retention at, synapses: vesicular transport and endosomal recycling, exocytic fusion, scaffolding and cytoskeletal anchoring, and lipid modification that tethers scaffolds to the membrane. Auxiliary subunits such as NETO1 and NETO2 govern kainate receptor composition and surface levels, GRIPAP1 and IQSEC2 act on AMPA receptor recycling and Arf-dependent trafficking, and palmitoyltransferases ZDHHC2 and ZDHHC3 modify synaptic scaffolds and receptor subunits. Small GTPase and MAPK signalling, adhesion molecules and proteolytic shedding by ADAM10 tune the process. Disruption weakens synaptic plasticity and is associated with intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy.

How many neurons a brain ends up with depends on how long its progenitors keep dividing before they differentiate, and this pathway covers the controls that set that balance. Both directions matter: too little proliferation gives microcephaly, while failure to exit the cycle expands the progenitor pool and predisposes to tumours such as medulloblastoma. Patterning transcription factors including PAX6, FOXG1, SIX3 and GLI3 define where and when progenitors divide, while Sonic hedgehog acting through SMO, Notch, and Wnt signalling via beta-catenin supply the extrinsic mitogenic and self-renewal cues. Spindle and centrosome proteins such as ASPM and WDR62 govern division orientation and symmetry, linking mitotic mechanics to cell fate choice. Niche-derived signals, chromatin regulators and microRNA-mediated repression add further layers, and several members are also active in adult neurogenic zones.

Muscle satellite cells sit quiescent beneath the basal lamina and must be held back from differentiating so that a reserve pool remains for future repair; this is the restraining arm of that decision, blocking or slowing the conversion of activated satellite cells into fusion-competent myocytes. Without such brakes the progenitor pool is spent, and regeneration after injury or in ageing muscle fails. Myostatin, a secreted TGF-beta family ligand, is the best-characterised member and signals through activin receptors to suppress myogenic commitment and limit muscle mass, which is why its loss produces hypermuscular phenotypes in cattle, mice and humans. Others act inside the cell or at the membrane: the NAD-dependent deacetylase SIRT2 links metabolic state to myogenic gene expression, a receptor tyrosine kinase reads ephrin cues from the niche, and homeodomain-family regulators tune the myogenic transcriptional programme. The pathway therefore sits within skeletal muscle stem cell self-renewal and repair.

Proteoglycans give cartilage, tendon and vascular wall their water-binding, load-bearing properties, and this pathway covers the signals that push cells to make more of them. Upregulating proteoglycan biosynthesis matters for chondrocyte matrix production, skeletal and musculoskeletal growth, and the composition of connective tissue; when the balance tips the wrong way the matrix becomes weak or disorganised, as in the arterial tortuosity caused by loss of the glucose transporter family member SLC2A10. The set links Wnt-responsive transcription, through beta-catenin and its partner TCF7L2, to expression of the enzymes that build glycosaminoglycan chains, alongside a musculoskeletal-enriched regulator induced during growth and repair. Also represented is control at the level of chain initiation itself, since PXYLP1 dephosphorylates xylose on the nascent linker region and so gates whether glycosaminoglycan synthesis proceeds.

Long bones grow by keeping the proliferating chondrocytes of the growth plate under tight numerical control, and this pathway covers the brakes on that expansion. Restraining chondrocyte division sets when cells stop dividing and begin hypertrophic differentiation, so it helps determine limb length and the timing of growth plate closure; loss of restraint contributes to skeletal overgrowth and cartilage tumours, while excessive braking yields chondrodysplasia and short stature. Bone morphogenetic protein receptors transmit signals that can limit as well as promote proliferation depending on context, and SMAD7 acts as an inhibitory SMAD that dampens transforming growth factor beta and BMP signal output. CCN3, a matricellular protein of the CCN family, is an antiproliferative regulator in cartilage, and a microRNA adds post-transcriptional control. The biology sits within endochondral ossification and cartilage homeostasis.

Growth of the skeleton in length depends on chondrocytes dividing in orderly columns within the growth plate before they mature and are replaced by bone, and this pathway covers the signals that drive that expansion of the chondrocyte pool. Too little proliferation shortens and disorganises the growth plate, producing dwarfism and chondrodysplasia; loss of control over it contributes to cartilage overgrowth and to the abnormal chondrocyte behaviour seen in osteoarthritic joints. The set couples transcriptional control of cartilage identity, through the master chondrogenic factor SOX9 together with LEF1 acting downstream of Wnt signalling and the nephrogenic factor SIX2, to matrix and secreted cues such as cartilage oligomeric matrix protein and lactoferrin. SIRT6 links the process to chromatin-based regulation and to skeletal ageing, placing this biology at the intersection of endochondral bone development and cartilage homeostasis.

Programmed cell death is not only a response to damage; sculpting an embryo requires cells to be deleted on schedule, and this is the apoptotic component of anatomical structure development. It removes interdigital webbing, trims excess neurons and nephric precursors, hollows out the lens and cardiac cushions, and prunes axons that reach the wrong target, so that organ shape and cell number come out right. The core machinery is mitochondrial: BAX and BAK1 permeabilise the outer membrane once the BH3-only protein BCL2L11 tips the balance, while TNF receptors TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF1B provide a death-receptor route. What makes it developmental is the input — BMP4 and BMP7, TGFB2, Notch and Wnt/LRP5 signalling, SLIT–ROBO guidance cues, and patterning transcription factors such as PAX2, PAX8, SIX3, NKX2-5 and FOXC1 — plus XKR scramblases that expose phosphatidylserine for clearance. Loss of these controls yields malformations of eye, kidney, heart and limb.

A lamellipodium is the flat, branched-actin sheet a cell pushes out at its leading edge, and this pathway covers the signals and actin regulators that decide when and where one forms, how broad it becomes, and when it is dismantled. Cell migration during wound healing, immune cell chemotaxis, axon guidance and tumour invasion all depend on this control. The core machinery is the Arp2/3 complex and its WAVE/WASP activators with their ABI, CYFIP and NCKAP subunits, switched on downstream of Rac1, Rac2 and CDC42 and of receptor and lipid signals through SRC and PI3K. Balancing factors set protrusion limits: cofilin and twinfilin turn over filaments, coronins and CARMIL proteins tune capping, ARPIN inhibits Arp2/3, and fascin bundles the resulting actin. Guidance cues such as SLIT2 and ephrin receptor signalling steer the process, linking protrusion to directional movement.

Cells crawl by extending a lamellipodium, a flat sheet of branched actin at the leading edge, and negative regulation of lamellipodium organization is how that protrusion is restrained, retracted or kept from forming in the wrong place. Damping protrusion sets the direction and speed of migration, so it matters for axon guidance, wound repair, immune cell trafficking and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. Several members act directly on the actin machinery: ARPIN antagonises Arp2/3-driven branched nucleation, cofilin severs and disassembles existing filaments, and ABI3 alters WAVE-complex output. Others deliver the signal from outside: SLIT2 and plexin-family receptors transduce repulsive guidance cues that collapse protrusions, while KANK1 links the restraint to adhesion and microtubule-associated control. Regulatory microRNAs and a secreted plasma factor add further suppression, placing this biology at the junction of cytoskeletal turnover and directional cell motility.

Migrating cells push forward by building a lamellipodium, a flat sheet of branched actin at the leading edge, and this pathway covers the signals and machinery that promote its formation and expansion. It underlies wound healing, immune cell chemotaxis, axon and dendrite growth, and epithelial sheet movement, and its overactivation contributes to tumour cell invasion. The small GTPases RAC1, RAC2 and CDC42, activated downstream of receptor and PI3K signalling, engage the WAVE regulatory complex, whose subunits CYFIP1, NCKAP1, ABI2, BRK1 and WASF2 in turn stimulate the ARP2/3 complex to nucleate branched filaments. Cofilin, twinfilin, coronins and capping-protein regulators of the CARMIL family control filament turnover and length, while fascin and villin-family actin-bundling proteins shape the protrusion. SRC and mTOR signalling tune the response to growth factors and adhesion.

regulation of lens fiber cell differentiation controls when and how fast lens epithelial cells exit the cell cycle and elongate into the transparent, crystallin-packed fiber cells that form the optical core of the eye. Getting the timing right is what makes the lens clear and correctly shaped; failure produces cataract, microphthalmia and anterior segment dysgenesis. The genes describe a balance between a differentiation-promoting growth factor signal and its brakes: FGF2 acting through receptor tyrosine kinase–ERK signalling drives fiber commitment, while Sprouty and Spred proteins dampen that output to prevent premature or excessive differentiation. Withdrawal from proliferation is enforced by the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p27 and p57, which couple cell cycle exit to elongation, and transcription factors such as FOXE3 and ZEB2 set the epithelial progenitor state upstream. The pathway thus links growth factor signalling, cell cycle arrest and terminal differentiation in an organ whose function is purely structural.

The transparent lens is built by epithelial cells at its equator withdrawing from the cell cycle and elongating into crystallin-packed fiber cells, and this pathway sets how readily and how fast that switch occurs. Getting the balance right determines lens shape and optical clarity; misregulation is associated with cataract and anterior segment malformation. Fibroblast growth factor signalling from the vitreous provides the differentiation cue, and much of the control here is restraint of it: Sprouty proteins and the Sprouty-related SPRED family dampen receptor tyrosine kinase output through RAS-ERK, tuning rather than abolishing the signal. Cell cycle exit is enforced by the CIP/KIP inhibitors p27 and p57, which couple proliferation arrest to fiber elongation, while the transcription factors FOXE3 and ZEB2 govern the lens epithelial state and the competence of cells to differentiate.

negative regulation of lens fiber cell differentiation restrains the conversion of lens epithelial cells into elongated, crystallin-packed fiber cells, so that differentiation happens only at the equatorial transition zone and not across the anterior epithelium. This brake preserves the proliferative epithelial pool that supplies new fibers throughout life, and its loss distorts lens shape and transparency, causing congenital cataract, anterior segment dysgenesis and microphthalmia. The mechanism is largely damping of growth factor input: Sprouty and Spred proteins intercept FGF- and other receptor tyrosine kinase-driven RAS-ERK signalling, the same cascade that otherwise drives fiber elongation, while the forkhead factor FOXE3 maintains epithelial identity and proliferation in the anterior lens and is itself mutated in human lens malformations. The pathway is therefore a spatial patterning device, coupling negative feedback on ERK signalling to the maintenance of an undifferentiated progenitor compartment.

The transparent lens forms only if fibre cell differentiation happens in the right place at the right time, and this pathway supplies the brake. Epithelial cells at the lens equator must be held in a proliferative, undifferentiated state until they are positioned correctly; premature elongation and crystallin accumulation distort lens architecture and cause cataract or anterior segment dysgenesis. The Sprouty and Sprouty-related SPRED proteins dampen receptor tyrosine kinase output, restraining the FGF-driven ERK signalling that would otherwise drive fibre commitment, while the forkhead transcription factor FOXE3 maintains the anterior lens epithelium and its proliferative capacity, with mutations causing congenital lens malformations. Together these factors illustrate how negative regulation of differentiation, rather than differentiation itself, sets the boundary between epithelium and fibre compartment and preserves the ordered cell arrangement on which optical clarity depends.

Entry into mitosis is a licensed step, and the controls over the G2/M phase transition decide whether a cell with damaged or incompletely replicated DNA is allowed to divide. The switch itself is the activation of cyclin B–CDK1: WEE1 and PKMYT1 kinases hold the complex inhibited by phosphorylation, CDC25 phosphatases remove those marks, and PLK1 and Aurora kinases drive commitment to mitosis. Damage sensing feeds directly into this decision through ATM and ATR, the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex, TOPBP1 and CLSPN, which activate CHEK1 and stabilise p53 to impose the G2 checkpoint, with CDKN1A sustaining arrest. An abscission checkpoint arm involving CHMP4C and VPS4 delays the final cut. Loss of this restraint permits division with unrepaired lesions, producing aneuploidy and genomic instability characteristic of tumours, and it is the basis for WEE1 and CHK1 inhibitor strategies in cancer.

Cells must not enter mitosis with unreplicated or damaged DNA, and negative regulation of the G2/M phase transition is the brake that holds them in G2 until repair is done. It works by restraining the mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase CDK1: WEE1 and PKMYT1 phosphorylate CDK1 inhibitorily, while the ATM and ATR kinases, activated by double-strand breaks and replication stress, signal through CHEK1 and its mediators CLSPN, TOPBP1 and ETAA1 to block the phosphatases that would remove those marks. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and the BRCA1-containing BRCC36 module sense and process breaks, and p21 (CDKN1A) reinforces arrest transcriptionally. A separate abscission checkpoint involving CHMP4C and AURKB delays the final cut. Loss of these restraints produces premature or catastrophic mitosis, chromosome missegregation and the genome instability characteristic of cancer, which is why WEE1 and CHK1 inhibitors are pursued therapeutically.

Entry into mitosis is a switch, and this is the set of activities that push it forward: positive regulation of the G2/M transition works by raising the activity of the mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase so that a cell committed to division actually begins chromosome condensation and spindle assembly. The core is the cyclin B–CDK1 complex, held inactive by inhibitory phosphorylation until CDC25A, CDC25B and CDC25C remove it; the anaphase-promoting complex inhibitor encoded by FBXO5 protects mitotic cyclins from premature destruction. Supporting members tie the decision to upstream events — replication licensing and origin firing through CDC7 and its partner, nucleotide supply through ribonucleotide reductase subunits, and chromatin and transcriptional inputs through BRD4, SIN3A and NPM1. Driving this transition without satisfying replication and damage checkpoints produces mitosis on damaged or under-replicated chromosomes, a route to aneuploidy and a common feature of proliferating tumour cells.

Material destined for degradation reaches the lysosome by maturation and fusion of late endosomes, and this late endosome to lysosome transport step decides whether internalised receptors, damaged organelles and autophagic cargo are actually broken down. The route depends on positioning the compartments correctly and then merging them: the small GTPase ARL8B recruits the tethering factor PLEKHM1 and components of the HOPS complex, including VPS39 and VPS41, which promote fusion, while VPS35 acts in retromer-dependent retrieval of cargo away from this degradative fate. A large contingent of ESCRT-III subunits with the VPS4A/VPS4B ATPases drives the membrane remodelling and scission that shapes multivesicular bodies and repairs damaged lysosomal membranes. Mutations in LRRK2 and C9orf72 impair this traffic, linking defective endolysosomal delivery to Parkinson's disease and to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with frontotemporal dementia.

Mitochondria translate their own genome, and the large subunit of the mitoribosome must be built from mitochondrially encoded 16S rRNA plus imported proteins before any of the thirteen respiratory chain subunits can be made. Assembly of this subunit therefore sits upstream of oxidative phosphorylation, and defects in it cause combined respiratory chain deficiency, cardiomyopathy and encephalopathy. The genes here cover the successive steps: RNA helicases such as DDX28 and DHX30 and the RNA-binding protein FASTKD2 organise nucleoid-adjacent granules where rRNA is processed and folded; MRM2 and MRM3 add 2'-O-methyl marks and NSUN4, in complex with MTERF4, methylates cytosine in the rRNA; and a set of GTPases including MTG1, MTG2 and GTPBP10 drive maturation checkpoints. MALSU1 with RCC1L and NDUFAB1 forms an anti-association module that keeps immature subunits from joining the small subunit prematurely.

Synaptic vesicles and their precursors must be moved along axonal microtubules to and from release sites, and this pathway covers the control of that trafficking rather than the transport machinery itself. Setting the rate and direction of vesicle movement determines how much releasable vesicle pool a distal synapse has, and so how reliably it can sustain neurotransmission. The genes involved point to two convergent themes: microtubule-based motor regulation, with MAP2 stabilising the cytoskeletal tracks and a lysosome-related BORC subunit influencing cargo positioning, and mitochondrial quality control, where the kinase PINK1 and the ubiquitin ligase parkin act together, alongside LRRK2, to couple organelle health and phosphorylation signals to axonal transport. Mutations in these same kinases and ligase cause familial Parkinson's disease, linking failure of presynaptic vesicle transport control to degeneration of dopaminergic neurons.

Before a cell commits to replicating its DNA it must pass the G1/S transition, the restriction point at which growth signals, nutrient status and DNA integrity are weighed; regulation at this step determines whether a cell proliferates, arrests or remains quiescent, and its loss is one of the most common events in cancer. The core switch is cyclin D- and cyclin E-dependent kinase activity acting on retinoblastoma family proteins, releasing E2F-DP transcription factors to induce replication genes such as CDC6 and ribonucleotide reductase subunits. Restraint comes from CDK inhibitors of the CDKN1 and CDKN2 families, p53-dependent induction of CDKN1A, PTEN-mediated damping of growth factor signalling, and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of cyclins by ligases including FBXW7 and CUL4. SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits, numerous microRNAs, and checkpoint kinases such as WEE1 tune the threshold further.

Cells commit irreversibly to DNA replication at the G1/S boundary, and negative regulation of this transition is what keeps that commitment conditional on growth signals, genome integrity and cell size. Its failure is a defining step in tumour formation, which is why so many of its components are tumour suppressors. The core brake is the retinoblastoma protein and its relatives RB1, RBL1 and RBL2 holding E2F-dependent transcription shut, reinforced by CDK inhibitors such as CDKN1A, CDKN2B and CDKN2D that block cyclin-CDK2 activity, and by p53-directed arrest after DNA damage. Additional restraint comes from PTEN dampening growth factor signalling, from ubiquitin-ligase-mediated destruction of cyclin D, from WEE1-type inhibitory kinase activity, and from a large complement of microRNAs that lower cyclin and CDK message levels. Differentiation factors including KLF4 feed into the same arrest.

Cells decide in G1 whether to commit to another round of division, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that decision forward by raising cyclin-dependent kinase activity at the G1/S boundary.
