Passing this restriction point commits a cell to DNA replication, so its inappropriate activation is one of the commonest routes to unchecked proliferation in cancer, while its restraint underlies quiescence and differentiation. D-type cyclins with cyclin E partners drive the kinase activity that inactivates retinoblastoma protein and releases E2F-dependent transcription, seen here in TFDP1 and in the replication licensing factor CDC6 and the ribonucleotide reductase subunits RRM1 and RRM2 that supply deoxynucleotides. Growth-factor and receptor signalling through EGFR and AKT1, MDM2-mediated restraint of p53, chromatin and transcription-elongation regulators, and a large complement of microRNAs all feed into the same commitment step.

This is the restraining side of microtubule protein recruitment: processes that keep a protein from accumulating on the microtubule lattice or its ends, or that strip it off once there. Such negative control matters because microtubule-binding proteins must be released as well as loaded for plus-end tracking, cargo handover, cilium assembly and mitotic spindle turnover to proceed rather than freeze in place. Two mechanisms are represented. Tau-tubulin kinase 2 phosphorylates microtubule-associated substrates, including CAP-Gly plus-end binding proteins, lowering their affinity for the polymer. The ABHD17 family of depalmitoylating serine hydrolases removes S-palmitoyl groups, altering membrane and cytoskeletal partitioning of their substrates. MAP1A, a structural microtubule-associated protein of neurons, contributes by occupying the lattice and competing with other binders. The combined effect is spatial and temporal limitation of who sits on a microtubule and for how long.

Every dividing cell must build a bipolar spindle, attach each chromosome to it, and take the structure apart again, and this is the microtubule cytoskeleton organization that serves mitosis. Its output is accurate chromosome segregation; when it fails, cells become aneuploid or multinucleated, a route to developmental microcephaly and to the chromosomal instability of tumours. Centrosome and spindle pole components such as pericentrin, CEP192, CDK5RAP2 and gamma-tubulin nucleate microtubules, TPX2 and Aurora A activate spindle assembly, and the kinetochore NDC80 complex with CENPE couples chromosomes to dynamic microtubule ends. Kinesins including KIF11 and KIF15 slide antiparallel microtubules to separate poles while dynein-dynactin with NUMA1 and LIS1 orients the spindle relative to the cell cortex. Central spindle regulators and ESCRT subunits then complete cleavage furrow ingression and abscission, linking spindle architecture to cytokinesis and to oriented division in tissues.

Most cells extend a single non-motile primary cilium, an antenna for Hedgehog and other developmental signals, and this pathway sets whether that organelle is built and how long it grows. Control begins at the mother centriole, where a kinase that phosphorylates distal appendage proteins licenses removal of capping factors and initiates axoneme extension, while centriolar proteins such as CEP135 and CPAP govern centriole structure and restrain excessive elongation. Septins form a diffusion barrier at the ciliary base that separates ciliary membrane from the rest of the plasma membrane, transport and trafficking factors including a BBSome subunit deliver cargo, and microtubule-associated proteins tune axoneme stability; the male germ cell kinase MAK limits photoreceptor outer segment length. Loss of these controls produces ciliopathies, with retinal degeneration, polycystic kidney disease and skeletal and neurodevelopmental defects.

Most quiescent human cells extend a single non-motile primary cilium, the antenna through which Hedgehog, PDGF and other signals are received, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote its assembly rather than merely permit it. Ciliogenesis begins when the mother centriole docks at the membrane and converts to a basal body, and the genes here act at that transition: CEP135 and CPAP build and set the length of the centriole itself, TTBK2 is recruited to the distal appendages to trigger removal of the capping protein that blocks axoneme extension, and WRAP73 contributes to basal body and spindle pole organisation. Septins form a diffusion barrier at the ciliary base that separates ciliary from plasma membrane. Loss of these activities gives ciliopathy phenotypes — retinal degeneration, as with the photoreceptor axoneme protein RP1, skeletal and neurodevelopmental defects, and disrupted Hedgehog patterning.

Cells must scale their antioxidant defences to the amount of oxidative damage they face, and this regulation of the response to oxidative stress sets how strongly and how long those defences are deployed. The central switch is the KEAP1-NFE2L2 pair: KEAP1 targets the transcription factor for ubiquitin-dependent degradation with a cullin-RING ligase component, and its release under electrophilic or oxidant stress allows induction of genes such as the cystine importer SLC7A11, which feeds glutathione synthesis. Sestrins, OXR1 and selenoprotein N add further buffering, while PINK1 and parkin remove damaged mitochondria that would otherwise keep generating reactive oxygen species. Lipid-handling and cofactor genes, including GCH1 for tetrahydrobiopterin, tune the redox environment itself. Too little of this control leaves neurons and other long-lived cells vulnerable to degeneration; too much sustains the antioxidant programme that lets tumour cells survive.

Cells need to damp their own antioxidant and stress-response programmes once a reactive oxygen challenge has passed, and negative regulation of the response to oxidative stress covers the brakes that keep that response proportionate. Persistent or excessive activation is costly: it reprogrammes metabolism, blunts redox signalling that cells use for normal growth cues, and in tumours a constitutively antioxidant state supports survival under stress. The clearest mechanism here is the KEAP1-based ubiquitin ligase, in which KEAP1 acts as the redox sensor and substrate adaptor and RBX1 supplies the ligase core, marking NRF2 for degradation so that antioxidant gene expression stays off in unstressed cells. Other members act on chromatin, on deubiquitination, and on oxidation resistance itself, tying this restraint to transcriptional control, protein turnover and neuronal survival under metabolic stress.

Autophagosome formation has to be held in check when nutrients are plentiful or when unrestrained self-digestion would damage a cell, and this pathway covers the brakes applied to that step. Suppressing autophagosome assembly keeps basal turnover matched to demand, and its loss shifts cells toward excessive sequestration of cytoplasm and organelles; conversely, too much suppression blocks clearance of damaged mitochondria and aggregated proteins, a defect linked to neurodegeneration through LRRK2 and PINK1. Inhibitory inputs act at several levels: chromatin and transcriptional regulators such as EHMT2 and NUPR1 limit expression of autophagy genes, PHF23 restrains the initiation machinery centred on BECN1, FEZ1 and FEZ2 interfere with early assembly, and membrane-trafficking components including SEC22B, SCFD1 and TMEM39A govern how much lipid and cargo reaches the nascent phagophore. Together these constitute the negative arm of autophagy initiation control.

Cells build long polymer fibers — actin filaments, microtubules, spectrin networks and sarcomeric arrays — and the regulation of supramolecular fiber organization covers everything that sets how fast they form, how long and how bundled they become, and when they are taken apart. This control determines cell shape, motility, adhesion, division and neurite outgrowth, and its failure underlies neurodegeneration, cardiomyopathy and defective immune cell migration. Rho-family GTPases with their many exchange factors and GAPs feed into effectors such as ROCK, PAK and LIM kinases, which act on cofilin and destrin to gate filament severing; profilins, capping proteins, gelsolin, tropomodulins and thymosin control monomer supply and filament ends; Arp2/3 with WAVE, WASH and WASP complexes nucleates branches. On the microtubule side, CAMSAPs, CLASPs, EB proteins, katanin, spastin and the augmin complex govern minus-end stability, severing and branched nucleation, while spectrins and tropomyosins organize the mature fiber lattice.</description>

Cells constantly restrain the growth of actin filaments, microtubules and other polymeric assemblies, and the negative regulation of supramolecular fiber organization gathers the machinery that caps, severs, sequesters and depolymerizes them. Setting limits on filament length and number is what makes the cytoskeleton dynamic rather than static: lamellipodia retract, spindles and cilia adopt defined geometry, sarcomere thin filaments stop at fixed length, and membrane-associated spectrin-adducin networks remain organized. Capping proteins and their CARMIL regulators block barbed-end elongation, tropomodulins and leiomodins cap pointed ends, gelsolin, cofilin and the slingshot phosphatases that reactivate it promote filament disassembly, and stathmins sequester tubulin while prefoldin chaperones its folding. Loss of such braking activity produces disordered protrusion, impaired cell migration and adhesion, and in the nervous system aberrant dendritic and axonal architecture; several members are also linked to neurodegeneration and myopathy.

Neuroepithelial cells are the founding cells of the neural tube, and this pathway covers the signals that push uncommitted ectoderm toward that fate and increase the rate at which it is adopted. Getting this right sets up the neural plate and its folding into a tube, so that later neural progenitors and the whole central nervous system have a starting population; disturbance contributes to neural tube closure defects. The genes point to two convergent inputs: bone morphogenetic protein ligands acting through receptor serine/threonine kinases to pattern dorsal ectoderm, and canonical Wnt output in which stabilised beta-catenin partners with LEF1 to drive transcription of fate-specifying targets. Nuclear import machinery and an mTORC1 scaffold contribute by controlling where signalling effectors go and how growth and translation are tuned during commitment.

Attaching a chain of ubiquitins to a substrate usually marks it for proteasomal destruction, but polyubiquitin chains also act as signalling scaffolds, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how much of that modification a protein receives. Tuning it determines protein half-life, the strength of inflammatory signalling and the threshold for cell death. Members span the machinery and its controllers: E2 conjugating enzymes and their dimerisation partners, including the UBE2N–UBE2V1/UBE2V2 pairs that build the K63-linked chains used for signalling rather than degradation; RING and BIR-domain ligases such as BIRC2 and XIAP; F-box substrate receptors like SKP2 and FBXO4 that select cell cycle targets; and the mitophagy ligase PRKN. Also present are upstream signalling proteins such as NOD2 and RIPK2, linking bacterial peptidoglycan sensing to ubiquitin-dependent NF-κB activation. Dysregulation contributes to inflammatory disease, apoptosis resistance in cancer and parkinsonism.

Polyubiquitin chains commit proteins to proteasomal destruction or reshape signalling complexes, so restraining chain assembly is a way of protecting substrates and tuning the pathways they serve. Negative regulation of protein polyubiquitination covers the diverse brakes on this step: proteins that shield a substrate from its ligase, that inhibit ligase or E2 activity, or that intercept assembled chains. Among the members, GPS2 blocks ubiquitin transfer within corepressor complexes and thereby stabilises signalling intermediates, TRIM44 is a ubiquitin-binding family member lacking ligase activity that acts to protect rather than mark substrates, and PLAA participates in ubiquitin-dependent membrane protein handling. Also represented are a microRNA and a mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase, indicating control at transcriptional and post-translational levels. The consequence is longer substrate half-life and dampened ubiquitin-dependent signalling, relevant to inflammation, DNA damage responses and centrosome regulation.

Attaching a polyubiquitin chain to a protein marks it for proteasomal destruction or, when the linkage differs, converts it into a signalling scaffold; this set covers the factors that raise the rate and extent of protein polyubiquitination. Positive regulation of this step determines how quickly cell cycle regulators such as cyclin D1 and p27 are cleared, how damaged mitochondria are tagged for autophagic removal by the parkin ubiquitin ligase, and how strongly innate immune signalling proceeds. The ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBE2N with its UEV partners UBE2V1 and UBE2V2 builds K63-linked chains that are not degradative but recruit kinase complexes, and the inhibitor-of-apoptosis ligases BIRC2 and XIAP together with RIPK2 use such chains downstream of the bacterial peptidoglycan sensor NOD2 to activate NF-κB. Loss of these activities is linked to inflammatory disease and to parkinsonism from failed mitochondrial quality control.

Control over how much sterol and other hydroxylated lipid a cell makes is exercised here, and most of the pathway is the feedback circuitry that keeps cholesterol synthesis matched to demand. Its output sets membrane composition, lipoprotein production and the supply of precursors for steroid hormones and bile acids; loss of restraint underlies hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. The core is sterol-sensing in the endoplasmic reticulum, where SCAP and INSIG1 retain or release SREBF1 and SREBF2 for proteolytic activation by the site-1 and site-2 proteases, while ERLIN proteins and the ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 impose degradative control. Energy status enters through AMPK, hormonal and G protein-coupled inputs through receptors such as PTH1R and LHCGR, and a set of microRNAs adds post-transcriptional tuning. Efflux transporters and apolipoproteins couple synthesis to cholesterol export, and CYP7A1 diverts sterol into bile acids.

Cells must stop making sterols when they already have enough, and this braking of alcohol — chiefly cholesterol — biosynthesis is how that is enforced. Without it, sterol synthesis runs unchecked, membranes and lipoproteins overload, and the lipid excess that underlies atherosclerosis follows. The core mechanism is feedback at the endoplasmic reticulum: when sterols accumulate, INSIG1 retains the SCAP–SREBP complex in the ER so the transcription factor is never processed to its active nuclear form, shutting off the genes for the mevalonate route. In parallel, ERLIN1 and ERLIN2 recognise sterol-loaded HMG-CoA reductase and the membrane ubiquitin ligase MARCHF6 marks rate-limiting enzymes for degradation, adding post-translational shutdown to transcriptional shutdown. Extracellular cholesterol return by APOE, BMP ligands, the transcriptional repressor REST, and several microRNAs that target biosynthetic transcripts provide further layers of restraint.

Cholesterol and other sterols are alcohols, and this grouping collects the signals that push their biosynthesis upward — the positive arm of control over alcohol biosynthetic processes. It matters because sterol supply sets membrane composition, steroid hormone output and bile acid production, and unchecked stimulation of the same route drives hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. The core machinery is the sterol-sensing transcriptional switch: SCAP escorts SREBF1 and SREBF2 precursors for cleavage by site-2 protease (MBTPS2), releasing transcription factors that turn on lipogenic and cholesterogenic genes. Layered on top are hormone and nucleotide receptors signalling through heterotrimeric G proteins and kinases such as PRKACA and MAPK1, the AMPK catalytic subunit PRKAA1 as an energy-sensing brake point, sterol transporters ABCG1 and ABCG4, the bile acid-committing enzyme CYP7A1, and microRNAs of the miR-183 cluster acting as post-transcriptional tuners.

Delivery and retention of proteins at the early endosome determines what an internalized receptor does next " be recycled to the surface, sorted into a degradative route, or held in a compartment where it can keep signalling. The early endosome is the first sorting station after endocytosis, so protein localization to it governs the duration of growth factor responses and the turnover of surface receptors. RAB5A is the defining GTPase that specifies this compartment and recruits its tethering and fusion machinery, while ARL8B links endosomal and lysosomal membrane traffic. Ligands such as EGF and VEGFA, with the co-receptor NRP1, enter this route and have their signalling output shaped by it. Membrane"cytoskeleton crosslinkers of the ezrin"radixin"moesin family, together with NF2 and ROCK2, couple endosomal cargo to cortical actin, and SORL1 acts as a sorting receptor whose failure is tied to amyloid precursor protein mishandling in Alzheimer disease.

Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic compartments of most excitatory synapses in the brain, and once formed they must be actively held in place; the regulation of dendritic spine maintenance covers the signals that set how long spines persist and therefore how stable a synaptic connection is. Because spine loss tracks cognitive decline, this control point matters for learning, memory and the early synaptic pathology of Alzheimer's disease, where APOE, APP and prion protein all act on spine stability, with Fyn kinase and GluN2B-containing NMDA receptors transducing the damaging signals. Structural upkeep depends on actin dynamics through cofilin and on scaffolding by Homer, while retromer subunit VPS35 supplies the endosomal trafficking that returns receptors and membrane to the spine. Microglial receptor signalling and transcriptional regulators contribute further tuning, linking spine persistence to immune and gene-expression inputs.

negative regulation of dendritic spine maintenance describes the processes that destabilise existing dendritic spines, the small postsynaptic protrusions that carry excitatory synapses. Spine loss is how circuits are pruned during refinement and learning, but it is also the structural correlate of cognitive decline: the genes here are the ones through which amyloid- cbeta and prion protein drive synapse elimination in neurodegenerative disease. Amyloid precursor protein and its processing, the APOE isoform background, and cellular prion protein converge on NMDA receptor signalling through GluN2B and the tyrosine kinase FYN, which in turn engages cofilin-dependent remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton that gives a spine its shape. A microRNA contributes post-transcriptional restraint of the same machinery. The pathway therefore links extracellular signals to actin depolymerisation, and its overactivation is the proximate cause of synaptic failure preceding neuronal death in Alzheimer's disease.

Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic compartments of most excitatory synapses, and their persistence is actively opposed as well as supported; negative regulation of dendritic spine maintenance covers the signals that destabilise and eliminate existing spines. Controlled spine loss refines circuits during development and underlies experience-dependent remodelling, but when it runs unchecked it produces the synapse loss that tracks most closely with cognitive decline in Alzheimer's disease. The genes here converge on that route: amyloid precursor protein and its cleavage products, the ApoE lipoprotein that governs amyloid handling, prion protein as a surface receptor, and the Fyn kinase–NMDA receptor GluN2B axis that transmits the signal inward. Cofilin acts at the endpoint, severing the actin filaments that give a spine its shape.

Dendritic spines are the postsynaptic protrusions that hold most excitatory synapses on principal neurons, and once formed they must be actively preserved; this pathway covers the signals that increase the stability and persistence of existing spines rather than making new ones. Spine maintenance sets how much synaptic memory a circuit can retain, and its loss is an early feature of Alzheimer's disease and of the dendritic simplification seen in schizophrenia. The genes here span extracellular and intracellular arms: the lipid transport protein APOE, whose variants influence synapse loss with age, insulin acting as a trophic signal at neuronal receptors, the scaffold NEDD9 linking adhesion to cytoskeletal remodelling, and the chromatin reader ZMYND8 together with the risk gene ZNF804A providing transcriptional support. The output is a spine cytoskeleton and adhesion complex reinforced against turnover.

Newly made secretory and membrane proteins leave the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated carriers bound for the Golgi, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate and extent of that export step. It matters because collagen, lipoproteins, hormones and cell-surface receptors all depend on efficient ER exit; when it falters, cargo backs up in the ER and triggers stress responses, and loss of one COPII cargo adaptor causes chylomicron retention disease with fat malabsorption. Mechanistically, a small GTPase of the SAR1 family initiates coat assembly at ER exit sites, SEC24 paralogues select distinct cargo, and the SEC13-SEC31 outer cage deforms the membrane into a budding vesicle. Additional regulators act on GPI-anchor remodelling, Rab GTPase cycling and SNARE-dependent tethering, linking cargo maturation and vesicle fusion to overall secretory throughput.

regulation of mitochondrial electron transport, NADH to ubiquinone controls the throughput of complex I, the entry point where electrons from NADH are passed to ubiquinone and protons are pumped to build the membrane potential that drives ATP synthesis. Tuning this step sets how much energy a cell extracts from fuel and how many reactive oxygen species escape in the process, so its misregulation contributes to oxidative damage and to the neuronal loss of Parkinson disease. The genes act at several levels: a hypoxia-induced microRNA and the alternative subunit NDUFA4L2 dampen complex I activity when oxygen is scarce, an iron-sulfur scaffold supplies the cofactors the enzyme requires, and PINK1, PARK7 and alpha-synuclein link complex I performance to mitochondrial quality control, redox defence and synaptic health. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of oxidative phosphorylation, hypoxic adaptation and neurodegeneration.

Complex I transfers electrons from NADH to ubiquinone, the entry step of the respiratory chain and the point where most mitochondrial proton pumping and much superoxide production begin; regulating its throughput sets how much oxidative phosphorylation a cell runs and how much reactive oxygen it makes. Tuning this step matters under low oxygen, when unrestrained electron flow into a poorly oxidized chain is damaging: hypoxia-induced factors including a microRNA and the complex I subunit paralogue NDUFA4L2 dampen electron entry, while ISCU supplies the iron-sulfur cofactors the enzyme depends on and its loss limits assembly. A second arm is quality control and stress protection, with PINK1 and PARK7 supporting complex I activity and mitochondrial integrity and alpha-synuclein accumulation impairing it. The convergence of these regulators explains why complex I dysfunction is a recurring feature of Parkinson's disease and of ischaemic tissue injury.

Newly internalised cargo passes first through the early endosome, and this pathway covers the processes that increase delivery of proteins to that compartment. Where a receptor or transmembrane protein ends up — recycled to the surface, sorted to lysosomes, or held in a signalling endosome — determines how long a growth factor signal lasts, so promoting early endosomal targeting is a way of controlling signal duration and receptor availability. Growth factors such as EGF and VEGFA drive internalisation of their own receptors, while the ERM proteins ezrin, radixin and moesin together with the related tumour suppressor merlin link membranes to the cortical actin cytoskeleton, and ROCK2 signalling reshapes that cortex during uptake. SORL1 acts as a sorting receptor that routes cargo, including amyloid precursor protein, through endosomes, connecting this trafficking step to neuronal protein handling and Alzheimer's disease risk.

Duplication of nuclear DNA during a mitotic cell cycle, so that each daughter cell inherits one complete copy of the genome. The genes here span the steps of that process: licensing of origins by CDT1 with its inhibitor geminin restricting it to once per cycle, helicase loading through the MCM2-7 subunits, activation via CDC45 and the GINS complex, priming and synthesis by DNA polymerase alpha, and ligation of nascent strands by LIG1. Nucleotide supply is supported by thymidine kinase, while RAD51, BRCA2 and the RECQL5 helicase protect and restart stalled or broken forks by homologous recombination. Because replication is the point at which mutations are fixed and chromosomes become vulnerable, control over it links cell proliferation to genome stability; its deregulation underlies replication stress and tumour development, and loss of fork-protection components causes chromosomal instability syndromes.

Neurofibrillary tangle assembly describes the formation of the intracellular filamentous inclusions of hyperphosphorylated tau that accumulate in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies, and whose distribution tracks the progression of cognitive decline better than amyloid burden does. Tau, encoded by MAPT, normally binds and stabilises axonal microtubules; when its phosphorylation state shifts, it detaches, misfolds and bundles into paired helical filaments that compromise transport and neuronal viability. The balance is set by kinases such as DYRK1A and the microtubule affinity-regulating kinase MARK2 acting against the phosphatase activity represented here by a PP2A catalytic subunit, with a microRNA contributing to tau dosage control. Chaperone activity of HSP90 triages misfolded tau between refolding and degradation, while APOE, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 link tangle formation to lipid handling and endosomal trafficking risk factors for late-onset dementia.

How much amyloid precursor protein is cleaved, and by which route, determines the amount of amyloid-beta a neuron releases, so the processes that tune APP catabolism sit directly upstream of plaque formation in Alzheimer's disease. Regulation operates at several levels: trafficking and sorting proteins such as SORL1, PICALM, BIN1 and the adaptor GGA3 control whether APP meets its secretases in endosomes, reticulon family proteins restrain BACE1, and GSAP influences gamma-secretase cleavage. Lipid and cholesterol handling through APOE, CLU and ABC transporters modifies both processing and clearance, while kinases including GSK3A and DYRK1A, the ROCK kinases and the isomerase PIN1 shift the balance between amyloidogenic and non-amyloidogenic cuts. Inflammatory input via TNF and interferon-gamma signalling, and a large set of microRNAs acting on APP and secretase transcripts, add transcriptional and post-transcriptional control over the same step.

negative regulation of amyloid precursor protein catabolic process describes the brakes on cleavage of amyloid precursor protein, the step that determines how much amyloid-beta a neuron releases. Because amyloid-beta accumulation initiates the plaque pathology of Alzheimer's disease, restraint of this processing is one of the main protective axes in the brain, and several of the genes here are among the strongest genetic risk loci for late-onset disease. The mechanisms are varied: reticulon proteins bind and sequester BACE1 away from its substrate, sortilin-related receptor SORL1 and trafficking adaptors such as BIN1 and GGA3 route the precursor through compartments where secretases cannot act, lipid and lipoprotein handling by APOE, CLU and ABCA7 modulates both cleavage and clearance, and a large panel of microRNAs suppresses secretase and precursor expression. Neurotrophic signalling through IGF1 and NTRK2 feeds into the same restraint.

Amyloid precursor protein is continuously cleaved, and how much of it is routed toward the amyloidogenic secretase pathway sets the supply of amyloid-beta peptide in the brain. This set covers the braking side of that process — factors that stop or slow APP catabolism and thereby limit amyloid-beta production, a control point whose loosening is tied to Alzheimer's disease risk. Several mechanisms converge: reticulon proteins bind and sequester BACE1 away from its substrate, the sorting receptor SORL1 and the trafficking adaptors BIN1 and GGA3 divert APP and BACE1 through endosomal and retrograde routes rather than cleavage-competent compartments, and the lipid-handling and chaperone proteins APOE, CLU and ABCA7 influence both processing and clearance. A large group of microRNAs, including the miR-29 family and miR-15/16 members, represses BACE1 and related transcripts post-transcriptionally. The pathway links membrane trafficking, lipid transport and small-RNA regulation to neuronal proteostasis.

Positive regulation of amyloid precursor protein catabolic process covers the influences that push amyloid precursor protein into its proteolytic routes, increasing the rate at which it is cleaved and, in the amyloidogenic direction, the amount of amyloid-beta peptide generated. This matters because amyloid-beta accumulation is the initiating lesion of Alzheimer's disease, and most of the genes here are recognised late-onset risk factors or drug targets: APOE and clusterin as lipoprotein chaperones, PICALM in endocytic trafficking of APP to the compartments where secretases act, and GSAP as a gamma-secretase activating partner. The set links this cleavage to several upstream inputs, including inflammatory signalling through TNF, interferon-gamma and RAGE with NF-kB and SP1 as transcriptional relays, ephrin-EphA4 and cholinergic receptor signalling at synapses, kinase activity via GSK3 and ROCK2, and caspase-3 cleavage of APP itself, tying amyloid production to neuroinflammation, membrane trafficking and neuronal stress.

Amyloid precursor protein is continuously cleaved by secretases, and the balance of those cleavages sets how much amyloid-beta peptide a neuron releases; this pathway covers the influences that push APP catabolism harder, raising amyloid-beta production and deposition in Alzheimer's disease. The genes act at several levels: gamma-secretase modulation by its activating protein GSAP, kinase input from GSK3A, ROCK2 and the Src-family kinase LYN, lipid and cholesterol handling by APOE, CLU and ABC transporters, endocytic trafficking of APP and secretase components through PICALM, and transcriptional drive via SP1 and the NF-kappaB subunit RELA downstream of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and interferon-gamma acting through its receptor. Ephrin-Eph signalling and the RAGE receptor add surface-initiated regulation. Together these tie amyloidogenic processing to cholesterol metabolism, membrane trafficking and neuroinflammation rather than to a single proteolytic step.

regulation of neurofibrillary tangle assembly controls whether hyperphosphorylated tau aggregates into the paired helical filaments and tangles that accumulate in Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies. Tangle burden tracks closely with neuronal loss and cognitive decline, so the balance struck here determines how quickly a neuron's microtubule cytoskeleton and axonal transport fail. The genes act at two levels: kinases and phosphatases that set tau's phosphorylation state, including DYRK1A, the MARK family that phosphorylates tau's microtubule-binding repeats, and the PP2A catalytic subunit that reverses these marks, plus a microRNA that limits tau expression itself. The remainder are lipid and trafficking proteins of the amyloid axis — APOE, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 — linking extracellular amyloid handling and endosomal sorting to intracellular tau pathology, and accounting for much of the common genetic risk for late-onset dementia.

Neurofibrillary tangles are intraneuronal aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau, and this pathway covers the influences that promote or restrain their formation, a process central to Alzheimer's disease and other tauopathies where tangle burden tracks with neuronal loss and cognitive decline. Control operates largely through tau phosphorylation balance: the kinases DYRK1A and MARK2 phosphorylate tau at sites that reduce microtubule binding and favour aggregation, while a catalytic subunit of protein phosphatase 2A reverses such marks. Post-transcriptional limits on tau production are set by microRNA regulation. Lipid and trafficking factors act from the other side, with APOE isoforms, clusterin and the sorting receptor SORL1 shaping amyloid handling, endosomal trafficking and glial responses that feed back onto tau pathology. Together these determine how quickly tau shifts from a microtubule-stabilising protein to a filamentous deposit.

Ubiquitin chains are removed as well as added, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise deubiquitinase activity on target proteins, tuning how long a ubiquitin signal lasts. Because ubiquitination controls both proteasomal degradation and non-degradative signalling, promoting its reversal changes protein half-life and switches signalling complexes off. Several of the components here converge on restraining NF- cEB-driven inflammation: TANK and TNIP1 are adaptors that help direct deubiquitinating activity toward ubiquitinated signalling intermediates downstream of innate immune receptors, and loss of this brake is associated with autoimmune and inflammatory disease. VCP, an AAA-ATPase segregase, extracts ubiquitinated substrates from membranes and complexes and works with associated deubiquitinases during protein quality control. The set therefore links ubiquitin chain editing to inflammatory signal termination, ribosome and stress surveillance, and proteostasis.

Organelles are not permanent structures; several must be taken apart on cue, and this pathway covers the controlled disaggregation of an organelle into its components. Its largest arm is ribosome disassembly during quality control, where stalled or collided ribosomes are recognised and split so that faulty nascent chains can be ubiquitinated and extracted: rescue and recycling factors such as PELO, HBS1L and ABCE1 separate the subunits, ZNF598 marks collisions, and LTN1 with NEMF and the VCP/UFD1/NPLOC4 segregase clears the trapped polypeptide, with parallel machinery acting on mitochondrial ribosomes. Other components dismantle the Golgi ribbon before mitosis under CDK1 and PLK activity, disassemble the primary cilium, and mobilise lipid droplets through perilipins and ATGL under AMPK control. Failure leaves aggregation-prone translation products and undivided organelles, contributing to proteotoxic stress and neurodegeneration.

Bone is built and remodelled continuously, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how fast and how far that development proceeds — setting skeletal size, shape and mineral content, with failures showing up as skeletal dysplasia, abnormal ossification or reduced bone mass. The genes act at several levels: osteocalcin, an osteoblast-secreted matrix protein whose activity depends on vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX, links bone matrix to mineral handling and endocrine signalling; lysyl oxidase cross-links collagen to give the matrix its tensile strength; GLI3 transmits hedgehog patterning signals that govern skeletal element formation; and the VEGF receptor KDR couples vascular invasion to endochondral bone growth. Chromatin-level regulation through the acetyltransferase KAT2A and additional membrane and matrix proteins modulate osteoblast differentiation, tying the programme to growth factor signalling, angiogenesis and extracellular matrix assembly.

Glycoproteins must be made, modified and disposed of at controlled rates, and this pathway covers the inputs that set those rates rather than the glycosyltransferase chemistry itself. Much of it concerns amyloid precursor protein processing: nicastrin, BACE2, the BRICHOS-domain ITM2 family, MESD and several microRNAs tune how a heavily glycosylated membrane protein is cleaved and cleared, linking this regulation to Alzheimer disease risk and to lipid transporters such as ABCA7. A second arm sets glycosaminoglycan and proteoglycan output, where FAM20B phosphorylates the xylose of the linker region and PXYLP1 removes that phosphate, a switch that decides whether chain elongation proceeds and thereby shapes cartilage and extracellular matrix. Secreted pentraxins, cystatin C, RAB1 proteins governing ER-to-Golgi traffic, and growth factor and chemokine signalling supply further control, placing this biology at the interface of secretory throughput and tissue remodelling.

This is the restraining side of glycoprotein metabolism: the set of activities that slow or block the synthesis, processing and turnover of glycoproteins. Much of the biology here converges on amyloid precursor protein, a glycoprotein whose proteolytic handling determines whether amyloid-beta accumulates in the brain. Membrane proteins of the BRICHOS/ITM2 family, the aspartyl protease homologue BACE2, cystatin C and the lipid transporter ABCA7 each limit amyloidogenic processing or the aggregation of its products, and a large complement of microRNAs adds post-transcriptional damping of the secretase machinery and its substrates. Also represented are modifiers of glycan chain initiation and glycosyltransferase activity, linking the pathway to proteoglycan and N-glycan output. Loss of this negative control shifts the balance toward amyloid deposition and altered glycan decoration of secreted and surface proteins, with consequences for neurodegeneration and connective tissue integrity.

Glycoproteins must be synthesised, modified and turned over at rates matched to cellular demand, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that metabolism upward — increasing the production, glycosylation or processing of glycoproteins and proteoglycans. It matters for the composition of the cell surface and extracellular matrix, for secretory output, and for the sulfation and chain length of proteoglycan glycosaminoglycans, where PXYLP1 acts as a phosphatase on xylose during chondroitin chain initiation. The genes span several routes into that output: chemokine signalling through CCL19, CCL21 and CCR7, growth factor input via IGF1, Wnt-responsive transcription through CTNNB1 and TCF7L2, phospholipase C signalling, and RAB1 GTPases driving ER-to-Golgi transport, the compartment where glycan maturation occurs. NCSTN links the set to regulated intramembrane proteolysis of membrane glycoproteins. Misregulation affects matrix quality, as in disorders of proteoglycan and collagen-associated glycan handling.

Regulation of opsonization controls how heavily microbes and dying cells are coated with complement proteins to mark them for phagocyte recognition and clearance. This tuning determines whether infections are cleared efficiently, whether apoptotic debris and immune complexes are removed without inflammation, and whether complement instead damages host tissue; deficiencies in these components predispose to encapsulated bacterial infection and to lupus-like autoimmunity. The genes cover the recognition arms that initiate deposition — mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins acting through the MASP proteases — together with the classical pathway components C2 and C4 and the alternative pathway amplifiers factor B and properdin, all converging on C3 as the opsonin deposited on the target surface. Counterbalancing them, C4b-binding protein restrains classical and lectin pathway activation, setting the ceiling on how much C3b accumulates.

Opsonization is the coating of microbes and dying cells with complement proteins and other tags so that phagocytes can recognize and engulf them; controlling how much of this coating occurs sets the balance between clearing pathogens and damaging host tissue. The genes here build the classical and lectin routes to C3 deposition: C2, C4A/C4B and C3 itself, factor B and properdin for the alternative amplification loop, and the recognition molecules mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins with their associated proteases MASP1 and MASP2. Regulation runs in both directions — properdin stabilizes the C3 convertase to boost surface tagging, while the C4b-binding protein chains restrain classical pathway convertase activity and limit deposition on host surfaces. Secreted phospholipase PLA2G5 contributes by modifying bacterial membranes. Loss of these components predisposes to pyogenic and meningococcal infection and to impaired clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris.

Tissue injury triggers a coordinated program of bleeding control, inflammation, re-epithelialization and matrix remodelling, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly and how long that program runs. Its tuning determines whether a wound closes cleanly, fails to heal as in chronic ulcers, or overshoots into fibrosis and scarring. Coagulation and fibrinolysis are heavily represented: fibrinogen chains, thrombin and its protease-activated receptors, plasminogen with its activators PLAT and PLAU, and serpin brakes such as SERPINE1 and antithrombin, alongside platelet surface proteins and thromboregulators like thrombomodulin and nitric oxide synthase. Other members drive the cellular phases, including growth factors and their receptors, integrin-linked adhesion and focal adhesion kinase signalling, tight junction and barrier proteins that restore epithelial continuity, cytokines such as TNF, IL10 and IL33, and a set of microRNAs that damp or sustain these responses. Neurite outgrowth inhibitor receptors extend the same logic to injury in nervous tissue.

Wound healing must be self-limiting, and this collection of brakes on the response to wounding keeps clotting, platelet activation, inflammation and tissue remodelling proportionate to the injury. Anticoagulant and fibrinolytic regulators dominate: protein C and its cofactor thrombomodulin, protein S, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, antithrombin-like serpins and plasminogen activator inhibitors that cap plasmin generation by tPA and uPA, alongside the contact-system and fibrinogen components whose activity they constrain. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase and prostacyclin-type signalling suppress platelet adhesion through receptors such as GP1BA, while PTEN, PTPN6, SMAD3 and STAT3 set limits on the growth-factor and cytokine drive from PDGF, FGF2, TNF and IL33 that fuels fibroblast migration and scarring. Myelin-associated Nogo receptors and axon guidance inhibitors extend the same logic to the injured nervous system, where they block regrowth. Loss of these restraints favours thrombosis, chronic inflammation and fibrosis.

Tissue injury triggers a coordinated programme of clotting, inflammation, re-epithelialisation and matrix remodelling, and this set covers the inputs that amplify that response to wounding rather than restrain it. Its output is haemostasis and closure: without adequate amplification, bleeding continues and wounds fail to heal; with excess, fibrosis and thrombosis follow. Coagulation and fibrinolysis components such as prothrombin, factor VII, tissue factor, plasminogen and its activators, together with the thrombin receptor and thrombomodulin, set the balance between clot formation and dissolution. Integrin and kindlin adhesion machinery, focal adhesion kinase and myosin light chain kinase drive platelet activation and keratinocyte migration, while growth factors, alarmins including HMGB1, NADPH oxidases, tight junction proteins and several microRNAs tune epithelial barrier restoration, angiogenesis and the inflammatory and oxidative signalling that accompanies repair.

negative regulation of leukocyte cell-cell adhesion covers the brakes that limit how strongly immune cells stick to one another, and therefore how readily lymphocytes form stable synapses and become activated. It is the machinery of peripheral tolerance: without it, T cells engage antigen-presenting cells unchecked and autoimmunity or chronic inflammation follows, while tumours exploit the same brakes to escape immune attack. The genes are dominated by inhibitory surface receptors and their ligands, including CTLA4, PDCD1 with CD274, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA and HAVCR2, which recruit phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN22 to damp antigen receptor signalling and integrin avidity. Complementing these are intracellular restraints — CBL and CBLB ubiquitin ligases, SOCS proteins, CSK, proteasome subunits — plus regulatory T cell programming through FOXP3, IL10 and TGFB1, and a large set of microRNAs tuning adhesion and activation thresholds.

Immune responses have to be damped as well as started, and this collection of brakes on leukocyte cell-cell adhesion covers the processes that reduce how often and how tightly lymphocytes stick to each other and to antigen-presenting cells. Loss of these restraints permits runaway T cell activation, autoimmunity and chronic inflammation; their exaggeration in tumours produces immune evasion. Much of the content is inhibitory receptor signalling at the immune synapse, where CTLA4, PDCD1 and its ligands CD274 and PDCD1LG2, LAG3, TIGIT, BTLA, HAVCR2 and the VSIR checkpoint recruit phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN22 and PTPN2 to blunt kinase signalling. Complementary arms include SOCS1-mediated cytokine feedback, ubiquitin ligases CBLB, ITCH and PELI1 with the RC3H1/RC3H2 RNA-decay system, immunosuppressive mediators IL10, TGFB1, IDO1 and arginases, galectins, and FOXP3-dependent regulatory T cell identity.

Immune cells must stick to one another to work: a T cell cannot be activated without forming a stable contact with an antigen-presenting cell, and leukocytes cannot leave the blood without arresting on endothelium. This programme covers the signals and molecules that increase such leukocyte cell-cell adhesion, and it underlies antigen presentation, lymphocyte priming in lymph nodes, and the recruitment of cells into inflamed tissue; when it is driven too hard it sustains chronic inflammation and autoimmunity, and when it fails immunodeficiency follows. MHC class I and class II molecules paired with CD4, CD28, ICOS and other costimulatory receptors build the immunological synapse, while selectins, ITGB2 and ITGA4 integrins with VCAM1 mediate rolling and firm attachment. Cytokines and chemokines such as IL2, IL12, TNF, CCL19 and CCL21 raise adhesiveness, and proximal kinases including LCK, ZAP70, SYK and VAV1 convert receptor engagement into cytoskeletal remodelling and transcriptional change.

Membrane rafts are cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich microdomains that concentrate receptors and signalling enzymes, and this pathway covers the delivery and retention of proteins within them. Sorting a protein into a raft changes what it can meet: clustering of signalling components there sets the threshold for immune receptor activation, adhesion, and ion pump distribution at the plasma membrane. The genes reflect several routes to raft residence — scaffolding by caveolin and flotillin, the raft-linking adaptor RFTN1 that positions B cell and innate immune receptors, and the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC2, whose addition of lipid chains to substrate proteins provides the membrane anchoring that raft partitioning depends on. Cholesterol availability is itself regulated here, since CYP46A1 hydroxylates cholesterol to permit its turnover in neurons. Loss of such localization mislocalizes receptors and blunts the signalling and trafficking events that depend on ordered lipid domains.

Meiosis halves the genome and shuffles it, and the processes gathered here are the steps that make that possible in oocytes and spermatocytes: commitment to the meiotic programme, programmed double-strand break formation, homologue pairing and recombination, and the two specialised divisions that follow. Failure produces infertility, arrested gametogenesis, or aneuploid eggs and embryos. A topoisomerase-like enzyme cuts DNA at hotspots chosen by a zinc-finger methyltransferase; meiosis-specific recombinases and mismatch-repair-related factors convert those breaks into crossovers, while the synaptonemal complex and HORMA-domain proteins hold homologues together and monitor progress. Cohesin with meiotic subunits, shugoshins, and separase enforce the stepwise loss of cohesion that separates homologues first and sisters second. Telomere attachment to the nuclear envelope, spindle and kinetochore components, and kinase-phosphatase switches controlling cyclin-dependent kinase activity time entry, arrest, and resumption of the divisions.

Somatic cell proliferation requires that a cell duplicate its genome once and segregate the copies equally, and the mitotic cell cycle process encompasses the ordered events that accomplish this: licensing and firing of replication origins, chromosome condensation and cohesion, spindle assembly, kinetochore attachment, anaphase and cytokinesis. Cyclins paired with cyclin-dependent kinases drive progression, while inhibitors such as CDKN1A and the retinoblastoma-E2F axis restrain entry; the anaphase-promoting complex with CDC20 or FZR1 triggers timed destruction of securin and mitotic cyclins. Aurora and Polo-like kinases, condensin and cohesin complexes, kinesins and dynein organize chromosomes and microtubules, and spindle checkpoint proteins including MAD2L1 and BUB1B delay separation until attachments are correct. DNA damage and replication checkpoints signalling through ATM, ATR and CHEK1 arrest the cycle for repair. Loss of these controls produces aneuploidy, genome instability and tumour growth.}

Cells decide not only which proteins to destroy but how fast, and this pathway covers the regulatory layer that tunes proteolysis during protein catabolism. Setting that rate governs the half-lives of cell cycle drivers, transcription factors and signalling intermediates, clears misfolded and damaged proteins, and when it fails leaves aggregates behind — the reason many components here are neurodegeneration genes such as PRKN, PINK1, LRRK2, ATXN3 and UBQLN2. The core machinery is the 26S proteasome, represented by its full complement of alpha and beta core subunits and ATPase and non-ATPase regulatory subunits, together with activator and inhibitor caps, shuttling ubiquitin receptors, the segregase VCP, and deubiquitinases that edit chains before commitment. Around it sit substrate-selecting ubiquitin ligases and adaptors including MDM2, FBXW7, STUB1, KEAP1 and SCF components, chaperones, kinases and sumoylation factors that mark, spare or accelerate individual targets, coupling degradation to growth signalling, oxidative stress responses and ER quality control.

negative regulation of proteolysis involved in protein catabolic process covers the braking mechanisms that protect proteins from destruction by the proteasome and lysosome, setting how long a given protein persists and therefore how strongly its signal is felt. Stabilising a substrate is as decisive as degrading it: p53 rescue by USP7, ribosomal protein RPL5/RPL11 restraint of MDM2, and CDKN2A-linked control of the nucleolar stress response all depend on blocking turnover, and their loss underlies tumour progression and neurodegeneration. Mechanisms represented here include deubiquitinases that reverse ubiquitin marks before commitment to degradation, proteasome inhibitors such as PSMF1 and shuttling cofactors like UBXN1 and SGTA that divert clients away from proteolysis, chaperone-based triage by BAG proteins and HSP90, and UFM1 pathway components. Together they tune protein quality control, developmental signalling, and stress adaptation by determining which substrates escape catabolism.

Protein degradation must be restrained as well as driven, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that spare a substrate from proteolysis during its catabolism. Stabilising a protein rather than destroying it sets the abundance of tumour suppressors, cell cycle regulators and signalling receptors, so these brakes decide the half-life of much of the proteome. Deubiquitinating enzymes such as USP7, USP9X, USP5, USP14 and UCHL5 strip ubiquitin chains before or at the proteasome, reversing the degradation signal; USP14 and the proteasome inhibitor PSMF1 act directly at the particle to damp its activity. Chaperone and cochaperone components including BAG6, SGTA, HSP90AB1 and UBX-domain adaptors triage misfolded clients away from immediate destruction, while ribosomal proteins RPL5, RPL11 and RPL23 stabilise p53 by sequestering MDM2. Loss of such restraint accelerates turnover of regulatory proteins and contributes to tumour suppressor loss and muscle atrophy.

Cells dispose of damaged, misfolded and short-lived regulatory proteins by tagging them for destruction, and this collection covers the factors that raise the rate of that proteolytic breakdown. Increasing flux through protein catabolism sets the lifetime of cell cycle regulators, transcription factors and signalling intermediates, clears the endoplasmic reticulum of terminally misfolded substrates, and removes aggregates that would otherwise be toxic to neurons. Represented are ubiquitin ligases and their substrate adaptors such as MDM2, FBXW7, KEAP1, STUB1, PRKN and SMURF1, the anaphase-promoting complex activators CDC20 and FZR1, ubiquitin-binding shuttles and chaperones including UBQLN1/2, BAG6, VCP and DNAJB2, proteasome ATPase subunits, and kinases such as GSK3B and CSNK1D that prime substrates by phosphorylation. Deubiquitinases and the ER-associated degradation machinery are also present, linking this activity to the unfolded protein response, Wnt and NRF2 signalling, and neurodegeneration.

regulation of extracellular matrix organization controls how much matrix a tissue builds, how it is cross-linked and assembled, and how fast it is broken down again. This balance determines tissue stiffness and architecture during development and wound healing, and its loss drives fibrosis of lung, liver, kidney and heart as well as the stromal remodelling that lets tumours invade. TGF-beta signalling through its receptors and SMAD3/SMAD4 is the dominant pro-matrix input, opposed by protease inhibitors such as TIMP3 and RECK that restrain metalloproteinase activity. Collagen and laminin receptors including the discoidin domain kinases DDR1/DDR2 and integrins let cells sense the matrix they have made and adjust output, while transcription factors such as SOX9, RUNX1 and PPARG set matrix programmes by cell type. Numerous microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, tune collagen and basement membrane gene expression post-transcriptionally.

Tissues control not just how much matrix they make but how it is assembled, cross-linked and turned over, and this regulatory layer determines whether a basement membrane forms correctly, a wound heals or a tissue scars. Signals acting here include TGF-beta ligands with their receptors and SMAD3/SMAD4 effectors, BMP2, interleukin-6 acting through STAT3, and Notch, converging on transcription factors such as RUNX1, SOX9, PPARG and PRDM5 that set the expression of structural components. Collagen VI, laminin chains and nidogen represent the matrix being organized, while TIMP3 and RECK restrain metalloproteinase activity, hyaluronan synthase and heparanase modify glycan scaffolds, and collagen receptors DDR1 and DDR2 report fibril state back to the cell. Numerous microRNAs, including the miR-29 family, tune these transcripts. Dysregulation drives fibrosis, aneurysm and connective tissue disorders, and supports tumour stroma remodelling.

negative regulation of extracellular matrix organization is the braking system on matrix assembly, restraining how much collagen and other structural protein is deposited and cross-linked around cells. It matters because unchecked matrix accumulation is fibrosis: the same restraint keeps vessel walls compliant, cartilage properly composed, and healing wounds from scarring excessively, while its loss underlies organ fibrosis and tumour desmoplasia. Two kinds of control appear here. Protease and protease-inhibitor balance is set by TIMP3, RECK, cystatin C, and the surface peptidases DPP4 and FAP, which curb metalloproteinase and collagen-processing activity. Layered on top is transcriptional and post-transcriptional damping, including TGFB1 signalling through the non-signalling decoy receptor TGFBR3, PPARG-driven suppression of myofibroblast programmes, NOTCH1, TNF receptor input, and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, that directly repress collagen and matrix transcripts.

The extracellular matrix is continuously built, cross-linked and remodelled, and this pathway covers the brakes on that process — the signals and inhibitors that limit how much matrix is assembled and organized. Restraint matters because unchecked matrix deposition and fibre cross-linking produce fibrosis, stiffened vessels and scarring, while excess proteolysis destroys tissue architecture; both extremes are pathological. The genes act at several levels: TIMP3 and RECK inhibit metalloproteinases that would otherwise cut matrix components, CST3 blocks cysteine proteases, and EMILIN1 and CHADL modulate fibre assembly and collagen deposition directly. Receptor-level control comes through TGFB1 signalling and its non-signalling decoy receptor TGFBR3, NOTCH1, PPARG and TNF receptors. A large group of microRNAs, notably the miR-29 family, post-transcriptionally represses collagen and matrix gene expression, making transcript-level damping as much a part of this control as protein inhibition.

The extracellular matrix is not assembled passively, and this pathway covers the signals and factors that drive matrix deposition, crosslinking and remodelling upward. It underlies wound healing, bone and cartilage formation, and vascular wall maintenance, and when it runs unchecked it produces the fibrosis seen in kidney, lung, liver and heart disease as well as the stiffened stroma that supports tumour invasion. Much of the drive comes through TGF-beta ligands acting via TGFBR1 and the SMAD3/SMAD4 transcriptional module, reinforced by BMP2, angiotensinogen, IL6 and STAT3; SOX9 and RUNX1 direct matrix gene programmes in cartilage and other lineages. Other members act on the matrix itself or on the cell's grip on it, including the collagen receptor DDR2, the collagen galactosyltransferase COLGALT1, the fibulin EFEMP1-family member EFEMP2, tenascin XB and the heparan sulfate-degrading enzyme heparanase, with microRNAs tuning the output.

Attaching a lipid to a protein changes where it sits in the cell and what it can bind, and this regulatory layer sets how often that happens. Two distinct branches appear here. One controls lipidation of the autophagy machinery: the kinase complex built from ULK1, ATG13, ATG101 and RB1CC1, together with the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase PIK3C3, governs conjugation of ATG8-family proteins to membrane phospholipid at the forming autophagosome, the step that commits a cell to degrading and recycling its own contents during starvation. The other concerns protein prenylation and palmitoylation, with the RAB3GAP1-RAB3GAP2 complex acting upstream of Rab GTPase prenylation and membrane targeting, and HHATL modulating hedgehog acyltransferase activity. Loss of these controls disrupts autophagic flux and the membrane anchoring of small GTPases and secreted morphogens, with consequences for neurodevelopment and eye development.

Reverse cholesterol transport moves excess cholesterol from peripheral tissues and macrophage foam cells onto HDL particles for delivery to the liver and excretion in bile, and the genes here set the pace at which that clearance runs. Because the process empties lipid-laden macrophages in the artery wall, its tuning bears directly on atherosclerosis risk. Regulation operates at two levels: transporter and receptor proteins that handle sterol efflux and lipoprotein uptake, including a broad-specificity ABC transporter and the hepatic endocytic receptor LRP1, and small non-coding RNAs that repress efflux machinery post-transcriptionally. The intronic microRNA encoded within the SREBF2 locus is the best-characterised of these brakes, limiting ABCA1-dependent efflux and coupling cholesterol export to sterol-sensing transcriptional control. Raising flux through this route is a long-standing therapeutic aim in cardiovascular disease.</description>

regulation of protein localization to plasma membrane controls how many copies of a given receptor, channel or transporter are displayed at the cell surface at any moment, and is therefore the main way cells set their sensitivity to hormones, growth factors and ions without changing gene expression. Insulin-stimulated glucose transporter delivery, receptor tyrosine kinase downregulation, and the WNK-dependent tuning of renal ion transporters all depend on it. The machinery spans clathrin adaptors and endocytic sorting proteins, Rab and Arf GTPases with SNAREs that direct exocytic vesicles to the surface, scaffolds and the ezrin-spectrin cortex that anchor cargo once it arrives, and palmitoyltransferases that provide the lipid modification licensing membrane residence. Kinases such as AKT1, PDPK1, CaMKII and protein kinase C isoforms couple upstream signals to these steps, and accessory chaperones govern the surface expression of specific receptors. Its failure produces signalling and trafficking disease.

How much of a given receptor, channel or transporter sits at the cell surface is set by trafficking rather than by transcription, and this pathway covers the processes that tune protein localization to the plasma membrane up or down. It determines hormone and growth factor sensitivity, synaptic receptor number, glucose and ion transport capacity, and adhesion, so its misregulation shows up as resistance to insulin signalling, altered receptor tyrosine kinase output in cancer, and channelopathies. Mechanistically it draws on clathrin-mediated endocytosis and its adaptors, Rab- and ARF-dependent recycling, SNARE-mediated exocytic fusion, and scaffolds that anchor cargo to the cortical cytoskeleton. Covalent modification contributes too: palmitoyl transferases and depalmitoylating enzymes control membrane attachment, while kinases including AKT, PDPK1, CaMKII, protein kinase C isoforms and the WNK family phosphorylate cargo or its adaptors to shift the balance between insertion and retrieval.

Whether a channel, transporter or receptor actually works depends on getting it to the cell surface, and this pathway covers the processes that increase delivery and retention of proteins at the plasma membrane. It sets the surface density of signalling receptors and ion pumps, so it governs hormone and growth factor responsiveness, excitability, and epithelial polarity; mislocalisation underlies drug resistance and channel-trafficking diseases. The genes span the steps involved: Rab and Arf GTPases with kinesin motors for vesicle transport, syntaxins for the final fusion event, palmitoyltransferases that add membrane anchors, scaffolds and cytoskeletal linkers such as ezrin, spectrin and DLG1 that tether cargo in place, and kinases including AKT1, PDPK1 and protein kinase C isoforms that signal for insertion. Receptor tyrosine kinases and integrins here are both cargo and regulators, illustrating how surface signalling reinforces its own trafficking.

When chromosomes condense for mitosis, a specific set of proteins must be delivered to and held at defined sites on them — centromeres, kinetochores and the inner centromere — and this targeting step is what makes accurate chromosome segregation possible. Cells that fail at it mis-attach microtubules, bypass the spindle assembly checkpoint and become aneuploid, a route to mitotic catastrophe and to the chromosomal instability seen in tumours. The genes involved span the recruitment hierarchy: a constitutive centromere component and the KNL1 scaffold build the platform, CDK1 and the kinases Aurora B and TTK/MPS1 phosphorylate substrates to license loading and to destabilise incorrect attachments, and BUB3, KNTC1, ZW10, ZWILCH and SPDL1 assemble the RZZ–dynein and checkpoint modules that signal unattached kinetochores. The same logic governs delivery of chromosomal passenger and condensation factors, linking protein targeting to cell cycle timing.

Mitochondria carry their own genome and transcribe it with a dedicated machinery, and controlling how much of that transcription happens sets the supply of the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded there, along with the mitochondrial rRNAs and tRNAs needed to translate them. Tuning this output matters because oxidative phosphorylation capacity must match demand; too little mitochondrial transcript output starves the respiratory chain of core subunits, while unrestrained initiation wastes resources and distorts the balance with nucleus-encoded partners. Regulation acts at several levels: TEFM promotes processive elongation by the mitochondrial RNA polymerase, MTERF3 restrains initiation at the heavy-strand promoter, MTRES1 protects transcript levels under stress, and the AMP-activated kinase subunit PRKAA1 links energy status to mitochondrial biogenesis. Chromatin-associated factors including KAT8 with KANSL subunits and the transcription factor THAP11 couple nuclear regulatory programmes to mitochondrial gene expression.

Contraction driven by actin filaments has to be tuned in strength, speed and timing, and this is the control layer that does the tuning — most clearly in heart muscle, where the genes here set how forcefully and how rhythmically myocytes shorten. Calcium handling dominates: ryanodine receptors release calcium from sarcoplasmic reticulum stores, SERCA pumps reclaim it, and phospholamban restrains SERCA until phosphorylation relieves the brake, so beta-adrenergic receptors, adenylyl cyclase, phosphodiesterases and CaMKII translate catecholamine signals into altered contractility. Sodium, potassium and TRPM4 channels together with HCN4 shape the action potential that triggers each cycle, while desmosomal and junctional proteins such as desmoplakin, plakophilin-2 and connexin-40 couple neighbouring cells mechanically and electrically. Sarcomeric components including MYBPC3 and troponin C set myofilament calcium sensitivity. Actin-based contractile movement in muscle and other motile cells can be dialled up, and this regulatory pathway describes the inputs that increase the rate or extent of such filament-based motion. It matters for vascular tone, airway calibre and cardiac performance, where the amount of force a cell generates has to be matched to demand rather than fixed. The genes converge on contraction control from several directions: a smooth muscle actin that forms the filaments themselves, a beta-adrenergic receptor that couples catecholamine signalling to the contractile apparatus, and a sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump plus a small regulatory peptide of the same pump that together set the calcium transient governing cross-bridge cycling. A transcription factor contributes by shaping the smooth muscle differentiation state on which contractility depends. Disturbed regulation here underlies arterial disease and cardiomyopathy.

Many regulators of the actin cytoskeleton only work once they are physically delivered to and held on actin filaments, and this pathway covers that targeting step. Positioning proteins at filaments and at the cortex determines where bundling, capping and severing activities act, and so shapes cell shape, adhesion, motility and the stability of dendritic spines and cell-cell contacts. The members here act as scaffolds and adaptors rather than as motors: spinophilin (PPP1R9B) tethers protein phosphatase 1 to F-actin so that dephosphorylation occurs at the cytoskeleton, filamin-interacting proteins link to the filamin-actin network, and LUZP1 associates with actin structures and the centrosome and basal body. Through such tethering, the pathway couples signalling enzymes and their substrates to specific cytoskeletal locations, feeding into cytoskeletal remodelling during migration, neuronal morphogenesis and ciliogenesis.

Mononuclear cell differentiation covers the maturation of lymphocytes and monocyte-derived cells from haematopoietic progenitors into the specialised effectors of adaptive and innate immunity. It determines whether an individual can mount antibody responses, reject infected cells, tolerate self tissue, or clear pathogens through phagocytes; its failure produces immunodeficiency, autoimmunity and leukaemia. Lineage-restricted transcription factors such as PAX5, SPI1, GATA3, TBX21, RORC, FOXP3 and BCL11B impose and maintain identity, acting alongside chromatin remodelling and epigenetic machinery. Antigen receptor assembly by RAG1/RAG2 with non-homologous end-joining factors, pre-receptor signalling through LCK, ZAP70, SYK and BTK, and Notch ligand-receptor interactions in the thymus drive stepwise commitment and selection. Cytokines and their JAK-STAT and SOCS circuits, together with costimulatory and checkpoint receptors including CD28, ICOS and CTLA4, set helper T cell polarisation, plasma cell and dendritic cell fates, and monocyte-macrophage differentiation.

regulation of autophagy of mitochondrion controls how aggressively a cell culls its own damaged mitochondria, setting the balance between clearing depolarised organelles and preserving respiratory capacity. Tuning this balance matters for neuronal survival, cardiac and muscle metabolism, and erythrocyte maturation; loss of control underlies recessive Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative syndromes. The core switch is the PINK1 kinase and the ubiquitin ligase Parkin, which mark outer-membrane proteins such as VDAC1 and the mitochondrial import channel for autophagic capture, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30 and by proteases including PARL and PPTC7 that limit signal accumulation. Receptor-mediated routes through BNIP3, BNIP3L and FKBP8 provide a ubiquitin-independent alternative used during hypoxia and developmental mitochondrial clearance, while AMBRA1, HDAC6 and the fission factor DNM1L couple recognition to autophagosome formation. Metabolic and lipid sensors such as CAMKK2, TSC2 and the SREBP factors set the threshold.

Damaged or surplus mitochondria are cleared by a selective form of autophagy, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower how much of that clearance happens. Tuning it matters because too little clearance leaves depolarised, ROS-producing organelles in place — a failure implicated in Parkinson's disease, where PINK1 and the ubiquitin ligase PRKN act as the best-characterised sensor–effector pair — while unchecked clearance depletes respiratory capacity. Regulation acts at several levels: the kinase and ligase pair is opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30 and modulated by phosphatases and chaperone-associated factors; receptor proteins such as BNIP3, BNIP3L and FKBP8 tether outer-membrane cargo to the autophagy machinery; and fission by DNM1L sizes organelles for engulfment. Metabolic and stress cues enter through AMPK-related kinases, hypoxia signalling and integrated stress response components, linking mitochondrial turnover to nutrient state and quality control.

negative regulation of autophagy of mitochondrion is the braking system on mitophagy, ensuring that healthy mitochondria are not stripped away when the machinery that recognises damaged ones is active. Sustaining the right mitochondrial mass matters for oxidative metabolism in muscle, neurons and heart; unrestrained turnover produces mitochondrial DNA depletion and encephalomyopathy, as seen with loss of FBXL4 or PPTC7. The genes act largely at the level of the PINK1-Parkin axis and its substrates: the deubiquitinase USP30 removes the ubiquitin marks that recruit autophagy receptors, ubiquitin ligase components target PINK1 and its adaptors for degradation, and phosphatase and protease activities limit the accumulation of the initiating kinase on the outer membrane. Additional inputs come from mTOR-linked nutrient signalling through TSC2 and from redox and lipid-handling proteins, tying mitochondrial quality control to overall growth and stress state.

Mitochondria are removed selectively by autophagy when they are damaged, but the process has to be restrained so that healthy organelles and basal mitochondrial mass are preserved; this is the braking side of mitophagy. Loss of that restraint depletes the mitochondrial network, and mutations in several of these genes cause encephalopathy with mitochondrial DNA depletion or early-onset parkinsonism. The brakes act at different points: a deubiquitinase opposes the ubiquitin marks that recruit autophagy receptors, a phosphatase and a ubiquitin ligase adaptor promote turnover of outer-membrane mitophagy receptors, and a substrate-recognition subunit working with a cullin-RING ligase limits receptor accumulation. Others set the threshold indirectly, through mTORC1 signalling, mitochondrial protease quality control, or redox and reactive oxygen species levels. The balance between this suppression and activation determines mitochondrial quality control in neurons and other long-lived cells.</description

regulation of calcium ion transmembrane transport controls how much calcium crosses membranes and when, setting the amplitude and timing of the calcium signals that drive muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release, secretion and gene expression. Because calcium is both a signal and a toxin, this regulation determines whether a cell contracts efficiently or dies of overload, and its failure underlies arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia-like excitation-contraction defects and excitotoxic neuronal death. The genes span the accessory and modulatory layer around the channels themselves: auxiliary subunits and anchoring proteins that tune L-type voltage-gated channels, junctophilins and triadin-calsequestrin complexes coupling surface excitation to ryanodine receptor release, sarcolipin and phospholamban restraining SERCA-driven reuptake, sodium-calcium exchange, and calmodulin-calcineurin and kinase feedback. Receptor inputs from purinergic, thrombin and neuropeptide receptors feed in, while BCL2-family and VDAC components link mitochondrial calcium handling to apoptotic commitment.

Cells use calcium as a signal, so the flux of calcium across membranes has to be tuned rather than simply allowed, and this pathway covers the modulators that set how much calcium enters the cytosol, when, and for how long. It governs cardiac and skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, neuronal excitability and transmitter release, immune cell activation, and hormone secretion; loss of control gives arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia-like dysregulation, excitotoxic neuronal death, and impaired contractility. Regulators act on voltage-gated channel complexes and their auxiliary subunits, on ryanodine receptor calcium release through junctophilins, triadin, calsequestrins, FKBP proteins and phospholamban-type inhibitors, on store-operated and TRP entry, and on sodium-calcium exchange and mitochondrial uptake. Calmodulin, calcineurin subunits, kinases such as PRKACA and CAMK2D, receptor and chemokine inputs, and several microRNAs feed into the same decisions, linking calcium handling to contraction, secretion, gene expression and apoptotic signalling.

Calcium entry must be switched off as decisively as it is switched on, and this collection covers the brakes: processes that reduce the rate or extent of calcium movement across membranes. Damping is what allows a cardiac myocyte to relax, a neuron to reset excitability, and mitochondria to avoid the calcium overload that triggers permeability transition and cell death. Mechanisms represented include calmodulin-dependent feedback inhibition of channels, calcineurin subunits acting downstream of the same signal, sarcolipin and phospholamban restraining the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump, FKBP1B stabilising the closed state of ryanodine receptors, MCUB acting as a dominant-negative subunit of the mitochondrial uniporter, and auxiliary proteins that suppress voltage-gated channel surface expression. Several microRNAs tune the same targets. Loss of this restraint produces arrhythmia, contractile dysfunction, excitotoxicity and apoptotic signalling through mitochondria.

Recruitment of cytosolic proteins onto the mitochondrial surface has to be limited as well as promoted, and this pathway covers the braking side: processes that reduce the rate or extent of protein targeting to mitochondria. The clearest context is mitophagy, where damaged organelles are tagged by PINK1-dependent recruitment of Parkin and other cytosolic factors; dampening that recruitment sets the threshold at which a mitochondrion is committed to degradation, and mis-setting it contributes to the neuronal vulnerability seen in Parkinson disease. Several members act through this route, including SIAH3, which restrains PINK1-driven recruitment, and the kinase LRRK2. Co-chaperone regulators of the BAG family link the process to HSP70-dependent protein handling and quality control, placing this negative regulation at the intersection of chaperone activity, apoptotic signalling and mitochondrial turnover.

Endoderm is the germ layer that gives rise to gut, liver, pancreas and lung epithelium, and the differentiation of cells into it must be timed and positioned correctly during gastrulation or organ primordia form in the wrong place or not at all. The genes here act as modulators rather than core effectors of that fate decision: a secreted Wnt antagonist tunes the Wnt/nodal signalling gradients that partition mesoderm from endoderm, a bHLH transcription factor of the nascent mesoderm helps set the boundary between the two lineages, a histone variant that marks facultative heterochromatin constrains which lineage programmes remain accessible, and fibrillar collagen V contributes to the extracellular matrix through which migrating cells receive positional cues. Together they illustrate how signalling, chromatin state and matrix context converge to raise or lower the rate at which cells adopt endodermal identity.

Melanosome assembly builds the pigment organelle of melanocytes and retinal pigment epithelium, the enclosed compartment where tyrosinase and its partners make melanin and store it safely away from the rest of the cytoplasm. Without it, pigment enzymes never reach a maturing organelle, and the result is oculocutaneous albinism with reduced visual acuity, alongside the bleeding and lung disease that follow when related lysosome-related organelles such as platelet dense granules also fail. The genes here define the sorting machinery: adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-3 select cargo into vesicles leaving the endosomal system, the BLOC-1/BLOC-2/BLOC-3 subunits encoded by the HPS genes direct tubular carriers to the nascent organelle, and the paralogous small GTPases RAB32 and RAB38 recruit tethering and motor effectors for delivery.
