Endonuclease G contributes a caspase-independent route from the mitochondrion, while CIDE-family proteins modulate DNA fragmentation activity. Upstream cues, including cytokine signalling through IL6 and transcriptional input from GATA factors, set the threshold at which this machinery engages. Failure to degrade apoptotic DNA properly leaves immunostimulatory chromatin behind and is linked to inflammation and autoimmunity, tying nuclease regulation to safe clearance of dying cells.

DNA is normally protected, but during apoptosis and related remodelling it must be actively destroyed, and this pathway describes the signals that switch that destruction on. Positive regulation of DNA catabolic process matters because chromosomal fragmentation is the committed end point of programmed cell death: without it, dying cells release intact genomic DNA, a potent trigger of autoimmune and inflammatory responses. The machinery here spans the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis, where BAX permeabilizes the outer membrane, the executioner protease CASP3 that inactivates inhibitors of nuclease activity, and ENDOG, a mitochondrial nuclease that relocates to the nucleus to cleave chromatin. Transcriptional and cytokine inputs such as GATA5 and IL6 tune how readily cells enter this state. The same nucleolytic endpoint governs turnover of damaged cells, tissue involution, and enucleation events during differentiation.

Complement can lyse cells outright once the membrane attack complex forms, so the killing must be aimed at pathogens and damaged cells while host tissue is spared; this pathway covers the controls that set how much complement-dependent cytotoxicity actually occurs. Membrane-anchored regulators such as CD55 and CD59 act on the cell surface, the former destabilising C3 and C5 convertases and the latter blocking assembly of the terminal pore, while soluble factor H and clusterin restrain the alternative pathway and the fluid-phase terminal complex. Complement receptors of the CR1 family bind and help dispose of opsonised particles. Anti-inflammatory and type 2 cytokines including IL4, IL10, IL13 and TGFB2 tune expression of these regulators. Loss of such restraint underlies paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and complement-mediated transplant and autoantibody injury, and tumour cells exploit it to resist therapeutic antibodies.</br>

Complement can lyse cells outright, and host tissue survives that threat only because it carries brakes on the terminal attack. Negative regulation of complement-dependent cytotoxicity covers the mechanisms that limit membrane attack complex formation and the killing that follows, protecting self cells from bystander damage during infection and inflammation. Membrane-anchored CD59 blocks the final assembly step by preventing C9 incorporation into the nascent pore, while clusterin binds soluble terminal complex components in the fluid phase, and CR1 acts earlier as a regulator of the C3 and C5 convertases. Cytokine input from IL4 and IL13 links this restraint to type 2 immune signalling and to the regulation of complement components by target cells. Loss of these controls produces intravascular haemolysis, as in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, and shapes how tumour cells resist antibody-based therapies.

New blood vessels usually form by sprouting from existing ones, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how often and how far such sprouts grow. Tight control matters because too little sprouting leaves ischaemic tissue unperfused and wounds unhealed, while too much feeds tumour growth and proliferative retinopathy. Pro-sprouting drive comes from VEGFA acting through PI3K-dependent signalling and from fibroblast growth factors, with integrin alpha5 and matrix remodelling permitting endothelial invasion; Notch ligand DLL1 and thrombospondin-1 restrain it, so that only selected tip cells sprout. Flow-responsive transcription factors KLF2 and KLF4 tie sprouting decisions to haemodynamics, and a large complement of microRNAs, including the miR-17~92 cluster and miR-126, tunes endothelial responsiveness. Junctional and cytoskeletal regulators such as TJP1 and RHOJ link the decision to sprout to the mechanics of vessel remodelling.

New blood vessels form when endothelial cells break their quiescence and sprout toward a growth-factor gradient; the braking systems described here keep that behaviour restrained, so that vessel density matches tissue demand and stalks do not branch without limit. Loss of such restraint contributes to tumour vascularisation and to proliferative retinal disease, while excessive restraint leaves ischaemic tissue poorly perfused. Several mechanisms converge: thrombospondin-1 and the metalloproteinase ADAMTS9 act as matrix-derived anti-angiogenic signals, the epsins EPN1 and EPN2 promote endocytic removal of VEGF receptors from the endothelial surface, flow-responsive KLF2 stabilises the quiescent phenotype, and SEMA6A and the RhoGAP STARD13 shape tip-cell guidance and motility. A large complement of microRNAs, including the miR-17~92 cluster, miR-34 family and miR-221, tunes sprouting post-transcriptionally, placing this control at the interface of mechanosensing, matrix remodelling and receptor turnover.

New blood vessels usually form by sprouting from existing ones, and this is the set of inputs that pushes that process forward — increasing how often endothelial tip cells are specified and how far sprouts extend. It matters wherever tissue outgrows its perfusion: wound healing, ischaemic muscle and heart, the menstrual cycle, and pathologically in tumour vascularisation and proliferative retinopathy, where excess sprouting is the disease. VEGFA and the fibroblast growth factors FGF1 and FGF2 supply the main pro-angiogenic cues; Notch ligand DLL1 and BMP signalling through SMAD1 and the modulator BMPER set tip-versus-stalk identity; integrin alpha-5, junctional proteins and transglutaminase couple sprouts to fibronectin-rich matrix; and KLF4, JAK1 and PDPK1 relay the transcriptional and kinase responses. Several microRNAs, notably miR-126, act as endothelial-enriched amplifiers of the same growth factor signalling.

regulation of wound healing, spreading of epidermal cells controls how quickly keratinocytes flatten, extend and migrate across a breach in the epidermis to re-establish the skin barrier. Its tuning determines whether a wound closes on schedule or persists as a chronic ulcer, and inappropriate activation contributes to hyperproliferative and invasive epithelial behaviour. The regulators act at the interface between adhesion and the cytoskeleton: kindlins couple integrins to the extracellular matrix and are required for keratinocyte anchorage, with kindlin-1 loss causing Kindler syndrome and skin fragility, while CLASP proteins and PHLDB2 stabilise microtubules at the leading edge to orient protrusion. Growth-factor input is set by the PTEN-mTOR axis, which gates the translational and metabolic capacity needed for spreading, and additional transcriptional and microRNA-level control adjusts the migratory response. The pathway therefore links cell-matrix signalling to directed epithelial sheet movement during tissue repair.

After skin injury, keratinocytes at the wound edge must flatten, polarise and migrate across the denuded surface, and this pathway tunes how fast and how far that epidermal spreading proceeds. It sets the pace of re-epithelialisation, so its dysregulation contributes to chronic non-healing ulcers at one extreme and to excessive or disorganised repair at the other. Control operates at two points. Integrin-associated kindlins link the migrating cell to the basement membrane and license adhesion turnover; loss of FERMT1 causes the skin fragility and blistering of Kindler syndrome. Meanwhile microtubule plus-end regulators such as CLASP1 and CLASP2 and the adhesion-associated PHLDB2 orient the cytoskeleton for directed movement, and the PTEN-mTOR axis couples phosphoinositide signalling and growth-factor input to the protein synthesis and lamellipodial dynamics that sustain forward crawling.

When skin is broken, keratinocytes at the wound edge flatten, polarize and migrate to close the gap; this pathway is the braking side of that response, damping the rate and extent to which epidermal cells spread. Restraint matters because unchecked migration would compromise the ordered re-epithelialization and adhesion needed for a stable barrier, and the same controls limit inappropriate motility in epithelia generally. Mechanistically the members converge on the microtubule-actin interface at the leading edge: the CLASP proteins and their partner PHLDB2 stabilize and tether microtubule plus ends to cortical sites and focal adhesions, coupling adhesion turnover to protrusion, while the phosphatase PTEN dephosphorylates PIP3 and thereby lowers PI3K-dependent polarity and protrusive signalling. The net effect is control of the timing and speed of epidermal wound closure rather than its initiation.

After skin injury, keratinocytes at the wound edge must flatten, spread and migrate across the denuded surface before the epidermal barrier can be restored, and this pathway covers the inputs that accelerate that spreading. Its outputs matter for re-epithelialisation: too little drives chronic, non-healing ulcers, while the same machinery contributes to skin fragility syndromes. Mechanistically, the kindlin proteins FERMT1 and FERMT2 bind integrin beta cytoplasmic tails and cooperate with talin to switch integrins to their high-affinity state, coupling the spreading cell to laminin- and fibronectin-rich wound matrix; loss of FERMT1 underlies Kindler syndrome, with blistering and poor epithelial repair. Growth-factor signalling through mTOR supports the protein synthesis and cytoskeletal remodelling that migration demands, and a microRNA and a transcriptional regulator tune the response, placing this biology at the intersection of cell adhesion, motility and tissue repair.

positive regulation of microvillus assembly promotes the building of the dense apical actin protrusions that form the brush border of intestinal and kidney epithelial cells, the surface where nutrient absorption, ion transport and digestive enzyme presentation occur. Loss of this drive leaves epithelia with stunted or disordered microvilli and impaired absorptive capacity, as seen in congenital microvillus inclusion disease. The genes trace a small GTPase relay: guanine nucleotide exchange factors activate the Ras-family GTPase RAP2A, which in turn engages the STE20-family kinases MST4 and TNIK to control apical actin organisation and the polarity machinery, including LKB1/STRAD-dependent brush border formation. The pathway therefore links polarity signalling at the apical membrane to cytoskeletal remodelling, coupling epithelial differentiation to the physical elaboration of absorptive surface area.

Absorptive epithelial cells of the gut and kidney tubule display a dense apical brush border, and this pathway drives the positive regulation of microvillus assembly that builds it, expanding the surface available for nutrient uptake and transport. The small GTPase RAP2A, loaded by its exchange factors RAPGEF2 and RAPGEF6, relays apical cues to Ste20-family kinases: STK26 (MST4) phosphorylates ezrin to link the plasma membrane to the underlying actin bundle, while the related kinase TNIK contributes to cytoskeletal remodelling beneath the apical surface. The net effect is polarized actin core formation and elongation of microvilli at the right membrane domain. Loss of signalling through this axis flattens the brush border and impairs the absorptive capacity of the epithelium, connecting Rap GTPase signalling to apical polarity, actin organization and epithelial differentiation.

Blood cell production from hematopoietic stem cells must be tuned continuously to demand, and the regulation of hemopoiesis covers the signals and transcriptional controls that set how many erythrocytes, platelets, granulocytes, macrophages, lymphocytes and osteoclasts are made. Lineage-determining transcription factors such as GATA1, TAL1, RUNX1, SPI1, GATA3 and MITF act with chromatin remodelling and acetyltransferase complexes to commit progenitors, while cytokines and their receptors — thrombopoietin acting through MPL, G-CSF through CSF3R, interleukin-7 through IL7R, plus IL2, IL15 and CSF1 — drive survival and expansion via JAK-STAT signalling, restrained by SOCS proteins and the phosphatase PTPN6. Notch ligands, BMP, TGF-beta and Wnt inputs, RNA-binding proteins and microRNAs add further layers. Loss of control produces cytopenias, immunodeficiency, bone marrow failure syndromes and leukemia; TNFSF11-TNFRSF11A signalling here links the same progenitor pool to bone remodelling.

Blood cell production has to be restrained as well as driven, and this pathway collects the brakes: processes that slow or block the proliferation, lineage commitment and terminal differentiation of haematopoietic progenitors and their lymphoid and myeloid descendants. Restraint sets steady-state blood counts, prevents exhaustion of stem cell pools, and its loss contributes to myeloproliferative expansion and leukaemia. The mechanisms span several levels: transcriptional repressors and lineage factors such as BCL6, ID2, GATA2, RUNX1 and CBFB that hold progenitors short of maturation; cytokine-signalling negative feedback through SOCS1 and phosphatases including INPP5D and PTPN2; BMP, Wnt-modulating and activin/inhibin ligands acting on the niche; inhibitory immune receptors of the LILRB family and CTLA4 with FOXP3-dependent suppression; cell cycle inhibition by CDKN2A and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of drivers by FBXW7 and the proteasome subunits. Microparticle regulators such as miR-125b and erythroferrone add post-transcriptional and systemic control, notably over erythropoiesis.

Blood and immune cells are replenished continuously from haematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, and this collection covers the signals and transcriptional machinery that drive that output upward — positive regulation of hemopoiesis. It matters because the pace of lineage commitment sets immune competence, platelet and myeloid supply, and bone remodelling; too little gives immunodeficiency and cytopenia, while unchecked activity contributes to leukaemia. Cytokines and their receptors (IL7–IL7R, IL2 receptor chains, CSF1, IL15, TNFSF11/RANKL) act through JAK-STAT effectors STAT5A and STAT5B to promote progenitor survival and expansion. Lineage-determining transcription factors including SPI1, RUNX1 with CBFB, GATA3, BCL6, ZBTB16 and SOX4 work alongside SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling subunits and the acetyltransferase EP300 to open lineage-specific loci. Antigen receptor assembly and proximal signalling components such as RAG1, LCK, ZAP70, SYK and BTK extend the programme into lymphocyte maturation, while RANKL–TRAF6 signalling drives osteoclast differentiation from myeloid precursors.

Spermidine is a polyamine that cells need for growth, translation (via hypusination of eIF5A), autophagy and nucleic acid stabilisation, but they largely acquire it from diet, gut bacteria and neighbouring cells rather than making all of it themselves. Moving spermidine across membranes therefore sets intracellular polyamine pools and links them to whole-body handling of these cations. The carriers here are organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family, expressed in liver, kidney, intestine and testis, which take up spermidine and related polyamines along with many drugs and endogenous cations; the same proteins govern hepatic and renal clearance of metformin, cisplatin and other charged xenobiotics, so genetic variation in them alters drug disposition. A related sugar-transporter-like carrier contributes further polyamine flux. Loss of uptake capacity limits polyamine availability and blunts the growth advantage that tumours gain from scavenging extracellular spermidine.

Cells tune how much of their ATP comes from oxygen-dependent mitochondrial metabolism rather than glycolysis, and this regulation of aerobic respiration covers the inputs that raise or damp that flux. It matters for matching energy supply to demand, for surviving hypoxia, and for limiting the reactive oxygen species that leak from an overdriven electron transport chain. The genes act at several levels: assembly and composition of respiratory complexes, mitochondrial transcription and iron cofactor supply, calcium and metabolite transport across the inner membrane, permeability transition control, and deacetylation of matrix enzymes by SIRT3. Hypoxic signals acting through MIR210 and NDUFA4L2 suppress complex activity, while quality-control factors such as PINK1, PARK7 and VCP protect it. Failure shows up as mitochondrial dysfunction in neurodegeneration, ischaemic injury and inflammatory states driven by TNF.

regulation of centriole elongation controls how long a growing centriole becomes, setting the length of the microtubule barrel that later templates a cilium or anchors a spindle pole. Centriole length must be reproducible: over-elongated or truncated centrioles distort centrosome number and function, disrupt cilium assembly, and are linked to microcephaly, dwarfism and ciliopathies. The genes act on the elongating daughter centriole through the cartwheel-to-microtubule interface, where CPAP (CENPJ) tunes tubulin addition at the distal end, CEP120 and CEP295 promote extension and centriole-to-centrosome conversion, and POC1B and POC5 stabilise the central and distal core. ESCRT-III components with the VPS4B ATPase contribute membrane-remodelling activity at the distal centriole, coupling length control to structural maturation. The pathway therefore sits within centrosome duplication and the licensing of ciliogenesis during the cell cycle.

Centrioles must reach a defined length during duplication, and this control step sets where the growing microtubule wall stops. Length matters because centrioles template centrosomes and, in ciliated cells, the basal body from which the axoneme extends; over- or under-elongated centrioles disturb spindle geometry and cilium formation, and mutations in the genes involved cause microcephalic dwarfism and ciliopathies. Regulation operates on the distal end of the procentriole, where CPAP, CEP120 and CEP295 promote extension of the centriolar microtubules while POC5, POC1B, CCDC15 and PPP1R35 build and stabilise the inner scaffold and cartwheel-associated structures that fix final length. Membrane remodelling factors CHMP2A and VPS4B connect this process to ESCRT-dependent activities at the centrosome, linking centriole size control to broader centrosome biogenesis and cell cycle progression.

Centrioles must reach a defined length to template cilia and to organize a functional centrosome, and this pathway covers the activities that drive and extend that growth. Elongation adds tubulin to the distal end of the procentriole after duplication, and proteins such as CEP120 and CPAP promote incorporation along the microtubule wall while CEP295 and PPP1R35 act in the maturation of a nascent centriole into a competent one; POC1B stabilizes the cartwheel-associated core. Getting length right matters because over-elongated or truncated centrioles produce defective basal bodies, abnormal spindle poles and mitotic errors, and mutations in several of these components cause ciliopathies, retinal dystrophy and microcephaly with short stature. The pathway therefore sits within centrosome biogenesis and cilium assembly rather than in microtubule dynamics generally.

Membrane phospholipids must be made, remodelled and turned over at rates matched to cell growth and organelle function, and this pathway covers the controls that set those rates. Its outputs include lung surfactant, where ABCA3 and LPCAT1 supply and remodel phosphatidylcholine for lamellar bodies, and the inner mitochondrial membrane, where tafazzin transfers acyl chains onto cardiolipin — loss of that step causes Barth syndrome with cardiomyopathy. Regulation operates at several levels: lipin phosphatidate phosphatase activity gates glycerolipid flux, myotubularin-family phosphatases dephosphorylate phosphoinositides, receptors and second-messenger enzymes such as serotonin and muscarinic receptors and PRKCD couple external signals to lipid turnover, and transcriptional inputs from XBP1 and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 tie phospholipid synthesis to secretory demand and lipid load. Lipoproteins, transporters and lipid-binding proteins add substrate supply.

negative regulation of phospholipid metabolic process covers the brakes cells apply to the synthesis and turnover of membrane phospholipids, keeping bilayer composition, lipid droplet formation and lipoprotein handling matched to demand rather than running unchecked. Restraint here matters because unbalanced phospholipid flux distorts membrane properties, drives ectopic lipid storage and feeds into atherosclerosis and hepatic steatosis. The genes act at several levels: LPIN1 phosphatidate phosphatase and LPCAT1 sit directly in glycerophospholipid remodelling and can limit precursor availability; APOC1 constrains lipase access to lipoprotein phospholipid and triglyceride; ABCA2 governs lipid movement across intracellular membranes, particularly in myelinating cells; platelet-derived growth factor ligands impose extracellular control, coupling growth factor signalling to suppression of lipid synthetic output; and a microRNA adds post-transcriptional damping. Together they represent negative feedback within lipid homeostasis rather than a linear biosynthetic route.

Membrane phospholipid pools are set by opposing synthesis and breakdown, and this collection represents the damping side of that balance curbing the rate at which phospholipids are made, remodelled or degraded. Restraining these fluxes matters for surfactant composition in the lung, for lipid droplet and membrane biogenesis in the liver and adipose tissue, and for keeping lipoprotein lipolysis in check: APOC1 inhibits lipase action on lipoprotein phospholipid and triglyceride, while LPCAT1 and LPIN1 sit at the acyltransferase and phosphatidate phosphatase steps whose activity determines how much phosphatidylcholine and diacylglycerol are produced. Regulation is exerted at several levels, including transcriptional and growth-factor input through PDGF ligands, sterol- and lipid-sensitive transport by ABCA2, and microRNA-mediated suppression of lipogenic transcripts. Loss of such brakes drives excess lipid accumulation and altered membrane composition.

Phospholipids are the building blocks of every cellular membrane and the source of lipid second messengers, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate of their synthesis, remodelling and breakdown. Upregulating phospholipid metabolism supports membrane expansion during secretory demand, surfactant production in the lung, and the release of signalling lipids. Several routes converge here: the serotonin receptors HTR2A, HTR2B and HTR2C couple through Gq to stimulate phospholipase C, PRKCD acts downstream of diacylglycerol, and the stress-activated transcription factor XBP1 drives lipid biosynthetic gene expression as part of the unfolded protein response and membrane biogenesis. ACSL3 activates fatty acids for incorporation into glycerolipids, TAFAZZIN remodels cardiolipin in mitochondria, NR1H4 provides bile acid dependent transcriptional control, and APOC2 promotes lipoprotein lipolysis. Loss of such stimulatory control disturbs membrane composition and lipid signalling.

The plasma membrane is not a passive sheet: its lipid asymmetry, curvature, cortical support and repair capacity are actively set, and regulation of plasma membrane organization covers the processes that tune how much of this remodelling happens. It matters for wound resealing, vesicle scission, phosphatidylserine exposure during cell death, and the stiffness or deformability of the cell surface. Here, a calcium-sensing annexin complex with S100A10 and AHNAK is recruited to damaged or curved membrane, flippases such as ATP8B1 and ATP10A maintain aminophospholipid asymmetry, and dynamin-2 with endophilin-family and actin regulators (gelsolin, WASL, MYH9) couple membrane geometry to the cortical cytoskeleton. Caspase-7 and FASLG link the same machinery to apoptotic surface changes that mark cells for clearance. Loss of individual components produces cholestasis, bleeding and platelet defects, and impaired membrane repair in muscle and epithelia.

Which proteins arrive at mitochondria, and how many, is actively tuned rather than fixed, and this regulatory layer controls mitochondrial quality, apoptotic commitment and organelle turnover. Much of it converges on the import machinery and on the PINK1-Parkin axis: import receptors and the TOM channel subunit TOMM7 govern entry, the rhomboid protease PARL cleaves imported PINK1 in healthy mitochondria so that its accumulation on depolarised outer membranes recruits the ubiquitin ligase Parkin, while SIAH3 and related factors restrain that step. Downstream ubiquitin conjugating and ligase activities, chaperones such as DNAJA1 and BAG-family cochaperones, and kinases including PRKAA1 and GSK3A modulate targeting and retention. A parallel arm controls recruitment of apoptotic and mitophagy effectors such as PUMA and BNIP3L to the outer membrane. Defects here underlie familial parkinsonism and impaired clearance of damaged mitochondria.

Mitochondria import most of their proteome from the cytosol, and this set covers the braking side of that traffic — processes that block or reduce delivery of proteins to the mitochondrion. Restraint matters because several of the cargoes concerned are damaging when they arrive: limiting recruitment of pro-apoptotic and mitophagy-initiating factors to the outer membrane keeps cells from committing to death or to organelle clearance unnecessarily. Co-chaperones of the BAG family act with HSP70-type partners, including DNAJA1, to sort clients in the cytosol and divert them from mitochondrial targeting, while SIAH3 interferes with PINK1-dependent recruitment steps. Also represented are proteins whose mislocalisation to mitochondria is itself pathogenic, notably tau and LRRK2, linking this regulation to neurodegeneration, where excess association of aggregation-prone proteins with mitochondria compromises respiration and membrane integrity.

Mitochondria import almost all of their proteins from the cytosol, and this pathway covers the events that increase the rate or extent of protein delivery to the organelle. It matters for building respiratory capacity, for recruiting apoptotic effectors such as the BH3-only protein PUMA to the outer membrane, and for stress responses in which cytosolic kinases and ubiquitin machinery redirect proteins to mitochondria. Components of the translocase of the outer membrane, including TOMM7 and the receptor TOMM70, provide the entry route, while PINK1 accumulation on depolarised mitochondria marks damaged organelles for clearance. Ubiquitin conjugating and ligase activities, SUMO activation, deubiquitinases, kinases such as CSNK2A2, GSK3A and the AMPK subunit PRKAA1, and autophagy adaptors modulate targeting and retention. Loss of this control compromises mitochondrial quality surveillance, mitophagy and the commitment step of apoptosis.

Hydrogen peroxide generated during oxidative stress can permeabilize mitochondria and commit a cell to death, and this pathway covers the controls that set how readily that happens. Tuning it decides whether a transient burst of peroxide is buffered or converted into caspase activation, which matters for neuronal survival, muscle and cardiac tolerance of ischaemia, and the resistance of tumour cells to oxidative therapy. Most of the components act as brakes: AKT1 signalling promotes survival, PARK7 and PINK1 protect mitochondria against oxidative damage and their loss causes recessive Parkinson's disease, and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrains permeabilization. RACK1 scaffolds the kinases involved, carbonic anhydrase III contributes antioxidant thiol capacity, and two microRNAs add post-transcriptional regulation. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of redox homeostasis and the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis rather than within either alone.

The p38 MAPK cascade drives stress and inflammatory responses, and shutting it down again limits cytokine output, apoptosis and tissue damage once a stress signal has passed. Negative regulation of this cascade keeps inflammation self-limiting; when it fails, chronic cytokine production and autoimmune or inflammatory disease follow. Several routes converge on the same end. Dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP1 and DUSP10 dephosphorylate the activating threonine and tyrosine of p38 itself, terminating the kinase. CYLD removes ubiquitin chains from upstream signalling intermediates, damping the kinase relay that feeds the cascade, while PTPN22 is a tyrosine phosphatase that restrains immune receptor signalling in lymphocytes and myeloid cells. Scaffolding and adhesion proteins, a microRNA and the myeloid receptor TREM2 contribute additional brakes, tying cascade attenuation to cell contact, transcript-level control and innate immune tone.

Potassium efflux sets the resting membrane potential and repolarizes excitable cells, so controlling how much potassium leaves through plasma membrane channels determines cardiac action potential duration, epithelial secretion and systemic potassium balance. The genes here act on that step rather than conducting the current themselves: accessory beta subunits such as KCNE3 and KCNE5 and the calcium-binding partner KCNIP2 alter the gating and kinetics of channels including the rapid delayed rectifier KCNH2, the scaffold DLG1 positions channels at the membrane, and the ubiquitin ligases NEDD4, NEDD4L and WWP2 target them for internalization and degradation, tuning surface density. The kinase WNK4 links this control to renal potassium secretion and blood pressure, while the atrial hormone precursor NPPA ties it to volume regulation. Loss of such regulation lengthens repolarization and produces long QT arrhythmia, or disturbs potassium handling and electrolyte homeostasis in the kidney.

Potassium efflux sets the resting potential and the pace of repolarisation, so damping it is one way cells tune excitability and volume. This is the braking arm: processes that reduce the rate or extent of potassium export across the plasma membrane, acting either on channel gating or on how many channels reach and remain at the surface. Accessory beta subunits such as KCNE3 and KCNE5 associate with pore-forming partners and shift their voltage dependence and kinetics, in some pairings suppressing current outright. The HECT-type ubiquitin ligases NEDD4, NEDD4L and WWP2 recognise channel substrates and mark them for internalisation and degradation, lowering surface density. KCNH2, the cardiac rapid delayed rectifier channel, is a substrate for such regulation, and its loss of surface expression underlies long QT syndrome and arrhythmia, linking this restraint to cardiac repolarisation and to epithelial transport.

The heartbeat depends on an electrical impulse spreading through the myocardium in a fixed sequence, and this pathway covers the processes that tune how fast and how far that impulse travels. Its outputs set heart rate, atrioventricular delay and the coordination of chamber contraction; disturbance produces arrhythmia, conduction block and sudden cardiac death. Much of the control is exerted on calcium handling: sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pumps and the ryanodine receptor RYR2 load and release the stores that drive each beat, plasma membrane calcium ATPases and sodium-calcium exchangers set the efflux, and TRPM4 contributes a calcium-activated depolarizing current whose mutation causes familial conduction disease. Gap junction connexins such as GJA5 provide the cell-to-cell coupling for propagation, ankyrin-B and EHD3 target these channels correctly, and transcription factors NKX2-5 and TBX5 specify the conduction system itself. Adrenergic input via protein kinase A and renin-angiotensin components layer neurohumoral modulation on top.

Sodium entry across the plasma membrane sets epithelial salt reabsorption, cell volume and, through it, extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure, so the rate of that entry is tuned rather than left constant. Regulators here act on sodium channels and sodium-coupled transporters: NEDD4L, a HECT-type ubiquitin ligase, marks the epithelial sodium channel for removal from the surface and thereby limits reabsorption, and variants in this control circuit contribute to salt-sensitive hypertension. STK39, a Ste20-family kinase, phosphorylates cation-chloride cotransporters to promote sodium and chloride uptake in kidney tubule cells, placing it in the WNK kinase signalling cascade. Post-transcriptional repression by microRNAs adds another layer of control over transporter abundance. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of renal physiology, blood pressure homeostasis and membrane trafficking of transport proteins.

Cells tune how quickly amino acids cross their membranes, and this regulatory layer sets the supply of substrates for protein synthesis, neurotransmitter pools and growth signalling rather than performing the transport itself. Control operates largely by governing where transporters sit and how stably they are held there: ACE2 and its kidney counterpart CLTRN act as obligatory chaperones that deliver neutral amino acid transporters to the apical surface of intestine and kidney, and their loss produces the aminoaciduria of Hartnup-like disease and impairs tryptophan uptake. Other members modulate glutamate transporter trafficking and activity, couple transport to Na+/K+ gradients set by ATP1A2, or link nutrient entry to integrin adhesion and inflammatory cytokine signalling. Leucine carriers such as SLC7A5 and the SLC43 family place this regulation directly upstream of mTORC1-dependent growth control, while circadian input imposes a daily rhythm on uptake capacity.

negative regulation of miRNA processing covers the mechanisms that block maturation of microRNAs, holding primary and precursor transcripts back from Drosha and Dicer cleavage so that the corresponding target mRNAs escape silencing. This restraint sets how much of any given microRNA a cell actually makes, and it matters most in development and cancer: the LIN28A and LIN28B RNA-binding proteins bind pre-let-7 and recruit terminal uridylyltransferase activity to mark it for decay, keeping stem and progenitor cells undifferentiated and, when reactivated in tumours, sustaining a proliferative state. Other routes act chemically or transcriptionally, as with methylation of pre-miRNA 5' monophosphates by BCDIN3D, which impairs Dicer loading, and inflammatory IL6-STAT3 signalling that feeds back onto microRNA biogenesis. The net effect is post-transcriptional control layered on top of gene expression, tuning differentiation, inflammatory responses, and metabolic programmes.

MicroRNA maturation is not automatic: precursor hairpins can be blocked before Drosha or Dicer cleaves them, and the pathway described here comprises the brakes on that route. Restraining processing of particular miRNAs keeps their targets expressed, which matters most in stem cells and in tumours, where release of the brake changes cell fate. LIN28A and LIN28B bind the terminal loop of pre-let-7 and recruit terminal uridylyltransferase activity so the precursor is degraded rather than matured, sustaining the pluripotency and proliferative programmes that let-7 would otherwise suppress; BCDIN3D methylates pre-miRNA 5' monophosphates to make them poor Dicer substrates. Inflammatory input through IL6 and STAT3 feeds into the same output, linking cytokine signalling to selective loss of tumour-suppressive miRNAs. The result is post-transcriptional control acting one layer above the miRNAs themselves.

MicroRNAs must be cut out of longer hairpin transcripts before they can silence their targets, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate of that maturation step. Because a single miRNA tunes many mRNAs, changing processing efficiency shifts whole gene expression programmes, and the best-characterised examples here link cell-surface signalling to the nuclear cleavage machinery. DGCR8 is the RNA-binding partner that presents primary miRNA hairpins to the Drosha nuclease, defining the site of regulation. BMP4 and TGFB1 act through receptor-activated SMADs that associate with the processing complex and accelerate maturation of specific miRNAs, a route important in vascular smooth muscle phenotype and fibrotic responses. Also represented are an RNA pseudouridine synthase acting on pri-miRNA and a kinase better known in inflammatory and death signalling, indicating that stress and cytokine pathways feed into miRNA output as well.

Cells acquire the branched-chain amino acid leucine from the extracellular space by carrier-mediated uptake, and this import step does more than feed protein synthesis: cytosolic leucine is the amino acid that mTORC1 senses, so the transporters here set how strongly growth signalling, translation and autophagy suppression respond to nutrient supply. Two systems carry the traffic. The heterodimeric system L exchangers pair the light chains SLC7A5 or SLC7A8 with the heavy chain SLC3A2 for obligatory antiport, trading intracellular glutamine or other neutral amino acids for leucine and related large neutral substrates including aromatic amino acids and thyroid hormones. SLC43A1 and SLC43A2 instead move leucine by facilitated, sodium-independent diffusion. Because tumours upregulate SLC7A5 to sustain anabolic demand, and because these carriers deliver amino acids across the blood-brain barrier and placenta, leucine import links systemic nutrient distribution to cellular growth control.

Glutamine is the cell's main carrier of carbon and nitrogen for biosynthesis, and its uptake across the plasma membrane sets how much is available for nucleotide and amino acid synthesis, glutathione production and anaplerotic feeding of the TCA cycle. The transporters here are sodium-coupled, using the inward sodium gradient to concentrate glutamine in the cytosol: SLC1A5 (ASCT2) exchanges neutral amino acids, while the SLC38 family members act as system A and system N carriers, some of them reversible and pH-sensitive. In the brain this import returns glutamine to neurons for glutamate and GABA resynthesis in the glutamine-glutamate cycle; in liver and kidney it supports ureagenesis and ammonia handling. Proliferating cells, including many tumours, become dependent on this step, and blocking glutamine entry starves mTORC1 signalling and growth.

Glycine taken up from the extracellular space across the plasma membrane serves two very different ends: it terminates inhibitory glycinergic neurotransmission at synapses, and it supplies cells with an amino acid used for protein synthesis, one-carbon metabolism and glutathione production. The transport is carried out by sodium- and chloride-coupled carriers of the neurotransmitter transporter family, including the neuronal and glial glycine transporters SLC6A9 and SLC6A5, the proline/glycine carrier SLC6A20, and the broad-specificity amino acid transporter SLC6A14 found in epithelia. Loss of presynaptic glycine reuptake causes hyperekplexia, an exaggerated startle disorder, while impaired renal and intestinal handling underlies iminoglycinuria; pharmacological block of glial uptake raises synaptic glycine at NMDA receptors. Regulator-of-G-protein-signalling proteins such as RGS2 and RGS4 are included as modulators that tune transporter activity downstream of receptor signalling.

Arginine must cross membranes to be used, and this transport underpins nitric oxide synthesis, polyamine production, urea cycle flux and the amino acid signals that cells read as nutrient sufficiency. Cationic amino acid transporters of the SLC7 family carry arginine, lysine and ornithine across the plasma membrane, some as uniporters and others as exchangers paired with a heavy chain; loss of the SLC7A7 exchanger in intestine and kidney causes lysinuric protein intolerance, with hyperammonaemia from a starved urea cycle. Mitochondrial carriers of the SLC25 group import ornithine and arginine into the matrix, and defects in the ornithine translocase SLC25A15 produce a urea cycle disorder. Lysosomal transport contributes too, including SLC38A9, which delivers arginine information to mTORC1 and links amino acid availability to growth control, while organic cation and multidrug carriers provide lower-specificity routes.

Where a protein ends up inside a cell determines what it can do, and this collection covers the braking mechanisms that keep proteins out of a compartment, off a membrane, or away from the cell surface. Restraint of this kind sets how many glucose transporters, ion channels and receptors reach the plasma membrane, how long signalling proteins are held in the cytoplasm rather than the nucleus, and how misfolded cargo is pulled back from the secretory route. Recurrent devices include 14-3-3 proteins that sequester phosphorylated clients, ER-associated degradation components such as VCP, derlins and OS9 that retrotranslocate rather than export, depalmitoylating hydrolases that release proteins from membranes, retromer and sorting nexins that divert cargo from the surface, and WNK kinases that suppress channel and cotransporter delivery. Loss of such negative control underlies insulin resistance, uncontrolled hormone secretion, hypertension and aberrant developmental signalling.

Proteins only work where they are put, and this collection covers the many ways cells actively increase the delivery or retention of a protein at a particular site: insertion of transporters and channels into the plasma membrane, recruitment of signalling molecules to receptors and the cytoskeleton, nuclear import and export, and secretory traffic. Such positive regulation of protein localization underlies insulin granule exocytosis, glucose transporter and calcium channel surface delivery, synaptic vesicle release, and receptor turnover; when it fails, hormones are not secreted and aggregation-prone proteins such as tau, alpha-synuclein and amyloid precursor protein are mishandled. Mechanistically the genes span COPII coat components and cargo receptors, importins and exportins, Rab and Arf GTPases with their regulators, chaperonin and HSP90 folding machinery, palmitoyl transferases and thioesterases that switch membrane anchoring, and kinases including PKA, PKC and AKT that trigger translocation downstream of extracellular cues.

Transforming growth factor beta controls whether a cell divides, differentiates, deposits matrix, or converts to a mesenchymal phenotype, and this collection covers the machinery that tunes how strongly a cell answers that cue. Setting the gain matters because too little restraint drives fibrosis, tissue stiffening and tumour-promoting immune suppression, while loss of responsiveness removes a brake on epithelial proliferation. Control operates at every level: latent ligand is stored and released by matrix-binding proteins such as LTBP1 and thrombospondin, accessory receptors including endoglin and betaglycan alter ligand access, and inhibitory SMAD6/SMAD7 with the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2 target receptors and activated SMAD2/SMAD3 for degradation, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP15. In the nucleus, SKI and SKIL together with SIN3A-HDAC corepressors or CREBBP/EP300 coactivators reset transcriptional output, and a large set of microRNAs adjusts component levels post-transcriptionally, feeding into ZEB-driven epithelial plasticity.

TGF-beta signalling drives growth arrest, extracellular matrix production and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and cells restrain it to avoid fibrosis, excessive scarring and the tumour-promoting arm of the pathway. This collection covers the brakes on that response: dampening how strongly a cell reacts to TGF-beta once the ligand is present. Much of the control is post-transcriptional, through microRNAs that target receptors, SMAD transducers and downstream effectors so that receptor engagement yields a smaller transcriptional output; several of the listed families are themselves TGF-beta induced, forming negative feedback. Protein regulators act alongside them, including the nuclear receptor PPARG, whose activation antagonises fibrogenic TGF-beta programmes in fibroblasts and mesangial cells, and the cytokine IL4, which reflects immune cross-talk. Loss of this restraint contributes to organ fibrosis, and its exaggeration removes the cytostatic protection TGF-beta normally provides in epithelia.

Cells amplify their sensitivity to TGF-beta when this set of positive regulators is engaged, tuning how strongly a given dose of ligand is converted into transcriptional change. The output matters for tissue fibrosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, smooth muscle and myofibroblast differentiation, and growth arrest, since TGF-beta is both a cytostatic signal and a driver of matrix deposition. Enhancement acts at several levels: thrombospondin-1 releases active ligand from its latent complex, accessory receptors and adaptors such as TGFBR3, GIPC1 and syntenin modulate receptor availability, the ubiquitin ligase RNF111 removes inhibitory SnoN/Ski repressors, and SMAD4 with coactivators CREBBP and EP300 plus CITED and SNW1 partners builds the transcriptional complex. Downstream effectors include the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors CDKN1C and CDKN2B and the transcription factors ZEB2 and myocardin. Overactivity feeds fibrotic disease and tumour-promoting TGF-beta signalling.

Regulation of dendrite extension controls how far and how fast a neuron's dendritic arbor grows, setting the receptive field over which a cell can collect synaptic input. Arbor size determines how many partners a neuron integrates, so mis-set growth contributes to intellectual disability, autism spectrum phenotypes and the dendritic simplification seen in neurodegeneration. The genes point to two convergent mechanisms: calcium sensing at membranes, through copines, synaptotagmins and the active-zone proteins RIMS1/2 and UNC13A, which couples electrical activity and vesicle delivery to where new membrane is added; and ubiquitin ligase control, through SMURF1, NEDD4L, RNF157, MUL1 and parkin, which prunes growth-promoting signalling and cytoskeletal regulators such as RhoA. Osteocrin, a secreted activity-induced factor in primate cortex, acts as an extrinsic brake. The pathway thus links neuronal activity to arbor morphology during development and plasticity.

How far a neuron's dendrites grow, and how fast, determines how many inputs it can receive, so the control of dendrite extension shapes the wiring and receptive properties of neural circuits; too little or too much arborisation is a recurring feature of intellectual disability and neurodegenerative disease. The genes here point to two recurring levers. One is ubiquitin ligase activity at the growing process -- NEDD4L, SMURF1, RNF157, MUL1 and parkin mark substrates for degradation and so set the local abundance of cytoskeletal and signalling regulators. The other is calcium-dependent membrane traffic: copine family calcium-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins, synaptotagmins, UNC13A and RIMS active-zone proteins couple calcium entry to vesicle delivery at the membrane, linking activity to growth. Calcium channel subunits and a Ras GTPase-activating protein place this regulation downstream of excitability and small GTPase signalling.

Extraembryonic membrane development covers the formation and maturation of the tissues that surround and support the embryo rather than contribute to it — the amnion, chorion, yolk sac and allantois — whose fusion and vascularisation establish the fetal side of the placenta. Failure here is a common cause of mid-gestation lethality even when the embryo proper is patterned normally, and of defects in chorioallantoic fusion and labyrinth formation. The genes involved span secreted signals and receptors that pattern these membranes, including BMP family ligands and the Wnt receptor FZD5, together with intracellular regulators such as the kinase MAP3K4 and the secretory pathway protein TMED2. Transcriptional and chromatin components contribute as well: ASCL2 acts in trophoblast lineages, the atypical E2F7 and E2F8 pair restrains proliferation and supports polyploidy, and DNMT3L links the programme to imprinting and DNA methylation.

regulation of IRE1-mediated unfolded protein response tunes one arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, setting how strongly and how long the ER stress sensor IRE1 fires when misfolded protein accumulates in the ER lumen. That tuning decides whether a stressed cell restores proteostasis by expanding chaperone and lipid capacity through XBP1 splicing, or instead crosses into apoptosis, which matters in secretory tissues such as plasma cells and pancreatic beta cells and in tumours adapting to ER stress. Regulation acts at several levels: the chaperone BiP and the co-chaperone ERdj3 hold or release IRE1 depending on lumenal folding load, FICD-mediated AMPylation resets BiP activity, UFM1 ligase components and Nedd8/COP9 subunits modify signal strength, membrane proteins such as TMBIM6 and TMEM33 dampen sensor oligomerisation, and BAX/BAK together with BH3-only proteins couple sustained signalling to mitochondrial cell death.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the sensor kinase IRE1 oligomerizes and activates an RNase output that splices XBP1 mRNA and expands ER folding and secretory capacity; the genes here set how strongly and how long that arm of the unfolded protein response fires. Tuning matters because sustained IRE1 signalling shifts the cell from adaptation toward apoptosis, a switch relevant to secretory cell physiology, metabolic stress and tumour survival under ER stress. Control operates at several levels: the ER chaperone BiP and the cochaperone ERdj4 restrain sensor activation, TMBIM6 and TMEM33 modulate it from the membrane, UFM1 ligation components including UFL1 and DDRGK1 act on the pathway, and a phosphatase, PTPN1, influences signal output. BCL-2 family members such as BAX, BAK1, PUMA and BIM couple prolonged stress to mitochondrial cell death.

The IRE1 arm of the unfolded protein response senses misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum and, through XBP1 mRNA splicing and stress kinase signalling, expands ER capacity or commits a cell to death; dampening that arm is how cells end the response once folding homeostasis returns and avoid the apoptotic output of chronic signalling. Restraint is imposed at the sensor itself. The ER chaperone BiP and the ERdj4 co-chaperone bind IRE1 and favour its inactive, monomeric state, while the ER membrane protein TMBIM6 (BI-1) and the UFM1-conjugation components UFL1 and DDRGK1 modulate IRE1 stability and activity. BFAR contributes anti-apoptotic regulation at the same membrane. The balance set here determines whether ER stress resolves adaptively or progresses to cell death, a switch relevant to secretory cell function, metabolic disease, and neurodegeneration.

When misfolded protein accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum, the sensor kinase IRE1 oligomerizes and activates its RNase and kinase outputs, splicing XBP1 mRNA to expand ER folding and degradation capacity and signalling onward to stress kinases. This set covers the inputs that turn that arm of the unfolded protein response up rather than down, setting how strongly a stressed cell commits to adaptation versus death. Proteins of the BCL-2 family, including BAX and BAK1 at the ER membrane and the BH3-only members PUMA and BIM, engage IRE1 directly and couple ER stress to apoptotic decisions; the scaffold DAB2IP links it to JNK activation, the phosphatase PTPN1 acts on the signalling output, and an ER-resident membrane protein and the ER chaperone AGR2 modulate sensor activity. Sustained amplification drives stress-induced cell death, relevant to secretory tissue loss in diabetes and neurodegeneration.

regulation of PERK-mediated unfolded protein response tunes one of the three arms of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, setting how strongly and how long a cell shuts down protein synthesis when unfolded proteins accumulate. The strength of this control decides whether ER stress ends in adaptation and recovery or in apoptosis, which matters for secretory cells such as pancreatic beta cells, for neurodegeneration, and for tumour cells surviving hypoxia and nutrient limitation. Regulation acts at several points: the chaperone BiP holds PERK inactive until it is recruited to misfolded clients, membrane proteins including TMEM33 and DDRGK1 modulate sensor activity, phosphatases and Akt-family kinases dampen signalling, and the GADD34/CReP regulatory subunits direct protein phosphatase 1 to dephosphorylate eIF2α and restart translation. BOK and ATAD3A link the same axis to mitochondria and cell death commitment.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the kinase PERK shuts down most translation and reprogrammes gene expression to restore folding capacity; the genes here set how strongly and how long that arm of the unfolded protein response runs. Tuning matters because sustained PERK signalling drives apoptosis, while blunted signalling leaves secretory cells unable to cope with folding load, and both extremes appear in neurodegeneration, diabetes and tumour adaptation to stress. The chaperone BiP (HSPA5) holds the sensor inactive until unfolded protein binds it; GADD34 (PPP1R15A) and its constitutive relative feed back through phosphatase targeting to reverse eIF2α phosphorylation and resume translation. Membrane proteins such as TMEM33 and the UFMylation adaptor DDRGK1 act at the ER to modulate sensor activity, while AKT isoforms and tyrosine phosphatases couple this stress branch to growth and insulin signalling.

negative regulation of PERK-mediated unfolded protein response restrains one arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, allowing cells to recover protein synthesis and survive after an episode of misfolded protein accumulation rather than remaining in translational arrest or progressing to apoptosis. PERK phosphorylates eIF2α to shut down cap-dependent translation; the genes here terminate that signal at several points. The chaperone BiP binds and holds PERK inactive when the ER lumen is not stressed, the phosphatase regulatory subunits GADD34 and CReP direct PP1 to dephosphorylate eIF2α, and NCK adaptors together with PTP1B and AKT signalling dampen PERK output and couple it to growth and insulin pathways. Set-point control of this kind determines whether ER stress ends in adaptation or cell death, and matters for secretory cells such as pancreatic β cells, lipid handling, and neurodegenerative disease.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the PERK arm of the unfolded protein response halts most translation and drives a stress transcriptional programme; dampening that arm is how cells recover protein synthesis and avoid committing to apoptosis when stress is transient or resolved. This negative regulation sets the duration and intensity of the response, and its loss leaves cells chronically translationally repressed, while excessive restraint permits unfolded protein load to go unchecked. The clearest mechanism is dephosphorylation of eIF2α by phosphatase regulatory subunits GADD34 and CReP, which closes the feedback loop initiated by PERK. The ER chaperone BiP holds PERK inactive under basal conditions, PTPN1 acts on the kinase's phosphotyrosine state, NCK adaptors and AKT isoforms couple growth and survival signalling to attenuation, and DDRGK1 links the pathway to ufmylation-dependent ER quality control.

Viruses depend on host machinery at every step, and host cells in turn have factors that either restrict or assist those steps; together these constitute the regulation of the viral life cycle. The balance decides whether an infection is aborted, becomes productive, or turns latent, and it shapes which viruses can cross into a given cell type. Restriction factors act at defined stages: entry and membrane fusion are blocked by interferon-induced transmembrane proteins, incoming capsids are recognised by TRIM proteins, genomes and transcripts are edited or degraded by APOBEC cytidine deaminases, ADAR, OAS-RNase L and zinc-finger antiviral protein, translation is shut down by PKR, and budding virions are tethered at the surface by BST2. Working the other way, proteases such as FURIN and TMPRSS2 prime viral glycoproteins, receptors including AXL, BSG and CD209 mediate uptake, cyclophilins chaperone capsids, and ESCRT components are appropriated for egress. Many of these genes are interferon-stimulated, linking innate sensing to direct antiviral effect.

Cells restrict viruses not only by killing infected neighbours but by interfering with the virus's own replication steps, and negative regulation of the viral life cycle covers the host activities that slow or block those steps. The best-defined member here is the interferon-induced tetherin BST2, which physically retains budding enveloped virions, including HIV-1 particles, at the plasma membrane so they cannot disseminate; viral accessory proteins such as Vpu exist largely to counteract it. Other contributors act on intracellular stages, including a TRIM-family protein of the kind that couples ubiquitin ligase activity to innate immune signalling, a cyclophilin that acts as a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase on retroviral capsid, a casein kinase 2 regulatory subunit, and a cytokine linked to antiviral inflammatory responses. Loss or viral antagonism of these restriction activities permits higher viral output and spread.

Viruses depend on host proteins at nearly every step, and this grouping collects host activities that promote rather than restrain the viral life cycle anging from attachment and entry through genome import, assembly and budding. Several members act as attachment or entry factors: lectins such as CD209 and CLEC4G capture glycosylated envelope proteins, the receptor tyrosine kinases AXL and TYRO3 mediate phosphatidylserine-dependent uptake, and the proteases TMPRSS2, TMPRSS4 and FURIN cleave envelope glycoproteins to license membrane fusion, with acid sphingomyelinase and the redox chaperone P4HB shaping the endosomal fusion step. Importins KPNA2 and KPNA6 carry viral components into the nucleus, while TSG101, VPS37B and VPS4A supply the membrane-scission machinery that virions borrow to bud from the cell. Because these factors determine host and tissue susceptibility, they are prime targets for antiviral inhibitors, and the same list includes TRIM proteins that modulate the outcome.

A T cell that meets an antigen-presenting cell must reorganise itself into a front and a back, concentrating receptors and signalling machinery at the contact site while remodelling the trailing edge, and this control layer sets how readily and how strongly that asymmetry is established. The same polarity underlies directed migration through tissue and interstitial crawling, so its loss leaves T cells unable to form stable immune synapses or reach their targets; mutations in DOCK8, an activator of Cdc42-type GTPases, cause a combined immunodeficiency in which lymphocytes crawl poorly and die during migration. Actin is the common substrate: gelsolin severs and caps filaments, the ABL family kinases couple receptor and adhesion signals to cytoskeletal rearrangement, RIPOR2 restrains RhoA-driven rear contraction, and membrane organisation by flotillin helps define the polarised domains.

Receptors work best when concentrated at the right patch of membrane, and the control of receptor clustering sets how densely they gather and how long they stay put. The clearest physiological read-out here is the neuromuscular junction: LRP4 with its chaperone MESD presents agrin signals that pack acetylcholine receptors beneath the nerve terminal, while dystroglycan, its glycosyltransferase LARGE1 and the laminin chains of the synaptic basement membrane anchor that specialisation. Failure of these steps produces congenital myasthenic and muscular dystrophy phenotypes with weak, fatigable transmission. In the central nervous system, FRRS1L, SHISA6 and SHISA7 act as auxiliary subunits that hold AMPA-type glutamate receptors at postsynaptic sites, tuning synaptic strength. Actin and adaptor components such as gelsolin, GIT1, SSH1 and the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC2 supply the cytoskeletal remodelling and lipid modification that make clusters stable or dispersible.

Receptors work better in groups, and this pathway covers the processes that promote receptor clustering, concentrating receptors into dense patches at specialised regions of the plasma membrane. The clearest example among these genes is the neuromuscular junction, where agrin acting through the LRP4 co-receptor and the dystroglycan complex drives acetylcholine receptors into high-density postsynaptic aggregates; without this, endplates fail to transmit and muscle weakness follows, as in congenital myasthenic syndromes. Laminin subunits and the glycosyltransferase LARGE1 supply the matrix scaffold and the matriglycan modification of dystroglycan that anchors it, with MESD assisting folding of the receptor itself. Other members act on membrane organisation and the actin cytoskeleton, including the tetraspanin CD81, the palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC2, the phosphatase SSH1 and the adaptor GIT1, linking clustering to synapse formation, adhesion and cell migration.

Bisphenol A is a synthetic monomer leached from polycarbonate plastics and resins that acts as a weak estrogen-receptor agonist and endocrine disruptor, and the response to bisphenol A covers the changes in gene expression and cell behaviour that follow such exposure. Much of the interest lies in epigenetic consequences: the maintenance methyltransferase DNMT1 and the de novo enzyme DNMT3A set cytosine methylation patterns, while methyl-CpG-binding proteins of the MBD family read those marks and recruit repressive chromatin complexes, so altered activity of these factors can shift developmental gene silencing in ways that persist after the chemical is gone. The presence of the glutamate transporter SLC1A1 points to effects on neuronal excitatory signalling and glutamate clearance. Together these components link environmental exposure to developmental programming, reproductive and metabolic disturbance, and neurobehavioural outcomes attributed to bisphenol A.

Sodium arsenite is a thiol-reactive metalloid that provokes oxidative and proteotoxic stress, and the response to it is a composite defence programme that determines whether an exposed cell adapts or dies. Two arms dominate. One is antioxidant and detoxifying: NFE2L2 escapes its normal degradation, accumulates in the nucleus and turns on genes for glutathione synthesis, NADPH supply and conjugative export, the same route that handles electrophiles generally. The other is the heat shock response, in which HSF1 drives chaperone expression to cope with proteins aggregating on arsenic-bound cysteines. Alongside these, stress-granule and RNA-handling behaviour of HNRNPA1, stress-activated p38-family signalling through MAPK13, apoptotic and transcriptional regulation by DAXX, and mRNA-destabilising control of inflammation by ZC3H12A shape the outcome. Arsenic exposure through contaminated drinking water causes skin, bladder and lung cancer, making the adequacy of this response a determinant of susceptibility.

Sodium arsenite is a proteotoxic and oxidative insult, and the cellular response to it is a stress programme that decides whether a cell repairs itself or dies. Arsenite exposure causes protein misfolding and reactive oxygen production, and the response protects the proteome while reshaping which messages get translated. HSF1 is the transcriptional core, driving heat shock protein genes that refold or triage damaged proteins; DAXX modulates stress-induced apoptotic and transcriptional outcomes. HNRNPA1 relocalises from the nucleus to the cytoplasm under arsenite and partitions into stress granules, the translationally silent condensates that form when initiation stalls, and p38-family kinase signalling contributes to this stress-activated output. ZC3H12A adds control over the stability of inflammatory transcripts. Together these activities link arsenic toxicity to proteostasis, RNA granule dynamics and inflammation, biology relevant to arsenic-associated tissue damage and carcinogenesis.

TORC2 is the mTOR complex that controls AKT activation, and so cell survival, glucose uptake, cytoskeletal organisation and cell migration; its regulation sets how strongly growth factor and insulin signals are converted into anabolic and pro-survival output. The genes here act on that tuning rather than on the kinase reaction itself: DEPTOR binds mTOR as an inhibitory subunit, deubiquitinases including USP9X, OTUD5 and OTUD7B alter the stability and assembly of complex components, a HSP90 co-chaperone adaptor contributes to complex maturation, and acetylation by EP300 modifies signalling proteins. AKT1 and its substrate kinase GSK3B, together with S6 kinase, sit downstream and feed back on complex activity, linking the two mTOR complexes. Persistently elevated signalling through this axis supports tumour cell growth and invasion, while loss of restraint on AKT distorts metabolic control.

Hepatocytes die by apoptosis during viral hepatitis, cholestatic injury, alcohol and drug toxicity, and fatty liver disease, and this regulatory programme sets how readily that happens. Tuning it matters because excessive hepatocyte loss drives inflammation, fibrosis and eventual cirrhosis, while too little clearance of damaged cells permits transformation and hepatocellular carcinoma. Control is exerted at two levels: direct interference with death receptor signalling, where CFLAR acts as a caspase-8 decoy blocking Fas- and TNF-initiated killing, and metabolic sensing, where the AMPK catalytic subunits encoded by PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 couple energy stress to survival decisions and the nuclear receptor PPARA links fatty acid oxidation to protection from lipotoxic death. The retinoblastoma protein contributes cell cycle-linked restraint. The result is a liver whose parenchymal mass can be defended or sacrificed according to nutrient state and injury signals.

Liver cells are exposed constantly to death signals — TNF and Fas ligand from resident immune cells, bile acids, drug metabolites, lipid overload — and hepatocytes survive this only because apoptosis is actively restrained. Suppressing hepatocyte apoptosis preserves liver mass and function; when the brake fails, the result is the hepatocyte dropout seen in fulminant hepatitis, cholestatic and alcoholic liver injury, and steatohepatitis, where repeated death drives inflammation, fibrosis and eventually cancer. The genes here act at different levels: CFLAR competes with caspase-8 at death receptor complexes to block initiation, the AMPK catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 couple energy stress to metabolic adaptation and survival, PPARA directs fatty acid oxidation and limits lipotoxic damage, and RB1 constrains death that would otherwise follow deregulated proliferation. Together they link survival control to hepatic metabolic state and regeneration.

Macrophage colony-stimulating factor instructs monocyte and macrophage survival, proliferation and differentiation, and also drives osteoclast formation; this pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly cells answer that cue. Setting the gain matters because too much signalling expands tumour-associated and inflammatory macrophage populations and accelerates bone resorption, while too little leaves tissues short of resident macrophages and microglia. Regulation acts at several levels: the ligand CSF1 itself sets available stimulus, the phosphatase PTPN2 dampens receptor-proximal tyrosine phosphorylation and downstream JAK-STAT output, and the adaptor STAP1 modulates kinase signalling. Innate immune receptors TLR2 and TLR4 cross-talk with this axis so that microbial sensing reshapes the myeloid response, and TREM2, a microglial and macrophage receptor, cooperates with colony-stimulating factor signalling to support survival — a link relevant to neurodegenerative disease.

Glia are motile cells: microglia patrol the parenchyma and converge on injury, and astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursors must reach their targets during development and repair. Control over how fast and how far these cells move is what this regulation of glial cell migration describes, and it determines whether damage is cleared and remyelinated or whether inflammatory cells accumulate where they do harm. Much of the input is chemotactic: neurons release fractalkine that acts on microglial CX3CR1, CCL3 signals through CCR2, CSF1 supports microglial survival and directed movement, and purinergic sensors such as P2RY12 and P2RX4 read extracellular nucleotides released by injured tissue as a "find-me" cue. TREM2 couples lipid recognition to cytoskeletal responses, while adaptors including CRKL and the microRNAs miR-221/222 tune the motile output. Dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, glioma invasion and chronic neuroinflammation.

Glia must move to the right place and then stop, and this pathway covers the braking side of that balance: processes that reduce the rate or extent of glial cell migration. Restraint matters during nervous system development, where astrocyte and oligodendrocyte precursors have to settle and differentiate rather than keep travelling, and it matters again in injury and tumour contexts, where loss of migratory control contributes to glioma invasiveness. The genes involved point to several ways of applying that brake, including a sodium pump beta subunit that also serves as an adhesion molecule mediating glial interactions with neurons, sphingolipid synthesis that shapes membrane composition and hence motility, and mitochondrial metabolic enzymes whose products influence cell state. Together they mark migration arrest as a distinct regulated step rather than a simple absence of movement.

Glial cells are not static: microglia patrol the brain, converge on injury and plaque, and astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursors relocate during development and repair, and this pathway covers the signals that drive that movement rather than restrain it. Chemokines and their receptors set the direction typified by CCL3 acting through chemokine receptors, CCR2 recruiting monocyte-derived cells, and fractalkine signalling from neurons to microglia. Purinergic sensing of extracellular nucleotides through P2RY12 and the ATP-gated channel P2RX4 lets microglia detect damage and extend processes toward it, while TREM2 supports the motility and survival of microglia around amyloid deposits and CSF1 sustains the lineage. Adaptor signalling via CRKL and microRNA control by the miR-221/222 pair tune the cytoskeletal response. Too little of this activity leaves lesions uncleared; too much contributes to neuroinflammation and glioma invasiveness.

Microglia switch from surveying the brain parenchyma to an activated, phagocytic and cytokine-secreting state, and this pathway covers the signals that set how readily and how strongly that switch is thrown. Tuning matters because too little activation leaves debris, dying neurons and plaques uncleared, while unrestrained activation drives chronic neuroinflammation and synapse loss in neurodegeneration. Neurons restrain microglia through the chemokine CX3CL1 acting on their receptor, whereas TREM2 and progranulin set the threshold for the phagocytic, lipid-handling response; loss-of-function variants in TREM2, GRN and LRRK2 shift microglia toward damaging states and are linked to dementia and Parkinson disease. Other members provide the output and feedback arms: CCL3 and IL6 recruit and amplify, cathepsins and cystatin F govern lysosomal proteolysis, and circadian and sphingolipid signalling gate responsiveness over time.

Microglia must be able to switch to a reactive, inflammatory state and also to be talked back down from it, and this pathway covers the braking signals that limit microglial activation in the healthy brain. Restraint matters because persistently activated microglia release cytokines, reactive oxygen species and complement, prune synapses inappropriately, and drive the chronic neuroinflammation seen in neurodegeneration. Neurons supply part of the brake directly: fractalkine, made by neurons, acts on microglial CX3CR1 to suppress reactive responses. Progranulin, secreted and delivered to lysosomes, keeps microglia quiescent, and its loss causes frontotemporal dementia with strongly activated microglia; the lysosomal cathepsin inhibitor cystatin F is induced in the same reactive states. A circadian factor and a lipoprotein receptor add transcriptional and lipid-handling control, linking microglial tone to metabolism and the daily clock.

Microglia are the brain's resident macrophages, and this pathway covers the signals that push them from a surveying state into an activated one, with enlarged morphology, phagocytic capacity and secretion of cytokines. Turning that switch up matters for clearing debris, amyloid and dying neurons, but sustained activation drives the neuroinflammation seen in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and demyelinating injury. The components illustrate the routes involved: TREM2 is the microglial surface receptor whose loss-of-function variants blunt responses to lipid and damage signals and raise dementia risk; CCL3 is a chemokine that recruits and stimulates further myeloid cells; LRRK2, a kinase mutated in familial Parkinson's disease, links this response to lysosomal and vesicle handling; cathepsin C and MMP8 are proteases acting on the extracellular and endolysosomal environment. A microRNA and tau-tubulin kinase activity add post-transcriptional and kinase-level control over the activation threshold.

Food intake is set by hypothalamic circuits that weigh energy stores and gut signals against the drive to eat, and the regulation of eating behavior covers the neuropeptides and receptors that tune how much and how often an animal feeds. Its failure produces obesity or wasting: loss-of-function variants in the melanocortin-4 receptor are the commonest monogenic cause of severe human obesity. Arcuate neurons form two opposing populations, one releasing the orexigenic peptides AGRP and NPY, the other producing POMC, whose cleavage yields the melanocortin agonist that suppresses feeding; CARTPT is co-expressed in the anorexigenic set. Peripheral ghrelin from the stomach signals hunger through its receptor GHSR, while CRH and neuromedin U act to restrain intake, and MGRN1 modulates melanocortin receptor signalling. The pathway links endocrine sensing of nutritional state to motivated behaviour and body weight homeostasis.

Food intake is held in check by a set of satiety signals acting mainly in the hypothalamus, and negative regulation of eating behavior is the arm of energy balance that terminates a meal and limits body weight gain. Loss of this restraint produces hyperphagia and early-onset obesity, most clearly when melanocortin signalling fails: POMC is cleaved to α-MSH, which acts on MC4R in paraventricular and other hypothalamic neurons to suppress appetite, and mutations in either gene cause severe inherited obesity in humans. CARTPT and neuromedin U act as additional anorexigenic peptides, while CRH links appetite suppression to the stress axis. NAPEPLD generates N-acylethanolamines, tying lipid-derived signalling to feeding, and TTC21B is required for hypothalamic cilia, whose disruption in ciliopathies also causes overeating. The pathway sits downstream of leptin and upstream of meal termination and metabolic rate.

Feeding is driven by a small set of orexigenic signals that report energy deficit to the hypothalamus and raise the drive to eat. Stomach-derived ghrelin acting through its receptor GHSR is the principal circulating hunger signal, stimulating arcuate neurons that co-release neuropeptide Y and agouti-related peptide; AGRP in turn antagonises melanocortin receptor signalling, lifting the tonic brake that leptin-responsive POMC neurons impose on appetite. MGRN1 shapes this melanocortin arm through receptor trafficking and ubiquitination, while kappa-opioid receptor signalling contributes hedonic and reward-related components of food intake. Positive regulation of eating behavior sets meal initiation, body weight set point and adaptation to fasting; excess drive contributes to obesity and hyperphagia, and its loss to cachexia and anorexia in chronic illness. These molecules are consequently targets for both appetite-suppressing and appetite-stimulating drugs.

Thyroid hormone in its active form, triiodothyronine, released from thyroglobulin, sets the pace of metabolism in nearly every tissue, and this pathway covers what a cell does once that hormone arrives: changes in gene expression, enzyme output, secretion and growth. Because T3 acts through nuclear receptors, the response is largely transcriptional, and the steroid receptor coactivators NCOA1 and NCOA2 are the bridge between a liganded receptor and the transcriptional machinery, determining how strongly target genes respond. Downstream consequences show up as altered glucose uptake through the transporter GLUT1, lysosomal glycosidase activity, and changed secretion of the activin/inhibin subunit INHBB, linking hormone sensing to fuel use, tissue remodelling and endocrine feedback. Too little or too much signalling here produces the developmental delay, altered basal metabolic rate and thermogenic changes seen in hypo- and hyperthyroidism.

positive regulation of vasculature development gathers the signals that drive new blood and lymphatic vessel formation, the process by which growing tissues, healing wounds, and tumours obtain a supply of oxygen and nutrients. Without it, embryonic vascular remodelling fails and ischaemic tissue cannot recover; in excess it feeds tumour growth, diabetic retinopathy, and inflammatory neovascularisation. The core drive comes from VEGF family ligands acting through KDR, FLT1, and neuropilin, angiopoietins through TEK and TIE1, and TGF-β/BMP inputs via ENG, ACVRL1, and GDF2 whose loss causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Hypoxia sensing through HIF1A, inflammatory and chemokine cues such as CXCL12-CXCR4, IL1B and complement receptors, matrix and integrin engagement, and a large set of microRNAs including MIR126 and MIR210 all converge on endothelial proliferation, migration, sprouting, and junctional remodelling, coupling metabolic and immune state to vessel growth.

Blood and lymphatic vessels are built and expanded by endothelial cells that proliferate, migrate and assemble into perfused tubes, and this collection captures the signals that drive that expansion forward. Such positive regulation of vasculature development underlies wound healing, placental and embryonic growth, and adaptation to hypoxia, and it is hijacked in tumour angiogenesis, diabetic retinopathy and inflammatory neovascularisation.
