The core drivers are the VEGF family acting through KDR, FLT1 and the co-receptor NRP1, angiopoietins signalling via TEK and TIE1, fibroblast growth factors, and a TGF-beta/BMP arm through ENG, ACVRL1 and SMAD1 whose loss causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Hypoxia sensing by HIF1A, chemokine cues such as CXCL12-CXCR4, integrin-mediated adhesion to remodelled matrix, nitric oxide production by NOS3, and a large set of endothelial microRNAs tune the response, alongside transcription factors including GATA2, ETS1 and SOX-independent lymphatic regulators such as FOXC2.

Programmed cell death of epithelial cells shapes glands, ducts and linings throughout development and turnover, removing cells that are damaged, displaced from their matrix, or surplus to a tissue's needs. Its failure permits the survival of transformed epithelium and underlies carcinoma; excessive activation contributes to degeneration of secretory tissues such as pancreatic beta cells, reflected here by insulin-lineage regulators including PDX1, NEUROD1 and the ER-stress gene WFS1. The genes span the core death machinery and its brakes — BID and BOK promoting mitochondrial permeabilization, BCL2L1 and the caspase-8 inhibitor CFLAR opposing it, with CASP6 executing cleavage of substrates including the epithelial keratins KRT8 and KRT18. Upstream inputs arrive from TGF-beta receptor signalling, JAK2 and IL6, energy sensing through AMPK subunits, and the Hippo kinases STK3/STK4 acting on YAP1, linking growth control and tissue size to epithelial survival decisions.

G protein-coupled receptors are removed from the cell surface by endocytosis after activation, and controlling how fast and how completely that happens sets how long a cell keeps responding to a hormone or peptide ligand. Regulation of this internalization step therefore governs desensitization, receptor recycling versus degradation, and the duration of downstream signalling. Here the apelin receptor and its two peptide agonists, apelin and the related early endogenous ligand, illustrate the ligand-driven arm: agonist binding promotes receptor uptake, and the balance between ligands tunes signalling in cardiovascular tone, fluid homeostasis and angiogenesis. Accessory proteins contribute the trafficking arm, including a calcium-binding partner that retains certain receptors at the membrane and a ubiquilin family protein linking receptor fate to ubiquitin-dependent sorting and degradation. Amyloid precursor protein is likewise handled through this endocytic machinery, tying receptor traffic to processing events relevant in neurons.</description>}</invoke>

Collagen fibrils give tendon, skin, blood vessel wall and cartilage their tensile strength, and their diameter, spacing and lateral packing are actively controlled rather than left to spontaneous self-assembly. Regulation of collagen fibril organization covers the factors that set how fast and how extensively fibrils form and align, and its failure produces connective tissue fragility, aberrant scarring and vessel wall disease. Matrix components act as fibril modifiers: tenascin XB and EMILIN1 shape the fibrillar network and its elastic partners, collagen VI microfibrils and a chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan-like protein decorate fibril surfaces, while EFEMP2 links fibril assembly to elastic fibre formation. COLGALT1 glycosylates collagen hydroxylysines during biosynthesis, altering what is delivered to the matrix, and miR-29b acts in the opposite direction by repressing collagen transcripts, so fibrillogenesis is tuned both inside and outside the cell.

Epithelial sheets are continually renewed, and the decision of an individual epithelial cell to die or survive is tuned rather than fixed; regulation of the epithelial cell apoptotic process covers the inputs that raise or lower that threshold. It matters for maintaining barrier integrity in gut, kidney, lung and mammary tissue, for involution and duct remodelling, and for the survival of pancreatic beta cells, whose loss underlies diabetes. The controls act at several levels: BOK belongs to the BCL-2 family at the mitochondrial commitment step, CFLAR restrains death-receptor caspase activation, and calpain activity is held in check by its endogenous inhibitor calpastatin. Transcriptional and stress inputs converge here too, including the PDX1/NEUROD1/WFS1 axis of beta-cell survival, YAP1-dependent growth signalling, energy sensing through AMPK subunits, cytokine signalling via IL6 and JAK2, chromatin regulators, and post-transcriptional repressors such as ZFP36 and selected microRNAs.

Epithelia are continually exposed to injury, stretch and metabolic stress, and their survival depends on active suppression of programmed cell death; this pathway groups the factors that restrain apoptosis in epithelial cells so that sheets remain intact and secretory tissues retain their cell mass. It matters most in the pancreatic beta cell, the kidney tubule and regenerating epithelium: loss of these brakes contributes to diabetes, cystic kidney disease and tissue atrophy, while their overactivity lets damaged epithelial cells persist and become tumorigenic. Mechanisms represented here are varied rather than linear. CFLAR blocks caspase-8 activation at the death receptor complex, CAST inhibits calpain proteases, and YAP1 drives pro-survival transcription downstream of Hippo signalling. Transcription factors such as PDX1, NEUROD1 and TCF7L2 maintain beta cell identity and viability, while WFS1 buffers endoplasmic reticulum stress and the AMPK subunits couple survival to energy status.

Epithelial sheets are maintained by balancing cell division against cell death, and this pathway covers the inputs that push epithelial cells toward apoptosis rather than survival. Raising the rate of epithelial cell death matters for involution of secretory tissue, turnover of gut and airway lining, elimination of damaged or virally infected cells, and the tissue loss seen in kidney injury, colitis and lung damage; too little of it permits epithelial tumour growth, too much strips barrier integrity. The contributing activities are varied rather than a single cascade: cytokine and kinase signalling through IL6 and JAK2, translation-initiation control via EIF2S1 during stress responses, chromatin and transcriptional regulators including HDAC3 and CARM1, secreted Wnt antagonism by SFRP4, phospholipase and calpain proteolytic activity, and microRNA-mediated tuning. Together they represent points at which apoptotic sensitivity of epithelium is set by growth factor, inflammatory and stress context.

Aldosterone is the adrenal mineralocorticoid that tells epithelia to retain sodium, and this is the set of cellular changes cells make when they receive it. The canonical response occurs in the distal nephron and collecting duct, where the hormone's transcriptional programme raises the abundance and open probability of the epithelial sodium channel subunits and the thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter, with SGK1 induced as the immediate effector kinase and STK39 phosphorylating the cotransporter; the net result is sodium reabsorption, potassium secretion and expansion of extracellular volume, which is why excess signalling drives hypertension and its blockade lowers blood pressure. Beyond salt handling, aldosterone stimulation elicits NADPH oxidase-dependent superoxide production, inflammatory and stress responses involving PARP1 and immune signalling components, and feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary stress axis through corticotropin-releasing hormone, linking mineralocorticoid excess to cardiac and vascular remodelling.

cellular response to aldosterone is how target cells react to the adrenal mineralocorticoid that governs sodium retention, potassium excretion and blood pressure. In the distal nephron, colon and airway epithelium, aldosterone binding to its nuclear receptor drives a transcriptional programme whose best-characterised output is SGK1, a kinase that relieves Nedd4-2-mediated degradation of the epithelial sodium channel and thereby raises the number of active ENaC subunits at the apical membrane. The result is increased electrogenic sodium reabsorption, water follows, and extracellular volume rises. The channel subunits themselves are among the responding genes, alongside HCN2 and mitochondrial AIFM1, linking the hormone to excitability and cell survival as well as transport. Excess signalling produces hypertension and hypokalaemia, while loss of channel function causes salt wasting, making this axis the target of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and amiloride-type diuretics.

Aldosterone is the adrenal mineralocorticoid that tells epithelia to retain sodium, and this describes how a target cell reacts once the hormone arrives. In the distal nephron and collecting duct the response sets sodium reabsorption, potassium secretion and therefore extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure; excessive signalling drives hypertension and hypokalaemia, while loss of the effectors causes salt wasting. The core output is the epithelial sodium channel, whose alpha, beta, gamma and delta subunits form the apical entry pathway for sodium. Induction of the kinase SGK1 is the classic transcriptional step downstream of the mineralocorticoid receptor, and it increases channel abundance at the membrane by restraining its ubiquitin-dependent removal. Additional members point to accompanying changes in cation conductance and mitochondrial apoptotic machinery, linking hormone sensing to epithelial transport capacity and cell survival.

VEGF is the principal driver of new blood vessel growth, and its output must be held down when tissue is adequately perfused; this pathway covers the processes that suppress VEGF production. Restraint of VEGF limits pathological angiogenesis in tumours, diabetic retinopathy and inflamed tissue, where excess ligand produces leaky, disorganised vessels. Almost all of the members are microRNAs that bind the VEGFA transcript or its upstream regulators, lowering message stability and translation; the miR-15/16 and miR-17~92 families, miR-34a, miR-146a and miR-200-related species recur in studies of endothelial and tumour cells. Seryl-tRNA synthetase acts differently, moonlighting in the nucleus to repress VEGFA transcription, a role established in vascular development. Together these brakes tune the balance between angiogenic drive and vessel quiescence, and their loss in cancer contributes to the angiogenic switch.

Pain sensitivity is not fixed; it is actively raised by signals that increase the gain of nociceptive pathways, and this positive regulation of pain perception is what turns injury or inflammation into heightened, persistent hurting. The genes here act mostly at the interface between primary sensory neurons and the dorsal horn. Tachykinin precursors give rise to substance P and related peptides released from peptidergic nociceptors, which act on neurokinin receptors to depolarize second-order neurons and promote central sensitization; neuromedin U is a further neuropeptide that facilitates nociceptive transmission. The metabotropic glutamate receptor GRM5 couples glutamate release to intracellular calcium signalling and sustained excitability in spinal and peripheral sensory circuits. Excessive drive through these routes contributes to hyperalgesia, allodynia and chronic pain states, making the same molecules long-standing analgesic drug targets.

Vasopressin released from the posterior pituitary tells the kidney to conserve water and sodium, and this pathway covers the cellular changes that follow when a cell detects the hormone. The response matters for blood pressure and plasma osmolality: without it, urine cannot be concentrated, as in diabetes insipidus, while excessive signalling drives water retention and hyponatraemia. Downstream of the G protein-coupled vasopressin receptors, adenylate cyclase raises cAMP and phospholipase C beta generates inositol phosphates and diacylglycerol, and these second messengers change transport protein abundance and activity at the apical membrane. Prominent among the effectors are the subunits of the epithelial sodium channel, whose surface expression in collecting duct principal cells sets sodium reabsorption and thereby the osmotic gradient for water movement. Transcriptional and cell cycle responses accompany the acute transport effects.

Microglia are the resident macrophages of the brain, and their directed movement toward sites of injury, infection or synaptic remodelling is what allows the CNS to mount a local immune response and clear debris. The genes here describe how that migration is steered: neurons release fractalkine, which acts on the microglia-restricted receptor CX3CR1 to control process motility and positioning; damaged cells release nucleotides that are sensed by P2RY12 and the ionotropic channel P2RX4, providing the chemotactic gradient that draws processes and cell bodies toward a lesion. CSF1 supports microglial survival and proliferation alongside recruitment, CCL3 amplifies chemokine-driven attraction, and TREM2 couples lipid and damage recognition to cytoskeletal reorganisation and phagocytic engagement. Loss of these cues leaves microglia unable to reach damaged synapses or plaques, a defect linked to neurodegeneration and impaired injury responses.

Microglia patrol the brain and must move toward sites of injury, infection or synaptic remodelling, and this pathway covers the signals that promote that movement. Nucleotides released from damaged or stressed cells are sensed by purinergic receptors, with P2RY12 acting as the principal sensor guiding process extension and chemotaxis toward ATP and ADP gradients, while ionotropic P2RX4 contributes to the activated state. Neuron-derived CX3CL1 and the chemokine CCL3 provide directional cues from injured tissue, CSF1 supports microglial survival and motility through its receptor, and TREM2 couples lipid and damage recognition to cytoskeletal reorganisation and migration. Loss of these inputs blunts recruitment to amyloid plaques and injury sites, and TREM2 variants that impair this response are linked to Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegenerative conditions, making microglial positioning a determinant of neuroinflammatory outcome.

Misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are recognised, pulled back across the membrane into the cytosol, and destroyed by the proteasome; this pathway sets how fast and how extensively that retrograde dislocation happens. Tuning it matters because too little clearance loads the ER with aggregation-prone cargo and triggers stress responses, while unchecked extraction destroys proteins that would otherwise fold successfully. Lectin-like sensors such as OS9 and ERLEC1 read demannosylated glycans generated by EDEM family mannosidases and commit substrates to disposal, Derlin channels and membrane adaptors including BCAP31 and UBAC2 organise the retrotranslocation site, and dedicated ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes mark substrates for extraction. Counterweights are built in: the deubiquitinase YOD1 trims chains during extraction and SVIP acts as an inhibitor of the machinery, so the pathway is a rheostat on ER protein quality control rather than a one-way route.

Motile cilia and flagella beat because a pair of central singlet microtubules and their projections sit at the core of the 9+2 axoneme, converting dynein activity into coordinated, directional waveforms. Building that central apparatus is what this pathway does, and its failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia: immotile or dyskinetic airway cilia, chronic sinopulmonary infection and bronchiectasis, hydrocephalus in some cases, and sperm flagellar defects with male infertility. HYDIN and SPAG17 are structural components of the central pair projections, while radial spoke and spoke-associated proteins such as RSPH9, CFAP91 and DNAJB13 connect the central apparatus to the outer doublets so that the spoke–central pair interaction can regulate dynein arms around the circumference. SPEF1 binds and bundles microtubules. The programme is a downstream output of the transcriptional network that specifies multiciliated and spermatogenic cells.

How much adipose tissue a body builds, and where, is set by regulators that tune the commitment of precursors to adipocytes and the extent to which those cells fill with lipid. This control determines fat mass and depot distribution, and its loss shifts an organism toward obesity and insulin resistance or, in the opposite direction, toward lipodystrophy and ectopic fat. The master adipogenic transcription factor PPARG sits at the centre, with coactivators NCOA1 and NCOA2 amplifying its output, SIRT1 and the energy sensor PRKAA1 restraining lipid storage in response to nutrient state, and KLF7 and SPI1 acting as negative regulators of differentiation. A CUL4-DDB1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase together with WDTC1 limits adipose expansion by degradative control, while LPL supplies fatty acids from circulating triglyceride and secreted factors such as ghrelin and activin-family ligands relay whole-body signals to the tissue.

negative regulation of adipose tissue development covers the brakes on fat tissue formation inhibitory inputs that block preadipocytes from committing to and completing adipogenesis. Its output is fat mass itself: weak restraint permits adipose expansion and obesity, while strong restraint limits lipid storage capacity and can push lipid into liver and muscle. Several distinct mechanisms converge here. A CUL4 DDB1 RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, with the adipose restricted adaptor WDTC1, targets adipogenic substrates for degradation, and loss of WDTC1 produces obesity. Activin signalling through ACVR2B, driven by the liver secreted, nutrient responsive ligand INHBE, transmits systemic metabolic state to fat depots. Transcriptional repression is supplied by KLF7 and by the myeloid factor SPI1, which antagonises the PPAR gamma C/EBP program, while PARP1 and a microRNA add chromatin and post transcriptional layers. The pathway sits at the interface of energy balance, insulin sensitivity, and lineage choice in mesenchymal progenitors.

Fat mass is set not only by how much adipogenesis occurs but by what restrains it, and this pathway covers the brakes on adipose tissue development. Suppressing the conversion of precursor cells into lipid-storing adipocytes limits fat expansion, and loss of these restraints promotes obesity and its metabolic consequences, including insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis. The genes act at several levels: a cullin-4 ubiquitin ligase scaffold with DDB1 and RBX1, partnered by the adipose-restricting substrate receptor WDTC1, targets proteins for degradation to hold adipogenic transcription in check; KLF7 and the myeloid transcription factor SPI1 oppose the PPARG/CEBP differentiation programme; PARP1 links nuclear NAD metabolism to adipocyte gene expression; and the activin family ligand INHBE, secreted by liver, signals through an activin type II receptor to influence fat accumulation. A microRNA contributes post-transcriptional repression of the same programme.

positive regulation of adipose tissue development covers the signals that promote the formation and expansion of fat tissue, the body's main store of energy and a major endocrine organ. Its output determines how much lipid the body can safely sequester, and shifts in it underlie obesity, altered insulin sensitivity, and the lipodystrophies in which fat fails to form at all. The central driver is the nuclear receptor PPARG, working with coactivators such as NCOA1 and NCOA2 to switch on the adipocyte transcriptional programme, while nutrient- and energy-sensing regulators including SIRT1, the AMPK subunit PRKAA1, and the bile acid receptor NR1H4 tune that programme to systemic metabolic state. Lipoprotein lipase supplies fatty acids for storage, and the gut hormone ghrelin links feeding behaviour and appetite to adipose accretion, tying preadipocyte differentiation to whole-body energy balance.

Fat tissue is built by expanding pools of preadipocytes that differentiate into lipid-storing adipocytes, and this grouping covers the signals that push that process forward, setting how much adipose mass a body accrues and how it partitions energy. Positive regulation of adipose tissue development matters for whole-body energy buffering, insulin sensitivity, and the endocrine output of fat; excessive drive contributes to obesity and metabolic disease, while insufficient adipogenesis produces lipodystrophy with ectopic fat and dyslipidaemia. The master adipogenic nuclear receptor PPARG acts with the coactivators NCOA1 and NCOA2 to install the adipocyte transcriptional programme, while lipoprotein lipase supplies fatty acids by hydrolysing circulating triglycerides. Nutrient- and hormone-sensing components tune the same output: ghrelin signals feeding status, and the AMP-activated kinase subunit PRKAA1 and the NAD-dependent deacetylase SIRT1 couple energy availability to adipocyte differentiation and lipid storage.

Excitable and non-excitable cells alike must limit how far and how often their membrane potential shifts toward positive values, and this pathway groups activities that oppose membrane depolarization, keeping resting potential stable and restraining excitability. Suppressing depolarization matters in two distinct settings: at the plasma membrane of muscle and neurons, where unchecked depolarization drives arrhythmia, hyperexcitability and calcium overload, and at the mitochondrial inner membrane, where loss of potential commits a cell to apoptosis. Members reflect both: BCL2 and its relative BOK act at mitochondria to control permeabilization and the collapse of the membrane potential, while caveolin-3 organizes the sarcolemmal membrane domains in which ion channels sit, and its mutation causes rippling muscle disease and cardiomyopathy. SRC-family signalling and a Frizzled receptor link surface receptor input to this restraint, placing the process at the junction of ion homeostasis and survival decisions.

positive regulation of membrane depolarization covers the processes that push a cell's membrane potential toward threshold, making excitation more likely or more frequent. It matters wherever electrical activity drives function: cardiac impulse conduction, neuronal firing, sperm hyperactivation, and immune cell activation. The genes act at several levels. Channels and channel partners set the depolarizing current directly, with TRPM4 conducting a calcium-activated cation current and RANGRF trafficking cardiac sodium channels to the surface, while ANK3 anchors sodium channels at the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier where action potentials are generated. P2RX7 depolarizes cells in response to extracellular ATP during inflammation. Others contribute through soluble signalling and transcription, including bicarbonate-sensing adenylate cyclase and CREB1-dependent gene expression. Loss of this control underlies arrhythmia and altered neuronal excitability.

Excitable cells signal by letting their membrane potential swing positive, and this pathway covers the processes that promote or intensify that depolarizing shift. It matters for setting the threshold and frequency of action firing in neurons and cardiomyocytes, and for the calcium entry that couples electrical events to secretion and contraction. The genes span the routes by which depolarization is driven and positioned: a calcium-activated nonselective cation channel that carries depolarizing current, an ATP-gated purinergic channel that opens a large cation pore during inflammatory and immune signalling, and a scaffolding ankyrin that clusters sodium channels at axon initial segments and nodes so that current arises where it is needed. Chaperone and modulatory factors influencing cardiac sodium channel trafficking also appear, linking this regulation to arrhythmia risk, while transcriptional and metabolic components suggest longer-term tuning of excitability rather than moment-to-moment gating.

Pericytes are the contractile mural cells that wrap capillaries, stabilize the endothelium, and control vessel diameter and permeability; their differentiation from unspecialized mesenchymal progenitors is what converts a raw endothelial tube into a mature, quiescent microvessel. Loss of this programme leaves capillaries leaky and prone to microaneurysm, and is a feature of diabetic retinopathy, blood-brain barrier failure and tumour vasculature. Endothelium-derived PDGFB recruits progenitors, TGFB2 and NOTCH1 signalling drive their commitment and quiescence, and transcription factors such as FOXC2 and OSR1 specify mural identity, with smooth muscle actin ACTA2 marking the acquired contractile phenotype. EPHA2 and the proton-sensing receptor GPR4 link the process to endothelial guidance cues and to local acidosis, situating pericyte specification within angiogenesis, vessel maturation and microvascular homeostasis.

TORC1 is the growth-promoting kinase hub that couples nutrient and energy status to protein synthesis and autophagy, and this set covers the braking machinery that shuts it down. When amino acids, glucose or growth factors are scarce, these components restrain anabolic spending and license autophagic recycling; losing them drives constitutive growth signalling, and germline lesions in several of them cause tuberous sclerosis, focal cortical dysplasia and familial epilepsies. The TSC1-TSC2-TBC1D7 complex acts as a GTPase-activating complex for RHEB, while GATOR1 subunits NPRL2, NPRL3 and DEPDC5 inactivate the Rag GTPases and are held in check by the KICSTOR scaffold including SZT2 and KPTN. Sestrins and CASTOR proteins sense leucine and arginine deprivation, AMPK subunits and LKB1 report low energy, and DEPTOR plus PRAS40 inhibit the complex directly. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and 14-3-3 proteins tune the stability and assembly of these regulators.

Cells commit to growth only when nutrients, amino acids and growth factor signals are all present, and this collection describes the inputs that switch TORC1 on. Active TORC1 drives ribosome biogenesis and protein synthesis through effectors such as S6 kinase while shutting down autophagy, so its activation determines cell size, anabolic metabolism and the balance between building and recycling. Much of the machinery works at the lysosomal surface: the Ragulator complex tethers Rag GTPases to the membrane, GATOR2 components including MIOS, WDR24, WDR59, SEC13 and SEH1L relieve inhibition imposed by amino acid sensors like CASTOR1, SESN2 and SAMTOR, and the transporter SLC38A9 reports arginine availability. Growth factor signalling converges separately through AKT1 onto the small GTPase RHEB. Ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases and kinases tune the output. Chronic overactivation underlies tumour growth and metabolic disease.

Misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are retrotranslocated to the cytosol and destroyed by the proteasome, and this set governs how fast and how far that disposal route runs. Tuning it matters because too little clearance lets toxic species accumulate and triggers stress-induced death, while excessive degradation destroys salvageable or functional membrane proteins, as happens to CFTR and to lipoprotein assembly intermediates. Control operates at several points: ubiquitin ligases and their regulators such as RNF185, STUB1 and the inhibitor SVIP set substrate commitment; deubiquitinases including ATXN3, USP13, USP14 and USP19 edit ubiquitin chains and can rescue substrates; UBQLN1, UBQLN2, BAG6 and SGTA shuttle and triage extracted clients toward the proteasome. Transcriptional arms feed in through XBP1 and HERPUD1, linking the unfolded protein response to degradative capacity, with NFE2L2 tying stress sensing to redox control.

negative regulation of ERAD pathway restrains the endoplasmic reticulum's own quality-control disposal system, which retrotranslocates misfolded secretory and membrane proteins to the cytosol for proteasomal destruction. Braking that machinery matters because unchecked degradation strips cells of proteins that are slow-folding but functional, and a tunable threshold determines whether a mutant channel or receptor reaches the surface or is destroyed. The genes act at successive steps: SGTA extracts and reshuffles substrates on the cytosolic face, deciding between triage and rescue; SVIP and the UBX-domain proteins bind p97/VCP and its E3 partners to blunt substrate handoff; and the deubiquitinases USP14 and USP25 remove ubiquitin marks before commitment to the proteasome. AQP11 contributes ER membrane homeostasis. Together these set the balance point of ER proteostasis and shape the unfolded protein response and disease-causing protein misfolding phenotypes such as cystic fibrosis.

Misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are normally retrotranslocated to the cytosol and destroyed by the proteasome, and this biology sets limits on that disposal route. Damping ER-associated degradation matters because the machinery is not perfectly selective: functional but slow-folding proteins, and regulated substrates whose levels must be tuned rather than cleared, get a chance to fold or act. The brakes work at several points. A small VCP-interacting protein and UBX-domain cofactors compete for the VCP/p97 retrotranslocation motor and its adaptors, the co-chaperone SGTA holds extracted substrates and opposes their commitment to degradation, and the deubiquitinases USP14 and USP25 trim ubiquitin chains to rescue substrates before proteasomal engagement. Loss of such restraint accelerates turnover of ER clients, and the water channel AQP11 links this control to renal proximal tubule integrity.

Misfolded proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are recognised, retrotranslocated to the cytosol and destroyed by the proteasome, and this pathway covers the factors that push that clearance route harder. Upregulating ER-associated degradation lets cells cope with folding stress, limits accumulation of aggregation-prone and orphan membrane proteins, and determines the turnover rate of substrates such as misfolded ion channels and lipoprotein components; chronic failure contributes to neurodegenerative and metabolic disease. The genes here act at several steps: membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases including RNF185 and RNFT1 tag substrates on the ER surface, the cytosolic chaperone STUB1 couples recognition to ubiquitination, BAG6 with SGTA holds extracted hydrophobic clients soluble, ubiquilins shuttle them to the proteasome, and the deubiquitinases ATXN3 and USP13 edit ubiquitin marks to license degradation. Transcriptional arms via XBP1 and NFE2L2 expand this capacity as part of the unfolded protein response.

Gut motility depends on smooth muscle in the stomach and intestine contracting in coordinated waves, and this pathway covers the signals that drive those contractions harder or more often. It matters for gastric emptying, propulsion of chyme, and the hunger-linked contractile bursts that occur between meals; when such prokinetic signalling fails, the result is gastroparesis, delayed transit and functional dyspepsia. Ghrelin, released by stomach endocrine cells, acts through its receptor GHSR on enteric neurons and muscle to stimulate motility while also driving appetite and growth hormone release, tying feeding behaviour to gut mechanics. Neuromedin U and spexin act as neuropeptide contractile stimuli on the same tissue. KIT marks the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells that generate slow waves and set the rhythm the muscle follows, linking this regulation to enteric neuromuscular organisation.

Response to forskolin captures how cells react to pharmacological activation of adenylyl cyclase, the standard experimental route to raising intracellular cAMP. Because forskolin bypasses receptors and acts directly on the cyclase, this response reports the downstream consequences of cAMP itself: PKA activation, CREB1-dependent transcription of immediate-early genes such as FOS and JUND, and phosphorylation-gated changes in transport and secretion. Several adenylyl cyclase isoforms are the direct targets, with inhibitory G protein signalling through GNAI1 and small GTPases like RAP1A setting the tone of the response. The functional outputs are concrete: CFTR chloride channel opening at the apical membrane, iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter in thyrocytes, and steroidogenic gene expression. This makes the pathway a readout of cAMP competence in epithelial secretion, endocrine hormone production and activity-dependent gene expression in neurons.

Forskolin is a diterpene that binds adenylate cyclase directly and raises intracellular cAMP without going through a receptor, so the cellular response to forskolin is essentially a readout of how a cell behaves when cAMP is forced upward. This makes it the standard experimental lever for probing protein kinase A signalling, and the genes involved are those of the cAMP axis itself: multiple adenylate cyclase isoforms that generate the second messenger, an inhibitory G protein alpha subunit that restrains them, and the transcription factor CREB1 with immediate-early targets such as FOS and JUND that convert a transient cAMP rise into changes in gene expression. Downstream consequences are concrete: cAMP-dependent gating of the CFTR chloride channel governs epithelial fluid secretion, and iodide uptake through the sodium-iodide symporter in thyroid follicular cells responds to the same signal, linking this stimulus to secretion, hormone synthesis and neuronal plasticity.

Midbrain dopaminergic neurons are the cells lost in Parkinson's disease, and their production from ventral neural progenitors depends on how strongly and for how long a handful of patterning signals are read. Controlling the pace and extent of dopaminergic neuron differentiation is what determines how many of these neurons a brain makes, and it is the step that protocols for generating replacement neurons from stem cells attempt to reproduce. Sonic hedgehog from the floor plate sets ventral identity, while WNT ligands acting through beta-catenin drive progenitor expansion and neurogenic conversion; secreted frizzled-related proteins and DKK1 restrain that WNT input, and GSK3B acts inside the pathway to limit signalling. FGF20 and the Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor TIAM1 contribute further pro-differentiation and cytoskeletal cues, linking extracellular gradients to the timing of neuronal commitment.

Proteins delivered to the lysosome (the vacuole in the broad sense) are degraded by acid hydrolases, and this pathway covers the controls that set how much of that degradation happens and to which substrates. It matters because the balance between recycling a receptor and destroying it determines signalling output, cholesterol and protein uptake, and the clearance of aggregation-prone material; when it fails, undegraded substrate accumulates and neurodegenerative and lysosomal storage phenotypes follow. Endocytic receptors such as LDLR, LRP1 and LRP2 supply cargo, while sorting factors including GGA3, the retromer subunit VPS35 and the deubiquitinase USP8 decide whether cargo is retrieved to the Golgi and surface or committed to the lumen. Ubiquitin ligases like MARCHF2 and RNF128 mark substrates for that fate, and lysosomal proteins including ATP13A2, GBA1 and MFSD8 shape the degradative environment itself.

Proteins delivered to the lysosome are usually destined for destruction, and this pathway covers the braking mechanisms that spare them, damping the rate and extent of vacuolar protein catabolism. The effect is largely a matter of sorting: cargo diverted away from the degradative lumen is recycled to the cell surface or the Golgi instead, so receptor levels, signalling output and membrane protein lifespan all depend on how strongly this restraint operates. A retromer subunit retrieves cargo from endosomes before it commits to lysosomal delivery, a deubiquitinase removes the ubiquitin marks that would otherwise consign a receptor to the lumen, and a lysosomal cation-transporting ATPase supports organelle homeostasis; loss of the latter causes juvenile parkinsonism with lysosomal dysfunction. Related activities stabilise growth factor receptors such as EGFR, linking this control to proliferative signalling and, when excessive, to tumour cell survival.

Enhancing protein breakdown in the vacuolar/lysosomal compartment is how cells clear surface receptors, extracellular ligands and misfolded membrane proteins rather than simply recycling them. The genes here act at the two steps that set the rate: capture and sorting. Endocytic receptors of the LDL receptor family — LDLR, LRP1 and LRP2 — bind lipoproteins, proteases and filtered plasma proteins and deliver them inward, a route that underlies cholesterol clearance and renal protein reabsorption; loss of LRP2 causes the proteinuria and developmental defects of Donnai–Barrow syndrome. Membrane-bound ubiquitin ligases such as MARCHF2 and RNF128 ubiquitinate transmembrane substrates to mark them for degradative rather than recycling itineraries, while the clathrin adaptor GGA3 sorts ubiquitinated cargo between endosomes and lysosomes. CD81 contributes membrane organisation to these trafficking events, linking receptor turnover to signalling shutdown and immune tolerance.

Chromosome ends must be masked so that the cell does not treat them as broken DNA, and regulation of telomere capping tunes how effectively that protective state is maintained. When capping fails, exposed ends trigger damage signalling, fusion and senescence or drive genome rearrangement in cancer. The shelterin component TRF2 is central to end protection, repressing inappropriate repair at the telomere, while poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases tankyrase 1 and 2 and the deubiquitinase USP7 modulate the abundance and turnover of telomeric proteins. Damage-response factors including ATM and the MRE11 interacting partners NBN and RAD50 sense and process uncapped ends, and nucleases and helicases such as the ERCC1-ERCC4 complex and RTEL1 resolve telomeric structures and limit overhang loss. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of DNA repair control, replicative lifespan and chromosome stability.</br>

Chromosome ends must be shielded from being read as broken DNA, and this set covers the processes that damp down or reverse telomere capping, keeping end protection under active control rather than permanently on. Loss of that control matters in both directions: unchecked capping can license inappropriate telomere extension and fusion resolution, while excess uncapping exposes ends to the DNA damage response, triggering senescence, apoptosis or end-to-end fusions and genome rearrangement. The players sit at the interface of telomere structure and double-strand break repair — the shelterin subunit TERF2, the MRE11-associated NBN and RAD50 of the MRN complex, the ATM kinase that signals damage at deprotected ends, the ERCC1-ERCC4 structure-specific endonuclease that cleaves 3' overhangs, and XRCC1-organised single-strand break repair. This regulation underlies replicative ageing, telomere-driven crisis, and the genome instability that accompanies tumour progression.

Chromosome ends must be disguised as normal DNA termini rather than double-strand breaks, and this pathway comprises the influences that increase the extent and reliability of telomere capping. When capping fails, exposed ends trigger a DNA damage response, end-to-end fusions and senescence or genome instability, so keeping the protective structure intact is part of how cells tolerate continued division. The proteins involved act at several points: the helicase RTEL1 unwinds T-loop and G-quadruplex structures so that replication through telomeric repeats finishes cleanly, single-stranded DNA-binding activity via NABP2 protects and processes the G-overhang, and the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases tankyrase 1 and 2 modify shelterin-associated TRF1 to regulate access of telomerase and other factors to the end. HNRNPD binds single-stranded telomeric DNA and RNA, linking capping to telomere length maintenance and replicative lifespan.

Regulation of telomere maintenance via telomere lengthening sets how far chromosome ends are extended, balancing the replicative capacity a cell needs against the unlimited division that underlies cancer. Too little activity gives progressive telomere erosion, senescence and the bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis of telomere biology disorders; too much supports tumour immortalisation. Control acts at several levels: the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD count telomere length and restrain telomerase access, while PINX1 and the tankyrases tune that restraint; CST components (CTC1, STN1, TEN1) with RTEL1 and PIF1 limit extension and resolve G-quadruplex and t-loop structures. Telomerase RNA itself is matured and stabilised by DKC1, NAF1, WRAP53, PARN and the nonsense-mediated decay factors SMG5/SMG6, and chaperonin and HSP90 complexes assist enzyme assembly. ATM, ATR and TP53 couple telomere state to damage signalling, and the SLX4 nuclease module handles recombination-based lengthening.

Chromosome ends shorten with every round of replication, and the processes that modulate how much telomere length is restored set the replicative lifespan of a cell. Positive and negative regulators are both represented: the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD cap the end and restrain telomerase access, the CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 terminates extension, and PINX1 inhibits telomerase directly, while tankyrases, chaperone activity from the CCT/TRiC subunits and HSP90, and RNA-binding and trafficking factors such as DKC1, NAF1, WRAP53, PARN and hnRNPs govern telomerase RNA maturation, holoenzyme assembly and recruitment. Helicases including RTEL1 and PIF1 and the SLX4 nuclease complex resolve end structures, and ATM, ATR and TP53 couple telomere state to damage signalling. Tight control matters because too little lengthening causes bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis, while unrestrained extension supports cancer cell immortality.

negative regulation of telomere maintenance via telomere lengthening is the braking system on telomere elongation, setting an upper limit on how far telomerase and recombination-based mechanisms can extend chromosome ends. Without these restraints telomeres over-elongate and become unstable, a permissive state for immortalisation in cancer; excessive braking instead shortens telomeres and drives premature senescence, as seen in bone marrow failure and telomere biology disorders. The shelterin complex, through POT1, TPP1, TRF1, TRF2 and TIN2, counts telomere repeats and blocks telomerase access, while CST components (CTC1-STN1-TEN1) terminate extension and hand ends to replication. PINX1 directly inhibits telomerase, PIF1 helicase displaces it, tankyrases and PARPs tune shelterin loading, and structure-specific nucleases such as SLX4-SLX1 and ERCC4 resolve or trim recombination intermediates at telomeres. RNA-binding and decay factors, PML bodies and p53 add further layers, linking end-length control to genome stability and cellular lifespan.

Telomeres must be kept long enough to protect chromosome ends but not allowed to elongate without limit, and this pathway covers the braking processes that restrain telomere lengthening. Restraint sets replicative lifespan: losing it contributes to the unchecked telomere elongation seen in cancers, while excessive braking drives premature telomere attrition and bone marrow failure or pulmonary fibrosis syndromes. Much of the control is exerted by the shelterin complex, where POT1, TPP1, TIN2 and the duplex-binding TRF1 and TRF2 proteins count telomere length and limit telomerase access, with PINX1 acting as a direct telomerase inhibitor and the CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 terminating telomerase action and coordinating fill-in synthesis. Structure-specific nucleases, the PIF1 helicase, poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases, RNA-binding and decay factors, and p53-dependent damage signalling supply further negative input, linking end protection to DNA replication and repair.

Chromosome ends shorten with every round of replication unless something actively adds sequence back, and this pathway covers the inputs that push telomere maintenance toward net lengthening. It sets the replicative lifespan of dividing cells: too little activity gives the progressive erosion seen in bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis syndromes, while sustained activation is one route by which tumours become immortal. The genes act at several levels — assembly and trafficking of telomerase RNP components through the chaperonin TRiC ring, HSP90 with its co-chaperone p23, dyskerin and WRAP53, plus PARN-dependent maturation of the RNA subunit; recruitment and access control at the telomere by POT1, tankyrase-mediated release of TRF1, and the RTEL1 helicase together with G-quadruplex-resolving activities; and the ATM and ATR damage kinases, which signal through the end structure itself. Single-stranded DNA-binding hnRNPs contribute to overhang handling.

Kainic acid is a glutamate analogue that overstimulates ionotropic glutamate receptors, and the cellular reactions it provokes are used experimentally to model excitotoxic injury and temporal lobe epilepsy. The changes grouped here span how neurons and surrounding glia adjust transcription, translation and excitability when glutamatergic drive becomes damaging. Translation initiation control through the alpha subunit of eIF2 links excitotoxic and integrated stress signalling to protein synthesis shutdown, while the Kv3-family potassium channel subunit KCNC2 sets the fast repolarisation that lets interneurons fire at high frequency and limits runaway activity. Lipocalin 2 is induced as part of the reactive glial and inflammatory response to seizure-associated damage, and spinophilin, a dendritic spine protein phosphatase-targeting scaffold, ties the response to synaptic remodelling. Together these represent the excitability, stress-response and structural arms of neuronal adaptation or death after excitotoxic challenge.

Whether a receptor, channel or transporter is present at the plasma membrane determines how a cell senses and responds to its surroundings, and this pathway covers the processes that tune how much protein reaches the cell periphery and how long it stays there. The controls it describes set glucose and ion transporter density, neurotransmitter receptor number at synapses, integrin-dependent adhesion, and growth factor receptor signalling output, so its misregulation contributes to insulin resistance, arrhythmia, altered excitability and unchecked receptor signalling in cancer. Mechanistically it draws together vesicle delivery and fusion through SNAREs and Rab11-dependent recycling, retromer-mediated retrieval from endosomes, clathrin adaptor-driven internalisation, cortical anchoring by ezrin, spectrin and band 4.1 proteins, palmitoylation by ZDHHC acyltransferases, and phosphorylation by kinases such as AKT1, CDK5, CaMKII and the WNK family that bias the balance between surface retention and removal.

Cells decide how much of a given protein sits at the plasma membrane, and this pathway covers the events that push that balance toward the cell periphery. It determines how many receptors, channels and transporters a cell displays, and so sets the gain of hormone and growth factor responses, the strength of cell adhesion, and excitability. The machinery spans vesicular delivery and recycling (RAB11A, ARF6, syntaxins STX3 and STX4, the retromer subunit VPS35, kinesin-mediated transport), cortical scaffolds and the membrane skeleton (ezrin, spectrin, 4.1 proteins, DLG1), palmitoylating enzymes of the ZDHHC family that tether cargo to membranes, and kinases such as AKT1, PDPK1 and several protein kinase C isoforms that act as the regulated switch. STAC proteins in this group traffic voltage-gated calcium channels, illustrating how surface delivery translates directly into physiological signalling. Mislocalisation of this kind underlies defective receptor signalling and altered ion handling.

Cells and tissues sense inorganic phosphate and adjust mineral handling accordingly, and the response to sodium phosphate stimulus captures that regulation: how bone and kidney read a phosphate load and answer with hormonal and enzymatic changes that keep mineralization on target. Failure of this control produces rickets and osteomalacia on one side and pathological calcification of soft tissue and vessels on the other. Osteocyte-derived FGF23 signals through FGFR1 with Klotho to lower serum phosphate by restraining renal reabsorption; PHEX, a membrane endopeptidase whose loss causes X-linked hypophosphatemia, governs FGF23 levels, while tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase hydrolyses pyrophosphate to permit hydroxyapatite deposition and ABCC6 acts as a systemic calcification inhibitor. RUNX2 drives the osteogenic transcriptional programme, linking phosphate sensing to osteoblast differentiation and to vascular smooth muscle transformation in chronic kidney disease.

cellular response to angiotensin describes how cells react when they encounter the vasoactive peptides cleaved from angiotensinogen, the effector arm of the renin-angiotensin system that sets blood pressure, sodium and water balance, and vascular tone. Its outputs are contraction of vascular smooth muscle, renal tubular ion transport, aldosterone release, and, chronically, cardiac and vascular remodelling; overactivity drives hypertension, fibrosis and heart failure, which is why receptor blockers and converting-enzyme inhibitors are mainstays of cardiovascular therapy. Angiotensin II acting mainly through the AGTR1 G-protein-coupled receptor mobilises calcium and activates protein kinase C isoforms, calcineurin, CaMKII, Src, Rho-kinases and NADPH oxidase, converging on NF-κB-driven transcription, oxidative stress and cytoskeletal reorganisation. Counter-regulatory branches through AGTR2 and the MAS1 receptor oppose these effects, and smooth-muscle microRNAs miR-143/145 tune the contractile phenotype that results.

Angiotensin peptides cleaved from angiotensinogen act on target cells to raise blood pressure, retain sodium, and remodel heart and vessel wall, and this describes how a cell responds once that peptide arrives. The response depends on the type 1 and type 2 receptors and the counter-regulatory MAS receptor, whose opposing outputs set whether the cell constricts and hypertrophies or relaxes; ACE and angiotensinogen themselves supply the ligand locally. Downstream, protein kinase C isoforms, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase, calcineurin, Src, Rho kinases and Rac1 with the NADPH oxidase subunit p22phox convert receptor occupancy into contraction, cytoskeletal remodelling, reactive oxygen production and NF-κB-driven inflammatory transcription, with natriuretic peptide induction as a feedback arm. Sustained signalling through this route underlies hypertension, cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, and is the target of receptor blockers and ACE inhibitors.

Cells alter their behaviour when exposed to compounds derived from L-phenylalanine ém a chemical family that includes tyrosine and the catecholamines built from it, as well as drugs and dietary phenylalanine analogues. The response is read out as changes in gene expression, enzyme induction and secretion, and the small group of genes here points to two recurring themes. One is oxidative defence: the catalytic and modifier subunits of glutamate-cysteine ligase set the rate of glutathione synthesis, and their induction is a standard reaction to the reactive quinones and radicals generated when catecholamines and related phenolic compounds oxidise. The other is protein and signalling adaptation, including a mitochondrial outer-membrane import receptor, a protein phosphatase 1 targeting subunit enriched at dendritic spines where catecholamine signalling converges, and altered output of a secreted coagulation factor. Together they illustrate how an aromatic amino acid metabolite acts as a stimulus rather than merely a nutrient.

Neuromuscular transmission depends on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors being packed densely into the postsynaptic membrane directly beneath the motor nerve terminal, and this regulatory programme sets how tightly that clustering occurs. Without it, endplates are diffuse and structurally immature, transmission fails, and the result is congenital myasthenia or fatigable weakness. The genes point to two converging inputs: nerve-derived agrin acting through the LRP4 co-receptor, whose folding and surface delivery require the chaperone MESD, with the adaptor CRKL relaying the signal to receptor anchoring downstream of muscle-specific kinase; and the synaptic basal lamina, where laminin subunits engage dystroglycan, itself dependent on LARGE1-mediated glycosylation for ligand binding. A Frizzled receptor links Wnt cues into the same postsynaptic assembly. This is synapse organisation in muscle rather than signalling for its own sake, and it explains why defects in dystroglycan glycosylation produce both muscular dystrophy and endplate abnormalities.

At the neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine receptors must be packed into dense clusters in the postsynaptic membrane directly beneath the motor nerve terminal, and this pathway covers the signals that promote and stabilise that clustering. Without it, transmission from nerve to muscle fails: receptor density falls, endplate potentials become too small to trigger contraction reliably, and the result is fatigable weakness of the kind seen in congenital myasthenic syndromes. Nerve-derived agrin acts through the muscle surface receptor LRP4 and its partner kinase to drive receptor aggregation, while the laminin subunits of the synaptic basement membrane and dystroglycan provide the extracellular anchor; LARGE1 builds the matriglycan sugar that lets dystroglycan bind laminin, and MESD chaperones LRP4 folding. Defects in the glycosylation arm also cause dystroglycanopathy muscular dystrophy, linking synaptic organisation to muscle membrane integrity.

Motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres must build and calibrate the synapse between them, and this regulatory programme sets how extensively that neuromuscular junction forms and matures. Without it, acetylcholine receptors fail to cluster beneath the nerve terminal, transmission is weak, and the result is congenital myasthenia, arthrogryposis or muscle weakness. The core instructive signal is neural agrin acting on the muscle receptor tyrosine kinase MuSK, which organises postsynaptic receptor clustering; COLQ anchors acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic basal lamina so released transmitter is cleared, and the vesicular acetylcholine transporter loads the neurotransmitter presynaptically. Additional control comes from transcription factors of the SIX family that pattern muscle and motor neuron identity, a ubiquitin ligase restraining axon terminal growth, and LIN7 scaffold proteins that position membrane proteins at the synapse. The pathway sits at the junction of synaptogenesis, axon guidance and muscle differentiation.

Xenophagy is the selective capture of intracellular bacteria and other invading microbes into autophagosomes for lysosomal destruction, and this pathway covers the signals that set how strongly and how fast that capture happens. It links innate immune recognition to the autophagy machinery: cytosolic peptidoglycan sensing through NOD1 and its kinase adaptor RIPK2 recruits autophagy factors to the bacterial entry site, while ubiquitin ligase activity marks the microbial surface for capture. LRSAM1 and a cullin-RING ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1 contribute ubiquitin tags, the LUBAC component RNF31 adds linear chains, and the receptor OPTN, phosphorylated by TBK1, bridges those tags to LC3 on the growing membrane. IRGM coordinates the response with broader autophagy control. Variants in IRGM and related components are associated with Crohn's disease and with impaired clearance of mycobacteria and Salmonella.

Positive regulation of xenophagy describes the signals that switch on selective autophagy of intracellular bacteria, the arm of innate immunity that encloses invading microbes in autophagosomes and delivers them to lysosomes. It matters because cells that fail to upregulate this route cannot clear pathogens such as Salmonella or Mycobacterium from their cytosol; variants in IRGM and OPTN are linked to Crohn's disease and to defective bacterial handling in the gut epithelium. Cytosolic peptidoglycan sensing by NOD1 with its kinase RIPK2 and the ubiquitin machinery of LRSAM1 and RNF31 tags bacterial surfaces, while TBK1 phosphorylates the autophagy receptor OPTN to strengthen its binding to ubiquitin and LC3. IRGM coordinates the core autophagy apparatus at the bacterial surface. The pathway therefore links pattern recognition and inflammatory signalling to autophagosome targeting and antibacterial defence.

Xenophagy is the selective autophagic capture and destruction of intracellular bacteria, and this set covers the events that switch it on and amplify it. It gives epithelial and myeloid cells a way to clear pathogens such as Salmonella and Mycobacterium that escape or damage their vacuoles, and its weakening is linked to Crohn's disease susceptibility and to mycobacterial persistence. Cytosolic peptidoglycan sensing through NOD1 with its kinase adaptor RIPK2, together with LUBAC-mediated linear ubiquitination, marks bacteria and recruits the autophagy machinery; the ubiquitin ligase LRSAM1 coats bacterial surfaces, while TBK1 phosphorylates the receptor optineurin to strengthen its grip on ubiquitinated cargo and on LC3. IRGM acts as a hub coordinating core autophagy factors at these sites. The output is delivery of bacteria to lysosomes and coupling of innate immune detection to autophagic degradation.

positive regulation of calcium ion transmembrane transport covers the mechanisms that increase calcium entry across membranes, converting extracellular signals into the cytosolic calcium rises that drive muscle contraction, secretion, immune activation and synaptic plasticity. The genes span the receptors that initiate such signals — purinergic P2X channels, thrombin and bradykinin receptors, chemokine receptor CXCR3, glutamate and dopamine receptors — together with the store-operated and TRPC channels, voltage-gated channel subunits, and scaffolding AKAPs that position kinases and phosphatases near channel pores. Downstream, calcineurin subunits decode the signal into transcriptional programs, while sorcin, calsequestrin and junctate tune release and refilling of internal stores. Apoptotic BAX and BAK contribute calcium fluxes that commit cells to death. Loss of this tuning underlies arrhythmia, impaired lymphocyte activation, and calcium overload injury in neurodegeneration and inflammation.

Raising calcium influx across membranes is how cells convert an external signal into a rapid, quantitative intracellular response, and the genes here are the accelerators of that step rather than the channels' basal machinery. Ligand-gated and store-operated routes are both represented: ATP-gated P2X channels, the NMDA receptor subunit GRIN1, and TRPC1/TRPC3 provide the conductive pathways, while G protein-coupled receptors for thrombin, neurotensin, apelin, bradykinin and chemokines acting through CXCR3 recruit phospholipase C signalling to open them. Scaffolds such as AKAP5 and AKAP6 position kinases next to channels, CACNB2 and sorcin tune voltage-gated and cardiac calcium handling, and calcineurin subunits read the resulting signal out to transcription. The same influx drives muscle contraction, synaptic plasticity, secretion, immune activation and, when sustained, the mitochondrial permeabilisation step of apoptosis via BAX and BAK1.

Telomeres can be shortened abruptly by excising the t-loop as an extrachromosomal telomeric circle, and this pathway controls how often that happens. Regulation of t-circle formation matters because unchecked looped-telomere excision causes sudden telomere truncation and genome instability, while controlled trimming limits excessive telomere elongation and is a hallmark of cancers using the alternative lengthening of telomeres mechanism. The shelterin component TRF2 protects the t-loop from inappropriate resolution, and the RTEL1 helicase disassembles the loop during replication so it is unwound rather than cut. When protection fails, the SLX4 scaffold with its SLX1 structure-specific endonuclease partners, together with the ERCC1 nuclease complex, resolves the branched telomeric junction and releases a circle. Ku (XRCC5) contributes by restraining recombination-driven excision at chromosome ends, linking this control to end-protection and double-strand break repair choice.

Matrix metalloproteinases remodel and degrade extracellular matrix, and how much enzyme cells release is controlled separately from how much they make. This regulation of matrix metallopeptidase secretion sets the balance between tissue repair and destruction: too much output drives cartilage and bone erosion in arthritis, plaque rupture, and tumour invasion, while too little impairs wound healing and leukocyte migration. Inputs come from several directions. Cell-surface basigin is a classic inducer of MMP release from neighbouring stromal cells, innate immune receptors TLR2 and TLR4 couple microbial and damage signals to protease output, and CD200 delivers an inhibitory signal to myeloid cells that restrains it. Several microRNAs, including miR-146a and miR-29b, tune the same output post-transcriptionally. The pathway therefore links inflammatory and metabolic cues to extracellular proteolysis and matrix turnover.

Matrix metalloproteinases degrade collagen and other extracellular matrix components once released from the cell, so restraining their secretion limits tissue breakdown during inflammation, wound healing and tumour invasion. This braking arm of matrix metalloproteinase secretion control keeps proteolysis proportionate: when it fails, unchecked enzyme release contributes to cartilage and bone erosion in arthritis, plaque instability in atherosclerosis, and stromal invasion by carcinoma cells. Much of the regulation here is post-transcriptional, through microRNAs that dampen inflammatory signalling and matrix-degrading output; miR-146a acts as a feedback limiter on innate immune activation downstream of Toll-like receptors, and miR-29 family members constrain matrix-related gene expression. The immune checkpoint ligand CD200 delivers an inhibitory signal to myeloid cells bearing its receptor, quieting macrophage activation, while the mitochondrial isocitrate dehydrogenase IDH2 links metabolic and redox state to this restraint.

regulation of intestinal absorption sets how much of the diet actually enters the body across the gut epithelium, tuning the uptake of sterols, lipids, iron and ions rather than the digestive step itself. It determines whole-body cholesterol and iron balance, and its failure produces sitosterolemia, iron overload or deficiency, and fat malabsorption. The heterodimeric sterol transporter ABCG5/ABCG8 pumps plant sterols and excess cholesterol back into the lumen, while SOAT2 esterifies cholesterol for packaging and CYP8B1 shapes the bile acid pool that solubilises lipid. Apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV, together with LPCAT3-dependent membrane phospholipid remodelling, control chylomicron assembly and secretion. Hepcidin restrains enterocyte iron export, leptin signals nutritional status back to the gut, and claudins 2 and 15 build the paracellular sodium and cation conductance that drives water and nutrient flux.

How much of a meal actually enters the body is set by control mechanisms acting at the intestinal epithelium, and regulation of intestinal absorption covers the signals and transporters that tune this uptake rather than performing it. The genes point mainly at lipid and sterol handling: the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer pumps absorbed plant and animal sterols back into the lumen, limiting cholesterol entry, while SOAT2 esterifies cholesterol for packaging and apolipoproteins A1, A2 and A4 build the chylomicrons and HDL that carry lipid onward. Bile acid composition, shaped by CYP8B1, determines how efficiently fat is emulsified, and LPCAT3 maintains the membrane phospholipid environment that enterocyte lipid transport depends on. Tight junction claudins govern paracrine ion and water flux, hepcidin restrains iron uptake, and leptin links nutritional status back to absorptive capacity. Loss of sterol export causes sitosterolemia; dysregulated lipid uptake feeds hypercholesterolemia.

Nutrient uptake across the gut epithelium is tuned rather than fixed, and this pathway covers the processes that raise the rate and extent of intestinal absorption, particularly of lipids and sterols. It matters for how much dietary fat and cholesterol actually enters the body, and so for plasma lipid levels, obesity risk and the efficiency of nutrition after feeding. The genes involved act largely on lipid handling in enterocytes and in the lumen: a bile acid-modifying hydroxylase shapes the composition of bile and hence micellar solubilisation of fat, an intestinal alkaline sphingomyelinase digests dietary sphingomyelin, a membrane acyltransferase incorporates polyunsaturated acyl chains into phospholipids to support chylomicron formation, and a sterol O-acyltransferase esterifies cholesterol for packaging and export. Together they link brush-border digestion to absorptive capacity and whole-body lipid balance.

The transition zone sits at the base of a cilium and acts as a gate, deciding which membrane and soluble proteins are allowed into the organelle and preventing ciliary components from leaking back into the cell body. Getting proteins delivered to and held at this zone is therefore what establishes ciliary compartment identity, and its failure underlies a spectrum of ciliopathies: Meckel and Joubert syndromes, nephronophthisis, and retinal degeneration. The genes involved form interdependent modules at the zone's Y-shaped links, including a B9-domain complex with MKS1, the tectonic and small transmembrane proteins TMEM107, TMEM216 and TMEM231, and a nephrocystin module with NPHP1, NPHP4 and RPGRIP1L; CEP290 anchors the assembly to the axoneme. Loss of one component destabilises recruitment of the others, so hedgehog signalling, photoreceptor outer segment maintenance and renal tubule architecture all depend on this gatekeeping.

Lipophagy is the selective autophagic delivery of lipid droplets to lysosomes for breakdown, and its regulation sets how quickly stored triglyceride is mobilised into free fatty acids for oxidation. This control matters most in liver and adipose tissue, where too little lipophagy allows droplets to accumulate as steatosis and too much drains lipid reserves and floods mitochondria with fatty acids. The genes here act as modulators rather than core autophagy machinery: adrenergic receptor signalling links catecholamine stimulation to droplet turnover, a stress-induced regulator of mTOR signalling couples nutrient and oxidative stress to autophagy initiation, the huntingtin scaffold supports selective autophagic cargo recognition, and the serine palmitoyltransferase subunits tie sphingolipid synthesis to autophagic lipid handling. Together they place lipophagy at the junction of hormonal signalling, nutrient sensing and lipid storage homeostasis.

Telomeres are chromosome ends that resemble broken DNA, so cells must decide when damage there triggers repair, resection or elongation and when it is left alone. This control of telomere maintenance following DNA damage keeps chromosome ends from being fused, over-resected or inappropriately recombined, and its failure produces telomere loss, fragile ends and premature senescence or genome instability. Much of the gene content is the INO80 chromatin remodelling complex, including its ATPase, the actin-related subunits, the RUVBL1/RUVBL2 AAA+ pair and accessory subunits, which slides nucleosomes to give repair factors access to end-proximal chromatin. Acting alongside it are the ERCC1-XPF structure-specific endonuclease, which cleaves branched DNA intermediates, the helicase RTEL1, which dismantles telomeric G-quadruplex and T-loop structures during replication, the base excision repair scaffold XRCC1, and the transcription factor YY1.

TORC2 is the mTOR-containing complex that phosphorylates AGC kinases such as AKT at the hydrophobic motif, coupling growth factor and lipid cues to cell survival, glucose uptake, cytoskeletal remodelling and cell migration; upregulating its activity is a route by which tumour cells sustain AKT-dependent proliferation and resist apoptosis. The genes here act as positive inputs to that complex rather than as its catalytic core: AKT1 is both the principal substrate and a feedback participant, TBK1 and SIK3 are kinases that promote mTOR complex output, the deubiquitinases OTUD5, OTUD7B and USP9X stabilise or license signalling components by trimming ubiquitin chains, and EP300 contributes acetylation-dependent regulation. NCKAP1L links the pathway to actin-based membrane dynamics in immune cells. Collectively they raise the rate and extent of TORC2 signalling, tuning anabolic growth, metabolic flux and cytoskeletal organisation.

Moving L-proline across membranes supplies cells with an amino acid used for protein synthesis, collagen production and, through its interconversion with glutamate, for redox and energy balance. The transport activity described here operates prominently at the intestinal and renal brush border, where proline and imino acids absorbed from the diet or reclaimed from the glomerular filtrate must cross the apical membrane. SLC6A20 is a sodium- and chloride-dependent imino acid carrier whose surface expression depends on accessory membrane proteins ACE2 and its kidney-enriched relative collectrin; loss of that partnership produces iminoglycinuria, the urinary loss of proline, hydroxyproline and glycine. Complementary routes include the broadly expressed sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporter SLC38A2 at the plasma membrane and a proton-coupled SLC36 family member associated with intracellular compartments, linking proline uptake to lysosomal amino acid efflux and nutrient signalling.

Alanine is a principal carrier of amino nitrogen between tissues, shuttling carbon and nitrogen from muscle to liver for gluconeogenesis and urea synthesis, and transmembrane transport of L-alanine is what allows cells to take it up or release it. The transporters here span several families with distinct driving forces: a sodium-dependent neutral amino acid exchanger of the SLC1 family, sodium-coupled system N/A carriers of the SLC38 group that are prominent in liver and placenta, and an obligatory exchanger formed by the SLC7A8 light chain with the SLC3A2 heavy chain, which trades intracellular amino acids for extracellular ones. Together they support hepatic nitrogen handling, placental nutrient supply to the fetus, renal and intestinal reabsorption, and the supply of small neutral amino acids for protein synthesis, serine and pyruvate metabolism, and cellular osmotic balance.

Where a transcript sits inside a cell determines where its protein appears, and regulation of intracellular mRNA localization tunes that placement. It matters for delivering mRNAs to neuronal processes and to mitochondria, for locally translated cytoskeletal and signalling proteins, and for keeping unwanted messages out of the translating pool. Several members form a complex that tethers mRNAs to mitochondrial surfaces for local translation, while the RNA-binding proteins act more directly on individual transcripts: a DEAH-box helicase resolves G-quadruplex structures that block transport and translation, a Pumilio-family repressor binds 3' UTR elements and directs dendritic targeting, and tandem zinc-finger proteins bind AU-rich elements to route cytokine and other unstable mRNAs toward decay granules. Together these activities link mRNA transport and storage in granules to compartmentalized protein synthesis, with consequences for neuronal function and for the control of inflammatory gene expression.

Cells adjust their behaviour when they encounter glycoproteins, whether as hormones acting on receptors or as misfolded glycosylated cargo that must be disposed of. This response covers both readings. One arm is receptor-mediated: the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor binds a glycoprotein hormone and drives thyroid follicular cell activity, including iodide uptake through the sodium-iodide symporter that underlies thyroid hormone synthesis and the clinical use of radioiodine. The other arm is quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, where EDEM1, EDEM2 and EDEM3 trim mannose residues from terminally misfolded glycoproteins to commit them to degradation, with MAN1A1 acting on N-glycans along the secretory route. Also represented are secreted glycoproteins that act as signals themselves, such as coagulation factor VII and the natriuretic peptide CNP, linking this biology to haemostasis and to skeletal growth control.

Dioxin is not metabolized readily, and cells respond to it through a dedicated ligand-activated transcriptional programme that both detoxifies foreign aromatic compounds and, when persistently engaged, drives the toxicity of this class of pollutants. Binding of 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzodioxin to the aryl hydrocarbon receptor moves it to the nucleus, where it acts as a transcription factor at xenobiotic response elements and induces phase I monooxygenase activity, most characteristically CYP1A1, along with genes affecting coagulation, matrix and cell adhesion such as F7 and SPP1, and neuroendocrine output such as vasopressin. TIPARP, an ADP-ribosyltransferase induced in the same programme, feeds back to restrain receptor activity and limit the response. Sustained activation underlies chloracne, hepatotoxicity, immune suppression, developmental defects and tumour promotion, and the same receptor normally handles dietary and microbial ligands in barrier tissues.

Phorbol esters such as phorbol 13-acetate 12-myristate mimic diacylglycerol and lock protein kinase C into an active state, and the cellular reaction to that stimulus is the classic experimental readout of the diacylglycerol–PKC branch of signalling downstream of receptors that activate phospholipase C. It matters because this axis drives immediate-early gene expression, proliferation, differentiation and secretory responses, and because sustained phorbol ester exposure is tumour-promoting in skin carcinogenesis models. The genes here span the arm of the response: conventional PKC alpha and the related kinase PRKD1 as proximal effectors, a sphingosine kinase feeding lipid second messengers, the immediate-early factor FOS and the antiproliferative BTG2 as transcriptional output, CDK4 linking the signal to cell cycle entry, the phagocyte oxidase subunit CYBA for oxidative burst, plus induced secreted products such as beta-defensins and inhibin beta B. Metabolic enzymes including FBP1 indicate transcriptional reprogramming beyond growth signalling alone.

response to ionomycin describes the cellular changes triggered when the calcium ionophore ionomycin floods the cytosol with Ca2+, bypassing receptors and directly engaging calcium-dependent signalling. Because ionomycin is a standard laboratory tool for mimicking antigen receptor or hormone stimulation, the genes responsive to it mark the downstream machinery of calcium signalling itself: calcineurin-NFAT-driven transcription, phospholipase C-linked inositol phosphate turnover through PLCB1, and membrane organisation at caveolae involving CAV3. In lymphocytes, this calcium surge drives activation programmes, with CD4 and the transcription factor ZNF683 tied to T cell effector and memory identity, while the RNase ZC3H12A degrades cytokine mRNAs to restrain the inflammatory output. Coupling to CDK4 links the calcium signal to cell cycle entry, making this a readout of how calcium converts stimulation into proliferation, secretion, and altered gene expression.

Ionomycin is a calcium ionophore used experimentally to bypass receptor signalling and raise cytosolic calcium directly, and the cellular responses it provokes report on how cells translate a calcium rise into changed gene expression, secretion and enzyme activity. The genes grouped here reflect that readout rather than a single linear cascade: a phospholipase C beta isoform that generates the inositol trisphosphate normally responsible for releasing stored calcium, a caveolar scaffold of muscle membranes, a cyclin-dependent kinase linking stimulation to cell cycle entry, and immune effectors including the T cell coreceptor CD4, the ribonuclease Regnase-1 that degrades inflammatory cytokine mRNAs, and the transcription factor Hobit associated with tissue-resident lymphocyte programmes. Together they mark calcium-dependent lymphocyte activation and its transcriptional and post-transcriptional control, the setting in which ionomycin is most often applied.

Resveratrol, a plant polyphenol found in grape skin and red wine, produces measurable changes in cell and tissue behaviour, and this pathway covers the responses cells mount to it covering gene expression, enzyme activity and secretion. The genes involved point to metabolic and vascular endpoints: hepatic glucose-6-phosphatase sets the final step of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, so its regulation bears on fasting glucose output, while the inwardly rectifying potassium channel subunits that form ATP-sensitive K+ channels couple metabolic state to membrane excitability in pancreatic beta cells and vascular smooth muscle, influencing insulin release and vessel tone. Reduced expression of the inflammatory cytokine TNF and altered levels of a small regulatory RNA implicated in fibrosis and proliferation reflect anti-inflammatory and growth-modulating effects, and steroid 5-alpha-reductase activity links the compound to androgen metabolism. Together these outputs underlie interest in resveratrol for metabolic and cardiovascular disease.

Cells monitor how much methionine they have because it is the source of S-adenosylmethionine, the universal methyl donor, and their response to a methionine stimulus couples nutrient supply to growth and methylation capacity. When methionine is plentiful, SAM produced by methionine adenosyltransferase accumulates and is read out by SAMTOR, a SAM sensor that acts upstream of mTOR complex 1 to permit anabolic signalling, protein synthesis and suppression of autophagy; methionine restriction reverses this and is one of the dietary interventions that extends lifespan in model organisms. Downstream consequences include arginine methylation of histones and RNA-binding proteins by PRMT1, glycan modification, and activation of the NRF2 antioxidant programme, reflecting the link between methionine metabolism, transsulfuration and glutathione synthesis. Tumour cells are often methionine-dependent, making this sensing axis relevant to cancer metabolism and dietary therapy.
