Cells that encounter amyloid-beta peptide mount a defined response, and this is the biology that determines whether that response is protective clearance or the chronic inflammation and synaptic loss seen in Alzheimer's disease. Neurons detect the peptide through surface receptors and channels ation including cellular prion protein, glutamate receptors such as GRIN1 and GRM5, the alpha-7 nicotinic receptor and ephrin receptors ation and transduce the signal via Fyn, CDK5 and GSK3B toward tau phosphorylation, calcium influx and excitotoxic dysfunction. Microglia and macrophages sense it through TREM2 with its adaptor TYROBP, plus TLR4, CD36 and RAGE, driving SYK signalling, TNF and adhesion molecule induction, and uptake by scavenger routes; LRP1 and matrix metalloproteinases contribute to clearance and degradation. Also present are the amyloid-generating machinery itself, BACE1, PSEN1 and APP, and microRNAs including MIR146A that tune the inflammatory arm.

Amyloid-beta peptide is not merely a deposit; cells detect it and respond, and those responses shape the course of Alzheimer's disease. The cellular response to amyloid-beta covers what neurons, microglia and endothelium do once the peptide is sensed: surface receptors including TLR4, CD36, RAGE and the TREM2-TYROBP pair on microglia trigger inflammatory gene expression, cytokine release and phagocytic clearance, while prion protein, ephrin receptors and glutamate receptors such as GRIN1 and GRM5 route the signal into synaptic depression and excitotoxic calcium entry through FYN, CDK5 and GSK3B. LRP1 and ABCC1 handle efflux and clearance, and BACE1, APP and PSEN1 set how much peptide is generated in the first place. Sustained engagement produces tau hyperphosphorylation, adhesion-molecule-driven leukocyte recruitment, oxidative stress and neuronal death, linking peptide sensing to neuroinflammation and synapse loss.

Ubiquitin ligases must be switched on and off at the right moment, and this control of ubiquitin protein ligase activity is what makes ubiquitin-dependent degradation a timing device rather than a constant drain on the proteome. The genes here point squarely at the anaphase-promoting complex, whose activity dictates when a cell leaves mitosis and whether it can re-enter S phase. Activating subunits CDC20 and FZR1 confer substrate specificity, while the pseudosubstrate inhibitor FBXO5 and the spindle checkpoint proteins MAD2L1 and MAD2L2 restrain the ligase until chromosomes are correctly attached; UBE2C and UBE2S are the cognate E2 enzymes that build and extend the ubiquitin chains. USP44 opposes ubiquitination to stabilise the checkpoint, and CDKN2A links the same circuitry to tumour suppression. Loss of this restraint produces premature sister chromatid separation, aneuploidy and genomic instability.

positive regulation of ubiquitin protein ligase activity describes the activating inputs that switch on ubiquitin ligases so that substrate proteins are tagged for proteasomal destruction at the right moment. The genes here point squarely at the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, the ligase that drives mitotic exit: CDC20 and FZR1 are its interchangeable substrate-recruiting activators, licensing degradation of securin and mitotic cyclins so sister chromatids separate and CDK activity falls, while CDC14B dephosphorylates regulatory sites to promote activator loading. UBE2C initiates ubiquitin attachment and UBE2S elongates K11-linked chains, converting a marked substrate into one the proteasome will accept. Timed, irreversible proteolysis of this kind gives the cell cycle its directionality; failure to activate the ligase stalls anaphase, while inappropriate activation causes premature loss of cyclins, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy.

Control over when a ubiquitin ligase is switched on determines when its substrates are destroyed, and here that control is aimed almost entirely at the anaphase-promoting complex, the ligase that drives cells out of mitosis. CDC20 and FZR1 are the substrate-recruiting activators that engage the complex at successive points, CDC20 during metaphase to trigger securin and cyclin B destruction and FZR1 in late mitosis and G1 to keep degradation running until S phase commits. UBE2C and UBE2S are the cooperating ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes that initiate and then elongate the lysine-11-linked chains that mark substrates for the proteasome, so their availability sets the ligase's effective output. Positive regulation of ubiquitin protein ligase activity in this setting therefore enforces the irreversibility of chromosome segregation and mitotic exit; its loss permits premature separation, aneuploidy and unscheduled proliferation.

ATP is not only an intracellular energy currency; once outside the cell it acts as a signalling molecule, and this pathway covers the directed movement of ATP out of cells and organelles. Extracellular ATP drives purinergic signalling through P2X and P2Y receptors, serving taste transmission, inflammatory and immune activation, and as a danger signal released from stressed or dying cells; its breakdown products feed adenosine signalling and, in mineralizing tissue, pyrophosphate that restrains ectopic calcification. Mechanistically, large-pore calcium homeostasis modulator channels provide voltage- and calcium-regulated conduits for ATP release, notably from type II taste cells, while a vesicular nucleotide transporter loads ATP into secretory vesicles for regulated exocytosis, and ANKH controls efflux of ATP and pyrophosphate at the plasma membrane. Loss of these routes blunts taste perception, nucleotide-dependent immune crosstalk, and control of tissue mineralization.

Adult tissues depend on pools of somatic stem cells that must divide without exhausting themselves or differentiating prematurely, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how large and how persistent those pools are. Getting the balance wrong leads either to tissue atrophy and failed regeneration or to unchecked self-renewal of the kind seen in tumours. The genes act largely at the level of transcription: MYC drives the proliferative and metabolic state of progenitors, TP63 sustains basal stem cells of stratified epithelia, PAX2, PAX8 and HNF1B specify and maintain nephron progenitors in the developing kidney, and the TAF5L and TAF6L subunits of a histone acetyltransferase-containing coactivator complex support the chromatin state permissive for self-renewal. BMP7 provides an extrinsic signal and miR-145 a post-transcriptional brake that favours differentiation, linking niche cues to progenitor identity.

negative regulation of somatic stem cell population maintenance describes the signals that push tissue stem and progenitor cells out of the self-renewing state and toward differentiation. This restraint sets the size of progenitor pools during organ development and in adult tissue turnover; when it fails, progenitors persist and expand inappropriately, a route to developmental malformation and to tumours that retain stem-like features. The genes here point squarely at nephron development, where BMP7 signalling and the PAX2/PAX8 and HNF1B transcription factor network drive cap mesenchyme progenitors into epithelial tubule fates rather than continued renewal, so that the nephron endowment is completed and the progenitor niche is exhausted on schedule. A microRNA arm, miR-145, adds post-transcriptional silencing of pluripotency and self-renewal transcripts, coupling exit from the stem state to commitment and terminal differentiation.

Stem cell pools must be shut down as well as sustained, and this is the side of the balance that limits self-renewal so that progenitors stop expanding and commit to differentiation. Restraining somatic stem cell maintenance sets the point at which a tissue stops growing and starts working; when the brake fails, progenitor compartments persist and expand, a route to developmental overgrowth and to tumours that retain stem-like character. The genes here point strongly at nephrogenesis: a secreted bone morphogenetic protein ligand signals to nephron progenitors, while paired-box transcription factors and a homeodomain factor of the tubular lineage drive epithelial differentiation of the renal mesenchyme, with a microRNA reinforcing exit from the self-renewing state by repressing pluripotency-associated transcripts. The theme is transcriptional and secreted-signal control of when renewal ends and lineage commitment begins.

Initiation is the step at which most protein synthesis is controlled, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise or lower the rate at which cytoplasmic ribosomes begin translating an mRNA. Through it, cells match protein output to nutrient supply, growth signals and stress: mTOR relays amino acid and growth factor availability to the cap-binding and 40S recruitment machinery, AKT2 feeds into the same axis, and the GAIT complex components including the glutamyl-prolyl-tRNA synthetase and a ribosomal protein silence specific inflammatory transcripts after interferon exposure. IMPACT restrains the kinase that phosphorylates eIF2 and so biases cells away from the integrated stress response. Methyladenosine marks written by METTL3 and read by YTHDF2 add a further layer, coupling mRNA modification and turnover to initiation efficiency. Loss of such control leaves growth, differentiation and stress adaptation uncoupled from the signals that should set them.

Cells can shut down the loading of ribosomes onto specific messages without altering transcription, and this negative control of cytoplasmic translational initiation is how that selective silencing is achieved. Its best-characterised example is the interferon-gamma-activated inhibitor of translation complex, in which a glutamyl-prolyl-tRNA synthetase, the glycolytic enzyme GAPDH, a ribosomal protein normally resident in the large subunit, and an hnRNP-family RNA-binding protein leave their usual duties and assemble on a 3' untranslated region element to block initiation on inflammatory transcripts such as ceruloplasmin. The arrangement illustrates moonlighting: housekeeping proteins repurposed as sequence-specific repressors that impose a timer on macrophage inflammatory output. A homeobox transcription factor also contributes, linking this repression to developmental and haematopoietic gene control. Loss of such restraint permits unchecked synthesis of inflammatory mediators.

Cells adjust how much protein they make largely at the start of translation, and this pathway covers the inputs that push cytoplasmic translational initiation up rather than down. Raising initiation rates lets cells grow, respond to nutrients and growth factors, and translate specific mRNAs on demand; losing that control limits growth or, when it runs unchecked, supports the elevated protein synthesis characteristic of tumour cells. The kinase arm acts through AKT2 and mTOR, which relieve inhibition of cap-dependent initiation and license ribosome loading downstream of growth factor and amino acid signals. Other members work on the message itself or on the initiation machinery: METTL3 deposits N6-methyladenosine marks that YTHDF2 reads to alter transcript fate, while adaptors such as NCK1 couple signalling complexes to initiation factors. The pathway therefore links extracellular signals and mRNA modification state to ribosome recruitment.

Vascular smooth muscle cells in a healthy artery are quiescent and contractile; restraining their proliferation is what keeps a vessel wall from thickening. When this brake fails, medial cells dedifferentiate and divide, producing neointimal hyperplasia after angioplasty, restenosis of grafts, arterial stiffening and the fibroproliferative cap of atherosclerotic plaque, and contributing to pulmonary and systemic hypertension. Several routes converge on the same outcome: cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors such as CDKN1A and CDKN1B block G1 progression, PTEN opposes phosphoinositide-driven growth signalling, cGMP-dependent protein kinase PRKG1 transmits nitric oxide and natriuretic peptide signals, and nuclear receptors including PPARG suppress proliferative gene expression. Myocardin and MEF2C with contractile targets like calponin and tropomyosin enforce the differentiated state, since contractile identity and quiescence are coupled. Adipokines, apelin and interleukin-10 act from outside the cell, and a large complement of microRNAs tunes the whole programme post-transcriptionally.

Vascular smooth muscle cells in a healthy artery are quiescent and contractile; the signals that push them back into the cell cycle drive the medial thickening seen in atherosclerosis, restenosis after angioplasty, pulmonary and systemic hypertension, and vein graft failure. This is the stimulatory side of that control, gathering the growth factors and cytokines that increase smooth muscle proliferation — PDGF-B, FGF2 and FGF9 acting through FGFR2, IGF1, endothelin-1, TNF — together with downstream kinases and transcriptional effectors such as JAK2, PAK1, MAP3K7, JUN and MEF2D. Matrix remodelling by MMP2 and MMP9 and the ER stress arm through ERN1 and XBP1 permit the phenotypic switch away from contraction, while a large complement of microRNAs, including the miR-221/222 pair and miR-21, tunes how strongly the cells respond. Telomerase reactivation and DNMT1-dependent methylation support sustained proliferative capacity.

Chaperone-mediated autophagy is a selective route by which individual cytosolic proteins bearing a KFERQ-like motif are recognised by HSC70, delivered to the lysosomal membrane and translocated for degradation, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how fast that happens. Its output matters for clearing damaged and aggregation-prone proteins, which is why several regulators here are tied to neurodegeneration: alpha-synuclein is both a substrate and, when mutated or overabundant, an inhibitor that blocks the lysosomal receptor; ATP13A2, a lysosomal polyamine transporter mutated in juvenile parkinsonism, supports degradative capacity; and GFAP at the astrocyte lysosomal surface participates in stabilising the translocation complex. Also represented are a lysosomal protease component, translation elongation factors that interact with the chaperone system, and kinase-mediated modulation. Loss of regulation shifts proteostatic load onto bulk autophagy and the proteasome, promoting protein aggregation with age.

Vascular smooth muscle cells are normally quiescent and contractile within the vessel wall, but they can be induced to migrate, and this directed movement rebuilds vessels during development and remodelling while also driving neointima formation in atherosclerosis, restenosis after angioplasty, and hypertensive vessel thickening. Growth factors such as PDGFB and FGF9 initiate the response, GNA12 and PAK1 together with DOCK-family Rac/Cdc42 exchange factors and the actin regulator SSH1 reorganise the cytoskeleton for protrusion, and the matrix metalloproteinase ADAMTS1 and collagen receptor DDR2 couple movement to extracellular matrix. Cyclic GMP signalling through PRKG1 and the myocardin-driven contractile programme restrain the switch to a motile phenotype, while stress-responsive factors including DDIT3, XBP1 and NFE2L2 modulate it. Numerous microRNAs, notably the smooth-muscle-enriched miR-143/145 and miR-21, tune this phenotypic plasticity.

Development sculpts tissues partly by deciding which cells die, and this pathway covers the countervailing signals that keep specific progenitor populations alive long enough to differentiate. The genes involved point to kidney and eye morphogenesis: BMP7 signalling from the ureteric bud sustains nephron progenitors in the metanephric mesenchyme, while PAX2 and PAX8 act as transcription factors that maintain their survival and epithelial commitment, and HNF1B supports tubule patterning. FOXC1 and FOXC2 restrain programmed cell death in periocular and mesenchymal lineages, and their loss produces anterior segment and lymphatic defects. When this survival programme fails, progenitors are lost prematurely rather than misplaced, giving renal hypodysplasia or agenesis, glaucoma-associated eye malformations, and other congenital structural disease. It represents the developmental arm of apoptosis control, balancing growth factor and transcriptional inputs against death signals at defined stages.

Programmed cell death is not only a response to damage but a sculpting tool during development, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the rate of developmental apoptosis so that surplus cells, misplaced cells and transient structures are removed on schedule. Too little of it leaves interdigital webbing, excess neurons, or cells that should have been deleted during lineage selection; too much thins tissues that need their cells. The members work at different levels: BAX permeabilises the outer mitochondrial membrane to release cytochrome c and commit a cell to death, the two tumour necrosis factor receptors carry extrinsic death-ligand signals, NOTCH1 and the vitamin D receptor couple cell-fate and hormonal cues to death sensitivity, PML organises nuclear bodies that concentrate pro-apoptotic responses, and a microRNA tunes the balance post-transcriptionally. Together they link morphogenesis and tissue remodelling to the core apoptotic machinery.

Tissues are sculpted during development as much by the cells that die as by those that divide, and this pathway covers the controls that set how much of that programmed death occurs. Its outputs are morphogenetic: nephron and ureteric bud formation, ocular anterior segment and cardiac outflow patterning, and the pruning of surplus progenitors, so loss of restraint here produces renal hypodysplasia, anterior segment dysgenesis and related malformation syndromes. Tissue-specifying transcription factors such as PAX2, PAX8, FOXC1, FOXC2 and HNF1B set survival thresholds in the lineages they specify, while NOTCH1 signalling, BMP7 and TGFB2 supply the intercellular cues that decide which cells persist. Execution runs through familiar apoptotic machinery — BAX at the mitochondrion and the TNF receptors TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF1B at the cell surface — with PML and vitamin D receptor signalling tuning sensitivity.

regulation of protein localization to nucleolus controls which proteins are recruited to or retained in the nucleolus, the nuclear compartment where ribosomes are built and where cells sequester regulatory factors during stress. Because nucleolar residence determines whether a protein is active, stored, or degraded, this control governs ribosome biogenesis capacity, cell growth rate, and telomere maintenance. The genes point to several arms of that control: NPM1 acts as a shuttling chaperone that ferries ribosomal and nucleolar clients, NVL is an AAA-ATPase acting with NMD3 in late pre-60S maturation and export, and PINX1 restrains telomerase by holding TERT in the nucleolus. Others link nucleolar trafficking to RNA polymerase I transcription and to chromatin-associated complexes. Loss of this regulation produces nucleolar stress, p53 stabilisation, and the ribosomopathy and leukaemia phenotypes seen with NPM1 mislocalisation.

The nucleolus is where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and pre-ribosomes are assembled, and proteins must be delivered into and retained within it for that work to proceed; regulation of protein localization to the nucleolus controls which factors accumulate there and for how long. This matters for setting ribosome output to growth demand, for sequestering regulatory proteins away from the nucleoplasm during stress, and for telomerase biology, since the catalytic subunit TERT is held in the nucleolus and released to telomeres, with PINX1 acting as an inhibitor of telomerase and a nucleolar partner. The chaperone NPM1 shuttles between nucleolus and nucleoplasm and is a hub for such trafficking, while the RNA polymerase I subunit POLR1A, the export adaptor NMD3 and the AAA-ATPase NVL tie the process to rRNA synthesis and large subunit maturation. Disturbed nucleolar targeting accompanies nucleolar stress signalling and is recurrent in cancer.

The nucleolus concentrates ribosome biogenesis and a set of stress- and telomere-related activities, and proteins reach it only through targeting signals and chaperone-like escorts; increasing that traffic is what this regulatory process does. Promoting nucleolar accumulation of a partner protein determines where it can act: nucleophosmin shuttles between nucleolus and nucleoplasm and helps retain client proteins there, NMD3 works in the export of the large ribosomal subunit, and PINX1 together with telomerase reverse transcriptase links nucleolar sequestration to control of telomere elongation, since holding telomerase in the nucleolus keeps it away from chromosome ends. Other members, including MCRS1 and the chaperone SIGMAR1, act as binding partners that drive or stabilise this relocalisation. Regulated nucleolar residence of this kind couples ribosome production, cell growth signalling and stress responses to the availability of specific proteins in the right compartment.

Vascular smooth muscle cells normally sit quiescent in the medial layer of arteries; when they migrate into the intima they drive neointimal thickening, restenosis after angioplasty, and the fibrous remodelling of atherosclerotic plaque. This pathway covers the restraining signals that hold that migration in check and help keep the cells in a contractile, differentiated state. Transcriptional inputs such as myocardin and MEF2C reinforce the contractile programme, cyclic GMP-dependent kinase signalling downstream of nitric oxide relaxes and quiets the cell, adiponectin acts as a vessel-protective adipokine, BMP4 and NRF2-dependent redox control modulate phenotype, and a large complement of microRNAs including miR-21, miR-34a, miR-145-family relatives and let-7b tune the cytoskeletal and growth-factor machinery that motility requires. Loss of this restraint favours a synthetic, migratory phenotype and pathological vascular remodelling.

Vascular smooth muscle cells are normally quiescent within the artery wall, but injury, growth factor exposure and inflammation push them into a migratory, synthetic state; this pathway covers the inputs that increase the rate and extent of that migration. It matters because medial-to-intimal movement of smooth muscle cells builds neointima after angioplasty or stenting, contributes to atherosclerotic plaque growth and remodelling, and is also part of normal vessel repair. Mitogenic and matrix cues are prominent: PDGFB acting through its receptor, FGF9, the collagen receptor DDR2, and the secreted metalloproteinase ADAMTS1 remodelling proteoglycan-rich matrix. Downstream, DOCK-family guanine nucleotide exchange factors, PAK1 and the cofilin phosphatase SSH1 drive actin turnover and lamellipodial protrusion, with MAP3K7, NR4A3 and XBP1 shaping the transcriptional response. A large complement of microRNAs, including the miR-143 and miR-221 axes, tunes the phenotypic switch.

Myofibroblasts are the contractile, matrix-secreting cells that close wounds and, when they persist, drive fibrosis of lung, liver, kidney and heart; this pathway covers the controls that set how readily fibroblasts and related precursors adopt that fate. Differentiation is normally transient and self-limiting, and loss of restraint converts a repair response into scarring with progressive loss of organ function. The regulators here act at several levels: a transcription factor of the AP-1 family shapes the profibrotic gene programme, the tumour suppressor RB1 and TP53INP1 link cell cycle and stress status to the decision, PARP1 couples chromatin and DNA damage signalling to it, and several microRNAs together with their target PDCD4 tune translation of the underlying transcripts. Most of this activity is downstream of TGF-beta and mechanical cues from the extracellular matrix.

Myofibroblasts are the contractile, matrix-secreting cells that close wounds, and their persistence after repair drives fibrosis of lung, liver, heart and kidney. This pathway covers the brakes on that conversion: signals that stop fibroblasts, pericytes or epithelial-derived cells from acquiring smooth muscle actin and a profibrotic secretory programme, or that limit how many do so. Several microRNAs act here by repressing transcripts downstream of TGF-beta, the dominant differentiation cue, while PDCD4 restrains translation and TP53INP1 links stress and p53 signalling to a less activated state. RB1 ties the decision to cell cycle control, and TSKU, a secreted small leucine-rich protein, modulates matrix and growth factor signalling outside the cell. Loss of these restraints favours scarring over regeneration, making them of interest as antifibrotic targets.

regulation of protein localization to cell cortex controls which proteins are recruited to the membrane-associated cortical layer, and thereby sets the geometry of cell division and the polarity of epithelia. Its output is spindle orientation: an LGN-Gαi-NuMA module docks dynein at defined cortical sites so that astral microtubules pull the spindle into position, deciding whether daughter cells divide symmetrically within the plane of an epithelium or asymmetrically to generate distinct fates. Membrane skeleton proteins of the band 4.1 family and the spinophilin scaffold anchor these complexes to cortical actin, while mitotic phosphorylation by PLK1 and inhibition by SAPCD2 restrict recruitment to the correct cell cycle stage and cortical region. Loss of this control produces misoriented divisions, disorganised epithelial and neuroepithelial architecture, and defects in progenitor self-renewal during development.

Where a protein sits at the cell cortex determines where the mitotic spindle points and how a dividing cell splits its fate, and this pathway controls the rate and extent of such cortical recruitment. Its best-understood output is spindle orientation: a Gi-family G protein subunit anchors the LGN scaffold GPSM2 at the plasma membrane, which in turn captures NuMA and, through it, dynein that pulls on astral microtubules. Polo-like kinase 1 phosphorylation and the negative regulator SAPCD2 restrict this complex to defined cortical domains during mitosis, while band 4.1 proteins and the spinophilin scaffold PPP1R9B link cortical cargo to the actin–membrane skeleton. Correct cortical targeting underlies asymmetric division, epithelial and neuroepithelial architecture, and progenitor pool maintenance; its failure produces misoriented divisions, disorganised epithelia and, in humans, deafness and retinal patterning defects.

Directing proteins to the cell cortex, the actin-rich layer just beneath the plasma membrane, is how cells mark where the membrane skeleton anchors and where the mitotic spindle should pull. Promoting this localization matters for oriented cell division and for the asymmetric divisions that generate distinct daughter fates in epithelia and neural progenitors; its failure misorients spindles and disrupts tissue architecture. A heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunit, a GoLoco-domain adaptor and a large coiled-coil nuclear/spindle protein together form the cortical force-generating module that captures astral microtubules through dynein, while band 4.1 family proteins link transmembrane proteins to spectrin-actin and a phosphatase-targeting subunit recruits protein phosphatase 1 to cortical actin structures. The theme is cortical polarity: building and stabilizing a submembrane platform that determines the geometry of division and cell shape.

The centrosome is the cell's dominant microtubule-organizing centre, and it works only if the right proteins are delivered to it and held there. Controlling protein localization to the centrosome therefore sets how much pericentriolar material accumulates, how the two centrioles stay linked, and how spindle poles and cilia are built; miscontrol contributes to abnormal spindles, chromosome missegregation and centrosome amplification in cancer. The genes here act through several routes: a rootletin-binding linker protein and a centrosomal recruitment factor organize the core, a kinase acting on microtubules localizes to centrosomes, GSK3B and APC couple the machinery to microtubule and polarity signalling, a polarity protein and a nucleoporin contribute positional cues, and RAB11A with its effector RAB11FIP3 provides recycling-endosome traffic toward the centrosome. Cofactors of the p97 segregase are also present, linking centrosomal protein content to ubiquitin-dependent extraction and turnover.

Centrosomes must recruit the right proteins to the right place at the right time to nucleate microtubules, anchor them, and duplicate once per cell cycle, and positive regulation of protein localization to the centrosome describes the inputs that promote that recruitment. It matters for spindle assembly, for cilium formation from the mother centriole, and for the polarized microtubule arrays that orient migrating and epithelial cells; when recruitment fails, centrosome cohesion and orientation are lost and division becomes error-prone. The genes involved span several routes to the same outcome: a centrosomal linker protein that holds duplicated centrosomes together, a kinase that acts at centrosomes and on microtubule-associated substrates, a nucleoporin that also associates with centrosomal structures, a dynein-adaptor that delivers cargo along microtubules, and polarity and Wnt-pathway components that couple cell polarity signalling to centrosome positioning.

Purine nucleobase transmembrane transport moves adenine, guanine, hypoxanthine and their nucleoside forms across cell membranes, supplying the salvage route by which cells recycle bases rather than synthesise them de novo. Tissues with little de novo capacity, such as bone marrow, gut epithelium and lymphocytes, depend on this uptake, and the same carriers determine how nucleoside analogue drugs enter cells, making them determinants of response to gemcitabine, cytarabine and antiviral therapy. Two carrier families do the work: concentrative sodium-coupled transporters that drive uptake against a gradient in absorptive epithelia, and equilibrative transporters that allow bidirectional flux and set extracellular adenosine levels for purinergic signalling. A nucleobase-selective permease and an aquaglyceroporin broaden the substrate range. Loss of the lysosomal equilibrative transporter causes histiocytosis and hearing loss, and blockade of the plasma membrane equilibrative route underlies the vasodilatory action of dipyridamole.

Purine bases such as adenine, hypoxanthine and guanine are largely insoluble in lipid and must be carried across membranes by dedicated transporters before cells can reuse them through salvage pathways rather than paying the cost of de novo synthesis. This transport activity supplies substrate for nucleotide pools in tissues with limited synthetic capacity, and it governs how effectively nucleoside and nucleobase analogue drugs enter cells. Two families dominate: sodium-coupled concentrative carriers that accumulate substrate against a gradient, and equilibrative carriers that move it down one bidirectionally, with an equilibrative family member also setting extracellular adenosine levels and the tone of adenosine receptor signalling. An additional facilitative carrier acts as the main nucleobase-preferring route, and a glycerol-permeable aquaporin channel contributes further purine permeability. Loss of function in this group causes lysosomal and immune disorders and alters chemotherapy and antiviral drug uptake.

Fibroblast growth factors act not only as mitogens but as directional cues, and this pathway covers the control of how strongly and how far cells migrate toward an FGF source. Such guided movement underlies angiogenic sprouting, wound repair, limb and skeletal patterning, and the recruitment of stromal and immune cells into tissue; when it is amplified it contributes to tumour vascularisation and invasion. Secreted ligands including FGF1, FGF2, FGF4, FGF16 and FGF18 set up the gradients that endothelial and mesenchymal cells read through FGF receptor signalling, while the chemokine CXCL13 links the same migratory response to lymphoid cell positioning. Superimposed on the ligands is post-transcriptional damping by microRNAs of the miR-15/16 and miR-424 families and miR-149, which lower FGF and receptor output and so tune the magnitude of the chemotactic response rather than switching it on.

Cells that migrate toward fibroblast growth factor gradients must eventually stop, and this pathway covers the braking influences that dampen chemotaxis toward FGF. Restraint of FGF-directed movement matters during vascular patterning and tissue repair, where unchecked endothelial and fibroblast migration contributes to aberrant angiogenesis and to tumour invasion; much of the interest in these regulators comes from their loss in cancer. The effectors here are largely post-transcriptional: several microRNAs, including the miR-15/16 family and miR-424, suppress FGF receptor signalling components and cell-cycle and migration transcripts, lowering the responsiveness of a cell to an FGF gradient rather than removing the ligand. A chemokine, CXCL13, also appears, indicating that competing chemoattractant signalling can redirect or blunt the FGF response. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of growth factor signalling, directed cell motility and microRNA-mediated gene silencing.

Excitatory synapse assembly is the process by which an axon and a dendrite recognise each other and build a functional glutamatergic contact, aligning presynaptic release sites with postsynaptic receptor scaffolds. It sets the number and strength of excitatory connections in the brain, and its disruption underlies autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia risk. Assembly is driven largely by trans-synaptic adhesion complexes: neurexins pairing with neuroligins, LRRTMs and cerebellins, latrophilins with FLRT/teneurin partners, and receptor phosphatases such as PTPRD and PTPRS engaging SLITRK and IL1RAP family ligands. C1QL and neuronal pentraxins act as secreted organisers that recruit and cluster glutamate receptors, while intracellular scaffolds including SHANK3 and CASKIN1 anchor the postsynaptic density. Guidance and growth cues -- Wnts, semaphorins, reelin, neurotrophin and FGF receptors -- plus PTEN and SRGAP2 control where and how many synapses form, tying assembly to dendritic morphogenesis and activity-dependent refinement.

Excitatory synapse assembly is the process by which glutamatergic contacts between neurons are built: axonal and dendritic membranes are brought together, adhesion complexes are stabilised, and receptor-bearing postsynaptic densities are organised opposite transmitter release sites. It sets the number and strength of excitatory connections in a circuit, and thereby learning capacity; disruption of its components is recurrent in autism, intellectual disability and schizophrenia. Much of the work is done by trans-synaptic adhesion pairs — presynaptic neurexins with postsynaptic neuroligins, LRRTMs and leucine-rich repeat proteins, presynaptic receptor phosphatases with their partners, and cerebellin and C1q-like proteins bridging to delta-type glutamate receptors. Scaffolds such as SHANK3 and CASKIN1 link adhesion to receptor clustering, while latrophilin adhesion GPCRs, Wnt ligands, reelin and PTEN provide instructive and permissive signals that specify where synapses form and how many persist.

Inhibitory synapse assembly builds and specifies the GABAergic and glycinergic contacts that restrain excitation in neural circuits, setting the excitation-inhibition balance whose disturbance underlies epilepsy, autism spectrum conditions and intellectual disability. Trans-synaptic adhesion drives the process: neuroligin-2 acts on the postsynaptic side to recruit inhibitory scaffolding, MDGA1 antagonizes that interaction to limit inhibitory contacts, and cerebellins, calsyntenins, dystroglycan and semaphorin/plexin pairs provide additional matching cues across the cleft. Clustering and stabilization of GABA-A receptors is the functional endpoint, with many alpha, beta and gamma subunits represented and LHFPL4 required for their synaptic retention. Activity-dependent control is layered on top, notably through the transcription factor NPAS4, which drives inhibitory synapse formation onto active neurons, while SRGAP2 and its human-specific paralog tune synaptic maturation rate and density.

Cajal bodies are nuclear compartments where spliceosomal snRNPs, scaRNPs and telomerase are assembled and modified, and delivering the right proteins into them is a prerequisite for that maturation work. This pathway covers the events that increase protein targeting to Cajal bodies, and it is dominated by the cytosolic chaperonin TRiC/CCT — all eight subunits including TCP1 and CCT2–CCT8 — which folds substrates such as the Cajal body scaffolding factor WRAP53/TCAB1 so that they can reach the body rather than aggregate. LARP7 and MEPCE, the stabilising and capping partners of the 7SK small nuclear RNP, link this to RNP biogenesis and to control of transcriptional elongation. When the chaperonin step fails, telomerase is not properly trafficked to Cajal bodies and telomeres shorten, the defect underlying dyskeratosis congenita caused by TCAB1 mutation.

Telomerase must be assembled and delivered to the right place before it can extend chromosome ends, and the trafficking of its RNA subunit to Cajal bodies is a control point in that route. Regulation of telomerase RNA localization to Cajal bodies determines how much active enzyme reaches telomeres during S phase, so defects here shorten telomeres and cause bone marrow failure and premature ageing syndromes such as dyskeratosis congenita, where DKC1 mutations destabilize the RNA. Control operates largely through RNA maturation and quality control: PARN trims the 3' end to a stable form, the exosome-associated nuclease EXOSC10 and the decapping enzyme DCP2 act on the same transcript in the opposing, degradative direction, and the chaperonin TRiC ring built from CCT subunits and TCP1 contributes folding capacity to the assembling ribonucleoprotein.

Telomerase must be assembled and delivered to the right nuclear compartment before it can extend chromosome ends, and Cajal bodies are the staging site where the telomerase RNA component accumulates en route to telomeres during S phase. Promoting that trafficking step keeps telomere length stable in stem and progenitor cells; when it fails, telomerase is mislocalized, telomeres shorten prematurely, and the result resembles telomere biology disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita with bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis. The activity here rests on two elements: dyskerin, the pseudouridine synthase that binds the H/ACA motif of the telomerase RNA and stabilizes it as part of the holoenzyme, and the eight-subunit cytosolic chaperonin ring, whose folding capacity supports biogenesis and correct assembly of the RNP components. This links protein folding quality control to nuclear RNA targeting and genome maintenance.

High voltage-gated calcium channels admit the Ca2+ that triggers muscle contraction, neurotransmitter release and activity-dependent gene expression, so damping their flux is how excitable cells keep calcium entry proportionate to demand. The processes gathered here reduce the frequency, rate or extent of calcium entry through these L-, P/Q- and related channel types, acting largely on channel abundance and availability at the membrane rather than on the pore itself. Membrane-remodelling and adaptor proteins such as BIN1 and SESTD1 influence channel trafficking and surface localisation, a small Ras-family GTPase of the RGK group suppresses channel activity through the auxiliary beta subunit, a ubiquitin ligase component links channel turnover to protein degradation, and a microRNA sets transcript levels. Loss of such restraint produces calcium overload, with consequences for cardiac excitability, arrhythmia, muscle function and neuronal survival.

Hydrogen sulfide is a gaseous signalling molecule produced endogenously from cysteine metabolism, and cells respond to it by altering ion channel behaviour, vascular tone, mitochondrial quality control and inflammatory output. The response matters because sulfide acts as a vasodilator and cytoprotective mediator: low concentrations relax smooth muscle and limit ischaemic injury, while excess is a mitochondrial poison. Among the effectors here, the sulfonylurea receptor subunit SUR2 confers sulfide sensitivity on ATP-sensitive potassium channels, hyperpolarizing smooth muscle and dilating vessels, and the VEGF receptor KDR couples sulfide exposure to endothelial proliferation and angiogenesis. PINK1 and parkin link the stimulus to mitophagy and the clearance of damaged mitochondria, a route relevant to neuronal survival, while TNF ties it to cytokine-driven inflammation. Together these reflect sulfide's dual role as a protective signal and a metabolic stressor.

Formation of the cranial skeleton — skull vault and base, mandible, and the pharyngeal and hyoid apparatus — depends on patterning neural crest and mesodermal progenitors into cartilage and bone in register with the face they will support. The pathway explains why its disruption yields craniosynostosis, cleft lip and palate, mandibulofacial and branchial arch syndromes rather than generalized skeletal disease. Nested homeodomain and forkhead regulators such as DLX2, HOXA2, PRRX1, TWIST1, MSX2 and SIX family factors assign identity to arch and vault territories, while FGF, BMP, Wnt/beta-catenin, TGF-beta, hedgehog-linked ciliary components and endothelin receptor signalling drive migration, proliferation and RUNX2-dependent osteoblast differentiation. Sutures remain patent through balanced FGFR2 and BMP antagonist activity, and enzymes of proteoglycan sulfation, retinoid production and folate metabolism supply the extracellular and metabolic context these signals require.

Excitatory glutamatergic synapses are built by matched pairs of adhesion molecules that bridge the cleft and nucleate pre- and postsynaptic specializations, and this pathway covers the signals that set how many such contacts form and how fast. The output determines excitatory drive onto a neuron, dendritic spine density, and the balance between excitation and inhibition that underlies learning and is disturbed in autism, intellectual disability and epilepsy. Presynaptic receptor phosphatases of the PTPRD and PTPRS type pair with postsynaptic leucine-rich repeat partners such as LRRTM2 and the LRFN/SALM and LRRC4 families, while secreted cerebellins bridge GRID2 to organize parallel fibre inputs. Calsyntenin, scaffold and adaptor proteins including CASKIN1 and CRIPT couple these contacts to postsynaptic density assembly, and FGFR1, WNT7A and kinase signalling tune synaptogenesis up or down during circuit refinement.

Cytokine and growth factor receptors that lack intrinsic kinase activity signal through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, and this pathway covers everything that tunes the amplitude and duration of that relay. Its set point determines how strongly cells respond to interferons, interleukins, growth hormone, prolactin and leptin, and therefore how immune responses are scaled, how the liver and adipose tissue read metabolic hormones, and how blood cell progenitors expand. Negative feedback is central: CISH and the SOCS proteins are STAT-induced inhibitors that bind receptors and JAKs, while phosphatases such as PTPN2, PTPRC and the adaptor SH2B3 dampen upstream kinase activity. Receptor chains (IFNAR1/2, IL7R, IL2RG, GHR, PRLR, LEPR pathway components), the kinases JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2, coactivators like EP300, and numerous microRNAs set the gain. Loss of restraint underlies myeloproliferative disease, chronic inflammation, and immunodeficiency when signalling fails.

Cytokine and growth factor receptors signal through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, and this braking machinery ensures that the response is transient rather than continuous. Sustained STAT activity drives inflammation, lymphoproliferation and oncogenic transcription, so the negative regulation of receptor signaling via STAT sets the duration and amplitude of responses to interleukins, leptin, adiponectin and interferons. Several mechanisms converge: SOCS family proteins and CISH are induced by STATs themselves and feed back to block JAK activity and target receptors for degradation, phosphatases including PTPN2, PTPRC and PTPRT strip activating phosphates from JAKs and STATs, adaptors such as SH2B3 and HGS limit receptor availability and trafficking, and caveolin-1 sequesters signalling components at the membrane. A large complement of microRNAs, among them miR-146a and let-7 members, lowers receptor and adaptor levels post-transcriptionally. Loss of these restraints underlies immune dysregulation and cytokine-driven tumour growth.

STAT transcription factors are switched on when cytokine and growth factor receptors engage JAK kinases, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise the amplitude or duration of that signalling. It determines how strongly cells respond to interleukins, interferons and hormones, shaping T helper differentiation, acute-phase and antiviral responses, haematopoiesis, growth and lactation. The ligands and receptors here span several STAT-coupled families: growth hormone and prolactin with their receptors, leptin, IL-6 and LIF, the IL-12/IL-23 axis driving Th1 and Th17 programmes, IL-10 and its receptor chains restraining inflammation, and TSLP acting through CRLF2 and IL7R. JAK2 relays most of these, KIT contributes receptor tyrosine kinase input, and EP300 supplies coactivator function at STAT-bound promoters. Excessive activation of this axis underlies chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and myeloproliferative and lymphoid neoplasia, which is why JAK inhibitors are therapeutically useful.

Membrane scission by ESCRT-III leaves behind a polymer that must be taken apart before the machinery can be reused, and ESCRT complex disassembly is that recycling step. It is what makes multivesicular body formation, cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope resealing and plasma membrane and lysosome repair repeatable rather than single-use events, so its failure stalls receptor downregulation and leaves cells connected by unresolved intercellular bridges. The CHMP proteins and IST1 form the helical filaments that constrict membrane necks; the AAA-ATPase VPS4A and VPS4B, stimulated by its cofactor VTA1, hydrolyses ATP to extract subunits from the filament and return them to the cytosol as soluble monomers. This remodelling also contributes to the constriction itself, coupling subunit turnover to the geometry of the neck. CHMP7 directs the same activity to the reforming nuclear envelope after mitosis.

Endothelial cells grip the basement membrane through integrin-mediated contacts, and tuning the strength of that grip determines whether a vessel wall stays quiescent or whether cells detach, migrate and sprout. Control over endothelial cell–matrix adhesion therefore sits upstream of angiogenesis, vascular remodelling and barrier integrity, and its dysregulation contributes to tumour vascularisation and vascular malformation. The genes here act at several levels: a small GTPase of the Ras family and its exchange factor partner signal toward integrin activation and adhesion turnover, a matrix metalloproteinase degrades elastin and other matrix components to loosen attachment, a lipid phosphatase modifies phospholipid signals at the cell surface, and fucosylation enzymes alter the glycans on adhesion receptors. A transcription factor acting with β-catenin and a microRNA add transcriptional and post-transcriptional control, linking adhesion state to Wnt signalling and to endothelial responses to flow.

Endothelial cells must grip their underlying basement membrane to build and stabilise blood vessels, and this pathway covers the signals that increase the strength or frequency of that cell-matrix attachment. Adhesion to laminin, collagen and fibronectin controls whether sprouting endothelium can migrate, form a lumen and then quiesce as a sealed monolayer; when it fails, vessels are leaky and structurally weak, a defect seen in hereditary connective tissue and vascular disease. The genes converge on integrin activation and adhesion turnover from several directions: a small GTPase and an associated Rab effector promote integrin-dependent attachment and spreading, a fucosyltransferase and its GDP-fucose supply enzyme modify surface glycans that mediate contact, a lipid phosphatase tunes lysophospholipid signalling at the cell surface, and a Wnt-responsive transcription factor sets the adhesive programme. Together they link vascular morphogenesis to the cytoskeletal and glycosylation machinery of the endothelium.

Cortical inhibitory interneurons are born far from where they will work, in the ventral telencephalic ganglionic eminences, and must travel tangentially into the cortex and then settle into the correct layer. Interneuron migration is the orderly movement that accomplishes this, and it determines how much GABAergic inhibition a cortical circuit ultimately has; when it fails, the resulting imbalance of excitation and inhibition manifests as epilepsy, intellectual disability and interneuronopathies such as those caused by ARX mutation. Transcriptional control dominates this biology: ARX and LHX6 specify and maintain the migratory GABAergic identity of medial ganglionic eminence-derived cells, with FEZF2 and SOX1 contributing to regional patterning and progenitor state. Guidance and motility also respond to extrinsic cues, including dopamine receptor signalling through DRD1 and DRD2 and contactin-mediated cell surface adhesion, linking neurotransmitter signalling to the positioning of cells before circuits form.

Midbrain dopaminergic neuron differentiation is the developmental programme that converts uncommitted neural progenitors of the ventral midbrain into the dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area — the cells that support voluntary movement, motivation and reward, and whose degeneration produces Parkinson's disease. The genes here show that the specification is largely WNT-driven: secreted ligands including WNT1, WNT3A and WNT5A act through Frizzled receptors and the LRP6 co-receptor, or through the atypical receptor RYK, to stabilise β-catenin and drive transcription, while DKK1 and the secreted frizzled-related proteins SFRP1 and SFRP2 restrain the same signals so that the progenitor domain is correctly sized and positioned. Downstream, the homeodomain factor LMX1A and the nuclear receptor NR4A2 impose dopaminergic identity, turning on the machinery for dopamine synthesis and transport. The pathway is also the template for deriving dopaminergic neurons from stem cells for cell-replacement therapy.

Cells constantly restrain where their proteins go, and this collection covers the braking side of protein targeting " trafficking, secretion, membrane insertion and nuclear or organellar delivery all being actively suppressed under defined conditions. Two themes dominate. One is endoplasmic reticulum quality control and retrotranslocation, where lectins and derlins such as OS9, ERLEC1, DERL2/3 with the ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes UBE2J1 and UBE2G2 divert misfolded cargo to degradation rather than allowing export, and SREBF1/INSIG1 hold sterol sensors in the ER until cholesterol falls. The other is regulated secretion and receptor surface delivery in neurons and endocrine cells: insulin release, dopamine and opioid receptor signalling, KATP channel subunits ABCC8 and KCNJ11, and Rab11 effectors that govern recycling. Several microRNAs and 14-3-3 proteins add post-transcriptional and sequestration-based restraint. Loss of such negative control underlies secretory disease, proteostasis collapse and neurodegeneration.

Proteins are only useful where they belong, and this grouping collects the regulatory inputs that increase the rate or extent of getting them there — secretion, vesicle-mediated delivery to the plasma membrane, import into organelles and the nucleus, and transport along the endomembrane system. Its breadth reflects how much physiology depends on regulated export: COPII components such as SEC13, SEC31A and the SEC24 paralogues with SAR1A/B build the carriers that leave the ER, while syntaxin and VAMP proteins, DOC2B and UNC13B govern the final fusion step. A large insulin-secretion module is prominent, with glucokinase, GLUT2, SLC30A8 and the beta-cell transcription factors PDX1, NKX6-1 and NEUROD1, alongside cAMP- and PKC-dependent kinases, small GTPases, centrosomal and cytoskeletal scaffolds, and ubiquitin-pathway and nuclear import factors. Failure of such control underlies secretory and trafficking disease, including diabetes and neurodegeneration.

Absorptive epithelial cells of the intestine and kidney proximal tubule present a dense, ordered array of microvilli whose packing multiplies the surface available for nutrient uptake, and brush border assembly is the process that organises those protrusions into that array. Rather than each microvillus standing alone, neighbouring tips are tethered to one another by calcium-dependent adhesion links built from two atypical cadherins, CDHR2 and CDHR5, which pair across the intermicrovillar space. Their cytoplasmic ends are held by a tripartite module of USH1C, ANKS4B and the actin-based motor MYO7B, with CALML4 as a light chain, which traffics the adhesion complex to microvillar tips along the actin core. Loss of this machinery leaves microvilli disordered and sparse, compromising absorptive capacity; related adhesion and scaffold proteins underlie congenital diarrhoeal disease and, in the inner ear, hair bundle organisation.

Bleomycin is a DNA-cleaving antitumour antibiotic that generates double-strand breaks and, in lung tissue, drives inflammation and fibrosis; the cellular response to bleomycin covers the transcriptional and repair changes cells mount when exposed to it. How well a cell tolerates this insult determines both the therapeutic window of the drug and the severity of its characteristic side effect, pulmonary fibrosis. The genes here point to two arms of that response. Replication-fork and DNA repair components, including the helicase DDX11 and the replisome-associated TIMELESS, help cells cope with breaks encountered during S phase and maintain fork stability. Alongside them sit an apoptosis regulator of the inhibitor-of-apoptosis family, an AP-1 family transcription factor that remodels gene expression after stress, and a collagen VI chain reflecting the extracellular matrix deposition that follows bleomycin-induced tissue injury.

regulation of endosome organization controls how endosomes are sized, shaped, matured and positioned as cargo moves from the plasma membrane toward lysosomes. This governs receptor downregulation, membrane protein turnover and the delivery of hydrolases and lipids to the degradative compartment, so its failure produces enlarged or stalled endosomes and the accumulation of undegraded substrates seen in neurodegeneration and lysosomal storage disease. The genes act at successive control points: RAB7A marks late endosomes and recruits tethering and motor machinery for maturation and transport, the phosphoinositide phosphatase SYNJ1 sets the lipid identity that determines coat and adaptor binding, TOM1 links ubiquitinated cargo to the sorting machinery, and SCARB2 chaperones glucocerebrosidase to the lysosome. The ubiquitin ligase PRKN adds a quality-control arm, tying endosomal membrane traffic to mitophagy and to Parkinson disease pathogenesis.

Endosomes must be shaped, matured and positioned correctly for material taken into a cell to reach lysosomes, be recycled to the surface, or be handed to autophagic membranes; regulation of endosome organization covers the inputs that set how fast and how far that remodelling goes. The genes here act at different points on that theme: a small GTPase that marks late endosomes and licenses their fusion with lysosomes, a lysosomal membrane protein needed for delivery of a glucocerebrosidase, a phosphoinositide phosphatase that controls membrane lipid identity during vesicle uncoating, an adaptor that engages ubiquitinated cargo and autophagic machinery, and a ubiquitin ligase linked to damaged-organelle clearance. Several are mutated in Parkinson disease and related neurodegeneration, reflecting how strongly neurons depend on accurate endosomal maturation and cargo sorting for synaptic vesicle recycling and protein turnover.

Leukocytes leaving the blood must first stick to the vessel wall, and this pathway covers the signals that dial that adhesion up or down. It sets how much inflammation a tissue receives: too little and infection goes uncontained, too much and the endothelium is damaged, as in atherosclerosis, sepsis and chronic inflammatory disease. Inflammatory input through TNF and IL6 acts via IRAK1 tTRAF6 and the NF- cappaB subunit RELA to induce the endothelial selectins SELE and SELP, while glycosyltransferases such as FUT7, ST3GAL4 and the sulfotransferases CHST2 and CHST4 build the sialyl-Lewis and sulfated ligands those selectins recognise. Integrins ITGA4 and ITGB2 convert rolling into firm arrest, chemokines including CXCL12 and CCL21 and the receptor CCR2 provide directional cues, and RHOA remodels the cytoskeleton. Restraining factors, notably KLF4 and a large complement of microRNAs led by MIR146A and MIR21, keep the endothelium quiescent.

negative regulation of leukocyte adhesion to vascular endothelial cell restrains the first committed step of inflammation, in which circulating leukocytes stick to the vessel wall before crossing into tissue. Keeping this step in check preserves endothelial quiescence; its loss drives chronic vascular inflammation and the leukocyte-rich lesions of atherosclerosis. Two kinds of brake appear here. The transcription factor KLF4 enforces an anti-inflammatory endothelial program, suppressing VCAM1 and E-selectin induction downstream of cytokine and shear-stress cues. A set of microRNAs, including MIR146A, MIR31 and let-7 family members, damp NF-κB signalling and directly limit adhesion molecule and chemokine output. Homeostatic chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21 and CCL25 contribute by redirecting leukocyte trafficking toward lymphoid and mucosal destinations rather than inflamed endothelium. Together these controls set the threshold at which vascular endothelium permits immune cell recruitment.

Leukocytes only stick to the vessel wall where they are needed, and this restraint on leukocyte adhesion to vascular endothelial cells keeps that from happening indiscriminately. Losing it tips the endothelium toward a chronically activated, adhesive state — the initiating step of atherosclerotic lesions and of inflammatory vascular injury. Two kinds of brake appear here. Transcriptional control by KLF4 maintains an anti-inflammatory endothelial phenotype, damping cytokine-driven expression of the selectins and immunoglobulin-family adhesion receptors that capture rolling leukocytes. Alongside it, a set of microRNAs including miR-146a, miR-31, miR-181 family members of the let-7 group and the miR-221/222 pair post-transcriptionally limit NF-κB signalling and adhesion molecule output. Homeostatic chemokines such as CXCL12, CCL21 and CCL25 contribute by guiding leukocyte traffic to lymphoid and mucosal tissue rather than to inflamed vessel walls.

Leukocytes leave the blood only where the endothelium tells them to, and this pathway covers the signals and surface chemistry that increase that sticking. It is the first committed step of inflammatory cell recruitment: without it, infected or injured tissue cannot be patrolled; with it running unchecked, the same adhesion drives atherosclerotic plaque formation, vasculitis and reperfusion injury. Inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL6 act through IRAK1-TRAF6 and NF-kB (RELA) to induce endothelial E- and P-selectin, while glycosyltransferases and sulfotransferases including FUT7, ST3GAL4, GCNT1 and CHST2/CHST4 build the sialyl-Lewis-x and sulfated glycans that selectins recognise, converting rolling into firm arrest. Integrins ITGA4 and ITGB2 on the leukocyte, chemokine sensing via CCR2, and RhoA-dependent cytoskeletal tension complete adhesion strengthening, with ephrin signalling and microRNAs tuning the endothelial side.

positive regulation of leukocyte adhesion to arterial endothelial cell describes signals that make the arterial wall sticky for circulating white blood cells, the initiating step of vascular inflammation and atherosclerotic plaque formation. Firm adhesion of monocytes and other leukocytes to activated endothelium precedes their transmigration into the intima, where they become foam cells; chronic activation of this process drives atherogenesis, while its absence protects arteries at branch points exposed to disturbed flow. TNF acts as the prototypical inflammatory input, upregulating endothelial adhesion molecules, and ALOX5 supplies leukotriene mediators from arachidonate that reinforce recruitment. Ephrin-B2 and EphA4 contribute juxtacrine cues at the endothelial surface that promote leukocyte attachment, and the flow-responsive microRNA miR-92a links shear stress sensing to a proinflammatory endothelial phenotype. The pathway sits at the interface of innate immunity, lipid mediator signalling and hemodynamic control of vessel wall biology.

Leukocytes are recruited into the arterial wall only where the endothelium has been licensed to capture them, and this pathway covers the signals that increase that capture. It is the initiating step of atherosclerotic lesion formation: monocytes sticking to activated endothelium at branch points and regions of disturbed flow accumulate as foam cells, so persistent upregulation here drives plaque growth and vascular inflammation. Inflammatory input from TNF induces adhesion molecule display on endothelial cells, while the 5-lipoxygenase route generates leukotrienes that amplify chemoattraction and adhesiveness. Ephrin-B2 and Eph receptor signalling contributes contact-dependent regulation at the arterial endothelial surface, and a flow-sensitive microRNA of the miR-17~92 cluster adds post-transcriptional control that links shear stress to endothelial activation. Together these inputs make endothelial adhesiveness a tunable, site-specific property rather than a constitutive one.

The heart's valves and septa begin as endocardial cushions, swellings of extracellular matrix into which endocardial cells migrate after losing their epithelial character. Control over how many cells undergo that epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and how fast, sets the size and shape of the cushions and therefore whether valve leaflets and the atrioventricular and outflow septa form properly; too little or too much activity yields septal defects and valve malformations, among the commonest congenital heart lesions. The regulators here are the transforming growth factor beta ligands TGFB1, TGFB2 and TGFB3 acting through the type I and type II receptor pair, with the accessory receptor endoglin tuning responsiveness in endothelial cells. Endoglin mutation instead causes hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, illustrating how the same receptor complex serves both cardiac cushion morphogenesis and vascular wall integrity.

Ventricular myocytes must return to resting potential on a tightly controlled schedule, and modulation of repolarization during the ventricular action potential sets how long each beat's plateau lasts. This determines the QT interval on the electrocardiogram and the refractory period that protects the ventricle from re-excitation; when repolarization is delayed or made unstable, early afterdepolarizations and torsade de pointes-type arrhythmias and sudden death can follow. Control is exerted on the repolarizing potassium currents and on the calcium handling that shapes the plateau: an accessory potassium channel subunit alters channel gating, a sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium-buffering protein constrains store release, nitric oxide synthase with its adaptor provides local nitrosative signalling to channels, a RING-finger protein influences channel trafficking, and two muscle-enriched microRNAs tune the levels of the underlying transcripts. The pathway thus links excitation-contraction coupling to electrical stability.

Each heartbeat ends with repolarization, the return of the cardiomyocyte membrane to its resting potential, and control over how fast that happens sets action potential duration, the QT interval, and the refractory period that prevents re-entrant arrhythmia. Modulating repolarization during the cardiac action potential is therefore a rhythm-safety function: too slow and the cell is vulnerable to early afterdepolarizations, long QT and torsades de pointes; too fast and short-QT phenotypes with atrial and ventricular fibrillation follow. The regulators here act largely on repolarizing potassium currents and on the calcium handling coupled to them, including an accessory potassium channel subunit, a sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium buffer, a cytoskeletal scaffold, and an adaptor that links neuronal nitric oxide synthase to channel signalling; several microRNAs tune the abundance of channel and handling proteins. Variants in these genes segregate with inherited repolarization disorders and sudden cardiac death.

Fungal pathogens are detected by innate immune receptors such as the C-type lectins that recognise beta-glucan and mannan on the fungal cell wall, and this pathway covers the processes that tune how strongly that antifungal response fires. Getting the setting right matters clinically: too little signalling leaves mucosal and systemic candidiasis and other invasive mycoses unchecked, while excess drives damaging inflammation in the lung and gut. Control is exerted largely at the level of CARD9-dependent signalling downstream of the lectin receptors, where ubiquitin ligase and deubiquitinase activities acting on the adaptor set the gain, with TRIM62 and USP15 opposing each other. A myeloid transcription factor, SPI1, contributes by specifying the macrophage and neutrophil populations that do the phagocytosis and killing, and a secreted phospholipase adds lipid-mediated antifungal activity.

Autophagosome organization is the building of the double-membraned vesicle that engulfs cytoplasmic cargo and delivers it to lysosomes for degradation, the committed step of macroautophagy. It lets cells survive starvation, clear damaged mitochondria and protein aggregates, and restrain intracellular bacteria; its failure underlies neurodegeneration, lysosomal storage disease and inflammatory bowel disease, and several members here are Parkinson's and hereditary spastic paraplegia genes. Nutrient status is read by mTOR and relayed to the ULK1/ULK2 initiation kinase complex with ATG13 and RB1CC1, which activates the class III PI3K complex of PIK3C3, BECN1 and ATG14 to generate PI3P on a nascent membrane. WIPI and ATG2 proteins then read that lipid and transfer lipid to expand the phagophore, while the ATG7-ATG3-ATG5/ATG12/ATG16L1 conjugation machinery lipidates LC3 and GABARAP family proteins onto it. ATG9 vesicles, TMEM41B, VMP1 and Rab and SNARE components supply membrane, sealing and subsequent fusion competence.

Control over how much sphingolipid and phospholipid a membrane contains, rather than the synthetic steps themselves, is what this regulatory layer provides. Cells tune the balance between ceramide, sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate because these lipids act as signals that decide between growth and death, and mis-set levels alter membrane order, lysosomal function and inflammatory tone. The ORMDL proteins restrain serine palmitoyltransferase to cap sphingolipid output, a brake whose genetic variation is linked to asthma risk; the sphingosine kinases SPHK1 and SPHK2 generate sphingosine-1-phosphate, pushing the balance toward survival and migration. Additional inputs come from an energy-sensing kinase subunit, a calcium-independent phospholipase, microRNAs and a lysosomal lipid-associated receptor, so nutrient state, calcium signalling and transcript stability all feed in. Failures here surface as sphingolipid storage and neurodegenerative disease, altered immune activation and disordered lipid handling.

Carboxylic acid transmembrane transport moves amino acids, monocarboxylates, di- and tricarboxylates, fatty acids and folate across plasma and organellar membranes, connecting extracellular nutrient supply to cytosolic and mitochondrial metabolism. It underlies intestinal and renal reabsorption, glutamate clearance at synapses, lactate shuttling between glycolytic and oxidative cells, and delivery of acyl groups and TCA-cycle intermediates into mitochondria. Carriers here span several families: monocarboxylate transporters of the SLC16 group, sodium-dependent and exchange-type amino acid carriers of the SLC1, SLC7 and SLC38 groups, vesicular glutamate transporters, mitochondrial SLC25 carriers for citrate, malate, aspartate/glutamate and carnitine, ABC transporters that import very-long-chain fatty acids into peroxisomes, and the pyruvate carriers MPC1/MPC2. Loss of individual members causes cystinuria, lysinuric protein intolerance, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, thyroid hormone transport defects and excitotoxic neurological disease, and tumours exploit these routes for glutamine and lactate flux.

Vascular smooth muscle cells switch between a contractile, differentiated state and a proliferative, synthetic one, and this pathway covers the inputs that push the balance either way. The contractile phenotype maintains vessel tone and wall integrity; loss of it drives neointima formation after injury, atherosclerotic plaque remodelling, arterial stiffening and aneurysm. Control is exerted at several levels: growth factor and receptor signalling through PDGFB, FGF9 and KIT; transcriptional programmes involving HEY2 in arterial identity and calcineurin-responsive NFATC factors; DNA methylation by DNMT1; extracellular matrix and TGF-beta-family context supplied by EFEMP2 and the endothelial co-receptor endoglin; and a substantial post-transcriptional layer, with miR-145 among the microRNAs that promote the contractile state and others favouring dedifferentiation. Redox and sulfur metabolism, via SOD2 and cystathionine gamma-lyase, and estrogen signalling through GPER1 also modulate the decision.

Vascular smooth muscle cells are not permanently fixed in their contractile state; they can be held back from, or driven out of, the differentiated phenotype, and this braking on vascular associated smooth muscle cell differentiation is what keeps arterial wall cells proliferative and migratory during development, injury repair and disease. Loss of contractile gene expression in favour of a synthetic, dedifferentiated phenotype underlies neointima formation after angioplasty, atherosclerotic plaque growth and hypertensive vessel remodelling. The machinery here is mixed: growth factor signals such as PDGF-B and FGF9 suppress maturation, calcineurin-responsive NFAT transcription factors and the Notch target HEY2 repress contractile programmes, DNMT1 supplies DNA methylation-based silencing, and a set of microRNAs including miR-21, miR-221 and miR-15b tune the same switch post-transcriptionally, with PDCD4 among their targets. Together they place smooth muscle plasticity under combined epigenetic, transcriptional and paracrine control.

Vascular smooth muscle cells give arteries their contractile tone and mechanical strength, and this pathway covers the inputs that push progenitors and dedifferentiated cells toward that mature contractile state. It matters because the switch is reversible: loss of differentiation markers lets smooth muscle cells adopt a synthetic, proliferative, migratory phenotype that drives neointima formation after injury, atherosclerotic plaque remodelling and arterial stiffening. Much of the positive regulation here is post-transcriptional, through microRNAs such as miR-145, miR-21 and miR-1, which reinforce contractile gene programmes and restrain proliferative ones. Additional contributions come from TGF-beta family receptor signalling via endoglin, extracellular matrix and elastic fibre assembly involving fibulin-4, oestrogen receptor signalling through GPER1, and redox and hydrogen sulfide-generating enzymes that shape the local signalling environment during vessel wall maturation and repair.

Tight junctions seal the space between neighbouring epithelial and endothelial cells, and their controlled dismantling is what allows a barrier to open — during wound repair, leukocyte passage, or inflammatory leak. Regulating the frequency and extent of tight junction disassembly therefore sets barrier permeability, and unchecked disassembly underlies vascular oedema, blood-brain barrier breakdown and the increased gut or airway permeability seen in inflammatory disease. Inflammatory input is represented here by interleukin-1 beta, a cytokine that acts on the junctional complex to loosen cell-cell contacts, while TGF-beta signalling through its type I receptor provides a second route that remodels junctions as part of epithelial plasticity. Myosin light chain kinase activity links these signals to actomyosin contraction at the perijunctional ring, the mechanical step that physically pulls junction strands apart, placing this biology at the interface of cytokine signalling and cytoskeletal tension.

Cells dispose of damaged mitochondria by tagging them for engulfment by autophagosomes, and this pathway sets how readily that clearance is triggered. Type 2 mitophagy proceeds without the usual reliance on autophagosome formation at the mitochondrion being driven by membrane potential collapse alone, and its regulation determines how much dysfunctional mitochondrial mass a neuron or muscle cell tolerates. The core sensing step is the kinase PINK1, which accumulates on depolarised outer membranes and recruits the ubiquitin ligase parkin to ubiquitinate outer-membrane substrates such as VDAC1; additional ligases including MUL1 and HUWE1, the deacetylase HDAC6 acting on transport of damaged cargo, the chaperone co-factor CDC37 and the protease HTRA2 tune the response up or down. Loss of this control underlies recessive Parkinson disease, and related lysosomal factors such as GBA1 and VPS13C link the same surveillance to neurodegeneration.

Cells dispose of damaged mitochondria by wrapping them in autophagosomes, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that selective clearance harder or faster. Keeping it responsive protects neurons in particular: loss-of-function mutations in PINK1 and in the ubiquitin ligase parkin cause recessive early-onset Parkinson's disease, and failure to remove depolarized organelles leaves cells exposed to oxidative damage and defective respiration. The machinery named here spans the signal and its amplification: a mitochondrial kinase retained on damaged membranes recruits parkin, import-channel components such as TOMM7 and the outer-membrane porin VDAC1 shape that retention and provide ubiquitination substrates, additional ligases including MUL1 and HUWE1 add ubiquitin marks, and HDAC6 helps cluster and traffic the tagged cargo. Metabolic and chaperone factors such as hexokinase 2 and CDC37 tune how readily the response is triggered, linking mitochondrial quality control to cellular energy state and proteostasis.

Meiosis only produces balanced gametes if chromosomes are held together until every kinetochore is correctly attached, and this braking activity — negative regulation of meiotic chromosome separation — is what imposes that delay. Loss of the restraint allows premature separation and aneuploid eggs or sperm, the leading cause of miscarriage and chromosomal disorders in humans. The genes here act largely through the spindle assembly checkpoint at the kinetochore: KNL1 is a scaffold at the outer kinetochore that recruits checkpoint components, TTK (MPS1) is the kinase that initiates checkpoint signalling in response to unattached kinetochores, and ZWINT links the kinetochore to the RZZ complex and dynein-dependent checkpoint silencing. MOS, the oocyte-specific MAP kinase kinase kinase, sustains metaphase arrest in vertebrate eggs, while CHFR contributes mitotic-stress checkpoint control through ubiquitin ligase activity. Together they couple attachment status to the timing of anaphase onset.

Cells that respond to acetylcholine do so through two very different receptor families, and this pathway covers both and what happens downstream. Nicotinic receptors are ligand-gated cation channels built from alpha, beta, delta, epsilon and gamma subunits; the muscle-type combination drives neuromuscular transmission, while neuronal assemblies such as those containing CHRNA4/CHRNB2 or CHRNA7 modulate synaptic excitability and are the targets of nicotine dependence. The five muscarinic receptors instead couple to G proteins, with Gq-linked signalling through PLCB1, IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release and PKC, and Gi-linked inhibition slowing heart rate and shaping neuronal firing. Acetylcholinesterase terminates the signal, agrin organises receptor clustering at the endplate, and secreted or membrane LY6/lynx-family modulators tune nicotinic sensitivity. Loss of these components underlies congenital myasthenic syndromes, and cholinergic tone is pharmacologically manipulated in dementia, asthma and anaesthesia.

Membrane invagination is the inward deformation of the plasma membrane that begins engulfment, and this pathway covers the signals that tune how readily and how extensively it happens. Most of the biology here is about phagocytic and endocytic uptake by macrophages, microglia and platelets: recognition receptors such as CD36, TREM2 and complement-derived opsonin signals mark a target, phospholipase C gamma and adaptor proteins convert that recognition into cytoskeletal and calcium signalling, and Rab-dependent trafficking supplies membrane to the forming cup. Inhibitory receptors and lipid-handling proteins set the threshold so that uptake is proportionate, and scramblase activity redistributes phospholipids to permit membrane bending. These controls determine clearance of apoptotic cells, oxidised lipids and debris; when they are weakened, as with TREM2 variants in microglia, defective clearance contributes to neurodegenerative and inflammatory disease.

Proteins delivered to lysosomes are degraded there, and this regulatory arm increases the rate at which that happens, largely by controlling how much substrate reaches the lysosomal lumen. Endocytic receptors of the LDL receptor family take up ligands at the cell surface and route them inward for hydrolysis: LDLR clears lipoprotein particles, LRP1 binds a broad set of ligands including proteases and their inhibitors, and LRP2 (megalin) retrieves filtered proteins in the kidney proximal tubule. Trafficking adaptors such as GGA3 sort cargo between endosomes and lysosomes, while the membrane-bound ubiquitin ligase MARCHF2 tags substrates for lysosomal disposal.
