Together these activities set the turnover of extracellular and membrane proteins, with consequences for plasma cholesterol handling, urinary protein reabsorption, and the clearance of aggregation-prone material.

Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks accurately by copying an intact sister template, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote it — raising the rate at which breaks are channelled into recombination rather than error-prone end joining. The choice matters for genome stability: loss of these promoting activities shifts repair toward mutagenic routes and underlies chromosome instability and cancer predisposition, while the same machinery is exploited by therapies that target recombination-deficient tumours. Much of the group is chromatin-directed, notably the NuA4/TIP60 acetyltransferase and associated helicase-like ATPases, which open nucleosomes around a break to allow resection and filament loading. Ubiquitin and SUMO ligases such as RNF8 and PIAS4 build the signalling marks that recruit repair factors, NBN reports the break through the sensing nuclease complex, PARP1 detects damage, and RAD51AP1 assists strand invasion by the recombinase itself.

Vascular smooth muscle cells are not terminally fixed: they can switch from a quiescent, contractile state to a proliferative, migratory, matrix-secreting phenotype, and control over that switch is what this pathway describes. The transition is useful for vessel repair but drives neointima formation after angioplasty, arterial stiffening and the fibroproliferative cap of atherosclerotic plaques, so modulating the rate of dedifferentiation determines whether a vessel heals or narrows. Several microRNAs act here as phenotypic gatekeepers, with miR-145 favouring the contractile programme and miR-221 and miR-214 tuning proliferation, while platelet-derived growth factor B supplies the extracellular cue from endothelium and platelets that pushes cells away from the contractile state. Olfactomedin-like OLFM2 contributes by influencing the transcriptional machinery governing contractile gene expression, linking growth factor signalling to smooth muscle identity.

Manchette assembly builds the transient microtubule- and actin-based skirt that encircles the nucleus of an elongating spermatid, anchored at the perinuclear ring below the acrosome. It shapes the sperm head and serves as a trafficking corridor delivering cargo from the cytoplasm to the growing flagellum and its basal body, so its failure produces malformed, headless or immotile sperm and male infertility of the teratozoospermia type. Genes here include the linker protein HOOK1 and MEIG1, which together recruit cargo to the manchette, the testis-specific actin-binding profilin PFN4, the kinase STK33, and several coiled-coil and centriolar satellite proteins such as CCDC181, CEP131 and CFAP53 that connect the structure to the centrosome and axoneme. The process sits at the junction of intraflagellar transport, cytoskeletal remodelling and nuclear condensation during spermiogenesis.

Regulation of connective tissue replacement controls how much scar tissue forms when an injured organ heals, setting the balance between repair and fibrosis. When it fails, functional parenchyma in lung, liver, kidney or heart is progressively displaced by collagen-rich matrix, the basis of pulmonary fibrosis, cirrhosis and post-infarct cardiac remodelling. The regulators here act at several levels: microRNAs of the miR-34, miR-15/16, miR-17 and miR-199/214 families tune the fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition and matrix gene output; the Rho-associated kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 transmit mechanical tension and actomyosin contractility into profibrotic transcription; calcineurin and RUNX1 couple calcium and injury signals to that program; PPARG and the advanced glycation end-product receptor AGER act as opposing brakes and accelerators, linking metabolic and inflammatory state to fibrotic outcome. The pathway therefore sits downstream of tissue injury and upstream of matrix deposition and organ stiffening.

Connective tissue replacement is the substitution of damaged parenchyma by fibrous matrix after injury, and the factors here set how far that scarring goes. Too little leaves wounds mechanically weak; too much produces the fibrosis that stiffens lung, liver, kidney and heart and drives organ failure, including the collagen-rich scar that replaces infarcted myocardium. Control operates at several levels: PPARG acts as a transcriptional brake on fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion, the ROCK1 and ROCK2 kinases transmit actomyosin tension and matrix stiffness into contractile and profibrotic gene programmes, calcineurin and RUNX1 couple calcium and lineage signals to the same output, and AGER links advanced glycation and damage-associated ligands to injury responses. A large set of microRNAs, among them the miR-34 and miR-15/16 families, miR-21-related regulators, miR-199 and miR-214, tunes these circuits post-transcriptionally, making fibrosis a quantitatively regulated outcome of wound healing rather than a fixed one.

Fibrosis is the replacement of damaged parenchyma with collagen-rich connective tissue, and this grouping covers the influences that drive that substitution forward rather than restrain it. Sustained activation underlies scarring in heart, liver, lung and kidney, where stiffened matrix displaces working tissue and organ function declines. Much of the control here is post-transcriptional: several microRNA families, including the miR-34 members and miR-15/16, tune the abundance of pro-fibrotic and survival transcripts in fibroblasts, myofibroblasts and neighbouring parenchymal cells, while miR-199a and miR-214 have been linked to fibroblast activation. On the effector side, the Rho-associated kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 couple cytoskeletal tension and actomyosin contractility to myofibroblast differentiation and matrix deposition, and calcineurin's catalytic subunit links calcium signalling to the transcriptional programmes of hypertrophic and fibrotic remodelling.

Regulation of cardiocyte differentiation governs how many cardiac progenitors become beating cardiomyocytes and when, setting the size, chamber identity and contractile character of the developing heart. Its outputs matter for congenital heart disease, for the failure of adult myocardium to regenerate after infarction, and for directed differentiation of stem cells into cardiac tissue. Control is exerted at several levels: BMP, WNT and TGF-beta ligands with their antagonists such as DKK1 provide the inductive and inhibitory cues; Notch components including DLL1 and HEY2 partition ventricular versus conduction fates; and the core transcriptional module of NKX2-5, TBX5, MEF2C, SOX6 and the SRF cofactor MYOCD drives the sarcomeric and ion-handling gene program. Chromatin modifiers such as HDAC3 and KAT2A, together with muscle-enriched microRNAs including miR-1 and miR-133, tune the timing and reversibility of commitment.

Cardiac muscle cells are specified from mesodermal progenitors during heart development, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast and how far that commitment proceeds. Its balance determines chamber identity, conduction versus working myocardium, and the size of the cardiomyocyte pool; misregulation underlies congenital heart malformations such as septal and outflow tract defects, and reactivation of the same circuitry shapes hypertrophic and regenerative responses in the adult heart. BMP and TGF-beta ligands signalling through SMAD4, Wnt ligands and the secreted antagonist DKK1, Notch through DLL1 and HEY2, and ephrin and growth factor receptor input converge on a core transcriptional module of NKX2-5, TBX5, MEF2C and the coactivator myocardin. Chromatin regulators including HDAC3 and a set of muscle-enriched microRNAs such as miR-1 and miR-133 tune the output, reinforcing commitment or restraining it.

Heart development depends as much on restraining cardiac fate as on promoting it, and this set represents the braking side: processes that stop or slow the differentiation of progenitors into cardiomyocytes and related cardiac cells. Holding progenitor pools undifferentiated allows the heart to grow to the right size and lets distinct chamber, conduction and outflow identities emerge in sequence rather than all at once; premature or excessive differentiation depletes the pool and contributes to septal, valve and chamber malformations. The repression runs through several routes — BMP and Wnt ligand-receptor signalling with the secreted Wnt antagonist DKK1 and the planar-cell-polarity protein PRICKLE1, Notch ligand DLL1 acting through the transcriptional repressor HEY2, SMAD4-dependent transcription, receptor tyrosine kinase input via EGFR and the adaptor FRS2, chromatin repression by HDAC3, and microRNA-mediated damping of cardiogenic transcripts.

This is the set of inputs that push a progenitor cell toward becoming a heart muscle cell, the step that builds the myocardium during development and that regenerative and stem-cell cardiology tries to recapitulate. Positive regulation of cardiocyte differentiation works through secreted morphogens such as BMP4, WNT3A and TGF-beta ligands that specify cardiac mesoderm, converging on the core transcriptional circuit of NKX2-5, TBX5, MEF2C and the smooth/cardiac muscle coactivator MYOCD, which switch on sarcomeric and contractile gene expression. Chromatin acetylation by KAT2A and a group of muscle-enriched microRNAs including miR-1 and miR-133 reinforce the commitment by silencing alternative fates and tuning proliferation versus maturation. Loss or mutation of the central factors, notably NKX2-5 and TBX5, produces septal and conduction defects and other congenital heart malformations, tying this regulatory layer directly to cardiac chamber and valve formation.

cellular response to L-glutamate covers what a cell does once glutamate, the main excitatory neurotransmitter of the vertebrate brain, engages its receptors: change synaptic strength, remodel the postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton, alter gene expression, and in excess die by excitotoxicity. It underlies learning and memory at glutamatergic synapses and is the point of failure in ischaemic neuronal death and in neurodegenerative disease. The genes span receptor and transducer: AMPA and NMDA receptor subunits such as GRIA1 and GRIN2D admit calcium and sodium, the tyrosine kinase FYN phosphorylates NMDA receptors to tune their gating, the calcium sensor hippocalcin couples the resulting calcium rise to receptor internalisation during long-term depression, and BAIAP2 links activity to dendritic spine morphology. Parkin ties glutamate signalling to synaptic protein turnover and mitochondrial quality control in neurons under excitatory load.

Glutamate is the main excitatory transmitter of the vertebrate brain, and the cellular response to it converts receptor occupancy into changes in excitability, synaptic strength, cytoskeletal shape and gene expression. This coupling underlies learning and memory, while excessive or prolonged glutamate signalling drives excitotoxic calcium overload in stroke and neurodegeneration. AMPA-type and NMDA-type ionotropic receptor subunits such as GRIA1 and GRIN2D provide the initial depolarising and calcium-permeable conductances; the Src-family kinase FYN phosphorylates receptor subunits and tunes their function, and the adaptor BAIAP2 links activated receptors to actin remodelling at dendritic spines. Hippocalcin acts as a neuronal calcium sensor that translates the resulting calcium rise into downstream effects including receptor internalisation, and parkin activity connects this signalling to protein turnover and neuronal survival. Together these components set the threshold between adaptive plasticity and glutamate-driven neuronal injury.

Synapses are not fixed structures; spines grow, shrink, and change shape as circuits adapt, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how much such structural remodelling occurs. It underlies activity-dependent plasticity, learning-related circuit refinement, and the maintenance of spine density in mature neurons, with loss of restraint linked to intellectual disability and autism-spectrum phenotypes. Most of the regulation converges on the actin cytoskeleton beneath the postsynaptic membrane: RHOA and RHOB set small GTPase tone, BAIAP2 and CYFIP1 couple signalling to actin nucleation and branching, CTTNBP2 anchors cortactin at spines, and PDXP dephosphorylates cofilin to promote filament severing. Receptor and trafficking components such as EPHA4, ITSN1 and the motor KIF5B tie extracellular guidance cues and cargo delivery into the same output, while ZDHHC17 provides palmitoylation-dependent scaffolding. The result is bidirectional tuning of synapse size and number rather than synapse formation itself.

Chromatin states must be reversed as well as written, and this grouping covers processes that restrain or reduce chromatin organization, keeping compaction and modification from spreading beyond their proper limits. Such counter-regulation lets genes stay accessible during differentiation and prevents heritable silencing of loci that must remain active. The genes act largely by removing repressive marks or opposing the enzymes that place them: KDM1A demethylates mono- and dimethylated histone H3 lysine 4, PHF8 and PHF2 are JmjC-domain histone demethylases, and L3MBTL3 links methylated-lysine reading to degradation of chromatin regulators. DNMT3L lacks catalytic activity itself and instead modulates de novo DNA methyltransferase partners, while KMT2A and SAMD1 tie the pathway to CpG-island promoter states. Loss of these activities contributes to intellectual disability syndromes and to leukaemias driven by misdirected chromatin modification.

Dendritic spines hold their shape, and change it, through the actin filaments packed beneath the postsynaptic membrane, and control over how that actin is remodelled sets how strongly a synapse can be potentiated or pruned. This regulation of postsynaptic actin cytoskeleton modification determines spine number and morphology during development and during activity-dependent plasticity, and its disruption is a recurring theme in intellectual disability and autism. Scaffolds link glutamate receptor complexes to nucleation machinery: BAIAP2 couples small GTPase signals to branched filament assembly, CYFIP1 restrains Arp2/3-driven polymerisation as part of the WAVE regulatory complex and also ties into local translational control, CTTNBP2 targets cortactin to spines, and RHOA signalling opposes spine growth. Together they convert synaptic activity into structural change at individual contacts rather than across the whole neuron.

Epithelial tubes are the structural basis of kidney nephrons, airways, glands and blood vessels, and this pathway covers the signals that promote their formation rather than the tube-building itself. Growth factors dominate: GDNF drives ureteric bud outgrowth and branching in kidney development, while EGF, FGF2 and VEGFA stimulate epithelial and endothelial cells to proliferate, migrate and organise into lumenised cords. These cues converge on intracellular signalling, with PI3K catalytic subunits relaying receptor activation to cytoskeletal and survival responses. Transcription factors act upstream and in parallel: SIX1 and SIX4 specify nephrogenic mesenchyme and sustain GDNF expression, and GATA3 is required for ureteric epithelium identity. Matrix components such as MMRN2 contribute to the extracellular environment guiding tube formation. Loss of these inputs causes renal agenesis or hypoplasia, branchio-oto-renal syndrome, and defective vascular and glandular tubulogenesis.

Cargo that reaches endosomes must sometimes be returned to the Golgi rather than degraded, and this set governs how strongly that retrograde endosome-to-Golgi route operates. Recycling of sorting receptors such as the mannose 6-phosphate receptor, of SNAREs, and of bacterial toxins depends on it, so tuning the pathway sets the balance between lysosomal enzyme delivery and lysosomal degradation of membrane proteins. Regulators here act at several levels: a P4-ATPase flippase and an Arf-related machinery including MON2 and its DOPEY partner shape tubule formation at the endosomal membrane, EIPR1 works with the CCC/retriever-associated sorting apparatus, and a deubiquitinase modulates the stability of trafficking components. The presence of LRRK2, RAB29 and parkin links this regulation to Parkinson disease, where mislocalised Rab phosphorylation and impaired membrane traffic converge on endolysosomal dysfunction in dopaminergic neurons.

Programmed death of vascular smooth muscle cells shapes how arteries remodel. Loss of these cells thins the medial layer and destabilises atherosclerotic plaques, contributing to aneurysm formation, plaque rupture and the vessel wall changes of hypertension and restenosis, while controlled apoptosis also prunes excess cells after injury-induced proliferation. The regulators here span several levels: the integrated stress response effector ATF4 and mitochondrial handlers such as MFN2, which restrains smooth muscle proliferation and promotes apoptosis, and the superoxide-detoxifying SOD2, which buffers the oxidative stress that triggers death. Growth and survival input comes from IGF1 signalling, amino acid supply through the transporter SLC7A5, and transcriptional control by PPARG, E2F3 and DNA methylation. A large microRNA component, including miR-21, miR-210 and miR-17, tunes the balance together with the translational repressor PDCD4, placing this decision downstream of redox, metabolic and mechanical cues in the vessel wall.

AMPK is the cell's low-energy sensor, and one route to switching it on runs through calcium: a rise in intracellular Ca2+ activates calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase kinases, which phosphorylate AMPK and so couple calcium signalling to catabolic metabolism, autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. Control over the strength and duration of this CAMKK-to-AMPK relay determines how readily a cell shifts from anabolic to energy-conserving behaviour. The genes here act as modulators rather than core components: huntingtin and LRRK2, both associated with neurodegeneration, and TREM2, the microglial receptor whose variants raise Alzheimer's disease risk and whose signalling supports microglial energy metabolism and survival. PCP4 modulates calmodulin, linking calcium-sensor availability to the upstream kinase step. Set at the wrong level, this cascade leaves neurons and immune cells unable to match fuel use to demand.

The aortic and pulmonary valves that guard the outflow tracts begin as endocardial cushions and must be remodelled into thin, layered leaflets that open and close for a lifetime. Semi-lunar valve development converts cushion mesenchyme into stratified fibrous tissue, and its failure produces bicuspid aortic valve, valve stenosis and outflow tract malformations, among the commonest congenital heart defects. Endocardial cells undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition under BMP and TGF-beta signalling, with SNAI1, SNAI2 and TWIST1 driving the transition and SMAD6 restraining it; Notch components including NOTCH1, JAG1, RBPJ and HEY targets specify valve endocardium, while NFATC1 governs leaflet elongation. Cardiac transcription factors GATA4, GATA5, NKX2-5 and TBX20 set the transcriptional context, SOX9 and ADAMTS proteases with elastin and EMILIN1 build and sculpt the extracellular matrix, and SLIT-ROBO with RhoA-ROCK signalling shapes cell behaviour and leaflet morphology.

Telomerase must be built before it can work, and this pathway covers the assembly of its catalytic and RNA components into a functional holoenzyme. Without it, telomeres shorten with each division, limiting the replicative lifespan of stem and progenitor cells; inherited defects in the assembly machinery cause bone marrow failure and dyskeratosis congenita with pulmonary and liver fibrosis, while excessive activity supports the unlimited proliferation of tumour cells. The RNA subunit is bound and stabilised co-transcriptionally by a dyskerin-containing H/ACA ribonucleoprotein core with NAF1 acting as an assembly factor, and the HSP90 chaperone system together with its co-chaperone p23 folds and loads the reverse transcriptase subunit. An AAA-ATPase contributes to maturation of the complex, and the damage-response kinases ATM and ATR link assembly and recruitment to telomere maintenance and genome surveillance.

regulation of morphogenesis of an epithelium covers the signals that set how far and how fast a sheet of epithelial cells folds, branches, buds or cavitates as an organ takes shape. It is the control layer on top of branching morphogenesis in kidney, lung, mammary gland, salivary gland and tooth, and its miscalibration produces renal agenesis and hypodysplasia, pulmonary hypoplasia and disordered ductal architecture. Most of the action is reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal signalling: FGF, WNT, hedgehog, TGF-beta/BMP and GDNF-RET cues, tuned by dedicated antagonists such as noggin, gremlin and SFRP1, are read out by transcription factors including PAX2, PAX8, GATA3, SIX1/SIX2 and SOX9 that specify branch tips and nephron progenitors. Cell-adhesion and junction components including beta-catenin, p120-catenin and connexin 43 translate these inputs into changes in cell shape, cohesion and epithelial-mesenchymal plasticity. Hormonal and inflammatory mediators modulate the same programmes in adult tissue remodelling.

Epithelial sheets acquire their shape by branching, folding, budding and cavitating, and this pathway covers the signals that set how far and how fast that remodelling goes. It is the control layer behind branching morphogenesis in the kidney, lung, salivary gland and mammary gland, so tuning it up or down changes nephron number, airway and ductal architecture, and the invasive behaviour that tumours reactivate. Much of the regulation is reciprocal crosstalk between epithelium and mesenchyme: FGF, WNT, hedgehog and TGF-beta/BMP ligands act with their antagonists, GREM1 and NOG restraining BMP while SFRP1 dampens WNT, and GDNF with its downstream ETV5 drives ureteric bud outgrowth under SIX1/SIX2 and PAX2 control. Adherens junction components such as CTNNB1 and CTNND1 link these cues to cell adhesion, cleft formation and collective epithelial movement, and steroid receptors add hormonal timing.

Epithelial sheets acquire their shape by folding, branching, budding and tube formation, and these processes must be restrained as well as driven; this pathway covers the braking influences on epithelial morphogenesis. Damping morphogenetic activity sets branch spacing in organs such as lung, kidney and mammary gland, terminates outgrowth once a structure is complete, and keeps epithelia from over-proliferating or dispersing inappropriately. The genes act at several levels: secreted BMP4 and BMP7 and non-canonical WNT5A signalling constrain branching and polarity decisions, the transcriptional repressor TBX2 limits target gene output, SULF1 edits heparan sulfate sulfation and thereby tunes availability of growth factors to their receptors, and p120-catenin (CTNND1) stabilises cadherin-based junctions that resist remodelling. Inflammatory input via TNF and post-transcriptional repression by miR-21 add further restraint. Loss of such control contributes to excess branching, fibrotic remodelling and epithelial tumour progression.

Epithelial sheets acquire their shape by branching, folding, tubulogenesis and lumen formation, and this grouping covers the signals that promote those rearrangements rather than restrain them. The output is organ architecture: ureteric bud branching and nephron induction in the kidney, mammary and lung branching, and duct elongation, so loss or misdirection of these cues gives renal hypodysplasia, absent or duplex ureters, and defective glandular development. Secreted ligands and their receptors drive it — GDNF, BMP4 opposed by the antagonists noggin and gremlin, WNT4 and other WNTs feeding into β-catenin, FGF2, EGF and VEGFA — while transcription factors including PAX2, PAX8, GATA3, LHX1, SIX1 and SOX9 read the signals out as tissue identity and competence to respond. Hedgehog transduction through SMO and TGFβ add further inductive input, linking growth-factor signalling to coordinated changes in epithelial proliferation, polarity and cell shape.

Regulation of aggrephagy controls how aggressively a cell routes misfolded, aggregated protein into autophagosomes for lysosomal destruction. This is the principal defence against toxic inclusions in long-lived cells such as neurones and muscle fibres, and its weakening underlies protein-aggregation diseases including Huntington disease and myofibrillar myopathy. The core machinery here is the chaperone-assisted selective autophagy module, in which HSPB8 and the co-chaperone BAG3 recognise unfolded client protein and hand it toward the microtubule motor adaptor HDAC6, which transports cargo along tubulin tracks to the perinuclear aggresome for engulfment. Casein kinase 2 phosphorylates the sequestosome-type receptors to strengthen ubiquitin binding, while acetylation by KAT5 and cycles of S-acylation and depalmitoylation tune adaptor localisation. Huntingtin itself acts as a scaffold in this selective autophagy route, linking cargo recognition to autophagosome formation.

Aggrephagy is the selective autophagic clearance of protein aggregates, and this is the control layer that sets how fast and how extensively it runs. It matters most in long-lived cells such as neurons and cardiomyocytes, where misfolded protein that escapes degradation accumulates into inclusions and drives neurodegenerative and myopathic disease. Regulation works by assembling aggregates into cargo that autophagy can recognise and move: a co-chaperone complex of BAG3 with the small heat shock protein HSPB8 routes clients away from refolding toward degradation, HDAC6 links ubiquitinated cargo to microtubule-based transport and delivery to the perinuclear aggresome, and kinase and acetyltransferase activities tune the efficiency of capture. Reversible S-acylation, added by a palmitoyltransferase and removed by a thioesterase, provides a further switch, and huntingtin itself participates both as a scaffold and as aggregation-prone cargo.

Aggregated, misfolded proteins that escape the proteasome must be packaged and delivered to lysosomes, and this pathway describes the signals that raise the rate of that selective autophagy of protein aggregates. It protects neurons, cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle from inclusion-body toxicity, and its impairment is linked to myopathies, cardiomyopathy and neurodegenerative disease. A chaperone co-chaperone pair built around the small heat shock protein HSPB8 and the scaffold BAG3 recognises aggregation-prone clients and routes them toward autophagic clearance rather than refolding; casein kinase 2 phosphorylation tunes cargo recognition by autophagy receptors, and huntingtin itself acts as a scaffold in the process whose polyglutamine-expanded form is also a cargo. The pathway therefore connects proteostasis and chaperone activity to lysosomal degradation, with transcriptional and acyltransferase inputs modulating how strongly it is engaged under stress.

Spliceosomal snRNAs such as U1 and U2 are made by RNA polymerase II from specialized promoters, and controlling how much of them is produced sets the cell's capacity for pre-mRNA splicing. Regulation of snRNA transcription by RNA polymerase II is carried out largely by a dedicated elongation complex in which ICE1 scaffolds ICE2 together with an ELL family subunit, directing polymerase activity to snRNA genes rather than to protein-coding ones and concentrating that activity at Cajal bodies. Related control comes from the 7SK small nuclear RNP, where LARP7 stabilizes 7SK and MEPCE caps it, restraining the P-TEFb kinase that licenses productive elongation. Additional factors here include the transcriptional regulator MYOD1 and the zinc-finger protein ZC3H8, linking snRNA output to broader programmes of gene expression and, when disrupted, to defects in RNA processing and neurodevelopment.

Neurotransmitter release depends on the right proteins arriving at, and staying in, the presynaptic terminal, and protein localization to the presynapse is the delivery and retention step that makes a bouton competent to signal. Because axon terminals sit far from the soma, cargo must be carried along microtubules: the kinesin-1 heavy chains KIF5A, KIF5B and KIF5C provide the motor, MAPK8IP3 acts as an adaptor linking cargo to that motor, and MAP1A stabilizes the microtubule tracks they run on. Scaffolding and vesicle-trafficking components such as DLG2 and the small GTPase RAB27B position receptors and secretory vesicles once cargo arrives, while WNT7A signalling through DVL1 instructs presynaptic assembly and clustering at nascent terminals. Disrupted axonal delivery of this kind underlies motor neuron degeneration and spastic paraplegia, and shapes synapse formation and plasticity during development.

Oxidative phosphorylation is not run flat out; its rate is tuned to demand and to oxygen availability, and this is the regulatory layer that raises or damps electron flow through the respiratory chain and the ATP synthesis coupled to it. Control operates on several fronts: a mitochondrially localized cyclin-CDK pair phosphorylates respiratory complex subunits to boost output during cell cycle progression, a hypoxia-induced microRNA and an alternative complex IV-associated subunit reprogramme the chain when oxygen is scarce, and a J-domain co-chaperone acts as a negative regulator of complex I activity. Others, including a coiled-coil-helix protein and a membrane protein influencing inner-membrane architecture and cristae organization, set the structural context in which supercomplexes work. Loss of this tuning shifts cells toward glycolysis or leaves them producing reactive oxygen species, a link reflected in the inclusion of alpha-synuclein and in Parkinsonian phenotypes.

Lymphoid progenitor cell differentiation is the step at which multipotent marrow progenitors commit to the B and T lineages, and the genes here modulate how fast and how far that commitment proceeds — setting the output of the thymus and the supply of naive lymphocytes. Notch signalling is the dominant input: NOTCH1 activation and its HES1/HES5 transcriptional repressor targets push progenitors toward T cell fate while restraining alternative lineages, and the RAS activators SOS1 and SOS2 relay pre-receptor signals that enforce developmental checkpoints. Metabolic and chromatin arms also regulate the transition, with FLCN and its partner FNIP1 coupling nutrient and mTORC1 status to B cell progression, ZBTB1 and ZNHIT1 acting on transcription and chromatin, and NUDT21 and PCID2 linking mRNA 3' processing and export to progenitor survival. Loss of these controls produces lymphopenia, blocked maturation, or leukaemic transformation.

Vascular smooth muscle cells in the arterial wall must persist for decades to maintain vessel tone and structural integrity, and this pathway covers the signals that hold their death programme in check. Survival of these cells preserves the fibrous cap of atherosclerotic plaques and limits medial thinning, while excessive loss contributes to plaque rupture, aneurysm and vessel calcification; conversely, over-suppression of apoptosis favours the neointimal thickening seen after angioplasty and in restenosis. Growth factor input through IGF1 activates pro-survival kinase signalling, the amino acid transporter SLC7A5 supports the nutrient supply and mTOR-linked anabolic state that sustains viability, and the DNA methyltransferase DNMT1 alters the epigenetic setting of death-related genes. Several microRNAs, including miR-21, miR-17 and the hypoxia-induced miR-210, act post-transcriptionally to damp apoptotic effectors, linking cell survival to injury and low-oxygen conditions in the vessel wall.

Vascular smooth muscle cells give arteries their tone and structural integrity, and controlled elimination of these cells shapes vessel remodelling after injury, in aneurysm, and within atherosclerotic plaques, where loss of the medial and cap smooth muscle population thins the fibrous cap and favours rupture. Positive regulation of vascular smooth muscle cell apoptosis covers the signals that raise the rate of that death, drawing together stress-responsive transcription, mitochondrial control and small RNA repression. The integrated stress-response factor ATF4 and the mitochondrial fusion GTPase MFN2 push cells toward mitochondrial apoptosis, PDCD4 and the nuclear receptor PPARG restrain growth and survival signalling, E2F3 links cell cycle drive to death, and the manganese superoxide dismutase SOD2 sets the redox context. Several microRNAs act as post-transcriptional tuners, making this a checkpoint on vascular wall cellularity rather than a single death route.

Where a protein sits determines what it can do, and this collection governs how proteins are delivered to, retained at, or removed from cellular membranes. It sets the surface density of receptors, channels and transporters, and so tunes how strongly a cell responds to hormones, growth factors and neurotransmitters; misrouting underlies receptor signalling defects, altered glucose and ion handling, and synaptic dysfunction. Mechanisms represented include clathrin-mediated endocytosis and adaptor capture, SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion, recycling through Rab11 compartments, and ESCRT-associated sorting. Lipid modification provides another layer: palmitoyl transferases of the ZDHHC family and depalmitoylating enzymes reversibly anchor substrates to bilayers, while PI3K products and kinase cascades recruit effectors such as AKT1 and PDPK1 to the inner face of the plasma membrane. Chaperone-like escorts, including MRAP for melanocortin receptors and MESD for Wnt coreceptors, ensure correct surface delivery, and scaffolds such as DLG1 and ezrin hold cargo in place once it arrives.

Membrane protein composition is set as much by what is kept off the membrane as by what is delivered there, and this pathway covers the processes that block, slow or reverse the arrival of proteins at cellular membranes. It matters for setting receptor and transporter density: WNK kinases restrain surface expression of ion cotransporters and channels and thereby blood pressure and salt handling, MRAP and MRAP2 govern trafficking of melanocortin receptors with consequences for appetite and adrenal signalling, and clathrin-coated pit components including clathrin heavy chain, the AP-2 mu subunit, PICALM, DAB2 and NUMB retrieve cargo by endocytosis rather than letting it accumulate at the plasma membrane. Depalmitoylating enzymes such as LYPLA1 remove the lipid anchors that hold proteins on bilayers, while CSK, phosphatase regulatory subunits and 14-3-3 sigma act as negative regulators of membrane recruitment in signalling. Loss of such restraint produces mislocalized receptors and dysregulated transport.

positive regulation of protein localization to membrane covers the mechanisms that drive or enhance delivery, insertion and retention of proteins at the plasma membrane and other membranes, setting how many receptors, channels and transporters a cell displays at any moment. Surface abundance, not just protein amount, determines signalling strength, ion flux, adhesion and synaptic transmission, so this control underlies insulin-responsive transport, receptor tyrosine kinase output, and excitation-contraction coupling. The machinery spans vesicle traffic and recycling (RAB11A, ARF6, AP2B1, syntaxins, KIF5B), scaffolds and cytoskeletal anchors (EZR, DLG1, SPTBN1, PDZK1, RACK1), lipid and kinase signalling through PI3K, AKT1, PDPK1 and PKC isoforms, chaperones and folding checkpoints such as MESD, and palmitoylating ZDHHC enzymes that tether cargo to bilayers. Failure lowers surface receptor density, and several members link this control to muscular dystrophy, neurodegeneration and tumour signalling.

Many receptors, channels and transporters only work once they reach the plasma membrane, and this pathway covers the processes that promote and accelerate their delivery to and retention in membranes. It determines how strongly cells respond to growth factors and neurotransmitters, how much calcium enters muscle, and how adhesion complexes are built, so its failure blunts signalling and mislocalises channels. The genes span several routes to the same end: vesicular trafficking and tethering through Rab and Arf GTPases, adaptor and SNARE proteins; cytoskeletal and scaffold anchoring by ezrin, spectrin and PDZ scaffolds; lipid and phosphoinositide signalling via PI3K, PDK1, AKT and protein kinase C isoforms; and palmitoylation by ZDHHC acyltransferases, which tethers substrates to the bilayer. Extracellular cues including WNT, laminins, integrins and receptor tyrosine kinases feed in, linking surface protein composition to adhesion, excitability and cell polarity.

Regulation of motile cilium assembly controls how readily a cell builds the beating cilia that drive fluid movement — clearing mucus from airways, circulating cerebrospinal fluid, propelling sperm, and establishing left-right asymmetry at the embryonic node. When this control fails, cilia are absent, short or immotile, producing the chronic sinopulmonary infection, hydrocephalus, infertility and situs defects characteristic of ciliary dyskinesia. The genes act at distinct stages: cytoplasmic assembly factors chaperone dynein arm subunits before they are loaded onto the axoneme, while Rab GTPases direct the vesicular traffic that delivers membrane and cargo to the growing ciliary base. LRRK2 kinase activity, acting on Rab substrates, restrains ciliogenesis, linking this regulation to Parkinson disease-associated signalling and to broader questions of how centrosome-derived structures are licensed to extend.

Motile cilia beat to move fluid and mucus across epithelial surfaces, drive sperm, and set left-right body asymmetry, and this pathway covers the controls that determine whether and how efficiently such cilia are built. Failure of motile ciliogenesis produces the picture of primary ciliary dyskinesia: chronic airway infection, hydrocephalus, situs inversus and infertility. The genes here act on membrane traffic and cytoplasmic assembly rather than on the axoneme itself. LRRK2 kinase signalling through RAB10 and RAB29 restrains ciliogenesis, a link that connects Parkinson's disease genetics to cilium formation, while ZMYND10 works in the cytoplasm to stabilise and assemble dynein arm complexes before they are imported into the growing axoneme. KATNIP contributes to trafficking and centriole-associated steps of cilium formation, placing this biology at the junction of vesicular transport and cytoskeletal assembly.

Centrosomes and related microtubule organizing centres work only if the right proteins are delivered to them, and this pathway covers the targeting and retention of cargo at the centriole, pericentriolar material and basal body. It determines whether a cell can build a bipolar spindle, nucleate and anchor microtubules, and assemble a cilium; failures show up as mitotic errors, microcephaly and ciliopathies. Much of the traffic runs through pericentriolar satellites, where PCM1 and CEP131 act as docking platforms serviced by dynein-associated adaptors such as HOOK3 and DCTN2, while RAB11A and its effector RAB11FIP3 bring in recycling-endosome-derived membrane. Scaffolds including CEP192, CEP250 and CEP350 recruit assembly and licensing factors, and kinases such as AURKA, CSNK1D, MARK4 and GSK3B time these recruitments, linking centrosome composition to cell cycle progression, centriole duplication and cell polarity.</description

Most human cells build a single non-motile, or primary, cilium from the mother centriole, and this assembly programme is how that antenna is made. The organelle concentrates receptors for Hedgehog, Wnt and other cues, and it is the light-sensing outer segment of photoreceptors, so failure of assembly produces the ciliopathies: retinal degeneration, cystic kidney disease, polydactyly, obesity and cerebellar malformation. Construction begins with centriolar and distal appendage proteins that dock the basal body, followed by transition zone gatekeeping that controls which membrane and soluble proteins enter the compartment. Intraflagellar transport complexes with the dynein-2 motor then move cargo along the axoneme, while a chaperonin-like octamer sorts membrane proteins into the cilium and small GTPase regulators including ARL13B govern ciliary signalling. Planar polarity and kinase components couple axoneme extension to tissue-level orientation.

Fertilization requires more than the meeting of gamete and egg: sperm must mature correctly, move through the female tract, bind and penetrate the zona pellucida, and fuse with the oocyte, and the genes here act to raise the efficiency with which those steps succeed. Their loss typically produces sterile or subfertile animals with structurally normal-looking gametes, which makes this biology a common explanation for unexplained infertility rather than for gross gonadal failure. The members span sperm flagellar and acrosomal components that set motility and the ability to traverse the egg coat, a serine protease family member needed for sperm migration into the oviduct and zona binding, a membrane protein acting in the reproductive tract, and a meiotic histone methyltransferase that directs recombination hotspot placement during germ cell development, tying gamete quality to successful conception.

Macrophages only work where they are needed, and this is the programme that gets them there — the directed movement of macrophages out of blood or tissue reservoirs toward sites of infection, injury, or tissue remodelling. It underlies inflammatory infiltration, wound healing, atherosclerotic plaque growth and tumour-associated macrophage accumulation, and its failure leaves infections uncleared and debris uncleaved. Chemoattractant receptors read the local signal: CCR2 responds to CCL2, CX3CR1 to fractalkine, C5AR1 and C3AR1 to complement fragments, and CSF1R to CSF1 or IL34, which also sustain macrophage survival and identity. Downstream, focal adhesion kinases PTK2 and PTK2B and ERK signalling couple receptor engagement to cytoskeletal remodelling and adhesion turnover, while matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP2 and MMP14 clear a path through extracellular matrix. Restraining signals through CD200R1 and purinergic and calcium-permeable channels tune how far and how fast cells travel.

Macrophages must be told where to go: to a wound, an infected tissue, a plaque, or a tumour, and the control of that movement is what this pathway describes. Chemoattractants set the direction — CCL2, CCL3 and CCL5 acting on classic chemokine receptors, fractalkine signalling through CX3CR1 for patrolling and tissue residency, complement fragments acting via C3AR1 and C5AR1 during inflammation, and chemerin through CMKLR1. Growth factor input from CSF1 and IL34 through CSF1R couples survival and differentiation to motility, while MIF and midkine act as additional migratory cues. Inside the cell, focal adhesion kinases PTK2 and PTK2B and ERK signalling translate receptor engagement into adhesion turnover and cytoskeletal advance, with MMP14 clearing matrix ahead of the cell. Restraining signals such as CD200–CD200R1 and purinergic sensing tune how far and how fast recruitment goes; imbalance drives chronic inflammatory and neuroinflammatory disease.

Macrophages must be held in place as well as recruited, and this collection covers the braking signals that stop, slow or restrain macrophage migration. Restraint matters because unchecked myeloid infiltration drives tissue damage in atherosclerosis, arthritis and chronic inflammation, while resolution of inflammation requires that recruited macrophages cease moving and adopt a local, reparative role. Inhibitory receptor engagement is one arm: CD200 on tissue cells binds CD200R1 on myeloid cells to damp their activation and motility. Secreted and extracellular contributions include the cytokine MIF and its relative DDT, complement C5-derived signals, the matrix glycoprotein EMILIN1 and a matrix metalloproteinase, together shaping how cells read chemotactic and adhesive cues. Additional control comes from microRNA-mediated repression of migratory transcripts, placing this biology at the interface of innate immune signalling, cell adhesion and inflammatory resolution.

Macrophages must be recruited from blood and moved through tissue to reach sites of infection, injury or dying cells, and this pathway covers the signals that increase that movement. Chemoattractants act through G protein-coupled receptors: complement fragments via C3AR1 and C5AR1, chemokines such as CCL2, CCL3 and CCL5, fractalkine, and chemerin acting on CMKLR1. Growth factor input from CSF1 and IL34 through their shared receptor CSF1R both sustains macrophage survival and directs migration, while nucleotide sensing through P2RY12 and P2RX4 and mechanical or osmotic cues through TRPV4 add positional information. Downstream, ERK signalling and focal adhesion kinase remodel adhesion and the actin cytoskeleton, and MMP14 clears a path through matrix. Enhanced recruitment drives inflammatory disease, atherosclerotic plaque growth and the accumulation of tumour-associated macrophages, whereas microglial receptors such as TREM2 tie the same machinery to neurodegeneration.

Newly made proteins destined for the secretory pathway must be delivered to the endoplasmic reticulum at the right moment, and this regulatory layer tunes how much and how fast that targeting happens. It matters because mistargeting leaves secreted and membrane proteins stranded in the cytosol, where they aggregate or are degraded, and because ER shape and capacity must match the load. The nascent polypeptide-associated complex subunits act at the ribosomal exit tunnel, screening emerging chains and influencing whether a translating ribosome engages ER targeting machinery rather than a cytosolic fate. Other members shape the membrane itself and its associated quality control, including a reticulon that stabilises tubular ER curvature and a UFMylation pathway component linked to ribosome quality control at the ER surface, while kinase signalling adjusts these steps to growth and stress conditions.

How often a growing vessel splits determines the density of a capillary bed, and regulation of blood vessel branching sets that frequency during development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation. Too little branching leaves tissue hypoxic; too much yields the leaky, disorganised networks seen in tumours and in proliferative retinopathy. The genes here act at several levels: secreted factors such as VEGFA, FGF2 and midkine provide the pro-angiogenic drive sensed by endothelial tip cells, while FKBPL acts as an anti-angiogenic brake on that drive. Junctional and signalling components including beta-catenin and p120-catenin couple endothelial cell-cell adhesion to the decision to sprout, and ABL1 kinase and the deacetylase SIRT6 modulate the transcriptional and cytoskeletal response. The pathway therefore links growth factor availability and adhesion state to vascular network architecture rather than to vessel formation as such.

Vascular networks expand not by lengthening existing tubes alone but by sprouting new branches, and this pathway covers the signals that raise the frequency and extent of that branching. It shapes how densely a growing or healing tissue is perfused, and it is co-opted by tumours to build their own blood supply. Secreted growth factors such as VEGFA, FGF2 and the heparin-binding factor midkine act on endothelial cells to trigger tip-cell selection, migration and proliferation, while intracellular players relay and modulate the response: the kinase ABL1 in cytoskeletal and adhesion signalling, beta-catenin coupling cadherin junctions to transcription, and the sirtuin SIRT6 acting through chromatin to tune endothelial gene expression. Too little branching leaves tissue ischaemic; too much contributes to tumour growth and proliferative retinopathy, making these regulators targets for both pro- and anti-angiogenic therapy.

negative regulation of vascular endothelial cell proliferation is the braking side of blood vessel growth: the set of signals that hold endothelial cells quiescent so that vessels stop expanding once a bed is adequately perfused. It matters because unrestrained endothelial division drives tumour angiogenesis, proliferative retinopathy and intimal lesions, while excessive braking impairs wound healing and collateral vessel formation. Restraint is imposed at several levels. A soluble decoy receptor for VEGF sequesters the principal endothelial mitogen, a basement membrane collagen fragment (tumstatin) signals anti-proliferative arrest from the matrix, and transcriptional regulators such as MEF2C and PPARG tune the endothelial growth program. A large complement of microRNAs, including the endothelial-enriched miR-126 and miR-34a, miR-15b and the miR-424/503 cluster, damp growth factor and cell cycle transcripts post-transcriptionally, coupling vessel quiescence to inflammatory and metabolic cues.

Blood vessel growth has to be switched off as well as on, and this is the restraining arm: processes that slow or stop proliferation of vascular endothelial cells so that vessel density matches tissue need. Losing this brake permits the excess endothelial expansion seen in tumour angiogenesis, diabetic retinopathy and vascular malformation, while excessive braking impairs wound healing and collateral vessel formation. The effectors here are largely post-transcriptional: a large family of microRNAs, including miR-34a, miR-15b, miR-424 and miR-503, damps expression of growth-promoting transcripts in endothelium. Protein components act on the same output by other means, notably a soluble-capable VEGF receptor (FLT1) that sequesters VEGF-A, the collagen IV alpha-3 chain whose tumstatin fragment is antiangiogenic, and the transcriptional regulators MEF2C and PPARG. Chemokine signalling via CCL2 links inflammatory cues into the same control of endothelial quiescence.

New blood vessels require endothelial cells to divide, and this pathway covers the signals that drive that division upward. It underlies angiogenesis during development, wound healing and exercise-induced vascular remodelling, and its excessive activation feeds tumour vascularisation, diabetic retinopathy and other neovascular disease, while insufficient drive limits collateral growth in ischaemic tissue. Growth factors acting through receptor tyrosine kinases, exemplified by FGF2 with FGFR1, engage phospholipase C gamma and the PDPK1-AKT axis to license S-phase entry, with STAT3 and SP1 converting those inputs into transcription of proliferative genes. Secreted and matrix-associated cues such as apelin, midkine and extracellular HMGB1, plus the sheddase ADAM17 and the ghrelin receptor, broaden the range of stimuli. A large set of microRNAs tunes the response post-transcriptionally, and SIRT6 links endothelial growth to metabolic and chromatin state.

regulation of blood-brain barrier permeability controls how tightly the cerebral vasculature seals the brain off from the circulation, and how that seal is loosened or reinforced. The barrier keeps plasma proteins, ions and immune cells out of neural tissue while permitting selective transport of nutrients; when regulation fails, vasogenic oedema, haemorrhagic transformation after stroke, and inflammatory infiltration in multiple sclerosis follow. The genes span both sides of the balance. Occludin and the zonula occludens scaffolds build and remodel the endothelial tight junctions themselves, while angiopoietin-1 signalling from pericytes stabilises them and VEGFA, acting on the same endothelium, drives permeability and angiogenic sprouting. A sulfonylurea receptor subunit links ion and water flux across the barrier to swelling after injury, and ZEB2 acts transcriptionally on endothelial junctional identity. This is barrier physiology as an actively tuned property rather than a fixed structure.

The brain keeps its extracellular environment far more tightly controlled than the rest of the body, and regulation of blood-brain barrier permeability is how that seal is tuned — determining which ions, metabolites, macromolecules and immune cells reach neural tissue. Loosening it underlies vasogenic oedema after stroke, trauma, tumours and neuroinflammation, while an intact barrier also blocks most therapeutic drugs from the CNS. Control acts largely at endothelial tight junctions, where occludin and the zonula occludens scaffolds ZO-1, ZO-2 and ZO-3 link junctional strands to the actin cytoskeleton. Opposing secreted signals set the state: angiopoietin-1 from pericytes and astrocytes stabilises junctions, whereas VEGFA drives permeability and leakage. Transcriptional input from ZEB2 can shift endothelial cells toward a mesenchymal, leakier phenotype, and endocytic and ion-transport components including SH3GL2 and the sulfonylurea receptor subunit ABCC8 modulate junction turnover and swelling.

The blood-brain barrier restricts what reaches neural tissue, and loosening it is a regulated event rather than simple damage: controlled increases in permeability allow passage of macromolecules, ions and immune mediators into the brain, and also govern how drugs gain access. The genes here are the core tight-junction machinery of brain microvascular endothelium — occludin as the transmembrane sealing protein, and the ZO family scaffolds ZO-1, ZO-2 and ZO-3 that anchor junctional strands to the actin cytoskeleton — together with angiopoietin-1, a Tie2 ligand from pericytes and astrocytes that signals endothelial junction stability. Modifying, redistributing or downregulating these junctional components opens the paracellular route. Excessive or sustained opening underlies vasogenic oedema, leukocyte infiltration and the barrier breakdown seen in stroke, multiple sclerosis, and neuroinflammation, linking this biology to cerebrovascular integrity and neurovascular unit function.

Regulation of protein localization to chromatin controls which proteins are loaded onto, retained at, or evicted from chromatin, and thereby sets where transcription, DNA repair and chromosome segregation actually occur. Cells depend on it to concentrate repair factors at damage sites, to license transcription elongation, and to clear chromatin-bound complexes once their job is done; failure produces stalled repair, persistent replication stress and mitotic errors. The genes act through several levers: kinases such as AURKB, CDK2, CDK9, VRK1 and nuclear JAK2 phosphorylate histones and chromatin clients to promote or block their binding; SUMO ligation by PIAS4 with the SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4 marks bound factors for extraction by the VCP segregase, opposed by the deubiquitinase VCPIP1; and SETD2, SIRT6 and the lineage factor SPI1 shape the histone landscape that recruits readers in the first place.

Whether a regulatory protein reaches chromatin, and how long it stays, determines which genes are transcribed, whether replication forks restart and whether damaged DNA is repaired, so the loading and eviction of chromatin-bound factors is itself a controlled step. The genes here modulate that recruitment through several routes: kinases such as AURKB, CDK2, CDK9, VRK1 and JAK2 phosphorylate histones and chromatin-associated substrates to create or destroy binding sites; SUMO ligase PIAS4 and the SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligase RNF4 mark factors for extraction, while the VCP ATPase and its deubiquitinase partner VCPIP1 physically remove ubiquitylated proteins from chromatin. SETD2 deposits H3K36 methylation read by downstream effectors, SIRT6 deacetylates histones to close regions off, and SPI1 acts as a lineage transcription factor whose own access is regulated. Failures of this layer distort transcription programmes and genome stability, and contribute to tumorigenesis.

Arteries are not simply larger vessels; they acquire a distinct identity, wall structure and branching pattern during development, and this regulatory programme sets how far and how fast that shaping proceeds. It matters for coronary and aortic patterning, for arteriovenous distinction, and for the remodelling that follows ischaemia or hypertension, with failure producing malformations in which arterial and venous beds are improperly connected. Notch signalling together with the ephrin ligand EFNB2 specifies arterial endothelium, endothelin-1 acts on vascular tone and smooth muscle recruitment, and NFATC3 and AKT3 relay calcium and phosphoinositide signals into endothelial gene expression. Several microRNAs tune the same outputs post-transcriptionally, damping or sustaining pro-arterial signalling. The pathway sits at the interface of endothelial specification, mural cell investment and vessel calibre control.

Arteries acquire their identity and shape during development, and this is the set of activities that push artery morphogenesis forward — driving arterial rather than venous specification of endothelium, sprouting, lumen formation and the recruitment of a muscular wall. Without such positive input, the arterial tree is malformed or fails to remodel, a route to congenital cardiovascular defects and to impaired collateral growth after ischaemia. Notch signalling with its arterial ligand ephrin-B2 marks and maintains arterial endothelium; endothelin-1 acts on vascular tone and on smooth muscle and neural crest contributions to the great vessels; AKT3 transmits growth-factor and shear-stress cues to endothelial survival and proliferation; calcineurin-responsive NFATC3 couples those cues to transcription. Midkine and reticulon-4 add growth-promoting and membrane-shaping influences. The processes involved connect angiogenesis, arteriovenous patterning and vessel wall assembly.

Cytosolic calcium rises are one of the most widely used cellular signals, and this pathway covers the control of how much calcium crosses the plasma membrane from outside the cell. Tuning that entry sets the gain of downstream responses ranging from lymphocyte activation and neuronal excitability to cardiac and smooth muscle behaviour, and misregulation produces either signalling failure or calcium overload and cell death. The members act at several levels: ligand-gated purinergic channels and a metabotropic glutamate receptor at retinal synapses shape the entry step itself, a calcium-activated potassium channel and a scaffolding protein that anchors kinases and phosphatases to channel complexes provide feedback on membrane potential and channel state, and the calcineurin catalytic and regulatory subunits decode the resulting calcium signal while feeding back on influx. Kinase activity, prion protein and microRNAs add further modulatory input.

Raising the rate at which calcium enters a cell from outside is one of the fastest ways to change its behaviour, since the resulting rise in cytosolic calcium triggers secretion, contraction, gene expression and lymphocyte activation. This pathway covers the processes that promote such calcium import across the plasma membrane, and it matters because sustained calcium entry, not just a transient spike, is what sustains downstream responses. Mechanistically it includes ligand-gated entry routes such as the ATP-gated P2X channels, a scaffolding protein that anchors kinases and phosphatases next to channels at the membrane, a metabotropic glutamate receptor of the retinal ON-bipolar pathway, and all subunits of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin, which both responds to calcium and feeds back to enhance further entry, notably in immune cell activation.

Whether a protein reaches an endosome determines whether a receptor is recycled to the surface, handed on for degradation, or held where it can keep signalling, so controlling protein localization to endosomes shapes how long and how strongly cells respond to growth factors. The genes here act at several points: acyl-protein thioesterases of the ABHD17 family remove palmitate from membrane-anchored substrates and release them from the plasma membrane, ubiquitin-pathway components such as ANKRD13A and DTX3L mark cargo for sorting, and the FERM-domain proteins ezrin, radixin, moesin and the tumour suppressor merlin, together with ROCK2, link membranes to the actin cortex where sorting compartments form. Ligands such as EGF and VEGFA drive receptor internalisation, while SORL1 routes cargo between endosomes and the Golgi. Failures in this trafficking control contribute to sustained oncogenic signalling and to amyloid handling in neurons.

Lysosomes must be built, sized, positioned and renewed in proportion to a cell's degradative load, and this regulatory layer sets how much lysosomal capacity a cell maintains. It matters because too little leads to storage of undigested material and neurodegeneration, while unchecked expansion supports tumour cell growth and invasion. Nutrient status is read at the lysosomal surface by mTOR together with the folliculin complex, which controls whether TFEB enters the nucleus and switches on the transcriptional programme for lysosome and autophagosome biogenesis; calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation, triggered by calcium released through the lysosomal channel MCOLN1, reinforces that switch. Other members act on membrane composition and trafficking, including SCARB2, which delivers glucocerebrosidase to the lumen, and progranulin and TMEM106B, whose loss causes lysosomal dysfunction in frontotemporal dementia. Autophagy initiation and innate immune restriction of intracellular pathogens draw on the same machinery.

Cells in mechanically stressed tissue such as skeletal muscle routinely tear their plasma membrane, and survival depends on resealing the wound within seconds; this pathway modulates how fast and how completely that repair proceeds. Calcium entering through the lesion is the trigger, and the genes here read that signal and marshal membrane and cytoskeleton to the site: annexin A2 with its S100A10 partner binds calcium and phospholipid and nucleates repair, the large scaffold AHNAK organises the subsarcolemmal complex, myosin-9 supplies contractile force to draw wound edges together, and a Rab GTPase with a synaptotagmin-like effector directs vesicles to the damaged surface for patching. Caspase-7 activity links wound responses to apoptotic decisions when damage exceeds what can be sealed. Impaired regulation of this process underlies muscular dystrophies characterised by defective sarcolemmal resealing.

Lipid droplets are the cell's neutral lipid stores, and their disassembly releases fatty acids for oxidation, membrane synthesis and signalling when energy is demanded. Breakdown of the droplet determines how much substrate reaches mitochondria during fasting or exercise, and defective mobilisation contributes to hepatic steatosis, ectopic lipid accumulation and insulin resistance, while unrestrained release drives lipotoxicity. Perilipins PLIN2 and PLIN3 coat the droplet surface and govern access of lipases to the triglyceride core; PNPLA2 (ATGL) catalyses the initial hydrolysis of triacylglycerol to diacylglycerol and free fatty acid. The AMP-activated kinase catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 couple droplet turnover to cellular energy charge, and additional regulation comes through choline kinase-dependent phospholipid supply for the droplet monolayer and acetyltransferase-mediated transcriptional control of the lipolytic programme.

Inhibitory synapses set the balance between excitation and inhibition in neural circuits, and this pathway governs how many of them form and how quickly. The genes act at the point of contact between a GABAergic or glycinergic terminal and its target, biasing nascent contacts toward an inhibitory identity rather than an excitatory one. Secreted and transmembrane organizers bridge the cleft and recruit postsynaptic scaffolds: LHFPL4 is required to cluster gephyrin and GABA-A receptors at inhibitory postsynaptic sites, calsyntenin-3 and cerebellin family ligands engage presynaptic adhesion partners, and semaphorin signalling through plexin receptors tunes contact formation. Shifting this regulation changes inhibitory tone, and loss of inhibitory synapse number is associated with epilepsy and with neurodevelopmental disorders in which circuits become hyperexcitable. The biology sits within synaptogenesis and activity-dependent circuit refinement.

Membranes must hold their contents in, and this pathway covers the processes that restrain permeability rather than increase it. Most of the genes act at the mitochondrion, where keeping the outer membrane sealed decides whether a cell lives: anti-apoptotic BCL2L1 and ARC/NOL3 oppose pore formation by the effectors BAK1 and BOK, so that cytochrome c and other apoptogenic factors stay sequestered and caspase activation never begins. Related members influence permeability transition and matrix solute exchange through the adenine nucleotide translocase SLC25A5, while BNIP3 links the same membrane to hypoxic stress and mitophagy. Antioxidant and stress components such as GCLC and HSPA1A raise the threshold for permeabilization, and endothelial factors RASIP1 and HEG1 extend the theme to vascular barrier integrity. Loss of this restraint drives ischaemic and degenerative cell death; its excess allows tumour cells to resist apoptosis.

positive regulation of membrane permeability describes processes that increase the passage of ions and proteins across membranes, and in this gene collection it is dominated by permeabilization of the mitochondrial outer membrane, the committed step of intrinsic apoptosis. When BAX, BAK1 and BOK oligomerize in the outer membrane, cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins escape into the cytosol and drive caspase activation; anti-apoptotic relatives such as BCL2L1 restrain them, while BH3-only proteins including BID and BCL2L11 tip the balance. Related components govern the permeability transition pore and its sensitizers, notably PPIF, VDAC2 and SPG7, linking calcium overload and oxidative stress to necrotic death. Also represented are BNIP3 and BNIP3L, which couple membrane permeabilization to mitophagy, plus kinases, microRNAs and transcription factors that set the threshold. Loss of control here underlies neurodegeneration, ischemic injury and tumour cell survival.

Increasing the passage of molecules across a membrane is, in this collection of genes, overwhelmingly about the mitochondrion: the controlled loss of outer membrane integrity that commits a cell to apoptosis, and the permeability transition of the inner membrane that collapses the proton gradient. BAX, BAK1 and BOK form the pores that release cytochrome c, BID and BCL2L11 activate them, BCL2L1 restrains them, and PPIF (cyclophilin D) sensitises the permeability transition pore, with VDAC2 and adenine nucleotide translocase at the interface. BNIP3 and BNIP3L couple the same membrane events to hypoxia and mitophagy, while GSK3 kinases, ATF2 and several miR-29 family members regulate the balance transcriptionally and post-transcriptionally. The outcome determines whether a damaged or stressed cell survives, and its failure underlies both tumour cell resistance to death and excess neuronal loss in ischaemia and neurodegeneration.

Positioning proteins and membrane-bound cargo in the perinuclear region of the cytoplasm concentrates degradative and sorting compartments around the centrosome and nucleus, which is how cells build aggresomes, cluster late endosomes and lysosomes, and keep recycling and autophagic traffic organized rather than dispersed at the cell periphery. Much of the work here is done by the FHF complex, in which AKTIP together with FHIP subunits and the HOOK proteins bridges cargo to microtubule motors so that vesicles can be drawn inward along microtubules toward the minus end. An ER-anchored ubiquitin ligase, RNF26, marks the perinuclear zone where endosomal adaptors dock, and the ubiquitin-binding receptor SQSTM1 gathers polyubiquitinated and misfolded protein into inclusions delivered for autophagic clearance. Loss of this inward positioning scatters organelles, slows cargo degradation, and impairs the sequestration of aggregation-prone protein implicated in neurodegeneration.

Membrane proteins delivered into endosomes are not necessarily destined for degradation; many are sorted back out and returned to the cell surface, and this pathway covers the control of that recycling step. How fast and how much cargo is returned sets the surface abundance of receptors, channels and transporters, so it determines the strength of signalling and of synaptic transmission rather than simply moving vesicles around. In neurons these regulators govern trafficking of glutamate receptors during synaptic plasticity: a scaffolding anchor tethers kinase and phosphatase activity near the membrane, a GTPase-activating protein shapes the endosomal tubules from which cargo departs, and a palmitoyl acyltransferase modifies recycling machinery to direct its membrane association. Other members link the process to copper handling and to sorting complexes that decide whether cargo returns or is retained intracellularly.

Mesoderm gives rise to heart, blood, bone, muscle and kidney, and the rate and extent to which progenitors commit to that fate must be tuned rather than simply switched on. Regulation of mesodermal cell differentiation sets this balance during gastrulation and in stem cell models of it, determining how many cells leave the pluripotent pool and when. The inputs are the classical patterning signals: WNT3A drives mesoderm induction while secreted antagonists DKK1 and SFRP2 restrain it, BMP receptor signalling through BMPR1A and FGF input via FGFR1 add graded positional information, and the transcription factor MESP1 marks and specifies nascent cardiovascular mesoderm. Gap junction communication through connexin 43 and post-transcriptional damping by microRNAs provide further control. Misregulation distorts germ layer proportions and underlies congenital heart and skeletal malformation.

The anaphase-promoting complex is the ubiquitin ligase that triggers chromosome separation and exit from mitosis by marking securin, cyclins and other substrates for proteasomal destruction; this pathway covers the inputs that decide when and how strongly it acts. Timing here sets the irreversibility of mitotic transitions, and misregulation produces premature separation, missegregated chromosomes and aneuploidy. Control runs largely through the two interchangeable substrate-specifying activators, CDC20 during mitosis and FZR1 (Cdh1) in late mitosis and G1, whose binding and availability determine which proteins are degraded and when. Mitotic kinases impose the schedule: PLK1 phosphorylation promotes activation, while CDK2-cyclin phosphorylation of the Cdh1 activator restrains the ligase as cells commit to a new S phase. AKT1 links growth and survival signalling to this degradation machinery, tying proliferative cues to cell cycle progression.

Developing circuits form more synapses than they keep, and the control of synapse pruning sets how many are eliminated and how fast, converting exuberant early connectivity into refined, functional circuits. Too little elimination leaves immature, overconnected networks implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders; too much, or reactivation of the same machinery in adulthood, contributes to synapse loss in neurodegeneration. The genes here span the recognition and execution sides of that process: secreted C1QL1 tags synapses for complement-dependent removal, TREM2 licenses microglial engulfment of tagged contacts, adhesion and guidance receptors such as ADGRB3, EPHA4, PLXNC1 and integrin β1 read local cues that mark a connection for retention or retraction, and NGEF couples Eph signalling to Rho-family control of the actin cytoskeleton. SARM1 links the same decisions to axonal degeneration, tying synapse elimination to neuron-intrinsic self-destruction programmes.

Synapses are not simply added as fast as possible; their number, size and placement are held in check by signals that restrain or dismantle them, and this negative regulation of synapse organization is what keeps circuits selective rather than saturated. Excessive connectivity impairs pruning and refinement during development, while inappropriate loss of restraint in the adult brain contributes to synapse dysfunction in degeneration. The genes here act largely as extracellular cues and their receptors: secreted Slit acting through Robo repels and limits contacts, Dkk1 antagonizes Wnt signalling at the synapse, non-canonical Wnt5a and ephrin receptor EphA7 shape spine remodelling, and adhesion molecules such as NEGR1 and calsyntenin set limits on synaptic adhesion. Apolipoprotein E and TLR2 tie the process to glial and lipid-dependent control of synapse elimination, with transcriptional input from NeuroD2 and NFATc4.

At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition a cell must release the cohesion holding sister chromatids together and pull them apart, and this is the set of activities that push that step forward. Getting it right gives each daughter a complete genome; getting it wrong produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and the chromosomal instability typical of tumours. Several arms converge: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator CDC20 and the E2 enzyme UBE2C ubiquitinates securin and cyclin B, freeing separase (ESPL1) to cleave cohesin; the chromosomal passenger complex of Aurora B, INCENP, survivin and borealin corrects faulty kinetochore attachments; condensin subunits compact chromatids so they can be resolved; and SKA components stabilise the kinetochore-microtubule interface. Relief of spindle assembly checkpoint restraint, including MAD2L1BP acting on MAD1/MAD2 signalling, is what licenses the transition to proceed.}

positive regulation of chromosome condensation describes the drive toward compacting interphase chromatin into the short, rigid mitotic chromosomes that can be gripped by the spindle and pulled apart intact. Without it chromosomes stay diffuse and tangled, sister chromatids fail to resolve, and anaphase produces bridges, breaks and aneuploid daughter cells. The genes are the condensin machinery: the SMC2-SMC4 ATPase heterodimer that forms the core motor, together with the kleisin and HEAT-repeat subunits that distinguish condensin I (NCAPD2, NCAPG, NCAPH) from condensin II (NCAPD3, NCAPG2, NCAPH2). These complexes extrude chromatin loops in an ATP-dependent manner, with condensin II acting early in the nucleus and condensin I gaining access after nuclear envelope breakdown. The same activity contributes to chromosome territory organisation, rDNA and repeat stability, and mitotic chromosome mechanical stiffness during cell division.

Before a cell can segregate its chromosomes, the long interphase chromatin fibres must be compacted into short, stiff, individualized bodies; this is the machinery that drives and promotes that compaction. The genes here are the subunits of the two condensin complexes: a shared SMC2-SMC4 ATPase heterodimer paired with either the kleisin and HEAT-repeat subunits of condensin I or their condensin II counterparts. Condensin II acts earlier and more nuclear, condensin I after nuclear envelope breakdown, together building mitotic chromosome shape by ATP-dependent DNA loop extrusion. Positive regulation of chromosome condensation therefore feeds directly into mitotic chromosome architecture, sister chromatid resolution and faithful segregation, and it also contributes to interphase genome organization. Loss or mutation of condensin subunits produces tangled, undercondensed chromosomes, anaphase bridges, micronuclei and aneuploidy, and in humans causes microcephaly.

Before a cell can divide it must build a bipolar microtubule spindle, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote and accelerate that assembly. Its output determines whether chromosomes are captured and segregated accurately, so weakness here produces monopolar or disorganised spindles, missegregation and aneuploidy, and in the developing brain depleted progenitor pools. Several members act at the centriole and centrosome, where the cartwheel components SASS6 and STIL and the centriolar protein CPAP (CENPJ) license procentriole formation and set centriole length, mutations in which cause microcephaly. Others work at the poles and on microtubules themselves: NUMA1 with cytoplasmic dynein heavy chain tethers and focuses minus ends, GPSM2 links cortical cues to spindle orientation, and SPAG5 (astrin) stabilises kinetochore-microtubule attachments. Together they connect centriole duplication, motor-driven pole organisation and cortical positioning to mitotic spindle formation.

regulation of 3'-UTR-mediated mRNA stabilization controls how long a transcript survives once it has been made, by tuning the RNA-binding proteins and modifying enzymes that act on 3' untranslated regions. This is post-transcriptional gene regulation at the level of message lifetime, and it sets the amplitude and duration of inflammatory cytokine output, neuronal mRNA availability, and muscle differentiation programmes. The genes represent the opposing arms of that control: stabilizing factors such as ARID5A, the neuronal HuD protein, QKI and RBM24 bind AU-rich or other 3'-UTR elements to protect transcripts, ZFP36 recruits deadenylation and decay machinery to destroy them, and the TENT4 non-canonical poly(A) polymerases add mixed adenosine-guanosine tails that block deadenylase progression. LARP4B links poly(A) status to translation, while METTL16-dependent methylation feeds m6A signals into the same decisions. Loss of this balance drives sustained cytokine expression and autoimmune or inflammatory pathology.

Whether a transcript survives or is destroyed is decided largely in its 3' untranslated region, and this pathway covers the control of that decision by RNA-binding proteins and RNA-modifying enzymes that either protect messages or license their decay. Setting mRNA half-life this way tunes inflammatory cytokine output, neuronal mRNA transport and translation, and muscle differentiation programmes without any change in transcription. Members act in opposing directions: ARID5A stabilises cytokine transcripts, while ZFP36 binds AU-rich elements in the same messages and hands them to deadenylases, and the terminal nucleotidyltransferases TENT4A and TENT4B add mixed poly(A) tails that resist deadenylation. QKI, RBM24, ELAVL4 and LARP4B bind specific 3'-UTR elements to extend transcript lifetime, coupling post-transcriptional control to cell identity. Loss of this restraint prolongs cytokine messages and drives chronic inflammation and autoimmunity.

positive regulation of 3'-UTR-mediated mRNA stabilization describes how RNA-binding proteins act on sequences in the 3' untranslated region to prolong a transcript's life, raising protein output without any change in transcription.
