This is the counterweight to the decay machinery that strips AU-rich and other destabilizing elements, and it sets the duration of inflammatory, neuronal and muscle gene expression programs; unchecked stabilization of cytokine mRNAs promotes autoimmunity. The genes act through distinct devices: ARID5A binds the IL6 3'-UTR and shields it from regulatory endoribonuclease attack, ELAVL4 is a neuronal Hu-family protein that stabilizes transcripts during differentiation, RBM24 does the same for myogenic and cardiac messages, LARP4B links poly(A)-binding protein to the translational apparatus, and the noncanonical polymerases TENT4A/TENT4B add mixed poly(A) tails whose guanosines resist deadenylation. Post-transcriptional control of this kind tunes cytokine responses, muscle development and synaptic plasticity.

How long a transcript survives is often decided by its 3' untranslated region, where RNA-binding proteins and modifying enzymes compete to protect or destroy the message. This pathway covers the protective side: factors that increase 3'-UTR-mediated mRNA stabilization, raising the abundance of specific transcripts without any change in transcription. RNA-binding proteins such as ELAVL4, RBM24 and ARID5A bind AU-rich and other regulatory elements in the 3'-UTR and shield bound mRNAs from deadenylation and decay, while LARP4B works at the poly(A) tail and interacts with the translation machinery, coupling stability to protein output. The non-canonical polymerases TENT4A and TENT4B add mixed poly(A) tails containing guanosine, which blocks processive deadenylation. Such control shapes inflammatory cytokine levels, muscle and neuronal differentiation programmes, and the speed with which cells reset gene expression after a stimulus.

The postsynaptic density is the protein lattice beneath an excitatory synapse that holds glutamate receptors in register with the presynaptic release site, and this pathway covers the signals that build, enlarge or dismantle it. Control over its organization sets synaptic strength and thus learning and memory, and its disruption is a recurring theme in autism, schizophrenia and neurodegeneration. Much of the regulation is adhesive and trans-synaptic: leucine-rich repeat proteins such as LRRTM2, LRFN1/4 and LRRC4B pair with presynaptic partners, receptor phosphatases PTPRD and PTPRS act as their receptors, and cadherin-2 stabilises the cleft. Cerebellin and the delta-2 glutamate receptor form a parallel organizing bridge, while kinases including PTK2B and actin regulation through cofilin translate these contacts into scaffold remodelling. Scaffold adaptors such as CASKIN1 and CRIPT link the machinery to PSD-95-based complexes, coupling adhesion to receptor anchoring and spine morphology.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount an adaptive response, and this pathway covers the machinery that tunes how strongly and how long that response runs. Setting the gain matters because the same signals can either restore folding capacity or commit a cell to death: chronic mis-tuning contributes to diabetes, neurodegeneration and Wolfram syndrome. The three sensor arms are represented by the kinase PERK, the endoribonuclease IRE1 and the transcription factor precursor ATF6, feeding XBP1 splicing, CHOP induction and chaperone genes such as BiP. Regulation comes from phosphatase-directed subunits that reverse translational shutdown, deubiquitinases and ER-membrane ubiquitin ligases that control retrotranslocation and degradation of misfolded substrates, and BCL-2 family members that decide whether prolonged stress triggers apoptosis. Cofactors including WFS1, MANF and SIGMAR1 modulate sensor output and calcium handling.

positive regulation of response to endoplasmic reticulum stress describes the機 mechanisms that amplify the unfolded protein response when misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER, determining whether a stressed cell restores proteostasis or is eliminated. This choice matters in secretory tissues such as pancreatic beta cells and plasma cells, and its dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, diabetes and tumour survival under hypoxia. The genes include the proximal stress sensors IRE1 and ATF6 with the downstream transcription factors XBP1 and CHOP, which drive chaperone and ERAD gene expression while also priming apoptosis. A second group carries out ER-associated degradation and retrotranslocation: membrane ubiquitin ligases, ubiquilins, the BAG6-SGTA chaperone system, deubiquitinases and CHIP. When adaptation fails, BAX, BAK, PUMA, NOXA and BIM commit the cell to mitochondrial apoptosis, linking ER quality control to cell fate decisions.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount the unfolded protein response, and this pathway covers the inputs that raise its activity — strengthening ER quality control, degradation of faulty proteins, and, if stress persists, commitment to death. It matters because the amplitude of this response decides whether a secretory cell such as a plasma cell or pancreatic beta cell adapts or is eliminated, and its dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, metabolic disease and tumour cell survival. Sensors ERN1 and ATF6 drive XBP1-dependent transcription and chaperone induction, while DDIT3 (CHOP) links prolonged stress to apoptotic effectors including BAX, BAK1, PMAIP1, BBC3 and BCL2L11. Membrane-embedded ubiquitin ligases, deubiquitinases, ubiquilins and cochaperones such as STUB1 and SGTA promote retrotranslocation and proteasomal clearance of ER substrates, tying stress signalling to protein degradation and to redox and metabolic regulators.

Some peptides can convert from soluble forms into ordered, insoluble fibrils, and this pathway covers the cellular controls that promote or restrain that conversion. It matters because amyloid deposition underlies Alzheimer's disease, where amyloid-beta derived from APP by presenilin-dependent cleavage accumulates in plaques, and type 2 diabetes, where islet amyloid polypeptide aggregates and destroys beta cells. Control operates at several levels: chaperone activity, including the small heat shock protein CRYAB and the prefoldin complex, keeps aggregation-prone species soluble; lipoprotein and receptor components such as APOE, clusterin and LDLR govern clearance and seeding of extracellular deposits; heparan sulfate proteoglycan in the basement membrane influences fibril nucleation. Microglial TREM2 signalling shapes how deposits are engulfed and compacted. APOE variants are the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease, tying this regulation directly to neurodegenerative outcome.

Negative regulation of amyloid fibril formation covers the cellular defences that keep aggregation-prone peptides soluble and block their assembly into ordered fibrils. It matters because failure of this restraint underlies the plaque pathology of Alzheimer's disease, islet amyloid in type 2 diabetes, and cataract-associated lens protein aggregation. Two arms are represented. Extracellular chaperones and lipoprotein components — clusterin, apolipoprotein E and its receptor LDLR — bind amyloid-beta, sequester it and route it toward clearance, while TREM2 licenses microglial recognition and phagocytosis of deposits; APOE and TREM2 variants are among the strongest genetic risk factors for late-onset dementia. Intracellularly, the small heat shock protein alpha-B crystallin and the six-subunit prefoldin complex act as holdases, capturing nascent or partially folded polypeptides before they nucleate. Together these activities set the threshold at which physiological peptides such as amylin become cytotoxic aggregates.

Peptides such as amyloid-beta and islet amyloid polypeptide readily misfold into ordered fibrils, and suppressing that conversion protects tissue from amyloid deposits. This restraining activity underlies why extracellular chaperones and lipoprotein handling matter in Alzheimer's disease and in islet amyloidosis of type 2 diabetes, where loss of the brake permits plaque growth, neuroinflammation and beta cell loss. Several distinct mechanisms converge here: the secreted chaperone clusterin and the small heat shock protein CRYAB bind partly folded intermediates and hold them soluble; apolipoprotein E and the LDL receptor govern clearance and trafficking of amyloidogenic peptide; microglial TREM2 supports uptake and compaction of deposits; and the cytosolic prefoldin complex, a co-chaperone for nascent chains, keeps aggregation-prone proteins on productive folding routes. Together they place amyloid suppression within general protein quality control and lipid-mediated clearance rather than in any single signalling cascade.

Amyloid fibrils form when peptides misfold and stack into ordered insoluble aggregates, and this pathway covers the processes that promote that conversion rather than oppose it. The genes involved are central to Alzheimer's disease: the amyloid precursor protein supplies the aggregating peptide, presenilin 1 is the catalytic core of the gamma-secretase complex that releases amyloid-beta from it, and the lipid transporter apolipoprotein E and the chaperone clusterin bind the peptide extracellularly and can nucleate or stabilise fibrils, with particular apolipoprotein E variants conferring the strongest common genetic risk for late-onset disease. Deubiquitination by USP8 contributes by altering trafficking and degradation of precursor protein, shifting how much substrate is available for processing. The net effect links protein quality control, secretase activity and extracellular chaperone behaviour to plaque deposition and neurodegeneration.

Cells end a calcium signal partly by pumping the ion back out across the plasma membrane, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast that export runs. Tuning it determines how long a calcium transient lasts, which shapes contraction and relaxation in muscle, transmitter release, and the resting calcium load a cell must tolerate; chronic failure of export leaves cytosolic calcium elevated and activates calcium-dependent proteases and cell death. Calmodulin, present here as all three genes encoding it, is the central sensor: calcium-loaded calmodulin binds the plasma membrane calcium ATPases and raises their transport rate, providing negative feedback proportional to the signal being terminated. Also represented are a microRNA and a 14-3-3 adaptor, indicating that export capacity is additionally set by transcript-level and protein-interaction control rather than by calcium occupancy alone.

Cells extrude calcium across the plasma membrane through ATP-driven pumps and exchangers, and restraining that export is one way a cell sets how long a calcium signal lasts and how much calcium it retains. Negative regulation of calcium efflux therefore shapes the amplitude and decay of cytosolic calcium transients that drive contraction, secretion and transcriptional responses. Calmodulin, encoded here by three near-identical genes, is the central calcium sensor whose binding to pump regulatory domains couples efflux activity to prevailing calcium levels; a 14-3-3 adaptor and a muscle-enriched microRNA add post-translational and post-transcriptional control over transporter abundance and function. Because sustained efflux would blunt signalling and deplete internal stores, this restraint matters most in excitable and contractile tissues, where mis-set calcium handling contributes to arrhythmia and impaired excitation-contraction coupling.

Fertility depends on germ cells expanding to the right number at the right time, and this pathway covers the signals that set the pace of germ cell proliferation in the developing and adult gonad. Prostaglandin D2 signalling is the dominant theme: a lipocalin-type and a hematopoietic synthase both generate PGD2, which acts through the DP2 receptor to influence germ cell behaviour and Sertoli cell support, a route also implicated in male gonadal differentiation. Alongside it sit factors required for spermatogenic cell survival and maturation — a rhomboid intramembrane protease whose loss causes germ cell apoptosis and male infertility, a calcium- and integrin-binding adaptor needed for spermatid development, and an endoplasmic reticulum peroxiredoxin that limits oxidative damage. Failure of this control yields hypospermatogenesis, reduced germ cell number and subfertility, linking lipid mediator signalling and redox balance to reproductive output.

Whether a bipotential gonadal ridge becomes a testis or an ovary, and how far it develops, is set by a small set of regulators whose dosage and timing this control programme adjusts. The outcome determines gonadal somatic cell identity — Sertoli versus granulosa — and with it hormone output, germ cell support and the entire downstream sexual phenotype, so perturbation produces disorders of sex development, gonadal dysgenesis, sex reversal and infertility. Early transcriptional input from WT1, NR5A1, CITED2 and ZFPM2 licenses gonad formation; SRY then drives SOX9 and DMRT1 to establish and maintain the testicular pathway, while WNT4 supports the ovarian alternative, the two arms mutually antagonistic even in adulthood. Oocyte-derived GDF9 shapes follicle growth, and insulin receptor signalling ties gonadal development to metabolic state.

Building a testis or ovary from the bipotential genital ridge depends on a small set of transcriptional regulators that must be switched on at the right time and dose, and this pathway covers the inputs that promote that gonadal programme. Its failure is a recognised cause of disorders of sex development: heterozygous loss of NR5A1 or WT1, translocations affecting SOX9, or deletion of SRY produce gonadal dysgenesis, sex reversal, and infertility, and WT1 mutations also link gonadal and kidney malformation. Mechanistically, WT1 and the transcriptional coregulators CITED2 and ZFPM2 act upstream to drive NR5A1 and SRY expression in the developing somatic gonad, SRY then activates SOX9 to commit supporting cells to Sertoli fate, and DMRT1 maintains that testicular identity afterwards. The programme sets up steroidogenic capacity and germ cell support for the rest of reproductive life.

Calcium entry through plasma membrane channels must be curtailed once a signal has been delivered, and this pathway covers the processes that damp or shut off such influx. Restraining calcium import protects cells from overload, which otherwise drives arrhythmia, excitotoxicity and mitochondrial calcium-triggered death, and it shapes the duration of calcium transients that control contraction, secretion and gene expression. The calcineurin holoenzyme dominates the protein component here: catalytic subunits paired with regulatory subunits form a calcium- and calmodulin-activated phosphatase that dephosphorylates channel-associated substrates and so feeds back on the influx that activated it. Alongside them sit microRNAs, including cardiac-enriched species, that lower the abundance of channel and transport components post-transcriptionally. Together the two layers give both rapid enzymatic feedback and slower transcript-level limitation of calcium entry, with particular consequence for cardiac and muscle excitability.

regulation of lipid localization controls where lipids go in the body and within cells — how cholesterol and fatty acids are loaded onto lipoproteins, effluxed from cells, stored in droplets, or mobilised for fuel. It sets circulating lipid levels and tissue lipid burden, so its failure produces atherosclerosis, hepatic steatosis, obesity and, for individual transporters, surfactant deficiency or ichthyosis. The genes span ABC-family lipid transporters and flippases, apolipoproteins and transfer proteins such as CETP and PLTP, scavenger and lipoprotein receptors including CD36, SCARB1 and LRP1, lipases and perilipin-coated droplet proteins, and the secretory machinery that packages lipoprotein cargo. Above these sit the nuclear receptors PPARs, LXRs and RXRA, SREBP-driven feedback with PCSK9, adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin, inflammatory cytokines, and a large complement of microRNAs including the miR-33 pair, which tune efflux and fatty-acid oxidation. It links whole-body energy balance to innate immune and macrophage foam-cell biology.

Lipids must be moved to the right place -- across membranes, out of cells, into lipoprotein particles, or into cytoplasmic droplets -- and this pathway covers the control of that placement rather than the chemistry of lipid synthesis. Its outputs determine reverse cholesterol transport, plasma lipoprotein levels, surfactant secretion, skin barrier lipid delivery and fat storage in adipocytes, so its failure underlies atherosclerosis, dyslipidaemia and lipid-laden macrophage foam cell formation. Mechanistically it combines ABC-family lipid exporters and flippases, apolipoprotein and lipase components of lipoprotein metabolism, scavenger and LDL-related receptors that take lipid up, and perilipins that gate access to stored triglyceride. Nuclear receptors such as the liver X receptors and PPARs, together with SREBP-responsive elements and a large complement of microRNAs including the miR-33 family, set how much of this transport machinery is made, tying lipid traffic to inflammation, hormonal signalling and energy status.

Cells must limit where lipids accumulate, and this collection of brakes on lipid localization covers the processes that reduce cholesterol and triglyceride deposition in cells and tissues. It matters most in the artery wall and in adipose tissue: when these restraints fail, macrophages become lipid-laden foam cells and atherosclerosis, hepatic steatosis and obesity-associated metabolic disease follow. Cholesterol efflux transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 move sterol onto apolipoprotein acceptors including APOE and APOA2, and are themselves induced by the liver X receptors NR1H2 and NR1H3, whose messages are in turn silenced by a large set of microRNAs, notably the MIR33 family. Lipolytic and lipid-handling enzymes, PPAR-family transcription factors, adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin, inflammatory cytokines including TNF and IL6, and PCSK9-dependent control of lipoprotein uptake all feed into how much lipid a given compartment retains.

Lipids must be moved between membranes, organelles, cells and tissues, and this collection captures the processes that increase that movement — cholesterol efflux, lipoprotein assembly and uptake, phospholipid translocation across bilayers, and the deposition and mobilisation of neutral lipid in droplets. It matters most for cholesterol homeostasis in macrophages and the liver: transporters such as ABCA1 and ABCG1 hand cholesterol and phospholipid to apolipoprotein acceptors including APOA1 and APOE, while scavenger receptors CD36, MSR1 and SCARB1 take lipid up, and failure of this balance produces foam cells and atherosclerosis. Nuclear receptors of the liver X and PPAR families with RXRA drive the transcriptional arm, flippases with their TMEM30A subunit and perilipins handle intracellular distribution, and secreted factors such as LPL, CETP, PLTP and adipokines act on circulating lipid. Surfactant secretion and skin barrier lipid transport depend on the same family of transporters.

Glutamatergic neuron differentiation is the route by which an uncommitted progenitor acquires the identity of an excitatory, glutamate-releasing neuron, the principal driver of excitatory transmission in the retina, cortex and cerebellum. Much of the biology here concerns retinal bipolar cells, which relay photoreceptor input onward: homeodomain factors such as VSX2 and VSX1 specify bipolar fate, PROX1 and PRDM1 partition progenitors among retinal cell classes, and phototransduction and synaptic components including RHO, GNAT2 and CABP4 mark the upstream photoreceptors whose ribbon synapses these neurons read. Others act at the excitatory synapse itself, with NRXN1 and the CBLN1-GRID2 pair organising presynaptic and postsynaptic partners in the cerebellum, alongside WNT7A signalling and OPHN1-dependent Rho regulation. Failure of these steps produces congenital retinal dysfunction, ataxia and intellectual disability, linking cell-fate choice to circuit wiring.

Amyloid fibril formation is the conversion of soluble proteins into insoluble, beta-sheet-rich fibres that resist degradation and accumulate in tissue, and it is the common endpoint of the degenerative amyloidoses. The proteins that do this are represented here — amyloid-beta released from APP by BACE1 and the presenilin-containing gamma-secretase, tau, alpha-synuclein, islet amyloid polypeptide in pancreatic islets, beta-2-microglobulin in dialysis-associated deposits, and the RNA-binding proteins FUS and TARDBP that aggregate in motor neuron disease. Whether a precursor fibrillises depends on the balance between chaperone and quality-control activity and the local environment: small heat-shock proteins such as CRYAB, the prefoldin subunits, clusterin, gelsolin and the SERF proteins modulate assembly, while ubiquitin ligases and deubiquitinases govern clearance of the substrates. Apolipoprotein E and TREM2 set glial handling of deposits, linking fibril burden to neuroinflammation and Alzheimer risk.</br>

Cells hold cytosolic calcium at nanomolar levels against a steep gradient, and export across the plasma membrane is how that resting level is restored after every signalling event. Without it, calcium transients fail to terminate, contraction and neurotransmission lose their timing, and sustained overload triggers protease activation and cell death. Two families do the work: plasma membrane calcium ATPases such as ATP2B1 and ATP2B3, which use ATP hydrolysis for high-affinity fine tuning, and sodium/calcium exchangers of the SLC8 family together with the potassium-dependent SLC24 exchangers, which use the inward sodium gradient for high-capacity extrusion during large loads. Calmodulin binding activates the pumps in proportion to calcium itself, providing feedback control, while accessory regulators tune exchanger activity. This chemistry shapes cardiac excitation-contraction coupling, neuronal calcium recovery, and photoreceptor light adaptation.

Muscle relaxation depends on clearing calcium from the cytosol after each contraction, and this pathway is the pump-driven return of that calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum store, where it is held ready for the next action potential. The SERCA ATPases ATP2A1 and ATP2A2 use ATP hydrolysis to move calcium against a steep gradient in fast skeletal, slow skeletal and cardiac muscle respectively; the rate at which they do so sets relaxation kinetics, diastolic filling and the size of the releasable store that determines contractile force. A family of small transmembrane peptides tunes the pump: phospholamban, sarcolipin and myoregulin inhibit it, while DWORF relieves that inhibition. Because reuptake governs both relaxation and store loading, reduced pump activity or excessive inhibition contributes to diastolic dysfunction and heart failure, and mutations in ATP2A1 cause Brody myopathy with delayed muscle relaxation after exercise.

Anterograde neuronal dense core vesicle transport delivers neuropeptides, neurotrophins and their processing machinery from the neuronal cell body outward along the axon to release sites at the presynapse. Because dense core vesicles cannot be made locally, this long-range delivery sets how much peptidergic and modulatory signalling a terminal can perform, and its disruption underlies hereditary spastic paraplegia and sensory-motor neuropathies caused by KIF1A mutations. Kinesin motors, chiefly KIF1A with contributions from KIF1C and the kinesin-1 heavy chain KIF5B, walk cargo toward microtubule plus ends; MAP2 and the axon initial segment protein TRIM46 organise and bundle the microtubule tracks with uniform polarity, giving motors an unambiguous directional cue as cargo leaves the soma. The pathway is thus a junction of intracellular trafficking, microtubule cytoskeletal organisation and neuronal polarity, and supports axon growth, synapse maintenance and neuromodulator secretion.

Neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines are packaged into dense core vesicles at the soma and must be carried the length of the axon before they can be released, and anterograde transport of these vesicles along axonal microtubules toward the presynaptic terminal is how they get there. Without it, peptidergic and modulatory signalling fails at the synapse even though the vesicles are made normally, a defect reflected in the hereditary spastic paraplegias and sensory-motor neuropathies caused by kinesin mutations. Kinesin-3 and kinesin-1 motors, including KIF1A and KIF5B, walk cargo along microtubule tracks whose polarity and bundling are set in the proximal axon, where TRIM46 organises parallel plus-end-out arrays and MAP2 associates with the dendritic and somatic cytoskeleton. The pathway thus links motor-driven cargo traffic to neuronal polarity and long-range intracellular delivery.

Dense core vesicles carry neuropeptides, neurotrophins and biogenic amines, and their position within a neuron determines where those cargoes can be released; retrograde transport of these vesicles is the movement back along axonal microtubules toward the soma, allowing recapture, recycling or degradation of vesicles and their contents rather than their accumulation at distal terminals. Because axons can be extremely long, this traffic depends on motor proteins running on a polarised microtubule track, and the kinesin motors named here — including KIF1A, KIF1B and KIF5A — are the transport machinery associated with dense core vesicle movement and its regulation in concert with dynein-driven minus-end travel. Disruption of these motors causes hereditary spastic paraplegia, distal neuropathies and axonal degeneration, underscoring how much long-term neuronal maintenance and peptidergic signalling rest on correctly directed vesicle logistics.

Cartilage homeostasis is the maintenance of a steady state in cartilage, balancing chondrocyte proliferation, survival and matrix turnover so that the tissue keeps its mechanical properties over a lifetime of loading. Loss of this balance underlies osteoarthritic cartilage degeneration and skeletal dysplasias. The genes here act at several levels: a secreted matrix glycoprotein organises collagen fibrils and stabilises the extracellular network, a cytokine-like factor promotes chondrogenic differentiation, and an intraflagellar transport component builds the primary cilium through which chondrocytes read mechanical and Hedgehog signals. Metal handling matters too, with a zinc-responsive transcription factor and a manganese and zinc transporter linking trace element supply to glycosyltransferase activity and proteoglycan synthesis. Together they tie matrix assembly, cell signalling and metabolic control to the long-term integrity of joint and growth plate cartilage.

Nerve growth factor instructs sympathetic and sensory neurons to survive, grow axons and differentiate, and the cellular response to it is what keeps those neurons alive and correctly wired; loss of the ligand or its receptor causes congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis and contributes to neurodegenerative decline. Binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase TRKA, with sortilin and the p75-associated machinery shaping the outcome, triggers PI3K-AKT and Rap1-ERK cascades through adaptors such as CRK, RAPGEF1 and SHOC2, converging on CREB1- and FOXO3-dependent transcription. A large part of the response is membrane traffic: ARF6, RAB35, EHD1, endophilin and USP8 govern receptor internalisation and retrograde signalling endosomes carried along microtubules to the soma. Downstream effects include cytoskeletal remodelling for neurite outgrowth via WASF1 and stathmin-2, regulation of tau, and induction of neuropeptides and related neurotrophins.

When a ribosome stalls on a damaged or aberrant mRNA, the partly made polypeptide must be destroyed rather than released, and ribosome-associated ubiquitin-dependent degradation is how cells do it. Without this surveillance, incomplete proteins accumulate and aggregate, and neurons are particularly vulnerable, so the pathway underlies proteostasis and protection from neurodegeneration. Collided ribosomes are recognised and ubiquitinated on the small subunit by ZNF598, which marks the event for resolution; the large subunit is then split away and the trapped nascent chain is polyubiquitinated by the E3 ligase listerin (LTN1) working with NEMF, which holds the chain on the 60S and appends destabilising C-terminal alanine and threonine tails. Cullin-RING components with KLHDC10 and elongin B/C target such degron-bearing products, while the VCP/p97 ATPase with its UFD1-NPLOC4 cofactor extracts substrates for proteasomal breakdown. An ASCC-based rescue arm handles alkylation-stalled ribosomes.

neuron projection extension is the long-distance outgrowth of an axon or dendrite from a developing neuron, the process by which the nervous system is physically wired and by which injured nerves attempt to regrow. Without it, cortical layering, commissure formation and target innervation fail, and the same machinery limits recovery after axonal injury. Guidance cues and their receptors dominate: semaphorins with plexins and neuropilins, slits, netrin, ephrin-like and Wnt ligands, and myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG signalling through the Nogo receptor. These converge on Rho-family effectors, PAK and LIM kinase, GSK3B and CDK5, which remodel the actin cortex and reorganise microtubules through MAP1B, tau, CLASP2 and shootin-driven adhesion coupling. Cell adhesion molecules including L1CAM, NRCAM and DSCAM, integrin-laminin contacts, and transcription factors such as LHX2 and POU4F2 set the growth competence of particular neuronal classes; several members are mutated in neurodevelopmental and motor neuron disease.

Neurons wire the nervous system by sending a single axon or dendrite over long distances to its target, and this pathway covers the machinery that drives and steers that growth. Without it cortical and spinal tracts fail to form, commissures misroute, and regeneration after injury stalls; several members are mutated in intellectual disability, autism and hereditary spastic paraplegia. Guidance cues and their receptors — netrin, slits, semaphorins with plexins and neuropilins, Wnts, and myelin-derived inhibitors signalling through the Nogo receptor — are read at the growth cone and converted by Rho-family effectors such as PAK1, LIMK1 and CDK5 into actin remodelling, while MAP1B, MAPT, CLASP2 and dynein regulators organise the microtubule core of the shaft. Adhesion molecules of the L1 and cadherin families, integrins and extracellular matrix provide traction, and vesicle trafficking supplies membrane to the advancing tip.

intrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway in response to hypoxia is the route by which a cell deprived of oxygen commits to mitochondrial apoptosis rather than continuing to adapt. It sets the threshold that decides infarct size in ischaemic heart and brain, and its suppression lets tumour cells survive the hypoxic cores of solid masses. Falling oxygen tension shifts the balance of BCL-2 family proteins at the outer mitochondrial membrane, where BNIP3 promotes permeabilisation and mitophagy while ARC (NOL3) and the BI-1 protein TMBIM6 restrain caspase activation and buffer ER calcium release. Counterbalancing survival input arrives through PI3K and MEK1 signalling and the ATF2-driven stress transcriptional response, with the ER chaperone HYOU1 and the mitochondrial kinase PINK1 protecting damaged organelles. When protection fails, mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation releases cytochrome c and triggers the execution phase.

When oxygen falls low enough that adaptation fails, cells can commit to death from within, and this hypoxia-triggered intrinsic apoptotic route is how that decision is transmitted to the mitochondrial execution machinery. It sets the threshold for cell loss in ischaemic tissue — infarcted myocardium, stroke penumbra, hypoxic tumour cores — and its suppression lets tumour cells survive an environment that should kill them. The balance is struck between pro-death and protective components: BNIP3 accumulates under hypoxia and permeabilises mitochondria, while ARC (NOL3) and the ER calcium-leak regulator TMBIM6 restrain caspase activation and limit calcium-driven death. PINK1 links the response to mitochondrial quality control, and kinase and lipid-kinase signalling through MAP2K1 and PIK3CB together with the transcription factor ATF2 determine whether hypoxic stress resolves in survival or apoptosis.

Ribosomes must pair each codon with the correct tRNA, and this pathway is the set of safeguards that keeps that pairing accurate. Most of its members build a single tRNA modification: the KEOPS complex — the OSGEP catalytic subunit with TP53RK, TPRKB, LAGE3 and GON7 — installs threonylcarbamoyladenosine at position 37 of tRNAs that read ANN codons, and CDKAL1 adds a methylthio group to that modified base in the lysine tRNA. Without these marks, tRNAs slip in the ribosomal A site, frameshifting and misreading rise, and the consequences are concrete: KEOPS mutations cause galloway-Mowat syndrome with nephrotic disease and microcephaly, while CDKAL1 variants impair proinsulin processing in beta cells and associate with type 2 diabetes. The ribosomal proteins RPS12 and RPS23 sit in the decoding centre itself, where substitutions alter stop-codon readthrough and error rates.

Repair of a chromosomal double-strand break depends on recruiting and holding the right proteins at the lesion, and this recruitment step determines both the speed and the choice of repair pathway. Phosphorylated H2AX marks chromatin flanking the break and is read by MDC1, which amplifies the signal and brings in the NBN-containing nuclease complex, TP53BP1, and the SLF1-SLF2 scaffold; RPA1 coats resected single-stranded DNA and TOPBP1 with RAD17 and RHNO1 couples damage to checkpoint kinase activation. CYREN and XRCC4 favour end-joining, SIRT6 and PARP3 modify chromatin and proteins locally to speed factor arrival, and IFFO1 anchors broken ends against drifting apart. Failure of this localised assembly leaves breaks unrepaired or misjoined, producing translocations, genome instability and the cancer predisposition and immunodeficiency seen when individual components are mutated.

Getting a protein into the nucleoplasm and holding it there is a prerequisite for the reactions that happen in the soluble nuclear interior, and this pathway covers that targeting and retention step. Much of the work is chaperone-dependent: the eight-subunit TRiC/CCT chaperonin folds newly made substrates into conformations competent for nuclear import and complex assembly, so its failure leaves clients aggregated or mislocalised in the cytoplasm. Other members act as assembly and trafficking factors for nuclear ribonucleoproteins, including the telomerase-associated proteins DKC1 and WRAP53, which route the telomerase complex to its nuclear sites, and LARP7 with MEPCE, which stabilise the 7SK snRNP that restrains RNA polymerase II elongation. Ribosome biogenesis and nucleolar stress factors such as NOP53 are also delivered this way, linking correct nucleoplasmic localisation to telomere maintenance, transcriptional control and growth regulation.</description>

Cells monitor leucine because it is the amino acid that most strongly licenses growth, and the cellular response to leucine starvation is how they stand down anabolism when it runs short. When leucine is abundant, sestrins release the GATOR2 complex and leucyl-tRNA synthetase and the Rag GTPases permit mTORC1 to dock at the lysosome; withdrawal reverses this, mTORC1 activity falls, protein synthesis and ribosome biogenesis are curtailed, and autophagy is de-repressed to recover amino acids from bulk cytoplasm. In parallel, uncharged tRNA accumulation drives a transcriptional arm through ATF4 and ATF2 that induces amino acid transporters, synthetases and stress-adaptive genes, including the sestrins themselves as a feedback loop. This surveillance couples nutrient supply to cell size, muscle protein balance and immune cell activation, and is the route by which leucine and its analogues influence mTOR-dependent growth control.

Transcripts that fail to be spliced or translated correctly must be destroyed rather than allowed to produce aberrant protein, and pre-mRNA catabolism is the route by which such unspliced precursors are broken down. The activity matters because it keeps nuclear and cytoplasmic pools of messenger RNA free of intron-containing or stalled species, contributing to the general surveillance that protects proteome quality. The genes here centre on a repressive complex in which GIGYF1 and GIGYF2 bind the cap-binding protein EIF4E2 and recruit the DEAD-box helicase DDX6, silencing translation and directing transcripts toward decay. ZNF598 is the ubiquitin ligase that marks collided ribosomes and initiates ribosome-associated quality control, coupling detection of problematic translation to transcript destruction. Together these link translational repression, deadenylation-dependent decay and RNA turnover in cytoplasmic granules.

Anti-Mullerian hormone signalling is how the fetal testis eliminates the precursor of the female reproductive tract: Sertoli-cell-derived AMH acting through its dedicated type II receptor drives regression of the Mullerian ducts, and loss of either the hormone or AMHR2 leaves genetically male individuals with a uterus and fallopian tubes, the persistent Mullerian duct syndrome. The same axis continues after development, restraining recruitment of primordial ovarian follicles and serving as a circulating index of ovarian reserve. Mechanistically it is a branch of TGF-beta family signalling: ligand binding assembles AMHR2 with a type I receptor kinase such as BMPR1A, which phosphorylates SMAD1 and SMAD5 so they accumulate in the nucleus and reprogramme transcription in duct mesenchyme and gonadal somatic cells. DKK3 acts alongside this output as a modulator of duct regression.

Neutrophils are the first leukocytes to reach an infected or injured tissue, and their migration from blood into that tissue is the opening move of acute inflammation; when it fails, bacterial and fungal infections go unchecked, while unrestrained recruitment drives tissue damage in sepsis, acute lung injury and chronic inflammatory disease. Chemoattractants set the direction: CXCL8 and related chemokines acting through CXCR1 and CXCR2, complement fragments through C5AR1 and C3AR1, and formyl-peptide and lipid cues. Signalling converges on PI3K gamma and delta, SYK, VAV exchange factors and Rac GTPases to polarize the cell and remodel actin. Selectin ligands built by FUT4 and FUT7, the beta2 integrin ITGB2 and junctional proteins such as PECAM1, CD99 and JAM3 support rolling, firm adhesion and passage between endothelial cells. S100A8/A9, IL1B and PRTN3 amplify the recruiting signal once neutrophils arrive.

This is the set of cellular changes triggered when a cell encounters insulin-like growth factor, the principal endocrine and paracrine driver of somatic growth. IGF signalling determines body and organ size, sustains muscle and bone mass, promotes survival of neurons and other post-mitotic cells, and, when chronically elevated, supports tumour cell proliferation and resistance to apoptosis. Ligand engagement of the receptor recruits adaptors such as CRK and converges on transcriptional output through CREB1, driving cell cycle entry via cyclin A and coupling growth factor input to metabolic and mitochondrial capacity. Parallel responses reshape the cytoskeleton and cell adhesion through cofilin and integrin beta-3, and intersect with extracellular matrix and TGF-beta signalling, so the response coordinates proliferation with migration and matrix remodelling. Growth hormone secretagogue receptor signalling ties the pathway to the somatotropic axis that sets circulating IGF1 levels.

Adjacent cells can share ions, metabolites and second messengers directly when their cytoplasms are joined by gap junction channels, and this gap junction-mediated intercellular transport lets a tissue behave as an electrically and metabolically coupled unit rather than as isolated cells. Each channel is built from connexin hexamers docked end to end across the intercellular space; the members here include lens connexins and the cochlear and epidermal connexins, alongside the lens-specific water channel MIP. The lens depends on this coupling especially heavily, because its fibre cells lose organelles and have no blood supply, so nutrients and antioxidants must be passed inward and waste outward through junctional channels. Mutations in these connexins cause inherited cataract, non-syndromic deafness, and palmoplantar keratoderma with hearing loss, illustrating how much transparency, epidermal differentiation and potassium recycling in the inner ear rely on direct cell-to-cell exchange.

The brain cannot synthesise all the lipids it needs, so fatty acids and their carriers must be moved across the endothelium of the blood-brain barrier in a controlled, directional way. This transport supplies docosahexaenoic acid and other long-chain fatty acids for membrane and myelin synthesis, and its loss has severe consequences: mutations in MFSD2A, the sodium-dependent lysophosphatidylcholine transporter of brain endothelium, cause microcephaly and also relax barrier tightness, since the same protein suppresses vesicular transcytosis. Uptake and handoff involve a scavenger receptor and fatty acid transport proteins at the luminal membrane, intracellular binding proteins that shuttle lipids across the cell, and apolipoprotein E to distribute lipid within the brain parenchyma. The pathway links peripheral lipid supply to neuronal and glial membrane maintenance, and its regulation shapes barrier permeability as well as brain lipid composition.

The fetal eye is nourished by a transient hyaloid vascular plexus that must be dismantled before vision begins, and its programmed regression clears the vitreous so light reaches the retina unobstructed; failure leaves persistent fetal vasculature, a cause of congenital cataract, retinal detachment and childhood blindness. The genes here place this remodelling under light- and neurotransmitter-dependent control: the atypical opsins OPN4 and OPN5 confer photosensitivity late in gestation, and this input is relayed through dopaminergic components — tyrosine hydroxylase for dopamine synthesis, the dopamine transporter, and the D2 receptor — together with glutamatergic release machinery. Downstream, the VEGF receptor FLT1 tunes the availability of VEGFA to endothelial cells, so that survival signalling drops and the hyaloid endothelium undergoes apoptosis on schedule. The pathway links sensory photoreception to developmental vascular pruning in the eye.

Formation of the brain during embryogenesis, from the initial patterning of the neural tube through the growth and regionalisation that produce a mature organ, is captured by this embryonic brain development programme. It sets up the midbrain-hindbrain boundary and its organiser activity, where WNT1 signalling through beta-catenin and the engrailed transcription factors EN1 and EN2 specify midbrain and cerebellar territory; loss of these functions deletes whole brain regions. Much of the remainder concerns the cilium and its trafficking machinery — CC2D2A, MKS1, IFT140 and the kinase TTBK2, which licenses ciliogenesis — linking defective cilia to cerebellar and hindbrain malformations of the Joubert and Meckel type. Additional components act in neuronal migration and cortical architecture, including the tubulin TUBB2B, in blood-brain barrier lipid transport via MFSD2A, and in spliceosomal and transcriptional coactivator functions whose mutation causes syndromic intellectual disability.

Calcitonin gene-related peptide, encoded by the alternatively spliced CALCA gene and its paralogue CALCB, is released from sensory nerve terminals and acts as one of the body's most powerful vasodilators; signalling through its receptor drives arterial and arteriolar relaxation, neurogenic inflammation and the transmission of pain, and is the pathway blocked by modern migraine therapeutics. The receptor is not a single protein but a complex: the calcitonin receptor-like receptor partners obligately with the accessory protein RAMP1 to acquire CGRP selectivity, with the related calcitonin receptor contributing to amylin-type pharmacology, and the assembled receptors can associate into higher-order oligomers. Ligand binding raises cyclic AMP and downstream kinase activity in smooth muscle, endothelium and neurons. Co-expression with the sensory sodium channel SCN11A places this signalling in nociceptor biology, linking peptide release to vascular tone, mast cell activation and headache.

Adrenomedullin is a secreted peptide that dilates blood vessels, stabilises endothelial barrier function and supports lymphatic and cardiovascular development, and this pathway covers how it is received at the cell surface. Signalling begins when adrenomedullin, or the related peptide intermedin, binds a receptor that is only functional as a pair: the class B G protein-coupled receptor CALCRL together with an accessory protein, RAMP2 or RAMP3, whose identity dictates whether the complex prefers adrenomedullin or calcitonin gene-related peptide. The assembled receptor couples through Gs to raise cyclic AMP, relaxing vascular smooth muscle and tightening endothelial junctions. Loss of the ligand or of RAMP2 in mice causes lethal hydrops and defective vessel formation, and the peptide rises sharply in sepsis and heart failure, where it is used as a marker of vascular stress. Tumours also exploit this axis to promote angiogenesis.

When a replication fork encounters a nick or lesion, the result is a one-ended double-strand break that cannot be rejoined end-to-end; repair instead copies the intact sister chromatid, and the crossover this generates is seen cytologically as a sister chromatid exchange. This route keeps replication from converting single-strand damage into chromosome loss, and its failure leaves cells dependent on error-prone alternatives, with the chromosomal instability and interstrand crosslink sensitivity characteristic of Fanconi anaemia. Physical proximity of the two sisters is a prerequisite, which is why cohesin subunits and the cohesin loading factor NIPBL appear alongside the recombination machinery. RAD51 performs strand invasion and template-directed synthesis, while the helicase RECQL5 restrains inappropriate recombination so that exchange occurs only where needed. The pathway sits at the junction of DNA replication, homologous recombination and sister chromatid cohesion during S and G2 phase.

Brain-derived neurotrophic factor acts on neurons to promote survival, dendritic growth and the lasting strengthening of synapses that underlies learning and memory, and the cellular response to it is what converts that extracellular signal into changes at the synapse. Binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase TrkB, encoded by NTRK2, triggers kinase cascades that reach both the translational machinery and the postsynaptic membrane. Local protein synthesis is gated through elongation factor eEF2 and its inhibitory kinase eEF2K, while AMPA receptor subunit GRIA1 trafficking and endophilin-dependent endocytic recycling adjust synaptic strength; actin remodelling via WASF1 reshapes spines, and microtubule-associated tau links the signal to the neuronal cytoskeleton. Blunted signalling of this kind is associated with depression, impaired plasticity and neurodegeneration, and the pathway is a point of convergence for antidepressant and exercise-induced effects on the brain.

response to insulin-like growth factor stimulus covers the cellular changes that follow IGF binding to its receptor — shifts in growth, survival, secretion and gene expression that drive somatic growth, tissue repair and neuronal maintenance. Loss of this responsiveness produces growth failure and reduced cell survival, while excessive signalling supports tumour proliferation. The genes trace the canonical survival arm through AKT1, which suppresses apoptotic effectors such as CASP3, alongside transcriptional output via XBP1, linking IGF input to endoplasmic reticulum stress adaptation and secretory capacity. Others place the response in specific tissues: PHEX ties IGF-related signalling to osteoblast function and phosphate handling in bone, while APP and BACE1 connect it to amyloid precursor processing in neurons, where IGF-driven survival signalling modulates neurodegenerative risk. The pathway therefore sits at the intersection of endocrine growth control, apoptosis suppression and tissue-specific differentiation.

Cells adjust growth, survival and metabolic activity when they encounter insulin-like growth factors, and this response captures the downstream consequences of that stimulus. IGF signalling acts through receptor tyrosine kinase engagement and AKT1 activation to promote anabolic metabolism, suppress apoptosis and drive proliferation and differentiation, which is why it governs somatic growth, bone and muscle mass, and tissue repair. The genes here point to several contexts in which IGF exposure changes cell behaviour: pro-survival kinase signalling that restrains caspase-3-dependent apoptosis, altered processing of amyloid precursor protein by the secretase BACE1, XBP1-dependent transcription linking the stimulus to endoplasmic reticulum stress and secretory capacity, and PHEX, a bone-expressed endopeptidase tied to phosphate handling in mineralised tissue. Excessive IGF-driven survival signalling supports tumour growth, while deficient responses limit growth and skeletal development.

Mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum are held in close apposition at contact sites, and the tethers that bridge the two membranes set how much calcium and lipid passes between them. These junctions matter because ER-released calcium taken up locally by mitochondria stimulates oxidative metabolism, while excessive transfer triggers permeability transition and apoptosis; contact spacing also influences mitochondrial division and autophagosome formation. The proteins here act on both the physical link and its calcium traffic: PDZD8 is a bona fide ER-mitochondrial tether, PACS2 controls ER-mitochondria apposition and calnexin localisation, PSEN2 and AHCYL1 modulate inositol trisphosphate receptor-dependent calcium release, ATP2A2 pumps calcium back into the ER lumen, and VMP1 acts in the opposite direction by promoting contact dissolution. Disrupted tethering is implicated in neurodegeneration and in insulin resistance, where mitochondrial calcium supply and lipid handling fail together.

Messenger RNAs carry more than the four standard bases: scattered uridines are isomerised to pseudouridine, a modification that alters base pairing, rigidifies the sugar-phosphate backbone and can change how a codon is read or how stable and translatable a transcript is. The enzymes that perform this conversion fall into several families — stand-alone synthases such as PUS1, PUS3 and PUS7, the TRUB and RPUSD groups, and DKC1, which also acts as the catalytic subunit of box H/ACA ribonucleoprotein particles that use guide RNAs to select sites. Several of these proteins are mitochondrial, linking the modification to organellar as well as cytoplasmic RNA. Because pseudouridylation tunes translation and transcript fate rather than changing the encoded sequence outright, it acts as a layer of post-transcriptional regulation; loss of individual synthases causes intellectual disability, mitochondrial myopathy with sideroblastic anaemia, and in the case of DKC1, dyskeratosis congenita.

Neurons and endocrine cells package neuropeptides, insulin-related hormones and monoamines such as serotonin and dopamine into dense core granules and release them only when cytosolic calcium rises. This regulated exocytosis sets the slower, modulatory layer of chemical signalling that tunes synaptic strength, appetite, stress responses and metabolic control, distinct from fast synaptic vesicle release. Granules must first be tethered and primed before they can fuse: priming factors of the CAPS and Munc13 families make granules fusion-competent, Munc18 proteins chaperone syntaxin and license SNARE complex assembly with SNAP25, and a Rab3 GTPase governs granule trafficking and docking at the plasma membrane. Synaptotagmin-family members contribute calcium sensing and granule composition. Loss of these steps blunts hormone and neuropeptide secretion; mutations in the Munc18-1 and Munc13-1 genes cause severe epileptic encephalopathies, and related family members act in immune cell granule release.

Once an axon or dendrite has grown, it must be held in place for the life of the cell, and neuron projection maintenance is the set of activities that preserves those processes in a stable structural and functional state rather than building them. Its failure is the basis of axonal degeneration and dying-back neuropathy, and several of the genes here are classical neurodegeneration loci: mutations in the dynactin subunit DCTN1 cause motor neuron disease, presenilin and amyloid precursor protein are central to Alzheimer pathology, the prion protein supports peripheral myelinated axon integrity, and defects in the peroxisomal transporter ABCD1 produce adrenoleukodystrophy with long-tract axonopathy. Mechanistically the contributions are heterogeneous: microtubule binding and dynein-based transport along the process, an ion pump that sustains the axonal membrane potential, lipid handling, and trophic input through insulin and ephrin receptor signalling.

Mitochondria are metabolically sealed off by two membranes, and transmembrane transport is what lets substrates, ions and metabolites cross them so that oxidative metabolism can proceed. Without these carriers the matrix cannot receive pyruvate, fatty acyl groups, amino acids or the precursors of haem, and energy production stalls. Pyruvate entry depends on the MPC1/MPC2 carrier; long-chain fatty acids are routed in by the carnitine shuttle, where CPT1 enzymes on the outer membrane and CPT2 on the inner face flank the acylcarnitine/carnitine translocase SLC25A20. Other members move ornithine and basic amino acids, glycine and serine for one-carbon and haem synthesis, glutathione, and iron for cluster and haem assembly, while porins provide the outer-membrane conduit for metabolites and uncoupling proteins dissipate the proton gradient as heat. Loss of individual carriers causes inherited metabolic disease, including fatty acid oxidation defects, hyperornithinaemia and sideroblastic anaemia.

ATP made by oxidative phosphorylation is useless to the cell unless it leaves the mitochondrion, and this transport step across the mitochondrial membranes is what couples respiration to work done in the cytosol. The adenine nucleotide translocases SLC25A4, SLC25A5, SLC25A6 and the testis-enriched SLC25A31 exchange matrix ATP for cytosolic ADP across the inner membrane, setting the rate at which the ATP synthase can be resupplied with substrate and contributing to proton leak and permeability transition. A second group, SLC25A23, SLC25A24 and SLC25A41, carries ATP-Mg for phosphate in a calcium-regulated manner, adjusting the total adenine nucleotide pool of the matrix rather than merely swapping one nucleotide for another. Loss of translocase function causes cardiomyopathy, myopathy and exercise intolerance, and the isoform composition of this transport shapes how tissues buffer energy demand.

Polyufmylation is the building of chains of the ubiquitin-like modifier UFM1 on a substrate protein, an extension of the simpler single-UFM1 tag. The conjugation machinery is minimal and dedicated: UBA5 activates UFM1 in an ATP-dependent step, transfers it to the E2-like carrier UFC1, and the UFL1 ligase, stabilised by its ER-membrane partner DDRGK1, attaches it to targets and elongates the chain. This system operates chiefly at the endoplasmic reticulum, where it supports the response to ER stress, ribosome quality control on the ER surface, and reticulophagy, and it is needed for erythroid maturation and haematopoiesis. Chain length affects how the modification is read and reversed, so polyufmylation adds a layer of signal encoding beyond mere tagging. Loss-of-function mutations in these components cause severe infantile encephalopathy and neurodevelopmental disease, underscoring how dependent secretory-pathway homeostasis is on this modification.

Glycosyltransferases work inside the Golgi and ER lumen, but their nucleotide-sugar donors are made in the cytosol, so UDP-N-acetylglucosamine must be carried across the organelle membrane before any glycan can be extended. The antiporters here perform that step, exchanging the incoming nucleotide sugar for UMP released by the transferase reaction, and thereby set the luminal supply that limits N-glycan branching, keratan and other glycosaminoglycan synthesis, and O-linked glycosylation. Specificity varies: some members also carry UDP-galactose, UDP-glucuronic acid or UDP-xylose, so the group as a whole governs delivery of several donors to the secretory pathway. Loss of individual transporters has clear consequences — defective SLC35D1 causes a lethal skeletal dysplasia through impaired cartilage proteoglycan synthesis, and SLC35A3 deficiency produces congenital malformation syndromes — placing this transport step upstream of glycoprotein and proteoglycan maturation and of extracellular matrix assembly.

potassium ion import across plasma membrane is the set of transporters and channels that move potassium from the extracellular space into the cytosol, sustaining the steep inward potassium gradient on which resting membrane potential, excitability and cell volume all depend. Its failure produces cardiac arrhythmia, seizures, renal salt-wasting and deafness. The principal engine is the Na+/K+-ATPase, whose catalytic alpha and glycosylated beta subunits are tuned by small FXYD regulators; alongside it, Na-K-2Cl and K-Cl cotransporters of the SLC12 family couple potassium entry to sodium and chloride fluxes and are controlled by WNK-activated kinases such as STK39. Inward-rectifier Kir channels, including the ATP-sensitive pores formed with sulfonylurea receptors, and HCN and KCNQ1 channels provide conductive routes, linking potassium handling to insulin secretion, glial buffering of neuronal activity, epithelial transport in kidney and stomach, and pacemaking in heart and neurons.

Cells hold potassium high inside and sodium high outside, and this uptake of potassium across the plasma membrane is what builds and maintains that gradient. On it depend the resting membrane potential, the excitability of neurons and muscle, cell volume regulation, and the reabsorption of salt and water in kidney and gut; loss of individual components causes cardiac arrhythmia, epilepsy, periodic paralysis, salt-wasting tubulopathies and hyperinsulinism. The Na+/K+-ATPase pump, built from catalytic alpha and glycosylated beta subunits and tuned by small FXYD regulators, drives uptake using ATP, while cation-chloride cotransporters bring potassium in with sodium and chloride under control of a WNK-responsive kinase. Inward-rectifying and other potassium channels, including ATP-sensitive channels paired with sulfonylurea receptors and hyperpolarization-activated pacemaker channels, allow inward flux that sets pacemaking and couples metabolism to secretion.

Ribosomal RNA genes exist in hundreds of copies, and only a fraction are transcribed at any time; nucleolar chromatin organization is how the silent fraction is established and held silent. Keeping surplus rDNA repeats packaged protects the repeat array from recombination and loss, and sets ribosome output to match growth demand, which is why the nucleolus is remodelled during nutrient stress, senescence and ageing. A nucleolar remodelling complex built from BAZ2A and the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeller SMARCA5 positions nucleosomes on promoters of inactive repeats, while SUV39H1 deposits repressive histone H3K9 methylation and the NAD-dependent deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT2 strip histone acetylation. Opposing demethylases including PHF2 and PHF8 relieve repression at active copies, and the histone variant macroH2A1 and BEND3 contribute to the heterochromatic state, so the pathway acts as a rheostat on ribosome biogenesis and genome stability.

Conditioned place preference is the associative learning by which an animal comes to seek out a neutral environment that has been paired with the rewarding internal state produced by a drug, and it is the behavioural readout most used to measure drug reward and relapse risk. The genes here converge on the mesolimbic dopamine circuitry that assigns incentive value to cues: glutamatergic transmission through the AMPA receptor subunit GRIA1 and the metabotropic receptor GRM5 supports the synaptic plasticity that encodes the association, while the glutamate transporter SLC1A1 and the serotonin transporter SLC6A4 shape the clearance of those signals. Neuropeptide and receptor components, including the CART peptide precursor, the kappa opioid receptor, neurotensin and tachykinin receptors, and sigma-1, modulate whether the experience is registered as appetitive or aversive. Dysregulation of this reward learning underlies addiction and compulsive drug seeking.

The presynaptic active zone is the small patch of nerve terminal membrane where synaptic vesicles dock and fuse, and building it is what makes neurotransmitter release fast and spatially precise. Organizing this structure determines how many vesicles are release-ready, how tightly calcium channels sit next to them, and therefore the strength and timing of synaptic transmission; disruption degrades release probability and short-term plasticity, and mutations in these scaffolds are linked to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders as well as retinal and hearing deficits. Large cytomatrix proteins such as Bassoon and Piccolo form the structural core, RIM family proteins and their ELKS/CAST partners tether calcium channels and prime vesicles through interaction with the vesicular GTPase RAB3A, and adhesion molecules including neurexin align the release site with the postsynaptic receptor field across the cleft.

Angiotensin peptides cleaved from angiotensinogen act on target cells to raise blood pressure, retain sodium, and remodel tissue, and this pathway covers the cellular responses they provoke. It matters for cardiovascular and renal physiology: sustained stimulation drives vasoconstriction, cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, and hypertension, which is why the converting enzyme and the type 1 receptor are among the most widely drugged targets in medicine. Angiotensinogen is processed by ACE, and signalling proceeds mainly through the AGTR1 receptor, opposed in many tissues by AGTR2 and by MAS1, with an adaptor restraining receptor output. Downstream, protein kinase C isoforms, calcium/calmodulin-dependent and Rho-associated kinases, Src, and Rac1-dependent NADPH oxidase subunits generate contractile and oxidative responses, while NF-kB subunits, SMAD3 and NFE2L2 convert the stimulus into inflammatory, fibrotic and antioxidant gene expression. Natriuretic peptide and transport proteins reflect the accompanying volume and electrolyte control.

Cells only work if the right proteins reach the right patch of membrane, and this is the machinery that delivers proteins to the cell periphery and holds them there. It determines where ion channels, transporters, receptors and adhesion molecules sit on the surface, and so underlies epithelial polarity, synaptic strength, cilium formation, insulin-responsive glucose uptake and renal salt handling; its failure produces ciliopathies, channelopathies and loss of tight-junction integrity. Delivery runs through post-Golgi sorting and exocyst-, Rab- and SNARE-dependent vesicle fusion, with clathrin adaptors and retromer recycling cargo back from endosomes. Retention depends on scaffolds: spectrin-ankyrin and band 4.1 networks, ezrin-radixin-moesin links to actin, PDZ scaffolds such as DLG4 and the NHERF proteins, and lipid anchoring by ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases. Polarity complexes including Crumbs and Scribble components specify which surface a cargo is targeted to.

Dorsal root ganglion development builds the clusters of sensory neurons flanking the spinal cord that carry touch, temperature, proprioception and pain signals from the periphery into the central nervous system. These ganglia arise from migrating neural crest cells, which must coalesce at the correct segmental positions, commit to sensory neuronal identity, and extend bipolar axons toward both peripheral targets and the dorsal spinal cord; failure produces sensory loss and misrouted afferents. Wnt-responsive beta-catenin signalling supports crest specification and ganglion formation, while the neuropilin co-receptors and the netrin receptor UNC5C read semaphorin and netrin guidance cues that steer migrating cells and growing axons, largely as repulsive signals. A POU-domain transcription factor contributes to neuronal differentiation, and neuron-specific beta-III tubulin marks the differentiating cells and supplies the microtubule backbone of their long processes.

Fast chemical neurotransmission depends on receptors that are themselves ion channels: ligand binding opens a pore directly, converting a synaptic signal into depolarization and calcium entry within milliseconds. This ligand-gated ion channel signaling underlies excitatory transmission at central synapses and, through serotonin type-3 receptors, also emetic and gut reflexes. AMPA, kainate, delta and NMDA-type glutamate receptor subunits form the channels, with NMDA receptors acting as coincidence detectors whose calcium flux drives synaptic strengthening, kinase and calpain activity, and activity-dependent transcription via factors such as MEF2C. Scaffolds including PSD-95 and SHANK1 cluster the receptors in the postsynaptic density, while neurexin-neuroligin adhesion aligns them with presynaptic release sites. Disturbed signalling here contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death, epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism, and shapes learning and memory.

The peripheral endoplasmic reticulum is not a uniform bag but a polygonal network of narrow tubules, and this pathway builds and maintains the membrane of that network. The shape matters because tubules are where the ER makes contacts with mitochondria, endosomes and the plasma membrane, where lipid transfer and calcium handoff occur, and where the ER is drawn out along axons to reach distant synapses. Two protein families do the work: reticulons and related hairpin-containing proteins such as ARL6IP1 wedge into one leaflet to impose high membrane curvature and stabilise tubules and sheet edges, while the atlastin GTPases catalyse homotypic fusion between tubule tips to generate the three-way junctions that make the network continuous. Mutations in atlastin-1, reticulon-2 and ARL6IP1 cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, linking tubular ER geometry to the survival of long corticospinal axons.

Leukemia inhibitory factor is an IL-6 family cytokine acting through the LIFR/gp130 receptor and JAK-STAT3, and this pathway covers the transcriptional and metabolic changes a cell makes when it receives that signal. The response sustains self-renewal of naive pluripotent stem cells, drives acute-phase and inflammatory gene expression, supports blastocyst implantation and decidualization, and contributes to neuronal and megakaryocyte differentiation. Immediate targets include the negative-feedback inhibitor SOCS3 and the pluripotency-associated factor KLF4, while transcriptional regulators such as CREB1, MYB, FOSL2 and KLF5 and Polycomb-associated proteins including EED, JARID2, MTF2 and PHC1 remodel chromatin to hold or release lineage programmes. Accompanying shifts in one-carbon and hexosamine metabolism, glycolysis, and iron uptake, together with SMAD7 and Sprouty-family brakes on other growth factor inputs, integrate the cytokine signal with the cell's broader growth and differentiation state.

Smell begins when a volatile chemical binds receptors on olfactory sensory neuron cilia and is converted into an electrical signal, and this is the cellular response to odorant stimulus that makes that conversion possible and keeps it graded rather than saturating. Cyclic nucleotide-gated channel subunits open in response to odour-evoked cAMP, admitting cations including calcium, while a potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchanger clears that calcium from the cilium to terminate and adapt the response. A ciliary protein required for normal olfactory transduction kinetics shapes response duration, and proteolytic activities contribute to tissue remodelling and maturation in the olfactory epithelium, which regenerates its neurons throughout life. Loss of these components blunts odour detection and adaptation, producing anosmia or reduced odour discrimination, with knock-on effects on feeding behaviour and avoidance of hazards.

Endothelins are short peptides released mainly by endothelium that act on G protein-coupled receptors to constrict vascular smooth muscle, remodel vessels, and guide the migration of neural crest derivatives; the cellular reaction to such a stimulus is what this pathway captures. Downstream consequences include changes in gene expression, contractility, and secretion, and loss of endothelin signalling through the receptor EDNRB produces aganglionic megacolon and pigmentation defects because enteric neurons and melanocytes depend on it. Signal relay here involves the adaptor CRK and the insulin-receptor substrate IRS2 linking receptor engagement to cytoskeletal and metabolic responses, protein kinase D1 transducing diacylglycerol-dependent signals, and a large complement of Kruppel-like transcription factors, including the endothelial shear-responsive KLF2 and KLF4, that translate the stimulus into transcriptional programmes for vascular tone, growth and differentiation.

Cells respond to lectins carbohydrate-binding proteins presented by pathogens, damaged cells or used experimentally as mitogens by switching on transcription, cytokine output and cytoskeletal rearrangement. The receptors here are themselves C-type lectins: Dectin-1 and Dectin-2 recognise fungal β-glucan and mannan on the surface of myeloid cells, while the NKG2 family paired with CD94 and the activating NKG2D receptor let natural killer cells read stress ligands on infected or transformed targets. Engagement recruits the ITAM adaptor DAP12 or an intrinsic ITAM-like motif, activating Src-family kinases LYN, FYN and SRC together with SYK, which drives PLCγ2, TAK1–IKK–NF-κB signalling through TRAF6 and PAK-dependent actin remodelling, with CREBBP and EP300 coactivating the resulting transcription. This is how antifungal immunity, NK cytotoxicity and lectin-induced lymphocyte activation are initiated.

Mammals defend body temperature and dispose of excess dietary energy by burning fuel for heat, and adaptive thermogenesis is the regulated form of that response to cold, feeding or stress. It is the defining function of brown and beige adipose tissue, and its capacity correlates inversely with obesity and insulin resistance in humans. Sympathetic noradrenaline acting on beta-adrenergic receptors raises cAMP, driving lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation while uncoupling protein 1 short-circuits the mitochondrial proton gradient so that substrate oxidation yields heat rather than ATP; creatine and calcium-cycling routes provide UCP1-independent alternatives. A transcriptional program built on PRDM16, PPARGC1A, EBF2 and thyroid hormone activation by the deiodinase DIO2 specifies and maintains thermogenic adipocytes, with chromatin modifiers, circadian factors, leptin and FGF21 signalling, and type 2 cytokines tuning the response to nutritional and environmental state.

Vacuolar localization covers the positioning of lysosomes and related secretory granules within the cell, which determines where degradation, nutrient sensing and regulated secretion actually happen. Cells that must release granule contents on demand – mast cells degranulating in response to IgE crosslinking, cytotoxic lymphocytes killing targets, platelets – depend on moving these organelles to the right membrane, and failures produce immunodeficiency and pigmentation disorders of the Chediak–Higashi and Hermansky–Pudlak type. The BORC complex with ARL8B recruits kinesins for anterograde transport along microtubules, while PLEKHM1, PLEKHM2 and dynein adaptors pull organelles inward; SNARE proteins such as VAMP7 and VAMP8 with UNC13D and STXBP2 then execute fusion. Positioning is coupled to metabolic state through the LAMTOR/Ragulator–FLCN–TFEB axis, and to receptor signalling via SYK, LYN and BTK downstream of Fc and KIT receptors.

Vacuolar localization covers the transport and anchoring of vacuolar and lysosome-related organelles at defined positions in the cytoplasm, a prerequisite for nutrient sensing, autophagosome–lysosome fusion and for regulated secretion of granule contents. Positioning is set by a multisubunit BORC complex acting through the small GTPase ARL8B to recruit kinesin motors such as KIF5B with its light chain, driving anterograde movement along microtubules, while dynein-side adaptors and PLEKHM1/PLEKHM2 pull organelles inward and couple them to fusion machinery including VPS33A/VPS33B and multiple VAMP SNAREs. Coordination with mTORC1 through the Ragulator subunit LAMTOR1, the FLCN complex and the transcription factor TFEB ties organelle position to metabolic state. The same machinery governs secretory lysosomes in mast cells and cytotoxic cells, where UNC13D, STXBP2 and Fc receptor–SYK–LYN signalling trigger degranulation; loss of these components causes pigmentation and immune deficiencies of the Hermansky-Pudlak and haemophagocytic type.

Chemokines are small secreted proteins that tell leukocytes where to go, and the cellular response to a chemokine stimulus converts that positional information into directed migration, adhesion, degranulation and changes in gene expression. This traffic control underlies immune surveillance, lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes and mucosa, neutrophil and monocyte recruitment to inflamed tissue, and the organisation of germinal centres; deranged versions of it drive chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and tumour metastasis, and one receptor here, CCR5, serves as an HIV entry co-receptor. Ligands of the CC, CXC, CX3C and C families engage seven-transmembrane receptors coupled through Gi proteins to Rho- and kinase-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling, with JAK2, LYN, PTK2B and MAPK1 among the downstream effectors. Atypical receptors that scavenge rather than signal shape the gradients, while WNK1-OXSR1-STK39 and SLC12A2 link migration to cell volume regulation.

Vascular smooth muscle cells in a healthy artery wall are largely quiescent and contractile, and their re-entry into the cell cycle is the central event in neointima formation, restenosis after angioplasty, atherosclerotic plaque growth and hypertensive vessel remodelling. This pathway covers the signals that drive or restrain that proliferation, together with the accompanying switch away from the contractile phenotype marked by calponin, tropomyosin and the myocardin-driven programme. Mitogens such as PDGF-B, FGF2, endothelin-1 and IGF1 act through receptor kinases and JAK2, while cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors p21 and p27, PTEN, PPARG and cGMP-dependent kinase signalling oppose growth. Matrix metalloproteinases and ADAMTS1 permit the migration that accompanies expansion, and a large complement of microRNAs, notably the miR-143/145-independent regulators miR-21, miR-221/222 and miR-146a, tunes the balance between quiescence and growth. Inflammatory and metabolic inputs including TNF, IL10 and adiponectin feed in.

Meiosis deliberately breaks its own chromosomes so that homologues can find each other, and repairing those breaks by homologous recombination is what generates crossovers, holds bivalents together, and shuffles parental alleles into gametes. The topoisomerase-like enzyme SPO11 makes the programmed double-strand breaks, PRDM9 marks where they occur by placing histone methylation at recombination hotspots, and the resected ends are loaded with the strand-exchange proteins RAD51 and the meiosis-specific DMC1 to invade the homologous chromosome. Accessory factors including HSF2BP, BRME1 and MCMDC2 tune recombinase assembly and intermediate processing, while TERB1, TERB2 and MAJIN tether telomeres to the nuclear envelope so chromosomes can move and pair. Failure here causes asynapsis, unrepaired breaks, apoptotic loss of germ cells, and human infertility or aneuploid eggs and sperm.

Short-term synaptic potentiation is the transient strengthening of transmitter release that occurs when action potentials arrive at a synapse in rapid succession, lasting tens to hundreds of milliseconds. It gives synapses with low initial release probability a use-dependent gain, allowing neurons to act as filters that respond preferentially to bursts and encode information in spike timing rather than rate alone; working memory, sound localisation and the temporal fidelity of cortical circuits all depend on such facilitation. Mechanistically it reflects residual presynaptic calcium acting on high-affinity sensors, with synaptotagmin-7 the calcium sensor for facilitation and PRRT2 shaping vesicle priming and release probability alongside the SNARE machinery. Loss of these presynaptic regulators produces paroxysmal disorders, dyskinesia and epilepsy, and disturbed short-term dynamics also accompanies altered secretase and lipid metabolism in neurons.

Short-term synaptic potentiation is the transient strengthening of transmitter release that follows a burst of closely spaced action potentials, lasting tens to hundreds of milliseconds and most evident at synapses whose initial release probability is low. It lets a synapse act as a high-pass filter, so that bursts of activity are conveyed more faithfully than isolated spikes, and it supplies the working-memory-like buffering that underlies temporal coding in cortical and cerebellar circuits. Mechanistically it depends on residual presynaptic calcium acting on high-affinity sensors and on regulators of vesicle priming and fusion: synaptotagmin-7 is the calcium sensor that sustains facilitation, while PRRT2 tunes release and vesicle availability at the active zone, and its loss causes paroxysmal dyskinesia and infantile epilepsy. Lipid composition and processing of membrane proteins by the gamma-secretase component nicastrin also shape presynaptic efficacy over this timescale.

Cells must detect when amino acids run short and switch from growth to conservation, and this starvation response is the machinery that makes the switch. Two arms dominate.
