Sensors that read leucine, arginine and S-adenosylmethionine levels (CASTOR1, SAMTOR, the sestrins) act through the Rag GTPases and their GATOR and KICSTOR regulators to determine whether mTORC1 is active at the lysosome; loss of amino acids releases the brake on autophagy, engaging BECN1 and LC3 and licensing TFEB-driven lysosomal gene expression. In parallel, uncharged tRNA activates the kinase GCN2 with its partner GCN1, phosphorylating eIF2α to dampen general translation while inducing ATF4 and downstream stress transcription factors that restore amino acid supply and transporters such as SLC38A2. Together these arms rebalance protein synthesis against protein breakdown, and their failure leaves cells unable to survive nutrient restriction or to tune growth to supply, with consequences for cancer metabolism and epilepsy-associated mTOR disorders.

Xenobiotic transport across blood-brain barrier describes how drugs, toxins and other foreign chemicals are moved into and, more often, out of the brain across the endothelium that seals the cerebral vasculature. It is the main reason the central nervous system is chemically protected, and the main reason many otherwise effective drugs never reach their targets there. Efflux pumps of the ATP-binding cassette family, notably P-glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein along with multidrug resistance-associated proteins, sit in the luminal membrane of brain capillary endothelial cells and expel substrates back into blood using ATP hydrolysis, while organic cation carriers of the solute carrier family mediate uptake steps. The same transporters govern chemotherapy resistance in tumours and drive clinically consequential drug-drug interactions, so their expression and induction shape neuropharmacology and neurotoxicant exposure alike.

The brain is shielded from circulating drugs and toxins by transporters in the endothelial cells that line its capillaries, and xenobiotic transport across the blood-brain barrier is the directed movement of such compounds through that interface. The barrier's gatekeeping explains why many otherwise potent drugs never reach their central targets, and why inhibiting or saturating these carriers alters neurotoxicity and CNS drug exposure. ATP-driven efflux pumps including P-glycoprotein, the multidrug resistance-associated proteins and the breast cancer resistance protein actively expel a chemically broad range of substrates back into blood, while organic cation transporters of the solute carrier family mediate uptake of small charged compounds. The same efflux proteins limit chemotherapy penetration into brain tumours and contribute to multidrug resistance, linking this barrier function to pharmacokinetics, detoxification and drug delivery strategy.

The retina is shielded from circulating solutes and immune cells by a barrier built at two levels: tight junctions between retinal capillary endothelial cells form the inner barrier, and the retinal pigment epithelium forms the outer one. Establishing this blood-retinal barrier is what keeps the photoreceptor environment stable and the neural retina dehydrated and transparent; when it breaks down, fluid and protein leak into the retina, as in diabetic macular oedema. The genes here reflect a Norrin-driven arm of this process, in which the ligand NDP acting through the co-receptor LRP5 stabilises beta-catenin to drive an endothelial barrier programme, including the tight junction protein claudin-5 and suppression of vesicular transcytosis via MFSD2A. Mutations in this ligand-receptor pair cause Norrie disease and familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, with defective retinal vascularisation and leakage.

When DNA is damaged, cells arrest the cycle until repair is complete, and this pathway tunes how strongly and how long that damage checkpoint is imposed. Setting the threshold correctly matters in both directions: too little restraint lets cells replicate and divide with broken or unreplicated DNA, driving mutation and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, while failure to release the arrest locks cells in senescence. Members act at several levels — the BRCA1–BARD1 ubiquitin ligase and its deubiquitinase partner BRCC3 with BABAM2 shape signalling at damage sites; ETAA1 stimulates ATR; the TELO2–TTI1–TTI2 complex stabilises ATR and ATM as PIKK client kinases; cullin–RING ligases with SKP1 and RBX1 impose ubiquitin-dependent turnover on checkpoint and repair factors. RPA2, RAD51 and BRCA2 tie the decision to replication fork protection and homologous recombination.

When DNA is damaged, cells must halt cycle progression long enough for repair to occur, and this pathway covers the inputs that turn that checkpoint on or make it stronger. Loss of such reinforcement lets damaged cells replicate and divide, feeding genomic instability of the kind that underlies cancer predisposition and sensitivity to genotoxic therapy. Much of the activity here converges on the apical damage-sensing kinases: TELO2, TTI1 and TTI2 form the TTT co-chaperone module that, with HSP90, stabilises newly synthesised PIKK-family kinases including ATM and ATR, so that checkpoint signalling can be mounted at all. CCAR2 contributes through regulation of deacetylase activity and damage-responsive transcription, while MAP3K20 links stress-activated kinase signalling to arrest and apoptotic outcomes. Together they set the threshold at which damage translates into cell cycle delay.

regulation of protein localization to cell surface controls how many copies of a given membrane protein are displayed on the plasma membrane at any moment, tuning a cell's sensitivity to its environment. Because receptors, ion channels and transporters only act where they are presented, this regulation sets synaptic strength, cardiac excitability, immune receptor signalling and hormone responsiveness; its failure underlies arrhythmias from mistrafficked sodium channels, receptor loss in metabolic disease, and skin barrier defects. The genes span the machinery that decides surface abundance: Rab11 and its effectors with ARF6 and GBF1 driving recycling and exocytic delivery, syntaxins executing the final fusion step, PICALM and SNX33 handling endocytic retrieval, NEDD4L ubiquitinating cargo for removal, chaperones such as HSP90 and RIC3 licensing folding and assembly, and scaffolds and adaptors including caveolin-3, GOPC and TYROBP that hold complexes in place. Growth factors and cytokines act as upstream cues.

How many copies of a receptor, channel or transporter sit on the plasma membrane is set not by transcription alone but by trafficking, and this pathway covers the processes that tune that surface abundance up or down. The stakes are concrete: surface density of sodium and potassium channels sets cardiac and neuronal excitability, surface receptor levels set the gain of growth factor and immune signalling, and mistrafficking underlies arrhythmia syndromes and skin barrier defects. The genes span the routes involved — small GTPases and their effectors such as ARF6, RAB11B and RAB11FIP5 driving recycling endosome delivery, GBF1 acting at the Golgi, SNX33 and PICALM affecting endocytic retrieval, the ubiquitin ligase NEDD4L marking channels for removal, chaperones including HSP90AB1 and RIC3 assisting folding and assembly, and SNARE proteins STX3 and STX4 executing fusion. Ligands and receptors in the list place this regulation downstream of signalling as well as upstream of it.

Whether a receptor or channel is present at the plasma membrane determines how strongly a cell responds to its environment, and negative regulation of protein localization to the cell surface is the set of processes that keep surface levels down by blocking delivery, diverting cargo, or pulling it back inside. This tuning sets receptor density for hormone and neurotransmitter signalling: reduced leptin receptor display blunts satiety signalling, and altered surface levels of glutamate receptors and ion channels change synaptic strength and cardiac or neuronal excitability. Mechanisms represented here include ARF6- and sorting nexin-dependent endosomal traffic, clathrin adaptor-mediated internalization through PICALM, ubiquitin ligase-driven downregulation by NEDD4L, retention or lysosomal routing via GOPC and ASTN2, and scaffolding by caveolin-3 and actinin in muscle. The overall effect is turnover and retention rather than synthesis, making surface abundance a continuously adjustable quantity.

How much of a given receptor, channel or transporter sits in the plasma membrane at any moment is set by trafficking, and this pathway covers the events that push that balance upward. Increased surface delivery determines how strongly a cell can respond to a ligand, conduct an ionic current, or present a signalling complex to its neighbours, so it underlies processes from cardiac excitability to immune receptor assembly. Mechanistically the members act at several steps: SNAREs such as STX3 and STX4 catalyse fusion of carrier vesicles with the plasma membrane, sorting nexins and COMMD1 direct cargo away from degradative routes, chaperones including HSP90AB1 stabilise client proteins for export, and dedicated accessories like RIC3 promote maturation of nicotinic receptors while RANGRF and GPD1L influence sodium channel delivery. Immune adaptors TYROBP, FCER1G and CD247 escort their partner receptors to the surface, linking this trafficking control to receptor-mediated activation.

Whether a bipotential gonad becomes a testis is decided by a small set of regulators, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how far and how fast that male programme proceeds. Its output determines Sertoli cell differentiation, seminiferous cord formation and the hormonal environment that masculinises the rest of the embryo; when it fails, the result is gonadal dysgenesis, sex reversal or ovotesticular development, sometimes with Wilms tumour or congenital diaphragmatic hernia depending on which gene is affected. Mechanistically, SRY acts with the nuclear receptor NR5A1 and cofactors including WT1, ZFPM2 and CITED2 to drive SOX9 expression, which reinforces the testicular fate, while WNT4 promotes the competing ovarian route. DMRT1 maintains the male identity after it is established, and DHX37 is required in early germ cell and gonadal development.

This is the broad set of controls that tune how fast, how far and in what direction a developing body builds its tissues. It covers the modulation of multicellular organismal development rather than any single organ programme, and its members set the pace of patterning, growth, differentiation and tissue remodelling from embryo through adult homeostasis. The major morphogen systems are all represented — WNT ligands with FZD receptors and LEF1/CTNNB1, Hedgehog through PTCH1, SMO and GLI factors, BMP/TGF-beta via SMADs, and Notch with JAG/DLL ligands and HES/HEY repressors — alongside lineage transcription factors (SOX, HOX, PAX, RUNX, GATA), chromatin remodellers such as the SWI/SNF and INO80 complexes, many microRNAs, and axon-guidance cues including slits, semaphorins and ephrins. Growth factors, cytokines and extracellular matrix components provide the environmental input. Disruption of these regulators produces congenital malformation, skeletal and neurodevelopmental syndromes, and contributes to cancer when developmental signalling is reactivated.

Organs acquire their shape through iterative branching, budding, folding and condensation of epithelium against mesenchyme, and this set covers the factors that tune how far, how fast and in what pattern that shaping proceeds. It matters because the same tuning determines nephron number in the kidney, branch density in lung, salivary gland and mammary tissue, tooth and hair placode spacing, and skeletal and craniofacial form; its disturbance underlies renal hypodysplasia, cleft and tooth agenesis syndromes, and polycystic kidney disease. Secreted cues dominate — BMPs with their antagonists noggin and gremlin, FGF7 and FGF10 signalling to FGFR1 through FRS2 with Sprouty feedback, hedgehog acting via smoothened, GDNF driving ureteric bud outgrowth, and WNT ligands read out through beta-catenin or planar cell polarity via VANGL2. Transcription factors including WT1, PAX8, SIX1/SIX2, SOX9 and GATA3 convert these gradients into progenitor fate and epithelial morphogenetic behaviour.

Stem cells must divide often enough to replenish a tissue but not so often that the pool is exhausted or transformed, and this pathway covers the inputs that set that rate. Its balance determines whether haematopoietic and other progenitor compartments are maintained for life, and its loss underlies both marrow failure and leukaemic expansion. The regulators here act at several levels: transcription factors and chromatin-associated proteins including ESRRB, PRDM15, MLLT3 and SOX17 sustain self-renewal programmes in pluripotent and blood progenitor states; SFRP2 tunes Wnt ligand availability in the surrounding niche; a microRNA and a CDK2-associated protein restrain cell cycle entry; and a mitochondrial protease component links organelle quality to proliferative capacity. Together they connect cell-extrinsic niche signals and intrinsic transcriptional identity to the decision to divide, and to whether the daughters remain stem cells or differentiate.

Stem cells must divide without differentiating, and the processes that tune how strongly that self-renewing state is held determine whether a tissue keeps a progenitor pool or exhausts it. Too much maintenance activity yields tumour-initiating cells; too little causes premature differentiation and failure of tissue renewal and regeneration. Much of the regulation here is chromatin-based: SWI/SNF-family remodellers built around SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and ARID1A, the Sin3-HDAC1/HDAC2 corepressor with RBBP4/RBBP7, non-canonical BAF components such as BRD9, and modifiers including TET1, KDM2B and SIRT6 set the accessibility of pluripotency and lineage loci. These act alongside transcriptional drivers of self-renewal such as MYC, PRDM14, ESRRB, TEAD4 and YAP1, Hippo input through SAV1, and secreted cues from NODAL, BMP7, WNT9B and Hedgehog signalling via SMO, plus post-transcriptional control by ELAVL1, the CCR4-NOT complex and microRNA regulation.

Homologous recombination is the accurate way to mend a double-strand break, but it is not always the right choice, and this set covers the braking mechanisms that suppress it. Restraint matters because recombination on an unreplicated or inappropriate template produces loss of heterozygosity and chromosome rearrangement, and because cell-cycle stage and chromatin context determine whether a break should instead be sealed by end joining. Several routes are represented: 53BP1 with RIF1 and the shieldin subunits blocks resection of broken ends and channels repair away from recombination, helicases such as RECQL5, HELB and FBH1 strip or antagonise RAD51 filaments, RADX and PARPBP tune filament stability, and POLQ commits ends to microhomology-mediated joining. Kinases including PLK1, CSNK2A1 and ABL1 and chromatin writers such as KMT5A and KAT5 impose additional control. Loss of this restraint underlies the synthetic lethal relationships exploited by PARP inhibitors in BRCA-mutant tumours.

regulation of cell-cell adhesion mediated by cadherin controls how tightly epithelial and endothelial cells hold onto one another, tuning the strength and turnover of cadherin-based junctions rather than building them. This tuning decides whether a tissue stays a coherent sheet or lets cells move: it governs epithelial integrity, junctional remodelling during morphogenesis and wound repair, endothelial barrier tightness, and the loss of adhesion that accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumour invasion. The regulators act at several levels. Secreted cues including TGFB1 with its inhibitor SMAD7, BMP6, WNT3A, WNT5A, VEGFA and Notch signalling reset cadherin expression and junctional state, while transcription factors such as FOXA1 and FOXA2 maintain epithelial identity. At the junction itself, scaffolds and adaptors such as afadin and ZO-1 couple cadherin complexes to the actin cytoskeleton, and PTPRU, PPM1F and the metalloprotease ADAM19 modify or cleave junctional components to loosen contacts.

Cadherin-based junctions hold epithelial and endothelial sheets together, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how strongly and where those junctions form. Adhesion strength is not fixed: it is dialled up as tissues differentiate and released during wound healing, developmental rearrangement, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, so its regulation sets the boundary between a sealed barrier and a migratory cell. The genes here act at several levels — junctional scaffolds such as afadin and ZO-1 that couple cadherin complexes to the cytoskeleton, a receptor phosphatase and a phosphatase acting on junctional signalling, a metalloproteinase and plasminogen-related proteolysis that can shed adhesive contacts, and developmental signals including TGFB1 with SMAD7, BMP6, NOTCH receptors, WNT3A, WNT5A and VEGFA that reprogramme adhesion transcriptionally. Loss of control here contributes to tumour invasion, vascular leak, and defective morphogenesis.

negative regulation of cell-cell adhesion mediated by cadherin covers the processes that loosen or dismantle cadherin-based junctions, converting a cohesive epithelium into cells able to move, divide apart, or change identity. This is how tissues remodel: it permits gastrulation and neural crest migration, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition during wound repair and fibrosis, endothelial junction opening for angiogenesis and leukocyte passage, and, when persistent, the loss of E-cadherin that precedes tumour invasion and metastasis. The genes act at several levels: secreted cues such as TGFB1, BMP6 and VEGFA that reprogram junctional gene expression, NOTCH1 and NOTCH4 signalling that specifies mesenchymal and endothelial states, EPCAM which antagonises cadherin-mediated adhesion at the membrane, and regulators of the actomyosin machinery such as PPM1F that control the contractile tension junctions require. Plasminogen contributes proteolytic clearance of the surrounding matrix and adhesion receptors.

Cadherin-based junctions must be loosened as well as built, and this collection covers the processes that dampen or dismantle cadherin-mediated cell-cell adhesion. Weakening these contacts allows epithelia to become migratory, endothelial barriers to become permeable, and neurons and their partners to remodel connections; the same programme is exploited during tumour invasion and metastasis, where loss of cadherin-dependent cohesion is a defining step. The regulators here act by several routes: TGFB1 and BMP6 signal transcriptional changes that shift cadherin repertoires and drive epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions, NOTCH1 and NOTCH4 modulate junctional stability in endothelium, VEGFA promotes vascular permeability with junction disassembly, EPCAM interferes with classical cadherin adhesion in epithelia, and plasminogen contributes proteolytic activity at the cell surface. PPM1F acts on cytoskeletal contractility that junctions depend on.

Cadherin-based junctions hold epithelial and other tissues together, and this pathway covers the inputs that strengthen them — increasing the rate or extent of cell–cell adhesion mediated by cadherin. Strong cadherin adhesion maintains epithelial sheets, polarity and tissue architecture; when it is weakened, cells detach, become motile and undergo the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transitions that underlie invasion and metastasis, so positive regulators act as brakes on that switch. The genes involved work at several levels: junctional scaffolds such as afadin and the tight-junction protein ZO-1 link adhesion receptors to the actin cytoskeleton, the receptor phosphatase PTPRU acts on cadherin–catenin complexes, secreted Wnt ligands including WNT3A and WNT5A signal toward junction assembly and catenin pools, SMAD7 restrains TGF-beta-driven junction loss, and FOXA1 and FOXA2 sustain the epithelial transcriptional programme that supplies junctional components.

Wnt ligands can signal without stabilizing β-catenin, instead steering cell polarity, oriented cell movement and cytoskeletal remodelling; this pathway covers the inputs that set how strongly and how long that branch runs. Tuning it matters for convergent extension during gastrulation, limb and palate outgrowth, planar polarity of epithelia and ciliated tissues, and vascular remodelling, and its dysregulation contributes to skeletal and craniofacial malformations, ciliopathy-associated phenotypes and tumour invasiveness. The regulators here act at several levels: WNT5A and WNT5B are the prototypical non-canonical ligands, RSPO3 potentiates and ZNRF3 restrains receptor availability, secreted frizzled-related proteins and DKK1 sequester ligands or block receptor engagement, and casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon, DVL-binding proteins such as DAAM2, DACT1, NKD1 and ANKRD6, and the adaptor DAB2 modulate downstream branch choice. Several members are also ciliary or basal-body proteins, tying polarity signalling to cilium function.

Wnt ligands can act through routes that bypass beta-catenin, controlling cell polarity, oriented cell movement and cytoskeletal remodelling, and this pathway covers the brakes applied to that non-canonical branch. Restraining it matters because unchecked planar polarity and Wnt/calcium signalling distort convergent extension during gastrulation, ciliary and skeletal patterning, and adipose and metabolic tissue behaviour. Two secreted frizzled-related proteins here act as decoys that bind Wnt ligands away from their receptors, with one of them linked to islet function and metabolic disease and the other to bone and cartilage phenotypes. Membrane-level control comes from a ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates frizzled receptors and drives their removal from the cell surface, lowering receptor availability. An intraflagellar transport component ties the regulation to the cilium, a compartment where Wnt responsiveness is set and dampened.

Wnt ligands can signal without stabilizing beta-catenin, instead steering cell polarity, oriented cell movement and cytoskeletal remodelling, and this is the set of influences that raise the output of that non-canonical branch. It matters for convergent extension during gastrulation, neural tube and limb morphogenesis, planar orientation of epithelial cells, and for chemotactic and invasive behaviour that is reactivated in tumours. WNT5A and WNT5B are the prototypical ligands here, acting through receptor complexes that engage RHO- and JNK-directed effectors rather than TCF-dependent transcription. Casein kinase 1 delta and epsilon phosphorylate pathway components including Dishevelled, setting branch choice; DAB2, ANKRD6 and NKD1 bias signalling away from the beta-catenin route; RSPO3 and glypican-3 modulate ligand reception at the cell surface, while SFRP1 and DKK1 are secreted modulators whose net effect depends on context. ABL1 links the pathway to cytoskeletal and adhesion control.

Whether a ubiquitylated protein is actually destroyed, and how fast, is tuned rather than fixed, and this regulatory layer sets the half-lives of transcription factors, cyclins, misfolded proteins and signalling intermediates. It governs cell cycle transitions, oxidative-stress responses, Wnt signalling output and the clearance of aggregation-prone substrates, and its failure underlies tumour suppressor loss and neurodegeneration. Control is exerted at several points: kinases such as GSK3B and casein kinases prime substrates for recognition, substrate adaptors and ligase components including FBXW7, MDM2, KEAP1, PRKN and STUB1 determine what is marked, and deubiquitinases such as USP7, USP14 and ATXN3 reverse or edit chains before the proteasome acts. Chaperones and shuttling factors including BAG proteins, VCP, RAD23A/B and ubiquilin deliver clients, while SUMOylation, acetylation and sirtuin activity modulate the machinery itself. Ribosomal proteins RPL5, RPL11 and RPL23 feed nucleolar stress into MDM2-p53 control.

Proteins tagged with ubiquitin are normally committed to destruction by the proteasome, and this pathway covers the opposing side of that decision: the mechanisms that stop, slow or reverse ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolism so that a substrate is spared. Sparing matters because it sets the half-life of regulators such as p53, MDM2, cyclins and developmental signalling components, and so determines whether a cell arrests, dies or proliferates. Several routes appear here. Deubiquitinases including USP7, USP5, USP14 and UCHL5 trim or remove chains, some acting directly at the proteasome to delay substrate processing. Cochaperones and UBX- or UBL-domain adaptors such as BAG6, SGTA and UBXN1 hold clients away from degradation or shuttle them elsewhere. Ribosomal proteins RPL5, RPL11 and RPL23 act as a nucleolar stress brake on MDM2. Kinases, acetyltransferases and O-GlcNAc transferase add modifications that mask degrons, linking protein stability to nutrient and damage signalling. Loss of this restraint destabilises tumour suppressors and underlies cancer and neurodegenerative proteostasis defects.

Regulated destruction of proteins by the ubiquitin-proteasome system sets the abundance and lifetime of most short-lived regulatory proteins, and this collection covers the factors that push that turnover upward. Enhancing ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis is how cells clear misfolded and damaged substrates, terminate signalling, and enforce irreversible transitions such as anaphase and mitotic exit, where the APC/C activators CDC20 and FZR1 act with mitotic kinases. Others deliver substrates to the machinery or build the ligases that mark them: SCF components including FBXW7 and RBX1, CRL2 adaptors, the E3s MDM2, PRKN, SMURF1 and STUB1, and chaperone-linked triage through VCP, BAG2 and HSPA1A. Kinases and scaffolds such as GSK3B, CSNK1 isoforms and AXIN prime substrates for recognition, as in beta-catenin and NRF2/KEAP1 control. Loss of this regulation stabilises oncoproteins and allows aggregation-prone proteins to persist, linking it to cancer and neurodegeneration.

Cortisol output from the adrenal cortex sets metabolic fuel mobilisation, blood pressure and the stress response, and the tone of that output is set not only by pituitary ACTH but by local signals that decide how much steroidogenic capacity the zona fasciculata carries. This regulatory layer tunes the rate and extent of cortisol biosynthesis, and its derangement produces adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing-type hypercortisolism or, in the opposite direction, glucocorticoid insufficiency. The genes involved include secreted morphogens of the BMP and WNT families together with the WNT modulator DKK3, which pattern adrenal zonation and progenitor renewal; the transcriptional repressor REST, which restrains steroidogenic gene expression; and H6PD, which supplies NADPH inside the endoplasmic reticulum so that 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 regenerates active cortisol from cortisone in peripheral tissues. The pathway therefore links developmental signalling and cofactor supply to endocrine steroid output.

Insulin-secreting beta cells arise from pancreatic endocrine progenitors, and this pathway covers the inputs that tune how many are made and how far their differentiation proceeds. Beta cell mass set during development and early life determines lifelong capacity to buffer blood glucose; too few functional beta cells, or cells that fail to complete their maturation programme, leads to diabetes. Lineage identity is imposed transcriptionally, with NKX6-1 specifying and maintaining the beta cell state and RFX3 supporting islet gene expression and ciliary function. Growth factor and nutrient signalling modulate this: AKT1 acting through GSK3 and through RHEB-dependent mTOR activation promotes beta cell growth and survival, with BAD linking metabolic input to apoptotic decisions. The circadian transcription factors CLOCK and BMAL1 tie islet development and secretory competence to daily feeding rhythms.

Epithelial sheets and tissues need a shared sense of direction within the plane of the sheet: hair cells in the cochlea orient uniformly, skin hairs and ependymal cilia point the same way, and cells intercalate directionally to elongate the body axis. Modulation of the planar cell polarity branch of Wnt signalling sets how strongly and where that non-canonical, Frizzled/Dishevelled-dependent output fires, as distinct from the beta-catenin route. Regulators here act at several levels: secreted modulators such as DKK1 and RSPO3 and the ubiquitin ligase ZNRF3 tune receptor availability, DACT1, NKD1 and ANKRD6 impinge on Dishevelled, and the endocytic adaptor DAB2 shifts receptor trafficking. Several members, including MKS1 and NPHP3, tie the pathway to ciliary structure, which is why disturbed polarity signalling appears in neural tube closure defects, ciliopathies and cystic kidney disease.

Planar cell polarity is the non-canonical arm of Wnt signalling that orients cells within the plane of an epithelium, and this pathway covers the inputs that turn it up. Its output is tissue-level organisation: coordinated hair and cilia orientation, convergent extension during gastrulation and neural tube closure, and oriented cell division, so loss of it produces shortened body axes and neural tube defects rather than the overgrowth typical of canonical Wnt failure. Several members act by biasing the choice between branches, since antagonists of the canonical route such as DKK1, NKD1, DAB2 and the diversin-like ANKRD6 free ligand and receptor for polarity signalling, while RSPO3 and the membrane-tethered proteoglycan GPC3 modulate how Wnt ligands are presented at the cell surface. ABL1 contributes cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase activity downstream, linking polarity cues to the actin cytoskeleton and directed cell movement.

Cells must replicate their genome exactly once per cycle, and this collection of brakes on DNA-templated DNA replication is how over-replication, re-firing of origins and replication under stress are prevented. Geminin binds and sequesters the licensing factor CDT1 so that origins cannot be reloaded after S phase begins, while FBXO5 (Emi1) restrains APC/C activity to keep that block in place; a cullin-RING ligase module built from CUL2, RBX1, elongin B and C with the substrate receptor LRR1 targets replisome components for degradation, contributing to replisome disassembly at termination. TIMELESS and TIPIN stabilise stalled forks and couple them to checkpoint signalling, and SLFN11 kills replication in cells suffering DNA damage, which underlies its influence on responses to chemotherapy. Loss of these controls produces re-replication, amplified genomic segments and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours.

positive regulation of DNA-templated DNA replication covers the inputs that license and accelerate genome duplication, determining when a cell commits to copying its DNA and how efficiently replication forks are established and sustained. Cells depend on it to complete S phase on schedule; too little activity stalls proliferation, while unrestrained activity drives re-replication, fork collapse and the genome instability characteristic of cancer. The core mechanism is kinase-driven origin firing: the CDC7 catalytic subunit paired with its DBF4 or DBF4B regulatory partners phosphorylates the replicative helicase, while CDK2 activity at the G1/S transition, aided by the cyclin A anchoring factor CIZ1, converts licensed origins into active forks. Chromatin remodellers such as INO80 and ATRX keep templates accessible at difficult loci, atypical E2F factors tune replication-associated transcription and endoreduplication, and SSBP1 supports mitochondrial DNA synthesis alongside the nuclear program.

Cells only copy their genomes when licensed to do so, and this collection covers the inputs that raise the rate or extent of DNA-templated DNA replication, whether by firing origins, driving entry into S phase, or sustaining fork activity. The core activating step is kinase-driven: CDC7 with its regulatory partners DBF4 and DBF4B phosphorylates the replicative helicase to convert licensed origins into active forks, while CDK2 couples this to cell cycle progression and CIZ1 helps position replication factors in nuclear foci. Chromatin contributors such as the INO80 remodelling complex and ATRX keep templates accessible and forks stable through difficult regions, and SSBP1 supports replication of mitochondrial DNA. Because unchecked origin firing produces re-replication and genome instability, these activators are balanced by repressive transcription factors, and their overactivity is a recurring feature of proliferating tumour cells.

regulation of leukocyte apoptotic process controls how many white blood cells live or die, setting the size and composition of the immune compartment during development, infection and resolution of inflammation. Too little death leaves autoreactive lymphocytes alive and favours autoimmunity or lymphoid malignancy; too much causes immunodeficiency and lymphopenia. The genes span both the survival and killing arms: cytokine and receptor inputs such as IL7R, IL2, JAK3 and STAT5A keep thymocytes and T cells alive, while BAX, PUMA, FADD, TP53 and RIPK3 execute or trigger death. Layered on top are transcriptional regulators (BCL6, FOXP1, MYC, glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3), microRNAs, chemokine cues that position cells in survival niches, and clearance receptors of the TAM family that recognise apoptotic cells. The pathway therefore underlies thymic selection, contraction of effector responses after antigen clearance, and immune tolerance.

Whether a leukocyte lives or dies by apoptosis determines the size of immune cell pools, the removal of self-reactive clones, and the resolution of inflammation once an infection is cleared. This regulatory layer sets the frequency and extent of leukocyte death: survival cytokine signalling through IL7R, IL2 and JAK3-STAT5A sustains developing and activated lymphocytes, while BAX, BBC3, TP53 and FADD-coupled receptor death routes execute or license killing. Antigen-receptor and kinase modules such as BTK, LYN, PRKCQ and PI3K catalytic subunits tune thresholds during thymic and B cell selection, and transcription factors including BCL6, FOXP1, MEF2C and RORC bias fate over longer timescales. Immunosuppressive mediators such as IL10, IDO1, CD274, galectins and glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3 promote deletion of effector cells. Too much death yields immunodeficiency and lymphopenia; too little permits autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy.

Leukocytes are produced in excess and normally die by apoptosis unless actively told to live; the negative regulation of leukocyte apoptotic process covers the survival signals that spare them. It sets the size and persistence of lymphocyte pools, allows thymocytes and developing B cells to survive selection, and sustains memory and effector cells during and after infection; too little of it causes lymphopenia and immunodeficiency, too much underlies autoimmunity and lymphoid malignancy. Survival is delivered by cytokine receptors and their kinases, notably IL7R signalling through JAK3 to STAT5A, by chemokine axes such as CXCL12, CCL19/CCL21 and CCR7 that couple positioning in lymphoid tissue to viability, by TNF-family costimulation, and by TAM receptors AXL and MERTK with their ligand GAS6. Transcriptional regulators including BCL6, FOXP1, RORC, HIF1A and the glucocorticoid-induced TSC22D3 tune the apoptotic threshold, linking this control to lymphocyte development, tolerance and immune homeostasis.

Immune responses must be terminated, and the clones that mount them removed, so signals that promote leukocyte apoptosis set the size and duration of an inflammatory episode and enforce self-tolerance. Positive regulation of the leukocyte apoptotic process spans intrinsic death machinery — p53 with its target PUMA and the pore-forming effector BAX — and extracellular cues delivered by other cells, including IL10, TGFB2, the chemokine CCL5, galectin-9 and PD-L1, which drive activated lymphocytes and granulocytes toward deletion. Metabolic and enzymatic brakes act here too: IDO1 tryptophan catabolism starves responding T cells, while P2RX7 couples extracellular ATP to death in purinergic sensing of tissue damage. Tuning of these signals by SIRT1, MYC, MEF2C and miR-34a links death sensitivity to differentiation state. Insufficient leukocyte clearance favours autoimmunity and lymphoid accumulation; excessive killing produces immunosuppression and lymphopenia, and tumours exploit several of these ligands to eliminate infiltrating lymphocytes.

Macrophages that have engulfed pathogens or accumulated lipid must eventually be cleared or retained, and control over macrophage apoptosis sets how long an inflammatory response persists. Tuning this survival decision matters in atherosclerotic plaque, where macrophage death drives necrotic core formation, and in infection, where premature loss of macrophages blunts bacterial killing. The genes here act at several levels: a chemokine and its receptor deliver extracellular survival signals, an intracellular bacterial sensor couples microbial recognition to cell fate, and interferon-regulatory and MEF2-family transcription factors shape the transcriptional response. A tumour suppressor acting through cell cycle arrest, an NAD-dependent deacetylase that restrains stress-induced death, an endoplasmic reticulum selenoprotein and a let-7 family microRNA add post-transcriptional and metabolic input, placing macrophage lifespan under combined inflammatory, stress and epigenetic regulation.

Macrophages that have entered an inflamed or infected tissue must survive long enough to clear pathogens and debris, and this pathway comprises the signals that hold their apoptotic programme in check. Prolonged macrophage survival sustains chronic inflammation and shapes lesions such as atherosclerotic plaque and granulomas, while premature death of these cells blunts innate defence and delays resolution. The chemokine CCL5 acting through its receptor CCR5 delivers a pro-survival signal, the pattern recognition receptor NOD2 links bacterial peptidoglycan sensing to survival as well as inflammatory output, and IRF7 ties antiviral transcription to cell fate. Additional inputs come from the ghrelin receptor GHSR, from a let-7 family microRNA acting post-transcriptionally, and from SELENOS, a selenoprotein of endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation that limits ER stress-driven death. Together these represent survival control within innate immune cell homeostasis.

Phosphate balance in the body depends on how much filtered phosphate the kidney reclaims, and this regulatory pathway sets the activity of the sodium-coupled phosphate carriers that do the reclaiming. Tuning that transport determines serum phosphate, and with it bone mineralization and the risk of rickets, osteomalacia, stone formation or ectopic calcification; loss-of-function in the proximal tubule cotransporter SLC34A1 causes renal phosphate wasting with hypercalciuria. Control operates at several levels: transcription factors including ATF4 and CEBPB alter cotransporter expression, a circadian repressor links phosphate handling to the daily feeding and excretion cycle, and the secreted frizzled-related protein SFRP4 acts as a phosphaturic signal that suppresses reabsorption. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of renal solute handling, endocrine mineral regulation by parathyroid hormone and FGF23, and skeletal homeostasis.

Superoxide generated by respiration, NADPH oxidases and uncoupled nitric oxide synthase must be disposed of quickly, and this pathway covers the control layer that sets how fast that clearance happens rather than the dismutation chemistry itself. Tuning it matters for vascular tone and endothelial health: when superoxide removal lags, nitric oxide is consumed to form peroxynitrite, signalling is distorted and oxidative damage accumulates. Several members act by supporting tetrahydrobiopterin supply, with GTP cyclohydrolase I catalysing the committed step and dihydrofolate reductase regenerating the reduced cofactor, so that nitric oxide synthase stays coupled and does not itself leak superoxide. NFE2L2 raises transcription of antioxidant and detoxification genes in response to electrophilic stress, while the matrix protein fibulin-5 and the scavenger receptor CD36 link extracellular and lipid-handling cues to superoxide burden in vessels.

Heart chambers reach their proper size because cardiac progenitors and cardiomyocytes are told to divide at defined times and places, and this pathway covers the signals that increase that proliferation during heart morphogenesis. Without it the ventricular wall stays thin and trabeculation fails, an embryonic-lethal defect that underlies forms of congenital heart disease and non-compaction cardiomyopathy. BMP10, secreted by trabecular myocardium, acts through receptor-activated SMAD signalling in which SMAD4 is the common mediator, sustaining myocyte growth; Notch signalling read out by the transcription factor RBPJ coordinates endocardial and myocardial cues, and SOX9 contributes to proliferation in valve and cushion mesenchyme. The kinase PIM1 promotes cardiomyocyte survival and cycling, while NACA supports the sarcomeric assembly that expanding myocardium requires. Together these inputs link developmental signalling to cell cycle entry in the forming chambers, valves and outflow tract.

Deciding how often a gene is read begins at the moment RNA polymerase is recruited to a promoter, and this pathway covers the processes that raise or lower the rate of transcription initiation. It sets the output of developmental, metabolic and stress-response genes, so its misregulation underlies both cancer and tissue-specific developmental defects. The core machinery is here in force: TBP with the full set of TAF subunits forming the promoter-recognition complex, general factor subunits GTF2A1 and GTF2A2, and essentially the entire Mediator complex, which bridges enhancer-bound activators to the polymerase. Sequence-specific factors such as MYC, JUN, CREB1, TP53, FOXO1, CEBPA, SRF, MITF and the HNF1 proteins supply the regulatory input, while DR1/DRAP1 repress TBP function and SUB1 acts as a coactivator. Transcription initiation is the committed step at which RNA polymerase is loaded onto a promoter, and holding it back is how cells keep genes off until the right signal arrives. This negative control over DNA-templated initiation sets basal expression levels, enforces developmental timing, and prevents inappropriate activation of growth and differentiation programmes. Several routes converge on it: the NC2 heterodimer of DR1 and DRAP1 binds TBP and blocks assembly of the preinitiation complex; HEY2 acts as a Notch-responsive repressor during cardiac and vascular patterning; CTNNBIP1 sequesters beta-catenin away from TCF/LEF to dampen Wnt-driven transcription; and the nuclear thyroid hormone receptor THRA silences target promoters when unliganded. SUMO1 and the SUMO ligase ZNF451 add repression through modification of transcription factors, while HMGB1 alters promoter architecture. Loss of such restraint contributes to unchecked proliferation, as deregulated MYC activity illustrates.

Getting RNA polymerase II to actually start at a promoter is the committed step of gene expression, and this pathway covers the machinery and factors that raise the rate at which it happens. Almost the whole general apparatus is here: TBP with its full complement of TAF subunits forming TFIID, the TFIIA subunits that stabilise TBP on the TATA box, the coactivator PC4, and essentially every subunit of the Mediator complex, which bridges promoter-bound polymerase to enhancers. Acting through them are sequence-specific activators — JUN, MYC, CREB1, SRF, TP53, NF-κB, and lineage factors such as CEBPA, HNF1A/HNF1B, MITF, NKX2-5 and TWIST1 — that recruit and stimulate initiation at their target genes. Also represented are chromatin and repair-coupled contributions, including the acetyltransferase KAT8 and transcription-coupled repair factors. Together these determine which genes are switched on during differentiation, growth signalling and stress responses.

Neurons must limit dendritic growth as well as promote it, and this pathway covers the processes that stop or reduce dendrite outgrowth, branching and arbor expansion. Restraining arborization is what gives each neuronal class its characteristic dendritic field, prevents excess or misplaced branches, and helps set the number and placement of synaptic inputs a cell receives; when such restraint fails, arbor shape and circuit wiring are altered, with consequences for cortical layering and reading and language disorders linked to neuronal migration genes. The genes involved act at several levels: guidance and adhesion receptors such as DCC and the atypical cadherin FAT3 read extracellular cues to suppress inappropriate branch formation, ARF6-dependent membrane trafficking shapes local cytoskeletal and surface delivery, and nuclear regulators including BCL11A and the arginine methyltransferase CARM1 tune the transcriptional programmes underlying dendritic morphogenesis.

How many neurons and glia a brain ends up with is decided largely by how long neural precursors keep dividing before they differentiate, and this pathway covers the signals that push that balance either way. Its output sets cortical size and layer composition, sustains adult neurogenic niches in the hippocampus and subventricular zone, and when it is disturbed produces microcephaly, cortical malformation and, at the other extreme, glioma-like overgrowth. Secreted cues converge on the precursor pool — Sonic hedgehog through SMO and GLI3, WNT ligands through Frizzled receptors and beta-catenin, FGF2, EGF, IGF1 and VEGF, alongside Notch–DLL4 lateral inhibition. These feed into transcriptional determinants such as PAX6, FOXG1, LHX2, ASCL1 and NR2E1, into cell cycle brakes including BTG2, and into spindle and centrosome proteins such as ASPM and WDR62 that govern division mode. Tumour suppressors NF1 and NF2 restrain the same proliferation.

The size of the brain depends as much on when neural precursors stop dividing as on how fast they divide, and negative regulation of neural precursor cell proliferation is the braking side of that balance. Curbing precursor expansion allows cells to exit the cycle and differentiate into neurons and glia on schedule, and it protects against the overgrowth and tumour formation seen when the brake fails — loss of the RAS GTPase-activating protein neurofibromin, for example, drives glial and neural progenitor overproliferation. The genes here act at several levels: antiproliferative and cell-cycle-exit factors such as BTG2 and CEND1, transcriptional regulators including PAX6, NR2E1, GATA2 and VAX1 that set regional identity while limiting self-renewal, chromatin and deacetylase activities, adhesion and integrin-linked signalling, secreted cues such as TGFB1 and WNT5A, and a microRNA that tunes neurogenic timing. Together they couple patterning to cell cycle withdrawal during cortical and neural tube development.

Expansion of the neural progenitor pool sets the size of the brain and the number of neurons and glia that can later be made, so signals that increase neural precursor cell proliferation govern cortical growth, ventricular zone thickness and the persistence of adult neurogenic niches. The genes here cover the mitogens and their receptors that keep progenitors cycling, including FGF2, EGF, IGF1, SHH acting through SMO and GLI3, WNT3A with beta-catenin, and Notch-Delta signalling, alongside transcription factors such as PAX6, FOXG1, LHX2 and ASCL1 that specify progenitor identity and proliferative competence. Others act on the mitotic apparatus itself: ASPM, WDR62 and ZNF335 operate at the centrosome and spindle, and their loss causes microcephaly through premature depletion of precursors. Too much proliferative drive instead underlies megalencephaly and contributes to brain tumour initiation.

Cells must match fatty acid uptake and intracellular movement to their demand for fuel and membrane lipid, and this regulatory layer sets how fast that transport runs. It matters for tissues that live on lipid oxidation, such as heart and skeletal muscle, and for the lipid overload that drives insulin resistance and steatosis when the controls fail. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases trap incoming fatty acids as CoA thioesters, maintaining the inward gradient and committing them to oxidation or storage, while a cytosolic fatty acid binding protein shuttles them between membranes and enzymes. Insulin signalling through AKT kinases and IRS2, and transcriptional control by the lipid-activated nuclear receptor PPARA, tune this capacity to nutritional state. Phospholipases release fatty acids from membrane stores, and inflammatory mediators including IL1B and MIF, plus purinergic and peptide hormone receptors, modulate flux in a tissue-dependent way.

Cells must limit how much fatty acid they take up and shuttle between compartments, and this negative regulation of fatty acid transport describes the brakes on that flux. Restraining uptake protects tissues from lipid overload, ectopic triglyceride accumulation and lipotoxic stress, processes that underlie insulin resistance and fatty liver when the brakes fail. Several components act through insulin signalling: the AKT1 and AKT2 kinases and the adaptor IRS2 couple hormonal input to the trafficking and abundance of transporters at the plasma membrane. Others work metabolically or structurally, including a long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase that esterifies imported fatty acids and so changes their availability, a mitochondrial fission factor linking organelle dynamics to lipid handling, and a secreted matrix protein that modulates CD36-dependent transport. Together they place fatty acid entry under hormonal and metabolic control rather than leaving it concentration-driven.

Fatty acids must move across membranes and between tissues to serve as fuel, signalling precursors, and storage substrate, and this pathway covers the signals that increase that flux. Boosting fatty acid uptake and trafficking matters for how muscle and heart meet energy demand, how adipose tissue loads lipid, and how inflamed tissue supplies substrate for lipid mediator synthesis. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases trap incoming fatty acids as CoA esters, which keeps the inward gradient steep and commits them to oxidation or esterification, while a cytoplasmic fatty acid binding protein shuttles them to their destinations. Secreted and cytosolic phospholipases liberate arachidonate from membrane phospholipids for prostaglandin production, and inflammatory and hormonal inputs including interleukin-1 beta, endothelin-1, oxytocin and purinergic receptor activation drive the process. Sustained stimulation contributes to lipid overload in metabolic and inflammatory disease.

Ovary formation and subsequent follicle maturation are tuned rather than simply switched on, and this regulatory layer sets how many follicles develop, how granulosa cells respond, and ultimately female fertility. Transcriptional regulators dominate: WT1 and the nuclear receptor NR5A1 (SF-1) govern gonadal ridge formation and steroidogenic gene expression, with ZFPM2 acting as a GATA cofactor in gonadal somatic cells; mutations in these genes cause gonadal dysgenesis and disorders of sex development. Oocyte-derived GDF9, a TGF-beta family ligand, drives granulosa cell proliferation and cumulus expansion, and its loss blocks folliculogenesis beyond the primary stage. Metabolic and stress inputs feed in through insulin receptor signalling, the adipokine resistin, and the stress-inducible regulator NUPR1, linking nutritional state to ovarian output — a connection evident in the ovarian dysfunction of insulin-resistant states.

Regulation of anoikis tunes the death programme that kills epithelial and other adherent cells when they lose contact with their proper extracellular matrix. This surveillance keeps cells in their correct tissue compartment, and escape from it is a prerequisite for tumour cells to survive in the circulation and seed metastases. The genes describe both arms of the control. Integrins such as ITGA5 and ITGB1, together with focal adhesion kinase, SRC and caveolin-1, sense attachment and convert it into PI3K-AKT survival signalling; the BCL2 family members BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 set the mitochondrial threshold that decides whether detachment is tolerated. Superimposed on these are transcriptional modulators, including SNAI2, NOTCH1 and the Groucho-family corepressors, which lower anoikis sensitivity during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Metastasis suppressors such as BRMS1 act on the opposite side, restoring susceptibility to detachment-induced death.

Cells that lose contact with the extracellular matrix normally die, and the tuning of that death programme — the regulation of anoikis — determines whether a detached epithelial cell survives or is eliminated. This surveillance keeps epithelia anchored and confines them to their proper tissue compartment; when it is dampened, detached cells persist, which is a prerequisite for invasion, circulation in the bloodstream and metastatic colonisation. Integrin engagement through fibronectin-binding subunits such as ITGA5 and ITGB1 sustains adhesion-dependent signalling via focal adhesion kinase, SRC and PI3K subunits, feeding into anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 that hold back mitochondrial permeabilisation. Set against these are suppressors of metastasis and transcriptional regulators including BRMS1, SNAI2, NOTCH1 and Groucho-family corepressors, which shift the threshold in either direction. The balance links cell adhesion and matrix sensing to apoptotic commitment.

Cells that lose contact with their proper extracellular matrix are meant to die, and anoikis is that form of apoptosis; increasing its frequency or extent keeps detached or misplaced cells from surviving where they do not belong. This matters most as a barrier to metastasis, since a tumour cell must evade anoikis to travel through blood or lymph and seed a distant site. Accordingly, several of the promoters here behave as metastasis suppressors: BRMS1 and MYBBP1A restrain metastatic colonisation through transcriptional and chromatin-associated repression, while PTRH2 sensitises cells to detachment-induced death downstream of integrin signalling, and SIK1 links loss of adhesion signalling to p53-dependent death. The pathway sits at the intersection of integrin-mediated survival signalling, apoptotic commitment, and epithelial tissue architecture, where anchorage dependence enforces normal tissue organisation.

Testosterone output from Leydig cells is not fixed; it is tuned by hormonal, nutritional and developmental inputs, and this regulatory layer sets circulating androgen levels that drive male sexual differentiation, spermatogenesis, muscle and bone mass, and libido. Too little produces hypogonadism and infertility; unchecked androgen synthesis contributes to virilisation and hormone-dependent disease. The genes here act at several levels: a transcription factor relays cyclic AMP signalling from gonadotropin receptors onto steroidogenic gene promoters, an aldo-keto reductase performs the final reduction step that converts androstenedione to testosterone, and a signalling axis linking bone to the gonad operates through a carboxylated osteoblast-derived hormone and its G protein-coupled receptor on Leydig cells. A WNT ligand contributes to gonadal development and sex determination, restraining steroidogenic commitment. Together these place androgen production within endocrine feedback, skeletal crosstalk and testis differentiation rather than in the steroid pathway alone.

Ribosome production begins with a long precursor transcript that must be cleaved, trimmed and chemically modified before mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNA can be assembled into subunits, and this pathway sets how fast and how completely that maturation proceeds. Because ribosome output scales with growth, control here couples nucleolar activity to proliferative demand, and its disruption triggers nucleolar stress and p53-dependent arrest, the basis of ribosomopathies. The genes act at distinct steps: BUD23 with its partner TRMT112 methylates 18S rRNA, DIMT1 dimethylates adenosines near the decoding site, the RIOK1 and RIOK2 kinases license late cytoplasmic pre-40S maturation, and UTP15, WDR43, WDR75 and HEATR1 work within small subunit processome complexes. Modifying enzymes including PRMT5 with WDR77, SIRT7, KAT2B and the deubiquitinase USP36 tune the machinery and the nucleolar transcription that feeds it.

Ribosome production begins with a long polycistronic pre-rRNA that must be methylated, cleaved and trimmed before it can be assembled into subunits, and this pathway covers the factors that raise the rate and efficiency of that maturation. It sets how fast a cell can build ribosomes, and therefore its growth capacity: nucleolar output of this kind is amplified in proliferating and tumour cells and falters in ribosomopathies. Members include small-subunit processome components such as UTP15, WDR43 and WDR75 and the large HEATR1 scaffold, which organize early cleavage of the pre-rRNA; BUD23 with its partner TRMT112 methylates 18S rRNA, while the atypical kinases RIOK1 and RIOK2 act late in cytoplasmic maturation of the 40S subunit. A PRMT5 interacting arginine methyltransferase module and the deacetylase SIRT7 link chromatin and nucleolar transcription to processing throughput.

Fertility depends on control points layered over every stage of reproduction, and this collection of regulators of the reproductive process sets the pace and extent of gonad formation, germ cell differentiation, meiosis, gamete maturation and fertilization. Sex determination and gonadal programming run through SRY, SOX9, NR5A1, WT1 and WNT4, while STRA8, MEIOSIN, DMRT1 and NANOS2 decide when germ cells enter meiosis; HORMAD1/2, PRDM9, SPATA22 and TRIP13 then govern recombination and its surveillance. Oocytes are held in prophase and released through the anaphase-promoting complex with its activators CDC20 and FZR1, opposed by CDC25 phosphatases, WEE2 and PKMYT1, and by oocyte-specific factors such as MOS, NLRP5 and NPM2. Zona pellucida glycoproteins, ASTL and sperm surface proteases set gamete recognition and block polyspermy. Growth factors including GDF9, BMPs, activins, LIF and IGF1 tune follicle development. Disruption produces infertility, gonadal dysgenesis and disorders of sex development.

negative regulation of reproductive process collects the brakes on fertility: the signals and checkpoints that hold gametes in arrest, block extra sperm from entering an egg, and restrain germ cell differentiation until the right moment. Without such restraint oocytes resume meiosis prematurely, polyspermy destroys the zygote, and germline stem cells are lost to precocious differentiation. Several mechanisms converge here. Cyclic nucleotide signalling through NPPC/NPR2, together with the kinases WEE2 and PKMYT1 and the APC/C inhibitors FBXO5 and FBXO43, keeps the oocyte in prophase and metaphase arrest, while spindle assembly checkpoint components and meiotic HORMA proteins police chromosome pairing and recombination. At fertilisation the astacin protease ASTL cleaves zona pellucida ZP2 to harden the coat. Others act on the male side, from epididymal protease inhibitors and semenogelins that suppress sperm motility to NANOS2 and DMRT1 blocking meiotic entry in spermatogonia.

Fertility depends as much on brakes as on drivers, and this collection captures the processes that suppress or restrain reproduction — holding oocytes in meiotic arrest, blocking polyspermy, limiting germ cell differentiation, and damping gonadal signalling. Much of it is meiotic arrest machinery: WEE2 and PKMYT1 inhibit the maturation-promoting kinase, FBXO43 and FBXO5 restrain the anaphase-promoting complex, and MOS-linked signalling keeps the egg at metaphase II until fertilisation. At the egg surface, zona pellucida glycoproteins and the protease ASTL harden the coat after sperm entry to prevent further binding. Other members restrain sperm function and capacitation, including epididymal and seminal inhibitors such as EPPIN and the semenogelins. Gonadal transcription factors and TGF-beta/BMP and WNT ligands set limits on germ cell fate and follicle activation. Loss of such restraint yields premature oocyte activation, aneuploid eggs, polyspermy, or depleted ovarian reserve.

This grouping covers the signals that drive reproduction forward — pushing germ cells into meiosis, specifying gonadal sex, maturing gametes, and preparing them for fertilisation. Its output is fertility itself, and disruption of individual members produces sex reversal, premature ovarian insufficiency, azoospermia or failed sperm–egg interaction. Several distinct layers appear together: the meiotic entry programme (STRA8 with MEIOSIN, DAZL, YTHDC2 and MEIOC as an RNA-binding switch, PRDM9 marking recombination hotspots), gonadal fate determination through SRY, SOX9, NR5A1, WT1, DMRT1 and WNT4, cell-cycle activators such as the CDC25 phosphatases and AURKA that license meiotic and mitotic divisions, and sperm-surface and acrosomal proteases with the zona pellucida proteins ZP3 and ZP4 that mediate gamete recognition. Neuroendocrine input arrives via tachykinins and their receptors, oxytocin and activins, linking hypothalamic control to gonadal function.

Appetite is held in check by a set of hypothalamic and hormonal signals that suppress food intake once energy stores are adequate, and negative regulation of feeding behavior is the arm of energy balance that produces satiety. Its failure causes hyperphagia and obesity, and in humans mutations in the melanocortin 4 receptor are the commonest single-gene cause of severe early-onset obesity. Proopiomelanocortin-derived melanocortins act on that receptor in the arcuate-to-paraventricular circuit, while CART peptide, neuromedin U, corticotropin-releasing hormone and urocortin reinforce anorexigenic tone through stress and neuroendocrine pathways. Peripheral signals feed in as well: insulin and the adipokine resistin report nutritional state to the brain, and neuropeptide Y and neuropeptide S receptors set the responsiveness of the orexigenic side. Ciliary protein TTC21B links this circuitry to hypothalamic neuronal signalling, connecting satiety control to body weight regulation and metabolic disease.

Appetite is actively driven, not merely permitted, and this pathway covers the signals that turn hunger into eating. Its core is the hypothalamic orexigenic circuit, where AGRP and NPY are co-released from arcuate neurons to increase food intake, AGRP acting as an antagonist and inverse agonist at melanocortin receptors so that the satiety arm of melanocortin signalling is switched off. Peripheral hunger cues feed in through the stomach hormone ghrelin acting on its receptor GHSR, and through the gut peptide INSL5 signalling via RXFP4; opioid signalling contributes hedonic drive to consumption. Also represented are modulators of melanocortin receptor trafficking and signalling, including MGRN1 and the endocytic adaptor SGIP1. Overactivity of this drive promotes hyperphagia and obesity, while its loss causes reduced intake and wasting, making it a focus of anti-obesity and cachexia therapeutics.

Fibroblasts are the connective-tissue cells that build and remodel extracellular matrix, and their survival decisions set how much matrix persists after injury; suppressing fibroblast apoptosis keeps these cells alive during wound repair, but sustained survival of activated fibroblasts is also what allows fibrosis and tumour stroma to accumulate. The genes here restrain that death programme through several routes: secreted GAS6 acts on receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to promote survival, phosphoinositide 3-kinase catalytic subunits feed the canonical PI3K-AKT survival axis, and an apoptosis inhibitor together with chromatin regulators and a microRNA tune the threshold at which caspase activation proceeds. A modulator of Wnt signalling is also represented, linking survival control to developmental signalling in mesenchyme. This anti-apoptotic arm therefore sits at the junction of tissue repair, scarring, and stromal expansion.

Fibroblasts that have done their job in wound healing or tissue remodelling must be cleared, and this pathway covers the signals that push them into programmed cell death. Driving fibroblast apoptosis limits scarring: when the pro-death programme fails, fibroblasts persist, keep depositing collagen, and the result is fibrosis of lung, kidney, heart or skin. The effectors here are largely mitochondrial. BCL2L11 and BID are BH3-only members of the BCL2 family that neutralise anti-apoptotic relatives and promote outer membrane permeabilisation and caspase activation, while the related kinases STK17A and STK17B act as apoptosis-promoting serine/threonine kinases. Other members modulate the decision more indirectly, through antiproliferative signalling, secreted Wnt antagonism, transcriptional control and microRNA-mediated repression of survival transcripts, linking growth arrest to commitment to death.

Receptor signalling has to be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and this collection of dampening mechanisms describes the negative regulation of signaling receptor activity: reducing how strongly, how often or how long an activated receptor can transmit. Without it, growth factor and hormone pathways run continuously, a state that underlies tumour growth and inflammatory signalling. Several routes converge on the same outcome. Components of the ESCRT machinery, including TSG101, VPS25 and CHMP6, sort ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation, with sorting nexins and ZFYVE28 acting on endosomal receptor trafficking; SOCS4 and SOCS5 attenuate receptor tyrosine kinase and cytokine receptor output; ERRFI1 restrains EGF receptor kinase activity. Secreted and accessory proteins such as CRHBP sequester ligand so that the receptor is never engaged, illustrating that suppression can act before, at, or after the receptor itself.

Cells must set how much DNA they make and when, and this regulatory layer tunes the rate and extent of DNA synthesis during replication, telomere extension and mitochondrial genome copying. Damage-responsive kinases ATM and ATR, together with p53 and the CDK inhibitor p21, restrain synthesis when the template is compromised, while cyclin A and the replication factor C clamp-loader subunits with their CHTF18/DSCC1 partners support processive polymerase loading. A large telomeric contingent is prominent: the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and ACD, the CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1, tankyrases and PINX1 limit telomerase access and telomere length, and DKC1, NAF1, WRAP53 and exonucleolytic factors such as PARN control telomerase RNA maturation and stability. Loss of this control produces overreplication, telomere shortening or elongation, and the genome instability underlying bone marrow failure syndromes and cancer.

This is the braking side of DNA synthesis: a collection of activities that hold back replication and telomere extension rather than promote them. Much of it is telomere biology, where the shelterin proteins POT1, TERF1, TERF2 and TINF2 and the CST complex (CTC1, STN1, TEN1, ACD) cap chromosome ends and restrain telomerase, with PINX1 and the PIF1 helicase acting as further inhibitors of telomere elongation; losing this restraint permits unchecked telomere lengthening and is a route to immortalisation in cancer, while excess inhibition drives premature senescence. A second arm is damage-responsive cell cycle arrest through TP53 and the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, which blocks S-phase entry after genotoxic stress. Several RNA-binding and RNA-turnover factors, including hnRNPs and exonucleolytic decay enzymes, contribute by limiting the transcripts and templates available. Together these controls set proliferative limits and protect genome stability.

Skeletal muscle growth and repair depend on expanding the pool of myoblasts before any of them fuse, and this pathway covers the signals that push that expansion — positive regulation of myoblast proliferation. Its output determines how much muscle is built during development and how well muscle regenerates after injury; when the proliferative phase is curtailed, satellite cells are depleted and repair fails, while unchecked proliferation without differentiation is a feature of rhabdomyosarcoma. The members act at several levels: IGF1 provides the classic extracellular growth stimulus, PAX7 marks and maintains satellite cells in a proliferative, undifferentiated state, SOX15 and MEIS2 act transcriptionally on progenitor genes, MEGF10 supports satellite cell proliferation at the membrane, and PPARD links the programme to metabolic state. The biology sits upstream of myogenic differentiation and fusion rather than within it.

Skeletal muscle growth and repair depend on keeping myoblasts dividing long enough to build a pool of progenitors, then stopping them so they can fuse and differentiate; this is the control point that sets that balance. It matters for muscle mass in development, for regeneration after injury, and for the self-renewal of satellite cells, whose identity is defined here by PAX7 while MYOD1 marks commitment to the myogenic programme. Growth factor input through IGF1 pushes proliferation, whereas myostatin restrains it, and loss of myostatin signalling produces the hypermuscular phenotypes seen in several species. Transcriptional regulators such as SOX15, MEIS2 and GATA6 and a large complement of muscle-enriched microRNAs including the miR-1 and miR-133 families tune the proliferation-to-differentiation switch. Failure of this regulation contributes to muscle wasting, poor regeneration and myopathy.

Neurotransmitter release is not simply switched on by an action potential; its probability, timing and short-term plasticity are tuned, and this tuning is what regulation of synaptic vesicle exocytosis describes. It sets how faithfully a synapse transmits during trains of activity and so underlies learning-related plasticity, with failures contributing to intellectual disability, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Calcium entry through presynaptic channels such as CACNA1B with its beta subunit is sensed by synaptotagmins, which trigger fusion, while active zone scaffolds including RIMS proteins, CASK and liprins position vesicles and channels together. Rab3 and its regulators control vesicle docking and priming, SV2 proteins and synapsin manage the reserve pool, and kinases and phosphatases such as CDK5, protein kinase C isoforms and calcineurin adjust release strength. Synaptic adhesion and Wnt signalling feed retrograde and trans-synaptic instructions into the same machinery.

Neurotransmitter release must be damped as well as triggered, and this pathway covers the braking side: processes that lower the probability or extent of synaptic vesicle fusion at the presynaptic terminal. Holding release below maximum sets the dynamic range over which a synapse can be potentiated, shapes short-term plasticity, and protects circuits from runaway excitation. The kinase CDK5, acting with its neuronal activator, phosphorylates presynaptic substrates and constrains the pool of vesicles available for fusion; the small GTPases RAP1A and RAP1B, with BRAF as a downstream effector, couple terminal signalling to this restraint. SYT4 is a calcium-binding synaptotagmin that, unlike the fast release sensor, acts as a negative modulator of secretion. FMR1, the fragile X protein, ties translational control at the synapse to release probability, and its loss produces the synaptic overexcitability characteristic of the disorder.

Neurotransmitter release at a synapse is graded, and this is the biology that pushes it upward — increasing the probability, rate or extent of synaptic vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane. Such positive regulation sets synaptic strength and underlies short-term facilitation and the potentiation that supports learning; loss of it weakens transmission and, for some components, produces epilepsy or movement and neurodevelopmental disorders. The mechanism is built around calcium: a presynaptic N-type voltage-gated calcium channel admits the Ca2+ that triggers fusion, synaptotagmin-1 senses it as the vesicular calcium sensor, and the calcineurin catalytic subunit couples calcium rises to dephosphorylation of release machinery. A bicarbonate-dependent anion transporter contributes by shaping presynaptic pH and ion balance, while a postsynaptic adhesion molecule signals back across the cleft to align and strengthen the release site.

Fast excitatory transmission at most central synapses depends on AMPA-type glutamate receptors, and how strongly a synapse responds is set largely by how many of these receptors reach the postsynaptic membrane and how they gate once there. Control over AMPA receptor activity is therefore the substrate of long-term potentiation and depression, and its disruption contributes to epilepsy, intellectual disability and cognitive decline. Auxiliary subunits dominate this regulation: TARPs of the CACNG family, cornichon homologues CNIH2 and CNIH3, and the Shisa-family proteins SHISA7 and PRRT1 chaperone receptors to the surface, slow deactivation and desensitisation, and anchor them at the density. Acting in parallel, the 19S proteasome regulatory particle links receptor number to ubiquitin-dependent turnover of synaptic scaffolds, while the kinase MINK1 feeds into cytoskeletal signalling at spines. Together these set synaptic gain and its activity-dependent plasticity.

Th17 cells defend mucosal surfaces against fungi and extracellular bacteria by producing IL-17, and the strength of that response has to be tuned tightly: too little permits chronic candidiasis, too much drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune tissue damage. This pathway covers the positive and negative controls on how many Th17 cells arise and how vigorously they act. Fungal recognition through the C-type lectins dectin-1 and dectin-2 feeds into CARD9 and NF-kB signalling in dendritic cells, which supply IL-23 and IL-12 family cytokines; IL-23R and downstream JAK3 signalling then sustain the programme, with BATF, JUNB and coactivators such as p300 and BRD4 shaping the transcriptional output. Restraint comes from RNA-level brakes including the endoribonuclease ZC3H12A and the Roquin proteins, and from competing lineage factors FOXP3, TBX21 and ZBTB7B that steer cells toward regulatory, Th1 or other fates instead.

Th17 cells drive inflammation at mucosal surfaces and are potent mediators of autoimmunity, so the brakes on a T-helper 17 type immune response matter as much as its induction. This is the set of restraining influences: cytokine signals such as IL-2 acting through JAK3 and STAT5A, and IL-27 receptor engagement, suppress the Th17 programme, while lineage-determining factors for competing fates, including FOXP3 for regulatory T cells, TBX21 for Th1 and ZBTB7B, antagonise RORγt-driven differentiation. Post-transcriptional control contributes heavily: the roquin proteins RC3H1 and RC3H2 and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A degrade mRNAs encoding inflammatory cytokines and costimulatory molecules, and mice lacking them develop spontaneous autoimmune inflammation. SMAD7 tempers TGF-beta input, and CD69 and galectin-1 limit effector activity locally. Loss of this restraint permits IL-17-mediated tissue damage in psoriasis, colitis and arthritis.

Th17 cells defend mucosal surfaces against extracellular bacteria and fungi by producing IL-17 and IL-22, and this pathway comprises the signals that amplify that response; when it runs unchecked it drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune inflammation, while its loss leaves patients prone to chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Fungal β-glucan and mannose recognition through dectin receptors CLEC7A and CLEC6A feeds into CARD9 and MALT1, linking innate sensing to NF-κB activation in dendritic cells and T cells. The resulting IL-23 (IL23A with the shared IL12B subunit) acts on IL23R and IL12RB1 to stabilise the Th17 program, and PRKCQ transmits T cell receptor signals toward the same end. Atypical IκB proteins NFKBIZ and NFKBID, the RNA-binding stabiliser ARID5A, BET proteins BRD2 and BRD4, and the acetyltransferase EP300 set the transcriptional and post-transcriptional gain on IL-17 output.

regulation of T-helper 17 cell differentiation controls how strongly naive CD4 T cells commit to the IL-17-producing effector program that defends mucosal surfaces against fungi and extracellular bacteria, and whose overproduction drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune inflammation. The genes span the inducing cytokine axis (IL-23 and its receptor with IL12RB1, signalling through JAK3), the transcription factors that impose or oppose the fate (BATF and JUNB as positive drivers, FOXP3, TBX21, ZBTB7B and STAT5A diverting cells toward regulatory, Th1 or other lineages), and coactivators such as EP300 and the bromodomain proteins BRD2/BRD4 that open the relevant enhancers. Restraint comes largely from post-transcriptional and NF-kB-proximal brakes: the Roquin proteins RC3H1/RC3H2 and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A degrade cytokine mRNAs, while NFKBIZ and MALT1 tune the strength of the signal. Balance here sets the threshold between protective mucosal immunity and tissue damage.

Th17 cells are the CD4 T-helper subset that makes IL-17 and defends mucosal surfaces against fungi and extracellular bacteria, and this regulatory programme sets how many of them a naive T cell pool produces. Too little leaves mucosal and skin immunity vulnerable; too much drives psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune inflammation, which is why IL-23 and its receptor are drug targets. Control operates at several levels: IL-23 and IL-12 family cytokines signalling through JAK3 and their shared receptor chain, transcription factors such as BATF, JUNB and NFKBIZ that build the effector state, and antagonists including FOXP3, TBX21 and ZBTB7B that divert cells toward regulatory, Th1 or other fates. Post-transcriptional brakes matter too: the RNA-binding ubiquitin ligases RC3H1 and RC3H2 and the ribonuclease ZC3H12A degrade transcripts encoding costimulatory and cytokine components, limiting runaway differentiation.

Th17 cells are the interleukin-17-producing effector CD4 T cells that defend mucosal surfaces against fungi and extracellular bacteria, and that drive psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and other autoimmune inflammation when they expand without restraint. The genes here push naive CD4 cells toward that fate. IL-23, made of a p19 subunit with the p40 subunit shared with IL-12, acts through a receptor pair including IL23R and IL12RB1 to stabilise and amplify the Th17 programme.
