The pathway ties skeletal remodelling to immune and endocrine signalling.

Bone mass is maintained by holding osteoclast formation in check, and this braking arm of osteoclast development limits how many bone-resorbing multinucleated cells arise from myeloid precursors. When the restraint fails, resorption outpaces formation and bone is lost, as in osteoporosis, inflammatory erosion and other high-turnover skeletal disease; excessive restraint instead gives dense, poorly remodelled bone. The genes involved act at several levels: a claudin tight-junction protein whose loss in the stomach alters systemic signals to bone, an extracellular matrix glycoprotein that sequesters TGF-beta family ligands and so tunes precursor differentiation, an F-box ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor that targets osteoclastogenic transcription factors for degradation, an inhibitory leukocyte immunoglobulin-like receptor that dampens ITAM-driven costimulation, and lactoferrin, an iron-binding secreted protein that suppresses precursor commitment while favouring osteoblasts. Together they place skeletal remodelling under immune, endocrine and matrix control.

Vasculogenesis is the de novo formation of blood vessels from mesodermal or endothelial progenitors, and the genes here tune how readily and how extensively that happens — setting the pace at which the first vascular plexus of the embryo and the yolk sac forms, and how progenitor-derived tubes are later remodelled. Too little or too much of this regulation gives embryonic lethality from failed vessel assembly, and in adults it shapes tumour and ischaemic neovascularisation. Control acts at several levels: VEGF sensing through the receptor KDR, adrenomedullin signalling via its receptor-modifying partner RAMP2 and the endothelial gene TMEM100, Notch-driven repressors HEY1 and HEY2 that bias arterial identity, HIF1AN as a brake on the hypoxia response, and small GTPase modules built from RAP1A, RAPGEF2, RRAS and ELMO proteins that direct endothelial migration, lumen formation and cell shape.

Vasculogenesis is the de novo formation of blood vessels from endothelial progenitors, and the genes that push it forward set how readily new vascular tubes are built during embryonic development and in response to low oxygen. Without this positive input, the primitive vascular plexus fails to form or remains unstable, a defect incompatible with embryonic survival and relevant to ischaemic tissue and tumour vascularisation. The VEGF receptor KDR marks and instructs endothelial precursors, CD34 identifies progenitor and endothelial populations, and adrenomedullin acting through the RAMP2-containing receptor complex supports endothelial survival and vascular integrity. Small GTPase signalling through RRAS, RAP1A and its exchange factor RAPGEF2 promotes endothelial adhesion and lumen formation, while oxygen sensing via the HIF pathway and TMEM100 downstream of BMP signalling couple vessel formation to developmental and metabolic cues.

Building a layered cortex requires newborn neurons to travel from their birthplace to their final position, and this pathway covers the signals that set how fast, how far, and in which direction they go. Reelin signalling, adhesion GPCRs, netrin-G and semaphorin-plexin guidance cues, and UNC5D-type repulsive receptors act on the actin and microtubule machinery through Rho-family regulators such as ARHGEF2 and SRGAP2 and through shootin and filamin at the leading process. Cul5-based ubiquitin ligase activity and CaMKII-dependent calcium signalling tune the response. When these controls fail, neurons stop or overshoot, producing lissencephaly, periventricular heterotopia, microcephaly and other cortical malformations with epilepsy and intellectual disability; the same logic governs GnRH neuron migration into the hypothalamus, whose failure causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

Neurons must stop moving in the right place, and this pathway covers the braking signals that halt or slow neuronal migration during cortical and hypothalamic development. Getting it wrong produces malformations of cortical development: loss of the adhesion GPCR ADGRG1, which reads extracellular matrix ligands including collagen III at the pial surface, causes bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria because migrating neurons overshoot the cortical plate. Other members act as stop or repulsion cues from neighbouring cells and glia, including the chemokine CX3CL1 and neuregulin signalling through the ERBB4 receptor, while SRGAP2 restrains cytoskeletal protrusion and NEXMIF links migration control to intellectual disability and autism. GNRH1 neurons illustrate the same requirement outside the cortex, where migration must terminate at the correct hypothalamic target. Together these arrest signals set final neuronal position, layering and connectivity.

Neurons are born far from where they will finally work, and this pathway covers the signals that promote and accelerate their migration to those destinations. It shapes the layering of the cerebral cortex and the positioning of interneurons and granule cells, and when it fails the result is malformed cortex — lissencephaly, periventricular heterotopia, microcephaly — with epilepsy and intellectual disability. Extracellular cues such as reelin, midkine and a semaphorin are read by migrating neurons and converted into cytoskeletal action: filamin A crosslinks actin, shootin‐1 couples actin flow to adhesion at the leading process, and Rho‐family regulators including a RhoA‐activating exchange factor and a Rac‐directed GAP steer growth‐cone and soma advance. Centrosomal and mitotic proteins such as WDR62 and KIF20B tie migration to the preceding rounds of progenitor division, so disruption at either step alters final neuronal placement.

Whether a cell dies or survives is set by tunable brakes and accelerators placed on the apoptotic signalling pathway, and this collection covers that regulatory layer rather than the execution machinery itself. It matters for tissue size control, elimination of damaged or infected cells, immune contraction and neuronal pruning; too much restraint permits tumour survival and chemoresistance, too little drives degeneration and ischaemic injury. Both routes are represented: death receptor signalling through FAS, FASLG, TNFSF10, FADD, RIPK1 and the inhibitor CFLAR, and the mitochondrial arm where BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 oppose BAX, BAK1, BID, BBC3 and BCL2L11 to control cytochrome c release and APAF1-dependent caspase activation. Upstream inputs include p53 and DNA damage sensing, ER stress effectors such as DDIT3, ATF4 and XBP1, redox enzymes, growth factor and AKT survival signalling, and numerous microRNAs that dampen these transcripts.

negative regulation of apoptotic signaling pathway covers the many brakes cells apply to their own death programs, setting the threshold at which stress, DNA damage, growth-factor withdrawal or receptor ligation actually triggers self-destruction. It determines which cells survive development, injury and inflammation, and its excess is a hallmark of cancer and chemoresistance, while its failure contributes to neurodegeneration and ischaemic tissue loss. Restraint is exerted at several levels: anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members such as BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 hold BAX and BAK in check at the mitochondrial outer membrane; CFLAR, TNFAIP3 and RIPK1-associated regulators blunt death-receptor signalling; and survival kinases and transcription factors including AKT1, NF-κB/RELA, STAT3, HIF1A and NFE2L2 induce chaperones, antioxidant enzymes and IAP-like inhibitors. Unfolded-protein-response effectors, mitochondrial quality-control proteins such as PINK1 and PRKN, and numerous microRNAs tune the same decision, linking survival to metabolic and redox state.

Cells constantly receive death-promoting cues, and this collection captures the braking systems that stop or blunt apoptotic signaling before commitment to death occurs. It underlies tissue homeostasis, survival of post-mitotic neurons and cardiomyocytes, wound repair and immune restraint, and its over-activity is a hallmark of cancer, where suppression of death signals confers chemoresistance; conversely, loss of the brakes contributes to neurodegeneration and ischemic injury. Mechanistically it spans several tiers: anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members (BCL2, BCL2L1, MCL1, NOL3) opposing BAX, BAK1 and BID at the mitochondrial membrane; decoy and adaptor inhibitors such as CFLAR and FAIM at death receptors; survival kinase cascades through AKT1, SRC, RAF1-MAP2K1 and STAT3; stress-response and antioxidant programmes driven by NFE2L2, HMOX1, SOD2, HSPB1 and the XBP1/ATF4 arms of the unfolded protein response; plus mitochondrial quality control by PINK1 and PRKN and a set of microRNAs tuning these outputs.

Cells that have been damaged, infected or rendered superfluous are removed by apoptosis, and this collection describes the inputs that push a cell over the threshold into that programme rather than away from it. It matters for tissue turnover, immune contraction and tumour suppression: too little and damaged cells persist as cancer, too much and tissues degenerate. Both routes to caspase activation are represented. Death receptors of the tumour necrosis factor family and their ligands recruit adaptors such as FADD, RIPK1 and TRAF2 to initiate signalling from the cell surface, while stress and DNA damage acting through TP53 and the transcription factor DDIT3 induce BH3-only proteins including BAX, BID, BBC3 and PMAIP1 that permeabilise mitochondria and engage APAF1. Also included are inhibitors of survival factors like MCL1, several microRNAs, and kinases and phosphatases that amplify these signals.

Death receptor signalling decides whether a cell survives a cytokine encounter, and this collection concerns the brakes and accelerators placed on that decision. Ligands of the tumour necrosis factor family, including FASLG, TNF and TNFSF10, engage receptors that nucleate a death-inducing complex around FADD and the initiator caspase platform, with RIPK1 as a switch point between killing and NF-kB-driven survival. Modulation occurs at every level: CFLAR competes with caspase recruitment, TNFAIP3 and CYLD edit ubiquitin chains on receptor complexes, BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 restrain the BID-dependent link to mitochondria, and survival kinases such as AKT1 and SRC raise the threshold for commitment. Growth factors, integrins and matrix contacts feed in as trophic inputs. Set too low, the pathway causes tissue atrophy and immune-mediated damage; set too high, it permits autoimmunity and tumour cell escape from immune killing.

Death receptors such as Fas and TNF receptor 1 can commit a cell to apoptosis within minutes of ligand binding, and this collection of brakes determines when that signal is aborted instead. Suppressing extrinsic apoptotic signalling is how activated lymphocytes survive their own cytokine environment, how epithelia tolerate inflammatory TNF, and how tumour cells evade immune killing; loss of these restraints produces tissue injury during inflammation. The mechanisms are layered: a caspase-8 decoy, FLIP, competes at the death-inducing complex; ubiquitin ligases and the deubiquitinase A20 reshape RIPK1 signalling toward survival rather than death; anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members block the mitochondrial amplification step; and survival kinase cascades through AKT, SRC and RAF1, driven by growth factors like HGF and IGF1, phosphorylate and neutralise death machinery. Antioxidant enzymes and heat shock proteins raise the threshold further, linking redox and proteostatic state to cell fate.

positive regulation of extrinsic apoptotic signaling pathway covers the processes that push a cell toward death initiated from outside rather than from mitochondrial stress, amplifying signals delivered by death ligands at the plasma membrane. It matters for immune surveillance and self-tolerance: cytotoxic lymphocytes use FASLG and TRAIL to kill infected or transformed targets, activation-induced death removes clonally expanded T cells, and TNF-family cues shape tissue involution and remodelling. Mechanistically, ligands of the TNF superfamily engage their receptors, promoting assembly of death-inducing complexes through FADD, RIPK1 and TRAF2, caspase-8 activation, and BID cleavage that recruits the mitochondrial arm for full commitment. Regulators here include deubiquitinases and phosphatases such as CYLD and PP2A subunits, Hippo kinases STK3/STK4, and tumour suppressors PML, WWOX and THBS1. Loss of this tuning permits survival of damaged cells and contributes to tumorigenesis, while excess drives inflammatory tissue injury.

Cells can be instructed to die by signals from outside, and this is the biology that strengthens that instruction. Death ligands of the tumour necrosis factor family, including TNF itself, FAS ligand, TRAIL and lymphotoxins, engage their receptors to nucleate a death-inducing complex in which FADD recruits and activates caspase-8; RIPK1 and TRAF2 set whether the outcome is death or survival signalling. Amplification onto the mitochondrial route occurs through BID cleavage and BH3 proteins such as NOXA, linking the two apoptotic arms. Positive regulators here span adaptors and scaffolds, phosphatases, Hippo kinases STK3/STK4, and tumour suppressors including PML and WWOX, alongside inflammatory input from TLR4 and inflammasome adaptor PYCARD. Enhancing this pathway underlies immune killing of infected and transformed cells and tissue involution, while its loss permits tumour survival and immune evasion.

Some receptors kill the cell that carries them unless they are occupied, and this pathway covers the controls on that default death programme — apoptosis triggered by an unliganded receptor rather than by a death ligand. Such dependence receptor signalling ties survival to the continued availability of a trophic cue, pruning neurons that fail to reach their targets and limiting inappropriately placed or angiogenic cells; its loss allows cells to survive outside their supportive niche, a permissive step in tumour growth and metastasis. Members include receptors whose ligand withdrawal is the death signal, such as the GDNF receptor RET, the netrin receptor UNC5B and GFRAL, alongside survival factors and growth cues (GDNF, NRG1, FGF10 with FGFR1, TGFB2) that suppress it. Downstream restraint comes from PI3K–AKT signalling, BCL2-family proteins including BCL2L1 and MCL1, and phosphatase and kinase modulators such as PP2A subunits and RIPK1.

Some receptors kill the cell that expresses them unless they are occupied, and this pathway covers the processes that enhance that unliganded death signal. It is the logic of dependence receptors: survival is conditional on a trophic cue being present, so cells that stray from a source of ligand, or tumour cells that outgrow it, are eliminated. RET is the clearest example here, signalling proliferation and survival when bound by GDNF-family ligands but promoting apoptosis when unoccupied. Support comes from phosphatase subunits such as PPP1CA and the PP2A scaffolds, which set the phosphorylation state of the receptor's downstream effectors, from the mitochondrial serine protease HTRA2, from the tumour suppressors NF1 and WWOX, and from TGF-beta superfamily members. The result is a tissue-sculpting and tumour-suppressive check that constrains where cells may survive during development and in the adult.

Cells decide whether to die from within by controlling permeabilization of the mitochondrial outer membrane, and this pathway covers the inputs that push that decision either way. Tuning it sets how readily damaged, stressed or oncogene-driven cells are eliminated; too little sensitivity permits tumour survival and chemoresistance, too much drives neurodegeneration and ischaemic tissue loss. The core is the BCL-2 family balance, where anti-apoptotic BCL2, BCL2L1 and MCL1 restrain BAX and BOK and are opposed by BH3-only proteins such as BID, BAD, BCL2L11 and the p53 targets PMAIP1 and BBC3. Converging on this balance are p53 and MDM2 after DNA damage, PI3K-AKT survival signalling, the integrated stress and unfolded protein responses through ATF4, DDIT3 and XBP1, redox enzymes including SOD1 and SOD2, mitochondrial quality control by PINK1 and PRKN, and numerous microRNAs that set the levels of the family members themselves.

Cells constantly restrain the mitochondrial, or intrinsic, route to apoptosis so that transient stress does not become a death sentence; this pathway collects the activities that block or damp that route. It sets the threshold at which DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, oxidative injury or endoplasmic reticulum stress are tolerated rather than lethal, and its overactivity is a hallmark of tumour cell survival and chemoresistance, while its loss contributes to neuronal and cardiac degeneration. Anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members such as BCL2 and BCL2L1 hold back mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation; survival kinase signalling through AKT1 and SRC, transcriptional programmes driven by STAT3, HIF1A and NFE2L2, chaperones and antioxidant enzymes including HSPB1 and SOD2, and unfolded protein response effectors such as XBP1 and HERPUD1 all feed in. Mitochondrial quality control proteins like PINK1, PRKN and OPA1 reinforce the block, as do several microRNAs.

Cells that have sustained irreparable DNA damage, sustained ER stress, or the loss of survival signals commit suicide through the mitochondrial arm of apoptosis, and this collection of activators is what pushes that decision past the point of no return. Positive regulation of intrinsic apoptotic signaling matters for tumour suppression, developmental sculpting of tissues, and the cytotoxic action of chemotherapy; when it is blunted, damaged cells persist and transform. The core effectors are BH3-only proteins such as BID, BAD, BCL2L11, PMAIP1 and BBC3 that neutralise anti-apoptotic guardians including MCL1, together with the pore-forming BAX and BOK that permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c. Upstream, TP53 and its cofactors transcriptionally induce several of these effectors, while stress sensors such as DDIT3 link unfolded protein responses to the same mitochondrial endpoint, and microRNAs tune the balance by repressing survival factors.

regulation of phosphatidylcholine biosynthetic process controls how much phosphatidylcholine a cell makes, setting the supply of the most abundant membrane phospholipid and of the surfactant lipid that keeps alveoli from collapsing. Output must be tuned to demand: membrane expansion during growth, lipid droplet and lipoprotein assembly, and the secretory burst of surfactant from alveolar type II cells. The genes act at distinct control points -- an acyl-CoA synthetase and a fatty acid binding protein govern the availability and channelling of activated fatty acyl substrates, a lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase performs the remodelling step that installs palmitate to generate dipalmitoyl-phosphatidylcholine, a calcium-dependent protease provides proteolytic modulation, and a small GTPase directs lamellar body biogenesis and trafficking. Loss of this regulation disturbs surfactant homeostasis and membrane lipid balance, with consequences for respiratory function and lipid storage.

Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid of cellular membranes and the main lipid of pulmonary surfactant, and this pathway covers the inputs that set how fast it is made. Control is exerted largely at the level of substrate supply and the final acylation step: an acyl-CoA synthetase activates long-chain fatty acids for incorporation, a cytosolic fatty acid binding protein shuttles them, and lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase 1 adds the second acyl chain, the reaction that generates the disaturated species enriched in surfactant. A Rab GTPase involved in lamellar body and secretory organelle biogenesis links this lipid output to alveolar type II cell secretion, while a calcium-dependent protease contributes proteolytic regulation. Tuning this route matters for membrane biogenesis and expansion, lipid droplet and lipoprotein assembly, and the surface-tension-lowering function of the lung; imbalance contributes to surfactant deficiency and to hepatic steatosis.

Chromosomes must be restrained as much as remodelled, and this collection of brakes on chromosome organization keeps telomeres capped, sister chromatids held together until the right moment, and segregation from proceeding before every kinetochore is attached. Shelterin components such as TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2, together with the CST complex, limit telomere elongation and block the recognition of chromosome ends as broken DNA, preventing fusions and the genome instability that drives cancer and telomere syndromes. A second arm is the spindle assembly checkpoint, where MAD1L1, MAD2L1, BUB1, BUB3 and the ROD-ZW10-Zwilch module inhibit CDC20 and hold the anaphase-promoting complex inactive, while separase restraint and WAPL-dependent cohesin removal time chromatid release. Chromatin remodellers, DNA damage sensors and Aurora B-containing passenger components add further negative control over condensation, repair intermediate resolution and error correction.

positive regulation of chromosome organization covers the activities that drive and accelerate the folding, condensation and end-protection of chromosomes, so that genetic material can be faithfully segregated at mitosis and telomeres remain stable across divisions. Loss of this control produces chromosome mis-segregation, aneuploidy, telomere attrition and the genome instability characteristic of cancer and premature ageing syndromes. Three activities dominate. Condensin subunits and their SMC ATPases, activated by mitotic kinases such as CDK1 and Aurora B, compact chromatin and build kinetochore-competent chromosomes alongside spindle checkpoint and SKA components. The shelterin complex with telomerase-associated factors and the RTEL1 helicase maintains and elongates telomeres. The INO80 remodelling complex, with RUVBL1/2, the acetyltransferase KAT5 and histone variants, restructures nucleosomes, while damage kinases ATM and ATR and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease couple break repair to chromatin reorganisation.

Chromosomes must be remodelled, compacted and capped at the right moments, and this collection of activators drives those changes forward. It matters for faithful mitosis, for keeping chromosome ends from being read as broken DNA, and for opening chromatin so repair and transcription machinery can reach damaged or silenced regions; loss of control here produces missegregation, aneuploidy, telomere attrition and premature senescence. Condensin subunits and the SMC-family cohesion and repair complexes drive mitotic chromosome condensation and sister chromatid handling, while the INO80 remodeller with its RUVBL1/RUVBL2 ATPases repositions nucleosomes. A shelterin module including TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2, together with telomerase-associated factors, governs telomere length and protection. Damage-responsive kinases such as ATM and ATR, mitotic kinases including AURKB and CDK1, and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex couple these rearrangements to checkpoint and repair signalling.

When intracellular calcium stores are depleted, cells refill them by opening plasma membrane channels, and this pathway tunes how strongly and how long that store-operated calcium entry runs. The set point matters for immune cell activation, secretion, muscle function and gene expression driven by sustained calcium signals; too little entry causes immunodeficiency and myopathy, while unrestrained entry is toxic. STIM1 is the endoplasmic reticulum sensor that detects store depletion and migrates to junctions with the plasma membrane to gate the channel, and much of the regulation acts on it: SARAF promotes slow inactivation, HOMER scaffolds and junctophilin organise the ER-plasma membrane contact sites where coupling occurs, and calsequestrin buffers luminal calcium to set the depletion signal itself. Mitochondrial and lysosomal transport contributes by shaping local calcium gradients near the channel.}

Cation channels rarely act alone: their opening probability, calcium sensitivity and surface delivery are set by accessory subunits and activating partners, and this positive regulation of cation channel activity collects the proteins that raise channel output. The consequences are concrete. STIM1 and STIM2 sense endoplasmic reticulum calcium depletion and directly gate ORAI channels to drive store-operated calcium entry, with CRACR2A and STIMATE tuning that coupling; loss of this arm produces immunodeficiency because lymphocyte activation depends on sustained calcium influx. STAC3 and the calcium channel beta subunit CACNB3 support voltage-gated calcium channel function in skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, where calsequestrin buffers luminal calcium, and STAC3 mutation causes a congenital myopathy. LRRC26 and related leucine-rich subunits shift BK potassium channel gating, while SCN1B modifies sodium channel behaviour in excitable tissue, linking this regulation to muscle contraction, neuronal firing and immune signalling.

Control over how much unsaturated fatty acid a cell makes, and how much of it is converted onward into signalling lipids, is exercised here. The output matters because unsaturated fatty acids set membrane fluidity and supply arachidonate for prostaglandins and other eicosanoids, so tuning this step shapes inflammation, vascular tone and lipid storage. Several members act by controlling substrate release and flux: secreted and activating phospholipase components liberate fatty acids from phospholipids, cyclooxygenase-2 commits arachidonate to prostaglandin synthesis, and peroxisomal transporters of the ABCD family govern very-long-chain fatty acid entry for beta-oxidation, with ABCD1 loss causing X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Inflammatory and hormonal inputs including interleukin-1 beta, endothelins and vasopressin acting through its receptor drive the process upward, while SIRT1 and a set of microRNAs restrain it, linking desaturation and eicosanoid output to nutrient state and transcriptional regulation.

This is the set of signals that push cells to make more unsaturated fatty acids, in practice largely the release and oxygenation of arachidonate into prostaglandins and related lipid mediators that drive inflammation, fever, pain, vascular tone and platelet behaviour. Inflammatory and hormonal inputs — interleukin-1 beta, endothelins, vasopressin acting through its V1A receptor, and the macrophage migration inhibitory factor receptor component CD74 — converge on phospholipase A2 activity, which liberates fatty acid from membrane phospholipids, and on cyclooxygenase-2, the inducible enzyme that commits that substrate to prostaglandin synthesis. Peroxisomal ABC transporters contribute by importing very long chain fatty acyl-CoAs for beta-oxidation and remodelling, linking this regulation to peroxisomal lipid handling whose loss causes adrenoleukodystrophy. Sustained activation of this arm underlies chronic inflammatory disease and is the target of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Caveolae are flask-shaped invaginations of the plasma membrane that internalise lipids, receptors and some pathogens and toxins, and the processes gathered here set how readily that route operates. Tuning caveolar uptake matters for membrane lipid and cholesterol handling, for mechanical buffering of the cell surface, and for signalling from receptors concentrated in these domains; muscle-specific caveolin CAV3 links the same machinery to sarcolemmal integrity, where loss causes myopathy and rippling muscle disease. Control is exerted at several points: the tyrosine kinase SRC phosphorylates caveolin and licenses budding, the adaptor ITSN1 couples the membrane to dynamin-dependent scission, and the ubiquitin ligase NEDD4L marks cargo and regulators for downregulation. CLN3 and PROM2 act on membrane composition and protrusion organisation, placing this regulation at the junction of endocytic traffic and plasma membrane architecture.

Malonyl-CoA sits at the switch point between burning fat and making it, and the reactions that produce and dispose of it set that balance. It is made by carboxylation of acetyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylases: the cytosolic enzyme supplies the two-carbon donor for fatty acid synthesis, while the mitochondrially anchored isoform generates malonyl-CoA as an inhibitory signal that blocks carnitine palmitoyltransferase and so shuts off fatty acid entry into mitochondria for oxidation. Malonyl-CoA decarboxylase runs the reaction back to acetyl-CoA, relieving that block; its loss causes a metabolic disorder with cardiomyopathy and developmental delay. Nudix hydrolases contribute by cleaving CoA esters, trimming the acyl-CoA pool. Together these activities govern lipogenesis, hepatic and cardiac fuel selection, and appetite signalling in the hypothalamus, and the carboxylases are long-standing targets for metabolic disease drugs.

Lipoxin A4 is a trihydroxylated arachidonic acid derivative that signals the resolution phase of inflammation, telling neutrophils to stop arriving, promoting macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, and restoring barrier function once an insult has passed; its metabolic turnover therefore sets how long an inflammatory episode lasts. Formation depends on sequential lipoxygenase action, with platelet-type 12-lipoxygenase and the 15-lipoxygenases inserting oxygen at distinct positions of arachidonate, often through transcellular cooperation between leukocytes, platelets and epithelium. Inactivation is equally decisive: omega-hydroxylation by a cytochrome P450 of the 4F family and reduction by prostaglandin reductase convert the mediator into inactive products, limiting its lifetime locally. Loss of adequate lipoxin production or its accelerated destruction is associated with non-resolving inflammation in asthma, periodontitis and chronic inflammatory disease, and the same enzymes shape related pro-inflammatory eicosanoid output.

Adipogenesis is the program by which preadipocytes become mature fat cells, acquiring the capacity to store energy as triglyceride and to signal systemic nutritional status. It defines white and brown adipose tissue, and its failure or dysregulation underlies lipodystrophy, obesity and insulin resistance. The transcriptional master switch PPARG, with nuclear receptor cofactors such as ESRRA, drives expression of the lipid-handling machinery: fatty acid uptake and transport via CD36, LPL and FABP4, glycerolipid synthesis through GPAM and DGAT1, lipid droplet coating by PLIN2 and CIDEA, and lipolysis via LIPE and MGLL. In parallel the cell expands its mitochondrial capacity, with respiratory chain subunits, TCA enzymes and beta-oxidation machinery supporting the high flux between storage and release. Mature adipocytes also become endocrine, secreting leptin, adiponectin and resistin to report fat stores to the brain and to modulate insulin sensitivity.

Adipogenesis is the differentiation of mesenchymal precursors into fat-storing adipocytes, the programme that builds white and brown adipose tissue and sets the body's capacity to buffer dietary lipid and to signal its energy state. Genes induced during this transition include the master nuclear receptor PPARG and its metabolic output: fatty acid uptake and trafficking (CD36, LPL, FABP4, SLC27A1), triglyceride synthesis and storage on lipid droplets (GPAM, DGAT1, PLIN2, CIDEA), and mobilisation by the lipases LIPE and MGLL. Mitochondrial expansion is prominent, with respiratory chain, TCA cycle and beta-oxidation enzymes, uncoupling protein UCP2 and coenzyme Q synthesis. Mature adipocytes also become endocrine cells, secreting leptin, adiponectin, resistin and angiogenic and inflammatory factors. Impaired adipocyte differentiation underlies lipodystrophy and contributes to the insulin resistance and ectopic lipid deposition of obesity.

Allograft rejection is the immune destruction of transplanted tissue, the response that limits graft survival and dictates lifelong immunosuppression after organ transplantation. It is driven by recognition of foreign MHC: donor HLA class I and class II molecules, together with the peptide-loading machinery TAP1/TAP2 and tapasin, are presented to recipient T cells whose receptor complex, CD3 chains, co-receptors CD4 and CD8, and proximal kinases LCK and ZAP70 convert that recognition into clonal expansion. Costimulation through CD28-CD80/CD86 and CD40-CD40L licenses the response, IL-2 and IL-12 with STAT1/STAT4 and IFN-γ polarise it, and chemokines such as CXCL9 and CCL5 recruit effectors into the graft. Killing proceeds through perforin, granzymes and Fas-FasLG, with macrophage and innate Toll-like receptor input amplifying inflammation. The same programme underlies graft-versus-host disease and, more broadly, cell-mediated immunity to non-self tissue.

Rejection of a transplanted organ is the immune system recognising donor tissue as foreign, and the genes induced during that response trace the whole arc from antigen presentation to cytotoxic destruction of graft cells. Donor MHC molecules and the peptide-loading machinery present alloantigen; T cell receptor complexes with their proximal kinases and adaptors transduce recognition; costimulatory pairs and interleukin-2 receptor subunits license clonal expansion. Interferon-gamma with its receptors and downstream transcription factors amplifies presentation and macrophage activation, while chemokines recruit further T cells, monocytes and B cells into the graft. Killing is carried out by granzymes, perforin and death receptor ligands. Counter-regulatory cytokines and suppressor-of-cytokine-signalling genes appear alongside, reflecting attempts at tolerance. The same programme underlies graft-versus-host disease and is the target of calcineurin inhibitors and costimulation blockade in clinical immunosuppression.

Androgen response is the transcriptional program switched on when testosterone or dihydrotestosterone binds the androgen receptor, driving male sexual differentiation, prostate and seminal vesicle secretory function, and muscle anabolism. Its outputs are the clinical language of prostate biology: KLK3 (PSA), KLK2, TMPRSS2, NKX3-1 and PMEPA1 are classic receptor targets, and continued firing of this program after castration underlies resistant prostate cancer, while loss of receptor signalling gives androgen insensitivity. The genes trace what the hormone actually instructs a cell to do: enter the cycle through CCND1 and CDK6, build membranes and secretory lipids via HMGCR, HMGCS1, SCD and FADS1, expand ER and glycosylation capacity, and buffer stress through FKBP5 and SGK1. Coregulators such as NCOA4, PIAS1, ZMIZ1 and UBE2I tune receptor output, linking steroid sensing to epithelial growth and differentiation.

Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone act through the androgen receptor to reprogramme transcription, and this is the transcriptional output that follows. It drives male sexual development and the secretory identity of the prostate, and its persistent reactivation underlies castration-resistant prostate cancer, which is why the programme is the target of antiandrogen therapy. Classic direct targets include the kallikreins KLK2 and KLK3 (prostate-specific antigen), the serine protease TMPRSS2, the prostate homeobox tumour suppressor NKX3-1, and the chaperone cofactor FKBP5. Downstream, the response couples hormone sensing to growth and anabolic metabolism: cyclins and CDK6 push cells through G1, while HMGCR, HMGCS1, INSIG1, SCD, FADS1 and ELOVL5 expand cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis. Coregulators such as PIAS1, ZMIZ1 and NCOA4, alongside kinases AKT1 and SGK1 and the feedback inhibitor PMEPA1, tune the strength and duration of the signal.

Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels from existing ones, the process that supplies oxygen and nutrients to expanding or healing tissue and that tumours co-opt to grow beyond a few millimetres. Its genes are those induced as endothelial cells are activated, migrate, and organise into tubes: VEGFA and PDGFA as the driving growth factors, FGFR1 and NRP1 as receptors reading those cues, JAG1 and JAG2 feeding Notch-based decisions about which cell leads a sprout and which follows, and integrin ITGAV with focal adhesion kinase PTK2 coupling adhesion to motility. Alongside them sits extensive remodelling of the surrounding matrix and basement membrane — collagens, versican, lumican, periostin, osteopontin, vitronectin and TIMP1 — plus coagulation and chemotactic mediators such as thrombomodulin and PF4. The programme underlies wound repair, ischaemic collateral formation, and tumour vascularisation.

New blood vessels sprout from existing ones whenever a tissue outgrows its oxygen supply, and this collection marks the genes induced as that programme runs. It underlies wound healing, the menstrual cycle and collateral growth after ischaemia, and it is co-opted by solid tumours, which cannot expand beyond a millimetre or two without recruiting a vasculature; the same biology drives retinopathy and is the target of anti-VEGF therapy. Hypoxia-driven VEGFA acts with PDGFA and FGFR1 signalling to mobilise endothelial cells, while neuropilin shapes the ligand response and JAG1/JAG2 Notch ligands sort tip from stalk cells. Much of the remainder is matrix and adhesion: collagens, versican, lumican, periostin, osteopontin, vitronectin and integrin alphaV give the sprout something to migrate through, with TIMP1 and serpins restraining the proteolysis that clears the way.

Apical junction covers the adhesive belt that seals and organises epithelial and endothelial sheets, giving tissues a barrier, a defined apical-basal axis, and the mechanical coupling needed to hold cells together under stress. Loss of these contacts underlies leaky epithelia, defective tissue polarity, and the invasive, motile behaviour of carcinoma cells during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The genes assemble the tight junction seal from claudins and scaffolding proteins such as ZO-1, the adherens junction from E-cadherin with catenins, nectins and desmosomal cadherins, and anchor both to a cortical network of actin, actinins, myosins, vinculin and zyxin. A polarity module including Crumbs3, PALS1, PAR6 and DLG1 positions the complex, while integrin, SRC, FAK, PTEN and small GTPase signalling links junction state to adhesion turnover, growth control and leukocyte trafficking through ICAMs and PECAM1.

Epithelial and endothelial sheets seal themselves and stay polarized through the apical junction complex, the belt of tight junctions, adherens junctions and associated cytoskeletal anchors that encircles the top of each cell. This organization creates the barrier that separates lumen from tissue, sets apical versus basolateral membrane identity, and restrains cell movement; its loss underlies leaky epithelia, edema, and the detachment and invasion seen when carcinoma cells undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Claudins and tight junction scaffolds such as ZO-1 build the paracellular seal, while E-cadherin with catenins and nectins mediates calcium-dependent adhesion and links to actin through vinculin, alpha-actinin and non-muscle myosin. Polarity proteins including CRB3, PALS1 and PAR6 position the complex, and integrins, laminins and adhesion receptors couple it to matrix and to neighboring cells. Src, FAK, Rho-family and MAPK signalling continuously remodel these contacts during wound healing, morphogenesis and leukocyte transmigration.

Apical surface groups proteins enriched at the apical membrane domain of polarized epithelial cells, the face that contacts the lumen or external environment and that must be kept molecularly distinct from the basolateral side. This asymmetry is what allows epithelia to perform vectorial transport, secretion and barrier function; when apical identity is lost, kidney tubules, bile canaliculi and gut epithelium fail, as in the ciliopathy-associated fibrocystin defects of polycystic kidney and liver disease or the bile transport failure caused by mutation of the flippase ATP8B1. Represented here are apical transporters and channels for phosphate, urate, ammonium, glucose and protons, GPI-anchored and raft-associated proteins such as MAL and flotillin that direct apical sorting, cytoskeletal and junctional organizers including shroom family actin regulators, and receptors and ectodomain sheddases that read signals from the luminal space.

Epithelial cells are functionally two-sided, and this collection describes the proteins enriched at the apical surface — the membrane facing a lumen, airway, or urinary space — where transport, sensing and polarity are established. Apical identity is what allows an epithelium to move solutes directionally, and its loss underlies cystic kidney disease, cholestasis and disorganised tumour architecture. The membership reflects that specialisation: an apical urate transporter and sodium-phosphate cotransporter of the renal brush border, the vacuolar ATPase subunit and ammonium transporter that acidify urine, a flippase required for bile canalicular function, and fibrocystin, whose mutation causes recessive polycystic kidney disease. Alongside these sit GPI-anchored and raft-associated proteins, ephrin and Eph receptors, a membrane-tethered protease-activating receptor, and the actin-regulating polarity protein shroom, linking apical membrane composition to cytoskeletal shaping and to signalling received from the lumen.

Apoptosis is the controlled self-destruction of cells that removes damaged, infected, or superfluous cells without inflaming the surrounding tissue. It sculpts developing organs, ends immune responses, and eliminates cells with irreparable DNA damage; too little of it permits tumour growth and autoimmunity, too much drives degeneration and ischaemic injury. Two converging routes are represented. Death receptor engagement by FAS, TNF, or TRAIL assembles a complex that activates caspase-8, restrained by FLIP and deubiquitinases such as CYLD. The mitochondrial route is set by the balance of BCL-2 family members, where BAX and BH3-only proteins including BID, BIM, and NOXA permeabilise the outer membrane, releasing cytochrome c and SMAC to activate caspase-9 and the executioner caspases-3, -6 and -7, with XIAP opposing them. Also present are p53-responsive stress genes, oxidative and ER-stress effectors, and the caspase substrates whose cleavage dismantles the nucleus and cytoskeleton.

Apoptosis is the orderly self-destruction of cells that lets tissues remove damaged, infected or surplus cells without inflammation, and its regulation sets the balance between degeneration and cancer. The core machinery here is the caspase cascade: initiators such as CASP8 and CASP9 activate the executioners CASP3, CASP6 and CASP7, which dismantle structural and nuclear substrates including lamin A/C, spectrin and keratin 18 and unleash DNA fragmentation. Two entry routes converge on this cascade — death receptor signalling through FAS and its ligand or TRAIL, and the mitochondrial route where BAX, BID, BIM and NOXA oppose BCL2L1 and MCL1 to release cytochrome c and SMAC/DIABLO, relieving XIAP inhibition. Stress and damage inputs enter through p21, GADD45, CHOP and JUN, while CFLAR, BIRC3 and antioxidant enzymes restrain commitment. Inflammatory caspases and cytokines link the programme to immune killing.

Bile acid metabolism converts cholesterol into the amphipathic detergents that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the gut, and in doing so provides the liver's main route for disposing of excess sterol. Loss of these steps causes cholestasis, fat malabsorption, and inherited bile acid synthesis defects with neurological and hepatic disease. The classic and alternative routes are represented by CYP7A1, CYP27A1, CYP7B1 and CYP8B1 together with the sterol-modifying reductases and dehydrogenases AKR1D1 and HSD3B7, while side-chain shortening depends on peroxisomal beta-oxidation, explaining the large peroxin and peroxisomal transporter component. Conjugation by SLC27A5 and sulfotransferases and export by ABC transporters complete the enterohepatic cycle. Output is fed back through the bile acid receptor FXR and its partners SHP, PXR and RXR, tying the pathway to lipid, sterol and xenobiotic transcriptional control.

Bile acids are cholesterol-derived detergents that drive intestinal fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption and act as hormones controlling their own synthesis; this pathway covers their production, modification and transport. Hepatic conversion begins with cholesterol hydroxylation by CYP7A1, CYP8B1 and the alternative route through CYP27A1 and CYP7B1, followed by steroid ring reduction by AKR1D1 and HSD3B7, then peroxisomal side-chain shortening that requires AMACR, SCP2, HSD17B4 and an intact peroxisome, hence the many PEX assembly factors. Conjugation by SLC27A5 and sulfation precede canalicular and basolateral export via ABC and organic anion transporters. Feedback runs through the bile acid receptor FXR and its target NR0B2, with RXR partners and PXR coordinating detoxification. Loss of these steps produces cholestasis, fat malabsorption and neurological disease, as seen in peroxisome biogenesis disorders and cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.

Cholesterol homeostasis is the program cells use to keep membrane sterol levels within a narrow range, balancing de novo synthesis, uptake and storage against demand. It matters because cholesterol sets membrane fluidity and raft organisation, supplies precursors for steroid hormones, bile acids and vitamin D, and because chronic mis-setting of this balance drives hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis. The core is the SREBF2-driven transcriptional response to sterol depletion, which switches on the entire mevalonate route from HMGCS1 and HMGCR through FDPS, FDFT1 and SQLE, then the post-squalene steps carried out by LSS, CYP51A1, EBP, NSDHL, SC5D and DHCR7, alongside LDLR for receptor-mediated lipoprotein uptake. Sterol transport proteins such as STARD4 and TMEM97 distribute the product between organelles, while accompanying fatty acid and lipid genes including FASN, SCD and LPL tie sterol supply to broader lipogenesis and to stress and growth signalling.

Cells must keep sterol supply matched to demand, and cholesterol homeostasis is the transcriptional programme that does it, switching on when membrane sterol falls and off when it is replenished. Its core is the mevalonate route to cholesterol, essentially complete here: HMGCS1 and HMGCR commit acetyl-CoA to mevalonate, MVK, PMVK and MVD activate and decarboxylate it, FDPS and FDFT1 build squalene, and SQLE, LSS, CYP51A1, EBP, NSDHL, SC5D and DHCR7 carry out the ring closure and side-chain modifications that finish the sterol. Uptake through the LDL receptor and intracellular transfer by STARD4 complement de novo synthesis, with SREBF2 coordinating the whole output and TMEM97 and TRIB3 acting as sterol-responsive regulators. Accompanying fatty acid and lipid genes such as FASN, SCD and LPL tie the response to broader lipogenesis. Loss of individual steps causes congenital sterol-synthesis disorders, and chronic dysregulation drives hypercholesterolaemia and atherosclerosis.

Coagulation covers the plasma protease cascade that seals vascular injury with a fibrin clot, together with the platelet and complement programs that accompany it. Its output is haemostasis: tissue factor exposure triggers sequential activation of factors X, IX and prothrombin, thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and platelets adhere and aggregate through von Willebrand factor, GP1BA and integrin αIIbβ3. Deficiency of single factors causes haemophilia and related bleeding disorders, while unchecked activation produces thrombosis, so the set is balanced by anticoagulant and fibrinolytic arms — antithrombin, protein C with thrombomodulin, plasminogen, tPA and urokinase, and their PAI-1 inhibitor. Also represented are complement components and matrix metalloproteinases with their TIMP inhibitors, reflecting how clotting is embedded in acute-phase liver output, innate immune defence, wound healing and extracellular matrix remodelling.

Blood coagulation stops bleeding at sites of vascular injury by converting soluble fibrinogen into a cross-linked fibrin clot on a platelet plug, and the same proteolytic network must be restrained so that clots do not spread or persist. Loss of individual components produces haemophilia and related bleeding disorders, while excess activity drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The programme spans the contact and tissue factor pathways through prothrombin to fibrin, the anticoagulant brake supplied by antithrombin, thrombomodulin, protein C and protein S, and fibrinolysis by plasminogen with its tissue and urokinase activators and their serpin inhibitors. Platelet adhesion and activation machinery contributes von Willebrand factor, glycoprotein Ib, integrin "IIb"3 and released chemokines such as platelet factor 4. Also represented are complement proteins and matrix metalloproteinases with their TIMP inhibitors, reflecting how clotting is coupled to inflammation and wound remodelling.

Complement is the humoral arm of innate immunity: a cascade of plasma proteases that recognises microbes and immune complexes, tags them for phagocytosis, recruits leukocytes, and punches lytic pores in target membranes. It also clears apoptotic debris and shapes antibody responses, so its failure leads to recurrent pyogenic infection, immune-complex disease, and — when its regulators fail — self-directed attack, as in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and macular degeneration. The classical initiators C1q, C1r/C1s, C2 and C4 converge with the alternative-pathway factor B on C3 cleavage, while factor H, CD46, CD55 and CD59 restrain amplification on host cells and CR1/CR2 transmit signals to phagocytes and B cells. The wider set places complement alongside the coagulation and kallikrein cascades, cathepsin and matrix metalloproteinase proteolysis, serpin inhibition, caspase-driven inflammasome activity, and inflammatory transcriptional programmes.

Complement is the innate immune system's rapidly deployed humoral arm: a cascade of plasma proteins that, once triggered by antibody-bound or microbial surfaces, opsonizes targets, recruits phagocytes, and assembles lytic pores in membranes. Its failure leaves hosts prone to encapsulated bacterial infection, while unrestrained activation drives haemolytic and kidney disease, which is why regulators such as CFH, CD46, CD55 and CD59 are as prominent here as the cascade components C1QA, C1R, C1S, C2, C3, CFB and C9. The broader picture drawn by these genes is proteolysis-driven host defence and inflammation: coagulation and kinin factors including thrombin, plasminogen and kallikrein intersect with the cascade, serpins and TIMPs restrain it, and cathepsins, granzymes, matrix metalloproteinases and caspases extend the theme, alongside receptor and kinase signalling that converts surface deposition into leukocyte activation and cytokine output.

DNA repair covers the surveillance and correction of DNA lesions that would otherwise become mutations, and the transcriptional and nucleotide-supply machinery that supports it. Its failure underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, Cockayne syndrome and the mutator phenotypes of cancer. The core here is nucleotide excision repair: XPC and DDB2 recognise helix-distorting damage, the TFIIH helicases ERCC2/ERCC3 open the duplex, ERCC1-ERCC4 and ERCC5 incise it, and replicative polymerases with PCNA, RFC and LIG1 fill and seal the gap. Base excision repair (MPG, POLB, FEN1), translesion synthesis (POLH, REV3L) and homologous recombination (RAD51, RAD52, RPA) handle other lesion classes, with TP53 coordinating the damage response. The large complement of RNA polymerase subunits, general transcription factors and elongation regulators reflects transcription-coupled repair, while nucleotide kinases and salvage enzymes maintain the dNTP pools that repair synthesis consumes.

Genomes are continuously damaged by UV, oxidation and replication errors, and this DNA repair programme restores the original sequence so that cells can divide without accumulating mutations; its failure underlies the sun sensitivity and cancer predisposition of xeroderma pigmentosum and related syndromes. Nucleotide excision repair is the most strongly represented arm, with damage recognition by XPC and DDB2, dual incision by ERCC1-ERCC4 and ERCC5, and the ERCC2/ERCC3-containing general transcription factor TFIIH coupling lesion verification to RNA polymerase II activity. Gap filling uses replicative polymerases with PCNA and RFC clamp loading, FEN1 and LIG1, while POLB, POLH and REV3L handle base excision and lesion bypass, and RAD51 and RAD52 act on strand breaks. Also present is the nucleotide salvage and kinase network that supplies balanced dNTP pools, plus TP53-directed damage response.

E2F targets is the transcriptional programme that commits a cell to divide: the genes switched on when Rb is phosphorylated and E2F factors are released at the G1/S transition. It supplies almost everything needed to copy a genome and segregate it — origin licensing and firing (the MCM2-7 helicase, ORC, GINS, CDC45-associated factors), replicative polymerases and clamp loaders, PCNA and ligase I, and the nucleotide-supply enzymes RRM2, TK1 and DUT. The same programme installs replication-coupled chromatin (ASF1, histone variants, DNMT1), the checkpoint and repair apparatus (ATR-CHEK1, BRCA1/2, MRE11-RAD50-NBN, mismatch repair), cohesin and condensin, and mitotic kinases and kinesins such as CDK1, AURKA/B and PLK1. Loss of Rb control makes these genes constitutively active, which is why this signature marks proliferating tumours; feedback through CDKN1A, TP53 and E2F8 restrains it.

Passing the restriction point commits a cell to divide, and the E2F transcription factors execute that commitment by switching on the genes needed to copy and segregate a genome. Released from retinoblastoma protein control when cyclin-dependent kinases phosphorylate it, E2F drives replication licensing and origin firing through the MCM helicase subunits, ORC and GINS components, and the polymerase, primase, PCNA and replication factor C machinery, together with the nucleotide-supplying enzymes thymidine kinase and ribonucleotide reductase. The same programme supplies mitotic effectors such as CDK1, cyclin B, Aurora kinases, PLK1 and cohesin and condensin subunits, plus mismatch repair, homologous recombination and checkpoint proteins including BRCA1, BRCA2, MSH2, CHEK1 and WEE1, so that replication stress is sensed rather than ignored. Deregulation of this axis by loss of retinoblastoma protein or CDK inhibitors underlies uncontrolled proliferation in most cancers.

Epithelial mesenchymal transition describes the conversion of a stationary, tightly adherent epithelial cell into a migratory, matrix-producing mesenchymal one. It is the program behind wound closure and tissue repair, and the same program, when persistent, drives organ fibrosis and allows carcinoma cells to invade and metastasise. Cells lose apical-basal polarity and E-cadherin junctions, switch to N-cadherin and vimentin, assemble an actomyosin contractile apparatus with ACTA2, TAGLN and MYL9, and acquire a fibroblast-like secretory phenotype. Much of the output is extracellular matrix: fibrillar collagens, fibronectin, fibulins, tenascin and versican, plus the enzymes that crosslink and remodel them, including LOX family members, prolyl hydroxylases and matrix metalloproteinases. TGFB1, WNT5A, Notch and integrin signalling feed transcription factors such as SNAI2, PRRX1 and FOXC2, while released chemokines and VEGFs recruit stroma and vasculature to the remodelling site.

Epithelial cells can abandon their apical-basal polarity and junctional attachments to become motile, matrix-producing mesenchymal-like cells, a conversion that closes wounds, drives organ fibrosis, and allows carcinoma cells to invade and metastasise. The programme is defined here by the products cells switch to making: fibrillar and basement membrane collagens, fibronectin, tenascin, versican and other proteoglycans, along with the enzymes that crosslink and mature them, including lysyl oxidases, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases and procollagen processing factors. Integrins, syndecans and CD44 re-engage the new matrix, matrix metalloproteinases and plasminogen activator machinery clear a path through it, and a contractile cytoskeleton of vimentin, smooth muscle actin, transgelin and myosin light chain kinase replaces the epithelial one. TGF-beta, WNT5A, FGF2 and inflammatory cytokines provide the inputs, with SNAI2 and PRRX1 among the transcription factors enforcing the mesenchymal state and cadherin switching to N-cadherin.

Estrogen response early is the first wave of transcription set off when estrogen binds its nuclear receptor in hormone-responsive tissue such as breast, endometrium and uterus. It drives the proliferative, secretory and differentiated phenotype of estrogen-dependent epithelium, and its persistent activation defines luminal breast cancers that depend on it for growth, making it the target of antiestrogens and aromatase inhibitors. Direct receptor-bound targets appear here: GREB1, PGR, TFF1, MYC and CCND1 link hormone sensing to cell cycle entry, while NRIP1, NCOR2 and FOXC1 feed back on receptor output and TFAP2C, XBP1 and GATA-like luminal factors sustain the differentiated state. Accompanying changes reprogram lipid synthesis, nutrient and amino acid transport, keratin and junction composition, and growth factor signalling through IGF1R, RET and AREG, coupling endocrine input to metabolism and survival.

Estrogen acting through its nuclear receptor rewires gene expression within minutes to hours, and the early response arm of that programme is the first wave of direct transcriptional targets. It drives proliferation and secretory differentiation in hormone-responsive tissues such as breast, endometrium and prostate epithelium, and its persistent activation underlies the growth of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, which is why these transcripts serve as readouts of receptor activity and of resistance to antihormonal therapy. Classic direct targets appear here, including the progesterone receptor, GREB1, trefoil factors, cyclin D1 and MYC, together with growth factor and receptor tyrosine kinase components such as AREG, IGF1R and RET that convert hormonal input into mitogenic signalling. Also represented are lipogenic enzymes, nutrient and amino acid transporters, keratins and junctional proteins, coregulators such as NRIP1 and NCOR2, and the chaperone-associated FKBP4/FKBP5 pair.

Estrogen response late captures the sustained, secondary phase of transcription that follows estrogen receptor activation in hormone-responsive tissues such as breast, endometrium and their tumours. Where the immediate response is dominated by direct receptor target genes, this later wave reflects the consequences: cells commit to proliferation, remodel their metabolism and secretory output, and acquire the differentiated epithelial phenotype that defines luminal breast cancer. Hallmarks include cell cycle drivers such as CCND1, CDC6 and TOP2A, the receptor's own feedback partners PGR, NRIP1 and NCOR2, chaperone and folding machinery including FKBP4, XBP1 and DNAJC12, and abundant secreted products such as TFF1, TFF3 and AGR2. Lipid and cholesterol synthesis enzymes, solute carriers and glycosylation enzymes point to the biosynthetic expansion that accompanies growth. Because this program sustains estrogen-driven tumour growth, it underlies both dependence on and resistance to endocrine therapy.

Estrogen acting through its nuclear receptor drives a two-phase transcriptional programme, and this is the delayed arm of it — the genes induced hours after hormone exposure, largely secondary to the immediate-early wave and dependent on new protein synthesis. It defines the hormone-responsive phenotype of breast, endometrial and other epithelia: proliferation, differentiation and secretory output. Characteristic members include the progesterone receptor and the secreted trefoil factors TFF1 and TFF3, along with cyclin D1 and replication and mitotic genes that carry cells into S phase, secretory and chaperone machinery such as XBP1 and FKBP4, and transporters, sulfotransferases and dehydrogenases that remodel metabolism. Because sustained signalling through this programme underlies the growth of estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, its activity reports hormone dependence and predicts response to antiestrogens and aromatase inhibition, while loss of response accompanies endocrine resistance.

Fatty acid metabolism covers the breakdown and synthesis of fatty acids and the accessory reactions that feed them into cellular energy production. It supplies ATP during fasting and exercise, generates ketone bodies for the brain, and builds the acyl chains needed for membranes and signalling lipids; when it fails, as in the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiencies, patients suffer hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Fatty acids are taken up via CD36 and binding proteins, activated by acyl-CoA synthetases, carried into mitochondria by the carnitine shuttle of CPT1A, CPT2 and SLC22A5, and cycled through beta-oxidation to acetyl-CoA, which enters the citric acid cycle or ketogenesis via HMGCS2. Peroxisomal oxidation handles very-long-chain substrates, FASN and elongases run the biosynthetic direction, and PPARA coordinates the whole programme transcriptionally with nutrient status.

Fatty acids are both a fuel and a building block, and this programme covers the enzymes that activate, break down, and synthesise them together with the mitochondrial machinery that finishes the job. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and the CD36 transporter feed fatty acids into carnitine-dependent mitochondrial import via CPT1A and CPT2, after which acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of differing chain-length specificity and the hydratase-dehydrogenase-thiolase steps of beta-oxidation yield acetyl-CoA for the citric acid cycle and, in liver, ketone bodies through HMGCS2 and HMGCL. Counterbalancing routes include FASN-driven lipogenesis, peroxisomal oxidation of very long and branched chains, and lipolysis by monoacylglycerol lipase, with PPARA coordinating the transcriptional response to fasting. The set matters for energy supply to heart and muscle during fasting, and defects in the dehydrogenases or carnitine transport cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and metabolic crisis.

G2M checkpoint covers the control point that decides whether a cell with replicated DNA is fit to enter mitosis, and the mitotic machinery it licenses. It keeps damaged or incompletely replicated chromosomes out of division, and its loss produces the chromosomal instability and aneuploidy characteristic of tumours, which is why many of these genes are proliferation markers and drug targets. Damage sensing through ATR-CHEK1 restrains the CDC25 phosphatases and so the CDK1-cyclin B kinase that triggers mitotic entry, while E2F-driven transcription supplies the required cyclins, replication licensing factors and kinases. Once the gate opens, the same program executes division: Aurora and Polo kinases, the chromosomal passenger complex, kinetochore and spindle assembly checkpoint proteins, condensin and cohesin, separase, and APC/C-directed ubiquitination that destroys mitotic regulators to allow anaphase and exit.

Before a cell commits to dividing, it must finish replicating its DNA, repair any damage, and assemble a bipolar spindle; the G2/M checkpoint enforces that order and delays mitotic entry until those conditions are met. Loss of this control produces mitosis on damaged or under-replicated chromosomes, missegregation, aneuploidy and the genomic instability characteristic of tumours, which is why many of these genes are proliferation markers and drug targets. The programme couples damage sensing through CHEK1 and the replication machinery to the CDK1-cyclin B switch, opposed by the CDC25 phosphatases and by CDKN1B, with E2F and MYB transcription factors supplying the mitotic gene expression. Downstream components build the kinetochore and spindle - Aurora kinases, PLK1, kinesins, condensins and cohesins - while the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2L1 and BUB1 hold back separase-driven anaphase until attachment is correct.

Glycolysis is the core route by which cells break glucose down to pyruvate for ATP and biosynthetic precursors, together with the reverse gluconeogenic and glycogen-handling reactions that keep blood glucose stable during fasting. Its output determines whether a cell can grow without oxygen, and cancer cells and hypoxic tissues depend on it heavily, exporting lactate through monocarboxylate transporters and stabilising the pathway through hypoxia-driven transcription. The classical enzymes are here in full – hexokinase, aldolase, GAPDH-family, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase, pyruvate kinase and lactate dehydrogenase – alongside pentose phosphate and polyol branches, malate–aspartate shuttle components, and the glycogen synthases and phosphorylases. A large set of glycosyltransferases, sulfotransferases and proteoglycan genes reflects the diversion of hexose intermediates into nucleotide sugars and glycan assembly, linking central carbon flux to extracellular matrix production, collagen hydroxylation and angiogenic signalling.

Glycolysis is the core route by which cells break glucose down to pyruvate and lactate to generate ATP without oxygen, and the reverse gluconeogenic and glycogen-handling reactions that let tissues store and release glucose. Its output sets how a cell copes with hypoxia and how fast it can proliferate: tumours and activated immune cells shift toward lactate production even when oxygen is available, and defects in the enzymes cause haemolytic anaemia, myopathy and glycogen storage disease. The canonical enzymes are here in full, from hexokinase and phosphofructokinase through aldolase, GAPDH, PGK1, enolase and pyruvate kinase to lactate dehydrogenase, with the lactate exporter SLC16A3 completing the flux. Alongside them sit the branches fed by glycolytic intermediates - pentose phosphate, hexosamine and nucleotide-sugar synthesis, glycosaminoglycan and collagen modification - and hypoxia-responsive regulators such as VEGFA, P4HA1 and EGLN3 that couple oxygen sensing to this metabolic state.

Hedgehog signaling is the transcriptional output of the Hedgehog morphogen pathway, the patterning system that assigns positional identity in the developing neural tube, limb and gut and that later governs stem cell maintenance and tissue repair. Its readout here is defined by the ligand SHH itself together with the receptor PTCH1 and the transcription factor GLI1, forming the ligand-receptor-effector loop whose derepression drives target gene expression; HEY1/HEY2 and the TLE corepressors mark the interface with Notch and Wnt-associated regulation. Many induced genes are neural guidance and adhesion molecules — L1CAM, NRCAM, SLIT1, UNC5C, neuropilins, VLDLR, DPYSL2 — linking Hedgehog activity to axon pathfinding, ventral neuronal specification through NKX6-1, and proliferation via CDK6 and VEGFA-driven angiogenesis. Loss of this signal causes holoprosencephaly and skeletal malformation; its constitutive activation underlies basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma.

Hedgehog signaling patterns the developing embryo and specifies cell fates along the neural tube, limb bud and many epithelia, and its transcriptional output is read out here as the set of genes induced when the pathway turns on. The ligand SHH relieves repression by the receptor PTCH1, allowing GLI transcription factors to accumulate and activate targets; GLI1 and PTCH1 themselves are induced, forming the feedback loops that shape the gradient. Downstream targets here lean heavily toward neural development and axon guidance — L1CAM, NRCAM, SLIT1, UNC5C, the neuropilins and CRMP/DPYSL family — alongside ventral progenitor identity (NKX6-1), Notch-linked repressors (HEY1, HEY2, TLE co-repressors), cell cycle entry via CDK6, and VEGFA-driven vascular growth. Loss of this signalling causes holoprosencephaly and midline defects, while its inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma.

Heme metabolism covers the synthesis, handling and breakdown of the iron-porphyrin cofactor together with the erythroid differentiation programme that consumes most of it. It matters because heme is the oxygen-binding centre of hemoglobin and the prosthetic group of respiratory and detoxifying enzymes, and because defects in its production cause porphyrias, sideroblastic anemia and hemolytic disease. The genes trace the biosynthetic route from ALAS2 through ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX to ferrochelatase, supported by mitochondrial iron and glycine importers such as SLC25A37 and SLC25A38, and by BLVRA/BLVRB on the degradative side. Alongside sit the transcription factors that build a red cell -- GATA1, KLF1, TAL1, NFE2 -- plus the membrane skeleton, blood group antigens, erythropoietin receptor signalling and the selective autophagy and nuclear extrusion steps that strip an erythroblast down to a hemoglobin-filled cell.

Heme metabolism couples the synthesis and turnover of the iron-porphyrin cofactor to the maturation of erythroblasts into red cells, the cell type that consumes most of the body's iron. Successive enzymes of the porphyrin route, beginning with the erythroid-specific ALAS2 and continuing through ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX to ferrochelatase, insert iron delivered by transferrin receptor uptake and the mitochondrial importer SLC25A37; defects cause sideroblastic anaemia and the porphyrias, while heme catabolism through biliverdin reductases feeds bilirubin production. Alongside the enzymes, the erythroid transcription factors GATA1, KLF1, TAL1 and NFE2 drive expression of globins, the band 3 anion exchanger, spectrin and ankyrin membrane skeleton components, and blood group antigens, and erythropoietin receptor signalling supports survival. Mitochondrial clearance by BNIP3L and ferritin delivery by NCOA4 complete terminal differentiation, linking this programme to iron homeostasis and oxidative stress defence.

Hypoxia is the transcriptional program cells switch on when oxygen falls below the level needed for oxidative phosphorylation, allowing survival by shifting energy production to glycolysis and by summoning new blood supply. It defines the behaviour of tissue at the core of solid tumours, of ischaemic myocardium and of the fetal placenta, and its persistent activation drives tumour angiogenesis, metastasis and therapy resistance. Stabilised HIF transcription factors, opposed by the VHL degradation route and by SIAH2 and prolyl hydroxylase feedback, induce nearly every glycolytic enzyme along with glucose transporters SLC2A1 and SLC2A3, PDK1 to divert pyruvate away from mitochondria, and VEGFA, ADM and PGF for vessel growth. Parallel outputs remodel extracellular matrix and glycosaminoglycans, restrain the cell cycle through CDKN1A, engage ER stress and autophagic clearance of mitochondria, and couple hypoxia to inflammatory and growth factor signalling.

Cells that run short of oxygen must switch their metabolism and call for new blood supply, and this hypoxia response is the transcriptional programme that does both. It sustains tissue under ischaemia, drives wound healing and placental development, and is hijacked by solid tumours to survive poorly perfused regions, making it a central axis of cancer biology. Induced genes are heavy in glycolysis and glucose handling into lactate into lactate glucose transporters, hexokinases, phosphofructokinase, GAPDH, PGK1, ALDOA, LDHA alongside PDK1, which restrains pyruvate entry into mitochondria. VEGFA, PGF, ADM and CXCR4 promote angiogenesis and cell recruitment; SERPINE1, LOX, P4HA1/2 and proteoglycan enzymes remodel matrix; CDKN1A and BNIP3L slow growth and prune mitochondria. VHL and the prolyl hydroxylases that set HIF stability, plus the demethylase KDM3A, tie oxygen sensing to chromatin and gene output.

IL2 STAT5 signaling is the transcriptional program switched on when interleukin-2 engages its receptor on lymphocytes and activates JAK-dependent STAT5, driving clonal expansion, survival and the differentiation of regulatory T cells. It is what allows an activated T cell to proliferate after antigen encounter, and its loss produces severe immunodeficiency, while unchecked signalling supports lymphoid leukemias and lymphomas. The response is self-reinforcing and self-limiting at once: IL2RA and IL2RB are themselves induced, sensitising cells to further cytokine, while CISH, SOCS1 and SOCS2 feed back to terminate the signal. Downstream targets include survival factors BCL2 and BCL2L1, cell cycle drivers MYC, CCND2 and PIM1, metabolic transporters and glycolytic enzymes supporting growth, and the regulatory T cell identity genes FOXP3-associated IKZF2, IKZF4, CTLA4 and TNFRSF18. Additional cytokines and receptors broaden the output into effector differentiation and immune tolerance.

Interleukin-2 acting through STAT5 is the main growth and survival signal for antigen-activated T cells, and this transcriptional programme is what that signal produces. It sustains clonal expansion after antigen encounter and maintains regulatory T cells, so its loss causes severe immunodeficiency while its unchecked activity drives lymphoproliferation; it is also the axis targeted by IL-2 based immunotherapy and by JAK inhibitors. Ligand binding to the IL2RA/IL2RB receptor chains activates JAK-STAT5, which induces its own brakes in CISH, SOCS1 and SOCS2, together with cell-cycle and anti-apoptotic effectors such as CCND2, CCND3, MYC, PIM1, BCL2 and BCL2L1. Much of the output defines activated and regulatory T cell identity: CTLA4, ICOS, TNFRSF4, TNFRSF18, IKZF2 and IRF4, alongside cytokines, chemokine receptors, adhesion molecules and nutrient transporters that support the metabolic demands of proliferation.

IL6 JAK STAT3 signaling is the inflammatory cytokine axis that converts interleukin-6 and related gp130 ligands into changes in gene expression, most visibly the hepatic acute phase response that raises proteins such as alpha-2-macroglobulin during infection and injury. It shapes fever, emergency myelopoiesis, leukocyte recruitment and the transition from innate to adaptive immunity, and its chronic overactivity drives autoimmune inflammation, cachexia and tumour-promoting inflammation, which is why the receptor is a therapeutic target. Ligand binding to IL6ST-containing receptor complexes activates JAK family kinases such as TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT3 for nuclear transcription, with adaptors GRB2 and PTPN11 linking to kinase cascades. Induced targets include further cytokines and chemokines, receptors for interferons and colony-stimulating factors, and the negative regulators SOCS1, SOCS3 and phosphatases that terminate the response.

Interleukin-6 acting through JAK kinases and STAT3 is the main route by which local inflammation is converted into a systemic response, driving the hepatic acute phase reaction, fever, emergency myelopoiesis and the recruitment of leukocytes to damaged tissue. Cytokine binding to the IL6 receptor and its shared signal-transducing subunit IL6ST activates TYK2/JAK, which phosphorylates STAT1/STAT3 for transcription of acute phase products such as alpha-2-macroglobulin and of feedback inhibitors SOCS1 and SOCS3; phosphatases including PTPN2 and PTPN11 and the adaptors GRB2 and CBL tune the output toward PI3K and MAPK branches as well. The induced programme is dominated by chemokines, additional cytokines and a broad panel of cytokine, interferon, TNF and Toll-like receptor receptors, amplifying inflammatory sensitivity. Sustained activity underlies chronic inflammatory disease, cachexia, cytokine storm and STAT3-driven tumour growth, and is the target of IL6 receptor and JAK inhibitors.

Inflammatory response is the coordinated reaction of tissue to infection or injury: recognition of danger, recruitment of leukocytes, and the vascular and metabolic changes that support them. It is what clears pathogens and initiates repair, and its failure to resolve underlies sepsis, atherosclerosis, arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease. The genes trace the full arc — pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2, CD14, NOD2 and the NLRP3 inflammasome that senses cytosolic danger; NF-κB components RELA and NFKB1 that convert these signals into transcription; the resulting cytokines IL1B, IL6, TNF-family ligands and interferon-driven effectors; and chemokines with their receptors that direct neutrophils, monocytes and lymphocytes into tissue. Adhesion molecules SELE and ICAM1, complement and formyl-peptide receptors, prostaglandin and sphingolipid mediators, and endothelial factors including F3 and SERPINE1 couple immune activation to changes in blood flow, permeability and coagulation, while IL10 restrains the response.

Inflammation is the coordinated tissue response to infection and injury: recognise the insult, recruit leukocytes, raise vascular permeability, and then resolve. The genes here map that programme end to end. Pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR2, NOD2 and the NLRP3 inflammasome scaffold detect microbial and damage signals; NFKB1 and RELA drive transcription, restrained by NFKBIA; and the output is a wave of cytokines and chemokines including IL1B, IL6, TNF-family ligands, CXCL8 and CCL2 acting through their matching receptors. Endothelial adhesion molecules ICAM1, SELE and SELL, complement receptors C3AR1 and C5AR1, prostanoid and purinergic receptors, and matrix and coagulation factors such as SERPINE1 and F3 execute recruitment and exudation. The same circuitry, when chronically engaged, underlies autoinflammatory disease, atherosclerosis, sepsis pathology and tumour-promoting inflammation, which is why IL-1 and IL-6 signalling are therapeutic targets.

Interferon alpha response is the transcriptional program a cell switches on when type I interferon binds its receptor, converting a warning signal from infected neighbours into an antiviral state. It is the first line of innate defence against viruses, and its chronic activation drives interferonopathies and contributes to lupus and other autoimmune disease. STAT2 and IRF9 relay the signal to interferon-stimulated response elements, and IRF7 amplifies it in a feed-forward loop, while USP18 and other negative regulators restrain it. The induced effectors act on many fronts: OAS1 and EIF2AK2 shut down viral RNA and translation, MX1, RSAD2, BST2 and the IFITM proteins block entry, replication and release, ISG15 with UBA7 and UBE2L6 tags proteins for antiviral modification, and immunoproteasome subunits with TAP1 and MHC class I enhance antigen presentation to recruit adaptive immunity.

Type I interferon alerts cells to viral infection, and the interferon alpha response is the transcriptional programme it switches on: dozens of genes that make a cell inhospitable to virus replication and better seen by the immune system.
