When a cell suffers DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, loss of attachment or cytoskeletal disruption, BH3-only proteins such as BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD, BMF and truncated BID are induced or released, and their BH3 helices dock into the hydrophobic groove of BCL-2 and BCL-XL. Sequestering these guardians frees BAX and BAK to permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c, committing the cell to caspase activation. The balance set here determines lymphocyte selection, tissue involution and the response to chemotherapy; tumours that overexpress BCL-2 survive by keeping BH3-only proteins bound, which is the rationale for BH3-mimetic drugs.

Whether a stressed cell dies is decided at the mitochondrial outer membrane, and this step is the switch: BH3-only proteins such as BIM, PUMA, NOXA, BAD, BMF and truncated BID bind the hydrophobic groove of the anti-apoptotic guardians BCL-2 and BCL-XL and neutralise them. Sequestering these guardians frees BAX and BAK to permeabilise the membrane, releasing cytochrome c and committing the cell to caspase activation. Each BH3-only protein reports a different insult — DNA damage and p53 activity induce PUMA and NOXA, growth factor withdrawal and kinase signalling control BAD phosphorylation, cytoskeletal and death receptor signals act through BMF and BID — so the balance of binding partners sets the apoptotic threshold. Tumours survive by overexpressing BCL-2 or BCL-XL, and BH3-mimetic drugs work by imitating exactly this association.

Mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization is the commitment step of intrinsic apoptosis, and this is the event in which the intermembrane space empties its apoptotic cargo into the cytosol. Once BAK and BAX oligomerize into pores in the outer membrane, cytochrome c escapes and nucleates apoptosome assembly with APAF1 and caspase-9, while SMAC/DIABLO and the serine protease HTRA2/Omi-related regulator ARTS neutralize inhibitor-of-apoptosis proteins so that effector caspases are freed from restraint. The result is coordinated: a signal to activate caspases plus removal of the brake on them. Cells that cannot permeabilize their mitochondria resist chemotherapy and developmental culling, which is why BCL-2 family control of this step is a drug target. The gasdermins listed here link the same caspase activity to membrane pore formation and secondary lytic death, connecting apoptosis to inflammatory cell death outcomes.

Apoptosome formation is the committing step of the intrinsic, mitochondrial route to apoptosis: once cytochrome c escapes the intermembrane space it binds APAF1, which undergoes ATP-dependent conformational change and oligomerises into a heptameric platform that recruits procaspase-9 through reciprocal CARD interactions. Bringing procaspase-9 monomers together on this wheel-like disk allows dimerisation and catalytic activation, and the activated caspase-9 then processes the effector caspases-3 and -7 that dismantle the cell. Because this step decides whether mitochondrial damage becomes death, it is heavily restrained: XIAP binds and inhibits caspase-9 until DIABLO, released alongside cytochrome c, sequesters it, while AVEN, APIP, UACA and ERK1/2 signalling further suppress APAF1 oligomerisation or caspase activation. Loss of this control contributes to chemotherapy resistance in tumours, whereas excess activity drives ischaemic and neurodegenerative cell loss.

The intrinsic apoptotic pathway commits a cell to death when caspase-9, gathered on the apoptosome, cleaves the executioner caspases-3 and -7 into their active forms. This step converts mitochondrial damage into irreversible dismantling of the cell: the executioner enzymes cut hundreds of substrates, driving chromatin fragmentation, cytoskeletal collapse and the surface changes that mark a corpse for phagocytosis. Cytochrome c released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space binds APAF1, which oligomerises into the wheel-like platform that recruits and activates procaspase-9, and the resulting holoenzyme performs the proteolytic maturation of procaspase-3 and procaspase-7. XIAP restrains the outcome by binding and inhibiting the active caspases, setting a threshold that must be overcome for death to proceed. Loss of this activation step allows damaged or virally infected cells to persist, and its suppression is a recurring feature of tumour cell resistance to chemotherapy.

This is the execution arm of intrinsic apoptosis: once mitochondria are permeabilised, cytochrome c reaches the cytosol and commits the cell to dismantling itself. The response matters because it is how damaged, infected or superfluous cells are removed during development and tissue turnover, and its blockade underlies chemotherapy resistance in tumours. Cytosolic cytochrome c binds APAF1, which in an ATP/dATP-dependent step oligomerises into the apoptosome and recruits procaspase-9; the activated initiator caspase then cleaves the effector caspases 3 and 7, which proteolyse hundreds of substrates to produce the familiar morphology of cell death. The outcome is set by inhibitors and their antagonists — XIAP restrains caspases-9, -3 and -7 until DIABLO, also released from mitochondria, displaces it, while AVEN and APIP dampen apoptosome assembly and ERK signalling supplies survival input.

Once mitochondria commit a cell to apoptosis, the remaining obstacle to death is XIAP, which clamps onto the executioner caspases and holds them inactive. SMAC/DIABLO removes that brake: released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space alongside cytochrome c, the dimeric protein engages the BIR2 and BIR3 domains of XIAP simultaneously and displaces it from caspase-3, caspase-7 and caspase-9, freeing the proteases to dismantle the cell. Cytochrome c meanwhile nucleates the APAF1 apoptosome that activates caspase-9, so the two mitochondrial outputs are complementary — one starts the cascade, the other prevents its suppression. This de-repression step sets the threshold for intrinsic apoptosis, and tumours that overexpress IAPs resist chemotherapy-induced death; small-molecule SMAC mimetics were designed to reproduce this interaction and restore caspase activity in cancer cells.

Once mitochondria are permeabilized during apoptosis, the cell must overcome the brake that inhibitor-of-apoptosis proteins place on its executioner proteases, and SMAC/DIABLO-mediated dissociation of IAP:caspase complexes is how that brake is released. SMAC is released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space alongside cytochrome c, which drives APAF1 oligomerization into the apoptosome and activation of caspase-9. SMAC's amino-terminal motif mimics the sequence caspase-9 uses to dock on the BIR3 domain of XIAP, so it competes caspase-9 free, while engagement of BIR2 blocks the XIAP linker region from occluding the active sites of caspase-3 and caspase-7. The result is derepression of both initiator and effector caspase activity and commitment to demolition. Tumours that overexpress XIAP resist this step, which is why SMAC-mimetic compounds were developed to restore apoptotic sensitivity.

Once executioner caspases are active, a cell is dismantled in an orderly way rather than bursting, and the apoptotic cleavage of cellular proteins is that dismantling step. Caspases 3, 6 and 7, activated downstream of caspase-8, cut a defined set of substrates that hold the cell together and hold it in place: adherens junction and desmosomal components such as E-cadherin, beta-catenin, desmogleins, desmoplakin and plakophilin, tight junction proteins including occludin and ZO-1/ZO-2, and cytoskeletal and nuclear scaffolds such as plectin, alpha-fodrin, gelsolin, vimentin, tau and the nuclear lamins. The result is loss of adhesion, membrane blebbing, nuclear envelope breakdown and chromatin condensation, with ACIN1 cleavage driving the latter. Some cuts amplify the response, as truncation of APC or of the IAP BIRC2 removes brakes on death, while ROCK1 cleavage generates a constitutively active kinase that powers blebbing.

Cells that have committed to apoptosis must overcome a standing brake on their own executioner enzymes, and this is the step that removes it. When mitochondria are permeabilised, cytochrome c drives apoptosome assembly with APAF1 and caspase-9, but the resulting active caspase-9 and the downstream executioners caspase-3 and caspase-7 are held in check by XIAP, an inhibitor of apoptosis protein that binds and suppresses them. SMAC/DIABLO, released from the intermembrane space alongside cytochrome c, binds XIAP and displaces it from these complexes, freeing the caspases to cleave their substrates and dismantle the cell; a SEPTIN4 isoform acts similarly. This relief of inhibition sets the threshold for intrinsic apoptosis, and its loss lets damaged or malignant cells survive signals that should kill them, which is why SMAC-mimetic drugs are used to resensitise tumours.

Once mitochondria are committed to death, the proteins they release into the cytosol carry out the killing, and this apoptotic factor-mediated response covers what those factors do. Pore formation by BAX and BAK permeabilises the outer membrane; cytochrome c then nucleates an apoptosome with APAF1 that recruits and activates caspase-9, which cleaves the executioner caspases CASP3 and CASP7 to dismantle the cell. Release of DIABLO relieves XIAP-mediated inhibition of those caspases, setting the threshold for whether a damaged cell dies or persists. Caspase-independent routes contribute nuclear DNA degradation, and caspase-3 cleavage of gasdermin E can convert the outcome to a lytic, inflammatory death. Inhibitory proteins such as AVEN and APIP, and survival signalling through ERK1/2, oppose the cascade. Loss of this control permits the survival of cells that should be eliminated, a route to tumorigenesis and chemotherapy resistance.

Opioid Signalling is the neuronal response to endogenous opioid peptides such as the enkephalins, endorphins and dynorphins, and to the opiate drugs that mimic them. It is the route through which morphine and related analgesics suppress pain perception and produce sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression and, on repeated exposure, tolerance and addiction. Opioid peptides derived from precursors including proopiomelanocortin and prodynorphin act on Gi-coupled receptors such as the mu receptor, whose activated alpha subunits inhibit adenylate cyclases while released beta-gamma dimers and parallel Gq-phospholipase C signalling raise inositol trisphosphate and calcium. The downstream consequences are changes in cAMP tone and in the balance of protein kinase A, protein kinase C, calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and opposing phosphatases, feeding into CREB-dependent transcription. Receptor phosphorylation by kinases such as GRK2 desensitises the response, a step central to the adaptations underlying opioid tolerance and dependence.

Opioid signalling is how endogenous peptides such as the enkephalins, endorphins and dynorphins — and the opiate drugs that mimic them — suppress pain perception, and it explains both the analgesia and the tolerance, dependence and addiction that follow repeated opioid use. The mu receptor couples through inhibitory G proteins and a full complement of beta and gamma subunits to lower adenylate cyclase output, so cAMP falls, protein kinase A activity drops, and neuronal excitability and transmitter release decline. Phospholipase C beta isoforms, inositol trisphosphate receptors and calcium release feed calmodulin-dependent kinases, calcineurin and protein kinase C, while phosphodiesterases, phosphatases and receptor kinase-mediated desensitisation set the duration of the response. Convergence on CREB and on striatal signalling proteins including DARPP-32 links acute receptor activation to the lasting transcriptional and synaptic changes of reward learning.

This is the route by which a rise in cAMP is converted into a change in gene expression. Hormones and neurotransmitters acting through G protein-coupled receptors stimulate adenylate cyclases, several of which are also tuned by calcium and calmodulin, and the cAMP produced binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A, releasing catalytic subunits that enter the nucleus and phosphorylate CREB on serine-133. Phosphorylated CREB recruits coactivators and drives transcription from cAMP response elements, supporting long-term synaptic plasticity and memory consolidation, circadian gene expression, gluconeogenic and lipolytic programmes, and hormone-driven differentiation. Anchoring and scaffolding restrict where the kinase acts, so signalling remains local despite a diffusible second messenger. Loss of regulatory subunit function causes endocrine tumour syndromes, and mutations affecting CREB-dependent transcription impair cognitive development.

A rise in intracellular calcium is converted into lasting changes in gene expression by this route, which links calmodulin-bound calcium sensing to the transcription factor CREB. It underlies activity-dependent transcription in neurons — the basis of long-term synaptic plasticity, memory consolidation and neuronal survival — and also shapes T cell activation and bone and immune gene programmes. Calmodulin, loaded with Ca2+, activates the upstream kinases CAMKK1 and CAMKK2, which phosphorylate CaMKIV; nuclear CaMKIV then phosphorylates CREB1 at Ser133, licensing recruitment of CBP-type coactivators and transcription of target genes. Importin-mediated nuclear import, represented here by KPNA2, delivers components to the nucleus, while the multifunctional CaMKII isoforms provide parallel cytoplasmic calcium decoding and cross-talk with cAMP, MAPK and Akt signalling. Loss of this coupling blunts stimulus-induced transcription and the persistence of synaptic change.

Calmodulin induced events describes what happens once calcium-loaded calmodulin engages its downstream effectors, converting a rise in cytosolic Ca2+ into changes in cyclic AMP, kinase activity and gene transcription. This crosstalk between the calcium and cAMP second-messenger systems underlies activity-dependent plasticity in neurons, learning and memory, and the tuning of hormone and neurotransmitter responses. Calmodulin directly regulates adenylyl cyclases, stimulating the calcium-sensitive isoforms such as AC1 and AC8 while inhibiting others, and simultaneously activates Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphodiesterases that degrade cAMP, so the net cyclic nucleotide signal is shaped in both directions. In parallel it activates the CaMKK-CaMKIV and CaMKII kinase cascades, which converge with protein kinase A and protein kinase C on CREB-dependent transcription. Loss of this integration degrades synaptic strengthening and the coupling of excitation to long-term transcriptional responses.

A rise in intracellular calcium is translated into lasting biochemical change largely through calmodulin, and the calmodulin-induced events described here are the downstream branch in which calcium-loaded calmodulin engages cyclic nucleotide machinery and kinases. Several adenylyl cyclases are calcium-sensitive, notably type 8, so calcium can raise or lower cAMP depending on which isoform a cell expresses; calmodulin-stimulated phosphodiesterases of the PDE1 family hydrolyse the same second messenger, setting the duration of the signal. cAMP then activates protein kinase A through its regulatory and catalytic subunits, while calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II isoforms and CaMKIV, activated via the upstream CaMK kinases, phosphorylate CREB and drive activity-dependent transcription. This convergence of calcium and cAMP underlies synaptic plasticity and memory formation, hormone secretion, and the tuning of receptor responsiveness, and it links membrane excitation to changes in gene expression.

Calcium-dependent activation of PDE1 phosphodiesterases links calcium signalling to the turnover of cyclic nucleotides, giving cells a way to terminate cAMP and cGMP signals when cytosolic Ca2+ rises. Calmodulin, loaded with Ca2+, binds the PDE1A, PDE1B or PDE1C enzyme and switches on hydrolysis of both cyclic nucleotides, opposing the synthetic output of adenylate and guanylate cyclases and shaping the amplitude and duration of downstream protein kinase A and G activity. Because the three isoforms are distributed differently across tissues, this crosstalk tunes striatal dopamine signalling and motor behaviour, smooth muscle and cardiac myocyte tone, and sperm function. These largely cytosolic enzymes are pharmacological targets in cognitive and movement disorders and in vascular disease, where inhibiting them sustains cyclic nucleotide signalling rather than initiating it.

phospho-PLA2 pathway is the activation step that releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids and so licenses eicosanoid production. It sets the pace of inflammatory lipid signalling: without it, cells cannot generate the prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive fever, pain, platelet aggregation, bronchoconstriction and leukocyte recruitment, and the same reaction supplies the acyl turnover that keeps membrane phospholipid composition in repair. The cytosolic, calcium-dependent enzyme cPLA2 cleaves the sn-2 ester bond, but only after ERK-family MAP kinase phosphorylates it and a calcium rise recruits it to the nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum membranes where downstream cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases reside. This places arachidonate release downstream of growth factor, cytokine and G protein-coupled receptor input, converting surface stimulation into a diffusible lipid mediator response, and makes the step a control point exploited by anti-inflammatory therapy.

Release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids is the committed first step in making eicosanoids, and this route describes how cytosolic phospholipase A2 is switched on by phosphorylation to do it. The consequence is inflammation: the arachidonate liberated here feeds cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase routes to prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive fever, pain, platelet aggregation and leukocyte recruitment, and the same activity supplies lysophospholipids for membrane acyl turnover and repair. Extracellular stimuli converge on ERK-family MAP kinase, which phosphorylates PLA2G4A; together with a rise in intracellular calcium this promotes translocation of the enzyme to perinuclear and endoplasmic reticulum membranes, where it hydrolyses the sn-2 ester bond. Because activation is a post-translational event, cells can mount a rapid lipid mediator response without new transcription, and this step is a point at which anti-inflammatory intervention acts upstream of the prostaglandin route.

Ca-dependent events covers what a cell does once cytosolic calcium rises: the steep gradient across the plasma membrane, maintained against a thousand-fold difference in concentration, lets brief Ca2+ influx act as a second messenger that reshapes enzyme activity and gene expression. This decoding underlies synaptic plasticity and learning, muscle and secretory responses, and hormone-driven changes in metabolism. Calmodulin is the central sensor, activating CaMKII isoforms, the CaMKK-driven kinase cascade, and CaMKIV, which enters the nucleus and phosphorylates CREB to switch on activity-dependent transcription. Calcium also converges on cyclic nucleotide signalling, stimulating or inhibiting particular adenylate cyclases, driving PDE1 phosphodiesterases, and thereby tuning PKA holoenzyme output; parallel branches engage conventional PKC isoforms and cytosolic phospholipase A2 for lipid mediator release. Dysregulated calcium decoding contributes to cardiac hypertrophy, excitotoxic neuronal injury, and impaired memory formation.

A rise in cytosolic Ca2+ is one of the cell's most widely used signals, and the calcium-dependent events described here are what converts that transient into lasting changes in enzyme activity and gene expression. Because free Ca2+ inside the cell is held far below the extracellular concentration, even brief influx is read as information. Calmodulin is the principal sensor: bound to Ca2+ it activates the CaMK family and the upstream kinases CAMKK1/2, stimulates or inhibits particular adenylate cyclases, and switches on Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphodiesterases that degrade cyclic nucleotides, so calcium and cAMP-PKA signalling are directly cross-wired. Downstream, CREB1 phosphorylation couples stimulation to transcription, while protein kinase C isoforms and cytosolic phospholipase A2 act on membrane lipid signalling. This logic underlies synaptic plasticity and learning, muscle and secretory responses, and hormone-driven metabolic control.

Calmodulin is the cell's general-purpose calcium sensor: a small EF-hand protein that binds up to four Ca2+ ions and, once loaded, changes shape to engage and activate a panel of downstream enzymes. This converts a transient rise in cytosolic calcium into lasting biochemical output, and it is how excitation is coupled to gene expression in neurons, to contractility, secretion and metabolic adjustment elsewhere. Calcium-calmodulin stimulates adenylyl cyclases that make cAMP and calcium-dependent phosphodiesterases that destroy it, so the pathway sets cAMP tone and thereby protein kinase A activity through its catalytic and regulatory subunits. In parallel it activates the CaMK arm, where upstream kinases CAMKK1 and CAMKK2 phosphorylate CAMK4 and CaMKII isoforms signal to CREB1-dependent transcription. Crosstalk with protein kinase C isoforms and receptor kinase regulation ties calcium sensing into synaptic plasticity, learning and memory.

Once a G protein-coupled receptor is engaged and the heterotrimer splits, the freed Galpha-GTP and Gbeta-gamma subunits carry the signal onward, and the G-protein mediated events that follow determine whether a cell raises cyclic AMP, releases calcium, or does neither. Which outcome occurs depends on the alpha subtype: Gs-like and Gi-like subunits stimulate or inhibit adenylyl cyclases, setting PKA holoenzyme dissociation and CREB-dependent transcription, while Gq-family members activate phospholipase C-beta to generate inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, opening IP3 receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum and recruiting protein kinase C. Calcium then feeds calmodulin, CaM kinases and phosphodiesterases that terminate the cyclic nucleotide arm, so the two branches shape each other. This is the general amplification and decoding layer beneath hormone, neurotransmitter and sensory responses, and mutations in its components cause endocrine and developmental disorders.

Activation of phospholipase C beta isoforms by Gq-family G proteins converts receptor occupancy into two intracellular signals: inositol trisphosphate, which opens IP3 receptor channels to release calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, and diacylglycerol, which recruits and activates protein kinase C. This branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling underlies smooth muscle contraction, secretion, platelet activation, synaptic plasticity and the calcium transients that shape gene expression. Downstream, calcium-loaded calmodulin drives CaMKII and the CaMKK-dependent kinases, feeding into CREB-mediated transcription, MAP kinase activity and arachidonic acid release via cytosolic phospholipase A2. The pathway is tightly interwoven with cyclic AMP signalling here: adenylate cyclases, protein kinase A subunits and calcium-calmodulin-stimulated phosphodiesterases let calcium raise or damp cAMP levels, while receptor kinase-mediated desensitisation limits the response. Dysregulated PLC beta signalling contributes to cardiac hypertrophy, hypertension and epilepsy.

Alkylating agents, whether environmental or endogenous, leave methyl adducts such as 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine on DNA bases, where they block base pairing and stall replication. ALKBH2-mediated reversal of alkylation damage erases these lesions directly, without excising the base or breaking the backbone, so no repair patch or strand gap is ever created. ALKBH2 is an iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase, a human counterpart of bacterial AlkB, that hydroxylates the offending methyl group; the unstable intermediate collapses and releases formaldehyde, regenerating the unmodified base. Longer adducts such as 1-ethyladenine are removed the same way, yielding acetaldehyde. Acting mainly on double-stranded DNA and enriched at replication foci, this repair route protects genome integrity and shapes cellular sensitivity to alkylating chemotherapy.

Alkylating agents, whether environmental or endogenous, leave methyl adducts on DNA bases that block base pairing and stall replication. Direct reversal by ALKBH3 erases two of the most damaging of these, 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine, restoring the unmodified base in a single oxidative step rather than excising and resynthesising the strand. The enzyme is an iron(II)- and alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase that hydroxylates the offending methyl group so it falls away as formaldehyde; an ethyl adduct is released as acetaldehyde. Because ALKBH3 works best on single-stranded DNA, repair of duplex substrates requires the ASCC complex, whose ASCC3 helicase unwinds the damaged region while ASCC1 and ASCC2 target the activity to sites of alkylation damage. This chemistry contributes to alkylation tolerance and shapes how tumour cells respond to methylating chemotherapy.

Electrical synapses let current pass directly from one neuron to the next, so signalling occurs essentially without the millisecond delay imposed by neurotransmitter release and receptor binding. Where the two membranes are apposed, aligned hemichannels from each cell dock to form a continuous aqueous pore, and ionic current plus small metabolites move passively down the electrical and concentration gradients. This kind of direct electrical transmission across gap junctions synchronises firing in coupled populations, which matters for rhythmic and oscillatory activity in retinal, hypothalamic and inferior olivary circuits. The connexins here, including the retinal connexin36-type channel of the amacrine and bipolar cell network, supply the junctional pores, while pannexins form single-membrane channels better known for releasing ATP as an extracellular signal. Loss of coupling degrades network synchrony and, in the retina, the coordinated relay of visual signals.

Transmission across Electrical Synapses is direct electrical coupling between neurons, in which current from one cell flows into the next through gap junctions rather than being converted into a chemical signal. Because no transmitter release or receptor binding intervenes, transmission is nearly instantaneous and bidirectional, which is what allows populations of neurons to fire in synchrony — as in the hypothalamic neurons that release hormones in coordinated bursts, in retinal circuits, and in developing networks where coupling shapes wiring. Each junction is built from two hemichannels, one contributed by each partner cell, assembled from connexins such as GJD2 and GJC1; related pannexin channels form large-pore conduits that release ATP and other signals to the extracellular space rather than joining two cytoplasms. Loss or misregulation of this coupling disrupts network rhythmicity and, for some connexins, causes inherited visual and neurological defects.

Some neurons communicate not by releasing transmitter but by passing current directly, and transmission across electrical synapses is that route. Where populations must fire together — hypothalamic neurosecretory cells, retinal networks, inhibitory interneurons — the near-instantaneous coupling it provides synchronises activity in a way chemical synapses cannot match, and it also allows small molecules and second messengers to be shared between coupled cells. The conduit is a gap junction built from two apposed hemichannels, one contributed by each cell, assembled from connexins; the neuronal connexin encoded by GJD2 forms much of the coupling in retina, while GJC1 and GJA10 contribute elsewhere. The related pannexins form single-membrane channels rather than cell-to-cell junctions, releasing ATP and other messengers into the extracellular space and linking this biology to purinergic signalling and inflammatory responses.

Chemical neurotransmission begins with an electrical event: the action potential invading a presynaptic terminal depolarizes its membrane, and that depolarization is converted into a chemical signal by the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels. The resulting local calcium influx is the trigger that drives synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the cleft, so the amplitude and timing of this step set synaptic strength and short-term plasticity. The channels involved are P/Q-, N- and R-type complexes built from a pore-forming alpha1 subunit (CACNA1A, CACNA1B, CACNA1E) together with auxiliary alpha2delta, beta and gamma subunits that control trafficking, surface density and voltage dependence. Mutations in these subunits cause episodic ataxia, familial hemiplegic migraine and epilepsy, and the alpha2delta proteins are the targets of gabapentinoid analgesics; autoantibodies against P/Q-type channels underlie Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

Chemical synaptic transmission depends on a repeating cycle in which transmitter is synthesized, loaded into synaptic vesicles, released by calcium-triggered exocytosis when the presynaptic terminal depolarizes, and then cleared from the cleft for reuse or degradation. This neurotransmitter release cycle sets the speed and fidelity of signalling between neurons; its failure produces epilepsy, movement disorders, myasthenic syndromes and excitotoxic neuronal death. Synthesis and recycling enzymes such as glutaminase, the glutamate decarboxylases and choline acetyltransferase supply glutamate, GABA and acetylcholine, while vesicular transporters concentrate transmitter using the proton gradient and plasma-membrane carriers for glutamate, GABA and choline retrieve it afterwards. Fusion itself uses the SNARE proteins syntaxin-1A, SNAP25 and VAMP2 with synaptotagmin-1 as calcium sensor, regulated by Munc18, Munc13, complexin, RAB3A and active-zone scaffolds that position vesicles at release sites.

Neurotransmitter clearance terminates chemical signalling at the synapse, removing transmitter from the cleft so that each presynaptic action potential produces one discrete postsynaptic response rather than sustained depolarisation. Without it receptors desensitise or are overdriven, which in cholinergic synapses means depolarising block of neuromuscular transmission, and in monoaminergic circuits altered mood, arousal and reward. Two strategies are represented: enzymatic destruction, by acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase at cholinergic synapses and by monoamine oxidase, catechol-O-methyltransferase and aldehyde dehydrogenase acting on dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin; and transport, with the dopamine and serotonin reuptake carriers returning transmitter to the presynaptic terminal and organic cation transporters providing lower-affinity uptake into surrounding cells. These proteins are the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants, MAO inhibitors and cholinesterase inhibitors, and of organophosphate poisoning, making the pathway central to neuropharmacology as well as to normal synaptic timing.

Synaptic transmission must stop as sharply as it starts, and neurotransmitter clearance is what terminates a signal once the postsynaptic receptors have been engaged. Excess transmitter is removed from the cleft by reuptake into the presynaptic terminal or surrounding glia, by diffusion away from the synapse, or by enzymatic breakdown; without it, receptors are continuously occupied and postsynaptic cells are overdriven. Cholinesterases hydrolyse acetylcholine at cholinergic synapses and the neuromuscular junction, while catechol-O-methyltransferase and monoamine oxidase A degrade catecholamines and serotonin, with aldehyde dehydrogenase disposing of the reactive aldehydes produced. Dedicated plasma membrane carriers recapture dopamine and serotonin, and organic cation transporters provide lower-affinity uptake. These proteins are the targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants, MAO inhibitors and anticholinesterases, and their variants shape monoamine tone, mood and cognition.

Synaptic transmission is terminated not by the neuron alone but by surrounding astrocytes, which clear released transmitter and return it in an inert form. This glial uptake and metabolism step keeps extracellular glutamate low enough to preserve signal-to-noise at the synapse and to prevent excitotoxic overactivation of NMDA receptors, a failure mode implicated in ischaemic injury, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. High-affinity sodium-dependent transporters on the astrocyte membrane, notably the excitatory amino acid transporters encoded by SLC1A2 and SLC1A3, drive glutamate into the glial cytoplasm, where glutamine synthetase converts it to glutamine. A neutral amino acid carrier then exports glutamine for reuptake by the presynaptic terminal, where it is reconverted to transmitter. The resulting glutamate-glutamine shuttle links neurotransmitter recycling to astrocytic nitrogen handling and to the metabolic coupling between neurons and glia.

When a presynaptic terminal releases neurotransmitter, the receiving cell must convert that chemical signal back into an electrical and biochemical one, and this postsynaptic arm of synaptic transmission is where that conversion happens. It sets the speed and strength of every synapse, and its plasticity underlies learning and memory, while mutations in its receptor subunits cause epilepsies, myasthenic syndromes, hyperekplexia and intellectual disability. Ligand-gated channels "" AMPA, NMDA and kainate glutamate receptors, GABA-A and glycine receptors, nicotinic and serotonin type 3 receptors "" mediate fast excitation and inhibition, while metabotropic GABA-B receptors act through G protein subunits, adenylate cyclases, phospholipase C and inwardly rectifying potassium channels. Downstream, calmodulin, CaMKII, PKA, PKC and ERK relay calcium entry to CREB-dependent transcription. Scaffolds such as PSD-95 family proteins, GRIP and PICK1, together with AP-2 adaptors, motors and tubulin, control receptor trafficking, anchoring and turnover at the postsynaptic density.

Transmission across chemical synapses is how one neuron passes information to another neuron, a muscle fibre or a gland cell, and it is the basis of all fast neural computation, movement and memory. An arriving action potential opens presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, and the calcium rise drives SNARE-mediated fusion of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles with the terminal membrane, using SNAP25, VAMP2, syntaxin, synaptotagmin and their priming partners. Vesicular and plasma-membrane transporters load and then reclaim glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine, dopamine and serotonin, while acetylcholinesterase and monoamine oxidase terminate signalling enzymatically. On the postsynaptic side, ionotropic AMPA, NMDA, kainate, GABA-A, glycine and nicotinic receptors change membrane potential directly, whereas metabotropic receptors act through G proteins, adenylate cyclases, phospholipase C and inwardly rectifying potassium channels; scaffolds such as DLG4 and kinases including CAMK2A tune receptor number and underlie synaptic plasticity. Disruption produces epilepsy, myasthenia and neuropsychiatric disease.

Neurons communicate with one another across synapses, and this large programme covers both arms of that communication: direct electrical coupling through gap junction and pannexin channels, and chemical transmission in which a presynaptic action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels, triggering SNARE-mediated fusion of neurotransmitter-filled vesicles. It underlies every behaviour the nervous system produces, from the neuromuscular junction to learning and memory, and its components are targets of anaesthetics, anticonvulsants and antidepressants. Glutamate, GABA, glycine, acetylcholine and serotonin act on ionotropic and metabotropic receptors whose scaffolds organise the postsynaptic density; transporters clear and recycle transmitter, while adhesion molecules such as neurexins and neuroligins specify which contacts form. Potassium channel families set excitability and repolarisation, and kinase cascades convert calcium entry into lasting changes in synaptic strength. Mutations in these channels, receptors and adhesion proteins cause epilepsy, myasthenia and autism spectrum disorders.

After initiating at a promoter, RNA polymerase II must be converted into a processive machine that can travel tens of kilobases through chromatin without falling off or stalling indefinitely; this conversion is the formation of the elongation complex, and it determines how efficiently genes are expressed and how transcription is coupled to RNA processing. The twelve-subunit polymerase, clamped on a DNA:RNA hybrid, is joined by TFIIF, the DSIF pair SPT4/SPT5 and the NELF complex, which impose promoter-proximal pausing until CDK9 in P-TEFb phosphorylates them and the polymerase C-terminal domain to release the enzyme. Elongation factors including TFIIS, ELL, the Elongin ABC complex, SPT6 and IWS1, and the histone chaperone FACT then suppress pausing, rescue backtracked polymerase and allow passage through nucleosomes, while the PAF1 complex and the cap-binding proteins make the moving polymerase a platform for capping, splicing and export. Failure here underlies transcriptional dysregulation in leukaemias driven by super elongation complex fusions.

Insulin and insulin-like growth factor receptors do not act on their targets directly; they phosphorylate the docking proteins IRS1 and IRS2, and IRS-mediated signalling is what happens next. Tyrosine-phosphorylated IRS presents binding sites that recruit the PI3K regulatory subunits, launching PIP3 production, PDPK1 activation and AKT-dependent control of glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid storage, protein synthesis and cell survival; PDE3B links the same branch to suppression of lipolysis. In parallel, GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1 loads RAS proteins and drives the RAF-MEK-ERK route toward growth and mitogenic gene expression, with GAB adaptors and the phosphatase PTPN11 amplifying the output. Related receptor tyrosine kinases, including the FGF receptors with their FRS2 adaptor and klotho co-receptors, feed the same core modules. Loss of IRS function or its inhibition by stress-induced TRIB3 produces insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

ERK1 and ERK2 drive proliferation, differentiation, inflammatory gene expression and cytoskeletal remodelling, and they can be switched on without the RAS-to-RAF route that textbooks emphasise. This RAF-independent activation of MAPK1/3 matters because cytokine receptors, immune receptors and stress signals reach the same terminal kinases through other MAP3 kinases, so tumours and inflammatory states can sustain ERK output while RAF is bypassed. Here interleukin-6 acting through its receptor and the shared IL6ST subunit engages JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 with the phosphatase adaptor PTPN11, converging on MEK1 and MEK2 and then on ERK1/2. Output is shaped as much by termination as initiation: a large family of dual-specificity phosphatases dephosphorylates the activation loop, PEA15 sequesters ERK in the cytoplasm, and CDK1 links activity to cell cycle timing. Active ERK enters the nucleus to phosphorylate Ets-family factors such as ELK1 and reprogramme transcription.

Activation of MAPK1, better known as ERK2, is the step that converts upstream signals into a kinase able to enter the nucleus and drive proliferative and differentiation gene programmes. The immediate activator is the dual-specificity kinase MAP2K2 (MEK2), which phosphorylates ERK2 on the threonine and tyrosine of its activation loop; only the dually phosphorylated kinase is active toward substrates such as transcription factors and ribosomal S6 kinases. Here the input comes from interleukin-6, which engages IL6R with the shared signal-transducing subunit IL6ST (gp130) and the associated Janus kinases JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2. The phosphatase-adaptor PTPN11 (SHP2) docks on activated gp130 and couples it to the Ras-MEK-ERK arm, so a cytokine classically read out through STAT3 also feeds growth and survival signalling. Persistent flux through this route contributes to inflammatory disease and to the growth of IL-6-dependent tumours.

Growth factor and insulin receptors must convert a phosphotyrosine signal at the membrane into activation of a small GTPase, and SOS-mediated signalling is that conversion step. The adaptor GRB2 binds phosphorylated docking sites — including the insulin receptor substrates IRS1 and IRS2 — and brings the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 to the inner face of the plasma membrane, where it catalyses GDP-for-GTP exchange on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS. Loading Ras with GTP launches the MAP kinase cascade that drives proliferation, differentiation and metabolic responses to insulin. Because this is the rate-limiting входной step for Ras output, mutations that lock SOS1 in an active state or that make Ras insensitive to hydrolysis cause developmental disorders such as Noonan syndrome and are among the most common oncogenic events in human cancer, which is why the exchange reaction itself is now a drug target.

Just after RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it enters a tightly supervised early elongation state, and this transition is where most human genes decide whether a transcript will actually be made. The polymerase carries TFIIF and the cap-binding complex on the nascent RNA's 5' end, while DSIF (SUPT4H1-SUPT5H) and the four-subunit NELF complex bind the hypophosphorylated enzyme and hold it in promoter-proximal pause a short distance downstream of the start site. TFIIH, with its CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module and the XPB and XPD helicases, phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and opens DNA, and the phosphatase FCP1 reverses CTD marks to recycle the enzyme. Pausing here is a regulated checkpoint that couples capping to elongation and sets the rate of inducible gene expression; the same TFIIH subunits also serve nucleotide excision repair, and their mutation causes xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy.

Replication forks must not be launched from damaged templates, and this RB1/E2F1-dependent brake is one way S-phase cells enforce that rule. When DNA damage occurs during S phase, a PP2A holoenzyme dephosphorylates RB1, and the unphosphorylated form is recruited to damage sites together with E2F1 and its DP partners, where it blocks initiation of new replication from those origins. The targets of the block are the enzymes that actually start a nascent strand: DNA polymerase alpha with its primase subunits, which synthesise the RNA-DNA primer at each origin. Suppressing initiation locally gives repair time to act and limits the replication of lesions into mutations and breaks. It also shows that the retinoblastoma protein does more than gate G1-to-S transcription, and its loss in tumours removes a genome-stability safeguard as well as a proliferation checkpoint.

Origins of DNA replication must be licensed exactly once per cell cycle, and this arm of E2F activity works in the opposite direction, blocking assembly of the pre-replication complex so that origins are not re-licensed after they have fired. E2F1 raises Cdc25A activity, which removes the inhibitory phosphorylation on Cdk1; the restored mitotic kinase, partnered with Cyclin B, then phosphorylates origin recognition complex subunits ORC1 through ORC6 and associated MCM helicase loading factors, dispersing the licensing machinery from chromatin. The effect couples the transcriptional programme that drives S phase entry to the mitotic kinase that forbids a second round of loading, preventing re-replication and the gene amplification and genomic instability that follow from it. It links E2F-dependent cell cycle commitment to the control of replication origin usage rather than to origin firing itself.

Cells commit to duplicating their genome only once per cycle, and the RB1:E2F axis is the switch that licenses that commitment. E2F1 with its DP partners drives transcription of the machinery S phase requires — origin recognition complex subunits, the MCM8 helicase, and the DNA polymerase alpha/primase heterotetramer that lays down initiating RNA-DNA primers — while RB1 binds E2F and holds those genes silent until cyclin-dependent kinase phosphorylation releases it. Beyond transcription, E2F1 acts directly at replication initiation, and the pathway is tuned by protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes and by mitotic CDK1-cyclin B activity, linking origin firing to cell cycle position. Loss of RB1 control uncouples proliferation from growth signals and is one of the most common events in human cancer, whereas intact signalling also couples replication to DNA damage responses and to exit from the cycle during differentiation.

Activation, translocation and oligomerization of BAX is the commitment step of mitochondrial apoptosis: the point at which a death signal becomes irreversible permeabilization of the outer mitochondrial membrane. Cells that cannot execute it survive damage they should not survive, a route to chemotherapy resistance and tumour persistence, while inappropriate activation drives excessive cell loss in ischaemic and degenerative injury. Cytosolic BAX is normally inert; cleaved BID, generated downstream of caspase-8 in receptor-initiated death signalling, engages BAX and exposes its membrane-insertion surfaces. BAX then translocates to the mitochondrion and oligomerizes into pores through which cytochrome c and other intermembrane proteins escape, seeding apoptosome assembly and caspase-9 activation. This is the node at which the extrinsic and intrinsic death pathways converge, and the step that BCL-2 family antagonists exist to restrain.

Commitment to apoptosis is decided at the mitochondrial outer membrane, and BAX activation is the step that makes the decision irreversible. In healthy cells BAX is largely cytosolic and inactive; once engaged by the activated, truncated form of BID, it changes conformation, translocates to the outer mitochondrial membrane and oligomerizes there to form the pores through which cytochrome c and other intermembrane space proteins escape into the cytosol. That release licenses apoptosome assembly and caspase activation, linking upstream death receptor and stress signals to the execution phase of cell death. Because BID is cleaved by caspase-8, this route connects extrinsic receptor signalling to the intrinsic mitochondrial pathway and amplifies it. Blocking BAX activation, whether by antiapoptotic BCL-2 family relatives or by tumour-associated loss of function, allows damaged cells to survive; excessive activation contributes to degenerative tissue loss.

BH3-only proteins are the sensors that decide whether a stressed cell should die, and their activation is the committing step of mitochondrial apoptosis. They respond to DNA damage, growth factor withdrawal, cytoskeletal detachment and developmental cues, and their loss permits survival of cells that should have been eliminated — a route to tumour persistence and therapy resistance. Each member is restrained differently until needed: BAD is phosphorylated by AKT and sequestered by 14-3-3 proteins, then freed by calcineurin-mediated dephosphorylation; BIM and BMF are tethered to dynein light chains on cytoskeletal structures; PUMA and NOXA are transcriptionally induced by p53 and its relatives p63 and p73, with E2F1 providing a proliferation-linked input; BID requires proteolytic cleavage. Once liberated they neutralise BCL-2 and BCL-XL, or engage BAX and BAK directly, releasing cytochrome c and triggering caspase activation.

When phospholipase C cleaves the membrane lipid PIP2, it generates two second messengers whose downstream consequences constitute this pathway: inositol trisphosphate, which opens ITPR1-3 channels to release calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, and diacylglycerol, which stays in the membrane and recruits effectors to it. DAG activates protein kinase C isoforms, the RasGRP guanine nucleotide exchange factors that link receptor stimulation to Ras signalling in lymphocytes, and TRPC3/6/7 cation channels. Its levels are set by termination routes: diacylglycerol kinases phosphorylate DAG back to phosphatidic acid, while diacylglycerol lipases convert it to the endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol, which is then degraded by MGLL and ABHD6/12. This output governs secretion, contraction, platelet and T cell activation, and synaptic retrograde signalling; unchecked DAG-driven PKC activity is the basis of phorbol ester tumour promotion.

Platelet granule release requires that syntaxin-4 on the plasma membrane be freed from a clamp before it can pair with vesicle SNAREs, and this disinhibition of SNARE formation is the switch that licenses fusion. Munc18-3 (STXBP3) binds syntaxin-4 in a closed conformation that cannot enter a fusion complex; conventional protein kinase C isoforms activated downstream of thrombin, collagen and other platelet agonists phosphorylate the pair and release the constraint, allowing syntaxin-4 to assemble with SNAP and VAMP partners and drive exocytosis of dense granule and alpha granule contents. The result is amplified recruitment and aggregation of platelets at a site of vascular injury, so the step sits at the interface of agonist signal transduction and regulated secretion. Related Munc18-syntaxin control governs insulin granule and immune cell granule release, and defective granule secretion produces bleeding tendency.

Platelets stick to exposed collagen at a damaged vessel wall largely through GPVI, and the activation cascade it triggers converts that contact into shape change, granule release and aggregation — the first step of haemostasis and a driver of arterial thrombosis. GPVI pairs with the FcR gamma chain, whose ITAM is phosphorylated by the Src-family kinases Fyn and Lyn, recruiting Syk and assembling a signalosome around the transmembrane adaptor LAT and the cytosolic adaptor SLP-76 (LCP2), much as immune receptors do in T and B cells. Syk output runs through PI3K subunits and PLC-gamma2 to calcium mobilisation and protein kinase C, while VAV exchange factors drive Rac, RhoA and CDC42 for cytoskeletal remodelling; SHP-1 and SHP-2 tune the response. The related receptor CLEC-2, ligated by podoplanin, feeds into the same machinery. Loss of GPVI gives a mild bleeding tendency, and its blockade is pursued as antithrombotic therapy.

Platelet degranulation is the secretory burst that turns an activated platelet into a source of clotting factors, adhesion proteins and growth factors at a site of vascular injury. It converts a mechanical plug into a biochemical hub: without it haemostasis fails and bleeding disorders such as grey platelet and storage pool disease follow, while excessive release drives thrombosis and feeds inflammation and wound repair. Alpha granules discharge fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, thrombospondin, P-selectin, PF4 and PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family growth factors together with protease inhibitors of the serpin group; dense granules release ADP, ATP, serotonin and calcium that recruit further platelets in an autocrine loop; lysosomal contents complete the repertoire. Fusion depends on SNARE and Munc18 machinery with Rab27 and synaptotagmin-like regulators, coordinated with integrin alphaIIb-beta3 activation, talin and kindlin, and cytoskeletal remodelling that drives granule centralisation.

When a vessel is injured, platelets not only plug the breach but empty their storage granules into it, and platelet degranulation is that secretory event. The released cargo amplifies platelet recruitment, supports coagulation, and initiates wound repair; loss of granule content or of the machinery that releases it causes bleeding disorders such as gray platelet and storage pool disease. Alpha granules supply adhesive and clotting proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen chains, factor V, thrombospondin and multimerin, along with protease inhibitors of the serpin family and growth factors such as PDGF, TGF-beta and VEGF family members that drive angiogenesis and fibrosis. P-selectin and CD63 move to the surface as granule membranes fuse, marking activation. Fusion itself depends on SNARE and regulatory proteins including STXBP2, VTI1B, RAB27B and SYTL4, while integrin alphaIIb-beta3 and the cytoskeletal proteins talin, kindlin-3 and filamin couple activation to secretion.

Once an antigen-engaged B cell receptor has generated its second messengers, this branch converts them into transcriptional programmes that decide whether the cell proliferates, survives or becomes tolerant. Diacylglycerol recruits protein kinase C beta, which acts through the CARD11/BCL10/MALT1 complex and TAK1 to activate the IKK complex; IkappaB proteins are then phosphorylated, polyubiquitinated and destroyed by the proteasome, freeing NF-kappaB subunits such as RELA, REL and NFKB1 to enter the nucleus. In parallel, calcium-loaded calmodulin activates the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFATC1-3 and permits their nuclear import, while RasGRP1 and RasGRP3 load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS to drive the MAP kinase arm. The abundance of proteasome and ubiquitin components reflects how much of the output depends on regulated protein degradation. Loss of these steps causes antibody deficiency, and their constitutive activation underlies several B cell lymphomas.

When a B cell receptor engages antigen, the resulting diacylglycerol and calcium signal must be converted into a transcriptional programme for survival, proliferation and antibody responses; this is the route that activates NF-kappaB in B cells. Protein kinase C beta phosphorylates CARMA1, which nucleates the CBM complex with BCL10 and MALT1, recruiting TAK1 and the IKK complex. IKK-beta phosphorylates the inhibitors IkB-alpha, -beta and -epsilon, marking them for SCF-betaTrCP ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction, so the accompanying ubiquitin genes and the full 26S proteasome are integral rather than incidental. Freed p50-RelA and c-Rel dimers enter the nucleus and drive target transcription. Loss of CARMA1, BCL10 or MALT1 causes combined immunodeficiency with unresponsive lymphocytes, while gain-of-function mutations in the same complex sustain constitutive NF-kappaB activity in B cell lymphomas.

B cell receptor engagement must be converted into a proliferative, differentiation-promoting signal, and RAS activation in B cells is the step that links receptor-proximal lipid signalling to the MAP kinase cascade. Antigen binding activates phospholipase C, generating diacylglycerol at the plasma membrane; the exchange factors RASGRP1 and RASGRP3 are recruited to that lipid and phosphorylated by protein kinase C, which switches on their catalytic activity. They then load HRAS, KRAS and NRAS with GTP by promoting release of bound GDP, and active RAS drives the RAF-MEK-ERK route toward transcriptional programmes for B cell survival, clonal expansion and antibody responses. This is one of the principal amplification points downstream of the antigen receptor, so its loss blunts humoral immunity, while inappropriate RAS-GRP activity contributes to lymphoid leukaemia and autoimmunity.

ISG15 antiviral mechanism is the arm of the type I interferon response that tags host and viral proteins with the ubiquitin-like modifier ISG15, restricting virus replication and tuning the interferon response itself. Loss of its regulation causes interferonopathy: the deconjugating enzyme USP18 is the brake, and its failure leads to runaway interferon signalling and severe disease. Conjugation follows the ubiquitin logic — activation by the E1 UBA7, transfer through UBE2L6, and ligation by HERC5, TRIM25 or ARIH1 — but the substrates are innate immune sensors and effectors such as RIG-I, MDA5, PKR, MX1, STAT1 and IRF3, whose activity or localisation is thereby altered. Translation initiation factors, importins and the nuclear pore complex appear as substrates too, linking ISGylation to control of protein synthesis and nucleocytoplasmic transport during infection, and to inhibition of viral budding.

Type I interferon signalling arms cells against viruses partly by inducing ISG15, a ubiquitin-like modifier, and the antiviral mechanism described here is the conjugation of ISG15 onto host and viral proteins. ISGylation restricts virus replication by altering the activity, stability or localisation of its targets, and interfering with viral budding and release; loss of the pathway leaves cells more permissive to infection, while its excess is restrained by the ISG15-specific protease USP18. The chemistry mirrors ubiquitination: UBA7 activates ISG15 at the cost of ATP, UBE2L6 carries it, and E3 ligases such as HERC5 and TRIM25 transfer it to substrates. Targets here include the sensors RIGI and MDA5, the effectors MX1/MX2 and the kinase EIF2AK2, transcription factors IRF3 and STAT1, and JAK1, along with translation initiation factors, importins and much of the nuclear pore complex, linking the response to protein synthesis and nucleocytoplasmic transport.

Antimicrobial mechanism of IFN-stimulated genes is the effector arm of interferon responses: once type I and type II interferons signal through JAK–STAT, hundreds of induced genes encode proteins that directly attack viruses and other intracellular pathogens while shaping the adaptive response that follows. It is what makes an interferon-primed cell resistant to infection, and its loss leaves patients vulnerable to severe viral disease. Distinct effector modules appear here: OAS enzymes and RNase L degrade viral RNA, PKR phosphorylates eIF2α to shut down translation initiation, IFIT proteins sequester foreign mRNA from the eIF3–ribosome machinery, MX GTPases trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins disrupt pathogen-containing vacuoles and license inflammasome activation. ISG15 conjugation, driven by UBA7, UBE2L6 and HERC5 and reversed by USP18, modifies both viral and host proteins, including nucleoporins and karyopherins that control nucleocytoplasmic traffic during infection.

Interferons do more than announce infection: through JAK cSTAT signalling they switch on hundreds of interferon-stimulated genes whose products attack viruses directly, and this is the effector arm of that response. Cells lacking it fail to restrict viral replication despite intact sensing, while excessive or unchecked activity drives interferonopathy and autoinflammation. Several distinct mechanisms are represented. Double-stranded RNA activates PKR, which phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α and shuts down protein synthesis, and the oligoadenylate synthetases, which generate second messengers that unleash RNase L to degrade RNA; the IFIT proteins sequester viral transcripts from the initiation machinery, MX1 and MX2 trap incoming nucleocapsids, and guanylate-binding proteins target intracellular pathogens. ISG15 is conjugated to substrates by a dedicated E1 cE2 cE3 cascade and removed by USP18, which also restrains further interferon signalling. Nuclear pore and cytoskeletal components reflect the trafficking steps these effectors intercept.

Prolactin, secreted by the pituitary and by tissues such as decidua, skin and exocrine glands, drives mammary gland development and lactation, and receptor loss leaves female mice infertile with no mammary outgrowth. The pathway describes how prolactin receptor engagement converts hormone binding into gene transcription. The receptor belongs to the cytokine receptor superfamily and has no catalytic activity of its own; it sits as a preformed dimer associated with JAK2, which is activated by transphosphorylation after ligand-induced conformational change and then phosphorylates receptor tyrosines. These create docking sites for STAT5A and STAT5B, the dominant effectors, whose dimerization and nuclear entry induce milk protein and proliferative genes. SH2B1 enhances JAK2 activity, the phosphatase PTPN11 is recruited to the receptor tail as a regulator, and an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase module targets signalling components for degradation. Growth hormone and placental lactogen signal through closely related receptors.

NODAL signalling is the embryonic patterning system that sets up the anterior-posterior and left-right axes and specifies mesoderm and endoderm during gastrulation; without it a mammalian embryo fails to form a primitive streak, and misregulation underlies laterality defects such as heterotaxy and situs inversus. NODAL is secreted as a proprotein and activated extracellularly by proprotein convertases including FURIN and PCSK6, then acts as a homodimer or as a more potent heterodimer with GDF1. It signals through a type I activin receptor (ACVR1B or ACVR1C) paired with a type II receptor (ACVR2A or ACVR2B) and an EGF-CFC coreceptor of the CRIPTO family, driving phosphorylation of SMAD2 and SMAD3, which complex with SMAD4, enter the nucleus and cooperate with FOXH1 to activate target genes. LEFTY1, LEFTY2, CER1 and DAND5 restrain the pathway, and its reactivation contributes to tumour stemness.

Fertilization is the union of sperm and egg that begins a new organism, and the genes here cover the final steps: sperm activation in the female tract, penetration of the egg's outer coat, and fusion of the two plasma membranes. Failure at any of these steps causes infertility, and several components are candidate targets for non-hormonal contraception. The zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4 form the egg coat that sperm must bind and traverse, aided by acrosomal enzymes such as acrosin and the hyaluronidase SPAM1. Hyperactivated motility depends on the sperm-specific CatSper calcium channel complex and on pH regulation through the proton channel HVCN1 and the potassium channel KCNU1. Membrane fusion itself requires sperm IZUMO1 engaging its oocyte receptor, with CD9 on the egg surface needed for fusion competence, while oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 conditions the gametes in transit.

Fertilization is the union of sperm and egg that restores diploidy and initiates embryonic development; failure at any of its steps is a cause of infertility and a target for contraceptive design. The genes here cover the sequential encounters: zona pellucida glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4 form the egg coat that sperm must recognize and penetrate, with the oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 modifying that coat, while acrosin and the hyaluronidase SPAM1 provide proteolytic and matrix-degrading activity for passage through the cumulus and zona. Hyperactivated motility depends on the sperm-specific CatSper calcium channel complex and on pH regulation through the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1 and the potassium channel KCNU1. Final membrane fusion requires sperm IZUMO1 engaging the oocyte surface, with tetraspanin CD9 needed on the egg side; ADAM family proteins contribute to sperm surface maturation and adhesion.

During the first meiotic division, homologous chromosomes must find each other and become held together along their full length before they can recombine and segregate correctly; meiotic synapsis is that pairing. Without it, crossovers fail, chromosomes missegregate, and the outcome is aneuploid gametes or infertility. Meiosis-specific cohesins such as REC8, STAG3 and SMC1B build axial elements along each chromosome, telomere-binding proteins tether chromosome ends to the inner nuclear membrane through SUN and nesprin bridges to drive homology search, and SYCP1 transverse filaments then zip the lateral elements to a central element containing SYCE1, SYCE2, SYCE3 and TEX12 to complete the synaptonemal complex. Chromatin regulation accompanies this: regions that remain unsynapsed recruit BRCA1 and ATR, and phosphorylation of H2AX silences them, the same mechanism that inactivates the sex chromosomes in male pachynema.

Macrophages kill ingested bacteria by flooding the phagosome with superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and reactive nitrogen species, and tolerance of this oxidative burst is what allows Mycobacterium tuberculosis to survive inside the very cell meant to destroy it, persisting for months or years and establishing latent infection. The defence is layered rather than reliant on any single enzyme: the thick, lipid-rich mycobacterial cell wall acts as a physical and chemical barrier, superoxide dismutases convert superoxide to peroxide, and the catalase-peroxidase KatG disposes of peroxide, while parallel systems detoxify nitrosative stress and sequester iron so that free metal cannot drive Fenton chemistry. Alkyl hydroperoxide reductase contributes but does not track with virulence. This antioxidant capacity underlies intracellular persistence and the failure of innate immunity to clear the pathogen; KatG is also the activator of the prodrug isoniazid, linking the same biology to drug resistance.

Iron is a nutrient that host and pathogen compete for, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis meets the shortage by chelation: it synthesises the membrane-associated siderophore mycobactin and the polar, secreted exomycobactin (exochelin) to capture iron in the hostile environment of the macrophage. On the human side of this contest, lactoferrin is the relevant player. Secreted in milk, mucosal fluids and neutrophil granules and taken up into phagocytes, it binds ferric iron with high affinity and so enforces nutritional immunity, holding free iron in macrophages to vanishingly low concentrations and limiting bacterial replication. The mycobacterial siderophores bind iron more tightly still and can strip it from lactoferrin, which is why iron acquisition by chelation contributes to persistence of the bacillus inside host cells and why iron overload worsens tuberculosis outcome.

When Mycobacterium tuberculosis is taken up by a macrophage, it enters a phagosome that is acidified, stripped of essential metal ions, and filled with reactive oxygen and nitrogen species before lysosomal enzymes arrive; the bacillus counters each of these pressures and settles into a non-replicating, dormant state, the basis of latent tuberculosis that can reactivate years later. On the host side, this arm of the response centres on nutritional immunity: lactoferrin, an iron-binding glycoprotein delivered from neutrophil secondary granules and mucosal secretions, withholds iron from the pathogen, limits iron-driven radical chemistry, and has direct antimicrobial and immunomodulatory activity. Restricting metal availability suppresses bacterial metabolic activity and replication rather than killing the organism outright, so the outcome is containment within granulomas rather than clearance, and the standoff between macrophage starvation tactics and mycobacterial adaptation determines whether infection stays latent.

Activated macrophages attack ingested bacteria with nitric oxide and peroxynitrite, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives in the late phagosome largely because it can blunt this chemistry. Tolerance to macrophage-derived nitric oxide is therefore one of the determinants of bacterial persistence, latent infection and the failure of innate immunity to clear the pathogen. Reactive nitrogen species damage DNA, iron-sulfur centres, thiols and methionine residues, and the bacterium answers each: base-excision and alkylation repair restore single-base lesions, abundant mycothiol and methionine-rich proteins act as sacrificial scavengers whose nitrosated products are subsequently reduced, and truncated haemoglobins together with peroxiredoxins reduce nitric oxide and peroxynitrite directly. Thioredoxins and NADPH-dependent reductases regenerate the oxidised thiol pools that keep this detoxification running. The same defences shape how host nitric oxide contributes to granuloma control rather than sterilisation.

Cell redox homeostasis is the set of reactions by which a cell keeps its thiol pools reduced and detoxifies peroxides and other reactive oxygen species generated by metabolism or by an attacking immune system. In Mycobacterium tuberculosis this capacity is what allows the bacillus to survive the oxidative and nitrosative burst inside activated macrophages, and it is therefore a persistent focus of drug discovery. Catalase and peroxiredoxins do the peroxide-destroying chemistry, but they are only regenerated by a relay of disulfide-exchange proteins such as thioredoxins and mycothiol-linked carriers, which ultimately draw electrons from NAD(P)H through reductases including TrxB and the dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase Lpd. Because the downstream peroxidases are extensively redundant, inhibition is most effective at these upstream NAD(P)H-dependent entry points, linking central carbon metabolism directly to antioxidant defence and intracellular persistence.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by neutralising the oxidative and nitrosative burst directed at it, and cell redox homeostasis is the network that makes this possible. Catalase and peroxiredoxin-type peroxidases destroy hydrogen peroxide and peroxynitrite, but they are not self-sufficient: each is re-reduced through relays of thiol-disulfide proteins such as thioredoxins, mycoredoxins and the lipoamide-bearing components of alpha-keto acid dehydrogenases, with electrons drawn ultimately from NADH or NADPH. Maintaining a reduced cytoplasmic thiol pool also supports biosynthetic reductions and protects iron-sulfur centres and DNA from damage. Because the peroxide-detoxifying arms are heavily redundant, inhibiting any single peroxidase is unlikely to be bactericidal; attention has instead turned to the upstream NAD(P)H-dependent reductases, including thioredoxin reductase and lipoamide dehydrogenase, that feed the entire cascade. Loss of this capacity leaves the bacterium vulnerable to host-derived oxidants.

After a neutrophil or macrophage engulfs a microbe, the phagosome is converted into a killing chamber, and the oxidative and nitrosative burst is the chemistry that does the killing. The membrane flavocytochrome formed by CYBA and CYBB, activated by the cytosolic factors NCF1, NCF2, NCF4 and the GTPase RAC2, transfers electrons from NADPH to oxygen to make superoxide, which dismutates to hydrogen peroxide; myeloperoxidase then converts peroxide to hypochlorous acid in neutrophils, while inducible nitric oxide synthase supplies nitric oxide that reacts with superoxide to form peroxynitrite. A voltage-gated proton channel and the vacuolar ATPase together set phagosomal pH and charge compensation, acidifying macrophage phagolysosomes for hydrolase activity, while SLC11A1 strips iron and manganese from the lumen. Loss of oxidase subunits causes chronic granulomatous disease, with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection and granuloma formation.

Fibroblast growth factor receptors normally translate FGF ligand binding into controlled proliferation, differentiation and skeletal patterning, and when that control is broken the receptors signal constitutively. Activating point mutations in FGFR1, FGFR2 and FGFR3 cause dwarfism syndromes such as achondroplasia and thanatophoric dysplasia and craniosynostosis syndromes including Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer and Muenke, by widening ligand specificity, forcing ligand-independent dimerisation through unpaired cysteines, or raising kinase activity. The same lesions recur somatically in cancer, notably FGFR3 in bladder carcinoma, alongside amplification and translocations that fuse the FGFR1 kinase domain to dimerisation domains from partners such as BCR, CNTRL, ZMYM2 or TRIM24 in myeloproliferative disease. Downstream output runs through FRS2, GRB2, SOS1 and RAS proteins, PI3K, PLCG1 and STAT factors, and the fusion-driven aberrant signalling here also engages transcription and mRNA-processing machinery.

Signaling by ERBB2 describes how the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB2 (HER2), which binds no ligand of its own, drives epithelial proliferation, survival and differentiation by partnering with ligand-bound EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4. It is the pathway amplified in HER2-positive breast and gastric cancer and the target of trastuzumab and lapatinib, and its output governs normal mammary, cardiac and neural development through neuregulin signalling. Inactive ERBB2 is held by HSP90 and CDC37 and localised basolaterally by ERBIN; heterodimerisation displaces these partners and permits trans-autophosphorylation of C-terminal tyrosines that recruit GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and PIK3R1, converging on RAS-RAF-MAP kinase, PI3K-AKT and phospholipase C gamma with PKC. Signal strength is set by counteracting machinery: phosphatases PTPN12 and PTPN18, Src-family and PTK6 kinases, and ubiquitin ligases RNF41, STUB1 and CUL5 that direct receptor degradation, with USP8 opposing them.

ERBB2 is the receptor tyrosine kinase that no ligand binds directly; it works instead as the preferred partner for EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4 once those receptors are engaged by EGF-family ligands or neuregulins, and the resulting heterodimers drive epithelial proliferation, survival and differentiation. Because a dimerization-ready receptor needs no ligand of its own, amplification of ERBB2 forces constitutive signalling and defines an aggressive subtype of breast and gastric cancer that is the target of receptor-directed antibodies and kinase inhibitors. Inactive receptor is held by HSP90 with CDC37, while ERBIN confines it to basolateral membrane in polarized epithelium. After dimerization, trans-autophosphorylated C-tail tyrosines recruit GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and PI3K, feeding the RAS-RAF-MAP kinase cascade, AKT signalling and phospholipase C gamma. Ubiquitin ligases including RNF41 and STUB1, deubiquitination by USP8, and phosphatases such as PTPN12 and PTPN18 set signal duration and receptor turnover.

ERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase that drives proliferation and survival when it dimerizes with other EGF receptor family members, and in cancer it is a principal oncogenic driver as well as a drug target. Amplification and overexpression produce constitutively active, ligand-independent HER2 homodimers, while co-overexpression with ERBB3 or mutations in the extracellular, transmembrane/juxtamembrane and kinase domains stabilize active dimers and raise signal intensity. The resulting output runs through GRB2, SHC1, SOS1 and GAB1 to RAS proteins and to PI3K, engaging the MAPK and AKT routes that support growth-factor-independent growth. HSP90 with its cochaperone CDC37 stabilizes the receptor kinase, and PTPN12 and ERBIN act as negative regulators. Which alteration is present determines response to trastuzumab, pertuzumab and tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and secondary mutations underlie acquired resistance in breast, gastric and lung tumours.

Regulation of gene expression by Hypoxia-inducible Factor is the transcriptional arm of the cellular oxygen-sensing system, the step at which low oxygen is converted into a new pattern of gene activity. It drives erythropoietin production and red cell mass, angiogenesis through VEGFA, pH control via carbonic anhydrase IX, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism, so tissues can survive ischaemia; constitutive activation of the same program sustains tumour vascularisation and is the basis of VHL-associated cancers. Stabilised HIF-alpha subunits (HIF1A, EPAS1, HIF3A) are imported into the nucleus, dimerise with ARNT, bind hypoxia-response elements, and recruit the coactivators CBP and p300 to build a productive transcription complex. Negative feedback through CITED2, which competes for coactivator binding, and mitochondrial targets such as HIGD1A that retune respiration, keep the response self-limiting and matched to oxygen availability.

Cells that run short of oxygen respond by rewiring transcription, and hypoxia-inducible factor is the switch that does it. When oxygen is plentiful the alpha subunits are degraded; when it falls they are stabilised, imported into the nucleus, and pair with the constitutive partner ARNT to bind hypoxia response elements, recruiting the CBP and p300 acetyltransferases to open target promoters. The output is an adaptive programme: erythropoietin to expand red cell mass, VEGFA to drive angiogenesis, carbonic anhydrase 9 to buffer pH, and mitochondrial adjustments through factors such as HIGD1A that tune respiration to available oxygen. CITED2 competes for the coactivators and damps the response, providing negative feedback. This axis governs development, wound healing and high-altitude adaptation, and its constitutive activation in kidney cancer and other tumours supplies the vascular supply that solid tumours depend on.

Cellular response to hypoxia is the transcriptional program that lets cells sense how much oxygen they have and adjust accordingly, driving erythropoietin production, angiogenesis through VEGFA, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism. It underlies adaptation to altitude, wound healing and ischaemia, and its constitutive activation through loss of VHL causes clear cell renal carcinoma and other highly vascularised tumours. Oxygen availability is read out by dioxygenases: the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1-3 and the asparaginyl hydroxylase HIF1AN use O2 as substrate to modify HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A. Proline hydroxylation recruits a VHL-CUL2-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase, committing HIF-alpha to proteasomal destruction, while asparagine hydroxylation blocks recruitment of the coactivators p300/CBP. When oxygen falls, hydroxylation stalls, HIF-alpha accumulates, dimerises with ARNT and activates its targets; LIMD1-AJUBA scaffolds and CITED2 tune the output.

Cells must sense how much oxygen they have and adjust transcription accordingly, and this hypoxia response is the mechanism, built around the HIF-alpha transcription factors HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A. It drives erythropoietin production to raise red cell mass, VEGFA-dependent angiogenesis, and a shift toward glycolytic metabolism with carbonic anhydrase 9 to manage the resulting acid load; tumours exploit it to vascularise themselves, and loss of VHL causes constitutive activation and renal cancer. Oxygen acts as a substrate for the prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1-3 and the asparaginyl hydroxylase HIF1AN: proline hydroxylation recruits a VHL-CUL2-RBX1-elongin ubiquitin ligase that marks HIF-alpha for proteasomal destruction, while asparagine hydroxylation blocks recruitment of the coactivators p300 and CBP. When oxygen falls, both reactions stall, HIF-alpha accumulates, dimerises with ARNT and activates its targets. LIMD1 and related scaffolds assemble the hydroxylase-VHL machinery.

Oxygen-dependent proline hydroxylation of Hypoxia-inducible Factor Alpha is the cell's oxygen sensor: it destroys the HIF transcription factor whenever oxygen is plentiful, and stops doing so when it is not. This switch controls erythropoietin production, angiogenesis, and the shift to glycolytic metabolism, and its failure underlies VHL disease, familial erythrocytosis, and the pseudo-hypoxic metabolic state of many tumours. Prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1/2/3 use molecular oxygen, iron and 2-oxoglutarate to modify conserved prolines in HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A; cytosolic EGLN2 (PHD2) sets the basal rate.
