Hydroxyproline creates a binding site for VHL within a cullin-RING E3 ligase built on Elongin B/C, CUL2 and RBX1, which polyubiquitinates HIF-alpha for rapid proteasomal degradation. LIMD1-family scaffolds assemble hydroxylase and ligase together. Under hypoxia the reaction stalls, HIF-alpha accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives the adaptive transcriptional response.

This is the oxygen sensor that keeps the hypoxic response switched off when oxygen is plentiful. Prolyl hydroxylases EGLN1, EGLN2 and EGLN3 use molecular oxygen, 2-oxoglutarate and iron to hydroxylate specific prolines in the HIF-alpha subunits HIF1A, EPAS1 and HIF3A; the modified proline creates a binding site for VHL within a cullin-RING ligase containing CUL2, RBX1, ELOB and ELOC, which polyubiquitinates HIF-alpha for destruction by the 26S proteasome. Because the reaction needs oxygen as a substrate, hypoxia stalls hydroxylation, HIF-alpha escapes degradation and enters the nucleus to drive erythropoietin, glycolytic and angiogenic gene expression. LIMD1, AJUBA and WTIP scaffold the hydroxylases with VHL to sharpen the response. Loss of VHL or EGLN1 function causes constitutive HIF signalling, underlying familial erythrocytosis, paraganglioma and clear cell renal carcinoma.

Mutations in EGFR that lock the receptor in its active conformation drive a large fraction of non-small-cell lung cancers and, through extracellular-domain substitutions, many glioblastomas. These ligand-responsive cancer variants still bind and respond to EGF but dimerize and autophosphorylate spontaneously, so growth and survival signalling runs continuously without a growth factor cue. Adaptors such as GRB2, SHC1, GAB1 and SOS1 couple the mutant receptor to RAS-family GTPases and the MAP kinase cascade, to PI3K and AKT, and to PLCG1, producing sustained proliferation and resistance to apoptosis. Signalling is also unusually long-lived: the HSP90 chaperone with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37 stabilises the mutant kinase and blunts CBL-mediated ubiquitination, delaying the receptor degradation that normally terminates wild-type responses. This biology underlies the clinical sensitivity of such tumours to reversible EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors and the resistance conferred by secondary kinase-domain changes.

ERBB4/HER4 is the receptor tyrosine kinase of the EGF receptor family that responds to neuregulins NRG1-NRG4 as well as EGF-like ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF, and its signalling shapes heart development, mammary differentiation and lactation, and the wiring and GABAergic function of cortical interneurons, with disrupted neuregulin-ERBB4 activity linked to schizophrenia risk. Ligand binding drives dimerisation and autophosphorylation, recruiting SHC1, GRB2 and SOS1 to RAS-MAPK and the PI3K subunits p85/p110 to AKT. Uniquely among these receptors, juxtamembrane isoforms are cleaved by ADAM17 and then by the presenilin-containing gamma-secretase complex, liberating a soluble intracellular domain that enters the nucleus as a co-regulator with STAT5A on beta-casein, with estrogen receptor, with YAP1 in Hippo output, and with NCOR1-TAB complexes repressing astrocyte genes. WWP1, ITCH and NEDD4 ubiquitinate the receptor and its fragments, while WWOX sequesters the released domain from the nucleus.

Dendritic cells that engulf microbes, dying cells or tumour debris must present peptides from that material on MHC class I, so that CD8 T cells can be primed against pathogens and tumours they never directly encountered. Cross-presentation of particulate antigens taken up into phagosomes is more efficient than presentation of soluble protein, and it underlies cytotoxic T cell priming during infection and antitumour immunity. The genes here cover the first two requirements: recognition and uptake of the particle, through the scavenger receptor CD36 and the integrin pair that mediates engulfment of apoptotic cells, and control of the phagosomal environment by the NADPH oxidase, whose membrane flavocytochrome and cytosolic regulatory subunits assemble on the phagosome. Oxidase activity alkalinizes the lumen and restrains proteolysis, preserving epitopes for loading on MHC class I by either vacuolar or cytosolic routes.

Cross-presentation lets dendritic cells and macrophages display peptides from engulfed extracellular material on MHC class I, priming cytotoxic T cells against tumours and against viruses that never infect the presenting cell itself. In the ER-phagosome model, endoplasmic reticulum membrane is delivered to the forming phagosome, so that the machinery normally confined to the secretory pathway operates on a phagocytic compartment. Sec61 channels export internalised antigen to the cytosol for degradation by the proteasome and immunoproteasome, TAP1/TAP2 pump the resulting peptides back in, and tapasin, calreticulin, ERp57 and beta-2 microglobulin assemble them onto class I heavy chains. SNAREs such as SEC22B, STX4 and SNAP23 direct the membrane fusion, while TLR and MyD88 signalling from the ingested cargo licenses the response.

Cross-presentation lets antigen-presenting cells, above all dendritic cells, display peptides from material they took up from outside on MHC class I, so that CD8+ T cells can be primed against viruses and tumours that never infected the presenting cell itself. Without it, cytotoxic immunity would be limited to directly infected cells, and the same route can instead impose tolerance to harmless self antigens. Exogenous cargo is captured by scavenger and lectin receptors such as CD36, MRC1 and langerin, or by Fc receptors, and delivered to phagosomes whose NADPH oxidase activity limits acidification and preserves epitopes. Cathepsins provide vacuolar processing, while the cytosolic arm routes antigen out through membranes for proteasome and immunoproteasome degradation, TAP-mediated transport, and loading onto MHC class I with calreticulin, tapasin, ERp57 and beta-2 microglobulin. SNARE and SEC61 components supply ER-derived machinery to the phagosome; Toll-like receptor signalling tunes the response.

Dendritic cells can present peptides from extracellular antigens on MHC class I, priming cytotoxic T cells against material the cell never synthesised itself. The endosomal/vacuolar route is one way this cross-presentation happens, and unlike the better-known cytosolic route it needs neither the proteasome nor TAP-mediated peptide transport: internalised protein is degraded by endosomal proteases, and the resulting peptides are loaded onto class I molecules directly within early and late endosomes. Cathepsin S and cathepsin L supply the proteolysis, an aminopeptidase trims peptide N-termini, and beta-2-microglobulin pairs with the classical and non-classical class I heavy chains that display the product. This matters for immunity to viruses that do not infect dendritic cells and for anti-tumour responses, and it explains why some epitopes survive only when processing stays out of the cytosol.

Dendritic cells can display peptides from antigens they took up from outside the cell on MHC class I, allowing CD8+ T cells to be primed against viruses and tumours that never infected the presenting cell itself. This route handles soluble exogenous antigens, which are captured less efficiently than particulate material and enter through selective receptors — the mannose receptor, langerin and the high-affinity IgG receptor FCGR1A — that deliver cargo into stable early endosomes rather than degradative lysosomes. From there antigen escapes to the cytosol and is trimmed by the proteasome; the 20S core, 19S regulatory subunits, the immunosubunits PSMB8, PSMB9 and PSMB10 and the PA28 activators PSME1/PSME2 generate peptides suited to class I loading. Without this pathway, cytotoxic responses to extracellular and cell-associated antigens, and cross-priming in antitumour immunity and vaccination, are lost.

In respiring tissues, red cells must load carbon dioxide and let go of oxygen, and this exchange is what makes systemic gas transport work. CO2 enters erythrocytes through aquaporin-1 and the Rh-associated glycoprotein channel, or is hydrated in plasma at the endothelial surface by membrane-anchored carbonic anhydrase IV; inside the cell, cytosolic carbonic anhydrases (chiefly CA2, with CA1) convert it rapidly to bicarbonate and protons. Bicarbonate leaves in exchange for chloride via the band 3 anion exchanger, while protons and CO2 bind histidines and N-terminal amino groups of haemoglobin, shifting it to a low-affinity conformation and promoting oxygen unloading — the Bohr effect. Cytochrome b5 reductases keep haem iron in the ferrous state so haemoglobin remains competent to bind oxygen. Loss of these activities gives methaemoglobinaemia, impaired acid-base buffering, or fragile, misshapen red cells.

Methionine salvage pathway regenerates methionine from 5'-methylthioadenosine, the sulfur-containing waste product released whenever cells make the polyamines spermidine and spermine. Because sulfur assimilation is energetically expensive, recycling this thioether lets cells sustain high polyamine synthesis and keep the S-adenosylmethionine pool available for methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins and small molecules. Six cytosolic reactions carry it out: a phosphorylase (MTAP) cleaves the nucleoside to 5-methylthioribose-1-phosphate, releasing adenine for purine salvage, then isomerase, dehydratase, enolase-phosphatase and dioxygenase steps convert the sugar to a 2-keto acid that is transaminated to methionine, largely by GOT1. Its clinical relevance is largely oncological: MTAP is co-deleted with CDKN2A in many tumours, and the resulting accumulation of the substrate creates a selective dependence exploited by PRMT5 and MAT2A inhibitors. The pathway also connects polyamine turnover to purine and one-carbon metabolism.

Polyamine synthesis consumes decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine and leaves behind 5'-methylthioadenosine, a byproduct that must be disposed of and whose sulfur is too costly to discard. The methionine salvage pathway solves both problems, running six cytosolic reactions that regenerate methionine from the methylthio group while releasing adenine back into nucleotide salvage. MTAP begins the route by phosphorolysing the thioether nucleoside; isomerase, dehydratase-enolase-phosphatase and dioxygenase steps then rearrange and oxidise the ribose-derived carbon skeleton, and a transamination by GOT1 completes methionine. Because recycling here spares the energy of assimilating sulfate, the pathway ties polyamine metabolism to the cell's methylation capacity through the methionine-S-adenosylmethionine cycle. MTAP is co-deleted with CDKN2A in many tumours, and the resulting accumulation of methylthioadenosine creates a metabolic vulnerability exploited in cancer therapy.

In the pulmonary capillaries a red cell has well under a second to load oxygen and unload the carbon dioxide it carried from the tissues, and this exchange is what makes respiration possible. As haemoglobin, built from alpha and beta globin chains, binds oxygen it releases protons held on histidine residues and carbon dioxide bound as carbamate to its N-termini. Plasma bicarbonate enters the erythrocyte through the band 3 anion exchanger and is dehydrated by cytosolic carbonic anhydrases I and II to water and carbon dioxide, which leaves the cell passively through aquaporin 1 and the Rh-associated glycoprotein channel; endothelial carbonic anhydrase IV converts bicarbonate directly in the plasma. The same chemistry runs in reverse in tissue capillaries, coupling gas transport to blood pH buffering; defects in band 3 or globins cause haemolytic anaemias.

Growth factor signalling through ERBB2 converges on the adaptor SHC1 to switch on RAS and the RAF/MAP kinase cascade, driving proliferation and survival in epithelial, cardiac and neural tissues; amplified ERBB2 in breast and gastric cancer makes this route a major oncogenic output and a drug target. ERBB2 has no ligand of its own and acts as the preferred partner for EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4, which bind EGF-family and neuregulin ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin, HB-EGF and NRG1-4. Dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation create phosphotyrosine docking sites on the receptor C-tails; SHC1 binds, is itself phosphorylated, and recruits GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS. Protein kinase C isoforms and the phosphatase PTPN12 modulate receptor output, tuning signal strength and duration.

ERBB4 is a receptor tyrosine kinase for neuregulins and several EGF-family ligands, and one branch of its output is the recruitment of phosphoinositide 3-kinase to the activated receptor. This arm supports cell survival, migration and differentiation in the nervous system, heart and mammary epithelium, where neuregulin-ERBB4 signalling guides neuronal migration, synapse formation, cardiomyocyte maturation and lactational differentiation; disrupted signalling has been linked to cardiomyopathy and to schizophrenia risk. Ligands such as NRG1-NRG4, betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF drive receptor dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation. Only the CYT1 splice isoforms retain the C-terminal tyrosine that docks the PI3K regulatory subunit p85 alpha; the p110 alpha catalytic subunit is then brought in, and the assembled kinase converts PIP2 to PIP3 to activate AKT. CYT2 isoforms lack this site, so alternative splicing determines whether a cell couples ERBB4 to survival signalling at all.

Neuregulins and EGF-family ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF activate the receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4, and one of the main routes out of the activated receptor is the adaptor SHC1, which converts receptor phosphorylation into RAS–MAP kinase signalling. This arm supports proliferation, survival and differentiation responses in neural, cardiac and mammary tissue, where neuregulin–ERBB4 signalling shapes synapse formation, heart development and lactational differentiation; disturbance of the axis is linked to schizophrenia susceptibility and to breast cancer. Mechanistically, ligand binding drives receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation of C-terminal tyrosines that dock SHC1 through its phosphotyrosine-binding domain. ERBB4 then phosphorylates SHC1, creating a site for GRB2, which brings the exchange factor SOS1 to the membrane so that HRAS, KRAS or NRAS are loaded with GTP and the RAF–MEK–ERK cascade is engaged.

Growth factor receptors of the ERBB family can steer cells toward motility and calcium-dependent responses rather than simply proliferation, and the PLCG1 arm of ERBB2 signalling is how that branch is engaged. Ligand-bound EGFR pairs with ERBB2 as a heterodimer, and phospholipase C gamma 1 docks on specific phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails, notably Y992 and Y1173 of EGFR. Once recruited and activated, PLCG1 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C. The output feeds into actin remodelling, cell migration and secretion, and contributes to the invasive behaviour of ERBB2-amplified breast tumours. Because this route depends on heterodimer formation rather than ERBB2 alone, it illustrates how receptor partner choice determines which second messengers a growth signal produces.

The receptor tyrosine kinase ERBB4 can act directly in the nucleus as well as at the cell surface, and nuclear signaling by ERBB4 is how neuregulin ligands are converted into changes in gene expression rather than kinase cascades alone. Neuregulin or EGF-family binding to juxtamembrane-A isoforms triggers ectodomain shedding by ADAM17, followed by gamma-secretase cleavage (presenilins with nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN) that liberates a soluble intracellular domain into the cytosol. This fragment shuttles transcription factors into the nucleus and serves as their co-factor: with TAB2 and the corepressor NCOR1 it suppresses astrocytic genes such as GFAP and S100B in neural precursors, with STAT5A it drives beta-casein transcription during lactation, and with estrogen receptor it promotes progesterone receptor and CXCL12 expression. Competing WW-domain partners YAP1 and the tumour suppressor WWOX set whether the fragment reaches the nucleus, linking this axis to mammary differentiation and breast cancer.

Signalling through the ERBB4 receptor tyrosine kinase, one of the EGF receptor family, is terminated by ubiquitin-dependent destruction of the receptor and its cleavage fragments, and this downregulation sets how much growth-factor input from neuregulins a cell converts into proliferation, differentiation or nuclear gene regulation. Excessive or unopposed ERBB4 signalling contributes to tumour growth, while the same restraint shapes heart and nervous system development where ERBB4 acts. WW-domain motifs in the receptor's cytoplasmic tail recruit the NEDD4-family E3 ligases WWP1, ITCH and NEDD4, which attach ubiquitin to intact ERBB4 and to its membrane-anchored and soluble intracellular cleavage products, routing them to proteasomal and lysosomal degradation. Ubiquitination of the soluble fragment limits the pool that can enter the nucleus to act as a transcriptional co-regulator. Binding by these ligases does not require receptor activation, and SRC-mediated phosphorylation modulates the outcome.

Growth factor receptors tell a cell to grow, take up nutrients and stay alive largely through this route, in which class IA PI3K converts PIP2 to the second messenger PIP3 and thereby activates AKT. Receptor tyrosine kinases for EGF, FGF, insulin, PDGF, HGF and SCF, together with adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1, IRS1/2 and PTPN11, relieve the p85 restraint on p110; PIP3 then recruits AKT to the membrane, where PDPK1 and the mTORC2 subunits RICTOR and MAPKAP1 phosphorylate its activation loop and hydrophobic motif. Active AKT inactivates FOXO transcription factors, BAD and GSK3, blocks TSC2 to switch on mTORC1 and drive protein synthesis, and restrains p53 via MDM2. The counterweights are prominent here: the lipid phosphatase PTEN, PHLPP and PP2A phosphatases, ubiquitin-proteasome control of PTEN, and microRNA and Polycomb repression of PTEN transcription. Loss of this braking, or activating PIK3CA mutation, makes the route one of the most frequently deregulated in cancer and in overgrowth syndromes.

Interleukin-7 signaling is the survival and growth input that lymphocytes depend on, supplied by fibroblastic reticular cells and other stromal cells in thymus, bone marrow and peripheral lymphoid tissue. Without it T cell development fails: loss-of-function mutations in the alpha chain IL7R or the shared common gamma chain IL2RG cause severe combined immunodeficiency, with profoundly reduced circulating T cells, and IL2RG defects additionally eliminate NK cells. Ligand binding assembles the IL7R:IL2RG heterodimer, juxtaposing JAK1 and JAK3 so they transactivate and phosphorylate a receptor tyrosine that recruits STAT5A/STAT5B for transcription of survival and cell cycle genes; PI3K regulatory subunits and IRS adaptors provide a parallel arm, and CISH, SOCS1 and SOCS2 impose negative feedback. Downstream targets include the recombinase genes RAG1 and RAG2, linking this cytokine to antigen receptor assembly. The same receptor alpha chain pairs with CRLF2 to serve TSLP.

This is the broad programme by which a fertilized egg and its descendants generate the specialized tissues of the body, spanning early embryonic patterning through terminal differentiation of individual cell types. Pluripotency factors such as POU5F1, NANOG and SOX2 hold early cells uncommitted; NODAL and its Lefty antagonists drive gastrulation and left-right asymmetry; HOX clusters, held in check by Polycomb complexes, assign position along the body axis. Later steps are represented by cardiogenic and myogenic transcription factors, pancreatic beta cell regulators including PDX1 and NEUROD1, adipogenesis through PPARG and CEBP factors, melanocyte and granulocyte differentiation, and keratinization with its keratins, late cornified envelope proteins and transglutaminases. Axon guidance by ephrins, semaphorins, netrins and Slit-Robo wires the nervous system. Failures produce congenital malformation, and reactivation of these regulators contributes to cancer.

Mitochondrial protein import delivers the roughly 1500 proteins encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes into the organelle that needs them, sorting each to the outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane or matrix. Essentially all mitochondrial function "" respiration, the citric acid cycle, metabolite exchange, heme and iron-sulfur chemistry "" depends on it, and defects in import components cause neuropathies, deafness-dystonia and cardiomyopathy. Precursors first engage the outer membrane translocase, with TOMM20 reading N-terminal presequences and TOMM70 recognising internal signals before TOMM40 forms the conducting pore. Downstream, SAMM50 inserts beta-barrels, TIMM22 handles carrier proteins such as the ADP/ATP translocases, and TIMM23 with its motor (HSPA9, TIMM44, PAM16, GRPEL) pulls presequence-bearing proteins into the matrix, where MPP peptidases trim them. Small TIM chaperones and the MIA40/GFER disulfide relay escort hydrophobic and cysteine-rich intermembrane space clients.

Almost the entire mitochondrial proteome is encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes, so mitochondria depend on a dedicated import and sorting system to acquire their roughly 1500 proteins and deliver each to the correct one of four destinations: outer membrane, intermembrane space, inner membrane, or matrix. Precursors first engage receptors such as TOMM20 and TOMM70 and cross the outer membrane through the TOMM40 channel, then are routed onward by the SAMM50 machinery for beta-barrel insertion, by TIMM22 for carrier proteins, or by the TIMM23 translocase for presequence-bearing inner-membrane and matrix proteins, with the HSPA9 chaperone and its GRPEL nucleotide exchange factors driving translocation and PMPCA/PMPCB and PITRM1 trimming targeting peptides. Small chaperone complexes containing TIMM8, TIMM9, TIMM10 and TIMM13 escort hydrophobic precursors, while CHCHD4 oxidatively traps cysteine-rich intermembrane space proteins. Defects impair respiratory chain assembly and cause neurodegenerative and metabolic disease.

Cytokine Signaling in Immune system is the collective language of immune communication: small secreted proteins that act locally and briefly at very low concentrations to coordinate immunity, inflammation, tissue repair and haematopoiesis. It determines whether an infection is cleared, how helper T cell subsets are polarised, how blood lineages expand from progenitors, and — when miscalibrated — drives autoimmunity, chronic inflammation and cytokine storm. Receptors of the interleukin, interferon, chemokine and TNF families transmit signals through JAK kinases to STAT transcription factors, through MyD88/IRAK and TRAF adaptors to NF-kB and MAP kinases, and through PI3K and Ras branches to survival and proliferation programmes. Negative regulators such as SOCS proteins, phosphatases and ubiquitin-dependent turnover terminate the response. Interferon arms additionally impose an antiviral state, inducing ISG15 conjugation, OAS/RNase L, MX and IFIT effectors, GBPs, and enhanced antigen presentation by MHC molecules.

Cytokine signaling in the immune system is the communication layer that coordinates immunity, inflammation and blood cell production: secreted interleukins, interferons, tumour necrosis factor family ligands, chemokines and haematopoietic growth factors act briefly and locally on specific surface receptors to instruct nearby cells to proliferate, differentiate, migrate or die. Loss or excess of these signals produces immunodeficiency, autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease, cytokine storm, and the antibody or receptor blockade targeted by modern biologics. Mechanistically the receptors coupled to JAK1/2/3 and TYK2 phosphorylate STAT1-6, which enter the nucleus through nuclear pore and karyopherin machinery and are restrained by SOCS proteins and phosphatases such as PTPN6; interleukin-1 and TNF receptor arms instead route through MYD88, IRAK kinases, TRAF adaptors and NF-kB, while interferon responses induce antiviral effectors including OAS enzymes, MX proteins, GBPs and ISG15 conjugation, alongside MHC class I and II antigen presentation.

Antigen-specific defence by B and T lymphocytes is captured here in its full breadth, from antigen capture and display to receptor signalling and antibody output. Dendritic cells and other antigen-presenting cells load peptides onto class I and class II MHC molecules with help from the peptide transporters, tapasin, lysosomal cathepsins and aminopeptidases, while lipid antigens go to CD1 proteins; cytosolic proteasomes supply the peptides. Engagement of the T cell receptor complex and CD79-associated B cell receptor recruits Lck, ZAP70, Syk and Btk, driving calcium entry through STIM/ORAI, calcineurin-NFAT, NF-kB and PI3K-Akt-mTOR responses, tuned by costimulatory and inhibitory receptors such as CD28, CTLA4, PD-1 and the KIR, SIGLEC and LILR families. Class switching and somatic hypermutation via AICDA diversify immunoglobulins. Defects here cause immunodeficiency, autoimmunity, or failed tumour surveillance.

Sprouty proteins act as a built-in brake on fibroblast growth factor signalling, limiting how long and how strongly the MAPK cascade fires after FGF stimulation. This feedback shapes branching morphogenesis in lung and kidney, limb outgrowth and bone growth, and its loss contributes to unrestrained growth factor signalling in cancer. SPRY2 is the best studied and most broadly expressed of the four human family members; it can sequester GRB2 and so block recruitment of the GRB2-SOS complex to the activated receptor, and can also dampen the pathway at the level of RAF activation, with ERK1/2 and the downstream kinase MNK1 as readouts. Sprouty activity is itself tightly controlled: SRC-dependent phosphorylation and dephosphorylation by protein phosphatase 2A subunits switch its inhibitory state, while CBL-mediated ubiquitination targets it for degradation, coupling the brake to the strength of the original signal.

ATP-sensitive potassium channels translate a cell's metabolic state into an electrical one, opening when ATP is low and closing when it is plentiful so that membrane potential tracks fuel availability. Each channel is an octamer of four inward-rectifier pore subunits, Kir6.1 or Kir6.2, with four sulphonylurea receptor subunits that are ABC-family proteins rather than transporters in the usual sense and that confer nucleotide and drug sensitivity. In pancreatic beta cells, glucose metabolism closes the channel, depolarises the membrane and triggers calcium-dependent insulin release; mutations that shift this balance cause neonatal diabetes or congenital hyperinsulinism, and the same complex is the target of sulphonylurea drugs. Related subunit combinations set tone in vascular smooth muscle and contribute to cardiac and neuronal protection during ischaemia, where loss of function is linked to cardiomyopathy and vasospasm.

Inhibitory neurotransmission is enforced in part by potassium channels that open in direct response to G protein subunits, and this is how metabotropic GABA-B receptors silence a neuron. When GABA binds the GABBR1/GABBR2 heterodimer, the coupled G protein dissociates and the released G beta-gamma dimer binds inwardly rectifying Kir3/GIRK channels, opening them so K+ flows out and the membrane hyperpolarises. The result is slow inhibitory postsynaptic current, reduced firing and presynaptic dampening of transmitter release; the same channels set resting conductance and rate in cardiac pacemaker cells, where muscarinic input slows the heart. Channel subunits include KCNJ3, KCNJ6 and KCNJ9 in brain and KCNJ5 in atrium, with many G beta and G gamma combinations supplying the activating ligand. Loss or gain of this signalling contributes to seizure susceptibility, aldosterone-producing adenomas and arrhythmia.

Calcium-activated potassium channels couple a rise in intracellular Ca2+ to potassium efflux, so that the cell answers its own calcium signal by repolarizing or hyperpolarizing the membrane. This negative feedback limits further Ca2+ entry through voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and sets how long a burst of excitation or secretion lasts. The large-conductance BK channel, formed by the KCNMA1 pore subunit with modulatory beta subunits that tune its calcium and voltage sensitivity, shapes action potential repolarization and relaxes vascular and airway smooth muscle; the small- and intermediate-conductance SK and IK channels encoded by the KCNN genes are gated by calmodulin-bound Ca2+ rather than voltage and generate the afterhyperpolarization that controls neuronal firing frequency, with the KCNN4 product also driving K+ loss in erythrocytes, epithelia and activated lymphocytes. Mutations produce paroxysmal movement disorders, hypertension, bladder overactivity and hereditary red cell dehydration.

Classical Kir channels are strongly inwardly rectifying potassium channels that let K+ flow in more readily than out, so they hold cells near the potassium equilibrium potential without opposing depolarization once an action potential has fired. In cardiac myocytes, Purkinje fibres and atrial and ventricular muscle they set a very negative resting membrane potential, permit the long plateau phase, and then supply the current for rapid terminal repolarization; similar channels stabilize excitability in neurons and skeletal muscle. Rectification is not intrinsic gating but block of the outward direction by intracellular Mg2+ and polyamines, which relieves as the membrane repolarizes. The Kir2 subfamily members encoded here assemble as homo- and heterotetramers; loss- and gain-of-function mutations in KCNJ2 cause Andersen-Tawil syndrome and short QT syndrome, linking these channels directly to arrhythmia and periodic paralysis.

Inhibitory neurotransmitters and hormones quiet excitable cells largely by opening G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels, which hyperpolarize the membrane and raise the threshold for firing. This is how GABA-B receptors produce slow inhibitory postsynaptic potentials in neurons, how acetylcholine slows the heart at the sinoatrial node, and how opioid and adrenergic receptors damp synaptic transmission. Agonist binding to a Gi/o-coupled receptor releases Gbeta-gamma dimers, and it is the Gbeta-gamma pair, not the alpha subunit, that binds the channel cytoplasmic domain and stabilizes the open state; activation requires membrane PIP2 and is terminated as the G protein heterotrimer reassembles. The channels are tetramers of Kir3 subunits, with Kir3.1/3.2 combinations dominant in brain and Kir3.1/3.4 in atrium. Mutations in Kir3.4 cause primary aldosteronism, and altered GIRK signalling contributes to arrhythmia, epilepsy and drug reward.

The four HCN subunits encode the hyperpolarization-activated, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels that carry the "funny" pacemaker current and set the rate of spontaneous firing in the heart and brain. Unusually, they open on hyperpolarization rather than depolarization, conducting a mixed inward Na+/K+ current in the diastolic voltage range that drives the slow depolarization taking a sinoatrial cell to its next action potential; direct cAMP binding to the channel's cyclic nucleotide-binding domain speeds activation, which is how sympathetic and vagal tone accelerate or slow the heart. HCN4 dominates in the sinoatrial node, with HCN1 and HCN2 prominent in neurons, where the same current shapes resting potential, dendritic integration and rhythmic burst firing. Loss-of-function mutations cause sinus bradycardia and arrhythmia, and HCN1 variants cause epilepsy; the cardiac current is the target of rate-lowering drugs such as ivabradine.

Inwardly rectifying potassium channels pass K+ more readily inward than outward, which lets them hold cells near the potassium equilibrium potential and set how easily an action potential can fire or terminate. They matter wherever resting excitability and K+ handling are controlled: cardiac myocytes, neurons, glia, and renal and retinal epithelia. The Kir subunits here span the classical strong rectifiers (KCNJ2, KCNJ12), the G protein-gated channels of the KCNJ3/KCNJ5/KCNJ6 family, ATP-sensitive channels formed by KCNJ8 or KCNJ11 with the sulfonylurea receptors ABCC8 and ABCC9, and transport channels such as KCNJ1, KCNJ10 and KCNJ16 that recycle K+ across epithelia. The accompanying G protein beta and gamma subunits, with GABA-B receptors, represent the membrane-delimited route by which inhibitory neurotransmitters open these channels and hyperpolarise the cell. Mutations cause Andersen-Tawil and Bartter syndromes, congenital hyperinsulinism and neonatal diabetes, and hyperaldosteronism.

Potassium transport channels of the inwardly rectifying Kir family set the potassium permeability of renal tubular membranes and determine how much potassium the kidney secretes or retains. Kir1.1, encoded by KCNJ1, forms homotetramers in the thick ascending limb and collecting duct, where it recycles potassium across the apical membrane to sustain sodium-potassium-chloride reabsorption and provides the secretory route that sets urinary potassium output; loss of function causes antenatal Bartter syndrome with salt wasting and hypokalaemic alkalosis. Kir4.1 and Kir5.1, products of KCNJ10 and KCNJ16, assemble as heterotetramers on the basolateral side of distal tubule cells, recycling potassium for the sodium pump and acting as a sensor that couples plasma potassium to sodium chloride transport. Mutations produce electrolyte disturbances with acid-base and, for KCNJ10, neurological and hearing deficits, reflecting the same channels' roles in glia and inner ear.

Potassium channels set the resting membrane potential of excitable cells and shape how quickly they repolarize after firing, so this family underlies the timing of neuronal action potentials, the duration of the cardiac ventricular plateau, smooth muscle tone, renal and cochlear K+ recycling, and glucose-triggered insulin release from pancreatic beta cells. Four structural classes are represented: voltage-gated pore-forming subunits with their accessory beta and silent partners, calcium-activated large- and small-conductance channels, two-pore-domain leak channels, and inwardly rectifying channels including the ATP-sensitive KATP pore that pairs with the sulfonylurea receptors ABCC8 and ABCC9. Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated HCN subunits generate pacemaker current in heart and brain. Included G protein beta and gamma subunits, with GABA-B receptors, capture the inhibitory route by which neurotransmitters open G protein-gated inward rectifiers. Mutations cause long QT syndrome, epilepsy, deafness, congenital hyperinsulinism and neonatal diabetes.

Voltage-gated potassium channels set the excitability of neurons, cardiac myocytes and skeletal muscle by opening in response to membrane depolarization and letting K+ flow out, repolarizing the membrane and shaping action potential width, firing frequency and refractory period. Pore-forming alpha subunits assemble as tetramers, often with cytoplasmic beta subunits and with silent or modifier subunits that only contribute to heterotetramers, generating a large repertoire of currents distributed across axons, nodes, dendrites and nerve terminals. Different families carry distinct duties: rapidly inactivating A-type currents, delayed rectifiers that allow fast-spiking interneurons to repolarize, the M-current that damps repetitive firing, and the cardiac repolarizing currents. Loss or gain of function in these channels underlies episodic ataxia, epilepsy, deafness and long and short QT syndromes, making them frequent targets of drugs and of unintended cardiac drug toxicity.

Two-pore-domain potassium channels carry the background leak current that sets and stabilises the resting membrane potential, opposing depolarisation and raising the threshold for firing in neurons, cardiac and smooth muscle, and secretory cells. Unlike voltage-gated channels they open largely independently of voltage and are tuned instead by extracellular and intracellular pH, membrane stretch, temperature, lipids, volatile anaesthetics and G protein-coupled receptor signalling, which lets them convert chemical and mechanical cues directly into changes in excitability. Each subunit contributes two pore-forming domains and dimerises to build one channel. Members span acid-sensitive, alkaline-activated, mechanosensitive and halothane-inhibited groups; KCNK3 and KCNK9 underlie anaesthetic sensitivity and chemoreception, KCNK18 mutations cause familial migraine with aura, and loss of KCNK3 is linked to pulmonary arterial hypertension through loss of vascular tone control.

Tandem pore domain halothane-inhibited K+ channel (THIK) describes a background potassium leak conductance that sets the resting membrane potential and dampens excitability in the cells that express it. Unlike its two-pore-domain relatives, this channel is insensitive to pH and temperature, and is instead closed by volatile anaesthetics such as halothane, which links it to anaesthetic action on neuronal excitability. The gene here, KCNK13, encodes a subunit whose open leak current provides steady potassium efflux and so opposes depolarising inputs. It is prominent in microglia, where the constitutive potassium conductance supports ramified surveillance behaviour, interleukin-1beta release and inflammasome-driven signalling, making it a control point for neuroinflammation. More broadly this belongs to potassium homeostasis and the regulation of resting potential, upstream of neurotransmitter and cytokine responses rather than part of any single receptor cascade.

Two-pore domain potassium channels provide the background leak current that sets a cell's resting membrane potential, and the halothane-inhibited member of this family, encoded by KCNK13, forms such a leak channel that is insensitive to the pH and temperature cues which gate other K2P subtypes. Each subunit contributes two pore-forming domains and four transmembrane segments, with two subunits dimerising to build a single potassium-selective pore that conducts outward current across essentially the whole voltage range. Volatile anaesthetics inhibit rather than activate this channel, distinguishing it from the anaesthetic-activated K2P channels and making it a candidate contributor to anaesthetic action on excitability. The channel is prominent in microglia, where the standing potassium conductance maintains the resting potential required for process motility, surveillance of brain parenchyma and inflammasome-dependent interleukin-1β release, linking background potassium leak to neuroinflammation.

TWIK channels are two-pore-domain potassium channels that set resting membrane potential by leaking K+ down its gradient, but unlike their relatives they pass remarkably little current. The three members here — KCNK1 (TWIK1), KCNK6 (TWIK2) and KCNK7 — share the signature architecture of two pore-forming domains in tandem within a single subunit, assembling as dimers with four pore domains in total, and show weak inward rectification. Their near-silence appears to reflect regulation rather than an inability to conduct: rapid endocytic retrieval from the plasma membrane into recycling endosomes keeps surface density low, and sumoylation further suppresses activity. TWIK1 contributes background K+ conductance in heart and kidney, where it can become permeable to Na+ under low external K+ and thereby depolarize cells, while TWIK2 has been linked to potassium efflux supporting inflammasome activation in macrophages.

TASK channels are two-pore-domain potassium leak channels whose open probability tracks extracellular pH, letting cells convert acidification into membrane depolarization. KCNK3 (TASK-1) and KCNK9 (TASK-3) are closely related subunits that assemble as homodimers and as heterodimers with biophysical and pharmacological properties distinct from either parent. Because they carry background potassium current, they set resting membrane potential and input resistance, and their inhibition by protons or by neurotransmitters acting through Gq-coupled receptors makes neurons more excitable. This underlies chemosensitivity in brainstem respiratory and carotid body cells, contributes to adrenal aldosterone secretion, and shapes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction; loss-of-function in KCNK3 causes pulmonary arterial hypertension, while KCNK9 is imprinted and its disruption causes a developmental disorder with hypotonia. The channels are also targets of volatile anaesthetics, linking this leak conductance to anaesthetic action.

TRESK, encoded by KCNK18, is the sole member of its branch of the two-pore-domain potassium channel family, and it sets the resting membrane potential of sensory neurons. Background potassium leak through such channels keeps neurons hyperpolarized and raises the threshold for firing, so TRESK acts as a brake on excitability in dorsal root and trigeminal ganglion neurons; loss-of-function variants have been linked to migraine with aura, consistent with a role in trigeminal nociceptive signalling. Unlike other leak channels, TRESK is opened by calcium signals: rising intracellular calcium activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates the channel's intracellular loop and increases current, while kinase-mediated phosphorylation and 14-3-3 binding suppress it. This places the channel downstream of G protein-coupled receptor and calcium signalling as a tunable regulator of neuronal excitability and pain sensitivity.

Alkaline pH-activated two-pore-domain potassium channels of the TALK group provide a background K+ leak whose conductance rises as extracellular pH becomes more basic, linking acid-base status directly to membrane potential. The two members here, TALK-1 and TALK-2, are encoded by KCNK16 and KCNK17 and are most prominent in pancreas and kidney epithelium. Because these channels open rather than close under alkaline conditions, they let cells that handle bicarbonate set their resting potential according to the pH of the fluid they face, supporting tubular bicarbonate reabsorption and the driving force for transepithelial transport. In pancreatic islets, TALK-1 hyperpolarizes beta cells and dampens the electrical activity that triggers insulin secretion, and variants at KCNK16 alter glucose tolerance and diabetes risk. The family belongs to the leak potassium channels rather than voltage- or ligand-gated classes.

TREK channels are two-pore-domain potassium leak channels that set the resting membrane potential and dampen excitability in neurons, and they do so as sensors of the cell's physical and chemical state. KCNK2 (TREK1), KCNK10 (TREK2) and KCNK4 (TRAAK) open in response to membrane stretch and convex deformation, depolarization, heat, intracellular acidosis, and polyunsaturated fatty acids such as arachidonic acid, making them a molecular link between mechanical force or lipid signals and potassium efflux. Because opening hyperpolarizes the cell, their activity raises the threshold for firing, which places them in mechanosensation and thermosensation by sensory neurons, in the control of pain signalling, and in neuronal protection during ischaemia and seizure, when acidosis and free fatty acids accumulate. They are also targets of volatile anaesthetics, and of antidepressant action through TREK1.

Sperm Motility And Taxes describes how mature sperm steer and change gear on their way to the egg, converting cues in the female reproductive tract into the hyperactivated flagellar beating and directional swimming that fertilization requires. Loss of these channels leaves sperm that swim but cannot penetrate the cumulus and zona, a recognized cause of male infertility. The core is the sperm-specific CatSper complex, a pH-sensitive, calcium-selective channel built from four pore subunits and auxiliary beta, gamma and delta partners in flagellar membrane domains; it admits the calcium that reshapes the beat. The proton channel HVCN1 alkalinizes the flagellum to open it, and the potassium channel KSper sets membrane potential. Progesterone released by cumulus cells acts as a short-range chemoattractant through this system, while fluid flow provides rheotactic guidance over longer distances, and the same calcium signals prime the acrosome reaction.

Sperm must change how they swim once inside the female reproductive tract, and the ion channels gathered here are what allow that switch. Their coordinated activity produces hyperactivated motility, the asymmetric high-amplitude flagellar beating needed to penetrate the cumulus mass and zona pellucida, and it underlies the steering behaviours that guide sperm toward the oocyte, whether chemotaxis toward progesterone released by cumulus cells or rheotaxis against fluid flow over longer distances. The CatSper complex, built from pore-forming subunits and accessory subunits arranged in flagellar nanodomains, is a pH-sensitive calcium-selective channel activated by progesterone and alkalinization; the voltage-gated proton channel HVCN1 extrudes protons to raise intracellular pH, while KCNU1 provides the sperm-specific potassium conductance that sets membrane potential. Loss-of-function mutations in these subunits cause male infertility and are associated with deafness-infertility syndrome.

Fertilisation requires a sperm to shed its acrosomal contents and then physically fuse with the egg, and this pathway covers both steps: the acrosome reaction triggered by zona pellucida binding and calcium entry, and the adhesion of the sperm head to the oocyte surface that follows. Cleavage of proacrosin to the active protease acrosin marks the reaction and helps the sperm penetrate the cumulus layer and zona pellucida. Only an acrosome-reacted sperm displays IZUMO1 on its equatorial membrane, where it engages the oocyte receptor JUNO, while the egg tetraspanin CD9 organises the membrane environment that permits fusion; the related IZUMO family members contribute to sperm surface complex formation. Loss of IZUMO1 or of oocyte CD9 leaves gametes able to bind but unable to fuse, producing infertility, which makes this step the decisive gate on conception.

GRB7 recruitment is one branch of growth factor signalling through the ERBB2 receptor, engaged when neuregulin binds ERBB3 and drives formation of a ligand-activated ERBB2-ERBB3 heterodimer. Phosphotyrosines in the ERBB3 C-terminal tail create the docking site for the adaptor GRB7, which carries no catalytic activity of its own but links the receptor complex to proliferative and migratory outputs. Through recruitment of SHC1 it contributes to RAS activation and cell growth, and when GRB7 is itself phosphorylated by integrin-activated focal adhesion kinase it feeds into VAV2-dependent RAC1 activation and cytoskeletal remodelling that supports cell motility. The downstream mechanisms remain incompletely defined. This arm matters clinically because GRB7 lies adjacent to ERBB2 on chromosome 17 and is co-amplified with it in breast cancer, coupling receptor overexpression to invasive behaviour as well as to proliferation.

Endocrine fibroblast growth factors lack the heparin-binding affinity that keeps other FGFs near their site of secretion, so they circulate as hormones and depend on a co-receptor to find their target tissues. Betaklotho supplies that specificity: by binding FGF19 and FGF21 and presenting them to particular FGF receptor isoforms, it restricts their action to liver, adipose and other betaklotho-expressing tissues. FGF19, released from the ileum after a meal, engages FGFR4 together with betaklotho in hepatocytes and suppresses bile acid synthesis by shutting down CYP7A1, closing the enterohepatic feedback loop; FGF21 acts largely through FGFR1c to alter glucose and lipid handling. Receptor selectivity is real chemistry rather than convention, since betaklotho favours 'c' splice isoforms and ignores 'b' forms. Loss of this co-receptor-dependent ligand binding deranges bile acid and metabolic control, and unchecked FGF19-FGFR4 signalling drives hepatocellular carcinoma.

Growth signalling through the ERBB2:ERBB3 heterodimer has to be switched off as well as switched on, and this negative feedback arm sets how much ERBB3 remains available at the cell surface. Neuregulin binding to ERBB3 and pairing with ERBB2 activates AKT; the same AKT activity phosphorylates and stabilises the deubiquitinase USP8, which reverses self-ubiquitination of the E3 ligase RNF41. Stabilised RNF41 then ubiquitinates ERBB3 and sends it for degradation, so receptor output limits its own duration. When RNF41 levels are low, ERBB3 persists on the membrane and sensitivity to neuregulin rises. Loss of this brake contributes to sustained PI3K/AKT signalling in breast and other epithelial cancers, where ERBB3 retention is one route to resistance against ERBB2-directed therapy, making receptor turnover part of the control of proliferation and survival.

Quiescent and early G1 cells must keep the genes that drive DNA replication switched off until a growth signal justifies their expression, and the DREAM complex is what holds them off. It assembles the MuvB core (LIN9, LIN37, LIN52, LIN54) with the repressive E2F4 or E2F5 bound to a DP partner and the p107/p130 pocket proteins, delivering histone deacetylase and chromatin-associated activity to promoters of replication and mitotic genes such as CDC6, CDC25A, PCNA and TOP2A. Loss of this repression lets cells enter S phase without proper licensing, a route to unscheduled proliferation and genome instability; conversely, cyclin-dependent kinase activity and MYC-driven transcription dismantle the complex so the activating E2Fs, including E2F1, can take over. The pathway therefore sets the threshold for the restriction point and for exit from and re-entry into the cell cycle.

Quiescent and early G1 cells must keep the genes that drive DNA replication and mitosis switched off, and this is the repressive arm of E2F control that does it. The pocket proteins p107 and p130 bind repressor E2Fs (E2F4, E2F5) paired with DP partners at promoters of cyclin A, CDK1, E2F1 and MYBL2, and recruit histone deacetylase HDAC1 together with the histone-binding protein RBBP4, so local chromatin stays deacetylated and transcription is silenced. The LIN9/LIN37/LIN52/LIN54 core seen here forms the MuvB module that, with p130, assembles the DREAM complex holding cell cycle genes down in G0. Loss of this restraint allows premature entry into S phase, and its bypass by cyclin-dependent kinase-driven pocket protein phosphorylation is the switch that commits cells to divide -- a step deregulated in most cancers.

Iron-sulfur cofactors are built inside the mitochondrial matrix before being handed to the enzymes that need them, and this assembly line supplies respiratory chain complexes, aconitase, lipoate synthase and, indirectly, cytosolic and nuclear Fe-S proteins involved in DNA repair and iron sensing. Mitoferrins move ferrous iron across the inner membrane, frataxin binds iron in the matrix, and the cysteine desulfurase NFS1 with its partner ISD11 (LYRM4) converts cysteine to alanine to generate the persulfide sulfur used for cluster building on the ISCU scaffold. Ferredoxin reductase and ferredoxin supply the reducing electrons, a dedicated HSP70-HSC20 chaperone step and the monothiol glutaredoxin GLRX5 release the nascent [2Fe-2S] cluster, and ISCA1/ISCA2 support conversion to larger [4Fe-4S] forms. Loss of frataxin causes Friedreich ataxia, and defects elsewhere give myopathy, sideroblastic anaemia and mitochondrial iron overload.

The positive limb of the circadian clock: BMAL1 partnered with CLOCK or its paralogue NPAS2 binds E-box elements and drives rhythmic transcription of downstream genes, setting the daily timing of behaviour, sleep, hormone release and metabolism. Output targets illustrate how broadly the clock reaches — vasopressin in the suprachiasmatic nucleus for neuropeptide signalling, NAMPT for NAD+ salvage, the repressors BHLHE40/BHLHE41 and the deadenylase NOCT, and coagulation and fibrinolysis factors such as F7 and SERPINE1, which underlie time-of-day variation in thrombotic risk. Activation requires coactivators and chromatin modifiers, including CREBBP, the p160 family NCOA1/NCOA2, the methyltransferase CARM1, MED1 and SWI/SNF and nuclear receptor corepressor-associated subunits, and intersects nuclear receptor signalling through PPARA:RXRA and KLF15. Loss of this arm flattens circadian gene expression and produces metabolic and sleep-wake disruption.

Most ABC transporters work at the plasma membrane or on secretory organelles, but a small subfamily resides in mitochondrial membranes, and these mitochondrial ABC transporters connect the organelle's interior chemistry to the rest of the cell. Their cargo traffic supports haem biosynthesis and the export or handling of iron-sulfur cluster intermediates, so they sit upstream of haemoglobin production in developing erythroid cells and of the cofactors required by respiratory complexes and cytosolic Fe-S enzymes. ABCB7 is the best characterised: loss-of-function mutations cause X-linked sideroblastic anaemia with ataxia, in which iron accumulates in mitochondria while haem synthesis falters. ABCB10 partners with mitoferrin in erythroid iron import and protects against oxidative stress, ABCB8 has been linked to mitochondrial iron export and cardiac protection, and ABCB6 contributes to porphyrin handling. Together they make iron and porphyrin distribution a transport problem as much as an enzymatic one.

ATP-driven lipid movement across membranes is what keeps cholesterol, phospholipids and fatty acids where cells can use them, and this group of ABC transporters carries out that traffic in lipid homeostasis. ABCA family members, prominent in monocytes and macrophages and induced when cells accumulate cholesterol, export phospholipid and sterol to acceptors such as apolipoprotein A-I to build HDL, so their failure promotes foam cell formation and atherosclerosis. ABCG1 and ABCG4 also efflux cellular cholesterol, while the ABCG5/ABCG8 heterodimer limits intestinal absorption and drives biliary sterol secretion; loss of that pair causes sitosterolemia. ABCD transporters, inserted into peroxisomes with help from the peroxin machinery, import very long chain fatty acids for beta-oxidation, and ABCD1 mutation gives X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. ABCA3 supplies surfactant lipid to lung lamellar bodies and ABCA12 the skin permeability barrier.

Raising cytosolic Ca2+ is the switch that converts agonist binding into a functional response in non-excitable cells, and in platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation during haemostasis. Two sources are combined. Phospholipase C-generated IP3 opens the ER channels ITPR1-3 to discharge internal stores; the resulting drop in store content is sensed by STIM1, which gathers at ER-plasma membrane contacts and gates the ORAI1/ORAI2 pore to produce store-operated Ca2+ entry that both sustains signalling and refills the store. Independently, ligand- and receptor-operated routes admit Ca2+ directly: the ATP-gated P2X family, with P2X1 prominent in platelets, and TRPC3/6/7 channels. Loss of STIM1 or ORAI1 function produces immunodeficiency and impaired platelet and lymphocyte activation, while excessive entry favours thrombosis, placing this step at the centre of secretion, adhesion and calcium-dependent enzyme control.

Apoptosis can be triggered by loss of anchorage or UV damage, and the release of BMF and its translocation to mitochondria is how those cues reach the cell death machinery. BMF is a BH3-only protein of the BCL-2 family that, once free, moves to the outer mitochondrial membrane to neutralise pro-survival relatives such as BCL-2 and BCL-XL, permitting BAX/BAK pore formation, cytochrome c release and caspase activation. In healthy cells BMF is held away from mitochondria by binding dynein light chain 2 (DYNLL2) within the myosin V motor complex, tethering it to the actin cytoskeleton. Stress-activated JNK (MAPK8) phosphorylates the light chain, breaking the interaction and liberating BMF. This makes the pathway a sensor of cytoskeletal integrity: detached epithelial cells die by anoikis, and failure of the arrangement allows survival of cells outside their proper niche, a step in tumour dissemination.

When DNA damage or oncogenic stress makes a cell unfit to continue, one of the decisive steps is induction of the BH3-only protein PUMA and its arrival at the mitochondrial outer membrane, where it neutralises BCL2-family survival proteins and permits BAX/BAK pore formation, cytochrome c release and caspase activation. This is the transcriptional arm of intrinsic apoptosis, and it explains much of why p53 kills cells rather than merely arresting them; loss of it lets damaged or oncogene-driven cells persist, a route to tumour survival and to resistance against genotoxic therapy. The BBC3 gene is transactivated by p53 and by its relatives p63 and p73, and independently by E2F1 acting with its DP dimerisation partners, linking deregulated cell cycle entry to death. ASPP family cofactors bias p53 toward proapoptotic targets such as this one rather than toward arrest genes.

Oxidative deamination by amine oxidases terminates the action of biogenic amines and clears amines taken in with food. Monoamine oxidases A and B, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, degrade serotonin, noradrenaline, adrenaline, dopamine and dietary tyramine, which is why their inhibitors are used as antidepressants and in Parkinson's disease, and why MAO inhibition makes tyramine-rich foods dangerous. Loss-of-function in MAOA is associated with aggressive behaviour and raised monoamine levels. The polyamine oxidases SMOX and PAOX act on spermine and acetylated polyamines, feeding the back-conversion arm of polyamine catabolism that controls cellular polyamine pools. All use an FAD cofactor: the amine is cleaved to an imine, hydrolysed to an aldehyde plus ammonia, and reoxidation of the flavin releases hydrogen peroxide, a source of oxidative stress that links these reactions to neuronal injury and iron-driven radical chemistry.

Arachidonic acid freed from membrane phospholipids by phospholipases can be routed down three enzymatic branches; the cyclooxygenase reactions are the branch that produces prostaglandins and thromboxanes. Prostaglandin H synthase carries out two sequential chemistries at one enzyme: a cyclooxygenase activity that oxygenates and cyclizes arachidonate to the hydroperoxy endoperoxide prostaglandin G2, and a peroxidase activity that reduces it to prostaglandin H2. That unstable intermediate is the common precursor from which downstream synthases and isomerases make PGE2, PGD2, prostacyclin and thromboxane A2, mediators of platelet aggregation, vascular tone, fever, pain, gastric mucosal protection and renal development. The constitutive isoform represented here, PTGS1, supports these housekeeping functions, while the inducible isoform dominates inflammation and tumour settings. Both are the targets of aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which explains the gastrointestinal and bleeding consequences of blocking this step.

The chromosomal DNA laddering that marks a dying cell comes from a nuclease held in check until apoptosis commits. In healthy nuclei the DNA fragmentation factor exists as a heterodimer in which DFFA (ICAD) chaperones and inhibits the catalytic subunit DFFB (CAD); once effector caspase-3 cleaves the inhibitor, the liberated nuclease cuts internucleosomal DNA into the oligonucleosomal fragments detected as apoptotic DNA degradation. Chromatin proteins tune the reaction: linker histone H1 variants and the HMG-box proteins HMGB1 and HMGB2 stimulate cleavage by making nucleosomal DNA accessible, while importin alpha/beta carry the complex into the nucleus where it acts. Destroying the genome irreversibly prevents a dying cell from being resuscitated or from passing on damaged DNA, and it prepares the corpse for clearance by phagocytes; failure leaves undigested DNA that can provoke inflammation and autoimmunity.

Death receptors of the tumour necrosis factor receptor family turn an extracellular ligand into an irreversible commitment to die, and this is the step where that decision is made. Binding of FasL or TRAIL to Fas or the TRAIL receptors, or engagement of TNFR1-associated adaptors, nucleates a death-inducing signalling complex in which FADD recruits procaspase-8 monomers through homophilic death effector domain contacts. Dimerization at the receptor, followed by autoprocessing, generates catalytically active caspase-8, which then cleaves downstream executioner caspases; cleavage alone is insufficient without the induced proximity. The pathway clears virally infected and damaged cells, enforces immune contraction after lymphocyte responses, and is a route by which cytotoxic lymphocytes kill. FLIP competes for the same adaptor and blocks activation, while RIPK1 and TRADD link the complex to survival and necroptotic alternatives; TLR4 adaptors can feed into the same caspase-8 platform.

Biogenic amines are oxidatively deaminated to aldehydes by MAOA and MAOB is the step that terminates the action of monoamine neurotransmitters and dietary amines, converting them to reactive aldehydes plus ammonia and hydrogen peroxide. It sets the tissue levels of serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline, tyramine and phenylethylamine, and so shapes mood, arousal and blood pressure; inhibiting it is the basis of an entire antidepressant class and of adjunct therapy in Parkinson disease, while the same inhibition creates the tyramine-cheese hypertensive reaction. Two flavin-dependent isozymes anchored to the outer mitochondrial membrane do the work, MAOA favouring serotonin and dominant in fibroblasts and gut, MAOB favouring phenylethylamine and dominant in platelets and glia. The aldehyde products are handed to aldehyde dehydrogenases for excretion, linking this reaction to downstream catecholamine catabolism and to oxidative stress in ageing neurons.

Neurotransmitters and dietary amines must be cleared as fast as they are made, and oxidative deamination by the two monoamine oxidases is the main route by which that happens. Anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane as flavin-dependent enzymes, MAOA and MAOB convert primary, secondary and tertiary amines to the corresponding aldehydes, releasing ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, after which aldehyde dehydrogenases finish the job to acids such as homovanillic and 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid. The two isoforms share most substrates, including dopamine, tyramine and tryptamine, but MAOA favours serotonin and noradrenaline while MAOB favours phenylethylamine. This turnover sets synaptic monoamine tone, protects against pressor amines absorbed from food, and generates peroxide that contributes to oxidative stress in ageing neurons. Inhibitors of these enzymes are used as antidepressants and in Parkinson disease, and loss of MAOA function is linked to aggressive behaviour and Brunner syndrome.

Polyamines such as spermine and spermidine drive proliferation, chromatin and nucleic acid interactions, and stress responses, and their intracellular levels are held within narrow limits by coordinated synthesis, uptake and catabolism. This catabolic step uses FAD-dependent polyamine oxidases to cleave polyamines back to shorter amines, generating hydrogen peroxide and an aldehyde as by-products. One enzyme acts on acetylated substrates in peroxisomes, completing the back-conversion route initiated by acetylation, while the other oxidises spermine directly and operates largely in the cytosol and nucleus. Because the products include reactive oxygen species and reactive aldehydes, flux through this route links polyamine turnover to oxidative stress, DNA damage and programmed cell death, and heightened activity accompanies inflammation and some tumours. The same enzymes also oxidise certain xenobiotic amines, placing polyamine degradation alongside monoamine oxidase chemistry in amine metabolism.

Cells must not separate their sister chromatids until every kinetochore is properly attached to the spindle, and this is the step that enforces the delay. Unattached kinetochores generate a signal that blocks the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, the multisubunit E3 ubiquitin ligase whose ubiquitination of securin and cyclin B, with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S, triggers chromatid separation and mitotic exit. Inhibition works either by direct binding of the mitotic checkpoint complex, built from MAD2L1, BUB1B and BUB3 together with CDC20, or by sequestering CDC20 so that it cannot act as the activating cofactor for the core APC/C subunits. Releasing this brake too early produces missegregated chromosomes and aneuploidy, a route to chromosomal instability in cancer; failure to release it at all arrests cells in mitosis, the basis of spindle-poison chemotherapy.

A single chromosome whose kinetochore has not yet captured spindle microtubules must be able to halt the entire cell, and this is the step that converts that local defect into a cell-wide block on mitotic exit. Amplification of the kinetochore-derived signal is what makes the spindle assembly checkpoint sensitive enough to prevent aneuploidy; when it fails, cells divide with unattached or misattached chromosomes and missegregate them. Unattached kinetochores, built on centromeric CENP proteins and the Mis12 and Ndc80 attachment complexes, recruit Mad1, Mad2, Bub1, BubR1 and Bub3 and act catalytically to generate a diffusible inhibitor that sequesters Cdc20 and keeps the anaphase-promoting complex off securin and cyclin B. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin, Plk1, the Rod-Zw10-Zwilch complex, dynein, depolymerising kinesins and PP1 and PP2A phosphatases tune attachment status and silence the signal once tension is achieved.

Inactivation of APC/C via direct inhibition of the APC/C complex is the braking mechanism of the spindle assembly checkpoint: it holds the anaphase-promoting complex switched off until every chromosome is correctly attached to the spindle, so that sister chromatids are not separated prematurely. Without this restraint, cyclin B and securin are destroyed too early, cells exit mitosis with unattached kinetochores, and chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy follow. Mechanistically, a cytosolic mitotic checkpoint complex of BUBR1, BUB3, MAD2 and the substrate-recognition subunit CDC20 binds the assembled APC/C directly, occluding substrate recruitment and blocking productive interaction with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S that build ubiquitin chains on its targets. The many ANAPC and CDC subunits represent the cullin-RING-like ubiquitin ligase itself, whose reactivation upon checkpoint satisfaction triggers anaphase and mitotic exit.

Cells must not separate their chromosomes until every kinetochore is properly attached, and this branch of the spindle assembly checkpoint enforces that delay by shutting down the anaphase-promoting complex outright. The APC/C is the ubiquitin ligase that, with its E2 partners UBE2C and UBE2S, marks securin and cyclin B for proteasomal destruction to trigger sister chromatid separation and mitotic exit. When attachment is incomplete, a cytosolic mitotic checkpoint complex containing BUBR1, BUB3, MAD2 and the APC/C activator CDC20 binds the ligase directly and blocks substrate recognition, so the ubiquitination of anaphase substrates never begins. The result is a metaphase arrest that buys time for correct spindle attachment. Loss of this restraint permits premature anaphase, chromosome missegregation and the aneuploidy characteristic of tumour cells, and it underlies the action of spindle poisons used as chemotherapy.

Cells must not divide until every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle, and this is the step that turns a single unattached kinetochore into a cell-wide stop signal. Mad1 recruited to the unattached site binds Mad2 and converts it to a closed, inhibitory conformation that is then released into the cytoplasm, where it sequesters CDC20 and blocks the anaphase-promoting complex, delaying chromosome segregation until attachment is complete. Amplification depends on the kinetochore platform itself: the constitutive centromere-associated network, the MIS12 and NDC80 complexes, KNL1-BUB1-BUB3, the RZZ complex with SPDL1, and the dynein machinery that strips checkpoint proteins once microtubules engage. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin corrects erroneous attachments, while PP1 and PP2A phosphatases oppose kinase marks. Loss of this surveillance produces aneuploidy and chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours.

This is the oxygen-dependent route by which cells extract most of their ATP from nutrients, spanning pyruvate handling, the citric acid cycle and respiratory electron transport. Pyruvate produced by glycolysis is imported into mitochondria by a dedicated carrier and oxidatively decarboxylated by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, whose activity is set by inhibitory kinases and opposing phosphatases; acetyl-CoA then feeds a cycle that regenerates NADH and FADH2 while supplying carbon skeletons for amino acid and lipid synthesis. Those reducing equivalents pass through complexes I-IV, requiring iron-sulfur cluster assembly, haem and copper insertion, and numerous assembly factors, and the resulting proton gradient drives the ATP synthase. Uncoupling proteins dissipate the gradient as heat, and sirtuins tune the enzymes involved. Defects in any subunit or assembly factor cause mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis, encephalomyopathy and cardiomyopathy, and tumour-associated loss of cycle enzymes reshapes metabolism.

Human metabolism encompasses the reactions that extract energy from dietary carbohydrate, fat and protein, build the molecules the diet does not supply, and chemically inactivate toxins made internally or absorbed from the environment. Together these routes set the body's fuel economy, and their inherited failures account for much of the catalogue of metabolic disease — glycogen storage disorders, urea cycle defects, fatty acid oxidation and lysosomal storage diseases, porphyrias. Glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation converge on mitochondrial ATP synthesis; fatty acid synthesis, β-oxidation, cholesterol and steroid production, nucleotide, amino acid, heme and vitamin pathways, glycosaminoglycan and sphingolipid processing, and phosphoinositide signalling lipids are all represented. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, sulfotransferases, glutathione transferases and glucuronosyltransferases handle xenobiotics. Nuclear receptors such as PPARs and SREBP-linked factors, plus insulin and glucagon signalling, coordinate whether substrates are burned or stored.

Stem cell factor, made by fibroblasts and endothelial cells as both soluble and membrane-bound forms, tells hematopoietic progenitors, mast cells, melanocytes and germ cells to survive, divide, migrate and differentiate. Its receptor KIT is a tyrosine kinase relative of the PDGF, CSF1 and FLT3 receptors; ligand-induced dimerization switches on its kinase and triggers recruitment of adaptors such as GRB2, GAB2 and the SH2B family, driving RAS-MAPK through SOS1 and HRAS/KRAS/NRAS, PI3K via its catalytic and regulatory subunits, Src-family and Tec-family kinases, and JAK2-STAT signalling to STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5. Output is tuned by the phosphatases PTPN11 and PTPN6, SOCS proteins, and CBL-mediated receptor ubiquitination and downregulation. Loss of this axis leaves animals anemic, mast-cell deficient, unpigmented and sterile, while activating KIT mutations underlie mastocytosis, gastrointestinal stromal tumours, some melanomas and germ cell tumours, making it a target of kinase inhibitor therapy.

Stem cell factor binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT drives survival, proliferation and migration of haematopoietic progenitors, mast cells, melanocytes, germ cells and the interstitial cells of Cajal, so the strength and duration of that signal must be actively limited. This pathway covers the brakes applied after ligand engagement: the phosphatase SHP-1 dephosphorylates activated receptor and its substrates, the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL tags KIT for ubiquitin-dependent internalisation and degradation, suppressor-of-cytokine-signalling proteins and the adaptors LNK and APS restrain downstream kinase output, and protein kinase C feeds back onto the receptor. Src-family kinases and the GRB2-SOS1 module illustrate the effector arm being tuned. Loss of this restraint matters clinically, since constitutively active KIT underlies gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute myeloid leukaemias, where negative regulation is bypassed rather than absent.

Regulation of signaling by NODAL is the brake on a TGF-beta family signal that patterns the early embryo, setting the anterior-posterior axis, specifying mesoderm and endoderm, and breaking left-right symmetry so that heart and viscera are placed correctly. Because NODAL acts as a graded morphogen, its range and duration matter as much as its presence, and the feedback antagonists encoded here supply that limit; loss of restraint produces laterality defects such as heterotaxy and congenital heart malformation. Mechanistically, LEFTY1 and LEFTY2 and the Cerberus/DAN proteins CER1 and DAND5 sequester mature NODAL in inactive heterodimers, while the LEFTYs additionally occupy the EGF-CFC coreceptors CRIPTO and CFC1 so they cannot present ligand to the activin type I and type II receptors. The result is a self-limiting reaction-diffusion circuit rather than a simple off switch.

NODAL is a TGF-beta family morphogen that patterns the early embryo, specifying mesoderm and endoderm and setting up left-right asymmetry, so the amount and location of its signalling must be held within narrow bounds. Regulation of signalling by NODAL describes how that restraint is imposed: the secreted antagonists LEFTY1 and LEFTY2 and the Cerberus/DAN proteins CER1 and DAND5 bind mature NODAL to form heterodimers that cannot engage its receptor, while LEFTY proteins additionally sequester the EGF-CFC coreceptors Cripto and Cryptic so they cannot assemble with the type I and type II activin receptors ACVR1B, ACVR1C, ACVR2A and ACVR2B. Blocking coreceptor assembly prevents SMAD2/3 activation downstream. Asymmetric expression of these inhibitors around the node converts a symmetric signal into laterality, and their loss produces midline and left-right patterning defects such as heterotaxy and situs inversus.

Collagen is the bulk of the extracellular matrix, and its controlled proteolysis is how tissues remodel during development, wound healing, bone turnover and tumour invasion; unchecked, the same chemistry drives arthritic cartilage loss, fibrotic scarring and metastatic spread. The interstitial collagenases MMP1, MMP8 and MMP13, together with the membrane-anchored MMP14, initiate attack by locally unwinding the triple helix and cutting each alpha chain at a single conserved Gly-Ile/Leu bond about three-quarters along its length. The nicked fibril becomes unstable and is then cleaved more broadly by gelatinases such as MMP2 and MMP9, neutrophil elastase, and lysosomal cathepsins including cathepsin K, which degrades bone collagen during osteoclastic resorption. Furin-mediated activation of latent proteinases and the ADAM sheddases contribute to regulating this activity. Substrates span the fibril-forming, basement membrane, network and FACIT collagen families.

Fat and muscle cells clear glucose from blood only when told to, and the switch is the movement of the GLUT4 glucose transporter from intracellular storage vesicles to the cell surface. Insulin, acting through AKT1 and AKT2, and in muscle also contraction acting through AMPK, triggers this translocation; its failure is the cellular definition of insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. AKT phosphorylates the RAB GTPase-activating proteins TBC1D1 and TBC1D4, which then bind 14-3-3 proteins and stop inactivating RAB8A, RAB10, RAB13 and RAB14, so these GTPases accumulate GTP. Vesicles travel on actin and microtubule tracks with myosins and kinesins, are tethered by the exocyst complex, and finally fuse when vesicular VAMP2 pairs with SNAP23 and syntaxin-4 at the plasma membrane. The pathway ties nutrient and energy sensing directly to regulated exocytosis and whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Beta defensins are small cationic, cysteine-rich peptides secreted by epithelia of skin, airway, gut and the male reproductive tract, where they form a chemical barrier against bacteria and fungi and supplement the slower adaptive response. Their killing depends on electrostatic attraction to negatively charged microbial membranes followed by permeabilization, described either as transmembrane pore formation or as detergent-like carpeting of the bilayer; some peptides additionally block cell wall synthesis. Six conserved cysteines and their disulfide pattern define the fold. Expression of several members, notably DEFB4A and DEFB103A, is induced by bacterial products sensed through Toll-like receptors such as the TLR1/TLR2 pair and by proinflammatory cytokines, so the output tracks infection. Beyond direct antimicrobial action these peptides act as chemoattractants through CCR6 and CCR2, recruiting memory T cells and immature dendritic cells and linking barrier defence to immune cell trafficking. Copy number variation across the locus contributes to differences in susceptibility to infection and to psoriasis.

Defensins are small cationic peptides that act as a first line of chemical defence at surfaces exposed to microbes, killing Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, fungi and some viruses largely by permeabilizing their membranes. Neutrophils, Paneth cells of the small intestine and epithelia of skin, airway and urogenital tract are the main sources; gut and neutrophil peptides are mostly constitutive, while epithelial beta-defensins are induced by inflammatory signals. Both alpha- and beta-defensin subfamilies are represented, each defined by a beta-sheet fold braced by three disulfide bonds, and each made as a precursor whose signal and pro-pieces are removed, with trypsin-like proteases such as PRSS2 and PRSS3 maturing intestinal alpha-defensins. Beyond direct killing, these peptides link innate to adaptive immunity, signalling through CCR2, CCR6 and Toll-like receptors to recruit monocytes and T cells, shape cytokine output and promote wound repair.

Alpha-defensins are small cationic, cysteine-rich antimicrobial peptides that provide a fast, non-clonal line of defence against bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses at mucosal surfaces and inside phagocytes. Human neutrophil peptides 1-4, encoded by DEFA1, DEFA3 and DEFA4, are packaged into azurophilic granules and kill ingested microbes by permeabilising their membranes, while HD5 and HD6 from intestinal Paneth cells shape the gut microbiota and protect crypt stem cells; HD6 additionally forms nanonets that entangle bacteria.
