The peptides are made as inactive propeptides and require proteolytic maturation, with trypsin-family proteases performing this cleavage in the small intestine. Their six conserved cysteines form a fixed disulfide pattern that stabilises a beta-sheet fold. Beyond direct microbicidal action they modulate host cells, binding targets such as CD4 to influence chemotaxis and HIV entry. DEFA1/DEFA3 copy number varies widely between individuals, altering neutrophil defensin content.

Tetrahydrobiopterin is the redox cofactor that aromatic amino acid hydroxylases and glycerol ether monooxygenase depend on, so its de novo synthesis, recycling and salvage set the capacity of cells to make dopamine, serotonin and to clear phenylalanine. Inherited failure of this route causes hyperphenylalaninemia together with brain monoamine neurotransmitter deficiency that phenylalanine restriction alone does not correct. Three enzymes build the cofactor from GTP -- GTP cyclohydrolase I, 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase and sepiapterin reductase -- with GCHFR imposing feedback control on the first step and dihydrofolate reductase salvaging the oxidised pterin. The same cofactor keeps endothelial nitric oxide synthase coupled to L-arginine oxidation; when it is depleted the enzyme generates superoxide instead of nitric oxide, and the resulting peroxynitrite drives endothelial oxidative stress, atherosclerosis and hypertension. Calmodulin, HSP90 and AKT1 phosphorylation tune the same synthase.

Sexual reproduction mixes two parental genomes, and this pathway spans the steps that make that possible: specification of germ cells, meiosis, gamete maturation, fertilization and the first events of embryogenesis. Failure at any step causes infertility, aneuploid gametes and pregnancy loss. Much of the gene content concerns meiotic recombination, where a topoisomerase-like enzyme (SPO11) introduces programmed double-strand breaks at hotspots chosen by PRDM9, and these are repaired by homologous recombination machinery including RAD51, DMC1, BRCA1/2 and the MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 mismatch-family complexes, with meiosis-specific cohesins (REC8, STAG3, SMC1B) and synaptonemal complex proteins (SYCP1-3, SYCE1-3) holding homologues together. Other components act at fertilization: sperm CatSper calcium channels drive hyperactivated motility, IZUMO1 and CD9 mediate sperm-egg fusion, and zona pellucida glycoproteins form the egg coat. Pluripotency and germline factors such as POU5F1, NANOG and NANOS3 link back to the earliest embryo.

Tissues remodel by cutting their own scaffolding, and degradation of the extracellular matrix is how that cutting is done. Matrix metalloproteinases, together with ADAMs, ADAMTS proteoglycanases, cathepsins, serine proteases and calpains, cleave collagens, laminins, fibronectin, elastin, fibrillins, aggrecan and basement membrane components such as nidogen and perlecan. This turnover permits wound healing, bone and cartilage remodelling, angiogenesis, ovulation and leukocyte migration, and it releases matrix-bound growth factors and sheds cell surface proteins including cadherin and CD44, so proteolysis also rewrites signalling. Activity is restrained by proenzyme forms whose prodomain cysteine ligates the catalytic zinc until removed, by activating proteases such as furin, and by tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases and alpha-2-macroglobulin. When the balance tips toward proteolysis the results are cartilage loss in arthritis, aneurysm, fibrosis and tumour invasion and metastasis; too little leaves matrix uncleared.

Every tissue is built on a scaffold of fibrous and adhesive proteins outside cells, and extracellular matrix organization covers how that scaffold is made, crosslinked, attached to cells and broken down again. Beyond mechanical support, it sets the microenvironment that steers proliferation, adhesion, migration, differentiation and survival, underlies wound repair, bone remodelling, angiogenesis and branching morphogenesis, and when deregulated drives fibrosis, invasive cancer and heritable connective tissue disease. Collagens are synthesised as procollagens, hydroxylated by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, trimmed by BMP1 and ADAMTS proteases, then crosslinked by lysyl oxidases; elastin with fibrillins forms elastic fibres, while laminins, nidogens, perlecan, fibronectin and tenascins link the network to integrins, syndecans, CD44, dystroglycan and discoidin domain receptors. Proteoglycans such as aggrecan, versican, decorin and lumican tether fibrils and hold water. Matrix metalloproteinases, ADAMs, cathepsins and plasmin remodel it, restrained by TIMPs and broad-spectrum inhibitors, and this proteolysis also liberates matrix-sequestered TGF-beta and other growth factors.

Collagen formation is the biosynthetic route that produces the body's most abundant protein family and the fibrils, networks and anchoring structures they build. Collagens make up the bulk of connective tissue, giving tendon, skin, bone, cartilage, cornea and basement membranes their tensile strength and their instructions to adherent cells; defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and Alport syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and chondrodysplasias. Alpha chains are co-translationally modified in the endoplasmic reticulum by prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, collagen galactosyltransferases and the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and chaperone activities of PPIB, P4HB and HSP47, then trimerise into procollagen. After secretion, N- and C-propeptides are removed by ADAMTS2/3/14 and BMP1-tolloid proteinases, and lysyl oxidases introduce covalent cross-links that lock fibrils together. The set also covers assembly of type IV networks, type VII anchoring fibrils, hemidesmosomal type XVII collagen with integrin alpha6beta4, plectin and laminin-332, and matrix metalloproteinase- and cathepsin-mediated turnover.

Collagen formation covers the synthesis, modification, secretion and extracellular assembly of the collagens, the most abundant proteins in the body and the structural backbone of skin, bone, cartilage, tendon, cornea, blood vessels and basement membranes. Nascent alpha chains are hydroxylated on proline and lysine by prolyl 4-hydroxylases and lysyl hydroxylases, glycosylated by collagen galactosyltransferases, and folded into triple helices with help from a dedicated chaperone complex including HSP47 and cyclophilin B; procollagen is then secreted, its propeptides trimmed by BMP1/tolloid and ADAMTS proteinases, and the resulting fibrils cross-linked by lysyl oxidases. Beyond fibril-forming types, the pathway builds basement membrane networks, anchoring fibrils and transmembrane collagen XVII within hemidesmosomes alongside laminin-332, plectin and integrin alpha6beta4. Defects give osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and Alport syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and chondrodysplasias, and remodelling by matrix metalloproteinases and cathepsins shapes wound healing and fibrosis.

Carbon dioxide and bicarbonate interconvert far too slowly on their own to keep up with respiration, and the carbonic anhydrases solve that by catalysing the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide into bicarbonate and a proton. This underlies CO2 transport in red blood cells, acid secretion by gastric parietal cells, bicarbonate reabsorption in the renal tubule, aqueous humour and cerebrospinal fluid production, and the supply of bicarbonate for urea and pyrimidine synthesis in mitochondria. Catalysis uses an active-site zinc that deprotonates a bound water; the resulting hydroxide attacks CO2, and a histidine or glutamate relay shuttles the proton to buffer. The family spans cytosolic, mitochondrial, membrane-anchored, secreted and tumour-associated forms, so isoform identity sets compartment and tissue. Loss of CA2 causes osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis, and inhibitors of this chemistry are used as diuretics and glaucoma drugs.

Respiration depends on red blood cells loading oxygen in the lung and unloading it in tissues while carrying carbon dioxide the other way, and this gas exchange chemistry is what makes that round trip efficient. Hemoglobin alpha and beta subunits bind oxygen cooperatively; carbon dioxide forms carbamates on hemoglobin's N-terminal amino groups and protons bind histidines, lowering oxygen affinity so that oxygen is released where tissue acidity and CO2 are highest, the Bohr effect. Most carbon dioxide instead moves as bicarbonate: cytosolic carbonic anhydrases I and II interconvert CO2 and bicarbonate, band 3 exchanges bicarbonate for chloride across the membrane, and aquaporin 1 and the Rh-associated glycoprotein provide gas and ammonium permeation, with carbonic anhydrase IV acting on the endothelial surface. Cytochrome b5 reductases keep heme iron reduced, since methemoglobin cannot carry oxygen. Defects cause hemolytic anemia, spherocytosis, distal renal acidosis, or cyanosis.

Membranes are not built once and left alone: the fatty acids esterified to phosphatidylcholine are continually swapped out, and this acyl chain remodelling of PC — the Lands cycle — is how a cell sets the final composition of its most abundant phospholipid. The balance of saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated chains determines membrane fluidity and curvature, the behaviour of embedded proteins, and the surfactant properties of lung alveolar lining, where a disaturated PC species is the key component. Phospholipases of the secreted, cytosolic and calcium-independent families cleave the sn-2 acyl chain to yield lysophosphatidylcholine plus a free fatty acid, and lysophospholipid acyltransferases such as LPCAT1-4 and MBOAT2 reacylate it with a different chain. Release of arachidonic acid by this step, particularly via cytosolic PLA2G4A, feeds eicosanoid production, linking membrane maintenance directly to inflammatory signalling.

Cardiolipin is the signature phospholipid of the mitochondrial inner membrane, and it acquires its characteristic, largely linoleoyl-rich acyl chain composition only after synthesis, through cycles of deacylation and reacylation. This remodeling of cardiolipin gives the lipid the shape and packing properties needed to support respiratory chain supercomplexes, cristae curvature, protein import and the initiation of apoptotic cytochrome c release. Phospholipases of the calcium-dependent and calcium-independent classes remove an acyl chain to yield monolysocardiolipin, which is then reacylated by transacylase and acyltransferase activities including tafazzin and LCLAT1, with mitochondrial trifunctional protein subunits contributing acyltransferase activity alongside their role in fatty acid oxidation; part of the cycle occurs at endoplasmic reticulum membranes. Loss of tafazzin function causes Barth syndrome, with cardiomyopathy, skeletal myopathy and neutropenia, showing how dependent heart and muscle are on correctly acylated cardiolipin.

Phosphatidylserine is made with a generic fatty acid composition and then edited, and acyl chain remodelling of PS is the deacylation-reacylation cycle that does the editing. Phospholipases A remove one fatty acid to leave lyso-PS, and lysophospholipid acyltransferases such as LPCAT3, LPCAT4 and MBOAT1 re-esterify the vacant position with a chosen acyl chain, MBOAT1 favouring oleoyl species. The result is a defined set of PS molecular species rather than one lipid, which matters because PS sits on the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane, recruits protein kinase C and other C2-domain and polybasic proteins, and when exposed on the outer surface marks apoptotic cells for clearance and supports coagulation. Membrane curvature, fluidity and the release of signalling lysolipids all follow from which chains are installed. Oxysterol-binding-related proteins in the set link this remodelling to intracellular lipid transfer between organelle membranes.

Membrane phospholipids are not made in their final form; their fatty acids are exchanged after synthesis, and acyl chain remodelling of phosphatidylethanolamine is the cycle that does this for PE. A phospholipase removes an acyl chain to leave lyso-PE, and a lysophospholipid acyltransferase re-esterifies a different fatty acid in its place, so the same headgroup can carry saturated, monounsaturated or polyunsaturated tails. This deacylation-reacylation cycle sets membrane fluidity and curvature, positions arachidonate and other polyunsaturated chains for release as eicosanoid precursors, and generates the asymmetric lipid composition of the bilayer. Secreted and cytosolic phospholipase A2 enzymes together with intracellular acyltransferases such as LPCAT3 and MBOAT2 carry out the two halves. The liberated free fatty acids feed inflammatory lipid mediator production, linking membrane lipid composition to signalling, lipoprotein assembly and susceptibility to lipid peroxidation.

Stored fat is not static: triacylglycerol and diacylglycerol are continuously broken down and rebuilt, and this remodeling of their acyl chains sets which fatty acids sit in the lipid droplet and how quickly they can be released for energy. The cycle turns on lipases and acyltransferases working against each other. PNPLA2, the principal triglyceride lipase of adipose tissue, hydrolyses TAG to DAG and can also transacylate DAG and 2-monoacylglycerol back to TAG, while DGAT1 and DGAT2 reacylate DAG to TAG at the endoplasmic reticulum and droplet surface. Monoacylglycerol lipase completes hydrolysis of 2-MAG to fatty acid and glycerol, a step that also terminates endocannabinoid signalling. Balanced futile cycling of this kind governs fuel export from adipocytes, hepatic lipid handling, and sebaceous lipid composition; its loss underlies neutral lipid storage disease and shapes susceptibility to fatty liver.

Phosphatidylinositol made de novo does not carry its final fatty acids; acyl chain remodelling of PI reshapes them after synthesis through a deacylation-reacylation cycle. A phospholipase removes the sn-2 acyl chain to give lyso-PI and free fatty acid, and an acyltransferase re-esterifies the position, in this case MBOAT7 preferentially installing arachidonate. The result is the arachidonate-rich PI pool that supplies substrate for phosphoinositide signalling and, when released rather than recycled, for eicosanoid production; secreted and cytosolic phospholipase A2 enzymes of the group I, II, IV, V and X families provide the hydrolytic step. Because remodelling sets membrane acyl composition and curvature as well as signalling lipid supply, its disturbance matters for inflammation and for liver fat handling, where MBOAT7 variants are linked to fatty liver disease and fibrosis.

Membrane phospholipids are not made in their final form; their fatty acid chains are swapped after synthesis, and acyl chain remodelling of phosphatidylglycerol is the deacylation-reacylation cycle that does this for PG. The cycle matters because PG composition determines the surface activity of pulmonary surfactant, where dipalmitoyl species are enriched, and because PG is the immediate precursor of cardiolipin in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2 remove a chain to leave lyso-PG, and acyltransferases including LPGAT1, LPCAT1 and LPCAT4 re-esterify it with a selected acyl-CoA; cardiolipin synthase draws remodelled PG into cardiolipin. Through this editing, cells tune membrane curvature, fluidity and the lipid environment of respiratory chain complexes, and also release free fatty acids that feed eicosanoid signalling. Defects in surfactant lipid composition and mitochondrial membrane function follow from its disruption.

Synthesis of CL produces cardiolipin, the signature dimeric phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which shapes cristae, stabilises respiratory chain supercomplexes and ADP/ATP carriers, and anchors cytochrome c until apoptotic signals release it. Cells depleted of cardiolipin lose oxidative phosphorylation efficiency and mitochondrial ultrastructure, and defects in its synthesis or subsequent remodelling underlie mitochondrial cardiomyopathies such as Barth syndrome. The committed step is carried out by cardiolipin synthase, CRLS1, an inner-membrane enzyme that condenses phosphatidylglycerol with CDP-diacylglycerol; the CDP-DAG substrate arises within mitochondria or is drawn from a pool imported from the endoplasmic reticulum, and phosphatidylglycerol phosphate formation limits the overall rate. Nascent cardiolipin is then remodelled with unsaturated acyl chains, linking this branch of glycerophospholipid metabolism to mitochondrial bioenergetics, membrane dynamics and the regulation of programmed cell death.

Cardiolipin is the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, and its synthesis there gives that membrane the curvature and charge needed to organize respiratory chain supercomplexes, the ADP/ATP carrier, and the machinery of cristae shaping, mitochondrial fusion and fission. The final committed step condenses phosphatidylglycerol with CDP-diacylglycerol, releasing CMP, and is carried out on the matrix face of the inner membrane by cardiolipin synthase; precursor CDP-diacylglycerol can be made locally or drawn from an endoplasmic reticulum pool. Newly made cardiolipin is subsequently remodelled to its mature, largely unsaturated acyl composition. Because oxidative phosphorylation, apoptotic cytochrome c release and mitophagy signalling all depend on this lipid, depletion or defective remodelling compromises bioenergetics and is associated with cardiomyopathy, neutropenia and neuromuscular disease, placing this route at the interface of lipid metabolism and mitochondrial function.

Phosphatidylserine is the principal anionic phospholipid of the cytoplasmic face of cellular membranes, and its synthesis is carried out by two base-exchange enzymes that swap L-serine for the head group of an existing phospholipid: one prefers phosphatidylcholine, the other phosphatidylethanolamine. Because these serine base-exchange reactions occur in the endoplasmic reticulum and associated mitochondria-contacting membranes, they set the supply of phosphatidylserine for transfer to other organelles and for decarboxylation into phosphatidylethanolamine. The product recruits signalling proteins with C2 and polybasic domains to the inner plasma membrane, supports protein kinase C activation, and when exposed on the outer surface marks apoptotic cells for phagocytosis and provides a platform for blood coagulation. Loss of feedback inhibition of PTDSS1 by phosphatidylserine causes Lenz-Majewski syndrome, a disorder of bone overgrowth, while PTDSS2 variants affect membrane lipid balance in a more tissue-restricted way.

Lysophosphatidylcholine is a single-chain lipid produced when membrane phosphatidylcholine is partially deacylated, and its hydrolysis is how cells dispose of it and recover its building blocks. Lysophospholipases strip the remaining fatty acid to give glycerophosphocholine, which a glycerophosphodiesterase then cleaves into choline and glycerol-3-phosphate. This matters on two counts: lysophosphatidylcholine is a detergent-like, pro-inflammatory lipid that damages membranes and signals through surface receptors if allowed to accumulate, and the choline released feeds back into phosphatidylcholine synthesis, acetylcholine production and one-carbon metabolism. Members of the cytosolic phospholipase A2 family carry lysophospholipase activity alongside their better-known release of arachidonic acid, while the lysosomal enzyme PLA2G15 handles degradation of lysophospholipids delivered by autophagy and endocytosis. The glycerophosphocholine step also governs this osmolyte's abundance in kidney medulla and muscle.

Phosphatidylglycerol is the direct precursor of cardiolipin, so its synthesis sets the lipid composition of the inner mitochondrial membrane and underwrites respiratory chain assembly, cristae shape and mitochondrial fusion and fission. The main route runs through CDP-diacylglycerol: phosphatidic acid is activated with CTP by CDS2, PGS1 condenses the activated lipid with glycerol-3-phosphate to give phosphatidylglycerophosphate, and the mitochondrial phosphatase PTPMT1 removes the phosphate to yield phosphatidylglycerol. A separate, non-mitochondrial contribution comes from phospholipase D enzymes, which transphosphatidylate phosphatidylcholine with glycerol and release choline. Loss of this route depletes cardiolipin and produces mitochondrial disease phenotypes, including cardiomyopathy and hearing loss, and in the lung phosphatidylglycerol is also a component of secreted surfactant, linking the pathway to both bioenergetics and alveolar function.

Membrane phospholipid turnover does not stop at the lysophospholipid stage, and the hydrolysis of lysophosphatidylethanolamine is the step that completes the breakdown of the ethanolamine-containing glycerophospholipids to their soluble building blocks. A phospholipase removes the remaining acyl chain to leave glycerophosphoethanolamine, which a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase then cleaves to free ethanolamine and glycerol-3-phosphate. Both products re-enter biosynthesis: ethanolamine is phosphorylated for phosphatidylethanolamine synthesis through the Kennedy pathway, while glycerol-3-phosphate feeds glycerolipid assembly or is oxidized for energy. The route therefore recycles headgroups and glycerol backbones rather than discarding them, and it limits the accumulation of lysophospholipids, which are detergent-like and destabilize membranes. GPCPD1, the phosphodiesterase acting here, also governs intracellular glycerophosphocholine levels in muscle, linking this catabolism to osmolyte handling and myogenic differentiation.

Synthesis of PA builds phosphatidic acid, the branch-point lipid from which all glycerophospholipids and triacylglycerol are made, and which doubles as a signalling lipid that recruits proteins and bends membranes. Cells that cannot make it cannot expand their membranes or store fat, and loss of the adipose-enriched acyltransferase AGPAT2 causes congenital generalized lipodystrophy. The core route acylates glycerol-3-phosphate, supplied by cytosolic and mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenases, to lysophosphatidic acid via GPAT enzymes at the endoplasmic reticulum and outer mitochondrial membrane, then to phosphatidic acid via AGPAT/LPAAT activity; the peroxisomal GNPAT route feeds ether lipid synthesis. Phospholipase D isoforms generate the same product directly from phosphatidylcholine, with PLD6 acting on mitochondrial membranes during fusion. Secreted and cytosolic phospholipases A2 together with reacylating enzymes remodel acyl chains, tailoring membrane composition and releasing arachidonate for eicosanoid production.

Phosphatidic acid is the branch point of glycerolipid metabolism: it is the precursor from which triacylglycerol and all the major phospholipids are built, and it also acts as a signalling lipid that recruits and activates effector proteins at membranes. Its synthesis begins when glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases esterify glycerol 3-phosphate, itself supplied by glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases, to give lysophosphatidic acid, which acyltransferases of the AGPAT family then acylate at the sn-2 position. A second route generates it directly by phospholipase D cleavage of phosphatidylcholine, while phospholipase A2 enzymes and reacylating acyltransferases feed acyl-chain remodelling cycles that set the fatty acid composition of the product. Output is tuned to nutritional state and underpins fat storage in adipocytes; loss of AGPAT2 causes congenital generalised lipodystrophy, and mitochondrial PLD6 acts in this chemistry at organelle membranes.

Bis(monoacylglycerol)phosphate, historically called lysobisphosphatidic acid, is the signature lipid of late endosomes and intraluminal vesicles, and its synthesis gives these compartments the membrane properties they need for cargo sorting and lipid degradation. Its negatively charged, unusual sn-1:sn-1' stereochemistry resists lysosomal lipases and creates a platform on which sphingolipid hydrolysis, cholesterol export and multivesicular body formation depend; loss of the lipid or its accumulation is seen in lysosomal storage disorders and in drug-induced phospholipidosis. Production begins with phosphatidylglycerol made in mitochondria and delivered through membrane contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum and late endosomes, since the acidic compartment cannot make it de novo. There the glycerophospholipid is deacylated by a phospholipase A2 activity, reacylated, and the phosphodiester linkage reoriented, yielding a lipid that is retained rather than turned over in the degradative pathway.

Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in mammalian membranes, and its synthesis sets membrane bilayer composition, lipoprotein secretion from liver, lung surfactant production and bile lipid output. The main route is the Kennedy pathway: choline is taken up by transporters of the SLC44 family, phosphorylated by choline kinases CHKA and CHKB, activated to CDP-choline by the rate-limiting cytidylyltransferases PCYT1A/PCYT1B, and condensed with diacylglycerol by CEPT1 or CHPT1. Diacylglycerol supply depends on the lipin phosphatidate phosphatases, while acyltransferase remodelling by LPCAT1 tailors the acyl chains, notably for surfactant. A second route methylates phosphatidylethanolamine three times via PEMT, chiefly in hepatocytes. Transfer proteins such as PCTP and STARD7 distribute the finished lipid between membranes. Loss of PCYT1A causes lipodystrophy and retinal dystrophy, and impaired flux underlies fatty liver and neonatal respiratory distress.

Phosphatidylinositol is made in the endoplasmic reticulum but consumed at other membranes, and shuttling PI and PC between ER and Golgi membranes is one way cells solve that geographic mismatch without relying on vesicles. The soluble carrier PITPNB binds a single PI molecule in a hydrophobic pocket, delivers it to the Golgi, and picks up phosphatidylcholine for the return trip, so the same protein running back and forth both supplies PI to Golgi membranes and removes PC from them. The PI delivered this way feeds local phosphoinositide kinases, supporting the PI4P pools that recruit coat and lipid-transfer machinery and sustain secretory traffic from the Golgi. Loss of this exchange cycle compromises Golgi structure and cargo export, linking non-vesicular lipid transfer to the maintenance of organelle lipid identity and to phosphoinositide signalling generally.

Glycerophospholipid biosynthesis builds the phospholipids that form every cellular membrane, and also supplies serum lipoprotein lipids, pulmonary surfactant, and the precursors of signalling molecules such as platelet-activating factor, eicosanoids and diacylglycerol. Synthesis begins from glycerol 3-phosphate, with acyltransferases and phosphatases generating lysophosphatidic acid, phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol; branches through CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine give phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while CDP-diacylglycerol feeds phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol and mitochondrial cardiolipin. Head-group exchange and methylation interconvert phosphatidylserine, ethanolamine and choline species. Because acyl chains are asymmetrically distributed, phospholipases and reacylating enzymes such as the LPCAT and MBOAT family continuously remodel membranes, setting fluidity and curvature, while transfer proteins and contact-site components distribute products between the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and endosomes. Defects cause lipodystrophy, surfactant deficiency, and cardiolipin-related cardiomyopathy including Barth syndrome.

Glycerophospholipids form the bilayer of every cellular membrane, supply the lipid backbone of serum lipoproteins and pulmonary surfactant, and serve as reservoirs for signalling molecules such as diacylglycerol, lysophosphatidic acid and eicosanoid precursors. Their biosynthesis begins from glycerol 3-phosphate, which is acylated in sequence to lysophosphatidic acid and phosphatidic acid; phosphatidate phosphatases of the lipin family divert flux to diacylglycerol for phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine production through choline and ethanolamine kinase and cytidylyltransferase steps, while CDP-diacylglycerol synthases feed phosphatidylinositol, phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin. Cardiolipin is made and remodelled in mitochondria, where tafazzin transfers acyl chains and its loss causes Barth syndrome. Phospholipases and lysophospholipid acyltransferases then remodel acyl chains to generate membrane asymmetry and polyunsaturate content, and transfer proteins move finished lipids between endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria and other compartments. Defects disturb lipid droplet formation, adipose development and surfactant function.

Phosphatidylethanolamine is the second most abundant phospholipid of mammalian membranes, and its synthesis supplies the cone-shaped lipid that lets bilayers curve during vesicle budding, cell division and autophagosome formation, as well as the ethanolamine donor for GPI anchors and the substrate for protein lipidation. Two routes are represented. In the cytidine-based route, ethanolamine kinases phosphorylate ethanolamine, PCYT2 activates phosphoethanolamine to CDP-ethanolamine as the rate-limiting step, and CEPT1 or SELENOI transfers the head group onto diacylglycerol generated by the lipin phosphatidate phosphatases. Independently, PISD decarboxylates phosphatidylserine on the inner mitochondrial membrane, the source of PE that mitochondria depend on for cristae architecture and respiratory function. Loss of PCYT2 or SELENOI causes hereditary spastic paraplegia-like neurodegeneration, and PISD mutation produces a skeletal dysplasia, placing this lipid supply behind membrane biogenesis in neurons and cartilage alike.

Phosphatidylinositol is the parent lipid of every phosphoinositide signalling molecule and of the inositol phospholipid anchors, so its de novo synthesis sets the supply available for PIP2 production, calcium signalling, membrane traffic and cytoskeletal regulation. Two enzymatic steps do the work: a CDP-diacylglycerol synthase activates phosphatidic acid with CTP to form the liponucleotide intermediate, and phosphatidylinositol synthase then condenses that intermediate with inositol, releasing CMP. Because synthesis occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum while phosphoinositides are consumed at the plasma membrane and other organelles, membrane-associated transfer proteins of the PITPNM family move PI between compartments and help replenish pools depleted by receptor-stimulated hydrolysis. This arrangement makes lipid supply and inter-organelle lipid shuttling inseparable, and it is particularly demanding in photoreceptors and other cells with rapid phospholipase C signalling.

Phosphoinositides are made and unmade where their precursor lipid is made, and at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane the interconversion of phosphatidylinositol with phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate sets the pool available to the rest of the cell. This matters because PI4P gradients across the ER and Golgi drive lipid transfer at membrane contact sites, and because the ER must keep its own PI4P low so that counter-transport of sterols and phosphatidylserine can run. Lipid kinases add the 4-phosphate, while the ER-resident phosphatase SACM1L and the myotubularin-family enzymes, including MTMR2 and its pseudophosphatase partner SBF1, remove phosphates and return the lipid to plain phosphatidylinositol. Loss of MTMR2 or SBF1 function causes demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy, showing how tightly membrane identity, lipid traffic and myelin maintenance depend on balanced phosphoinositide turnover.

Inositol phosphate metabolism generates and interconverts the soluble inositol phosphates that carry intracellular signals, beginning with the inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate released when phospholipase C cleaves PI(4,5)P2 to trigger calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum. Beyond that classical second messenger, successive kinase and phosphatase steps build a large family of higher species — IP4, IP5, IP6 and the energetic pyrophosphates IP7 and IP8 — which tune insulin secretion, phosphate and iron sensing, vesicle traffic, chromatin regulation and mRNA export. The genes span the phospholipase C isozymes, the multikinases IPMK, IPPK and IP6K1-3, diphosphoinositol pyrophosphate kinases and hydrolases, and the 5-phosphatases and PTEN-family enzymes that reverse the pathway; inositol synthase and monophosphatases recycle free myo-inositol, the latter being the target of lithium. Because synthesis shuttles between cytosol and nucleus, nucleoporins appear as the transport route. Loss of individual enzymes causes Lowe syndrome, and disrupted signalling in cancer and neurological disease.

Soluble inositol phosphates are the second messengers and signalling currency generated when phospholipase C cleaves membrane PI(4,5)P2, and this metabolic network builds and dismantles them. The immediate product, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, releases calcium from intracellular stores and so drives secretion, contraction, fertilisation and lymphocyte activation; successive kinases and phosphatases then convert it into a large family of higher species, including the energetic pyrophosphates IP7 and IP8, that regulate phosphate sensing, insulin secretion, vesicle traffic and mRNA export. Inositol trisphosphate 3-kinases, a multikinase, IPPK, IP6 kinases and diphosphoinositol phosphatases of the NUDT family set the balance, while myo-inositol monophosphatases recycle free inositol and are the presumed targets of lithium. Lipid phosphatases such as PTEN, OCRL and synaptojanin link the soluble pool back to phosphoinositide turnover; nucleoporins appear because inositol phosphate species shuttle between cytosol and nucleus and modulate nuclear transport.

Phosphoinositide metabolism converts a minor membrane lipid, phosphatidylinositol, into seven interconvertible phosphorylated species that act as address labels on organelle membranes and as second messengers. Because each compartment carries its own signature lipid, this chemistry tells vesicles, sorting machinery and cytosolic effectors where they are: PI4P marks the Golgi and supports secretory vesicle budding, PI(4,5)P2 dominates the plasma membrane where it organises actin, endocytosis and exocytosis, and PI3P defines early endosomes. Opposing kinases and phosphatases set these levels locally — class I, II and III PI3Ks with their regulatory subunits, PI4 kinases, PIP5 and PIP4 kinases, PIKFYVE with VAC14 and FIG4, against PTEN, the myotubularins, SAC1, OCRL, synaptojanins and INPP4/INPP5 enzymes. Pleckstrin-homology and FYVE-domain proteins read the output. Loss of this control underlies PTEN- and PI3K-driven cancers, myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, Lowe syndrome and ciliopathies.

Phospholipid metabolism builds, remodels and degrades the lipids that make up cellular membranes, setting membrane fluidity, curvature and leaflet asymmetry while generating the lipid second messengers that organelles use as identity tags. The enzymes here cover glycerophospholipid synthesis from glycerol-3-phosphate through acyltransferases and phosphatidate phosphatases, head-group attachment via CDP-choline and CDP-ethanolamine routes, phosphatidylserine synthesis and its decarboxylation to phosphatidylethanolamine, and cardiolipin production and acyl remodelling in mitochondria. A large phosphoinositide arm couples lipid kinases and phosphatases with PH-domain effectors and transfer proteins to mark endosomes, lysosomes and the plasma membrane for traffic and signalling. Phospholipases release fatty acids and lysophospholipids that feed eicosanoid production and membrane repair. Defects produce myotubular and Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathies, Lowe syndrome, Barth syndrome and lipodystrophy, and this chemistry is a hub for growth-factor signalling and cancer.

Receptor-driven hydrolysis of the membrane lipid PIP2 by phospholipase C gamma splits one lipid into two second messengers, and DAG and IP3 signaling is how that split is converted into cellular action. IP3 opens the ITPR1-3 channels of the endoplasmic reticulum to release stored calcium, while DAG remains in the membrane to recruit and activate protein kinase C isoforms. Released calcium binds calmodulin and switches on the CaMK2 kinases and CaMK4 via the CaMKK enzymes, and also feeds into cyclic nucleotide control through calcium-sensitive adenylyl cyclases and PDE1 phosphodiesterases, converging with protein kinase A on CREB1-dependent transcription. This branching output shapes synaptic plasticity and learning, immune receptor responses, secretion and contraction; sustained or unregulated flux through it contributes to hypertrophic growth and excitotoxic calcium overload.

Meiosis halves the genome: a diploid germ cell undergoes two successive divisions to yield four haploid gametes, and in the process shuffles parental alleles so that each gamete is genetically unique. Failure produces aneuploid eggs and sperm, miscarriage, and infertility. The defining events occur in prophase of meiosis I, when SPO11 introduces programmed double-strand breaks at hotspots specified by the PRDM9 methyltransferase, and the breaks are repaired by homologous recombination using DMC1 and RAD51 with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 directing a subset toward crossovers. Homologues are held together by the synaptonemal complex, built from SYCP1-3 and the SYCE proteins, while meiosis-specific cohesin subunits REC8, STAG3 and SMC1B keep sister chromatids linked until anaphase II. Telomere-bound proteins and SUN-KASH bridges tether chromosome ends to the nuclear envelope to drive pairing, and ATM/ATR checkpoint signalling monitors the whole process.

Multicellular tissues hold together and coordinate their cells through direct contact, and this is the biology of those contacts: cadherin-based adherens junctions, claudin-sealed tight junctions, nectin and other immunoglobulin-superfamily recognition receptors, and integrin-based adhesion to laminin in hemidesmosomes. It sets epithelial polarity and barrier function, guides axons and builds synapses during development, and defines specialised structures such as the glomerular slit diaphragm, where nephrin and podocin assemble a modified adherens junction whose failure causes congenital nephrotic syndrome. Junctional receptors couple to catenins, alpha-actinin, vinculin, filamin and the actin cytoskeleton, and to Rho-family GTPases, Src and focal adhesion kinases that convert adhesion into signalling; polarity complexes containing Par proteins, PRKCI and Crumbs partners position the junctions. Signal regulatory proteins interacting with CD47 restrain myeloid migration and phagocytosis, marking self to macrophages.

Activin signalling is a branch of the TGF-beta family that drives follicle-stimulating hormone production in the pituitary and patterns early embryos into mesoderm and endoderm. Activin dimers assembled from INHBA and INHBB subunits first engage type II receptors ACVR2A or ACVR2B, which recruit and phosphorylate the type I receptors ACVR1B or ACVR1C; these in turn phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3, which pair with SMAD4 and move to the nucleus to switch on target genes, with FOXH1 acting as a forkhead partner for the SMAD complex at mesendodermal promoters. Output is restrained by secreted antagonists follistatin and FSTL3 and by the inhibin alpha subunit, which forms competing dimers, while TGFBR3 modulates ligand presentation. The same axis governs reproductive endocrine feedback, wound and tissue repair, and, when deregulated, tumour growth and cachexia.

Cells that are not dividing must actively keep their proliferation genes switched off, and this describes how that silence is imposed during quiescence and the earliest part of G1. The pocket proteins p130 and p107 partner with the repressive E2F family members E2F4 and E2F5 together with a DP dimerization subunit, and p130 joins the MuvB core (LIN9, LIN37, LIN52, LIN54) to build the conserved DREAM repressor. Recruitment of the deacetylase HDAC1 and the chromatin adaptor RBBP4 keeps promoters of S-phase and mitotic genes, including cyclins E and A, CDC6, CDC25A, PCNA, MYBL2 and TOP2A, in a closed state until cyclin-dependent kinase activity phosphorylates the pocket proteins and releases them. DYRK1A phosphorylation of LIN52 is what licenses DREAM assembly. Loss of this restraint permits unscheduled entry into S phase and is a common route into tumour cell proliferation.

Phase II - Conjugation of compounds is the second stage of xenobiotic biotransformation, in which transferase enzymes attach polar groups from cofactors onto drugs, dietary chemicals, hormones and the reactive metabolites generated by phase I oxidation, making them water-soluble and readily excreted in bile or urine. It determines drug half-life, and its failure or genetic variation causes hyperbilirubinaemia, thiopurine and irinotecan toxicity, and susceptibility to chemical carcinogens; occasionally conjugation instead bioactivates a compound. The main routes are glucuronidation by microsomal UGTs, sulfonation by cytosolic SULTs, glutathione conjugation by the GST family, methylation by COMT, TPMT and NNMT, acetylation by NAT1 and NAT2, and amino acid conjugation by glycine N-acyltransferases. Also included is the supply and recycling of the cofactors themselves — UDP-glucuronic acid, S-adenosylmethionine, and glutathione synthesis and turnover through the gamma-glutamyl cycle — which can limit overall conjugating capacity.

Drugs, dietary chemicals and endogenous metabolites are cleared from the body by attaching a water-soluble group to them, and this conjugative arm of biotransformation is where that happens. By adding glucuronate, sulfate, glutathione, acetyl, methyl or amino acid groups, transferases make lipophilic compounds excretable in bile and urine and usually abolish their activity, though some conjugates are more reactive than the parent compound. The chemistry is spread across families: microsomal UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, cytosolic sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases, N-acetyltransferases and methyltransferases using S-adenosylmethionine, alongside the enzymes that synthesise and recycle the cofactors themselves, including glutathione synthesis and UDP-sugar supply. Cofactor availability often limits throughput. Variation here shapes individual drug response and toxicity, as with bilirubin handling by UGT1A1 and thiopurine inactivation by TPMT, and failure to conjugate reactive intermediates leaves them free to damage protein and DNA.

Methylation is a Phase II conjugation route that caps drugs, xenobiotics and small endogenous molecules with a methyl group, altering their activity and clearance. It is quantitatively minor next to glucuronidation and sulfonation, but pharmacologically decisive: catechol O-methyltransferase terminates dopamine and catecholamine signalling and is a target in Parkinson's therapy, while thiopurine methyltransferase deficiency causes life-threatening toxicity from azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine. All the reactions draw on S-adenosylmethionine, made from methionine and ATP by methionine adenosyltransferase isoforms, and leave S-adenosylhomocysteine, which is hydrolysed to homocysteine and remethylated by the cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase system, linking xenobiotic handling to one-carbon and folate metabolism. Substrates include phenols and catechols, aliphatic and aromatic amines, thiols, nicotinamide and arsenic species, the last methylated by AS3MT during arsenic detoxification. Cytosolic monomeric transferases carry out most of this chemistry.

Methylation is a phase II conjugation route that caps nucleophilic groups on drugs, neurotransmitters and other small molecules, and although it handles less traffic than glucuronidation or sulfonation, it determines the fate of several clinically important compounds. Methionine adenosyltransferases build the universal methyl donor S-adenosylmethionine, cytosolic methyltransferases pass its methyl group to catechols, amines and thiols, and the resulting S-adenosylhomocysteine is hydrolysed by AHCY to homocysteine, which methionine synthase and its reductase partner remethylate to close the cycle. Substrate-named enzymes give the pathway its character: COMT inactivates dopamine and other catecholamines, TPMT methylates thiopurine drugs, NNMT acts on nicotinamide, and AS3MT methylates arsenic during its detoxification. Because activity depends on cofactor supply and on common variants in these transferases, the pathway links one-carbon metabolism to differences in drug tolerance, thiopurine toxicity, and catecholamine turnover.

Acetylation is a phase II drug-metabolism route in which cytosolic N-acetyltransferases transfer an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA onto the nitrogen of aromatic amines and hydrazines, converting them to amides. It is the preferred conjugation pathway for such compounds, and it determines how quickly people clear drugs including isoniazid, sulfonamides and hydralazine, as well as how they handle arylamine carcinogens from tobacco smoke and industrial exposure. Two enzymes, NAT1 and NAT2, act through a ping-pong mechanism in which the acetyl group is parked on an active-site cysteine before delivery to the substrate. Unlike glucuronidation or sulfation, acetylation masks an amine with a non-ionizable group, so products are often less water soluble than the parent. Common NAT2 variants split populations into slow and fast acetylators, a classic pharmacogenetic difference underlying drug toxicity and bladder cancer susceptibility.

Acetylation is a phase II drug-metabolising route in which cytosolic N-acetyltransferases transfer an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA onto the nitrogen of aromatic amines and hydrazines, converting them to the corresponding amides. It is the main way the body handles arylamine drugs and carcinogens, including isoniazid, sulfonamides, hydralazine and procainamide, and unlike glucuronidation or sulfation it masks a basic amine with a non-ionisable group, so products are often less water-soluble than the parent compound. Two enzymes carry the activity, NAT1 and NAT2, working through a two-step ping-pong mechanism in which a catalytic cysteine is acetylated before the acceptor amine binds. Common NAT2 variants define slow and fast acetylator phenotypes, whose frequencies differ markedly between populations and which alter both drug toxicity, such as isoniazid-related adverse effects, and susceptibility to arylamine-associated cancers. Aliphatic amines are not substrates.

Sulfonation in the cytosol is a phase II conjugation route that attaches a sulfate group from the donor PAPS onto hydroxyl and amine groups of small molecules, generating water-soluble sulfate esters that are readily excreted and whose biological activity is usually switched off. It governs the clearance of drugs, dietary phenols, catecholamines and environmental chemicals, and it sets hormone tone: SULT1E1 inactivates estrogens, while SULT2A1 produces the circulating sulfated steroid reservoir DHEA-S in adrenal cortex and liver. The reaction can also bioactivate certain procarcinogens into reactive electrophiles, so the same chemistry that detoxifies can produce DNA-damaging species. Family members differ in tissue distribution and substrate preference rather than in chemistry, acting as dimers with broad and overlapping specificity, and nucleotidases that hydrolyse the PAP by-product keep the donor cycle turning. Related transferases sulfate protein tyrosines in the secretory pathway.

Amino acid conjugation is a phase II route by which carboxylic acid-containing xenobiotics and endogenous acids are coupled to an amino acid, usually glycine or glutamine, converting them into more polar, readily excreted amides. It is the pathway that detoxifies benzoate to hippurate and handles salicylate, valproate and bile acid intermediates, and it also clears medium-chain acyl groups that accumulate when fatty acid oxidation is impaired, which is why glycine conjugation capacity shapes tolerance to several drugs and organic acidurias. Mechanistically the acid is first activated to a CoA thioester by mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, and an N-acyltransferase then transfers the acyl group onto the amino group of the acceptor amino acid. A related chemistry acting on aromatic hydroxylamines instead forms unstable N-esters that decompose to electrophilic nitrenium and carbonium ions, so this conjugation can bioactivate as well as detoxify.

Glucuronidation is the dominant phase II conjugation route by which the liver and gut make drugs, hormones and waste metabolites water-soluble enough to leave the body in bile or urine. Membrane-bound UDP-glucuronosyltransferases of the microsomal face transfer glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronate onto hydroxyl, carboxyl, amine and sulfate groups, adding charge and polarity that favour biliary and renal excretion. The co-substrate is generated from UDP-glucose by UGP2 and UGDH and delivered into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen by nucleotide-sugar transporters, with UXS1 diverting the same intermediate toward xylose. Individual isoforms define physiology: UGT1A1 clears bilirubin, and its loss causes the unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia of Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes, while UGT1A6 handles acetaminophen and UGT2B7 morphine. Bacterial beta-glucuronidase in the gut can reverse the conjugation, returning the parent compound for reabsorption and prolonging its residence.

Glutathione conjugation is the major phase II route for disposing of reactive electrophiles, and it determines how well a cell tolerates drugs, carcinogens, reactive oxygen species and lipid peroxidation products such as 4-hydroxynonenal. Glutathione S-transferases of the alpha, mu, pi, theta, zeta, omega and kappa classes, together with membrane-bound microsomal forms, catalyse nucleophilic attack of the glutathione cysteine thiol on epoxides, activated alkenes and other electrophilic carbon, sulfur or nitrogen centres, giving less reactive, more water-soluble thioethers for biliary and urinary excretion. The pathway also includes supply and turnover of the cofactor itself: glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits and glutathione synthetase build the tripeptide, while gamma-glutamyl transferases, cyclotransferases and dipeptidases recycle it through the gamma-glutamyl cycle. Common deletions of GSTM1 and GSTT1 alter individual susceptibility to chemical carcinogens, and GST overexpression contributes to chemotherapy resistance; some substrates are instead bioactivated to toxic species.

Elastic fibre formation builds the resilient, recoiling component of connective tissue in large arteries, lung parenchyma, skin and ligament, allowing these organs to stretch under pulsatile load and spring back over a lifetime with almost no turnover. Tropoelastin monomers coacervate and are deposited on a template of fibrillin-rich microfibrils, then locked together by lysyl oxidase family enzymes, which oxidise lysine side chains to allysine and generate the desmosine cross-links unique to elastin. Fibulins, EMILINs, microfibril-associated glycoproteins and a fibronectin scaffold organise deposition at the cell surface, with integrins providing the receptors that position assembly. Latent TGF-beta binding proteins tether TGF-beta and BMP growth factors into the same matrix, so the fibre doubles as a reservoir controlling their release. Mutations in fibrillin-1 cause Marfan syndrome and thoracic aneurysm, in fibrillin-2 congenital contractural arachnodactyly, and fibulin or LTBP4 defects produce cutis laxa.

Fibronectin matrix formation is the assembly of secreted fibronectin dimers into the fibrillar network that surrounds and connects cells, providing the scaffold on which much of the rest of the extracellular matrix is built. Cells cannot organise collagen or fibrillin microfibrils without it, and its loss compromises adhesion, migration, wound healing and vascular development. Assembly is cell-driven: alpha5beta1 integrin engages the RGD and synergy sites in fibronectin's type III repeats, and the resulting conformational change and applied tension expose self-association sites so that additional dimers polymerise into fibrils. The fibril then serves as a template and binding surface for interstitial and basement membrane collagens, fibrin, heparan sulfate proteoglycans and fibulin, and its turnover is set by matrix metalloproteinase activity. Alternative splicing of the extra type III and variable regions tunes which integrins and partners a given fibronectin engages, distinguishing cellular from plasma forms.

Fibronectin matrix formation is the step that converts soluble fibronectin dimers into the fibrillar network that surrounds cells and acts as the template on which the rest of the extracellular matrix is built. It matters because collagen deposition, fibrillin microfibril assembly and cell adhesion all depend on this scaffold; without it, matrix turnover accelerates and tissue architecture, wound repair and developmental morphogenesis fail. Assembly is cell-driven rather than spontaneous: FN1 dimers, joined by C-terminal disulfide bonds, engage alpha5beta1 integrin through the RGD and synergy sites, and the resulting tension and conformational change expose self-association surfaces so that further dimers add to growing fibrils. Type III modules lack internal disulfides and unfold under applied force, giving the fibril its elasticity. The polymerized network then binds and organizes fibrillar and basement membrane collagens, linking integrin-mediated mechanics to matrix composition.

Polo-like kinase mediated events describes how PLK1 drives the commitment step into mitosis, converting a G2 cell into a dividing one. Its output is the abrupt activation of cyclin B-CDK1, the switch that triggers nuclear envelope breakdown, chromosome condensation and spindle assembly; cells that cannot execute it arrest in G2, and its deregulation is a common feature of proliferating tumours. PLK1 achieves the switch by activating CDC25 phosphatases while inhibiting the opposing kinases WEE1 and MYT1, and CDK1 itself primes these substrates so that the polo-box domain can dock on them, making the circuit self-amplifying. A transcriptional arm reinforces it: PLK1 phosphorylates FOXM1, which together with MYBL2 and the MuvB core drives expression of mitotic genes including PLK1 and cyclin B, closing a positive feedback loop on the G2/M transition.

Entry into mitosis is a switch, and Polo-like kinase 1 is one of the levers that throws it. PLK1-mediated events tip the balance of activity on cyclin B-bound CDK1 from inhibited to active, committing a cell to divide; loss of this control delays or blocks mitotic entry, while excess PLK1 activity lets cells through with damaged DNA and is common in tumours. PLK1 phosphorylates and stimulates the activating phosphatase CDC25C while inactivating the inhibitory kinases WEE1 and MYT1, and CDK1 in turn creates the phosphopeptide docking sites that PLK1's polo-box domain reads, so the two kinases reinforce each other. A second loop runs through transcription: PLK1 activates FOXM1, which together with the MYBL2-MuvB complex drives expression of G2/M genes including PLK1 and the cyclins themselves.

Interferon-gamma switches on ceruloplasmin in monocytes and macrophages, and then shuts it off again: roughly sixteen hours after induction, translation of the ceruloplasmin message is silenced so that the inflammatory output is self-limiting rather than open-ended. The silencing is carried out by RPL13A, a large-subunit ribosomal protein that is phosphorylated, released from the 60S subunit, and redirected to a structured element in the transcript's 3' UTR, where it blocks recruitment or scanning by the initiation machinery. Because circularization of the mRNA through cap-bound eIF4E/eIF4G and poly(A)-bound PABPC1 places the 3' UTR next to the initiation complex, a 3' repressor can reach the 5' end. The accompanying eIF2, eIF3, eIF4 factors and the full complement of 40S and 60S proteins are the cap-dependent initiation apparatus being targeted, making this a model of transcript-selective, extraribosomal control of inflammatory gene expression.

Once a ribosome has engaged an mRNA start codon, elongation is the repetitive step that reads the message codon by codon and builds the polypeptide, and it accounts for most of the energy and time a cell spends making protein. Aminoacyl-tRNAs are delivered as ternary complexes with eEF1A and GTP; correct codon-anticodon pairing triggers GTP hydrolysis and eEF1A release, the ribosome's peptidyl transferase center joins the incoming amino acid to the growing chain, and eEF2 with GTP then drives translocation by exactly three nucleotides, shifting peptidyl-tRNA to the P site and deacylated tRNA to the E site. The large and small subunit ribosomal proteins listed here form the platform on which this occurs, together with the eEF1B complex that recycles eEF1A to its GTP form. Elongation rate sets protein output and co-translational folding, and mutations in ribosomal proteins underlie ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

Elongation is the repetitive core of protein synthesis: once a ribosome has initiated on an mRNA, it adds one amino acid at a time until a stop codon is reached, and this cycle accounts for most of the energy a growing cell spends. The set comprises the small and large cytoplasmic ribosomal subunit proteins together with the elongation factors EEF1A1, which delivers aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site, and EEF2, which drives translocation of the ribosome along the mRNA. Peptide bond formation itself is catalysed by the large subunit's RNA centre, leaving a deacylated tRNA in the P site and a nascent chain one residue longer. Output is tuned to growth signals and stress, and mutations in individual ribosomal proteins cause ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia; EEF2 is also the target of diphtheria toxin.

Notch signalling lets a cell take instruction directly from its neighbour, and it is the main way tissues make binary fate decisions: which progenitor differentiates and which stays a stem cell, which inner-ear cell becomes a hair cell and which its support, how somites are segmented, and how T-cell and blood lineages are specified. Receptors NOTCH1-4 are matured by furin cleavage and decorated in the secretory pathway by O-fucose and O-glucose transferases and Fringe enzymes, which tune responsiveness to DLL and JAG ligands presented on adjacent cells; ligand pulling triggers ADAM10/17 shedding and gamma-secretase cleavage, releasing the intracellular domain to join RBPJ and Mastermind and switch corepressors such as NCoR, TLE and histone deacetylases for coactivators, inducing HES and HEY repressors, MYC and CCND1. Output is limited by NUMB, ubiquitin ligases including MIB1, ITCH and FBXW7, proteasomal turnover and microRNAs. Dysregulation drives T-cell leukaemia, CADASIL and Alagille syndrome.

Linear chromosomes end in TTAGGG repeats with a G-rich 3' overhang, and telomere maintenance is the set of activities that replenishes and protects those ends so cells can keep dividing. Because lagging-strand replication and nucleolytic processing shorten telomeres each cycle, critically short ends trigger a DNA damage response and replicative senescence; loss of these functions underlies bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis syndromes, while reactivation supports the unlimited proliferation of tumours. The telomerase ribonucleoprotein, built around the reverse transcriptase TERT with dyskerin, NHP2, NOP10 and GAR1, uses an RNA template to add repeats. Shelterin components TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2, ACD and TERF2IP sequester the end from end-joining and recombination, while the CST complex, polymerase alpha-primase, the replicative polymerases, RPA, PCNA, RFC, FEN1 and ligase I fill in the C strand, and helicases such as WRN, BLM and RTEL1 resolve telomeric structures. Nucleosome assembly with histone variants completes chromatin at the end.

Adjacent cells exchange ions, metabolites and second messengers directly through gap junctions, and this pathway covers how those channels are built, delivered, gated and removed. Connexin subunits oligomerise into six-subunit hemichannels, travel along microtubules to the plasma membrane, dock head-to-head with a partner hemichannel on the neighbouring cell, and are later internalised by clathrin-mediated endocytosis involving adaptor and dynamin components, actin and myosin VI. Turnover is rapid, and Src-dependent phosphorylation of connexins such as GJA1 closes channels and promotes their removal, while scaffolds like ZO-1 organise plaque edges. Different connexins serve different tissues, so failures produce tissue-specific disease: GJB2 mutations cause deafness, GJB1 an X-linked demyelinating neuropathy, GJA8 and GJA3 cataract, and GJA5 cardiac conduction defects. Coordinated electrical and metabolic coupling in heart, lens, cochlea and myelinating glia depends on this regulated trafficking.

Purine and pyrimidine nucleotides supply the building blocks of DNA and RNA, the cell's short-term energy currency, second messengers such as cAMP, and the backbones of cofactors like NAD and FAD, and this metabolism is how the body makes, recycles and disposes of them. De novo synthesis runs through multifunctional enzymes including CAD, GART and UMPS to the branch points guarded by IMPDH and ADSL, while salvage routes such as HPRT1, APRT and the thymidine and deoxycytidine kinases reclaim bases and nucleosides released by nucleic acid turnover. Ribonucleotide reductase, using thioredoxin-based reducing power, couples deoxyribonucleotide supply to S phase, and sanitising enzymes remove damaged or non-canonical nucleotides before they reach DNA. Catabolism through PNP and xanthine dehydrogenase ends in uric acid; its failure causes gout, and defects in ADA cause severe combined immunodeficiency. These same pathways activate nucleoside-analogue antiviral and antitumour drugs.

Mitochondrial biogenesis is how a cell builds new mitochondria and matches its respiratory capacity to demand, the adaptation that lets exercised muscle gain endurance and that fails in metabolic disease, heart failure and ageing. Calcium influx and energy depletion are the initiating signals: AMPK senses a falling ATP:AMP ratio, p38 MAPK and CaMKIV respond to contraction and calcium, and both converge on the coactivator PGC-1alpha, with PGC-1beta and PPRC acting similarly. PGC-1alpha binds no DNA itself but partners with NRF1, GABP, ESRRA and nuclear receptors such as PPARA/RXRA to drive nuclear genes for oxidative phosphorylation subunits, the MICOS cristae-shaping complex, protein import machinery and antioxidant enzymes. It also switches on TFAM, TFB2M and POLRMT, coupling nuclear transcription to replication and expression of the mitochondrial genome, while sirtuins and corepressors such as NCOR1 tune the response.

Cells match their respiratory capacity to demand by building new mitochondria, and this programme is how exercise, calcium influx and energy depletion are converted into more mitochondrial protein. It underlies endurance adaptation in muscle, thermogenic and oxidative tissue function, and its blunting accompanies ageing, insulin resistance and metabolic disease. Falling ATP and rising AMP activate AMPK, while contraction-linked calcium signals act through CaMKIV and CREB and through p38 kinases; these converge on the coactivator PGC-1alpha and its relatives PGC-1beta and PPRC1, which do not bind DNA themselves but partner with NRF1, GABP, ESRRA, PPARA and RXRA to switch on nuclear genes for mitochondrial components. Targets include the mitochondrial transcription and replication machinery, TFAM, TFB1M/TFB2M, POLRMT, TWNK and SSBP1, plus ATP synthase subunits, matrix enzymes such as SOD2 and IDH2, mitochondrial sirtuins, and MICOS proteins that shape cristae during remodelling.

Once a transcript has been capped, spliced and polyadenylated, it must physically cross the nuclear envelope before it can be translated, and this route carries mature mRNAs whose export does not depend on the histone-specific stem-loop binding protein. It is the general bulk mRNA export path, and it couples nuclear processing quality control to cytoplasmic protein synthesis: transcripts that fail to acquire the right adaptors are retained and degraded rather than exported. The cap is held by the nuclear cap-binding complex of NCBP1 and NCBP2, while ALYREF acts as an adaptor that loads the export receptor NXF1 onto the message. Translocation then occurs through the nuclear pore complex, whose scaffold, transmembrane and phenylalanine-glycine-repeat nucleoporins, together with TPR and RANBP2 on the nuclear and cytoplasmic faces, provide the permeability barrier and docking sites the receptor traverses. Cytoplasmic release exchanges the nuclear cap complex for EIF4E, licensing translation.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are the exception among metazoan transcripts: they end in a conserved stem-loop rather than a poly(A) tail, and once that end has been made by the U7 snRNP-directed cleavage machinery the transcript must still reach the cytoplasm. This pathway covers nuclear export of the mature, stem-loop-bound histone message, which supplies the bulk histone protein needed to package newly replicated DNA during S phase. The stem-loop binding protein SLBP stays bound to the 3' end and accompanies the mRNA through the pore, acting in place of the poly(A)-binding proteins used by other transcripts, while cap-binding subunits, the export adaptor ALYREF and the receptor NXF1 hand the ribonucleoprotein to the nuclear pore complex. The remaining nucleoporins, together with RANBP2, TPR and RAE1, form the translocation channel and its filaments. Loss of this coupling uncouples histone supply from replication and destabilises chromatin assembly.

Most human genes are spliced, but a minority — histones, interferons and others — are transcribed without introns, and their mRNAs must still be licensed for export. This pathway describes how such a transcript acquires export competence through 3' end formation rather than splicing, and it matters because only correctly processed mRNA reaches the ribosome; unprocessed or prematurely released transcripts are retained and degraded in the nucleus. The cleavage and polyadenylation machinery, together with symplekin, defines the mRNA 3' end, while the cap-binding complex marks the 5' end. The adaptor ALYREF recruits the export receptor NXF1, which ferries the ribonucleoprotein through the nuclear pore complex; the bulk of the gene list is the pore itself, from the structured Y-complex scaffold to the phenylalanine-glycine repeat nucleoporins and the basket protein TPR that provide the permeability barrier and docking sites. Cytoplasmic release hands the capped message to EIF4E for translation initiation.

Not all human genes have introns; histone genes, heat shock genes and many others are transcribed as intronless units, and their mature mRNAs must still reach the cytoplasm to be translated. This route delivers them. Because no splicing occurs, the export adaptors are recruited instead through 3' end processing and cap binding: cleavage and polyadenylation factors such as CPSF subunits, FIP1L1 and WDR33 with symplekin, the nuclear cap-binding complex NCBP1/NCBP2, and for replication-dependent histone messages the stem-loop binding protein SLBP. ALYREF then loads the export receptor NXF1, which ferries the ribonucleoprotein through the nuclear pore complex, whose nucleoporins, the basket protein TPR and RANBP2 make up most of the machinery here; EIF4E marks the transition to cytoplasmic translation. The pathway couples transcript maturation to nucleocytoplasmic transport, and defects in individual nucleoporins cause tissue-restricted disease such as triple-A syndrome.

Only fully processed messenger RNAs are allowed to leave the nucleus, and this pathway is the route by which an mRNA made from an intron-containing gene is licensed and moved to the cytoplasm for translation. Splicing itself leaves the marks that permit export: the exon junction complex deposited near spliced junctions, cap-binding proteins at the 5' end, and SR proteins that accompany the transcript. The TREX complex and its adaptors, including ALYREF and CHTOP, load the export receptor NXF1 with its cofactor NXT1, which ferries the ribonucleoprotein through the nuclear pore built from the nucleoporins listed here, with RNA helicases and GLE1 driving release on the cytoplasmic face. Coupling export to correct processing keeps intron-retaining and improperly capped RNAs out of the cytoplasm, and defects in pore or export components cause neurological and developmental disease.

Matrix metalloproteinases are secreted or membrane-anchored zinc proteases that remodel the extracellular matrix and, as it turns out, cleave a large set of non-matrix substrates including cytokines, growth factor binding proteins and cell surface receptors. Because their activity is destructive and largely irreversible, they are made as latent proenzymes, and proteolytic removal of the propeptide is the committed regulatory step described here. Different family members are unlocked by different activators: the proprotein convertase furin acts on membrane-type enzymes in the secretory pathway, while plasmin generated from plasminogen, neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, mast cell chymase and tryptase, and pancreatic trypsins and chymotrypsins activate others extracellularly, often in cascades where one MMP activates the next. TIMP1 and TIMP2 restrain the resulting activity. The balance shapes wound healing, morphogenesis and tissue homeostasis, and its loss underlies arthritis, atherosclerosis, ulceration and tumour invasion.

Bile salts secreted into the gut are not discarded: almost all are recaptured in the ileum and returned to the liver for re-export, so that a small pool can be reused many times a day to emulsify dietary fat and absorb fat-soluble vitamins. This enterohepatic circulation depends on a relay of transporters — apical uptake into enterocytes by SLC10A2, cytosolic carriage by the ileal bile acid binding protein FABP6, basolateral efflux through ABCC3 and the OSTα/OSTβ heterodimer, transit in portal blood bound to albumin, and hepatocyte uptake by the sodium-dependent taurocholate carrier SLC10A1 with contributions from organic anion transporting polypeptides. In the hepatocyte, SLC27A5 activates bile acids as CoA thioesters and BAAT conjugates them to glycine or taurine before ABCB11 pumps them back into bile. The nuclear receptor FXR, partnered with RXRα and coactivators, senses the returning flux and restrains further synthesis; loss of these steps causes cholestasis and fat malabsorption.

Carboxylic acid drugs and metabolites are cleared by amino acid conjugation, a two-step phase II route that turns them into water-soluble amides for urinary excretion. This is how benzoate, phenylacetate and salicylate are detoxified, and it is exploited therapeutically: benzoate and phenylacetate are given in urea cycle disorders precisely because conjugation with glycine or glutamine drains waste nitrogen through an alternative path. First, medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases of the ACSM family activate the free acid to its coenzyme A thioester at the expense of ATP, largely in liver and kidney mitochondria. Glycine N-acyltransferase and its GLYATL relatives then transfer the acyl group onto the amino group of glycine or glutamine, releasing CoA. The same chemistry disposes of acyl-CoA species that accumulate in fatty acid oxidation defects, linking xenobiotic metabolism to mitochondrial CoA homeostasis and nitrogen handling.

Gamma-carboxylation of protein precursors is the vitamin K-dependent modification that makes coagulation factors able to bind calcium and dock onto membrane surfaces, and it is the step targeted by warfarin. Without it, prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S and protein Z circulate but cannot assemble on phospholipid at a site of injury, producing bleeding disorders; loss of the carboxylase itself causes a combined deficiency of all these factors. In the endoplasmic reticulum, a single enzyme recognises a propeptide motif on the amino-terminal side of a glutamate cluster and processively converts each glutamate to gamma-carboxyglutamate before releasing the substrate. The same modification serves biology beyond clotting: osteocalcin in bone mineralisation and Gas6 in growth factor-like signalling depend on it, linking vitamin K status to haemostasis, skeletal and vascular function.

Several secreted proteins only work after a cluster of glutamate residues near their amino terminus is converted to gamma-carboxyglutamate, which creates the calcium-binding surface that lets them dock onto membrane phospholipid. This vitamin K-dependent modification of protein precursors is what makes coagulation possible: prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, together with the anticoagulant regulators protein C, protein S and protein Z, all require it, as do the growth factor-like GAS6 and the bone matrix protein osteocalcin. A single enzyme in the endoplasmic reticulum, gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, recognises a propeptide motif on its substrates and processively carboxylates the whole cluster before release. Loss of carboxylase activity, or vitamin K deficiency, produces combined clotting factor deficiency and bleeding; pharmacological blockade of vitamin K recycling is the basis of warfarin anticoagulation.

Vitamin K-dependent proteins acquire gamma-carboxyglutamate residues in the endoplasmic reticulum, and this step moves the finished precursors forward along the secretory route to the Golgi for further processing and eventual secretion. The cargo defines the biology: prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X drive coagulation, protein C and its cofactor protein S restrain it, protein Z modulates factor Xa, osteocalcin binds mineral in bone, and GAS6 acts as a ligand for TAM receptor tyrosine kinases in cell survival and clearance of apoptotic cells. Their gamma-carboxylated glutamates confer calcium-dependent binding to phospholipid membranes, which is what makes coagulation reactions local and surface-restricted. Anterograde COPII-mediated traffic is therefore a required leg of the journey from translation to plasma; blocking carboxylation with vitamin K antagonists yields circulating but non-functional forms and anticoagulation.

Removal of aminoterminal propeptides from gamma-carboxylated proteins is the maturation step that converts vitamin K-dependent proteins into functional secreted factors. It matters because the proteins involved are the backbone of blood coagulation and its control -- prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S and protein Z -- along with osteocalcin in bone mineralisation and GAS6 in cell survival signalling. The propeptide is the recognition element that lets gamma-glutamyl carboxylase modify glutamate residues in the Gla domain; once carboxylation is complete the propeptide has no further use. Furin, a Golgi-resident proprotein convertase that cleaves after a basic Arg-X-Lys/Arg-Arg motif, excises it, and the trimmed proteins move on to secretion or the plasma membrane. Uncleaved precursors are still released but function poorly, so this step gates the activity rather than the output of the clotting cascade.

Vitamin K-dependent proteins acquire gamma-carboxyglutamate residues in the endoplasmic reticulum using a propeptide that serves as the recognition signal for the carboxylase; once carboxylation is complete that propeptide must be cut away, and removal of the aminoterminal propeptides from gamma-carboxylated proteins is the maturation step that makes them functional. Furin, a Golgi-localized endopeptidase that cleaves after a basic Arg-X-Lys/Arg-Arg motif, performs the cut; uncleaved precursors are still secreted but work poorly. The substrates define the output: prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X drive coagulation, protein C, protein S and protein Z restrain it, osteocalcin binds bone mineral, and GAS6 signals through TAM receptors. Because the propeptides themselves have no known onward role, this is essentially a licensing event linking post-translational carboxylation to haemostasis, bone mineralization and cell survival signalling.

Gamma-carboxylation, transport, and amino-terminal cleavage of proteins is the vitamin K-dependent maturation step that turns newly synthesized clotting factors into functional, calcium- and membrane-binding proteins. Prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X, protein C, protein S, protein Z and Gas6 all carry a glutamate-rich Gla motif near their amino termini; the ER enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase adds carboxyl groups to these residues using reduced vitamin K, after which the propeptide is removed by furin as the protein traverses the Golgi. Only the carboxylated form docks onto phospholipid surfaces at a site of vascular injury, so loss of this processing abolishes both coagulation and its anticoagulant braking arm — the basis of warfarin action and of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. The same chemistry matures osteocalcin, linking the pathway to bone mineralization and Gas6-driven cell survival signalling.

Several secreted proteins acquire calcium-binding ability only after a vitamin K-dependent modification made as they transit the secretory pathway. Gamma-carboxylation converts glutamate residues in an amino-terminal Gla motif into gamma-carboxyglutamate, which lets the mature protein bind calcium and dock onto membrane phospholipid surfaces; removal of the propeptide by a furin-type protease in the Golgi completes maturation. Most of the substrates run the coagulation cascade and its brakes — prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X, together with the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z — so loss of the carboxylase or of its vitamin K cofactor produces bleeding disorders, and this chemistry is the target of warfarin-class anticoagulants. Other clients extend the theme beyond haemostasis: osteocalcin in bone mineralization and Gas6 in receptor tyrosine kinase signalling and apoptotic cell clearance.

Cytosolic DNA from viruses or damaged cells must be detected and converted into an antiviral transcriptional response, and ZBP1 (also called DAI) is one sensor proposed to do this, driving type I interferon induction and NF-kB activation. Once engaged, ZBP1 recruits the kinase TBK1 to phosphorylate IRF3, which dimerises and enters the nucleus to switch on interferon-beta; in parallel, RIPK1 and RIPK3 couple the sensor to the IKK complex (CHUK, IKBKB, IKBKG), whose phosphorylation of IkB inhibitors frees RELA-containing NF-kB dimers to drive inflammatory gene expression. The same RIPK3 interaction links this sensor to necroptotic cell death, an alternative route for eliminating infected cells. Its contribution to DNA sensing is contested, since depleting it has little effect in many cells, and its restricted tissue expression suggests it acts in a cell-type-specific manner rather than as a universal cytosolic DNA sensor.
