IRF3 mediated activation of type 1 IFN is the terminal step by which cells that have detected foreign DNA in their cytosol switch on interferon-beta and related type I interferon genes, arming neighbouring cells with an antiviral state and shaping the ensuing adaptive response. The cytosolic DNA sensor ZBP1/DAI recruits the kinase TBK1 together with IRF3 to its C-terminal region, where IRF3 is phosphorylated, dimerises and enters the nucleus to transactivate interferon promoters; IRF7 contributes secondarily in this branch. The pathway is held in check by negative regulation of TBK1 itself, with NLRP4 delivering the E3 ligase DTX4 to target TBK1 for degradation, so that interferon output is transient. Loss of restraint here drives interferonopathy and autoimmunity, while loss of signalling leaves cells vulnerable to DNA virus infection.

Detection of cytosolic DNA from viruses or damaged cells culminates in IRF3-mediated induction of type I interferon, the transcriptional response that arms neighbouring cells against infection before adaptive immunity engages. The DNA sensor ZBP1/DAI recruits the kinase TBK1 together with IRF3 to its C-terminal region, and TBK1 phosphorylates IRF3 so that it dimerises, enters the nucleus and drives IFN-beta and IFN-alpha4 transcription; IRF7 contributes only partially in this branch. Because sustained interferon output is damaging, the response is restrained by negative regulation of TBK1 itself: NLRP4 recruits the E3 ubiquitin ligase DTX4 to mark TBK1 for degradative ubiquitination, terminating signalling. The balance between these arms determines antiviral competence on one side and, when regulation fails, interferon-driven autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease on the other.

Hydrogen sulfide is a signalling molecule at low concentrations and a respiratory poison at higher ones, so cells that break down cysteine and other sulfur amino acids must dispose of the sulfide they generate. Mitochondrial sulfide oxidation to sulfate does this, converting the gas through persulfide, thiosulfate and sulfite intermediates to sulfate for excretion. Sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase in the inner membrane performs the committed step, passing electrons into the respiratory chain while transferring sulfur to an acceptor; a persulfide dioxygenase and sulfurtransferases handle the intermediates, and sulfite oxidase completes the route. A dicarboxylate carrier supports exchange across the inner membrane. Loss of the persulfide dioxygenase ETHE1 causes ethylmalonic encephalopathy, with sulfide accumulating in tissue and inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase, while sulfite oxidase deficiency produces severe neonatal neurological disease, underlining how tightly sulfur catabolism must be coupled to detoxification.

Cysteine and homocysteine are useful but toxic in excess, and their catabolism sets the sulfur amino acid pool while generating taurine and hydrogen sulfide as products the body uses elsewhere. Taurine is needed for bile salt conjugation and osmotic balance; hydrogen sulfide acts as a vasodilatory and mitochondrial signalling molecule, so this route links amino acid disposal to cardiovascular and neurological function. One branch oxidizes cysteine via cysteine dioxygenase and decarboxylation by CSAD or GADL1 toward taurine and hypotaurine; another releases sulfide through cystathionine gamma-lyase and transfers or oxidizes it using sulfurtransferases, the mitochondrial sulfide:quinone oxidoreductase, a persulfide dioxygenase, and sulfite oxidase, with thioredoxin and a dicarboxylate carrier supporting the mitochondrial steps. Loss of the sulfide-clearing arm causes ethylmalonic encephalopathy, and sulfite oxidase deficiency produces severe neonatal neurodegeneration.

Cysteine formation from homocysteine is the animal branch of transsulfuration, the only route by which the sulfur of methionine-derived homocysteine is committed to cysteine and, through it, to glutathione and taurine synthesis. It also disposes of homocysteine, so its failure raises plasma homocysteine and causes classical homocystinuria, with lens dislocation, skeletal changes and thromboembolic risk. Two vitamin B6-dependent cytosolic enzymes carry out the conversion: cystathionine beta-synthase condenses homocysteine with serine to give cystathionine, and cystathionine gamma-lyase cleaves it to cysteine plus alpha-ketobutyrate. Both enzymes additionally generate hydrogen sulfide from cysteine and homocysteine, making this chemistry the principal source of a gaseous mediator that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and modulates neuronal signalling. Activity is tuned by S-adenosylmethionine, linking sulfur amino acid disposal to methylation status and to antioxidant capacity.

Sulfur amino acid metabolism links methionine, cysteine, homocysteine and taurine, and in humans it is where the methyl donor economy meets antioxidant and sulfide chemistry. Methionine activation by MAT1A yields S-adenosylmethionine for cellular methylation; AHCY and the remethylation enzymes MTR with its reductase partner, plus the betaine-dependent BHMT route, regenerate methionine, while CBS and CTH commit homocysteine irreversibly through transsulfuration to cysteine, the precursor of glutathione. Cysteine is further oxidized by CDO1 and decarboxylated by CSAD or GADL1 toward taurine and hypotaurine, and ADO controls the cysteamine branch. A parallel salvage arm recycles methylthioadenosine back to methionine via MTAP, APIP and ADI1, and sulfide generated along the way is disposed of by SQOR, ETHE1 and sulfite oxidase. Loss of CBS causes homocystinuria; blocks in sulfite oxidation are neonatally lethal.

This is the broad collection of routes by which cells detect extracellular cues and convert them into changes in behaviour, encompassing receptor tyrosine kinases for growth factors such as EGF, FGF, insulin, PDGF and VEGF, G protein-coupled receptors for hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines and sensory ligands, TGF-beta and BMP receptors acting through SMADs, WNT signalling via beta-catenin and its destruction complex, NOTCH activation by proteolytic release of its intracellular domain, Hedgehog signalling through PTCH and SMO at the cilium, and integrin-mediated adhesion signalling. Shared downstream machinery includes RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascades, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, phospholipase C and calcium, cyclic nucleotide production and degradation, and Rho family GTPases with their GEFs, GAPs and actin regulators. The output is control of proliferation, differentiation, survival, migration, cytoskeletal organisation and metabolism; dysregulation at almost any node drives cancer and developmental disorders.

After an HIV-1 particle fuses with the cell, its conical capsid must be partially disassembled before the viral genome can be copied, and this uncoating step converts the incoming core into a functional reverse transcription complex containing the diploid RNA genome, tRNA-Lys primer, reverse transcriptase, integrase, nucleocapsid, Vpr and matrix, freed from the plasma membrane. Timing matters in both directions: premature loss of the capsid shell exposes viral nucleic acid to cytosolic sensors and nucleases, while failure to disassemble blocks nuclear entry and integration. Cytosolic pH and dilution of capsid subunits appear to drive the process, aided by matrix and Nef and by association of the transiting nucleoprotein complex with actin microfilaments. The host peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A binds the capsid protein directly and tunes core stability, which is why capsid-cyclophilin interactions are pursued as antiviral targets.

HIV-1 replicates by commandeering host machinery at every step, and the human proteins it borrows are collected here as the viral life cycle from entry through budding. Infection begins when the virion engages CD4 together with the chemokine co-receptors CCR5 or CXCR4, after which reverse transcription and integration deliver the provirus into host chromatin, with host factors such as PSIP1 (LEDGF/p75), BANF1 and the non-homologous end-joining proteins Ku70/Ku80, XRCC4 and LIG4 assisting integration and gap repair. The late phase runs almost entirely on host transcription: RNA polymerase II, TBP and the TAFs, TFIIH, negative elongation factors and the P-TEFb cyclin-CDK9 pair that Tat hijacks to relieve promoter-proximal pausing. Viral RNAs are capped, exported through the nuclear pore complex and via CRM1/RanGTP, and progeny particles bud using the ESCRT machinery and VPS4 ATPases. Understanding these dependencies underlies antiretroviral drug design and latency reversal strategies.

The last steps in the HIV replication cycle: an assembled, immature particle pinches off from the plasma membrane and its Gag polyprotein is processed into the mature, infectious virion. Budding and maturation of the HIV virion depend almost entirely on borrowed host machinery, which is why they are attractive antiviral targets. Gag's late domain recruits TSG101 within ESCRT-I, together with VPS28, VPS37 and MVB12 subunits, and also PDCD6IP (ALIX); these adaptors nucleate CHMP4 and CHMP2 filaments that constrict the membrane neck, after which the AAA-ATPase VPS4A/VPS4B with its cofactor VTA1 disassembles the polymers and completes fission. Ubiquitin and NEDD4-family ligase activity tune this recruitment, while the incorporated peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A binds capsid and influences core maturation and subsequent infectivity. The same membrane-scission chemistry normally builds multivesicular bodies and closes the cytokinetic midbody.

Reverse Transcription of HIV RNA converts the single-stranded RNA genome delivered by an incoming HIV-1 particle into double-stranded DNA, the obligatory step that allows the virus to integrate into a host chromosome and establish lifelong infection; it is the target of the nucleoside and non-nucleoside inhibitors that form the backbone of antiretroviral therapy. In the cytosol of the newly infected cell, the viral reverse transcriptase heterodimer, whose active subunit carries both a primer-dependent DNA polymerase and an RNase H domain, copies the genome from a tRNA primer, degrades the RNA of the resulting hybrids, and performs two template switches so that long terminal repeats are duplicated at both ends of the product. The host contribution here is cyclophilin A, a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase recruited by the capsid that shapes core uncoating and the fidelity and timing of DNA synthesis.

Conversion of the HIV-1 RNA genome into double-stranded DNA is the step that commits a newly infected cell to harbouring a provirus, and it is the target of the largest class of antiretroviral drugs. In the cytosol of the new host cell, the viral reverse transcriptase heterodimer copies genomic RNA into a minus-strand DNA using a host tRNA primer, degrades the RNA of the resulting RNA:DNA hybrids through its RNase H activity, and completes a plus strand, with two template-switching events that duplicate the long terminal repeats at both ends of the product. The linear duplex is then available for integration into host chromatin. Host factors participate as well: the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A binds incoming capsid, influencing uncoating and the efficiency of early reverse transcription, and links this stage to innate sensing of the viral core.

Retroviral replication only becomes productive once the reverse-transcribed viral DNA is covalently joined to a host chromosome, and integration of the provirus is that step: the point at which HIV infection becomes permanent in a cell and the basis of the latent reservoir that antiretroviral therapy cannot clear. Viral integrase carries out 3' end processing and strand transfer, but the host supplies much of the surrounding machinery represented here. Importin alpha and the chromatin proteins BANF1 and HMGA1 act on the preintegration complex and its nuclear entry, PSIP1/LEDGF tethers integrase to transcriptionally active chromatin and steers target-site selection, and PPIA binds capsid during early uncoating. The gap repair that completes integration and generates the short duplication of flanking cellular DNA draws on nonhomologous end joining factors including the Ku heterodimer, XRCC4 and LIG4. These host dependencies are targets for integrase strand-transfer inhibitors and related strategies.

Everything HIV does before it can express its own genes happens here: attachment and entry, uncoating, reverse transcription of the RNA genome into cDNA, nuclear import of the resulting nucleoprotein complex, and integration of viral DNA into a host chromosome. Because integration is irreversible, this phase establishes the latent reservoir that makes infection lifelong and resists therapy. Entry depends on CD4 together with a chemokine receptor coreceptor, either CCR5 or CXCR4, whose usage determines viral tropism and explains why CCR5 loss confers resistance. Host factors are co-opted throughout: cyclophilin A acts on the incoming capsid, an importin supports transport into the nucleus, and chromatin proteins including BANF1, HMGA1 and the tethering factor LEDGF/PSIP1 steer the preintegration complex toward transcribed genes. Nonhomologous end-joining and ligation enzymes then repair the breaks flanking the integrated provirus.

Once HIV-1 has integrated its genome, the late phase of its life cycle turns that provirus into new virions, and it does so almost entirely with borrowed host machinery. Viral gene expression begins with RNA polymerase II and the general initiation factors assembled on the integrated LTR promoter; the viral Tat protein then captures the CDK9/cyclin T kinase to phosphorylate the polymerase C-terminal domain and the negative elongation and DSIF factors, converting stalled short transcripts into full-length message. Capping, elongation through the FACT and elongin complexes, and Rev-directed export of unspliced and partially spliced RNAs through nucleoporins, RAN-cycle components and XPO1 deliver Gag, Pol and Env transcripts to the cytoplasm. Myristoyltransferases, cyclophilin A, furin and the ESCRT machinery with VPS4 ATPases then support particle assembly and membrane scission. These dependencies define the steps targeted by transcriptional silencing and latency-reversal strategies.

Before a mammalian cell divides, the Golgi ribbon that normally sits stacked beside the centrosome must be taken apart so that both daughters inherit the organelle, and this disassembly is itself a requirement for mitotic entry. The pericentriolar stacks are first unlinked in G2, then fragment through prophase and metaphase as stacking is lost and secretory traffic halts. Mitotic kinases drive the change: CDK1 with cyclin B phosphorylates the cis-Golgi proteins GM130 and GRASP65, and the latter is further phosphorylated by PLK1, blocking the trans-oligomers that glue cisternae together. GM130 phosphorylation prevents USO1/p115 binding, so ER-to-Golgi carriers can no longer dock and anterograde transport ceases; RAB1 and RAB2A mark the tethering steps that are suspended. ERK1/ERK2 act on GRASP55, which partners golgin-45 in medial cisternae. Golgi inheritance and spindle organization both depend on this reorganization.

Synthesis of dolichyl-phosphate mannose generates the lipid-linked mannose donor that all mannose-transfer reactions in the endoplasmic reticulum depend on. Without it, cells cannot build the dolichol-pyrophosphate oligosaccharide used for N-linked glycosylation, cannot complete the glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor that tethers a large class of surface proteins, and cannot O-mannosylate alpha-dystroglycan or C-mannosylate thrombospondin repeats; loss-of-function mutations cause congenital disorders of glycosylation with muscular dystrophy-like features. Cytosolic GDP-mannose is transferred onto dolichyl phosphate at the cytosolic face of the ER membrane, after which the product flips so its mannose faces the lumen and becomes available to the glycosyltransferases there. The reaction is carried out by a three-subunit ER membrane complex in which DPM1 is the catalytic mannosyltransferase and DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it, coupling substrate supply to membrane localisation.

Most mannose that ends up on secreted and membrane proteins arrives through a single lipid-linked donor, dolichyl-phosphate mannose, and this two-step route is how that donor is made. It feeds the lipid-linked oligosaccharide used for N-linked glycosylation, the GPI anchor precursor, and protein O- and C-mannosylation, so its output is required for essentially all glycoprotein traffic through the secretory pathway. A mannosyltransferase transfers mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate at the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane; the product then flips so the sugar faces the lumen, where downstream transferases can use it. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit and DPM2 and DPM3 are membrane subunits that stabilise and localise the complex. Loss of any of the three causes congenital disorders of glycosylation with muscular dystrophy and neurological involvement, reflecting undermannosylated alpha-dystroglycan.

Many cell surface proteins are held on the membrane not by a transmembrane helix but by a lipid anchor, and this endoplasmic reticulum pathway builds that anchor. Starting from phosphatidylinositol, enzyme complexes add N-acetylglucosamine, deacetylate it, then extend a mannose chain and decorate it with ethanolamine phosphate groups to create the structure that will later be transferred onto the C-terminus of a nascent protein. The products anchor complement regulators such as CD55 and CD59, alkaline phosphatases, folate receptors and prion protein. Loss of the first glycosyltransferase step in a haematopoietic clone strips erythrocytes of complement protection and causes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, while hypomorphic mutations in the mannosyltransferase and ethanolamine phosphate transferase steps produce inherited glycosylation disorders with epilepsy, intellectual disability and skeletal anomalies. Variant anchors carrying an extra mannose or ethanolamine may serve tissue-specific modification.

The urokinase plasminogen activator receptor reaches the cell surface only as a lipid-anchored protein, and this pathway is the step that attaches it. In the endoplasmic reticulum membrane a five-subunit GPI transamidase complex, comprising the catalytic PIGK subunit together with GPAA1, PIGS, PIGT and PIGU, recognises the C-terminal signal of the nascent receptor, cleaves it, and replaces it with a preassembled glycosylphosphatidylinositol moiety. A subsequent deacylation by PGAP1 remodels the anchor so the conjugate can leave the ER for the Golgi and the plasma membrane. Anchoring matters because surface uPAR concentrates plasminogen activation at the cell periphery, driving pericellular proteolysis, matrix remodelling, cell migration and invasion; it is also the substrate for phospholipase-mediated shedding of soluble receptor. Defects in the shared transamidase machinery cause inherited GPI-anchor deficiency disorders affecting many surface proteins.

HIV infection of CD4-positive T cells and macrophages destroys the helper T cell compartment and leaves patients open to opportunistic infection, and the virus accomplishes this almost entirely by commandeering normal host machinery. Entry depends on CD4 together with the chemokine receptors CCR5 or CXCR4 and Src-family kinases such as LCK and FYN in the T cell receptor environment. The reverse-transcribed genome enters the nucleus through the nuclear pore and Ran-dependent import, and integrated provirus is transcribed by RNA polymerase II with TBP/TAF general factors; Tat recruits the CDK9-cyclin T kinase to overcome negative elongation factor and release paused polymerase. Capped, exported transcripts yield virions that bud using the ESCRT complexes and VPS4 ATPases. Accessory proteins subvert host defence and degradation, Vif directing a cullin-RING ligase and the proteasome against the cytidine deaminase APOBEC3G, and Nef and Vpu rerouting CD4 and MHC class I through clathrin adaptor trafficking.

HIV-1 encodes only a handful of accessory proteins, and this collection describes how they hijack host machinery to complete the viral life cycle. Vpr and Rev exploit the nuclear pore complex and the Ran-dependent karyopherin system, with exportin-1 carrying incompletely spliced viral RNA to the cytoplasm so that structural genes can be translated. Nef redirects CD4 and MHC class I from the cell surface using clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-2, shielding infected cells from cytotoxic T lymphocytes, and engages Src-family kinases such as LCK, FYN and HCK to alter T cell signalling. Vif recruits a Cullin5-ElonginB/C-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase to degrade the cytidine deaminase APOBEC3G through the proteasome, preventing hypermutation of reverse transcripts. Tat with CCNT1 and CDK9 drives transcriptional elongation. Together these interactions determine immune evasion, restriction factor escape, and the CD4 T cell depletion underlying AIDS.

Glycosaminoglycan metabolism covers the building and breakdown of the long sulfated sugar chains "— hyaluronan, chondroitin and dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and keratan sulfate — that fill the extracellular matrix, cushion joints, stiffen cartilage and bone, and coat cell surfaces where they capture growth factors and guide signalling. Except for hyaluronan, the chains are assembled on core proteins such as the syndecans, glypicans, aggrecan, versican and perlecan, starting from a xylose-initiated tetrasaccharide linker laid down by xylosyltransferases and galactosyltransferases, then extended by polymerases including the EXT1–EXT2 heparan sulfate complex and decorated by sulfotransferases using PAPS made by PAPSS1 and PAPSS2. Epimerases convert glucuronate to iduronate, tuning chain flexibility. Turnover proceeds through hyaluronidases, heparanase and a suite of lysosomal exoglycosidases and sulfatases; loss of these degradative enzymes causes the mucopolysaccharidoses, while linker and sulfation defects produce skeletal dysplasias and connective tissue disease.

Many cell-surface proteins are tethered to the membrane not by a transmembrane helix but by a lipid glycan, and this pathway builds that tether and attaches it. Synthesis of GPI-anchored proteins begins in the endoplasmic reticulum, where a series of PIG-family enzymes add glucosamine, mannoses donated via dolichol-phosphate-mannose, and ethanolamine phosphate side chains to phosphatidylinositol; a multisubunit transamidase containing PIGK, PIGS, PIGT, PIGU and GPAA1 then cleaves the signal peptide from the nascent client and ligates the anchor, after which PGAP1-mediated deacylation permits export to the Golgi. The clients define the pathway's reach — alkaline phosphatases, folate and lipoprotein-lipase-binding receptors, Thy-1, uPAR, LY6 and LYPD proteins, contactins and IgLON adhesion molecules, and sperm and inner-ear proteins. Inherited defects in the biosynthetic enzymes cause epilepsy and developmental disorders with hyperphosphatasia, while somatic PIGA loss underlies paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

Almost all of the ATP a human cell spends is made here, at the final step of oxidative phosphorylation, where the proton gradient built by the respiratory chain is cashed in for chemical energy. Protons flowing back into the mitochondrial matrix through the membrane-embedded F0 sector turn its rotor, and the rotation drives conformational cycling of the catalytic beta subunits in the F1 head, which bind ADP and phosphate, form ATP, and release it. The complex is a mosaic of nuclear-encoded subunits together with mitochondrially encoded ATP6 and ATP8, linked by central and peripheral stalks that hold the catalytic core against rotation. Because energy supply everywhere depends on this coupling, mutations in individual subunits or assembly factors cause complex V deficiency, presenting as encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy, and the same machinery can run in reverse to consume ATP when the membrane potential collapses.

Mitochondrial DNA carries genes for respiratory chain subunits and the rRNAs and tRNAs needed to translate them, and none of it is expressed unless transcription can be started at the mitochondrial promoters. This initiation step therefore sets the supply of oxidative phosphorylation components and ultimately cellular ATP output. The polymerase POLRMT is a single-subunit enzyme related to bacteriophage RNA polymerases, but unlike them it cannot recognise promoter DNA alone. TFAM, which also packages the mitochondrial genome into nucleoids, binds upstream of the promoter and bends the DNA, while TFB2M joins the polymerase and helps melt the duplex to form an open complex ready for RNA synthesis. The paralogue TFB1M is primarily a small-subunit rRNA adenine dimethyltransferase acting in mitoribosome biogenesis. Loss or imbalance of these factors depletes mitochondrial transcripts and causes respiratory deficiency, and TFAM levels track mtDNA copy number.

Macroautophagy is the bulk self-digestion route by which a cell encloses cytoplasm, protein aggregates, damaged organelles or invading microbes in a double-membrane autophagosome and delivers it to lysosomes for degradation. It buffers starvation by recycling amino acids and lipids, and also serves development, clearance of dying cells, antigen presentation and defence against toxins; its failure contributes to neurodegeneration, Crohn's disease and cancer. Nutrient and energy status is read by mTORC1 on lysosomes, through Rag GTPases, RHEB and the TSC complex, opposed by AMPK, which together set the activity of the ULK1-ATG13-RB1CC1 initiation complex. PIK3C3 with BECN1 and ATG14 makes PI3P that WIPI proteins sense, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades, ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 and lipidated LC3/GABARAP, build and mark the growing phagophore. Cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN, PINK1-PRKN-driven mitophagy, dynein-microtubule transport and ESCRT-mediated closure complete the route.

Macroautophagy is the bulk self-digestion route by which a cell sequesters cytoplasm, organelles, protein aggregates and intracellular microbes into a double-membraned autophagosome and delivers them to lysosomes for breakdown, recycling amino acids and lipids during starvation and clearing damaged components at all times. Loss of this capacity underlies neurodegeneration from accumulated aggregates, contributes to Crohn's disease and to cancer, and impairs development and immune presentation. Nutrient and energy status is read by mTORC1 on lysosomes, with Rag GTPases, Ragulator and the TSC1/TSC2-Rheb module opposing AMPK to set the activity of the ULK1-ATG13-RB1CC1-ATG101 initiation complex. PI3P made by the PIK3C3-BECN1 complex recruits WIPI proteins, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades (ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1, then ATG7/ATG3 lipidating LC3 and GABARAP proteins, reversed by ATG4) build and mark the growing phagophore. Cargo receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN link ubiquitinated substrates to LC3, notably in PINK1/parkin-driven mitophagy, while dynein and microtubules move autophagosomes and ESCRT subunits assist membrane closure and fusion.

Mitochondrial transcription termination sets the boundary of the ribosomal RNA transcription unit in mitochondrial DNA, and in doing so determines how much rRNA a cell makes relative to the mRNAs encoding respiratory chain subunits. Mitochondria must build their own ribosomes in vast excess over individual messages, and the imbalance is achieved partly by stopping transcription just past the 16S rRNA gene rather than letting polymerase continue along the heavy strand. MTERF1 accomplishes this by binding a short sequence within the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene immediately downstream of 16S rRNA, blocking read-through from the upstream ribosomal promoter. Termination therefore acts together with initiation site selection to control stoichiometry of mitochondrial gene expression, upstream of oxidative phosphorylation capacity; the same tRNA-Leu region is the site of mutations associated with mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic units, and the heavy strand carries two overlapping ones: a short unit covering the two rRNA genes and flanking tRNAs, and a longer one spanning nearly the whole strand. Because ribosomes must be built in far greater numbers than any single respiratory chain subunit, the rRNA unit is transcribed much more heavily, and that imbalance is set in part by where transcription stops. MTERF1 provides the stop signal: it binds a short sequence within the tRNA-Leu(UUR) gene just past the 16S rRNA gene and terminates the ribosomal unit there, so most polymerase molecules are released before entering the downstream protein-coding genes. Control of termination therefore shapes the stoichiometry between mitochondrial ribosome components and the mRNAs encoding oxidative phosphorylation subunits, linking this step to mitochondrial gene expression and respiratory capacity.

When hormones such as glucagon or adrenaline raise cAMP, protein kinase A tetramers dissociate and the freed catalytic subunits phosphorylate enzymes that set the direction of glucose metabolism. This is the switch that turns a fed, glucose-storing liver or muscle cell into one that mobilises glycogen and exports glucose, and its loss would leave tissues unable to respond to fasting or stress. Phosphorylation of the bifunctional 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase lowers fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, relieving stimulation of glycolysis and favouring gluconeogenesis, while parallel targeting of glycogen synthase and the phosphorylase activation cascade shifts glycogen handling toward breakdown. The kinase also phosphorylates the carbohydrate-responsive transcription factor ChREBP, keeping it out of the nucleus and shutting down transcription of glycolytic and lipogenic genes. Three catalytic subunit isoforms provide the enzymatic activity, linking G protein-coupled receptor signalling to both acute enzyme control and longer-term metabolic gene expression.

Glucagon is the hormone that defends blood glucose during fasting, and this signalling route is how its message reaches the enzymes of hepatic glucose production. When glucose falls, pancreatic alpha cells release glucagon, which binds its G protein-coupled receptor on hepatocytes and switches the liver from storing fuel to exporting it: glycogen is broken down, gluconeogenesis is driven forward, and glycolysis and glycogen synthesis are suppressed. The receptor couples through the stimulatory G protein Gs, with its beta and gamma partners, to adenylate cyclases that raise cAMP; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A, freeing catalytic subunits to phosphorylate metabolic enzymes and transcriptional regulators. Its counterpoise with insulin sets fasting glycaemia, and excessive glucagon action contributes to the hyperglycaemia of type 2 diabetes, making the receptor a drug target.

Stored fat is mobilised by hydrolysing triacylglycerol into free fatty acids and glycerol, and this triglyceride catabolism sets how much lipid fuel reaches the blood during fasting, exercise or stress. The rate-limiting step is hormone-sensitive lipase, which is switched on when catecholamines, ACTH or glucagon raise cAMP and protein kinase A phosphorylates both the lipase and perilipin on the lipid droplet surface; insulin opposes this, and protein phosphatase 1 subunits reverse the phosphorylations to shut the pathway down. Phosphorylation of perilipin releases the coactivator ABHD5 and opens the droplet to enzyme access, while fatty acid binding proteins escort the released fatty acids away from the site of hydrolysis and monoacylglycerol lipase completes the final step. The same lipase also hydrolyses cholesteryl esters, supplying substrate for steroid hormone synthesis. Dysregulated lipolysis contributes to insulin resistance, ectopic lipid accumulation and type 2 diabetes.

Protein kinase A is the main effector that converts a rise in cAMP into protein phosphorylation, and its activation step is how hormonal and neurotransmitter signals received at G protein-coupled receptors are translated into changes in metabolism, gene transcription, secretion and synaptic strength. In the resting state the kinase is an inactive tetramer: a dimer of regulatory subunits, in RI or RII forms, clamps two catalytic subunits. Adenylate cyclases, several of which are tuned by calcium bound to calmodulin, generate cAMP; binding of two cAMP molecules to each regulatory subunit triggers a conformational change that releases free, catalytically competent kinase. Anchoring proteins hold the holoenzyme near particular substrates so that the released activity acts locally. Mutations in the RIalpha regulatory subunit cause Carney complex, and unrestrained catalytic subunit activity drives adrenal and liver tumours, showing how tightly this release must be controlled.

When cellular ATP falls, AMP-activated protein kinase shuts down anabolic spending, and one of its targets is the glucose-responsive transcription factor ChREBP. Phosphorylation of ChREBP blocks its ability to occupy carbohydrate response elements, so transcription of glycolytic and lipogenic enzymes drops and the liver stops converting sugar into fat while energy is scarce. The arrangement links nutrient sensing to lipid synthesis: the AMPK heterotrimer of catalytic, beta and gamma subunits is switched on by the upstream kinase LKB1 when the AMP:ATP ratio rises, and adiponectin acting through its receptors ADIPOR1 and ADIPOR2 provides a hormonal route to the same kinase. Loss of this restraint contributes to hepatic steatosis and the dyslipidaemia of insulin resistance, which is why adiponectin signalling and AMPK activation are pursued as metabolic drug targets.

Whole-body fuel handling is coordinated by hormones that tell tissues whether to store nutrients or mobilise them, and this module captures that integration of energy metabolism around insulin and glucagon. Its failure underlies the hyperglycaemia of diabetes and the inability to defend blood glucose during fasting. One arm covers regulation of insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells: glucose uptake and metabolism close the ATP-sensitive potassium channel formed by KCNJ11 and ABCC8, depolarisation opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and SNAP25, VAMP2, STX1A and STXBP1 drive granule fusion, with GLP1R and adrenergic inputs tuning the response through adenylate cyclases and phospholipase C. In liver, glucagon receptor signalling raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates phosphofructokinase-2/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase and the lipogenic transcription factor ChREBP; insulin opposes this by way of pentose phosphate metabolites and PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation, while AMPK reports energy scarcity and restrains fatty acid synthesis through ACACA and FASN.

Insulin does more than push glucose into cells; it reshapes carbon flux so that glycolytic intermediates accumulate and feed the non-oxidative arm of the pentose phosphate pathway, raising cytosolic xylulose-5-phosphate. The two enzymes that carry this step, transketolase and transaldolase, interconvert fructose-6-phosphate, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, sedoheptulose-7-phosphate, ribose-5-phosphate and xylulose-5-phosphate, balancing sugar phosphates for nucleotide synthesis and NADPH-dependent biosynthesis. Xylulose-5-phosphate then acts as a signal rather than just a metabolite: it stimulates protein phosphatase 2A, which promotes formation of fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, an allosteric activator of phosphofructokinase 1 and therefore of glycolytic commitment. The result is a feed-forward loop linking the fed state to glycolysis and lipogenic gene expression in liver and adipose tissue. Transketolase depends on thiamine pyrophosphate, which is why this arm falters in thiamine deficiency.

When glucose is abundant, the carbohydrate-responsive transcription factor ChREBP switches on the genes that convert surplus sugar into fat, coupling the fed state to lipogenesis in liver and adipose tissue. Dephosphorylation in response to feeding signals permits nuclear entry, where ChREBP (MLXIPL) heterodimerizes with its obligate partner MLX and occupies carbohydrate response elements in target promoters. The resulting programme includes liver pyruvate kinase, which drives glycolytic flux to pyruvate, together with ATP-citrate lyase, acetyl-CoA carboxylase and fatty acid synthase, which supply cytosolic acetyl-CoA and elongate it into palmitate, and an acyltransferase step toward triglyceride assembly. This is the transcriptional arm of de novo lipogenesis that acts in parallel with insulin-driven SREBP signalling, and its overactivity contributes to hepatic steatosis and hypertriglyceridemia, while loss impairs the storage of dietary carbohydrate as fat.

High glucose is converted into a transcriptional signal for lipogenesis through PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation of key metabolic factors, chiefly the carbohydrate response element binding protein ChREBP encoded by MLXIPL. When glucose flux raises xylulose-5-phosphate from the pentose phosphate pathway, this phosphatase activity is stimulated, and dephosphorylated ChREBP moves into the nucleus, partners with MLX, and occupies carbohydrate response elements to switch on glycolytic and fatty acid synthesis genes in liver and adipose tissue. The same phosphatase acts on the bifunctional 6-phosphofructo-2-kinase/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, coupling the signal to glycolytic flux control. Catalytic subunits together with scaffolding and regulatory subunits assemble the holoenzyme that confers substrate specificity. This is the nutrient-sensing counterpart to insulin-driven lipogenic transcription, and its overactivity contributes to hepatic steatosis and dyslipidaemia.

Keratan sulfate is a glycosaminoglycan built from repeating N-acetylglucosamine-galactose units, and its synthesis and turnover shape the tissues that must stay transparent or resist compression. Corneal clarity depends on keratan sulfate proteoglycans such as lumican, keratocan and mimecan spacing collagen fibrils correctly, while in cartilage the chains decorate aggrecan and, being heavily hydrated, let joints absorb load; fibromodulin and PRELP tie the same chemistry to collagen organisation. Chain elongation alternates B3GNT-type GlcNAc transfer with B4GALT galactosylation, with sulfation by corneal and cartilage sulfotransferases including CHST6 and CHST3 and capping by sialyltransferases. Lysosomal breakdown runs through GALNS, GNS, GLB1 and the hexosaminidases, and loss of these degradative steps causes keratan sulfate accumulation in Morquio syndrome, with skeletal dysplasia, dental defects and corneal clouding.

Heparan sulfate and heparin metabolism covers the building, editing and breakdown of the sulfated sugar chains carried by proteoglycans such as the syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin. These chains sit on cell surfaces and in basement membranes, where their sulfation pattern determines which growth factors, morphogens, chemokines and coagulation factors are captured and presented, so the pathway shapes angiogenesis, development, blood clotting and tumour invasion. Chain elongation is carried out by EXT and EXTL glycosyltransferases, after which N-deacetylase/N-sulfotransferases and 2-O-, 6-O- and 3-O-sulfotransferases write the code, and an epimerase converts glucuronic to iduronic acid. Turnover requires heparanase to cleave chains and a set of lysosomal exoenzymes including IDUA, IDS, NAGLU, HGSNAT and SGSH; loss of any of these blocks stepwise degradation and causes mucopolysaccharidoses, in which undegraded glycosaminoglycan accumulates in lysosomes with skeletal and neurological consequences.

Grouped here are irreversible finishing steps that convert newly made proteins into functional ones: vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation, hypusine formation, diphthamide synthesis, side-chain hydroxylation and the activation of sulfatases. Each has a distinct physiological readout. GGCX carboxylates glutamate residues in prothrombin, factors VII, IX and X and the anticoagulants protein C and S, plus bone Gla protein, so loss of this chemistry causes bleeding or defective mineralisation and is the basis of warfarin action. DHPS and DOHH build hypusine on eIF5A, without which translation elongation past proline stretches fails; the DPH enzymes install diphthamide on eEF2, the residue that diphtheria toxin exploits. Jumonji-family and prolyl/asparaginyl hydroxylases modify ribosomal proteins, splicing factors and translation factors, while SUMF1 generates the formylglycine residue that all arylsulfatases need for lysosomal sulfate-ester hydrolysis; its failure causes multiple sulfatase deficiency.

Cell Cycle is the ordered program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, the basis of all tissue growth, renewal and, in germ cells, gamete production. Progression is driven by cyclin-dependent kinases whose partners oscillate in abundance, opposed by CDK inhibitors, the RB-E2F transcriptional switch, and phosphatases such as PP2A, with irreversibility imposed by ubiquitin ligases including the anaphase-promoting complex and SCF feeding the proteasome. Origin licensing by ORC/MCM and replisome assembly execute S phase; centrosomes, gamma-tubulin nucleated spindles, kinetochores, cohesin and condensin execute mitosis, monitored by the spindle assembly checkpoint and by ATM/ATR-CHEK damage checkpoints. Also included are nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, telomere maintenance by telomerase, centromeric chromatin assembly, and meiotic recombination and synapsis. Loss of these controls yields aneuploidy, genomic instability and cancer.

Cell division requires that the genome be copied exactly once and then split evenly between two daughters, and the cell cycle is the ordered programme that enforces this. Oscillating cyclin-CDK activity drives the transitions: cyclin D- and E-associated kinases inactivate RB to release E2F-dependent transcription at the G1/S boundary, origin licensing and firing proceed through ORC, CDC6, CDT1 and the MCM helicase with the replicative polymerases, and mitotic CDK1-cyclin B with Aurora and Polo kinases builds the spindle, kinetochores and condensed chromosomes. Counter-regulation comes from CDC25 phosphatases, WEE1, PP2A holoenzymes, CDK inhibitors such as p21 and p27, and ubiquitin-dependent destruction by the anaphase-promoting complex, SCF and the proteasome. Checkpoint kinases ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and CHEK2 halt progression when replication stalls or spindle attachment is faulty. Related activities include telomere maintenance, nuclear envelope and pore reassembly, cytokinetic abscission, and the meiotic recombination and synapsis machinery of germ cells. Loss of this control underlies aneuploidy and cancer.

This is an umbrella grouping of human disease biology, assembled from the molecular standpoint that illness arises when pathways are perturbed in one of three ways: microbial proteins are introduced into host processes, human proteins acquire altered function through mutation or aberrant modification, or normal proteins are made in abnormal amounts. The membership spans nearly every major cellular system, which is the point: oncogenic growth factor receptor and RAS-MAPK-PI3K signalling (EGFR, FGFR1-4, KRAS, BRAF, PTEN), DNA repair and checkpoint failure (BRCA1/2, MSH2, MLH1, ATM, TP53), congenital glycosylation and lysosomal storage defects, transporter disorders including CFTR and many SLC and ABC carriers, coagulation and complement deficiencies, extracellular matrix and collagen disease, innate immune and interferon signalling exploited during infection, and inherited errors of amino acid, carbohydrate and cobalamin metabolism. It organises variant proteins as extensions of their corresponding normal reactions, linking genotype to the specific step that fails.

Mutant and overexpressed forms of the epidermal growth factor receptor drive proliferation in lung adenocarcinoma, glioblastoma and other tumours, and this pathway describes EGFR signalling in cancer as a counterpart to the normal ligand-controlled receptor. Wild-type EGFR is activated transiently by EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, betacellulin and related ligands, then dimerises, autophosphorylates and recruits GRB2, SOS1 and SHC1 to activate RAS proteins, along with GAB1, PI3K subunits and PLCG1. Cancer variants, including kinase-domain mutants and the extracellular deletion variant EGFRvIII, signal without ligand or without restraint; they also escape the CBL-dependent ubiquitination that normally routes activated receptor for degradation, and depend on the HSP90/CDC37 chaperone system for stability. The result is sustained growth, survival and motility signalling, and the basis for treatment with EGFR kinase inhibitors and receptor antibodies.

PKA activation in glucagon signalling is the step that converts a hormonal signal of fasting into intracellular kinase activity, allowing the liver to raise blood glucose when it falls. Glucagon acting through its Gs-coupled receptor releases GNAS, which stimulates adenylate cyclase to make cAMP from ATP. Protein kinase A rests as an inactive tetramer of two catalytic and two regulatory subunits; cAMP binding to the regulatory subunits releases free catalytic monomers that phosphorylate targets driving glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenic gene expression via CREB, and suppression of glycolysis and lipogenesis. The multiple adenylate cyclase and regulatory subunit isoforms give tissue-specific tuning of signal strength and duration. Because this module is the general cAMP relay, it also transmits many other Gs-coupled hormone signals, and mutations in GNAS or the regulatory subunit PRKAR1A cause endocrine tumour syndromes.

When blood glucose falls, glucagon acts on hepatocytes to mobilise stored fuel, and this step is where the hormonal signal becomes an intracellular one. The stimulatory G protein alpha subunit encoded by GNAS switches on membrane adenylate cyclases, which convert ATP into cyclic AMP. Protein kinase A rests as a tetramer of two catalytic and two regulatory subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits, the complex dissociates, and free catalytic monomers phosphorylate targets that drive glycogen breakdown, gluconeogenic gene expression and lipolysis. Several adenylate cyclase and regulatory subunit isoforms exist with distinct tissue distributions and cAMP sensitivities, tuning the amplitude of the response. Loss or gain of function in this cascade disturbs glucose homeostasis, and activating GNAS mutations or regulatory subunit loss cause endocrine tumour syndromes, underscoring that cAMP output must be held within narrow limits.

Reverse transcription of the HIV-1 genome begins with minus-strand DNA synthesis, in which the viral reverse transcriptase copies the single-stranded RNA genome into a complementary DNA strand using a host lysine tRNA captured from the cell as primer. This step converts the incoming retroviral genome into the DNA form that can later be integrated into host chromatin, and it is the target of nucleoside and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors that form the backbone of antiretroviral therapy. Synthesis occurs in two stages separated by transfer of the nascent strand to the opposite genome end, while the RNase H activity of the same enzyme degrades the RNA template, sparing polypurine tracts that will prime plus-strand synthesis. The host peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A, carried into the cell with the capsid, influences uncoating and the efficiency of this early replication step.

The second half of HIV-1 reverse transcription, in which plus-strand DNA is copied from the newly made minus-strand to yield the linear double-stranded provirus that integration requires. Two polypurine tracts spared from RNase H degradation — one central within pol, one just upstream of U3 — serve as primers, and their removal, along with removal of the tRNA primer used for minus-strand initiation, plus a second strand transfer, generates a duplex carrying complete long terminal repeats at both ends. Both the polymerase and RNase H activities reside in domains of the reverse transcriptase heterodimer, making this step a target of antiretroviral nucleoside and non-nucleoside inhibitors. The host peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A, carried into the cell within the capsid, promotes efficient reverse transcription and uncoating, illustrating the dependence of the viral replication cycle on host factors.

When a retrovirus such as HIV-1 reverse transcribes its genome, only some of the linear cDNA integrates; the rest is circularised, and 2-LTR circle formation is the route by which the two blunt viral DNA ends are joined head-to-head in the nucleus. The product is a dead-end episome rather than a template for productive infection, which makes its abundance a convenient readout of how much viral DNA has reached the nuclear compartment and a marker used to track reverse transcription and nuclear import in infected cells. The joining is done not by viral enzymes but by the host non-homologous end-joining machinery: the Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer recognises and protects the ends, and XRCC4 with DNA ligase IV seals them. Chromatin and cofactor proteins including BANF1, HMGA1 and the integrase-binding factor PSIP1 associate with the incoming pre-integration complex. Loss of the end-joining components abolishes circle formation while leaving integration largely intact, and has been linked to the cytotoxicity of retroviral infection.

HIV-1 Nef strips immune receptors from the surface of an infected cell by linking them to the clathrin adaptor machinery, and this rerouting is a large part of why Nef is needed for full viral virulence and progression to disease. CD4, CD8, CD28 and MHC class I are pulled into AP-1 and AP-2 dependent endosomal and lysosomal itineraries rather than recycling to the plasma membrane, with ARF1, the vacuolar ATPase subunit ATP6V1H and the sorting connector PACS1 contributing to adaptor recruitment and trafficking. Loss of surface MHC class I, presented with beta-2-microglobulin, hides the infected cell from cytotoxic T lymphocytes, while removal of CD4 and the costimulatory receptor CD28 weakens contacts with antigen-presenting cells and limits superinfection. LCK signalling from the T cell receptor complex is disrupted in parallel, so viral immune evasion here is achieved entirely by subverting normal receptor endocytosis and sorting.

HIV-1 Nef strips the costimulatory receptor CD28 from the surface of infected T cells, blunting the second signal that normally accompanies antigen recognition and licenses full T cell activation, interleukin-2 production and clonal expansion. By removing CD28 alongside its better-known targets CD4 and MHC class I, the viral accessory protein leaves infected cells poorly responsive to antigen-presenting cells and harder for the immune system to clear, contributing to the persistent immune dysfunction of infection. Mechanistically Nef acts as a connector rather than an enzyme: a dileucine-based sorting motif in its flexible loop engages the clathrin adaptor complex through its mu subunit, hijacking normal endocytic cargo selection so that CD28 is captured in clathrin-coated pits, internalised at an accelerated rate and delivered to lysosomes for degradation instead of recycling.

Nef mediated downregulation of MHC class I complex cell surface expression describes how HIV-1 hides infected cells from cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Class I molecules such as HLA-A, paired with beta-2 microglobulin, normally display viral peptides at the plasma membrane so that CD8 T cells can kill the infected cell; the viral accessory protein Nef prevents this display, and its loss leaves infected cells far more vulnerable to immune killing, making the pathway a determinant of viral persistence and of vaccine and immunotherapy strategy. Mechanistically Nef acts as a connector in the endosomal system, linking the short cytoplasmic tail of MHC class I to the sorting adaptor PACS1 and to clathrin adaptor protein complex 1 subunits, so that internalised class I is rerouted to the trans-Golgi network and endosomes rather than recycled to the surface. It is a hijacking of ordinary intracellular protein sorting for immune evasion.

HIV-infected cells survive cytotoxic T lymphocyte surveillance in part by stripping MHC class I from their surface, and the viral accessory protein Nef is what drives this immune evasion. Class I molecules, made up of an HLA heavy chain paired with beta-2 microglobulin, normally display cytosolic peptides for CD8 T cell inspection; removing them leaves infected cells without the signal that marks them for killing, while other ligands that would trigger NK cells are left comparatively untouched. Mechanistically, Nef bridges the cytoplasmic tail of the class I heavy chain to the sorting connector PACS1 and to the clathrin adaptor AP-1 complex, whose large, medium and small subunits are all represented here. Rather than being degraded at the cell surface, the receptor is rerouted from the trans-Golgi and endosomes away from the plasma membrane, so newly synthesised molecules never reach it.

Nef and signal transduction describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Nef rewires host T cell and macrophage signalling to make infected cells better hosts for the virus. This matters because Nef-mediated signalling raises T cell activation and cytokine output, recruits resting T cells to sites of infection, and contributes to the pathogenicity that distinguishes Nef-competent virus in vivo. Myristoylated Nef partitions into cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains where signalling mediators concentrate, and its proline-rich motif engages SH3 domains of Src-family kinases such as LCK, FYN and the myeloid kinase HCK. Through a DOCK2-ELMO1 guanine nucleotide exchange module it activates RAC1, and it assembles a complex that activates PAK2, feeding into actin remodelling and TCR-proximal signalling downstream of the CD247 chain. The result is altered activation thresholds, chemokine secretion and enhanced viral replication rather than a normal antigen response.

HIV-1 Nef rewires host signal transduction to make infected cells more permissive and to recruit new targets for infection. Anchored in cholesterol-rich membrane microdomains by N-terminal myristoylation and engaging SH3 domains through its proline-rich motif, Nef captures Src-family kinases such as Lck, Fyn and the myeloid kinase Hck, positioning itself at the T cell receptor complex where the CD3 zeta chain (CD247) initiates activation signalling. It also forms a complex with the serine/threonine kinase PAK2, acting through the Rac1 GTPase and its DOCK2-ELMO1 exchange machinery to remodel the actin cytoskeleton and lower the threshold for cell activation, with enhanced interleukin-2 output during T cell stimulation. In macrophages the same accessory protein co-opts CD40 ligand signalling to release chemokines that draw resting T cells into contact and infection, linking viral pathogenesis to normal lymphocyte activation and migration control.

HIV-1 encodes Nef, a small myristoylated accessory protein made early in infection that is not required for virus assembly but largely determines how aggressively the virus replicates and how fast disease progresses — Nef-deleted SIV and HIV are strikingly attenuated. Its contribution to replication and pathogenesis works through host trafficking and signalling machinery: by engaging clathrin adaptor complexes AP-1 and AP-2 together with ARF1 and PACS1, Nef redirects CD4 and MHC class I molecules such as HLA-A and its β2-microglobulin partner away from the cell surface, blunting CD4 helper function and shielding infected cells from cytotoxic T lymphocytes. In parallel Nef binds Src-family kinases including LCK, FYN and HCK and activates a PAK2–RAC1 module with the DOCK2/ELMO1 exchange complex, perturbing T cell receptor and CD28 signalling, actin remodelling and cell motility while raising virion infectivity.

HIV-1 makes all of its proteins from a single transcript, and the virus can only build capsid and envelope if unspliced and partially spliced RNAs reach the cytoplasm despite the cellular rule that incompletely spliced pre-mRNA stays in the nucleus. Rev-mediated nuclear export of HIV RNA is how that rule is bypassed: Rev binds the Rev response element in the viral RNA and, through its leucine-rich nuclear export signal, recruits the karyopherin exportin-1 together with RanGTP, delivering the cargo through the nuclear pore. The machinery involved is entirely host: the nucleoporin scaffold and channel of the pore complex, the cytoplasmic and basket filaments, and the Ran gradient set by its GTPase-activating protein and cytoplasmic exchange factor, which supplies directionality and releases cargo. Without it, only early regulatory transcripts are exported and virion production stalls, making this step a target for antiviral strategies.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the body, and its biosynthesis together with the modifying enzymes that mature it determines whether skin, bone, cartilage, blood vessels and basement membranes have tensile strength. Procollagen alpha chains from across the family — fibrillar types I, II, III, V and XI, network-forming type IV, anchoring type VII and the FACIT and beaded-filament collagens — enter the endoplasmic reticulum, where prolyl 4-hydroxylases and their P4HB partner, prolyl 3-hydroxylases, lysyl hydroxylases (PLOD1-3), collagen galactosyltransferases, the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase PPIB and the collagen-specific chaperone HSP47 stabilise and fold the triple helix. After secretion, BMP1 and tolloid-like proteases with their PCOLCE enhancers remove C-propeptides while ADAMTS2, 3 and 14 cleave N-propeptides, releasing tropocollagen for fibril assembly. Defects here cause osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos and dermatosparactic syndromes, epidermolysis bullosa and Alport syndrome.

AKT2 is the insulin-responsive member of the AKT/PKB family of AGC-family serine/threonine kinases, and its activation is the step that converts a lipid signal at the plasma membrane into control of glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, cell survival and growth. Recruitment depends on its pleckstrin homology domain binding PIP3 generated by PI3-kinase downstream of insulin and growth factor receptors; PDPK1 then phosphorylates the activation-loop threonine, while phosphorylation of the C-terminal hydrophobic motif is required for full catalytic output. The process is held in check by binding partners rather than only by lipid turnover: THEM4 and TRIB3 associate with AKT2 and restrain its activity. Because AKT2 predominates in muscle, liver and adipose tissue, loss-of-function mutations cause severe insulin resistance and diabetes, whereas persistent activation contributes to tumour growth and resistance to apoptosis.

MTOR signalling is the cell's central decision point for growth: it reads nutrient abundance, energy charge and growth factor input, and sets the balance between anabolic programmes such as protein synthesis and catabolic ones such as autophagy. Its dysregulation underlies cancer, obesity-related metabolic disease and diabetes, and the tuberous sclerosis genes TSC1 and TSC2 act here as brakes on the pathway. Amino acid sufficiency is sensed at the lysosome, where the Rag GTPases, the Ragulator complex and the transporter SLC38A9 recruit mTORC1 for activation by RHEB; energy stress acts oppositely through the LKB1-STRAD-CAB39 module and AMPK. Activated mTORC1 phosphorylates S6 kinase and 4E-BP1 to license cap-dependent translation, while AKT relays growth factor signals and feeds back on the complex. Rapamycin binding via FKBP1A inhibits this arm selectively.

mTOR signalling is how a cell decides whether conditions are good enough to grow. The mTOR kinase sits in two complexes: mTORC1, with RPTOR and MLST8, integrates amino acid availability, energy charge and growth factor input to drive protein synthesis and suppress autophagy, while a RICTOR-containing complex responds to growth factors. Amino acids act through the lysosomal Ragulator-Rag GTPase platform and the transporter-like sensor SLC38A9 to recruit mTORC1 to the lysosome, where RHEB activates it; the TSC1-TSC2 complex opposes this as a GTPase-activating protein for RHEB, and AMPK, activated by the LKB1-STRADA-CAB39 module under low energy, brakes growth. Outputs include S6K1 and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation, releasing eIF4E for cap-dependent translation, plus effects on elongation via eEF2 kinase and on miRNA silencing machinery. Dysregulation underlies tumour growth, insulin resistance and hamartoma syndromes, and rapamycin selectively blocks mTORC1.

Insulin's ability to shut down fat breakdown depends on PDE3B signalling, the step at which insulin-activated AKT lowers cAMP inside the cell. In adipocytes, hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells, cAMP drives protein kinase A and thus lipolysis and glycogen breakdown; degrading it converts a hormonal signal into suppression of these catabolic programmes and favours triglyceride storage. Mechanistically, phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate generated downstream of the insulin receptor recruits AKT to the plasma membrane, where phosphorylation activates it; AKT2, the isoform most associated with metabolic tissues, then phosphorylates the membrane-associated cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterase PDE3B, stimulating hydrolysis of 3',5'-cyclic AMP. This is one of the principal anti-lipolytic arms of insulin action, and its blunting contributes to the elevated free fatty acid flux and insulin resistance seen in type 2 diabetes and obesity.

Growth factor and insulin signalling switches cells from catabolism to growth, and one of the steps that makes this possible is AKT-mediated shutdown of the TSC complex. TSC1 and TSC2 (hamartin and tuberin) together act as a GTPase-activating protein for the small GTPase RHEB, driving it into its GDP-bound state and thereby keeping mTORC1 off; when AKT phosphorylates TSC2 at multiple sites, TSC2 activity falls and its association with TSC1 is disrupted, leaving free TSC2 open to ubiquitination and degradation. RHEB then accumulates in its GTP-bound form and activates mTORC1, licensing protein synthesis, ribosome biogenesis and cell growth. Loss-of-function mutations in either subunit cause tuberous sclerosis complex, a multi-system disorder of benign tumours and hamartomas, and constitutive mTORC1 signalling through this axis contributes to tumorigenesis. The complex also tempers the negative feedback by which S6K1 dampens insulin-driven PI3K/AKT signalling.

Cells must keep membrane sterol levels within narrow limits, and this is the feedback circuit that senses when cholesterol is scarce and switches on the genes that make it. When sterols are plentiful, the escort protein SCAP holds SREBP precursors in the endoplasmic reticulum through cholesterol- and oxysterol-dependent binding to INSIG1/INSIG2; when sterols fall, SCAP instead engages Sec24 of the COPII coat and the complex moves to the Golgi, where two proteases release the transcription factor's N-terminal domain for importin-mediated nuclear entry. There, together with SP1, NF-Y subunits and coactivators such as CREBBP, NCOA1/2 and MED1, it drives the mevalonate pathway and downstream sterol synthesis enzymes including HMGCR, SQLE and DHCR7, plus lipogenic genes FASN, SCD and acetyl-CoA carboxylases. SREBF2 favours cholesterol synthesis and SREBF1 lipogenesis; the axis underlies statin responsiveness, hepatic steatosis and dyslipidaemia.

Toll Like Receptor 4 (TLR4) Cascade is the innate immune sensing route for bacterial lipopolysaccharide, the pathway that lets macrophages, dendritic cells and endothelium detect Gram-negative infection and mount inflammation; its overactivation produces the cytokine storm, coagulopathy and organ failure of septic shock. LPS is delivered to TLR4 with the help of LBP, CD14 and MD-2, and the receptor then uses two adapter arms. At the plasma membrane TIRAP and MyD88 recruit IRAK4/IRAK1, TRAF6 and the TAK1-IKK axis, driving NF-kB and MAPK/AP-1 output and pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF and IL-6. After dynamin-dependent endocytosis, TRAM and TRIF engage TBK1/IKKe and IRF3 for type I interferon and delayed NF-kB activation. Endogenous ligands including HMGB1 and S100 proteins feed the same circuit in sterile inflammation, while SIGIRR, IRAK3, SOCS1 and ubiquitin-editing enzymes restrain it. Output also includes co-stimulatory molecules that shape adaptive immunity.

Detection of bacterial lipopolysaccharide by innate immune cells runs through the TLR4 cascade, the signalling route that converts contact with Gram-negative outer membrane into inflammation, fever and, when unrestrained, septic shock with disseminated coagulation and organ failure. LPS is delivered to the receptor by LBP, CD14 and the co-receptor MD-2 (LY96), after which TLR4 uniquely engages two adapter arms: TIRAP with MyD88 at the plasma membrane, recruiting IRAK4/IRAK1 and TRAF6 to drive IKK-dependent NF-kB activation and MAP kinase output through TAK1, p38, JNK and ERK toward AP-1 and CREB target genes; and, after dynamin-dependent endocytosis, TRAM with TRIF, which signals via TBK1/IKKe and IRF3 to induce type I interferons and a delayed NF-kB response. Endogenous ligands such as HMGB1, S100 proteins and serum amyloid A feed the same circuit in sterile inflammation, while SIGIRR, IRAK3, SOCS1, A20-binding proteins and phosphatases restrain it. Ubiquitin conjugation and SCF-mediated IkB degradation set the timing throughout.

Detection of Gram-negative bacteria begins with a handoff: lipopolysaccharide-binding protein extracts LPS from bacterial membranes or intact organisms and transfers it to CD14 on the surface of macrophages, monocytes and neutrophils, which concentrates the lipid and passes it to the MD2:TLR4 receptor complex for signalling. This step sets the sensitivity of innate immune sensing, allowing responses to picomolar endotoxin; without it, much higher LPS loads are needed to trigger inflammatory gene expression, while unrestrained amplification of the same route drives the cytokine storm and vascular collapse of Gram-negative sepsis. LBP acts as a soluble opsonin and CD14 as the opsonic receptor, existing both as a GPI-anchored membrane form and as a shed soluble form that confers LPS responsiveness on cells lacking the anchored protein. The pathway is the gateway to TLR4-dependent NF-κB activation.</br>

Phosphoinositides are the plasma membrane's addressing system: the pattern of phosphates on the inositol headgroup tells cytosolic proteins where the cell surface is and what is happening there. Synthesis of PIPs at the plasma membrane is the set of lipid kinases and phosphatases that write and erase those marks, converting PI4P to PI(4,5)P2 through PIP5K enzymes and, downstream of receptor activation, generating PI(3,4,5)P3 via class I PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits. Opposing phosphatases including PTEN, SHIP family 5-phosphatases, INPP4 enzymes, OCRL, synaptojanins and the myotubularin family reverse these steps, with catalytically dead myotubularins acting as partners that tune the active ones. The resulting lipids recruit PH-domain effectors and control endocytosis, actin remodelling, ion channel gating and growth signalling; loss of control underlies cancer, Lowe syndrome, and myotubular and demyelinating neuropathies.

Endosomes are identified by the phosphoinositides in their limiting membrane, and the switch that converts an early endosome into a late one is the conversion of PI(3)P into PI(3,5)P2. This lipid change reprogrammes which effectors can dock, allowing cargo destined for degradation to progress toward lysosomes while recycling cargo is withdrawn; it also governs endosome size, multivesicular body formation and the fission events that keep the compartment from swelling. A lipid kinase acting on the 5-position of PI(3)P generates PI(3,5)P2 within a complex that also contains the opposing 5-phosphatase and a scaffold, so synthesis and turnover are coupled and the pool is kept small and locally controlled. Loss of this interconversion causes vacuolated, enlarged endosomes and failure of lysosomal delivery, and underlies neurodegenerative and myopathic disease in which endolysosomal traffic breaks down.

Phosphoinositides mark membranes with lipid identity codes that tell trafficking machinery where it is, and this step moves phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate out of the late endosomal membrane and delivers it to the Golgi. Because PI(3,5)P2 is made on late endosomes and lysosomes, where it governs endolysosomal maturation, ion channel activity and membrane fission, its appearance on Golgi membranes links the degradative arm of the endomembrane system to the secretory and retrograde pathways. Transport of this kind lets a locally synthesised lipid signal act at a distance, supporting the reciprocal traffic between endosomes and the Golgi that recycles receptors and sorting machinery. More broadly, the pathway belongs to phosphoinositide interconversion and turnover, the lipid-based coding system on which organelle identity, vesicle budding and vacuolar homeostasis depend.

PIPs transport between Golgi and plasma membranes describes the vesicular delivery of phosphoinositide-rich membrane from the trans-Golgi network to the cell surface, a route that sets the lipid identity of each compartment. Phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate generated on Golgi membranes by PI4-kinases recruits lipid transfer and coat proteins, drives cargo sorting into secretory carriers, and is then carried with those carriers to the plasma membrane, where it is converted onward to PI(4,5)P2. That surface pool underlies exocytosis, endocytic vesicle formation, actin attachment to the membrane, and signalling through phospholipase C and PI3-kinase. Because organelle-specific phosphoinositide gradients tell peripheral proteins where they are, disrupting this flow blurs the boundary between Golgi and plasma membrane and impairs constitutive secretion and receptor signalling. The pathway sits at the intersection of lipid metabolism and membrane traffic.

Phosphoinositides mark organelle membranes with a lipid identity code, and the movement of these species between the Golgi and the plasma membrane keeps that code aligned with vesicular traffic. Secretory carriers budding from the trans-Golgi network carry phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate with them to the cell surface, so the same lipid that recruits clathrin adaptors and lipid-transfer proteins at the Golgi becomes a substrate pool at the plasma membrane, where further phosphorylation yields PI(4,5)P2. That surface pool governs endocytosis, actin attachment to the membrane, ion channel gating and signalling through phospholipase C, while the Golgi pool governs cargo sorting and export. Because delivery and retrieval are balanced by kinases, phosphatases and membrane contact sites, disturbances in this traffic distort secretion and surface signalling rather than any single enzymatic step, linking lipid distribution directly to the organisation of the secretory pathway.

The Golgi is identified as a compartment partly by the phosphoinositides in its membranes, and generating them there is what allows lipid-binding coat proteins, tethers and transfer proteins to be recruited to the right face of the right cisterna. Phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate dominates: type III kinases PI4KA and PI4KB, the latter recruited by ARF1, and membrane-anchored type II kinases PI4K2A and PI4K2B phosphorylate phosphatidylinositol, while the phosphatase SACM1L removes the same phosphate to set a gradient that drives sterol and ceramide exchange at contact sites with the ER. Class II and class III PI 3-kinases supply PI3P, PIKFYVE with its VAC14 and FIG4 partners converts it to PI(3,5)P2, and 5-phosphatases including OCRL and INPP5E reverse those steps. This lipid code governs secretory traffic and sorting, and its disruption underlies Lowe syndrome and ciliopathies.

Endosomes are labelled with phosphoinositide lipids that tell trafficking machinery where a membrane is and how mature it is, and the synthesis of PIPs at the early endosome membrane is how that code is written and erased. PI3P, made largely by the class III kinase PIK3C3 with its regulatory partner PIK3R4, recruits FYVE- and PX-domain effectors for cargo sorting and autophagosome formation, and is further phosphorylated by PIKFYVE within a complex with the scaffold VAC14 and the phosphatase FIG4 to give PI(3,5)P2, which governs endolysosome size, acidification and fission. Opposing this, myotubularin-family 3-phosphatases such as MTM1 and MTMR2 and the inositol 4-phosphatases INPP4A/B turn the signal off. Loss of balance here causes myotubular myopathy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy and neurodegeneration with swollen, undigested endosomal compartments.

Late endosomes carry a distinctive phosphoinositide signature that tells trafficking machinery where a membrane is in the endocytic pathway, and this pathway makes and edits those lipids. PI3P, generated by the class III kinase VPS34 with its regulatory partners, recruits FYVE- and PX-domain effectors for cargo sorting and autophagosome formation; PIKFYVE phosphorylates it further to PI(3,5)P2, which governs endosome maturation, lumenal acidification and lysosome reformation. The dominant reactions here are removals: myotubularin-family 3-phosphatases strip PI3P to phosphatidylinositol, some members acting only as catalytically dead regulatory subunits, while FIG4 within the PIKFYVE-VAC14 complex turns PI(3,5)P2 back to PI3P, and other routes yield PI5P. Balance matters clinically: myotubularin loss causes centronuclear myopathy and demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, and FIG4 mutations cause neurodegeneration with vacuolated neurons.

Phosphoinositides mark membranes with identity, and their movement between compartments is one way a cell keeps track of where a membrane came from and where it is going. This step follows phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate as it leaves the plasma membrane and appears on the early endosome membrane, a relocation that accompanies clathrin-mediated endocytosis and the maturation of a nascent vesicle into a sorting endosome. PI(3,4)P2 is generated at the cell surface downstream of growth factor and receptor signalling and recruits effectors bearing lipid-binding modules that shape membrane curvature and drive vesicle scission; carrying it inward transfers that recruiting capacity to the endosomal face. Because endosomal phosphoinositide composition determines which cargo is recycled, degraded or signalled from, this transfer sits upstream of receptor downregulation and of the spatial control of PI3K-dependent signalling.

Phosphoinositides are membrane-identity lipids: which one is present on a given organelle determines which effector proteins are recruited there, so their movement between compartments helps define organelle identity and traffic. This step concerns phosphoinositide transport between early endosome and Golgi membranes, in particular the export of phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate from the early endosomal membrane to the Golgi. PI(3,5)P2 is generated on endosomes by phosphorylation of PI3P and governs endosome maturation, cargo sorting and lysosomal ion channel activity; delivering it to Golgi membranes links the endosomal system to retrograde traffic and to the interconversion network that regenerates other phosphoinositide species. Movement of these lipids between organelles is part of the broader control of vesicular transport and membrane signalling, where imbalance disrupts endolysosomal sorting and degradative capacity.

Toll-like receptors sitting at the plasma membrane, principally TLR4 with its LY96/CD14 co-receptors and the TLR2 heterodimers with TLR1 or TLR6, sense bacterial lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides and endogenous danger signals such as S100 proteins and HMGB1, and convert that recognition into inflammatory gene expression. The MyD88:MAL(TIRAP) cascade is how they do it: TIRAP recruits MyD88 to the receptor, MyD88's death domain assembles the IRAK kinases into a Myddosome, and IRAK phosphorylation passes the signal to TRAF6, whose K63-linked ubiquitin chains built with UBE2N/UBE2V1 activate the TAK1-TAB complex. From there the IKK complex frees NF-kB from IkB while parallel MAP kinase branches drive JNK, p38 and ERK toward AP-1, together inducing cytokines. Pelino ligases, SIGIRR, SOCS1, IRAK3 and phosphatases restrain the output; too little gives susceptibility to pyogenic infection, too much drives septic and chronic inflammation.

Ceramide and its derivatives are built from scratch here, starting with condensation of serine and palmitoyl-CoA by serine palmitoyltransferase and continuing through reduction, N-acylation by a family of ceramide synthases with distinct acyl-chain preferences, and desaturation or hydroxylation of the sphingoid backbone. De novo sphingolipid biosynthesis supplies the structural lipids of membranes and myelin, the ceramide that signals stress and apoptosis, and the sphingosine-1-phosphate that governs lymphocyte egress and vascular integrity. Output is controlled by ORMDL proteins, which restrain the first committed step in response to sphingolipid load, and products leave the endoplasmic reticulum via a dedicated ceramide transfer protein working with VAP tethers at membrane contact sites, or as sphingomyelin made in the Golgi. Sphingosine kinases and plasma membrane exporters release the phosphorylated signalling forms; mutations in the pathway cause hereditary sensory neuropathy and skin barrier disease.

Glycosphingolipids are ceramide-based lipids carrying sugar headgroups; they populate the outer face of the plasma membrane, organise lipid rafts, define blood group and ganglioside antigens, and are especially abundant in myelin and neuronal membranes. Their metabolism covers both branches of the cycle: glucosylceramide and galactosylceramide synthases commit ceramide to the glycolipid route, and a series of galactosyl-, N-acetylgalactosaminyl- and sialyltransferases elaborate the globoside, lacto and ganglioside series, while sulfotransferases add sulfate to make sulfatides. Breakdown runs in the lysosome, where exoglycosidases and their activator proteins strip sugars in sequence before ceramidase and sphingomyelinase release sphingosine. This catabolic arm is the origin of the sphingolipidoses — Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs, Krabbe, metachromatic leukodystrophy — in which undegraded substrate accumulates and causes progressive neurodegeneration and organomegaly.

Bacterial lipopolysaccharide sensed by TLR4 triggers two waves of signalling, and this one proceeds without MyD88: after receptor internalisation, the bridging adapter TRAM (TICAM2) recruits TRIF (TICAM1) to the endosomal receptor complex. From there the cascade splits, driving TBK1/IKBKE-dependent phosphorylation of IRF3 to induce type I interferons, TRAF6- and TAK1-dependent activation of NF- cB and the p38, JNK and ERK MAP kinase arms for pro-inflammatory cytokines, and, through RIPK1, FADD and caspase-8, a route to apoptotic or necroptotic death.
