This arm shapes the interferon component of the innate response to Gram-negative infection and contributes to endotoxin-driven inflammation and septic shock; deubiquitinases, phosphatases and IkB proteins restrain it, since unchecked output is damaging. Co-receptors CD14 and MD-2 (LY96) are required for ligand delivery to TLR4.

Mitochondrial Uncoupling describes how cells deliberately waste the proton gradient built by respiratory electron transport, dissipating it as heat instead of capturing it as ATP. This is the basis of adaptive thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, which warms small mammals in the cold, protects newborns during the cold stress of birth, and drives arousal from hibernation; regulated leak also limits reactive oxygen species production and, in pancreatic beta cells, tempers insulin secretion. The carriers involved belong to the SLC25 mitochondrial transporter family, folded on the same six-helix architecture as the adenine nucleotide translocase, which itself conducts protons. UCP1 leak is held off by purine nucleotides and released by fatty acids mobilised after adrenergic stimulation, most plausibly through a fatty-acid cycling mechanism. A separate route works through the secreted enzyme PM20D1, which makes and breaks N-acyl amino acids such as oleoyl-phenylalanine that uncouple mitochondria without UCPs.

Not all of the proton gradient made by respiratory electron transport is spent on ATP synthesis; mitochondrial uncoupling deliberately leaks protons back into the matrix so that substrate oxidation continues while the energy is released as heat. This is the basis of adaptive non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue, which warms small mammals in the cold, supports newborns through the cold stress of birth, and rouses hibernators. UCP1 is the dominant carrier there, one of a family of inner-membrane transporters that includes UCP2, UCP3, the brain and kidney carriers SLC25A14 and SLC25A27, and the adenine nucleotide translocase SLC25A4, which itself conducts protons. UCP1 conductance is held down by purine nucleotides and released by fatty acids mobilised after adrenergic stimulation, most likely through fatty acid cycling. A secreted enzyme, PM20D1, makes N-acyl amino acids such as oleoyl-phenylalanine that uncouple independently of UCPs. Controlled leak also lowers reactive oxygen species output and modulates beta-cell insulin secretion, linking this biology to energy balance and oxidative stress.

Cells only commit to growth when nutrients, energy, oxygen and growth factor signals all permit it, and mTORC1-mediated signalling is the node where those inputs converge on the decision to build new protein and mass. The kinase mTOR, with raptor and mLST8, is recruited to lysosomal membranes by Rag GTPase heterodimers anchored through the Ragulator complex, where amino acid availability is read out in part by the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9; there the small GTPase Rheb, held in check by the tuberous sclerosis GAP complex downstream of insulin and AMPK signals, switches the kinase on. Active mTORC1 phosphorylates S6 kinase and the 4E-BP translational repressor, releasing eIF4E and cap-dependent translation initiation, and blocks autophagy. PRAS40 restrains the complex, and FKBP12 mediates rapamycin inhibition. Persistent activation drives tumour growth, hypertrophy and metabolic disease.

Sulfatases cannot work until a cysteine in their active site is converted to formylglycine, and this maturation step is what switches the arylsulfatase family on. The enzymes that depend on it desulfate sulfolipids, glycosaminoglycans and steroid sulfates, mostly in lysosomes and the endoplasmic reticulum, so the modification sits upstream of turnover of sulfated macromolecules and of steroid hormone availability. SUMF1 performs the oxygen-dependent cysteine oxidation in the ER lumen and is required for the activity of all family members; its paralogue SUMF2 can restrain that activation, giving a way to tune sulfatase output. Loss of SUMF1 disables every sulfatase at once, producing multiple sulfatase deficiency with the combined features of metachromatic leukodystrophy, mucopolysaccharidoses and ichthyosis, while single-enzyme failures such as ARSA or steroid sulfatase give their own storage or skin disorders.

Neurotrophins — NGF, BDNF, NT-3 and NT-4 — are secreted in small amounts by target tissues and instruct neurons to survive, differentiate, grow axons and remodel synapses; signalling by NTRKs is how that instruction is read. NTRK1, NTRK2 and NTRK3 are receptor tyrosine kinases with distinct ligand preferences that dimerize and trans-autophosphorylate on ligand binding, creating docking sites for SHC, FRS2, GRB2/SOS, GAB1 and PLCG1. From there RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK, PI3K and small GTPase routes converge on CREB, ELK1, SRF and immediate-early genes such as FOS, EGR family members, ARC and VGF, linking trophic support to activity-dependent plasticity and learning. Clathrin and AP-2 components carry activated receptors into signalling endosomes for retrograde transport from axon terminals. Loss of NTRK1 signalling causes congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis; unliganded NTRK3 acts as a dependence receptor triggering BAX- and caspase-9-dependent death, and NTRK gene fusions drive several cancers.

The complement cascade is the blood's rapid surveillance system: soluble proteins circulating as inactive precursors that detect microbes, immune complexes and dying cells and convert that recognition into opsonization, inflammation and lysis. Three entry routes converge on C3 cleavage — the classical route through C1q/C1r/C1s bound to antibody-antigen complexes, the lectin route through mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins with their associated MASP proteases, and the spontaneous alternative route amplified by factor B, factor D and properdin. C3 convertases deposit C3b for phagocyte receptors, release C3a and C5a that signal through C3AR1 and C5AR1 to recruit leukocytes, and switch to C5 convertases that assemble C6–C9 into the membrane attack complex. Restraint is equally important: factor H, C4b-binding protein, factor I, CD46, CD55 and CD59 protect host membranes, and their loss causes haemolytic disease, atypical uraemic syndrome and macular degeneration.

Lectin pathway of complement activation is one of the three routes into the complement cascade, and the one that lets innate immunity recognise microbes directly by their sugar coats rather than by antibody. It provides antibody-independent opsonisation and lysis of bacteria, fungi and altered host cells, and contributes to clearance of apoptotic debris; deficiency of mannose-binding lectin or MASP2 predisposes to recurrent pyogenic infection in infancy, while excessive activation drives ischaemia-reperfusion and ischaemic tissue injury. Calcium-dependent collagenous lectins – MBL, the ficolins, and the CL-K1/CL-L1 heterocomplex – oligomerise and bind repetitive carbohydrate and acetylated patterns on target surfaces, triggering conformational activation of associated MASP proteases. MASP2 then cleaves C4 and C2 to build the C4b:C2a C3 convertase, converging on the same downstream cascade as the classical pathway. MASP1 amplifies this and also cross-talks with coagulation by acting on fibrinogen and factor XIII.

Innate immune recognition of carbohydrate patterns on microbes and dying cells triggers the lectin pathway of complement activation, one of three routes into the complement cascade and a first line of antibody-independent defence. Calcium-dependent recognition molecules — mannose-binding lectin, the ficolins FCN1, FCN2 and FCN3, and the collectin heterocomplex of COLEC10 and COLEC11 — circulate as oligomers bound to MBL-associated serine proteases. Binding to sugar arrays on a target surface rearranges the complex so that MASP1 and MASP2 become active; MASP2 then cleaves C4 and C2 to build the C3 convertase that deposits opsonins, recruits phagocytes and drives lytic pore formation. MASP1 additionally activates MASP2 and cross-talks with coagulation by acting on fibrinogen and factor XIII. Deficiency of MBL2 or MASP2 predisposes to recurrent respiratory infection in childhood, while COLEC10 and COLEC11 loss causes the developmental 3MC syndrome.

Complement is the humoral arm of innate defence, and its initial triggering is the recognition step that decides whether the cascade fires at all. Three routes converge on the same outcome: antibody bound to a target engages the C1 complex of C1QA/B/C with the serine proteases C1R and C1S; carbohydrate patterns on microbes are read by mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins acting through MASP1 and MASP2; and spontaneously generated C3b deposited on foreign surfaces recruits factor B, factor D and properdin. Each route cleaves C4 and C2, or B, to build C3 and C5 convertases, marking the surface for phagocytosis and lysis while releasing inflammatory fragments. The many immunoglobulin heavy and light chain segments here reflect the antibody repertoire that supplies classical-pathway targets. Failure of early components predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and to lupus-like autoimmunity from poor clearance of immune complexes and dying cells.

The terminal pathway of complement is the shared killing step in which all three complement activation routes converge to punch a hole in a target membrane. It lyses Gram-negative bacteria such as Neisseria, and people lacking C5 through C9 suffer recurrent meningococcal disease, while uncontrolled activation damages host cells in haemolytic disease and glomerulonephritis. Cleavage of C5 exposes a C6 binding site; the resulting C5b6 recruits C7, which reveals lipid-binding surfaces and anchors the complex in the bilayer. C8, a trimer of C8A, C8B and C8G, then nucleates recruitment and unfurling of multiple C9 molecules into a ring-shaped pore. Sublytic pores also signal, driving inflammatory responses rather than immediate death. Clusterin binds nascent complexes in fluid phase and blocks assembly, one of the brakes that confines lysis to the intended surface.

The first committed step of complement activation by the classical and lectin routes is the assembly of a protease complex able to cleave C4 and C2, generating the C3 convertase C4b2a that marks a surface for opsonisation, inflammation and lysis. This is how antibody-coated and carbohydrate-coated microbes, immune complexes and dying cells are flagged for clearance; loss of it predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and impaired clearance of self debris, while unchecked activation drives tissue damage. In the classical arm, C1q recognises IgG or IgM bound to antigen, or C-reactive protein, and the change in conformation activates C1r, which cleaves C1s to yield the active C4/C2-cleaving enzyme. In the lectin arm, mannose-binding lectin, ficolins and collectins CL-K1/CL-L1 bind pathogen sugar patterns and activate the associated serine proteases MASP1 and MASP2 to the same end. The large immunoglobulin variable and constant repertoire reflects the antibody specificities that trigger the classical route.

Neurotrophin binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase can be routed into a calcium and lipid second-messenger response, and PLC-gamma1 signalling is that route. Activated TrkA, engaged by nerve growth factor, phosphorylates phospholipase C-gamma1, which hydrolyses PIP2 to inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores while DAG and the rising calcium together activate protein kinase C isoforms and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases. The output matters for sensory and sympathetic neurons: the arm supports neurotrophin secretion itself, neurite outgrowth, synaptic modulation and nociceptor sensitisation, which is why NGF-TrkA activity is a target in pain. Loss-of-function mutations in this receptor cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis, showing how much peripheral sensory development depends on this branch running alongside the Ras-MAPK and PI3K outputs of the same receptor.

Growth factor receptors convert ligand binding into RAS activation, and this route describes how nerve growth factor acting through its receptor tyrosine kinase TrkA does so. Receptor autophosphorylation recruits Shc adaptors, which bind GRB2 and the exchange factor SOS1; SOS1 loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, launching the kinase cascades that drive neuronal differentiation, neurite outgrowth and survival of sympathetic and sensory neurons. Signalling through Shc is essentially the same for NGF and EGF and produces only fast, transient ERK activation, so it cannot by itself account for the sustained MAPK output that distinguishes an NGF response. Active RAS also engages RALGDS to switch on the RAL GTPases, while p38 family kinases and their MAPKAPK2/3 substrates and the SRC kinase provide parallel and modulating branches. Loss or constitutive activation of these components underlies both neurotrophin-dependent developmental defects and RAS-driven cancers.

Nerve growth factor is made as a precursor and must be trimmed before it can act as a mature neurotrophin, and NGF processing is the set of proteolytic steps that decide which form a cell secretes. This matters because the pro-form and the mature form have opposing consequences: mature NGF binds TrkA to support survival, axon growth and the maintenance of sympathetic and sensory neurons, while uncleaved pro-NGF favours p75-mediated death signalling. After signal peptide removal in the endoplasmic reticulum the pro-protein dimerises and moves through the Golgi to the trans-Golgi network, where subtilisin-like proprotein convertases including furin, PCSK5 and PCSK6 excise the pro-domain at a basic cleavage site. Mature dimers are routed to secretory vesicles for constitutive release; incompletely processed pro-NGF can also be secreted, a balance implicated in neurodegeneration and in pain sensitisation.

Without the viral Tat protein, transcription from the integrated HIV-1 promoter depends entirely on the host machinery, and this pathway describes how RNA polymerase II is converted from a promoter-paused state into a productive elongation complex on the viral template. Elongation and chromatin factors including ELL, the elongin complex, TCEA1 and FACT then sustain processive synthesis, while the nuclear cap-binding complex engages the nascent transcript.

Transcription of the integrated HIV-1 provirus begins with host RNA polymerase II, and the formation of the HIV-1 early elongation complex is the step at which the newly initiated polymerase is captured in a paused, promoter-proximal state that the viral Tat protein later releases. Because this pause sets the switch between latency and productive replication, it is central to how the virus establishes a reservoir. RNA Pol II CTD phosphorylation and interaction with CE during HIV infection describes the earliest committed step of transcript maturation on the integrated HIV provirus: marking the polymerase so that the nascent viral RNA is capped. Because the host machinery transcribes the provirus, viral messages depend entirely on this step for stability, nuclear export and translation, and its loss aborts viral gene expression. Shortly after initiation, the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7 with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners phosphorylates Serine 5 of the heptad repeats on the POLR2A C-terminal domain. The capping enzyme guanylyltransferase RNGTT and the cap methyltransferase RNMT dock on this phosphorylated tail, which also stimulates guanylyltransferase activity, coupling capping to elongation alongside the DSIF subunit SUPT5H. The arrangement restricts cap addition to polymerase II products and links promoter clearance to co-transcriptional RNA processing.

Newly initiated RNA polymerase II transcripts are capped while still being made, and this step links the polymerase to the capping enzymes during transcription of the integrated HIV provirus. Capping protects the nascent 5' end from exonucleases and marks the transcript for export and translation, so viral mRNAs depend on it as host mRNAs do. The mechanism runs through the heptapeptide repeats of the largest polymerase subunit: the TFIIH-associated kinase CDK7, with its cyclin H and MNAT1 partners, phosphorylates serine 5 of the C-terminal domain near the promoter, and the phosphorylated tail is bound directly by the guanylyltransferase and the cap methyltransferase, which stimulates guanylyl transfer. The elongation factor SPT5 contributes to coupling capping with early elongation. This phosphorylation mark is the timing signal that restricts capping to polymerase II products.

The integrated HIV-1 provirus is transcribed by the host's own RNA polymerase II machinery, and initiation at the viral LTR promoter is the step that converts a silent provirus into a productive infection. Host general factors assemble on the TATA box: TBP and its associated factors recognise the promoter, TFIIB positions the start site, TFIIF delivers polymerase, and TFIIE recruits TFIIH, whose ERCC3 helicase melts the duplex to form the open complex while the CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain. Formation of the first phosphodiester bond marks initiation and triggers TFIIB release, though the early complex is unstable and often releases short abortive transcripts before committing to elongation. Because this stage is entirely host-encoded and precedes Tat-dependent elongation, it sets the basal level of viral gene expression that determines latency versus active replication.

Transcription of the integrated HIV-1 provirus depends on host RNA polymerase II, and promoter escape is the step at which the enzyme, having made its first phosphodiester bonds at the viral LTR, breaks its grip on the promoter and commits to productive elongation. Until this transition succeeds, the polymerase abortively initiates and releases short transcripts, so escape sets how much viral RNA is made and contributes to the difference between latent and actively replicating infection. The machinery is the general initiation apparatus: TBP with its TAF partners in TFIID, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE and TFIIF, the twelve-subunit polymerase core, and TFIIH, whose helicase subunits ERCC2 and ERCC3 open and translocate the DNA while the CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain. The same steps drive escape at cellular promoters, and TFIIH doubles as a nucleotide excision repair factor.

Productive transcription of the integrated HIV-1 provirus depends on escape from a promoter-proximal pause, and this pathway covers the elongation step that the viral Tat protein commandeers. Without Tat, RNA polymerase II initiates normally at the viral LTR but disengages early, yielding short abortive transcripts and latent, non-productive infection; Tat binding to the nascent TAR RNA recruits the positive transcription elongation factor complex of CDK9 and cyclin T1, whose kinase activity phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the DSIF subunits SPT4 and SPT5, converting the paused complex into a processive one and relieving negative elongation factor restraint. The set also includes the TFIIH kinase module, general elongation factors such as ELL and the elongin components, the FACT histone chaperone for chromatin passage, and cap-binding proteins, so host elongation machinery is what the virus subverts. This step is a target for latency-reversal and antiviral strategies.

Transcription of the HIV genome is the step at which an integrated HIV-1 provirus becomes a productive infection: the virus has no polymerase of its own for this job and borrows the host RNA polymerase II machinery to copy its genome into mRNAs and into the RNA packaged by new virions. Blocking or failing to activate it is what distinguishes latent, therapy-resistant reservoirs from replicating virus. Initiation depends on cellular factors recruited to the 5' LTR, with TBP and the TAF-containing general machinery, TFIIH and its CDK7 kinase positioning polymerase at the promoter. The rate-limiting control is elongation: NELF and DSIF pause the polymerase shortly after initiation, and the viral Tat protein binds the nascent TAR stem-loop to deliver P-TEFb (CCNT1-CDK9), which phosphorylates SPT5 and the polymerase tail to license processive elongation, capping, and co-transcriptional splicing.

An integrated HIV-1 provirus is transcribed by the host's own RNA polymerase II machinery, so viral gene expression is essentially a hijacking of cellular transcription, and the balance between silence and activity at the viral promoter determines whether an infected cell stays latent or produces virus. Sequences in the 5' long terminal repeat recruit TBP and the TAF-containing general factors, TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and the TFIIH helicase-kinase module, which positions polymerase and phosphorylates its C-terminal domain. Polymerase then pauses just downstream, held by NELF and DSIF; escape into productive elongation requires the viral Tat protein binding the nascent TAR stem-loop and recruiting P-TEFb (CDK9 with cyclin T1). Capping enzymes, the nuclear cap-binding complex, elongin and ELL elongation factors, and the FACT histone chaperone complete the cycle, yielding transcripts that serve as mRNA and as packaged genomic RNA.

HIV-1 depends on a single viral protein to convert a stalled polymerase at its promoter into a processive one, and this step — assembly of the Tat-containing elongation complex — is what allows full-length viral transcripts to be made rather than short abortive ones. Without it the provirus stays latent, which is why this transition is central both to viral replication and to latency-reversal strategies. Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent transcript and recruits P-TEFb, the cyclin T1–CDK9 kinase, which phosphorylates the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain together with the pausing factors DSIF (SUPT4H1/SUPT5H) and NELF, releasing the paused enzyme. The complex also carries general factors TFIIF and TFIIH, elongin and ELL elongation activities, TFIIS, the FACT histone chaperone, and cap-binding proteins, mirroring normal host promoter-proximal pause release hijacked for viral gene expression.

HIV-1 transcription from the integrated provirus depends on the viral Tat protein converting a stalled polymerase into a processive one, and this step describes how RNA polymerase II pauses by backtracking a few nucleotides on the viral template and then resumes elongation. Without it the virus makes only short abortive transcripts, which is the molecular basis of proviral latency and of the reservoir that resists antiretroviral therapy. Tat recruits the P-TEFb kinase pair, cyclin T1 with CDK9, which phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the DSIF subunits SPT4 and SPT5, relieving repression imposed by the NELF complex. Elongation factors including ELL and the elongin ELOA-ELOB-ELOC module, together with TFIIF and TFIIS, stimulate escape from the backtracked state, while the FACT histone chaperone allows passage through chromatin. The same machinery governs promoter-proximal pausing at host genes.

Without the viral Tat protein, RNA polymerase II that initiates at the HIV-1 promoter clears the start site but cannot continue, so the provirus yields only short, abortive transcripts instead of full-length viral RNA. This block is the molecular basis of proviral latency: integrated HIV-1 stays transcriptionally silent and invisible to immune clearance until Tat accumulates and rescues elongation. The arrest uses the same brakes that pause polymerase on host genes early in elongation, namely the DSIF heterodimer of SUPT4H1 and SUPT5H together with the four-subunit NELF complex, acting on the twelve-subunit polymerase core with general factor TFIIF and the cap-binding proteins NCBP1 and NCBP2 on the nascent 5' end. Phosphatase and kinase activity on the polymerase C-terminal domain, including CTDP1, normally sets the balance, but here relief of pausing requires the viral transactivator, making Tat the switch between latency and productive replication.

HIV transcription depends on the viral Tat protein converting a stalled polymerase at the integrated provirus into a processive one, and this pathway covers the arrest step and its rescue. RNA polymerase II transcribing the viral long terminal repeat can backslide by roughly seven to fourteen nucleotides into an arrested state from which it cannot resume; TFIIS (TCEA1) binds the enzyme and stimulates intrinsic cleavage of the nascent transcript so that a new 3' end is aligned with the active site and elongation restarts. The surrounding machinery is the standard elongation apparatus that Tat hijacks: the NELF complex and DSIF (SUPT4H1/SUPT5H) impose pausing, P-TEFb (CDK9 with cyclin T1) relieves it by phosphorylation, and elongin, ELL and the FACT histone chaperone support movement through chromatin. Efficient viral gene expression, and hence exit from latency, rests on this cycle.

Tat-mediated elongation of the HIV-1 transcript explains how HIV-1 converts a stalled polymerase at its own promoter into a productive one, and it is the step that determines whether an integrated provirus stays latent or produces virus. RNA polymerase II can initiate at the viral LTR without help, but DSIF and NELF arrest it after a few dozen nucleotides, yielding only abortive short transcripts. The viral transactivator Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent leader RNA and tethers P-TEFb (cyclin T1 with CDK9), which hyperphosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and the SPT5 and RD subunits of the pausing factors, releasing NELF from TAR and licensing processive elongation together with elongin, ELL, FACT and capping factors. Because this switch controls proviral output, it is the mechanistic basis of latency reversal strategies and of CDK9-directed antiviral approaches.

HIV-1 cannot make full-length viral RNA on its own: polymerases that initiate at the proviral promoter stall soon after and release short abortive transcripts, so the virus depends on its Tat transactivator to convert them into processive elongation complexes. This step sets the switch between latency and productive replication, and blocking it is the rationale behind CDK9-directed antiviral strategies. Tat binds the TAR stem-loop in the nascent leader RNA and tethers the P-TEFb kinase, cyclin T1 with CDK9, to the paused polymerase. CDK9 hyperphosphorylates the RNA polymerase II carboxy-terminal domain and also modifies the SPT5 subunit of DSIF and the RD subunit of NELF, relieving their negative effect on elongation. The remaining machinery here is the host's own: the general initiation and TFIIH kinase components, elongation factors such as ELL and the elongin complex, FACT histone chaperones, and the nuclear cap-binding proteins.

Transcription of the integrated HIV provirus depends on RNA polymerase II reading through the viral long terminal repeat, and the polymerase frequently stalls or backslides on the template rather than moving steadily forward. Elongation arrest and its recovery determine whether viral transcripts are completed or abandoned, which in turn sets the balance between latent infection and productive replication. Negative elongation factor subunits together with the DSIF components SUPT4H1 and SUPT5H hold the polymerase in a paused state near the promoter; the CDK9 cyclin T kinase releases it by phosphorylating the polymerase C-terminal domain and the pausing factors, a step the viral Tat protein commandeers. When the enzyme backslides irreversibly, TCEA1 (TFIIS) rescues it by stimulating cleavage of the nascent transcript to regenerate an aligned 3' end, while elongin and FACT components help the polymerase traverse chromatin.

Transcription of the integrated HIV-1 provirus by host RNA polymerase II is not continuous: the enzyme backtracks a few nucleotides and stalls shortly after initiation, and viral gene expression depends on whether that stall is resolved. This pausing and recovery step during HIV elongation is the rate-limiting control point that separates latent infection from productive replication, which is why it is a target for strategies aiming either to silence or to flush out the viral reservoir. The negative elongation factor complex together with DSIF (SPT4/SPT5) imposes the pause, while the positive transcription elongation factor kinase CDK9 with its cyclin T partner phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain and DSIF to release it. Elongin and ELL factors suppress transient stalling, TFIIS-family TCEA1 rescues backtracked polymerase, and the FACT histone chaperone (SSRP1, SUPT16H) lets the enzyme traverse chromatin.

Nef Mediated CD4 Down-regulation describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Nef strips its own entry receptor from the surface of an infected cell. Removing CD4 prevents newly made Env from being captured by receptor on the producer cell, so virions are released efficiently and remain infectious, and it simultaneously blunts helper T cell signalling and superinfection. CD4 carries a dileucine-based internalization signal that is normally masked by bound Lck; Nef displaces the kinase, exposes the motif, and links CD4 to the AP-2 clathrin adaptor complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits together with an ARF1- and V-ATPase-associated step drive endocytosis. Internalized receptor is then routed away from recycling toward lysosomal degradation, with COPI coatomer implicated in the final sorting. The pathway is a textbook case of a viral protein hijacking clathrin-mediated endocytosis and receptor trafficking for immune evasion.

HIV-1 Nef strips CD4 from the surface of infected cells, and this down-regulation serves the virus: without CD4 on the plasma membrane the receptor cannot engage newly made Env on budding particles, so virions are released more efficiently and are more infectious, and the cell is also protected from superinfection. CD4 carries its own internalization signal in its cytoplasmic tail, but that signal is masked while the tail is bound by the Src-family kinase Lck; Nef displaces this interaction and links CD4 to the clathrin adaptor AP-2 complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits drive endocytosis. Internalized CD4 is then routed onward, with ARF1-dependent coat recruitment and vacuolar ATPase-dependent acidification contributing to delivery into the lysosomal degradation route. The same trafficking machinery normally handles receptor turnover, and immune evasion here is a hijacking of it.

This is a mechanistic account of how uncoupling proteins dissipate the mitochondrial proton gradient, the basis of non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue. Rather than conducting protons directly, the carrier is proposed to work through fatty acid cycling: a protonated long-chain fatty acid flips across the inner membrane and releases its proton into the matrix, and UCP1 then transports the resulting fatty acid anion back to the cytosolic face, so that repeated rounds amount to net proton leak. The consequence is that substrate oxidation produces heat instead of ATP, a capacity recruited on cold exposure and of interest for energy balance and obesity. The related carriers UCP2 and UCP3, together with the brain and kidney homologues of this mitochondrial carrier family, are expressed far more widely and are linked to control of reactive oxygen species and fatty acid handling rather than thermogenesis proper.

Trafficking and processing of endosomal TLR governs how the nucleic acid-sensing Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 reach the compartment where they can work, and why they respond to viral and bacterial DNA and RNA rather than to the cell's own. Restricting these receptors to acidified endolysosomes, and requiring an irreversible activation step there, is the main safeguard against autoreactive interferon responses; loss of that control underlies lupus-like autoimmunity, while loss of the trafficking machinery itself causes susceptibility to herpes encephalitis and pyogenic infection. Newly made receptors are held in the endoplasmic reticulum with the chaperones gp96 and CNPY3, then escorted outward by the multipass membrane protein UNC93B1. In the endolysosome, cathepsins and asparagine endopeptidase cleave the TLR7 and TLR9 ectodomains, generating the fragment competent to bind ligand and signal to the cytosol.

Nucleic-acid-sensing Toll-like receptors TLR3, TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 detect viral and bacterial RNA and DNA, but only after they have been delivered to acidified endolysosomes and, in some cases, trimmed by proteases. This trafficking and processing step is what keeps innate immune sensing pointed at pathogens rather than at the cell's own DNA and RNA: compartment restriction plus a requirement for proteolytic maturation means self nucleic acids released outside endosomes go unseen, and loss of that discipline contributes to lupus-like interferon-driven autoimmunity. Newly made receptors fold in the endoplasmic reticulum with the chaperones HSP90B1 and CNPY3, and UNC93B1 escorts them onward; in the endolysosome, cysteine cathepsins such as CTSB, CTSL and CTSS together with asparagine endopeptidase cleave the TLR7 and TLR9 ectodomains to yield signalling-competent receptors. Mutations in UNC93B1 abolish endosomal TLR responses and predispose to herpes encephalitis.

Unmethylated CpG DNA is a signature of bacteria and viruses rather than of host chromatin, and the TLR9 cascade is how innate immune cells read it. Unlike surface receptors, TLR9 works from endosomes and lysosomes, so delivery of internalised DNA to that compartment — supported by endosomal trafficking and the transporter SLC15A4 with its adaptor TASL — is part of the recognition step itself. Engaged receptor recruits MyD88 and the IRAK kinases, which act through TRAF6 and ubiquitin conjugation to activate the TAK1–IKK axis and the p38, JNK and ERK arms, driving NF-κB, AP-1, CREB and IRF7 to produce inflammatory cytokines and type I interferon. Phosphatases, pellino ligases, IκB proteins and deubiquitinases restrain the output. Excess signalling against self DNA contributes to lupus and other interferon-driven autoimmunity, while the same route is exploited therapeutically by CpG adjuvants.

Toll Like Receptor 10 (TLR10) Cascade describes innate immune signalling through one of the least understood Toll-like receptors, expressed mainly on B cells and dendritic cells as a heavily N-glycosylated surface protein that homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2. Its ligands remain undefined, but engagement recruits the MyD88 adaptor and the shared downstream module used by most TLRs: IRAK kinases, Pellino ubiquitin ligases, TRAF6-directed polyubiquitin chains, and the TAK1-TAB complex, which branches into IKK-driven degradation of IkB inhibitors to release NF-kB, and into the p38, JNK and ERK cascades that activate AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. The output is transcription of inflammatory cytokines and immune activation genes, tuned by DUSP phosphatases, PP2A and IkB-related brakes. Because TLR10 can restrain responses from other TLRs, it contributes to setting the threshold and resolution of inflammation rather than only amplifying it.

TLR10 is an innate immune receptor of the Toll-like family expressed in a restricted way, mainly on B cells and dendritic cells, whose ligands remain poorly defined; it homodimerizes and can pair with TLR1 and TLR2, and signals through the MyD88 adaptor. The downstream cascade described here is the shared MyD88-dependent route that converts receptor engagement into inflammatory gene expression: IRAK4, IRAK1/2 and Pellino ligases assemble with TRAF6 and the TAK1-TAB complex, K63-linked ubiquitin chains built by UBE2N/UBE2V1 relay the signal, and the IKK complex frees NF-kB from IkB while parallel MAP kinase branches activate p38, JNK, ERK and the AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors. DUSP phosphatases, PP2A subunits and deubiquitinases restrain the output. The result is cytokine production and antigen-presenting cell activation; TLR10 itself is generally regarded as a dampener of inflammatory TLR responses.

Double-stranded RNA appearing inside endosomes is a signature of viral replication, and the TLR3 cascade is how cells read that signal and mount an antiviral and inflammatory response. Unlike most Toll-like receptors, TLR3 does not use MyD88; it signals through the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), which recruits RIP1 and TRAF3/TRAF6 and branches into two outputs. One branch drives TBK1 and IKK-epsilon to phosphorylate IRF3 and IRF7, inducing type I interferons; the other engages the TAK1–TAB complex and the IKK trimer to degrade IkappaB and release NF-kappaB, with parallel activation of p38, JNK and ERK toward AP-1 and MEF2 target genes. Ubiquitin conjugation and removal, phosphatases and negative regulators such as SARM1 and A20-binding partners set the amplitude and shut the response down. This arm of innate immunity protects against viral infection, and its dysregulation contributes to susceptibility to herpes encephalitis and to interferon-driven autoinflammation.

Toll Like Receptor 5 (TLR5) Cascade is the innate immune response to bacterial flagellin, the structural protein of flagella, and it lets gut epithelium, macrophages and dendritic cells detect motile bacteria that have breached the mucosal barrier. Because TLR5 sits only on the basolateral face of intestinal epithelial cells, the response is triggered by invading pathogens rather than by luminal commensals, and its loss shifts susceptibility to enteric infection and mucosal inflammation. Ligand binding recruits MyD88 and the IRAK1/IRAK4 kinases, with Pellino proteins and TRAF6-driven ubiquitin chains activating the TAK1 complex; this branches into IKK-mediated degradation of IkB and NF-kB nuclear entry, and into the p38, JNK and ERK modules that turn on AP-1, CREB, ELK1 and MEF2 to drive cytokine and chemokine transcription. Phosphatases, deubiquitinases and IkB-like inhibitors damp the output, keeping antibacterial signalling self-limiting.

TLR5 is the innate immune sensor for bacterial flagellin, the conserved building block of flagella, and its signalling cascade lets epithelium and myeloid cells raise an inflammatory alarm when motile bacteria breach a barrier. Because TLR5 sits on the basolateral face of intestinal epithelial cells, the response is triggered by invading pathogens rather than by luminal commensals, and variation in this route affects susceptibility to enteric infection and inflammatory bowel disease. Ligand binding recruits MYD88 and the IRAK kinases, which act through TRAF6-directed ubiquitin chains and the TAK1-TAB complex to split into two outputs: IKK-mediated phosphorylation and degradation of IkB, freeing NF-kB, and MAP kinase modules that drive JNK, p38 and ERK to activate AP-1, CREB and ELK1. Phosphatases, deubiquitinases and Pellino ligases shape the amplitude, keeping cytokine output proportionate and self-limiting.

Innate immune cells detect bacteria by their surface molecules, and the TLR1:TLR2 heterodimer is the receptor pair that senses triacylated lipopeptides from mycobacteria and Neisserial PorB, among other microbial products. Engagement on monocytes and macrophages licenses pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion and, in some settings, apoptosis, making this cascade an early determinant of whether an infection is contained or provokes damaging inflammation. Ligand binding recruits MYD88 and TIRAP to the receptor's TIR domains, assembling an IRAK1/IRAK4 complex that activates TRAF6 and non-degradative ubiquitin chains; the TAK1-TAB module then drives the IKK complex to release NF-kB from its IkB inhibitors, and in parallel activates JNK, p38 and ERK to switch on AP-1, CREB and MEF2 target genes. Negative regulators including IRAK3, SIGIRR, SOCS1 and phosphatases of the DUSP and PP2A families restrain the output, and endogenous ligands such as S100 proteins and HMGB1 can drive sterile inflammation through the same route.

Single-stranded RNA in the endosome is read as evidence of viral infection, and the TLR7/8 cascade is how that signal becomes an interferon and cytokine response. TLR7 acts mainly in plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells, TLR8 in monocytes, macrophages and myeloid dendritic cells, sensing GU-rich viral RNA from influenza, HIV-1 and coronaviruses; loss-of-function TLR7 variants blunt type I interferon induction and predispose to severe viral disease. Engaged receptors recruit MyD88 with IRAK4, IRAK1 and TRAF6, whose ubiquitin-dependent signalling activates the TAK1-IKK axis to release NF-kB and drives MAP kinase branches through p38, JNK and ERK toward AP-1 and CREB target genes, while IRF7 and IRF5 direct interferon transcription. Phosphatases, deubiquitinases and negative regulators such as PPP2, DUSPs, USP18 and N4BP1 restrain the output, since unchecked nucleic-acid sensing drives autoimmune inflammation. Imidazoquinolines such as imiquimod exploit this route therapeutically.

Innate immune cells detect Gram-positive bacteria and mycobacterial diacylated lipopeptides through a TLR2 heterodimer with TLR6, and this recognition event triggers the inflammatory response that contains such infections. Ligand binding, assisted by CD14 and CD36, recruits MyD88 and the IRAK kinases, which activate TRAF6-dependent polyubiquitination and the TAK1 complex. From there the signal splits: IKK subunits phosphorylate IκB proteins to free NF-κB for nuclear entry, while MAP kinase modules drive p38, JNK and ERK toward AP-1, CREB and MEF2 target genes encoding cytokines and antimicrobial effectors. Because unrestrained output is damaging, the cascade carries its own brakes, including the decoy kinase IRAK3, the inhibitory receptor SIGIRR, SOCS1, phosphatases and ubiquitin editing. Loss of signalling leaves hosts susceptible to pyogenic infection; excess contributes to sepsis and chronic inflammation, sustained partly by endogenous S100 and HMGB1 alarmins.

Innate immunity is the body's inborn, non-specific defence: it detects conserved microbial features and tissue damage within minutes and acts without prior exposure or clonal selection, providing the first barrier against infection and the signals that later recruit adaptive responses. The genes here span its main arms. Pattern-recognition receptors including Toll-like receptors, cytosolic NOD proteins, RIG-I-like helicases and the DNA sensor cGAS with STING1 converge through adaptors such as MYD88, TICAM1 and MAVS on IRAK/TRAF-driven NF-kB and IRF activation, yielding inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons. Inflammasome components including NLRP3, PYCARD and CASP1 mature IL1B and IL18 and drive gasdermin-dependent pyroptosis. Complement cascades, ficolins, collectins and pentraxins opsonise targets, while neutrophil granule contents - defensins, cathepsins, myeloperoxidase, lactoferrin and the NADPH oxidase subunits - support phagocytosis and microbial killing. Fc and lectin receptors, integrins and actin-regulatory machinery execute engulfment and degranulation; excess or deficient output gives autoinflammation or susceptibility to infection.

Influenza infection describes the full cycle by which an orthomyxovirus with a segmented, negative-sense RNA genome takes over a human cell, the biology behind seasonal epidemics and the pandemics that have killed on the scale of 1918. Because influenza transcribes and replicates its genome in the nucleus, the host contribution is dominated by nuclear transport and gene expression machinery: importin alpha/beta receptors, RAN and exportin-1, and essentially the whole nuclear pore complex, which ferry the viral ribonucleoprotein in and newly assembled genomes out. Host RNA polymerase II and cleavage/polyadenylation factors are hijacked for cap-snatching, ribosomal proteins are commandeered for viral protein synthesis, and chaperones such as calnexin, calreticulin and HSP90 fold viral glycoproteins. Countermeasures also appear here, including the double-stranded RNA sensor kinase PKR and ISG15, which the virus in turn antagonises.

This is the whole of human immune defence at its broadest scope, spanning the rapid innate response that meets a new pathogen within hours and the slower, antigen-specific adaptive response that clears it and remembers it. Innate components here include pattern-recognition receptors of the Toll-like, NOD-like, RIG-I-like and C-type lectin families feeding through adaptors such as MYD88, MAVS and STING1 into NF-kB and interferon regulatory factors; complement cascades; inflammasome assembly and caspase-1-driven IL-1 maturation; and the antimicrobial peptides, defensins, proteases and NADPH-oxidase machinery of neutrophil granules and phagosomes. Adaptive arms cover antigen processing and presentation on MHC class I and II, T and B cell receptor signalling through LCK, ZAP70, SYK and BTK, immunoglobulin gene segments and class-switch recombination, costimulation and checkpoint receptors, and the cytokine-JAK-STAT networks that shape effector differentiation. Failure produces immunodeficiency, autoinflammation or autoimmunity.

Virus Assembly and Release is the final stage of the influenza replication cycle, in which newly made viral components converge at the apical plasma membrane of polarized airway epithelial cells and bud off as infectious particles. The directionality of this step matters clinically: apical release sends progeny virions into the airway lumen for transmission and spread along the respiratory tract, whereas basolateral budding used by other enveloped viruses favours systemic dissemination, so budding polarity helps set tissue tropism and pathogenesis. Envelope glycoproteins accumulate at the same polar surface from which particles emerge, effectively marking the maturation site. Before reaching it, hemagglutinin and neuraminidase must be folded and quality-controlled in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the lectin chaperones calreticulin and calnexin perform this glycoprotein-specific surveillance, linking host secretory-pathway folding machinery to the production of functional virions.

Influenza virions are built and released at the apical surface of polarized airway epithelial cells, and the site of budding helps set tissue tropism and pathogenesis: envelope glycoproteins accumulate at the same polar membrane from which particles pinch off, so the virus emerges into the airway lumen rather than into underlying tissue. Before that can happen, the viral membrane proteins must be folded and glycosylated correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin are the quality-control step that does it, binding monoglucosylated N-glycans on nascent glycoproteins and retaining them until they attain a transport-competent conformation. The host secretory pathway is therefore co-opted for assembly and release, with chaperone-assisted maturation determining how much functional hemagglutinin and neuraminidase reach the plasma membrane and thus the infectivity of progeny virions.

Influenza enters a cell by endocytosis, but the genome only becomes available for replication once the virion is taken apart inside the endosome, and this fusion and uncoating step is the point at which infection is either established or blocked. Endosomal acidification triggers an irreversible conformational change in the viral hemagglutinin, exposing the HA2 fusion peptide, which inserts into the endosomal membrane; several HA trimers acting together pull the two bilayers into a fusion pore. In parallel, the viral M2 proton channel lets H+ into the virion interior, loosening M1 matrix interactions so that the ribonucleoprotein complexes are freed rather than remaining tethered. The released ribonucleoproteins pass into the cytosol and are imported to the nucleus for transcription. Whether fusion occurs in early or late endosomes depends on the pH threshold of the particular HA, and blocking the M2 channel with amantadine or rimantadine stalls uncoating.

Influenza virus replicates its genome in the nucleus, and the incoming viral ribonucleoproteins must be actively delivered there before any viral RNA synthesis can begin. Each of the eight genome segments is coated by nucleoprotein and capped by the polymerase subunits, forming a particle far too large to diffuse through the nuclear envelope; import therefore depends entirely on host machinery. Nuclear localization signals on the viral proteins are read by importin alpha and importin beta, which dock the cargo at the nuclear pore complex and thread it through the central channel, with directionality set by the Ran GTPase gradient. The host contribution here is the pore itself: the structural Y-complex scaffold, the transmembrane anchors, the FG-repeat nucleoporins that form the permeability barrier, and basket and cytoplasmic filament components such as TPR and RANBP2. This step makes nucleocytoplasmic transport a determinant of influenza infectivity and a candidate point of antiviral intervention.

Influenza Viral RNA Transcription and Replication describes how influenza A virus copies its segmented negative-strand genome inside the host cell nucleus, the step that commits an infected cell to producing progeny virions and the target of polymerase inhibitors such as baloxavir. The viral polymerase subunits and nucleoprotein, imported through the nuclear pore, use genomic RNA as template both for capped, polyadenylated messenger RNAs and for full-length complementary RNA that seeds new genome copies; the balance shifts toward genome replication and export of ribonucleoprotein complexes late in infection. Because the virus cannot make its own caps or translate its own mRNAs, the pathway is built almost entirely from hijacked host machinery: RNA polymerase II and its associated factors provide capped primers, importins and the full nuclear pore complex handle traffic in and out of the nucleus, and the cytoplasmic ribosome translates the resulting transcripts.

Influenza A is a negative-strand RNA virus that, unusually, replicates in the host nucleus, and this pathway covers the synthesis of viral mRNA and the vRNA/cRNA replication intermediates that sustain infection. Because the virus encodes only a polymerase and nucleoprotein, it must borrow the cell wholesale: host RNA polymerase II supplies the capped nascent transcripts whose 5' ends are snatched to prime viral mRNA, and its largest subunit is degraded as a consequence, shutting down host transcription. Import of polymerase subunits and nucleoprotein and export of assembled ribonucleoproteins run through the nuclear pore complex and karyopherin-mediated transport, which is why nucleoporins and importins figure here, while the cytoplasmic ribosome translates the resulting viral messages. Chaperones such as HSP90 assist polymerase assembly. These dependencies are the basis of host-directed antiviral strategies and of interferon-driven restriction of viral gene expression.

Influenza replicates its genome in the host nucleus, so newly made viral ribonucleoproteins — vRNA wrapped in NP trimers with the polymerase subunits — must be exported to the cytoplasm before virions can assemble at the plasma membrane; this step sets the pace of the infectious cycle and is a point at which host defences and antivirals can intervene. The complexes are far too large to leak out, so the virus borrows the cell's own export route: matrix protein M1 bridges the RNP to NEP/NS2, which docks onto the exportin CRM1 (XPO1) and its RanGTP gradient. Passage then proceeds through the nuclear pore complex, represented here by its scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporins together with RANBP2, TPR, NUP98 and NUP153. The pathway is a clear case of a virus subverting nucleocytoplasmic transport rather than encoding its own.

Influenza virions attach to sialylated receptors at the cell surface but cannot cross the plasma membrane directly; entry into the host cell requires endocytic uptake, which delivers the particle to an acidified endosome where low pH triggers hemagglutinin-mediated fusion and release of the viral genome. This step sets the host range and tropism of the virus at the level of the cell it can productively infect, and it is the point at which entry inhibitors and endosomal acidification blockers act. Several routes have been described, including caveolar uptake, macropinocytosis and clathrin-independent internalization, but the dominant path is through clathrin-coated pits, represented here by the clathrin heavy and light chains that polymerize into the coat lattice. The pathway is therefore a virus co-opting ordinary receptor-mediated endocytosis, the same machinery cells use for nutrient and receptor internalization.

Influenza NS1 is the virus's main countermeasure against the host antiviral response, and this describes how it bends host machinery to that purpose. Two host activities are hit hardest: nuclear export of cellular mRNA and the interferon-induced defences that would otherwise shut down viral protein synthesis. Through its effector domain NS1 engages the 30 kDa subunit of the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor and nuclear poly(A)-binding protein, blocking 3' end processing so host transcripts are neither matured nor exported; the nucleoporins, the NUP62 and NUP107-160 subcomplexes, RAE1 and NUP98 among them, together with importin alpha and beta carriers, define the transport route that is both exploited for NS1 import and obstructed for host mRNA. The dsRNA-binding domain sequesters viral replication intermediates from PKR and the ISG15 and GBP1 arms of interferon signalling, tipping the balance toward productive infection.

Influenza A infection kills host cells partly by turning the cell's own death machinery against it, and this virus-induced apoptosis shapes both viral spread and the tissue damage seen in severe influenza. Two routes are captured here. Viral surface and matrix proteins, including neuraminidase and the M1 and M2 proteins, convert latent host TGF-beta1 to its active form, and that activated cytokine drives pro-apoptotic signalling in infected epithelium while also modulating the local immune response. Separately, the small accessory protein PB1-F2 targets mitochondria and engages the adenine nucleotide translocator encoded by SLC25A6, destabilising the inner membrane and promoting cytochrome c release through the intrinsic death pathway. Apoptosis in this setting is double-edged: it limits replication in some cells yet contributes to epithelial destruction and the inflammatory pathology of influenza pneumonia.

Influenza enters a cell by endocytosis, but its genome only reaches the cytosol if the viral envelope merges with the endosomal membrane, and that fusion step is the point of no return in infection. Acidification of the maturing endosome protonates hemagglutinin, triggering an irreversible refolding that releases the hydrophobic fusion peptide of the HA2 subunit and drives it into the endosomal bilayer. HA2 is then anchored in two membranes at once, its transmembrane segment in the viral envelope and its fusion peptide in the host membrane; collapse of the extended intermediate pulls the two leaflets together, and several hemagglutinin trimers acting in concert open a pore through which the viral ribonucleoprotein passes. This pH-triggered conformational switch explains why endosomal acidification inhibitors and stalk-directed antibodies block infection, and it is the archetype for class I viral fusion machinery generally.

The final step of influenza virus budding, in which newly formed particles are cut free from the cell that made them. Hemagglutinin on the virion surface binds sialic acid-terminated glycans on the plasma membrane, so a budded particle whose envelope has already pinched off remains tethered to its host cell; the viral neuraminidase cleaves those terminal sialic acids and frees it. The same enzymatic activity strips sialic acid from the virion's own glycoproteins, preventing progeny particles from clumping together and keeping them infectious as they spread to new cells. Because release limits how much infectious virus leaves an infected cell, this reaction sets the pace of viral dissemination within the airway and is the target of neuraminidase-inhibiting antivirals such as oseltamivir and zanamivir, drugs whose efficacy is eroded by resistance mutations in the enzyme.

Budding is the final step of influenza virus assembly, the point at which a newly built particle pinches off from the plasma membrane of an infected cell and becomes able to spread to a new host cell. Without it, viral components accumulate at the cell surface but no infectious progeny are released, which is why this step is a target for antiviral strategies. Accumulation of the matrix protein M1 beneath the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane is thought to initiate bud formation, which proceeds until the ribonucleoprotein core is fully enveloped; scission then requires fusion of the membrane at the neck of the bud. Particle shape, spherical or filamentous, maps genetically to the M segment, while host determinants such as epithelial polarity and the actin cytoskeleton shape filamentous virions, making release a joint viral-host process.

An influenza virion is only fully infectious if it carries one copy of each of the eight negative-sense genome segments, so the step that loads viral ribonucleoproteins into a budding particle sets the ratio of infectious to defective virus and constrains how readily segments from different strains reassort. Two explanations compete. Under random incorporation, every vRNP has an equal chance of capture, and packaging more than eight — around a dozen — yields the roughly ten percent fully infectious fraction seen experimentally. Under selective incorporation, coding-region sequences at the 5' and 3' ends of each segment act as packaging signals, reported for all segments except the one encoding the matrix and ion channel proteins, directing assembly through specific RNA–RNA and protein–RNA contacts. Electron micrographs showing eight discrete rod-like cores in cross-section favour a selective, ordered arrangement within the assembling envelope.

Influenza A virus does not merely compete with its host for resources; its NS1 protein actively dismantles host gene expression, and the inhibition of host mRNA processing and RNA silencing is one arm of that attack. By binding the 30 kDa subunit of the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor and the nuclear poly(A)-binding protein, NS1 blocks 3' end cleavage and poly(A) tail elongation of cellular pre-mRNAs, so transcripts remain unprocessed and trapped in the nucleus. Splicing is impaired as well. The consequence is a general shutdown of host protein synthesis, including the interferon and antiviral effector messages that would otherwise limit infection, while viral mRNAs made by the viral polymerase bypass the blockade. NS1 additionally sequesters double-stranded RNA, suppressing RNA-based silencing and sensing. This host shutoff contributes to influenza virulence.

Influenza virus makes its envelope proteins in the host secretory pathway, and assembly of viral components at the budding site is the step where hemagglutinin, neuraminidase and the M2 ion channel converge on the apical plasma membrane so that infectious particles can form. Newly made HA and NA are translated on membrane-bound ribosomes and must be folded and glycosylated correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum before HA can trimerize; the lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin represented here perform that quality control, retaining incompletely folded glycoproteins and permitting only properly assembled forms to move on. Golgi transit adds palmitoylation and proteolytic maturation of HA into its HA1 and HA2 subunits, after which transmembrane-domain sorting signals direct the proteins to cholesterol- and sphingolipid-rich raft microdomains from which budding preferentially occurs. Host chaperone capacity is therefore a determinant of virion production.

Influenza virus makes its mRNAs in the host nucleus, and this transcription programme is how the virus converts its segmented negative-strand genome into protein-coding messages that the cell's own ribosomes will translate. Because the viral polymerase cannot cap its own transcripts, it steals methylated caps from nascent host mRNAs: the PB2 subunit binds the cap while PB1 cleaves the host message a short distance downstream, and the resulting fragment primes viral RNA synthesis. Poly(A) tails are added not by host cleavage machinery but by polymerase stuttering on a uridine tract near the template's 5' end, keeping viral messages translatable even when host polyadenylation is shut off. Host RNA polymerase II supplies the capped primers, and the nuclear pore complex, represented here by a large set of nucleoporins and their scaffolds, governs the nuclear import and export steps on which the whole cycle depends.

Influenza virus replicates its genome in the host nucleus, and before new virions can form, each negative-sense genomic RNA segment must be packaged with nucleoprotein and matrix protein M1 into a ribonucleoprotein complex competent for export to the cytoplasm. Assembly of viral RNP complexes in the nucleus is therefore the step that converts newly synthesised genome copies into exportable, packageable cargo, and it is a point at which the host can interfere. Such complexes are found throughout the nucleoplasm and also at the nuclear periphery in association with the nuclear matrix and chromatin, particularly those containing M1. The inducible chaperone HSPA1A represents the host contribution here: stress-induced Hsp70 binds M1 and impedes productive vRNP formation and nuclear egress, restraining the output of infectious particles and linking cellular stress responses to the efficiency of viral replication.

NEP/NS2 Interacts with the Cellular Export Machinery describes how influenza virus gets its newly replicated genome out of the host nucleus, the step that allows progeny ribonucleoproteins to reach the plasma membrane and be packaged into virions. Influenza replicates its RNA in the nucleus, so nuclear egress is a hard requirement for the viral life cycle and a point at which the virus is entirely dependent on host machinery. The viral nuclear export protein acts as an adaptor, bridging the matrix protein M1 coating the ribonucleoprotein to the exportin XPO1/CRM1, which in turn engages RanGTP and the nucleoporins of the nuclear pore complex. The gene complement is essentially the pore itself — the Y-complex scaffold, the FG-repeat channel nucleoporins, the cytoplasmic filaments and basket, plus RAN and RAE1 — illustrating viral subversion of normal receptor-mediated nucleocytoplasmic transport.

Influenza virus replicates its genome in the host nucleus, so newly made viral ribonucleoprotein complexes must be exported to the cytoplasm before virions can assemble at the plasma membrane. The viral nuclear export protein NEP/NS2 makes this possible by acting as an adaptor: it binds the viral matrix protein M1 coating the vRNP and simultaneously engages the host export receptor CRM1/exportin-1 (XPO1), which recognises leucine-rich export signals and releases cargo in a RAN-GTP-dependent manner. The resulting complex then translocates through the nuclear pore, whose scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporins, together with RANBP2, TPR and RAE1, form the permeability barrier and docking sites for receptor-cargo transit. This hijacking of a normal nucleocytoplasmic transport route is a step at which the viral life cycle can be blocked, and it illustrates how a small viral protein can redirect host machinery built for cellular RNA and protein export.

After an influenza particle is taken into the cell by endocytosis, it must dismantle itself to release its genome, and uncoating of the influenza virion is that step. Without it, the segmented ribonucleoprotein complexes never reach the nucleus and no viral transcription or replication occurs, which is why this stage is a drug target. Acidification of the endosome triggers a conformational change in hemagglutinin that fuses the viral and endosomal membranes, while the M2 ion channel conducts protons into the particle interior, loosening the matrix protein M1 from the ribonucleoproteins so they can escape into the cytosol. Amantadine and rimantadine block the M2 channel, and weak bases or ionophores that raise endosomal pH prevent hemagglutinin activation. Freed ribonucleoproteins are then imported through nuclear pores using the host nucleocytoplasmic transport machinery, within roughly half an hour of adsorption.

Bacterial peptidoglycan fragments that reach the cytosol are detected by the intracellular sensors NOD1 and NOD2, which convert that detection into an inflammatory transcriptional response. NOD1 is broadly expressed while NOD2 is largely confined to monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells and intestinal Paneth cells, and loss-of-function NOD2 variants are among the strongest genetic risks for Crohn's disease, linking this sensing to intestinal barrier defence and antimicrobial peptide output. Ligand-bound receptors oligomerise and engage the kinase RIPK2 through reciprocal CARD interactions; K63-linked polyubiquitination of RIPK2, supported by TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair, recruits the TAB-bound MAP3K7 complex and, with NEMO and the IKK subunits CHUK and IKBKB, drives NF-kappaB release plus p38 MAPK activation. The deubiquitinases TNFAIP3 and CYLD and the ligase ITCH restrain the output, keeping cytokine production proportionate.

Intracellular sensing of microbial and damage signals by nucleotide-binding domain, leucine-rich repeat containing receptors gives cells a way to detect invaders that have already breached the plasma membrane, complementing surface Toll-like receptors. Two output arms dominate: NOD1 and NOD2 recognize peptidoglycan fragments and signal through the kinase RIPK2, ubiquitin machinery and the TAK1-IKK axis to activate NF-kappaB and p38 MAP kinases, driving cytokine and antimicrobial peptide expression; NLRP1, NLRP3, NLRC4 and the DNA sensor AIM2 instead nucleate inflammasomes with the adaptor PYCARD/ASC, which recruits and activates caspase-1 to mature IL-1 family cytokines and trigger inflammatory cell death. Regulators including TNFAIP3, CYLD, pyrin, TXNIP and the P2RX7-pannexin axis set the activation threshold. Gain-of-function or loss of restraint in these receptors underlies hereditary periodic fever syndromes, familial Mediterranean fever, Crohn disease susceptibility and gouty inflammation.

Clostridial neurotoxicity is the interruption of neurotransmitter release by botulinum and tetanus toxins after they enter neurons. The resulting paralysis takes different forms: botulinum toxins silence motor nerve terminals and cause flaccid weakness, whereas tetanus toxin disrupts inhibitory signalling in spinal circuits and produces sustained muscle contractions. Toxins bind neuronal membrane components, including exposed synaptic vesicle proteins such as SV2 or synaptotagmin, and enter through vesicle recycling. Acidification permits their protease domain to reach the cytosol, where it cleaves selected SNARE proteins: SNAP25, syntaxin or VAMP, depending on the toxin. These proteins normally bring synaptic vesicles and the plasma membrane together for fusion, so their cleavage prevents neurotransmitter release even when a nerve impulse arrives.

Influenza virus builds its envelope proteins in the host secretory pathway, and this step moves the folded, assembled forms of them out of the endoplasmic reticulum toward the Golgi. Haemagglutinin has trimerised, neuraminidase has formed its tetramer, and the M2 proton channel has assembled as a tetramer before export; only correctly oligomerised molecules leave the ER, so quality control here determines how much functional envelope protein reaches the cell surface for budding. Once in the Golgi the proteins acquire mature glycans and, in the case of haemagglutinin, become available for proteolytic priming, while M2 must reach the plasma membrane to acidify incoming virions in later infections. The transport itself uses the host's conventional ER-to-Golgi vesicular route, making viral envelope maturation dependent on ordinary anterograde secretory traffic.

Influenza A virus blunts the host's first line of antiviral defence by preventing infected cells from making type I interferon, and the viral NS1 protein is the agent of this inhibition of IFN-beta. Because double-stranded RNA generated during viral replication is the signature that cytosolic sensors read as infection, NS1 binds and sequesters dsRNA so that the signalling cascades converging on IRF3, NF-kB and AP-1 never assemble the enhanceosome at the IFN-beta promoter. Mutations that abolish RNA binding cripple this antagonism, yet a compensatory substitution restores much of the phenotype without restoring RNA binding, indicating that NS1 also suppresses interferon induction by other routes, including interference with host RNA processing and with the sensing machinery itself. The outcome is delayed innate immunity, wider viral spread, and a major determinant of influenza virulence and host range.

Toll-like receptor cascades are how innate immune cells detect conserved microbial structures — lipopolysaccharide, lipopeptides, flagellin, double-stranded and single-stranded RNA, CpG DNA — and convert that detection into inflammation, antimicrobial defence and instruction of adaptive immunity. Ten human receptors share a leucine-rich repeat sensing region and a cytoplasmic TIR domain; accessory and delivery factors such as CD14, LY96, LBP, CNPY3 and UNC93B1 determine what each receptor sees and where. Signalling runs through two adaptor routes: a MyD88/IRAK4–IRAK1 axis used by most receptors, and a TICAM1 (TRIF) route used by TLR3 and, via TICAM2, TLR4. Both converge on TRAF6-directed ubiquitin chains, the TAK1 and IKK kinases, and thence NF-κB, AP-1 and p38/JNK, or on TBK1–IKKε to activate IRF3/IRF7 for type I interferon. Negative regulators including IRAK3, SIGIRR, SOCS1 and TNIP2 restrain the output, since unchecked signalling drives septic shock and autoimmunity.

Double-stranded RNA sensed by TLR3 at the endosome signals through the adaptor TICAM1 (TRIF), and this branch describes how RIPK1 is recruited and ubiquitinated so that the IKK complex can be assembled on it. The outcome is NF- fkB activation alongside the TBK1-dependent arm that drives type I interferon, giving virally infected cells both an inflammatory and an antiviral transcriptional response. Mechanistically, TRAF6 together with the cIAP proteins BIRC2 and BIRC3 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair build polyubiquitin chains on RIPK1, which serve as a scaffold for the CHUK/IKBKB/IKBKG trimer; free and ribosomal-protein-fused ubiquitin precursors supply the chain material. RIPK1 sits at a decision point here, since the same adaptor can instead engage RIPK3 and necroptotic death when ubiquitination or caspase activity is compromised, linking innate immune sensing to programmed cell death.

Cytosolic detection of viral RNA is how most cells first recognise that they are infected, and the RIG-I-like receptors DDX58 (RIG-I) and IFIH1 (MDA5) are the sensors that do it, triggering type I interferon production and an antiviral state in the infected cell and its neighbours. RIG-I favours short 5'-triphosphorylated duplexes from influenza and other negative-strand viruses, MDA5 long duplexes from picornaviruses. Both signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, recruiting TRAF ubiquitin ligases and the kinases TBK1 and IKKepsilon, which phosphorylate IRF3 and IRF7 so they enter the nucleus and switch on IFNB1 and the IFN-alpha genes; parallel IKK activity releases NF-kB. Ubiquitin chemistry dominates the control layer, with TRIM25 and RNF135 promoting sensor activation and CYLD, TNFAIP3 and RNF125 restraining it. Loss of restraint produces interferonopathies and autoimmunity; loss of signalling leaves severe viral susceptibility.

PKR is the double-stranded RNA-activated kinase that shuts down translation during viral infection by phosphorylating the initiation factor eIF2-alpha, and this pathway concerns how that alarm is switched off. Restraint matters in both directions: viruses from poxviruses to influenza encode decoy RNAs and pseudosubstrates that block PKR, and the sheer number of such countermeasures is a measure of how costly the kinase is to a virus. Host cells likewise need mechanisms to limit PKR, since unchecked eIF2-alpha phosphorylation arrests protein synthesis, triggers stress granule formation and pushes cells toward apoptosis. Because PKR also feeds into interferon and inflammatory signalling, its inhibition sets the threshold for the antiviral translational shutoff and for the integrated stress response more generally, linking innate nucleic acid sensing to control of protein synthesis.

Nerve growth factor does more than switch its receptor on briefly: through prolonged ERK activation it converts a transient ligand encounter into a lasting transcriptional programme that drives neuronal differentiation, neurite outgrowth and survival of sympathetic and sensory neurons, in contrast to the short ERK pulses that favour proliferation. Ligand-bound TrkA recruits the scaffolds FRS2 and ARMS/Kidins220, which assemble adaptors of the CRK family together with the exchange factor C3G (RAPGEF1). C3G loads GTP onto Rap1, and Rap1-GTP engages B-Raf rather than the more transient Ras-Raf route, sustaining phosphorylation of MEK1/MEK2 and then ERK1/ERK2; a 14-3-3 subunit stabilises components of the relay. Duration of signalling, not merely its presence, determines the outcome here, and loss of TrkA signalling in humans causes congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis.

Whether a cell lives or dies has to be decided continuously during development and tissue turnover, and tipping this balance the wrong way contributes to autoimmunity, neurodegeneration and cancer. The regulation of apoptosis described here works largely through ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis: ubiquitin precursors and ribosomal fusion proteins supply the tag, and the full 26S proteasome, both the 20S catalytic core and the 19S regulatory particle with its deubiquitinase and ATPase subunits, destroys the substrates. Setting the abundance of pro- and anti-apoptotic regulators by degradation means commitment to death can be imposed or averted without new transcription. Alongside this, processing of the mitochondrial fusion GTPase OPA1 by the protease OMA1 remodels cristae and licenses cytochrome c release, and caspase cleavage of the kinase PAK2 drives apoptotic morphological changes such as membrane blebbing.

Many hormones and neurotransmitters act by raising intracellular cAMP, and this adenylate cyclase activating route is the step that generates that second messenger. Stimulatory G protein alpha subunits, here represented by the olfactory- and striatum-enriched GNAL, engage membrane adenylyl cyclases, which convert ATP to cAMP; the resulting cAMP activates protein kinase A and downstream phosphorylation cascades that alter metabolism, ion channel behaviour, secretion and gene transcription through CREB. The nine transmembrane cyclase isoforms differ in tissue distribution and regulation — calcium/calmodulin stimulation of ADCY1 and ADCY8 supports hippocampal synaptic plasticity and learning, while ADCY5 and ADCY6 dominate cardiac contractility responses to adrenergic input. Loss or gain of function in these enzymes produces movement disorders, dystonia, deafness and altered cardiac output, and the pathway is the point at which many drugs and toxins set cellular tone.

Many hormones and neurotransmitters act by turning cAMP production down rather than up, and this is the route they use: receptors coupled to Gi-type alpha subunits bind and inhibit adenylate cyclase, lowering cAMP and reducing protein kinase A activity toward its substrates. The output is a brake on cAMP-dependent transcription, ion channel gating, secretion and metabolic mobilisation, so the same second messenger system can be pushed in either direction depending on which receptor is engaged. Opioid, adrenergic alpha-2, muscarinic and dopamine D2 receptors all converge here, which is why this inhibitory arm underlies analgesia, presynaptic feedback restraint of neurotransmitter release, and the actions of antipsychotics. The nine membrane-bound cyclase isoforms differ in tissue distribution and in sensitivity to calcium and Gbeta-gamma, giving cell-type-specific tuning of how strongly cAMP falls.

Hepatocytes phosphorylate incoming glucose with glucokinase, and this pathway describes how that first committed step of hepatic glucose disposal is held in reserve until glucose actually arrives. Glucokinase regulatory protein binds glucokinase to form an inactive complex that is imported through the nuclear pore, sequestering the enzyme away from its substrate; fructose 6-phosphate and sorbitol 6-phosphate promote the interaction while fructose 1-phosphate opposes it. A rise in glucose dissociates the complex and releases the enzyme back to the cytosol, so that phosphorylation begins promptly after a meal without futile cycling between glucose and glucose 6-phosphate during fasting. The large nucleoporin contingent reflects the translocation step through the nuclear pore complex. Variants in the regulatory protein influence fasting glucose, triglycerides and liver fat, and glucokinase mutations cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young and hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia.

TGF-beta ligands restrain epithelial proliferation, drive extracellular matrix production and enforce immune tolerance, and this receptor complex is how that instruction reaches the genome. Latent TGF-beta held by latent-binding proteins is released, processed by furin and presented by integrins to TGFBR2, which recruits and phosphorylates TGFBR1; the activated receptor, docked on endosomes via the SARA adaptor, phosphorylates SMAD2 and SMAD3, which partner with SMAD4 and move to the nucleus to activate or repress targets such as SERPINE1, JUNB and collagen while shutting down MYC and inducing CDKN2B for cytostasis. Co-repressors including SKI, TGIF and histone deacetylases, phosphatases such as PPM1A, inhibitory SMAD7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases, and deubiquitinases like USP15 set signal duration. Loss of this growth-inhibitory arm underlies epithelial tumour progression, while excess output produces fibrosis; germline receptor mutations cause aortic aneurysm syndromes.

Sustained rather than transient ERK activity is what tells a neuron to differentiate instead of merely divide, and FRS2-mediated activation is the adaptor route that produces it. Docked at an activated receptor tyrosine kinase — here the NGF receptor TrkA — tyrosine-phosphorylated FRS2 recruits CRKL and the exchange factor C3G (RAPGEF1), which loads GTP onto Rap1A. Rap1A engages B-Raf rather than Raf-1, and the resulting endosomal signal drives MEK1/MEK2 and then ERK1/ERK2 over hours, with 14-3-3 binding stabilising the kinase complexes. The prolonged kinase output allows ERK to accumulate in the nucleus and turn on differentiation genes, underlying neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival in sympathetic and sensory neurons.
