The same adaptor serves FGF receptors in development, and activating lesions in BRAF or amplification of FRS2 make this branch oncogenic.

Neurotrophin signalling can either pulse or persist, and the ARMS-mediated route is one way a nerve growth factor signal is converted into sustained ERK activation rather than a transient one — the difference between a transcriptional programme for neurite outgrowth and differentiation and a brief metabolic response. NGF binding to the TrkA receptor triggers tyrosine phosphorylation of KIDINS220/ARMS, a multi-transmembrane adaptor anchored at the neuronal plasma membrane, which recruits CRK adaptors and guanine nucleotide exchange activity toward Rap1. GTP-loaded RAP1A engages BRAF at endomembranes, and a 14-3-3 protein stabilises the active kinase, giving prolonged MAPK cascade output. This branch underlies neuronal survival, axon and dendrite growth, and synaptic maturation, and loss of the adaptor disrupts nervous system and cardiovascular development.

Nerve growth factor does not only switch on the classical ERK cascade; it also drives sustained p38 MAPK signalling, and the two arms together push a neuronal precursor toward neurite outgrowth and differentiation rather than mere proliferation. This is the signalling logic behind the classic response of PC12 cells to NGF, where duration of kinase activity, not just its presence, decides differentiation. Downstream of the receptor, Ras proteins and the Ral branch acting through RalGDS, together with the tyrosine kinase SRC, feed into the stress-activated p38 isoforms, which in turn phosphorylate the MAPKAPK2 and MAPKAPK3 kinases and converge with ERK on CREB phosphorylation and immediate-early gene induction. The same kinases serve inflammatory and stress responses elsewhere, so the neurotrophin context is what gives this output its developmental meaning, linking growth factor sensing to transcriptional programmes for neuronal maturation and survival.

HIV-1 encodes its envelope glycoprotein and the accessory protein Vpu on a single bicistronic mRNA, and their synthesis and maturation on the rough endoplasmic reticulum is the step that gives the virion its fusion machinery. Env is inserted cotranslationally into the ER membrane, heavily N-glycosylated, folded and assembled into trimers, then carried through the secretory pathway toward the plasma membrane where assembly and budding occur. In the trans-Golgi network the host proprotein convertase furin cleaves the gp160 precursor into the receptor-binding gp120 and the transmembrane fusion subunit gp41, which remain non-covalently associated; without this cleavage the spike cannot mediate entry into CD4-positive target cells. Vpu, made from the same transcript, counteracts host restriction and downregulates CD4. The pathway illustrates how viruses co-opt cellular glycosylation, trafficking and proteolytic maturation machinery, and it defines the spike that neutralizing antibodies and entry inhibitors target.pn

Chromosome ends must be hidden from the DNA damage machinery while remaining accessible to the enzymes that maintain them, and the packaging of telomere ends is how that compromise is struck. Telomeric repeats are wrapped in nucleosomes built from core histone H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 variants, and the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, TERF2IP, POT1, TINF2 and ACD bind the duplex repeats and the 3' G-rich single-stranded overhang. Together they fold the terminus into higher-order arrangements, including the lariat-like t-loop formed when the overhang invades the double-stranded tract, masking the free end so it is not read as a break and fused or resected. This capping is coordinated with C-strand resection, telomerase-mediated elongation and fill-in synthesis. Loss of end protection triggers senescence, chromosome fusions and genome instability, and underlies telomere syndromes and cancer-associated immortalisation.

Chromosome ends shorten with every round of replication, and telomere extension by telomerase is the counter-mechanism: a reverse transcriptase, TERT, uses an internal RNA template to add TTAGGG repeats onto the G-rich 3' overhang, then translocates and repeats the cycle. This activity sets replicative lifespan — it is normally restricted in somatic tissue, sustains stem and germ cells, and is reactivated in most cancers, while loss-of-function in the RNA-binding accessory proteins DKC1, NOP10, NHP2 and GAR1, or in the assembly factors SHQ1 and WRAP53, causes dyskeratosis congenita and short-telomere syndromes with bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis. Access to the substrate is governed by the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, TINF2, ACD and POT1, which both recruit and restrain the enzyme, and the helicases RTEL1 and PIF1 together with a CDK2-cyclin and phosphatase module tie elongation to replication and the cell cycle.

The first step of HIV infection is attachment to a susceptible cell and fusion of the viral and host membranes, which delivers the viral core into the cytoplasm and determines which cells the virus can infect. The envelope glycoprotein trimer, built from a surface subunit that binds receptor and a transmembrane subunit that drives fusion, engages CD4 on helper T cells and macrophages; the resulting conformational change exposes a site for a chemokine receptor coreceptor, CCR5 or CXCR4, whose usage defines viral tropism and explains why loss-of-function CCR5 alleles confer resistance. Coreceptor engagement releases the fusion peptide into the target bilayer and the collapse of the transmembrane subunit into a hairpin pulls the two membranes together. Host cyclophilin A, a peptidyl-prolyl isomerase, acts on the incoming capsid and shapes early post-entry events. This step is the target of entry inhibitors and of neutralizing antibodies.

Glucuronidation is how the body converts bilirubin, steroids, bile acids and many drugs into water-soluble conjugates for excretion, and it depends on a supply of the activated sugar donor UDP-glucuronate. Formation of this active cofactor begins with glucose 1-phosphate and UTP, which UGP2 joins into UDP-glucose; UGDH then oxidises the sugar at C6 to yield UDP-glucuronate. Because the conjugating enzymes face the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, nucleotide-sugar transporters of the SLC35D family carry the donor across the ER membrane to reach them. The same pool feeds proteoglycan and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, and UXS1 decarboxylates UDP-glucuronate to UDP-xylose, the sugar that initiates glycosaminoglycan chains on core proteins. Loss of the transport step disturbs cartilage matrix formation and causes skeletal dysplasia, linking this small biosynthetic route to both detoxification and connective tissue structure.

This is the antibody-triggered entry point to the complement cascade, the step that converts antigen recognition by IgG or IgM into enzymatic amplification on a target surface. It underlies opsonisation and lysis of bacteria, clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris, and is the effector arm exploited by therapeutic antibodies; its loss predisposes to encapsulated bacterial infection and, in the case of C1q deficiency, to lupus-like autoimmunity from uncleared self material. C1q, built from six trimeric subunits of C1QA, C1QB and C1QC arranged like a bunch of tulips, engages clustered Fc regions of bound immunoglobulin heavy and light chains, or alternatively C-reactive protein on damaged membranes. The conformational change autoactivates the associated C1r protease, which cleaves C1s, launching downstream cleavage of C4 and C2 and formation of the classical pathway C3 convertase.

Alternative complement activation is the arm of complement that needs no antibody and no lectin to get started: it runs continuously at low level and amplifies wherever C3b lands on a surface that fails to protect itself. This makes it the immune system's default surveillance mechanism against bacteria and other foreign surfaces, and the reason host cells must actively display regulators; loss of that restraint drives haemolysis in paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria and renal injury in atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome and C3 glomerulopathy. Mechanistically, deposited C3b recruits factor B, which factor D cleaves to leave the Bb catalytic subunit as a surface-bound C3 convertase; properdin binds and stabilises this short-lived complex, and addition of a further C3b converts it into a C5 convertase that initiates the terminal lytic sequence. The loop is inherently self-amplifying, feeding back on classical and lectin activation alike.

The alternative complement pathway provides continuous, antibody-independent surveillance of surfaces, amplifying complement deposition on microbes and other targets that lack host regulatory proteins. It matters because it converts a low-level spontaneous reaction into rapid opsonisation and lytic attack, and because its dysregulation drives conditions such as atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, C3 glomerulopathy and age-related macular degeneration. Mechanistically it is a positive feedback loop centred on C3b: once C3b attaches covalently to surface sugars, factor B binds it and is cleaved by factor D into Ba and Bb, leaving the C3bBb complex as a C3 convertase. Properdin stabilises this otherwise short-lived enzyme on the target surface, and addition of a further C3b converts it into a C5 convertase that initiates membrane attack. Serine protease granzyme M is also assigned here, linking cytotoxic granule activity to this arm of innate humoral defence.

Exit from mitosis requires that cyclin B1 be destroyed, and this is the ubiquitin-dependent step that does it. Until cyclin B1 is degraded, CDK1 remains active, sister chromatids cannot separate cleanly and the cell cannot decondense chromosomes, reassemble the nuclear envelope or divide; premature destruction, conversely, would let cells leave mitosis with unattached kinetochores. The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a large multisubunit ubiquitin ligase built from ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 subunits, acquires substrate specificity when the activator Cdc20 binds and recognises the destruction box of cyclin B1. Ubiquitin is transferred through E2 enzymes, with UBE2C priming chains and UBE2S elongating them, marking cyclin B1 for proteasomal proteolysis at the spindle. The spindle assembly checkpoint restrains Cdc20 until metaphase, making this reaction the licensing point for anaphase and the irreversible commitment to mitotic exit.

The anaphase-promoting complex paired with its activator Cdh1 keeps cells in a low-CDK state after mitosis, and one of its substrates is Cdh1 itself. This self-directed ubiquitination limits how long the complex stays active during G1 and quiescence, allowing cyclin and other substrate levels to rise again so that S phase can be entered on schedule; persistent Cdh1 activity blocks proliferation, while its premature loss permits untimely accumulation of mitotic regulators and genome instability. Mechanically, the multisubunit cullin-like ligase built from ANAPC1-ANAPC11, CDC16, CDC23 and CDC27 uses FZR1 as its substrate-recruiting adaptor, works with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S to build ubiquitin chains, and delivers the modified Cdh1 to the 26S proteasome for destruction. It is an autoregulatory timer within cell cycle control rather than a separate signalling route.

Progression through mitosis requires the anaphase-promoting complex to be switched on at the right moment, and that switch is thrown by destroying its inhibitor. Emi1 (FBXO5) binds and restrains APC/C with its activators Cdc20 and Cdh1 (FZR1) through interphase, keeping cyclins and securin stable so that DNA replication is licensed only once; in early mitosis it must be removed. Cdk-mediated phosphorylation of a DSGxxS motif creates a phosphodegron recognised by beta-TrCP (BTRC), the substrate receptor of an SCF ubiquitin ligase built on Cul1 and Skp1. Polyubiquitin chains assembled from ubiquitin precursors then target Emi1 to the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory particle subunits make up most of this route. Loss of timely Emi1 destruction leaves APC/C inhibited, blocking mitotic exit, while its stabilisation elsewhere promotes re-replication and genomic instability.

APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins is the ubiquitin-dependent destruction programme that makes cell cycle transitions irreversible: it triggers sister chromatid separation, drives exit from mitosis, and keeps G1 free of mitotic regulators until a new round of replication is licensed. The anaphase-promoting complex is a multisubunit E3 ligase that, with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S, builds ubiquitin chains on substrates bearing destruction or KEN box motifs, marking them for the 26S proteasome. Securin degradation releases separase to cleave cohesin, while loss of cyclin B inactivates CDK1. Activity is timed by mitotic phosphorylation, by the exchange of the CDC20 and CDH1/FZR1 activators, by EMI1/FBXO5 inhibition, and by spindle checkpoint proteins including MAD2 and BUBR1 that sequester CDC20 until kinetochores are attached. Failure produces premature anaphase, aneuploidy and genomic instability characteristic of tumour cells.

Mitosis is irreversible because the proteins that drive it are destroyed rather than merely switched off, and APC/C-mediated degradation of cell cycle proteins is the ubiquitin ligase machinery that does the destroying. By targeting securin and the mitotic cyclins for proteasomal proteolysis, it permits separase to cleave cohesin so sister chromatids part, then lowers CDK1 activity so cells exit mitosis; continued activity through G1 keeps cyclins low until the next S phase commitment. The multisubunit core (ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 subunits) works with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S to build ubiquitin chains read by the 26S proteasome. Substrate choice is set by the exchangeable activators CDC20 and FZR1/Cdh1, which recognise destruction- and KEN-box motifs; mitotic kinases such as PLK1 and Aurora, the inhibitor EMI1/FBXO5, and spindle checkpoint proteins MAD2L1, BUB3 and BUB1B restrain activation until chromosomes are correctly attached. Loss of this timing produces aneuploidy.

Sister chromatids stay glued together until the cell is certain every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle, and this step is the trigger that releases them. Securin binds and holds the protease separase inactive; once the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied at metaphase, the anaphase-promoting complex loaded with its Cdc20 specificity factor ubiquitinates securin, and the 26S proteasome destroys it. Freed separase then cleaves the cohesin subunit that encircles the chromatids, allowing anaphase to proceed. The machinery here is a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase built from the ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 subunits, the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S that build and elongate the ubiquitin chains, and the full proteasome. Premature or failed securin degradation causes chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and securin itself is a transforming oncoprotein overexpressed in pituitary and other tumours.

As cells leave mitosis and enter G1, the anaphase-promoting complex switches coactivators from Cdc20 to Cdh1 (FZR1) and keeps destroying mitotic regulators so that the next cycle starts from a clean slate. Cdh1-directed ubiquitination targets Cdc20 itself, the mitotic kinases Plk1 and Aurora A and B, securin, Skp2 and other substrates, which are then degraded by the 26S proteasome; the core APC/C subunits, the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S that build K11-linked chains, and the full proteasome are all represented here. Substrate order is set by how processively each one acquires a chain, with distributive substrates cycling on and off and subject to deubiquitination. Sustained low mitotic kinase and cyclin activity allows origin licensing and holds G1, and loss of this control drives premature S-phase entry, re-replication and chromosome instability in cancer.

Cdc20:Phospho-APC/C mediated degradation of Cyclin A removes cyclin A at the start of mitosis, an early and distinctive step in the ordered destruction of mitotic regulators that drives cells through division. Cyclin A partners CDK1 and CDK2 to drive S phase entry and mitotic commitment; its timely clearance is required for normal chromosome segregation and for resetting the licensing of the next replication cycle, and its stabilisation contributes to genomic instability in tumours. Mechanistically, mitotic phosphorylation of the anaphase-promoting complex allows Cdc20 to load and target cyclin A for polyubiquitination by UBE2C and UBE2S, followed by degradation in the 26S proteasome. Notably this happens while the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins BubR1, Bub3 and Mad2 still restrain the same ligase from destroying securin and cyclin B, making cyclin A a checkpoint-insensitive substrate and setting the sequence of mitotic exit events.

Cyclin A drives S-phase entry and early mitotic events, and must be removed before chromosomes can be segregated correctly; its timed destruction in early mitosis is what this route accomplishes. The anaphase-promoting complex, phosphorylated by mitotic kinase activity and loaded with its Cdc20 substrate adaptor, ubiquitinates cyclin A with the help of the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S, and the 26S proteasome degrades the polyubiquitinated cyclin. Notably this happens while the spindle assembly checkpoint is still engaged: checkpoint proteins such as BUBR1, BUB3 and MAD2 restrain the same ligase from destroying securin and cyclin B, so cyclin A turnover precedes anaphase. Failure to clear cyclin A leaves CDK1 activity inappropriately high, disturbing mitotic progression and the following replication cycle.

Sulfation requires an activated sulfate donor, and this pathway makes and delivers it. Inorganic sulfate taken up by anion transporters of the SLC26 family is condensed with two molecules of ATP by the bifunctional synthases PAPSS1 and PAPSS2 to give PAPS, the universal sulfonate donor for cytosolic sulfotransferases acting on steroid hormones, thyroid hormone, catecholamines and drugs, and for Golgi sulfotransferases that sulfate glycosaminoglycans. Because synthesis is cytosolic while proteoglycan assembly is not, dedicated nucleotide-sugar-type transporters SLC35B2 and SLC35B3 import PAPS into the Golgi lumen. Loss of PAPSS2 or of the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 undersulfates cartilage chondroitin sulfate and causes recessive skeletal dysplasias, linking this small metabolic route to cartilage matrix integrity, bone growth, hormone inactivation and xenobiotic clearance.

Glutathione is the cell's main small-molecule thiol antioxidant and the sulfur donor for detoxifying electrophiles, and its synthesis and recycling keep that pool replenished. Glutamate and cysteine are joined in an ATP-dependent step by glutamate-cysteine ligase, a catalytic subunit with a modifier subunit that tunes its feedback inhibition, and glycine is then added by glutathione synthetase; because this ligase step is rate-limiting, cysteine availability sets how much glutathione a cell can make. Recycling proceeds through the gamma-glutamyl cycle: membrane gamma-glutamyl transferases strip the gamma-glutamyl group from extracellular glutathione and its conjugates so that constituent amino acids can be reimported, while cytosolic cyclotransferases and a cation-dependent dipeptidase complete turnover of the intermediates, and 5-oxoprolinase reopens the ring at the cost of ATP. Loss of capacity here leaves cells vulnerable to oxidative stress and drives ferroptotic death; inherited defects cause haemolytic anaemia and oxoprolinuria.

Telomeres are replicated in two stages, and this step is the handoff that makes the second one possible: once primase and DNA polymerase alpha have laid down short primers on the telomeric C-strand, the clamp loader Replication Factor C binds the primer-template junction, displaces the poorly processive pol alpha-primase complex, and loads the PCNA sliding clamp so that polymerase delta can extend the strand processively. Without this exchange, C-strand fill-in after telomerase-mediated G-strand extension stalls, leaving telomeres with excessive single-stranded overhangs that are read as damage. The CST complex components CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 recruit and stimulate the priming step at chromosome ends, while shelterin proteins including TRF1, TRF2, POT1 and TIN2 provide the telomeric context and restrain inappropriate repair. The biology links chromosome end maintenance to conventional lagging-strand replication and underlies telomere length homeostasis in dividing cells.

Telomeres are replicated in two halves: telomerase extends the G-rich strand, and the complementary C-strand must then be filled in by conventional lagging-strand synthesis. This pathway covers the processive part of that job, in which DNA polymerase delta, held to the template by the PCNA clamp, extends each Okazaki fragment along the telomeric template. As the growing fragment meets the RNA-DNA primer ahead of it, the displaced 5' flap is coated by replication protein A and trimmed by FEN1 or DNA2, with the BLM and WRN helicases helping resolve the G-rich structures that stall polymerases there, and LIG1 sealing the nick. Shelterin components including TRF1, TRF2, POT1 and TIN2 organise the chromosome end and set how much of it is copied. Defects cause telomere shortening and fragility, underlying premature ageing syndromes and genome instability.

After telomerase extends the G-rich telomeric overhang, the complementary C-strand must be filled in, and this lagging-strand synthesis at chromosome ends is what converts a single-stranded extension into duplex telomeric DNA of stable length. Without it telomeres shorten or leave persistent single-stranded tracts that are read as damage, triggering senescence or fusion; mutations in the CST complex (CTC1, STN1, TEN1), which recruits polymerase alpha-primase here, cause Coats plus and dyskeratosis-like bone marrow failure syndromes. Mechanistically the reaction uses the conventional replication apparatus: primase lays RNA primers, the clamp loader and PCNA license polymerase delta for processive extension, flap endonuclease and DNA2 trim displaced 5' flaps, and ligase I seals Okazaki fragments, with the helicases WRN and BLM resolving telomeric secondary structure. The shelterin proteins POT1, TRF1 and TRF2 govern access to the end.

After telomerase extends the G-rich telomere overhang, the complementary C-strand must be filled in, and that fill-in begins with primer synthesis. Here the polymerase alpha-primase complex, with its two primase subunits and two polymerase subunits, lays down a short RNA primer and extends it into DNA at the chromosome end, converting a single-stranded overhang into duplex telomeric DNA. The CST complex of CTC1, STN1 and TEN1 recruits and stimulates this activity, while the shelterin proteins POT1, TPP1, TRF1, TRF2, RAP1 and TIN2 coat the telomere, set how much telomerase-mediated extension occurs, and are reported to restrain priming through TRF1. Coordinating C-strand initiation with G-strand elongation keeps telomere length and end structure stable; failure leaves eroded or unprotected ends that trigger DNA damage signalling, senescence, and the bone marrow failure and telomere-shortening syndromes linked to CST and shelterin mutations.

When the lagging C-strand of a telomere is synthesized, strand-displacement synthesis by DNA polymerase delta leaves a single-stranded flap that must be cut away before the nick can be sealed; removal of this flap intermediate completes maturation of the newly copied telomeric DNA. Failure to process such flaps leaves unligated nicks and unprotected single-stranded DNA, inviting telomere shortening, fragility and inappropriate DNA damage signalling. Two nucleases do the cutting: FEN1 trims short flaps held against the PCNA-polymerase delta holoenzyme, while DNA2, aided by the WRN helicase, handles long flaps, and replication protein A coating of the displaced strand dictates which of the two acts. The shelterin proteins POT1, TRF1, TRF2, TIN2, TPP1 and RAP1 provide the telomeric context, coupling this step to chromosome end protection and to the replication of repetitive, structure-prone sequence.

Retroviruses bud from a small fraction of the membrane available to them, and this step explains how HIV Gag reaches the inner face of the plasma membrane — the basolateral surface in polarized cells — rather than internal membranes. Getting targeting right determines where virions form and therefore how efficiently infectious particles are released. Gag is co-translationally modified by N-myristoyltransferase, whose fatty acid tail, together with a basic matrix patch, anchors the polyprotein to the lipid bilayer. Gag then engages ESCRT-I, the TSG101–VPS28–VPS37–MVB12/UBAP1 complex that normally sorts ubiquitinated cargo into multivesicular bodies, so the virus borrows a cellular membrane-deformation and scission machinery for budding. Ubiquitin itself is a recurring feature of these interactions. The same chemistry links viral assembly to endosomal sorting, protein lipidation and the topology of membrane fission.

Retroviruses such as HIV-1 build their particles from a single polyprotein: Gag supplies the matrix, capsid and nucleocapsid layers, while occasional ribosomal frameshifting yields the Gag-Pro-Pol precursor that carries protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase at a fixed low ratio to Gag. This arrangement lets one transcript generate both the bulk structural protein and the enzymes, and the translated Gag captures free viral genomes elsewhere in the cytoplasm rather than the RNA it came from. Maturation of the assembling particle depends on host machinery represented here by the ESCRT-I complex — TSG101 with VPS28, the VPS37 subunits and MVB12/UBAP1 — which Gag recruits through its late domain, together with ubiquitin, to pinch off the budding virion at the plasma membrane. N-myristoyltransferase activity directs Gag to that membrane. Blocking these steps traps immature, non-infectious particles at the cell surface.

Complement activation converges here: the three initiating routes all build convertases that cleave C3 and then C5, the step that turns pathogen recognition into effector activity. Cleavage of C3 releases C3a, a fluid-phase anaphylatoxin that recruits and activates leukocytes, and deposits C3b on the target surface as an opsonin for phagocyte complement receptors. Surface C3b nucleates further convertases in an amplification loop and, once incorporated, shifts substrate preference to C5, whose cleavage yields the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, the seed of the membrane attack complex. The classical convertase uses C4 and C2 fragments, the alternative route uses factor B, and properdin stabilises the alternative convertase against decay. Deficiency of C3 or C5 brings recurrent pyogenic and neisserial infection, while unrestrained activation drives haemolytic and inflammatory disease.

Lipids travel through blood packaged into lipoprotein particles, and this pathway covers the whole life cycle of those particles: assembly, remodeling in the circulation, and receptor-mediated clearance. Chylomicrons built in enterocytes carry dietary fat, hepatic VLDL exports triacylglycerol, and HDL returns cholesterol from peripheral tissues to the liver. Assembly requires apolipoprotein B loaded with lipid by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, while ABCA1 and ABCG1 efflux cholesterol and phospholipid onto nascent HDL, which LCAT then matures by esterifying cholesterol. In plasma, lipoprotein lipase anchored by GPIHBP1 and regulated by angiopoietin-like proteins and apoC-II/apoC-III hydrolyzes triglyceride, and CETP and PLTP exchange lipids between particles. Remnants are removed by LDL receptor and relatives through clathrin-coated pits, with PCSK9 and the ubiquitin ligase MYLIP setting receptor abundance. Defects underlie familial hypercholesterolemia, chylomicronemia, abetalipoproteinemia, and atherosclerotic risk.

Assembly Of The HIV Virion is the late stage of the retroviral life cycle in which a new, infectious particle is built at the host plasma membrane, packaging two copies of genomic RNA, a host tRNA-Lys primer, the envelope glycoprotein, and the Gag and Gag-Pro-Pol polyproteins that carry protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase. Without it, infected cells produce no transmissible progeny, which is why this step is a drug target alongside entry and enzymatic inhibitors. The process is almost entirely dependent on borrowed host machinery: N-myristoyltransferase directs Gag to the membrane, cyclophilin A is recruited onto capsid to license later uncoating, furin matures Env, and ubiquitin together with the ESCRT-I complex of TSG101, VPS37 subunits, UBAP1 and MVB12 provides the membrane-scission activity normally used for multivesicular body formation, here hijacked to pinch off the budding virion.

Late in HIV replication, the virus gathers everything a new particle needs to be infectious: two copies of genomic RNA, a primer tRNA, the envelope glycoprotein, the Gag polyprotein and the Gag-Pro-Pol precursor carrying protease, reverse transcriptase and integrase. Assembly of the HIV virion is essentially a hijacking of host membrane and trafficking machinery at the plasma membrane. Gag is myristoylated by N-myristoyltransferase to anchor it to the inner leaflet, the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase cyclophilin A is recruited through the capsid domain and incorporated into particles, and the envelope precursor is matured by a cellular proprotein convertase of the furin family. Budding depends on the ESCRT-I complex, TSG101 with VPS28, VPS37 subunits, MVB12 and UBAP1, together with ubiquitin, normally used for sorting cargo into multivesicular bodies. Blocking these interactions traps immature particles at the cell surface, a recognised antiviral vulnerability.

A retrovirus only becomes a permanent part of its host when its reverse-transcribed DNA is joined covalently to a chromosome, and this step — integration of viral DNA into host genomic DNA — converts infection into a lifelong provirus that cannot be cleared by antiviral drugs. The preintegration complex enters the nucleus, selects a target, and catalyses strand transfer by direct transesterification of both viral DNA ends into target strands, leaving short gaps and overhangs that host DNA repair enzymes must seal. Site selection is not sequence-specific but strongly biased toward active transcription units, a bias imposed by PSIP1/LEDGF/p75, which binds integrase at one end and chromatin at the other and tethers the complex there. Chromatin proteins including BANF1 and HMGA1 associate with the complex and with target nucleosomes, whose bent DNA is preferentially used. This chemistry is the target of integrase inhibitors.

Interactions of Vpr with host cellular proteins describes how the HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr subverts host machinery to help the virus replicate in non-dividing cells and to reshape the infected cell's fate. Its main partners here are the nuclear pore complex and nuclear import factors contributing to docking and translocation of the viral pre-integration complex through the nuclear envelope, alongside importin-alpha, the chromatin tethers BANF1, HMGA1 and PSIP1/LEDGF that accompany the incoming genome. A second arm engages the adenine nucleotide translocators of the inner mitochondrial membrane, promoting membrane permeabilization and release of apoptogenic factors. Vpr additionally arrests cells at the G2/M boundary by driving inhibitory Tyr15 phosphorylation of CDK1, a block that depends on PP2A and differs from the canonical DNA damage checkpoint. Together these activities link nucleocytoplasmic transport, cell cycle control and apoptosis to viral pathogenesis and CD4 T cell loss.

HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr is a small virion-packaged protein that rewires host machinery to favour infection, and the contacts it makes with cellular proteins explain three of its activities: nuclear delivery of the viral pre-integration complex, arrest of the host cell in G2/M, and induction of apoptosis. Most of the host partners here are components of the nuclear pore complex — the scaffold and linker nucleoporins, the FG-repeat channel proteins, the transmembrane ring, and the basket with TPR and NUP153 — together with an importin-alpha and chromatin-associated factors such as BANF1, HMGA1 and the integration cofactor PSIP1/LEDGF, consistent with docking of the incoming complex at the pore and transit into the nucleus. The adenine nucleotide translocases of the inner mitochondrial membrane provide a separate route, where Vpr binding promotes permeabilization and release of pro-apoptotic factors. Blocking mitotic entry via Cdk1 hyperphosphorylation prolongs a cell state favourable to viral gene expression.

HIV-1 transcription stalls shortly after initiation unless the viral Tat protein recruits host machinery to release the paused polymerase, and this hijacking of cellular factors is what allows the integrated provirus to make full-length transcripts rather than short abortive ones. The two host components here, cyclin T1 and the kinase CDK9, form the positive transcription elongation factor P-TEFb; Tat binds cyclin T1 and, together with the TAR RNA element in the nascent transcript, tethers the kinase to the elongation complex. CDK9 then phosphorylates the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain and the negative elongation factors that hold it in place, converting a paused polymerase into a processive one. The same complex controls pause release at host genes, so productive viral gene expression depends on borrowing a general control point of eukaryotic transcription, and blocking it suppresses viral replication.

When a replication fork stalls, the cell must stop making new forks and delay mitosis until the problem is resolved, and this is the checkpoint that does it. Activation of ATR in response to replication stress begins with persistent single-stranded DNA coated by the RPA trimer, which recruits ATR together with its partner ATRIP; in parallel the RAD17-RFC clamp loader deposits the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 ring, and claspin brings in CHK1 so that ATR can phosphorylate and amplify it. Activated CHK1 drives degradation or sequestration of CDC25 phosphatases, leaving CDK2 and mitotic CDKs in their inhibited, tyrosine-phosphorylated state. The downstream targets are the replication machinery itself — ORC subunits, CDC6, CDC45, the MCM helicase and the CDC7-DBF4 kinase that licenses origin firing. Loss of this surveillance produces under-replicated DNA, fork collapse and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours.

Exit from mitosis requires that the anaphase-promoting complex change its partner: the switch from APC/C:Cdc20 to APC/C:Cdh1 in late anaphase extends ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis to a broader set of substrates and holds cells in G1 with low Cdk activity. This handover is what makes mitotic exit irreversible, prevents premature entry into the next S phase, and guards against re-replication and chromosome missegregation. The core ubiquitin ligase is a large multisubunit assembly built from the ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 scaffold and cullin-RING catalytic subunits, working with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and the chain-elongating UBE2S. Mitotic Cyclin:Cdk phosphorylation activates the Cdc20-bound form while keeping Cdh1 (FZR1) inhibited; as Cdk activity falls, the phosphatase CDC14A dephosphorylates Cdh1 so it can bind and activate the complex, sustaining degradation of cyclins and other mitotic regulators through G1.

The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome is the ubiquitin ligase that times mitotic exit, and its substrate choice depends entirely on which activator is bound; regulation of APC/C activators between G1/S and early anaphase is how a cell keeps that switch aligned with the cell cycle. Cdc20 accumulates as cells enter mitosis and engages the core complex only in M phase, where it is restrained by the spindle checkpoint proteins Mad2 and BubR1 until chromosomes are correctly attached; Cdh1 (FZR1) takes over in G1 and is excluded at other times by Cdk1- and Cdk2-dependent phosphorylation and by the inhibitor Emi1 (FBXO5), itself destroyed through SCF/beta-TrCP. Plk1 and the cyclins feed into this timing, and the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S build the chains that route substrates to the proteasome. Loss of control produces premature sister chromatid separation and aneuploidy.

Mitosis ends only when the proteins that sustained it are destroyed, and this is the step that destroys them. Once mitotic kinases phosphorylate the anaphase-promoting complex, the activator Cdc20 docks onto the core to form APC/C:Cdc20, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase that, with E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S, polyubiquitinates cyclin A, cyclin B and securin for proteasomal destruction. Loss of securin frees separase to cleave cohesin so sister chromatids can part, while cyclin B loss inactivates CDK1 and permits mitotic exit and cytokinesis. The ligase is held in check until chromosomes are correctly attached: BUB1B, BUB3 and MAD2L1 sequester Cdc20 as part of spindle checkpoint surveillance. Mistiming here yields premature separation, aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours, placing this irreversible proteolytic switch at the heart of cell cycle control.

The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome is the ubiquitin ligase that triggers sister chromatid separation and mitotic exit, and phosphorylation of its subunits is the switch that licenses it to do so. Mitotic kinases — cyclin B–CDK1 and PLK1 — modify several APC/C subunits, notably the TPR-containing scaffold components such as CDC27, CDC16 and CDC23, relieving autoinhibition so that the activator Cdc20 can bind and direct substrate recognition. Only then can the complex, working with E2 enzymes including UBE2C for chain initiation and UBE2S for K11-linked chain elongation, ubiquitinate securin and cyclin B for proteasomal destruction at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition. This creates a feedback arrangement in which CDK1 activity ultimately drives its own cyclin's degradation. Failure to impose this control causes premature or delayed anaphase, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and the step is held in check by the spindle assembly checkpoint.

Entry into mitosis requires that the ubiquitin ligase APC/C be released from inhibition, and phosphorylation of Emi1 is the switch that does it. Emi1, encoded by FBXO5, binds and restrains APC/C during interphase, holding cyclins and securin stable so that S phase and G2 proceed without premature destruction of mitotic regulators. Once cells commit to division, Cdk1 in complex with cyclin B and the kinase Plk1 phosphorylate Emi1, creating a phosphodegron that targets it for ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis. Loss of the inhibitor allows APC/C, working with its activators CDC20 and later FZR1/Cdh1, to drive cyclin B and securin turnover and thus anaphase and mitotic exit. The same relationship makes Emi1 stability a determinant of genome stability: failure to restrain APC/C in interphase causes re-replication and endoreduplication, while failure to remove Emi1 blocks mitotic progression.

Exit from mitosis depends on destroying, in a set order, the very proteins that drove cells into it. At the prometaphase-to-metaphase transition the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome is switched on by mitotic kinase phosphorylation of its core subunits and by binding of its activator Cdc20, converting it into an active ubiquitin ligase that, with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S, builds polyubiquitin chains for proteasomal destruction. Cyclin A and the kinase Nek2 go first, then cyclin B and securin, so that Cdk1 activity falls and separase is freed to cleave cohesin for sister chromatid separation. Spindle checkpoint proteins including Mad2, BubR1 and Bub3 restrain Cdc20 until kinetochores are properly attached, coupling proteolysis to chromosome alignment. Loss of this control produces premature anaphase, aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours.

Before a replication fork can copy DNA, the parental duplex must be opened, and this step converts a licensed origin into an active fork. The MCM2-7 ring, loaded onto origins in late mitosis as part of the pre-replication complex, is the replicative helicase, but it is inert until CDC45 and the four-subunit GINS complex join it to form the active CMG helicase at the G1/S transition. CMG then translocates along the leading-strand template, unwinding the parental strands and providing the single-stranded template for polymerases and primase. Because helicase loading and activation are separated in time, this arrangement enforces once-per-cell-cycle replication and prevents re-initiation. Loss or misregulation of these subunits causes fork stalling, replication stress and genome instability; MCM8 additionally supports homologous recombination repair and meiotic functions, with mutations linked to premature ovarian insufficiency.

Conjugation of salicylate with glycine is the main route by which the body disposes of aspirin. Once aspirin is hydrolysed to salicylate, this two-step mitochondrial pathway converts it to salicyluric acid, a water-soluble product cleared by the kidneys, and accounts for the majority of salicylate elimination. A medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetase family (ACSM2A/2B, ACSM4, ACSM5) first activates salicylate to its CoA thioester at the expense of ATP, and a glycine N-acyltransferase (GLYAT, with related GLYATL enzymes) then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, releasing free coenzyme A. Because the route has limited capacity, it saturates at high doses, which is why salicylate kinetics become dose-dependent and toxicity escalates in overdose. The same enzymes handle benzoate and other xenobiotic and medium-chain acids, linking drug detoxification to amino acid and mitochondrial acyl-CoA metabolism.

Aspirin is hydrolysed in the body to salicylate, and conjugation of salicylate with glycine is the main route by which that salicylate is disposed of, producing salicyluric acid for renal excretion and accounting for the majority of aspirin metabolites. Because the pathway saturates at higher doses, it sets the point at which salicylate elimination shifts from first-order to capacity-limited kinetics, contributing to toxicity in overdose. Two steps are required. Mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, including the ACSM2A/ACSM2B pair and related ACSM4 and ACSM5, use ATP to activate salicylate as its coenzyme A thioester, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate. Glycine N-acyltransferase then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, regenerating free CoA; the related GLYATL enzymes carry out analogous amino acid conjugations of other acyl-CoA substrates. The same chemistry detoxifies benzoate and endogenous acyl-CoAs, placing this arm of drug metabolism alongside glucuronidation and ring hydroxylation.

Conjugation of benzoate with glycine is the two-step detoxification route that turns benzoic acid, a common dietary and food-preservative compound, into hippuric acid for urinary excretion. It was among the first drug-metabolism pathways ever described, and because each molecule of hippurate carries away a nitrogen atom, sodium benzoate has been given therapeutically to drain ammonia in patients with urea cycle defects. Mitochondrial medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases first activate benzoate to benzoyl-CoA at the expense of ATP; glycine N-acyltransferases then transfer the acyl group onto glycine, releasing the water-soluble conjugate. Related transferase family members handle other acyl acceptors and aromatic acids, linking this chemistry to bile acid and phenylacetate handling. The pathway sits within phase II xenobiotic conjugation and mitochondrial CoA-thioester metabolism, and it competes with glycine's other uses when substrate loads are high.

Benzoate, common in the diet and as a food preservative, is detoxified by conjugation with glycine to form hippuric acid, which is readily excreted in urine. This two-step route was among the first detoxification pathways ever described, and it was used clinically to drain nitrogen in patients with urea cycle defects, since each conjugate carries an amino group out of the body. Medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSM1 and ACSM2B first activate benzoate to benzoyl-CoA at the expense of ATP; mitochondrial glycine N-acyltransferase GLYAT then transfers the acyl group onto glycine, releasing free CoA. The related GLYATL enzymes handle other acyl donors and related amine acceptors, extending the same chemistry to bile acid and arylalkanoic conjugation. The pathway sits in hepatic and renal phase II metabolism, and its capacity limits tolerance of benzoate loads and ammonia-scavenging therapy.

Conjugating phenylacetate with glutamine converts a small aromatic acid into phenylacetylglutamine, a water-soluble product that the kidney clears in urine and that carries two nitrogen atoms out of the body with it. This gives the route its clinical value: phenylbutyrate and phenylacetate are given as nitrogen-scavenging drugs in urea cycle disorders, where ammonia cannot be disposed of normally, and the conjugate provides an alternative exit for waste nitrogen. The first step is activation, in which a medium-chain acyl-CoA synthetase uses ATP and coenzyme A to make phenylacetyl-CoA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate; ACSM1 and ACSM2B both catalyse this efficiently, though their relative contributions in liver are unsettled. A mitochondrial glutamine N-acyltransferase, distinct from the glycine-conjugating enzyme, then transfers the acyl group to glutamine. This places the pathway within hepatic phase II conjugation and xenobiotic elimination.

HIV-1 cannot complete its replication cycle unless intron-containing viral RNAs escape the nucleus, and the viral Rev protein achieves this by hijacking the host's nucleocytoplasmic transport machinery. Rev enters the nucleus bound to importin-beta with nucleophosmin, docking at the nuclear pore through contacts with phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins; RanGTP then displaces the cargo, and the exportin CRM1 together with RanGTP assembles on Rev bound to the Rev response element, carrying unspliced and singly spliced transcripts through the pore. In the cytoplasm RanBP1 and RanGAP1 trigger GTP hydrolysis and complex disassembly, while nuclear RCC1 regenerates RanGTP, sustaining the compartmental Ran nucleotide gradient that gives transport its direction. The genes here are largely the nuclear pore complex itself, from the Y-complex scaffold to the transmembrane and basket components, illustrating how a small viral adaptor exploits an entirely cellular route.

Sympathetic and sensory neurons extend axons far from their cell bodies, and they learn whether a target has been reached by carrying the message home. Retrograde neurotrophin signalling is that journey: NGF bound to its receptor kinase TrkA is internalized at the distal nerve terminal and travels back along microtubules inside a signalling endosome, still ligand-bound and still active, to trigger transcriptional responses at the soma. The outcome is target-dependent survival, appropriate innervation, synaptogenesis and maintenance of connectivity; loss of the axis causes neuronal death and, in the case of NGF-TrkA, congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis. The machinery here is largely that of endocytic uptake -- clathrin heavy and light chains with the AP-2 adaptor complex, dynamins and endophilin for vesicle scission -- coupled to dynein-based minus-end transport. Caveolar and pincher-mediated routes offer alternative entry points.

Retroviral replication requires that reverse-transcribed viral DNA be inserted into a host chromosome, and this pathway describes the abortive outcome in which the integrase machinery attacks a target site within the viral DNA itself. The resulting covalent rearrangement yields circular viral DNA forms that can no longer serve as integration substrates, so every autointegration event is a dead end that lowers the effective titre of infection. The host barrier-to-autointegration factor BANF1, a small DNA-bridging protein of the pre-integration complex, is thought to coat and compact the viral DNA so that it is a poorer intramolecular target, while HMGA1 and the chromatin-tethering factor PSIP1 (LEDGF/p75) also associate with the complex and influence where integration occurs. The balance between productive chromosomal integration and self-destructive circularisation therefore sets how efficiently an incoming provirus is established.

Growth factor cues reaching the cell surface are converted into decisions to divide, survive, migrate or differentiate, and epidermal growth factor receptor signalling is one of the main routes by which that happens; it drives epithelial renewal and wound repair, and when the receptor is mutated, amplified or chronically stimulated it becomes a principal oncogenic driver in lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers, and the target of antibody and kinase-inhibitor therapy. Ligands such as EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin and HBEGF, several released by ADAM10 and ADAM17 shedding, promote receptor dimerisation and tyrosine trans-autophosphorylation. The resulting phosphotyrosines recruit SHC1, GRB2 with SOS1 to activate RAS and the MAP kinase cascade, GRB2-GAB1 to assemble PI3K and AKT signalling, and PLCG1 for diacylglycerol and IP3 output. Attenuation is built in: CBL-mediated ubiquitination, clathrin and endophilin-dependent internalisation with ESCRT components, LRIG1, sprouty proteins and phosphatases limit signal duration.

Chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate are long sulfated sugar chains attached to core proteins, and this pathway covers both their construction and their breakdown. The chondroitin chains give cartilage its resistance to compression, while dermatan sulfate predominates in skin, blood vessels, heart valves and tendon, where it organises collagen and influences wound repair, fibrosis and coagulation. Chain elongation by polymerising glycosyltransferases alternates glucuronic acid with N-acetylgalactosamine; a family of sulfotransferases places sulfate at specific ring positions to create the binding motifs that growth factors and matrix proteins read, and epimerases convert glucuronic to iduronic acid to yield dermatan. The core proteins here include aggrecan-family proteoglycans such as versican, brevican and neurocan plus decorin and biglycan. Lysosomal exoglycosidases and sulfatases then degrade the chains; loss of these steps causes mucopolysaccharidoses with skeletal, corneal and neurological disease.

The centrosomal kinase Nek2A, which promotes splitting of duplicated centrosomes and contributes to spindle assembly, is one of the earliest substrates destroyed as cells enter mitosis. Its removal during prometaphase illustrates that the anaphase-promoting complex bound to its activator Cdc20 can be active before the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied: unlike securin and cyclin B, Nek2A docks directly onto the complex through a C-terminal motif and is polyubiquitinated even while checkpoint proteins such as Mad2, BubR1 and Bub3 hold Cdc20 in an inhibited mitotic checkpoint complex. The core cullin-like and TPR subunits of the ubiquitin ligase, together with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S, build the chains that commit the kinase to proteasomal destruction. Timely turnover of Nek2A restricts centrosome-associated kinase activity to a narrow window, and its persistence perturbs centrosome behaviour and chromosome segregation fidelity.

Even while the spindle assembly checkpoint is still active and holding sister chromatids together, a subset of substrates is already being destroyed by the anaphase-promoting complex bound to its activator Cdc20. This early, checkpoint-insensitive activity degrades cyclin A and the kinase Nek2A, which is how cyclin A/CDK1 activity falls as cells enter mitosis and how centrosomal Nek2A is cleared, timing events that would otherwise wait for full checkpoint satisfaction. The multisubunit APC core, together with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S, builds ubiquitin chains that route substrates to the 26S proteasome, whose complete subunit set is represented here. Checkpoint proteins Mad2, BubR1 and Bub3 restrain the same ligase toward securin and cyclin B, so this arm illustrates how substrate-selective ubiquitination orders mitotic progression and protects against chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy.

This is the step that converts a ligand-bound, autophosphorylated EGF receptor into active RAS, and it is the canonical textbook route from a growth factor at the cell surface to proliferation. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises the receptor and triggers phosphorylation of its cytoplasmic tail. The adaptor GRB2 docks on those phosphotyrosines through its SH2 domain while holding the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 through its SH3 domains, so receptor binding delivers SOS1 to the plasma membrane next to HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, where it promotes GDP-to-GTP exchange. Output feeds the MAP kinase cascade and downstream transcriptional programmes for growth and survival. Because the link is so direct, activating EGFR or RAS mutations drive lung, colorectal and other carcinomas, and determine whether receptor-blocking therapy can work.

SRP-dependent cotranslational protein targeting to membrane delivers newly made secretory and membrane proteins into the endoplasmic reticulum while they are still being translated, and it is the entry point for the entire secretory pathway covering hormones, antibodies, receptors, and lysosomal enzymes. A hydrophobic signal sequence emerging from the ribosome is captured by the signal recognition particle, which pauses elongation and escorts the ribosome to the SRP receptor at the ER membrane; the ribosome is then handed to the SEC61 translocon, translation resumes, and the chain threads into the lumen, where signal peptidase and translocon-associated subunits complete processing and stabilise the nascent chain. Nearly the full complement of large and small ribosomal subunit proteins participates, reflecting that this is cytosolic translation redirected to a membrane. Defects impair secretion and provoke ER stress, and ribosomal protein loss causes ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Secreted proteins, membrane proteins and the contents of the entire endomembrane system are made on ribosomes that dock at the endoplasmic reticulum, and this is the route by which they get there. Translation begins in the cytosol like any other, but once a hydrophobic signal sequence emerges from the ribosomal exit tunnel the signal recognition particle binds it, pauses elongation, and delivers the whole ribosome-mRNA-nascent chain complex to its receptor at the ER membrane. Handover to the Sec61 translocon channel reorients the growing peptide into the lumen, translocon-associated and translocating-chain accessory components stabilise the engaged ribosome, and signal peptidase subunits clip the signal sequence so elongation can finish inside the ER. The large complement of cytosolic ribosomal subunits reflects that the translating ribosome itself is part of the machinery. Loss of this targeting step strands secretory cargo in the cytosol, blocking glycosylation, disulfide bonding and onward traffic.

DARPP-32 is the switch that lets dopamine-responsive neurons, especially striatal medium spiny neurons, convert transient receptor signals into lasting changes in the phosphorylation state of downstream targets, and it underlies the actions of antipsychotics, psychostimulants and drugs of abuse as well as normal motor and reward learning. Dopamine acting through cAMP and protein kinase A phosphorylates DARPP-32 (PPP1R1B) at Thr34, turning it into a strong inhibitor of protein phosphatase 1; phosphorylation at Thr75 by Cdk5 instead makes it inhibit PKA, so the same protein can amplify or damp cAMP signalling depending on which site is modified. Phosphodiesterases of the PDE4 family terminate the cAMP signal, while protein phosphatase 2A and the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin remove the regulatory phosphates, placing DARPP-32 at the intersection of dopaminergic and glutamatergic calcium input.

Growth factor stimulation of the EGF receptor must be converted into a lipid signal if a cell is to activate the AKT survival and growth arm, and assembly of the GAB1 signalosome is how that conversion happens. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or HB-EGF — activates EGFR, which binds GRB2; GRB2 in turn brings in the scaffold GAB1, and GAB1 recruits the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1 together with the catalytic subunit PIK3CA. The assembled complex phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, triggering AKT-dependent proliferation and resistance to apoptosis. GAB1 also docks the phosphatase PTPN11 and links to SRC-family kinase activity, itself restrained by CSK and the adaptor PAG1, while paxillin ties the complex to adhesion signalling. Excessive flux through this node is a recurring feature of EGFR-driven cancers.

Ligand-bound EGFR has to convert a phosphotyrosine signal into RAS activation, and the adaptor SHC1 provides one of the two routes by which it does so. SHC1 docks on phosphorylated receptor tails through its SH2 and PTB domains, becomes tyrosine phosphorylated itself, and then recruits GRB2 together with the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1; SOS1 loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, launching the MAPK cascade that drives proliferation, survival and epithelial migration. The pathway can be triggered by any of the receptor's ligands, including EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, epiregulin, betacellulin and HB-EGF, several of which are shed from the membrane by proteolysis. Because this is the principal mitogenic output of EGFR, activating mutations in the receptor or in RAS lock it on and are among the commonest drivers of lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers.

HIV-1 must strip CD4 from the surface of the cells it infects, because retained receptor would trap newly made envelope glycoprotein and allow superinfection; Vpu-mediated degradation of CD4 is how the virus accomplishes this. The accessory protein Vpu acts as an adaptor in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, binding the cytoplasmic tail of newly synthesised CD4 on one side and the substrate receptor beta-TrCP on the other, thereby hijacking a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase whose SKP1 subunit completes the complex. Polyubiquitin chains built from the ubiquitin precursors present here mark CD4 for retrotranslocation and destruction by the 26S proteasome, represented by its full complement of core particle and regulatory particle subunits. The result is loss of the helper T cell receptor that defines CD4 lineage identity, enhanced infectivity of progeny virions, and a clear example of a pathogen redirecting host protein quality control.

APOBEC3G is a host cytidine deaminase that, when packaged into budding virions, hypermutates the minus-strand viral cDNA during reverse transcription, converting cytidine to uracil and producing G-to-A changes and premature stop codons that cripple the provirus. HIV-1 escapes this restriction through its accessory protein Vif, which binds APOBEC3G and delivers it for destruction, and this counter-defence is what allows the virus to replicate in lymphocytes and macrophages. Vif acts as a substrate adaptor for a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase built on CUL5, RBX1 and the Elongin B/C pair, directing polyubiquitin chains onto APOBEC3G so that the 26S proteasome, with its 20S catalytic core and 19S regulatory particle, degrades it in the producer cell. The pathway illustrates hijacking of host ubiquitin-proteasome machinery to neutralise intrinsic antiviral immunity, and makes the Vif-APOBEC3G interface an antiviral drug target.

Cells that HIV-1 infects carry a built-in defence against it: the cytidine deaminase APOBEC3G, expressed in T lymphocytes and macrophages, is packaged into budding virions through an RNA-dependent interaction with the viral nucleocapsid and travels with the particle into the next cell. There, during reverse transcription, it deaminates cytidine to uracil in the minus-strand viral DNA, producing G-to-A hypermutation across the plus strand so that the resulting provirus is crippled or the DNA is degraded before integration. This is a form of innate, cell-autonomous antiviral immunity directed at retroviruses and retroelements generally. HIV-1 counters it with Vif, which targets APOBEC3G for degradation, and the balance between the two shapes viral fitness and sequence evolution. Host factors of the reverse transcription and pre-integration complex, including PPIA, the lens epithelium-derived growth factor PSIP1, and BANF1, act in the same compartment.

HIV-1 Rev must reach the nucleus to perform its job of exporting unspliced and partially spliced viral RNAs, and this pathway describes how the host import machinery delivers it there. Rev carries an arginine-rich nuclear localization signal embedded in its RNA-binding domain, which is recognized by importin-beta (KPNB1) and by nucleophosmin/B23 (NPM1), a chaperone that normally escorts ribosomal proteins into the nucleus. The resulting complex docks at the nuclear pore through importin-beta contacts with phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins and translocates through the central channel, with the full pore scaffold, cytoplasmic filaments and nuclear basket contributing. Inside the nucleus, RanGTP generated by the chromatin-bound exchange factor RCC1 binds importin-beta and dissociates the complex, releasing Rev. The example illustrates how a small viral protein hijacks the compartmentalization of eukaryotic cells, and the Ran gradient that gives nucleocytoplasmic transport its direction.

Chromosome ends shorten with every round of replication, and telomere extension is how dividing cells restore them. It sustains the proliferative capacity of stem, germ and progenitor cells, is reactivated in most cancers to grant unlimited division, and when deficient produces the short-telomere syndromes: bone marrow failure, pulmonary fibrosis and dyskeratosis congenita. The telomerase holoenzyme centres on the reverse transcriptase TERT with its RNA template, stabilised by dyskerin and the H/ACA proteins NHP2, NOP10 and GAR1, with trafficking aid from WRAP53 and assembly chaperones. Access to the 3' overhang is controlled by the shelterin proteins TRF1, TRF2, POT1, TPP1 and TIN2, which also limit elongation. The extended G-strand is then converted to duplex DNA by conventional lagging-strand machinery — primase, polymerase alpha and delta, RPA, RFC, PCNA, FEN1 and ligase I — with CST and helicases such as WRN, BLM and RTEL1 resolving telomeric secondary structure.

HIV-1 accessory protein Vpr can kill infected and bystander cells, and one route by which it does so is to breach the mitochondrial outer membrane directly. Vpr binds the adenine nucleotide translocator — the ADP/ATP carriers encoded by SLC25A4, SLC25A5 and SLC25A6 in the inner membrane — and this interaction is proposed to act on the permeability transition pore complex, collapsing the mitochondrial membrane potential and permeabilizing the membranes. The consequence is release of cytochrome c and other apoptogenic factors such as apoptosis-inducing factor into the cytosol, triggering caspase activation and intrinsic apoptosis. Because these carriers normally exchange ADP for ATP to supply the cell with energy from oxidative phosphorylation, their subversion links viral protein activity to loss of bioenergetic function, and contributes to the T cell depletion that characterises HIV infection.

Vpr-mediated nuclear import of PICs describes how HIV-1 delivers its reverse-transcribed genome across the nuclear envelope, the step that allows the virus to integrate and establish infection in non-dividing cells such as macrophages that never disassemble their nuclear membrane. The accessory protein Vpr docks the pre-integration complex at the nuclear pore, apparently by binding nucleoporins directly, while importin-alpha and the host chromatin factors BANF1, HMGA1 and the tethering protein PSIP1 (LEDGF) contribute to complex stability and eventual targeting to chromatin. The gene complement is essentially the whole nuclear pore complex — the Y-shaped NUP107–160 scaffold, the central FG-repeat channel nucleoporins, the transmembrane ring, and the cytoplasmic and nuclear basket filaments RANBP2 and TPR — illustrating how a virus subverts constitutive nucleocytoplasmic transport for its own replication cycle.

HIV-1 must deliver its reverse-transcribed genome into the nucleus of a non-dividing cell, and the accessory protein Vpr contributes to that step by docking the pre-integration complex at the nuclear envelope so that its cargo can cross into the nucleoplasm. This is what allows the virus to infect terminally differentiated macrophages and resting T cells, where no mitotic breakdown of the nuclear envelope is available, and it sets up the integration that makes infection permanent. The host contribution here is essentially the whole nuclear pore complex: the structural Y-complex scaffold, transmembrane and channel nucleoporins, and the peripheral filaments RANBP2 and TPR that Vpr and importin alpha engage. Other host factors in the complex include the lens epithelium-derived growth factor PSIP1, which tethers integrase to chromatin, together with BANF1 and HMGA1.

ZBP1 is a cytosolic sensor of intracellular DNA and Z-form nucleic acids, and one output of its engagement is transcriptional induction of inflammatory genes through NF-kB. This arm of innate immune sensing lets infected cells announce viral or bacterial nucleic acid in the cytoplasm by producing cytokines, chemokines and pro-survival factors, complementing the interferon and cell-death responses that the same sensor can trigger. Signal transfer depends on RHIM-mediated interaction with the kinases RIPK1 and RIPK3, which recruit the IKK complex (CHUK/IKBKB with the regulatory subunit IKBKG); IKK phosphorylation of IkB proteins such as NFKBIA frees RELA-containing dimers to enter the nucleus. Related adaptors for Toll-like receptor routes, including TICAM1 and MYD88, converge on the same kinase module. Deregulated ZBP1 signalling contributes to interferonopathy-like inflammation and to the balance between survival and necroptotic death.

Serotonergic signalling depends on packaging serotonin into synaptic vesicles and releasing it in response to an action potential, and this release cycle is the step at which that happens. It supports mood, sleep, appetite and gut motility regulation, and it is the point of action of drugs that block vesicular monoamine loading; loss of release capacity underlies depressive and anxiety states as well as impaired intestinal secretion from enterochromaffin cells. A vesicular monoamine transporter concentrates serotonin using the proton gradient, synapsins tether the reserve pool, and Rab3A with active-zone scaffolds such as RIM1 and liprins positions vesicles at the release site. Depolarisation admits calcium, synaptotagmin-1 senses it, and the SNARE proteins syntaxin-1A, SNAP25 and VAMP2 with Munc18 and complexin drive fusion, making this a specialised instance of general calcium-triggered exocytosis.

Noradrenergic neurons signal by packaging norepinephrine into synaptic vesicles and releasing it in response to action potentials, a cycle that drives sympathetic control of heart rate, blood pressure and smooth muscle tone as well as arousal and attention in the brain. Dopamine is taken up into reacidified vesicles by the vesicular monoamine transporter SLC18A2 and converted to norepinephrine inside the vesicle lumen; the loaded vesicle is then docked, primed and fused at the active zone. Fusion is carried out by the SNARE proteins STX1A, SNAP25 and VAMP2 under control of the calcium sensor synaptotagmin, complexin, Munc18 and Munc13, with RAB3A and active-zone scaffolds RIMS1 and liprins organising release sites. Transporters of the organic cation family clear released amine, and monoamine oxidase A degrades it. Disrupted handling of this cycle underlies autonomic failure and is the target of antidepressant and antihypertensive drugs.

Fast cholinergic transmission begins when acetylcholine binds a pentameric nicotinic receptor and opens an intrinsic cation channel, depolarizing the postsynaptic membrane and, for calcium-permeable forms, raising intracellular calcium. This is the step that converts motor nerve firing into muscle contraction at the neuromuscular junction, relays signalling through autonomic ganglia, and modulates release of other transmitters at presynaptic terminals throughout the brain. The genes here encode the alpha, beta, delta, epsilon and gamma subunits whose combinations and stoichiometry set each receptor's ligand sensitivity and ion selectivity; the gamma-to-epsilon switch marks the maturation of the endplate receptor. Alpha7-containing receptors are notably calcium-permeable and rapidly desensitizing, while alpha4beta2 receptors mediate much of nicotine's central action and underlie dependence. Mutations in muscle subunits cause congenital myasthenic syndromes, and these receptors are the autoantigen in myasthenia gravis.

Innate immune cells detect gram-positive bacteria, bacterial and mycoplasmal lipoproteins and mycobacterial cell wall products through the TLR2 cascade, which converts that recognition into inflammatory gene expression and antimicrobial defence. TLR2 pairs with TLR1 or TLR6 and uses accessory molecules such as CD14 and CD36 to broaden ligand range, then signals through the adaptors MyD88 and TIRAP to IRAK1/4 and TRAF6, whose ubiquitin chains activate the TAK1–TAB complex. From there the IKK complex frees NF-κB by degrading IκB, while parallel MAP kinase arms (p38, JNK, ERK) drive AP-1, CREB and MEF2 targets. Endogenous alarmins including S100 proteins and HMGB1 feed the same route during sterile injury. Negative regulators such as IRAK3, SIGIRR, SOCS1 and phosphatases restrain output, and loss of that restraint favours excessive inflammation and septic tissue damage; the pathway also drives oxidative stress responses and cell death.

Nef Mediated CD8 Down-regulation is one of the immune-evasion tricks by which HIV rewires host membrane traffic: the viral accessory protein Nef strips the CD8 beta-chain from the surface of infected cells, blunting the cytotoxic T lymphocyte responses that would otherwise clear them. Nef is a membrane-associated adaptor that also removes CD4, CD28 and MHC class I, and here it links the cytoplasmic tail of CD8 beta, through an FMK motif, to the clathrin adaptor complex AP-2 assembled from its alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits, together with a V-ATPase subunit that assists Nef-dependent sorting. The receptor is thereby routed into accelerated clathrin-mediated endocytosis, while the alpha-chain is spared. The same Nef determinants required for CD4 removal are needed here, and the activity is conserved across HIV-1, HIV-2 and SIV, connecting receptor internalisation to persistence of infection.

HIV-1 uses its accessory protein Nef to strip immune recognition molecules from the surface of infected cells, and one target is the beta chain of the CD8 alpha-beta receptor on cytotoxic T lymphocytes. Loss of surface CD8 beta blunts the co-receptor function that lets killer T cells engage peptide-MHC class I efficiently, contributing, alongside Nef-driven removal of CD4 and MHC class I, to viral escape from cell-mediated immunity. Mechanistically Nef acts as a connector to the clathrin adaptor AP-2 complex, whose alpha, beta, mu and sigma subunits are all represented here, accelerating endocytosis of CD8 beta through a short cytoplasmic FMK motif; a subunit of the vacuolar ATPase participates in the trafficking step. The same Nef determinants required for CD4 removal are needed here, and the activity is conserved across HIV-1, HIV-2 and SIV.

Growth factor receptors must be switched off as reliably as they are switched on, and this pathway describes how ligand-activated EGFR is removed from the cell surface and destroyed so that signalling is limited in strength and duration. Loss of this braking system leaves the receptor chronically active, a route to transformation exploited by many epithelial tumours. After EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin or another ligand triggers autophosphorylation, the RING ubiquitin ligase CBL is recruited directly and through GRB2 and attaches ubiquitin to the receptor. The adaptor SH3KBP1 (CIN85) links CBL to endophilins, which bend membranes during clathrin-coated pit formation, while EPS15 and epsin read the ubiquitin mark and HGS/STAM sort the cargo into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation rather than recycling. Phosphatases such as PTPN12 and Sprouty proteins add further negative feedback on receptor and downstream kinase output.

Cytosolic DNA is a danger signal, and this is the route by which cells convert it into an antiviral and antibacterial transcriptional response. The ER-resident adaptor STING is engaged after cyclic dinucleotides are produced by cGAS or after DNA sensors such as IFI16 and DDX41 detect foreign nucleic acid, and it then traffics from the ER through the Golgi to perinuclear vesicles. There its C-terminal tail acts as a scaffold for TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 and, in some settings, STAT6, driving type I interferon and chemokine genes. The output governs immunity to DNA viruses, HIV, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Plasmodium, and is restrained at several points: TREX1 degrades cytosolic DNA, NLRC3 and NLRP4 dampen signalling, and ubiquitin ligases including DTX4 and TRIM21 tune adaptor and kinase stability. Loss of this restraint produces interferonopathies and autoimmunity, while nucleic-acid repair proteins including MRE11 and the DNA-PK components link genome damage to the same interferon output.

DNA in the cytosol is a sign of infection or of a cell's own genome gone astray, and the sensors gathered here are how cells detect it and respond with interferon. Recognition by cGAS and its adaptor STING, together with IFI16, DDX41, ZBP1, LRRFIP1 and DNA-PK subunits, converges on TBK1-mediated phosphorylation of IRF3 and on IKK-dependent NF-kB activation, driving type I interferon and inflammatory gene transcription. A parallel arm through AIM2 assembles an inflammasome that activates caspase-1 and matures IL-1beta and IL-18. RNA polymerase III offers an indirect route, transcribing AT-rich DNA into an RNA ligand for RIG-I-like signalling. The exonuclease TREX1 clears cytosolic DNA to keep the system quiet; when it fails, or when self-DNA persists, chronic interferon output produces autoinflammatory and lupus-like disease. This surveillance also shapes antiviral defence, antitumour immunity and responses to DNA damage.

Signaling by cytosolic FGFR1 fusion mutants describes the oncogenic signalling that drives 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome, an aggressive stem-cell disorder presenting with eosinophilia and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma that progresses rapidly to acute myeloid leukaemia and is currently curable only by allogeneic transplantation. Chromosomal translocations at 8p11 fuse the FGFR1 intracellular kinase domain to N-terminal partners such as ZMYM2, BCR, CUX1, CPSF6, TRIM24, LRRFIP1 or centrosomal proteins, each contributing a dimerization module. The resulting cytosolic kinase dimerizes without ligand and fires constitutively, so growth factor control is lost entirely. Because the fusions lack the membrane anchor and the FRS2 docking site, output is skewed toward PI3K and JAK-STAT arms, with STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5 activation and GRB2:GAB2 recruitment sustaining anti-apoptotic, prosurvival signalling and rendering haematopoietic progenitors independent of IL3. This is a paradigm for receptor tyrosine kinase fusion-driven leukaemogenesis.

Chromosomal translocations at 8p11 fuse the intracellular kinase domain of FGFR1 to N-terminal partners that supply a dimerization module, producing cytosolic fusion kinases that signal without ligand and drive the aggressive 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome, which presents with eosinophilia and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma and progresses rapidly to acute myeloid leukemia. Because the fusion lacks the receptor's transmembrane and extracellular regions, it sits in the cytoplasm and is constitutively dimerized by its partner, among them ZMYM2, BCR, CUX1, TRIM24, CPSF6, LRRFIP1 and centrosomal proteins. Downstream output favours phospholipase C-gamma, PI3K through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, and STAT family transcription factors including STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5, with GRB2 and GAB2 adaptors contributing weaker MAPK activation. The net effect is cytokine-independent, anti-apoptotic proliferation of haematopoietic progenitors, illustrating how loss of ligand control over a receptor kinase becomes leukaemogenic.

Gene amplification can drive cancer simply by putting too much receptor on the cell surface, and signaling by FGFR1 amplification mutants is the clearest example: copy-number gain at the 8p11 locus raises fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 levels without altering the kinase domain itself. The overexpressed receptor fires at a low ligand-independent level yet remains responsive to exogenous FGF, so aberrant autocrine or paracrine stimulation from the tumour or its stroma amplifies proliferation and survival output through the usual RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLC-gamma arms. Amplification is reported in squamous lung, breast, oesophageal, bladder, prostate and ovarian cancers and in rhabdomyosarcoma, making it a biomarker for FGFR-directed kinase inhibitors, though neighbouring 8p11 genes may contribute and causality is not settled in every tumour type.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 is a receptor tyrosine kinase that couples FGF ligands to proliferation, migration and differentiation signals in developing bone, brain and many epithelia. Point mutations that render it constitutively active shift this normally ligand-controlled output toward chronic signalling: a germline substitution at proline 252 in the ligand-binding region increases affinity for FGFs and causes Pfeiffer syndrome, a craniosynostosis disorder with premature suture fusion and digit anomalies, while the same residue is hit somatically in melanoma and lung cancer. Separate kinase-domain substitutions found in glioblastoma lie at positions whose equivalents in other FGFR family members produce skeletal dysplasias. The activating mutants still engage the secreted FGF ligands listed here, so the biology is one of amplified rather than rewired signalling, feeding into RAS-MAPK and PI3K routes that control skeletal patterning and tumour growth.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 normally requires ligand binding to dimerize, but point mutations, gene amplification and chromosomal translocations convert it into a constitutively active kinase, and activation of mutant FGFR1 in this way drives both congenital and neoplastic disease. Germline changes produce craniosynostosis and Kallmann syndromes, while somatic events underlie glioblastoma, lung and breast cancers and the myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms associated with 8p11 rearrangements.
