The fusion partners here an assortment of centrosomal, nuclear and coiled-coil proteins such as ZMYM2, CNTRL, CEP43, BCR, CPSF6 and TRIM24 contribute dimerization interfaces that force the kinase domain into a signalling-competent state without FGF ligand, although added ligand can amplify output. Downstream, GRB2 and GAB2 adaptors couple to PI3K through PIK3CA and PIK3R1, and STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5 are also engaged, converting unscheduled receptor firing into sustained proliferation and survival.

Germline and somatic changes in the fibroblast growth factor receptor FGFR2 make the receptor signal when it should not, and the consequences run from malformed skulls to cancer. Activating point mutations underlie craniosynostosis syndromes such as Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Apert and Jackson-Weiss, in which premature suture fusion and limb anomalies follow from excess signalling during skeletal development; the same kinase is activated by point mutation in endometrial cancer, by amplification in diffuse gastric and some breast cancers, and by fusion with partners that supply dimerization domains. Mutant receptors gain activity in several ways: ligand-independent dimerization, broadened affinity for the FGF ligand family represented here, heightened intrinsic kinase activity, or escape from internalization and degradation when C-terminal exons are lost. Because signalling remains kinase-dependent, these lesions are targets for FGFR inhibitors. The transcription and mRNA capping machinery included reflects transcriptional output downstream of receptor activation.

FGFR4 is the least characterised of the four fibroblast growth factor receptors, and unlike its relatives it has not been tied to congenital skeletal or craniofacial syndromes; its clinical interest comes instead from somatic mutations found in tumours such as rhabdomyosarcoma. Activation of mutant FGFR4 describes how these altered receptors signal outside normal control: substitutions in the coding sequence favour ligand-independent dimerisation and raise autophosphorylation of the intracellular kinase domain, so downstream cascades run without a fibroblast growth factor being present. Because wild-type FGFR4 normally couples growth factor availability to proliferation, survival and migration, and in the liver to bile acid feedback, constitutive firing of the receptor supports tumour cell growth and invasion. The receptor is therefore pursued as a kinase-inhibitor target, with mutation status shaping response.

FGFR3 normally restrains the proliferation of growth-plate chondrocytes in response to fibroblast growth factors, and point mutations that lock the receptor into a signalling state convert that brake into a constitutive signal. Substitutions in the extracellular ligand-binding domain, the transmembrane segment and the kinase domain allow dimerisation and tyrosine kinase activation without ligand, so the receptor fires irrespective of the FGF ligands — FGF1, FGF2, FGF8, FGF9, FGF18 and relatives — that would ordinarily control it. In the skeleton this produces the dominantly inherited dwarfing conditions, achondroplasia and the lethal thanatophoric dysplasias, through premature arrest of chondrocyte expansion and ossification. The same alleles act as oncogenic drivers in bladder and cervical carcinoma, head and neck and breast tumours, and multiple myeloma, where sustained receptor output feeds MAPK and PI3K signalling and makes FGFR3 a target for kinase inhibition.

Cells build and renew their subcellular compartments continuously, and organelle biogenesis and maintenance covers how that is done for the structures whose numbers and integrity must be controlled: centrioles, cilia, and mitochondria. Centriole duplication and elongation depend on a kinase-driven licensing step and a large complement of centrosomal scaffolds, pericentriolar material and the tubulins and augmin components that nucleate microtubules; failures cause microcephaly and centrosome amplification in cancer. The same platform matures into a basal body that templates a cilium, with intraflagellar transport trains, dynein and kinesin motors, transition-zone gatekeepers and small GTPases delivering cargo for Hedgehog and photoreceptor signalling, and mutations here produce the ciliopathies, including Bardet-Biedl, nephronophthisis and polycystic kidney disease. Multiciliated airway differentiation is imposed by dedicated transcription factors and microRNAs. In parallel, coactivator and nuclear-receptor circuits drive mitochondrial biogenesis, mitochondrial genome transcription, cristae architecture and ATP synthase assembly, matching respiratory capacity to demand.

Higher inositol phosphates made in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen must reach the nucleus, where IP4 and IP5 serve as substrates for further phosphorylation and as signalling molecules in their own right. This transport step links lipid-derived second messenger metabolism to nuclear events, since nuclear inositol polyphosphates influence mRNA export, chromatin remodelling and transcriptional regulation, and feed the kinase cascade that ultimately produces IP6 and the inositol pyrophosphates governing phosphate sensing and vesicle traffic. Inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases are distributed across the cytosol and nucleoplasm, so the pools they act on depend on movement of these charged, membrane-impermeant metabolites out of the ER lumen. How that movement occurs, whether by a dedicated carrier or by transfer during membrane continuity between the ER and the nuclear envelope, has not been resolved.

Synthesis of pyrophosphates in the cytosol builds the most highly phosphorylated inositol messengers, the diphosphoinositol polyphosphates IP7 and IP8, from IP5 and IP6. These molecules act as intracellular energy and phosphate sensors: they pyrophosphorylate target proteins non-enzymatically and compete with soluble inositol phosphates for binding pockets, tuning insulin secretion and sensitivity, vesicle trafficking, telomere length, phosphate homeostasis through the SPX-domain machinery, and Akt signalling. Loss of the kinases blunts these controls, and mice lacking one of them are lean and insulin-hypersensitive. Sequential kinases handle each step: IPPK and ITPK1 supply the IP6 precursor, IP6 kinases add a beta-phosphate at the 5-position, and the diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases PPIP5K1 and PPIP5K2 phosphorylate the 1-position to make IP8. A family of diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases reverses the reactions, so the pool turns over rapidly and levels track cellular metabolic state.

Inositol pyrophosphates are high-energy signalling molecules made in the cytosol by adding further phosphates to the already fully phosphorylated inositol ring, giving diphospho- and triphosphoinositol species such as 5-IP7 and IP8. They act as metabolic and phosphate-status sensors, tuning insulin secretion and sensitivity, phosphate homeostasis, vesicle trafficking, telomere length and the response to DNA damage, partly by pyrophosphorylating target proteins and partly by competing with inositol phosphate binding sites on effectors such as the Akt PH domain. Inositol hexakisphosphate kinases generate IP7 from IP6, while diphosphoinositol pentakisphosphate kinases add the second pyrophosphate to make IP8; upstream, IPPK and ITPK1 supply the precursor pool. Diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases of the Nudix family reverse these reactions, so cytosolic levels reflect a continuous synthesis-degradation cycle. Loss of IP6K1 in mice impairs growth, fertility and insulin signalling.

Inositol phosphates are small, highly charged signalling molecules, and several of the kinases that make them work in the nucleus, so the products must reach the cytosol to act on calcium release, phosphate sensing, vesicle traffic and other targets. This step describes that movement of inositol phosphates between nucleus and cytosol, which keeps nuclear synthesis coupled to cytoplasmic signalling; the transport mechanism itself is not well defined. The proteins assigned to it are the constituents of the nuclear pore complex: the scaffold Y-complex members such as NUP107, NUP133 and SEC13, transmembrane anchors including NDC1 and POM121, the FG-repeat channel nucleoporins NUP62 and NUP98 that form the permeability barrier, and the basket components TPR and NUP153. Passage of a small metabolite through this aqueous channel is therefore treated as diffusion across the pore rather than carrier-mediated transport.

Free myo-inositol is the starting material for all inositol lipids and inositol phosphates, and the cytosolic steps that generate IP2, IP and inositol are how cells recover it after receptor-stimulated phospholipase C signalling. A cascade of position-specific phosphatases strips phosphates from higher inositol phosphates and from lipid-derived species, ending with inositol monophosphatases that release free inositol; inositol-3-phosphate synthase provides a de novo route from glucose 6-phosphate, and an oxygenase route feeds inositol catabolism. The activity matters because it terminates calcium-mobilising and PI3K-derived signals while replenishing substrate for PIP2 resynthesis. Several members are disease genes: loss of the 5-phosphatase OCRL causes Lowy oculocerebrorenal syndrome, synaptojanin supports clathrin-mediated synaptic vesicle recycling, and INPP4B acts as a tumour suppressor. Lithium's inhibition of inositol monophosphatases places this recycling route in mood-disorder pharmacology.

Higher inositol phosphates made in the cytosol do not stay there: IP4, IP5 and IP6 also appear in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, and their movement between cytosol and ER lumen is the step that puts them there. This matters because inositol polyphosphates act as soluble signals and as counter-ions and cofactors, influencing calcium handling, nuclear and secretory-pathway functions, and the pools from which further pyrophosphorylated inositol messengers are drawn; compartmentalisation determines which of these uses a given pool can serve. Mechanistically the traffic is poorly defined, and is represented simply as myo-inositol-headgroup transmembrane transport across the ER membrane by a carrier that has not been identified molecularly. Conceptually it belongs with inositol phosphate metabolism and the wider problem of how charged small-molecule messengers cross intracellular membranes rather than being confined to the cytosol.

Synthesis of IPs in the nucleus builds the higher inositol phosphates inside the nucleus, generating soluble signalling molecules that act on transcription, mRNA export, chromatin remodelling and DNA repair rather than on membranes. These compounds also serve as a phosphate and energy reservoir, since the pyrophosphorylated forms can donate a high-energy phosphate directly to target proteins, coupling inositol phosphate levels to nutrient and phosphate sensing. A sequential kinase route does the work: a multikinase with relaxed specificity phosphorylates inositol trisphosphate and its products toward IP5, a dedicated 2-kinase completes IP6, and two inositol hexakisphosphate kinases add the diphosphate groups of IP7 and IP8. Output from this route influences apoptotic sensitivity, insulin secretion and telomere length control, and loss of individual kinases disturbs growth, ribosome biogenesis and nuclear RNA trafficking.

Inositol phosphates are not confined to membranes; a soluble, highly phosphorylated series is built inside the nucleus, and these molecules act as diffusible signals and phosphate donors rather than as lipid second messengers. Their production couples cellular phosphate and energy status to chromatin and RNA metabolism, with roles in mRNA export, transcriptional control, DNA repair and apoptosis, and it shapes how cells sense and store phosphate. In this nuclear branch, a multikinase phosphorylates lower inositol phosphates to IP4 and IP5, a 2-kinase completes IP6, and two inositol hexakisphosphate kinases add a high-energy pyrophosphate to generate IP7 and IP8, which can transfer phosphate to target proteins. Loss of individual kinases alters growth signalling and stress responses, and the same enzymes influence insulin secretion and tumour cell survival, placing nuclear inositol polyphosphate synthesis upstream of both gene expression and metabolic regulation.

Inositol polyphosphates made in the nucleus must reach other compartments to act, and this step describes their movement between the nucleoplasm and the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum, in particular the import of the fully phosphorylated species IP6. Such highly charged small molecules cannot cross membranes unaided, so their distribution depends on carriers or channels that have not been identified; the transport is inferred from the appearance of IP6 inside the ER rather than from a known transporter. The point of the traffic is signalling reach: inositol phosphates generated downstream of phospholipase C and successive inositol phosphate kinases regulate calcium handling, mRNA export, chromatin-associated processes and vesicle trafficking, and delivering them into the ER lumen places them alongside the cell's main internal calcium store and its protein folding machinery.

IP3 and IP4 transport between cytosol and nucleus describes the movement of the soluble inositol phosphate second messengers inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and inositol 1,3,4,5-tetrakisphosphate from the cytoplasm into the nucleoplasm, where a distinct pool of inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases acts on them. This matters because nuclear inositol phosphates control local calcium release, chromatin remodelling, mRNA export and transcriptional output, so calcium signalling initiated at the plasma membrane can be relayed into nuclear responses. The route is the nuclear pore complex, represented here by the full scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporin repertoire together with the basket and cytoplasmic filament components. Because these metabolites are small, passage may be simple diffusion through the pore channel rather than carrier-mediated transport. The pathway thus links phosphoinositide signalling downstream of phospholipase C to nucleocytoplasmic exchange and nuclear envelope architecture.

Inositol phosphate signalling is not confined to the cytoplasm: the nucleus maintains its own pool of inositol trisphosphate and tetrakisphosphate, which feed nuclear kinases and phosphatases and influence chromatin regulation, mRNA export and calcium release from nuclear envelope stores. Movement of IP3 and IP4 between cytosol and nucleoplasm supplies that pool, and it occurs across the nuclear pore complex, whose scaffold, transmembrane and FG-repeat nucleoporins are represented here alongside the Y-complex components, the central channel proteins, the basket formed by TPR and NUP153, and cytoplasmic filament elements such as RANBP2 and NUP214. Whether these small, highly charged metabolites simply diffuse through the pore's permeability barrier or are carried by a dedicated transporter is unresolved. Pore integrity therefore sets the boundary conditions for nuclear inositol phosphate signalling, and nucleoporin defects disturb nucleocytoplasmic exchange broadly, as in triple A syndrome caused by loss of AAAS.

Receptor-driven calcium signalling begins when phospholipase C cleaves membrane PIP2 to release inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, and the cytosolic inositol phosphate kinases and phosphatases collected here decide how long that signal lasts and what it becomes. The many PLC isoforms differ in how they are switched on al by G protein-coupled receptors, by tyrosine kinase receptors through PLCG1 and PLCG2, or by calcium itself al so the same second messenger reports on very different stimuli. Inositol trisphosphate 3-kinases such as ITPKA and ITPKB convert IP3 into inositol tetrakisphosphate, while 5-phosphatases including OCRL, INPPL1, INPP5D and synaptojanin strip phosphates and terminate signalling. The resulting pool of IP3 and IP4 species controls store release of calcium, membrane trafficking and lipid identity; loss of OCRL causes Lowe syndrome, and INPP5D shapes immune receptor thresholds.

Inositol phosphates made or accumulated in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen must reach the cytosol to act, and this transport step across the ER membrane connects the two pools. It matters because cytosolic IP3 is the ligand that opens ER calcium release channels, and higher phosphorylated species such as IP5 feed the kinase cascades that generate IP6 and inositol pyrophosphates, which in turn tune phosphate sensing, vesicle traffic and nuclear signalling. Movement of IP3 and IP5 out of the lumen therefore determines how much signalling inositol phosphate is available to receptors and to the enzymes that further modify them, linking lipid-derived second messenger production to calcium mobilisation. The carriers responsible have not been identified, so the step is defined by the substrates translocated and the compartments involved rather than by a characterised transport protein.

Highly phosphorylated inositols act as diffusible signals and phosphate donors inside the nucleus, where they influence chromatin regulation, mRNA export and transcription, so the cell must move inositol hexakisphosphate and the pyrophosphorylated form IP7 between cytosol and nucleus rather than making them only where they are used. This passage across the nuclear envelope is attributed to the nuclear pore complex, and the components here are its parts: the structural Y-complex scaffold with NUP107, NUP133, NUP85, SEC13 and SEH1L, the transmembrane ring anchors NDC1 and the POM121 proteins, the phenylalanine-glycine channel nucleoporins NUP62, NUP54 and NUP98 that form the permeability barrier, and peripheral elements such as NUP153, NUP50, RANBP2 and TPR on the cytoplasmic filaments and nuclear basket. How these small, densely charged metabolites are selected and translocated is not established, so the pathway is best read as the conduit rather than a defined carrier mechanism.

Higher inositol phosphates are best known as cytosolic signalling and phosphate-storage molecules, but a branch of their metabolism runs inside the endoplasmic reticulum lumen, where inositol polyphosphates are trimmed rather than built up. This compartmentalised turnover is carried out by multiple inositol polyphosphate phosphatase MINPP1, a broadly acting histidine phosphatase that removes phosphate groups from IP4, IP5 and IP6 to generate lower inositol phosphate species. Because the enzyme is separated from the cytosolic kinases that generate its substrates, its activity is thought to shape the pool of inositol phosphates available when membrane integrity is lost or substrates enter the secretory pathway, with consequences for calcium signalling and phosphate handling. Loss of MINPP1 function in humans causes a severe pontocerebellar hypoplasia, linking this lumenal dephosphorylation step to brain development.

Insulin-secreting beta cells arise during fetal pancreas development through a staged progression from budding endoderm epithelium to endocrine-committed progenitors to hormone-producing islet cells, and the transcriptional circuitry that drives it determines how much beta-cell mass a person is born with. Disruption of these regulators causes monogenic diabetes: heterozygous loss of HNF1A, HNF4A, HNF1B or PDX1 underlies maturity-onset diabetes of the young, and PDX1 or PTF1A loss can abolish the pancreas entirely. Notch signalling through RBPJ, HES1 and Mastermind-like coactivators holds progenitors in a proliferative undifferentiated state, while transient NEUROG3 expression commits cells to the endocrine fate and switches on a network including NEUROD1, NKX2-2, NKX6-1, PAX4, PAX6, RFX6 and INSM1. Downstream targets such as INS, IAPP, GCK and the glucose transporter SLC2A2 give the mature beta cell its glucose-sensing and secretory identity, with MAFA and FOXO1 tuning function postnatally.

Ligand-bound PDGF receptors autophosphorylate on tyrosines, and those phosphotyrosines become docking sites that convert receptor activation into intracellular responses — the downstream signal transduction step that makes PDGF a driver of fibroblast, smooth muscle and pericyte proliferation, migration and survival during development, angiogenesis and wound repair. SH2-domain proteins read the phosphorylated receptor tail: PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits generate lipid second messengers, PLCG1 releases diacylglycerol and IP3, SRC adds further tyrosine phosphorylation, the phosphatase PTPN11 and the adaptor GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1 route the signal to HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, while RASA1 acts as a Ras GTPase-activating protein to restrain it. CRK, NCK and BCAR1 link to cytoskeletal and adhesion control, and STAT family factors carry signal to the nucleus. Persistent PDGFR signalling through these routes contributes to fibrosis and to tumours bearing receptor fusions or activating mutations.

Platelet-derived growth factor signalling drives the proliferation, survival and migration of mesenchymal cells — fibroblasts, pericytes and vascular smooth muscle — and so underlies wound healing, vessel wall investment and connective tissue formation; its persistent activation feeds fibrosis, atherosclerotic intimal thickening and glioma growth, and receptor-activating mutations cause gastrointestinal stromal and other tumours. Four ligand chains dimerise and, for PDGF-C and -D, require proteolytic processing by furin or plasminogen-derived proteases before they can engage the alpha and beta receptor tyrosine kinases. Receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation create docking sites for GRB2–SOS1 and RAS proteins, PI3K subunits, PLCG1, SRC, the phosphatase PTPN11 and the adaptors CRK and BCAR1, coupling the receptor to growth, cytoskeletal remodelling and STAT-dependent transcription. Extracellular matrix components, including collagens and thrombospondins, sequester and present ligand, tying the response to the surrounding matrix.

TRKA receptor activation is the first step by which nerve growth factor instructs sensory and sympathetic neurons to survive, extend axons and express pain-sensing machinery; loss of NGF or its receptor NTRK1 causes congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis, while inappropriate activation drives pain sensitization and NTRK-fusion tumours. Mature NGF binds the TRKA ectodomain as a dimer, dimerizing the receptor and triggering trans-autophosphorylation of its cytoplasmic kinase domain, which creates docking sites for adaptors feeding into the RAS-ERK, PI3K-AKT and PLC-gamma routes. An alternative, ligand-independent route is represented here: the G protein-coupled receptors for adenosine and for pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide can transactivate TRKA and the related TRKB, apparently through intracellular cAMP-dependent signalling rather than neurotrophin binding, though the physiological weight of this crosstalk remains unsettled.

Neurotrophin receptors are usually switched on by nerve growth factor binding at the cell surface, but TRKA can also be activated without any neurotrophin at all, through signals arriving from G protein-coupled receptors. Adenosine acting on the A2a receptor and the neuropeptide PACAP acting on its type I receptor both raise cyclic AMP and, over the course of an hour or more, lead to tyrosine phosphorylation of TRKA and TRKB at an intracellular site thought to be the Golgi, with contributions from SRC-family kinase activity and intracellular calcium and a requirement for new transcription and protein synthesis. Unlike ligand-driven signalling, this slow transactivation route favours AKT over the ERK arm, biasing the outcome toward neuronal survival. It offers a way for neuromodulators and metabolic stress signals such as extracellular adenosine to keep neurons alive when trophic factor supply is limited.

Nerve growth factor acting through its receptor tyrosine kinase NTRK1 (TRKA) tells sensory and sympathetic neurons to survive, grow axons and differentiate, and loss-of-function mutations in this receptor or its ligand cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis. Ligand binding dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, which recruits SHC and FRS2 adaptors with GRB2/SOS to activate RAS family GTPases and the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, alongside PI3K and PLCG1 arms; the scaffold KIDINS220 and CRK/RAPGEF1-RAP1 routes shape how sustained the output is. Clathrin and AP-2 components with dynamins internalise the activated receptor, converting fast plasma-membrane signalling into the slower endosomal signalling that neuronal differentiation requires. ERK and p38 kinases then drive RSK, CREB, ELK1/SRF and MEF2 to induce immediate-early genes such as FOS and EGR family members, while DUSP phosphatases and PP2A limit the response. Brief signalling favours proliferation; prolonged signalling favours neurite outgrowth and neuropeptide expression.

Nerve growth factor signals the survival and differentiation of sympathetic and sensory neurons, and it does so by binding and activating the receptor tyrosine kinase TRKA. Secreted NGF homodimers engage TRKA, dimerising the receptor and triggering autophosphorylation of its cytoplasmic tyrosines, which creates docking sites for adaptors that feed into RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and PLC-gamma routes; the same ligand also binds the shared neurotrophin receptor p75NTR, and a joint NGF-p75NTR-TRKA complex can form, tuning ligand affinity and downstream output. Activated receptor-ligand complexes are internalised and carried retrogradely from axon terminals to the soma, coupling target-derived trophic supply to neuronal gene expression. Loss-of-function mutations in either partner cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis, reflecting failure of nociceptive and autonomic neuron development, while this axis also drives sensitisation of pain fibres in inflammation.

Entry into S phase requires that the brakes on cyclin-dependent kinases be removed, and this is the route by which they are destroyed. The CDK inhibitors p27 (CDKN1B) and p21 (CDKN1A) restrain cyclin E/A-CDK2 through G1; their ubiquitination by the SCF ubiquitin ligase using Skp2 as the substrate receptor, together with the small accessory protein Cks1, targets them to the 26S proteasome, and the resulting rise in CDK activity commits the cell to replication. Recognition is phosphorylation-dependent, notably at Thr187 of p27 by cyclin E/A-CDK2, creating a feed-forward loop in which residual kinase activity eliminates its own inhibitor. Skp2 levels are themselves timed by degradation earlier in G1, restricting this arm of proteolysis to late G1 onward. Skp2 overexpression lowers p27 in many tumours, linking this degradation step to loss of proliferative control.

Neurotrophin binding to its receptor must be converted into a lasting nuclear signal if a neuron is to differentiate, extend axons and survive, and signalling to ERKs is the route that does it. Nerve growth factor acting through TrkA recruits adaptors such as SHC proteins, FRS2 and the scaffold KIDINS220, which assemble GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1 to load RAS GTPases; RAS then engages BRAF and the MEK1/MEK2 kinases that phosphorylate ERK1 and ERK2. A parallel arm running through CRK adaptors and the exchange factor C3G activates RAP1 on early endosomes, giving a sustained signal where RAS output from the plasma membrane and coated vesicles is transient - a difference that distinguishes differentiation from mere proliferation. Related RIT and RAL GTPases and stress-activated p38 kinases broaden the output. Constitutive activation of these components underlies many cancers and developmental RASopathies.

Nerve growth factor acting through its receptor tyrosine kinase TrkA does not signal only through classical RAS; it also engages the RAS-family GTPases RIT1 and RIT2, and this branch feeds preferentially into p38 MAP kinase. The route matters for neuronal differentiation and neurite outgrowth, the characteristic response of sympathetic and sensory neurons to neurotrophin stimulation. RIT1 and RIT2 resemble RAS across the core effector region but lack the C-terminal prenylation motif that anchors RAS at the plasma membrane, so their membrane targeting and localisation differ; RIT1 is broadly expressed while RIT2 is largely neuronal. Once GTP-loaded, they recruit BRAF and drive the downstream MAP kinase cascade toward p38 as well as ERK activation. Germline RIT1 mutations cause a Noonan-like RASopathy, and the same gene is somatically mutated in lung adenocarcinoma and myeloid disease.

Dietary starch and disaccharides must be broken down to monosaccharides before they can be absorbed, and this is the route by which most dietary calories enter the body. Salivary and pancreatic amylases begin the work in the lumen, cleaving amylose and amylopectin into maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins. Completion occurs at the brush border of small intestinal enterocytes, where membrane-anchored enzymes release glucose, galactose and fructose for uptake by intestinal sugar transporters. Sucrase-isomaltase handles sucrose and branched dextrins, maltase-glucoamylase the linear oligomers, lactase the milk sugar lactose, and trehalase the disaccharide trehalose. Loss of lactase expression after weaning produces lactose intolerance, and congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhoea after starch or sucrose intake. The associated chitinases act on chitin rather than starch, reflecting the broader glycoside hydrolase activity of the gut and secretory tissues.

Cellular hexose transport is how glucose, fructose and galactose cross plasma membranes, and it sets the terms for whole-body sugar handling: dietary absorption in the small intestine, reabsorption in the kidney tubule, delivery across the blood-brain barrier, insulin-stimulated uptake into muscle and fat, and release of glucose from liver into blood. Two families do the work. The SLC2 (GLUT) proteins carry hexoses passively down their concentration gradient, with tissue-restricted isoforms such as GLUT1 for brain endothelium, GLUT2 for hepatocyte and enterocyte basolateral flux, GLUT4 for insulin-responsive tissues and GLUT5 for fructose. The SLC5 (SGLT) proteins instead couple sugar uptake to the sodium gradient, allowing enterocytes and proximal tubule cells to absorb glucose against a gradient. Intracellular phosphorylation traps the sugar, making uptake effectively unidirectional except where glucose 6-phosphatase is expressed. Mutations cause GLUT1 deficiency epilepsy, renal glycosuria and glucose-galactose malabsorption, and SGLT2 is a major diabetes drug target.

Sugars cannot cross membranes unaided, so every tissue depends on carrier proteins to move glucose, fructose and galactose into and out of cells. Cellular hexose transport covers the two families that do this work: the facilitative GLUTs of the SLC2 family, which allow sugar to follow its concentration gradient, and the sodium-coupled SGLTs of the SLC5 family, which concentrate glucose and galactose against a gradient using the sodium electrochemical potential. Together they mediate dietary sugar absorption across the intestinal epithelium, glucose reclamation from the renal filtrate, delivery of fuel to the brain across the blood-brain barrier, and insulin-regulated uptake into muscle and fat via GLUT4. Loss of individual carriers produces distinct disease: GLUT1 deficiency causes infantile epilepsy, GLUT2 mutation causes Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, and SGLT2 is the target of glucose-lowering drugs that force renal glucose excretion.

Porphyrin metabolism covers the making and unmaking of the tetrapyrrole ring that holds iron in heme, the cofactor that lets hemoglobin carry oxygen, cytochromes pass electrons, and catalase and peroxidases dispose of hydrogen peroxide. Synthesis begins with condensation of glycine and succinyl-CoA by an erythroid-specific or housekeeping aminolevulinate synthase, proceeds through ALAD, HMBS, UROS, UROD, CPOX and PPOX, and ends when ferrochelatase inserts ferrous iron; partial blocks at these steps cause the porphyrias, in which accumulated intermediates provoke photosensitivity and neurovisceral attacks. Further tailoring by COX10 and COX15 yields heme A for cytochrome oxidase. On the catabolic side heme oxygenases open the ring to release iron, carbon monoxide and biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases convert to bilirubin for glucuronidation by UGT1A1 and biliary export by ABCC2 and related transporters. The route links iron economy, erythropoiesis and hepatic bile pigment handling; failure of conjugation or export produces jaundice.

Heme is the iron-containing tetrapyrrole that lets hemoglobin carry oxygen and lets cytochromes, catalase and P450 enzymes do redox chemistry, and its biosynthesis is concentrated in erythroid precursors and hepatocytes. The route begins in mitochondria with condensation of succinyl-CoA and glycine by ALA synthase, whose erythroid-specific form ALAS2 sets the pace of red cell heme supply while ALAS1 serves other tissues. Four cytosolic steps build and decarboxylate the tetrapyrrole ring through porphobilinogen, uroporphyrinogen III and coproporphyrinogen III, after which the intermediates return to mitochondria for side-chain oxidation and insertion of ferrous iron by ferrochelatase. Enzyme deficiencies cause the porphyrias, in which accumulated photoreactive porphyrins damage skin or neurotoxic precursors provoke acute attacks; ALAS2 loss instead gives sideroblastic anemia. Transport proteins handle porphyrin and heme efflux, and downstream heme a synthesis feeds cytochrome c oxidase assembly.

Heme degradation disposes of the heme released when red cells are broken down, several hundred milligrams a day, while salvaging its iron for reuse. It matters because free heme is a pro-oxidant and because the pathway's end product, bilirubin, must be conjugated and excreted; blocks at successive steps produce the jaundice of hemolysis, Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes, and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia. Microsomal heme oxygenases open the porphyrin ring, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and yielding biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases reduce to bilirubin. Albumin carries bilirubin in blood, hepatic organic anion transporters take it up, cytosolic binding proteins and glutathione transferases shuttle it, UDP-glucuronosyltransferase conjugates it with glucuronic acid, and ABC-family efflux pumps export the conjugate into bile. The inducible oxygenase HMOX1 also makes this route a cytoprotective response to oxidative and inflammatory stress.

Senescent red cells release several grams of hemoglobin daily, and heme degradation is the route by which its porphyrin ring is dismantled, its iron salvaged, and the remainder excreted. Heme oxygenases HMOX1 and HMOX2 open the ring at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, releasing iron and carbon monoxide and yielding biliverdin, which biliverdin reductases BLVRA and BLVRB reduce to bilirubin. Because bilirubin is lipophilic and neurotoxic, it travels bound to albumin, is taken up by hepatocytes through organic anion transporters of the SLCO family, held by cytosolic binding proteins, conjugated with glucuronic acid by UGT1A1, and pumped into bile by ABCC2 and related efflux pumps. Loss of conjugating capacity produces the unconjugated hyperbilirubinemias, from benign Gilbert syndrome to kernicterus, while the inducible oxygenase arm also serves as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory stress response.

Fibroblast growth factors and their four receptor tyrosine kinases form a signalling system that instructs cell fate, proliferation, migration and survival throughout development and in adult tissue repair, bone growth and phosphate homeostasis. Ligands require heparan sulfate, or the Klotho co-receptors KL and KLB for the endocrine FGF19/FGF23 branch, to assemble productive receptor dimers; receptor autophosphorylation then creates docking sites for GRB2, SHC1, FRS2 and PTPN11, launching RAS-ERK signalling through HRAS/KRAS, BRAF and MAPK1/3, PI3K via PIK3CA and PIK3R1, and PLCG1. Adhesion molecules such as the FLRT proteins offer a ligand-independent route used in neural contexts. Output is tuned by negative regulators including SPRY2, SPRED proteins, CBL-mediated ubiquitination and phosphatase PP2A, while ESRP and hnRNP splicing factors switch FGFR2 between its epithelial b and mesenchymal c isoforms. Germline mutations cause craniosynostosis, dwarfism and Kallmann syndrome; somatic activation drives many carcinomas.

Fibroblast growth factors bind FGFR3 at the cell surface and dimerize it, switching on the receptor's tyrosine kinase activity; unusually among growth factor receptors, the output restrains rather than promotes growth, acting as a brake on chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plates of long bones. Ligand binding and activation of FGFR3 therefore sets skeletal proportion: constitutively activating mutations shorten bones, producing achondroplasia and the milder hypochondroplasia, while the same lesions acquired somatically drive multiple myeloma and bladder and cervical carcinoma. Selectivity comes from which FGFs an FGFR3 splice variant can engage, with heparan sulfate needed for stable complex formation. FGF23 stands apart as an endocrine, bone-derived phosphate-regulating hormone whose secretion depends on O-glycosylation by GALNT3, linking this receptor family to renal phosphate handling as well as to local skeletal growth control.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 sits at the interface between epithelium and mesenchyme, and the step described here is the one that switches it on: binding of a fibroblast growth factor ligand, with heparan sulfate and secreted FGF-binding proteins controlling how much free ligand reaches the receptor. Which ligands bind depends on alternative splicing of the receptor's third immunoglobulin loop, so the same gene reads epithelial ligands such as FGF7 and FGF10 in one isoform and mesenchymal ligands such as FGF2, FGF8 and FGF18 in the other. Ligand-driven dimerisation triggers kinase transactivation and downstream growth, survival and patterning signals. The consequences are developmental: dominant activating mutations in this receptor cause Crouzon, Apert, Pfeiffer and Jackson-Weiss craniosynostosis, in which cranial sutures fuse prematurely, while the same signalling governs limb, lung and skin morphogenesis.

FGFR1 ligand binding and activation is the first step in fibroblast growth factor signalling through receptor 1, the event that converts an extracellular FGF gradient into a receptor dimer poised to fire. It governs limb and craniofacial patterning, skeletal growth, olfactory bulb and GnRH neuron development, and phosphate homeostasis; loss-of-function mutations in FGFR1 or its partner anosmin cause Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while activating changes drive craniosynostosis and several cancers. Which of the paracrine FGFs binds is set by alternative splicing of the receptor's third immunoglobulin domain and by heparan sulfate, with anosmin and TGFBR3 acting as accessory co-receptors and GIPC1 shaping trafficking. The endocrine ligand FGF23 instead requires Klotho, linking the receptor to renal phosphate handling. Ligand capture here dictates the downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLC-gamma responses, and FGFR1 also reaches the nucleus to influence transcription directly.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 becomes a signalling receptor when one of a large family of FGF ligands, presented with a heparan sulfate or Klotho co-receptor, binds its extracellular immunoglobulin domains and drives receptor dimerisation and kinase activation. This ligand binding and activation step sets the specificity of the whole pathway: alternative splicing of FGFR1 and the restricted expression of individual FGFs determine which cells respond, so the same downstream cascade can direct proliferation, migration, or differentiation depending on context. The biology governs limb and craniofacial patterning, skeletal growth, and, through FGF8 and the extracellular protein anosmin-1 encoded by ANOS1, the migration of GnRH neurons — loss of which causes Kallmann syndrome with hypogonadism and anosmia. FGF23 with Klotho instead signals phosphate handling. Co-receptors and adaptors such as betaglycan and GIPC1 modulate ligand availability and receptor trafficking; aberrant FGFR1 activation recurs in cancer.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 binds a distinct subset of FGF ligands at the cell surface and converts them into intracellular signals; the receptor is prominent in mature skeletal muscle, and losing its signalling disrupts limb muscle formation in vertebrates. Ligand binding and activation of FGFR4 begins when a paracrine FGF, together with heparan sulfate, dimerises the receptor and triggers trans-autophosphorylation of its kinase domains, feeding into the RAS-MAPK and PI3K routes that drive proliferation, differentiation and survival. FGFR4 is also the endocrine arm of this family: with the coreceptor beta-Klotho it responds to FGF19 to suppress hepatic bile acid synthesis, and it can partner FGF23 in phosphate handling. Ligands here range from FGF1 and FGF2 to the developmental FGF8/FGF17/FGF18 group and muscle-associated FGF6. Aberrant FGFR4 activity contributes to rhabdomyosarcoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.

Alternative splicing of the third immunoglobulin-like domain of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 produces two isoforms with distinct ligand preferences, and FGFR1b ligand binding and activation covers the subset of FGFs that engage the epithelial 'b' form. This selectivity is how epithelium and mesenchyme talk to each other without crosstalk: mesenchymally produced FGF3, FGF7-family and FGF10 signal to epithelial receptors, driving branching morphogenesis, limb and craniofacial outgrowth, and wound repair, while FGF1 binds both isoforms. Ligand engagement requires heparan sulfate, and betaglycan (TGFBR3) can act as a heparan sulfate proteoglycan co-receptor; dimerisation then activates the receptor tyrosine kinase and downstream RAS-ERK, PI3K and PLCγ output. The PDZ adaptor GIPC1 contributes to receptor trafficking. Mutations altering isoform choice or ligand affinity underlie craniosynostosis and Kallmann syndrome, and aberrant FGFR1 signalling recurs in cancer.

FGFR3b is the epithelial splice variant of fibroblast growth factor receptor 3, and this step describes which fibroblast growth factors actually engage it and switch it on. The choice of ligand matters because FGFR3 signalling restrains chondrocyte proliferation in growth plates and supports epithelial and skeletal patterning; gain-of-function receptor mutations cause achondroplasia and related dwarfing skeletal dysplasias, while activating lesions in epithelia contribute to bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma. Binding of FGF1, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 or FGF20, with heparan sulfate as a co-factor, dimerises the receptor and juxtaposes its kinase domains for trans-autophosphorylation, creating docking sites that feed into the RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLC-gamma routes. The affinities of these ligands differ widely, so the isoform's response is set by which factors a tissue secretes rather than by the receptor alone.

FGFR3 is expressed as alternatively spliced isoforms with different ligand preferences, and the mesenchymal-type 'c' variant binds a distinct set of fibroblast growth factors to initiate receptor dimerisation and kinase activation. FGFR3c signalling restrains chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, so its activity sets limits on long bone elongation; activating mutations cause achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, while loss of signalling produces skeletal overgrowth, and somatic mutations drive bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma. Paracrine ligands including FGF1, FGF2, FGF4, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 and FGF20 engage the receptor together with heparan sulfate, whereas the endocrine ligand FGF23 requires a Klotho co-receptor and acts in phosphate homeostasis; GALNT3 glycosylates FGF23 to protect it from proteolytic inactivation before secretion. Ligand binding is the committed step upstream of downstream growth and differentiation signalling.

FGFR1c is the mesenchymal splice variant of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1, and this step describes which fibroblast growth factors actually engage it and drive receptor dimerisation and kinase activation. The choice of ligand determines the downstream output, since FGFR1c signalling shapes limb and skeletal patterning, cranial suture closure, midline and olfactory development, and, through FGF23, renal phosphate handling. Loss of this signalling arm underlies Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, in which the extracellular matrix protein anosmin-1 encoded by ANOS1 acts as a cofactor for ligand presentation; activating mutations instead cause craniosynostosis. Ligands including FGF1, FGF2, FGF4, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17 and FGF20 bind with differing affinity, often requiring heparan sulfate or, for FGF23, a Klotho-type cofactor, while betaglycan and the adaptor GIPC1 modulate receptor availability and trafficking.

Phosphate balance between bone and kidney depends on this receptor pairing: the bone-derived hormone FGF23 signals to the kidney only when the FGFR1c splice form of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 is partnered with the transmembrane protein Klotho. FGFR1c alone binds FGF23 too weakly to respond, so Klotho acts as the obligate co-receptor that converts a generic growth factor receptor into a high-affinity endocrine FGF23 receptor and thereby restricts hormone action to Klotho-expressing tissue, chiefly the renal tubule. Ligand binding and receptor dimerisation launch downstream kinase signalling that suppresses phosphate reabsorption and lowers active vitamin D synthesis. Excess FGF23 signalling produces hypophosphataemic rickets and osteomalacia, while loss of Klotho or FGF23 causes hyperphosphataemia, vascular calcification and premature ageing phenotypes; the axis is also central to mineral disturbance in chronic kidney disease.

FGFR2c ligand binding and activation is the ligand-recognition step of one specific fibroblast growth factor receptor splice variant, the mesenchymal 'c' isoform of FGFR2, whose engagement drives skeletal patterning, osteoblast differentiation and suture closure in the developing skull. Alternative splicing of the third immunoglobulin-like domain determines which FGFs a cell can hear, so the c isoform responds to a mesenchyme-facing panel including FGF1, FGF2, FGF4, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 and the endocrine ligand FGF23, while the epithelial b isoform reads a different set. Ligand binding, stabilised by heparan sulfate or by Klotho co-receptors for endocrine ligands, dimerises the receptor and triggers kinase transactivation feeding into RAS-MAPK, PI3K and PLCgamma output. Mutations that relax this isoform-restricted binding underlie craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, and aberrant FGFR2 signalling recurs in cancer.

The FGFR2c splice variant is the mesenchymal form of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2, and this step covers which fibroblast growth factors actually bind it and switch it on. Ligand selection here is what makes FGF signalling tissue-specific: alternative splicing of the receptor's third immunoglobulin-like domain gives FGFR2c a preference for FGF2, FGF4, FGF6, FGF8, FGF9, FGF17, FGF18 and related ligands, whereas the epithelial FGFR2b form responds to a different group, and the reciprocal epithelial-mesenchymal exchange of ligands drives limb outgrowth, skeletal patterning and organ branching. FGF23 acts in this family as an endocrine regulator of phosphate handling and requires a Klotho co-receptor. Binding assembles a ligand-receptor complex with heparan sulfate, dimerises the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation of its cytoplasmic kinase, initiating downstream growth and differentiation signalling. Mutations that alter FGFR2 ligand binding or activation cause craniosynostosis syndromes, and the receptor is amplified in several cancers.

FGFR2b is the epithelial splice variant of fibroblast growth factor receptor 2, and this step covers which fibroblast growth factors actually engage it and switch it on. The pairing matters because FGFR2b on epithelium reads signals sent by mesenchyme: FGF7, FGF10, FGF22 and FGF3 are among the ligands selective for this isoform, and their action drives branching morphogenesis of lung, salivary gland, limb bud ectoderm, skin and hair follicles, as well as epithelial repair. Loss of FGF10 or FGFR2b function causes limb and lacrimal/salivary gland agenesis in humans, while receptor activating mutations and isoform switching feature in cancer. Broader-specificity ligands such as FGF1 and FGF2 also activate the receptor, and secreted FGF binding proteins act as extracellular chaperones that release heparan-sulfate-bound FGFs to reach it, initiating receptor dimerisation and tyrosine kinase signalling.

Gap junction channels begin as connexons, hexameric hemichannels formed when six connexin subunits oligomerize in the secretory pathway before reaching the plasma membrane and docking with a connexon on a neighbouring cell. This assembly step sets the permeability and gating of the resulting channel, and so determines what small metabolites, ions and second messengers can pass directly between coupled cells. Six identical subunits give a homomeric connexon; mixtures of compatible connexins give heteromeric ones, and compatibility appears restricted within the alpha or beta subgroups, with short sequence determinants contributing to selectivity. Depending on the connexin and the cell type, oligomerization occurs after insertion into the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, or in the trans-Golgi network. The connexins involved here, including Cx43, Cx32 and Cx26, underlie cardiac and glial coupling, peripheral nerve myelin integrity and cochlear function, and their mutation causes deafness and demyelinating neuropathy.

Gap junctions form only after their subunits have travelled the classical secretory route, and this pathway covers that journey: connexins are inserted into the ER membrane, pass through the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and Golgi to the trans-Golgi network, and reach the plasma membrane as hexameric connexons ready to dock with a partner hemichannel on an apposed cell. The step that distinguishes connexins from ordinary cargo is oligomerization, and where it happens depends on the isoform and the cell: Cx32 assembles during or soon after ER insertion, Cx26 in the intermediate compartment, and Cx43 only in the trans-Golgi network. Delivery of these three subunits supports direct cytoplasmic coupling in heart and skin, myelinating Schwann cells, and the cochlea; trafficking and assembly defects underlie X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, hereditary deafness and skin disorders.

Gap junctions let neighbouring cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers directly, coordinating cardiac and smooth muscle contraction, lens transparency, cochlear homeostasis, myelin function and epidermal differentiation. Gap junction trafficking covers the life cycle that puts these channels where they are needed: connexins are made at the endoplasmic reticulum, oligomerize into hexameric connexons, transit the Golgi, and are carried on microtubules to the plasma membrane, where they diffuse laterally and aggregate into plaques that dock with connexons on the apposing cell. Turnover runs through clathrin-mediated internalization, with adaptor, dynamin and actin-based motor components such as AP2M1, DAB2, DNM2 and MYO6 driving uptake of channel plaques for lysosomal and proteasomal degradation. The large connexin family here, including GJA1, GJB2 and GJC2, explains why mutations in individual members cause tissue-specific disease: deafness, cataract, peripheral neuropathy, skin disorders and cardiac conduction defects.

Microtubule-dependent trafficking of connexons from Golgi to the plasma membrane is the delivery step that lets cells build gap junctions, the channels through which coupled cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers. Connexin hexamers assembled in the Golgi are packaged into secretory vesicles and moved outward in saltatory fashion along curvilinear microtubules, then docked at the surface where they pair with connexons on a neighbouring cell to form an open channel. The genes reflect this dependence on the tubulin cytoskeleton, with alpha- and beta-tubulin isotypes providing the tracks and connexin 43 the cargo. Because gap junction plaques turn over rapidly, continuous microtubule-based supply sets the level of intercellular coupling in heart, lens, skin and glia, and disruption of connexin delivery underlies conduction defects, cataract and hearing loss.

Gap junction channels must be delivered to the cell surface before neighbouring cells can couple electrically and metabolically, and this step carries newly assembled connexons from the Golgi to the plasma membrane along microtubules. The cargo is connexin 43 (GJA1), which oligomerises into hexameric connexons in the secretory pathway and is then moved in vesicles that travel in saltatory fashion along curvilinear microtubule tracks, docking at the membrane where they can join a partner hemichannel on an apposed cell. The remainder of the machinery is the alpha- and beta-tubulin heterodimer pool that builds those tracks. Because connexin 43 turns over within hours, continuous microtubule-based delivery sets how much coupling a tissue has, which matters for cardiac conduction, lens transparency and coordinated contraction; disrupted trafficking or connexin mutation reduces junctional plaques and produces arrhythmia and cataract.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic channels that let neighbouring cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers, the basis of electrical coupling in heart and nerve, coordinated contraction, lens transparency, cochlear ion homeostasis and epidermal differentiation. Connexins are synthesised at the endoplasmic reticulum, oligomerise into homomeric or heteromeric hexameric connexons, traverse the Golgi, and are stored in trans-Golgi membranes before microtubule-based delivery to the plasma membrane; there they diffuse laterally and dock with partner hemichannels on the apposed cell, aggregating into ordered plaques. Cx43-containing junctions reciprocally capture and stabilise microtubule plus ends, which explains the prominence of alpha- and beta-tubulins alongside the connexin family here. Mutations in individual connexins cause deafness, peripheral neuropathy, congenital cataract, palmoplantar keratoderma and arrhythmia, each reflecting the tissue where that isoform carries coupling.

Gap junction assembly builds the direct cytoplasmic channels that let neighbouring cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers, giving tissues electrical and metabolic continuity dash synchronous contraction in heart and uterus, ionic recycling in the cochlea, lens transparency, and myelin homeostasis in Schwann cells and oligodendrocytes. Connexin polypeptides are made at the endoplasmic reticulum and oligomerize into hexameric hemichannels, which traverse the Golgi, are stored in trans-Golgi membranes and then delivered to the plasma membrane along microtubules, accounting for the large tubulin component here. Once inserted, connexons diffuse laterally, dock with partners on the apposing cell and cluster into plaques, and Cx43-based junctions in turn capture microtubule plus-ends. Different connexin genes serve different tissues, and their mutation causes deafness, skin disorders such as erythrokeratodermia, cataract, X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and cardiac conduction defects.

Gap junctions form only after connexin hexamers, the connexons, reach the cell surface, and the delivery step that moves assembled hemichannels from the Golgi to the plasma membrane is what this pathway covers. It matters because direct electrical and metabolic coupling between neighbouring cells depends on where and how fast new channels arrive: cardiac conduction relies on connexin 43 reaching intercalated discs, and cochlear connexin 26 supports potassium recycling in the inner ear, with loss-of-function mutations causing arrhythmia-prone hearts and congenital deafness. Post-Golgi carriers roughly 50-200 nm across ferry connexons outward along a dense complement of alpha- and beta-tubulins, and microtubule plus ends can target connexin cargo directly to nascent junctional plaques. A microtubule-independent route also appears to operate, so channel delivery is regulated trafficking rather than passive diffusion, and it sets the turnover and placement of intercellular channels.

Connexin channels turn over unusually fast, with half-lives of only a few hours, so gap junctional communication between cells is controlled as much by removal of channels as by their delivery. This route retrieves connexin43 and the plaques it forms from the plasma membrane and commits them to lysosomal and proteasomal destruction, allowing coupling to be rapidly rescaled during wound healing, cardiac remodelling, tissue differentiation and mitosis. Internalisation uses the clathrin machinery: a clathrin coat assembled from heavy and light chains with the AP-2 mu subunit and the alternative cargo adaptor DAB2, scission by the dynamins, and inward movement supported by myosin VI and the actin cytoskeleton. The resulting double-membrane annular junction is then degraded. Phosphorylation of connexins and their partner interactions set the pace, and failure to clear channels appropriately disturbs electrical and metabolic coupling in heart and epithelia.

Pre-NOTCH Processing in the Endoplasmic Reticulum is the quality-control and cofactor-installation step that makes a newly synthesised NOTCH receptor competent to signal, long before it ever meets a ligand. NOTCH signalling governs cell-fate decisions across development from somite and vascular patterning to lymphocyte lineage choice and intestinal secretory differentiation so failure at this step blocks all of it. Within the ER lumen, two dedicated glycosyltransferases decorate conserved serines and threonines in the tandem EGF repeats of the NOTCH1-4 precursors: POFUT1 adds O-fucose at a C2-X(4-5)-S/T-C3 motif, and POGLUT1, the mammalian counterpart of Drosophila Rumi, adds O-glucose at a C1-X-S-X-P-C2 motif. These sugars stabilise EGF repeat folding, permit ER exit, and set the receptor's later sensitivity to Delta- and Jagged-type ligands, with the fucose serving as the substrate for Fringe-mediated tuning. Loss of POGLUT1 causes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy and Dowling-Degos disease.

Before a NOTCH receptor can respond to ligand, its extracellular EGF repeats must be sugar-modified in the endoplasmic reticulum, and this early processing step determines whether the receptor folds correctly and reaches the surface in a signalling-competent form. All four human NOTCH precursors are substrates. An O-fucosyltransferase adds fucose to serine or threonine residues at a defined position between the second and third cysteines of an EGF repeat, while an O-glucosyltransferase adds glucose to serines in a separate consensus site; the fucose later serves as the acceptor for Fringe-mediated elongation that tunes ligand preference. Loss of either modification cripples NOTCH output, with consequences for the lineage decisions, somite and vascular patterning, and progenitor maintenance that depend on NOTCH, and mutations in the glucosyltransferase cause a form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy.

Before any Notch receptor can respond to a ligand, it has to be made, and this pathway covers the steps that set how much NOTCH1-4 protein a cell has: transcription of the receptor genes, their repression by microRNAs, and the co-translational targeting of nascent peptides to the endoplasmic reticulum for processing en route to the cell surface. Receptor abundance sets the gain of Notch signalling, which governs cell fate choices in development, neurogenesis, vascular and biliary formation, and lymphocyte differentiation; mutation of individual receptors causes CADASIL, Alagille syndrome and T-cell leukaemia. Transcription of the NOTCH genes is driven by activators including RBPJ with Mastermind-like coactivators, E2F factors, RUNX1 and JUN, with histone acetyltransferase activity from EP300, CREBBP and KAT2A/KAT2B on chromatin. Opposing this, p53-induced miR-34 family members and other microRNAs acting through Argonaute-TNRC6 complexes silence NOTCH transcripts, and the partially duplicated NOTCH2NL genes further modulate signalling output.

Before a NOTCH receptor can respond to ligand on a neighbouring cell, it must be matured in the Golgi, and this processing step sets how strongly and to which ligands it will respond. FURIN cleaves the ~300 kDa precursor into extracellular and transmembrane-intracellular fragments that reassociate as a calcium-stabilised heterodimer, the form displayed at the cell surface. Trafficking to and through the Golgi is quality-controlled by SEL1L in the ER and TMED2 in the Golgi membrane and promoted by the GTPase RAB6A, while SERCA calcium pumps supply the luminal calcium the heterodimer requires. Fringe glycosyltransferases LFNG, MFNG and RFNG elongate O-fucose on the EGF repeats, extended further by B4GALT1 and ST3GAL sialyltransferases; this sugar code raises affinity for Delta-like ligands and lowers it for Jagged, biasing lateral inhibition, somite segmentation and angiogenic tip-cell selection.

Before a NOTCH receptor can respond to a ligand on a neighbouring cell, it must be transcribed, translated, glycosylated and cleaved into a functional heterodimer, and this maturation route covers all four human receptors. Because NOTCH signalling governs binary cell-fate decisions in development, stem cell maintenance, T cell specification and vascular patterning, the quality of receptor synthesis sets the gain of every downstream decision. Transcription of the NOTCH genes is controlled by factors including RBPJ-associated complexes, RUNX1, E2F/TFDP and p53, with the acetyltransferases EP300, CREBBP and KAT2A/KAT2B acting on chromatin, while a large set of microRNAs loaded into Argonaute-containing silencing complexes damps translation of NOTCH messages. In the endoplasmic reticulum POFUT1 adds O-fucose and POGLUT1 adds O-glucose to EGF repeats; Golgi fringe enzymes elongate the fucose to tune ligand preference, and FURIN cleavage yields the cell-surface heterodimer.

Cells build cholesterol from acetyl-CoA when dietary supply is insufficient, and the product is needed for membrane fluidity, lipid raft organisation, bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D. The route runs through the mevalonate pathway -- HMG-CoA synthase and the rate-limiting, statin-targeted HMG-CoA reductase, then the kinases and decarboxylase that generate isoprenoid units -- to squalene via farnesyl diphosphate synthase and squalene synthase, then to lanosterol through squalene epoxidase and lanosterol synthase. Post-lanosterol demethylation, isomerisation, desaturation and reduction steps convert sterol intermediates to cholesterol, with DHCR24 reducing the C24 double bond either late (Bloch route) or early, and DHCR7 acting last in the alternative route. Transcription is controlled by SREBF1/2 in response to sterol depletion. Enzyme defects cause malformation syndromes such as Smith-Lemli-Opitz, CHILD syndrome and chondrodysplasia punctata, showing how sterol intermediates shape development.

Gap junctions built from connexin 43 let adjacent cells share ions, metabolites and second messengers directly, coordinating electrical coupling in heart and smooth muscle and metabolic cooperation in many epithelia; regulation of gap junction activity determines how open that conduit is. Coupling is not fixed but gated by phosphorylation of the connexin cytoplasmic tail. The tyrosine kinase Src binds connexin 43 and phosphorylates it, displacing the scaffold protein ZO-1 from the channel's carboxy-terminal binding site and closing the junction; serine phosphorylation by protein kinase C and by MAP kinases similarly promotes channel gating and turnover of the connexin. Loss of coupling is a recurring feature of transformed cells, and in the heart reduced or mislocalised connexin 43 favours conduction slowing and arrhythmia, so this control step links growth-factor and oncogenic kinase signalling to tissue-level communication.

Spliceosomal snRNPs are the particles that recognize and excise introns, and snRNP assembly is how they are built: a small nuclear RNA is joined to a ring of seven Sm proteins to make a stable core. Newly made snRNAs are capped, bound by the cap-binding complex with PHAX, and exported through the nuclear pore, so a large share of the machinery here is nucleoporins and transport factors including RANBP2, TPR and the importin-like snurportin. In the cytoplasm the SMN complex, with its Gemin partners, selects genuine snRNAs and loads the Sm core, assisted by methylation of Sm proteins by the PRMT5-WDR77 methylosome; hypermethylation of the cap by TGS1 then licenses re-import of the mature particle. Loss of SMN1 reduces this assembly capacity and causes spinal muscular atrophy, linking pre-mRNA splicing competence to motor neuron survival.

Bile acid and bile salt synthesis is the liver's main route for disposing of cholesterol, converting roughly half a gram of it each day into amphipathic detergents that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the intestine. The dominant path starts with 7alpha-hydroxylation of cholesterol by CYP7A1, followed by ring modification through HSD3B7, AKR1D1 and the AKR1C reductases, CYP8B1 branching toward cholic acid, then peroxisomal side-chain shortening by ACOX2, AMACR and the multifunctional HSD17B4, and finally conjugation to taurine or glycine by BAAT and export across the canalicular membrane by ABCB11. Alternative oxysterol routes via CYP27A1, CYP46A1 and CH25H begin outside the liver and matter more for cholesterol and brain sterol homeostasis than for bile salt output. The bile acid receptor FXR with RXRA feeds back on the pathway; failure of individual steps causes cholestasis, fat malabsorption and neurological disease.

Digestion of dietary lipid is the extracellular breakdown of fat in the gut lumen, the step that converts triacylglycerols and cholesterol esters from food into free fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, glycerol and cholesterol that enterocytes can absorb. Without it fat passes through undigested, producing steatorrhoea, weight loss and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins that ride along with dietary lipid; this is the defect seen in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and in cystic fibrosis. Digestion begins in the stomach with acid-stable gastric lipase and is completed in the small intestine by pancreatic triacylglycerol lipase, whose activity on bile-salt-coated emulsion droplets requires the cofactor colipase, together with carboxyl ester lipase and related pancreatic lipase-family proteins that act on cholesterol esters and other substrates. The pathway sits upstream of chylomicron assembly and whole-body lipid and energy supply.

Fat arriving in the diet is largely triacylglycerol and cholesterol ester, neither of which can cross the intestinal epithelium intact, so digestion of dietary lipid is the step that converts them into absorbable free fatty acids, monoacylglycerols, glycerol and cholesterol. Gastric lipase begins the hydrolysis in the acidic stomach, and pancreatic triacylglycerol lipase completes it in the duodenum, where colipase anchors the enzyme to the bile-salt-coated surface of emulsified fat droplets that would otherwise inhibit it. Carboxyl ester lipase broadens the range of substrates to cholesterol esters and fat-soluble vitamin esters, while the related pancreatic lipase regulatory proteins modulate this lipolytic activity. The products are taken up by enterocytes for resynthesis and chylomicron packaging. Loss of pancreatic lipase output, as in pancreatic insufficiency, produces steatorrhoea and deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins.

Influenza virus replicates its segmented negative-strand genome in the host cell nucleus, and vRNA synthesis is the step that regenerates full-length genomic RNA from the complementary positive-sense cRNA intermediate. Without it the infected cell produces only messenger RNA and antigenomic copies, and no progeny genomes are available for packaging into virions. The reaction mirrors cRNA synthesis in reverse: cRNA coated with viral nucleoprotein serves as template for the trimeric viral polymerase, and the nascent vRNA is encapsidated by nucleoprotein as it emerges, yielding ribonucleoprotein complexes competent for further replication, transcription and nuclear export. Evidence places this assembly in the nuclear matrix as well as the nucleoplasm. Host nuclear proteins participate, including PARP1, illustrating how the virus co-opts chromatin-associated machinery to amplify its genome, a dependence of interest for antiviral strategies.

Viral mRNA Translation is the step at which influenza hands its transcripts to the host protein synthesis machinery, converting viral genetic information into the ten or more proteins needed to build progeny virions. Because the virus encodes no ribosome of its own, this dependence on host 40S and 60S subunits makes translation the point where infection is most exposed to antiviral defence and to therapeutic interference. Conserved viral 5' untranslated regions favour ribosome recruitment, assisted by the cellular RNA-binding protein GRSF1, while NS1 together with the host chaperone P58(IPK) keeps the stress kinase PKR inactive so that eIF2alpha is not phosphorylated and initiation continues. Host mRNA translation is simultaneously suppressed, redirecting ribosomes toward viral messages. The PB1 segment additionally yields PB1-F2 from an alternative reading frame, expanding the coding capacity of a compact genome.

Influenza virus encodes no ribosomes of its own, so every viral protein is made by the host translation apparatus; this step converts spliced and unspliced viral mRNA in the cytoplasm into the roughly ten polypeptides that build new particles, including the surface glycoproteins HA and NA, the polymerase subunits PB1, PB2 and PA, nucleoprotein, matrix proteins and NS1. The bulk of the gene content is the cytoplasmic 40S and 60S ribosomal subunit proteins that carry out initiation and elongation. Conserved viral 5' untranslated sequences favour recruitment of this machinery, aided by the host G-rich sequence factor GRSF1, while the co-chaperone P58(IPK) restrains the antiviral kinase PKR so that initiation is not shut down by the interferon-induced translational block. Host protein synthesis falls at the same time, making this the point where the virus captures a central cellular process to its own ends.

Influenza virus must copy its segmented negative-sense genome, and cRNA synthesis is the step that produces the full-length positive-sense replicative intermediate from which new vRNA genomes are made. It is distinct from viral mRNA production by the same polymerase: transcription steals a methylated cap from host transcripts to prime synthesis and terminates by stuttering on a sub-terminal poly-U tract to add a poly(A) tail, whereas replication must initiate de novo, unprimed, and read through that signal to the very 5' end of the template. Free nucleoprotein accumulating during infection appears to switch the polymerase into this processive, unprimed mode and to encapsidate the nascent product, though the mechanism is not fully resolved. The switch from transcription to replication sets the timing of genome amplification and thus the yield of progeny virions.

Influenza virus packages each of its eight negative-sense RNA segments into a viral ribonucleoprotein, in which the RNA is coated by nucleoprotein and bound at its ends by the trimeric viral polymerase. Because this assembly happens in the host nucleus, the virus depends on cellular import and chaperone machinery to get its polymerase subunits and nucleoprotein there and to fold them into a functional complex; an importin-beta family carrier of the nuclear import system and the HSP90 chaperone contribute to that step. The assembled particle is the unit that transcribes capped viral mRNA using host cap snatching, replicates the genome through a complementary RNA intermediate, and is finally exported to the cytoplasm for packaging into budding virions. Blocking this host-dependent assembly stalls the infectious cycle before genome replication, which makes the host factors involved candidate antiviral targets.

Androgen biosynthesis converts cholesterol-derived precursors into testosterone and dihydrotestosterone, the hormones that drive male sexual differentiation in utero, virilisation at puberty, spermatogenesis, and much of adult sexual behaviour. Loss of steps in this route causes disorders of sex development: defects in 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 or in 5α-reductase type 2 leave 46,XY individuals undervirilised at birth, while excess activity underlies hyperandrogenism. The pathway runs in testicular Leydig cells and the adrenal cortex, where CYP17A1 performs both hydroxylation and lyase chemistry on pregnenolone and progesterone, 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoforms interconvert Δ5 and Δ4 steroids, and terminal reductases generate the active ligands for the nuclear androgen receptor. Output is set from above by pituitary luteinising hormone and by proopiomelanocortin-derived ACTH, tying gonadal and adrenal steroid production to hypothalamic–pituitary control.

Estrogen biosynthesis converts androgen precursors into the estrogens that drive reproductive tract development, the ovarian cycle, mammary gland growth, and bone and lipid homeostasis in both sexes. Its committed step is aromatization: the cytochrome P450 aromatase CYP19A1 removes the C19 methyl group of androstenedione and testosterone to yield estrone and estradiol, and this reaction is the target of aromatase inhibitors used against hormone-dependent breast cancer. Interconversion of the weak and potent forms is set by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases, with HSD17B1 favouring reduction of estrone to estradiol while HSD17B2 oxidizes estradiol back, so local tissue potency depends on their balance rather than on circulating hormone alone. Additional short-chain and aldo-keto reductases contribute reductive steps. Loss of aromatase causes estrogen deficiency with virilization, delayed epiphyseal closure and tall stature; excess local synthesis sustains estrogen-driven tumour growth.</description>

The liver disposes of excess cholesterol and produces the detergents that make dietary fat absorbable, and the classic route begins when CYP7A1 hydroxylates cholesterol at the 7alpha position. Downstream of 7alpha-hydroxycholesterol the pathway divides: 12alpha-hydroxylation by CYP8B1 commits intermediates to cholate, while reduction by AKR1D1 and the AKR1C reductases leads to chenodeoxycholate, with the ratio set largely by hydroxylase abundance. Completing either product requires several compartments — side-chain oxidation by mitochondrial CYP27A1, peroxisomal beta-oxidation through ACOX2, the bifunctional HSD17B4 and SCP2, and racemization by AMACR — before BAAT conjugates the acids to glycine or taurine and ABCB11 exports the salts into bile. The bile acid receptor FXR, with RXRA and coactivators, feeds back to restrain synthesis. Loss of individual steps causes cholestasis, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption and neonatal liver disease.

Myelin in the adult central nervous system actively blocks axons from regrowing, and this receptor complex is how that block is imposed. Myelin-derived inhibitors including Nogo, myelin-associated glycoprotein and oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein bind a tripartite receptor made of the Nogo receptor, LINGO1 and the p75 neurotrophin receptor, converting extracellular contact with myelin into growth cone collapse. The signal converges on RHOA: p75NTR engagement releases RHOA from its cytoplasmic inhibitor RHOGDI, allowing exchange-factor-driven loading with GTP and downstream actin-myosin contraction that retracts the growth cone and halts elongation. The same receptor also restrains sprouting and stabilises circuits after development ends. Because axonal growth inhibition of this kind limits recovery from spinal cord injury and stroke, blocking the receptor or RHOA activity is a long-standing strategy for promoting regeneration.

Nerve growth factor binding to the p75 neurotrophin receptor can promote neuronal survival rather than death, and NF-kB activation is the arm of p75NTR signalling that delivers that pro-survival output. The response is selective for mature NGF; BDNF and NT-3 engaging the same receptor do not trigger it, so the pathway helps explain how one receptor produces opposite fates depending on which ligand and co-receptors are present. Mechanistically, the receptor's intracellular tail recruits a scaffold built on the adaptor p62/SQSTM1, atypical protein kinase C, TRAF6 and interleukin receptor-associated kinase components, generating polyubiquitin signals that activate the IKK complex; phosphorylated IkB-alpha is degraded and p50/p65 dimers enter the nucleus to drive survival gene transcription. This determines whether sympathetic and sensory neurons live or are pruned during development, and it links neurotrophin sensing to the same ubiquitin-dependent logic used by innate immune receptors.

Neurotrophin receptors can kill as well as sustain neurons, and this is the death arm: NGF or proNGF binding to the p75 receptor (NGFR) recruits the adaptor NRAGE (MAGED1), which couples the receptor to Rho-family GTPase exchange factors and on to c-Jun N-terminal kinase. JNK then drives apoptosis on two fronts, turning on pro-apoptotic transcription and acting directly on the mitochondrial machinery through BH3-only proteins such as BAD and BIM. This route helps prune surplus neurons and axons during nervous system development, where cells that fail to secure adequate trophic support are eliminated, and it is reactivated after injury and in neurodegenerative conditions where proNGF accumulates. The large complement of Dbl-family exchange factors, including TRIO, TIAM1 and the VAV proteins, reflects Rac1-dependent signalling shared with cytoskeletal remodelling, so the same wiring links receptor occupancy to both morphology and survival decisions.

Nerve growth factor does not only promote survival and differentiation; through its low-affinity receptor p75NTR it can also stop cells dividing, and this arm of p75NTR signalling works through the zinc finger protein SC1/PRDM4. The outcome matters for Schwann cells and neural progenitors, where exit from the cell cycle is a prerequisite for differentiation and myelination, and for tumour contexts in which loss of this brake permits continued proliferation. On NGF binding, SC1 associates with the receptor complex and translocates to the nucleus, where its PR/SET domain and recruited class I histone deacetylases repress transcription, lowering cyclin E levels and blocking progression through G1 into S phase.
