This makes the pathway a link between a neurotrophin signal at the membrane and chromatin-level control of proliferation, distinct from the apoptotic and survival outputs of the same receptor.

Neurotrophin binding to the p75 receptor can act through lipid rather than protein second messengers, and this is the arm that generates ceramide. Nerve growth factor engaging p75NTR activates a neutral sphingomyelinase, which cleaves membrane sphingomyelin to release ceramide, a bioactive lipid that reorganises membrane microdomains and engages downstream kinases and phosphatases. The outcome is strikingly context-dependent: in oligodendrocytes the same signal drives apoptosis, in neocortical subplate neurons it supports survival, and at low levels in hippocampal neurons it promotes axonal outgrowth. This makes ceramide signalling one route by which a single neurotrophin receptor decides between death and growth, relevant to developmental pruning of neurons, myelinating glia survival, and injury responses in the nervous system.

The neurotrophin receptor p75NTR is not only a ligand-binding receptor but a substrate for regulated intramembrane proteolysis, and its stepwise cleavage converts a surface receptor into diffusible signalling fragments. This matters for how neurons decide between survival and death: p75NTR shapes responses to NGF and BDNF alongside the TRK receptors, and mediates growth cone collapse to myelin-associated inhibitors in the injured nervous system. Shedding of the extracellular domain is carried out by the metalloproteinase ADAM17, leaving a membrane stub that is cut within the bilayer by the gamma-secretase complex of presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2. The liberated intracellular domain can engage adaptors such as TRAF6 and promote NF-kappaB activation through p50 and RelA, linking receptor processing to transcriptional output. The same protease pair also handles Notch and amyloid precursor protein, placing this route in a shared family of cleavage-activated receptor signalling.

Whether a growing axon extends or stalls depends in part on p75NTR, which regulates axonogenesis by setting the activity state of the small GTPase RHOA and hence the rigidity of the growth cone actin cytoskeleton. Active, GTP-bound RHOA stiffens actin and collapses growth cones, so control over it determines whether neurites elongate during development or regenerate after injury. The outcome depends on what binds the receptor: neurotrophin engagement, as by NGF, releases RHOA inhibition of growth by favouring the GDP-bound state held by the dissociation inhibitor ARHGDIA, whereas myelin-derived inhibitors such as MAG, OMG and the reticulon NOGO act through a receptor complex of p75NTR with the NOGO receptor and LINGO1 to activate RHOA and arrest extension. This axis explains much of why central nervous system axons fail to regrow through myelin-rich scar tissue.

Neurotrophins such as NGF act not only through TRK tyrosine kinase receptors but also through p75NTR, and p75 NTR receptor-mediated signalling is the branch that decides between survival, apoptosis, differentiation and control of axon growth depending on cellular context. It matters because pro-forms of the neurotrophins bind p75NTR preferentially and drive neuronal death, so proteolytic maturation of the ligand sets the balance between trophic support and degeneration, and because the same receptor serves as the Nogo receptor co-partner that converts myelin-derived cues into growth cone collapse. Lacking catalytic activity, the receptor signals by recruiting adaptors: TRAF6, MYD88/IRAK1 and RIPK2 feed NF-kB activation, MAGED1 and BEX3 link to JNK and caspase-dependent death, and regulated intramembrane cleavage by ADAM17 and the gamma-secretase complex liberates the intracellular domain. A large complement of Rho-family exchange factors couples the receptor to RhoA and Rac1, linking it to cytoskeletal control of neurite outgrowth and to hippocampal synaptic depression.

Neurons cannot excrete cholesterol directly, so they convert it to 24-hydroxycholesterol, which crosses the blood-brain barrier and is degraded to bile acids in the liver. This route contributes only a small fraction of the total bile acid pool but provides the main outlet for surplus brain cholesterol, and its impairment is linked to cholesterol accumulation and neurodegenerative change. CYP46A1 performs the brain-specific 24-hydroxylation; in hepatocytes CYP39A1 adds the 7alpha-hydroxyl, HSD3B7 isomerises and oxidises the A ring, and AKR1D1 with the AKR1C reductases reduce it, before CYP27A1 initiates side-chain oxidation. Activation to a coenzyme A thioester, peroxisomal beta-oxidation involving AMACR and the transporter ABCD3, and conjugation to glycine or taurine yield cholate and chenodeoxycholate. The chemistry spans cytosol, mitochondria and peroxisomes, tying sterol disposal to bile formation and intestinal lipid absorption.

Cholesterol is disposed of largely by conversion to bile acids, and the acidic route beginning with 27-hydroxycholesterol is the minor branch of that conversion, initiated outside the liver rather than within it. A mitochondrial sterol 27-hydroxylase acting in macrophages and other extrahepatic cells oxidises the cholesterol side chain, producing an oxysterol that leaves the cell and travels to the liver; this provides a way for lung phagocytes and similar cells to unload excess cholesterol. In hepatocytes an oxysterol 7alpha-hydroxylase, 3beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, 12alpha-hydroxylase and reductases of the aldo-keto reductase family remodel the ring system, after which peroxisomal side-chain shortening and conjugation to glycine or taurine yield cholate and chenodeoxycholate. The bile acid receptor FXR with RXR and nuclear receptor coactivators feeds back on this output, restraining 7alpha-hydroxylase transcription. Loss of 27-hydroxylase causes cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis.

Aldosterone, the body's main mineralocorticoid, sets renal sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion and thereby extracellular fluid volume and blood pressure; its synthesis in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex is the pathway described here. Pregnenolone is oxidised and isomerised to progesterone by 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase enzymes, CYP21A2 adds a 21-hydroxyl to give deoxycorticosterone, and the zona glomerulosa-specific aldosterone synthase CYP11B2 completes the conversion through 11-beta-hydroxylation and 18-oxidation. Loss of CYP21A2 causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia with salt wasting, CYP11B2 deficiency gives isolated hypoaldosteronism, and excess output underlies primary aldosteronism and hypertension. The pathway sits downstream of angiotensin II and potassium signalling in the glomerulosa cell, and its steroidogenic capacity is supported by gonadotropin subunits that share the broader endocrine control of steroid-producing tissues.

Cortisol is the body's principal glucocorticoid, setting blood glucose, blood pressure, and the stress and inflammatory response, and it is made in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex from pregnenolone. The route runs through 3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase/isomerase and 17alpha-hydroxylase activity to 17alpha-hydroxyprogesterone, then CYP21A2 hydroxylation to 11-deoxycortisol and a final CYP11B1 step yielding cortisol. Output is driven by pituitary ACTH cleaved from proopiomelanocortin, most circulating hormone travels bound to corticosteroid-binding globulin, and interconversion of cortisol with inactive cortisone by the two 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases determines how much active hormone reaches receptors in liver, adipose and kidney. Loss of CYP21A2 causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia, with cortisol deficiency and shunting of precursors into androgens; related enzymes serve the parallel mineralocorticoid branch.

Bile acid and bile salt metabolism is the route by which the liver disposes of cholesterol by converting it into detergents that emulsify dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins in the small intestine. Roughly half a gram of cholesterol is committed to this pathway daily, making it a principal arm of whole-body cholesterol homeostasis; its failure causes cholestasis, fat malabsorption, and progressive liver injury. Synthesis begins with 7alpha-hydroxylation of cholesterol by CYP7A1, or alternatively with oxysterols made in extrahepatic tissues by CYP27A1 and CYP46A1, followed by ring modification, peroxisomal side-chain shortening, and conjugation to taurine or glycine by BAAT. Dedicated transporters then complete the enterohepatic circulation: canalicular export via ABCB11, ileal uptake by SLC10A2, and hepatic reuptake through sodium-dependent and organic anion transporters. The nuclear receptor FXR with RXRA senses bile salt levels and feeds back on synthesis and transport.

Converting cholesterol into bile salts is the body's main route for disposing of sterol and, at the same time, the way it makes dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins absorbable. Roughly half a gram of cholesterol is spent this way each day in the liver, secreted into bile, used as detergent in the small intestine, and then almost entirely reclaimed and recirculated. The classic route begins with 7alpha-hydroxylation by CYP7A1, followed by ring modification, side-chain oxidation and peroxisomal beta-oxidation, before conjugation to taurine or glycine by BAAT. Alternative routes start from oxysterols made in extrahepatic tissues by CYP27A1 or CYP46A1, contributing little to the bile salt pool but helping clear cholesterol from brain and periphery. Dedicated transporters export salts into bile and take them up again in ileum and hepatocyte, while the nuclear receptor FXR with RXRA feeds back on synthesis. Defects cause cholestasis, fat malabsorption and bile acid synthesis disorders.

Vascular endothelial growth factors and their receptors drive the formation of blood and lymphatic vessels, both during embryonic vasculogenesis and in adult angiogenesis, wound healing and tumour vascularization; blockade of this axis is the basis of anti-angiogenic cancer therapy, while its overactivity contributes to retinal neovascularization and inflammatory vascular disease. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, VEGFC and placental growth factor engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 together with neuropilin co-receptors, and receptor autophosphorylation recruits adaptors such as SHB, NCK, SRC and PLCG1. Downstream branches raise cytosolic calcium through IP3 receptors, activate PKC-RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR arms, and stimulate endothelial nitric oxide synthase for vasodilation and permeability. Rho-family GTPases with WAVE complex, PAK and focal adhesion components remodel actin and VE-cadherin junctions, producing endothelial survival, proliferation and directed migration.

Neuropilin interactions with VEGF and VEGFR describes how the neuropilin co-receptors NRP1 and NRP2 capture VEGF family ligands and present them to the signalling receptors VEGFR1 (FLT1) and VEGFR2 (KDR), tuning the strength of angiogenic signalling. This matters for the formation and remodelling of blood and lymphatic vessels during development, for wound healing, and for tumour vascularisation, where neuropilin levels help determine how strongly endothelial cells respond to a given amount of growth factor. Neuropilins have short cytoplasmic tails and no kinase activity; they work as ligand-binding cofactors, with NRP1 favouring VEGF-A165, VEGF-B and PlGF-2 and NRP2 also binding VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, the latter linking it to lymphatic endothelium. The same receptors serve axon guidance through semaphorins, placing this module at the intersection of vascular patterning and neuronal wiring.

Neuropilins are short-tailed cell-surface receptors that bind selected VEGF family ligands and hand them to the signalling VEGF receptors, so this set describes how ligand presentation tunes endothelial responsiveness during blood and lymphatic vessel growth. NRP1 captures the heparin-binding isoform VEGF-A165 along with VEGF-B and PlGF-2, while NRP2 additionally binds VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, and both associate laterally with KDR (VEGFR-2) or FLT1 (VEGFR-1) to raise their affinity for particular ligands rather than to signal by their own kinase activity, since they have none. The consequence is isoform-selective control of endothelial proliferation, migration and sprouting, with NRP1 weighted toward arterial and angiogenic vessels and NRP2 toward veins and lymphatics. Loss of neuropilin function disrupts vascular patterning in development, and the same co-receptor interface is exploited in tumour angiogenesis and targeted by anti-angiogenic strategies.

Blood and lymphatic vessels form where VEGF ligands meet their receptor tyrosine kinases, and the pairing rules between them determine which kind of vessel grows. VEGF-A acting on VEGFR-2 drives endothelial proliferation, migration and permeability in angiogenesis, while VEGF-C and VEGF-D signalling through VEGFR-3 specifies and expands lymphatic endothelium; placental growth factor and VEGF-B bind only VEGFR-1, which also acts as a decoy that limits how much VEGF-A reaches VEGFR-2. Each active ligand is a homodimer, and alternative splicing and proteolytic processing tune receptor preference and matrix binding, with neuropilin co-receptors raising affinity without signalling themselves. This ligand-receptor layer sets the level of the signal that follows, and it underlies wound healing, tumour vascularisation, diabetic retinopathy and macular degeneration, making these proteins the targets of anti-angiogenic drugs.

Rho family small GTPases act as molecular switches that tell a cell what shape to take and where to move, and signalling through them underlies lamellipodia and stress fibre formation, cell-cell and cell-matrix adhesion, cytokinesis, phagocytosis and neuronal morphogenesis; its deregulation contributes to tumour invasion and metastasis. Classical members such as RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 cycle between GTP- and GDP-bound states under the opposing control of exchange factors, GTPase-activating proteins and cytosolic dissociation inhibitors, while Rnd, RhoH and RhoBTB proteins lack appreciable hydrolysis and act constitutively. Active GTPases engage kinases including ROCK1/2, PAK family members and PKN proteins, plus IQGAPs, formins and WASP/WAVE-Arp2/3 machinery, driving actin polymerisation and myosin-based contractility. Related branches here connect to microtubule motors and kinetochore function during mitosis, membrane trafficking, SRF-dependent transcription, and assembly of NADPH oxidase complexes for superoxide production.

Non-coding RNAs make up the bulk of transcriptional output, and their maturation requires dedicated processing and trafficking machinery rather than the route taken by messenger RNAs. The genes here center on one well-defined branch of that biology: biogenesis of the spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs. Newly transcribed snRNAs are capped and bound by the nuclear cap-binding complex with PHAX, exported through the nuclear pore, and assembled in the cytoplasm into Sm-core particles by the SMN complex with its Gemin subunits, aided by the PRMT5-WDR77-CLNS1A methylosome that symmetrically dimethylates Sm proteins. TGS1 then converts the cap to trimethylguanosine, which snurportin recognizes to reimport the particle for splicing. The extensive nucleoporin and RanBP2 content reflects the bidirectional pore transit this cycle demands. Loss of SMN1 function depletes these particles and causes spinal muscular atrophy, linking snRNP assembly to motor neuron survival.

Degradation of beta-catenin by the destruction complex is the off-switch of canonical Wnt signalling: in unstimulated cells it continuously destroys cytoplasmic beta-catenin so that Wnt target genes stay silent. This restraint sets the threshold for Wnt-driven proliferation and stem cell renewal in tissues such as intestinal crypts, and its loss through APC or AXIN mutation stabilises beta-catenin and drives colorectal and other cancers. A scaffold of APC, axin and AMER1 presents beta-catenin to casein kinase 1 and GSK3-beta for sequential N-terminal phosphorylation, creating a phosphodegron read by the beta-TrCP-SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase; polyubiquitinated beta-catenin is then dismantled by the 26S proteasome, with PP2A subunits and the deubiquitinase ZRANB1 tuning complex output. Absent nuclear beta-catenin, TCF/LEF factors remain bound to TLE/Groucho and CtBP corepressors, keeping targets such as MYC repressed.

When no Wnt ligand is present, cytoplasmic beta-catenin is kept at low levels by a dedicated destruction complex, and this restraint is what prevents constitutive transcription of Wnt target genes such as MYC. The scaffolds AXIN1/AXIN2 and the tumour suppressor APC hold beta-catenin so that casein kinase 1 alpha and GSK3B phosphorylate its N-terminal degron; the beta-TrCP-containing SCF ligase, with CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1, then polyubiquitinates it for proteasomal destruction. Protein phosphatase 2A subunits and the deubiquitinase ZRANB1 tune the complex, while FRAT proteins and AMER1 act on GSK3B and Axin availability. In parallel, TCF/LEF factors sit on target promoters with TLE/Groucho and CtBP corepressors and HDAC1, holding them silent. Loss of APC or stabilizing mutations in beta-catenin break this control and drive colorectal and other cancers, linking the pathway to intestinal stem cell renewal and development.

Small GTPases of the RHO family switch on a diverse panel of downstream effectors, and this collection of RHO GTPase effectors is where their signals become physical changes in the cell. The outputs determine cell shape, adhesion, motility, division and host defence, so loss of individual effectors produces immunodeficiency, cytokinesis failure or defective wound healing. RHOA-family GTPases activate ROCK1/2, which drive myosin light chain phosphorylation and actomyosin contractility, and also engage PKN kinases, citron kinase, rhotekin and rhophilins; RAC1 and CDC42 activate PAK kinases, WASP/WAVE-ARP2/3 actin nucleation, formins and IQGAP scaffolds that couple actin to cadherin-catenin junctions and microtubules. Related branches cover kinesin- and dynein-based transport, kinetochore and spindle assembly during mitosis, GOPC-dependent trafficking of CFTR to the plasma membrane, and RAC-dependent assembly of NADPH oxidase complexes for superoxide production in phagocytes. Actin remodelling also feeds SRF-dependent transcription.

VEGF binds to VEGFR leading to receptor dimerization is the initiating step of angiogenic signalling: secreted VEGF family ligands engage their receptor tyrosine kinases on endothelial cells, bringing two receptor chains together so their kinase domains can trans-autophosphorylate. This event sets in motion endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and therefore governs blood vessel formation in development, wound healing, and tumour neovascularisation, where it is the target of anti-VEGF therapeutics. Ligand identity determines the output: VEGFA and the placental growth factor PGF act through VEGFR-1 (FLT1) and VEGFR-2 (KDR), while VEGFC and VEGFD signal through VEGFR-3 (FLT4) to drive lymphatic endothelial development. Homodimers predominate, though VEGFR-1/VEGFR-2 heterodimers form, and VEGFR-2 carries most angiogenic activity in vivo while VEGFR-1 largely restrains ligand availability.

Blood and lymphatic vessels grow where endothelial cells receive a vascular endothelial growth factor signal, and that signal begins with ligand binding to a VEGF receptor and the receptor pairing up. The step initiates cascades that drive endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and increased vascular permeability, and it is the point at which tumours recruit their own blood supply and the target of anti-angiogenic drugs. Secreted ligands including VEGFA, VEGFB, placental growth factor and the lymphangiogenic VEGFC and VEGFD engage the receptor tyrosine kinases FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences; receptors mainly form homodimers, though FLT1-KDR heterodimers occur. KDR carries most angiogenic signalling in vivo, FLT1 acts largely as a modulating or decoy receptor, and FLT4 specifies lymphatic endothelium. Loss or dysregulation underlies vascular malformations, lymphoedema and pathological neovascularisation in retinopathy and cancer.

WNT ligands are secreted glycoproteins that tell cells what to become, when to divide, and which way to point, and the signalling they initiate governs embryonic patterning, adult tissue renewal and stem cell maintenance in crypts, skin and bone. In the beta-catenin-dependent branch, WNT binding to Frizzled receptors with LRP5/6 co-receptors disables the destruction complex of APC, AXIN, GSK3 and casein kinase 1, so beta-catenin escapes proteasomal degradation and partners with TCF/LEF transcription factors to drive targets such as MYC and AXIN2. Tuning comes from secreted antagonists like DKK1, SFRPs and sclerostin, from RNF43/ZNRF3 receptor turnover opposed by R-spondins acting through LGR receptors, and from tankyrase-mediated AXIN destabilisation. Beta-catenin-independent branches signal through Frizzled, ROR and RYK to Rho-family GTPases, PKC and calcineurin-NFAT, orienting planar cell polarity and convergent extension. Loss of restraint on this pathway underlies colorectal cancer; deficits cause skeletal and developmental defects.

Gap junctions must be removed as well as built, and annular gap junction formation is how a cell retires them: an intact plaque, containing connexin hemichannels contributed by both neighbouring cells, is drawn into the cytoplasm as a double-membrane vesicle rather than being disassembled at the surface. This turnover sets the lifetime of direct intercellular coupling and allows plaques to be renewed, or communication to be shut down, during wound healing, differentiation and mitosis. The machinery is that of clathrin-mediated endocytosis adapted to an unusually large cargo: the adaptor DAB2 and the AP-2 complex link connexin 43 to clathrin lattices, dynamins pinch off the internalising membrane, and actin provides the pulling force. The internalised annular structures are then routed to lysosomal or autophagic degradation, making connexin turnover a determinant of how strongly tissues remain electrically and metabolically coupled.

Cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone and the estrogens all begin as cholesterol, and the metabolism of steroid hormones is the tissue-specific route from that precursor to each active hormone. It sets the body's handling of stress and glucose, its sodium and water balance, and sexual differentiation and fertility; enzyme defects here cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia, aldosterone-driven hypertension, and disorders of sex development. The rate-limiting step is delivery of cholesterol into mitochondria by STAR and related lipid-transfer proteins, after which the side-chain cleavage enzyme CYP11A1, fed electrons by ferredoxin and ferredoxin reductase, makes pregnenolone. Downstream cytochromes P450 and hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases then hydroxylate, oxidize and aromatize the steroid nucleus, with CYP19A1 generating estrogens and 5-alpha-reductases making dihydrotestosterone. Pituitary tropic hormones drive the pathway, a plasma binding globulin controls free hormone availability, and HSD11B enzymes tune local glucocorticoid action in target tissues.

Every steroid hormone in the body begins as pregnenolone, and pregnenolone biosynthesis is the committed first step that converts cholesterol into a hormone precursor. It sets the overall output of the adrenal cortex and gonads, so its loss causes lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia, with absent cortisol, aldosterone and sex steroids. Cholesterol drawn from lipid droplets or lysosomes must reach the inner mitochondrial membrane, and this transport, not enzyme abundance, is rate-limiting; STAR delivers cholesterol across the outer membrane under acute trophic hormone control, with related lipid-transfer modules such as STARD3 and STARD4 and the outer-membrane translocator protein TSPO contributing to sterol movement. There, the side-chain cleavage enzyme CYP11A1 performs three successive oxidations to cleave the cholesterol side chain, fed with electrons by ferredoxin and ferredoxin reductase. Pregnenolone then returns to the cytosol for tissue-specific elaboration into mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens.

In cells not receiving a Wnt signal, beta-catenin is kept scarce by being continuously marked for destruction, and this phosphorylation cascade is the marking step. It sets the threshold for Wnt-dependent transcription, so its loss allows beta-catenin to accumulate, enter the nucleus and drive TCF/LEF target genes constitutively — the defining lesion of most colorectal cancers, where APC or beta-catenin itself is mutated. Mechanistically, the scaffolds APC, AXIN1 and AMER1 assemble a destruction complex in which casein kinase 1 alpha phosphorylates beta-catenin at Ser45, priming GSK3 to modify Thr41, Ser37 and Ser33 in turn; the doubly phosphorylated N-terminal degron is then recognised for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation. Protein phosphatase 2A subunits and the GSK3-binding proteins FRAT1/FRAT2 tune the output, linking the cascade to developmental patterning and stem cell renewal.

When ERBB2 heterodimerizes with EGFR or ERBB4 after growth factor binding, phosphotyrosines in the receptor C-terminal tails become docking sites for the adaptor GRB2, and this is the step that converts ligand binding into RAS-dependent proliferation. GRB2 arrives bound to SOS1, a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, which in turn switches on RAF and the downstream MAP kinase cascade controlling cell cycle entry, growth and survival. The ligands feeding into this route are the EGF-family and neuregulin growth factors, so the same adaptor step serves epithelial proliferation, cardiac and neural development, and wound repair. Because ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancers raises the number of signalling-competent dimers, GRB2 recruitment is a principal route by which these tumours sustain constitutive MAP kinase output, and it underlies resistance when RAS is mutated downstream.

Growth factor receptors of the ERBB family route part of their output into the PI3K-AKT axis, and this branch of ERBB2 signalling is how heterodimers containing ERBB2 promote cell survival, growth and metabolic activity. It matters clinically because ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancer, together with activating PIK3CA mutations, makes tumour cells dependent on this arm for survival and shapes response to HER2-directed therapy. Neuregulins bind ERBB3 or ERBB4 and EGF-family ligands such as betacellulin, epiregulin and HB-EGF bind EGFR, driving heterodimerisation with ERBB2 and tyrosine phosphorylation of the receptor tails. The p85 regulatory subunit docks directly on phosphorylated ERBB3 or ERBB4 CYT1 tails, or indirectly via GRB2 and GAB1 when the partner is EGFR, recruiting the p110 catalytic subunit to generate PIP3 and activate AKT at the membrane.

Humans cannot make vitamin B12 and must extract it from food, so cobalamin transport and metabolism is the relay that carries the vitamin from the gut lumen to two cytosolic and mitochondrial enzymes that need it. Gastric intrinsic factor binds dietary cobalamin after pancreatic proteases release it from haptocorrin, the cubilin-amnionless receptor with megalin takes the complex into ileal enterocytes and reabsorbs it in kidney, and transcobalamin II carries it in blood to the CD320 receptor on target cells. Lysosomal export and cytosolic processing by MMACHC and MMADHC then split the traffic: methylcobalamin supports methionine synthase in remethylating homocysteine, while adenosylcobalamin, made with MMAB and MMAA, supports methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in propionate catabolism. Inherited blocks at any step cause megaloblastic anaemia, homocystinuria, methylmalonic acidaemia and neurological degeneration.

Folate metabolism supplies the one-carbon units used to build purines and thymidylate and to remethylate homocysteine for methylation reactions, so it sits upstream of both DNA synthesis and the methyl donor economy. Dietary folate enters cells through a reduced folate carrier and an intestinal proton-coupled transporter, is carried into mitochondria by a mitochondrial folate transporter, and is retained intracellularly by polyglutamylation via FPGS; dihydrofolate reductase regenerates tetrahydrofolate and is the target of antifolate chemotherapy. Parallel cytosolic and mitochondrial arms, using paired serine hydroxymethyltransferases and methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase/cyclohydrolase enzymes, interconvert formyl, methylene and methyl folates, while MTHFR commits carbon to methionine synthesis and the ALDH1L formyltetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases release excess one-carbon load as CO2. Deficiency or variant activity underlies megaloblastic anaemia, hyperhomocysteinaemia and neural tube defects, and the mitochondrial arm is a hallmark of proliferating and tumour cells.

Biotin is a vitamin humans cannot make, so dietary uptake and reuse determine whether five carboxylase enzymes can work at all. Intestinal and cellular entry occurs through the sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter SLC5A6, whose interaction with PDZD11 helps position it at the membrane; holocarboxylase synthetase then attaches biotin covalently to lysine residues on apocarboxylases, and biotinidase releases it again from biocytin and degraded enzymes so the cofactor can be salvaged rather than lost. The recipients set the metabolic stakes: acetyl-CoA carboxylases commit carbon to fatty acid synthesis, pyruvate carboxylase feeds gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis, and propionyl-CoA and 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylases handle odd-chain fatty acid and branched-chain amino acid breakdown. Loss of holocarboxylase synthetase or biotinidase causes multiple carboxylase deficiency, with organic acidaemia, ketolactic acidosis, rash and neurological damage, treatable with biotin supplementation.

Coenzyme A is the acyl-group carrier that makes fatty acid oxidation and synthesis, the citric acid cycle, ketone body handling and acetylation chemistry possible, and cells build it from dietary pantothenate in five steps. Pantothenate kinases (PANK1-3) commit the vitamin by phosphorylating it, the rate-limiting and feedback-regulated step, after which cysteine is added and decarboxylated by PPCS and PPCDC to give pantetheine phosphate; the bifunctional COASY then adenylylates and phosphorylates it to finish CoA, with DCAKD a related kinase domain protein. The reactions run in the cytosol and mitochondrial intermembrane space, and a carrier delivers CoA into the matrix where much acyl metabolism occurs. Loss of PANK2 causes pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and COASY mutations produce a related neurodegenerative disorder, linking cofactor supply to neuronal survival.

Vitamin D (calciferol) metabolism converts a sterol made in skin or taken in the diet into a hormone that controls intestinal calcium absorption, renal calcium handling and bone mineralisation; loss of the activating steps causes rickets and osteomalacia, while loss of inactivation produces hypercalcaemia and nephrocalcinosis. Cholecalciferol travels bound to vitamin D binding protein, is 25-hydroxylated in liver by CYP2R1, and is then 1-alpha-hydroxylated by renal CYP27B1 to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Delivery into proximal tubule cells depends on receptor-mediated endocytosis by megalin and cubilin with their adaptor and on lysosomal proteolysis of the carrier. The active hormone signals through the nuclear vitamin D receptor, whose transcriptional output extends beyond mineral homeostasis to immune function, differentiation and apoptosis, and which is modulated by SUMO conjugation. CYP24A1 terminates signalling by C23/C24 oxidation.

Nicotinate metabolism is how cells obtain and renew NAD+ and NADP+, the hydride carriers used by nearly every redox enzyme and the substrate consumed by sirtuins, ADP-ribosyltransferases and NAD+ glycohydrolases. Three routes converge: de novo synthesis from tryptophan-derived quinolinate via QPRT, the Preiss-Handler route from dietary nicotinate taken up by transporters and activated by NAPRT, and salvage of nicotinamide by NAMPT or of nicotinamide riboside by NMRK1/2. Nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferases in three isoforms complete the reaction in nucleus, cytosol and mitochondria, while NADK phosphorylates NAD+ to the NADPH pool supporting biosynthesis and antioxidant defence. Consumption by CD38, BST1 and PARP enzymes, methylation by NNMT, and mitochondrial NAD+ import by SLC25A51 set the steady-state level. Declining NAD+ availability is linked to axonal degeneration, metabolic disease and ageing, and tumour dependence on salvage enzymes is a drug target.

Thiamin cannot be made or stored by human cells, so vitamin B1 metabolism is the route by which dietary thiamin is taken up, delivered to the compartments that need it, and converted into the coenzyme form that central carbon metabolism depends on. Thiamin pyrophosphate, generated by thiamin pyrophosphokinase, is the cofactor for pyruvate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complexes, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase, linking this pathway to oxidative decarboxylation, the citric acid cycle and the pentose phosphate pathway. Carriers of the SLC19 family move thiamin across plasma membranes while a mitochondrial transporter supplies the organelle, and a triphosphatase regulates the thiamin triphosphate pool. Dietary deficiency causes beriberi and, in alcoholism, Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome; inherited transporter defects cause thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anaemia and biotin-thiamine-responsive basal ganglia disease, both treatable with supplementation.

Humans cannot make vitamin C, so everything depends on taking it up from the diet and recycling what has been oxidised. Ascorbate serves as an antioxidant and as the reductant that keeps copper- and iron-dependent enzymes turning over, including collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, and the dioxygenases that demethylate DNA and histones; without adequate supply, collagen matures poorly and scurvy follows. Sodium-dependent transporters bring in reduced ascorbate, while glucose transporters carry the fully oxidised form, dehydroascorbate, into cells. Inside, dehydroascorbate is reduced back to ascorbate by glutathione-dependent transferases, and the one-electron intermediate monodehydroascorbate is returned by a cytochrome b5 and its NADH-dependent reductase. This salvage loop greatly extends the useful life of a vitamin that the body neither synthesises nor stores well, coupling the antioxidant pool to glutathione and NADH status.

Riboflavin (vitamin B2) is not used directly but converted into the flavin cofactors FMN and FAD, which serve as hydrogen carriers in over a hundred redox reactions across fatty acid oxidation, the respiratory chain, amino acid catabolism and folate and vitamin B6 handling. Vitamin B2 metabolism covers its uptake from the diet, where dietary flavoproteins are degraded and the free vitamin absorbed, and its stepwise activation: riboflavin kinase phosphorylates riboflavin to FMN, and FAD synthase adenylylates FMN to FAD. Three membrane transporters (SLC52A1-3) move riboflavin into cells and across the intestinal and placental barriers, and loss of the SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 carriers causes Brown-Vialetto-Van Laere syndrome, a riboflavin-responsive motor neuropathy. Phosphatases such as ENPP1 and ACP5 reverse the activation steps, releasing FMN and riboflavin, which is the main excreted form in humans.

Humans cannot make the B vitamins or vitamin C, so dietary forms must be absorbed, carried into cells and converted into the coenzymes that intermediary metabolism runs on. This pathway covers that conversion: thiamine to thiamine pyrophosphate for decarboxylases, riboflavin to FMN and FAD, nicotinamide and niacin to NAD through salvage and de novo routes, pantothenate to coenzyme A, pyridoxine to pyridoxal phosphate, folate to its polyglutamylated one-carbon carriers, cobalamin to the cofactors used by methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and sulfuration of the molybdenum cofactor. Dedicated transporters and binding proteins handle uptake, including intrinsic factor with cubilin and amnionless in the ileum and specific carriers for folate, riboflavin, thiamine and ascorbate. Defects produce recognisable disease: thiamine-responsive anaemia, megaloblastic anaemia with homocystinuria, methylmalonic acidaemia, biotinidase deficiency and neurodegeneration from disrupted coenzyme A synthesis. Biotin-dependent carboxylases and NAD-consuming enzymes act as the downstream consumers.

Vitamins are dietary organic compounds that human cells cannot make in sufficient amounts, and this branch of metabolism converts them into the active cofactors that intermediary metabolism depends on, then regenerates those cofactors as they are consumed. It underlies energy production, one-carbon and amino acid metabolism, vision, bone formation and blood coagulation, and its failure produces deficiency diseases from megaloblastic anaemia to methylmalonic acidaemia and bleeding disorders. Uptake and delivery come first: dedicated transporters and carriers move folate, thiamine, riboflavin, biotin, pantothenate and ascorbate across membranes, while intrinsic factor, cubilin-amnionless and transcobalamins route cobalamin to intracellular processing. Kinases and synthetases then build the working forms tgeneratethiamine pyrophosphate, FAD, NAD, coenzyme A, pyridoxal phosphate, tetrahydrofolate and its one-carbon derivatives, adenosyl- and methylcobalamin, molybdopterin, and reduced vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation. Retinoid and lipoprotein-associated handling covers the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

Proteoglycans carry their sugar chains on a shared anchor, and building the glycosaminoglycan-protein linkage region is the committed first step that converts a bare core protein into a substrate for chondroitin/dermatan sulfate or heparan sulfate polymerization. Xylosyltransferases attach xylose to specific serines, two galactoses are added, and a glucuronic acid completes the tetrasaccharide; the identity of the next hexosamine then decides which chain type is made. A kinase-phosphatase pair acting on the linker xylose tunes how efficiently elongation proceeds, and UDP-xylose is supplied by decarboxylation of UDP-glucuronate. The core proteins served include the cell-surface syndecans and glypicans, the basement membrane and matrix components perlecan, agrin, versican, decorin and biglycan, and the brain-enriched lecticans. Loss of these steps compromises extracellular matrix assembly, growth factor presentation and cartilage and bone development, and underlies a group of linkeropathy skeletal and connective tissue disorders.

NOTCH1 signalling lets one cell instruct its immediate neighbour, and it decides fates in almost every tissue: T-lymphocyte commitment, arterial versus venous endothelium, neural progenitor maintenance, gut secretory lineages. Because it is a short, contact-dependent route with no amplification step, its output is dose-sensitive; activating NOTCH1 mutations drive T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while loss-of-function underlies Alagille-like vascular and skeletal disease and tumour suppression in squamous epithelia. Ligands of the Delta-like and Jagged families, presented in trans and themselves controlled by MIB and NEURL ubiquitin ligases, trigger ADAM10/ADAM17 shedding and gamma-secretase cleavage by the presenilin-nicastrin complex. The released intracellular domain enters the nucleus, converts RBPJ from a repressor bound to NCoR, TLE and histone deacetylases into an activator with MAML proteins and p300/CBP, and induces HES, HEY and MYC. FBXW7-directed ubiquitination and NUMB-driven endocytic sorting terminate the signal.

NOTCH2 signalling lets a cell read the identity of its immediate neighbours, and the decisions it drives build bile ducts, shape bone remodelling and tune lymphocyte programmes. Delta-like and Jagged ligands presented on an adjacent cell, made competent by ubiquitin ligases such as MIB1 and the neuralized-family enzymes, trigger shedding of the NOTCH2 ectodomain by ADAM10 and then cleavage within the membrane by the gamma-secretase complex of presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN. The released intracellular domain enters the nucleus and, with RBPJ and a mastermind-like coactivator plus CREB1 and the EP300 acetyltransferase, switches on targets including the HES1 and HES5 repressors, FCER2 and granzyme B. Contactin 1 and midkine also engage the receptor. Loss-of-function mutations in NOTCH2 or JAG1 underlie Alagille syndrome, while C-terminal truncations that stabilise signalling cause the progressive bone loss of Hajdu-Cheney syndrome.

Growth factor receptors recruit lipid kinase activity to the membrane, and the resulting PIP3 signal activates AKT to keep cells alive, grow, and remodel their shape. In neurons this is the dominant survival arm downstream of nerve growth factor acting through its receptor tyrosine kinase TrkA: signalling suppresses the cytoplasmic apoptotic machinery, shifts transcription toward survival genes, and adjusts metabolism to match. Class IA PI3K here is a heterodimer of a p110 catalytic subunit with a p85 regulatory subunit, coupled to receptors directly or through IRS adaptors that also carry insulin and IGF input. Consequences extend beyond survival: axon diameter and branching depend on it, RhoA and the actin cytoskeleton are regulated downstream, and mTOR activation promotes translation of selected mRNAs. Loss of this signalling contributes to neuronal degeneration, while its constitutive activation is a common oncogenic event.

Once growth factor signalling activates AKT at the plasma membrane, the kinase acts on a set of cytosolic substrates that together tilt the cell toward survival, growth and cell cycle entry. This is the arm of PI3K signalling that suppresses apoptosis: inhibitory phosphorylation of BAD frees anti-apoptotic BCL-2 proteins, phosphorylation of caspase-9 blunts its activation, and modification of MDM2 promotes degradation of p53. Parallel events relieve brakes on proliferation and on protein synthesis — the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27 are retained in the cytoplasm, GSK3 isoforms are switched off, and phosphorylation of TSC2 and of the mTORC1 subunit PRAS40 permits TOR kinase activity, which in turn feeds back to support AKT. IKK phosphorylation links the same input to NF-κB-dependent survival transcription. Constitutive flux through these steps is a common feature of tumours with PI3K–AKT pathway mutations.

Growth factor and insulin signalling ends in changes to gene expression, and one route is activated AKT entering the nucleus to phosphorylate transcription factors there. This is how a cell converts a survival or nutrient signal into a decision not to die: AKT phosphorylation of the forkhead factors FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 blocks their activity, driving them out of the nucleus and silencing the apoptotic, cell-cycle-arrest and stress-resistance genes they otherwise switch on. AKT also phosphorylates CREB1, favouring recruitment of coactivators and transcription of survival genes, and modifies the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A1 to curb its pro-apoptotic behaviour. All three AKT isoforms contribute. Because these are the nuclear outputs of PI3K signalling, their constitutive engagement in tumours with PI3K or PTEN lesions suppresses apoptosis and supports proliferation, while insufficient signalling shifts metabolism toward the catabolic, stress-adapted FOXO programme.</description>

Neurotrophins such as NGF and BDNF act on their receptors at the cell surface, but the lasting consequences — neuronal differentiation, survival, dendritic growth and the synaptic changes underlying learning — require the signal to reach the nucleus and rewrite gene expression. That step is what nuclear events downstream of neurotrophin signalling accomplish: ERK and p38 family kinases, together with the ribosomal S6 kinase family, phosphorylate transcription factors including CREB1, ELK1 in partnership with SRF, ATF1/ATF2 and MEF2 proteins, recruiting the p300 acetyltransferase to activate transcription. The immediate result is induction of immediate-early genes — FOS, FOSB, JUNB, the EGR family, ARC and VGF — many themselves transcription factors that drive a second, delayed-early wave. Phosphatases of the DUSP family and PP2A subunits restrain the cascade, while CDK5 with its neuronal activators and the repressor REST tune the neuronal output. Disruption affects neuronal plasticity and survival.

Nerve growth factor acting through its receptor tyrosine kinase TrkA does more than promote survival of sympathetic and sensory neurons; one branch of its output converges on the transcription factor STAT3, best known as the acute-phase response factor of cytokine signalling. Recruitment and tyrosine phosphorylation of STAT3 downstream of activated NTRK1 allows it to dimerise and enter the nucleus, where it drives immediate early gene transcription and gene programmes associated with exit from the cell cycle and neurite extension. This route helps explain how a single neurotrophin can switch a responsive cell from proliferation to differentiation and process outgrowth, linking growth factor reception at the membrane to lasting changes in neuronal morphology. The same axis is co-opted in tumours where NTRK1 is rearranged or constitutively active, and loss of NGF-TrkA signalling underlies congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis.

Once ERK enters the nucleus its signal is converted into changes in gene expression, and the ERK/MAPK targets described here are the substrates that perform that conversion. They determine whether a growth factor stimulus produces proliferation, differentiation or a stress response, which is why this step sits downstream of RAS in most growth-factor-driven cancers. ERK1/ERK2, together with related kinases such as p38 and ERK5, phosphorylate transcription factors including ELK1 and the MEF2 family, and activate a second tier of kinases — the RSK family and MSK — that broaden the output to chromatin and immediate-early gene promoters. Equally represented is the shutdown machinery: dual-specificity phosphatases dephosphorylate the kinase activation loop, several of them induced by ERK itself as negative feedback, while protein phosphatase 2A subunits reverse substrate phosphorylation, keeping the response transient rather than sustained.

Neurons must report back to the nucleus that their distant axon terminals have found trophic support, and ERK5 signalling is the arm of neurotrophin response that carries out this retrograde message. Ligand-bound, phosphorylated TRK receptors are internalised at distal axons and trafficked as signalling endosomes to the cell body, where MEK5 phosphorylates and activates ERK5, which enters the nucleus and switches on transcription factors such as MEF2 to sustain neuronal survival. This route is distinguished from the ERK1/2 cascade, which responds to stimulation at the cell body and drives different nuclear targets; ERK5 activation does not require RAS and its MEK5 partner shows a vesicle-associated distribution consistent with travelling with the receptor. Loss of such target-derived survival signalling leaves developing neurons unsupported, and the pathway underlies the matching of neuron numbers to their innervation targets.

Lymphocytes decide whether a cell they touch is healthy self, stressed, infected or malignant, and immunoregulatory interactions between a lymphoid and a non-lymphoid cell are where that decision is made at the cell surface. Killer cell receptors of the immunoglobulin-like and C-type lectin families read MHC class I and its relatives, so loss of HLA-A/B/C during viral infection or tumour progression releases inhibition, while stress-induced ligands such as MICA, MICB and the ULBPs actively flag damaged cells to NKG2D. Inhibitory receptors carrying ITIM motifs and activating receptors coupling through DAP10 and DAP12 set the net signalling balance. Alongside recognition, selectins, IgSF adhesion molecules such as ICAMs and VCAM1, and integrins govern where lymphocytes arrest and enter tissue; Fc receptors and complement receptor CD21 with CD19 bring antibody- and complement-coated antigen to the same synapse. These contacts underlie self-tolerance, tumour surveillance and the checkpoints exploited therapeutically.

PPAR-alpha is the fatty acid-activated nuclear receptor that lets liver and heart switch to burning lipid during fasting, and this pathway describes how it turns target genes on. Bound to an RXR partner at peroxisome proliferator response elements, the liganded receptor exchanges corepressor complexes containing NCOR1/NCOR2, HDAC3 and TBL1X for coactivators such as NCOA1-3, CREBBP/EP300, MED1 and PGC-1alpha, then recruits the full Mediator complex to engage RNA polymerase II. The genes induced cover mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis (ACADM, ACOX1, CPT1A, CPT2, HMGCS2), fatty acid uptake and trafficking (CD36, FABP1, SLC27A1, ACSL1), lipid droplet and lipolysis control (PLIN2, G0S2, ANGPTL4), and HDL apolipoproteins APOA1, APOA2 and APOA5. Related receptors and clock factors, including LXRs, FXR, ESRRA and BMAL1/CLOCK, share this coregulator machinery and tie lipid catabolism to circadian and cholesterol signals. Fibrate drugs act here to lower triglycerides.

Vitamin B5 (pantothenate) metabolism supplies cells with coenzyme A, the thiol cofactor required for fatty acid synthesis and oxidation, the citric acid cycle, sterol and ketone body metabolism, and protein acylation. Because coenzyme A itself is degraded outside cells and not transported across plasma membranes, each cell imports pantothenate through a sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter and rebuilds the cofactor internally: pantothenate kinases commit the vitamin by phosphorylation, cysteine is added and decarboxylated, and a bifunctional enzyme completes adenylylation and phosphorylation. Vanins hydrolyse pantetheine to regenerate pantothenate, while phosphodiesterases and nudix hydrolases degrade CoA, and mitochondrial carriers distribute it between compartments so that cytosolic, matrix and peroxisomal pools can be set independently. A phosphopantetheinyl transferase instead loads the prosthetic arm onto fatty acid synthase. Loss of the neuronal kinase PANK2 causes an iron-accumulating neurodegeneration.

Growth factor signalling through PI3K to AKT drives cell growth, survival and metabolic anabolism, and must be turned off as reliably as it is turned on; negative regulation of the PI3K/AKT network is how that braking is achieved. The central event is removal of the lipid second messenger PIP3, chiefly by the tumour suppressor phosphatase PTEN, which reverses PI3K catalysis and prevents membrane recruitment of AKT. Additional restraint acts on AKT itself: PHLPP1 and PHLPP2 dephosphorylate its hydrophobic motif, protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes oppose activating phosphorylation, and TRIB3 and THEM4 bind and inhibit the kinase. Also represented are the upstream inputs being restrained — receptor tyrosine kinases for EGF, FGF, PDGF, HGF and insulin, immune receptor and Toll-like adaptors, and the lipid kinases that supply substrate. Loss of this brake gives constitutive AKT activity, a common route to tumorigenesis and therapy resistance.

Neurotrophin signalling ends, in part, at the nucleus, where phosphorylation of CREB on serine 133 converts a resting transcription factor into an activator of genes that keep neurons alive, grow their axons, and consolidate synaptic change into lasting memory. Loss of this step leaves neurotrophin-dependent neurons unable to mount the survival and growth transcription programme that nerve growth factor normally triggers, including in axons signalling retrogradely back to the cell body. The kinases that carry out the modification sit downstream of the MAP kinase cascades: the RSK family members RPS6KA1, RPS6KA2 and RPS6KA3 and the ERK/p38-activated MSK1 (RPS6KA5), together with the p38 effector MAPKAPK2. MSK1 additionally phosphorylates the related factor ATF1, and its activity tracks NGF-induced CREB phosphorylation more closely than that of the RSKs. Serine 133 phosphorylation then permits coactivator recruitment and target gene transcription.

Roughly a quarter of newly made proteins must leave the endoplasmic reticulum, and anterograde transport from the ER to the Golgi is the first leg of that journey. It supports secretion of hormones, clotting factors and matrix proteins, and delivery of receptors and surface molecules to the plasma membrane; when it fails, cargo is retained and disease follows, as in factor V/VIII deficiency from loss of the LMAN1–MCFD2 cargo receptor or in ER-retained mutant alpha-1 antitrypsin. Cargo is concentrated at ER exit sites by the COPII coat, with SAR1 and SEC23/24 inner and SEC13/31 outer layers assembled on SEC16 and TANGO1 scaffolds, and carried to the intermediate compartment. RAB1, p115, golgins, the TRAPP complex and SNAREs including STX5, BET1 and SEC22B drive tethering and fusion, while COPI, ARF1, KDEL receptors and dynein-dynactin on microtubules return escaped ER residents and receptors.

Membrane trafficking is the set of routes by which a cell moves proteins, lipids and sugars between its organelles and the cell surface, and it underlies secretion, nutrient uptake, receptor signalling and the maintenance of organelle identity. Newly made cargo leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated carriers, is processed and glycosylated in the Golgi, and is sorted at the trans-Golgi network into carriers that fuse with the plasma membrane; retrieval by COPI and retrograde carriers balances this outward flow. Clathrin and adaptor complexes with dynamin drive endocytosis, Rab GTPases with their activating and inactivating regulators specify compartments, SNAREs and NSF execute fusion, ESCRT components sort ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies, and kinesin, dynein and myosin motors carry vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks. Defects cause lysosomal and pigmentation disorders, hypercholesterolaemia, bleeding diatheses and neurodegeneration, and impair regulated events such as insulin-stimulated glucose transporter delivery.

Cargo that has finished transiting the Golgi must be sorted and packaged for onward delivery, and vesicle budding at the trans-Golgi network is where that decision is made. It sends lysosomal hydrolases to the endolysosomal system, recycles receptors, and dispatches secretory and plasma membrane proteins along microtubules to the cell surface. Heterotetrameric adaptor complexes, chiefly AP-1 and its relatives AP-3 and AP-4, recognise sorting signals in transmembrane cargo such as the mannose-6-phosphate receptors and sortilin, recruit clathrin triskelia to curve the membrane, and hand off to dynamin and accessory factors for scission and uncoating, with ARF1 and GBF1 licensing coat assembly. Related machinery builds lysosome-related organelles including melanosomes and platelet granules, so defects here cause Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, mislocalised hydrolases and lysosomal storage disease, and spastic paraplegia.

Long-chain fatty acids cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane as CoA esters, and the carnitine shuttle is how they get in to be burned. Tissues that rely on fat oxidation during fasting or exercise cannot sustain ATP output without it: loss of the carnitine transporter SLC22A5, the translocase SLC25A20, or CPT2 causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Carnitine is taken up from plasma, an outer-membrane acyltransferase (CPT1A in liver, CPT1B in muscle) converts acyl-CoA to acylcarnitine, the inner-membrane carrier exchanges it for free carnitine, and CPT2 regenerates acyl-CoA for beta oxidation. The step is the main control point for fuel choice, since malonyl-CoA made by acetyl-CoA carboxylases inhibits CPT1; AMP-activated protein kinase subunits and nuclear receptors such as PPARD with RXRA tune this so that fatty acid synthesis and oxidation do not run at once.

Bone morphogenetic proteins are TGF-beta family ligands that pattern bone, cartilage, blood vessels, heart, kidney and lung, and signalling by BMP is how those instructions reach the nucleus. Secreted ligands such as BMP2, BMP10 and GDF2 engage a type II receptor (BMPR2, ACVR2A/B) paired with a type I kinase (BMPR1A, BMPR1B, ACVRL1); the constitutively active type II kinase phosphorylates the type I GS domain, which then phosphorylates the receptor-regulated SMAD1, SMAD5 and SMAD9. These partner with the shared co-SMAD SMAD4 and, with ZFYVE16 aiding endosomal trafficking, direct transcription of target genes. Output is tuned by extracellular antagonists including noggin, cerberus and gremlin, by inhibitory SMAD6/SMAD7 recruiting the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1/2, and by the corepressor SKI. Loss of control underlies vascular malformations such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, heterotopic ossification, skeletal disorders and cancer.

Signaling by ALK covers the anaplastic lymphoma kinase, a neural receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor family whose activation drives proliferation and survival, and whose deregulation is one of the best-known oncogenic drivers in anaplastic large cell lymphoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, neuroblastoma and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumours. Physiologically it is expressed in the developing central and peripheral nervous system, where the ALKAL1/ALKAL2 ligands, and possibly the heparin-binding factors pleiotrophin and midkine, induce receptor dimerisation, trans-autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHC1, FRS2 and IRS1. From there signals flow into RAS-MAPK, PI3K and JAK3-STAT3 routes, with STAT3 turning on MYC, MYCN, HIF1A, PRDM1 repression and PD-L1 expression through cooperating chromatin regulators. Chromosomal rearrangements producing NPM-ALK or EML4-ALK fusions, or activating point mutations, make this signalling constitutive and ligand-independent, the basis for ALK inhibitor therapy.

ALK is a receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor family, expressed mainly in the developing central and peripheral nervous system, where its activation by the secreted ligands ALKAL1 and ALKAL2 contributes to neuronal differentiation; in mice and flies it also acts as a determinant of resistance to weight gain. Its importance in humans is largely oncogenic: chromosomal rearrangements that fuse the kinase domain to dimerization-competent partners, as well as amplification and activating point mutations, drive anaplastic large cell lymphoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, neuroblastoma and other tumours, making the kinase a major drug target. Ligand binding or fusion-driven dimerization triggers transautophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHC1, FRS2 and IRS1, feeding RAS, PI3K and SRC signalling. Parallel JAK3-STAT3 activation reprogrammes transcription, inducing MYC, MYCN and HIF1A and, via chromatin repressors including HDACs, SIN3A and DNMT1, silencing genes such as PRDM1 while raising PD-L1 expression.</br>

Canonical WNT signalling ends at the nucleus, where TCF/LEF factors switch on target genes, and this branch covers everything from ligand binding to that transcriptional output. It sets cell fate in development, maintains intestinal and other adult stem cell compartments, and drives colorectal and many other cancers when its brakes fail. WNT ligands engaging Frizzled receptors with LRP5/6 disable the destruction complex of APC, AXIN and GSK3B, so beta-catenin escapes proteasomal degradation, enters the nucleus, displaces TLE/Groucho repressors from TCF7L2 and partners, and recruits BCL9, PYGO and histone-modifying coactivators to induce MYC, AXIN2 and TERT. Tuning comes from secreted antagonists such as DKKs, SFRPs and sclerostin, from RSPO-LGR signalling that blocks the receptor ubiquitin ligases RNF43 and ZNRF3, and from tankyrase-mediated turnover of axin.

Dishevelled proteins are the first cytoplasmic relay in WNT signalling, and their activation converts ligand binding at a Frizzled receptor into a membrane platform that ultimately stabilises beta-catenin and reprogrammes transcription during development, stem cell maintenance and tissue regeneration. Kinases including casein kinase 1 epsilon and the casein kinase 2 holoenzyme phosphorylate DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3, which already carry basal phosphate before stimulation; phosphorylated Dishevelled then docks on the conserved cytoplasmic motif of Frizzled and oligomerises through its DIX domain to recruit AXIN away from the destruction complex. Dishevelled also engages phosphoinositide kinases, including a type I phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate 5-kinase, so that local PI(4,5)P2 production drives LRP6 clustering and phosphorylation. Because this step licenses downstream signal amplification, its dysregulation contributes to WNT-driven tumours and to developmental patterning defects.

This is the nuclear endpoint of WNT signalling: stabilized beta-catenin enters the nucleus, binds TCF/LEF factors such as TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2 and LEF1 sitting on WNT response elements, and converts them from repressors into activators of target genes including MYC, AXIN2 and TERT. The switch controls stem and progenitor self-renewal, crypt and limb patterning, and is constitutively engaged in colorectal and other cancers where beta-catenin escapes degradation. Mechanistically, beta-catenin displaces Groucho/TLE corepressors and HDAC1 from TCF/LEF and uses its armadillo repeats and C-terminus as a scaffold: BCL9/BCL9L with PYGO bind the N-terminal repeats, while histone acetyltransferases CREBBP/EP300 and KAT5, the MLL-family methyltransferase complex (KMT2B with WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, DPY30, MEN1), the SWI/SNF ATPase SMARCA4 and PAF components are recruited to open chromatin and fire transcription. Histone substrates are the ultimate targets of these modifying activities.

This is the switch step that converts ligand binding at a G protein-coupled receptor into an intracellular signal. An agonist-occupied receptor acts as a nucleotide exchange factor for the heterotrimer, replacing GDP with GTP on the Galpha subunit, which then separates from the Gbeta-gamma dimer so that both can engage effectors; intrinsic GTP hydrolysis by Galpha terminates the cycle and allows reassembly, while the receptor turns over further heterotrimers and amplifies the input. The Galpha members here are the Gq/11 family, which drives phospholipase C, inositol trisphosphate and calcium release, paired with a broad repertoire of Gbeta and Ggamma subunits whose combinations tune effector selectivity. Opioid receptor signalling by endogenous peptides derived from prodynorphin and proopiomelanocortin illustrates the physiology, linking analgesia, reward and neuroendocrine control to this nucleotide exchange event.

Metabolism of nitric oxide: NOS3 activation and regulation governs how endothelial cells make nitric oxide, the diffusible messenger that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, sets blood pressure and vascular tone, and restrains platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion. Loss of endothelium-derived NO is the defining feature of endothelial dysfunction and contributes to hypertension and atherosclerosis. Because NO cannot be stored, output is controlled entirely at the enzyme. Calcium-loaded calmodulin binds NOS3 to permit electron flow from its reductase domain to heme, while HSP90 and AKT1-mediated phosphorylation raise activity and caveolin-1 sequestration lowers it. N-myristoylation and palmitoylation by NMT1/NMT2 and ZDHHC21, reversed by acyl-protein thioesterase, target the enzyme to caveolae and traffic it between plasma membrane, Golgi and perinuclear membranes, with NOSIP and NOSTRIN redirecting it. Cofactor supply through tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis and DDAH1-mediated clearance of the inhibitor ADMA further tune arginine turnover.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase makes the diffusible gas that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, and this pathway covers how that enzyme is switched on, positioned and restrained. NO produced here sets blood pressure and vascular tone, damps platelet aggregation and leukocyte adhesion, and its loss defines endothelial dysfunction in hypertension and atherosclerosis. Activity requires calcium-loaded calmodulin and is tuned by phosphorylation, with AKT1 and the HSP90 chaperone promoting output while caveolin-1 sequesters and inhibits the enzyme in caveolae. Membrane targeting depends on N-myristoylation by NMT1/NMT2 and palmitoylation by ZDHHC21, reversed by the thioesterase LYPLA1, while NOSIP and NOSTRIN redistribute the enzyme away from the plasma membrane. Substrate and cofactor supply matters too: DDAH1 destroys the endogenous inhibitor asymmetric dimethylarginine, and SPR contributes to tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis, without which the enzyme uncouples.

Once procollagen trimers reach the extracellular space, they must be trimmed, aligned and locked together; this is the step where collagen fibrils and the other multimeric collagen assemblies are built, and it sets the tensile strength of tendon, bone, cartilage, skin and blood vessel wall. Propeptides are removed by bone morphogenetic protein 1 and tolloid-like proteinases, with PCOLCE enhancing C-propeptide cleavage, after which tropocollagen self-assembles in quarter-stagger register and is covalently stabilised by lysyl oxidases. Minor collagens such as types V, XI and IX nucleate or coat fibrils and limit their diameter, while non-fibrillar types form hexagonal networks, beaded filaments and the type VII anchoring fibrils that, with laminin-332 and integrin α6β4, tether epidermis to dermis. Cathepsins and matrix metalloproteinases remodel these structures; defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta, Ehlers-Danlos syndromes and epidermolysis bullosa.

Blood pressure and salt balance are set in part by a cascade of peptide hormones cut successively out of a single liver-secreted prohormone. Renin, released by juxtaglomerular cells when perfusion falls, cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and angiotensin-converting enzyme on endothelial surfaces trims this to angiotensin II, the vasoconstrictor that drives sodium and water retention and aldosterone secretion; drugs blocking renin or ACE are mainstays of hypertension therapy. The conversion of angiotensinogen to angiotensins is not a single route: mast cell chymase, cathepsin G and cathepsin Z generate angiotensin II locally, while ACE2 and neprilysin produce angiotensin-(1-7), which acts through the MAS receptor to oppose angiotensin II. Aminopeptidases A and N further shorten the peptide to angiotensins III and IV with their own receptors, and the prorenin receptor enhances renin catalysis at membranes. Imbalance among these arms contributes to hypertension, cardiac and renal fibrosis.

Keratan sulfate is a sulfated glycosaminoglycan attached to proteoglycan core proteins, and its biosynthesis determines the spacing and hydration of collagen fibrils in the cornea and cartilage. Corneal transparency depends on it: loss-of-function mutations in the corneal GlcNAc-6-O-sulfotransferase CHST6 cause macular corneal dystrophy, with progressive corneal clouding, while the same polymers in cartilage contribute to the compressive resilience of the matrix. The chain is built by alternating addition of galactose and N-acetylglucosamine through beta-1,4-galactosyltransferases and beta-1,3-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases, then sulfated on both sugars by carbohydrate sulfotransferases, with capping by sialyltransferases terminating elongation. Nucleotide-sugar supply to the Golgi lumen is required for these transfers. The carrier proteins are small leucine-rich proteoglycans of the extracellular matrix -- lumican, keratocan, fibromodulin, mimecan and PRELP -- alongside the large cartilage proteoglycan aggrecan.

Keratan sulfate chains on proteoglycans of cornea and cartilage are turned over in lysosomes, and this degradative route is where they are dismantled residue by residue. Because the core proteins are Asn-linked glycoproteins, breakdown proceeds by sequential exo-glycosidase and sulfatase action from the non-reducing end: sulfate groups are removed by GALNS and GNS, terminal galactose by acid beta-galactosidase (GLB1), and N-acetylglucosamine by the beta-hexosaminidase A and B isoenzymes built from HEXA and HEXB subunits. Each step must precede the next, so loss of any one enzyme stalls the whole chain and leaves partially digested fragments accumulating in lysosomes, the basis of mucopolysaccharidosis IVA, Morquio B and related storage diseases with skeletal and corneal involvement. The substrates themselves include aggrecan and the small leucine-rich proteoglycans lumican, keratocan, fibromodulin, osteoglycin and PRELP, which organise collagen fibrils and corneal transparency.

Chondroitin sulfate glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis builds the long, negatively charged sugar chains that give cartilage, blood vessel wall and brain extracellular matrix their hydration, compressive resistance and ability to bind growth factors. The chains are polymerised onto a tetrasaccharide linker on proteoglycan core proteins — aggrecan-family members such as versican, brevican and neurocan, plus decorin, biglycan and the cell-surface proteoglycans CSPG4 and CSPG5 — by GalNAc transferases (CSGALNACT1/2) and the chondroitin synthase and polymerising-factor complexes (CHSY1, CHSY3, CHPF, CHPF2) that alternate GalNAc with glucuronic acid. A family of Golgi sulfotransferases then decorates the chain at the GalNAc 4- and 6-positions and at glucuronate, and the resulting sulfation pattern dictates binding specificity. Loss of CHSY1 causes a skeletal dysplasia with brachydactyly, and chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans deposited after CNS injury inhibit axon regrowth.

DS-GAG biosynthesis builds dermatan sulfate, the glycosaminoglycan that gives skin, tendon, blood vessels and cornea their tensile strength and hydration, and that decorates proteoglycans controlling collagen fibril spacing, growth factor availability and neural matrix organisation. Chains of alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and uronic acid are elongated on the tetrasaccharide linker of core proteins such as decorin, biglycan, versican and the brain proteoglycans brevican and neurocan. Dermatan sulfate identity comes from epimerisation of glucuronic to iduronic acid by DSE and DSEL, followed by sulfotransferase action: CHST14 adds 4-O-sulfate to GalNAc, CHST15 makes the 4,6-disulfated form, and UST sulfates uronic acid at position 2. This sulfation pattern encodes binding specificity for heparin cofactor II and for FGF and HGF signalling. Loss of CHST14 or DSE causes musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with joint laxity, fragile skin and skeletal malformation.

Dermatan sulfate chains are built on proteoglycan core proteins and give connective tissue its tensile and hydrating properties, while also shaping growth factor and chemokine availability in the extracellular matrix. Synthesis extends the tetrasaccharide linker with alternating N-acetylgalactosamine and uronic acid, then diversifies the chain: epimerases encoded by DSE and DSEL convert glucuronic acid to iduronic acid, which is what distinguishes dermatan sulfate from chondroitin sulfate, and sulfotransferases such as CHST14, CHST15 and UST add sulfate to the 4- and 6-positions of GalNAc or to the uronic acid 2-position. The finished chains decorate small leucine-rich proteoglycans like decorin and biglycan and the large hyalectans versican, neurocan and brevican, controlling collagen fibril assembly, skin and vascular integrity, and neural matrix organisation. Defects in the epimerase or the 4-O-sulfotransferase cause a form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with joint laxity and fragile skin.</description>

Heparan sulfate chains coat nearly every cell surface and fill basement membranes, where their patterned sulfation creates binding sites that concentrate growth factors, morphogens, chemokines and coagulation factors and dictate how cells read those signals. Synthesis of these glycosaminoglycans starts on a core protein — syndecans, glypicans, perlecan or agrin — with EXT1 and EXT2 polymerising the alternating glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine backbone. The chain is then tailored: NDST enzymes remove acetyl groups and add N-sulfate, an epimerase converts glucuronic to iduronic acid, and 2-O-, 6-O- and 3-O-sulfotransferases install the sulfates that define specific ligand-binding motifs, one of which generates the antithrombin-binding sequence of heparin, made by mast cells. Loss of EXT function causes hereditary multiple exostoses, and defects in these proteoglycans disrupt skeletal growth, neuromuscular junction assembly and filtration barriers.

Amplification of the FGFR2 gene drives ligand-independent growth signalling in a subset of cancers, notably around a tenth of gastric cancers — where it marks poor-prognosis diffuse tumours — and a small fraction of breast cancers. Sheer overexpression of the receptor tyrosine kinase, rather than any change in its intrinsic catalytic activity, is what produces constitutive downstream output toward proliferation and survival. Amplified alleles frequently carry deletions of C-terminal exons, removing sequences needed for receptor internalisation and degradation, so the protein persists at the cell surface and signals without fibroblast growth factor stimulation. Because the driver is receptor dosage and stability rather than a kinase-domain change, these tumours remain responsive to FGFR-directed small-molecule inhibitors, which makes amplification status a predictive biomarker as well as an oncogenic mechanism.

Engagement of the T cell receptor by peptide presented on MHC class II is the decision point at which a naive T cell commits to proliferate, differentiate and acquire effector function, and it underlies both protective cellular immunity and, when miscalibrated, autoimmunity and immunodeficiency. Clonotypic alpha/beta chains paired with invariant CD3 and zeta subunits have no catalytic activity of their own, so signalling begins with Lck, held in check by Csk and the phosphatases CD45, PTPN22 and PTPRJ, phosphorylating receptor ITAMs to recruit ZAP-70. ZAP-70 phosphorylates the adaptors LAT and SLP-76, nucleating a complex that activates phospholipase C gamma, PI3 kinase and Vav-directed actin remodelling through WASP, PAK kinases and Ena/VASP proteins. Protein kinase C theta then drives the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 complex to the IKK complex, and proteasomal degradation of IkB releases NF-kB for transcription of activation genes.

HS-GAG degradation is the lysosomal breakdown of heparan sulfate chains released from proteoglycans, the turnover arm of proteoglycan homeostasis. It matters because heparan sulfate cannot be digested by a single enzyme: exoglycosidases and sulfatases must act in strict sequence from the non-reducing end, and loss of any one step causes undegraded fragments to accumulate in lysosomes, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses — Hurler, Hunter and the Sanfilippo subtypes — with skeletal, visceral and neurodegenerative consequences. The substrates are the cell surface and matrix proteoglycans themselves: syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin, whose sugar chains tune growth factor and morphogen signalling. Cathepsin L and heparanase initiate the process by shedding and internally cleaving the chains, after which iduronidase, iduronate sulfatase, sulfamidase, acetyl-CoA transferase and alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase strip the resulting oligosaccharides residue by residue.

Heparan sulfate chains on cell-surface and matrix proteoglycans are constantly turned over, and this pathway covers their breakdown from intact proteoglycan to free sugars. Syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin are internalised, their core proteins clipped by cathepsin L, and the heparan sulfate chains cut into fragments by heparanase before delivery to the lysosome. There a strictly ordered set of exo-acting enzymes works from the non-reducing end: iduronate 2-sulfatase and alpha-L-iduronidase remove iduronic acid residues and their sulfate, sulfamidase and the acetyl-CoA-dependent transferase HGSNAT handle glucosamine nitrogen, and NAGLU releases N-acetylglucosamine. Because each step requires the previous one, loss of any single enzyme halts the chain and undegraded fragments accumulate, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses — Hunter, Hurler, and Sanfilippo syndromes — with skeletal, visceral and neurological disease.

CS/DS degradation is the lysosomal breakdown of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate chains released from extracellular matrix proteoglycans, the disposal arm of glycosaminoglycan turnover. Proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan, versican and the brain-specific aggrecan family members brevican and neurocan are continuously internalised and dismantled, and the sugar chains must be taken apart sugar by sugar. Hyaluronidases first fragment the long polymers, then exoenzymes act in strict order: sulfatases including ARSB and IDS remove sulfate groups, and glycosidases such as GUSB, GLB1, IDUA and the beta-hexosaminidase subunits HEXA/HEXB cleave the exposed terminal residues. Because each step depends on the one before, loss of any single enzyme halts the chain and undegraded fragments accumulate, producing mucopolysaccharidoses with skeletal, corneal, visceral and neurological damage. The pathway thus links matrix remodelling to lysosomal catabolic capacity.

Chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate chains on proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan, versican, brevican and neurocan are continuously turned over, and their final breakdown happens in the lysosome. Endoglycosidases of the hyaluronidase family cleave the chains internally, after which exo-acting enzymes strip the ends one residue at a time: sulfatases including arylsulfatase B and iduronate 2-sulfatase remove sulfate groups, while beta-glucuronidase, alpha-L-iduronidase, beta-galactosidase and the beta-hexosaminidase subunits release the terminal sugars. Because each step depends on the one before it, loss of a single enzyme halts the whole sequence and partially digested glycosaminoglycan accumulates, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses and related lysosomal storage disorders with their skeletal, visceral and neurological consequences. This catabolism supports extracellular matrix remodelling and the general homeostasis of glycoconjugate turnover.

When a T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC class II on an antigen-presenting cell, the proximal signal must be converted into new gene expression before the cell can proliferate and secrete effector cytokines. This downstream arm of T cell receptor signalling carries that conversion, principally by activating NF-kappaB alongside NFAT and AP-1.
