PI3K recruited to the synapse generates PIP3, opposed by the lipid phosphatases PTEN and SHIP, and PDK1 together with diacylglycerol activates PKC-theta, the one PKC isoform that translocates to the immunological synapse. PKC-theta phosphorylates CARD11, which oligomerises and recruits BCL10 and MALT1; TRAF6 then builds K63 ubiquitin chains that engage TAK1 and the IKK complex. IKK-beta phosphorylates IkB-alpha, marking it for SCF-betaTrCP-directed proteasomal destruction so RELA/NFKB1 enters the nucleus. Defects here produce combined immunodeficiency, while chronic activation of this axis drives lymphoid malignancy.

The first biochemical step after a T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC is phosphorylation of the CD3 and TCR zeta ITAMs, which converts antigen recognition into an intracellular signal and thereby sets the threshold for T cell activation, thymic selection and tolerance. Before stimulation the Src-family kinase LCK, carried by the CD4 coreceptor, is held inactive by CSK, which phosphorylates its C-terminal inhibitory tyrosine while docked on the raft adaptor PAG1 and also sequesters the phosphatase PTPN22. Engagement of MHC class II displaces CSK, the receptor phosphatase PTPRC removes the inhibitory phosphate, and LCK trans-autophosphorylates its activation loop before marking the paired tyrosines of each ITAM in CD3 delta, epsilon and gamma and in the zeta chain, creating docking sites for ZAP-70. Opposing phosphatases such as PTPRJ tune the output; variants in PTPN22 predispose to autoimmunity.

Early in T cell activation, the kinase ZAP-70 is drawn from the cytosol to the immunological synapse, the contact zone where a T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC class II on an antigen-presenting cell. This recruitment step converts antigen recognition into an intracellular signal, and without it helper T cells cannot be activated at all: loss of ZAP-70 causes a severe combined immunodeficiency, while variants of the phosphatase PTPN22 that blunt its restraint of this step predispose to autoimmunity. Phosphorylated ITAM motifs in the CD3 chains and the zeta chain form docking sites for the tandem SH2 domains of ZAP-70; the CD4-associated kinase LCK then phosphorylates the activation loop, and trans-autophosphorylation completes activation so that the adaptor LAT can be phosphorylated. PTPN22 dephosphorylates ZAP-70 to damp the response, making this a tightly thresholded gate on antigen-driven signalling.

When a T cell receptor engages peptide-MHC, the resulting tyrosine phosphorylation must be converted into diffusible signals the cell can act on; this step generates those second messengers. Its output determines whether a T cell proliferates, differentiates and mounts an immune response, and loss of its components produces severe immunodeficiency. After the receptor complex and its CD3 chains are engaged with coreceptor and MHC class II, LCK and ZAP70 phosphorylate the membrane adaptor LAT and the cytosolic adaptor LCP2/SLP-76, which with GRAP2 nucleate a signalosome. Recruited there, phospholipase C-gamma1 is activated by ITK and ZAP70 and hydrolyses PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, driving protein kinase C, NF-kB and calcium release. The same platform couples to actin regulators including WAS, NCK1, PAK kinases and Ena/VASP proteins that shape the immunological synapse.

Antigen receptor engagement on T and B cells raises cytosolic calcium, and this is the step that converts that calcium signal into new gene expression. Calcium-loaded calmodulin activates the phosphatase calcineurin, built from a catalytic subunit and a calcium-binding regulatory subunit, which then strips inhibitory phosphates from NFAT transcription factors. Dephosphorylation uncovers their nuclear localisation signals, so NFATC1, NFATC2 and NFATC3 move from cytosol to nucleus and, together with partners such as AP-1, drive the cytokine genes that underlie lymphocyte activation and clonal expansion. The pathway matters clinically because it is the point of attack for transplant immunosuppression: cyclosporin A and FK-506 act through the immunophilins cyclophilin A and FKBP1A to block calcineurin and shut down NFAT-dependent transcription. The same calcineurin-NFAT axis also operates in muscle, bone and cardiac hypertrophy.

ERKs are inactivated is the off-switch for ERK signalling, the step that converts a growth factor stimulus into a transient pulse rather than a permanent one. Because ERK output drives proliferation, differentiation and survival decisions, the duration and location of its activity determines the cellular response, and loss of shutdown contributes to unchecked growth in cancers with hyperactive RAS-RAF input. Inactivation works by removing the activating phosphates from the threonine and tyrosine of the activation loop: dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7 act on cytoplasmic ERK1/2, DUSP4 acts in the nucleus, and the serine/threonine phosphatase PP2A holoenzyme contributes through its catalytic and regulatory subunits, with VRK3 serving as a scaffold for nuclear dephosphorylation. Since ERK itself induces transcription of these phosphatases, the arrangement forms a negative feedback loop that sets signal amplitude and timing.

Growth factor signalling through ERK must be switched off as well as on, and this is the shut-off arm: phosphatases strip the activating phosphates from the Thr-Xaa-Tyr motif in the activation loop of ERK1, ERK2 and ERK5, returning the kinases to a resting state. Because ERK activity drives proliferation, differentiation and survival gene programmes, the duration and amplitude of the signal determine the cellular outcome, and loss of this braking step contributes to unchecked mitogenic signalling in cancer. Dual-specificity phosphatases such as DUSP6 and DUSP7, which act largely on ERK in the cytoplasm, and nuclear DUSP4, remove both phosphates, while the PP2A holoenzyme built from catalytic, scaffolding and B56 regulatory subunits contributes serine/threonine dephosphorylation; VRK3 acts as a scaffold promoting phosphatase action on ERK. Since ERK itself induces DUSP transcription, the arrangement forms a negative feedback loop.

Leukocytes must be captured from flowing blood and moved across the vessel lining to reach inflamed or injured tissue, and the cell surface interactions at the vascular wall described here are what make that possible. Selectins and their glycoprotein ligands, notably SELE, SELP, SELL and SELPLG, mediate reversible tethering and rolling, after which integrins such as ITGAL/ITGB2 and ITGAM convert rolling into firm adhesion on endothelium or on platelets already deposited at a site of injury. Junctional and immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion molecules including PECAM1, F11R, JAM2/JAM3, CD99 and ESAM control endothelial cell contacts and guide transendothelial migration, while Src-family kinases, phosphatases and PI3K/Ras adaptors relay adhesion into intracellular signalling. Related interactions cover thrombin- and protein C-dependent endothelial anticoagulant control, angiopoietin-TEK signalling, SIRPA-CD47 recognition, and amino acid transporter heterodimers at the plasma membrane. Dysregulation contributes to atherosclerosis, thrombosis and chronic inflammatory injury.

Hippo signalling sets organ size by deciding whether cells keep dividing or stop and die, and its loss is a route to tissue overgrowth and cancer. A three-tier kinase cascade carries the decision: autoactivated STK3 and STK4, partnered with SAV1, phosphorylate LATS1 and LATS2 together with their MOB1A/MOB1B cofactors, and the LATS kinases in turn phosphorylate the transcriptional co-activators YAP1 and WWTR1 (TAZ). Phosphorylated YAP1 and TAZ are captured by 14-3-3 proteins and held in the cytosol; unphosphorylated, they enter the nucleus and drive proliferative and anti-apoptotic transcription. Many of these contacts use WW domains and PPxY motifs. The pathway is tied to cell junctions and density sensing through angiomotins and the tight-junction proteins ZO-1 and ZO-2, is amplified when caspase-3 clips inhibitory tails off the MST kinases, and intersects Wnt signalling via sequestration of DVL2.

Antibody-coated microbes and debris are cleared by monocytes, macrophages and neutrophils that recognise the Fc portion of bound IgG, and this Fcgamma receptor-dependent phagocytosis links humoral immunity to physical destruction of targets; it also underlies the action of therapeutic antibodies and, when misdirected at self, drives tissue injury in autoimmune cytopenias. Clustering of FCGR1A, FCGR2A or FCGR3A by IgG immune complexes triggers Src-family kinases such as LYN, HCK and FGR to phosphorylate receptor ITAMs, recruiting SYK and BTK and activating PI3K, phospholipase C gamma and VAV-family exchange factors. Calcium release through IP3 receptors and activation of CDC42 and RAC1 then drive WASP- and WAVE-dependent Arp2/3 actin nucleation, cofilin and PAK/LIMK turnover, and myosin-based contraction, extending pseudopods that zipper around the particle and seal it into a phagosome. Loss of WAS function compromises this engulfment.

Antibody-coated targets are cleared by phagocytes, and this is the step that converts IgG binding into an intracellular signal. Clustering of Fc gamma receptors by IgG immune complexes brings their ITAM-bearing chains together, SRC-family kinases such as LYN, HCK, FGR and FYN phosphorylate those motifs, and the tandem SH2 domains of SYK dock on the phosphotyrosines to propagate signalling toward actin remodelling and engulfment of the particle. The receptors here span the high-affinity FCGR1A and the lower-affinity FCGR2A and FCGR3A, paired in some cases with shared ITAM subunits, while the large complement of immunoglobulin heavy, kappa and lambda variable and constant region genes represents the IgG ligands that form the complexes. This activation underlies opsonised phagocytosis, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity, and the efficacy of therapeutic antibodies; it also drives tissue damage in immune-complex diseases.

Phagocytes engulf antibody-coated particles by extending pseudopods around them, and this branch of actin regulation builds the phagocytic cup that does the swallowing. It is how macrophages and neutrophils clear opsonized bacteria and apoptotic debris, and its failure leaves antibody-dependent clearance ineffective. Immunoglobulin-coated targets are recognized by Fc gamma receptors, whose engagement recruits SYK and the tyrosine kinase BTK and activates the GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 through VAV family exchange factors and the DOCK1-ELMO module. Active GTPases relieve autoinhibition of WASP, N-WASP and WAVE complex components, including the CYFIP-ABI-NCKAP1 assembly, which in turn switch on ARP2/3-dependent branched actin nucleation. Cofilin, LIMK1, PAK1 and unconventional myosins shape filament turnover and contractile closure, so cup formation couples immune receptor signalling to directed membrane deformation.

Phagocytes engulf antibody-coated particles by remodelling membrane lipids at the site of contact, and this lipid signalling arm of phagocytosis converts receptor engagement into the actin and calcium changes that close a phagocytic cup. IgG bound to a target is recognised by Fc gamma receptors, whose ITAM tails recruit the kinase SYK; downstream, class I PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits generate PI(3,4,5)P3, while phospholipase C gamma isoforms cleave PI(4,5)P2 to diacylglycerol and IP3. IP3 opens ER inositol trisphosphate receptors so that local cytosolic calcium rises around the forming cup, and DAG activates protein kinase C isoforms; phospholipase D and phospholipase A2 activities supply phosphatidic acid and arachidonic acid, and phosphatidate phosphatases return the products to diacylglycerol. Together these mediators drive particle ingestion and phagosome maturation, the basis of antibody-dependent clearance of microbes and opsonised cells.

YAP1 and its paralogue WWTR1 (TAZ) are the transcriptional output of Hippo signalling: when the kinase cascade is off, they enter the nucleus and drive genes that promote proliferation, survival and growth, so tissues reach and hold the right size. Neither binds DNA directly; both work as co-activators for TEAD family factors, with TAZ also partnering RUNX2 in osteoblast differentiation and TBX5, and the cardiac factors GATA4 and NKX2-5 linking this output to heart gene programmes such as natriuretic peptide and the matricellular target CCN2. Acetyltransferase and HIPK kinase components modulate the complex. Hippo phosphorylation instead traps both proteins in the cytosol; loss of that restraint, or YAP amplification, produces organ overgrowth, fibrotic matrix production and is a recurrent driver of mesothelioma and other cancers.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 normally restrains chondrocyte proliferation during endochondral bone growth, and activation of mutant forms of the receptor converts that brake into a constitutive growth signal. Germline gain-of-function changes produce the autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasias, including achondroplasia and thanatophoric dysplasia, while the same or analogous substitutions arising somatically drive bladder carcinoma, cervical cancer and other tumours. Some mutants remain dependent on FGF ligands, several of which are represented here as paracrine and endocrine agonists that engage the receptor with heparan sulfate or Klotho cofactors; others dimerize and signal without ligand. In multiple myeloma a translocation places the gene under immunoglobulin heavy chain control, and fusion proteins in lung, bladder and glioblastoma dimerize through partner-derived domains. Output flows through RAS-ERK and PI3K-AKT to sustain proliferation, survival and transformation.

A chromosomal rearrangement joining chromosome 4 to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14 places FGFR3 under the control of the strong IGH enhancer, and this t(4;14) event defines a recurrent subgroup of about 15% of multiple myelomas with generally poor prognosis. The consequence is gross overexpression of a receptor tyrosine kinase that normally restrains chondrocyte proliferation in growth plates but here drives plasma cell growth and survival, signalling either without ligand or with exaggerated responses to fibroblast growth factors. In a minority of cases activating point mutations in FGFR3 accompany the translocation, further uncoupling the kinase from control. The breakpoint also deregulates the neighbouring histone methyltransferase gene MMSET, so both a signalling and a chromatin lesion arise together. Sensitivity of such myeloma lines to FGFR3 kinase inhibitors makes this an example of oncogene activation by regulatory-element capture with direct therapeutic implications.

Gain-of-function point mutations in FGFR2 turn a ligand-controlled receptor tyrosine kinase into a constitutively or hypersensitively signalling one, and the consequences are visible in the skeleton and skin: dominantly inherited craniosynostosis syndromes including Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Jackson-Weiss, Apert and Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata, plus somatic activation in roughly a sixth of endometrial cancers and some ovarian and gastric tumours. Most substitutions leave intrinsic kinase chemistry intact but subvert control of it, clustering in the third Ig-like domain where unpaired cysteines drive ligand-independent dimerization, or in the IgII-IgIII linker where they broaden the range and affinity of FGF ligands accepted, including partners normally reserved for the alternative splice isoform. The accompanying FGF family members are those ligands. Because FGFR2 signalling governs osteoblast differentiation, suture patency and epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalk in development, its deregulation yields premature bone fusion and proliferative disease.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase makes the nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, restrains platelet adhesion and leukocyte recruitment, and sets basal blood pressure; losing its output is a defining feature of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension, atherosclerosis and diabetes. eNOS activation describes how the enzyme is switched on rather than how it is transcribed. N-myristoylation and palmitoylation by ZDHHC21 target it to caveolae, where caveolin-1 holds it inactive until a rise in intracellular calcium loads calmodulin onto the enzyme and displaces the inhibitor; depalmitoylation reverses the lipid anchor. AKT1 phosphorylation of the reductase-domain serine raises activity and calcium sensitivity, while HSP90 acts as an activating chaperone. Cofactor and substrate supply matter as much as modification: sepiapterin reductase provides tetrahydrobiopterin, and DDAH1 degrades methylarginines that would otherwise compete with L-arginine and uncouple the enzyme toward superoxide.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase must sit at the right membrane to make the nitric oxide that relaxes vascular smooth muscle, and NOSTRIN-mediated eNOS trafficking is how endothelial cells pull it away from that site. NOSTRIN binds eNOS and moves it from the plasma membrane into intracellular vesicular compartments, lowering nitric oxide output; because endothelium-derived nitric oxide controls vessel tone, platelet adhesion and permeability, this relocalisation is a way of tuning vascular relaxation, and its dysregulation belongs to the broader picture of endothelial dysfunction in hypertension and atherosclerosis. Mechanistically NOSTRIN trimerises and uses its SH3 domain as an adaptor, gathering eNOS together with dynamin-2 and the N-WASP homologue encoded by WASL; dynamin drives vesicle fission while N-WASP recruits the Arp2/3 complex to nucleate actin. Caveolin-1 places the process in caveolae, linking nitric oxide signalling to caveolar endocytosis and actin remodelling.

Endothelial nitric oxide synthase must sit in plasma membrane caveolae to make nitric oxide efficiently, and NOSIP-mediated trafficking is one way that localisation is taken away from it. By binding the carboxy-terminal region of the eNOS oxygenase domain, this nucleocytoplasmic shuttling protein pulls the enzyme off caveolae and onto the cytoskeleton, where its output of nitric oxide falls. The consequence is felt in the vasculature: nitric oxide from endothelium relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelet aggregation and limits leukocyte adhesion, so relocalising its source is a way to tune vascular tone and blood pressure without changing how much enzyme is present. Because NOSIP accumulates in the cytoplasm during G2, this represents a point where cell cycle position feeds into endothelial signalling output, and it illustrates control of an enzyme by compartment rather than by transcription.

MicroRNAs are short RNAs that tune the output of most human genes, and their biogenesis is the multi-step route from a transcribed hairpin to a loaded silencing complex. The pathway sets how strongly hundreds of mRNAs are translated and degraded, shaping differentiation, proliferation and stress responses; loss of the processing machinery is embryonically lethal, and its disruption is a recurrent feature of tumours. RNA polymerase II generates a primary transcript whose hairpin is cropped in the nucleus by DROSHA with its partner DGCR8, exported by Exportin-5 in a Ran-GTP-dependent step, and cut by DICER1 with TARBP2 or PRKRA to a short duplex. One strand is discarded and the guide strand is retained by an Argonaute protein, of which AGO2 alone can slice highly complementary targets, forming the effector complex that directs post-transcriptional silencing.

COPII-mediated vesicle transport is the first step of the secretory pathway: it captures newly made proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum and delivers them to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment, so that everything a cell secretes or puts on its surface can leave the ER. Its failure underlies bleeding disorders through defective export of factors V and VIII, as well as skeletal and neurological disease. Cargo is concentrated at ER exit sites organised by SEC16, where the Sar1 GTPase recruits the inner SEC23/SEC24 adaptor layer and the outer SEC13/SEC31 cage to deform the membrane into a vesicle. Cargo receptors such as LMAN1 with its partner MCFD2 select specific glycoproteins, while TRAPP complexes, Rab1 and the SNAREs STX5, BET1, SEC22B and YKT6 with NSF and SNAP proteins drive uncoating, tethering and fusion at the acceptor membrane.

Everything a cell secretes or puts on its surface leaves the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII-coated vesicles, and this pathway is the export step that starts the secretory route. Cargo is concentrated at ER exit sites organized by SEC16, where the small GTPase SAR1B recruits the inner SEC23/SEC24 adaptor layer and the outer SEC13/SEC31 cage, budding vesicles that uncoat and fuse with the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment. Selective receptors such as LMAN1 with its partner MCFD2 capture particular clients, and mutations in either cause combined factor V and factor VIII deficiency; alpha-1 antitrypsin, collagen VII and blood clotting factors all depend on this traffic. Delivery is completed by RAB1 activation through the TRAPP complex, the tether USO1, and SNARE-mediated fusion involving STX5, BET1, SEC22B and the NSF/SNAP machinery that recycles them.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is the committed step that converts glycolytic pyruvate into acetyl-CoA, and its regulation decides whether a cell burns glucose or conserves it. Switching the complex off spares glucose during fasting and shifts tissues onto fat oxidation; keeping it on allows glucose carbon to feed the TCA cycle for ATP and to supply acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis. Control is by reversible phosphorylation of the E1 alpha subunit: four kinases (PDK1-4) inactivate the complex in response to hormonal and nutritional state, while two magnesium-dependent phosphatases (PDP1, PDP2, with the regulatory subunit PDPR) reactivate it. SIRT4 further restrains activity. Loss-of-function mutations in the core subunits cause pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency with lactic acidosis and neurological disease, and persistent PDK activity underlies the glycolytic metabolism of many tumours.

Humans cannot make linoleic acid or alpha-linolenic acid and must take them from the diet, so the conversion of these two essential fatty acids into their long-chain derivatives determines the supply of arachidonic acid, EPA and DHA. Alternating desaturation by FADS1 and FADS2 and two-carbon elongation by the ELOVL enzymes, with ACSL1 activating fatty acids as CoA thioesters, builds chains up to 24 carbons; the final step to DHA requires a round of peroxisomal beta-oxidation, which explains the presence of the ABCD1 transporter, ACOX1, the bifunctional HSD17B4, thiolase and SCP2. The products matter because they are membrane constituents of brain and retina and the precursors of prostaglandins, leukotrienes and related lipid mediators that set the tone of inflammatory responses. The relative flux through the omega-3 and omega-6 branches, which share these enzymes, influences cardiovascular and neurological health, and defects in the peroxisomal steps cause severe inherited disease.

Linoleic acid is an essential omega-6 fatty acid taken in from the diet, mainly vegetable oils, and its metabolism converts it into the longer, more unsaturated fatty acids the body cannot make from scratch ation arachidonic acid above all, the precursor of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes. The route supports skin barrier integrity and hair growth, bone and reproductive health, and membrane phospholipid composition. Alternating desaturation and elongation steps take place in the endoplasmic reticulum, where FADS2 introduces the delta-6 double bond, FADS1 the delta-5, and ELOVL5 and ELOVL2 add two-carbon units; the final shortening of a 24-carbon intermediate to 22:5(n-6) requires transport into peroxisomes, via the ABCD1 transporter, for one round of beta-oxidation. Acyl-CoA synthetase activity supplies the activated thioester substrates. Variation in the desaturase locus shifts circulating lipid profiles and inflammatory mediator supply.

Alpha-linolenic acid metabolism converts a dietary omega-3 fatty acid that humans cannot make into the long-chain products that matter physiologically, eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid. DHA is enriched in retinal and neuronal membranes, and EPA-derived mediators restrain inflammation, so the efficiency of this route shapes cardiovascular, neurological and visual health and is why dietary omega-3 intake is monitored at all. The chemistry alternates desaturation and two-carbon elongation on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane: FADS2 introduces the delta-6 double bond, FADS1 the delta-5, and ELOVL5 and ELOVL2 extend the chain. Making DHA requires an extra detour, since the 24-carbon intermediate must be imported into peroxisomes and shortened by one round of beta-oxidation involving acyl-CoA oxidase, the bifunctional enzyme HSD17B4 and thiolase before the finished product returns for membrane incorporation.

Hypusine is an amino acid found in exactly one protein, the translation factor eIF5A, and this two-step modification is what makes that factor functional. Ribosomes stall on stretches of consecutive prolines and on other awkward sequences; hypusinated eIF5A rescues them, so the pathway sits at the heart of translation elongation and termination, cell proliferation and viability. Deoxyhypusine synthase first transfers the aminobutyl moiety of the polyamine spermidine onto a specific lysine of eIF5A using NAD+, and deoxyhypusine hydroxylase then adds a hydroxyl group using molecular oxygen to complete hypusine. This makes eIF5A activity directly dependent on polyamine supply, linking spermidine metabolism to protein synthesis capacity. Loss-of-function mutations in the synthase cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability and seizures, and the paralogue eIF5A2 is amplified in several cancers.

Cell death signalling via NRAGE, NRIF and NADE is the apoptotic arm of neurotrophin receptor p75 (NGFR) signalling, the route by which developing neurons that fail to secure trophic support, or neurons injured in the adult nervous system, are eliminated. Mature NGF and, more potently, proneurotrophins engage p75NTR, while TrkA signalling opposes the same outcome, so the balance between the two receptors sets neuronal survival during target-field competition and after axonal damage. Death signalling proceeds through the adaptors TRAF6, NRAGE/MAGED1 and NRIF with ubiquitin-dependent steps, activation of Rac via guanine nucleotide exchange factors, and JNK-dependent induction of BIM, BAD and caspase-2/-3. Gamma-secretase cleavage of the receptor releases an intracellular fragment that carries NRIF to the nucleus for transcriptional events. Dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration and to neuronal loss following ischaemia or trauma.

Neurons are eliminated during development and after injury when the p75 neurotrophin receptor, rather than TrkA, dominates the response to nerve growth factor or its unprocessed precursor, and this receptor-initiated death programme is what the intracellular adaptors NRAGE, NRIF and NADE carry forward. It matters because it sculpts the size of neuronal populations to match their targets and contributes to neuronal loss after axotomy and in degenerative injury. Ligand-bound NGFR recruits TRAF6 and MAGED1 (NRAGE), engages Rac1 through an array of Rho-family exchange factors, and activates JNK, converging on BAD, BIM and caspase-3 to dismantle the cell. In parallel, gamma-secretase components including presenilins and nicastrin cleave the receptor so that its intracellular domain, with NRIF, can reach the nucleus and drive transcriptional events; ubiquitin and SQSTM1 support the signalling scaffold.

Nerve growth factor and its unprocessed precursor proNGF both engage the p75 neurotrophin receptor, but with opposite consequences for a neuron's fate. Mature NGF signalling through TRKA promotes survival and neurite growth, whereas proNGF cannot bind TRKA and instead selects p75NTR when a sortilin-family co-receptor is present at the cell surface, converting receptor engagement into an apoptotic cascade. This discrimination lets the balance between precursor and processed neurotrophin, and the availability of the co-receptor, determine whether a sensory or sympathetic neuron lives or dies. The death arm is implicated in neuronal loss after axonal injury and in neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer's dementia, where proNGF accumulates. The same logic applies to proBDNF, making pro-neurotrophin binding to p75NTR a general switch within neurotrophin signalling rather than a property of NGF alone.

When nerve growth factor binds the p75 neurotrophin receptor rather than a Trk receptor, the outcome can be death instead of survival, and NADE modulates that death signalling branch. This is the route by which developing sympathetic and sensory neurons that fail to secure adequate trophic support are eliminated, and it contributes to neuronal loss after injury and in neurodegeneration. The adaptor NADE, encoded by BEX3, is recruited to the p75 receptor intracellular region selectively after NGF engagement, whereas BDNF, NT3 and NT4/5 do not trigger the response. Recruitment leads to caspase activation, with initiator caspase-2 feeding into effector caspase-3 and the dismantling of the cell. The 14-3-3 protein epsilon binds NADE and tunes how readily apoptosis proceeds, making this a regulated checkpoint rather than an automatic consequence of receptor occupancy.

Neurotrophin receptor p75 can kill the cell it signals in, and this route is how that decision is carried into the nucleus. It shapes developmental pruning of sympathetic neurons and retinal cells, where neurotrophin or proneurotrophin withdrawal and receptor engagement determine which neurons survive, and it contributes to neuronal loss after injury. Ligand binding to p75 recruits an adaptor and ubiquitin-ligase complex built around TRAF6 and the scaffold SQSTM1, leading to polyubiquitination of the zinc-finger DNA-binding protein NRIF; JNK activity participates in the death signal. Gamma-secretase, comprising presenilin with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2, cleaves the p75 intracellular domain and releases it, permitting NRIF translocation into the nucleus, where it is thought to act as a transcription factor that commits the neuron to apoptosis. Regulated proteolysis and ubiquitin signalling thus convert a surface receptor event into a nuclear death programme.

p75NTR recruits signalling complexes describes how the neurotrophin receptor p75, on binding NGF, assembles an adaptor platform at the plasma membrane that turns on NF-kB and thereby favours neuronal survival. p75NTR is unusual in that the same receptor can drive apoptosis through JNK or survival through NF-kB depending on which complex it recruits, so this branch sets the balance that determines whether developing and injured neurons live, and it shapes responses to axonal damage and neurodegenerative stress. Mechanistically, the ligand-bound receptor gathers RIP2, MyD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62/SQSTM1 and atypical PKC iota, allowing TRAF6 to build polyubiquitin chains that activate the IKK complex and release NF-kB for nuclear entry. The pathway is a clear example of ubiquitin-dependent scaffolding borrowed from innate immune signalling and used in the nervous system.

Neurotrophin binding to the p75 neurotrophin receptor turns the receptor's cytoplasmic tail into a docking platform, and the complexes it recruits determine whether a neuron survives, grows, or dies. Because p75NTR has no catalytic activity of its own, everything depends on which adaptors arrive: here the assembly built around NGF-bound receptor gathers RIPK2, MYD88 and IRAK1 together with the scaffold p62 and atypical protein kinase C iota, converging on TRAF6. TRAF6 acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and the polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin genes in this module drives activation of the IKK complex through IKBKB, freeing NF-kB to enter the nucleus and switch on survival and inflammatory transcription. This arm of neurotrophin signalling opposes the pro-apoptotic outputs of the same receptor, and its balance shapes developmental neuronal pruning, axon growth and injury responses.

Nerve growth factor acting through the p75 receptor does more than promote neurite growth: it engages NF-kB to keep neurons alive, and this survival arm is the pathway described here. Ligand-bound NGFR recruits TRAF6 together with the scaffold SQSTM1 and the kinase IRAK1, and polyubiquitin chains built from the ubiquitin precursors in this set relay the signal to the IKK subunit IKBKB. Phosphorylation of the inhibitor NFKBIA marks it for degradation, freeing the p50/p65 dimer of NFKB1 and RELA to enter the nucleus and switch on anti-apoptotic and pro-survival transcription, including HES family genes that restrain dendritic branching. The same circuitry balances the death signalling that p75 can otherwise initiate, so its output helps determine which developing sympathetic and sensory neurons survive and how elaborately they arborise.

Axon extension depends on keeping the RHOA branch of cytoskeletal control switched off at the growth cone, and this is how neurotrophin signalling achieves that. Unliganded p75 neurotrophin receptor holds RHOA in a complex that keeps it active and the actin cytoskeleton contracted, restraining elongation; binding of nerve growth factor releases RHOA to its GDP-dissociation inhibitor, which sequesters the inactive GTPase in the cytosol and permits growth cone advance. The outcome is stimulation of axonal growth by relief of an inhibitory brake rather than by a positive growth signal, and the same receptor can instead limit outgrowth when it engages myelin-associated inhibitors. This switch shapes how developing and regenerating neurons navigate, and its failure contributes to the poor regrowth of injured central axons.

Several hormones and neurotransmitters are built by decorating a single aromatic amino acid, and this pathway covers those routes: tyrosine to dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline, tyrosine on thyroglobulin to thyroid hormone, and tryptophan to serotonin and then melatonin. The products set heart rate and blood pressure, basal metabolic rate and growth, mood, and the daily sleep-wake rhythm. Tyrosine hydroxylase and DDC generate dopamine, DBH and PNMT extend it to the adrenal catecholamines, while TPH1/TPH2 and the sequential action of AANAT and ASMT produce pineal melatonin. Thyroid synthesis requires iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter, peroxide from a DUOX-DUOXA complex, iodination by thyroid peroxidase under TSH control, and iodide recycling; deiodinases then activate or inactivate the hormone in peripheral tissues. Defects cause congenital hypothyroidism, catecholamine deficiency states and dysautonomia.

The glycoprotein hormones are the heterodimeric pituitary and placental hormones that drive reproduction and thyroid function: follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone and chorionic gonadotropin. All four share a common alpha subunit, encoded by CGA, paired through disulphide bonds with a distinct beta subunit (FSHB, LHB, TSHB or CGB3) that determines which receptor is engaged and therefore whether the signal drives follicle maturation, ovulation and steroidogenesis, thyroid hormone synthesis, or maintenance of the corpus luteum in early pregnancy. Carbohydrate side chains on the mature dimers govern circulating half-life and potency. The inhibin and activin subunits included here act as gonadal feedback regulators of FSH output, inhibin restraining it and activin promoting it. Loss of individual beta subunits produces selective hypogonadism or congenital hypothyroidism rather than global endocrine failure, illustrating the modular design of this hormone family.

Dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline are made from the amino acid tyrosine in a short, strictly ordered enzymatic sequence, and catecholamine biosynthesis is what gives dopaminergic, noradrenergic and adrenergic cells their identity. The products govern movement and reward in the brain, sympathetic control of heart rate and vascular tone, and the adrenal stress response. Tyrosine hydroxylase performs the rate-limiting ring hydroxylation to L-DOPA using tetrahydrobiopterin, aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase converts L-DOPA to dopamine, dopamine beta-hydroxylase acts inside secretory vesicles to yield noradrenaline, and phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase adds a methyl group to form adrenaline, largely in adrenal medullary chromaffin cells. Which product a cell releases is set by which of these enzymes it expresses. Loss of tyrosine hydroxylase or the decarboxylase causes infantile dopamine-deficient movement disorders, and degeneration of the neurons that run this route underlies the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis converts dietary tryptophan into two signalling molecules that set mood, sleep and circadian timing. Serotonin acts as a neurotransmitter in the central nervous system and as a peripheral hormone affecting gut motility, platelet function and vascular tone, while its conversion to melatonin in the pineal gland communicates night length to the rest of the body. Tryptophan hydroxylase performs the rate-limiting hydroxylation, in a neuronal form and a peripheral/pineal form, and the aromatic amino acid decarboxylase step yields serotonin itself. In the pineal gland, an N-acetyltransferase whose activity rises at night acetylates serotonin, and an O-methyltransferase completes melatonin synthesis, making the acetylation step the principal gate on nocturnal melatonin output. Disturbance of this route is linked to depression, migraine and disordered sleep, and the enzymes lie upstream of the drug targets used to treat them.

Peptide hormone biosynthesis covers how endocrine peptides are made as inactive precursors and converted into the circulating signals that control reproduction, growth, metabolism and the stress response. Two themes dominate here: the glycoprotein hormones, in which a shared alpha subunit encoded by CGA pairs with a distinct beta subunit — chorionic gonadotropin, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone or thyrotropin — so that subunit choice determines which receptor and which target tissue responds; and the proteolytic maturation of a polyprotein precursor, where the prohormone convertase PCSK1 cleaves proopiomelanocortin into corticotropin and related melanocortin and opioid peptides. Inhibin and activin subunits contribute the feedback arm that tunes pituitary gonadotropin output. Loss of convertase activity or of POMC-derived peptides produces adrenal insufficiency and severe early-onset obesity, while defective gonadotropin subunits cause hypogonadism and infertility.

Thyroxine biosynthesis is the making of thyroid hormone by follicular cells of the thyroid, the process that sets basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, growth and neurodevelopment throughout life; its failure causes congenital hypothyroidism, goitre and cretinism, and its dysregulation underlies common thyroid disease. Pituitary thyrotropin, a heterodimer of a shared glycoprotein alpha subunit with TSHB, drives the programme. Iodide is concentrated from plasma by the sodium-iodide symporter SLC5A5, delivered to the apical membrane, and oxidised by thyroid peroxidase using hydrogen peroxide generated by the DUOX1/DUOX2 oxidases with their maturation factors DUOXA1/2. Iodination and coupling of tyrosines occurs on thyroglobulin, which is endocytosed and degraded in lysosomes to liberate T4 and T3, while iodotyrosine deiodinase recycles iodide. In peripheral tissues the selenodeiodinases DIO1, DIO2 and DIO3 activate T4 to T3 or inactivate it, tuning local hormone action on nuclear receptors.

Thyroid hormone sets basal metabolic rate, drives growth and brain development, and its supply depends on thyroxine biosynthesis in thyroid follicular cells. Thyrotropin, the pituitary glycoprotein hormone made of a shared alpha subunit and TSHB, stimulates follicular cells to concentrate iodide from plasma through the sodium-iodide symporter SLC5A5 and to iodinate tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin at the apical membrane. Thyroid peroxidase catalyses iodination and coupling using hydrogen peroxide generated by the dual oxidases DUOX1 and DUOX2 with their maturation factors DUOXA1 and DUOXA2. Iodotyrosine deiodinase salvages iodide from uncoupled residues, while the selenoenzymes DIO1, DIO2 and DIO3 set local hormone activity by converting T4 to active T3 or to inactive metabolites. Loss of any of these steps causes congenital hypothyroidism, goitre and, untreated, irreversible developmental delay; released T3 acts through nuclear receptors to reprogramme target gene expression.

Glutamatergic transmission depends on clearing the transmitter from the synaptic cleft quickly, and astrocytic glutamate-glutamine uptake and metabolism is how that clearance is coupled to transmitter resupply. Astrocyte processes wrapped around the synapse take up released glutamate through the high-affinity excitatory amino acid transporters EAAT2 and EAAT1 (SLC1A2, SLC1A3), keeping extracellular levels low enough to preserve signal fidelity and to prevent the excitotoxic overstimulation of NMDA receptors implicated in ischaemia, epilepsy and motor neuron degeneration. Inside the astrocyte, glutamine synthetase (GLUL) amidates glutamate to the non-excitatory carrier glutamine, which a system N transporter (SLC38A1) releases to the extracellular space for neuronal reuptake and reconversion to glutamate. The cycle thus links astrocytic amino acid and nitrogen handling to neuronal neurotransmitter pools and to the energetic coupling between the two cell types.

Fast excitatory transmission in the brain depends on packaging glutamate into synaptic vesicles and releasing it in a calcium-triggered burst, and this release cycle is the machinery that accomplishes it. Glutaminase converts glutamine to glutamate in the presynaptic cytosol, a vesicular transporter (SLC17A7/VGLUT1) concentrates it into vesicles, and after exocytosis high-affinity excitatory amino acid transporters on neurons and astrocytes clear the cleft to end the signal and prevent excitotoxic damage. Release itself proceeds through docking and priming at the active zone, organized by Munc18/STXBP1, Munc13 and RIM-liprin scaffolds, followed by assembly of a SNARE complex of VAMP2, syntaxin-1A and SNAP25; synaptotagmin-1 senses the calcium rise and complexin clamps and synchronizes fusion. Mutations in these components cause epileptic encephalopathies and movement disorders, and the cycle underlies synaptic plasticity, learning and the balance of excitation across circuits.

Regulation of gene expression in late stage (branching morphogenesis) pancreatic bud precursor cells describes the transcriptional program that keeps pancreatic epithelial progenitors proliferating within branching ducts while parcelling out the first endocrine cells. It sets the size of the progenitor pool from which islet beta cells eventually arise, so its failure underlies pancreatic hypoplasia and neonatal diabetes; mutations in HNF1B cause maturity-onset diabetes of the young with renal cysts. ONECUT1 sustains HNF1B and ONECUT3 expression and drives epithelial proliferation as PDX1 and NKX6-1 levels fall. Superimposed on this, Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ, mastermind-like coactivators and the histone acetyltransferases CBP/p300 and GCN5/PCAF maintains HES1, which represses NEUROG3 and enforces lateral inhibition. Cells escaping this repression accumulate NEUROG3 and exit the cycle to begin endocrine differentiation, linking chromatin-level coactivation to cell fate choice in organ development.

During the branching morphogenesis stage of pancreatic development, committed but still undifferentiated epithelial precursors in the growing ductal tree must be kept proliferating until a subset is released to become hormone-producing endocrine cells. This transcriptional programme sets that balance, and its disruption limits beta cell number, an origin of neonatal diabetes and pancreatic hypoplasia. ONECUT1 sustains expression of ONECUT3 and HNF1B, which maintain the epithelial progenitor state and duct formation, while NEUROG3 induction marks the commitment of individual cells to the endocrine lineage. Notch signalling through NOTCH1, RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators, with the acetyltransferases CREBBP, EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, drives the repressor HES1 to restrain NEUROG3 and hold neighbouring cells as progenitors, so that lateral inhibition rations differentiation across the branching epithelium.

Mature pancreatic beta cells are defined by a transcriptional programme that keeps insulin, glucokinase and the GLUT2 glucose transporter expressed at the levels needed for glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. Regulation of gene expression in beta cells is dominated by PDX1 and HNF1A, which sustain this identity by driving insulin, amylin, the liver/pancreas pyruvate kinase and further transcription factors including HNF4A, HNF4G and FOXA3. PDX1 itself is positioned downstream of MAFA, FOXA2 and PAX6 and is restrained through AKT-dependent signalling, with FOXO1 linking nutrient and insulin signals back to the network; NEUROD1, NKX2-2, NKX6-1 and RFX6 act in lineage specification and maintenance. Loss of individual factors produces monogenic diabetes, and erosion of the programme underlies the dedifferentiation and secretory failure seen in type 2 diabetes, making this circuitry the basis of glucose homeostasis.

Regulation of gene expression in endocrine-committed (NEUROG3+) progenitor cells describes the transcriptional step at which a pancreatic duct-like progenitor stops being a generic epithelial cell and commits to becoming a hormone-secreting islet cell. It is the gateway to the beta, alpha, delta and PP lineages, so loss of the initiating factor abolishes islet formation altogether and causes neonatal diabetes with malabsorptive diarrhoea, since related endocrine cells of the gut depend on the same factor. Transient expression of neurogenin 3 activates a downstream tier of regulators — PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and INSM1 — which reinforce endocrine identity, suppress alternative acinar and ductal programmes, and steer subprogrammes toward particular hormone fates; PAX4 in particular biases cells toward beta and delta rather than alpha character. This cascade sits within pancreatic organogenesis and is the template followed when stem cells are directed toward insulin-producing cells in vitro.

Pancreatic endocrine cells arise from a transient population of progenitors that switch on neurogenin 3, and this transcriptional programme is what commits those cells away from duct and acinar fates toward the hormone-producing islet lineages. Without it no beta, alpha, delta or PP cells form; loss-of-function mutations in humans cause congenital malabsorptive diarrhoea with permanent neonatal diabetes, and the same programme is the target of efforts to make beta cells from stem cells. NEUROG3 acts as a short-lived pioneer factor that directly induces a second tier of regulators, including PAX4, NEUROD1, NKX2-2 and the zinc-finger factor INSM1, which together consolidate endocrine identity, drive exit from the cell cycle, and bias progenitors toward particular hormone subtypes. The pathway illustrates how a brief pulse of one factor is converted into a stable differentiated state.

The pancreas begins as a pair of buds of endoderm whose cells are already committed to become the exocrine acini, ducts and islets, and this transcriptional programme is what specifies and maintains that early precursor state. Much of it is inferred from mouse embryology, where loss of the founding factors causes pancreatic agenesis or severe hypoplasia; in humans, mutations in the same genes underlie pancreatic and beta-cell developmental disorders, including diabetes arising from failed islet formation. HNF1B, ONECUT1 and PDX1 act in the nascent bud, and together with mesenchymal FGF10 signalling they drive expression of a second tier that includes PTF1A, ONECUT3, NR5A2 and NKX6-1. These downstream factors begin to separate the acinar and endocrine fates, so the network functions as the hierarchical link between endodermal patterning and later hormone- and enzyme-producing cell identity.

PECAM-1/CD31 is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor concentrated at endothelial cell junctions and present on platelets and leukocytes, where its interactions govern leukocyte transendothelial migration, T cell activation, platelet responses and angiogenesis. It engages partners both homophilically, through its extracellular Ig domains, and heterophilically, including with the integrin alphaV/beta3 pair. Its main signalling role is inhibitory: Src-family kinases such as SRC, FYN, LYN, LCK and YES1 phosphorylate tyrosines in the cytoplasmic ITIM motifs, creating docking sites for the SH2-domain phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 and the inositol phosphatase SHIP1, which damp immunoreceptor and integrin signalling and limit PLCgamma-dependent activation. This restraint sets thresholds for platelet aggregation and immune cell activation, while junctional PECAM-1 contributes to endothelial barrier maintenance and mechanosensing of shear stress, linking the receptor to vascular inflammation and thrombosis.

Basigin (CD147) is an immunoglobulin-superfamily transmembrane glycoprotein on epithelial and many other cell surfaces that acts both as an adhesion receptor and as an obligatory chaperone for membrane transporters. Its interactions matter because they set the surface level of the monocarboxylate transporters that export lactate from glycolytic cells, and because basigin engagement on neighbouring fibroblasts drives matrix metalloproteinase production and angiogenic VEGF signalling, a combination that supports tumour invasion and metastasis. Partners here include the MCT lactate/pyruvate carriers, the heavy chain 4F2hc with its LAT-family amino acid exchangers, Na+/K+-ATPase beta subunits, caveolin-1, beta1 integrin pairs, and cyclophilin A, which binds the N-terminal Ig-like domain. Homophilic contacts between basigin molecules on apposed cells, plus binding to L1CAM and MAG, link this hub to adhesion, energy metabolism, migration and development.

Blood vessels need a signal that tells endothelial cells to stay quiescent, stay attached to each other, and survive, and the Tie2 receptor tyrosine kinase encoded by TEK provides it. Angiopoietin-1 and angiopoietin-4 bind and trigger receptor autophosphorylation, while angiopoietin-2 acts largely as a competing ligand that loosens this restraint and primes vessels for sprouting or regression; the balance between them governs vascular stability, permeability, and angiogenic remodelling during development, wound healing, and tumour growth. Phosphorylated Tie2 becomes a docking platform: SHC1, GRB2 with SOS1 and the PTPN11 phosphatase route signals to RAS proteins and the MAP kinase cascade, while p85 regulatory and p110 catalytic PI3K subunits drive AKT-dependent endothelial survival. Loss or mutation of this axis underlies venous malformations, and its dysregulation contributes to sepsis-associated vascular leak and tumour vasculature.

Gene Silencing by RNA covers the small non-coding RNA systems that switch off genes after transcription, giving cells a layer of control that tunes protein output, defends the genome against transposons, and shapes development and differentiation. Loss of this machinery derails stem cell programmes, causes male infertility through transposon activation in germ cells, and contributes to cancer through widespread microRNA deregulation. Mechanistically, primary microRNA transcripts made by RNA polymerase II are cropped by Drosha with DGCR8, exported by exportin-5, diced by DICER1, and loaded into Argonaute proteins with TNRC6 partners to repress translation and destabilise target mRNAs; short interfering RNAs use the same effector step. A parallel germline branch built on PIWI proteins, Tudor-domain factors, MOV10L1 and mitochondrial PLD6 generates piRNAs that silence retroelements, while angiogenin and ELAC2 cleavage of tRNAs yields a further class of regulatory small RNAs.

Small non-coding RNAs let cells repress genes sequence-specifically, tuning developmental programmes, restraining transposons and buffering gene dosage. This silencing-by-RNA biology covers how microRNAs, small interfering RNAs, PIWI-interacting RNAs and tRNA-derived fragments are made and how they act. Primary microRNA transcripts made by RNA polymerase II are cropped in the nucleus by Drosha with its partner DGCR8, exported by exportin-5, and cut by Dicer; the resulting guide strand loads onto an Argonaute protein, which with a TNRC6 scaffold blocks translation and destabilises target mRNAs, or cleaves fully complementary targets. In germ cells a separate branch loads piRNAs onto PIWIL proteins with Tudor-domain and MOV10L1 helicase cofactors, methylated at their 3' end by HENMT1, to silence retrotransposons and safeguard spermatogenesis; loss of this arm causes germ cell loss and infertility. Angiogenin-cleaved tRNA fragments add a further layer of repression.

Growth factor and insulin signalling suppresses a stress- and starvation-driven transcriptional programme, and AKT-mediated inactivation of FOXO1A is the step that accomplishes it. In the absence of signalling, FOXO1 shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm with enough nuclear residence to drive genes for gluconeogenesis, autophagy, cell cycle arrest and apoptosis; once insulin or growth factors activate the AKT isoforms downstream of PI3K, the kinases phosphorylate FOXO1 at several sites, promoting 14-3-3 binding and its exclusion from the nucleus, so the programme is switched off. This is the branch of insulin action that lowers hepatic glucose output and permits growth and survival, and its loss of control contributes to insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia. Because FOXO1 restrains proliferation, constitutive AKT activity in tumours keeps this tumour-suppressive factor cytoplasmic and inert.

PAK2 is unusual among the p21-activated kinases in being a caspase substrate: cleavage during apoptotic signalling releases a constitutively active C-terminal fragment, PAK-2p34, that accumulates in the nucleus and drives cell death rather than the survival and cytoskeletal responses of the full-length kinase. This pathway describes how that death-promoting fragment is restrained. The Rho GTPase-activating protein PS-GAP, encoded by ARHGAP10, binds the cleaved kinase directly, suppresses its catalytic activity and redistributes it from the nucleus to the perinuclear region, so the amount of active PAK-2p34 available to signal apoptosis is set by how much of it is captured. The interaction matters because it makes the apoptotic outcome of PAK2 cleavage tunable rather than automatic, linking caspase processing, kinase localization and Rho family regulation at the decision point between stress survival and death.

Caspase cleavage of PAK-2 releases a constitutively active kinase fragment, PAK-2p34, that drives programmed cell death, so how long that fragment survives determines whether a stress-exposed cell dies. Turnover by proteasome-mediated degradation sets this threshold: the cleaved fragment, unlike full-length PAK-2, is polyubiquitinated and destroyed by the 26S proteasome, keeping apoptotic signalling from proceeding unless the fragment is stabilized. The machinery involved is the general ubiquitin-proteasome system — ubiquitin supplied as free and ribosomal fusion precursors, the 20S core of alpha and beta subunits that carries the peptidase activity, and the 19S regulatory particle with its ATPases and ubiquitin-receptor and deubiquitinating subunits that recognize, unfold and translocate the substrate. Placing the pro-apoptotic fragment under proteolytic control links cytoskeletal and stress kinase signalling to the cell's decision to commit to death.

Stimulation of the cell death response by PAK-2p34 describes how a normally growth-promoting kinase is converted, by caspase cleavage, into a pro-apoptotic effector that helps execute the morphological program of cell death. Under stress, active caspase-3 cuts PAK-2 to release the constitutively active carboxy-terminal fragment PAK-2p34, which autophosphorylates at Thr402, loses its nuclear export signal and accumulates in the nucleus, where it drives cell rounding and chromatin condensation. This makes PAK-2 unusual among p21-activated kinases: full-length PAK-2 supports survival and cytoskeletal remodelling downstream of Rac and Cdc42, while its cleaved form commits the cell to dying. The fragment is restrained by proteasomal turnover and by binding the GAP PS-GAP, which inhibits it and relocalizes it to the perinuclear region, and it may suppress cap-dependent translation initiation by phosphorylating Mnk1 during apoptosis.

Apoptotic commitment involves not only the destruction of structural proteins but the conversion of a kinase into a pro-death enzyme, and that is what happens here. Caspase-3 cleaves the p21-activated kinase PAK-2, releasing a constitutively active catalytic fragment, PAK-2p34, that drives the morphological hallmarks of dying cells: cell rounding, loss of adhesion, and condensation of apoptotic chromatin. Cleavage removes the nuclear export signal, so the fragment autophosphorylates and accumulates in the nucleus. Its activity is held in check by proteasomal turnover and by binding to a GTPase-activating protein that both inhibits the kinase and redistributes it to the perinuclear region. Downstream, PAK-2p34 has been implicated in shutting down cap-dependent translation initiation during apoptosis. The pathway illustrates how stress signalling and caspase proteolysis converge to make an ordinarily growth- and cytoskeleton-related kinase execute cell death.

Lipophilic chemicals — drugs, plant alkaloids, industrial compounds, and endogenous steroids, bile acid precursors and eicosanoids — would accumulate in tissue unless converted into water-soluble products that bile and urine can carry away. Biological oxidations covers that biotransformation, concentrated in liver but active in gut, kidney and lung, and it determines drug half-life, drug–drug interactions and the toxicity of carcinogens. A functionalization phase dominated by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases with their reductase partner POR, plus alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, flavin monooxygenases, monoamine oxidases, esterases and epoxide hydrolase, exposes or installs a reactive handle; conjugating transferases then cap it with glucuronide, sulfate, glutathione, acetyl or methyl groups, with glutathione and SAM supply enzymes feeding the cofactors. Aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling through ARNT induces much of this machinery. When functionalization outruns conjugation, electrophilic intermediates attack DNA and protein, the basis of chemical carcinogenesis and idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity.

The cytochrome P450 superfamily, organised here by the kinds of substrate its members oxidise, carries out most phase I biotransformation in humans and much of the oxidative chemistry of endogenous lipids. These heme-thiolate monooxygenases transfer one atom of molecular oxygen to a substrate using electrons from NADPH, delivered by the flavoprotein reductase POR in the endoplasmic reticulum or by the ferredoxin/ferredoxin reductase couple in mitochondria. One arm clears drugs, procarcinogens and other xenobiotics, with CYP3A4, CYP2D6 and CYP2C9 explaining much of the variation in drug response and toxicity, and inducible CYP1A1/CYP1A2 controlled by the aryl hydrocarbon receptor with ARNT. Other members are committed to specific endogenous routes: steroidogenesis and cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, oestrogen formation by aromatase, bile acid synthesis from cholesterol, vitamin D activation and inactivation, retinoic acid clearance, cholesterol biosynthesis, and eicosanoid formation including thromboxane and prostacyclin. Loss of individual enzymes causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia, rickets and bile acid disorders.

Fat-soluble vitamins only become hormones after enzymatic tailoring, and this small group of cytochrome P450 enzymes performs both the activating and the inactivating steps for vitamins D and A. Dietary vitamin D is 25-hydroxylated in liver by CYP2R1 and then converted to the active hormone calcitriol by the renal 1α-hydroxylase CYP27B1, which sets calcium and phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation; loss of CYP27B1 causes vitamin D-dependent rickets. CYP24A1 opposes this by 24-hydroxylating calcitriol for degradation, and its failure produces hypercalcaemia. In parallel, the CYP26 enzymes hydroxylate retinoic acid, clearing the vitamin A-derived morphogen and thereby shaping the concentration gradients that pattern the hindbrain, limbs and germ cells. Together these reactions determine how long each vitamin-derived signal persists at its nuclear receptor.

Long-chain fatty acids and their oxygenated derivatives are turned over by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, and this hydroxylation determines both how such lipids are cleared and what signalling molecules they become. The CYP4 family dominates the reaction, adding a hydroxyl at the terminal (omega) carbon to convert arachidonic acid into 20-HETE, a vasoconstrictor that helps set renal and vascular tone, and to inactivate leukotriene B4 and related eicosanoids so that inflammation resolves. Other members contribute epoxygenase activity, notably the heart-enriched CYP2J2, which generates vasodilatory epoxyeicosatrienoic acids, while an alcohol dehydrogenase supports related oxidation steps. Skin-expressed CYP4F22 hydroxylates ultra-long-chain fatty acids for ceramide synthesis, and its loss causes congenital ichthyosis; variants in the omega-hydroxylases have been linked to blood pressure regulation and to warfarin and vitamin K handling.

Before most drugs, toxins and lipophilic xenobiotics can be conjugated and excreted, they must first be given a reactive chemical handle, and this functionalization step is what phase I metabolism provides. It determines how long a drug persists, which metabolites reach tissues, and whether a compound is detoxified or converted into something that attacks DNA and protein — the route by which polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and paracetamol become hazardous. Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases dominate, supported by the reductase POR, cytochrome b5 and, for mitochondrial forms, ferredoxin and its reductase; flavin-containing monooxygenases, monoamine oxidases, alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, molybdenum-containing MTARC enzymes, epoxide hydrolase and carboxylesterases add oxidation and hydrolysis of esters, amides and epoxides. Ligand-activated transcription factors including the aryl hydrocarbon receptor with ARNT, and RXRA with FXR, induce these enzymes. Many members also handle endogenous substrates — steroid, bile acid, vitamin D, retinoic acid and prostanoid metabolism — explaining pharmacogenetic variation in drug response.

Aromatic amines can be N-hydroxylated or N-dealkylated by CYP1A2 describes a hepatic phase I biotransformation step that determines the fate of arylamine and heterocyclic amine compounds taken in from tobacco smoke, cooked meat and many drugs. Its consequences cut both ways: N-dealkylation clears substrates such as caffeine, theophylline, clozapine and tacrine, while N-hydroxylation of aromatic amines generates reactive hydroxylamines that are further conjugated and can bind DNA, linking this reaction to bladder and colorectal carcinogen activation. CYP1A2 is one of the most abundant cytochrome P450s in liver, uses NADPH-derived electrons and molecular oxygen at a heme iron centre, and is induced through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor by the same polycyclic aromatic compounds it metabolizes. Variation in its activity, from genetic polymorphism, smoking or inhibitors, is a major source of interindividual differences in drug clearance and chemical susceptibility.

Aromatic amines taken in from cooked meat, tobacco smoke and industrial exposures are chemically inert until a liver enzyme attacks their nitrogen, and CYP1A2 is the cytochrome P450 that performs this step, either N-hydroxylating the amine or stripping an alkyl group from it. The consequence is double-edged: N-dealkylation generally clears drugs such as caffeine, theophylline, clozapine and tacrine, so variation in this activity sets their plasma levels and dosing, while N-hydroxylation of heterocyclic and arylamines creates hydroxylamines that are further conjugated into DNA-binding electrophiles, linking this route to bladder and colorectal carcinogenesis. The enzyme sits in hepatic endoplasmic reticulum, draws electrons from NADPH via cytochrome P450 reductase, and is strongly induced through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling, which is why smoking accelerates clearance of its drug substrates. It also oxidizes steroids and fatty acids as part of general phase I metabolism.

Miscellaneous substrates gathers the cytochrome P450 enzymes whose in vivo substrates and physiological assignments remain unsettled, alongside a few with better-defined but hard-to-classify chemistry. These heme-thiolate monooxygenases sit in the endoplasmic reticulum, draw electrons from NADPH via P450 reductase, and oxidize lipophilic compounds, so their activities bear on drug clearance, eicosanoid turnover, and skin and vascular physiology. The group includes CYP2D6, the highly polymorphic enzyme that determines metabolism of a large share of prescribed drugs and defines poor and ultrarapid metabolizer phenotypes; CYP4F2 and CYP4A11, which omega-hydroxylate arachidonic acid and leukotriene B4 to regulate blood pressure and terminate inflammatory signalling; and CYP4F22, required for making the acylceramides of the epidermal permeability barrier, whose loss causes lamellar ichthyosis. Others, such as CYP2W1 and CYP2S1, catalyze P450-type reactions in vitro but await confirmed endogenous roles.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes acting on miscellaneous substrates are those whose oxidative chemistry is demonstrable but whose physiological substrates and regulation remain incompletely defined, so they sit outside the tidy classes of steroid, bile acid or eicosanoid metabolism. Their importance is nonetheless concrete: CYP2D6 oxidises a large share of clinically used drugs and its polymorphisms drive interindividual differences in dose response, while CYP4F2 and CYP4A11 hydroxylate arachidonic acid and related lipids to influence vascular tone and blood pressure, and CYP4F22 is required for the ultra-long-chain fatty acid processing that builds the epidermal permeability barrier, with loss-of-function causing ichthyosis. Others, including CYP2S1, CYP2U1, CYP2W1 and CYP4B1, are expressed in epithelia, brain or tumours and perform monooxygenation of fatty acids and xenobiotics whose in vivo significance is still being established.

Endogenous sterols covers the cytochrome P450 reactions that build cholesterol, convert it to bile acids and steroid hormones, and dispose of it, keeping whole-body cholesterol input and output balanced. When this balance fails, cholesterol accumulates and drives atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, while loss of individual enzymes causes bile acid deficiency, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Mechanistically, a lanosterol demethylase acts within the biosynthetic route, while 7alpha-, 24-, 25- and 27-hydroxylases initiate the neutral and acidic bile acid pathways and clear sterols from tissues such as brain; mitochondrial side-chain cleavage and the 11beta- and 21-hydroxylases divert cholesterol into glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and sex steroids, supported by ferredoxin and its reductase as the electron supply. Output is controlled transcriptionally through the bile acid receptor FXR with RXR and nuclear receptor coactivators, and through aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes acting on endogenous sterols set the balance between cholesterol made, converted and disposed of, and that balance determines circulating lipid levels, bile flow, and the supply of steroid hormones. One branch runs biosynthesis, where a lanosterol 14-alpha demethylase step is required to reach cholesterol; another converts cholesterol into bile acids, with the classical route initiated by cholesterol 7-alpha hydroxylase and alternative routes through sterol 27- and 25-hydroxylation, feedback-controlled by the bile acid receptor FXR with RXR. A third branch, in adrenal cortex, gonads and placenta, cleaves the cholesterol side chain and hydroxylates intermediates to make glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids and oestrogens, supported by adrenodoxin and its reductase as the electron relay. Brain-specific 24-hydroxylation allows sterol export across the blood-brain barrier. Loss of individual enzymes causes congenital adrenal hyperplasia, bile acid synthesis defects and hypercholesterolaemia-linked cardiovascular disease.

Eicosanoids are the short-range lipid mediators made from arachidonic acid, and they set vascular tone, platelet behaviour, renal salt handling and the intensity of inflammatory responses. Arachidonate is routed through cyclooxygenase, lipoxygenase and cytochrome P450 branches; the enzymes here represent the P450-dependent oxygenations and the P450-family isomerases that finish prostanoid synthesis. CYP4A and CYP4F monooxygenases hydroxylate arachidonic acid to 20-HETE, a vasoconstrictor that influences blood pressure and tubular transport, and the same CYP4F enzymes inactivate leukotriene B4, limiting neutrophil recruitment. Prostacyclin synthase and thromboxane synthase convert the cyclooxygenase product prostaglandin H2 into opposing signals, one favouring vasodilation and platelet inhibition, the other platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction. Related activities extend to bile acid 12-alpha-hydroxylation and to omega-hydroxylation of very long chain lipids needed for skin barrier formation, where loss of CYP4F22 causes congenital ichthyosis.

Foreign chemicals that enter the body — drugs, plant alkaloids, solvents, combustion products — are largely disposed of by a small group of microsomal cytochrome P450 enzymes with deliberately loose substrate specificity, and this xenobiotic oxidation step determines how long a compound persists and what it becomes. Phase I hydroxylation and dealkylation by enzymes such as CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9 and CYP2E1 introduces handles for conjugation and excretion, but can also bioactivate procarcinogens and generate reactive metabolites that damage liver tissue. Common polymorphisms in these genes underlie much of the inter-individual variation in drug clearance and adverse reactions. Transcriptional control is built in: the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, partnered with ARNT, senses planar aromatic compounds and induces CYP1A1 and CYP1A2, while AHRR provides negative feedback. Expression is centred on liver but extends to lung, gut and other exposed epithelia.

The branch point of bile acid synthesis that decides which primary bile acid the liver makes is set by 12-alpha-hydroxylation of sterol intermediates. The microsomal cytochrome P450 sterol 12-alpha-hydroxylase acts on 7-alpha-hydroxylated C27 intermediates derived from cholesterol, and its activity determines the ratio of cholic acid to chenodeoxycholic acid in the bile acid pool. That ratio matters physiologically because the two acids differ in hydrophobicity, in how efficiently they solubilise dietary lipid and cholesterol for absorption, and in how strongly they signal through the bile acid receptor FXR. Expression is confined to hepatocytes and is suppressed by bile acid feedback, so the step also serves as a regulated output of cholesterol disposal. Shifts in 12-alpha-hydroxylated bile acids track with insulin resistance and hepatic steatosis.

CYP2E1-mediated oxidation handles small, often volatile molecules that other drug-metabolising enzymes ignore: ethanol, benzene, carbon tetrachloride, vinyl chloride, halothane and acetaminophen. Because the products are frequently more reactive than the parent compound, this chemistry determines individual susceptibility to solvent and industrial chemical toxicity rather than simply clearing it — the classic case being conversion of acetaminophen to NAPQI, which depletes glutathione and causes hepatic necrosis in overdose. The reaction cycle is poorly coupled, so electrons leak to oxygen and generate reactive oxygen species that damage mitochondria and DNA and set off lipid peroxidation, a route by which chronic ethanol exposure, which induces the enzyme, injures the liver. Related family 2 cytochromes P450 accompanying it, including CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP2B6, cover overlapping ranges of drug and xenobiotic substrates and are major sources of pharmacogenetic variability.

Epigenetic regulation of gene expression is the set of heritable chromatin states that lock in which genes a cell may express, without altering DNA sequence. It is what makes a fat cell stay a fat cell and a lineage-inappropriate gene stay silent through division, and its breakdown underlies developmental syndromes and the aberrant silencing of tumour suppressors in cancer. The machinery covers writers, erasers and readers: Polycomb complexes deposit H3K27me3 and PRC1-mediated H2A ubiquitination, DNMT1 with UHRF1 propagates cytosine methylation while TET enzymes and TDG reverse it, SET1/MLL and WDR5-containing methyltransferases and KAT2B-type acetyltransferases activate, and Sin3/NuRD and NCoR deacetylase complexes repress. Related arms tune ribosomal RNA transcription to metabolic demand, drive nuclear receptor-directed adipocyte differentiation through PPARG and coactivators, and silence retroelements via KRAB zinc fingers, TRIM28, SETDB1 and the HUSH complex.

Heritable control of which genes a cell expresses, without altering DNA sequence, is what allows one genome to produce many stable cell identities. This epigenetic regulation of gene expression writes, reads and erases covalent marks on DNA and histones: DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B transfer methyl groups to cytosine while TET1-3 with TDG reverse that mark by oxidation and base excision; PRC2 subunits EZH2/EZH1, EED and SUZ12 deposit H3K27 trimethylation, and SETDB1, EHMT2 and SUV39H1 generate H3K9 methylation for silencing. Coactivator acetyltransferases, SIN3/NuRD/CoREST deacetylase complexes, SWI/SNF remodellers, COMPASS methyltransferases with WDR5 and the Mediator complex tune promoter output, including metabolic programmes such as PPARG-driven adipocyte differentiation and nutrient-responsive ribosomal RNA transcription. KRAB zinc fingers with TRIM28, the HUSH complex and piRNA machinery keep retroelements transcriptionally silent. Loss of these activities causes developmental syndromes and is pervasive in cancer.

Once NOTCH1 is cleaved at the membrane, its released intracellular domain becomes a short-lived transcription factor, and this is the step at which a cell-surface contact between neighbouring cells is converted into a change in gene expression. The domain enters the nucleus and binds RBPJ, evicting a corepressor complex built on NCOR1/NCOR2, TBL1X/TBL1XR1 and histone deacetylases. Recruitment of a mastermind-like protein completes a heterotrimeric coactivator complex and brings in the acetyltransferases EP300, CREBBP and KAT2A/KAT2B, switching on HES1, HES5, HEY family repressors and MYC — outputs that hold progenitors undifferentiated in neurogenesis, somitogenesis and lymphopoiesis. The same complex builds in its own shutoff: CDK8–cyclin C phosphorylates the PEST domain, marking it for FBXW7-dependent ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, while HIF1A binding stabilises it under low oxygen. PEST and FBXW7 mutations that defeat this turnover drive T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.

Notch signalling lets a cell read the identity of its immediate neighbours, and this pathway covers the step in which ligand engagement of NOTCH1 at the cell surface is converted into a nuclear signal. It underlies binary fate decisions throughout development and adult tissue renewal involving neurogenesis, oligodendrocyte maturation, angiogenic tip-versus-stalk choice and lymphocyte specification; constitutive activation of the same machinery drives T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Delta- and Jagged-family ligands presented in trans (DLL1, DLL4, JAG1, JAG2) are ubiquitinated by Mindbomb and Neuralized E3 ligases and endocytosed, mechanically unfolding the receptor to expose a site cut by ADAM10 or ADAM17. The resulting fragment is cleaved within the membrane by the gamma-secretase complex (presenilins, nicastrin, APH1, PSENEN), releasing the NOTCH1 intracellular domain to act as a transcriptional regulator. Non-canonical activators such as CNTN1 and DNER act through Deltex proteins, while cis-expressed ligands, DLK1, NUMB and ITCH-mediated ubiquitination restrain signalling.

Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 lays down the initiating mark of heritable gene silencing, trimethylating lysine 27 of histone H3 to keep developmental regulators off in cells where they do not belong. This is how lineage decisions are made stable and inherited through division; its loss or hyperactivity underlies developmental syndromes and cancers, and gain-of-function EZH2 mutations drive lymphoma. The catalytic subunit EZH1 or EZH2 works only within a core containing EED and SUZ12, with RBBP4/RBBP7 and accessory factors such as JARID2, AEBP2, MTF2 and the PHF1/PHF19 Polycomb-like proteins shaping recruitment to CpG-rich, unmethylated promoters; EZHIP restrains catalysis. The resulting H3K27me3 is read by PRC1, which ubiquitinates H2A and locks in repression. PRC2 also associates with DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B, linking histone methylation to CpG DNA methylation and longer-term epigenetic memory.

This is the broad programme of RNA polymerase II transcription regulation in human cells "— how protein-coding genes are switched on and off to give each cell type its identity. It spans the core machinery (Pol II subunits, TBP and the TAF-containing initiation complex, TFIIF and TFIIH, elongation and negative elongation factors, the Mediator adaptor complex) together with the sequence-specific activators and repressors that read promoters and distal enhancers: nuclear receptors, p53 family and its target genes, E2F/RB, SMADs, RUNX, GATA, TCF/LEF, TEAD/YAP, Notch–RBPJ with Mastermind, and a very large complement of KRAB zinc-finger repressors. Coregulators supply the chromatin chemistry — p300/CBP and other acetyltransferases, HDACs, NCoR/SIN3 corepressors, Polycomb and Trithorax methyltransferases, SWI/SNF and NuRD remodellers. Combinatorial use of these parts sets developmental fate, metabolic and stress responses, and cell-cycle entry; its corruption is a recurring route to cancer.
