Dopaminergic neurons signal by packaging dopamine into synaptic vesicles and releasing it in response to action potentials, and this release cycle is what supports reward learning, motor control and motivated behaviour; its loss in midbrain neurons underlies the motor deficits of Parkinson's disease, and its pharmacological manipulation is how psychostimulants and antipsychotics act. A vesicular monoamine transporter loads cytosolic dopamine into vesicles using the proton gradient, synapsins tether the reserve pool to the cytoskeleton, and active-zone scaffolds built from RIM, liprins and their partners position vesicles at release sites. Docking and priming depend on Munc18 and Munc13 acting with the SNARE proteins syntaxin-1A, SNAP-25 and VAMP2, while synaptotagmin-1 serves as the calcium sensor and complexin clamps the assembled complex until calcium arrives, giving fast, synchronous exocytosis into the cleft.

EGFR interacts with phospholipase C-gamma is the branch of epidermal growth factor receptor signalling that converts ligand binding at the cell surface into calcium and protein kinase C signals. It gives growth factors control over rapid, membrane-proximal events such as cytoskeletal remodelling, motility and secretion, alongside the longer-term proliferative output of the receptor, and it is one of the arms exploited when EGFR is amplified or mutated in carcinoma and glioma. Any of several ligands -- EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or HB-EGF -- dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites that recruit PLC-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once phosphorylated, the enzyme hydrolyses PIP2 to IP3 and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores and activating protein kinase C isoforms, thereby linking receptor tyrosine kinase activity to phosphoinositide turnover.

Growth factor binding to the EGF receptor does more than switch on kinase cascades; one branch of its output runs through phospholipid turnover, and that is what this pathway captures. Any of several ligands — EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin or heparin-binding EGF — dimerises and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma1 through its SH2 domains. Once tyrosine phosphorylated at the membrane, PLCG1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, so a single receptor event raises cytosolic calcium released from internal stores and activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling in epithelia, and inappropriate output from this arm contributes to the growth and invasiveness of EGFR-driven carcinomas.

Elastic fibres give skin, lung, arteries and ligaments their ability to stretch and recoil, and the molecules that decorate them determine how well they are built and what signals they hold. Fibrillin microfibrils and the elastin core are surrounded by accessory proteins — fibulins, EMILINs, microfibril-associated proteins, vitronectin and fibronectin — that guide tropoelastin deposition onto the microfibril scaffold and crosslink the assembling fibre. The same scaffold acts as a reservoir for growth factors: latent TGF-beta binding proteins tether TGF-beta isoforms in an inactive complex, and BMPs including BMP2, BMP4, BMP7 and GDF5 are similarly sequestered, with integrins such as alphaV-beta6 and alphaV-beta8 releasing active TGF-beta under mechanical strain. Loss of these interactions underlies Marfan syndrome, cutis laxa and aortic aneurysm, where failed matrix assembly is compounded by unrestrained growth factor signalling.

Antigen-presenting cells - dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells - display peptides from internalized proteins on MHC class II heterodimers so that CD4+ helper T cells can survey them, the step that licenses antibody production, class switching and most adaptive responses to extracellular pathogens; failure of it causes bare lymphocyte syndrome, while particular HLA-DR and HLA-DQ alleles predispose to autoimmunity. Newly made alpha-beta dimers leave the endoplasmic reticulum in COPII vesicles bound to the invariant chain CD74, which blocks the groove and routes them to endosomes. There, cathepsins and legumain degrade the invariant chain and the ingested antigen, and HLA-DM catalyses peptide exchange while HLA-DO modulates it. Clathrin and AP-1/AP-2 adaptors, dynamins, Rab7 with RILP, and dynein, kinesin and tubulin components move the compartments and deliver loaded complexes to the cell surface.

Arachidonic acid can be routed away from the cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase branches into a third fate: epoxidation by cytochrome P450 enzymes to yield epoxyeicosatrienoic acids. These EETs act as autocrine and paracrine mediators that relax vascular smooth muscle, contribute to endothelium-derived hyperpolarization, and temper inflammation, so the balance of their production and breakdown influences blood pressure, coronary and renal blood flow, and vascular injury responses. Epoxygenases including CYP2J2 and the CYP2C family attack each of the four double bonds to give the 5,6-, 8,9-, 11,12- and 14,15-regioisomers, while CYP1 family enzymes contribute additional oxidative metabolism of the substrate. The signal is terminated by soluble epoxide hydrolase, encoded by EPHX2, which adds water across the epoxide to form the far less active dihydroxyeicosatrienoic acids; inhibiting this step is a strategy for prolonging EET action.

Arachidonic acid oxidation at carbon 5 generates a family of signalling lipids that recruit and activate leukocytes, and this branch produces them: 5-lipoxygenase, held at the nuclear envelope by its membrane-bound activating protein, inserts oxygen to give 5-hydroperoxy-eicosatetraenoic acid, which is reduced to 5S-HETE by glutathione peroxidases or dehydrogenated further to 5-oxo-ETE. These products are chemoattractants for eosinophils and neutrophils acting through the OXE receptor, so the pathway shapes the intensity of allergic and inflammatory responses in asthma, rhinitis and atherosclerosis. The same 5-lipoxygenase step is the gateway to leukotrienes, and leukotriene C4 synthase conjugates glutathione to divert flux toward the cysteinyl leukotrienes that drive bronchoconstriction. Peroxidase and paraoxonase-family activities limit accumulation of the hydroperoxide intermediate, tying eicosanoid output to cellular redox and lipid-peroxide handling.

Leukotrienes and the related eoxins are lipid mediators made from arachidonic acid that drive the inflammatory side of asthma, allergy and leukocyte recruitment: they constrict bronchial smooth muscle, raise vascular permeability, and attract and activate granulocytes. Synthesis begins when 5-lipoxygenase, positioned on the nuclear envelope by its activating protein ALOX5AP, converts arachidonate to the unstable epoxide LTA4; this is either hydrolysed by LTA4H to the chemoattractant LTB4 or conjugated to glutathione by LTC4S to give LTC4, which is exported by the transporter ABCC1 and trimmed by gamma-glutamyl transferases and dipeptidases to LTD4 and LTE4. Eoxins arise instead through 15-lipoxygenase. Omega-oxidation by CYP4F enzymes and reduction by PTGR1 terminate signalling, while MAPKAPK2 phosphorylates and activates ALOX5. These steps are the targets of anti-leukotriene asthma drugs.

Hepoxilins are short-lived lipid mediators made from arachidonic acid, and their production marks one branch of the 12-lipoxygenase route that runs parallel to the better-known prostaglandin and leukotriene pathways. They act on neutrophil recruitment across epithelia, insulin secretion, vascular tone and neuronal signalling, and their overproduction contributes to inflammatory recruitment at mucosal surfaces. The chemistry begins with arachidonate 12-lipoxygenase, which oxygenates arachidonic acid at C-12 and then converts the hydroperoxide intermediate into hepoxilin A3 or B3, each carrying an 11,12-epoxide plus a hydroxyl at C-8 or C-10 respectively. That epoxide is unstable: hydrolysis, either spontaneous in acidic conditions or catalysed by a hepoxilin-selective epoxide hydrolase, opens it to the corresponding diols trioxilin A3 and B3, which terminates signalling. This makes hepoxilin and trioxilin formation part of eicosanoid metabolism in platelets, skin and epithelial tissue.

Lipoxins are arachidonate-derived mediators that actively switch off inflammation, telling neutrophils to stop arriving and macrophages to clear apoptotic cells and debris so tissue can return to baseline. Their synthesis requires two cell types cooperating: 5-lipoxygenase, working with its membrane partner ALOX5AP, generates leukotriene A4 in neutrophils, which platelets take up and convert through 12-lipoxygenase into the trihydroxy, conjugated-tetraene lipoxins A4 and B4. A parallel route starts from 15-hydroperoxy or 15-hydroxy arachidonate made by 15-lipoxygenase and handed to 5-lipoxygenase in monocytes and neutrophils, while aspirin-acetylated cyclooxygenase-2 yields 15R-epimeric lipoxins of comparable potency. The same branch point feeds leukotriene C4 synthase and pro-inflammatory cysteinyl leukotrienes, so the balance matters. Dehydrogenase and reductase steps inactivate these eicosanoids, limiting their duration; failure to generate lipoxins is linked to persistent inflammation in asthma and chronic inflammatory disease.

Arachidonic acid oxidised at carbon 12 gives rise to a family of lipid mediators that act in platelet function, inflammation and skin barrier formation. The route begins with 12- and 15-lipoxygenases inserting molecular oxygen to form the hydroperoxide 12S-HpETE, after which the pathway splits: glutathione peroxidases reduce the hydroperoxide to the stable alcohol 12S-HETE, while a hydroperoxide isomerase instead rearranges it into epoxy-alcohol hepoxilins. 12S-HETE modulates platelet and leukocyte responses and is prominent in tumour cell behaviour, whereas hepoxilins influence insulin secretion, pain signalling and vascular permeability. The epidermis-type enzymes ALOX12B and ALOXE3 act as a pair to generate epoxy-alcohols required for the cornified lipid envelope, and loss of either causes autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis. The peroxidase branch also limits the lipid peroxidation that these hydroperoxides would otherwise propagate.

Arachidonate metabolism converts a 20-carbon fatty acid released from membrane phospholipids into the eicosanoids that signal pain, fever, inflammation, bronchoconstriction, platelet aggregation and vascular tone, acting locally and briefly before being degraded. Because free arachidonate is scarce, flux begins with phospholipase A2 cleavage of phospholipids, and the enzymes a cell expresses decide which mediators it can make. Cyclooxygenases generate the prostaglandin endoperoxide that downstream synthases convert to prostaglandins D, E and I, plus thromboxane; lipoxygenases with their activating protein produce leukotriene A4, which is hydrolysed to LTB4 or conjugated to glutathione to form the cysteinyl leukotrienes, later trimmed by peptidases. Cytochrome P450 epoxygenases and omega-hydroxylases yield epoxyeicosatrienoic and hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids, with soluble epoxide hydrolase and dehydrogenases terminating signalling. This chemistry is the target of aspirin, other anti-inflammatory drugs and antileukotriene asthma therapy.

Arachidonic acid can be oxygenated at carbon 15 to yield a family of signalling lipids, and the synthesis of 15-eicosatetraenoic acid derivatives is that branch of eicosanoid metabolism. Arachidonate 15-lipoxygenases, the reticulocyte-type ALOX15 and the epidermal ALOX15B, insert molecular oxygen to give the hydroperoxide 15-HpETE, which glutathione peroxidases including GPX1, GPX2 and the phospholipid-directed GPX4 reduce to the stable alcohol 15-HETE; further oxidation of the hydroxyl group gives 15-oxoETE. Cyclooxygenase-2 can also generate 15-hydroperoxy products from arachidonate. The outputs matter because they feed into anti-inflammatory and pro-resolving mediator production, act as ligands for nuclear receptors, and influence monocyte and macrophage behaviour, airway and skin biology. Because ALOX15 attacks esterified fatty acids in membranes, this chemistry also links to peroxide-driven membrane damage and the lipid peroxidation that GPX4 normally restrains.

Coenzyme Q10, present in human tissues mostly as its reduced form ubiquinol, is the lipid electron carrier that shuttles electrons from respiratory complexes I and II to complex III, and also serves as a cofactor for other dehydrogenases, a chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes, and a participant in oxygen sensing. Its biosynthesis builds the molecule in two halves: PDSS1 and PDSS2 make the decaprenyl tail, a mitochondrial dioxygenase-like enzyme (HPDL) feeds production of the 4-hydroxybenzoate head group from tyrosine catabolism, and COQ2 joins them in the inner membrane. Ring hydroxylations, O- and C-methylations and a decarboxylation are then carried out by COQ3-COQ7 and COQ9 acting as a membrane-associated multienzyme assembly, with the atypical kinases COQ8A and COQ8B supporting it; STARD7 distributes the product to other membranes. Loss of any core step causes coenzyme Q10 deficiency, ranging from lethal neonatal multisystem disease and nephropathy to adult myopathy, sometimes responsive to supplementation.

Arachidonic acid can be oxidised at its terminal carbons by heme-thiolate cytochrome P450 enzymes, and the resulting 16- to 20-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids act as lipid mediators in their own right rather than as intermediates. The best characterised product, 20-HETE, constricts renal and cerebral arterioles, modulates tubular sodium transport and blood pressure, and promotes vascular smooth muscle proliferation, so this branch of arachidonate metabolism links membrane lipid release to circulatory and renal homeostasis; variants in the omega-hydroxylases CYP4A11 and CYP4F2 are associated with hypertension and altered vascular tone. Unlike the lipoxygenases, which abstract hydrogen using a non-heme iron, these monooxygenases use a heme-iron centre and NADPH-derived electrons to insert oxygen at unactivated sp3 omega-carbons. Family members such as CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP1B1 contribute overlapping hydroxylase activity alongside their roles in xenobiotic oxidation.

Hyaluronan metabolism covers the synthesis, turnover and clearance of the one glycosaminoglycan that is unsulfated, unattached to any core protein, and made at the plasma membrane rather than in the Golgi. Its enormous hydrated polymers give connective tissue, skin, cartilage and joint fluid their lubrication, compressive resilience and space-filling bulk, and they also serve as a signalling matrix: fragment size determines whether hyaluronan is quiescent or pro-inflammatory and pro-migratory. Hyaluronan synthases extrude the growing chain outward, while hyaluronidases, CEMIP and lysosomal exoglycosidases such as GUSB and hexosaminidase degrade it, with acidification and sialic acid export supporting the lysosomal step. Receptors including CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the scavenger STAB2 mediate cell adhesion, motility and lymphatic uptake for systemic clearance. Dysregulated production accompanies tumour invasion, fibrosis and inflammatory tissue remodelling.

Hyaluronan is the one glycosaminoglycan made without sulfation and without a protein core, and its metabolism covers both its synthesis at the plasma membrane and its turnover. Because the polymer holds enormous volumes of water, it gives cartilage, skin and connective tissue their compressive resilience and lubrication, and its fragmentation into short oligosaccharides converts a structural filler into a signal that drives inflammation, angiogenesis and cell migration. Membrane synthases extrude growing chains directly into the extracellular space, while hyaluronidases and CEMIP cleave them; the receptors CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the scavenger STAB2 mediate binding, migratory signalling and clearance through lymphatics and liver. Internalised fragments are degraded in lysosomes by beta-glucuronidase and hexosaminidases, with the sialin transporter exporting the released sugars. Dysregulated turnover accompanies tumour invasion, fibrosis and joint degeneration.

Cells match their mitochondrial content to energy demand by turning on a nuclear transcriptional programme, and this is the circuit that does it: transcriptional activation of mitochondrial biogenesis coordinates expression of the hundreds of nuclear-encoded proteins that must be imported for respiration, and of the machinery that replicates and transcribes mitochondrial DNA itself. It underlies the adaptation of muscle to exercise, brown fat to cold, and liver to fasting; its blunting accompanies insulin resistance, heart failure and neurodegeneration. PPARGC1A acts as a coactivator rather than a DNA-binding factor, working through NRF1, GABPA/GABPB1 (NRF2), ESRRA and PPARA/RXRA with CREBBP and mediator components to induce TFAM, TFB1M/TFB2M, POLRMT, TWNK and SSBP1. Calcium-driven CAMK4, CREB1 with CRTC coactivators, MEF2C/D and ATF2 raise PPARGC1A transcription, while NR1D1 and NCOR1-HDAC3 repress it, linking biogenesis to circadian and nutrient state.

Mitochondrial biogenesis is turned on when a cell senses that it is running short of energy, and phosphorylation of the coactivator PGC-1alpha is the switch that couples that sensing to transcription. In exercising muscle this is how contraction and fuel depletion translate into more mitochondria, greater oxidative capacity and a shift toward fat oxidation; blunted PGC-1alpha activation accompanies inactivity, insulin resistance and mitochondrial myopathy. Falling ATP and rising AMP activate the AMP-activated protein kinase heterotrimer, built here from a catalytic alpha subunit with regulatory beta and gamma subunits, which phosphorylates PGC-1alpha directly. In parallel, p38 MAP kinases activated downstream of contraction and calcium signalling modify the same target. PGC-1alpha binds no DNA itself, instead docking onto nuclear receptors and other transcription factors to drive respiratory chain and oxidative gene programmes; SIRT1-dependent deacetylation reportedly follows phosphorylation.

Phenylketonuria is the metabolic disease that follows loss of phenylalanine hydroxylase activity, the liver enzyme that converts dietary phenylalanine to tyrosine using tetrahydrobiopterin as cofactor. When this step fails, phenylalanine accumulates in blood and tissues and is diverted into side products such as phenylpyruvate and phenyllactate, while tyrosine becomes a diet-dependent requirement. High circulating phenylalanine competes for transport into the brain and disturbs neurotransmitter synthesis and myelination, so untreated infants develop severe, irreversible intellectual disability, seizures and microcephaly; this is why newborn screening and lifelong phenylalanine-restricted diet are standard care. The amount of alternative catabolites produced varies between individuals carrying the same enzyme defect, indicating modifying genetic influences outside the hydroxylase itself, with transaminases and lactate dehydrogenase carrying the overflow chemistry. The pathway sits at the entry point of aromatic amino acid degradation.

Cells read their surroundings largely through integrins, the alpha/beta heterodimeric receptors that physically couple the extracellular matrix to the cytoskeleton and convert contact into decisions about adhesion, migration, survival and differentiation. This interface holds epithelia on their basement membranes, lets platelets bind fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor to arrest bleeding, and lets leukocytes stick to endothelium before entering tissue; its ligands and receptors are accordingly implicated in blistering skin disease, bleeding disorders, fibrosis and tumour invasion. The receptor repertoire divides by ligand preference: collagen-binding alpha1, alpha2, alpha10 and alpha11 with beta1; laminin and RGD receptors recognising fibronectin, vitronectin, osteopontin and thrombospondin; and the beta2/beta7 leukocyte integrins that pair with ICAMs, VCAM1 and MAdCAM-1 for cell-cell rather than matrix adhesion. Collagens of many types, fibrillin, perlecan, agrin and tenascin supply the matrix side, alongside co-receptors such as CD44 and CD47.

Hyaluronan, the unbranched glycosaminoglycan that gives connective tissue, cartilage and skin their hydration and space-filling bulk, is turned over remarkably fast — roughly a third of the body's pool each day — and this is the route by which it is dismantled. Receptors including CD44, HMMR, LYVE1 and the liver sinusoidal scavenger STAB2 bind the polymer and bring it into cells or clear it from lymph and blood. Cell-surface and lysosomal hyaluronidases such as HYAL2 and HYAL1, plus CEMIP and the sperm enzyme SPAM1, cut the chain into short oligosaccharides, which beta-glucuronidase and hexosaminidases reduce to glucuronic acid and N-acetylglucosamine for reuse. Acidification and sialic acid export support the lysosomal step; failure leaves undegraded glycosaminoglycan in a storage-disease pattern, and fragment accumulation alters inflammation and matrix remodelling.

Abacavir is an antiretroviral nucleoside analogue that must reach the cytosol to be phosphorylated into its active form, and how much of it gets there depends on the opposing action of uptake and efflux carriers at the plasma membrane. Movement of abacavir across membranes therefore sets intracellular drug exposure and contributes to variation in efficacy and toxicity between patients. Facilitated entry is handled by the organic cation transporters SLC22A1, SLC22A2 and SLC22A3, expressed in liver, kidney and other tissues where they also handle endogenous cations and many cationic drugs. Working against them, the ATP-driven exporters ABCB1 and ABCG2 pump abacavir back out, limiting accumulation in enterocytes, hepatocytes and the blood-brain barrier. This balance is a general theme of xenobiotic disposition, where transporter expression and polymorphism shape pharmacokinetics and drug-drug interactions.

Abacavir is a nucleoside analogue used against HIV-1, and its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion determine both how much active drug reaches infected cells and how much reaches tissues where it can cause harm. The parent compound is a prodrug: organic cation transporters of the SLC22 family carry it into hepatocytes and other cells, while the efflux pumps ABCB1 and ABCG2 limit intracellular exposure and shape tissue penetration. Intracellular activation proceeds through phosphorylation and deamination to carbovir monophosphate, which cytosolic nucleotide kinases and phosphatases such as NT5C2 further process toward carbovir triphosphate, the species that terminates reverse transcription. Competing routes inactivate the drug: alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises it toward a 5'-carboxylate, and glucuronidation gives the other major excreted form. Variation in these transport and metabolic steps underlies differences in efficacy and toxicity between patients.

Abacavir is a guanosine analogue used against HIV, and its handling in the body determines both whether it works and how it is cleared. The drug is a prodrug: cellular kinase and phosphotransferase steps, with a 5'-nucleotidase contributing to the phosphate balance, convert it stepwise while a deaminase removes the cyclopropylamino group to give carbovir monophosphate, which is further phosphorylated to the triphosphate that terminates reverse transcription. The remainder is inactivated rather than activated — alcohol dehydrogenase oxidises the 5'-hydroxyl toward the carboxylate derivative, and glucuronidation gives the other major urinary product, so the two together account for most excreted drug. Because activation and elimination compete, variation in these enzymes shapes intracellular triphosphate levels and therefore antiviral potency, and the pathway sits within broader nucleoside and purine salvage metabolism.

Prostaglandins and thromboxanes, collectively the prostanoids, are short-lived lipid mediators made on demand from arachidonate, and they set local tone for inflammation, pain, fever, platelet aggregation, vascular calibre, gastric mucosal protection, renal blood flow and labour. Their synthesis is the target of the most widely used drugs in medicine: aspirin and other NSAIDs block the two cyclooxygenases, PTGS1 being constitutive and PTGS2 induced at sites of stress and injury. Both convert arachidonate to the unstable intermediate PGH2, which downstream synthases then divert along competing branches — PTGES isoforms to PGE2, PTGDS and HPGDS to PGD2, PTGIS to vasodilatory prostacyclin, and TBXAS1 to pro-aggregatory thromboxane. Reductases and the dehydrogenase HPGD act on these products, terminating or reshaping signalling. Which mediator predominates depends on cell type, so shifting the balance between endothelial and platelet output has cardiovascular consequences.\n

When red cells lyse inside blood vessels, the hemoglobin and heme they spill are toxic: heme intercalates into membranes, oxidizes lipoproteins, and supplies redox-active iron that drives Fenton chemistry and oxidative injury. Scavenging of heme from plasma is the extracellular clearance system that prevents this. Liver-derived haptoglobin captures hemoglobin dimers, and the complex is taken up through CD163 on monocytes and macrophages for degradation and iron recycling. Once haptoglobin is saturated, heme released from methemoglobin is buffered by albumin and handed to hemopexin, which delivers it to hepatocytes via the endocytic receptor LRP1. Apolipoprotein A-I and the AMBP-derived alpha-1-microglobulin contribute additional heme and radical handling. Immunoglobulin chains appear because plasma antibodies associate with these carriers in circulation. Overwhelming this capacity, as in sickle cell disease or transfusion reactions, produces hemolysis-driven vascular and renal damage.

Natural killer cells and myeloid cells read their environment through receptors that have no signalling tail of their own, and DAP12 supplies it. Encoded by TYROBP, this small ITAM-bearing adapter homodimer pairs with activating KIRs, NKG2C/CD94, NKG2D, TREM1 and TREM2, SIRP-beta, CLEC5A and several Siglecs by a salt bridge between oppositely charged transmembrane residues, then recruits SYK and ZAP70-family kinases once Src kinases such as LCK and FYN phosphorylate its motifs. Downstream, LAT and SLP-76 scaffolds feed PI3K, PLC-gamma, VAV-RAC and RAS-ERK signalling, producing cytotoxic granule release, cytokine output, phagocytosis and osteoclast maturation. Recognition of MHC class I molecules by activating KIR and NKG2C links the pathway to missing-self and viral surveillance. Loss of DAP12 or TREM2 causes Nasu-Hakola disease with bone cysts and presenile dementia, and TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's risk through impaired microglial responses.

FMO oxidises nucleophiles is a phase I drug-metabolising route that converts soft nucleophilic heteroatoms — nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus — into more polar N-, S- and P-oxides, priming xenobiotics, dietary amines and many therapeutics for conjugation and excretion. It works alongside cytochrome P450s in liver, kidney and lung microsomes but by a distinct chemistry: NADPH first reduces the bound FAD, molecular oxygen adds to give a stable C4a-hydroperoxyflavin, and this pre-activated enzyme simply waits for a substrate to present a lone pair, transferring one oxygen and releasing water. Because activation precedes substrate binding, the enzymes are broadly promiscuous and, unlike P450s, are not induced by their substrates. FMO3 dominates in adult liver, and its loss causes trimethylaminuria, in which unoxidised dietary trimethylamine accumulates and produces a strong fish-like body odour.

Flavin-containing monooxygenases make up the second major family of microsomal drug-oxidising enzymes, working alongside the cytochrome P450s to oxygenate soft nucleophiles. By adding oxygen to nitrogen, sulfur or phosphorus atoms, they convert amines, sulfides and related xenobiotics into N-oxides, S-oxides and P-oxides that are more polar and readily excreted, and they detoxify dietary and bacterially derived compounds absorbed from the gut. Catalysis runs in an unusual order: NADPH reduces the bound FAD cofactor, molecular oxygen is captured as a flavin hydroperoxide, and only then does the substrate encounter the activated oxygen, so these enzymes are neither substrate-inducible nor dependent on substrate binding for activation. FMO1, FMO2 and FMO3 carry this nucleophile-oxidising activity, with the hepatic FMO3 form dominant in adults; its loss leaves trimethylamine unoxidised and produces the fish-odour syndrome trimethylaminuria, and variation across the family shapes individual drug clearance.

Scavenger receptors clear unwanted or damaged material from blood and tissue fluid, and this binding-and-uptake step is how that waste is recognised and committed to endocytosis. Macrophages, liver sinusoidal endothelium and other clearance cells use these receptors to remove modified lipoproteins, free haemoglobin, advanced glycation products, apoptotic debris, collagen fragments and immunoglobulin, protecting tissue from oxidative and inflammatory injury; unchecked uptake of oxidised LDL by macrophage receptors such as MSR1 and CD36 instead drives foam cell formation and atherosclerosis. Specificity ranges from dedicated pairings, as when CD163 captures haptoglobin-haemoglobin complexes to salvage haem iron, to broad polyanion recognition by class A receptors, MARCO and SCARA5. Stabilin family members and LRP1 handle hyaluronan, collagen propeptides and chaperone-bound cargo. Ligand internalisation feeds lysosomal degradation, iron recycling into ferritin, and antigen handling that links this route to innate immune defence.

TGF-beta controls growth arrest, extracellular matrix production and immune tolerance, and cells must be able to switch that signal off; the negative-feedback arm that terminates TGF-beta receptor signaling does exactly this, and its loss underlies fibrosis and the runaway matrix deposition and tumour-promoting signalling seen when the pathway is chronically active. Activated SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 induces the inhibitory SMAD7, which returns to the receptor complex and blocks further SMAD2/3 recruitment. SMAD7 acts as a platform: it brings the PP1 catalytic subunits via the regulatory subunit PPP1R15A to dephosphorylate TGFBR1, and recruits the HECT ubiquitin ligases SMURF1, SMURF2 and NEDD4L to ubiquitinate the receptor for proteasomal and lysosomal destruction. Deubiquitinases USP15 and UCHL5 oppose this, STUB1 turns over SMAD3, PMEPA1 sequesters SMADs, MTMR4 dephosphorylates them on endosomes, and the pseudoreceptor BAMBI blunts receptor activation.

TGF-beta controls growth arrest, extracellular matrix production, immune tolerance and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and this is the route by which the ligand reaches the nucleus: receptor engagement activating the SMAD transcription factors. Latent TGF-beta is processed by furin and held in the matrix by latent-binding proteins and fibrillin until integrins, notably the alphaV-containing pairs, release the active dimer. Ligand binding assembles TGFBR2 with TGFBR1, whose kinase is restrained by FKBP1A until trans-phosphorylation of its GS domain; the endosomal anchor SARA then presents SMAD2 and SMAD3 for C-terminal phosphorylation, after which they partner SMAD4 and move to the nucleus. Inhibitory SMAD7 with the ubiquitin ligases SMURF1/2 and NEDD4L, the decoy receptor BAMBI, PP1 phosphatases and deubiquitinases such as USP15 tune output. Loss or distortion of this signalling underlies fibrosis, aortic aneurysm syndromes and tumour progression.

Epithelial cells hold their apical junctions together and stay immobile; TGF-beta signalling at the tight junction is one route by which they lose that state and acquire migratory, mesenchymal character. The same ligand restrains proliferation in normal tissue, but in advanced cancer this junctional arm promotes invasion and metastasis, and it also operates in developmental morphogenesis and fibrosis. The type I receptor TGFBR1 is held at tight junctions through PARD6A, part of the PAR polarity complex with PARD3 and atypical PKC zeta. Ligand-activated TGFBR2 phosphorylates both TGFBR1 and PARD6A, and phosphorylated PARD6A recruits the ubiquitin ligase SMURF1, which ubiquitinates RHOA locally and targets it for degradation. Loss of RHOA at the junction dismantles the apical complex, including cingulin and JAM-A, dissolving epithelial polarity independently of SMAD-mediated transcription.

TGF-beta and activin signals end in the nucleus, where phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 partnered with SMAD4 read target promoters and set the transcriptional output that arrests the cell cycle, drives extracellular matrix production and enforces epithelial differentiation. This is the step that produces the classic responses to TGF-beta: induction of the CDK inhibitor CDKN2B and of PAI-1 and collagen, and repression of MYC. The heterotrimer has little intrinsic activating power and works through partners, recruiting p300 for histone acetylation and CDK8/CDK9-cyclin modules that phosphorylate the SMAD linker, while corepressors SKI, SKIL, TGIF1/2 and NCOR-HDAC1 shut transcription down. Duration of signalling is limited by the phosphatase PPM1A and by ubiquitin ligases including SMURF2 and NEDD4L, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP9X. Loss of this control underlies TGF-beta resistance in carcinoma and fibrotic matrix deposition.

TGF-beta and activin signals are carried into the nucleus by SMAD2/3 bound to SMAD4, and this branch of the pathway shuts that signal off, setting how long and how strongly target genes such as the plasminogen activator inhibitor gene respond. Several mechanisms converge: the repressors SKI and SKIL, along with TGIF1 and TGIF2, occupy SMAD complexes on promoters and bring in NCOR co-repressors and histone deacetylase HDAC1; the phosphatase PPM1A removes the receptor-added C-terminal phosphates so SMAD2/3 returns to the cytosol; PARP1 poly(ADP-ribosyl)ates SMAD3 and SMAD4 to weaken DNA binding; and ubiquitin ligases including NEDD4L, SMURF2, RNF111 and TRIM33 either destroy the SMADs or strip SKI/SKIL away, with USP9X reversing SMAD4 monoubiquitination. The balance determines whether cells arrest, differentiate or escape growth control, and SKI/SKIL overexpression blunts TGF-beta responses in cancer.

This is the nuclear endpoint of TGF-beta and activin signalling: once receptor kinases phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3, they assemble with SMAD4 into a heterotrimer that enters the nucleus and sets gene expression. The output is largely growth-inhibitory and matrix-building, which is why this step underlies TGF-beta's cytostatic programme and, when subverted, tumour progression and fibrosis. Working with partners rather than alone, the complex cooperates with SP1 to induce the CDK inhibitor CDKN2B and with an RBL1/E2F4/5/TFDP repressor complex to shut down MYC transcription, while also driving SERPINE1, JUNB and collagen expression; WWTR1 promotes its nuclear accumulation. Induction of SMAD7 closes a negative feedback loop, itself limited by the ubiquitin ligase RNF111. CDK8- and CDK9-cyclin pairs phosphorylate the SMAD linker regions, boosting activity while marking the complex for ubiquitin-dependent turnover, and TGIF corepressors and HDAC1 dampen the response.

Gastrin is a gut hormone that drives growth and acid secretion in the stomach, and one way it produces growth signals is by borrowing the epidermal growth factor receptor rather than signalling through its own receptor alone. This transactivation route links a G protein-coupled, Gq-type receptor to the classic receptor tyrosine kinase pathway, and its persistent activation is part of why hypergastrinaemia promotes gastric mucosal hyperplasia and contributes to gastric and colorectal tumour growth. Diacylglycerol generated downstream of Gq activates protein kinase C alpha, which turns on matrix metalloproteinase 3; the protease sheds the membrane-anchored precursor of heparin-binding EGF, releasing mature ligand that binds EGFR on the same or neighbouring cells. Activated EGFR then recruits GRB2 and SOS1 to load the RAS GTPases, feeding proliferative MAPK signalling.

Daylight and colour vision depend on cones regenerating their visual chromophore far faster than rods, and the cone retinoid cycle is the route that supplies it. Unlike the rod pathway, which depends on the retinal pigment epithelium, this one runs through Müller glia in the retina: all-trans-retinol released from cone outer segments is taken up, isomerised directly to 11-cis-retinol, esterified for storage, and later hydrolysed and returned to the cone, where oxidation yields 11-cis-retinal for reloading onto opsin. The three cone opsins tuned to long, medium and short wavelengths make colour discrimination possible, and the interphotoreceptor retinoid-binding protein RBP3 and the cellular retinaldehyde-binding protein RLBP1 carry and protect retinoids between cells. Rapid turnover here is what allows light and dark adaptation within minutes; defects cause impaired dark adaptation and retinal degeneration.

Sight begins when a photon strikes a visual pigment in a rod or cone outer segment and is converted into an electrical signal, and this is the cascade that does it. Rhodopsin and the cone opsins carry an 11-cis-retinal chromophore whose photoisomerisation activates transducin, which relieves inhibition of cGMP phosphodiesterase; falling cGMP shuts the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels, hyperpolarising the cell and reducing glutamate release onto bipolar neurons. Recovery and adaptation depend on rhodopsin kinase, arrestin, RGS9 and the calcium-sensitive guanylate cyclase activators that restore cGMP. Because vertebrates cannot make retinal de novo, the set also covers dietary vitamin A uptake, lipoprotein and retinol-binding-protein transport, and the retinoid cycle enzymes of the pigment epithelium that regenerate 11-cis-retinal. Mutations across these steps cause retinitis pigmentosa, Leber congenital amaurosis, Stargardt disease, congenital stationary night blindness and colour vision defects.

NOTCH2 intracellular domain regulates transcription is the nuclear output step of NOTCH2 signalling: after ligand-induced cleavage, the released intracellular domain enters the nucleus and switches on genes that specify cell fate. It matters for bile duct and kidney development, for marginal-zone B cell identity, and for cytotoxic lymphocyte function; its dysregulation contributes to B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and, through loss-of-function, to Alagille syndrome. Mechanistically the intracellular domain converts RBPJ from a repressor into an activator by recruiting a Mastermind-like coactivator and histone acetyltransferase EP300 at RBPJ-binding elements. Targets include the HES1 and HES5 repressors shared with NOTCH1, and others that are NOTCH2-selective, notably FCER2/CD23A, whose overexpression marks leukaemic B cells and can be mimicked by Epstein-Barr virus EBNA2. At the granzyme B promoter the complex cooperates with phosphorylated CREB1 to support CD8+ T-cell killing.

Once NOTCH2 is cleaved at the membrane, its released intracellular domain travels to the nucleus and becomes a transcription factor subunit, and this step is where NOTCH2 signalling actually changes gene expression. The cleaved domain binds the DNA-binding protein RBPJ and a mastermind-like coactivator, converting RBPJ from a repressive to an activating complex on RBPJ-binding promoter elements. Direct targets include the HES1 and HES5 repressors shared with other Notch receptors, plus targets that distinguish NOTCH2: the low-affinity IgE receptor FCER2/CD23, whose overexpression is a hallmark of B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and is mimicked by Epstein-Barr virus EBNA2, and granzyme B, activated jointly with phosphorylated CREB1 and the acetyltransferase EP300 to support CD8+ T-cell cytotoxicity. The same output contributes to bile duct and kidney development.

Hyaluronan, the unsulfated glycosaminoglycan that fills joint fluid, skin and other extracellular matrix, must be continually broken down as well as made, and the lysosomal hyaluronidase HYAL1 performs that degradation by hydrolysing the beta-1,4 linkages between N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronate in internalised hyaluronan fragments. Loss of this single activity causes mucopolysaccharidosis type IX, or Natowicz syndrome, a very rare lysosomal storage disorder in which hyaluronan accumulates in serum and tissues. Affected individuals develop periodically painful soft-tissue masses around the joints, acquired short stature and erosion of the hip joint, while joint mobility and intelligence remain unaffected fffff fffff a strikingly mild phenotype for a mucopolysaccharidosis, probably because other hyaluronidases and the cell-surface degradation route partly compensate. The pathway situates hyaluronan turnover within lysosomal glycosaminoglycan catabolism and matrix remodelling.

Glycosaminoglycans turn over continuously in cartilage, skin, cornea and other connective tissues, and their breakdown depends on a sequence of lysosomal sulfatases, glycosidases and an acetyltransferase that trim the chains one residue at a time. When any one step is missing, partially degraded dermatan, heparan, keratan or chondroitin sulfate accumulates in lysosomes and spills into blood and urine, producing the mucopolysaccharidoses: progressive skeletal dysplasia, coarse facies, joint and corneal disease, organomegaly, cardiac and airway involvement, and in several forms neurodegeneration and shortened life. The enzymes here map onto specific syndromes — iduronidase and iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency give Hurler and Hunter disease, sulfamidase, acetyl-CoA:glucosaminide acetyltransferase and alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase give Sanfilippo subtypes, and arylsulfatase B or galactosamine-6-sulfatase loss gives Maroteaux-Lamy and Morquio. They illustrate how one blocked catabolic step becomes multisystem storage disease.

Sanfilippo syndrome type B is a lysosomal storage disease caused by loss of alpha-N-acetylglucosaminidase, the enzyme that removes terminal non-reducing N-acetylglucosamine residues during stepwise lysosomal degradation of heparan sulfate. When this single step fails, partially digested heparan sulfate accumulates in lysosomes throughout the body, but the consequences fall most heavily on the nervous system: affected children show progressive cognitive decline, behavioural disturbance and seizures with comparatively mild skeletal and visceral involvement, and survival is usually limited to the second or third decade. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the many distinct mutations described in the gene account for a broad range of residual activity and clinical severity. The biology situates this disorder within glycosaminoglycan catabolism and lysosomal function generally, alongside the other mucopolysaccharidoses that block successive steps of the same degradative sequence.

Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome is an inherited lysosomal storage disease that results when the stepwise breakdown of dermatan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate stalls for want of a single enzyme. Arylsulfatase B, the N-acetylgalactosamine 4-sulfatase encoded by ARSB, removes the 4-sulfate group from terminal N-acetylgalactosamine residues of these glycosaminoglycans inside the lysosome; without that step the chain cannot be degraded further and partially digested sugar accumulates in connective tissue, cartilage, heart valves, cornea and meninges. The consequences are skeletal dysplasia and short stature, joint stiffness, corneal clouding, valvular heart disease and airway and spinal cord compression, typically with intelligence spared, and undegraded chondroitin sulfate appears in urine. It is inherited recessively, and enzyme replacement addresses the deficiency directly, placing this biology within lysosomal glycosaminoglycan catabolism and extracellular matrix turnover.

Morquio syndrome A is a lysosomal storage disorder of glycosaminoglycan turnover, inherited recessively, in which cartilage and bone bear the brunt of the defect. It follows loss of N-acetylgalactosamine 6-sulfatase, the lysosomal enzyme that removes 6-sulfate groups from N-acetylgalactosamine 6-sulfate residues of chondroitin sulfate and from galactose 6-sulfate residues of keratan sulfate. Without this desulfation step, stepwise degradation of these chains stalls, partially digested keratan sulfate accumulates within lysosomes of chondrocytes and other cells, and excess is excreted in urine. The clinical consequence is a severe osteochondrodysplasia with short trunk, spinal instability and odontoid hypoplasia, corneal clouding and hearing loss, while intelligence is typically spared; severe forms shorten life into early adulthood. It illustrates how one missing sulfatase activity within sequential lysosomal catabolism translates into a skeletal disease.

Heparan sulfate is degraded stepwise in the lysosome, and one step in that chain requires the non-reducing terminal glucosamine to be N-acetylated before an exoglycosidase can remove it. That transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA is performed by the lysosomal membrane enzyme HGSNAT, and its loss causes the autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease Sanfilippo syndrome type C. Because the sugar chain cannot be trimmed further, partially degraded heparan sulfate accumulates in cells and tissues, with neurons especially vulnerable. The clinical picture is dominated by progressive central nervous system degeneration with developmental regression, behavioural disturbance and seizures, while somatic features stay comparatively mild; death typically follows in the second or third decade. The pathway situates glycosaminoglycan catabolism within lysosomal function and illustrates how a single missing modification blocks an entire degradative sequence.

Beta-glucuronidase deficiency, known clinically as mucopolysaccharidosis type VII or Sly syndrome, is the failure of a single lysosomal exoglycosidase step in the stepwise degradation of glycosaminoglycans, including hyaluronan as well as dermatan, keratan and chondroitin sulfate. GUSB removes terminal glucuronic acid residues; without it, partially degraded chains accumulate in lysosomes throughout connective tissue, liver, bone and brain. The consequences are those of lysosomal storage generally: hepatomegaly, dysostosis and coarse facial features, corneal and cardiac involvement, and variable cognitive impairment, with the most severe alleles presenting as non-immune hydrops fetalis and the mildest compatible with adult survival. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and residual enzyme activity largely sets where a patient falls on this spectrum. The defect illustrates how turnover of extracellular matrix polysaccharides depends on an ordered series of lysosomal hydrolases, each indispensable to the next.

Heparan sulfate glycosaminoglycans are continually turned over in the lysosome by an ordered series of exo-enzymes, and each step must occur before the next can proceed. Hunter syndrome is the block at one of those steps: loss or deficiency of iduronate-2-sulfatase, encoded on the X chromosome and therefore affecting mainly males, leaves the 2-sulfate group on L-iduronate residues in place and halts further degradation of heparan sulfate, dermatan sulfate and heparin. The undegraded fragments accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body and spill into urine. Clinically this produces hepatosplenomegaly, thickened heart valves, obstructive airway disease, joint stiffness and skeletal deformity, and in severe forms progressive neurological decline and death in childhood, while attenuated forms allow survival into adulthood. The disorder illustrates how a single missing sulfatase activity disables an entire catabolic route.</description>

Heparan sulfate is dismantled inside the lysosome by an ordered series of exo-enzymes, and alpha-L-iduronidase performs one obligatory step: removal of non-reducing terminal alpha-L-iduronic acid residues. When IDUA activity is lost, the degradative chain stalls and undegraded heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body, spilling into urine. This is the biochemical basis of mucopolysaccharidosis type I, inherited recessively and graded by residual enzyme activity from severe Hurler syndrome through Hurler-Scheie to the attenuated Scheie form. Storage produces hepatosplenomegaly, short stature with skeletal dysplasia, coarse facial features, corneal clouding and retinopathy, cardiac and airway disease, and in the severe form progressive neurological decline with death in childhood. Because a single missing glycosidase blocks turnover of abundant extracellular matrix polysaccharides, the disorder is treatable in principle by supplying the enzyme or the cells that make it.

Heparan sulfate is dismantled inside lysosomes by an ordered sequence of exoenzymes, and each step must occur before the next can proceed. Sanfilippo syndrome type D is the autosomal recessive disease that follows loss of N-acetylglucosamine 6-sulfatase, the enzyme encoded by GNS, which removes the 6-sulfate group from terminal N-acetylglucosamine 6-sulfate residues. Without it, partially degraded heparan sulfate accumulates in lysosomes and is excreted in urine, with the burden falling most heavily on neurons: affected children show progressive intellectual deterioration and behavioural disturbance with comparatively mild skeletal and visceral involvement, and survival is typically limited to the second or third decade. Keratan sulfate, whose beta-linked N-acetylglucosamine 6-sulfate can be released by beta-hexosaminidase A, does not build up. The disorder belongs to the mucopolysaccharidoses, a family of lysosomal glycosaminoglycan storage diseases.

Sanfilippo syndrome type A is the lysosomal storage disease that follows loss of N-sulphoglucosamine sulphohydrolase, encoded by SGSH, the enzyme that removes the sulfate from the terminal N-sulphoglucosamine residue at the non-reducing end of heparan sulfate. Because this step opens the way for all subsequent exoglycosidase and sulfatase action, its absence stalls stepwise heparan sulfate breakdown entirely, and partially degraded chains accumulate inside lysosomes across tissues and spill into urine. Neurons are the least tolerant of this burden, so the clinical picture is dominated by progressive central nervous system degeneration beginning in early childhood, with developmental regression, behavioural disturbance and death in the second decade, while somatic features stay comparatively mild. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and this defect represents one of four enzymatically distinct forms of mucopolysaccharidosis III affecting the same catabolic route.

Morquio syndrome B is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by loss of acid beta-galactosidase activity, the step that removes terminal galactose residues from keratan sulfate and other glycoconjugates during lysosomal degradation. When that cleavage fails, keratan sulfate accumulates inside cells and is excreted in excess in urine, producing skeletal dysplasia with short stature and joint and spinal abnormalities, plus corneal clouding, while intelligence and the central nervous system remain unaffected. The single enzyme responsible, GLB1, also acts on gangliosides and glycoproteins, so different mutations in the same gene instead give rise to the neurodegenerative GM1 gangliosidoses, with the residual activity and substrate preference determining which phenotype appears. This disorder illustrates how one exoglycosidase step in glycosaminoglycan turnover supports cartilage and connective tissue integrity, and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Anchoring fibrils are the structures that hold the epidermis onto the dermis, and their formation explains why skin resists shearing. Collagen VII, the product of COL7A1, is secreted as procollagen that dimerizes tail-to-tail; bone morphogenetic protein 1, with the related tolloid-like proteinases, cleaves the C-propeptide, after which the processed antiparallel dimers aggregate laterally into fibrils. These fibrils span from the lamina densa of the basement membrane into the papillary dermis, where they engage laminin-332 (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2) and collagen IV networks above and fibrillar collagen I below, linking the two compartments into one mechanical unit. Loss or mutation of collagen VII causes dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, in which blisters form beneath the basement membrane after minor trauma; defects in the laminin-332 chains underlie a junctional form of the same disease.

Growth factor receptors converge on class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase to tell a cell to grow, take up nutrients, and stay alive, and constitutive activation of PI3K/AKT signalling is among the most common events in human cancer. Receptor tyrosine kinases for EGF-family, FGF, PDGF, HGF and stem cell factor ligands, together with adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1, IRS1 and PTPN11, relieve p85 inhibition of the p110 catalytic subunit, generating PIP3 that recruits PDPK1 and AKT to the membrane; mTORC2 components and PDPK1 complete AKT activation. Active AKT then suppresses FOXO transcription factors, BAD and caspase-9, inactivates GSK3 and TSC2 to drive mTORC1-dependent growth, and destabilises p53 via MDM2. PTEN degrades PIP3 and opposes the whole axis, so its mutation, deletion or silencing, like activating PIK3CA and AKT1 mutations, locks the pathway on and underlies both sporadic tumours and hamartoma syndromes.

Constitutive Signaling by Aberrant PI3K in Cancer describes how tumours lock the PI3K/AKT axis into the "on" state without any growth factor being present, giving cells continuous survival, growth and metabolic signalling. Gain-of-function mutations in PIK3CA, encoding the p110alpha catalytic subunit, or in PIK3R1, encoding the p85alpha regulatory subunit, are among the most common events in breast, endometrial and colorectal cancer, and they make tumours dependent on, and treatable by, PI3K and AKT inhibitors. Helical-domain and SH2-domain mutations break the inhibitory clamp p85 normally holds on p110 while the two subunits stay bound; catalytic-domain mutations favour an active kinase conformation. Either way PIP3 is generated and AKT is engaged ligand-independently. The surrounding receptor tyrosine kinases, ligands and adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1, IRS1 and PTPN11 mark the normal upstream input that the mutant enzyme bypasses.

Class I PI3Ks normally fire only when a growth factor receptor is engaged, and the resulting PIP3 signal drives AKT-dependent growth, anabolic metabolism and survival. Gain-of-function mutations in the p110alpha catalytic subunit or the p85alpha regulatory subunit uncouple this from ligand, so the kinase produces PIP3 and activates AKT constitutively — one of the most common oncogenic events in breast, endometrial and colorectal cancer, and the rationale for PI3K and AKT inhibitors. Helical-domain and nSH2/iSH2 mutations break the inhibitory contact between the two subunits while keeping them bound, whereas catalytic-domain mutations favour an intrinsically active conformation. The surrounding machinery defines what is bypassed: receptor tyrosine kinases and their ligands from the EGF, FGF, PDGF, HGF and neurotrophin families, adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1/2, IRS1/2 and PTPN11, and Src-family and Rac components that couple receptors to lipid kinase activation.

Newly secreted collagen only becomes load-bearing once neighbouring molecules are locked together, and the crosslinking of collagen fibrils supplies that covalent stabilisation. It gives tendon, bone, skin, cornea and blood vessel wall their tensile strength and renders mature collagen insoluble; when it fails, tissues are fragile and mechanically weak, and when it runs excessively it contributes to fibrosis and tumour stiffening. Procollagen propeptides are first removed by proteinases such as BMP1 and the tolloid-like enzymes, assisted by the enhancer protein PCOLCE, allowing type I molecules to pack into microfibrils. Lysyl oxidase and its LOXL relatives then oxidatively deaminate telopeptide lysine or hydroxylysine residues, and the resulting aldehydes react spontaneously to yield aldimine or ketoimine links that mature into trivalent pyridinolines and pyrroles. In type IV collagen basement membrane networks, peroxidasin instead forms sulfilimine bonds between chains.

Cellular responses to stress collects the programs cells use to survive perturbations of their internal and external environment — oxygen shortage, heat, oxidants and electrophiles, nutrient and amino acid deprivation, misfolded protein burden, heme deficiency — and to shut down proliferation permanently when damage cannot be repaired. Tissue homeostasis depends on it, and its components are the levers of ageing, tumour suppression and adaptation to ischaemia. The genes trace several coordinated arms: HIF stabilisation by prolyl hydroxylases and VHL driving hypoxic transcription; KEAP1–NFE2L2 control of glutathione, thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin antioxidant defence; HSF1 with HSP70, HSP90 and small chaperones in proteostasis and steroid receptor maturation; PERK, ATF6 and IRE1–XBP1 in the unfolded protein response; eIF2α kinases restraining translation; mTORC1 regulation by Rag GTPases and sestrins under starvation; and p53, CDK inhibitors, telomere proteins and Polycomb complexes enforcing senescence and its inflammatory secretion.

Cells constantly meet insults from outside and from their own metabolism — low oxygen, heat, oxidants, misfolded proteins, nutrient shortage, heme or amino acid deficiency — and this collection of cellular stress responses is how they adjust to survive or withdraw from the cell cycle. Its outputs maintain tissue homeostasis; its failure underlies degeneration, ischemic injury and, when senescence programmes are bypassed, tumour growth. Oxygen sensing runs through prolyl hydroxylases and VHL-dependent turnover of HIF1A/EPAS1, which switch on erythropoietin, VEGFA and glycolytic and respiratory adaptations. Heat shock factor HSF1 with HSP90, HSP70 and small chaperones restores proteostasis, while ER stress sensors ATF6, ERN1/XBP1 and PERK-family kinases converge on EIF2S1 phosphorylation, ATF4 and CHOP to throttle translation. KEAP1–NFE2L2 drives antioxidant and glutathione genes; mTORC1 with Rag GTPases, GATOR and sestrins gauges nutrients; p53, CDKN1A and polycomb–telomere components enforce senescence.</description>

As cells enter mitosis, interphase chromatin must be compacted into discrete, mechanically robust chromosomes before they can be captured by the spindle and segregated; the prophase condensation step initiates that transformation. Condensin II, built from the SMC2/SMC4 ATPase core with NCAPD3, NCAPG2 and NCAPH2, acts first in the nucleus, loading onto chromatin in part through recognition of monomethylated histone H4 by NCAPD3. Two events raise that mark at mitotic entry: the methyltransferase KMT5A peaks at G2/M, while CDK1/cyclin B1 phosphorylates the demethylase PHF8 and evicts it from chromatin. Condensin II is itself activated by successive CDK1 and PLK1 phosphorylation, with RB1 and MCPH1 modulating its chromatin association. Failure of this programme yields tangled, undercondensed chromosomes, missegregation and aneuploidy, and MCPH1 loss causes premature condensation and primary microcephaly.

Phosphate bond hydrolysis by NUDT proteins is the cell's nucleotide sanitation and housekeeping system, clearing damaged or surplus nucleotides before they can be used. Its main payoff is genome and proteome fidelity: NUDT1 (MTH1) destroys 8-oxo-dGTP and other oxidised purine nucleotides so they are never incorporated into DNA or mRNA, and NUDT15 and NUDT18 act on related oxidised or modified substrates, while NUDT16 additionally trims inosine-containing nucleotides and RNA caps. Loss of this surveillance raises mutation rates and mistranslation under oxidative stress. Other members handle metabolic intermediates: NUDT5 and NUDT9 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, preventing spontaneous non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and feeding nucleotide and NAD-related salvage, and ADPRM cleaves ADP-ribose-derived phosphoesters. The shared Nudix motif coordinates the magnesium ion used for catalysis. NUDT15 activity also governs how patients tolerate thiopurine drugs.

Nudix hydrolases keep the cellular nucleotide pool clean, and the phosphate bond hydrolysis they carry out is best understood as sanitation: damaged or surplus nucleotides are cleaved before they can be used as substrates. Oxidised, deaminated or methylated purine nucleoside di- and triphosphates are degraded by enzymes such as NUDT1, NUDT15 and NUDT18, preventing their incorporation into DNA as mutations or into mRNA as mistranslated protein. NUDT16 acts on inosine- and other modified guanine-containing nucleotides, while NUDT9 and NUDT5 hydrolyse ADP-ribose, limiting non-enzymatic ADP-ribosylation of proteins and the accumulation of a potent second messenger; ADPRM degrades ADP-ribose 1''-phosphate from tRNA splicing. Because these enzymes also destroy nucleotide analogues, their activity sets tolerance to thiopurine and other nucleoside-based chemotherapies, and NUDT15 variants cause severe drug toxicity.

Mitochondria run a very short electron relay that moves reducing equivalents from NADPH to small iron-sulfur proteins, and this NADPH-to-ferredoxin transfer is what supplies electrons to two otherwise unrelated jobs: steroid hormone synthesis and the building of iron-sulfur cofactors. A single flavoprotein reductase, FDXR (adrenodoxin reductase), oxidises NADPH and reduces either of two [2Fe-2S] ferredoxins. FDX1 serves the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzymes of the adrenal cortex and gonads, feeding the side-chain cleavage and hydroxylation steps that generate cortisol, aldosterone and sex steroids; FDX2 instead delivers electrons to the cysteine desulfurase scaffold complex where nascent clusters are assembled, and so supports respiratory chain subunits, lipoate synthesis and cellular iron sensing. Loss of the FDX2 arm produces mitochondrial myopathy with deficient iron-sulfur enzymes, while the FDX1 arm is rate-limiting for adrenal steroid output.

Growth factor control of body size, tissue growth and metabolism runs largely through the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor, a tyrosine kinase activated when IGF1 or IGF2 binds its extracellular alpha subunits. Receptor autophosphorylation recruits IRS adaptors and SHC1, which assemble GRB2-SOS complexes to fire the RAS-RAF-ERK cascade driving proliferation, and engage the p85-p110 PI3 kinase to generate lipid second messengers that activate PDK1 and AKT for survival, protein synthesis and suppression of apoptosis. Shared adaptors such as FRS2, GAB1/2 and PTPN11 link the same machinery to fibroblast growth factor receptors and FLT3, and negative regulators including TRIB3 restrain AKT output. Excess signalling through this axis supports tumour growth and resistance to therapy, while loss causes growth retardation; reduced flux is also tied to extended lifespan in model organisms.

Selenium is needed in trace amounts but toxic in excess, and converting it into selenosugars for excretion is how the body disposes of the surplus. Once dietary selenium has been reduced to hydrogen selenide and the demands of selenoprotein synthesis are met, the remaining pool is diverted into conjugates rather than allowed to accumulate. Selenide or selenite reacts with glutathione, and methylation together with transfer onto an N-acetylgalactosamine sugar yields methylseleno-hexosamine derivatives that are water-soluble and readily cleared by the kidney. These selenosugars, alongside trimethylselenonium ion at higher intakes, are the main urinary selenium metabolites and serve as markers of selenium status. The route links selenium homeostasis to glutathione-dependent detoxification and methyl group metabolism, and its capacity sets the margin between adequate intake and selenosis.

Dietary selenium arrives mostly as organic forms — selenomethionine, selenocysteine and methylselenocysteine — none of which can be used directly; this route funnels them into hydrogen selenide, the common donor from which selenophosphate and then selenocysteine-containing proteins such as the glutathione peroxidases and thioredoxin reductases are built. Selenomethionine is handled by the same enzymes that run methionine and homocysteine metabolism, with methionine adenosyltransferase, the methyltransferases that regenerate homocysteine, and AHCY feeding the trans-selenation arm; cystathionine beta-synthase and cystathionine gamma-lyase then convert selenohomocysteine onward, while selenocysteine lyase cleaves free selenocysteine to release selenide. Because selenium enters through transsulfuration, selenium status is coupled to sulfur amino acid and methyl-group supply. Inadequate flux limits selenoprotein synthesis and antioxidant defence; excess selenide drives redox toxicity, which is why methylated selenium species are the preferred excretory endpoint.

Selenium reaches the body as selenite, selenate, selenomethionine or selenocysteine, and selenoamino acid metabolism is the route by which all of these converge on selenide, the common donor used to build selenocysteine and, through it, the selenoproteins that support antioxidant defence and thyroid hormone metabolism. Selenocysteine lyase and cystathionine gamma-lyase release selenium from dietary and recycled forms, methyltransferases and methionine-cycle enzymes handle methylselenol, and excess selenium leaves as methylated or sugar-conjugated species, so the same chemistry sets both nutritional sufficiency and the narrow margin before selenium toxicity. Selenocysteine itself is made on its own tRNA: a kinase phosphorylates the seryl intermediate and SEPSECS converts it to selenocysteinyl-tRNA, which a dedicated elongation factor and a SECIS-binding protein deliver to ribosomes that recode a UGA codon. The large ribosomal and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase complement reflects this translational step.

Metabolism of ingested H2SeO4 and H2SeO3 into H2Se converts dietary inorganic selenium into the single reduced form the cell can actually use. Hydrogen selenide is the obligatory precursor for selenophosphate and thus for the selenocysteine inserted into glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and iodothyronine deiodinases; without this reduction step, ingested selenate and selenite cannot support antioxidant defence, thyroid hormone activation or male fertility, and selenoprotein synthesis fails. Selenate is first activated by the bifunctional PAPS synthases PAPSS1 and PAPSS2, borrowing the sulfate assimilation machinery, and the adenylylated intermediate is reduced onward. Selenite is reduced more directly at the expense of NADPH-dependent thiol systems, with thioredoxin reductase 1 and glutathione reductase supplying reducing equivalents through thioredoxin and glutathione. The chemistry is redox-costly and generates reactive intermediates, which is one reason selenium is beneficial at trace levels and toxic in excess.

Dietary selenium arrives largely as inorganic selenate and selenite, but the only form the cell can use for selenoprotein synthesis is hydrogen selenide, and this reductive route makes the conversion. Without it, selenocysteine cannot be charged onto its dedicated tRNA, and the whole selenoprotein family — glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases, iodothyronine deiodinases — fails to be made, with consequences for antioxidant defence and thyroid hormone activation. Reduction proceeds stepwise: the bifunctional sulfate-activating enzymes PAPSS1 and PAPSS2 adenylate selenate as they would sulfate, a reductase step acts on the activated intermediate, and thiol-based reducing systems built on thioredoxin reductase 1 and glutathione reductase, fed by NADPH, carry selenite through to selenide. The chemistry borrows the sulfur assimilation machinery, reflecting the close similarity of selenium and sulfur. Excess selenium is toxic, so flux through this pathway also matters for handling overload.

Selenium is required in trace amounts but toxic in excess, and methylation of methylselenol is the route by which the body disposes of the surplus. Methylselenol sits at the hub of selenium metabolism, released from selenoamino acids and selenium-containing compounds; it is reactive and redox-active, capable of generating superoxide and depleting glutathione, so its concentration must be kept low. Successive S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation by indolethylamine N-methyltransferase converts it to volatile dimethylselenide, exhaled on the breath and responsible for the garlic odour of selenium poisoning, and then to the charged trimethylselenonium ion, which is excreted in urine. This disposal arm balances the alternative fate of methylselenol, incorporation into selenoproteins, and is part of the broader picture of how methylselenol levels determine both selenium toxicity and the antiproliferative effects attributed to selenium supplementation.</description>

Selenocysteine synthesis builds the 21st amino acid on its own tRNA and delivers it into growing proteins, supplying the catalytic residue of glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and the deiodinases. Through these selenoproteins it underwrites cellular antioxidant defence, redox signalling and thyroid hormone activation; loss of the pathway causes selenoprotein deficiency syndromes with abnormal thyroid hormone metabolism, myopathy, and, for SEPSECS mutations, progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy. Serine is first charged onto tRNA(Sec) by seryl-tRNA synthetase, phosphorylated by PSTK, and converted to selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec) by SEPSECS using selenophosphate from SEPHS2. Because UGA normally terminates translation, incorporation is a recoding event: SECISBP2 binds a SECIS element in the 3' untranslated region and recruits the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC to the ribosome, so the full complement of large and small subunit ribosomal proteins is integral to the process.

Selenocysteine is the 21st amino acid and the catalytic residue of glutathione peroxidases, thioredoxin reductases and the deiodinases, so its synthesis is what allows the cell to build selenoproteins and defend itself against peroxides. Unusually, the amino acid is made on its own tRNA rather than free: seryl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNA(Sec) with serine, PSTK phosphorylates it, SEPHS2 generates the selenium donor selenophosphate, and SEPSECS converts the phosphoseryl intermediate into selenocysteinyl-tRNA(Sec). Delivery is equally specialised — the dedicated elongation factor EEFSEC and the SECIS-binding protein SECISBP2 recode an in-frame UGA codon from stop to selenocysteine, which is why the large and small ribosomal subunit proteins accompany this chemistry. Loss of SEPSECS causes progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy, and SECISBP2 defects disturb thyroid hormone metabolism, linking selenium handling to brain development and endocrine function.

DAP12 is the short transmembrane adaptor that gives activating receptors on myeloid cells and NK cells a way to signal, and the pathway built on it drives target-cell killing, cytokine release, phagocytosis and microglial responses to damage. Receptors including TREM2 and the NKG2C/CD94 and NKG2D complexes have no signalling tails of their own; they pair with DAP12 (TYROBP), whose ITAM tyrosines are phosphorylated by Src-family kinases such as LCK and FYN to create a docking site for SYK. SYK then phosphorylates the membrane scaffold LAT, assembling GRB2:SOS, GADS/SLP76, VAV, PI3K and phospholipase C-gamma, which together activate RAS-ERK and AKT, mobilise calcium and remodel actin through RAC1. Loss of DAP12 or TREM2 function causes Nasu-Hakola disease and predisposes to Alzheimer's disease, reflecting the pathway's role in microglial survival and clearance.

Cells that need to build membranes or store energy must turn on the enzymes of lipid synthesis, and this is the transcriptional step that does it: nuclear forms of SREBF1 and SREBF2 bind sterol regulatory elements in target promoters and switch on the cholesterol and fatty acid biosynthetic programmes. The outputs are the mevalonate and sterol pathway enzymes — HMGCS1, HMGCR, MVK, SQLE, LSS, DHCR7 — and the lipogenic set including FASN, ACACA/ACACB, SCD and ELOVL6, linking the pathway to membrane supply, lipoprotein metabolism and hepatic steatosis when it runs unchecked. SREBFs are weak activators alone and depend on partners: the NF-Y trimer and SP1 at neighbouring promoter sites, coactivators such as CREBBP, NCOA1/2/6, MED1 and CARM1, and nuclear receptor input via PPARA and RXRA. SREBF1 favours fatty acid genes, SREBF2 the cholesterol arm, so that sterol sensing upstream is translated into selective metabolic output.

Growth factor signalling through the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor drives cell growth, survival and metabolic anabolism, and its overactivity is a recurrent feature of cancers where it supports proliferation and resistance to therapy. Binding of IGF1 or IGF2 triggers receptor autophosphorylation and recruitment of the IRS1/2/4 and SHC1 scaffolds, which couple the receptor to two branches: PI3K, through its p85 regulatory and p110 catalytic subunits, generates lipid second messengers that activate AKT via PDPK1, while GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1 loads GTP onto RAS and launches the RAF-MAPK cascade. Additional adaptors such as GAB1/2 and the phosphatase PTPN11 amplify the signal, and negative regulators including TRIB3 restrain AKT output. Receptor tyrosine kinases of the FGF and FLT3 families, with FRS2, converge on the same adaptor and effector modules, underlining a shared architecture for mitogenic signalling.

IRS-related events triggered by IGF1R describes how insulin-like growth factor signalling is converted into the two major growth-promoting cascades of the cell. Ligand-bound IGF1R phosphorylates the insulin receptor substrate scaffolds IRS1, IRS2 and IRS4, which then recruit PI3K regulatory and catalytic subunits and the GRB2:SOS complex, launching PI3K-PDK1-AKT survival and metabolic signalling alongside RAS-RAF-MAPK proliferative signalling. This axis drives somatic growth, anabolic metabolism, cell survival and tissue regeneration, and its inappropriate activation is a recurrent feature of cancers, where IGF1R and IRS levels correlate with resistance to therapy. Shared adaptors such as FRS2, GAB1/2, PTPN11 and the RAS isoforms link this route to closely related receptor tyrosine kinase inputs including FGF receptors and FLT3, while negative regulators such as TRIB3 and feedback on IRS phosphorylation set the duration of the response.

Growth factor signalling through the type 1 insulin-like growth factor receptor is routed largely through IRS scaffold proteins, and this branch is what converts IGF1 and IGF2 binding into cell growth, survival and anabolic metabolism during development and tissue maintenance. The activated receptor phosphorylates IRS1, IRS2 and IRS4 on tyrosines, creating docking sites for the PI3K regulatory subunits and for GRB2:SOS; the first arm generates PIP3 and activates AKT via PDPK1, the second loads RAS proteins to drive the RAF-MAPK cascade. Additional adaptors such as GAB1/GAB2, FRS2 and the phosphatase PTPN11 shape the output, and negative regulators including TRIB3 restrain AKT. The same adaptor logic is shared with fibroblast growth factor receptors and FLT3, which is why those ligands and receptors appear alongside. Overactive signalling here supports tumour proliferation and resistance to therapy, while impairment produces growth deficiency and insulin-like resistance.

Insulin-like growth factor signalling drives body and tissue growth, and this branch is how the activated IGF1 receptor reaches the RAS-MAPK route that tells cells to proliferate. When IGF1 or IGF2 binds, the receptor tyrosine kinase autophosphorylates and recruits the adaptor SHC1, phosphorylating it on tyrosines that create a docking site for GRB2 in complex with the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1; SOS1 then loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, launching the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade toward growth-promoting transcription. This axis accounts for much of the mitogenic, as opposed to metabolic, output of IGF receptor activation, and it operates alongside the IRS-dependent PI3K arm. Persistent flux through it supports tumour cell proliferation and resistance to therapy, which is why IGF1R is a recurring oncology target; loss of IGF signalling instead causes growth deficiency.

Vision begins when 11-cis-retinal bound to opsin absorbs a photon; the retinoid cycle regenerates that chromophore between the photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium, and inherited defects in its components cause a spectrum of blinding disease. Mutations here underlie Stargardt macular degeneration and fundus flavimaculatus through the photoreceptor flippase ABCA4, whose failure allows toxic bisretinoid adducts to accumulate as lipofuscin, as well as retinitis punctata albescens and Bothnia dystrophy from loss of the retinaldehyde-binding protein RLBP1, and retinal dystrophies from the dehydrogenases RDH5 and RDH12 that interconvert retinol and retinaldehyde. Upstream steps in vitamin A supply are equally vulnerable: retinol esterification by LRAT, circulating transport on RBP4 with transthyretin, and cellular uptake through the receptor STRA6, whose disruption gives Matthew-Wood syndrome with microphthalmia. Cone opsin gene defects in the same context produce colour vision deficiency.

Rod photoreceptors see in dim light because their chromophore is continuously regenerated: after a photon isomerizes 11-cis-retinal bound to rhodopsin, the spent all-trans-retinal must be recycled back to the 11-cis form before the cell can respond again. This canonical retinoid cycle of twilight vision shuttles retinoids between the photoreceptor outer segment and the retinal pigment epithelium, where reduction to all-trans-retinol, esterification by LRAT, hydrolysis and isomerization by RPE65, and reoxidation by RDH5 restore the usable chromophore, with carrier proteins such as RBP3, RLBP1 and RBP1 solubilizing these hydrophobic intermediates and serum RBP4 and STRA6 supplying vitamin A from the circulation. ABCA4 clears retinal adducts from disc membranes. Loss of these steps underlies Stargardt disease, retinitis pigmentosa, fundus albipunctatus and delayed dark adaptation, and permits toxic bisretinoid accumulation.

High-affinity IgE receptor signalling is how mast cells and basophils convert antigen recognition into an immediate allergic response, and it underlies type I hypersensitivity, from urticaria and allergic rhinitis to asthma and anaphylaxis. Antigen cross-links IgE bound to the receptor's alpha chain, and the beta and gamma chains, through their ITAM motifs, are phosphorylated by LYN and FYN, recruiting SYK.
