Phosphorylated LAT and NTAL/LAT2 nucleate scaffolds bearing GRB2, LCP2/SLP76, GADS and GAB2, engaging PI3K, BTK and phospholipase C gamma; the resulting IP3 opens ITPR channels to release stored calcium, while DAG and RASGRP-driven RAS activation feed ERK, JNK and p38. Calcium-loaded calcineurin dereprsses NFAT, and a CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 module with TAK1 and IKK drives NF-kB, requiring ubiquitin conjugation and proteasomal degradation of IkB. Output is degranulation, eicosanoid synthesis, cytokine production, adhesion and survival.

Entering mitosis requires not only that CDK1 phosphorylate its substrates but that the opposing phosphatase be silenced, and the Greatwall kinase MASTL is the switch that does it. Without this arm, mitotic substrates are dephosphorylated as fast as they are marked, and cells fail to enter or sustain mitosis and exit prematurely, with consequences for chromosome segregation fidelity. CDK1-cyclin B1 and autophosphorylation activate MASTL at mitotic entry; active MASTL then phosphorylates the small, heat-stable proteins ARPP19 and ENSA, converting them into potent inhibitors of PP2A holoenzymes carrying the B55-delta regulatory subunit. With that phosphatase held off, CDK1 phosphorylation of mitotic targets accumulates and the mitotic state is maintained until cyclin degradation reverses the balance. The pathway thus couples kinase and phosphatase control into a bistable commitment to division.

A2E is the bisretinoid pigment that accumulates as lipofuscin in retinal pigment epithelial cells, and its formation links the daily chemistry of vision to slow, irreversible retinal damage. After photoisomerization, all-trans-retinal released in photoreceptor outer segment discs condenses with phosphatidylethanolamine; a second retinal adduct and further rearrangement yield the di-retinoid-pyridinium-ethanolamine fluorophore. Because outer segment tips are shed daily and phagocytosed by the pigment epithelium, A2E is delivered into RPE lysosomes, where no catabolic route is known and the compound simply builds up, photosensitizing the cell, damaging membranes and contributing to macular degeneration and Stargardt disease. The phospholipase D-type enzyme acting on N-acylphosphatidylethanolamine represents the lipid-processing chemistry surrounding this pathway, and lipofuscin accumulation more broadly marks aging and neurodegenerative tissue. Limiting retinal clearance failure is the main way cells restrain the process.

The irreversible step of mitosis, in which paired sister chromatids are pulled apart and delivered one copy to each daughter cell; errors here produce aneuploid daughters and are a route to chromosome instability in tumours and to miscarriage-causing trisomies. Cohesin rings holding the sisters together (SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21, STAG1/2) are protected at centromeres by shugoshin until the spindle checkpoint is satisfied. The anaphase-promoting complex with CDC20 then ubiquitinates securin, which is destroyed by the proteasome, freeing separase to cleave RAD21 and dissolve centromeric cohesion. The genes assembled here span the machinery the event depends on: the constitutive centromere-associated network and the kinetochore MIS12 and NDC80 complexes, checkpoint proteins MAD1/MAD2/BUB1/BUB3, Aurora B with the chromosomal passenger complex, dynein, kinesins and tubulins, and the phosphatases that reverse mitotic phosphorylation as chromatids move poleward.

Establishment of Sister Chromatid Cohesion is the step in S phase that converts the transient, dynamic loading of cohesin onto chromatin into a stable embrace of the two newly replicated sister chromatids. Without it sisters cannot be held together until anaphase, and chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploidy; mutations in these components underlie cohesinopathies such as Roberts syndrome. Cohesin itself is a ring of SMC1A, SMC3 and RAD21 with a STAG1 or STAG2 subunit, and its residence on DNA reflects a tug of war between loading and the release activity of WAPL bound to PDS5A/PDS5B. Replication-coupled acetylation of SMC3 by ESCO1 and ESCO2 permits recruitment of sororin (CDCA5), which displaces WAPL and locks the ring in place. This licensing underpins faithful chromosome segregation, and also feeds into DNA repair and chromatin looping.

After DNA replication, each chromosome exists as two identical copies that must stay physically linked until anaphase, and this is how that linkage is made permanent. Cohesin — a ring of SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and a STAG subunit — loads onto chromatin from telophase onward but cycles on and off, with WAPL driving release. During S phase the acetyltransferases ESCO1 and ESCO2 acetylate SMC3, which together with PDS5A/PDS5B allows CDCA5 (sororin) to bind and displace WAPL, locking cohesin onto replicated DNA. Stable cohesion gives the spindle the resistance it needs to biorient sister kinetochores, so its failure produces premature sister separation, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy. Mutations in ESCO2 and cohesin subunits underlie cohesinopathies such as Roberts syndrome and Cornelia de Lange syndrome, and the same complex also shapes interphase genome architecture and supports recombinational repair.

Sister chromatids must be held together from replication until anaphase, and this depends first on getting the cohesin ring onto DNA. As chromosomes decondense in telophase, the ring of SMC1A, SMC3 and RAD21 with its STAG1 or STAG2 subunit is deposited on chromatin by the NIPBL-MAU2 loading complex, while PDS5A/PDS5B and WAPL ride along as regulators that also permit ring opening and release. Beyond chromosome segregation, chromatin-bound cohesin organises interphase genome folding and enhancer-promoter contacts, so the amount loaded sets both mitotic fidelity and transcriptional output. Loss of MAU2 strips cohesin from the chromatin fraction. Mutations in NIPBL, SMC1A or SMC3 cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome, with facial and limb malformations, growth restriction and intellectual disability, and STAG2 loss recurs in cancer.

Activin, a TGF-beta family dimer built from inhibin beta subunits, drives reproductive, metabolic and tissue-remodelling responses, and follistatin-mediated antagonism sets how much of that signal ever reaches a receptor. Follistatin and the related follistatin-like-3 protein wrap around activin A and activin B dimers with essentially irreversible affinity, occluding the surfaces needed for type II receptor engagement and so blocking downstream SMAD2/3 activation. The two binders are interchangeable in a test tube but not in an animal: loss of follistatin causes perinatal death with muscle and skeletal defects, while loss of follistatin-like-3 is compatible with life but shifts glucose handling and islet biology. This buffering explains why follistatin acts as a growth-promoting factor in muscle and why the same ligand trap is exploited pharmacologically. It is one arm of extracellular control over TGF-beta superfamily signalling, alongside inhibin and receptor-level regulation.

Vision depends on a continuous supply of 11-cis-retinal to opsins in photoreceptors and on the machinery that converts photon capture into a neural signal; mutations in either arm produce inherited retinal disease. The genes here cover retinoid delivery and recycling between photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium — retinol-binding proteins and transthyretin carrying vitamin A in plasma, a membrane receptor for its cellular uptake, an acyltransferase esterifying retinol, and dehydrogenases interconverting retinal and retinol — together with the cone opsins that absorb light. Loss of the photoreceptor flippase ABCA4 allows retinoid adducts to accumulate as lipofuscin, causing Stargardt macular degeneration; other defects give retinitis pigmentosa, fundus albipunctatus, Leber congenital amaurosis, or colour-vision anomalies from cone pigment variation. These disorders illustrate how failure of chromophore regeneration leads to progressive photoreceptor degeneration and blindness.

Vision in dim light begins when a single photon is converted into an electrical signal in a rod photoreceptor, and this is the amplifying cascade that does it. Light isomerises the 11-cis-retinal chromophore bound to rhodopsin, switching the receptor to its active metarhodopsin II state, which catalytically activates many copies of the heterotrimeric G protein transducin. Transducin alpha relieves inhibition of the PDE6 catalytic complex by its gamma subunit, cGMP is hydrolysed, and cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels built from CNGA1 and CNGB1 close. The rod hyperpolarises and reduces tonic glutamate release onto bipolar cells, so photon number is encoded as a graded voltage; a sodium-calcium-potassium exchanger shapes the accompanying calcium fall that feeds back on recovery, while arrestin binding quenches activated rhodopsin. Mutations in these components cause retinitis pigmentosa and congenital stationary night blindness.

Before a cell can split its chromosomes evenly, the glue holding replicated sisters together must be released in two stages, and this stepwise resolution of sister chromatid cohesion is what makes accurate segregation possible. In prometaphase, CDK1 and PLK1 phosphorylate the cohesin subunits RAD21 and STAG2 and the cohesin stabiliser sororin (CDCA5), freeing WAPL to strip cohesin from chromosome arms while centromeric cohesion is spared: shugoshin proteins SGO1 and SGO2 recruit PP2A-B56 phosphatase to the kinetochore, where dephosphorylation of STAG2 keeps centromeric cohesin intact until anaphase. The accompanying centromere and kinetochore components, the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes, spindle checkpoint proteins, dynein, kinesins and tubulins, place this within the attachment of chromosomes to the mitotic spindle. Premature or incomplete resolution produces lagging chromosomes, aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours and in cohesinopathies.

Once the nuclear envelope breaks down at the start of prometaphase, cytoplasmic condensin I gains access to chromatin and drives the hypercondensation that turns prophase chromosomes into the compact, mechanically robust rods that a spindle can segregate. Without this step chromosome arms remain long and tangled, sister chromatids fail to resolve cleanly, and anaphase produces bridges and missegregation. The complex is a pentamer of the ATPase subunits SMC2 and SMC4, shared with condensin II, together with NCAPD2, NCAPG and NCAPH; ATP-dependent activity introduces positive supercoils and compacts DNA loops. Timing comes from mitotic phosphorylation: CDK1 bound to cyclin B modifies the non-SMC subunits to switch the complex on, while casein kinase 2 marks placed during interphase must be removed for full activity. Condensin I has also been linked to cohesin loss from chromosome arms, tying compaction to sister chromatid resolution.

The phototransduction cascade converts a single absorbed photon into an electrical signal in rod photoreceptors, making dim-light vision possible; mutations in its components cause retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness and Leber congenital amaurosis. Light isomerizes the 11-cis-retinal chromophore of rhodopsin, which activates the G protein transducin; the freed alpha subunit stimulates PDE6 to hydrolyse cGMP, closing CNGA1/CNGB1 cation channels and hyperpolarizing the outer segment. The hyperpolarization reaches the synapse, shuts voltage-gated calcium channels, and reduces tonic glutamate release onto bipolar cells. Equally represented is the shutoff and recovery arm that resets sensitivity for the next photon: rhodopsin kinase and arrestin quench the receptor, an RGS9 complex terminates transducin, and calcium sensing through recoverin, guanylate cyclase activating proteins and the NCKX1 exchanger restores cGMP synthesis. Lipid modification and N-terminal processing enzymes anchor and mature the cascade's membrane-associated subunits.

Vision begins when a photon isomerizes the retinal chromophore bound to rhodopsin, and this cascade converts that single molecular event into an electrical signal a rod photoreceptor can send to the retina. Activated opsin turns on the G protein transducin, whose alpha subunit releases the inhibitory gamma subunits of PDE6 so that cGMP is hydrolysed; cGMP-gated cation channels built from CNGA1 and CNGB1 then close and the cell hyperpolarizes, reducing glutamate release at the synapse. Equally important is shutoff and recovery: rhodopsin kinase and arrestin quench the receptor, an RGS9 complex accelerates transducin deactivation, and calcium sensed by recoverin and the guanylate cyclase activators GUCA1A/B feeds back on cyclase activity to restore cGMP and set light adaptation. Mutations in these components underlie retinitis pigmentosa, congenital stationary night blindness and Leber congenital amaurosis.

Inactivation, recovery and regulation of the phototransduction cascade is the shut-off arm of vision in rod and cone photoreceptors: after a photon has been counted, activated rhodopsin, transducin and phosphodiesterase 6 must all be quenched and cGMP restored so the CNG channels reopen and the cell can respond to the next photon. Without it photoreceptors cannot adapt to background light or recover sensitivity, and mutations in these components cause congenital stationary night blindness, Oguchi disease, cone dystrophies and Leber congenital amaurosis. Rhodopsin kinase phosphorylates the bleached pigment and arrestin caps it, with recoverin gating kinase activity as a calcium sensor; an RGS9 complex accelerates GTP hydrolysis on the transducin alpha subunit to silence PDE6; and calcium-sensitive guanylate cyclase activators drive GUCY2D to resynthesise cGMP. Lipid and terminal modifications of the subunits determine their membrane targeting and turnover.

After a rod or cone has responded to light, it must switch off and reset before it can report the next photon, and this shutoff-and-recovery arm of phototransduction is what makes vision fast, reproducible and able to adapt to background light. Activated rhodopsin is quenched by rhodopsin kinase phosphorylation followed by arrestin capping, with recoverin gating the kinase in a calcium-dependent way; the transducin-PDE6 complex is turned off by a GTPase-activating assembly of RGS9 with its membrane anchor and G-beta-5. Falling calcium through the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel releases guanylate cyclase activating proteins to stimulate retinal guanylate cyclase, restoring cGMP and reopening the channels. Lipid modification and N-terminal processing enzymes supply the myristoylation and farnesylation that hold these components at the disc membrane. Mutations in the cyclase, its activator, arrestin or PDE6 subunits cause stationary night blindness, cone dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa.

Interaction With Cumulus Cells And The Zona Pellucida covers the first physical encounter between a fertilizing sperm and the egg's protective coverings, the step that decides whether fertilization happens at all and whether it happens with a single sperm. The mammalian oocyte is wrapped in cumulus cells set in a hyaluronan-rich matrix and, beneath that, the zona pellucida built from the glycoproteins ZP1-ZP4. Sperm hyaluronidase (SPAM1) lets an acrosome-intact sperm penetrate the cumulus layer, after which ZP glycoproteins mediate species-restricted binding and trigger the acrosome reaction; ADAM family sperm surface proteins and the galactosyltransferase B4GALT1 contribute to adhesion, while oviductal glycoprotein OVGP1 modifies the zona in the reproductive tract. The same matrix blocks polyspermy and shields the early embryo until implantation. Defects in ZP genes cause empty follicle syndrome and female infertility.

Before a sperm can fuse with an egg it must cross two barriers, and this pathway covers those first encounters: passage through the hyaluronan-rich cumulus cell layer and binding to the zona pellucida. The zona is built from four glycoproteins, ZP1-ZP4, which mediate species-specific sperm recognition, trigger the acrosome reaction in bound sperm, block fertilization by more than one sperm, and shield the cleaving embryo until implantation. A hyaluronidase on the sperm surface, SPAM1, digests the cumulus matrix, while ADAM-family sperm proteins and glycan-modifying enzymes such as B4GALT1 and the oviduct-secreted glycoprotein OVGP1 shape adhesive recognition between the gametes. Mutations in the zona genes cause empty follicle and zona-defect infertility in women, and these same molecules are the basis of immunocontraceptive strategies and of diagnostic sperm-binding assays.

The metaphase and anaphase stages of mitosis are where a cell commits to dividing its duplicated genome equally, and errors here produce aneuploid daughter cells, a hallmark of tumours and of congenital chromosomal disorders. Chromosomes align on the metaphase plate through kinetochores built on centromeric chromatin marked by the CENPA nucleosome, attached to spindle microtubules by the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes and tracked by motors and plus-end regulators. Until every kinetochore is properly attached, the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1, ZW10/ZWILCH) restrains the anaphase-promoting complex. Once satisfied, the APC/C with CDC20 directs ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction of securin and mitotic cyclins, freeing separase to cleave cohesin and allowing sister chromatids to move apart. The same transition drives nuclear envelope and nuclear pore reassembly, with lamins, LEM-domain proteins and ESCRT-III components sealing the new nuclei.

Reactive oxygen species, whether generated by mitochondrial dysfunction downstream of oncogenic RAS or by prolonged interferon-beta exposure, can push a cell into an irreversible proliferative arrest, and oxidative stress induced senescence is the route by which that happens. It is a tumour-suppressive barrier: cells that sustain oxidative damage withdraw permanently from the cycle rather than propagate it, at the cost of accumulating senescent cells in ageing tissue. Oxidised thioredoxin releases MAP3K5 (ASK1), which activates the MKK3/MKK6-p38 and MKK4/MKK7-JNK arms; p38 substrates MAPKAPK2/3 and MAPKAPK5 phosphorylate BMI1 and p53 respectively, while JNK-driven AP-1 induces the H3K27me3 demethylase KDM6B. Both converge on de-repression of the CDKN2A locus by evicting Polycomb complexes, raising p16INK4A to block CDK4/6-mediated RB inactivation and p14ARF to stabilise p53 against MDM2.

Cells that have permanently exited the cell cycle do not fall silent; they secrete a program of cytokines, chemokines and growth-factor binding proteins known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. This secretome reinforces the arrest in the cell that makes it, recruits immune cells to clear damaged cells, and—when it persists—drives chronic inflammation, tissue ageing, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and growth of neighbouring premalignant cells. Here the transcriptional control is the focus. DNA damage signalling raises CDKN1A, which restrains CDK2 and leaves the APC/C ubiquitin ligase with its FZR1 activator competent to degrade the histone methyltransferases EHMT1 and EHMT2, de-repressing the silenced IL6 and CXCL8 promoters. Oncogenic RAS–MAPK signalling activates CEBPB, which cooperates with NF-kappa-B subunits at the same promoters, while IL6–STAT3 and IL1A feed back to sustain output. AP-1 components FOS and JUN drive IL1A and IGFBP7, and INK4/CIP-family inhibitors lock in the arrest.

Cellular Senescence is the permanent exit from the cell cycle that a cell adopts when it sustains DNA damage, exhausts its telomeres, or experiences oncogene activation, and it is one of the body's main barriers to tumour formation. Senescent cells accumulate with age and drive tissue decline through the inflammatory secretome they release. The genes trace the routes in: telomere capping by the shelterin complex and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN sensor feeding ATM to p53, and the p16/p21 inhibitors that shut down CDK4/6 and CDK2 to keep RB1 bound to E2F. Downstream, HIRA and ASF1A restructure chromatin into heterochromatic foci while Polycomb complexes and EZH2 silence proliferative genes, and stress kinase signalling through p38 with NF-kB and CEBPB switches on the secretory programme of IL6, IL1A and CXCL8 that reinforces arrest and alters neighbouring cells.

Cellular senescence is the permanent withdrawal of a damaged or oncogene-stressed cell from the division cycle, a barrier against tumour formation that also drives tissue ageing as senescent cells accumulate. Triggers converge on two arrest circuits: the p53-p21 axis engaged by DNA damage sensing through ATM and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and by telomere uncapping when shelterin components such as TRF1, TRF2 and POT1 are lost, and the p16/p15-RB axis that keeps CDK4/6-cyclin D and E2F targets silenced. Chromatin is remodelled into senescence-associated heterochromatic foci with HIRA-ASF1A histone chaperoning, Polycomb repressors and lamin B1 loss, while stress-activated p38 and JNK kinases with NF-kB, CEBPB and STAT3 drive the senescence-associated secretory phenotype -- IL6, IL1A and IL8 among them -- which reinforces arrest locally and can promote inflammation and invasiveness in neighbouring cells.

Formation of Senescence-Associated Heterochromatin Foci (SAHF) is the chromatin remodelling step that makes cellular senescence permanent. When DNA damage or telomere attrition forces a cell out of the cycle, each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin that silences proliferation-promoting genes, so the arrest cannot be reversed by growth signals; this is a barrier to tumourigenesis and a feature of ageing tissue. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 first accumulates in PML nuclear bodies, then relocates to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and macroH2A while H3K9 methylation and HP1 mark the compacted domains. HMGA proteins and linker histone H1 redistribution drive the architectural change, and loss of lamin B1 accompanies it. Focus formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, linking it to CDKN1A-mediated cell cycle exit.

Cells that have sustained irreparable DNA damage or critically short telomeres exit the cell cycle for good, and the assembly of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci is how that exit is made permanent. Each chromosome condenses into a single punctate focus of facultative heterochromatin bearing H3K9 methylation, with telomeric and centromeric regions pushed to the periphery, and proliferation-promoting genes driven by E2F are locked in a silent state. A conserved histone chaperone complex of HIRA, ASF1A, UBN1 and CABIN1 stages at PML nuclear bodies before relocating to the forming foci, depositing histone H3.3 and remodelling chromatin; linker H1 variants, HMGA proteins and loss of lamin B1 accompany the structural reorganisation. Formation depends on intact RB1 and TP53 signalling, with CDKN1A enforcing the arrest. This chromatin endpoint underlies tumour suppression by senescence and contributes to the altered nuclear architecture of aged tissue.

Cells that acquire a strong oncogenic signal, typically hyperactive RAS/RAF/ERK output or unrestrained E2F activity following loss of RB1, respond by permanently withdrawing from the cell cycle rather than proliferating. This oncogene-induced senescence is one of the body's first barriers to tumour formation, and its failure allows an initiating mutation to expand into a growing lesion. The response converges on the CDKN2A locus, whose two distinct products enforce arrest by separate routes: p16INK4A blocks CDK4 and CDK6 so RB1 stays hypophosphorylated and E2F target genes remain silent, while p14ARF destabilises MDM2 and thereby stabilises TP53 and its arrest programme. ERK-phosphorylated ETS1 and ETS2 drive p16INK4A transcription, ID1 opposes them, and related inhibitors including p15INK4B contribute. A microRNA-24/Argonaute arm sets a translational ceiling on both transcripts, tuning how readily cells commit to arrest.

Cells that have sustained irreparable double-strand breaks, or whose telomeres have eroded through replicative exhaustion, exit the cell cycle permanently rather than risk propagating damage, and this DNA damage and telomere stress induced senescence is the route by which they do it. It is a barrier to tumourigenesis and, accumulating with age, a source of tissue dysfunction. Critically short telomeres lose their shelterin cap — TERF1, TERF2, POT1, TINF2 and their partners — and are read as broken DNA by the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex, which recruits and activates ATM. ATM phosphorylates TP53, which transactivates CDKN1A to inhibit CDK2–cyclin E and enforce G1/S arrest alongside RB1. The many histones, linker H1 variants, HMGA proteins, lamin B1, the HIRA–UBN1–ASF1A chaperone complex and the KAT5 acetyltransferase reflect the accompanying chromatin reorganisation that locks the arrest in place.

Toll-like receptors 3 and 4 do more than switch on inflammatory transcription: through the adaptor TRIF they can also commit an infected or stressed cell to die. This gives innate immunity a way to eliminate cells harbouring viruses or responding to bacterial lipopolysaccharide, and it shapes how much tissue damage accompanies infection. TRIF (TICAM1), assisted at the receptor by TICAM2, CD14 and the LPS co-receptor MD-2, recruits RIPK1 and the FADD-caspase-8 module, so that receptor engagement feeds into the same death-inducing complex used by TNF and Fas. Active caspase-8 drives apoptosis; when its activity is lost or blocked, signalling is diverted to RIPK3-dependent necroptosis, a lytic and strongly pro-inflammatory outcome. The reciprocal suppression of these two programmed cell death routes determines which form of death follows TRIF-mediated signalling.

Many cytosolic and nuclear enzymes need a 4Fe-4S cofactor to work, and cytosolic iron-sulfur cluster assembly is the route by which those clusters are built outside the mitochondrion and delivered to them. Its clients are heavily weighted toward genome maintenance: the DNA polymerase catalytic subunit POLD1, the nucleotide excision repair helicase ERCC2/XPD, and the helicases BRIP1 and RTEL1 all depend on it, so loss of the pathway produces replication stress, defective repair and genome instability. Clusters are assembled on a scaffold formed by the NUBP1-NUBP2 pair, with electrons supplied through a diflavin reductase and CIAPIN1, then handed to apoproteins by a targeting complex built around CIAO1, MMS19 and CIAO2B. The process remains tied to mitochondria, which export a sulfur-containing intermediate through the transporter ABCB7; failure of that step underlies sideroblastic anaemia with ataxia.

Regulation of PLK1 Activity at G2/M Transition governs the switch that commits a cell to mitosis, setting the moment at which centrosomes mature, spindle assembly begins, and the nuclear envelope breaks down. PLK1 must be turned on at the right time and place and then turned off again; failure of this timing produces spindle defects, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and PLK1 is a target of anti-mitotic cancer drugs. Aurora A, activated on centrosomes with the help of AJUBA, phosphorylates PLK1 on T210 in a reaction requiring BORA, which PLK1 then marks for SCF/beta-TrCP-mediated destruction so that other substrates can be engaged. A negative feedback arm runs through optineurin, released from RAB8-positive Golgi membranes, which promotes activation of MYPT1-containing myosin phosphatase to dephosphorylate T210. The accompanying centrosomal, gamma-tubulin, augmin and dynein components are the machinery this control acts upon.

Entry into mitosis depends on switching on PLK1, the kinase that ripens centrosomes, drives mitotic entry and later governs cytokinesis, and this pathway describes how its activity is turned on and off at the G2/M transition. Aurora A kinase, itself activated by AJUBA-assisted autophosphorylation at the centrosome, phosphorylates PLK1 on Thr210 with BORA as a cofactor; active PLK1 then phosphorylates BORA to mark it for SCF/beta-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination and destruction, freeing the kinase for its mitotic substrates. A negative-feedback limb runs through optineurin, which leaves Golgi-associated RAB8 for the nucleus and promotes myosin phosphatase activation, dephosphorylating Thr210 to shut PLK1 down. The accompanying centriolar, gamma-tubulin, augmin and dynein components place this control on the maturing centrosome and spindle poles. Deregulation couples centrosome amplification and chromosome missegregation to tumorigenesis, and PLK1 is a drug target.

Leptin is the adipocyte-derived hormone that reports the size of the body's fat stores to the brain, and signalling through its receptor sets food intake, energy expenditure and neuroendocrine function accordingly. Loss of either the hormone or the receptor produces severe early-onset obesity and hyperphagia, while common obesity is marked instead by resistance to the signal; the same axis modulates immune cell activity, angiogenesis and tumour growth. The receptor has no intrinsic kinase activity and is constitutively associated with JAK2, which autophosphorylates on ligand binding and phosphorylates receptor tyrosines. These recruit STAT3 and STAT5, which dimerise and drive transcription, and the phosphatase-adaptor PTPN11, which feeds the MAPK route; SH2B1 couples JAK2 to IRS1/IRS2 and PI3K/AKT. Induced SOCS3 terminates the response.}

Truncating mutations that remove the C-terminal PEST degron of NOTCH1 turn a normally self-limiting developmental signal into a persistent oncogenic one, and they are among the most common lesions in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Normally, ligands such as DLL1, DLL4 and JAG1 on a neighbouring cell trigger sequential cleavage by ADAM proteases and the presenilin-containing gamma-secretase complex, releasing the intracellular domain NICD1, which enters the nucleus, binds RBPJ with a MAML coactivator and displaces NCOR/HDAC corepressors to switch on HES, HEY and MYC transcription. The SCF ubiquitin ligase using the substrate receptor FBXW7 then recognises the phosphorylated PEST region and targets NICD1 for proteasomal destruction. PEST-domain mutants escape this step, so NICD1 accumulates and drives sustained proliferative transcription, explaining why such tumours are sensitive to gamma-secretase inhibition.

NOTCH1 is a cell-surface receptor that converts contact with a neighbouring cell into a transcriptional response, and in cancer that response becomes self-sustaining. Oncogenic NOTCH1 mutations occur in the majority of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemias, either in the heterodimerization domain, which allows the intracellular domain to be released without ligand, or in the C-terminal PEST domain, which escapes destruction and so accumulates; loss of the ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor FBXW7 has the same effect and is found in the alternative genotype. Normally, DLL and JAG ligands on adjacent cells trigger ADAM10/17 and gamma-secretase cleavage, freeing an intracellular fragment that partners RBPJ and MAML coactivators to switch corepressor complexes for acetyltransferases at target genes such as HES, HEY and MYC. Persistent output drives proliferation and survival of immature T lymphocytes, making this signalling an oncogenic driver rather than a developmental cue.

Activated NOTCH1 must be destroyed on a short timescale for its transcriptional output to stay pulsatile, and the ubiquitin ligase FBXW7 is the substrate receptor that does it. Working as the recognition subunit of an SCF complex with SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1, FBXW7 binds phosphorylated degrons in the C-terminal PEST region of the NOTCH1 intracellular domain and marks it for proteasomal degradation. Loss-of-function mutations in FBXW7 remove that timer, so cleaved NOTCH1 persists and drives its proliferative target genes continuously. This is a recurrent lesion in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where it is largely mutually exclusive with truncating PEST-domain mutations in NOTCH1 itself two routes to the same stabilised oncoprotein. The pathway illustrates how oncogenic signalling can arise from failed protein turnover rather than altered ligand or receptor activity, and it links tumour suppressor function to controlled proteolysis.

Truncating mutations that remove the NOTCH1 PEST domain leave ligand binding and proteolytic activation intact but make the released intracellular fragment abnormally stable, so the receptor signals constitutively. Normally, after Delta- and Jagged-family ligands trigger cleavage by ADAM proteases and the gamma-secretase complex, the liberated NICD1 enters the nucleus, converts RBPJ from a repressor into an activator with Mastermind-like coactivators and acetyltransferases, and induces HES and HEY genes plus MYC before being phosphorylated and marked by the FBXW7-SKP1-CUL1 ubiquitin ligase for proteasomal destruction. Loss of the PEST degron blocks that turnover, prolonging target gene transcription. Because the pathway sets thymocyte fate and proliferative drive, such mutants are recurrent drivers of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, illustrating how signal termination rather than initiation can be the step that fails in cancer.

FBXW7 is the substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF ubiquitin ligase, and its loss of function in cancer removes the timer that limits NOTCH1 signalling. Normally, once the NOTCH1 intracellular domain has activated its target genes, CDK8 phosphorylates a degron in the PEST domain; FBXW7 binds that phosphodegron and, with SKP1, CUL1 and the RING protein RBX1, ubiquitinates the domain for proteasomal destruction. Missense mutations in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia hit conserved arginines in the WD40 substrate-binding pocket that contact the phosphothreonine, acting dominant-negatively so that the complex assembles but cannot engage its substrate. The intracellular domain then persists and drives transcription of proliferative NOTCH targets well beyond its usual short half-life. This places regulated proteolysis at the centre of how a developmental signal is kept transient, and explains why a ubiquitin ligase behaves as a tumour suppressor in T-cell leukemia.

Cholinergic neurons signal by loading acetylcholine into synaptic vesicles and releasing it in response to action potentials, and this release cycle supports neuromuscular transmission, autonomic ganglionic signalling, and attention, arousal and memory circuits in the brain. Choline is taken up by a high-affinity transporter, acetylated by choline acetyltransferase, and concentrated into vesicles by a vesicular acetylcholine transporter; the loaded vesicles are then tethered at the active zone and primed by scaffolding and priming factors including RIMS1, UNC13B and the liprins. Calcium entry is sensed by synaptotagmin, which triggers fusion through the SNARE proteins SNAP25, syntaxin-1A and VAMP2 under the control of complexin and STXBP1. Loss of choline supply or of the fusion machinery produces myasthenic weakness and epileptic encephalopathies, and degeneration of these neurons is a feature of Alzheimer disease.

The rounding, blebbing and detachment that mark a dying cell come largely from executioner caspases dismantling the cytoskeleton, and this branch of apoptosis accounts for those morphological changes. Once CASP8 activates the effector caspases CASP3, CASP6 and CASP7, they cleave structural and linker proteins rather than signalling molecules: the spectrin-actin cortex is broken by cutting alpha-spectrin (SPTAN1) and adducin (ADD1), gelsolin is cleaved to a fragment that severs actin filaments constitutively, and the intermediate filament and cross-linking scaffold is degraded through vimentin, plectin and GAS2. Cleavage of the microtubule-associated protein tau and of the actin-binding adaptor DBNL extends the same logic to neuronal and membrane-associated structures. The result is irreversible loss of cell shape and adhesion, packaging the cell for phagocytosis, and the cleavage fragments generated here are widely used as markers of apoptotic execution.

Insulin processing is the route by which a pancreatic beta cell converts newly made preproinsulin into crystalline, secretion-ready insulin granules poised beneath the plasma membrane. It defines the secretory identity of the beta cell, and defects in it produce hyperproinsulinaemia and diabetes. In the endoplasmic reticulum, P4HB and ERO1B install three disulfide bonds in proinsulin; the folded hormone traffics to the Golgi and complexes with zinc, supplied by the granule transporter SLC30A8, and calcium. Within immature granules the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 cleave proinsulin at two sites and carboxypeptidase E trims the ends, releasing mature insulin and C-peptide. Kinesin-1 motors move granules along microtubules and myosin Va with RAB27A and MYRIP carry them through cortical actin, after which the exocyst tethers them and syntaxin-1A with VAMP2 drives calcium-triggered fusion.

Pancreatic beta cells make insulin as an inactive precursor, and insulin processing is the sequence of folding, cleavage and packaging that converts preproinsulin into the mature hormone held ready for release. Without it, glucose cannot be cleared after a meal, and defects in the granule machinery contribute to diabetes. In the endoplasmic reticulum, disulfide bond formation assisted by protein disulfide isomerase (P4HB) and the oxidase ERO1B produces correctly folded proinsulin, which travels to the Golgi and complexes with zinc supplied by transporters such as SLC30A8. Within immature granules, the prohormone convertases PCSK1 and PCSK2 cut proinsulin and carboxypeptidase E trims the ends, liberating insulin and C-peptide, which crystallise with zinc and calcium. Kinesins and myosin Va, with RAB27A and MYRIP, move granules to the cell cortex, where exocyst components dock them and SNAREs including STX1A and VAMP2 drive calcium-triggered exocytosis.

A rare chromosomal translocation in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia fuses the NOTCH1 locus to T-cell receptor beta regulatory sequences, placing a truncated receptor beginning near residue M1580 under lymphoid transcriptional control. The resulting protein lacks most of the extracellular ligand-binding region but retains the transmembrane and intracellular portions, so it is constitutively poised for cleavage and nuclear signalling; overexpression of this mutant drives a leukaemia-like disease in mice, and normal NOTCH1 signalling is otherwise what specifies T-cell fate in the thymus. Signalling still proceeds through the canonical steps represented here: ligands of the Delta-like and Jagged families presented by neighbouring cells, ectodomain shedding by the metalloproteases ADAM10 and ADAM17, and subsequent intramembrane proteolysis releasing the intracellular domain to activate transcription. The pathway links cell-contact-dependent developmental signalling to oncogenic transformation of thymocytes.

A rare chromosomal translocation in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia fuses part of the NOTCH1 gene to the T-cell receptor beta promoter, driving expression in T cells and their precursors of a truncated receptor that begins at residue 1580 and has lost nearly the whole extracellular region. Because the EGF and LIN12 repeats that normally engage DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 and JAG2 are gone, the protein cannot bind ligand, yet its cleavage sites are permanently exposed: ADAM10 or ADAM17 and then gamma-secretase process it without any signal, releasing the NOTCH1 intracellular domain, which accumulates in the nucleus and switches on target genes of T lymphocyte development. This uncouples a developmental decision from the cell contacts that should license it, and retroviral expression of similar truncations in mouse bone marrow produces T-ALL-like disease, making the lesion an oncogenic driver rather than a passenger.

Stimuli-sensing channels covers the ion channels that convert physical and chemical stimuli — heat, cold, acid, mechanical pressure, taste, light-driven signals — into electrical and calcium signals a cell can act on. They define sensory neurons and taste cells, set thresholds for pain and itch, and their mutation causes inherited pain syndromes, retinal degeneration, muscle disease and epithelial transport disorders. TRP family members act as polymodal detectors of temperature, capsaicin, menthol and osmotic stress, while acid-sensing channels report tissue acidification during inflammation and ischaemia. A second theme is calcium itself as the stimulus: ryanodine receptors with triadin and calsequestrin release stores for muscle contraction, and bestrophins, anoctamins and tweety homologs open calcium-activated chloride currents. Epithelial sodium channels under WNK and SGK control, chloride channels and mucolipins extend the same logic to salt handling, endolysosomal function and, through RIPK3–MLKL, membrane permeabilisation during necroptosis.

Sensation begins at the membrane, where stimuli-sensing channels convert heat, cold, acid, mechanical force, irritant chemicals, taste and light-driven signals into ionic current. TRP channels dominate this repertoire: TRPV1 responds to capsaicin and noxious heat, TRPM8 to cold and menthol, TRPA1 to reactive irritants, and TRPM5 supports taste transduction, while TRPV5/TRPV6 and TRPM6/TRPM7 handle epithelial calcium and magnesium uptake. Acid-sensing channels detect extracellular protons during inflammation and ischaemia, contributing to pain. Calcium-gated and calcium-permeable components broaden the theme, including bestrophins and anoctamins as anion channels, ryanodine receptors releasing store calcium with calsequestrin and triadin, and endolysosomal mucolipins and two-pore channels. Chloride channels, ENaC subunits with their WNK, SGK and NEDD4L regulators, and NALCN set epithelial transport and background excitability. Mutations cause pain syndromes, retinal and renal disease, and myopathies.

Cells find their correct positions in a developing embryo largely by touching their neighbours, and EPH-ephrin signaling is the contact-dependent system that turns those touches into movement or repulsion. It guides axons to their targets, sets boundaries between tissue compartments, patterns blood vessels and bone, and in the nervous system tunes dendritic spine formation and elimination during synaptic maturation and plasticity. Because both receptor tyrosine kinases and their GPI-anchored or transmembrane ephrin ligands sit in the membrane, signals travel in both directions, forward into the receptor-bearing cell and in reverse into the ligand-bearing one. Downstream, Src-family kinases and guanine nucleotide exchange factors switch RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 to reshape actin through ARP2/3, cofilin, LIM kinases, ROCK and myosin II, while metalloproteinase and gamma-secretase cleavage plus clathrin-mediated endocytosis terminate adhesion so contacting cells can separate. Misregulation contributes to tumour invasion and defective neural wiring.

NOTCH1's heterodimerization domain holds the receptor's two subunits together after furin cleavage and keeps the proteolytic cascade locked until a ligand pulls the negative regulatory region open. Mutations in this domain, common in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, destabilize that interface so the receptor is cleaved and signals without proper ligand control, driving the transcriptional programme that expands immature T-cell progenitors. The steps represented here are the ones such mutants exploit: DLL and JAG ligands on the sending cell, their ubiquitination by MIB and NEURL E3 ligases together with ubiquitin precursors, and the ADAM10/ADAM17 metalloproteases that make the S2 cut releasing the membrane-tethered fragment for subsequent intramembrane cleavage. Because signalling becomes ligand-independent yet still requires proteolysis, this biology underlies both the leukemogenic effect of these alleles and the rationale for targeting the cleavage machinery therapeutically.

Notch signalling normally requires a ligand on a neighbouring cell to pull the receptor apart and expose it to proteolysis, and the heterodimerization domain is what holds the extracellular and transmembrane halves together until then. Leukemia-associated mutations in that domain loosen the association so that cleavage by ADAM10 or ADAM17 and subsequent gamma-secretase processing release the intracellular domain spontaneously, without DLL or JAG engagement, giving continuous transcriptional output. This constitutive signalling by HD domain mutants is a common driver of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where sustained Notch activity keeps thymocyte progenitors proliferating and blocks normal differentiation. The mutant receptors remain ligand-responsive, so canonical components are retained here: DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 and JAG2 ligands, the ubiquitin ligases MIB1, MIB2 and NEURL1 that license ligand activity, and ubiquitin itself. Pharmacological blockade of the proteolytic steps is the therapeutic handle.

Mast cells release histamine and other mediators when IgE bound to the high-affinity receptor FcERI is cross-linked by allergen, and the transmembrane adaptor LAT2 (also called NTAL or LAB) tunes how much calcium enters during that response. The pathway matters because the size of the calcium signal sets the extent of degranulation and cytokine output, and therefore the intensity of allergic and anaphylactic reactions. IgE heavy and light chain variable regions bind antigen and engage the receptor's alpha and beta subunits together with the signalling gamma chain; the Src-family kinases LYN and FYN and the tyrosine kinase SYK then phosphorylate raft-resident LAT2, which recruits GRB2 and GAB2 and activates class IA PI3K to generate the lipids that drive store release and influx. LAT2 acts both cooperatively with and in opposition to the related adaptor LAT, giving it a dual positive and negative influence on mast cell activation.

Recognition of microbes by the innate immune system begins with pattern-binding proteins in plasma, and ficolins are the arm of this surveillance that reads repetitive carbohydrate and acetylated patterns on pathogen and apoptotic cell surfaces to trigger the lectin pathway of complement. Humans have three: M-ficolin, secreted locally by monocytes and neutrophils, and L- and H-ficolin, which circulate in blood. Each assembles into trimers and larger oligomers built from a collagen-like stalk and a C-terminal fibrinogen-like recognition domain, and circulates in complex with the MBL-associated serine proteases MASP1 and MASP2. Target binding activates these proteases, which cleave C4 and C2 to build a C3 convertase, leading to opsonization, inflammation and clearance of dying cells. Deficiency, particularly of H-ficolin, predisposes to recurrent bacterial infection in newborns and immunocompromised patients.

When IgE bound to the high-affinity Fc epsilon receptor on mast cells and basophils is cross-linked by allergen, one arm of the response produces cytokines rather than immediate granule release, and MAPK activation downstream of this receptor is that arm. It sustains the late phase of allergic inflammation in asthma, urticaria and anaphylaxis, so blocking IgE engagement of the receptor damps it. Receptor aggregation activates the SYK and LYN kinases, which phosphorylate the transmembrane adaptor LAT and recruit GRB2, SLP-76 and phospholipase C gamma; the exchange factors SOS1 and VAV load GTP onto RAS and RAC. RAS drives the RAF-ERK cascade to ERK1 and ERK2, while RAC and MAP3K1 feed the JNK branch through MAP2K4 and MAP2K7, converging on FOS and JUN to switch on inflammatory gene transcription.

Allergic reactions begin when IgE bound to its high-affinity receptor on mast cells and basophils is cross-linked by antigen, and the calcium signal that follows is what actually triggers granule release of histamine and other mediators. Calcium mobilization downstream of the IgE receptor therefore sits at the heart of immediate hypersensitivity, anaphylaxis, asthma and urticaria. Receptor subunits, including the IgE-binding alpha chain and the signalling gamma and beta chains, recruit the kinases LYN and SYK, which with adaptors such as LAT and LCP2 and the Tec-family kinase BTK activate phospholipase C-gamma1 and -gamma2. These cleave PIP2 to generate IP3 and DAG; IP3 opens the ITPR1-3 channels of the endoplasmic reticulum, and the ensuing sustained rise in cytosolic calcium both drives degranulation and activates calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT family factors so they enter the nucleus and switch on cytokine genes.

Cross-linking of the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells and basophils by allergen-bound IgE drives transcription of proinflammatory cytokines, and this arm of the response routes that signal to NF-kB. It is the branch that sustains allergic inflammation beyond the immediate degranulation burst, underlying asthma, atopic dermatitis and anaphylactic tissue responses. Receptor subunits including FCER1A and the signalling chains FCER1G and MS4A2 engage LYN, and diacylglycerol together with rising calcium recruits PKC-theta and RasGRP guanine nucleotide exchange factors. PKC-theta assembles the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 complex, which through TRAF6 and TAK1 with its TAB partners activates the IKK complex. Phosphorylated IkB-alpha is then ubiquitinated by an SCF-betaTrCP ligase and destroyed by the proteasome, freeing NFKB1-RELA dimers to enter the nucleus. The large complement of immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable segments reflects the IgE ligand that initiates the cascade.

Pluripotent stem cells stay pluripotent partly by actively silencing the transcription factors that would commit them to a germ layer, and this repressive arm of the OCT4-SOX2-NANOG core network is how that silencing is imposed. The three factors co-occupy hundreds of promoters in human embryonic stem cells, activating the self-renewal programme at some and shutting down lineage specifiers at others; the targets here belong to the repressed class. Among them are drivers of trophectoderm and extraembryonic fate such as CDX2 and GATA6, mesendoderm and primitive streak regulators including EOMES and GSC, endoderm-associated HHEX, and the WNT antagonist DKK1. Loss of this repression, or withdrawal of the factors themselves, releases differentiation into definitive endoderm, mesoderm or trophoblast, which is why the network is central to embryonic development and to reprogramming somatic cells to induced pluripotency.

Human embryonic stem cells stay undifferentiated and keep dividing because a small core of transcription factors continuously reinforces its own expression and switches on growth-promoting targets. In this arm of that network, OCT4 (POU5F1), SOX2 and NANOG co-occupy promoters and activate a proliferation-associated programme, while repressing differentiation genes through separate targets. The activated set includes the factors' own genes, forming interlocking positive feedback, along with the TGF-beta/nodal co-receptor CRIPTO, the growth factor FGF2 that supports self-renewal in culture, STAT3, and the pluripotency-associated regulators SALL4, ZIC3, FOXD3, DPPA4 and NR6A1. Loss of any core member collapses the state and pushes cells toward lineage commitment, which is why these same factors are the reprogramming tools used to generate induced pluripotent stem cells, and why their reactivation in somatic tissue is associated with tumour stem-cell phenotypes.

NOTCH1 alleles carrying mutations in both the heterodimerization and PEST domains drive oncogenic Notch signalling, most notably in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where the two lesions occur on the same allele and combine to raise transcriptional output far beyond either alone. HD mutations destabilize the negative regulatory region so the receptor is cleaved by ADAM proteases and gamma-secretase without ligand engagement, while PEST truncations remove the degron recognized by the SCF-FBXW7 ubiquitin ligase, so the released intracellular domain persists. Accumulated NOTCH1 assembles with RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators, displaces NCOR-HDAC corepressors, and recruits p300/CBP and the CDK8 module to activate HES and HEY repressors together with MYC, sustaining proliferation of immature T cells. This explains why gamma-secretase inhibition and FBXW7 status matter therapeutically in Notch-driven leukemia.

Oncogenic NOTCH1 alleles that combine a heterodimerization-domain mutation with a truncating PEST-domain lesion drive ligand-independent, unusually durable Notch output, and their combination in cis is the classic genetic lesion of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. The two defects attack opposite ends of the receptor's life cycle: destabilizing the heterodimerization domain permits spontaneous metalloprotease and gamma-secretase cleavage and release of the intracellular fragment without a DLL or JAG ligand, while loss of the PEST degron blocks FBXW7-directed ubiquitination by the SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 complex, so the released fragment persists. The stabilized fragment assembles with RBPJ and a MAML coactivator and recruits acetyltransferases such as CREBBP and EP300 in place of NCOR-HDAC corepressors, sustaining transcription of HES and HEY repressors and MYC. The result is continuous proliferative signalling in immature T cells, and the pathway underpins the rationale for gamma-secretase inhibition in leukaemia.

Abnormal conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to 2-hydroxyglutarate describes the neomorphic activity acquired by isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 when its arginine 132 residue is mutated, an event found in the majority of low-grade gliomas and secondary glioblastomas as well as in other cancers. The normal cytosolic enzyme oxidizes isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while generating NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence; the mutant instead consumes NADPH to reduce 2-oxoglutarate to the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate, which accumulates to millimolar levels. Because 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including the TET DNA demethylases, JmjC histone demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, the metabolic lesion is transmitted to the epigenome, producing the hypermethylation phenotype and blocked differentiation characteristic of these tumours. This links central carbon metabolism directly to chromatin state, and makes the mutant enzyme a tractable drug target.

Cancer-associated mutations at arginine 132 of the cytosolic isocitrate dehydrogenase IDH1 convert a routine metabolic step into the production of an oncometabolite. Wild-type IDH1 oxidatively decarboxylates isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+, supplying both a citric acid cycle intermediate and cytosolic NADPH for redox defence and lipid synthesis. The mutant enzyme instead reduces 2-oxoglutarate using NADPH to give 2-hydroxyglutarate, which builds up to millimolar levels in the cytosol. Because 2-hydroxyglutarate closely resembles 2-oxoglutarate, it competitively inhibits dioxygenases that depend on it, including histone and DNA demethylases and prolyl hydroxylases, producing the hypermethylated, differentiation-blocked state characteristic of IDH1-mutant tumours. The alteration is frequent in gliomas and glioblastomas and also occurs in acute myeloid leukaemia, and it serves both as a diagnostic marker and as a drug target for mutant-selective inhibitors.

Contact between neighbouring cells is converted into a transcriptional decision when NOTCH2 meets a Delta-like or Jagged ligand presented on the surface of an adjacent cell. This is one of the receptor-specific branches of Notch signalling, and it governs cell fate choices in liver bile duct formation, marginal zone B cell development, bone remodelling and vascular smooth muscle; loss of JAG1-NOTCH2 signalling underlies Alagille syndrome, and truncating NOTCH2 mutations cause Hajdu-Cheney syndrome. Ligand engagement, reinforced by E3 ubiquitin ligases such as MIB1 and Neuralized that ubiquitinate the ligand and drive its endocytosis, exposes the receptor to ADAM10 cleavage at S2 and then to the gamma-secretase complex of presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN at S3. The freed intracellular domain NICD2 moves to the nucleus to regulate transcription. Contactin 1 and midkine are reported non-canonical activators.

Peptide hormones are made as inactive precursors and only become signals after regulated cutting, modification, packaging and, eventually, destruction; this metabolism sets how much active hormone reaches a target tissue. Precursors such as proinsulin, proopiomelanocortin, proglucagon, progastrin-releasing peptide and proghrelin enter the secretory pathway, are cleaved by the granule endoproteases PCSK1 and PCSK2 with carboxypeptidase E trimming, and are stored in granules whose zinc supply and exocyst-, kinesin-, Rab27/myosin-Va- and syntaxin/VAMP-dependent transport deliver them to the surface. Ghrelin additionally requires octanoylation by MBOAT4 and is deacylated in blood by butyrylcholinesterase. Extracellular peptidases then shape activity: renin and ACE generate angiotensin II to drive vasoconstriction, sodium retention and aldosterone release, ACE2 and neprilysin produce alternative fragments, and DPP4 inactivates the incretins GLP-1 and GIP. Glycoprotein hormone subunits and lineage factors such as PAX6 and ISL1 link this biology to endocrine cell identity, diabetes and blood pressure control.

Before a cell can divide its chromosomes, it must dismantle the membrane that keeps them separate from the cytoplasm. Nuclear envelope breakdown in late prophase disassembles nuclear pore complexes, depolymerises the lamina, and strips membrane away from chromatin, giving spindle microtubules access to kinetochores so that the genome can be partitioned into two daughter cells. Mitotic kinases drive it: the CDK1-cyclin B complex together with PLK1 and the NEK family phosphorylate nucleoporins such as NUP98, NUP53 and the NUP107 scaffold to dissolve the pore, while lamins A/C and B1 are phosphorylated and depolymerise. Chromatin is released when VRK1 phosphorylates BANF1, weakening its bridging of DNA to LEM-domain inner membrane proteins including emerin, LEMD2 and LAP2. Lipin phosphatases and CTDNEP1 tune membrane lipid composition for envelope remodelling, and the whole process reverses at mitotic exit to rebuild two nuclei.

Entry into mitosis requires a relay of kinase activations that prepare the centrosomes and spindle, and this NIMA-family branch supplies part of it. NEK9 sits at the head of the cascade: mitotic CDK1 paired with cyclin B phosphorylates it, PLK1 adds further phosphorylation, and activated NEK9 then phosphorylates and switches on the smaller kinases NEK6 and NEK7. Their downstream work supports centrosome separation, bipolar spindle assembly and progression through mitosis, so loss or misregulation produces spindle defects and chromosome missegregation, a route to aneuploidy. The arrangement makes these kinases effectors that convert the master mitotic signals of CDK1 and PLK1 into localized spindle-building activity, and places them within the broader control of the G2/M transition and cell division rather than in interphase signalling.

SUMOylation is a reversible post-translational modification in which small ubiquitin-like modifier proteins are attached to lysine residues of target proteins, changing their partners, localisation and stability rather than marking them for destruction. Because most substrates are nuclear, the main consequences are for gene expression, chromatin state, DNA repair and chromosome segregation. Precursor SUMO is matured by SENP proteases, activated by the SAE1-UBA2 E1 complex, passed to the single E2 enzyme UBE2I, and conjugated with help from E3 ligases such as the PIAS proteins, RANBP2 and TOPORS; SENP enzymes also remove or trim the modification, and SUMO2/3 chains create binding sites for proteins with SUMO-interaction motifs. Substrates here include nuclear receptors and their coregulators, Polycomb components, DNA repair factors, topoisomerases, cohesin and the SMC5/6 complex, PML and p53, and much of the nuclear pore. Disrupted SUMO cycling perturbs genome stability and transcriptional control.

At the end of mitosis each daughter cell must rebuild a single intact nucleus around its chromosomes, and this is the step that starts that process. In late anaphase and telophase the small DNA-bridging protein BANF1 coats the coalescing chromosome mass, cross-linking DNA so that separate chromosomes are gathered into one compartment rather than several micronuclei; failure here produces fragmented nuclei and the genome instability that follows. BANF1 recruits LEM-domain inner nuclear membrane proteins such as emerin, LAP2beta, LEM2 and MAN1, together with the lamin B receptor and A- and B-type lamins, drawing membrane onto chromatin. Timing is set by phosphorylation: mitotic CDK1-cyclin B and the VRK1/VRK2 kinases keep BANF1 and lamins dispersed, while PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation and the ANKLE2 module license reassembly. Mutations in these lamina components underlie laminopathies and microcephaly.

Nuclear Envelope (NE) Reassembly rebuilds the nucleus at the end of mitosis, enclosing the separated sister chromatids in a sealed membrane with functional pores so that each daughter cell regains a compartment distinct from the cytoplasm. Without it, nucleocytoplasmic transport cannot be re-established, chromatin is exposed to cytoplasmic surveillance, and micronuclei or aberrant nuclear shapes arise. Reassembly is driven by reversal of mitotic phosphorylation: CDK1-cyclin B activity is extinguished and PP2A dephosphorylates lamins and inner nuclear membrane proteins such as emerin, LBR and LEM-domain proteins, while BANF1, counter-regulated by VRK kinases, tethers membranes to chromatin. Nucleoporin subcomplexes reassemble around ELYS-marked chromatin, and the RAN-RCC1-RanGAP gradient with importin-β restores directional transport. ESCRT-III components with VPS4 and the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin clear spindle microtubules and anneal the membrane, completing the diffusion barrier in telophase.

At the end of mitosis each daughter cell must rebuild a nucleus, and nuclear envelope reassembly is the step that restores the boundary between chromatin and cytoplasm. Beginning in late anaphase and finishing in telophase, membrane is recruited to decondensing chromatin, inner nuclear membrane and lamina proteins such as lamins, emerin, LBR and the LEM-domain proteins reaccumulate, and nuclear pore complexes are built and inserted so that regulated nucleocytoplasmic transport and the Ran gradient are re-established. Reversal of mitotic CDK1-cyclin B phosphorylation by protein phosphatase 2A, together with the chromatin-binding protein BANF1 and VRK kinases, times lamina reattachment, while ESCRT-III subunits with CHMP7, spastin and VPS4 sever residual spindle microtubules and seal remaining holes. Incomplete sealing leaves micronuclei and ruptured envelopes, a route to DNA damage, chromosomal instability and inflammatory cytosolic DNA sensing.

Laminins are trimeric glycoproteins that form the scaffold of every basement membrane, and their interactions with cell surface receptors and neighbouring matrix components are what anchor epithelia, muscle fibres, nerves and blood vessels to the sheet beneath them. Alpha, beta and gamma chains assemble through C-terminal coiled-coil contacts; the alpha-chain globular domain then engages integrins, while short-arm domains bind additional integrin isoforms so a single laminin can be tethered at both ends. Nidogens bridge laminin to type IV collagen networks, and perlecan supplies proteoglycan links, building a cross-linked membrane that also presents growth factors and guides cell polarity and migration. Integrins such as alpha6beta4 couple these ligands to epithelial anchoring junctions. Loss of specific chains or receptors produces junctional epidermolysis bullosa, congenital muscular dystrophy and glomerular basement membrane disease, while type IV collagen partners underlie Alport and related syndromes.

Syndecans are heparan sulfate proteoglycans that sit in the plasma membrane and let cells read the extracellular matrix, and their interactions decide how firmly a cell adheres, how it migrates, and how strongly it responds to growth factors. The four core proteins have distinct territories s s- syndecan-1 on epithelia and endothelium, syndecan-2 on mesenchymal and smooth muscle cells, syndecan-3 in the nervous system, syndecan-4 broadly s s- and their sugar chains capture fibronectin, vitronectin, thrombospondin, tenascin-C, collagens, FGF2 and TGF-beta. Because the same ligands engage integrins, syndecans act as adhesion coreceptors, cooperating with beta1, beta3 and beta5 integrin pairs and linking through cytoplasmic partners such as CASK, alpha-actinin and protein kinase C to the actin cytoskeleton and focal adhesion signalling. Proteolytic shedding releases ligand-binding ectodomains that compete with cell-surface receptors, a source of soluble effectors in inflammatory exudates, wound repair and tumour growth.

Cells read their surrounding matrix through receptors other than integrins, and this branch of membrane-extracellular matrix engagement covers those routes: the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, syndecan proteoglycans, and the discoidin domain receptors. It matters because it mechanically couples the basement membrane to the internal cytoskeleton and converts matrix contact into cytoskeletal and growth factor signalling. Dystroglycan binds laminin and agrin outside the cell while dystrophin or utrophin, sarcoglycans, syntrophins and dystrobrevins link it to actin inside; loss of these links makes muscle fibres tear under contraction, the basis of muscular dystrophies and several congenital myopathies. Syndecans bind fibronectin, thrombospondin and heparin-binding growth factors such as FGF2 and PDGF, modulating integrin and receptor behaviour and remodelling actin via protein kinase C. Discoidin domain receptors are collagen-activated tyrosine kinases that feed back onto matrix turnover, relevant to fibrosis and tumour invasion.

Proteoglycans give the extracellular matrix its bulk, hydration and load-bearing properties, and this pathway covers their core proteins, the partners they bind, and the receptors that read them. In cartilage, aggrecan and link protein assemble with hyaluronan into enormous aggregates that resist compression, while small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as decorin, biglycan, lumican and fibromodulin bind collagen fibrils and tune their diameter and spacing; decorin and biglycan also sequester TGF-beta, coupling matrix structure to growth factor availability. Basement membrane perlecan and agrin work with laminins, type IV collagen and dystroglycan, and agrin signalling through LRP4 and MuSK clusters acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. Integrins transmit these matrix cues into cells. Mutations in the collagen, laminin and matrilin components cause chondrodysplasias, Alport syndrome, muscular dystrophies and connective tissue fragility, and remodelling of these molecules accompanies fibrosis and tumour invasion.

Scavenger receptors of class B clear modified lipoproteins, apoptotic cells and released danger signals from the extracellular space, activity that sets tissue cholesterol flux and limits inflammation driven by debris. The class is defined structurally by two transmembrane segments flanking a large extracellular loop, an arrangement shared by CD36 and SCARB1 that leaves both termini cytoplasmic. SCARB1 binds HDL and mediates selective uptake of cholesteryl esters, underpinning reverse cholesterol transport and steroidogenic substrate supply, while CD36 takes up oxidised LDL and long-chain fatty acids and contributes to macrophage foam cell formation in atherosclerosis. The same receptors engage endogenous ligands released from stressed or dying cells, including HMGB1, S100A9, peroxiredoxin 1 and the acute-phase protein serum amyloid A, linking lipid handling to innate immune sensing. Secreted CD5L and SSC5D are related soluble scavenger molecules acting in the same clearance context.

Class A scavenger receptors are trimeric surface proteins of macrophages and related phagocytes that bind and internalise a broad range of polyanionic ligands for degradation, giving innate immunity a non-opsonic route to clear bacteria, modified lipoproteins, apoptotic debris and altered self proteins. Receptors such as MSR1, MARCO, SCARA5 and COLEC12 share a coiled-coil stalk, a collagenous stretch and in some members a cysteine-rich domain, and it is these extracellular regions that set ligand specificity. Captured cargo includes apolipoproteins and modified LDL, collagens, ferritin light and heavy chains, and chaperones such as calreticulin and GRP94 displayed on stressed or dying cells. The uptake of oxidised lipoproteins by macrophages drives foam cell formation in atherosclerosis, while loss of this scavenging weakens bacterial clearance and the handling of extracellular iron and matrix turnover.

Class F scavenger receptors clear unwanted extracellular material from tissue and blood, and this route defines what SCARF1, an endothelial and macrophage surface protein with multiple extracellular EGF-like domains, takes up. Its recognised cargo is unusual for a scavenger receptor: besides modified lipoproteins carrying apolipoprotein B, it binds chaperones displayed outside the cell, including calreticulin, HSP90 and related stress proteins such as HSPH1 and the ER-resident HYOU1. Because surface or released chaperones mark dying and stressed cells, this binding links scavenging to the disposal of apoptotic debris and to the handling of chaperone-bound antigen, feeding material toward degradation and antigen presentation. The related SCARF2 shares the domain architecture but appears to serve cell adhesion rather than ligand capture. Loss of such clearance routes contributes to lipid accumulation in vessel walls and to autoimmunity driven by uncleared cell corpses.</description>

Class H scavenger receptors are the stabilin proteins STAB1 and STAB2, very large transmembrane receptors built from fasciclin, EGF-like and hyaluronan-binding domains that clear unwanted macromolecules from blood by endocytosis. They are the main clearance receptors of liver sinusoidal endothelium and of subsets of macrophages, taking up hyaluronan, advanced glycation end products, modified lipoproteins and matrix glycoproteins and delivering them to lysosomes for degradation. Ligands captured here include apolipoprotein B-containing particles and the matricellular protein SPARC, linking this scavenging to lipoprotein turnover and to remodelling of extracellular matrix. Loss of stabilin-mediated uptake raises circulating hyaluronan and matrix protein levels and can lead to glomerular and hepatic deposition, while stabilin-1 on macrophages also contributes to clearance of dying cells and to the anti-inflammatory tone of tissue-resident phagocytes.

SUMO modification changes where a protein goes, what it binds, and how long it lasts, and every SUMO conjugation event begins with the step described here: activation of the modifier by the heterodimeric E1 enzyme formed by UBA2 and SAE1. Using ATP, the enzyme adenylates the C-terminal glycine of mature SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3, releasing pyrophosphate, and then transfers the modifier onto a catalytic cysteine in UBA2 as a high-energy thioester, priming it for handoff to the E2 conjugating enzyme and onward to substrates. Because this single entry point serves the whole sumoylation system, it governs nuclear transport, transcriptional repression, DNA damage responses, chromosome segregation and the formation of nuclear bodies. Loss of E1 activity is not tolerated by dividing cells, and the enzyme is pursued as a drug target in cancers dependent on high sumoylation flux.

SUMO is transferred from E1 to E2 (UBE2I, UBC9) is the committed handoff step of protein SUMOylation, the modification that controls nuclear transport, chromatin organisation, DNA damage responses, transcriptional repression and the integrity of nuclear bodies. Activated SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3, carried as a thioester on cysteine-173 of the UBA2 subunit of the SAE1-UBA2 activating enzyme, is passed by transthiolation to cysteine-93 of UBC9. UBC9 is the sole conjugating enzyme for all SUMO paralogues, so every SUMOylation event in the cell funnels through it; substrate choice is then set by E3 ligases, or, for targets such as RanGAP1 that present a consensus motif directly to UBC9, by no E3 at all. RWDD3 (RSUME) enhances the reaction by binding UBC9 and increasing thioester formation, linking SUMO conjugation to hypoxic and stress signalling.

SUMOylation modifies thousands of nuclear proteins to control their localisation, partner binding and stability, and the step described here is the handoff that loads the modifier onto the only conjugating enzyme available for it. The activating heterodimer of SAE1 and UBA2 charges SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3 as a thioester, and that thioester is passed by transthiolation from a cysteine in UBA2 to the active-site cysteine of UBC9 (UBE2I), which then delivers SUMO to substrate lysines. Because UBC9 is the sole E2 for this pathway, the transfer is an obligatory bottleneck for all SUMO conjugation, including substrates such as RanGAP1 that need no E3 ligase; RWDD3 stimulates the reaction. Downstream consequences include nucleocytoplasmic transport, chromosome segregation, DNA damage responses and transcriptional repression, and loss of UBC9 is not tolerated by dividing cells.

Before a SUMO protein can be attached to anything, it must be cut. SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO3 are made as precursors carrying extra C-terminal residues, and only after these are removed is the diglycine motif exposed that allows conjugation to lysines on target proteins. This maturation step gates the entire sumoylation system, which governs nuclear transport, transcriptional repression, DNA damage responses, chromosome segregation and the assembly of nuclear bodies. The endopeptidases SENP1, SENP2 and SENP5 perform the cleavage with distinct preferences, SENP1 favouring SUMO1 and SENP2 and SENP5 favouring SUMO2, and they occupy different compartments: SENP1 shuttles but is largely nuclear, SENP2 associates with the nucleoplasmic face of the nuclear pore, and SENP5 concentrates in the nucleolus. The same enzymes also deconjugate SUMO, so they set the supply of mature modifier and its turnover.

Attaching the small ubiquitin-like modifier SUMO to DNA damage response and repair factors tunes their activity, stability and ability to recruit partners, and it is one of the main ways a cell converts a break in its chromosomes into an organised repair reaction. Without it, damage signalling fails to amplify at the lesion and repair factors are not assembled or removed on schedule, a route to genome instability and cancer predisposition. The E2 enzyme UBE2I works with PIAS-family E3 ligases and the SMC5/6-associated NSMCE2 ligase, much of this happening at nuclear pore and PML body platforms built from nucleoporins, RANBP2 and SP100. Substrates named here span double-strand break signalling and repair (BRCA1, MDC1, RNF168, RPA1, XRCC4, RAD52), the RecQ helicases BLM and WRN, cohesin subunits, Polycomb components, and base and nucleotide excision factors such as TDG and XPC.

Attachment of SUMO to lysines on target proteins is a reversible mark that tunes protein behaviour rather than destroying it, and the E3 ligase step is where substrate choice is made. Most targets are nuclear, so this modification shapes transcription, chromatin state, DNA repair and nuclear transport: it usually dampens a factor's activity by blocking partner binding, competing with ubiquitylation or phosphorylation, or recruiting proteins bearing SUMO-interacting motifs. The conjugating enzyme UBE2I carries SUMO and can transfer it alone, while ligases such as the PIAS family, RANBP2 and the SMC5/6-associated NSMCE2 accelerate or direct transfer. Substrates here include nuclear receptors and their coregulators, p53 and MDM2, DNA methyltransferases, Polycomb components, topoisomerases, cohesin subunits, and repair factors recruited to damage sites. RANGAP1 SUMOylation at the nuclear pore and stress-induced SUMO2/3 conjugation illustrate constitutive versus inducible use.

Plasmacytoid dendritic cells are the body's main source of type I interferon during viral infection, and cytosolic DEx/H-box helicases give them a way to recognise foreign DNA and convert that recognition into interferon and inflammatory cytokine output. DHX36 and DHX9 bind unmethylated CpG DNA — preferring the A and B classes respectively — and associate with MyD88, the adaptor shared with the endosomal Toll-like receptors, so that sensing converges on the same signalling machinery. From there the response splits: IRF7 drives transcription of type I interferon genes, while NF-κB subunits including RELA, NFKB1 and NFKB2 drive proinflammatory cytokines. Although this helicase family is better known for RNA metabolism and for the RNA sensors RIG-I and MDA5, these two members act as DNA sensors, contributing to antiviral defence and, when inappropriately engaged by self DNA, to interferon-driven autoinflammation.

Cells infected by viruses or intracellular bacteria must convert detection of foreign nucleic acid into interferon output, and this route describes one way that happens. LRRFIP1 binds cytosolic double-stranded RNA and DNA, and in macrophages responding to vesicular stomatitis virus or Listeria it promotes interferon-beta production by acting through beta-catenin. Stabilised beta-catenin is recruited to the interferon-beta promoter with IRF3, where it serves as a transcriptional cofactor and brings in the histone acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300 to allow efficient transcription. This links a Wnt-pathway effector to antiviral transcription rather than to cell fate, and it amplifies the type I interferon response that establishes the interferon-stimulated antiviral state in neighbouring cells. Loss of this amplification lowers interferon output and permits greater replication of intracellular pathogens.

Cytosolic DNA signals infection or genome damage, and the sensing pathway that detects it must be tuned tightly enough to mount interferon responses without attacking the host's own nucleic acids. This regulatory layer controls the STING centric route: the adaptor recruits the kinase TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 to drive type I interferon transcription, while ubiquitin conjugates and several RING and TRIM ligases set the amplitude and duration of the response. TRIM56 and TRIM32 promote signalling through ubiquitination of the adaptor, whereas a DTX4-containing complex directs TBK1 for degradation, and the helicase DDX41 and the sensor ZBP1 contribute additional DNA recognition. TREX1, a cytosolic DNA exonuclease, removes self-DNA before it can trigger the pathway; its loss causes interferonopathies such as Aicardi-Goutières syndrome, illustrating why restraint here matters as much as detection.
