Removing acetyl groups from histone lysines restores the positive charge on nucleosome tails, tightens chromatin and switches genes off, and this deacetylation step is how repressive chromatin states are established and maintained. The zinc-dependent enzymes that catalyse it — HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC3, HDAC8 and HDAC10 here — have no DNA-binding capacity of their own and work as catalytic cores of multisubunit corepressor complexes recruited to promoters: HDAC1/2 with RBBP4/7 and MTA proteins plus CHD4 in the nucleosome remodelling deacetylase complex, with SAP30 and SUDS3 in Sin3, and with the demethylase KDM1A, RCOR1 and the neuronal repressor REST; HDAC3 partners NCOR1/NCOR2 with TBL1X and GPS2 to silence nuclear receptor targets. The balance against acetyltransferases sets transcriptional output in differentiation, metabolism and inflammation, and these enzymes are the targets of approved deacetylase inhibitors that force differentiation, cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in tumour cells.

PKMTs methylate histone lysines is the writing arm of the histone methylation code: SET-domain lysine methyltransferases, plus the SET-independent DOT1L, transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine onto specific lysines of histones H3 and H4, marking chromatin as active or silent. These marks decide which genes a cell can express, and thereby lineage identity, developmental patterning, X inactivation, heterochromatin integrity and meiotic recombination hotspot choice; their loss or hyperactivity underlies overgrowth syndromes, leukaemias driven by KMT2A fusions, and NSD2- or EZH2-dependent tumours. Specificity is enzyme-encoded and often complex-dependent: SUV39H1, EHMT2 and SETDB1 lay down repressive H3K9 methylation, EZH2 within Polycomb repressive complex 2 with SUZ12 and EED makes H3K27 methylation, SETD1/KMT2 enzymes with the WDR5-RBBP5-ASH2L-DPY30 core mark H3K4 at promoters, NSD proteins and SETD2 mark H3K36 over transcribed bodies, and KMT5 enzymes methylate H4K20. Several members additionally methylate non-histone substrates such as NF-κB subunits.

Histone lysine methylation is one of the main ways chromatin is marked to say whether a gene should be read, and this pathway covers the enzymes that write those marks. Protein lysine methyltransferases transfer a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine onto the epsilon-amino nitrogen of specific lysines in histones H3 and H4, mostly through a SET domain, with DOT1L as the exception. Different enzymes are strikingly selective for site and for the number of methyl groups added: SUV39H1, EHMT2 and SETDB1 deposit repressive H3K9 methylation, EZH2 within a Polycomb complex with EED and SUZ12 marks H3K27, KMT2/SETD1 complexes with WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 methylate H3K4 at active promoters, SETD2 and the NSD proteins act on H3K36, and KMT5A-C on H4K20. The resulting marks steer transcription, heterochromatin formation, DNA repair and mitotic chromosome behaviour, and mutation or translocation of these writers is a recurrent driver of leukaemia and other cancers and of developmental overgrowth syndromes.

HDMs demethylate histones removes methyl marks from histone lysines, making methylation a reversible signal rather than a permanent one and allowing cells to switch genes on and off during differentiation, development and stress responses. Two chemically distinct enzyme families do the work: KDM1A/B are FAD-dependent amine oxidases that need a protonatable lysine amine and therefore act only on mono- and dimethylated substrates, while the larger Jumonji C family are Fe(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that also strip trimethyl groups, releasing formaldehyde, succinate and CO2. Individual enzymes are site-specific, erasing activating H3K4 and H3K36 marks (KDM5, KDM2), repressive H3K9 marks (KDM3, KDM4) or H3K27 marks (KDM6A/B), so their balance sets promoter and heterochromatin states. Their dependence on oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate links chromatin to metabolic status, and mutations cause intellectual disability syndromes and drive cancers.

Histone methylation is not a permanent mark, and the demethylases that erase it make chromatin states reversible, allowing genes to be switched between active and repressed as cells differentiate or respond to signals. Two chemically distinct groups do the work: KDM1A and KDM1B are FAD-dependent amine oxidases limited to mono- and dimethylated lysines, while the Jumonji C family (KDM2-KDM7, PHF2, PHF8 and relatives) are iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that also clear trimethyl marks, releasing formaldehyde along with succinate and carbon dioxide. Their specificities partition the histone code: KDM5 enzymes remove the activating H3K4me2/3 mark, KDM4 and KDM3 target repressive H3K9 methylation, and KDM6A/KDM6B strip H3K27me3 to lift Polycomb silencing. JMJD6 acts on methylated arginine and as a lysyl hydroxylase. Because these enzymes require oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate, they couple metabolism to transcription, and mutations in KDM6A, KDM5C and PHF8 cause intellectual disability syndromes and cancer.

Adding acetyl groups to lysines on histone tails loosens chromatin and marks it for readers that promote transcription, and this is the enzymatic step that writes those marks. Acetylation from these enzymes underlies promoter and enhancer activation, DNA repair, replication-coupled chromatin assembly and dosage compensation; mistargeting of the writers is a recurrent event in leukaemia and other cancers, and the p300/CBP branch is mutated in developmental syndromes. Members fall into the GCN5/PCAF, MYST and p300/CBP families, represented here by KAT2A and KAT2B, the MYST enzymes KAT5, KAT6A, KAT7 and KAT8, and the coactivators CREBBP and EP300. Nearly all act within multisubunit assemblies rather than alone: SAGA-type complexes with TADA and TAF-like subunits, NuA4/TIP60 with TRRAP and the RUVBL ATPases, MSL, and the ELP elongator complex. Partner subunits set substrate and lysine preference, so complex composition determines which histones and non-histone targets are acetylated.

Methylation of arginine residues on histone tails by protein arginine methyltransferases sets a chromatin mark that helps decide whether a gene is transcribed. Type I enzymes such as PRMT1, PRMT3, PRMT6 and CARM1 produce asymmetric dimethylarginine, while PRMT5 with its partner WDR77 produces the symmetric form, and PRMT7 can stop at monomethylation; no demethylase for these marks is known, so they are unusually stable. The marks act combinatorially with lysine acetylation and methylation on the same tails, one modification priming or blocking another, which is why H3R2 and H3K4 methylation are mutually exclusive. Readers and remodellers translate the signal: components of the SWI/SNF complex, the WDR5 scaffold, and DNMT3A link arginine methylation to nucleosome remodelling and DNA methylation. Through these routes the pathway shapes transcriptional coactivation, cell cycle gene expression including cyclin D1, and differentiation, and is frequently deregulated in cancer.

SUMO proteins are made as precursors that cannot be attached to anything until their C-terminal extensions are trimmed, and this maturation and charging step is what makes the entire sumoylation system available to the cell. Protein modification by SUMO governs nuclear transport, transcriptional repression, DNA repair, chromosome segregation and the integrity of nuclear bodies, so a block at this first step disables all of it. SUMO-specific proteases cleave the propeptides to expose the diglycine terminus, with individual enzymes preferring particular SUMO paralogues and occupying distinct nuclear compartments cleoplasm for SENP1 and SENP2, nucleolus for SENP5. Mature SUMO is then adenylated and bound as a thioester by the heterodimeric E1 activating enzyme formed by SAE1 and UBA2, and passed to the single E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2I, whose activity RWDD3 enhances before transfer to substrates.

Glycogen storage diseases covers the inherited failures of glycogen synthesis, branching, and breakdown that disrupt the body's main short-term glucose reserve. Because liver glycogen buffers blood glucose between meals and muscle glycogen fuels exertion, these defects present as fasting hypoglycaemia, exercise intolerance, hepatomegaly, or myopathy, with severity depending on which tissue-specific isoform is lost. The genes trace the whole cycle: glycogenin priming and glycogen synthase elongation, branching enzyme shaping the polymer, lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase degrading it, and the glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit with its endoplasmic reticulum transporter releasing free glucose into blood. Damage also comes from what accumulates — poorly branched, insoluble polyglucosan bodies. Laforin and malin, a phosphatase and ubiquitin ligase pair that keep glycogen soluble, cause a fatal progressive myoclonic epilepsy when mutated, and G6PC3 loss produces congenital neutropenia rather than a metabolic crisis.

Glycogen is the body's rapidly mobilizable glucose store, and its regulated synthesis and breakdown keeps blood glucose stable during fasting and supplies fuel to muscle and brain during exercise and stress. Inherited defects in the enzymes that build, branch, or release glycogen cause the glycogen storage diseases, whose presentations range from fasting hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly to myopathy, cardiomyopathy and neutropenia. Loss of the liver or muscle glycogen synthases blocks storage outright; deficiency of glucose-6-phosphatase or its endoplasmic reticulum glucose-6-phosphate transporter traps glucose inside hepatocytes, while loss of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase leaves undegraded glycogen in lysosomes. Defects in the branching enzyme or in glycogenin, the self-glucosylating protein that primes new chains, yield structurally abnormal or absent glycogen. Failure of the laforin-malin pair, a phosphatase and a ubiquitin ligase acting with ubiquitin on overphosphorylated glycogen, produces insoluble polyglucosan and progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

Glucose-6-phosphatase sits inside the endoplasmic reticulum, so the glucose-6-phosphate generated in the cytosol by glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis must first be carried across the ER membrane; SLC37A4 is the transporter that does this, exchanging cytosolic glucose-6-phosphate for luminal orthophosphate and thereby delivering substrate to the phosphatase that releases free glucose into the blood. Loss-of-function mutations cause glycogen storage disease type Ib, in which the liver and kidney cannot mobilise stored glycogen into circulating glucose: patients suffer fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and hyperlipidaemia. Because the trapped hexose phosphate also perturbs neutrophil metabolism, this form is distinguished from type Ia by neutropenia, impaired neutrophil function and inflammatory bowel disease. The pathway therefore links hepatic glucose output and whole-body fasting tolerance to a single ER membrane antiporter step.

Attaching the small ubiquitin-like modifier SUMO to a transcription factor is one of the main ways cells tune how strongly a gene programme runs without changing the amount of factor present. Transcription factors are overrepresented among SUMO targets, and the usual consequence is dampened activation: modified factors bind DNA less well, are sequestered into inactive nuclear bodies, or recruit repressive partners such as histone deacetylase-containing complexes. The outcome is not uniform, and p53 is the classic case where SUMOylation can instead favour activity, linking this modification to the DNA damage and tumour suppressor circuitry that also includes MDM2, CDKN2A and TP53BP1. The single E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2I works with PIAS-family E3 ligases to transfer SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3 onto substrates including MITF, FOXL2, HIC1, SP3 and the AP-2 factors, so defects skew developmental and pigmentation gene expression.

Ubiquitin ligases are themselves regulated by a second modification, and this pathway covers the attachment of SUMO to enzymes of the ubiquitin system. The consequences differ by target: SUMOylation promotes nuclear import of MDM2, the ligase that marks p53 for degradation, so it feeds into control of the p53 tumour suppressor response, while SUMO conjugation on VHL abolishes its ligase activity, linking the modification to hypoxia signalling and to VHL-associated tumour predisposition. Other targets are ligases recruited to damaged chromatin, where SUMO and ubiquitin marks are laid down together to assemble repair factors. Modification is carried out by the SUMO E2 UBE2I with PIAS-family and RANBP2 E3 activity, and the strong representation of nuclear pore components reflects the pore and PML bodies as the sites where much SUMO conjugation and the associated nucleocytoplasmic transport occur.

Before a WNT morphogen can pattern a tissue, it must be built, lipid-modified and escorted out of the cell that makes it, and this biogenesis and trafficking route is what makes secreted WNT signalling possible at all. The nineteen human WNTs act over short and long ranges to drive proliferation, cell polarity, migration and tissue renewal through beta-catenin-dependent and non-canonical routes, so failure at the production end silences all of them at once. In the endoplasmic reticulum the acyltransferase PORCN attaches palmitoleate to a conserved serine, a modification required for both secretion and receptor binding; the dedicated sorting receptor WLS then carries WNT to the cell surface. A retromer complex of VPS26A, VPS29 and VPS35 with SNX3 retrieves WLS to the Golgi for reuse. Loss of PORCN causes focal dermal hypoplasia, and the pathway is the target of porcupine inhibitors in WNT-driven cancers.

Access to DNA packaged in nucleosomes is controlled largely by covalent marks placed on and removed from histone tails, and this pathway gathers the enzymes that write and erase them together with the core and variant histones they act upon. The outcome is cell-type-specific gene readability: which genes are open in a given tissue, how developmental programmes are locked in, and how silenced regions stay silent. Acetyltransferases and deacetylases, SET-domain and DOT1L methyltransferases, JmjC and LSD1-family demethylases, arginine methyltransferases and arginine deiminases act within large multiprotein assemblies -- SAGA-like and NuA4/TIP60 acetylation modules, MLL/COMPASS complexes with WDR5 and RBBP5, Polycomb repressive complex 2 built on EZH2, SUZ12 and EED, NuRD, and SWI/SNF remodellers -- alongside corepressors such as NCOR1 and SIN3-associated subunits. Mutation of these enzymes is a recurrent driver of leukaemias, solid tumours and intellectual disability syndromes.

Cells must destroy stray DNA in their own cytoplasm, and regulation by TREX1 is how that housekeeping is done. TREX1 is a 3'-to-5' exonuclease anchored to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane that chews back unpaired nucleotides on single- and double-stranded DNA ends, clearing DNA derived from damaged chromatin, retroelements and reverse transcription. Removing this substrate keeps cytosolic DNA sensors quiet, so loss-of-function mutations produce chronic type I interferon signalling and antibodies to DNA, as seen in Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, familial chilblain lupus and systemic lupus erythematosus. The same activity can work against the host during retroviral infection by degrading viral cDNA before it is sensed. TREX1-deficient cells also show an expanded lysosomal compartment and altered mTORC1-TFEB control, linking the enzyme to interferon-independent induction of interferon-stimulated genes and placing it at the boundary between genome debris disposal and innate immune tolerance of self.

Virus infection normally triggers interferon production, but it also drives a separate, interferon-independent arm of the antiviral response that recruits leukocytes to the infected tissue. Here STAT6 acts as the transcription factor for that arm: rather than being turned on by IL-4 or IL-13 through JAK kinases, it is recruited to the endoplasmic reticulum adaptor STING and phosphorylated by TBK1 during RNA or DNA virus infection. Phosphorylated STAT6 dimerizes, enters the nucleus, and drives transcription of the chemokines CCL2, CCL20 and CCL26, which attract monocytes, lymphocytes and eosinophils. This couples cytosolic nucleic acid sensing directly to immune cell recruitment, running parallel to the IRF3-dependent type I interferon output of the same STING-TBK1 module, and links innate viral detection to the inflammatory cell infiltration seen in airway and antiviral immune responses.

Detection of cytosolic DNA from viruses, bacteria or damaged self is converted into an antiviral transcriptional response through IRF3, and this branch of innate immunity is what allows a newly infected cell to warn its neighbours before adaptive immunity arrives. Sensors including IFI16, DDX41 and the Ku70/Ku80-DNA-PK components engage the adaptor STING1, whose C-terminal tail scaffolds TBK1 together with IRF3; TBK1 phosphorylates IRF3, driving its dimerisation, nuclear entry and induction of type I interferon and interferon-stimulated genes. The pathway is held in check by negative regulators such as NLRC3 and NLRP4, by DTX4-directed ubiquitin-mediated turnover of TBK1, and by the exonuclease TREX1, which degrades cytosolic DNA before it can be sensed. Loss of that restraint produces chronic interferon signatures and autoinflammatory disease, while defective signalling leaves severe susceptibility to DNA virus infection.

The last step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is the release of free glucose from glucose-6-phosphate, and glycogen storage disease type Ia is what happens when the enzyme that performs it fails. Glucose-6-phosphatase sits in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane of liver, kidney and intestinal cells with its catalytic site facing the lumen, hydrolysing glucose-6-phosphate delivered by a companion transporter into glucose and inorganic phosphate for export to the blood. Loss-of-function mutations trap carbon inside the hepatocyte: fasting hypoglycaemia becomes severe and early, glycogen and fat accumulate to give hepatomegaly, and the diverted hexose phosphate feeds lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia and hypertriglyceridaemia, with later risk of renal disease and hepatic adenomas. The defect therefore illustrates how whole-body blood glucose homeostasis between meals depends on a single hepatic phosphatase step.

Severe congenital neutropenia type 4 is the disease that follows loss of G6PC3, a glucose-6-phosphatase isoform embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane that hydrolyses glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose and inorganic phosphate. Unlike the liver-restricted enzyme of glycogen storage disease type I, this isoform is expressed broadly, so its inactivation does not produce fasting hypoglycaemia or lactic acidaemia; instead neutrophils and their marrow precursors are selectively vulnerable. Without the enzyme, phosphorylated glucose analogues such as 1,5-anhydroglucitol-6-phosphate accumulate, poisoning glycolysis in cells that depend heavily on it, and granulocyte progenitors die by endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis. Patients present with profound neutropenia and recurrent bacterial infection, often with congenital heart and urogenital malformations and prominent superficial veins, linking a housekeeping step of intracellular glucose release to myeloid cell survival.

Transient receptor potential channels are the cell's general-purpose sensors: tetrameric cation channels, mostly Ca2+-permeable, that convert heat, cold, acid, mechanical force, oxidants and lipid messengers into membrane depolarisation or a rise in cytosolic calcium. They underlie somatosensation and nociception (the capsaicin and menthol receptors TRPV1 and TRPM8, the irritant sensor TRPA1), taste and light-independent retinal signalling, epithelial Ca2+ and Mg2+ uptake in gut and kidney via TRPV5, TRPV6 and TRPM6/TRPM7, and lysosomal ion flux through the mucolipins. Mutations cause channelopathies spanning skeletal dysplasia, mucolipidosis type IV, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, night blindness and hereditary neuropathies. Several members sit downstream of receptor-operated phospholipase C signalling, and TRPM7 gating is coupled to the RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL necroptotic machinery, linking channel-mediated calcium entry to regulated cell death and inflammation.

Fat cells need a way to sense when energy substrates are already abundant and stop releasing more, and the hydroxycarboxylic acid-binding receptors provide it. These three closely related, gene-clustered G protein-coupled receptors respond to intermediary metabolites: lactate acts on HCAR1, the ketone body 3-hydroxybutyrate on HCAR2, and a medium-chain beta-hydroxy fatty acid on HCAR3, which is confined to higher primates. All three signal through Gi proteins in adipocytes, lowering cyclic AMP and suppressing lipolysis, so that exercise-derived lactate or fasting ketones feed back to restrain free fatty acid output. HCAR2 and HCAR3 are also carried by neutrophils, macrophages and other immune cells, linking metabolite levels to inflammatory tone, and HCAR2 is the target through which nicotinic acid lowers plasma lipids and causes cutaneous flushing.

Vitamin B12 must be absorbed from food, carried in blood, taken into cells, stripped of its upper ligand and delivered as two distinct cofactor forms before any enzyme can use it, and inherited defects anywhere along that route produce the cobalamin deficiency disorders. Loss of the cytosolic arm starves methionine synthase and its reactivating reductase, trapping folate as methyltetrahydrofolate, blocking purine and thymidylate synthesis, and causing megaloblastic anaemia with hyperhomocysteinaemia; loss of the mitochondrial arm leaves methylmalonyl-CoA mutase without adenosylcobalamin and causes methylmalonic aciduria with acidotic crises. Intrinsic factor, the cubilin-amnionless receptor and transcobalamin handle uptake and transport; lysosomal export and the processing enzymes generate usable cofactor. Because methionine feeds myelin, neurotransmitter and DNA methylation chemistry, these defects present with neurological as well as haematological disease.

Vitamins must come from the diet, and inherited blocks in their uptake or conversion into active cofactors cause disease even when intake is adequate. This grouping of defects in vitamin and cofactor metabolism centres on cobalamin and biotin handling. Dietary B12 is captured by intrinsic factor, taken up in the ileum through the cubilin-amnionless receptor, carried in blood on transcobalamin and delivered via CD320, then released from lysosomes and processed by the MMACHC/MMADHC route into methylcobalamin for methionine synthase and adenosylcobalamin for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Failure at any step produces homocystinuria, methylmalonic aciduria, megaloblastic anaemia and neurological injury. In parallel, biotinidase recycles biotin and holocarboxylase synthetase attaches it to the carboxylases of gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis and leucine and propionate catabolism, so defects there cause multiple carboxylase deficiency with organic acidaemia.

Aerobic metabolism unavoidably produces superoxide, hydrogen peroxide and related oxidants, and detoxification of reactive oxygen species is the set of enzymes that converts them to water and oxygen before they damage lipids, proteins and DNA. The same chemistry sets the amplitude and duration of peroxide signalling, so these enzymes both protect cells and shape redox-sensitive responses; their failure contributes to oxidative stress in neurodegeneration, inflammation and ageing. Three superoxide dismutases act in distinct compartments — cytosol, mitochondrial matrix and extracellular space — and hand hydrogen peroxide to catalase, glutathione peroxidases and peroxiredoxins. Thioredoxins and glutathione reductase, with their NADPH-dependent reductases, regenerate the reduced peroxidases each cycle. Also represented are the sources: NADPH oxidase subunits and endoplasmic reticulum oxidoreductases that generate peroxide deliberately, plus copper chaperones that load superoxide dismutase with its metal cofactor.

Before a cell can divide, the barrier that separates nucleus from cytoplasm has to be taken apart, and nuclear pore complex disassembly is the step that permeabilizes the nuclear envelope at mitotic entry. Its consequence is practical: chromosomes become accessible to spindle microtubules and the nucleocytoplasmic transport barrier is abolished, so regulators that were segregated by compartment mix. The trigger is phosphorylation. Mitotic CDK1 with its B-type cyclin partners, together with the NIMA-family kinases NEK6 and NEK7 acting downstream of NEK9, modify nucleoporins, and the FG-repeat nucleoporin NUP98 that helps form the permeability barrier is among the first to dissociate. The remaining subcomplexes—the NUP107-NUP160 scaffold ring, the NUP62 channel nucleoporins, transmembrane components such as POM121 and NDC1, and the cytoplasmic and basket proteins RANBP2 and TPR—then disperse, to be reassembled after anaphase.

SMAD4 is the shared partner that receptor-activated SMAD2 and SMAD3 must recruit to carry TGF-beta and BMP signals into the nucleus and switch on growth-inhibitory transcription, so its loss removes one of the main brakes on epithelial proliferation. The gene was originally found homozygously deleted in pancreatic cancer, and inactivation by deletion or point mutation is common there and in biliary and colorectal tumours; inherited mutations cause juvenile polyposis with hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps and a raised cancer risk. Most cancer-associated substitutions fall in the MH2 domain, which mediates heterotrimer formation with phosphorylated SMAD2/SMAD3 and also SMAD4 homotrimers linked to protein stability; MH1 mutations instead disrupt DNA binding. The result in each case is a signalling complex that cannot assemble or cannot engage target promoters, leaving cells insensitive to TGF-beta cytostatic control and cooperating with other lesions during tumour progression.

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and tumours frequently escape that restraint by disabling the receptor-activated SMADs that carry the signal. Loss of SMAD2/3 function in cancer, best characterised in colorectal tumours, removes the growth-inhibitory arm of TGF-beta signalling while leaving other receptor outputs intact. In the intact route, ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates TGFBR1, which phosphorylates the C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 presented by the anchoring protein SARA (ZFYVE9); phosphorylated SMADs then form transcriptionally active heterotrimers with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to drive cytostatic gene programmes. Cancer-associated mutations cluster in the MH2 oligomerisation domain and in that phosphorylation motif, preventing complex assembly. Mouse genetics separates the consequences: Smad3 loss can initiate intestinal tumours, whereas Smad2 loss mainly accelerates progression to large, invasive carcinomas.

Signaling by TGF-beta Receptor Complex in Cancer describes how a growth-inhibitory pathway is dismantled during tumorigenesis. In normal epithelium, TGF-beta ligand binding brings together the type II and type I receptor kinases, which phosphorylate SMAD2 and SMAD3; these partner with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to switch on cell cycle inhibitors such as p15 and p21, driving cytostasis, differentiation and apoptosis. Loss of this brake is one of the more common events in cancer, through SMAD4 deletion in pancreatic tumours, TGFBR2 frameshifts in microsatellite-unstable colorectal cancer, and inactivating changes in TGFBR1, SMAD2 or SMAD3. Accessory components set the threshold for signalling, with FKBP1A restraining the unliganded type I receptor and the SARA anchor presenting SMADs at the membrane. Paradoxically, tumours that survive with intact receptors exploit the pathway later, using it to induce epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasion.

TGF-beta acting through its receptor complex normally restrains epithelial growth, driving cell cycle arrest, differentiation and apoptosis, and cancers commonly dismantle this brake. Ligand binding brings the type II receptor together with the type I receptor, whose kinase is held in check by FKBP1A until activation; the anchoring protein ZFYVE9 presents SMAD2 and SMAD3 for phosphorylation, after which they partner with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to control transcription of growth-inhibitory targets. Deletion or loss-of-function mutation of SMAD4 is the classic route to escape and is especially frequent in pancreatic cancer, while inactivating lesions in SMAD2, SMAD3, TGFBR1 or TGFBR2 disable the same axis in colorectal and other tumours. In advanced disease the residual pathway can switch roles, promoting epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasiveness, so its output is context-dependent rather than uniformly suppressive.

SMAD2/3 Phosphorylation Motif Mutants in Cancer describes how tumours escape the growth-suppressive arm of TGF-beta signalling by destroying the site at which the pathway's messengers are switched on. Normally ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates TGFBR1, which phosphorylates the C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 after the adaptor SARA presents them at the receptor; the phosphorylated proteins then trimerise with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to drive cytostatic and differentiation programmes. Cancer-associated substitutions, truncations or deletions of the two terminal serines leave SMAD2/3 receptor-bound but permanently unphosphorylated, so no active complex forms and target genes such as those enforcing cell cycle arrest are never induced. The result is loss of contact inhibition and TGF-beta insensitivity, a recurrent event in colorectal, pancreatic and other epithelial tumours where this arm behaves as a tumour suppressor.

TGF-beta signalling normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and cancers frequently escape that restraint by breaking the step at which the receptor writes its signal onto its effectors. Ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and activates the TGFBR1 kinase, which phosphorylates the conserved C-terminal Ser-Ser-X-Ser motif of SMAD2 and SMAD3 after the anchoring protein ZFYVE9 presents them at the membrane; phosphorylated SMAD2/3 then assemble heterotrimers with SMAD4 and enter the nucleus to direct growth-inhibitory transcription. Cancer-associated mutants of this phosphorylation motif substitute, delete or truncate the critical serines, so the receptor complex can no longer activate them, the heterotrimer never forms, and the antiproliferative arm of the pathway is silenced. Loss of this input contributes to tumour growth and to the switch of residual TGF-beta signalling toward invasion, while leaving receptor activation itself intact.

TGF-beta signalling restrains epithelial proliferation, and it does so by delivering activated SMAD2 and SMAD3 into a heterotrimeric complex with the shared partner SMAD4 that enters the nucleus and directs transcription of growth-inhibitory and differentiation genes. Cancer-associated mutations in the SMAD4 MH2 domain destroy this last step: the protein is still made but can no longer trimerise, so receptor-level signalling is received and then goes nowhere. Hotspot substitutions cluster in two surfaces of the domain, the L1 loop that mediates subunit-subunit contacts within the trimer and a basic pocket including the L3 loop arginine that reads the C-terminal phosphoserine motif of activated R-SMADs. Loss of function here is common in pancreatic and colorectal carcinoma and in juvenile polyposis, releasing epithelium from TGF-beta-imposed cytostasis and altering tumour-stroma and immune crosstalk.

TGF-beta signalling restrains epithelial proliferation, and cancers escape that restraint by breaking the step in which receptor-phosphorylated SMAD2 and SMAD3 partner with SMAD4. Cancer-associated missense mutations in the MH2 domain of SMAD2 and SMAD3 target the interface used for heterotrimer assembly, so the activated R-SMADs can no longer form the complex that enters the nucleus and drives transcription of growth-inhibitory and differentiation genes. The affected residues mirror positions in SMAD4 that are themselves recurrently mutated, including aspartate and arginine contacts at the trimer interface and a proline in the same region. The consequence is loss of cytostatic TGF-beta responses while other arms of the pathway persist, a combination seen most clearly in colorectal cancer, where SMAD pathway inactivation accompanies adenoma-to-carcinoma progression.

Glycogen synthesis builds the branched glucose polymer that liver and muscle draw on between meals and during exercise, making it the body's short-term fuel reserve and a buffer for blood glucose. Glucose 6-phosphate is isomerised to glucose 1-phosphate by phosphoglucomutase and activated as UDP-glucose by UGP2; glycogenin then self-glucosylates to prime a chain, glycogen synthase (the muscle GYS1 or liver GYS2 isoform) extends it in inkage, and branching enzyme GBE1 introduces the -1,6 branches that make the particle soluble and rapidly mobilisable. A targeting subunit recruits protein phosphatase 1 to activate synthase, while laforin and malin restrain excessive or poorly branched glucan and mark substrates for ubiquitin-dependent turnover; their loss causes Lafora body epilepsy. Defects in branching or in either synthase isoform produce glycogen storage diseases with hepatic, muscular or cardiac failure.

Biotin is the cofactor that lets five human carboxylases work, and this grouping covers what happens when the enzymes that attach and recover it fail. Holocarboxylase synthetase transfers biotin onto acetyl-CoA carboxylase, pyruvate carboxylase, propionyl-CoA carboxylase and methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, while biotinidase releases biotin from dietary biocytin and from degraded carboxylases so it can be reused. Loss of either step disables all of them at once, producing multiple carboxylase deficiency: gluconeogenesis, fatty acid synthesis, and the catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine all stall, and patients present with ketolactic acidosis, organic aciduria, hyperammonemia, rash, alopecia, hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay. Because humans cannot synthesise biotin, the same phenotypes follow severe malnutrition or avidin-rich raw egg white. Both inherited forms respond to biotin supplementation, which is why newborn screening looks for them.

Vitamin B12 absorbed from the gut must be carried in blood to the tissues that use it, and transcobalamin II is the plasma protein that performs that delivery, binding cobalamin and handing it to cells through receptor-mediated uptake. When TCN2 is defective, circulating B12 may appear adequate yet cells are starved of the cofactor needed by methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so one-carbon metabolism and propionate catabolism both stall. The resulting autosomal recessive deficiency presents in infancy with failure to thrive, megaloblastic anaemia and pancytopenia, reflecting the dependence of rapidly dividing haematopoietic precursors on thymidine synthesis; untreated children develop intellectual disability and neurological abnormalities as myelin maintenance fails. It illustrates how a transport defect, rather than a dietary shortfall or an enzymatic lesion, can produce functional vitamin deficiency, and why treatment requires cobalamin doses high enough to bypass the missing carrier.

Dietary vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed on its own; it must be escorted through the gut by intrinsic factor, the glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells that binds cobalamin and delivers it to the cubilin-amnionless receptor in the ileum for uptake into portal blood. Loss-of-function mutations in the intrinsic factor gene CBLIF (gastric intrinsic factor, GIF) abolish this carrier step and cause hereditary intrinsic factor deficiency, an autosomal recessive congenital pernicious anaemia in which infants and young children develop megaloblastic anaemia, low serum B12 and neurological signs despite normal gastric acid secretion and no autoimmune gastritis. Because cobalamin is the cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, the resulting deficiency stalls one-carbon and propionate metabolism, impairing DNA synthesis in erythroid precursors and myelin maintenance. The defect responds to parenteral B12, bypassing absorption entirely.

Dietary vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum only as a complex with intrinsic factor, taken up by the cubilin-amnionless receptor at the brush border; loss of functional amnionless disables that receptor and causes recessive hereditary megaloblastic anemia 1, the Norwegian form of Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome. Amnionless is the transmembrane anchoring and trafficking subunit that escorts cubilin to the apical membrane and drives endocytosis of the bound intrinsic factor-cobalamin complex, so its defect leaves gastric intrinsic factor and cubilin themselves intact but the uptake step non-functional. Without absorbed cobalamin, methionine synthase stalls, folate is trapped as methyltetrahydrofolate, and thymidylate supply for DNA replication fails, producing megaloblastic erythropoiesis, and often proteinuria because the same receptor reabsorbs filtered proteins in the kidney. Patients require parenteral B12 for life, and untreated disease brings neurological injury alongside the anemia.

Defective CUBN causes MGA1 describes what happens when the intestine cannot absorb vitamin B12. Cubilin, working with amnionless as the cubam receptor complex on the ileal brush border, binds gastric intrinsic factor carrying dietary cobalamin and internalises it by endocytosis; loss-of-function mutations in cubilin abolish this uptake and cause recessive hereditary megaloblastic anemia 1, also known as Imerslund-Gräsbeck syndrome, typically with proteinuria because the same receptor reclaims filtered proteins in the kidney proximal tubule. Cobalamin deficiency stalls methionine synthase, trapping folate as methyltetrahydrofolate and starving thymidylate synthesis, so erythroid precursors cannot replicate DNA and arrest as large immature megaloblasts. Neurological deterioration accompanies the anemia. The pathway thus links receptor-mediated nutrient transport at an epithelial surface to one-carbon metabolism and proliferation in the bone marrow, and is corrected by parenteral B12.

Dietary vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum only as a complex with intrinsic factor, and cubilin is the receptor that takes that complex up. Loss-of-function mutations in CUBN cause recessive hereditary megaloblastic anemia of the Imerslund-Grasbeck type, in which cobalamin malabsorption starves B12-dependent reactions, stalls folate cycling, and limits thymidylate supply so that erythroid precursors cannot complete DNA replication and enlarge without dividing. Cubilin works at the apical enterocyte membrane together with amnionless, whose partner protein anchors and traffics the receptor, while gastric intrinsic factor supplies the ligand; defects in any of these produce overlapping disease, and because the same receptor complex mediates proximal tubule protein reabsorption, patients often also show benign proteinuria. The condition links a single transport step to systemic one-carbon metabolism and haematopoiesis, and responds to parenteral B12.

Methionine synthase reductase keeps the cobalamin cofactor of methionine synthase in its active, reduced methylcobalamin state, and when it fails the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine stalls. Loss of this reductase activity produces homocystinuria with megaloblastic anaemia, the cblE disorder, typically presenting in infancy with developmental delay, feeding problems and haematological abnormality. Mechanistically, methionine synthase transfers a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, but its enzyme-bound cobalamin is occasionally oxidised to an inactive cob(II)alamin form; the reductase performs reductive remethylation using S-adenosylmethionine to restore catalysis. Without that repair cycle, homocysteine accumulates in blood and urine while methionine and downstream S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation are depleted, and folate becomes trapped as the methyl form, linking this step to one-carbon metabolism, nucleotide synthesis and erythropoiesis. Treatment centres on hydroxocobalamin with betaine as an alternative methyl donor.

Methionine synthase remethylates homocysteine to methionine using a methyl group from 5-methyltetrahydrofolate and a cobalamin cofactor, linking folate one-carbon metabolism to the supply of S-adenosylmethionine for methylation of DNA, RNA, proteins and lipids. Loss-of-function mutations in MTR cause the cblG form of methylcobalamin deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder presenting with homocystinuria, megaloblastic or macrocytic anaemia, developmental delay and neurological impairment, because homocysteine accumulates while methionine and reduced folate become unavailable for methyl transfer. The enzyme's cobalt centre is periodically oxidised and inactivated, and the partner reductase MTRR restores it by reductive methylation; defects in that reductase give a clinically overlapping condition. Together these two steps explain why cobalamin and folate status converge on a single reaction whose failure is read out as elevated plasma homocysteine.

Adenosylcobalamin is the cofactor that methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs to convert methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA, the step that lets propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains and the branched-chain amino acids valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine enter the citric acid cycle. Loss of MMAB, the mitochondrial ATP:cob(I)alamin adenosyltransferase that attaches the adenosyl group to the reduced cobalamin ring, leaves the mutase itself intact but without its cofactor, and produces cblB-type methylmalonic aciduria. Methylmalonic acid and propionyl-CoA accumulate, and affected newborns present with life-threatening metabolic ketoacidosis, hyperammonaemia, failure to thrive and neurological injury unless acidosis is corrected quickly. Because the lesion is in cofactor synthesis rather than the enzyme, many patients respond biochemically to pharmacological vitamin B12, distinguishing this defect from mutase deficiency itself.

Vitamin B12 taken up by cells must be stripped of its upper-axial ligand and then routed either to mitochondria for adenosylcobalamin synthesis or to the cytosol for methylcobalamin synthesis; MMADHC is the branch-point protein that directs cobalamin down these two arms, working with the dealkylating/decyanating enzyme MMACHC. Loss-of-function mutations in MMADHC produce cobalamin D disease, in which both coenzymes are depleted, crippling methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase. The metabolic consequence is combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria, with accumulation of methylmalonic acid and homocysteine and failure of the methionine cycle that supplies methyl groups. Affected infants present with feeding difficulty, developmental delay, hypotonia, megaloblastic anaemia and metabolic acidosis. Which domain of MMADHC is disrupted determines whether one branch or both are lost, so the same gene yields isolated or combined biochemical phenotypes.

Vitamin B12 taken up by cells arrives as a variety of cobalamin forms that must be stripped of their upper axial ligand before they can be converted into the two active coenzymes, methylcobalamin for cytosolic methionine synthase and adenosylcobalamin for mitochondrial methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. MMACHC performs this processing step, dealkylating alkylcobalamins and reductively decyanating cyanocobalamin in the cytosol. When MMACHC is defective, both coenzymes fall short and the cblC form of combined methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria follows, the commonest inherited disorder of cobalamin handling. Methylmalonic acid and homocysteine accumulate while methionine synthesis falters, producing feeding difficulty and failure to thrive, megaloblastic anaemia, developmental delay and seizures, progressive retinopathy, and in severe cases thrombotic microangiopathy. The disease illustrates how a single trafficking and tailoring enzyme gates two otherwise separate branches of intermediary metabolism.

Defective MMAA causes MMA, cblA type describes the loss of a mitochondrial chaperone that keeps the vitamin B12-dependent enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase supplied with its adenosylcobalamin cofactor. That enzyme carries propionyl-CoA derived from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains and the branched-chain amino acids valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine into the citric acid cycle as succinyl-CoA. When MMAA fails, the mutase cannot acquire or retain its cofactor, methylmalonyl-CoA is not isomerised, and methylmalonic acid accumulates in blood and urine. Infants and young children present with life-threatening metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, failure to thrive and neurological injury, with later risk of renal impairment. Because the defect lies in cofactor handling rather than in the apoenzyme itself, this form of methylmalonic aciduria is typically responsive to pharmacological hydroxocobalamin, distinguishing it from mutations in the mutase gene.

Propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol and the branched-chain amino acids is disposed of through methylmalonyl-CoA, and the mitochondrial enzyme MMUT converts that intermediate to succinyl-CoA using adenosylcobalamin as cofactor. MMAA is the GTPase-like chaperone that delivers and maintains the cobalamin cofactor on MMUT, and loss of MMAA function leaves the mutase without a usable cofactor. The result is cblA-type methylmalonic aciduria: methylmalonic acid builds up in blood and urine, and infants and young children suffer metabolic acidotic crises with vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia and risk of death, together with longer-term renal and neurological damage. Because the defect is in cofactor handling rather than in the enzyme itself, many patients respond to pharmacological vitamin B12, distinguishing this form from mutase-deficient methylmalonic acidaemia and linking it to the broader mitochondrial cobalamin utilisation route.

Loss of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase activity blocks the final step by which propionyl-CoA derived from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains and the amino acids valine, isoleucine, methionine and threonine is converted to succinyl-CoA for entry into the citric acid cycle. When the mutase is defective, methylmalonic acid and its precursors accumulate, producing methylmalonic aciduria of the mut type, a disorder of organic acid metabolism that presents in newborns with metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, vomiting, encephalopathy and renal damage, and is often fatal without protein restriction and carnitine therapy. The mitochondrial enzyme requires adenosylcobalamin as cofactor, and MMAA is the accessory GTPase that delivers and protects this cobalamin on the mutase; mutations in either gene therefore impair the same catalytic step. This places the defect at the junction between amino acid catabolism, vitamin B12 handling and mitochondrial energy production.

Cells acquire vitamin B12 from blood by taking up transcobalamin-bound cobalamin through the CD320 receptor, and loss of that receptor produces methylmalonic aciduria of the transcobalamin receptor type. Without receptor-mediated endocytosis of the transcobalamin–cobalamin complex, cobalamin never reaches the lysosome for release and onward conversion to the two active cofactor forms, so both B12-dependent enzymes lose activity: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in mitochondria and cytosolic methionine synthase. The consequence detected on newborn screening is elevated methylmalonic acid together with raised homocysteine, reflecting blocked propionate catabolism and stalled remethylation of homocysteine to methionine. The clinical picture is often mild or transient compared with other inherited cobalamin disorders, but the pathway illustrates how a single uptake receptor gates intracellular B12 supply for branched-chain amino acid, odd-chain fatty acid and one-carbon metabolism.

Death receptor engagement by FAS ligand or TRAIL assembles a complex in which FADD clusters procaspase-8 for autoprocessing; regulation by c-FLIP sets the threshold at which that step commits a cell to apoptosis. Encoded by CFLAR, the c-FLIP proteins carry the same death effector domains as procaspase-8 but lack a functional catalytic site, so they compete for recruitment to FADD at the receptor and block caspase-8 maturation. The short forms are straightforwardly protective, while the long form can favour partial caspase-8 activation at low abundance and inhibition at high abundance, also feeding signalling through RIPK1, TRADD and TRAF2 toward survival and inflammatory outputs rather than death. Because c-FLIP levels are often raised in tumours, this checkpoint underlies resistance to TRAIL- and FAS-directed killing by cytotoxic lymphocytes, and its loss sensitises cells to receptor-driven apoptosis.

Cells meet heat, oxidative insult and proteotoxic stress by switching on a transcriptional programme that makes more chaperones, and the control of HSF1-mediated heat shock response determines when that switch is thrown and how quickly it is turned off again. Keeping HSF1 inactive under normal conditions matters as much as activating it: chronic activation supports tumour cell proteostasis, while blunted induction leaves neurons vulnerable to aggregated protein. HSP70 family members and their DNAJ and BAG co-chaperones bind HSF1 and hold it monomeric, a repression relieved when unfolded substrates compete for them; trimerisation, nuclear import through the nuclear pore complex with the carrier HIKESHI, and DNA binding follow. Kinases including GSK3B and the ERK1/2-MAPKAPK2 axis, together with SIRT1-dependent deacetylation and ubiquitin-mediated turnover, tune the amplitude and duration of the response.

Glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, androgen and progesterone receptors can only bind their hormones if a chaperone machine holds them in a receptive conformation, and this ATP-driven HSP90 cycle for steroid hormone receptors in the ligand-bound state does exactly that. It determines whether a cell responds to cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone or progesterone, and so sits upstream of stress metabolism, salt handling and reproductive gene programmes; it is also why HSP90 inhibitors destabilise these receptors in hormone-driven cancers. Newly made receptors are delivered from HSP70 and its DNAJ co-chaperones to HSP90 through the adaptor STIP1, which is displaced on ATP binding by the immunophilins FKBP4 or FKBP5, while PTGES3 stabilises the high-affinity conformation. ATP hydrolysis releases the hormone-bound receptor, which is then carried toward the nucleus along microtubules by cytoplasmic dynein and its dynactin cofactor to dimerise and transactivate target genes.

Cells respond to heat, oxidants, and other proteotoxic insults by mounting the heat shock response, and HSF1 activation is the switch that turns it on. Without it, misfolded proteins accumulate unchecked and cells die under stress; constitutive activation instead supports the proteotoxic tolerance of tumour cells, making this a target in cancer. HSF1 sits in cytoplasm and nucleus as an inactive monomer held in check by chaperones including HSP90 and HSP70 family members; stress releases it, and it trimerises, accumulates in the nucleus, and binds heat shock elements to drive transcription of chaperones and co-chaperones such as DNAJB1, HSPB1, HSPH1 and ubiquitin. Feedback is built in: newly made chaperones, together with HSBP1, return HSF1 to the monomeric state, while acetylation and deacetylation, translation elongation factor and RNA-binding inputs, and RPA-mediated promoter access tune the amplitude of the response.

Heat, hypoxia, oxidants and other proteotoxic insults denature proteins faster than a cell can refold them, and the cellular response to heat stress is the emergency programme that restores proteostasis. Its centrepiece is HSF1, held inactive as a monomer by HSP90 and HSP70/DNAJ chaperones and by inhibitory phosphorylation; on stress it is released, trimerizes with help from eEF1A1, accumulates in the nucleus and binds heat shock elements to drive transcription of chaperones such as HSPA1A/B, HSPB1, CRYAB, DNAJB1 and HSPH1, together with BAG cofactors, the HSP70 nuclear importer HIKESHI, and ubiquitin for disposal of damaged protein. Kinases and acetylation machinery including MAPK, GSK3B, CAMK2, SIRT1 and CREBBP/EP300 tune HSF1 output, while nucleoporins support the nuclear trafficking the response requires. The same circuitry underlies thermotolerance, buffers neurodegenerative aggregation, and is chronically co-opted to support tumour cell survival.

The heat shock response must be switched off as well as on, and the attenuation phase is how cells terminate it once chaperone capacity again matches the load of unfolded protein. Sustained HSF1 activity is costly and, left unchecked, supports the proteostasis addiction seen in tumours, while premature shutdown leaves damaged proteins unresolved. Attenuation proceeds by several converging routes: newly made HSPA1A/HSPA1B and DNAJB1, no longer occupied by exposed hydrophobic surfaces, bind HSF1 trimers and silence them; HSP90 complexes with FKBP4 and PTGES3 favour the inactive state; HSBP1 engages the trimer and blocks DNA binding and transactivation; and acetylation by the p300/CBP acetyltransferases reduces HSF1 occupancy at heat shock elements. Trimers then leave the promoter and revert to monomers. Downstream chaperone products such as HSPB1, HSPH1 and SERPINH1 mark the response being wound down.

When cells are heated or otherwise stressed, HSF1 binds heat shock elements in chromatin, but binding alone does not switch genes on; converting DNA-bound HSF1 into an active transcription factor is the step captured here, and it determines how quickly a cell mounts the heat shock response. Release of an internal regulatory region and stress-induced serine phosphorylation license two acidic activation domains that stimulate both initiation and elongation, with CREBBP and EP300 supplying coactivator acetyltransferase activity and mTOR complex components among the kinases implicated. The output is a burst of chaperone synthesis — HSPA1A/B, DNAJB1, HSPH1, HSPB1 and the small crystallins — that refolds damaged proteins, while HSP90 and HSPA8 feed back to restrain HSF1 and HSBP1 helps terminate the response. This circuit underlies proteostasis, thermotolerance, and the chaperone addiction of many tumours.

Biotin is a cofactor for the carboxylases of fatty acid synthesis, gluconeogenesis and amino acid catabolism, and it is not discarded after use: the vitamin is cleaved from biocytin and from dietary protein-bound biotin so it can be reused. Biotinidase performs that release, and loss-of-function mutations in BTD abolish recycling, producing a secondary biotin deficiency and juvenile-onset multiple carboxylase deficiency. Affected infants typically present between the second and fifth months with seizures, hypotonia, skin rash, alopecia, hearing and optic nerve damage, and organic acid accumulation reflecting stalled carboxylase reactions. Because the block is in cofactor supply rather than the apoenzymes themselves, pharmacological oral biotin corrects the metabolic and neurological consequences, and newborn screening for enzyme activity allows treatment before irreversible injury occurs. The condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

Five human carboxylases need a biotin molecule covalently attached to work, and holocarboxylase synthetase is the single enzyme that performs that attachment. When mutations disable it, all five enzymes fail at once, producing early-onset multiple carboxylase deficiency: metabolic acidosis, organic aciduria, lethargy, hypotonia, seizures and a characteristic dermatitis appearing from the newborn period through early childhood. The affected substrates span central metabolism — pyruvate carboxylase for gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis, propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunits and methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase subunits for amino acid and odd-chain fatty acid catabolism, and acetyl-CoA carboxylase for fatty acid synthesis. Active-site mutations lower biotin affinity and can be overcome with pharmacological oral biotin, giving full biochemical and clinical reversal; mutations elsewhere instead weaken recognition of the apocarboxylase substrates, respond only partially, and carry a worse long-term outlook.

Autodegradation of the E3 ubiquitin ligase COP1 is the switch that releases p53 from constitutive destruction after DNA damage, allowing the tumour suppressor to accumulate and impose cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis. In unstressed cells COP1 continuously ubiquitinates p53 and keeps its levels low; loss of this restraint, or conversely COP1 overexpression in breast and ovarian cancers, distorts the damage response. The mechanism is self-directed: the damage-activated kinase ATM phosphorylates COP1 on Ser387, COP1 dissociates from p53 and ubiquitinates itself, and the polyubiquitinated ligase is delivered to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle and regulatory subunits carries out the degradation. Ubiquitin precursors supply the conjugated tag. This is a case of a ligase destroying itself to stabilise its substrate, coupling genotoxic stress sensing to proteasomal control of p53 abundance.

In unstressed cells p53 is held at low levels by ubiquitin ligases that mark it for destruction, and COP1 is one of them; this route describes how COP1 itself is eliminated so that p53 can accumulate after genotoxic stress. The switch matters because it converts DNA damage sensing into a stable p53 response that drives cell cycle arrest, senescence or apoptosis, and its loss permits damaged cells to keep dividing. The damage-activated kinase ATM phosphorylates COP1 on Ser387, which triggers COP1 autoubiquitination; polyubiquitin supplied by the ubiquitin precursor genes is then read by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of 20S core and 19S regulatory subunits carries out degradation. Removing the ligase abrogates p53 ubiquitination, making this a self-limiting brake within tumour suppressor control and a point at which COP1 overexpression can blunt p53 in cancer.

Notch signalling decides cell fate between neighbouring cells, and its final step is a switch at the DNA: the CSL factor RBPJ sits on target promoters and flips from repressor to activator. This transcriptional output, converging on HLH-family targets such as HES and HEY genes, governs neurogenesis, lymphocyte lineage choice, vascular and cardiac development, and intestinal secretory versus absorptive fate; its corruption drives T-cell leukaemia, while NOTCH3 mutation causes the small-vessel disease CADASIL. In unstimulated cells RBPJ, with the bifunctional adaptor SKIP (SNW1), recruits NCOR1/NCOR2, TBL1 proteins and histone deacetylases to keep targets silent. Receptor cleavage frees the Notch intracellular domain, which displaces the corepressors, binds RBPJ and recruits a Mastermind-like coactivator, and the ternary complex then brings in CREBBP and the acetyltransferases GCN5 and PCAF to open chromatin. Mastermind also nucleates the kinase-dependent shutoff that limits signal duration.

Regulation of ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) is the feedback circuit that keeps polyamine synthesis in check, and it is the textbook case of ubiquitin-independent proteasomal degradation. ODC catalyses the committed step in making putrescine, spermidine and spermine, polyamines required for proliferation and translation; unrestrained ODC activity is transforming, and the enzyme is a downstream effector of MYC. When polyamines accumulate they promote a ribosomal frameshift that produces antizyme, which binds ODC, inhibits it, and exposes a C-terminal degron so that the 26S proteasome destroys the enzyme without ubiquitin tagging while releasing antizyme for further rounds. Antizyme also blocks polyamine uptake, and an antizyme inhibitor sequesters it to relieve the brake. The presence of the full core and regulatory particle subunits, together with NQO1, reflects how directly proteolysis and its redox-linked stabilisation set cellular polyamine levels.

Polyamines such as putrescine and spermidine are needed for growth and translation but are toxic in excess, so cells cap their supply at the committed step: ornithine decarboxylase. This feedback circuit keeps polyamine pools within a narrow range, and its loss contributes to the elevated polyamine levels characteristic of transformed and rapidly proliferating cells. When polyamines rise they promote a ribosomal frameshift that produces antizyme (OAZ1, OAZ2, OAZ3), which binds ODC1 and exposes a C-terminal degron; the heterodimer is then destroyed by the 26S proteasome without ubiquitination, the antizyme subunit being released to act again. Antizyme additionally blocks polyamine uptake, while the antizyme inhibitor AZIN1 sequesters antizyme to relieve repression. NQO1 and the proteasome activator-associated subunits shown here place the reaction in the context of ubiquitin-independent turnover of short-lived regulatory enzymes.

Thyroid hormone action on target tissues is set less by the gland than by local enzymatic conversion, and the three iodothyronine deiodinases perform that conversion. The thyroid secretes mostly T4, a reservoir with little intrinsic activity; outer-ring deiodination by DIO1 and DIO2 removes an iodine to yield T3, the form that binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors and drives transcription of genes for basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, growth and neurodevelopment. DIO3 does the opposite, catalysing inner-ring deiodination to generate inactive reverse T3 and T2, and so shields tissues such as the placenta and fetal brain from excess hormone. Because these selenoenzymes are expressed differently across liver, thyroid, brown fat, brain, pituitary and placenta, each tissue tunes its own intracellular T3 supply, contributing to pituitary feedback on thyrotropin output. Disturbed deiodinase activity underlies the low-T3 state of severe illness and selenium deficiency, and altered hormone availability during development.

Agmatine is a small amine made by decarboxylating arginine and removed by hydrolysis to putrescine and urea, and this short route sets its level in brain and other tissues. Agmatine acts as a candidate neuromodulator, binding imidazoline and alpha-2 adrenergic sites and blocking NMDA receptors and nitric oxide synthase, which underlies interest in it for pain, mood, seizure and neuroprotection; its turnover also links arginine handling to polyamine supply, connecting the early inflammatory use of arginine for nitric oxide with the later proliferative and repair phase that needs polyamines. Two activities define the pathway: an arginine decarboxylase step, attributed in humans to AZIN2, and agmatinase (AGMAT), a mitochondrial manganese enzyme that clears agmatine and feeds putrescine into spermidine and spermine synthesis. Flux here therefore tunes both neuronal signalling and polyamine-dependent growth.

Polyamines are small polycations required for proliferation, translation and chromatin function, and their levels are held within a narrow range by a retroconversion route that runs the biosynthetic pathway backwards. This interconversion of polyamines lets cells convert spermine back to spermidine and spermidine back to putrescine rather than relying only on synthesis and export. The cytosolic acetyltransferase SAT1 attaches an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to spermidine or spermine, and the peroxisomal FAD oxidase PAOX then cleaves the acetylated intermediate, releasing an aminoaldehyde and hydrogen peroxide. SMOX acts directly on spermine without prior acetylation, also generating peroxide. Because SAT1 is strongly and rapidly inducible, it is the main throttle on polyamine pools, coupling polyamine turnover to acetyl-CoA use and to oxidative stress; excess flux through the oxidases contributes to DNA damage and inflammatory tissue injury.</description>}Here's the JSON:. {

Polyamine metabolism supplies putrescine, spermidine and spermine, small polycations that bind nucleic acids and membranes and are required for the proliferation of essentially every cell, for translation (including hypusine modification of eIF5A) and for ion channel regulation. Output is controlled at the committed step: ornithine decarboxylase converts ornithine to putrescine, and decarboxylated S-adenosylmethionine from AMD1 provides the aminopropyl groups added by spermidine and spermine synthases. Arginine can instead be decarboxylated to agmatine, which AGMAT hydrolyses to putrescine. Levels are held in a narrow range by unusually rapid turnover: antizymes target ODC1 for ubiquitin-independent destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose subunits form much of this pathway, while antizyme inhibitors sequester them. A back-conversion arm through SAT1 acetylation with SMOX and PAOX oxidation drains excess and generates hydrogen peroxide. Sustained overproduction is characteristic of tumours, making ODC1 a chemopreventive target.

A dying cell must let go of its neighbours, and caspase cleavage of cell adhesion proteins is how that detachment is executed. This is the step that turns an apoptotic commitment into the visible morphology of apoptosis: loss of epithelial contact, cell rounding, collapse of the keratin intermediate filament network, and eventual shedding of the corpse from a sheet without breaching the barrier. Executioner caspase-3 targets all three junction types — desmosomal cadherins and their plakin and plakophilin linkers, E-cadherin and its partner beta-catenin at adherens junctions, and occludin with the ZO scaffolds at tight junctions. Because these substrates anchor the cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane, their proteolysis simultaneously severs mechanical coupling and frees cytoplasmic pools of signalling molecules such as beta-catenin. In epithelia, this controlled dismantling permits cell turnover while the tissue retains its sealing function.

Amino acid transport across the plasma membrane moves amino acids into and out of cells, and it is what allows dietary protein absorbed in the intestine to be reclaimed in the kidney proximal tubule and delivered to tissues for protein synthesis, neurotransmitter and glutathione production, and nitrogen handling. Physiologists first defined these activities as transport "systems" distinguished by substrate preference, pH dependence and coupling to sodium, chloride or exchange of a counter-amino acid; the carriers are members of several solute carrier families, including sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporters, cationic transporters, proton-coupled carriers, and heteromeric exchangers built from a heavy chain such as SLC3A1 or SLC3A2 paired with a light chain. Loss of individual members causes recognisable transport diseases, including cystinuria, Hartnup disorder and lysinuric protein intolerance, while SLC7A11 and SLC7A5 link this uptake to redox balance, ferroptosis and mTORC1 nutrient sensing.

Cells cannot make protein, glutathione or neurotransmitters without first importing the relevant amino acids, and amino acid transport across the plasma membrane is the set of carriers that does this. It underlies dietary absorption in the intestine, reabsorption from the glomerular filtrate in the kidney proximal tubule, and delivery of substrates to every tissue; loss of individual carriers causes distinct aminoacidurias, including cystinuria from failure of the cystine/dibasic carrier formed by SLC3A1 with SLC7A9 and Hartnup disorder from loss of the neutral amino acid transporter SLC6A19. The transporters here span several families with different mechanisms: sodium- and chloride-coupled symporters, proton-coupled carriers, obligate exchangers such as the SLC7 members that heterodimerise with the heavy chain SLC3A2, and facilitative uniporters. Their combined activity sets intracellular amino acid pools, which in turn feed nutrient sensing and growth signalling.

Dismantling of the nuclear lamina is one of the committed steps of apoptosis, converting a reversible stress response into an irreversible collapse of nuclear architecture. The lamina is a meshwork of intermediate filament proteins, here A-type and B-type lamins, that lines the inner nuclear membrane, gives the nucleus its shape and mechanical stiffness, and anchors chromatin and nuclear pore complexes. During execution of cell death, activated caspase-6 cleaves lamins at a conserved site in their rod domain, so the filament network can no longer polymerise. The nucleus shrinks and fragments, chromatin condenses, and the cell breaks into the apoptotic bodies cleared by phagocytes. Without this cleavage, nuclei resist condensation and apoptotic disassembly stalls, linking caspase proteolysis directly to the nuclear morphology used to recognise dying cells.

Integrin signalling couples cells to the extracellular matrix and turns that physical attachment into decisions about adhesion, migration, survival and proliferation, with the platelet receptor alphaIIb-beta3 serving as the best-worked example. Its function is bidirectional: agonists at a site of vascular injury act through Rap1 GTPases and their exchange factors, together with the adaptor RIAM, to recruit talin to the beta3 tail, which breaks the interaction holding the receptor bent and low-affinity. The primed receptor binds fibrinogen and von Willebrand factor, cross-linking platelets into an aggregate; ligand engagement then signals back inward through Src, Syk, FAK and the Cas-Crk module, plus PI3K-dependent AKT activation, driving cytoskeletal contraction and clot retraction. Loss of the receptor or of talin-mediated activation causes bleeding disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, while the same machinery on adherent cells underlies matrix-dependent anchorage and survival.

Integrins report the state of the extracellular matrix to the cell interior, and this step is how that report reaches the MAP kinase cascade: GRB2 with its exchange factor SOS1 couples an adhesion complex to Ras, converting matrix attachment into proliferative and survival signalling. The context is the activated platelet or adherent cell, where fibrinogen chains, fibronectin and von Willebrand factor engage the ITGA2B/ITGB3 receptor whose cytoplasmic tail is held by talin, with RAP1A/RAP1B and the adaptor APBB1IP acting upstream to bring the receptor into its high-affinity state. Clustering activates focal adhesion kinase (PTK2) and SRC, which phosphorylate sites that recruit the GRB2:SOS pair; loss of this linkage leaves cells attached but unable to translate adhesion into growth-factor-like ERK output, a requirement for anchorage-dependent growth, migration and platelet aggregation.

Diseases associated with glycosaminoglycan metabolism covers the inherited disorders that arise when the sugar chains of proteoglycans cannot be built, sulfated, or broken down correctly. Because glycosaminoglycans attached to core proteins such as aggrecan, versican, decorin, perlecan and the syndecans and glypicans give cartilage, bone, skin and basement membranes their tensile and hydration properties and tune growth factor signalling, defects produce skeletal dysplasias, connective tissue fragility, corneal clouding and neurodegeneration. Loss of the linker-region enzymes B4GALT7, B3GALT6 or B3GAT3 causes Ehlers-Danlos-like and multiple joint dislocation syndromes; EXT1 and EXT2 mutations give hereditary multiple exostoses; sulfotransferase and sulfate transporter defects such as CHST3, CHST6, CHST14 and SLC26A2 underlie chondrodysplasias, macular corneal dystrophy and skin laxity; and hexosaminidase deficiency blocks ganglioside and GAG catabolism in Tay-Sachs and Sandhoff disease. Overgrowth syndromes follow glypican loss.

Glycosaminoglycan chains attached to proteoglycan cores fill the extracellular matrix, hold water in cartilage and cornea, and tether growth factors at cell surfaces, so inherited defects in making or breaking them produce recognisable skeletal, connective tissue and neurological disease. Failures at the linkage-region glycosyltransferases that start a chondroitin or heparan sulfate chain, such as B4GALT7, B3GALT6 and B3GAT3, cause forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia; loss of the EXT1/EXT2 heparan sulfate polymerase gives hereditary multiple exostoses. Sulfation defects are equally damaging: CHST6 mutations cause macular corneal dystrophy, CHST3 and CHST14 alter chondroitin and dermatan sulfation, and PAPSS2 and the sulfate transporter SLC26A2 limit sulfate donor supply, producing chondrodysplasias. On the catabolic side, deficiency of the HEXA or HEXB hexosaminidase subunits blocks ganglioside and GAG degradation. Affected substrates include aggrecan, perlecan, decorin, glypicans and syndecans.

Proteoglycans carry their glycosaminoglycan chains on a shared tetrasaccharide linker built onto a core protein serine, and B4GALT7 adds the first galactose of that linker. When this galactosyltransferase is defective, linker assembly fails across the whole proteoglycan repertoire, producing the progeroid form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: aged facial appearance, short stature, osteopenia, hypermobile joints, hypotonic muscle, loose elastic skin and poor wound healing. The affected acceptors span the matrix and cell surface — small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as decorin and biglycan, the large aggregating lecticans versican, aggrecan-like brevican and neurocan, basement membrane perlecan and agrin, and the syndecan and glypican families that tune growth factor signalling. Loss of their sugar chains degrades collagen fibril organisation, matrix hydration and morphogen presentation, explaining why a single glycosylation step shapes connective tissue integrity and development so broadly.

Defective SLC26A2 causes chondrodysplasias describes what happens to skeletal development when cartilage cells can no longer import sulfate. SLC26A2 is the sulfate transporter that supplies chondrocytes with the intracellular SO4(2-) needed to sulfate the glycosaminoglycan chains of aggrecan and other matrix proteoglycans; that sulfation gives cartilage its fixed negative charge, water retention and compressive resilience. Loss-of-function mutations undersulfate the growth plate matrix, disorganise the extracellular matrix and derail endochondral ossification, producing a graded series of autosomal recessive chondrodysplasias from diastrophic dysplasia through atelosteogenesis type II to perinatally lethal achondrogenesis type 1B. The pathway therefore links a single anion transport step to bone elongation, joint formation and limb and thoracic proportion, and illustrates how sulfur assimilation feeds directly into extracellular matrix biosynthesis in a tissue that depends on it absolutely.

Cartilage stiffness and resilience depend on proteoglycans whose glycosaminoglycan chains are heavily sulfated, and chondrocytes obtain the sulfate for that modification by importing it from outside the cell. SLC26A2 is the sulfate transporter that performs this uptake, exchanging extracellular sulfate for intracellular anions; loss of its activity starves the cell of the substrate needed to make the sulfate donor used in Golgi sulfotransferase reactions. The result is undersulfated matrix proteoglycan, disorganised extracellular matrix, and failure of the growth plate to build normal skeletal elements. Recessive mutations therefore cause a graded family of chondrodysplasias, from diastrophic dysplasia with clubfoot and joint deformity, through atelosteogenesis type II, to lethal achondrogenesis type 1B. The biology links a single anion transport step to skeletal growth, connecting sulfur metabolism with cartilage matrix assembly.

Sulfation of cartilage proteoglycans depends on a supply of the universal sulfate donor PAPS, and PAPSS2 is the enzyme that makes it, combining ATP sulfurylase and APS kinase activities to activate inorganic sulfate. Loss-of-function mutations cause spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia Pakistani type, in which undersulfated chondroitin leaves growth-plate cartilage mechanically inadequate: affected individuals have short stature from birth, bowed lower limbs, mild brachydactyly, kyphoscoliosis, abnormal gait and enlarged knee joints, with epiphyseal dysplasia and milder metaphyseal change. Because the same donor is used by cytosolic sulfotransferases acting on steroids, deficiency also impairs DHEA sulfation, and some patients show premature pubarche and androgen excess. The condition illustrates how a single metabolic cofactor links skeletal matrix assembly to hormone inactivation, and places PAPS synthesis upstream of all sulfoconjugation reactions in the body.

Proteoglycans acquire their glycosaminoglycan chains through a common linker tetrasaccharide, and the glucuronyltransferase B3GAT3 adds the terminal glucuronic acid that allows heparan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate polymerisation to begin. When B3GAT3 activity is lost, that step fails for a whole class of core proteins, producing an autosomal recessive disorder of multiple joint dislocations with short stature, craniofacial dysmorphism and congenital heart defects, clinically reminiscent of Larsen syndrome. The affected acceptors span the matrix and cell surface: perlecan, agrin, the small leucine-rich proteoglycans decorin and biglycan, the hyalectans versican, brevican and neurocan, and the syndecan and glypican families. Their chains organise collagen fibrils and basement membranes, tether growth factors and morphogens, and shape skeletal and cardiac development, which explains why a single sugar transfer defect manifests as connective tissue and cardiovascular malformation.

Chondroitin sulfate is the dominant glycosaminoglycan of cartilage, and its sulfation pattern determines how proteoglycans bind water, growth factors and matrix partners. Carbohydrate sulfotransferase 3 places sulfate at the 6-position of N-acetylgalactosamine residues on chondroitin chains attached to core proteins such as aggrecan-family proteoglycans, versican, brevican, neurocan, decorin and biglycan. When this transfer fails, the resulting undersulfated chains cannot support normal cartilage and joint capsule mechanics, producing spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with congenital joint dislocations: severe progressive kyphoscoliosis, dislocated joints, early arthritic degeneration and short stature in adults. The same modification also shapes chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans of the nervous system, where sulfation influences perineuronal matrix and axon guidance. The biology therefore sits at the junction of Golgi carbohydrate modification, extracellular matrix assembly and skeletal development, and illustrates how a single sugar modification governs connective tissue integrity.
