Dermatan sulfate gets its characteristic sulfation pattern from carbohydrate sulfotransferase 14, which adds sulfate to the 4-position of N-acetylgalactosamine in the growing chain; when the enzyme is defective, proteoglycans that should carry dermatan sulfate are made with incorrectly sulfated glycosaminoglycan instead. The consequence is the musculocontractural form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, in which collagen fibrils are poorly organised and connective tissue fails mechanically, producing craniofacial dysmorphism, congenital contractures of the fingers and thumbs, clubfoot, progressive kyphoscoliosis, muscular hypotonia, skin hyperextensibility and tissue fragility. The affected core proteins span the small leucine-rich proteoglycans decorin and biglycan, which bind and space collagen fibrils, and the large aggregating and cell-surface proteoglycans versican, brevican, neurocan and CSPG4, linking this sulfation step to extracellular matrix assembly in skin, tendon, bone and nervous tissue.

Defective CHSY1 causes TPBS describes what happens to proteoglycan assembly when chondroitin sulfate cannot be polymerised properly, and the skeletal and neurological disease that follows. CHSY1 elongates the chondroitin chain by alternately transferring glucuronate and N-acetylgalactosamine onto core proteins such as versican, aggrecan-family lecticans (brevican, neurocan), decorin, biglycan and the cell-surface proteoglycans CSPG4 and CSPG5. These glycosaminoglycan chains give cartilage and other extracellular matrices their water-binding, load-bearing properties and steer growth-factor and Notch signalling during limb patterning and neural development. Loss-of-function mutations produce temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome, in which affected children show shortened digits with extra phalanges, growth retardation, sensorineural deafness and intellectual disability. The pathway therefore links a single glycosyltransferase step in the Golgi to skeletal morphogenesis, matrix integrity and perineuronal net formation in the nervous system.

Chondroitin sulfate chains are built by alternating addition of glucuronate and N-acetylgalactosamine onto a linker tetrasaccharide, and CHSY1 is a principal polymerizing enzyme of that reaction. When CHSY1 is defective, chain elongation fails and the proteoglycans that depend on it are left with truncated glycosaminoglycan decoration, producing temtamy preaxial brachydactyly syndrome dash congenital anomalies with short digits, extra phalanges, sensorineural deafness, growth retardation and intellectual disability. The affected acceptors span the cartilage and nervous-system matrix: versican, biglycan and decorin in skeletal and connective tissue, brevican, neurocan and CSPG5 in brain perineuronal and interstitial matrix, and CSPG4 on pericytes and glial progenitors. Because chondroitin sulfate controls matrix hydration, growth-factor availability and Notch-dependent limb patterning, loss of its synthesis affects skeletal morphogenesis as much as tissue mechanics, linking a single glycosyltransferase step to digit formation and hearing.

TGF-beta normally acts as a brake on epithelial proliferation, and tumours frequently escape it by destroying the type II receptor that binds the ligand. Loss of TGFBR2 function is a defining event in colorectal cancer: in microsatellite-unstable tumours, short insertions or deletions in a coding adenine repeat cause frameshifts and premature termination of both alleles, while microsatellite-stable tumours more often carry missense changes in the kinase domain that cripple catalytic activity; promoter methylation silences the gene in some lymphomas. Because TGFBR2 must bind TGF-beta1 and then recruit and phosphorylate TGFBR1 to initiate SMAD signalling, its loss aborts the pathway at its first step, removing growth arrest and differentiation cues from the epithelium. Mouse studies confirm the consequence, with intestinal Tgfbr2 deletion accelerating carcinogen- and Apc-driven adenoma and carcinoma formation.

TGF-beta normally restrains the proliferation of epithelial cells, and colorectal tumours with microsatellite instability escape that restraint by mutating the receptor that receives the signal. A short adenine repeat in the coding sequence of the type II TGF-beta receptor is a hotspot for slippage when mismatch repair is defective, and the resulting one- or two-base deletions shift the reading frame and introduce a premature stop codon. Most mutant transcripts are cleared by nonsense-mediated decay; any truncated protein made fails to reach the cell surface, so TGFB1 can no longer engage a functional receptor complex or signal through it. The consequence is loss of TGF-beta-mediated growth inhibition, one of the recurring routes by which mismatch-repair-deficient colon cancers acquire a proliferative advantage, and an illustration of how repeat-tract instability converts a tumour suppressor pathway into a mutational target.

TGFBR2 Kinase Domain Mutants in Cancer describes how loss-of-function missense mutations in the kinase domain of the type II TGF-beta receptor free tumour cells from the growth-suppressive arm of TGF-beta signalling. Normally, TGFB1 binds TGFBR2, which recruits and transphosphorylates TGFBR1 to activate SMAD-dependent transcription that halts epithelial proliferation; a receptor with a dead kinase domain cannot complete this step, so the cytostatic response is lost while the ligand remains present. Such mutations occur in roughly a fifth of microsatellite stable colorectal cancers, typically affecting both alleles, and in esophageal carcinoma the mutant receptor can act dominant-negatively over the wild-type protein. They are distinct from the frameshift inactivation seen in mismatch-repair-deficient tumours, and they mark an early escape from tumour suppression in epithelial carcinogenesis.

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and tumours frequently escape that restraint by damaging the receptor that receives the signal. Missense changes in the kinase domain of the type II TGF-beta receptor, TGFBR2, occur in a substantial minority of microsatellite stable colorectal cancers and in esophageal carcinoma, and they abolish the growth-inhibitory response to TGFB1 while leaving the ligand and the type I receptor intact. In the normal sequence, TGFB1 binding brings TGFBR2 and TGFBR1 into a heteromeric complex in which TGFBR2 kinase activity transphosphorylates TGFBR1 to launch SMAD-dependent transcription of cell cycle inhibitors. Kinase-domain mutants cannot perform that step; some appear to act dominant-negatively by sequestering partners in a non-signalling complex. Loss of this cytostatic arm removes a tumour-suppressive brake on epithelial cells, which is one route by which colorectal and esophageal tumours acquire unchecked proliferation.

Corneal transparency depends on keratan sulfate proteoglycans whose highly sulfated chains keep collagen fibrils thin, evenly spaced and regularly ordered. The Golgi sulfotransferase CHST6 places sulfate on carbon 6 of terminal N-acetylglucosamine residues in keratan sulfate; when it is defective, poorly sulfated or unsulfated keratan accumulates inside keratocytes and in the stromal matrix, and the result is macular corneal dystrophy type I — bilateral, progressive clouding of the cornea beginning early in life with reduced corneal sensitivity, often requiring transplantation. The proteins that carry or accompany these chains are small leucine-rich proteoglycans of the stroma, including keratocan, lumican, mimecan, fibromodulin, osteomodulin and PRELP, alongside the large aggregating proteoglycan aggrecan. Their shared role in collagen fibrillogenesis explains why a single carbohydrate modification step governs whether the cornea remains optically clear.

Lysosomal breakdown of glycoconjugates requires removal of terminal N-acetylgalactosamine, and the alpha subunit encoded by HEXA supplies that activity within the beta-hexosaminidase A heterodimer that degrades GM2 ganglioside and related glycosaminoglycan-derived substrates. Loss-of-function mutations in this subunit cause GM2 gangliosidosis type 1, Tay-Sachs disease, in which undegraded ganglioside accumulates in lysosomes of neurons. The classical infantile form brings early neurodegeneration with progressive paralysis, dementia and blindness and death in the first few years of life, while rarer juvenile- and adult-onset forms reflect residual enzyme activity. The defect illustrates how a single hydrolase step limits the whole catabolic route: the partner beta subunit is intact, but without a functional alpha subunit the A isoenzyme cannot act on its charged substrate, placing this lesion among the lysosomal storage disorders of sphingolipid and carbohydrate turnover.

Heparan sulfate chains decorate proteoglycans at the cell surface and in basement membranes, where they shape gradients of growth factors and morphogens, anchor matrix architecture, and contribute to coagulation, angiogenesis and tumour spread. Their backbone is polymerised in the Golgi by a complex of two exostosin glycosyltransferases that alternately add N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronate to the growing chain. Loss-of-function mutations in EXT2 remove that activity and cause hereditary multiple exostoses type 2, an autosomal dominant disorder in which cartilage-capped bony outgrowths form at the growth plates, deforming the legs, forearms and hands and occasionally progressing to chondrosarcoma. The acceptor proteins left unmodified are the ones listed here: the syndecan family of transmembrane proteoglycans, the GPI-anchored glypicans, and the secreted perlecan and agrin of basement membranes, linking a single Golgi enzyme defect to skeletal patterning.

Sialylation of glycoprotein glycans by ST3GAL3 adds sialic acid in alpha-2,3 linkage to terminal galactose on N- and O-glycans, and the Golgi enzyme's loss in humans causes disease of the developing brain: recessive intellectual disability and a severe early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with profound developmental impairment. The substrates illustrated here are the small leucine-rich proteoglycans and related extracellular matrix proteins of cartilage and other connective tissue -- aggrecan, lumican, fibromodulin, keratocan, osteoglycin, osteomodulin and PRELP -- whose keratan sulfate and other glycan chains receive terminal sialic acid, contributing to the sialyl Lewis a determinant. Terminal sialic acid governs glycan charge, protein half-life and recognition by lectins and selectins, so defective capping alters matrix glycoprotein properties and, in neural tissue, the glycosylation needed for normal cognitive development and seizure control.

Galactose transfer onto N-glycans is the step that converts an immature, trimmed glycan into a mature complex chain, and loss of that activity produces a type II congenital disorder of glycosylation. B4GALT1 encodes the beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase responsible; defective enzyme leaves serum glycoproteins hypogalactosylated, detectable as abnormal transferrin isoforms, and causes a multisystem disease with dysmorphic features, hydrocephalus, hypotonia, myopathy and coagulation abnormalities. The accompanying substrates are extracellular matrix proteoglycans and small leucine-rich repeat proteins / aggrecan, lumican, fibromodulin, keratocan, osteoglycin, osteomodulin and PRELP / whose keratan sulfate and complex N-glycan chains depend on this galactosylation. Their undergalactosylation links the enzymatic lesion to defects in cartilage, cornea and connective tissue, illustrating how a single Golgi glycosylation step shapes matrix assembly, protein stability and development across many organs.

Beta-hexosaminidase removes terminal N-acetylgalactosamine residues from GM2 ganglioside, glycosaminoglycan fragments and other GalNAc-terminated glycoconjugates inside the lysosome, and HEXB encodes the beta subunit shared by both the alpha-beta heterodimeric and beta-only forms of the enzyme. Because the beta subunit is common to both, its loss disables more hydrolytic activity than loss of the alpha subunit alone, affecting both ganglioside turnover and the degradation of GalNAc-bearing glycosaminoglycans. Loss-of-function mutations cause GM2-gangliosidosis type 2, or Sandhoff disease, an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder in which undegraded GM2 accumulates in neurons and produces early blindness with macular cherry-red spots, macrocephaly, and relentless motor and cognitive regression, usually fatal in early childhood. The defect illustrates how a single lysosomal exoglycosidase step limits the catabolism of membrane glycolipids and matrix polysaccharides in the nervous system.

Heparan sulfate chains decorate cell-surface and basement membrane proteoglycans, where they hold growth factors, morphogens and coagulation and angiogenic regulators in place; loss of EXT1 function blocks their synthesis and causes disease. EXT1 partners with EXT2 as a Golgi-membrane glycosyltransferase complex that elongates the chain by adding alternating N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronate to the growing polymer. Without adequate EXT1 activity, the core proteins named here — syndecans, glypicans, perlecan and agrin — carry defective or shortened chains, and signalling gradients that pattern the growth plate go awry. The clinical result is hereditary multiple exostoses type 1, cartilage-capped bony outgrowths that deform forearms, hands and legs, with occasional malignant progression to chondrosarcoma; when the neighbouring TRPS1 gene is also lost, the contiguous deletion produces trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II. This places heparan sulfate chain initiation upstream of skeletal development and matrix organisation.

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and loss of that brake through kinase-domain mutations in the type I receptor TGFBR1 is one route by which tumours escape it. Ligand-bound TGFBR2 recruits and phosphorylates TGFBR1, which in turn phosphorylates the receptor-regulated SMADs SMAD2 and SMAD3, with the FYVE-domain adaptor ZFYVE9 presenting them at the membrane; the activated complex then moves to the nucleus to impose cytostatic transcription. Truncating and splice-site lesions in the kinase domain produce receptors that reach the cell surface but cannot signal, or transcripts destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay, while missense changes leave partially active or unstable protein. The consequence is failed SMAD phosphorylation and unchecked growth, seen in multiple self-healing squamous epithelioma as well as breast, ovarian and head-and-neck carcinoma, placing this defect within growth-factor control of epithelial homeostasis.

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, so tumours often escape by breaking the receptor that receives the signal; loss of function of TGFBR1 is one such escape route, less common than inactivation of TGFBR2 or SMAD4 but documented in pancreatic and biliary duct cancer, lymphoma, breast and ovarian cancer, and in the self-healing squamous tumours of Ferguson-Smith disease. Mutations cluster in the ligand-binding extracellular domain and in the serine/threonine kinase domain, either preventing TGFB1 capture within the heteromeric receptor complex with TGFBR2 or abolishing phosphorylation of the receptor-regulated effectors SMAD2 and SMAD3. Accessory proteins normally governing receptor activity, including the inhibitory FKBP1A bound to the unstimulated receptor and the SARA adaptor ZFYVE9 that presents SMADs at early endosomes, are left without a functional kinase. The result is failure of growth arrest signalling, which cooperates with other tumour suppressor losses such as APC in intestinal tumorigenesis.</response>

TGF-beta normally restrains epithelial proliferation, and loss of that brake is one route to skin and gut cancers. Mutations in the ligand-binding domain of the type I receptor TGFBR1 disrupt this restraint by preventing the receptor from engaging TGF-beta1 presented with the type II receptor TGFBR2, so no active heterotetrameric receptor complex forms and the downstream SMAD-mediated transcriptional response that enforces cytostasis is never triggered. In the inherited setting these variants cause multiple self-healing squamous epithelioma (Ferguson-Smith tumour), an autosomal dominant condition in which tumours commonly lose the remaining wild-type allele, consistent with tumour-suppressor behaviour; comparable somatic ligand-binding domain mutations occur in oesophageal carcinoma. The immunophilin FKBP1A, which binds the unstimulated receptor's GS region and holds it inactive until ligand arrives, marks the step that these mutants never get past.

Transcriptional Regulation by TP53 is the gene expression programme a cell runs when it detects DNA damage, oncogene activation, oxidative stress or nutrient imbalance, and it is the main barrier between a damaged cell and a tumour. TP53 binds response elements as a tetramer and, with coactivators such as EP300/CREBBP and repressive complexes such as NuRD, switches on arrest genes like CDKN1A and GADD45A, apoptotic effectors including BAX, PUMA, NOXA and the TRAIL receptors, DNA repair and checkpoint factors, and metabolic regulators such as TIGAR, SCO2 and the sestrins that tune glycolysis, respiration and mTOR signalling. Its own activity is set by ATM/ATR and checkpoint kinase phosphorylation, acetylation and methylation marks, and MDM2/MDM4-mediated degradation. Loss or mutation of TP53 in roughly half of human cancers removes this coordination of arrest, senescence, repair and death.

TP53 is the transcription factor that converts cellular stress — DNA damage, oncogene activation, nutrient or oxidative imbalance — into a decision about whether a cell continues dividing, pauses, ages out, or dies. Transcriptional regulation by TP53 therefore sits at the centre of tumour suppression, and its loss through mutation in roughly half of human cancers removes the barrier that keeps damaged cells from proliferating. Damage sensors and checkpoint kinases such as ATM, ATR, CHEK1 and CHEK2 stabilise p53 against MDM2-directed degradation, while acetyltransferases, methyltransferases and prolyl isomerases tune which promoters it occupies. The output programmes are broad: CDKN1A and 14-3-3 proteins enforce cell cycle arrest; BAX, PMAIP1, BBC3 and death receptors commit cells to apoptosis; TIGAR, SCO2, glutaminase and sestrins redirect glycolysis, respiration and mTOR signalling; and DNA repair, antioxidant and miRNA-processing effectors support recovery when damage is survivable.

When an integrin engages an extracellular matrix ligand, the adhesion it forms must be converted into a growth and motility signal, and this is the branch that carries it to the MAP kinase cascade. Clustering of the platelet integrin αIIbβ3 on fibrinogen, fibronectin or von Willebrand factor, stabilised on the cytoplasmic side by talin and the Rap1 GTPases with their effector RIAM, assembles a focal adhesion kinase–Src complex. Src-dependent phosphorylation of the docking protein p130Cas creates binding sites for the adaptor Crk, and the resulting Cas–Crk module couples adhesion to Ras–ERK activation and to Rac-driven cytoskeletal remodelling. The output is spreading, migration and, in platelets, firm aggregation and clot retraction; loss of the integrin or its activation machinery causes bleeding disorders, while the same signalling axis is exploited by invasive tumour cells.

Seven-transmembrane receptors form the largest receptor family in the human genome, and signaling by GPCR is how cells read light, odorants, tastants, hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines, lipid mediators and nucleotides at the plasma membrane and convert them into intracellular change. This breadth explains why the family underlies vision, olfaction and taste, autonomic and endocrine control, platelet activation, leukocyte chemotaxis and inflammation, and why it is the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. Ligand binding triggers nucleotide exchange on heterotrimeric G proteins, whose alpha subunits of the Gs, Gi, Gq and G12/13 classes act on adenylate cyclases, phospholipase C beta, PI3K and Rho GTPase exchange factors, raising cyclic AMP, inositol phosphates, calcium and diacylglycerol and engaging protein kinases A and C, calmodulin-dependent kinases and ERK. Signals are terminated by RGS proteins, phosphodiesterases, and receptor kinases with arrestins that desensitize and internalize the receptor. Frizzled, Smoothened and taste receptors extend the family into developmental patterning and sensory reception.

The rhodopsin-like receptors, class A/1, are by far the largest family of G protein-coupled receptors and the one most heavily exploited by drugs, from beta-blockers and antihistamines to opioid analgesics and antipsychotics. Together with their ligands they let cells read almost every kind of extracellular chemical signal: photons captured by rhodopsin and the cone opsins, biogenic amines such as adrenaline, dopamine, serotonin, histamine and acetylcholine, peptide hormones including vasopressin, oxytocin, angiotensin, somatostatin and the melanocortins, lipid mediators such as prostaglandins, leukotrienes, sphingosine-1-phosphate and cannabinoids, nucleotides, protons, free fatty acids, and the full chemokine system with its receptors and decoy receptors. All couple through heterotrimeric G proteins to change cyclic nucleotide levels, calcium and kinase activity, so this group underlies vision, neurotransmission, endocrine control of reproduction and metabolism, vascular tone, platelet activation, and leukocyte recruitment during inflammation.

Secretin-family (class B/2) G protein-coupled receptors read a large group of peptide hormones and translate them into cyclic AMP and calcium signals, chiefly through Gs and the heterotrimeric G protein subunits represented here. The hormones involved govern whole-body physiology: glucagon, GIP and GLP-1 set insulin secretion and glucose handling, parathyroid hormone and calcitonin with their receptors control calcium and bone remodelling, corticotropin-releasing hormone and urocortins drive the stress axis, growth hormone-releasing hormone controls pituitary output, and secretin, VIP and PACAP act on gut and neural targets. Accessory RAMP proteins redirect the calcitonin receptor-like receptor toward adrenomedullin and CGRP, the basis of migraine therapeutics, while GLP-1 receptor agonists treat diabetes and obesity. Also grouped in this structural class are the adhesion receptors, Frizzleds serving as Wnt receptors, and Smoothened with Patched in Hedgehog signalling, linking the family to developmental patterning as well as endocrine control.

Growing axons find their targets by reading gradients of secreted cues, and netrin-1 signaling is the archetype of that guidance: the same ligand attracts some axons and repels others depending on which receptor the growth cone displays. Attraction runs through DCC and neogenin, repulsion through the UNC5 family, and loss of these interactions misroutes commissural axons across the midline and disrupts neuronal migration during nervous system development. Downstream, receptor engagement recruits Src-family and focal adhesion kinases, the phosphatase PTPN11, adaptors such as NCK1 and DOCK1, and Rho-family GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 with the exchange factor TRIO, remodelling actin via ABLIM proteins, WASL and myosin-X; TRPC channels and phospholipase C couple the signal to calcium entry. Related repulsive systems are represented by SLIT ligands with ROBO1 and by RGM proteins, and the DSCAM adhesion receptors participate in the same guidance decisions.

The kidney's filtration barrier depends on the slit diaphragm, a specialised junction between podocyte foot processes, and nephrin family interactions are what hold that structure together. Nephrin, an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor expressed prominently in podocytes, engages itself homophilically across the slit and heterophilically with KIRREL1, KIRREL2 and KIRREL3 on the opposing cell, defining the pore that retains plasma protein. On the cytoplasmic side podocin, CD2AP, MAGI2, CASK, IQGAP1, alpha-actinins and spectrins couple the receptor to the actin cytoskeleton, so that adhesion and foot process shape are mechanically linked; NCK adaptors and WASL direct local actin polymerisation. Tyrosine phosphorylation by the Src-family kinase FYN recruits PI3K subunits and drives AKT-dependent survival signalling. Loss of nephrin or podocin collapses the barrier, giving congenital nephrotic syndrome and steroid-resistant proteinuria.

Semaphorins are secreted and membrane-bound guidance cues that tell migrating cells and growing axons where not to go, and their interactions with plexin and neuropilin receptor complexes shape axon pathfinding, cortical wiring, vascular patterning, bone remodelling and immune cell contacts. Binding typically collapses the growth cone: plexins act on small GTPases of the Rho and Ras families, with RhoA-ROCK, Rac1-PAK and LIM kinase feeding onto cofilin and non-muscle myosin II to disassemble actin and retract protrusions, while CDK5 and GSK3B phosphorylate collapsin response mediator proteins to destabilise microtubules and integrin-talin adhesions are weakened. Neuropilin-1 serves as a ligand-binding co-receptor for class 3 semaphorins, and receptor tyrosine kinases such as MET and ERBB2 can be recruited to switch responses toward attraction or invasion. Immune-restricted members signal through CD72 and TREM2-TYROBP, linking this guidance chemistry to myeloid and lymphocyte regulation.

Sidekick-1 and sidekick-2 are immunoglobulin superfamily adhesion molecules that let a developing neuron find the right synaptic partner rather than merely the right neighbourhood. Each is expressed by a distinct, non-overlapping subset of retinal neurons, and each binds itself: homophilic adhesion between a presynaptic and a postsynaptic cell carrying the same sidekick concentrates the pair at a shared synapse and stabilises it. Because retinal interneurons and ganglion cells stratify their processes into narrow laminae of the inner plexiform layer, this matching translates into lamina-specific wiring, and loss of SDK2 disrupts the circuit that computes the direction of visual motion. These interactions therefore represent adhesion used as a targeting code, a general strategy by which cell-surface recognition proteins convert overlapping neurite arbors into selective, functional neuronal circuits.

L1CAM interactions cover the adhesive and signalling functions of the L1 family of immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors — L1, CHL1, NrCAM and neurofascin — which guide axon outgrowth, fasciculation and neuron-neuron adhesion during nervous system development. Loss-of-function mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and corpus callosum agenesis with spasticity and intellectual disability, illustrating how much of cortical wiring depends on this adhesion. Extracellularly the receptors engage contactins, NCAM, neurocan, laminin, beta1 and other integrins, and neuropilins, and cooperate with FGF and EGF receptors; intracellularly their conserved tails bind ankyrins, which couple them through spectrin to the actin and tubulin cytoskeleton. That link clusters voltage-gated sodium channels and KCNQ subunits at axon initial segments and nodes of Ranvier. Src, PAK1/RAC1, casein kinase 2 and ERK signalling, together with clathrin\/AP-2-mediated endocytosis, control receptor turnover and growth-cone motility.

NCAM signaling for neurite out-growth describes how the neural cell adhesion molecule converts cell-cell and cell-matrix contact into the intracellular signals that drive axon extension, neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. It builds and maintains nervous system wiring; loss of this adhesion-coupled signalling impairs neurite growth and activity-dependent remodelling. NCAM1 acts partly by activating FGFR1 and partly by nucleating a cytoplasmic complex with Fyn, Src and focal adhesion kinase, regulated by the phosphatase RPTPalpha, feeding through Grb2/SOS to Ras and ERK1/2 and on to MSK1 and CREB-dependent transcription of growth and survival genes. Polysialylation by ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 tunes adhesive strength, spectrin cytoskeletal links anchor the receptor, and collagens and other matrix components, voltage-gated calcium channels and GDNF-family ligands with their GFRA receptors act as partners and parallel inputs to the same growth programme.

Growing axons decide where to extend by reading cell-surface adhesion cues, and NCAM signalling for neurite outgrowth is one of the main routes by which that contact is converted into growth. It shapes how neurons differentiate, extend processes and remodel synapses, and it underlies aspects of learning-related plasticity and nervous system wiring. Homophilic NCAM1 engagement, modulated by polysialylation from ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4, recruits the Src-family kinase Fyn together with focal adhesion kinase, and also transactivates FGFR1; GRB2/SOS coupling to Ras drives ERK1/2 and, via MSK1, CREB-dependent transcription of genes for axon growth and neuronal survival. RPTP-alpha supplies the dephosphorylation step that activates Fyn. Spectrin scaffolds link the receptor to the submembrane cytoskeleton, while collagens, agrin and neurocan represent the extracellular matrix context, and GDNF-family ligands with their GFRA co-receptors provide a parallel NCAM-dependent input. Voltage-gated calcium channels couple adhesion to calcium entry.

Peptide ligand-binding receptors are the arm of the rhodopsin-like G protein-coupled receptor family that reads short peptides and proteins rather than small amines or lipids, and through them the body coordinates pain, appetite, blood pressure, water balance, reproduction and inflammation. The grouping pairs ligands with their receptors: chemokines with the CC, CXC and CX3C receptors that steer leukocyte trafficking and lymphoid organisation, opioid peptides derived from proenkephalin, prodynorphin and proopiomelanocortin with the opioid receptors, somatostatin, neuropeptide Y, tachykinins, galanin, orexins, ghrelin and kisspeptin with their cognate receptors, and vasoactive peptides such as angiotensin, endothelin, bradykinin and vasopressin with theirs. Thrombin acts here by cleaving protease-activated receptors, and complement fragments C3a and C5a signal through their own receptors, while atypical chemokine receptors scavenge ligand instead of signalling. These receptors are among the most heavily exploited drug targets, in analgesia, hypertension, obesity and HIV entry blockade.

Biogenic amines act as neurotransmitters and hormones, and the amine ligand-binding receptors are the rhodopsin-like G protein-coupled receptors through which they signal. Adrenergic, muscarinic acetylcholine, dopamine, histamine and serotonin receptor families here set heart rate and vascular tone, bronchial and smooth muscle contraction, gastric acid secretion, wakefulness, mood, reward and motor control; trace amine receptors respond to tyramine, phenylethylamine and related compounds, with one family member also detecting volatile amine odours. Ligand binding in a pocket within the seven-transmembrane bundle shifts the receptor to an active conformation that couples to Gs, Gi/o or Gq, raising or lowering cAMP or mobilising calcium, and is followed by arrestin-mediated desensitisation. Because these receptors dominate autonomic and central signalling, they are among the most heavily drugged proteins in medicine, targeted by beta-blockers, antipsychotics, antihistamines, bronchodilators and antiemetics.

Endocrine control of reproduction and thyroid function runs through a small family of rhodopsin-like G protein-coupled receptors that recognise peptide and glycoprotein hormones. The glycoprotein hormones follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone and chorionic gonadotropin each pair a shared alpha subunit, encoded by CGA, with a distinct beta subunit, and act on large extracellular leucine-rich domains of FSHR, LHCGR and TSHR to drive cAMP signalling in granulosa and Sertoli cells, Leydig and theca cells, and thyroid follicular cells respectively. Upstream, gonadotropin-releasing hormone acting through GNRHR in pituitary gonadotropes sets the pulsatile drive for gonadotropin secretion. Loss-of-function mutations in these ligands or receptors cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, infertility and congenital hypothyroidism, while activating receptor mutations underlie precocious puberty and toxic thyroid nodules; the same receptors are the targets of fertility therapeutics.

DSCAM and its paralogue DSCAML1 are immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptors on the neuronal surface, and their interactions guide growing axons and set the spacing of neurites and cell bodies in the developing nervous system. Both engage in homophilic binding, cell to cell, which mediates self-recognition and the repulsion that keeps sister branches and like neurons from overlapping; loss of this activity disrupts dendritic tiling and retinal mosaic arrangement. DSCAM also cooperates with the netrin receptor DCC in responding to the secreted guidance cue netrin-1, linking adhesive contact to the attractive turning of commissural axons at the midline. The gene lies in the chromosome 21 region associated with Down syndrome, though a direct causal contribution remains unproven. Overall this is cell-surface adhesion feeding into axon pathfinding, lamina targeting and the wiring precision of neural circuits.

Growing axons are steered as much by being pushed away from the wrong territory as by being drawn to the right one, and ROBO receptor signalling is the repulsive arm of that decision. SLIT proteins binding ROBO1 and ROBO2 collapse or turn growth cones at the midline, keeping commissural axons from recrossing and setting the position of major spinal and forebrain tracts; ROBO3 responds instead to NELL2, while related guidance cues such as netrin with DCC and CXCL12-CXCR4 shape the same trajectories. The output is cytoskeletal: ABL kinases, Ena/VASP proteins, profilins, CLASPs, and Rho-family GTPases with their PAK effectors and SRGAP inactivators remodel actin and microtubules in the turning tip. Receptor levels are themselves controlled, through ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, deubiquitination by USP33, and translational and nonsense-mediated decay machinery, alongside LIM-homeodomain transcription factors that specify which neurons express which ROBO. Beyond neurons, this signalling also guides endothelial behaviour during vessel formation.

WNT signalling ends by dismantling the beta-catenin/TCF transactivating complex in the nucleus, and this shutdown sets how long and how strongly target genes such as those driving proliferation and stem-cell maintenance stay on. Loss of these brakes leaves TCF-dependent transcription constitutively active, the situation in colorectal and other cancers where APC is mutated. Several mechanisms converge: CTNNBIP1 (ICAT) and Chibby bind beta-catenin directly and block its contact with TCF/LEF and coactivators, Chibby together with 14-3-3 proteins and the exportin XPO1 driving nuclear export; Groucho/TLE repressors and HDAC1 or CTBP1 reoccupy TCF sites; nuclear APC helps disassemble the complex. Numerous SOX factors also antagonise or redirect beta-catenin-TCF output. The coactivator side that is displaced includes BCL9, Pygopus and the WDR5-containing MLL methyltransferase module, and ubiquitin-dependent turnover completes the return to the off state.

WNT ligands acting through beta-catenin and TCF/LEF transcription factors drive stem cell maintenance, patterning and bone accrual, and secreted antagonists set the limits of that signalling in space and time. Two mechanistic classes are represented here. Secreted frizzled-related proteins such as SFRP1 and SFRP2, and WNT inhibitory factor WIF1, sequester WNT ligands themselves, preventing engagement of frizzled receptors and shaping how far a WNT gradient spreads across a tissue. Dickkopf proteins DKK1, DKK2 and DKK4, together with the transmembrane partners KREMEN1 and KREMEN2, and the osteocyte product sclerostin instead target the co-receptors LRP5 and LRP6, disrupting formation of the ligand-induced frizzled-LRP complex. This arm has direct clinical weight: loss of sclerostin causes high bone mass, and antibodies against it are used to treat osteoporosis. Excess antagonism restrains regeneration, while its loss permits inappropriate pathway activation.

N-linked glycans are built on a dolichol-phosphate carrier in the endoplasmic reticulum, transferred to asparagine residues of nascent proteins, and then trimmed and rebuilt in the Golgi; inherited defects in these steps cause congenital disorders of glycosylation. Because glycans govern protein folding and quality control, cell adhesion and recognition, protease resistance and immune function, patients typically present with multisystem disease: developmental delay, hypotonia, coagulation abnormalities, liver and gut involvement. Mannosyltransferases and glucosyltransferases of the ALG family, together with the GlcNAc-1-phosphate transferase DPAGT1 and the flippase RFT1, account for assembly-stage defects, while MOGS, MAN1B1, MGAT2 and B4GALT1 disrupt processing and terminal elaboration. Lysosomal sialidase and beta-galactosidase deficiencies, with the protective protein cathepsin A, cause glycan degradation to fail instead, producing sialidosis, galactosialidosis and GM1 gangliosidosis.

Diseases of glycosylation collects the inherited defects that disrupt attachment and elaboration of sugar chains on proteins and lipids, the congenital disorders of glycosylation. Because nearly every secreted and membrane protein is glycosylated, these defects produce multisystem disease, most often psychomotor retardation, seizures, coagulopathy and skeletal or connective tissue abnormality; N-glycosylation defects such as PMM2-CDG are the largest group and are detected by abnormal transferrin isoforms. The genes trace each affected step: nucleotide-sugar supply and galactose metabolism, dolichol synthesis and the ALG enzymes that build the lipid-linked precursor, oligosaccharyltransferase-associated processing, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan underlying muscular dystrophies, O-fucosylation that tunes Notch, and assembly of proteoglycan linkage regions on syndecans, glypicans and lecticans. Lysosomal glycan degradation defects and mucin-type O-glycosylation belong here too. Treatment remains largely supportive.

Congenital disorders of glycosylation are inherited failures to build or attach glycans, and because nearly every secreted and membrane protein is glycosylated, the consequences are multisystem: psychomotor retardation, coagulopathy, liver and skeletal disease, and in the N-linked forms a diagnostic shift in the isoelectric focusing pattern of plasma transferrin. The genes here span the routes that can break. Lipid-linked oligosaccharide assembly on dolichol and its transfer and trimming account for classic N-glycosylation defects such as PMM2-CDG and the ALG deficiencies; O-mannosylation enzymes including POMT1, POMT2 and POMGNT1 modify dystroglycan and, when lost, cause muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy; O-fucose and O-glucose modification of Notch receptors tunes Notch signalling; and defects in the xylose-galactose-galactose linker built by B4GALT7, B3GALT6 and B3GAT3 disrupt proteoglycan assembly on decorin, perlecan, syndecans and the aggrecan-versican family, producing skeletal and connective tissue fragility. Nucleotide-sugar supply, sulfation and lysosomal glycan catabolism are affected likewise. Treatment remains largely supportive.

Lafora disease is an inherited progressive myoclonic epilepsy of late childhood in which seizures and relentless neurological decline follow the accumulation of insoluble, abnormally branched and phosphorylated glycogen, forming Lafora bodies in brain, muscle, liver and heart. It is best understood as a glycogen storage disorder: preventing glycogen synthesis in mouse models prevents the disease. Normal glycogen turnover depends on laforin (EPM2A), a glucan phosphatase on cytosolic glycogen granules that removes the phosphate groups occasionally introduced during chain elongation by glycogen synthase (GYS1) acting on the glycogenin (GYG1) core, and on malin (NHLRC1), a ubiquitin ligase that polyubiquitinates laforin, with ubiquitin supplied by the conjugation pool, marking it for proteasomal degradation. Recessive loss of either protein leaves glycogen over-phosphorylated and poorly soluble, and the resulting deposits underlie neurodegeneration. The glycogen-targeting subunit PPP1R3C links the process to phosphatase-driven activation of synthesis.

Dopamine signalling is terminated not only by reuptake but by chemical destruction of the transmitter, and this route begins with catechol-O-methyltransferase. After the dopamine transporter returns dopamine to the cytosol, COMT transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine onto the 3-hydroxyl of the catechol ring to give 3-methoxytyramine, which monoamine oxidase A then oxidatively deaminates, yielding homovanillic acid as the end product measured clinically as an index of dopamine turnover. Because COMT clears dopamine where transporter density is low, this arm matters most in prefrontal cortex, and common functional variation in the enzyme is linked to differences in executive function; the pathway is also the reason COMT inhibitors extend the action of L-DOPA in Parkinson's disease. A related transmembrane O-methyltransferase, TOMT, shares the methyltransferase chemistry but acts in hair cell mechanotransduction rather than catecholamine turnover.

Enzymatic degradation of Dopamine by monoamine oxidase terminates dopamine signalling after the neurotransmitter is taken back up into presynaptic terminals and glia, setting how long and how strongly dopaminergic transmission acts on motor control, reward and executive function. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, oxidatively deaminates dopamine to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid, which catechol-O-methyltransferase then methylates to homovanillic acid, the principal dopamine metabolite excreted in urine and measured in cerebrospinal fluid. The reaction generates hydrogen peroxide and reactive aldehydes, linking catecholamine turnover to oxidative stress in substantia nigra neurons. Both enzymes are pharmacological targets: MAO inhibitors and COMT inhibitors prolong dopamine action in Parkinson's disease and depression, while common COMT variants alter prefrontal dopamine tone and cognitive performance.

Dopamine signalling ends when the transmitter is broken down, and this route accounts for its enzymatic degradation by monoamine oxidase in neurons and surrounding tissue. Dopamine taken back up from the synapse is oxidatively deaminated by monoamine oxidase at the outer mitochondrial membrane, producing an aldehyde that is further oxidised to 3,4-dihydroxyphenylacetic acid; catechol-O-methyltransferase then methylates a hydroxyl group to give homovanillic acid, the excreted end product measured as an index of dopamine turnover. By limiting how long dopamine persists, this catabolism sets the gain of dopaminergic transmission in motor control, reward and prefrontal cognition, and its inhibition is deliberately exploited in Parkinson's disease and depression. The deamination step also generates hydrogen peroxide and reactive aldehydes, linking dopamine breakdown to oxidative stress in dopaminergic neurons; common variation in these enzymes alters catecholamine tone and behaviour.

Dopaminergic signalling is terminated not by the receptor but by removal of transmitter from the extracellular space, and this pathway covers that clearance step. The sodium-dependent dopamine transporter encoded by SLC6A3 pumps released dopamine back into the presynaptic terminal, limiting the duration and spatial spread of the signal and recycling transmitter for repackaging into vesicles. Dopamine that is not reused is inactivated enzymatically: catechol-O-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group to the catechol hydroxyl, while monoamine oxidase A oxidatively deaminates the amine, together with a related methyltransferase activity. Because this machinery sets synaptic dopamine tone, it determines the targets of psychostimulants such as cocaine and amphetamine, of MAO inhibitors used as antidepressants, and it shapes susceptibility to movement disorders, attention deficit phenotypes and disturbances of reward and motivation.

Cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that loads each tRNA with its correct amino acid, setting the accuracy of the genetic code before a ribosome ever reads a codon. Without faithful charging, mistranslated proteins accumulate and translation stalls; inherited mutations in these synthetases cause peripheral neuropathies, leukodystrophies and multisystem developmental disease. Each enzyme activates its cognate amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the tRNA 3' end, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate, with inorganic pyrophosphatase pulling the reaction forward. Eight of the human enzymes, including the bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl synthetase and those for arginine, lysine, methionine and isoleucine, assemble with the AIMP scaffolding proteins into a multisynthetase complex that channels charged tRNAs toward elongation factors and the ribosome. Released components of that complex moonlight in angiogenesis, inflammation and stress signalling, linking translational supply to cell state.

Every round of protein synthesis in the cytoplasm begins with charging a tRNA with its matching amino acid, and cytosolic tRNA aminoacylation is the step that establishes the accuracy of the genetic code. A family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, one for most amino acids plus a bifunctional glutamyl-prolyl enzyme, activates the amino acid with ATP and transfers it to the 3' end of a nuclear-encoded tRNA, releasing AMP and pyrophosphate; a pyrophosphatase removes the latter to keep the reaction favourable. Eight of these enzymes assemble with the accessory factors AIMP1, AIMP2 and EEF1E1 into a multi-synthetase complex thought to channel charged tRNAs to translating ribosomes, and several components moonlight in angiogenesis, inflammation and DNA damage signalling. Mutations in individual synthetases such as GARS1 and AARS1 cause peripheral neuropathies and multisystem developmental disorders, reflecting how narrowly translation tolerates mischarging.

Every round of protein synthesis begins with charging a tRNA with its matching amino acid, and tRNA aminoacylation is the step that sets the genetic code's accuracy at the chemical level. Each synthetase activates its amino acid with ATP to form an aminoacyl adenylate, then transfers it to the 3' end of the cognate tRNA, releasing AMP; pyrophosphatases such as PPA1 and PPA2 destroy the released pyrophosphate and make the reaction effectively irreversible. Proofreading domains hydrolyse misactivated amino acids rather than pass them to the ribosome. Separate nuclear genes supply cytosolic and mitochondrial enzymes for most amino acids, so mitochondrial translation depends on its own set, and several cytosolic enzymes sit in a multi-synthetase complex with AIMP scaffolding subunits that also carry signalling roles. Mutations cause peripheral neuropathies, leukoencephalopathies and mitochondrial disease.

Mitochondria translate their own thirteen respiratory chain subunits, and that translation depends on charging the mitochondrially encoded tRNAs with their correct amino acids. A dedicated set of nuclear-encoded aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases is imported into the matrix to do this, each ligating one amino acid to its cognate tRNA using ATP and releasing AMP and pyrophosphate; an inorganic pyrophosphatase clears the byproduct and keeps the reaction favourable. Most of these enzymes are distinct gene products from their cytosolic counterparts, though the glycine, lysine and glutamine enzymes are made as dual-localised isoforms from a single gene. Because accurate charging sets the fidelity and rate of mitochondrial protein synthesis, mutations in individual synthetases cause oxidative phosphorylation deficiency with strikingly tissue-specific presentations, including leukoencephalopathies, cardiomyopathy, sensorineural deafness and ovarian failure.

Tachykinins are short neuropeptides that end in a shared C-terminal motif and act on three G protein-coupled receptors, NK1, NK2 and NK3, to excite neurons, dilate blood vessels and contract smooth muscle. This ligand-receptor pairing underlies rapid gut contraction, from which the peptides take their name, and also pain and itch transmission, neurogenic inflammation, vomiting, airway and bladder tone, and hypothalamic control of reproductive hormone release. Two genes supply the ligands: TAC1 encodes substance P and neurokinin A, while TAC3 encodes neurokinin B, whose signalling through TACR3 is required for normal GnRH secretion, so loss-of-function mutations cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Receptor coupling drives phospholipase C, calcium mobilisation and depolarisation in target cells. NK1 blockade is used clinically against chemotherapy-induced nausea, and antagonists of these receptors have been pursued as antidepressants, anxiolytics and antipsychotics.

Chemokine receptors bind chemokines is the ligand-recognition step that tells leukocytes where to go. Chemokines secreted at sites of infection, injury or within lymphoid tissue form gradients, and G protein-coupled receptors on the cell surface read them, triggering intracellular calcium flux, cytoskeletal remodelling and directed chemotaxis. This underlies neutrophil recruitment to inflamed tissue, the homing of naive T cells and dendritic cells into lymph nodes via CCR7, B cell positioning in germinal centres through CXCR5, and haematopoietic stem cell retention in marrow through the CXCL12-CXCR4 axis. Ligand-receptor pairing is subfamily-restricted but highly redundant, with many chemokines binding several receptors. Atypical receptors such as ACKR2 and ACKR3 bind without conventional signalling, instead scavenging ligand to shape gradients. Misuse of these receptors permits HIV entry, and their dysregulation drives chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and tumour metastasis.

Leukocytes find their way to infection, injury and lymphoid tissue by reading gradients of secreted chemoattractant proteins, and the binding of chemokines to their G protein-coupled receptors is the recognition step that sets that migration in motion. Ligands of the CC, CXC, CX3C and XC families engage matching receptors such as CCR1-CCR10, CXCR1-CXCR6, CX3CR1 and XCR1, triggering calcium flux, integrin activation and directed chemotaxis. The pairings define immune cell behaviour: CCR7 with CCL19 and CCL21 routes dendritic cells and naive T cells into lymph nodes, CXCR4 with CXCL12 retains progenitors in bone marrow, and CXCR1/CXCR2 with CXCL8 recruits neutrophils to inflamed tissue. Atypical receptors including ACKR2, ACKR3 and ACKR4 bind ligands without conventional signalling, scavenging them to shape gradients. This signalling underlies inflammation, lymphoid organisation, HIV entry and tumour metastasis.

Loss of Nlp from mitotic centrosomes describes a switch in centrosome behaviour at mitotic entry: the interphase microtubule-anchoring factor Nlp is evicted so the centrosome can be rebuilt as a high-capacity spindle pole. This maturation step is what allows a cell to nucleate the dense microtubule arrays needed for bipolar spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation; when it fails, spindles are disorganised and aneuploidy or mitotic arrest follows. Mechanistically, Plk1 activated at G2/M phosphorylates Nlp, displacing it from gamma-tubulin ring complexes, while pericentriolar scaffolds such as pericentrin, CDK5RAP2, CEP192 and AKAP9 recruit gamma-TuRC through NEDD1 and the augmin (HAUS) complex amplifies nucleation. Dynein-dynactin, centrin, NEK2 and centriolar proteins including CEP135, CEP152 and PLK4 tie the process to centriole duplication and pole separation, linking it to broader cell cycle control and ciliopathy-associated centrosome biology.

As cells enter mitosis they rebuild the centrosome into a high-capacity microtubule nucleating hub, and one step in that conversion is the loss of Nlp from mitotic centrosomes. Nlp binds gamma-tubulin ring complexes during interphase and helps organize the interphase microtubule array; when Plk1 is activated at mitotic onset it phosphorylates Nlp and drives it off the centrosome, clearing the way for a mitotic scaffold that nucleates the spindle. The accompanying machinery is the pericentriolar matrix and its regulators — pericentrin, AKAP9, CDK5RAP2 and NEDD1 recruiting gamma-tubulin, centrins and the CEP proteins of the centriole wall, the augmin (HAUS) complex, and dynein–dynactin with CDK1, PLK4 and NEK2 as kinase controls. Correct handover matters for bipolar spindle assembly and accurate chromosome segregation; failure promotes spindle disorganization and aneuploidy, and mutations in these centrosomal components cause microcephaly and ciliopathies.

As cells enter mitosis, interphase centrosomes must be converted into high-capacity microtubule nucleating poles, and this maturation step is what the recruitment of mitotic centrosome proteins and complexes accomplishes. Without it the spindle cannot be built with two robust poles, and errors produce multipolar or misoriented spindles, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy; many of the components are mutated in microcephaly, dwarfism and ciliopathies because the same scaffolds also organise the centriole and cilium. Pericentrin, CEP192, CEP152 and CDK5RAP2 form the pericentriolar scaffold that loads gamma-tubulin ring complexes through NEDD1 and the MZT and TUBGCP subunits, while PLK1, CDK1, NEK2 and casein kinase 1 drive the timing of assembly. Dynein-dynactin with LIS1 and NDE1, the augmin HAUS complex, and plus-end regulators such as ch-TOG and CLASP1 then anchor and amplify microtubules at the poles.

As a cell enters mitosis the centrosome is remodelled, and part of that remodelling is subtractive: proteins that organized the interphase microtubule array and held the two centrioles together are displaced or released so the organelle can switch to high-output spindle pole nucleation. Loss of these factors permits centriole disengagement and separation, converting a single interphase microtubule-organizing centre into two spindle poles. Mitotic kinases drive the change, with NEK2 phosphorylating the cohesion linker components C-Nap1 and rootletin, and PLK1 and CDK1 acting on anchoring and appendage proteins; dynein-dynactin and the HAUS/augmin complex, gamma-tubulin with NEDD1, and pericentrin-AKAP9 scaffolds are among the machinery reorganized. The same proteins double as ciliary base and centriole duplication components, which is why mutations in many of them cause ciliopathies, microcephaly and spindle orientation defects.

As cells approach mitosis, the centrosome is rebuilt into a far more powerful microtubule organizing centre, and this maturation at the G2/M transition determines whether a bipolar spindle can form and chromosomes can be segregated accurately. Pericentriolar scaffolds such as pericentrin, CEP192, CDK5RAP2 and CEP152 expand and recruit the gamma-tubulin ring complex with its NEDD1 and MZT adaptors, so that nucleation capacity rises sharply; the augmin complex adds microtubule-dependent nucleation, while dynein-dynactin and end-binding proteins anchor and stabilise the resulting array. Mitotic kinases drive the switch, with PLK1 and CDK1 activating recruitment and NEK2 dissolving the CEP250-based linker that holds duplicated centrosomes together. Failure of these steps yields disorganised or multipolar spindles and aneuploidy, and mutations in the same centriolar proteins cause microcephaly, ciliopathies and retinal degeneration, reflecting the shared role of this apparatus in cilium formation.

When the nuclear envelope breaks down at mitotic onset, the nuclear matrix protein NuMA is released into the cytoplasm and delivered to the forming spindle poles, where it builds an insoluble crescent that tethers microtubule minus ends into a focused, bipolar array. Without this pole-focusing activity spindles splay apart, chromosome segregation becomes error-prone, and cells risk aneuploidy. Ran-GTP frees NuMA from importin to license its mitotic function, and dynein-dynactin motors together with the dynein regulators NDE1 and LIS1 transport it poleward. The accompanying machinery is that of the centrosome and pericentriolar material itself: gamma-tubulin ring components and their adaptors nucleate microtubules, the augmin complex generates branched microtubules within the spindle, scaffolds such as pericentrin, CEP192 and CDK5RAP2 organise the poles, and CDK1, PLK1 and PLK4 provide the mitotic phosphorylation control. This is the structural foundation on which spindle assembly and centrosome maturation depend.

Metabolism of serotonin is the catabolic route that terminates serotonin signalling and clears the amine from neurons, platelets and the gut. It sets how long serotonin persists after release and how much is available to receptors, so its output influences mood, aggression, sleep, appetite and intestinal motility; the end product, 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid, is the urinary marker used clinically to gauge serotonin turnover and to detect carcinoid tumours. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane, oxidatively deaminates serotonin to 5-hydroxyindole acetaldehyde, releasing hydrogen peroxide, and mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase then oxidises that reactive aldehyde to the stable acid. Loss of MAOA function causes excess monoamine accumulation and a syndrome of impulsive aggression, and the enzyme is the target of antidepressant monoamine oxidase inhibitors, placing this pathway at the heart of neurotransmitter inactivation.

Serotonin signalling must be terminated as well as initiated, and the metabolism of serotonin is the two-step oxidative route that destroys the transmitter after reuptake and converts it into an excretable acid. Monoamine oxidase A, anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane of neurons, enterochromaffin cells, liver and platelets, oxidatively deaminates serotonin to 5-hydroxyindole acetaldehyde, releasing hydrogen peroxide and ammonia; mitochondrial aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH2 then oxidises the reactive aldehyde to 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid, the urinary metabolite measured clinically as an index of serotonin turnover and of carcinoid tumour burden. This clearance sets synaptic and circulating serotonin tone, which is why monoamine oxidase inhibitors are antidepressants and why combining them with serotonergic drugs risks serotonin excess. Loss-of-function of the enzyme raises serotonin and has been linked to impulsive aggression, placing amine catabolism upstream of mood and behaviour.

Serotonin signalling shapes mood, appetite, sleep, sensory processing and motor output, and its duration is set not by synthesis but by how quickly the transmitter is taken back out of the synaptic cleft and destroyed. The plasma membrane serotonin transporter SLC6A4 drives sodium-coupled reuptake into the presynaptic terminal, terminating the signal and recycling transmitter for repackaging; it is the target of SSRI antidepressants and of several stimulants. Recaptured serotonin that is not revesiculated is oxidatively deaminated by monoamine oxidase A on the outer mitochondrial membrane to an aldehyde intermediate, which aldehyde dehydrogenase ALDH2 converts to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid for excretion. Loss or inhibition of these steps raises extracellular serotonin and prolongs receptor occupancy, with consequences for anxiety, aggression and impulse control, and the urinary acid metabolite serves as a clinical readout of serotonin turnover.

Cells match growth to the energy they can afford, and this is the circuit that does it: when ATP falls and AMP rises, AMPK is switched on and mTOR complex 1 is switched off, halting protein synthesis and other costly anabolic work until fuel is restored. Activation requires the tumour suppressor kinase LKB1 bound to STRAD and MO25, which phosphorylates the AMPK catalytic subunits; adenine nucleotide binding to the gamma subunits protects that phosphorylation from PP2C-type phosphatases. Active AMPK phosphorylates TSC2, and the TSC1:TSC2 complex acts as a GTPase-activating protein that drives Rheb to its GDP-bound state, leaving mTOR and Raptor inactive at the lysosome, where Rag GTPases, the Ragulator subunits and the amino-acid sensor SLC38A9 provide the parallel nutrient input. Loss of LKB1 or TSC function uncouples growth from supply and underlies inherited tumour syndromes.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, translation of the transcription factor ATF4 rises and it switches on a transcriptional programme that either restores proteostasis or commits the cell to death. This arm of the unfolded protein response, acting downstream of PERK-mediated eIF2alpha phosphorylation, drives expression of the ER-associated degradation factor HERPUD1, the amino acid biosynthetic enzyme asparagine synthetase, the growth regulator IGFBP1, the inflammatory mediators IL-8 and MCP-1, and the pro-apoptotic factor CHOP (DDIT3), with ATF3 providing feedback. ATF4 works combinatorially with C/EBP family partners and the NF-Y trimer at promoter elements, while ATF6 contributes a parallel branch. The mRNA decay machinery included here, the cytoplasmic exosome core with DIS3, deadenylases and the destabilizing factor KHSRP, sets how long these stress transcripts persist. Chronic activation contributes to secretory cell loss in diabetes and neurodegeneration.

One of the three arms of the unfolded protein response, this branch restores folding capacity in a stressed endoplasmic reticulum by inducing chaperone genes. ATF6-alpha sits in the ER membrane held there by the chaperone BiP (HSPA5); when BiP is recruited to unfolded proteins, ATF6-alpha is released, moves to the Golgi and is cut successively by the site-1 and site-2 proteases (MBTPS1, MBTPS2). The liberated cytosolic fragment enters the nucleus and, with the NF-Y trimer binding ER stress response elements, switches on genes for BiP, GRP94 (HSP90B1), calreticulin and the transcription factor XBP1, whose splicing extends the response. Output overlaps with the ATF4/CHOP axis, so the same stress that rebuilds folding capacity can tip toward apoptosis if unresolved. The pathway supports secretory cells such as plasma cells and hepatocytes, and is implicated in metabolic and neurodegenerative disease.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the IRE1 arm of the unfolded protein response splices XBP1 mRNA to produce an active transcription factor, and the spliced product then drives a broad expansion of ER folding and processing capacity. This is the adaptive, pro-survival output of ER stress signalling: cells that cannot mount it fail at secretion-heavy tasks such as antibody production, insulin secretion and collagen deposition, and tip instead toward apoptosis. Spliced XBP1 binds the CCACG half of ER stress response elements together with the CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, inducing chaperones and co-chaperones (DNAJB9, DNAJB11, DNAJC3, HYOU1), oxidoreductases (PDIA5, PDIA6), degradation components for terminally misfolded substrates (EDEM1, SYVN1), translocon-associated and trafficking factors (SSR1, SERP1, SRPRA, SEC31A, KDELR3), plus WFS1, whose loss causes Wolfram syndrome.

PERK regulates gene expression is the translational arm of the unfolded protein response, the branch that reacts to endoplasmic reticulum stress by shutting down new protein synthesis and rewiring transcription to match. It buys a stressed cell time to clear misfolded protein, and its failure underlies the diabetes and skeletal dysplasia of Wolcott-Rallison syndrome as well as the secretory cell death seen in chronic ER stress. The ER-resident kinase EIF2AK3 is released from BiP (HSPA5) when unfolded protein accumulates, dimerises, and phosphorylates eIF2alpha, globally suppressing initiation while paradoxically favouring translation of ATF4. ATF4 with CHOP (DDIT3), CEBPB/CEBPG and NFY then drives chaperone, amino acid transport and pro-apoptotic genes, including ASNS and HERPUD1. Loss of short-lived cyclin D1 arrests the cell cycle in G1, and exosome-mediated mRNA decay factors shape which transcripts survive the response.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the kinase PERK is released from the chaperone BiP, dimerizes and phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2alpha on Ser52, shutting down most cap-dependent translation while permitting selective expression of stress-response genes. This arm of the unfolded protein response lowers the load of newly synthesized protein entering the ER, depletes short-lived proteins such as Cyclin D1 to stall the cell cycle in G1, and drives a transcriptional programme through ATF4 together with CHOP (DDIT3), ATF3 and C/EBP and NF-Y factors, inducing chaperones, amino acid supply enzymes such as asparagine synthetase, and inflammatory mediators. Prolonged signalling tips the outcome from adaptation toward apoptosis. mRNA decay machinery, including deadenylases and the exosome complex, shapes the resulting transcript levels. Loss of PERK function in humans causes Wolcott-Rallison syndrome with infantile diabetes, reflecting the demands of secretory cells.

When unfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, the sensor kinase IRE1alpha activates chaperones as one arm of the unfolded protein response, expanding the ER's folding, quality-control and secretory capacity so that a stressed cell can survive rather than die. Release of the luminal chaperone BiP (HSPA5) lets IRE1alpha (ERN1) oligomerize and autophosphorylate, and its cytosolic endoribonuclease domain excises an intron from XBP1 mRNA; the spliced message encodes a transcription factor that, with NF-Y at ER stress response elements, drives ER-resident chaperones and foldases such as DNAJB9, DNAJB11, DNAJC3, PDIA5/PDIA6 and HYOU1, ERAD components including EDEM1 and the ubiquitin ligase SYVN1, and machinery for protein targeting, glycosylation and COPII trafficking. The output matters for secretory cells under high load: loss of this branch compromises plasma cell and pancreatic beta cell function, and WFS1 links ER stress handling to diabetes with optic atrophy.

When misfolded protein accumulates in the endoplasmic reticulum, cells mount the unfolded protein response, a stress programme that restores folding capacity or, failing that, commits the cell to death. It matters most in professional secretory cells — plasma cells, pancreatic beta cells, chondrocytes, hepatocytes — whose normal differentiation depends on it, and its failure underlies diabetes, neurodegeneration and skeletal dysplasias. Three sensors act in parallel: IRE1 (ERN1) dimerizes and splices XBP1 mRNA unconventionally to yield an active transcription factor; membrane-tethered ATF6 and related CREB3 factors travel to the Golgi for cleavage by site-1 and site-2 proteases, releasing their cytosolic transcriptional domains; and PERK (EIF2AK3) phosphorylates eIF2α to throttle translation while inducing ATF4 and CHOP (DDIT3). Outputs include ER chaperones such as BiP (HSPA5), GRP94 and calreticulin, disulfide isomerases, ERAD components including SYVN1 and EDEM1, and expanded secretory and mRNA-decay machinery.

When misfolded proteins accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum, one arm of the unfolded protein response cleaves ATF6-alpha and releases its cytosolic bZIP fragment to the nucleus, where it turns on the chaperone genes that restore folding capacity. This transcriptional output is what lets secretory cells such as plasma cells, hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells expand their ER and survive heavy client protein loads; when it fails, chronic ER stress pushes cells toward apoptosis. The activated fragment recognises the CCACG motif of ER stress response elements and works together with the heterotrimeric CCAAT-binding factor NF-Y, whose three subunits are represented here, to drive targets including the ER chaperones BiP (HSPA5), GRP94 (HSP90B1) and calreticulin, as well as XBP1 and the stress regulators ATF4 and CHOP, linking adaptive folding capacity to cell fate decisions.

White fat cells arise from preadipocytes through an ordered transcriptional cascade, and this programme is what gives the body its main lipid store and its largest endocrine organ. Its output includes leptin and adiponectin, the lipid droplet coat protein perilipin, the fatty acid binding protein FABP4, lipoprotein lipase, the CD36 fatty acid transporter and insulin-responsive glucose uptake via GLUT4, so failure or distortion of the programme underlies lipodystrophy, obesity and insulin resistance. Early, transient induction of CEBPB and CEBPD activates PPARG together with EBF1 and KLF5; PPARG then heterodimerises with RXRA and, in a reinforcing loop with CEBPA, locks in the mature state. Ligand binding swaps corepressor complexes containing NCOR1/NCOR2, HDAC3 and TBL1X for coactivators such as p300, CREBBP and the NCOA proteins, and recruits the Mediator complex to engage RNA polymerase II. WNT ligands, TGFB1 and TNF oppose differentiation.

Insulin-like growth factors I and II circulate almost entirely bound to a family of six high-affinity binding proteins, and this system determines how much IGF actually reaches its receptors on target tissues. It sets the half-life of the hormones in blood, restrains their insulin-like hypoglycaemic activity, and governs growth, bone remodelling and tissue repair; loss of the ternary complex component ALS or of IGFBP proteolysis causes growth failure and altered IGF bioavailability. Most IGF travels in a large complex of IGFBP3 with IGFALS that cannot cross the endothelium, while smaller binary complexes with IGFBP1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 distribute to tissues. Release requires limited proteolysis: PAPPA and PAPPA2 cleave IGFBP4 and IGFBP5, and kallikreins, thrombin, plasmin and matrix metalloproteinases act on others. Extracellular matrix and secreted-protein components here also reflect the secretory and ER folding machinery that produces these factors.

Glycogen synthesis begins with glycogenin building a short glucose chain on itself, and that self-glucosylated primer is what glycogen synthase then extends into the branched storage polymer of muscle and other tissues. Glycogen storage disease type XV arises when GYG1 encodes a protein that cannot be autoglucosylated, so no primer is available and muscle glycogen fails to accumulate; patients present with muscle weakness, exercise intolerance and cardiac involvement, with abnormal polyglucosan-like deposits in some fibres. The two participants define the initiation step itself: glycogenin transfers UDP-glucose to its own tyrosine residue and remains attached at the core of the granule, while muscle glycogen synthase encoded by GYS1 elongates the alpha-1,4 chain. The defect illustrates how energy storage in skeletal muscle depends on a single priming reaction rather than on bulk polymer-forming capacity.

Glucagon-like Peptide-1 (GLP1) regulates insulin secretion is the incretin arm of glucose homeostasis: a hormone released by intestinal L-cells after a meal reaches pancreatic beta cells and amplifies their insulin output in proportion to circulating glucose. This glucose-dependence is why the axis is exploited therapeutically in type 2 diabetes, and its blunting contributes to the impaired postprandial insulin response of the disease. GLP-1 binds its Gs-coupled receptor, freeing Gs-alpha to stimulate adenylyl cyclases and raise cAMP, which acts through two branches. PKA, anchored near its targets by AKAPs, closes potassium channels to depolarize the cell, mobilizes ER calcium through IP3 receptors, and drives PDX-1 and CREB-dependent insulin gene transcription. In parallel, the cAMP-activated exchange factors Epac1 and Epac2 signal via Rap1A to prime secretory granules for exocytosis and support beta cell proliferation and survival.

The incretin effect — why an oral glucose load releases far more insulin than the same glucose given intravenously — rests on this signalling route, in which intestinal L-cell-derived GLP-1 amplifies glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells. It is the target of the GLP-1 receptor agonists and DPP-4 inhibitors used in type 2 diabetes, and its potentiation of secretion is glucose-dependent, so it raises insulin output without provoking hypoglycaemia. GLP-1 binding to its Gs-coupled receptor frees the Gs alpha subunit to stimulate adenylate cyclases, and the resulting cAMP acts through two effectors: protein kinase A, whose catalytic subunits are released from regulatory subunits and organised by anchoring proteins, and the exchange factors Epac1 and Epac2, which load GTP onto Rap1A. Downstream, potassium channel closure, IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release from the endoplasmic reticulum, and granule priming drive exocytosis, while transcriptional effects support beta cell mass.

The sense of smell begins when a volatile odorant binds one of several hundred odorant receptors displayed on the cilia of olfactory sensory neurons in the nasal epithelium, and this olfactory signaling pathway converts that binding event into an electrical message sent to the olfactory bulb. Each mature neuron expresses a single receptor gene, so receptor choice defines the neuron's odour identity and the map it projects centrally; loss of the transduction machinery produces anosmia. Activated receptors engage an olfactory-specific heterotrimeric G protein whose alpha subunit GNAL stimulates adenylate cyclase ADCY3; the resulting cAMP opens cyclic nucleotide-gated channels built from CNGA2, CNGA4 and CNGB1, admitting sodium and calcium, and calcium then drives chloride efflux through ANO2 to amplify depolarization. Accessory factors RTP1, RTP2 and REEP1 help receptors escape the endoplasmic reticulum and reach the surface, while LHX2 and EBF1 support the neuronal programme.

GLP-1 is the principal incretin hormone: released from intestinal L cells after a meal, it amplifies glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppresses glucagon, slows gastric emptying and promotes satiety, which is why its receptor agonists and inhibitors of its degrading enzyme are mainstays of type 2 diabetes and obesity therapy. This pathway covers the whole life cycle of the hormone. TCF7L2 with beta-catenin, together with CDX2 and PAX6, drives transcription of the proglucagon gene GCG; signal peptidase complex subunits process the nascent precursor, and the prohormone convertase PCSK1 cleaves proglucagon within secretory granules to yield the active GLP-1 forms. Secretion is triggered by nutrients sensed through the free fatty acid receptors FFAR1 and FFAR4, a lipid-sensing receptor and taste-type G protein subunits, and modulated by leptin and gastrin-releasing peptide. Circulating hormone is short-lived because DPP4 trims two N-terminal residues and inactivates it. Variants in TCF7L2 are a major diabetes risk locus.

Membranes keep the cytoplasm separate from the outside world, and this broad transport programme is how cells then obtain nutrients, ions, metals and lipids across those barriers and between organelles. It covers the solute carrier families that move sugars, amino acids, neurotransmitters, nucleosides, bicarbonate and organic anions; ATP-driven pumps such as the sodium/potassium and calcium ATPases, vacuolar proton pumps and the ABC exporters; channels for chloride, water, cations and calcium release including aquaporins, TRP channels, ryanodine receptors and the mitochondrial calcium uniporter; plus iron and copper handling through transferrin, ferritin and ferroportin, and lipoprotein-mediated cholesterol and triglyceride traffic. Together they set membrane potential, cell volume, pH and metal homeostasis, and their failure underlies cystic fibrosis, renal salt-wasting and tubular disorders, Wilson disease and haemochromatosis, and dyslipidaemias.

ATP-binding cassette transporters use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to pump substrates across membranes against their concentration gradients, and this family-wide transport activity underlies bile and cholesterol secretion, lipid loading of surfactant and skin barrier lipids, chloride conductance at epithelial surfaces, peroxisomal import of very-long-chain fatty acids, mitochondrial iron and heme handling, and the efflux of drugs that produces multidrug resistance in tumours. Individual failures are well-defined diseases: CFTR mutations cause cystic fibrosis, ABCA4 causes retinal degeneration, ABCD1 causes adrenoleukodystrophy, and ABCG5/ABCG8 loss causes sitosterolemia. Alongside the transporters themselves, the set covers their biogenesis and quality control — peroxisomal membrane targeting via PEX3 and PEX19, and ER-associated degradation of misfolded transporters through SEL1L, derlins, VCP, ubiquitin and the 26S proteasome — so that defective channels such as ΔF508 CFTR are retrotranslocated and destroyed rather than reaching the cell surface.

Glycogen storage disease type 0 (muscle GYS1) describes what happens to muscle when it cannot build glycogen at all. Glycogen is the fuel store that skeletal muscle draws on during bursts of contraction and that the heart uses as a metabolic buffer, so loss of muscle glycogen synthase leaves patients with exercise intolerance, syncope on exertion, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, sometimes presenting as sudden cardiac death in childhood. Normally glycogenin self-glucosylates to form the protein primer, and glycogen synthase 1 then extends that primer by adding glucose residues in alpha-1,4 linkage from UDP-glucose, with branching enzyme introducing the branch points that make the particle compact and rapidly mobilised. When the synthase step fails, the primer cannot be elongated and no particle forms, distinguishing this defect from the storage diseases in which abnormal glycogen accumulates. It sits at the anabolic end of carbohydrate metabolism, downstream of insulin signalling.

Muscle stores glucose as glycogen for rapid use during contraction, and this disease state describes what happens when that store cannot be built. Glycogenin initiates a glycogen particle by autoglucosylating itself, and glycogen synthase 1, the isoform of skeletal muscle and heart, extends the chain by adding glucose units from UDP-glucose to the growing polymer. Loss of GYS1 activity abolishes muscle glycogen synthesis, so fibres cannot draw on an internal fuel reserve when demand outstrips glucose delivery; patients show exercise intolerance, muscle pain, and a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that can cause sudden cardiac death in childhood. Unlike the liver form, fasting hypoglycaemia is not the presenting problem. The condition marks glycogen as the substrate for anaerobic glycolysis in working muscle rather than simply a systemic glucose buffer.

Steroid hormones, thyroid hormone, retinoids, vitamin D, oxysterols and fatty acid derivatives act largely by changing gene expression, and the nuclear receptor transcription pathway is how that happens.
