These DNA-binding receptors switch between repression and activation depending on ligand: unliganded receptors recruit the NCOR1 or NCOR2 corepressor proteins, which nucleate silencing complexes at target promoters, while ligand binding triggers a conformational change that swaps the corepressor for MED1 and the Mediator coactivator complex, coupling the receptor to RNA polymerase II. The family spans reproductive and stress endocrinology (AR, ESR1, PGR, NR3C1), metabolic and lipid sensing (PPARs, NR1H3, NR1H4, HNF4A), xenobiotic handling (NR1I2, NR1I3), circadian control (NR1D1, RORs) and development (RARs, RXRs, NR5A1). Ligand-dependent switching makes these receptors among the most tractable drug targets, and their dysregulation underlies hormone-driven cancers, metabolic syndrome and endocrine disorders.

Not every WNT signal works by stabilising beta-catenin. This branch of WNT signalling instead shapes cell shape, polarity and movement, and it underlies convergent extension during gastrulation, neural tube closure, oriented cell division in epithelial sheets, and the planar alignment of structures such as inner ear hair cells; its failure produces neural tube and skeletal defects and contributes to tumour invasion. Ligands such as WNT5A and WNT11 act through Frizzled receptors and the alternative receptors ROR1, ROR2 and RYK, using Dishevelled as the shared hub. One arm engages VANGL2, PRICKLE1, SCRIB, DAAM1 and Rho-family GTPases to polarise the cytoskeleton; another runs through heterotrimeric G proteins and phospholipase C to release calcium from the endoplasmic reticulum, activating protein kinase C, CaMKII and calcineurin-NFAT. Receptor turnover by clathrin-mediated endocytosis, ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome sets signal strength, and NLK-mediated inhibition of TCF/LEF antagonises the beta-catenin arm.

The liver stores glucose as glycogen after a meal and releases it between meals; glycogen storage disease type 0 is what happens when that store is never built. Glycogenin 2 primes a new glycogen particle by attaching the first glucose units to itself, and liver glycogen synthase then elongates the chain with UDP-glucose. When the hepatic synthase is lost, hepatocytes cannot deposit glycogen at all, so the liver has nothing to mobilise during fasting. Affected children show fasting hypoglycaemia with ketosis and, paradoxically, postprandial hyperglycaemia and lactate elevation, since ingested glucose cannot be diverted into storage. Unlike the other glycogenoses, the liver is not enlarged and no abnormal polysaccharide accumulates, because the defect is in synthesis rather than breakdown. It illustrates how tissue-specific isoforms of glycogen metabolism separate hepatic glucose buffering from muscle's own supply.

Glycogen is only soluble and only rapidly mobilised because it is branched, and branching enzyme is what puts the alpha-1,6 linkages in. Working alongside glycogenin, which primes the chain, and glycogen synthase, which extends it in alpha-1,4 linkage, the branching enzyme transfers terminal glucose blocks to create the branch points that give the granule its structure. When branching enzyme activity is lost, cells in liver, muscle, heart and nervous tissue accumulate a poorly soluble amylopectin-like polysaccharide with long unbranched chains, which is toxic rather than usefully stored. The resulting glycogen storage disease type IV ranges from fatal infantile liver cirrhosis to adult polyglucosan body disease with neuropathy and myopathy, depending on how much residual enzyme activity the mutation leaves. It illustrates how polymer architecture, not just glucose quantity, determines whether glycogen can be safely stored and retrieved.

Most hormones, neurotransmitters, chemokines, lipid mediators and sensory stimuli act through seven-transmembrane receptors, and GPCR downstream signalling is what converts that binding into intracellular change. It underlies heart rate and vascular tone, neurotransmission, hormone release, chemotaxis of leukocytes, vision and taste, and it is the target of a large share of prescribed drugs. Ligand-bound receptors activate heterotrimeric G proteins, whose alpha subunits and the released beta-gamma dimer engage distinct effector arms: Gs stimulates and Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclases to set cAMP and protein kinase A activity, Gq activates phospholipase C beta to generate inositol phosphates and diacylglycerol, mobilising calcium through IP3 receptors and activating protein kinase C, and G12/13 works through RhoGEFs and Rho kinases on the cytoskeleton. Signalling converges on MAP kinases, PI3K and calcium-dependent kinases and phosphatases, and is terminated by RGS proteins, GRK phosphorylation, arrestin recruitment and phosphodiesterase-mediated cyclic nucleotide breakdown.

Two hypothalamic nonapeptides, vasopressin and oxytocin, and the G protein-coupled vasopressin-like receptors they act on, link neuroendocrine output to water balance, blood pressure, and reproduction. Both hormones are made in hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary into the circulation. Vasopressin acting on the renal V2 receptor drives aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption in the collecting duct, so loss of this signalling produces diabetes insipidus with dilute, copious urine, while V1A receptors mediate vascular smooth muscle constriction and V1B receptors on pituitary corticotrophs support ACTH release during stress. Oxytocin acting on its receptor triggers uterine contraction at parturition and milk ejection during nursing, and the same receptor contributes to social and affiliative behaviour. Signalling is largely through Gq-driven calcium mobilisation, with the V2 receptor instead raising cyclic AMP, making these receptors targets for antidiuretics, vasopressors and labour induction.

T cells need two signals to respond: antigen recognition through the T cell receptor, and a second costimulatory input delivered by CD28 family receptors engaging B7 ligands on antigen-presenting cells. This second layer sets the threshold for activation and decides between full effector responses, anergy and tolerance, which is why it is the target of checkpoint blockade and of CTLA-4-based immunosuppression. Stimulatory CD28 and ICOS drive PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, Src-family and adaptor-mediated amplification of receptor signals, and transcription by NF-κB, AP-1 and MYC, while CTLA-4, PD-1 and BTLA recruit phosphatases such as PTPN6 and PTPN11 to dampen the same circuitry. Also represented here is control of checkpoint ligand and receptor abundance: PD-L1 glycosylation and ER quality control, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, microRNA repression, and Polycomb and MLL/WRAD chromatin regulation of the loci encoding these receptors.

Excitatory synapses form where a presynaptic terminal is physically matched to a postsynaptic site, and the type IIa receptor-type tyrosine-protein phosphatases are among the adhesion molecules that make that match. PTPRD, PTPRF (LAR) and PTPRS sit in the presynaptic membrane with immunoglobulin-like and fibronectin III domains facing the cleft, and bind trans-synaptically to postsynaptic partners including IL1RAP and IL1RAPL1, the neurotrophin receptor NTRK3, the leucine-rich repeat protein LRRC4B, and the Slitrk family. Each pairing specifies where a synapse forms and how presynaptic release machinery is assembled, with intracellular liprin-alpha and liprin-beta scaffolds (the PPFIA and PPFIBP proteins) organising the active zone. Mutations in IL1RAPL1, PTPRD and SLITRK genes are linked to intellectual disability, autism and Tourette syndrome, placing this adhesion code behind normal circuit wiring. These phosphatases also mediate cell-matrix contacts and axon guidance responses.

A T cell that recognises antigen through its receptor still needs a second, confirmatory signal to commit to a full response, and CD28 co-stimulation supplies it. Engagement of CD28 by CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells drives interleukin-2 production, clonal expansion and survival, so that antigen encountered without co-stimulation yields anergy or tolerance instead of immunity; the same axis is exploited therapeutically, since CTLA4 competes for the same ligands and dampens the response. Mechanistically, Src-family kinases including LCK and FYN phosphorylate the CD28 tail, recruiting PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits to generate PIP3, which activates PDPK1 and AKT and feeds mTOR complexes containing RICTOR, MLST8 and MAPKAP1. VAV1 with GRB2 and GRAP2 links the receptor to RAC1, CDC42 and PAK kinases for cytoskeletal remodelling, while protein phosphatase 2A subunits restrain the pathway.

CD28 dependent PI3K/Akt signaling is the costimulatory arm of T cell activation: engagement of CD28 by CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells recruits PI3K and turns on Akt, converting antigen recognition into a full productive response rather than tolerance or anergy. Without this second signal a T cell that has seen antigen fails to make IL-2, does not survive or divide, and cannot mount the metabolic expansion that effector function requires; the same axis is what checkpoint molecules such as CTLA-4 and PD-1 oppose. Mechanistically, a YMNM motif in the CD28 tail binds the p85 regulatory subunit, PI3K generates PIP3, and PDK1 together with mTORC2 activates Akt, which then drives anti-apoptotic signalling, NF-kB-directed cytokine transcription, cell cycle entry, and mTOR-dependent growth and nutrient uptake. Src-family kinases LCK and FYN link this to proximal receptor phosphorylation.

A T cell that has engaged antigen still needs a second signal to commit, and CD28-dependent PI3K/Akt signalling supplies much of it. Binding of CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells to CD28 creates a phosphotyrosine motif, phosphorylated with help from the Src-family kinases LCK and FYN, that docks the p85 regulatory subunit of PI3K. The catalytic subunits then generate PIP3 at the inner membrane, recruiting PDPK1 and AKT, whose activation is completed by mTORC2 (mTOR with RICTOR, MAPKAP1, MLST8 and PRR5). Active AKT drives IL-2 transcription, blocks apoptosis, permits cell cycle entry and reprograms metabolism toward the biosynthesis a growing effector cell requires. Tuning comes from inhibitors such as TRIB3 and THEM4. Loss of this costimulatory arm produces anergy or tolerance; its blockade is the basis of costimulation-blocking immunosuppressants, while excess contributes to autoimmunity.

A T cell that has engaged antigen needs a second, costimulatory input before it commits to full activation, and CD28 engagement by CD80 or CD86 on antigen-presenting cells supplies it. One arm of that costimulation runs through the guanine nucleotide exchange factor Vav1, which CD28 keeps phosphorylated and membrane-localized far longer than T cell receptor engagement alone can. Vav1 loads the small GTPases Rac1 and Cdc42 with GTP, and these in turn engage PAK kinases to remodel the actin cytoskeleton, drive immune synapse formation, polarization and integrin-mediated adhesion, and feed JNK and p38 signaling toward AP-1 and NFAT-dependent cytokine genes. The Src-family kinases Lck and Fyn and the adaptor Grb2 couple receptor occupancy to Vav1. Without sustained costimulation of this kind, antigen encounter yields anergy or deletion rather than clonal expansion, the principle exploited by costimulation-blocking immunosuppressants.

Hypothalamic neuropeptides that set arousal, feeding and pain tone act through this set of ligand-receptor pairings. Orexin (hypocretin), cleaved into two peptides from a single precursor, engages the receptors HCRTR1 and HCRTR2 to sustain wakefulness and drive food seeking; loss of orexin neurons or of HCRTR2 signalling produces narcolepsy with cataplexy, and the receptors are the target of dual-antagonist hypnotics. Neuropeptide FF, acting at NPFFR1 and NPFFR2, modulates opioid analgesia and contributes to opioid tolerance while also influencing feeding and blood pressure. QRFP (26RFa) signals through QRFPR to stimulate appetite and affect energy balance and bone mass. All three systems work through G protein-coupled receptors on central neurons, converting peptidergic input into changes in cyclic nucleotide and calcium signalling, and together they link hypothalamic peptide release to sleep-wake state, nociception and metabolic drive.}

Activated T cells and regulatory T cells upregulate CTLA-4, and co-inhibition through it is the brake that keeps an ongoing T cell response from running into autoreactivity. Loss of this restraint causes lethal lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, while blocking it deliberately with antibodies unleashes antitumour T cell responses; the same axis governs tolerance to transplanted tissue. CTLA-4 binds the B7 ligands CD80 and CD86 with higher avidity than CD28 does, stripping away costimulation, and it also signals inward: Src-family kinases including LCK and FYN phosphorylate its cytoplasmic tail, recruiting the phosphatase SHP-2 (PTPN11) and protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes that dephosphorylate TCR-proximal substrates and damp AKT activation. The result is reduced IL-2 output and arrest in G1, and because CTLA-4-bearing cells deplete ligand from antigen-presenting cells, the suppression extends to neighbouring T cells.

NADPH regeneration supplies the reducing power that biosynthesis and antioxidant defence run on, outside of the pentose phosphate pathway's canonical route. NADPH is consumed by fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, by glutathione and thioredoxin reductases that neutralise peroxides, and by cytochrome P450 reactions, so cells maintain a high NADPH:NADP+ ratio in every compartment where those reactions occur. Cytosolic and peroxisomal isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1) carries much of this load, oxidatively decarboxylating isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate while reducing NADP+; cytosolic aconitase (ACO1) feeds it by interconverting citrate and isocitrate, linking NADPH output to citrate exported from mitochondria. The same aconitase doubles as the iron-regulatory protein IRP1, tying this reducing-equivalent supply to cellular iron sensing. A parallel arm in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen sets the local NADPH balance that steroid-modifying reductases depend on.

Reducing power for biosynthesis and antioxidant defence comes largely from NADPH, and this route regenerates it outside the mitochondrion by oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to 2-oxoglutarate. Cytosolic and peroxisomal isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1) performs the NADP+-dependent step, while aconitase (ACO1) supplies its substrate by isomerising citrate exported from mitochondria to isocitrate. The NADPH produced supports fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis, regeneration of reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and detoxification of peroxides, which matters in peroxisomes where beta-oxidation generates oxidative load. Related NADP+/NADPH balancing in the endoplasmic reticulum lumen sustains reductive reactions there. Because IDH1 also links this chemistry to 2-oxoglutarate availability for dioxygenases, mutations that alter its catalytic output reshape cellular redox state and metabolite-dependent epigenetic signalling, as seen in gliomas and myeloid malignancies.

Phytanic acid, a branched-chain fatty acid released by ruminant breakdown of chlorophyll and taken up in dairy fat and meat, cannot be handled by ordinary beta-oxidation because a methyl group sits at the beta carbon. Alpha-oxidation of phytanate solves this in the peroxisomal matrix: the acid is first activated to its CoA ester by a very-long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase, hydroxylated by the 2-hydroxylase PHYH, cleaved by the thiamine-dependent lyase HACL1 to formyl-CoA and a fatty aldehyde, and the aldehyde oxidised by ALDH3A2 to pristanic acid, which enters peroxisomal beta-oxidation. A peroxisomal solute carrier supplies cofactors for these steps. Loss of PHYH causes phytanic acid to accumulate in plasma and tissues, producing the retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy and ataxia of Refsum disease, while ALDH3A2 deficiency underlies Sjogren-Larsson syndrome. Phytanic acid also acts as a nuclear receptor ligand, linking dietary lipid to transcriptional control of fat metabolism.

Glyoxylate is a reactive two-carbon aldehyde produced in liver peroxisomes and mitochondria during the breakdown of glycine, glycolate and hydroxyproline, and the reactions that handle it determine whether it is safely recycled or oxidised to oxalate. Detoxification depends on transamination of glyoxylate to glycine by the peroxisomal alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase and on its reduction to glycolate by glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase; loss of either enzyme causes primary hyperoxaluria, with calcium oxalate deposition, kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis and renal failure. Defects in the hydroxyproline route through HOGA1 produce a third form. Glycine itself is degraded by the mitochondrial glycine cleavage system, where GLDC, AMT, GCSH and the shared dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase release one-carbon units to folate; its failure causes nonketotic hyperglycinemia. Related activities include D-amino acid oxidase, peroxisomal hydroxyacid oxidase and the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex linking this chemistry to central carbon metabolism.

Branched-chain fatty acids from dairy and ruminant fat cannot be handled by the mitochondrial route, so the peroxisome degrades them. Beta-oxidation of pristanoyl-CoA takes the product of phytanic acid alpha-oxidation through three rounds of oxidation, hydration, dehydrogenation and thiolytic cleavage, releasing acetyl-CoA and two propionyl-CoA units and leaving 4,8-dimethylnonanoyl-CoA. Because the methyl branches create chiral centres, an alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) converts the (R)- to the (S)-stereoisomer that the branched-chain acyl-CoA oxidase can use, while a multifunctional enzyme (HSD17B4) provides hydratase and dehydrogenase activities and sterol carrier protein 2 supplies the thiolase step. Carnitine acyltransferases then esterify the shortened chain and the propionyl and acetyl groups for export to mitochondria, where oxidation is completed. Loss of racemase or oxidase activity causes accumulation of branched-chain fatty acids and bile acid intermediates with neuropathy and liver disease.

Attaching the small protein SUMO to transcription cofactors is a way of tuning gene expression without touching DNA itself. Cofactors such as the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300, the nuclear receptor coactivators NCOA1 and NCOA2, and corepressors including NCOR2, SIN3A and CTBP1 do not bind promoters directly but are recruited by DNA-bound factors; modifying them generally dampens their activity, so SUMOylation of a coactivator like PPARGC1A lowers transcription while SUMOylation of a repressor such as the methyl-CpG reader MBD1 relieves it. The E2 enzyme UBE2I works with PIAS-family and other ligases to transfer SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3 onto substrates that include Polycomb repressive components (RNF2, BMI1, CBX and PHC proteins) and the silencing corepressor TRIM28. The pathway thereby shapes metabolic gene programmes, heterochromatin maintenance and developmental repression, and contributes to how nuclear bodies and repressive complexes assemble.

PD-1 co-inhibition is the brake that T cells apply to their own activation, limiting autoimmunity and tissue damage but also enforcing the exhausted, unresponsive state of tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes that checkpoint-blockade antibodies are designed to release. Engagement of PD-1 by PD-L1 or PD-L2 presented alongside peptide-MHC class II recruits the tyrosine phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 to the synapse, where they dephosphorylate CD3 chains and LCK-dependent intermediates and dampen PI3K-AKT output, cutting IL-2 production, survival signalling and effector differentiation. Much of the biology here concerns how the ligand itself is controlled: PD-L1 abundance is set by transcription factors including HIF1A, MYC, NF-κB, STAT1/3 and IRF1, by YAP/TAZ-TEAD and Wnt-β-catenin inputs, by chromatin regulators such as the PRC2 and MLL-WDR5 complexes, by numerous microRNAs acting through Argonaute complexes, and post-translationally by N-glycosylation, casein kinase 2 and GSK3β phosphorylation, and ubiquitin-proteasome and ER-associated degradation.

Actin and tubulin cannot reach their native shapes unaided, and the handoff from prefoldin to the CCT/TriC chaperonin is the step that commits newly made subunits to productive folding. Prefoldin, a jellyfish-shaped hexamer built from PFDN1, PFDN2, PFDN4, PFDN5, PFDN6 and VBP1, captures nascent actin and tubulin chains as they leave the ribosome, holds them in a folding-competent state, and docks onto the cytosolic chaperonin ring so the substrate is delivered directly into the folding cavity. CCT itself is an eight-subunit double ring whose ATP-driven cycle then completes folding and releases polymerization-competent monomers. Because the products are the building blocks of microtubules and actin filaments, this transfer sets the supply of cytoskeletal subunits available for mitotic spindle assembly, cell shape, motility and intracellular transport, and its disruption compromises cytoskeletal integrity and proteostasis alike.

Actin and tubulin cannot fold on their own; they depend on a dedicated relay of chaperones, and without it a cell cannot build microtubules or actin filaments, so mitotic spindles, cilia, axonal transport and cell shape all fail. Nascent actin and tubulin chains leaving the ribosome are captured by prefoldin, a hexameric jellyfish-shaped co-chaperone assembled from PFDN1-PFDN6 and VBP1, which holds them in a folding-competent state and delivers them to the cytosolic chaperonin TRiC/CCT. That double-ring ATPase, built from eight paralogous subunits including TCP1 and CCT2-CCT8, encloses the substrate and uses ATP-driven cycles to release correctly folded actin and the many alpha- and beta-tubulin isotypes that feed into microtubule assembly. The cooperation of prefoldin and TRiC/CCT thus sits upstream of all cytoskeletal function, and mutations in chaperonin subunits cause neuropathy and developmental disorders.

Newly synthesised alpha- and beta-tubulin cannot reach their native state unaided, and the cytosolic chaperonin CCT/TriC is what gives them a chance to try. The eight-subunit ring, built from CCT1-CCT8 (TCP1 through CCT8), captures unfolded tubulin in an ATP-dependent cavity and releases quasi-native folding intermediates; because these intermediates are unstable, a series of downstream tubulin cofactors is needed to complete folding and to join alpha and beta chains into the heterodimer that polymerises into microtubules. Every process that depends on microtubules therefore depends on this step upstream of it: mitotic spindle assembly, intracellular transport, cilia and axonal architecture. The many alpha- and beta-tubulin isotypes here, including neuronal TUBB3 and TUBB4A, are all clients, and mutations that impair their folding or dimerisation cause cortical malformations and other tubulinopathies.

Post-chaperonin tubulin folding pathway completes the manufacture of the alpha/beta tubulin heterodimer, the building block from which every microtubule is assembled. Nothing about mitotic spindles, intracellular transport, cilia or neuronal axons works unless this step delivers correctly folded, GTP-competent dimers, and mutations in its cofactors cause cortical malformations and neurodegeneration. After the CCT/TriC chaperonin releases partly folded alpha and beta tubulin monomers, five dedicated cofactors take over: TBCA and TBCB capture the individual subunits, TBCE holds alpha tubulin while TBCD holds beta tubulin, and entry of TBCC into the assembled supercomplex triggers GTP hydrolysis on beta tubulin to discharge the native dimer. The small GTPase ARL2 regulates this machinery, which also acts in reverse as a tubulin-sequestering and degradation route, setting the size of the soluble dimer pool available for polymerisation.

Microtubules can only be built from correctly folded alpha/beta tubulin heterodimers, and this is the route by which those dimers are finished after the chaperonin releases partly folded monomers. Everything that depends on microtubules — mitotic spindles, intracellular transport, cilia, axonal architecture — rests on a supply of assembly-competent dimer, and on the same machinery to sequester or recycle free monomer so that unpolymerized tubulin does not poison assembly. Five cofactors act in sequence: TBCA and TBCB capture newly released beta and alpha subunits, TBCD and TBCE present them to one another, and arrival of TBCC triggers GTP hydrolysis on beta tubulin to discharge the native heterodimer, with ARL2 also binding the cofactor complex. Numerous alpha and beta tubulin isotypes are handled this way. Loss of TBCE causes hypoparathyroidism with growth retardation, and TBCD mutations produce early encephalopathy.

Fatty acids longer than 18 carbons cannot be handled by mitochondria, so they are shortened first in peroxisomes, where beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids trims them to acetyl-CoA and medium-chain acyl-CoAs such as octanoyl-CoA that are then exported for mitochondrial oxidation. The route begins with activation to a CoA thioester and transport across the peroxisomal membrane by an ABC half-transporter; ACOX1 introduces the double bond in the oxidase step that generates hydrogen peroxide, a bifunctional hydratase-dehydrogenase and a thiolase complete each cycle, and auxiliary enzymes isomerize or reduce unsaturated intermediates while thioesterases free CoA. Its importance is clearest when it fails: loss of the transporter causes X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy with accumulation of saturated very long chain fatty acids and demyelination, and bifunctional protein deficiency produces severe neonatal peroxisomal disease. The pathway also supplies lipid precursors and links to malonyl-CoA turnover.

Actin cannot reach its native state on its own; nascent beta-actin chains must be folded by the cytosolic chaperonin CCT/TriC, and the output of this reaction is the soluble monomeric actin that feeds every microfilament in the cell. Without it, cytoskeletal assembly, cell shape, motility, division and intracellular transport all fail, which is why this chaperone is required in essentially all dividing cells. The chaperonin is a double-ring barrel of eight distinct subunits (TCP1 and CCT2-CCT8, with CCT6B a testis-enriched paralogue) that encloses a single substrate in its central cavity. Unfolded actin is handed over from prefoldin without nucleotide exchange, then folded through ATP binding and hydrolysis that cycles the rings between open and closed states, releasing folded monomer. Tubulin and a set of other stringent substrates depend on the same machine, linking actin biogenesis to general cytoskeletal proteostasis.

Newly made actins, tubulins and many other proteins cannot reach their native shape unaided, and chaperonin-mediated protein folding is the route by which they do. The eight-subunit CCT/TRiC complex, encoded by TCP1 and CCT2-CCT8, forms two back-to-back rings whose central cavity encloses non-native substrate and folds it in cycles of ATP hydrolysis, without needing a separate co-chaperonin. Substrates arrive from the ribosome via the prefoldin complex or Hsp70 machinery, and because only a fraction reach the native state per round, polypeptides are repeatedly recaptured. Output is the cytoskeleton itself: alpha and beta tubulins need further cofactors to assemble heterodimers, and beta-propeller clients such as the G-protein beta subunits and F-box/WD40 proteins depend on the same cavity. Consequently microtubule dynamics, heterotrimeric G-protein signalling and SCF ubiquitin ligase assembly all rest on this folding capacity, and its overload contributes to protein aggregation disease.

The cytosolic chaperonin TRiC/CCT is a two-ringed ATP-driven folding chamber that takes on newly synthesised polypeptides as they emerge from the ribosome and brings them to their native state. Substrate capture during biosynthesis matters because TRiC clients are proteins that do not fold spontaneously: actin and tubulin, WD40-repeat and beta-propeller proteins, and multisubunit assemblies that must reach a competent conformation before they can be incorporated. Here the eight paralogous subunits encoded by TCP1 and CCT2-CCT8 form the ring, and the clients include F-box proteins that supply substrate recognition to SCF ubiquitin ligases, cyclin E, and regulators such as STAT3, TP53 and HDAC3. This links folding capacity directly to cell cycle progression, ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis and transcriptional control; loss of chaperonin function causes broad proteostasis collapse and aggregation of obligate clients.

Striated Muscle Contraction is the force-generating cycle of skeletal and cardiac muscle, converting chemical energy into shortening of the sarcomere and thus into movement, posture and the pumping of blood. A rise in cytosolic calcium is read by the troponin complex (TNNC, TNNI, TNNT), which shifts tropomyosin off the actin filament and uncovers myosin binding sites; myosin heads then bind, pivot, release ADP and rebind ATP, ratcheting thin and thick filaments past one another. Titin, nebulin, tropomodulins, alpha-actinin and telethonin set filament length and anchor the lattice at the Z-disc, while dystrophin and desmin transmit force to the membrane and cytoskeleton. Because the geometry is so exacting, mutations in these components cause hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, nemaline myopathy, distal arthrogryposis and muscular dystrophy, and the isoform composition here distinguishes cardiac, fast and slow fibre types.

Skeletal and cardiac muscle shorten and generate force through the sarcomere, the repeating array of thin and thick filaments that gives striated muscle contraction its name and its banded appearance. Calcium released during excitation binds the troponin complex (troponin C, I and T isoforms), shifting tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites so that myosin heads can attach, pivot, release ADP and reset on a fresh ATP; repeated cycles slide the filaments past one another. Structural and scaffolding proteins set the geometry this chemistry depends on: titin and nebulin act as molecular rulers, alpha-actinin and telethonin build the Z-disc, tropomodulins cap thin filament ends, myosin-binding proteins tune crossbridge kinetics, and dystrophin and desmin transmit force to the membrane and cytoskeleton. Mutations in these components underlie hypertrophic and dilated cardiomyopathies, nemaline myopathy and muscular dystrophy.

Acetylcholine acts on two receptor families, and the muscarinic arm is the G protein-coupled one, comprising the five receptors M1-M5. Through them the parasympathetic nervous system slows the heart, drives smooth muscle contraction in gut, airway and bladder, stimulates glandular secretion, and modulates cortical and striatal circuits underlying learning, attention and movement. The receptors split by coupling: M2 and M4 signal through Gi/o, lowering cyclic AMP and opening potassium channels to dampen excitability, while M1, M3 and M5 signal through Gq/11 to phospholipase C, generating inositol phosphates and calcium release. This pharmacology makes them targets of atropine-like antagonists and of agents for overactive bladder, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and bradycardia, and of efforts to treat cognitive and psychotic symptoms in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease and schizophrenia. Antimuscarinic side effects of many psychiatric drugs arise here.

Histamine acts as a local mediator of immune and inflammatory responses, a regulator of gastric acid secretion and gut function, and a neurotransmitter in the brain, and it does all of this through four G protein-coupled histamine receptors. H1 drives the bronchoconstriction, vascular leak and itch of allergic reactions and is the target of antihistamines; H2 on gastric parietal cells raises cyclic AMP to stimulate acid secretion and is blocked by drugs used for ulcer and reflux disease; H3 acts largely as a presynaptic autoreceptor and heteroreceptor in the central nervous system, restraining histamine and other transmitter release and thereby influencing arousal, sleep-wake cycling and appetite; H4 is expressed mainly on immune cells such as mast cells, eosinophils and dendritic cells, where it promotes chemotaxis. Together they couple a single amine to signalling outputs ranging from smooth muscle tone to leukocyte recruitment.

Dopamine acts on five G protein-coupled receptors that translate dopaminergic transmission into changes in neuronal excitability, and through them into motor control, reward learning, motivation and pituitary hormone release. The D1-like receptors, D1 and D5, couple to Gs and raise cyclic AMP, driving protein kinase A signalling in striatal and cortical neurons; the D2-like receptors, D2, D3 and D4, couple to Gi/Go, lower cyclic AMP and also act presynaptically as autoreceptors that restrain dopamine synthesis and release. This opposing pair of arms sets the balance between direct and indirect basal ganglia output pathways. Loss of dopaminergic input to these receptors produces the motor signs of Parkinson's disease, and their signalling is the target of antipsychotics, which block D2-like receptors, and of stimulants and dopamine agonists. Variation here is repeatedly implicated in schizophrenia, addiction and attention disorders.

Serotonin acts as a slow modulator rather than a fast point-to-point transmitter, and the receptors that read it set mood, anxiety, sleep and wakefulness, appetite, thermoregulation, aggression, sexual behaviour, gut motility and vascular tone. Nearly all of these receptors are G protein-coupled: the 5-HT1 family signals through Gi/o to lower cyclic AMP and, as autoreceptors on raphe neurons, damps serotonergic firing itself; the 5-HT2 family couples to Gq and phospholipase C; and 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 couple to Gs and raise cyclic AMP. This receptor layer is the pharmacological target of antidepressants, atypical antipsychotics, anxiolytics and the triptan antimigraine drugs, which act at 5-HT1B/1D on cranial vessels and trigeminal terminals. Disordered signalling through these receptors is implicated in depression, anxiety, psychosis, and in the case of 5-HT2B agonism, valvular heart disease.

Adrenoceptors are the G protein-coupled receptors through which adrenaline and noradrenaline impose the sympathetic "fight-or-flight" state on the body: faster and stronger cardiac contraction, redistribution of blood flow, airway relaxation, pupil dilation and mobilization of glucose and fat stores. The nine subtypes split into three functional groups with opposing intracellular logic. The alpha1 receptors (ADRA1A, ADRA1B, ADRA1D) couple through Gq to phospholipase C, raising calcium and constricting vascular smooth muscle; the alpha2 receptors couple to Gi and lower cAMP, acting largely presynaptically to restrain further noradrenaline release; the beta receptors (ADRB1, ADRB2, ADRB3) couple to Gs and raise cAMP, driving cardiac stimulation, bronchodilation and lipolysis. This pharmacology underlies beta-blockers, alpha-blockers and inhaled beta2 agonists in hypertension, heart failure and asthma.

Diseases associated with O-glycosylation of proteins collects the congenital disorders that arise when sugars fail to be attached to serine and threonine residues of secreted and membrane proteins. O-glycosylation comes in several flavours defined by the first sugar added, and each has its own disease signature: loss of O-mannosylation of dystroglycan by POMT1, POMT2, POMGNT1, B4GAT1 or LARGE1 breaks the link between muscle fibres and their basement membrane and produces congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye malformation; loss of O-fucosylation and its B3GLCT-dependent glucose extension on thrombospondin repeats of ADAMTS and ADAMTSL proteins causes Peters-plus syndrome and connective tissue disease, while altered fucosylation of Notch receptors disturbs somite and vascular patterning. Mucin-type GalNAc glycosylation, built by C1GALT1 with its chaperone and the GALNT enzymes, gives mucins their protective gel properties, and its failure is linked to tumoral calcinosis and epithelial barrier defects.

Sugars added to serine and threonine residues shape mucus, muscle attachment and developmental signalling, and the inherited defects grouped here are the congenital disorders of glycosylation that follow when O-linked chains are built incorrectly. Three branches are represented. Mucin-type GalNAc glycosylation, elaborated by the C1GALT1 galactosyltransferase with its obligate chaperone C1GALT1C1 and by GALNT enzymes, decorates the secreted and membrane mucins that protect epithelial surfaces; loss of GALNT3 activity causes hyperphosphatemic familial tumoral calcinosis. Peroxisomes handle lipids that mitochondria cannot: very long chain fatty acids, the branched-chain isoprenoid derivatives phytanate and pristanate, and the ether-lipid backbone of plasmalogens. Peroxisomal lipid metabolism shortens and oxidises these substrates so they can be finished elsewhere, and supplies precursors for membrane phospholipids and bile acid side-chain modification. Loss of it is not a subtle metabolic shift but a cause of severe neurodevelopmental and demyelinating disease, including adrenoleukodystrophy when the membrane transporter ABCD1 fails to import very long chain acyl-CoAs, and Refsum disease when phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase cannot initiate alpha-oxidation. Inside the organelle, acyl-CoA oxidases introduce the first double bond using molecular oxygen and generating hydrogen peroxide, a multifunctional enzyme performs hydration and dehydrogenation, and thiolases cleave the chain; racemase and carnitine acyltransferase activities set stereochemistry and export products for mitochondrial completion.

Macrophages and other myeloid cells must decide what to engulf, and the signal regulatory protein family provides one of the checks on that decision. SIRPA on the phagocyte binds CD47 displayed on the surface of healthy cells, delivering a "don't eat me" signal that restrains phagocytosis; tumours exploit this by overexpressing CD47, which is why blocking the interaction is being pursued therapeutically. Ligand engagement clusters SIRPA and recruits the tyrosine phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 to its cytoplasmic tail, dampening signalling that would otherwise drive engulfment and migration, with adaptors such as SKAP2 and FYB1, the kinases SRC, PTK2 and PTK2B, and GRB2 shaping the output. Lung collectins SP-A and SP-D also engage SIRPA to hold alveolar macrophages in a resting state, while SIRPB1 signals instead through the activating adaptor TYROBP and SIRPG binds CD47 weakly.

Protein folding is the chaperone-assisted process by which newly synthesised polypeptides reach their native shape in a crowded cytosol where spontaneous folding would fail or aggregate. Without it cells cannot build a microtubule cytoskeleton, assemble signalling complexes, or clear misfolded species, and aggregation-prone proteins accumulate. The genes centre on the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC/CCT, an ATP-driven double-ring cage that binds unfolded substrates and releases them through cycles of nucleotide hydrolysis, working with the prefoldin co-chaperone that captures nascent chains on the ribosome and delivers them to the cage. Its principal clients are actin and the alpha/beta tubulins, which are then matured by tubulin-specific cofactors into polymerisation-competent heterodimers, and the G-protein beta subunits, whose folding gates assembly of heterotrimeric G proteins for receptor signalling. Cell cycle regulators and ubiquitin ligases link folding capacity to quality control and protein turnover.

Newly synthesized polypeptides rarely reach their native shape unaided in the crowded cytosol; protein folding by molecular chaperones is what converts them into functional protein. The dominant machinery here is the eukaryotic chaperonin TRiC/CCT, a double-ring ATPase built from eight paralogous subunits, fed by the prefoldin co-chaperone that captures nascent chains at the ribosome and delivers them. Cycles of ATP-driven substrate binding and release stabilize productive intermediates rather than adding information. Two obligate clients dominate the substrate list: actin and the alpha/beta tubulins, whose folding is completed by tubulin-specific cofactors before heterodimer assembly, and the G protein beta subunits, which acquire their propeller fold on CCT before pairing with gamma subunits for receptor signalling. Consequently cytoskeletal dynamics, mitosis and heterotrimeric G protein signalling all depend on this chaperone capacity, and its overload contributes to protein misfolding and aggregation.

Eicosanoids — prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes made from arachidonic acid and related 20-carbon fatty acids — act locally, and the cell-surface receptors that bind them determine which tissues respond. These eicosanoid ligand-binding receptors are almost all G protein-coupled, and through them a lipid released by one cell sets vascular tone, bronchial smooth muscle contraction, platelet aggregation, fever, pain sensitisation and leukocyte recruitment in its neighbours. The prostanoid group covers receptors for prostaglandin E2 (PTGER1-4), D2, F2α, prostacyclin and thromboxane A2, the last two forming the antagonistic pair that balances clotting and vasodilation. Cysteinyl leukotriene and leukotriene B4 receptors drive bronchoconstriction and neutrophil chemotaxis, and an oxoeicosanoid receptor responds to 5-oxo-ETE. Because these receptors sit at the receiving end of the cyclooxygenase and lipoxygenase routes, they are the targets of antiplatelet therapy and of asthma drugs.\n

Leukotrienes are lipid mediators made from arachidonic acid during inflammation, and this family of G protein-coupled receptors is how target cells read them. Two receptors respond to leukotriene B4 and act mainly on neutrophils and other leukocytes, driving chemotaxis, adhesion and recruitment to injured or infected tissue. Two others respond to the cysteinyl leukotrienes LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4, contracting airway smooth muscle, increasing vascular permeability and promoting mucus secretion and eosinophil influx; this arm underlies the bronchoconstriction of asthma and the nasal symptoms of allergic disease, and is blocked therapeutically by receptor antagonists such as montelukast. A related orphan receptor in the same group has been linked to oligodendrocyte maturation. Signalling proceeds through heterotrimeric G proteins to calcium mobilisation and altered cyclic AMP, coupling lipid mediator release to acute inflammatory and allergic responses.

Prostanoid ligand receptors are the cell-surface G protein-coupled receptors through which prostaglandins and thromboxane act, converting locally released lipid mediators into changes in vascular tone, platelet behaviour, inflammation, pain sensitivity, fever and smooth muscle contraction. Arachidonic acid released from membranes is cyclised by cyclooxygenase to PGH2 and then tailored by tissue-specific synthases into PGD2, PGE2, PGF2alpha, prostacyclin and TXA2; the receptors named here read that output. DP1/DP2, the four EP subtypes, FP, IP and TP couple to different G proteins, so the same ligand family can raise or lower cAMP, mobilise calcium, and produce opposing effects such as prostacyclin-mediated vasodilation versus thromboxane-driven platelet aggregation. This branch explains why COX inhibitors relieve pain and inflammation yet perturb gastric protection, renal perfusion, uterine contraction and cardiovascular risk, and DP2 antagonism is exploited in allergic airway disease.

Prostanoids made downstream of cyclooxygenase — PGD2, PGE2, PGF2alpha, prostacyclin and thromboxane A2 — act on cells through a family of prostanoid ligand receptors, and these receptors are what convert local lipid mediator production into changes in vascular tone, platelet aggregation, pain sensitivity, fever, uterine contraction and inflammatory cell recruitment. They are G protein-coupled receptors with opposing outputs: the prostacyclin receptor and the EP2/EP4 subtypes raise cAMP to relax smooth muscle and restrain platelets, while the thromboxane receptor and FP and EP1 receptors mobilise calcium to constrict vessels and promote aggregation, so the balance between them sets haemostatic and vascular set points. Two DP receptors mediate PGD2 actions, with the second recruiting eosinophils, basophils and Th2 cells in allergic airway disease. This receptor layer explains the therapeutic effects of aspirin and NSAIDs, which act by removing their ligands.

Adrenaline signalling through Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor is the inhibitory arm of adrenergic control, the route by which adrenaline and noradrenaline damp rather than stimulate cellular activity. It sets the negative feedback that limits noradrenaline release at sympathetic nerve terminals, suppresses insulin secretion while promoting glucagon release, contracts gastrointestinal sphincters and vascular smooth muscle, and lowers the threshold for platelet aggregation. Because of the presynaptic autoreceptor function, agonists at these receptors are used clinically as antihypertensives, sedatives and analgesics. The three receptor subtypes are G protein-coupled receptors that preferentially engage Gi/Go heterotrimers; the released alpha subunit inhibits adenylate cyclase so that cAMP falls and protein kinase A activity declines, while liberated beta-gamma subunits act on potassium and calcium channels. The pathway therefore opposes beta-adrenergic signalling within the same catecholamine response.

Adrenaline acting on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors is the arm of catecholamine signalling that damps rather than drives cAMP production. The three receptor subtypes encoded here couple preferentially to Gi/Go heterotrimers, so agonist binding inhibits adenylate cyclase and lowers cyclic AMP, while the released G protein subunits also regulate potassium and calcium channels. The physiological consequences are broad: suppression of insulin secretion and promotion of glucagon release from pancreatic islets, contraction of gastrointestinal sphincters, platelet aggregation, and presynaptic autoinhibition of noradrenaline release at sympathetic and central synapses. That last negative feedback loop is why alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine and dexmedetomidine lower sympathetic outflow and blood pressure and produce sedation and analgesia, and why the subtypes differ in their vascular versus neuronal contributions to autonomic tone.

Nitric oxide made from L-arginine by the endothelial, neuronal and inducible synthases acts as a diffusible messenger that relaxes vascular smooth muscle and restrains platelets, and its activation of soluble guanylate cyclase is how that message is read inside the target cell. The heterodimeric cyclase (GUCY1A1 with GUCY1B1 and related subunits) binds NO at its haem and raises cGMP, which activates protein kinase G. PKG phosphorylates the inositol trisphosphate receptor-associated regulator IRAG1 to suppress IP3 receptor-mediated calcium release, and large-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels built from KCNMA1 and its beta subunits hyperpolarise the membrane, both lowering cytosolic calcium. Multiple phosphodiesterases, notably PDE5A, terminate the signal by hydrolysing cGMP and are the point of pharmacological intervention in erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Weak cGMP control leaves platelets hyperaggregable and predisposes to thrombosis and hypertension.

Platelets release ADP from their dense granules when they are activated, and ADP acting back on the P2Y12 receptor is what converts a weak, reversible clump into a stable thrombus. This amplification loop is required for aggregation triggered by every other platelet agonist fcollagen, thrombin, thromboxane, adrenaline, serotonin f and it is the target of the thienopyridine antiplatelet drugs used after coronary stenting; loss-of-function variants cause a bleeding tendency. P2RY12 couples to Gi, so agonist binding releases an inhibitory alpha subunit that lowers adenylate cyclase output and cAMP, relieving protein kinase A restraint on cytoplasmic calcium, while the liberated beta-gamma dimer engages its own effectors. The many G protein alpha, beta and gamma subunits here represent the interchangeable heterotrimer components through which this receptor, and Gi-coupled receptors generally, act. Downstream consequences include granule secretion, thromboxane generation and integrin activation.

Chemoattractant receptors coupled to Gi release free G beta:gamma dimers, and one of the things those dimers do is switch on PI3K gamma at the plasma membrane. This is the route by which neutrophils and other leukocytes convert a chemokine gradient into directed migration and a respiratory burst, and it is a target of interest for inflammatory and allergic disease. The lipid kinase is a heterodimer of the p110 gamma catalytic subunit with a p101 or p84 regulatory partner; membrane recruitment by beta:gamma both activates it and delivers it to PIP2, which it phosphorylates to PIP3. PIP3 then recruits PDK1 and AKT for survival and metabolic signalling, while RhoA links the same input to actin and cytoskeletal remodelling. Loss of this arm blunts leukocyte chemotaxis without disturbing receptor-proximal G protein coupling itself.

Metabolism of proteins spans the entire life of a polypeptide, from its synthesis on cytosolic and mitochondrial ribosomes through folding, covalent modification, trafficking and eventual destruction. It is the layer of cell biology that determines how much of each protein exists, where it sits, and what chemical decorations tune its activity, and its failure underlies congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, neurodegenerative amyloid disease and cancers driven by defective degradation. The genes cover aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and initiation and elongation factors, chaperonin and prefoldin folding machinery, ER translocation and signal peptidase, N- and O-linked glycosylation, GPI anchoring, gamma-carboxylation, sulfation and methylation, RAB prenylation with COPI/COPII and exocyst transport, and the ubiquitin, SUMO and NEDD8 conjugation systems feeding cullin-RING ligases, deubiquitinases and the proteasome. Peptide hormone processing by furin and PCSK enzymes, surfactant secretion, and amyloid fibre formation are downstream outcomes of the same machinery.

This is the full life cycle of a cellular protein, from synthesis through maturation to destruction, and nearly every compartment contributes. Ribosomal subunits, initiation and elongation factors and aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases translate mRNA in the cytosol, while a parallel mitochondrial apparatus of mitoribosomal proteins and mitochondrially encoded subunits supplies the respiratory chain. Chaperonins and prefoldin fold nascent chains; signal recognition particle, the signal peptidase and oligosaccharyltransferase route and glycosylate secretory proteins, with COPI/COPII, TRAPP, SNARE and RAB components moving them onward. Covalent modification is broadly represented: N- and O-glycosylation, GPI anchoring, gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, sulfation, methylation, ubiquitination by cullin-RING and other ligases, SUMOylation, neddylation, and reversal by deubiquitinases. Proprotein convertases liberate peptide hormones such as insulin and POMC products; misfolded substrates are cleared by ER-associated degradation and the proteasome. Failures here underlie congenital glycosylation disorders, surfactant deficiency, and amyloid diseases.

Rap1 signalling governs how cells stick to their surroundings and to each other, acting as the switch that converts intracellular second messengers into integrin activation, cadherin-based junction assembly and controlled cell adhesion. Its outputs matter for platelet aggregation, leukocyte arrest on endothelium, T cell contact with antigen-presenting cells and endothelial barrier integrity; loss of the hematopoietic exchange factor RASGRP2 causes a bleeding disorder from platelet integrin failure. Rap1A and Rap1B cycle between GDP- and GTP-bound states at endosomal and plasma membranes, loaded by cAMP-responsive exchange factors (RAPGEF3/4) and diacylglycerol- and calcium-sensitive RasGRPs, and switched off by RAP1GAP family GAPs and SIPA1. Protein kinase A and PKG feed directly into this circuit, linking hormonal and nitric oxide signalling to adhesion. Rap1 also modulates ERK output through RAF1, tuning proliferative signalling alongside its adhesive role.

Rap1 signalling controls how cells stick to their surroundings: the GTPases RAP1A and RAP1B, when loaded with GTP, recruit effectors that switch integrins to a high-affinity state, so this branch of Ras-superfamily signalling governs platelet aggregation, leukocyte adhesion and arrest on endothelium, cell junction integrity and cell shape. Activation is set by opposing regulators. Exchange factors load GTP in response to second messengers, with RAPGEF3 and RAPGEF4 acting as direct cAMP sensors and RASGRP1 and RASGRP2 responding to diacylglycerol and calcium downstream of antigen and collagen receptors; RAP1GAP, RAP1GAP2 and SIPA1 accelerate GTP hydrolysis and shut the switch off. PKA and cGMP-dependent kinase feed in from hormonal and nitric oxide inputs, phosphorylating regulators, while RAF1 and 14-3-3 proteins link Rap1 to ERK-directed growth signalling. Loss of RASGRP2 function causes a platelet adhesion bleeding disorder.

When platelets first stick to a damaged vessel wall they release ADP, ATP and thromboxane A2, and this amplification step is how a handful of adherent platelets recruit many more and convert local adhesion into a growing thrombus. It underlies normal haemostasis and, when unchecked, arterial thrombosis; the ADP receptor P2Y12 is the target of clopidogrel and related antiplatelet drugs, while the thromboxane receptor TBXA2R lies downstream of the aspirin-sensitive arm. Mechanistically, secreted nucleotides act on P2Y1 and P2Y12, and thromboxane on its own receptor, all coupling through heterotrimeric G proteins: Gq-family alpha subunits raise calcium and activate phospholipase C, Gi subunits lower cyclic AMP, and released beta:gamma dimers signal in their own right. Src and p38 signalling together with cytosolic phospholipase A2 feed back to sustain thromboxane production, integrin activation and aggregation.

Healthy vascular endothelium releases prostacyclin continuously, and its action at the Gs-coupled prostacyclin receptor PTGIR keeps platelets quiescent and vessels relaxed. This signalling is the principal brake on spontaneous thrombosis: receptor engagement raises cAMP, activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and blocks the rise in cytoplasmic calcium that platelet activation and granule secretion require, while smooth muscle relaxation lowers vascular tone. The genes here are PTGIR together with the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit GNAS and a full complement of beta and gamma subunits that form the heterotrimer transducing receptor occupancy to adenylate cyclase. The output opposes thromboxane A2, the other major eicosanoid arm, and the set point between them governs bleeding versus clotting tendency. Loss of prostacyclin tone contributes to pulmonary arterial hypertension and to the thrombotic risk seen when prostanoid synthesis is pharmacologically shifted.

EphB receptors bound by membrane-anchored ephrin-B ligands on a neighbouring cell signal into the receptor-bearing neuron, and this forward signalling shapes dendritic spines during central nervous system development. It converts contact between cells into synapse formation: filopodia become motile, find a partner, shorten, and mature into mushroom-shaped spines, with NMDA receptor subunits recruited to the new postsynaptic site. The output is cytoskeletal. Clustered receptors engage Src-family kinases and focal adhesion kinase, and recruit guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as intersectin and kalirin that load CDC42 and RAC1; these drive Arp2/3-dependent actin branching and PAK signalling, while a parallel RHOA-ROCK-LIMK arm phosphorylates cofilin to stabilise existing filaments. Loss of this signalling leaves spines immature and synapses sparse, and the same receptors guide axons and set tissue boundaries elsewhere.

Growing axons steer by retreating from repulsive cues, and ephrin-A binding to EPHA receptors is one of the main signals that makes a growth cone collapse and pull back. This repulsion keeps axons out of territories rich in ephrin-A and is how topographic maps, such as the retinal projection onto the superior colliculus, acquire their graded order; losing it produces mistargeted projections. Ligand engagement clusters EPHA receptors and recruits Src-family kinases, which phosphorylate and switch the exchange factor ephexin (NGEF) toward RHOA activation while Cdc42 and Rac1 signalling falls. Active RHOA drives ROCK1 and ROCK2 to phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains, and non-muscle myosin II contracts the actin network faster than it can extend. The net shift from protrusion to contraction disassembles filopodia and lamellipodia, converting a receptor-ligand contact into directed axon retraction.

Ephrin signaling is bidirectional: when a B-type ephrin on one cell meets an EPH receptor on another, the receptor transmits a forward signal and the ligand itself transmits a reverse signal back into its own cell. This two-way readout of cell-cell contact steers growth cones, sets tissue boundaries, and shapes dendritic spines; loss of it misroutes corpus callosum and retinal axons and, for ephrin-B1, produces craniofrontonasal developmental defects. Reverse signaling works two ways. Src-family kinases including FYN and SRC phosphorylate conserved tyrosines on the ephrin cytoplasmic tail, recruiting the adaptor NCK2 and, through GIT1, ARHGEF7 and PAK kinases, converting the contact into RAC1-dependent actin and myosin light chain remodeling. Alternatively the C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages scaffolds such as syntenin, coupling adhesion to junctional and synaptic organization rather than to kinase output.

Contact between an EPH receptor-bearing cell and an ephrin-bearing cell usually ends in withdrawal rather than sticking, and this contact-dependent repulsion is how growth cones, axon branches and migrating cells are steered away from inappropriate territory. It patterns retinotopic maps, guides commissural and corticospinal axons, keeps tissue boundaries sharp, and its loss produces mis-wired projections and disordered cell segregation. Because the trans-cellular EPH-ephrin interaction is of high affinity, adhesion must be actively dismantled: transmembrane and secreted proteases including ADAM10 and matrix metalloproteinases cleave the ligand or receptor, gamma-secretase components process the remaining stub, and clathrin- and AP-2-dependent endocytosis with dynamin internalises intact receptor-ligand complexes. Src-family kinases transmit the signal, while RAC1 activated through TIAM1 and VAV exchange factors drives the actin remodelling that collapses the growth cone and retracts the membrane.

Muscle contraction covers how a rise in cytosolic calcium is converted into actin-myosin sliding and mechanical force in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle, together with the electrical events that time it. It underlies every heartbeat, voluntary movement, and the tone of blood vessels, airways and gut; its components are the genes mutated in cardiomyopathies, congenital myopathies and inherited arrhythmia syndromes such as long QT and Brugada. Depolarization through voltage-gated sodium and L-type calcium channels triggers ryanodine receptor-mediated release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, calcium binds troponin C or, in smooth muscle, calmodulin to activate myosin light chain kinase, and SERCA pumps, calsequestrin, phospholamban and sodium-calcium exchange terminate the signal. Potassium channels and their accessory subunits set resting potential and repolarization, while titin, dystrophin, actinins and costameric adhesion proteins transmit force to the sarcolemma. Natriuretic peptide and cGMP signalling provide relaxation and vasodilatory control.

Every heartbeat, breath and voluntary movement depends on calcium-triggered sliding of actin and myosin filaments, and this module covers that force generation across skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle together with the electrical signalling that times it. Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, calcium release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum amplify the signal, and calcium binding to troponin relieves tropomyosin inhibition so that myosin heads engage actin; in smooth muscle, myosin light chain kinase phosphorylation of myosin sets tone instead. Relaxation follows from calcium pumps, phospholamban-regulated reuptake, sodium-calcium exchange and nitric oxide-cyclic GMP signalling. Sodium and potassium channels with their auxiliary subunits shape the cardiac action potential's depolarization, plateau and repolarization phases and its propagation. Mutations in these sarcomeric, cytoskeletal and channel components cause cardiomyopathies, arrhythmias including long QT syndrome, and muscular dystrophies.

When a G-protein-coupled receptor activates a heterotrimer, the beta:gamma dimer released alongside the alpha subunit is itself a signalling module, not merely a brake on alpha. G-protein beta:gamma signalling carries receptor input to phospholipase C beta isoforms, generating inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol for calcium release, and to the gamma isoform of PI3K with its regulatory subunits, producing PIP3 that recruits PDK1 and AKT for survival and metabolic responses. A parallel arm engages Rho-family GTPases and their regulators, with CDC42, RHOA, a Rac exchange factor and PAK1 reshaping the actin cytoskeleton. This is the route by which chemokine receptors direct leukocyte chemotaxis and by which BTK links receptor occupancy to B-cell activation, and the many beta and gamma genes provide combinatorial dimers whose tissue distribution tunes which effectors a given receptor reaches; retinal transducin subunits serve phototransduction.

Activation of AMPA receptors is the fast step of excitatory neurotransmission: glutamate released at a synapse binds AMPA-type ionotropic receptors and opens a cation channel within milliseconds, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane and setting the pace of nearly all excitatory signalling in the brain. Changes in the number and composition of these receptors at the synapse are the physical substrate of long-term potentiation and depression, and hence of learning and memory; their overactivation contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death. The four subunits GRIA1-GRIA4 assemble as homomeric or heteromeric tetramers whose properties are tuned post-transcriptionally. RNA editing of the GluR2 pore residue makes receptors calcium-impermeable, so glutamatergic neurons typically carry sodium-only channels while GABAergic interneurons carry calcium-permeable ones. Alternative splicing of cytoplasmic tails and flip/flop exons further sets desensitisation and closing kinetics, generating functionally distinct receptors across synapses.

Fast excitatory transmission at glutamatergic synapses depends on AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors, and their activation by synaptically released glutamate produces the millisecond depolarization that carries most information flow in the brain. The four subunits GRIA1-GRIA4 assemble as homomeric or heteromeric tetramers whose properties are tuned by subunit composition, RNA editing and alternative splicing: an edited GluR2 subunit places arginine in the pore and renders the channel calcium-impermeable, so receptors lacking it pass calcium as well as sodium, as is typical of GABAergic interneurons. Flip/flop variants and long or short cytoplasmic tails set desensitization, resensitization and channel closing rates and govern trafficking. Regulated insertion and removal of these receptors underlies long-term potentiation and depression, and hence learning and memory; excessive calcium entry through GluR2-lacking receptors contributes to excitotoxic neuronal death, while subunit mutations cause intellectual disability and epilepsy.

The strength of an excitatory synapse is set largely by how many AMPA-type glutamate receptors sit in the postsynaptic membrane, and their regulated delivery and removal is the substance of long-term potentiation and depression. Bursts of presynaptic activity raise postsynaptic calcium, activating CaMKII and protein kinase C isoforms that phosphorylate GluA1 and GluA2; the receptors are then held, recycled or internalized depending on which scaffolds and adaptors bind them. PSD-95 and related membrane-associated guanylate kinases anchor receptors at the density, TARP auxiliary subunits encoded by the CACNG genes chaperone them to the surface and tune gating, GRIP and PICK1 retain internal pools, clathrin adaptor complex AP-2 and myosin VI drive endocytic removal, and NSF supports receptor insertion. Because this trafficking implements synaptic plasticity, it underlies learning and memory and is disrupted in intellectual disability, addiction and neurodegeneration.

Fast excitatory transmission in the brain depends on glutamate binding to AMPA-type ionotropic receptors, whose Na+ influx depolarises the postsynaptic membrane and permits coincident NMDA receptor activation; the resulting changes in AMPA receptor number and efficacy are the physical substrate of learning and memory. The four GluA subunits assemble as tetramers held at the synapse by TARP auxiliary subunits (the CACNG proteins), PDZ scaffolds such as PSD-95 and GRIP, and the actin-linked adaptor EPB41L1. Calcium entry activates CaMKII and protein kinase C, which phosphorylate GluA1 to raise channel conductance and drive receptor delivery, strengthening the synapse as in long-term potentiation. Conversely, PICK1-dependent GluA2 phosphorylation, clathrin adaptor-mediated endocytosis and myosin VI-driven internalisation remove receptors during long-term depression. Disturbed AMPA receptor trafficking contributes to epilepsy, intellectual disability and excitotoxic neuronal injury.

Growing axons are steered as much by repulsion as by attraction, and Sema3A is one of the classic repellents: growth cones that meet it collapse and turn away, which is how sensory and cortical projections are kept out of inappropriate territory and how peripheral nerve and dendrite patterning is set. Signal reception requires neuropilin-1 as the ligand-binding subunit together with a plexin-A family receptor, and the PAK-dependent arm of the response converts that binding into actin disassembly. Rac1 recruited to the receptor complex activates group I PAK kinases, which phosphorylate LIMK1; LIMK1 in turn phosphorylates cofilin, blocking its actin-severing and depolymerising activity and remodelling filaments in the collapsing growth cone. Src-family and Fes kinases and HSP90 chaperones support signal transmission. Loss of this route leaves axons insensitive to a major guidance cue and mistargeted.

Growing axons are steered as much by being pushed away as by being pulled, and Sema3A repulsion is the classic example: the secreted cue binds neuropilin-1, which pairs with a plexin-A family receptor to transduce the signal and collapse the growth cone. The route described here works by switching off substrate adhesion, so a neurite loses traction on the extracellular matrix and turns away; the same logic restrains migration of non-neuronal cells. Plexin GAP activity toward R-Ras lowers integrin affinity for ligand, while Rnd1 and Rac1 gate plexin activation and cytoskeletal remodelling, FARP2 acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, and Src-family and Fes kinases relay phosphorylation. Talin and the lipid kinase PIP5K1C link the output to focal adhesion assembly. Disrupting it misroutes axons and disturbs wiring of the peripheral and central nervous systems.

Growing axons steer by retracting from repellent cues, and the collapsin response mediator proteins are the cytosolic step that converts one such cue, Sema3A, into a change in the growth cone cytoskeleton. Sema3A binds a receptor made of neuropilin-1 together with a plexin-A, and the plexin's cytoplasmic tail holds CRMP family members (CRMP1 and the related DPYSL proteins) close to the kinases that modify them. Sequential phosphorylation by Fyn-recruited Cdk5 with its neuronal activator p35, by Fes, and by GSK3beta strips CRMPs of their ability to bind tubulin heterodimers, so microtubule assembly stalls and F-actin depolymerises, collapsing the growth cone and turning the axon away. This axon guidance and neuronal differentiation machinery patterns cortical and sensory projections, and CRMP phosphorylation by the same kinases is a recurring feature of neurodegenerative and regenerative failure in injured nerves.

Parasympathetic input to the pancreas amplifies insulin release during a meal, and this cholinergic arm explains why insulin output is larger when food is anticipated and ingested than when the same glucose load is given intravenously. The potentiation is conditional on glucose already being elevated, so the nerve signal boosts rather than initiates secretion, and loss of this vagal control blunts the early phase of the insulin response. Acetylcholine acts on the M3 muscarinic receptor of beta cells, which couples through Gq-family alpha subunits to phospholipase C beta. Hydrolysis of PIP2 yields IP3, releasing calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores to drive granule exocytosis, and diacylglycerol, which recruits and activates protein kinase C alpha at the membrane. PKC alpha phosphorylates MARCKS, an actin- and membrane-binding substrate linked to granule trafficking and the mobilisation of insulin vesicles for release.

Sympathetic activation shuts down insulin release so that glucose stays available during stress and exercise, and this catecholamine brake on the pancreatic beta cell is how adrenaline and noradrenaline achieve it. The signal begins at alpha-2 adrenergic receptors (ADRA2A, ADRA2C), which couple to inhibitory heterotrimeric G proteins; the released Gi alpha subunits suppress secretory granule exocytosis directly and open ATP-sensitive potassium channels to repolarize the cell, while the liberated beta-gamma dimer closes L-type voltage-gated calcium channels built from CACNA1C/CACNA1D with their auxiliary subunits and inhibits adenylyl cyclases, lowering cytosolic calcium and cAMP. The net effect opposes the glucose-triggered depolarization and calcium influx that normally drive granule fusion. Variants in ADRA2A have been linked to impaired insulin secretion and type 2 diabetes risk, and alpha-2 agonists suppress insulin output pharmacologically.

Fasting liver survives by burning fat, and this transcriptional programme is what licenses it to do so. Activated by fatty acid ligands and by fibrate drugs given for hypertriglyceridaemia, PPARalpha heterodimerises with RXR and occupies peroxisome proliferator response elements at genes for fatty acid uptake and transport (CD36, FABP1, SLC27A1), mitochondrial and peroxisomal beta-oxidation (CPT1A, CPT2, ACADM, ACOX1), ketogenesis (HMGCS2) and lipoprotein handling (APOA1, APOA2, ANGPTL4). Ligand binding swaps corepressor complexes containing NCOR1/2, HDAC3 and SIN3 for coactivators — CREBBP/EP300, the NCOA family, PGC-1 coactivators and the full Mediator complex — to engage RNA polymerase II. Related nuclear receptors and circadian factors here place hepatic lipid catabolism within cholesterol, bile acid and day-night control; loss of the pathway causes fasting hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and steatosis.

Circulating fatty acids amplify how much insulin a beta cell releases in response to glucose, coupling nutrient availability in the blood to the hormonal control of metabolism. Two routes converge: the fatty acid receptor FFAR1 (GPR40) on the beta cell surface signals through Gq-family alpha subunits to phospholipase C beta isoforms, generating inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol that raise intracellular calcium and prime the exocytotic machinery; in parallel, fatty acids taken up via the scavenger receptor CD36 are activated to acyl-CoA esters by long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases, and these lipid intermediates potentiate granule release. Acute potentiation of this kind sustains insulin output after a fat-containing meal, whereas chronic lipid excess contributes to beta cell dysfunction and type 2 diabetes, which has made FFAR1 an attractive target for insulin secretagogue drugs.

Incretin synthesis, secretion, and inactivation describes how the small intestine converts a meal into a hormonal signal that primes the pancreas for the glucose about to arrive. GLP-1 from L cells and GIP from K cells amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release, and this gut-to-islet axis explains why oral glucose is far more insulinotropic than intravenous glucose; its loss contributes to type 2 diabetes, and it is the target of DPP4 inhibitors and GLP-1 mimetics. Preproglucagon and proGIP are made in enteroendocrine cells specified by transcription factors including PAX6, ISL1, CDX2 and TCF7L2, processed by signal peptidase and the prohormone convertase PCSK1, and released in response to fatty acids and phospholipids sensed through FFAR1, FFAR4 and GPR119 acting via heterotrimeric G proteins. Circulating peptides are then clipped within minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, keeping the signal brief and meal-locked.

Gut endocrine cells sense a meal and release hormones that amplify insulin secretion before blood glucose has fully risen, and incretin synthesis, secretion and inactivation covers that whole life cycle. Proglucagon in intestinal L cells and GIP in K cells are made as precursors, cleaved by the signal peptidase complex and by the prohormone convertase PCSK1 to yield active GLP-1 and GIP; transcription factors including CDX2, PAX6, ISL1, GATA4 and TCF7L2, with beta-catenin, specify these cells and drive hormone gene expression. Secretion is triggered by nutrients acting through long- and medium-chain fatty acid receptors FFAR1 and FFAR4, the lipid sensor GPR119, taste-type G protein subunits, and by gastrin-releasing peptide and leptin. Circulating incretins are then truncated within minutes by dipeptidyl peptidase IV, the reason DPP4 inhibitors lower glucose in type 2 diabetes.

GIP is one of the two incretin hormones: released from enteroendocrine K cells of the upper small intestine after a meal, it travels in the blood to pancreatic beta cells and amplifies glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, so that oral glucose provokes far more insulin than the same load given intravenously. This route covers the hormone's whole life cycle. Transcription factors including PAX6, ISL1 and GATA4 specify the K cell and drive expression of the GIP gene; the signal peptidase complex processes the nascent preprohormone in the endoplasmic reticulum, and prohormone convertase PCSK1 cleaves proGIP within secretory granules to the mature peptide. Lipid and nutrient sensors such as FFAR1 and GPR119 couple luminal fat to granule release. Circulating GIP is short-lived because DPP4 removes two N-terminal residues and inactivates it — the basis for DPP4-inhibitor therapy in type 2 diabetes.

Sema4D (CD100) is a membrane-bound guidance cue that, acting through plexin-B1, tells a cell whether to hold onto its substrate or let go and move — the basis of axon repulsion and growth cone collapse, endothelial migration during angiogenesis, and bone and immune cell behaviour. Engagement of plexin-B1 by dimeric Sema4D remodels the actin cytoskeleton: the receptor's intrinsic R-Ras GAP activity lowers RRAS-dependent integrin adhesion, while associated RhoGEFs (ARHGEF11/12) and the Rho GTPases RHOA/B/C drive ROCK1/2 and LIMK1/2, phosphorylating myosin regulatory light chains and driving nonmuscle myosin II contractility. RND1 and RAC1 provide opposing inputs, and ARHGAP35 restrains Rho signalling, so the same ligand can collapse a neurite or promote endothelial motility depending on context. Receptor tyrosine kinases MET and ERBB2 can couple to plexin-B1, linking this axis to invasive growth and tumour cell migration.

Loss of phosphomannomutase 2 activity causes the most common congenital disorder of glycosylation, PMM2-CDG or Jaeken syndrome. The enzyme interconverts mannose 6-phosphate and mannose 1-phosphate in the cytosol, the committed step toward GDP-mannose and dolichol-phosphate-mannose, the mannose donors used to build the lipid-linked oligosaccharide that is transferred onto asparagine residues of nascent secretory and membrane proteins. When the supply of activated mannose falls, N-glycan precursors are assembled incompletely and glycoproteins are underoccupied, detectable clinically as serum and cerebrospinal fluid transferrin lacking sialic acid. Affected infants show psychomotor retardation, cerebellar hypoplasia, coagulation and endocrine abnormalities, and multisystem disease, illustrating how broadly development depends on protein N-glycosylation. The defect lies upstream of the endoplasmic reticulum glycan assembly line rather than in the glycosyltransferases themselves.

Mannose 6-phosphate is the entry point for the mannose donors used in protein N-glycosylation, and the cytosolic isomerase MPI supplies it by converting fructose 6-phosphate, linking glycolytic flux to glycan synthesis. When MPI activity is lost, mannose 6-phosphate becomes limiting for GDP-mannose and dolichol-phosphate-mannose, the donors for mannosyl transfer onto lipid-linked oligosaccharides, so serum glycoproteins are secreted underglycosylated. The resulting congenital disorder of glycosylation, MPI-CDG, spares the nervous system, unlike the commoner phosphomannomutase deficiency, and instead presents with diarrhoea, failure to thrive, protein-losing enteropathy, hepatic involvement and coagulopathy, and can be fatal untreated. Because hexokinase can phosphorylate dietary mannose directly and bypass the missing isomerase step, oral mannose supplementation corrects glycosylation, making this one of the few treatable glycosylation defects.

Sialic acid metabolism builds, activates, installs and recycles the negatively charged nine-carbon sugars that cap most cell-surface glycans. These terminal sialic acids determine how cells are recognised: they form the ligands for selectins and Siglecs, mask glycans from galectins and complement, carry the polysialic acid that lets developing neurons remodel their contacts, and serve as attachment sites for influenza and other pathogens. Synthesis begins with GNE and NANS generating N-acetylneuraminate, CMAS activates it to CMP-Neu5Ac in the nucleus, and SLC35A1 imports the donor into the Golgi, where a large family of ST3GAL, ST6GAL, ST6GALNAC and ST8SIA transferases attaches it in linkage-specific fashion. Turnover runs in reverse: neuraminidases NEU1-NEU4 release sialic acid in lysosomes and at the plasma membrane, SLC17A5 exports it, and NPL degrades it. Loss of these steps causes sialic acid storage disease, sialidosis and GNE myopathy, and altered sialylation accompanies tumour invasion and immune evasion.
