Sialic acids cap the outer ends of glycan chains on cell-surface glycoproteins and glycolipids, and sialic acid metabolism covers how the most abundant human form, N-acetylneuraminate, is made, activated, attached, recycled and broken down. The resulting negatively charged termini govern cell-cell recognition, immune self-marking through Siglec binding, neural development via polysialylated adhesion molecules, and serve as attachment sites exploited by influenza virus and bacterial toxins. GNE and NANS commit UDP-GlcNAc to the pathway, CMAS activates the sugar as CMP-Neu5Ac in the nucleus, a dedicated transporter delivers it into the Golgi, and families of sialyltransferases transfer it in alpha2,3, alpha2,6 or alpha2,8 linkage, the last generating polysialic acid. Lysosomal sialidases and a sialic acid exporter return free sugar to the cytosol for reuse or degradation. Loss of these steps causes inclusion body myopathy, sialidosis and free sialic acid storage disease, and altered sialylation accompanies tumour metastasis.

Sialic acid biosynthesis begins with a single bifunctional enzyme, GNE, which converts UDP-N-acetylglucosamine to N-acetylmannosamine and then phosphorylates it, committing the cell to making Neu5Ac for the terminal sugars of glycoproteins and glycolipids. Because sialic acid caps most cell-surface glycans, the rate of this step sets how heavily cells are sialylated, and CMP-Neu5Ac feeds back on the epimerase domain to keep production matched to demand. Mutations that abolish that feedback cause sialuria, with free Neu5Ac accumulating in cytoplasm and spilling into urine — distinct from sialidoses, where the stored sugar is protein-bound. Loss-of-function mutations instead reduce sialylation and cause adult-onset distal myopathies, Nonaka myopathy and inclusion body myopathy 2, in which muscle wastes progressively and biopsies show rimmed vacuoles with beta-amyloid deposits despite no neurological involvement.

Loss-of-function mutations in GFPT1 cause a congenital myasthenic syndrome with tubular aggregates, a limb-girdle pattern of fatigable weakness in which muscle biopsies show abnormal fibre morphology and characteristic tubular aggregates, and patients typically improve on acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. GFPT1 catalyses the first, rate-limiting step of hexosamine biosynthesis, converting fructose 6-phosphate and glutamine toward UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, the donor sugar for N- and O-linked glycosylation and other glycan modifications. Flux through this step therefore sets the availability of substrate for glycosylating the receptors, adhesion molecules and synaptic proteins on which neuromuscular junction assembly and transmission depend, linking central carbon and amino acid metabolism to synaptic function. Disease-associated missense changes need not abolish catalytic activity outright; reduced GFPT1 protein in patient muscle points to unstable or poorly translated product, so the defect is one of enzyme dosage limiting hexosamine supply to the endplate.

SUMO conjugation is itself regulated by SUMO, and this self-directed branch of the pathway covers modification of the machinery that attaches SUMO to other proteins. The sole SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBE2I (UBC9) and the E3 ligases PIAS4, RANBP2 and TOPORS all carry SUMO marks, which tune their catalytic activity and their placement within the nucleus and at nuclear bodies. Because RANBP2 sits in the cytoplasmic filaments of the nuclear pore, much of this chemistry occurs at the pore itself, and the nucleoporin scaffold listed here comprises the Y-complex, central channel FG repeats, the transmembrane ring and the TPR basket that anchor the ligase. The result is a feedback layer that sets how strongly and where substrates are SUMOylated, with consequences for nucleocytoplasmic transport, mitotic spindle checkpoint signalling, chromosome segregation and the DNA damage response.

Non-canonical WNT ligands such as WNT5A and WNT11 bind Frizzled receptors and raise intracellular calcium rather than stabilising beta-catenin, and this calcium arm of WNT signalling shapes dorsoventral polarity, convergent extension movements and organ morphogenesis in vertebrates. Ligand-bound FZD couples to heterotrimeric G proteins, whose released beta-gamma subunits and Galpha activate phospholipase C beta and phosphodiesterases; inositol trisphosphate then opens ITPR channels on the endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting calcium flux engages calmodulin, CaMK2, protein kinase C and the phosphatase calcineurin, which dephosphorylates NFAT for nuclear entry, while TAK1 and NLK act to dampen TCF/LEF-driven transcription downstream of beta-catenin. This antagonism makes the route a brake on canonical WNT output, and its misregulation is implicated in inflammatory responses and in tumour invasion and metastasis.

Cells in an epithelial sheet need to know not just up from down but which way is forward, and this non-canonical WNT branch, planar cell polarity and its morphogenetic output convergent extension, supplies that in-plane orientation. It narrows and lengthens tissue during gastrulation, closes the neural tube, orients hair follicles and stereociliary bundles in the inner ear, and patterns the limb bud; loss of components such as VANGL2 produces neural tube defects and deranged hair cell orientation. Non-canonical ligands including WNT5A, WNT5B and WNT11 act through FZD receptors or the single-pass receptors RYK and ROR1/ROR2, and signal via DVL proteins, DAAM1, PRICKLE1, SCRIB and PARD6A to RHOA and RAC GTPases that remodel actin and drive polarized cell movement. Asymmetric protein distribution is enforced by clathrin/AP-2 endocytosis and by SMURF-directed ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover of polarity components.

Nuclear receptors translate hormones, lipids and xenobiotics into transcriptional programmes, and attaching SUMO to them is one of the main ways cells set how strongly those programmes run. SUMOylation of intracellular receptors generally dampens their output: modification of receptors such as the glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors, estrogen and progesterone receptors, PPARs, retinoid, thyroid and vitamin D receptors, and the liver X and farnesoid X receptors can weaken DNA binding, recruit or retain corepressors, alter subnuclear localisation, block dimerisation, or compete with other modifications at the same residues. The androgen receptor and RORA are notable exceptions where the mark can favour activity. SUMO1 to SUMO3 are conjugated through the E2 enzyme UBE2I with PIAS family E3 ligases providing specificity, and the resulting repression is important for restraining inflammatory gene expression, with consequences for metabolic and hormone-driven disease.

Hundreds of hormones, neurotransmitters and lipid mediators act through receptors coupled to the Gq family of heterotrimeric G proteins, and this branch of receptor signalling is how those ligands raise intracellular calcium. Receptor occupancy releases activated Gq, which stimulates phospholipase C beta isoforms to cleave PIP2 into diacylglycerol and IP3; IP3 receptors then empty endoplasmic reticulum calcium stores while DAG activates protein kinase C, feeding onward into Ras-ERK cascades, RhoGEFs such as Trio and Kalirin, and calcium-gated TRPC channels. Diacylglycerol kinases and lipases terminate the DAG signal, RGS proteins accelerate Gq deactivation, and receptor kinases desensitise the receptors. The receptor repertoire here spans muscarinic, adrenergic alpha-1, angiotensin, endothelin, thrombin and serotonin 2 receptors, underlying smooth muscle contraction, vasoconstriction, secretion, neuronal excitability and platelet activation and aggregation.

G alpha (12/13) signalling events is the branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling that reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, converting hormone and lipid mediator binding at the cell surface into changes in cell shape, adhesion and contractility. It drives platelet shape change and aggregation downstream of thromboxane receptors, smooth muscle tone downstream of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, and the migration and invasion programs co-opted by tumour cells, with GNA13 mutation a recurrent event in lymphoma. Activated GNA12 or GNA13 engages RhoGEFs such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF11 and ARHGEF12, loading GTP onto RHOA, RHOB and RHOC; Rho-kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 then promote stress fibre and focal adhesion assembly. Many additional exchange factors for Rho, Rac and Cdc42 are recruited through this hub, linking the pathway to axon guidance via plexin receptors, cytokinesis and cell proliferation. Receptors using this route generally also couple to Gq.

Some G protein-coupled receptors, including alpha-1 adrenergic and thromboxane A2 receptors, signal through the G alpha 12/13 family to reshape the actin cytoskeleton rather than to raise calcium or cyclic AMP. This route governs cell shape, stress fiber and focal adhesion formation, adhesion, migration and proliferation, and underlies platelet shape change, vascular smooth muscle tone, neurite retraction and the invasive behaviour of tumour cells. Activated GNA12 and GNA13, with released beta-gamma subunits, engage Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF11, ARHGEF12 and AKAP13, which load GTP onto RhoA, RhoB and RhoC; the Rho kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2 then drive actomyosin contractility. Many other exchange factors acting on Rac and Cdc42 broaden the output. Because G12/13-coupled receptors almost always also couple to Gq, Rho activation is the practical readout of this branch.

Semaphorin 4D acting through plexin-B1 tells a cell to let go and turn away, converting an extracellular guidance cue into loss of integrin-mediated adhesion and collapse of the leading edge. This repulsive signalling shapes axon guidance and growth cone steering, and the same receptor pair is co-opted in vascular and tumour settings, where plexin-B1 partners with the receptor tyrosine kinase MET. Ligand binding allows Rnd1 to engage plexin-B1 and switch on its intracellular GTPase-activating domain, which lowers active R-Ras; the resulting drop in PI3K and Akt output relieves inhibition of GSK-3beta, which phosphorylates and inactivates the microtubule assembly factor CRMP2. In parallel, recruitment of p190RhoGAP transiently reduces RhoA-GTP, and Rac1 activity is redirected, so that actin and microtubule dynamics at the periphery favour retraction rather than protrusion.

Sema4D binding to plexin-B1 reshapes the actin cytoskeleton, driving endothelial cell migration in angiogenesis while causing growth cones of responding neurons to collapse and retract, so the same ligand steers vessel and axon guidance in opposite directions depending on context. Plexin-B1 acts as a receptor whose cytoplasmic tail recruits the RhoA-specific exchange factors ARHGEF11 and ARHGEF12 and binds the small GTPase RND1, and in endothelium its association with ERBB2 couples receptor occupancy to RhoA, RhoB and RhoC activation. Active RhoA engages ROCK1 and ROCK2, which phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains such as MYL9 and MYL12B and activate LIM kinases; the resulting non-muscle myosin II contractility builds stress fibres, stabilizes focal adhesions and integrin-mediated adhesion in migrating cells, or in neurons collapses the peripheral actin network. This branch is Rho-dependent and distinct from the R-Ras-directed arm of plexin signalling.

Semaphorins are guidance cues that tell migrating cells and growing axons where not to go, and plexins are their principal receptors; beyond the canonical class 3 to plexin-A route, a broad set of other semaphorin interactions couples transmembrane and GPI-anchored semaphorins to plexins of the A, B, C and D subfamilies and to non-plexin partners. These contacts steer axon repulsion and fasciculation, vascular patterning, bone remodelling and immune cell behaviour. Specificity comes from the receptor combination: SEMA4D acting through CD72 on B cells, SEMA4A and SEMA6 family members engaging plexin-A receptors, SEMA7A signalling through integrin alpha1/beta1 rather than a plexin, and SEMA6D working with the TREM2-TYROBP adaptor pair in myeloid cells. SEMA3E-PLXND1 restricts endothelial sprouting. Loss of these cues produces miswired circuits, disordered vessel branching and altered immune activation.

The number of AMPA-type glutamate receptors held at a synapse sets its strength, and the trafficking of GluR2-containing AMPA receptors is how neurons adjust that number and control calcium permeability, since inclusion of the GluR2 subunit makes the channel calcium-impermeable. This underlies hippocampal synaptic plasticity and long-term depression, and its failure contributes to excitotoxic calcium overload. The GluR2 C-terminus is a hub for competing interactions: GRIP1 and GRIP2 anchor receptors at the postsynaptic membrane, PICK1 drives internalization and surface delivery, NSF sustains synaptic receptor levels, and the AP-2 adaptor complex couples receptors to clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Protein kinase C isoforms phosphorylate GluR2 at serine 880, releasing GRIP and favouring PICK1 binding, which switches receptors from anchored to mobile. Constitutive recycling between synapse and endosome, and activity-driven subunit exchange, both depend on this balance.

Extracellular nucleotides act as signals as well as metabolites, and P2Y receptors are the G protein-coupled receptors that read them. ATP, ADP, UTP, UDP and UDP-glucose released from damaged, stressed or activated cells bind these receptors to report tissue injury and coordinate responses to it: platelet aggregation, smooth muscle tone, epithelial chloride and fluid secretion, microglial chemotaxis, and inflammatory cell recruitment. Coupling determines the output, with some members raising inositol phosphates and calcium through Gq and others lowering cAMP through Gi. P2RY12 on platelets is the ADP receptor blocked by clopidogrel and related antithrombotics, while P2RY2 agonism has been pursued for mucosal hydration. Several related orphan receptors sit in the same family branch, including GPR17 and lysophospholipid receptors, reflecting shared ancestry rather than shared ligand.

Adenosine accumulates when tissues are stressed, hypoxic or metabolically taxed, and the four P1 receptors are how cells read that signal. Acting as G protein-coupled receptors for extracellular adenosine, they tune cardiac work to oxygen supply, dilate coronary vessels, dampen neuronal excitability and restrain inflammation, which is why this is the system caffeine blocks and why adenosine terminates supraventricular tachycardia in the clinic. The A1 subtype couples to inhibitory G proteins and lowers cyclic AMP, slowing atrioventricular conduction and suppressing transmitter release; A2A and A2B raise cyclic AMP, with A2A shaping striatal dopamine signalling and suppressing T cell and myeloid activation in tumours and injured tissue; A3 acts mainly on mast cells and other immune populations.

Nucleotide-like (purinergic) receptors are the cell-surface sensors for extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP, UDP-sugars and adenosine, molecules that leak or are released from stressed, dying and activated cells and so act as signals of tissue damage and metabolic state. Through them, purine and pyrimidine nucleotides control vascular tone, platelet aggregation, inflammatory cytokine secretion, nociception and apoptosis; P2RY12 is the target of antiplatelet drugs such as clopidogrel, and adenosine receptors mediate caffeine's stimulant action and adenosine's brake on cardiac conduction and immune activation. The genes here are the G protein-coupled arm of the family: P2Y receptors coupling to Gq and phospholipase C or to Gi, the four adenosine receptors tuning cyclic AMP up or down, and related orphan and lysophospholipid receptors of the same structural branch. Signalling converges on calcium release, cAMP and downstream regulation of secretion, chemotaxis and cell survival.

Extracellular ATP, ADP, UTP and adenosine act as signals reporting cell damage, stress and nucleotide release, and this family of nucleotide-like purinergic receptors is how cells read them. The set covers the G protein-coupled arm: four adenosine receptors that tune vascular tone, inflammation, neuronal excitability and cardiac rate, and the P2Y receptors that respond to nucleotides. Some couple through Gq to phospholipase C and calcium release, others through Gi to lower cyclic AMP, so a single nucleotide can produce opposing outcomes depending on which receptor a cell expresses. P2RY12 on platelets drives ADP-dependent aggregation and is the target of widely used antithrombotic drugs. Related orphan and lysophospholipid-responsive receptors are grouped here by sequence kinship. Collectively these receptors shape vascular reactivity, immune cytokine secretion, platelet activation and apoptotic responses to nucleotide release.

G beta:gamma signalling through PLC beta is the branch of G protein-coupled receptor signalling in which the released beta:gamma dimer, rather than the alpha subunit, directly stimulates phospholipase C beta to generate second messengers. It converts receptor occupancy into a rise in cytosolic calcium and protein kinase C activity, and it is the dominant route by which chemokine and chemoattractant receptors on leukocytes trigger chemotaxis, degranulation and the respiratory burst. Mechanistically, the beta:gamma dimer binds the pleckstrin homology domain of PLC beta and increases hydrolysis of PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, the latter opening ER calcium stores; PLCB3 responds most strongly, followed by PLCB2 and PLCB1. Combinatorial pairing of multiple beta and gamma subunits, including retinal transducin gamma subunits, gives tissue-specific tuning of this output, and loss of the neuronal GNB5 subunit causes intellectual disability with cardiac arrhythmia.

Free G protein beta:gamma dimers, released when a receptor-activated heterotrimeric G protein dissociates, act as signalling molecules in their own right, and one of their direct effectors is phospholipase C beta. Engagement of the enzyme's pleckstrin homology domain stimulates hydrolysis of the membrane lipid PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, so that IP3 releases calcium from intracellular stores while DAG recruits and activates protein kinase C. This gives Gi- and Go-coupled receptors, which do not stimulate PLC through their alpha subunits, a route to calcium mobilisation; it underlies chemokine-driven leukocyte activation, platelet responses and taste transduction, where the hematopoietic isoform PLCB2 and the gustatory gamma subunit GNG13 operate. The various beta and gamma subunits combine combinatorially, and the beta isoforms differ in sensitivity, with PLCB3 the most responsive and PLCB1 the least.

Platelet homeostasis is the resting state that keeps circulating platelets quiescent until vessel injury demands otherwise, and its loss tips the balance toward thrombosis or, in the other direction, bleeding. Healthy endothelium releases prostacyclin and nitric oxide, which act on platelets through the prostacyclin receptor and soluble guanylate cyclase to raise cyclic nucleotides; protein kinase G and its substrate IRAG then suppress inositol trisphosphate receptor-mediated calcium release, while phosphodiesterases set the duration of the signal. Much of the remaining machinery governs cytosolic calcium itself: SERCA and plasma membrane calcium pumps and sodium-calcium exchangers remove it, STIM1 with ORAI channels and TRPC and P2X purinergic channels admit it. Calcium-activated potassium channels, PECAM1, and phosphatases including SHP-1 and PP2A add inhibitory tone, linking endothelial vasodilator signalling to platelet activation thresholds and vascular smooth muscle relaxation.

Reduction of cytosolic Ca++ levels is the clearance arm of calcium signalling: it returns free cytoplasmic Ca2+ to its resting nanomolar concentration after a signalling spike, which is what allows the next spike to be interpreted as information rather than noise. Sustained elevation instead triggers protease and phospholipase activation, mitochondrial overload and cell death, and in heart and muscle it manifests as impaired relaxation and arrhythmia. Two routes do the work: SERCA pumps (ATP2A1-3) pump Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic and endoplasmic reticulum for reuse, while plasma membrane Ca2+ ATPases (ATP2B1-4) and the Na+/Ca2+ exchangers (SLC8A1-3) extrude it across the cell surface, the exchangers trading the sodium gradient for high-capacity efflux. Calmodulin tunes pump activity to the calcium load, and sorcin modulates the release channels, coupling clearance to excitation-contraction cycling.

Calcium signals must be terminated as sharply as they are generated, and this pathway is how a cell clears calcium from its cytosol after a transient. Pumps of the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum family reload internal stores, plasma membrane calcium ATPases extrude calcium against its gradient using ATP, and sodium/calcium exchangers move it out in exchange for inbound sodium, a lower-affinity but high-capacity route that dominates in cardiac myocytes. Calmodulin senses the rising ion and stimulates the plasma membrane pumps, giving feedback control over the recovery phase; sorcin modulates calcium handling in excitable cells. Restoring resting calcium sets the rate of muscle relaxation, resets neuronal excitability and secretory cells for the next stimulus, and prevents the sustained overload that triggers protease and phospholipase activation and cell death. Failure contributes to heart failure, arrhythmia and hereditary deafness.

Platelets only aggregate, change shape, secrete their granules and expose procoagulant phosphatidylserine when cytosolic Ca2+ rises, so the control of that rise and its reversal sets the threshold for haemostasis and thrombosis. In the resting state, calcium is kept low by pumps: plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPases extrude it, SERCA isoforms sequester it into the dense tubular system, and sodium-calcium exchangers of the SLC8 family provide an additional exit route. On agonist stimulation, phospholipase C-derived IP3 opens IP3 receptor channels on that store; store depletion is sensed by STIM1, which gates Orai channels in the plasma membrane to sustain store-operated entry. Receptor-operated entry through the ATP-gated P2X1 channel and TRPC channels adds further influx, and calmodulin and sorcin tune the response. Loss of STIM1 or Orai1 function blunts platelet activation and confers bleeding, while excessive signalling favours thrombus formation.

cGMP made by guanylate cyclases in response to nitric oxide or natriuretic peptides is the messenger that relaxes smooth muscle, restrains platelets and tunes neuronal excitability, and this pathway covers what happens once it has been made. Its central reader is cGMP-dependent protein kinase, present as the smooth-muscle PRKG1 and the epithelial and neuronal PRKG2, which phosphorylates targets that lower cytosolic calcium: IRAG1 in complex with the IP3 receptor ITPR1 to curb calcium release from internal stores, and large-conductance calcium-activated potassium channels built from KCNMA1 with beta subunits to hyperpolarise the membrane. Signal duration is set by phosphodiesterases that hydrolyse cGMP, among them PDE5A, whose pharmacological inhibition sustains vasodilation and is used to treat erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Loss of this braking arm favours vasoconstriction and excessive platelet aggregation.

Hormones and neurotransmitters that raise intracellular cAMP do so through receptors coupled to the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit, and this branch of G protein-coupled receptor output is what converts those extracellular signals into protein kinase A activity. It underlies adrenergic control of heart rate and airway tone, thyroid and gonadal stimulation by pituitary glycoprotein hormones, parathyroid hormone action on bone and kidney, incretin-driven insulin release, and melanocortin control of pigmentation and appetite. Ligand-bound receptor activates GNAS, which stimulates adenylate cyclase isoforms; cAMP then releases catalytic PRKACA/PRKACB subunits from their regulatory partners, while phosphodiesterases hydrolyse the second messenger and set signal duration. Receptor kinases and arrestins desensitise the receptor, and c-Src provides a tyrosine kinase arm. Loss- and gain-of-function mutations in GNAS cause pseudohypoparathyroidism, fibrous dysplasia and endocrine tumours.

ADP released from platelet dense granules acts as an autocrine amplifier of haemostasis, and the P2Y1 purinoceptor is the arm of that response that starts shape change and the first, reversible wave of aggregation. It works with the Gi-coupled P2Y12 receptor, the target of clopidogrel and related antithrombotics; both must be engaged for full, irreversible aggregation and thrombus stabilisation, so loss of either leaves a bleeding tendency while excess signalling favours arterial thrombosis. P2Y1 couples to Gq family alpha subunits (GNAQ, GNA11, GNA14, GNA15) with a wide range of beta and gamma partners, mobilising calcium from internal stores. Downstream, p38 MAP kinase and Src-family signalling converge on cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonic acid for thromboxane synthesis and recruiting further platelets. The pathway therefore links nucleotide sensing to integrin activation, granule secretion and clot formation.

Many G protein-coupled receptors work by lowering cyclic AMP rather than raising it, and G alpha (i) signalling is that inhibitory arm. Receptor-activated Gi subunits suppress adenylate cyclase, so less cAMP is made from ATP and protein kinase A activity falls, while the released beta-gamma dimer acts on its own effectors including phospholipase C beta and channel and kinase targets; Gi can also engage the tyrosine kinase Src. The receptors that use it span opioid, adrenergic alpha-2, muscarinic M2/M4, somatostatin, cannabinoid, adenosine, chemokine and taste and visual pigment families, which is why this route governs analgesia, neurotransmitter release, heart rate slowing, leukocyte chemotaxis and sensory transduction. RGS proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis to terminate signalling, and phosphodiesterases, phosphatases and CREB-directed kinases shape the downstream cAMP and calcium response. Drugs from opioids to chemokine receptor blockers act here.

Signalling through G alpha (z) is a slow, pertussis toxin-resistant branch of inhibitory G protein signalling that lowers cAMP and shapes platelet and neuronal responses to catecholamines and opioids. Receptors such as the alpha-2 adrenergic receptors couple through this subunit, which inhibits several adenylyl cyclase isoforms and so reduces protein kinase A activity, while the released beta-gamma dimer acts on its own effectors. The distinguishing feature is kinetic: GTP hydrolysis by G alpha (z) is exceptionally slow, so signals persist unless terminated by RGS proteins, and phosphorylation by protein kinase C provides a further layer of control. G alpha (z) also engages Rap1GAP, linking receptor input to attenuation of Rap1 signalling. Loss of this pathway disturbs epinephrine-driven platelet aggregation and alters behavioural responses to neuroactive drugs, placing it at the interface of haemostasis and central neuromodulation.

Growing axons steer toward sources of netrin-1, and DCC is the receptor that converts that gradient into attraction, guiding commissural axons across the midline and wiring the two halves of the nervous system together. Loss of this attractive signalling leaves midline crossing incomplete, as seen in congenital mirror movements and agenesis of the corpus callosum. DCC itself has no catalytic activity; instead the kinases FAK, Src and Fyn associate with its cytoplasmic tail and, on netrin binding, phosphorylate it and recruit adaptors such as NCK1 and DOCK1. These feed the Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 and the exchange factor TRIO, while WASL and the actin-binding ABLIM proteins remodel filaments in the growth cone. The output is asymmetric actin polymerisation and filopodial extension on the netrin-facing side, turning a diffusible cue into directed growth-cone motility.

Growing axons are steered by the same guidance cue in opposite directions depending on which receptor they display, and netrin-mediated repulsion is the arm that turns netrin-1 into a turning-away signal. It shapes the trajectories of commissural and other projecting neurons, and the same receptors act in vascular patterning and as regulators of cell survival, since UNC5 family members are dependence receptors that trigger death when unoccupied by ligand. Netrin binding to UNC5A-D promotes phosphorylation within the receptor's ZU-5 domain, with Src-family kinase activity and the phosphatase SHP2 relaying the signal to the actin cytoskeleton of the growth cone. Long-range repulsion additionally requires cooperation with DCC, whose cytoplasmic domain pairs with UNC5, whereas UNC5 alone suffices at short range. Loss of this steering causes misrouted commissures and defective neural wiring.

Some receptors do not simply stay silent when unoccupied: they actively kill the cell, making survival conditional on continued ligand supply. The netrin-1 receptors DCC and UNC5 behave this way, and caspase activation via these dependence receptors in the absence of ligand is thought to prune neurons that fail to reach netrin-rich targets during axon guidance, and to suppress tumours by killing cells that stray from their normal environment. When netrin-1 is present the same receptors direct attraction or repulsion of growing axons; when it is absent, DCC is cleaved and recruits caspase-9, which activates caspase-3 without cytochrome c release or apoptosome assembly. UNC5 death signalling instead works through adaptors such as MAGED1 and the death-associated protein kinases DAPK1-3. Loss of this ligand-dependence contributes to survival of cancer cells that have lost netrin signalling.

Growing axons steer by reading guidance cues, and netrin-1 is one of the strongest attractants for commissural axons crossing the midline of the developing spinal cord. Whether a growth cone turns toward or away from netrin depends on the second messengers it generates, so this signalling sets the wiring of long-range connections; loss of the pathway leaves axons unable to reach their targets, and the netrin receptor DCC is also mutated in congenital mirror movements and corpus callosum agenesis. Netrin binding to DCC engages phospholipase C gamma, aided by phosphatidylinositol transfer, to produce IP3 and diacylglycerol. IP3 releases calcium from endoplasmic reticulum stores while diacylglycerol directly gates TRPC3 and TRPC6; store depletion recruits other TRPC channels, and the resulting calcium influx at the growth cone, tuned by cyclic nucleotide levels, determines attraction versus repulsion.

Adherens junction interactions establish and hold the calcium-dependent, homotypic cell-cell contacts that give epithelia and endothelia their sheet-like integrity, polarity and coordinated movement. The core events are trans-dimerization of cadherins and of nectin-family adhesion receptors across the intercellular gap, coupled inside the cell through catenins, plakoglobin, vinculin and alpha-catenin to the actin cytoskeleton, with Rho-family GTPases such as RAC1 and CDC42 and their activators shaping the junction as it matures. Src-family and casein kinase phosphorylation, proteolytic shedding and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover regulate receptor availability, while transcriptional repressors including SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST, together with polycomb and histone-deacetylase activity and microRNAs, silence E-cadherin during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. This explains why the pathway underlies embryonic cell sorting and contact inhibition of growth, and why its loss accompanies tumour invasion and metastasis.

NCAM1 interactions describes the binding partnerships of the neural cell adhesion molecule, an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor that also transduces signals across the membrane. It governs how neurons and glia stick to each other and to matrix, how axons grow and are guided, and how synapses remodel, so it underpins neural development, learning-related synaptic plasticity, and regeneration after injury. NCAM1 engages in homophilic cis- and trans-binding and in heterophilic contacts with collagens and other extracellular matrix and proteoglycan components such as agrin and neurocan, with contactin and prion protein, and with the GDNF family ligands through GFRA co-receptors, making it an alternative signalling receptor for neurotrophic factors. Downstream, it couples to voltage-gated calcium channel subunits to influence neurite outgrowth. Polysialylation by ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4 weakens adhesion and switches NCAM1 toward permitting migration and plasticity.

NCAM1 is a neural cell adhesion molecule that both glues cells together and signals, and its interactions shape how neurons and glia migrate, extend axons, and remodel synapses during development and learning. Homophilic binding between NCAM1 molecules on adjacent cells is tuned by polysialylation, added by the sialyltransferases ST8SIA2 and ST8SIA4, which bulks up the extracellular domain and weakens adhesion to favour plasticity and cell movement; loss of this modification stiffens circuits and has been linked to schizophrenia risk. Heterophilic partners broaden the output: fibrillar and basement membrane collagens and the proteoglycans agrin and neurocan tie NCAM1 to the extracellular matrix, GDNF family ligands with their GFRA co-receptors couple it to neurotrophic survival signalling, and voltage-gated calcium channel subunits link adhesion to excitability and transmitter release. Contactin-2 and prion protein complete a set of neuronal surface associations governing adhesion, proliferation, differentiation and neurite outgrowth.

Lysophospholipids released by membrane turnover act as extracellular messengers, and the receptors for lysosphingolipids and lysophosphatidic acid are how cells read them. Signalling through the S1P receptors governs lymphocyte egress from lymph nodes, vascular barrier integrity and angiogenesis — the basis for S1P receptor modulators used in multiple sclerosis — while the LPA receptors drive cytoskeletal contraction, wound healing, fibrosis and tumour cell migration. These are G protein-coupled receptors coupling mainly through Gi and Gq to inhibit adenylyl cyclase, mobilise endoplasmic reticulum calcium and engage Rho, with downstream effects of suppressed apoptosis and increased proliferation. Also represented are the phospholipid phosphatase-related proteins, membrane proteins concentrated in neurons that shape local availability of these lipid mediators and influence axon outgrowth and dendritic spine formation.

Opsins are the light-detecting G protein-coupled receptors that let the eye convert photons into neural signals. Each is a seven-transmembrane protein bound to a retinal chromophore whose photoisomerization changes receptor conformation and activates a heterotrimeric G protein, and for rod and cone opsins this launches the phototransduction cascade in which transducin stimulates cGMP phosphodiesterase and the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes. Rhodopsin supports dim-light vision while the long-, middle- and short-wavelength cone pigments provide colour discrimination; mutations in them cause retinitis pigmentosa, night blindness and colour vision defects, and loss of the transducin subunits gives stationary night blindness or achromatopsia. Melanopsin serves non-image-forming roles, entraining circadian rhythms and driving the pupillary light reflex, while encephalopsin, neuropsin and the retinal G protein-coupled receptor and peropsin act in extraocular light sensing or in regenerating retinal for the visual cycle.

Calcitonin-like ligand receptors handle a family of related peptide hormones "calcitonin, amylin, CGRP, adrenomedullin and intermedin " that between them control calcium and bone turnover, appetite and nutrient intake, vascular tone and lymphatic and vascular development. Signalling runs through two class B G protein-coupled receptors, the calcitonin receptor and the calcitonin receptor-like receptor, generally raising cyclic AMP in target cells. Ligand selectivity is not set by the receptor alone: three receptor activity-modifying proteins escort these receptors to the surface and reshape their binding pockets, so that the calcitonin receptor with a RAMP becomes an amylin receptor, while the calcitonin receptor-like receptor pairs with RAMP1 for CGRP and with RAMP2 or RAMP3 for adrenomedullin. CGRP signalling through this route drives the neurogenic vasodilation targeted by migraine therapeutics, while amylin aggregation in islets and adrenomedullin loss in endothelium illustrate the pathology at either end.

Tight junctions seal the space between neighbouring epithelial and endothelial cells, and the interactions described here are the ones that build the sealing strands and anchor the polarity machinery to them. Without them an epithelium cannot hold a solute gradient across itself: leaky junctions underlie renal magnesium wasting, deafness, skin barrier failure and breakdown of the blood-brain barrier. The strands themselves are polymers of claudins, a large family whose members differ in whether they occlude the paracellular route or form selective pores for ions, so the mix expressed by a tissue sets its permeability. Junctional adhesion molecule A contributes adhesion, while PAR-3, PAR-6 isoforms with atypical PKC iota and the CRB3-PALS1-PATJ module are recruited to the apical junction, where they specify the apical membrane domain, maintain the boundary separating it from the basolateral surface, and feed into control of proliferation and morphogenesis.

Glucagon-type ligand receptors are the class B, secretin-like G protein-coupled receptors through which peptide hormones released by gut, pancreas and hypothalamus set blood glucose, appetite, digestive secretion and growth. Glucagon acting on its receptor mobilises hepatic glucose between meals, while the incretins GIP and GLP-1 potentiate insulin release after a meal, making the GLP-1 receptor one of the most exploited drug targets in diabetes and obesity; GLP-2 signalling supports intestinal mucosal growth, secretin and VIP receptors drive pancreatic and epithelial fluid and bicarbonate secretion, and the growth hormone-releasing hormone receptor governs pituitary somatotroph output, with loss-of-function causing dwarfism. All couple through heterotrimeric G proteins, chiefly the stimulatory alpha subunit encoded by GNAS together with an assortment of beta and gamma subunits, raising cyclic AMP in the target cell. PACAP and its receptor extend the same chemistry to neuroendocrine and stress responses.

Class C G protein-coupled receptors sense small molecules that report on the chemical environment anging from synaptic glutamate and GABA to extracellular calcium, amino acids and nutrients in food. They matter because they tune rather than trigger: the eight metabotropic glutamate receptors and the GABA-B heterodimer of GABBR1 and GABBR2 modulate synaptic strength and underlie forms of plasticity, GRM6 carries the ON-bipolar response in retina, and the calcium-sensing receptor CASR sets parathyroid hormone release and renal calcium handling, with loss-of-function mutations causing familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. Sweet and umami taste arises from TAS1R pairings, while the TAS2R bitter receptors detect potentially toxic compounds and shape dietary aversion. These receptors share a large clamshell-shaped extracellular ligand-binding domain, function as dimers, and signal through the seven-transmembrane bundle, which also hosts allosteric drug sites of pharmacological interest.

Cell-cell adhesion is often built from pairs of immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors that recognise a different partner across the gap rather than a copy of themselves, and trans-heterodimerization between nectins and nectin-like molecules is the clearest example. These mismatched pairings, such as nectin-1 with nectin-3 or nectin-2 with nectin-3, generate stronger and more selective contacts than like-with-like binding and set up asymmetric junctions between two different cell types — Sertoli cell with spermatid, photoreceptor with glial process, neuron with neuron at the synapse. The contacts they nucleate recruit afadin and cooperate with cadherins to organise adherens junctions and tight junctions. The same molecules serve outside epithelia: CADM1 and the poliovirus receptor engage activating receptors including CD226, CD96 and CRTAM on T and NK cells, so this adhesion chemistry also governs immune cell recognition, and nectin-1 and nectin-2 double as herpesvirus entry receptors.

Cell-cell junction organization builds and maintains the contacts that hold epithelial and endothelial sheets together, giving tissues mechanical integrity and a selective paracellular barrier. Adherens junctions initiate contact through classical cadherins such as CDH1 linked by catenins and vinculin to actin; claudins and JAM-A seal tight junctions that control passage of water, ions and small solutes; desmosomal plakoglobin ties the intermediate filament network between neighbouring cells. Nectins, CADMs and the PAR3-PAR6-aPKC and Crumbs-PALS1-PATJ modules position these junctions and set apical-basal polarity, with Rho-family GTPases and Src-family kinases remodelling them dynamically. Transcriptional repressors including SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST, along with miR-200 family regulation and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of junctional components, dismantle adhesion during epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Loss of this organization underlies barrier failure, disrupted morphogenesis and wound repair, and the invasive behaviour of carcinomas.

Epithelial sheets hold together through three adhesion systems — adherens junctions, tight junctions and desmosomes — and this pathway covers how they are built, remodelled and controlled. Junction organization sets the permeability barrier of skin, gut, kidney tubule and endothelium, establishes apical-basal polarity, and its loss underlies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, wound healing failure and invasive tumour spread. Classical cadherins and nectins nucleate contacts and link through catenins, vinculin and plakoglobin to actin, while claudins and junctional adhesion molecules create the paracellular seal and select which ions and small solutes pass. Polarity complexes containing PARD3, PARD6 and atypical PKC, together with Rho-family GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 and their exchange factors, position junctions correctly. Cadherin levels are further set by proteasomal turnover, N-glycosylation and signal peptide processing, and by transcriptional repressors such as SNAI1, SNAI2, ZEB1 and TWIST1 acting with histone-modifying and microRNA machinery.

Ghrelin is the hunger hormone: released mainly by gastric X/A-like cells, it rises with fasting, peaks before a meal, and acts on the growth hormone secretagogue receptor in hypothalamus and pituitary to stimulate appetite and growth hormone release, linking gut nutrient status to energy balance and somatic growth. Its maturation is unusual among peptide hormones. Preproghrelin enters the secretory pathway through signal peptidase cleavage, and the acyltransferase MBOAT4 attaches an octanoyl or decanoyl group to serine-3, a modification without which the peptide cannot activate its receptor. Prohormone convertase 1/3 then releases mature acyl ghrelin and C-ghrelin. Secretion is restrained by insulin, leptin, glucagon and glucose and promoted by IGF1, while circulating butyrylcholinesterase and platelet-activating factor acetylhydrolase strip the acyl chain to give des-acyl ghrelin, terminating receptor signalling. This axis is of interest in obesity, cachexia and metabolic disease.

Regulation of insulin secretion describes how pancreatic beta cells convert nutrient and hormonal signals into graded release of insulin, the master control on postprandial glucose disposal. Its failure, through loss of channel function or blunted incretin amplification, produces neonatal diabetes, hyperinsulinism, or the impaired first-phase secretion that marks type 2 diabetes. Glucose entering through GLUT transporters is catabolised to raise ATP, closing KATP channels built from KCNJ11 and ABCC8; the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium channels open, and calcium triggers SNARE-dependent exocytosis of insulin granules via syntaxin, SNAP25, VAMP2 and the calcium sensor synaptotagmin V. Layered on this trigger are G protein-coupled modulators: GLP-1 and GIP receptors and muscarinic and fatty acid receptors raise cAMP or IP3 to amplify release through PKA, Epac and PKC, while adrenergic Gi signalling suppresses it. Voltage-gated potassium channels repolarise and terminate each burst.

Pancreatic beta cells set the amount of insulin released into blood, and the tuning of that release keeps postprandial glucose within narrow limits; its failure underlies type 2 diabetes, while mutations in the KATP channel subunits SUR1 and Kir6.2 cause congenital hyperinsulinism or neonatal diabetes. Glucose entering through GLUT transporters is catabolised to raise ATP, closing KATP channels so the membrane depolarises and L-, P/Q-, R- and T-type voltage-gated calcium channels admit calcium, which drives SNARE-mediated fusion of docked granules through syntaxin-1A, SNAP25, VAMP2 and the calcium sensor synaptotagmin V. On top of this trigger, amplifying and inhibitory inputs converge via G proteins: incretin and muscarinic receptors raise cAMP or generate IP3 for calcium release, acting through protein kinase A and the Epac exchange factors, while adrenergic alpha-2 receptors coupled to Gi suppress secretion. Free fatty acid sensing adds a further amplifying arm.

Axon guidance is how a growing neuron finds its target, and it is the process that builds the wiring diagram of the nervous system; when it fails, commissures fail to cross the midline, sensory and motor projections mistarget, and cortical layering is disrupted. Motile growth cones read attractive and repulsive cues in their environment through dedicated receptor families "netrins acting on DCC and UNC5, Slits on Robo, semaphorins on plexins and neuropilins, and ephrins on Eph kinases" together with adhesion molecules such as L1CAM, NCAM1 and contactins and with extracellular matrix laminins, collagens and integrins. Signals converge on Rho-family GTPases, PAK and ROCK kinases, cofilin, Ena/VASP and the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton to steer or collapse the growth cone. Local protein turnover by the proteasome, receptor endocytosis, and translational control tune responsiveness, and the same cues are redeployed in tumour cell migration and angiogenesis.

Wiring the nervous system depends on axon pathfinding: growth cones at the tips of extending axons read attractive and repulsive cues in their surroundings and translate them into directional cytoskeletal remodelling, so that projections reach their correct targets and form functional circuits. The canonical cue families are all represented — netrins acting through DCC and UNC5 receptors, Slits through Robo, semaphorins through plexins and neuropilins, and ephrins through Eph kinases — alongside adhesion molecules such as L1CAM, NCAM1 and contactins, Reelin signalling through VLDLR and DAB1, and extracellular matrix laminins, collagens and integrins. Downstream, Rho-family GTPases, PAK and ROCK kinases, LIM kinases, cofilin, profilin, Arp2/3 and tubulins execute actin and microtubule turnover, while proteasomal degradation, endocytic adaptors and local regulation of translation tune receptor levels. Failures produce commissural and cortical malformations, and the same cues are redeployed in tumour cell migration and angiogenesis.

Bicarbonate is the body's main pH buffer, generated from the carbon dioxide of respiratory oxidation, but as a charged ion it cannot cross membranes without help. Bicarbonate transporters provide that route and so set intracellular and systemic acid-base balance, drive CO2 carriage by red cells, and support secretion of alkaline fluids by kidney, pancreas, stomach and salivary epithelia. The SLC4 family splits into two functional arms: electroneutral chloride/bicarbonate exchangers, including the erythrocyte anion exchanger SLC4A1 (band 3) and its epithelial relatives SLC4A2 and SLC4A3, and sodium-coupled bicarbonate cotransporters such as the renal SLC4A4, which reclaims filtered bicarbonate in the proximal tubule. AHCYL2 belongs with them as an IRBIT-type regulatory partner rather than a transporter. Loss of these activities causes distal renal tubular acidosis, hereditary spherocytosis and proximal acidosis with ocular and neurological defects.

Vitamins, nucleosides and a range of related small molecules cannot diffuse across membranes and must be carried by dedicated solute carriers; this group of transport steps supplies them to the cytosol and to the secretory organelles. The sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter encoded by SLC5A6 brings in biotin, pantothenate and lipoate, making it upstream of carboxylase and coenzyme A-dependent metabolism. Concentrative and equilibrative nucleoside transporters of the SLC28 and SLC29 families feed nucleotide salvage and also determine cellular uptake of nucleoside-analogue cancer and antiviral drugs. SLC35 family antiporters move nucleotide sugars such as CMP-sialic acid, UDP-galactose and GDP-fucose into the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum lumen in exchange for nucleoside monophosphates, so their loss causes congenital disorders of glycosylation and leukocyte adhesion deficiency. Related members carry acetyl-CoA into the Golgi, adenine nucleotides across the inner mitochondrial membrane, and long-chain fatty acids for energy and lipid synthesis.

Cells must move sugars, amino acids, ions, vitamins, nucleosides, metals and drugs across membranes that they cannot cross unaided, and the solute carrier superfamily provides most of that traffic. SLC-mediated transmembrane transport works by conformational cycling rather than by pumping or by an open pore, using existing ion gradients to drive uphill uptake or exchange, and it sets the terms for intestinal absorption, renal reabsorption, neurotransmitter clearance at synapses, and hepatic drug handling. Members here include glucose carriers of the GLUT and SGLT families, glutamate and GABA transporters, cation-chloride cotransporters, bicarbonate and sodium-proton exchangers that hold pH and cell volume steady, mitochondrial carriers for ATP/ADP and citrate, zinc and iron transporters, Golgi nucleotide-sugar antiporters supplying glycosylation, and organic anion transporting polypeptides. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, Bartter syndrome, glucose transporter deficiency and other inherited transport disorders.

Metals are needed as enzyme cofactors and signalling ions but are toxic in excess, so cells rely on dedicated solute carrier transporters to move them across the plasma membrane and into and out of organelles. This group of metal ion SLC transporters covers iron, zinc, copper, manganese and magnesium handling together with sodium-coupled calcium and proton exchange. Divalent metal transporters of the SLC11 family take up dietary iron and manganese, ferroportin is the only known cellular iron exporter and works with the ferroxidases ceruloplasmin and hephaestin, SLC31A1 imports copper, and the ZIP and ZnT families import and sequester zinc respectively. Sodium/calcium exchangers and sodium/proton exchangers set cytosolic calcium and pH, with calmodulin and sorcin modulating exchanger activity. Mutations cause acrodermatitis enteropathica, hemochromatosis, manganese-related dystonia and neonatal diabetes, and intestinal absorption of these metals depends on this transport.

Cells that use calcium as a signal must clear it again quickly, and sodium/calcium exchangers do that by harnessing the inward sodium gradient to drive calcium out. This low-affinity, high-capacity extrusion complements the calcium pumps and dominates recovery in excitable tissues: the cardiac exchanger NCX1 (SLC8A1) moves the bulk of calcium out of myocytes between beats, and reversal of its direction during ischaemia and reperfusion contributes to calcium overload and arrhythmia. The potassium-dependent branch (SLC24 family) serves photoreceptor light adaptation and neuronal signalling, and one member, SLC24A5, supplies melanosomes and is a major determinant of human skin pigmentation; a mitochondrial relative, SLC8B1, governs calcium efflux from that organelle. Calmodulin and sorcin appear here as calcium-binding regulators that tune exchanger and coupled channel activity, linking transport to excitation-contraction coupling.

Metabolism constantly generates acid, and the sodium/proton exchangers of the SLC9 family are the main route by which cells get rid of it, trading extracellular sodium entry for proton efflux without net charge movement, powered by the inward sodium gradient set up by the Na+/K+-ATPase. Beyond cytoplasmic pH, this activity governs cell volume, sodium and fluid absorption, and the luminal acidity of intracellular compartments. The plasma membrane members differ in distribution and role: SLC9A1 is broadly expressed and couples pH control to volume regulation and growth signalling, while SLC9A2 and SLC9A3 drive electroneutral sodium uptake across intestinal and renal epithelia, where loss of SLC9A3 causes congenital sodium diarrhoea. SLC9A6 through SLC9A9 instead acidify or alkalinize endosomes and the trans-Golgi network, tuning vesicular trafficking; mutations in these are linked to X-linked intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Arachidonic acid, the precursor of prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes, can be liberated not only from phospholipids but also from diacylglycerol, and this route additionally generates the principal endocannabinoid of the nervous system. Diacylglycerol lipases alpha and beta hydrolyse DAG produced by phosphoinositide breakdown – in platelets this DAG is almost entirely arachidonate-bearing – to yield 2-arachidonoylglycerol, an agonist of cannabinoid receptor 1 that mediates retrograde suppression of neurotransmitter release at synapses. Monoacylglycerol lipase, together with the serine hydrolases ABHD6 and ABHD12, then degrades 2-AG to glycerol and free arachidonate, terminating cannabinoid signalling and feeding the eicosanoid pool. The balance between synthesis and hydrolysis sets endocannabinoid tone and links lipid second-messenger signalling to inflammation, pain and neuroprotection; loss of ABHD12 causes a neurodegenerative disorder with ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.

Cation-coupled chloride cotransporters of the SLC12 family move chloride across membranes together with sodium, potassium, or both, without net charge transfer, and in doing so set intracellular chloride, cell volume, and the direction of transepithelial salt movement. They ride on gradients built by the Na+/K+-ATPase: sodium-driven members load chloride into the cell, while the potassium-driven members extrude it. This determines whether GABA and glycine receptors hyperpolarize or depolarize a neuron, and the developmental shift from NKCC1 to the neuronal KCC2 underlies maturation of inhibitory signalling; loss of KCC2 or of KCC3 causes epilepsy and peripheral neuropathy. In the kidney, the thiazide-sensitive NCC of the distal tubule and the loop diuretic-sensitive NKCC2 of the thick ascending limb reabsorb salt, and their mutation causes Gitelman and Bartter syndromes; these are the direct targets of thiazide and loop diuretics used to treat hypertension and oedema.

Long double-stranded RNA, whether from a virus or from transcribed repeats and transposons in the genome, is converted here into the short guides that silence matching transcripts. siRNA biogenesis is the entry point of RNA interference, giving cells a sequence-specific way to suppress parasitic nucleic acids and providing the basis for experimental and therapeutic gene knockdown. DICER1 cleaves the duplex into 21-25 nucleotide products while bound to TARBP2 or PRKRA within a RISC-loading complex, and the duplex is handed to an Argonaute protein; of the four human Argonautes, AGO2 is the one with slicer activity and is found largely on the cytosolic face of the rough endoplasmic reticulum as well as in the nucleus. The passenger strand is discarded, and the translin-associated nuclease pair TSN and TSNAX contributes to processing the discarded RNA.

Small RNAs give cells a sequence-specific way to shut off messages that have already been made, tuning the output of hundreds of genes and enforcing the developmental and stress programmes that microRNAs control. An Argonaute protein loaded with a microRNA or siRNA guide scans mRNAs for complementarity; when the match is exact, AGO2, the only human Argonaute with endonuclease activity, slices the target, while imperfect pairing instead represses translation and speeds deadenylation and decay. AGO1, AGO3 and AGO4 lack cleavage activity and work only through this second route. The TNRC6 scaffolds bind Argonaute and recruit the deadenylase and decapping machinery that carries out the silencing, concentrating the complex in cytoplasmic foci. The same guide-directed recognition can also feed back on chromatin to silence transcription. Loss of this post-transcriptional silencing deregulates proliferation and differentiation, and Argonaute-microRNA circuits are broadly disturbed in cancer.

Ribosome production is the cell's largest biosynthetic commitment, so rRNA transcription must track nutrient supply; SIRT1 provides that link by negatively regulating rRNA expression when energy is scarce. Acting as an NAD-dependent histone deacetylase, SIRT1 senses a high NAD/NADH ratio during glucose limitation and, together with nucleomethylin (RRP8) and the H3K9 methyltransferase SUV39H1, forms a nucleolar silencing complex that deacetylates and dimethylates histone H3 on ribosomal DNA chromatin. Recognition of pre-existing H3K9me2 by the complex allows the repressive mark to spread across adjacent nucleosomes, closing the rDNA repeats to the RNA polymerase I machinery represented here by TBP and the SL1 subunits TAF1A-TAF1D. The result is coordinated restraint of ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation under metabolic stress, a form of energy-dependent nucleolar silencing linked to caloric restriction responses, nucleolar stress signalling and cellular ageing.

Only about half the ribosomal RNA gene copies in a nucleus are transcriptionally active at any time, and this pathway describes how ERCC6 (CSB) and the histone methyltransferase EHMT2 (G9a) keep that active fraction switched on, setting the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth. CSB is recruited through TTF1 bound at the Sal box terminator of rRNA repeats and brings in G9a, which dimethylates histone H3 lysine 9 across the transcribed region; CBX3 (HP1gamma) reads that mark and reinforces polymerase I output, a loop that persists only while transcription continues. The accompanying nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase components, including CHD3/CHD4, HDAC1/2, MTA and RBBP4/7 subunits, act on the same chromatin to shape rRNA gene state. Loss of CSB function deregulates polymerase I transcription and contributes to the growth failure and neurodegeneration of Cockayne syndrome.

Ribosome production is expensive, and cells keep only a fraction of their hundreds of rRNA gene copies transcriptionally active; the nucleolar remodeling complex is how the rest are shut down and kept that way. TIP5 (BAZ2A) partnered with the ATP-dependent remodeller SNF2H repositions the promoter nucleosome into a silent configuration, guided to rDNA by a promoter-associated noncoding RNA bound through its TAM domain and by an interaction with transcription termination factor TTF-I at a promoter-proximal site. Recruitment of SIN3-associated HDAC1 and HDAC2 removes histone acetylation, and DNMT1 and DNMT3B together with the methyl-CpG reader MBD2 impose heritable CpG methylation, locking copies off across cell divisions. The silenced state opposes the RNA polymerase I machinery and its SL1/UBTF initiation factors listed here, setting rRNA output, nucleolar organisation and genomic stability of the repeat array; loss of this restraint accompanies unchecked growth in cancer.

Phosphate balance in the body depends on how much dietary phosphate is absorbed and how much filtered phosphate the kidney reclaims, and the type II Na+/Pi cotransporters do both jobs. The three SLC34 proteins sit in the apical brush-border membrane of epithelial cells, using the inward sodium gradient established by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase to drive uptake of divalent phosphate against its own gradient. NaPi-IIa and NaPi-IIc handle reabsorption in the renal proximal tubule and are the main targets of parathyroid hormone and FGF23, which trigger their removal from the membrane to promote phosphaturia; NaPi-IIb mediates intestinal absorption and is also abundant in lung alveolar type II cells. Loss of SLC34A1 or SLC34A3 causes renal phosphate wasting with hypophosphataemic rickets, nephrocalcinosis and stones, while SLC34A2 mutations underlie pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, linking this transport step to bone mineralisation and surfactant phospholipid turnover.

Epithelia move chloride, bicarbonate, sulphate and oxalate across their apical membranes, and the SLC26 family provides much of that inorganic anion exchange. Their output sets luminal pH and fluid composition in intestine, kidney, pancreatic duct, airway and inner ear, and shapes the sulphate supply needed for proteoglycan sulphation in cartilage. The family splits by function: selective sulphate transporters such as SLC26A1 and SLC26A2, chloride/bicarbonate exchangers including SLC26A3, SLC26A4 and SLC26A6, and members that behave more like anion channels, such as SLC26A7 and SLC26A9. Loss of individual members causes recognisable disease -- congenital chloride diarrhoea, diastrophic dysplasia, Pendred syndrome with deafness and goitre from defective iodide and bicarbonate handling, and kidney stones from disturbed oxalate excretion. Several also cooperate with CFTR, coupling this exchange to cAMP-regulated chloride secretion.

Sodium-coupled phosphate cotransporters bring inorganic phosphate into cells against its electrochemical gradient, supplying the phosphate needed for ATP and nucleotide synthesis, membrane phospholipids, protein phosphorylation and skeletal mineralisation. They also set whole-body phosphate balance: the SLC34 members reclaim filtered phosphate in the renal proximal tubule and absorb it across the intestine and lung, so their loss causes hypophosphataemic rickets, nephrolithiasis and pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, while the ubiquitous SLC20 (PiT1/PiT2) transporters handle housekeeping uptake and, in vascular smooth muscle, drive calcification when phosphate is high; PiT2 mutations cause familial brain calcification. All are secondary-active symporters that couple phosphate influx to the inward sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase, and their surface abundance is tuned by parathyroid hormone, FGF23 and vitamin D. A related SLC17 carrier mediates apical anion efflux in kidney and liver.

Phosphate is needed for bone mineral, nucleotides, phospholipids and every phosphorylation reaction, and cells cannot take up this charged anion without help. Sodium-coupled phosphate cotransporters supply that uptake, exploiting the inward sodium gradient maintained by the Na+/K+-ATPase to drive phosphate across the plasma membrane against its electrochemical gradient. The SLC34 members handle bulk transepithelial handling: NPT2a and NPT2c in the renal proximal tubule brush border set urinary phosphate excretion and are the target of PTH and FGF23 regulation, while NPT2b mediates dietary absorption in the small intestine and phosphate supply for surfactant in lung. The SLC20 pair, PiT1 and PiT2, are broadly expressed housekeeping importers serving cellular metabolism. Loss of function causes hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis, pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, and, for PiT2, familial brain calcification.

Proton/oligopeptide cotransporters are the SLC15 family carriers that move di- and tripeptides across membranes using an inward proton gradient, and they are how the body absorbs dietary protein after luminal digestion has reduced it to short peptides. PEPT1 in the small intestinal brush border, together with its kidney counterpart, accounts for the bulk of amino acid nitrogen uptake and reabsorption, and its broad substrate tolerance makes it the route by which beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors and peptidomimetic prodrugs enter the body, a fact routinely exploited in drug design. The related PHT1 and PHT2 work instead on lysosomal and endosomal membranes of immune cells, where peptide and histidine transport delivers bacterial products such as muramyl dipeptide and shapes endosomal Toll-like receptor and NOD signalling; variants in this arm are linked to lupus and inflammatory disease susceptibility.

Dietary protein is absorbed largely as di- and tripeptides rather than free amino acids, and the proton-coupled oligopeptide cotransporters of the SLC15 family are what move those peptides across membranes. PEPT1 in the small intestinal brush border drives bulk uptake of digestion products using the inwardly directed proton gradient maintained by sodium/hydrogen exchange, and its broad substrate tolerance makes it the route by which beta-lactam antibiotics, ACE inhibitors and peptidomimetic prodrugs reach the bloodstream, a property exploited in oral drug design. The related PHT1 and PHT2 proteins sit in lysosomal and endosomal membranes of immune cells, where they export histidine and bacterial peptide fragments into the cytosol; this delivery of muramyl dipeptide and related ligands to NOD sensors, and the trafficking role of PHT1 in endosomal Toll-like receptor signalling, links peptide transport to innate immune activation and to lupus susceptibility.

Sphingolipid metabolism builds, remodels and degrades the sphingoid-based lipids that give membranes their structure and that double as signalling molecules controlling apoptosis, stress responses and lymphocyte trafficking. Cells depend almost entirely on de novo synthesis, beginning with serine palmitoyltransferase condensing serine and palmitoyl-CoA, followed by reduction, N-acylation by a family of ceramide synthases with distinct chain-length preferences, and desaturation to ceramide. Ceramide is then transferred from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi by CERT for conversion to sphingomyelin, or glucosylated by UGCG to seed glycosphingolipids and gangliosides. Sphingomyelinases, ceramidases and sphingosine kinases run the salvage arm, generating sphingosine 1-phosphate that is exported by transporters such as SPNS2 to establish the gradients guiding T cell egress. Lysosomal hydrolases and their saposin activators complete catabolism; their loss causes Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs and metachromatic leukodystrophy.

Sphingolipids are membrane lipids built on a long-chain amino alcohol backbone, and their metabolism covers both the making and the breaking of ceramide, sphingomyelin, glucosyl- and galactosylceramides, sulfatides and gangliosides. Beyond structure, intermediates of the route act as signals: ceramide promotes stress responses and apoptosis, while sphingosine 1-phosphate, made by sphingosine kinases and exported by transporters such as SPNS2 and MFSD2B, guides lymphocyte egress and vascular integrity. De novo synthesis starts with serine palmitoyltransferase subunits condensing serine with palmitoyl-CoA, is restrained by ORMDL proteins, and proceeds through ketodihydrosphingosine reduction, ceramide synthase acylation and desaturation; CERT1 with VAPA/VAPB then delivers ceramide to the Golgi for sphingomyelin synthase. Catabolism runs through sphingomyelinases, glycosidases, sulfatases and ceramidases in the lysosome with activator proteins, and loss of individual steps causes the sphingolipidoses, including Gaucher, Fabry, Tay-Sachs, Krabbe and Niemann-Pick disease.

A small family of cytoplasmic RNA-binding proteins, IGF2BP1-3 (also called IMPs or VICKZs), grabs thousands of protein-coding transcripts and decides how long they survive, where in the cell they are translated, and how efficiently. This control matters most in contexts of rapid growth and movement: the proteins are highly expressed in embryonic tissues, guide localized translation of mRNAs such as beta-actin at the leading edge of migrating cells, and are re-expressed in many cancers, where they stabilize oncogenic messages including MYC and drive proliferation and invasion. Recognition depends on a CAUH sequence motif read by tandem KH domains, and binding generally shields the transcript from decay rather than silencing it. The imprinted noncoding RNA H19 is part of this circuitry, reflecting the family's link to the imprinted IGF2/H19 locus and to growth regulation.

Growing axons decide whether to cross the midline, and RAC1 activation is how a repulsive guidance cue is converted into remodelling of the actin cytoskeleton at the growth cone. A low level of RAC1 activity sustains axon outgrowth, so the pathway is less an on-off switch than a set point that shapes where a growth cone advances and where it turns away; loss of this control produces midline crossing errors and mispatterned commissural tracts. SLIT2 binding to the ROBO1 receptor exposes cytoplasmic motifs that recruit the adaptors NCK1 or NCK2, which bring the dual-specificity exchange factors SOS1 and SOS2 to the membrane, where they load GTP onto RAC1. Active RAC1 then engages PAK family serine/threonine kinases, linking receptor occupancy to actin and adhesion dynamics, and placing this repulsion step within broader Rho-family control of cell shape and motility.

Axons that connect the two halves of the nervous system must cross the midline exactly once, and SLIT–ROBO signalling is the switch that makes a single crossing possible. Before crossing, commissural axons are drawn to the floor plate by Netrin-1 acting on the DCC receptor, while ROBO3 dampens the repulsive receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 so that midline-derived SLIT1, SLIT2 and SLIT3 are ignored; the secreted cue NELL2, read through ROBO3, keeps growth cones steered toward the midline from the motor column side. Once inside the floor plate, SLIT-bound ROBO associates with DCC and silences the attractive netrin response, ROBO3 is downregulated and alternatively spliced, and the axon is expelled contralaterally and barred from re-crossing. SRC-family kinase activity couples these receptors to cytoskeletal remodelling. Loss of ROBO3 underlies horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis, in which hindbrain axons fail to cross.

Growing axons steer by retracting from repellent cues, and this branch of SLIT–ROBO signalling provides the switch that does it: inactivation of CDC42 and RAC1 collapses the actin-based protrusions at the leading edge of a growth cone. Repulsive guidance of commissural and cortical axons, midline crossing decisions, and the positioning of neurons during cortical development all depend on it, and disruption of SRGAP-family genes is associated with intellectual disability and defective neuronal migration. Mechanistically, SLIT2 binding to ROBO1 exposes a cytoplasmic motif that recruits SLIT/ROBO-specific GAPs, SRGAP1–3 and the Vilse/CrossGAP orthologue ARHGAP39, which stimulate GTP hydrolysis on CDC42 and RAC1 and so return these small GTPases to their inactive GDP-bound state. Lowering Rho GTPase activity withdraws the filopodial and lamellipodial drive, linking a receptor at the membrane to cytoskeletal remodelling and directed motility.

Proton-coupled neutral amino acid transporters move small neutral amino acids such as glycine, alanine and proline across membranes together with a proton, using the inward proton gradient rather than sodium as the driving force. This makes them well suited to acidic environments: one member works at the apical surface of the intestine and kidney proximal tubule, absorbing dietary and filtered imino acids and glycine, while the other also operates in lysosomes, exporting amino acids generated by protein degradation back to the cytosol. Loss of the kidney transporter causes iminoglycinuria, the benign urinary loss of glycine and proline, and the lysosomal route contributes to amino acid sensing and recycling that feeds growth signalling. Transport is electroneutral symport with low substrate specificity, favouring short, unbranched amino acids and their derivatives.

Organic anions — carboxylates, sialic acid, and the di- and tricarboxylate intermediates of central metabolism — cannot cross membranes unaided, and this group of carriers moves them across the lysosomal, plasma and mitochondrial membranes. The transport supports short-chain fatty acid and lactate uptake in intestine and kidney, catabolism of sialylated glycoconjugates, and the shuttling of citrate, malate and 2-oxoglutarate between mitochondrion and cytosol that links the citric acid cycle to fatty acid and sterol synthesis and to the malate–aspartate shuttle. Most carriers couple anion flux to sodium, protons or the exchange of a counter-anion rather than to ATP. Loss of the lysosomal sialic acid exporter SLC17A5 causes free sialic acid storage disease with hypomyelination and developmental regression, while defects in the mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 produce 2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, illustrating how tightly neurological function depends on anion compartmentalisation.

Growing axons are steered away from the midline when the secreted cue SLIT binds ROBO receptors, and the ABL kinases sit at the point where that repellent signal is converted into cytoskeletal change. This determines whether commissural axons cross the midline once or recross inappropriately, and the same receptor-kinase axis is reused in epithelial polarity and in tumour cell migration. ABL1 and ABL2 act in two directions at once: they phosphorylate effectors that reorganise the growth cone, and they phosphorylate ROBO1 itself, tuning how sensitive the receptor remains to further SLIT. Their partners span both major cytoskeletal systems, with the cyclase-associated proteins CAP1 and CAP2 governing actin filament turnover and CLASP1/CLASP2 acting on microtubule plus ends, so filopodial collapse and microtubule behaviour are coordinated rather than controlled separately.

Thromboxane A2 is the platelet-derived eicosanoid that drives aggregation and vasoconstriction, and its actions all run through the TP receptor, the target of the antiplatelet drug class that blocks it. Signalling through TP shapes haemostasis, and its overactivity contributes to thrombosis, hypertension and bronchoconstriction, while pharmacological interruption of thromboxane production or receptor engagement is standard cardiovascular prophylaxis. TP exists as two splice variants differing in their cytoplasmic tails, one first described in platelets and placenta and the other in endothelium. Ligand binding couples the receptor to Gq-family alpha subunits, stimulating phospholipase C and raising intracellular calcium to trigger shape change and granule release; coupling to G13 instead activates Rho and Rac for cytoskeletal remodelling. The assortment of beta and gamma subunits here reflects the combinatorial heterotrimers available to this G protein-coupled receptor.

Cells accumulate myo-inositol far above plasma levels because they need it as the backbone of phosphatidylinositols and the inositol phosphate second messengers, and as an organic osmolyte that protects against hyperosmotic stress. Three carriers from the glucose transporter superfamily do this work: SLC5A3 and SLC5A11 drive uptake using the inward sodium gradient, coupling two Na+ ions per inositol, while SLC2A13 couples transport to protons instead. SLC5A11 additionally accepts D-chiro-inositol, broadening substrate range beyond myo-inositol. Expression is prominent in kidney medulla, brain and placenta, tissues where osmotic load or inositol lipid turnover is high, and transcription of the sodium-coupled carriers rises under tonicity stress. Loss of inositol accumulation compromises volume regulation and starves phosphoinositide signalling of its precursor, with consequences for neural tube closure and renal medullary function.

Deadenylation-dependent mRNA decay is the normal end of an mRNA's life: after rounds of translation, the poly(A) tail is trimmed and the transcript is destroyed. This sets mRNA half-life and therefore how long a gene's message can be translated, making it the main route by which cells clear transcripts during differentiation, stress responses and immune activation. Tail shortening happens stepwise, first by PAN2-PAN3 and then by the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex or PARN, stripping the poly(A)-binding protein platform that protects the message. The stripped body is then degraded from either end: Lsm1-7 recruits the DCP1-DCP2 decapping enzyme so XRN1 can chew 5' to 3', or the exosome with its SKI helicase partners degrades 3' to 5', leaving a capped remnant cleared by the scavenger decapping enzyme. Decapping factors such as DDX6, EDC3 and PATL1 tie this decay to P-body assembly and translational repression.

Most cytoplasmic mRNAs are retired by deadenylation-dependent decay, the default route that ends a transcript's working life after rounds of translation and thereby sets mRNA half-life, message abundance and the speed with which a cell can change its expression programme. Shortening of the poly(A) tail begins with the PAN2-PAN3 pair and is completed by the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose CNOT6/6L and CNOT7/8 nuclease modules, or by PARN, stripping the platform that poly(A)-binding protein and initiation factors use to keep the message stable and translatable. The trimmed body is then destroyed from either end: the Lsm1-7 ring and decapping factors DCP1-DCP2 with DDX6, EDC3 and EDC4 expose the 5' end to XRN1, or the exosome with its helicase-containing cofactors degrades 3' to 5', leaving a cap fragment cleared by DCPS. Much of this occurs in cytoplasmic granules, and its regulation underlies developmental and immune transcript turnover.

Deadenylation of mRNA is the first and usually rate-limiting step in mRNA decay: trimming the 3' poly(A) tail that, together with its bound poly(A)-binding protein and the cap-binding initiation complex, keeps a transcript stable and efficiently translated. Shortening the tail therefore both silences a message and commits it to degradation, which is how cells set transcript half-lives and dismantle regulatory programs after a signal ends. Trimming proceeds in two phases, with the PAN2-PAN3 complex shortening long tails and the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex or PARN completing the job to an oligo(A) stub. CCR4-NOT couples this to transcription and to microRNA- and RNA-binding-protein-directed repression, while terminal uridylyl transferases mark shortened tails for decapping and exonucleolytic destruction.
