Related deadenylases impose rhythmic control on gene expression, and PARN-type activity governs tail length and translational timing in oocytes.

Shortening of the poly(A) tail is the first and usually rate-limiting step in cytoplasmic mRNA turnover, and it sets how long a transcript remains translatable. Because the tail bound by poly(A)-binding protein cooperates with the cap-binding initiation machinery to promote translation, trimming it both silences a message and commits it to decay, making deadenylation of mRNA a general lever for controlling gene expression after transcription. Two exonuclease steps are represented: the PAN2-PAN3 complex performs initial trimming, then the multisubunit CCR4-NOT complex, whose catalytic subunits are CNOT6/6L and CNOT7/8 assembled on the CNOT1 scaffold, or the separate PARN enzyme completes it. Terminal uridylyltransferases mark short-tailed transcripts for destruction. This machinery shapes responses to developmental and circadian cues, oocyte maturation, and the clearance of unstable regulatory transcripts.

mRNA decay by 3' to 5' exoribonuclease is one of the two main routes by which cells destroy messenger RNAs once they are deadenylated, setting transcript half-life and thus the duration of any gene's expression. It also clears aberrant and surplus transcripts, so its loss produces accumulation of defective RNA and is linked to cerebellar hypoplasia and multiple myeloma through mutations in exosome subunits and DIS3. The exosome, a barrel of nine EXOSC proteins capped by the processive ribonuclease DIS3, threads the oligoadenylated 3' end through its central channel and degrades it to mononucleotides; the cytoplasmic SKI complex with HBS1L feeds RNA into that channel, including messages stalled on ribosomes. What remains is a short capped fragment, which the scavenger decapping enzyme DCPS hydrolyses, releasing m7GMP for recycling by downstream nucleotidases.

Messenger RNAs that have been deadenylated must be destroyed, and one of the two routes for doing so chews the transcript inward from its 3' end. This keeps transcript levels matched to need, clears aberrant and no-longer-wanted mRNAs, and sets the lifetime of regulated messages such as those bearing destabilising elements. The nine-subunit exosome barrel provides the channel, with DIS3 supplying the hydrolytic exoribonuclease activity, while a cytoplasmic cofactor complex built from SKIC2, SKIC3 and SKIC8 together with the GTPase-like HBS1L feeds substrate RNA into it from ribosomes. Degradation stops short of the 5' end, leaving a capped oligonucleotide that the scavenger decapping enzyme DCPS hydrolyses to release 7-methylguanosine monophosphate for recycling. Loss of exosome subunits causes neurological and skeletal disease, reflecting how closely RNA turnover is tied to gene expression control.

Most cytoplasmic mRNAs are destroyed by the 5'-to-3' exoribonuclease route, which sets transcript half-life and so determines how quickly a cell can change its protein output after a signal, a stress, or a developmental cue. After deadenylation, the heptameric LSM1-7 ring binds the shortened 3' end and, with the scaffold PATL1, delivers the message to the decapping machinery: DCP2 is the catalytic subunit that hydrolyses the 7-methylguanosine cap, supported by DCP1A/B and the enhancers EDC3, EDC4 and the RNA helicase DDX6, which also represses translation of the bound message. Removal of the cap exposes a free 5' monophosphate that XRN1 processively degrades. These factors concentrate in processing bodies, linking translational silencing to irreversible turnover, and the same activity clears aberrant transcripts and enforces the rapid decay of cytokine and cell-cycle mRNAs.

Platelets stick to a damaged vessel wall before they do anything else, and the GPIb-IX-V complex is the receptor that makes that first contact possible. Its four subunits (GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9 and GP5) bind von Willebrand factor immobilised on exposed subendothelial collagen, an interaction that works best under the high shear of arterial flow and tethers a resting platelet long enough for firm adhesion and activation to follow. Loss or defect of the complex causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome, with giant platelets and bleeding; inappropriate engagement at a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque drives the arterial thrombi behind heart attack and stroke. Signalling from the cytoplasmic tail runs through filamin A to the actin cytoskeleton and recruits Src, PI3K regulatory subunit and 14-3-3, while the receptor also docks thrombin for presentation to protease-activated receptors, amplifying activation.

During fasting, triglyceride stores in fat are broken down and the glycerol backbone must reach the liver to be reused; aquaporin-mediated glycerol transport from adipocytes to the liver provides that route. Glycerol is too polar to cross membranes quickly on its own, so aquaglyceroporins act as passive channels that let it follow its concentration gradient. AQP7 in the adipocyte plasma membrane releases glycerol into the blood, and AQP9 in hepatocytes takes it up, where it is phosphorylated and fed into gluconeogenesis to help maintain blood glucose between meals. This connects lipolysis in adipose tissue to hepatic glucose output, and interruption of it causes glycerol to accumulate in fat cells, promoting triglyceride re-synthesis and adipocyte hypertrophy; altered expression of these channels has been linked to obesity and insulin resistance.

Body water balance is set in the kidney by how much of the glomerular filtrate is reabsorbed, and vasopressin is the hormone that tunes it. Aquaporin-1 handles the bulk of constitutive water reabsorption in the proximal tubule and descending limb of Henle, moving water across both apical and basolateral surfaces back to the blood. Fine control happens in the collecting duct, where circulating vasopressin binds the V2 receptor, and Gs-coupled adenylate cyclases raise cAMP to activate protein kinase A. Phosphorylated aquaporin-2 is then trafficked from storage vesicles to the apical membrane by Rab11 and myosin Vb-dependent machinery, with aquaporin-3 and -4 completing exit basolaterally. Loss of receptor or channel function causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, with dilute polyuria and dehydration; inappropriate signalling instead produces water retention and hyponatraemia.

Passive transport by Aquaporins is the family of membrane channels that let water, and in some cases small neutral solutes, cross cell membranes down an osmotic gradient far faster than simple diffusion permits. It sets the water permeability of epithelia and so underlies urine concentration in the kidney, cerebrospinal fluid production and brain fluid balance, secretion by salivary, lacrimal and airway glands, bile flow, and lens transparency; loss of individual members causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, cataract, and renal cyst formation. Each monomer forms a narrow pore whose asparagine-proline-alanine motifs enforce selectivity, and four monomers assemble into a tetramer. The aquaglyceroporins AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 additionally conduct glycerol and urea, linking this transport to lipolysis and hepatic gluconeogenesis, while AQP6 conducts anions and AQP8 ammonia. AQP2 trafficking to the apical membrane is the regulated step in vasopressin-driven water reabsorption.

Water crosses membranes far faster than lipid permeability allows because aquaporins provide dedicated channels for it, and this family of channels is how epithelia and other tissues move fluid down osmotic gradients without expending energy. Each subunit folds into six transmembrane helices whose two asparagine-proline-alanine motifs line a narrow pore that admits water while excluding protons and ions; four subunits assemble into a tetramer. Selectivity varies across the family: the aquaglyceroporins AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 also pass glycerol, some conduct urea, AQP8 passes ammonia, and AQP6 conducts anions such as nitrate. The consequences are physiological rather than metabolic: AQP1 and AQP2 underlie renal water reabsorption and vasopressin-responsive urine concentration, AQP4 governs brain water balance, AQP0 keeps lens fibre cells transparent, and loss of these channels produces cataract, diabetes insipidus or renal cyst formation.

Circulating low-density lipoprotein does not by itself trigger platelets, but at normal plasma concentrations it lowers their threshold for activation, so that thrombin, collagen or ADP produce a larger aggregation response. This sensitization links dyslipidaemia to the prothrombotic tendency seen in atherosclerosis. The apolipoprotein B component of LDL is recognised by ApoER2 (LRP8), a splice variant of the apolipoprotein E receptor family, whose engagement recruits the Src-family kinase Fgr and leads to phosphorylation of p38 MAP kinase on its activation loop. Active p38 phosphorylates cytosolic phospholipase A2, releasing arachidonate for thromboxane production and amplifying granule release and aggregation. The signal is self-limiting: LDL also promotes PECAM-1 signalling, which recruits the phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 together with protein phosphatase 2A holoenzymes to dephosphorylate p38 and terminate the primed state.

Newly made lysosomal enzymes are not secreted; they are diverted at the trans-Golgi network into clathrin-coated carriers that deliver them to the endosomal-lysosomal system, and lysosome vesicle biogenesis is that diversion step. Without it, acid hydrolases escape into the extracellular space and the lysosome cannot degrade the macromolecules it receives, a failure mode shared with lysosomal storage disease. Cargo bearing mannose 6-phosphate is captured by its receptor, which recruits the AP-1 adaptor complex and clathrin triskelia; ARF1 licenses coat assembly on the membrane, dynamin and endophilin contribute to scission, and uncoating chaperones recycle the machinery. SNAREs including VAMP7 and VAMP8 then fuse the carriers with their target compartment. An AP-4 adaptor arm handles a distinct set of trans-Golgi cargoes, and mutations in its subunits cause hereditary spastic paraplegia, linking this sorting route to neuronal maintenance.

At the exit face of the Golgi, cargo destined for secretion, for lysosomes, or for the cell surface is packaged into coated vesicles, and this budding step sets where each protein ends up. It serves the final legs of the secretory pathway, delivering hydrolases to lysosomes, receptors and transporters to the plasma membrane, and neurotransmitter and hormone cargo to regulated release sites. Clathrin, its heavy and light chains, adaptor complexes of the AP1, AP3 and AP4 families, and the small GTPase ARF1 recruit coats to trans-Golgi membranes; sorting receptors such as sortilin and the mannose-6-phosphate/IGF2 receptor select cargo; auxilin-family and dynamin activities drive scission and uncoating, and SNAREs including VAMP2, VAMP7 and VAMP8 fuse the resulting carriers. BLOC-1 subunits link this machinery to lysosome-related organelle biogenesis, so defects produce pigmentation, platelet and neurodevelopmental disease.

The SLC13 family carries out sodium-coupled uptake of sulphate and of di- and tri-carboxylates such as succinate, citrate and alpha-ketoglutarate across the plasma membrane, using the inward sodium gradient to concentrate these anions inside cells. The two sulphate transporters represented here, NaS1 and NaS2, set the body's sulphate supply: NaS1 in the renal proximal tubule reabsorbs filtered sulphate and determines plasma sulphate levels, while NaS2 works at placental and choroid plexus barriers to deliver sulphate to the fetus and brain. That sulphate is the substrate for sulphonation of glycosaminoglycans, proteoglycans, steroids and xenobiotics, so loss of transport causes hyposulphataemia with consequences for cartilage and bone growth, detoxification capacity and fetal development. The carboxylate-transporting relatives instead feed citric acid cycle intermediates into renal, hepatic and neuronal metabolism.

Lactate and pyruvate must cross plasma membranes for cells to export the end products of glycolysis or import them as fuel, and proton-coupled monocarboxylate transport is how that traffic occurs. It underlies the lactate shuttle between glycolytic and oxidative tissues, muscle handling of lactate during exercise, ketone body uptake by brain, and the acid export that lets tumour cells sustain high glycolytic flux, making these carriers drug targets in cancer and immunometabolism. Members of the SLC16A family carry a monocarboxylate together with a proton, so transport direction follows the substrate and pH gradients rather than ATP. MCT1 and MCT4 (SLC16A1, SLC16A3) reach the surface only in complex with basigin, while MCT2 depends instead on embigin, so the chaperone partner determines where and whether transport activity appears. Loss-of-function in SLC16A1 causes exercise-induced myopathy and disturbed ketone handling.

Lysosomal breakdown of sialylated glycoproteins and oligosaccharides begins with removal of the terminal sialic acid, and loss of that step causes sialidosis. The lysosomal sialidase NEU1 performs the cleavage, but it is catalytically inert unless held in a multienzyme complex with the protective protein cathepsin A, which stabilises it, and with beta-galactosidase, which strips the newly exposed galactose; mutations that destroy NEU1 activity or its assembly into this complex block degradation. Undigested sialylated glycopeptides then accumulate in lysosomes and bound N-acetylneuraminic acid is excreted, distinguishing this defect from sialuria, where free sialic acid is stored. The milder type I disease presents as cherry-red spot myoclonus syndrome with ataxia and visual loss, while type II begins earlier with dysmorphism, skeletal dysplasia, organomegaly and intellectual disability, illustrating how glycan catabolism supports neuronal and connective tissue maintenance.

Pancreatic beta cells amplify glucose-stimulated insulin release when fatty acids are available, and part of that amplification comes from burning the fatty acids rather than from surface receptor signalling. Long-chain fatty acids enter through the scavenger receptor CD36, are activated to their coenzyme A thioesters by acyl-CoA synthetases such as ACSL3 and ACSL4, and the resulting acyl-CoAs can be carried into mitochondria for beta oxidation. The ATP generated raises the cytosolic ATP:ADP ratio, closing ATP-sensitive potassium channels, depolarising the membrane and opening voltage-gated calcium channels so that insulin granules fuse. This nutrient-sensing arithmetic links circulating lipid supply to insulin output; chronic fatty acid excess distorts it, contributing to beta cell lipotoxicity and the secretory failure of type 2 diabetes. The same enzymes operate throughout the body, but their combination and localisation here tie lipid catabolism directly to hormone secretion.

Pancreatic beta cells secrete more insulin when glucose is accompanied by long-chain free fatty acids, and roughly half of that amplification runs through the fatty acid receptor FFAR1 (GPR40) rather than through intracellular fatty acid metabolism. The receptor couples to the Gq/11 family of heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunits, which activate beta isoforms of phospholipase C; hydrolysis of membrane phosphoinositides yields inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, and the resulting release of calcium from intracellular stores reinforces the calcium rise that drives granule exocytosis. This lipid-sensing arm of nutrient-stimulated insulin release links circulating fat to glycemic control and has been pursued pharmacologically as a way to boost secretion only when glucose is elevated, with implications for type 2 diabetes and for how chronic lipid exposure alters beta cell function.

Zinc is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, yet free cytosolic zinc must be held within a narrow range, and the zinc transporters described here are how cells do it. Two opposing families act together: ZIP proteins of the SLC39 family move Zn2+ into the cytosol, either from outside the cell or out of organelle stores, while ZnT proteins of the SLC30 family move it the other way, across the plasma membrane or into secretory vesicles, the Golgi and the ER. The division of labour is tissue-specific and consequential: intestinal uptake by SLC39A4 fails in acrodermatitis enteropathica, SLC30A8 loads zinc into pancreatic beta-cell insulin granules and carries diabetes risk variants, and SLC30A3 supplies zinc to synaptic vesicles. Beyond nutrition, these carriers shape protein folding in the secretory pathway, metallothionein induction and zinc-dependent signalling.

Free zinc in the cytosol must be kept low, and the SLC30 (ZnT) carriers are the exporters that do it, either pushing zinc across the plasma membrane or loading it into secretory and vesicular compartments where it is stored or used. This efflux and compartmentalization arm of zinc homeostasis complements the importers that bring zinc in, and it determines how much zinc is available to metalloenzymes and transcription factors versus sequestered away from them. The members here illustrate the range: a plasma membrane exporter that protects against zinc overload, a transporter that concentrates zinc into mammary secretory vesicles for milk, one that fills zinc-rich glutamatergic synaptic vesicles in brain, a Golgi-localized carrier, and the pancreatic beta cell transporter that loads insulin granules, whose variants shift type 2 diabetes risk.

Growth cones advance by gripping the substrate at the front and letting go at the back, and the recycling of the adhesion molecule L1 is how that asymmetry is maintained. L1CAM links immobile extracellular ligands to retrograde actin flow through ERM proteins such as ezrin, radixin and moesin, so that cytoskeletal movement is converted into forward traction; without this, axon outgrowth and neuronal migration fail, and L1CAM mutations cause X-linked hydrocephalus and corpus callosum agenesis. A tyrosine-based sorting motif in the L1 cytoplasmic tail is read by the AP-2 clathrin adaptor only when unphosphorylated, so SRC-mediated phosphorylation retains L1 at the peripheral membrane while dephosphorylation at the central domain licenses clathrin- and dynamin-dependent endocytosis. Internalized L1 is then carried anterogradely along microtubules, with kinesin motors and shootin-1, back to the leading edge for reuse.

Post NMDA receptor activation events describes what a glutamatergic synapse does with the calcium that floods through an activated NMDA receptor, and it is the molecular basis of long-term potentiation, learning and memory. Calcium entering the dendritic spine binds calmodulin and switches on CaMKII, CaMKIV and the CaMKK kinases, engages adenylate cyclases and PKA, and recruits Ras-GRF proteins to drive ERK signalling; these converge on phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133, so that a transient electrical event is converted into transcription of genes that stabilise the strengthened synapse. In parallel, scaffolding by PSD-95 family proteins, Rac1/GIT1 signalling and remodelling of tubulin and actin-associated cytoskeleton reshape the spine itself. Neuregulin-ErbB4 signalling modulates the response. Dysregulation of this cascade underlies excitotoxic neuronal death and contributes to cognitive and psychiatric disorders.

Calcium entering a dendritic spine through the NMDA receptor is the trigger that converts brief synaptic activity into lasting change, and the events downstream of NMDA receptor activation are how that calcium signal is decoded. They underlie long-term potentiation, and with it learning and memory; disturbance of these steps contributes to intellectual disability, epilepsy and neurodegeneration. Calmodulin-dependent kinases, adenylate cyclases with cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and the Ras-ERK route each converge on phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133, switching on transcription of genes that consolidate the synapse. In parallel, scaffolding proteins of the PSD-95 family anchor the receptor to signalling enzymes, AMPA receptor subunits are inserted and modified to strengthen transmission, and Rac1 with its regulators remodels the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton so the spine changes shape. Neuregulin-ERBB4 signalling tunes the process.

NMDA receptors act as coincidence detectors at excitatory synapses: they open only when glutamate and a co-agonist are bound and the postsynaptic membrane is simultaneously depolarised enough to expel the Mg2+ ion that plugs the pore at rest. Relieving that voltage-dependent block lets Ca2+ enter the spine, and this Ca2+ signal is what converts patterned activity into long-term potentiation, synapse strengthening and memory; too little underlies cognitive and psychotic phenotypes, too much drives excitotoxic neuronal death in ischaemia. The depolarisation typically comes from Na+ flux through neighbouring AMPA receptors built from GRIA1-4. Obligatory GRIN1 subunits combine with GRIN2A-D to set gating and Mg2+ sensitivity, while PSD-95 family scaffolds, densin and alpha-actinin anchor the receptors in the postsynaptic density and couple incoming Ca2+, via calmodulin, to CaMKII activation.

This is the transcriptional output step of canonical WNT signalling: stabilized beta-catenin enters the nucleus, partners with a TCF/LEF family DNA-binding factor at promoters and enhancers, and converts those sites from repressed to active. It is how a WNT signal at the cell surface becomes a change in gene expression, and it controls stem and progenitor proliferation, cell fate choices during embryogenesis, and the renewal of tissues such as intestinal crypt epithelium. Targets include cell cycle and growth regulators such as MYC, lineage factors such as RUNX3, and feedback components like AXIN2 that limit further signalling; most other targets are cell- and tissue-restricted. Without beta-catenin, TCF7, TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 act largely as repressors, so the switch depends on beta-catenin availability. Constitutive activation of this step, through APC or CTNNB1 mutation, drives colorectal and other cancers.

Before a cell can segregate its chromosomes, the meshwork of lamin filaments lining the inner nuclear membrane must come apart, and this depolymerization of the nuclear lamina is the step that allows nuclear envelope breakdown in mitotic prophase. The lamina gives the nucleus its mechanical integrity and tethers chromatin through inner-membrane partners such as emerin, LEMD2, LEMD3 and thymopoietin, so its disassembly releases both structure and chromatin anchoring at once. Lamin head-to-tail polymers are dissolved by phosphorylation: the CDK1-cyclin B1 kinase modifies lamin N-termini while PRKCA and PRKCB act on the C-termini. PKC recruitment depends on lipid signalling, with the CTDNEP1-CNEP1R1 phosphatase activating lipins to generate diacylglycerol at the envelope. Mutations in the lamins themselves underlie laminopathies affecting muscle, nerve and adipose tissue, and the same filaments must be rebuilt after anaphase.

VEGFA-VEGFR2 Pathway is the principal driver of angiogenesis, the sprouting of new blood vessels from existing ones. Vascular endothelial growth factor A acting on the receptor tyrosine kinase VEGFR2 (KDR) makes endothelial cells proliferate, survive, migrate and become more permeable; loss of the receptor blocks blood island and endothelial development and is embryonic lethal, and the same axis is exploited by tumours to recruit their blood supply, which is why it is a major anti-angiogenic drug target. Receptor autophosphorylation recruits SRC, SHB and PLCG1 and branches into PI3K-AKT-mTOR survival signalling, eNOS activation and vasodilation, p38-MAPKAPK2 stress signalling, and Rho-family GTPase control of the actin cytoskeleton through WAVE complexes, PAK and ROCK. Integrin αvβ3, focal adhesion components and VE-cadherin junctional proteins couple this to adhesion, motility and barrier control.

New blood vessels sprout from existing ones under the control of vascular endothelial growth factor A acting on its endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase VEGFR2 (KDR), and this axis is the principal driver of angiogenesis in development, wound healing, tumour growth and diabetic retinopathy; loss of the receptor kills mouse embryos for lack of endothelial and blood island formation, while blocking the ligand is standard anti-angiogenic therapy. Ligand binding triggers receptor autophosphorylation and recruitment of adaptors such as SHB, NCK and SRC, feeding PLCG1-calcium-PKC signalling, RAS-p38 MAPK activation through MAPKAPK2 and HSPB1, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR survival signalling. Rho-family GTPases with WAVE complex and PAK/ROCK effectors remodel actin for endothelial migration and sprouting, focal adhesion and VE-cadherin junction components govern adhesion and permeability, and eNOS activation supplies nitric oxide for vasodilation.

Proteoglycans carry their chondroitin/dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate chains on a shared tetrasaccharide linker, and B3GALT6 adds the second galactose of that linker; when the enzyme is defective the linker cannot be completed and glycosaminoglycan chains fail to be built on core proteins. The consequences are skeletal and connective tissue disease: progeroid Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 2, with lax skin, joint hypermobility and impaired wound healing, and spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia with joint laxity type 1, with spinal deformity, severe joint laxity and respiratory compromise. The affected substrates span the matrix and cell surface — small leucine-rich proteoglycans such as decorin and biglycan, the large aggregating versican, brevican and neurocan, basement membrane perlecan and agrin, and the syndecan and glypican families that tune growth factor signalling. Loss of their sugar chains degrades matrix assembly, collagen fibril organisation and cartilage and bone growth.

Zinc is required by hundreds of transcription factors, hydrolases and structural proteins, and the ZIP transporters of the SLC39 family are the route by which it enters the cytosol — either across the plasma membrane from outside the cell or out of intracellular stores such as the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi. Their activity sets the cytosolic labile zinc pool that enzymes, zinc-finger proteins and zinc-dependent signalling draw upon, complementing the ZnT exporters that move zinc the other way. The physiological stakes are clear from human disease: loss of the intestinal transporter SLC39A4 causes acromelanoderma, the zinc-deficiency disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica, SLC39A8 and SLC39A14 defects disturb manganese as well as zinc handling and produce neurological and glycosylation disease, and SLC39A13 loss affects connective tissue. Several members, including SLC39A6 and SLC39A10, belong to the LIV-1 subfamily and have been linked to epithelial growth and breast cancer behaviour.

Chemical synapses work only because transmitter is loaded into vesicles before release and cleared from the cleft afterwards, and these solute carriers do both jobs. Plasma membrane symporters of the SLC6 family use sodium and chloride gradients to recapture GABA, glycine, dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and proline into neurons and surrounding glia, terminating the signal and recycling the transmitter; they are the direct targets of antidepressants, psychostimulants and anticonvulsants, and loss of the glycine transporter SLC6A5 causes hyperekplexia. On the vesicle side, the vesicular glutamate transporters SLC17A6/7/8 and the vesicular GABA/glycine transporter SLC32A1 fill synaptic vesicles using the proton gradient, and their expression effectively defines whether a neuron is excitatory or inhibitory. Mitochondrial glutamate carriers and organic cation transporters extend the same logic to metabolic compartmentation and lower-affinity monoamine clearance, linking synaptic transmission to amino acid handling throughout the nervous system.

Long-lasting synaptic change requires that a brief electrical event be converted into new gene expression, and this is one of the routes that does it. Calcium entering a postsynaptic neuron through NMDA receptors binds calmodulin, which stimulates the calcium-sensitive adenylate cyclases ADCY1 and ADCY8 to make cAMP. Rising cAMP dissociates the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A from its catalytic subunits, freeing kinase activity that reaches the nucleus and phosphorylates CREB1 on the serine that licenses recruitment of transcriptional coactivators. The resulting CREB1-driven transcription supplies the proteins needed to consolidate late-phase long-term potentiation and durable memory; loss of the calcium-stimulated cyclases impairs learning and hippocampal plasticity in particular. The same cAMP-PKA module is used broadly for hormone and neurotransmitter signalling, but here its input is synaptic calcium and its output is activity-dependent transcription.

Neuronal activity at NMDA receptors must be converted into lasting changes in gene expression if a synaptic change is to outlive the stimulus, and this calcium-to-nucleus route is how that happens. Calcium entry loads calmodulin, and the CaMKII gamma isoform, together with an importin, escorts the calcium/calmodulin complex into the nucleus rather than acting only as a local synaptic kinase. There CaMKK1 and CaMKK2 activate the nuclear kinase CaMKIV, which phosphorylates CREB1 on its regulatory serine and switches on CREB-dependent transcription of plasticity genes. The output supports maintenance of long-term potentiation and the consolidation of memory, linking a brief synaptic event to a transcriptional programme. Disruption of this cascade impairs learning and is implicated in intellectual disability and neurodegenerative cognitive decline, placing it at the junction of calcium signalling and activity-dependent transcription.

Synapses convert electrical activity into lasting changes in gene expression, and this route is how calcium entering through NMDA receptors reaches the nucleus to phosphorylate CREB1 and switch on activity-dependent transcription. The resulting programme supports long-term potentiation, dendritic remodelling and memory consolidation; its disruption is linked to intellectual disability and to the RSK3-dependent syndromes affecting cognition. Mechanistically, Ca2+ passing through GRIN1-containing receptors held in place by PSD-95 family scaffolds binds calmodulin and engages the exchange factors RASGRF1/2, loading HRAS, KRAS and NRAS with GTP, while CaMKII subunits reinforce the cascade at the level of RAF. ERK1/2 then activate ribosomal S6 kinases, which phosphorylate CREB1 at serine 133 to recruit coactivators. The pathway thus couples glutamatergic transmission to neuronal plasticity rather than to proliferation, and is a point where scaffold integrity determines signalling output.

NMDA receptor activation and the postsynaptic events that follow are how an excitatory synapse converts coincident presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic depolarization into a lasting change in its own strength, the cellular basis of learning and memory. The receptor itself is a heteromer of an obligatory GRIN1 subunit with GRIN2/GRIN3 partners, gated by glutamate plus glycine and unblocked from Mg2+ only when the membrane depolarizes; the resulting Ca2+ entry is the signal. Calcium bound to calmodulin drives CaMKII and CaMKK-dependent kinases, Ca2+-sensitive adenylate cyclases and PKA, Ras exchange factors and ERK, converging on AMPA receptor delivery and on CREB-dependent transcription. Scaffolds of the PSD-95 family, CASK-LIN7 complexes and the kinesin KIF17 position receptors, while tubulins and actin regulators remodel the spine. Dysregulation underlies excitotoxic neuronal death, epilepsy, and cognitive and psychiatric disorders.

Synaptic strengthening begins with calcium entering a postsynaptic spine, and this pathway is the step that converts that calcium signal into small GTPase activity capable of driving lasting change. Glutamate binding and depolarization open the NMDA receptor, whose GRIN1/GRIN2 subunits are tethered by PSD-95 family scaffolds and associated cytoskeletal and spine proteins into a signalling platform. Incoming Ca2+ is bound by calmodulin, which engages CaMKII holoenzymes and the guanine nucleotide exchange factors RasGRF1 and RasGRF2; these promote GDP-to-GTP exchange on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, launching downstream kinase cascades that alter AMPA receptor trafficking and gene expression. The result is long-term potentiation and the synaptic plasticity underlying learning and memory. Because the same receptor admits calcium during excitotoxic insults, this coupling also links glutamate overstimulation to neuronal injury, and its disruption features in cognitive and neurodevelopmental disorders.

Fatty acids are not only fuel but signals, and the free fatty acid receptors are the cell-surface G protein-coupled receptors that read them. FFAR1 responds to medium- and long-chain fatty acids and potentiates glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, making it a target for type 2 diabetes drugs; FFAR4 is activated by long-chain species and mediates anti-inflammatory and insulin-sensitising effects in macrophages and adipose tissue. FFAR2 and FFAR3 instead sense short-chain carboxylates such as acetate, propionate and butyrate produced by gut microbial fermentation, linking the microbiome to enteroendocrine hormone release, appetite, colonic epithelial function and neutrophil recruitment. The related GPR31 responds to a hydroxylated eicosanoid. Coupling through Gq or Gi alters intracellular calcium and cyclic AMP, translating dietary and bacterial lipid availability into metabolic, endocrine and immune responses relevant to obesity and inflammatory disease.

RSK activation describes how the ribosomal S6 kinases are switched on at the end of the RAS-ERK cascade, converting growth factor and mitogen signals into phosphorylation of substrates that drive protein synthesis, cell growth, survival and transcription. It is the step that couples ERK activity to targets such as ribosomal protein S6 pathway components, CREB and pro-apoptotic BAD, and its loss in the brain matters: mutations in RSK2 cause Coffin-Lowry syndrome, with cognitive impairment and skeletal anomalies, consistent with high RSK expression in synaptically active brain regions. Activation is multi-step and mostly membrane-localised: ERK1/2 phosphorylate the C-terminal kinase domain and linker, enabling autophosphorylation, while PDK1 phosphorylates the N-terminal kinase domain to complete activation. The four human isoforms differ in behaviour, with RSK4 showing constitutive activity independent of growth factor stimulation.

RSK activation converts growth factor signalling through RAS and the ERK cascade into a kinase that acts on translation, transcription and survival machinery. The four human isoforms, RSK1-4, are switched on by a two-input mechanism: the ERK enzymes MAPK1 and MAPK3 phosphorylate sites in the C-terminal kinase domain and linker, which licenses autophosphorylation, while PDPK1 phosphorylates the activation loop of the N-terminal domain to give full catalytic output. Activation occurs mainly at the plasma membrane but also in cytoplasm and nucleus, and RSK4 is unusual in showing high basal activity even without growth factor stimulation. The output matters physiologically: RSK2 is abundant in synaptically active brain regions, and loss-of-function mutations in it cause Coffin-Lowry syndrome with cognitive impairment and skeletal abnormalities. Because RSKs sit downstream of RAS, their activity also contributes to proliferative signalling in tumours.

Ammonium is both a waste product of amino acid catabolism and a toxin, and the Rhesus glycoproteins provide the membrane channels that let cells and epithelia move it across lipid bilayers rather than relying on passive diffusion of NH3. Three human members carry this function: the erythroid RhAG, which associates with the Rh blood group antigens in the red cell membrane and gave the family its immunological name, and the non-erythroid RhBG and RhCG, which are expressed in kidney tubule, liver and other epithelia. They are structurally related to the microbial and plant ammonium permeases, forming trimeric channels that conduct NH4+ or NH3 depending on the electrochemical gradient. In the collecting duct this transport underlies urinary ammonium excretion and thus systemic acid-base balance, linking nitrogen disposal to renal acid handling; loss of RhAG in red cells also perturbs membrane structure and cation permeability.

Neutrophils and other phagocytes detect bacterial and mitochondrial N-formylated peptides through a small family of Gi-coupled formyl peptide receptors, and this sensing directs chemotaxis toward infection or tissue damage, degranulation and the respiratory burst. The three receptors, encoded by a gene cluster, are strikingly promiscuous: besides formylated peptides such as fMLF they respond to host-derived agonists including serum amyloid A, a cleavage product of amyloid precursor protein, a chemokine-derived peptide, and a mitochondrially encoded humanin peptide, while annexin A1 and a heme-binding protein-derived peptide act at these same receptors. Because some ligands drive inflammation and others promote its resolution, signalling here sets the balance between recruiting leukocytes and shutting recruitment down, which matters in bacterial sepsis, sterile injury responses and chronic inflammatory disease. The receptors are also entry points for pharmacological control of neutrophil trafficking.</br>

Relaxin family peptides are insulin-related heterodimeric hormones that act through four G protein-coupled receptors, and this ligand-receptor system governs reproductive physiology, connective tissue remodelling and aspects of appetite and stress behaviour. Relaxin-2, the main circulating form in humans, signals through RXFP1 to soften and remodel collagen-rich tissues such as the cervix and pubic symphysis, promote vasodilation and increased renal blood flow in pregnancy, and restrain fibrosis. INSL3 acting on RXFP2 drives testicular descent, and loss of either partner causes cryptorchidism. Relaxin-3 and INSL5 instead engage RXFP3 and RXFP4, which resemble somatostatin-type peptide receptors and couple to inhibitory G proteins; the relaxin-3/RXFP3 axis operates in brain circuits controlling arousal and feeding, while INSL5 is made by colonic enteroendocrine cells. RXFP1 and RXFP2 are leucine-rich-repeat receptors distinguished by a large ectodomain.

L1 family adhesion molecules are anchored to the underlying membrane skeleton through ankyrins, and this link determines where adhesion and excitability machinery sit on a neuron's surface. Ankyrin-G, ankyrin-B and ankyrin-R bind the cytoplasmic tails of L1CAM, neurofascin and NrCAM and tether them, together with voltage-gated sodium channels and KCNQ2/KCNQ3 potassium channels, to spectrin-actin networks built from alpha and beta spectrins. Coupling restrains lateral diffusion in the plasma membrane and strengthens homophilic adhesion, which in turn supports axon guidance, branching and synaptogenesis of cortical inhibitory neurons, and concentrates sodium channels at axon initial segments and nodes of Ranvier so that action potentials initiate and propagate reliably. Mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and spastic paraplegia, while ankyrin and channel defects underlie epilepsy, cardiac arrhythmia and hereditary spherocytosis.

The adhesion molecule L1CAM does more than glue neurons together: it acts as a receptor that converts contact with the extracellular environment into decisions about axon growth, guidance and cell migration. This signalling underlies neurite extension and pathfinding during nervous system development, and loss-of-function mutations in L1CAM cause X-linked hydrocephalus and related syndromes with corticospinal tract and corpus callosum defects. On the cell surface L1 partners with beta1- and beta3-containing integrins, triggering Src-family kinase activity, the exchange factor VAV2, RAC1 and PAK1, and thence the MEK1/2-ERK1/2 cascade that drives motility and outgrowth. L1 also serves as an obligate co-receptor with neuropilin-1 for semaphorin 3A-induced growth cone collapse, so the same molecule can mediate repulsion or, through homophilic trans binding, attraction. Association with FGFR1 and casein kinase 2 phosphorylation add further layers of control.

Smooth Muscle Contraction is the contractile program of the non-striated muscle that lines blood vessels, airways, gut, bladder and uterus, setting vascular tone, peristalsis and airway calibre; its dysregulation underlies hypertension, asthmatic bronchoconstriction and vasospasm. Contraction is triggered not by neural command alone but by hormones, paracrine mediators, local chemistry and mechanical load, all converging on a rise in cytosolic calcium. Calcium entering through T-type channels binds calmodulin, activating myosin light chain kinase, which phosphorylates the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin and licenses cross-bridge cycling on actin; a parallel arm relieves caldesmon's block of the thin filament, analogous to troponin control in striated muscle. Because the filaments attach to dense bodies and focal adhesions rather than sarcomeres, sliding pulls talin, vinculin, paxillin and integrin anchorages inward, shortening the whole cell. Nitric oxide-driven soluble guanylate cyclase and phosphodiesterase-5 oppose this, providing relaxation.

Smooth muscle contraction generates the force that narrows blood vessels, moves food through the gut, and controls airway, bladder and uterine tone, responding to autonomic nerves, hormones, local mediators and stretch rather than to voluntary command. Calcium entry, here through low-voltage T-type channels, loads calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase to phosphorylate the regulatory light chains of smooth muscle myosin and permit actin cross-bridge cycling; a parallel caldesmon-dependent arm modulates the actin filament in a manner analogous to troponin. Because the contractile apparatus is anchored not to sarcomeres but to dense bodies and focal adhesions built on talin, vinculin, paxillin and integrins, shortening squeezes the whole cell. Relaxation runs through nitric oxide-stimulated soluble guanylate cyclase and cGMP, the target of phosphodiesterase 5 inhibitors. Dysregulation underlies hypertension, vasospasm, asthmatic bronchoconstriction and bowel dysmotility.

Water crosses most membranes far faster than lipid permeability allows because aquaporin channels are there, and this pathway covers their tetrameric water and solute conduction plus the hormonal control of one of them. Selectivity comes from NPA motifs lining each monomer's pore; the aquaglyceroporins AQP3, AQP7, AQP9 and AQP10 also pass glycerol and urea, linking adipocyte triglyceride breakdown to hepatic gluconeogenesis, while AQP0/MIP maintains lens transparency and AQP4 governs brain water balance. The bulk of the gene list describes how vasopressin sets renal water reabsorption: hormone binding to the V2 receptor on collecting duct cells activates Gs, adenylate cyclases and cAMP-dependent protein kinase, and AQP2-bearing vesicles are trafficked on RAB11 and myosin Vb to the apical membrane. Loss of this axis produces diabetes insipidus with dilute, unconcentrated urine.

TAK1-dependent IKK and NF-kappa-B activation describes how innate immune and inflammatory receptor signals are converted into new gene expression, driving cytokine, chemokine and survival gene transcription. NF-kappa-B dimers such as RELA/NFKB1 are held inactive in the cytoplasm by IkB proteins; the IKK complex (CHUK, IKBKB, IKBKG) phosphorylates IkB, triggering its degradation and freeing NF-kappa-B to enter the nucleus. Upstream, receptor engagement builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains via TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 pair, recruiting the MAP3K7 (TAK1)-TAB1/TAB2/TAB3 kinase module that activates IKK. Inputs include cytosolic NOD1/NOD2-RIPK2 sensing of bacterial peptidoglycan, IRAK-coupled Toll-like receptor signalling, and RAGE ligands such as HMGB1 and S100 proteins. Negative regulators including NKIRAS proteins, N4BP1, NLRX1 and deubiquitinases limit output, since sustained activation produces chronic inflammation and supports tumour cell survival.

Inflammatory and innate immune receptors converge on releasing NF-kappa-B from cytoplasmic restraint, and TAK1-dependent IKK and NF-kappa-B activation is the relay that does it. Resting cells keep NFKB1, NFKB2 and RELA bound to inhibitory IkB proteins such as NFKBIA and NFKBIB; the IKK complex of CHUK, IKBKB and the regulatory subunit IKBKG phosphorylates IkB, triggering its degradation so the dimers enter the nucleus and switch on cytokine, chemokine and survival genes. Upstream, receptor engagement — including intracellular bacterial sensing through NOD1, NOD2 and RIPK2, IRAK1-coupled receptors, and alarmins like HMGB1 and S100 proteins acting via AGER — builds non-degradative ubiquitin chains using TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 pair that recruit and activate MAP3K7 with its TAB adaptors. Ubiquitin precursors and deubiquitinases set the duration of the response. Overactivity drives chronic inflammation and autoinflammatory disease, while loss cripples host defence.

Hemidesmosomes anchor the basal cells of stratified and pseudostratified epithelia to the underlying basement membrane, and type I hemidesmosome assembly builds the classical version found in skin. The junction ties the keratin intermediate filament network inside the cell to laminin-332 outside it, so that mechanical stress on the epidermis is transmitted through the tissue rather than shearing the cell layer off its matrix. Integrin alpha6beta4 and collagen XVII span the membrane, plectin and the dystonin/BP230 plakin link them to keratin 5/keratin 14 filaments, and tetraspanin CD151 helps organize the integrin. Loss of these components causes epidermolysis bullosa with blistering and fragile mucosae, and autoantibodies against collagen XVII or BP230 produce bullous pemphigoid. Despite their stability, these complexes disassemble rapidly during cell division, differentiation and migration.

Nearly every secreted and membrane protein is N-glycosylated, and this pathway builds the sugar tree that starts the process. On the cytoplasmic and then luminal faces of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, a stepwise series of glycosyltransferases assembles a fourteen-sugar oligosaccharide on the lipid carrier dolichol phosphate, which is then transferred en bloc to asparagine residues of nascent polypeptides as they enter the secretory pathway. Supporting arms supply the nucleotide-sugar and dolichol substrates: mannose and GlcNAc activation through phosphomannomutase, phosphoglucomutase-like and UDP-GlcNAc pyrophosphorylase steps, dolichol synthesis and recycling, sialic acid production, and transporters that carry activated sugars into the lumen. The glycans shape protein folding, quality control, cell-cell recognition and developmental timing. Loss-of-function mutations in these steps, PMM2 most commonly, cause congenital disorders of glycosylation, with multisystem neurological, hepatic and coagulation disease.

Protein N-glycosylation cannot begin without a lipid anchor, and dolichyl-phosphate synthesis supplies it. Dolichol is a long polyisoprenoid made from mevalonate-derived isoprene units, and its phosphorylated form sits in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane holding the growing N-glycan on the cytoplasmic face, where the sugar chain is assembled before transfer to nascent proteins. The route branches off cholesterol and isoprenoid metabolism at mevalonate decarboxylation, extends the chain through the cis-prenyltransferase subunits DHDDS and NUS1, reduces the polyprenol to dolichol via SRD5A3 and DHRSX, and phosphorylates it through the kinase DOLK; a phosphatase step recycles dolichyl diphosphate released once a glycan is handed off. Loss of these steps produces congenital disorders of glycosylation, with hypoglycosylated serum proteins, developmental delay, epilepsy and eye and muscle involvement, illustrating how much of glycoprotein biosynthesis depends on lipid supply.

Most proteins that enter the endoplasmic reticulum are decorated with sugars on asparagine residues, and asparagine N-linked glycosylation is the machinery that builds, attaches and remodels those glycans. It matters because the glycan is both a folding aid and a quality-control tag: it keeps hydrophobic secretory proteins soluble, recruits chaperones such as calnexin and calreticulin, and marks terminally misfolded glycoproteins for retrotranslocation and proteasomal destruction. A dolichol-linked 14-sugar precursor is assembled by the ALG enzymes and transferred en bloc by the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, then trimmed by glucosidases and mannosidases before COPII vesicles, tethering and Golgi transferases elaborate hybrid and complex glycans with branching GlcNAc, galactose, fucose and sialic acid. Nucleotide-sugar supply, transporters and vesicle trafficking components are integral to the route. Mutations across these steps cause congenital disorders of glycosylation, typically with neurological, hepatic and coagulation defects.

GDP-mannose is the activated sugar donor that supplies mannose to glycosylation, and its synthesis links central carbohydrate metabolism to the assembly of N-glycans, O-mannosyl glycans, GPI anchors and C-mannosylated proteins. Fructose 6-phosphate drawn from glycolysis is isomerised to mannose 6-phosphate by mannose phosphate isomerase, converted to mannose 1-phosphate by phosphomannomutase, and condensed with GTP by the GDP-mannose pyrophosphorylase subunits GMPPA and GMPPB; hexokinase feeds the route by phosphorylating free mannose taken up by the cell. GDP-mannose then serves the first five mannose transfers onto the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor and the synthesis of dolichol-phosphate-mannose for later transfers. Because supply of this donor is limiting, defects here cause congenital disorders of glycosylation: PMM2 mutations give the commonest form, while GMPPB deficiency produces dystroglycanopathy with muscular dystrophy.</description

UDP-N-acetylglucosamine is the activated sugar donor that cells must make before they can build almost any glycoconjugate, and this route is how it is produced from fructose 6-phosphate, glutamine, acetyl-CoA and UTP. Its product feeds the first committed steps of the N-glycan precursor on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, later modifications of glycoproteins, O-GlcNAc modification of nuclear and cytoplasmic proteins, and glycosaminoglycan and GPI anchor synthesis, so flux here couples nutrient supply to glycosylation capacity. The amidotransferases encoded by GFPT1 and GFPT2 catalyse the rate-limiting transfer of glutamine's amide nitrogen onto fructose 6-phosphate, followed by acetylation, phosphomutase-mediated isomerisation by PGM3, and uridylyltransfer by UAP1; a salvage arm recycles free GlcNAc through NAGK. Loss of GFPT1 or PGM3 activity causes congenital myasthenic syndrome and an immunodeficiency with hyper-IgE, illustrating how tightly neuromuscular and immune function depend on adequate donor supply.

Before any protein can be N-glycosylated, the cell must manufacture the activated sugar donors and the lipid carrier that deliver each monosaccharide, and that supply chemistry is what this branch of N-glycan biosynthesis covers. Cytosolic enzymes convert fructose-6-phosphate and other hexoses into GDP-mannose, UDP-GlcNAc, CMP-sialic acid, GDP-fucose and related donors, while a parallel route builds dolichol from the isoprenoid pathway and phosphorylates it, so that mannose and glucose can be loaded onto dolichyl-phosphate and delivered to the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Nucleotide-sugar transporters move donors into the Golgi, where sialyltransferases and their sialidase counterparts set the terminal decoration of glycans. Loss of individual steps causes congenital disorders of glycosylation, PMM2 deficiency being the commonest, with multisystem neurological and developmental disease; GFPT1 and GMPPB defects instead present as myasthenia or muscular dystrophy.

Cells grip the extracellular matrix at focal adhesions, and the PINCH-ILK-PARVIN complex is one of the modules that must be delivered there for integrin-based adhesion to mature into a functional, force-bearing link. Its recruitment matters because it couples the short cytoplasmic tail of the beta1 integrin to the actin cytoskeleton, supporting cell spreading, migration, survival signalling and the mechanical integrity of tissues; loss of ILK in mice disrupts adhesion assembly and is embryonically lethal. ILK acts as a pseudokinase scaffold, binding integrin beta tails on one side and alpha-parvin on the other, while paxillin provides docking at the adhesion plaque. Mutual interaction among the complex members is required but not sufficient for targeting, so additional adhesion-resident partners contribute to positioning it. This is the adaptor layer of integrin adhesion rather than a catalytic cascade.

Cells read the extracellular matrix through adhesion receptors and convert that contact into decisions about shape, movement, survival and differentiation. Cell-extracellular matrix interactions are built on integrins, represented here by the beta-1 subunit, whose short cytoplasmic tails recruit cytoplasmic adaptors that physically couple the membrane to actin filaments and to signalling. A central module pairs the pseudokinase ILK with PINCH proteins and parvins, working alongside kindlin-2, filamins, actinin, paxillin and migfilin at focal adhesions; downstream effectors such as a Rac/Cdc42 exchange factor, TESK1 and VASP tune actin dynamics, lamellipodial protrusion and adhesion turnover, allowing cells to spread and migrate. Signals travel in both directions, so matrix composition and stiffness are reported inward while integrin activation state is projected outward. This biology underlies tissue assembly and wound repair, and its subversion contributes to tumour invasion and to muscle and skin fragility disorders.

Cells attached to extracellular matrix must convert integrin engagement into actin rearrangement in order to spread, migrate and sense substrate stiffness, and the PINCH-ILK-parvin module is the adaptor hub that performs this conversion at focal adhesions. Loss of its components impairs adhesion maturation and spreading, with consequences for wound healing, vascular and muscle integrity, and tumour cell invasion. The scaffold itself is built from LIMS1 (PINCH), integrin-linked kinase and the parvins PARVA and PARVB, which link the integrin tail to F-actin; alpha-actinin and paxillin anchor it into the adhesion plaque, while ARHGEF6 couples the complex to Rho-family GTPase signalling and TESK1 acts on cofilin-dependent actin turnover. RSU1 binds PINCH and feeds into stress-activated kinase signalling, illustrating how this platform is simultaneously structural and regulatory in cytoskeletal remodeling.

Interleukin-1 family signaling is the core alarm circuit of innate immunity: eleven related cytokines, including IL-1 dalpha/beta, IL-18, IL-33 and the IL-36 group, that announce infection, injury and cell death and drive fever, neutrophil recruitment, and downstream T helper responses. Its failure or over-activity underlies autoinflammatory fevers, gout, sepsis pathology, pustular psoriasis and asthma, and it is the target of anakinra and canakinumab. Most of these cytokines lack a secretion signal and are made as precursors, so activity is gated by inflammasome caspase-1 cleavage and gasdermin-D mediated release, and restrained by decoy receptors, antagonists such as IL1RN and IL18BP, and negative regulators including SIGIRR and IRAK3. Cytokine binding pairs a specific receptor with a shared accessory chain, assembling MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 to trigger ubiquitin-dependent IKK activation, proteasomal degradation of IκB, NF-κB transcription, and parallel p38, JNK and ERK output.

The interleukin-1 family drives the acute inflammatory response: fever, neutrophil recruitment, acute-phase protein production, and the alarm signalling that follows infection or tissue damage. Eleven related cytokines, including IL1A, IL1B, IL18, IL33 and the IL36 proteins, pair with heterodimeric receptors such as IL1R1, IL18R1 and IL1RL1 that share the IL1RAP co-receptor, while IL1RN, IL1R2, IL18BP and SIGIRR act as decoys or antagonists that keep the response bounded. IL1B and IL18 are made as inactive precursors and require inflammasome caspase-1 cleavage before release, linking this signalling to pyroptotic cell death through gasdermin D. Activated receptors recruit MYD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6, and through TAK1 and the IKK complex trigger ubiquitin- and proteasome-dependent degradation of IkB, freeing NF-kB, alongside p38, JNK and ERK activation. Excessive output underlies autoinflammatory syndromes, gout and psoriasis, and is blocked therapeutically by receptor antagonism.

Cell junction organization builds and maintains the contacts that hold epithelia and other tissues together and anchor cells to their surrounding matrix. It is what makes an epithelial sheet a barrier: tight junctions seal the paracellular space and set apical-basal polarity, adherens junctions and nectin-based contacts couple neighbouring cells to their actin cytoskeletons, and hemidesmosomes rivet basal keratinocytes to the laminin-332 of the basement membrane. Loss of these links causes blistering skin disease, renal magnesium wasting, and the detachment and motility that accompany epithelial-mesenchymal transition. The genes span cadherins and catenins, claudins and junctional adhesion molecules, the PAR-Crumbs polarity modules, integrin α6β4 with plectin and collagen XVII, and integrin-linked kinase adhesomes, together with the transcriptional repressors SNAI1, ZEB1/2 and TWIST that dismantle junctions and the proteasomal and glycosylation machinery that controls junction protein turnover and maturation.

Epithelia and endothelia only work as barriers and coherent sheets because their cells are physically linked to one another and to the basement membrane, and cell junction organization is the assembly, remodelling and turnover of those links. Tight junctions built from claudins and JAM-A seal the paracellular space and set ion selectivity; classical cadherins with alpha- and beta-catenin, p120 and plakoglobin form adherens junctions; nectins and nectin-like adhesion molecules nucleate contacts; and integrin alpha6beta4 with collagen XVII, plectin, laminin-332 and keratins 5/14 anchors basal keratinocytes through type I hemidesmosomes, loss of which causes blistering skin disease. Integrin-linked kinase, kindlin, parvin, paxillin, vinculin and talin-associated adaptors couple adhesion to actin and to Rho-family GTPases, while Crumbs and Par polarity complexes position junctions apicobasally. Transcriptional repressors such as SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST dismantle this programme during epithelial-mesenchymal transition and tumour invasion.

NrCAM is an L1-family adhesion receptor that helps axons find their targets and helps assemble the specialized membrane domains of myelinated nerve, including the node of Ranvier; it is also needed for normal eye development, and its loss is associated with axon guidance and lens defects. Its interactions fall into three groups. Through a cytoplasmic ankyrin-binding segment it couples the adhesive surface to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton, clustering receptors at nodes. A C-terminal PDZ-binding motif engages membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffolds of the SAP97/SAP102/PSD-95 family, linking NrCAM into postsynaptic and submembrane protein networks. Extracellularly it binds the GPI-anchored contactin axonin-1/TAG-1 to promote neurite outgrowth, and partners with neuropilin-2 in the receptor complex that converts class 3 semaphorin cues into repulsive axon turning. Together these contacts make NrCAM a bridge between guidance signalling and cytoskeletal organisation.

CHL1, a close homolog of L1, is an immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptor on subsets of neurons and glia that supports neuronal survival, neurite extension and the steering of growing axons. Unlike other L1 family members it does not bind itself homophilically, so its signalling depends on partners: contactin-6 in trans, beta1-containing integrin heterodimers engaged through RGD and DGEA motifs in its Ig domains, and neuropilin-1, through which it converts secreted Semaphorin-3A into a repulsive turning or collapse response in the growth cone. Its cytoplasmic tail contacts ankyrin, linking adhesion to the spectrin cytoskeleton, and a chaperone interaction is also part of its handling at the membrane. These contacts translate extracellular guidance cues into cytoskeletal change during nervous system wiring, and CHL1 loss is associated with abnormal axon targeting and neurodevelopmental deficits.

Neurofascin interactions describes the adhesive contacts made by neurofascin, an L1-family immunoglobulin cell adhesion molecule that organizes the node of Ranvier and the paranodal junction and directs axonal subcellular targeting and synapse formation. These contacts hold the myelinating glial cell to the axon and cluster the machinery that makes saltatory conduction possible; their disruption slows nerve conduction and is a feature of demyelinating neuropathy and autoimmune attack on nodal antigens. The neuronal 186 kDa isoform partners with NrCAM and links through ankyrin to the axonal spectrin cytoskeleton, while the glial 155 kDa isoform engages the contactin-CASPR complex to build the paranode. A carboxy-terminal PDZ class I motif recruits syntenin-1, coupling adhesion to intracellular scaffolding, and the same adhesive signalling promotes neurite outgrowth and, with doublecortin, microtubule-dependent neuronal migration during development.

Neurofascin is an L1-family immunoglobulin adhesion molecule whose interactions organize specialized axonal membrane domains, and this adhesive biology is what allows nodes of Ranvier and axo-glial junctions to form and hold together so that saltatory conduction works. Distinct isoforms act on either side of the junction: the neuronal 186 kDa form clusters at nodes with NrCAM and is anchored to the spectrin-based cytoskeleton through ankyrin, while the glial 155 kDa form works with contactin and its associated protein CNTNAP1 to build the paranodal septate-like junction with the myelinating cell. A C-terminal class I PDZ-binding motif recruits syntenin-1, linking adhesion to intracellular scaffolding and trafficking, and the presence of doublecortin reflects the roles these contacts play in axon subcellular targeting, neurite outgrowth and synapse formation during neural development. Disruption of these contacts causes paranodal disorganization and conduction failure, and neurofascin is an autoantigen in inflammatory neuropathy.

The interleukin-12 family — IL-12, IL-23, IL-27 and IL-35 — links antigen-presenting cells to T and NK cell effector programmes, and is where cell-mediated immunity against intracellular bacteria, mycobacteria and viruses is set in motion. IL-12, a heterodimer of IL12A and IL12B, drives Th1 differentiation and interferon-gamma production, which feeds back to elicit more IL-12; IL-23 with its receptor sustains Th17 responses, while IL-27 and IL-35 restrain inflammation. All members share paired receptor chains related to gp130, so ligand binding brings JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 together to phosphorylate STAT4, STAT1 and STAT3, which then reprogramme transcription. Loss of IL12B or IL12RB1 leaves patients unable to make interferon-gamma and prone to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection, whereas excess signalling contributes to rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and inflammatory bowel disease, making these subunits established therapeutic targets.

Interleukin-17 signaling is the arm of mucosal and skin immunity that mobilizes neutrophils and antimicrobial defence against bacteria and fungi, and the same circuit drives the tissue inflammation of psoriasis, spondyloarthritis and other autoimmune disease, which is why its cytokines and receptors are drug targets. Family members including IL17A, IL17F, IL17C and IL25 bind heterodimeric receptors built from IL17RA with IL17RC, IL17RB or IL17RE on epithelial cells, fibroblasts and keratinocytes. Engaged receptors recruit an adaptor and TRAF6, with ubiquitin conjugation and a TAK1-TAB module converging on IKK-dependent NF-kB release and on the ERK, JNK and p38 cascades, whose kinases activate AP-1, CREB/ATF, ELK1 and MEF2 transcription factors and MAPKAPK2/3. Output genes encode defensins, IL6, chemokines, G-CSF and matrix metalloproteases; phosphatases of the DUSP and PP2A families and SCF-mediated degradation of IkB set the strength and duration of the response.

Interleukin-1 processing converts inactive cytoplasmic precursors of the interleukin-1 family into mature, secreted cytokines, the step that licenses fever, neutrophil recruitment and the acute inflammatory response. Because pro-IL1B and pro-IL18 lack signal peptides, they bypass the ER-Golgi route and instead require proteolytic maturation by caspase-1 assembled on an inflammasome scaffold, with gasdermin D pores providing a conduit for release; alternative routes through secretory lysosomes, shed microvesicles and neutrophil proteases such as cathepsin G also contribute, and calpain-like activity processes pro-IL1A. Transcription of the precursors themselves depends on NF-kB subunits, so pathogen or damage sensing controls both substrate supply and its cleavage. This two-step control keeps a potent cytokine latent until warranted; its dysregulation drives the periodic fever syndromes and gout-like inflammation treated by IL-1 blockade.

Interleukin-1 processing is the step that converts an inactive cytoplasmic precursor into a released, receptor-competent inflammatory cytokine, and it sets the threshold for fever, neutrophil recruitment and the acute-phase response. Unlike most cytokines, pro-IL1B and pro-IL1A lack a signal peptide and cannot leave through the ER-Golgi route, so activation and export are coupled: inflammasome-activated caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL1B and pro-IL18 to their mature forms, and also cleaves gasdermin D, whose pore both releases the cytokines and can commit the cell to pyroptosis. Neutrophil cathepsin G offers a caspase-independent route to processing extracellularly, while NF-kB subunits supply the transcriptional arm that makes precursor available in the first place. Excessive flux through this pathway drives the autoinflammatory fevers and gout-like inflammation treated by IL-1 blockade.

Interleukins are secreted proteins that let immune and tissue cells instruct one another, acting locally on neighbouring or on the producing cell itself to coordinate host defence, haematopoietic output, inflammation and wound repair. Signaling by interleukins spans the receptor families collected here: shared-chain cytokine receptors feeding JAK kinases and STAT transcription factors, the IL-1 and IL-17 receptor families working through MyD88, IRAK kinases and TRAF6 to activate NF-kB and MAP kinases, and receptors coupling to PI3K, Ras-ERK and adaptor proteins such as GRB2 and SHC1. Output is transcriptional, inducing chemokines, adhesion molecules, matrix proteases, prostaglandin and nitric oxide synthases, and survival factors, and is restrained by SOCS proteins, phosphatases, decoy and antagonist receptors, and proteasomal turnover of IkB. These circuits define helper T cell subsets and macrophage states; their dysregulation drives autoinflammatory disease, autoimmunity, cytokine storm and immunodeficiency, and several members are direct drug targets.

Other interleukin signaling gathers the cytokine-receptor systems that regulate immune cell production and mucosal antiviral defence but fall outside the major interleukin families. Interleukins are small secreted proteins acting on nearby cells or on the cell that made them, and collectively they govern haematopoietic homeostasis, tissue growth and repair, and layered host defence against pathogens; loss of individual axes here produces specific immunodeficiencies. Two well-defined arms are represented: colony-stimulating factor signalling, in which CSF1 and IL34 act through CSF1R to specify macrophages and microglia while CSF3 drives neutrophil production, and interferon-lambda signalling through IFNLR1 with IL10RB, which restricts viral infection at epithelial barriers via JAK1 and TYK2. Also included is regulated secretion of cytokines and granule contents, using SNARE proteins such as VAMP2, STX3, STX4 and STXBP2, alongside CD4- and caspase-linked lymphocyte responses.

Interleukins are small secreted proteins that act on nearby or the same cell through surface receptors, coordinating tissue growth and repair, blood cell production and host defence; here the focus falls on interleukin-like cytokines handled outside the main receptor families. Colony-stimulating factors and their receptors drive myeloid output, with CSF1 and IL34 both acting through CSF1R to specify macrophage and microglial survival, while IL34 additionally engages PTPRZ1 and syndecan-1. CSF3 signalling through CSF3R sustains granulopoiesis. Interferon lambda uses a receptor pair of IFNLR1 with IL10RB and the JAK1/TYK2 kinases to protect epithelial barriers from viral infection. Also represented are IL16, released from its precursor by caspase-3 cleavage and binding CD4, and IL32, which lacks a defined receptor. The SNARE and syntaxin components indicate the regulated vesicle fusion required to release these cytokines.

Once ERK, JNK and p38 are activated at the end of a MAP kinase cascade, much of their output is delivered in the nucleus, where they phosphorylate transcription factors and so convert a transient growth factor, cytokine or stress signal into a change in gene expression. This is how mitogens drive immediate-early gene induction and cell cycle entry, and how stress signals trigger inflammatory or apoptotic transcription; persistent activation of the same targets underlies much oncogenic signalling. ERK and p38 phosphorylate ternary complex factor ELK1 to switch on FOS, while downstream kinases of the RSK and MAPKAPK families relay the signal to CREB, ATF and MEF2 family factors, and AP-1 components FOS and JUN are themselves direct substrates. Termination is built in: dual-specificity phosphatases strip the activating phosphates from the kinases, and protein phosphatase 2A subunits reverse substrate phosphorylation, setting signal duration.

MAP kinase activation converts receptor engagement at the cell surface into changes in gene expression, and it is the route by which growth factors, microbial products and stress signals reach the nucleus. Three parallel branches are represented here s-- ERK1/2, p38 and the JNKs s-- each activated by dual phosphorylation of a Thr-Xaa-Tyr motif through a tiered relay in which a MAP3K phosphorylates a dual-specificity MAP2K, which then phosphorylates the MAPK. TAK1 with its TAB partners, assembled on K63-linked ubiquitin downstream of TRAF6, IRAK kinases and the NOD1/NOD2-RIPK2 module, feeds both this cascade and IKK-dependent NF- s-B activation during innate immune responses. Output kinases such as MAPKAPK2 and the RSK family, and transcription factors including FOS, JUN, ELK1, ATF2, CREB1 and MEF2, execute the response, while DUSP phosphatases and PP2A terminate it. Dysregulated ERK signalling drives many cancers.

Inflammatory and stress signals converge on the kinase TAK1, and one of the routes out of it is the p38 stress-activated cascade, which sets the tone of cytokine production and the cell's response to infection, oxidative injury and heat. Here TAK1 in complex with its TAB1-TAB3 partners is switched on downstream of innate immune receptors, including the intracellular bacterial sensors NOD1 and NOD2 acting through RIPK2, and of TLR/IL-1 receptor signalling through IRAK1/2 and TRAF6, with non-degradative polyubiquitin chains built by UBE2N/UBE2V1 serving as the activating scaffold. TAK1 then phosphorylates the activation loops of MKK3 and MKK6, which in turn phosphorylate p38alpha and p38beta; these activate MAPKAPK2 and MAPKAPK3, stabilising cytokine mRNAs and phosphorylating HSP27 and stress-responsive transcription factors. Loss of control at this node contributes to chronic inflammation and to granulomatous disease when NOD2 signalling is disturbed.

JNK (c-Jun kinases) phosphorylation and activation mediated by activated human TAK1 is the stress- and inflammation-triggered arm of MAP kinase signalling that converts innate immune receptor engagement into changes in gene expression and cell fate. It decides whether a cell exposed to inflammatory cytokines, bacterial peptidoglycan sensed by NOD1/NOD2, UV or heat shock proliferates, survives, or undergoes apoptosis, and it drives the transcriptional programmes downstream of c-Jun and AP-1. Upstream adaptors such as IRAK1 and RIPK2 recruit TRAF6, which together with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains; these are read by the TAB1/TAB2/TAB3 subunits that activate the kinase TAK1. Activated TAK1 phosphorylates the dual-specificity kinases MKK4 and MKK7, which in turn activate JNK1, JNK2 and the largely neuronal JNK3. Isoform-specific substrate choice explains why the same module can promote either death or survival.

Stress and inflammatory signals are converted into a transcriptional response through the stress-activated JNK kinases, and this route describes their phosphorylation and activation downstream of active TAK1. The output determines whether a cell undergoes apoptosis, survives, or proliferates, and it drives AP-1-dependent cytokine production, so chronic engagement contributes to inflammatory disease while loss blunts innate immune responses. Upstream, pattern recognition by NOD1 and NOD2 recruits the kinase RIPK2, and interleukin-1/Toll-like receptor input through IRAK1 and IRAK2 converges on TRAF6, which together with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains. These are read by the TAB2 and TAB3 adaptors that, with TAB1, position TAK1 (MAP3K7) for autoactivation. TAK1 then phosphorylates the dual-specificity kinases MKK4 and MKK7, which activate JNK1, JNK2 and the largely neuronal JNK3 by dual phosphorylation of their activation loop.

AP-1 is not a single protein but a family of bZIP dimers — Jun with Jun, Fos or ATF partners — that bind sequence-specific sites in target promoters and convert transient stimuli into changes in gene expression. Its activation decides whether a cell proliferates, differentiates, migrates, survives or dies, which is why the same dimer pool reads out differently depending on subunit abundance, dimer composition, cell type and the nature of the stimulus. Here the immediate mechanism is phosphorylation by MAP kinases: the JNK family (MAPK8, MAPK9, MAPK10) and p38 isoforms (MAPK11, MAPK14) act on JUN and ATF2, while ERK1 and ERK2 feed into FOS, raising transactivation potential and stabilising the proteins. This links growth factor, stress and inflammatory signalling to transcriptional output, and its dysregulation contributes to oncogenic transformation and chronic inflammation.

Short-lived mRNAs encoding cytokines, growth factors and cell cycle regulators carry AU-rich elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and BRF1/ZFP36L1 is one of the tandem zinc-finger proteins that recognizes those elements and commits the transcript to decay. By binding and destabilizing such mRNAs, it sets the duration of inflammatory and proliferative gene expression after a stimulus and contributes to lymphocyte development and quiescence; loss of this braking activity leaves transcripts inappropriately stable. Once bound, BRF1 delivers the message to the general degradation machinery — decapping by DCP1A/DCP2, 5'-to-3' digestion by XRN1, and 3'-to-5' digestion by the multisubunit exosome with its DIS3 nuclease. The activity is switched off by phosphorylation: AKT1 and the stress-activated kinase MAPKAPK2 modify BRF1, and 14-3-3 binding then sequesters it so that RNA binding no longer triggers decay, linking signalling to mRNA turnover.

Short-lived mRNAs encoding cytokines, cell cycle regulators and proto-oncogenes carry AU-rich elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and AUF1, the protein also known as hnRNP D0, is one of the factors that reads these elements and commits the transcript to decay. This control keeps inflammatory output transient, so that messages for interleukin-1 beta, TNF, GM-CSF and inducible nitric oxide synthase, along with those for cyclin D1, MYC, FOS, p21 and BCL2, are cleared rather than accumulating; loss of such restraint underlies chronic inflammation and unchecked proliferation. AUF1 dimers bind U-rich sequences and oligomerize, recruiting translation and mRNA-binding partners such as eIF4G1, poly(A)-binding protein and the chaperones HSPA8 and HSPB1. The assembled complex is ubiquitinated and degraded by the 26S proteasome, and this proteolysis is coupled, by unclear means, to destruction of the bound message.

Inflammatory messages must be switched off as well as on, and this is one of the main ways cells do it: tristetraprolin binds AU-rich elements in the 3' untranslated regions of short-lived transcripts such as TNF, GM-CSF, IL-2 and FOS, and delivers them to the decay machinery. The bound mRNA is deadenylated and destroyed from both ends, by the 3'-to-5' exosome complex with its DIS3 ribonuclease, by the 5'-to-3' exonuclease XRN1, and after removal of the cap by DCP1A and DCP2. Signalling controls the switch: the p38-activated kinase MAPKAPK2 phosphorylates tristetraprolin, creating a 14-3-3 binding site that keeps it out of stress granules and spares its target transcripts, transiently prolonging cytokine output. Loss of this braking mechanism in mice produces cachexia, arthritis, dermatitis, autoimmunity and myeloid hyperplasia, illustrating how post-transcriptional turnover limits inflammation.

Many short-lived transcripts — cyclins, inflammatory enzymes, immediate-early genes — carry AU-rich destabilizing elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and their half-lives are set by which proteins occupy those elements. HuR (ELAVL1) is the ubiquitously expressed member of the Hu/ELAV family that binds such elements and stabilizes the bound mRNA, thereby raising output of COX-2, cyclin A, cyclin B1, cyclin D1 and c-Fos and coupling post-transcriptional control to proliferation and inflammatory responses; it can additionally repress or promote translation of its targets. Binding begins in the nucleus, and export to the cytoplasm proceeds through the CRM1/exportin-1 route with nucleoporin and ligand support from the pp32 and APRIL adaptors. Phosphorylation by protein kinase C alpha and delta enhances binding and stabilization. Under lethal stress HuR accumulates in the cytoplasm and is cleaved by executioner caspases, and the fragments favour apoptosis.
