Transcripts encoding cytokines, growth factors and other short-lived regulators carry AU-rich elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and the proteins that bind those elements set how long the message survives. This is how a cell terminates an inflammatory response on schedule; loss of control produces sustained TNF and other cytokine output and contributes to chronic inflammation and malignancy. Destabilising factors such as ZFP36, KHSRP and HNRNPD recruit deadenylases and hand the body of the message to the cytoplasmic exosome or to decapping and 5'-to-3' decay, while ELAVL1 binding the same elements protects the transcript instead. The balance is set by signalling: the p38 pathway acting through MAPKAPK2 phosphorylates ZFP36, promoting 14-3-3 binding and sequestration, and nucleocytoplasmic transport and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover of the binding proteins add further layers to post-transcriptional gene regulation.

Short-lived transcripts encoding cytokines, growth factors and cell cycle regulators carry AU-rich elements in their 3' untranslated regions, and KSRP is one of the proteins that reads those elements and condemns the message to rapid decay. This route sets how long an inflammatory or proliferative signal persists after transcription stops; losing it leaves transcripts such as cytokine mRNAs abnormally stable, a route to chronic inflammation and unrestrained growth signalling. Bound KSRP recruits the deadenylase PARN to shorten the poly(A) tail, the decapping enzyme DCP2 to strip the 5' cap, and the multisubunit exosome with its DIS3 ribonuclease to degrade the body of the message 3' to 5'. Kinases set the switch: Akt phosphorylation at serine 193 creates a 14-3-3zeta binding site that sequesters KSRP in the nucleus and blocks decay, while p38 MAPK signalling likewise tempers its destabilizing activity.

Ionotropic activity of kainate receptors covers fast excitatory neurotransmission through one of the three families of glutamate-gated ion channels, distinct from AMPA and NMDA receptors in its slower kinetics and its prominent presynaptic role in tuning transmitter release and short-term plasticity. Tetramers assembled from GRIK1-GRIK5 subunits open a cation pore on glutamate binding; whether the channel passes Ca2+ depends on subunit composition and on RNA editing at the Q/R site of GluK1 and GluK2, so editing status directly sets calcium signalling in the postsynaptic spine. PDZ scaffolds of the DLG/PSD-95 family anchor the receptors at synapses, while calmodulin and neurocalcin provide calcium-sensor feedback onto channel behaviour. These receptors shape hippocampal mossy fibre transmission and interneuron excitability, and their dysregulation is linked to epilepsy and intellectual disability.

Kainate receptors are one of the three families of ionotropic glutamate receptors, and their ionotropic activity converts synaptic glutamate release into fast cation flux across the postsynaptic membrane. They shape excitatory transmission at a subset of synapses and also act presynaptically to modulate release, making them contributors to synaptic plasticity, network excitability and seizure susceptibility. Tetramers assemble from GRIK1-GRIK3 subunits combined with the high-affinity GRIK4 and GRIK5 subunits, and whether the resulting channel passes calcium as well as sodium depends on subunit composition and on RNA editing of the GluR5 and GluR6 subunits at the pore-lining Q/R site. Membrane-associated guanylate kinase scaffolds of the DLG family anchor the receptors within the postsynaptic density, while calmodulin and neurocalcin provide calcium-sensing regulation of channel behaviour and localisation.

Kainate receptors are ionotropic glutamate receptors that shape fast excitatory transmission and presynaptic control of release at central synapses, and whose ion selectivity is decided after transcription rather than by the gene itself. Channels built from GRIK1 and GRIK2 subunits that have been RNA-edited at the pore-lining Q/R site conduct sodium but exclude calcium, so their activation by glutamate depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane without delivering a calcium signal. Editing of GRIK2 at two further positions in the same region reinforces this loss of calcium permeability. The distinction matters because calcium-permeable glutamate receptors can drive excitotoxic injury and plasticity, whereas the sodium-permeable forms contribute mainly to depolarization and to modulation of transmitter release. Editing efficiency varies with development and brain region, making this a tunable determinant of neuronal excitability and vulnerability.

Kainate receptors are ionotropic glutamate receptors built from GRIK1-GRIK5 subunits, and a subset of them conduct calcium as well as sodium. Whether a given receptor is calcium-permeable depends on RNA editing: when GRIK1 or GRIK2 transcripts are left unedited at the Q/R site, glutamate binding opens a channel through which Ca2+ enters the postsynaptic or presynaptic terminal, converting a fast depolarising signal into a calcium signal that can engage kinases, gene expression and synaptic plasticity. Editing therefore acts as a dial on excitatory calcium influx, and excessive influx contributes to excitotoxic neuronal injury in ischaemia and seizure. Scaffolding proteins of the membrane-associated guanylate kinase family, including PSD-95 and its relatives DLG1 and DLG3, position and stabilise these receptors at synapses, while calmodulin and neurocalcin provide calcium-sensing feedback onto receptor and downstream signalling.

Kainate receptors are one of the three families of ionotropic glutamate receptors, and their activation by glutamate shapes fast excitatory transmission and, presynaptically, how much glutamate is released at all. The tetrameric channels assembled from GRIK1-GRIK5 subunits pass Na+, K+ and in some combinations Ca2+, depolarising the postsynaptic membrane; the same receptors also act non-canonically through pertussis toxin-sensitive G proteins, so that receptor occupancy recruits G protein beta and gamma subunits and phospholipase C beta isoforms to mobilise calcium from intracellular stores. Calmodulin and neurocalcin read out the resulting calcium signal, while PSD-95 family scaffolds anchor the receptors at the synapse and couple them to downstream partners. This dual ionotropic and metabotropic output makes kainate receptors modulators of synaptic strength and network excitability, and their dysregulation contributes to epileptic seizure activity and excitotoxic neuronal injury.

Signalling through the interleukin-2 family — IL2, IL9, IL15 and IL21, cytokines whose receptors share the common gamma chain — governs how lymphocytes decide to proliferate, survive or differentiate after antigen encounter. It sustains effector and memory T cells, licenses NK cell development and cytotoxicity, and supports regulatory T cells through the high-affinity IL2 receptor; loss of the gamma chain or of JAK3 causes severe combined immunodeficiency, while the same axis is exploited therapeutically to expand or restrain immune responses. Ligand binding juxtaposes receptor chains bearing JAK1 and JAK3, which phosphorylate docking sites recruiting STAT5A and STAT5B, with STAT1, STAT3 and STAT4 engaged by particular members. Parallel branches run through PI3K regulatory and catalytic subunits, GRB2–SOS–SHC1 toward Ras, and adaptor GAB2, with the phosphatase SHP-1 and inositol phosphatases SHIP1/SHIP2 damping output. Related beta-chain-sharing receptors for IL3, IL5 and GM-CSF use much of the same machinery.

Pluripotent stem cells self-renew indefinitely and can give rise to every somatic lineage, and the transcriptional circuitry described here is what holds them in that state. It defines the inner cell mass of the early embryo and is the programme reactivated when adult cells are reprogrammed to induced pluripotency, so its logic underlies embryonic stem cell culture and regenerative medicine. At its centre, POU5F1 (OCT4), SOX2 and NANOG bind each other's promoters in a self-reinforcing loop, then act combinatorially to switch on genes supporting rapid proliferation while repressing differentiation regulators such as CDX2, GATA6 and EOMES. Auxiliary factors including PRDM14, SALL4, ZIC3, FOXD3 and LIN28A reinforce the network, and it is tuned by extrinsic cues: FGF2 and Nodal/TGF-beta signalling through SMAD2/SMAD4, JAK-STAT3 input, and hypoxia sensed via HIF-family subunits. Loss of the loop triggers exit from pluripotency and lineage commitment.

After DNA replication finishes, a cell spends G2 growing and preparing its machinery before committing to division, and the G2/M transition is the switch that makes that commitment irreversible. The decision matters because entering mitosis with unreplicated or damaged DNA, or with a single centrosome, produces missegregated chromosomes and aneuploidy. CDK1 paired with cyclin B is the master kinase here, held inactive by inhibitory phosphorylation from WEE1 and PKMYT1 and released by CDC25 phosphatases, with Aurora A, its cofactor BORA, and PLK1 driving activation and feedback. In parallel, duplicated centrosomes mature and separate through a large complement of centriolar and pericentriolar proteins, gamma-tubulin ring components and the augmin complex, arming them for bipolar spindle assembly. Transcriptional input from FOXM1, MYBL2 and the DREAM components, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, and p53-CDKN1A checkpoint restraint set the timing of entry.

Regulation of mitotic cell cycle covers the timed destruction of cell cycle proteins that makes mitosis irreversible and unidirectional. Its central actor is the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase that, together with E2 enzymes and the 26S proteasome, degrades securin and mitotic cyclins so that sister chromatids separate, CDK1 activity collapses, and cells exit into G1. Substrate choice is dictated by the co-activators CDC20 and CDH1, and by inhibitors such as EMI1 and the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2, BUB3 and BUBR1, which hold the ligase off until every kinetochore is attached. Mitotic kinases including PLK1, Aurora A and Aurora B, and the SCF ligase acting on CDK inhibitors, feed into the same switch. Loss of this control produces chromosome missegregation, aneuploidy and the genomic instability characteristic of tumours.

Mitosis is timed by destruction rather than synthesis, and regulation of the mitotic cell cycle here centres on ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis that makes each transition irreversible. The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome, a multisubunit ubiquitin ligase built from ANAPC and CDC16/23/27 subunits, works with the E2 enzymes UBE2C and UBE2S and the 26S proteasome to degrade securin and the mitotic cyclins, thereby releasing separase to cleave cohesin, inactivating CDK1 and permitting sister chromatid separation and mitotic exit. Its two substrate adaptors act in sequence: CDC20 during metaphase, FZR1 from anaphase into G1, with the spindle assembly checkpoint proteins MAD2L1, BUB3 and BUB1B restraining CDC20 until all kinetochores are attached. Kinases including PLK1, AURKA and AURKB and the inhibitor FBXO5 tune the timing. Loss of this control produces premature separation, aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours.

Mitotic G1 phase and G1/S transition covers the interval in which a cell decides whether to divide, and the commitment step that makes that decision irreversible once DNA replication begins. It sets the restriction point that mitogens act on, and its loss is among the most common events in cancer. In quiescent and early G1 cells the pocket proteins p130 and p107 with E2F4/5 and the MuvB core assemble repressive DREAM complexes that silence cell cycle genes, while RB1 restrains E2F1-3. Mitogen-driven D-type cyclins with CDK4/6, then cyclin E-CDK2, phosphorylate RB1 and release E2F-dependent transcription of replication factors -- MCM helicase subunits, ORC and CDC6/CDT1 licensing proteins, polymerases, PCNA and nucleotide-synthesis enzymes. INK4 and Cip/Kip inhibitors oppose these kinases, and SCF-proteasome degradation of p27 and CDT1 enforces the switch and prevents re-replication.

Between one division and the next, a cell spends G1 deciding whether to replicate its DNA at all, and this G1 phase and G1/S transition programme is where that commitment is made or deferred into quiescence. Mitogen-driven D-type cyclins with CDK4 and CDK6, followed by cyclin E-CDK2, phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein and release E2F1-3 to switch on genes for nucleotide synthesis and replication, while pocket proteins p107 and p130 with E2F4/E2F5 and the MuvB subunits hold those promoters off in resting cells. INK4 and Cip/Kip inhibitors restrain the kinases, and ubiquitin-proteasome and SCF-mediated degradation makes the transition irreversible by clearing inhibitors and licensing factors. Downstream, origin recognition, CDC6, CDT1 and the MCM helicase license origins for firing. Loss of this restraint point, through RB1 inactivation, CDKN2A deletion or cyclin D and MYC amplification, is among the most common routes into cancer, and it is the target of CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy.

N-linked glycosylation begins on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, where a lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor is built sugar by sugar before transfer to nascent proteins. ALG2 is the bifunctional alpha-1,3/1,6-mannosyltransferase that adds two mannose residues early in that assembly line, and when its activity is lost the precursor stalls, glycoproteins leave the secretory pathway underglycosylated, and the result is the congenital disorder of glycosylation known as ALG2-CDG (CDG-1i). Affected individuals show the multisystem picture typical of type I CDG: poor neurological development and psychomotor delay, dysmorphism, hypotonia, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how many secreted and membrane proteins depend on correct glycan occupancy. Separate hypomorphic ALG2 alleles impair neuromuscular transmission and cause a congenital myasthenic syndrome with proximal limb weakness, linking precursor biosynthesis to synaptic function at the motor endplate.

N-linked glycosylation begins with the transfer of N-acetylglucosamine from UDP-GlcNAc onto dolichol phosphate at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the first committed step in building the lipid-linked oligosaccharide later transferred to nascent proteins. DPAGT1 catalyses that step, and when its activity is lost the entire downstream assembly line is starved of substrate, so serum and membrane glycoproteins emerge under-glycosylated. Hypomorphic mutations cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation with impaired nervous system development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, dysmorphism, coagulation defects and immunodeficiency. Milder alleles instead present as a congenital myasthenic syndrome with tubular aggregates, in which poor glycosylation of acetylcholine receptor subunits and other synaptic proteins degrades neuromuscular transmission, producing proximal limb weakness, frequent falls and, in infants, poor head control. The pathway illustrates how a single glycosyltransferase step sets the ceiling for protein quality control and secretion throughout the body.

N-linked glycosylation begins on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, where a lipid-linked oligosaccharide is built stepwise on dolichol phosphate before being transferred en bloc to nascent proteins. ALG1 is the beta-1,4-mannosyltransferase that adds the first mannose to chitobiosyldiphosphodolichol, and loss of its activity stalls precursor assembly so that glycoproteins leave the ER with missing or truncated glycans. The resulting congenital disorder of glycosylation, ALG1-CDG, is among the most severe of this family: affected infants show underglycosylated serum glycoproteins, impaired nervous system development, psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, often with death in early childhood. Because virtually every secreted and membrane protein depends on this precursor, the defect illustrates how a single early step in glycan biosynthesis constrains multisystem development rather than one organ.

Assembly of the lipid-linked precursor that donates N-glycans to newly made proteins begins on the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and ALG11 carries out two steps of it, adding the fourth and fifth mannose residues in alpha-1,2 linkage to Man3GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol. These are the final additions before the growing glycan is flipped into the ER lumen for completion and transfer to nascent polypeptides. Loss-of-function mutations in ALG11 truncate the precursor and produce congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ip, in which serum glycoproteins are underglycosylated. Affected individuals show early-onset developmental delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how broadly protein N-glycosylation is required for secreted and membrane protein folding, stability and function across tissues.

Attachment of SUMO to chromatin regulators is a way of tuning gene silencing without changing the proteins' abundance, and it shapes how repressive complexes are built and where they sit in the nucleus. Targets here include Polycomb repressive components such as RING1, RNF2, BMI1 and the chromobox proteins CBX2/4/8, the PRC2 subunit SUZ12, histone deacetylases HDAC1/2/4, the heterochromatin protein CBX5, and the matrix-attachment factors SATB1 and SATB2, so the modification touches both histone-modifying activity and higher-order chromatin architecture. Conjugation runs through the single E2 UBE2I with PIAS1/PIAS2 ligases transferring SUMO1, SUMO2 or SUMO3. The prominence of nucleoporins and RANBP2 reflects SUMOylation occurring at the nuclear pore and the coupling of chromatin state to nuclear periphery positioning, linking transcriptional repression, developmental gene control and stable cell identity.

Thrombin signalling through proteinase activated receptors (PARs) is how the coagulation protease thrombin acts as a cell-signalling agonist rather than just a fibrin-generating enzyme, and it is the main route by which platelets are activated at a site of vascular injury. Loss or blockade of this route blunts platelet secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, which is why PAR1 is a target of antithrombotic drugs; excessive signalling contributes to thrombosis, inflammation and vascular remodelling. Thrombin cleaves the receptor N-terminus, and the tethered new terminus self-activates the receptor, which couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent shape change. Beta-gamma subunits engage lipid kinases and channels, while Src and ERK activation, partly via sheddase-released growth factor ligands, link thrombin to proliferation. Arrestins terminate and redirect the response.

Thrombin, the protease at the end of the coagulation cascade, also acts as a hormone-like signal by cleaving proteinase-activated receptors on the cell surface, and this route is how a clotting signal becomes a cellular response. In platelets it drives shape change, granule secretion, integrin activation and aggregation, making it central to haemostasis and to arterial thrombosis; the same receptors mediate thrombin's effects on endothelium, smooth muscle and inflammatory cells. Activation is irreversible and unusual: thrombin clips the receptor N-terminus, and the new tethered ligand folds back to activate the receptor, which then couples through Gq and G12/13 heterotrimers to phospholipase C beta, calcium mobilisation, protein kinase C and Rho-dependent cytoskeletal remodelling. Beta-arrestins terminate and redirect signalling, while Src and ERK link receptor activation to growth and differentiation responses. PAR1 is the dominant human thrombin receptor, with PAR4 contributing at higher concentrations.

Attaching SUMO to RNA-binding proteins retunes how they engage nucleic acids and partner proteins, which is how cells adjust mRNA packaging, snoRNP assembly and RNA-dependent transcriptional output without changing protein levels. Modification of HNRNPC lowers its affinity for single-stranded nucleic acid, SUMOylation of NOP58 is needed for snoRNA binding within nucleolar ribonucleoprotein particles, and modified HNRNPK is required for it to coactivate p53-driven transcription, linking this chemistry to stress responses and growth arrest. The conjugating enzyme UBE2I transfers SUMO1 or SUMO2 to substrates, with the nuclear pore-associated ligase RANBP2 and a Polycomb-associated ligase activity providing substrate specificity; the accompanying nucleoporins mark the pore as the site where much nuclear SUMOylation occurs and where modified cargo is handled during nucleocytoplasmic transport. Such reversible marking couples RNA metabolism to nuclear organisation.

Defective RFT1 causes CDG-1n describes what happens to protein N-glycosylation when the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor cannot be moved into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. RFT1 is required for flipping Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol from the cytosolic face of the ER membrane to the lumenal face, where the remaining mannose and glucose residues are added before the finished glycan is transferred to nascent polypeptides. Loss of this step stalls precursor maturation and leaves serum glycoproteins such as transferrin hypoglycosylated, the diagnostic hallmark of a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. Affected individuals show early-onset developmental delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, seizures, sensorineural deafness, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how broadly secreted and membrane glycoproteins depend on an intact assembly line. The pathway sits at the interface of dolichol-linked sugar biosynthesis and ER quality control.

N-linked glycosylation begins on the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, so the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor must be flipped into the ER lumen before the remaining sugars can be added and the finished glycan transferred to nascent proteins. RFT1 is required for this translocation step, though the mechanism by which the bulky dolichol-linked intermediate crosses the bilayer remains unsettled. Loss of RFT1 function stalls precursor maturation and yields a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation, in which serum glycoproteins such as transferrin are incompletely occupied by glycans. The resulting multi-system disease presents in infancy with developmental delay, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, seizures, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, illustrating how broadly secreted and membrane protein function depends on this single early lipid-linked oligosaccharide flipping event in the secretory pathway.

Cells within an epithelial sheet coordinate a common orientation in the plane of the tissue, and the defining feature of this planar cell polarity is that its core components segregate to opposite sides of each cell. The asymmetry orients hair cells of the inner ear, aligns hair follicles and cilia, and drives the convergent extension movements that close the neural tube; its loss produces neural tube defects and disordered stereociliary bundles. Frizzled receptors with Dishevelled occupy one membrane domain while Vangl2 and Prickle occupy the other, each complex excluding the other. Non-canonical Wnt5a input and scaffolds such as Scribble and Par6 feed into this partitioning, and the ubiquitin-proteasome system is integral to it: the ligases SMURF1 and SMURF2 target Prickle1 for degradation, so proteolysis maintains the polarized boundary rather than merely turning signalling off.

Attachment of small ubiquitin-like modifiers to replication and chromosome-segregation machinery tunes how cells copy and separate their DNA without breaking it. SUMOylation of the sliding clamp PCNA restrains inappropriate recombination and double-strand break formation at replication forks, an outcome that matters because the alternative is genome rearrangement; modification of topoisomerases I and II is induced when these enzymes are trapped on DNA by inhibitors, as happens during chemotherapy. A second branch acts on the chromosomal passenger complex — Aurora A and B kinases, survivin, borealin and INCENP — where the modification is required for accurate chromosome segregation. The reaction runs through the single SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBE2I with PIAS-family ligases, and much of it is organised at the nuclear pore, whose nucleoporins together with RANBP2 and RANGAP1 provide the platform where substrates are modified as they pass.</description>

AXIN is the scaffold that holds together the destruction complex which phosphorylates and marks beta-catenin for disposal, so how much AXIN a cell contains sets how strongly Wnt signalling is damped. Its turnover through the ubiquitin-proteasome system is therefore a tuning knob on Wnt output, with consequences for stem cell maintenance, developmental patterning and colorectal tumorigenesis, where loss of destruction-complex function drives constitutive beta-catenin activity. Two routes converge here: the HECT ligase SMURF2 ubiquitinates AXIN directly, while the tankyrases TNKS and TNKS2 poly-ADP-ribosylate AXIN1 and AXIN2 to create a mark recognised by the RING ligase RNF146, which then attaches ubiquitin. Polyubiquitinated AXIN is delivered to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits carries out recognition, deubiquitination and proteolysis. Tankyrase inhibitors exploit this axis to stabilise AXIN and suppress Wnt-driven growth.

Dishevelled proteins are the hub adaptors that relay Wnt signals from Frizzled receptors to both the beta-catenin and planar cell polarity branches, so the amount of DVL present sets how strongly a cell can respond to Wnt. Turnover of DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 keeps that responsiveness in check; when it fails, Wnt output runs high, a state associated with excess proliferation in cancer and with defects in polarity and morphogenesis. Ubiquitin ligase activity marks DVL for destruction: a CUL3-RBX1 complex directed by the substrate adaptor KLHL12, together with HECW1, builds polyubiquitin chains that the 26S proteasome recognises through its ubiquitin receptor subunits and degrades using its core peptidase and ATPase rings. Separately, the antagonist DACT1 binds DVL and routes it to the lysosome, giving two independent routes for dialling Wnt signalling down.

This is the switch that turns canonical WNT signalling on. In unstimulated cells a destruction complex built around AXIN1, APC, GSK3beta and casein kinase 1 keeps beta-catenin phosphorylated and targeted for degradation; when WNT binds a Frizzled/LRP5-LRP6 receptor pair, DVL proteins polymerise at the membrane and pull AXIN and GSK3beta away, so the complex falls apart and beta-catenin accumulates and enters the nucleus to drive target gene transcription. Phosphorylation of the LRP6 tail creates a feed-forward docking site, while PP2A subunits dephosphorylate AXIN and loosen its grip on its partners, and FRAT proteins sequester GSK3beta. Because AXIN is limiting, its relocation is the rate-determining step. The output governs embryonic patterning, stem cell renewal in intestinal crypts and bone mass; constitutive beta-catenin stabilisation through APC or AXIN loss underlies colorectal cancer.

How strongly a cell responds to WNT depends on how many Frizzled receptors sit on its surface, and ubiquitination of FZD is the main way that number is set. The transmembrane E3 ligases ZNRF3 and RNF43 attach ubiquitin to Frizzled proteins and drive them, together with the LRP5/LRP6 co-receptors, into lysosomal degradation, damping signalling; the deubiquitinase USP8 removes those marks and returns receptors to the plasma membrane. R-spondins tune the balance by binding LGR4/5/6 and clearing the two ligases from the surface, so RSPO acts as a WNT potentiator for both canonical and non-canonical outputs rather than as a ligand itself. This circuit governs stem cell niches in intestinal crypts and elsewhere, and loss-of-function mutations in RNF43 or RSPO gene fusions leave WNT signalling constitutively high in colorectal and pancreatic tumours.

When no WNT ligand is present, the genes that WNT would otherwise switch on are actively held off, and this repression is what keeps proliferation and cell-fate programmes such as MYC and AXIN2 silent in resting tissue. Its loss contributes to the constitutive target-gene activation seen in colorectal and other cancers. The DNA-binding step is carried out by TCF/LEF factors (TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2, LEF1), which in the absence of nuclear beta-catenin recruit Groucho-family corepressors TLE1-4 rather than coactivators. TLE proteins do not touch DNA themselves; they oligomerize through a glutamine-rich N-terminal domain, contact the core transcription machinery and histones, and bring in histone deacetylase activity, with CtBP corepressors acting alongside. The short TLE5 protein retains the oligomerization domain but lacks the C-terminal interaction module and behaves as a dominant negative, setting the threshold at which WNT signalling can relieve repression.

DNA methyltransferases are themselves regulated by covalent modification, and attachment of SUMO to DNMT1, DNMT3A and DNMT3B is one way the cell tunes where and how strongly cytosine methylation is deposited. This matters because methylation patterns set at imprinted loci, repetitive elements and silenced promoters must be both established de novo and copied faithfully at each replication fork; mis-set patterns underlie imprinting disorders and the promoter hypermethylation seen in tumours. SUMO1 is transferred by the sole E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2I, with CBX4 acting as the SUMO ligase; modification alters the catalytic output of DNMT1 and reshapes the protein interactions of DNMT3A rather than marking the enzymes for destruction. The accompanying Polycomb repressive complex 1 components — RING1, RNF2, BMI1, PCGF2, chromobox and PHC subunits — place this chemistry within a broader repressive chromatin network that links histone ubiquitination to DNA methylation.

N-linked glycosylation begins with a lipid-linked oligosaccharide built stepwise on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and several of the later mannose additions draw their sugar from dolichyl-phosphate-mannose rather than directly from GDP-mannose. MPDU1 is the membrane protein that makes this donor accessible to the mannosyltransferases that extend the growing oligosaccharide and to the enzymes that mannosylate glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors. When MPDU1 function is lost, the donor and the transferases themselves remain present and apparently competent, yet the transfer reactions fail, leaving truncated precursors and hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins. The resulting congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1f is a multisystem disease with impaired neurological development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, dysmorphism, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, illustrating how broadly protein glycosylation is required across secreted and cell-surface proteomes rather than in any single tissue.

Defective DPM1 causes DPM1-CDG describes the loss of dolichol-phosphate mannose synthesis and the multisystem congenital disorder of glycosylation that follows. The DPM complex supplies the single mannose donor used inside the endoplasmic reticulum for N-glycan precursor assembly, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan, C-mannosylation, and GPI anchor biosynthesis, so when it fails many unrelated glycoproteins are made incomplete at once. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit, transferring mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate, while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it in the ER membrane. Hypomorphic DPM1 mutations produce hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins together with severe developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia and dysmorphism, a phenotype overlapping muscular dystrophy because dystroglycan glycosylation is also lost. The pathway sits at the junction of lipid-linked sugar donor supply and protein quality in the secretory route.

Dolichol-phosphate mannose is the mannose donor used inside the endoplasmic reticulum for N-linked glycan assembly, GPI anchor synthesis, C-mannosylation and O-mannosylation of proteins such as alpha-dystroglycan, and it is made by a three-subunit enzyme in the ER membrane. DPM1 is the catalytic subunit, transferring mannose from cytosolic GDP-mannose onto dolichyl phosphate, while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it in the membrane. Loss-of-function mutations in DPM1 starve all of these downstream glycosylation routes of their donor and produce a congenital disorder of glycosylation, recognisable as hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins together with severe developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia and a muscular dystrophy-like picture. The pathway therefore links a single lipid-linked sugar intermediate to the quality and function of a large fraction of secreted and membrane proteins.

Dolichol-phosphate mannose is the mannose donor that the endoplasmic reticulum uses for N-glycosylation, O- and C-mannosylation, and GPI anchor assembly, and it is made by a three-subunit ER membrane enzyme in which DPM1 carries the catalytic transfer from cytosolic GDP-mannose to dolichyl phosphate while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it. Loss-of-function mutations in the DPM3 subunit destabilise the complex and cause DPM3-CDG, a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins, developmental delay, hypotonia, dysmorphism, and coagulation and immune problems. Because alpha-dystroglycan depends on O-mannosylation for its matrix-binding glycan, the shortage of donor sugar also produces muscular dystrophy, placing this defect at the intersection of the glycosylation disorders and the dystroglycanopathies and illustrating how one shared metabolic intermediate supports several unrelated glycan pathways.

Dolichol-phosphate mannose is the mannose donor used inside the endoplasmic reticulum for N-glycan precursor assembly, O-mannosylation of proteins such as alpha-dystroglycan, GPI anchor biosynthesis and C-mannosylation, and it is made by a three-subunit enzyme in which DPM1 carries the catalytic mannosyltransferase activity while DPM2 and DPM3 anchor and stabilise it in the ER membrane. Loss-of-function changes in the DPM2 subunit destabilise the complex, cutting the supply of this donor and producing a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins. Affected individuals show a multisystem type I phenotype: impaired nervous system development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia with muscle involvement, dysmorphism, seizures, coagulation abnormalities and immune deficiency. The pathway therefore links a single lipid-linked sugar carrier to the integrity of nearly every glycosylation route that begins in the ER.

N-linked glycosylation begins with a lipid-linked oligosaccharide built stepwise on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and ALG9 is the alpha-1,2-mannosyltransferase that adds the seventh and ninth mannose residues to that precursor. When ALG9 activity is lost, the pathway stalls and truncated dolichol-linked intermediates bearing six or eight mannoses accumulate, so the mature fourteen-sugar glycan cannot be transferred efficiently onto nascent proteins. The result is a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation, ALG9-CDG, in which serum glycoproteins are underglycosylated and patients show impaired nervous system development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how many secreted and membrane proteins depend on correct glycan occupancy for folding and function. This biology sits at the start of the secretory pathway's quality control, upstream of glycoprotein maturation in the Golgi.

N-linked glycosylation begins with a lipid-linked oligosaccharide built stepwise on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and ALG3 performs one specific step in that assembly: it transfers the sixth mannose, the first donated by dolichol-phosphate-mannose, onto the Man5GlcNAc2 intermediate on the lumenal face. When ALG3 activity is lost, the precursor stalls as a truncated structure that is transferred inefficiently and incompletely to nascent proteins, so serum and membrane glycoproteins are underglycosylated. The result is ALG3-CDG, a congenital disorder of glycosylation type I presenting with impaired brain development and microcephaly, severe psychomotor retardation, seizures, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, and variable coagulation and immune deficits. Because the affected chemistry supplies the glycan used by essentially all secreted and cell-surface glycoproteins, the defect is multisystem rather than organ-specific, and it also feeds into endoplasmic reticulum quality control, where glycans direct folding and degradation decisions.

Before any N-glycan can be attached to a protein, a fourteen-sugar precursor must be built step by step on a dolichol lipid carrier in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. ALG12 performs one of those steps, adding the eighth mannose in alpha-1,6 linkage to the growing lipid-linked oligosaccharide using dolichol-phosphate-mannose as donor. When the enzyme is defective, an incomplete precursor is transferred to nascent proteins, leaving serum glycoproteins hypoglycosylated and producing the congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ig. Because N-glycosylation shapes folding, quality control, secretion and receptor function across nearly every tissue, the consequences are multisystemic: impaired nervous system development, psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency. The pathway illustrates how a single mannosyltransferase step in ER precursor assembly gates the entire secretory glycoproteome.

Before any N-linked glycan can be transferred to a nascent protein, a lipid-linked precursor must be built to completion on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and ALG6 performs the step that adds the first glucose to the mannose-nine intermediate. Glucosylation is what marks the precursor as finished, allowing efficient transfer by oligosaccharyltransferase and later serving as the signal read by the calnexin/calreticulin folding cycle. When ALG6 activity is lost, the unglucosylated precursor accumulates, transfer becomes inefficient, and serum glycoproteins are secreted with unoccupied glycosylation sites. The resulting congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ic is the second most common of these diseases after PMM2 deficiency, and like other type I forms it produces psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, dysmorphic features, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency, reflecting how broadly protein N-glycosylation is required across developing tissues.

Before a protein can be N-glycosylated, a lipid-linked oligosaccharide must be built to completion on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and ALG8 performs one step of that assembly: it transfers the second glucose onto the dolichol-linked Glc1Man9GlcNAc2 precursor. Loss of this glucosyltransferase activity stalls the precursor at the monoglucosylated form, so the truncated donor is transferred poorly to nascent polypeptides and serum glycoproteins circulate underglycosylated. The result is ALG8-CDG, a congenital disorder of glycosylation type I presenting as multisystem disease with impaired nervous system development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, dysmorphism, protein-losing enteropathy, coagulation factor deficiencies and immunodeficiency. Because glucose capping of the precursor also governs recognition by the glycan-dependent quality control and folding machinery of the ER, defects here couple a biosynthetic block to widespread secretory protein dysfunction rather than to any single organ.

Attachment of the small ubiquitin-like modifiers SUMO1 and SUMO3 to components of the NF-kappaB system tunes how strongly and how long inflammatory and innate immune genes are transcribed. Normally NF-kappaB dimers such as RELA are held in the cytosol by the inhibitor NFKBIA until the IKK complex phosphorylates it and triggers its destruction; SUMOylation intersects this switch at several points. Modification of NFKBIA competes with the ubiquitin-dependent degradation that would otherwise free the transcription factor, and modification of RELA itself damps target gene output, whereas SUMOylation of NFKB2 is needed for the processing step that generates the mature p52 subunit of the non-canonical arm. The E2 conjugating enzyme UBE2I works with PIAS-family and other SUMO ligases, including TOPORS, while regulatory subunits such as IKBKG and the kinase IKBKE link the modification to pathogen sensing. Loss of this restraint favours chronic inflammation and tumour-promoting signalling.

N-glycosylation depends on a lipid carrier, dolichol, and the final step of making it is the NADPH-dependent reduction of polyprenol's alpha-isoprene unit by polyprenol reductase in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. When this reductase is defective, dolichol supply falls and the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor that donates glycans to nascent proteins cannot be built efficiently, so serum glycoproteins circulate under-glycosylated. The clinical consequence is a congenital disorder of glycosylation of type I, with impaired nervous system development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, coagulation abnormalities and immunodeficiency; allelic mutations produce Kahrizi syndrome, combining intellectual disability with cataracts, iris coloboma, kyphosis and coarse facial features. The pathway situates isoprenoid lipid metabolism directly upstream of protein quality control and secretion, illustrating how a single reductase step constrains glycosylation across many tissues.

Defective DOLK causes DOLK-CDG describes what happens when cells cannot make dolichyl phosphate, the lipid carrier on which nearly all protein glycosylation is built. Dolichol kinase phosphorylates dolichol at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, and the resulting dolichyl phosphate serves as the anchor for assembling the lipid-linked oligosaccharide used in N-glycosylation, as the mannose donor for O-mannosylation, and as a substrate in GPI anchor biosynthesis. Loss-of-function mutations therefore starve several glycosylation routes at once, producing a congenital disorder of glycosylation with hypoglycosylated serum glycoproteins, dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures and often death in infancy. Because O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan depends on the same lipid pool, some patients also show muscular dystrophy-like features, illustrating how a single lipid-modifying step upstream of the secretory pathway constrains protein maturation across many tissues.

Dolichol kinase converts dolichol to dolichyl phosphate in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the lipid carrier on which the oligosaccharide precursor for N-linked glycosylation is built and which also supplies O-mannosylation and GPI anchor synthesis. When DOLK activity is lost, dolichyl phosphate becomes limiting and glycan transfer to nascent proteins fails across many substrates at once, producing the underglycosylated serum glycoproteins that define a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. The resulting DOLK-CDG is a severe multisystem disease, with dilated cardiomyopathy, ichthyosis, seizures, hypotonia and developmental failure, and death frequently occurs in infancy. Because the affected step sits upstream of all dolichol-dependent glycosylation rather than within one glycan branch, the defect illustrates how a single lipid-activating kinase governs secretory protein maturation, membrane protein folding and cell surface anchoring throughout the body.

Defective DHDDS causes RP59 describes how loss of function in the first committed step of dolichol synthesis produces an inherited blinding retinal degeneration. Dolichol is the lipid carrier on which the N-linked glycan is built before transfer to nascent proteins, so cells that secrete or traffic heavily glycosylated membrane proteins depend on a steady supply; rod photoreceptors, which manufacture enormous amounts of rhodopsin, are especially vulnerable. The active enzyme is a heterodimer of the catalytic subunit DHDDS with the NUS1-encoded partner, working at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane to add isopentenyl pyrophosphate units head-to-tail onto farnesyl pyrophosphate until a polyprenyl chain of roughly 17-23 isoprene units is reached. Mutations that impair this cis-prenyltransferase activity cause retinitis pigmentosa 59, with night blindness, progressive loss of peripheral then central vision, and pigment deposits reflecting rod loss followed by cone loss.

Dolichol is the lipid carrier on which N-linked glycans are built before transfer to nascent glycoproteins, and the first committed step of its synthesis is carried out by a two-subunit cis-prenyltransferase at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, comprising the catalytic DHDDS subunit and the NUS1-encoded partner. Together they add isopentenyl pyrophosphate units head-to-tail onto farnesyl pyrophosphate to give polyprenyl pyrophosphate, the precursor of the 17-23 isoprene dolichols used in glycosylation. Loss-of-function mutation in the catalytic subunit underlies retinitis pigmentosa 59, an inherited pigment retinopathy in which rod photoreceptors degenerate first and cones follow, producing night blindness, progressive loss of mid-peripheral and then central vision, and pigment deposits in the fundus. Rhodopsin is among the glycoproteins dependent on adequate dolichol supply, linking a general biosynthetic lipid pathway to photoreceptor survival.

WNT signalling drives stem and progenitor self-renewal in epithelia, and its inappropriate activation is one of the most common routes to human cancer — nearly all sporadic colorectal tumours carry an activating lesion in this route, and mis-regulation also occurs in liver, kidney, stomach and many other solid tumours. Normally, in the absence of ligand a destruction complex built around APC, AXIN1, AMER1, GSK3B and casein kinase 1 alpha phosphorylates beta-catenin and targets it for degradation; loss of these tumour suppressors, or stabilising mutations in beta-catenin itself, leaves the protein free to enter the nucleus and drive TCF/LEF-dependent transcription of growth genes. Ligand supply and receptor turnover matter too: PORCN lipidates WNTs, the ubiquitin ligase RNF43 removes Frizzled receptors, secreted DKK antagonists act with KREMEN proteins on LRP5/6, and tankyrases destabilise AXIN. Non-canonical branches contribute polarity and motility changes that favour invasion and metastasis.

Glycoproteins that fail to fold correctly in the secretory pathway must be recognised and disposed of, and trimming of their N-linked glycans is the timer that marks them for disposal. The ER mannosidase MAN1B1 removes a single mannose residue from the B branch of the high-mannose glycan on persistently misfolded substrates, generating the signal that commits them to lectin-mediated extraction and proteasomal destruction rather than further folding attempts. Loss-of-function mutations in MAN1B1 blunt this quality-control step, allowing aberrant glycoproteins to escape degradation and perturbing Golgi morphology and glycan processing; the clinical consequence is an autosomal recessive, non-syndromic intellectual disability of moderate to severe degree, sometimes with obesity and facial dysmorphism. The condition illustrates how neurodevelopment depends on glycoprotein folding surveillance, placing this reaction within ER-associated degradation and the broader congenital disorders of glycosylation.

Complex N-glycans on secreted and membrane proteins acquire their second antenna when a Golgi enzyme adds N-acetylglucosamine to the alpha-1,6 mannose arm of the core structure; MGAT2 performs this branching step, and its loss defines congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIa. Without this transfer, glycoproteins remain monoantennary, cannot be extended into the normal biantennary complex forms, and reach the circulation underglycosylated, which is how the condition is detected in serum transferrin. Because so many receptors, adhesion molecules, clotting factors and plasma proteins depend on complex glycan structure, the consequence is multisystem: psychomotor retardation, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies and immune dysfunction. This lesion belongs to the processing and trimming class of glycosylation defects, downstream of the endoplasmic reticulum assembly of the oligomannose precursor and within Golgi N-glycan maturation.

Loss of beta-1,4-galactosyltransferase 1 activity gives rise to a type II congenital disorder of glycosylation, in which N-glycans attached to proteins are made but cannot be properly elongated. The enzyme normally adds galactose to terminal N-acetylglucosamine on growing complex glycans in the Golgi, the step that creates the acceptor for later sialylation; without it, glycoproteins leave the secretory pathway truncated, which is detected clinically as abnormal serum transferrin on isoelectric focusing. Because so many secreted and membrane proteins depend on complete glycan processing, the consequences are multisystem: dysmorphic features, hydrocephalus, muscular hypotonia, developmental delay and a coagulation defect reflecting poorly glycosylated clotting factors. This places the defect among the Golgi glycan trimming, elongation and processing disorders rather than among failures of lipid-linked oligosaccharide assembly and transfer in the endoplasmic reticulum.

N-linked glycosylation begins when a 14-sugar lipid-linked oligosaccharide is transferred onto nascent proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, and the first trimming step removes the outermost alpha-1,2-linked glucose. The ER enzyme mannosyl-oligosaccharide glucosidase (MOGS, also called glucosidase I) performs that cut, which is a prerequisite for further glucose removal, for the calnexin/calreticulin folding and quality-control cycle that reads mono-glucosylated glycans, and for subsequent mannose trimming and Golgi glycan extension. Loss of this activity causes the congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIb, one of the glycan processing and trimming defects, in which serum glycoproteins are underglycosylated and abnormal tetrasaccharides are excreted in urine. Affected infants show a multisystem presentation with hypotonia, dysmorphism, hepatomegaly, seizures, immune abnormalities and early lethality, illustrating how broadly secretory protein maturation depends on this single trimming reaction.

Glucose residues that cap the N-glycan precursor are not transferred directly from UDP-glucose; they must first be loaded onto a lipid carrier, and synthesis of dolichyl-phosphate-glucose is that loading step. ALG5 catalyses the transfer of glucose from UDP-glucose onto dolichol phosphate at the cytosolic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, after which the product is flipped into the lumen and used for the three terminal glucosylations of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide destined for newly synthesised proteins. Those glucoses are what the oligosaccharyltransferase and the calnexin/calreticulin quality-control system read, so the pathway feeds directly into glycoprotein folding surveillance. NUDT14 provides the opposing activity, hydrolysing the sugar nucleotide-like donor to release glucose 1-phosphate and thereby limiting carrier availability. Defects in ALG5 cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation with polycystic kidney disease.

Chromatin organization is the packaging of genomic DNA with histones into nucleosomes and the continual remodelling of that packaging to control which sequences are readable. It sets the accessibility of DNA for transcription, replication and repair, and thereby defines cell identity; mutations in its components underlie many developmental syndromes and are among the most common lesions in cancer. The machinery falls into recognisable groups: core and variant histones themselves; writers and erasers of histone marks such as acetyltransferases, deacetylases, methyltransferases and demethylases; readers bearing bromo-, chromo- and PHD domains; and ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, CHD and NuRD families that slide, evict and exchange nucleosomes. Polycomb and Trithorax complexes impose heritable repression or activation, while histone chaperones and elongation factors keep chromatin restored behind polymerases. The output is epigenetic memory that persists through division and is reset during differentiation.

Genomic DNA in the nucleus is packaged with histones into nucleosomes, and chromatin organization is the set of activities that build, mark and move those nucleosomes so that DNA can be read, copied and repaired while remaining protected. Core histones of all four classes plus variants such as H2A.X and H3.3 provide the substrate; deposition is coupled to replication and to transcription-associated histone exchange. Writers and erasers of epigenetic marks set the accessibility state: acetyltransferases including EP300, CREBBP and KAT5-containing complexes, histone deacetylases with NuRD and NCoR corepressors, lysine methyltransferases such as KMT2A-D, EZH2 within Polycomb repressive complex 2, SUV39H enzymes and demethylases of the KDM families, alongside arginine methyltransferases and deiminases. ATP-dependent remodellers of the SWI/SNF, CHD and INO80-related families reposition nucleosomes. Mutations in these subunits are widespread in cancer and in developmental syndromes affecting growth and neural patterning.

AXIN1 and AXIN2 are the scaffolds that hold together the beta-catenin destruction complex, and signalling by AXIN mutants describes what happens when that scaffold is lost. Normally AXIN docks APC, the AMER1 adaptor, casein kinase 1 and GSK3 beta alongside beta-catenin so the kinases can phosphorylate it for ubiquitin-mediated degradation, with protein phosphatase 2A subunits tuning the complex; this keeps cytoplasmic beta-catenin low and WNT target genes off in the absence of ligand. Truncating or expression-abrogating mutations in AXIN1 remove the interaction domains needed for this assembly, so beta-catenin escapes destruction and drives constitutive transcription of proliferative targets. AXIN1 therefore behaves as a tumour suppressor, and its biallelic inactivation is found in hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal cancer and medulloblastoma, making this a route to ligand-independent WNT pathway activation in cancer.

Beta-catenin is normally kept scarce: a destruction complex built on APC, AXIN1 and AMER1 presents it to CK1alpha and GSK3beta, which phosphorylate a cluster of serines and threonines in its N-terminus (S33, S37, T41, S45) and thereby mark it for ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction, with PP2A subunits tuning the reaction. Signalling by CTNNB1 phospho-site mutants describes what happens when those acceptor residues are altered by exon 3 mutations in cancer. The protein can no longer be tagged for turnover, so it accumulates even without a WNT ligand, enters the nucleus and partners with LEF1/TCF factors to drive transcription of proliferative targets such as MYC and CCND1. This constitutive, ligand-independent WNT output is a recurrent driver in colorectal, hepatocellular and endometrial tumours, and it renders cells insensitive to upstream regulation of the pathway.

In unstimulated cells the beta-catenin destruction complex keeps WNT target genes off, and APC is the scaffold that holds it together, binding AXIN1, GSK3beta, casein kinase 1 alpha, PP2A subunits and beta-catenin so that beta-catenin is sequentially phosphorylated, ubiquitinated and degraded. Signaling by APC mutants describes what happens when that scaffold is broken: truncating frameshift mutations remove the SAMP motifs and the 15 and 20 amino acid repeats needed for AXIN binding and beta-catenin turnover, so beta-catenin accumulates in the cytoplasm and drives constitutive transcription of proliferative WNT targets. This is the initiating lesion in the great majority of sporadic and familial colorectal tumours, and the membrane-associated APC partner AMER1 is itself mutated in related cancers. Stabilising mutations in beta-catenin's own phosphodegron produce the same outcome and occur in tumours that retain wild-type APC.

AMER1/WTX normally helps the beta-catenin destruction complex keep WNT signalling off, and mutant forms of it release that brake. The protein binds beta-catenin directly through its C-terminal half and works alongside APC, AXIN1, casein kinase 1 alpha and GSK3B, whose sequential phosphorylation of beta-catenin marks it for ubiquitin-dependent degradation; protein phosphatase 2A subunits in the same complex tune those phosphorylation events. Loss of AMER1, whether by whole-gene deletion or by nonsense and missense changes that truncate the protein before its beta-catenin-binding region, stabilises cytoplasmic beta-catenin and raises transcription of WNT target genes. Because this pathway controls progenitor proliferation in the developing kidney, such lesions are recurrent in Wilms tumour, placing AMER1 among the tumour suppressors whose failure converts a degradation machine into a source of constitutive growth signalling.

Cells must keep balanced pools of all eight ribo- and deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates for transcription, replication, repair and energy metabolism, and the interconversion of nucleotide di- and triphosphates is the step that does the balancing. Nucleoside monophosphate kinases such as the adenylate kinases, guanylate kinase, CMPK1 and thymidylate kinase add the second phosphate, drawing almost always on ATP, while the broadly specific NME family transfers the terminal phosphate to make triphosphates. Because these reactions sit near equilibrium and overlap in substrate preference, an excess of one nucleotide can be redistributed to replenish scarcer ones. Ribonucleotide reductase, with its thioredoxin and glutaredoxin reducing systems, diverts diphosphates into the deoxy series, and dUTPase and dCTP pyrophosphatase remove species that would otherwise be misincorporated into DNA. Imbalance here causes replication stress, mutagenesis and mitochondrial DNA depletion.

Kainate receptors sitting on axon terminals tune how much glutamate or GABA a synapse releases, acting as autoreceptors and heteroreceptors that set synaptic gain and short-term plasticity rather than simply carrying current. What distinguishes this presynaptic role is that it proceeds without ion flux through the channel: the receptor, here built around GRIK3-containing assemblies, couples instead to heterotrimeric G proteins, so that liberated beta-gamma subunits stimulate phospholipase C beta isoforms. The resulting inositol trisphosphate mobilises calcium from internal stores, and that local calcium rise promotes vesicle fusion and transmitter release. This metabotropic mode of kainate receptor signalling shapes excitatory-inhibitory balance in hippocampal and cortical circuits, contributes to the regulation of network excitability, and is of interest because disturbed kainate receptor function is linked to epilepsy and to psychiatric and mood disorders.

De novo pyrimidine biosynthesis builds the uracil ring from scratch, supplying the UMP precursor from which all other pyrimidine nucleotides — CTP, UTP and the thymidine nucleotides of DNA — are derived. Proliferating cells depend on it to keep pace with replication and RNA synthesis, which is why it is a drug target in cancer, autoimmunity and antiparasitic therapy. Atoms are drawn from glutamine, bicarbonate and aspartate: a single multifunctional cytosolic protein carries out the first three steps through to dihydroorotate, the inner mitochondrial membrane enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase oxidises that intermediate while feeding electrons to the respiratory chain, and a bifunctional cytosolic enzyme joins orotate to PRPP and decarboxylates the product to UMP. This last step links pyrimidine supply to ribose-phosphate availability. Loss of the bifunctional enzyme causes hereditary orotic aciduria, with megaloblastic anaemia and orotate excretion.

The recognition step by which G protein-coupled receptors, the largest receptor superfamily in the human genome and the largest single class of drug targets, detect their agonists. The ligands here span almost every mode of chemical communication: peptide and protein hormones such as vasopressin, oxytocin, glucagon, parathyroid hormone and the opioid precursors; biogenic amines acting at adrenergic, muscarinic, dopamine, serotonin and histamine receptors; chemokines pairing with chemokine receptors to direct leukocyte traffic; lipid mediators including prostanoids, leukotrienes, sphingosine-1-phosphate and lysophospholipids; nucleotides, free fatty acids, protons, calcium and amino acids; light captured by rhodopsin and cone opsins; and sweet, umami and bitter tastants. Rhodopsin-like, secretin-like and clamshell-domain glutamate-family receptors each bind ligands differently, and accessory subunits such as the RAMPs reshape specificity. Occupancy is then relayed through heterotrimeric G proteins to endocrine, neural, cardiovascular, sensory and inflammatory responses, which is why this interface dominates pharmacology.

Mucin-type O-glycosylation begins when a GalNAc transferase adds N-acetylgalactosamine to serine or threonine residues of a secreted or membrane protein in the Golgi, and GALNT3 is the isoform whose loss causes hyperphosphatemic familial tumoral calcinosis. Its heavily glycosylated substrates include the mucin family represented here, from gel-forming secreted mucins such as MUC2, MUC5AC and MUC5B to membrane-tethered MUC1, MUC4 and MUC16, whose dense O-glycan coats give mucus its viscosity and protect epithelial surfaces. GALNT3 also glycosylates the phosphaturic hormone FGF23, shielding it from proteolytic cleavage; without this protection intact FGF23 falls, renal phosphate reabsorption rises, and calcium phosphate crystals deposit progressively in skin, soft tissue and bone. Affected individuals show hyperphosphatemia and may suffer painful long-bone swellings with cortical hyperostosis, linking a glycosyltransferase defect to systemic mineral homeostasis.

Alpha-dystroglycan links muscle and neural cell membranes to the extracellular matrix, and it can only bind laminin, agrin and perlecan if its O-mannosyl glycans are extended with a long matriglycan polymer. LARGE1 builds that polymer, alternating xylose and glucuronic acid onto a primer whose terminal glucuronic acid is added by B4GAT1. When LARGE1 activity is lost, alpha-dystroglycan is hypoglycosylated and cannot engage the basement membrane, so myofibres detach and degenerate and neuronal migration in the developing brain fails. The resulting dystroglycanopathies span a severity range: congenital muscular dystrophy with brain and eye malformations and profound developmental delay at the severe end, and a milder form with intellectual disability, white matter changes and structural brain abnormalities. This places the pathway at the intersection of glycan biosynthesis, muscle membrane integrity and cortical development.

Alpha-dystroglycan must carry an unusual O-mannosyl glycan to bind laminin and other extracellular matrix ligands, and POMGNT1 performs one step of building it: adding N-acetylglucosamine in beta-1,2 linkage to O-linked mannose on the dystroglycan core protein. This glycan chain is what tethers the basal lamina to the cytoskeleton in skeletal muscle, brain and peripheral nerve, so when POMGNT1 is defective the receptor is made but cannot engage its ligands. The result is a congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy whose severity tracks residual enzyme activity, from the severe type A3 form with brain and eye malformations including muscle-eye-brain disease, through an intermediate type B3 with mental retardation, to a milder limb-girdle type C3. The biology sits within Golgi glycosyltransferase-mediated protein O-mannosylation and matrix receptor maturation rather than within muscle contraction itself.

Alpha-dystroglycan must be O-mannosylated to bind laminin and other extracellular matrix ligands, and the first committed step of that modification is performed by a heterodimeric enzyme in which POMT1 and POMT2 must both be present for activity. The resulting glycan chain lets dystroglycan tether the basal lamina to the cytoskeleton in skeletal muscle, brain and peripheral nerve, maintaining sarcolemmal integrity during contraction and guiding neuronal migration in the developing cortex. Loss-of-function mutations in POMT2 abolish mannosyl transfer to serine and threonine residues of dystroglycan, stripping it of matrix binding and producing a graded spectrum of congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy: the severe form with brain malformation and eye anomalies, an intermediate congenital form with intellectual disability, and a milder limb-girdle presentation. This places the defect within protein glycosylation disorders rather than within muscle structural protein deficiency.

Vertebrae and ribs are laid down by the rhythmic segmentation of paraxial mesoderm into somites, a process timed by Notch signalling, and loss-of-function mutations in lunatic fringe produce the recessive segmentation disorder spondylocostal dysostosis type 3, with disorganised, fused and malformed vertebrae and ribs and a shortened trunk. LFNG is a Golgi-resident glycosyltransferase that adds an N-acetylglucosamine residue in beta1,3 linkage onto O-linked fucose on the EGF repeats of the Notch receptors, and this sugar elongation retunes receptor responsiveness, lowering affinity for Jagged-type ligands relative to Delta-type ones. That biased ligand sensitivity sharpens the oscillatory Notch activity of the segmentation clock and the boundary formation that follows. When the enzyme is catalytically dead or mislocalised away from the Golgi, Notch receptors carry unmodified O-fucose, segmentation timing is lost, and the axial skeleton forms incorrectly.

Mucin-type O-glycosylation normally extends beyond the first sugar: a galactosyltransferase adds galactose to O-linked GalNAc to build the core 1 structure on which longer glycans are elaborated. That enzyme, C1GALT1, only folds and stays active in complex with its dedicated chaperone C1GALT1C1, so loss of the chaperone silences the enzyme and leaves the truncated Tn antigen exposed on mucins and other glycoproteins. Somatic mutation of C1GALT1C1 produces Tn polyagglutination syndrome, in which erythrocytes displaying Tn are agglutinated by naturally occurring anti-Tn antibodies, causing haemolysis and cytopenias. The same truncated glycan is a tumour-associated marker found across human carcinomas, where incomplete glycosylation of secreted and membrane mucins such as MUC1, MUC2 and MUC16 alters cell adhesion, immune recognition and mucosal barrier properties.

Alpha-dystroglycan must be O-mannosylated to bind laminin and other extracellular matrix ligands, and the first committed step of that modification is carried out by a protein O-mannosyltransferase complex in which POMT1 and POMT2 are both required for activity. The resulting glycan chain lets dystroglycan link the basal lamina to the cytoskeleton in skeletal muscle, brain and peripheral nerve. Loss-of-function mutations in POMT1 leave dystroglycan hypoglycosylated and unable to engage matrix, producing the congenital muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathies: the severe type A form with brain malformation and eye anomalies of Walker-Warburg and muscle-eye-brain type, an intermediate type B with muscular dystrophy and intellectual disability, and a milder limb-girdle type C presenting later with proximal weakness. The graded severity tracks how much residual mannosyltransferase activity survives, making this a dosage-sensitive glycosylation step underlying muscle and neuronal migration integrity.

Proteins carrying thrombospondin type 1 repeats — the ADAMTS proteases and ADAMTSL proteins, thrombospondins, semaphorins 5A/5B, spondins, properdin and related secreted factors — depend on an unusual sugar for correct folding and export. B3GLCT, an ER-membrane beta-1,3-glucosyltransferase, adds glucose to O-linked fucose on these repeats, completing a glucose-fucose disaccharide that acts as a folding checkpoint and licenses secretion from the ER lumen. When B3GLCT is defective, TSR-containing clients are retained or degraded rather than delivered to the extracellular matrix, and the resulting loss of matrix remodelling and guidance activity produces Peters plus syndrome, a recessive disorder with anterior eye chamber malformation, short stature, developmental delay and orofacial clefting. The pathway links ER glycosylation-based quality control to extracellular matrix assembly, procollagen processing, angiogenesis and axon guidance during development.

Mucins protect the gut lining, and their protective properties depend on dense O-linked glycosylation added in the Golgi. GALNT12 initiates that glycosylation by transferring N-acetylgalactosamine onto serine and threonine residues of mucin polypeptides, and it is expressed mainly in the digestive tract, including stomach, small intestine and colon. When GALNT12 function is lost, mucins such as MUC2, MUC5AC, MUC13 and the membrane-tethered MUC1 and MUC17 are underglycosylated, weakening the mucus barrier and altering the cell surface properties that govern adhesion and signalling in epithelial cells. Inherited GALNT12 variants have been linked to susceptibility to colorectal cancer, arising as malignant lesions of the colonic and rectal wall, placing this initiating glycosyltransferase step within the broader relationship between epithelial glycosylation, barrier maintenance and tumour development.

Cells tune their sensitivity to Wnt ligands partly by controlling how many receptors sit at the surface, and this route removes the Frizzled-4 receptor from the plasma membrane in response to WNT5A. Because FZD4 is the receptor through which Norrin and Wnt ligands drive retinal and inner-ear vascular development, its removal sets an upper limit on that signalling; loss-of-function in the FZD4 receptor axis causes familial exudative vitreoretinopathy. WNT5A acting as a non-canonical ligand engages protein kinase C, whose phosphorylation of the scaffold Dishevelled-2 licenses receptor uptake. Internalization then proceeds through the classical endocytic machinery: beta-arrestin 2 bridges phosphorylated DVL2 to the AP-2 adaptor complex and clathrin triple heavy and light chains, delivering FZD4 into coated vesicles. The pathway illustrates how receptor trafficking, rather than ligand availability alone, shapes the balance between canonical and non-canonical Wnt output.

Three haematopoietic cytokines — IL-3, IL-5 and GM-CSF — share a receptor family in which each ligand-specific alpha chain pairs with a common beta subunit, and signalling through it drives the production, survival and activation of myeloid cells. IL-3 acts on multipotent marrow progenitors, IL-5 governs eosinophil maturation and B cell differentiation, and GM-CSF supports granulocyte, macrophage and dendritic cell output, including the alveolar macrophages whose loss causes pulmonary alveolar proteinosis; the same axis underlies emergency myelopoiesis during infection and autocrine growth in some acute myeloid leukaemias. The receptor chains have no catalytic activity, so JAK1 and JAK2 phosphorylate the beta subunit, creating docking sites for STAT5A/STAT5B, Shc–Grb2–SOS1 and PI3K subunits, with Src-family kinases, GAB2 and VAV1 broadening the response. Phosphatases such as PTPN6, PTPN11 and the inositol phosphatase INPP5D, together with CBL-mediated ubiquitination, restrain the output.

WNT5A acts on cells without stabilizing beta-catenin, and the receptor internalization step described here is how that non-canonical output is generated. When WNT5A binds FZD2 or FZD5 together with the ROR1/ROR2 tyrosine kinase-like co-receptors, the complex is taken from the plasma membrane into clathrin-coated vesicles, a step required for downstream RAC activation and the cytoskeletal remodelling that drives polarized cell migration, convergent extension and planar tissue organization. The AP-2 adaptor subunits and clathrin heavy and light chains named here provide the endocytic machinery, coupling ligand binding to cargo selection and vesicle budding. Receptor uptake is thus not merely signal termination but a prerequisite for signal output. Loss of ROR2 function causes skeletal malformation syndromes, and this arm of WNT signalling is reactivated in invasive tumour cells, where it favours motility over proliferative beta-catenin responses.

Attaching sugars to serine and threonine residues of secreted and membrane proteins is one of the commonest post-translational modifications, and it determines whether those proteins fold, are secreted, resist proteases or bind partners at all. Several distinct routes are represented here: mucin-type glycosylation, in which a large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases initiates chains that are elongated by core and branching enzymes and capped by sialyltransferases, builds the dense glycan shield of gel-forming and membrane mucins that protects gut and airway epithelium and is remodelled in cancer. O-mannosylation by POMT1/POMT2 and the glycosyltransferases acting downstream, including FKTN, FKRP and LARGE, creates the matriglycan on dystroglycan that anchors muscle to laminin; its loss causes congenital muscular dystrophies with brain and eye involvement. O-fucosylation of thrombospondin repeats, seen in ADAMTS proteases and thrombospondins, supports secretion of extracellular matrix regulators. Nucleotide-sugar transporters supply the donors.

O-glycosylation of TSR domain-containing proteins is the sugar modification that licenses secreted matrix and guidance proteins to fold and leave the cell. Proteins built from thrombospondin type 1 repeats — thrombospondins, the ADAMTS metalloproteases and ADAMTS-like proteins, F-spondin, properdin, semaphorins 5A/5B — depend on it for quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum, and its loss causes Peters plus syndrome, with eye, skeletal and craniofacial defects. POFUT2 recognises a CSX(S/T)CG consensus within folded TSR domains and attaches fucose to the conserved serine or threonine; B3GLCT then adds glucose to build the rare Glc-beta-1,3-Fuc disaccharide. Because the fucosyltransferase acts only on properly folded repeats, the modification doubles as a folding checkpoint that governs secretion. The client proteins in turn shape extracellular matrix assembly, procollagen processing, angiogenesis, complement activation, axon guidance and von Willebrand factor cleavage.

Secreted and matrix proteins built from thrombospondin type 1 repeats are sugar-modified inside the endoplasmic reticulum before they ever reach the extracellular space, and this O-glycosylation of TSR domain-containing proteins acts as a folding and secretion checkpoint. POFUT2 attaches fucose to a serine or threonine within the CSX(S/T)CG consensus of a properly folded repeat, and B3GLCT then adds glucose to build the rare Glc-beta1,3-Fuc disaccharide. Substrates include thrombospondins, properdin of the complement alternative pathway, spondins, several semaphorins, and the large ADAMTS metalloprotease and ADAMTSL families that process procollagen and proteoglycans. Because the modification stabilises the repeat, its loss leaves substrates retained and degraded rather than secreted; B3GLCT mutations cause Peters plus syndrome, with skeletal, eye and craniofacial defects that echo the connective-tissue roles of ADAMTS proteases in matrix assembly, angiogenesis and wound healing.

Mitophagy is the selective autophagic removal of mitochondria, the quality-control route that clears damaged or surplus organelles before they leak reactive oxygen species and pro-apoptotic factors. It also serves programmed elimination: paternal mitochondria after fertilisation, and the wholesale clearance of functional mitochondria during erythrocyte and lens fibre maturation. The best-defined arm depends on the kinase PINK1, which accumulates on depolarised outer membranes, phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits the E3 ligase Parkin; ubiquitin chains built with UBE2D and UBE2N conjugating enzymes on TOM complex subunits, VDAC channels and mitofusins are then read by the receptors OPTN and SQSTM1, whose TBK1- and casein kinase 2-dependent phosphorylation strengthens LC3 binding. Hypoxia engages the receptor FUNDC1 instead. ULK1 and the ATG5-ATG12 conjugation machinery build the engulfing membrane. Loss of PINK1 or Parkin causes early-onset Parkinson disease.

Mitophagy is the selective clearance of mitochondria by autophagy, the route by which cells dispose of damaged or surplus organelles and keep the mitochondrial population functional. It matters for quality control in neurons, for programmed loss of mitochondria during erythrocyte and lens maturation, and for maternal inheritance of mitochondrial DNA through destruction of sperm-derived mitochondria; failure of the kinase PINK1 or the ubiquitin ligase PRKN causes recessive Parkinson disease. Loss of membrane potential stabilises PINK1 on the import channels, where it phosphorylates ubiquitin and recruits PRKN to ubiquitinate outer-membrane substrates including the translocase components, mitofusins and the porins. Ubiquitin-binding receptors such as OPTN and SQSTM1, assisted by TBK1 and casein kinase 2 phosphorylation, then link the tagged organelle to LC3 and the ATG5-ATG12 conjugation machinery, while the hypoxia-responsive receptor FUNDC1 provides a receptor-mediated alternative under low oxygen.

Cells dispose of individual damaged mitochondria rather than whole populations, and PINK1-PRKN mediated mitophagy is the quality-control route that selects them. Depolarized mitochondria fail to import the kinase PINK1 through the TOM translocase, so it accumulates on the outer membrane, autophosphorylates, and phosphorylates both ubiquitin and the ubiquitin-like domain of the E3 ligase Parkin, switching Parkin on. Parkin then ubiquitinates outer-membrane substrates such as the fusion GTPases MFN1 and MFN2 and the porins VDAC1-3, and the resulting chains, further phosphorylated by PINK1 in a feedforward loop, are read by cargo receptors SQSTM1 and OPTN with help from TBK1. These tether the organelle to LC3 and the ATG5-ATG12 machinery for engulfment and lysosomal degradation. Loss-of-function mutations in PINK1 or PRKN cause early-onset recessive Parkinson disease.

Anthrax toxicity arises from a bacterial binary toxin system in which one subunit ferries two enzymes into host cells. Protective antigen binds the cell-surface receptors ANTXR1 and ANTXR2, is cleaved by furin, and oligomerises into a prepore that captures lethal factor and edema factor; clathrin-mediated endocytosis, assisted by ALIX, delivers the complex to endosomes, where acidification converts the oligomer into a translocation pore that releases both enzymes into the cytosol.
