There lethal factor, a zinc protease, clips the N-termini of MAP2K family kinases (MEK1/2, MKK3/4/6/7), collapsing ERK, JNK and p38 signalling in macrophages and endothelium, while edema factor, activated by host calmodulin, generates cAMP unrelentingly. The combination disables innate immune responses, drives vascular leak and oedema, and accounts for the lethality of systemic anthrax; the receptor and furin steps are the points targeted by antitoxin strategies.

Necroptosis is a lytic, inflammatory form of programmed cell death that acts as a backup when caspase-8 activity is blocked, for example by viral inhibitors, and it matters because the ruptured cell spills damage-associated molecules that drive inflammation in ischaemic injury, neurodegeneration and inflammatory disease. Death ligands such as TNF, FasL and TRAIL signalling through their receptors and the FADD/TRADD adaptors normally favour apoptosis; when caspase-8 with its regulator CFLAR cannot cleave RIPK1 and RIPK3, the two kinases instead oligomerize through their homotypic interaction motifs into a necrosome. RIPK3 then phosphorylates the pseudokinase MLKL, which assembles into higher-order species, traffics to the plasma membrane and permeabilizes it. Ubiquitin ligases and chaperone-associated quality control components, including the IAP proteins, ITCH, PELI1, STUB1 and HSP90 with CDC37, set how much RIPK1 and MLKL signal is licensed, while ESCRT-related and flotillin proteins influence membrane repair and shedding.

Regulated necrosis is cell death that ends in membrane rupture and spillage of cytoplasmic contents, yet is driven by defined genetic programmes rather than passive collapse. Because lysis releases alarmins such as HMGB1 and mature IL-1β and IL-18, these routes are intensely inflammatory and shape host defence against pathogens, sterile tissue injury, ischaemic damage and autoinflammatory disease. Two arms dominate here. In necroptosis, death receptor and TNF-family signalling through FADD, TRADD and RIPK1 assembles a RIPK1-RIPK3 necrosome when caspase-8 and its regulators CFLAR and the ubiquitin ligases BIRC2/3 and XIAP fail to restrain it; phosphorylated MLKL then permeabilises the plasma membrane, with ESCRT-III components attempting repair. In pyroptosis, inflammatory caspases 1, 4 and 5 cleave gasdermin D, while caspase-3 and granzyme B liberate gasdermin E, forming pores that drive swelling and cytokine release.

CASP8 activity is inhibited describes the switch that decides whether a cell receiving a death signal dies by apoptosis or by necroptosis. Caspase-8, recruited through FADD to ligated death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors, normally both drives the apoptotic protease cascade and cleaves RIPK1 and RIPK3, thereby suppressing regulated necrosis. When its proteolytic activity is blocked — by pan-caspase inhibitors, by the short FLIP isoform encoded by CFLAR, or by viral FLIP mimics — RIPK1 and RIPK3 survive intact, assemble a necrosome and kill the cell by membrane rupture instead. The distinction matters physiologically: apoptosis is immunologically quiet, whereas necroptosis spills contents and inflames tissue, and this route serves as a backup defence when viruses disable caspases. Loss of caspase-8 restraint underlies inflammatory tissue damage and embryonic lethality in animal models.

Death receptor engagement can end in either apoptosis or necroptosis, and the decision hinges on whether caspase-8 is allowed to work. When CASP8 activity is inhibited, the apoptotic route is closed and signalling is redirected toward RIPK1/RIPK3-dependent regulated necrosis, an inflammatory form of death that releases cellular contents rather than packaging them quietly. Ligands such as FASLG and TRAIL cluster their receptors, FAS and the TRAIL receptors, and recruit FADD or TRADD together with TRAF2 to assemble a platform where procaspase-8 dimerises. Catalytically inactive CFLAR (c-FLIP) short forms, viral FLIP mimics and pharmacological caspase inhibitors block full processing of the protease, so RIPK1 escapes the cleavage that would normally restrain it. This switch matters for antiviral defence, where pathogens suppress caspase-8 and provoke necroptosis instead, and for the inflammation seen when caspase-8 function is lost.

When VEGF acts on VEGFR2, one of the immediate consequences is that blood vessels dilate and leak, and this arm of VEGFR2 signalling explains how that happens. Loosening of endothelial junctions allows plasma protein extravasation and provides the matrix and space into which new vessels sprout, so it is an early step in angiogenesis as well as the basis of oedema in tumours, diabetic retinopathy and inflammation. Two outputs converge here. AKT, activated with PDPK1 and the mTORC2 components RICTOR and MLST8, phosphorylates endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which with calmodulin, HSP90 and caveolin-1 releases nitric oxide to relax smooth muscle. In parallel, VAV proteins activate RAC1 and the PAK kinases to trigger endocytosis of VE-cadherin, dismantling the adherens junction with its catenin and plakoglobin partners and opening the paracellular barrier.

VEGFR2 mediated cell proliferation is the arm of vascular endothelial growth factor signalling that drives endothelial cells to divide, supplying the new cells needed for angiogenesis during development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation. VEGFA binding to KDR triggers autophosphorylation of Tyr1175, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting diacylglycerol and IP3-mediated calcium release through ITPR channels activate protein kinase C isoforms. Rather than using the canonical GRB2-SOS route, this cascade reaches RAS by relieving GAP-mediated suppression, while PKC alpha can also phosphorylate RAF directly, feeding the MEK/ERK module that licenses S-phase entry. Calmodulin, PDPK1, SRC and sphingosine kinase shape the calcium and lipid second-messenger context. Because endothelial proliferation depends on this route, it is the target of anti-VEGF therapies in cancer and retinal disease, and its loss blocks vessel growth.

Endothelial cells divide in response to VEGF, and this is the branch of VEGFR2 signalling that drives that proliferation — the basis of angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumour vascularisation, and the target of anti-VEGF drugs. VEGFA binding to the KDR receptor triggers Src-dependent phosphorylation of the receptor tail, which recruits and activates phospholipase C gamma; the resulting inositol trisphosphate opens IP3 receptor channels on the endoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium that, with calmodulin, cooperates with diacylglycerol to activate conventional protein kinase C isoforms. PKC then feeds into the Ras/Raf/MEK/ERK cascade, either by phosphorylating Raf directly or by acting on Ras itself — here through relief of GTPase-activating protein restraint rather than exchange-factor recruitment. Sphingosine kinase and PDPK1 add further lipid and kinase input, linking the same receptor to survival as well as growth.

Active removal of DNA methylation lets cells erase an epigenetic mark rather than wait for it to be diluted by replication, and it is how imprints are erased in primordial germ cells and how the paternal genome is demethylated in the zygote. The TET dioxygenases oxidize 5-methylcytosine stepwise to 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine; thymine DNA glycosylase then excises the formyl- and carboxyl-modified bases, leaving an abasic site that base excision repair restores to unmodified cytosine. The oxidized intermediates are themselves abundant marks in embryonic stem cells and neurons, where TET1 expression tracks neuronal activity, while TET3 acts in oocytes and zygotes. TET2 predominates in haematopoietic stem cells and behaves as a tumour suppressor, its loss-of-function mutations being recurrent in myeloid malignancy. The pathway thus links chromatin state, developmental reprogramming and DNA repair chemistry.

A grouping of transport and binding events that do not yet fit an established route, held together by the movement of ions, metals and small solutes across membranes and by carrier-like binding proteins. Several coherent themes emerge: magnesium handling by the NIPA/NIPAL family, the mitochondrial carrier MRS2 and the MAGT1/TUSC3 subunits that double as oxidoreductase components of the oligosaccharyltransferase complex; ammonium conduction by the Rhesus glycoproteins RHAG, RHBG and RHCG in erythrocytes, liver and kidney; volume-regulated anion and osmolyte efflux through LRRC8 heteromers; and lysosomal cystine export by cystinosin, whose loss causes cystinosis. Adducins and dematin link the erythrocyte membrane skeleton to actin, while caseins, prolactin-induced protein and zinc-alpha-2-glycoprotein act as secreted ligand- or mineral-binding proteins. Together these activities support ion homeostasis, acid-base balance, cell volume control and membrane mechanical stability.

Ribosome production begins with RNA polymerase I transcribing the rRNA genes in the nucleolus, and only about half of the several hundred repeats are active at any time; positive epigenetic regulation of rRNA expression is how a growing cell opens more of them. Active repeats carry unmethylated DNA and acetylated histones, and the output sets how many ribosomes a cell can build, tying this chromatin control directly to growth rate, cell size and the hyperactivated ribosome biogenesis seen in tumours. ERCC6 (CSB) acts as a recruiting hub, bringing in the acetyltransferase KAT2B to modify histones H3 and H4 at the promoter and the methyltransferase EHMT2 to mark transcribed regions, while the B-WICH remodelling complex built on SMARCA5, BAZ1B, nuclear actin and MYO1C repositions nucleosomes. Pol I subunits with the SL1/TBP initiation factors then assemble on the cleared promoter; NuRD components and histone deacetylases provide the opposing restraint.

Ribosome production sets the pace of cell growth, and this chromatin-remodelling route raises output by opening the rDNA repeats so that RNA polymerase I can transcribe them efficiently. The B-WICH assembly, built around the ATP-dependent remodeller SMARCA5 with BAZ1B, nuclear myosin MYO1C, actin, DDX21, DEK, MYBBP1A, ERCC6 and SF3B1, binds active ribosomal RNA genes and also the polymerase III-transcribed 5S rRNA and 7SL RNA genes. By sliding nucleosomes and recruiting histone acetyltransferases such as EP300, KAT2A and KAT2B, it converts the surrounding histones to an acetylated, transcriptionally permissive state that favours loading of the SL1 promoter-selectivity factor (TAF1A-TAF1D with TBP) and the Pol I catalytic core. The result is coordinate control of rRNA and signal recognition particle RNA synthesis, linking nucleolar activity to growth signals, with GSK3B among the kinases modulating the response.

Only about half of a cell's ribosomal RNA gene copies are transcribed at any time; the rest are held silent, and this epigenetic silencing of rRNA expression sets how much ribosome production a cell can afford. Because ribosome biogenesis consumes a large share of nuclear transcription, keeping a reserve of repressed repeats links growth rate to nutrient and energy status and protects the tandem rDNA arrays from recombination and instability. Silenced copies carry methylated promoter DNA and H3K9 methylation instead of acetylated histones. The NoRC complex, built on BAZ2A with the chromatin remodeller SMARCA5, slides a nucleosome over the transcription start site and brings in HDAC1/HDAC2 and the DNA methyltransferases DNMT1 and DNMT3B; SIRT1 with the methyltransferase SUV39H1 couples deacetylation to H3K9 dimethylation. The repressed state acts on the Pol I machinery, UBTF and the SL1 TAFs that would otherwise fire these promoters.

Botulinum toxin type D toxicity disrupts communication between nerve cells and their targets by preventing synaptic vesicles from releasing neurotransmitters. At motor nerve terminals, this can block acetylcholine release and cause flaccid paralysis, although type D is only rarely associated with human botulism and its route from the human gut into circulation is not established. The toxin binds neuronal gangliosides and synaptic vesicle protein 2 (SV2), enters through vesicle uptake, and delivers its light chain into the cytosol. This protease cleaves VAMP1 and VAMP2, vesicle membrane proteins required for fusion with the presynaptic membrane. Without these components, neurotransmitter-filled vesicles cannot discharge their contents, interrupting chemical signalling across the synapse despite continued neuronal activity.

Botulinum toxin type B causes botulism by stopping motor neurons from releasing acetylcholine, leaving muscles unable to contract and, in severe cases, impairing breathing. After ingestion, a protective protein complex helps the toxin survive the gut and cross the intestinal lining into circulation. At nerve terminals, its heavy chain binds membrane gangliosides and synaptotagmin proteins SYT1 and SYT2 exposed during synaptic vesicle recycling. The toxin is taken into an acidifying vesicle, allowing its light chain to enter the cytosol. This protease cleaves VAMP2, a vesicle protein needed for fusion with the presynaptic membrane. Neurotransmitter-filled vesicles can no longer discharge their contents, producing prolonged flaccid paralysis until functional release machinery is restored.

Botulinum toxin type A causes botulism by stopping acetylcholine release from motor nerve endings, leaving muscles unable to contract and potentially causing respiratory paralysis. After ingestion, associated bacterial proteins protect the toxin in the gut and help it cross the intestinal epithelium into the circulation. At nerve terminals, the toxin binds gangliosides and synaptic vesicle proteins SV2A, SV2B or SV2C exposed during vesicle recycling, then enters acidifying vesicles. Acidification allows the heavy chain to deliver the light chain into the cytosol, where it cleaves SNAP25. Because SNAP25 is part of the machinery that fuses synaptic vesicles with the plasma membrane, its cleavage prevents neurotransmitter exocytosis despite continued nerve activity. The result is failure of neuromuscular transmission rather than direct muscle damage.

Botulinum toxin type C poisoning disables neurotransmitter release by preventing synaptic vesicles from fusing with neuronal membranes. At motor nerve terminals, loss of acetylcholine secretion can produce flaccid paralysis, although type C is only rarely implicated in human botulism. The toxin binds neuronal surface gangliosides, enters through vesicular uptake, and delivers its proteolytic light chain into the cytosol. This protease cleaves SNAP25 and the syntaxin 1 proteins encoded by STX1A and STX1B, disrupting the SNARE machinery that couples synaptic vesicles to membrane fusion. Without functional fusion machinery, electrical impulses reach nerve terminals but cannot trigger normal neurotransmitter secretion. The cellular mechanism of toxicity is established, whereas a route by which this toxin enters the human circulation from the gut has not been defined.

Botulinum neurotoxin type F blocks neurotransmitter release from nerve terminals, preventing muscles from receiving signals to contract. Its action can produce flaccid paralysis and, if respiratory muscles are affected, respiratory failure, although type F is an uncommon cause of human botulism. The toxin binds neuronal surface gangliosides and synaptic vesicle protein 2 (SV2), then enters nerve terminals through synaptic vesicle recycling. Vesicle acidification enables its light chain to reach the cytosol, where it cleaves VAMP1 and VAMP2, proteins required for synaptic vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane. Disabling this fusion machinery prevents acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions, interrupting communication between motor neurons and muscle without directly damaging the muscle itself.

Tetanus toxin intoxication is the route by which a wound-dwelling Clostridium blocks inhibitory neurotransmission, producing the rigidity and spasms of tetanus. The toxin is a disulfide-linked heavy chain-light chain dimer that circulates from the infection site, binds gangliosides and protein receptors at nerve terminals, and is internalised into clathrin-coated vesicles that travel by retrograde transport to the neuronal cell body and onward to inhibitory interneurons. Acidification of the vesicle lumen refolds the heavy chain into a channel through which the light chain translocates, and reduction of the interchain disulfide frees it into the cytosol. There it acts as a zinc-dependent metalloprotease with a single decisive substrate, VAMP2, a synaptobrevin of the SNARE complex; its cleavage prevents synaptic vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane, so neurotransmitter release fails and disinhibited motor neurons fire uncontrollably.

Botulinum neurotoxin type G disables neurotransmitter release from neurons, a mechanism capable of interrupting communication between motor nerves and muscle. If sufficient toxin reaches motor nerve terminals, loss of acetylcholine secretion can cause flaccid paralysis, although type G is rarely associated with human disease and a route from the gut into circulation has not been established. The toxin binds neuronal gangliosides and synaptotagmin 1 (SYT1), enters synaptic vesicles, and delivers its light chain into the cytosol. This protease cleaves VAMP1 and VAMP2, vesicle-associated proteins required for membrane fusion, preventing synaptic vesicles from releasing their neurotransmitter. The resulting disruption of vesicle fusion blocks chemical synaptic transmission without requiring destruction of the affected neuron.

Botulinum toxin type E causes flaccid paralysis by preventing motor neurons from releasing acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions, leaving muscles unable to contract. Severe intoxication can compromise breathing. After ingestion in contaminated food, the toxin is protected during passage through the gut, crosses the intestinal epithelium, and reaches peripheral nerve terminals through the circulation. Its heavy chain binds neuronal gangliosides and synaptic vesicle proteins SV2A and SV2B exposed during vesicle recycling. Endocytosis and vesicle acidification allow the light chain to cross into the neuronal cytosol, where reduction of an interchain disulfide releases it. The light chain then cleaves SNAP25, a component of the membrane fusion machinery, blocking synaptic vesicle exocytosis and neurotransmitter release.

Myogenesis is the formation of skeletal muscle, in which proliferating myoblasts exit the cell cycle, commit to a muscle fate, and fuse into multinucleated myotubes; it builds muscle during development and rebuilds it from satellite cells after injury, so its failure underlies muscle hypoplasia and poor regeneration. The pathway is centred on the myogenic bHLH factors MyoD, Myf5, myogenin and MRF4, which heterodimerize with E proteins such as E12/E47, HEB and ITF-2 to occupy E boxes in muscle-specific promoters, acting combinatorially with MEF2 family MADS-box factors to drive the contractile gene program. Upstream, the transmembrane co-receptor CDO, together with Boc, neogenin and netrin-3, works within N- and M-cadherin adhesion complexes at myoblast contacts; through the scaffolds JLP and Bnip-2 it engages Cdc42 and p38 MAPK signalling, which hyperphosphorylates E proteins and potentiates bHLH heterodimer activity, coupling cell-cell adhesion to differentiation.

Skeletal muscle is built when proliferating myoblasts exit the cycle, switch on muscle-specific genes and fuse into multinucleated myotubes, and this account of myogenesis focuses on the co-receptor CDON and its partners as an entry point into that transition. Loss of this programme underlies failures of muscle formation and regeneration, and the same transcription factors are reactivated by satellite cells after injury. CDON acts with the related Boc, neogenin and its ligand netrin-3, and N-, R- and M-cadherins with catenins at sites of myoblast contact, linking adhesion to differentiation. Through the scaffolds BNIP2 and JLP it engages Cdc42 and the p38 MAPK cascade, which promotes heterodimer formation between the myogenic bHLH factors MyoD, myogenin, Myf5 and MRF4 and E proteins such as E12/E47 and HEB. These heterodimers act at E boxes together with MEF2 family factors to drive muscle gene expression.

Immune defence fails in two directions, and diseases of the immune system cover both: too little response, giving recurrent or invasive infection, and too much, giving autoinflammation and tissue damage. The genes here center on inherited defects in innate sensing and its downstream signalling — Toll-like receptors for bacterial lipopeptides, lipopolysaccharide, flagellin, single-stranded RNA and double-stranded RNA, their co-receptors and chaperone UNC93B1, the adaptors MYD88, TIRAP and TICAM1, the kinase IRAK4, and the NF-kB module of IKK subunits, NFKBIA and the RELA/NFKB1 transcription factors. Loss of IRAK4 or MYD88 leaves children prone to pyogenic bacterial disease; BTK mutation abolishes B cell development and antibody production; hypomorphic IKBKG causes ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency. Also represented are contact-activation and complement regulators, notably SERPING1, whose deficiency causes hereditary angioedema, alongside endogenous alarmins such as HMGB1 and S100A8/A9 that drive sterile inflammation.

Dietary selenium only becomes biologically useful once it is converted into a reduced, transferable form, and the handling of ingested methylseleninic acid is one route into that pool. Methylseleninic acid is reduced in two steps, first to methylselenenic acid and then to methylselenol, the volatile monomethylated selenide that serves as the proximal donor for selenoprotein synthesis and as the species responsible for much of selenium's redox and growth-inhibitory activity in cells. Thioredoxin reductase, an NADPH-dependent selenoenzyme itself, carries out both reductions, so the same enzyme system that maintains thioredoxin in its reduced state also feeds selenium metabolism. This links nutritional selenium status to cellular antioxidant defence: too little selenium limits selenoprotein production, while high methylselenol generation drives oxidative stress and apoptosis, the basis of interest in selenium compounds as chemopreventive agents.

Newly made glycoproteins entering the endoplasmic reticulum carry a uniform N-glycan that the cell reads as a folding report card. Sequential trimming of glucose residues by glucosidases I and II converts the glycan into a monoglucosylated tag recognized by the lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin, which, with the associated oxidoreductase PDIA3, hold the substrate in a folding-permissive environment. Removal of the final glucose releases the client; if it is still misfolded, UGGT1/UGGT2 re-add a glucose and send it around the cycle again. Slow mannose trimming by MAN1B1 and the EDEM proteins acts as a timer, committing persistent failures to lectins such as OS9 and the SEL1L–HRD1 machinery for retrotranslocation, VCP-driven extraction, deglycosylation by NGLY1 and proteasomal destruction. This quality control sets the balance between secretion and degradation, and its enzymes are mutated in congenital disorders of glycosylation.

Cytosine methylation is the chemical mark that lets a cell keep a stable record of which genes it should not express, and it is copied to daughter cells at each division. Three active methyltransferases transfer methyl groups from S-adenosylmethionine to cytosine, mostly in CG dinucleotides: DNMT1 acts on hemimethylated sites generated by replication and so maintains existing patterns, while DNMT3A and DNMT3B, aided by the catalytically inactive DNMT3L, place new marks during the genome-wide remethylation that follows early embryonic and germline erasure. UHRF1 recognises hemimethylated DNA and modified histones and recruits DNMT1 to replicating chromatin, which explains why core histones accompany the enzymes here and links methylation to histone marks. Methylated promoters and CG islands are silenced, supporting imprinting, X inactivation and repression of repeats; aberrant patterns and DNMT3A mutations are recurrent in cancer and overgrowth syndromes.

Diphtheria toxin kills human cells by shutting down protein synthesis, and the route it takes into the cytosol is built entirely from host components. The bacterium itself stays in the throat or a skin lesion, so the systemic damage of diphtheria reflects this uptake and intoxication process in distant tissues such as heart and nerve. The toxin's B fragment binds proheparin-binding EGF-like growth factor (HBEGF) at the cell surface, with CD9 enhancing binding, and is taken into endosomes; acidification triggers B to insert as a channel through which the A fragment is threaded. Cytosolic HSP90 chaperones and thioredoxin reductase complete translocation and reduce the interchain disulfide, releasing fragment A. Free A then ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, arresting translation and killing the cell. The same receptor-mediated delivery is exploited by engineered toxin-fusion therapeutics.

Many bacterial diseases are caused not by the bacterium itself but by secreted toxins that enter host cells and sabotage them, and the uptake and actions of bacterial toxins covers that shared route of intoxication. Each toxin is bipartite: one moiety binds a surface receptor and delivers the second, catalytic moiety into the cytosol. The host proteins here are the doors and the targets. Anthrax toxin uses the receptors ANTXR1 and ANTXR2, is activated by the protease furin, and its lethal factor cleaves MAP kinase kinases to shut down MAPK signalling; diphtheria toxin enters via HBEGF and ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EEF2 to halt translation; botulinum and tetanus neurotoxins bind synaptic vesicle proteins and synaptotagmins, then cleave SNAP25, syntaxins and VAMPs to block neurotransmitter release; heat-stable enterotoxin activates GUCY2C to drive secretory diarrhoea. The outcomes are paralysis, tissue necrosis, arrested protein synthesis and fluid loss.

TCF7L2 is the DNA-binding transcription factor that converts a WNT signal into gene expression in intestinal epithelium, and its activity is normally held in check by corepressors. Signaling by TCF7L2 mutants describes what happens when that restraint is lost: around half of colorectal cancers with microsatellite instability carry frameshift mutations in TCF7L2, typically truncating the C-terminal region through which it binds the corepressors CTBP1 and CTBP2. The truncated protein no longer colocalizes with CTBP, so target promoters escape repression and TCF-dependent reporters are more strongly activated, biasing cells toward the proliferative WNT programme that drives adenoma formation. Because the mutations arise in repeat tracts, they reflect defective mismatch repair rather than direct selection of an activating lesion, and they illustrate how loss of a transcriptional brake can substitute for gain-of-function signalling upstream in the pathway.

Beta-catenin levels are normally held low by a cytoplasmic destruction complex, and this pathway describes what happens when GSK3beta is aberrantly spliced so that it can no longer be recruited into that complex. In chronic myeloid leukemia stem cells, in-frame loss of the AXIN- and FRAT-binding regions produces a GSK3beta protein that fails to phosphorylate beta-catenin efficiently, so beta-catenin escapes recognition by the ubiquitin ligase machinery, accumulates in the nucleus, and drives TCF/LEF-dependent transcription and self-renewal. The remaining components named here are the scaffold and kinase parts of the intact complex: APC and AXIN1 as scaffolds, AMER1 as a membrane-associated partner, casein kinase 1 alpha as the priming kinase, and protein phosphatase 2A subunits that tune complex activity. The result is constitutive Wnt output uncoupled from ligand, linking a splicing defect to leukemic progression.

Wnt ligands signal through a Frizzled receptor together with the co-receptor LRP5, and normal control of that signal depends on being able to switch the co-receptor off. Secreted DKK antagonists bind the LRP5 extracellular domain and, with the transmembrane KREMEN proteins, drive the co-receptor off the cell surface, damping beta-catenin accumulation. A splice variant of LRP5 found in breast and parathyroid tumours deletes the region required for this inhibition, so the mutant co-receptor remains responsive to Wnt whatever the level of DKK1. The consequence is a constitutive rise in active, unphosphorylated beta-catenin, sustained TCF/LEF-dependent transcription, and a proliferative advantage that is no longer restrained by extracellular feedback. This illustrates how oncogenic activation of Wnt signalling can arise at the receptor tier rather than through the more familiar destruction-complex or beta-catenin mutations, and why antagonist-based therapy would fail against such tumours.

WNT ligands cannot leave the cell that makes them unless they are first lipid-modified, and the drug LGK974 blocks precisely that step by inhibiting PORCN. PORCN is a membrane-bound O-acyltransferase of the endoplasmic reticulum that attaches a palmitoleoyl group to a conserved serine of WNT proteins; without this fatty acyl chain, WNTs are not loaded onto the chaperone that escorts them to the surface, are not secreted, and cannot engage Frizzled receptors on neighbouring cells. Inhibiting the enzyme therefore shuts down ligand-driven WNT signalling at its source, upstream of beta-catenin stabilisation and TCF/LEF-dependent transcription. This is of interest because inappropriate WNT pathway activity drives tumour growth in several tissues, and cancers that depend on autocrine or paracrine WNT ligand production, rather than on downstream mutations, are candidates for such pharmacological blockade.

Cells limit their own sensitivity to WNT by destroying the receptors that detect it, and RNF43 together with its relative ZNRF3 is the ubiquitin ligase that does so, tagging Frizzled proteins for removal from the plasma membrane so that WNT signalling output is capped. Frameshift truncations of RNF43 abolish this brake, leaving FZD4, FZD5, FZD6 and FZD8 and the co-receptors LRP5 and LRP6 to accumulate and respond excessively to ligands such as WNT3A. Such loss-of-function alleles recur in pancreatic and colorectal tumours, where they drive proliferation through beta-catenin-dependent transcription. Because the resulting growth still requires ligand, these tumours remain sensitive to blockade of WNT secretion by porcupine inhibitors, unlike cancers driven by downstream APC or beta-catenin lesions. This makes receptor turnover a decisive control point in intestinal and pancreatic stem cell self-renewal and a therapeutic vulnerability.

Pompe disease, or glycogen storage disease type II, follows from loss of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase activity, the single enzyme able to digest glycogen that reaches the lysosome. Glycogen delivered by autophagy is normally hydrolysed to glucose there; when the enzyme is absent or crippled by mutation, structurally normal glycogen accumulates inside swollen lysosomes and poisons the cell mechanically rather than by any toxic metabolite. Severity tracks residual enzyme activity: near-complete loss presents in infancy with cardiomyopathy and generalised tissue involvement, while partial activity gives later-onset disease largely confined to cardiac and skeletal muscle, with progressive weakness and respiratory failure. The substrate itself is built on glycogenin, the protein primer that nucleates glycogen chains, linking cytoplasmic glycogen synthesis to this lysosomal disposal route. It remains the model case for enzyme replacement therapy in a lysosomal storage disorder.

Caspase activation via extrinsic apoptotic signalling pathway is the route by which a cell is instructed from outside to kill itself, allowing immune cells to eliminate infected or transformed targets and allowing tissues to remove cells that have lost their positional cues. Death ligands such as FasL and TRAIL cluster their receptors, which recruit adaptors including FADD and TRADD into a death-inducing complex that dimerises and activates the initiator caspases-8 and -10; these cleave executioner caspase-3 directly or cleave Bid to amplify the signal through mitochondria. FLIP and RIPK1 set the threshold, determining whether ligation instead yields survival or necroptotic signalling, and TLR4 adaptors feed into the same node. A second arm operates through dependence receptors such as DCC and UNC5, which trigger caspase activation when their netrin ligand is absent, coupling neuronal and epithelial survival to trophic supply and suppressing tumour growth.

Cells can be instructed to die by signals arriving from outside, and this extrinsic route converts receptor engagement at the plasma membrane into activation of the caspase proteases that dismantle the cell. It underlies immune killing of infected and transformed targets, deletion of autoreactive lymphocytes, and the sculpting of tissues by removing cells that lack trophic support; its failure permits tumour survival and autoimmunity, while excess drives tissue injury. Death ligands such as FasL and TRAIL cluster Fas or TRAIL receptors, which recruit FADD and TRADD together with RIPK1 and TRAF2, allowing procaspase-8 to dimerise and cleave executioner caspase-3, with FLIP acting as a competitive brake. Toll-like receptor 4 with its TRIF adaptors feeds into the same machinery. Dependence receptors including DCC and UNC5 homologues take the opposite logic, triggering apoptosis when their ligands are absent.

Tumour necrosis factor acting on TNFR1 does not commit a cell to any one fate; the proapoptotic arm of TNFR1 signalling is the branch that kills it, and whether that branch is taken decides whether inflammation resolves or becomes tissue damage. The receptor first assembles a membrane complex containing TRADD, TRAF2, RIPK1 and the linear ubiquitin ligase components SHARPIN, RBCK1 and RNF31 that favours survival through NF- infB. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD, OTULIN-like enzymes, TNFAIP3 and OTUD7B strip those chains, releasing a cytosolic death-inducing complex in which FADD recruits procaspase-8 for dimerisation and autoprocessing, launching the effector caspase cascade. The inhibitors BIRC2, BIRC3 and XIAP set the threshold, so their loss or pharmacological mimicry sensitises cells to TNF killing, a principle exploited against tumours and disrupted in inflammatory disease.

Programmed cell death is the controlled elimination of cells that sculpts tissues during development and keeps cell numbers in check afterwards; when it fails, damaged or autoreactive cells persist and tumours and autoimmunity follow, while excess killing drives degeneration and inflammatory injury. Death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors recruit FADD, RIPK1 and caspase-8, and the fate of the cell pivots on whether caspase-8 is activated or blocked by CFLAR and IAPs. Active caspase-8 engages BID and the BCL2 family at mitochondria, releasing cytochrome c to drive APAF1–caspase-9 and the executioner caspases that cleave lamins, cytoskeletal proteins and DFFA to fragment DNA. Blocked caspase-8 instead permits RIPK3–MLKL necroptosis, while inflammasome caspases cleave gasdermin D and IL-1 family cytokines for pyroptosis.

Whether a cell exposed to TNF-alpha survives and mounts an inflammatory response or instead dies is decided at the level of TNFR1, and the checkpoints that make that decision are the substance of TNFR1 signalling regulation. The receptor recruits TRADD, RIPK1, FADD and TRAF2 into complexes whose composition is set largely by ubiquitin editing: the linear ubiquitin assembly machinery of RNF31, RBCK1 and SHARPIN, together with cIAP1/2 and XIAP, builds chains that license IKK-driven NF-kappaB activation and a pro-survival, pro-inflammatory transcriptional programme. Opposing deubiquitinases including CYLD with its partner SPATA2, A20 and OTULIN dismantle those chains and restrain signalling, while caspase-8 and its pseudo-substrate regulator CFLAR govern the switch to apoptosis, and RIPK1 cleavage sets the threshold for cell death. Loss of this balance produces chronic inflammation, autoinflammatory disease and NF-kappaB-addicted tumours.

When TNF-alpha engages TNFR1, one of the outcomes is transcriptional activation of NF-kappaB, and this arm decides whether the stimulated cell survives inflammation or dies. The receptor recruits the adaptor TRADD together with the kinase RIPK1, which is then decorated with K63-linked and, through the LUBAC components HOIP, HOIL-1 and SHARPIN, linear ubiquitin chains. These chains serve as a scaffold that docks the TAK1 kinase complex with its TAB regulatory subunits and the IKK complex of CHUK, IKBKB and NEMO, leading to IkB phosphorylation and destruction and to release of NF-kappaB, which induces inflammatory mediators and antiapoptotic proteins such as cIAP1/2, XIAP and FLIP while restraining sustained JNK activity. Deubiquitinases including A20 and CYLD reverse these chains as negative feedback; loss of that restraint gives chronic inflammation, autoimmunity and tumour-promoting signalling, while excess ubiquitin editing pushes cells toward apoptosis and necroptosis.

Hedgehog ligands are secreted morphogens that pattern the embryo, and their biogenesis is the set of processing and release steps that turn a precursor protein into an active signal. The three mammalian ligands direct limb, notochord and neural tube organization (SHH), bone and cartilage growth (IHH), and germ cell and peripheral nerve sheath development (DHH); loss of processing causes holoprosencephaly and skeletal malformation. The precursor cleaves itself, and the N-terminal fragment is modified with cholesterol and, via the acyltransferase HHAT, with palmitate. These lipids tether the ligand in membrane rafts, so long-range spread requires untethering by the transmembrane protein DISP2 with secreted SCUBE2, by shedding, or by packaging into lipoprotein particles and vesicles. Quality control is part of the picture: misfolded precursor is retrotranslocated through the SEL1L–SYVN1 machinery with VCP and degraded by the proteasome, and secreted NOTUM and glypicans tune ligand availability.

Signaling by Hedgehog is the morphogen pathway that patterns the developing embryo — limb buds, neural tube, skeleton — and later sustains stem cell compartments in adult tissues. Its loss causes congenital malformations such as holoprosencephaly and skeletal dysplasias, while inappropriate activation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. The genes trace the full circuit: ligand maturation and release by palmitoylation and SCUBE2, reception by Patched and co-receptors GAS1, CDON and BOC, and relief of Patched's inhibition of Smoothened. Output converges on the GLI transcription factors, whose fate depends on PKA and CK1 phosphorylation, SUFU sequestration, and ubiquitin-proteasome processing to repressor or degraded forms. Much of this occurs in the primary cilium, explaining the presence of intraflagellar transport, kinesin, tubulin and ciliary base components — the reason many ciliopathies present as Hedgehog patterning defects.

Hedgehog signalling converts a secreted morphogen gradient into patterned gene expression, and it is what tells cells in the limb bud, neural tube and developing skeleton which position they occupy; in adults it maintains stem and progenitor compartments. Loss of output causes birth defects such as holoprosencephaly and polydactyly, while inappropriate reactivation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Ligands SHH, IHH and DHH are lipid-modified and released, then bind the receptor PTCH1, relieving its inhibition of Smoothened. Signalling is organised at the primary cilium, so intraflagellar transport components, the anterograde kinesin motor, retrograde dynein and tubulins are integral rather than incidental. In the off state, GPR161 raises cAMP and protein kinase A, GSK3 and casein kinase 1 prime GLI proteins for processing by the ubiquitin-proteasome system into repressors; SUFU sequesters them. Activation preserves full-length GLI activators, with SPOP, ITCH and SMURF ligases tuning the response.

Synthesis of diphthamide-EEF2 builds a modified histidine found on just one protein in the cell, elongation factor 2, the GTPase that drives ribosomal translocation during translation elongation. Without this modification translation elongation loses fidelity and speed, and loss of the pathway in humans causes developmental disorders with microcephaly and short stature; the same residue is the target that diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates to shut down protein synthesis and kill the cell. Four enzymatic steps are involved: an iron-sulfur radical-SAM-like complex of DPH1, DPH2, DPH3 and DNAJC24 transfers a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to histidine 715, DPH5 methylates it, DPH7 demethylates the carboxylate to give diphthine, and DPH6 amidates that carboxyl group. The pathway thus links one-carbon metabolism and iron-sulfur cofactor biology to the accuracy of ribosomal protein synthesis.

Translation elongation depends on a single unusual amino acid: histidine 715 of eukaryotic elongation factor 2 is rebuilt into diphthamide, and no other protein in the cell carries this modification. The pathway matters because EEF2 drives GTP-dependent translocation of tRNA and mRNA through the ribosome, and because the finished diphthamide is the residue that diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates to shut down protein synthesis and kill the cell. Construction proceeds in four committed steps: a radical-SAM complex built from DPH1 and DPH2, with the small iron-sulfur protein DPH3 and its partner DNAJC24, transfers a 3-amino-3-carboxypropyl group from S-adenosylmethionine; DPH5 methylates it; DPH7 removes a methyl group to yield diphthine; and DPH6 amidates the carboxylate. Loss of these enzymes impairs translational fidelity and causes developmental disorders with craniofacial and neurological features.

Mismatch Repair corrects single-base mismatches and small insertion/deletion loops that escape the proofreading of DNA replication, and it is the main guardian of microsatellite stability. Loss of it produces the hypermutable, microsatellite-unstable tumours of Lynch syndrome, most characteristically colorectal and endometrial cancer, and also confers resistance to some thiopurine and alkylating agents. Recognition is by MutS complexes: MSH2 paired with MSH6 detects single mismatches and one- or two-base loops, while MSH2 with MSH3 handles larger loops. The activated sensor engages MLH1:PMS2 and the replication clamp PCNA, which marks the nascent strand; MLH1:PMS2 nicks it and EXO1 excises a tract around the error. RPA protects the resulting gap, DNA polymerase delta resynthesises, and LIG1 seals the nick. Expression and activity peak in S phase, tying the pathway directly to the replication fork.

Replication is accurate but not perfect, and mismatch repair is the system that removes the base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that polymerases leave behind, raising replication fidelity by orders of magnitude. Loss of it produces microsatellite instability and a hypermutator phenotype; germline defects in MSH2, MSH6, MLH1 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome with its high risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer, and MMR status now guides immunotherapy decisions. Recognition is by MutS heterodimers, MSH2:MSH6 for single mismatches and short loops and MSH2:MSH3 for larger loops, which then engage MLH1:PMS2 and the replication clamp PCNA to nick the newly made strand. EXO1 excises a tract containing the error, RPA coats the gap, polymerase delta resynthesizes and LIG1 seals the nick, tying the repair directly to S-phase replication.

Replication inevitably leaves behind mispaired bases and small insertion-deletion loops, and this branch of post-replicative mismatch repair is the route by which single base mismatches and one- to two-nucleotide loops are found and corrected. Its loss raises the spontaneous mutation rate genome-wide, destabilises microsatellites, and underlies Lynch syndrome and a large fraction of sporadic mismatch-repair-deficient tumours, which is also why such tumours respond to immune checkpoint blockade. Recognition falls to the MSH2:MSH6 heterodimer, with MSH6 contacting the mismatch; ADP-to-ATP exchange licenses sliding along DNA and recruitment of downstream partners. PCNA marks the newly synthesised strand, the MLH1:PMS2 endonuclease nicks it, EXO1 resects a gap of hundreds of nucleotides that RPA protects, and DNA polymerase delta resynthesises before ligase I seals the product. Abundance of this complex relative to the MSH2:MSH3 form shapes overall repair specificity.

Replication slippage at repetitive sequences leaves small insertion-deletion loops in the new strand, and the MSH2:MSH3 heterodimer known as MutS-beta is the sensor that finds them, recognising unpaired loops of two or more nucleotides rather than single base-base mismatches. Repair of these lesions keeps microsatellites stable; losing it produces the microsatellite instability and mutator phenotype characteristic of Lynch syndrome and many sporadic colorectal and endometrial tumours. Lesion binding triggers ADP-for-ATP exchange and a sliding clamp conformation that engages PCNA, the MLH1:PMS2 endonuclease and EXO1. PCNA marks the nascent strand for excision, MLH1:PMS2 nicks it, EXO1 widens the nick into a gap of hundreds of nucleotides protected by RPA, and DNA polymerase delta resynthesises the strand before LIG1 seals the remaining nick. Because MutS-beta is far less abundant than MSH2:MSH6, shifts in their ratio alter repair fidelity.

CTNNB1 S33 mutants aren't phosphorylated describes how cancer-associated substitutions at serine 33 of beta-catenin escape the destruction signal that normally limits WNT signalling. Serine 33 is one of the GSK3-beta target residues in the beta-catenin N-terminal degron; when it is mutated, the protein cannot be marked for ubiquitin-dependent turnover, so it accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives constitutive transcription of WNT target genes such as MYC and CCND1, promoting proliferation. The machinery involved is the axin-APC destruction complex, including AXIN1, AMER1, casein kinase 1 alpha, GSK3-beta and PP2A subunits that tune the phosphorylation state of the complex. Loss of this control point underlies tumours of the liver, endometrium, stomach and central nervous system, and makes this pathway a paradigm for oncogenic stabilisation of a transcriptional coactivator by degron mutation.

Beta-catenin levels are normally held down by a destruction complex that marks the protein for degradation, and mutation of serine 33 removes one of the phosphate acceptor sites that makes this possible. Because GSK3B cannot phosphorylate the altered residue, beta-catenin escapes recognition by its ubiquitin ligase, accumulates, and moves into the nucleus where it partners with TCF/LEF factors to drive a constitutive WNT transcriptional programme of proliferation and stem-like gene expression. The machinery that fails here is the scaffolded complex of APC, AXIN1 and AMER1 together with casein kinase 1 and protein phosphatase 2A subunits that tune its activity. Such stabilizing substitutions are recurrent driver events in hepatocellular carcinoma, medulloblastoma and other central nervous system tumours, endometrial and gastric cancers, illustrating how loss of a single phosphodegron site converts a regulated signal into an oncogenic one.

Beta-catenin levels are normally held low by a destruction complex that marks the protein for ubiquitin-dependent degradation, and serine 37 is one of the residues that must be phosphorylated for that to happen. When CTNNB1 carries a mutation at S37, GSK3 can no longer modify the site, the protein escapes recognition by its ubiquitin ligase, and stabilized beta-catenin accumulates and enters the nucleus to drive constitutive WNT target gene transcription. The scaffold that performs the doomed phosphorylation is represented here in full: APC and AXIN1 with the AMER1 adaptor, casein kinase 1 alpha priming the site cluster, GSK3B extending it, and multiple PP2A catalytic, scaffolding and B56 regulatory subunits tuning the output. Such mutations are recurrent oncogenic events in colorectal, hepatic, ovarian and brain tumours, where they lock cells into a proliferative WNT-driven state independent of ligand.

Beta-catenin levels are normally held low by a destruction complex that marks it for degradation, and cancer-associated mutations at serine 45 of CTNNB1 escape this control. Serine 45 is the site phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 alpha, and that mark primes GSK3-beta to phosphorylate threonine 41 and then serines 37 and 33, creating the phosphodegron recognised by the ubiquitin ligase machinery. Mutation of the priming residue blocks the whole cascade, so beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives constitutive Wnt target gene transcription regardless of ligand. The scaffolds APC, AXIN1 and AMER1 assemble the kinases with PP2A subunits that tune the reaction. Such substitutions are recurrent in colorectal and hepatocellular carcinoma, soft tissue tumours and Wilms tumour, and illustrate how loss of a single phosphorylation step converts a regulated developmental signal into an oncogenic driver.

Beta-catenin levels are normally held low by a destruction complex that marks the protein for degradation, and mutation of threonine 41 removes one of the phosphosites that makes this possible. Because T41 is a GSK3 target within the N-terminal degron, the mutant escapes sequential priming by casein kinase 1 alpha and GSK3B, avoids recognition by the ubiquitin ligase machinery, and accumulates in the nucleus, where it partners with TCF/LEF factors to drive constitutive transcription of Wnt targets such as MYC and CCND1. The scaffolds and regulators involved — APC, AXIN1, AMER1 and the PP2A holoenzyme subunits — assemble and tune the complex that the mutant defeats. This is a ligand-independent, oncogenic activation of Wnt signalling, found in hepatocellular carcinoma, medulloblastoma and tumours of the pituitary, endometrium, colon and skin, and it illustrates how loss of a single phosphorylation site converts a signalling intermediate into a driver.

Vitamin A is useless to a cell until it is converted into an active retinoid, and this pathway covers that conversion and the transcriptional response it drives. Retinol is oxidised to retinal by alcohol and retinol dehydrogenases, then irreversibly oxidised to retinoic acid by the ALDH1A enzymes; cytoplasmic binding proteins such as CRABP2 and FABP5 chaperone the ligand to nuclear receptors, where RAR-RXR heterodimers switch on target genes governing embryonic patterning, growth, neurogenesis, epithelial differentiation and immune function. Signal duration is set by catabolism, with the CYP26 enzymes hydroxylating retinoic acid to oxidised metabolites destined for conjugation, and DHRS3 returning retinal to retinol. Retinoid tone also intersects with fuel metabolism through PPARD and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex and its kinases. Excess or deficiency of this signalling is teratogenic, and the same receptors are pharmacological targets in acute promyelocytic leukaemia and skin disease.

Sonic hedgehog is made as a precursor that must cleave itself and acquire lipid modifications before it can be secreted as the active signalling ligand that patterns the neural tube, limbs and craniofacial midline. Mutant SHH proteins that fail this autocatalytic processing never fold correctly, and instead of being exported they are recognised in the endoplasmic reticulum and destroyed, so no functional ligand reaches receiving cells — a route to holoprosencephaly and related midline brain and face malformations. Disposal follows the standard ER-associated degradation route: lectin-like sensors such as OS9 and ERLEC1 detect the misfolded glycoprotein and deliver it to the SEL1L–SYVN1 ubiquitin ligase complex with the DERL2 membrane channel, VCP extracts the ubiquitinated substrate into the cytosol, and the 26S proteasome degrades it. Quality control here acts as a gatekeeper on morphogen availability during development.

Hedgehog ligands are lipid-modified at both ends, which glues them to the membrane of the cell that made them; getting them off that membrane is what converts a short-range, contact-dependent cue into a morphogen that can pattern tissue at a distance. Release of Hh-Np from the secreting cell governs how far Sonic, Indian and Desert Hedgehog travel, and therefore neural tube patterning, limb bud outgrowth, skeletal growth plate control and gonadal development. Cholesterol and palmitate anchor the processed ligand in sterol-rich membrane domains where glypicans such as GPC5 stabilise it and promote lateral spread. Dispersal then depends on dedicated carriers, including the transporter-like DISP2 and the secreted adaptor SCUBE2, and on proteolysis: NOTUM acts on glypican anchoring, while the metalloprotease ADAM17 sheds the lipidated termini. Failure of ligand release blunts gradient formation and the developmental fields that depend on it.

All-trans-retinoic acid is the hormone form of vitamin A, and this route is how cells make it from stored or circulating retinol. The product is a ligand for nuclear retinoic acid receptors, so the flux through these enzymes sets the transcriptional dose of retinoid signalling that patterns the embryonic body axis, limbs and hindbrain, maintains epithelial differentiation and spermatogenesis, and drives myeloid maturation. Conversion is two-step: short-chain dehydrogenases/reductases such as RDH10 and DHRS9 oxidise retinol to retinaldehyde, a reversible step opposed by reductases including DHRS3, and then the aldehyde dehydrogenases ALDH1A1, ALDH1A2 and ALDH1A3 commit it irreversibly to retinoic acid, with alcohol dehydrogenases contributing. Binding proteins hold and deliver the retinoid, while CYP26 enzymes degrade it, so synthesis and catabolism together create the concentration gradients that direct development.

Mitochondria make their own thirteen proteins, all of them subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, and translation initiation is the step that sets each of those messages in frame on the mitochondrial ribosome. Because mitochondrial mRNAs carry essentially no untranslated leader and no Shine-Dalgarno-like element, start codon selection depends on the small 28S subunit together with MTIF3 and GTP-bound MTIF2, which position a formylmethionyl-tRNA generated by the formyltransferase MTFMT; the large 39S subunit then joins and the factors are released on GTP hydrolysis. The ribosome works at the matrix face of the inner membrane, with the insertase OXA1L threading nascent hydrophobic products into the bilayer as they emerge. Defects in the small and large subunit proteins, in MTFMT, or in the initiation factors cause combined respiratory chain deficiency, presenting as infantile encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy or Leigh syndrome.

Mitochondrial translation is the organelle's own protein synthesis system, which makes just thirteen proteins — all hydrophobic core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase — yet without it oxidative phosphorylation cannot be assembled and cells lose aerobic energy production. Everything else, including the ribosome itself, is nuclear-encoded and imported. Mitoribosomes are protein-rich 55S particles built from small and large subunit proteins around short mitochondrial rRNAs, and they work at the matrix face of the inner membrane, where OXA1L co-translationally inserts nascent chains into the bilayer. Initiation uses formylated methionyl-tRNA and dedicated factors, elongation cycles through TUFM, TSFM and GFM1, and termination and recycling require MTRF1L, MRRF and GFM2, with separate rescue factors clearing stalled or non-stop complexes. Mutations in ribosomal proteins, translation factors and the mitochondrial tRNAs cause encephalomyopathies, cardiomyopathy and other mitochondrial diseases.

Only thirteen human proteins are made inside mitochondria, and all of them are hydrophobic subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation complexes, so mitochondrial translation sets the ceiling on a cell's capacity for respiration and ATP synthesis. The machinery is bacterial in ancestry but heavily remodelled: a protein-rich 55S mitoribosome built from small and large subunit proteins around short rRNAs, the full set of mitochondrially encoded tRNAs, and dedicated factors for each step. Initiation requires formylation of methionyl-tRNA and the factors MTIF2 and MTIF3, elongation cycles through TUFM with GTP regenerated by TSFM and translocation by GFM1, and termination and recycling use MTRF1L with MRRF and GFM2. Nascent chains are inserted co-translationally into the inner membrane via OXA1L, and quality-control factors clear stalled peptidyl-tRNAs. Mutations in ribosomal proteins, tRNAs or translation factors cause mitochondrial disease with encephalopathy, cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis.

Negative regulation of TCF-dependent signaling by DVL-interacting proteins is a brake on canonical WNT signalling that acts at the level of Dishevelled, the hub that relays receptor activation into stabilisation of beta-catenin and TCF/LEF-driven transcription. Restraining this step keeps proliferative and stem-cell programmes in check; unchecked beta-catenin output underlies colorectal and other cancers, while loss of the DVL-binding protein CCDC88C (Daple) causes congenital hydrocephalus, and CXXC4 (Idax) levels tune WNT responsiveness in development and tumours. Mechanistically, DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 recruit AXIN away from the destruction complex after WNT stimulation; direct binding by CXXC4 through its DIX-interacting region and by CCDC88C sequesters DVL and blocks that recruitment, so the destruction complex continues to degrade beta-catenin. This sits alongside phosphorylation and regulated degradation as ways cells set the gain of WNT signalling.

Dishevelled proteins sit at the hub of WNT reception, and one way cells set the ceiling on WNT output is by sequestering them. This branch describes negative regulation of TCF-dependent signalling by DVL-interacting proteins: CXXC4 (Idax) and CCDC88C (DAPLE) bind DVL1, DVL2 and DVL3 directly and dampen their ability to relay signal from activated receptors, so less beta-catenin escapes destruction and fewer TCF/LEF target genes are switched on. Because WNT/beta-catenin activity governs stem cell renewal, body axis patterning and tissue growth, restraint at the DVL step matters as much as activation does; loss of CCDC88C causes congenital hydrocephalus, and unchecked TCF-dependent transcription is a hallmark of colorectal tumourigenesis. DVL is also the point where canonical and planar-cell-polarity WNT branches diverge, so its interactors influence which route a WNT signal takes.

Hedgehog ligands only signal after extensive maturation: autocatalytic cleavage of the precursor, cholesterol addition to the new C-terminus, and N-terminal palmitoylation by the acyltransferase HHAT, which together yield the secreted, lipid-modified active form. When disease-associated mutations in SHH, IHH or DHH block this processing, or when HHAT is lost, ligand secretion is abrogated and the pathway falls silent in the tissues that depend on it. The consequences are developmental: SHH variants of this kind underlie holoprosencephaly with midline brain and craniofacial malformation, while failure of DHH palmitoylation causes gonadal dysgenesis. Misprocessed precursors are instead retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and cleared by ER-associated degradation, and the recognition, retrotranslocation and ubiquitin-proteasome components here carry out that disposal, coupling quality control of a secreted morphogen to its complete loss of activity.

The thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA are all core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, and this is the step that builds them: the repeating cycle by which the mitochondrial ribosome adds one amino acid at a time to a growing chain. Without it a cell cannot assemble complexes I, III, IV or V from its own genome, and mutations in the machinery cause infantile encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy and lactic acidosis. Each round begins with TUFM delivering an aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site with GTP hydrolysis, followed by peptide bond formation and GFM1-driven translocation, with TSFM acting as the nucleotide exchange factor that recharges TUFM. The small and large subunit proteins, the mitochondrial rRNAs and the tRNA together form the ribosome, which docks at the inner membrane so that hydrophobic products are inserted co-translationally with help from OXA1L.</description>

The thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA are all core subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, and each one must be released intact from the mitoribosome before it can be inserted into the inner membrane. Termination of mitochondrial translation is that release step: a release factor reads the stop codon in the A site, GTP is hydrolysed, and the large subunit's peptidyl transferase centre cleaves the finished polypeptide from its tRNA. MTRF1L handles the standard UAA and UAG stops, while the unusual AGA and AGG codons ending MT-CO1 and MT-ND6 are dealt with separately. A recycling factor together with GFM2 then strips the remaining tRNA and mRNA and splits the 55S ribosome into 28S and 39S subunits for reuse. The mitoribosomal proteins listed here provide the machine, and OXA1L receives the nascent chains; defects in these components cause infantile mitochondrial disease with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency.

DNA mismatch repair corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that escape the replicative polymerases, and when it fails the genome accumulates mutations fastest at repetitive tracts, producing the microsatellite instability that defines this class of disease. Germline defects in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2 underlie Lynch syndrome and hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, with related presentations including Muir-Torre and Turcot syndromes and childhood brain tumours; MSH3 loss contributes to endometrial cancer susceptibility. Mechanistically, MSH2 pairs with MSH6 to recognise single-base substitutions and one-base loops, or with MSH3 for larger loops, sliding along duplex DNA until a lesion is engaged; the MLH1-PMS2 heterodimer is then recruited to license strand excision and resynthesis with exonuclease, clamp-loader and single-strand binding factors. Tumours arising this way carry heavy mutational loads and are characteristically responsive to immune checkpoint blockade.

Aflatoxin B1, a mold toxin contaminating maize and groundnuts, is only dangerous after the body chemically alters it, and this pathway covers both that bioactivation and the routes that dispose of the product. Hepatic cytochrome P450s, principally CYP3A4 with contributions from CYP1A2 and CYP2A13, oxidise AFB1 to the exo-8,9-epoxide, which attacks guanine N7 to form DNA adducts and drives the signature mutations of hepatocellular carcinoma; other P450 products such as AFQ1 and AFM1 are far less genotoxic. Competing with adduct formation, aldo-keto reductases reduce the dialdehyde derived from the hydrolysed epoxide, and microsomal glutathione transferases conjugate the epoxide to glutathione. The conjugate is then trimmed by gamma-glutamyltransferases, dipeptidases and aminoacylases to a mercapturic acid for urinary excretion. The balance between activation and conjugation, which varies with genotype and diet, sets individual liver cancer risk.

Adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) normally works inside the beta-catenin destruction complex, which keeps cytoplasmic beta-catenin low when no WNT ligand is present; loss of that restraint drives the constitutive WNT signalling that initiates most colorectal tumours. Full-length APC carries a reversible K63-linked polyubiquitin modification, and this non-degradative ubiquitin mark supports assembly of the destruction complex with axin, GSK3 and CK1 so that beta-catenin can be phosphorylated and routed for proteasomal destruction. Truncating mutations of APC, the germline lesion in familial adenomatous polyposis and a common somatic event in sporadic colorectal cancer, remove the region required for this modification. The unmodified truncated protein cannot nucleate a functional complex, beta-catenin accumulates, and TCF/LEF target genes such as MYC and CCND1 are transcribed inappropriately, locking intestinal epithelial cells into a proliferative, stem-like state.

APC is the scaffold that lets the beta-catenin destruction complex work, and truncating mutations in its central mutation cluster region remove the SAMP repeats through which it binds AXIN1. Because the resulting proteins can no longer assemble APC with AXIN1, CSNK1A1, GSK3B and the PP2A subunits, beta-catenin escapes priming phosphorylation and degradation, accumulates, and drives constitutive WNT target gene transcription — the initiating lesion in familial adenomatous polyposis and the majority of sporadic colorectal cancers. AMER1 (WTX) normally helps recruit APC to the membrane and to the complex, and its loss has similar consequences. This is a disease-state counterpart to normal WNT signal termination: rather than a regulated switch responding to ligand, the pathway is locked on, coupling loss of a tumour suppressor scaffold to unchecked intestinal epithelial proliferation and adenoma formation.

When Wnt signalling is off, cytoplasmic beta-catenin is captured by a scaffolded complex and marked for degradation, keeping the pathway's transcriptional output silent. AXIN1 is the scaffold that holds that destruction complex together, bringing APC, casein kinase 1, GSK3 beta and protein phosphatase 2A subunits into proximity so beta-catenin is sequentially phosphorylated and routed to the proteasome. Missense changes in AXIN1 that damage its protein-protein interaction surfaces prevent assembly of a functional complex, so beta-catenin escapes turnover, accumulates, and drives constitutive Wnt target gene expression. This is a recurrent oncogenic route in hepatocellular carcinoma, colorectal cancer and medulloblastoma, and it illustrates how loss of a scaffold rather than of a catalytic enzyme is enough to release growth control. The associated APC-binding partner AMER1 is likewise mutated in Wnt-driven tumours.

Loss of AMER1 (WTX) removes a scaffolding component from the beta-catenin destruction complex, and the result is constitutive Wnt pathway output. Whole-gene deletions of AMER1 are found in roughly 12% of Wilms tumors, the commonest pediatric kidney cancer, alongside nonsense and missense lesions, which marks the gene as a tumor suppressor whose failure drives inappropriate nephrogenic progenitor proliferation. Normally AMER1 binds beta-catenin directly through its C-terminal half and helps assemble the axin-APC-GSK3 complex at the membrane, promoting phosphorylation and proteasomal turnover of cytoplasmic beta-catenin. When AMER1 is depleted, beta-catenin accumulates and beta-catenin/TCF target transcription rises, as seen with reporter assays after siRNA knockdown. This places AMER1 deletion among the several ways that Wnt signalling escapes negative regulation in cancer, the same endpoint reached by APC or CTNNB1 mutation.

Beta-catenin is normally kept at low levels by a cytoplasmic destruction complex in which AXIN1 acts as the scaffold, bringing together APC, GSK3 and CK1 so that beta-catenin is phosphorylated, ubiquitinated and degraded. Deletions removing the N-terminal exons of AXIN1 compromise its expression and leave the complex unable to assemble, so beta-catenin escapes turnover, enters the nucleus and drives TCF/LEF-dependent transcription of growth-promoting targets such as MYC and cyclin D1. Loss of this scaffold therefore produces constitutive WNT signalling in the absence of ligand, and such deletions were found in hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines, where elevated TCF reporter activity reflects the unrestrained pathway. AXIN1 behaves as a tumour suppressor in this setting, placing it alongside APC mutation and stabilising beta-catenin mutations as routes to aberrant WNT activation in liver and colorectal cancer.

Truncations of AMER1 destabilize the destruction complex describes how loss-of-function mutations in a scaffold of the beta-catenin destruction complex switch on Wnt signalling inappropriately. AMER1/WTX normally binds beta-catenin directly through its C-terminal half and helps assemble the complex with APC, AXIN1, CSNK1A1, GSK3B and PP2A subunits, which together phosphorylate beta-catenin and mark it for ubiquitin-dependent degradation. Nonsense and frameshift mutations that remove the beta-catenin-binding region leave a protein that can no longer support this turnover, so beta-catenin accumulates, enters the nucleus and drives TCF/LEF target gene transcription. Depleting AMER1 has the same effect, identifying it as a tumour suppressor. The clinical consequence is Wilms tumour, a paediatric kidney cancer in which AMER1 truncations are recurrent, placing this biology within Wnt-driven control of nephron progenitor proliferation and differentiation.

Beta-catenin is kept low in unstimulated cells by a cytoplasmic destruction complex built on APC and AXIN1, in which casein kinase 1 and GSK3B phosphorylate beta-catenin to mark it for ubiquitin-mediated degradation, with PP2A subunits acting as regulatory counterweights. AMER1/WTX is a membrane- and complex-associated scaffold that binds beta-catenin through its C-terminal half and helps hold this assembly together. Truncating nonsense and frameshift mutations remove that beta-catenin-binding region, destabilizing the destruction complex so that beta-catenin escapes turnover, enters the nucleus and drives TCF/LEF target gene expression. This is a loss of tumour suppressor function: AMER1 truncations recur in Wilms tumour, a paediatric kidney cancer, and illustrate how constitutive Wnt pathway output arises from scaffold failure rather than ligand stimulation.

Many drugs, neurotransmitters and metabolites carry a positive charge at physiological pH and cannot cross membranes unaided; transport of organic cations by SLC carriers moves them into and out of cells and so sets much of hepatic and renal drug handling. The SLC22 organic cation transporters OCT1-3 work electrogenically, without sodium coupling, and bidirectionally, taking up substrates such as metformin, cisplatin and cationic neurotoxins at the sinusoidal and basolateral surfaces of liver and kidney. Related SLC22 members handle more specific cargo: one imports carnitine for mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, another the antioxidant ergothioneine, and variants in these are linked to inflammatory bowel disease and systemic carnitine deficiency. Efflux across the apical membrane into urine and bile is completed by the MATE proteins SLC47A1 and SLC47A2, making this route a determinant of drug clearance and drug-drug interactions. Urea channels are also represented here.

DNA mismatch repair corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops that escape replicative polymerase proofreading, and MLH1 is the obligate partner in the heterodimer that licenses this correction. Together with PMS2 it forms the MutL-homologous complex that is recruited to mismatches recognised by the MutS-like sensors, coordinating strand discrimination, excision and resynthesis through its latent endonuclease activity and its coupling to PCNA and the replication machinery. Loss of MLH1 function destabilises PMS2 and abolishes repair, producing microsatellite instability and a hypermutator phenotype with characteristic frameshifts in repetitive coding sequences. Germline heterozygous mutation underlies hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, or Lynch syndrome, predisposing to colorectal, endometrial and other epithelial tumours; somatic promoter hypermethylation silences MLH1 in sporadic mismatch repair-deficient cancers. Such tumours accumulate neoantigens and are characteristically responsive to immune checkpoint blockade.

XAV939 stabilizes AXIN describes the pharmacological brake that can be applied to Wnt/beta-catenin signalling by protecting the pathway's rate-limiting scaffold from destruction. AXIN1 and AXIN2 assemble the beta-catenin destruction complex with GSK3beta and APC, and their abundance sets how much beta-catenin escapes phosphorylation and degradation to drive transcription; because tumours with APC or beta-catenin lesions depend on that escape, restoring AXIN levels is an attractive way to shut down constitutive Wnt output in colorectal cancer. The poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases tankyrase 1 and 2 normally PARsylate AXIN, marking it for ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover. XAV939 occupies their catalytic sites, so AXIN protein accumulates without any change in transcript levels, GSK3beta-AXIN complexes increase, beta-catenin is phosphorylated and cleared, and beta-catenin-dependent proliferation is suppressed.

AXIN proteins are the limiting scaffold of the destruction complex that phosphorylates beta-catenin and keeps Wnt target genes off, and their abundance is set by poly-ADP-ribosylation. The two tankyrases, TNKS and TNKS2, modify AXIN1 and AXIN2, marking them for ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation and thereby raising the threshold for Wnt signalling. Blocking the tankyrase catalytic site with the small molecule XAV939 stabilizes AXIN without changing its transcription, restores GSK3beta-AXIN complexes, increases beta-catenin phosphorylation and lowers beta-catenin-dependent transcription. This is the rationale for targeting tankyrase in colorectal cancers driven by APC loss, where the pathway is constitutively active; growth of such cells is suppressed in culture. The biology illustrates how a post-translational modification controls the stability of a scaffold and so the output of a developmental signalling route.

Lipid metabolism covers the synthesis, breakdown, transport and interconversion of the hydrophobic molecules that store energy, build membranes and carry signals. It supplies ATP through fatty acid beta-oxidation and ketone bodies, provides cholesterol and phospholipids for bilayers, makes bile acids that solubilize dietary fat, and generates steroid hormones, eicosanoids, phosphoinositides and sphingolipids used as messengers. The genes here span the enzymatic routes — fatty acid synthase and elongases, the mevalonate pathway to cholesterol, mitochondrial and peroxisomal oxidation, serine palmitoyltransferase and ceramide synthases, phospholipases and phosphoinositide kinases and phosphatases, cytochrome P450s and hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases — together with the transcriptional control that tunes them, including SREBP processing, PPAR–RXR and liver X receptor signalling, and lipid droplet and transfer proteins. Defects cause lysosomal lipid storage diseases, peroxisomal disorders, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis, and underpin insulin resistance and fatty liver.

Between beats, a cardiac myocyte sits at a stable negative voltage of roughly -85 to -95 mV, and the resting membrane potential of phase 4 is what holds it there. This quiescent baseline sets excitability: it keeps sodium channels available for the next upstroke, prevents spontaneous firing in working myocardium, and makes the diastolic interval possible. The potential is set almost entirely by potassium, because the membrane is far more permeable to K+ than to other ions, so the transmembrane K+ gradient dictates the voltage. Inward rectifier channels such as KCNJ2 conduct strongly near rest and clamp the potential close to the potassium equilibrium, while two-pore domain leak channels of the KCNK family provide background K+ conductance that is modulated by pH, stretch and anaesthetics. Loss-of-function in the inward rectifiers destabilises repolarisation and causes inherited arrhythmia syndromes with conduction and rhythm disturbance.

Rapid repolarisation is the phase of the cardiac action potential in which potassium efflux returns the myocyte membrane to its resting negative potential, ending the plateau and setting the duration of the ventricular refractory period. Its timing determines the QT interval, and both loss- and gain-of-function changes in the channels involved cause long and short QT syndromes with risk of torsades de pointes and sudden death. The current is carried by voltage-gated potassium channels: KCNQ1 underlies the slow delayed rectifier, KCNH2 the rapid delayed rectifier, and KCNA5 an ultra-rapid component largely confined to atrial myocytes and relevant to atrial fibrillation. Small single-span KCNE subunits assemble with these pores to shift their gating kinetics and voltage dependence, while the scaffold AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to KCNQ1 so that repolarisation can be tuned by adrenergic input during increased heart rate.

Cardiac conduction is the ordered electrical activation of atria and ventricles that sets heart rate, rhythm, and the timing of contraction, and its failure produces long QT and Brugada syndromes, atrial fibrillation, conduction block, and sudden arrhythmic death. The cardiac action potential is built by sequential ion fluxes: voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits and FGF-homologous factor modulators drive rapid depolarisation; L-type calcium channels sustain the plateau; and delayed rectifier and transient outward potassium channels, including KCNQ1/KCNE1 and KCNH2 with KCNIP-regulated Kv4 currents, restore the resting potential set by inward rectifiers and Na+/K+-ATPase. Coupled to this are the calcium handling proteins of excitation-contraction coupling -- ryanodine receptors, SERCA with phospholamban, calsequestrin, and sodium-calcium exchange -- plus CaMKII and PKA arms that adapt beat-to-beat behaviour to autonomic tone, and transcription factors such as NKX2-5 and TBX5 that specify the conduction system.

Each heartbeat begins as an electrical event, and cardiac conduction is the ordered generation and spread of the action potential that makes atria and ventricles contract in sequence and lets rate adjust to autonomic tone. Voltage-gated sodium channels such as SCN5A with their beta subunits drive rapid depolarisation; L-type calcium channels sustain the plateau that supports contraction; delayed rectifier and transient outward potassium channels, including KCNQ1 with KCNE1 and KCNH2, restore the resting potential set largely by inward rectifiers and the sodium pump. Calcium handling by ryanodine receptors, SERCA pumps regulated by phospholamban, and sodium-calcium exchangers couples excitation to mechanical output, while calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA tune the response. Transcription factors including NKX2-5 and TBX5 specify the conduction system itself. Mutations in these channels underlie long QT and Brugada syndromes, conduction block, and sudden arrhythmic death.
