The upstroke of the cardiac action potential, phase 0 rapid depolarisation, is the instant in which an excitable cell commits to firing: membrane potential swings from roughly -90 mV to positive values within milliseconds, setting conduction velocity through the myocardium and, in turn, the coordination of each heartbeat. Voltage-gated sodium channels open first and carry the large inward current, with SCN5A dominant in working myocardium and its beta subunits plus modulators such as fibroblast growth factor homologous factors and RANGRF tuning gating and channel trafficking. L-type calcium channels built from CACNA1C with auxiliary alpha2delta, beta and gamma subunits then admit Ca2+, linking excitation to contraction, while calmodulin and CaMKII isoforms provide calcium-dependent feedback onto both channel families. Loss- or gain-of-function mutations in these channels underlie Brugada syndrome, conduction block, long QT syndrome and inherited pain and epilepsy disorders.

Phase 2 - plateau phase is the long depolarized shoulder of the cardiac action potential, the interval that keeps ventricular myocytes contracting and sets the refractory period that protects the heart from re-excitation. It is held by a near balance between inward Ca2+ current through L-type channels and outward K+ current through the slow delayed rectifier. The L-type channel is a multi-subunit complex in which the CACNA1C pore is tuned by beta, alpha2delta and gamma subunits; the Ca2+ that enters triggers sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ release and excitation-contraction coupling. On the repolarizing side, KCNQ1 requires KCNE accessory subunits to generate slow kinetics, and is anchored with kinase signaling by the scaffold AKAP9. Loss or gain of function in these channels lengthens or shortens the plateau, producing long QT and short QT syndromes and arrhythmic risk.

The long plateau that distinguishes cardiac from nerve action potentials comes from a near-balance between inward and outward current, and this phase 2 biology is what keeps ventricular myocytes depolarized long enough for calcium-induced calcium release to drive a full contraction and for the refractory period to prevent re-excitation. Depolarization is sustained by Ca2+ entry through L-type channels built around the CACNA1C pore-forming subunit with beta, alpha2delta and gamma accessory subunits that tune trafficking and gating, and it is opposed by the slow delayed rectifier carried by KCNQ1 in partnership with KCNE subunits that convert the channel's kinetics to the slow, non-inactivating current needed here. The scaffold AKAP9 anchors kinase signalling to KCNQ1 so that adrenergic stimulation shortens the plateau as heart rate rises. Mutations in these subunits underlie congenital long QT syndromes and arrhythmic sudden death.

Phase 1 - inactivation of fast Na+ channels is the brief early repolarization that follows the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, producing the characteristic notch before the plateau. It sets the height and duration of the plateau and thereby the timing of calcium entry and contraction; loss or excess of this current reshapes repolarization and predisposes to arrhythmias such as Brugada syndrome and to the electrical remodelling seen in heart failure. Once fast sodium channels inactivate, a transient net outward current dominated by potassium efflux briefly drives the membrane back toward negative potentials. The Kv4 family channels carry this fast transient outward current, and their kinetics, surface expression and recovery from inactivation are tuned by calcium-sensing KChIP accessory subunits, which also underlie the gradient of notch amplitude across the ventricular wall.

Immediately after the upstroke of the cardiac action potential, fast sodium channels inactivate and a brief net outward current produces the notch of early repolarization, known as phase 1. This transient outward current, carried largely by potassium with a chloride contribution, sets the height and duration of the plateau that follows and therefore shapes calcium entry and contractile force; its remodelling in hypertrophy and heart failure prolongs repolarization and predisposes to arrhythmia. The channels responsible here are the Kv4 family pore-forming subunits KCND1, KCND2 and KCND3, which open and inactivate rapidly at depolarized potentials. Their kinetics, trafficking and surface density are governed by the calcium-binding KChIP accessory proteins KCNIP1-4, whose association slows inactivation and speeds recovery. In pacemaker cells the equivalent phase reflects rapid potassium efflux together with closure of L-type calcium channels.

Small RNAs are best known for silencing messenger RNAs in the cytoplasm, but the same machinery also works in the nucleus, where it can switch target genes on or off at the level of transcription itself. Argonaute proteins loaded with microRNAs are carried across the nuclear envelope by importin-8 and by RAN-dependent import of the shuttling scaffold TNRC6A, then engage chromatin and RNA polymerase II at loci whose sequences match the guide RNA. The outcome depends on the chromatin marks recruited: DNA cytosine methylation with histone H3 lysine-9 and lysine-27 methylation accompany transcriptional gene silencing, whereas H3 lysine-4 methylation accompanies RNA activation, which is why core histones and the full polymerase II complex accompany the Argonautes here. Nuclear small RNAs have additionally been linked to alternative splicing choices and to the response to DNA double-strand breaks, extending guide-RNA specificity into genome maintenance.

Natriuretic peptide signalling is the heart's own endocrine brake on blood pressure and volume, and this grouping covers the physiological factors that set how much of that hormone is made and received. Atrial and C-type natriuretic peptides are synthesised as precursors, cleaved to active form by the transmembrane protease corin, and cleared or degraded by neprilysin, the target of heart-failure drugs that spare the peptide. Their guanylyl cyclase receptors NPR1 and NPR2 raise cGMP to drive natriuresis, vasodilation and, for CNP, endochondral bone growth. Transcriptional control links the pathway to cardiac identity: GATA4, NKX2-5 and TBX5 act combinatorially on the NPPA promoter with coactivators and HIPK kinases, so the same factors that pattern the developing heart also tune its hormonal output during hypertrophy and pressure overload.

Ion homeostasis covers the pumps, exchangers and channels that set intracellular ion gradients in excitable cells, with the cardiac myocyte as the central case. Each heartbeat requires calcium to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, bind troponin, and then be cleared again within a fraction of a second, while sodium and potassium gradients are restored so the cell can repolarise and fire again. Ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors provide release, SERCA pumps with their regulators phospholamban and sarcolipin provide reuptake, calsequestrin and triadin buffer and gate the store, and the sodium-potassium ATPase together with sodium-calcium exchange and plasma membrane calcium pumps handles trans-sarcolemmal balance. Calmodulin, CaMKII and PKA tune these fluxes to sympathetic drive. Store-operated entry via STIM1 and ORAI refills depleted stores. Mutations here cause catecholaminergic arrhythmia, malignant hyperthermia and cardiomyopathy.

Cardiac muscle contracts and relaxes on a beat-to-beat cycle, and that requires the ion gradients underlying the action potential and the calcium transient to be restored after every excitation — the substance of ion homeostasis in cardiac conduction. Sodium/potassium ATPase subunits with their FXYD regulators maintain the transmembrane sodium and potassium gradients that set resting potential, while sodium/calcium exchangers, plasma membrane calcium pumps and the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPases clear cytosolic calcium after release through ryanodine receptors and inositol trisphosphate receptors. Calsequestrin, triadin and junctin organise the release complex; phospholamban and sarcolipin restrain SERCA until phosphorylation by protein kinase A or calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase II relieves them, and STIM–ORAI components refill stores. ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits couple metabolic state to excitability. Disruption produces arrhythmia, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, and impaired relaxation in heart failure.

Defective TPMT causes TPMT deficiency describes what happens to thiopurine drug handling when the enzyme that inactivates these drugs is lost. Thiopurines such as 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine are mainstays of treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia, inflammatory bowel disease and autoimmune conditions, and their safety depends on S-methylation by thiopurine methyltransferase, a cytosolic SAM-dependent methyltransferase that diverts drug away from conversion into cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides. Inherited variants that reduce or abolish TPMT activity shift metabolism toward those nucleotides, so a standard dose becomes an overdose and patients suffer profound myelosuppression. The trait is co-dominant: roughly one person in 300 has negligible activity and several percent are intermediate metabolisers, making TPMT genotyping one of the earliest and most widely adopted examples of pre-emptive pharmacogenetic dose adjustment in clinical practice.

Thiopurine drugs such as 6-mercaptopurine and azathioprine, used against childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and in immunosuppression for inflammatory disease, are inactivated largely by S-methylation. The enzyme responsible, thiopurine methyltransferase, transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to the thiol sulfur, diverting the drug away from conversion into cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides. Loss-of-function variants produce TPMT deficiency, in which methylation capacity is reduced or absent and standard doses drive excessive accumulation of active metabolites in haematopoietic cells, causing severe myelosuppression. The trait is co-dominant: heterozygotes with intermediate activity need reduced doses, while rare homozygotes tolerate only a small fraction of the usual amount. This makes the pathway one of the clearest examples of pharmacogenetic variation guiding dose selection, and genotyping or enzyme assay before thiopurine treatment is standard practice.

Bile acid synthesis depends on oxidation of the cholesterol side chain, and the mitochondrial sterol 27-hydroxylase encoded by CYP27A1 performs that first oxidation step on cholestanetriol and related sterol intermediates. When the enzyme is defective, chenodeoxycholic acid production falls, feedback restraint on the pathway is lost, and unoxidised intermediates such as cholestanol accumulate in tissues. The resulting disease, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, is a rare inherited sterol storage disorder in which deposits form in tendons, lens and brain, producing juvenile cataracts, tendon xanthomas, premature atherosclerosis and slowly progressive neurological deterioration with ataxia and cognitive decline. Because the block is enzymatic and upstream products drive the damage, replacing the missing bile acid can suppress accumulation, which makes this one of the treatable inborn errors of cholesterol catabolism and links mitochondrial sterol hydroxylation directly to neurological health.

S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase is the only route in human cells for disposing of S-adenosylhomocysteine, the product left behind by every S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferase and a potent feedback inhibitor of those same enzymes. By hydrolysing it to homocysteine and adenosine, the cytosolic NAD+-bound tetramer keeps the methylation potential high and links the methionine cycle to homocysteine remethylation and transsulfuration. Loss-of-function mutations in AHCY block this step, so S-adenosylhomocysteine and methionine accumulate and transmethylation of DNA, proteins, phospholipids and creatine synthesis is throttled. The resulting disorder, hypermethioninemia with S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase deficiency, presents in infancy with failure to thrive, hypotonia and psychomotor delay, myopathy and cardiomyopathy, abnormal hair and teeth, and raised creatine kinase and liver enzymes, reflecting how broadly methyl-group transfer supports development.

Glutathione is made and broken down through the gamma-glutamyl cycle, and one step of that cycle converts 5-oxo-L-proline back to L-glutamate so the amino acid can re-enter synthesis. The ATP-dependent cytosolic homodimer 5-oxoprolinase catalyses this ring-opening reaction; when the enzyme is defective, 5-oxoproline accumulates and spills into urine, producing 5-oxoprolinase deficiency. The condition is extremely rare, and whether it amounts to a disease at all remains debated: reported individuals show persistent 5-oxoprolinuria with variable and often absent clinical findings, in contrast to the metabolic acidosis seen with glutathione synthetase defects. The pathway matters mainly as an interpretive anchor for organic acid screening, distinguishing an inherited enzymatic block from acquired causes of 5-oxoprolinuria such as acetaminophen exposure, and as a window on how glutamate is recycled during glutathione turnover.

Glutathione is the cell's main thiol buffer, and the rate-limiting step in making it is the ligation of glutamate to cysteine by glutamate-cysteine ligase, a heterodimer of the catalytic subunit GCLC and the regulatory subunit GCLM. Loss-of-function variants in the catalytic subunit impair this first committed step of the gamma-glutamyl cycle and cause hemolytic anemia due to gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase deficiency, in which erythrocytes deprived of glutathione are especially vulnerable to oxidant stress. Affected individuals show hemolysis together with generalized glutathione depletion, myopathy, late-onset spinocerebellar degeneration and peripheral neuropathy, illustrating how dependent long-lived neurons and muscle are on thiol-based antioxidant defence. The regulatory subunit lowers the enzyme's Km for glutamate and relieves feedback inhibition by glutathione, tying flux to redox demand and to stress-responsive transcription of both subunits.

Loss-of-function mutations in cytochrome P450 1B1 underlie inherited glaucoma, and this is the biology that connects a drug- and steroid-metabolising enzyme to eye development. CYP1B1 is a monooxygenase that oxidises structurally diverse substrates including steroids, fatty acids and xenobiotics, and bioactivates some procarcinogens; among its characteristic reactions is 4-hydroxylation of estradiol-17beta. In the anterior eye the enzyme is needed for normal formation of the trabecular meshwork and aqueous humour outflow structures, plausibly through the oxidised metabolites it generates as local signals. When activity is defective, outflow is impaired and intraocular pressure rises, producing primary congenital glaucoma, some primary open-angle glaucoma, and Peters anomaly. The consequence is a progressive optic neuropathy with visual field loss that becomes irreversible blindness, making this enzyme defect a developmental as well as a metabolic disorder.

Defective UGT1A1 causes hyperbilirubinemia describes what happens when the liver cannot glucuronidate bilirubin, the yellow end product of heme catabolism. UGT1A1 is the sole enzyme that attaches glucuronic acid to lipophilic unconjugated bilirubin, converting it into a water-soluble form that can be excreted in bile; without this step bilirubin accumulates in blood and, at high concentrations, crosses into the brain to cause kernicterus. Loss-of-function and promoter variants produce a graded spectrum of disease, from the benign, common Gilbert syndrome and transient neonatal jaundice through Crigler-Najjar type 2 to the type 1 form, which requires phototherapy or liver transplantation. Because the same enzyme conjugates drugs and other lipophilic xenobiotics, reduced activity also alters clearance of compounds such as irinotecan's active metabolite, linking bilirubin handling to pharmacogenetic toxicity risk.

Bilirubin, the lipophilic end product of heme catabolism, must be made water-soluble before the liver can excrete it into bile, and UGT1A1 is the only enzyme that performs this step. It transfers glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid onto bilirubin in the hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum, converting it to mono- and diglucuronides that enter bile; the same enzyme conjugates various drugs and other lipophilic compounds as part of phase II xenobiotic clearance. When UGT1A1 activity is reduced or absent, unconjugated bilirubin accumulates in blood and tissues. The consequences scale with the severity of the defect, from the benign intermittent jaundice of Gilbert syndrome and transient neonatal hyperbilirubinemia through Crigler-Najjar type 2 to type 1, where near-total loss of conjugation causes kernicterus and neurological damage unless bilirubin is removed by phototherapy or transplantation.

Retinoic acid is the active derivative of vitamin A and a potent regulator of cell growth, patterning and differentiation, so the amount of it in a tissue must be limited as precisely as it is made. CYP26C1 is one of the cytochrome P450 enzymes that terminate retinoid signalling by 4-hydroxylating retinoic acid, and it is distinctive in acting on the 9-cis isomer as well as the all-trans form, funnelling both toward inactive polar metabolites. When the enzyme is defective, retinoic acid clearance in the developing face fails and signalling persists where it should decline, producing focal facial dermal dysplasia type 4, a rare congenital condition marked by symmetrical scar-like facial skin lesions. The pathway therefore sits on the catabolic side of retinoid homeostasis, linking morphogen degradation to craniofacial development.

Defective CYP4F22 causes ARCI5 describes what happens to the skin barrier when a single keratinocyte cytochrome P450 enzyme is lost. CYP4F22 acts in the 12(R)-lipoxygenase arm of arachidonic acid metabolism, omega-hydroxylating trioxilin A3 and related fatty acid derivatives, and it is also the omega-hydroxylase that generates the ultra-long-chain acylceramides needed to build the epidermal lipid lamellae. That lipid layer is what holds water in the stratum corneum, so mutations that inactivate the enzyme give autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis type 5, with scaling, hyperkeratosis and defective barrier function from birth. The same lipoxygenase route yields 12- and 15-HETE products that modulate keratinocyte proliferation and differentiation, linking this metabolic step to proliferative skin disease more broadly and placing it within epidermal lipid biosynthesis and terminal keratinocyte maturation.

Loss-of-function mutations in the keratinocyte cytochrome P450 CYP4F22 cause autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis type 5, in which the skin barrier fails and newborns present with thick scaling and, in severe cases, a collodion membrane. The enzyme acts in the 12(R)-lipoxygenase branch of arachidonic acid metabolism, hydroxylating trioxilin A3 and related eicosanoid intermediates; it also contributes to synthesis of the ultra-long-chain fatty acid species that form acylceramides in the stratum corneum. Because these lipids create the water-impermeable lamellar membranes of the outer epidermis, defective CYP4F22 activity leaves the cornified envelope unable to retain hydration, and the resulting compensatory hyperproliferation links this oxidative lipid processing to proliferative skin disease more broadly. The biology sits at the junction of epidermal differentiation, lipid barrier assembly, and eicosanoid signalling in keratinocytes.

Glutathione is the cell's main thiol antioxidant, and the final step of its synthesis — ligating glycine onto gamma-glutamylcysteine — is carried out by glutathione synthetase. Loss-of-function mutations in GSS cause glutathione synthetase deficiency, an autosomal recessive disorder in which cells cannot maintain their reduced glutathione pool and so lose buffering against oxidative injury. Red cells are among the first to suffer, giving haemolytic anaemia, while accumulating gamma-glutamylcysteine is diverted to 5-oxoproline, producing 5-oxoprolinuria and metabolic acidosis; severe cases add progressive central nervous system damage and recurrent bacterial infection. The defect sits within the gamma-glutamyl cycle, the route by which glutathione is made, exported, degraded and its constituent amino acids recycled, and it illustrates how disrupting one enzyme both removes an antioxidant and creates a toxic intermediate. Severity ranges from mild haemolysis to neurological disease.

Aminoacylase 1 is the cytosolic zinc metalloenzyme that recycles amino acids from N-acetylated protein degradation products, hydrolysing N-acetyl-L-amino acids (all but N-acetyl-aspartate) back to the free amino acid plus acetate, and also cleaving N-acetylcysteine-S-conjugates generated during mercapturic acid detoxification. Because it is widely expressed and sits at the end of protein turnover, loss of its activity blocks salvage of acetylated residues and leaves them to be excreted. Inactivating mutations cause aminoacylase-1 deficiency, in which large amounts of several N-acetylated amino acids appear in urine and affected children present with encephalopathy, psychomotor delay and seizures, though the clinical picture is variable. The defect illustrates how a single step in amino acid catabolism and cofactor-dependent hydrolysis links protein recycling to neurological development.

Aldosterone is the adrenal steroid that drives renal sodium retention and potassium excretion, and its final synthesis depends on a single mitochondrial enzyme, CYP11B2, which carries corticosterone through 18-hydroxylation to 18-hydroxycorticosterone and then oxidises it to aldosterone. Loss-of-function mutations in this enzyme cause corticosterone methyloxidase type 1 deficiency, an autosomal recessive defect of aldosterone biosynthesis in which plasma aldosterone is undetectable while the immediate precursor 18-hydroxycorticosterone remains low or normal, distinguishing it from the type 2 form where precursor accumulates. Affected infants present with salt wasting, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, dehydration and failure to thrive, with compensatory renin elevation. The biology sits at the terminal step of the mineralocorticoid branch of adrenal steroidogenesis in the zona glomerulosa, linking cholesterol-derived steroid synthesis to blood pressure and electrolyte homeostasis.

Defective CYP24A1 causes HCAI concerns the loss of the body's main off-switch for active vitamin D, and the calcium overload that follows. CYP24A1 is the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 that initiates catabolism of calcitriol by 24-hydroxylation, starting the route to calcitroic acid, a water-soluble metabolite cleared in bile; it is itself induced by calcitriol, forming a feedback loop that limits hormone action on intestinal calcium absorption and bone. When the enzyme is inactivated by mutation, calcitriol persists, calcium absorption runs unchecked, and affected infants present with hypercalcemia, suppressed parathyroid hormone, failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration and nephrocalcinosis, sometimes with kidney stones later in life. The defect illustrates that vitamin D endocrine balance depends as much on timely degradation as on synthesis, and it sits within steroid and xenobiotic hydroxylation metabolism more broadly.

Active vitamin D must be destroyed as well as made, and the mitochondrial enzyme CYP24A1 begins that destruction by 24-hydroxylating calcitriol and its precursor, committing them to a side-chain oxidation route that ends in water-soluble calcitroic acid for biliary excretion. Because calcitriol drives intestinal calcium absorption, this catabolic step is the brake on vitamin D signalling and is itself induced by calcitriol, forming a negative feedback loop that limits hormone exposure. Loss-of-function mutations remove that brake and cause idiopathic infantile hypercalcemia, in which persistently elevated calcitriol produces excessive calcium uptake, suppressed parathyroid hormone, failure to thrive, vomiting, dehydration, nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones, sometimes unmasked by ordinary vitamin D supplementation. The pathway situates vitamin D turnover within calcium and phosphate homeostasis and within mitochondrial cytochrome P450 sterol metabolism.

Loss-of-function mutation of CYP2U1 underlies autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 56, a hereditary neurodegenerative condition in which the long corticospinal axons degenerate and patients develop slowly progressive weakness and spasticity of the lower limbs, often with childhood onset. The normal enzyme is a cytochrome P450 monooxygenase that hydroxylates arachidonic acid, docosahexaenoic acid and other long-chain fatty acids, producing hydroxylated eicosanoid and docosanoid derivatives that serve as lipid signalling molecules. When this hydroxylation fails, fatty acid-derived signalling and membrane lipid handling in neurons are disturbed, with reported consequences for mitochondrial function; the resulting defect is expressed as a length-dependent axonopathy rather than a generalised metabolic crisis. The pathway therefore links neuronal lipid oxidation chemistry to maintenance of the motor tracts that control gait, and places CYP2U1 among the fatty acid metabolism genes whose failure causes inherited spastic paraplegia.

Monoamine oxidase A sits on the mitochondrial outer membrane and, using FAD as cofactor, oxidatively deaminates serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline and adrenaline, setting the rate at which these neurotransmitters are degraded and thereby their concentrations in brain and peripheral tissues. Loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked MAOA gene cause Brunner syndrome, in which affected males show mild intellectual disability without dysmorphic features together with impulsive aggression, sleep disturbance and other behavioural abnormality; urinary and plasma monoamines and their metabolites are correspondingly deranged. The defective enzyme illustrates how catabolic control of biogenic amines, rather than their synthesis or release, governs mood, arousal and behavioural restraint. The same activity accounts for clearance of dietary amines such as tyramine, and is the target of monoamine oxidase inhibitors used as antidepressants.

Bile acid synthesis from cholesterol proceeds by two routes, and the alternative acidic route depends on the microsomal enzyme 25-hydroxycholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase to add a 7-alpha hydroxyl group to oxysterol intermediates. Loss of that activity blocks the pathway and causes two very different diseases: hereditary spastic paraplegia type 5A, in which oxysterols such as 25- and 27-hydroxycholesterol accumulate in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid and long corticospinal axons degenerate, producing slowly progressive lower-limb weakness and spasticity; and congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 3, a neonatal presentation with severe cholestasis, cirrhosis and failure of hepatic synthetic function in which hepatic enzyme activity is undetectable. The pathway therefore links cholesterol catabolism and bile acid production to both liver function and the maintenance of motor neuron axons, illustrating how oxysterol excess rather than bile acid deficiency alone can be neurotoxic.

Vitamin D becomes a hormone only after two hydroxylations, and the final, rate-limiting one is performed in the kidney mitochondrion by the 1-alpha-hydroxylase CYP27B1, which converts circulating calcidiol into calcitriol. Calcitriol binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor and drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone remodelling, and programmes of cellular differentiation, so this single enzymatic step sets whether the body can mineralise its skeleton. Loss-of-function mutations in CYP27B1, most of them missense, abolish activation despite normal substrate supply and cause vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1A: hypocalcaemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism, bowed limbs, growth failure and defective bone mineralisation from infancy. The biochemical signature is low calcitriol with preserved calcidiol, distinguishing it from dietary deficiency and from receptor defects, and the condition responds to replacement with the active hormone rather than with vitamin D itself.

Retinoic acid is a potent morphogen, and tissues protect themselves from excess of it by destroying it locally. CYP26B1 is the cytochrome P450 that performs this clearance, hydroxylating all-trans retinoic acid at carbon 4 to begin its catabolism and so setting the sharp concentration gradients that pattern limbs, craniofacial structures and the hindbrain. Its high expression in cerebellum and pons is consistent with shielding neural tissue from retinoid damage. When the enzyme is defective, retinoic acid accumulates where it should be cleared and skeletal patterning fails, producing radiohumeral fusions with additional skeletal and craniofacial anomalies. The condition illustrates that vitamin A signalling is controlled as much by degradation as by synthesis, and it links ligand turnover directly to nuclear retinoic acid receptor output and the differentiation programmes those receptors drive during development.

Bilirubin, the lipophilic end product of heme catabolism, must be glucuronidated in the liver before it can be excreted in bile, and UGT1A4 is one of the UDP-glucuronosyltransferase isoforms that performs this conjugation. When UGT1A4 activity is lost or reduced, unconjugated bilirubin accumulates in blood, producing the inherited unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia syndromes: mild, largely benign jaundice in Gilbert syndrome, and the far more severe Crigler-Najjar types 1 and 2, where bilirubin can cross into the brain and cause kernicterus. The same endoplasmic reticulum enzyme transfers glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronate onto amine and hydroxyl groups of many drugs and endogenous steroids, so defective alleles also alter xenobiotic clearance. This places the defect within phase II drug metabolism and hepatic bile pigment handling rather than in heme synthesis itself.

Defective CYP11B1 causes AH4 describes the loss of the final hydroxylation step of adrenal cortisol synthesis and the disease that follows. Mitochondrial cytochrome P450 11B1 converts 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol in the adrenal zona fasciculata, so when the enzyme is inactivated the gland cannot complete glucocorticoid production; ACTH feedback is lost, the cortex becomes hyperplastic, and precursors are shunted into adrenal androgens. This is 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency, the second most common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia after 21-hydroxylase deficiency, inherited recessively and presenting with virilization of affected girls, precocious pseudopuberty in boys, and hypertension driven by accumulated 11-deoxycorticosterone acting on the mineralocorticoid receptor. The pathway situates steroid hormone biosynthesis within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and explains why a single mitochondrial monooxygenase defect disturbs both salt balance and sexual development.

The final step of cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex is 11-beta-hydroxylation of 11-deoxycortisol, carried out by the mitochondrial cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP11B1. When this activity is lost, cortisol cannot be made, feedback restraint on pituitary ACTH is removed, and the adrenal cortex is driven to hyperplasia while steroid precursors are shunted into androgen production. The resulting disorder, adrenal hyperplasia 4, is a recessive form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia and the second most common after 21-hydroxylase deficiency, accounting for a small percentage of cases. Affected individuals show virilization from androgen excess together with hypertension, the latter reflecting accumulation of 11-deoxycorticosterone, which acts as a mineralocorticoid and promotes sodium retention. This places the defect within adrenal steroidogenesis and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that governs it.

Trimethylamine, released by gut bacteria from dietary choline and carnitine and also present in fish, is absorbed and detoxified in the liver by the flavin-containing monooxygenase FMO3, which N-oxygenates it to the odourless trimethylamine N-oxide. This single hepatic step is what normally prevents a volatile, strongly fishy-smelling amine from accumulating and being excreted in urine, sweat and breath. When FMO3 activity is lost through inherited loss-of-function variants, unoxidised trimethylamine escapes into body fluids and produces trimethylaminuria, or fish-odour syndrome, a benign but socially and psychologically disabling condition often exacerbated by choline-rich meals and managed largely by dietary restriction. The same NADPH- and FAD-dependent oxygenation contributes to phase I metabolism of drugs and other nitrogen- and sulfur-containing xenobiotics, so defective FMO3 also alters handling of those substrates, and the trimethylamine N-oxide produced has been linked to cardiovascular risk.

Cartilage matrix depends on a steady supply of nucleotide sugars inside the endoplasmic reticulum, and SLC35D1 is the transporter that delivers them. Sitting in the ER membrane, it carries UDP-glucuronic acid and UDP-N-acetylgalactosamine from the cytosol, where they are made, into the lumen, where glycosyltransferases use them to build the alternating disaccharide backbone of chondroitin sulfate. Because proteoglycan chains give growth-plate cartilage its water-binding bulk and mechanical resilience, loss of this import step starves the assembly line at its substrate supply. Recessive loss-of-function mutations cause Schneckenbecken dysplasia, a lethal skeletal dysplasia marked by extremely short limbs, a narrow thorax and the characteristic snail-shaped ilia that give the condition its name. The defect illustrates how a single compartmental transport activity, rather than any enzyme of the biosynthetic route itself, can govern glycosaminoglycan output and skeletal development.

Defective CYP21A2 causes AH3 describes the loss of steroid 21-hydroxylase activity that underlies the commonest form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, accounting for more than nine in ten cases. The enzyme, a microsomal cytochrome P450 of the adrenal cortex, hydroxylates progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone at carbon 21, the committed step toward both aldosterone and cortisol. When it fails, cortisol output falls, negative feedback on the pituitary is lost, and rising ACTH drives adrenal hypertrophy and a backlog of precursors, chiefly 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which is shunted into androgen synthesis. The clinical consequences follow directly: virilization of affected females, salt wasting when mineralocorticoid synthesis is also lost, and in milder allelic forms later-onset hyperandrogenism. This places the defect within adrenal steroidogenesis and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis that regulates it, and makes 17-hydroxyprogesterone the basis of newborn screening.

Steroid 21-hydroxylase sits at a branch point of adrenal steroid synthesis, converting progesterone and 17-hydroxyprogesterone into the precursors of aldosterone and cortisol. When the enzyme is defective, the resulting adrenal hyperplasia 3 accounts for the great majority of congenital adrenal hyperplasia: cortisol output falls, feedback restraint on pituitary ACTH is lost, and the adrenal cortex enlarges while precursors such as 17-hydroxyprogesterone accumulate. Because those precursors are shunted into androgen synthesis, affected females are virilized and both sexes may show accelerated growth and early puberty; severe alleles also impair mineralocorticoid production and present as salt-wasting adrenal crisis in infancy. Milder, partially active variants produce late-onset hyperandrogenism. The clinical spectrum tracks residual enzyme activity, which makes this a mutation-severity-graded microsomal cytochrome P450 defect in adrenal cortical hormone output.

Glutathione does not cross membranes intact; it is broken down outside the cell, and gamma-glutamyltransferase 1 performs the committed first cut, removing the gamma-glutamyl group from extracellular glutathione and from glutathione S-conjugates to yield glutamate and cysteinylglycine. This salvage step recovers cysteine, the limiting precursor for intracellular glutathione resynthesis, and it also starts the route by which xenobiotic conjugates are converted to mercapturic acids for urinary excretion. The enzyme is a membrane-anchored heterodimer of heavy and light chains generated by autocatalytic cleavage, positioned on the cell surface of kidney, biliary and other epithelia. Loss-of-function mutations affecting either chain cause glutathionuria, a recessive disorder in which glutathione accumulates in plasma and spills into urine, reflecting failure of the gamma-glutamyl cycle's extracellular arm and of cysteine recycling.

The liver converts dietary methionine into S-adenosylmethionine, the universal methyl donor for transmethylation of DNA, proteins, phospholipids and small molecules, and the hepatic enzyme methionine adenosyltransferase I/III encoded by MAT1A performs that ATP-dependent step. When the enzyme is defective, methionine cannot be efficiently activated and accumulates in blood, producing methionine adenosyltransferase deficiency, an inborn error of amino acid metabolism marked by isolated persistent hypermethioninemia. Most affected individuals are clinically mild and detected on newborn screening, but severe deficiency can lower methyl group supply enough to impair myelination and cause neurological signs, and it perturbs downstream transsulfuration and glutathione synthesis. The defect illustrates how a single liver-enriched isoform gates entry into the methionine cycle, linking amino acid catabolism to methylation capacity and to homocysteine handling.

Every steroid hormone begins with the same reaction: cleavage of the cholesterol side chain to pregnenolone by the mitochondrial enzyme CYP11A1, working with the ferredoxin reductase and ferredoxin partners that shuttle electrons from NADPH to the P450. When mutations disable this first committed step, no cortisol, aldosterone or sex steroids can be made, producing congenital adrenal insufficiency with 46,XY sex reversal. Affected infants present with salt loss and adrenal crisis, high ACTH and plasma renin reflecting absent negative feedback, and low or undetectable adrenal steroids; genetically male fetuses fail to virilise because testicular testosterone synthesis is equally blocked, and complete loss of function is associated with prematurity. Milder alleles retaining partial activity give later-onset adrenal failure. The defect therefore illustrates how a single mitochondrial electron-transfer-dependent oxidation gates the entire steroidogenic output of adrenal cortex and gonad.

Defective CYP27B1 causes VDDR1B describes the loss of vitamin D activation that produces vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1B, a hereditary failure to make the active hormone despite adequate vitamin D intake or sun exposure. Cholecalciferol made in skin is itself inert; it must be hydroxylated at carbon 25 in the liver by the microsomal cytochrome P450 CYP2R1 to give calcidiol, and then at the 1-alpha position to give calcitriol, the ligand for the nuclear vitamin D receptor. Through that receptor calcitriol drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation, and programmes of cellular differentiation and proliferation. When the 25-hydroxylase step is crippled by mutation, circulating calcidiol is low, hormone-dependent gene expression is not engaged, and children develop hypocalcaemia and the skeletal deformities of rickets, correctable by supplying the hydroxylated metabolite.

Vitamin D3 made in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol is inert until it is hydroxylated twice: at carbon 25 in the liver by the microsomal cytochrome P450 CYP2R1 to give calcidiol, and then at the 1-alpha position to give calcitriol, the hormone that binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor and drives intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, bone mineralisation, and programmes of cellular differentiation and proliferation. This pathway describes loss of that activation step, which produces vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1B. Because the substrate cannot be converted to the circulating 25-hydroxy form, patients have a selective deficiency of active hormone despite adequate vitamin D intake or sun exposure, with hypocalcaemia, defective growth plate and bone mineralisation, and the skeletal deformities of rickets; the defect is bypassed clinically by supplying hydroxylated vitamin D metabolites rather than cholecalciferol.

Cortisol and the sex steroids both require a single microsomal cytochrome P450, CYP17A1, which carries out 17-alpha-hydroxylation of pregnenolone and progesterone and then the 17,20-lyase cleavage that yields DHEA and androstenedione. Loss-of-function mutations block this step in the adrenal cortex and gonads and cause adrenal hyperplasia 5, a recessive form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Because precursors are shunted into the mineralocorticoid arm, affected individuals develop low-renin hypertension with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis alongside mild cortisol deficiency, while absent androgen and estrogen synthesis leaves genetic males undervirilised and genetic females without pubertal ovarian function. The two catalytic activities can fail separately, so some patients show combined 17-alpha-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase deficiency and others an isolated lyase defect, which makes this enzyme the branch point between glucocorticoid and sex steroid production.

Biotransformation converts drugs, toxins and endogenous lipids into forms that can be used or excreted, and inherited defects in the enzymes that do this work cause a recognisable group of metabolic disorders. Phase 1 functionalisation is dominated here by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases with their electron-supplying ferredoxin and ferredoxin reductase partners, covering steroidogenesis (including 21-hydroxylase and aldosterone synthase, whose loss gives congenital adrenal hyperplasia and mineralocorticoid deficiency), vitamin D activation and catabolism, bile acid and retinoic acid turnover, and skin barrier lipid processing. Phase 2 conjugation adds glutathione synthesis and recycling, sulfur amino acid and methionine metabolism, thiopurine methylation, and glucuronidation, where UGT1A1 deficiency produces the unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia of Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes. Flavin monooxygenase failure causes trimethylaminuria, and monoamine oxidase A loss disturbs neurotransmitter breakdown and behaviour, illustrating how broadly these lesions present.

Aromatase, encoded by CYP19A1, performs the final step of estrogen biosynthesis, converting androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol, and is therefore the sole route by which the body makes estrogens from androgen precursors. Its activity in ovary, placenta, adipose tissue, bone and brain sets the local and circulating estrogen tone that drives female sexual development, ovulation, pregnancy, epiphyseal closure and bone mass in both sexes. Loss-of-function changes abolish estrogen synthesis, producing virilization of affected females and continued growth with delayed bone maturation; conversely, rearrangements that place the gene under strong heterologous promoters cause excess enzyme activity and the aromatase excess syndrome, with prepubertal gynaecomastia, accelerated bone age and short adult stature in males. This pathway represents the mutant enzyme's failure to carry out the androgen-to-estrogen conversion within steroid hormone metabolism.

Pro-opiomelanocortin is a precursor cleaved into several hormones, among them corticotropin (ACTH), which acts on the adrenal cortex through its receptor MC2R to drive cortisol output, while related cleavage products such as alpha-melanotropin act on melanocortin receptors to control appetite and pigmentation. When ACTH is defective or POMC processing fails, this axis collapses in a characteristic way: early-onset severe obesity from loss of central satiety signalling, adrenal insufficiency from absent cortisol stimulation, and red hair from unopposed pigment switching. Cortisol itself supports gluconeogenesis, immune restraint and the handling of fats, proteins and carbohydrates, so its loss affects stress responses and fuel metabolism broadly. This links a single prohormone, and the receptor that reads its ACTH product, to energy balance, steroidogenesis and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal control.

Thromboxane A2 is the short-lived lipid mediator that makes platelets aggregate and constricts vascular and airway smooth muscle, and thromboxane-A synthase is the enzyme that makes it, converting prostaglandin H2 from the arachidonic acid cascade into TXA2. Balanced against endothelial prostacyclin, this activity sets the haemostatic tone of the circulation, and it also feeds into osteoclast differentiation and activation, linking eicosanoid signalling to bone remodelling. Loss-of-function variants in TBXAS1 cause Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia, a recessive disorder in which the diaphyses of long bones become abnormally dense while the marrow fails to regenerate blood cells, producing a steroid-responsive aregenerative anaemia. The disease illustrates how a single prostanoid branch point governs both platelet function and the osteoblast-osteoclast balance that keeps the marrow cavity open for haematopoiesis.

Germ cells must keep transposons from mobilising in the genome they pass to the next generation, and piRNA biogenesis supplies the small RNAs that enforce that silence. Long precursor transcripts are made by RNA polymerase II from piRNA clusters, individual transposons and intergenic regions, then processed without Dicer: the mitochondrial phospholipase D PLD6 generates mature 5' ends, an exonuclease trims the 3' end, and HENMT1 adds a 2'-O-methyl mark that stabilises the 26-30 nucleotide product. Loaded PIWI proteins split the labour, with PIWIL1 and PIWIL2 acting in cytoplasmic cleavage and a ping-pong amplification loop, while PIWIL4 with TDRD9 enters the nucleus to direct DNA methylation of target loci. Tudor-domain partners, the helicase MOV10L1, MAEL and chaperone activity organise these complexes in germ granules. Loss of the pathway derepresses L1 elements and arrests spermatogenesis, causing male infertility.

Toll-like receptors let the innate immune system recognise microbial products and host damage signals, and when the cascade they trigger is broken the consequences are clinically stark. Loss-of-function in MyD88 or IRAK4, the shared adaptor and kinase downstream of most TLRs, leaves children unable to mount inflammation against pyogenic bacteria such as pneumococcus and staphylococcus, while defects in TLR3 or its trafficking chaperone UNC93B1 and the adaptor TRIF selectively predispose to herpes simplex encephalitis. Mutations in the IKK complex and NF-kB subunits blunt cytokine induction more broadly and cause combined immunodeficiency syndromes, and a recurrent activating MyD88 mutation drives constitutive NF-kB signalling in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. The receptors and co-receptors here, including CD14, MD-2, CD36 and the TLR1/2/6 heterodimer partners, together with ligands such as HMGB1, S100A8/A9 and fibrinogen, define the sensing step whose failure produces susceptibility to infection, sterile inflammation, autoimmunity or malignancy.

Sensing of double-stranded RNA, a replication intermediate of most viruses, by the endosomal receptor TLR3 drives type I and type III interferon induction; when this sensor is defective, the consequence in humans is herpes simplex encephalitis. TLR3 is expressed widely, including in neurons, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes, and central nervous system cells appear to depend on it almost exclusively for antiviral interferon responses against herpes simplex virus type 1. Children carrying loss-of-function TLR3 alleles therefore suffer a narrow susceptibility: peripheral blood cells still mount normal interferon output, presumably through cytosolic RNA sensors such as RIG-I and MDA5, but intrinsic control of viral replication in brain tissue fails and a life-threatening focal encephalitis can follow an otherwise ordinary infection. It is a textbook example of an inborn error of immunity in which one receptor guards one organ against one pathogen.

Nucleic-acid-sensing Toll-like receptors are made in the endoplasmic reticulum but only work once they reach endosomes, and UNC93B1 is the multipass membrane chaperone that escorts them there. When UNC93B1 is defective, TLR3 cannot be delivered to its signalling compartment, so double-stranded RNA from a replicating virus goes unrecognised and type I and type III interferon induction fails. The clinical consequence is herpes simplex encephalitis: children with this inherited deficiency are otherwise largely healthy but cannot contain HSV-1 in the central nervous system, where patient-derived neurons and oligodendrocytes show blunted interferon responses and permit rapid viral replication. The same chaperone is required by TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9, so responses to imidazoquinolines and CpG DNA are also lost. This is innate antiviral immunity viewed as a trafficking problem, and it illustrates tissue-restricted susceptibility arising from a general signalling defect.

Recognition of bacterial cell-wall products by TLR2 and TLR4 depends on the adaptor MyD88, and loss-of-function mutations in MYD88 cause an inherited immunodeficiency in which this arm of innate sensing fails. Affected children suffer recurrent invasive infection with pyogenic bacteria such as pneumococcus and Staphylococcus aureus, often with strikingly little fever or acute-phase response, because signalling that would normally drive cytokine production is abolished. Normally, lipopeptides engaging TLR2 with its TLR1 or TLR6 partner, or LPS captured by CD14 and the MD-2 co-receptor for TLR4, trigger receptor dimerisation and TIR-domain recruitment of MyD88, which oligomerises and recruits IRAK kinases into a Myddosome to activate NF-kB and AP-1. Endogenous alarmins including HMGB1 and S100A8/A9, and fibrinogen chains, act through the same receptors, so sterile inflammatory signalling is blunted alongside antibacterial defence.

Sensing of viral double-stranded RNA in the central nervous system depends on TLR3 and its adaptor TRIF, encoded by TICAM1, and children who inherit defective TICAM1 alleles can develop herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis during primary infection. This is one of a group of single-gene lesions in the TLR3-to-interferon axis that leave general immunity largely intact yet cripple antiviral defence in neurons and other resident brain cells, allowing an otherwise commonplace infection to destroy the temporal lobe. TLR3 in endosomes recruits TRIF, which nucleates signalling toward IRF3 and NF-kB and the production of type I and type III interferons; both dominant-negative and recessive TRIF defects blunt this output. The example illustrates how interferon induction, rather than adaptive immunity, sets tissue-specific susceptibility to a particular virus.

Sensing of viral double-stranded RNA in the central nervous system depends on TLR3 signalling through the adaptor TRIF, and TRAF3 is the cytoplasmic link that carries that signal onward to interferon induction. Loss of TRAF3 function cripples this arm of innate antiviral defence and, like TLR3 deficiency itself, leaves otherwise healthy children unable to contain herpes simplex virus type 1 in the brain, producing herpes simplex encephalitis while immunity to most other pathogens remains intact. TRAF3 acts as an adaptor shared by toll-like receptors and members of the TNF receptor superfamily, coupling receptor engagement to the kinases that activate IRF3 and drive type I and type III interferon production. The narrow clinical phenotype illustrates how a single interferon-inducing route can be non-redundant in one tissue and dispensable elsewhere.

Loss of IKBKB, the catalytic beta subunit of the IKK complex, causes a severe combined immunodeficiency in which infants present with early, life-threatening bacterial, viral and fungal infections and failure to thrive despite normal-looking B and T cell counts. The IKK complex — the two kinases CHUK (IKK-alpha) and IKBKB (IKK-beta) together with the regulatory scaffold IKBKG (NEMO) — phosphorylates inhibitors of NF-kappaB so they are degraded and NF-kappaB can enter the nucleus. Without IKBKB this relay downstream of antigen receptors, Toll-like receptors and TNF-family receptors is silent, so lymphocytes fail to be activated: circulating T and B cells remain almost entirely naive, regulatory T cells and gamma delta T cells are missing, and immunoglobulin levels are low. The disorder illustrates how a single kinase subunit couples innate and adaptive receptor engagement to lymphocyte maturation and tolerance.

Flagellin from motile bacteria is detected at the cell surface by TLR5, which signals through the adaptor MyD88 to mount an inflammatory response; this describes what happens when MyD88 is lost. Ligand-bound TLR5 dimerizes and recruits MyD88 via TIR-domain contacts, and MyD88 then oligomerizes through its death domain to nucleate a Myddosome with IRAK4 and IRAK1/2, driving NF-kB and AP-1 activation and cytokine output. Autosomal recessive MyD88 deficiency, caused by variants that abolish the protein or cripple its oligomerization and IRAK4 binding, leaves flagellin-stimulated blood cells unable to produce cytokines. Affected children suffer recurrent invasive pyogenic infections, notably pneumococcal disease, with blunted fever and acute-phase responses that make infection hard to recognize clinically. The defect illustrates how one adaptor couples innate pattern recognition to protective inflammation, and how its loss produces a narrow but severe primary immunodeficiency.

NEMO, the regulatory subunit encoded by IKBKG, partners with the catalytic kinases IKK alpha and IKK beta to form the IKK complex that switches on canonical NF-kB signalling. When Toll-like receptors sense microbial products, the signal converges on this complex, which phosphorylates IkB and targets it for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation, freeing NF-kB to enter the nucleus and drive inflammatory cytokines, adhesion molecules and anti-apoptotic genes. Because IKBKG is X-linked and indispensable, hypomorphic alleles rather than null ones survive in males, and the resulting partial loss of IKK function produces anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency: absent sweat glands, abnormal teeth and hair reflecting failed NF-kB-dependent development of ectodermal appendages, alongside recurrent bacterial infection from blunted innate responses to TLR stimulation. Related mutation classes instead cause incontinentia pigmenti or add osteopetrosis and lymphedema.

NF-kB transcription factors sit inactive in the cytoplasm bound to IkB proteins until an inflammatory or microbial signal arrives; the IKK complex, built from CHUK (IKKalpha), IKBKB (IKKbeta) and the regulatory subunit IKBKG (NEMO), then phosphorylates IkBalpha, marking it for ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction so that p50/p65 and p52-containing dimers can enter the nucleus and drive inflammatory, antimicrobial and developmental gene programmes. Hypermorphic heterozygous mutations in NFKBIA remove the phosphorylation sites, so IkBalpha is never degraded and continues to sequester NF-kB dimers. The result is autosomal dominant anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency: absent or abnormal teeth, hair and sweat glands, reflecting the requirement for NF-kB downstream of ectodysplasin signalling in skin appendage development, together with recurrent bacterial infection and impaired antibody responses from the blunted innate and adaptive immune signalling.

Flagellin from motile bacteria is sensed at the cell surface by TLR5, which dimerises and recruits MyD88 to nucleate a Myddosome with IRAK4 and IRAK1/2, driving NF-kB and AP-1 activation and the output of inflammatory cytokines such as TNF, IL-6 and IL-1beta. This depicts what happens when IRAK4 is lost: inherited, recessive loss-of-function mutations either abolish IRAK4 protein through nonsense alleles or block its death-domain interaction with MyD88 through missense changes, so the receptor engages its adaptor but no signal is transmitted. Affected children suffer recurrent invasive pyogenic infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus, and their leukocytes fail to make cytokines or shed CD62L after flagellin stimulation. Because IRAK4 sits downstream of almost all Toll-like receptors, including the closely related TLR10, the defect is broad rather than TLR5-specific, and it illustrates how one kinase gates innate antibacterial immunity.

Innate immune cells detect bacterial lipopeptides and lipopolysaccharide through TLR1/2, TLR2/6 and TLR4 with their co-receptors CD14, CD36 and MD-2, and relay that recognition through the adaptors MyD88 and TIRAP to the kinase IRAK4, which drives NF-kB and AP-1 and the output of TNF, IL-6 and IL-1beta. Inherited loss of IRAK4 function breaks this relay: recessive null or MyD88-binding-defective alleles leave leukocytes unable to make inflammatory cytokines or shed CD62L after stimulation with lipopeptide or LPS agonists, and children present in infancy with recurrent pyogenic infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus. The defect is selective rather than global, since MyD88-independent TLR4 branches and RNA-sensing antiviral routes remain largely intact, which is why viral immunity is broadly preserved. Endogenous ligands such as HMGB1, S100A8/A9 and fibrinogen chains feed the same receptors in sterile inflammation.

Recognition of fungal beta-glucans by the myeloid lectin receptor Dectin-1 shapes antifungal immunity, and one arm of that response is a slow, sustained wave of noncanonical NF-kB activity distinct from the rapid canonical burst. Downstream of SYK, the kinase NIK (MAP3K14) accumulates and activates IKKalpha (CHUK), which primes the NFKB2 p100 precursor for ubiquitin-dependent partial proteasomal processing to mature p52; an SCF complex with beta-TrCP and the 26S proteasome carry out the limited degradation, supported here by ubiquitin and E2/E3 components. Resulting p52:RELB dimers enter the nucleus and set the character of the ensuing T cell response, inducing the chemokines CCL17 and CCL22 that recruit Th2 and regulatory T cells while repressing IL12B and thereby dampening Th1 polarization. The balance between this route and canonical RELA-driven transcription determines whether fungal encounter yields inflammatory or tolerogenic output.

Dectin-1 is the myeloid receptor for fungal beta-glucans, and one branch of its signalling converts recognition of a fungal cell wall into a calcium-dependent transcriptional response. Spleen tyrosine kinase engagement activates phospholipase C-gamma 2, generating inositol trisphosphate that opens the IP3 receptor channels ITPR1, ITPR2 and ITPR3 on the endoplasmic reticulum and releases stored calcium into the cytosol. Calcium-loaded calmodulin then activates the phosphatase calcineurin, built here from catalytic PPP3CA or PPP3CB with the PPP3R1 regulatory subunit, which dephosphorylates cytoplasmic NFATC1, NFATC2 and NFATC3 and permits their nuclear entry. The resulting transcription drives interleukin-2 and other cytokines that shape dendritic cell and macrophage responses to Candida and related fungi. AHCYL1 tunes IP3 receptor sensitivity. Loss of this arm blunts antifungal immunity and the instruction of adaptive T cell responses.

Myeloid cells recognise fungi largely by sensing beta-1,3-glucan in the cell wall, and Dectin-1 is the receptor that does it, coupling that recognition to phagocytosis, reactive oxygen production and inflammatory gene expression. Loss of this route, or of its adaptor CARD9, leaves people vulnerable to chronic mucocutaneous and invasive fungal disease, while excessive signalling drives Th17-skewed inflammation. Engagement of clustered glucan triggers Src- and Syk-dependent tyrosine signalling through an ITAM-like tail, activating PLCG2 to raise calcium through inositol trisphosphate receptors; calcineurin then dephosphorylates NFAT transcription factors, and a CARD9-BCL10-MALT1 complex with TRAF6 and the TAK1-IKK axis releases canonical NF-kB by ubiquitin- and proteasome-dependent degradation of NFKBIA. A parallel NIK-driven non-canonical arm mobilises RelB. Outputs include IL-1beta and the chemokines CCL17 and CCL22, linking antifungal innate defence to dendritic cell instruction of adaptive immunity.

Phosphoglucomutase 1 sits at the junction between glycogen metabolism and glycan synthesis, interconverting glucose-6-phosphate and glucose-1-phosphate in the cytosol so that glucose carbon can be routed either into glycogen or into UDP-glucose and the other nucleotide sugars that donate residues to N-glycans. Loss of this isomerisation step starves the glycosylation machinery of donor substrates, and the resulting condition, PGM1-CDG, presents with hypoglycaemia, exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis alongside the features typical of congenital disorders of glycosylation: cleft palate and other dysmorphism, hypotonia, developmental delay, cardiomyopathy, coagulation factor abnormalities and abnormal transferrin glycoforms in serum. Because the block is in substrate supply rather than in a glycosyltransferase, the disorder is partly correctable by dietary galactose, which feeds UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose pools through an alternative route.

Before any sugar can be attached to a protein or lipid, it must first be activated as a nucleotide sugar or loaded onto a dolichol carrier, and inherited defects in that supply line cause the congenital disorders of glycosylation grouped here as diseases of glycosylation precursor biosynthesis. Because the shortage is upstream of all glycan assembly, the consequences are multisystem: PMM2 deficiency, the commonest form, produces cerebellar hypoplasia, coagulation abnormalities and failure to thrive, while GALT and GALK1 lesions cause classic galactosemia and cataract. Other members build the lipid carrier itself — the cis-prenyltransferase subunits DHDDS and NUS1, dolichol kinase, and the polyprenol reductase SRD5A3 — or make mannose-donor substrates through the DPM synthase complex and phosphomannose isomerase. GFPT1 and GNE feed hexosamine and sialic acid production, and their mutation yields congenital myasthenic syndrome and inclusion body myopathy respectively.

Dietary galactose, released mainly from the lactose in milk, is funnelled into glycolysis through the Leloir pathway, and galactokinase performs its first committed step by phosphorylating D-galactose to galactose 1-phosphate at the expense of ATP. When this cytosolic enzyme is deficient, the block described here as type II galactosemia follows: galactose accumulates in blood and tissues and is diverted to the alternative aldose reductase route, generating galactitol. Because galactitol is trapped inside lens fibre cells and draws in water osmotically, the cardinal consequence is cataract, congenital or infantile in severe deficiency and presenile in milder heterozygous or partial states. Unlike the classic form of galactosemia caused by loss of the next enzyme, liver and kidney injury is largely absent, and dietary galactose restriction prevents or reverses the lens opacity.

Dietary galactose is converted to glucose derivatives through the Leloir pathway, and the loss of its third step produces epimerase-deficiency galactosemia, also called type III galactosemia. The cytosolic enzyme GALE, active as an NAD+-bound homodimer, reversibly interconverts UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose, and also epimerises UDP-N-acetylglucosamine to UDP-N-acetylgalactosamine, so it supplies the activated sugar donors used for glycoprotein, glycolipid and glycosaminoglycan synthesis as well as clearing galactose. When GALE activity is deficient, galactose and UDP-galactose handling fails and glycosylation substrate pools shift, with clinical consequences ranging from a nearly benign state detected only in red blood cells to generalised enzyme loss with early cataracts, liver damage, deafness and developmental impairment. The two presentations are now understood as ends of a continuum of residual activity rather than separate diseases, placing this defect among the inherited disorders of carbohydrate metabolism.

Milk sugar has to be converted into a usable form, and the uridylyltransferase step of the Leloir pathway is where that conversion turns on a single enzyme. GALT transfers uridine monophosphate from UDP-glucose onto galactose-1-phosphate, yielding UDP-galactose and glucose-1-phosphate, so that dietary galactose can enter glycolysis and supply the activated galactose used in glycoproteins and glycolipids. When the enzyme is defective, classic galactosemia follows as an autosomal recessive disease: galactose-1-phosphate and its side products accumulate from the first milk feeds, and newborns develop jaundice, liver dysfunction, cataracts and, if untreated, intellectual disability. Dietary galactose restriction limits the acute crisis but does not prevent all long-term outcomes, which places this reaction at the centre of newborn screening for inherited carbohydrate metabolic disorders.

Organic anion transport by SLC22 transporters is the kidney's route for clearing small anionic waste products and drugs from the blood into the urine, and for reclaiming solutes the body needs to keep. It sets the plasma half-life of diuretics, NSAIDs, beta-lactam antibiotics, antivirals and methotrexate, and it governs urate handling: URAT1 (SLC22A12) reabsorbs uric acid at the proximal tubule brush border, and its variants shift serum urate and gout risk, while SLC22A11 (OAT4) contributes to the same balance. OAT1 and OAT3 (SLC22A6, SLC22A8) sit basolaterally and drive uptake from blood in exchange for intracellular dicarboxylates such as alpha-ketoglutarate, coupling secretion indirectly to the sodium gradient. Because these carriers are polyspecific and share substrates, they are a principal site of drug-drug interaction and of nephrotoxic accumulation, and they also export uremic toxins and hormone conjugates.

Renal handling of small anions depends on a family of polyspecific organic anion transporters in the SLC22 family, and this pathway describes the transport step by which they move endogenous metabolites and anionic drugs across kidney epithelial membranes. The carriers OAT1 and OAT3, encoded by SLC22A6 and SLC22A8, work at the basolateral membrane of the proximal tubule, exchanging intracellular dicarboxylate for organic anions to load substrates for secretion into urine; OAT4 and OAT7 handle further substrates, while URAT1 (SLC22A12) reabsorbs urate from the tubular lumen and sets serum uric acid levels, so its loss causes hypouricaemia and its overactivity contributes to gout. Because diuretics, NSAIDs, antivirals and beta-lactams are substrates, these transporters determine drug clearance, nephrotoxic accumulation and clinically important transporter-mediated drug interactions, and they are the point of action of uricosuric agents.

When Hedgehog ligand is absent, the transcriptional activator GLI1 is not merely trimmed but destroyed outright, and this complete proteasomal degradation of GLI1 keeps the pathway's output off in unstimulated cells. Loss of that restraint underlies the ligand-independent Hedgehog target gene expression seen in basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma and other tumours where GLI1 acts as an oncogenic driver. Protein kinase A catalytic subunits phosphorylate GLI1, priming recognition by the SCF ubiquitin ligase containing the F-box protein BTRC together with SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1; the HECT ligase ITCH, assisted by NUMB, provides a second route to ubiquitination. Polyubiquitinated GLI1 is then delivered to the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory particle subunits make up most of this machinery, while SUFU sequesters GLI1 and limits its access to the nucleus. GLI1 differs from GLI3 in lacking the sequences that permit partial processing to a repressor.

Degradation of GLI2 by the proteasome is the off-switch that keeps Hedgehog target genes silent when no ligand is present. GLI2 is the principal transcriptional activator of the pathway, and cells that fail to destroy it acquire constitutive Hedgehog output, a route to medulloblastoma, basal cell carcinoma and developmental patterning defects of the neural tube and limb. In unstimulated cells SUFU sequesters GLI2 while PKA primes a cluster of serines that CK1 and GSK3 then extend, creating a phosphodegron recognised by the SCF-beta-TrCP ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1. Polyubiquitinated GLI2 is delivered to the 26S proteasome and largely destroyed outright, in contrast to the related GLI3, whose C-terminal processing determinant domain directs partial proteolysis to a repressor form. Pathway activation blocks this phosphorylation cascade and spares GLI2.

Hedgehog signalling depends on keeping its transcriptional activators silent until a ligand arrives, and this route is how the activator GLI2 is disposed of when no signal is present. Unlike GLI3, which is clipped to a stable repressor, most GLI2 is destroyed outright, so that basal target gene expression stays low and developmental patterning of the neural tube, limb and other Hedgehog-dependent tissues remains faithful; loss of this restraint contributes to tumours such as basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Sequential phosphorylation by protein kinase A, casein kinase 1 and GSK3 creates a phosphodegron recognised by the beta-TrCP-containing SCF ubiquitin ligase, built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1, which polyubiquitinates GLI2 for complete proteolysis by the 26S proteasome. SUFU sequesters GLI2 in the cytoplasm and promotes its turnover, linking receptor state to activator abundance.

When Hedgehog ligand is absent, the transcription factor GLI3 is not destroyed outright but clipped by the proteasome into a shorter repressor form, GLI3R, which occupies Hedgehog target promoters and keeps the pathway silent. This default-off state is what makes Hedgehog signalling an instructive morphogen cue in limb bud patterning, digit number, neural tube dorsoventral identity and craniofacial development; loss of processing causes constitutive pathway output and underlies polydactyly syndromes, while GLI3 mutations produce Greig cephalopolysyndactyly and Pallister-Hall. Processing is driven by ordered phosphorylation: PKA catalytic subunits prime a cluster of sites, allowing casein kinase 1 and GSK3 beta to phosphorylate adjacent residues, creating a degron recognised by the BTRC-SKP1-CUL1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase. Polyubiquitinated GLI3 engages the 26S proteasome, whose regulatory and core particles degrade the C-terminal activation domain while sparing the DNA-binding N-terminus. SUFU binds and stabilises GLI3 throughout.

In the absence of Hedgehog ligand, cells actively hold the pathway silent, and this Hedgehog 'off' state is what keeps target genes such as those driving ventral neural tube and limb patterning switched off until a morphogen gradient says otherwise; its failure produces polydactyly, holoprosencephaly-like patterning defects and, when SUFU or PTCH1 restraint is lost, basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. Unliganded PTCH1 keeps SMO out of the primary cilium, while the orphan receptor GPR161 signals through Gs and adenylyl cyclases to raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A. PKA, with casein kinase 1 and GSK3B, primes GLI3 and GLI2 for beta-TrCP/SCF-mediated ubiquitination and partial proteasomal processing into truncated repressors, with SUFU sequestering full-length GLI. All of this depends on ciliary trafficking, so IFT-A and IFT-B components, the KIF3A kinesin, dynein-2 and tubulins are integral rather than accessory.

The hindbrain is built as a series of transient segments, the rhombomeres, and each segment's identity is set by which of the anterior HOX genes (paralog groups 1-4) is switched on there. Activation of these genes during early embryogenesis gives rise to the cranial nerves, branchial arch derivatives and neural crest patterning of the head and neck; mutations in HOXA1, HOXA2 or HOXB1 cause facial palsy, hearing loss, microtia and eye movement defects. A somite-derived retinoic acid gradient read by RAR/RXR heterodimers initiates HOXA1 and HOXB1 expression, which then feeds into EGR2 and MAFB to set successive rhombomere boundaries, with HOX proteins acting combinatorially with TALE partners such as PBX1, MEIS1 and PKNOX1. Onset is controlled at chromatin: Polycomb components including EZH2, EED and SUZ12 hold clusters silenced in a bivalent state, while trithorax-related MLL/COMPASS subunits, KDM6A demethylase activity and CBP/p300 acetylation license sequential, colinear transcription by RNA polymerase II.

Cilium assembly builds the microtubule-based projections that let cells sense their surroundings and move fluid across epithelial surfaces. The primary cilium is the antenna for Hedgehog signalling, while motile cilia clear airway mucus, drive cerebrospinal fluid flow and establish left-right asymmetry; photoreceptor outer segments and olfactory sensory cilia are specialized variants, reflected here by rhodopsin and cyclic-nucleotide-gated channel subunits. A centriole-derived basal body docks at the membrane through distal appendage proteins, a transition zone with nephrocystins, MKS and tectonic components forms a diffusion barrier, and tubulins are polymerized at the tip. Cargo moves by intraflagellar transport: kinesin-2 with the IFT-B complex carries material outward, dynein-2 with IFT-A returns it, and BBSome subunits sort membrane proteins. Transcriptional control by FOXJ1, RFX factors and multiciliate regulators specifies ciliated cells. Mutations in these components cause ciliopathies, including polycystic kidney disease, retinal degeneration and Bardet-Biedl syndrome.

Sialic acid released by lysosomal breakdown of glycoproteins and glycolipids has to leave the lysosome to be reused or excreted, and sialin, the proton-driven lysosomal transporter encoded by SLC17A5, is the exporter that does it. When the transporter is defective, free N-acetylneuraminic acid accumulates in lysosomes and spills into urine, producing the autosomal recessive sialic acid storage disorders: Salla disease, with hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia and intellectual disability, and the far more severe infantile form, in which storage causes early organomegaly, dysmorphism and death. Export depends on the acidic proton electrochemical gradient across the lysosomal membrane, coupling this step to organelle acidification. The disorders illustrate how a single failed catabolite efflux route converts normal glycoconjugate turnover into a progressive neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disease, with white matter and myelin particularly vulnerable.

Melanin production in pigment cells depends on getting calcium into and out of the organelles where the pigment is made, and SLC24A5 is the potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchanger that does this job in melanocytes. Sitting in trans-Golgi membranes, it trades one calcium and one potassium ion for four sodium ions, shaping the local calcium environment that melanosome maturation and tyrosinase-dependent melanin synthesis require. It is also one of the small number of loci that account for normal variation in human skin colour. Loss-of-function variants reduce or abolish melanin in skin, hair and eyes, producing oculocutaneous albinism type 6, in which hypopigmentation is accompanied by ocular features such as reduced visual acuity, nystagmus and foveal hypoplasia, since retinal development depends on pigment in the eye.

Sialic acid caps many N- and O-glycans and glycolipids, but the enzymes that attach it work inside the Golgi while its activated donor, CMP-sialic acid, is made in the nucleus and cytosol. The SLC35A1 transporter bridges that gap, carrying CMP-sialic acid into the Golgi lumen in exchange for CMP, and it is the sole route by which sialyltransferases obtain substrate. Loss-of-function mutations cause a congenital disorder of glycosylation, CDG2F, in which serum proteins are under-sialylated and patients show neurological impairment, developmental delay, bleeding tendency from defective platelet and von Willebrand factor glycans, and immunodeficiency with impaired leukocyte selectin ligands. The defect illustrates how nucleotide-sugar supply, rather than glycosyltransferase activity itself, sets the ceiling on terminal glycan maturation and on the cell-surface recognition events that depend on sialylation.

KCC3, encoded by SLC12A6, is an electroneutral K+/Cl- cotransporter that moves potassium and chloride out of cells in a 1:1 ratio, serving cell volume regulation, transepithelial salt handling and the setting of intracellular chloride in neurons, where it helps determine whether GABA and glycine signals are inhibitory. The transporter is broadly expressed, with prominent roles in brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerve, kidney, heart and muscle. Loss-of-function mutations cause the autosomal recessive disorder of corpus callosum agenesis with peripheral neuropathy, in which failure of KCC3-dependent volume and ion homeostasis in axons and Schwann cells produces severe progressive sensorimotor neuropathy, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features and variable absence of the corpus callosum. The phenotype illustrates how a housekeeping ion cotransporter becomes indispensable for axonal maintenance and commissural tract development.

Whole-body phosphate balance is set largely by how much filtered phosphate the kidney reclaims, and SLC34A1 is the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter in the proximal tubule brush border that does most of that reclaiming, moving divalent phosphate together with three sodium ions using the inward sodium gradient. When the transporter is defective, phosphate is lost into the urine rather than returned to the blood, producing the hypophosphatemia, hyperphosphaturia and hypercalciuria that define hypophosphatemic nephrolithiasis/osteoporosis type 1. The consequences follow from phosphate's two main uses: mineral is not available for bone matrix, so patients demineralise and develop osteoporosis, while the altered urinary mineral load favours calcium-containing kidney stones. The same transporter is the point at which parathyroid hormone and phosphatonin signalling act to tune renal phosphate excretion, linking this single carrier to endocrine control of skeletal mineralisation.

Defective SLC36A2 causes iminoglycinuria (IG) and hyperglycinuria (HG) describes the loss of a kidney amino acid reabsorption step, the event that lets glycine and the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline escape into urine. SLC36A2 encodes the proton-coupled amino acid transporter PAT2, which uses the inward proton gradient of the proximal tubule brush border to recover filtered glycine and proline with high affinity; it is also expressed in muscle.
