When the transporter is inactivated, reabsorption fails and patients present with iminoglycinuria, an autosomal recessive trait, or the milder hyperglycinuria in which only glycine is lost. Penetrance and the exact urinary profile depend on the accompanying activity of related tubular transporters SLC6A18, SLC6A19 and SLC6A20, so the phenotype behaves as a polygenic threshold rather than a simple single-gene defect. Both conditions are generally benign, illustrating the redundancy of renal amino acid transport.

Reabsorption of glycine, proline and hydroxyproline from the glomerular filtrate depends on proton-coupled amino acid transporter 2, encoded by SLC36A2, which works at the apical membrane of the proximal tubule and uses the inward proton gradient to drive high-affinity uptake of these small amino acids; the same transporter is also expressed in muscle. When the transporter is defective, these substrates escape recovery and appear in urine, producing iminoglycinuria, an autosomal recessive defect of renal imino acid and glycine transport, or the milder hyperglycinuria in which glycine alone is lost. Both conditions are generally benign, and their severity is shaped by co-inherited variants in partner transporters of the same reabsorptive system, so the phenotype behaves as a digenic or polygenic trait rather than a simple single-gene loss.

Defective RHAG causes regulator type Rh-null hemolytic anemia (RHN) describes what happens to red blood cells when the glycoprotein that organises the Rhesus antigen complex is lost. RHAG is an erythroid-specific member of the SLC42 ammonium transporter family and is required for cell-surface expression of the Rh polypeptides; without it the entire complex fails to assemble and the Rh-null phenotype results. Affected red cells are stomatocytic or spherocytic, leak cations, lose normal membrane phospholipid asymmetry, and are cleared prematurely, producing chronic hemolytic anemia of variable severity. RHAG itself is thought to move ammonium across the erythrocyte membrane, preventing toxic NH3/NH4+ accumulation and contributing to systemic nitrogen handling. The pathway therefore links a single transporter defect to red cell membrane architecture, blood group serology, and inherited hemolysis.

The Rh-associated glycoprotein is an erythroid membrane transporter of the Rhesus family that carries ammonium/ammonia across the red cell membrane and, just as importantly, acts as the chaperone required for surface assembly of the whole Rh antigen complex. Loss-of-function mutations in RHAG produce the regulator type of Rh-null disease, in which Rh antigens are absent or severely reduced from the erythrocyte surface even though the genes encoding them are intact. The resulting Rh-deficiency syndrome is a chronic hemolytic anemia: red cells become stomatocytic or spherocytic, show disturbed cation fluxes and abnormal membrane phospholipid asymmetry, and are cleared prematurely. The pathway links solute transport across the erythrocyte membrane to the structural integrity of the red cell, and explains why blood group antigen expression can fail through a defective accessory subunit rather than the antigen itself.

Glucose reaches the brain by facilitated diffusion across the blood-brain barrier, and SLC2A1 (GLUT1) is the transporter that carries it there and into red blood cells, astrocytes and endothelium. Its affinity for glucose is high relative to normal blood levels, so uptake continues steadily regardless of glycaemic swings — a property the brain depends on because it cannot store fuel. Loss-of-function variants cause GLUT1 deficiency syndrome 1, in which cerebrospinal fluid glucose falls and infants develop epileptic encephalopathy, acquired microcephaly, developmental delay, spasticity and movement disorders; milder alleles produce paroxysmal exertion-induced dyskinesia or isolated seizures. The transporter works as a homotetramer of channel-forming subunits, and defective monomers can act dominantly. Because the defect is fuel delivery rather than fuel metabolism, a ketogenic diet supplying ketone bodies as an alternative substrate is the standard treatment.

Neutral amino acids taken in with food are absorbed across the brush border of the small intestine and reclaimed from the glomerular filtrate in the proximal tubule, and B(0)AT1, encoded by SLC6A19, is the sodium-coupled transporter that performs both jobs. Loss-of-function mutations abolish this uptake and cause Hartnup disorder, in which tryptophan and other neutral amino acids are lost in urine and stool; because tryptophan is the precursor for niacin and serotonin, affected individuals can show pellagra-like photosensitive rash, cerebellar ataxia and psychiatric disturbance, typically episodic and provoked by poor diet or intercurrent illness. Certain variants instead contribute to the milder aminoaciduria phenotypes iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria. Transport depends on the inward sodium gradient and on accessory proteins including ACE2 and collectrin for correct apical membrane delivery, placing this pathway within epithelial nutrient absorption and renal solute reabsorption.

Alveolar type II cells must clear the phosphate released as surfactant phospholipids are broken down and recycled, and they do so through the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter SLC34A2, which moves inorganic phosphate across the apical membrane together with sodium ions. When the transporter is lost through inactivating mutation, phosphate accumulates in the alveolar space and precipitates with calcium, filling the lungs with innumerable calcium phosphate microliths. This is pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis, a rare recessive disorder that progresses slowly over decades toward restrictive lung disease and respiratory failure, often with few symptoms until imaging reveals diffuse sand-like calcification. The same transporter is expressed more modestly in intestinal, pancreatic, prostatic and renal epithelia, where it contributes to phosphate handling, so the disease illustrates how a general solute-transport function becomes indispensable in one organ because of the phosphate load that surfactant turnover imposes.

Pendrin is an anion exchanger that trades chloride for bicarbonate, iodide and other anions at the apical membrane of thyroid follicular cells, inner ear epithelium and kidney intercalated cells. In the cochlea it conditions endolymph, setting the ionic composition and pH on which hair cell mechanotransduction depends, and in the thyroid it helps move iodide toward the follicular lumen for thyroid hormone synthesis. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC26A4 cause Pendred syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder combining congenital sensorineural deafness, usually with malformation of the bony labyrinth such as an enlarged vestibular aqueduct, and goitre with variable hypothyroidism; milder alleles give nonsyndromic hearing loss alone. The disease illustrates how a single epithelial transporter links iodide handling for hormone production to fluid homeostasis required for hearing.

Uric acid is the terminal product of purine breakdown in humans, and the kidney decides how much of it is kept rather than lost in urine. GLUT9, the class II facilitative transporter encoded by SLC2A9, performs the reabsorption step in proximal tubule epithelium, moving urate back across the tubular cell with a secondary, low-rate capacity for fructose and glucose; it is also expressed in liver. Loss-of-function variants cause renal hypouricemia type 2, in which urate reabsorption fails and serum urate falls abnormally low while urinary urate excretion rises. Although often asymptomatic, affected individuals are prone to exercise-induced acute kidney injury and to urate nephrolithiasis. The same transporter sits at the opposite end of the spectrum from hyperuricemia and gout, making it a principal determinant of serum urate set point and of purine end-product handling overall.

Dietary iron enters the body through the duodenum, where ferrous iron crosses the apical membrane of enterocytes before being released to the portal circulation; the proton-coupled divalent metal transporter encoded by SLC11A2, also known as DCT1 or NRAMP2, performs that apical uptake step and also moves iron out of the endosome after transferrin receptor-mediated uptake in erythroid precursors. Loss-of-function mutations produce hypochromic microcytic anemia with iron overload, in which red cells are small and poorly hemoglobinized because developing erythroblasts cannot acquire usable iron, yet serum iron is high and the liver accumulates heavy iron deposits, with bone marrow stainable iron and sideroblasts absent. The disorder illustrates how iron distribution rather than total body iron determines erythropoietic success, and connects intestinal absorption, transferrin cycling, and heme synthesis in a single transport activity.

Macrophages that recycle iron from senescent red cells must export it back to plasma, and ferroportin (SLC40A1) is the only cellular iron exporter that does this job. When it fails, iron recovered from haem breakdown is trapped in reticuloendothelial cells and body iron handling becomes deranged, producing type 4 hemochromatosis — an iron overload disorder in which decades of progressive deposition damage liver, heart, pancreas and joints, causing cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, arthritis and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Export requires a partner: the copper-dependent ferroxidase ceruloplasmin colocalises with ferroportin, stabilises it at the cell surface, and oxidises the exported ferrous iron so that it can be loaded onto transferrin. Loss-of-function or trafficking-defective ferroportin variants therefore block the macrophage arm of systemic iron recycling rather than intestinal absorption, which distinguishes this condition from the more common HFE-related disease.

Defective SLC4A1 causes hereditary spherocytosis type 4 (HSP4), distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA) and dRTA with hemolytic anemia (dRTA-HA) covers the disease consequences of losing band 3, the chloride/bicarbonate exchanger that is the most abundant protein of the red cell membrane and the basolateral bicarbonate exit route of kidney alpha-intercalated cells. In erythrocytes it both carries CO2 as bicarbonate during gas exchange and anchors the spectrin-ankyrin cytoskeleton to the lipid bilayer; mutations that destabilise this link produce spherical, fragile cells that are cleared by the spleen, giving hereditary spherocytosis with haemolytic anaemia. In the collecting duct the same exchanger supports net acid secretion, so loss-of-function or mistrafficked variants leave the kidney unable to acidify urine, causing distal renal tubular acidosis with metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis, sometimes together with haemolysis. Normal sequence variation at this locus defines the Diego blood group.

Band 3, the erythrocyte anion exchanger encoded by SLC4A1, swaps chloride for bicarbonate across the membrane and is the most abundant protein of the red cell surface, where it also anchors the spectrin-based cytoskeleton and defines the Diego blood group. The same protein sits in the basolateral membrane of kidney collecting duct alpha-intercalated cells, exporting bicarbonate to blood as protons are pumped into urine. Loss-of-function or mistrafficked variants therefore produce two distinct clinical pictures: membrane destabilisation gives hereditary spherocytosis type 4, with rigid spherical erythrocytes and haemolytic anaemia, while defective renal handling causes distal renal tubular acidosis, an inability to acidify urine that leads to metabolic acidosis, hypokalaemia, nephrocalcinosis and rickets or osteomalacia. Some alleles combine both, presenting as distal renal tubular acidosis with haemolytic anaemia, and inheritance may be dominant or recessive depending on the mutation.

Defective SLC9A9 causes autism 16 (AUTS16) describes what follows when the endosomal sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE9 is lost or impaired, a defect linked to susceptibility to autism spectrum disorder with associated epilepsy and attention deficits. NHE9 sits in the membrane of late and recycling endosomes, where it leaks protons back out in exchange for sodium or potassium and so sets the luminal pH of that compartment. Because endosomal acidity governs how quickly cargo is sorted and returned to the cell surface, this housekeeping activity determines the surface residence of glutamate transporters and synaptic receptors in neurons and glia. Mutations that reduce exchange activity over-acidify endosomes, slow recycling, and alter excitatory synaptic signalling, connecting a general ion-homeostasis function to the reciprocal social interaction, communication, and stereotyped behaviour phenotypes that define the pervasive developmental disorders.

The endosomal sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE9, encoded by SLC9A9, sets the luminal pH of recycling and late endosomes by trading luminal protons for cytosolic sodium or potassium, countering the acidification driven by the vacuolar ATPase. Because compartment pH governs how fast receptors and transporters are returned to the cell surface, this housekeeping activity has particular consequences in neurons and glia, where it influences surface levels of glutamate transporters and synaptic receptor recycling. Loss-of-function and truncating variants in the gene confer susceptibility to autism 16, a form of the prototypic pervasive developmental disorder marked by impaired reciprocal social interaction and communication, restricted and stereotyped interests, and developmental abnormalities evident before age three; the same locus has been linked to attention deficit and epilepsy phenotypes, illustrating how over-acidified endosomes disturb neurodevelopmental signalling.

Carnitine is the carrier that allows long-chain fatty acids to enter mitochondria for beta-oxidation, and cells cannot make enough of it to meet demand, so they depend on uptake from plasma. OCTN2, encoded by SLC22A5, is the sodium-dependent high-affinity carnitine transporter that performs this uptake and, in the kidney, reabsorbs filtered carnitine to keep systemic levels high; it is prominent in heart, skeletal muscle and placenta. Loss-of-function mutations cause systemic primary carnitine deficiency, an autosomal recessive fatty-acid oxidation disorder in which carnitine is wasted in the urine and tissue stores fall. Affected children present with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, myopathy and cardiomyopathy that progresses to fatal heart failure if untreated, yet the phenotype is largely reversible with oral carnitine supplementation, making this transport step a treatable link between membrane transport and mitochondrial energy production.

Reabsorbing filtered bicarbonate in the kidney proximal tubule is how the body defends blood pH, and the electrogenic sodium-bicarbonate cotransporter NBCe1, encoded by SLC4A4, carries out the basolateral exit step that completes it, moving one Na+ with three HCO3- out of the tubular cell into blood. Loss-of-function mutations block this exit, so bicarbonate is wasted in urine and a permanent isolated proximal renal tubular acidosis develops, accompanied in this recessive syndrome by short stature, intellectual disability, and ocular disease including bilateral glaucoma, cataracts, and band keratopathy. The eye findings reflect the same transporter's role in bicarbonate movement across corneal endothelium and ciliary epithelium, where it supports aqueous humour formation and intraocular pressure homeostasis. The protein also contributes to bicarbonate secretion in pancreatic duct and other epithelia, making systemic acid-base balance dependent on a single carrier.

Tooth enamel is the hardest tissue in the body, and its mineralization depends on ameloblasts pumping large amounts of calcium into the developing enamel matrix. SLC24A4 encodes NCKX4, a potassium-dependent sodium/calcium exchanger that couples the inward movement of four Na+ ions to the extrusion of one Ca2+ together with one K+, and it is strongly induced in ameloblasts during the maturation stage when mineral is deposited and the matrix is hardened. Loss-of-function mutations that diminish or abolish this transport activity cause an autosomal recessive hypomineralized form of amelogenesis imperfecta, in which enamel forms at near-normal thickness but remains soft, discoloured and prone to rapid wear and fracture. The same gene carries common variants associated with blond versus brown hair and blue versus green eye colour, linking this calcium exchanger to pigmentation variation as well as to biomineralization.

Hexokinase 1 catalyses the first and irreversible step of glycolysis, phosphorylating glucose to glucose-6-phosphate using ATP, and it is the predominant hexokinase in tissues that depend on glucose for their function, including brain, erythrocytes, platelets, lymphocytes and fibroblasts. Loss-of-function mutations in HK1 cause hexokinase deficiency, a rare autosomal recessive disorder whose main clinical feature is nonspherocytic haemolytic anaemia. Red cells are especially vulnerable because they have no mitochondria and no alternative route to ATP: reduced flux through this committed entry step starves glycolysis, depletes ATP and 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, and shortens erythrocyte survival. The defect illustrates how a single rate-determining kinase governs glucose commitment to energy production and to downstream branches such as the pentose phosphate pathway that supply reducing power against oxidative stress.

Conjugated bilirubin leaving the hepatocyte into bile is partly re-entering the liver from blood, and the basolateral organic anion transporter SLCO1B3 (OATP1B3) is one of the two carriers that perform that hepatic reuptake. Loss of this uptake step, described here as defective SLCO1B3 causing Rotor-type hyperbilirubinemia, leaves conjugated bilirubin to spill into plasma and urine, producing a mild autosomal recessive jaundice that appears soon after birth or in childhood without hemolysis; the clinically relevant syndrome requires simultaneous loss of the related OATP1B1 carrier. Because the same transporter takes up bile salts, thyroid hormone conjugates, and many drugs including statins and methotrexate, its failure also alters hepatic drug clearance. The biology sits at the sinusoidal entry point of heme catabolism, upstream of glucuronidation and canalicular biliary excretion.

Iron leaving a cell must be oxidised before plasma transferrin can accept it, and the plasma ferroxidase ceruloplasminemia is named for is what performs that step. Ceruloplasmin, a copper-loaded glycoprotein secreted by the liver, oxidises ferrous to ferric iron at the cell surface and keeps the iron exporter ferroportin stable there; loss-of-function mutations in CP therefore block iron export rather than iron uptake. The result is aceruloplasminemia, a recessive disorder in which iron is trapped in tissues while serum iron and transferrin saturation fall, producing accumulation in brain, liver, pancreas and retina with retinal degeneration, diabetes and progressive neurological deterioration. It is counted among the syndromes of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and is distinct both from hemochromatosis, which spares the brain, and from copper-handling diseases such as Wilson and Menkes disease.

Loss of function in SLC33A1 explains an inherited form of lower-limb spasticity, spastic paraplegia 42, in which corticospinal motor axons degenerate and weakness and spasticity of the legs progress at variable rates. The gene encodes the acetyl-CoA transporter AT1, which moves cytosolic acetyl-CoA across the membrane into the Golgi lumen, supplying the acetyl donor that resident acetyltransferases use to O-acetylate sialic acid residues on gangliosides and glycoproteins. Without that supply, the acetylation status of cell-surface glycoconjugates is altered, a modification that long neurons appear especially to depend on. Other mutations in the same transporter produce a recessive syndrome combining congenital cataracts, hearing loss and neurodegeneration with low serum copper and ceruloplasmin, linking Golgi acetyl-CoA import to both motor and sensory function.

Glutamate released at synapses must be cleared quickly, and the astrocytic transporter SLC1A3 (EAAT1/GLAST) does much of that clearing in the cerebellum, with additional expression in frontal cortex, hippocampus and basal ganglia. Uptake is driven by the sodium electrochemical gradient, with co-transport of Na+ and a proton and counter-transport of K+, allowing glutamate to be moved into cells against its concentration gradient and returned to neurons through the glutamate-glutamine cycle. Loss-of-function mutations reduce this clearance capacity, so extracellular glutamate lingers and neurons become hyperexcitable; the resulting disorder, episodic ataxia type 6, features attacks of ataxia together with seizures and hemiplegic episodes. The same failure illustrates why transporter activity protects against glutamate excitotoxicity, linking a single astrocyte membrane carrier to the control of excitatory signalling and neuronal survival in the central nervous system.

Nucleosides released inside lysosomes by the degradation of nucleic acids must be returned to the cytosol for salvage, and the equilibrative nucleoside transporter ENT3, encoded by SLC29A3, is the lysosomal membrane carrier that does this. It moves purine and pyrimidine nucleosides bidirectionally and also handles nucleoside-analogue drugs such as cladribine, cordycepin, tubercidin and zidovudine, so transporter activity influences how these agents reach their intracellular targets. Loss-of-function mutations cause the autosomal recessive histiocytosis-lymphadenopathy plus syndrome, in which patients show overlapping features of several histiocytic disorders: infiltration by pigmented histiocytes, lymphadenopathy, hyperpigmentation, insulin-dependent diabetes, hearing loss and cardiac anomalies. The disease phenotype points to macrophage and histiocyte biology as particularly dependent on lysosomal nucleoside export, with undischarged lysosomal contents driving abnormal accumulation and activation of these cells.

Loss of function in the imprinted organic cation transporter-like protein ORCTL2, encoded at chromosome 11p15.5, links a membrane transport defect to tumour predisposition. The intact protein is a proton-coupled antiporter for organic cations such as chloroquine and quinidine, expressed most strongly in kidney, liver and colon and more weakly in heart, brain and lung, and it is thought to export xenobiotics and potentially genotoxic compounds from cells. Mutation or transcriptional silencing accompanies lung cancer and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and the locus lies within the region whose imprinting is disrupted in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, where Wilms' tumour, rhabdomyosarcoma and hepatoblastoma risk is raised. How the transporter restrains growth is unsettled; proposals centre on retention of DNA-damaging substrates and on altered handling of chemotherapeutic cations, placing this biology at the junction of solute transport, genomic imprinting and tumour suppression.

SLC1A1 encodes EAAT3 (EAAC1), a sodium-dependent high-affinity transporter that pulls glutamate and aspartate into cells against their concentration gradient, cotransporting Na+ and H+ while exporting K+. In brain it clears synaptic glutamate as part of the glutamate-glutamine cycle, protecting neurons from excitotoxic death; in the apical membrane of kidney proximal tubule and intestine it reclaims filtered dicarboxylic amino acids. When the transporter is defective, both roles fail. Loss-of-function changes such as R445W and I395del cause dicarboxylic aminoaciduria, in which glutamate and aspartate are wasted in the urine, while variants and deletions affecting the gene confer susceptibility to schizophrenia 18, consistent with the synaptic and glutamatergic disturbances seen in psychotic illness. The gene therefore links excitatory neurotransmitter handling to renal amino acid reabsorption, and its impairment illustrates how a single carrier serves quite different organs.

Defective SLC2A10 causes arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) describes what happens when a cell loses GLUT10, a high-affinity glucose transporter of the class III facilitative carrier family, and why that loss is felt in the arterial wall rather than in metabolism. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC2A10 cause arterial tortuosity syndrome, an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder in which the aorta and other large arteries become elongated, twisted, aneurysmal and prone to dissection, often with early death, alongside joint laxity and skin hyperextensibility. GLUT10 is expressed most strongly in liver and pancreas but present broadly, and is thought to supply dehydroascorbate to intracellular compartments; its absence disturbs redox balance and TGF-beta signalling in vascular smooth muscle, degrading elastic fibre assembly in the extracellular matrix. The pathway therefore links sugar transport to arterial structural integrity.

Arterial tortuosity syndrome follows loss of function of GLUT10, the high-affinity glucose transporter encoded by SLC2A10 and one of the class III facilitative sugar carriers. GLUT10 is most abundant in liver and pancreas but present at lower levels in most tissues, and its transport activity is thought to supply dehydroascorbate or glucose to intracellular compartments where redox balance and collagen and elastin processing depend on ascorbate. When both alleles are defective, the elastic fibre architecture of large arteries is abnormal and vessels become elongated and corkscrew-like, with aneurysm, stenosis and dissection; affected individuals also show joint laxity, skin hyperextensibility and craniofacial features, and death may occur early in life. The gene lies in a chromosomal interval linked to type 2 diabetes susceptibility, connecting sugar transport to connective tissue integrity and vascular wall mechanics.

Muscle, red cells and glia constantly export or import lactate, pyruvate and ketone bodies, and MCT1 is the proton-coupled carrier that moves them across the plasma membrane. Loss-of-function changes in SLC16A1 cause symptomatic deficiency in lactate transport, in which lactate cannot leave exercising muscle; the cytoplasm acidifies and fibres break down, releasing myoglobin and creatine kinase after exertion, so that otherwise healthy carriers are limited at extreme workloads. Functional transport requires the accessory glycoprotein basigin (CD147), which chaperones MCT1 to the surface and stabilises it there. The same carrier supplies energy metabolites from astrocytes and oligodendrocytes to axons, linking its failure to axonal degeneration, and its high expression on glycolytic tumour cells governs uptake of monocarboxylate-mimicking drugs such as 3-bromopyruvate. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of energy metabolism and acid-base homeostasis.

Blood urate levels are set largely in the kidney, where most filtered urate is recovered rather than excreted, and URAT1 encoded by SLC22A12 is the apical exchanger in proximal tubule cells that performs that reabsorption, swapping urate for intracellular organic anions such as lactate. Loss-of-function mutations cause renal hypouricemia type 1, in which urate escapes into the urine, serum urate falls to very low levels, and patients are prone to exercise-induced acute kidney injury and urolithiasis. Because urate is both an end product of purine catabolism and a circulating antioxidant that precipitates when concentrated, this single transport step links purine metabolism to gout risk at one extreme and to antioxidant deficiency at the other, and it is the target of uricosuric drugs used to lower serum urate.

Galactose cannot be added to glycans unless its activated donor, UDP-galactose, is first carried from the cytosol into the Golgi lumen, and SLC35A2 is the transporter that does this, exchanging UDP-Gal (and UDP-GalNAc) for UMP across the Golgi membrane. Loss of function starves lumenal glycosyltransferases of substrate, so N-glycans stall as truncated GlcNAc-terminated structures and mucin-type O-glycans remain GalNAc-terminated, a biochemical signature shared with other congenital disorders of glycosylation in which serum glycoproteins are under-glycosylated. The clinical consequence, CDG type 2M, presents in infancy with developmental delay, hypotonia, ocular abnormalities and brain malformations, and the same X-linked defect underlies a severe early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with tonic seizures and spasms. The pathway illustrates how nucleotide-sugar supply, rather than the glycosyltransferases themselves, can limit secretory protein maturation and neurodevelopment.

Glucokinase acts as the glucose sensor of the pancreatic beta cell and the gatekeeper of hepatic glucose uptake, phosphorylating glucose to glucose-6-phosphate as the committed first step of glycolysis. Unlike the other hexokinases, it has a low affinity for glucose and is not strongly inhibited by its product, so its activity tracks blood glucose across the physiological range and couples rising glucose to ATP production and insulin release. Loss-of-function mutations raise the threshold at which beta cells secrete insulin, producing maturity-onset diabetes of the young type 2: mild, stable, non-progressive fasting hyperglycaemia presenting in childhood or early adulthood that usually needs no pharmacological treatment. Impaired hepatic glycogen storage after meals accompanies the secretory defect.

Loading glutamate into synaptic vesicles is what allows a neuron to release it, and the vesicular transporter encoded by SLC17A8 (VGLUT3) does this job using the proton electrochemical gradient built by the vacuolar H+-ATPase rather than a sodium gradient. Its most striking requirement is in the cochlea: inner hair cells depend on this transporter to fill their vesicles and transmit sound-evoked signals to afferent auditory nerve fibres. When the transporter is defective, that synapse falls silent and the result is autosomal dominant deafness 25, a non-syndromic sensorineural hearing loss; mice lacking the gene are congenitally deaf and hearing can be restored by gene replacement. The same transporter also operates in restricted neuronal populations and astrocytes of the central nervous system, contributing to excitatory glutamatergic transmission and the wider glutamate-glutamine cycle.

Defective SLC24A1 causes congenital stationary night blindness 1D (CSNB1D) describes what happens to rod photoreceptors when they cannot expel calcium after light stimulation. SLC24A1 encodes NCKX1, a sodium/calcium-potassium exchanger enriched in rod outer segments that trades four Na+ for one Ca2+ and one K+, providing the calcium efflux arm of phototransduction. Light closes the cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and continued exchange by NCKX1 lowers outer segment calcium, which resets guanylate cyclase and channel sensitivity so that rods recover and adapt to changing illumination. Loss-of-function mutations block this recalibration, and affected individuals inherit an autosomal recessive, non-progressive impairment of night vision with a Riggs-type electroretinogram reflecting reduced rod response amplitude. The condition illustrates how calcium homeostasis in a sensory cell, rather than the excitatory signal itself, sets the dynamic range of vision in dim light.

Rod photoreceptors recover from a flash of light by clearing calcium from the outer segment, and the exchanger encoded by SLC24A1 is what does that clearing. It carries one Ca2+ and one K+ out in exchange for four Na+ entering, using both the sodium and potassium gradients so that calcium can be extruded against a steep gradient; the resulting fall in cytosolic calcium resets cyclic nucleotide synthesis and channel sensitivity, which is the basis of light adaptation and of the rod's ability to respond to a second stimulus. Loss-of-function mutations cause congenital stationary night blindness 1D, an autosomal recessive, non-progressive condition in which patients see poorly in dim light and show a Riggs-type electroretinogram indicating that rod phototransduction itself is impaired rather than the downstream bipolar cell connection.

Fucose must be delivered into the Golgi lumen as GDP-fucose before any fucosyltransferase can use it, and SLC35C1 is the transporter that does this. Loss-of-function mutations cause the congenital disorder of glycosylation type 2C, also known as leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II: without luminal GDP-fucose, glycoproteins lose their fucose-dependent epitopes, most conspicuously the sialyl-Lewis X ligands that neutrophils need to roll on selectins at inflamed endothelium. The result is recurrent bacterial infection with persistently high circulating neutrophil counts that cannot reach tissue, alongside the Bombay-like blood group phenotype, growth failure, dysmorphic features and marked psychomotor retardation. The defect illustrates how a single nucleotide-sugar transport step upstream of Golgi glycan maturation determines leukocyte trafficking and neurodevelopment; some patients respond partially to oral fucose supplementation, which raises cytosolic substrate levels for residual transporter activity.

Dopamine signalling at the synapse is terminated by pumping the transmitter back into the presynaptic neuron, and the sodium-dependent dopamine transporter DAT, encoded by SLC6A3, is the pump that does it. By clearing released dopamine from the cleft it sets the duration and amplitude of dopaminergic transmission and replenishes the vesicular pool, which matters most in the nigrostriatal circuits that control voluntary movement. Loss-of-function mutations disable this reuptake and cause infantile parkinsonism-dystonia, in which affected children develop hypokinesia, rigidity and dystonic movements from the first months of life, with a characteristic rise in dopamine metabolites relative to the parent transmitter. The transporter couples dopamine influx to the inward sodium and chloride gradients, and is also the site of action of cocaine and amphetamines, so defective clearance links transporter biology to both inherited movement disorder and psychostimulant pharmacology.

Branched N-glycans can only be extended inside the Golgi if the donor sugar is delivered there, and SLC35A3 is the transporter that does it, moving UDP-N-acetylglucosamine from the cytosol into the Golgi lumen in exchange for UMP. The imported donor supplies the Golgi glycosyltransferases that add successive GlcNAc branches to maturing N-glycans. When the transporter is defective, cells make far fewer tetraantennary structures and accumulate abnormally under-branched glycoproteins, even though the serum glycome can look unremarkable — a reminder that congenital glycosylation defects are not always visible in circulating proteins. The clinical consequence is arthrogryposis with intellectual disability and seizures, linking a single Golgi solute carrier to joint contractures and neurodevelopmental impairment, and placing this step within congenital disorders of glycosylation.

ATP-binding cassette transporters use ATP hydrolysis to pump lipids, bile salts, ions, metals, vitamin B12 derivatives and drugs across membranes, and mutations in roughly a third of the human family cause defined disease. Collected here are those disease-linked transporters together with the quality-control machinery that disposes of the misfolded mutant proteins. Loss of ABCA1 abolishes cholesterol efflux to apolipoprotein A-I in Tangier disease; CFTR defects cause cystic fibrosis; ABCB11 and ABCB4 mutations produce cholestasis; ABCG5/ABCG8 restrict dietary sterol absorption in sitosterolaemia; ABCC8 and KCNJ11 form the pancreatic KATP channel controlling insulin secretion; ABCD1 underlies X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. Many mutant alleles fail to fold in the endoplasmic reticulum and are retained by lectin-like sensors, routed through SEL1L, derlins and RNF5/RNF185 ubiquitin ligases, extracted by VCP and degraded by the proteasome, so the clinical phenotype reflects degradation as much as transport loss.

Absorption of salt and water by the intestine depends on an apical chloride/bicarbonate exchanger in the colon and ileum, and loss of that exchanger is the basis of congenital secretory chloride diarrhea. SLC26A3, historically called down-regulated in adenoma, takes up luminal chloride in exchange for bicarbonate, working alongside sodium/hydrogen exchange so that NaCl and fluid are reclaimed from stool; the bicarbonate it secretes also helps set luminal pH and mucus properties. When the transporter is defective, chloride remains in the lumen and draws water with it, producing watery chloride-rich stools from birth, dehydration, potassium loss and metabolic alkalosis, with maternal polyhydramnios before delivery. The same exchanger sits in the sperm midpiece membrane, where chloride/bicarbonate handling during epididymal maturation contributes to fertility, so carriers of certain alleles may show subfertility in addition to intestinal disease.

Salt reclaimed in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidney is taken up by the thiazide-sensitive sodium-chloride cotransporter encoded by SLC12A3, the final fine-tuning step in renal sodium handling and a determinant of blood pressure and body fluid volume. Loss-of-function mutations in this transporter cause Gitelman syndrome, an autosomal recessive salt-wasting disorder in which patients develop hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with hypomagnesemia and low urinary calcium, and may suffer episodes of muscle weakness, tetany, abdominal pain and vomiting. Reduced apical NaCl uptake drives compensatory distal potassium and hydrogen secretion, explaining the electrolyte picture. The phenotype overlaps the loop-transporter defects of Bartter syndrome but is milder and more distal in origin. Because this same cotransporter is the target of thiazide diuretics, the disease effectively reproduces chronic pharmacological blockade of distal salt reabsorption.

Dietary zinc must cross the intestinal brush border before it can reach any tissue, and the ZIP4 transporter encoded by SLC39A4 is the apical carrier that performs this uptake in the duodenum and jejunum. Loss-of-function mutations block that step and cause acrodermatitis enteropathica of the zinc-deficiency type, an inherited disorder in which infants develop a characteristic perioral and acral dermatitis, diarrhoea, alopecia, growth retardation, impaired immune function and neurobehavioural disturbance, all reversible with oral zinc supplementation. Because zinc is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and for zinc-finger transcription factors, failure of absorption is felt most acutely in rapidly renewing tissues such as skin, gut epithelium and lymphocytes. Normally the transporter is itself regulated by zinc status, being trafficked to the apical membrane when supply is low, linking whole-body zinc homeostasis to intestinal cell surface expression.

Glycine acts as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord and brainstem, and its signal is switched off by sodium- and chloride-dependent reuptake into presynaptic terminals. The transporter GLYT2, encoded by SLC6A5 and enriched in the medulla and spinal cord, performs that clearance and refills inhibitory vesicles with glycine, so loss-of-function mutations starve glycinergic synapses of transmitter. The result is hyperekplexia type 3, or startle disease: neonatal hypertonia, an exaggerated and non-habituating startle to touch or sound, and apnoeic episodes that can be life-threatening, though symptoms often ease during the first year. The condition illustrates how inhibitory neurotransmission restrains spinal motor reflexes, and places presynaptic transmitter recycling, rather than receptor signalling itself, at the root of this form of impaired glycinergic inhibition.

The endosomal sodium/hydrogen exchanger NHE6, encoded by SLC9A6, leaks protons back out of early and recycling endosomes in exchange for Na+ or K+, setting the luminal pH at which receptors are sorted, ligands released and cargo returned to the plasma membrane. Because neurons depend on endosomal recycling for synapse growth, receptor trafficking and glutamatergic signalling, loss of this activity over-acidifies the compartment and disrupts neuronal arborisation and synaptic maintenance. Loss-of-function mutations cause the X-linked syndromic intellectual disability of Christianson type, in which affected males show profound intellectual disability, epilepsy, ataxia, microcephaly and postnatal neurodegeneration, a presentation often mistaken for Angelman syndrome. The transporter is expressed widely but is most abundant in brain, heart and skeletal muscle, linking endosomal pH homeostasis to neurodevelopmental disease rather than to any single signalling route.

SLC6A14 is a sodium- and chloride-coupled plasma membrane transporter with unusually broad specificity, carrying neutral and cationic amino acids plus beta-alanine into cells, with each amino acid imported alongside two sodium ions and one chloride. Because its substrates include tryptophan, the transporter can influence how much precursor is available for serotonin synthesis, and through that route appetite regulation and body weight; sequence variants in the gene have been linked to obesity susceptibility in some populations, and the locus lies on the X chromosome. Expression is high in lung and low or absent in intestine and kidney, so its amino acid supply role is tissue-biased rather than general. The same transporter is exploited by proliferating cells for amino acid nutrition, and impaired transport activity illustrates how a single solute carrier defect can register as a metabolic rather than a transport disorder.

Defective SLCO2A1 causes primary, autosomal recessive hypertrophic osteoarthropathy 2 (PHOAR2) concerns loss of the prostaglandin transporter PGT, the carrier that moves prostaglandins across the plasma membrane and thereby terminates their signalling. SLCO2A1 is expressed nearly everywhere and handles PGD2, PGE1, PGE2 and PGF2A, taking up circulating prostaglandins for cytoplasmic degradation and contributing to release of newly synthesised mediators. When the transporter fails, PGE2 accumulates in tissue and plasma and its receptors are chronically stimulated, driving bone remodelling and soft tissue overgrowth. The result is primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, a rare recessive genodermatosis with thickened facial and limb skin, digital clubbing, periostosis and painful joint swelling, more severe in males. The condition illustrates that prostaglandin inactivation by transport is as much a control point in eicosanoid signalling as synthesis by cyclooxygenases, and explains why COX inhibitors relieve symptoms.

Prostaglandins act locally and must be cleared from tissue and circulation once they have signalled, and the prostaglandin transporter encoded by SLCO2A1 is the carrier that performs this uptake. It is broadly expressed and moves PGE1, PGE2, PGD2 and PGF2alpha across the plasma membrane, supporting both the release of newly synthesised prostaglandins and their delivery to intracellular degradation by 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase. Loss-of-function mutations block that uptake, so PGE2 accumulates and drives sustained signalling in skin, periosteum and vasculature. The result is primary autosomal recessive hypertrophic osteoarthropathy type 2, a rare genodermatosis with thickened facial skin, digital clubbing and periosteal new bone formation, more often symptomatic in males. The condition illustrates how eicosanoid signalling is terminated by transport rather than by receptor shutdown alone, and overlaps clinically with deficiency of the degrading enzyme itself.

Thyroid hormone synthesis begins with the thyrocyte concentrating iodide from the blood, and the sodium/iodide symporter NIS, encoded by SLC5A5, is the transporter that does it, coupling inward sodium movement down its electrochemical gradient to active iodide uptake across the basolateral membrane. When this transport fails, the gland can no longer trap iodide against a plasma gradient, thyroglobulin iodination is starved of substrate, and too little T4 and T3 is made. The result is thyroid dyshormonogenesis type 1, a form of congenital hypothyroidism presenting with goitre and, untreated, impaired growth and neurodevelopment, since thyroid hormone drives brain maturation and basal metabolic rate. The same transporter underlies diagnostic radioiodine scanning and radioiodine therapy of thyroid cancer, so loss-of-function variants also predict poor isotope uptake.

Phosphate recovered from the glomerular filtrate is reclaimed at the apical brush border of the kidney proximal tubule, and the sodium-dependent cotransporter encoded by SLC34A3 (NaPi-IIc) carries out part of that reabsorption, moving two sodium ions with each phosphate in an electroneutral step driven by the inward sodium gradient. Loss-of-function mutations cause hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria, an autosomal recessive disorder in which phosphate is wasted into the urine, serum phosphate falls, and bone mineralisation fails, producing rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults. Because hypophosphatemia here is not driven by excess FGF23, circulating 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rises appropriately and drives intestinal calcium absorption, giving the hypercalciuria and predisposition to nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis that distinguish this condition from FGF23-mediated phosphate wasting. The pathway links renal solute transport to systemic mineral homeostasis and skeletal growth.

Defective SLC2A2 causes Fanconi-Bickel syndrome (FBS) describes what happens when cells lose their bidirectional exit route for glucose, galactose and fructose. SLC2A2 (GLUT2) is a low-affinity facilitative hexose transporter placed at the basolateral membrane of intestinal and renal proximal tubule epithelium and in hepatocytes and pancreatic beta cells, where it lets dietary sugars taken up apically pass into the circulation, allows the liver to move glucose in either direction according to fed or fasting state, and lets beta cells sense ambient glucose before secreting insulin. Loss-of-function mutations produce Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, in which hepatic and renal glycogen accumulates, the proximal tubule leaks glucose, phosphate, amino acids and bicarbonate, and galactose and glucose utilisation is impaired, causing rickets, hepatomegaly and growth failure. The pathway thus links transepithelial sugar absorption to whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Fanconi-Bickel syndrome is what follows loss of the low-affinity hexose transporter GLUT2, encoded by SLC2A2, and it shows how much whole-body sugar handling depends on a single facilitative carrier. GLUT2 moves glucose, galactose and fructose bidirectionally across the plasma membrane down their concentration gradients, sitting basolaterally in intestinal and renal proximal tubule epithelium to release dietary and reabsorbed sugars into blood, allowing the liver to take up or export glucose as feeding state demands, and serving pancreatic beta cells as part of the glucose-sensing step that sets insulin release. When the transporter is defective, glucose is trapped intracellularly and stored as glycogen, giving hepatorenal glycogen accumulation, proximal tubular wasting, rickets and stunted growth with impaired glucose and galactose utilisation.

Water balance depends on vasopressin, a nine-residue hormone cleaved from the AVP precursor in hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary when plasma osmolarity rises or blood volume falls. Acting through its receptors, it drives aquaporin-2 trafficking to the apical membrane of kidney collecting duct cells so that water is reabsorbed rather than lost in urine, and it also raises vascular tone and stimulates pituitary ACTH release through the AVPR1A and AVPR1B subtypes. Mutations in the AVP gene disrupt folding and processing of the prohormone, so that mature hormone is not secreted and cannot reach its receptors; this failure of ligand availability, not receptor defect, underlies autosomal dominant familial neurohypophyseal diabetes insipidus, with unremitting thirst, compulsive drinking and passage of large volumes of dilute urine, and reflects the progressive loss of magnocellular neurons that accumulate misfolded precursor.

Reabsorption of glycine and the imino acids proline and hydroxyproline from the kidney filtrate depends on a small set of apical sodium-dependent transporters, and SLC6A20 encodes one of them, SIT1, which carries proline, N-methylated amino acids and glycine into intestinal and renal epithelial cells. A common coding variant, the T199M substitution, reduces this transport capacity, and when it accompanies loss-of-function mutations in the principal proline transporter it contributes to hyperglycinuria and iminoglycinuria, benign conditions in which glycine alone, or glycine together with proline and hydroxyproline, is spilled into the urine. The phenotype is therefore polygenic: SLC6A20 behaves as a modifier alongside other neutral amino acid transporters of the same brush border, and the case illustrates how amino acid salvage at epithelial surfaces sets urinary composition rather than causing systemic disease.

Solute carriers are the membrane transporters that move sugars, amino acids, ions, metals, nucleosides, vitamins and organic anions across plasma and organelle membranes, and this collection gathers those in which loss-of-function mutations cause recognisable human disease. The clinical range shows how much depends on them: glucose transporter defects cause epileptic encephalopathy and renal glycosuria, thiazide- and loop-sensitive salt transporters underlie Gitelman and Bartter syndromes, divalent metal and ferroportin transporters cause iron overload or anaemia, amino acid carriers cause cystinuria and lysinuric protein intolerance, nucleotide-sugar transporters cause congenital glycosylation disorders, and thyroid iodide uptake failure causes hypothyroidism. Alongside the carriers themselves are accessory subunits and the nuclear pore complex, whose nucleocytoplasmic transport channel represents a distinct route of macromolecular movement with its own nephrotic and neurological disease phenotypes. Together they frame epithelial absorption, reabsorption in the kidney and intestine, and neurotransmitter clearance as transporter-dependent physiology.

Salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle depends on the apical Na-K-2Cl cotransporter NKCC2, encoded by SLC12A1, which moves one sodium, one potassium and two chloride ions together into the tubular cell and thereby generates the medullary osmotic gradient used to concentrate urine. Loss-of-function mutations abolish this transport and cause antenatal Bartter syndrome type 1, an autosomal recessive salt-wasting disorder in which hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis and hypercalciuria appear in infancy alongside polyuria, polydipsia, failure to thrive and muscle weakness. The same transporter is the target of loop diuretics, so the disease phenotype resembles chronic furosemide exposure. Defective cotransport also removes the driving force for paracellular calcium and magnesium recovery, linking this single carrier to whole-body electrolyte, volume and acid-base homeostasis.

Traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm passes through the nuclear pore complex, and TPR forms the basket on its nuclear face, anchoring filaments that guide mRNA export and protein import. This pathway frames what happens when TPR is defective: the basket scaffold fails, nucleocytoplasmic transport is degraded, and rearrangements involving TPR are associated with susceptibility to papillary thyroid carcinoma, the commonest thyroid malignancy. The illustrative cargo here is the glucokinase-glucokinase regulatory protein complex, whose nuclear sequestration controls hepatic glucose phosphorylation according to fructose and glucose levels; its shuttling depends on an intact pore. The remaining members are the pore's own parts, from the structural Y-complex scaffold and transmembrane ring through the FG-repeat channel nucleoporins and the cytoplasmic filament proteins that handle export. Together they connect pore architecture to gene expression, metabolic regulation, and oncogenesis.

Long-chain fatty acids enter cells through fatty acid transport proteins, and SLC27A4 (FATP4) is the member that combines transport with acyl-CoA synthetase activity, activating the very-long-chain fatty acids needed to build epidermal ceramides. It is the major intestinal long-chain fatty acid transporter and is also expressed in brain, kidney, liver, heart and, importantly, in keratinocytes, where it supports formation of the skin permeability barrier during epidermal development. Loss-of-function mutations cause ichthyosis prematurity syndrome, a keratinisation disorder presenting with premature birth, thickened epidermis, neonatal respiratory complications and lifelong non-scaly ichthyosis. The defect illustrates how lipid uptake and activation feed directly into barrier lipid synthesis: without functional FATP4, cornified envelope lipids are abnormal and the epidermis cannot restrict water loss, linking a single transport step to whole-organ skin function.

Noradrenaline released at sympathetic and central synapses is cleared largely by reuptake into the releasing neuron, and the sodium- and chloride-coupled norepinephrine transporter encoded by SLC6A2 does that work, recapturing the transmitter for vesicular storage and reuse and thereby setting how long and how strongly adrenergic signalling persists. The transporter is found in noradrenergic neurons of the central nervous system and in the adrenal gland, and it is the target of tricyclic antidepressants, reboxetine and cocaine. When the transporter is defective, synaptic clearance fails and circulating norepinephrine rises abnormally, producing orthostatic intolerance: lightheadedness, tachycardia and fatigue on standing that resolve on sitting or lying down. The condition illustrates how autonomic control of heart rate and vascular tone during postural change depends on transmitter reuptake rather than on release alone.

Defective SLCO1B1 causes hyperbilirubinemia, Rotor type (HBLRR) describes what happens to bilirubin handling when hepatocytes lose the transporter that takes it up from blood. SLCO1B1 (OATP1B1) sits on the sinusoidal, basolateral face of the hepatocyte and imports unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin along with bile acids, and it is the route by which conjugated bilirubin secreted into plasma is recaptured for biliary excretion. When it fails, together with its paralogue, that reuptake step is lost and conjugated bilirubin accumulates in the circulation, producing Rotor syndrome: an autosomal recessive, benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with mild jaundice appearing in infancy or childhood and no hemolysis. The same transporter clears many drugs, so its loss or reduced activity also alters statin and methotrexate pharmacokinetics, linking heme catabolite disposal to hepatic drug uptake more broadly.

Bilirubin generated by heme breakdown must be taken up from blood into hepatocytes before it can be conjugated and excreted in bile, and the organic anion transporter SLCO1B1 on the sinusoidal (basolateral) hepatocyte membrane performs that uptake, including the re-uptake of conjugated bilirubin that has leaked back into plasma. Loss of functional SLCO1B1 blocks this hepatic clearance step and produces Rotor-type hyperbilirubinaemia, an autosomal recessive conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in which mild jaundice appears after birth or during childhood without haemolysis and with otherwise normal liver histology. Because the same transporter carries statins, methotrexate and other anionic drugs across the sinusoidal membrane, its activity also sets hepatic first-pass drug uptake, and reduced-function variants raise systemic drug exposure. The pathway sits at the entry point of hepatobiliary elimination, upstream of glucuronidation and canalicular export.

Defective SLC20A2 causes idiopathic basal ganglia calcification 1 (IBGC1) concerns loss of a sodium-dependent inorganic phosphate transporter and the brain calcification that follows. SLC20A2 encodes PiT2, which co-transports two sodium ions with each phosphate and, together with the related PiT1, performs housekeeping phosphate uptake from interstitial fluid — a function that also shapes extracellular matrix, cartilage and vascular mineralisation. When PiT2 activity is reduced, phosphate is not cleared efficiently from the brain interstitium and cerebrospinal fluid, and calcium phosphate deposits accumulate in vessel walls and pericapillary spaces of the basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum. Inheritance is autosomal dominant; carriers range from wholly asymptomatic to presenting with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance. The pathway links solute carrier–mediated phosphate homeostasis to neurodegeneration and to the broader biology of ectopic tissue calcification.

Cells take up inorganic phosphate from extracellular fluid through sodium-coupled cotransporters, and PiT2, encoded by SLC20A2, performs this housekeeping uptake with two sodium ions carried per phosphate. In the brain its activity keeps interstitial phosphate low enough that calcium phosphate does not precipitate around small vessels. Loss-of-function mutations cause idiopathic basal ganglia calcification type 1, an autosomal dominant condition in which mineral deposits accumulate in vascular and pericapillary spaces of the basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum. Carriers range from wholly asymptomatic to presenting with parkinsonism, dystonia, cognitive decline and psychiatric disturbance, so the clinical picture is variable even within families. The same transporter family also contributes to matrix, cartilage and vascular calcification elsewhere in the body, placing this defect within the wider problem of phosphate handling and ectopic mineralisation.

Reabsorbing cystine and the dibasic amino acids from the glomerular filtrate falls to a single heterodimeric transporter in the proximal tubule, and its failure through mutation of SLC3A1 causes the inherited disorder cystinuria. The heavy subunit rBAT (SLC3A1) is disulfide-linked to the catalytic light subunit b(0,+)AT (SLC7A9), which exchanges extracellular cystine, arginine and lysine for intracellular neutral amino acids such as leucine; rBAT is required for trafficking the complex to the apical brush border of kidney and small intestinal epithelium. When transport is lost, cystine remains in the tubular lumen, and because it is poorly soluble at urinary pH it precipitates as recurrent stones, producing obstruction, pyelonephritis and, in severe cases, renal failure. Loss-of-function alleles in the light subunit gene cause the clinically similar type B form, placing both genes in one epithelial amino acid reabsorption route.

Cholinergic neurons cannot make their own choline, so they must retrieve it from the synaptic cleft after acetylcholine is hydrolysed, and the high-affinity, sodium- and chloride-dependent choline transporter encoded by SLC5A7 performs that retrieval at the presynaptic terminal. Because choline uptake is the rate-limiting step in acetylcholine synthesis, this transport step sets how much transmitter can be reloaded into vesicles during sustained firing, making it part of the neurotransmitter release and recycling cycle rather than a peripheral metabolic detail. Loss-of-function mutations impair transmission at the neuromuscular junction and cause distal hereditary motor neuronopathy 7A, in which anterior horn motor neurons degenerate selectively and patients develop progressive distal wasting and weakness of the legs, sometimes with vocal cord paresis, while sensory function is spared. Motor endplate function thus depends directly on presynaptic choline salvage.

Solutes, ions and lipids cross membranes by three routes: ATP-driven pumps, channels that let substrates flow down their gradients at very high rates, and transporters that move specific substrates through conformational cycles. Inherited defects in these proteins produce a broad family of transmembrane transporter disorders, and the genes here map onto recognisable diseases: CFTR in cystic fibrosis, ABCB11 and ABCB4 in cholestasis, ABCD1 in adrenoleukodystrophy, SLC2A1 in glucose transporter deficiency with seizures, SLC12A3 and SLC12A1 in renal salt-wasting tubulopathies, SLC40A1 and SLC11A2 in iron handling, and KCNJ11 with ABCC8 in neonatal diabetes and hyperinsulinism. Much of the accompanying machinery explains how mutant transporters are handled rather than how they work: misfolded substrates are retained in the endoplasmic reticulum and routed to ubiquitin-dependent degradation by the proteasome via VCP, SEL1L and derlins, so loss of function frequently reflects premature disposal of the protein.

HOX genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that assign positional identity along the head-to-tail axis of the embryo and later pattern structures such as the hindbrain and limbs. Their activation during differentiation follows the order of the genes within each cluster, so that 3' genes switch on earliest and most anteriorly, and errors in this sequence produce homeotic transformations and segmentation defects. Retinoic acid is the principal initiating signal here, acting through RAR/RXR heterodimers that recruit coactivators such as CREBBP, EP300 and NCOA6 while releasing NCOR1-HDAC3 repression at target promoters and recruiting RNA polymerase II. Activation requires resolving bivalent chromatin: Polycomb components EZH2, EED and SUZ12 maintain H3K27 trimethylation and repression, KDM6A removes that mark, and trithorax-related KMT2C/KMT2D with the WDR5-RBBP5-ASH2L-DPY30 module deposit H3K4 methylation. CTCF boundaries, and cofactors PBX1 and MEIS1, shape the resulting expression domains.

Cilium assembly begins when a mother centriole converts into a basal body and docks at the plasma membrane, and this anchoring step sets up the ciliary base from which the axoneme extends. Distal appendage proteins such as CEP83, CEP89, SCLT1, FBF1 and CEP164 form the transition fibres that tether the basal body to the membrane, while CEP290, the MKS/B9 module (MKS1, B9D1, B9D2, TMEM216, TMEM67), tectonic proteins and the nephrocystin group (NPHP1, NPHP4, RPGRIP1L, IQCB1) build the transition zone, a diffusion barrier that controls which proteins and lipids enter the ciliary compartment. Rab8 and Rab11 with their exchange factor deliver vesicles that supply ciliary membrane, and kinases including TTBK2 and PLK1 together with CP110/CEP97 removal license axoneme growth. Pericentriolar and dynein-dynactin components position the organelle. Mutations here cause ciliopathies such as Joubert, Meckel and nephronophthisis syndromes.

VxPx cargo-targeting to cilium is the sorting route that delivers selected membrane proteins from the trans-Golgi network to the ciliary membrane, giving the cilium its distinct receptor and channel composition. It matters because the cilium cannot synthesize its own membrane proteins: photoreceptor outer segments depend on it to load rhodopsin and cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and kidney epithelia depend on it for polycystin-1 and -2, so failure produces retinal degeneration and polycystic kidney disease. Cargo bearing a C-terminal VxPx-like motif is captured by ARF4 at the Golgi, together with ASAP1 and GBF1, and packaged into carriers whose delivery is controlled by a RAB11-RAB3IP-RAB8A cascade. Docking and fusion at the base of the cilium require the octameric exocyst complex, which tethers the vesicles at the periciliary membrane. The pathway thus links Golgi export and polarized vesicle traffic to ciliary signalling capacity.

Cilia and the outer segments of photoreceptors are built from membrane proteins made in the secretory pathway, and this route is how those proteins get there. Cargo bearing a short VxPx-type signal in its cytoplasmic tail is captured by the small GTPase ARF4 at the trans-Golgi network, together with an ARF GAP and a GEF, and packaged into carriers that are then handed off through a RAB11-to-RAB8 conversion mediated by the exchange factor Rabin8 and delivered at the ciliary base with help from the exocyst complex. The cargoes define why it matters: rhodopsin and cyclic nucleotide-gated channel subunits for phototransduction, polycystin-1 and -2 for renal tubule mechanosensing. Mislocalisation of rhodopsin underlies forms of retinitis pigmentosa, while polycystin trafficking failure causes polycystic kidney disease, linking this targeting step to ciliopathy in general.

Cilia have a protein and lipid composition unlike the rest of the plasma membrane, and they acquire it because membrane and peripheral proteins are actively sorted and delivered to the periciliary region at the ciliary base rather than diffusing there. This targeted delivery determines whether receptors such as Smoothened, somatostatin and melanin-concentrating hormone receptors, the polycystins, and rhodopsin and the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels of photoreceptors reach the compartment where they signal; when it fails the result is ciliopathy, including Bardet-Biedl syndrome, polycystic kidney disease and retinal degeneration. A Golgi-based module built around ARF4, the ARF-GAP ASAP1, RAB11A with its effector FIP3, and the RAB8A exchange factor RAB3IP recognises VxPx-bearing cargo, while the exocyst tethers vesicles for fusion. ARL6 delivers the BBSome as a cargo adaptor, and ARL3 with UNC119B or PDE6D releases lipid-modified cargo such as NPHP3 and INPP5E. Tubulins and their acetylation and deacetylation enzymes supply the axonemal track.

Cilia concentrate specific membrane receptors, and BBSome-mediated cargo targeting is how many of those receptors get there. The BBSome is a stable eight-subunit coat-like complex built from Bardet-Biedl syndrome proteins, including BBS1, BBS2, BBS4, BBS5, BBS7, BBS9, TTC8 and BBIP1, which are rich in TPR and beta-propeller repeats. It acts as the principal effector of the small GTPase ARL6/BBS3, which recruits it to the membrane at the ciliary base so that cargo is coupled to intraflagellar transport and delivered across the transition zone. Assembly of the complex itself requires a chaperonin-like module of BBS6/MKKS, BBS10 and BBS12 acting with CCT/TRiC subunits, while LZTFL1 restrains entry. Cargoes such as Smoothened, somatostatin receptor 3 and melanin-concentrating hormone receptor 1 depend on it, linking failures to Bardet-Biedl syndrome with obesity, retinal degeneration, polydactyly and renal disease.

Cilia have no internal protein synthesis, so every axonemal subunit, membrane receptor and signalling component must be ferried in and out along the microtubule track — the job of intraflagellar transport. This bidirectional shuttling builds and maintains primary and motile cilia, and its loss underlies the ciliopathies: polycystic kidney disease, skeletal dysplasias, retinal degeneration and situs defects, together with failure of Hedgehog signalling, which depends on trafficking of its components through the cilium. Trains of IFT-B subunits such as IFT88, IFT52 and IFT81 carry cargo outward under heterotrimeric kinesin-2 (KIF3A/KIF3B with KIFAP3), while IFT-A components including IFT122, IFT140, WDR19 and WDR35 return with cytoplasmic dynein-2, built around DYNC2H1 and its light and intermediate chains. Tubulin isotypes supply the axonemal track and a major transported cargo. Mutations in anterograde components abolish cilia; retrograde defects produce short, bulging cilia stuffed with stalled particles.

Pyroptosis is a lytic, inflammatory form of programmed cell death in which gasdermin family proteins punch pores in the plasma membrane, killing the cell and spilling its contents to alert neighbouring tissue. It defends against intracellular bacteria and viruses by destroying their replication niche, and drives the cytokine release behind septic shock, inflammatory bowel disease and sterile inflammation after stroke when it runs unchecked. Inflammatory caspases CASP1, CASP4 and CASP5 cleave GSDMD downstream of inflammasome assembly, while apoptotic CASP3, acting below BAX/BAK-dependent mitochondrial cytochrome c release or granzyme B delivered by cytotoxic lymphocytes, cleaves GSDME to convert an apoptotic signal into a lytic one; neutrophil elastase provides another route to GSDMD activation. The liberated N-terminal fragments oligomerise into pores that conduct mature IL-1β, IL-18 and the danger signal HMGB1, with ESCRT-III subunits repairing damaged membrane to limit death, and IRF and p53-family factors shaping the response transcriptionally.

Myeloid and dendritic cells recognise fungi, mycobacteria and damaged host cells through the Dectin-2 family of C-type lectin receptors, an innate sensing arm that drives antifungal immunity and shapes Th17-biased responses independently of Toll-like receptors. Members such as CLEC6A and CLEC4E bind mannosylated and glycolipid patterns on fungal hyphae and mycobacterial cell walls, while CLEC4D and CLEC10A extend the ligand range and CLEC4C marks plasmacytoid dendritic cells. These short-tailed receptors lack signalling motifs of their own and instead pair with the FcR gamma chain, recruiting Src-family kinases and SYK to activate phospholipase C-gamma2 and downstream NF-kB-dependent TNF and IL6 production; CLEC4A is the inhibitory exception. Heavily glycosylated mucins are recognised ligands for lectin receptors of this type, linking the pathway to surveillance of mucosal glycan surfaces. Loss of this recognition predisposes to invasive fungal infection.

C-type lectin receptors are surface pattern-recognition receptors on dendritic cells, macrophages and neutrophils that read carbohydrate structures on fungi, mycobacteria and viruses and translate that recognition into innate defence and instruction of T cell responses. Dectin-1, dectin-2, mincle, MCL, DC-SIGN and CD301 engage glycan ligands, including the mucin-type O-glycans and secreted mucins that also form the barrier these receptors survey. Signalling runs mainly through the Fc receptor gamma chain and Syk to PLC-gamma2 and the CARD9-BCL10-MALT1 complex, activating the IKK complex and TAK1 so that NF-kB subunits are released following ubiquitin- and proteasome-dependent degradation of IkB; calcium flux through calcineurin activates NFAT in parallel. The output is phagocytosis, respiratory burst, inflammasome assembly, dendritic cell maturation and cytokine and chemokine release that biases helper T cell differentiation. Loss of CARD9 causes inherited susceptibility to invasive fungal infection.

Dendritic cells read the sugar coats of microbes, and the C-type lectin receptor CD209, better known as DC-SIGN, is one of the sensors that does it. Its mannose-binding activity captures Mycobacterium tuberculosis and HIV-1, and it also serves as an adhesion receptor for ICAM2 on endothelium and ICAM3 on T cells, tuning the immune response to the pathogen encountered. Rather than working alone, signalling from this receptor reshapes Toll-like receptor output at the level of NF-kB: Src-family kinases and Ras proteins activate RAF1, which leads to phosphorylation of RELA on serine 276 and its subsequent acetylation by CREBBP and EP300. Phosphorylated RELA both enhances canonical transcription and sequesters RELB into non-DNA-binding dimers, suppressing the non-canonical arm. The result is a pathogen-tailored cytokine profile, which pathogens such as HIV-1 exploit to blunt dendritic cell activation.

Some ciliary membrane proteins are anchored not by a transmembrane domain but by an N-terminal myristoyl group, and this route delivers them from the cytosol into the cilium. Cargoes such as nephrocystin-3 and cystin-1 depend on it, and their mislocalisation underlies nephronophthisis and polycystic kidney disease, while failure of the GTPase arm of the same system causes X-linked retinitis pigmentosa. The lipid anchor is shielded in a hydrophobic pocket of the solubilising carrier UNC119B, which ferries the cargo across the transition zone. Inside the cilium, the ARF-like GTPase ARL3, stimulated by its GTPase-activating protein RP2, triggers release of the myristoylated protein into the ciliary membrane and frees the carrier to exit and be reused. ARL3 additionally coordinates intraflagellar transport complexes with their kinesin motors, linking cargo delivery to ciliary trafficking more broadly.

The primary cilium maintains a phosphoinositide composition distinct from the rest of the plasma membrane, and delivery of the 5-phosphatase INPP5E is how that distinction is established. INPP5E hydrolyses PI(4,5)P2 in the ciliary membrane, keeping the shaft enriched in PI4P, which in turn controls which signalling proteins are retained in or excluded from the organelle and underlies proper Hedgehog responsiveness. Newly prenylated INPP5E is bound and solubilised by the prenyl-binding chaperone PDE6D, which carries it to the ciliary base; the atypical ciliary GTPase ARL13B then acts as the release factor that discharges the cargo into the cilium, where ARL13B also supports intraflagellar transport. Loss of either ARL13B or INPP5E causes Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies, with cerebellar and retinal malformation, kidney cysts and polydactyly.

Protein kinases N are Rho effectors: RHOA, RHOB, RHOC and RAC1 bind N-terminal antiparallel-coiled-coil motifs of PKN1, PKN2 and PKN3, relieving autoinhibition and positioning them for activation-loop phosphorylation by PDPK1. Through this route Rho GTPase signalling is converted into control of the actomyosin cytoskeleton, mitotic timing and nuclear transcription. Downstream of PKN activity sit non-muscle myosin heavy and light chains together with the myosin phosphatase holoenzyme and its inhibitor CPI-17, so contractility is set by the balance of kinase and phosphatase acting on myosin light chain. A second branch acts on cell cycle entry into mitosis via CDC25C, whose phosphorylation creates 14-3-3 binding sites that sequester it. In prostate cells PKN1 cooperates with the androgen receptor and histone-modifying enzymes including the demethylases KDM1A and KDM4C to drive expression of target genes such as the kallikreins, linking cytoskeletal signalling to hormone-dependent transcription and prostate cancer.

Androgen-driven transcription in prostate cells depends on more than hormone binding; the chromatin around target promoters must be licensed for output. Here the kinase PKN1, once phosphorylated on a threonine in its activation loop, binds ligand-activated androgen receptor and raises transcription of the kallikrein genes KLK2 and KLK3, the latter encoding prostate-specific antigen, the standard serum marker of prostate disease. Activated PKN1 helps assemble a productive receptor complex with the coactivator NCOA2, then travels with the receptor onto androgen-responsive promoters, where it phosphorylates histone tails. That mark recruits the demethylases KDM4C and KDM1A, whose removal of repressive histone methylation opens the promoters for elevated expression. The many core histone genes present mark the chromatin substrate, and the axis is of interest because sustained androgen receptor output sustains prostate cancer growth.

Active RHO-family GTPases recruit and switch on citron kinase, a ROCK-related serine/threonine kinase that couples small GTPase signalling to actomyosin contractility and to the completion of cell division. Its best-defined output is phosphorylation of the myosin regulatory light chain on the same residues targeted by ROCK, promoting assembly of contractile non-muscle myosin II filaments; opposing dephosphorylation by the myosin phosphatase holoenzyme, with its PPP1R12 targeting subunits, sets the balance. At the cleavage furrow and midbody, citron kinase acts with the kinesin KIF14 and the microtubule-bundling protein PRC1 so that the ingressing ring is stabilised and abscission proceeds; loss of this activity produces binucleate cells and, in the brain, underlies microcephaly with defective neurogenesis. A nervous-system splice form lacking the kinase domain instead resides in the postsynaptic density with the scaffold PSD-95. RHOA-dependent citron activity also shapes Golgi organisation via the actin cytoskeleton.

This branch of Rho GTPase signalling links the small GTPases to microtubule-based transport by way of kinectin. Active, GTP-loaded RHOA, RHOG, RAC1 and CDC42 bind KTN1, an endoplasmic reticulum membrane protein that engages the cargo-binding region of kinesin-1 and stimulates its microtubule-dependent ATPase activity. The output is directed movement of membrane cargo: RHOG acting through kinectin and kinesin drives microtubule-dependent cellular protrusions and contributes to lysosomal positioning and transport, so the pathway couples cytoskeletal signalling to organelle distribution and cell shape rather than to actin remodelling alone. The kinesin-1 components here are the heavy chains KIF5A and KIF5B together with light chains KLC1-KLC4, which are the adaptors through which cargo is selected. Downstream steps beyond GTPase-kinectin and kinectin-kinesin binding remain incompletely defined.

IQGAP scaffolds are how active RHO-family GTPases get translated into changes in cell shape, motility and adhesion. When RAC1 and CDC42 are loaded with GTP they are captured by the GAP-related domain of IQGAP1, IQGAP2 or IQGAP3, which, despite the domain's name, lacks catalytic activity and instead locks the GTPases in their active state, prolonging their signalling. The same scaffolds bind F-actin through a calponin homology domain and tune the balance between monomeric and filamentous actin, an interaction switched off when calmodulin occupies the IQ repeats — giving calcium a direct say in cytoskeletal remodelling. IQGAP1 also links to microtubules and their plus-end tracking machinery to set front-rear polarity and build lamellipodia, and binds E-cadherin with alpha- and beta-catenin to modulate adherens junction stability. This convergence on migration and junctional turnover underlies wound healing and is exploited during tumour invasion.

TNFR1-mediated ceramide production is the lipid arm of tumour necrosis factor signalling: when TNF-alpha engages TNFR1, sphingomyelinases hydrolyse membrane sphingomyelin to ceramide, converting a cytokine signal into a second messenger that biases cells toward growth arrest, stress responses and apoptosis. This route contributes to inflammatory tissue injury and to the cytotoxicity of TNF, and it links receptor engagement directly to membrane composition rather than to transcription. Neutral sphingomyelinases such as SMPD2 and SMPD3 act at the plasma membrane and are recruited through the adaptor NSMAF, which bridges them to a dedicated activating region of the receptor, with RACK1 as a scaffolding partner; the receptor death domain and its adaptors instead drive caspase-dependent activation of the acidic, lysosomal enzyme.
