Downstream metabolism of ceramide to sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate reverses the signal, so the balance of these lipids sets whether a cell dies or survives.

Tumour necrosis factor does not only trigger caspase activation; it also remodels membrane lipids, and TNFR1-mediated ceramide production is the branch that converts receptor engagement into a sphingolipid signal. Sphingomyelinases hydrolyse sphingomyelin to ceramide, which acts as a second messenger favouring growth arrest and apoptosis, while its downstream conversion to sphingosine-1-phosphate has the opposite, pro-survival effect; the balance between these lipids helps set whether a TNF-stimulated cell dies or persists. Neutral, magnesium-dependent sphingomyelinases such as SMPD2 and SMPD3 act at the plasma membrane and are recruited to a dedicated cytoplasmic region of TNFR1 through the adaptor NSMAF, with RACK1 as a scaffolding partner; an acid, lysosomal sphingomyelinase is engaged instead via the death domain and caspase cleavage. The pathway links inflammatory cytokine signalling to lipid-mediated control of proliferation, stress responses and cell death.

How much CFTR chloride channel reaches the cell surface is decided in the Golgi, and RHO GTPase control of CFTR trafficking is one switch that makes that decision. CFTR conducts chloride and bicarbonate across the apical membrane of airway, intestinal and ductal epithelia, so its surface abundance sets fluid and mucus hydration; loss of functional channel causes cystic fibrosis, and many disease mutants are lost to degradation rather than being intrinsically inactive. The Golgi-resident PDZ scaffold GOPC (also called PIST or CAL) binds the CFTR C-terminus and, on its own, routes the channel toward lysosomal destruction. The small GTPase RHOQ, better known as TC10, binds GOPC in its GTP-loaded state and redirects the GOPC:CFTR complex to the plasma membrane instead, rescuing channel expression. The pathway therefore links GTPase signalling to post-Golgi sorting and to the pharmacological problem of stabilising mutant CFTR.

Cells generate shape change, traction and contractile force by tuning actin filament stability and myosin motor activity, and this is the branch of RHO signalling that does it. Active, GTP-loaded RHOA, RHOB or RHOC bind the RHO-binding domain of the kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2, relieving an autoinhibitory fold made by their pleckstrin homology region and switching on kinase activity. The activated kinases phosphorylate LIM kinases 1 and 2, which in turn phosphorylate cofilin and so block actin depolymerisation, stabilising filaments. In parallel they phosphorylate myosin regulatory light chains to drive non-muscle myosin II, and phosphorylate the MYPT1 targeting subunit of myosin light chain phosphatase to prevent that phosphorylation being reversed -- two routes converging on sustained actomyosin contraction. The output underlies cell migration, polarity, stress fibre assembly, cytokinesis and smooth muscle tone, and the kinases are drug targets in vascular and fibrotic disease.

Cells change shape, spread and migrate by remodelling actin and tuning actomyosin contractility, and the conventional p21-activated kinases PAK1-3 are the point where small GTPase signals are converted into those mechanical changes. Active, GTP-loaded RAC1 and CDC42 bind the CRIB domain, breaking the autoinhibited PAK dimer and permitting activation-loop autophosphorylation. The released kinase then phosphorylates LIMK1, which in turn restrains cofilin-mediated actin filament severing, and acts on myosin regulatory light chains, myosin light chain kinase, the myosin phosphatase targeting subunits, filamin A, cortactin and the merlin tumour suppressor. The net effect is coordinated control of lamellipodial protrusion, stress fibre and focal adhesion turnover, and non-muscle and smooth muscle myosin II contractility. Beyond the cytoskeleton these kinases feed MAPK cascades, survival signalling and cell cycle progression, and their overactivity is a recurring feature of invasive tumours and of neurodevelopmental disease linked to PAK3.

Beyond arresting the cell cycle and triggering apoptosis, p53 acts as a metabolic governor, and this transcriptional programme is how it does it. By steering cells away from fermentative glucose use toward mitochondrial respiration and by holding down oxidative stress, it opposes the metabolic rewiring typical of tumours, and its loss contributes to the glycolytic, Warburg-type phenotype of cancer cells. p53 induces TIGAR to lower glycolytic flux and NADPH-linked ROS, SCO2 and other cytochrome c oxidase components to sustain oxidative phosphorylation, GLS2 for glutamine-fuelled respiration, and RRM2B for deoxyribonucleotide supply and mitochondrial DNA maintenance. It restrains growth signalling by transactivating PTEN, the sestrins and DDIT4, which converge on AMPK, the TSC1:TSC2 complex, Rheb and mTORC1 to reduce protein synthesis. Thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin components tie the programme to antioxidant defence, a function some cancer-associated p53 mutants retain.

Hedgehog signalling begins at the cell surface, where secreted ligands engage their receptor and co-receptors, and this ligand-receptor step sets whether the pathway is on or off. It patterns the neural tube, limb bud, gut and skeleton during development and is reactivated in basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma when receptor-level control fails; loss of ligand function underlies holoprosencephaly. Sonic, Indian and Desert Hedgehog all bind Patched, which in the unliganded state sits in the primary cilium and restrains Smoothened, keeping GLI transcription factors in their processed repressor forms. Ligand binding triggers Patched internalisation and releases that restraint. The co-receptors CDON and BOC, both transmembrane glycoproteins with calcium-dependent ligand binding, and the GPI-anchored GAS1 capture ligand and present it to Patched, acting with partial redundancy, while HHIP binds Hedgehog proteins to dampen signalling.

When a Hedgehog ligand such as SHH, IHH or DHH engages the PTCH1 receptor, the pathway switches from repression to activation, and this active state is what patterns the neural tube, limb bud, gut and many other embryonic fields, and later sustains stem cell compartments. Ligand binding relieves PTCH1 inhibition of Smoothened, which accumulates in the primary cilium; kinesin KIF3A-dependent transport and the ciliary protein KIF7 reorganise the tip, GPR161 is removed, and SUFU releases GLI2 and GLI3. Freed full-length GLI proteins escape the partial proteasomal processing that would otherwise generate the GLI3 repressor, enter the nucleus and induce targets including GLI1, an obligate activator. Coreceptors GAS1, CDON and BOC promote ligand capture while HHIP sequesters it; ubiquitin ligases such as SPOP, ITCH and the cullin-RING machinery set GLI levels. Loss of flux causes holoprosencephaly and polydactyly syndromes, while inappropriate activation drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma.

Post-replicative mismatch repair corrects base-base mispairs and small insertion-deletion loops left behind by DNA polymerases, and loss of it produces the microsatellite instability and mutator phenotype seen in several cancers. MSH3 partners MSH2 in the MutS beta heterodimer, which recognises mismatched or looped-out DNA and, together with the MutL alpha heterodimer, licenses excision and resynthesis of the newly made strand. MutS beta is the arm of the system most responsible for repairing larger insertion-deletion loops, work it shares only partly with the MSH6-containing heterodimer, so MSH3 deficiency destabilises repetitive tracts in particular. Defective repair through this route underlies susceptibility to endometrial cancer and contributes to instability at di- and tetranucleotide repeats, linking replication fidelity to tumour suppression and to the somatic expansion of repeat sequences.

Defective Mismatch Repair Associated With MSH2 describes what happens to genome maintenance when MSH2, the human counterpart of bacterial MutS, is lost or altered. MSH2 is the obligate partner in the mismatch-recognition heterodimers that scan newly replicated DNA: with MSH6 it detects base-base mispairs and small insertion-deletion loops, and with MSH3 it handles larger loops, after which downstream excision and resynthesis restore the correct sequence. Without functional MSH2 these lesions persist, replication errors accumulate at repetitive tracts, and tumours acquire the microsatellite instability and hypermutator phenotype used to diagnose them. Inherited heterozygous mutations cause hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, with related presentations including the sebaceous tumours of Muir-Torre syndrome and, in biallelic form, childhood-onset mismatch repair cancer syndrome. The same defect also removes a barrier to tolerating certain chemotherapeutics while sensitising tumours to immune checkpoint blockade.

Mismatch repair corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops left behind by DNA replication, and MSH2 is the common subunit of the complexes that recognise them: it pairs with MSH6 to form MutSalpha, which handles single-base mismatches and short loops, and with MSH3 to form MutSbeta, which handles larger insertion-deletion heterologies. Loss of functional MSH2 therefore disables mismatch recognition altogether, the initiating step that licenses downstream excision and resynthesis. Cells with defective mismatch repair of this kind accumulate mutations and show microsatellite instability, particularly at repetitive sequences in coding regions. Inherited pathogenic MSH2 variants underlie Lynch syndrome, with high lifetime risk of colorectal and endometrial cancer, and the associated Muir-Torre and constitutional mismatch repair deficiency phenotypes. The resulting hypermutated, neoantigen-rich tumours are characteristically responsive to immune checkpoint blockade, making repair status a clinically actionable marker.

Loss of MSH6 function disables one branch of DNA mismatch repair, the proofreading system that removes base-base mispairs and small insertion-deletion loops left behind by replication. MSH6 partners with MSH2 to form the MutS-alpha heterodimer, the sensor that recognises G/T and related mismatches and recruits downstream repair machinery; without it, errors escape correction and accumulate. Cells lacking MSH6 characteristically destabilise mononucleotide repeat tracts, producing a comparatively subtle microsatellite instability signature rather than the broad instability seen when MLH1 or MSH2 is lost. Germline MSH6 defects cause hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, though typically as atypical Lynch families with later disease onset and a weaker cancer family history. The pathway links replication fidelity to tumour suppression, and its failure produces the hypermutator phenotype that also shapes tumour immunogenicity and treatment response.

Mismatch repair corrects base-base mismatches and small insertion-deletion loops left behind by DNA polymerases, and the endonuclease-bearing partner of that system is PMS2, which pairs with MLH1 to form the MutL alpha heterodimer that is recruited after MutS proteins recognise a mismatch and that nicks the error-containing strand so it can be excised and resynthesised. When PMS2 is lost or truncated, MutL alpha cannot be assembled and repair becomes defective: replication slippage at short repeats goes uncorrected, tumours acquire a microsatellite-instability-high phenotype, and immunohistochemistry shows absent PMS2 staining. Inherited defects of this kind underlie a subset of Lynch syndrome and hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer, with associated brain tumours in Turcot syndrome and supratentorial primitive neuroectodermal tumours. The same repair deficiency raises mutational burden genome-wide, which is why such cancers respond well to immune checkpoint blockade.

The p53 tumour suppressor decides whether a damaged cell arrests, repairs itself, senesces or dies, and regulation of TP53 activity is how that decision is set. In unstressed cells p53 is kept scarce: the ubiquitin ligase MDM2, with MDM4 and other ligases, marks it for proteasomal destruction, while deubiquitinases such as USP7 oppose this. DNA damage sensing through ATM, ATR with its partner ATRIP, the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp and TOPBP1 activates CHEK1 and CHEK2, and phosphorylation at the amino terminus blocks MDM2 binding and stabilises the protein. Further marks tune output rather than amount: acetylation by EP300 and KAT5 favours transcription, methylation by SMYD2, EHMT2 or KMT5A can silence it, HIPK2 phosphorylation biases towards apoptotic targets, and PIN1 isomerisation licenses cofactor binding. Loss of this control underlies much of human cancer.

When damage or stress cannot be repaired, p53 commits the cell to die, and it does so largely by turning on a transcriptional programme of cell death genes. This output is the arm of p53 tumour suppression that eliminates cells with irreparable genomic damage; its loss allows damaged cells to persist and is a route to tumour development and to resistance against DNA-damaging therapy. Targets span both apoptotic routes: death receptors such as FAS and the TRAIL receptors DR4 and DR5 for extrinsic signalling, and BH3-only proteins BAX, BID, PUMA and NOXA that permeabilise mitochondria for intrinsic signalling, together with caspases and cytosolic caspase-activating platforms including APAF1, PIDD1 and NLRC4, the latter linking to inflammatory death. ATM-dependent phosphorylation stabilises p53 beforehand, ASPP cofactors select particular promoters, and antiapoptotic targets such as TRIAP1 and survivin temper the response so recovery remains possible. The relatives TP63 and TP73 can drive overlapping targets.

N-linked glycosylation begins on the cytoplasmic face of the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, where a lipid-linked oligosaccharide is built stepwise on dolichol phosphate. ALG14 partners with ALG13 to form the UDP-GlcNAc transferase that adds the second N-acetylglucosamine to this growing precursor, a step without which the full 14-sugar donor cannot be assembled and transferred to nascent proteins. Loss-of-function variants such as p.P65L and p.R104* leave this activity defective, and the resulting glycosylation deficit is felt most acutely at the neuromuscular junction, where correct glycosylation of acetylcholine receptor subunits and associated synaptic proteins is needed for reliable transmission. The consequence is a congenital myasthenic syndrome with fatigable weakness that preferentially involves proximal limb muscles, illustrating how a general biosynthetic defect in the secretory pathway can present as a selectively synaptic disease.

Hedgehog ligands act on cells by relieving the repression that Patched imposes on Smoothened, and activation of SMO is the switch that converts ligand binding into a transcriptional response. It governs embryonic patterning of the neural tube, limb and skeleton, and hair follicle and stem cell maintenance; constitutive SMO activity drives basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma, which is why SMO is the target of Hedgehog pathway inhibitors. SHH, IHH or DHH engage PTCH1 together with co-receptors such as CDON, BOC and GAS1, freeing SMO to accumulate in the primary cilium via intraflagellar transport involving KIF3A. Phosphorylation of the SMO C-terminal tail by GRK2 and casein kinase 1 alpha, with beta-arrestin recruitment, stabilizes the active conformation, while an EVC-EVC2-EFCAB7-IQCE complex confines active SMO to a proximal ciliary zone. The outcome is release of GLI transcription factors from SUFU-mediated restraint.

This is the transcriptional output step of Hedgehog signalling: once ligand binding blocks the proteolytic processing that would otherwise generate truncated repressors, full-length GLI1, GLI2 and GLI3 accumulate, enter the nucleus and occupy consensus GLI sites in target promoters. The genes switched on include much of the pathway's own machinery — the receptors PTCH1 and PTCH2, the co-receptor BOC, the secreted antagonist HHIP and GLI1 itself — so induction simultaneously amplifies and restrains the signal through feedback. The program patterns the neural tube, limb bud and many other embryonic fields, and sustains stem and progenitor compartments after birth. Activating GLI output interprets morphogen concentration as graded gene expression; when it escapes control, through loss of PTCH1 restraint or GLI amplification, the result is basal cell carcinoma, medulloblastoma and other Hedgehog-driven tumours. Activation complexes recruit acetyltransferase, Mediator and elongation-associated factors.

A truncated form of the epidermal growth factor receptor lacking its ligand-binding domain, EGFRvIII, is the commonest EGFR alteration in glioblastoma and drives growth without any external cue. Because it cannot bind ligand yet dimerizes and autophosphorylates spontaneously, the receptor signals constitutively, and because it fails to phosphorylate the docking tyrosine used by the CBL ubiquitin ligase, it escapes the receptor downregulation that normally terminates such signalling. Stability of the mutant depends on HSP90 with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which is why these tumours are sensitive to chaperone inhibition. Adaptors including GRB2, SOS1, SHC1 and GAB1 route the active receptor into RAS/RAF/MAP kinase and PI3K/AKT cascades, with possible PLCG1 involvement, producing proliferation and survival signals that give mutant-bearing cells a selective advantage.

EGFRvIII is a truncated epidermal growth factor receptor lacking its ligand-binding domain, the commonest EGFR variant in glioblastoma and a recurring lesion in other tumours, where gene amplification drives it to high levels. Because it dimerizes and autophosphorylates without ever binding EGF, it delivers growth and survival signalling continuously rather than in response to extracellular cues, and this ligand-independent output sustains proliferation, invasion and resistance to therapy. The phosphorylated receptor recruits the familiar adaptors — GRB2 with SOS1 and SHC1 to activate HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, GAB1 with the PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits, and PLCG1 — feeding the MAPK, PI3K/AKT and phospholipase C arms. HSP90 with its CDC37 cochaperone stabilises the mutant kinase, while the ubiquitin ligase CBL normally limits receptor levels; escape from such downregulation is part of why the variant signals persistently and marks it as an oncogenic driver.

Certain cancer-associated mutations in EGFR, either in its kinase domain or as point substitutions in the extracellular region, let the receptor fire without ligand while still retaining the ability to bind EGF, so that available ligand pushes output higher still. These ligand-responsive variants drive lung adenocarcinoma and other epithelial tumours and are the targets of EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, whose efficacy depends on which mutation is present. Signalling proceeds through the normal adaptors: GRB2 with SOS1 toward RAS and the MAP kinase cascade, GAB1 and PI3K toward AKT, SHC1, and PLCG1 for calcium and diacylglycerol. HSP90 with its co-chaperone CDC37 stabilizes the mutant kinase, making the variants chaperone-dependent, while CBL-mediated ubiquitination normally terminates signalling through receptor degradation.

Amplification of the EGFR locus makes tumour cells hypersensitive to ordinary growth factor cues: the receptor is structurally normal, but there is simply too much of it, so ligand binding drives proliferation and survival signalling far beyond what the same stimulus would produce in normal tissue. This is a common route to EGFR pathway activation in glioblastoma, lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers, and it is why receptor-blocking antibodies and kinase inhibitors work in some of these tumours. The ligand repertoire here spans the whole family that engages EGFR directly, from EGF and TGFA to amphiregulin, epiregulin, epigen, betacellulin and heparin-binding EGF, several of which are themselves produced by the tumour or its stroma to create autocrine loops. Downstream, dimerised receptors autophosphorylate and recruit adaptors that feed into MAPK and PI3K growth programmes.

Many epithelial tumours drive their own growth by overexpressing wild-type EGFR and responding to the full set of its ligands, and this pathway describes how that ligand-driven signalling can be blocked therapeutically. EGFR binds EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, betacellulin, epiregulin, epigen and heparin-binding EGF, each triggering receptor dimerisation, kinase activation and downstream proliferation and survival signalling through RAS-MAPK and PI3K routes. Antibody antagonists such as cetuximab occupy the extracellular ligand-binding site, preventing this activation in colorectal and head and neck cancers where receptor levels are high. Small-molecule covalent kinase inhibitors can also suppress the receptor, but because wild-type EGFR supports normal skin and gut epithelium, inhibiting it broadly produces dose-limiting toxicity. The pathway therefore frames the therapeutic window between tumour dependence on amplified EGFR signalling and the physiological requirement for the same receptor in healthy tissue.

Abasic sites arise constantly in DNA, both spontaneously and as intermediates left behind by glycosylases that excise damaged bases, and they must be cleaned up before replication turns them into mutations or strand breaks. This branch of base excision repair resolves them without the usual AP endonuclease step: NEIL1 and NEIL2, bifunctional glycosylases with beta/delta lyase activity, incise the strand and leave a 3' phosphate and a 5' deoxyribose phosphate. DNA polymerase beta trims the 5'dRP but is blocked by the 3' phosphate, so the phosphatase activity of PNKP must restore a 3'-hydroxyl before a single replacement nucleotide can be inserted and the nick sealed by the XRCC1-scaffolded LIG3 complex. The route matters for handling oxidative lesions, including those generated by OGG1, and for limiting mutagenesis in transcribed and replicating DNA.

Base excision repair removes damaged and abasic bases, and when the 5' end of the resulting nick cannot be trimmed by a simple one-nucleotide patch, the cell switches to long-patch repair using the replication machinery. This PCNA-dependent branch keeps oxidative and alkylation damage from becoming mutations or strand breaks, and it operates most readily in S phase, when replication factors are abundant. After the AP endonuclease APEX1 incises the abasic site, DNA polymerase beta adds the first nucleotide and displaces the intractable 5' abasic sugar phosphate; the clamp loader RFC loads PCNA, and polymerase delta or epsilon extends strand-displacement synthesis with RPA coating the displaced flap. FEN1 excises that flap and DNA ligase I seals the patch. The same clamp, clamp loader and polymerases serve genome replication, so this route links damage repair directly to replicative synthesis.

Dietary fructose, from fruit, sucrose and added sweeteners, is handled largely by the liver along a route distinct from glycolysis at its entry steps, and the way it bypasses the main regulated step of glucose breakdown is why heavy fructose intake is linked to fatty liver, raised triglycerides and insulin resistance. Ketohexokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, aldolase B splits it into dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde, and triokinase and glycerate kinase feed the fragments back into central carbon metabolism toward pyruvate and lipogenesis. Loss of aldolase B causes hereditary fructose intolerance, and ketohexokinase deficiency the benign condition essential fructosuria. Fructose is also made endogenously from glucose by the polyol pathway, in which aldose reductase and sorbitol dehydrogenase act in sequence; this supplies seminal fructose and, under hyperglycaemia, contributes to diabetic tissue damage.

Fructose biosynthesis is the two-step polyol route that converts glucose to fructose through sorbitol, and it is the source of the fructose that dominates seminal fluid and fuels sperm motility. Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol using NADPH, and sorbitol dehydrogenase oxidises sorbitol to fructose using NAD+; the pathway therefore runs independently of insulin and accelerates whenever intracellular glucose rises. That property makes it a central mechanism of diabetic tissue injury: in lens epithelium, peripheral neurons, kidney and retina, flux through aldose reductase depletes NADPH needed for glutathione regeneration, traps osmotically active sorbitol, and shifts cytosolic redox balance, contributing to cataract, neuropathy and microvascular disease. The same enzymes are abundant in seminal vesicle and epididymal tissue, where the output is a physiological energy substrate rather than a hazard, and aldose reductase inhibition remains a therapeutic strategy in diabetic complications.

Fructose biosynthesis in human tissues runs through the two-step polyol pathway, in which aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol using NADPH and sorbitol dehydrogenase then oxidizes sorbitol to fructose with NAD+. This route supplies the high fructose concentrations of seminal fluid, where it serves as an energy substrate for sperm, and it operates in epididymal and seminal vesicle tissue as well as in the eye lens, kidney, peripheral nerve and retina. Because the first enzyme is not insulin-regulated and has a low affinity for glucose, flux rises steeply in hyperglycaemia, consuming NADPH, depleting glutathione regeneration capacity and accumulating osmotically active sorbitol. This makes the pathway a recognized contributor to diabetic complications such as cataract, neuropathy, retinopathy and nephropathy, and a target of aldose reductase inhibitors. It also links glucose disposal to fructose metabolism and to cellular redox balance.

Vesicle-mediated transport is the cell's internal courier system: proteins, lipids and other cargo move between compartments and to and from the cell surface inside membrane-bounded carriers, either dissolved in the vesicle lumen or embedded in its membrane. It underlies secretion of hormones, antibodies and matrix proteins, uptake of lipoproteins and iron by scavenger and endocytic receptors, receptor downregulation, and delivery of hydrolases to lysosomes; its failure produces disorders of bleeding, pigmentation, cholesterol handling and neurodegeneration. Cargo selection and budding use coat complexes such as COPII at ER exit sites, COPI for retrograde traffic, and clathrin with AP adaptors at the plasma membrane and trans-Golgi; dynamin severs the neck, motors and cytoskeletal tracks move the carrier, and Rab GTPases with their GEFs and GAPs, tethers like TRAPP, COG and the exocyst, and SNARE-driven fusion complete delivery. ESCRT components route ubiquitinated receptors into multivesicular bodies.

Vesicle-mediated transport is the system by which cells move proteins, lipids and extracellular cargo between compartments inside membrane-bounded carriers, and it underlies secretion, receptor uptake, lysosomal delivery and the maintenance of organelle identity. Its failure blocks hormone and antibody secretion, leaves receptors such as LDLR, TFRC and EGFR uncleared from the surface, and causes storage and pigmentation disorders. The genes here cover the full itinerary: COPII components with SAR1B and the SEC23/24 subunits bud carriers from the ER, COPI and the Golgi-associated conserved oligomeric Golgi and TRAPP complexes handle intra-Golgi and retrograde steps, clathrin with AP-1 and AP-2 adaptors, dynamins and endophilins drive endocytosis, and ESCRT subunits with TSG101 and VPS4 sort ubiquitinated cargo into multivesicular bodies. Rab GTPases with their GEFs and TBC-domain GAPs specify identity, SNAREs and NSF execute fusion, and kinesin, dynein and myosin motors carry vesicles along cytoskeletal tracks.

Lactose is the principal sugar of milk, and its synthesis in the Golgi of lactating mammary epithelium is what makes milk an osmotically driven, carbohydrate-rich secretion; because lactose draws water into the secretory vesicle, the rate of this single reaction effectively sets milk volume. Free glucose is delivered into the Golgi lumen by a facilitative hexose transporter, and there a galactosyltransferase joins it to UDP-galactose to give lactose and UDP. The specificity switch is the defining feature: B4GALT1 normally galactosylates glycoprotein and glycolipid acceptors, but binding of the mammary-restricted regulatory subunit alpha-lactalbumin, itself a milk protein, reorients its preference toward free glucose. Lactation therefore depends on hormonal induction of LALBA rather than on new enzymes, linking this short biosynthetic route to secretory differentiation of the breast and to infant nutrition.

Phospholipase C-mediated cascade: FGFR1 is the branch of fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 signalling that converts ligand binding into calcium and protein kinase C signals, shaping limb and skeletal patterning, neuronal and craniofacial development, and, through Klotho-dependent FGF23 responses, phosphate handling in the kidney. Loss or distortion of this output contributes to craniosynostosis syndromes, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and FGFR1-driven cancers. Mechanistically, one of the FGF ligands together with heparan sulfate dimerises FGFR1 and triggers trans-autophosphorylation; a specific phosphotyrosine in the receptor tail recruits PLCG1 via its SH2 domains, and the receptor kinase phosphorylates and activates it. Activated PLC-gamma hydrolyses PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing stored calcium and engaging calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases and PKC. This arm runs in parallel with the FRS2-RAS-ERK and PI3K routes, allowing the same receptor to specify distinct cellular outcomes.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR1 trigger receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, and one of the branches that follows runs through phospholipase C-gamma. This arm converts growth factor binding at the cell surface into a calcium and lipid second-messenger signal, feeding the proliferation, migration and differentiation responses that FGF signalling drives in limb and skeletal development, neuronal patterning and wound repair. Phosphotyrosines on the activated receptor tail create docking sites read by the SH2 domains of PLCG1, which is then phosphorylated and activated in place; it cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and engaging protein kinase C and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases. The ligand repertoire here spans classical paracrine FGFs and the endocrine FGF23, whose action on FGFR1 requires the co-receptor klotho and governs phosphate handling. Aberrant FGFR1 activity underlies skeletal dysplasias and several cancers.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2, once bound by one of its many FGF ligands and autophosphorylated, recruits phospholipase C-gamma through an SH2 domain interaction and phosphorylates it, launching a phospholipase C-mediated cascade that converts receptor occupancy into a calcium signal. Activated PLC-gamma1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and engaging protein kinase C and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases. This arm of FGFR2 output works alongside the RAS-MAPK and PI3K routes to shape proliferation, migration and differentiation, and the ligand repertoire here spans FGFs acting in limb and craniofacial development, branching morphogenesis of lung and salivary gland, and, in the case of FGF23, phosphate homeostasis. Activating FGFR2 mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, while loss of signalling impairs epithelial-mesenchymal patterning.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 signals through several branches, and this one converts receptor activation into a calcium and lipid second-messenger response. On ligand binding, FGFR3 dimerises and autophosphorylates, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites that recruit phospholipase C-gamma through its SH2 domains; the receptor kinase then phosphorylates and activates it. Activated PLC-gamma1 cleaves phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and engaging protein kinase C and calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases. The ligands here span the canonical FGF families and a hormone-like member, FGF23, that acts on phosphate handling. FGFR3 output governs chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, and activating mutations in the receptor cause achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, while the same receptor is recurrently mutated in bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 4, engaged by FGF ligands and in some cases the co-receptor beta-Klotho, recruits phospholipase C-gamma to an autophosphorylated tyrosine on its cytoplasmic tail, launching the phospholipase C-mediated arm of FGF signalling. This branch converts receptor activation into second messengers: PLCG1 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, the latter releasing calcium from intracellular stores while DAG activates protein kinase C, feeding into calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase signalling. The output shapes proliferation, differentiation, migration and cell survival during development and tissue repair, and through endocrine ligands such as FGF19 and FGF23 links FGFR4 to bile acid and phosphate homeostasis. The SH2 domain of PLC-gamma provides the docking specificity, one of several competing effector routes downstream of the receptor; aberrant FGFR4 signalling contributes to hepatocellular and other cancers.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR1 trigger receptor dimerization and activation-loop autophosphorylation, and the intracellular events that follow convert that ligand cue into decisions about proliferation, differentiation, migration and survival. This branch of FGFR1 signalling drives limb and skeletal patterning, brain and craniofacial development, and phosphate homeostasis through the FGF23-Klotho axis; germline mutation causes Kallmann syndrome and skeletal dysplasias, while aberrant activation supports tumour growth. Phosphotyrosines on the receptor and on the closely associated docking proteins FRS2 and FRS3 nucleate a complex containing GRB2, SOS1, the phosphatase PTPN11 and GAB1, routing signal into RAS-family GTPases and the MAP kinase cascade and into PI3K-mediated survival signalling. SHC1 provides a parallel adaptor route and PLCG1 binds a distinct C-terminal site to generate diacylglycerol and inositol phosphates. FLRT proteins modulate receptor output at the cell surface.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR1 drive proliferation, migration and patterning decisions in development, and one route from the activated receptor to the RAS-MAPK module runs through the adaptor SHC1. This SHC-mediated cascade downstream of FGFR1 matters because RAS-ERK output is what converts an FGF gradient into changes in growth and cell fate; germline FGFR1 mutations cause skeletal dysplasias and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and the same signalling is co-opted in tumours. Mechanistically, FGF ligands together with the co-receptor Klotho engage FGFR1 and trigger tyrosine phosphorylation of the p46 and p52 SHC1 isoforms, though the receptor association appears indirect and may require SRC activity. Phosphorylated SHC1 then binds GRB2 and the exchange factor SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, providing an adaptor-based alternative to the FRS2-dependent route into the MAPK pathway.</description>}Y

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR1 do more than drive proliferation; one of their main outputs is a survival signal that keeps cells from dying, and it runs through PI3-kinase and AKT. Ligand-bound, dimerised FGFR1 autophosphorylates and recruits the docking protein FRS2, which assembles GRB2, the phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) and the scaffold GAB1 at the membrane; GAB1 brings in the p110/p85 PI3-kinase heterodimer, whose lipid product recruits PDK1 and AKT. Active AKT suppresses pro-apoptotic factors and inhibits GSK-3β, reinforcing the anti-apoptotic state, and also feeds growth and metabolic control. The many FGF ligands here, together with Klotho as a co-receptor for FGF23, indicate how context and cofactors select which tissue responds. This arm of FGFR1 output matters in skeletal and craniofacial development, and its constitutive activation by receptor amplification or mutation supports tumour cell survival.

Fibroblast growth factors instruct cells to divide, migrate and adopt positional identity during development, and much of that instruction passes through FGFR1 by way of the FRS scaffolds. When ligand binding activates the receptor kinase, FRS2 or FRS3 is phosphorylated on tyrosines and recruits GRB2 and the phosphatase PTPN11/SHP2, which together load SOS1 onto RAS and drive sustained ERK activation rather than a transient pulse. This branch of FGFR1 output governs limb and craniofacial patterning, skeletal growth, and the hypothalamic-pituitary control of reproduction; loss-of-function mutations in the receptor or its ligands cause Kallmann syndrome and craniosynostosis, while gain-of-function lesions in RAS or SHP2 produce overlapping developmental syndromes and cancer. The presence of klotho reflects the endocrine arm, in which FGF23 signals through FGFR1 to set phosphate handling.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR2 do more than drive proliferation: through the phosphoinositide 3-kinase arm of the receptor's output they keep cells alive, and this survival signalling is what allows growth factors to protect tissues from apoptosis. Ligand-bound, dimerised FGFR2 phosphorylates the docking protein FRS2, which recruits GRB2 and the phosphatase SHP2 to assemble a complex with GAB1; GAB1 then brings in the p85 regulatory and p110alpha catalytic subunits of PI3K. The resulting PIP3 recruits PDK1 and AKT, and active AKT suppresses pro-apoptotic effectors and inhibits GSK-3beta, adding further anti-apoptotic tone. The same axis contributes to migration, metabolism and growth. Because FGFR2 is used in limb, skeletal and craniofacial development and in epithelial maintenance, mutations that alter its signalling cause craniosynostosis syndromes, while amplification sustains survival signalling in gastric and breast cancers.

When an FGF ligand dimerizes and activates FGFR2, autophosphorylation of the receptor's cytoplasmic tail converts ligand binding into intracellular instructions for growth, movement and differentiation; this is the downstream signaling of activated FGFR2. The output governs limb bud outgrowth, branching morphogenesis of lung and salivary gland, keratinocyte behaviour and cranial suture and palate development, which is why FGFR2 mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, and why activating lesions recur in gastric, endometrial and breast tumours. Mechanistically, the long juxtamembrane region binds the FRS2/FRS3 adaptors, which recruit GRB2 with the phosphatase PTPN11 and the exchange factor SOS1 to load the RAS proteins and drive MAP kinase signalling, while GAB1 brings in PI3K for AKT-dependent survival. SHC1 provides a parallel route to RAS, and PLCG1 binds the receptor directly to generate diacylglycerol and mobilize calcium.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR2 trigger receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, and one route from the activated receptor to the RAS-ERK module runs through the adaptor SHC1. This branch matters because FGFR2 output governs limb and craniofacial patterning, lung and mammary branching morphogenesis, keratinocyte behaviour and wound repair; activating mutations in the receptor cause craniosynostosis syndromes and recur in endometrial and gastric cancers, while gene fusions drive cholangiocarcinoma. Mechanistically, phosphorylated SHC1 provides docking sites for GRB2, which brings the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 to the membrane to load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS and so initiate the MAP kinase cascade that reaches transcriptional targets controlling proliferation and differentiation. Whether SHC1 contacts the receptor directly is unsettled; association may be indirect, possibly requiring SRC activity, making this a supplementary rather than exclusive input to RAS.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR2 must convert receptor autophosphorylation into a lasting cytoplasmic signal, and the FRS scaffolds are how that happens. FRS2 and its relative FRS3 dock at the activated receptor, become tyrosine phosphorylated, and recruit GRB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11/SHP2; GRB2 in turn brings in the exchange factor SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS to drive sustained ERK activation, while GRB2's other partners feed into PI3K signalling and receptor ubiquitination. The output governs proliferation, survival and differentiation in epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, and FGFR2 with its many ligands shapes limb, lung, skeletal and craniofacial development. Activating FGFR2 mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, and the same axis is amplified in gastric and breast cancers, where SHP2 and RAS-ERK dependence makes it a drug target.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR3 drive proliferation and differentiation decisions in chondrocytes, keratinocytes and other cells, and the adaptor SHC1 provides one route from the activated receptor to RAS. In this arm of FGFR3 output, FGF-stimulated phosphorylation of the p46 and p52 forms of SHC1 creates docking sites for GRB2, which brings the exchange factor SOS1 to the membrane so that HRAS, KRAS and NRAS are loaded with GTP and the downstream MAPK cascade fires. Whether SHC1 contacts the receptor directly is unsettled; the association may be bridged by SRC family kinases rather than by the receptor itself. The biology matters because FGFR3 restrains growth plate expansion, and activating mutations cause achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, while the same RAS-MAPK output underlies FGFR3-driven bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 relays ligand binding into RAS-ERK activation through the FRS scaffolds, and this branch of FGFR3 output governs how chondrocytes in the growth plate proliferate and differentiate. Its tone sets bone length: activating FGFR3 mutations that drive excess signalling here cause achondroplasia and thanatophoric dysplasia, while the same receptor is a recurrent oncogenic driver in bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma. Mechanistically, receptor autophosphorylation recruits FRS2 or FRS3, which are themselves tyrosine phosphorylated and then dock GRB2 and the phosphatase PTPN11/SHP2; GRB2 brings the exchange factor SOS1 to the membrane to load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, giving the sustained ERK activation characteristic of FRS-dependent signalling. A broad set of FGF ligands, including FGF1, FGF9 and FGF18, initiates the cascade with heparan sulfate as cofactor.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3, once bound by its ligands and dimerized, autophosphorylates and converts extracellular FGF availability into instructions about proliferation, differentiation and survival. In cartilage this receptor acts mainly as a brake on chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate, and activating mutations produce achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, while the same mutations drive bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma. Downstream of the activated receptor, phosphotyrosines and the long juxtamembrane segment recruit the docking proteins FRS2 and FRS3, which assemble GRB2, the phosphatase PTPN11 and GAB1 into a complex. From there SOS1 loads GTP onto RAS proteins to fire the MAP kinase cascade, PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits generate lipid second messengers for AKT-dependent survival, SHC1 provides a parallel adaptor route, and PLCG1 hydrolyses PIP2 to mobilise calcium and activate protein kinase C.

Fibroblast growth factors acting through FGFR3 recruit the phosphoinositide 3-kinase route to AKT, and the main consequence is survival: growth-factor-stimulated cells resist apoptosis because AKT, activated downstream of PI3K and PDK, suppresses pro-apoptotic effectors and inhibits GSK-3beta. Ligand binding to FGFR3 assembles a docking platform in which the adaptor FRS2 recruits GRB2 and the phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11), bringing GAB1 to the receptor; GAB1 then binds the p85 regulatory subunit (PIK3R1) so that the p110alpha catalytic subunit (PIK3CA) generates PIP3 at the membrane. Because FGFR3 governs chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation in the growth plate, this survival and growth signalling is central to skeletal development, and activating receptor mutations cause achondroplasia and related dysplasias; the same PI3K-AKT output contributes to FGFR3-driven tumours such as bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma.

Fibroblast growth factors acting through FGFR4 drive proliferation, differentiation and metabolic responses, and the FRS scaffolds are how that receptor talks to RAS. Once FGFR4 is activated by ligand, FRS2 or FRS3 is phosphorylated on tyrosines and recruits GRB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11/SHP2; GRB2 brings in the exchange factor SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS and sets off sustained ERK activation. The same adaptor platform couples to PI3K and to ubiquitin-dependent receptor downregulation, so FRS2 both transmits and limits the signal. FGFR4 with its co-receptor beta-Klotho is the liver receptor for FGF19, linking this route to bile acid feedback, while FGF23 signalling through FGFR4 relates to phosphate handling. Aberrant FGFR4 output contributes to hepatocellular and other carcinomas, making the receptor a drug target.

Downstream signaling of activated FGFR4 describes what happens inside the cell once fibroblast growth factors bind and activate FGFR4, converting receptor autophosphorylation into proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation decisions. This particular receptor, partnered with the coreceptor beta-Klotho, transmits the hepatic FGF19 signal that suppresses bile acid synthesis, and its overactivity through amplification or activating mutation drives rhabdomyosarcoma and hepatocellular carcinoma. Mechanistically, phosphotyrosines on the receptor tail and the long juxtamembrane docking site recruit FRS2 and FRS3, which assemble GRB2, SOS1 and the phosphatase SHP2 to load RAS proteins with GTP and trigger the MAP kinase cascade; GAB1 recruitment engages PI3K and AKT-dependent survival signalling, while phospholipase C-gamma generates diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate for calcium and PKC responses. The same adaptor logic serves all FGF receptors, with ligand and coreceptor availability determining tissue-specific output.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 binds FGF ligands and, once its kinase is autophosphorylated, converts that event into the intracellular programmes that drive proliferation, survival, migration and differentiation. This receptor is also the metabolic arm of the family: with the coreceptor beta-Klotho it responds to endocrine FGFs such as FGF19 and FGF23 to control bile acid synthesis and phosphate handling, and its aberrant activation is implicated in hepatocellular and rhabdomyosarcoma tumours. Downstream signalling of activated FGFR4 proceeds through docking proteins FRS2 and FRS3, which recruit GRB2, the phosphatase SHP2 and GAB1, feeding the SOS1-RAS-ERK route and PI3K-AKT survival signalling; SHC1 provides a parallel adaptor link and phospholipase C-gamma generates diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate. Ligand identity, coreceptor availability and adaptor choice together determine which of these outputs dominates.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR4 trigger receptor dimerisation and tyrosine phosphorylation, and one branch of the resulting output runs through the adaptor SHC1 to the RAS-MAPK module. SHC1 becomes phosphorylated after FGF stimulation and associates with GRB2 and the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS to drive proliferative and differentiation signals; whether SHC1 contacts the receptor directly or is recruited indirectly, possibly via SRC, is not settled. FGFR4 is distinctive in partnering with the co-receptor beta-Klotho to receive endocrine ligands such as FGF19 and FGF23, linking this cascade to bile acid and phosphate homeostasis in liver and kidney as well as to classical paracrine FGF responses. Sustained FGFR4 signalling through RAS effectors contributes to hepatocellular and rhabdomyosarcoma tumour growth, making the receptor a drug target.

Fibroblast growth factors binding FGFR4 can keep a cell alive as well as make it divide, and the PI-3-kinase arm of that receptor's output is the survival branch. Phosphoinositide production at the membrane recruits PDK1 and activates AKT, which suppresses pro-apoptotic factors and inhibits GSK-3beta, so growth factor availability is translated into resistance to apoptosis; loss of the signal leaves cells dependent on other survival inputs. Activated FGFR4 assembles a docking complex through FRS2, GRB2, GAB1 and the phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11), which brings the p110alpha/p85 kinase pair encoded by PIK3CA and PIK3R1 to the receptor. Ligand identity sets the context: klotho-beta acts as coreceptor for FGF19 and FGF23, linking hepatic bile acid and phosphate endocrine signalling to this receptor, while classic FGFs such as FGF1, FGF2 and FGF8 act locally in development and tissue repair. FGFR4 amplification and pathway-activating mutations support tumour cell survival.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 transmits mitogenic and developmental cues, and the negative regulation of FGFR1 signalling is what keeps that output brief and proportionate. Without it, sustained receptor activity drives inappropriate proliferation and patterning errors; gain-of-function or escape from feedback underlies skeletal dysplasias, craniofacial and gonadotropin-releasing hormone neuron defects, and FGFR1-driven cancers. Ligand-bound receptor recruits FRS2, GRB2, PTPN11 and SRC to fire the RAS-ERK cascade, and the same cascade then dampens itself: activated MAPK1/MAPK3 phosphorylate FRS2 to reduce its tyrosine phosphorylation, SPRY2 intercepts GRB2-dependent coupling, and protein phosphatase 2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylations. In parallel, the E3 ligase CBL ubiquitinates the receptor with ubiquitin supplied by UBB, UBC and ribosomal ubiquitin precursors, committing it to endocytosis and degradation. Several inhibitors are themselves induced by the pathway, forming transcriptional negative feedback.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 drives proliferation, differentiation and morphogenesis in bone, limb and epithelial tissues, and its output must be switched off promptly once a ligand has been read; the negative regulation of FGFR2 signaling collects the brakes that do this. Activated receptor recruits FRS2, GRB2, PTPN11 and SRC to fire the RAS-BRAF-ERK cascade, and that cascade then feeds back on itself: ERK-dependent phosphorylation dampens FRS2 signalling competence, Sprouty proteins such as SPRY2 interrupt adaptor coupling, phosphatase subunits reset phosphorylation states, and the CBL ubiquitin ligase with ubiquitin precursors tags the receptor for internalisation and degradation. Because several inhibitors are themselves induced by the pathway, the system is self-limiting. Loss of this restraint underlies craniosynostosis and skeletal dysplasia syndromes caused by activating FGFR2 mutations, and sustained FGFR2 output contributes to gastric and breast tumour growth.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 transmits growth and differentiation cues, most conspicuously as a brake on chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, and its output must be switched off promptly; the negative regulation of FGFR3 signaling is the set of feedback devices that does this. Ligand-bound receptor recruits the FRS2 adaptor with GRB2 and the phosphatase PTPN11 to drive BRAF and the ERK kinases MAPK1/MAPK3, and the same cascade then turns on its own inhibitors. The ubiquitin ligase CBL, working with ubiquitin and ubiquitin-ribosomal fusion precursors, tags the receptor for internalisation and degradation, SPRY2 intercepts signalling at the adaptor level, ERK-dependent phosphorylation of FRS2 dampens further recruitment, and PP2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylations. Loss of this restraint underlies achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, and activating FGFR3 lesions recur in bladder carcinoma and myeloma.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 4 transmits signals from FGF ligands into RAS-ERK activation, and the feedback circuits that shut this output down are what keep the response transient and dose-appropriate. Negative regulation of FGFR4 signaling matters because sustained receptor output drives proliferative and metabolic programmes; FGFR4 in particular, paired with the co-receptor beta-Klotho, mediates FGF19 and FGF23 signalling that controls bile acid synthesis and phosphate handling, and its deregulation is implicated in liver cancer. Restraint is imposed at several levels: the E3 ligase CBL ubiquitinates the activated receptor and routes it for endocytic degradation, ERK-mediated phosphorylation of the adaptor FRS2 blunts further recruitment of GRB2 and PTPN11, Sprouty proteins interfere with signal propagation to BRAF, and protein phosphatase 2A subunits reverse activating phosphorylation. Several inhibitors are themselves induced by the pathway, forming delayed negative feedback.

Signaling by FGFR1 describes how fibroblast growth factors, held in place by heparan sulfate proteoglycans, activate one particular receptor tyrosine kinase to direct cell fate, proliferation, migration and survival across development. It patterns the limb bud, skeleton and brain, and drives GnRH neuron migration, so loss-of-function mutations in the receptor or its partner anosmin cause Kallmann syndrome and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, while amplification and fusion of the receptor drive squamous lung cancer and other tumours. Ligand binding dimerises the receptor and autophosphorylates its tail, creating docking sites for FRS2, GRB2 and SHC1 that launch RAS-RAF-ERK output, alongside PI3K-AKT via GAB1 and PLCG1-mediated calcium signalling. Feedback through SPRY, SPRED, PTPN11 and CBL-mediated ubiquitination limits the response, and Klotho co-receptors redirect the same kinase toward endocrine FGF23 control of phosphate homeostasis.

FGFR1 is one of four fibroblast growth factor receptor tyrosine kinases, and signalling through it directs cell fate, proliferation, migration and survival during development and in tissue repair. It patterns limb and craniofacial structures, drives olfactory and GnRH neuron development — loss of FGFR1 or its partner anosmin causes Kallmann syndrome with hypogonadism and anosmia — and, with Klotho as co-receptor, transduces FGF23 signals that lower phosphate. Ligands such as FGF1, FGF2 and FGF8 act together with heparan sulfate to dimerise the receptor; autophosphorylated tyrosines then recruit FRS2, GRB2, SHC1, PTPN11 and GAB1, feeding into RAS–RAF–ERK, PI3K and PLC-gamma outputs. Sprouty and SPRED proteins, protein phosphatase 2A subunits, and CBL-mediated ubiquitination restrain the response, while adhesion molecules of the FLRT family provide ligand-independent activation on neuronal membranes. Amplification and activating fusions of FGFR1 occur in several cancers.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 is one of four FGF receptor tyrosine kinases, and signalling through it coordinates epithelial tmesenchymal communication during limb, craniofacial, lung and skin development; activating mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes such as Apert and Crouzon, while amplification drives gastric and breast cancers. FGFs, working together with heparan sulfate, dimerise the receptor and trigger autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for adaptors including FRS2, GRB2, SHC1 and GAB1 that feed into RAS ERK signalling via SOS1, HRAS/KRAS and MAPK1/3, into PI3K through PIK3CA and its regulatory subunit, and into PLCG1. SHP2, SPRY2, CBL-mediated ubiquitination and phosphatase activity restrain the output. A distinctive feature here is ligand specificity set by mutually exclusive splicing of the third immunoglobulin domain: the epithelial IIIb and mesenchymal IIIc isoforms are chosen by ESRP1/2 and hnRNP-type splicing regulators acting with the transcription machinery, determining which FGFs a given cell can respond to.

FGFR3 is one of four fibroblast growth factor receptor tyrosine kinases, and signalling through it sets limits on growth — most visibly in the growth plate, where it restrains chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation. Activating mutations cause achondroplasia and related skeletal dysplasias, while the same kinase is amplified or mutated in bladder carcinoma and multiple myeloma; loss-of-signalling affects bone elongation in the opposite direction. Heparan sulfate–assisted binding of FGF ligands such as FGF1, FGF2, FGF8, FGF9 and FGF18 dimerises the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for FRS2, GRB2, SHC1 and GAB1. From there SOS1 and RAS proteins drive BRAF and the ERK1/2 kinases, while PI3K and PLCG1 form parallel arms controlling survival and shape. Negative regulation is built in: SPRY2 dampens RAS-ERK output, protein phosphatase 2A subunits and PTPN11 tune the cascade, and CBL-directed ubiquitination routes the receptor to degradation. FGF23 with GALNT3 links the family to phosphate handling.

FGFR4 is one of four fibroblast growth factor receptor tyrosine kinases, and signalling through it links FGF ligands to control of proliferation, differentiation, survival and metabolism. It is distinctive in serving as the liver receptor for the endocrine ligand FGF19, which with the co-receptor beta-Klotho suppresses bile acid synthesis; other family members such as FGF23 and the paracrine FGFs act on receptor forms too. Ligand binding, aided by heparan sulfate, drives receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for FRS2, GRB2, SHC1 and GAB1; the adaptors assemble complexes that route signal into RAS-driven ERK activation via SOS1, HRAS/KRAS and BRAF, into PI3K, and into PLCG1-dependent second messengers. Negative regulation by SPRY2, the phosphatase PP2A and CBL-mediated ubiquitination limits output. Aberrant FGFR4 activity contributes to hepatocellular carcinoma, rhabdomyosarcoma and other cancers, making it a therapeutic target.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 relays FGF ligand signals into growth and differentiation decisions, and when that relay is stuck on, the consequences are developmental or malignant. Germline activating mutations cause autosomal dominant craniosynostosis syndromes — Pfeiffer, Apert, Crouzon, Jackson-Weiss, Beare-Stevenson — in which cranial sutures fuse prematurely and, in some cases, digits fuse as well; the same or similar changes arising somatically, together with FGFR2 amplification, drive gastric, endometrial and breast cancers, while loss-of-function alleles occur in melanoma. Aberrant signalling by FGFR2 in disease works through the normal receptor output: ligand binding drives docking of FRS2, GRB2, GAB1 and SOS1, activating RAS–MAPK and PI3K, with PLCG1 as a parallel arm. Mutant receptors can also gain or lose ligand specificity across the FGF family, and aberrant transcriptional responses via RNA polymerase II are part of the downstream consequence.

FGFR4 is the least studied fibroblast growth factor receptor, and although its mutations are not linked to developmental syndromes, somatic changes in it drive cancer signalling. Activating kinase-domain substitutions such as N535K and V550E occur in a subset of rhabdomyosarcomas and can transform fibroblasts, a Y367C change has been found in breast cancer, and the common G388R variant tracks with faster progression, recurrence and metastasis in breast, colorectal and prostate tumours. Aberrant signalling by FGFR4 in disease runs through the same effectors the normal receptor uses: FRS2 and GRB2 with SOS1 load the RAS proteins and drive the MAP kinase cascade, GAB1 recruits PI3K to promote AKT-dependent survival and growth, and PLCG1 couples the receptor to calcium and diacylglycerol. The result is ligand-independent proliferative and survival signalling, making the receptor a candidate for kinase-inhibitor therapy.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose normal job is to read FGF ligands and convert them into proliferation, survival and patterning cues; when that control is lost, the same wiring drives skeletal malformation and cancer. Germline point mutations in the extracellular ligand-binding region raise FGF affinity and cause craniosynostosis syndromes such as Pfeiffer syndrome, while somatic events — gene amplification in breast, lung and squamous tumours, and chromosomal translocations — produce ligand-independent signalling. The fusion partners here, including BCR, ZMYM2, CNTRL, CPSF6, CEP43 and TRIM24, contribute dimerization domains that force constitutive kinase activity, the basis of the 8p11 myeloproliferative syndrome that progresses to leukaemia. Downstream, the activated receptor recruits FRS2, GRB2, SOS1 and GAB adaptors to RAS-MAPK, engages PI3K through PIK3CA and PIK3R1, and activates PLCG1 and STAT transcription factors, explaining why these lesions are targets for kinase inhibition.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 normally restrains chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate, and when its signalling is switched on inappropriately the consequences are skeletal and oncogenic. Germline activating mutations in the transmembrane or kinase domains cause achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, the lethal thanatophoric dysplasias and SADDAN, with phenotype severity tracking the degree of receptor activation; a mutation in the linker between immunoglobulin domains raises ligand affinity and produces craniosynostosis instead. Somatically, an extracellular S249C change is found in about half of bladder cancers, a translocation places the gene under immunoglobulin heavy chain control in multiple myeloma, and fusions with the spindle protein TACC3 yield constitutively active kinase. In each case the receptor recruits FRS2, GRB2, SOS1 and GAB1 to drive RAS-ERK and PI3K-AKT output, with PLCG1 as an additional branch, so ligand-independent dimerisation converts a growth-restricting receptor into a proliferative driver.

Dietary iron enters the body at the duodenal enterocyte, and the last step of that journey is the export of ferrous iron across the basolateral membrane into portal blood. Ferroportin, encoded by SLC40A1, is the only known cellular iron exporter and performs this efflux, working alongside the membrane-bound ferroxidase hephaestin, which stabilises it and oxidises the released iron for loading onto transferrin. When ferroportin is defective, iron handling at the gut-blood interface and in macrophages is deranged and the result is the iron overload disorder type 4 hemochromatosis, in which decades of accumulating iron deposit in liver, heart, pancreas, joints and endocrine tissue and produce cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, diabetes, cardiomyopathy, arthritis and hypogonadism. This export step is also the target of hepcidin, the hormone through which systemic iron demand controls absorption.

When a replication fork meets a damaged base it stalls, and translesion synthesis by DNA polymerase kappa is one of the routes that lets replication continue past the lesion rather than collapse. POLK is a Y-family polymerase particularly suited to copying past oxidised bases such as thymine glycol and 8-oxoguanine and past bulky adducts formed by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, so it limits fork breakage and the chromosomal damage that follows, at the cost of introducing mutations. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader and marked using the ubiquitin pool encoded by UBB, UBC and the ribosomal fusion genes; RPA coats the exposed single strand. POLK acts with REV1 and the REV3L-MAD2L2 polymerase zeta complex, which extends the nucleotide inserted opposite the lesion, making this a damage-tolerance rather than a repair pathway.

When a replication fork meets a damaged base it stalls, and DNA polymerase iota provides one way past the block: translesion synthesis by POLI lets replication continue across lesions that the high-fidelity polymerases cannot copy, trading accuracy for completion of the genome. This tolerance matters because unrescued stalled forks collapse into breaks and cell death, though the same error-prone copying contributes to mutation load. POLI is unusual in favouring Hoogsteen rather than Watson-Crick pairing, flipping template purines to a syn conformation so that adducted or edge-damaged G and A can still be read. Recruitment depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA, loaded by the replication factor C clamp loader onto RPA-coated DNA, together with REV1 as a scaffold. Because POLI extends poorly beyond the inserted nucleotide, polymerase zeta (REV3L with MAD2L2) carries out the extension step.

Termination of translesion DNA synthesis ends the emergency mode a replication fork enters when it meets a DNA lesion, and returns synthesis to the accurate replicative machinery. This matters because the Y-family polymerases that copy past damage — POLH, POLI, POLK and REV1 — are error-prone, so leaving them on the template beyond the lesion is a direct source of mutation and genome instability of the kind seen in cancer. Recruitment of these enzymes depends on monoubiquitinated PCNA at K164; deubiquitination by enzymes such as USP10 and USP43 strips that mark, evicts the bypass polymerase and licenses a switch back to polymerase delta or epsilon with RFC and RPA at the fork. ISG15 conjugation, driven by UBA7, TRIM25 and UBE2L6, provides a parallel brake, and PCLAF modulates polymerase access to PCNA. The pathway is thus the mutagenesis-limiting arm of DNA damage tolerance.

Translesion synthesis lets a replication fork copy past a damaged base, but the Y-family polymerases that do it are error-prone, so cells must switch back to accurate replication as soon as the lesion is passed. Terminating translesion DNA synthesis is that switch, and its failure raises the mutation burden carried forward into daughter cells, a route toward the mutational signatures seen in tumours. Monoubiquitinated PCNA recruits the bypass polymerases eta, iota, kappa and REV1; removing that ubiquitin mark, by deubiquitinases including USP10, evicts them and restores processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon loaded via replication factor C on RPA-coated template. An ISG15 arm, acting through UBA7, UBE2L6 and TRIM25, modifies PCNA and PCLAF to help disengage the bypass machinery, linking interferon-inducible conjugation to the fidelity of damage tolerance and to normal fork restart.

Dietary glucose and galactose are absorbed across the intestinal brush border against their concentration gradient, and the sodium/glucose cotransporter SGLT1 encoded by SLC5A1 does that work, coupling the inward movement of two Na+ ions to the uptake of one sugar molecule and using the sodium gradient set by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase as its energy source. The transporter is concentrated in the microvilli of small intestine and kidney tubule, where it also recovers filtered glucose. Loss-of-function mutations cause congenital glucose/galactose malabsorption, an autosomal recessive disease in which unabsorbed sugars retain water in the gut lumen and newborns develop severe osmotic diarrhoea that is fatal unless glucose and galactose are withdrawn from the diet. The same transporter is upregulated in several cancers, where sustained glucose entry can suppress autophagic cell death.

Hereditary fructose intolerance is what happens when the liver cannot process the fructose it takes up. Dietary fructose is phosphorylated to fructose 1-phosphate, and aldolase B, encoded by ALDOB, is the enzyme that cleaves this intermediate to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and glyceraldehyde so the carbons can enter glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. When aldolase B activity is lost through recessive mutation, fructose 1-phosphate accumulates and sequesters phosphate and adenine nucleotides, inhibiting gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown. Affected infants develop hypoglycaemia, vomiting, lactic acidosis, liver and kidney injury after fructose or sucrose exposure, and the illness can be fatal, though it is controlled simply by lifelong exclusion of fructose and sorbitol from the diet. The condition illustrates how a single step of hepatic carbohydrate metabolism governs tolerance of a common dietary sugar.

Dietary fructose is normally trapped in the liver by phosphorylation at its first carbon, and essential fructosuria is the benign condition that follows when this first step fails. Ketohexokinase, the fructokinase encoded by KHK, converts fructose to fructose-1-phosphate and commits it to hepatic fructolysis, where aldolase B and triokinase feed the carbons into glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Without ketohexokinase activity, ingested fructose is not phosphorylated, persists in blood, and is excreted in urine, giving a positive urinary reducing-sugar test but no liver injury, hypoglycaemia or other symptoms; it is usually discovered incidentally. This distinguishes it from hereditary fructose intolerance, where the block lies one step further on and fructose-1-phosphate accumulates toxically. The same enzymatic step is of wider interest because ketohexokinase-driven fructose metabolism bypasses the regulated points of glycolysis and contributes to lipogenesis and uric acid production.</description

Alkylating agents, whether endogenous metabolites or chemotherapy drugs, can transfer a methyl group to the O6 position of guanine, creating a base that pairs ambiguously with both cytosine and thymine and therefore seeds G:C to A:T transition mutations at the next round of replication. Direct reversal by MGMT removes this lesion before it is copied, restoring guanine in a single step without excising the base or nicking the backbone. The protein accepts the methyl group onto an active-site cysteine and is thereby inactivated, so each molecule acts only once and the cell's capacity is set by how much of it is present. Silencing of the gene by promoter hypermethylation is common in glioma and other tumours, raising mutational load but also sensitising those tumours to alkylating chemotherapy such as temozolomide, which makes this repair route a prognostic and predictive marker in oncology.

Hedgehog ligands only signal properly once they are lipid-modified, and the acyltransferase HHAT attaches palmitate to the N-terminus of the processed Hh precursor in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. The G278V substitution destroys this activity, so Sonic, Indian and Desert Hedgehog are secreted without their acyl chain and fail to activate Patched-Smoothened signalling in receiving cells at normal potency. Because Desert Hedgehog from Sertoli cells drives fetal Leydig cell differentiation and testosterone production, loss of palmitoylation produces syndromic 46,XY disorder of sex development with testis dysgenesis, alongside skeletal and neurological features attributable to reduced Indian and Sonic Hedgehog output. The defect illustrates how a single post-translational lipid modification gates an entire developmental morphogen family, affecting ligand membrane association, release and range rather than its transcription or proteolytic maturation.

Almost all glucose filtered by the kidney is recovered before urine leaves the proximal tubule, and SGLT2, encoded by SLC5A2, does the bulk of that work. Sitting in the apical membrane of the S1 and S2 segments, it is a low-affinity, high-capacity sodium-glucose cotransporter that moves one Na+ with each glucose, using the inward sodium gradient as the driving force, and accounts for roughly 98% of renal glucose reabsorption, with SGLT1 handling the remainder. Loss-of-function variants cause familial renal glucosuria, an autosomal recessive condition in which glucose appears in the urine despite normal blood glucose and otherwise intact tubular function; genotype-phenotype correlation is loose because reabsorptive capacity varies. The same transport step is targeted pharmacologically in type 2 diabetes, where inhibiting it deliberately induces glucosuria to lower plasma glucose.

RAS proteins are active only while bound to GTP, and GTPase-activating proteins end that signal by accelerating the intrinsic hydrolysis of GTP to GDP. This shutoff sets how long growth factor receptors can drive the RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K routes toward proliferation and survival, so its loss produces constitutive RAS signalling even when RAS itself is unmutated. Around a dozen GAPs act on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, including neurofibromin, the p120 and synaptic family members, and several calcium- or lipid-regulated variants, giving tissue- and stimulus-specific control; SPRED proteins recruit neurofibromin to the membrane where RAS resides. GAP abundance is itself limited by ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, with a cullin-RING ligase and the 26S proteasome represented here. Inactivating mutations in this arm cause neurofibromatosis type 1, Legius syndrome and developmental disorders, and contribute to tumour progression.

Cholinergic neurons cannot make their own choline, so they must recapture it from the synaptic cleft, and the high-affinity, sodium- and chloride-dependent choline transporter encoded by SLC5A7 is what performs that recapture at presynaptic terminals. Because choline uptake is the rate-limiting step in acetylcholine synthesis, the transporter sets how much neurotransmitter can be resupplied during sustained firing, most consequentially at the neuromuscular junction. Loss-of-function variants that impair this transport underlie distal hereditary motor neuronopathy 7A, in which motor neurons of the spinal anterior horn degenerate selectively and patients develop progressive distal muscle wasting and weakness of the legs, with vocal cord involvement, while sensory function is spared. The biology sits at the junction of solute carrier-mediated membrane transport, presynaptic neurotransmitter recycling, and the maintenance of motor unit function.

FGFRL1 is a fifth fibroblast growth factor receptor that binds FGF ligands through an extracellular region resembling FGFR1-4 but has no intracellular kinase domain, so it cannot signal on its own; its role is to tune what FGFR1 does. Because fibroblast growth factor signalling drives limb, skeletal, kidney and diaphragm development, the amount of ligand available to kinase-competent receptors matters, and loss of FGFRL1 in humans and mice produces diaphragmatic and skeletal defects. Two non-exclusive models are represented here: FGFRL1 may act as a decoy that sequesters ligands such as FGF2, FGF8, FGF10 and FGF18 away from FGFR1, or it may help nucleate receptor complexes and raise ERK1/2 output. The accompanying SPRED proteins act as negative regulators downstream, dampening RAS-ERK activation, which places this biology within the feedback control of growth factor signalling rather than its initiation.

Neutral amino acids taken in with food, or filtered by the kidney, must be recovered from the lumen by a dedicated sodium-coupled transporter at the apical brush border, and the loss of that activity is the basis of Hartnup disorder. The transporter B(0)AT1, encoded by SLC6A19, carries tryptophan, methionine, leucine and other neutral amino acids into enterocytes and proximal tubule cells together with a sodium ion, the sodium gradient providing the driving force. When mutations impair its folding, trafficking or transport cycle, neutral amino acids are lost in urine and stool; reduced tryptophan availability limits niacin synthesis and produces pellagra-like rashes, episodic cerebellar ataxia and psychiatric disturbance, typically precipitated by poor diet. Related SLC6A19 variants contribute to iminoglycinuria and hyperglycinuria, linking this carrier to epithelial amino acid reabsorption more broadly.

Dietary sugars must be broken to monosaccharides at the brush border before they can be absorbed, and loss of either of the two enzymes that do this job causes carbohydrate malabsorption. Lactase, the hydrolytic domain of lactase-phlorizin hydrolase on the external face of small intestinal enterocyte microvilli, cleaves the lactose that dominates breast milk; congenital deficiency presents in nursing newborns with severe diarrhoea and is managed with lactose-free formula, and is distinct from the common post-weaning decline in lactase expression behind adult lactose intolerance. Sucrase-isomaltase completes the digestion of starch-derived di- and oligosaccharides left by amylases, so its deficiency manifests after weaning. In both cases undigested sugar stays in the lumen, drawing water osmotically and feeding bacterial fermentation, with bloating, gas and diarrhoea as the result.

Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase sits in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, where it interconverts ribose 5-phosphate and ribulose 5-phosphate and so links the sugar rearrangements that feed transketolase and transaldolase to the ribose supply used for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis. When RPIA activity is lost, this reversible isomerisation fails: ribitol and D-arabitol, polyol products of the pentose pool, accumulate in body fluids and brain, and affected individuals develop a slowly progressive leukoencephalopathy with developmental delay, seizures and peripheral neuropathy. The disorder is exceptionally rare and is recognised biochemically by the polyol pattern on magnetic resonance spectroscopy and urine analysis. The pathway illustrates how a single step in cytosolic carbohydrate metabolism, normally buffered by the reversibility of the pentose phosphate reactions, becomes rate-limiting for white matter integrity when the isomerase is defective.

Cells must keep free zinc within narrow limits and neutralise heavy metals such as cadmium before they poison thiol-containing enzymes, and the zinc-sensing transcription factor MTF1 is the switch that mounts that response. Loaded with zinc, MTF1 enters the nucleus and binds metal response elements bearing a TGCRCNC core in the promoters of metallothioneins, zinc transporters and other stress-response genes, activating or repressing them according to promoter context. Its six zinc fingers differ in zinc affinity, so graded metal occupancy recruits different subsets of targets, giving a dose-scaled rather than all-or-none output. This makes MTF1 the hub of metal detoxification and zinc buffering, linked to oxidative and hypoxic stress responses and to the metal handling that tumour cells exploit for survival. Targets here include the zinc-binding LIM-domain protein CSRP1 and beta-synuclein.
