Zinc, copper and iron are needed as enzyme cofactors but are toxic when free, displacing other metals from proteins or driving uncontrolled redox chemistry, so cells maintain a transcriptional response to metal ions that buffers them. The zinc-sensing transcription factor MTF1 is the hub: cytosolic MTF1 binds zinc, moves to the nucleus and occupies metal response elements, inducing metallothioneins and glutamate-cysteine ligase for sequestration while repressing importers that would bring in more metal. Cadmium and copper act indirectly, displacing zinc from metallothioneins so that the liberated zinc activates MTF1. The many metallothionein isoforms here, including the brain-enriched MT3, bind metals through cysteine-rich domains and serve in heavy-metal detoxification, zinc storage and delivery, and thiol redox balance. Loss of this capacity leaves cells vulnerable to oxidative damage and heavy-metal poisoning, and the same system shapes zinc availability during growth and immune activation.

Antifungal defence depends on myeloid cells converting recognition of fungal β-glucan into mature interleukin-1β, the cytokine that drives protective TH17 responses at mucosal surfaces and in skin; people who cannot mount this response suffer chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis. Engagement of the β-glucan receptor dectin-1 signals through spleen tyrosine kinase to a CARD9-BCL10-MALT1 assembly, which activates NF-κB (RELA with NFKB1) and switches on transcription of pro-IL1B. MALT1 then nucleates a second complex with caspase-8 and the adaptor ASC that cleaves the pro-cytokine directly, a noncanonical inflammasome that needs neither caspase-1 nor internalisation of the pathogen. Some fungi additionally engage the classical NLRP3-caspase-1 route, so the two processing mechanisms can operate in parallel. The pathway links pattern recognition at the cell surface to the transcription and proteolytic maturation steps that together set IL-1β output.

Reabsorption of proline, hydroxyproline and glycine from the kidney filtrate depends on a small set of apical transporters, and loss of their combined activity leaves these amino acids in the urine. SIT1, encoded by SLC6A20, is the sodium- and chloride-coupled imino acid carrier of intestinal and renal brush border membranes, taking up L-proline, N-methylated amino acids such as pipecolate, and glycine. A common coding variant substituting methionine for threonine at position 199 reduces transport and acts as a modifier that pushes carriers toward hyperglycinuria, in which only glycine is spilled, or the broader iminoglycinuria phenotype, in which proline and hydroxyproline are lost as well. These are generally benign inherited aminoacidurias whose penetrance reflects the combined dosage of several transporters acting in series with the main proline carrier, illustrating how a digenic or polygenic transport defect produces a graded renal phenotype.

Dopamine signalling at the synapse is terminated by re-uptake of the transmitter into the presynaptic terminal, and the sodium- and chloride-coupled dopamine transporter DAT, encoded by SLC6A3, is the carrier that does it. By clearing dopamine from the cleft, it both limits the duration of receptor activation and recycles transmitter for repackaging into vesicles, setting striatal dopamine tone; it is also the target of cocaine and amphetamines. Loss-of-function mutations that misfold or mistraffic the protein, or abolish its transport activity, cause infantile parkinsonism-dystonia, in which affected children present in the first months of life with hypokinesia, rigidity and dystonic movements, with grossly abnormal dopamine metabolite ratios in cerebrospinal fluid. The disorder illustrates that defective transmitter clearance, not defective synthesis or release, is sufficient to produce a severe dopaminergic movement disorder resistant to levodopa.

Cationic amino acids absorbed in the gut or reclaimed from the glomerular filtrate must be moved out of epithelial cells across the basolateral membrane to reach the blood, and this is the step that fails in lysinuric protein intolerance. The transporter is a heterodimer of the catalytic light subunit SLC7A7 (y+LAT1) with the glycoprotein heavy subunit SLC3A2, which exchanges intracellular arginine, lysine or ornithine for extracellular leucine together with sodium; under normal amino acid gradients the net direction is export of the cationic substrate. When SLC7A7 is defective, dibasic amino acids are wasted in urine and poorly absorbed from the intestine, starving the urea cycle of arginine and ornithine so that ammonia accumulates after protein meals and orotic acid appears in urine. Affected infants refuse protein, vomit and fail to thrive, and may develop hepatosplenomegaly, haematological abnormalities and neurological involvement.

Defective amino acid transport by SLC7A9 causes cystinuria (CSNU) describes what happens in the kidney when the transporter that recovers cystine from urine stops working. Normally SLC7A9 pairs with the glycoprotein SLC3A1 to form a heterodimeric exchanger in the apical membrane of proximal tubule cells, taking up cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine in exchange for neutral amino acids, sodium-independently, so that these residues are reabsorbed rather than lost. When mutations disable the light subunit, cystine remains in the tubular fluid, and because oxidised cysteine is poorly soluble it precipitates into recurrent urinary stones, with obstruction, infection and occasionally renal failure. This is the type B form of an inherited aminoaciduria, mechanistically parallel to loss of the heavy subunit, and illustrates how epithelial solute retrieval sets urinary composition.

Cystine filtered by the glomerulus is normally recovered almost completely in the proximal tubule, and this reabsorption depends on a two-subunit transporter at the apical membrane: the light chain SLC7A9 (b(0,+)AT/BAT1) disulfide-linked to the heavy chain SLC3A1 (rBAT), which chaperones it to the surface. Together they carry out sodium-independent, high-affinity uptake of cystine and the dibasic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine in exchange for neutral amino acids. Loss-of-function mutations in SLC7A9 produce type B cystinuria, the counterpart of type A caused by SLC3A1 defects. Because cystine is poorly soluble in acidic urine, the unreabsorbed load precipitates as recurrent stones, leading to obstructive uropathy, pyelonephritis and, occasionally, chronic kidney damage. The pathway illustrates how epithelial solute recovery, rather than synthesis or catabolism, sets urinary amino acid composition.

Metallothioneins are small cysteine-rich proteins that clamp divalent metal ions through thiolate bonds, and this metal binding is how cells buffer zinc and neutralise toxic heavy metals such as cadmium, mercury and excess copper. Each protein holds up to seven metal ions in two clusters, forming a reservoir from which zinc can be released to transcription factors and enzymes, and the thiol-rich surface also scavenges reactive oxygen and electrophiles. The MT1 isoforms have expanded in primates into a family of closely related proteins expressed widely and induced by metal load, glucocorticoids and oxidative stress; MT3 is prominent in brain, where zinc handling at synapses and metal-linked neurodegeneration make this chemistry relevant, and MT4 is restricted to stratified epithelia. Loss of this buffering capacity leaves cells vulnerable to heavy metal toxicity and disordered zinc distribution.

Glucuronate released from the turnover of glucuronidated proteins and glycosaminoglycans is not discarded; formation of xylulose-5-phosphate is the route that salvages it back into central carbon metabolism, feeding the pentose phosphate pathway and, through it, glycolysis and NADPH-dependent biosynthesis. The conversion proceeds stepwise through L-gulonate, 3-dehydro-L-gulonate, L-xylulose, xylitol and D-xylulose, alternating reductions and oxidations that consume and regenerate NADPH and NAD, before a final kinase step commits the sugar as a phosphorylated pentose. An aldo-keto reductase opens the pathway, a lactonase-family enzyme and dicarbonyl/L-xylulose reductase handle the intermediate pentoses, and sorbitol dehydrogenase supplies the polyol oxidation. Loss of the L-xylulose reductase step causes pentosuria, a benign inherited condition in which L-xylulose accumulates in urine, marking this as a quantitatively minor but chemically distinctive branch of sugar metabolism.

Melanin biosynthesis is the pigment-making programme of melanocytes, carried out inside melanosomes and delivered to neighbouring keratinocytes so that the epidermis, hair, eye and inner ear acquire colour and protection from ultraviolet light. Tyrosinase performs the committing oxidation of tyrosine, and dopachrome tautomerase and TYRP1 act downstream to steer intermediates toward black-brown eumelanin, which absorbs light and quenches reactive oxygen species, rather than the pro-oxidant reddish pheomelanin; the balance between the two depends on tyrosinase activity and on how much tyrosine and cysteine are available. OCA2 and SLC45A2 set melanosomal ion and pH conditions that permit the enzymes to work. Loss of any of these genes causes oculocutaneous albinism with hypopigmentation, photosensitivity and visual deficits, and milder variants underlie normal variation in skin, hair and eye colour and melanoma risk.

Essential pentosuria is a harmless inherited metabolic quirk in which large amounts of the pentose sugar L-xylulose appear in the urine, historically one of the first recognised human biochemical variants and notable mainly because it can be mistaken for diabetes on older sugar-based urine tests. It arises when both copies of the gene for L-xylulose reductase, DCXR, are inactivated by loss-of-function mutations, as occurs at appreciable frequency in Ashkenazi Jewish and Lebanese populations. This NADPH-dependent enzyme normally reduces L-xylulose to xylitol as part of the glucuronate/xylulose pathway, a branch of sugar metabolism that disposes of glucuronate derived from UDP-glucuronic acid and feeds carbon back toward the pentose phosphate pool. Blocking the step leaves L-xylulose with no route onward, so it accumulates and is cleared renally without metabolic consequence, making this a benign trait rather than a disease.

Essential pentosuria is a harmless inherited condition in which large amounts of the pentose sugar L-xylulose appear in the urine, inherited recessively and found mainly in Ashkenazi Jewish and Lebanese families. It arises when L-xylulose reductase, encoded by DCXR, is inactivated by mutation, so the NADPH-dependent reduction of L-xylulose to xylitol cannot occur. That step belongs to the glucuronate–xylulose pathway, a branch of carbohydrate metabolism that disposes of glucuronate derived from UDP-glucuronic acid and feeds carbon back toward the pentose phosphate pool; blocking it causes the unused pentose to spill into urine rather than any metabolic crisis. The trait matters chiefly as an interpretive problem, since the urinary reducing sugar can be mistaken for glycosuria and prompt an unnecessary diagnosis of diabetes, and it illustrates how a metabolic dead end can be tolerated without disease.

Sialic acid is added to glycans in the Golgi lumen, but it is activated in the cytosol as CMP-Neu5Ac and must be carried across the Golgi membrane before any sialyltransferase can use it. SLC35A1 is that carrier, exchanging CMP-sialic acid inward for CMP outward, so loss of its function starves the Golgi of donor substrate and leaves secreted and surface glycoproteins under-sialylated. The result is congenital disorder of glycosylation type 2F, one of the severe inherited defects of protein glycosylation, presenting with impaired nervous system development, psychomotor delay, hypotonia, bleeding tendency and immunodeficiency; poor sialylation of selectin ligands compromises leukocyte adhesion and of platelet glycoproteins compromises clotting. The defect sits at the substrate-supply step of terminal glycan maturation rather than in the transferases themselves, and affects N-glycans, O-glycans and glycolipids alike.

Diseases of carbohydrate metabolism collects the inherited defects that break the route from dietary sugar to usable energy and to glycan turnover. It matters because each block produces a recognisable clinical syndrome: lactase or sucrase-isomaltase deficiency causes osmotic diarrhoea and carbohydrate intolerance; aldolase B or ketohexokinase loss underlies hereditary fructose intolerance and benign fructosuria; glucose-6-phosphatase and its transporter, glycogen synthase, branching enzyme and glycogenin failures give the glycogen storage diseases, with acid maltase deficiency causing Pompe disease; laforin and malin mutations produce Lafora body epilepsy. Pentose phosphate pathway defects in transaldolase and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase impair NADPH and nucleotide precursor supply, while loss of dicarbonyl reductase in glucuronate catabolism yields harmless pentosuria. Lysosomal sulfatases, glycosidases and hyaluronidase are included because failure to degrade glycosaminoglycans produces the mucopolysaccharidoses, with ubiquitin genes reflecting degradative quality control.

Inherited defects in carbohydrate handling span the whole route from a meal to usable energy, and this collection of diseases of carbohydrate metabolism covers failures at each step. Loss of intestinal brush-border enzymes such as lactase or sucrase-isomaltase leaves disaccharides undigested and causes osmotic diarrhoea, while ketohexokinase and aldolase B mutations produce benign fructosuria or the hepatotoxic, hypoglycaemic syndrome of hereditary fructose intolerance. Glycogen storage disorders arise when synthesis or mobilisation breaks down: glycogenin and glycogen synthase deficiencies, branching enzyme loss, acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency in Pompe disease, and failure of glucose-6-phosphatase or its transporter, which uncouples the liver from fasting glucose output. Laforin and malin mutations yield insoluble polyglucosan and progressive myoclonic epilepsy. Pentose phosphate pathway lesions in transaldolase and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase, lysosomal glycosaminoglycan degradation defects, and dicarbonyl reductase loss causing essential pentosuria complete the spectrum.

Growth factor receptors and the second messenger cascades beneath them tell cells when to divide, survive, migrate and differentiate, and most of the recurrent lesions of human cancer land somewhere in this circuitry. Gathered here are the molecular consequences of mutation and fusion in that machinery: activating changes in receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, ERBB2, FGFR1-4, KIT, MET, PDGFRA and ALK, oncogenic RAS and RAF alleles feeding the MAP kinase module, PIK3CA mutation with loss of PTEN driving AKT-mTOR output, and breakpoint fusions that tether kinase domains to partners like EML4 or BCR. Also represented are corrupted developmental signalling arms - WNT with truncated APC and stabilised beta-catenin, NOTCH cleaved by gamma-secretase, TGF-beta receptors and SMADs - plus the ubiquitin-proteasome and chromatin-modifying steps that normally limit these signals. Germline defects in the same components cause developmental syndromes including RASopathies and skeletal dysplasias.

This is the broad collection of host processes hijacked or mobilised during infectious disease, covering bacterial, viral and parasitic invasion of human cells. It matters because the same core machinery that runs normal cell biology is what pathogens subvert: receptor-mediated entry and clathrin/actin-driven uptake, nuclear pore transport, host transcription by RNA polymerase II with Mediator and elongation factors, spliceosome and 3' end processing, ribosomes and cap-dependent translation, N-glycosylation and signal peptide cleavage, ubiquitin-proteasome turnover, and ESCRT-dependent membrane budding. Entry factors such as ACE2, TMPRSS2, CTSL, CD4 and CXCR4 sit alongside toxin receptors and clostridial toxin targets. Countervailing host defence is represented by Toll-like and cytosolic nucleic acid sensors, interferon induction and effectors, inflammasome and complement components, which together determine whether infection is cleared or becomes disease.

Branched actin networks that push out lamellipodia, drive phagocytosis and immune synapse formation, and propel intracellular pathogens are built when RHO family GTPases activate WASP and WAVE nucleation-promoting factors. CDC42 binding relieves the autoinhibitory clamp between the GTPase-binding and VCA regions of WASP and N-WASP, freeing them to deliver monomeric actin to the ARP2/3 complex, whose seven subunits are all represented here. RAC1 instead acts on the WAVE regulatory complex, in which WAVE1-3 sit with ABI, NCKAP1, CYFIP and BRK1 until a conformational change permits ABL1-mediated activating phosphorylation. Adaptors such as NCK1, GRB2, WIP family proteins and the kinases PTK2 and BTK couple surface receptors to this machinery. Loss of WASP function causes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, an X-linked immunodeficiency reflecting how much leukocyte motility, spreading and degranulation depend on regulated actin nucleation.

Small GTPases of the RHO family switch on diaphanous-related formins, and this is how a cell converts RHO signalling into actual actin filaments. The formins are autoinhibited until an active GTPase such as RHOA, RHOC, RAC1 or CDC42 breaks the internal clamp; the released FH2 domain then nucleates and elongates unbranched actin, with the proline-rich FH1 domain recruiting profilin-bound actin monomers to speed the process. The outputs are diverse: lamellipodia and phagocytic cups, stress fibres, actin coats that drive endosome motility, a link from WNT/dishevelled signalling to cytoskeletal reorganisation, and relief of MRTF/SRF-dependent transcription as unpolymerised actin is consumed. One isoform acts in mitosis, where CDC42-activated formin activity helps kinetochores capture astral microtubules, which brings the kinetochore, dynein, tubulin and spindle-checkpoint machinery into the same axis. Deregulation contributes to tumour cell motility and invasion, and formin loss is linked to premature ovarian failure.

RHO GTPases Activate Rhotekin and Rhophilins covers one branch of RHOA/RHOB/RHOC signalling in which the activated GTPase engages scaffold effectors rather than kinases, linking RHO activity to actin organisation, cell polarity and membrane traffic. These effectors matter because they determine where RHO output is delivered: rhotekin binds GTP-loaded RHOA, RHOB and RHOC, restrains their GTPase activity, contributes to septin assembly and polarity establishment, drives SRF-dependent transcription, and can suppress apoptosis through NF-kappaB. A lymphocyte-restricted relative broadens the family into immune cells. Rhophilins pair an N-terminal RHO-binding domain with BRO1 and PDZ modules, so they couple RHO to protein kinase C signalling and, through PDZ partners such as TAX1BP3 and LIN7B, to junctional and polarity complexes; RHOB recruits rhophilin-2 onto endosomes, relevant to thyroid cell function. Together they shape cytoskeletal remodelling, motility and epithelial architecture.

Active RHOA, RHOB and RHOC do their work by recruiting effectors, and rhotekin and the rhophilins are one such set of GTP-dependent binding partners that link RHO signalling to the actin cytoskeleton, cell polarity and membrane traffic. Rhotekin binds the GTP-loaded forms of all three GTPases and dampens their hydrolysis, and has been tied to septin organization, serum response factor-driven transcription, and NF-kappaB-dependent survival; a lymphocyte-restricted relative remains poorly characterized. Rhophilin-1 and rhophilin-2 pair an N-terminal GTPase-binding region with a BRO1 domain and a C-terminal PDZ domain, the latter engaging PDZ-containing partners such as TAX1BP3 and the scaffold LIN7B, and RHOB recruits rhophilin-2 onto endosomes. Through these effectors RHO activity is translated into cell shape, motility and directed membrane organization rather than into a single enzymatic output.

A subset of TNF-family receptors, TNFR2 among them, signals not through the fast canonical NF-kB route but through the slower non-canonical arm that generates RelB:p52 dimers. This branch drives survival and proliferation rather than apoptosis, supports regulatory T cell function and B cell survival, and builds lymphoid tissue, bone and skin appendages; loss of individual components causes immunodeficiency, hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia or disordered osteoclast formation. The switch is controlled by protein stability: in resting cells cIAP1/2 with TRAF2 and TRAF3 target the kinase NIK for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal destruction. Receptor ligation redirects that ubiquitin ligase activity onto TRAF3, NIK accumulates and phosphorylates IKKalpha, which marks p100 for beta-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination and partial proteasomal processing to p52. Related receptors including CD40, BAFF-R, RANK, LTbetaR and EDAR feed into the same output, explaining the prominence of proteasome and ubiquitin components here.

RHO GTPases Activate NADPH Oxidases describes how the small GTPases RAC1 and RAC2, in their GTP-bound state, switch on membrane NADPH oxidase complexes to generate superoxide. This is the reaction behind the neutrophil respiratory burst that kills ingested bacteria and fungi — loss of the NOX2 subunits CYBB, CYBA or the cytosolic factors NCF1/NCF2 causes chronic granulomatous disease — and the same chemistry supplies superoxide as a second messenger downstream of VEGF receptor signalling in endothelial cells during angiogenesis. Assembly requires RAC:GTP to dock directly on the flavocytochrome and on NCF2, joined by NCF1 and NCF4 after priming by protein kinase C isoforms, p38 and ERK MAP kinases, phosphoinositide kinases and the S100A8/A9 arachidonate carrier. Related NOX1 and NOX3 complexes use NOXO1 and NOXA1 in place of the phagocyte factors, extending RAC-dependent reactive oxygen production to epithelia and the inner ear.

Superoxide is made deliberately by NADPH oxidase complexes, and small GTPases of the RHO family are the switch that turns them on. When RAC1 or RAC2 loaded with GTP docks onto the membrane flavocytochrome and its cytosolic partners, electrons pass from NADPH to oxygen and superoxide is released into a phagosome or across the plasma membrane. In neutrophils this burst is the chemistry that kills ingested bacteria and fungi; loss of the catalytic subunit or of the p47/p67/p40 assembly causes chronic granulomatous disease with recurrent infection and granuloma formation. In endothelium the same output acts as a second messenger that amplifies VEGF receptor signalling during angiogenesis. Assembly is licensed by phosphorylation, with kinases including protein kinase C isoforms and ERK/p38 MAP kinases modifying the cytosolic factors, and S100A8/A9 and PIN1 contributing to subunit handling. Related oxidases NOX1 and NOX3 are activated through homologous adaptors.

Inherited metabolic disorders arise when a single enzyme, transporter or cofactor-handling protein fails, so that a substrate accumulates to toxic levels or a required product is never made. The genes here span the routes most often affected: carbohydrate handling and glycogen storage, galactose and fructose metabolism, urea cycle and amino acid catabolism including phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency, branched-chain ketoacid breakdown, cobalamin uptake and trafficking, lysosomal degradation of glycosaminoglycans and sphingolipids, N- and O-linked glycosylation together with dystroglycan and proteoglycan assembly, cytochrome P450-dependent steroid and vitamin D oxidations, and pulmonary surfactant production. Clinical consequences range from neonatal hyperammonaemia, hypoglycaemia and intellectual disability to skeletal dysplasia, congenital muscular dystrophy and respiratory failure. Also included are a somatic isocitrate dehydrogenase change found in gliomas and proopiomelanocortin defects that cause early-onset obesity, linking metabolic failure to both neoplasia and energy balance.

Ligand-receptor pairing between the tumour necrosis factor superfamily and its receptors is the first committed step in a set of signalling events that shape inflammation, lymphocyte costimulation and controlled cell death. These interactions decide whether a T cell receiving antigen proliferates and survives, whether a B cell matures, whether an osteoclast forms, and whether a target cell is instructed to die. The set includes the classic inflammatory receptors TNFRSF1A and TNFRSF1B, costimulatory pairs such as CD27 with CD70 and TNFSF4/TNFSF9 with their receptors, the B cell survival factor TNFSF13B, the bone remodelling ligand TNFSF11, and ectodysplasin with EDAR and the adaptor EDARADD, which patterns hair, teeth and sweat glands. Soluble decoy receptors such as TNFRSF11B and TNFRSF6B tune the output by sequestering ligand. Disturbance of these axes underlies septic shock, autoimmunity, graft rejection, ectodermal dysplasia and immunodeficiency, and several pairs are drug targets.

Turning on a RAF kinase is the step that converts active RAS at the membrane into a running MAPK cascade, and it is where growth factor signals are committed to proliferation, differentiation and survival. The three isoforms ARAF, BRAF and RAF1 share a RAS-binding and cysteine-rich region, inhibitory phosphosites that hold the kinase closed through 14-3-3 binding, and a C-terminal kinase domain preceded by an acidic motif required for activity. Activation demands release from that closed state by phosphatase action, with the SHOC2-MRAS-PP1 holoenzyme and PP2A subunits performing the key dephosphorylations, membrane recruitment by RAS, and homo- or heterodimerization so one monomer allosterically primes another; scaffolds such as KSR1 assemble RAF with MEK1/2. BRAF contributes most to ERK output, and its mutation is among the commonest oncogenic events in melanoma, thyroid and colorectal cancer, while germline lesions in these regulators cause Noonan-spectrum developmental syndromes.

Growth factors, cytokines and hormones tell cells whether to divide, differentiate, survive, senesce or move, and the RAF/MAP kinase cascade is the route by which those instructions reach the nucleus. Receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs, KIT, MET, PDGFR and RET, together with cytokine receptors, recruit adaptors GRB2 and SHC and the exchange factor SOS1 to load RAS with GTP at membranes; GTP-bound HRAS, KRAS or NRAS then engages BRAF, ARAF or RAF1, which phosphorylate MEK1/2, which phosphorylate ERK1/2. Output is shaped by scaffolds and modulators including KSR1/2, SHOC2, CNKSR and IQGAP1, by RAS GAPs such as NF1 and RASA1, by DUSP phosphatases and PEBP1, and by prenylation and palmitoylation enzymes that place RAS at the right membrane. Activating mutations in RAS and BRAF make this among the most frequently corrupted signalling routes in cancer, and germline lesions cause developmental RASopathies.

This is the core relay of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, the step at which activated RAF kinases phosphorylate the activation loops of MEK1 and MEK2, which in turn phosphorylate ERK1 and ERK2. Because ERK then acts on hundreds of cytoplasmic and nuclear substrates, including transcription factors, this junction converts growth factor and adhesion signals into decisions about proliferation, differentiation and survival, and its constitutive activation by mutant RAS or BRAF drives much of human cancer. Signalling does not occur freely in the cytosol: scaffolds such as KSR1/KSR2, IQGAP1, CNKSR proteins, 14-3-3 and late endosomal Rab-interactor components assemble the kinases into complexes that set specificity, timing and subcellular location, while PEBP1 acts as an inhibitory brake. Integrin and fibrinogen components with talin, vinculin and SRC place this activation step downstream of platelet and cell-adhesion signalling as well.

Constitutive Signaling by AKT1 E17K in Cancer describes how a single recurrent point mutation locks a central growth-and-survival kinase into the active state, driving tumours of the breast, bladder, ovary and endometrium independently of upstream receptor input. Substitution of glutamate 17 by lysine in the pleckstrin homology domain lets AKT1 bind PIP2 rather than requiring PI3K-generated PIP3, so the kinase sits constitutively at the plasma membrane where PDPK1 and the mTORC2 complex (MTOR, RICTOR, MLST8, MAPKAP1, PRR5) phosphorylate it. The consequence is unrestrained output through the normal AKT substrate repertoire: inhibition of the pro-apoptotic BAD and CASP9, phosphorylation and nuclear exclusion of FOXO transcription factors, stabilisation of MDM2 against p53, inactivation of GSK3 and TSC2 to unleash mTORC1-driven protein synthesis, and blockade of the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27. This bypass of PI3K shapes tumour responses to pathway-targeted inhibitors.

AKT sits at the centre of growth factor signalling, and a single glutamate-to-lysine change at position 17 of AKT1 turns that node on permanently, driving the survival and proliferation programmes that underlie breast, ovarian and other cancers. Normally AKT must wait for PI3K to generate PIP3 before its PH domain docks at the membrane; the E17K substitution lets the kinase bind the abundant lipid PIP2 instead, so membrane recruitment no longer reports on receptor activity. Once there it is phosphorylated by PDPK1 and by the rapamycin-insensitive mTOR complex containing RICTOR, MLST8 and MAPKAP1, and becomes constitutively active. The downstream consequences are the familiar ones: FOXO transcription factors and GSK3 are inactivated, BAD and caspase-9 are silenced to block apoptosis, MDM2 is activated against p53, TSC2 is relieved so mTORC1 drives translation, and CDKN1A and CDKN1B are held away from the cell cycle machinery.

PTEN is the lipid phosphatase that removes the 3-phosphate from PIP3, and its loss of function in cancer is one of the most common routes by which tumour cells acquire constitutive growth signalling. Without it, PIP3 accumulates at the plasma membrane and AKT is chronically activated, driving proliferation, cell survival, growth through mTOR, and resistance to apoptosis and to therapies that act upstream. Inactivation occurs many ways: point mutations that cripple the phosphatase domain, deletion of one or both alleles, promoter methylation, and overexpression of microRNAs that suppress PTEN mRNA, with even partial dosage reduction being consequential. Germline loss underlies the hamartoma tumour syndromes, in which benign overgrowths coexist with elevated breast, thyroid and endometrial cancer risk, while somatic loss is frequent in glioblastoma, prostate and endometrial tumours. This places the gene among the classical tumour suppressors restraining phosphoinositide signalling.

Growth factor signalling through RAF-MEK-ERK must be transient, and negative feedback regulation of the MAPK pathway is how activated ERK shuts down its own upstream activators. Once ERK1 and ERK2 are phosphorylated by MEK1 and MEK2, they phosphorylate inhibitory sites on RAF1, BRAF, MEK1 and the exchange factor SOS, weakening receptor coupling to RAS, destabilising RAF dimers and desensitising the cascade to further stimulation. This converts a graded input into a pulsed, self-limiting output and sets the duration of ERK activity, which determines whether a cell proliferates, differentiates or arrests. Loss of the feedback is a recurring theme in cancer: oncogenic BRAF signals independently of it, and relief of ERK-mediated feedback on RAF and receptor signalling underlies the rebound of pathway activity seen after treatment with RAF and MEK inhibitors.

Negative regulation of MAPK pathway is the braking system on RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signalling, setting how strongly and for how long growth factor cues are transmitted. Because the same inputs can drive proliferation, differentiation, or senescence depending on signal duration, these brakes determine cell fate, and their loss is a route to oncogenic ERK hyperactivation. Several mechanisms converge: ERK-dependent feedback phosphorylation of RAF and of MAP2K1 T292 dampens kinase output, PP2A and PP5 strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region, priming PKA/AKT-mediated rephosphorylation that restores 14-3-3 binding and the inactive conformation, and PEBP1 uncouples RAF1 from its MEK substrates. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, themselves ERK-inducible, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, while GAP-stimulated GTP hydrolysis returns RAS to its GDP-bound state. Scaffolds, ubiquitin, and KSR1 tune complex assembly.

Growth factor signalling through RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK must be switched off as reliably as it is switched on, and negative regulation of the MAPK pathway is how the duration, amplitude and location of that signal are set. Without it, sustained ERK activity drives inappropriate proliferation and transformation, which is why many of these brakes are lost or bypassed in cancer. ERK itself feeds back onto RAF and onto MAP2K1 at T292, priming the PP2A holoenzyme and PP5 to strip activating phosphates from the RAF activation loop and N-terminal acidic region; subsequent phosphorylation restores 14-3-3 (YWHAB) binding and returns RAF to an autoinhibited state. PEBP1 sequesters RAF1 away from its MEK substrates, and scaffolds and modifiers such as KSR1, BRAP and PAQR3 constrain complex assembly and membrane localisation. Nuclear and cytoplasmic dual-specificity phosphatases, many of them ERK-induced, dephosphorylate ERK and stress-activated MAPKs, closing the loop.

Necroptosis is a lytic, inflammatory form of programmed cell death that runs when caspase-8 activity is blocked, and the controls over it decide whether a stressed cell dies quietly or spills its contents and alerts the immune system. Keeping that balance right matters for development and tissue homeostasis; losing it contributes to autoimmunity, neurodegeneration, ischemia/reperfusion injury, steatohepatitis and cancer. Death receptor engagement through FAS or the TRAIL receptors assembles FADD and caspase-8 with RIPK1, where cFLIP and caspase-8 cleavage suppress the necroptotic route. When suppression fails, RIPK1 and RIPK3 form the necrosome and phosphorylate MLKL, which oligomerizes and permeabilizes the plasma membrane. Ubiquitin ligases including the cIAPs, XIAP, ITCH, PELI1 and the chaperone-linked CHIP set the threshold by marking RIPK1 and RIPK3 for restraint or degradation, with HSP90 and CDC37 required for kinase stability.

NIK-->noncanonical NF-kB signaling is the slower, longer-lasting arm of NF-kB activation, here triggered downstream of the fungal-recognition receptor Dectin-1 and SYK, and it shapes which cytokines a dendritic cell or macrophage makes in response to a pathogen. Where canonical signalling is rapid and transient, this branch builds over hours and sustains transcription, inducing chemokines such as CCL17 and CCL22 while repressing IL12B and thereby biasing the ensuing T helper response. Mechanistically, stabilised NIK (MAP3K14) activates IKKalpha, which phosphorylates the NFKB2 p100 precursor; an SCF-betaTrCP ubiquitin ligase and the 26S proteasome then process p100 to mature p52, releasing p52:RELB dimers into the nucleus. The same axis governs lymphoid organogenesis and B cell survival, and its dysregulation drives lymphoid malignancy and immunodeficiency.

The noncanonical NF-kB route is the slower, longer-lasting arm of NF-kB signalling, and it controls transcription of chemokines and immune modulators that shape the character of an inflammatory response rather than simply switching it on. Downstream of receptors such as the fungal sensor Dectin-1 acting through SYK, and of several TNF receptor family members, stabilised NIK (MAP3K14) phosphorylates IKK-alpha (CHUK), which marks the NFKB2 p100 precursor for recognition by a SKP1-CUL1-beta-TrCP ubiquitin ligase. Instead of being destroyed, p100 is partially processed by the 26S proteasome to mature p52, releasing p52:RELB dimers into the nucleus where they induce genes such as CCL17 and CCL22 while repressing IL12B. Neddylation components and polyubiquitin precursors supply the conjugation chemistry. This pathway underlies lymphoid organ development, B cell survival, and dendritic cell polarisation of T helper responses; its constitutive activation drives multiple myeloma and lymphoma.

A subset of tumour necrosis factor receptor superfamily members signals through the non-canonical NF-kB route, and this branch is what builds and maintains lymphoid tissue rather than simply reacting to infection. Lymphotoxin-beta receptor signalling organises lymph node and splenic microarchitecture, BAFF receptor sustains mature B cell survival, CD40 licenses B cell responses to helper T cells, and RANK drives osteoclast differentiation and bone remodelling; loss of these outputs produces immunodeficiency, absent germinal centres or osteopetrosis. Mechanistically these receptors share a TRAF-binding motif that recruits TRAF2 and TRAF3 together with the ubiquitin ligases BIRC2 and BIRC3, a complex that constitutively degrades the kinase NIK. Ligand engagement destroys this complex, allowing NIK to accumulate and direct processing of the NF-kB2 precursor p100 into p52, which enters the nucleus with RelB to activate transcription.

Protein repair reverses two kinds of spontaneous chemical damage to proteins that would otherwise accumulate with age, restoring function to already-folded polypeptides rather than degrading and replacing them. Reactive oxygen species oxidise methionine side chains to sulfoxides, altering enzyme activity and structure; the methionine sulfoxide reductases MSRA and MSRB1-3 reduce the S- and R-diastereomers respectively, using a catalytic cysteine, an internal disulfide intermediate, and regeneration by NADPH-dependent thioredoxin. Because each cycle consumes an oxidant equivalent, these enzymes double as catalytic antioxidants alongside peroxiredoxins and superoxide dismutases. Separately, PCMT1 methylates isoaspartyl residues formed by spontaneous asparagine deamidation, driving them back through a succinimide intermediate to normal aspartate linkages. Loss of these activities accelerates oxidative and age-related protein damage, with the selenoprotein MSRB1 linking the system to selenium status and immune redox control.

Proteins accumulate chemical damage simply from living in an oxidizing, aqueous environment, and a small set of enzymes reverses two of the commonest lesions rather than letting the damaged protein be degraded. Reactive oxygen species oxidize methionine side chains to methionine sulfoxide, altering folding and activity; the methionine sulfoxide reductases restore them, with MSRA acting on the S-diastereomer of free and protein-bound substrate and the MSRB enzymes on protein-bound R-sulfoxide in cytosol, mitochondria and secretory compartments. Each cycle consumes an oxidizing equivalent, so these reductases double as catalytic antioxidants, regenerated through thioredoxin and NADPH. Separately, spontaneous deamidation of asparagine creates isoaspartyl bonds that distort the backbone, and PCMT1 methylates them to drive conversion back to normal aspartate. Loss of such protein repair capacity contributes to the protein damage that accompanies oxidative stress, neurodegeneration and ageing.

ATP-sensitive potassium channels couple a cell's metabolic state to its membrane excitability, and in heart and smooth muscle that channel is built from the pore-forming inward rectifier subunit KCNJ11 together with the regulatory sulfonylurea-receptor subunit ABCC9. Rising ADP/ATP ratios open the channel, hyperpolarising the membrane; channel closure depolarises it, recruiting voltage-gated calcium channels and raising intracellular calcium, so the complex sets the threshold for contraction and provides protection during ischaemia and metabolic stress. Mutations in ABCC9 that disturb this nucleotide sensing produce distinct human disease: dilated cardiomyopathy 10 with ventricular dilation, poor systolic function and heart failure; familial atrial fibrillation 12 with disorganised atrial activity, stasis and thromboembolic risk; and Cantu syndrome, where gain of channel activity gives hypertrichosis, macrosomia, skeletal dysplasia and cardiomegaly through excessive vascular smooth muscle relaxation.

Hepatocytes must pump bile salts across their canalicular membrane against a steep gradient, and ABCB11, the bile salt export pump, is the transporter that does it, using ATP hydrolysis to drive bile salt secretion into bile. This step sets bile flow and keeps intracellular bile acid concentrations below toxic levels. When mutations impair the pump, bile salts are retained in the liver, and the resulting cholestasis takes two clinically distinct forms: progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2, in which chronic retention drives hepatocyte and bile duct injury, inflammation, fibrosis and cirrhosis with end-stage liver disease in childhood and a raised risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, and benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis type 2, with self-limiting episodes that resolve over weeks or months. Loss of function can reflect misfolding and failed trafficking as well as defective transport, linking this disease biology to bile acid homeostasis, lipid absorption and drug-induced cholestasis.

Hepatocytes protect their own bile ducts by secreting phospholipid alongside bile salts, and ABCB4 (MDR3) is the canalicular floppase that performs this step, translocating phosphatidylcholine into bile in an ATP-dependent manner. The exported phospholipid forms mixed micelles with bile salts and cholesterol, blunting the detergent action of bile acids and keeping cholesterol in solution. When the transporter is defective, bile becomes phospholipid-poor and directly injurious: canalicular membranes and biliary epithelium are damaged, bile flow fails, and cholesterol crystallises. The resulting phenotypes span a spectrum of cholestatic liver disease, from progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3 with early ductular injury and fibrosis, through the reversible intrahepatic cholestasis of the third trimester of pregnancy, to adult cholesterol gallstone disease. This places the transporter at the centre of bile formation, biliary lipid homeostasis and susceptibility to cholelithiasis.

Defective CFTR causes cystic fibrosis describes what happens to a misfolded chloride channel that never reaches the cell surface. CFTR normally conducts chloride across airway, pancreatic, intestinal and sweat gland epithelia, setting the hydration and salt content of secretions; when mutant forms such as F508del fail quality control, secretions become thick and poorly cleared, producing chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, male infertility and salty sweat. The genes trace the disposal route rather than the channel's function: lectin-like sensors and the SEL1L adaptor recognise the misfolded protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, derlins and ERLIN proteins mark it for retrotranslocation, RNF5 and RNF185 ubiquitinate it, the VCP ATPase extracts it, and the 26S proteasome degrades it. This is endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation acting as the proximate cause of disease, and the target of corrector therapies.

CFTR is a cAMP-regulated chloride channel in the apical membrane of epithelia, and the chloride and bicarbonate it moves set the hydration and pH of airway, pancreatic, intestinal and biliary secretions. When mutation prevents the protein from folding, as with the common F508del allele, the channel never reaches the surface and cystic fibrosis follows: thick unclearable mucus and chronic lung infection, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, meconium ileus, biliary disease, salty sweat and male infertility. The genes here trace the fate of the misfolded protein rather than the channel's transport function — lectin-like ER quality control and retention factors such as OS9, ERLEC1 and the SEL1L complex, membrane ubiquitin ligases RNF5 and RNF185, the VCP ATPase and derlin channels that retrotranslocate the substrate, and the ubiquitin and 26S proteasome machinery that degrades it. Loss of function is thus a disposal problem imposed by endoplasmic-reticulum-associated degradation.

Bilirubin, the coloured end product of heme breakdown, is conjugated with glucuronate in hepatocytes and must then be pumped across the canalicular membrane into bile. That export step is carried out by the ATP-dependent transporter ABCC2 (MRP2), which moves mono- and di-glucuronosyl bilirubin with high affinity along with glutathione conjugates, sulfates and a broad range of other organic anions, making it a principal route of phase III elimination for drugs and toxins. When ABCC2 is lost or misfolded and fails to reach the apical membrane, conjugated bilirubin refluxes into plasma: the result is Dubin-Johnson syndrome, a benign autosomal recessive conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with a darkly pigmented liver and characteristically abnormal organic anion clearance. The defect illustrates how biliary secretion, rather than conjugation itself, limits bilirubin disposal.

Whole-body sterol balance depends on the body's ability to reject plant sterols while retaining cholesterol, and that discrimination is performed by a single heterodimeric transporter. ABCG5 and ABCG8 are half transporters that pair in the endoplasmic reticulum and traffic to the apical surface of enterocytes and the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, where they use ATP to pump sterols back into the gut lumen and into bile. Loss-of-function mutations in ABCG8 abolish this selectivity: dietary sitosterol and campesterol are absorbed largely unchecked and poorly excreted, producing sitosterolemia with xanthomas, haematological abnormalities and premature coronary atherosclerosis. Variants that alter transporter activity more subtly instead shift biliary cholesterol saturation and predispose to cholesterol gallstones, the basis of gallbladder disease 4. The pathway therefore links intestinal sterol uptake, hepatobiliary secretion and cardiovascular risk.

Plant sterols such as sitosterol are taken in with every meal but are normally kept out of the body by an active pumping step in the gut and liver. That step is carried out by ABCG5 paired with ABCG8: two ATP-binding cassette half transporters that heterodimerize in the endoplasmic reticulum, traffic to the apical membrane of enterocytes and hepatocytes, and push non-cholesterol sterols back into the intestinal lumen and into bile. When ABCG5 is defective, this discrimination between cholesterol and phytosterols is lost, so dietary sitosterol is absorbed and poorly excreted. The resulting sitosterolemia presents with raised plasma sterols, xanthomas, haematological abnormalities and premature coronary atherosclerosis. The pathway places sterol efflux at the centre of whole-body cholesterol balance and explains why biliary secretion is the principal route for eliminating absorbed sterols.

The first step in making high density lipoprotein is the export of cellular cholesterol and phospholipid onto lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I, and this is what fails when ABCA1 is defective, causing Tangier disease. ABCA1 is an ATP-driven plasma membrane transporter that presents intracellular cholesterol, including cholesterol delivered from cytosolic vesicles, at the outer face of the membrane for pick-up by APOA1; the active transporter is palmitoylated, phosphorylated and largely tetrameric. Loss-of-function mutations abolish this efflux, so nascent HDL is never assembled and plasma HDL is nearly absent, while cholesteryl esters accumulate in macrophages and other tissues, producing enlarged orange tonsils, hepatosplenomegaly and neuropathy. Because reverse cholesterol transport begins here, impaired ABCA1 activity links directly to the low-HDL phenotype common in coronary heart disease and to foam cell formation in atherosclerosis.

The outermost layer of skin keeps water in and pathogens out by means of lipid lamellae packed between corneocytes, and loading those lipids into lamellar granules depends on the keratinocyte transporter ABCA12. When ABCA12 is defective, glucosylceramides and other barrier lipids are never delivered to the extracellular space of the stratum corneum, the lamellar structure fails to form, and desquamation and cornification are grossly disordered. The resulting autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis 4B, also known as harlequin ichthyosis, is the most severe of the congenital ichthyoses: affected newborns are encased in thick armour-like plates separated by deep fissures, are frequently premature, and suffer catastrophic transepidermal water loss, temperature instability and infection. This is lipid transport read out directly as epidermal barrier physiology, linking an ATP-binding cassette transporter to terminal keratinocyte differentiation and neonatal survival.

Synapses are built and tuned by proteins that bridge the pre- and postsynaptic membranes, and the leucine-rich glioma inactivated proteins do this as secreted ligands for ADAM family cell-surface receptors. LGI1 binding to ADAM22 and ADAM23 organises a transsynaptic complex that recruits postsynaptic scaffolding through PSD-95 and couples to AMPA receptor auxiliary subunits of the stargazin/TARP family, while presynaptic syntaxins link the assembly to vesicle fusion machinery. The interaction sets excitatory transmission strength and neuronal excitability, and LGI4 signalling to ADAM22 on Schwann cells drives peripheral myelination. Loss of function matters clinically: LGI1 mutations cause autosomal dominant lateral temporal lobe epilepsy, autoantibodies against LGI1 produce limbic encephalitis with seizures, and disrupted LGI4-ADAM22 signalling causes congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. These interactions therefore underpin nervous system development, synaptic maturation, and control of network excitability.

MAPK family signalling cascades convert extracellular cues "a growth factor, a cytokine, a stress "into changes in gene expression, proliferation, differentiation, metabolism and survival. This is the route by which receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs, KIT, MET, RET and PDGFRs and cytokine receptors talk to the nucleus, and its constitutive activation through RAS or RAF mutation is among the commonest events in human cancer; germline lesions in NF1, SPRED1 or SHOC2 cause developmental RASopathies. Adaptors including GRB2, SHC and FRS2 with the exchange factors SOS1 and RASGRP load RAS-family GTPases, which recruit ARAF/BRAF/RAF1 to phosphorylate MAP2K1/2 and thence ERK1/2; scaffolds such as KSR and CNKSR organise the tiers. GAPs, DUSP phosphatases, PP2A, RAF inhibitory protein and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover set signal duration, while palmitoylation and prenylation enzymes control GTPase membrane targeting. Atypical members ERK3/ERK4 with MAPKAPK5 are also represented.

Defective ABCC8 can cause hypo- and hyper-glycemias concerns the pancreatic beta-cell ATP-sensitive potassium channel and the glucose-sensing function it performs. This channel, built from the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8 together with the pore-forming subunit KCNJ11, couples metabolic state to membrane potential: as glucose oxidation raises the ATP:ADP ratio the channel closes, the beta cell depolarises, voltage-gated calcium entry follows, and insulin granules fuse with the plasma membrane. Because the channel sets the threshold for secretion, mutations shift glycemia in either direction. Loss-of-function alleles leave the cell chronically depolarised and secreting insulin regardless of glucose, producing familial hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia and leucine-sensitive hypoglycemia; gain-of-function alleles hold the channel open and cause neonatal or transient neonatal diabetes and adult non-insulin-dependent diabetes. The same subunit is the binding site for sulfonylurea drugs used to stimulate insulin release.

Insulin release from pancreatic beta cells is timed by an ATP-sensitive potassium channel built from the sulfonylurea receptor ABCC8 and the pore-forming subunit KCNJ11. When glucose metabolism raises the ATP:ADP ratio, the channel closes, the membrane depolarises, voltage-gated calcium entry follows, and insulin granules fuse with the plasma membrane; when the ratio falls the channel opens and secretion is silenced. Mutations in ABCC8 break this coupling in either direction. Loss of channel function leaves beta cells persistently depolarised and secreting insulin regardless of blood glucose, producing familial hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia and leucine-sensitive hypoglycaemia of infancy. Gain of function holds the channel open, blunting depolarisation and insulin output, and underlies permanent and transient neonatal diabetes as well as susceptibility to non-insulin-dependent diabetes. The same channel is the target of sulfonylurea drugs and of diazoxide, so genotype guides treatment.

Vitamin B12 taken up by cells is delivered to lysosomes, and it must cross the lysosomal membrane before it can be converted into the two cofactor forms the body uses. This export step depends on the ABC transporter ABCD4 working together with the lysosomal membrane protein LMBRD1, which helps target the transporter and couples it to downstream cytosolic processing. When ABCD4 is defective, cobalamin is trapped in the lysosome and cells cannot make adenosylcobalamin for mitochondrial methylmalonyl-CoA mutase or methylcobalamin for cytosolic methionine synthase. The resulting inborn error, methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria of the cblJ type, presents in infancy with feeding difficulty, poor growth, hypotonia, lethargy, anaemia and developmental delay, reflecting the haematological and neurological dependence on B12-dependent one-carbon and propionate metabolism.

ABCB6 is an ATP-binding cassette transporter that moves porphyrins across membranes, supplying intermediates for haem synthesis; it acts as a homodimer and has been localised to the outer mitochondrial membrane as well as to endolysosomal compartments, where it also underlies the Langereis blood group antigen. Loss-of-function variants cause isolated colobomatous microphthalmia 7, in which the optic fissure fails to fuse properly during eye morphogenesis and the eyeball remains abnormally small, sometimes with associated defects of the anterior segment. This links a transport step in porphyrin and haem metabolism to ocular development, since the closure of the optic fissure is one of the early patterning events of the central nervous system. Defective ABCB6 therefore illustrates how a single metabolite transporter can be required for organ morphogenesis rather than only for biosynthetic flux.

Defective ABCA3 causes SMDP3 describes what happens to the lung when a single lipid transporter fails. ABCA3 sits in the limiting membrane of lamellar bodies in alveolar type II cells and pumps phospholipids and cholesterol into them, so that surfactant lipids and the surfactant proteins can be packaged together and secreted into the airspace. That secreted film lowers surface tension at the air-liquid interface and keeps alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration. Loss-of-function mutations produce pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3: lamellar bodies are absent or replaced by small vesicles with electron-dense inclusions, surfactant is not delivered, and lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveoli. Newborns present with severe, usually fatal respiratory distress, and milder alleles underlie childhood interstitial lung disease. The biology places surfactant production within ABC-transporter-mediated lipid trafficking and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis.

Pulmonary surfactant lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface and keeps the lungs from collapsing at end-expiration, and ABCA3 is the lipid transporter that loads the phospholipids and cholesterol needed to build it into lamellar bodies of alveolar type II cells. There, lipids and surfactant proteins are packaged into bilayer stacks for secretion into the airspace. When ABCA3 function is lost, normal lamellar bodies fail to form and are replaced by small vesicles with electron-dense inclusions, surfactant secretion collapses, and lipoproteinaceous material accumulates in the alveoli. The resulting disorder of surfactant metabolism, pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 3, presents as severe and usually fatal neonatal respiratory distress, with milder mutations underlying childhood interstitial lung disease. This links ABC-transporter-mediated lipid translocation directly to lung development and neonatal respiratory physiology.

Air breathing depends on a lipoprotein film that lowers surface tension at the alveolar air-liquid interface, and surfactant metabolism covers how alveolar type II cells make, secrete, recycle and degrade it. Without adequate surfactant, alveoli collapse at low lung volumes: premature infants whose type II cells are immature develop respiratory distress syndrome, and inherited defects cause interstitial and chronic lung disease or alveolar proteinosis. Phosphatidylcholine- and phosphatidylglycerol-rich lipids are loaded into lamellar bodies by the transporter ABCA3, while the hydrophobic proteins SFTPB and SFTPC, matured by proteases such as napsin A and cathepsin H, organise the film; the hydrophilic collectins SFTPA1/2 and SFTPD additionally opsonise inhaled microbes as part of innate lung defence. Transcription factors including NKX2-1 and GATA6 drive this programme before birth, and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor receptor subunits support macrophage-mediated surfactant clearance.

Very long-chain fatty acids can only be broken down in peroxisomes, and they must first be carried across the peroxisomal membrane. ABCD1, a half ABC transporter also known as adrenoleukodystrophy protein, performs that import step, delivering VLCFA-CoA substrates to peroxisomal beta-oxidation. When mutations disable it, the fatty acids are not degraded but instead further elongated by ELOVL1, so saturated VLCFAs accumulate in plasma, adrenal cortex and nervous tissue. The consequence is X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, in which adrenal insufficiency combines with inflammatory cerebral demyelination or a slower progressive myelopathy; clinical severity varies widely among carriers of the same mutation, implicating modifier genes and environment. This places the defect at the intersection of lipid catabolism, membrane transport and myelin maintenance, and explains why plasma VLCFA measurement serves as the diagnostic and newborn-screening marker.

Innate immune cells translate detection of bacterial products and inflammatory cytokines into cytokine output, and MAP3K8 (TPL2)-dependent activation of ERK1/2 is one route by which they do it, driving TNF-alpha, prostaglandin and chemokine production in monocytes and macrophages. In resting cells TPL2 is sequestered in a stoichiometric complex with ABIN2 (TNIP2) and the NF-kB precursor p105 (NFKB1), which stabilizes the kinase while keeping it catalytically silent. Stimulation activates the IKK complex, and IKKbeta phosphorylation of p105 marks it for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal processing through an SCF-type ligase using SKP1, CUL1 and the beta-TrCP subunits, releasing TPL2 to phosphorylate MEK1 and thereby ERK1/2. The freed kinase is itself short-lived, so signalling is self-limiting; the liberated p50 fragment contributes to NF-kB-driven transcription. Whether the output is net pro- or anti-inflammatory depends on cell type and stimulus, and the kinase is a drug target for inflammatory disease.

ERK1 and ERK2, encoded by MAPK3 and MAPK1, are the terminal kinases of the classical mitogen-activated cascade, and MAPK1/MAPK3 signaling is how growth factors, cytokines and adhesion cues are converted into decisions to proliferate, differentiate, migrate or survive. Receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR, FGFRs, KIT, MET, PDGFRs and RET recruit GRB2/SHC adaptors and SOS or RASGRP exchange factors to load RAS with GTP; RAF kinases then activate MAP2K1/2, which phosphorylate ERK, with scaffolds (KSR1/2, SHOC2, CNKSR), prenylation and palmitoylation enzymes controlling membrane localisation. Output is restrained by RASA1 and neurofibromin as RAS GTPase-activating proteins, SPRED proteins, DUSP phosphatases, PP2A and proteasomal turnover. Cytokine receptor chains and JAK kinases feed in as parallel inputs, and synaptic scaffolds and NMDA receptor subunits couple the cascade to neuronal plasticity. Activating mutations in this route underlie many cancers and the developmental RASopathies.

Single strand annealing is a mutagenic route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that falls back on direct pairing of repeated sequences rather than faithful copying from a homologous template. It matters because it salvages breaks that cannot be repaired accurately, at the cost of deleting one repeat and everything between them, and because its use reshapes genomes in tumours where accurate recombination is compromised. Breaks first activate ATM and are extensively resected by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1, then by EXO1 or DNA2 with the BLM and WRN helicases, generating long 3' single-stranded tails that RPA coats and that trigger ATR-TOPBP1-9-1-1 checkpoint signalling. RAD52 heptamers, phosphorylated by ABL1, anneal homologous repeats in opposing tails and simultaneously block invasive RAD51 filament formation, committing the break away from homologous recombination. The ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease trims displaced 3' flaps before ligation seals the product.

HDR through MMEJ (alt-NHEJ) is a backup route for sealing DNA double-strand breaks that trades accuracy for speed, and it becomes the dominant repair choice when higher-fidelity options are saturated or genetically lost. It matters most in tumours: cells deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, depend on it to survive, which is why DNA polymerase theta is pursued as a drug target, and its error-prone action leaves a distinctive scar of deletions, base substitutions and translocations that drives genome instability. Mechanistically the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP performs limited end resection without the CDK-dependent BRCA1 recruitment that would commit the break to recombination; PARP1 or PARP2 then load POLQ, which anneals short microhomologies in the 3' overhangs and extends them, while FEN1 trims displaced flaps and LIG3-XRCC1 ligates the remaining nicks. ATM activation suppresses this route.

Microhomology-mediated end joining, also called alternative nonhomologous end joining, is a mutagenic backup route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks that operates when high-fidelity repair is saturated or genetically compromised. It matters clinically because tumours deficient in homologous recombination, such as BRCA-mutant cancers, lean on it to survive, which is why polymerase theta and PARP are drug targets there. Repair begins with limited end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex together with CtIP, generating 3' single-stranded overhangs that are not licensed for recombination. PARP1 or PARP2 and DNA polymerase theta then align the two ends through short microhomologous tracts, POLQ extends by strand-displacement synthesis, FEN1 trims the displaced 5' flaps, and LIG3 with XRCC1 seals the remaining nicks. The outcome is invariably a deletion spanning the sequence between microhomologies, plus frequent base substitutions and occasional chromosomal translocations.

Homologous recombination repair is the error-free route for mending DNA double-strand breaks, using an intact sister chromatid as the template, and it operates mainly in S and G2 phase when that template exists. Cells that lose it accumulate chromosomal rearrangements and become dependent on more mutagenic repair; germline loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 predisposes to breast and ovarian cancer, and the resulting deficiency is what makes tumours sensitive to PARP inhibitors. Mechanistically, the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP and nucleases such as EXO1 and DNA2 resect break ends to long 3' single-stranded tails, which RPA coats and BRCA2 hands over to RAD51 to form the invasive nucleofilament. Strand invasion generates a D-loop extended by replicative polymerases and PCNA, and the resulting joint molecules are dissolved by the BLM-TOP3A-RMI complex or cut by structure-specific resolvases. ATM, ATR and checkpoint clamp components couple the repair to cell cycle arrest.

Toll-like receptors detect microbes, but they also respond to host molecules released or exposed when tissue is injured, and this endogenous-ligand arm of TLR signalling is how sterile damage becomes inflammation. Nuclear HMGB1, the calprotectin subunits S100A8 and S100A9, fibrinogen chains, oxidised lipoproteins and surfactant proteins act as damage-associated molecular patterns, engaging TLR2 and TLR4 with their heterodimer partners TLR1 and TLR6, aided by the accessory proteins CD14, LBP, MD-2 and the scavenger receptor CD36. The output is inflammatory gene expression and recruitment of phagocytes to clear debris and drive repair; the gasdermins listed link pyroptotic membrane rupture to further DAMP release, creating feed-forward loops. Persistent or citrullination-modified ligands sustain this signalling inappropriately, contributing to rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, and inflammation-associated cancer.

MAPK6 and MAPK4, better known as ERK3 and ERK4, are atypical MAP kinases distinguished by a single Ser-Glu-Gly phospho-acceptor site in place of the usual Thr-X-Tyr motif, so they are not switched on by classical MAP kinase kinases. Instead they are phosphorylated downstream of class I p21-activated kinases acting under RAC1 and CDC42, linking small GTPase signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling rather than to the growth-factor cascades of conventional ERKs. Their best-established substrate is MAPKAPK5, which promotes HSPB1-dependent rearrangement of F-actin and thereby cell migration; a second arm acts through the NCOA3 coactivator and the ETV4 transcription factor to drive matrix metalloproteinase expression and invasiveness, and both arms are implicated in tumour progression. MAPK6 is unusually short-lived, and ubiquitin-proteasome degradation together with microRNA-mediated silencing sets its abundance, making turnover a principal means of control.

Alveolar type II cells recycle phosphate from the airspace for surfactant synthesis, and they do so through the sodium-dependent phosphate cotransporter NaPi-2b encoded by SLC34A2, which moves divalent phosphate across the apical membrane together with three sodium ions in an electrogenic step driven by the sodium gradient. The same transporter operates, less abundantly, in intestinal, pancreatic, prostatic and renal epithelia, where it contributes to dietary and systemic phosphate handling. When SLC34A2 function is lost, phosphate liberated in alveolar fluid is no longer cleared and precipitates with calcium as microscopic calcium phosphate concretions, producing pulmonary alveolar microlithiasis. Affected individuals are often asymptomatic for years before a slowly progressive decline in gas exchange and lung compliance, which can end in respiratory failure. This links a single epithelial transport activity to surfactant metabolism and to the prevention of ectopic mineralisation in the lung.

Pulmonary surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension so that the lung does not collapse at the end of each breath, and genetic defects in its production, packaging and clearance cause a spectrum of severe neonatal and childhood lung disease. Alveolar type II cells synthesise the hydrophobic proteins SFTPB and SFTPC, which are processed and loaded with phospholipid into lamellar bodies by the transporter ABCA3; loss of any of these gives fatal respiratory distress in newborns or chronic interstitial lung disease later. The collectins SFTPA1, SFTPA2 and SFTPD add innate immune surveillance to the same secreted film, binding pathogens and aiding their clearance. On the disposal side, alveolar macrophages depend on GM-CSF receptor subunits CSF2RA and CSF2RB to catabolise surfactant, and their failure produces pulmonary alveolar proteinosis; SLC34A2 mutations cause alveolar microlithiasis through defective phosphate handling.

Surfactant protein A2 is one of the pulmonary collectins secreted by alveolar type II cells into the airway, where it helps organise surfactant lipids at the air-liquid interface, regulates surfactant turnover, and opsonises inhaled microbes for clearance. Mutations that disturb the folding of SFTPA2 prevent its secretion: the misfolded protein is retained in the endoplasmic reticulum rather than reaching the alveolar lumen, so its contribution to surfactant homeostasis is lost and the type II cell bears a chronic burden of unfolded protein. The consequence is familial idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, in which repeated alveolar epithelial injury drives progressive scarring, breathlessness and declining gas exchange, typically fatal from respiratory failure within a few years of diagnosis. This links defective SFTPA2 to alveolar epithelial secretory failure as an initiating event in interstitial lung disease.

Surfactant protein B is a small hydrophobic peptide, cleaved from a larger precursor in alveolar type II cells, that lets phospholipid films spread across the air-liquid interface and lowers surface tension so alveoli do not collapse at end-expiration. When SFTPB is mutated, the mature peptide is lost and the pathway of surfactant assembly fails at two points: lamellar bodies form abnormally and the SFTPC precursor is left partially processed and inactive, so floccular lipoprotein material accumulates in air spaces instead of a functional film. The result is pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 1, a rare disorder of surfactant homeostasis, and a severe respiratory distress syndrome that presents in newborns and premature infants and is typically fatal without transplantation. This biology links intracellular processing of a secreted proprotein to alveolar mechanics and neonatal lung function.

Surfactant protein C is made by alveolar type II cells as a propeptide that must fold, traffic through the secretory pathway and be proteolytically trimmed before the mature hydrophobic peptide joins the lipid film that lowers surface tension and keeps alveoli from collapsing at end-expiration. Mutations that disrupt folding, routing or processing of pro-SFTPC produce a dominant disease mechanism in which the misfolded proprotein is retained in type II cells rather than simply being absent. The retained precursor triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, reactive oxygen species generation and autophagy, injuring and killing the cells that renew the alveolar epithelium. The result is impaired surfactant homeostasis with floccular material filling alveoli, seen as interstitial lung disease and as respiratory distress in newborns.

Alveoli stay open at the end of each breath because type II epithelial cells secrete a phospholipid-rich surfactant that lowers surface tension, and ABCA3 is the lipid transporter that loads that material into lamellar bodies, the secretory organelles from which surfactant is released. It moves phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol, the dominant surfactant lipids, from the endoplasmic reticulum membrane into the limiting membrane of the lamellar body, where they are packaged with the surfactant proteins. When ABCA3 is defective, lamellar bodies fail to mature and surfactant is deficient or abnormal, producing pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 3: fatal respiratory distress in full-term newborns in severe cases, and chronic childhood interstitial lung disease in milder ones. This places the transporter at the centre of alveolar lipid handling and neonatal lung function.

Ubiquitin marks are reversible, and deubiquitination is the erasing step that decides whether a tagged protein is destroyed, relocated, or simply switched off. It recycles ubiquitin and keeps the pool long-lived, trims inappropriate degradation tags as a quality-control check, processes ubiquitin precursors encoded as fusions and polyproteins, and clears unanchored chains from the proteasome. Cysteine-protease families — USP, UCH, OTU, JOSD and Josephin enzymes — together with JAMM/MPN metalloproteases such as the proteasome subunit PSMD14 and the BRCC36 complex, cleave isopeptide bonds and are themselves tuned by oxidation of the catalytic cysteine and by cofactors like WDR48. The targets define the consequences: chromatin ubiquitylation on histone H2A/H2B, NF-kB and RIG-I-like antiviral signalling, TGF-beta/SMAD output, p53-MDM2, DNA repair, receptor sorting on endosomes and damaged-mitochondrion clearance.

Alveolar macrophages clear and recycle pulmonary surfactant, and they depend on GM-CSF signalling through a receptor built from an alpha subunit (CSF2RA) and a shared beta subunit (CSF2RB) to acquire that capacity. Loss-of-function mutations in the beta subunit cause pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction 5, also called hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, in which macrophages fail to take up and degrade surfactant lipid and protein; the alveoli fill with floccular surfactant material, gas exchange deteriorates, and respiratory failure follows. The surfactant components involved here — the hydrophobic proteins SFTPB and SFTPC, the collectins SFTPA1, SFTPA2 and SFTPD, and SFTA3 — are secreted by type II pneumocytes to lower alveolar surface tension and support innate defence, then internalised by macrophages via clathrin-coated vesicles. The pathway therefore links haematopoietic cytokine signalling to lung lipid homeostasis rather than to surfactant synthesis itself.

Alveolar macrophages clear and recycle pulmonary surfactant, and they can only do so when GM-CSF signalling licenses their maturation and catabolic function. The receptor is a heterodimer of a ligand-binding alpha subunit and a shared signalling beta subunit; loss-of-function mutations in the alpha subunit gene block this input, so surfactant lipids and the surfactant proteins A, B, C and D accumulate in alveoli instead of being taken up and degraded. The resulting disorder, pulmonary surfactant metabolism dysfunction type 4 or hereditary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, fills airspaces with floccular lipoproteinaceous material and impairs gas exchange, presenting as progressive hypoxaemic lung disease in children. The same surfactant components maintain alveolar surface tension and innate defence, so their mishandling links macrophage growth-factor signalling to respiratory failure, with misfolded proprotein forms provoking ER stress, oxidative stress and autophagy in alveolar epithelium.

Removal of ubiquitin from substrates is what keeps the ubiquitin pool recyclable and lets tagged proteins escape destruction, and the UCH family of deubiquitinases performs one arm of that job. These are cysteine (thiol) proteases with an N-terminal catalytic domain; the compact members UCHL1 and UCHL3 trim small adducts and peptides from the ubiquitin C-terminus, regenerating free ubiquitin, while the larger UCHL5 and BAP1 disassemble polyubiquitin chains within multiprotein assemblies. UCHL5 works at the 26S proteasome through the ADRM1 receptor and also within the INO80 chromatin remodelling complex, coupling chain editing to degradation and nucleosome mobilization; BAP1 acts with ASXL proteins, HCFC1, FOXK transcription factors and OGT to deubiquitinate histone H2A and regulate transcription, and is a tumour suppressor lost in mesothelioma and uveal melanoma. UCHL1 is abundant in neurons and linked to neurodegeneration. Related activity extends to NEDD8 processing.

Deubiquitinating enzymes built around a Josephin domain form one of the smaller cysteine protease families that edit ubiquitin signals, comprising ataxin-3, its paralogue ATXN3L, and JOSD1 and JOSD2. By trimming polyubiquitin chains rather than simply erasing them, these enzymes influence whether a tagged protein is committed to proteasomal degradation, and they appear tuned to chain length, acting preferentially on longer conjugates. Ataxin-3 works alongside the shuttle factors RAD23A and RAD23B and the ATPase VCP at the interface between ubiquitinated substrates and the proteasome, and it can counteract the ubiquitin ligase parkin, linking this activity to mitochondrial quality control and protein homeostasis. Ubiquitin itself is supplied by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes. The pathway is of particular medical interest because a polyglutamine expansion in ataxin-3 causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 3, or Machado-Joseph disease.

Ubiquitin conjugation is reversible, and the ubiquitin-specific processing proteases are the largest family of enzymes that undo it, trimming or removing ubiquitin chains so that substrate proteins escape proteasomal destruction, change localisation, or alter signalling output. More than fifty human USPs share a catalytic domain built around a Cys-box and His-box triad, with variable insertions and terminal extensions that provide substrate selectivity either directly or through scaffolds and cofactors such as the WDR48/WDR20 partners of USP12 and USP46. Their targets span most regulatory biology represented here: p53 and MDM2 stability, transforming growth factor beta receptors and SMADs, NF-kappaB components downstream of TRAF adaptors, innate immune sensors, histone H2A and H2B deubiquitination in chromatin regulation, mitochondrial outer membrane proteins, endosomal sorting, and the proteasome itself, where USP14 edits chains at the 19S regulatory particle. Loss or overactivity of individual members drives tumorigenesis and inflammatory disease, making them attractive drug targets.

Ubiquitin chains are not permanent marks, and the ovarian tumour domain family of deubiquitinases is one of the main ways cells erase them. These enzymes matter most as brakes on inflammation: A20, working with its TNIP adaptors, strips chains from RIPK1, NEMO and TRAF6 to shut down NF-κB signalling downstream of TNF and the NOD receptors, and loss of this restraint underlies autoimmune and autoinflammatory disease. Related members tune antiviral signalling through RIG-I, MDA5 and MAVS, where TRIM25-deposited chains are removed to set the interferon threshold. Others act on tumour suppressors and cytoskeletal and cell cycle regulators such as PTEN, p53, APC and RhoA. Chain-linkage selectivity is the organising principle: individual members prefer K48, K11, K63 or K29/K33 linkages, so each reverses a distinct signal rather than ubiquitination in general, and some engage E2 enzymes directly.

Metalloprotease DUBs are the zinc-dependent deubiquitinases of the JAMM/MPN+ family, which strip ubiquitin from substrates rather than adding it, and so decide whether a ubiquitin signal is read or erased.
