They matter at three junctions: PSMD14 in the proteasome lid removes chains from doomed substrates so they can be threaded into the proteolytic chamber, STAMBP and STAMBPL1 act with STAM on endosomes to recycle ubiquitin from receptors destined for lysosomal degradation, and BRCC3 within the BRCA1-A complex, with ABRAXAS1, BABAM1/2 and UIMC1, trims K63 chains on histone H2A to control how DNA double-strand break repair factors are retained at damage sites. MYSM1 similarly deubiquitinates H2A to permit transcription. Catalysis uses a zinc-activated water and a conserved glutamate acting as general base. BRCC3 also licenses NLRP3 inflammasome activation, and loss of these enzymes causes microcephaly-associated neurodegeneration and defective genome maintenance.

Zinc-dependent JAMM/MPN-domain deubiquitinases remove ubiquitin from substrates, and this metalloprotease branch of the DUB superfamily handles most of the K63-linked chains that act as signals rather than degradation marks. Their activity decides whether a ubiquitinated protein is degraded, sorted to lysosomes, or used to recruit repair factors. PSMD14 sits in the proteasome 19S lid and strips chains from substrates as they are unfolded and fed into the core, recycling free ubiquitin. BRCC3 works within the BRCA1-A complex with ABRAXAS1, BABAM1/2 and UIMC1 to trim K63 chains on damaged chromatin, tuning the DNA double-strand break response; the same enzyme also acts on NLRP3 during inflammasome activation. STAMBP and STAMBPL1 deubiquitinate cargo at endosomes alongside STAM during receptor sorting, while MYSM1 removes monoubiquitin from histone H2A to permit transcription. Catalysis uses a zinc-activated water and a conserved glutamate general base.

Pseudoxanthoma elasticum follows from loss of ABCC6, a liver- and kidney-enriched member of the multidrug resistance-associated protein branch of ABC transporters that exports organic anions across the plasma membrane. Its physiological output is systemic: ABCC6 activity in hepatocytes promotes release of pyrophosphate into the circulation, and pyrophosphate is the main soluble inhibitor of hydroxyapatite deposition in soft tissue. When the transporter is defective, circulating anti-mineralization capacity falls and calcium phosphate accumulates on elastic fibres, which fragment and calcify in skin, arterial walls and the Bruch membrane of the retina. Patients develop characteristic yellow skin papules, peripheral arterial disease and choroidal neovascularization with progressive central vision loss. This links a single anion efflux step in the liver to the control of ectopic calcification throughout connective and vascular tissue.

B cells must respond to antigen without responding to self, and CD22 is the brake that sets how much B cell receptor signalling is enough. Acting as a sialic-acid-binding lectin of the Siglec family, it recognises alpha2,6-linked sialylated glycans on B cell surface proteins and, when the receptor is cross-linked, is phosphorylated on its cytoplasmic inhibitory tyrosine motifs by the Src-family kinase LYN. Those phosphorylated motifs recruit the tyrosine phosphatase SHP-1 (PTPN6), which dephosphorylates components of the receptor complex and damps the calcium flux that would otherwise drive activation. The signalling unit itself is surface immunoglobulin, built from heavy and light chain variable and constant regions, paired with the CD79A/CD79B signalling heterodimer. Loss of this threshold-setting permits hyperresponsive B cells and autoimmunity, and CD22 is exploited clinically as a B-cell-directed therapeutic target.

A single unrepaired double-strand break can kill a cell or, worse, be mended wrongly and leave a translocation behind, so the repair of DNA double-strand breaks underwrites both genome stability and tumour suppression. Breaks arise from ionizing radiation and radiomimetic drugs, from collapsed replication forks, and deliberately during meiotic recombination and antigen receptor assembly. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex detects the lesion and activates ATM, which phosphorylates histone H2AX and marks the chromatin; ubiquitin and SUMO ligases such as RNF8 and RNF168 then recruit MDC1, TP53BP1 and BRCA1 to decide the outcome. End resection by CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2 commits the break to homology-directed repair through RAD51, BRCA2 and PALB2, while Ku70:Ku80 with DNA-PKcs, Artemis and LIG4 rejoins ends directly in any cell cycle phase. Checkpoint kinases CHEK1 and CHEK2 hold division back meanwhile; loss of these factors causes cancer predisposition and radiosensitivity syndromes.

Homologous recombination repair of a double-strand break proceeds through a D-loop, in which the resected broken end invades an intact homologous duplex and primes repair synthesis; resolution of D-loop structures is the step that dismantles this joint molecule and determines whether repair is conservative or exchanges genetic material. Two routes exist: displacement of the extended strand so it anneals back to its original partner, which avoids crossovers, or maturation into Holliday junctions that must be cut or unwound. Helicase-topoisomerase activity involving BLM, TOP3A and the RMI subunits dissolves double junctions, while structure-specific nucleases such as MUS81-EME1, SLX1-SLX4 and GEN1 cleave them. Upstream, the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and BRCA1-BARD1 promote resection and BRCA2-PALB2 load RAD51 with its paralogues. Failure leaves unresolved intermediates, sister chromatid entanglement and chromosomal rearrangements, and mutations here cause breast and ovarian cancer predisposition and Bloom syndrome.

Double-strand breaks that sever both DNA strands are repaired most accurately when an intact homologous sequence, usually the sister chromatid, is copied to restore the lost information. Homology directed repair covers this template-guided route and its lower-fidelity relatives: error-free homologous recombination, single-strand annealing between direct repeats, and microhomology-mediated end joining, which uses polymerase theta and readily creates deletions and translocations. Repair begins with break sensing by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and ATM, histone H2AX phosphorylation and ubiquitin-driven focus assembly through RNF8, RNF168 and BRCA1, then nucleolytic resection to 3' single-stranded tails that RPA coats and ATR monitors. BRCA2 and PALB2 load RAD51 for strand invasion, followed by repair synthesis, branch migration and resolution of joint molecules by BLM-TOP3A or structure-specific nucleases. Loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or the RAD51 paralogues causes genome instability and hereditary breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer, and underlies PARP inhibitor sensitivity.

A double-strand break is the most dangerous lesion a genome can sustain, and this pathway is the first step by which a cell notices one. The MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex binds the broken ends and holds them together, and its recruitment converts a physical break into a signal: the acetyltransferase KAT5 acetylates ATM, which autophosphorylates and switches from an inactive dimer to an active monomeric kinase. Active ATM then phosphorylates the substrates that arrest the cell cycle and assemble repair factors at the lesion, so detection and the damage response are coupled at their origin. Import of components into the nucleus depends on karyopherin-mediated transport. Loss of this sensing step underlies ataxia-telangiectasia and the related Nijmegen breakage and MRE11-deficiency syndromes, with radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency, chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition.

Homologous recombination repair of a double-strand break can end without exchanging chromosome arms, and synthesis-dependent strand annealing is the route that achieves it. After the invading strand has been extended using the sister chromatid as template, the extended strand is displaced from the D-loop and reanneals with its original partner, so repair restores sequence without generating a crossover — the outcome that protects cells from loss of heterozygosity and gross rearrangement. Upstream components carry out end resection and filament assembly: the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex with CtIP, EXO1, DNA2 and the BLM–TOP3A–RMI1–RMI2 dissolvasome, then BRCA1–BARD1, PALB2 and BRCA2 loading RAD51 and its paralogues. The helicase RTEL1 promotes D-loop disassembly, remaining gaps are filled by polymerase-mediated synthesis, and nicks are ligated. Loss of these factors underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition and sensitivity to crosslinking agents.

A DNA double-strand break must be converted into a signal that stops the cell cycle and marshals repair machinery, and this is the step that builds that signal at the break. The MRN complex (MRE11:RAD50:NBN) senses broken ends and activates ATM, which phosphorylates histone H2AX on serine 139; the resulting gamma-H2AX mark spreads over flanking chromatin and docks MDC1, creating ionizing radiation-induced foci. Ubiquitin ligases RNF8 and RNF168, with HERC2 and ubiquitin conjugating enzymes, modify histones to retain downstream factors, recruiting UIMC1/RAP80 and the BRCA1-A complex, while removal of the KDM4A/KDM4B demethylases and NSD2-dependent H4K20 methylation license 53BP1 binding. ATM then phosphorylates BRCA1:BARD1, 53BP1 and CHEK2, enforcing checkpoint arrest via TP53 and biasing repair toward homologous recombination or end joining. Loss of these components underlies radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

Double-strand breaks that sever both DNA strands are repaired accurately only when an intact homologous sequence is available as a template, and this homology-directed route covers both that accurate option and its error-prone fallback. Loss of it underlies breast and ovarian cancer predisposition and the sensitivity of BRCA-mutant tumours to PARP inhibition. ATM is activated at the break and phosphorylates histone H2AX, seeding ubiquitin- and SUMO-dependent recruitment of MDC1, RNF8/RNF168 and BRCA1-containing complexes into repair foci. MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1, DNA2 and BLM resect the ends to long 3' single-stranded tails, which RPA coats, triggering ATR-CHEK1 checkpoint signalling. BRCA2 and PALB2 then load RAD51 to invade a sister chromatid for templated synthesis by polymerase delta, with resolvases such as MUS81-EME1, GEN1 and the BLM-TOP3A dissolvasome processing joint molecules. Where the tails share direct repeats, RAD52-mediated single-strand annealing joins them at the cost of deleting the intervening sequence.

Homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks begins with strand invasion, and the branched D-loop that results must be taken apart before chromosomes can segregate. How it is dismantled determines the genetic outcome: the BLM-TOP3A-RMI1-RMI2 helicase-topoisomerase complex dissolves double Holliday junctions to give non-crossover products and suppresses sister chromatid exchange, while nucleolytic resolvases such as GEN1 and the SLX1A-SLX4 partnership with MUS81-EME1/EME2 cleave them and yield crossovers. Crossovers in mitotic cells risk loss of heterozygosity, exposing recessive mutations in tumour suppressors, so the choice between routes is a genome-stability decision. The upstream context is present too: MRE11-RAD50-NBN and CtIP-driven resection with EXO1 and DNA2, ATM signalling, BRCA1-BARD1 and BRCA2-PALB2 loading of RAD51 with its paralogues, and SPIDR with FIGNL1-FIRRM biasing recombination toward the non-crossover path. Mutation of these factors underlies Bloom syndrome and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous lesions a genome can suffer, and nonhomologous end joining is the route that repairs them by re-ligating the two ends directly, without a homologous template. It works throughout the cell cycle, dominates in G1, and is the mechanism that seals the programmed breaks of antigen receptor gene rearrangement — loss of its ligase or nuclease components causes radiosensitivity and severe combined immunodeficiency. Break recognition by the MRE11–RAD50–NBN complex activates ATM, which phosphorylates H2AX; ubiquitin signalling through RNF8, RNF168 and UBE2N builds the foci that recruit 53BP1 with RIF1 and PAXIP1, blocking end resection and steering repair away from homologous recombination. The Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer with DNA-PKcs synapses the ends, ARTEMIS trims overhangs, TDP1 and TDP2 clear blocking adducts, polymerases mu and lambda fill short gaps, and XRCC4–LIG4 with XLF completes ligation, sometimes with small deletions.

Homologous DNA Pairing and Strand Exchange is the search-and-invasion step of homologous recombination, the error-free route for repairing DNA double-strand breaks and collapsed replication forks using an intact sister chromatid as template. Cells that cannot execute it accumulate chromosomal rearrangements, and inherited loss of BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 predisposes to breast, ovarian and pancreatic cancer while also conferring the sensitivity to PARP inhibitors exploited therapeutically. Mechanistically, MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2 resect break ends to 3' single-stranded overhangs coated by RPA; BRCA2 and PALB2 then load RAD51 in place of RPA, and the resulting nucleofilament, stabilised by RAD51B-RAD51C-RAD51D-XRCC2 and stimulated by RAD51AP1, invades homologous duplex DNA to form a D-loop. ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp couple the process to checkpoint signalling, while BLM-TOP3A-RMI resolves the joint molecules formed.

Repairing a DNA double-strand break by homologous recombination requires the broken end to find its intact sister chromatid, and homologous DNA pairing and strand exchange is the search-and-invasion step that makes this possible. Without it, breaks are repaired by error-prone routes or not at all, producing the chromosomal instability and cancer predisposition seen when BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 are lost; the same dependency underlies the sensitivity of such tumours to PARP inhibition. Resected 3' single-stranded overhangs, generated by MRE11-RAD50-NBN with CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2, are first coated by RPA; BRCA2 with PALB2 then replaces RPA with RAD51, whose nucleofilament is stabilised by RAD51B-RAD51C-RAD51D-XRCC2 and stimulated by RAD51AP1. Invasion of the homologous duplex forms a D-loop, engaged further by RAD51C-XRCC3 and by BLM-TOP3A-RMI helicase-topoisomerase activity. ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and checkpoint clamp components couple the process to cell cycle arrest.

A double-strand break is the most dangerous lesion a genome can sustain, and the response described here is how cells detect one and convert that detection into repair and cell-cycle arrest. Failure produces chromosomal translocations, genomic instability and cancer predisposition, which is why several of its components are classic tumour suppressors. Breaks are sensed by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex, which activates the ATM kinase; ATM phosphorylates histone H2AX, and MDC1 binding spreads the mark along flanking chromatin. RNF8 and RNF168 then ubiquitinate nearby histones with UBE2N, recruiting TP53BP1 and the BRCA1-BARD1-containing complexes that choose between repair routes, while SUMO ligase PIAS4, the deubiquitinase BRCC3 and proteasomal turnover shape the signal. Checkpoint output runs through CHEK2 and TP53 to arrest division, and chromatin remodellers and demethylases make the damaged region accessible.

Before a broken chromosome can be repaired using a sister chromatid as template, the two DNA ends must be trimmed back to leave long single-stranded 3' tails, and this end-processing step is what commits a double-strand break to homology-directed repair rather than to blunt-end joining. Resection proceeds in two stages: the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease complex with CtIP and BRCA1-BARD1 initiates trimming, then EXO1 or DNA2 working with the BLM or WRN helicases extends it over kilobases. CDK2-cyclin A activity restricts initiation to S and G2 phases when a sister chromatid exists, while ATM-dependent phosphorylation and ubiquitin and SUMO marks laid on chromatin histones by RNF8, RNF168 and associated ligases organise factor recruitment around the break. RPA-coated overhangs then recruit ATR-ATRIP with TOPBP1, RAD17-RFC and the RAD9-HUS1-RAD1 clamp to activate CHEK1 checkpoint signalling. Loss of these steps underlies chromosomal instability and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer predisposition.

Repair of a double-strand break by homologous recombination requires a search for an intact sister template, and this presynaptic step builds the tool that performs the search. Resection nucleases and helicases acting with the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and CtIP generate long 3' single-stranded tails, which RPA coats to remove secondary structure. BRCA2, working with BRCA1-BARD1 and licensed by checkpoint kinase signalling through ATM, ATR and CHEK1, then loads RAD51 onto that ssDNA in place of RPA, nucleating the helical nucleoprotein filament that will invade duplex DNA. Paralogue complexes containing RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D and XRCC2 stabilise the filament. The same events sustain the damage checkpoint via the 9-1-1 clamp and its loader. Loss of these factors causes error-prone repair, chromosomal instability and hereditary breast, ovarian and Fanconi-type cancer predisposition, and underlies sensitivity to PARP inhibition.

About a quarter of the human proteome leaves the endoplasmic reticulum, and before it can go it must be selected and packed at high density into the 60-90 nm COPII vesicles that carry it to the ERGIC. Cargo concentration in the ER is that selection step, and it determines how efficiently secreted and membrane proteins reach the rest of the cell. Transmembrane cargo binds directly to one of the four SEC24 isoforms of the inner coat, while soluble lumenal cargo is captured by transmembrane receptors — the lectin LMAN1 with its partner MCFD2, p24 proteins such as TMED2 and TMED10, and CNIH/Erv-family adaptors — which grip cargo in the lumen and coat components in the cytosol, then return to the ER in COPI vesicles. Oversized cargo such as fibrillar collagen requires MIA3 and MIA2, which stay behind in the ER membrane. Loss of these receptors causes combined factor V/VIII deficiency and defects in collagen secretion.

Bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts must be found before they can be cut out, and damage recognition in global genome nucleotide excision repair is the search step that scans the entire genome rather than only transcribed strands. Two sensors cooperate: an XPC complex with RAD23A or RAD23B and centrin-2 probes for destabilised base pairing and binds the undamaged strand, while the UV-DDB ubiquitin ligase built on DDB2, DDB1, a cullin-4 scaffold and RBX1 engages the lesion itself and helps retain XPC there. Ubiquitin transfer, modulated by the COP9 signalosome, and PARP1/PARP2 activity mark the site, and INO80 chromatin remodelling opens nucleosomal DNA for access. Loss of these factors underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer, placing this step upstream of the incision and resynthesis stages of repair.

Bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV photoproducts are removed anywhere in the genome by global genome nucleotide excision repair, and this step builds the machinery that actually cuts them out. Once damage-sensing proteins XPC with its partners and the UV-DDB complex mark the site, the transcription factor TFIIH is recruited; its helicase subunits ERCC2 and ERCC3 open a bubble around the lesion while XPA verifies that real damage is present and RPA coats the undamaged strand to shield it. The endonucleases ERCC5 and the ERCC1-ERCC4 heterodimer then dock to form the incision complex that excises the damaged oligonucleotide. Assembly is tuned by PARP1/PARP2, ubiquitin ligase activity of CUL4-DDB1-RBX1, and SUMO conjugation with SUMO-targeted ubiquitylation. Loss of these factors underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.

The final stage of global genome nucleotide excision repair restores an intact duplex after a bulky, helix-distorting lesion such as a UV photoproduct has been cut out. Dual incision leaves a gap of roughly 27-30 nucleotides held by replication protein A; the clamp loader RFC deposits PCNA, and DNA polymerase delta, epsilon or the Y-family polymerase kappa copies the undamaged strand to refill it. LIG1 seals the remaining nick during replicative repair, while LIG3 in complex with the scaffold XRCC1 performs ligation in non-cycling cells, giving the step two routes depending on proliferative state. Ubiquitin contributed by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes supports PCNA modification and turnover of repair factors. Without this gap-filling and sealing, incision leaves persistent single-strand breaks, and defective nucleotide excision repair underlies xeroderma pigmentosum and its extreme sunlight-induced cancer risk.

Nucleotide Excision Repair removes bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions — UV photoproducts such as cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and 6-4 photoproducts, and chemical adducts from agents like benzopyrene and aflatoxin — restoring template integrity for replication and transcription. Loss of it causes xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer, as well as Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy. Two branches feed a common core: global genome repair, where XPC-RAD23 and the DDB1-DDB2 ubiquitin ligase scan the whole genome, and transcription-coupled repair, where an RNA polymerase II stalled at damage recruits ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. The TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 open the duplex, XPA and RPA verify and orient it, and ERCC1-ERCC4 with ERCC5 excise the damaged oligonucleotide before PCNA, RFC and replicative polymerases resynthesise and ligases seal the gap. Ubiquitin, SUMO and chromatin remodelling regulate throughout.

Bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV photoproducts and chemical adducts from benzopyrene or aflatoxin are removed by nucleotide excision repair, which cuts out a short damage-containing oligonucleotide and resynthesises the gap. Loss of this capacity underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer, as well as Cockayne syndrome and trichothiodystrophy, linking repair failure directly to mutation rate and tumour risk. Two branches share most machinery: global genome repair surveys the whole genome using XPC with RAD23 partners and the DDB1-DDB2 damage sensor, while transcription-coupled repair is triggered when RNA polymerase II stalls at a lesion and engages ERCC6, ERCC8 and UVSSA. The TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 open the duplex, ERCC5 and the ERCC1-ERCC4 nuclease incise, and replicative polymerases with PCNA, RPA and ligases restore the strand. Ubiquitin, SUMO and CUL4-based ligases regulate factor turnover throughout.

Bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers and chemical adducts are removed from anywhere in the genome by global genome nucleotide excision repair, the transcription-independent arm of excision repair. Loss of it causes xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sunlight sensitivity and skin cancer, which shows how much survival of UV exposure depends on this route. Damage is found by XPC with RAD23A/B and centrin-2, assisted in chromatin by a DDB1-DDB2-CUL4-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase whose activity is tuned by the COP9 signalosome; SUMO and poly(ADP-ribose) marks and INO80 chromatin remodelling improve access to nucleosomal DNA. TFIIH with its CDK7 kinase module and XPA then verify the lesion and open a bubble, RPA coats the undamaged strand, XPG and ERCC1-XPF incise either side, and polymerases delta, epsilon or kappa with PCNA, RFC and ligase fill and seal the gap.

Dual Incision in GG-NER is the cutting step of global genome nucleotide excision repair, the pathway that removes bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV-induced cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers from anywhere in the genome. Its loss underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition. After damage recognition by the DDB2-containing cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase and XPA, and unwinding by the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3, the lesion sits in an open bubble stabilised by RPA. ERCC1-ERCC4 cuts 5' to the damage first, allowing repair synthesis to begin, and ERCC5 then cuts 3', releasing a 27-30 nucleotide fragment. Gap filling uses PCNA loaded by replication factor C together with polymerases delta, epsilon or kappa, coupling lesion removal directly to restoration of an intact duplex.

Global genome nucleotide excision repair removes bulky, helix-distorting lesions such as UV photoproducts and chemical adducts from anywhere in the genome, and the dual incision step is the committed cut that releases them. Once the damage-verification factors XPA, RPA and the TFIIH helicases ERCC2/ERCC3 have opened a bubble around the lesion, the ERCC1-ERCC4 endonuclease cuts 5' to the damage and ERCC5 cuts 3', excising a roughly 27-30 nucleotide fragment. The resulting gap is immediately filled, so replication factor C, PCNA and DNA polymerases delta, epsilon and kappa are recruited as part of the same transaction. Damage recognition by the DDB1-DDB2 complex with cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase components, plus PARP1/PARP2, marks lesions in chromatin for this processing. Loss of these incision activities underlies xeroderma pigmentosum, with extreme sun sensitivity and skin cancer predisposition.

Post-translational protein modification covers the covalent changes that convert newly synthesised polypeptides into functional, correctly located and appropriately short-lived proteins. Without it secreted and membrane proteins cannot fold or reach the cell surface, signalling cannot be switched off, and damaged or surplus proteins accumulate; congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, coagulation defects and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria all arise from failures within it. One branch builds sugar chains in the endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi — dolichol-linked N-glycan assembly and transfer, mucin-type O-glycosylation, O-mannosylation of dystroglycan, sialylation — alongside GPI anchor synthesis, vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, sulfatase formylglycine activation and secretory-pathway kinases. Another branch attaches ubiquitin, SUMO or NEDD8 through E1, E2 and cullin-RING enzymes, reversed by deubiquitinases, to control proteasomal degradation, DNA damage responses and transcription. Further arms handle prenylation of RAB GTPases, tubulin polyglutamylation, hypusination of eIF5A, and non-histone methylation.

Most proteins only become functional after translation, when enzymes attach sugars, lipids, small chemical groups or other proteins to specific residues. This broad programme of post-translational protein modification determines where a protein goes, how long it lasts and what it can do. N- and O-linked glycosylation and GPI anchoring, built through the ALG, PIG, GALNT and sialyltransferase enzymes, mark secreted and membrane proteins and support quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum; geranylgeranylation licenses RAB GTPases for vesicle traffic; vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX activates clotting factors; sulfatases are switched on by formylglycine generation; and tubulin is tailored by polyglutamylation, tyrosination and detyrosination. A large ubiquitin, SUMO and NEDD8 arm, including cullin-RING ligases, deubiquitinases and the proteasome, sets protein stability and signalling output. Defects cause congenital disorders of glycosylation, muscular dystrophies, bleeding disorders, lysosomal storage disease and cancer.

Centromere identity is epigenetic rather than sequence-encoded, and it is maintained by depositing new CENPA-containing nucleosomes at the centromere once per cell cycle, in late telophase and early G1. Without this replenishment, the CENPA mark is diluted by DNA replication, the kinetochore cannot be built, and chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploidy. Licensing is performed by the Mis18 complex, including MIS18A, MIS18BP1 and OIP5, which primes centromeric chromatin for the chaperone HJURP; HJURP binds newly made CENPA–H4 tetramers and delivers them for assembly, with NPM1, the histone-binding proteins RBBP4 and RBBP7, and the RSF chromatin remodelling activity of RSF1 and SMARCA5 assisting maturation and stabilisation. The resident constitutive centromere-associated network, including CENPC, CENPN, CENPT-W-S-X and the CENPH-I-K-M module, reads existing CENPA nucleosomes and both recruits new ones and nucleates the outer kinetochore. Bulk H2A, H2B and H4 histones supply the surrounding chromatin context.

Oxidation of NADH and FADH2 by the mitochondrial respiratory chain is how cells convert the reducing equivalents made by the Krebs cycle and fatty acid beta-oxidation into a proton gradient across the inner membrane, the immediate driving force for ATP synthesis. Electrons pass from complex I (the many NDUF subunits) and succinate dehydrogenase through ubiquinone to the cytochrome bc1 complex (UQCR subunits, cytochrome c1) and cytochrome c, then to cytochrome c oxidase, where oxygen is reduced to water. Also represented are the assembly factors and cofactor pathways that make this possible: heme a and copper delivery by COX10/COX15-type and SCO/COX17 proteins, iron-sulfur cluster building via NFS1, ISCU and frataxin, electron entry from fatty acid oxidation through the ETF system, and the malate-aspartate shuttle carriers that import cytosolic reducing equivalents. Defects cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome and lactic acidosis.

Inflammasomes are cytosolic sensor complexes that convert detection of microbial products, cytosolic DNA and cell damage into a burst of inflammatory cytokine release. They matter because they are the checkpoint that licenses mature IL1B and IL18 output: Toll-like receptor signalling induces the inactive pro-cytokines, and only a second, inflammasome-activating stimulus permits their cleavage, so excess activity drives gout, cryopyrin-associated periodic fevers, familial Mediterranean fever and other autoinflammatory states. Distinct sensors define the subtypes — NLRP3 responding to potassium efflux and ATP acting through P2RX7 and pannexin channels, NLRC4 to bacterial flagellin and secretion systems, AIM2 to double-stranded DNA — and each oligomerizes to recruit procaspase-1, directly or through the adaptor PYCARD, so that induced proximity drives autoprocessing into active caspase-1. Pyrin, PSTPIP1, thioredoxin and TXNIP tune assembly, and released IL1B and IL18 feed back onto NF-kappaB-driven inflammation.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors sitting at or near nerve terminals act as a volume control on transmitter release, letting cholinergic input tune the output of glutamatergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic synapses rather than carrying the signal itself. This presynaptic modulation underlies the reinforcing effects of nicotine, and receptors built from alpha4 and beta2 subunits, or containing alpha6 and beta3, are the ones through which nicotine drives dopamine release in reward circuits; variation at the alpha5-alpha3-beta4 cluster is tied to smoking behaviour and dependence. All the subunits here are ligand-gated cation channels that assemble as pentamers, and their cation selectivity sets the mechanism: direct calcium entry can suffice for release, while sodium-dominated flux depolarises the terminal and recruits voltage-gated calcium channels. Homomeric alpha7 channels instead seed calcium-induced calcium release from internal stores via ryanodine and IP3 receptors, amplifying a small influx into a release-competent local signal.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors sitting in the postsynaptic membrane convert acetylcholine release into a fast depolarizing current, and they are how the nervous system drives muscle contraction and how fast cholinergic transmission is achieved at ganglionic and central synapses. The pathway covers the pentameric ligand-gated cation channels assembled from alpha and beta subunits, including the muscle-type receptor built from CHRNA1 with beta, delta and either the fetal gamma or adult epsilon subunit, neuronal heteromers such as alpha4-beta2, and homomeric alpha7 channels whose high calcium permeability lets them influence downstream signalling as well as excitability. Ion selectivity varies with subunit composition, from predominantly sodium-carrying to strongly calcium-permeable. Loss or autoimmune blockade of the muscle receptor causes congenital myasthenic syndromes and myasthenia gravis, while neuronal subunit variants affect nicotine dependence and epilepsy susceptibility.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated cation channels that convert a pulse of acetylcholine into an immediate electrical signal. The subunit combinations here form receptors with high sodium permeability and little calcium flux, so their opening depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane rather than delivering calcium directly; the depolarization then recruits voltage-gated calcium channels and the downstream signalling that follows a rise in cytosolic calcium. These subunits build the receptors of the neuromuscular junction, where the fetal gamma subunit is replaced by epsilon after birth, and the ganglionic and neuronal receptors assembled from alpha3, beta2, beta4 and alpha4 that mediate fast autonomic transmission and nicotine's actions in the brain. Loss or autoimmune attack on the muscle receptor causes myasthenic weakness, while mutations in the neuronal subunits underlie nocturnal frontal lobe epilepsy and shape nicotine dependence.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated cation channels, and a subset of the postsynaptic forms carries substantial calcium current in addition to sodium, so that acetylcholine release raises intracellular Ca2+ rather than merely depolarising the cell. This distinguishes highly calcium permeable postsynaptic nicotinic receptors from purely depolarising neurotransmission: the calcium entry engages second messenger and kinase cascades that facilitate long-term potentiation and other forms of synaptic plasticity, linking cholinergic input to learning, attention and memory. The alpha7 subunit assembles homopentamers with the greatest calcium permeability, while alpha4 with beta2 forms the high-affinity nicotine-binding receptors of the brain; other alpha and beta subunits combine into autonomic ganglionic and muscle-type channels. These receptors are the targets of nicotine, underlie tobacco dependence, and variants in the subunit genes are tied to epilepsy, smoking behaviour and cognitive decline.

Highly calcium permeable nicotinic acetylcholine receptors describes the subset of nicotinic receptor assemblies that admit substantial Ca2+ along with Na+ when acetylcholine or nicotine binds, converting a fast ionotropic signal into a second-messenger event. This matters because Ca2+ entry through these channels drives presynaptic neurotransmitter release, activates calcium-dependent kinases and gene transcription, and supports neuronal survival and plasticity; the same receptors mediate nicotine reinforcement and are implicated in addiction, and in epilepsy and cognitive decline. Permeability is set by subunit composition: homopentamers of the alpha7 type are the most Ca2+-permeable, while heteromeric combinations of alpha3 with beta2 or beta4 that incorporate the accessory alpha5 subunit come next, and alpha4/beta2 receptors carry less. The pathway thus links cholinergic transmission in brain and autonomic ganglia to calcium signalling rather than to depolarisation alone.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are ligand-gated cation channels, and certain subunit combinations pass enough calcium that acetylcholine acts less like a simple depolarizing signal and more like a second-messenger trigger. This matters at presynaptic terminals, where calcium entry through these channels promotes release of glutamate, dopamine and other transmitters, and in neurons where it engages calcium-dependent kinases, gene expression and synaptic plasticity. Permeability is set by composition: homomeric alpha7 receptors are the most calcium-permeable, while heteromers built from alpha3 with beta2 or beta4 plus the accessory alpha5 subunit come next, with alpha5 variants altering calcium flux and desensitization. The subunits here also form the receptors of autonomic ganglia and the muscle endplate. Because this calcium signalling underlies nicotine reinforcement and neuronal survival, these channels are studied in addiction, cognitive decline and inflammatory regulation.

Every protein-coding gene must first have RNA polymerase II placed correctly on its promoter and licensed to begin, and this is the set of events that gets it there and through the first few nucleotides. TATA-binding protein and the TAF subunits of TFIID recognise promoter DNA, and TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and the TFIIH helicase/kinase module assemble with the twelve-subunit polymerase into a pre-initiation complex; TFIIH opens the duplex and its CDK7 subunit phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain. Early complexes are unstable and repeatedly release short transcripts until the nascent RNA reaches a few nucleotides, after which the enzyme commits to escape. Accompanying factors govern the immediate next step: NELF and DSIF impose promoter-proximal pausing, CDK9-containing kinase complexes and elongation factors such as the PAF1 complex, FACT and ELL release it, and cap-binding proteins engage the new 5' end. Defects here underlie transcription-coupled repair disorders and leukaemic fusion proteins.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a lesion in the transcribed strand, cells assemble the pre-incision complex of transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair, the step that verifies the damage and opens the DNA before cutting. This route clears bulky, transcription-blocking lesions from active genes, and its loss causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with premature ageing, neurodegeneration and failure to resume transcription after UV rather than cancer predisposition. ERCC6 (CSB) recognises the stalled polymerase and brings in ERCC8 (CSA) within a CUL4A/CUL4B-DDB1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase regulated by the COP9 signalosome; UVSSA delivers the deubiquitinase USP7 to protect ERCC6 from degradation. XPA arrives with the ten-subunit TFIIH complex, whose ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases unwind the damaged duplex, while the XAB2 complex and the elongation factor TCEA1 help the polymerase backtrack so repair proteins can reach the lesion.

Bulky, helix-distorting DNA lesions such as UV photoproducts stall elongating RNA polymerase II, and transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair is the route by which such damage is removed from the transcribed strand of active genes so that RNA synthesis can resume. Loss of this repair arm causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with UV hypersensitivity, growth failure and neurodegeneration, while the parallel global-genome branch remains intact. A stalled polymerase recruits CSB (ERCC6), which brings in CSA (ERCC8) within a CUL4-DDB1-RBX1 ubiquitin ligase regulated by the COP9 signalosome; UVSSA with the deubiquitinase USP7 protects CSB from turnover. TFIIH, XPA, RPA and the XAB2 complex assemble a pre-incision complex, TCEA1 promotes polymerase backtracking, and ERCC1-XPF and XPG excise the damaged oligonucleotide. Replicative polymerases with PCNA and RFC fill the gap, and LIG1 or LIG3-XRCC1 seals it.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky lesion in a transcribed strand, transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair removes the damage so that gene expression can resume; the dual incision step is where the damaged oligonucleotide is actually cut out. Loss of this route causes Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, with photosensitivity, developmental failure and neurodegeneration rather than the cancer predisposition typical of the global-genome branch. Stalled polymerase must first backtrack to expose the lesion, aided by ERCC6 and ERCC8-dependent remodelling and ubiquitination, UVSSA, TCEA1-stimulated nascent RNA cleavage, and the helicase subunits of TFIIH. The ERCC1:ERCC4 endonuclease then incises 5' of the lesion and ERCC5 3' of it, on a substrate stabilised by XPA and the RPA trimer, leaving a gap that replicative polymerases with PCNA and clamp loader refill.

When RNA polymerase II stalls at a bulky, helix-distorting lesion, transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair removes the damaged strand; this final stage refills and seals the resulting single-stranded gap so transcription can resume. Loss of the pathway underlies Cockayne syndrome and UV-sensitive syndrome, where neurons and other non-dividing cells accumulate transcription-blocking damage and degenerate. After dual incision, RPA coats the gap, the clamp loader RFC deposits PCNA, and DNA polymerases delta or epsilon, or the translesion polymerase kappa, synthesize the repair patch; ligase I or ligase III with its partner XRCC1 then seals the nick. The stalled polymerase complex, the CSA and CSB proteins with UVSSA and a cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase, and the TFIIH helicases provide the damage-recognition and unwinding context, linking genome maintenance directly to ongoing gene expression.

Transfer RNAs leave transcription as bare polymers and are only made functional by chemical decoration of their bases and sugars; this is the nuclear and cytosolic arm of that work. Methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, deaminases, thiolation and queuosine or wybutosine enzymes act at dozens of positions, with anticodon-loop marks tuning codon reading accuracy and wobble decoding while modifications in the core stabilise the L-shaped fold and protect tRNA from degradation. Accurate, efficient translation and the fidelity of ribosomal frame maintenance depend on it. The KEOPS complex components contribute the universal threonylcarbamoyl-adenosine mark, and 5-methylcytosine deposited by NSUN2 also gates stress-induced tRNA fragment production. Loss-of-function mutations in these enzymes cause intellectual disability syndromes, microcephaly, Galloway-Mowat syndrome and anaemias, and variants in CDKAL1 associate with type 2 diabetes through impaired insulin secretion.

Phenylalanine tRNA carries an unusually elaborate tricyclic base immediately 3' of its anticodon, and building it is what this route accomplishes. The bulky wybutosine at position 37 stacks against the codon-anticodon duplex, stabilizing pairing at the ribosomal A site and suppressing +1 ribosomal frameshifting, so loss of the modification degrades translational accuracy; the same chemistry is exploited by HIV, whose reverse transcription primes on modified tRNA(Phe). Six sequential steps convert the genomically encoded guanosine: TRMT5 methylates N1, the radical SAM enzyme TYW1 condenses pyruvate onto it to form the imidazoline ring of 4-demethylwyosine, TYW2 transfers an aminocarboxypropyl group, TYW3 and LCMT2 add methyl and methoxycarbonyl groups, and TYW5 hydroxylates the product. The pathway illustrates how tRNA anticodon-loop modification, rather than the tRNA sequence itself, tunes decoding fidelity.

Interstrand crosslinks covalently tie the two DNA strands together and block replication forks; the Fanconi anemia pathway is how cells unhook and repair them. Loss of it causes a syndrome of skeletal malformation, bone marrow failure, leukemia predisposition and extreme sensitivity to crosslinking agents, and it handles crosslinks generated endogenously by reactive aldehydes from normal metabolism. A multisubunit core complex built from FANCA, FANCB, FANCC, FANCE, FANCF, FANCG, FANCL and FANCM with associated FAAP and CENPS/CENPX partners acts as an E3 ligase that, with the UBE2T conjugating enzyme, monoubiquitinates the FANCD2-FANCI pair after ATR-ATRIP signalling at the stalled fork; USP1 with WDR48 reverses the mark to reset the system. Ubiquitinated FANCD2 recruits structure-specific nucleases including SLX4-SLX1, FAN1, MUS81-EME1 and ERCC1-ERCC4 to incise the lesion, after which polymerase nu bypasses it and the resulting break is resolved by recombination.

Interleukin-6 family signaling transmits a group of structurally related cytokines — IL6, IL11, LIF, oncostatin M, CNTF, cardiotrophins and IL31 — into changes in gene expression that shape inflammation, acute-phase protein production by the liver, haematopoiesis, neuronal survival, bone remodelling and metabolic control. Chronic output from this route drives rheumatoid arthritis, cytokine storm and tumour-promoting inflammation, which is why IL6 and its receptor are antibody drug targets. Each cytokine binds a private receptor chain but most converge on the shared transducer gp130 (IL6ST), alone or paired with LIFR or OSMR, while IL31 instead uses IL31RA. Receptor assembly activates associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1 for nuclear translocation and target gene transcription. SOCS3, the phosphatase PTPN11 and CBL-mediated receptor turnover restrain the response. Soluble IL6R permits trans-signalling on cells lacking IL6R, redirecting IL6 from regenerative toward pro-inflammatory outcomes.

Cytokines of the interleukin-6 family drive inflammation, hepatic acute-phase protein production, hematopoiesis, neuronal and glial survival, metabolic control and, when chronic, tumour promotion and autoimmune tissue damage; blocking IL6 or its receptor is now standard therapy in rheumatoid arthritis and cytokine storm. The family is unified by the shared signal-transducing subunit gp130 (IL6ST), which pairs with ligand-specific chains such as IL6R, IL11RA, CNTFR, LIFR or OSMR to read out IL6, IL11, LIF, oncostatin M, CNTF, cardiotrophin and cardiotrophin-like cytokine; IL31 is the exception, signalling through IL31RA. Receptor assembly activates associated Janus kinases (JAK1, JAK2, TYK2), which phosphorylate STAT3 and STAT1 for dimerisation, nuclear entry and target gene transcription. Shed or spliced soluble IL6R permits trans-signalling on gp130-bearing cells that lack IL6R, biasing responses toward inflammation, while SOCS3, PTPN11 and CBL impose negative feedback.

Interleukin-10 signaling is the main brake on inflammation by activated macrophages and dendritic cells, and without it mucosal immunity runs unchecked causing colitis and other exaggerated inflammatory responses in mice and, in humans, early-onset inflammatory bowel disease. IL10 binds a receptor built from IL10RA and IL10RB chains that carry JAK1 and TYK2; these kinases phosphorylate the receptor tail and then STAT3, which dimerizes, enters the nucleus and drives an anti-inflammatory transcriptional programme. The output is suppression of antigen-presenting cell activation: reduced MHC class II and CD80/CD86 costimulation and lowered output of TNF, IL1, IL6, IL8, IL12 and a wide range of chemokines such as CCL2, CCL3, CCL5 and CXCL10, together with induction of restraining factors including IL1RN and soluble decoy receptors. Effects on T cells are largely indirect, following from the dampening of myeloid cell activation, while IL10 can promote B cell and NK responses.

Glycine is the smallest amino acid, and its breakdown by the glycine cleavage system is the main route by which cells dispose of excess glycine while feeding one-carbon units into folate metabolism for nucleotide and methyl group synthesis. The reaction is carried out by a mitochondrial multienzyme complex: the pyridoxal phosphate-dependent decarboxylase GLDC releases CO2, the lipoyl-bearing carrier protein GCSH shuttles the remaining aminomethyl group, the aminomethyltransferase AMT transfers a one-carbon unit to tetrahydrofolate and liberates ammonia, and the flavoprotein dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase DLD reoxidises the lipoamide arm. DLD is shared with other lipoamide-dependent mitochondrial dehydrogenase complexes, which is why 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase subunits appear alongside. Loss of GLDC, AMT or GCSH causes nonketotic hyperglycinemia, in which glycine accumulates in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid and produces encephalopathy and seizures in newborns.

Transfer RNAs are made as longer precursors, and nuclear tRNA processing converts them into functional adaptors before they can serve translation. Without it, ribosomes lack charged tRNAs and protein synthesis fails; mutations in several of these steps cause pontocerebellar hypoplasia, sideroblastic anaemia with immunodeficiency, and other developmental disorders. The RNase P ribonucleoprotein, built around a catalytic RNA with protein subunits such as POP1 and RPP30, trims the 5' leader, while ELAC2 removes the 3' trailer and TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA end required for aminoacylation. Intron-containing pre-tRNAs are cleaved by the TSEN endonuclease complex and the exon halves rejoined by an RTCB-containing ligase complex. Mature tRNAs are then delivered to the cytosol by exportin-t with RAN, which accounts for the nucleoporins and nuclear pore components accompanying the processing enzymes here.

Mitochondria transcribe each strand of their circular genome as a single long polycistronic RNA, so every mRNA, rRNA and tRNA must be liberated by cutting that transcript apart. tRNA processing in the mitochondrion performs those cuts and finishes the products, supplying the complete set of 22 organelle-encoded tRNAs that mitochondrial translation of respiratory chain subunits depends on. A protein-only RNase P complex, built from the catalytic subunit PRORP with TRMT10C and HSD17B10, cleaves 5' ends, while the mitochondrial form of ELAC2 acts as RNase Z at 3' ends; because tRNAs punctuate the transcript, these cleavages simultaneously release the flanking mRNAs and rRNAs. TRNT1 then adds the universal CCA acceptor end needed for aminoacylation. Mutations in these enzymes or in the tRNA genes themselves impair oxidative phosphorylation and cause encephalomyopathies affecting energy-demanding brain and muscle.

Growth factor receptors of the ERBB family do more than drive proliferation: when ERBB2 partners with EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4 after ligand binding, it also steers where a cell goes. This motility arm matters for epithelial wound closure and morphogenesis, and its hyperactivation in ERBB2-amplified breast cancer contributes to invasion and metastasis rather than growth alone. Ligands such as EGF, betacellulin, heregulins and HB-EGF trigger receptor dimerisation and phosphorylation, creating a docking site for MEMO1. MEMO1 in turn holds active RHOA and its effector DIAPH1, a formin, at the plasma membrane, so that actin polymerisation and microtubule capture are coordinated at the leading edge. The result is directed lamellipodial protrusion and stabilised cell polarity, linking receptor tyrosine kinase signalling to cytoskeletal remodelling and migration.

IL4 and IL13 are the defining cytokines of type 2 immunity, driving Th2 differentiation, B cell class switching to IgE, and the alternative activation of macrophages that supports antiparasite defence and wound repair; when dysregulated they underlie allergy, asthma and tissue fibrosis. Both act through shared receptor chains — IL4R paired with the common gamma chain on haematopoietic cells, or with IL13RA1 on non-haematopoietic cells such as epithelium, fibroblasts and smooth muscle — while IL13RA2 acts as a high-affinity decoy. Receptor engagement activates JAK1, JAK2, JAK3 and TYK2 and principally STAT6, with STAT1 and STAT3 contributing, and an IRS-linked arm feeding PI3K/AKT for growth and survival. Transcriptional output includes GATA3, IRF4, FCER2 and eotaxin-type chemokines, adhesion molecules, matrix metalloproteinases and collagen, linking this signalling to eosinophil recruitment, IgE production and remodelling; SOCS1 and SOCS3 restrain it.

The thirteen proteins of the respiratory chain that are made inside mitochondria are translated using only 22 mitochondrially encoded tRNAs, and those tRNAs must be chemically decorated before they can decode mRNA accurately. Nucleus-encoded enzymes imported into the matrix carry out this modification: some, such as PUS1 and TRIT1, also act on cytosolic tRNAs, while MTO1, TRMU and TRMT61B work only in mitochondria. Modifications at the anticodon wobble position tune codon recognition, those near the 3' end affect aminoacylation, and core modifications stabilise tRNA folding. GTPBP3, MTO1 and TRMU together build the mammalian-specific 5-taurinomethyl-2-thiouridine at position 34, and mutations in them cause infantile mitochondrial disease with cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis and hearing loss. TRMT10C with HSD17B10 forms a methyltransferase subcomplex that also participates in processing mitochondrial tRNA ends alongside the RNase P protein PRORP, linking maturation to modification.

GDP-fucose biosynthesis supplies the activated sugar donor that all fucosyltransferases require, and so determines whether a cell can fucosylate its glycoproteins and glycolipids at all. Fucose caps on glycans build selectin ligands for leukocyte rolling, ABO and Lewis blood group antigens, and the O-fucose modifications that tune Notch receptor responsiveness, so loss of donor supply produces immunodeficiency with recurrent infection and developmental defects, as in congenital disorders of glycosylation. Most GDP-fucose is made de novo from GDP-mannose by a dehydratase and a bifunctional epimerase/reductase; a smaller salvage route recovers free fucose taken up or released by lysosomal turnover through a kinase and a pyrophosphorylase, with a mutarotase feeding the correct anomer in. A dedicated Golgi transporter then delivers the nucleotide sugar to the lumenal compartment where glycan assembly occurs, linking cytosolic metabolism to secretory pathway modification.

Fucose attached to glycoproteins and glycolipids underlies selectin-mediated leukocyte rolling, Notch signalling, ABO/Lewis blood group antigens and much of glycan-based cell recognition, and every fucosyltransferase that installs it depends on the activated sugar donor made here. GDP-fucose biosynthesis proceeds by two routes: a dominant de novo pathway in which GMDS dehydrates and GFUS epimerises and reduces GDP-mannose, and a minor salvage route in which free fucose taken up or released by glycan turnover is phosphorylated by FCSK and adenylyl/guanylyl-transferred by FPGT, with FUOM handling fucose anomer interconversion. The product must then reach the Golgi lumen, which is the job of the transporter SLC35C1; its loss causes leukocyte adhesion deficiency II, with recurrent infection, impaired neutrophil recruitment and developmental delay. The pathway thus links central sugar nucleotide metabolism to immune trafficking and developmental signalling.

A family of cytokines that all converge on the shared receptor subunit gp130 (IL6ST), or its relative OSMR/IL31RA, to control inflammation, acute-phase responses, haematopoiesis, bone remodelling, neuronal survival and embryo implantation. Ligand recognition is modular: non-signalling alpha chains such as CNTFR and IL11RA capture their cytokine and present it to a signal-transducing chain, gp130, LIFR or OSMR, whose dimerisation brings JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 into position to phosphorylate the receptor tails and launch STAT3-dominated transcription alongside MAPK and PI3K output. CLCF1 acts with CRLF1 as a secreted composite ligand for CNTFR, and loss of either causes cold-induced sweating and Crisponi syndrome, while LIF/LIFR signalling is required for uterine receptivity. Excess signalling through this route drives chronic inflammatory disease, cachexia and tumour-promoting inflammation; IL31 acting on IL31RA with OSMR instead evokes itch.

rRNA modification in the nucleus and cytosol installs the roughly 200 chemical marks that turn newly transcribed ribosomal RNA into a functional ribosome. The modified nucleotides cluster in the peptidyl transferase A and P sites, the polypeptide exit tunnel and the subunit interface, so their loss degrades translational accuracy and ribosome assembly; mutations in the machinery cause ribosomopathies such as dyskeratosis congenita and are exploited by proliferating tumour cells. Two guide-RNA-directed systems dominate: box H/ACA particles containing DKC1, GAR1, NHP2 and NOP10 convert uridine to pseudouridine, while box C/D particles built around fibrillarin, NOP56, NOP58 and SNU13 add 2'-O-methyl groups, each snoRNA base-pairing with pre-rRNA to select its target. Stand-alone enzymes contribute base methylation and acetylation, including BUD23, NOP2, DIMT1, TSR3 and NAT10. Much of this occurs within the nucleolar small-subunit processome, coupling modification to pre-rRNA cleavage and ribosome biogenesis.

Newly transcribed ribosomal RNA is chemically decorated at roughly 200 positions before it can work, and this nucleolar and cytoplasmic modification programme installs those marks. They cluster in the functional heart of the ribosome s dash the peptidyl transferase A and P sites, the polypeptide exit tunnel, and the subunit interface dash so their loss degrades translational accuracy and ribosome assembly rather than any single metabolic route. The two dominant marks are pseudouridine, made by box H/ACA particles built around the DKC1 pseudouridine synthase with GAR1, NHP2 and NOP10, and 2'-O-methylation by box C/D particles containing the fibrillarin methyltransferase with NOP56 and NOP58; guide snoRNAs base-pair with pre-rRNA to select each target nucleotide. Base methylations and acetylation are added by standalone enzymes such as BUD23, DIMT1, NOP2 and NAT10. Many components sit in the small subunit processome alongside UTP and WDR proteins, linking modification to cleavage; mutations cause dyskeratosis congenita and other ribosomopathies.

Transaldolase links the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway back to glycolysis, reversibly transferring a three-carbon unit between sedoheptulose 7-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate to yield fructose 6-phosphate and erythrose 4-phosphate. This traffic lets cells balance ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis against NADPH production and glycolytic carbon flow. When TALDO1 is mutated, the reaction fails, seven-carbon sugars and polyols such as sedoheptulose and erythritol accumulate in body fluids, and patients present in infancy with hepatosplenomegaly, liver fibrosis and cirrhosis, coagulopathy, kidney involvement and growth failure. The defect illustrates how a single step in sugar rearrangement supports redox defence: loss of flexible NADPH supply leaves tissues, particularly liver, vulnerable to oxidative damage. Transaldolase deficiency is one of the rare inborn errors of pentose phosphate metabolism, detected by urinary polyol profiling.

Ribosome production begins with a single long 47S precursor transcript that must be trimmed, modified and folded into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs; this is the dominant route by which that happens, starting in the nucleolus and finishing in the cytoplasm. Its output sets the cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth, and defects in it cause the ribosomopathies, including Diamond-Blackfan anemia and Treacher Collins syndrome, while nucleolar stress from blocked processing stabilises p53. Small-subunit processome components such as the UTP proteins, WDR43 and NOL11 assemble co-transcriptionally, box C/D snoRNP factors including fibrillarin, NOP56 and NOP58 direct 2'-O-methylation, and endo- and exonucleases such as XRN2, the RNA exosome and NOB1 make the successive cuts. Ribosomal proteins of both subunits join during these steps, and cytoplasmic kinases RIOK1 and RIOK2 act in final 40S maturation.

When DNA damage or other stress stabilizes p53, one of its first outputs is a transcriptional programme that halts the division cycle, buying time for repair and preventing damaged genomes from being passed to daughter cells. Loss of this arm of the p53 response allows proliferation with unrepaired lesions and is central to tumour development. The classic G1 effector is CDKN1A (p21), which binds and inhibits CDK2 in complex with cyclin E or A to block S-phase entry, while induced E2F7 represses E2F1 target genes. G2 arrest is imposed by GADD45A, which inhibits Aurora kinase A, by SFN (14-3-3sigma), which sequesters the CDK1-cyclin B1 complex outside the nucleus, and by repression of CDC25C with E2F4. Additional targets including BTG2, acting through the CCR4-NOT deadenylase complex, and PLK2, PLK3 and PLAGL1 reinforce or resolve the arrest, and prolonged signalling can redirect cells toward apoptosis.

Ribose 5-phosphate is the sugar backbone of nucleotides, and in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway it is made by isomerising ribulose 5-phosphate. This step, catalysed reversibly by ribose-5-phosphate isomerase, links glucose oxidation to nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis and allows pentose phosphates to be recycled back into glycolysis. Loss of that activity through mutation of RPIA defines an extremely rare inborn error of metabolism presenting as a slowly progressive leukoencephalopathy, with developmental regression, seizures and accumulation of polyol sugars such as ribitol and D-arabitol detectable in body fluids and brain tissue. The disorder illustrates how white matter is particularly vulnerable to disturbed pentose metabolism, and how a defect in one isomerase step can leave the oxidative arm of the pathway intact while starving cells of correctly configured ribose units.

Transaldolase sits in the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway, where it reversibly shuttles a three-carbon unit between sugar phosphates so that cells can balance ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis against glycolytic intermediates and NADPH-generating flux. Loss-of-function mutations in TALDO1 block the interconversion of fructose 6-phosphate and erythrose 4-phosphate into sedoheptulose 7-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, so seven-carbon sugars and polyols such as sedoheptulose and erythritol accumulate in urine and plasma while downstream carbon flow stalls. The resulting transaldolase deficiency presents in newborns with hepatosplenomegaly, cirrhosis and coagulopathy, often with intrauterine growth restriction and renal and cardiac involvement, and is thought to reflect both toxic metabolite build-up and impaired NADPH-dependent antioxidant defence in the liver. It illustrates how a single reversible step in central carbohydrate metabolism supports redox homeostasis and biosynthetic precursor supply.

The non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway reshuffles sugar phosphates so that cells can balance ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis against glycolytic intermediates, and two of its enzymes are mutated in inherited metabolic disease. Ribose-5-phosphate isomerase interconverts ribulose-5-phosphate and ribose-5-phosphate; its deficiency is an extremely rare, slowly progressive leukoencephalopathy in which polyol and sugar-phosphate intermediates accumulate and white matter development fails. Transaldolase transfers a three-carbon unit between fructose-6-phosphate and erythrose-4-phosphate to yield sedoheptulose-7-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate; loss of this step causes congenital liver disease with hepatosplenomegaly, fibrosis and characteristic sedoheptulose and polyol excretion. Both disorders illustrate how blocking carbon flow between the pentose phosphate pathway and glycolysis leaves toxic intermediates behind and compromises tissues dependent on NADPH supply and ribose provision.

Mitochondrial ribosomes are built from two rRNAs encoded by the organelle's own genome, and those transcripts must be chemically modified before they can support translation. Methylation and pseudouridylation of 12S and 16S rRNA tune the decoding site and the peptidyl transferase centre, so that the mitoribosome can synthesise the thirteen respiratory chain subunits made inside the organelle; without them assembly stalls and oxidative phosphorylation fails. TFB1M dimethylates adjacent adenosines in the small subunit rRNA and NSUN4 adds 5-methylcytidine, while MRM1, MRM2 and MRM3 install 2'-O-methyl groups on the large subunit, two of them in the A-loop that contacts aminoacyl-tRNA. Pseudouridine synthases of the RPUSD and TRUB families, together with NGRN, RCC1L and FASTKD2, act in RNA granules where modification is coupled to mitoribosome assembly. Loss of these enzymes causes mitochondrial disease, and TFB1M variants are linked to aminoglycoside-induced deafness.

Synapses acquire their identity and strength through adhesion across the cleft, and the neurexin interaction with neuroligins is the best-studied example of this trans-synaptic bridge. Presynaptic neurexins bind postsynaptic neuroligins and LRRTMs to align transmitter release sites with receptor clusters, so that vesicle fusion is read out efficiently by the opposing membrane; the pairing also helps specify whether a contact becomes excitatory glutamatergic or inhibitory GABAergic. On the presynaptic side the adhesion complex links through CASK, Mint adaptors and the release machinery of syntaxin, MUNC18 and synaptotagmin calcium sensors, while postsynaptically it couples to PDZ scaffolds PSD-95, SHANKs, GKAPs and Homer, which anchor NMDA receptors and metabotropic glutamate receptors. Loss of these molecules in mice causes severe deficits in synaptic transmission, and human mutations in neurexins, neuroligins and SHANK3 are recurrent causes of autism and intellectual disability.

Synapses are asymmetric adhesive junctions, and the trans-synaptic protein pairings described here are how a presynaptic terminal and a postsynaptic density recognize each other, align, and mature into a functional contact. Adhesion molecules spanning the cleft — neurexins with neuroligins, LRRTMs, SLITRKs and LRFNs, and receptor phosphatases of the PTPRD/PTPRF/PTPRS group — bind heterophilically and then recruit intracellular scaffolds through their cytoplasmic tails. On the postsynaptic side PSD-95 family proteins, SHANKs, DLGAPs and HOMERs organize glutamate receptors, clustering AMPA and NMDA subunits and coupling metabotropic receptors to signalling; presynaptically, CASK, liprins, Munc18 and synaptotagmins position the release machinery opposite them. This matching determines excitatory versus inhibitory identity and synaptic strength, and underlies learning-related plasticity. Mutations in neurexins, neuroligins, SHANK3 and IL1RAPL1 are recurrent causes of autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.

When DNA is damaged, the tumour suppressor p53 does more than arrest the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis: it raises the supply of repair proteins themselves. Direct p53 targets here include the mismatch repair genes MSH2, MLH1 and PMS2, the nucleotide excision repair damage sensor DDB2, and FANCC of the interstrand crosslink repair pathway, so that repair capacity scales with genotoxic stress. A second, indirect arm runs through induction of cyclin K, the activating partner of CDK12 and CDK13; the kinase phosphorylates the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain and sustains productive elongation across unusually long repair genes such as BRCA1, ATM, ATR, FANCD2, FANCI, MDC1 and CHEK1. Accordingly the gene list is rich in polymerase II subunits, general transcription and elongation factors, and chromatin passage machinery. Loss of this coupling leaves double-strand break and crosslink repair underpowered, a route to genomic instability and cancer.

Choline catabolism converts dietary choline into a methyl donor, linking a nutrient best known as a phospholipid and acetylcholine precursor to one-carbon metabolism. Transporters bring choline into cells and mitochondria, where choline dehydrogenase oxidises it to betaine aldehyde and an aldehyde dehydrogenase completes conversion to betaine. Betaine then donates a methyl group to homocysteine through betaine-homocysteine methyltransferase, regenerating methionine independently of folate and helping keep homocysteine low; the resulting dimethylglycine is demethylated in two flavin-dependent mitochondrial steps by dimethylglycine and sarcosine dehydrogenases, feeding one-carbon units back to tetrahydrofolate before renal clearance. This route matters most in liver and kidney, where it supports methylation capacity and osmolyte balance. Disrupting it raises homocysteine, alters choline availability for membrane synthesis, and contributes to hepatic steatosis; the same substrate can instead be diverted by gut microbes toward trimethylamine.

Neutrophil degranulation is the effector step of innate antimicrobial defence: activated neutrophils fuse their storage granules with the plasma or phagosomal membrane, discharging antimicrobial and proteolytic cargo onto microbes and simultaneously delivering new receptors to the cell surface. It underlies bacterial and fungal killing at inflammatory sites, and its dysregulation drives tissue injury in sepsis, ARDS and chronic inflammatory disease, while loss of granule proteins or trafficking components causes congenital neutropenia and specific granule deficiency. The cargo spans azurophil enzymes such as myeloperoxidase, elanase, proteinase 3 and defensins, secondary and gelatinase granule proteins including lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and MMP8/MMP9, and lysosomal hydrolases. Their release depends on Rab GTPases, SNAP/VAMP fusion machinery, RAB27A-UNC13D-dependent exocytosis and cytoskeletal remodelling. Mobilised membrane proteins such as integrins, Fc and formyl-peptide receptors and the NADPH oxidase subunits then reprogramme how the cell senses and responds to its environment.

Neutrophils are the most abundant circulating leukocytes and the first responders to bacterial and fungal infection; degranulation is how they deliver their arsenal, fusing preformed granules with the plasma or phagosomal membrane to release antimicrobial and proteolytic cargo and to display new receptors at the cell surface. Azurophil granules supply myeloperoxidase, elastase, cathepsin G, proteinase 3, azurocidin, defensins and bactericidal permeability-increasing protein; specific and gelatinase granules contribute lactoferrin, lipocalin-2, matrix metalloproteinases and components of the NADPH oxidase, while secretory vesicles bring integrins, complement and Fc receptors, formyl-peptide receptors and adhesion molecules that retune the cell to its surroundings. Rab GTPases, SNAREs and Munc13-4 with cytoskeletal and motor components drive the trafficking step. Excessive release damages host tissue in sepsis, vasculitis and chronic inflammatory lung disease, whereas defective granule biogenesis or oxidase assembly causes recurrent infection.

Complex I, the entry point of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, oxidises NADH generated by glycolysis and the TCA cycle and uses the energy released to pump protons across the inner membrane, feeding the gradient that drives ATP synthesis. Its biogenesis is the stepwise construction of a ~45-subunit enzyme from separately made parts: seven hydrophobic core subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA and inserted into the membrane with help from OXA1L, and nuclear-encoded subunits of the NDUFA, NDUFB, NDUFS and NDUFV families imported from the cytosol. Modules for NADH oxidation, iron-sulfur electron relay and proton translocation are preassembled and then joined, with dedicated assembly factors such as NDUFAF1-8, ACAD9, ECSIT, TIMMDC1 and TMEM126B acting transiently, while NUBPL and chaperones supply the flavin and Fe-S cofactors. Defects in subunits or assembly factors cause isolated complex I deficiency, presenting as Leigh syndrome, encephalomyopathy and optic neuropathy.

Host defence can starve microbes of the metals they need, and metal sequestration by antimicrobial proteins is the arm of innate immunity that does it. Because nearly all bacteria and fungi require iron, zinc and manganese as enzyme cofactors, withholding these ions at inflamed or colonised surfaces restricts growth without killing host cells — a strategy often called nutritional immunity. Lactoferrin binds iron in milk, tears and neutrophil granules, while lipocalin 2 intercepts bacterial siderophores and so blocks siderophore-mediated iron capture. The calprotectin heterodimer of S100A8 and S100A9, released abundantly by neutrophils, chelates zinc and manganese, and the related psoriasin proteins act as zinc-binding antimicrobials in skin and epithelia. These factors shape the composition of mucosal and skin microbial communities, and pathogens counter them with high-affinity metal uptake systems; the same proteins are widely used as markers of gut and joint inflammation.

BRAF is the RAF-family kinase that couples active RAS to the MEK-ERK cascade, and cancer-associated substitutions outside the hotspot V600 position raise its activity only modestly. These moderate kinase activity BRAF mutants matter clinically because, unlike the strongly activating class, they still require RAS binding and dimerisation with a partner RAF to drive ERK output, so they remain sensitive to upstream input and behave differently towards RAF inhibitors, which can paradoxically promote dimer-driven signalling. The genes here assemble that context: the three RAS isoforms and RAP1 GTPases as activators, ARAF and RAF1 as dimerisation partners, MAP2K1/2 and ERK1/2 as the downstream module, and scaffolds and modulators including KSR1/2, CNKSR proteins, IQGAP1, 14-3-3 and the RAF inhibitory protein PEBP1. Integrin, talin and fibrinogen components place this signalling downstream of adhesive and platelet receptor engagement, with SRC, CSK and CaMK isoforms tuning the response.

Oncogenic BRAF alleles that carry greatly elevated intrinsic kinase activity, of which the V600E substitution accounts for the large majority, drive the MAP kinase cascade without an upstream signal. Because these mutants mimic activation-loop phosphorylation or lock the kinase in its active conformation, they phosphorylate MEK1/2 and thence ERK1/2 constitutively, act largely as monomers independent of RAS binding or dimer formation, and transform cells. This wiring explains the near-mutual exclusivity with RAS mutations and the low RAS activity of such tumours, and it underlies melanoma, hairy cell leukemia, papillary thyroid, colorectal and ovarian cancers, as well as the clinical logic of selective RAF inhibitors and the resistance that follows. Scaffolds and modulators including KSR1/2, CNKSR proteins, IQGAP1, 14-3-3 and the RAF inhibitory protein PEBP1 shape output, with integrin and SRC-associated components linking adhesion to the same cascade.

Oncogenic RAS proteins are the most common driver lesions in human cancer, and this pathway covers what happens downstream when they are mutated. Substitutions at glycine 12, glycine 13 or glutamine 61 in KRAS, NRAS or HRAS cripple GTP hydrolysis, locking the GTPase in its active state so that growth signalling continues without receptor input; KRAS mutations predominate in colorectal, pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancer. The immediate consequence traced here is constitutive engagement of the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, with ARAF, BRAF and RAF1 recruited to the membrane alongside scaffolds and modulators such as KSR1/2, CNKSR, IQGAP1, BRAP and the RAF inhibitor RKIP, feeding into MAP2K1/2 and ERK1/2. Related RAP1 and integrin-associated components place this signalling in the context of adhesion and cytoskeletal control, which together with proliferation and survival outputs underlies transformation.

Chromosomal rearrangements that fuse the kinase domain of BRAF or RAF1 to an unrelated N-terminal partner create constitutively active kinases, and the signalling they drive underlies pilocytic astrocytoma, thyroid and prostate carcinoma, melanoma and other tumours in which no RAF point mutation is found. The fusion removes the RAF N-terminal regulatory region, which normally holds the kinase autoinhibited and makes its activation dependent on RAS binding and membrane recruitment; many partners, such as KIAA1549, FAM131B, AGK, QKI and SND1, contribute coiled-coil or other dimerization elements that force the kinase domain into the active dimer. The result is RAS-independent, sustained phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2, feeding proliferation and survival programmes and suppressing apoptotic effectors like BIM. Scaffolds and regulators including KSR1/2, CNKSR proteins, 14-3-3 and RKIP shape the output, and the rearrangements confer distinct sensitivity to RAF and MEK inhibitors.

Neurofibromin is the GTPase-activating protein that accelerates intrinsic hydrolysis of GTP on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, and losing it leaves RAS locked in its active, GTP-bound state. This is the mechanism behind neurofibromatosis type 1, where germline NF1 inactivation drives neurofibromas, optic gliomas, and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, and behind sporadic cancers such as glioblastoma and melanoma that delete or truncate NF1. Because a GAP does not activate its target but switches it off, NF1 deletions, missense and frameshift mutations that reduce protein levels or abolish GAP activity produce constitutive signalling into the RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K routes, with unchecked proliferation and survival. SPRED proteins recruit neurofibromin to the plasma membrane, so their loss mimics NF1 loss and causes Legius syndrome. The pathway frames RAS regulation as a problem of negative control rather than receptor input.

Kinase-dead or drug-occupied BRAF can switch from a signal transmitter into a signal amplifier, and this paradoxical activation of RAF signalling explains why BRAF inhibitors given to cells with wild-type or kinase-impaired BRAF raise rather than lower ERK output. The consequence is clinical: skin tumours and secondary malignancies arise in treated patients, and RAS-mutant cancers carrying impaired BRAF alleles such as D594V gain, not lose, proliferative drive. Mechanistically, inhibitor binding or loss of catalytic activity disrupts autoinhibitory contacts between the kinase domain and the N-terminal regulatory region, favouring RAS binding and side-to-side dimerisation with CRAF; because inhibitor occupies only one protomer of the dimer, the partner is transactivated and phosphorylates MEK1/2, driving ERK1/2. Scaffolds and modulators including KSR1/2, CNKSR proteins, 14-3-3, PEBP1 and RAP1 shape dimer assembly, placing the effect within normal RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK growth control and integrin- and SRC-linked adhesion signalling.

Growth factor signals reach the nucleus through the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade, and this route is one of the most frequently corrupted in human cancer: activating mutations in KRAS, NRAS or HRAS occur in roughly a third of tumours, BRAF substitutions in many melanomas and thyroid cancers, and loss of the RAS GAP NF1 achieves the same end by removing a brake. Oncogenic MAPK signalling describes these lesions together with the machinery that normally restrains them – SPRED proteins, DUSP phosphatases that dephosphorylate ERK, and RKIP encoded by PEBP1 – plus scaffolds such as KSR1/2, SHOC2 and CNKSR that set the efficiency of RAF activation. Chromosomal rearrangements producing fusion partners like KIAA1549-BRAF or AGK-BRAF act by the same logic. Persistent ERK output drives proliferation and blocks apoptosis, partly by suppressing BIM, and defines the tumours treated with RAF and MEK inhibitors.
