Antimicrobial peptides is the innate chemical defence that epithelia, neutrophils and secretions use to kill bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses directly, without waiting for adaptive immunity. It keeps skin, gut, airway and reproductive surfaces colonised but not invaded, and its failure underlies conditions such as atopic dermatitis, Crohn's-like Paneth cell deficiency and recurrent skin infection. Most members are small cationic amphipathic peptides — alpha- and beta-defensins, cathelicidin, histatins, dermcidin, RNase family peptides — that bind anionic microbial membranes electrostatically and disrupt the bilayer. Several are made as inactive precursors and require proteolysis by neutrophil serine proteases such as elastase, cathepsin G and proteinase 3 to become active. A second arm is nutritional immunity: calprotectin (S100A8/A9), lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and copper transporters withhold or weaponise zinc, iron and copper at inflamed sites. Many of these peptides also act as chemoattractants, recruiting leukocytes and shaping the ensuing inflammatory response.

Antimicrobial peptides are the chemical arm of innate host defence at epithelial surfaces and inside phagocytes, killing bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses directly and shaping the inflammatory response that follows. Most are small cationic amphipathic molecules "" defensins, cathelicidin, histatins, hepcidin-like LEAP2 "" that bind anionic microbial membranes electrostatically, insert into the bilayer and permeabilise it; others act enzymatically, as with lysozyme cleaving peptidoglycan, or by sequestering nutrients, as lactoferrin, lipocalin-2 and the calprotectin subunits S100A8/A9 starve microbes of iron, zinc and manganese while copper handling by ATP7A and ATOX1 supports metal-based killing in phagosomes. Several precursors, including dermcidin in sweat and cathelicidin, require proteolytic processing by neutrophil serine proteases or kallikreins to become active. Beyond direct lysis, these peptides recruit and modulate neutrophils, monocytes and T cells through chemokine receptors and Toll-like receptor engagement. Deficient or dysregulated production underlies skin infection, periodontal disease and altered gut barrier immunity.

When damage is too severe to repair, TP53 commits a cell to die, and one arm of that decision is transcriptional: TP53 regulates genes that control mitochondrial outer membrane permeability and cytochrome c release. Induction of BAX, BID, PMAIP1 (NOXA) and BBC3 (PUMA) tips the balance of BCL2-family proteins toward pore formation, releasing cytochrome c to assemble the apoptosome and activate caspases; BNIP3L, STEAP3 and AIFM2 act in the same direction, while TRIAP1 restrains the step. Upstream, ATM-dependent phosphorylation, the acetyltransferase CREBBP, and ASPP cofactors encoded by PPP1R13B and TP53BP2 tune which promoters are engaged, and TP53INP1 promotes the serine-46 phosphorylation required for TP53AIP1 induction. The related factors TP63 and TP73 can substitute at some targets. Loss of this output lets damaged cells survive, a route to chemotherapy resistance and tumour progression.

When p53 is activated by DNA damage or oncogenic stress it turns on a large transcriptional programme, and part of that programme consists of cell death genes whose contribution to apoptosis is real but mechanistically unresolved. This arm of p53-dependent apoptosis matters because it determines how much killing a damaged cell receives beyond the well-characterised mitochondrial effectors, and because its targets are altered in tumours that retain wild-type p53. Induced products include the Bcl-2 family member BCL2L14, the transcriptional repressor BCL6, the quinone oxidoreductase-like TP53I3, the stress-regulated NDRG1, the tetraspan membrane protein PERP, and subunits of Rab geranylgeranyltransferase. Also present are the ASPP-family p53 cofactors, which modulate promoter selection, the apoptosis inhibitor survivin as a repressed target, and the p53 relatives TP63 and TP73, which share many of these response elements and can substitute for p53 in driving them.</response>

When DNA damage or other stress activates p53, part of its response is to stock the cell with the machinery needed to execute its own death, and this arm of the p53 programme sets the transcription of caspases and the platforms that activate them. It raises the threshold-lowering components rather than triggering death directly, so a cell that has already been primed dies faster and more decisively once a second signal arrives; loss of this output contributes to the apoptosis resistance of p53-mutant tumours. Targets include APAF1, the core of the apoptosome that activates caspase-9 downstream of mitochondrial cytochrome c release; PIDD1 and its adaptor CRADD, which assemble the caspase-2 activating complex; NLRC4 and CASP1, linking to inflammasome-driven pyroptosis; and the executioner caspase CASP6 and initiator CASP10 of death receptor signalling. ATM acts upstream as the damage sensor, and the p53 relatives TP63 and TP73 share overlapping target promoters.

Damaged cells can be told to die by signals from outside as well as from within, and one arm of the p53 response makes them more sensitive to that external verdict. Acting as a transcription factor, TP53 — with help from its relatives TP63 and TP73 and the ASPP cofactors encoded by PPP1R13B and TP53BP2, which bias p53 toward pro-apoptotic promoters — raises expression of the death receptors FAS and the TRAIL receptors DR4 and DR5, along with the decoy receptors DcR1 and DcR2 that tune the response. The secreted target IGFBP3 has been proposed to act through TMEM219 as a further death-inducing ligand–receptor pair. By loading the cell surface with receptors that feed into caspase-8 activation, this programme links genotoxic stress to extrinsic apoptosis and to immune killing, and its loss in TP53-mutant tumours contributes to resistance to both chemotherapy and TRAIL-based agents.

A single FGFR2 gene yields two receptors with different ligand preferences, and the choice between them is made by alternative splicing of mutually exclusive exons encoding the C-terminal half of the third immunoglobulin-like domain. Epithelial cells make FGFR2 IIIb, which responds to FGF7 and FGF10, while mesenchymal cells make FGFR2 IIIc; the resulting asymmetry lets the two compartments signal to each other during limb, skeletal and branching organ development, and loss of the epithelial isoform accompanies epithelial-mesenchymal transition in tumour progression. Decision-making is combinatorial and co-transcriptional, occurring on nascent transcripts made by RNA polymerase II and capped by the nuclear cap-binding complex. Silencing elements around the IIIb exon recruit PTBP1, hnRNPA1 and hnRNPM to favour IIIc, whereas the epithelial-restricted regulators ESRP1 and ESRP2, together with RBFOX2 and hnRNP H/F, promote IIIb inclusion.

When a macrophage engulfs a bacterium, it fights back partly by manipulating metal chemistry inside the phagosome, and this ion influx and efflux at the host-pathogen interface is that battleground. Metals such as iron, manganese, zinc and copper are obligatory enzyme cofactors for both host and microbe, yet in excess they drive damaging redox cycling, so the host can attack either by starvation or by poisoning. Here the copper arm is represented: the cytosolic chaperone ATOX1 hands copper to the ATP7A pump, which relocates toward the phagosomal membrane and loads copper into the vacuole at toxic concentrations, with PDZD11 assisting pump trafficking. In parallel, the divalent cation transporter SLC11A1 (NRAMP1) withdraws manganese and iron from the phagosome, depriving the pathogen of cofactors. Variants in these components alter susceptibility to intracellular infections such as mycobacteria and Salmonella, and the same logic underlies attempts to treat infection by disturbing microbial metal balance.

TP53 Regulates Transcription of Genes Involved in G2 Cell Cycle Arrest describes how the p53 tumour suppressor halts cells at the G2/M boundary after genotoxic stress, buying time for DNA repair before mitosis and preventing damaged chromosomes from being segregated. Loss of this arm of the p53 response permits mitotic entry with unrepaired lesions, driving aneuploidy and tumorigenesis. p53 works in two directions: it activates GADD45A, with help from the acetyltransferase EP300 and the arginine methyltransferases PRMT1 and CARM1, and GADD45A then inhibits Aurora kinase A; and it induces SFN (14-3-3-sigma), aided by the target ZNF385A, which sequesters the CDK1-cyclin B1 complex outside the nucleus. In parallel, p53 acting with the repressor E2F4 and its DP and retinoblastoma-family partners shuts down CDC25C transcription, removing the phosphatase needed to activate CDK1. SFN additionally restrains BAX, coupling arrest to apoptosis avoidance.

When DNA damage is detected in the second gap phase, cells must hold off mitosis until repair is finished, and p53-driven transcription is one route to that arrest. The tumour suppressor switches on GADD45A and SFN (14-3-3-sigma) while shutting down CDC25C, the phosphatase that would otherwise dephosphorylate and activate the CDK1-cyclin B1 complex driving entry into mitosis. GADD45A binds and inhibits Aurora kinase A; SFN sequesters CDK1-cyclin B1 in the cytoplasm, and because it also binds BAX it can restrain apoptosis at the same time. Induction of GADD45A depends on coactivators and chromatin modifiers including EP300 and the arginine methyltransferases PRMT1 and CARM1, while repression of CDC25C involves E2F4 with pocket proteins RBL1/RBL2 and DP partners. Loss of this checkpoint permits division with unrepaired lesions, producing the aneuploidy and genomic instability typical of p53-mutant cancers.

When p53 is activated by damage or stress, it turns on a broad transcriptional programme that halts proliferation, and this arm covers cell cycle target genes whose contribution to the outcome is still only partly understood. The antiproliferative factor BTG2 is one such target: it docks onto the multi-subunit CCR4-NOT complex and stimulates its mRNA deadenylase activity, linking p53 to the control of transcript stability, though how this enforces growth arrest is unresolved. Two polo-like kinases, PLK2 and PLK3, are also induced directly; PLK2 acts at centrosomes and helps cells survive spindle damage, while PLK3 influences nuclear accumulation of the mitotic phosphatase CDC25C. RGCC and the zinc finger protein PLAGL1 round out the group, both implicated in arrest or apoptosis and frequently lost in tumours, situating this biology within the p53-dependent tumour suppression response.

When DNA is damaged, cells must stop before replicating a corrupted genome, and this is the arm of the p53 response that holds them at the G1/S boundary. Its best-known output is CDKN1A (p21), among the earliest genes induced by TP53, which binds and inhibits CDK2 partnered with cyclin E or cyclin A and so blocks entry into S phase; loss of this brake is one route by which damaged cells proliferate and become transformed. TP53 also induces the atypical repressors E2F7 and E2F8, which shut down E2F1-driven transcription of replication genes, and the cofactor ZNF385A, which biases p53 toward arrest rather than apoptosis. The decision is reversible and tuned: PCBP4, itself p53-induced, destabilises CDKN1A mRNA under prolonged stress, releasing G1 arrest and pushing cells toward G2 arrest or death, while ARID3A can act in either direction.

How much p53 protein a cell contains sets the threshold for arresting the cell cycle or dying after DNA damage, and the TP53 gene is itself transcriptionally controlled. Here the regulation is a negative feedback loop: PRDM1 (BLIMP1), whose own transcription is driven by p53, binds the TP53 promoter and represses it, probably by recruiting repressive histone methylation. The result is a self-limiting response in which p53 activity curtails its own production, keeping tumour suppressor output proportionate to the insult rather than permanently high. The protein that emerges acts as a homotetramer, so the amount made also influences how readily functional complexes assemble on target promoters. Because the same PRDM1 factor drives plasma cell differentiation, this loop links terminal B cell maturation to damped p53 expression, and its disturbance contributes to lymphoid malignancy.

Whether a stressed cell pauses, senesces, or kills itself depends largely on how p53 is phosphorylated, and this is the set of kinase inputs that decide. Marks on the N-terminal serines S15 and S20, placed by ATM and ATR after double-strand breaks or stalled forks and by the checkpoint kinases CHEK1 and CHEK2, block MDM2 binding and so stabilise p53 instead of letting it be ubiquitinated and destroyed. Other sites steer output rather than abundance: S46, modified by HIPK2 with TP53INP1 or by ATM-activated DYRK2, favours apoptotic target genes; MAPKAPK5 acts at S37 during oncogene-induced senescence; casein kinase II with the FACT complex works at S392. Conversely, CDK2 and Aurora A phosphorylate S315 and TFIID components modify T55, both enhancing MDM2-driven turnover. Also present are the MRN complex, RPA and 9-1-1 sensors that generate the damage signal, and AMPK subunits coupling metabolic stress to p53.

Regulation of TP53 Degradation sets how much p53 protein a cell keeps, and therefore whether damaged or oncogene-stressed cells arrest, senesce or die. In unstressed cells p53 is held at low levels by continuous ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover, so that growth is not needlessly restrained; loss of this restraint is embryonic lethal, while its excess is a common route to tumours that retain wild-type p53. The E3 ligase MDM2, itself a p53 target gene, forms the core negative feedback loop and works with its partner MDM4, both also subject to auto- and cross-ubiquitination. Kinase inputs tune the loop: AKT and SGK1 downstream of mTORC2 promote MDM2 nuclear entry, CDK1/CDK2 and PP2A adjust its affinity, and ATM with CHEK2 uncouple MDM2 from p53 after double-strand breaks. ARF sequesters MDM2 during oncogenic stress, and USP2 and USP7 reverse ubiquitination.

The tumour suppressor p53 is kept at low levels in healthy, unstressed cells, and controlling its turnover is what allows the protein to be silent normally yet surge within minutes of damage. The E3 ubiquitin ligase MDM2, itself induced by p53, ubiquitinates p53 for proteasomal destruction and acts with its partner MDM4 (MDMX) as a heterodimer; both ligases also ubiquitinate each other and themselves. Growth signalling through mTORC2, PDPK1, AKT and SGK1 promotes nuclear entry of MDM2, while CDK1/CDK2 phosphorylation weakens its grip on p53. DNA double-strand breaks activate ATM and CHEK2, which phosphorylate p53 to block MDM2 binding and mark MDM4 for degradation, stabilising p53. Counterweights include a PP2A complex recruited by cyclin G1, the deubiquitinases USP2 and USP7, and p14-ARF, which sequesters MDM2 under oncogenic stress. Loss of this balance underlies MDM2-amplified and ARF-deleted cancers with intact p53.

Regulation of TP53 Activity through Acetylation controls how strongly the p53 tumour suppressor turns on its target genes, and which of them it chooses. Acetylation is the switch that converts a stabilised p53 protein into an active transcription factor, so this layer of control decides whether a damaged cell arrests, dies, or shifts its metabolism, and its loss lets tumours tolerate p53 that is present but inert. EP300 acetylates lysine 382 with help from BRD7, enhancing promoter binding at CDKN1A, MDM2 and TIGAR; KAT6A acting with PML modifies the same residue plus lysine 120 in the DNA-binding domain, where MYST-family marks bias the arrest-versus-apoptosis decision. The NuRD complex, recruited through MTA2 and carrying HDAC1/2, reverses these marks and dampens p53 output. Acetylation in the DNA-binding domain also uncouples transactivation from repression and feeds into reactive oxygen species control and ferroptosis.

Whether p53 arrests a damaged cell or kills it depends heavily on which of its lysines are acetylated, and this is the branch of p53 regulation that sets that choice. Acetylation in the DNA-binding domain and at the C-terminal K382 strengthens promoter occupancy and drives targets such as the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A, the MDM2 feedback loop, and genes governing energy metabolism, reactive oxygen species and ferroptosis. EP300 acts with the bromodomain protein BRD7, while the MYST-family acetyltransferase KAT6A works together with PML and BRPF/ING/MEAF6 scaffolding subunits. The opposing reaction comes from the NuRD chromatin remodelling complex — CHD3/CHD4, MTA2, MBD3, RBBP4/7 and HDAC1/2 — which deacetylates p53 and damps its output. Loss of this tuning blunts tumour suppression after genotoxic stress.

Once p53 is activated by stress it must choose between halting the cell cycle and killing the cell, and that choice is largely made by the co-factors it binds. Regulation of TP53 activity through association with co-factors therefore sets the outcome of DNA damage responses, and its distortion lets damaged cells survive and divide, a route to tumour formation. ZNF385A and POU4F1 bias p53 toward arrest genes such as CDKN1A, while the ASPP proteins PPP1R13B and TP53BP2 and the related factor POU4F2 favour pro-apoptotic targets; PPP1R13L acts as the inhibitory member of the ASPP family and blunts apoptotic output. PHF20 recognises methylated p53 and competes with MDM2-mediated degradation, extending the protein's half-life. AKT kinases feed survival signalling into the same decision, and the paralogues TP63 and TP73 share overlapping co-factor partners.

Regulation of TP53 Activity through Methylation tunes the tumour suppressor p53 after it has been stabilised, deciding which of its target programmes -- cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, or none -- actually gets transcribed. This is a layer of control that determines whether a cell damaged by genotoxic stress pauses, dies, or continues dividing with mutations, and its subversion contributes to tumours that retain wild-type p53. Lysine and arginine methyltransferases write opposing marks on the p53 C-terminal regulatory region: SETD9 methylation at K372 stabilises and activates it, PRMT5 acting in an ATM-activated complex with TTC5, JMY and p300 biases output toward arrest genes, while SMYD2, the EHMT1-EHMT2 complex and KMT5A-directed recruitment of the chromatin compaction factor L3MBTL1 silence transcription. These marks interact with the parallel MDM2- and MDM4-driven ubiquitination route that controls p53 abundance, integrating damage signalling from ATM and CHEK2 into a graded response.

The tumour suppressor p53 decides whether a damaged cell arrests, repairs itself or dies, and methylation of its own lysine and arginine residues is one of the switches that sets which target genes it turns on. Because the marks can either stabilise and activate p53 or silence it, this layer of control helps determine whether DNA damage produces cell cycle arrest or is tolerated, and its subversion favours tumour growth. After ATM and CHEK2 sense damage, PRMT5 is recruited with TTC5, JMY and the acetyltransferase EP300 and methylates arginines that bias p53 toward arrest genes, while SETD9 methylation of K372 raises p53 stability and activity. Opposing marks placed by SMYD2 and by the EHMT1-EHMT2 complex repress transcription, and KMT5A-generated monomethylation recruits the chromatin compaction factor L3MBTL1. Ubiquitin and the MDM2-MDM4 axis link these marks to p53 turnover.

Keratinization is the differentiation programme that turns a living keratinocyte into the tough, dead, water-impermeable corneocyte of skin, hair, nail and other stratified epithelia. It builds the barrier that keeps water in and microbes and allergens out; its failure produces ichthyoses, palmoplantar keratodermas, epidermolysis bullosa simplex, monilethrix and hair-shaft defects, and Netherton syndrome. Type I and type II keratins pair as obligate heterodimers into 10 nm intermediate filaments whose bundles anchor at desmosomes through desmogleins, desmocollins, plakophilins, plakoglobin and desmoplakin, giving epithelial sheets mechanical continuity. In the granular layer, filaggrin, involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases beneath the plasma membrane, while kallikrein proteases restrained by SPINK inhibitors, plus caspase-14 and calpain, execute cornification and controlled desquamation. Hair-specific keratins and keratin-associated proteins form the disulfide-rich hair shaft.

Keratinization is the terminal differentiation programme that converts a living keratinocyte into a flattened, cross-linked corneocyte, giving skin, hair, nails and other stratified epithelia their mechanical strength and barrier function. Type I and type II keratins pair as heteropolymeric intermediate filaments that bundle into tonofilaments and anchor at desmosomes through desmogleins, desmocollins, plakophilins, plakoglobin, desmoplakin and the plakin family, distributing tension across the tissue. In the upper layers, filaggrin and trichohyalin aggregate filaments, while involucrin, loricrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins are cross-linked by transglutaminases into the cornified envelope; hair keratin-associated proteins supply the disulfide-rich matrix of the hair shaft. Kallikrein proteases, balanced by SPINK and cystatin inhibitors, and caspase-14 govern desquamation and filaggrin processing. Mutations in these components cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, palmoplantar keratodermas, ichthyoses, Netherton syndrome, monilethrix and pemphigus-related blistering.

How much p53 protein a cell contains is set largely after transcription, and this control circuit explains why an unstressed cell holds almost none while a damaged one accumulates it rapidly. Keeping p53 low permits normal proliferation; failure to relieve that restraint blunts the DNA damage response and allows transformed cells to survive, which is why the degradation machinery is itself a drug target. The core mechanism is ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal turnover driven by the E3 ligase MDM2, acting alone or with its partner MDM4, with RNF34 and RFFL ubiquitinating the phosphorylated form and the deubiquitinase USP7 opposing turnover to stabilise p53. Damage-activated kinases ATM and CHEK2 phosphorylate p53 near its MDM2-binding surface, and p14-ARF from the CDKN2A locus sequesters MDM2 during oncogenic stress. AKT and mTOR complex components, cyclin-CDK pairs and PP2A subunits feed growth and phosphatase signals into the same set point.

Vitamin K exists in the body to serve one chemical purpose: it is the cofactor that lets a carboxylase convert specific glutamate residues into gamma-carboxyglutamate, a modification that creates calcium-binding sites in proteins. Without it, clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, the bone protein osteocalcin, and GAS6 are secreted in non-functional form, producing haemorrhage and defective bone mineralisation. Dietary phylloquinone and bacterial menaquinones arrive in tissues by lipoprotein trafficking; UBIAD1 then prenylates menadiol with geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate to generate MK4, the active hydroquinone used in liver and osteoblasts. Each carboxylation event oxidises the cofactor to an epoxide, so the vitamin must be recycled: VKORC1 reduces the epoxide back to usable MK4, with the related VKORC1L1 of less settled physiological role. This reductase is the target of warfarin, and its variants explain much of the inherited variation in anticoagulant dosing.

Vitamins A, D, E and K cannot be absorbed or moved through the blood without lipid carriers, and the metabolism of fat-soluble vitamins covers both their uptake from the diet and their conversion into usable forms. Dietary carotenoids are cleaved by BCO1 and BCO2 to retinal, which is reduced and esterified by LRAT for storage, while retinol-binding proteins and transthyretin carry retinol to target tissues. Vitamin K quinone is prenylated by UBIAD1 and recycled by the VKORC1 reductases that regenerate the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, the step blocked by warfarin. Absorption depends on pancreatic lipase and colipase, chylomicron apolipoproteins, lipoprotein lipase tethered by GPIHBP1, and LDL-receptor-family and proteoglycan receptors for particle clearance. TTPA selects alpha-tocopherol for export; its loss causes vitamin E deficiency with ataxia, and retinoid failure impairs vision and epithelial maintenance.

The MET receptor tyrosine kinase responds to hepatocyte growth factor/scatter factor and converts that cue into cell growth, survival, scattering and invasive motility. It drives placental and liver development, muscle precursor migration and motor neuron survival, and is redeployed in wound healing and liver regeneration; overexpression or activating mutation makes it a recurrent oncogenic driver and a drug target, and Listeria exploits it to enter host cells. Ligand binding dimerizes the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for GRB2, SHC1 and the scaffold GAB1 that route signals to PI3K, RAS-ERK, STAT3, RAC1, RAP1 and focal adhesion kinase. Proteolytic activators such as HGFAC and HPN and their inhibitors SPINT1/2 control ligand maturation, while CBL-mediated ubiquitination, ESCRT components and phosphatases including PTPN1/PTPN2 and PTPRJ terminate signalling. Engagement of integrins, laminins, fibronectin and collagens ties receptor output to matrix adhesion.

Turning on the MET receptor tyrosine kinase is a two-step affair, and this pathway covers both: the proteolytic maturation of hepatocyte growth factor and the ligand-driven dimerization of MET itself. The output is a signal that drives epithelial cell survival, scattering, motility and branching morphogenesis, and that underpins liver and placental development as well as wound repair and tissue regeneration. HGF is secreted as an inert single-chain precursor and must be cleaved by a membrane-anchored serine protease such as hepsin or by the extracellular activator HGFAC; the Kunitz-domain inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restrain those proteases and so set how much active ligand is available. Mature HGF engages the SEMA and PSI domains of MET, promoting receptor pairing and trans-autophosphorylation that both raises kinase activity and creates docking sites for adaptors. Excessive MET activation is a recurrent driver of invasive carcinoma.

Negative regulation of MET activity is the brake on signalling by the hepatocyte growth factor receptor, terminating the proliferative, motility and survival programme that MET otherwise drives in epithelial cells. Its loss underlies sustained MET signalling in invasive carcinomas, and mutations that uncouple MET from these controls are transforming. Two mechanisms dominate. Phosphatases strip activating phosphates: PTPRJ removes the Y1349 docking site needed for GAB1 recruitment, while PTPN1 and PTPN2 dephosphorylate the kinase activation loop to blunt catalytic output. In parallel, the E3 ligase CBL, recruited with GRB2 and CIN85, ubiquitinates activated MET at the membrane or in early endosomes, committing it to ESCRT-dependent sorting through HGS, STAM and USP8 and lysosomal destruction; endophilins and EPS15 supply the endocytic step. LRIG1 drives degradation of unstimulated receptor, setting basal MET levels independently of ligand.

The HGF receptor MET drives proliferation, motility and epithelial morphogenesis, so signalling through it must be terminated once the ligand has been sensed; negative regulation of MET activity is how the cell sets the duration and amplitude of that response, and its loss underlies the sustained MET signalling seen in invasive and metastatic carcinomas. Two mechanisms dominate. Tyrosine phosphatases strip activating phosphates: PTPRJ acts on the site that docks the GAB1 adaptor, while PTPN1 and PTPN2 dephosphorylate the kinase activation loop to blunt catalytic output. In parallel, the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL, recruited with GRB2 and SH3KBP1, ubiquitinates activated MET and commits it to clathrin- and endosome-dependent trafficking, with EPS15, endophilins, and the HGS-STAM sorting complex delivering it to lysosomal degradation; USP8 deubiquitination counterbalances this, and LRIG1 promotes turnover of unstimulated receptor.

The final stretch of cholesterol synthesis converts zymosterol to cholesterol, and it can run by two routes that differ only in when the side-chain double bond is reduced. In the Bloch route that reduction comes last, so the sterol nucleus is demethylated, isomerised and desaturated first and desmosterol is the immediate precursor; DHCR24 then completes the molecule. This branch predominates in liver and most tissues, whereas skin favours the alternative order and accumulates 7-dehydrocholesterol as a substrate for vitamin D photosynthesis. The enzymes act in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and include a lanosterol 14-demethylase, the C-4 demethylation complex, a sterol isomerase and the C-5 desaturase, with 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase shared between routes. Because cholesterol is needed for membranes, bile acids and steroid hormones, defects here cause malformation syndromes such as Smith-Lemli-Opitz, CHILD syndrome and chondrodysplasia punctata.

Zymostenol biosynthesis via lathosterol (Kandutsch-Russell pathway) is one of the two alternative routes by which post-squalene intermediates are converted to cholesterol, and the one that predominates in skin. It differs from its counterpart only in timing: the side-chain double bond is reduced first, by DHCR24, so all subsequent steps proceed on saturated sterols. From there the standard sequence follows — CYP51A1 demethylation at C14, TM7SF2 reduction of the resulting Δ9(11) bond, and the MSMO1/NSDHL/HSD17B7 triad that removes the two C4 methyl groups — yielding zymostenol and then lathosterol. Because this branch generates 7-dehydrocholesterol in keratinocytes, it supplies the substrate for UV-driven vitamin D3 formation. Flux through both routes is set transcriptionally by SREBF1 and SREBF2 in response to sterol depletion, tying the pathway to membrane lipid homeostasis; loss of its enzymes causes skeletal and skin malformation syndromes.

Cholesterol can be built along two routes that differ only in when the side-chain double bond is reduced; the Kandutsch-Russell route reduces it first, so the sterol intermediates are saturated and pass through zymostenol and lathosterol rather than desmosterol. This branch predominates in skin, where it feeds 7-dehydrocholesterol, the precursor that ultraviolet light converts into vitamin D, and it supplies membrane cholesterol and the raw material for steroid and bile acid synthesis generally. The early reduction is carried out by DHCR24, after which the shared post-squalene enzymes act on the saturated series: CYP51A1 removes the C14 methyl, TM7SF2 reduces the resulting double bond, and MSMO1, NSDHL and HSD17B7 together strip the two C4 methyl groups. Output is set transcriptionally by the sterol-responsive regulators SREBF1 and SREBF2, and defects in these steps cause congenital skin and skeletal disorders.

PTEN is the phosphatase that drains PIP3 and so restrains PI3K–AKT–mTOR signalling; because even modest reductions in its dose permit growth, survival and tumour formation, cells control how much PTEN they make, where it sits and how long it lasts. Transcription is repressed epigenetically when SALL4 recruits the Mi-2/NuRD deacetylase complex or EVI1 recruits Polycomb, and by JUN, SNAI1/SNAI2 and the NR2E1:atrophin complex, while TP53, ATF2, EGR1 and PPARG drive it up. A set of microRNAs including the miR-17~92 family, miR-21-related species, miR-214 and miR-205 silence the mRNA through Argonaute-containing complexes, and the PTENP1 pseudogene transcript sponges them away. Protein levels and localisation are then set by ubiquitin ligases such as NEDD4, WWP2, STUB1, XIAP and MKRN1 feeding the proteasome, opposed by the deubiquitinases USP7, USP13 and OTUD3, with casein kinase 2 and FRK phosphorylation tuning stability and activity.

Spliceosomal small nuclear RNAs must be made before any pre-mRNA can be spliced, and most of them — U1, U2, U4, U5 and the minor-spliceosome U11, U12 and U4atac — are made by RNA polymerase II using a promoter and termination system distinct from that of protein-coding genes. These genes are among the most heavily transcribed in the nucleus, and their output sets the capacity of both major and minor splicing; mutations affecting minor snRNA production cause developmental disorders such as microcephalic osteodysplastic dwarfism. Activators binding a distal element, including POU2F1, SP1 and ZNF143, promote loading of the multisubunit SNAPc complex onto the proximal sequence element, which clears nucleosomes and recruits TBP with general initiation factors and polymerase II. CDK7 and P-TEFb phosphorylation of the polymerase C-terminal domain, reversed in part by RPAP2 and SSU72, recruits the Integrator cleavage complex and the elongation factors that generate a correct snRNA 3' end for capping and nuclear export.

Newly made secretory proteins leaving the endoplasmic reticulum are collected in the ER-to-Golgi intermediate compartment, and COPI-mediated anterograde transport carries them onward to the cis-Golgi while returning ER residents in the opposite direction. This step sets the pace of secretion for cargo such as insulin and for surface proteins including CD55, CD59 and the folate receptor, and its disruption causes Golgi fragmentation and congenital glycosylation and skeletal disorders. The ARF1 GTPase, activated by the exchange factor GBF1 and switched off by ARFGAP proteins, recruits the seven-subunit coatomer to form vesicles that are moved along microtubules by dynein and its dynactin cofactor. Rab1, the tether p115, golgins, the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex and a syntaxin-5-containing SNARE set with NSF and SNAPs then dock and fuse the carriers, while KDEL receptors and p24 family cargo adaptors select what travels.

Formation of the cornified envelope is the terminal differentiation programme by which epidermal keratinocytes convert themselves into flattened, dead corneocytes, building the water-impermeable, mechanically tough outer barrier of skin, hair and oral epithelium. Loss of it causes ichthyosis, peeling skin and Netherton syndrome, and leaves the body vulnerable to dehydration, infection and allergen entry. Transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich and late cornified envelope proteins into a rigid submembranous shell, to which keratin filaments and ceramide lipids are covalently anchored; filaggrin and trichohyalin aggregate the keratin cytoskeleton. Desmosomal cadherins, plakins and plakophilins are crosslinked into corneodesmosomes that glue cornified cells together, while kallikrein and other proteases, restrained by SPINK inhibitors, later dissolve those junctions for orderly desquamation. Caspase-14 and calpain drive the accompanying organelle and nuclear breakdown, a specialised, calcium-gradient-controlled form of programmed cell death.

The outermost skin barrier is built by a specialized form of programmed cell death in which upper-epidermal keratinocytes convert themselves into flattened corneocytes. Formation of the cornified envelope creates a heavily crosslinked protein shell coated with covalently bound lipids, giving the stratum corneum its rigidity and its resistance to water loss and microbial entry. Transglutaminases crosslink loricrin, involucrin, small proline-rich proteins and late cornified envelope proteins into that shell, while keratin filaments and filaggrin or trichohyalin aggregates fill the cell interior and anchor to it. Desmosomal cadherins, plakins and corneodesmosin are incorporated to hold cornified cells together, and kallikrein-family proteases balanced by SPINK inhibitors later dissolve those junctions to allow orderly shedding. Loss of individual components causes ichthyosis, palmoplantar keratoderma, Netherton syndrome and hair or nail defects, and barrier failure predisposes to atopic disease.

Vitamin A reaches the eye and other peripheral tissues bound to a dedicated carrier, and this pathway covers what happens when that delivery step fails. Retinol-binding protein, secreted by the liver, picks up all-trans-retinol from hepatic stores and circulates with it in complex with transthyretin, which keeps the small carrier from being filtered by the kidney and releases retinol at target cells. Because the retinal pigment epithelium and photoreceptors depend on this supply to regenerate visual chromophore, loss-of-function mutations in the carrier cause retinol-binding protein deficiency, with impaired night vision, a xerophthalmic fundus and progressive atrophy of the pigment epithelium. The defect illustrates how retinoid homeostasis links liver storage to vision and to retinoid signalling in tissues generally, rather than to any single enzymatic conversion.

COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde traffic is the return arm of the early secretory pathway, recycling membrane, cargo receptors and escaped resident proteins from the cis-Golgi back to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and the ER. Without it the ER loses its chaperones and lipid and protein balance across the two organelles collapses, disrupting secretion and quality control. Vesicle formation begins with the ARF1 activator GBF1, which recruits the seven-subunit COPI coat; ARFGAP proteins and p24/TMED cargo receptors shape the coat and select cargo, while KDEL receptors capture escaped chaperones such as BiP for return. Carriers move along microtubules using kinesin motors and tubulin tracks, then are captured at the ER by the NRZ tethering complex (NBAS, RINT1, ZW10) working with ER SNAREs STX18, USE1, BNIP1 and SEC22B, with NSF and SNAPs recycling the fusion machinery. Rab1 GTPases coordinate tethering and fusion.

Secretory traffic leaks: ER residents such as chaperones escape forward to the Golgi, and the machinery that carries them back is COPI-dependent Golgi-to-ER retrograde transport. By recovering escaped proteins and recycling the membrane, receptors and SNAREs consumed by anterograde flow, it keeps the ER competent for folding and quality control and maintains the compartmental identity of the early secretory pathway. KDEL receptors capture the escaped chaperones at the cis-Golgi and concentrate them into vesicles whose coat is the heptameric COPI complex, recruited by ARF GTPases activated by GBF1 and disassembled with help from ARFGAP proteins; p24/TMED components and cargo receptors such as SURF4 contribute to sorting. Motor and microtubule components move the carriers, which are captured at the ER by the NRZ tethering complex with ZW10, RINT1 and NBAS acting alongside ER SNAREs STX18, USE1, BNIP1 and SEC22B, with NSF and SNAPs recycling the fusion machinery.

Proteins that escape or must be recycled from the Golgi return to the endoplasmic reticulum by more than one route, and this one works without a COPI coat. It retrieves resident Golgi glycosylation enzymes such as the polypeptide GalNAc transferases and is the path exploited by Shiga and Shiga-like toxins to reach the ER and then the cytosol, making it the entry step for their lethality. Cargo travels in long membrane tubules rather than coated vesicles, generated under the control of RAB6 and pulled along microtubules by the dynein-dynactin motor with Bicaudal-D proteins as the adaptors linking motor to membrane. Tubule formation requires membrane curvature supplied by phospholipase A activity that converts phospholipids to lysophospholipids, balanced by reacylation, so the lipid-modifying enzymes help set whether tubules or vesicles form. It supports Golgi enzyme homeostasis and compartment identity.

Cargo entering the Golgi at its cis face must move through biochemically distinct cisternae in order, while the enzymes that decorate it stay where they belong; intra-Golgi traffic is the vesicle flow in both directions that accomplishes both. Anterograde movement carries newly synthesized secretory and membrane proteins toward the trans-Golgi network, and retrograde movement returns resident glycosylation enzymes to their home cisternae, sustaining cisternal maturation and the ordered glycan processing performed by mannosidases such as MAN1A1 and MAN2A1. ARF1 and its cytohesin-family activators drive COPI carrier formation, Golgi-localized SNAREs including STX5, GOSR1/2 and YKT6 give each step its specificity, and NSF with its SNAP proteins recycles them; the conserved oligomeric Golgi complex and golgins tether membranes. Because structure and transport are inseparable here, loss of COG subunits disorganizes the stack and causes congenital disorders of glycosylation.

Membrane traffic runs in both directions, and retrograde transport at the trans-Golgi network is the return leg: vesicles arriving from endosomes and the plasma membrane dock and fuse there, recycling resident Golgi proteins such as TGOLN2 and returning mannose-6-phosphate receptors (M6PR, IGF2R) so that newly made lysosomal hydrolases can keep being sorted. Without it, hydrolase delivery fails and Golgi glycosylation enzymes are lost, which is why defects in the GARP complex (VPS51-VPS54) or in COG subunits cause congenital glycosylation disorders and neurodevelopmental disease. Incoming vesicles are captured by long coiled-coil golgins such as GOLGA4, GCC1 and GCC2, anchored via ARL1 and ARFRP1, under the control of RAB6 for early endosome-derived carriers and RAB9 with RHOBTB3 for late endosomal ones; fusion then proceeds through SNAREs including STX6, STX16 and VTI1A and the NSF-SNAP disassembly machinery. Shiga and cholera toxins exploit this same route to reach the cytosol.

Secretory cargo does not simply flow forward through the Golgi; the resident glycosylation enzymes, cargo receptors and vesicle machinery that act on it must be continuously recycled backwards, and that is what intra-Golgi and retrograde Golgi-to-ER traffic accomplishes. It keeps the cis-, medial- and trans-cisternae biochemically distinct so that glycans are built in the correct sequential order, returns escaped ER residents via KDEL receptors, and retrieves mannose-6-phosphate receptors after they deliver hydrolases toward lysosomes. Mechanistically, COPI coat subunits recruited by ARF1 and its activator GBF1, with ARFGAPs terminating the cycle, bud the carriers; RAB1 and RAB6 direct them; long golgins together with the multisubunit conserved oligomeric Golgi and GARP tethers capture them; and Golgi SNAREs with NSF-driven disassembly complete fusion. Dynein, kinesins and microtubules position the ribbon and move the vesicles. Loss of tether subunits causes congenital glycosylation disorders with skeletal and neurological disease.

Nuclear phosphoinositides act as a stress signal that tunes how strongly p53 responds, and this route links phosphatidylinositol-5-phosphate levels to acetylation of the tumour suppressor. When cells are stressed, nuclear PI5P rises because the PIP4K2 kinases that consume it by phosphorylating PI5P to PI(4,5)P2 are inhibited, while phosphatase activity can regenerate it. PI5P is read by the PHD finger of ING2, retaining ING2 in the nucleus, where it binds p53 and brings in the acetyltransferase p300 to acetylate it. Acetylated p53 is more stable and more competent to activate targets driving growth arrest and apoptosis, with the stress kinase MAP2K6 and the prolyl isomerase PIN1 feeding into the same response. The pathway matters because it sets the threshold for p53-dependent tumour suppression, and loss of PIP4K or ING2 function blunts or distorts that output in cancer.

Growth factor receptors signal through PI3K to AKT to promote cell survival, growth and metabolic anabolism, and this pathway describes how the lipid phosphatidylinositol-5-phosphate, the phosphatase PP2A and the immediate-early protein IER3 set the strength and duration of that output. Receptor tyrosine kinases and their ligands — EGFR and its neuregulin and epiregulin family agonists, FGF receptors, insulin receptor, KIT, MET, PDGF receptors, FLT3 — recruit adaptors such as GRB2, GAB1/2, IRS1/2 and PTPN11 to activate class I PI3K, generating PIP3 and phosphorylating AKT. PI5P, made and consumed by PIP4K and PIP5K enzymes, feeds PI(4,5)P2 supply and restrains dephosphorylation of AKT1 by PP2A holoenzymes containing B56 regulatory subunits; ERK1/ERK2 and IER3 contribute inhibitory phosphorylation of PP2A. Because this brake determines how long AKT stays active, its loss biases cells toward the proliferation and survival characteristic of tumours with hyperactive PI3K signalling.

Heterotrimeric G proteins cannot signal unless their beta subunits are folded correctly and paired with a gamma partner, and that folding is not spontaneous. The cytosolic chaperonin TRiC/CCT, an eight-subunit barrel, binds nascent G-protein beta chains, and the phosducin-like protein PDCL (PhLP1) acts as a co-chaperone that completes folding, releases the finished subunit and hands it to a gamma subunit to form the obligate beta:gamma dimer. Without this step, receptor-coupled signalling at the plasma membrane has no functional beta:gamma module for effector regulation or for Galpha-q family recruitment. The beta 5 subunit follows a variant route, folding into dimers with R7-family RGS proteins that regulate signalling in neurons and photoreceptors rather than with gamma. Casein kinase 2 phosphorylation of PDCL tunes its chaperone activity, linking G-protein biogenesis to the assembly quality control that precedes all G-protein-coupled receptor signalling.

Membrane glycerophospholipids are not permanent structures; this catabolic route dismantles them down to glycerophosphodiesters and then cleaves those to glycerol phosphate plus a free head group such as choline. The released choline matters physiologically: in kidney medulla cells it accumulates as an organic osmolyte that buffers the extreme salt and urea concentrations of the concentrating nephron, and elsewhere it feeds phosphatidylcholine resynthesis and acetylcholine supply. Two classes of enzyme do the work. Phospholipase-type esterases, including the neuropathy target esterase PNPLA6 and its relative PNPLA7, strip acyl chains from the glycerol backbone, while glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterases such as GDE1, GDPD1, GDPD3 and GDPD5 hydrolyse the remaining phosphodiester bond. Their tissue distributions and substrate preferences differ, linking the same chemistry to osmotic protection, membrane remodelling, developmental events and, when PNPLA6 fails, axonal degeneration.

Assembly of the ORC complex at the origin of replication is the licensing step that marks where DNA replication will begin, and it determines that each origin fires once and only once per cell cycle. Without it cells cannot load the replicative helicase, and hypomorphic subunit mutations cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome with dwarfism and microcephaly. ORC1 acts first, recognising G-rich, largely nucleosome-free origin DNA near transcription start sites and reading the H4K20me2 mark on flanking nucleosomes; it then nucleates assembly by joining a preformed ORC2-ORC3-ORC5-ORC4 module, remodelling an autoinhibitory ORC2 winged-helix domain that otherwise blocks the central DNA channel, with ORC6 added last and loosely. Importin-mediated nuclear import brings subunits and histones to chromatin. ORC1 is degraded on S-phase entry, coupling origin choice to once-per-cycle control upstream of pre-replication complex formation.

Every round of DNA replication begins by marking where it will start, and the origin recognition complex is what does the marking. Loading ORC onto chromatin licenses origins for later firing, so that each stretch of the genome is copied once and only once; defects in its subunits cause the dwarfism and microcephaly of Meier-Gorlin syndrome, reflecting how tightly growth depends on faithful origin licensing. Assembly is ordered: an ORC2-ORC3 heterodimer recruits ORC5 and ORC4, ORC1 joins to relieve an autoinhibited conformation that otherwise blocks the DNA-binding channel, and ORC6 attaches weakly. ORC1 binds origin DNA on its own, favouring G-rich and guanine-quadruplex-forming sequences near transcription start sites, and reads neighbouring nucleosomes carrying dimethylated histone H4 lysine 20. Importins carry subunits into the nucleus, and ORC1 degradation at S phase entry prevents relicensing.

CDC6 association with the ORC:origin complex is the first committed step in licensing a replication origin: CDC6 loads onto the origin recognition complex bound at chromatin, creating the platform onto which MCM helicases are later deposited to form the pre-replicative complex. Without this step no origin can fire, and cells fail to duplicate their genome; conversely, unrestrained CDC6 loading permits re-licensing within a single cycle, causing re-replication, amplification and genomic instability of the kind seen in tumours. CDC6 acts as an AAA+ ATPase switch, working with the six-subunit ORC ring to sense and clamp origin DNA, with MCM8 among the helicase-family partners recruited. Cell cycle control is enforced on CDC6 itself, through E2F-driven expression in G1 and phosphorylation-triggered nuclear exclusion and ubiquitin-mediated degradation once S phase begins, restricting replication to once per division.

Loading of CDC6 onto origin-bound ORC is the licensing step that makes a replication origin competent to fire, and it is where the cell enforces the rule that each stretch of DNA replicates only once per cycle. The six-subunit origin recognition complex marks origins in chromatin; CDC6, an AAA+ ATPase related to the ORC subunits, joins it in late M and G1 to create the platform that subsequently recruits CDT1 and the MCM2-7 helicase, with ATP binding and hydrolysis acting as the switch that commits helicase loading. CDC6 abundance is set by E2F-driven transcription in G1 and curtailed after S-phase entry through phosphorylation, nuclear exclusion and ubiquitin-mediated degradation, so that reloading cannot occur. Loss of this control permits re-replication and gene amplification, linking origin licensing to genome stability and to proliferative control in cancer.

Assembly of the pre-replicative complex is the licensing step that marks replication origins for a single round of DNA synthesis, and it determines that each chromosome is copied exactly once per cell cycle. Loss of this control produces re-replication, amplification and genome instability, while insufficient licensing blocks S phase entry entirely. From late mitosis through G1, the origin recognition complex binds chromatin and, with CDC6 and CDT1, loads the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer around DNA. Timing is imposed from outside: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator FZR1 and the ubiquitin-proteasome system degrade licensing inhibitors and the components themselves, geminin sequesters CDT1 after firing, and importins deliver factors into the nucleus. Nucleosome components reflect the chromatin context in which origins are selected, linking histone deposition to where replication begins.

Before a cell can replicate its DNA, every origin must be licensed exactly once, and assembly of the pre-replicative complex is that licensing step. It runs from late mitosis through G1, when the origin recognition complex (ORC1-6) marks chromosomal origins and CDC6 with CDT1 loads the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer; only at the G1/S transition is that helicase activated to unwind DNA. Restricting licensing to a window when CDK activity is low is what prevents re-replication, and loss of the restriction produces polyploidy and genome instability; germline ORC and CDT1 defects cause Meier-Gorlin syndrome. The controls are largely degradative and inhibitory: the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator FZR1, ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes and the 26S proteasome clear geminin and mitotic cyclins to open the window, while geminin itself sequesters CDT1 once S phase begins. Importin-mediated nuclear import and chromatin context complete the setting.

Mitotic prophase is the entry step of mitosis, when a cell dismantles its interphase architecture and builds the machinery that will segregate chromosomes. Its outputs are condensed, individualized chromosomes, a disassembled nuclear envelope and nuclear pore complexes, a fragmented Golgi, and duplicated centrosomes separating toward opposite poles to nucleate the spindle; without them, chromatids cannot be captured or pulled apart, and aneuploidy or mitotic failure follows. Cyclin B–CDK1 drives the transition, with PLK1, NEK9–NEK6/7 and the MASTL–ENSA/ARPP19 arm restraining PP2A so mitotic phosphorylations persist. Condensin II subunits including SMC2, SMC4 and NCAPD3 compact chromatin alongside histones and their modifiers, while phosphorylation of lamins, LEM-domain proteins and nucleoporins breaks the envelope open. Golgi tethers and lipins reorganize membranes, coupling organelle inheritance to the onset of division.

Prometaphase is the window of mitosis in which the nuclear envelope breaks down, kinetochores mature on centromeres, and spindle microtubules capture chromosomes and pull them toward the metaphase plate. Getting this right determines whether daughter cells inherit an accurate chromosome complement; errors here produce aneuploidy and chromosomal instability of the kind seen in tumours and in developmental disorders. The machinery assembles in layers: CENP proteins build the inner kinetochore on CENP-A chromatin, the MIS12 and NDC80 complexes form the outer plate that grips dynamic microtubule ends, and tubulin, gamma-tubulin ring components and augmin nucleate and organise the spindle from centrosomes. Aurora B with INCENP and survivin corrects mis-attachments, while MAD1, MAD2, BUB1 and BUBR1 hold the spindle assembly checkpoint to restrain CDC20 until every chromosome is bioriented. Cohesin, condensin and dynein-dynactin contribute chromosome cohesion, compaction and poleward transport.

The switch from metaphase to anaphase is the irreversible commitment step of mitosis: once sister chromatids separate, division must be completed, so the cell delays it until every chromosome is properly attached to the spindle. The transition is driven by ubiquitin-dependent destruction of mitotic cyclins and of securin, releasing the protease that cleaves cohesin and allowing chromatids to move to opposite poles. Control converges on the anaphase-promoting complex, whose activity is restrained by the inhibitor encoded by FBXO5 (Emi1) and relieved as mitosis proceeds, while the kinase PLK1 contributes phosphorylation events that license inhibitor turnover and coordinate centrosome, spindle and cohesin behaviour. Premature or delayed passage through this point produces chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, linking the step to genomic instability in cancer and to the action of antimitotic drugs.

Mitotic anaphase is the step at which sister chromatids are finally pulled apart and delivered to the two nascent daughter cells; getting it wrong produces aneuploid progeny, a hallmark of tumours and of miscarriage-causing chromosome imbalance. The trigger is ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis: once the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied, the anaphase-promoting complex with its activator CDC20 marks securin and mitotic cyclins for destruction by the proteasome, freeing separase to cleave the cohesin subunit RAD21 that holds sisters together. Kinetochore assemblies built on centromeric CENP proteins and the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes couple chromosomes to spindle microtubules, while kinesins, dynein and microtubule regulators generate and shape the movement. Falling CDK1 activity then permits nuclear envelope and nuclear pore reassembly, lamina reformation, and the membrane remodelling that completes division.

The closing act of mitosis, in which two separated chromatid sets are enclosed in reforming nuclear envelopes and the mother cell is physically split in two by an actomyosin ring that constricts at the cell equator. Getting this right is what keeps chromosome number stable; failed abscission or a misplaced division plane yields binucleate, tetraploid cells of the kind that seed aneuploidy in tumours. Two activities dominate here: central spindle assembly and midbody formation, driven by kinesins such as KIF23 and KIF20A under Polo-like kinase 1 control, and the reloading of cohesin onto decondensing chromatin. Cohesin subunits SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and the STAG paralogues, together with the NIPBL-MAU2 loader, the PDS5 proteins and the releasing factor WAPL, re-establish sister chromatid linkage and genome organisation for the daughter cells' next interphase.

M phase is the part of the cell cycle in which a cell divides its duplicated chromosomes and then splits in two, proceeding through prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase before cytokinesis. Getting it right is what keeps chromosome number constant; errors produce aneuploidy, micronuclei and the genomic instability typical of tumours. The genes here cover the machinery that does the work: CDK1-cyclin B and Aurora B/INCENP kinase activity, centrosome and gamma-tubulin ring assembly of the spindle, kinetochore and outer-plate complexes such as NDC80 and MIS12, condensin and cohesin with separase cleaving cohesin at anaphase, and the spindle assembly checkpoint (MAD1/MAD2, BUB1, BUB3) restraining the anaphase-promoting complex and its proteasomal destruction of securin and cyclin B. Also included are nuclear envelope and pore disassembly and reformation, Golgi partitioning, and ESCRT-dependent abscission of the midbody.

G2 phase is the gap between the end of DNA replication and entry into mitosis, the interval in which a cell grows, synthesises protein, and stockpiles the cytoplasmic material that two daughter cells will need. It is also when replication is verified before chromosome segregation is allowed, so its regulation determines whether damaged or incompletely replicated DNA is carried into mitosis. The genes here represent the cyclin-dependent kinase activity that carries cells through this window: A-type cyclins partnering CDK2 after the S-phase transition, with E2F transcription factors driving the periodic expression of replication and cell cycle genes that underlies the switch. Loss of control over this interval, through deregulated E2F activity or cyclin A overexpression, shortens the delay before mitosis and contributes to the genome instability characteristic of tumour cells.

Eukaryotic cells must fire each replication origin exactly once per cycle, and displacing Orc1 from chromatin after origins have fired is one of the safeguards that enforces this. Once S phase begins, cyclin A–CDK2 phosphorylates Orc1, which is released from the origin recognition complex bound at chromatin and targeted for ubiquitination by an SCF-type cullin–RING ligase built on CUL1, RBX1 and SKP1 with the SKP2 substrate receptor, then degraded by the 26S proteasome. Because ORC together with CDC6, CDT1 and the MCM2-7 helicase is required to license origins, removing Orc1 prevents re-formation of pre-replicative complexes on DNA that has already been copied. Loss of this restraint permits re-replication, gene amplification and the chromosomal instability that accompanies tumour development, placing the step within cell cycle control and genome maintenance rather than replication itself.

DNA replication initiation is the step that gets DNA synthesis started, solving the problem that no DNA polymerase can begin a chain from scratch. Every chromosome duplication in every dividing cell depends on it, and defects in these polymerases cause replication stress, genome instability, and developmental syndromes such as microcephalic primordial dwarfism. The primase subunits PRIM1 and PRIM2, held in complex with the POLA1 catalytic subunit and its POLA2 partner, lay down a short RNA primer and extend it with a stretch of DNA, creating a substrate that processive polymerases can take over. DNA polymerase epsilon, with its POLE2, POLE3 and POLE4 accessory subunits, then elongates the leading strand. The same priming activity is reused repeatedly on the lagging strand, linking initiation to Okazaki fragment synthesis and to S-phase progression.

Every new DNA strand has to be started, and DNA polymerases cannot begin one on bare template. Initiation of DNA replication solves this by laying down a short RNA primer that can then be extended, a step required at each origin and at the start of every Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand. The polymerase alpha-primase complex does both jobs: the primase subunits synthesize a few nucleotides of RNA, and the associated catalytic and accessory polymerase alpha subunits extend it with a short stretch of DNA before handover to a processive replicase. The polymerase epsilon subunits here carry out leading-strand synthesis once initiation has occurred. Because priming licenses S-phase DNA synthesis, defects in these subunits impair replication fidelity and proliferation, and mutations in them are linked to hypermutated tumours and developmental growth disorders.

Licensed replication origins sit dormant until the G1/S transition, when activation of the pre-replicative complex converts them into working replication forks and commits the cell to duplicating its genome exactly once. The origin recognition complex, ORC1-ORC6, marks origins and, with CDC6 and CDT1, loads the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer; geminin blocks further CDT1 activity so that loading cannot recur after firing, which is how re-replication and the resulting amplification and genome instability are prevented. Firing requires two kinases, CDK2 with its cyclin partner and the CDC7-DBF4 pair, which together license recruitment of CDC45 and MCM10, unwinding of duplex DNA, coating of the exposed single strands by replication protein A, and priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase before polymerase epsilon begins processive synthesis. ORC's ATPase cycle is thought to act as the switch coupling origin melting to initiation.

Before a cell can copy its genome it must first mark where copying will start and license each origin exactly once, and that preparation happens in G1, well ahead of S phase. The origin recognition complex binds chromatin, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase as an inactive double hexamer, and CDC7-DBF4 together with CDK2 then convert this licensed state into an active replisome with CDC45, MCM10, the single-strand binding RPA complex, and polymerases alpha/primase and epsilon. Licensing is restricted to one round per cycle: geminin sequesters CDT1, and the anaphase-promoting complex with its ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes and the proteasome destroys licensing factors and mitotic regulators. Histones are supplied for packaging the new strands. Loss of this control produces re-replication, origin firing defects and genome instability, and underlies developmental disorders of replication licensing.

Origins of replication must fire once and only once per cell cycle, and the controlled inactivation of Cdc6 after S phase entry is one of the switches that enforces this. Cdc6 is a loading factor for the MCM helicase at licensed origins; once cyclin E- or cyclin A-bound CDK2 phosphorylates it, Cdc6 is exported from the nucleus and, in its APC/C-recognised form, ubiquitylated and destroyed by the 26S proteasome. The gene complement reflects that two-step logic: the cyclin-CDK kinases, the full anaphase-promoting complex with its Cdh1/FZR1 substrate-recognition subunit, ubiquitin and E2 conjugating enzymes, and the proteasomal core and regulatory particles. Preventing Cdc6 from reloading helicases onto already-replicated DNA blocks re-replication, and loss of this restraint produces gene amplification, unscheduled endoreduplication and the genome instability characteristic of tumour cells.

Once an origin of replication has fired, it must be marked as used so that no stretch of chromosome is copied twice in a single cell cycle. Switching origins to a post-replicative state is how that restriction is imposed: the licensing factors that permitted initiation are inactivated, displaced from chromatin, or destroyed, leaving the origin incompetent until the next G1. Cyclin-dependent kinase activity with cyclin E or A phosphorylates Cdc6 and ORC1, targeting them for ubiquitin-dependent degradation by the proteasome through SCF-type and anaphase-promoting complex ubiquitin ligases, while geminin sequesters CDT1 and the MCM2-7 helicase is redistributed away from the origin. Loss of this control permits re-replication, giving rise to gene amplification and the genome instability characteristic of tumour cells, so the pathway is best understood as the enforcement arm of once-per-cycle DNA replication.

DNA replication begins with a short, error-prone primer and must hand off to a processive enzyme before large amounts of genome can be copied, and polymerase switching is that hand-off. Pol alpha-primase lays down an RNA-DNA initiator but cannot extend it far, so the clamp loader RFC recognises the primer-template junction, displaces the priming complex, and loads the PCNA ring around the duplex. PCNA then acts as a sliding clamp that tethers DNA polymerase delta for rapid, high-fidelity elongation, and RFC leaves once loading is complete. This exchange sets the accuracy and speed of chromosomal replication and recurs at every Okazaki fragment on the lagging strand; the same clamp platform recruits repair and ligation factors, linking replication to mismatch repair and lesion bypass.

At a replication fork, one of the two new DNA strands can be copied continuously in the same direction the fork moves, and leading strand synthesis is that continuous copying. It supplies the bulk of newly duplicated genome during S phase, and its fidelity determines the mutation rate a dividing cell passes to its descendants. Synthesis begins with the polymerase alpha-primase complex, which lays an RNA primer extended by a short stretch of DNA; the clamp loader, an ATP-dependent five-subunit complex, then opens the sliding clamp PCNA and deposits it on the primed template. PCNA tethers DNA polymerase delta so that it extends many kilobases without dissociating, and the polymerase's own 3'-to-5' exonuclease excises misinserted nucleotides. Loss of proofreading or clamp loading raises replication errors and genome instability, a route to tumour-associated hypermutation.

Removal of the Flap Intermediate is the step in lagging-strand DNA replication that gets rid of the RNA-DNA initiator segment left by primase, so that adjacent Okazaki fragments can be joined into a continuous daughter strand. Without it, replication leaves nicks and unligated flaps that become double-strand breaks, and cells accumulate the genome instability and repeat-expansion mutations associated with loss of flap endonuclease activity. Strand-displacement synthesis by DNA polymerase delta, held on the template by the PCNA clamp, peels the primer made by DNA polymerase alpha-primase into a single-stranded flap. Short flaps are clipped directly by FEN1; longer ones become coated by replication protein A, which blocks FEN1 and instead recruits the DNA2 nuclease/helicase to trim the flap to a size FEN1 can finish. The nicked product is then sealed by ligase, completing Okazaki fragment maturation.

During lagging-strand replication, each Okazaki fragment begins as an RNA-DNA primer laid down by pol alpha-primase, and that primer must be displaced and cut away before the fragments can be joined into continuous DNA. Removal of the flap intermediate is that cutting step: strand-displacement synthesis by DNA polymerase delta on a PCNA-loaded primer-template generates a single-stranded 5' flap, which is trimmed by flap endonuclease 1 when short, or shortened first by the DNA2 nuclease/helicase when the flap grows long enough to be coated by replication protein A. RPA binding is what dictates the handoff between the two nucleases. Efficient flap processing keeps replication from leaving unligatable nicks and single-stranded gaps, so defects here feed genome instability, repeat expansion and replication-associated DNA damage; the same nucleases also serve long-patch base excision repair.

Replication of the lagging strand cannot run continuously, so it is built from short Okazaki fragments that must each be primed, extended, trimmed and sealed. Processive synthesis on the lagging strand is what turns those fragments into an intact daughter strand, and errors in the process leave nicks, flaps and unligated gaps that become double-strand breaks and genome instability. Primase together with DNA polymerase alpha lays down an RNA-DNA primer, which is then exchanged for polymerase delta held on the DNA by the sliding clamp PCNA. As the polymerase advances it displaces the primer as a single-stranded flap; short flaps are cut by the FEN1 endonuclease, longer RPA-coated flaps are processed with DNA2, and LIG1 joins the resulting nick to the preceding fragment. The pathway sits at the heart of S-phase chromosome duplication.

Because DNA polymerases only extend in one direction, the strand running against the movement of the replication fork must be copied in pieces, and lagging strand synthesis is how those pieces are made and stitched together. It determines whether a replicated chromosome ends up as continuous, primer-free duplex DNA; failures leave nicks, unligated flaps and single-stranded gaps that drive genome instability and mutation. Pol alpha with its primase subunits lays down an RNA-DNA primer, the clamp loader complex deposits PCNA, and polymerase delta takes over for processive extension of each Okazaki fragment while replication protein A coats displaced single strands. Strand-displacement synthesis generates a 5' flap that is trimmed by FEN1, with DNA2 processing longer flaps, and DNA ligase I seals the remaining nick. This is the core of chromosomal DNA replication in S phase.

DNA strand elongation is the synthetic phase of genome duplication: the moving replication fork where template strands are unwound and copied, producing the two daughter genomes that mitosis will separate. Its fidelity determines whether cells inherit an intact genome, and stalling or collapse here is a principal source of the replication stress and chromosomal instability that drive cancer. Because polymerases work in one direction only on an antiparallel duplex, one strand is copied continuously and the other in short pieces. The MCM helicase with CDC45 and the GINS complex opens the duplex, RPA coats the exposed single strands, and primase-polymerase alpha lays down primers that RFC-loaded PCNA hands to polymerase delta for processive extension. Okazaki fragments are then matured by flap removal through FEN1 and DNA2 and sealed by ligase I.

Once a replication fork is established, the genome is copied by DNA strand elongation, the synthesis phase that must duplicate every base accurately and at speed before mitosis. Because the duplex is antiparallel and polymerases work in one direction only, the leading strand is extended continuously while the lagging strand is built as short fragments that are later joined. The machinery here covers each step: the MCM helicase with CDC45 and the GINS subunits unwinds the parental duplex, single-stranded DNA is protected by the RPA heterotrimer, primase lays RNA primers extended by polymerase alpha, and clamp loader RFC installs PCNA to make polymerase delta processive. Flap endonuclease FEN1 with the DNA2 nuclease/helicase trims displaced primer flaps and LIG1 seals the nicks. Errors or stalling here generate fork collapse, replication stress and the genome instability underlying cancer predisposition.

Cells commit to replicating their DNA at the G1/S boundary, and the phosphorylation of G1/S regulators by active Cyclin E:Cdk2 complexes is what makes that commitment irreversible. Cyclin E, induced as cells approach S phase, binds and activates Cdk2, which then hyperphosphorylates the retinoblastoma protein, completing the inactivation begun by Cyclin D:Cdk4/6 and freeing E2F transcription factors to drive expression of replication genes. The same kinase phosphorylates Cdk inhibitors of the p21/p27 family, marking them for ubiquitin-dependent destruction and removing the brake on its own activity, so the transition behaves as a self-reinforcing switch. Because this step converts graded growth signals into an all-or-none decision to replicate, its deregulation through cyclin E amplification or loss of retinoblastoma protein function is a common route to uncontrolled proliferation in cancer.

Cells commit irreversibly to DNA replication at the G1/S boundary, and the cyclin E-associated events of that transition are what set the timing. Cyclin E partners with CDK2, whose activity is held back by inhibitory phosphorylation from WEE1 and by the CIP/KIP inhibitors p21 and p27, and released when CDC25A removes the phosphate and CDK7-containing activating kinase completes maturation. Active cyclin E:CDK2 phosphorylates RB1 and related pocket proteins, dismantling repressive DREAM/E2F complexes and freeing E2F-DP transcription factors to drive replication genes. Ordered destruction is equally part of the mechanism: SKP1-CUL1-SKP2 ubiquitin ligase activity and the 26S proteasome degrade p27 and limit cyclin E accumulation. When that restraint fails, cells enter S phase prematurely with under-licensed origins, producing replication stress, genomic instability and a route to tumour formation.

Commitment to DNA replication is decided in late G1, when E2F transcription factors switch on the genes a cell needs to copy its genome. G1/S-specific transcription is what makes that switch: E2F1 with its DP partners activates origin licensing factors such as ORC1, CDC6, CDT1 and CDC45, the replisome components PCNA and the DNA polymerase alpha catalytic subunit, nucleotide-supply enzymes including RRM2, TYMS, DHFR and thymidine kinase, and the cyclins and CDC25A that drive the transition forward. Restraint comes from retinoblastoma-family proteins RBL1 and RBL2, repressive E2Fs, and the DREAM complex with its LIN components, histone deacetylase and RBBP4, which silence these promoters in quiescence. Loss of this restraint gives unscheduled proliferation and is a common route into cancer.

The G1/S transition is the commitment step of the cell cycle, the point at which a cell stops responding to growth signals and begins to copy its genome. Cyclin E-CDK2 and cyclin A-CDK2 drive the switch, inhibited by the CDK inhibitors p21 and p27 and by Wee1-mediated phosphorylation that CDC25A reverses. Upstream, cyclin D-CDK4 and CDK7-containing activating kinase relieve repression of E2F-DP transcription factors by RB and the related pocket proteins within the DREAM/LIN complex, switching on genes for replication licensing (ORC, CDC6, CDT1, the MCM helicase), polymerases and primase, and nucleotide supply enzymes such as thymidylate synthase, TK1 and ribonucleotide reductase. Timely destruction of cyclin E, p27 and the licensing inhibitor geminin requires SCF-type ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome. Loss of this control, through RB inactivation or cyclin/MYC overexpression, underlies unchecked proliferation in cancer.

The decision to commit to DNA replication is made in G1, and cyclin D-associated events are how growth signals are converted into that commitment. D-type cyclins partner with CDK4 and CDK6, whose activity is set by CDK-activating kinase phosphorylation (CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1), by assembly factors p21 and p27, and by INK4 inhibitors such as p16 that block CDK4/6 outright. The active kinases phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein and its relatives p107 and p130, dislodging repressive E2F4/E2F5 complexes and freeing activating E2F1-3 with their DP partners to transcribe replication genes, including cyclin E. Sequestration of p27 and its SKP2-dependent ubiquitin-mediated degradation then license cyclin E-CDK2 and the G1/S transition. Loss of this restraint, through cyclin D amplification or p16 and RB1 inactivation, is among the commonest routes to unchecked proliferation in cancer.

G1 Phase is the interval in which a cell decides whether to divide, and the point at which growth signals are converted into an irreversible commitment to replicate DNA. Its failure is the most common route into cancer: loss of the retinoblastoma protein or of the INK4 inhibitors, or amplification of D-type cyclins, removes the restriction point altogether. Mechanistically, cyclin D partners with CDK4 and CDK6 to begin phosphorylating Rb and its relatives p107 and p130, releasing E2F-DP heterodimers to transactivate the genes needed for S phase, including cyclin E. Cyclin E-CDK2 then completes Rb inactivation in a feedback loop. The pathway is tuned by CIP/KIP proteins p21, p27 and p57, by CDK-activating kinase and PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation, and by SKP1-CUL1-SKP2 ubiquitin ligase activity that degrades inhibitors once the decision is made.

G1 phase is the interval in which a cell decides whether to commit to another division, and this decision point is where growth signals, nutrient status and damage checks are integrated before DNA replication becomes irreversible. D-type cyclins partnered with CDK4 and CDK6, and later cyclin E with CDK2, progressively phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein and its relatives p107 and p130, releasing E2F-DP transcription factor complexes to switch on the genes needed for S phase entry. Opposing this are the INK4 family inhibitors and the Cip/Kip proteins p21, p27 and p57, whose degradation through SKP1-CUL1-SKP2 ubiquitin ligase activity, together with CDK-activating kinase and phosphatase input, sets the timing of the transition. Loss of this restraint, by p16 deletion, cyclin D amplification or RB1 mutation, is among the most common events in human cancer.

Synthesis of DNA is the duplication of the genome during S phase, the step that gives each daughter cell a complete and accurate copy of its chromosomes. Its control determines whether cells proliferate on schedule or accumulate the re-replication and replication stress that drive genome instability and cancer. Origins licensed in late M and G1 by the origin recognition complex, CDC6 and CDT1 are loaded with MCM2-7 helicase, which CDC45 and the GINS proteins activate; primase and DNA polymerase alpha lay down primers, and polymerases delta and epsilon extend them with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, while RPA coats single strands and FEN1 with DNA ligase I finish Okazaki fragment maturation. Cyclin E- and A-CDK2 activity, geminin, and ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex restrict firing to one round per cycle.

Duplication of the genome in S phase is what this pathway accomplishes: origins licensed in late mitosis and G1 are fired once, and once only, to copy every chromosome before division. Origin recognition complex proteins load CDC6 and CDT1, which deposit the MCM2-7 helicase; CDK2 paired with cyclin E and then cyclin A, together with CDC45 and the GINS tetramer, converts these into active replisomes.
