Primase and DNA polymerase alpha lay down primers, RFC loads the PCNA clamp for processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon, and FEN1 with LIG1 matures Okazaki fragments while RPA coats exposed single strands. Re-replication is prevented by geminin and by ubiquitin-proteasome destruction of licensing factors through SCF-SKP2 and the anaphase-promoting complex. Loss of this control produces endoreduplication, replication stress and the genome instability that underlies tumour development.

S phase is the interval in which a cell copies its genome, producing two sister chromatids from every chromosome and committing itself to division. Origins licensed in G1 by the origin recognition complex, CDC6 and CDT1 are fired once cyclin E- and cyclin A-CDK2 activity rises, converting loaded MCM2-7 hexamers into active CMG helicases with the GINS proteins and CDC45; RPA coats unwound DNA while polymerases alpha, delta and epsilon, primase, PCNA, the clamp loader, FEN1 and ligase I synthesise and join nascent strands. Cohesin rings with SMC1A, SMC3, RAD21 and the ESCO acetyltransferases hold the new copies together for later segregation. Timing is enforced by E2F-RB transcription, the DREAM complex, CDK inhibitors p21 and p27, WEE1, CDC25 phosphatases, and ubiquitin-proteasome destruction of cyclin E, geminin and licensing factors, which prevents re-replication. Loss of this control produces replication stress, genome instability and cancer.

The switch that commits a cell from completed DNA replication into mitosis is driven by CDK1 partnered with A- and B-type cyclins. This transition sets the timing of nuclear envelope breakdown, mitotic spindle assembly and Golgi disassembly, and its misregulation permits entry into mitosis with unreplicated or damaged DNA, a route to chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy. Activity is held back by the inhibitory kinases WEE1 and PKMYT1, which phosphorylate CDK1, and released by the CDC25 phosphatases, while the CDK7–cyclin H–MNAT1 activating kinase supplies the stimulatory phosphorylation. PLK1, with its cofactor BORA and upstream Aurora input, reinforces the switch, and PP2A holoenzymes with their regulatory and methylation-control subunits oppose it. Cyclin A:CDK1 acts largely in the nucleus while cyclin B complexes act in cytoplasm and at Golgi membranes, so localisation helps dictate substrate choice; FOXM1 sustains the transcription of mitotic genes.

The G2/M transition is the commitment step that converts a cell that has finished replicating its DNA into a cell in mitosis, and it sets the timing of centrosome maturation, spindle assembly, nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome condensation. The switch is CDK1 paired with A- and B-type cyclins, held inactive by inhibitory phosphorylation from WEE1 and PKMYT1 and released by the CDC25 phosphatases, with AURKA, BORA and PLK1 providing the feed-forward activation and PP2A and PP1 subunits opposing it. Much of the downstream output is structural: gamma-tubulin ring components and their MZT partners, centriole and pericentriolar proteins such as PLK4, CEP192 and PCNT, the augmin complex, TPX2, CKAP5 and dynein/dynactin nucleate and organise the microtubule array, while SCF-type ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome remove regulators on schedule. The DREAM/FOXM1 and p53-p21 arms tune entry, and their loss underlies checkpoint override and genomic instability in cancer.

Cell Cycle, Mitotic is the complete program by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, the basis of tissue growth, renewal and development; its deregulation is the defining feature of cancer and its errors generate aneuploidy. Progression is timed by cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins, restrained by CDK inhibitors and the RB-E2F and DREAM transcriptional switches that decide whether a quiescent cell re-enters division. Downstream steps are represented in depth: licensing of origins by ORC, CDC6 and CDT1, MCM helicase loading and replisome-driven synthesis in S phase, WEE1/CDC25 control of CDK1 at G2/M, centrosome maturation and gamma-tubulin-nucleated spindle assembly, kinetochore and cohesin function under spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope breakdown and reformation, and APC/C-driven ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of securin and cyclin B that triggers anaphase and cytokinesis.

The mitotic cell cycle is the ordered programme by which a cell duplicates its genome and partitions it equally into two daughters, passing through G1, S, G2 and M with quiescence as an alternative exit. Its fidelity determines tissue growth and renewal, and its deregulation through cyclin, CDK inhibitor and retinoblastoma-pathway lesions is a hallmark of cancer. Cyclin-dependent kinases paired with D, E, A and B cyclins drive the transitions, restrained by CDK inhibitors, WEE1 and phosphatases and reset by ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis through SCF and the anaphase-promoting complex with the proteasome. Origin licensing on ORC and MCM proteins commits cells to replication; centrosome maturation, gamma-tubulin nucleation, kinetochore assembly, cohesin and condensin, spindle checkpoint surveillance, nuclear envelope and Golgi breakdown, and ESCRT-dependent abscission complete division.</description>}

DNA Replication is the duplication of the genome that must happen once, and only once, before every cell division; its fidelity and its licensing controls are what keep cells from accumulating mutations or amplifying chromosome segments. Origin recognition complex subunits, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase onto origins, and CDK2- and CDC7/DBF4-dependent phosphorylation converts these licensed origins into active replisomes containing CDC45 and GINS. Elongation then requires RPA on single-stranded DNA, primase and polymerase alpha for priming, polymerases delta and epsilon with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC, and FEN1, DNA2 and ligase I for maturation of nascent strands. Re-replication is prevented by geminin and by ubiquitin-proteasome and APC/C-mediated destruction of licensing factors, tying replication directly to cell cycle progression; mitochondrial polymerase gamma and its accessory factors duplicate mtDNA in parallel.

Duplicating the genome once, and only once, per cell cycle is the task of DNA replication, and the fidelity of this process determines whether daughter cells inherit an intact genome or accumulate the mutations and rearrangements that drive cancer. Origin recognition complex subunits mark start sites, CDC6 and CDT1 load the MCM2-7 helicase, and CDC7-DBF4 together with CDK2-cyclin E/A activate it; GINS and CDC45 convert it into the active replisome. Priming by DNA polymerase alpha-primase gives way to processive synthesis by polymerases delta and epsilon on RPA-coated template, with PCNA and the clamp loader RFC coordinating elongation and FEN1, DNA2 and LIG1 finishing lagging-strand joins. Licensing is restricted to one round by geminin inhibition of CDT1 and by ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis through SCF and anaphase-promoting complex activity, while histones supply chromatin for the new strands. Mitochondrial polymerase gamma and TWNK extend the same logic to mitochondrial DNA.

Death receptor signalling only becomes lethal once procaspase-8 molecules are brought together, and this dimerization step is the switch that converts ligand binding into an active protease. When Fas ligand or TRAIL engages Fas or the TRAIL receptors, adaptors such as FADD, with TRADD, RIPK1 and TRAF2 contributing at the TNF-family receptor level, recruit procaspase-8 through death effector domain interactions into the death-inducing signalling complex. Local concentration drives pairing of two zymogen monomers, repositioning the inter-subunit linker so that each molecule cleaves its partner and generates a mature initiator caspase that then cleaves executioner caspases. The cellular FLIP protein CFLAR heterodimerizes with procaspase-8 and limits full processing, setting the threshold between apoptosis, survival and suppression of RIPK1-driven necroptosis. Failure here underlies immune cells that cannot be deleted, lymphoproliferative disease, and tumour resistance to death ligand therapy.

Cells that enter mitosis with broken chromosomes tear them apart, so damage detected in G2 must delay division until repair is done. This checkpoint enforces that delay by keeping the mitotic kinase CDK1, in complex with cyclin B, inactive through inhibitory phosphorylation on threonine 14 and tyrosine 15. Double-strand breaks recruit the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and activate ATM, while resected single-stranded DNA coated by RPA recruits ATR with ATRIP and the RAD9-RAD1-HUS1 clamp loaded by RAD17. Histone H2AX phosphorylation, MDC1 binding and RNF8/RNF168 ubiquitination build the repair focus that holds BRCA1 and TP53BP1. The effector kinases CHEK1 and CHEK2 then inactivate the CDC25C phosphatase, which 14-3-3 proteins sequester, and p53 reinforces arrest transcriptionally. Loss of this restraint produces mitotic catastrophe and the chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours.

Mitosis must not begin while DNA replication is still under way, and this G2/M replication checkpoint is what enforces that order. When forks stall or replication is incomplete, the signal converges on the mitotic kinase CDK1 and keeps it off: the kinases WEE1 and PKMYT1 phosphorylate CDK1 on Thr14 and Tyr15, so the cyclin B-CDK1 complex accumulates but stays catalytically silent and cannot phosphorylate the substrates that drive nuclear envelope breakdown, chromosome condensation and spindle assembly. A-type cyclins partner CDK1 through late S and G2 and feed into the same timing decision. Losing this restraint lets cells divide with unreplicated chromosomes, producing segregation errors and altered ploidy, the kind of genome instability that underlies tumour progression and makes WEE1 inhibition an approach to killing checkpoint-dependent cancer cells.

Before a cell commits to mitosis it must confirm that its DNA is intact and that replication finished exactly once, and the G2/M checkpoints enforce that decision. Loss of this surveillance lets cells divide with broken or partly copied chromosomes, producing the genome instability that underlies cancer predisposition and the sensitivity of tumours to DNA-damaging therapy. Damage is sensed by the ATM and ATR kinases with their partners, amplified through histone H2AX phosphorylation, ubiquitin-dependent recruitment of mediators such as MDC1, BRCA1 and 53BP1, and end resection that generates RPA-coated single-stranded DNA. The signal converges on CHEK1 and CHEK2, which inactivate CDC25 phosphatases and promote their degradation by the proteasome, so that WEE1 and PKMYT1 inhibitory phosphorylation keeps CDK1-cyclin B inactive. Licensing factors including ORC subunits, CDC6 and the MCM helicase restrict origin firing to one round per cycle; severe damage instead engages p53.

In unstressed cells the tumour suppressor p53 is kept scarce, continuously ubiquitinated by MDM2 (with MDM4 and COP1 as further negative regulators) and destroyed by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here along with ubiquitin itself. DNA damage reverses this: ATM, activated by double-strand breaks, phosphorylates p53 on Ser-15 and, through CHEK2, on Ser-20, while also modifying MDM2, so that the p53-MDM2 interaction is disrupted and p53 escapes turnover. ARF, encoded at the CDKN2A locus, sequesters MDM2 in response to oncogenic signalling, and PHF20 binding contributes to accumulation. The resulting rise in p53 levels licenses transcription of cell cycle arrest, repair and apoptotic targets. Loss of this stabilization step, common in cancers with amplified MDM2 or silenced ARF, leaves cells with wild-type p53 that never accumulates.

After DNA damage, p53 halts the cell cycle before a damaged genome can be replicated, and the transcriptional activation of p53 responsive genes is how that decision is carried out. The key output here is p21, whose induction by p53 binds and inactivates the G1/S cyclin-CDK complexes, leaving Rb unphosphorylated, E2F sequestered, and cells arrested at the G1/S transition; cells lacking p21 fail to arrest after damage. Accessory RNA- and protein-binding partners such as PCBP4 and ZNF385A modulate p53 target selection and p21 message stability, tuning whether the response is arrest or apoptosis. This transcriptional arm of the DNA damage response is the main tumour-suppressive function of p53, and its loss permits proliferation with unrepaired lesions, a route to genomic instability and cancer.

Cells that have sustained DNA double-strand breaks must not copy a damaged genome, and the p53-dependent G1 DNA damage response is the brake that stops them before S phase. Its loss is among the most common events in human cancer, allowing mutations to be fixed and propagated. Normally p53 is kept scarce by MDM2, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags it for proteasomal destruction; the many proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes here represent that constitutive turnover. After damage, ATM and the downstream kinase CHEK2 phosphorylate both p53 and MDM2, breaking the interaction and stabilising p53 so it can act as a transcription factor. Induction of the CDK inhibitor p21 then blocks cyclin E- and cyclin A-CDK2 complexes, holding the cell in G1 for repair. If damage is irreparable, the same p53 activation drives apoptosis instead.

When DNA is damaged before replication begins, cells hold themselves at the boundary between G1 and S phase until the lesions are repaired, and p53 is the switch that imposes that delay. Loss of this checkpoint lets damaged templates be copied, and the resulting mutations and chromosomal instability underlie much of human cancer; TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in tumours for exactly this reason. Damage sensed by ATM and its effector kinase CHEK2 leads to phosphorylation of p53, which blocks its MDM2- and MDM4-directed ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction, so p53 accumulates and transactivates CDKN1A. The resulting p21 protein inhibits cyclin E- and cyclin A-CDK2 complexes, preventing the phosphorylation events that would otherwise commit the cell to S phase. Ubiquitin and the 26S proteasome appear throughout as the machinery that sets p53 levels.

Ubiquitin-Mediated Degradation of Phosphorylated Cdc25A removes the phosphatase that switches on CDK2, and so enforces the G1/S checkpoint after DNA damage or replication stress. CDC25A normally strips inhibitory phosphates from CDK2 to license S-phase entry; destroying it keeps CDK2 phosphorylated on Tyr15 and halts the cell cycle until damage is resolved. Failure of this route allows replication to proceed on a damaged template, and CDC25A stabilisation is oncogenic. Mechanistically, checkpoint kinases CHEK1 and CHEK2, together with GSK3B, PLK3 and stress-activated p38 kinases, prime CDC25A; NEK11 or casein kinase I then completes a phosphodegron recognised by the SCF complex through the F-box proteins BTRC or FBXW11, with CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1 building the ligase. Polyubiquitinated CDC25A is then destroyed by the 26S proteasome, linking damage sensing to proteolytic control of cell cycle progression.

CDC25A is the phosphatase that removes inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation from CDK2 to let cells enter S phase, and destroying it is how the DNA damage checkpoint imposes a G1/S arrest. When replication stress, ionizing radiation or UV activates CHEK1 and CHEK2, they phosphorylate CDC25A; priming phosphorylation by GSK3B, PLK3 or p38 kinases is followed by casein kinase I and NEK11 to complete a phosphodegron recognised by the beta-TrCP subunit of an SCF cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1. Polyubiquitinated CDC25A is then dismantled by the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory subunits make up most of this route. Loss of this control lets cells replicate damaged DNA; CDC25A stabilisation or overexpression bypasses the arrest and is associated with genomic instability and tumour progression. The same degradation also operates in unstressed cycling and differentiating cells.

Cells that suffer DNA damage in G1 must stop before replicating a damaged template, and the fastest route to that arrest does not wait for p53-driven transcription. Within minutes of ultraviolet or ionizing radiation, the activating phosphatase CDC25A is phosphorylated and then destroyed by the ubiquitin-proteasome system, so CDK2 bound to cyclin E or A stays in its inhibitory tyrosine-phosphorylated state and S phase entry is blocked. CHEK1 drives this response after UV and CHEK2 after ionizing radiation, with contributions from casein kinase 1, GSK3B, p38 kinases, PLK3 and NEK11; an SCF complex built on CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and BTRC/FBXW11 transfers ubiquitin and the 26S proteasome degrades the target. The arrest is reversible, buying time for repair, and precedes the slower p21-dependent block. CDC25A overexpression bypasses it and is seen in aggressive tumours.

A cell that enters S phase with damaged DNA copies the damage, so the G1/S DNA damage checkpoint halts progression before replication starts and buys time for repair or, if damage is irreparable, commits the cell to arrest or death. Loss of this control is a route to mutation accumulation and cancer, and several of its components are among the most frequently altered genes in tumours. Damage sensed by ATM and the CHEK1/CHEK2 kinases feeds into two arms: stabilisation of TP53, normally kept low by MDM2-directed ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, which transcriptionally induces the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A; and p53-independent inhibition of CDK2-cyclin E/A through phosphorylation and SCF-mediated destruction of the activating phosphatase CDC25A. The ubiquitin-proteasome machinery listed here supplies the degradative steps that set the timing and reversibility of the arrest.

Chromosome segregation is stochastic at the level of individual kinetochore-microtubule attachments, and the mitotic spindle checkpoint is what keeps a cell from dividing before every chromosome is properly attached, preventing aneuploidy. An unattached kinetochore generates a diffusible inhibitory signal built around MAD1, MAD2, BUB1, BUBR1 and BUB3, which sequesters CDC20 and blocks the anaphase-promoting complex from ubiquitinating securin and cyclin B, so sister chromatids stay together and mitotic exit is delayed. The genes here cover the platforms on which this happens: the constitutive centromere-associated network, the MIS12 and NDC80 complexes that bind microtubules, the RZZ complex and dynein that strip checkpoint proteins once attachment forms, Aurora B and the chromosomal passenger complex that correct erroneous attachments, and phosphatase and kinesin activities that tune tension. Chronic failure produces chromosomal instability characteristic of tumours.

Cell cycle checkpoints are the surveillance systems that hold division in check until the previous step has been completed correctly, and they are the reason somatic cells maintain a stable genome while tumour cells generally do not. Damage sensors and the apical kinases ATM and ATR, with CHEK1 and CHEK2 downstream, delay CDK activation at the G1/S and G2/M transitions, acting through TP53 and CDKN1A, through degradation of CDC25A phosphatases, and through inhibitory phosphorylation by WEE1 and PKMYT1, with 14-3-3 proteins sequestering mitotic regulators. At mitosis, unattached kinetochores built on the centromere and NDC80/MIS12 networks generate a MAD2/BUB-dependent signal that restrains CDC20 and the anaphase-promoting complex until every chromosome is bioriented. Ubiquitin ligases and the proteasome execute the resulting decisions. Loss of these controls produces aneuploidy, replication stress and the mutational tolerance that underlies cancer predisposition.

Committing to DNA replication is an irreversible step, and the events surrounding cyclin A:Cdk2 activity at S phase entry are what make it so. Cyclin A accumulates late in G1 and binds Cdk2, and the resulting kinase phosphorylates Rb, the APC/C activator Cdh1, and the inhibitors p21 and p27, dismantling the restraints that hold cells in G1 and allowing E2F-dependent transcription of replication genes. Activation requires the CDK-activating kinase (Cdk7 with cyclin H and MAT1) and removal of inhibitory tyrosine phosphate by Cdc25 phosphatases, opposing Wee1. Degradation of p27 and p21 by the SCF complex with the Skp2 substrate receptor, acting through the proteasome, completes the switch. Loss of this control underlies unscheduled proliferation in cancer, where cyclin E, Myc and Skp2 overexpression or Rb loss uncouple S phase entry from growth signals.

Cells that have sustained DNA damage must stop dividing long enough to repair it, and transcriptional activation of the cell cycle inhibitor p21 is how that halt is imposed. p21, encoded by CDKN1A, binds and inhibits cyclin-dependent kinase complexes so that the retinoblastoma protein stays unphosphorylated and cells arrest before S phase or in G2; the same protein contributes to senescence and to differentiation-associated withdrawal from the cycle. Induction occurs both with and without p53, but the best-characterised route is direct binding of p53 to elements in the CDKN1A promoter after genotoxic stress. RNA-binding and p53 cofactor proteins such as PCBP4 and ZNF385A shape how strongly and for how long the message accumulates, biasing the outcome toward arrest rather than apoptosis. Loss of this arm of the damage response permits replication of a damaged genome and underlies tumour progression.

Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without any need for oxygen. It is the universal core of energy metabolism: red blood cells and other cells lacking mitochondria depend on it entirely, proliferating and tumour cells lean on it for biosynthetic carbon, and inherited defects in pyruvate kinase or phosphofructokinase cause haemolytic anaemia and exercise intolerance. Hexokinases and glucokinase trap glucose, phosphofructokinase-1 commits it in the pathway's irreversible flux-setting step, and aldolase, GAPDH, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the split and payoff phases. Control is layered on top: PFKFB bifunctional kinases set fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, glucokinase regulatory protein sequesters GCK in the hepatocyte nucleus, and PKA and protein phosphatase 2A tune enzyme activity to hormonal state. Downstream, pyruvate feeds mitochondrial oxidation or lactate production.

Glycolysis is the cytosolic route that breaks glucose 6-phosphate down to pyruvate, yielding ATP and NADH without oxygen and feeding carbon to mitochondrial oxidation, lactate production, or biosynthesis. It is the sole ATP source for erythrocytes and a dominant one in proliferating and tumour cells; inherited defects in pyruvate kinase, phosphofructokinase or triosephosphate isomerase cause haemolytic anaemia and exercise intolerance. Hexokinases and glucokinase commit glucose, phosphofructokinase-1 catalyses the irreversible control step, and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, phosphoglycerate kinase, enolase and pyruvate kinase complete the payoff phase, with several steps represented by tissue-specific isoforms. Flux is set by allosteric and hormonal control: the bifunctional PFKFB kinase/phosphatases govern fructose 2,6-bisphosphate levels, while PKA phosphorylation and protein phosphatase 2A subunits tune the enzymes, and glucokinase regulatory protein sequesters glucokinase. Nucleoporins and nuclear transport components appear alongside, reflecting regulated shuttling of these factors.

Glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) mobilises stored glucose, supplying muscle with fuel during contraction and liver with glucose for export to maintain blood sugar between meals. The chemistry is identical in all tissues but the isozymes differ, so liver and muscle glycogen serve different physiological ends: PYGL output feeds glucose release into the circulation, while PYGM output stays in the myocyte as glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis. Phosphorylase clips glucose 1-phosphate from branch ends and is switched on by phosphorylase kinase, a calmodulin-containing complex of PHKA/PHKB/PHKG subunits that links hormonal and calcium signals to fuel release; debranching enzyme handles the residual four-residue stubs, and phosphoglucomutase converts the product to glucose 6-phosphate. A parallel lysosomal route uses acid alpha-glucosidase. Loss of individual steps causes the glycogen storage diseases, with hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly or exercise intolerance depending on the isozyme affected.

Glycogen is the cell's rapidly mobilizable glucose store, and glycogenolysis is how it is released: in liver to maintain blood glucose between meals, in muscle to fuel contraction locally. The chemistry is the same everywhere but the control is not, with tissue-restricted phosphorylase isoforms (liver PYGL, muscle PYGM, brain PYGB) and distinct phosphorylase kinase subunits linking hormonal and calcium signals, through calmodulin as the kinase's delta subunit, to distinct physiological outcomes. Phosphorylase cleaves glucose 1-phosphate from branch ends, the bifunctional debranching enzyme clears the last residues of each branch releasing one free glucose, and phosphoglucomutase converts glucose 1-phosphate to glucose 6-phosphate for glycolysis or export. A parallel lysosomal route degrades glycogen via acid alpha-glucosidase. Defects cause glycogen storage diseases, including Pompe, Cori and McArdle disease, with hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly or exercise intolerance.

When dietary glucose runs out, liver and kidney cells make it from scratch, and gluconeogenesis is that route: pyruvate arising from lactate, alanine and other amino acids is built back up into glucose 6-phosphate and released as free glucose to keep blood sugar available to brain and red cells during fasting. Pyruvate carboxylase fixes CO2 to give oxaloacetate in mitochondria, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (cytosolic and mitochondrial isoforms) commits it to phosphoenolpyruvate, and the reversible glycolytic enzymes — enolase, phosphoglycerate kinase and mutase, GAPDH, aldolase, triose phosphate isomerase — run backwards toward fructose 1,6-bisphosphate. Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase and the glucose 6-phosphatase system, with its endoplasmic reticulum transporter, catalyse the irreversible, hormonally regulated steps. Defects cause glycogen storage disease and fasting hypoglycaemia; excessive flux contributes to hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes.

Pyruvate is the hub where glycolysis, the TCA cycle, gluconeogenesis and amino acid metabolism meet, and the reactions around it decide whether a cell burns glucose oxidatively, ferments it to lactate, or rebuilds it into glucose. Pyruvate kinase generates pyruvate at the end of glycolysis; mitochondrial carriers MPC1 and MPC2 import it; the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex with its E2 and E3 subunits commits it to acetyl-CoA for oxidation and for fatty acid, sterol and ketone body synthesis. Flux through that step is set by the balance of inhibitory PDK kinases and activating PDP phosphatases, a switch exploited in tumours and reset by fasting and exercise. Alternatively, lactate dehydrogenases regenerate NAD+ when oxygen or mitochondria are lacking, while pyruvate carboxylase and the malic enzymes feed anaplerosis and gluconeogenesis. Deficiencies of PDHA1 or pyruvate carboxylase cause lactic acidosis and encephalopathy.

Glucose metabolism covers the fate of dietary sugar once it enters a cell: trapping as glucose 6-phosphate by hexokinases or the liver/beta-cell glucokinase, breakdown through glycolysis to pyruvate, and in liver and kidney the reverse route of gluconeogenesis. It supplies most of the ATP used by red blood cells and is the brain's near-obligate fuel, so defects are severe — pyruvate kinase or phosphoglycerate kinase deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia, aldolase B deficiency causes fructose intolerance, and loss of glucose-6-phosphatase function with its transporter partner underlies glycogen storage disease. Flux is set by phosphofructokinase together with the bifunctional PFKFB enzymes that make and degrade fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, and by hormonal control through protein kinase A and phosphatase 2A. Nuclear pore components appear here because transport of glucose-responsive regulators across the nuclear envelope couples these reactions to transcription.

Dietary fructose, whether free or released from sucrose, enters central metabolism by a route quite separate from glycolysis of glucose, and this fructose catabolism happens mainly in liver with smaller contributions from kidney and small intestine. Ketohexokinase phosphorylates fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, aldolase B cleaves that to dihydroxyacetone phosphate and free D-glyceraldehyde, and triokinase phosphorylates the glyceraldehyde to glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, delivering both products into glycolysis and, in the fed liver, into lipogenesis. Because the first step bypasses the regulated control point of glycolysis, high fructose loads are processed without feedback restraint, depleting ATP and phosphate and driving hepatic fat synthesis and urate production. Loss of aldolase B causes hereditary fructose intolerance, with hypoglycaemia and liver injury after fructose ingestion, while ketohexokinase deficiency is benign essential fructosuria. Minor side routes handle glyceraldehyde through oxidation and glycerate phosphorylation.

Dietary galactose, released mainly from milk lactose in the intestine, is funnelled into central carbohydrate metabolism by galactose catabolism, largely in the liver. The route matters because it is the only efficient way to convert this sugar into a glycolytic intermediate, and because each of its steps is a recognised inherited disease: deficiency of the galactokinase GALK1 causes cataracts, loss of the uridylyltransferase GALT causes classic galactosemia with liver failure and neurological damage, and GALE defects disturb the UDP-sugar pool needed for glycoprotein and glycolipid synthesis. Mechanistically, GALM epimerises beta-galactose to the alpha anomer, GALK1 phosphorylates it, GALT exchanges it onto UDP-glucose to release glucose 1-phosphate, GALE regenerates UDP-glucose, and PGM1 feeds glucose 6-phosphate onward. AKR1B1 diverts excess galactose to galactitol, the sorbitol-pathway product implicated in cataract formation.

Urea cycle is the liver's route for disposing of excess nitrogen, converting ammonia into urea for excretion in urine while also generating arginine. It is what keeps blood ammonia low, and inherited defects in any step cause hyperammonemia with encephalopathy, the classic urea cycle disorders presenting in neonates. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and dedicated ornithine/citrulline carriers of the inner membrane shuttle intermediates to the cytosol, where argininosuccinate synthase and lyase and finally arginase release urea and regenerate ornithine. Flux is set by N-acetylglutamate, an allosteric activator of the first enzyme whose synthesis rises with arginine, so abundant free amino acids drive their own nitrogen disposal. Acetylation control by SIRT5 adds a further layer, linking ureagenesis to fasting and dietary protein load.

Excess nitrogen from amino acid breakdown is toxic as ammonia, and the urea cycle is how the liver converts it into urea for renal excretion while regenerating arginine. Four core reactions span two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I condenses ammonia and bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase joins the product to ornithine to give citrulline, and cytosolic argininosuccinate synthase and lyase then build and cleave argininosuccinate to release arginine and fumarate, linking the cycle to the TCA cycle. Arginase completes the turn, yielding urea and ornithine, which is returned to the matrix by mitochondrial ornithine carriers. Flux is set allosterically by N-acetylglutamate, whose synthesis rises with arginine, so abundant amino acids accelerate ureagenesis; deacetylation by SIRT5 tunes carbamoyl phosphate synthetase activity. Inherited deficiency of any step causes hyperammonemia with encephalopathy, the classic urea cycle disorders.

Proline catabolism converts the amino acid proline into glutamate, linking protein turnover and collagen breakdown to the citric acid cycle and to nitrogen handling. The route is short: a mitochondrial inner-membrane proline dehydrogenase oxidises proline to Δ-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate, which opens to glutamate gamma-semialdehyde; this intermediate is either oxidised by ALDH4A1 with NAD+ to glutamate and NADH, or transaminated with glutamate to give ornithine and alpha-ketoglutarate, feeding urea-cycle and polyamine precursors. Because the first step passes electrons directly to the respiratory chain, proline serves as a respiratory fuel and a source of reactive oxygen species, which is how it contributes to p53-linked stress responses and to metabolic flexibility in tumours. Loss of PRODH causes hyperprolinaemia type I, and ALDH4A1 deficiency causes hyperprolinaemia type II with accumulation of pyrroline-5-carboxylate; a related enzyme, PRODH2, prefers hydroxyproline derived from collagen.

Leucine, isoleucine and valine cannot be made by human cells, are abundant in muscle protein, and are disposed of by this catabolic route when protein is broken down or dietary intake exceeds need. Degradation begins with reversible transamination by cytosolic and mitochondrial branched-chain aminotransferases, followed by irreversible oxidative decarboxylation through the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, whose flux is set by a kinase that inhibits it and a phosphatase that relieves that inhibition. Distinct acyl-CoA dehydrogenases then commit each carbon skeleton to its own arm, converging on acetyl-CoA, acetoacetate and succinyl-CoA, so the products feed the citric acid cycle in muscle and ketone body or glucose synthesis in liver. Loss of the dehydrogenase complex causes maple syrup urine disease, and defects in downstream steps such as isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase or methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase produce organic acidurias; blunted flux also accompanies insulin resistance.

Histidine catabolism disposes of surplus dietary histidine and connects it to glutamate and one-carbon metabolism. The main route runs from histidase (HAL), which deaminates histidine to urocanate, through urocanase and imidazolonepropionase to formiminoglutamate, which formimidoyltransferase-cyclodeaminase then resolves by transferring a formimino group onto tetrahydrofolate and releasing glutamate. Loss of HAL causes histidinemia, while FTCD deficiency raises formiminoglutamate excretion and disturbs folate handling. Branches of the same amino acid feed distinct physiology: decarboxylation by HDC produces histamine for gastric acid secretion, allergic and neuronal signalling, with amine oxidase and histamine N-methyltransferase terminating its action; carnosine synthase and its methyltransferase build the histidine-containing dipeptides carnosine and anserine that buffer pH and scavenge carbonyls in skeletal muscle and brain.

Propionyl-CoA arises in mitochondria from the breakdown of isoleucine, valine, methionine and threonine, from odd-chain fatty acid beta-oxidation, and from cholesterol side chains, and this route disposes of it by converting it in three steps to succinyl-CoA, a citric acid cycle intermediate. That conversion lets these carbons be oxidized for energy or fed into gluconeogenesis, and it also prevents a reactive acyl-CoA from accumulating. A biotin-dependent carboxylase built from PCCA and PCCB subunits forms methylmalonyl-CoA, MCEE epimerizes it, and the adenosylcobalamin-dependent mutase MMUT rearranges it to succinyl-CoA, with MMAA assisting cofactor delivery and mutase reactivation. Loss of carboxylase or mutase function causes propionic and methylmalonic acidaemia, in which propionyl-CoA-derived metabolites build up and provoke metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia and neurological injury, tying this mitochondrial matrix pathway directly to amino acid and vitamin B12 handling.

Lysine is an essential amino acid that cannot be made or stored, so surplus lysine must be degraded, and this catabolic route disposes of it while delivering purely ketogenic carbon. The main saccharopine pathway runs in mitochondria: a bifunctional enzyme condenses lysine with alpha-ketoglutarate and then splits the product to glutamate and alpha-aminoadipate semialdehyde, which is oxidised to alpha-ketoadipate, decarboxylated by a dehydrogenase complex sharing subunits with the citric acid cycle enzyme, and processed through glutaryl-CoA to acetoacetyl-CoA for ketone body formation during fasting. A parallel pipecolate branch and handling of hydroxylysine and saccharopine-related metabolites feed the same intermediates, with a carrier moving oxoadipate across the inner membrane. Blocks here cause pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy and glutaric aciduria type I, in which accumulating glutaryl-CoA-derived acids injure the basal ganglia.

Tryptophan catabolism degrades the essential amino acid through the kynurenine route, in roughly seven enzymatic steps to aminomuconate semialdehyde, which can either be fully oxidised to acetyl-CoA or diverted toward de novo NAD+ synthesis. The pathway matters on two counts: it supplies the cell's NAD+ precursor quinolinic acid, and it depletes tryptophan locally while generating kynurenines that suppress T cell proliferation, which is how tumours and placental tissue enforce immune tolerance. Entry is controlled by the heme dioxygenases, hepatic TDO2 responding to substrate load and cortisol and IDO1/IDO2 induced by interferon-gamma at sites of inflammation; KMO, KYNU and HAAO carry the intermediates onward, while ACMSD determines how much flux escapes NAD+ synthesis. Transporters including the LAT1 heterodimer bring tryptophan across the membrane. Shared intermediates also feed serotonin production, and dysregulated kynurenine metabolites are implicated in neurodegeneration and mood disorders.

Carnitine is the carrier that lets long-chain fatty acids cross into the mitochondrial matrix for beta-oxidation, so cells that burn fat for energy depend on an adequate supply, and shortfalls present as metabolic disease with impaired fasting tolerance. Most carnitine comes from the diet, but it can also be made de novo in four steps from trimethyllysine, itself released when proteins bearing S-adenosylmethionine-methylated lysines are degraded. A mitochondrial hydroxylase acts first on trimethyllysine, an aldolase step releases the aldehyde, a dehydrogenase oxidises it to gamma-butyrobetaine, and a final dioxygenase hydroxylates that intermediate to carnitine. Only liver and kidney carry out this last step appreciably, so muscle and other high-demand tissues rely on export and plasma-membrane uptake transporters. Loss of the first enzyme is associated with a disorder of carnitine biosynthesis linked to neurodevelopmental phenotypes.

Creatine metabolism gives muscle, brain and other energetically demanding tissues a rapidly mobilizable phosphate reservoir that buffers ATP during bursts of demand. Synthesis begins in kidney with GATM transferring an amidino group from arginine to glycine, and is completed in liver by GAMT, which methylates the intermediate using S-adenosylmethionine; the product circulates and is taken up by consumer tissues through the sodium- and chloride-dependent transporter SLC6A8, with related SLC6 family carriers acting at the blood-brain barrier and in glia. Inside cells, creatine kinases shuttle high-energy phosphate between mitochondria and sites of ATP use, with cytosolic and mitochondrial isoforms specialized for brain and for muscle. Phosphocreatine decays spontaneously to creatinine, which the kidney excretes and clinicians use as a measure of renal filtration. Inherited defects in synthesis or transport cause cerebral creatine deficiency, with intellectual disability, seizures and speech delay.

This is the broad hub through which the body handles amino acids: synthesising the nonessential ones, degrading surplus or muscle-derived residues to carbon skeletons that feed gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis during fasting, and disposing of their nitrogen as urea. It also covers metabolism of amino acid derivatives — creatine, carnitine, polyamines, choline and betaine, melanin, thyroid hormone, catecholamines and serotonin — plus selenocysteine synthesis and its dedicated insertion machinery. Urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, OTC and ASS1, branched-chain dehydrogenase subunits, phenylalanine and tyrosine catabolism through PAH and HGD, and the kynurenine route of tryptophan breakdown are represented, alongside ribosomal proteins, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases and the proteasome, linking supply of amino acids to protein synthesis and turnover. Inherited defects here produce phenylketonuria, hyperammonaemia, maple syrup urine disease, homocystinuria and albinism.

This route branches off glycolysis at glucose 6-phosphate and supplies two things cells cannot make efficiently elsewhere: cytoplasmic NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defence, and ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide and nucleic acid synthesis. An oxidative branch, with G6PD committing the first step and PGLS and PGD completing it, releases CO2 and generates NADPH; a reversible non-oxidative branch built on RPE, RPIA, transketolase and transaldolase interconverts pentose, tetrose and heptose phosphates and returns carbon to fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, so net flux follows demand rather than a fixed direction. PRPS enzymes convert ribose 5-phosphate into PRPP for purine, pyrimidine and histidine metabolism. G6PD deficiency is the most common human enzymopathy and leaves erythrocytes unable to regenerate glutathione, causing haemolysis on oxidative challenge; transaldolase and ribose-5-phosphate isomerase defects cause rarer metabolic disease.

Ethanol, whether swallowed or generated by gut microbes, is disposed of largely by the liver, and this oxidation route is what converts it to a usable two-carbon fuel rather than letting a toxic intermediate accumulate. Alcohol dehydrogenases in the cytosol convert ethanol to acetaldehyde with reduction of NAD+, aldehyde dehydrogenases oxidize acetaldehyde to acetate, and acetyl-CoA synthetases condense acetate with coenzyme A to yield acetyl-CoA for oxidation or lipid synthesis. Class I enzymes such as ADH1B and ADH1C, along with mitochondrial ALDH2, carry most of the flux, and common variants in them explain much of the population variation in drinking response: the inactive ALDH2 allele causes acetaldehyde build-up and the flushing reaction, and aldehyde exposure is linked to liver injury and upper gastrointestinal cancer. The large NADH load generated also shifts hepatic redox balance toward fat accumulation.

This is the broad accounting of how the body handles sugars: glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, glycogen synthesis and breakdown, the pentose phosphate pathway, fructose and galactose conversion into glucose, lactose synthesis in the lactating breast, and the building and lysosomal turnover of glycosaminoglycans and proteoglycans. Together these routes supply ATP, maintain blood glucose between meals, and provide ribose-5-phosphate and NADPH for nucleotide synthesis and redox defence. Hexokinases and glucokinase commit glucose by phosphorylating it, phosphofructokinases and the PFKFB enzymes set glycolytic flux, and glucose-6-phosphatase releases free glucose from liver. Sulfotransferases, glycosyltransferases and sulfatases decorate and degrade chondroitin, heparan and keratan sulfate chains on matrix proteoglycans. Inherited defects give glycogen storage diseases, galactosemia, fructose intolerance, haemolytic anaemia and the mucopolysaccharidoses.

The citric acid cycle is the mitochondrial hub where acetyl-CoA from carbohydrate, fatty acid, ketone body and amino acid catabolism is fully oxidized to CO2, yielding NADH, FADH2 and one high-energy phosphate bond per turn to feed the respiratory chain. It also supplies carbon skeletons for amino acid, heme and lipid synthesis, so its intermediates matter beyond energy. Eight core reactions run from citrate synthase through aconitase, isocitrate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenases, succinyl-CoA synthetase, succinate dehydrogenase, fumarase and malate dehydrogenase; three steps are freely reversible and become relevant in insulin secretion and tumour metabolism. Several enzymes need iron-sulfur cofactors, which explains the presence of cluster assembly factors and frataxin, and succinate dehydrogenase requires dedicated maturation factors. Loss of fumarase or succinate dehydrogenase causes accumulation of oncometabolites and predisposes to paraganglioma and renal cancer, while SIRT3 deacetylation tunes flux.

Biosynthetic reactions that split ATP into AMP and pyrophosphate are close to reversible on their own; hydrolysis of the released pyrophosphate into two phosphate ions is what makes them go. By keeping intracellular pyrophosphate low, these enzymes pull nucleic acid, protein, lipid and polysaccharide synthesis forward at the cost of a second high-energy bond, and they also limit the pyrophosphate available for extracellular mineralization chemistry. Two inorganic pyrophosphatases carry most of this activity in human cells, one cytosolic and one in the mitochondrial matrix, where loss of the latter compromises oxidative phosphorylation and has been linked to cardiomyopathy. LHPP contributes pyrophosphatase activity as well and additionally removes phosphate from phosphohistidine residues, an activity tied to its behaviour as a tumour suppressor. The pathway is best understood as thermodynamic housekeeping that underwrites anabolism generally.

Every RNA polymerase II transcript acquires a 7-methylguanosine cap at its 5' end within the first few nucleotides of synthesis, and this co-transcriptional modification determines whether the message survives and is used. The cap blocks 5'-to-3' exonucleolytic decay, is required for export from the nucleus, promotes splicing of the first intron, and serves as the landing site for translation initiation, allowing communication with the poly(A) tail so a transcript can be translated repeatedly. Chemistry proceeds in steps: a triphosphatase and guanylyltransferase activity, both carried by RNGTT, convert the nascent 5' triphosphate and add GMP through an unusual 5'-5' linkage, after which RNMT with its activating partner RAMAC methylates the added guanine. Capping is coupled to transcription through the polymerase II C-terminal domain, its CDK7-containing kinase, the elongation factor SUPT5H, and the nuclear cap-binding pair NCBP1 and NCBP2.

Nearly all human protein-coding genes are interrupted by introns, and the major mRNA splicing pathway is how those introns are excised and exons joined to produce translatable mRNA. Without it no functional transcript reaches the cytoplasm, and mutations in its components cause retinitis pigmentosa, myelodysplastic syndromes and craniofacial disorders, while the branch-site recognition subunit SF3B1 is a recurrent cancer driver and drug target. Splicing occurs co-transcriptionally on the RNA polymerase II machinery: U1 snRNP marks the 5' splice site while SF1 and the U2AF heterodimer read the branch point and polypyrimidine tract, U2 snRNP then engages the branch point, and arrival of the U4/U6.U5 tri-snRNP builds a spliceosome that is remodelled by DEAH-box helicases and the PRPF19 complex through successive activated states. U6 snRNA forms the catalytic centre for two transesterifications; SR proteins and hnRNPs modulate site choice, and the spliced product leaves bearing exon junction complex subunits.

A small minority of human introns, fewer than one in two hundred, are removed not by the standard spliceosome but by the U12-dependent minor pathway described here. These introns carry divergent splice-site consensus sequences and depend on their own snRNAs — U11, U12, U4atac and U6atac — together with dedicated proteins such as RNPC3, ZRSR2, ZCRB1, ZMAT5 and the SNRNP25/35/48 subunits, while U5 and much of the core machinery, including PRPF8, SNRNP200, EFTUD2 and the SF3B complex, are shared with major splicing. Because the affected introns sit in genes governing DNA replication, cytoskeletal organisation and signalling, the pathway paces expression of a functionally coherent set of targets, and its splicing is comparatively slow and rate-limiting. Mutations in its unique components cause developmental disorders including microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism and Roifman syndrome, and ZRSR2 loss recurs in myelodysplastic syndrome. Association with RNA polymerase II and cap-binding factors places the process cotranscriptionally.

Human protein-coding genes are interrupted by introns, and mRNA splicing removes them and joins the flanking exons so that a translatable message can be exported from the nucleus. Without it no functional mRNA is made, and errors in it generate truncated or mislocalised proteins; mutations in core factors such as PRPF8, PRPF31 and SF3B1 cause retinitis pigmentosa and recur in myelodysplastic syndromes and other cancers. The reaction is carried out by the spliceosome, a dynamic ribonucleoprotein machine built from U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 snRNPs together with Sm and LSm cores, SF3A/SF3B subcomplexes and the PRP19/CDC5L activation complex, with DEAH-box ATPases driving the conformational rearrangements of each cycle. A minor U12-dependent spliceosome handles a small class of introns. SR proteins and hnRNPs select sites and thereby direct alternative splicing, while coupling to RNA polymerase II and deposition of the exon junction complex link splicing to transcription, export and surveillance.

mRNA 3'-end processing completes every protein-coding transcript: an extended primary RNA is cleaved at a site downstream of the stop codon and the upstream fragment receives a poly(A) tail of roughly 250 residues, giving the mRNA the stability, export competence and translational efficiency it needs in the cytoplasm. The cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor complex recognises the polyadenylation signal, CstF binds downstream sequences, symplekin scaffolds the machinery, and poly(A) polymerase with PABPN1 builds the tail; the downstream product is degraded by XRN2, which also drives transcription termination. Coupling to the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, to spliceosomal and hnRNP/SR factors, and to the TREX export complex explains why cleavage, last-intron splicing, termination and export are mutually dependent. Choice among alternative polyadenylation sites reshapes 3' UTRs and their regulation; major histone mRNAs are cleaved without polyadenylation.

Nearly every eukaryotic mRNA acquires its 3' end not by the polymerase stopping cleanly but by endonucleolytic cleavage of a longer transcript followed by addition of a poly(A) tail, and this processing determines transcript stability, export competence and translatability as well as which of several alternative last exons a gene uses. Recognition of the polyadenylation signal by the CPSF complex, with CPSF3 as the nuclease, is coordinated with downstream element binding by CSTF subunits, symplekin scaffolding, poly(A) polymerase and the nuclear poly(A)-binding protein that sets tail length. Coupling to the RNA polymerase II C-terminal domain, to spliceosomal snRNP and SR/hnRNP proteins, and to the exon junction and TREX export machinery ties 3'-end formation to splicing and mRNA release, while PCF11 and the XRN2 exonuclease drive transcription termination. Misregulated site choice shortens 3' UTRs and removes microRNA control in cancer.

Site-specific C-to-U editing rewrites a single cytidine in a mature transcript, and its best-understood use is in the intestine, where deamination of one base in apolipoprotein B mRNA converts a glutamine codon to a premature stop and yields the truncated ApoB-48 protein instead of full-length ApoB-100. That choice determines whether lipoproteins are assembled for dietary fat absorption and chylomicron secretion or for hepatic VLDL output, so the edit sits upstream of plasma lipid handling and atherogenic lipoprotein levels. The chemistry is a hydrolytic cytidine deamination performed by APOBEC1 together with its RNA-binding complementing factor A1CF, which recognises a mooring sequence downstream of the target base; editing occurs in the nucleus on pre-mRNA around splicing and polyadenylation. Related APOBEC family deaminases act mainly on DNA cytidines in antibody diversification and retroviral restriction, and their off-target activity is a source of mutational damage.

Only fully processed mRNA should reach the ribosome, and transport of mature transcript to the cytoplasm is the step that enforces it, moving spliced, capped and polyadenylated messages through the nuclear pore while retaining unfinished ones behind. Export is not directed by a sequence motif but by the proteins deposited during transcription and processing: the exon junction complex with MAGOH, RBM8A and EIF4A3, the cap-binding pair NCBP1/NCBP2, SR proteins, the TREX complex with its THOC subunits and ALYREF, and cleavage/polyadenylation factors. These recruit the NXF1-NXT1 export receptor, which docks on the phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins of the pore scaffold, with DDX39B and GLE1-stimulated helicase activity releasing cargo on the cytoplasmic face. Coupling export to processing gives spatial and temporal control over translation, and defects in pore components cause developmental and neurological disease.

Nascent transcripts made by RNA polymerase II are not usable messages until they are capped, spliced, cleaved, polyadenylated and exported, and this maturation of capped, intron-containing pre-mRNA is what converts genomic information into translatable mRNA. Because human genes average about nine introns, most of this work begins co-transcriptionally, with splicing factors recruited while the polymerase is still elongating, so transcription kinetics set the pace of intron removal. The machinery includes the U1, U2, U4/U6 and U5 snRNPs with their Sm and LSm cores, SR proteins and hnRNPs that select splice sites and shape alternative splicing, the cleavage and polyadenylation and cleavage-stimulation factors that define the 3' end, m6A writers, and the TREX/exon-junction and nuclear pore components that license nuclear export. Mutations in spliceosomal subunits such as PRPF8, PRPF31 and SF3B1 cause retinitis pigmentosa and recur in myelodysplastic syndromes, underscoring how sensitive tissues are to splicing fidelity.

tRNA processing turns raw polymerase transcripts into the mature, decoding-competent tRNAs that every ribosome depends on, in both the nucleus and the mitochondrial matrix. Precursors carry 5' leaders, 3' trailers and sometimes introns; RNase P (the RNA-based nuclear enzyme and the wholly proteinaceous mitochondrial PRORP/TRMT10C complex) removes the leader, ELAC2 trims the trailer, the TSEN endonuclease and RTCB-containing ligase excise and rejoin exons, and TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA that permits aminoacylation. Dozens of enzymes then install methyl, pseudouridine, thiol, queuosine, wybutosine and threonylcarbamoyl marks, many at the anticodon, tuning decoding accuracy and speed. Nucleoporins and exportin XPOT with RAN move tRNAs between compartments, including retrograde return to the nucleus for quality control. Defects cause mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, microcephaly, pontocerebellar hypoplasia, sideroblastic anemia and altered type 2 diabetes risk, reflecting how tightly translational fidelity constrains tissue function.

Newly transcribed tRNAs are not usable until their ends are trimmed, introns removed, a CCA tail added, and dozens of nucleotides chemically modified; tRNA processing carries out that maturation for both nuclear and mitochondrially encoded tRNAs and so sets the fidelity and capacity of translation. RNase P complexes remove 5' leaders, ELAC2 or its mitochondrial counterpart cuts 3' trailers, the TSEN endonuclease and RTCB-containing ligase handle intron removal, and TRNT1 adds the untemplated CCA end. A large family of methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, deaminases, thiolases and queuosine or wybutosine enzymes then decorates the anticodon loop and body, tuning codon reading. Nucleoporins and exportin-t move tRNAs between nucleus and cytosol. Defects cause microcephaly, intellectual disability, anaemia and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy.

rRNA processing converts the long precursor transcripts of ribosomal RNA into the mature 18S, 5.8S and 28S species of the cytosolic ribosome, and the 12S and 16S species of the mitochondrial ribosome, so that ribosomal proteins can be assembled into functional subunits. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and growth, this is one of the most energy-consuming activities of a proliferating cell, and its disruption triggers nucleolar stress and p53 stabilisation; inherited defects cause ribosomopathies such as dyskeratosis congenita and Diamond-Blackfan anaemia. Work proceeds in the nucleolus through ordered endonucleolytic and exonucleolytic cleavages by the exosome, XRN2 and NOB1, guided assembly of small nucleolar ribonucleoproteins containing fibrillarin or dyskerin that direct 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation, and a large cohort of UTP and WD-repeat processome factors, with final maturation steps completed in the cytoplasm.

Ribosomes are built from rRNA that must be carved out of long precursor transcripts, chemically modified, and folded together with ribosomal proteins before a subunit can translate anything. In the nucleolus, a single 47S precursor is trimmed by endonucleases and exonucleases into the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs, with snoRNP-guided pseudouridylation and 2'-O-methylation plus base methylation and acetylation installed as cleavage proceeds. Large assemblies of processing factors, RNA helicases and the exosome complex act on the precursor, while the ribosomal proteins of the 40S and 60S subunits join and final maturation steps occur in the cytoplasm. A parallel set of enzymes processes and modifies the 12S and 16S rRNAs cut from mitochondrial polycistronic transcripts, supporting mitochondrial translation. Because ribosome output sets the ceiling on cell growth, defects in these factors cause ribosomopathies such as bone marrow failure and craniofacial syndromes, and the pathway is heavily exploited by proliferating tumour cells.

Translation initiation is the step at which a ribosome is recruited to an mRNA and positioned on its start codon, and it is the principal point at which protein synthesis rates are set. Most cellular mRNAs are read by cap-dependent scanning: the cap-binding complex containing eIF4E, eIF4G and the helicase eIF4A engages the 5' end, poly(A)-binding protein circularises the message, and a 43S complex built from the 40S subunit, eIF3 and the eIF2-GTP-initiator tRNA ternary complex scans the 5'UTR until an AUG in good context is recognised, after which eIF5 and eIF5B drive joining of the 60S subunit. Ternary complex supply is regulated by the eIF2B guanine-nucleotide exchange factor and by eIF2α phosphorylation during stress, while 4E-BP1 sequesters eIF4E downstream of growth signalling. Some viral and cellular mRNAs bypass scanning entirely using internal ribosome entry sites when cap-dependent initiation is shut off. Mutations in ribosomal proteins and initiation factors cause ribosomopathies and leukodystrophy.

Every round of protein synthesis begins with loading a small ribosomal subunit onto an mRNA, and this step is where that happens: the 43S preinitiation complex, made of the 40S subunit, the eIF2-GTP-initiator tRNA ternary complex and the multisubunit eIF3, is recruited to the capped 5' end of a message. The cap-binding eIF4F assembly — eIF4E, the scaffold eIF4G and the DEAD-box helicase eIF4A, assisted by eIF4B and eIF4H — unwinds 5' structure, while poly(A)-binding protein circularises the transcript and eIF4G contacts eIF3 to bridge mRNA and ribosome; eIF1A stabilises the resulting complex before scanning to the start codon. Because this is the rate-limiting stage of translation, it is the point at which growth factor, nutrient and stress signals set global protein output, and its deregulation supports oncogenic transcript-selective translation.

Cap-dependent translation begins when the 5' cap of an mRNA is recognised and the message is prepared for loading onto a small ribosomal subunit. This step sets the rate of protein synthesis for most cellular mRNAs and is the point at which growth factor and nutrient signalling control how much protein a cell makes. eIF4E must first be freed from the inhibitory 4E-BP, after which it joins the scaffold eIF4G and the helicase eIF4A to form the cap-binding complex; eIF4B and eIF4H stimulate unwinding of secondary structure near the 5' end, while poly(A)-binding protein links the two ends of the message. The activated mRNA is then bound by the 43S pre-initiation complex their small subunit proteins, eIF3 subunits, the ternary eIF2-GTP-Met-tRNA complex and eIF1A committing the transcript to scanning and start codon selection.

Before a new round of translation can begin, the 80S ribosome left over from the previous round must be taken apart and the small subunit kept free of the large one. Generating a pool of free 40S subunits is the recycling step that makes initiation possible: eIF3, in its many subunits, together with eIF1A binds the 40S interface surface and acts as an anti-association factor, preventing premature rejoining with the 60S subunit so that the small subunit remains available to load initiator tRNA and mRNA. The full complement of small- and large-subunit ribosomal proteins is represented because it is the intact subunits themselves that are separated. This traffic control sets how quickly cells can translate, links protein synthesis capacity to growth signalling, and when ribosomal protein genes are mutated or haploinsufficient gives rise to ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

Formation of the ternary complex, and subsequently, the 43S complex is the first committed step of cap-dependent translation initiation, the point at which a cell decides how much protein it will make. Initiator methionyl-tRNA is loaded onto GTP-bound eIF2 to form the ternary complex, which then docks with the 40S small ribosomal subunit already carrying the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and eIF1A, producing the 43S preinitiation complex that goes on to scan mRNA for the start codon. Because eIF2's alpha subunit is the substrate of stress-activated kinases, this step is the main throttle on global protein synthesis during amino acid deprivation, ER stress, heme deficiency and viral infection, and its regulation drives the integrated stress response. The ribosomal small subunit proteins listed here supply the platform on which assembly occurs.

Every round of cap-dependent translation begins by loading an initiator methionyl-tRNA onto the small ribosomal subunit, and this is the step that does it. The GTP-bound trimeric factor eIF2, made of its alpha, beta and gamma subunits, captures Met-tRNAi to form the ternary complex; that complex then joins a 40S subunit already carrying the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and eIF1A, producing the 43S preinitiation complex that will later engage mRNA and scan for the start codon. Because eIF2 activity is the target of the integrated stress response, phosphorylation of its alpha subunit shuts ternary complex formation down and globally suppresses protein synthesis during amino acid deprivation, ER stress or viral infection. The abundant small-subunit ribosomal proteins listed here supply the 40S platform, and defects in them cause ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Choosing where to begin translating is the step that decides which protein an mRNA makes, and ribosomal scanning and start codon recognition is how that choice is made. After the 43S complex loads near the capped 5' end, the small subunit tracks along the leader in the 5'-to-3' direction until the initiator methionyl-tRNA anticodon pairs with an AUG in good context, producing the 48S complex that is then committed to subunit joining. The DEAD-box helicase eIF4A with eIF4B and eIF4H unwinds leader structure, the cap-binding eIF4E/eIF4G module and the multisubunit eIF3 tether the machinery to the message, and eIF1, eIF1A, the eIF2 GTPase carrying the initiator tRNA, and eIF5 together enforce codon fidelity. Small-subunit ribosomal proteins form the mRNA channel and exit site. Errors here shift reading frames, allow leaky or upstream initiation, and underlie translational control of growth and stress responses.

GTP hydrolysis and joining of the 60S ribosomal subunit is the final commitment step of translation initiation, the point at which a scanning 43S complex parked on a start codon becomes an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. Everything a cell makes as protein depends on this handoff, and its regulation sets global protein synthesis rates during growth, stress and differentiation. Once the initiator methionyl-tRNA base-pairs with AUG, eIF5 triggers hydrolysis of eIF2-bound GTP, releasing phosphate and destabilising the initiation factors; eIF5B then catalyses docking of the large subunit and, on hydrolysing its own GTP, departs. The genes reflect this composite event: the eIF2 trimer and the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold, cap-binding and helicase components of eIF4F, and the full complement of 40S and 60S ribosomal proteins. Mutations in these ribosomal proteins underlie ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

This is the final step of translation initiation, the point at which a scanning 43S complex that has found its start codon is converted into an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. Once the initiator methionyl-tRNA is base-paired with AUG in the P site, eIF5 triggers hydrolysis of GTP bound to the eIF2 trimer, committing the site selection and releasing eIF2 and the other initiation factors, including the multisubunit eIF3 scaffold and the cap-binding eIF4F group. eIF5B then promotes joining of the 60S subunit and, after hydrolysing its own GTP, leaves the assembled ribosome. Because every protein made in the cytoplasm passes through this handover, it sets the rate of protein synthesis and growth; it is the step suppressed when eIF2 is phosphorylated during the integrated stress response, and mutations in the large and small subunit proteins involved cause ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anaemia.

Every round of translation initiation consumes a molecule of GTP on eIF2, and the factor must be recharged before it can deliver another initiator methionyl-tRNA to the ribosome. Recycling of eIF2:GDP is that recharging step: the five-subunit eIF2B complex binds the spent trimeric eIF2 and acts as a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, releasing GDP so GTP can rebind and regenerate active eIF2. Because eIF2B is far less abundant than eIF2, this step sets the ceiling on global protein synthesis and is the control point of the integrated stress response: when the alpha subunit of eIF2 is phosphorylated by stress kinases, it becomes an inhibitor rather than a substrate, sequestering eIF2B and shutting down bulk translation while favouring stress-responsive messages. Mutations in eIF2B subunits cause vanishing white matter leukoencephalopathy.

Nearly all protein synthesis in human cells begins with recognition of the 7-methylguanosine cap at the 5' end of an mRNA, and this cap-dependent initiation route is where the ribosome is loaded and the start codon chosen. It sets the overall rate of translation and is the main point at which growth signals, nutrient supply and stress are converted into changes in protein output. The cap-binding protein eIF4E, together with the scaffold eIF4G, a helicase and poly(A)-binding protein, activates the message; eIF2 in its GTP form delivers initiator methionyl-tRNA to the 40S subunit alongside eIF3, and after scanning and codon recognition GTP hydrolysis permits 60S joining to form an elongation-competent 80S ribosome. Regulation acts through 4E-BP1 sequestering eIF4E and through the eIF2B guanine nucleotide exchange factor, the target of the integrated stress response. Ribosomal protein mutations cause bone marrow failure syndromes, and eIF4E-driven initiation is frequently elevated in cancer.

Protein synthesis ends when a stop codon reaches the ribosomal A site, and this step converts a stalled elongation complex into a released polypeptide and recyclable subunits. Accurate termination sets the true C-terminus of every protein; failure to terminate causes readthrough into 3' untranslated sequence, extended and often misfolded products, and it is the same recognition event that triggers surveillance of premature stop codons. Recognition is carried out by eRF1, encoded by ETF1, which reads all three stop codons and catalyses hydrolysis of the peptidyl-tRNA ester bond, working with the GTPase eRF3 (GSPT1 and GSPT2) that couples codon recognition to efficient release. The full complement of large and small subunit ribosomal proteins provides the decoding centre and peptidyl transferase centre in which this occurs, with HEMK2 and TRMT112 methylating the eRF1 catalytic motif to tune release activity.

Translation is the decoding of mRNA into protein, the step at which genetic information becomes the working machinery of the cell, and it consumes a large share of cellular energy and biosynthetic capacity. Cytosolic ribosomal subunits, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, and initiation, elongation and release factors carry out initiation at the start codon, cyclic peptide-bond formation, and stop-codon-triggered release and recycling; cap-binding and eIF2 regulation make this the main point at which growth signals and stress restrain protein output. Included are the co-translational branches: signal recognition particle capture of secretory and membrane proteins for insertion through the ER translocon and cleavage by signal peptidase, and a separate mitochondrial system in which bacterial-like mitoribosomes synthesise the thirteen respiratory chain subunits encoded by mtDNA. Quality-control components resolve stalled ribosomes and degrade aberrant nascent chains. Defects cause ribosomopathies, anaemias and mitochondrial disease.

Translation is the step where genetic information becomes protein, and this collection covers the whole of it: cytosolic initiation, elongation and termination, aminoacylation of tRNAs, co-translational targeting to the endoplasmic reticulum, and the separate translation system inside mitochondria. Cytosolic ribosomal subunits work with cap-binding and scaffolding initiation factors, the eIF2 complex and its guanine nucleotide exchange factor eIF2B, elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2, and release factor eRF1 with ABCE1 for recycling. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases exist as distinct cytosolic and mitochondrial enzymes, and mutations in either class cause neuropathies and mitochondrial disease. Signal recognition particle, its ER receptor, the Sec61 translocon and signal peptidase route secretory and membrane proteins into the ER. Mitoribosomal proteins, formylmethionine-tRNA machinery, TUFM and OXA1L build the thirteen hydrophobic respiratory chain subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Quality control components resolve stalled ribosomes and degrade aberrant nascent chains through ubiquitination and the proteasome.

Glycosyltransferases work inside the Golgi and endoplasmic reticulum lumen, but their activated sugar donors are made in the cytosol, so transport of nucleotide sugars across those membranes is what makes glycosylation possible at all. The SLC35 carriers perform this step, acting as antiporters that bring in a nucleotide sugar and return the corresponding nucleoside monophosphate to the cytosol. Individual members handle distinct donors: CMP-sialic acid, UDP-galactose, UDP-N-acetylglucosamine, GDP-fucose, UDP-glucuronic acid and UDP-N-acetylgalactosamine among them. Their output is the sugar chains of glycoproteins, glycolipids and proteoglycans, so loss of a single transporter narrows one branch of glycan synthesis with specific consequences — defective sialylation, impaired fucosylation with leukocyte adhesion failure, or disrupted proteoglycan sulfation and cartilage formation. These transporters are therefore rate-limiting suppliers for secretory-pathway glycan assembly and a recognised cause of congenital disorders of glycosylation.

Rather than build every pyrimidine nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released when DNA and RNA are degraded and phosphorylate them back to nucleotide monophosphates, which then re-enter the interconversion routes that feed replication and repair. Pyrimidine salvage keeps nucleotide pools balanced at far lower energetic cost than de novo synthesis and is the dominant supply route in tissues with limited biosynthetic capacity, including mitochondria, where thymidine kinase 2 supplies dTMP for mitochondrial DNA; its loss causes mitochondrial DNA depletion and myopathy. Uridine-cytidine kinases act on the ribonucleosides, thymidine and deoxycytidine kinases on the deoxy forms, while phosphorylases and cytidine deaminase recycle or interconvert bases upstream. The same enzymes determine the activation and breakdown of nucleoside-analogue drugs, making this chemistry a determinant of chemotherapy and antiviral response.

Pyrimidine catabolism disposes of uracil and thymine released from nucleotide turnover and dietary nucleic acids, converting them in three steps each to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate, which are excreted in urine or transaminated further. Upstream, nucleotidases such as NT5E and NT5C dephosphorylate pyrimidine monophosphates and phosphorylases including UPP1 and thymidine phosphorylase remove the sugar, feeding free bases into the degradative arm. There dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase reduces the ring, dihydropyrimidinase opens it, and beta-ureidopropionase releases the final amino acid with ammonia and CO2. The route matters clinically because it is the same one that clears fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutics: DPYD deficiency causes severe, sometimes fatal 5-fluorouracil toxicity, and inherited defects at each step produce neurological disease with pyrimidine accumulation. Mitochondrial AGXT2 can divert the end products toward branched-chain amino acid and short-chain fatty acid metabolism.

Ribosome production begins with transcription of the rRNA genes by RNA polymerase I, and before that polymerase can be loaded the nucleosomal rDNA promoter must be made accessible. This opening step sets how many rRNA genes are active, and therefore the cell's capacity for ribosome biogenesis and growth, which is why it is tuned to nutrient and proliferative signals and is deranged in cancer and in ribosomopathies. The upstream binding factor UBTF binds and bends promoter DNA, displacing histones to create a nucleosome-free region; its phosphorylation, with MAPK3 among the kinases implicated, governs productive engagement with the polymerase I initiation complex. Core histones of all four classes represent the chromatin being remodelled, while MBD2 and PHF6 act on the repressive side, keeping a fraction of rDNA repeats silent. The output is an initiation-competent promoter rather than any metabolic product.

Ribosome production begins with transcription of the rRNA genes, and RNA polymerase I transcription initiation is the step that sets how many ribosomes a cell will build — a rate that scales directly with growth, and one that is raised in proliferating and tumour cells. At the rDNA promoter the selectivity factor SL1, built from TBP with the Pol I-specific TAF1A–TAF1D subunits, forms a platform together with the architectural activator UBTF; phosphorylation of UBTF and the adaptor RRN3 then license loading of the multisubunit polymerase, whose POLR1 catalytic core shares several small subunits with Pol II and Pol III. Initiation output is tuned by reversible acetylation of the basal machinery through the KAT2A/KAT2B acetyltransferases opposed by HDAC1/HDAC2 within NuRD-type chromatin remodelling complexes, while the terminator-binding factor TTF1 links promoter events to rDNA chromatin state and nucleolar organisation.

Ribosome production begins with rRNA transcription, and promoter escape by RNA polymerase I is the step where an assembled initiation complex commits to processive synthesis. Cells tune this step to match ribosome supply to growth demand, so it sits at the heart of nucleolar function and of growth control; its dysregulation accompanies rapid proliferation in cancer and underlies ribosomopathies. The polymerase I catalytic core with its specific subunits engages rDNA through the SL1 complex of TBP and TAF1A/TAF1B/TAF1C together with the activator UBTF, and the initiation factor RRN3 dissociates as the enzyme clears the promoter and enters elongation, unlike polymerase II initiation there is no requirement for ATP-driven promoter melting. Shared small polymerase subunits, TFIIH components including CDK7-cyclin H and the helicases ERCC2/ERCC3, chromatin-bound histones and PHF6 provide the nucleolar chromatin context in which escape occurs.

Once RNA polymerase II has made the first phosphodiester bond of a transcript, it must break its grip on the promoter and commit to elongation; promoter escape is that transition, and it sets how much messenger RNA any gene actually yields. Without it the enzyme idles at the start site, aborting short transcripts, so escape is one of the main points at which activators and repressors control gene expression. The step requires the full twelve-subunit polymerase together with the general factors assembled at the TATA-binding protein and TFIID core, and depends on the TFIIH complex, whose CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase carboxy-terminal domain while its ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicase subunits help open and translocate promoter DNA. Those same TFIIH subunits serve nucleotide excision repair, and their mutation underlies xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy.

Every protein-coding gene must be found, marked, and opened before it can be read, and this is the step that does it: assembly of the RNA polymerase II pre-initiation complex on a core promoter and the melting of duplex DNA to expose the template strand. Without it there is no messenger RNA and no regulated gene expression, so all inducible and developmental transcription programmes converge here. TBP and the TAFs of TFIID recognise promoter elements, TFIIA and TFIIB stabilise that platform, TFIIF delivers the twelve-subunit polymerase, and TFIIE recruits TFIIH, whose ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicase subunits unwind the promoter while the CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 module phosphorylates the polymerase CTD to license escape. The same TFIIH subunits serve nucleotide excision repair, and their mutation causes xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy.
