RNA polymerase III makes the short, abundant, untranslated RNAs a cell needs constantly dash tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others dash and chain elongation is the productive phase in which the enzyme, having opened its promoter and escaped initiation, processively extends the transcript to its termination signal. Because tRNA and 5S rRNA supply are set here, the output of this polymerase scales with ribosome production and growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and other neurodevelopmental disease, while activating lesions raise its output in cancer. The sixteen-subunit enzyme is built from a catalytic core of the largest and second-largest subunits together with subunits shared with the other nuclear polymerases, plus a Pol III-specific subcomplex that handles promoter opening and RNA cleavage. Alternative forms of one subunit distinguish enzyme variants with differing gene preferences and a role in cytosolic DNA sensing.

De novo purine ribonucleoside monophosphate biosynthesis builds the purine nucleotides from scratch, assembling the ring stepwise on activated ribose-5-phosphate (PRPP) using nitrogen from glutamine and aspartate, carbon from glycine, bicarbonate and a folate-borne formyl group. The product, IMP, is then branched to AMP by an adenylosuccinate synthetase and lyase pair, or to GMP through IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthase. Cells need this route to supply DNA and RNA precursors, ATP and GTP for energy and signalling, and cofactors, so flux rises sharply in proliferating and rapidly dividing tissue; it is the reason IMP dehydrogenase inhibitors suppress lymphocyte expansion and why antifolates cripple nucleotide supply. Several steps are carried out by multifunctional enzymes that cluster into a metabolon, and inherited deficiency of adenylosuccinate lyase causes a neurodevelopmental disorder with seizures and autistic features.

Nucleotide synthesis begins with an activated sugar, and this is the step that makes it: phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase transfers pyrophosphate from ATP onto ribose 5-phosphate to give 5-phospho-alpha-D-ribose 1-diphosphate (PRPP), requiring magnesium and stimulated by inorganic phosphate. PRPP is the common entry point for de novo purine and pyrimidine synthesis, for salvage of hypoxanthine, guanine and uracil, and for NAD and histidine-related ribosylations, so flux through this reaction sets how much nucleotide a proliferating cell can make. The enzyme works as a multimer and is feedback-inhibited by purine nucleotides; variants that escape that restraint drive purine overproduction, hyperuricaemia and gout, while loss-of-function mutations in the widely expressed PRPS1 cause X-linked deafness and neuropathy syndromes. PRPS2 is also broadly expressed and coupled to growth signalling, whereas PRPS1L1 transcription is largely testis-restricted.

Transcription by RNA polymerase II ends with cutting the nascent transcript free and giving it a mature 3' end, and this is the step that defines where one gene's mRNA stops and determines its stability, export and translatability. Cleavage and polyadenylation factors recognise the poly(A) signal and downstream sequence — the CPSF subunits with WDR33 and FIP1L1, the CSTF trimer, and NUDT21 with CPSF6/CPSF7 — while symplekin scaffolds the machinery, PCF11 and CLP1 link cleavage to polymerase release, and PAPOLA adds the tail that PABPN1 coats. Replication-dependent histone mRNAs take the alternative route: they are cleaved without polyadenylation using a U7 snRNP built on LSM10 and LSM11 with Sm proteins, and end in a stem-loop bound by SLBP. Choice of poly(A) site also generates alternative 3' ends, coupling termination to post-transcriptional regulation and to cell cycle-restricted histone supply.

Transcription of protein-coding genes by RNA polymerase II is the step at which genetic information is converted into messenger RNA, and essentially every cell decision — proliferation, differentiation, stress response, circadian timing — is implemented through it. The twelve-subunit polymerase, led by POLR2A, is positioned at promoters by TBP and the TAF-containing TFIID complex together with the general factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH, whose CDK7 kinase phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license promoter escape. Elongation control follows: NELF and DSIF impose promoter-proximal pausing until CDK9-containing P-TEFb releases the polymerase, while PAF1, FACT and elongation factors sustain processive synthesis through chromatin, and cleavage/polyadenylation and Integrator complexes terminate transcripts. Layered on this core are Mediator, chromatin remodellers and modifiers, and a very large repertoire of sequence-specific regulators — nuclear receptors, p53, Notch effectors, KRAB zinc fingers — that set gene-specific output. Deregulation here underlies much of cancer and developmental disease.

Ribosome production begins with RNA polymerase I making a single long precursor rRNA in the nucleolus, and transcription of that gene must be stopped cleanly at the end of the repeat so the polymerase can be recycled and the transcript released. In this termination step the DNA-binding factor TTF1 occupies a terminator element downstream of the rRNA gene and stalls the elongating enzyme; the release factor PTRF/CAVIN1 then acts on the paused complex to free both the nascent pre-rRNA and polymerase I from the template. The gene set accordingly includes the full polymerase I catalytic core and its shared subunits, the SL1 promoter-selectivity complex with TBP and the TAF1 proteins, the nucleolar activator UBTF, and TFIIH components that couple this transcription to repair. Output here sets the ceiling on ribosome biogenesis, cell growth and proliferation.

Ribosome production begins with RNA polymerase I transcription of the tandemly repeated ribosomal DNA genes in the nucleolus, which yields the 45S precursor that is cleaved into the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs. Because rRNA synthesis sets the ceiling on how many ribosomes a cell can build, this is the step at which growth rate is matched to nutrient and proliferative signals, and its hyperactivation accompanies the enlarged nucleoli of tumour cells. The multisubunit polymerase core (POLR1A/POLR1B plus subunits shared with the other nuclear polymerases) is recruited to the CORE and upstream control elements of the rDNA promoter by UBTF, the TBP-containing selectivity factor built from TAF1A-TAF1D, and the initiation factor RRN3, with TTF1 acting at termination. Base Excision Repair removes and replaces individual damaged bases, and is the main defence against the most common forms of DNA damage a cell sustains: oxidised, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionising radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Loss of its components drives mutation accumulation and cancer predisposition, as with MUTYH-associated polyposis. A family of glycosylases each recognising particular lesions — OGG1, UNG, NTHL1, the NEIL enzymes, TDG, MPG — cleaves the glycosidic bond to leave an abasic site, which APEX1 incises. Repair then proceeds either as single-nucleotide replacement by polymerase beta with XRCC1 and LIG3, or as longer-patch synthesis using PCNA, replicative polymerases, RFC and FEN1. PARP1/PARP2 signal strand breaks and recruit repair factors, and end-processing by PNKP prepares ligatable termini. Repair also operates on damage arising in chromatin and at telomeres.

Base excision repair handles the most common everyday damage to DNA ": oxidized, deaminated and alkylated bases produced by mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, ionizing radiation, lipid peroxidation and inflammatory oxidants. Without it, mutation rates rise and lesions such as 8-oxoguanine are mispaired during replication; loss of MUTYH predisposes to colorectal adenomatous polyposis, and the route is also how uracil and thymine glycol are cleared from the genome. Repair begins with one of several damage-specific glycosylases ": UNG, OGG1, NTHL1, SMUG1, TDG, MPG and the NEIL enzymes ": which cleave the glycosidic bond and leave an abasic site. APEX1 and PNKP process the resulting ends, then either POLB with XRCC1 and LIG3 fills a single nucleotide, or PCNA, RFC, replicative polymerases, FEN1 and LIG1 replace a longer patch. PARP1 and PARP2 signal the strand break and recruit the scaffold, and chromatin and telomere-binding proteins set the context in which this repair occurs.

Chromosome Maintenance covers the specialised chromatin structures that keep linear chromosomes stable and functional across divisions: the centromere, which directs kinetochore assembly and accurate segregation, and the telomere, which caps chromosome ends so they are not read as broken DNA. Loss of either causes aneuploidy, end-to-end fusions, or replicative senescence, and mutations in these components underlie telomere biology disorders such as dyskeratosis congenita and premature ageing syndromes. Centromere identity is epigenetic rather than sequence-encoded: HJURP and the MIS18 complex deposit the histone H3 variant CENP-A outside S phase, seeding the constitutive centromere-associated network. At telomeres, shelterin proteins including TRF1, TRF2 and POT1 protect the repeat tract, telomerase with its dyskerin-containing RNP extends it, and the CST complex together with lagging-strand replication and helicase activities completes end processing.

Chromosome maintenance covers the two places on a chromosome that cannot be copied by ordinary replication alone: the centromere and the telomere. Both must be rebuilt every cycle or chromosomes missegregate and ends fuse or erode, outcomes that underlie aneuploidy, premature ageing syndromes and the immortalisation of tumour cells. At centromeres, replication-independent deposition of the histone H3 variant CENP-A by its chaperone HJURP, with the MIS18 complex and ATRX/DAXX-type remodellers, marks the site epigenetically and nucleates the constitutive centromere-associated network that builds the kinetochore. At telomeres, the shelterin proteins TRF1, TRF2, POT1, TPP1 and TIN2 cap the repeat tract and license the telomerase holoenzyme, whose RNA-binding partners include dyskerin, NOP10, NHP2 and GAR1; CST components plus lagging-strand polymerases, RPA, RFC-PCNA and helicases such as WRN and BLM finish the C-strand and resolve G-quadruplexes.

Cell-surface receptors of the TNF receptor family that carry a cytoplasmic death domain decide whether a cell dies or survives when it meets its ligand. Death receptor signaling through TNFR1, the TRAIL receptors and CD95/FAS assembles a death-inducing complex in which FADD recruits and activates caspase-8, launching caspase-3-dependent apoptosis largely without mitochondrial input; the caspase-8 homologue CFLAR and the IAPs BIRC2/3 and XIAP set the threshold, so failure to die underlies tumour survival and autoimmunity while excess killing drives tissue injury. The same receptors recruit TRADD, RIPK1 and TRAF2/6 toward IKK-dependent NF- cappaB and JNK activation, tuned by ubiquitin editing enzymes including CYLD, TNFAIP3 and OTULIN and by the LUBAC components SHARPIN and RNF31. A distinct neuronal arm operates through p75NTR with LINGO1 and Nogo receptor partners, regulating Rho GTPase exchange factors to restrain axon growth and remodel synapses.

When a replication fork meets a base lesion it cannot read, the high-fidelity polymerases delta and epsilon stall, and DNA damage bypass lets the cell finish copying the genome rather than collapse the fork. Tolerance comes at a cost in accuracy: the low-fidelity Y-family enzymes POLH, POLI, POLK and REV1, together with the POLZ complex of REV3L and MAD2L2, insert nucleotides opposite damaged templates and extend past them, and they lack proofreading exonuclease activity, so bypass is a major source of mutation. The switch is controlled by ubiquitin: RAD18 with UBE2B monoubiquitinates PCNA at stalled forks to recruit translesion polymerases, while USP1 with its partner WDR48 reverses the mark, and a CUL4-DDB1 ligase and VCP-dependent extraction act alongside RPA and the clamp loader. Loss of this route underlies the sun-sensitive, cancer-prone variant form of xeroderma pigmentosum and shapes mutational signatures and chemotherapy resistance.

DNA Repair is the collective machinery that keeps the genome intact against damage from radiation, reactive metabolites, chemical adducts and errors of replication. Its failure drives mutation accumulation, cellular senescence and cancer, and inherited defects in its components underlie Fanconi anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, ataxia-telangiectasia and Lynch syndrome; because dividing cells have little time to repair, the same machinery determines the response to DNA-damaging chemotherapy and PARP inhibitors. The genes span all the major routes: glycosylases and APEX1 with POLB and XRCC1-LIG3 in base excision repair, MSH2/MLH1/PMS2 mismatch correction of nascent strands, XPC-DDB2 and the TFIIH helicases in nucleotide excision repair, direct reversal by MGMT and ALKBH enzymes, FANC proteins unhooking interstrand crosslinks, translesion polymerases that permit damage bypass, and BRCA1/BRCA2-RAD51 recombination versus DNA-PK-mediated end joining at double-strand breaks. Overlaid are ATM/ATR checkpoint signalling, ubiquitin, SUMO and PARP marks, chromatin remodelling, and p53-directed arrest or apoptosis.

Genomes are damaged continuously by radiation, reactive metabolites, spontaneous base loss and replication errors, and DNA repair is the collection of enzyme systems that finds and mends those lesions so that genetic information is passed on intact. Its failure underlies cancer predisposition and premature ageing syndromes, and inherited defects in its components cause Fanconi anemia, xeroderma pigmentosum, Lynch syndrome and ataxia telangiectasia; its inhibition is also the basis of many chemotherapies. Distinct routes handle distinct damage: glycosylases such as OGG1 and UNG initiate base excision repair, XPC and the ERCC helicases excise bulky helix-distorting adducts, MSH2-MLH1 complexes correct replication mismatches, MGMT and AlkB-family enzymes reverse alkylation directly, BRCA1/2 with RAD51 drive homologous recombination while Ku and LIG4 mediate end joining, and FANC proteins unhook interstrand crosslinks. Damage sensing by ATM, ATR and TP53, ubiquitin and SUMO signalling on chromatin, and translesion polymerases coordinate repair with replication, checkpoints and apoptosis.

Oxidised and alkylated purines are removed from DNA by depurination, the opening move of base excision repair: a purine-specific DNA glycosylase hydrolyses the N-glycosidic bond linking the damaged base to deoxyribose, releasing the free base and leaving an abasic site for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps. Without it, 8-oxoguanine and alkylated bases persist and mispair, driving G:C to T:A transversions; loss of MUTYH, which excises adenine mispaired opposite 8-oxoG, causes an inherited adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer predisposition, while OGG1, MPG and NEIL3 handle oxidised guanine, alkylpurines and hydantoin or interstrand crosslink lesions. The accompanying core histones and the shelterin proteins TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2 place this chemistry in chromatin and at telomeres, where guanine-rich repeats are especially oxidation-prone and repair must occur without triggering a damage response.

Depyrimidination is the first committed step of base excision repair for damaged pyrimidines: a lesion-specific DNA glycosylase cuts the glycosidic bond between an altered base and its deoxyribose, releasing the free base and leaving an abasic site for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase action. This is how cells erase uracil from cytosine deamination or misincorporated dUTP, thymine glycol and other oxidised pyrimidines, and T:G mismatches at methylated CpGs; failure raises mutation rates and, in the case of MBD4 and TDG, disturbs epigenetic demethylation and predisposes to cancer. UNG, SMUG1, TDG, MBD4, NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes each cover distinct lesion spectra. The reaction occurs on chromatin, so core histones frame the substrate, while shelterin components including TRF1, TRF2, POT1 and TIN2 mark telomeric DNA as a repair context requiring special handling.

The first step of base excision repair when the damaged base is a pyrimidine: a lesion-specific DNA glycosylase cuts the N-glycosidic bond linking the altered base to deoxyribose, releasing the free base and leaving an abasic site for downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase action. This depyrimidination step is how cells erase deaminated cytosine (uracil), thymine glycol, hydroxymethyl- and formyl-pyrimidines and mismatched thymine arising from spontaneous hydrolysis, oxidation and alkylation, preventing the mutations that would otherwise accumulate at every cell division. Uracil-directed glycosylases such as UNG, SMUG1, TDG and MBD4 act alongside the oxidative-damage enzymes NTHL1 and the NEIL family, while OGG1 overlaps with purine lesions. Histone components place the chemistry in chromatin, and the telomeric shelterin proteins mark telomeres as a site where such repair is specially controlled. Loss of these activities drives base substitution signatures and cancer predisposition.

Base-Excision Repair, AP Site Formation is the opening step of the repair route that removes small, non-bulky base damage from DNA: a glycosylase recognises an aberrant base, cleaves the bond linking it to deoxyribose, and leaves behind an abasic (AP) site that downstream incision, gap-filling and ligation steps resolve. This is how cells cope with the constant chemical erosion of their genome by oxidation, alkylation, deamination and spontaneous base loss, and losing it raises mutation rates; inherited MUTYH defects, for example, cause adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer, while UNG and TDG activities also serve programmed processes such as antibody diversification and DNA demethylation. Distinct glycosylases cover distinct lesions, from oxidised purines handled by OGG1 and the NEIL enzymes to uracil, thymine mismatches and alkylated bases. Damage recognition occurs in chromatin, and the accompanying histones and telomere-capping proteins mark where this scanning takes place and where it must be restrained.

Every day cells sustain thousands of small base lesions — oxidised guanine, deaminated cytosine, alkylated purines, uracil misincorporated during replication — and base excision repair removes them before they become mutations. The first step is the recognition and excision of the damaged base itself, generating the abasic (AP) site that downstream nucleases, polymerases and ligases then resolve. Dedicated DNA glycosylases each police a lesion class: UNG and SMUG1 remove uracil, TDG and MBD4 act on deaminated bases at CpG sites, MPG on alkylated purines, OGG1, NTHL1 and the NEIL enzymes on oxidised bases, and MUTYH excises adenine mispaired with 8-oxoguanine, a defence whose loss causes adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer. Repair occurs in chromatin, so histones are intrinsic to the substrate, and shelterin components including TERF1, TERF2, POT1 and TINF2 govern how this chemistry proceeds at telomeres.

When a damaged or mismatched base is excised by a DNA glycosylase, the DNA is left with an abasic site whose sugar-phosphate remnant must be cleared before the gap can be filled; this is the short-patch, single-nucleotide replacement arm of base excision repair. Without it, abasic sites and their 5'-deoxyribose phosphate residues persist as blocking, mutagenic lesions that stall replication and drive base substitutions, which is why this chemistry underlies genome stability against oxidative and alkylation damage. APEX1 displaces the glycosylase from its product and incises the backbone on the 5' side of the base-free deoxyribose, creating a nick with a 3'-hydroxyl. DNA polymerase beta is then recruited to the resulting gap and uses its lyase activity to release the 5'dRP group, leaving a clean single-nucleotide gap for fill-in synthesis and ligation.

Every day each cell loses thousands of bases to spontaneous hydrolysis or to glycosylase excision of damaged ones, leaving abasic sites that stall polymerases and become strand breaks if left alone; resolution of these AP sites is the completion step of base excision repair that restores an intact double helix. The endonuclease APEX1 nicks the backbone 5' to the lesion and displaces the glycosylase, after which one of two routes finishes the job: short-patch repair, in which DNA polymerase beta removes the sugar remnant, inserts a single nucleotide and the XRCC1-ligase III complex seals the nick; or long-patch strand-displacement synthesis by polymerase delta or epsilon with PCNA, RPA and RFC, with FEN1 clipping the flap and ligase I closing it. PARP1/PARP2 mark the break and help recruit repair factors. Loss of this capacity drives mutation accumulation, and defects in MUTYH or NTHL1 predispose to colorectal and other cancers.

Alkylating agents, whether environmental or chemotherapeutic, leave methyl and ethyl adducts on DNA bases that mispair or block replication, and direct reversal removes them in a single enzymatic step without excising the base or cutting the strand. MGMT transfers the methyl group from O6-methylguanine onto its own cysteine, inactivating itself in the process, which is why MGMT promoter silencing sensitises glioma to temozolomide and MGMT activity confers resistance. ALKBH2 and ALKBH3 are iron- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases that oxidatively remove methyl groups from 1-methyladenine, 3-methylcytosine and related lesions, releasing formaldehyde; ALKBH3 works with the ASCC helicase complex to unwind duplex DNA and expose single-stranded substrates. Related demethylases acting on RNA, FTO and ALKBH5, use the same chemistry on methylated nucleotides. The pathway keeps mutation rates and replication stress low and shapes tumour response to alkylating chemotherapy.

Alkylating agents leave methyl groups on ring nitrogens of DNA bases, notably 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine, which block base pairing and stall replication. Direct reversal by DNA dioxygenases erases these lesions without cutting the backbone or excising the base: iron(II)- and 2-oxoglutarate-dependent enzymes hydroxylate the offending alkyl group, which then falls off as formaldehyde, restoring the original sequence intact. ALKBH2 works mainly on double-stranded DNA at replication forks, while ALKBH3 prefers single-stranded substrates and is delivered to them with help from the ASCC helicase complex, whose ASCC3 subunit unwinds duplex DNA to expose the lesion. Related family members act on RNA rather than DNA, reflecting a shared chemistry applied to different nucleic acid marks. Loss of this repair route sensitises cells to chemotherapeutic alkylators and raises mutation burden, placing it alongside base excision repair and alkyltransferase-mediated defence against genotoxic methylation.

RNA Polymerase III Transcription Termination is the final step in making the short, abundant non-coding RNAs that sustain protein synthesis and RNA processing — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and RNase P RNA. Ending each round cleanly matters because polymerase III transcribes very short genes at high rates; failure to release transcript and DNA would trap the enzyme and starve the cell of translational capacity. Termination is directed by a simple cis signal, a run of thymidines on the non-template strand, which destabilises the elongation complex without dedicated release factors, and the polymerase's own subunits, including POLR3A, POLR3B and the shared core shared with polymerases I and II, determine termination efficiency and recycling into reinitiation. The released transcript is bound by La protein (SSB), which protects the nascent 3' oligo(U) end and channels it into maturation.

RNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs in bulk tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others and this step ends each round of synthesis, freeing the transcript and the DNA template so the enzyme can recycle onto a new gene. Termination is driven almost entirely by the polymerase itself: a run of thymidines on the non-template strand is enough to destabilise the elongation complex, without the dedicated release factors or extensive cis-elements that other polymerases require. The seventeen-subunit enzyme is represented here in full, including subunits shared with polymerases I and II and the alternative catalytic-region paralogues POLR3G and POLR3GL. Released nascent transcripts bearing 3' oligo-U are captured by the La protein SSB, which protects them from exonucleolytic trimming and guides folding and maturation. Output from this machinery sets the ceiling on translational capacity and cell growth.

RNA polymerase III transcription supplies the cell with its short, untranslated workhorse RNAs — all tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL RNA of the signal recognition particle, RNase P RNA and 7SK — and so sets the ceiling on translational capacity and growth. Output scales with proliferation, and mutations in the polymerase subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies, while unchecked activity accompanies transformation. Because the enzyme cannot read promoters itself, recognition is delegated: TFIIIA binds the internal 5S element, the multisubunit TFIIIC complex binds A- and B-box elements of tRNA genes, and the SNAPc complex with ZNF143 and POU2F1 serves gene-external type 3 promoters upstream of U6. Each route converges on TFIIIB — TBP with BDP1 and either BRF1 or BRF2 — which docks the polymerase, opens the DNA and directs initiation; La protein binds the nascent transcripts' uridylate tails during maturation.

This is the broad programme by which DNA is read into RNA and that reading is controlled, covering all four human RNA polymerases and the regulatory layers built on top of them. It determines which proteins a cell makes, and therefore cell identity, growth rate and the capacity to respond to hormones, stress and DNA damage; its derangement underlies much of cancer and of developmental syndromes. Polymerase I subunits with UBTF and RRN3 drive ribosomal RNA synthesis in the nucleolus, Polymerase II with general factors, Mediator, elongation and capping/cleavage-polyadenylation machinery produces mRNA, Polymerase III with TFIIIB/TFIIIC components makes tRNAs and 5S RNA, and POLRMT with TFAM and TFB2M transcribes the mitochondrial genome. Superimposed are sequence-specific activators and nuclear receptors, KRAB zinc fingers with TRIM28, chromatin writers and erasers such as the Polycomb, SWI/SNF, HDAC and DNA methyltransferase complexes, p53-centred damage responses, and miRNA biogenesis feeding Argonaute-based silencing.

Ketone body metabolism is the fasting fuel switch: the liver converts surplus acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into water-soluble acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, exports them, and extrahepatic tissues burn them for energy. This spares glucose during prolonged fasting, exercise, or ketogenic diets and keeps the brain, which cannot oxidize fatty acids, supplied when carbohydrate is scarce. Synthesis runs through mitochondrial HMGCS2 and HMGCL, with BDH1 setting the acetoacetate/beta-hydroxybutyrate ratio according to mitochondrial redox state; acetone arises by spontaneous decarboxylation. Utilization requires OXCT1 (SCOT) and ACAT1 to regenerate acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle, and because liver lacks SCOT the hepatic route is effectively one-way. Cytosolic AACS and ACSS3 route ketone carbon into lipid synthesis instead. Inherited defects in these steps cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia or ketoacidotic crises, and uncontrolled flux underlies diabetic ketoacidosis.

During fasting, the liver converts fat-derived acetyl-CoA into water-soluble fuels that can circulate and spare glucose, and ketone body metabolism covers both their synthesis and their oxidation elsewhere. Hepatic mitochondria condense acetyl-CoA through a thiolase and the rate-setting HMG-CoA synthase HMGCS2, then HMGCL cleaves HMG-CoA to acetoacetate, which BDH1 reduces to beta-hydroxybutyrate; acetone arises by spontaneous decarboxylation. Because liver lacks the CoA transferase OXCT1, synthesis is effectively one-way, and the exported ketones are taken up by brain, heart and skeletal muscle, where OXCT1 and thiolase regenerate acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. Cytosolic AACS instead activates acetoacetate for lipid synthesis. This fuel switch sustains the brain during starvation and on ketogenic diets; inherited defects in the synthesizing or utilizing enzymes cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia or recurrent ketoacidotic crises, and uncontrolled flux underlies diabetic ketoacidosis.

Rather than build purine rings from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released by nucleic acid turnover and reattach them to ribose phosphate, an energetically cheap route that supplies much of the adenine and guanine nucleotide pool. Purine salvage matters most where de novo synthesis is weak: loss of HPRT1, which recycles hypoxanthine and guanine, causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease, while ADA deficiency poisons lymphocytes with deoxyadenosine metabolites and produces severe combined immunodeficiency. APRT handles adenine, nucleoside phosphorylase and deaminases feed bases back into the pool, and kinases such as ADK, DCK and DGUOK phosphorylate ribo- and deoxyribonucleosides, the last two also activating nucleoside analogue drugs. AMP deaminases and GMP reductases interconvert the adenine and guanine branches, linking salvage to purine balance and to urate production.

Purine catabolism is the route by which cells dispose of excess purine nucleotides, degrading them stepwise to urate for excretion in urine. In humans and other hominoids the pathway stops at uric acid, since urate oxidase has been lost, so the poorly soluble end product can crystallise in joints and kidneys and cause gout and urate nephropathy. Nucleotidases and phosphatases of the NT5 and NUDT families strip phosphates from mono- and diphosphorylated purines, purine nucleoside phosphorylase releases hypoxanthine and guanine from their nucleosides, guanine deaminase converts guanine to xanthine, and xanthine dehydrogenase oxidises hypoxanthine to xanthine and then to urate. Several of the same hydrolases sanitise the nucleotide pool by removing oxidised or otherwise damaged purines before they are incorporated into DNA or RNA, linking waste disposal to genome integrity and to the handling of thiopurine drugs.

IRS activation is the first committed step downstream of the insulin receptor, converting hormone binding into a phosphotyrosine platform that the rest of insulin signalling docks onto. It is what allows insulin to lower blood glucose by driving glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, and growth-promoting gene expression; loss or chronic inhibitory phosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 is a molecular basis of insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, and IRS2 failure in particular compromises pancreatic beta cell mass. Mechanistically, insulin-bound receptor autophosphorylates, and IRS1 engages the juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain while its PH domain grips membrane phospholipids. The receptor kinase then phosphorylates multiple IRS tyrosines, releasing the scaffold to recruit PI3K and Grb2-SOS and thereby branch into AKT and MAP kinase cascades. GRB10 binds the activated receptor as a negative regulator, tuning signal output.

Insulin's message gets past the receptor only through a docking protein, and IRS activation is that step: the activated insulin receptor recruits IRS1 or IRS2 and phosphorylates them on multiple tyrosines, converting them into membrane-associated scaffolds that assemble downstream effectors. This is what couples insulin binding to PI3K-dependent glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis, and to the Ras-MAP kinase arm controlling growth and gene expression. IRS1 engages the receptor's juxtamembrane phosphotyrosine through its PTB domain, with its PH domain anchoring it to membrane phospholipids, then releases once phosphorylated so that SH2-containing partners can bind. GRB10 competes at the receptor and dampens the output, one of several brakes on the pathway. Loss or serine-phosphorylation-driven inactivation of IRS proteins underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes, making this node the main site where metabolic signalling is tuned.

Signal attenuation is the shut-off phase of insulin action, the step that makes the hormonal signal transient and proportional to circulating insulin rather than self-sustaining. After the insulin receptor and its ligand are internalised, insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen and endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases dephosphorylate the receptor and its docking substrates, so that IRS1 and IRS2, SHC1, GRB2-SOS1 and the downstream ERK module can no longer be recruited and the assembled signalling complexes collapse. Adaptors such as GRB10 contribute by dampening receptor output. Termination matters because sustained receptor phosphorylation would uncouple glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid synthesis, and growth signalling from feeding; conversely, excessive or premature attenuation through phosphatase and adaptor activity contributes to insulin resistance. The pathway therefore sets signal duration and sensitivity in metabolic tissues and links receptor trafficking to endocrine control.

Insulin signalling must be switched off as well as on, and signal attenuation is the step that returns a stimulated cell to baseline after an insulin pulse. Once ligand and receptor dissociate inside the endosome and insulin is degraded in the endosomal lumen, endosome-associated protein tyrosine phosphatases strip phosphate from the activated insulin receptor and from its docking substrates. Dephosphorylation of IRS1 and IRS2 releases the adaptors and exchange factors they recruit — GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 — so the complexes that feed the ERK arm through MAPK1 and MAPK3 fall apart, and the adaptor GRB10 contributes further negative regulation of the receptor. Loss of this shutdown leaves growth and metabolic signalling running without a hormonal cue, while excessive attenuation blunts insulin action and contributes to insulin resistance, making it part of how glucose homeostasis is kept responsive.

Insulin binding to its receptor triggers receptor autophosphorylation, and the cascade that follows converts a hormonal signal about nutrient availability into glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid storage, and growth. Phosphotyrosines on the receptor recruit IRS1 and IRS2 or SHC1, which branch into two routes: GRB2-SOS1 loading of RAS proteins and the ERK1/2 kinases toward proliferative and transcriptional output, and PI3K with its regulatory subunits generating the lipid that activates PDPK1 and AKT2 for the metabolic arm, including PDE3B-mediated suppression of lipolysis. Adaptors and modulators such as GAB1/2, PTPN11, GRB10 and TRIB3 tune the strength of the response, and receptor internalisation into endosomes terminates it. Blunted flux through this cascade underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Related receptor tyrosine kinases, notably the FGF receptors with FRS2 and the klotho co-receptors, feed the same downstream machinery.

Insulin acts on cells through a receptor tyrosine kinase, and signalling by the insulin receptor is how a rise in blood glucose is converted into glucose uptake, glycogen and lipid storage, and suppression of lipolysis; its blunting underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. Insulin binding triggers receptor autophosphorylation and tyrosine phosphorylation of IRS1/IRS2 and SHC1, which recruit PI3K subunits and PDPK1 to activate AKT2 (driving GLUT4 delivery and PDE3B-mediated antilipolysis) or engage GRB2-SOS1 and RAS to reach ERK1/2. Signalling continues after internalisation: vacuolar ATPase-driven endosomal acidification releases insulin for degradation by insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin D, and phosphatases such as PTPN1 and PTPRF, together with GRB10 and TRIB3, terminate or restrain output. Related receptor kinases, including FGF receptors with their klotho co-receptors and FLT3, share the same adaptor and effector modules.

RNA Polymerase III Abortive And Retractive Initiation describes the false starts that precede productive synthesis of tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA and other short non-coding transcripts. Before Pol III commits to elongation it repeatedly makes and releases short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent RNA back into the active site, a proofreading-like cycle that sets how efficiently the polymerase clears its promoter and therefore how much translational and splicing capacity a cell builds. The machinery is the full Pol III enzyme with its shared and specific subunits, loaded by TFIIIB (TBP with BRF1 or BRF2 and BDP1), the six-subunit TFIIIC that reads internal A- and B-box promoters, TFIIIA for 5S genes, and the SNAPc complex with ZNF143 and POU2F1 at type 3 external promoters; La protein binds the released transcripts. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies growth signalling and oncogenic transformation.

RNA polymerase III makes the small structural RNAs a cell needs constantly — tRNAs, 5S rRNA, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others — so the rate at which it commits to productive synthesis sets the ceiling on protein synthesis and ribosome production. This step describes what happens immediately after the enzyme opens promoter DNA: the polymerase repeatedly synthesises and releases very short oligonucleotides, and can retract the nascent transcript, before it escapes the promoter and elongates processively. Promoter recognition upstream of this depends on distinct assembly factors for the different promoter classes — the multisubunit TFIIIC complex with TFIIIA at 5S genes, TBP-associated BRF1 and BDP1 at tRNA genes, and BRF2 with the SNAPc complex and ZNF143 at U6-type type 3 promoters. The La protein binds the uridylate-rich 3' ends of the released products. Deregulated Pol III output accompanies oncogenic growth, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy.

When DNA is damaged, cells must not enter mitosis with broken chromosomes, and this is the arm of the G2/M checkpoint that enforces the block by keeping the mitotic kinase switched off. Chk1 and Chk2, activated downstream of the damage-sensing ATR and ATM kinases, phosphorylate the Cdc25C phosphatase, creating 14-3-3 binding sites so that the adaptor proteins sequester it away from the nucleus; in parallel the Wee1 kinase is favoured, maintaining inhibitory tyrosine phosphorylation on CDK1. The net result is that cyclin B:CDK1, and the related cyclin A complexes, remain inactive and mitotic entry is delayed until repair is complete. Loss of this restraint permits premature chromosome condensation, mitotic catastrophe and genomic instability, and the same circuitry explains why checkpoint kinase and Wee1 inhibitors sensitise tumour cells to DNA-damaging treatment.

mRNA Editing: A to I Conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans, in which adenosine deaminases acting on RNA convert adenosine to inosine within double-stranded regions of pre-mRNA. Because the ribosome and spliceosome read inosine as guanosine, editing recodes codons, alters splice sites, and diversifies the proteome beyond what the genome encodes. It is most active in brain, where recoding of the GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit at the Q/R site makes the receptor impermeable to calcium and protects neurons from excitotoxicity, and where editing of the 5-HT2C serotonin receptor tunes G-protein coupling. ADAR and ADARB1 carry out this chemistry through paired double-stranded RNA-binding domains and a catalytic deaminase domain, with duplex structure formed by intronic complementary sequences specifying which adenosines are targeted. Editing of endogenous duplexes also marks them as self, restraining innate immune sensing of cellular RNA.

Adenosine-to-inosine conversion is the most common form of RNA editing in humans, rewriting transcripts after they are made so that a single gene can yield proteins of different function. Because the ribosome reads inosine as guanosine, editing within coding sequence changes amino acids: the best-known case recodes a glutamine to arginine in the GluA2 AMPA receptor subunit, making the assembled receptor impermeable to calcium and protecting neurons from excitotoxic damage. Editing of serotonin 5-HT2C receptor transcripts similarly tunes G-protein coupling efficiency. The reaction is carried out by double-stranded RNA-specific adenosine deaminases, ADAR and ADARB1, which recognise duplex structure in pre-mRNA formed with complementary intronic sequence rather than a linear consensus. Activity is highest in brain, and beyond recoding, widespread editing of repetitive duplexes marks transcripts as self and restrains innate immune sensing of endogenous RNA.

Most human genes are spliced, but a minority are transcribed as intronless units whose capped pre-mRNAs must be matured by 3' end formation alone, and this pathway covers how those transcripts are finished and made export-competent. Two outcomes are possible. Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are cleaved rather than polyadenylated: the U7 small RNP, built on the specialised Sm-like proteins LSM10 and LSM11 together with core Sm subunits, is guided with ZNF473 and the stem-loop binding protein SLBP to generate the conserved histone 3' stem-loop, coupling histone supply to S phase. All other intronless transcripts acquire a poly(A) tail through the canonical machinery - CPSF and CstF subcomplexes, symplekin, PCF11, poly(A) polymerase and PABPN1 - with the nuclear cap-binding complex marking the 5' end. Because no 3' splice site is available to license cleavage, alternative signals must activate polyadenylation, tying transcript stability and nuclear export to end processing.

Some messenger RNAs do not say what the genome says: specific bases are chemically converted after transcription, so one gene can yield proteins of different sequence. This substitution-type mRNA editing is the form used in humans, and it matters because it diversifies coding capacity and tunes transcript fate without changing DNA. Adenosine deaminases acting on RNA, ADAR and ADARB1, convert adenosine to inosine in double-stranded regions, which is read as guanosine and alters codons in targets such as neurotransmitter receptors while also marking endogenous duplex RNA so it is not mistaken for a viral trigger of interferon responses. On the cytidine side, APOBEC1 with its cofactor A1CF deaminates cytidine to uridine in apolipoprotein B mRNA, creating a stop codon and a shortened protein that reshapes lipid transport; related APOBEC3 deaminases act on viral and retroelement nucleic acids. Both reactions release ammonia.

Some mRNAs are rewritten after transcription, and formation of the editosome is the assembly step that makes one such rewrite possible: a cytidine deaminase is brought together with an RNA-binding specificity factor and the target transcript so that a single cytidine can be converted to uridine. The best-understood outcome is in apolipoprotein B mRNA, where APOBEC1 acting with its complementation factor A1CF creates a premature stop codon and yields the shorter ApoB-48 protein used for intestinal chylomicron assembly, while the unedited transcript gives the hepatic ApoB-100 that carries LDL cholesterol. Editing site selection depends on the factor that recognises the sequence context rather than on the deaminase alone. Related family members act instead on DNA cytidines in antiviral defence and antibody diversification, and their mistargeting is a recognised source of mutational damage in cancer genomes.

Adenosine bases in double-stranded RNA can be hydrolytically deaminated at the C6 position, converting them to inosine and releasing ammonia. Because the ribosome and the splicing machinery read inosine as guanosine, this chemistry recodes transcripts after they are made: it changes codons, creates or destroys splice sites, alters microRNA targeting, and destabilises long duplexes in untranslated regions and repeat elements. The two enzymes responsible act on structured RNA rather than free nucleosides, and their editing of endogenous double-stranded RNA marks it as self, preventing cytosolic sensors from launching an interferon response; loss of this self-marking underlies Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and related interferonopathies. Site-selective editing in the brain tunes glutamate and serotonin receptor properties, so the reaction matters for neuronal excitability as well as for innate immune tolerance, and its dysregulation is recurrent in cancer.

De novo fatty acid synthesis and activation supplies cells with the acyl chains used for membrane phospholipids, storage triglycerides, protein lipidation and energy, and it is the route by which excess dietary carbohydrate is converted into fat. Citrate exported from mitochondria is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase to cytosolic acetyl-CoA, carboxylated by acetyl-CoA carboxylase to malonyl-CoA, and condensed iteratively by fatty acid synthase to palmitate. Elongation of palmitate to longer chains occurs at the endoplasmic reticulum through the ELOVL condensing enzymes working with the ketoacyl reductase, dehydratase and trans-enoyl reductase steps, while stearoyl-CoA desaturases introduce the first double bond. Long-chain acyl-CoA synthetases and fatty acid transport proteins then thioesterify free fatty acids to CoA, committing them to downstream lipid metabolism. This biology is upregulated in many tumours and underlies inherited disorders of very-long-chain lipid synthesis affecting retina, skin and nervous system.

This is the step that lets a death receptor signal reach the mitochondrion. When Fas or TNF-family receptors engage, caspase-8 in the receptor complex cleaves the BH3-only protein BID, and the resulting truncated fragment is N-myristoylated by N-myristoyltransferase and targeted to the outer mitochondrial membrane. There it promotes BAX and BAK oligomerization and neutralizes anti-apoptotic BCL-2 relatives, so cytochrome c release and apoptosome-driven caspase activation amplify a signal that began at the cell surface. Granzyme B delivered by cytotoxic lymphocytes cleaves BID at a distinct site, giving killer cells the same route into the mitochondrial death machinery. The pathway therefore couples the extrinsic and intrinsic arms of apoptosis, and matters most in cells whose receptor-initiated caspase activity is too weak to kill without mitochondrial amplification, such as hepatocytes during immune-mediated liver injury.

Triglyceride biosynthesis is how cells package fatty acids into a neutral, osmotically inert storage form, filling the lipid droplets of adipose tissue and supplying the triacylglycerol exported in intestinal chylomicrons and hepatic VLDL. It is the anabolic counterpart of lipolysis and the point at which surplus dietary and de novo fatty acids are taken out of circulation; when it fails or runs unchecked the result is lipodystrophy at one extreme and hepatic steatosis and insulin resistance at the other. The route begins with glycerol phosphate, produced by glycerol kinase or from glycolysis, which is acylated by glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases and further acylated to phosphatidic acid. Lipin-family phosphatidate phosphatases then dephosphorylate phosphatidic acid to diacylglycerol, a branch point shared with phospholipid synthesis, and DGAT1 and DGAT2 add the final acyl chain. An alternative monoacylglycerol pathway, via MOGAT enzymes, dominates in enterocytes resynthesising fat absorbed from the gut lumen.

Once a cell has committed to die, the execution phase carries out the demolition that makes apoptosis recognisable: chromatin condenses, DNA is cut into fragments, the nucleus and other organelles break down, and the cell shrinks, blebs and detaches from its neighbours. Effector caspases 3, 6 and 7, activated downstream of initiator caspase 8, cleave a defined set of structural and regulatory substrates rather than degrading the proteome wholesale. Targets include the nuclear lamins and lamin-associated factors, cytoskeletal and membrane-anchoring proteins such as vimentin, plectin, spectrin, gelsolin and adducin, junctional components including desmosomal cadherins, plakophilin, occludin and tight-junction scaffolds, and the inhibitor of the DNA fragmentation nuclease, whose cleavage releases nuclease activity. ROCK1 and PAK2 cleavage drives membrane blebbing, while DNM1L participates in mitochondrial fragmentation. Orderly execution keeps dying cells packaged for phagocytosis, limiting inflammation during tissue turnover.

Killing by death receptor engagement begins here: FasL binding to the Fas receptor triggers apoptosis in the target cell, the route cytotoxic T cells and NK cells use to delete infected and tumour cells and the route by which activated lymphocytes are removed once an immune response ends. Ligand binding clusters the receptor, whose cytoplasmic death domain recruits the adaptor FADD, which in turn brings in the initiator caspases CASP8 and CASP10; their proximity-induced activation launches the caspase cascade, either directly or by amplification through mitochondrial permeabilisation. Loss of this signalling causes lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity, as unwanted lymphocytes survive, and contributes to tumour escape from immune attack; excessive Fas signalling instead drives hepatocyte death. The same receptor complex can also, in modified form, feed into inflammatory and necroptotic outcomes.

TRAIL signaling is an extrinsic apoptosis route in which the TNF-family ligand TRAIL kills target cells by engaging death receptors on their surface. It matters because it preferentially destroys transformed and virus-infected cells while sparing most normal tissue, making it an arm of immune surveillance by NK cells and cytotoxic lymphocytes and a long-standing target for cancer therapeutics. Ligand binding clusters TNFRSF10A and TNFRSF10B, whose cytoplasmic death domains recruit the adaptor FADD and procaspase-8 and -10 into a death-inducing signalling complex; local dimerisation activates the initiator caspases, which then cleave effector caspases or BID to amplify the signal through mitochondria. Sensitivity is set by competing components: cFLIP occupies the complex without catalytic activity, and decoy receptors such as TNFRSF10D bind ligand without transmitting death, mechanisms tumours exploit to acquire resistance.

TRAIL signalling is one of the extrinsic routes to apoptosis, in which a TNF-family ligand kills a target cell from outside by engaging death receptors on its surface. It contributes to immune surveillance of tumour and virus-infected cells, and its selectivity for transformed cells over normal ones has made the pathway a template for cancer therapeutics. Ligand binding to the death receptors TRAIL-R1 and TRAIL-R2 clusters their cytoplasmic death domains, which recruit the adaptor FADD and, through it, procaspase-8 and procaspase-10 into a death-inducing signalling complex where the initiator caspases dimerise and self-cleave. The catalytically inactive homologue CFLAR competes for the same platform and blocks caspase activation, and a receptor lacking a functional death domain further buffers the response. Resistance at these checkpoints determines whether cells survive TRAIL exposure.

Fibrinolysis clears a clot once it has served its purpose, and this is the route by which crosslinked fibrin is degraded to soluble fragments. Without it, thrombi persist and occlude vessels; with too much of it, bleeding follows, which is why the pathway is the target of thrombolytic drugs and of antifibrinolytic agents. The zymogen plasminogen is converted to the serine protease plasmin by tissue-type plasminogen activator acting on the fibrin surface, or by urokinase bound to its receptor on cell membranes, the latter route serving tissue remodelling, cell migration and inflammation more than intravascular clot removal. Assembly on a surface is itself regulatory: an annexin A2/S100A10 complex provides a cell-surface docking site, while free enzyme in plasma is inefficient. Serpins including plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and alpha-2-antiplasmin, together with histidine-rich glycoprotein, restrain both the activators and plasmin itself.

Cyclin D must be destroyed once it has done its job, and ubiquitin-dependent degradation of cyclin D is how cells impose a time limit on G1 Cdk4/Cdk6 activity. Because cyclin D levels set the threshold for Rb phosphorylation and commitment to division, failure to clear the protein leaves the kinase active and the G1 restriction point permeable, a state common in cancers where cyclin D1 is amplified or stabilised. Phosphorylation of threonine-286 by GSK3-beta marks the cyclin for nuclear export and ubiquitin conjugation, after which the polyubiquitinated protein is delivered to the 26S proteasome; the core alpha and beta subunits of the catalytic chamber, the ATPase ring, and the ubiquitin-receptor components of the 19S lid carry out recognition and proteolysis, with ubiquitin supplied from the several precursor and ribosomal fusion genes. Loss of cyclin D at the end of G1 hands control to the E-type cyclins for S phase entry.

Fatty acids longer than 20 carbons are built by adding two carbons at a time to dietary or de novo-made palmitate and stearate, and this elongation supplies the acyl chains of sphingolipids and ceramides, the lipids of skin barrier, retina and myelin, and precursors for eicosanoid hormones that drive and resolve inflammation. Unlike cytosolic de novo synthesis by one multifunctional enzyme, synthesis of very long-chain fatty acyl-CoAs is carried out by separate endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins: acyl-CoA synthetases such as the ACSL and ACSBG families first activate the fatty acid with coenzyme A, ELOVL condensing enzymes add malonyl-CoA-derived carbons, HSD17B12 reduces the 3-oxoacyl intermediate, HACD dehydratases remove water, and TECR performs the final trans-2,3-enoyl-CoA reduction. Differing tissue expression and chain-length preferences among these families give each tissue its own acyl chain profile; loss of individual elongation steps causes retinal degeneration, ichthyosis and neurological disease.

When a vessel wall is breached, the subendothelial collagen beneath is exposed to flowing blood, and platelet capture on that surface is the first step in building a haemostatic plug. Without it bleeding continues unchecked, as in von Willebrand disease or Bernard-Soulier syndrome; with it in the wrong place, arterial thrombosis follows plaque rupture. Von Willebrand factor bridges collagen to the platelet GPIb-IX-V complex, an interaction that becomes stronger as shear stress rises and so tethers platelets under arterial flow; the protease ADAMTS13 trims multimers to keep this in check. Integrin alpha2-beta1 then provides firm, magnesium-dependent attachment to a collagen recognition motif, while GPVI paired with the FcR gamma chain converts collagen contact into activation, using Src kinases Fyn and Lyn to phosphorylate ITAM tyrosines and recruit Syk. Adhesion, mechanosensing, and outside-in signalling are thus inseparable here.

TNF signaling is the inflammatory response cells mount to tumor necrosis factor alpha, released by macrophages, T cells and many non-immune tissues after injury or infection. It decides whether a stimulated cell survives and inflames or dies, and its dysregulation drives rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis, which is why TNF blockade is a mainstay of therapy. Ligand binding to TNFR1 nucleates a complex of TRADD, TRAF2, RIPK1 and the ubiquitin ligases cIAP1/2 and LUBAC; the ubiquitin chains they build recruit the TAK1 and IKK complexes, activating NF-kappaB and MAP kinase programs that induce anti-apoptotic proteins and cytokines. Deubiquitinases such as CYLD, A20 and OTULIN restrain this output. When survival signalling is blocked, RIPK1 assembles with FADD and caspase-8 to trigger apoptosis, or with RIPK3 for necroptosis, while sphingomyelinase-derived ceramide adds a parallel pro-apoptotic arm.

TNF signaling decides, cell by cell, whether an inflammatory stimulus ends in survival or death. TNF-α released from immune and stromal cells engages TNFR1 (TNFRSF1A), and the receptor assembles TRADD, TRAF2 and RIPK1 with ubiquitin ligases including BIRC2/3 and the linear ubiquitin chain complex (RNF31, RBCK1, SHARPIN). Those chains recruit the TAK1–TAB and IKK complexes, which activate NF-κB and MAP kinase output, driving pro-inflammatory cytokine production and anti-apoptotic proteins such as cFLIP and XIAP. Deubiquitinases — CYLD with SPATA2, A20, OTULIN — restrain this, and when the survival arm fails, RIPK1 moves into a FADD:caspase-8 platform for apoptosis or the RIPK3 necrosome. Sphingomyelinase-derived ceramide adds a parallel pro-apoptotic signal. Dysregulation underlies chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease, the target of anti-TNF therapy.

Plasmalogens are ether-linked phospholipids that make up a large share of membrane phospholipid in brain, heart and myelin, and their synthesis begins in the peroxisome. The committed steps start from dihydroxyacetone phosphate: an acyltransferase esterifies it with a long-chain acyl-CoA, a synthase exchanges that acyl chain for a fatty alcohol to create the defining ether bond, and a reductase converts the product to an alkylglycerophosphate that is finished in the endoplasmic reticulum into the vinyl-ether plasmalogens. Because the first two enzymes are peroxisomal, plasmalogen deficiency is a hallmark of peroxisome biogenesis disorders, and mutations in the acyltransferase or synthase themselves cause rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, with skeletal shortening, cataracts and severe neurodevelopmental impairment. The lipids contribute to membrane fluidity, myelin stability and protection against oxidative damage.

Transcription from mitochondrial promoters produces all RNA made inside mitochondria: the 13 respiratory chain subunits, 2 rRNAs and 22 tRNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA. Because the organelle cannot import these transcripts, this step sets how much oxidative phosphorylation machinery a cell can build, and its failure causes mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis, myopathy and neurodegeneration. The system is minimal and bacteriophage-like rather than nuclear: a single-subunit RNA polymerase, POLRMT, is recruited to the light-strand and heavy-strand promoters in the non-coding control region by TFAM, which also packages the circular genome into nucleoids, and by the initiation factor TFB2M, which melts the promoter. Each strand is transcribed as a polycistronic precursor that is later cleaved into individual tRNAs and mRNAs. MTERF1 terminates transcription past the rRNA genes, helping explain why ribosomal RNAs accumulate far above mRNA levels. The same promoter region couples transcription to mitochondrial DNA replication priming.

Mitochondria carry their own genome and must transcribe it themselves, and transcription from mitochondrial promoters is how the thirteen respiratory chain subunits, two rRNAs and twenty-two tRNAs encoded there are expressed. Without it oxidative phosphorylation cannot be assembled, and defects in this machinery cause mitochondrial depletion and multisystem energy-failure disease. A dedicated single-subunit RNA polymerase, POLRMT, is recruited to the light- and heavy-strand promoters in the non-coding control region by TFAM, which bends and packages the DNA, together with the initiation factor TFB2M that melts the template. Each promoter yields a long polycistronic precursor that is later cleaved into individual mRNAs and tRNAs. MTERF1 binds near the tRNA-Leu gene and terminates the rRNA-containing unit, helping explain why ribosomal RNAs accumulate far above mRNA levels. The same factors couple transcription to mitochondrial DNA copy number and replication priming.

RNA Polymerase II Transcription Initiation is the moment at which a promoter-bound polymerase makes its first phosphodiester bond, committing the cell to synthesising a messenger RNA. Every protein-coding gene depends on it, and it is the step at which most regulatory signals converge, so defects in its components cause developmental and repair disorders — mutations in the TFIIH helicases ERCC2 and ERCC3 underlie xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy. TBP and the TAFs of TFIID recognise the promoter, TFIIA, TFIIB and TFIIF position the twelve-subunit polymerase, and TFIIE with TFIIH melts the duplex using ATP hydrolysis to expose the template strand in the active site. The open complex is unstable and yields abortive dinucleotide products until escape succeeds; TFIIB then leaves, and the CDK7–cyclin H kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license promoter clearance and elongation.

Every protein-coding gene begins its expression here: RNA polymerase II, guided to a promoter by TBP and the TAF subunits of TFIID and by the general factors TFIIA, TFIIB, TFIIE, TFIIF and TFIIH, melts the DNA duplex and makes the first phosphodiester bond. Opening the promoter places the template strand in the catalytic center, and the resulting open complex is unstable, reverting to the closed state and releasing short abortive transcripts until a stable elongating polymerase escapes; TFIIB leaves once synthesis starts. The helicase subunits ERCC2 and ERCC3 within TFIIH drive strand opening using ATP hydrolysis, while the CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain to license the transition to elongation and capping. Because TFIIH is shared with nucleotide excision repair, mutations in its subunits cause xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy, and TAF defects give tissue-restricted developmental disease.

After RNA polymerase II clears a promoter it pauses, and the transition into productive transcription elongation is where most metazoan genes are actually controlled. This step sets how fast and how far the polymerase travels through a gene, and it couples synthesis to capping, splicing and export, so its failure produces truncated or unprocessed transcripts rather than simply less mRNA. The twelve-subunit polymerase is held in a paused state by the NELF complex together with DSIF (SUPT4H1-SUPT5H), and release requires P-TEFb (CDK9 with cyclin T) to phosphorylate Ser2 of the polymerase C-terminal domain, while TFIIH-associated CDK7 marks Ser5 earlier and CTDP1 reverses CTD marks. Elongation factors TFIIS, ELL and elongin help the enzyme resume after arrest, the PAF1 complex and the FACT histone chaperone let it pass nucleosomes, and the nuclear cap-binding proteins join nascent RNA. Several components are recurrent leukaemia fusion partners.

Haemostasis depends on platelets recognising vascular injury, switching to an adhesive and procoagulant state, and sticking to one another to plug the breach; excessive or misplaced activation produces arterial thrombosis, while loss of its components causes bleeding disorders such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Platelet activation, signaling and aggregation begins when collagen engages GPVI and the GPIb-IX-V complex binds von Willebrand factor, and when thrombin cleaves protease-activated receptors and secreted ADP acts on P2Y1 and P2Y12. Src-family kinases, Syk, PLC-gamma2, PI3K and protein kinase C raise intracellular calcium through IP3 receptors, driving Rap1- and talin/kindlin-dependent activation of integrin alphaIIbbeta3 for fibrinogen binding, cytoskeletal remodelling and shape change. Alpha and dense granules then release fibrinogen, P-selectin, thrombospondin and growth factors, amplifying recruitment and exposing a procoagulant phospholipid surface.

A rise in cytosolic calcium is the switch that converts a resting platelet into a secreting, aggregating one, and this pathway covers what follows that signal at a wounded vessel wall. Calcium, together with diacylglycerol generated by phospholipase C from PIP2, activates protein kinase C isoforms such as PRKCA and PRKCB, which drive granule release and integrin activation. The bulk of the genes are cargo: alpha-granule contents including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen chains, thrombospondin, platelet factor 4, factor V, growth factors (PDGF, VEGF, TGF-beta) and protease inhibitors, plus dense and lysosomal markers like CD63 and LAMP2. SNARE and Rab machinery (STX4, STXBP2, VTI1B, RAB27B) executes membrane fusion, while talin and kindlin-3 with ACTN and filamin link the activated ITGA2B/ITGB3 receptor to a remodelling cytoskeleton. Defects impair haemostasis and wound repair; excess promotes thrombosis.

When a vessel wall is breached, platelets must stick to the damaged surface and then to each other to seal it; platelet aggregation is that plug-forming step, and without it bleeding continues, while inappropriate activation produces the occlusive thrombi of heart attack and stroke. Tethering begins with the GPIb-IX-V complex capturing von Willebrand factor on exposed collagen, and firm adhesion follows when integrin alphaIIb-beta3 switches to a high-affinity state and cross-links neighbouring platelets through fibrinogen chains and fibronectin. Inside the platelet, RAP1B loading by CalDAG-GEFI and cAMP-responsive exchange factors, together with talin binding to the beta3 tail, drives that conformational change, while Src-family and SYK kinases, FAK and adaptor scaffolds transmit force and receptor occupancy back into the cytoskeleton. Thrombin and adrenergic receptors amplify the response, linking coagulation and sympathetic tone to plug stability.

Every protein-coding gene begins its expression here: RNA polymerase II must be placed at a promoter, the DNA duplex opened, and the first short RNA made before productive elongation can begin. TBP and the TAF subunits of TFIID recognise promoter DNA, TFIIA and TFIIB stabilise that recognition and set the start site, TFIIF delivers the twelve-subunit polymerase, and TFIIE recruits TFIIH, whose ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicase subunits melt the template while the CDK7–cyclin H–MNAT1 kinase module phosphorylates the polymerase C-terminal domain. Those phosphorylation marks release the enzyme from initiation factors, and promoter clearance is complete once the growing transcript is stably held in the active site. This step is where most regulated gene control converges, since activators and repressors act by promoting or blocking assembly of this complex; the same TFIIH subunits also serve nucleotide excision repair, and their mutation causes xeroderma pigmentosum and trichothiodystrophy.

RNA polymerase III makes the short untranslated RNAs a cell needs in bulk "ribosomal 5S rRNA, all tRNAs, U6 snRNA, 7SL and others" so initiation at its promoters sets the ceiling on protein synthesis capacity and is tightly coupled to growth signalling; mutations in polymerase III subunits and its initiation factors cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and other developmental disorders. Promoter recognition takes three forms. Gene-internal A/C blocks in 5S genes are read by GTF3A with the multisubunit TFIIIC complex; internal A and B boxes in tRNA genes are bound by TFIIIC alone; and upstream type 3 promoters use the SNAP complex, TBP and ZNF143 with POU2F1 at the distal enhancer. Each route converges on TBP-containing TFIIIB, built from BDP1 with BRF1 or BRF2, which recruits the polymerase"whose subunits are partly shared with polymerases I and II"and opens the DNA to begin synthesis.

Ribosome production depends on a steady supply of 5S ribosomal RNA, and this is the route by which RNA polymerase III is loaded onto the 5S rRNA gene, the classic type 1 promoter with its internal control region. Assembly is strictly ordered: the nine-zinc-finger factor TFIIIA binds the internal promoter first, creating a platform for the multisubunit TFIIIC complex, which in turn positions a TBP-containing TFIIIB built around BRF1 and BDP1 upstream of the start site; TFIIIB then recruits the polymerase itself, whose catalytic core (POLR3A, POLR3B) is completed by subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Output from this pathway sets the ceiling on ribosome assembly and is tied to growth control, and mutations in polymerase III subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and impair innate sensing of cytosolic DNA.

Transfer RNAs and other short non-coding RNAs are made by RNA polymerase III, and type 2 promoters are the internal A-box/B-box arrangement found in tRNA and Alu-type genes. Initiation here begins with the multisubunit TFIIIC complex binding the two internal boxes directly, without needing the TFIIIA zinc-finger factor required at 5S rRNA promoters. TFIIIC then recruits TFIIIB, built from BRF1, BDP1 and TBP, which positions the polymerase over the start site; once TFIIIB is stably engaged, it alone can sustain repeated rounds of transcription. The seventeen-subunit enzyme includes catalytic POLR3A and POLR3B plus subunits shared with polymerases I and II. Output from this system sets the cell's translational capacity, is tuned to growth and nutrient signals through mTOR and MYC, and mutations in its subunits cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophies and related neurodevelopmental disease.

A handful of small non-coding RNAs, notably the spliceosomal U6 snRNA, are made by RNA polymerase III from gene-external promoters that look more like those of polymerase II genes than like classical tRNA promoters. Initiation from these metazoan-specific type 3 promoters supplies the U6 and related transcripts on which pre-mRNA splicing and other RNA processing depend, so the cell's capacity to mature its own messages is set here. Recognition begins at the proximal sequence element by the five-subunit SNAPc complex (SNAPC1-SNAPC5), which cooperates with the polymerase III-specific TFIIIB variant built on BRF2, BDP1 and TBP bound at a TATA box; together they load the seventeen-subunit polymerase, whose core shares several small subunits with polymerases I and II. Upstream enhancer elements add POU2F1 at an octamer motif and the zinc-finger factor ZNF143 at the SPH element to raise output.

Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing recodes transcripts after they are made, and the ADAR enzymes that carry it out must first engage double-stranded RNA in a complex, the editosome, before deamination can occur. This is the assembly step for that machinery: ADAR1 and ADAR2 recognise duplex structures in pre-mRNA and other RNAs and convert adenosine to inosine, which the ribosome and splicing machinery read as guanosine. The consequences are twofold. Editing of coding sequence changes protein function, most famously in glutamate and serotonin receptor subunits, tuning neuronal excitability. Editing of repetitive duplexes in untranslated regions marks endogenous RNA as self, preventing MDA5 from triggering an interferon response; loss of this activity causes Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome and related interferonopathies. How the enzymes are recruited to particular targets, and what other subunits join them, remains poorly defined.

Newly initiated messenger RNAs are capped while still attached to the polymerase, and this step is what couples capping to the C-terminal domain of RNA polymerase II. Phosphorylation of the CTD heptad repeats at serine 5 by the CDK7-cyclin H-MNAT1 kinase module of TFIIH, acting just downstream of the promoter, creates the docking surface for the capping machinery: the guanylyltransferase RNGTT and the cap methyltransferase RNMT with its activating subunit RAMAC, with the elongation factor SUPT5H also contributing. Tethering the enzymes to the phosphorylated CTD restricts the 7-methylguanosine cap to polymerase II transcripts and links promoter clearance to the transition into productive elongation. The resulting cap protects the transcript from exonucleases and is required for splicing, export and translation initiation; the same TFIIH subunits, including the ERCC2 and ERCC3 helicases, serve nucleotide excision repair.

During fasting, prolonged exercise or a ketogenic diet, the liver exports beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate as circulating fuels, and utilization of ketone bodies is how extrahepatic tissues burn them. Brain, heart, skeletal muscle and kidney depend on this route when glucose is scarce, since ketones cross the blood-brain barrier and spare glucose and muscle protein. Mitochondrial BDH1 oxidizes beta-hydroxybutyrate back to acetoacetate, the CoA transferases OXCT1 and OXCT2 transfer CoA from succinyl-CoA to form acetoacetyl-CoA, and the thiolase ACAT1 cleaves it into two acetyl-CoA for entry into the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Because the liver lacks the CoA transferase step, it cannot consume the ketones it makes. Loss of OXCT1 or ACAT1 causes ketoacidosis crises in infancy, the latter also disrupting isoleucine catabolism. Acetone is a dead end, exhaled or excreted rather than recovered.

Synthesis of Ketone Bodies is the liver's route for converting fat-derived acetyl-CoA into acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, water-soluble fuels that circulate to heart, skeletal muscle and brain when carbohydrate is scarce. It is what allows fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate feeding to spare glucose for tissues that depend on it, and its loss causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and encephalopathy in infancy. Inside hepatocyte mitochondria, thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA units, HMG-CoA synthase 2 adds a third, and HMG-CoA lyase cleaves the intermediate to acetoacetate, which BDH1 reduces to beta-hydroxybutyrate using the NADH generated by beta-oxidation. HMGCS2 is the rate-setting, hormonally controlled step, induced by fasting and repressed by insulin. Related activating enzymes allow acetoacetate and acetate to be recaptured for lipogenesis. Unrestrained flux through this route, as in untreated diabetes, produces ketoacidosis.

When carbohydrate is scarce, the liver converts acetyl-CoA from fatty acid oxidation into ketone bodies that circulate as fuel, and this ketogenic route is what allows heart and skeletal muscle to burn acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate while the limited glucose supply is reserved for the brain. In hepatic mitochondria, a thiolase condenses two acetyl-CoA units to acetoacetyl-CoA, the mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase HMGCS2 adds a third to form HMG-CoA, HMG-CoA lyase cleaves it to acetoacetate, and BDH1 reduces that to beta-hydroxybutyrate; an acetoacetyl-CoA synthetase can also recapture ketone-derived carbon for lipid synthesis. Output rises during fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate feeding. In untreated diabetes, unrestrained fatty acid oxidation drives production beyond peripheral oxidative capacity, acidifying the blood and impairing oxygen delivery, while inherited defects of the lyase or synthase cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemic crises.

Fatty acids are burned for energy by repeated rounds of a four-step spiral that shortens the acyl chain by two carbons each turn, and this segment covers one such turn: myristoyl-CoA (C14) is converted to lauroyl-CoA (C12) with release of acetyl-CoA, plus FADH2 and NADH that feed the respiratory chain. The cycle matters most in heart, skeletal muscle and liver during fasting, when fat oxidation supplies ATP and ketone bodies. A long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase introduces the double bond, and the membrane-bound mitochondrial trifunctional protein, built from HADHA and HADHB subunits, carries out the hydration, NAD+-dependent oxidation and thiolytic cleavage in succession. Loss of trifunctional protein activity causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis, and maternal carriage of an affected fetus is linked to acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

Saturated fatty acids delivered into the mitochondrial matrix are dismantled two carbons at a time by the beta-oxidation spiral, the main route by which heart, skeletal muscle and liver generate ATP during fasting and sustained exercise, and the source of acetyl-CoA for hepatic ketogenesis. Each turn runs four reactions: an acyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidation feeding electrons to the respiratory chain, hydration of the resulting enoyl-CoA, a second NAD+-dependent oxidation, and thiolytic cleavage releasing acetyl-CoA plus a shortened acyl-CoA. Chain length is covered by a family of dehydrogenases spanning very long to short substrates, while the trifunctional protein subunits handle the long-chain hydratase, dehydrogenase and thiolase steps. Inherited deficiencies, most commonly of the medium-chain dehydrogenase, cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis during catabolic stress, and are screened for in newborns.

Most dietary fat is unsaturated, and mitochondrial beta-oxidation of unsaturated fatty acids is the set of accessory reactions that lets cis double bonds pass through a spiral built for trans intermediates. Without these steps, chains such as linoleoyl-CoA would stall part-way through degradation and fail to yield acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle and ketogenesis, compromising energy supply in heart, liver and muscle during fasting and exercise. An enoyl-CoA isomerase repositions an inconveniently placed double bond into the 2-trans configuration usable by the hydratase, while 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase uses NADPH to resolve intermediates carrying two double bonds before isomerisation returns them to the cycle. The core spiral itself is supplied by acyl-CoA dehydrogenases of differing chain-length preference and by the trifunctional protein subunits that carry out hydration, dehydrogenation and thiolytic cleavage; inherited defects in these cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy.

Mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation is how cells extract energy from fat, and it sustains the heart, skeletal muscle and liver during fasting, exercise and any period when glucose is scarce; hepatic ketone bodies made from its acetyl-CoA feed the brain. Once acyl-CoAs are delivered into the matrix by the carnitine system, a repeating four-step spiral of oxidation, hydration, second oxidation and thiolysis clips off two carbons per turn, yielding NADH and FADH2 for the respiratory chain plus acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. Chain-length-specific acyl-CoA dehydrogenases (very-long, long, medium, short) begin each round, and the trifunctional protein subunits HADHA/HADHB together with HADH and ECHS1 complete it; enoyl-CoA isomerase and 2,4-dienoyl-CoA reductase reroute unsaturated substrates. Accompanying thioesterases regulate acyl-CoA pools, while propionyl-CoA carboxylase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase steps handle odd-chain products. Inherited defects cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis.

Fatty acids are burned for energy by repeated rounds of a four-step spiral, and the conversion of palmitoyl-CoA to myristoyl-CoA is the first such round for this 16-carbon substrate, shortening it by two carbons and releasing acetyl-CoA plus reducing equivalents for the respiratory chain. The chemistry matters most in heart, skeletal muscle and liver during fasting or sustained exercise, when fat rather than glucose supplies ATP and hepatic ketone bodies.
