Dehydrogenation of the acyl-CoA is carried out by very long chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, after which the mitochondrial trifunctional protein, an inner-membrane complex of HADHA and HADHB subunits, performs hydration, NAD+-dependent 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA oxidation and thiolytic cleavage. Inherited deficiency of either enzyme causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy, rhabdomyolysis and accumulation of long-chain acylcarnitines, and is screened for in newborns.

Fatty acids are burned for energy two carbons at a time, and this is one turn of that mitochondrial spiral: the twelve-carbon lauroyl-CoA is shortened to decanoyl-CoA, which re-enters the cycle for further rounds. The acetyl-CoA released feeds the TCA cycle and, in liver, ketone body synthesis, making this chemistry the backbone of energy supply during fasting and sustained exercise, particularly in heart and skeletal muscle. Four sequential reactions do the work: an acyl-CoA dehydrogenase introduces a double bond and passes electrons to the respiratory chain via electron transfer flavoprotein, enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water, a 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidises the hydroxyl to a ketone, and a thiolase cleaves off acetyl-CoA. The trifunctional protein subunits carry the last two activities for longer chains. Inherited defects in these steps cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis under metabolic stress.

Fatty acids are burned for energy two carbons at a time, and this segment is the fourth turn of the mitochondrial beta-oxidation spiral, shortening decanoyl-CoA to octanoyl-CoA while yielding acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle plus FADH2 and NADH for respiration. The four chemical steps are dehydrogenation by the medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase ACADM, hydration by the crotonase ECHS1, NAD-dependent oxidation of the 3-hydroxyacyl group by HADH, and thiolytic cleavage by the alpha/beta subunits of the mitochondrial trifunctional protein. This chemistry matters most during fasting and sustained exercise, when muscle, heart and liver depend on fat rather than glucose; ketone body production for the brain depends on it too. Loss of ACADM is the common inherited defect, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic crises during fasting, while HADH and trifunctional protein deficiencies cause related cardiomyopathy and myopathy.

Fatty acids are burned for energy by repeated four-step cycles that shorten the acyl chain by two carbons each turn; this round takes the eight-carbon octanoyl-CoA to hexanoyl-CoA inside the mitochondrion, feeding acetyl-CoA to the TCA cycle and, in liver, to ketone body synthesis during fasting. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase introduces the double bond, ECHS1 hydrates it, HADH oxidises the hydroxyl to a ketone, and the thiolase activity of the membrane-associated trifunctional protein cleaves off acetyl-CoA. Because chain-length-specific enzymes handle successive passes, loss of the medium-chain dehydrogenase blocks the spiral at this point, causing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic crisis during fasting or illness; it is among the most common inherited disorders detected by newborn screening. Defects in the hydratase or hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase steps give distinct encephalopathic and hypoglycaemic presentations.

Fatty acids are dismantled two carbons at a time in the mitochondrial matrix, and this late turn of the beta-oxidation spiral shortens six-carbon hexanoyl-CoA to four-carbon butanoyl-CoA, feeding acetyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle and ketogenesis. It matters most when glucose is scarce, sustaining hepatic, cardiac and skeletal muscle energy supply during fasting and prolonged exercise. Four chemical steps recur: short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase introduces a double bond, enoyl-CoA hydratase adds water across it, short-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase oxidises the hydroxyl to a ketone, and a thiolase of the membrane-bound trifunctional protein cleaves off acetyl-CoA. Inherited defects at these short-chain steps cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and metabolic crisis with fasting; HADH loss also produces hyperinsulinism, and ECHS1 deficiency gives a Leigh-like encephalopathy reflecting its parallel role in valine catabolism.

The last turn of the mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation spiral takes the four-carbon butanoyl-CoA through to acetyl-CoA, completing the breakdown of long-chain fat into fuel for the citric acid cycle and for hepatic ketone body synthesis during fasting. Short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase introduces a double bond, the enoyl-CoA hydratase ECHS1 adds water across it, and the short-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase HADH oxidises the hydroxyl to a ketone, giving acetoacetyl-CoA, which a thiolase cleaves into two acetyl-CoA. Because this step sits at the end of the spiral, its failure blocks energy production from fat most acutely when glucose is scarce. Inherited deficiency of the short-chain dehydrogenase causes accumulation of butyryl carnitine detectable on newborn screening, while HADH loss produces hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia, linking this segment of fatty acid catabolism to insulin secretion as well as to fuel supply.

After insulin binds its receptor and the complex is internalised, the cell must decide the fate of both partners, and insulin receptor recycling is the route that destroys the hormone while returning the receptor to the cell surface. This sets how long a cell stays insulin-responsive and how quickly circulating insulin is cleared, so it bears directly on insulin sensitivity and on the resistance seen in type 2 diabetes. The vacuolar ATPase, represented here by the full complement of V0 and V1 subunits, pumps protons into the endosome; the resulting acidic pH releases insulin from the receptor, and the freed hormone is degraded by insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin D. Phosphatases such as PTP1B and PTPRF strip phosphates from the receptor's activated kinase domain, terminating downstream signalling and restoring a ligand-free receptor to the plasma membrane for another round of stimulation.

Centromeres are defined not by DNA sequence but by chromatin, and this pathway builds that chromatin: replication-independent deposition of the histone H3 variant CENP-A into nucleosomes at centromeric loci, together with the constitutive centromere-associated network that reads it. Because CENP-A-marked chromatin is the platform on which kinetochores are built each mitosis, its assembly determines where spindle microtubules attach; failure produces merotelic or lost attachments, chromosome missegregation and aneuploidy, and CENP-A overexpression and ectopic loading are recurrent features of tumours. The dedicated chaperone HJURP delivers new CENP-A, licensed by a Mis18-containing complex that restricts loading to a window outside S phase, while CENP-C and the CENP-T/W/S/X and CENP-H/I/K/M modules anchor outer kinetochore components such as KNL1. Canonical core histones, histone-binding subunits like RBBP4/7 and NPM1, and ATP-dependent remodellers including SMARCA5 and RSF1 supply general nucleosome deposition and spacing.

SLBP Dependent Processing of Replication-Dependent Histone Pre-mRNAs generates the mature messages for the core histones needed during S phase, and it does so without polyadenylation: instead of a poly(A) tail, these transcripts end in a conserved stem-loop produced by a single endonucleolytic cleavage. This is how a dividing cell matches histone supply to the amount of DNA it is replicating, and coupling of the pathway to the cell cycle keeps free histone from accumulating outside S phase. Stem-loop binding protein occupies the hairpin on the nascent transcript, while the U7 snRNP — built on Sm proteins plus the U7-specific LSM10 and LSM11 — base-pairs with the downstream element; ZNF473 bridges the two to position the cleavage machinery, with the cap-binding complex marking the 5' end. Stem-loop binding protein then accompanies the mature mRNA to the cytoplasm and directs its rapid destruction when replication ends.

Replication-dependent histone mRNAs are the one major class of eukaryotic mRNA that is not polyadenylated; instead their 3' ends are made by a single endonucleolytic cleavage that leaves a conserved stem-loop, and this SLBP-dependent processing of histone pre-mRNAs is how that end is generated. Coupling histone supply to S phase depends on it, since the same stem-loop and its bound protein later control mRNA stability and translation, and failure to restrict histone synthesis to replication disrupts chromatin assembly. Stem-loop binding protein engages the nascent transcript, while the U7 snRNP base-pairs with a downstream element through its snRNA. That particle carries a distinctive core in which Lsm10 and Lsm11 replace two of the canonical Sm proteins, and the zinc-finger protein encoded by ZNF473 bridges Lsm11 to SLBP to recruit it. The nuclear cap-binding proteins link processing to transcription and export.

Most human genes contain introns, but a subset — replication-independent histone-like transcripts, many stress and immune response genes, and single-exon genes generally — are transcribed without them and must have their 3' ends made by cleavage and polyadenylation alone, without splicing to help recruit the machinery. This processing defines where a transcript ends, licenses its export from the nucleus, and sets its stability and translatability; failure leaves read-through RNAs that are degraded or interfere with downstream transcription. A cleavage and polyadenylation specificity complex recognises the AAUAAA signal through WDR33 and CPSF4, with CPSF3 acting as the endonuclease, while cleavage stimulation factor subunits bind the downstream GU-rich element and CFIm subunits NUDT21, CPSF6 and CPSF7 influence poly(A) site choice. PAPOLA then adds the tail, measured and protected by PABPN1, with the cap-binding complex and PCF11 tying the event to termination.

Long-chain fatty acids must cross the plasma membrane before they can be burned for energy or converted into signalling lipids, and this uptake step supplies heart and skeletal muscle with fuel while feeding the eicosanoid and hormone precursors that shape inflammation, clotting, blood pressure and immune responses. Members of the SLC27A family encode fatty acid transport proteins; of these, FATP1, FATP4 and FATP6 have demonstrated transport activity and prefer substrates longer than ten carbons, with FATP4 prominent in intestinal absorption and FATP6 in the heart. Because free fatty acids and related hydrophobic ligands are poorly soluble, small extracellular carriers of the lipocalin family, including apolipoprotein D, bind and shuttle them between cells and tissues. Defects in this handling disturb lipid distribution, skin barrier lipid composition and tissue energy supply.

Cells that cannot make nucleotides from scratch depend on salvaging nucleosides and free purine and pyrimidine bases from the extracellular space, and this transport across the plasma membrane is how they get them. Two carrier families do the work: equilibrative transporters such as SLC29A1 and SLC29A2 move substrates down their concentration gradients in either direction, while the concentrative SLC28A1, SLC28A2 and SLC28A3 proteins couple uptake to inward sodium flux, with differing preferences for purine versus pyrimidine nucleosides. In kidney and intestinal epithelia, apical concentrative and basolateral equilibrative carriers together achieve net absorption. The same proteins set extracellular adenosine levels, shaping its signalling on vascular tone and neurotransmission, and they determine cellular uptake of nucleoside analogue antiviral and anticancer drugs, so their expression influences chemotherapy response. Related mitochondrial adenine nucleotide carriers and ARL2-associated regulators accompany this nucleoside traffic.

The NLRP1 inflammasome was the first such complex to be defined, and it links sensing of microbial and toxin-derived danger signals to the maturation of interleukin-1 family cytokines. Assembly brings procaspase-1 into a platform built on NLRP1, whose C-terminal CARD extension can engage the protease directly, with the adaptor ASC augmenting the interaction; the activated caspase then cleaves pro-IL-1beta to drive inflammation and can trigger pyroptotic cell death. Activation requires potassium efflux and binding of ribonucleoside triphosphates, ATP being most effective, together with magnesium. The antiapoptotic proteins BCL2 and BCL2L1 bind NLRP1 and restrain its oligomerisation, tying inflammasome output to the machinery that governs mitochondrial apoptosis. Polymorphism in the rodent paralogues determines susceptibility to anthrax lethal toxin, and human NLRP1 variants underlie inflammatory skin and autoinflammatory disease.

Innate immune cells sense damage and infection through the NLRP3 inflammasome, a cytosolic sensor complex that converts diverse danger signals into mature IL-1 beta and IL-18 and into inflammatory cell death. NLRP3 oligomerizes with the adaptor PYCARD (ASC) to recruit and autoactivate procaspase-1, which cleaves the cytokine precursors; chaperone activity from HSP90 and SUGT1 holds the sensor in a signalling-competent but inactive state, while TXNIP release from thioredoxin links oxidative stress to activation. Extracellular ATP acts through the P2RX7 receptor and the pannexin channel PANX1, whereas crystalline and particulate irritants such as silica and urate require phagocytosis. Output is amplified by NF-kB-driven transcription of the components themselves. Gain-of-function NLRP3 mutations cause hereditary periodic fever syndromes with uncontrolled IL-1 beta production, and related regulators including pyrin and PSTPIP1 underlie neighbouring autoinflammatory diseases.

Cytosolic double-stranded DNA is a danger signal: it should not be there, and its presence marks infection by DNA viruses or intracellular bacteria, or catastrophic damage to the cell's own genome. The AIM2 inflammasome is the sensor that converts that signal into an inflammatory response. AIM2 binds dsDNA through its HIN domain and, once engaged, uses its pyrin domain to recruit the adaptor ASC, which polymerises into a single large speck. That platform clusters procaspase-1 and drives its autoprocessing, and active caspase-1 then cleaves pro-IL-1beta and pro-IL-18 into secreted cytokines and cleaves gasdermin D to trigger pyroptosis, a lytic death that destroys the replicative niche. This arm of innate immunity is non-redundant for DNA sensing in macrophages, and its inappropriate activation by self-DNA contributes to autoinflammatory and autoimmune disease.

Cytosolic surveillance for bacterial invasion is carried out in part by the IPAF inflammasome, built around the NLR sensor NLRC4 and caspase-1. It gives macrophages and intestinal epithelium a way to detect Gram-negative bacteria that breach the vacuole or inject effectors through type III and type IV secretion systems, sensing flagellin and the structurally related secretion-system rod protein delivered into the cytosol, with NAIP proteins acting as the direct ligand-binding partners. Because NLRC4 carries a CARD domain, it can recruit procaspase-1 directly, although the adaptor ASC raises maximal caspase-1 activity for organisms such as Salmonella, Shigella and Pseudomonas. Active caspase-1 matures IL-1 family cytokines and triggers pyroptosis, killing the infected cell and exposing bacteria to other defences. Gain-of-function NLRC4 mutations cause autoinflammatory disease with macrophage activation syndrome.

Interferon gamma signaling is the arm of cytokine signalling that licenses macrophages to kill intracellular pathogens and raises the visibility of infected or transformed cells to T cells. Secreted mainly by activated T and NK cells, IFNG binds a preassembled IFNGR1/IFNGR2 receptor that has no catalytic activity of its own and instead recruits JAK1 and JAK2 to phosphorylate STAT1, which drives transcription from gamma-interferon activation sequences. The output is visible in the gene list: upregulation of class I and class II MHC molecules together with B2M and the class II transactivator CIITA, the guanylate-binding proteins and TRIM family effectors that restrict pathogens, adhesion molecules such as ICAM1 and VCAM1, and IRF-family transcription factors that broaden the response. SOCS1, SOCS3, PIAS1 and phosphatases including PTPN2 and PTPN6 terminate it; loss of receptor or STAT1 function causes susceptibility to mycobacterial disease, while chronic activation contributes to autoimmunity.

Interferon gamma drives macrophage activation, antigen presentation and antimicrobial defence, and because sustained signalling through it is damaging, the pathway is switched off almost as soon as it is turned on. Regulation of IFNG signalling describes that braking. Ligand binding to the IFNGR1/IFNGR2 receptor pair activates JAK1 and JAK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 for dimerisation and nuclear entry; three classes of negative regulator then intervene. SOCS1 and SOCS3, themselves induced by the response, bind receptor and kinase to block further phosphorylation; the SH2-domain phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN11, PTPN2 and PTPN1 remove activating phosphates from receptor, JAKs and STAT1; and PIAS1 with SUMO1 acts on activated STAT1 in the nucleus to limit transcription. Loss of restraint here contributes to chronic inflammation and autoimmunity, while loss of the receptor or STAT1 leaves patients vulnerable to mycobacterial infection.

Long-lived proteins incubated with sugars acquire irreversible glycation adducts, and signalling through the advanced glycosylation endproduct receptor AGER (RAGE) is how cells sense them and respond with inflammation. Because these adducts accumulate with age and hyperglycaemia, this axis links diabetes to its vascular, renal and neurological complications, and sustains the chronic inflammatory tone of atherosclerosis. AGER is an immunoglobulin-superfamily pattern recognition receptor with a promiscuous ligand set: besides glycation adducts it binds amyloid-beta from APP, the nuclear alarmin HMGB1 released by damaged cells, serum amyloid A, galectin-3, and proinflammatory S100 proteins such as S100B and S100A12. Ligand binding drives NF-kappaB into the nucleus and raises its synthesis, producing a self-amplifying inflammatory loop, while ERK1/2 association engages MAPK and JNK cascades. Downstream consequences include cytokine output, leukocyte recruitment, cell motility and amyloid-beta transport into the brain.

Organic anion transporting polypeptides move amphipathic anions across plasma membranes without needing a sodium gradient, and they are the entry gate through which bile salts, steroid and hormone conjugates, prostaglandins, peptides and a long list of drugs reach the inside of cells. Their tissue distribution sets the pharmacology: liver-enriched carriers such as SLCO1B1 and SLCO1B3 take statins, methotrexate and bilirubin conjugates out of portal blood for hepatic clearance, so variants in them raise plasma drug levels and underlie statin myopathy risk and forms of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Others serve local needs — SLCO1C1 and the related thyroid hormone carrier SLC16A2 deliver thyroxine and T3 across brain barriers, with loss of the latter causing severe X-linked psychomotor retardation, while SLCO2A1 handles prostaglandin uptake and degradation. Together this family governs drug disposition, drug–drug interactions, and hormone availability to target tissues.

Interconversion of 2-oxoglutarate and 2-hydroxyglutarate clears a metabolite that cells must not allow to accumulate. Both stereoisomers of 2-hydroxyglutarate arise as low-level byproducts of other routes -- plausibly lysine breakdown or aminolevulinate metabolism -- and are oxidised back to 2-oxoglutarate in the mitochondrial matrix, returning the carbon to the citric acid cycle. Two FAD-dependent dehydrogenases handle this with strict stereospecificity, D2HGDH acting on the R enantiomer and L2HGDH on the S enantiomer, while ADHFE1 reversibly couples R-2-hydroxyglutarate with succinate semialdehyde to yield 4-hydroxybutyrate and 2-oxoglutarate. Inherited loss of either dehydrogenase produces D- or L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with variable epilepsy, developmental delay and leukoencephalopathy. The accumulating acid inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, linking this small housekeeping route to chromatin demethylation and hypoxia signalling.

2-Hydroxyglutarate is a metabolic dead end that cells must clear, and this small mitochondrial route returns both of its stereoisomers to 2-oxoglutarate so the carbon can enter the citric acid cycle. Two FAD-dependent dehydrogenases do the oxidation with opposite stereospecificity: D2HGDH acts on the R(-) isomer and L2HGDH on the S(-) isomer. ADHFE1 provides a separate, reversible link, transferring reducing equivalents between R(-)-2-hydroxyglutarate and succinate semialdehyde to yield 4-hydroxybutyrate and 2-oxoglutarate, tying this chemistry to GABA-related metabolism. Inherited loss of either dehydrogenase causes D- or L-2-hydroxyglutaric aciduria, with accumulation of the acid and variable encephalopathy, seizures and developmental delay. The interest in these reactions is broader than the rare diseases, since 2-hydroxyglutarate competitively inhibits 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases that control DNA and histone demethylation.

Gastrin is the hormone that drives gastric acid secretion, but it is also a growth factor for gastrointestinal epithelium, and this route describes how it reaches the nucleus: binding of the G17 and G34 peptides to the cholecystokinin B receptor activates protein kinase C and a Ras-to-ERK cascade that ends in CREB1 phosphorylation by p90 ribosomal S6 kinases. The transcriptional output favours proliferation, survival, angiogenesis and invasion, and includes matrix metalloproteinase and growth factor genes. Signalling is amplified by transactivation of EGFR through shedding of heparin-binding EGF, so a gut hormone borrows a receptor tyrosine kinase circuit. Gastrin overexpression accompanies Helicobacter-associated gastritis, hypergastrinaemia from acid suppression, and gastric and colorectal tumours, where sustained CREB-dependent transcription contributes to epithelial transformation rather than to acid physiology alone.

Phosphoinositides are not confined to membranes; a distinct pool is made and turned over inside the nucleus, where it links stress signalling to chromatin regulation, transcription and cell survival rather than to vesicle traffic. Nuclear synthesis of PIPs centres on the balance between phosphatidylinositol 5-phosphate and PI(4,5)P2. A type I PI(4,5)P2 4-phosphatase relocates to the nucleus under stress and removes the 4-phosphate to generate PI5P, while PIP4K2A, PIP4K2B and PIP4K2C dimers consume PI5P by phosphorylating it back to PI(4,5)P2, normally holding PI5P low. Stress-activated p38 MAP kinase phosphorylates and inhibits PIP4K2B, allowing PI5P to accumulate and act as a signal read by chromatin-binding effectors such as PHD-finger proteins. Through this switch the pathway couples stress kinase activity to nuclear lipid messengers, with consequences for stress-responsive gene expression, apoptosis and tumour cell metabolism.

PTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that becomes active downstream of ERBB2, linking growth factor receptor engagement at the plasma membrane to proliferation, migration and survival signalling in epithelial cells. The relationship matters in breast cancer, where ERBB2 amplification and elevated PTK6 co-occur and PTK6 reinforces mitogenic output and resistance to ERBB2-directed therapy. Ligands of the EGF family — EGF, betacellulin, epiregulin and heparin-binding EGF acting on EGFR, and the neuregulins acting on ERBB3 and ERBB4 — drive receptor dimerisation, and ERBB2 serves as the preferred heterodimer partner that couples these complexes to PTK6 activation. Because EGFR and MET also heterodimerise with ERBB2, signals apparently arising from those receptors may be relayed through ERBB2 rather than reaching PTK6 directly. Activated PTK6 then phosphorylates substrates governing cytoskeletal dynamics, STAT-dependent transcription and anti-apoptotic signalling.

PTK6 (BRK) is an intracellular tyrosine kinase that acts downstream of ERBB family receptors and other growth factor receptors, and its aberrant expression in breast and other epithelial tumours makes this signalling largely a cancer-relevant circuit rather than a normal-tissue one. Activation feeds several outputs at once: STAT3-dependent transcription, RHO-family GTPase control through RAC1 and RHOA that drives motility and adhesion turnover at focal complexes, crosstalk with AKT1 and RAS effectors, and phosphorylation of the CDK inhibitor CDKN1B so that cyclin-CDK pairs can push cells through G1. PTK6 also stabilises EGFR by opposing its CBL- and ubiquitin-dependent downregulation, prolonging receptor output. Hypoxia-responsive factors raise PTK6 levels, while PTPN1, SRMS and SOCS3 restrain its activity. Nuclear substrates including SAM68-family proteins and SFPQ link the kinase to RNA-binding proteins, a branch whose function remains unclear.

Two lipid products of the skin and of membranes share a common first step, and this pathway covers both. Waxes are esters of long-chain fatty acids with long-chain fatty alcohols, secreted by sebaceous glands to keep the skin surface supple and resistant to drying and abrasion; plasmalogens are ether-linked phospholipids abundant in myelin, heart and brain whose loss causes severe peroxisomal developmental disease. Both routes begin with reduction of palmitoyl-CoA to hexadecanol by the peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA reductases FAR1 and FAR2. The alcohol is either esterified to an acyl-CoA by the wax synthases AWAT1 and AWAT2, or condensed onto the glycerone-phosphate backbone generated by GNPAT and the alkylglycerone-phosphate synthase AGPS to build the characteristic ether bond. Peroxisomal localisation of the early steps explains why plasmalogen deficiency is a hallmark of peroxisome biogenesis disorders.

Threonine is an essential amino acid, and its catabolism sets how much of the dietary supply is burned for energy rather than used for protein synthesis. In humans the route runs through the cytosol: serine dehydratase and its close relative, which also act as threonine deaminases, remove the amino group to give 2-oxobutanoate, a carbon skeleton that feeds into propionyl-CoA and ultimately the citric acid cycle. The reactive enamine/imine intermediate generated by deamination is handled by RIDA, a reactive intermediate deaminase that converts 2-iminobutanoate to 2-oxobutanoate and so limits damage to other enzymes. The alternative mitochondrial dehydrogenase route to glycine and acetyl-CoA used by many mammals is effectively lost in people, the human gene being inactivated, which explains why threonine breakdown in liver depends on these few cytosolic activities and shifts with nutritional state.

The intracellular tyrosine kinase PTK6 (BRK) is best known at the plasma membrane and cytoplasm of epithelial cells, but it also acts in the nucleus, where it phosphorylates RNA-binding proteins and thereby links tyrosine kinase signalling to the handling of nascent transcripts. Its nuclear substrates are the SAM68 family of KH-domain proteins — KHDRBS1, KHDRBS2 and KHDRBS3 — together with the splicing factor SFPQ, all of which bind RNA and influence alternative splicing, mRNA export and transcript stability. Tyrosine phosphorylation of these proteins alters their RNA-binding and self-association properties, offering a route by which growth factor signalling could reshape splice-site selection. PTK6 is overexpressed in breast and other carcinomas, so this nuclear branch of its activity is of interest in tumour biology, though the physiological consequences of the modifications for RNA processing remain undefined.

PTK6, a non-receptor tyrosine kinase related to SRC but lacking a membrane anchor, tunes how strongly epithelial cells respond to growth factors, and its overexpression in breast and prostate tumours sustains proliferative signalling. Rather than initiating signals itself, it prolongs and amplifies those from receptor tyrosine kinases: by interfering with CBL-directed ubiquitination and the ARAP1-dependent trafficking that would otherwise internalise and degrade activated EGFR, it keeps receptor output high, and it similarly potentiates signalling through IGF1R and ERBB3. Downstream, it influences AKT1 activation and so the survival and growth arm of the response, while phosphorylating the adaptor DOK1 to mark it for ubiquitin-mediated destruction, removing a brake on receptor signalling. The polyubiquitin and ribosomal ubiquitin precursor genes present reflect the proteasomal degradation steps through which this control over receptor abundance is exerted.

PTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, normally epithelial, that is overexpressed in breast and other carcinomas, where it pushes cells through the G1/S transition. It does this by removing a brake rather than adding an accelerator: PTK6 phosphorylates the CDK inhibitor p27 (CDKN1B), inactivating it and promoting its turnover, so cyclin D1-CDK4 and cyclin E1-CDK2 complexes remain active and phosphorylate the retinoblastoma protein. PTK6 also suppresses CDKN1B transcription by restraining the forkhead factor FOXO3, giving a second, slower route to the same outcome. The result is shortened G1 and sustained proliferation, which is why this kinase is studied as a driver of tumour growth and a candidate drug target. The pathway sits at the point where growth-factor and tyrosine kinase signalling meet the core cyclin-CDK machinery of cell cycle control.

PTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase related to SRC that couples adhesion and growth factor cues to cytoskeletal remodelling, and through it a cell acquires motility and invasive behaviour — a reason PTK6 overexpression is noted in breast and prostate carcinomas. Acting on RHO-family GTPase signalling, it promotes RAC1 activity while restraining RHOA, shifting the balance from contractility toward lamellipodial protrusion. The listed effectors trace how this happens: phosphorylation of the focal adhesion proteins paxillin and BCAR1 (p130Cas) recruits CRK, which with the DOCK1–ELMO complex acts as a RAC1 exchange factor, while the GAPs RASA1 and ARHGAP35 (p190RhoGAP) are inhibitory nodes that PTK6 modulates. Relieving RASA1 restraint sustains RAS activity, and downstream MAP kinase output, including ERK5, links the same kinase to proliferative and survival signalling alongside migration.

PTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase of epithelial tissues that promotes proliferation and survival downstream of growth factor receptors such as EGFR/ERBB, and its overexpression in breast and other carcinomas makes restraint of its activity consequential. Down-regulation of PTK6 works through two opposing tyrosine modifications on the kinase itself. PTPN1 (PTP1B), an endoplasmic reticulum-anchored protein tyrosine phosphatase, removes the phosphate from the activation-loop tyrosine Y342 and thereby lowers catalytic output. SRMS, a related Src-family-like kinase, phosphorylates the C-terminal inhibitory tyrosine Y447, which favours the closed, autoinhibited conformation in which the phosphotyrosine engages the kinase's own SH2 domain. Together these events set the ceiling on PTK6 signalling to substrates controlling epithelial growth and migration, and their loss leaves the kinase constitutively active.

Control of PTK6 abundance links oxygen sensing to the activity of a non-receptor tyrosine kinase that promotes proliferation, migration and survival in epithelial cells and is re-expressed in breast and other carcinomas. Under low oxygen the hypoxia-inducible factors HIF1A and EPAS1 bind the PTK6 gene and drive its transcription, while the protein is additionally stabilised by hypoxia through a HIF-independent route; in normoxia PTK6 is ubiquitinated and turned over, so the kinase accumulates chiefly when tissue oxygen falls. Steroid receptor signalling feeds into the same output, with the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1 and the coregulator PELP1 contributing to PTK6 induction. Because hypoxic tumour regions are where this induction occurs, the pathway offers a route by which the microenvironment amplifies growth-factor and kinase signalling and contributes to therapy resistance and metastatic behaviour.

PTK6 (BRK) is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase of epithelial cells that, among its other outputs, drives transcription through STAT3, linking kinase activity at the membrane to programmes of proliferation and survival. The adapter STAP2 brings kinase and transcription factor together, so that PTK6 phosphorylates STAT3 on the tyrosine required for its dimerisation and nuclear entry; STAT5 can be activated similarly. Once in the nucleus STAT3 induces SOCS3, which in turn binds and restrains PTK6 and blunts further STAT3 phosphorylation, a negative feedback loop that limits the duration of the signal. Because PTK6 is overexpressed in breast and prostate carcinomas and other epithelial tumours, persistent signalling along this route contributes to growth factor-independent proliferation, and loss of the SOCS3 brake removes a natural limit on it.

Synaptic adhesion-like molecules describes how the SALM/LRFN family of cell-surface adhesion proteins builds and matures excitatory synapses, determining where dendrites and axons contact each other and which receptors are held at the contact site. This is the final step of synapse assembly, and it sets the strength and composition of glutamatergic transmission that underlies learning; disruption of these adhesion systems is linked to autism spectrum and other neurodevelopmental disorders. Each SALM carries extracellular leucine-rich repeats, an Ig and fibronectin III domain, and in most members a cytoplasmic PDZ-binding tail that docks onto PSD-95 family scaffolds (DLG1/3/4). Through this link they cluster NMDA (GRIN1, GRIN2A-D) and AMPA (GRIA1-4) receptors in the postsynaptic density, while trans-synaptic binding to presynaptic receptor tyrosine phosphatases PTPRD, PTPRS and PTPRF drives synapse induction, neurite outgrowth and branching.

Excitatory synapses only work once glutamate receptors are concentrated opposite the presynaptic terminal, and the SALM/LRFN family of leucine-rich repeat adhesion proteins is one of the systems that puts them there. These single-pass transmembrane proteins span the synaptic cleft through extracellular leucine-rich repeats, an Ig-like domain and a fibronectin III domain, while most members end in a cytoplasmic motif that binds PSD-95 family scaffolds (DLG1, DLG3, DLG4), tethering AMPA-type (GRIA1, GRIA3/4) and NMDA-type (GRIN1 with GRIN2A-D) receptors to the postsynaptic density. Presynaptic receptor phosphatases of the PTPRD/PTPRF/PTPRS group act as their trans-synaptic partners, coupling adhesion to synapse assembly. Beyond receptor recruitment, these molecules shape neurite outgrowth, dendritic branching and synapse maturation, and variants in family members have been linked to autism spectrum and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

Extracellular ATP and ADP act as signalling molecules, and the eight-member NTPDase family sets how long they persist by hydrolysing nucleoside tri- and diphosphates down to monophosphates. By clearing these agonists, phosphate bond hydrolysis by NTPDase proteins controls the stimulation of P2X and P2Y purinergic receptors and feeds substrate toward adenosine production, shaping platelet aggregation and haemostasis, inflammatory and immune responses, and neurotransmission and nervous system development. ENTPD1 on endothelium and regulatory T cells is the best-characterised plasma membrane member, alongside ENTPD2, ENTPD3 and ENTPD8; ENTPD4 and ENTPD7 face the lumen of intracellular organelles, while ENTPD5 and ENTPD6 can be shed as soluble enzymes. All are transmembrane glycoproteins whose catalytic apyrase-conserved regions require divalent magnesium or calcium and attack the terminal phosphate through an activated water molecule, with differing preferences among nucleotide substrates.

Butyrophilins and their butyrophilin-like relatives are immunoglobulin-superfamily surface proteins structurally akin to the B7 co-stimulatory molecules, and through interactions with T cells they tune whether an encounter with an antigen-presenting or epithelial cell drives activation or restraint. They shape T cell development, co-stimulation and inhibition, and variants in several members are linked to autoimmune and inflammatory disease, sarcoidosis and inflammatory bowel disease among them. BTN3A1 is the sensor that allows human gamma-delta T cells bearing the Vgamma9Vdelta2 receptor to detect phosphoantigens accumulating in infected or transformed cells, with BTN2A1 contributing direct receptor binding; gut BTNL molecules similarly select intraepithelial gamma-delta subsets. The prototypic BTN1A1 works instead in lactation, where together with xanthine dehydrogenase and periplakin it governs budding of milk fat globules from the mammary epithelial apical membrane.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 normally drives proliferation and differentiation in bone, cranial suture and epithelial tissues, and an aberrant splice form of it acts as a brake on that signalling. In an Apert syndrome model, mis-splicing joins exon 7 to exon 10 to produce FGFR2 IIIa TM, a truncated receptor lacking the normal transmembrane and kinase arrangement that escapes nonsense-mediated decay and reaches the cell surface or the extracellular space. Because it retains ligand-binding capacity, it can soak up FGF1 and FGF2 and pair unproductively with full-length receptors, damping downstream growth factor responses in vitro and in vivo. The accompanying RNA polymerase II subunits, general transcription factor components and the nuclear cap-binding proteins reflect the transcription and capping steps that generate this alternatively spliced, decay-resistant transcript, placing the variant's origin in splice-site choice rather than receptor mutation alone.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase drives the proliferation, survival, scattering and morphogenesis of epithelial cells, and much of that output runs through RAS. This branch describes how activated MET converts receptor phosphorylation into GTP loading on HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, and thence into sustained ERK activity that reprogrammes gene expression for motility and growth. The receptor does not contact RAS directly: phosphotyrosines on MET recruit the adaptors GRB2 and SHC1, or scaffolds such as RANBP9, which in turn bring in the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1 to catalyse GDP-to-GTP exchange. Signalling continues from endosomes after receptor internalisation, and binding of MUC20 or RANBP10 to MET dampens the response. Constitutive activity of this axis, through MET amplification or mutation, sustains invasive growth in carcinoma and is a target of kinase inhibitor therapy.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase MET triggers a survival and growth response, and one major branch of it runs through PI3K to AKT. This arm supports epithelial cell survival, motility and tissue regeneration in liver, kidney and skin, and is a principal reason MET-driven tumours resist apoptosis and invade. Activated MET autophosphorylates and recruits GRB2, which brings the multi-site adaptor GAB1 to the receptor; MET then phosphorylates GAB1 to create docking sites for the PI3K regulatory subunit PIK3R1. The associated PIK3CA catalytic subunit converts PIP2 to PIP3 at the membrane, recruiting AKT for activation and thereby suppressing pro-apoptotic effectors and promoting mTOR-dependent growth. MET amplification or activating mutation, or excess HGF in the stroma, keeps this signal on and is targeted by MET kinase inhibitors.</description>

Ubiquitination is the tagging of proteins with the 76-residue protein ubiquitin, a mark that determines whether a protein is destroyed, relocated, or switched into a new activity. It underlies protein quality control, the DNA damage response, immune signalling and cell cycle progression, and its misregulation contributes to cancer and neurodegeneration. Ubiquitin is first liberated from polyubiquitin and ubiquitin–ribosomal fusion precursors encoded by UBB, UBC, UBA52 and RPS27A, with deubiquitinases such as OTULIN, USP5, UCHL3, USP7 and USP9X generating monomers. The E1 enzymes UBA1 and UBA6 adenylate and thioesterify ubiquitin, pass it to one of many E2 conjugating enzymes, and E3 ligases position the target so ubiquitin is joined, usually to a lysine. Chain linkage dictates outcome: K48 chains route substrates to the proteasome, K63 chains build signalling scaffolds. Represented branches include ERAD at the ER membrane, histone H2B monoubiquitination with the PAF1 complex, and replication-fork template switching via RAD18 and PCNA.

The role of GTSE1 in G2/M progression after G2 checkpoint describes how a cell that has arrested in G2 to repair DNA damage dismantles the arrest and commits to mitosis. This recovery step decides whether a damaged cell dies by p53-driven apoptosis or resumes proliferation, and its deregulation contributes to cancer cell survival, invasiveness and taxane resistance. GTSE1 is a microtubule-associated protein expressed maximally in G2; through binding tubulin and the plus-end tracking protein MAPRE1 it influences microtubule dynamics and cell migration, until CDK1-associated mitotic phosphorylation displaces it at prometaphase. PLK1 phosphorylation instead drives GTSE1 into the nucleus, where it binds TP53 and promotes its MDM2-dependent export and proteasomal destruction, lowering apoptotic and arrest gene output. Paradoxically GTSE1 also stabilises the CDK inhibitor CDKN1A together with an HSP90-FKBPL chaperone complex, linking checkpoint recovery to ubiquitin-proteasome protein turnover.

After DNA damage arrests cells in G2, they must eventually silence the arrest signal and re-enter mitosis, and GTSE1 is one route by which that recovery happens. GTSE1 is a microtubule-associated protein expressed maximally in G2; through binding tubulin and the plus-end tracker MAPRE1 (EB1) it decorates growing microtubule tips, an activity linked to cell migration and to the invasiveness of breast cancer lines that mis-express it in G1. PLK1 phosphorylation drives GTSE1 into the nucleus, where it binds TP53 and, with MDM2, promotes p53 export and proteasomal destruction, blunting apoptosis and arrest gene expression so that CDK1-cyclin B can fire. GTSE1 also binds CDKN1A (p21) together with HSP90 and FKBPL to extend its half-life, a combination implicated in paclitaxel resistance. Mitotic phosphorylation near the EB1-binding site releases GTSE1 from microtubule ends in prometaphase.

Signaling by MST1 describes the activation of macrophage-stimulating protein and its receptor RON, a growth factor axis that shapes how macrophages and epithelia respond to injury and infection. It tunes inflammation in two phases, first driving macrophage chemotaxis and phagocytosis and later damping their inflammatory output so tissue repair can proceed; the same receptor is overexpressed in epithelial cancers, where it promotes invasive growth. The ligand is secreted by the liver as an inactive single-chain precursor of the kringle family, related to hepatocyte growth factor and plasminogen, and must be cleaved by a membrane serine protease such as hepsin at sites of coagulation or inflammation. The HAI-type inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2 restrain that proteolysis, setting how much active ligand reaches the receptor. Receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation then create a docking site for GRB2, PI3K and SRC, coupling to survival, motility and wound-healing programmes.

Macrophage-stimulating protein (MST1), a kringle-domain relative of hepatocyte growth factor made by the liver, circulates as an inactive single-chain precursor until proteolysis converts it to the active dimer that engages its receptor tyrosine kinase RON (MST1R) on macrophages and epithelial cells. Signaling by MST1 shapes the inflammatory response to bacterial infection and tissue injury: it first drives macrophage chemotaxis and phagocytosis, then restrains further macrophage activation, so the pathway both starts and limits inflammation and contributes to wound healing and epithelial repair. Activation requires cleavage, here supplied by the membrane serine protease hepsin (HPN), whose activity is held in check by the Kunitz-type inhibitors SPINT1 and SPINT2; ligand binding then promotes receptor dimerisation, autophosphorylation and recruitment of SH2 adaptors. RON is overexpressed in many epithelial cancers, where this axis supports tumour progression and invasion.

Chromosomal rearrangements that fuse FGFR2 to a partner gene create receptors that signal without ligand, and this constitutive output drives tumour growth in cholangiocarcinoma as well as lung, breast and thyroid cancers. FGFR2 accepts the widest range of 3' partners of any fibroblast growth factor receptor, among them BICC1, AHCYL1, CIT, CCDC6 and AFF3; because many of these contribute coiled-coil or other dimerization domains, the chimeric protein self-associates, autophosphorylates its kinase domain and fires the normal downstream cascades — RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT, PLC-gamma and STAT signalling — continuously rather than in response to FGF ligand. What is normally a tightly controlled input into proliferation, survival, migration and developmental patterning becomes an unregulated proliferative signal. Because the kinase domain is retained intact, these fusions are actionable: tumours carrying them are selectively sensitive to FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and resistance typically arises through secondary kinase-domain mutations.

Chromosomal rearrangements that fuse the FGFR3 kinase to partner proteins such as TACC3 create constitutively active receptors, and this oncogenic signalling drives tumours of the bladder, lung and brain, including glioblastoma. The partner contributes a coiled-coil or other dimerization module, so the kinase oligomerizes and autophosphorylates without any fibroblast growth factor ligand, escaping the normal control that restricts FGFR3 activity to sites of ligand availability. Downstream output is skewed rather than simply amplified: RAS-ERK and PI3K-AKT signalling is engaged to promote proliferation and transformation, while phospholipase C gamma is not recruited because the fusion truncates its docking site. Because TACC3 normally works at the mitotic spindle, the fusion can also perturb chromosome segregation. These fusions remain sensitive to FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, making them actionable in precision oncology.

Chromosomal rearrangements can fuse the FGFR1 receptor tyrosine kinase to partner genes in a way that leaves the kinase at the plasma membrane rather than in the cytosol, and these plasma membrane FGFR1 fusions drive constitutive growth factor signalling without ligand. Such fusions, joining FGFR1 to partners including BAG4 and the endoplasmic reticulum protein ERLIN2, have been found in glioblastoma, breast cancer and non-small cell lung cancer, where they support anchorage-independent growth and continuous receptor autophosphorylation. Because the fusion retains an intact kinase domain but loses normal ligand and dimerisation control, downstream mitogenic cascades that ordinarily respond to fibroblast growth factors are switched on permanently, promoting proliferation and transformation. Tumours carrying these fusions are correspondingly sensitive to FGFR kinase inhibitors, making the rearrangement both a driver lesion and a therapeutic target in oncogenic receptor signalling.

Free oligosaccharides released from misfolded glycoproteins must be taken apart completely, and lysosomal oligosaccharide catabolism performs the final mannose-trimming steps of that disposal route. N-linked glycans added in the ER direct protein folding and trafficking; when quality control rejects a glycoprotein, the glycan is cleaved off and degraded stepwise, first in the cytosol and then within the lysosome. Acidic alpha-mannosidases remove alpha-linked mannose residues and a beta-mannosidase cleaves the remaining mannose-GlcNAc linkage, reducing the chain to monosaccharides that can be recycled. Incomplete digestion matters clinically: loss of the lysosomal alpha-mannosidase causes alpha-mannosidosis, and loss of beta-mannosidase causes beta-mannosidosis, both storage disorders in which even disaccharide remnants accumulate and produce neurological and skeletal disease. The pathway therefore links glycoprotein turnover to lysosomal catabolism and sugar salvage.

RET signaling is how neural crest, kidney and germline precursors read the GDNF family of neurotrophic cues, and it decides whether those cells survive, migrate and extend axons. It builds the enteric nervous system, drives ureteric bud branching during kidney development, and sustains spermatogonial self-renewal; loss of function causes Hirschsprung's disease and renal agenesis, while activating mutations give multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 and rearrangements give papillary thyroid carcinoma. GDNF, neurturin, artemin and persephin each act through a preferred GPI-anchored co-receptor of the GFRA family, which presents the ligand to the RET tyrosine kinase either from the same cell or from a neighbouring one. Autophosphorylated RET then recruits adaptors and scaffolds — GRB2, SHC1, the DOK and GAB proteins, FRS2, PTPN11 — to engage RAS-MAPK, PI3K, PLC-gamma and SRC, coupling extracellular trophic support to growth, motility and survival programmes.

VENTX is a human homeobox transcription factor, absent in rodents, whose amphibian and fish counterparts pattern dorsoventral mesoderm and which in humans acts mainly in blood. Transcriptional regulation by VENTX restrains proliferation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and pushes them toward myeloid differentiation; losing it expands the stem and multipotent progenitor pool, while high expression in acute myeloid leukemia supports blast growth, and VENTX also shapes tumour-associated macrophages. It works by direct promoter control: switching on the cell cycle inhibitors TP53 and p16INK4A and the macrophage colony-stimulating factor receptor CSF1R, and repressing cyclin D1 and interleukin-6, thereby intersecting Wnt/beta-catenin-TCF/LEF output and NF-kB-driven inflammatory signalling. Associated repressive histone methyltransferases, anaphase-promoting complex subunits and ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes place the resulting arrest within chromatin silencing and cell cycle proteolysis, with microRNA-loaded Argonaute complexes adding post-transcriptional control of cyclin D1.

Aurora kinase A drives centrosome maturation and spindle assembly, and its abundance must be held in check as cells enter mitosis; here an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase using FBXL7 as its substrate-recognition subunit tags centrosome-associated AURKA for destruction by the 26S proteasome. The core ligase contributes SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1, ubiquitin is supplied by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes, and the full complement of proteasome alpha, beta, ATPase and regulatory particle subunits carries out degradation. Excess FBXL7 arrests cells at the G2/M transition and triggers apoptosis, so its own level is limited by a second SCF complex built around FBXL18, which recognises an FQ motif in FBXL7 and routes it to the same proteasome. The arrangement makes mitotic entry dependent on competing ubiquitin ligases that set kinase dosage, linking spindle control to timed proteolysis.

Membrane traffic is timed by Rab GTPases switching between GTP- and GDP-bound states, and the TBC-domain Rab GTPase-activating proteins are the family that terminates the active state. By accelerating GTP hydrolysis on a specific Rab at a specific membrane, these GAPs decide where a vesicle coat, tether or motor is released, so endosome maturation, recycling to the plasma membrane, Golgi traffic and autophagosome formation all depend on them. The substrates here span the early endosomal Rab5 proteins, recycling Rab4, Rab11 and Rab35, Golgi Rab6, and late endosomal/lysosomal Rab7, with GGA adaptors and Rabaptin-5 representing the effector side of the switch. Several members have wider jobs: TBC1D7 works with TSC1 and TSC2 to restrain mTORC1 growth signalling, while TBC1D14 and TBC1D15 act at ULK1- and LC3/GABARAP-marked autophagic and mitochondrial membranes. Loss of individual GAPs causes epilepsy, deafness and trafficking disease.

Mitotic spindle assembly depends on switching on Aurora kinase A at the right place and time, and the activation of AURKA by TPX2 is that switch. TPX2, released from importin control once the nuclear envelope breaks down, binds AURKA and locks it in an active conformation that favours autophosphorylation on T288 and shields that site from phosphatase removal, concentrating active kinase at centrosomes and on spindle microtubules near poles. Active AURKA then drives centrosome maturation, microtubule nucleation and bipolar spindle formation alongside PLK1, CDK1, the gamma-tubulin nucleating machinery, augmin (HAUS) complex members, dynein-dynactin and a large complement of centrosomal scaffold proteins such as pericentrin, CEP192 and CEP152. Loss of this activation step yields misassembled or monopolar spindles and chromosome missegregation; AURKA and TPX2 are both frequently overexpressed in tumours, making them targets of mitotic inhibitors.

Aurora kinase A drives centrosome maturation and bipolar spindle assembly, and its overexpression is a recurrent feature of breast cancer; PHLDA1 acts as a brake on it. The two proteins bind each other, and the outcome of that encounter depends on phosphorylation state: unmodified PHLDA1 promotes ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction of AURKA, whereas AURKA-mediated phosphorylation of PHLDA1 triggers loss of PHLDA1 protein. The arrangement is a mutual-destruction switch in which whichever partner gains the upper hand eliminates the other. Restoring PHLDA1 suppresses the transformed phenotypes that elevated AURKA produces, so silencing of PHLDA1 is one route by which tumours sustain high Aurora A activity. The interaction links mitotic kinase control to apoptotic sensitivity and tumour progression, and it sits within the broader logic of degradation-based regulation of cell cycle kinases.

Interleukin-20 family signaling is the axis by which immune cells instruct epithelial tissue, driving antimicrobial defence, barrier integrity and wound repair at skin, gut and lung surfaces. IL19, IL20, IL22, IL24 and IL26 belong to the broader IL10 family but share receptor subunits (IL20RA, IL20RB, IL22RA1 with IL10RB) that are expressed largely on epithelial and stromal cells rather than leukocytes, so these cytokines act outward from the immune system instead of within it. Binding activates JAK1/JAK2/TYK2 and predominantly STAT3, inducing antimicrobial peptides, mucins and proliferation, with SOCS3 and the soluble decoy IL22RA2 limiting the response. Excess signalling produces the keratinocyte hyperproliferation of psoriasis, while deficiency compromises mucosal healing and pathogen containment. The related interferon-lambda ligands and IFNLR1 use the shared IL10RB chain to drive STAT1/STAT2-dependent antiviral protection of the same epithelia.

The IL20 subfamily of cytokines "IL19, IL20, IL22, IL24 and IL26" lets leukocytes speak to epithelial cells, and signalling through this family is how barrier tissues mount antimicrobial defence and repair themselves after injury. Skin, gut and lung epithelium respond by producing defensins and mucins, proliferating and restoring barrier integrity; excessive IL22 or IL20 signalling instead drives keratinocyte hyperproliferation and the epidermal changes of psoriasis, while loss of IL22 responses leaves mucosal surfaces vulnerable to infection. Receptors are heterodimers built from shared chains including IL20RA, IL20RB, IL22RA1 and IL10RB, with the secreted decoy IL22RA2 sequestering IL22 to limit responses. Ligand binding activates receptor-associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT3 predominantly alongside STAT1 and STAT5, with SOCS3 imposing negative feedback. The closely related lambda interferons use IL10RB with IFNLR1 for antiviral epithelial protection.

Membrane and protein that move forward from the endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi must be balanced by a return flow, and Golgi-to-ER retrograde transport is that return route. It recycles cargo receptors and SNAREs for reuse, retrieves escaped ER residents such as chaperones bearing KDEL signals through KDEL receptors, and maintains the size, lipid composition and glycosylation competence of both compartments. Two arms operate: COPI-coated vesicles, whose coat subunits are recruited by ARF1 under control of the GBF1 exchange factor and ARFGAP proteins, and a RAB6-dependent tubular route. Carriers travel along microtubules using dynein-dynactin and kinesin motors with BICD adaptors, then fuse at the ER through the syntaxin-18 complex with SEC22B, USE1, ZW10 and NBAS, driven by NSF and SNAP proteins. Loss of components disrupts secretory homeostasis and causes developmental and multisystem disease.

Before a clathrin-coated pit can bud, the cell must decide which surface proteins go inside it, and cargo recognition is that selection step. It sets the surface levels of receptors such as the transferrin receptor, LDL receptor, EGFR and G protein-coupled receptors, and so governs nutrient uptake, cholesterol clearance, synaptic vesicle recycling and the desensitisation of hormone signalling; defects in the sorting signals or their readers underlie familial hypercholesterolaemia and disturbed receptor turnover. Clathrin-associated sorting proteins are recruited to the inner leaflet by phosphoinositides and read short motifs in cytoplasmic tails: the tetrameric AP-2 adaptor binds tyrosine- and dileucine-based signals, while epsins, Dab2, ARH, stonins, beta-arrestins and PICALM serve their own cargoes, including ubiquitinated receptors. By binding clathrin and one another, these adaptors bridge cargo into the growing coat, linking selection to vesicle assembly.

Clathrin-mediated endocytosis is the principal route by which cells internalise plasma membrane proteins and the material bound to them, forming clathrin-coated vesicles that deliver cargo to early endosomes. It supplies cells with nutrients and lipids through receptors for transferrin, LDL and mannose-6-phosphate, recycles synaptic vesicle components after neurotransmitter release, and sets the surface levels of signalling receptors, so that internalisation of activated EGFR or beta-arrestin-bound GPCRs both attenuates and redirects their signalling from the membrane onto endosomes. Coat formation begins with adaptors that read PI(4,5)P2 and cytoplasmic sorting motifs — the AP-2 tetramer plus sorting proteins such as DAB2, PICALM and epsins — which recruit clathrin triskelia and bend the membrane through ENTH and BAR domains. Actin and dynamin GTPases drive constriction and scission, and HSPA8 with auxilin uncoats the vesicle, returning clathrin for reuse. Ubiquitination marks many cargoes for degradation rather than recycling.

Cells continually pull patches of plasma membrane inward as clathrin-coated vesicles, and this route is how they take up nutrients such as transferrin-bound iron and LDL cholesterol, retrieve synaptic vesicle components after exocytosis, and control how long activated receptors keep signalling. Ligand-bound receptor tyrosine kinases such as EGFR and G protein-coupled receptors are internalised through it, determining whether they are recycled or handed to the degradative endosomal machinery, so the pathway sets the amplitude and location of downstream signalling as much as it clears cargo. A coated pit begins with PI(4,5)P2-binding initiators and the AP-2 adaptor tetramer, which together with sorting adaptors like epsin, DAB2 and PICALM read cytoplasmic sorting motifs and couple cargo capture to clathrin lattice assembly. BAR-domain proteins and actin nucleation bend the neck, dynamin GTPases sever it, and HSPA8 with auxilin strips the coat for reuse.

Cells normally destroy HIF1A when oxygen is plentiful, so the hypoxia transcriptional programme stays off; this route overrides that rule, letting tumour cells accumulate HIF1A and switch on glycolytic and angiogenic genes even in normoxia. Growth factor HBEGF drives EGFR to pair with the glycoprotein GPNMB, and a long non-coding RNA scaffold brings the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase PTK6 (BRK) together with HIF1A and LRRK2 at the receptor complex. PTK6-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation of HIF1A blocks its oxygen-dependent recognition and degradation, stabilising the factor and enhancing its transcriptional output. The arrangement links receptor tyrosine kinase signalling at the plasma membrane to hypoxia-response gene expression without any change in oxygen tension, and has been described as a driver of triple-negative breast cancer metabolism and growth, making the lncRNA-kinase interaction an attractive target.

Mature neurons are post-mitotic, and this pathway describes how loss of control over CDK5 forces them back toward cell cycle activity and death, a sequence implicated in Alzheimer's disease and other neurodegeneration. Amyloid-beta, excitotoxicity, ischemia and oxidative stress raise intracellular calcium and activate calpains, which cleave the CDK5 activator p35 into the longer-lived, unanchored p25; the resulting CDK5:p25 complex is constitutively active and mislocalized to cytoplasm and nucleus, where it reaches substrates the kinase normally never sees. Among these are the CDC25 phosphatases, whose phosphorylation both boosts their activity and frees them from 14-3-3 sequestration, allowing inappropriate activation of mitotic and G1 CDKs. Downstream consequences include FOXO3-driven expression of pro-apoptotic BIM and FasL, altered antioxidant enzymes, and breakdown of nuclear lamina and Golgi architecture, culminating in neuronal apoptosis.

Neurodegenerative diseases share a common outcome — progressive neuronal dysfunction and death, usually with deposits of misfolded protein such as beta-amyloid, tau, alpha-synuclein, TDP-43 or prion protein, whose anatomical distribution defines the clinical syndrome. The mechanism drawn out here is the amyloid precursor protein-triggered deregulation of CDK5 that links amyloid pathology to neuronal death in Alzheimer's disease. Calcium influx activates calpain, which cleaves the CDK5 activator p35 to a stable p25 fragment; the resulting long-lived, mislocalised CDK5 phosphorylates targets it would not normally reach, including lamins, the Golgi protein GM130, FOXO3 and the phosphatases of the CDC25 family, driving Golgi fragmentation, nuclear envelope breakdown, aberrant cell cycle re-entry and transcription of pro-apoptotic effectors such as BIM and FasL. Oxidative stress handled by peroxiredoxins and SOD2 feeds the same loop, and calpastatin restrains it.

Growth factor signalling through ERBB2 must be switched off as well as on, and downregulation of ERBB2 signaling is the set of brakes that limits how long the receptor and its heterodimers can drive RAS and PI3K-AKT output. Loss of these brakes contributes to breast and gastric cancers in which ERBB2 is amplified or abnormally stabilised. Two mechanisms dominate. Ubiquitin ligases mark the receptor for proteasomal destruction: STUB1 and CUL5 act on non-activated ERBB2, often in concert with the HSP90-CDC37 chaperone system on which the receptor depends, while RNF41 ubiquitinates ERBB3 and thereby clears activated ERBB2-ERBB3 dimers, a step opposed by the deubiquitinase USP8. Separately, the PEST-family phosphatases PTPN12 and PTPN18 strip phosphotyrosines from the ERBB2 tail so adaptors cannot dock. Ligands such as EGF and the neuregulins, and the ERBIN scaffold, set the context in which this attenuation operates.

The AP-2 (TFAP2) family of transcription factors comprises five related proteins that bind GC-rich palindromic elements as dimers and shape embryonic development, particularly of neural crest derivatives, craniofacial structures, heart, placenta and mammary epithelium. Loss of their activity in animals produces neural crest, cardiac and adrenal defects, while sustained activity in adult tissue supports proliferation at the expense of terminal differentiation. Transactivation depends on CITED cofactors, chiefly CITED2, which dock on the helix-span-helix domain and bring in the acetyltransferase coactivators EP300 and CREBBP; KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the transactivation domain to dampen output, and SUMOylation via UBE2I imposes a further brake. Target genes explain much of the clinical interest: ESR1, ERBB2, EGFR, KIT and TGFA drive luminal breast cancer phenotypes, chorionic gonadotropin subunits are induced in placenta, PITX2 serves left-right patterning, VEGFA is repressed, and TFAP2A and TFAP2C act oppositely on the CDKN1A locus.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase drives epithelial cell scattering, motility, wound repair and morphogenesis, and the same axis is hijacked in carcinomas where MET is amplified or mutated. One branch of that output runs through the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN11 (SHP2). Activated, autophosphorylated MET recruits GRB2, which brings in the multisubstrate adaptor GAB1; GAB1 in turn docks PTPN11 at the receptor complex, where it becomes tyrosine phosphorylated after HGF stimulation. PTPN11 recruited in this way sustains ERK1/2 activation downstream of MET and supports recruitment and activation of sphingosine kinase, linking receptor engagement to lipid second messenger production and cell scattering. The phosphatase also acts back on MET itself, dephosphorylating receptor tyrosines, so this arm both propagates and limits growth factor signalling toward proliferation and migration.

Reelin is a large secreted glycoprotein that tells migrating neurons where to stop, setting up the layered architecture of the cortex, hippocampus and cerebellum, and it continues to tune dendritic growth and synaptic strength in the adult brain. Loss of this signalling produces profound cortical lamination defects and cerebellar hypoplasia, and altered reelin expression is reported in autism, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and Alzheimer's disease. Mechanistically, reelin binds the lipoprotein receptors VLDLR and ApoER2 on the neuronal surface, clustering them so that the intracellular adaptor DAB1 is phosphorylated by Src-family kinases such as FYN; phosphorylated DAB1 then recruits further adaptors, including SH3KBP1, and reorganises the cytoskeleton and adhesion machinery that determine migration arrest and process outgrowth. The pathway therefore links an extracellular positional cue to cytoskeletal control, bridging brain development and ongoing synaptic plasticity.

The liver exports fat to the rest of the body as very low-density lipoprotein, and VLDL assembly is the endoplasmic reticulum process that builds those particles. It sets how much triglyceride and cholesterol enters the circulation, making it the origin of the lipoprotein cascade that yields intermediate- and low-density particles, and a point at which failure causes either fatty liver or severe hypolipidaemia. Apolipoprotein B-100 is lipidated as it is translocated into the rough ER lumen, a step requiring microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, which works as a heterodimer with the ER oxidoreductase and chaperone P4HB (protein disulfide isomerase). Further lipid loading in the smooth ER produces a mature particle that also carries apolipoproteins C-I and C-IV before transit through the Golgi and secretion. Loss of the transfer protein causes abetalipoproteinaemia, with fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

VLDLR internalisation and degradation controls how many very low density lipoprotein receptors remain on the cell surface, and therefore how efficiently triglyceride-rich lipoproteins and remnant particles are cleared from blood. Because receptor number sets clearance capacity, the rate of this catabolic route influences circulating lipid levels and cardiovascular risk, and it is the same logic exploited therapeutically by antibodies against the secreted convertase PCSK9. Two destruction mechanisms converge: PCSK9 binds the receptor extracellularly and routes it, via clathrin- and AP-2-dependent endocytosis, to lysosomal degradation rather than recycling, while the LXR-induced E3 ubiquitin ligase IDOL (MYLIP) ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail to trigger its turnover. The nuclear receptors LXRα and LXRβ thus couple intracellular sterol abundance to receptor removal, making this a feedback arm of cholesterol and lipoprotein homeostasis alongside receptor-mediated lipid uptake in liver and other tissues.

The very low density lipoprotein receptor clears triglyceride-rich lipoproteins from plasma, and how quickly it is internalised and destroyed sets how much receptor is available at the cell surface — one of the determinants of circulating lipid levels. Two routes converge on the same outcome. The secreted convertase PCSK9 binds the receptor and, rather than cleaving it, escorts it through clathrin-coated pit endocytosis — clathrin heavy and light chains with the AP-2 adaptor complex — into lysosomal degradation. In parallel, the E3 ubiquitin ligase encoded by MYLIP (IDOL), induced by the sterol-sensing nuclear receptors LXRα and LXRβ, ubiquitinates the receptor's cytoplasmic tail and commits it for destruction, linking intracellular sterol abundance to receptor turnover. Loss of these controls raises receptor numbers and lowers plasma lipoproteins, which is why PCSK9 blockade is used therapeutically in hypercholesterolaemia.

Every ubiquitin-dependent event in a cell -- proteasomal degradation, DNA damage tolerance, mitotic progression, receptor sorting, NF-kB control -- begins with a supply of free, activated ubiquitin, and this is the pathway that generates it. Ubiquitin is not made as a monomer: the UBB and UBC genes encode head-to-tail polyubiquitin, while UBA52 and RPS27A encode ubiquitin fused to a ribosomal protein, so deubiquitinases including USP5, OTULIN, UCHL3, USP7 and USP9X must first liberate monomers. The E1 enzymes UBA1 and UBA6 then adenylate the C-terminal glycine and capture ubiquitin as a thioester on an active-site cysteine, passing it by transthiolation to one of many E2 conjugating enzymes, which cooperate with E3 ligases to choose substrates and chain linkages. Individual E2s specialise: UBE2C and UBE2S work with the anaphase-promoting complex, UBE2A and UBE2B in replication-coupled repair. Loss of UBA1 activity causes severe neuromuscular and inflammatory disease.

Ubiquitin ligases of the E3 class carry out the substrate-selection step of protein ubiquitylation, receiving ubiquitin from a charged E2 conjugating enzyme and attaching it, usually through a lysine side chain, to a chosen target. This determines which proteins are degraded by the proteasome, which are routed to lysosomes, and which are simply marked to recruit partners, so it governs protein quality control, signalling turnover and chromatin regulation alike. The linkage used encodes the outcome: K48 chains for proteasomal destruction, K63 chains as scaffolds in DNA damage responses. Several branches are represented here, including ERAD components that retrotranslocate misfolded ER proteins with VCP, the RNF20/RNF40 pair with UBE2A/UBE2B that monoubiquitylates histone H2B alongside the PAF1 transcription elongation complex, RAD18- and HLTF-dependent PCNA modification in DNA damage tolerance, and peroxin ligases that recycle the PEX5 import receptor.

Negative regulation of activity of TFAP2 (AP-2) family transcription factors describes how the AP-2 transcription factors are held in check, setting limits on programmes they drive in neural crest, craniofacial and limb development, epidermal differentiation, and breast epithelium. Losing this restraint matters: unopposed AP-2 activity contributes to tumour progression, and mutations in the inhibitor KCTD1 cause scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects, while KCTD15 restrains neural crest induction. Repression works at several levels. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the transactivation domain of AP-2 homo- and heterodimers and block transcription directly. SUMOylation by UBE2I with SUMO1 dampens the activity of TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, linking their output to a reversible post-translational switch. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C in the cytoplasm, and transcription of TFAP2A itself can be repressed by CREB and E2F1.

AP-2 family transcription factors drive programmes of neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and mammary development, and their output must be restrained as well as switched on; this pathway covers the mechanisms that damp AP-2 activity. KCTD1 and KCTD15 bind the AP-2 transactivation domain and block transcriptional activation, a brake whose loss in KCTD1 mutation causes scalp-ear-nipple syndrome and renal defects. SUMO conjugation through the E2 enzyme UBE2I attaches SUMO1 to TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C, converting them into weaker activators and influencing epithelial differentiation and cancer stem cell traits in breast tumours. The tumour suppressor WWOX sequesters TFAP2C outside the nucleus, preventing it from reaching its targets. Together these controls set the dosage of AP-2 signalling, which matters because both excess and deficiency distort embryonic patterning and epithelial gene expression.

AP-2 transcription factors act high in developmental hierarchies, and one of their outputs is the control of other transcription factors that pattern the embryo. Here TFAP2A and TFAP2C, as homodimers and possibly heterodimers, cooperate with the transcriptional coactivator CITED2 to stimulate expression of PITX2, a homeodomain factor that establishes left-right asymmetry and directs outflow tract and valve formation in the developing heart. Because PITX2 sits downstream, loss of this input reproduces laterality defects and congenital cardiac malformations seen when CITED2 or the AP-2 factors are disrupted; TFAP2A mutation in humans also causes branchio-oculo-facial syndrome, reflecting the family's wider role in neural crest and craniofacial development. The relationship illustrates how a coactivator-dependent dimeric factor converts positional signals into a downstream regulatory programme rather than directly into structural gene expression.

The AP-2 family of transcription factors controls gene programmes in neural crest, craniofacial, limb, skin and placental development, and their loss produces recognizable malformation syndromes — branchio-oculo-facial syndrome from TFAP2A mutation, Char syndrome from TFAP2B — while TFAP2C is a driver of trophoblast and germ cell identity and is co-amplified with HER2 in breast cancer. Activation of these factors begins with dimerization through the helix-span-helix motif and binding of a basic region to palindromic GC-rich elements, though individual members prefer variant sites. Transactivation depends on partners: CITED family co-factors, CITED2 most avidly, dock on the helix-span-helix domain and bring in the acetyltransferase co-activators EP300 and CREBBP, and YEATS4 raises TFAP2B DNA binding, whereas WWOX sequesters AP-2 proteins and dampens their output. Mouse CITED2 loss recapitulates neural crest, cardiac and adrenal defects expected from failed AP-2 activation.

The AP-2 transcription factors TFAP2A, TFAP2B and TFAP2C control a battery of growth factor and receptor genes, and through them the proliferative behaviour of epithelial and placental cells. Their targets read as a map of breast cancer biology: the estrogen receptor ESR1, the receptor tyrosine kinases ERBB2, EGFR and KIT, and the ligand TGFA are all directly stimulated, while VEGFA transcription is repressed, linking these factors to angiogenic output as well as to mitogenic signalling. Cooperating partners modulate the response, with YY1 association raising the rate of ERBB2 transcription and the bromodomain coactivator ATAD2 contributing to target gene activation. In placenta the same factors drive both chorionic gonadotropin subunits, supporting trophoblast hormone production. Overexpression of TFAP2C in estrogen-receptor-positive breast and endometrial tumours makes this circuitry a determinant of hormone-responsive tumour phenotype.

AP-2 transcription factors set how strongly a cell brakes its own division by controlling the p21 cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor gene. Because p21 restrains CDK-cyclin complexes at the G1/S transition and is a principal effector of growth arrest and senescence, the balance struck here determines whether cells proliferate or pause, and it is frequently skewed in tumours. Two closely related family members act in opposition at the same locus: TFAP2A binds the CDKN1A promoter and activates it, while TFAP2C represses it, recruiting MYC together with the histone demethylase KDM5B, which strips activating methylation from promoter histones to shut transcription down. The result is a switch in which the relative abundance of the two paralogues, rather than an external signal, dictates p21 levels, linking developmental transcription factor programmes to cell cycle entry and to differentiation-associated exit from the cycle.

rRNA processing in the mitochondrion generates the 12S and 16S ribosomal RNAs that build the mitoribosome, the machine that translates the thirteen mitochondrially encoded subunits of the respiratory chain and ATP synthase. Without it oxidative phosphorylation fails, and mutations in the responsible nuclear enzymes cause infantile mitochondrial disease with lactic acidosis and cardiomyopathy. Because the mitochondrial genome is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, the rRNAs must first be excised: the tRNAs punctuating them are cleaved at their 5' ends by the proteinaceous RNase P complex and at their 3' ends by ELAC2, releasing the flanking rRNAs. Nucleus-encoded enzymes acting in the matrix then install a small set of methylated and pseudouridylated nucleotides, and MTERF4-NSUN4 and RCC1L-containing complexes couple modification to assembly of the large and small mitoribosomal subunits.

Mitochondria make their own ribosomes, and the 12S and 16S rRNAs at their core must first be cut out of a single long polycistronic transcript of the heavy strand and then chemically decorated. This rRNA processing in the mitochondrion sets the ceiling on how much respiratory chain protein a cell can synthesise, since the mitochondrial genome encodes core subunits of complexes I, III, IV and the ATP synthase. Endonucleolytic release depends on the RNase P-like complex of PRORP, TRMT10C and HSD17B10 acting at tRNA 5' ends and on ELAC2 at 3' ends, with FASTKD2 and RNA granule components aiding folding and maturation. Methyltransferases including TFB1M, NSUN4 and the MRM enzymes, plus pseudouridine synthases, install the handful of modifications needed for subunit assembly. Defects impair mitochondrial translation and cause infantile encephalomyopathy, cardiomyopathy and deafness.
