Ribosome production begins with a single long 47S transcript that must be trimmed, chemically modified and folded before it can carry the 18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNAs into working subunits. Maturation of rRNA in the nucleolus and, for a few late steps, the cytosol therefore sets the cell's capacity for protein synthesis and growth. Endonucleases and exonucleases including XRN2, the RNA exosome and NOB1 remove spacer sequences, while snoRNP components such as fibrillarin, DKC1, NOP56 and NOP58 direct 2'-O-methylation and pseudouridylation at guide-RNA-specified sites, and helicases and U3-associated assembly factors remodel the pre-ribosome. Ribosomal proteins of both subunits join co-transcriptionally, and cytoplasmic kinases and TSR1/LTV1 license the final 40S maturation cleavage. Defects cause ribosomopathies, among them Diamond-Blackfan anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita, and unassembled ribosomal proteins activate p53 through nucleolar stress.

Retinoic acid pushes cells out of cycle and into differentiation, and part of how it does so is by shutting down genes that support growth. In this arm of the response, the transcription factor TFAP2A accumulates after retinoic acid treatment and acts as a repressor rather than an activator, partnering with the nucleolar chaperone nucleophosmin (NPM1) at target promoters. The repressed targets are growth- and proliferation-associated: the mitochondrial chaperonin HSPD1, the rRNA methyltransferase NOP2, and the cell cycle transcription factor MYBL2, the latter two used as proliferation markers. Repression is thought to work through NPM1-dependent recruitment of the histone deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, deacetylating promoter chromatin. The complex also occupies the NPM1 promoter itself, consistent with the fall in NPM1 levels after treatment, giving a self-limiting loop that links retinoid signalling to withdrawal from proliferation.

RAB geranylgeranylation is the lipid modification step that licenses the RAB family of small GTPases to work on membranes, and so underpins essentially all vesicular traffic through the secretory and endolysosomal system. Newly made RABs are soluble and inert; attachment of one or two geranylgeranyl groups to C-terminal cysteines gives them the hydrophobic anchor needed to dock on target compartments, cycle on and off with GDI, and recruit sorting adaptors, tethers and motors. The reaction is carried out by a trimeric geranylgeranyltransferase in which RABGGTA and RABGGTB provide catalysis while the escort proteins CHM (REP1) or CHML present GDP-bound substrate and then chaperone the prenylated RAB to its membrane. Loss of CHM impairs prenylation of a subset of RABs and causes choroideremia, a progressive retinal degeneration, illustrating how one shared modification step supports compartment-specific trafficking across more than sixty RABs.

RAB GTPases only work on membranes, and geranylgeranylation is the lipid modification that puts them there. Newly made RABs are soluble and inert until one or two C-terminal cysteines receive twenty-carbon geranylgeranyl groups, after which they can dock on the endosomes, Golgi cisternae, secretory granules and autophagic membranes whose identity they define. The reaction is carried out by a trimeric prenyltransferase: the catalytic RABGGTA/RABGGTB heterodimer plus an escort protein, CHM or its paralogue CHML, which binds the GDP-loaded substrate, presents it for modification, and then delivers the prenylated GTPase to its target compartment. Once installed, the RAB cycles between GTP-bound membrane-associated and GDI-bound cytosolic states under GEF and GAP control, recruiting tethers, sorting adaptors and motors. Loss of CHM causes choroideremia, a progressive retinal degeneration, illustrating how underprenylation of particular RABs disables trafficking in specific tissues.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor makes cells move, and the route from receptor to movement runs through focal adhesion kinase. MET activates PTK2 signaling only when PTK2 is engaged simultaneously by MET and by integrins contacting the extracellular matrix, so the pathway couples a soluble growth factor cue to the adhesive state of the cell; SRC phosphorylation is required for PTK2 to reach full activity. The matrix side is supplied by fibronectin, fibrillar and fibril-associated collagens and the laminin chains that build basement membranes, read out through collagen- and laminin-binding integrins that pair alpha subunits with beta1. The output is adhesion turnover and directed migration, as in wound epithelialisation and branching morphogenesis, and the same axis drives invasion and metastasis when MET is amplified or HGF is supplied by tumour stroma.

One arm of the unfolded protein response reads the folding load in the endoplasmic reticulum and answers it by making more chaperones, and ATF6B is the weaker of its two transcription factors. In resting cells ATF6B sits in the ER membrane with its lumenal domain held by the chaperone HSPA5 (BiP); when misfolded protein accumulates, HSPA5 lets go, Golgi targeting signals are exposed, and the protein moves to the Golgi. There the sequential proteases MBTPS1 (S1P) and MBTPS2 (S2P) clip it, freeing a cytoplasmic fragment carrying a bZIP domain and a nuclear localisation signal that enters the nucleus and drives chaperone and ER-quality-control genes. Because it activates transcription only weakly and heterodimerises with the stronger ATF6, it can dampen rather than amplify the response, tuning how much secretory capacity a stressed cell builds.

The CREB3/OASIS family of membrane-anchored transcription factors couples the secretory pathway to gene expression, allowing tissues with heavy secretory loads to expand their capacity. Each member sits in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane through a transmembrane segment, carrying a bZIP dimerization and DNA-binding module plus an activation domain on the cytosolic side. When these factors move to the Golgi they are cleaved in turn by the resident proteases MBTPS1 and MBTPS2, a regulated intramembrane proteolysis event that frees the cytosolic fragment to enter the nucleus and switch on target genes. Individual members act in distinct tissues: CREB3L1 in osteoblast collagen secretion, CREB3L2 in cartilage, CREB3L3 in hepatic lipid and acute-phase gene control, with CREBRF opposing this output. Several are induced by ER stress but, unlike ATF6, do not sense unfolded protein via BiP release. Loss of CREB3L1 causes osteogenesis imperfecta.

Listeria monocytogenes invades non-phagocytic cells such as intestinal epithelium and hepatocytes by hijacking a growth factor receptor, and InlB-mediated entry is the route it uses. The bacterial surface protein InlB acts as a mimic of hepatocyte growth factor: its leucine-rich repeats dimerize, forcing dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation of the MET receptor tyrosine kinase and switching on the RAS/MAPK and PI3K/AKT outputs normally reserved for HGF. Phosphorylated MET recruits GRB2 and through it the E3 ligase CBL, whose monoubiquitination of the receptor commits it to clathrin-mediated internalization; the adaptor SH3KBP1 (CIN85) with endophilins, EPS15 and the HGS/STAM complex then carry the receptor, and the attached bacterium, into the cell. This is receptor downregulation machinery subverted for bacterial uptake, and it underlies the ability of Listeria to cross epithelial barriers and cause invasive listeriosis.

The receptor tyrosine kinase MET, activated by hepatocyte growth factor, controls epithelial cell scattering, wound closure and invasive growth, and its coupling to tensin proteins at focal adhesions links that signal to how a cell grips and pulls on its substrate. At adhesion sites MET associates with tensin family members whose expression tends to be reciprocal: TNS4 stabilises the receptor and favours motility, while TNS3 predominates in less migratory states. Because tensins bridge the cytoplasmic tail of beta-1 integrin to the actin cytoskeleton, this interaction places growth factor signalling directly onto the adhesion machinery that determines migration speed and direction. Elevated TNS4 accompanies MET-driven invasion in carcinomas, making this branch of MET signalling relevant to metastatic behaviour rather than to proliferation alone.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase reshapes the cytoskeleton and makes epithelial cells move, and this branch of MET signalling is how that happens: activation of the small GTPases RAP1 and RAC1. The output is cell scattering, lamellipodium formation, spreading and integrin-dependent adhesion, processes used in wound healing, liver regeneration and embryonic morphogenesis, and hijacked by carcinomas for invasion and metastasis. Mechanistically, the activated receptor recruits GRB2 and the scaffolding adaptor GAB1, whose phosphorylated tyrosines bind the SH2/SH3 adaptors CRK and CRKL. These adaptors in turn dock guanine nucleotide exchange factors at the membrane: RAPGEF1 loads GTP onto RAP1A and RAP1B to strengthen adhesion, while DOCK7 acts on RAC1 to drive actin polymerisation at the leading edge. Sustained signalling through this axis is a feature of MET-amplified tumours.

MET receptor recycling is the route by which the activated hepatocyte growth factor receptor is returned to the cell surface rather than degraded, sustaining the motility and survival signals that drive epithelial wound healing, tissue regeneration and, when deregulated, tumour invasion and metastasis. After HGF binding, MET is internalised and sorted by GGA3 through RAB4-positive early endosomes back to the plasma membrane, with ARF6 supporting the membrane trafficking step. Recycling does more than replenish surface receptor: MET continues to signal from endosomes through its GAB1, GRB2 and CRK/CRKL adaptor complex, and this endosomal phase is what converts a transient ligand encounter into prolonged ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 activation. The balance between this recycling arm and ubiquitin-dependent degradative sorting sets how long and how strongly a cell responds to HGF, and oncogenic MET mutants that escape degradative sorting are shunted into this pathway.

After hepatocyte growth factor binds MET, the activated receptor is internalised rather than simply switched off, and its route through the endosomal system determines how long and how strongly it signals. Recycling of MET back to the plasma membrane sustains ERK1/ERK2 and STAT3 output, supporting the motility, scattering and invasive growth responses that HGF elicits in epithelial cells and that are hijacked in carcinoma progression. Endocytosed receptor is sorted by the adaptor GGA3 through RAB4A/RAB4B-marked early recycling endosomes and returned to the surface with help from ARF6, while adaptors GRB2, GAB1 and the CRK/CRKL pair remain bound and continue to relay signals from the endosome itself. Diverting MET toward degradation instead of recycling shortens the response, so this trafficking step acts as a control point on receptor tyrosine kinase signal duration.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the MET receptor tyrosine kinase triggers one branch of downstream signalling in which STAT3 is recruited and activated, linking a growth factor cue at the cell surface to changes in transcription that drive scattering, morphogenesis and invasive growth. STAT3 docks at a phosphorylated tyrosine in the MET carboxy-terminal tail, directly or via a scaffold, and is itself phosphorylated on Y705, which allows dimerization, nuclear entry and target gene expression; SRC activity contributes to this phosphorylation, and continued signalling from endosomes after MET internalization sustains it. The output is anchorage-independent proliferation and increased motility, which is why this axis is scrutinized in carcinomas where MET is amplified or HGF is produced in an autocrine loop. In normal physiology the same route supports epithelial repair, liver regeneration and branching morphogenesis.

Hepatocyte growth factor binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase MET triggers a scattering programme in which epithelial cells loosen their contacts, spread and migrate through matrix "" the basis of wound repair and branching morphogenesis, and of the invasive phenotype seen when MET is amplified or mutated in carcinoma. Activated MET recruits the scaffold GAB1 together with GRB2, SRC, and the CRK/CRKL adaptors, which through RAPGEF1 and DOCK7 load RAP1A/B and RAC1 with GTP to drive lamellipodial actin remodelling. The receptor also associates physically with integrin heterodimers such as ITGA3/ITGB1 and signals to focal adhesion kinase PTK2, coupling growth factor input to adhesion turnover on the collagen, laminin and fibronectin substrates represented here. Tensins TNS3 and TNS4 act at these adhesions, TNS4 stabilising MET itself and reinforcing motility.

RAB GTPases mark the identity of intracellular membranes, and they can only recruit effectors when loaded with GTP, so the exchange factors that swap GDP for GTP decide when and where a trafficking step happens. Activation converts a soluble GDI-bound RAB into a membrane-attached organizer of vesicle budding, motility, tethering and fusion, governing endocytosis, recycling, Golgi transport, autophagy and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis such as melanosome and granule formation. The exchange factors are structurally heterogeneous: DENN-domain proteins acting on RAB35 and others, VPS9-domain proteins including RABGEF1 and the RIN family that switch on RAB5, the multisubunit TRAPP complex serving RAB1, and heterodimers like RIC1:RGP1. Escort proteins CHM/CHML deliver newly prenylated RABs to membranes; loss of CHM causes choroideremia, and mutations in RAB3GAP and TRAPP subunits cause developmental and skeletal disease.

Listeria monocytogenes entry into host cells describes how this food-borne bacterium hijacks normal receptor endocytosis to get inside non-phagocytic cells, the step that lets it cross the intestinal, placental and blood-brain barriers and cause meningoencephalitis or sepsis in newborns and immunocompromised adults. Two bacterial surface internalins do the work by mimicking host ligands: InlA engages E-cadherin, pulling on the junctional complex of beta-catenin and p120-catenin, while InlB engages the MET receptor tyrosine kinase and activates PI3K/AKT signalling. Both routes converge on the machinery that normally internalises these receptors — Src-family kinases, Cbl and CBLL1 ubiquitin ligases with polyubiquitin, GRB2 and CIN85 adaptors, the ESCRT-0 components HRS and STAM, endophilins and EPS15 — so clathrin-mediated uptake and actin remodelling deliver the bacterium into a vacuole. Subsequent filopod formation spreads it between cells while evading immune detection.

Listeria monocytogenes is a food-borne intracellular pathogen that invades non-phagocytic cells by hijacking host surface receptors, and this entry step is what lets it cross the intestinal, placental and blood-brain barriers to cause gastroenteritis in healthy adults and meningoencephalitis or sepsis in newborns and immunocompromised people. Two routes converge on the same host endocytic machinery: the bacterial surface protein InlA engages E-cadherin, pulling on the junctional complex with beta-catenin and p120-catenin, while InlB engages the MET receptor tyrosine kinase and switches on PI3K/AKT signalling. In both cases Src-family kinase activity, Cbl- and CBLL1-mediated ubiquitination of the receptor, and clathrin-associated adaptors such as EPS15, endophilins and the ESCRT-0 components HGS and STAM drive receptor internalisation, with the resulting membrane and actin remodelling engulfing the bacterium. The pathway is essentially receptor endocytosis and adherens-junction turnover subverted for bacterial uptake.

InlA-mediated entry of Listeria monocytogenes into host cells describes how a food-borne bacterium hijacks an adhesion receptor to get inside epithelial cells, the step that lets Listeria cross the intestinal barrier and reach the placenta and brain in listeriosis. The bacterial surface protein internalin binds E-cadherin on the host cell surface and mimics the signalling that normally follows cell-cell contact: SRC kinase is activated and phosphorylates E-cadherin and its bound catenins, creating docking sites for the ubiquitin ligase Hakai. Ubiquitination of the junctional complex drives clathrin- and caveolin-dependent endocytosis, and SRC-directed actin remodelling through cortactin and ARP2/3 pulls the bacterium in with the receptor. The same machinery governs physiological turnover of adherens junctions, so this route is subversion of normal junction endocytosis rather than a dedicated uptake system.

Listeria monocytogenes crosses the intestinal epithelium by exploiting a junctional adhesion receptor, and InlA-mediated entry describes how the bacterial surface protein internalin A binds host E-cadherin and turns adherens junction turnover into a route of invasion. This is the step that allows a food-borne organism to reach the bloodstream, placenta and central nervous system, causing listeriosis in pregnancy and in immunocompromised people. Engagement of E-cadherin activates SRC, which phosphorylates the cadherin and its associated beta-catenin and p120-catenin; the ubiquitin ligase CBLL1 (Hakai) then docks on the phosphorylated receptor and ubiquitinates it, marking the complex for clathrin- and caveolin-dependent endocytosis with accompanying actin remodelling. Because the same phosphorylation and ubiquitination steps operate during normal cadherin internalisation, the pathway doubles as a model for how junctional adhesion is dismantled and recycled in epithelia.

Protein methylation is the transfer of methyl groups onto lysine and arginine residues of proteins other than histones, a widespread post-translational mark that tunes protein activity, stability and partner binding rather than being a metabolic end in itself. Through it, cells modulate signal transduction outputs including MAPK, WNT, BMP, Hippo and JAK-STAT, and coordinate chromatin remodelling, transcription, translation and DNA repair; methylation frequently crosstalks with phosphorylation, ubiquitination and with histone marks. The enzymes here are dedicated methyltransferases acting on defined substrates: calmodulin is trimethylated by CAMKMT, the translation apparatus is marked on elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2 and on ribosomal protein RPS2, chaperones and the AAA-ATPase VCP are modified by METTL21A and VCPKMT, and mitochondrial electron transfer flavoprotein is methylated by ETFBKMT. Loss of individual enzymes, such as CAMKMT, causes developmental and neurological disease.

Methyl groups added to lysine and arginine side chains tune the behaviour of proteins well beyond histones, and protein methylation of non-histone substrates regulates signalling through routes such as MAPK, WNT, BMP, Hippo and JAK-STAT, as well as chromatin remodelling, transcription, translation and DNA repair. The enzymes here are largely seven-beta-strand methyltransferases acting on defined targets: a calmodulin-specific lysine methyltransferase modifies calmodulin, dedicated enzymes methylate elongation factors eEF1A and eEF2, another modifies the electron transfer flavoprotein beta subunit, and further members act on the AAA-ATPase VCP and on Hsp70-family chaperones, while an arginine methyltransferase modifies ribosomal protein S2. The pattern shows methylation being used to set the activity of the translational apparatus, chaperone and protein-quality-control machinery, calcium signalling and mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation, with crosstalk to other post-translational marks integrating these responses.

Regulatory T cells keep immune responses from turning on self tissue, and their identity is set by a transcriptional circuit in which RUNX1 and FOXP3 control Treg development. RUNX1, acting with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, drives transcription of FOXP3 itself; FOXP3 protein then binds back to the RUNX1:CBFB complex and redirects it. Inflammatory effector genes such as IL2 and IFNG, which RUNX1 would otherwise switch on, are repressed, while the surface hallmarks of the suppressive lineage are induced: the IL-2 receptor alpha chain, CTLA4 and GITR, with NFATC2 cooperating at these promoters. RUNX1:CBFB also activates the complement receptor CR1, whose appearance on activated T cells favours Treg generation. Loss of FOXP3 abolishes this programme and produces fatal multi-organ autoimmunity, and weakened Treg output underlies autoimmune disease and allergy more broadly.

Vitamin E transport is the intracellular handling step that determines how much alpha-tocopherol, the body's principal vitamin E, reaches the circulation and peripheral tissues. Because tocopherols are lipophilic, they cannot diffuse freely through the cytosol and depend on dedicated carrier proteins; in hepatocytes this task falls to alpha-tocopherol transfer protein, which selectively binds alpha-tocopherol taken up from lipoproteins and directs it for secretion into nascent VLDL rather than degradation. This selectivity explains why alpha-tocopherol predominates in plasma over other dietary tocopherol forms. The pathway sustains the antioxidant protection of membrane lipids, particularly in neurons and erythrocytes, and its loss causes ataxia with isolated vitamin E deficiency, a progressive spinocerebellar degeneration with peripheral neuropathy and retinopathy that responds to high-dose supplementation. It belongs with the broader trafficking of fat-soluble vitamins and lipoprotein metabolism.

Alpha-tocopherol, the predominant and most biologically active form of vitamin E in humans, is a lipophilic antioxidant that cannot move freely through the aqueous cytosol and depends on a dedicated carrier to reach its destinations. This transport step occurs mainly in hepatocytes, where the alpha-tocopherol transfer protein binds tocopherol taken up from dietary lipoproteins and directs it toward secretion into circulating very low density lipoproteins, thereby setting plasma vitamin E levels and the supply available to peripheral tissues, including neurons. Selective retention of the alpha isoform over other tocopherols and tocotrienols explains why body stores are dominated by a single vitamer. Loss of this carrier causes ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, a progressive spinocerebellar and peripheral neuropathy attributable to unchecked lipid peroxidation in membranes, and it responds to high-dose tocopherol supplementation.

RUNX3 is a Runt-domain transcription factor that partners with CBFB to control cell fate decisions in the immune system and to restrain proliferation in epithelia. It drives CD8+ lineage commitment in thymocytes, shapes innate lymphoid and intestinal T cell programmes, and induces integrin genes such as ITGAL and ITGA4 that support leukocyte adhesion; loss of RUNX3, frequently through promoter hypermethylation, is associated with gastric, colorectal, oesophageal and breast cancers. Its growth-suppressive output runs largely through TGF-beta signalling, where cooperation with SMAD3 and SMAD4 enforces cell cycle arrest via CDKN1A, and through antagonism of proliferative programmes: RUNX3 opposes NOTCH target activation with RBPJ and MAML co-activators, blocks TEAD:YAP1/WWTR1 promoter binding, and intersects with WNT-driven TCF/LEF and MYC transcription. Acetyltransferases and HDAC4 tune its activity, while ubiquitin ligases including SMURF1 and SMURF2 and the proteasome set its abundance.

RUNX2 is the master transcription factor of bone formation, and the programme it directs converts mesenchymal progenitors into osteoblasts and drives chondrocyte maturation, so that both intramembranous and endochondral skeletal elements form. Loss of one functional copy causes cleidocranial dysplasia, with clavicular and cranial defects and delayed tooth eruption, while its misregulation contributes to osteosarcoma and to bone metastasis of breast cancer. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 turns on osteoblast genes such as osteocalcin, type I collagen and SP7/osterix, and stimulates Indian hedgehog to pace growth-plate maturation. Its own transcription is set by DLX5, MSX2, NKX3-2, TWIST1 and steroid receptors including ESR1 and the glucocorticoid receptor, and it autorepresses. Activity is further tuned by SOX9, RB1 and HDAC binding, by kinase phosphorylation, and by ubiquitin ligases SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2 that route it to the proteasome. RUNX2 also represses CDKN1A, linking it to proliferation control and cell migration genes.

RUNX1 is the transcription factor that lets blood form: with its obligate partner CBFB it drives self-renewal of haematopoietic stem cells and the commitment of myeloid, megakaryocytic, T regulatory and B lymphoid progenitors, and its translocation or mutation is among the commonest lesions in acute leukaemia. CBFB does not touch DNA itself; it stabilises the Runt domain on the double helix and relieves RUNX1 autoinhibition. From there RUNX1 recruits coactivators and chromatin machinery — CREBBP/EP300 acetyltransferases, SWI/SNF remodellers, MLL-family and WDR5-containing methyltransferase complexes — or represses targets through Sin3/HDAC1 and Polycomb components, while proteasomal turnover and kinase phosphorylation set its level and activity. Target genes include lineage factors such as GATA1, SPI1, TAL1, PAX5 and FOXP3, platelet genes, and cytokines like IL2 and CSF2; RUNX1 also acts in breast epithelium and nociceptive sensory neurons.

GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter of the mammalian brain, and its synthesis is the single step that defines a neuron as GABAergic. Two glutamate decarboxylases convert glutamate to GABA, linking the excitatory and inhibitory transmitter pools through a decarboxylation that also consumes a proton. The two isoforms are not interchangeable: the 65 kDa enzyme is largely membrane-associated near release sites and is coupled to vesicular loading by the vesicular GABA transporter, so the GABA it makes is preferentially packaged for synaptic release, while the 67 kDa enzyme is more cytosolic, saturated with its pyridoxal phosphate cofactor, and supplies GABA for metabolic and trophic roles beyond neurotransmission. Loss or reduction of this capacity shifts cortical circuits toward excitation, a feature of epilepsy; the 65 kDa enzyme is also a major autoantigen in type 1 diabetes and stiff-person syndrome.

GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the mammalian central nervous system, and this pathway covers its full life cycle: synthesis, vesicular loading, calcium-triggered release, clearance from the synaptic cleft, and catabolism. Inhibitory tone set here constrains network excitability, and its loss underlies epilepsy, anxiety states and movement disorders. Two glutamate decarboxylases, GAD1 and GAD2, generate GABA from glutamate, and the vesicular inhibitory amino acid transporter SLC32A1 concentrates it into synaptic vesicles. Release depends on the SNARE proteins VAMP2, SNAP25 and syntaxin-1A acting with the priming factor STXBP1, the calcium sensor synaptotagmin-1, complexin and active-zone RIM1. Plasma membrane transporters of the SLC6 family recover GABA and related osmolytes into neurons and glia, after which transamination by ABAT and oxidation by ALDH5A1 feed carbon into the TCA cycle; ALDH5A1 deficiency causes succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase disease.

Inhibitory signalling at GABAergic synapses is switched off largely by clearing the transmitter from the extracellular space, and this reuptake step sets how long and how far GABA acts. The carriers involved are sodium- and chloride-dependent plasma membrane transporters of the neurotransmitter transporter family: GAT1 (SLC6A1) dominates uptake into presynaptic terminals, where recovered GABA is reloaded into vesicles, while GAT3 (SLC6A11) and the betaine/GABA transporter BGT1 (SLC6A12) and GAT2 (SLC6A13) contribute uptake into astrocytes and at non-synaptic sites. GABA taken up by astrocytes is catabolised rather than reused, and glutamine returned to neurons regenerates the transmitter pool. Because these transporters limit ambient and tonic inhibition, they are drug targets in epilepsy — tiagabine blocks GAT1 — and loss-of-function variants in SLC6A1 cause myoclonic-atonic epilepsy and developmental delay.

Alpha-dystroglycan is the cell-surface receptor that anchors muscle fibres, neurons and peripheral nerves to their basal lamina, and it only binds laminin if it carries the right sugars. The O-mannosylation of dystroglycan therefore determines whether the link from extracellular matrix through the membrane to dystrophin and the cytoskeleton can bear mechanical load. Mannose is added to serine and threonine residues by the POMT1/POMT2 complex and then extended along three branches, with POMGNT1, POMGNT2 and POMK, B3GALNT2, B4GAT1 and the LARGE enzymes building the matriglycan that laminin actually recognises; fukutin, FKRP and CRPPA supply and transfer the ribitol phosphate step, while nucleotide-sugar transporters feed the reactions. Loss of any of these leaves dystroglycan hypoglycosylated and causes dystroglycanopathies, congenital muscular dystrophies often accompanied by brain and eye malformations; altered glycosylation is also seen in tumours.

Estrogen-responsive gene expression in breast epithelium is shaped not only by the hormone receptor itself but by the transcription factors it recruits, and RUNX1 acting on estrogen receptor mediated transcription is one such partnership. RUNX1, together with its obligate cofactor CBFB, binds directly to ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha and co-occupies the regulatory regions of a subset of estrogen target genes, among them the glycerolipid synthesis enzyme GPAM, the substrate adaptor KCTD6, and the Wnt pathway scaffold AXIN1. This gives RUNX1 a say in which genes respond to estrogen, linking hormone signalling to lipid metabolism and Wnt regulation rather than to proliferation alone. The relationship matters clinically: RUNX1 is a recurrently altered tumour suppressor in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, and high GPAM expression tracks with better overall survival.

Alpha-dystroglycan carries O-mannose glycans that link the muscle and brain cell surface to laminin and other basement membrane ligands, and this branch of the pathway builds the core M2 form of those glycans. Synthesis begins with protein O-mannosyltransferases POMT1 and POMT2 adding mannose to dystroglycan serines and threonines; POMGNT1 then attaches beta-1,2-GlcNAc to form core M1, and the branching enzyme MGAT5B adds a beta-1,6-linked GlcNAc to generate core M2. These branched structures are concentrated in brain and prostate, where they constitute a small fraction of protein O-glycans yet contribute to neural cell adhesion and migration. Defective O-mannosylation of dystroglycan underlies the dystroglycanopathies, congenital muscular dystrophies whose severe forms combine muscle degeneration with cobblestone lissencephaly and eye malformations, illustrating how a glycan modification rather than the protein itself determines receptor function.

DAG1 core M3 glycosylations builds the sugar chain on alpha-dystroglycan that lets muscle and brain cells grip their basement membrane. Matriglycan is the actual binding site for laminin, agrin and perlecan, so this modification, not the protein alone, creates the mechanical link between the extracellular matrix and the cytoskeleton in skeletal muscle and at the pial surface of the developing brain. Assembly is strictly ordered: POMT1 and POMT2 transfer mannose to specific threonines, POMGNT2 adds beta-1,4-GlcNAc, B3GALNT2 completes the GalNAc-GlcNAc-Man linker, and POMK phosphorylates the mannose 6-position to license further elongation. Loss of any step abolishes ligand binding and produces dystroglycanopathy, ranging from limb-girdle muscular dystrophy to Walker-Warburg syndrome with cobblestone lissencephaly and eye malformations, illustrating that a glycan can be the functional unit of a receptor.

Alpha-dystroglycan must be sugar-coated before it can work, and the core M3 glycosylation route is how that coat is built on specific threonines of its mucin-like domain. The finished structure, matriglycan, is what lets dystroglycan bind laminin, agrin and perlecan in the basement membrane and so anchor muscle fibres and neurons to the extracellular matrix; when the pathway fails, the link breaks and the result is dystroglycanopathy, ranging from limb-girdle muscular dystrophy to Walker-Warburg syndrome with brain and eye malformations. Assembly is strictly ordered: a protein O-mannosyltransferase complex transfers mannose to threonine, POMGNT2 adds beta-1,4-GlcNAc, B3GALNT2 caps it with GalNAc, and POMK phosphorylates the mannose to license further elongation into the ribitol-phosphate and glucuronate-xylose polymer. This is post-translational maturation in the secretory pathway serving cell-matrix adhesion.

Alpha-dystroglycan is heavily decorated with O-mannose glycans, and the core M1 branch is one of the routes that mannose can take once it is attached. The pathway begins with a protein O-mannosyltransferase complex, POMT1 with POMT2, transferring mannose to serine and threonine residues in the mucin-like domain of dystroglycan; POMGNT1 then adds beta-1,2-linked N-acetylglucosamine, defining core M1 as distinct from the beta-1,6-branched M2 and the phosphorylated M3 structures. M1 chains do not themselves bind laminin and the other extracellular matrix ligands that anchor muscle fibres and neurons to their basement membranes, but they serve as precursors for M2 and support maturation along the M3 route that carries the matriglycan binding site. Loss of these glycosyltransferases produces dystroglycanopathies, congenital muscular dystrophies frequently accompanied by brain and eye malformations.

RUNX1 is the master transcription factor of definitive blood formation, and the many layers that set its abundance and activity determine whether hemogenic endothelium yields hematopoietic stem cells and whether progenitors mature into T cells, megakaryocytes and other lineages; dosage matters so much that haploinsufficiency causes familial platelet disorder with leukemia predisposition, and translocations disrupting the gene drive acute myeloid leukemia. Transcription proceeds from two alternative promoters used differently across development, while a panel of microRNAs including miR-17, miR-20a, miR-18a and miR-27a engage the 3'UTR through Argonaute and TNRC6 silencing complexes to limit translation. Protein activity is then tuned by partners and modifications: heterodimerization with CBFB is required for DNA binding and transactivation, D-type cyclins and CDK6 antagonize that step, SRC-family tyrosine phosphorylation is reversed by the phosphatase PTPN11, and PML directs subnuclear localization.

Cells clear damaged or surplus mitochondria by tagging them directly for engulfment, and receptor-mediated mitophagy is the ubiquitin-independent route in which proteins anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane bind LC3 themselves through a short W/F/Y-x-x-L/I motif. This matters for matching mitochondrial mass to metabolic demand, for limiting oxidative damage, and for developmental programmes such as reticulocyte maturation, where failure to eliminate mitochondria blocks red cell formation; defective turnover contributes to cardiac and neurodegenerative pathology. Signalling controls whether the receptor engages: in normoxia Src kinase and casein kinase 2 phosphorylate FUNDC1 to keep affinity for LC3 low, while hypoxia inactivates them and the mitochondrial phosphatase PGAM5 dephosphorylates the receptor, strengthening LC3 binding. ULK1 is recruited to the mitochondrion, and the ATG5-ATG12 conjugation machinery supplies LC3 lipidation for autophagosome growth around the cargo.

Digestion is the luminal breakdown of dietary macromolecules into absorbable units — monosaccharides, fatty acids, monoacylglycerols and cholesterol, and amino acids and dipeptides — the step on which all nutrient uptake in the small intestine depends. Salivary and pancreatic amylases cleave starch to maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins, which brush-border hydrolases on enterocyte microvilli finish: sucrase-isomaltase, maltase-glucoamylase, lactase and trehalase release glucose, galactose and fructose. Gastric and pancreatic lipases, aided by colipase and carboxyl ester lipase, hydrolyse triacylglycerols and cholesterol esters, while gastric pepsin and pancreatic proteases, secreted as proenzymes and activated by proteolysis in the gut lumen, degrade protein. Loss of individual enzymes produces defined intolerances and malabsorption, as in lactase deficiency or pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. Guanylin and uroguanylin acting through guanylate cyclase C couple this process to intestinal fluid and electrolyte secretion.

Food arrives as polymers that no cell can absorb, and digestion is the extracellular chemistry that reduces dietary starch, fat and protein to monosaccharides, fatty acids and amino acids at the intestinal surface. Salivary and pancreatic amylases cleave starch to maltose and limit dextrins, which brush-border enzymes on enterocyte microvilli finish: sucrase-isomaltase, maltase-glucoamylase, lactase and trehalase release glucose, galactose and fructose. Gastric and pancreatic lipases, aided by colipase and bile-salt-stimulated carboxyl ester lipase, hydrolyse triacylglycerols and cholesterol esters. Most of these enzymes are secreted as inactive precursors and become active only in the lumen. Loss of individual activities is directly clinical: lactase decline causes lactose intolerance, pancreatic lipase deficiency causes fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea. Guanylin and uroguanylin acting on intestinal guanylate cyclase C link the process to fluid and electrolyte secretion that keeps the lumen suitable for absorption.

RUNX1 regulates expression of components of tight junctions describes a transcriptional program that sets how tightly epithelial and endothelial sheets seal against paracellular leak. Acting as the DNA-binding partner of core binding factor beta, RUNX1 occupies the promoters of TJP1, OCLN and CLDN5 and drives their transcription, so the scaffolding protein ZO-1, occludin and the endothelium-selective claudin-5 accumulate at junctional strands. Because claudin-5 is the principal determinant of barrier tightness in brain microvessels, this circuit helps maintain blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier integrity; loss of RUNX1 input, for example when miR-18a represses it in glioma vasculature, lowers junctional gene expression and increases permeability. The link places a haematopoietic and developmental transcription factor upstream of cell-cell adhesion and vascular barrier function, with consequences for oedema, inflammatory infiltration and the delivery of drugs across compromised barriers.

Tight junctions seal the space between adjacent endothelial and epithelial cells and set how much solute can cross a barrier; here that barrier programme is placed under transcriptional control by RUNX1. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX1 binds the promoters of the genes for ZO-1, occludin and claudin-5 and raises their expression, so the scaffolding protein and the two integral junctional membrane proteins that form the seal are produced together. The relevance is barrier permeability: in brain endothelium these three products are core constituents of the blood-brain and blood-tumour barrier, and loss of RUNX1 output, as occurs when the microRNA miR-18a represses it, loosens the junctions and increases passage across the barrier in glioma. This links a transcription factor best known in haematopoiesis to endothelial barrier integrity and to the problem of drug delivery into tumours.

Platelets arise from megakaryocytes, and the transcription factor RUNX1 with its partner CBFB sets the gene programme that makes them. The complex is induced as progenitors commit to the megakaryocytic lineage and switched off as they turn erythroid, and it cooperates with GATA1 and its partner ZFPM1 at megakaryocyte promoters. Which coregulators are recruited decides the outcome: arginine methylation by PRMT1 favours an activating complex with the acetyltransferases EP300 and KAT2B and WDR5-containing methyltransferase complexes, whereas unmethylated RUNX1 binds SIN3A/SIN3B with HDAC1 and PRMT6 to repress. Targets include the integrin ITGA2B and GP1BA for adhesion and aggregation, THBS1, the alpha-granule chemokine PF4, MYL9, PRKCQ, NFE2 and NR4A3, plus MIR27A, which feeds back on RUNX1 translation. Loss of RUNX1 function causes familial platelet disorder with thrombocytopenia and predisposition to leukaemia.

Cells sense foreign aromatic chemicals and respond by inducing the enzymes that metabolise them, and aryl hydrocarbon receptor signalling is the transcriptional route that links the two. It is how exposure to dioxins such as TCDD and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons like benzo(a)pyrene raises Phase I and Phase II detoxification capacity, including the cytochromes P450 CYP1A1 and CYP1B1 and quinone oxidoreductase; the same induction can bioactivate procarcinogens, so the pathway underlies both chemical clearance and dioxin toxicity. Before ligand binds, AHR is held in the cytosol with HSP90, the co-chaperone p23 and the AIP immunophilin-like protein. Ligand binding triggers nuclear entry, release of the chaperones, and dimerisation with ARNT so the pair can occupy xenobiotic response elements. The repressor AHRR competes for ARNT and damps the response, giving the system built-in negative feedback.

Estrogens coordinate development, reproduction, bone and lipid metabolism, and vascular and neuronal function, and estrogen receptor-mediated signaling is how their message is read inside target cells. Ligand-bound ESR1 and ESR2, released from HSP90-based chaperone complexes, act as nuclear receptors that recruit coactivators such as NCOA1-3, p300/CBP and the mediator subunit MED1, along with chromatin-modifying enzymes and cohesin, to assemble RNA polymerase II on target promoters and enhancers; lineage factors FOXA1 and GATA3 direct where the receptor binds, and outputs include CCND1, MYC, PGR, GREB1 and TFF1, driving proliferation and differentiation. A separate membrane-proximal arm, involving palmitoylation, caveolins, SRC, G protein subunits and PI3K-AKT and MAPK cascades, produces rapid responses such as eNOS activation. This circuitry underlies hormone-dependent breast cancer growth and is the target of antiestrogen therapy, while microRNA-loaded argonaute complexes add post-transcriptional control.

Blood formation requires stem cells to stop renewing themselves and commit to a lineage, and RUNX1, acting with its partner CBFB, is one of the transcription factors that makes that decision. Its best-defined target here is SPI1 (PU.1): RUNX1 brings the histone methyltransferase KMT2A to the SPI1 promoter and upstream regulatory element, depositing activating H3K4 trimethylation, and the resulting PU.1 expression restrains stem cell self-renewal while enabling myeloid and lymphoid commitment. RUNX1 also sits within a TAL1-containing complex with LMO1/LMO2, LDB1, GATA factors and E-proteins that drives MYB transcription, a configuration that in T-ALL promotes proliferation and blocks apoptosis. Proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes reflect the degradation that limits RUNX1 levels, ITCH and CDK7-containing kinase activity among its regulators. Loss or translocation of RUNX1 underlies familial platelet disorder and acute myeloid leukemia.

Skin epithelium must balance stem cell maintenance against terminal differentiation, and the transcription factor RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, tilts that balance in keratinocytes by repressing a small set of target genes. One is the protease inhibitor SERPINB13, which restrains cathepsin-family proteases such as cathepsin L and V that participate in epidermal differentiation and desmosomal remodelling; its loss is common in head and neck cancers. RUNX1 also represses SOCS3 and SOCS4, the negative feedback inhibitors of JAK-STAT signalling, so removing them raises STAT3 activity. Sustained STAT3 output favours proliferation and self-renewal in hair follicle and epithelial stem cell compartments, which is why this circuit is implicated in tumour initiation and in squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. The pathway thus links lineage-specific transcriptional repression to cytokine signalling strength and protease balance in stratified epithelium.

RUNX1, partnered with CBFB, is the master transcription factor of definitive blood formation, and its output depends heavily on which chromatin co-factors it brings to a promoter. Here RUNX1 is shown engaging partners whose net effect on target genes remains ambiguous, a state of affairs that matters because the same complex can activate or silence the same promoter depending on context. HIPK2 phosphorylates both RUNX1 and the acetyltransferase EP300 bound to the complex, and leukemia-associated CBFB mutations disrupt this modification. RUNX1:CBFB also associates with polycomb repressive complex 1 subunits, including RING1/RNF2 with CBX and PHC proteins, found at many RUNX1 targets acting as co-activators or co-repressors. Direct contacts with SWI/SNF subunits such as SMARCA4, SMARCB1 and ARID1A recruit nucleosome remodelling. Casein kinase 2 subunits add further phosphorylation input, tying hematopoietic gene control to chromatin state.

B cells need a functioning antigen receptor signalling apparatus, and part of that apparatus is put in place transcriptionally before any antigen is ever seen. Here RUNX1 controls transcription of genes acting in B cell receptor signalling, most directly the B lymphoid tyrosine kinase BLK, which propagates receptor engagement into the intracellular kinase cascades that drive B cell development, differentiation and antibody responses. RUNX1 works as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, which stabilises DNA binding, and cooperates at the BLK promoter with the ETS-family factors ELF1 and ELF2 and with PAX5, the transcription factor that commits and maintains the B lymphoid lineage. This convergence of lineage-determining and general ETS regulators on a single kinase gene illustrates how haematopoietic transcription factors specify signalling competence; RUNX1 itself is a recurrent target of leukaemic translocation and mutation.

RUNX1 regulates transcription of genes involved in differentiation of myeloid cells describes how the master haematopoietic transcription factor RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, directs myeloid progenitors toward mature granulocytes, macrophages, erythrocytes and platelet-producing megakaryocytes. This programme sets the output of adult blood production; disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB by translocation or point mutation blocks differentiation at the progenitor stage and is among the most common lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorder. Mechanistically the RUNX1:CBFB heterodimer binds target promoters and recruits the histone acetyltransferase CREBBP to activate transcription, inducing the growth factor GM-CSF (CSF2) that drives proliferation and survival of myeloid progenitors, the lectin galectin-3 whose levels rise through maturation, and protein kinase C-beta, which governs myeloid cell apoptosis. It links lineage-specifying transcription to cytokine signalling and survival control.

Myeloid progenitors in the bone marrow must be instructed to become granulocytes, monocytes, erythrocytes or platelet-producing megakaryocytes, and RUNX1 is the transcription factor that issues much of that instruction. Acting as a heterodimer with its non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, it occupies target promoters and recruits the acetyltransferase CREBBP to open chromatin and drive transcription. Among the genes switched on are CSF2, encoding GM-CSF, a cytokine that supports growth, survival and maturation across several myeloid lineages; LGALS3, whose galectin-3 product rises as myeloid cells mature; and PRKCB, a protein kinase C isoform governing myeloid cell apoptosis. Because this programme sets the balance between progenitor self-renewal and differentiation, loss or translocation of RUNX1 or CBFB stalls maturation and is a recurrent cause of acute myeloid leukaemia and familial platelet disorders.

The transcription factor RUNX1, working with its obligate partner CBFB, directs the haematopoietic gene programme, and part of that programme is the cell's ability to send and receive interleukin-family signals. Through this arm of its output RUNX1 turns on the gene for the leukemia inhibitory factor receptor, which transmits signals from an interleukin-6 family cytokine and contributes to blood cell production, embryo implantation, placental development and neural differentiation. Together with the ETS-family co-activator ELF1, the RUNX1:CBFB heterodimer also drives transcription of interleukin-3, a growth factor for multipotent progenitors and myeloid lineages. Because cytokine responsiveness and proliferative signalling are set here, disruption of RUNX1 or CBFB — as happens in familial platelet disorder and in the recurrent translocations of acute leukaemia — leaves progenitors with a miscalibrated response to interleukin cues.

RUNX1, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, is a lineage-defining transcription factor best known in blood development, and part of what it does is set the level of WNT signalling by transcribing WNT pathway components directly. This matters because the strength of WNT input decides whether progenitors self-renew or differentiate, and because RUNX1 is a recurrent target of translocation and mutation in leukaemia and a modifier of breast cancer behaviour. Two targets illustrate opposite arms of the same control. With the regulatory T cell factor FOXP3 as cofactor, the complex drives RSPO3, a secreted R-spondin that potentiates WNT receptor signalling and has oncogenic activity in breast tissue. With ligand-activated estrogen receptor alpha, it instead induces AXIN1, a scaffold of the destruction complex that restrains beta-catenin. Hormonal and immune context therefore determines whether RUNX1 amplifies or dampens WNT output.

Regulation of RUNX2 expression and activity controls the master transcription factor that commits mesenchymal progenitors to the osteoblast lineage and drives chondrocyte maturation, so its output sets bone formation, skeletal patterning and, when dosage is wrong, cleidocranial dysplasia or osteoporotic bone loss. Control operates at several levels. Two alternative promoters respond to distinct inputs: estrogen receptor alpha and ESRRA with its coactivators PPARGC1A or PPARGC1B, which switch the same receptor between activation and repression, the glucocorticoid receptor mediating dexamethasone-induced suppression, and the homeodomain and bHLH factors DLX5/DLX6, MSX2, NKX3-2 and TWIST1, plus RUNX2 autoregulation. Protein activity is then tuned by partners that enhance or sequester it, CBFB heterodimerization and SATB2 versus HIVEP3 and non-phosphorylated STAT1, which blocks nuclear import. Finally, the E3 ligases SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2 direct RUNX2 to proteasomal degradation, keeping osteogenic drive proportional to BMP signalling.

RUNX2 is the master transcription factor for osteoblast differentiation and bone formation, and this pathway covers how much of it is made and how active it is once made. The dosage matters clinically: loss of one functional copy causes cleidocranial dysplasia, with defective clavicles and delayed cranial suture closure, while sustained activity drives skeletal mineralization and chondrocyte maturation. Transcription is driven from two alternative promoters, stimulated by estrogen receptor alpha, the homeodomain factors DLX5 and DLX6, and TWIST1, and repressed by the glucocorticoid receptor NR3C1, MSX2 and NKX3-2; estrogen-related receptor alpha switches between activation and repression depending on whether PGC1-alpha or PGC1-beta is bound. Protein-level control adds heterodimerization with CBFB and cooperation with cofactors, cytoplasmic sequestration by unphosphorylated STAT1, and polyubiquitination by SMURF1, WWP1, STUB1 and SKP2-containing cullin-RING ligases followed by proteasomal degradation.

Osteoblasts are made, not born, and RUNX2 acting with its partner CBFB is the transcriptional switch that commits mesenchymal progenitors to the bone-forming lineage and drives the genes that build mineralized matrix. Loss of this programme gives cleidocranial dysplasia and failed ossification, while its output — type I collagen, osteocalcin, and the cartilage-associated matrix protein UCMA — defines the skeleton's organic scaffold and its endocrine activity. RUNX2 cooperates with SP7 (Osterix) and SATB2 at target promoters, and is tuned by a dense layer of regulation: MAPK phosphorylation and SRC/YES1-dependent YAP1 binding respectively promote and restrain activity at the osteocalcin promoter, activated androgen receptor and HDAC recruitment block DNA binding, Notch effectors HEY1 and HES1 and the zinc finger ZNF521 repress it, and ubiquitin-dependent turnover limits its abundance. The pathway sits at the junction of skeletal development, hormonal signalling and matrix production.

Invadopodia are actin-rich membrane protrusions through which tumour cells attach to and locally digest the extracellular matrix, the step that lets a cell leave its tissue of origin and invade. Their normal-cell counterparts, podosomes, perform the same adhesion-and-degradation function in monocytic cells, endothelium and smooth muscle, and appear in Src-transformed fibroblasts; the invadopodium name is reserved for the cancer version. Each protrusion has an actin core ringed by adhesion and scaffolding proteins, and matures by recruiting pericellular proteases that cleave matrix components at the contact site. The scaffold TKS5 links phosphoinositide-marked membrane to the actin machinery and to ADAM-family transmembrane metalloproteases, which supply the proteolytic activity and shed cell-surface substrates. This coupling of cytoskeletal protrusion to focal matrix breakdown underlies invasion, metastasis and matrix remodelling during tissue growth.

Long bones form by endochondral ossification, in which cartilage is progressively replaced by bone, and the step at which chondrocytes stop proliferating and become hypertrophic is controlled by RUNX2. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 drives transcription of Indian hedgehog and of markers of the hypertrophic state such as type X collagen, coupling chondrocyte maturation to the parathyroid hormone-related peptide feedback loop that sets growth plate length. GLI2 transduces the hedgehog signal, while HDAC4 restrains RUNX2 activity and so delays hypertrophy; loss of this brake causes premature ossification, and loss of RUNX2 function blocks maturation and limb elongation. The same factor governs osteoblast differentiation, making it the shared switch for skeletal patterning, and its haploinsufficiency underlies cleidocranial dysplasia.

Skeletal formation depends on a master transcription factor that turns mesenchymal progenitors into osteoblasts and drives chondrocytes through hypertrophy, and this is the programme RUNX2 runs during bone development. Without it, flat bones of the skull never ossify and long-bone development stalls at cartilage; losing one functional copy in humans gives cleidocranial dysplasia, with delayed sutures, absent clavicles and dental defects. Acting with its partner CBFB, RUNX2 induces matrix and osteoblast genes such as COL1A1, SP7 and BGLAP, whose product osteocalcin also acts as a hormone influencing glucose handling and fertility, and drives IHH to pace chondrocyte maturation. Its output is tuned by BMP-activated SMAD1:SMAD4 complexes, by Notch effectors HEY1 and HES1, by class II histone deacetylases, by Hippo effectors YAP1 and WWTR1, and by kinases including SRC and ERK. Deregulation of these controls features in osteosarcoma.

RUNX2 is the master transcription factor of osteoblast differentiation, but the same factor also drives a migratory and invasive gene programme in bone and in tumour cells that colonise it. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX2 turns on ITGA5, which mediates attachment to fibronectin and helps breast cancer cells adhere within bone, ITGBL1, which modulates TGF-beta signalling and contributes to RUNX2-driven bone metastasis, and MMP13, a collagenase that degrades fibrillar collagen during skeletal remodelling and permits immune cells and cancer cells to move through matrix. AKT kinases phosphorylate RUNX2 and raise its transcriptional output, linking growth factor and PI3K signalling to this migratory programme. The same targets support endothelial cell movement during retinal angiogenesis and stem cell migration, so the pathway spans normal tissue morphogenesis and metastatic invasion.

RUNX2 regulates genes involved in differentiation of myeloid cells describes a transcriptional step in blood cell maturation, in which RUNX family factors drive expression of galectin-3, a lectin whose levels rise as myeloid progenitors mature and which shapes cell adhesion, phagocyte behaviour and inflammatory responses. RUNX2 and its close relative RUNX1 both bind the LGALS3 promoter, and each acts as a heterodimer with the non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB, which stabilises DNA contact and is required for RUNX activity in haematopoiesis. RUNX1 is the classical master regulator of definitive blood formation, while RUNX2 is better known in osteoblast specification, so this shared target illustrates how one factor family is redeployed across lineages. Sustained galectin-3 output from this circuit is a feature of pituitary tumours and gliomas, where it supports growth and invasion.

The transcription factor RUNX2, best known for driving osteoblast commitment, also acts on genes of the myeloid programme, and this arm of its activity is captured by its control of galectin-3. Together with its paralogue RUNX1 and the shared non-DNA-binding partner CBFB, which stabilises RUNX binding to DNA and is required for its transcriptional output, RUNX2 stimulates transcription of LGALS3. Galectin-3 is present in myeloid progenitors and accumulates as those cells mature, contributing to adhesion, phagocyte behaviour and inflammatory responses. Because the same RUNX-CBFB module governs haematopoietic differentiation more broadly, misregulation here links lineage-specifying transcription to disease: galectin-3 is abundantly expressed in pituitary tumours and glioma, and RUNX1-CBFB disruption is a recurrent event in leukaemia. The pathway therefore connects a core developmental transcription complex to the maturation state and secreted lectin output of myeloid cells.

Events associated with phagocytolytic activity of PMN cells is the oxidative killing step inside the neutrophil phagosome, the reaction that converts engulfed bacteria into a chemically hostile environment they cannot survive. It is the effector end of innate antimicrobial defence: loss of this oxidant output leaves patients with recurrent bacterial and fungal infection, as in chronic granulomatous disease. After NADPH oxidase discharges superoxide into the vacuole, dismutation yields hydrogen peroxide, and heme peroxidases — myeloperoxidase above all, with lactoperoxidase acting at mucosal surfaces — use that peroxide with chloride and other halides to generate hypochlorous acid and related microbicidal species. Because the oxidase moves charge and protons directionally, voltage-gated proton flux must compensate to keep the membrane from depolarising, and the neutrophil phagosome stays alkaline rather than acidifying as a macrophage phagosome does, tuning the environment to peroxidase chemistry.

Neutrophils kill ingested bacteria inside the phagosome by generating oxidants, and this pathway covers the heme peroxidase step that converts the initial respiratory burst product into the most microbicidal species. NADPH oxidase releases superoxide into the vacuole, where it dismutates to hydrogen peroxide; myeloperoxidase, the abundant azurophil granule enzyme that gives pus its green colour, uses that peroxide with chloride to make hypochlorous acid and related chloramines that destroy bacterial proteins and membranes. The related lactoperoxidase carries out equivalent halide and thiocyanate oxidation chemistry in secretory settings. Because oxidase activity is vectorial, proton flux must balance the charge and the neutrophil phagosome stays alkaline rather than acidifying as macrophage phagosomes do. Loss of myeloperoxidase impairs oxidative killing, while unrestrained release of these oxidants damages host tissue and contributes to inflammatory injury and vasculitis.

Growth arrest imposed by TGF-beta depends on turning on the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, and RUNX3-driven transcription of CDKN1A is one route by which that happens. It matters most in gastric and other epithelia, where loss of this control removes a brake on proliferation: mice lacking Runx3 become insensitive to TGF-beta and develop gastric epithelial hyperplasia, and RUNX3 silencing is a recurrent event in gastric cancer. Mechanistically, TGFB1 signalling activates a SMAD3:SMAD4 complex that RUNX3 binds and cooperates with at the CDKN1A promoter; the RUNX3 heterodimer also engages the tumour suppressor ZFHX3 to reinforce induction. RUNX3 can additionally act as a co-factor for TP53, boosting p53-dependent target genes including CDKN1A, linking this transcriptional node to both cytokine-driven and damage-driven cell cycle arrest.

The transcription factor RUNX3 acts as a brake on NOTCH signalling, and losing that restraint is one route by which liver cells become tumorigenic. RUNX3 works at two points. It occupies the promoter of JAG1 and represses transcription of this NOTCH ligand, lowering the signal available to neighbouring cells. It also joins the coactivator complex assembled on cleaved NOTCH1 intracellular domain with RBPJ, Mastermind-like proteins and the acetyltransferases CREBBP/EP300 and KAT2A/KAT2B, and blocks activation of the target gene HES1. Because HES1 is a repressor that sustains progenitor states and blocks differentiation, this interference pushes cells toward differentiation and away from proliferation. RUNX3 silencing, common in hepatocellular carcinoma and gastric cancer, releases NOTCH output and links its tumour suppressor function directly to developmental cell-fate signalling.

Regulation of RUNX3 expression and activity controls the abundance, localisation and partner binding of a transcription factor that acts as a tumour suppressor in gastric and pancreatic epithelium and as a lineage determinant in cytotoxic T cells and dendritic cells. Loss of RUNX3 output, most often by CpG methylation of its downstream promoter or by protein destabilisation, removes a brake on epithelial proliferation and is common in solid tumours. Control operates at several levels: dual promoters and alternative splicing generate isoforms with different transactivating capacity, TGF-beta signalling through SMAD4 drives transcription, and hypoxia silences it via histone methylation and deacetylation. The protein is only active as a heterodimer with CBFB and with EP300 as coactivator; SRC-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation traps it in the cytosol, while MDM2, SMURF1 and SMURF2 direct it to the proteasome for ubiquitin-dependent degradation.

RUNX3 is a transcription factor that acts as a tumour suppressor in epithelial tissues and directs lymphocyte and dendritic cell differentiation, and the control of its expression and activity determines how much of it is available in the nucleus at any time. Its loss, most often through methylation of a CpG island at the internal promoter or through hypoxia-driven silencing, is a recurrent event in gastric and other solid tumours. Transcription responds to TGF-beta/SMAD input and to autoregulation; alternative promoter use and splicing yield isoforms differing in Runt-domain function. Once made, RUNX3 must heterodimerise with CBFB to bind DNA and recruits the acetyltransferase EP300 to activate targets such as CDKN2A. Activity is curtailed by SRC-mediated tyrosine phosphorylation, which blocks nuclear entry, and by polyubiquitination via MDM2, SMURF1 and SMURF2 followed by proteasomal degradation, the reason the 26S proteasome subunits and ubiquitin genes feature here.

Infectious gastroenteritis is inflammation of the stomach and small intestine caused by viruses, bacteria, parasites or fungi, producing diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain and the dehydration that makes it a leading cause of childhood death worldwide; oral rehydration rather than drugs is the mainstay of care. The molecular entry point represented here is the intestinal brush-border receptor guanylate cyclase C, normally activated by the endogenous peptides guanylin and uroguanylin to raise cGMP and drive chloride and fluid secretion into the lumen. Heat-stable enterotoxin from enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, a major cause of traveller's and infant diarrhoea, mimics these peptides and locks the cyclase on, and the PDZ scaffold NHERF4 organises the receptor with downstream effectors at the apical membrane. Sustained cGMP signalling opens CFTR, and the resulting unchecked salt and water efflux is the secretory diarrhoea itself.

How much PTEN protein a cell makes is set in part after transcription, by microRNAs that bind its mRNA and repress translation. Because PTEN is the phosphatase that reverses PI3K signalling by dephosphorylating PIP3, small changes in its abundance shift AKT activity, growth and survival, and modest loss of PTEN is enough to promote tumour formation. Members of the miR-17/miR-19/miR-20/miR-106 families along with miR-21, miR-22, miR-25, miR-26a, miR-93, miR-205 and miR-214 target the PTEN transcript through Argonaute proteins, GW182-family scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10 in silencing complexes. The repression is itself buffered by competing endogenous RNAs, notably transcripts of the pseudogene PTENP1, which titrate these microRNAs away and raise PTEN output. Amplification or overexpression of the microRNAs, or loss of the pseudogene, lowers PTEN in cancers without mutating the gene.

PTEN is the phosphatase that drains PIP3 and restrains PI3K-AKT signalling, so how much PTEN protein a cell makes sets its threshold for growth-factor-driven growth and survival; controlling transcription of the PTEN gene is therefore one of the main ways tumours lose tumour suppression without mutating the gene itself. Repression runs through chromatin: SALL4 recruits the Mi-2/NuRD complex (CHD3/CHD4, MTA and MBD3 subunits with HDAC1/2 and RBBP4/7) to the promoter, while EVI1/MECOM brings in Polycomb repressive complexes, PRC2 with EZH2 and SUZ12 depositing the H3K27 mark and PRC1 ring finger and CBX proteins reading it. Additional negative input comes from JUN, the NR2E1:atrophin complex, and the EMT factors SNAI1 and SNAI2; TP53, EGR1, ATF2, PPARG and MAF1 drive expression upward. Collagen chain trimerization is the step inside the endoplasmic reticulum where three procollagen polypeptides select one another and lock into register, the decision that sets the composition of every collagen molecule the cell will secrete. Everything downstream depends on it: only a correctly registered trimer can zip into a triple helix and go on to build fibrils, basement membrane networks, or the anchoring and beaded filaments of skin, cartilage and vessel wall. Recognition is carried by the C-propeptides, which choose homotrimeric or heterotrimeric partners, and in type III collagen a C-terminal disulfide bond permanently ties the chains together before helix formation propagates toward the N-terminus. Mutations in these propeptide domains misassemble the trimer and cause osteogenesis imperfecta, chondrodysplasias and other heritable connective tissue and basement membrane disorders, making chain selection a quality checkpoint on extracellular matrix production.

Every collagen molecule begins as three separate polypeptide chains that must find each other and lock into the correct combination before a triple helix can form, and this trimerization step is where that selection happens. C-terminal propeptide domains mediate the initial association, choosing which chains pair with which, aligning them in register, and nucleating helix formation that then propagates toward the N-terminus like a zipper; disulfide bonds stabilize the assembly. The chains represented here cover the fibril-forming collagens of skin, bone and cartilage, the network-forming basement membrane type IV chains, and the fibril-associated, anchoring and transmembrane collagens. Because composition is decided at this point, propeptide mutations produce misassembled or retained procollagen and underlie osteogenesis imperfecta, chondrodysplasias, Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, Alport syndrome and epidermolysis bullosa, making correct chain choice a prerequisite for extracellular matrix integrity.

PTEN is a lipid phosphatase that shuts down PI3K-AKT signalling, and small changes in how much of it a cell makes shift the balance between growth and restraint, so dosage control at the mRNA level has direct consequences for tumour suppression. Competing endogenous RNAs provide that control: transcripts sharing microRNA binding sites with PTEN mRNA, most notably the pseudogene PTENP1, act as decoys that soak up shared microRNAs and relieve repression of the parent transcript. The microRNAs involved belong to the miR-17/20/106 and miR-19 families of the oncogenic miR-17-92 cluster, which engage PTEN through Argonaute proteins loaded into silencing complexes with GW182 family scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10. Loss or deletion of the decoy transcripts lowers PTEN protein and favours transformation, illustrating how non-coding RNA abundance can titrate a tumour suppressor without altering its gene.

Regulation of PTEN localization controls where the tumour suppressor PTEN acts, and thereby whether it restrains PI3K-AKT signalling at the membrane or performs its distinct nuclear duties in chromosome stability and cell cycle control. Compartment choice matters as much as protein level: cancers can inactivate PTEN functionally by excluding it from the nucleus while leaving the gene intact. Monoubiquitination by the E3 ligases NEDD4 and XIAP marks PTEN for nuclear import, while the deubiquitinase USP7 removes that mark and returns PTEN to the cytosol; PML opposes USP7 to keep PTEN nuclear. Because polyubiquitination of the same protein instead routes it to proteasomal degradation, the ubiquitin pool shared by these reactions couples PTEN trafficking to PTEN turnover, making this a post-translational switch on growth-factor signalling output and tumour suppression.

PTEN is the phosphatase that drains PIP3 and so restrains PI3K-AKT signalling, but where it sits in the cell decides what it can do: only cytosolic PTEN reaches the plasma membrane lipid pool, while nuclear PTEN contributes to chromosome stability and growth suppression. Control of PTEN localization works through a ubiquitin switch. The E3 ligases NEDD4 and XIAP attach a single ubiquitin to PTEN, which drives its import into the nucleus; the deubiquitinase USP7 removes that mark and returns PTEN to the cytosol, with PML opposing USP7 action to keep PTEN nuclear. Because the modification is mono- rather than polyubiquitination, the outcome is trafficking rather than proteasomal destruction. Tumours exploit this layer: mislocalized PTEN leaves AKT signalling unopposed even when the protein is intact and abundant, an alternative to outright loss of the tumour suppressor gene.

PTEN is the phosphatase that removes the 3-phosphate from PIP3 and thereby restrains PI3K-AKT signalling, so how much of it is present and how active it is sets the threshold for cell growth, survival and insulin responsiveness; even modest reductions in PTEN dose promote tumour formation. Control of PTEN stability and activity operates largely through the ubiquitin-proteasome system: E3 ligases including NEDD4, WWP2, STUB1, XIAP, MKRN1 and RNF146 (acting with the poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases TNKS and TNKS2) mark PTEN for degradation by the 26S proteasome, whose subunits make up much of this machinery, while the deubiquitinases USP13 and OTUD3 reverse those chains and spare the protein. Other inputs alter catalysis rather than abundance: TRIM27-mediated ubiquitination of the C2 domain and PREX2 binding suppress lipid phosphatase activity, casein kinase 2 phosphorylation of the tail stabilises but slightly dampens PTEN, and the kinase FRK both protects it from NEDD4 and raises its activity. The result feeds directly back on AKT.

Mitochondria take up calcium from the cytosol and return it, and this flux couples cytosolic signalling to the pace of oxidative metabolism. Matrix calcium allosterically stimulates pyruvate, isocitrate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenases, so uptake raises NADH supply when a cell is working harder; excessive or sustained loading instead favours permeability transition and release of apoptotic cofactors, a route implicated in ischaemic and neurodegenerative injury. Voltage-dependent anion channels in the outer membrane pass calcium to the intermembrane space, particularly at contact sites with the endoplasmic reticulum, and the uniporter complex carries it across the inner membrane driven by membrane potential, with the pore-forming MCU regulated by MCUB, the EF-hand gatekeepers MICU1-3 and the essential subunit SMDT1. Efflux runs through the sodium/calcium exchanger SLC8B1 and LETM1. Inner-membrane proteases and prohibitin scaffolds shape the complex's assembly and turnover.

RUNX3 is a transcription factor that shapes immune cell identity and the adhesion machinery leukocytes need to leave the bloodstream. Acting with its obligate partner CBFB, it drives development of tissue-resident innate lymphoid cells of the ILC1 and ILC3 lineages, which guard mucosal surfaces against pathogens, by inducing the nuclear receptor RORC. In parallel it activates the integrin genes ITGAL (CD11a) and ITGA4 (CD49d), which mediate transendothelial migration during immune and inflammatory responses and provide co-stimulation to T cells. A shorter RUNX3 isoform lacking the DNA-binding Runt domain cannot transactivate these targets and accumulates as monocyte-derived dendritic cells mature, dampening inflammatory gene output. RUNX3 also raises expression of osteopontin (SPP1), a matrix protein that promotes invasiveness, linking this programme to pancreatic cancer progression as well as to normal mucosal immunity and leukocyte trafficking.

Cristae formation shapes the inner mitochondrial membrane into the folded invaginations that house the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, and it sets how much oxidative phosphorylation a cell can perform. Cristae multiply membrane surface area and create local proton pockets of high membrane potential; when their architecture collapses, respiration falls, apoptotic cytochrome c is mobilised more readily, and mitochondrial disease and cardiomyopathy follow. Two mechanisms dominate. The MICOS complex, built around IMMT (MIC60) with CHCHD3, CHCHD6, APOO and MICOS10/13, plus cardiolipin-rich membrane, imposes negative curvature at cristae junctions and tethers them to outer-membrane machinery such as SAMM50 and the metaxins, keeping the two membranes in register. At the opposite end, dimers and rows of F1Fo ATP synthase bend the membrane sharply at cristae tips. OPA1 interactions link this architecture to fusion and junction width.

Cristae are the folded invaginations of the inner mitochondrial membrane that carry the respiratory chain and ATP synthase, and shaping them is what gives a mitochondrion the membrane area and local proton gradients needed for efficient oxidative phosphorylation. The inward curvature at crista bases is set by the MICOS complex, built around MIC60/IMMT with MIC19 and MIC25, MIC27 and MIC10, which bridges to the outer membrane through SAMM50 and the metaxins and, with OPA1, stabilises crista junctions; cardiolipin-rich membrane contributes the same bending. At crista tips, dimers and higher oligomers of F1Fo ATP synthase impose sharp curvature, so the many ATP synthase subunits here act structurally as well as catalytically. Loss of MICOS subunits or of ATP synthase oligomerisation flattens cristae into concentric sheets, lowers respiratory output, releases sequestered cytochrome c and underlies mitochondrial encephalomyopathies and altered apoptotic sensitivity.

Mitochondrial calcium uptake through the uniporter must be gated, and the maturation of SMDT1 (EMRE) is the quality-control step that decides whether a gated channel gets built. EMRE is the small subunit that couples the pore-forming MCU to its MICU1/MICU2 regulators, MICU3 in neurons, so any EMRE that escapes regulation would allow unchecked calcium entry, matrix overload and permeability transition. The precursor is delivered with its transit peptide bound by MAIP1 in complex with the m-AAA protease AFG3L2 and SPG7, which shields it while the matrix processing peptidase subunits PMPCA and PMPCB remove the presequence. Mature EMRE not incorporated with MICU subunits is degraded by AFG3L2, and unprocessed precursor is cleared by the inner-membrane protease YME1L1. Prohibitins and stomatin-like scaffolds organise these proteases, linking uniporter assembly to broader inner-membrane proteostasis; AFG3L2 and SPG7 defects cause ataxia and spastic paraplegia.

Interleukin-12 drives naive CD4+ T cells toward the Th1 fate, and this pathway captures the gene and protein output of that instruction, transmitted through JAK-STAT signalling with STAT4 as the central transcription factor. The functional readouts are the hallmark Th1 cytokine IFNG alongside IL10, which together set the balance between cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens and its restraint; loss of this axis leaves people prone to mycobacterial and salmonella infection, while excess activity contributes to autoimmune inflammation. Downstream of transcription, the proteomic response reorganises the cell rather than simply adding cytokines: actin and membrane cytoskeletal regulators such as cofilin, moesin, CDC42 and PAK2 shift with motility and immune synapse formation, heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins and chaperonin subunits with altered RNA handling and folding load, and superoxide dismutases, peroxiredoxin-like and glutathione transferase activities with redox adjustment during lymphocyte activation and proliferation.

RUNX3 acts as a brake on WNT-driven proliferation, and its loss helps explain why this transcription factor behaves as a tumour suppressor in gastrointestinal epithelium. When WNT signalling stabilises beta-catenin, the protein enters the nucleus and partners with TCF/LEF factors such as TCF7, TCF7L1, TCF7L2 and LEF1 to switch on growth-promoting target genes, chief among them cyclin D1 and MYC, which together push cells through the G1 restriction point. RUNX3 binds the beta-catenin:TCF/LEF complex directly and prevents it from occupying the CCND1 and MYC promoters, so the transcriptional output of the pathway is attenuated without blocking beta-catenin stabilisation itself.
