Silencing or mislocalisation of RUNX3 therefore leaves these complexes free to drive proliferation, linking this regulatory step to epithelial growth control and to carcinogenesis in the stomach and colon.

Neddylation is the covalent attachment of the ubiquitin-like protein NEDD8 to substrate proteins, and it is the switch that turns on cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, the largest family of E3 enzymes in the cell. Because these ligases select most proteins destined for proteasomal destruction, neddylation sets the pace of cell cycle progression, hypoxic and oxidative stress responses, and turnover of transcription factors such as HIF1A and NFE2L2; blocking it is the basis of investigational anticancer drugs. Mature NEDD8 is generated by UCHL3 or SENP8 processing, activated by the NAE1-UBA3 E1, and carried by UBE2M or UBE2F to RBX1- or RBX2-containing cullin scaffolds, with DCUN1D proteins boosting transfer. Neddylation of a cullin promotes ubiquitin chain building, while the COP9 signalosome removes NEDD8 and CAND1 then exchanges substrate receptors -- the F-box, BTB, DCAF and SOCS-box adaptors -- reconfiguring each ligase for new targets.

Neddylation attaches the ubiquitin-like protein NEDD8 to substrate lysines, and its principal job is to switch on cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, the largest family of enzymes that mark proteins for proteasomal destruction. Through this switch the cell controls cell cycle progression, the hypoxic response via HIF1A and VHL, oxidative stress signalling via KEAP1 and NFE2L2, and cytokine signalling via SOCS/ASB adaptors, so blocking it stabilises hundreds of short-lived regulators at once — the basis of NAE1/UBA3 inhibitors used as anticancer drugs. NEDD8 is first matured by UCHL3 or SENP8, then activated by the NAE1-UBA3 E1 heterodimer and passed to UBE2M or UBE2F, which work with RBX1- or RBX2-containing cullin scaffolds; DCUN1D proteins boost the transfer. The COP9 signalosome removes NEDD8, after which CAND1 promotes exchange of substrate-receptor subunits such as the F-box, DCAF, BTB and SOCS-box adaptors, letting the ligases be rebuilt for new targets that are then degraded by the proteasome.

The Hippo pathway effectors YAP1 and its paralogue WWTR1 (TAZ) drive growth-promoting transcription by partnering with TEAD family DNA-binding factors, and one of their canonical outputs is CCN2 (connective tissue growth factor), a matricellular protein that fuels proliferation, matrix production and fibrosis. RUNX3 acts here as a brake: by binding the TEAD:YAP1 complex it blocks its loading onto the CCN2 promoter, damping transcription of this growth factor. The interaction links a classical tumour-suppressor RUNX transcription factor to organ-size and contact-inhibition control, and helps explain why loss or silencing of RUNX3, common in gastric and other epithelial cancers, permits unrestrained YAP-driven target gene expression. The balance set at TEAD-bound enhancers thus determines whether epithelial cells proliferate and remodel their surroundings or remain quiescent, placing this regulation at the intersection of Hippo signalling, tissue repair and tumour suppression.

RUNX family transcription factors cross-regulate one another, and here RUNX3 acts on the RUNX1 gene itself: bound with its obligate partner CBFB, RUNX3 occupies Runx response elements in the distal P1 promoter of RUNX1 and represses its transcription. This negative feedback sets the balance between two related master regulators whose combined output shapes haematopoietic stem cell emergence, lymphocyte and megakaryocyte differentiation, and gut epithelial homeostasis. Because neither factor binds DNA efficiently alone, the shared non-DNA-binding subunit CBFB determines how much of either complex is available, and shifting occupancy of the P1 promoter changes which RUNX1 isoform predominates. Loss of this restraint matters clinically: RUNX1 dosage is sensitive, its disruption underlies familial platelet disorder and recurrent leukaemic translocations, while RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric and other epithelial cancers.

This is a tumour-suppressive transcriptional switch in which RUNX3, acting with its obligate partner CBFB, turns on p14-ARF from the CDKN2A locus and so raises the barrier to oncogenic transformation. p14-ARF sequesters MDM2 and stabilises p53, meaning that loss of this arm allows cells carrying activating lesions such as mutant KRAS to proliferate instead of arresting or dying; RUNX3 silencing is common in gastric and other epithelial cancers. The control is acetylation-dependent: the acetyltransferase p300 modifies RUNX3, acetylated RUNX3 is read by the bromodomain protein BRD2, and this complex drives p14-ARF transcription. Cyclin D1 opposes the response by delivering the deacetylase HDAC4 to RUNX3, stripping the mark and muting induction, which couples the output to cell cycle state. TGF-beta signalling feeds into the same node, linking growth-inhibitory cues to p53 pathway activation.

RUNX3 regulates BCL2L11 (BIM) transcription is the step that converts a TGF-beta signal into a death decision, by switching on the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. It explains how TGF-beta suppresses tumours and how epithelial and lymphoid cells are eliminated when growth-inhibitory cues persist; loss of RUNX3 by promoter methylation or deletion in gastric and lung cancers removes this output and leaves cells resistant to TGF-beta-induced apoptosis. Mechanistically, receptor-activated SMAD3 with SMAD4 accumulates in the nucleus and cooperates with the lineage transcription factor RUNX3 and the forkhead factor FOXO3 at the BCL2L11 promoter, so that the response depends on the coincidence of TGF-beta signalling and low survival-kinase activity, since AKT excludes FOXO3 from the nucleus. The induced BIM then neutralises BCL2-family survival proteins and commits mitochondria to permeabilisation.

TGF-beta can instruct a cell to die rather than divide, and one route to that outcome is transcriptional induction of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only protein BIM. Here RUNX3 drives BCL2L11 transcription, acting on the gene's promoter together with receptor-activated SMAD3 and its partner SMAD4 and with the forkhead factor FOXO3. The BIM protein that results neutralises anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members and promotes BAX/BAK-dependent mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation, committing the cell to the intrinsic apoptotic programme. This arm of TGF-beta signalling contributes to the cytokine's tumour-suppressive behaviour in epithelial and gastric tissue and to apoptotic culling in lymphocytes; RUNX3 silencing by promoter methylation, or loss of SMAD signalling, removes this death output and allows cells that should have been eliminated to survive. It links growth factor signal transduction directly to the apoptotic machinery.

E2F6 is the atypical, repressive member of the E2F transcription factor family: it binds E2F consensus sites as a heterodimer with TFDP1 or TFDP2 but lacks both a transactivation domain and the pocket-protein interface, so it cannot be relieved by retinoblastoma-family binding. Its role is to hold down E2F-responsive genes required for DNA synthesis and repair — among them E2F1, RRM2, RAD51, BRCA1 and RBBP8 — during S phase rather than in quiescence. Repression is enforced through recruitment of polycomb and related chromatin machinery, including a PRC1-like complex containing PCGF6, L3MBTL2, MGA and MAX, core PRC2 subunits, and the H3K9 methyltransferases EHMT1/EHMT2. Under replication stress, CHEK1-dependent phosphorylation evicts E2F6 from target promoters so repair and fork-restart genes can be induced; loss of this switch converts stalled forks into DNA damage. Homeotic skeletal transformations in E2f6-null mice underscore the polycomb connection.

Every transcript made in the nucleus must be processed, checked, moved and eventually destroyed, and this superpathway of RNA metabolism gathers that whole life cycle. It determines how much of each protein a cell makes and which protein isoform, so its failures produce spliceosomopathies, ribosomopathies such as Diamond-Blackfan anemia, and retinitis pigmentosa from defective splicing factors. Nascent messages are capped, spliced by the U1-U6 snRNPs with SF3B and PRPF components, cleaved and polyadenylated by the cleavage/polyadenylation and cleavage stimulation complexes, then exported through the TREX-nuclear pore route. Quality control and turnover follow: nonsense-mediated decay via UPF1 and the SMG proteins, deadenylation by the CCR4-NOT complex, decapping, exosome-mediated degradation, and AU-rich element binding proteins that set message half-life. Parallel arms cover snRNP assembly, ribosomal RNA maturation, tRNA modification and splicing, and mitochondrial RNA processing.

Cells continuously read their surroundings — nutrients, oxygen tension, metals, oxidants, heat, misfolded protein burden, mechanical force — and mount programmes that either restore homeostasis or shut growth down, and this collection of cellular responses to stimuli spans that whole range. It underlies development, tissue maintenance and defence against noxious agents; when the responses fail or run constitutively, the consequences include ischaemic injury, oxidative damage, secretory-cell death and tumour progression. Represented here are oxygen sensing through prolyl hydroxylases, VHL and the HIF transcription factors; antioxidant defence via KEAP1–NFE2L2 with peroxiredoxins, superoxide dismutases and glutathione enzymes; metal handling through MTF1 and metallothioneins; heat shock and chaperone induction under HSF1; the unfolded protein response arms ATF6, ERN1/XBP1 and PERK–eIF2α; amino-acid and growth-factor sensing by mTORC1 at the lysosome; and senescence enforced by p53, CDKN2A and Polycomb-regulated chromatin, with proteasomal turnover integrating many of these outputs.

Microtubules are marked chemically on the flexible carboxyterminal tails that alpha- and beta-tubulins project from the filament surface, and these marks tune how motors, severing enzymes and microtubule-associated proteins read the lattice. Two reversible cycles dominate: glutamate chains are added by tubulin tyrosine ligase-like enzymes and trimmed by cytosolic carboxypeptidases of the AGBL/AGTPBP1 family, while alpha-tubulin cycles between tyrosinated and detyrosinated states through the ligase TTL and the vasohibin-SVBP complexes that remove the terminal tyrosine. The resulting tail code influences microtubule stability and rigidity and is read differently in axonemes, centrioles, neuronal axons and the mitotic spindle. Loss of the deglutamylase AGTPBP1 causes neurodegeneration in Purkinje cells, and disruption of these enzymes or of the tubulin isotypes themselves produces ciliopathy, infertility and cortical malformation phenotypes.

Nucleotide catabolism is the disposal arm of nucleotide metabolism: it degrades purine and pyrimidine bases and dismantles nucleoside phosphates once they are no longer needed. Purines flow through nucleosidase and phosphorylase steps to hypoxanthine and xanthine and finally to uric acid via xanthine dehydrogenase, an endpoint peculiar to humans and great apes and the direct cause of gout and urate nephropathy when overproduced or underexcreted. Pyrimidines are reduced and ring-opened by DPYD, DPYS and UPB1 to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate, feeding remnants into amino acid and short-chain fatty acid catabolism; loss of DPYD makes fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy toxic. In parallel, ecto-nucleotidases and 5'-nucleotidases set extracellular purinergic signalling and adenosine tone, while NUDT hydrolases and SAMHD1 sanitise the nucleotide pool, removing oxidised or excess triphosphates that would otherwise be incorporated into DNA.

Nucleotides that are no longer needed, or that have been chemically damaged, are broken down and their bases either recycled or excreted; this catabolic route sets the disposal end of nucleotide balance. Purine degradation runs through nucleoside phosphorylase and xanthine dehydrogenase to uric acid, which humans excrete rather than degrade further, so overload produces gout and urate stones. Pyrimidines take a separate three-step route via dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase and dihydropyrimidinase to beta-alanine and beta-aminoisobutyrate, with a mitochondrial transaminase feeding carbon into branched-chain and short-chain fatty acid metabolism. Parallel hydrolase families guard nucleotide quality and pool size: nucleoside triphosphate pyrophosphatases and NUDT sanitizers remove oxidized or non-canonical triphosphates, SAMHD1 depletes dNTPs, and ecto-nucleotidases with 5'-nucleotidases strip phosphates to terminate extracellular purinergic signalling. Variants here govern toxicity of fluoropyrimidine and thiopurine drugs.

Cells that divide must make their own nucleotides, and this de novo biosynthetic route builds purine and pyrimidine ribonucleotides from small metabolites rather than recycling bases. On the purine side, a series of steps adds atoms from glutamine, glycine, aspartate, bicarbonate and formyl-tetrahydrofolate onto phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate to give IMP, which is then branched to AMP via adenylosuccinate intermediates or to GMP via IMP dehydrogenase and GMP synthase. Pyrimidines begin with a multifunctional cytosolic enzyme carrying carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, aspartate transcarbamylase and dihydroorotase activities, followed by a mitochondrial inner-membrane dehydrogenase that oxidises dihydroorotate, and a bifunctional enzyme that produces UMP; UMP then feeds all other pyrimidines including thymidylate. Output rises with proliferation, which makes these enzymes targets of antimetabolite and immunosuppressive drugs, and inherited deficiencies cause orotic aciduria and neurodevelopmental disease.

Nucleotide salvage recycles the nucleosides and free bases released by RNA and DNA breakdown back into nucleotide monophosphates, sparing the cell the energetic cost of building purine and pyrimidine rings from scratch. It matters most in tissues with little de novo capacity: brain neurons depend on hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, and its loss causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome with hyperuricaemia and severe neurological disease, while adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency destroys lymphocyte development and causes immunodeficiency. Phosphoribosyltransferases reattach bases to ribose phosphate, kinases such as ADK, UCK1/2, TK1, TK2 and DGUOK phosphorylate nucleosides, and deaminases, phosphorylases and AMP deaminases route intermediates between the purine and pyrimidine pools or toward degradation. Because DNA turnover is normally low, deoxyribonucleotide salvage runs slowly, but the mitochondrial kinases TK2 and DGUOK supply dNTPs for mitochondrial DNA replication, and the same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs.

Rather than build every nucleotide from scratch, cells recover the bases and nucleosides released by RNA and DNA turnover and phosphorylate them back into monophosphates that re-enter the nucleotide pools. This salvage route is far cheaper in energy than de novo synthesis and is the main supply for cells with limited biosynthetic capacity, such as neurons and lymphocytes, and for mitochondria, which must maintain their own deoxyribonucleotide pools. Phosphoribosyltransferases reattach purine bases to ribose phosphate, while kinases such as thymidine kinase, deoxycytidine kinase and deoxyguanosine kinase act on nucleosides; phosphorylases and deaminases run the catabolic side, degrading or interconverting bases. Loss of HPRT1 causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, adenosine deaminase deficiency causes severe combined immunodeficiency, and mutations in the mitochondrial kinases produce mtDNA depletion syndromes. The same enzymes activate nucleoside analogue drugs.

Many secreted and extracellular proteins carry phosphate groups added after they leave the ribosome, and post-translational protein phosphorylation within the secretory pathway is how those groups get there. The Golgi-resident casein kinase FAM20C modifies serines in Ser-x-Glu motifs on substrates as varied as caseins, enamel and dentin matrix proteins (amelogenin, enamelin, DMP1, MEPE, osteopontin), coagulation and complement factors, plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen, and the hormone FGF23; FAM20A acts as its pseudokinase partner and allosteric activator. Phosphorylation tunes mineral binding, protease susceptibility and receptor interaction, so the output is read out in bone and tooth mineralization, phosphate homeostasis, blood clotting and extracellular matrix assembly. Loss of FAM20C causes lethal osteosclerotic bone dysplasia with hypophosphatemia, while FAM20A deficiency produces enamel renal syndrome, linking this Golgi chemistry directly to skeletal and dental disease.

Metabolism of steroids covers the making of cholesterol and everything the body builds from it: bile acids and salts, adrenal and gonadal steroid hormones, and active vitamin D. It supplies membrane sterol, the detergents needed for fat and fat-soluble vitamin absorption, the hormones that set stress responses, salt balance, and sexual development, and the endocrine control of calcium. Cholesterol is assembled from HMG-CoA through the mevalonate route, then tailored by cytochrome P450 enzymes, hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases and reductases in mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and peroxisomes, with cholesterol delivered to side-chain cleavage by STAR. Bile acid conjugates are exported and recaptured by dedicated transporters, and vitamin D circulates on a binding protein to reach the VDR. Output is matched to demand by SREBP cleavage-activating protein and INSIG sensing of ER sterol, and by nuclear receptor feedback. Defects cause skeletal malformation syndromes, cholestasis, adrenal hyperplasia, and hypercholesterolaemia.

Everything built on the four-ring sterol skeleton is made and disposed of here: cholesterol itself, the bile acids that emulsify dietary fat, the steroid hormones that set sex, stress and salt balance, and active vitamin D. The synthetic route runs from HMG-CoA through mevalonate and squalene to lanosterol and cholesterol, with HMGCR as the rate-limiting and statin-targeted step. Side-chain cleavage by CYP11A1 after STAR-dependent delivery of cholesterol into mitochondria opens the hormone branches, elaborated by hydroxylases and hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases; hepatic 7alpha-hydroxylation initiates bile acid formation, and dedicated transporters handle uptake and export. Supply is matched to demand by SREBP cleavage under SCAP and INSIG control, with nuclear receptor feedback through FXR and VDR. Defects cause hypercholesterolaemia, cholestasis, adrenal insufficiency and rickets.

Intestinal absorption is the step at which digested food actually enters the body: transporters on the surface of small-intestinal enterocytes move sugars and sterols out of the gut lumen and pass them to the portal circulation. It sets how much dietary energy and cholesterol a person acquires, and its manipulation is therapeutic — ezetimibe blocks the NPC1L1 sterol transporter to lower plasma LDL, while SGLT inhibitors act on the same transporter family used here for sugar uptake. Absorption is vectorial: the apical sodium-glucose cotransporter SGLT1 drives glucose and galactose uptake against a gradient using the sodium electrochemical gradient, GLUT5 carries fructose by facilitated diffusion, and GLUT2 exports all three across the basolateral membrane. Loss of SGLT1 causes glucose-galactose malabsorption with osmotic diarrhoea, illustrating how directly this pathway supports whole-body nutrition and fluid balance.

Dietary nutrients only become available to the body once they cross the enterocyte, and intestinal absorption in the small intestine is where that crossing happens. Sugars and sterols are taken up across the apical brush border and released into the portal circulation across the basolateral membrane, so this step sets postprandial blood glucose and how much dietary cholesterol reaches the liver. Glucose and galactose enter against their gradient through a sodium-coupled cotransporter driven by the sodium gradient, fructose enters by facilitated diffusion through a dedicated carrier, and a basolateral facilitative transporter completes the exit of all three. Sterol uptake is selective, and the apical protein responsible is the target of ezetimibe, a drug used to lower plasma cholesterol. Loss of these transporters causes glucose-galactose malabsorption and osmotic diarrhoea, linking the pathway to whole-body carbohydrate and lipid homeostasis.

Intestinal lipid absorption is the step at which dietary and biliary sterols cross the brush border of the small intestine and enter the body, setting how much cholesterol arrives from the gut rather than from endogenous synthesis. NPC1L1, a sterol-sensing membrane protein concentrated at the apical surface of enterocytes, mediates this uptake, and its loss-of-function variants lower circulating LDL cholesterol and reduce coronary risk. The same transporter takes up plant sterols, so its activity determines the sterol composition of chylomicrons and, together with biliary efflux, the balance that keeps phytosterols from accumulating. Because this route feeds directly into whole-body cholesterol homeostasis and lipoprotein production, it is pharmacologically exploited: ezetimibe blocks NPC1L1 and is used with statins to treat hypercholesterolaemia. The protein also cycles between the plasma membrane and endocytic compartments in response to sterol availability.

Dietary cholesterol and plant sterols must cross the brush border of the small intestine before they can enter the body's lipid pools, and intestinal lipid absorption at this step is controlled largely by a single sterol transporter, NPC1L1. Positioned on the apical membrane of enterocytes, it binds sterols and carries them into the cell by clathrin-mediated endocytosis, after which they are packaged with triglyceride into chylomicrons for delivery to the liver and periphery. This uptake sets how much of the daily sterol load reaches plasma, which is why blocking it lowers circulating LDL cholesterol; the transporter is the direct target of ezetimibe. It also excludes phytosterols, and loss of that selectivity underlies sitosterolemia-like sterol accumulation.

Excess tyrosine cannot be stored, so it is dismantled to intermediates that feed central metabolism. This five-step degradative route converts tyrosine to fumarate and acetoacetate, making it both a glucogenic and a ketogenic amino acid and linking amino acid disposal to the citric acid cycle and ketone body formation. Transamination by cytosolic tyrosine aminotransferase yields 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, which is oxidised and ring-cleaved by 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase and homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase; maleylacetoacetate is then isomerised by a glutathione transferase-family isomerase and hydrolysed by fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase. The pathway is most active in liver and kidney. Blocks at individual steps produce the tyrosinemias and alkaptonuria, with accumulated intermediates causing liver and renal tubular damage or ochronotic pigment deposition in cartilage; the dioxygenase step is the target of drug therapy that diverts flux away from toxic downstream metabolites.

Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid, and its conversion to tyrosine is both the main source of tyrosine in the body and the entry point for disposing of any excess. The route matters because every step has a human disease attached to it: loss of phenylalanine hydroxylase, or of the enzymes that recycle its tetrahydrobiopterin cofactor, causes phenylketonuria and neurological damage from accumulated phenylalanine, while blocks further along give tyrosinaemia and alkaptonuria. After hydroxylation, tyrosine is transaminated to 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, which is oxidised and isomerised through homogentisate and maleylacetoacetate to fumarate and acetoacetate, feeding carbon into the citric acid cycle and ketone body pools. Cofactor regeneration by the pterin-4a-carbinolamine dehydratase and dihydropteridine reductase steps keeps the hydroxylase running, linking this catabolism to biopterin-dependent catecholamine synthesis.

Aspartate and asparagine metabolism links the amino acid pool to the TCA cycle and to gluconeogenesis, letting cells build these two amino acids from glutamate, oxaloacetate and ammonia and, during fasting, feed their carbon skeletons back into glucose synthesis. Cytosolic and mitochondrial aspartate aminotransferases interconvert aspartate and oxaloacetate while transferring nitrogen from glutamate, and the aspartate-glutamate carriers of the inner membrane move aspartate outward as part of the malate-aspartate shuttle that transfers reducing equivalents into mitochondria; loss of the liver-type carrier causes citrin deficiency with hyperammonaemia. Asparagine synthetase consumes glutamine and ATP to amidate aspartate, and its induction under amino acid stress explains why leukaemic cells lacking it are killed by asparaginase therapy. Related reactions handle N-acetylaspartate, abundant in brain, whose failed hydrolysis by aspartoacylase produces Canavan disease.

Dietary macromolecules are useless until hydrolysed to absorbable units, and digestion and absorption is the pathway that performs both steps across the gastrointestinal lumen and the enterocytes of the small intestine. Salivary and pancreatic amylases attack starch, brush-border disaccharidases such as sucrase-isomaltase, lactase, maltase-glucoamylase and trehalase finish the job at the membrane, and the released monosaccharides cross apically via the sodium-glucose cotransporter SLC5A1 and fructose carrier SLC2A5 before leaving basolaterally through SLC2A2. Gastric and pancreatic lipases with colipase liberate fatty acids, while NPC1L1 mediates sterol uptake and is the target of ezetimibe. Loss of individual components produces recognisable disease: lactase decline causes lactose intolerance, and pancreatic lipase deficiency causes fat malabsorption and steatorrhoea. Guanylin and uroguanylin acting on guanylate cyclase C set luminal fluid and electrolyte balance alongside nutrient handling.

Chylomicron assembly is how the small intestine packages dietary fat for export, building the large triacylglycerol-rich lipoproteins that carry fat-soluble nutrients from the gut into lymph and then blood. Without it dietary lipid cannot leave the enterocyte: fat accumulates in intestinal cells and patients present with steatorrhoea, failure to thrive, and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins, as in abetalipoproteinaemia and chylomicron retention disease. Each particle is built around a single molecule of apolipoprotein B-48, which is lipidated in the endoplasmic reticulum by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein together with its disulfide isomerase partner, then loaded with triacylglycerol, phospholipid and cholesterol and decorated with exchangeable apolipoproteins A-I, A-II, A-IV, C-II, C-III and E. A dedicated COPII component, SAR1B, moves the oversized particle out of the ER, and the surface apolipoproteins subsequently direct lipase activation and hepatic remnant clearance.

Dietary fat absorbed by the small intestine cannot travel through blood or lymph unless it is packaged, and chylomicron assembly is the enterocyte process that builds those packages. Each nascent particle nucleates on a single molecule of apolipoprotein B-48, onto which microsomal triglyceride transfer protein — a heterodimer with protein disulfide isomerase — loads triacylglycerol, phospholipid and cholesterol as the apolipoprotein is translocated into the endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Exchangeable apolipoproteins A-I, A-II and A-IV join the surface, with apoC-II, apoC-III and apoE added or acquired to control later lipolysis by lipoprotein lipase and hepatic clearance of remnants. The particle then leaves the ER in specialized vesicles requiring the COPII component SAR1B before secretion into lymph. Loss of the transfer protein causes abetalipoproteinemia, and SAR1B defects cause chylomicron retention disease, both producing fat malabsorption and deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins.

Assembly of active LPL and LIPC lipase complexes describes how the two lipases that strip triglycerides from circulating lipoproteins are matured, positioned and switched off. This is the step that releases fatty acids from chylomicrons and VLDL for uptake by adipose, heart and skeletal muscle, and its failure causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia and chylomicronaemia. Lipoprotein lipase must be glycosylated, folded with the ER chaperone LMF1 and dimerised before GPIHBP1 shuttles it across capillary endothelium to heparan sulfate on the luminal surface; hepatic lipase follows a similar maturation route and is stabilised by heparin binding. Activity is then tuned by apolipoprotein cofactors such as APOC2 and APOA5, by inhibitory angiopoietin-like proteins, and by proprotein convertases that cleave ANGPTL3 and inactivate the enzyme. CREB3L3 coordinates transcription of the lipase together with its cofactors and FGF21, linking the pathway to fasting and hepatic lipid handling.

Circulating triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL can only be delivered to tissues after they are hydrolysed at the capillary wall, and this pathway covers how the two lipases that do it, lipoprotein lipase and hepatic lipase, are built, transported and switched off. LPL folding and dimerisation depend on the ER chaperone LMF1, after which GPIHBP1 ferries the enzyme across endothelial cells and holds it on the luminal surface; apolipoprotein C-II acts as an activating cofactor while APOA5 and APOC3-like modulators tune the reaction. Angiopoietin-like proteins 3, 4 and 8 inactivate LPL, in part through proprotein convertase cleavage by furin and related proteases, providing fasting and tissue-specific control of fuel partitioning. Transcription of LPL and its cofactors is driven by the hepatic factor CREB3L3. Loss of LPL, its chaperone, GPIHBP1 or APOC2 causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia with pancreatitis, and the inhibitory arm is an active target for lipid-lowering therapy.

High-density lipoprotein particles carry cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver for conversion to bile salts and excretion, and supply substrate to the adrenals and gonads for steroid hormone synthesis. HDL assembly is the first step in that reverse cholesterol transport route: newly synthesized apolipoprotein A-I is processed from its proprotein form and acquires phospholipid and free cholesterol to form nascent discoidal particles, which mature into spherical HDL as they take up further lipid from cells with excess cholesterol. The lipid efflux step depends on the ABCA1 transporter, whose loss causes Tangier disease with near-absent circulating HDL and cholesterol-laden tissue macrophages; protein kinase A subunits and palmitoylation contribute to regulating transporter activity and trafficking. Because apoA-I is recycled after delivering its cargo, the pathway sustains continuous lipid flux and shapes atherosclerosis risk.

Lipids are too hydrophobic to travel freely in blood, so they are packaged into lipoprotein particles, and plasma lipoprotein assembly is where those particles are built. Enterocytes construct chylomicrons to export dietary fat, hepatocytes construct very low density lipoproteins to export triacylglycerol they have synthesized, and nascent high density lipoprotein is formed when lipid-poor apolipoprotein A-I acquires cholesterol and phospholipid. The core step is lipidation of apolipoprotein B by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, assisted by the disulfide isomerase subunit that keeps it stable in the endoplasmic reticulum, followed by COPII-dependent export requiring SAR1B; ABCA1 supplies lipid for the HDL route. Exchangeable apolipoproteins of the C and E classes load onto the particles and later dictate their receptor and lipase targeting. Loss of assembly components causes abetalipoproteinaemia, chylomicron retention disease or Tangier disease, with fat malabsorption and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

Plasma lipoprotein remodeling covers the changes circulating lipoproteins undergo after secretion, converting triglyceride-rich chylomicrons and VLDL into remnants, IDL and LDL, and maturing nascent HDL into spherical particles. This is how dietary and hepatic fat is delivered to muscle and adipose tissue and how excess cholesterol is returned to the liver, so its dysfunction produces hypertriglyceridemia, familial chylomicronemia, low HDL states and premature atherosclerosis. Endothelial lipases, chiefly lipoprotein lipase anchored by GPIHBP1 and activated by APOC2 while inhibited by APOC3 and angiopoietin-like proteins, hydrolyze core triacylglycerol; hepatic and endothelial lipases act on remnants and HDL. Lipid and apolipoprotein exchange is carried out by CETP and PLTP, and LCAT esterifies HDL cholesterol to drive particle maturation. Apolipoprotein E acquisition marks remnants for hepatic LDL receptor uptake, linking remodeling to clearance and whole-body lipid homeostasis.

Once lipoproteins enter the circulation they are continuously rebuilt, and plasma lipoprotein remodeling is the set of lipase, transfer and apolipoprotein exchange reactions that converts newly secreted particles into the forms tissues can use and the liver can clear. Triglyceride-rich chylomicrons and VLDL are hydrolysed at the capillary endothelium by lipoprotein lipase, anchored there by GPIHBP1 and matured by LMF1/LMF2, releasing fatty acids for muscle and fat and yielding remnants and LDL that are taken up via apoB/apoE receptors. Apolipoproteins set the pace: APOC2 activates the lipase while APOC3 and the angiopoietin-like inhibitors restrain it. On HDL, LCAT esterifies cholesterol, CETP and PLTP shuttle esters and phospholipids between particles, and lipid-poor apoA-I is regenerated for further efflux. Defects produce severe hypertriglyceridaemia, chylomicronaemia, abetalipoproteinaemia and atherogenic dyslipidaemia, placing this chemistry at the centre of cardiovascular risk.

Chylomicron remodeling is the rapid maturation of dietary fat-carrying lipoproteins in the bloodstream, converting newly secreted intestinal chylomicrons into remnant particles that the liver can clear within an hour of a meal. It delivers fatty acids from food to muscle and adipose tissue and keeps postprandial triglyceride levels transient. Circulating particles exchange surface apolipoproteins with HDL, acquiring apoC-II and apoE while retaining apoB-48. ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which is anchored to the capillary endothelial surface by GPIHBP1 and hydrolyses the triacylglycerol core; apoC-III and apoA-V tune this rate. The shrunken, apoE-enriched remnant is then taken up by hepatic LDL and remnant receptors. Loss of lipoprotein lipase, its endothelial anchor, or apoC-II causes severe hypertriglyceridaemia with chylomicronaemia and pancreatitis, and remnant accumulation is atherogenic.

Chylomicrons carry dietary fat out of the intestine, and their remodeling in the circulation is how that fat is delivered to muscle and adipose tissue and the leftover particle returned to the liver. Newly secreted particles exchange apolipoproteins with HDL, gaining apoC-II and apoE, and are then stripped of most of their triacylglycerol by lipoprotein lipase, which GPIHBP1 captures from the interstitium and displays on the capillary endothelial surface. ApoC-II activates the lipase while apoC-III and apoA-V tune its rate, so that the resulting remnant, retaining apoB-48 and enriched in apoE, is cleared by hepatic LDL and remnant receptors within an hour. Loss of lipase activity or of its endothelial anchor causes severe fasting chylomicronemia with pancreatitis, and inefficient remnant clearance contributes to atherogenic postprandial lipemia.

High-density lipoprotein carries cholesterol from peripheral tissues back to the liver, and its clearance is the terminal step of reverse cholesterol transport, determining both plasma HDL levels and how much cholesterol is delivered for biliary excretion or steroidogenesis. Circulating particles dock on the scavenger receptor SR-BI (SCARB1) at the hepatocyte and steroidogenic cell surface, which does not internalize the whole particle but extracts its cholesteryl ester cargo, leaving a remodelled, lipid-poor pre-beta HDL. The apolipoprotein A-I released in this way is recovered chiefly in the kidney, where the cubilin transporter complex with amnionless binds and endocytoses it at the proximal tubule brush border, limiting urinary loss of apolipoprotein. Loss of this route raises HDL cholesterol while paradoxically impairing its delivery, and cubilin-amnionless defects also disrupt intestinal vitamin B12 uptake and cause tubular proteinuria.

Dietary fat leaves the gut packaged in chylomicrons, and chylomicron clearance is how the remnants of those particles are removed from blood after their triacylglycerol has been delivered to muscle and adipose tissue. Failure of this route leaves remnant lipoproteins circulating, the basis of type III hyperlipoproteinemia and a contributor to atherosclerotic risk. Depleted particles retain apolipoprotein B and acquire apolipoprotein E, which serves as the ligand recognised by the LDL receptor on hepatocytes. Hepatic lipase, held at the sinusoidal surface by heparan sulfate proteoglycans, further hydrolyses remnant lipid and assists particle capture. Receptor-bound remnants are then internalised by clathrin-mediated endocytosis, a step that depends on the adaptor LDLRAP1 to link the receptor tail to the coat machinery. The pathway represents the final, hepatic stage of dietary lipid transport and feeds cholesterol back into hepatic metabolism.

Circulating LDL particles, each built around a single apolipoprotein B-100 molecule, are removed from blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis, and this clearance sets plasma cholesterol concentration. Hepatocytes carry out most of it: the LDL receptor captures apoB-containing particles in clathrin-coated pits, with the adaptor protein complex AP-2 and the receptor-specific adaptor LDLRAP1 driving internalization, after which the particle is delivered to lysosomes and the receptor recycles to the surface. Lysosomal acid lipase hydrolyses cholesteryl esters, NPC1 and NPC2 export the liberated cholesterol from the lysosome, and ACAT enzymes re-esterify it for storage. PCSK9 opposes the whole route by directing the receptor to degradation rather than recycling. Loss of receptor function, or of its adaptor, causes familial hypercholesterolaemia and premature atherosclerosis, while lysosomal lipase or NPC defects trap lipid inside cells.

Low-density lipoprotein particles are not static once secreted; their lipid cargo and protein composition continue to be reworked in plasma, and this remodeling sets how much cholesterol circulates and how atherogenic it is. Each particle carries a single apolipoprotein B-100 molecule, whose lipidation during assembly depends on microsomal triglyceride transfer protein together with its protein disulfide isomerase subunit. In the circulation, cholesteryl ester transfer protein docks onto LDL and exchanges cholesteryl esters for triacylglycerol, a swap that routes peripheral cholesterol back toward the liver and is modulated by apolipoprotein F. Alternatively, apolipoprotein(a) binds covalently to apoB-100 to create lipoprotein(a), a particle cleared poorly by the LDL receptor and an inherited risk factor for atherosclerosis, aortic valve stenosis and thrombosis. These steps make LDL remodeling a determinant of plasma lipid balance and cardiovascular risk.

Removal of lipid-carrying particles from the bloodstream is how cholesterol and triglyceride delivered by the gut and liver are finally taken back into cells, and plasma lipoprotein clearance sets circulating cholesterol concentration and therefore atherosclerotic risk. Triglyceride-rich chylomicrons and VLDL acquire apolipoproteins C and E, are stripped of triacylglycerol by endothelial and hepatic lipases, and the remnants are captured by LDLR or VLDLR; LDL itself binds LDLR in clathrin-coated pits, with LDLRAP1 and the AP-2 adaptor complex driving internalisation to endosomes, where receptors recycle and particles pass to lysosomes for hydrolysis by LIPA and cholesterol export via NPC1 and NPC2. HDL is handled differently, docking on SCARB1 and the CUBN–AMN complex. Receptor availability is tuned by PCSK9-mediated degradation, MYLIP ubiquitination and liver X receptor transcription; loss of LDLR function produces familial hypercholesterolaemia.

Triglyceride-rich VLDL particles exported by the liver must eventually be taken up by peripheral tissues, and VLDL clearance covers the receptor-mediated capture and internalization step that ends a particle's time in the circulation. This delivers fatty acid energy to muscle and adipose tissue and keeps plasma triglyceride levels in check; when uptake is inefficient, remnant particles persist and contribute to hypertriglyceridaemia and atherogenic dyslipidaemia. Recognition depends on apolipoprotein B on the particle surface, read by cell-surface receptors including the VLDL receptor and the lipolysis-stimulated lipoprotein receptor, alongside an apoB-binding receptor. Small exchangeable apolipoproteins of the apoC family ride on the particle and modulate how readily it is bound and cleared, so the pathway links hepatic lipid export to peripheral lipid utilization and sits within broader lipoprotein metabolism and cardiovascular risk.

Mature HDL particles are not static cargo containers: their lipid and protein composition is continually reworked in plasma, and this remodeling sets how much cholesterol moves from peripheral tissues back to the liver for biliary excretion and to steroidogenic tissues for hormone synthesis. The transporter ABCG1 delivers intracellular cholesterol to the outer face of the plasma membrane where circulating HDL can take it up, together with phospholipid. On the particle surface, LCAT, activated by apoA-I, esterifies cholesterol using phosphatidylcholine, burying the ester in the core and releasing lysophosphatidylcholine, which drives particle maturation and further uptake. CETP exchanges cholesteryl ester and triglyceride with apoB-containing lipoproteins, PLTP transfers phospholipid between particles, and endothelial lipase hydrolyses HDL phospholipid. Exchangeable apolipoproteins including apoC-II, apoC-III and apoE bind reversibly, linking HDL to triglyceride metabolism. Variation here shapes HDL cholesterol levels and atherosclerosis risk.

Phenylalanine is an essential amino acid that must be disposed of when supplied in excess, and this pathway performs that disposal while generating tyrosine, the precursor of catecholamines, thyroid hormone and melanin. Phenylalanine hydroxylase carries out the committing hydroxylation using tetrahydrobiopterin as cosubstrate; loss of this enzyme causes classic phenylketonuria, in which phenylalanine accumulates to neurotoxic levels and untreated infants suffer irreversible intellectual disability, hence its place in newborn screening and lifelong dietary restriction. Because the cofactor is oxidized to a carbinolamine during turnover, it must be recycled: a dehydratase and a reductase regenerate tetrahydrobiopterin, and defects in these regeneration steps produce hyperphenylalaninaemia with additional deficits in biogenic amine synthesis. Transaminase and amino acid oxidase activities provide alternative routes that convert phenylalanine to phenylpyruvate and related keto acids.

G beta:gamma signalling through BTK is one of the routes by which G-protein coupled receptors talk to a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, linking chemokine and other GPCR inputs to the kinase that B cells depend on for development and antigen receptor signalling. Loss of BTK function causes X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, in which B cell maturation arrests and antibody production fails; the kinase is also the target of inhibitors used in B cell malignancies. Mechanistically, when a receptor-activated G alpha subunit dissociates, the freed beta-gamma dimer works together with membrane PIP3 to recruit BTK to the inner face of the plasma membrane, where the dimer stimulates its catalytic activity. Activated BTK then releases and phosphorylates downstream substrates, including phospholipase C gamma, coupling heterotrimeric G-protein signalling to calcium mobilisation and immune cell activation.

When a G-protein coupled receptor is activated, the beta-gamma dimer released from the alpha subunit is itself a signalling entity, and one of its targets is the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase BTK. Together with the membrane lipid PIP3, beta-gamma recruits BTK to the plasma membrane and stimulates its catalytic activity, after which the active kinase leaves the complex and phosphorylates its own substrates. This links heterotrimeric G-protein signalling, including chemokine receptor input, to the kinase that drives B lymphocyte development, differentiation and antigen receptor responses; loss of BTK function blocks B cell maturation and antibody production, the basis of X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, while its overactivity in B cell malignancies makes it a drug target. The many beta and gamma subunit genes here reflect combinatorial dimers assembled in different tissues rather than parallel routes to the same kinase.

Glutamate and glutamine metabolism sits at the junction of carbon and nitrogen handling. Glutamate is the hub through which amino groups from most amino acids enter and leave metabolism, and glutamine is the body's main circulating nitrogen carrier, so these reactions determine whether nitrogen is stored harmlessly, released as ammonia, or routed to urea synthesis in liver. The same chemistry feeds carbon skeletons into the TCA cycle and, during fasting, into gluconeogenesis. Glutamine synthetase condenses ammonia with glutamate, glutaminases reverse the step, and glutamate dehydrogenase interconverts glutamate and 2-oxoglutarate while transamination by aspartate aminotransferase balances amino and keto acid pools. Branches lead to proline via the pyrroline-5-carboxylate enzymes and to ornithine through ornithine aminotransferase. Because ammonia is neurotoxic and glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter, defects here produce hyperammonaemia, hyperinsulinism, and neurological disease.

Alanine metabolism links protein turnover to glucose and energy production by interconverting alanine and pyruvate. When muscle breaks down protein during fasting or exercise, amino groups are transferred to pyruvate to form alanine, which travels through the blood to the liver; there the reaction runs in reverse, releasing pyruvate for gluconeogenesis and nitrogen for urea synthesis. This alanine cycle lets peripheral tissues export both carbon and waste nitrogen safely, and it supports blood glucose between meals. The chemistry is carried by cytosolic and mitochondrial alanine aminotransferases, which use pyridoxal phosphate and couple the reaction to the glutamate/2-oxoglutarate pair, tying alanine handling to the wider transamination network. Leakage of these enzymes from damaged hepatocytes is the basis of serum transaminase measurement, the standard clinical readout of liver injury.

Alanine metabolism in humans turns essentially on a single reversible reaction: the transfer of an amino group between alanine and 2-oxoglutarate to give pyruvate and glutamate. This interconversion links protein turnover to energy metabolism, because it lets muscle export the nitrogen from degraded amino acids as a harmless carrier in the blood while delivering a three-carbon skeleton to the liver for gluconeogenesis, the basis of the glucose-alanine cycle during fasting and exercise. Two alanine aminotransferases carry out the step, one cytosolic and one mitochondrial, both using pyridoxal phosphate. Their release from damaged hepatocytes is why serum alanine aminotransferase is the standard clinical marker of liver injury, and the mitochondrial isoform's activity is also relevant to insulin secretion and hepatic glucose output.

Cells store surplus fat as lipid droplets, cytosolic organelles with a neutral lipid core of triglyceride and sterol esters bounded by a phospholipid monolayer, and this pathway covers how those droplets are made and sized. The capacity matters for adipocyte function, hepatic fat handling and the buffering of lipotoxic free fatty acids; when it is deranged the result is fatty liver, aberrant lipolysis and altered energy balance. Droplet biogenesis begins at the endoplasmic reticulum, where the fat storage-inducing transmembrane proteins FITM1 and FITM2 bind and partition triglyceride toward budding droplets. CIDEA and CIDEC sit at contact sites between adjacent droplets and drive net neutral lipid transfer from smaller to larger ones, enlarging stores and limiting lipolytic release. HILPDA, induced under hypoxia, promotes lipid accumulation, while the droplet-associated dehydrogenase HSD17B13 is strongly upregulated in nonalcoholic fatty liver disease.

When a G protein-coupled receptor fires, the released beta-gamma dimer is not merely a leftover of alpha subunit activation but a signalling module in its own right, and one of its outputs is activation of the small GTPase CDC42 to remodel the actin cytoskeleton and set cell shape and polarity. This route lets extracellular cues reshape epithelial apical-basal polarity, directed migration and chemotaxis. Mechanistically, the kinase PAK1 is held in the cytosol in complex with the exchange factor ARHGEF6 (alpha-PIX); beta-gamma recruits this pair to the plasma membrane, where ARHGEF6 loads GTP onto CDC42, and active CDC42 in turn stimulates PAK1, giving a local feed-forward loop at the membrane. The many beta and gamma subunit genes present reflect combinatorial dimers that diversify which receptors feed into this output, linking receptor stimulation to cytoskeletal and polarity control rather than to second-messenger production.

Fatty acid metabolism covers the synthesis, activation, elongation, desaturation and oxidative breakdown of fatty acids, together with the conversion of polyunsaturated fatty acids into eicosanoid signalling molecules. It supplies much of the body's energy between meals, provides the acyl chains for membrane lipids and storage triglycerides, and generates the prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes that drive inflammation, platelet aggregation and vascular tone. Cytosolic synthesis runs from acetyl-CoA through carboxylases and the fatty acid synthase complex; degradation requires CoA activation by acyl-CoA synthetases, carnitine-dependent import into mitochondria, and spiral beta-oxidation, with very-long-chain and branched substrates handled peroxisomally. Cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases and cytochrome P450s branch arachidonate toward mediators, while thioesterases, AMP-activated kinase subunits and nuclear receptors set flux. Inherited defects cause hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, cardiomyopathy and peroxisomal disease, and the lipogenic arm is central to fatty liver and metabolic syndrome.

Fatty acid metabolism supplies much of the body's energy currency, builds the acyl chains used in membranes and storage lipids, and generates the eicosanoid signals that shape inflammation, vascular tone and platelet behaviour. Synthesis runs from acetyl-CoA through carboxylation by ACACA/ACACB and the multifunctional fatty acid synthase, followed by elongation and desaturation steps that set chain length and unsaturation. Degradation requires activation to acyl-CoA, carnitine-dependent transport into mitochondria via CPT1/CPT2, and repeated rounds of beta-oxidation, with very-long-chain and branched substrates handled peroxisomally. A third arm oxygenates arachidonic acid through cyclooxygenases, lipoxygenases and cytochrome P450s to yield prostaglandins, thromboxane, leukotrienes and related mediators. Nuclear receptors and AMP-activated kinase subunits tune flux to nutritional state. Inherited defects cause fatty acid oxidation disorders with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and cardiomyopathy, while excess flux and eicosanoid overproduction contribute to steatosis, atherosclerosis and chronic inflammation.

Enzymes are only as capable as the cofactors they carry, and this branch of metabolism covers how those cofactors are made — built de novo, derived from dietary vitamins, or recycled back to their active oxidation state. Two routes dominate here. One assembles coenzyme Q, the lipid electron carrier of the respiratory chain and a membrane antioxidant: a polyprenyl diphosphate synthase pair generates the tail, and the COQ proteins hydroxylate, methylate and decorate the quinone head at the inner mitochondrial membrane, with loss of function causing primary CoQ10 deficiency, encephalomyopathy and steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. The other makes and regenerates tetrahydrobiopterin through GTP cyclohydrolase, pyruvoyl-tetrahydropterin synthase, sepiapterin reductase and dihydrofolate reductase; this pterin is required by aromatic amino acid hydroxylases for dopamine and serotonin synthesis and by endothelial nitric oxide synthase, whose coupling with calmodulin, HSP90 and AKT1 sets vascular NO output.

Triglyceride metabolism links dietary and newly synthesized fatty acids to the body's main form of energy storage, and its balance sets whether fat is deposited in adipose tissue or released as fuel for other organs. Synthesis runs from fatty acyl-CoA through phosphatidic acid, which lipin phosphatases convert to diacylglycerol, and finally to triacylglycerol via DGAT1 and DGAT2; glycerol kinases and glycerol-3-phosphate acyltransferases feed the backbone, and fatty acid binding proteins shuttle the lipid substrates. Breakdown is mobilized on the surface of cytosolic lipid droplets, where perilipins and the coactivator ABHD5 control access of hormone-sensitive lipase and monoacylglycerol lipase. Catecholamine, ACTH and glucagon signalling through PKA phosphorylates and activates this lipolytic machinery, while insulin-directed protein phosphatase 1 activity reverses it. The same lipase also hydrolyses cholesteryl esters to supply steroidogenesis. Dysregulation underlies obesity, insulin resistance, hepatic steatosis and inherited lipid storage disease.

RHOA GTPase cycle describes how the founding member of the RHO GTPase family is switched between GDP- and GTP-bound states, and what that switch controls: the actomyosin cytoskeleton and cell contractility. Through it cells adhere, migrate, divide, traffic vesicles, sense mechanical force and adjust gene expression, making it the hub of mechanotransduction in endothelium and smooth muscle, of neurite outgrowth and axon retraction, and of immune cell motility. Exchange factors such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF12 and TRIO load GTP; a large family of ARHGAP proteins, DLC1 and myosin-IX GAPs terminate signalling; ARHGDIA sequesters the inactive pool. Active RHOA engages ROCK1/2, citron kinase, PKN kinases, formins and rhotekin to drive stress fibre assembly and cytokinetic furrow ingression. RHOA is recurrently mutated in lymphoma and gastric cancer, and bacterial toxins hijack it to subvert the host cytoskeleton.

RHOA switches between GTP- and GDP-bound states, and this cycle is how cells set the tension and shape of their actin cytoskeleton. Contractile actomyosin structures, stress fibres, focal adhesions and the cleavage furrow of dividing cells all depend on it, as do cell migration, adhesion, vesicle traffic and mechanically driven changes in gene expression. Large families of exchange factors such as ARHGEF1/2/12, VAV and TRIO load GTP in response to upstream receptors, while ARHGAP and DLC1-type GTPase-activating proteins terminate signalling and RHOGDIs hold inactive RHOA in the cytosol. Active RHOA engages ROCK1/2, PKN kinases, citron and formins including DIAPH1 to drive myosin activation and actin polymerisation. The cycle underlies vascular tone, neuronal process outgrowth and immune cell function; its components are mutated in cancer, and bacterial toxins subvert RHOA to remodel the host cytoskeleton.

Intestinal hexose absorption is the step that moves dietary sugars out of the gut lumen and into the bloodstream, completing carbohydrate digestion and supplying the body with its main circulating fuel. Without it, glucose, galactose and fructose remain in the intestine, drawing water osmotically and causing the diarrhoea and dehydration seen in congenital glucose-galactose malabsorption and fructose intolerance. Uptake is vectorial: on the luminal brush border of enterocytes, SGLT1 (SLC5A1) couples glucose and galactose entry to the inward sodium gradient set by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, while GLUT5 (SLC2A5) carries fructose by facilitated diffusion. Sugars then exit across the basolateral membrane through GLUT2 (SLC2A2) into portal blood. The same transporters shape postprandial glycaemia and incretin release, and GLUT2 mutations cause Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, linking this absorptive route to whole-body glucose homeostasis.

Dietary starch and sugars are digested to free hexoses in the gut lumen, and this transport route moves that glucose, galactose and fructose across the intestinal epithelium into the bloodstream, making carbohydrate calories available to the rest of the body. Uptake is vectorial: on the brush border facing the lumen, SLC5A1 (SGLT1) couples glucose and galactose entry to the inward sodium gradient, allowing absorption against a concentration gradient, while SLC2A5 (GLUT5) carries fructose by facilitated diffusion. On the basolateral membrane, SLC2A2 (GLUT2) releases all three sugars to the portal circulation. Loss of SGLT1 causes glucose-galactose malabsorption with osmotic diarrhoea in infancy, and GLUT2 defects underlie Fanconi-Bickel syndrome; SGLT1-dependent sodium and water flux is also the basis of oral rehydration therapy. The same transporters link intestinal absorption to postprandial glycaemia and incretin release.

Cells that consume oxygen quickly need it buffered and shuttled inside the cytosol, and the cytosolic globins do that job. Myoglobin stores and ferries oxygen in cardiac and skeletal muscle, sustaining oxidative metabolism during contraction; neuroglobin performs a comparable role in neurons; cytoglobin is found in fibroblasts and smooth muscle of connective tissue. Each binds molecular oxygen reversibly at a heme iron, with myoglobin pentacoordinate and neuroglobin and cytoglobin hexacoordinate, the second histidine dissociating to admit oxygen, carbon monoxide or nitric oxide. Through these same hemes the globins shape nitric oxide balance and therefore vascular tone: oxygenated forms scavenge NO by oxidation, while deoxygenated forms reduce nitrite back to NO under hypoxia. This links intracellular oxygen transport to redox protection, hypoxic tolerance and blood flow regulation rather than to bulk oxygen carriage in blood.

Glycogen is the body's rapidly mobilisable glucose store, abundant in liver, where it buffers blood sugar between meals, and in skeletal muscle, where it fuels contraction. Its metabolism runs in two directions: glucose 6-phosphate is isomerised by phosphoglucomutase and activated as UDP-glucose, glycogenin primes a short glucose chain on itself, glycogen synthase extends it, and branching enzyme introduces the alpha-1,6 branch points that make the polymer soluble and rapidly accessible. Breakdown reverses this through glycogen phosphorylase, activated by phosphorylase kinase in response to hormonal and calcium signals, with debranching enzyme clearing the branch points; a lysosomal route depends on acid alpha-glucosidase. Tissue-specific isozymes of synthase, phosphorylase and the kinase subunits allow liver and muscle to be regulated independently. Loss of individual steps produces the glycogen storage diseases, including Pompe and McArdle disease, while laforin and malin defects cause Lafora progressive myoclonic epilepsy.

Interleukin-15 signalling sustains natural killer cells and memory CD8 T cells, giving them the survival and proliferative signals they need to persist long after an infection has cleared; loss of it leaves mice and people short of NK cells, while excess IL15 drives inflammatory disease such as coeliac enteropathy and some T/NK leukaemias. The high-affinity receptor is a heterotrimer of IL15RA with the shared IL2RB and common gamma chain, so IL15 and IL2 converge on the same kinases and are distinguished largely by the alpha subunit and by trans-presentation, in which a neighbouring cell displays bound IL15 to the responding lymphocyte. Engagement activates JAK1 and JAK3, which phosphorylate STAT5A, STAT5B and STAT3 for transcriptional output, while GAB2 with GRB2, SHC1 and the SOS exchange factors routes the signal into RAS-MAPK growth responses.

Interferon-inducible sensing of double-stranded RNA by the oligoadenylate synthetase family is one of the fastest cell-intrinsic brakes on viral replication. OAS1, OAS2 and OAS3 bind viral duplex RNA and polymerise ATP into 2'-5'-linked oligoadenylates, an unusual second messenger whose only major job is to dimerise and activate ribonuclease L. Activated RNase L then cleaves single-stranded RNA at U-rich sites, destroying viral and host transcripts alike, shutting down translation and pushing heavily infected cells toward death; ABCE1 restrains the nuclease, and PDE12 degrades the 2-5A signal, so the response is self-limiting rather than runaway. OASL lacks synthetase activity and instead works through RIG-I to amplify interferon induction. Loss or variation in these genes alters susceptibility to flaviviruses and other RNA viruses, and excessive signalling contributes to interferon-driven autoinflammation.

Interleukin-35 signalling is the inhibitory arm of the IL-12 cytokine family: a heterodimer of the EBI3 and IL12A subunits, secreted largely by regulatory T cells, that dampens inflammatory responses rather than driving them. It restrains effector T cell proliferation, promotes conversion of conventional T cells into suppressive regulatory populations, and contributes to the tolerance that prevents autoimmunity, while also being exploited by tumours and chronic infections to blunt immune attack. The cytokine engages a receptor built from IL12RB2 and IL27RA, with gp130 (IL6ST) available as an alternative chain, and transmits through receptor-associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2 to phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT4 and, in some contexts, STAT3. Calnexin appears here through its chaperone role in folding and assembling the subunits in the endoplasmic reticulum. Loss of this restraint tips the balance towards unchecked inflammation.

Guidance cues steer growing axons and restrain cell motility by reshaping the actin cytoskeleton, and this branch of SLIT-ROBO signalling does so by raising RHOA activity. When SLIT2 binds the ROBO1 receptor, the receptor engages the unconventional myosin MYO9B and blocks its RHOA GTPase-activating function; with GTP hydrolysis on RHOA suppressed, the active GTP-bound pool rises. The consequence is ROCK activation and phosphorylation of the myosin regulatory light chain, generating the actomyosin contractility that cranial motor neuron axons require to follow SLIT cues correctly. The same output limits cell migration and invasion, and loss of this restraint has been linked to increased invasiveness of lung cancer cells. It illustrates how a receptor can raise small GTPase activity by inhibiting an inhibitor rather than recruiting an exchange factor.

Cortical neurons acquire their input capacity by elaborating dendritic arbors, and this branching programme sets how many synapses a pyramidal cell can receive and therefore how cortical circuits are wired. The same secreted guidance cue family that repels growing axons is reused here for a constructive purpose: SLIT1 binds the transmembrane receptors ROBO1 and ROBO2 on cortical dendrites and, instead of causing retraction, promotes the formation of new branch points. The cytoplasmic adaptor NCK2 couples activated ROBO to the actin regulatory machinery and is required for the branching response, illustrating how the interpretation of a guidance signal depends on which effector is engaged in which compartment. Disturbed regulation of cortical dendrite branching yields simplified arbors and altered connectivity of the kind associated with neurodevelopmental and intellectual disability phenotypes, placing this signalling within cytoskeletal control of neuronal morphogenesis.

Interleukin-9 signaling is the growth and survival cue that a small T helper subset uses to amplify allergic and mucosal immune responses, and it also sustains mast cell expansion and airway mucus production in asthma. IL9 binds its private alpha chain, IL9R, which pairs with the shared common gamma chain, IL2RG, the same subunit used by receptors for IL2, IL4, IL7, IL15 and IL21; loss of that subunit abolishes IL9-driven proliferation and, more broadly, causes severe combined immunodeficiency. Receptor dimerisation brings together the tyrosine kinases JAK1 and JAK3, which phosphorylate STAT1, STAT3 and the two STAT5 proteins; these dimerise as STAT5 homodimers and STAT1:STAT3 heterodimers, move to the nucleus, and drive anti-apoptotic and proliferative transcription. Excess signalling through this axis is implicated in allergic inflammation, and in lymphoid malignancies dependent on autocrine IL9.

MECP2 reads methylated DNA in neurons and sets the transcriptional tone of the mature nervous system; loss-of-function mutations in this X-linked gene cause most cases of Rett syndrome, while duplication of the locus produces its own neurological disorder, so both too little and too much are damaging. The protein binds 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine and can either repress or activate, recruiting the SIN3A-HDAC1/2 and NCoR/SMRT co-repressor complexes or partnering with CREB1 at stimulated promoters. Its targets are the machinery of synaptic function and plasticity: BDNF, the GABA-synthesizing enzymes GAD1 and GAD2, glutamate and NMDA receptor subunits, opioid receptors, transcription factors such as MEF2C and RBFOX1, and tyrosine phosphatases that temper receptor kinase signalling. Neuronal activity-dependent phosphorylation through calcium/calmodulin kinases modulates MECP2 binding, and interaction with DROSHA-DGCR8 and Argonaute components links it to microRNA output.

Rett syndrome follows loss of function of MECP2, the methyl-CpG-binding protein that links DNA methylation to transcriptional control in neurons. Girls with these mutations develop normally for the first year and then regress, losing speech and purposeful hand use and acquiring stereotypies, seizures and breathing abnormalities — evidence that MECP2 is needed to maintain mature neuronal function rather than to build the brain. Wild-type MECP2 reads methylated and hydroxymethylated cytosine and recruits corepressor machinery, including the NCoR/SMRT complex with its histone deacetylase and TBL1 subunits, as well as SIN3A-HDAC1, to damp transcription of target genes such as BDNF. Neuronal activity further tunes this through calcium- and kinase-dependent phosphorylation involving calmodulin, CaMKIV and PKA. Disease mutations variously abolish methylated-DNA binding, corepressor recruitment, or activity-dependent phosphorylation at threonine 308.

Pervasive developmental disorders, which overlap closely with the autism spectrum, appear in early childhood as impairments of social interaction, communication and behaviour, and can arise from mutations in genes governing brain development, from environmental insults, or from both together. The annotated example here is Rett syndrome, caused by loss of function of the methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2, an X-linked chromatin reader that couples DNA methylation to transcriptional control in neurons. MECP2 recruits corepressor machinery — the SIN3A and NCOR complexes with their HDAC1/HDAC3 deacetylases, TBL1X/TBL1XR1 and GPS2 — to methylated promoters, and its activity is tuned by activity-dependent phosphorylation through calcium/calmodulin and PKA signalling. A central target is BDNF, whose regulated expression supports synapse maturation and activity-dependent plasticity; disrupting this circuit yields the developmental regression, motor and cognitive deficits characteristic of the disorder.

The TRKB receptor tyrosine kinase, encoded by NTRK2, is the principal receptor for brain-derived neurotrophic factor and neurotrophin-4, and signalling through it supports neuronal survival, dendrite and axon growth, synapse maturation and the activity-dependent plasticity underlying long-term potentiation and learning. Loss or haploinsufficiency of this route causes obesity with developmental delay and impaired nociception, and reduced BDNF-TRKB tone is linked to mood disorders and neurodegeneration. Ligand binding dimerizes the receptor and drives trans-autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for adaptors such as SHC1, GRB2, FRS2 and GAB1 with PTPN11, which route the signal into RAS-ERK, PI3K-AKT and PLCgamma-calcium cascades. Parallel outputs include SRC- and FYN-dependent tyrosine phosphorylation of the NMDA receptor subunit GRIN2B at synapses, CDK5 activity, and Rac1 activation via TIAM1 and DOCK3 to remodel the actin cytoskeleton during neurite outgrowth and growth cone guidance.

Erythropoietin signalling is how the body matches red cell production to oxygen supply: the kidney releases EPO when tissue oxygen tension falls, and the hormone acts on erythroid progenitors to keep them alive and dividing as they mature into erythrocytes. Loss of this axis produces the anaemia of renal failure, while its pharmacological stimulation is the basis of recombinant EPO therapy. EPO binds a pre-dimerised receptor that is already associated with the tyrosine kinase JAK2, LYN and the scaffold IRS2; JAK2 activation phosphorylates the receptor tail and creates docking sites that branch into four outputs — STAT5A/STAT5B-driven transcription of survival genes, PI3K–AKT, RAS–ERK through SHC1, GRB2 and SOS1, and phospholipase C gamma with downstream PKC. The survival and proliferative arms dominate in erythroid cells, but receptor expression in endothelium and neural tissue lets the same cascade act as a broader anti-apoptotic and growth signal.

Most cancers keep their telomeres from eroding by reactivating telomerase, but a minority instead copy telomeric DNA from one chromosome end to another using homologous recombination, a route known as alternative lengthening of telomeres. This gives tumour cells unlimited replicative potential without any telomerase activity, and it is common in osteosarcoma and other sarcomas, certain brain tumours and neuroblastoma, where it carries prognostic and therapeutic weight. The chromatin remodelling partners ATRX and DAXX, which deposit histone H3.3 at telomeric and other heterochromatin, normally suppress recombination at chromosome ends; loss-of-function mutation in either is the characteristic lesion in these tumours and permits recombination-directed telomere synthesis. Recruitment of recombination machinery to telomeres, aided by nucleosome remodelling complexes, then drives strand invasion and templated extension, linking telomere maintenance to DNA repair rather than to a dedicated reverse transcriptase.

Receptors at the cell surface rarely act directly on their targets; instead they generate diffusible second messengers inside the cell, and this collection of routes covers how those messengers are made, read and turned off. Adenylate cyclases convert ATP to cAMP that activates protein kinase A holoenzymes, phosphodiesterases degrade it, inositol trisphosphate receptors release calcium from ER stores, calcium-calmodulin engages CaMK kinases, and diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C isoforms. The largest arm here is phosphoinositide signalling: class I PI3 kinases acting downstream of growth factor, cytokine and antigen receptors produce PIP3, recruiting AKT via PDK1, with PTEN and the PHLPP phosphatases reversing the signal and TSC2, RHEB and the Rag-Ragulator machinery relaying it to mTOR. The outputs are proliferation, metabolism, survival through BAD and FOXO factors, and transcriptional change via CREB, and their deregulation is among the commonest events in cancer and diabetes.

Not all tyrosine phosphorylation in signalling comes from receptors themselves: cytosolic non-receptor tyrosine kinases are recruited to membrane receptors and complexes and act as the catalytic subunit that propagates the signal onward. Grouped into families such as SRC, ABL, SYK, JAK, TEC, FAK and the BRK/PTK6 group, they feed into the same growth, adhesion and survival routes used by receptor kinases, which is why their deregulation is a recurrent theme in leukaemia and solid tumours. Here the emphasis falls on PTK6/BRK and its relative SRMS acting alongside EGFR-family receptors and their ligands, with outputs through RAS proteins, STAT3, AKT and cell cycle regulators including cyclins, CDK2/CDK4 and p27, plus adhesion and Rho-family GTPase control via paxillin, BCAR1 and CRK-DOCK1-ELMO complexes. Negative regulation comes from CBL-directed ubiquitination, SOCS3 and the phosphatase PTPN1.

Lipophilic hormones and metabolites act largely by binding nuclear receptors, ligand-gated transcription factors that convert the presence of a steroid, retinoid, oxysterol or fatty acid into a change in gene expression. This branch of signalling sets reproductive tissue growth, cholesterol and lipid handling, and developmental patterning, and its deregulation underlies hormone-dependent breast cancer, dyslipidaemia and retinoid-related birth defects. Receptors such as the estrogen receptors, progesterone receptor, retinoic acid receptors and the liver X receptors bind DNA as dimers, frequently with RXR partners, and switch between corepressor complexes containing NCOR1/2 and HDACs and coactivators such as the p160 family, CREBBP/EP300 and Mediator, which remodel chromatin and recruit RNA polymerase II. Chaperone complexes with HSP90 and FKBP immunophilins hold unliganded steroid receptors competent for hormone binding and nuclear import. Ligand supply and clearance are themselves encoded here, through retinaldehyde dehydrogenases and CYP26 enzymes, alongside rapid membrane-initiated signalling via SRC, PI3K and MAPK cascades and target genes governing sterol efflux and lipogenesis.

Cell surface receptor tyrosine kinases are how cells read growth factors, and signalling by receptor tyrosine kinases is the route from an extracellular cue to decisions about proliferation, survival, differentiation, migration and metabolism. The receptor families here include the EGF/ERBB, FGF, PDGF, VEGF, insulin/IGF, NTRK, MET, KIT and ALK receptors, each binding its own ligands, dimerising and autophosphorylating cytoplasmic tyrosines that recruit adaptors such as GRB2, SHC, FRS2, IRS and GAB. Those complexes launch RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascades, PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling and PLC-gamma/PKC and STAT outputs, with feedback from phosphatases, SPRY/SPRED proteins, SOCS, CBL-mediated ubiquitination and clathrin-dependent endocytosis setting signal duration. Mutation or amplification of these receptors drives many carcinomas and leukaemias and makes them prime drug targets, while loss disrupts development, angiogenesis and glucose homeostasis.

The TGF-beta superfamily of secreted ligands — TGF-betas themselves, BMPs, activins and inhibins, nodal-related factors, GDFs and anti-Mullerian hormone — instructs cells on whether to divide, differentiate, migrate or deposit matrix, and signalling by TGFB family members underlies embryonic patterning, bone and cartilage formation, vascular integrity, immune restraint and wound healing. Ligand dimers assemble hetero-tetrameric complexes of type II and type I serine/threonine kinase receptors; the type II kinase transphosphorylates the type I receptor, which phosphorylates receptor-SMADs — SMAD2/3 for TGF-beta and activin, SMAD1/5/9 for BMP — that partner with the shared SMAD4 and, with cofactors such as p300, SKI/SKIL, TGIF and corepressors, set transcription of targets including SERPINE1, MYC, CDKN2B and myogenic factors. Output is tuned by latency-conferring LTBPs and integrin-mediated activation, extracellular antagonists such as noggin, follistatin and gremlin, inhibitory SMAD6/7 with SMURF ubiquitin ligases, and phosphatase and deubiquitinase feedback. Loss of this control drives fibrosis, vascular malformation, skeletal disease and cancer progression.

Every vesicle that leaves one compartment must know where to go, and the RAB family of small GTPases supplies that address code, making RAB regulation of trafficking the control layer over secretion, endocytosis, recycling, autophagosome maturation and lysosome-related organelle biogenesis. More than fifty RABs are represented here, each cycling between an inactive GDP-bound form held in the cytosol by GDI chaperones and an active GDP-to-GTP exchanged form docked on a specific membrane, where it recruits sorting adaptors, tethers and motors. Activation is driven by dedicated exchange factors – DENN-domain proteins, the multisubunit TRAPP and MON1–CCZ1 complexes, RABGEF1 – and reversed by TBC-domain GTPase-activating proteins, while prenylation by machinery involving the Rab escort proteins CHM and CHML anchors RABs to bilayers. Loss of individual components causes choroideremia, Griscelli and Hermansky–Pudlak syndromes, hereditary spastic paraplegia and intellectual disability, illustrating how tissue-specific cargo delivery depends on this shared switch.

Interleukin-38 signalling is an anti-inflammatory arm of the IL-1 cytokine family, acting as a brake on the IL-17 and IL-22 responses that drive psoriatic and other chronic inflammatory skin and joint disease. The ligand IL1F10 is made by keratinocytes and released from apoptotic cells, so it links cell death to dampened local immunity. It engages IL1RL2, the receptor otherwise used by the IL-36 cytokines, and also IL1RAPL1, whose outcome depends on N-terminal processing: the full-length protein induces IL-6, while the truncated form binds with higher affinity and suppresses it, with the JNK kinase MAPK8 and AP-1 transcription factors relaying the signal. This makes proteolytic maturation, rather than expression alone, the switch that sets whether the response is agonist or antagonist.

Interleukin-37 signaling is the braking arm of the interleukin-1 cytokine family, a dedicated anti-inflammatory circuit that restrains innate immune activation and limits tissue damage from excessive cytokine output. Loss of this restraint tips the balance toward chronic inflammation and autoimmunity, while its engagement dampens responses in macrophages, dendritic cells and epithelium. IL37 is made as a precursor and cleaved by caspase-1, after which it acts on two fronts: extracellularly it binds IL18R1 together with the decoy receptor IL18BP and recruits the inhibitory co-receptor SIGIRR, triggering STAT3 and PTEN phosphorylation while suppressing NF-kappaB; intracellularly the processed form partners with SMAD3 and moves to the nucleus to drive transcription of protein tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN6 and PTPN11 that strip activating phosphates from inflammatory signalling nodes.
