The net effect is broad, sustained suppression of proinflammatory cytokine production.

Interleukin-37 is the braking cytokine of the IL-1 family: rather than driving inflammation, it damps it, limiting cytokine output from macrophages, dendritic cells and other innate immune cells and protecting tissue from endotoxin shock, autoimmune injury and excessive inflammatory signalling. The precursor is cleaved by caspase-1, and both full-length and processed forms are secreted or bind IL-18 binding protein, which sequesters IL-18 and blunts its pro-inflammatory arm. Extracellular IL-37 engages IL-18 receptor 1 together with the inhibitory co-receptor SIGIRR, favouring STAT3 phosphorylation and PTEN activity while suppressing NF-kB-driven transcription. An intracellular route also operates: processed IL-37 associates with SMAD3 and moves to the nucleus, where it promotes expression of non-receptor tyrosine phosphatases such as PTPN6 and PTPN11 that dephosphorylate kinases in innate signalling cascades. The net effect is transcriptional and post-translational restraint of inflammation.

Estradiol acts within seconds to minutes through estrogen receptors held at the plasma membrane, a mode of action independent of the receptors' role as nuclear transcription factors. This extra-nuclear estrogen signaling underlies rapid physiological responses: endothelial nitric oxide production and vasodilation via NOS3, neuronal effects on cognition, stress and reproductive behaviour, and proliferative and anti-apoptotic responses that matter in hormone-dependent breast cancer. Membrane localization requires palmitoylation of ESR1 by the acyltransferases ZDHHC7 and ZDHHC21 and arginine methylation by PRMT1, after which the receptor nucleates complexes with SRC, caveolins, heterotrimeric G proteins and PI3K regulatory subunits. Signal flow proceeds into RAS-RAF-MAPK and PI3K/AKT outputs, converging on CREB1, FOS and ELK1, cyclin D1 and BCL2, with matrix metalloproteinase-driven shedding of EGFR ligands providing crosstalk to growth factor receptor and GPCR pathways.

Glycoproteins that fail to fold correctly in the endoplasmic reticulum are sorted in a specialised subregion, the ER quality control compartment, which decides between another attempt at folding and disposal. This triage protects cells from accumulating misfolded secretory and membrane proteins, and its output feeds ER-associated degradation, the route whose failure underlies ER stress and several conformational diseases. The decision is written in the N-glycan: UGGT1 and UGGT2 re-add glucose to nearly-native glycoproteins, sending them back for another round of calnexin and calreticulin binding, while ER mannosidase I and the EDEM proteins progressively trim mannose residues until reglucosylation is no longer possible. Trimmed substrates are captured by lectins such as OS9 and delivered to the SEL1L-HRD1 complex and related membrane ubiquitin ligases for retrotranslocation, ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction.

Newly made glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum are held by the lectin chaperones calnexin and calreticulin, which bind monoglucosylated N-glycans and give the client repeated chances to fold correctly before it leaves the ER. This quality-control cycle determines which secreted and membrane proteins reach the cell surface, and its outcome underlies diseases where a single mutation makes an otherwise functional protein undegradable or undeliverable. Glucosidase II trims the glycan to release the client, while the folding sensors UGGT1 and UGGT2 re-add glucose to still-unfolded substrates and return them to the chaperones; the thiol oxidoreductase PDIA3 works alongside to rearrange disulfides. Persistent failures are trimmed by mannosidases of the EDEM family, recognised by OS9, and routed through the SEL1L–HRD1 complex and other ER membrane ubiquitin ligases for retrotranslocation and proteasomal destruction, linking folding to ER-associated degradation.

SLIT ligands and their ROBO receptors steer growing axons away from inappropriate territory, most visibly at the midline, and set the paths of commissural projections, so the amount of each protein a neuron displays at a given moment determines how it responds to guidance cues. This pathway covers how those levels are set, at every step from gene to functional receptor. LIM-homeodomain factors such as LHX2, LHX3, LHX4, LHX9 and ISL1, together with HOXA2, drive ROBO and SLIT transcription in a cell-type-dependent way; the RNA-binding protein MSI1 boosts translation of ROBO3 mRNA, with ribosomal subunits, cap-binding and nonsense-mediated decay components supplying the translational machinery. Protein abundance is then tuned by ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP33 which stabilises ROBO1, while dystroglycan and a collagen IV chain anchor secreted SLITs where they are needed. Misregulation contributes to axon guidance defects and to invasive behaviour in cancer.

Axon guidance receptors of the ROBO family steer growing axons away from midline Slit sources, and their cytoplasmic tails can be coupled to local kinase and phosphatase activity through a scaffold. The binding of AKAP5 to ROBO2 and to the ROBO3.1 isoform brings protein kinase A, protein kinase C and the calcium/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase calcineurin into the immediate vicinity of the receptor, so that guidance signalling is read out alongside cAMP and calcium cues rather than in isolation. PKC recruited in this way phosphorylates ROBO3.1. Such anchoring is the general strategy AKAP proteins use to confine broadly acting kinases to defined membrane microdomains, and in neurons it links receptor engagement at the growth cone to cytoskeletal remodelling and decisions about midline crossing. The downstream consequences of the ROBO-AKAP5 interaction itself remain undefined, with the complex demonstrated in brain tissue.

Interleukin-18 signaling is an innate-to-adaptive amplifier: the cytokine, made as an inactive precursor and cleaved by caspase-1 or extracellular proteases such as elastase and cathepsin G, drives interferon-gamma production by Th1 cells, macrophages and NK cells and boosts NK cytotoxicity, with synergy from IL12 and related Th1 cytokines. Mature IL18 binds IL18R1 first, then recruits the accessory subunit IL18RAP to form a high-affinity complex whose paired Toll/IL-1 receptor domains recruit the MyD88-type adaptors used by IL-1 family receptors. Restraint is built in: soluble IL18BP sequesters mature IL18, IL37 engages IL18BP and IL18RAP to block signaling, and TIR-less receptor variants act as decoys. Depending on context the response can skew toward IL4 and IL13 and toward leukotriene generation via ALOX5. Unchecked activity underlies macrophage activation syndrome, autoinflammatory and inflammatory bowel disease.

NOTCH3 signalling is the arm of Notch communication used chiefly by vascular smooth muscle cells, lymphocytes and neural progenitors, and it decides whether those cells survive, stay undifferentiated, or adopt a particular fate. Its importance is clearest when it goes wrong: inherited gain-of-function NOTCH3 mutations cause CADASIL, in which smooth muscle cells degenerate from small cerebral arteries and young adults suffer strokes and white matter disease, while NOTCH3 amplification supports proliferation in breast and ovarian tumours and contributes to epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and to T-cell leukaemia. Mechanistically, delta-like and jagged ligands presented by a neighbouring cell, and ubiquitinated by MIB and NEURL ligases, trigger successive cleavage by ADAM10 and the gamma-secretase complex. The released intracellular domain enters the nucleus, binds RBPJ with mastermind-like coactivators and acetyltransferases such as EP300, and switches on HES and HEY repressors, along with PTCRA in developing thymocytes.

RHO GTPase cycle describes how the RHO family of small GTPases is switched on and off, and it sets the pace of actin cytoskeleton remodelling throughout the body. Because RHOA, RAC1, CDC42 and their relatives govern cell shape, adhesion, migration, cytokinesis and polarity, this cycle underlies neuronal morphogenesis, leukocyte motility and the phagocyte oxidase burst, endothelial and vascular homeostasis, and epithelial junction integrity; its dysregulation drives tumour invasion, congenital immunodeficiency and neurodevelopmental disease, and it is hijacked by bacterial toxins. Nucleotide state is controlled by three regulator classes: GDIs sequester GDP-bound GTPases in the cytosol, Dbl- and DOCK-family GEFs load GTP at the membrane, and a large complement of GAPs accelerates hydrolysis. Activated forms engage effectors such as ROCK, PAK, formins, WASP/WAVE components and IQGAPs. Atypical members including the Rnd, RhoBTB, RhoH and RhoU/V groups bypass this cycle and act constitutively.

Rho family GTPases are the switches that let cells rebuild their actin cytoskeleton on demand, and their nucleotide cycle is what sets the timing. Cell migration, adhesion, polarity establishment, cytokinesis and vesicle traffic all depend on it, which is why the same machinery shapes neuronal morphogenesis, leukocyte function and vascular tone, and why its deregulation contributes to invasion and metastasis, immunodeficiency and neurological disease. Classical members such as RHOA, RAC1 and CDC42 alternate between GTP-bound active and GDP-bound inactive states: numerous exchange factors of the DBL and DOCK families load GTP, a large family of GAPs accelerates hydrolysis, and GDIs such as ARHGDIA sequester the inactive protein in cytosol. Activated forms then engage effectors including ROCK kinases, PAKs, formins and WASP/WAVE complexes. Atypical relatives, among them the RND proteins, RHOH and RHOBTB members, lack appreciable hydrolysis and are regulated instead through expression and degradation.

RHOB cycles between GDP- and GTP-bound states to control actin organisation, membrane traffic and cell survival, and this switch is what the regulators and effectors here act upon. Unlike its close relatives RHOA and RHOC, RHOB carries a distinctive C-terminus whose prenylation and palmitoylation send it to endosomes as well as the plasma membrane, giving it roles in endocytic trafficking, receptor turnover and apoptosis alongside cytoskeletal control; these activities matter for immune cell behaviour, endothelial barrier function, angiogenesis and pulmonary gas exchange, and RHOB has been reported to act as both tumour suppressor and oncogene. Exchange factors such as NET1, ECT2 and the ARHGEF family load GTP, GAPs including DLC1 and ARHGAP1 accelerate hydrolysis, and a GDI sequesters the inactive form. Active RHOB engages ROCK1/2, PKN kinases, rhotekin and formins such as DIAPH1 to drive contractility and cell adhesion and migration.

RHOC is a small GTPase of the RHOA subfamily whose switching between GDP- and GTP-bound states controls actomyosin contractility, cell adhesion and directed migration; its overactivity is strongly associated with tumour cell invasion and metastatic spread. The RHOC GTPase cycle assembles the regulators that set that switch: numerous Dbl-family exchange factors such as ARHGEF1, ARHGEF11/12 and VAV2 load GTP, GAPs including ARHGAP1, DLC1 and STARD13 accelerate hydrolysis back to the inactive state, and ARHGDIA sequesters the prenylated GTPase in the cytosol between rounds of signalling. Active RHOC engages effectors that reshape the cytoskeleton — ROCK1 and ROCK2 kinases, formins such as DIAPH1 and FMNL2/3, protein kinase C-related kinases PKN1-3, citron kinase and the cytokinetic regulators ANLN and RACGAP1 — linking the cycle to stress fibre formation, cleavage furrow ingression, membrane trafficking and junctional organisation.

CDC42 GTPase cycle describes the switching of the Rho-family GTPase CDC42 between GDP- and GTP-bound states and the machinery that controls it, the core system by which cells establish and maintain polarity. Its output is directional actin assembly: apical membrane and lumen formation in epithelia, junction maturation, filopodia, phagocytic cups, neuronal growth cone guidance, and polarized membrane trafficking and secretion, including insulin release. Exchange factors of the DOCK, FGD, intersectin and VAV families load GTP, numerous RhoGAPs terminate signalling, and GDIs hold inactive CDC42 in the cytosol; active CDC42 engages PAK kinases, WASP/N-WASP with WIP partners to trigger Arp2/3 nucleation, formins, IQGAPs and the PAR6 polarity complex. Because many upstream exchange factors are oncogenes, deregulated cycling drives tumour cell invasion and metastasis, while loss of individual regulators causes intellectual disability and immunodeficiency.

CDC42 is the Rho-family GTPase that tells a cell which way is up: its cycling between GDP- and GTP-bound states sets cell polarity, drives filopodia and actin remodelling, and organizes apical membrane and lumen formation, junction maturation and directed migration. The switch is controlled by guanine nucleotide exchange factors such as the FGD, DOCK and intersectin families that load GTP, GAPs of the ARHGAP, SRGAP and DLC classes that accelerate hydrolysis, and GDIs that sequester the prenylated GTPase in the cytosol. Active CDC42 engages effectors including PAK kinases, WASP and N-WASP with their WIP partners, formins, IQGAP scaffolds and the polarity protein PAR6, linking it to Arp2/3-dependent actin nucleation, vesicle trafficking, adhesion and cell cycle progression. Because many upstream exchange factors are oncogenes, deregulated CDC42 cycling promotes tumour invasion and metastasis, and it also contributes to insulin secretion and diabetic kidney injury.

RAC1 is a small GTPase that switches between GDP- and GTP-bound states to control actin remodelling, lamellipodia formation, cell adhesion and migration, and the assembly of superoxide-generating NADPH oxidases. Its regulated cycling matters for neuronal development and dendritic spine morphogenesis underlying learning, phagocyte killing, contraction-stimulated glucose uptake in muscle, pancreatic beta-cell secretion, intestinal barrier repair, skin wound healing and vascular homeostasis; chronic hyperactivation, mutation or amplification of RAC1 is common in solid tumours, and bacterial toxins that cause diarrhoea target it directly. The cycle is set by DOCK- and Dbl-family exchange factors such as TIAM1, TRIO and VAV proteins that load GTP, by numerous ARHGAP-family and IQGAP-related GTPase-activating proteins that terminate signalling, and by RHO GDP-dissociation inhibitors that sequester the inactive form. Active RAC1 then engages PAK kinases, the WAVE/WASP actin nucleation machinery, PI3K subunits, and the NOX/p67phox-p47phox oxidase components.

RAC2 is the hematopoietic Rho-family GTPase, and its switching between GDP- and GTP-bound states governs how leukocytes crawl, adhere, degranulate and kill. The cycle matters most in neutrophils, where GTP-loaded RAC2 joins the phagocyte NADPH oxidase with the cytochrome subunits CYBA and CYBB and the cytosolic factors NCF1, NCF2 and NCF4 to generate the respiratory burst; loss-of-function and dominant RAC2 mutations cause primary immunodeficiency with poor neutrophil motility and microbicidal failure. It also controls adhesion and mobilisation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and mast cell migration. Activation is driven by exchange factors of the VAV, DOCK, TIAM1, TRIO and PREX1 families acting downstream of antigen, chemokine and integrin receptors; ARHGAP-family proteins and BCR/ABR terminate signalling, and ARHGDIA sequesters the inactive form. Effectors include PAK kinases, the WAVE regulatory complex and PI3K, linking the cycle to actin branching and lamellipodium formation.

RHOD is a Rho-family GTPase whose activity cycle shapes the actin cytoskeleton and the movement of endosomes and other vesicles through the cytoplasm. It is unusual among Rho proteins: it has high intrinsic nucleotide exchange and effectively auto-activates, so no exchange factors or dissociation inhibitors are known, and its off-switch depends instead on GTPase-activating proteins. Several such GAPs appear here alongside effectors that connect the switch to actin and membrane behaviour, including formins of the DIAPH family, WHAMM, the p21-activated kinases PAK5 and PAK6, and PI3-kinase regulatory subunits. Downstream consequences include actin-dependent positioning and motility of RAB7A-marked late endosomes, control of stress fibres and cell adhesion, and coupling to plexin receptors during guidance signalling. Through these outputs RHOD contributes to cell shape, migration and intracellular membrane traffic.

RHOQ (TC10), a CDC42-subfamily Rho GTPase, cycles between GDP- and GTP-bound states on exocytic vesicles and recycling endosomes, and its activity is needed for vesicles to fuse with the plasma membrane. This makes the RHOQ GTPase cycle the switch that couples membrane delivery to stimulus: in adipocytes it acts downstream of insulin to permit glucose transporter-containing vesicles to reach the cell surface, so glucose uptake depends on it, and it has also been linked to membrane addition during axon outgrowth. Exchange factors such as ARHGEF7 and ARHGEF9 load GTP, while a large set of RhoGAPs including ARHGAP1, DLC1 and SRGAP2 terminate signalling; unusually, the RhoGDIs that sequester most family members do not bind it. Active RHOQ engages effectors shared with CDC42 cluding PAK kinases, IQGAPs, CDC42EP septin-binding proteins and WASL, linking it to actin remodelling, trafficking machinery such as SNAP23 and VAMP3, and polarity proteins.

RHOH is an atypical Rho-family small GTPase of haematopoietic cells that works as a constitutively GTP-loaded adaptor rather than a switch, and the cycle described here is really about how much of it is present and where. It is needed for T cell development and for coupling the T cell receptor to downstream kinases, and loss-of-function mutations in humans cause T cell defects with susceptibility to beta-papillomavirus infection and the flat warts of epidermodysplasia verruciformis; the gene is also disrupted by mutation and translocation in lymphoma. Because RHOH lacks intrinsic hydrolytic activity and needs no exchange factor, regulation falls to guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors that sequester it in the cytosol, to phosphorylation by TCR-proximal kinases such as LCK and ZAP70, and to lysosomal degradation after receptor engagement. Associated GTPase-activating proteins and PAK and ROCK kinases act as candidate effectors linking it to cytoskeletal control.

RHOG is a RAC-related small GTPase that cycles between GDP- and GTP-bound states to control actin remodelling, and this cycle sets whether a cell can polarise, adhere and move. Cells depend on it for lamellipodium formation, phagocytic engulfment and leukocyte migration, and its overuse contributes to invadopodia and cancer cell invasiveness; it also feeds into VEGF-driven angiogenic responses. Activation is driven by exchange factors including TRIO, KALRN, VAV family proteins and ARHGEF26, while ARHGAP-family proteins accelerate GTP hydrolysis and RHOGDI proteins hold the inactive GTPase in the cytosol. Downstream, RHOG signals largely through the DOCK1-ELMO2 module to activate RAC1, engaging PAK kinases, the WAVE regulatory component CYFIP1 and PI3K to reorganise the cytoskeleton. Integrin and ephrin receptor inputs, together with trafficking and membrane partners, link the cycle to adhesion and endomembrane dynamics.

RHOJ is a small GTPase of the CDC42 subfamily, closely related to RHOQ and CDC42, and its activation cycle shapes the actin cytoskeleton during cell movement. The pathway matters most in endothelium, where RHOJ is highly expressed and controls lamellipodia formation, endothelial motility and tube formation, acting downstream of VEGF signalling to drive retinal and tumour angiogenesis; it also contributes to adipocyte differentiation and to cancer cell migration. Like other RHO proteins it alternates between GDP- and GTP-bound states, switched on by exchange factors such as ARHGEF7 and TRIO and switched off by GAPs of the ARHGAP family, with no GDI partner yet identified. In its active form it engages effectors that remodel actin and membranes, including PAK kinases, CDC42BPA/B, formins, WAS and WASL with WIPF2, and FNBP1 family BAR proteins, linking the switch to protrusion, vesicle traffic and polarity.

RHOBTB2 is an atypical Rho-family protein that, unlike conventional small GTPases, is not thought to toggle between GTP- and GDP-bound states; instead its tandem BTB and BACK domains let it work as a substrate adaptor for CUL3-based ubiquitin ligases, so its GTPase cycle is really a protein-degradation module. Through CUL3 it directs turnover of client proteins, restrains proliferation, favours apoptosis and contributes to vesicle traffic, and it is expressed most strongly in brain and heart. Loss of the gene, originally identified as deleted in breast cancer, is common across tumours, and missense changes that break the CUL3 interaction cause developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. The associated proteins point to its cellular setting: cytoskeletal and actin-regulatory components such as actin, actinin, drebrin, tropomodulin and twinfilin, the CCT chaperonin subunits, HSP90 with its cochaperone CDC37, the kinase STK38, and several RNA-binding and splicing factors.

Mitochondria must be delivered to the places in a cell that need ATP or calcium buffering — axon terminals, growth cones, immune synapses — and the RHOT2 GTPase cycle is part of how that positioning is controlled. RHOT2 (MIRO-2) sits in the outer mitochondrial membrane and, with its calcium-binding EF hands and tandem GTPase domains, acts as the receptor that links the organelle to cytoskeletal motors. Through the TRAK1 and TRAK2 adaptors it couples mitochondria to kinesin and dynein for bidirectional microtubule transport, while MYO19 provides actin-based movement; the mitofusins MFN1 and MFN2 tie this machinery to outer-membrane fusion and network shape. RAP1GDS1 acts as the nucleotide exchange activity, and no GAP is needed because intrinsic hydrolysis is fast. RHOT2 also localizes to peroxisomes and shapes their motility, and this transport machinery is disrupted in neurodegenerative disease.

RHOU GTPase cycle describes the regulation and effector engagement of RHOU (Wrch-1), an atypical Rho family GTPase that controls actin cytoskeletal remodelling, cell adhesion turnover and directed migration. Unlike canonical family members, RHOU exchanges nucleotide rapidly on its own and lacks appreciable hydrolysis, so it sits largely GTP-loaded and is governed instead by expression level, lipid modification and membrane localisation rather than by exchange factors; associated GAPs appear to act as effectors linking it to CDC42 and other Rho signalling. Downstream, PAK kinases, GIT/PIX adaptors, NCK and SRC couple RHOU to focal adhesion disassembly, JNK and PI3K-AKT activation, while partners such as PARD6A and VANGL1 tie it to cell polarity and planar polarity signalling. This output shapes embryonic morphogenesis, including cardiac and intestinal development, and contributes to epithelial migration and invasive behaviour in cancer.

RHOU, also called Wrch-1, is an atypical member of the Rho family, and its regulatory cycle differs from the classic switch: it exchanges nucleotide rapidly on its own and hydrolyses GTP poorly, so it sits largely in the active GTP-bound form without needing exchange factors. Control therefore falls to lipid-anchored membrane targeting, an autoinhibitory proline-rich N-terminus, and binding partners rather than to timed inactivation. Through effectors shared with CDC42 -- PAK kinases, GIT/ARHGEF adaptors, IQGAP1, and PI3K regulatory subunits together with SRC and NCK -- this cycle shapes actin and spectrin-based cytoskeletal organisation, focal adhesion turnover and cell migration, and feeds into JNK and AKT signalling. RHOU acts during embryonic development, contributing to cardiac and intestinal morphogenesis, and the presence of several RhoGAPs among its interactors suggests cross-talk with other Rho GTPases rather than simple inactivation.

RHOBTB1 is an atypical Rho-family protein that, unlike canonical small GTPases, is not thought to toggle between GTP- and GDP-bound states; its GTPase cycle instead describes a scaffolding module built from the GTPase domain plus tandem BTB domains and a C-terminal BACK domain. Through those BTB domains it engages cullin-3, acting as a substrate adaptor for ubiquitin ligase complexes, and the associated proteasome-pathway and COP9 signalosome components here point to regulated protein turnover as its main output. RHOBTB1 sits on early endosomes and helps shape endosomal-lysosomal architecture, consistent with partners such as the minus-end myosin MYO6 and cytoskeletal proteins vimentin and drebrin, alongside the Rho effector kinases ROCK1 and ROCK2. It is broadly expressed, with high levels in smooth muscle-rich and endocrine tissues, and contributes to a cascade controlling vascular tone and blood pressure; its loss in tumours suggests tumour-suppressive function.

RAC3 is a vertebrate-specific Rho-family GTPase closely related to RAC1 but concentrated in neurons, where its cycling between GDP- and GTP-bound states shapes actin-driven neurite outgrowth, growth cone dynamics and cortical development; loss-of-function and activating mutations cause intellectual disability with brain malformations, and overexpression drives proliferation, migration and invasion in tumours. The cycle itself is set by opposing regulators: exchange factors such as TIAM1, TRIO, VAV2 and PREX1 load GTP, a large family of GAPs including ARHGAP1, ARHGAP35 and SRGAP2 accelerate hydrolysis, and a GDI sequesters the inactive, prenylated pool in the cytosol. Active RAC3 engages effectors that remodel the cytoskeleton and membranes — the WAVE regulatory complex components WASF1/2, CYFIP1, NCKAP1 and ABI1/2 that nucleate branched actin through Arp2/3, PAK kinases, IRSp53-family membrane benders, and the NADPH oxidase subunits that generate superoxide — linking the pathway to cell shape, adhesion, motility and redox signalling.

RHOV, also called Chp, is an atypical Rho-family GTPase that appears constitutively active because of unusually fast intrinsic nucleotide exchange; no exchange factors or GTPase-activating proteins specific to it are known, so its nucleotide cycle is set largely by its own chemistry and by the effectors it engages. Expressed at low levels and prominent in embryonic tissue, it acts downstream of WNT signalling in neural crest formation and shapes cell adhesion by influencing E-cadherin and beta-catenin at adherens junctions. Effector partners here include PAK kinases, the mixed-lineage kinase MAP3K11 and the adaptor SH3RF1 feeding JNK activation, alongside GIT/ARHGEF7 complexes, PAR6 polarity proteins, NCK adaptors, IQGAP1 and spectrin and tropomyosin components that link the GTPase to actin and junctional cytoskeleton. Signalling through this route can drive apoptosis in some cells, and RHOV overexpression marks lung adenocarcinoma, where it behaves as an oncogene.

RHOT1 GTPase cycle describes the nucleotide-dependent switching of Miro-1, an atypical Rho-family GTPase anchored in the outer mitochondrial membrane that determines where mitochondria go inside a cell. It is the calcium- and nucleotide-sensitive adaptor that couples organelles to the cytoskeleton, and its failure is felt most acutely in neurons, where mitochondria must be delivered along long axons to synapses; disrupted Miro-dependent trafficking and turnover accompanies Parkinson's disease and other neurodegeneration, while raised RHOT1 is protective after ischaemic stroke. Loaded with GTP through exchange by RAP1GDS1, Miro-1 recruits the TRAK1 and TRAK2 adaptors that link kinesin and dynein motors to mitochondria, and the actin motor MYO19 for short-range positioning. The same machinery acts on peroxisomes and helps shape ER-mitochondria contact sites, tying organelle transport to fission, fusion and mitophagy. Its high intrinsic hydrolysis rate makes a GAP unnecessary.

Mitochondria must be delivered to the places in a cell that need ATP and calcium buffering, and the RHOT1 GTPase cycle is how they are attached to the cytoskeleton for that journey. RHOT1, also called MIRO-1, sits in the outer mitochondrial membrane with calcium-sensing and GTP-binding domains facing the cytosol, and switches between nucleotide states with high intrinsic hydrolysis activity; no GAP or GDI partner is required, while RAP1GDS1 acts as an exchange factor. Its effectors determine the outcome: the TRAK1 and TRAK2 adaptors couple mitochondria to kinesin and dynein for microtubule-based transport, prominently in axons, while MYO19 links them to actin. The same protein influences mitochondrial fission and fusion, peroxisome motility, and ER-mitochondria contact sites, and its clearance during damage-induced mitophagy connects this switch to neurodegenerative disease and to protection in ischemic injury.

NOTCH3 is the Notch family receptor most associated with vascular smooth muscle and pericytes, and its activation converts contact with a neighbouring cell's ligand into a direct change in gene transcription. Loss or mutation of this route disrupts mural cell identity and arterial wall integrity; dominant NOTCH3 mutations cause CADASIL, an inherited small-vessel disease of the brain. Signalling begins when DLL1, DLL4, JAG1 or JAG2, ubiquitinated by MIB and NEURL ligases on the sending cell, pull on the receptor and expose its S2 site. ADAM10 cleaves there, and the resulting membrane-tethered fragment is cut within the membrane by the gamma-secretase complex of presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN, freeing the intracellular domain to enter the nucleus and act as a transcription factor. Output is tuned negatively by WWP2-directed ubiquitination and lysosomal degradation, by TACC3 binding, and by EGFR-mediated phosphorylation, while YBX1 offers a ligand-independent stimulus.

When NOTCH3 is cleaved at the membrane, its released intracellular domain travels to the nucleus and converts a contact-dependent signal into a change in gene expression. There it joins the DNA-binding factor RBPJ together with a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1, MAML2 or MAML3) and recruits histone acetyltransferases such as CREBBP/EP300 and the GCN5/PCAF pair, switching RBPJ-bound promoters from repression to activation. Direct targets include the HES and HEY family repressors, which keep progenitors undifferentiated, the pre-T-cell receptor chain PTCRA during thymocyte development, FABP7 in radial glia supporting neuronal migration, the semaphorin receptor PLXND1, and PBX1, DLGAP5 and WWC1. Unlike NOTCH1, NOTCH3 favours single rather than paired RBPJ sites. Sustained output from this transcriptional module drives T-cell lymphomagenesis and is amplified in ovarian cancer, while NOTCH3 signalling elsewhere maintains vascular smooth muscle identity.

NOTCH4 is the endothelial-biased member of the Notch receptor family, and signalling through it shapes blood vessel formation and patterning, controlling arterial-venous identity, sprouting behaviour and endothelial survival. Ligands DLL4 and JAG1 on neighbouring cells trigger ADAM10 shedding and gamma-secretase cleavage by the presenilin-nicastrin-APH1-PEN2 complex, releasing the intracellular domain, which enters the nucleus and joins RBPJ and a Mastermind-like coactivator with p300/CBP to switch on HES and HEY repressors, VEGFR3 (FLT4) and smooth-muscle actin. Output is limited on several fronts: AKT1 phosphorylation holds the receptor in the cytoplasm, and FBXW7-directed ubiquitination feeds the activated domain to the proteasome, which explains the large complement of proteasome subunits and SCF components here. NOTCH4 can also restrain NOTCH1 maturation in the same cell. Aberrant activation, first found through proviral insertion at this locus, drives mammary tumorigenesis, anti-estrogen resistance in breast cancer and progression of gastric and head-and-neck carcinomas.

NOTCH4 is the Notch receptor most associated with endothelium and vascular development, and once its intracellular domain is released it acts directly as a transcriptional regulator in the nucleus. Bound to the DNA-binding factor RBPJ together with a mastermind-like coactivator and histone acetyltransferases such as CREBBP, EP300 and the GCN5/PCAF pair, it converts RBPJ from a repressive to an activating complex. Targets include the canonical Notch effectors HES1, HES5, HEY1 and HEY2, which act as repressors of differentiation programmes, plus the lymphatic and angiogenic receptor FLT4 and smooth muscle alpha actin, linking this arm of Notch signalling to arterial, venous and lymphatic specification and mural cell identity. The released domain also binds activated SMAD3 and dampens TGF-beta-driven transcription, a crosstalk that shapes endothelial responses and, when deregulated, contributes to vascular malformation and mammary tumourigenesis.

NOTCH4 is the Notch receptor of the vascular endothelium, and its activation converts contact with a neighbouring cell into a transcriptional change that shapes arterial identity, sprouting and vessel remodelling. Ligands presented by adjacent endothelial cells, DLL4 and JAG1, engage NOTCH4 and trigger the standard two-step proteolysis: ADAM10 removes the ectodomain, and the gamma-secretase complex built from presenilin, nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 cuts within the membrane to liberate the NOTCH4 intracellular domain. That fragment travels from cytosol to nucleus and works as a transcription factor, with 14-3-3 protein binding contributing to its handling en route. Notably, the ligand response is seen in endothelial cells rather than fibroblast or kidney lines, implying context-dependent co-factors. Dysregulated NOTCH4 signalling is linked to arteriovenous malformation and to tumour angiogenesis.

Detection of double-stranded RNA by the endosomal receptor TLR3 does more than switch on interferon genes: through its adaptor TRIF (TICAM1) it can also commit the infected cell to death, removing a replication niche from the virus. This TLR3-driven, TRIF-dependent death programme runs through a complex of RIPK1, FADD and caspase-8, which normally executes apoptosis and, by cleaving RIPK1 and RIPK3, actively restrains the alternative route. When caspase-8 activity is lost or blocked, as happens with many viral caspase inhibitors, RIPK1 and RIPK3 instead assemble a necrosome and the cell undergoes necroptosis, a lytic and inflammatory outcome. The two branches suppress one another, so the balance between them sets whether antiviral cell death is immunologically silent or releases damage signals; the same wiring operates downstream of TLR4, TNF receptors and Fas.

TICAM1-dependent activation of IRF3/IRF7 is the branch of Toll-like receptor signalling that turns detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial LPS into type I interferon production. It gives cells their first line of antiviral defence: without it, TLR3- and TLR4-driven interferon-beta induction fails and viral replication proceeds unchecked, while excessive activity contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity. Engaged receptors recruit the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), which with TRAF3 and its ubiquitin-dependent scaffolding assembles and activates the IKK-related kinases TBK1 and IKBKE. These kinases phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7, allowing them to dimerise, enter the nucleus and transactivate interferon and interferon-stimulated genes. TANK and OPTN act as adaptors and brakes on kinase output, and PI3K-Akt input is required for full IRF3 phosphorylation and promoter binding. TBK1 and IKBKE are partially redundant here.

Detection of viral double-stranded RNA by TLR3, and of bacterial LPS by TLR4, converges on the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1) to switch on type I interferon production, the first line of antiviral defence at the cell surface and in endosomes. TICAM1 recruits TRAF3, whose ubiquitin-dependent scaffolding assembles and activates the related kinases TBK1 and IKKε; these phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7, allowing them to dimerize, enter the nucleus and drive IFNβ and interferon-stimulated genes. TANK and OPTN act as modulators that restrain or tune kinase output, and polyubiquitin contributed by UBB, UBC and ribosomal ubiquitin precursors supplies the non-degradative chains required for complex assembly. TBK1 and IKKε are partly redundant, so loss of both abolishes IRF3 activation. Defects here blunt interferon responses and predispose to severe viral infection, while unchecked signalling contributes to interferon-driven autoinflammation.

Toll-like receptor 3 senses double-stranded RNA and signals through the adaptor TICAM1 (TRIF) to launch inflammatory gene expression, and this step is where that signal is converted into kinase activity. TRAF6, acting as a ubiquitin ligase with E2 partners, builds Lys63-linked polyubiquitin chains that are read by the ubiquitin-binding regulatory subunits TAB2 and TAB3; these chains cluster and allosterically activate the kinase MAP3K7 (TAK1) held with TAB1. Activated TAK1 then phosphorylates the IKK subunits, driving IkB degradation and NF-kB nuclear entry, and feeds the MKK3/6 and MKK4/7 branches to switch on p38 and JNK. The output is transcription of type I interferon-associated and proinflammatory cytokine genes during viral infection. Notably, the polyubiquitin chains can act unanchored rather than covalently attached, making ubiquitin here a signalling ligand rather than a degradation tag.

Interleukin-36 signalling is an epithelial alarm system: keratinocytes and other barrier epithelia release IL36 alpha, beta and gamma on injury or microbial exposure, driving local production of chemokines, antimicrobial peptides and neutrophil recruitment. The three agonists engage a receptor formed by IL1RL2 together with the shared accessory chain IL1RAP, assembling a Toll/IL-1 receptor complex that signals through MyD88-dependent NF-kB and MAP kinase activation in the manner of other IL-1 family cytokines. Restraint is built in: the secreted antagonist IL36RN and the related IL1F10 bind the receptor without productive signalling, and the agonists require N-terminal proteolytic processing before they become potent. Loss-of-function mutations in IL36RN remove that brake and cause generalised pustular psoriasis, and the axis is implicated more broadly in plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis and inflammatory disease of the gut and airway.

Interleukin-33 signaling is how tissues announce that cells have been damaged. IL33 is an interleukin-1 family alarmin held constitutively in the nuclei of endothelial and epithelial cells, bound to heterochromatin, and released passively when those cells are injured or die rather than by regulated secretion. Once extracellular it engages the receptor IL1RL1 (ST2) together with the accessory co-receptor IL1RAP, triggering an IL-1-like signalling cascade that activates mast cells, group 2 innate lymphoid cells, eosinophils and Th2 lymphocytes. This axis drives type 2 immunity and tissue repair, and its overactivity underlies asthma, allergic inflammation and fibrotic remodelling, while a soluble ST2 variant lacking transmembrane and cytoplasmic regions sequesters the cytokine and serves as a cardiovascular biomarker. Inflammatory proteases such as cathepsin G and neutrophil elastase cleave the N-terminus, altering potency and blocking nuclear re-entry.

Interleukin-33 signalling is how a tissue reports its own damage. IL33 is an IL-1 family alarmin made constitutively by endothelial and epithelial cells and stored in the nucleus bound to chromatin, and it is not actively secreted; necrosis or mechanical injury releases it, so its appearance outside a cell is itself the danger signal. Extracellular IL33 binds the receptor IL1RL1 (ST2) and recruits the shared accessory co-receptor IL1RAP, forming a complex that drives IL-1-type inflammatory signalling toward NF- fB-dependent gene expression. The main responders are type 2 immune cells, including mast cells, ILC2s and Th2 cells, which makes this axis a driver of allergic airway inflammation, asthma and helminth defence, and a contributor to cardiac and mucosal injury responses. Inflammatory proteases trim the N-terminus and alter potency, and a soluble ST2 variant lacking the transmembrane region acts as a decoy.

Noncanonical activation of NOTCH3 describes how the NOTCH3 receptor can be switched on without a classical DLL or JAG ligand on a neighbouring cell, instead responding to the secreted RNA-binding protein YBX1. This matters in inflammation and vascular remodelling: mesangial cells and monocytes release YBX1 as an extracellular mitogen, and NOTCH3 is the Notch paralogue that specifies vascular smooth muscle and pericyte identity, with its mutation causing CADASIL and its overactivity driving proliferative disease. YBX1 binding to NOTCH3 triggers regulated intramembrane proteolysis by the gamma-secretase complex, whose presenilin catalytic subunit acts with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 to release the intracellular domain. That fragment moves to the nucleus and turns on Notch target transcription, coupling an inflammatory extracellular signal directly to a cell-fate and growth programme normally reserved for cell-contact-dependent signalling.

NOTCH3 signalling is usually switched on by Delta-like or Jagged ligands presented by a neighbouring cell, but it can also be triggered without them. In this noncanonical route, extracellular YBX1 — an RNA-binding protein normally involved in mRNA processing that is released by mesangial cells and monocytes during inflammation — binds the NOTCH3 receptor and acts as a soluble mitogen. Ligand engagement licenses cleavage by the gamma-secretase complex, whose catalytic presenilin subunit works with nicastrin, APH1 and PEN-2 to release the NOTCH3 intracellular domain, which travels to the nucleus and turns on NOTCH3 target genes. Because NOTCH3 governs vascular smooth muscle and pericyte identity, this inflammation-linked input offers a way for injury signals to drive proliferative, fibrotic remodelling in the kidney and vessel wall independently of cell-cell contact.

Estrogen-dependent gene expression is the transcriptional program switched on when estrogen binds its nuclear receptors, and it accounts for much of the hormone's control over reproductive tissue, bone density, and lipid and metabolic physiology. It also defines hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer, where sustained receptor output drives proliferation and is the target of antiestrogen and aromatase therapy. Ligand-bound ESR1 dimers act at estrogen response elements or are tethered through partners such as SP1, AP-1 factors and RUNX1, with pioneer factors FOXA1 and GATA3 opening chromatin beforehand to license binding at distal enhancers looped to promoters by cohesin. Recruited coactivators including NCOA1-3, EP300/CREBBP, CARM1 and PRMT1 deposit activating histone marks and assemble general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II, while KDM1A, HDAC1 and NRIP1 impose repression. Outputs include TFF1, GREB1, CCND1, MYC and progesterone receptor, with microRNA-linked Argonaute complexes tuning the response.

Estrogen controls growth and differentiation of the breast, uterus, bone and other tissues by switching on defined transcriptional programmes, and this ligand-dependent gene expression is the route by which the hormone acts. Estrogen-bound ESR1 dimers bind estrogen response elements directly or are tethered through partners such as SP1, AP-1 components and RUNX1, and pioneer factors including FOXA1 and GATA3 open chromatin beforehand to determine which sites are usable. Recruited coactivators such as NCOA1-3, the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300, arginine methyltransferases CARM1 and PRMT1, and the Mediator subunit MED1 deposit active chromatin marks and assemble general transcription factors with RNA polymerase II, while HDAC1 and KDM1A and corepressors such as NRIP1 and TLE3 restrain output; cohesin supports enhancer-promoter looping. Target genes include TFF1, GREB1, PGR, MYC and CCND1, and the same circuitry drives hormone-dependent breast cancer and is the target of endocrine therapy.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and the D-series resolvins are among the lipid mediators that do it: they are made from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid and act on immune cells to halt neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, and return tissue to homeostasis without immunosuppression. Failure to generate these pro-resolving signals leaves inflammation smouldering, a state linked to chronic airway, vascular and metabolic disease. In the lipoxygenase route described here, DHA is oxygenated at carbon 17 to a 17(S)-hydroperoxide, reduced by a glutathione peroxidase, and then acted on by 5-lipoxygenase to give epoxide intermediates that are hydrolysed — with epoxide hydrolase activity of LTA4H contributing — to the 17(S)-epimers RvD1 through RvD6. Dehydrogenation by HPGD begins their inactivation, limiting how long the signal persists. The same enzymes serve pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis, so substrate availability shapes the switch.

Acute inflammation must be actively switched off, and the D-series resolvins and related mediators made from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid are among the signals that do it. Formed at sites of injury or infection where DHA arrives with edema fluid and endothelial cells interact with leukocytes, these specialized pro-resolving mediators limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and return tissue to homeostasis without immunosuppression; their inadequate production is associated with chronic, non-resolving inflammation. Synthesis begins with oxygenation of DHA by lipoxygenases such as ALOX15, ALOX5 and ALOX12, by cyclooxygenase-2 (including its aspirin-acetylated form), or by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, followed by epoxide hydrolysis, peroxide reduction, glutathione conjugation and dehydrogenation steps that dictate which resolvin, protectin or maresin-type product results.

Biosynthesis of specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs) generates the lipid signals that actively end an inflammatory episode rather than merely dampening it, and its failure leaves inflammation to smoulder into chronic disease of the vessel wall, joint, gut, airway and brain. As acute inflammation matures, leukocytes undergo a lipid mediator class switch: the same enzymatic machinery that made leukotrienes and prostaglandins is redirected onto polyunsaturated fatty acids released by phospholipase A2 to yield lipoxins from arachidonate and resolvins, protectins and maresins from the omega-3 fatty acids EPA, DHA and DPA. Lipoxygenases (ALOX5 with its activating protein, ALOX12, ALOX15), cyclooxygenase-2 including its aspirin-acetylated form, cytochrome P450 epoxygenases, epoxide hydrolases, LTA4H, LTC4S and dehydrogenases such as HPGD and PTGR1 supply successive oxygenation, hydrolysis and reduction steps. The products stop neutrophil recruitment, promote nonphlogistic macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, and drive tissue regeneration back to homeostasis.

Acute inflammation must be actively switched off, and the biosynthesis of specialized proresolving mediators is how that happens: lipoxins, resolvins, protectins and maresins are made from arachidonic acid and the ω-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA once the initial burst of leukotrienes and prostaglandins has done its work. These mediators stop further neutrophil recruitment, recruit monocytes, and drive non-inflammatory clearance of apoptotic neutrophils by macrophages, so tissue returns to homeostasis instead of drifting into the chronic inflammation behind atherosclerosis, arthritis, asthma and inflammatory bowel disease. The chemistry is oxygenation followed by hydrolysis, reduction and further oxidation: lipoxygenases ALOX5 with its partner ALOX5AP, ALOX12 and ALOX15 install hydroperoxides, LTA4H and LTC4S process epoxide intermediates, cytochromes P450 and EPHX2 diversify products, and PTGS2 — particularly when aspirin-acetylated — yields epimeric forms.

Acute inflammation does not simply fade; it is actively switched off by lipid mediators made from omega-3 fatty acids, and the E-series resolvins are the branch derived from eicosapentaenoic acid. These specialized pro-resolving mediators limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, and restore tissue homeostasis, so weak resolution favours persistent inflammation of the kind seen in arthritis, colitis and atherosclerosis. Synthesis begins at sites of inflammation where endothelial cells meet leukocytes: cyclooxygenase-2, particularly when acetylated by aspirin, or cytochrome P450 activity oxygenates EPA at C18, after which lipoxygenases such as ALOX5 and ALOX15 act, and epoxide hydrolysis by LTA4H, peroxide reduction by GPX4, and dehydrogenation by HPGD determine whether RvE1, RvE2 or RvE3 results. The same enzymes otherwise make pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, so substrate supply shapes the outcome.

Biosynthesis of protectins produces a family of specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid, providing the signals that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blunting it. Protectin D1 and its neural counterpart neuroprotectin D1 limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, and protect neurons and retinal pigment epithelium from oxidative injury; without such mediators, acute inflammation fails to resolve and becomes chronic tissue damage. Synthesis begins when 15-lipoxygenase oxygenates DHA, and the resulting epoxide intermediate is hydrolysed, with leukotriene A4 hydrolase and cytochrome P450 activities contributing to the conversion steps; a second lipoxygenase route yields protectin DX, and aspirin-acetylated cyclooxygenase supports an epimeric form. Induction of 15-lipoxygenase marks the class switch away from prostaglandin and thromboxane production toward resolution.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and protectins are among the omega-3-derived lipid mediators that do it. Made from docosahexaenoic acid, these specialized pro-resolving mediators limit leukocyte recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, and protect tissue from collateral damage; when generated in neural tissue the principal species is termed neuroprotectin D1, which guards retinal and brain cells against oxidative and inflammatory injury. Synthesis begins with 15-lipoxygenase acting on DHA to give an epoxide intermediate that is hydrolysed to protectin D1, while a second lipoxygenase reaction yields the double dioxygenation product protectin DX. Aspirin-acetylated cyclooxygenase and cytochrome P450 activity route the pathway toward epimeric forms. Induction of 15-lipoxygenase marks the handoff from prostaglandin and thromboxane production to resolution, and failure of this switch leaves inflammation unresolved and chronic.

Maresin biosynthesis converts the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid into specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators that actively switch off inflammation rather than merely blocking its start. Named for macrophage mediators resolving inflammation, maresins limit neutrophil influx, promote efferocytosis of dying cells, and act on vascular smooth muscle and endothelium to blunt TNF-driven monocyte adhesion and reactive oxygen species production, largely by dampening NF-kB-dependent transcription; they also confer analgesia and support tissue repair. Lipoxygenase action on DHA generates epoxide and hydroperoxide intermediates that are further processed by cytochrome P450 enzymes and by soluble epoxide hydrolase (EPHX2), which opens epoxides to dihydroxy products and thereby shapes the balance of mediators formed. Related 14,21-dihydroxy-DHA species arise through transcellular metabolism by leukocytes and platelets and can restore the reparative behaviour of macrophages in diabetic wounds. Failure of this resolution programme leaves inflammation chronic.

Inflammation does not simply fade out; it is actively switched off by lipid mediators made from long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids, and docosapentaenoic acid is one of the substrates feeding that programme. Conversion of the n-3 and n-6 isomers of this C22:5 fatty acid into mono-, di- and tri-hydroxylated products yields specialised pro-resolving mediators structurally and functionally parallel to the resolvins, protectins and maresins derived from DHA and EPA. Lipoxygenases acting at the 5-, 12- and 15-positions, together with cyclooxygenase-2 in its aspirin-modified mode, introduce the oxygen atoms, with neutrophils and macrophages as the principal producing cells. The resulting mediators limit neutrophil recruitment and promote clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, so that resolution is completed rather than allowed to persist as chronic inflammation and tissue damage.

Inflammation does not simply fade out; it is actively switched off by specialized pro-resolving lipid mediators, and the E-series 18(S)-resolvins are the branch of that programme derived from the omega-3 fatty acid eicosapentaenoic acid. These mediators limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and help restore tissue homeostasis, which is part of why dietary fish oil and low-dose aspirin have anti-inflammatory effects. Oxygenation of EPA at carbon 18 in the S configuration, by cytochrome P450 activity or by aspirin-acetylated cyclooxygenase-2 acting as a lipoxygenase, generates the precursor; further lipoxygenation by ALOX5 or ALOX15, peroxide reduction, epoxide hydrolysis by LTA4H and dehydrogenation by HPGD then determine whether RvE1, RvE2 or RvE3 is produced. The same enzymes otherwise make leukotrienes, so substrate supply shifts the balance between initiating and resolving inflammation.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and the D-series resolvins are among the lipid mediators that do it — promoting macrophage clearance of apoptotic neutrophils, blocking further neutrophil recruitment, and restoring tissue homeostasis after infection or injury. This route makes the 17(R) epimers of RvD1-6 from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid, starting from cyclooxygenase-2 that has been acetylated by aspirin, which diverts the enzyme from prostaglandin synthesis to 17(R)-hydroxylation of DHA. That intermediate is then handled by 5-lipoxygenase to form epoxide and hydroperoxy species, with a peroxidase step and hydrolase activity generating the individual resolvins. Because the epimeric products resist rapid inactivation, this chemistry accounts for part of aspirin's anti-inflammatory benefit beyond simple prostaglandin blockade, and failure of such pro-resolving signalling leaves inflammation unresolved and chronic.

Interleukin-2 signaling is the growth and survival input that antigen-stimulated T cells use to expand, and the same input that keeps the immune system from turning on itself. Originally named T cell growth factor, IL-2 also sensitizes activated T cells to activation-induced cell death and sustains regulatory T cells, so loss of the cytokine or its receptor produces lymphoproliferation and autoimmunity rather than simple immunodeficiency. Activated T cells upregulate the high-affinity alpha chain, which captures IL-2 and recruits the constitutively expressed beta and common gamma chains; the gamma chain is shared with the IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21 receptors, and its mutation causes X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency. Receptor-associated JAK1 and JAK3 phosphorylate tyrosines on the beta chain tail, recruiting SHC1 toward MAPK and PI3K signalling and phosphorylating STAT5A and STAT5B, which dimerize and drive proliferative gene expression in the nucleus.

Interleukin-12 signalling is how dendritic cells, macrophages and neutrophils instruct lymphocytes to mount a type 1 response. The cytokine is a p35/p40 heterodimer encoded by IL12A and IL12B, and it drives naive CD4 T cells toward the Th1 fate while boosting the cytotoxic output of NK cells and CD8 T cells; the interferon gamma it elicits makes this axis central to defence against intracellular bacteria and mycobacteria, and it also carries anti-angiogenic activity. Signalling runs through an IL12RB1/IL12RB2 receptor pair related to gp130, with receptor-associated TYK2, JAK1 and JAK2 phosphorylating STAT4 as the principal transcriptional output; IL10 restrains the response. Loss of receptor or JAK function underlies susceptibility to disseminated mycobacterial and salmonella infection. Accompanying cytoskeletal, chaperone and redox proteins reflect the activated-lymphocyte state that IL-12 induces.

Interleukin-1 signaling converts a danger signal into inflammation. IL1A and IL1B released from activated myeloid cells engage IL1R1, which recruits the accessory chain IL1RAP to form a competent receptor; the natural antagonist IL1RN and the non-signaling decoy IL1R2 set the threshold, and blocking this axis is the basis of therapy for autoinflammatory syndromes, gout and rheumatoid arthritis. The receptor's cytoplasmic TIR domain nucleates MYD88, IRAK4 and IRAK1, with IRAK3 acting as a brake and Pellino ligases plus the UBE2N/UBE2V1 pair building K63 ubiquitin chains on the complex. TRAF6 then recruits TAK1 with TAB1/2/3, activating the IKK complex so that phosphorylated IkappaB is degraded by the proteasome and NF-kappaB p65/p50 enters the nucleus, while parallel MKK3/4/6 and TPL2 branches drive p38, JNK and ERK. Output is transcription of cytokines, chemokines and acute-phase genes such as SAA1, coordinating fever, leukocyte recruitment and tissue remodeling.

Interleukin-23 signaling sustains the inflammatory T cell programmes that defend mucosal surfaces and, when unchecked, drive autoimmune disease. The cytokine is a heterodimer of IL23A paired with IL12B, the subunit it shares with IL-12, and is released mainly by activated macrophages and dendritic cells in skin, gut mucosa and lung. It acts through a receptor built from IL23R and the shared IL12RB1 chain, expressed on memory T cells, NK cells and monocytes. Engagement activates JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate the receptor to create docking sites for STAT3 and STAT4; STAT3 in particular drives IL-17 production and the maintenance of Th17 cells, alongside interferon-gamma induction and proliferation of memory T cells. Excess signalling underlies psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease and arthritis, which is why this axis is targeted therapeutically by antibodies against the p19 and p40 subunits.

Interleukin-27 signalling lets antigen-presenting cells restrain an ongoing immune response: the cytokine both promotes early type 1 differentiation and, more prominently, dampens inflammation by limiting Th17 development and inducing IL-10-producing regulatory T cells, which is why its loss tends toward immunopathology and unchecked tissue damage during infection. The active cytokine is a heterodimer of the p28 subunit with EBI3, secreted mainly by activated macrophages and dendritic cells, and it engages a receptor pairing the private chain IL27RA with the shared gp130 subunit used by IL-6-family cytokines. Receptor assembly activates associated JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT3; the balance between these two transcription factors largely determines whether the response is inflammatory or suppressive. Calnexin contributes to folding and quality control of the subunits in the endoplasmic reticulum before secretion.

Interleukin-21 signaling links follicular helper T cells, NKT and TH17 cells to the lymphocytes they instruct, driving germinal centre B cell differentiation into plasma cells and memory cells, sustaining CD8 T and NK cell effector function, and shaping TH17 responses. Its output matters clinically at both extremes: loss of the receptor causes a combined immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses, while excess IL21 drives autoantibody production and autoimmunity. The cytokine engages IL21R paired with the common gamma chain shared by the IL2 and IL4 receptor families; the gamma chain is needed for full signalling capacity. Receptor-associated JAK1 and JAK3 then phosphorylate STAT proteins, with STAT1 and STAT3 dominating in T cells, NK cells and macrophages, STAT4 contributing in NK cells, and STAT5A/STAT5B responses prominent in B-lineage cells. Cell-type-specific STAT usage explains the pleiotropy of a single cytokine.

MECP2 reads methylated and hydroxymethylated cytosine in neuronal DNA and translates that mark into stable patterns of gene expression, and this event describes what happens when that reading fails. Missense changes in its methyl-CpG binding domain, roughly between residues 90 and 162, leave the protein intact but unable to engage 5-hydroxymethylcytosine-containing DNA, so target loci are no longer bound and their transcription escapes normal restraint. Because 5hmC is abundant in mature neurons and enriched at actively regulated genes, loss of this interaction disproportionately affects the brain, where MECP2 supports synaptic maturation and activity-dependent transcription. Mutations of this kind underlie Rett syndrome, an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder in which early development appears normal before acquired skills regress. The pathway illustrates how chromatin-mark recognition, rather than enzymatic activity, can be the point of disease.

Neuronal activity normally leaves a mark on the chromatin reader MECP2: depolarization raises calcium, calmodulin-activated CaMKIV phosphorylates MECP2 at threonine 308, and this modification tunes MECP2's interaction with transcriptional corepressor machinery so that activity-dependent genes can be induced. Loss of phosphorylation at T308 describes what happens when Rett syndrome-associated missense mutations near this site prevent the modification from being installed, uncoupling MECP2 from the signals that report synaptic activity. The consequence is misregulated activity-dependent transcription in neurons, contributing to the arrested development, loss of acquired speech and motor regression characteristic of MECP2-related disease. The kinases represented here place the event downstream of calcium/calmodulin signalling, with cAMP-dependent protein kinase also acting on MECP2, and link neuronal excitation to epigenetic control of gene expression rather than to DNA methylation itself.

MECP2 reads methylated CpG DNA and translates that mark into transcriptional repression by recruiting the NCoR/SMRT corepressor complex, whose core includes NCOR1 or NCOR2 as scaffolds together with HDAC3, GPS2 and the TBL1X/TBL1XR1 subunits that deliver histone deacetylase activity to chromatin. This bridging function is required for normal neuronal maturation and synaptic gene regulation, and it is the activity destroyed by missense mutations clustered in the MECP2 transcriptional repression domain. Such changes leave DNA binding intact but abolish the interaction with the corepressor, so methylated targets escape deacetylation and repression. The consequence is Rett syndrome, an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder marked by regression of speech and hand use after an initially normal infancy. The pathway illustrates how a single protein-protein interface couples DNA methylation to chromatin-modifying enzymes and how its loss produces disease without loss of the protein itself.

MECP2 reads DNA methylation and translates it into transcriptional repression in neurons, and the loss of its ability to bind 5mC-DNA is a direct molecular cause of Rett syndrome. Missense changes clustered in the methyl-CpG binding domain leave the protein intact but unable to recognise methylated CpG, including the methylated CpA marks abundant in brain, so it no longer docks at target promoters. Because MECP2 normally recruits a corepressor complex containing SIN3A and the histone deacetylase HDAC1, failure of binding leaves chromatin at those sites hyperacetylated and target genes inappropriately expressed; BDNF is the best-studied example of a neuronal gene whose activity-dependent regulation depends on this interaction. The consequence is disordered synaptic maturation and activity-dependent gene expression rather than neuronal loss, which is why the disorder is progressive yet potentially reversible in principle.

MECP2 reads methylated DNA and tunes neuronal gene expression, and the layers that set how much of it is present and what it does are the subject here. Loss or misdosage of MECP2 causes Rett syndrome, so the controls on its level and activity matter as much as the protein itself. Its mRNA is silenced post-transcriptionally by miR-132 acting through Argonaute-containing silencing complexes, placing MECP2 downstream of activity-dependent neurotrophin signalling. Activity also acts directly: calcium-dependent kinases including CaMK IV and PKA, along with HIPK2 and AURKB, phosphorylate MECP2 at distinct sites that shift its chromatin association and its choice of partner. Through those partners MECP2 can repress, via the NCoR/SMRT and SIN3A complexes with HDAC1/2, or activate together with CREB1. Interactions with FOXG1, huntingtin and the lamin B receptor further shape its function and nuclear positioning.

The methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2 sets the transcriptional tone of maturing neurons, and one arm of that control is the direct regulation of the receptors, channels and transporters through which neurons sense and respond to their surroundings. Loss of MECP2 function causes Rett syndrome, in which apparently normal early development gives way to regression, and duplication of the gene is equally damaging, so the dosage of these target genes matters. Targets here include the AMPA receptor subunit GRIA2 and NMDA receptor subunits GRIN2A and GRIN2B, which shape excitatory synaptic transmission and its developmental switch; opioid receptors OPRK1 and OPRM1; the receptor tyrosine kinase MET and NOTCH1; the cation channel TRPC3 and glucose transporter SLC2A3. MECP2 acts with CREB1 and, through SIN3A and the histone deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, can repress as well as activate. Tyrosine phosphatases PTPN1 and PTPN4 provide indirect control of receptor kinase signalling.

MECP2 is the methyl-CpG-binding protein whose loss causes Rett syndrome, and much of its neuronal function comes down to setting the expression level of secreted signalling molecules that shape synapses and circuit activity. Here it governs transcription of neuronal ligands: the neurotrophin BDNF, which supports synaptic maturation and activity-dependent plasticity; corticotropin-releasing hormone, tied to stress responsiveness and anxiety behaviour; the neuropeptide somatostatin, marking an inhibitory interneuron population; and the Notch ligand DLL1, which influences neural progenitor fate. MECP2 can act in either direction at these promoters, recruiting the SIN3A corepressor with HDAC1 to deacetylate histones and dampen transcription, or cooperating with CREB1 to drive activity-dependent expression. Because ligand dosage rather than presence is what is tuned, both loss and duplication of MECP2 produce neurodevelopmental disease, linking chromatin readout of DNA methylation to synaptic and neuroendocrine output.

MECP2 is a methyl-CpG-binding nuclear protein that tunes neuronal gene expression, and one of its outputs is the level of other transcriptional regulators. By acting on the promoters of factors such as CREB1 and MEF2C, together with the splicing regulator RBFOX1 and the nuclear receptor PPARG, it sets the transcriptional tone for activity-dependent neuronal maturation, synapse refinement and dendritic complexity. MECP2 can both repress and activate these targets depending on context, so its loss does not silence a single gene but shifts a whole regulatory layer. That dependency explains why MECP2 mutation causes Rett syndrome, in which early development appears normal before acquired speech and motor skills regress, and why duplication of the locus is equally damaging. The PPARG link extends its reach beyond neurons to adipocyte differentiation and metabolic gene programmes.

Inhibitory neurotransmission depends on a steady supply of GABA, and the methyl-CpG-binding protein MECP2 helps set that supply by directly and positively driving transcription of the two glutamate decarboxylase genes, GAD1 and GAD2, whose products convert glutamate to GABA. This link places MECP2, a reader of DNA methylation that tunes neuronal gene expression, upstream of the excitation-inhibition balance of cortical and subcortical circuits. Loss of MECP2 from GABA-releasing neurons lowers GABA content and reproduces much of the Rett syndrome phenotype, including breathing irregularity, stereotypies and motor and social deficits, while its loss specifically in parvalbumin interneurons blunts sensory-evoked responses and impairs motor learning along with maturation of interneuron membrane properties and expression of parvalbumin, GABA-A receptor subunits and potassium channels. The pathway thus connects epigenetic transcriptional control to inhibitory circuit function and neurodevelopmental disease.

Inflammation does not simply fade out; it is actively switched off by specialized pro-resolving mediators, and this route builds the E-series resolvins RvE1, RvE2 and RvE3 from the omega-3 fatty acid eicosapentaenoic acid in the 18(R) configuration. These lipids restrain neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and help return inflamed tissue to homeostasis, which is a large part of why dietary fish oil and low-dose aspirin have anti-inflammatory effects. An initial 18-hydroxylation, attributable to cytochrome P450 activity or to aspirin-acetylated cyclooxygenase-2 acting as a lipoxygenase, is followed by lipoxygenase steps through ALOX5 and ALOX15, peroxide reduction by the glutathione peroxidase GPX4, and epoxide hydrolysis by LTA4H, the same enzyme set that otherwise generates leukotrienes. Impaired resolution favours chronic, non-healing inflammation.

Liver X receptor signalling through NR1H2 (LXRβ) and NR1H3 (LXRα) lets cells sense how much cholesterol they hold and respond by getting rid of the excess. Oxysterols formed in proportion to cellular cholesterol bind these nuclear receptors, which act as permissive heterodimers with RXR on response elements in target genes. Activation drives efflux transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1 toward HDL, biliary sterol export via ABCG5/ABCG8, lipoprotein remodelling (APOE, CETP, PLTP), and the MYLIP/IDOL route that degrades LDL receptors; it also induces SREBF1, FASN and SCD, so agonists raise triglycerides and can cause hepatic steatosis. Unliganded receptors are held down by NCOR1/NCOR2, HDAC3 and TBL1X complexes and released to coactivators such as EP300 and NCOA1, with lysine demethylases and a set of microRNAs including miR-33 adding further layers. The pathway underpins reverse cholesterol transport, bile acid handling and anti-inflammatory tone in macrophages, and is a target in atherosclerosis.

BDNF activates NTRK2 (TRKB) signaling is the initiating step by which brain-derived neurotrophic factor engages its receptor tyrosine kinase to support neuronal survival, dendritic and axonal growth, and activity-dependent synaptic plasticity. It is the molecular basis of much of long-term potentiation and hippocampal learning, and of the trophic support that keeps central neurons alive; disrupted BDNF-TRKB signalling is implicated in depression, where several antidepressants converge on this receptor, and in neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental disorders. Mechanistically, secreted mature BDNF binds the extracellular domain of NTRK2, driving receptor dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation of conserved tyrosines in the cytoplasmic tail. Those phosphotyrosines become docking sites for adaptors and enzymes that launch the downstream cascades governing growth, differentiation, and transcriptional responses, placing this event upstream of neurotrophin-driven PI3K, MAPK, and phospholipase C signalling in neurons.

Brain-derived neurotrophic factor acting on its receptor tyrosine kinase TRKB is the main way neurons are told to survive, grow and strengthen their synapses. This ligand-receptor pair supports the differentiation and maintenance of cortical, hippocampal and sensory neurons, underlies activity-dependent synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation, and contributes to appetite and body-weight control through hypothalamic circuits; loss or reduced signalling is linked to obesity, developmental delay and impaired learning, and altered BDNF-TRKB tone is implicated in depression and antidepressant response. Mechanistically, BDNF binding drives receptor dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation of tyrosines in the cytoplasmic tail, creating docking sites for adaptors that launch RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and phospholipase C-gamma cascades, coupling extracellular neurotrophin availability to gene expression, local protein synthesis, dendritic growth and receptor trafficking at the synapse.

Neurotrophin-3 can engage TRKB, the receptor tyrosine kinase encoded by NTRK2, even though its preferred partner is TRKC and TRKB's high-affinity ligands are BDNF and NT-4. This low-affinity pairing belongs to the broader neurotrophin system that governs survival, differentiation and synaptic plasticity of neurons in the developing and adult nervous system, and it offers a route by which NT-3 secreted in a given territory can influence TRKB-bearing cells. Ligand binding promotes receptor dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation of conserved tyrosine residues in the cytoplasmic kinase domain, the step that normally creates docking sites for adaptors feeding into MAPK, PI3K/AKT and PLC-gamma cascades. Activation through this route is inefficient compared with BDNF-driven TRKB signaling, and the consequences downstream of it remain poorly characterized, so it is best read as a minor, cross-reactive arm of neurotrophin receptor activation.

Biosynthesis of DPAn-3 SPMs produces the specialised proresolving mediators derived from the omega-3 fatty acid n-3 docosapentaenoic acid, the lipid signals that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blunting it. Resolution of an inflammatory episode requires such mediators to stop neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, and restore tissue homeostasis; when they are lacking, inflammation persists and becomes chronic, as in atherosclerosis, arthritis and non-healing wounds. DPAn-3 sits between eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid in the omega-3 elongation route, and its oxygenation follows the same enzymatic logic used to make DHA-derived resolvins, protectins and maresins: lipoxygenases (ALOX5, ALOX12, ALOX15) and cyclooxygenase-2 insert oxygen at defined positions, with subsequent epoxide formation and hydrolysis generating the n-3 DPA series. This links dietary fish-oil intake directly to the enzymatic control of inflammatory resolution.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and the omega-3 fatty acid DPAn-3 is one substrate from which the lipid signals that do the switching are made. Its conversion into specialised proresolving mediators yields n-3 docosapentaenoic acid analogues of the resolvins, protectins and maresins built from DHA, which limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and return tissue to homeostasis rather than merely blocking inflammatory signalling. DPAn-3 itself sits between EPA and DHA in the omega-3 elongation and desaturation route, so the same oxygenases act on it: lipoxygenases introduce oxygen at specific carbons to give hydroperoxy intermediates that are further converted to epoxide and dihydroxy products, with cyclooxygenase-2 in its aspirin-acetylated form providing an alternative entry. Failure of this resolution arm is associated with persistent, non-resolving inflammation in chronic disease.

Inflammation does not simply fade out; it is actively switched off by specialised proresolving mediators made enzymatically from long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids. Described here is the route that converts the omega-6 isomer of docosapentaenoic acid, DPAn-6, into such mediators, structural and functional analogues of the resolvins derived from DHA and EPA. Lipoxygenases carry the chemistry: the 12-lipoxygenase and 15-lipoxygenase activities encoded by ALOX12 and ALOX15 oxygenate the substrate at defined positions, generating hydroperoxy intermediates that are further converted to di- and tri-hydroxylated products. These act on leukocytes to limit neutrophil recruitment and promote macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells and debris, returning tissue to homeostasis. Because DPAn-6 accumulates when omega-3 supply is low, this branch links dietary fatty acid balance to the capacity for resolution, and its failure favours persistent, chronic inflammation.

Biosynthesis of DPAn-3-derived protectins and resolvins generates specialised pro-resolving lipid mediators that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blunting it, limiting neutrophil recruitment, promoting macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and protecting tissue during the resolution phase of an inflammatory response. The substrate, omega-3 docosapentaenoic acid, is an intermediate on the route from eicosapentaenoic to docosahexaenoic acid, and its oxygenation by 15-lipoxygenase to a 17(S)-hydroperoxy intermediate opens the same sequence of oxygenation, reduction and hydrolysis steps that converts DHA into D-series resolvins and protectins; 5-lipoxygenase supplies the second oxygenation for resolvin formation. The resulting mediators act on nanomolar-affinity receptors with anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective potency comparable to their DHA counterparts. This arm of lipoxygenase metabolism explains part of the benefit attributed to dietary omega-3 fatty acids, and its failure leaves inflammation unresolved and chronic.

Inflammation does not simply fade; it is actively switched off by lipid mediators made from omega-3 fatty acids, and this route generates that class of signals from the intermediate docosapentaenoic acid, DPAn-3. The products are resolvins and protectins, specialised pro-resolving mediators that limit neutrophil recruitment, promote macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and protect tissue during resolution, with potency comparable to their docosahexaenoic acid-derived counterparts. Synthesis begins when 15-lipoxygenase oxygenates DPAn-3 to a 17(S)-hydroperoxy intermediate; further oxygenation by 5-lipoxygenase together with reduction and epoxide hydrolysis yields the finished mediators. Because DPAn-3 sits between eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid, dietary omega-3 status feeds directly into this output, and weak resolution signalling is one way acute inflammation becomes chronic.

Biosynthesis of DPAn-3-derived maresins produces specialised pro-resolving lipid mediators that actively terminate inflammation rather than merely blocking it, promoting macrophage clearance of apoptotic cells, tissue repair and pain relief.
