The substrate, omega-3 docosapentaenoic acid, sits between eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid in the long-chain omega-3 series and serves as an alternative mediator precursor in its own right. Platelet-type 12-lipoxygenase oxygenates it at carbon 14 to a hydroperoxy intermediate, which is converted through epoxide formation, reduction and hydrolysis into maresin-like dihydroxy products that parallel the DHA-derived maresins in structure and potency; 5-lipoxygenase contributes to related routes from the same substrate pool. This chemistry links dietary fish-oil fatty acids to the resolution phase of the inflammatory response, and its failure underlies the persistent, non-resolving inflammation seen in chronic inflammatory and metabolic disease.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and maresins are among the lipid mediators that do it. Here they are made not from docosahexaenoic acid but from the omega-3 fatty acid docosapentaenoic acid (DPAn-3), an intermediate on the route from eicosapentaenoic to docosahexaenoic acid, giving a parallel family of specialised pro-resolving mediators with comparable anti-inflammatory and tissue-protective potency. Platelet-type 12-lipoxygenase (ALOX12) oxygenates DPAn-3 at carbon 14 to a 14(S)-hydroperoxy intermediate, which is then converted through further oxygenation, reduction and epoxide hydrolysis into the maresin series; 5-lipoxygenase (ALOX5) contributes related oxygenation chemistry from the same substrate pool. Products of this kind promote resolution of inflammation, macrophage clearance of debris and apoptotic cells, and repair of injured tissue, linking dietary omega-3 intake to the termination phase of the inflammatory response rather than its initiation.

Neurotrophin-4 is one of two ligands, alongside BDNF, that switch on the receptor tyrosine kinase TRKB, and this ligand-receptor pair supports the survival, differentiation and synaptic plasticity of neurons that depend on TRKB signalling. Ligand binding drives receptor dimerization and trans-autophosphorylation of tyrosine residues in the cytoplasmic tail, which then act as docking sites for adaptors and enzymes that launch the downstream cascades shared by neurotrophin receptors, including RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and PLC-gamma routes toward growth, anti-apoptotic signalling and activity-dependent changes at synapses. Because NTF4 and BDNF engage the same receptor, their signalling overlaps but differs in availability and in how efficiently the receptor is desensitized. Loss of TRKB activation compromises neuronal trophic support and is implicated in neurodegeneration, obesity and mood disorders, while aberrant activation contributes to tumour cell survival.

Omega-3 docosahexaenoic acid is the precursor for a family of sulfido-peptide lipid mediators that actively terminate inflammation and promote repair rather than simply blocking inflammatory signals. Macrophages convert DHA-derived epoxide intermediates into glutathione conjugates, producing the maresin, protectin and resolvin conjugates in tissue regeneration. The conjugation step uses the same enzymes that make cysteinyl-leukotrienes from arachidonic acid: leukotriene C4 synthase and a cytosolic glutathione S-transferase attach glutathione across the epoxide, and the products are structurally analogous to LTC4 but opposite in action, driving macrophage phenotype switching, bacterial clearance and regrowth of damaged tissue. This shared chemistry places resolution and pro-inflammatory eicosanoid production on branches of one enzymatic route, with substrate availability determining which is made; failure to generate these mediators is associated with chronic, non-resolving inflammation and delayed wound healing.

Inflammation must be actively switched off, and the 13-series resolvins are among the lipid mediators that do the switching. Derived from the omega-3 fatty acid n-3 docosapentaenoic acid, an intermediate between eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acid, these specialised pro-resolving mediators speed the clearance of infection: in bacterially infected animals they accelerate resolution and improve survival, and on human and mouse phagocytes they promote bacterial uptake while restraining inflammasome activity. Their synthesis depends on physical contact between neutrophils and vascular endothelium. Cyclooxygenase-2 in endothelial cells first generates a 13(R)-hydroxy precursor, which passes to the adjacent neutrophil where 5-lipoxygenase converts it to the four resolvins RvT1-RvT4. This transcellular route places resolution of the innate immune response alongside, rather than after, its initiation, and links dietary omega-3 intake to the termination of acute inflammation.

Neurons read BDNF and neurotrophin-4 as survival and growth cues through the receptor tyrosine kinase TRKB, and one of the main routes by which that signal reaches the nucleus is RAS activation. This arm supports neuronal survival, dendritic and axonal growth, and activity-dependent synaptic plasticity underlying learning and memory; loss of BDNF-TRKB output is linked to depression, obesity and hyperphagia, and to neurodegenerative decline. Ligand binding dimerizes and autophosphorylates the receptor, creating a phosphotyrosine docking site for the adaptor SHC1, which recruits GRB2 together with the guanine nucleotide exchange factor SOS1. SOS1 then loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, and active RAS:GTP feeds the MAP kinase cascade and other effectors that drive transcriptional programmes for differentiation and growth. The pathway is a defined branch of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling in the nervous system.

BDNF or neurotrophin-4 binding to the TRKB receptor tyrosine kinase sets off several parallel branches of neurotrophin signalling, and this one routes through phospholipase C-gamma. Receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation create a phosphotyrosine docking site that recruits PLCG1, which is then phosphorylated and cleaves membrane PIP2 into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate. Those second messengers raise intracellular calcium from internal stores and activate protein kinase C, coupling neurotrophin availability to calcium-dependent kinases and transcriptional responses in neurons. This arm of TRKB output is the one most closely tied to synaptic plasticity: it supports long-term potentiation in the hippocampus, dendritic and synaptic maturation, and activity-dependent refinement of circuits. Loss or attenuation of BDNF-TRKB signalling through this route is associated with impaired learning and memory, obesity and hyperphagia, and features of depression and neurodegenerative disease.

Acute inflammation must be actively switched off, and macrophages in the resolution phase do this partly by making peptide-conjugated lipid mediators from docosahexaenoic acid. The maresin conjugates in tissue regeneration are one such family: they enhance phagocytosis and bacterial clearance, dampen proinflammatory mediator output, and drive repair and regrowth of damaged tissue, so their loss favours persistent, non-resolving inflammation. Biosynthesis begins with a 13,14-epoxide intermediate derived from docosahexaenoic acid, which is conjugated to glutathione by leukotriene C4 synthase or the cytosolic glutathione transferase GSTM4 to give MCTR1. Sequential peptide trimming by a gamma-glutamyl transferase and then a dipeptidase yields MCTR2 and MCTR3. The chemistry parallels cysteinyl leukotriene formation but is directed toward resolution rather than inflammation, placing these enzymes at a branch point in eicosanoid and docosanoid metabolism.

Resolution of acute inflammation is an active process, and the sulfido-conjugated mediators built from the omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid are among its effectors. Protectin and resolvin conjugates in tissue regeneration are made by activated macrophages and neutrophils, where they limit further leukocyte recruitment, promote clearance of apoptotic cells and bacteria, and drive repair of damaged tissue rather than merely dampening inflammatory signalling. Biosynthesis begins with lipoxygenase oxygenation of docosahexaenoic acid at the 17- and 7-positions to give epoxide intermediates, which are then conjugated to glutathione by leukotriene C4 synthase, the same membrane enzyme that conjugates the leukotriene A4 epoxide to form cysteinyl leukotrienes. Downstream peptidase trimming yields the cysteinyl-glycine and cysteinyl forms. Insufficient production of these mediators is associated with inflammation that fails to resolve and with delayed tissue regeneration.

Erythropoietin drives red blood cell production by keeping erythroid progenitors alive and dividing, and one of the main survival arms it engages is phosphoinositide-3-kinase. Loss of this signalling contributes to anaemia of renal failure and to ineffective erythropoiesis, while constitutive activation of the same receptor-kinase module underlies polycythaemia. Hormone binding dimerises the erythropoietin receptor and activates the associated JAK2 kinase, with LYN contributing additional tyrosine phosphorylation. Class I PI3K, through its p85-type regulatory subunit, is then recruited in three ways: directly to a phosphotyrosine on the receptor tail, or indirectly through the phosphorylated scaffolds IRS2 and GAB1. Once membrane-localised, the catalytic subunit converts PIP2 to PIP3, creating docking sites that bring AKT to the membrane for activation. The output is suppression of apoptosis and support of progenitor expansion and metabolism.

Erythropoietin activates Phospholipase C gamma (PLCG) is one branch of the signalling that erythropoietin triggers in red cell progenitors, converting hormone binding into a calcium and protein kinase C response that supports erythroblast survival, proliferation and terminal maturation. Loss of erythropoietin signalling causes anaemia, while its overactivation drives erythrocytosis. Mechanistically, EPO dimerises its receptor and activates the receptor-associated kinase JAK2; the Src-family kinase LYN, recruited alongside adaptors such as IRS2, phosphorylates PLCG1 or PLCG2 docked on phosphotyrosines of the receptor tail. Activated phospholipase C gamma hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, releasing calcium from intracellular stores, and to diacylglycerol, which engages protein kinase C isoforms. This arm runs in parallel with STAT5, PI3K and RAS-MAPK outputs of the same receptor, adding calcium-dependent control to erythropoiesis.

Erythropoietin drives red cell production by keeping erythroid progenitors alive and proliferating, and one branch of that signal works through phospholipase C gamma. When erythropoietin binds its receptor, the receptor dimerizes and JAK2 is activated, creating phosphotyrosine docking sites; PLCG1 or PLCG2 is recruited to the activated receptor complex and phosphorylated by the Src-family kinase LYN, with IRS2 serving as an additional scaffold. Activated phospholipase C cleaves membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate into inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate, which releases calcium from intracellular stores, and diacylglycerol, which activates protein kinase C. The resulting calcium and PKC signals feed into transcriptional and survival responses that expand the erythroid compartment during hypoxia or blood loss. Loss of erythropoietin or receptor signalling causes anaemia, while gain-of-function receptor and JAK2 lesions produce erythrocytosis and myeloproliferative disease.

Erythropoietin drives the survival and maturation of red cell progenitors, and the STAT5 branch of its receptor signalling is how that survival message reaches the genome. When EPO binds its receptor, the associated kinase JAK2 is activated and phosphorylates tyrosines on the EPOR cytoplasmic tail; STAT5A and STAT5B dock there and are themselves phosphorylated by JAK2 and the Src-family kinase LYN. Phosphorylated STAT5 releases from the receptor, dimerizes, enters the nucleus and switches on anti-apoptotic and proliferative genes that allow erythroblasts to complete terminal differentiation. The adaptor IRS2 links the same receptor to additional growth signalling. Loss of this axis causes anemia, while constitutive JAK2 activity uncouples it from hormone control and produces polycythemia and other myeloproliferative disease; recombinant EPO therapy works through exactly this route.

Erythropoietin drives the survival and proliferation of erythroid progenitors, and one of the routes by which its receptor signals is activation of RAS, coupling the hormone to the MAPK proliferative cascade that expands red cell precursors during hypoxic stress or blood loss. Binding of EPO to its receptor activates JAK2 and the SRC-family kinase LYN, which phosphorylate the receptor tail and create docking sites for adaptors. CRKL recruited to the phosphorylated receptor is itself phosphorylated and engages SHC1, which in turn binds GRB2 together with a guanine nucleotide exchange factor, either SOS1 or VAV1. These exchange factors load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, switching them into their active state; RAPGEF1 and IRS2 provide additional adaptor links. Defective signalling through this arm contributes to anaemia, while constitutive JAK2 or RAS activity underlies erythrocytosis and myeloproliferative disease.

Resolution of inflammation is an actively driven programme, not simply the fading of an inflammatory signal, and maresin-like specialised proresolving mediators are among the lipid signals that drive it. These 14,21-dihydroxy docosahexaenoic acids, including MaR-L1 and MaR-L2, are generated by leukocytes, platelets and macrophages from the omega-3 fatty acid DHA, and they act as autocrine and paracrine cues that push macrophages from a proinflammatory state toward a reparative, tissue-remodelling one. The oxygenation steps here are carried out by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases such as CYP1A2, CYP2C8, CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, which hydroxylate DHA-derived intermediates. When this output falls, as in diabetic skin, macrophage phenotype switching stalls, low-grade inflammation persists and wounds fail to close; supplying the mediators restores reparative macrophage behaviour.

Omega-3 fatty acids do more than serve as structural lipids: in macrophages and neutrophils responding to inflammation and oxidative stress, they are enzymatically converted into electrophilic oxo-derivatives that actively drive resolution. Formation of these electrophilic ω-3 PUFA oxo-derivatives begins when 5-lipoxygenase and cyclooxygenase-2 oxygenate EPA, DHA or n-3 docosapentaenoic acid to hydroxy or epoxy intermediates, which cellular dehydrogenases then oxidise to α,β-unsaturated ketones. Because these products are electrophiles, they form reversible adducts with cysteine thiolates and with histidine and lysine amines on target proteins, switching on the Nrf2 antioxidant response, heat shock proteins and PPARγ while damping NF-κB-driven cytokine transcription. The result is an anti-inflammatory and cytoprotective signal rather than simple blockade of arachidonate eicosanoids, and it offers a mechanistic account of why dietary fish oil alters inflammatory tone; related oxo-derivatives also show antileukemic activity.

BDNF and the related neurotrophin NTF4 keep neurons alive and support synaptic growth largely by engaging the receptor tyrosine kinase TRKB, and one of the main branches leaving the activated receptor is the lipid kinase route described here. Autophosphorylated NTRK2 recruits GRB2 with the scaffold GAB1, which brings class IA PI3K — its p110α catalytic and p85α regulatory subunits — to the membrane, where PIP2 is phosphorylated to PIP3. The resulting PIP3 pool recruits and activates AKT, suppressing apoptotic effectors and switching on mTOR-dependent protein synthesis needed for neurite outgrowth, dendritic arborisation and long-term potentiation. This arm accounts for much of neurotrophin-dependent neuronal survival; reduced BDNF–TRKB output is associated with depression, impaired plasticity and neurodegeneration, while excess signalling through the same PI3K components contributes to tumour growth.

BDNF and neurotrophin-4 acting on the TRKB receptor support neuronal survival, dendritic growth and activity-dependent synaptic plasticity, and one route by which the activated receptor reaches the RAS pathway runs through the docking adapters FRS2 and FRS3. Both bind the juxtamembrane region of ligand-bound NTRK2 and are then phosphorylated by the receptor's kinase domain, creating phosphotyrosine sites that assemble a signalling platform; the FRS3 branch remains sparsely characterised. Phosphorylated FRS2 recruits the GRB2 adapter with its associated SOS1 exchange factor, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, while the phosphatase PTPN11 is brought in to sustain and amplify this output toward ERK-dependent transcription. Loss or weakening of this coupling blunts neurotrophin-driven differentiation and long-term potentiation, and BDNF-TRKB signalling deficits are linked to mood disorders, obesity and neurodegeneration.

The liver X receptors LXRα and LXRβ are oxysterol-activated nuclear receptors that read cellular cholesterol status and, among other outputs, switch acetyl-CoA away from sterol synthesis and into fatty acid synthesis. Through this arm they drive hepatic lipogenesis: heterodimers with retinoid X receptors bind response elements in target promoters to induce SREBF1, the master transcriptional regulator of fatty acid synthesis, and act directly on lipogenic genes such as fatty acid synthase and stearoyl-CoA desaturase, alongside ANGPTL3, which restrains lipoprotein lipase and raises circulating triglycerides. NRIP1 serves as a corepressor-type coregulator tuning the response. This explains why LXR agonists lower cholesterol yet cause hypertriglyceridaemia and hepatic steatosis, while loss of both receptors cuts hepatic lipogenesis dramatically and confers resistance to diet-induced obesity, making this pathway central to whole-body lipid partitioning.

Cells sense cholesterol overload through oxysterols, and the liver X receptors NR1H3 (LXRα) and NR1H2 (LXRβ) convert that signal into a transcriptional programme that unloads excess sterol. Acting as heterodimers with retinoid X receptors on target promoters, they drive expression of the membrane transporters ABCA1 and ABCG1, which pump cholesterol and phospholipid onto apolipoprotein acceptors in macrophages, and ABCG5/ABCG8, which limit intestinal absorption and promote biliary excretion. Induction of APOE and the APOC1/APOC2/APOC4 cluster, plus PLTP and CETP, supplies the lipoprotein machinery for reverse cholesterol transport back to the liver. Gene activation requires exchange of NCOR1/NCOR2 corepressor complexes containing HDAC3, GPS2 and TBL1X for coactivators such as NCOA1 and the acetyltransferase EP300, with lysine demethylases contributing chromatin changes. Counterbalancing microRNAs, notably the MIR33 family within sterol regulatory genes, act through Argonaute complexes to restrain efflux. Failure of this circuit promotes macrophage foam cell formation and atherosclerosis.

NR1H2 & NR1H3 regulate gene expression to limit cholesterol uptake is the arm of sterol sensing that shuts off LDL import when a cell already has enough cholesterol. The liver X receptors LXRalpha and LXRbeta bind oxysterols generated from excess cholesterol and, as heterodimers with RXRA or RXRB, switch on a transcriptional program that lowers sterol load. Here the induced target is MYLIP (IDOL), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor and drives its lysosomal degradation, reducing lipoprotein uptake independently of the SREBP-2 route that controls LDLR transcription. This feedback complements LXR-driven cholesterol efflux and suppression of biosynthesis, and it sets circulating LDL levels, making the receptor-degradation step relevant to hypercholesterolaemia, atherosclerosis and the response to lipid-lowering therapy.

When cells accumulate sterols, oxysterols generated from excess cholesterol bind the liver X receptors NR1H3 and NR1H2, which then act with retinoid X receptor partners as heterodimeric transcription factors to shut down further cholesterol acquisition. This arm of the response limits cholesterol uptake by inducing MYLIP, also called IDOL, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates the cytoplasmic tail of the LDL receptor and consigns it to degradation, so fewer receptors remain at the surface to internalise LDL particles. The result is post-translational control of LDL receptor abundance that is independent of the sterol-regulated transcription of the receptor itself, and complementary to the other LXR outputs promoting cholesterol efflux and suppressing synthesis. Because LDL receptor levels set plasma LDL cholesterol, this circuit is of interest in atherosclerosis and in understanding variation in lipid-lowering responses.

Adipose triglyceride stores are the body's main energy reserve, and their controlled hydrolysis to free fatty acids and glycerol supplies fuel between meals. The liver X receptors LXRα (NR1H3) and LXRβ (NR1H2), acting as ligand-activated heterodimers with retinoid X receptors, are expressed in mature adipocytes and set the transcriptional tone for basal lipolysis and fatty acid oxidation in fat. Their direct targets include perilipin 1, the lipid droplet coat protein that governs access of the triglyceride lipases ATGL and hormone-sensitive lipase to stored lipid, so receptor activation raises glycerol and fatty acid release without altering hormone-stimulated lipolysis. LXRα is induced during adipocyte differentiation and is the dominant isoform in this response; its loss in white adipose tissue reduces lipolytic and oxidative capacity and increases adiposity, linking these nuclear receptors to whole-body energy balance and obesity.

NGF-stimulated transcription is the nuclear output of nerve growth factor signalling: the wave of gene expression that converts a transient kinase signal at the TrkA receptor into the lasting decision of a neuronal precursor to stop dividing and grow neurites. It supports sympathetic and sensory neuron differentiation and survival, and the same machinery underlies activity-dependent gene expression in mature neurons, so it links extracellular trophic cues to synaptic plasticity and memory. Sustained ERK signalling activates CREB, ELK1 and SRF, which drive immediate early genes including FOS, FOSB, JUNB and the EGR family; these encode transcription factors that in turn switch on delayed response genes such as VGF and TPH1, with EP300 and CHD4 shaping chromatin and REST and the ID proteins restraining neuronal programmes. CDK5 and its p35/p39 activators couple the response to cytoskeletal remodelling during neurite extension.

Nerve growth factor binding to its receptor ends in the nucleus, and NGF-stimulated transcription is the gene expression response that converts a trophic signal into a lasting change in neuronal identity — cell cycle exit, neurite outgrowth and survival of sympathetic and sensory neurons. The first wave is immediate early genes: FOS, FOSB, JUNB, EGR1-4 and ARC are switched on within minutes by pre-existing factors such as CREB1, ELK1, SRF, ATF1 and ATF2 acting with the p300 acetyltransferase, without any need for new protein synthesis. Many of these products are themselves transcription factors, so they impose a slower, delayed wave that includes neuropeptide and neurotransmitter enzymes such as VGF and tryptophan hydroxylase, the NAB corepressors that restrain EGR activity, ID proteins, and CDK5 with its neuronal activators. REST and ASCL1 set how permissive the neuronal programme is. This is the logic underlying activity-dependent plasticity as well as differentiation.

BDNF binding to its receptor TrkB (NTRK2) recruits the Src-family kinase FYN, an arm of neurotrophin signalling that tunes synaptic strength and neuronal excitability rather than simply promoting survival. Through this route BDNF raises protein levels of AMPA receptor subunits without changing their transcripts, and FYN phosphorylation of voltage-gated sodium channels damps sodium currents; FYN also phosphorylates the NMDA receptor subunit GRIN2B, linking the receptor to glutamatergic plasticity and to seizure susceptibility. A DOCK3-RAC1 module downstream provides actin and cytoskeletal remodelling for growth-cone and spine dynamics, and the same signalling supports oligodendrocyte myelination and contributes to ERK1/2 activation. The relationship is reciprocal: FYN and SRC activated by other receptors, including G protein-coupled receptors, can phosphorylate NTRK2 and heighten its kinase activity, allowing unrelated inputs to sensitise neurons to BDNF.

Brain-derived neurotrophic factor acting through its receptor TRKB does more than promote neuronal survival; one branch of that signal reorganises the actin cytoskeleton at the growth cone, and this is the route by which NTRK2 activates RAC1. The output is axon outgrowth, growth cone advance and regeneration after injury, so loss of the link limits the capacity of injured central axons to regrow. Mechanistically, BDNF binding to NTRK2 recruits the atypical guanine nucleotide exchange factor DOCK3, either through the Src-family kinase FYN associated with the activated receptor, or via RHOG-GTP with ELMO as partner. DOCK3 then loads GTP onto RAC1, driving lamellipodial actin polymerisation and microtubule assembly. The same signalling supports dendritic and synaptic remodelling, connecting neurotrophin availability to structural plasticity in the nervous system.

BDNF binding to its receptor TRKB drives dendritic growth and synaptic strengthening, and one arm of that response runs through the neuronal kinase CDK5. Activated NTRK2 recruits CDK5 bound to its activator p35 and phosphorylates CDK5 on Tyr15 to stimulate its catalytic activity; CDK5 in turn phosphorylates a serine in the TRKB juxtamembrane region (S479 in human), a modification required for BDNF-evoked dendrite elaboration, hippocampal long-term potentiation and spatial memory. The signal is relayed to the actin cytoskeleton through the Rac1 exchange factor TIAM1 and Rac1 activation, linking receptor phosphorylation to growth cone and dendritic remodelling, with possible effects on AKT/mTOR output and PSD-95 levels. The same TRKB-CDK5 relationship contributes to inflammation-induced thermal pain hypersensitivity, placing it in nociceptor sensitization as well as activity-dependent plasticity.

Peroxisomal protein import delivers the entire folded matrix proteome of the peroxisome from the cytosol across a single membrane, and so builds the organelle's capacity for fatty acid beta-oxidation, glyoxylate and D-amino acid detoxification, hydrogen peroxide breakdown by catalase, and ether-phospholipid synthesis. Its failure causes Zellweger spectrum disease, neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy and rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata, in which enzymes such as ACOX1, PHYH, AGXT and GNPAT are made but never reach their compartment. Cargo carries a C-terminal PTS1 read by PEX5 or an N-terminal PTS2 read by PEX7, and the loaded receptor docks at a membrane translocation module of PEX13, PEX14 and the RING proteins PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12. Uniquely, substrates cross without unfolding. Receptor recycling drives the cycle: PEX5 is mono-ubiquitinated on a cysteine, extracted by the PEX1-PEX6 AAA-ATPase with PEX26, then deubiquitinated by USP9X.

Peroxisomes carry out fatty acid beta-oxidation, glyoxylate detoxification, hydrogen peroxide breakdown and plasmalogen synthesis, but they make none of their own matrix enzymes; peroxisomal protein import is how roughly four dozen cargo proteins reach the lumen from the cytosol. Cargo need not unfold to cross, which is unusual among translocation systems. Cytosolic receptors recognise targeting motifs on cargo — PEX5 binding the common C-terminal signal, PEX7 the alternative signal found on a few enzymes such as phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase and thiolase — and dock at a membrane module built from PEX13, PEX14 and the RING proteins PEX2, PEX10 and PEX12. The receptor is then mono-ubiquitinated, extracted by the PEX1–PEX6 AAA-ATPase ring with PEX26, and deubiquitinated by USP9X for reuse. Loss of these steps causes Zellweger spectrum disease and rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata.

Peroxisomal enzymes arrive in the organelle as full-length precursors, and a trypsin-like serine protease resident in the matrix trims a subset of them once import is complete. TYSND1-mediated processing of peroxisomal proteins matures the core machinery of fatty acid beta-oxidation and ether lipid synthesis: the thiolase ACAA1, acyl-CoA oxidase ACOX1, the multifunctional enzyme HSD17B4, the sterol carrier protein SCP2, phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase. Cleavage depends on a histidine-aspartate-serine catalytic triad. Without it, some of these enzymes are poorly retained in the peroxisome and both beta-oxidation of fatty acids and degradation of the branched-chain lipid phytanic acid fall off. The consequences extend beyond metabolism: mice lacking the protease produce sperm without acrosomal caps and males are sterile, tying peroxisomal lipid handling to spermatogenesis.

Blood group systems biosynthesis builds the surface antigens that determine transfusion compatibility. Mismatched donor red cells are attacked by recipient antibodies, so the products of this pathway dictate who can safely receive whose blood, and variation in them is linked to susceptibility to infection, thrombotic and cardiovascular risk, and tumour-associated carbohydrate changes. Most of these antigens are oligosaccharides added stepwise onto glycolipid and glycoprotein scaffolds: galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases extend the core chains, the ABO transferase adds the A or B terminal sugar, and fucosyltransferases generate H, Secretor and Lewis structures, with FUT2 activity also determining whether antigens appear in saliva, milk and other secretions. Inactivating or altered alleles convert one antigen into another or abolish expression, as in the O phenotype. The Rhesus proteins contribute a protein-based antigen system central to haemolytic disease of the newborn.

Blood group antigens are the inherited surface markers that determine transfusion compatibility, and their biosynthesis is largely a matter of carbohydrate chemistry: glycosyltransferases add specific sugars in defined order to oligosaccharide chains carried on red cell glycoproteins and glycolipids. The ABO transferase transfers N-acetylgalactosamine or galactose to the H antigen made by fucosyltransferases, while other fucosyltransferases, beta-1,3-galactosyltransferases and sialyltransferases build Lewis, secretor and related structures that also appear in saliva, milk and other secretions. RHD and RHCE instead encode protein antigens, the basis of Rh incompatibility and haemolytic disease of the newborn. Inherited variation in these enzymes creates new antigens or abolishes expression, explaining why mismatched transfusion provokes immune destruction of donor cells, and why blood type associates with susceptibility to certain infections, cardiovascular and malignant disease.

The ABO blood group antigens are carbohydrate structures displayed on red cell surfaces, epithelia and endothelia, and their biosynthesis determines the blood types that govern transfusion compatibility, organ transplant matching and forensic typing. Building them is a two-step glycosylation problem: an alpha-1,2-fucosyltransferase adds fucose to a galactose-terminated precursor chain to create the H antigen, with FUT1 acting mainly on type 2 chains of red cells and endothelium and FUT2 on type 1 chains in secretory glands, explaining why most people also carry these antigens in saliva and other fluids. The ABO locus then encodes a glycosyltransferase that caps H with N-acetylgalactosamine to give A, with galactose to give B, or is inactive, leaving unmodified H as blood group O. Loss of fucosyltransferase activity yields the rare Bombay and para-Bombay phenotypes, in which no H, A or B can be made. Naturally arising antibodies against absent antigens make mismatched transfusion hemolytic.

Neurotrophin-3 acting on its receptor tyrosine kinase TRKC is a survival and differentiation signal for defined classes of neurons, most notably proprioceptive sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglia and the muscle spindle afferents that report limb position. Loss of either partner removes proprioception and produces severe movement and gait abnormalities, and altered signalling through this pair has been linked to cardiac and neural developmental defects. Mechanistically, the ligand binds the receptor's extracellular domain, drives receptor dimerization, and triggers trans-autophosphorylation of conserved tyrosines in the cytoplasmic kinase domain; these phosphotyrosines then recruit adaptor and enzyme complexes that launch Ras-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and PLC-gamma cascades. Activation thereby couples an extracellular trophic cue to neuronal survival, axon growth, synapse formation and neurotransmitter phenotype, placing it within the broader neurotrophin receptor family alongside NGF and BDNF signalling.

NTRK3 (TRKC) is the receptor tyrosine kinase for neurotrophin-3, and signalling through it supports the survival, differentiation and connectivity of sensory neurons, proprioceptive afferents and other neural populations, as well as cardiac and vascular development. Ligand binding dimerizes the receptor and triggers trans-autophosphorylation, creating docking sites that recruit SHC1, GRB2 and SOS1 to activate RAS proteins, IRS1 and the PI3K subunits PIK3CA and PIK3R1 for survival signalling, and PLCG1 for calcium and protein kinase C output; SRC participates in the kinase cascade. Without ligand the receptor behaves as a dependence receptor, engaging BAX and caspase-dependent death so that neurons lacking trophic support are eliminated. The receptor phosphatases PTPRO and PTPRS dampen signalling by dephosphorylating NTRK3, while trans-synaptic binding of PTPRS to the receptor ectodomain helps organize synapses. Chromosomal fusions of NTRK3 drive several cancers.

Neurotrophin-3 binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase TRKC recruits and phosphorylates phospholipase C-gamma 1, one of the branches by which this receptor converts a neurotrophic signal into a cellular response. The output matters for neuronal survival, differentiation and synaptic function: NT-3/TRKC signalling supports proprioceptive sensory neurons and cerebellar and hippocampal populations, and its loss produces defects in limb proprioception and movement coordination. Once phosphorylated on its activation-loop tyrosines, the receptor provides a docking site for PLCG1, whose SH2 domains engage the phosphorylated tail; activated PLCG1 hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate to inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, releasing calcium from intracellular stores and activating protein kinase C. This arm runs in parallel to the Ras-MAPK and PI3K routes from the same receptor, and aberrant TRKC activity, including gene fusions, drives tumour growth.

Neurotrophin-3 binding to the receptor tyrosine kinase TRKC launches a RAS-dependent branch of neurotrophin signalling that supports the survival, differentiation and motility of responsive neurons, including proprioceptive sensory neurons that depend on this ligand-receptor pair for their development. Once the receptor autophosphorylates, the adaptor SHC1 and the GRB2-SOS1 pair are recruited to phosphotyrosines on its cytoplasmic tail; SOS1 acts as the guanine nucleotide exchange factor that loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, which in turn feeds the RAF-MEK-ERK cascade and the transcriptional changes that accompany neuronal differentiation. Sustained ERK output downstream of this receptor has also been linked to cytoskeletal remodelling and increased cell migration. Because the same module drives growth when misregulated, NTRK3 rearrangements and overexpression occur in several tumours, making this arm of signalling a therapeutic target.

RHOF GTPase cycle describes the activation state and downstream effectors of RHOF (RIF), a vertebrate-specific Rho-family GTPase that builds unbranched actin bundles. Its output is visible as filopodia, stress fibres, the microvilli that let lymphocytes scan endothelium, and dendritic spines in neurons, so it shapes how cells probe and adhere to their surroundings and how synapses are formed. Unusually, RHOF appears constitutively GTP-loaded, with no known exchange factor or dissociation inhibitor, so timing is set almost entirely by GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP1, ARHGAP5 and ARHGAP21 and by effector availability. The principal effectors are the diaphanous formins DIAPH1-3, which nucleate and elongate linear filaments, together with BAIAP2L1/2 membrane-deforming adaptors, actin capping and crosslinking proteins, and PI3K regulatory subunits. The set thus links a small GTPase switch to filopodial protrusion, cell shape and immune cell surface architecture.

RHOF (RIF) is a vertebrate-specific Rho-family GTPase that drives actin remodelling, and its regulatory cycle determines how cells build finger-like filopodia and contractile stress fibres. This output shapes cell surface architecture: microvillar protrusions on lymphocytes, dendritic spines in neurons, and the exploratory protrusions used in migration and cell-cell contact. Unusually, RHOF appears to sit largely in the GTP-loaded active state without a known exchange factor and without dissociation inhibitors, so the balance is set mainly by GTPase-activating proteins such as ARHGAP1, ARHGAP5, ARHGAP21 and SRGAP2, together with effectors that execute the cytoskeletal change. Chief among these are the formins DIAPH1, DIAPH2 and DIAPH3, which nucleate and elongate unbranched actin filaments, alongside I-BAR proteins BAIAP2L1 and BAIAP2L2 that deform membrane into protrusions, plus actin crosslinking and capping components including ACTN1 and CAPZB.

Glutathione conjugates formed during detoxification of electrophiles such as aflatoxin epoxides must be trimmed before they can leave the body as mercapturic acids, and gamma-glutamyltransferase 1 performs the first cut. This membrane-bound heterodimer, assembled from a heavy and a light chain, removes the gamma-glutamyl residue from extracellular glutathione or its conjugates, releasing free glutamate and cysteinylglycine; the latter is further degraded to supply cells with cysteine and thereby feed intracellular glutathione synthesis. Loss-of-function mutations in either chain cause glutathionuria, an autosomal recessive condition in which glutathione accumulates in plasma and spills into urine because the extracellular arm of the gamma-glutamyl cycle is broken. The defect links xenobiotic conjugate clearance to sulfur amino acid salvage and to the cell's capacity to maintain antioxidant defences.

Water balance in the body depends on a hypothalamic hormone reaching the kidney: arginine vasopressin, cleaved from its precursor and released from the posterior pituitary in response to rising plasma osmolality or falling blood volume, binds the type 2 vasopressin receptor on collecting duct cells, raises cAMP through Gs, and drives aquaporin-2 water channels to the apical membrane so that urine is concentrated. This disease pathway captures what happens when mutant vasopressin fails to engage its receptor. Loss of that ligand-receptor step leaves aquaporin-2 in intracellular stores, so dilute urine is passed in large volumes and thirst becomes unrelenting. The result is familial neurohypophyseal diabetes insipidus, an autosomal dominant disorder in which mutant precursor misfolds and hormone output from the neurohypophysis progressively fails, distinguishing it from nephrogenic forms where the kidney itself cannot respond.

Neurotrophins are secreted growth factors that keep neurons of the peripheral and central nervous system alive, direct their differentiation, and tune synaptic strength; their expression and processing determines how much active ligand ever reaches a receptor. NGF and its relatives are made as pre-pro-proteins, lose a signal peptide on entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, dimerise, and are then cleaved at a basic-residue site by proprotein convertases such as furin, PCSK5 and PCSK6 to release the mature dimer. The cut matters because the precursor and the mature form signal differently: mature neurotrophin engages the TRK receptor tyrosine kinases to promote survival and growth, whereas uncleaved pro-neurotrophin preferentially acts through the p75 receptor and can drive apoptosis and synaptic weakening. Regulated cleavage, in the secretory pathway or extracellularly, therefore sets the balance between trophic support and neuronal loss.

Rhesus blood group biosynthesis accounts for the red cell surface antigens that determine whether transfused blood is tolerated and whether a pregnancy risks hemolytic disease of the newborn. Two closely related, highly polymorphic genes do the work: RHD encodes the D antigen, the most immunogenic of the Rh determinants and the one meant by "Rh factor", while RHCE encodes the polypeptide carrying the C/c and E/e specificities. Both are multipass erythrocyte membrane proteins that assemble with Rh-associated glycoprotein and other components into a complex linked to the spectrin-based skeleton, so they contribute to the deformability and mechanical stability of the red cell as well as to its antigenic identity. Deletions, recombination between the two loci, and point variants generate dozens of further antigens, making this the most complex blood group system and the basis for Rh genotyping in transfusion medicine and antenatal care.

Lewis blood group biosynthesis builds the fucosylated glycan antigens carried on secreted mucins and glycoproteins of glandular epithelia, which are then adsorbed onto red cells rather than made by them. Two fucosyltransferases set the phenotype: FUT3 fucosylates type 1 chains to give Lewis A, and FUT2, present in secretors, adds a further fucose to yield Lewis B; FUT4, FUT5, FUT6, FUT7 and FUT9 act on type 2 chains to make Lewis X and Y. Upstream beta-1,3-galactosyltransferases supply the type 1 acceptor backbone, while ST3GAL sialyltransferases generate the sialylated forms. Sialyl-Lewis X and A are the minimal carbohydrate ligands for L-, E- and P-selectin, so this glycosylation route governs leukocyte and platelet trafficking in inflammation and haemostasis. Its upregulation in tumours produces the CA19-9 marker and promotes adhesion and metastasis.

Type I interferon alpha/beta signalling is the cell-autonomous alarm system against viral infection: interferons secreted by infected or sensing cells act on neighbours to put them into an antiviral state before the virus arrives. All the alpha subtypes and interferon beta converge on one receptor, IFNAR1 with IFNAR2, which uses JAK1 and TYK2 to phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2; with IRF9 these form the ISGF3 complex, while STAT1 homodimers drive a separate set of promoters, and importins carry the complexes into the nucleus. The output is hundreds of effectors that block translation and degrade RNA (PKR, the OAS enzymes with RNase L), restrict entry and budding (the IFITM proteins, tetherin, MX GTPases), tag proteins with ISG15, and raise MHC class I to expose infected cells. SOCS proteins, USP18 and phosphatases terminate the response; failures cause interferonopathies or susceptibility to severe viral disease.

Meiotic recombination exchanges DNA segments between homologous chromosomes during gamete formation, generating the genetic diversity of sexual reproduction and, just as importantly, the physical links that let homologs pair, synapse and segregate correctly. Failure produces aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. Programmed double-strand breaks are made by SPO11 at hotspots specified by the histone methyltransferase PRDM9, then resected by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN nuclease with ATM signalling and RPA coating the resulting 3' overhangs. RAD51 and the meiosis-specific recombinase DMC1, assisted by BRCA2 and the MND1-PSMC3IP complex, drive homology search and strand invasion; most intermediates resolve without crossover, while MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 channel a minority into chiasmata. FIGNL1-FIRRM restrains recombinase dynamics, and nucleosome remodelling with H2AX phosphorylation frames the chromatin context, including silencing of the unsynapsed X-Y body.

Meiotic recombination is how homologous chromosomes exchange DNA during gamete formation, shuffling alleles between parental chromosomes and, just as importantly, physically tethering each homolog pair so that the first meiotic division segregates them correctly. Without at least one crossover per bivalent, chromosomes missegregate, producing aneuploid eggs and sperm, infertility and pregnancy loss. The process begins with programmed double-strand breaks made by SPO11, whose covalent attachment to the DNA is removed nucleolytically before the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex and its partner RBBP8 resect the ends. RPA-coated 3' overhangs are handed to the RecA-like strand exchange proteins RAD51 and DMC1, aided by MND1 and PSMC3IP, which invade the homolog. Most intermediates resolve without crossover; a minority mature through MSH4-MSH5 and MLH1-MLH3 into chiasmata. PRDM9 marks hotspots by methylating histones, targeting breaks to defined genomic positions.

Cytokine receptors for IL-2, IL-3, IL-5 and GM-CSF drive lymphocyte and myeloid progenitor proliferation and survival, and one arm of their output runs through the adaptor SHC rather than through STAT transcription factors alone. After ligand binding assembles the shared receptor chains and activates JAK kinases, SHC1 is phosphorylated on tyrosines within the receptor complex and becomes a docking platform: GRB2 with the exchange factor SOS1 engages Ras and the Raf-MEK-ERK cascade to license cell cycle entry, while GAB2 recruits class IA PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits for survival and metabolic signalling. The inositol phosphatases INPP5D and INPPL1 and the tyrosine phosphatase PTPN6 bind the same phosphotyrosines and damp the response, so this interleukin receptor SHC signaling module sets how strongly a cytokine translates into growth. Its deregulation underlies cytokine-dependent leukaemic proliferation and eosinophil-driven inflammation.

Receptor signalling has to be switched off as well as on, and the E3 ubiquitin ligase CBL is one of the main devices for doing so, acting as a negative regulator that tags activated signalling proteins for ubiquitination and proteasomal destruction. In haematopoietic cells this restrains PI3K output: CBL binds the p85 regulatory subunit through SH3 and SH2 contacts, and phosphorylation of a specific CBL tyrosine by Src-family kinases such as FYN, HCK and LYN strengthens the interaction, increasing PI3K ubiquitination and turnover. CBL also sits in adaptor complexes with GRB2, CRK/CRKL and the exchange factor RAPGEF1, so its phosphorylation redistributes adaptor binding and reshapes downstream signalling rather than simply stopping it. Cytokine receptors including those for IL-3, IL-2 and IL-4, and antigen receptor kinases such as SYK, feed into this circuit; loss of the brake favours sustained growth signalling and leukaemic transformation.

Regulation of IFNA/IFNB signaling describes the brakes on type I interferon responses, the arm of innate immunity that arms cells against viral infection. Interferon alpha and beta signalling must be transient: sustained JAK-STAT output through IFNAR1/IFNAR2 drives inflammation, cytopenias and interferonopathy, and loss of these restraints underlies autoimmune disease and, in the case of USP18 or ISG15 deficiency, lethal interferon toxicity. Negative control operates at every tier of the cascade. The phosphatases PTPN6, PTPN11 and PTPN1 strip activating phosphates from JAK1, TYK2 and STAT1/STAT2; SOCS1 and SOCS3 bind and inhibit the receptor-associated kinases while targeting components for degradation; USP18 displaces JAK1 from IFNAR2, and nuclear inhibitors of activated STATs limit transcription. Because several of these regulators are themselves interferon-induced, the pathway forms a self-limiting feedback loop that sets the duration and amplitude of antiviral gene expression.

Type I interferon signalling must be shut down as promptly as it is switched on, and this is the braking system for it. Interferon alpha and beta binding to the IFNAR1/IFNAR2 receptor activates JAK1 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2 to drive antiviral gene expression; the negative regulators here set how strong and how brief that response is. Tyrosine phosphatases including PTPN1, PTPN6 and PTPN11 dephosphorylate receptor-associated kinases and STATs, SOCS1 and SOCS3 suppress JAK activity, and USP18 binds IFNAR2 to block its engagement with JAK1 independently of its deubiquitinase activity. Loss of this restraint produces sustained interferon-stimulated gene expression, the basis of type I interferonopathies such as USP18-deficient pseudo-TORCH syndrome, while excessive damping permits viral replication.

Interferon signaling is the cell-intrinsic and immunological response to viral infection and tumor cells, in which secreted type I (IFN-alpha/beta) and type II (IFN-gamma) interferons act on IFNAR and IFNGR receptors to place tissues into an antiviral state and to raise antigen presentation. Receptor engagement activates JAK1, JAK2 and TYK2, which phosphorylate STAT1 and STAT2; with IRF9 these form a trimeric complex that drives transcription from interferon-stimulated response elements, while STAT1 dimers act at gamma-activated sequences. The induced effectors do the actual work: MX GTPases, OAS enzymes with RNase L, PKR-mediated shutdown of translation initiation, ISG15 conjugation via UBA7 and UBE2L6, tetherin, IFITMs, guanylate-binding proteins, and elevated MHC class I and II. Nucleoporins and importins carry activated STATs into the nucleus, and SOCS proteins, USP18 and phosphatases restrain the response; failure of this restraint underlies interferonopathies and autoimmunity, while loss of signaling brings severe susceptibility to viral and mycobacterial infection.

Mucins are the gel-forming glycoproteins that coat airway, gut and ocular epithelia, and their O-linked glycosylation is what makes them work: hundreds of sugar chains added to serine and threonine residues in the tandem-repeat domains hold water, lubricate surfaces, and build the mucus barrier that separates tissue from microbes and digestive contents. Synthesis begins in the Golgi when a large family of polypeptide GalNAc transferases attaches the initiating GalNAc; C1GALT1 with its chaperone C1GALT1C1 extends this to the core 1 structure, branching enzymes such as GCNT1 and GCNT3 generate cores 2 and 4, and elongation by beta-3 and beta-4 glycosyltransferases is terminated by sialylation or sulfation. Defective or truncated glycosylation thins the protective layer and is seen in colitis and cystic fibrosis-like airway disease, while shortened, sialylated forms on MUC1 and MUC16 are classic tumour-associated antigens.

Degradation of GABA clears the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter after it has acted, and recycles its carbon into the citric acid cycle. This two-step route sets the size of the GABA pool available for inhibitory synaptic transmission, so its failure produces neurological disease: loss of succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase activity causes a rare inherited disorder marked by developmental delay, ataxia, hypotonia and seizures, with accumulation of GABA and of the abnormal metabolite gamma-hydroxybutyrate. Both reactions occur in the mitochondrial matrix of neurons and astrocytes. 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase transfers the amino group to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding succinic semialdehyde and glutamate, and ALDH5A1 oxidises the semialdehyde to succinate, which enters mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. The shunt therefore links neurotransmitter turnover directly to energy production, and the aminotransferase is the target of the antiepileptic drug vigabatrin.

The main inhibitory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system is cleared by catabolism as well as by reuptake, and GABA degradation is the route that disposes of it while feeding its carbon back into energy metabolism. In the mitochondrial matrix, 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase transfers the amino group of GABA to 2-oxoglutarate, yielding succinic semialdehyde and glutamate; succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase then oxidises the aldehyde to succinate, which enters the citric acid cycle. This short two-step shunt links neurotransmitter turnover to oxidative metabolism in neurons and astrocytes, and sets the size of the GABA pool available for inhibitory signalling. Loss of the dehydrogenase step causes succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase deficiency, in which the intermediate is diverted to gamma-hydroxybutyrate and patients present with developmental delay, hypotonia, ataxia and seizures; aminotransferase deficiency is likewise a severe infantile encephalopathy.

Membrane proteins destined for destruction rather than recycling are recognised on endosomes by their attached ubiquitin and packaged into intralumenal vesicles of multivesicular bodies, which then fuse with lysosomes for degradation. This sorting route terminates signalling from activated growth factor receptors, and the same machinery is reused for cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope resealing and budding of enveloped viruses such as HIV. Ubiquitylated cargo is captured by HGS and STAM, passed through TSG101- and VPS-containing complexes that concentrate it and deform the membrane, and finally enclosed by CHMP subunits that polymerise into spirals driving neck constriction and scission; the AAA-ATPase VPS4, with VTA1, disassembles the filaments for reuse. Loss of function compromises receptor downregulation and lysosomal delivery, and CHMP2B mutations cause frontotemporal dementia, linking this pathway to neuronal proteostasis.

Cells acquire iron for haem synthesis, iron-sulfur cluster assembly and dozens of redox enzymes, and this iron uptake and transport route describes how it crosses membranes and how the amount taken up is matched to need. Transferrin loaded with ferric iron binds its receptor and is endocytosed; vacuolar ATPase-driven acidification of the endosome releases the metal, a ferrireductase such as STEAP3 reduces it, and the divalent metal transporter DMT1 moves it into the cytosol, from where it is directed largely to mitochondria. Alternative entry occurs as haem or as siderophore-bound iron via lipocalin-2 and its receptor. Export through ferroportin requires ferroxidases such as ceruloplasmin and hephaestin, ferritin stores the surplus, and haem oxygenases liberate iron from haem. Iron-responsive regulators IREB2 and ACO1, together with the FBXL5-dependent degradation that senses iron, tune the system; its failure produces haemochromatosis, anaemia and iron-loading disease.

Nearly all iron taken up by dividing cells and by erythroid precursors arrives bound to transferrin, and this is the route by which it gets inside. Diferric transferrin binds its receptor at the plasma membrane and the complex is internalized into early and recycling endosomes; the vacuolar H+-ATPase, represented here by the full set of V0 and V1 subunits, acidifies the lumen, which weakens iron binding. Ferric iron is then reduced by an endosomal metalloreductase such as STEAP3 and exported to the cytosol through a divalent metal transporter, while the receptor and apo-transferrin escape lysosomal degradation and return to the surface for reuse. HFE and TFR2 tune receptor occupancy and link uptake to hepatic hepcidin-mediated control of systemic iron. Loss of STEAP3 or of receptor recycling capacity causes hypochromic microcytic anaemia; defects in the same proton pump subunits underlie osteopetrosis and distal renal tubular acidosis.

Cytosolic sensing of viral RNA has to be converted into interferon gene transcription, and this is the branch that does it. After RIG-I or MDA5 engages double-stranded RNA and is ubiquitinated by TRIM25 or related ligases, the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS aggregates and recruits TRAF3 through its TRAF-interaction motif. TRAF3 then scaffolds the kinases TBK1 and IKK-epsilon, which phosphorylate IRF3 and IRF7; the phosphorylated factors dimerize, enter the nucleus, and with the CBP/p300 acetyltransferases drive transcription of IFNB1 and other type I interferons. SIKE1 restrains TBK1 to keep the output from running unchecked. Loss of this arm leaves cells unable to mount an early interferon response and prone to severe viral disease, while inappropriate activation contributes to interferonopathies and autoimmune inflammation.

Nonsense-mediated decay is the surveillance system that destroys mRNAs whose translation terminates too early, preventing accumulation of truncated proteins. It shapes the phenotype of a large share of human disease alleles: roughly a third of nonsense and frameshift mutations are silenced this way, turning what would be a dominant-negative truncated product into a simple loss of transcript, while about a tenth of normal transcripts are also routine substrates, making this a general controller of mRNA abundance. Mechanistically, the translating ribosome and release factors eRF1 and eRF3 (ETF1, GSPT1/2) mark the stop codon; if an exon junction complex core of EIF4A3, MAGOH, RBM8A and CASC3 remains downstream, UPF1 is engaged with UPF2 and UPF3 and phosphorylated by SMG1, recruiting the endonuclease SMG6 or SMG5:SMG7 with decapping and deadenylation activities, with PP2A subunits resetting UPF1 for further cycles. Mutations in UPF3B cause X-linked intellectual disability.

Cells detect viral RNA in the cytosol and answer with type I interferon; this branch describes how TRAF6 feeds into that answer by activating the transcription factor IRF7. The sensors RIG-I and MDA5, primed by ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM25 and RNF135, signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, where the pathway splits: a TRAF3-dependent arm and a TRAF6-dependent arm that converge on IRF7 to drive the many IFNA genes and IFNB1, with CREBBP/EP300 acting as transcriptional coactivators. The kinases TBK1 and IKBKE, with the adaptor TANK, phosphorylate the IRFs, while SIKE1 restrains this kinase activity. Loss of TRAF6 leaves IRF3 largely intact but cripples IRF7 and NF-kB activation, reducing interferon and IL-6 output and permitting greater RNA virus replication. Excessive signalling here contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity.

Cytosolic sensing of viral RNA has to do more than switch on interferon; it also needs an inflammatory arm, and TRAF6-mediated NF-kB activation supplies it. The RNA helicases RIG-I and MDA5 signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, and the ubiquitin ligase TRAF6 together with MAP3K1 routes that signal into the canonical IKK complex of CHUK, IKBKB and IKBKG. Phosphorylated IkB inhibitors are degraded, freeing RELA-containing NF-kB dimers to enter the nucleus and drive cytokine genes, while parallel MAP kinase activity engages AP-1; both contribute to optimal type I interferon induction. Ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM25 and RNF135 license RIG-I upstream, and RAS-like NKIRAS proteins damp IkB turnover. Ligands of the receptor AGER, including HMGB1 and S100 proteins, converge on the same NF-kB output, linking sterile danger signals to antiviral and inflammatory transcription.

Cytosolic sensing of viral RNA has to end in gene expression, and this is one route by which it does: downstream of RIG-I and MDA5 signalling through mitochondrial MAVS, the death-domain adaptors FADD and RIPK1 dock onto the C-terminal region of MAVS and recruit the initiator caspases 8 and 10, which drive NF-kB activation rather than apoptosis. The output is transcription of inflammatory cytokines and survival genes that accompany the interferon response to infection, so the arm matters for how strongly a virus-infected cell inflames its surroundings. The death effector domain prodomains of the caspases appear to work as a scaffold that brings in the IKK complex, whose catalytic and regulatory subunits IKKalpha, IKKbeta and IKKgamma release NF-kB from inhibition. Ubiquitin ligases such as TRIM25 and RNF135 act upstream, modifying RIG-I so that it can signal at all.

Cytosolic sensing of viral RNA by RIG-I (RIGI/DDX58) and MDA5 (IFIH1) triggers type I interferon production, and this arm of the response exists to switch that output off again. Unrestrained interferon amplification — the sensors are themselves interferon-inducible, so their signalling feeds back onto their own expression — produces cellular toxicity and underlies interferonopathies and autoimmunity, so the brakes described here are as much a part of antiviral defence as the sensors. Most act through ubiquitin: E3 ligases such as RNF125 and ITCH mark the receptors or adaptors for degradation, while deubiquitinases including CYLD, TNFAIP3 and OTUD5 strip the activating chains needed for MAVS-dependent signalling to TBK1/IKBKE and IRF3. ISG15 conjugation, the ATG5–ATG12 conjugate, NLRX1 and NLRC5 add further dampening, and PCBP2 and PIN1 restrain the adaptor and the transcription factor respectively.

P-type ATPases use ATP hydrolysis, via a phosphorylated aspartate intermediate and cycling between E1 and E2 conformations, to move ions and lipids uphill across membranes. Together they set the electrochemical gradients that cells live by: the Na+/K+ pumps maintain membrane potential and drive secondary transport and action potentials, SERCA pumps and plasma membrane Ca2+ ATPases clear cytosolic calcium to terminate contraction and signalling, gastric H+/K+ pumps acidify the stomach, and copper-transporting ATPases load cuproenzymes and excrete excess copper. Accessory subunits and regulators tune these pumps, including the beta and FXYD subunits of the sodium pump and phospholamban and sarcolipin, which restrain SERCA in muscle, with calmodulin and CaMKII providing calcium-dependent control. A separate branch, the P4-type flippases, translocates aminophospholipids to establish membrane asymmetry. Loss of individual pumps causes neurological disease, hemiplegic migraine, parkinsonism, cholestasis, Menkes and Wilson disease.

Activation of IRF3, IRF7 mediated by TBK1, IKKε (IKBKE) is the step that converts detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial LPS into type I interferon production. Toll-like receptors 3 and 4 signal through the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), with TICAM2, CD14 and MD-2 (LY96) supporting LPS recognition, and recruit TRAF3 and TANK to assemble a complex in which TBK1 and IKBKE phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7. Phosphorylation drives their dimerization and nuclear entry, where they switch on IFNβ and interferon-stimulated genes that restrict viral replication and shape antiviral and inflammatory responses. The two kinases act partly redundantly, and their output is tuned by negative and modulatory regulators such as SARM1, optineurin, SHP2 and polyubiquitin. Loss of this arm leaves cells unable to mount an interferon response and susceptible to viral infection, while persistent activation contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity.

Detection of viral double-stranded RNA or bacterial lipopolysaccharide must be converted into type I interferon output, and this step is where that conversion happens. Signals from TLR3 and TLR4 pass through the adaptor TRIF (TICAM1), with TICAM2, CD14 and the LPS co-receptor MD-2 (LY96) serving the surface-receptor arm, to recruit TRAF3 and the related kinases TBK1 and IKKε (IKBKE). These kinases phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7, driving their dimerization and nuclear entry so that interferon-β and downstream antiviral genes are transcribed. The two kinases overlap in function, and only loss of both abolishes IRF3 activation. Scaffolds and regulators including TANK, optineurin, SARM1 and polyubiquitin tune the response, while excessive or deficient signalling leads respectively to interferon-driven inflammation or failure of innate antiviral defence.

Innate immune receptors of the interleukin-1 and Toll-like receptor families must convert ligand binding into NF-kappaB-driven transcription of inflammatory genes, and the step in which IRAK1 recruits the IKK complex is where the receptor-proximal signal is physically coupled to the kinase that frees NF-kappaB. Rather than depending on IRAK1 catalytic activity, this handoff is built on ubiquitin: Pellino E3 ligases (PELI1-3) together with TRAF6 and the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair attach Lys63-linked chains to IRAK1, and these chains are read by the NEMO subunit (IKBKG), bringing the CHUK/IKBKB catalytic kinases into the same complex as TRAF6 and the TAK1 module. The result is IKK activation, IkappaB degradation and p65 phosphorylation at Ser536. Differently modified IRAK1 also feeds interferon-regulatory-factor and STAT outputs, so this node apportions innate signalling between inflammatory and antiviral programmes.

Innate immune receptors that sense bacterial lipopolysaccharide must convert ligand binding into inflammatory gene expression, and RIP1-mediated recruitment of the IKK complex is the step that links the TRIF adaptor arm of Toll-like receptor signalling to NF-kB. Without it, cells fail to induce proinflammatory cytokines in response to endotoxin; excessive signalling drives septic inflammation. Downstream of TLR4 with its coreceptors CD14 and MD-2, the TRIF-related adaptors recruit RIPK1 together with TRAF6, which acts as a ubiquitin ligase with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair to build non-degradative polyubiquitin chains; the cIAP proteins BIRC2 and BIRC3 also ubiquitinate RIPK1. These chains provide a scaffold that brings in the IKK catalytic subunits CHUK and IKBKB with the regulatory subunit IKBKG, leading to IkB phosphorylation and NF-kB release. This branch is separable from TRIF-driven IRF3 activation, and RIPK1 and RIPK3 here also connect the receptor to programmed necrosis.

Innate immune receptors of the Toll-like and IL-1 receptor families must convert ligand binding into NF-kB and MAPK activation, and this step is where that conversion is committed. IRAK2, rather than IRAK1, engages TRAF6 through two binding motifs and drives its K63-linked polyubiquitination, using ubiquitin supplied by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes present here. The resulting chains are read by TAB2 and TAB3, which recruit and, with TAB1, activate the MAP3K7 kinase (TAK1). Activated TAK1 then phosphorylates the IKK complex and MAP kinase kinases, branching signalling toward inflammatory gene transcription and stress kinase output. Loss of IRAK2 function blunts NF-kB induction downstream of these receptors, and the same node is targeted by viral immune evasion proteins, making it a control point for how strongly a cell mounts an inflammatory response to microbial products.

Bacterial lipopolysaccharide sensed by TLR4 triggers two waves of signalling, and the TRIF (TICAM1)-dependent arm is the one that runs from the endosome to deliver type I interferon alongside inflammatory cytokines. It matters because it sets the tone of innate antibacterial defence and, when overdriven, contributes to septic shock and sterile inflammation driven by endogenous ligands such as HMGB1 and S100 proteins. LPS is handed to the receptor by CD14 and LY96, and the bridging adaptor TICAM2 recruits TICAM1, whose proline-rich region binds TRAF3 and TRAF6. TRAF3 with TBK1 and IKBKE phosphorylates IRF3 and IRF7 for interferon transcription, while TRAF6 feeds the TAK1-TAB complex into IKK-dependent NF-kappa-B release and into JNK and p38 MAP kinase cascades. The C-terminal region instead engages RIPK1, FADD and caspase-8, coupling receptor engagement to apoptosis or RIPK3-driven death when NF-kappa-B survival signalling fails.

When lipopolysaccharide engages TLR4 with its co-receptors CD14 and MD-2, the receptor must convert that recognition event into inflammatory gene expression, and this step is where the signal is committed to kinase activation. TRAF6, working with ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes, builds Lys63-linked polyubiquitin chains that are read by the TAB2 and TAB3 subunits of the TAK1 complex; chain binding clusters and activates the kinase MAP3K7 (TAK1), which then drives IKK-dependent NF-kB release and the JNK and p38 MAP kinase arms. The output is transcription of cytokines and other innate immune effectors during bacterial infection. Adaptors including TICAM1 and TICAM2 route the receptor toward this branch, while SARM1 acts as a negative regulator. Loss of the pathway leaves cells unresponsive to endotoxin; unchecked activity contributes to septic shock and chronic inflammation, and ubiquitin here is a non-degradative scaffold rather than a degradation tag.

Three human enzymes — sulfite oxidase, xanthine oxidase and aldehyde oxidase — are inactive without a molybdenum cofactor, and this conserved biosynthetic route builds it from GTP in several steps. The consequences of failure are severe: molybdenum cofactor deficiency leaves sulfite oxidase dead, sulfite and S-sulfocysteine accumulate, and affected infants suffer intractable seizures, neurodegeneration and early death, while loss of xanthine oxidase activity disturbs purine catabolism and urate production. MOCS1 converts GTP to cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate, MOCS2 encodes the two-subunit molybdopterin synthase that inserts the dithiolene sulfurs, MOCS3 with the cysteine desulfurase NFS1 supplies and recycles that sulfur, and gephyrin performs the final molybdenum insertion — the same protein that clusters glycine and GABA-A receptors at inhibitory synapses. MOCOS then adds the terminal sulfur required by xanthine and aldehyde oxidase, a refinement shared with plants.

Newly folded secretory and membrane proteins leave the endoplasmic reticulum and travel to the Golgi, where their N-glycans are trimmed and rebuilt into mature complex forms before onward delivery. This route supports essentially all secretion: insulin, coagulation factors V and VIII, alpha-1-antitrypsin and glycoprotein hormones all depend on it, and defects produce bleeding disorders and congenital glycosylation diseases. Cargo is captured into COPII-coated vesicles at ER exit sites by SAR1/SEC23-SEC24 and SEC13-SEC31, with LMAN1 and its partner MCFD2 acting as a glycan-reading receptor for selected cargo while bulk flow needs no signal. Vesicles move along microtubules using dynein-dynactin, are tethered by TRAPP complexes, RAB1 and golgins, and fuse via SNAREs such as STX5 and BET1. COPI and KDEL receptors return escaped ER residents, and mannosidases, MGAT and sialyl- and galactosyltransferases then remodel the attached sugars.

Neurotrophin-3 binding to its receptor tyrosine kinase TRKC triggers a survival arm of neurotrophin signalling in which the activated receptor engages PI3K, and this is the route by which NTRK3 signals through PI3K. It supports the survival, differentiation and process outgrowth of neurons that depend on NT-3, including proprioceptive sensory neurons, and the same output drives transformation when NTRK3 is fused to ETV6 in secretory breast carcinoma and congenital fibrosarcoma. Mechanistically, the p110 catalytic and p85 regulatory subunits of PI3K associate with the ligand-activated receptor, generating PIP3 and activating AKT, the principal effector that suppresses apoptosis and promotes growth. Efficient coupling requires SRC kinase activity and the adaptor IRS1, which bridges receptor to PI3K, though how the complex assembles is not fully resolved.

Developing sensory neurons are made to depend on a trophic factor for their survival, and NTRK3 acting as a dependence receptor is how that requirement is enforced. Supplied with its ligand NT-3, the receptor signals growth and survival; deprived of it, the same receptor actively kills the cell, so that neuron numbers are matched to the targets available during nervous system development. Unliganded NTRK3 is cleaved by caspases to release a killer fragment, which partners with NELFB (COBRA1) and inserts into the mitochondrial outer membrane. There, together with BAX, it promotes membrane permeabilisation and cytochrome c release, committing the cell to apoptosome-dependent death. This ligand-withdrawal killing is one route into intrinsic apoptosis, and loss of it would leave excess sensory neurons; conversely, tumour cells suppress it to survive without trophic support.

Class I peroxisomal membrane protein import builds the peroxisomal membrane itself, delivering the transporters, docking receptors and division factors that make an otherwise empty vesicle a functioning organelle. Without it peroxisomes cannot import matrix enzymes or fatty acid substrates, and the result is the severe peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum. Newly synthesised membrane proteins are captured in the cytosol by the chaperone-receptor PEX19, which recognises positively charged transmembrane segments, then dock at PEX3 on the peroxisomal surface and are inserted without ATP or GTP hydrolysis. PEX3 itself is handled differently, docking with PEX16, and both can enter the ER or mitochondrial outer membrane, from which pre-peroxisomal vesicles bud and fuse to seed new organelles. Cargoes include the ABCD fatty acid transporters, the PEX13/PEX14 matrix import docking complex, and PEX11B and FIS1 for peroxisome division, linking membrane assembly to beta-oxidation and ether lipid synthesis.

Peroxisomes cannot build themselves without first installing their membrane proteins, and class I peroxisomal membrane protein import is the route most of them take. The cytosolic chaperone-receptor PEX19 captures newly made membrane proteins, recognising signals within their transmembrane segments, and delivers them to PEX3 in the peroxisomal membrane, where insertion proceeds without ATP or GTP hydrolysis; PEX3 itself is handled by PEX19 together with PEX16, and both can enter the ER membrane co-translationally so that budded vesicles seed new peroxisomes. The cargoes placed this way define what the organelle can do: fatty acid transporters such as ABCD1 and ABCD3, small solute pores, division factors including PEX11B and FIS1, and the docking and ubiquitin-ligase components that import matrix enzymes. Loss of these steps yields peroxisome biogenesis disorders of the Zellweger spectrum, with failed β-oxidation and impaired ether lipid synthesis.

Negative regulation of NOTCH4 signaling restrains the output of a Notch receptor whose activity is concentrated in endothelium, where it shapes arterial-venous identity, sprouting and vessel remodeling; unchecked NOTCH4 activation disrupts vascular development and contributes to breast tumorigenesis, while loss of its brakes is embryonically lethal in mice. Control acts on the cleaved intracellular fragment rather than on ligand binding. AKT1 phosphorylates the fragment so that 14-3-3-zeta sequesters it in the cytosol, keeping it away from the transcriptional complexes it would otherwise coactivate. Phosphorylated fragment is also recognized by FBXW7 within an SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1, ubiquitinated, and destroyed by the 26S proteasome, whose subunits make up the bulk of the machinery here. Additional inhibition comes from TACC3 binding and from MDM2-dependent degradation downstream of p53, tying Notch dosage to growth and stress signaling.

NOTCH4 is the endothelial-biased Notch receptor, and restraining its output keeps angiogenesis and vascular remodelling in check; loss of that restraint gives excess Notch activity, disordered vessel development and, in mammary and other epithelia, oncogenic transformation. Signalling is shut down after receptor cleavage, by preventing the released NOTCH4 intracellular domain from reaching the nucleus and by destroying it. AKT1-mediated phosphorylation creates a binding site for 14-3-3-zeta (YWHAZ), which sequesters the fragment in the cytosol, while the F-box protein FBXW7 within an SCF complex built on SKP1, CUL1 and RBX1 recognises the phosphorylated fragment and polyubiquitinates it for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here. Binding to the centrosomal coiled-coil protein TACC3 provides a further inhibitory interaction. This is ubiquitin-proteasome control of a developmental transcriptional switch.

Oxidative attack on DNA constantly creates damaged bases such as 8-oxoguanine and ring-opened pyrimidines, and base excision repair removes them by cutting the damaged base out and restoring the correct one. Defects in the DNA glycosylases that initiate this repair define an inherited cancer predisposition: biallelic loss of MUTYH, which excises adenine mispaired opposite 8-oxoguanine, causes adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer, while NTHL1 deficiency produces a multi-tumour syndrome, and OGG1, the glycosylase for 8-oxoguanine itself, and the NEIL enzymes that clear oxidised pyrimidines and hydantoin lesions carry variants linked to tumour risk and to other oxidative stress-related disease. Because the lesions they remove are mutagenic rather than blocking, failure of this repair route shows up as characteristic G:C to T:A transversion signatures in tumour genomes, placing these diseases at the junction of genome maintenance and redox stress.

Defective Base Excision Repair Associated with MUTYH describes what happens when the adenine DNA glycosylase MUTYH fails, removing a safeguard against oxidative mutagenesis and predisposing carriers to colorectal adenomas and cancer. Oxidation of guanine to 8-oxoguanine, or incorporation of 8-oxo-dGTP from the nucleotide pool, creates templates that direct misinsertion of adenine; MUTYH excises that mispaired adenine from the nascent strand so base excision repair can restore the correct cytosine. When its catalytic activity or its partnerships with other repair proteins are lost, the mispairs are fixed as G:C to T:A transversions, which accumulate in APC and KRAS and drive tumour formation. Biallelic germline mutations produce MUTYH-associated polyposis, a recessive syndrome resembling familial adenomatous polyposis but with later onset and fewer polyps, alongside duodenal, gastric and other extracolonic tumours. Distinct isoforms distribute the enzyme between nucleus and mitochondria.

Oxidative damage turns guanine into 8-oxoguanine, which pairs with adenine during replication and fixes G:C to T:A transversions into the genome unless the misincorporated adenine is removed. The adenine DNA glycosylase encoded by MUTYH performs that removal, excising adenine mispaired with guanine or 8-oxoguanine on the nascent strand and initiating base excision repair to restore the correct base. When this activity is lost through biallelic germline mutation, the mutational signature accumulates in genes such as APC and KRAS, producing MUTYH-associated polyposis: multiple colorectal adenomas and a high lifetime risk of colorectal cancer, with additional duodenal, gastric, skin and breast tumours reported.
