Defective repair arises both from missense changes that cripple glycosylase catalysis, including the recurrent Y165C and G382D substitutions, and from variants that leave catalysis intact but disturb partner interactions or subcellular targeting between nucleus and mitochondria.

FLT3 is a class III receptor tyrosine kinase carried by hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and by dendritic cell precursors, and its signalling tells those cells to survive, divide and differentiate. Loss of the pathway depletes dendritic cells and early lymphoid progenitors; constitutive activation by internal tandem duplication is one of the commonest lesions in acute myeloid leukaemia and the reason FLT3 kinase inhibitors exist. Binding of FLT3 ligand dimerises the receptor and triggers autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for GRB2, GAB2 and the PI3K regulatory subunit, which drive RAS-MAPK and AKT signalling, while STAT5A/B are phosphorylated directly. The output is suppression of the pro-apoptotic protein BIM and of FOXO3 and p27, favouring cycle entry. Counter-regulation is prominent here: CBL-mediated ubiquitination, the phosphatases PTPN11 and PTPRJ, SOCS proteins and adaptors such as SH2B3 and SLA restrain the receptor, and their failure sustains leukaemic growth.

Oxidative damage converts guanine to 8-oxoguanine, which pairs with adenine during replication and fixes G:C to T:A transversions unless the misinserted adenine is removed. MUTYH is the DNA glycosylase that recognises the 8-oxoguanine:adenine mispair and excises the adenine, initiating base excision repair on the nascent strand; it is the last line of defence against mutations arising from reactive oxygen species. Inherited biallelic MUTYH variants cause MUTYH-associated polyposis, an autosomal recessive colorectal adenoma and carcinoma syndrome resembling familial adenomatous polyposis, in which tumours carry characteristic transversion signatures in APC and KRAS. Defective substrate binding describes the subset of disease alleles, including missense changes in the catalytic and iron-sulfur cluster domains and truncating variants, whose failure lies in engaging the mispaired lesion in the first place, not only in slow catalysis.

Oxidative damage converts guanine to 8-oxoguanine, which mispairs with adenine during replication; the base excision repair glycosylase MUTYH excises that misinserted adenine so the template can be restored to G:C rather than fixed as a G→T transversion. Inherited biallelic loss of this activity causes MUTYH-associated polyposis, a recessive colorectal adenoma and carcinoma syndrome resembling familial adenomatous polyposis but without APC mutation, and tumours accumulate a characteristic transversion mutational signature. Defective substrate processing describes the disease alleles themselves: missense changes in the catalytic and iron-sulfur cluster regions, in-frame insertions and deletions, nonsense and frameshift truncations, affecting both the nuclear and mitochondrial isoforms. Many retain partial adenine binding but cleave slowly, and in some the deficit is compounded by weakened recognition of the 8-oxoG:A mispair, leaving oxidative lesions unrepaired in proliferating epithelium.

Most organellar proteins are made in the cytosol and must be delivered to the compartment where they work; protein localization is the collection of targeting and import routes that get them there. Presequences and internal signals engage the TOM receptors of the mitochondrial outer membrane, after which cargo is sorted onward by SAM to the outer membrane, by the TIM22 and TIM23 translocases and small TIM chaperones to the inner membrane and intermembrane space, or pulled into the matrix by the HSP70-based import motor and trimmed by the processing peptidase. Peroxisomal matrix enzymes travel a distinct route in which PEX5 and PEX7 carry folded cargo to a docking and RING complex, with receptor recycling by ubiquitination; PEX19 and PEX3 insert membrane proteins, and tail-anchored proteins use the GET pathway. Failure produces peroxisome biogenesis disorders such as Zellweger syndrome, adrenoleukodystrophy and mitochondrial disease.

Tail-anchored proteins carry their single transmembrane segment so close to the C-terminus that it only emerges from the ribosome after translation ends, so they cannot use the standard cotranslational route and need dedicated post-translational delivery to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane. This insertion pathway builds much of the machinery of vesicle traffic and membrane biology, including SNAREs such as VAMP2, STX1A and STX5, cytochrome b5, emerin and subunits of the translocon itself. A cytosolic chaperone, SGTA, captures the hydrophobic tail on release and passes it via the BAG6-UBL4A-GET4 complex to the ATPase GET3 (ASNA1), which docks at the GET1(WRB)-CAMLG receptor in the ER membrane for ATP-dependent insertion. The same handover is a quality-control decision point: substrates that fail to transfer are held by BAG6 and ubiquitinated for proteasomal destruction, preventing aggregation-prone membrane proteins from accumulating in the cytosol.

Human cytomegalovirus is a betaherpesvirus carried for life by most adults, usually silently, but capable of causing congenital deafness and neurological damage, a mononucleosis-like illness, and disseminated pneumonitis, colitis or retinitis in transplant recipients and other immunocompromised hosts. The host proteins collected here trace the steps of productive infection: capsids released into the cytoplasm are carried along microtubules by cytoplasmic dynein to the nuclear pore, where the nucleoporin scaffold and its channel components allow genome delivery into the nucleoplasm. There the incoming genome is silenced by repressive host machinery — PML and DAXX bodies, TRIM28, the Polycomb complex with EZH2, SUZ12 and EED, and histone deacetylase corepressor complexes — which the virus must counteract to begin immediate-early transcription. Late in the cycle, ESCRT components including TSG101, the CHMP proteins and VPS4A drive budding into intracellular membranes and envelopment of progeny virions.

After human cytomegalovirus fuses with the cell, the early events of infection carry the incoming capsid from the cytoplasm to the nucleus and set up viral gene expression. This stage determines whether infection proceeds to productive replication or is silenced into latency, the basis of lifelong persistence and of disease in transplant recipients and congenitally infected infants. Dynein motors move the capsid along microtubules to the nuclear envelope, where the nuclear pore complex mediates delivery of the genome, which then circularizes. Tegument proteins arriving with the capsid counteract host defences: they antagonize repressive chromatin placed on the incoming genome by PML nuclear body components such as DAXX, together with TRIM28, HDAC-containing corepressors and Polycomb subunits including EZH2 and SUZ12. Host transcription factors, among them CREB1, ELK1 and NF-κB, are engaged to drive immediate early and then delayed early viral transcription.

NMDA receptors are the glutamate-gated, calcium-permeable channels that make excitatory synapses plastic, and this pathway covers how they are built and delivered to the neuronal surface. Each channel is a tetramer of two obligatory GluN1 subunits with GluN2A-D and/or GluN3 partners; the combination chosen in the endoplasmic reticulum sets ligand sensitivity, conductance, synaptic versus extrasynaptic placement and the downstream signalling the receptor supports, and it shifts with development, brain region and activity. Assembled receptors move in vesicles along microtubules, with a kinesin motor and a CASK-Lin7-Mint adaptor complex linking cargo to tubulin tracks, while PSD-95 family scaffolds, densin-180 and alpha-actinin anchor and stabilise receptors in the postsynaptic density alongside CaMK2 isoforms that read the resulting calcium influx. Mistrafficking or mutation of GRIN subunits produces epileptic encephalopathy and intellectual disability, and receptor loss underlies aspects of neurodegeneration and excitotoxicity.

The late phase of human cytomegalovirus infection covers viral DNA replication, expression of structural late genes, and the packaging and release of progeny virions, and it is the point at which a latently or early-infected cell becomes a factory producing infectious particles. Host machinery is co-opted throughout: nucleoporins of the nuclear pore complex, including the Y-complex, transmembrane POM121 and the RANBP2/TPR peripheral components, mediate traffic of viral genomes, capsids and mRNAs across the nuclear envelope, while core histones supply the chromatin context in which the viral genome is transcribed and replicated. ESCRT components TSG101, the CHMP proteins and the VPS4A ATPase drive the membrane scission events used for secondary envelopment and egress, the same topology-reversing budding chemistry used by multivesicular body formation. Blocking these steps limits virion output, which is relevant to congenital infection and to disease in transplant and immunocompromised patients.

Autophagy is how cells digest their own contents, delivering proteins, lipids, damaged organelles and intracellular microbes to the lysosome for breakdown and recycling of building blocks. It sustains cells through nutrient starvation, clears aggregation-prone proteins and defective mitochondria, and its decline underlies neurodegeneration, while its exploitation supports tumour cell survival. Nutrient and energy status is read by mTORC1 with its Rag GTPase and Ragulator anchors opposing AMPK, and the balance is relayed to the ULK1-ATG13-RB1CC1 initiation complex and the BECN1-PIK3C3 lipid kinase that marks the nascent phagophore for WIPI proteins. Two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems, built around ATG7, ATG3, ATG10 and the ATG12-ATG5-ATG16L1 complex, lipidate LC3 and GABARAP family proteins onto the growing membrane, where receptors such as SQSTM1, NBR1 and OPTN dock ubiquitinated cargo. PINK1 and parkin select damaged mitochondria, chaperones including HSPA8 with LAMP2 route substrates for chaperone-mediated uptake, and ESCRT components and microtubule motors complete membrane closure and lysosomal delivery.

Lipophagy is the selective autophagy of lipid droplets, the route by which cells mobilise stored triglyceride into free fatty acids for mitochondrial oxidation when nutrients are scarce. It supplies energy during fasting, keeps hepatocytes from accumulating fat, and its failure contributes to steatosis and the lipid overload seen in fatty liver disease and ageing tissues. Access to the droplet core is gated by its protein coat: perilipins PLIN2 and PLIN3 shield stored lipid, and their recognition by the chaperone HSPA8 and delivery to lysosomal degradation strips the surface so that autophagic membranes can engulf the droplet. The AMP-activated protein kinase subunits present here provide the nutrient sensor that triggers the process, coupling a falling energy charge to both autophagy initiation and lipolysis. Lipophagy therefore links autophagic membrane traffic to whole-body lipid and energy homeostasis.

Cells store neutral lipid in droplets and must mobilise it when nutrients run short; lipophagy is the autophagic route to that mobilisation, delivering droplet triglyceride to lysosomes for hydrolysis into free fatty acids that feed mitochondrial beta-oxidation. It matters most in hepatocytes, where failure of droplet turnover contributes to steatosis and fatty liver disease, and it links lipid stores to the cell's energy-sensing machinery. The droplet surface is coated by perilipins, and PLIN2 and PLIN3 must be removed before autophagic components can engage the droplet; the chaperone HSPA8 recognises these coat proteins and routes them for chaperone-mediated degradation. The AMP-activated protein kinase subunits present here provide the starvation signal: rising AMP activates the kinase, which promotes autophagy initiation and suppresses lipogenesis, coupling nutrient scarcity to breakdown of stored fat.

Chaperone Mediated Autophagy is the selective route by which single cytosolic proteins are delivered to the lysosome for degradation, one protein at a time rather than in bulk vesicles. It lets cells clear damaged, oxidised or misfolded proteins and remodel their proteome during nutrient stress, and its decline with age contributes to the accumulation of aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration; PARK7, a Parkinson disease gene, is among its substrates. The cytosolic chaperone HSPA8, with HSP90 co-chaperones, recognises a KFERQ-like pentapeptide motif in target proteins and brings them to the lysosomal surface, where LAMP2A oligomerises to form a translocation channel and the substrate is unfolded and passed into the lumen. Lipid droplet proteins such as perilipins are removed this way to permit lipolysis, and cytoskeletal and ubiquitin components modulate lysosomal positioning and substrate flux.

Chaperone-mediated autophagy is the selective route by which single cytosolic proteins, rather than bulk cargo in vesicles, are delivered across the lysosomal membrane and degraded. It lets cells dispose of individual damaged or misfolded proteins and mobilise amino acids during nutrient stress, and its decline with age is linked to accumulation of aggregation-prone proteins in neurodegeneration. Substrates carrying a KFERQ-like recognition motif are bound by the cytosolic chaperone HSPA8 with HSP90 co-chaperones, brought to the lysosomal surface, and threaded through a translocation complex formed by the LAMP2A receptor, whose multimerisation is the rate-limiting step. Cytoskeletal and lipid-droplet proteins such as GFAP, vimentin and the perilipins regulate or populate the lysosomal membrane microenvironment, while PARK7 and centrosomal and ciliary proteins are among the substrates cleared, connecting this pathway to proteostasis, lipid mobilisation and organelle turnover.

FOXO-mediated transcription is how cells respond at the level of gene expression to scarcity and stress: when growth factors and insulin are absent, FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 enter the nucleus and switch on programmes for stress resistance, cell cycle arrest, apoptosis and catabolic metabolism. Insulin/PI3K signalling through AKT phosphorylates these factors so that 14-3-3 proteins sequester them in the cytoplasm, making the pathway a direct read-out of nutrient and growth-factor availability. Target genes tell the story: antioxidant enzymes such as catalase, SOD2 and thioredoxin; the cell cycle inhibitors CDKN1A and CDKN1B; the pro-apoptotic BH3 proteins PUMA and BIM; gluconeogenic enzymes PCK1 and G6PC1 with the coactivator PPARGC1A; and the muscle atrophy ubiquitin ligases FBXO32 and TRIM63. Cofactors including CREBBP/EP300, SIRT1 and SIN3A-HDAC complexes tune output. This circuitry underlies hepatic glucose production, disuse muscle wasting, hypothalamic feeding control, and the link between insulin signalling and longevity.

FOXO transcription factors drive programmes of stress resistance, autophagy, gluconeogenesis, apoptosis and cell cycle arrest, and growth factor signalling switches those programmes off by moving the factors out of the nucleus. This is the main output of insulin and PI3K/AKT signalling onto metabolic and longevity gene expression: when insulin is present, hepatic glucose production and catabolic gene expression are suppressed, and when signalling is lost the factors return to chromatin. AKT1, AKT2 and AKT3 phosphorylate FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 at conserved sites, producing a conformational change that exposes a nuclear export signal; 14-3-3 proteins such as YWHAB, YWHAZ and stratifin then bind the phosphorylated factors and hold them in the cytosol, away from their target promoters. FOXO6 lacks the export signal and stays nuclear, so phosphorylation instead dampens its transcriptional activity. Loss of this control contributes to insulin resistance and tumour suppression escape.

When growth factor and insulin signalling falls silent, FOXO transcription factors move into the nucleus and switch on genes that kill the cell. This FOXO-driven transcription of cell death genes prunes neurons deprived of nerve growth factor, eliminates enteric nervous system precursors that lack RET signalling, and underlies much of the tumour-suppressive character of FOXO proteins; PI3K/AKT activity in cancer keeps FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 out of the nucleus and blocks it. The induced targets are the apoptotic machinery itself: the BH3-only proteins BIM and PUMA, the death ligand FASLG, the transcriptional repressor BCL6, plus PINK1 and the kinase STK11. Coactivators CREBBP and EP300 and the trimeric NF-Y complex work with FOXO at these promoters, while CITED2 and the stress-induced factor DDIT3 modulate the response, tying nutrient and stress sensing to a decision to die.

FOXO-mediated transcription of oxidative stress, metabolic and neuronal genes is the transcriptional output of FOXO factors when insulin signalling is low, turning fasting and stress into coordinated changes in antioxidant defence, fuel supply, appetite and muscle mass. It matters because it keeps blood glucose steady between meals, protects neurons from reactive oxygen species, and, when chronically active, drives muscle wasting and contributes to insulin resistance and neurodegeneration. FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6 bind insulin-responsive elements to induce mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and catalase, the gluconeogenic enzymes PCK1 and G6PC, and IGFBP1, while repressing glucokinase and SREBF1 through SIN3A-HDAC complexes to limit lipogenesis. In hypothalamic neurons they raise NPY and AGRP and silence POMC to stimulate feeding; in skeletal muscle they induce the atrophy ubiquitin ligases FBXO32 and TRIM63. Insulin-driven PI3K/AKT signalling shuts the programme off, with PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and SMAD partners tuning it.

FOXO transcription factors act as the nuclear output of insulin and growth factor signalling, and this branch covers their direct control of oxidative stress defence, fuel metabolism and neuronal gene programmes. When insulin is low, as in fasting, PI3K/AKT no longer restrains FOXO1, FOXO3, FOXO4 and FOXO6, which then drive hepatic gluconeogenesis through PCK1 and G6PC1 while repressing glucokinase via a SIN3A:HDAC corepressor complex and repressing SREBF1 to hold back lipogenesis; IGFBP1 and resistin further tune systemic insulin sensitivity. In hypothalamic neurons the same factors raise the orexigenic peptides NPY and AGRP and repress POMC, linking nutrient status to appetite. Antioxidant targets SOD2 and catalase, with contributions from cofactors such as PPARGC1A, SIRT3 and ataxin-3, limit superoxide and peroxide burden and support neuronal survival in neurodegeneration. FOXO6 also induces PLXNA4 during cortical radial glia migration, and FBXO32 and TRIM63 induction underlies starvation-induced muscle wasting.

Cells can degrade cytosolic proteins and organelles by pinching them directly into the boundary membrane of late endosomes, a route known as late endosomal microautophagy. It runs alongside macroautophagy and chaperone-mediated autophagy, providing bulk turnover under nutrient stress such as nitrogen starvation while also handling selected clients: the chaperone HSPA8 recognises KFERQ-containing substrates and delivers them for internalisation. The membrane deformation and scission work is done by ESCRT machinery, with TSG101, VPS28, VPS37 and MVB12 subunits building the recognition complexes and the CHMP proteins polymerising to complete invagination, so ubiquitin supplied by UBB, UBC and the ribosomal ubiquitin precursors marks cargo for capture. Substrates range from lipid droplet coat proteins to cytoskeletal and cytosolic proteins including PARK7 and vimentin, linking this pathway to proteostasis, lipid mobilisation and protection against aggregate accumulation.

When a cell exits mitosis it must rebuild the gateways through which every protein and RNA will pass, and postmitotic reformation of the nuclear pore complex is how the daughter nuclei regain a functional nuclear envelope. Without it there is no nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization: transport receptors cannot deliver cargo, and chromatin stays exposed to cytoplasmic machinery. Assembly begins in late anaphase as nascent membranes wrap chromatin, with ELYS seeding the NUP107-160 scaffold ring, followed by membrane-anchored nucleoporins such as NDC1 and POM121 and the central channel FG proteins. A chromatin-bound RAN gradient times the process: RCC1 generates RAN:GTP locally, which strips nucleoporins from importin-beta and transportin, while cytoplasmic RANGAP1, modulated by SUMO conjugation, restricts activation to the reforming nucleus.

Transcriptional regulation of granulopoiesis describes how a hematopoietic stem cell in the bone marrow is committed, step by step, to become a neutrophil or other granulocyte, the most abundant leukocytes in blood and the front line of antibacterial defence. Loss of this program produces neutropenia and recurrent infection, while its corruption by fusion proteins involving RUNX1, KMT2A or the retinoic acid receptor underlies myeloid leukemia. RUNX1 and its CBFB partner induce SPI1, which activates CEBPA; CEBPA then drives GFI1, KLF5, CSF3R and IL6R, autoregulates, and restrains proliferation by repressing MYC and by binding CDK2 and CDK4 so that progenitors differentiate rather than divide. CEBPE and SPI1 switch on the granule proteins used for microbial killing. During infection, G-CSF and GM-CSF signalling through STAT3 substitutes CEBPB for CEBPA, relieving MYC repression to expand progenitors in emergency granulopoiesis, with chromatin and histone-level changes accompanying commitment.

Neutrophils and the other granulocytes are the most abundant leukocytes in blood, and this transcriptional programme is how hematopoietic stem cells are routed through multipotent and common myeloid progenitors into granulocyte-monocyte progenitors and on to mature, granule-laden cells. RUNX1 with core binding factor induces SPI1 (PU.1), which turns on CEBPA; CEBPA then autoregulates and drives CEBPE, GFI1, KLF5 and the receptors CSF3R and IL6R, while simultaneously repressing MYC and binding CDK2 and CDK4 to curb proliferation so that differentiation can proceed. Under infection, G-CSF signalling through STAT3 favours CEBPB, relieving MYC repression and expanding progenitors in emergency granulopoiesis. Retinoic acid receptors, MYB, GATA2, TAL1, FLI1, EP300 and chromatin/histone components shape the underlying promoter landscape. Disruption of these factors underlies congenital neutropenia and the differentiation block of acute myeloid leukemia, including PML-RARA-driven disease.

Oxygen metabolism constantly damages DNA bases, and NTHL1 is the glycosylase that begins their removal: it excises oxidized pyrimidines and purines such as thymine glycol, cytosine glycol and formamidopyrimidine lesions, as well as dihydrouracil arising from cytosine deamination, initiating base excision repair at the abasic site it leaves behind. When both copies of the gene carry loss-of-function mutations, this first step fails, unrepaired oxidative lesions are copied by polymerases, and cells accumulate C>T transitions at non-CpG sites. The clinical consequence is a recessive tumour predisposition syndrome with adenomatous polyposis and colorectal cancer resembling MUTYH-associated polyposis, extended to breast, bladder, skin, uterine and brain tumours. Overexpression is also deleterious, destabilising the genome in non-transformed epithelial cells, so the defective repair here reflects loss of correctly dosed glycosylase activity rather than the enzyme's absence alone.

Oxidative attack on DNA leaves ring-opened formamidopyrimidines, thymine glycol and deaminated bases that mispair or stall replication, and base excision repair is the route by which these lesions are excised. NEIL1 is one of the glycosylases that initiates that route, recognising oxidised purines and pyrimidines and cutting them out while its associated beta/delta lyase activity nicks the backbone so downstream repair can finish the job. When NEIL1 is defective this initiating step fails and oxidative lesions persist, producing genomic instability. Naturally occurring low-frequency variants illustrate the consequences: a glycine-to-aspartate substitution with crippled catalytic activity is linked to primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma, an in-frame deletion found in gastric cancer cannot process thymine glycol, and a truncation removing the nuclear localisation signal strands the protein in the cytosol away from its substrate. Loss of expression, including by promoter hypermethylation, accompanies several cancers, and murine deficiency also produces a metabolic-syndrome phenotype.

Excitatory synapses must switch off NMDA receptor signalling as reliably as they switch it on, because sustained calcium entry through these channels drives excitotoxic damage and corrupts the timing rules of synaptic plasticity. This negative regulation of NMDA receptor-mediated transmission works at two levels. Calcium-loaded calmodulin binds the activated receptor directly, shortening channel open time and displacing the actinin ACTN2 that tethers receptor subunits to the postsynaptic cytoskeleton, thereby loosening anchoring within a scaffold built from PSD-95 family proteins and densin-180. Downstream, the phosphatases PPM1E and PPM1F dephosphorylate autoactivated calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinases, including CaMKII isoforms and CaMK4, terminating the kinase signalling that would otherwise persist after calcium falls. Together these steps limit the duration and spatial spread of NMDA receptor signals during learning-related plasticity and protect neurons from calcium overload.

FOXO transcription factors decide whether a stressed cell mounts an antioxidant and repair response, arrests its cycle, or dies, and acetylation is one of the switches that sets that choice. Under oxidative stress the acetyltransferases CBP, p300 and PCAF add acetyl groups to FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4, shifting which target promoters they favour and altering their nuclear retention in a way that can override the phosphorylation-driven nuclear exclusion imposed by insulin and growth factor signalling. The NAD-dependent deacetylases SIRT1 and SIRT3 reverse these marks, linking FOXO output to cellular energy and redox state; thioredoxin and its inhibitor TXNIP tie the same factors to the thiol redox environment. Through this regulation FOXO proteins govern stress resistance, metabolic adaptation, muscle atrophy programmes and tumour suppression, and the axis is central to how longevity signalling is interpreted at the level of gene expression.

When growth factor and insulin signalling wane, FOXO transcription factors escape cytoplasmic sequestration and enter the nucleus to shut down proliferation, and their transcription of cell cycle genes is how that arrest is enacted. FOXO1, FOXO3 and FOXO4 induce the CDK inhibitors p21 (CDKN1A) and p27 (CDKN1B), the pocket protein RBL2/p130 that helps maintain quiescence, the anti-proliferative genes CCNG2 and BTG1, GADD45A, caveolin-1, and KLF4. The output is withdrawal into G0 rather than division, a brake on erythroid progenitors, lymphocytes and neuroepithelial progenitors of the developing telencephalon, where FOXG1 opposes this arrest. TGF-beta input converges here: activated SMAD2/3 with SMAD4 partners with FOXO to drive p21 and, in muscle, myostatin, coupling cytostasis to differentiation. Loss of this arm of FOXO activity removes a tumour-suppressive restraint on growth factor-driven proliferation and stem cell exhaustion.

Calcium entering a synapse through activated NMDA receptors is converted here into a change in actin architecture, the step that lets excitatory synapses grow and remodel during learning. Calmodulin binds the incoming calcium and activates the upstream kinases CAMKK1 and CAMKK2, which phosphorylate and switch on cytosolic CaMKI; CaMKI in turn stimulates ARHGEF7 (beta-Pix), a guanine nucleotide exchange factor that loads GTP onto the small GTPase RAC1. Active RAC1 drives actin polymerisation in dendritic spines, promoting spine enlargement and new synapse formation. The scaffold GIT1 holds the exchange factor at the postsynaptic site so that this RAC1 activation stays local to the stimulated spine. This branch of NMDA receptor signalling links synaptic activity to structural plasticity, and disturbances in it are associated with intellectual disability and altered spine morphology.

Calcium entering excitatory synapses through NMDA receptors does more than depolarise a neuron; it can switch on a metabolic sensor kinase and thereby reshape the dendrite. In the route from NMDA receptor activation to AMP-activated protein kinase, calcium bound to calmodulin stimulates CAMKK2, which phosphorylates the AMPK catalytic subunits PRKAA1 and PRKAA2 within their heterotrimeric complexes with regulatory beta and gamma subunits, activating the kinase without a change in the cell's AMP:ATP ratio. Activated AMPK phosphorylates the microtubule-associated protein tau, altering its association with tubulin and destabilising the cytoskeleton that supports dendritic spines. Excessive signalling along this arm causes spine loss and is one route by which beta-amyloid oligomers exert synaptotoxicity in Alzheimer's disease, tying synaptic activity, neuronal energy sensing and tau pathology together.

Peripheral nerves conduct rapidly because Schwann cells wrap axons in compacted, lipid-rich myelin, and the transcriptional switch driven by EGR2 (Krox20) together with SOX10 and POU3F1 is what converts an immature Schwann cell into a myelinating one. Loss or mutation of these regulators and their targets produces the demyelinating neuropathies of the Charcot-Marie-Tooth spectrum, with conduction slowing and sensorimotor deficits. The programme turns on structural myelin proteins such as MPZ, MBP, PMP22 and MAG, the gap junction GJB1 that permits radial diffusion across the sheath, and periaxin and dystrophin-related complexes that link the abaxonal membrane to a laminin-rich basal lamina. It simultaneously raises cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis through SREBF2, HMGCR and CYP51A1 to supply membrane lipid. Axonal and basal lamina cues feed in via the receptor ADGRG6 and YAP/TAZ-TEAD transcription, while NAB corepressors and chromatin factors tune EGR2 output.

Long-term potentiation is the cellular basis of learning and memory: a brief burst of synaptic activity leaves an excitatory synapse lastingly stronger. Calcium entering through NMDA receptors binds calmodulin and activates calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II, which docks onto the NMDA receptor subunit GRIN2B and phosphorylates AMPA receptor subunits such as GRIA1, increasing their conductance and driving more receptors into the postsynaptic membrane. Scaffolding proteins of the PSD-95 family, together with densin-180 and actinin, hold receptors, kinases and Src in the postsynaptic density where this chemistry must occur, and neurogranin buffers calmodulin to set the threshold for induction. Neuregulin–ERBB4 signalling tunes the same synapses. Disrupted potentiation is a recurring theme in intellectual disability, epilepsy, schizophrenia and the early synaptic failure of Alzheimer's disease, and NMDA receptor autoantibodies attack this machinery directly.

NR1H2 & NR1H3 regulate gene expression to control bile acid homeostasis describes how the liver X receptors, sensors of cellular sterol excess, tune the synthesis, transport and disposal of bile acids. This matters because bile acids are both the route by which cholesterol leaves the body and detergents that damage hepatocytes and enterocytes when they accumulate; the pathway links sterol sensing to safe handling of that load. Activated by oxysterol ligands, NR1H2 and NR1H3 heterodimerise with retinoid X receptors on target promoters, exchanging NCOR1 and NCOR2 corepressor complexes for coactivators such as NCOA1. Among the induced genes are the ileal bile acid binding protein FABP6, which shuttles bile acids during enterohepatic recirculation, and UGT1A3, which glucuronidates hydrophobic bile acids into polar products cleared in urine. The pathway sits within nuclear receptor control of lipid metabolism and hepatic detoxification.

Liver X receptors, encoded by NR1H3 (LXR alpha) and NR1H2 (LXR beta), sense cellular oxysterols and reprogram transcription to unload excess sterol; one arm of that program tunes how bile acids are made, carried and disposed of. This matters because bile acids are both detergents needed for fat absorption and potentially cytotoxic molecules, so their levels must be held within a narrow range to avoid cholestatic liver injury. Ligand-bound LXRs heterodimerise with retinoid X receptors (RXRA, RXRB) and switch from corepressor complexes containing NCOR1 and NCOR2 to coactivators such as NCOA1, driving target genes including the glucuronosyltransferase UGT1A3, which conjugates hydrophobic bile acids into polar forms suitable for urinary excretion, and the ileal bile acid binding protein FABP6, which shuttles bile acids during enterohepatic recycling.

When mitochondria release cytochrome c into the cytosol, it nucleates the apoptosome with APAF1 and recruits caspase-9 to initiate the intrinsic death programme; this pathway covers the brakes and accelerators applied at that step, which decide whether a stressed cell dies or recovers. Setting the threshold matters because too little restraint kills neurons and too much lets damaged cells persist as tumours. XIAP binds and inhibits processed caspase-9 until DIABLO, released from the mitochondrial intermembrane space, displaces it. Additional modulators act earlier: APIP and AVEN restrain APAF1 oligomerisation, CARD8 and UACA interfere with apoptosome assembly, and ERK1/ERK2 signalling from survival cues phosphorylates caspase-9 to blunt its activity. The net result is a switch that is committed only when pro-death input outweighs these inhibitory layers.

Defective Base Excision Repair Associated with NEIL3 describes what happens when the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 cannot excise oxidized bases, the first step of base excision repair. NEIL3 prefers single-stranded and quadruplex DNA and removes hydantoin lesions from oxidized guanine as well as thymine glycol, work that matters most at telomeres and ahead of replication forks, where unrepaired lesions block polymerases; it also unhooks psoralen- and abasic-site interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anemia route. A catalytically dead D132V variant leaves oxidative lesions in place and predisposes homozygous carriers to autoimmune disease, while loss of the enzyme causes telomere attrition, impaired proliferation of neural stem cells with learning and memory deficits, and worse outcomes after myocardial infarction and in atherosclerotic plaque, some of these through transcriptional rather than repair functions. The pathway thus links oxidative genome maintenance to stem cell renewal and vascular disease.

Oxidative attack on DNA leaves lesions that must be excised before they block replication or cause mutation, and the glycosylase NEIL3 is the enzyme that initiates that removal in a particular niche: single-stranded DNA, telomeric repeats, and replication forks. It cleaves hydantoin products of guanine oxidation and thymine glycol, and also unhooks certain interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anaemia route, so loss of activity leaves both oxidative base damage and crosslinks unresolved. Failure of this arm of base excision repair has consequences beyond mutagenesis: an inactivating variant predisposes to autoimmune disease, depletion accelerates telomere loss, and deficiency limits proliferation of neural stem cells and adult hippocampal neurogenesis, with learning and memory deficits. Expression rises in failing heart and atherosclerotic plaque, where its protective role appears only partly explained by DNA repair.

Protein hydroxylation is the enzymatic addition of hydroxyl groups to specific amino acid side chains, a modification that tunes how proteins fold, interact, and are read by the translation and transcription machinery. It matters because these oxygenases sense oxygen and 2-oxoglutarate directly: their activity links cellular metabolic and oxygen status to protein function, and losses cause defects ranging from impaired ribosome fidelity to abnormal blood clotting. Members of the JmjC and related 2-OG-dependent oxygenase family hydroxylate proline, lysine, asparagine, arginine, aspartate, and histidine residues on targets that include ribosomal proteins such as RPS23 and RPL8, translation factors, splicing factors, and developmentally regulated GTPases. Aspartyl/asparaginyl hydroxylase acts on EGF-like domains of secreted proteins including coagulation factor IX, while JMJD6 modification of splicing and elongation regulators couples this chemistry to gene expression control.

Protein hydroxylation adds a hydroxyl group to specific proline, lysine, asparagine, aspartate, arginine or histidine side chains, a modification made by 2-oxoglutarate-dependent oxygenases that consume oxygen and iron and so report on cellular oxygen and metabolite supply. Outside collagen maturation, which is handled separately, these marks tune the ribosome and the translational apparatus: ribosomal proteins such as RPS23, RPL8 and RPL27A are hydroxylated by enzymes including OGFOD1 and RIOX1/RIOX2, affecting translational fidelity and stop-codon readthrough, while JMJD4 hydroxylates the release factor ETF1 to promote efficient termination. Other members act on splicing and RNA-binding proteins such as U2AF2 and on the GTPases DRG1 and DRG2, and ASPH hydroxylates aspartate in EGF-like domains of secreted proteins including coagulation factor IX. Collectively the pathway links oxygen availability to gene expression, protein synthesis and cell growth, and several of these oxygenases are overexpressed in tumours.

Oxidised bases such as thymine glycol are removed from DNA by base excision repair, and NTHL1 is the bifunctional glycosylase that recognises and excises them before they are read as mutations during replication. Defective NTHL1 substrate processing describes what happens when the D239Y variant, arising from a common coding polymorphism, is present: the altered protein still docks onto oxidatively damaged DNA but cannot efficiently cleave the damaged base, so it occupies lesions without repairing them. Because it competes with wild-type enzyme for the same substrates, it behaves as a dominant negative, and its expression in non-transformed human and mouse mammary epithelial cells raises genomic instability and drives neoplastic transformation. Whether carrying one copy of this allele increases human cancer risk remains unsettled, in contrast to the biallelic loss-of-function mutations that cause a recognised adenomatous polyposis and tumour predisposition syndrome.

Defective NTHL1 substrate binding describes the loss of a DNA glycosylase that normally initiates base excision repair of oxidised pyrimidines, and the tumour predisposition that follows. NTHL1 recognises lesions such as thymine glycol and 5-hydroxyuracil generated by reactive oxygen species, excises the damaged base, and leaves an abasic site for downstream APE1, polymerase beta and ligase steps to restore the sequence. Truncating germline mutations, exemplified by the Gln90 nonsense allele, remove the DNA-binding and glycosylase domains so that damaged bases are never engaged, leaving oxidative lesions to be misread during replication and producing a characteristic mutational signature of C-to-T transitions. Inherited biallelically, these alleles cause an autosomal recessive tumour syndrome with adenomatous polyposis, colorectal and breast cancer and multiple other neoplasms, placing this glycosylase step among the genome-stability caretakers whose failure permits mutation accumulation.

NTHL1 is the DNA glycosylase that initiates base excision repair of oxidized pyrimidines, recognizing lesions such as thymine glycol in duplex DNA and excising the damaged base so that downstream AP endonuclease, polymerase and ligase steps can restore the sequence. Loss of substrate binding by truncated NTHL1 protein removes that first recognition step: the germline nonsense and frameshift alleles found in patients delete the DNA-binding and glycosylase regions, leaving oxidative base damage unrepaired and driving a characteristic mutational signature of C>T transitions. Biallelic inheritance causes a tumour predisposition syndrome with adenomatous colorectal polyposis, colorectal and breast cancer, and a broad spread of other malignant and benign tumours. The biology situates oxidative genome maintenance upstream of cancer avoidance, and illustrates how a defect in lesion recognition, rather than in catalysis alone, is sufficient to abolish repair.

Cellular senescence is a permanent exit from the cell cycle that acts as a barrier to tumour formation, and its disruption is the disease-relevant side of that biology. When senescence fails, cells carrying activated oncogenes or oxidative damage keep dividing and progress toward malignancy; when senescent cells instead accumulate and escape immune clearance, their inflammatory secretions drive tissue damage in atherosclerosis, osteoarthritis and diabetes and create a permissive niche for neighbouring tumour cells. The central lesion here is loss of function at the CDKN2A locus, which encodes two distinct tumour suppressors: p16INK4A, an inhibitor of the cyclin D-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6 that otherwise phosphorylate RB to license S-phase entry, and p14ARF, which stabilises p53. Losing either arm allows evasion of oncogene-induced and stress-induced senescence, which is why CDKN2A deletion is among the most frequent events in human cancer and CDK4/6 inhibition is a therapeutic strategy.

Strong oncogenic signalling normally drives cells into an irreversible growth arrest, and the p16INK4A arm of that response is what makes the arrest stick. p16INK4A binds CDK4 and CDK6 and blocks their pairing with D-type cyclins, so retinoblastoma-family proteins stay unphosphorylated and E2F-dependent entry into S phase is denied. Loss of this brake lets precancerous cells continue dividing under oncogenic stress instead of senescing, one of the commonest events in human cancer. Its gene locus is frequently deleted or silenced by promoter hypermethylation, and point, nonsense, frameshift and splice-site mutations produce inhibitors that no longer engage CDK4 or CDK6; germline defects underlie familial melanoma. Because the same locus encodes p14ARF in an alternate reading frame, deletions often disable p53 stabilisation as well, removing two tumour-suppressive routes at once.

When an oncogene such as mutant RAS is switched on, normal cells respond by halting the cell cycle permanently, a barrier known as oncogene-induced senescence. One arm of that barrier depends on p16INK4A, encoded by CDKN2A, binding CDK4 and blocking its ability to pair with D-type cyclins and phosphorylate RB, so the RB-E2F brake stays engaged. Missense substitutions and small insertions or deletions in CDKN2A that leave the protein expressed but unable to contact CDK4 abolish this restraint: CDK4 remains active, RB is inactivated, and cells continue to divide despite oncogenic signalling. Such alleles underlie familial melanoma and recur in sporadic pancreatic, lung and head and neck tumours, and the same lesions relieve p16INK4A-mediated suppression of NF-kB signalling. The defect represents a tumour-suppressor failure at the interface of cell cycle control and senescence rather than a gain of proliferative signalling.

Cells that acquire an activating oncogenic lesion normally respond by arresting permanently rather than proliferating, and p16INK4A is one of the brakes that enforces that arrest. Encoded by CDKN2A, it binds CDK4 and CDK6 and blocks their cyclin D-dependent phosphorylation of RB, holding the cell at the G1 restriction point and locking in the senescent state. Missense substitutions and truncations that destroy the interaction surface leave the kinases free, so oncogene-induced senescence is never established and a mutant cell continues to divide; loss of p16INK4A also relieves its restraint on NF-kB signalling. This route of senescence evasion underlies the strong cancer predisposition seen with germline CDKN2A mutation, most familiarly in melanoma, and explains why the same axis is targeted therapeutically by CDK4/CDK6 inhibitors.

Prolonged oxidative stress normally pushes a cell into permanent cell cycle arrest, and the p16INK4A inhibitor encoded at the CDKN2A locus is the switch that enforces it. When that switch is broken, damaged cells keep dividing instead of senescing, an early and common step in melanoma, pancreatic and many other cancers. Wild-type p16INK4A binds CDK4 or CDK6 and blocks their assembly with D-type cyclins, so retinoblastoma-family proteins remain unphosphorylated and S-phase entry is held shut. Loss of p16INK4A function through gene deletion, promoter hypermethylation, or missense, nonsense and splice-altering mutations frees CDK4/6 to drive proliferation despite oxidative damage. Because the same locus encodes p14ARF in an alternative reading frame, larger deletions also disable p53 stabilisation, coupling failure of oxidative stress-induced senescence to loss of two tumour suppressor arms at once.

Oxidative stress normally pushes damaged cells into permanent growth arrest, and p16INK4A is the brake that enforces it by binding CDK4 and blocking phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein, so the cell cannot pass the G1 restriction point. Missense changes and small indels in CDKN2A that leave the protein intact but unable to engage CDK4 break this contact, allowing cells carrying oxidative damage to keep cycling instead of senescing. The result is one route by which tumours escape a tumour-suppressive fate: CDKN2A is among the most frequently inactivated loci in human cancer, notably melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma and glioma, and germline lesions underlie familial melanoma. Beyond cell cycle control, loss of p16INK4A function also relieves its restraint on NF-kB-driven transcription, adding an inflammatory and survival-promoting component to the consequences of defective p16INK4A-CDK4 binding.

Evasion of Oxidative Stress Induced Senescence Due to Defective p16INK4A binding to CDK4 and CDK6 describes how tumour cells escape a barrier that normally halts proliferation permanently. Oxidative stress and other damaging signals induce p16INK4A, which clamps the CDK4 and CDK6 kinases, prevents RB phosphorylation, and locks cells out of S phase in a stable senescent state. Missense substitutions and truncations of CDKN2A abolish the physical interaction with these kinases, so the cyclin D-CDK4/6 module remains active and stressed cells keep dividing rather than withdrawing from the cycle. This loss underlies familial melanoma and is one of the most common events in sporadic cancers; the same mutations also relieve p16INK4A-mediated restraint of NF-kB signalling, adding an inflammatory component. The pathway sits at the interface of cell cycle control, redox stress responses, and tumour suppression, and explains the rationale for CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy.

Oxidative stress normally pushes cells into permanent cell cycle arrest, and p16INK4A is the brake that enforces it by binding CDK4 and CDK6 and blocking their phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein. Missense substitutions and truncations of CDKN2A that destroy this binding let the kinases remain active, so cells that have accumulated reactive oxygen damage continue to proliferate instead of entering senescence. This escape from a tumour-suppressive barrier is one reason CDKN2A is among the most frequently inactivated loci in human cancer, notably in familial melanoma, pancreatic carcinoma and glioma. Loss of p16INK4A function also relieves its restraint on NF-kB-dependent transcription, adding an inflammatory and survival-promoting component to the phenotype. The biology sits at the junction of redox stress sensing, G1/S checkpoint control and the senescence programme that limits the lifespan of damaged cells.

Liver X receptors sit at the junction of lipid sensing and glucose production, and through NR1H2 and NR1H3 they tune the transcription of gluconeogenic genes so that hepatic glucose output falls when sterol levels are high. Activated NR1H3, working as a heterodimer with a retinoid X receptor partner such as RXRA or RXRB, represses the gluconeogenic enzymes phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PCK1) and glucose-6-phosphatase in liver while inducing the insulin-responsive glucose transporter GLUT4 in adipose tissue, a combination that lowers fasting glucose and improves peripheral uptake. The corepressor NRIP1 contributes to the repressive arm. The two receptors are not interchangeable: basal NR1H2 is required for glucocorticoid receptor-driven induction of PCK1, whereas ligand-activated NR1H3 opposes it, so the balance between them sets how strongly stress hormones can drive hepatic gluconeogenesis. This makes the axis a target of interest in type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome.

Cells that run short of amino acids must stop making protein they cannot finish, and the kinase EIF2AK4 (GCN2) is the sensor that makes that decision. It monitors uncharged tRNA accumulating at the ribosome, helped by the ribosome-associated GCN1 and restrained by IMPACT, and on activation trans-autophosphorylates and then phosphorylates serine-52 of EIF2S1, the alpha subunit of the initiation factor that delivers initiator tRNA. The result is a general drop in cap-dependent initiation coupled to selective translation of ATF4, whose upstream open reading frames make it favoured under these conditions. ATF4 with CEBPB, CEBPG, ATF3, DDIT3 and TRIB3 then drives transcription of amino acid supply and stress genes such as asparagine synthetase. This is one of four kinase arms of the integrated stress response, and it governs nutrient adaptation, dietary amino acid avoidance behaviour, and tumour survival under amino acid restriction.

When the ERBB2 (HER2) gene is amplified, the receptor accumulates far above its normal level and begins to pair with itself rather than waiting for a growth factor and a partner receptor. These homodimers signal constitutively, driving proliferation through recruitment of SHC1 and GRB2, the exchange factor SOS1, and activation of HRAS, KRAS and NRAS into the RAF/MAPK cascade, while the PI3K/AKT arm is comparatively unaffected. Receptor stability depends on the HSP90 chaperone with its co-chaperone CDC37, and the output is restrained by ERBIN, which sequesters the receptor basolaterally, and by the phosphatase PTPN12. This ligand-independent activity underlies HER2-positive breast and gastric cancer and explains why the receptor is a drug target: therapeutic antibodies such as trastuzumab bind preferentially to the homodimeric form.

GPER1 signaling describes rapid, membrane-initiated responses to estrogen that do not require the nuclear estrogen receptors. This route matters because it explains how oestrogen can raise cAMP and activate MAPK within minutes, and why some receptor-negative breast cancers, as well as vascular and metabolic tissues, remain oestrogen-responsive; it is of interest as a drug target in hormone-dependent cancer and blood pressure control. The receptor couples through heterotrimeric G proteins, with G alpha s stimulating the adenylate cyclase family and thereby protein kinase A holoenzymes, while released G beta gamma dimers and G alpha i contribute to a separate arm. Downstream, integrin alpha5/beta1 engagement with fibronectin together with Src and the adaptor SHC1 drives transactivation of EGFR, linking a G protein-coupled receptor to growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase output, cell proliferation, adhesion and migration.

Glycolytic flux is set largely at phosphofructokinase-1, and the cell tunes that enzyme not by changing its amount but by changing the concentration of its allosteric activator, fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. The bifunctional PFKFB enzymes both make and degrade this signalling metabolite, so their phosphorylation state decides whether a tissue burns glucose or spares it for gluconeogenesis. Hormonal control runs through this node: glucagon raises cAMP and activates protein kinase A catalytic subunits, which phosphorylate the liver isoform to favour the bisphosphatase activity and lower the activator, while insulin-directed dephosphorylation by protein phosphatase 2A holdoenzymes reverses the switch and restores glycolysis. Tissue-specific isoforms give the system different set points in liver, heart and proliferating cells, where the inducible PFKFB3 supports the high glycolytic rates of tumours and activated immune cells.

Estrogen does not act only through nuclear transcription; a rapid, membrane-proximal arm of its signalling recruits atypical protein kinase C zeta, and in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer cells this route contributes to hormone-dependent proliferation. Unlike conventional protein kinase C isoforms, PRKCZ lacks a calcium-binding C2 domain and is indifferent to diacylglycerol and phorbol esters, responding instead to PIP3 made by PI3 kinase, with PDPK1 phosphorylating its activation loop. Activated PRKCZ then feeds into Ras proteins and onward to ERK, linking a steroid hormone stimulus to the classical mitogenic MAP kinase cascade and to cell cycle entry. The pathway matters because it explains part of the proliferative response to estrogen that is independent of direct gene transcription, and because it couples growth factor-like lipid signalling to the Ras-ERK axis exploited in hormone-driven tumour growth and endocrine therapy resistance.

Estrogen acting at the membrane triggers fast kinase signalling, and this pathway covers how those signals are converted into lasting changes in gene expression. Membrane-associated estrogen receptor engages ERK/MAPK and PI3K-AKT cascades, which phosphorylate transcription factors such as ELK1, SRF, CREB1 and FOS to drive immediate-early transcription, while AKT phosphorylates FOXO3 and promotes its nuclear export, relieving repression of proliferation and apoptosis genes. The result is induction of cyclin D1 and BCL2 and cytoplasmic sequestration of the CDK inhibitor p27, favouring cell cycle entry and survival. A feed-forward limb induces EGFR ligands including amphiregulin, TGFA, epiregulin and HBEGF, so estrogen amplifies its own growth-factor signalling. This crosstalk underlies hormone-driven proliferation in breast epithelium and contributes to endocrine therapy resistance in estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer, where EGFR-MAPK output can substitute for direct receptor transcription.

Neurons translate electrical activity into lasting changes in their connections, and the calcium-dependent transcription factor NPAS4 is one of the fastest routes from stimulation to new gene expression. Induced within minutes of activity as an immediate early gene, it sets the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses onto a stimulated cell, a homeostatic adjustment that underlies circuit formation, plasticity and long-term memory; loss of this response degrades memory formation and has been linked to seizure susceptibility and neuroinflammatory injury. NPAS4 is a bHLH-PAS protein that must heterodimerize with ARNT or ARNT2 and recruit CREBBP to drive targets including BDNF, PLK2, IQSEC3 and SYT10, while CDK5 and ERK signalling, MDM2-dependent turnover and microRNA silencing machinery constrain its output. Related programmes involve FOS, SRF and REST, and the same factor supports pancreatic beta cell function and insulin gene expression under stress.

Macrophages normally respond to intracellular infection by killing themselves, stripping the pathogen of its niche and delivering its antigens to dendritic cells. Mycobacterium tuberculosis counters this by secreting effectors that blunt host programmed cell death, and the suppression of apoptosis described here is the host-side machinery those effectors engage: kinases of the ERK cascade and glycogen synthase kinase signalling that set the threshold for death versus survival, ubiquitin ligases and a nuclear RNA-binding regulator, and a granule protease that can process death signals. The outcome is a phagocyte kept alive as a replicative compartment, allowing bacilli to expand intracellularly and evade the antigen presentation that cross-presentation from apoptotic cells would otherwise drive. Tipping the balance back toward macrophage apoptosis, rather than necrosis, favours bacterial containment and underlies interest in host-directed tuberculosis therapy.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside the cells sent to destroy it, and this pathway covers the host-pathogen encounter in the macrophage that decides between latent carriage and active disease. Roughly a quarter of the world's population harbours the bacterium in a non-replicating persistent state; when immune control lapses it resumes growth, kills the phagocyte and spreads. The genes trace recognition through TLR2, uptake into phagosomes marked by RAB5A and RAB7A, and the maturation steps the bacterium blocks — vacuolar ATPase-driven acidification, endosomal sorting and lysosomal fusion — alongside CORO1A, which the pathogen exploits to retain actin at the vacuole. Antimicrobial effectors such as NOS2 and lactoferrin, MHC class I antigen presentation via B2M, ubiquitin and ERK/MAPK signalling to the nucleus are all part of the response, and their subversion underlies tuberculosis persistence and reactivation.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis damages the phagosomal membrane it sits within, and whether the bacterium escapes into the cytosol or is contained depends on how quickly the phagocyte can patch that injury. This step describes the bacterial counter-move: secreted mycobacterial proteins engage and block host membrane repair components, so the sensing of damage by the phagocyte is not translated into effective resealing. The host factor targeted here, HGS (Hrs), is a subunit of the ESCRT-0 complex that recognises ubiquitinated cargo on endosomal membranes and nucleates the downstream ESCRT machinery used for membrane scission and wound repair. Interfering with it leaves the phagosome permeabilised, permitting cytosolic access, inflammasome activation and bacterial persistence, and it links intracellular infection outcome to the general cellular machinery for endosomal sorting and damaged-membrane repair.

NEIL3-mediated resolution of ICLs is a repair route that removes interstrand crosslinks, the lesions that covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription. Cells that cannot clear such crosslinks stall replication forks and accumulate chromosome breakage, the defect underlying Fanconi anemia and the basis for the cytotoxicity of psoralen and crosslinking chemotherapeutics. Here the glycosylase NEIL3 acts at a converged replication fork and cleaves the N-glycosyl bond of the crosslinked base directly, unhooking psoralen-induced and abasic-site-derived crosslinks without incising the phosphodiester backbone. Because no double-strand break is generated, this route bypasses the Fanconi anemia nuclease machinery and homologous recombination altogether, offering a faster, less mutagenic option. It represents a specialised extension of base excision repair into replication-coupled crosslink tolerance and genome maintenance.

Interstrand crosslinks covalently tie the two strands of the double helix together and block both replication and transcription until they are removed. This route unhooks certain crosslinks directly, using the DNA glycosylase NEIL3 to cleave one of the two glycosidic bonds holding the lesion in place, converting the crosslink into a pair of more tractable single-strand lesions that base excision repair and downstream replication can handle. It acts on psoralen-induced crosslinks and on those arising spontaneously from abasic sites reacting with an opposing base, and it does so without the Fanconi anaemia machinery, so it avoids the double-strand break intermediates and incisions that nuclease-dependent crosslink repair requires. Acting at stalled replication forks, it offers cells a rapid, low-risk first option for crosslink removal, with the Fanconi anaemia route as backup when the lesion resists unhooking.

Phagocytes kill ingested bacteria in part by flooding the phagosome with nitric oxide, and inhibition of nitric oxide production describes how an intracellular pathogen blunts that attack by interfering with the host enzyme that makes it. Inducible nitric oxide synthase is transcribed in response to interferon-gamma and microbial ligands, so its output depends on transcription factors being carried into the nucleus by the importin alpha/beta system represented here by KPNA1 and KPNB1. Blocking that nuclear import step, or the synthase itself, lowers reactive nitrogen output before phagosome-lysosome fusion and allows bacteria such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis to survive inside macrophages. The biology sits at the junction of innate antimicrobial effector chemistry, cytokine-driven gene induction, and pathogen subversion of host signalling, and its failure on the host side translates into persistent intracellular infection.

Prevention of phagosomal-lysosomal fusion describes how Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by arresting the maturation of the phagosome that engulfed it. Normally a phagosome acquires RAB5A and then RAB7A, gains phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate, recruits tethering and sorting factors such as HGS and VPS33B, and fuses with lysosomes to destroy its contents; blocking this step gives the bacterium a protected replicative niche and explains the chronic, latent character of tuberculosis. Shed lipoarabinomannan inserts into lipid rafts of the phagosomal membrane, mycobacterial phosphatases strip PI3P and so disable RAB5 effector recruitment, the actin-associated protein coronin-1A is subverted, and VPS33B-dependent fusion is inhibited, with ubiquitin contributing to turnover of the affected trafficking machinery. The result is a host-pathogen interface where innate antimicrobial killing and antigen delivery to degradative compartments both fail.

Intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis survive inside macrophages by arresting the phagosome before it can merge with lysosomes, and this blockade of phagosomal-lysosomal fusion is what lets the bacterium persist in the very cell meant to destroy it. Normally a phagosome matures by exchanging early markers for late ones, acquiring RAB5A and then RAB7A, recruiting tethering and sorting factors including HGS and the fusion mediator VPS33B, and finally delivering its contents to an acidic, hydrolase-rich lysosome. Shed bacterial cell wall lipoarabinomannan inserts into the phagosomal membrane and disrupts these steps, retaining the actin-associated protein coronin-1A, interfering with VPS33B, and depleting the phosphoinositide signal that RAB5A effectors require. Ubiquitin contributed here reflects the ubiquitin-dependent sorting and degradative control that accompanies phagosome maturation. The outcome is a non-fusogenic replicative niche and failed bacterial killing.

Once a macrophage engulfs a microbe, killing it depends on dropping the pH of the phagosome by loading the membrane with proton-pumping V-ATPase, which primes the compartment for fusion with lysosomes and activates acid hydrolases. Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages precisely because it prevents this step: the phagosome it occupies stalls near pH 6.5 and never becomes a degradative phagolysosome, giving the bacterium a replicative niche and underlying the chronic, latent character of tuberculosis. Blockage of phagosome acidification is centred here on the V-ATPase regulatory subunit ATP6V1H, whose recruitment to the phagosomal membrane the pathogen subverts, so that fewer functional pumps are delivered and the proton gradient is not established. The failure links bacterial effector activity to innate antimicrobial defence, antigen processing, and the maturation of endocytic compartments generally.

Macrophages use autophagy to digest damaged organelles, aggregated proteins, and intracellular bacteria that escape or perforate the phagosome, delivering them to lysosomes for degradation. Suppression of autophagy describes how Mycobacterium tuberculosis blunts this defence: as the bacillus damages the phagosomal membrane and becomes visible to the autophagic machinery, it interferes with the signalling and trafficking steps that would otherwise route it to a degradative compartment, buying time to replicate before exiting the cell. The small GTPase RAB7A marks late endosomes and autophagosomes and is required for their maturation and fusion with lysosomes, a step the pathogen blocks. DUSP16 is a MAP kinase phosphatase acting on JNK, linking stress-kinase signalling to autophagic induction. The outcome is a permissive intracellular niche and persistent infection rather than bacterial clearance.

Manipulation of host energy metabolism describes how Mycobacterium tuberculosis rewires the glycolytic machinery of the macrophage it infects, turning an immune cell into a nutrient-rich niche. Secreted bacterial proteins stimulate the activity of host glycolytic enzymes, here represented by phosphoglycerate kinase and enolase, which together carry the payoff phase of glycolysis. The consequence is increased glucose uptake and, because flux through the pathway is unbalanced, accumulation of dihydroxyacetone phosphate, a precursor that feeds glycerolipid synthesis. The infected phagocyte therefore builds lipid, contributing to the foamy macrophage phenotype characteristic of tuberculous granulomas and supplying fatty acids that the bacillus uses as its preferred carbon source. This is host-pathogen metabolic subversion rather than signalling: by shifting central carbon metabolism, the bacterium secures nutrients and blunts effective macrophage killing, favouring persistence.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis does not simply survive inside a macrophage; it rewires the cell's metabolism to suit itself. Bacterial secreted proteins stimulate host glycolytic enzymes, and this manipulation of host energy metabolism raises glucose uptake and flux through the pathway, causing dihydroxyacetone phosphate to accumulate and feeding glycerolipid synthesis. The result is the lipid-laden foamy macrophage characteristic of tuberculous granulomas, a nutrient-rich niche in which the bacterium persists. The host enzymes affected, enolase and phosphoglycerate kinase, catalyse consecutive steps of the glycolytic payoff phase, converting 3-phosphoglycerate onward toward phosphoenolpyruvate and generating ATP; enolase also functions at the cell surface as a plasminogen receptor. This is an example of a pathogen redirecting central carbon metabolism of the immune cell that is meant to destroy it, and it links infection biology to macrophage lipid handling and immunometabolism.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives by shaping the immune response that should destroy it, and this modulation of the host immune system is why infection can persist for decades inside macrophages rather than being cleared. The bacterium blunts adaptive priming while steering its own uptake into phagocytes, where it can control the maturation of the compartment it occupies. Cell wall components engage host surface receptors directly: the mannose receptor MRC1 binds mycobacterial lipoarabinomannan to mediate non-opsonic phagocytosis, while TLR2 recognition of lipoproteins is exploited to skew cytokine output and to interfere with MHC class I and class II antigen presentation, in which B2M participates. Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like proteins here reflect the ubiquitin-dependent processing and degradative steps that accompany antigen handling and receptor turnover. The net effect is an intracellular niche and dampened T cell surveillance.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis survives inside macrophages by blocking phagosome maturation, but the phagosome is only a temporary refuge: once bacterial numbers build up to a few dozen per cell, the bacilli break out. Rupture of the phagosomal membrane, driven by secreted bacterial virulence factors, exposes the bacteria to the cytosol and damages mitochondria; depletion of NAD+ then tips the infected macrophage away from controlled apoptosis and into necrosis, lysing the cell and releasing bacteria to infect new phagocytes. This escape route explains why the bacterial population stays roughly constant during chronic infection, with rapid replication balanced by death, and why necrotic macrophage death rather than apoptosis favours the pathogen. It links intracellular bacterial persistence to host cell death decisions, granuloma breakdown and the tissue destruction that makes pulmonary tuberculosis transmissible.

Phagosomes normally mature by acidifying, acquiring oxidative and nitrosative killing capacity, and fusing with lysosomes to destroy engulfed microbes. Mycobacterium tuberculosis blocks this progression, and the resulting suppression of phagosomal maturation converts a degradative compartment into a protected replicative niche, which is why the bacterium persists inside macrophages and establishes latent infection. The pathway assembles the host machinery that is targeted: the small GTPases RAB5A and RAB7A that mark early and late phagosome identity, the tethering factor VPS33B and the ESCRT component HGS that drive fusion with lysosomal compartments, the vacuolar ATPase subunit ATP6V1H required for lumenal acidification, and inducible nitric oxide synthase for antimicrobial radical production. Retention of coronin-1A on the phagosome and interference with importin-dependent nuclear transport and ubiquitin signalling further stall maturation, linking membrane trafficking to the outcome of innate immune killing.

When a macrophage engulfs Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the bacterium lands in a phagosome that is acidifying, metal-starved and filling with reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, and is destined to fuse with lysosomes. This pathway covers that host-pathogen confrontation and the bacterial countermeasures that make tuberculosis a persistent, sometimes latent, infection rather than a cleared one. The host side is recognisable in the genes: Rab5 and Rab7 mark early-to-late phagosome conversion, VPS33B and HGS act in membrane tethering and endosomal sorting, a vacuolar ATPase subunit drives lumenal acidification, and NOS2 supplies nitric oxide. Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-ligase components support targeting of the bacterial compartment for autophagic capture, while ERK signalling and coronin-1A, which Mtb exploits to block lysosomal delivery, illustrate how arrest of phagosome maturation permits intracellular survival and later reawakening.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis that escapes the phagosome into the cytosol of macrophages and other phagocytes triggers a necrosis-like death of the host cell, and this route of killing serves the bacterium rather than the host. Where apoptosis of an infected macrophage sequesters bacilli in membrane-bound bodies that can be cleared by neighbouring cells, lytic death spills viable organisms into the extracellular space, seeding new phagocytes and driving tissue damage in the granuloma. The switch from contained apoptotic death to membrane rupture is therefore a determinant of whether infection is controlled or progresses to cavitary disease and transmission. Cytosolic access depends on mycobacterial secretion machinery that permeabilises the phagosomal membrane, after which mitochondrial injury, loss of plasma membrane integrity and release of bacteria and inflammatory contents follow. This makes host cell death modality a central variable in tuberculosis pathogenesis and in host-directed therapy.

Iron is scarce in the host because it is locked into transferrin, lactoferrin and heme, and enterobacterial pathogens overcome that barrier by secreting enterobactin, the catecholate siderophore with the highest known affinity for ferric iron. Iron assimilation using enterobactin lets bacteria extract iron from host binding proteins and even strip it from competing chelators, supplying the metal needed for respiration, DNA synthesis and oxidative stress defence, and thereby underwriting growth during infection. Apo-siderophore is exported, binds Fe(III) in the extracellular space, and the loaded complex is recaptured by dedicated outer-membrane and periplasmic transport systems before the iron is released intracellularly. The host counters with lipocalin-2, which sequesters enterobactin directly, and this reciprocal capture and counter-capture is one of the clearest arenas of nutritional immunity and host-pathogen coevolution at the level of metal acquisition.

Metal ion assimilation from the host describes how bacterial pathogens strip iron and other trace metals from human tissue in order to grow, and how the host tries to withhold them. Iron is scarce in the body because it is locked inside heme and carrier proteins, so enterobacteria secrete siderophores such as enterobactin, salmochelin, yersiniabactin and aerobactin to capture ferric ion at high affinity, take up the loaded complexes through dedicated outer-membrane receptors, and separately import ferrous iron under acidic or anaerobic conditions. Hemolysins lyse erythrocytes and free hemoglobin, whose alpha and beta globin chains yield heme that is imported and degraded to release the metal. Zinc, manganese, cobalt, nickel and copper are scavenged by analogous transporters. This nutritional tug-of-war is a determinant of virulence, and the host counters it with nutritional immunity through iron and manganese sequestration.

Bacterial pathogens colonising a mammalian host must extract iron and other transition metals from tissues in which those metals are deliberately kept scarce, and this metal ion assimilation from the host determines whether an infection can establish. Iron is the limiting nutrient: it circulates complexed in heme within hemoglobin, whose alpha and beta globin chains are represented here as the host-derived substrate. Hemolysins lyse erythrocytes and release hemoglobin, from which heme is captured, imported and degraded to liberate Fe2+, while free ferric iron is scavenged by high-affinity siderophores such as enterobactin, aerobactin, yersiniabactin and salmochelin and taken up as chelate complexes. Distinct transport systems handle zinc, manganese, cobalt, nickel and copper. Because host nutritional immunity works by sequestering exactly these ions, the acquisition machinery is concentrated in pathogenic strains and behaves as a virulence determinant.

Mucosal surfaces clear microbes by flushing and shedding them, so a pathogen that cannot hold on cannot colonize; bacterial attachment to epithelial cells is the step at which that clearance is defeated. The host molecules listed here are the docking sites: fibronectin, type IV and type V collagens, and the full range of laminin chains that make up the basement membrane, together with the epithelial surface proteins EpCAM and uroplakin 1A. Bacterial adhesins, displayed on the cell surface or at the tips of pili, bind these extracellular matrix and junctional components, anchoring enterobacteria and other pathogens to intestinal, respiratory and urogenital epithelium. Adhesion of this kind is the first virulence step in urinary tract infection and diarrhoeal disease, preceding invasion, toxin delivery and biofilm formation, and it explains why matrix exposure at sites of epithelial injury increases susceptibility to infection.

Antimicrobial drugs work by attacking bacterial structures and processes that human cells lack or build differently — cell wall synthesis, the ribosome, DNA replication and folate metabolism — and the combined view of antimicrobial action and antimicrobial resistance sets those drug targets alongside the bacterial countermeasures that blunt them. This matters because the same targets define both therapeutic success and its loss: enzymes that hydrolyse or chemically modify a drug, efflux pumps that expel it, target mutations or ribosomal methylation that lower its affinity, and altered porins that keep it out of the cell. Resistance determinants often travel on plasmids and transposons, so selection during treatment spreads them between organisms rather than only within a lineage. Understanding which step a drug blocks, and how that step can be protected, is the basis of combination therapy, resistance surveillance and the search for new antibacterial chemistry.

Antimicrobials are compounds that kill microorganisms or halt their growth, whether given to a patient as antibiotics, antifungals or antiparasitics, applied to skin as antiseptics, or used on surfaces as disinfectants. Their action is the basis of treating infectious disease, and its erosion through resistance returns routine infections and surgery to lethality. The logic is simple: permanently blocking any pathway the microbe cannot do without is sufficient to kill it, so drugs are aimed at targets the host either lacks or builds differently. Broad-spectrum agents therefore hit processes conserved across a whole taxonomic group, most often ribosomal protein synthesis, cell wall and membrane construction, nucleic acid replication, or folate metabolism, while narrower agents exploit organism-specific enzymes. Selectivity for the symbiont over host cells sets both the therapeutic window and the toxicity of these compounds.

Cells only commit to growth when building blocks are available, and this is the amino acid arm of that decision: nutrient sufficiency at the lysosomal surface licenses mTORC1 to drive protein and lipid synthesis and to shut off autophagy. Sensors read individual amino acids directly — sestrins bind leucine, CASTOR1 binds arginine, SAMTOR reads S-adenosylmethionine as a proxy for methionine — and their release from GATOR2 relieves inhibition of the GATOR1 complex, a GTPase-activating protein for the Rag GTPases. Ragulator tethers the RagA/B–RagC/D heterodimer to the membrane alongside the v-ATPase, and the transporter SLC38A9 acts as an arginine-dependent exchange factor, so that mTORC1 is recruited to meet RHEB and be activated. Loss of GATOR1 subunits causes focal epilepsy; FLCN mutation causes Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome.

Tuberculosis therapy depends on a handful of drugs that shut down pathways Mycobacterium tuberculosis cannot do without, and this pathway covers both how those compounds act inside the infected host and how the bacillus evades them. Isoniazid and ethionamide are prodrugs activated by mycobacterial enzymes to block mycolic acid synthesis for the cell envelope; rifampicin blocks RNA polymerase; fluoroquinolones poison DNA gyrase; aminoglycosides and other translation inhibitors bind the ribosome. Because the targets are essential and conserved, resistance arises mainly by mutating the drug target, losing the activating enzyme, modifying or effluxing the compound, or by drug tolerance in slow-growing, granuloma-resident and biofilm-like populations.
