The consequence of failure is clinical: multidrug- and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis, long regimens, and treatment relapse, making this biology central to infectious disease control and antimicrobial stewardship rather than to any single host process.

Enterobacteriaceae are ordinary gut residents, yet pathogenic strains invade tissue, secrete toxins, and spread to the urinary tract, airways, peritoneum, meninges and bloodstream, making them a leading cause of diarrhoea, urinary tract infection, pneumonia and sepsis, increasingly hard to treat as resistance plasmids circulate. The host side of infection with enterobacteria shows up here as the surfaces bacteria grab and breach and the defences mounted against them: basement membrane and matrix components such as the collagen IV and laminin families, fibronectin, and epithelial proteins including EpCAM and a urothelial uroplakin serve as adhesion and invasion substrates for fimbriae and bacterial proteases. Against cytosolic bacteria and their lipopolysaccharide, guanylate-binding proteins coat pathogen-containing vacuoles and license caspase-4 to trigger inflammasome-driven pyroptosis, while ubiquitin and a conjugating enzyme support targeting of bacteria for degradation. Calmodulin and haemoglobin chains reflect toxin activation and iron acquisition during infection.

Wax biosynthesis produces the esters of long-chain fatty alcohols and long-chain fatty acids that coat the skin surface, keeping it supple and resistant to water loss and abrasion. In humans this chemistry is concentrated in sebaceous glands and the meibomian glands of the eyelid, where wax esters dominate the secreted lipid film; loss of these lipids leaves skin dry and the tear film unstable. Two steps are defined enzymatically: peroxisomal fatty acyl-CoA reductases FAR1 and FAR2 reduce activated fatty acids to fatty alcohols, and the acyl-CoA wax alcohol acyltransferases AWAT1 and AWAT2 esterify those alcohols in the endoplasmic reticulum. An unidentified transport step must move alcohols between the two compartments, since co-expression of the reductases and transferases is sufficient to make non-sebaceous cells produce wax. FAR1 also supplies alcohols for ether lipid synthesis.

Wax esters are long-chain fatty alcohols esterified to long-chain fatty acids, and their synthesis supplies the sebaceous lipids that waterproof skin and hair and protect the surface from drying and abrasion. The route has two characterized enzymatic steps in humans. Fatty acyl-CoA reductases FAR1 and FAR2, anchored in the peroxisomal membrane, reduce activated fatty acids to fatty alcohols; the alcohols then reach the endoplasmic reticulum, where the acyltransferases AWAT1 and AWAT2 condense them with acyl-CoA to give the finished ester. How alcohols move between the two compartments is unresolved, but co-expression of a reductase with an acyltransferase is sufficient to make non-sebaceous cells produce wax, arguing the transfer step is not limiting. The same reductase activity also feeds ether lipid and plasmalogen synthesis, linking sebum production to peroxisomal lipid metabolism more broadly.

STAT5A and STAT5B are closely related transcription factors that convert cytokine and growth factor signals at the cell surface into programmes of survival, proliferation and differentiation, most conspicuously in haematopoietic progenitors and lymphocytes. STAT5 activation depends on receptor-associated tyrosine kinase activity: here the receptor FLT3, engaged by its ligand FLT3LG, autophosphorylates and recruits the adaptors GRB2 and GAB2 together with the phosphatase PTPN11, building a signalling platform from which STAT5 is tyrosine phosphorylated, dimerises and moves to the nucleus to drive genes such as those for cyclins and anti-apoptotic BCL2 family members. Because this output is growth-promoting, it is a frequent target of oncogenic hijacking; internal tandem duplication of FLT3 in acute myeloid leukaemia produces ligand-independent, constitutive STAT5 signalling and is one basis for kinase inhibitor therapy in that disease.

Gram-negative bacteria make lipopolysaccharide through a heptose sugar intermediate, and host cells exploit that intermediate as an unmistakable signature of bacterial invasion. Alpha-protein kinase 1 is the cytosolic receptor for it: ADP-heptose binds ALPK1 directly, activating its kinase domain so it phosphorylates the adaptor TIFA. Phosphorylated TIFA oligomerizes into a signalling platform that recruits and activates TRAF6, whose ubiquitin ligase activity builds polyubiquitin chains that engage TAB2/TAB3 and thereby switch on the TAK1 (MAP3K7) kinase complex with its TAB1 partner. TAK1 then drives NF-κB into the nucleus and turns on proinflammatory cytokine and chemokine genes. This surveillance operates in epithelial cells of the gut and stomach, shaping responses to Helicobacter, Shigella and Burkholderia; loss of ALPK1 abolishes the inflammatory reaction, while activating mutations cause autoinflammatory disease with uveitis and hearing loss.

Loss of p14ARF function disables the intrinsic, mitochondrial route to apoptosis and is one way tumours escape p53-dependent death. p14ARF is one of two proteins encoded in overlapping reading frames at the CDKN2A locus, and it normally couples oncogenic stress to p53 stabilisation; beyond that nuclear role it also travels to mitochondria, where binding to the matrix protein C1QBP supports permeabilisation of the outer membrane and caspase activation. Cancer-derived missense changes in the arginine-rich C-terminus abolish the C1QBP interaction, so stressed cells that should commit to apoptosis instead survive and propagate damage. Because the reading frames differ, many of these substitutions leave p16INK4A intact, separating the apoptotic defect from the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor arm of the same locus. The result is a tumour-suppressor failure specific to programmed cell death rather than to cell cycle arrest.

Cells that should die and do not are the substrate of cancer, and this collection covers how programmed cell death goes wrong in disease and thereby permits malignant survival and resistance to chemotherapy. Loss of TP53 function, silencing of BH3-only genes such as BCL2L11 by DNA methyltransferases and Polycomb repressive complex 2 components including EZH2, SUZ12 and EED, and altered caspase regulation all raise the threshold for death. Also represented is regulated necrosis: RIPK1, RIPK3 and MLKL acting downstream of death-receptor adaptors FADD, TRADD and TRAF2, with gasdermin E linking caspase cleavage to lytic, inflammatory death. Calpains, CDK5 and its activator, lamins and nuclear histone substrates mark the execution stage where chromatin and the nuclear envelope are dismantled. Failure at any step shifts the balance between tumour suppression, inflammation and survival.

Cells that acquire an activated oncogene normally respond by entering an irreversible growth arrest, and p14ARF is one of the sensors that enforces it. Encoded by an alternative reading of the CDKN2A locus that is independent of p16INK4A, p14ARF binds the ubiquitin ligase MDM2 and prevents it from degrading p53, so that oncogenic stress is converted into stable p53 accumulation and oncogene-induced senescence. This arm of the tumour suppressor response fails when exon 1beta is deleted, when splice donor mutations abolish the ARF transcript, or when frameshift and missense changes strip the protein of its MDM2-interacting and nucleolar localisation capacity; mislocalisation of otherwise wild-type p14ARF to the cytosol has the same effect. Cells that escape senescence this way continue to proliferate with an active oncogene, a route to familial and sporadic melanoma and to aggressive thyroid papillary carcinoma.

Cells that accumulate oxidative damage normally exit the cell cycle permanently, and p14ARF is one of the switches that enforces this. Encoded by an alternative reading frame of the CDKN2A locus, p14ARF sequesters the ubiquitin ligase MDM2 so that p53 escapes degradation and accumulates, imposing oxidative stress induced senescence as a barrier to the proliferation of damaged cells. Loss of this arm of the locus lets such cells continue dividing. Mutations that truncate or misfold the protein, delete its dedicated first exon, or disrupt its splice donor site abolish p53 stabilization while leaving the separate p16INK4A product intact, and mislocalization of otherwise wild-type protein out of the nucleus and nucleolus has the same effect. The resulting senescence evasion underlies familial melanoma predisposition and contributes to aggressive thyroid papillary carcinoma, placing this biology within tumour suppression by the p53 network.

Aggrephagy is the selective autophagic clearance of protein aggregates that the proteasome cannot handle, and it is the cell's last defence against the accumulation of misfolded, insoluble protein. Its failure underlies inclusion-body diseases of neurons, where aggregated species persist and become toxic. Misfolded proteins are tagged with ubiquitin, recognised by HDAC6, and hauled along microtubules by the dynein motor complex to the microtubule-organizing centre, where centrosomal and intermediate filament components such as pericentrin and vimentin enclose them in a single aggresome that is then engulfed by autophagosomes. The pathway is coordinated with the heat shock response through HSF1 and HSP90, and draws in AAA-ATPase and E3 ligase activity via VCP and parkin, linking it to mitochondrial quality control. Substrates include misfolded CFTR and aggregation-prone neurodegeneration proteins, making this a central arm of cytoplasmic proteostasis.

When misfolded proteins outpace what the proteasome can handle, cells sequester them into a single perinuclear inclusion and clear it by autophagy — the route known as aggrephagy. This gives cells a disposal option for aggregation-prone species that cannot be threaded into a proteasome, and its failure underlies inclusion-body pathology in neurodegeneration and the retention of misfolded CFTR. Ubiquitin tags on the substrate, added and extended with the help of conjugating enzymes, are read by HDAC6, which links cargo to dynein motors that haul it along microtubules toward the centrosome; tubulins, pericentrin and centrin mark that destination. There the material is caged by vimentin intermediate filaments to form an aggresome. Chaperone and unfoldase activity from HSP90, VCP and the HSF1-driven stress response, together with PRKN and PARK7, feeds the inclusion into autophagic degradation, tying protein quality control to microtubule transport.

Newly made glycoproteins arriving in the cis-Golgi have their N-glycans reshaped before they can be built into the complex and hybrid structures found on mature secreted and surface proteins. Trimming and elongation here is the committed step of that conversion: class I α-1,2-mannosidases remove up to four mannose residues from the Man9 structure delivered by the endoplasmic reticulum, and an N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase then adds the first GlcNAc to the trimmed core, licensing all downstream branching in the medial and trans-Golgi. Endomannosidase provides an alternative entry route by excising glucose-bearing mannose from glycans that escaped glucose removal in the ER, salvaging them into the main itinerary. Some glycans bypass trimming altogether and travel on as oligomannose forms. The balance struck at this bifurcation determines glycan heterogeneity on receptors, adhesion molecules and therapeutic glycoproteins.

RAS proteins are only able to signal when they are correctly anchored to membranes, and RAS processing is the series of lipid and proteolytic modifications that puts them there. A newly made RAS polypeptide is farnesylated by the farnesyltransferase subunits FNTA and FNTB, then trimmed at its C-terminus by RCE1 and carboxymethylated by ICMT, after which HRAS and NRAS acquire palmitoyl groups via the ZDHHC9-GOLGA7 acyltransferase complex. Depalmitoylating hydrolases of the ABHD17 family and LYPLA1 reverse that step, so cycles of acylation continuously redistribute RAS between Golgi and plasma membrane, while PDE6D and ARL2 solubilise and deliver prenylated cargo. Ubiquitination adds a further layer of control on localisation. Without these steps RAS cannot recruit or activate RAF, and the same enzymes have been pursued as indirect ways to disable oncogenic KRAS signalling in tumours.

EML4 and NUDC in mitotic spindle formation describes how a microtubule-binding protein and its partner are handed off at mitotic entry to build a spindle capable of capturing chromosomes. It matters because accurate attachment of microtubule ends to kinetochores and alignment of chromosomes at the metaphase plate determine whether daughter cells inherit a correct genome; failure produces missegregation and aneuploidy. In interphase EML4 binds and stabilises microtubules, but phosphorylation by the NEK6/NEK7/NEK9 kinase module releases it, permitting the dynamic microtubule turnover a spindle requires. Through its WD40 repeats EML4 recruits NUDC to kinetochores, where it acts alongside the constitutive centromere proteins, the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes, the RZZ and spindle assembly checkpoint machinery, dynein with its LIS1/NDEL1 regulators, and Aurora B. The N-terminal region of EML4 is also the fusion partner that creates constitutively active ALK in a subset of non-small cell lung cancers.

Cells entering mitosis must convert a stable interphase microtubule array into a dynamic spindle that captures every chromosome, and EML4 together with NUDC is required for that switch, for attaching spindle microtubule ends to kinetochores, and for aligning chromosomes at the metaphase plate. EML4 is a WD40-repeat protein that binds and stabilizes interphase microtubules; phosphorylation by the NEK6 and NEK7 kinases at mitotic entry releases it from microtubules, while its WD40 repeats recruit NUDC to kinetochores. The surrounding machinery here is the kinetochore itself — centromeric CENP proteins, the NDC80 and MIS12 complexes, spindle assembly checkpoint components, depolymerizing kinesins, dynein with its NDE1/NDEL1 and LIS1 regulators, Aurora B and PP2A phosphatase modules, and α/β-tubulins. Errors produce misaligned chromosomes and aneuploidy; rearrangement fusing EML4 to ALK drives a recurrent subset of non-small cell lung cancer.

Maturation of N-linked glycans requires that the high-mannose structure delivered from the endoplasmic reticulum be cut back before complex sugars can be added, and this trimming step is the committed entry into that route. In the cis-Golgi, alpha-1,2-mannosidases remove the outer alpha-1,2-linked mannose residues from Man9, Man8 or Man7 GlcNAc2 to leave Man5GlcNAc2, the substrate that GlcNAc transferase activity then extends toward hybrid and complex glycans. Three calcium-dependent class I enzymes, MAN1A1, MAN1A2 and MAN1C1, carry out the reaction; they differ in tissue distribution and in the order in which they attack the three mannose branches, but converge on the same five-mannose product. Because glycan structure governs receptor half-life, cell adhesion, immune recognition and lysosomal targeting, this trimming shapes the surface and secreted glycoproteome rather than any single protein.

Response of EIF2AK1 (HRI) to heme deficiency is the arm of the integrated stress response that matches globin synthesis to heme supply during red cell formation. It matters because without it, developing erythroblasts keep translating globin they cannot fold, producing heme-free aggregates, ineffective erythropoiesis and anemia under iron deficiency; the same axis influences fetal hemoglobin levels and is of interest in hemoglobinopathies. HRI binds heme at two sites, and loss of heme from the kinase insert domain releases inhibition, allowing autophosphorylation and phosphorylation of eIF2-alpha. This dampens general translation, especially of ribosomal proteins, while selectively promoting translation of upstream-ORF mRNAs such as ATF4, ATF5 and DDIT3. ATF4 then drives amino acid and redox genes including ASNS and CHAC1, feedback regulators GADD34 and TRIB3, and GRB10 to restrain mTORC1; unresolved stress tips toward CHOP-dependent apoptosis. HRI is also activated by oxidative, heat and osmotic stress.

Developing red cells must make globin only as fast as heme is available, and this heme-sensing arm of the integrated stress response is how they match the two. EIF2AK1, the heme-regulated inhibitor, binds heme at two sites; when heme dissociates from the kinase insert domain the kinase autophosphorylates and phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eIF2, damping general translation while favouring mRNAs with upstream open reading frames. The result is induction of ATF4, ATF5 and DDIT3 together with partner factors CEBPB and CEBPG and targets such as ASNS, CHAC1 and TRIB3, plus GRB10 to restrain mTORC1 and PPP1R15A to reverse the phosphorylation and end the response. Losing this control leaves heme-free globin to aggregate, and in iron deficiency produces ineffective erythropoiesis and anemia; the same kinase also responds to oxidative, heat and osmotic stress and influences fetal hemoglobin levels.

Humans cannot make pyridoxal 5'-phosphate de novo, so all of it comes from dietary pyridoxine, pyridoxal and pyridoxamine, and vitamin B6 activation to pyridoxal phosphate is the salvage route that converts these vitamers into the usable cofactor. PLP is the working group of transaminases and of decarboxylases that make GABA, serotonin and dopamine, and of enzymes in heme synthesis, glycine cleavage and transsulfuration, so the supply of active cofactor sets the capacity for amino acid and neurotransmitter metabolism. Only two committed steps are needed: pyridoxal kinase phosphorylates the free vitamers, and pyridoxine 5'-phosphate oxidase oxidizes the pyridoxine and pyridoxamine phosphates to PLP; an aldehyde oxidase also handles pyridoxal turnover. Loss of the oxidase step causes neonatal epileptic encephalopathy that responds to PLP rather than pyridoxine, showing how directly brain excitability depends on this conversion.

RAS proteins act as binary switches that relay growth factor signals from receptors to the MAPK and PI3K routes, and they only work because the switch turns off. Exchange factors load GTP; GTPase activating proteins accelerate the intrinsically slow hydrolysis that returns the protein to its GDP-bound off state. Oncogenic substitutions break the off step of the RAS GTPase cycle, chiefly at glycine 12, glycine 13 and glutamine 61, where the altered residues obstruct nucleophilic attack on the gamma phosphate of GTP; rarer changes speed GDP release or blunt GAP responsiveness. Either way the protein accumulates in the GTP-bound form and drives proliferative signalling without a ligand. Mutations in KRAS, NRAS and HRAS are among the most common drivers in pancreatic, colorectal and lung cancer and in melanoma, and they also underlie developmental RASopathies.

Oncogenic point mutations in HRAS, KRAS or NRAS lock the GTPase in its GTP-loaded state, so that signaling downstream of RAS mutants proceeds without upstream receptor input. This is one of the commonest routes to human cancer, driving proliferation, resistance to apoptosis and transformation in pancreatic, colorectal and lung tumours, and it explains why blocking growth factor receptors above the lesion fails. Constitutive RAS:GTP recruits the RAF kinases ARAF, BRAF and RAF1 to the membrane, where scaffolds and modulators such as KSR1/2, CNKSR proteins, 14-3-3 and the RAF inhibitor PEBP1 govern dimerisation and activity, and MAP2K1/2 then phosphorylate ERK1 and ERK2. Calcium-calmodulin and CaMKII inputs, SRC and its negative regulator CSK, and RAP1 with integrin-adhesion components including talin, vinculin and IQGAP1 feed into and shape the same output.

Signaling by MAP2K mutants describes how activating mutations in MEK1 and MEK2 lock the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade into a constitutively active state, driving proliferation independently of upstream growth factor input. Such mutations appear at low frequency across many cancers, including melanoma, lung and colorectal tumours, and in the germline they cause developmental disorders of the RASopathy family such as Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes, where dysregulated ERK output distorts craniofacial, cardiac and skin development. Mechanistically the mutant kinases escape the autoinhibitory constraints normally imposed by their regulatory helix and by RAF-dependent activation, so they phosphorylate ERK1 and ERK2 persistently, sustaining transcriptional programs for cell cycle entry and survival. Because these variants can also confer resistance to RAF-directed therapy, they matter clinically for the choice and sequencing of MAPK pathway inhibitors.

MEK1 and MEK2 are the kinases that sit between RAF and ERK, and mutations that lock them in an active state drive constitutive output through this arm of the RAS-ERK cascade. Signaling by MAP2K mutants describes that deregulated state: altered MAP2K1 or MAP2K2 phosphorylate the ERK1 and ERK2 kinases regardless of upstream input, sustaining proliferative and survival transcription programmes without growth factor stimulation. Such alleles arise somatically at low frequency across many tumour types, including melanoma, lung and colorectal cancer and histiocytic neoplasms, and also in the germline, where they produce Noonan and cardiofaciocutaneous syndromes and related RASopathies with their characteristic cardiac, craniofacial and skin features. Because mutations in the negative-regulatory and allosteric regions can bypass RAF dependence, they are a recognised route to resistance against RAF- and MEK-directed inhibitors, making the identity of the mutation clinically consequential.

ERBB2 (HER2) is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose amplification drives an aggressive subset of breast and gastric cancers, and blocking it is one of the clearest successes of targeted cancer therapy. Two drug classes converge on this receptor: small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib, which occupy the ATP-binding site and shut down catalytic activity, and monoclonal antibodies such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab, which bind the extracellular domain to prevent dimerisation and promote receptor downregulation. Loss of signalling removes the proliferative and survival input normally relayed to PI3K/AKT and MAPK cascades. The accompanying chaperone machinery, HSP90 with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, stabilises ERBB2 and is itself a drug target, while ERBIN binds the receptor and restrains its signalling. Resistance commonly arises through kinase-domain mutation or bypass activation of related receptors.

Cancer-associated mutations in ERK2 (MAPK1) illustrate how a signalling terminus can be locked on without a new upstream input. Such variants are uncommon but recurrent in cervical carcinoma and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, where they sustain output from the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK cascade that drives proliferation, survival and differentiation decisions. Mutant ERK generally still requires activating phosphorylation by MEK on its activation loop, but escapes the phosphatases that would normally shut it off. Those phosphatases are the dual-specificity MAP kinase phosphatases represented here, including the cytoplasmic ERK-directed DUSP6 and DUSP7 and the JNK/p38-preferring DUSP8, DUSP10 and DUSP16, which remove phosphate from the threonine and tyrosine of the TxY motif. Resistance to this dephosphorylation prolongs ERK activity and contributes to tumour growth and to reduced sensitivity to inhibitors acting upstream in the pathway.

RAF1 (CRAF) sits between RAS and the MEK-ERK kinases, and mutations that loosen its autoinhibition make that relay fire without upstream input. Germline changes clustered in the regulatory CR2 region and in the CR3 activation segment cause Noonan and related RASopathies, with craniofacial, cardiac and growth features, and similar lesions appear at low frequency in tumours. Normally RAF1 is held shut by 14-3-3 binding to phosphorylated CR2 serines; mutants lose this restraint, dimerise with BRAF or ARAF, and drive MAP2K1/2 and ERK1/2 activation that sustains proliferation and survival programmes. Scaffolds such as KSR1/2 and CNKSR proteins organise the cascade, while RAS and RAP1 GTPases, SRC and CSK, calmodulin and CaMKII set its output. Integrin and cytoskeletal partners including talin, vinculin, IQGAP1 and fibrinogen chains link this signalling to adhesion and platelet function.

Oxygen metabolism constantly converts guanine to 8-oxoguanine, a lesion that mispairs with adenine and drives G:C to T:A transversions unless it is excised, and OGG1 is the glycosylase that recognizes it and starts base excision repair by cleaving the damaged base from the deoxyribose. When OGG1 activity is lost or weakened, this first and committing step of the repair route fails, 8-oxoguanine persists through replication, and mutations accumulate genome-wide. A common coding polymorphism that reduces activity is associated with elevated breast and lung cancer risk, inactivating mutations appear in several tumour types and in Alzheimer's disease, and mice lacking the enzyme are cancer-prone. Defective repair of this kind links oxidative stress directly to genome instability, and places OGG1 among the caretaker functions whose failure permits, rather than causes, transformation.

Oxidative attack on DNA converts guanine to 8-oxoguanine, a lesion that mispairs with adenine and fixes G:C to T:A transversions unless it is removed. The glycosylase OGG1 finds this lesion in duplex DNA, flips it out, and excises the damaged base to start base excision repair, which then replaces the missing nucleotide. Defective substrate binding by OGG1 describes variants that fail at the recognition step: missense changes reported in Alzheimer's disease patients bind 8-oxoguanine-containing DNA poorly, so the lesion is left in place even though the rest of the repair pathway is intact. The consequence is a rising burden of oxidative DNA damage and mutation in tissues with high oxygen consumption, a link that connects this repair activity to neurodegeneration and to cancer predisposition more generally.

Oxygen radicals convert guanine in DNA to 8-oxoguanine and ring-opened FapyG, lesions that mispair with adenine and generate G:C to T:A transversions unless removed. OGG1 is the DNA glycosylase that finds these oxidised bases and cleaves them out to begin base excision repair; defective substrate processing by mutant OGG1 describes the loss of that first catalytic step. Variants affecting substrate recognition and the glycosylase active site, including R46Q, R131Q, R154H and R229Q, retain little or no capacity to excise 8-oxoguanine, and some also fail on FapyG; a truncating frameshift removes the activity outright. The common S326C polymorphism is itself oxidation-sensitive, so its repair capacity falls exactly when oxidative stress is highest. The consequence is an accumulating mutational burden linked to cancer predisposition, tying antioxidant defence to genome stability.

Oxidative attack on DNA produces 8-oxoguanine, a lesion that mispairs with adenine and drives G-to-T transversions unless it is excised; the glycosylase OGG1 initiates that repair by removing the damaged base and handing the abasic site to the rest of the base excision repair route. Alternative splicing determines where the enzyme works: the beta isoform carries an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence and lacks the C-terminal nuclear localization signal, so it is delivered to mitochondria rather than the nucleus, where it may contribute to repair of the mitochondrial genome. Mislocalization is the defect described here: a G12E substitution reported in kidney cancer disrupts the targeting sequence and prevents import, leaving the protein unable to reach mitochondrial DNA. The theme is compartment-specific genome maintenance against oxidative damage, and its loss as a route to mutagenesis and tumour development.

Hereditary angioedema arising from defective factor XII describes how mutant FXII drives the recurrent, potentially fatal swelling of skin, gut mucosa and upper airway that defines this disorder. Normally the contact system's plasma proteases are held in check by the C1 inhibitor, so bradykinin release from high molecular weight kininogen stays limited; in the rare form with normal C1 inhibitor activity, substitutions at threonine 328 in the FXII proline-rich region alter glycosylation and create a new cleavage site attacked by plasmin, thrombin or factor XIa. The resulting truncated FXII both converts prekallikrein to kallikrein more readily and is a better kallikrein substrate, so the reciprocal activation loop with KLKB1 accelerates beyond what inhibition can restrain. Excess bradykinin then acts on B2 receptors of postcapillary venules, raising vascular permeability and causing fluid efflux into tissue.

Plasma contact activation runs as a self-amplifying loop: factor XII bound to a negatively charged surface autoactivates, converts prekallikrein to kallikrein, and kallikrein in turn activates more factor XII while cleaving high molecular weight kininogen to release bradykinin. Bradykinin acting on its B2 receptor on endothelium raises vascular permeability and drives fluid into tissue. C1-esterase inhibitor, the serpin encoded by SERPING1, is the brake on every one of these proteases, and heterozygous loss of it or expression of a non-functional protein causes hereditary angioedema, inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Patients suffer recurrent, unpredictable swelling of skin, gut mucosa and upper airway, where laryngeal attacks can be fatal. The same contact system feeds the intrinsic coagulation cascade through factor XI, linking uncontrolled kinin generation to inflammation and clotting rather than to histamine-driven allergy.

Leishmania parasites are taken up by macrophages and survive inside the very cell meant to destroy them, and this collection of host processes covers that encounter: receptor-mediated uptake, the killing mechanisms switched on afterwards, and the signalling the parasite subverts to persist. The outcome determines whether infection resolves or progresses to cutaneous or visceral leishmaniasis. Opsonised promastigotes engage Fc gamma receptors and complement receptors, with immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable regions supplying the opsonising antibody and C3 the complement arm; Src-family and Syk kinases, BTK, VAV exchange factors and Rac1/CDC42 then drive Arp2/3- and WASP/WAVE-dependent actin remodelling for phagocytic cup closure. Killing depends on NADPH oxidase components and inflammasome assembly through NLRP3, PYCARD, caspase-1 and gasdermin D, releasing IL-1beta and IL-18. Countering this, adenylate cyclase/PKA signalling, adenosine and purinergic receptors, heme oxygenase and IL-10 deactivate the macrophage, tilting the balance toward parasite replication.

Sensory processing of sound is hearing at the level of the cochlea: how mechanical vibration is converted into neural signals by the hair cells of the organ of Corti. It defines the inner and outer hair cell phenotypes, and mutations in its components are the commonest causes of inherited deafness, from Usher syndrome to auditory neuropathy. Stereocilia built on tightly regulated actin bundles are linked tip-to-tip by cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15; deflection tensions these links and gates a mechanotransduction channel formed with TMC1/TMC2, TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2, depolarising the cell. In inner hair cells, voltage-gated calcium entry triggers otoferlin-dependent glutamate release at ribbon synapses scaffolded by RIBEYE, bassoon and piccolo onto spiral ganglion afferents. Outer hair cells instead amplify motion through voltage-driven prestin conformational change, tuned by potassium channels and by cholinergic efferent feedback through the CHRNA9/CHRNA10 receptor. Noise overexposure damages these structures, causing temporary or permanent hearing loss.

Hearing begins when cochlear hair cells convert mechanical vibration into electrical signals, and this is the machinery that makes that conversion possible. Inner hair cells act as the sensory receptors that drive auditory nerve firing, while outer hair cells amplify motion of the organ of Corti; loss of either causes sensorineural deafness, and many of these genes are mutated in inherited hearing loss and Usher syndrome. Stereocilia built from actin, espin, and unconventional myosins are linked tip to tip by cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15, whose tension gates a mechanoelectrical transduction channel containing TMC1/TMC2 with TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2. Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels at ribbon synapses, where otoferlin triggers glutamate release onto spiral ganglion neurons. Prestin drives voltage-dependent outer hair cell length changes, and potassium and calcium pumps plus cholinergic olivocochlear feedback restore and tune the resting state.

The retinoblastoma protein is the gatekeeper of the G1/S transition: by binding activating E2F factors and their DP partners, it keeps genes for DNA replication switched off until a cell has committed to divide. Loss of that restraint is one of the most common events in human cancer, producing unscheduled S-phase entry and proliferation independent of growth signals; germline RB1 defects cause retinoblastoma, and viral oncoproteins such as papillomavirus E7 achieve the same effect by displacing E2F from RB1's pocket region. Normally the switch is set by D- and E-type cyclins with CDK4, CDK6 and CDK2, which progressively phosphorylate RB1, opposed by the CIP/KIP inhibitors p21, p27 and p57. When RB1 is mutated or deleted, E2F1-3 target genes are transcribed constitutively, decoupling replication from upstream signalling and checkpoint control.

RAF kinases are held inactive in part by an inhibitory phosphorylation on their N-terminal region that recruits 14-3-3 proteins, and the MRAS-SHOC2-PP1 holoenzyme is the phosphatase module that strips this mark to license RAF activation and downstream MEK-ERK signalling. MRAS, a RAS-family GTPase, provides membrane targeting and substrate presentation, SHOC2 acts as the regulatory subunit, and PP1 catalytic subunits perform the dephosphorylation of RAF1, BRAF and ARAF. Because this step sets the threshold for growth factor signalling through the MAPK cascade, mutations in any subunit alter RAF output: gain-of-function and loss-of-function changes in MRAS, SHOC2 and PPP1CB underlie Noonan syndrome and related RASopathies, with developmental, cardiac and craniofacial features, and are found at low frequency in cancers. The complex is a point where GTPase signalling and reversible phosphorylation converge on kinase autoinhibition.

Extracellular adenosine, generated when stress, injury or infection releases ATP that is then dephosphorylated by ectonucleotidases, acts as a brake on inflammation, and ADORA2B is the low-affinity receptor that reads high adenosine concentrations and converts them into anti-inflammatory cytokine production. Engagement of this G protein-coupled receptor couples through Gs-containing heterotrimers to adenylate cyclases, raising cAMP, activating protein kinase A and its regulatory subunits, and phosphorylating CREB1 to drive transcription of IL6 and other mediators that dampen macrophage and monocyte killing responses. The same signalling limits tissue damage during ischaemia and injury, but is exploited by pathogens: monocyte ADORA2B expression and adenosine levels track with IL10 output and heavier Leishmania burdens, and with worse lesion development. The pathway therefore sits at the interface of purinergic sensing of cell damage, cAMP-dependent transcriptional control, and the resolution phase of innate immune responses.

Extracellular nucleotides act as danger signals during infection, and this purinergic arm of the macrophage response to Leishmania converts ATP released by stressed or injured tissue into inflammasome activation and parasite killing. ATP-gated channels P2RX7 and P2RX4 admit cation flux that, together with NLRP3, PYCARD and caspase-1, drives maturation of IL-1β and IL-18 and gasdermin D-dependent pyroptosis, eliminating intracellular parasites along with the host cell. NF-κB subunits supply the transcriptional priming step for the cytokine precursors, while TXNIP release from thioredoxin links oxidative stress to sensor assembly. The response is self-limiting: ectonucleotidases ENTPD1 and NT5E hydrolyse ATP to adenosine, which shifts signalling toward anti-inflammatory output and permits parasite persistence. Complement C3 and its receptor tie the cascade to opsonic recognition, and mutations in pyrin or PSTPIP1 cause hereditary autoinflammatory fever syndromes through the same machinery.

The retinoblastoma protein restrains entry into S phase by clamping the activating transcription factors E2F1, E2F2 and E2F3 together with their DP partners, keeping genes for DNA replication switched off until a cell has committed to divide. Cancer-associated mutations in the RB1 pocket domain abolish this binding, so the E2F-DP complexes remain free and drive replication gene expression regardless of growth signals; the loss underlies retinoblastoma and contributes to many sporadic tumours. Normally the switch is timed by phosphorylation: D-type cyclins with CDK4 or CDK6, then cyclin E with CDK2, progressively inactivate RB1, while the CIP/KIP inhibitors p21, p27 and p57 oppose those kinases. Defective RB1 binding short-circuits this restriction point, uncoupling proliferation from the upstream signals and checkpoints that would otherwise arrest the cell cycle in G1.

The retinoblastoma protein restrains cell cycle entry by binding E2F transcription factors and repressing genes needed for S phase, work it can only do inside the nucleus. Certain cancer-associated RB1 alleles truncate or disrupt the C-terminal nuclear localization signal, so the mutant protein is synthesized but stranded in the cytoplasm, away from E2F and from chromatin-modifying partners it normally recruits. The result is functional loss of the checkpoint even when a protein product is present: E2F target genes are expressed without mitogenic licence, and cells progress through the restriction point inappropriately. This defective nuclear translocation of RB1 mutants accounts for a subset of hereditary and sporadic retinoblastoma and contributes to tumour predisposition in osteosarcoma and other cancers, illustrating how mislocalization, rather than altered catalysis or binding, can inactivate a tumour suppressor.

Factor VIII is the cofactor that lets activated factor IX convert factor X to Xa on the surface of activated platelets, amplifying thrombin generation enough to sustain a clot. When F8 is missing, reduced or mutated, this amplification fails and the result is hemophilia A, an X-linked bleeding disorder ranging from bleeding after trauma or surgery to spontaneous joint and muscle haemorrhage. The biology described here covers the routes by which mutant factor VIII causes disease: misfolding and poor secretion from hepatocytes and endothelium, weakened binding to von Willebrand factor so the circulating protein is cleared too fast, impaired thrombin-mediated activation, and defective assembly with factor IXa. Tyrosylprotein sulfotransferases contribute the post-translational sulfation needed for normal factor VIII interactions, linking secretory processing quality control to coagulation competence.

Hearing begins when cochlear inner hair cells convert mechanical sound vibration into an electrical signal and pass it to auditory nerve fibres; loss of any step causes sensorineural deafness, and many of these genes are the classic nonsyndromic and Usher syndrome deafness loci. Apical stereocilia, built and maintained by actin, espins, unconventional myosins and the ankle/tip-link scaffolds whirlin, harmonin and TRIOBP, are arranged in a graded bundle whose tip links pair CDH23 with PCDH15. Deflection tensions these links and opens a mechanotransduction channel containing TMC1 or TMC2 with TMIE, LHFPL5 and CIB2, admitting potassium and calcium from endolymph and depolarizing the cell. Voltage-gated Cav1.3 channels then drive calcium entry at ribbon synapses, where RIBEYE, bassoon and piccolo tether vesicles and otoferlin couples calcium to glutamate release. Calcium pumps and BK and KCNQ4 potassium channels repolarize the cell, shaping temporal precision.

Outer hair cells of the cochlea act as a mechanical amplifier: they shorten and lengthen in time with sound, boosting the vibration of the organ of Corti so that inner hair cells can detect faint tones with sharp frequency tuning. Loss of this electromotility leaves hearing insensitive and poorly tuned, and mutations in these genes cause both syndromic and non-syndromic deafness. Sound deflects apical stereocilia, straining tip links built from cadherin 23 and protocadherin 15 and gating a mechanoelectrical transduction channel containing TMC1 or TMC2 with TMIE, CIB2 and LHFPL5; the resulting K+ and Ca2+ influx changes membrane voltage, and prestin in the lateral wall converts that voltage change into a conformational length change. Repolarization depends on KCNQ4 and the calcium pump ATP2B2, while myosins, espin, radixin and other actin regulators build and maintain the stereociliary bundle itself. Cholinergic receptor subunits mediate efferent feedback that damps amplification.

CD163 is a macrophage scavenger receptor that clears haemoglobin-haptoglobin complexes from tissue, and its high expression marks the anti-inflammatory, resolving macrophage state seen in intracellular infections such as leprosy and leishmaniasis and in chronic inflammatory disease. Induction by IL-10 drives the receptor to the surface, where it limits oxidative damage from free haem and contributes to tissue repair rather than pathogen killing. The receptor is also shed: the metalloprotease ADAM17, whose maturation and trafficking depend on furin cleavage and the iRhom protein RHBDF2, releases a soluble ectodomain under inflammatory stimulation, with p38 signalling promoting the cut. Circulating soluble CD163 tracks macrophage activation and is used as an inflammation biomarker, while proposed activities include bacterial opsonisation and dampening of T-cell proliferation, placing this axis alongside IL-6 and IL-10 in setting the balance between inflammation and its resolution.

Leishmania survives inside the very cells meant to kill it, and this pathway describes the anti-inflammatory macrophage state that makes that possible. Repair-type, Th2-associated macrophages mount weak oxidative and nitrosative killing, so parasites persist and lesions become chronic rather than resolving. Two routes converge here. Opsonising IgG, represented by an extensive repertoire of heavy and light chain variable and constant regions, engages Fc gamma receptors on the phagocyte; receptor clustering signals through Src-family kinases such as LYN, FYN, HCK and FGR together with SYK and phospholipase C gamma isoforms, driving calcium release via inositol trisphosphate receptors and MAPK14 activity, and culminating in IL10 and IL6 output that dampens classical activation. In parallel, G protein-coupled input including adenosine and cysteinyl leukotriene receptors sets adenylate cyclase and protein kinase A tone. The scavenger receptor CD163 marks the permissive, alternatively activated phenotype that shelters the parasite.

Defective DNA double strand break response due to BRCA1 loss of function describes what happens to genome maintenance when cancer-associated mutations disable BRCA1, the tumour suppressor whose germline loss underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome and confers added risk of pancreatic, stomach, fallopian tube and prostate tumours. BRCA1 normally directs homology-directed repair of double-strand breaks, so cells lacking its function accumulate chromosomal rearrangements and genomic instability, and Brca1-null embryos die early. The mechanism turns on the N-terminal RING domain, which heterodimerises with BARD1 to stabilise BRCA1 and confer E3 ubiquitin ligase activity; mutations in this domain abolish BARD1 binding and exclude BRCA1 from the break response, though whether ligase activity itself is required for tumour suppression remains unsettled. The resulting repair deficiency defines the vulnerability exploited by PARP inhibition and platinum chemotherapy.

Loss of BRCA1 function cripples the cell's ability to repair DNA double-strand breaks by homologous recombination, and the consequence is the hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome: early-onset breast and ovarian tumours, with smaller excesses of pancreatic, gastric, prostate and fallopian tube cancer in carriers. BRCA1 acts at breaks as an obligate heterodimer with BARD1, an interaction made through its N-terminal RING domain that stabilises the protein and confers E3 ubiquitin ligase activity; its C-terminal BRCT repeats read phosphorylated partners in the damage response. Cancer-associated RING mutations abolish BARD1 binding, leaving BRCA1 unable to join the repair reaction. Cells then accumulate chromosomal rearrangements and copy-number change, the genomic instability that drives tumour initiation, and become dependent on alternative repair routes -- the basis for the sensitivity of such tumours to PARP inhibition and crosslinking agents.

Rather than bulk self-digestion, cells can pick out a single damaged organelle or protein aggregate and deliver only that to the lysosome. This targeted quality control keeps mitochondria, peroxisomes, lipid droplets and misfolded protein deposits from accumulating, and its failure is tied to Parkinson's disease and other neurodegeneration. Cargo is first marked: PINK1 accumulates on depolarised mitochondria and activates the ubiquitin ligase PRKN, which decorates outer-membrane proteins such as TOMM20, MFN1/2 and the VDAC channels with ubiquitin, opposed by the deubiquitinase USP30. Receptors including SQSTM1, OPTN, NBR1, FUNDC1 and peroxisomal PEX5 bridge the tagged cargo to LC3 on the forming phagophore, while ATG5-ATG12, ULK1 and AMPK subunits drive autophagosome assembly. Dynein motors and microtubules, with HDAC6 and VCP, concentrate aggregates for aggrephagy and move vesicles toward lysosomal fusion.

FCGR3A-mediated IL10 synthesis describes how immune complexes of IgG engaging Fcγ receptors on macrophages drive production of interleukin-10, the principal brake on inflammation. This output limits and terminates inflammatory responses and shapes differentiation of several immune cell types, but the same circuit can be exploited by pathogens: IgG-opsonized Leishmania amastigotes trigger FcγR-dependent IL-10 that suppresses the killing capacity of phagocytes, favouring persistent cutaneous infection. Mechanistically, IgG heavy and light chain variable and constant regions form the ligand; receptor clustering activates Src-family kinases (LYN, FYN, HCK, FGR) and SYK, then phospholipase Cγ and inositol trisphosphate receptor-driven calcium release with calmodulin, alongside adenylate cyclase–cAMP–protein kinase A signalling that converges on CREB1 to transactivate the IL10 gene. It is a clear example of antibody-mediated feedback linking humoral immunity to myeloid anti-inflammatory programming.

IgG immune complexes engaging Fc gamma receptors on macrophages drive production of the anti-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-10, an arm of Fc receptor signalling that restrains rather than amplifies inflammation. This output limits and terminates inflammatory responses and shapes differentiation of other immune cells, but it can be exploited: IgG-opsonized Leishmania amastigotes trigger it to suppress the killing machinery of phagocytes, favouring parasite survival in cutaneous leishmaniasis. Receptor crosslinking by immunoglobulin heavy and light chains recruits Src-family kinases and SYK, activating phospholipase C gamma and inositol trisphosphate receptor-mediated calcium release, while adenylate cyclases and protein kinase A raise cAMP and converge on CREB1 to transcribe IL10. The same circuitry operates alongside Toll-like receptor input, so the balance between activating and immunoregulatory signals determines whether a macrophage clears or harbours an opsonized pathogen.

Leishmania parasites exploit the very phagocytic machinery meant to destroy them, and this pathway captures the host side of that infection: antibody-opsonised promastigotes are recognised by Fc receptors on macrophages and drawn into a phagosome whose maturation the parasite then delays, buying time to convert into the aflagellated amastigote form that replicates inside the parasitophorous vacuole. The gene complement reflects two linked processes. A large repertoire of immunoglobulin heavy, kappa and lambda variable and constant region segments provides the opsonins that engage FCGR3A, while Src-family and Syk/BTK kinases, the adaptors GRB2, CRK, NCK1 and VAV exchange factors, and Rho GTPases CDC42 and RAC1 relay that engagement to actin. Downstream, WASP/WAVE complexes with CYFIP, ABI and NCKAP subunits activate the ARP2/3 complex to polymerise actin, and myosins drive the membrane remodelling that internalises the parasite. The outcome is intracellular persistence and the pathology of cutaneous and visceral leishmaniasis.

Leishmania parasites enter their host by being eaten: macrophages engulf promastigotes and amastigotes, and the parasite then survives inside the very vacuole meant to destroy it, so the route of uptake helps decide whether infection is cleared or established as cutaneous or visceral leishmaniasis. Opsonising immunoglobulins and Fc gamma receptors such as FCGR3A provide one entry route, triggering Src-family kinases (LYN, HCK, FGR, FYN) and SYK, with BTK, adaptors GRB2, CRK and NCK1, and the guanine nucleotide exchange factors VAV1-3 and the DOCK1-ELMO complex activating RAC1 and CDC42. These GTPases drive WASP/WAVE-family nucleation-promoting factors and the ARP2/3 complex to build the branched actin network, while myosins and focal adhesion kinase supply force and adhesion signalling for pseudopod extension and phagosome closure. The same actin machinery serves ordinary phagocytosis and cell migration.

Macrophages that have taken up Leishmania attempt to destroy the parasite inside the phagosome, and the killing mechanisms available to them centre on oxidative attack: assembly of an NADPH oxidase that generates superoxide and downstream reactive oxygen species, alongside reactive nitrogen intermediates and autophagic capture of intracellular organisms. Whether this succeeds determines if infection is cleared or becomes the long-lasting intracellular residency characteristic of leishmaniasis. The genes here link non-canonical WNT input to oxidase output: WNT5A acting through FZD7 and dishevelled proteins, with RAC1 and the NOX1 organiser and activator subunits NOXO1 and NOXA1 plus the membrane component CYBA forming the superoxide-generating complex, and JNK signalling to AP-1 reinforcing the inflammatory transcriptional response. The same chemistry that kills pathogens damages host tissue, so its control matters to lesion severity as well as parasite burden.

Antibody-coated particles are cleared by phagocytes that recognise the IgG Fc region, and FCGR3A-mediated phagocytosis is the engulfment route that follows. It underlies clearance of opsonised microbes, including IgG-coated Leishmania amastigotes during established infection, and the same receptor drives antibody-dependent cytotoxicity exploited by therapeutic antibodies. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable and constant regions supply the opsonin; receptor clustering recruits Src-family kinases such as LYN, FGR and HCK together with SYK and BTK, and adaptors GRB2, CRK, NCK1 and the VAV and DOCK1-ELMO exchange factors. These converge on RAC1 and CDC42, which through WASP, WAVE proteins and the ARP2/3 complex nucleate branched actin, while myosins provide the force to extend pseudopods and close the phagosome. Rac and Cdc42 activity also switches on the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, coupling internalisation to oxidative killing of the ingested target.

Cell recruitment (pro-inflammatory response) is the arm of innate immunity that summons leukocytes to a site of infection and arms them for killing, illustrated here by macrophage encounters with Leishmania. A strong pro-inflammatory burst in acute infection limits parasite load, while a distorted chemokine and cytokine balance permits parasite persistence or drives immunopathology, so the same machinery sets both host defence and tissue damage. Mechanistically the genes centre on the inflammasome: NLRP3 with the adaptor PYCARD and caspase-1 matures IL-1β and IL-18 and cleaves gasdermin D for pyroptotic release, with TXNIP and pyrin among the sensors and modifiers. Extracellular ATP acting through P2RX7 and P2RX4, its hydrolysis by CD39 and CD73, and complement C3–C3AR1 signalling provide the upstream cues, converging on NF-κB-driven transcription of chemoattractant cytokines.

Pro-inflammatory cell recruitment is how an infected tissue calls in leukocytes that can kill intracellular pathogens, and it sets the balance that decides whether an infection such as Leishmania is contained or becomes chronic. A strong early response limits parasite load by bringing in cells with enhanced microbicidal capacity, while a distorted chemokine and cytokine network drives immunopathology or permits parasite survival. Much of the output here is inflammasome-driven: NLRP3 with the adaptor PYCARD and caspase-1 matures IL-1beta and IL-18, and gasdermin D executes the pore-forming, pyroptotic release step; TXNIP and pyrin add further activation inputs. Extracellular nucleotide signalling through P2RX7 and P2RX4 and its termination by ENTPD1 and NT5E tunes the threshold, alongside complement C3 acting on C3AR1 and NF-kB-dependent transcription of the cytokines themselves.</description>

Leishmania survives inside the very macrophages meant to destroy it, and this pathway describes how the parasite bends host signalling toward its own growth and persistence. Opsonised parasites engage Fc gamma receptors, whose ligands here are the full repertoire of immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable and constant regions, recruiting Src-family and Syk kinases and phospholipase C gamma to drive calcium release through inositol trisphosphate receptors. Rather than triggering microbicidal output, this signalling favours anti-inflammatory IL-10 and IL-6 production and cAMP generation through adenylate cyclases, G protein subunits and protein kinase A, blunting killing. Adenosine and cysteinyl leukotriene receptors, the scavenger receptor CD163, and shedding by ADAM17 with its regulator RHBDF2 add further immunomodulatory input. The outcome is impaired antigen presentation and a small persisting parasite reservoir, the basis of chronic and relapsing leishmaniasis.

Leukotriene C4 is a cysteinyl leukotriene made from arachidonic acid, and its action through cysteinyl leukotriene receptors links lipid mediator production to type 2 immunity by driving release of interleukin-4 from eosinophils. This output matters for allergic inflammation and asthma, where cysteinyl leukotrienes constrict airways, promote mucus and vascular leak, and reinforce the Th2 cytokine environment; receptor antagonists of this axis are established asthma drugs. Alongside the surface receptors CYSLTR1 and CYSLTR2, the gamma-glutamyl transferases GGT1 and GGT5 and the dipeptidases DPEP1 and DPEP2 convert LTC4 onward to LTD4 and LTE4, setting which ligand and which receptor dominate. The IL-4-inducing signal is attributed to an intracellular cysteinyl leukotriene receptor acting without the Gq heterotrimeric protein used by the classical receptors, so eicosanoid signalling here is compartmentalised rather than purely extracellular.

Signaling by ERBB2 KD Mutants describes how point mutations and small insertions in the kinase domain of ERBB2 (HER2) convert a growth factor receptor into a constitutively active oncogenic driver. Such mutations are found in breast, lung, gastric and bladder cancers, often without gene amplification, and they define tumours that may respond to HER2-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors, while secondary mutations at the gatekeeper threonine cause acquired resistance. Mutant ERBB2 heterodimerizes more readily with EGFR and ERBB3 in the presence of neuregulins and EGF-family ligands, increasing autophosphorylation and prolonging recruitment of GRB2, SHC1, SOS1 and GAB1 to drive RAS-ERK signalling, and of PI3K subunits to drive PI3K-AKT survival signalling, with PLCG1 as an additional effector. Folding and stability of the mutant receptor still depend on the HSP90:CDC37 chaperone system, and ERBIN restrains its localization. The net output is ligand-hypersensitive proliferation and cellular transformation.

Point mutations and small insertions in the kinase domain of ERBB2 (HER2) make the receptor signal without normal restraint, and these variants drive breast, lung, gastric and bladder cancers even where the gene is not amplified. Substitutions such as L755S, V777L, D769H, V842I and L869R raise intrinsic kinase activity and favour heterodimerization with EGFR or ERBB3, so ligands of the EGF and neuregulin families feed more strongly into growth signalling. The activated dimers recruit GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 to load RAS proteins and engage the MAP kinase route, and recruit GAB1 with PI3K subunits to activate PI3K-AKT signalling, with PLCG1 as an additional effector. HSP90 with CDC37 stabilizes the mutant kinase, and secondary gatekeeper changes at T798 confer resistance to HER2-directed inhibitors.

Pexophagy is the selective autophagic removal of peroxisomes, the organelles that break down branched and very-long-chain fatty acids and detoxify hydrogen peroxide. Because damaged peroxisomes leak reactive oxygen species rather than clearing them, their timely disposal sets the cell's oxidative tone and adjusts peroxisome number to shifting nutrient supply. Recognition depends on ubiquitination of peroxisomal membrane proteins, notably the import receptor PEX5, which is read by the autophagy receptors NBR1 and p62/SQSTM1; these tether the organelle to LC3 on the forming phagophore for delivery to the lysosome. The deubiquitinase USP30 opposes the tagging step and restrains turnover, while ATM signalling links oxidative and ROS-sensing cues, alongside hypoxic signalling through EPAS1, to the decision to degrade. Defective pexophagy leaves dysfunctional peroxisomes accumulating, with consequences for lipid catabolism, redox balance and metabolic adaptation.

Pexophagy is the selective autophagy route that clears surplus or damaged peroxisomes, keeping the organelle population matched to metabolic demand. Because peroxisomes both oxidise branched and very-long-chain fatty acids and generate and detoxify hydrogen peroxide, failure to remove dysfunctional ones allows reactive oxygen species to accumulate, while excessive turnover starves cells of lipid catabolism; the balance shifts with nutrient supply and oxidative stress. Targeting works through ubiquitination of peroxisomal membrane proteins, notably the import receptor PEX5, which recruits the autophagy receptors SQSTM1/p62 and NBR1; these bind LC3 on the forming autophagosome and deliver the organelle to the lysosome. The mitochondrial deubiquitinase USP30 opposes tagging by removing ubiquitin, and ATM signalling links oxidative and stress cues to receptor engagement, placing peroxisome quality control within the broader ubiquitin-dependent organelle turnover system.

HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase amplified or mutated in breast, gastric and other cancers, and blocking it with antibodies such as trastuzumab or with small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors is standard therapy. Point mutations and small insertions within the ERBB2 kinase domain, including L755S, V777L, T798M, L869R and the G778 insertion, change how the receptor engages these drugs and give rise to resistance, so that tumours signal through HER2 despite treatment. The accompanying machinery reflects how such mutant receptors are held in a signalling-competent state: the HSP90 chaperone with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37 stabilises the mutant kinase domain, while ERBIN binds HER2 and constrains its localisation and activity. Understanding this behaviour matters for choosing between antibody and kinase-inhibitor strategies, and explains why irreversible inhibitors or chaperone blockade are pursued when resistance emerges.

Resistance of ERBB2 KD mutants to trastuzumab explains why some HER2-driven breast and gastric cancers fail to respond to the monoclonal antibody trastuzumab even though the receptor is the drug's intended target. Trastuzumab binds the extracellular domain of ERBB2 and blocks its dimerisation and downstream growth signalling, but activating point mutations in the receptor's kinase domain drive signalling from within the cell, where an extracellular antibody cannot reach, so proliferative signalling through the MAPK and PI3K routes continues unabated. Stability of the mutant receptor depends on the HSP90 chaperone system together with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which makes such tumours sensitive to HSP90 inhibition and to small-molecule kinase inhibitors instead; the scaffold ERBIN modulates receptor localisation and signal output. The pathway is a template for acquired and intrinsic targeted-therapy resistance.

Trastuzumab is a therapeutic antibody directed against the extracellular region of the HER2 receptor, and it works in breast and gastric cancers that overexpress the intact receptor. Mutations in the ERBB2 kinase domain, however, activate signalling from inside the cell and so blunt the benefit of an antibody that acts at the surface, making this a route to acquired or intrinsic drug resistance and a reason patients are stratified by mutation rather than by receptor level alone. The mutant receptor remains dependent on chaperone support, with HSP90 and its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37 stabilising the folded kinase domain, while ERBIN binds HER2 and constrains its localisation and output. The biology sits at the junction of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, chaperone-dependent oncoprotein stability, and the rationale for kinase inhibitors or HSP90 blockade when antibody therapy fails.

Point mutations in the kinase domain of ERBB2 (HER2) can blunt the effect of the reversible tyrosine kinase inhibitor sapitinib, so that receptor signalling continues in tumours treated with the drug. This matters clinically in breast, gastric and lung cancers driven by ERBB2, where such substitutions predict which patients will fail targeted therapy and drive selection of alternative or covalent inhibitors. The mutant receptor still dimerises and autophosphorylates, feeding growth and survival signalling downstream of the receptor tyrosine kinase, and its stability at the membrane depends on the HSP90AA1 chaperone with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which protect kinase-domain mutants from degradation. ERBIN binds the receptor's carboxy-terminal tail and constrains its localisation and signalling output. Together these interactions explain why drug binding alone does not extinguish ERBB2 activity in the resistant setting.

Kinase-domain mutations in ERBB2 can blunt the effect of the ATP-competitive inhibitor tesevatinib, and this pathway captures that drug-resistant signalling state. It matters clinically because ERBB2-mutant breast, lung and gastric tumours are treated with small-molecule kinase inhibitors, and mutations that alter the ATP pocket or stabilise the active conformation allow receptor signalling to continue in the presence of drug, driving relapse. The mutant receptor remains dependent on chaperoning for folding and stability: HSP90 with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37 holds the kinase domain in a signalling-competent form, which is why chaperone inhibition is an alternative way to remove resistant receptors. ERBIN binds ERBB2 and influences its localisation and downstream output. Sustained signalling through the resistant receptor feeds the growth and survival routes normally engaged by ERBB2 dimers, keeping proliferation active despite treatment.

Certain point mutations in the kinase domain of ERBB2 (HER2) drive breast, lung and gastric cancers yet blunt the benefit of the irreversible tyrosine kinase inhibitor neratinib, and this pathway captures that drug-resistant signalling state. The mutant receptor still dimerizes and autophosphorylates, sustaining growth and survival output despite covalent inhibitor binding, so tumours progress on therapy and require alternative HER2-directed strategies. Stability of the mutant kinase depends on chaperoning by HSP90 together with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which explains why HSP90 inhibition can strip resistant receptors from the cell; ERBIN binds ERBB2 and influences its localisation and signalling. The biology sits at the intersection of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, chaperone-dependent protein quality control, and the clinical problem of acquired and intrinsic resistance to targeted kinase inhibitors.

Osimertinib is a covalent EGFR-family kinase inhibitor, and mutations in the ERBB2 kinase domain can blunt its effect, so tumours driven by those alleles keep signalling despite treatment. This matters clinically in lung and breast cancers, where insertions and point mutations in the ERBB2 kinase domain predict which patients will fail a targeted agent and need an alternative inhibitor. The mutant receptor remains dimerisation-competent and continues to fire growth and survival signalling through downstream cascades, and its stability depends on the HSP90 chaperone machinery acting with the kinase-specific cochaperone CDC37, which explains why HSP90 inhibition is explored as a way around the resistance. ERBIN binds ERBB2 and contributes to its localisation and regulation. The pathway is therefore an example of acquired or intrinsic resistance to receptor tyrosine kinase inhibition in cancer therapy.

Afatinib is an irreversible inhibitor that binds covalently within the ERBB2 kinase domain, and certain kinase-domain mutations of ERBB2 blunt that inhibition, allowing receptor signalling to continue during treatment. This matters clinically in breast, gastric and lung cancers driven by ERBB2 mutation rather than amplification, where acquired or intrinsic resistance limits the durability of targeted therapy. The mutant receptor remains dependent on chaperoning by HSP90 and its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which stabilise the kinase domain in a foldable, signalling-competent state, making HSP90 inhibition a rational way to counter resistance. ERBIN binds the receptor and influences its localisation and signalling output. Continued ERBB2 activity sustains downstream growth and survival signalling, so the pathway sits at the intersection of receptor tyrosine kinase oncogenesis, protein quality control, and the pharmacology of drug resistance.

Point mutations in the kinase domain of ERBB2 can render the receptor insensitive to the small-molecule inhibitor AEE788, so tumours carrying them continue to signal for growth and survival despite treatment. This matters clinically because ERBB2-driven breast, gastric and lung cancers are selected for kinase-targeted therapy on the assumption that the mutant receptor is druggable, and resistance of these mutants narrows the options. The mutant receptors retain catalytic activity and remain stabilised as client proteins of the HSP90 chaperone together with its kinase-specific co-chaperone CDC37, which supports their folding and steady-state levels, while ERBIN binds ERBB2 and influences its localisation and signalling output. The persistence of chaperone-dependent, active mutant receptor underlies continued downstream proliferative signalling and points to chaperone inhibition as an alternative to competing for the ATP site.

Lapatinib is a reversible tyrosine kinase inhibitor used against ERBB2-driven breast and gastric cancers, and certain point mutations in the ERBB2 kinase domain blunt its effect, allowing receptor signalling and tumour growth to continue during treatment. This pathway captures that drug-resistant state: mutant ERBB2 retains catalytic activity and downstream output despite drug exposure, so patients carrying these alleles derive little benefit and require alternative or irreversible inhibitors. Stability of the mutant receptor depends on chaperoning by HSP90 together with its kinase-specific cochaperone CDC37, a dependency that makes HSP90 inhibition an attractive way to degrade resistant ERBB2. ERBIN binds the receptor's carboxy-terminal tail and influences its localisation and signalling in polarised cells. The biology sits at the junction of growth factor receptor signalling, protein quality control, and acquired resistance to targeted cancer therapy.

Missense substitutions in the extracellular dimerization arm of ERBB2 — notably G309A, G309E and S310F — drive ligand-independent oncogenic signalling without gene amplification, and they occur in breast, bladder, lung and other carcinomas where they mark tumours likely to respond to trastuzumab or to kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib. The altered contact surface favours heterodimerization with EGFR, in one case stabilized by intermolecular disulfide bonds, so the mutant receptor is constitutively partnered and trans-phosphorylated on C-terminal tyrosines. Those phosphosites recruit GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 to activate RAS–ERK, engage GAB1 with the PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits to activate AKT, and bind PLCG1, while HSP90 and its cochaperone CDC37 maintain mutant receptor stability. The net output is proliferation, survival and increased phosphorylation of migration regulators, placing this among receptor tyrosine kinase pathways subverted in cancer.

Cancer-associated missense changes in the transmembrane and juxtamembrane segments of ERBB2 turn a receptor that normally needs a partner and a ligand into one that signals on its own, and this pathway describes the oncogenic signalling that follows. Substitutions such as V659E, G660D, S653C and R678Q favour an active dimer interface or lock the kinase in its active conformation, so the receptor trans-autophosphorylates its C-terminal tyrosines and those of EGFR and ERBB3 partners even without growth factor input from EGF, neuregulins or other family ligands. Phosphorylated tails recruit GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 to drive RAS-ERK output and engage PLCG1, giving sustained proliferative and survival signalling; HSP90 and CDC37 chaperone the mutant kinase. Which mutant is present determines response to trastuzumab, pertuzumab, lapatinib, neratinib or afatinib, making this biology directly relevant to targeted treatment choice in breast, gastric and lung tumours.

Point mutations in the transmembrane and juxtamembrane domains of ERBB2 (HER2) alter how the receptor dimerizes and signals, and in doing so change how tumours respond to HER2-directed drugs. This matters clinically in breast, lung and other carcinomas, where antibody and kinase-inhibitor therapy is chosen on the assumption that HER2 activation depends on ligand-driven heterodimerization. Substitutions such as V659E and G660D favour ligand-independent, self-associating dimers, so the blocking antibody pertuzumab fails to suppress them, whereas the juxtamembrane R678Q variant remains sensitive. Mutant receptor stability and signalling competence depend on the HSP90 chaperone with its kinase-specific cochaperone CDC37, while ERBIN binds the juxtamembrane region and constrains receptor localization and output. The biology sits at the intersection of receptor tyrosine kinase activation, chaperone-supported oncoprotein folding, and acquired or intrinsic resistance to targeted therapy.

Cochlear outer hair cells amplify sound mechanically, and descending cholinergic fibres from the medial olivocochlear system turn that amplification down. This efferent brake sets the dynamic range of hearing, sharpens frequency selectivity, and protects the cochlea from acoustic overexposure; loss of it leaves hearing more vulnerable to noise damage and less able to extract signals from background. Acetylcholine released onto the hair cell binds a distinctive nicotinic receptor built from CHRNA9 and CHRNA10 subunits, unusual in being blocked rather than activated by nicotine, and the resulting calcium influx opens calcium-activated potassium channels nearby: small-conductance SK2 channels and large-conductance BK channels formed by KCNMA1 with its KCNMB1 subunit. Potassium efflux hyperpolarizes the cell, reducing the voltage-driven electromotility of prestin and the slower cytoskeletal changes that underlie outer hair cell contraction.

Hemophilia B is the bleeding disorder that follows when coagulation factor IX is missing or non-functional, and this pathway captures how disease-associated F9 variants break the intrinsic arm of clotting. Factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent zymogen whose glutamate residues are carboxylated by GGCX so it can bind calcium and anionic membrane surfaces; activation by factor XIa yields FIXa, which assembles with factor VIIIa, calcium and phospholipid on platelet membranes to convert factor X to Xa and sustain thrombin generation. Platelet glycoprotein Ib-V-IX components provide the adhesive surface where this assembly occurs. Mutant factor IX may be poorly secreted or processed, fail to form the membrane complex, or cleave factor X inefficiently. Residual activity sets severity, from trauma-related bleeding in mild cases to spontaneous joint, muscle and intracranial hemorrhage when levels fall below one percent.

When a cell exits mitosis, the nuclear envelope must be rebuilt around the decondensing chromosomes and every remaining hole closed before nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalisation can be restored. Sealing of the reforming envelope by ESCRT-III accomplishes this at the fenestrations left in the mitotic ER-derived sheets that do not resolve into nuclear pore complexes. The inner nuclear membrane protein LEMD2 recruits CHMP7, which nucleates polymers of CHMP4 and CHMP2/CHMP3 subunits together with IST1; these filaments constrict the aperture in reverse-topology fashion and are then remodelled and disassembled by the AAA+ ATPase VPS4A. Because spindle microtubules still thread through the closing gaps, the microtubule-severing enzyme spastin is engaged to cut them, and the abundant tubulin subunits reflect that substrate. Defects in this step leave persistent envelope gaps, DNA damage and mislocalised nuclear contents, and the same machinery reseals envelope ruptures in interphase.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose activating mutations drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute leukaemias, and much of the treatment of those diseases rests on small-molecule inhibition of the mutant receptor. Dasatinib binds KIT in an inactive conformation and suppresses receptors mutated in the juxtamembrane region or the activation loop, but substitutions at valine 654 in the ATP-binding pocket reshape the drug contact surface so that inhibition is only partial. Such secondary mutations typically arise under treatment pressure and restore ligand-independent signalling to the proliferation and survival routes downstream of KIT, including RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT. Understanding which mutant alleles remain drug-resistant matters directly for choosing among the several type II inhibitors used sequentially in KIT-driven cancer.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor whose activating mutations drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute leukaemias, and whose inhibition by imatinib is the basis of targeted therapy in these diseases. Imatinib works because it binds the inactive conformation of the kinase, which is still adopted by receptors carrying juxtamembrane exon 11 mutations that release normal autoinhibition. Imatinib-resistant KIT mutants escape this constraint: secondary substitutions in the ATP-binding pocket or in the activation loop either block drug contact or stabilise the active conformation, so the receptor signals constitutively through growth and survival pathways despite continued treatment. Such variants typically emerge as polyclonal subpopulations during therapy and explain relapse, motivating second-line inhibitors chosen according to the specific resistance mutation present.

Oncogenic forms of the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and a subset of acute myeloid leukaemias, and the binding of tyrosine kinase inhibitors to these mutant kinases is the basis of their targeted treatment. Primary mutations typically fall in the juxtamembrane region encoded by exon 11, which normally holds the kinase autoinhibited; losing that restraint gives ligand-independent, constitutive signalling toward proliferation and survival, and such receptors are efficiently blocked by imatinib. Secondary mutations acquired under therapy remodel the ATP-binding pocket or the activation loop and exclude the first-line drug, yet remain susceptible to alternative inhibitors such as sunitinib and regorafenib. Which inhibitor engages which mutant therefore depends on the structural consequence of each substitution, making this drug-binding biology the practical link between tumour genotype and sequential treatment choice in KIT-driven disease.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor that drives mast cell, germ cell, melanocyte and hematopoietic progenitor development, and gain-of-function mutations in it cause gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute leukemias. Masitinib is a type II inhibitor, active against wild-type and juxtamembrane-mutant KIT as well as PDGFR and FGFR3, and the masitinib-resistant KIT mutants are those substitutions that escape it. Type II inhibitors bind only the inactive kinase conformation, so mutations in the activation loop or within the ATP-binding cleft either lock the kinase in an active conformation or block drug contact, leaving downstream signalling to RAS-MAPK, PI3K and STAT pathways switched on despite treatment. Such alleles arise both de novo and as acquired secondary mutations under therapy, and they explain a substantial share of clinical relapse, motivating inhibitors with different conformational preferences.

Activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis, some acute myeloid leukaemias and melanomas, and blocking the kinase with type II inhibitors such as nilotinib is the mainstay of treatment; this describes the mutant forms of KIT that resist that drug. Nilotinib binds only the inactive conformation of the kinase, so substitutions that stabilise the active state or reshape the ATP pocket restore ligand-independent signalling through the RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT routes that support proliferation and survival.
