Effectiveness varies by mutated region: juxtamembrane and kinase-domain changes in exons 11, 13, 17 and 18 confer partial or complete resistance, and the gatekeeper substitution T670I abolishes drug binding outright. Such mutations explain secondary relapse on therapy and guide the choice of alternative KIT inhibitors, making them a practical illustration of how kinase conformation dictates targeted drug response.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours are driven by activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT, and regorafenib is a type II inhibitor used after imatinib fails. This biology concerns the subset of KIT variants that remain active despite regorafenib, and it matters because it defines the point at which third-line kinase inhibition stops working and tumour growth resumes. Regorafenib binds the inactive kinase conformation and so retains activity against gatekeeper substitutions in exon 14 and most activation-loop changes in exons 17 and 18, but secondary mutations in the ATP-binding pocket and juxtamembrane region can restore signalling through the mutant receptor. The result is sustained ligand-independent KIT autophosphorylation and downstream proliferative and survival signalling, illustrating how sequential secondary mutations in one oncogenic kinase shape the order and limits of targeted therapy.</br>

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase that normally requires stem cell factor binding and receptor dimerization before it fires, and it drives the survival and proliferation of mast cells, hematopoietic progenitors, germ cells, melanocytes and the interstitial cells of Cajal. Signaling by kinase domain mutants of KIT describes what happens when substitutions in the catalytic domain and activation loop, encoded by exons 13, 14 and 17, lock the kinase in an active conformation: the receptor autophosphorylates and engages downstream growth and anti-apoptotic routes without ligand and without dimerizing. The result is ligand-independent proliferation, and these alleles are recurrent in mastocytosis, myeloproliferative disease, acute myeloid leukemia, melanoma and germ cell tumors. In gastrointestinal stromal tumors they are uncommon as founding lesions but arise as secondary mutations that restore kinase activity and confer resistance to imatinib, which explains why they matter for treatment choice.

Sunitinib-resistant KIT mutants describes forms of the KIT receptor tyrosine kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with sunitinib, the drug most often given when a KIT-driven cancer has already escaped imatinib. It matters because gastrointestinal stromal tumours and some mast cell and myeloid neoplasms depend on constitutively active KIT for growth and survival, and the sequence of mutations acquired in the kinase domain dictates which inhibitor still works. Sunitinib binds the inactive conformation of the kinase, so substitutions in the activation loop that favour the active state, and certain gatekeeper changes at the ATP pocket, abolish binding while leaving downstream signalling to PI3K-AKT and MAPK intact. This is clonal drug resistance in the classic sense: selection of pre-existing secondary mutations under therapy, driving the choice of later-line kinase inhibitors.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, and activating mutations in it drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some acute leukaemias. Such tumours are usually treated first with imatinib, and sunitinib is given second line when resistance emerges; this pathway captures the subset of KIT alleles that resist sunitinib as well. Resistance arises because substitutions in the kinase domain, particularly in the activation loop, reshape the pocket so the drug can no longer hold the receptor in the inactive conformation it requires, leaving the kinase constitutively autophosphorylated and signalling to proliferation and survival effectors without ligand. Clinically this defines the point at which second-line therapy fails and later-generation inhibitors with different conformational preferences are needed.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose normal activation by stem cell factor drives the growth and survival of interstitial cells of Cajal, mast cells, melanocytes, germ cells and haematopoietic progenitors. Its juxtamembrane segment, encoded by exon 11, folds back onto the kinase to hold it off in the absence of ligand; deletions and point mutations there destroy this autoinhibitory clamp, so the receptor dimerises and phosphorylates itself without stem cell factor and signals constitutively through the RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT routes. Such lesions are the commonest initiating events in gastrointestinal stromal tumour and occur at lower frequency in acute myeloid leukaemia, mast cell disease and melanoma, converting a growth-factor-dependent proliferation programme into an autonomous one. Because the kinase domain itself remains in a druggable conformation, these mutants are characteristically sensitive to imatinib, unlike activation-loop mutants that arise as resistance.

The receptor tyrosine kinase KIT drives growth of gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and some leukaemias, and small-molecule inhibitors of it are standard therapy; this biology concerns the subset of mutant KIT proteins that sorafenib cannot shut down. Sorafenib is a type II inhibitor, meaning it binds only the inactive, DFG-out conformation of the kinase, so it still blocks many KIT variants altered in the ATP-binding cleft or the juxtamembrane region. Substitutions at aspartate 816 in the activation loop, however, stabilise the active conformation and abolish the binding site the drug requires, leaving the receptor constitutively signalling to RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT pathways despite treatment. The practical consequence is primary or acquired clinical resistance, and the need to select inhibitors that accommodate the active-state kinase for D816-mutant disease.

KIT is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose activating mutations, typically in the juxtamembrane region, drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours and contribute to melanoma and acute myeloid leukaemia by locking the receptor into ligand-independent growth signalling. Such tumours initially respond well to imatinib, the first tyrosine kinase inhibitor approved for cancer, and this dependence on a single oncogenic kinase is what makes targeted therapy work. Resistance is the recurring clinical problem described here: most patients relapse as secondary mutations arise in the ATP-binding pocket or the kinase activation loop, sterically or energetically blocking drug binding or favouring the active kinase conformation that the inhibitor cannot engage. The result is restored downstream proliferative and survival signalling despite continued treatment, motivating second- and third-line inhibitors chosen according to which resistance mutation a tumour has acquired.

The receptor tyrosine kinase KIT, activated by stem cell factor, sustains haematopoietic stem cells, erythroid progenitors, mast cells, melanocytes and the interstitial cells of Cajal that pace gut motility. When mutations in its juxtamembrane or kinase domains make the receptor active without ligand, the same outputs drive tumour growth: gastrointestinal stromal tumours most often, and a minority of acute myeloid leukaemias, melanomas, mastocytosis and germ cell tumours. Constitutively phosphorylated KIT recruits GRB2 and SOS1 to load RAS proteins and fire the MAP kinase cascade, engages PI3K regulatory and catalytic subunits for survival signalling, and activates SRC-family kinases such as SRC, FYN, LYN and LCK together with JAK2 and STAT3 and STAT5. Because the oncogenic dependence runs through the kinase itself, these tumours are treated with imatinib and later-generation KIT inhibitors, and resistance arises from further mutations in the same domains.

Inhibition of DNA recombination at telomere is the protective packaging that stops chromosome ends from being mistaken for double-strand breaks. Telomeres look like broken DNA, and unless they are capped they recruit break-repair machinery, triggering damage signalling, senescence, and end-to-end fusions by non-homologous or microhomology-mediated joining. The shelterin complex — TRF1, TRF2, RAP1, TIN2, TPP1 and POT1 — binds telomeric repeats and blocks both recombination and checkpoint activation, while the ATRX-DAXX chaperone deposits histone H3.3 to keep telomeric chromatin repressive and limit transcription by RNA polymerase II of telomeric RNA. Loss of this restraint, especially ATRX inactivation, permits homologous recombination between telomeres and drives alternative lengthening of telomeres, a telomerase-independent route to replicative immortality used by roughly 5-15% of cancers. The pathway therefore sits at the junction of chromosome-end maintenance, chromatin state, and tumour suppression.

Chromosome ends look like double-strand breaks, and this pathway is how cells stop them from being treated as such. Shelterin — TRF1, TRF2, RAP1, TIN2, TPP1 and POT1 — caps telomeric repeats, suppressing end-joining fusions and blocking homologous recombination between telomeres, while the ATRX-DAXX chaperone deposits histone H3.3 to keep telomeric chromatin repressive and limit transcription by RNA polymerase II through the repeats. When capping or chromatin organisation fails, damage signalling at short telomeres drives replicative senescence, uncapped ends fuse to produce dicentric chromosomes and genome instability, and recombination-based alternative lengthening of telomeres can be unleashed. ALT, common in ATRX- or DAXX-deficient tumours such as sarcomas and gliomas, gives cancer cells telomerase-independent immortality. The pathway therefore links chromatin state at chromosome ends to ageing, DNA repair choice and tumour suppression.

KIT is the receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, and mutations in its juxtamembrane, extracellular or kinase domains lock it into a constitutively phosphorylated, ligand-independent state that drives gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and subsets of acute myeloid leukaemia and melanoma. Signalling from these activated mutant receptors recruits the same effectors as the normal receptor but without restraint: GRB2 with SOS1 loads the RAS proteins to fire the MAPK cascade, class IA PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits engage the PI3K/mTOR axis, and JAK2 together with SRC-family kinases such as SRC, LYN, FYN, LCK and YES1 feeds STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5 activation. The combined output sustains proliferation, blocks apoptosis and remodels the actin cytoskeleton. Because the oncogenic drive depends on kinase activity, these mutants are the targets of imatinib and related inhibitors, and secondary kinase-domain mutations are a route to resistance.

Telomeres must be kept from engaging the homologous recombination machinery, and the ATRX-DAXX complex is one of the guards that enforces this. DAXX is the histone chaperone partner that, with the ATRX remodeller, deposits histone H3.3 into telomeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin, keeping the repeats packaged and suppressing recombination between them. When DAXX carries loss-of-function mutations, that chromatin deposition fails and telomeres become substrates for recombination-based copying, producing the alternative lengthening of telomeres phenotype: heterogeneous, elongated telomeres maintained without telomerase. This route to telomere maintenance is found in a subset of tumours, notably pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, sarcomas and gliomas, and accounts for cases with ALT hallmarks that lack ATRX lesions. The biology links histone variant chaperoning and heterochromatin maintenance directly to replicative immortality in cancer.

Telomeres must be kept from engaging the homologous recombination machinery, and when that restraint fails cancer cells can maintain their chromosome ends without telomerase. Loss-of-function mutations in ATRX produce exactly this defect: the chromatin remodeller, acting with its partner DAXX, normally deposits the histone variant H3.3 into telomeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin, and that chromatin state suppresses recombination between telomeric repeats. Without functional ATRX-DAXX, telomeric chromatin becomes permissive, recombination-based copying of telomere sequence proceeds, and cells adopt alternative lengthening of telomeres as their route to unlimited replicative capacity. ATRX inactivation is common in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours, gliomas and osteosarcomas, which are typically telomerase-negative and ALT-positive, so this failed inhibition links chromatin assembly at repetitive DNA to immortalisation and genome instability in tumours.

Telomeres must be kept from recombining with one another, and loss of that restraint is how some cancers acquire limitless replicative capacity. The ATRX-DAXX chromatin remodelling complex normally enforces it, binding subtelomeric chromatin, depositing the histone variant H3.3 at telomeric repeats and holding down transcription of the telomeric repeat-containing noncoding RNA TERRA. When this inhibition of telomeric DNA recombination fails, telomeres become substrates for homology-directed exchange and tumours switch on alternative lengthening of telomeres, maintaining chromosome ends without telomerase. Loss-of-function mutation of ATRX, and less often DAXX, is a recurrent feature of ALT-positive sarcomas, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours and gliomas, frequently alongside H3.3, IDH and TP53 alterations. The pathway therefore links heterochromatin assembly at chromosome ends to genome stability and to a telomerase-independent route to cellular immortalisation.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptors PDGFRA and PDGFRB normally guide the development and upkeep of mesenchymal tissues such as vascular smooth muscle, kidney, gut, skin and lung, and this pathway covers what happens when their signalling is corrupted in human disease. Activating point mutations, gene amplification, ligand overproduction, or fusions that join the kinase domain to partners such as ETV6, FIP1L1, GOLGA4, KANK1 or STRN produce a receptor that fires without ligand, driving proliferation and survival through RAS-MAPK, PI3K and STAT arms. The downstream players here are the familiar oncogenic ones: GRB2 and SOS1 coupling to HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits, and STAT1/STAT3. Clinically this underlies a fraction of gastrointestinal stromal tumours, hypereosinophilic and other myeloid neoplasms, and gliomas, and it explains why these tumours respond to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

Bleeding stops because platelets plug a damaged vessel and a protease cascade converts fibrinogen into a stable fibrin mesh; disorders of hemostasis are what happens when that balance tips. Loss-of-function in the coagulation factors produces hemophilia A and B and related factor deficiencies, while defects in the platelet glycoprotein Ib-V-IX complex or in von Willebrand factor impair platelet adhesion to exposed collagen, giving Bernard-Soulier and von Willebrand disease. Tipping the other way, failure of the protein C/protein S anticoagulant arm or of the von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease ADAMTS13 drives thrombosis and microangiopathy. Also represented are defects in post-translational steps that factors require, including vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation and tyrosine sulfation, and contact-system dysregulation in which excess bradykinin raises venular permeability and causes hereditary angioedema.

Blood clotting depends on activated factor IX, which pairs with activated factor VIII on activated platelet membranes to form the intrinsic tenase complex and convert factor X to factor Xa, the step that drives thrombin generation. Because this complex sets the pace of coagulation, changes in factor IX activity shift the balance between bleeding and clotting: loss of function produces haemophilia B, whereas gain of function tips the system toward thrombosis. Here a substitution of leucine for arginine in factor IX, the Padua variant, yields a protease with markedly increased clotting activity within the factor VIIIa complex, so that defective factor IX causes thrombophilia rather than bleeding, presenting as venous thrombosis. The same hyperactive variant is exploited deliberately in gene therapy for haemophilia B, where its potency allows correction at low expression levels.

Defective F8 accelerates dissociation of the A2 domain describes a molecular mechanism of hemophilia A in which mutant coagulation factor VIII is secreted and activated normally but falls apart too quickly, shortening the burst of clotting activity needed to stop bleeding. Activated factor VIII is a non-covalent heterotrimer whose A2 subunit is held at the A1-A2 and A2-A3 interfaces by intersubunit hydrogen bonds; it serves as the cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic factor X-activating complex, amplifying thrombin generation on platelet surfaces. Missense substitutions at these interfaces, such as R550H, A303E, S308L and the R717 variants, weaken those contacts so A2 dissociates prematurely and factor VIIIa decays, collapsing factor Xase activity. Patients therefore show a mild to moderate bleeding phenotype with near-normal antigen levels but discordantly low functional clotting activity.

Activated factor VIII works only as long as it stays assembled: its A2 domain is held non-covalently against the A1 and A3 domains, and once A2 drifts away the cofactor is spent. Because factor VIIIa is the cofactor that lets factor IXa activate factor X on the platelet surface, its lifetime sets how much thrombin a wound can generate. Certain hemophilia A missense substitutions in F8 sit at the A1-A2 and A2-A3 contact surfaces and break the hydrogen bonds that keep the subunit docked; the protein is secreted and can be activated normally but decays far faster than wild type, so intrinsic pathway factor X activation collapses prematurely. The result is a bleeding disorder driven by cofactor instability rather than absent protein, a distinct molecular phenotype from null or secretion-defective mutations and one reason clotting activity can be low despite measurable antigen.

Factor VIII circulates bound to von Willebrand factor as an inactive procofactor and only becomes useful to coagulation once thrombin cuts it at specific arginines, releasing it from its carrier and generating the activated heterotrimer that partners factor IXa to activate factor X. When those cleavage sites are altered by mutation, this activation step fails: the protein is present in plasma at normal or near-normal levels but cannot be switched on, so intrinsic pathway amplification is lost and patients have mild to moderate haemophilia A with joint and soft-tissue bleeding. Defective thrombin cleavage of factor VIII therefore represents a functional rather than quantitative deficiency, distinguishing it from mutations that abolish synthesis or secretion, and it explains why clotting factor activity assays can disagree with antigen measurements in affected individuals.

Coagulation factor VIII is secreted into plasma with a very short independent half-life, and it survives in circulation only because von Willebrand factor binds it and shields it from premature clearance and proteolysis. When mutations in the F8 gene disrupt that interaction at the factor VIII light chain, circulating factor VIII levels fall even though the protein is made and secreted, producing hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder marked by joint and soft-tissue bleeding and prolonged bleeding after injury. Defective F8 binding to von Willebrand factor therefore illustrates a carrier-dependent mechanism of plasma protein stability rather than a catalytic defect: the released cofactor normally acts on activated platelet surfaces to accelerate factor X activation by factor IXa within the intrinsic tenase complex, so its loss blunts thrombin generation and clot propagation.

Defective F8 binding to the cell membrane describes a molecular lesion in blood coagulation: mutant factor VIII that can no longer dock onto phospholipid surfaces, and therefore cannot assemble the intrinsic clotting machinery where it is needed. Normally thrombin-activated FVIIIa binds phosphatidylserine exposed on activated platelets through its C1 and C2 discoidin domains, serving as the cofactor that concentrates factor IXa and accelerates factor X activation by orders of magnitude. Hemophilia A variants clustered in these membrane-binding domains, including substitutions and deletions such as A2220P and Q2330P, leave the protein expressed but functionally inert, so tenase complex formation fails and thrombin generation is inadequate. The clinical consequence is X-linked hemophilia A with spontaneous joint and soft-tissue bleeding, illustrating how coagulation depends on correct localisation of enzyme complexes to membranes rather than on enzyme activity alone.

Activated factor VIII works only when it is docked on a phospholipid surface, where it serves as the cofactor that accelerates factor IXa-mediated activation of factor X in the intrinsic clotting pathway. Membrane attachment is mediated by the C2 domain of factor VIII, which inserts hydrophobic loops into the exposed phosphatidylserine of activated platelets, concentrating the tenase complex at the site of injury. Missense and small deletion variants in this region, including changes at the C2 domain such as A2220P and Q2330P, leave a protein that can still be secreted and thrombin-cleaved but binds membranes poorly, so tenase assembly fails. The result is haemophilia A, an X-linked bleeding disorder with delayed, unstable clot formation, joint and soft-tissue haemorrhage, and a phenotype whose severity tracks how much residual cofactor function survives.

Blood clotting depends on the intrinsic tenase complex, in which activated factor VIII serves as the cofactor that accelerates factor IXa-catalysed conversion of factor X to factor Xa on a membrane surface; without this amplification, thrombin generation is too slow to stabilise a clot. Missense substitutions in a short segment of the factor VIII A2 domain leave the protein present and normally processed but unable to properly engage factor IXa, so the assembled complex generates little factor Xa. The result is mild to moderate haemophilia A, a bleeding disorder in which antigen levels can appear near normal while functional activity is low, illustrating how cofactor defects rather than protein absence explain discordant clinical assays. This defective cofactor behaviour places the lesion squarely in the amplification step of coagulation.

Coagulation factor VIII is made in the liver as a large multidomain glycoprotein that circulates bound to von Willebrand factor and acts as the cofactor for factor IXa in the intrinsic tenase complex, amplifying thrombin generation at a wound. When F8 mutations block the protein's passage through the secretory route, plasma factor VIII is absent or reduced and hemophilia A follows, with joint and soft-tissue bleeding proportional to the residual activity. Normally the nascent chain enters the endoplasmic reticulum, is signal-cleaved and N-glycosylated, folds with help from calnexin, calreticulin and BiP, and is carried to the Golgi by a cargo receptor complex for complex glycan maturation, O-glycosylation and tyrosine sulfation. Missense changes that cause misfolding, ER retention and degradation, or that abolish the sulfation needed for tight von Willebrand factor binding, all reduce secreted functional factor VIII.

Telomeres must be replenished each division or they erode, and disorders of telomere maintenance sit at both extremes of that requirement. When cancer cells reactivate telomerase or switch on recombination-based alternative lengthening of telomeres, they escape replicative senescence and become effectively immortal; when germline defects leave telomeres too short, the result is a telomere syndrome such as dyskeratosis congenita or Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome, with bone marrow failure, pulmonary and liver fibrosis, mucocutaneous abnormalities and cancer predisposition. ATRX and DAXX form a histone chaperone complex that deposits H3.3 at telomeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin; loss-of-function mutations in either are strongly associated with the alternative lengthening phenotype in gliomas, neuroendocrine tumours and sarcomas, permitting recombination at telomeric repeats. The pathway therefore links chromatin structure at chromosome ends to genome stability, replicative lifespan and tumour immortalization.

N-fatty-acyl amino acids are circulating lipid signals that raise energy expenditure, and the synthesis and breakdown of oleoyl-phenylalanine is the best-characterised example. The secreted enzyme PM20D1 works extracellularly and catalyses a reversible condensation, joining oleate to L-phenylalanine to form oleoyl-phe with release of water; hydrolysis is thermodynamically favoured, yet PM20D1 expression raises oleoyl-phe levels in serum and in culture medium. Leucine, isoleucine and other long-chain unsaturated fatty acids including arachidonate serve as less efficient substrates. The product acts on mitochondria, stimulating uncoupled respiration without requiring UCP1, with the adenine nucleotide translocases SLC25A4 and SLC25A5 implicated as targets. In mice, elevated oleoyl-phe accompanies increased energy expenditure and better glucose handling, placing this chemistry alongside brown-fat thermogenesis and making it of interest for obesity and metabolic disease.

Blood clotting depends on a brief amplification step in which activated factor IX, held on a membrane surface with its cofactor factor VIII, cleaves factor X to generate factor Xa and drive thrombin production. This describes what happens when that step fails because a mutant factor IX cannot perform the cleavage: missense substitutions in the serine protease domain leave the zymogen able to be activated but catalytically incompetent toward its substrate, so the tenase complex forms without producing factor Xa. The result is haemophilia B, an X-linked bleeding disorder whose severity tracks residual protease activity, ranging from prolonged bleeding after injury to spontaneous joint and muscle haemorrhage. Because the same reaction is the convergence point for the intrinsic pathway, loss of factor VIII produces a clinically similar disease, and treatment centres on replacing the missing clotting factor activity.

Defective F9 secretion describes the failure of coagulation factor IX to reach the bloodstream, one of the molecular routes to haemophilia B. Factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent serine protease made by hepatocytes and secreted into plasma, where activated factor IX together with factor VIII drives factor X activation in the intrinsic arm of coagulation; when circulating levels fall, thrombin generation is inadequate and patients suffer recurrent joint and soft-tissue bleeding. Mutations spread across the F9 gene can compromise not only catalytic activity but the earlier steps of protein biogenesis — folding, stability, and export through the secretory pathway — so that mutant protein is retained intracellularly and accumulates rather than being released. This links a bleeding disorder to quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum and secretory trafficking, and explains cases where antigen levels are low despite intact coding of the active site.

Coagulation factor IX is a vitamin K-dependent protease made by hepatocytes and released into plasma, where it works with factor VIII to activate factor X and sustain thrombin generation at a site of injury. Defective secretion of factor IX describes the situation in which mutant F9 protein is synthesised but fails to traverse the secretory pathway efficiently, so it accumulates intracellularly and circulating levels fall rather than the protein being simply inactive. The result is haemophilia B, an X-linked bleeding disorder whose severity tracks residual plasma factor IX activity, with joint and soft tissue haemorrhage in severe cases. Because the defect lies in folding, stability and export rather than catalysis, it connects the biology of blood clotting to quality control in the endoplasmic reticulum and to the post-translational modifications, including gamma-carboxylation and propeptide processing, that a secreted clotting factor must pass through.

Coagulation factor IX must be cleaved by factor XIa on the platelet surface to become an active protease and sustain thrombin generation; when that activation step fails, the result is haemophilia B, an X-linked recessive bleeding disorder with prolonged joint and soft-tissue bleeding. Point mutations at the FIX activation cleavage sites, such as substitutions of Arg191 and Arg226, leave the zymogen resistant to proteolysis by factor XIa, while mutations in the 18-residue propeptide prevent its removal before secretion, so FIX circulates uncleaved and with a destabilized calcium-dependent conformation that is only slowly activated. The glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex subunits included here reflect the platelet receptor scaffold that localizes factor XI-dependent FIX activation to the site of vessel injury, tying this defect to the amplification phase of the intrinsic coagulation cascade.}

Coagulation factor IX must have glutamate residues in its N-terminal Gla domain converted to gamma-carboxyglutamate before it can bind calcium, dock onto membrane phospholipid surfaces, and participate in the intrinsic pathway of clotting. This modification is carried out by the vitamin K-dependent gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which recognizes factor IX through its propeptide; point mutations in that propeptide weaken the interaction so the enzyme carboxylates too few residues and the propeptide is subsequently cleaved poorly. The resulting variants circulate still bearing their propeptide and are activated only sluggishly, producing a functionally deficient protein despite near-normal antigen levels. Defective gamma-carboxylation of factor IX is one molecular route to hemophilia B, with bleeding that tracks the severity of the carboxylation defect, and it illustrates how propeptide-directed recognition links vitamin K metabolism to hemostasis.

Macrophages infected with Leishmania induce WNT5A, and its engagement of the FZD7 receptor helps the cell restrain intracellular parasite numbers. This is a non-canonical, beta-catenin-independent branch of Wnt signalling: receptor-bound Dishevelled proteins recruit Rac1 and drive JNK-dependent activation of JUN, the same axis that reorganises the cytoskeleton during planar cell polarity. Here the output is oxidative rather than morphogenetic, with assembly of an NADPH oxidase complex from NOX1 with its cytosolic organisers and the p22phox subunit generating reactive oxygen species inside the infected macrophage. The same WNT5A-FZD7 circuit is strongly induced in macrophages during rheumatoid arthritis, atherosclerosis, obesity and tumour-associated inflammation, so this signalling links antimicrobial defence to chronic inflammatory disease and marks a possible point of therapeutic intervention in visceral leishmaniasis.

Signaling by cytosolic PDGFRA and PDGFRB fusion proteins describes how chromosomal rearrangements convert platelet-derived growth factor receptors into constitutively active oncogenic kinases, driving myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia and related myeloproliferative disorders. Because these tumours respond dramatically to imatinib, recognising the fusion has direct therapeutic consequences. In each case the receptor's extracellular and transmembrane portions are lost and the cytosolic kinase domain is joined to the N-terminal oligomerisation region of an intracellular protein — the RNA 3' processing factor FIP1L1 in the case of PDGFRA, and coiled-coil or scaffold partners such as striatin for PDGFRB. Forced dimerisation activates the kinase without ligand, so growth factor control is bypassed and downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K and STAT signalling runs continuously, producing autonomous proliferation and survival of haematopoietic progenitors rather than normal mesenchymal growth responses.

Chromosomal rearrangements can fuse the cytoplasmic kinase domain of the platelet-derived growth factor receptors PDGFRA or PDGFRB to the N-terminal region of an unrelated intracellular protein, and the resulting chimeras signal without ever binding ligand. Because the partner contributes an oligomerization surface, the kinase dimerizes constitutively and fires downstream growth and survival routes — RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT activation — driving proliferation independently of normal receptor control. Such fusions underlie myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, chronic myelomonocytic leukaemia and related myeloproliferative disease; the FIP1L1 fusion to PDGFRA, in which an RNA 3'-end processing factor supplies the fusion partner, is the best characterised example, while PDGFRB recruits many rarer partners including striatin and WDR48. Clinically these tumours matter because the constitutive kinase remains sensitive to imatinib and related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, making fusion detection directly actionable.

PDGFRA is a type III receptor tyrosine kinase whose intracellular juxtamembrane segment normally holds the kinase autoinhibited until ligand-induced dimerization and transautophosphorylation open it. Mutations in the transmembrane, juxtamembrane and kinase domains — most often at V561, N659 and D842, plus short activation-loop deletions — break that restraint, so the receptor phosphorylates itself and fires continuously without ligand. This ligand-independent output drives gastrointestinal stromal tumours, some melanomas and haematological malignancies, and the position of the mutation determines whether tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib can bind; D842V is notoriously resistant. Phosphotyrosines on the mutant receptor recruit GRB2 and SOS1 to activate RAS and the MAP kinase cascade, engage PI3K regulatory and catalytic subunits for AKT signalling, and dock STAT1 and STAT3 for transcriptional responses. Some mutants signal from Golgi membranes rather than the cell surface, altering which effectors they reach.

Signaling by membrane-tethered fusions of PDGFRA or PDGFRB covers the oncogenic receptor tyrosine kinases created when chromosomal rearrangements join a dimerization-competent partner to a platelet-derived growth factor receptor that keeps its transmembrane anchor. These fusions drive myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia, as well as some gliomas and sarcomas, and they matter clinically because the resulting kinase is constitutively active yet remains sensitive to imatinib and related inhibitors. Partners such as ETV6, GOLGA4, KANK1, BIN2 and KDR contribute self-association domains that force the kinase domains together at the plasma membrane, bypassing the requirement for PDGF ligand and producing ligand-independent autophosphorylation. The downstream output is the normal PDGFR program -- PI3K/AKT, RAS-MAPK, PLCG and STAT signalling toward proliferation and survival -- but run continuously, converting a growth factor response into autonomous clonal expansion of the affected hematopoietic or mesenchymal cell.

Chromosomal rearrangements can fuse the kinase domain of the platelet-derived growth factor receptors PDGFRA or PDGFRB to an unrelated partner protein, producing constitutively active oncogenic kinases; a subset of these retain the receptor transmembrane segment and so remain anchored at the plasma membrane rather than becoming cytosolic. Partners such as ETV6, KANK1, GOLGA4, BIN2 and KDR contribute self-association domains that drive ligand-independent dimerization and autophosphorylation, switching on the downstream growth and survival routes normally used by PDGF receptors, including RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT signalling. The resulting unchecked proliferative signal underlies myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms, notably chronic eosinophilic leukaemia and myeloproliferative disease with eosinophilia, as well as some gliomas. Because the lesion is a driver kinase, these fusions are typically sensitive to imatinib and related tyrosine kinase inhibitors, making their detection clinically actionable.

Cancer-associated mutations in the extracellular, ligand-binding portion of the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha can disrupt glycosylation and normal trafficking, so that the receptor never reaches the plasma membrane yet fires anyway. The Y288C substitution and an in-frame deletion of exons 8 and 9, found in glioblastoma and other tumours, leave the kinase trapped largely in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane where it autophosphorylates without ligand. From that aberrant compartment the receptor recruits the same effectors as the wild-type protein: GRB2 with SOS1 to load RAS proteins and drive MAPK output, PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits for the AKT arm, and STAT1 and STAT3 for transcriptional responses. The result is ligand-independent proliferative and survival signalling, illustrating how mislocalisation rather than kinase-domain mutation can constitute an oncogenic gain of function and complicate targeting with antibodies directed at the cell surface.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha is a receptor tyrosine kinase whose activating mutations drive gastrointestinal stromal tumours and a subset of other cancers, and the ATP-competitive inhibitor imatinib is the standard first-line treatment for such tumours. Certain PDGFRA alleles, however, escape that drug. The activation-loop substitution D842V, the most frequent PDGFRA mutation in GIST, stabilises the active kinase conformation that imatinib cannot bind, while the gatekeeper change T674I obstructs the drug-binding pocket directly and S601P also confers resistance. These imatinib-resistant mutant receptors signal constitutively without ligand, sustaining proliferative and survival signalling through the usual downstream routes. Clinically they explain primary and acquired treatment failure, and they define the patient groups for whom alternative inhibitors with different binding modes are required, making mutation genotyping part of therapeutic decision-making.

Sunitinib-resistant PDGFR mutants describes forms of the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha kinase that continue to signal despite treatment with sunitinib, the second-line inhibitor used when imatinib fails in PDGFR- and KIT-driven tumours. This matters clinically because gastrointestinal stromal tumours and related malignancies are driven by constitutively active PDGFRA, and sequential kinase inhibition is the mainstay of therapy; mutations that alter the ATP-binding pocket or the activation loop reduce drug affinity while leaving the receptor's ligand-independent kinase activity intact. The consequence is sustained autophosphorylation and downstream RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT signalling, driving proliferation and survival of tumour cells during therapy. Such alleles define acquired or primary resistance and dictate the choice of later-generation inhibitors, making this an example of oncogenic receptor tyrosine kinase signalling escaping pharmacological control.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours and related cancers are frequently driven by activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase PDGFRA, and the small-molecule inhibitor sunitinib is given as second-line therapy when imatinib fails. This biology captures the subset of PDGFRA variants that remain active despite sunitinib binding, so that receptor autophosphorylation and downstream proliferative and survival signalling through RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT continue unchecked. Resistance typically arises from substitutions in the activation loop, notably at the D842 position, which stabilise the active kinase conformation that type II inhibitors such as sunitinib cannot engage; other changes alter the ATP pocket or gatekeeper contacts. Clinically this explains why genotyping the receptor, rather than tumour histology alone, determines which inhibitor is likely to work, and motivates conformation-selective agents for patients whose disease escapes both imatinib and sunitinib.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumours are driven by activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinases KIT and PDGFRA, and are treated with kinase inhibitors that occupy the ATP site; regorafenib is one such type II inhibitor used in advanced disease. Its efficacy depends on the particular allele present, because type II inhibitors bind only the inactive, DFG-out conformation of the kinase. The most common PDGFRA alteration, the activation-loop substitution D842V, stabilises the active conformation and is therefore only weakly inhibited, so tumours carrying it progress despite treatment. Constitutive PDGFRA signalling continues to drive proliferation and survival through the downstream RAS-MAPK and PI3K routes. Describing regorafenib-resistant PDGFRA mutants in these terms explains why genotyping the receptor guides drug choice and why conformation-selective agents were developed for this allele.

Sorafenib is a type II kinase inhibitor used in hepatocellular and renal carcinoma and as second-line therapy for imatinib-refractory tumours, but point mutations in PDGFRA can render the receptor insensitive to it. This describes those sorafenib-resistant PDGFR mutant forms, which matter clinically because they explain relapse in gastrointestinal stromal tumours and other PDGFRA-driven cancers after an initial response. Type II inhibitors bind only the inactive, DFG-out conformation of the kinase; activating substitutions in the activation loop or juxtamembrane region shift the receptor toward the active state or alter the drug-binding pocket, so the mutant kinase continues to signal through downstream growth and survival routes including RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT. Recognising which PDGFRA alleles confer this resistance guides the choice of alternative inhibitors, and illustrates how receptor tyrosine kinase conformation dictates targeted-therapy response.

Platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha is an oncogenic driver in gastrointestinal stromal tumours, where it is mutated in roughly a tenth of cases in a pattern mutually exclusive with KIT, and also in some haematological malignancies and melanoma. Unlike KIT, its activating changes cluster in the kinase activation loop rather than the juxtamembrane region, and both PDGFRA and PDGFRB additionally form oncogenic fusion proteins through translocation. This biology matters clinically because tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy depends on the receptor sampling an inactive conformation: type II drugs such as imatinib bind only that state. Secondary mutations that shift the equilibrium further toward the constitutively active kinase confer resistance, blunting first- and second-line type II inhibitors and motivating the search for type I agents that engage the active conformation. The result is tumour growth signalling that escapes targeted therapy.

Activating mutations in the platelet-derived growth factor receptor drive ligand-independent proliferative signalling and underlie a subset of gastrointestinal stromal tumours and related neoplasms; the therapeutic question is whether a given mutant receptor can still be caught by a small-molecule kinase inhibitor. PDGFRA is a class III receptor tyrosine kinase of the dual-switch type, cycling through phosphorylation and conformational steps between an autoinhibited state and a fully active one, and this equilibrium determines drug sensitivity. Type II inhibitors engage the inactive conformation next to the ATP cleft, while type I agents bind the active form. Juxtamembrane mutations disrupt the autoinhibitory loop yet leave enough inactive receptor for type II binding, whereas activation-loop substitutions favour the active state; the common D842V change shifts the equilibrium so far toward activation that type II inhibitors lose efficacy, explaining clinical resistance and the need for conformation-matched drugs.

Coagulation factor VIII must be tyrosine-sulfated in the Golgi before it can work properly, and loss of sulfation at Tyr1699 in the acidic region of the light chain is one molecular route to hemophilia A. The two Golgi tyrosylprotein sulfotransferases transfer sulfate from PAPS onto specific factor VIII tyrosines during transit through the secretory pathway; the modification at this site is needed for high-affinity binding to von Willebrand factor, which chaperones factor VIII in plasma and protects it from premature clearance and proteolysis. Mutation of the acceptor tyrosine leaves a secreted but poorly stabilized protein, so circulating factor VIII activity is low despite adequate synthesis, producing a mild to moderate bleeding phenotype. This sits within the broader post-translational maturation of factor VIII required for the intrinsic pathway of blood clotting.

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor drives the production, survival and mobilisation of neutrophils, and this receptor pathway is how that signal is read inside granulocyte precursors and mature neutrophils. Dimeric CSF3 binds CSF3R, a receptor with no intrinsic kinase activity that instead relies on constitutively bound JAK1 and the Src-family kinase LYN; receptor dimerisation triggers tyrosine phosphorylation and recruitment of JAK2, SYK, HCK and TYK2. Phosphorylated STAT1, STAT3 and STAT5 dimerise and enter the nucleus to drive myeloid gene expression, while GRB2, SHC1 and the phosphatase PTPN11 route the signal into RAS-ERK proliferation and GAB2 into PI3K survival signalling. SOCS1 and SOCS3 terminate the response, nucleating an elongin-cullin-RING ubiquitin ligase that marks the receptor for degradation. Germline and somatic CSF3R mutations underlie severe congenital neutropenia, chronic neutrophilic leukaemia, and progression to acute myeloid leukaemia.

Building a nervous system requires neural progenitors to generate neurons and glia, then guiding those neurons' axons to correct targets and wrapping them in myelin, and this broad nervous system development programme collects those steps. Its failure underlies cortical malformations, agenesis of commissural tracts, and inherited peripheral neuropathies. Guidance is the dominant theme: netrin, slit, semaphorin, ephrin and GDNF-family ligands act through DCC/UNC5, ROBO, plexin/neuropilin, EPH and RET receptors, converging on Rho-family GTPases, PAK, ROCK, LIMK and cofilin to steer actin and microtubule remodelling in the growth cone. Reelin with VLDLR and DAB1 positions migrating neurons; CDK5, DCX and spectrin–ankyrin scaffolds set neurite polarity and axonal domains; sodium and calcium channels excite the maturing axon; MPZ, PMP22, MBP and SOX10 serve myelination. Ribosomal and proteasome components, and nonsense-mediated decay factors, support the local translation and protein turnover these decisions depend on.

Cell division is gated at the G1/S transition, and mutations in the regulators that enforce that gate underlie a large fraction of human cancer. This grouping of mitotic cell cycle diseases centres on the retinoblastoma protein RB1 and the machinery that controls it: D- and E-type cyclins with CDK4, CDK6 and CDK2 phosphorylate RB1, releasing E2F transcription factors and their DP partners to drive S-phase gene expression, while CDKN1A, CDKN1B and CDKN1C restrain those kinases. Loss of RB1 or amplification of cyclins removes the restriction point entirely. The anaphase-promoting complex with its coactivator FZR1 and E2 enzymes such as UBE2C and UBE2S degrades mitotic regulators and is itself opposed by SKP2. ATRX and DAXX link the same territory to chromatin deposition and telomere maintenance, connecting these lesions to cancer predisposition syndromes and neurodegeneration.

Cells must respond to damage and metabolic insult, and one outcome of that response is senescence, a permanent withdrawal from the cell cycle that prevents damaged cells from dividing. When this arm of the stress response fails, damaged cells keep proliferating and malignant transformation follows; conversely, senescent cells that persist and are not cleared fuel inflammation and create a tissue environment favourable to tumour growth, and contribute to atherosclerosis, osteoarthritis, chronic lung disease and diabetes. The genes here define the core brake: the CDKN2A product p16INK4A binds the cyclin D-dependent kinases CDK4 and CDK6 and blocks their phosphorylation of RB, keeping E2F-driven S-phase genes silent. Loss-of-function mutation or deletion of CDKN2A, and mutations in CDK4 or CDK6 that prevent inhibitor binding, disable senescence entry and are recurrent events in melanoma and many other cancers. Senotherapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors target this axis pharmacologically.

Cells constantly repair damaged or mismatched DNA, and inherited or acquired loss of that capacity produces the genetic instability behind familial cancer syndromes, premature ageing disorders and much of the mutational burden of sporadic tumours. Three repair routes dominate here: mismatch correction by MLH1, PMS2, MSH2 and MSH6, whose failure causes microsatellite instability, hypermutation and Lynch syndrome while also rendering tumours immunogenic and responsive to checkpoint blockade; base excision repair by glycosylases such as OGG1, MUTYH, NTHL1 and NEIL1 that remove oxidised or mispaired bases; and homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks, requiring BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, the RAD51 paralogues and the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex. Damage sensing and signalling through ATM, ATR-ATRIP, TOPBP1 and the 9-1-1 clamp, together with end resection and RecQ helicases WRN and BLM, links defective repair to senescence, apoptosis, radiosensitivity, immunodeficiency and neurodegeneration.

Double-strand breaks are the most lethal form of DNA damage, and inherited or acquired loss of the machinery that repairs them produces a recognizable group of disorders that combine developmental failure with cancer predisposition. When break sensing and homologous recombination fail, cells die, senesce, or survive with chromosomal rearrangements that drive malignant transformation. The genes concerned span damage signalling through ATM and the ATR-ATRIP-TOPBP1 axis with its 9-1-1 clamp, end resection by the MRE11-RAD50-NBN complex with CtIP, EXO1 and DNA2, filament formation by RAD51 with its paralogs, and the BRCA1:BARD1 and BRCA2-PALB2 modules that load RAD51 onto RPA-coated single-stranded DNA. Corresponding clinical syndromes include ataxia telangiectasia, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, Seckel syndrome, Bloom and Werner syndromes, Fanconi anemia, and hereditary breast and ovarian cancer; the same genes are recurrently mutated somatically in sporadic tumours, which underlies sensitivity to PARP inhibition.

Inherited disease of the neuronal system, as annotated here, centres on visual phototransduction failing because the retinoid cycle breaks down. Photoreceptors cannot regenerate 11-cis-retinal on their own; they depend on retinol delivery from the circulation and on recycling of all-trans-retinal through the retinal pigment epithelium. Mutations in the genes that carry out these steps cause retinal degeneration — Stargardt disease from defective ABCA4-mediated clearance of retinoid adducts from photoreceptor discs, fundus albipunctatus and retinitis pigmentosa from impaired retinol dehydrogenases and retinaldehyde-binding protein, and night blindness or maculopathy where retinol uptake by STRA6 from its RBP4–transthyretin carrier is lost. Defects in the cone opsins instead alter spectral sensitivity and produce colour vision deficiency. The unifying theme is toxic retinoid accumulation and chromophore starvation in a tissue that must recycle its light-absorbing cofactor continuously.

Mendelian developmental disorders arise when germline mutations in single genes derail the formation of organs and organ systems, producing conditions such as Rett syndrome, congenital myopathies, pancreatic agenesis, heterotaxy, lipodystrophy, anophthalmia, limb malformations and congenital neutropenia. The genes gathered here centre on the transcriptional arm of that problem, and specifically on MECP2, the methyl-CpG-binding regulator whose loss causes Rett syndrome: MECP2 reads methylated DNA and recruits corepressor machinery built around SIN3A, HDAC1/HDAC3, NCOR1/NCOR2 and the TBL1X adaptors, while also acting with the KMT2D-WDR5-RBBP5-ASH2L-DPY30 methyltransferase complex at active promoters. Neuronal activity feeding through calmodulin, CAMK4 and PKA modulates MECP2 and BDNF expression, linking synaptic signalling to chromatin state. Failure of this epigenetic control impairs postnatal brain maturation, motor skills, cognition and communication rather than gross body plan.

This is the full replication cycle of SARS-CoV-1, the coronavirus behind the 2003 severe acute respiratory syndrome outbreak, together with the host responses it triggers and subverts. Entry begins when the spike protein engages ACE2 and is primed by host proteases such as TMPRSS2 and cathepsin L, allowing membrane fusion and release of the genome; translation of the input RNA on host 40S ribosomes yields polyproteins whose self-cleavage products remodel ER membranes into double-membrane vesicles housing the replicase-transcriptase, and new virions bud into the ERGIC. Innate sensing through RIG-I/MDA5-MAVS, TLR7 and STING converges on TBK1, IRF3 and NF-kB to induce interferon-stimulated effectors, while viral proteins block these steps. Inflammasome activation, ESCRT membrane remodelling, chaperone and glycosylation machinery, and 14-3-3 and ubiquitin systems are also engaged, explaining the inflammatory lung injury of the disease.

Coronavirus infection begins with attachment and entry, the step at which the viral spike glycoprotein engages a host surface receptor and then drives fusion of the viral envelope with a cellular membrane so that the nucleocapsid reaches the cytosol. Because receptor recognition decides which cells and which species a coronavirus can infect, this step sets host range and tissue tropism, and it is the target of neutralising antibodies and entry inhibitors. ACE2, a cell surface carboxypeptidase of the renin-angiotensin system, serves as the receptor for SARS-like coronaviruses and HCoV-NL63. Spike must also be cleaved to become fusion-competent: the surface serine protease TMPRSS2 primes it at the plasma membrane, while the endosomal cysteine protease cathepsin L does so after endocytosis. The AAA ATPase VCP contributes to escape from early endosomes, completing delivery of the genome for replication.

Potential therapeutics for SARS collects the molecular targets through which candidate drugs act against SARS-CoV-1 and SARS-CoV-2 infection, either by blocking viral entry and replication or by damping the destructive host inflammatory response that drives severe COVID-19. It matters because most agents repurposed during the pandemic were developed for other RNA viruses or for autoimmune disease, and their usefulness depends on which human proteins they hit. Targets here span the entry machinery, including ACE2, furin and clathrin-adaptor endocytosis; interferon and cytokine receptor signalling through JAK/TYK2 and STAT2; B cell receptor kinases such as BTK and SYK; nucleotide synthesis via IMPDH; and chromatin regulators including BRD4 and the NuRD and CoREST complexes. Also represented are off-target liabilities and the pharmacokinetic strategy of inhibiting cytochrome P450 enzymes to sustain antiviral plasma levels, as exploited in ritonavir-boosted nirmatrelvir therapy, plus neutralising antibody variable regions.

Drug candidates aimed at SARS coronavirus infection fall into two broad groups, and the protein targets here reflect both: machinery the virus needs to enter and mature, and host pathways whose overactivation causes the lung injury and cytokine storm of severe disease. Viral entry factors include the receptor ACE2, the protease FURIN that cleaves spike, and clathrin adaptor subunits used for endocytosis. On the host side, Janus kinases with interferon and interleukin-6 receptors, Bruton tyrosine kinase with B cell receptor adaptors, and kinases such as RIPK1 and ROCK1/2 are targeted by anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agents, while HSP90, immunophilins, IMPDH nucleotide synthesis, and a NuRD/CoREST corepressor module represent off-target or repurposing interactions. Neutralizing antibody variable regions are also represented. Anticipated liabilities, including inhibition of unrelated essential proteins, are part of the same picture, as is deliberate cytochrome P450 blockade to extend antiviral half-life.

The first step a coronavirus takes after uncoating is to translate its own replicase from the incoming genome, then build the membrane-bound machine that copies it. Cap-dependent translation of ORF1a yields polyprotein pp1a, and a slippery sequence with a downstream pseudoknot directs a fraction of ribosomes into dash 1 frameshifting to extend into ORF1b; autoproteolysis by the papain-like and main proteases releases the nonstructural proteins, including the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. Several nsps remodel host membranes into double-membrane vesicles that anchor and shield the replication-transcription complex from innate immune sensing. Formation of these vesicles draws on host membrane-shaping and autophagy-related machinery, including the class III PI3-kinase complex with its regulatory subunits and beclin-1, LC3, and ESCRT-III charged multivesicular body proteins, which explains why these host factors govern viral RNA replication efficiency.

Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronaviruses enter and replicate in human cells by co-opting host machinery, and this pathway traces that life cycle from attachment through immune evasion. Entry begins with binding of the spike protein to the ACE2 receptor, with proteolytic priming by TMPRSS2, furin or cathepsin L, followed by clathrin-mediated uptake and endosomal trafficking. Once inside, the virus depends on endoplasmic reticulum glycosylation and secretory transport for structural protein maturation, ribosomal subunits and translation factors for subgenomic mRNA synthesis, and palmitoylation for spike assembly. Viral proteins in turn blunt host defence: interferon induction through RIG-I/MDA5 and MAVS, nuclear pore transport of STAT1, and nucleocapsid sequestration of stress granule proteins are all targeted. The accompanying inflammasome, Toll-like receptor, IL-17 and antibody components reflect the innate and humoral responses whose dysregulation drives severe COVID-19 and acute respiratory distress.

Virion Assembly and Release is the final step of the coronavirus replication cycle, in which newly made structural proteins and genomic RNA are packaged into infectious particles and exported from the cell; blocking it aborts spread even when replication itself proceeds normally. Assembly happens at the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment rather than the plasma membrane, and depends on the host secretory and retrieval machinery: retention signals in the cytoplasmic tails of the viral membrane and spike proteins engage COPI and related coats, so the proteins cycle between compartments and concentrate at the budding site. Homotypic interaction of M protein builds a lattice that bends the membrane and recruits E, S and the helical nucleocapsid, fixing a particle roughly 100 nm across with defined protein stoichiometry. Completed virions then traverse the secretory route for release, making membrane trafficking the effective bottleneck for viral egress.

The last step of a coronavirus replication cycle is building new particles and getting them out of the cell, and it happens not at the plasma membrane but on membranes of the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment. Structural proteins are concentrated there by retrieval signals in their cytoplasmic tails that engage host coat machinery such as COPI, so that repeated anterograde and retrograde trafficking keeps them at the budding site. Assembly begins with self-association of the membrane protein M into a lattice that bends the membrane and recruits the spike, envelope and nucleocapsid proteins, the latter delivering the helical ribonucleoprotein containing the genomic RNA. The result is a roughly 100 nm enveloped particle with spike trimers, abundant M, and packaged nucleocapsid, plus small amounts of accessory proteins, which then exits through the secretory route to infect new cells.

Coronaviruses copy their RNA genome in cytoplasmic replication-transcription complexes, and this arm of the SARS-CoV-1 life cycle covers the synthesis of new genomic RNA and of the nested subgenomic messages from which structural and accessory proteins are translated. A negative-sense antigenome is made first and used as template for progeny genomes, while the polymerase can jump between transcription-regulatory sequences to generate the shorter subgenomic RNAs; nucleocapsid protein acts as an RNA chaperone during these template switches, and host kinase activity on it tunes the balance between long and short products. Host RNA-binding proteins are co-opted at this step, including the DEAD-box helicase DDX5 and the zinc-finger protein ZCRB1, which engages the viral 5' untranslated region. Output from these reactions sets viral load, so the interactions represented here are candidate points for antiviral intervention.

KIT is the receptor tyrosine kinase for stem cell factor, driving the proliferation and survival of mast cells, melanocytes, germ cells, haematopoietic progenitors and the interstitial cells of Cajal. Its extracellular region contains five Ig-like domains; the membrane-proximal fifth domain does not bind ligand but holds the two receptor chains together after stem cell factor has brought them into contact, so that the cytoplasmic kinase domains can trans-phosphorylate. Mutations in this domain, encoded by exons 8 and 9, mimic that stabilised dimer interface and allow the receptor to signal without ligand, feeding constitutive input into RAS-MAPK, PI3K-AKT and STAT pathways. Such extracellular-domain mutants are found in gastrointestinal stromal tumours, mastocytosis and acute myeloid leukaemia, and differ from juxtamembrane and kinase-domain mutants in their sensitivity to tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

Macrophages, monocytes, osteoclasts and microglia depend on CSF1 signalling for their production, survival and maintenance, and this receptor tyrosine kinase route is what translates that cytokine cue into cell behaviour. CSF1, or the alternative ligand IL34, dimerises CSF1R and triggers trans-autophosphorylation of its cytoplasmic tyrosines, creating docking sites for SH2-domain effectors: PI3K via its p85 regulatory subunit, GRB2 bound to SOS1 feeding KRAS and the ERK cascade, PLCG2, SHC1, GAB scaffolds, the phosphatase PTPN11, and SRC-family kinases such as LYN, HCK and FYN. The output is proliferation of phagocyte precursors, macrophage survival, motility and an anti-inflammatory bias, with STAT1 and STAT3 recruited as well. CBL-mediated ubiquitination and inositol phosphatases including INPP5D damp the response. Loss of signalling impairs bone resorption and tissue macrophage populations, while excess drives tumour-associated macrophage accumulation, making CSF1R a drug target.

FLT3 is a type III receptor tyrosine kinase that drives proliferation and survival of haematopoietic progenitors when engaged by its ligand, and it is one of the most frequently mutated genes in acute myeloid leukaemia. Aberrant FLT3 signalling in disease arises from internal tandem duplications in the juxtamembrane region, missense changes in the kinase domain, or rare translocations that fuse FLT3 to partners such as ETV6, ZMYM2, GOLGB1 or SPTBN1; all of these dispense with ligand and leave the receptor constitutively active. Output flows through GRB2, SOS1, PTPN11 and GAB2 to RAS and the MAP kinase cascade, through PIK3CA/PIK3R1 to PI3K, and through STAT5A/STAT5B to targets including PIM1, CDKN1A and the survival protein BCL2L1, while CBL-dependent ubiquitination normally limits receptor output. The pathway is the rationale for FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitors, whose benefit is eroded by secondary mutations and bypass signalling.

Replication of the SARS-CoV-1 genome produces new viral RNA for packaging into infectious particles and sustains the RNA templates used to make viral proteins. Without this copying step, infection cannot propagate between cells. After entry, the positive-sense RNA genome is copied into a complementary negative strand by a membrane-associated viral replication-transcription complex. This negative strand then serves as a template for new positive-sense genomes and subgenomic RNAs. The viral polymerase carries out RNA synthesis, a helicase resolves RNA structures, and proofreading exonuclease activity limits copying errors. Viral RNA capping supports RNA stability and helps shield it from host innate immune detection. Host proteins involved in RNA processing and cellular regulation provide the environment in which this viral machinery operates.

Viral nucleoprotein maturation prepares an abundant structural protein for genome packaging and production of new virus particles. Disruption of this process can prevent nucleoprotein from reaching the assembly site and impair virion formation. During infection, nucleoprotein is present in the cytosol and at the plasma membrane before undergoing phosphorylation and SUMO modification. GSK3-family kinases participate in phosphorylation, while UBE2I is the conjugating enzyme that attaches SUMO1 to target proteins. These modifications promote nucleoprotein trimerization and its movement to the Golgi, where viral budding occurs. PARP-family proteins connect this process with host ADP-ribosylation machinery, which regulates protein function during infection. Together, these modification and trafficking steps prepare nucleoprotein for incorporation into assembling virions, connecting host protein-processing machinery to viral particle production.

Coronaviruses build new particles not at the plasma membrane but in the compartment between endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, and the membrane (M) protein is what organises that site. Maturation of protein M covers its insertion into ER membranes, partial N-glycosylation of its short ectodomain, and its passage to and accumulation in the Golgi complex, where the mature form adopts the conformation needed for lattice formation. Oligomerised M recruits the Spike glycoprotein and other structural components to budding sites in the ERGIC, determining particle shape and ensuring that Spike is retained in virions rather than trafficking onward to the cell surface. Because assembly depends on host secretory-pathway machinery, glycosylation enzymes and vesicular transport, this step links viral morphogenesis to normal membrane protein biogenesis and is a point at which egress can be blocked.

Maturation of the SARS coronavirus 3a protein gives a viral membrane accessory protein its O-linked sugar coating as it moves through the host secretory system. The mature protein can associate with membrane protein M and enter virions, although 3a is not required to build the particle; it also forms tetrameric, ion-permeable channels. Host GALNT1 initiates glycosylation by attaching N-acetylgalactosamine to exposed serine or threonine residues, while Golgi sialyltransferases add terminal sialic acids to suitable glycans. These modifications produce a sialylated extracellular surface on 3a and connect its maturation to host glycan processing. They distinguish 3a from the viral M protein, which carries N-linked sugars, without establishing that any one glycosylation step is required for channel activity or viral assembly.

Maturation of protein E covers the post-translational processing of the small envelope protein of a coronavirus after its synthesis on host ribosomes, a step that determines whether virions can assemble and bud correctly from intracellular membranes. Protein E is palmitoylated and ubiquitinated, oligomerises into trimers with ion-channel or porin activity, and accumulates in the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment rather than the plasma membrane, where it contributes to membrane curvature during particle formation and to the ion permeability that shapes secretory-pathway pH. The host contribution here is ubiquitin itself, supplied by the polyubiquitin genes and by the ribosomal protein fusion precursors, illustrating how viruses conscript the ubiquitin system for the modification and turnover of their own structural proteins. Loss of E maturation yields poorly assembled, attenuated virus, which is why it is examined as an antiviral and vaccine-attenuation target.

Coronavirus envelope (E) protein is a small membrane protein that must be modified after synthesis before it can perform its role in virion assembly and budding, and the maturation of protein E covers those post-translational steps. Following translation, E is palmitoylated and ubiquitinated; the host ubiquitin precursors represented here, including the ribosomal fusion proteins RPS27A and UBA52 and the polyubiquitin products of UBB and UBC, supply the ubiquitin that is conjugated to it. Matured E oligomerises into trimers with ion-conducting porin-like activity and remains in internal membranes of the secretory pathway rather than reaching the plasma membrane, consistent with its function at the endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi intermediate compartment where particles bud. This illustrates how viral structural proteins are routed through host modification and ubiquitin systems, which also govern their turnover and immune detection.

SARS-CoV spike maturation converts newly synthesized spike into a folded, glycosylated homotrimer displayed on the viral envelope. This surface protein binds host receptors and drives membrane fusion, so defective maturation can impair viral entry. In the host endoplasmic reticulum, N-linked glycans are added and trimmed by MOGS and the GANAB-PRKCSH glucosidase II complex, allowing calnexin (CANX) to assist spike folding and quality control. Subsequent processing, including MGAT1-dependent initiation of complex N-glycan formation in the Golgi, remodels the spike's carbohydrate coat. Spike also undergoes palmitoylation, which supports its membrane-associated function. Together these modifications and folding steps produce trimeric spike competent for incorporation into new virions and participation in infection.

Viral envelope glycoproteins fold in the endoplasmic reticulum using the same host quality-control machinery that handles the cell's own secretory proteins, and the maturation of spike protein is a well-studied illustration of it. After co-translational transfer of the N-linked glycan, glucosidase I trims the outermost glucose and the glucosidase II complex — its catalytic subunit paired with the regulatory beta subunit — removes the next, generating the monoglucosylated form that calnexin recognises. That lectin chaperone holds the nascent chain in the ER, promotes correct disulphide pairing and oligomerisation, and retains misfolded species for further cycles or degradation. Subsequent trimming and the action of the Golgi GlcNAc transferase that initiates complex N-glycans convert high-mannose chains into mature glycans. The same steps govern folding of receptors, adhesion molecules and secreted enzymes; their disruption causes congenital disorders of glycosylation and, for kidney cyst genes, polycystic liver disease.

After a coronavirus has replicated its genome, its subgenomic messenger RNAs are read out to make the proteins that build new particles — spike, envelope, membrane and nucleocapsid — and this step converts viral transcripts into the structural components of the virion. Because spike, envelope and membrane are membrane proteins, their synthesis is coupled to the endoplasmic reticulum, where host machinery for co-translational folding and glycan processing takes over: the calnexin cycle and glucosidase activities of MOGS, GANAB and PRKCSH oversee folding quality control, while N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase, sialyltransferase and polypeptide GalNAc-transferase enzymes elaborate N- and O-linked glycans that shield the spike from antibodies. Nucleocapsid is instead made on free cytosolic ribosomes and is modified by host kinases GSK3A/GSK3B, by SUMOylation through UBE2I and SUMO1, by ubiquitin, and by ADP-ribosyltransferases of the PARP family, several of which are interferon-induced antiviral effectors. These modifications tune assembly, RNA binding and immune evasion.

Coronaviruses translate their incoming genome as two long polyproteins, and this maturation step converts them into the individual non-structural proteins that build the viral replication-transcription complex. Nothing else in the infection can proceed without it: the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, helicase, proofreading exonuclease and capping enzymes exist only as polyprotein segments until they are cut free, which is why the responsible proteases are prime antiviral drug targets. Cleavage is autocatalytic and ordered, beginning with papain-like protease activity within nsp3 that releases the amino-terminal products, after which the liberated main protease trims the remaining junctions efficiently. Two of the products, nsp3 and nsp4, are also glycosylated; both are membrane-anchored and together remodel host endoplasmic reticulum membranes into the double-membrane vesicles where viral RNA synthesis is sequestered from cytosolic innate immune sensors.

Interferon-induced proteins with tetratricopeptide repeats give infected cells a way to recognise viral RNA by what its 5' end lacks and to stop it being translated. IFIT1 distinguishes self from non-self transcripts by cap 2'-O-methylation, binding cap-0 and 5'-triphosphate RNA in a channel between its repeat domains and sequestering it from the cap-binding initiation machinery; IFIT5 favours uncapped triphosphate RNA. IFIT3 partners IFIT1 to sharpen this discrimination and stabilise it, while IFIT2:IFIT3 complexes block messages with short 5' UTRs. The accompanying 40S subunit proteins and the full eIF3 complex, including the EIF3E subunit engaged by IFIT1 and IFIT2, mark the target: assembly of the 43S pre-initiation complex. Viruses counter by methylating their caps, folding protective 5' stem-loops, or, as in vaccinia, recruiting SKP1-CUL1 ubiquitin ligases to degrade IFITs.

Cytosolic lipopolysaccharide from invading Gram-negative bacteria is sensed directly by caspase-4 and caspase-5, which serve as their own receptors and thereby form the non-canonical inflammasome, bypassing the caspase-1-dependent route and TLR4 entirely. This arm of innate immunity converts detection of a bacterium that has escaped into the cytosol into pyroptosis, a lytic inflammatory death that destroys the replicative niche and alerts neighbouring cells. LPS binding drives caspase dimerization and autoprocessing; the active protease cleaves gasdermin D within its linker, freeing an N-terminal fragment that oligomerizes into plasma membrane pores through which mature IL-18 and IL-1 family cytokines escape as the cell swells and ruptures. Guanylate-binding proteins promote bacterial surface disruption to expose LPS, while SERPINB1 restrains caspase activity. Overactivation drives sepsis and inflammatory pathology; loss impairs clearance of intracellular pathogens.

Necroptosis is a lytic, inflammation-provoking form of programmed cell death that serves as a backup when apoptosis is blocked, and pathogens have evolved both to trigger and to suppress it. Here the focus is on how microbes modulate RIPK1-dependent regulated necrosis in the host: RIPK1 and RIPK3 engage through their RIP homotypic interaction motifs to form a necrosome, RIPK3 phosphorylates MLKL, and oligomerised MLKL permeabilises the plasma membrane, spilling damage-associated molecular patterns that drive antiviral and antibacterial inflammation. Caspase-8 normally restrains this route by cleaving RIPK1, so viral and bacterial effectors that inhibit caspase-8 or mimic RIP homotypic interaction motifs shift the outcome either way. The balance struck determines whether infected cells die immunogenically to alert the host or survive as a replication niche, and the same axis underlies inflammatory tissue damage.

Cells leaving mitosis must shut down cyclin-dependent kinase activity and stay out of S phase, and the retinoblastoma protein contributes to this by controlling the abundance of SKP2. When RB1 is lost or inactivated, as it is in retinoblastoma, small cell lung cancer and many other tumours, this arm of mitotic exit control fails and proliferation continues unchecked. Normally RB1 promotes APC/C-dependent ubiquitination and destruction of SKP2, the substrate-recognition subunit of an SCF ubiquitin ligase that otherwise targets the CDK inhibitor p27Kip1; removing SKP2 lets p27Kip1 accumulate and restrain CDK activity. The machinery involved is the anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome with its many ANAPC and CDC subunits, the activator FZR1, and E2 enzymes including UBE2C and UBE2S that build the ubiquitin chains. This links ubiquitin-proteasome degradation directly to tumour suppression at the mitosis-to-G1 transition.

Loss of the retinoblastoma protein removes the brake on entry into S phase, and the consequences of RB1 defects explain both the childhood eye tumour retinoblastoma and frequent somatic inactivation in bladder, small-cell lung, ovarian and bone cancers. Normally RB1 binds the activating E2F transcription factors E2F1, E2F2 and E2F3 with their DP partners and keeps DNA replication genes silent until cyclin D-CDK4/6 and cyclin E-CDK2 phosphorylate it, a step opposed by the CDK inhibitors p21, p27 and p57. When RB1 is deleted or truncated, E2F targets are transcribed regardless of growth signals and the G1/S restriction point is bypassed. RB1 also promotes APC/C-dependent destruction of SKP2, allowing p27 to accumulate during mitotic exit, so its loss additionally destabilises orderly cell cycle exit and genome integrity.

Gonads arise from a bipotential ridge, and the transcriptional programme that drives testis differentiation is what tips that tissue toward male development rather than ovary. Its failure or partial activation produces disorders of sex development, including XY gonadal dysgenesis and sex reversal. WT1, GATA4 with its cofactor ZFPM2, and the nuclear receptor NR5A1 switch on SRY from the Y chromosome in somatic cells of the genital ridge; SRY with NR5A1 then induces SOX9, which sustains its own expression and specifies Sertoli cells that enclose germ cells in testis cords. Feed-forward loops through FGF9 and prostaglandin D2 synthase reinforce SOX9, while DMRT1 locks in the male state and represses the ovarian regulators FOXL2 and WNT4. Downstream effectors include AMH, which drives Müllerian duct regression, and the hedgehog ligand DHH, needed for testis architecture.

Interferon-induced IFIT proteins restrict viruses by recognizing foreign RNA 5′ ends — triphosphorylated or lacking 2′-O-methylation of the cap — and sequestering them from the translation machinery, so successful viruses must neutralize this arm of innate immunity.
