Loss of the p16/p14ARF locus product and mutation of TP53 uncouple oncogenic and genotoxic stress from the transcription of pro-apoptotic effectors such as BCL2L11, leaving damaged cells alive. In neurons, calpain-mediated cleavage of CDK5R1 to p25 converts CDK5 into a chronically active, mislocalized kinase that phosphorylates targets including FOXO3, JUN, lamins and Golgi proteins, tipping the cell toward death; calpastatin restrains this. Oxidative stress enzymes and amyloid precursor protein place the dysregulation in a context of redox imbalance and neurodegeneration.

MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by hepatocyte growth factor to drive cell scattering, motility, invasive growth and survival, and it becomes oncogenic when amplified or mutated so that it signals excessively or without ligand. Because MET activation also emerges as an escape route in tumours treated against related receptors such as EGFR, blocking it matters both as a primary therapy and as a way to overcome acquired resistance. Pharmacological inhibition of MET activation covers the two ways this axis is drugged: monoclonal antibodies that intercept HGF or occupy the receptor ectodomain and prevent ligand-induced dimerisation, and small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitors that block catalytic activity and downstream phosphorylation. The outcome is loss of MET autophosphorylation and of the adaptor recruitment that would otherwise feed proliferative and invasive signalling in solid tumours carrying MET-driven lesions.

Defective APRT disrupts adenine salvage describes what happens when the single enzyme that recycles free adenine into AMP is lost. Adenine is released continuously as a by-product of metabolism, notably polyamine synthesis, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase normally captures it in one step by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP, feeding it back into the purine nucleotide pool. With the enzyme inactive, adenine is instead oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, a compound so poorly soluble that it precipitates in the urinary tract. The consequence is not nucleotide shortage, since de novo synthesis compensates, but crystal nephropathy: recurrent stones, tubular injury and progressive renal failure, sometimes presenting only after transplant loss. This places purine salvage failure among the inherited crystalline kidney diseases, and explains why treatment targets the oxidising enzyme rather than the missing one.

Adenine released by polyamine synthesis and nucleic acid turnover is normally recycled rather than degraded, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase performs that salvage step by transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto free adenine to give AMP. When the enzyme is defective, this purine salvage route fails and adenine is instead oxidised by xanthine dehydrogenase to the highly insoluble metabolite 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as crystals in urine and renal tissue. The clinical consequence is APRT deficiency: radiolucent kidney stones, crystalline nephropathy, and progressive renal failure that can recur after transplantation unless xanthine oxidoreductase is inhibited. The biology sits within purine metabolism, where salvage pathways spare the energetic cost of de novo nucleotide synthesis, and it illustrates how loss of a single recycling enzyme causes disease through toxic accumulation of the unsalvaged substrate rather than through nucleotide shortage.

Cells recycle purine bases rather than build them from scratch, and loss of that recycling capacity defines the nucleotide salvage defects. Three enzymes carry the identity of this biology: adenine phosphoribosyltransferase, hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, and adenosine deaminase. When adenine cannot be reattached to ribose phosphate, it is instead oxidised to poorly soluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which crystallises in the kidney and causes stones and progressive renal failure. When hypoxanthine and guanine cannot be salvaged, purines are shunted to urate, producing the hyperuricaemia, gout, and the self-injurious neurological disease of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Failure to deaminate adenosine and deoxyadenosine allows dATP to accumulate to levels toxic to developing lymphocytes, giving one of the classic forms of severe combined immunodeficiency. Together these illustrate how salvage of purines governs uric acid balance, renal health, and immune development.

Purine bases released by nucleic acid turnover are normally recycled rather than discarded, and hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase is the enzyme that does it, transferring a phosphoribosyl group from PRPP onto hypoxanthine to make IMP and onto guanine to make GMP. Loss of this salvage activity forces the cells to depend entirely on energetically costly de novo purine synthesis, while the unsalvaged bases are oxidized by xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase to urate. The consequences in humans are striking: partial deficiency produces gout and urate nephropathy from overproduction, and near-complete deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan disease, with hyperuricaemia, dystonia, cognitive impairment and compulsive self-injurious behaviour reflecting the particular reliance of basal ganglia dopaminergic neurons on purine recycling. The pathway links nucleotide economy to neurodevelopment and to renal handling of uric acid.

Adenosine deaminase converts adenosine and deoxyadenosine to inosine and deoxyinosine, the committed step that lets cells dispose of purine nucleosides through the salvage and degradation route toward uric acid. When ADA activity is lost, this deamination step fails and the unprocessed substrates accumulate, with deoxyadenosine being phosphorylated to dATP that poisons ribonucleotide reduction and DNA synthesis. Developing thymocytes and lymphocytes are the cells least able to tolerate this, so the consequence of defective (deoxy)adenosine deamination is severe combined immunodeficiency, with profoundly reduced T, B and NK cells, recurrent infection from infancy, and additional skeletal, neurological and pulmonary features reflecting the enzyme's ubiquitous expression. The disorder is treatable by enzyme replacement, transplantation or gene therapy, making it a model for how a single metabolic clearance reaction sustains adaptive immunity.

Every specialized cell in the body traces back to a zygote through a series of committed steps, and developmental cell lineages organize those steps as ordered transitions from stem or progenitor states to mature cell types, each state defined by its anatomical location and marker profile. The value is practical: knowing the regulators that drive a given step is what makes directed differentiation, regenerative medicine and the interpretation of tumour cell states possible. The molecules gathered here are the extrinsic side of that control — basement membrane and interstitial matrix components such as fibrillar collagens, fibronectin, vitronectin and the laminin chains, together with diffusible regulators including EGF, TGFA, amphiregulin, several FGFs, CSF1, prolactin and interferon gamma. Laminin-332 chains LAMA3, LAMB3 and LAMC2 illustrate the point: they anchor basal keratinocytes to the dermis, and their loss causes junctional epidermolysis bullosa.

Skin and its appendages develop and renew through growth-factor signalling between epithelium and the mesenchyme beneath it, and this small set of ligands captures that instructive crosstalk for the integumentary system. Epidermal keratinocytes stratify and form a barrier, while hair follicles, sweat and sebaceous glands, and the mammary gland arise as invaginating placodes whose branching and secretory maturation depend on the same cues. Amphiregulin, EGF and TGF-alpha act through the EGF receptor to drive keratinocyte proliferation and ductal outgrowth; FGF10 from mesenchyme signals to epithelial FGFR2b to initiate and elongate buds; prolactin drives lobuloalveolar differentiation and milk secretion in the mammary gland, a modified apocrine gland. Loss or excess of these signals produces failed appendage formation, impaired lactation and defective wound repair, and the same EGFR axis is a recurrent driver in epithelial tumours.

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase normally strips the sugar from inosine, deoxyinosine, guanosine and deoxyguanosine, releasing hypoxanthine or guanine for salvage back into nucleotides and clearing the products of nucleic acid turnover. When the enzyme is defective, this phosphorolysis step fails and its substrates build up; deoxyguanosine is rephosphorylated to dGTP, which poisons ribonucleotide reductase and blocks DNA synthesis in dividing cells. T lymphocytes, with their high deoxynucleoside kinase activity and demanding proliferative programme, are the most vulnerable, so loss of activity produces a profound T cell deficiency with variable B cell involvement, recurrent infection, and in many patients neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The disorder sits alongside adenosine deaminase deficiency as an inborn error of purine catabolism causing combined immunodeficiency, and illustrates how a single salvage reaction supports lymphoid development.

Purine nucleoside phosphorylase carries out a step in purine salvage and degradation, converting inosine and guanosine to hypoxanthine and guanine so that ribose is recovered and the bases are either reused or oxidised onward to uric acid. Loss of this activity is the archetypal nucleotide catabolism defect: deoxyguanosine and its nucleotides accumulate and are especially toxic to developing lymphocytes, producing a severe combined immunodeficiency with profound T cell depletion and, in many patients, neurological impairment and autoimmunity. The biochemistry illustrates why purine turnover must be kept in balance -- blocked degradation distorts the deoxynucleotide pool and stalls DNA replication in proliferating cells. Because the same chemistry limits nucleoside-analogue drugs, the enzyme is also a pharmacological target, linking inherited metabolic failure to immune development and purine homeostasis.

Diseases of nucleotide metabolism covers the inherited enzyme deficiencies that break purine salvage and catabolism, showing what happens when cells must rely on de novo synthesis alone. Loss of adenosine deaminase or purine nucleoside phosphorylase allows toxic deoxynucleosides to accumulate in lymphocytes, killing developing T cells and causing severe combined immunodeficiency; ADA deficiency was the first target of human gene therapy. Loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase diverts hypoxanthine and guanine to uric acid instead of recycling them into IMP and GMP, producing hyperuricaemia, gout and, when complete, the neurological and self-injurious features of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency leaves adenine to be oxidised to insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as kidney stones. Together these reactions link nucleotide economy to immune development, urate handling and renal function.

Purine nucleotides are salvaged rather than built from scratch in most tissues, and inherited loss of the salvage and catabolic enzymes produces a recognisable group of diseases of nucleotide metabolism. Adenosine deaminase and purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiencies allow toxic deoxynucleotides to accumulate in lymphocytes, causing severe combined immunodeficiency with absent T, B and NK cell function. Loss of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase, which recycles hypoxanthine and guanine onto ribose phosphate, diverts purines to uric acid and gives the hyperuricaemia, gout and self-injurious neurological disease of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency instead leaves adenine to be oxidised to insoluble 2,8-dihydroxyadenine, which precipitates as kidney stones and can destroy renal function. Together these enzymes show how purine recycling supports immune cell development, uric acid balance and neuronal function.

When SARS-CoV-1 infects a cell, one of its first acts is to take over protein synthesis, and this pathway describes how the viral nonstructural protein 1 and nucleocapsid protein shut down host translation. The consequence is twofold: the cell stops making the interferon and antiviral effector proteins it needs to respond to infection, while viral RNAs continue to be translated, tilting the outcome toward productive replication and contributing to the blunted innate immune response seen in severe coronavirus disease. Mechanistically, nsp1 binds the small ribosomal subunit, whose 40S proteins dominate this set alongside RPSA and the ubiquitin-ribosomal fusion product encoded by FAU, obstructing the mRNA entry channel so that capped host transcripts cannot be loaded or scanned; associated factors such as the elongation factor EEF1A1 and the RNA-binding protein HNRNPA1 link the hijacked ribosome to viral RNA metabolism.

SARS-CoV-1 does not merely replicate in a host cell; several of its proteins latch onto host signalling hubs and bend them toward viral advantage, which helps explain the apoptosis, fibrosis and inflammatory injury seen in severe respiratory disease. The membrane protein binds PDPK1 and prevents it from activating Akt, removing a survival signal and sensitising infected cells to death. The nucleocapsid protein engages SMAD3, blocking its partnership with SMAD4 so that TGF-beta-driven apoptosis is lost while transcription of the fibrosis effector PAI-1 is enhanced, with EP300 and SP1 contributing at the promoter. Nucleocapsid also contacts the proteasomal ATPase subunit PSMC6, altering regulated protein degradation, and the SUMO-conjugating enzyme UBE2I, perturbing sumoylation and cell cycle control. Viral 3a binds caveolin-1, linking virus uptake and structural protein trafficking. Multiple 14-3-3 proteins act as phosphoserine-binding scaffolds through these interactions.

Drug ADME describes what the body does to a drug rather than what the drug does to the body: its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion, the four stages that set circulating drug concentration, duration of action and dose requirements. This is the biology behind interindividual variation in drug response, drug-drug interactions and toxicity, and polymorphisms in these genes underlie clinical pharmacogenetics. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and cation families and nucleoside carriers move compounds into hepatocytes, enterocytes and renal tubule cells; cytochrome P450 monooxygenases and esterases perform oxidative and hydrolytic conversion; UDP-glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases, N-acetyltransferases and thiopurine methyltransferase conjugate metabolites for elimination; and ATP-binding cassette efflux pumps export them into bile, urine and gut lumen. Plasma proteins such as albumin govern distribution, while purine salvage enzymes activate thiopurine and antimetabolite prodrugs.

The fate of a drug in the body — how it is absorbed, distributed, chemically transformed and excreted — determines its dose, duration of action and toxicity, and this collection of absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion steps is where that pharmacokinetic handling is carried out. Uptake transporters of the organic anion and organic cation families, together with nucleoside carriers, move compounds into hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, while ABC efflux pumps including ABCB1 and ABCG2 export them back to blood, bile or urine and set oral bioavailability and blood–brain barrier access. Between the two, cytochrome P450 oxidations and hydrolysis by carboxylesterases generate metabolites that UGT glucuronosyltransferases, sulfotransferases, glutathione S-transferases and N-acetyltransferases conjugate for elimination; thiopurine and purine-handling enzymes such as TPMT, HPRT1 and XDH activate or inactivate antimetabolite drugs. Common variants in these genes underlie much interindividual variation in drug response and adverse reactions.

Azathioprine is a thiopurine prodrug used as an immunosuppressant in inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis and transplant rejection, and its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion determine both its benefit and its toxicity. Glutathione transferases release 6-mercaptopurine from the parent drug, after which competing routes decide its fate: xanthine dehydrogenase and the methyltransferase TPMT inactivate it, while HPRT1 channels it into nucleotide synthesis, where IMPDH and GMPS then kinases such as GUK1 and the NME phosphotransferases build cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides. These are incorporated into DNA and RNA, block de novo purine synthesis, and antagonise RAC1 signalling downstream of VAV exchange factors to drive apoptosis of activated T cells. Nucleoside transporters of the SLC28 and SLC29 families mediate uptake, ABCC4 and ABCC5 efflux the metabolites, and inherited variation in TPMT or NUDT15 causes severe myelosuppression, making this pathway a standard example of pharmacogenetic dose adjustment.

Aspirin's absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion determine how much acetylsalicylate reaches its targets, the cyclooxygenase enzymes, and how quickly it is cleared as salicylate. Nearly all of an oral dose is taken up across intestinal mucosa, favoured by the larger surface and less acidic conditions of the small intestine, with monocarboxylate and organic anion transporters such as SLC16A1, SLCO2B1 and SLC22A7 moving drug and metabolites across membranes and ABCC2/ABCC3 effluxing conjugates. Circulating drug rides largely on albumin. Carboxylesterases CES1 and CES2, together with butyrylcholinesterase, hydrolyse the acetyl group to yield salicylate, which is then conjugated with glycine by GLYAT-family enzymes, using acyl-CoA synthetases, to salicylurate, or glucuronidated by a broad set of UGTs; cytochromes P450 contribute minor hydroxylation. Variation in these steps shapes dose response, drug interactions and gastric toxicity.

Several mainstay therapeutics — nitrogen mustards and other alkylating agents, platinum compounds such as cisplatin, mitomycin C, and the psoralens used with ultraviolet light in psoriasis and severe atopic dermatitis — kill or arrest dividing cells by covalently joining the two strands of the DNA duplex. Such drug-induced interstrand crosslinks are the most cytotoxic lesion a cell can carry, because a tethered duplex cannot be unwound and so blocks both replication fork progression and transcription. Their repair depends on the Fanconi anemia pathway, which recognises stalled forks, unhooks the crosslink through coordinated nuclease incisions, and completes restoration by translesion synthesis and homologous recombination. The balance between lesion formation and this repair capacity sets therapeutic response: tumours with defective crosslink repair are hypersensitive, whereas restored repair underlies acquired chemoresistance, and patients with inherited Fanconi anemia show extreme toxicity to these agents.

Plasmacytoid dendritic cells sensing viral nucleic acids produce large amounts of type I interferon, and this branch of endosomal Toll-like receptor signalling is how they do it. TLR7 and TLR8 recognise single-stranded RNA and TLR9 recognises CpG DNA; both recruit MyD88, which nucleates a complex containing IRAK4, IRAK1 and TRAF6 together with IRF7 itself. TRAF6, acting with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 ubiquitin-conjugating pair and free ubiquitin, builds non-degradative polyubiquitin chains that license kinase activity, and IRAK1-dependent phosphorylation of IRF7 drives its nuclear translocation and transcription of IFN-alpha and IFN-beta genes. Unlike IRF3, IRF7 is the interferon regulator dedicated to this receptor set. Loss of MyD88 or IRAK4 leaves patients vulnerable to pyogenic infection, while excessive IRF7 output through these receptors contributes to interferon-driven autoimmunity such as lupus.

Endosomal sensing of microbial nucleic acids by TLR7, TLR8 and TLR9 triggers an inflammatory transcriptional response, and this is the branch that converts receptor engagement into NF-kB and MAP kinase activity. It drives production of type I interferon-associated and proinflammatory cytokines during viral and bacterial infection, and its misfiring underlies nucleic acid-driven autoimmunity such as lupus. MyD88 recruits IRAK4 and IRAK1, which engage the ubiquitin ligase TRAF6; TRAF6 builds polyubiquitin chains with the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair to activate the TAK1 (MAP3K7) complex with its TAB adaptors. TAK1 then phosphorylates the IKK complex, releasing NF-kB from IkB after its SCF-dependent degradation, and in parallel feeds the JNK, p38 and ERK cascades that activate AP-1 factors such as JUN and FOS. Pellino ligases, DUSP phosphatases, PP2A subunits and deubiquitinases set the amplitude and duration of the response.

Endosomal sensing of viral nucleic acids by TLR7, TLR8 or TLR9 must be converted into inflammatory gene transcription, and this step is where the receptor-proximal kinase IRAK1 hands the signal to the IKK complex that frees NF-kappaB. Rather than depending on IRAK1 catalytic activity, the handoff runs through non-degradative Lys63-linked polyubiquitin: the UBE2N/UBE2V1 conjugating pair, TRAF6 and the Pellino E3 ligases decorate IRAK1, and those chains are read by the NEMO regulatory subunit, docking the CHUK/IKBKB kinases with TAK1 so IkappaB can be phosphorylated and destroyed. The outcome is transcription of type I interferon and proinflammatory cytokine genes during antiviral defence; the same axis drives autoantibody-associated inflammation when self nucleic acids trigger it inappropriately.

Nucleic-acid-sensing Toll-like receptors sit in endosomes rather than at the cell surface, and this MyD88-dependent cascade initiated on the endosome is how detection of single-stranded RNA by TLR7/8 or unmethylated CpG DNA by TLR9 is converted into an antiviral and inflammatory response. Ligand binding recruits MyD88 and the IRAK kinases, which engage TRAF6 and the ubiquitin machinery to activate the TAK1 complex; from there the signal branches to IKK-driven degradation of IkB and release of NF-kB, and to the p38, JNK and ERK arms with their downstream AP-1, CREB and MEF2 transcription factors, while IRF7 drives type I interferon. Phosphatases, Pellino ligases, deubiquitinases and IkB-like inhibitors set the amplitude and duration. Plasmacytoid dendritic cell interferon output depends on it, and chronic activation by self nucleic acids contributes to lupus and other autoimmune inflammation.

Endosomal Toll-like receptors sensing microbial nucleic acid must convert ligand binding into inflammatory gene expression, and this step is where that signal is committed to the kinase cascade. After TLR7/8 or TLR9 engagement, IRAK2 rather than IRAK1 drives TRAF6 to build K63-linked polyubiquitin chains, using ubiquitin supplied by the polyubiquitin and ribosomal fusion genes present here. Those chains are read by the TAB2 and TAB3 subunits, which together with TAB1 assemble and activate the TAK1 kinase MAP3K7, the branch point that feeds both IKK-dependent NF-kB activation and the JNK and p38 MAP kinase arms. The output is transcription of cytokines and type I interferon responses underlying antiviral and antibacterial defence. IRAK2 mutants lacking TRAF6-binding motifs fail to activate NF-kB, and the poxvirus A52 protein exploits this node to blunt host inflammation; excess signalling here contributes to autoimmune nucleic-acid sensing.

The sense of smell begins with hundreds of odorant-binding G protein-coupled receptors, and this pathway covers how a single one of them is chosen for expression in each olfactory sensory neuron and then delivered to the ciliary membrane where odorants are detected. Because each neuron expresses just one receptor and projects to a matched glomerulus in the olfactory bulb, this one-receptor-per-neuron choice is what makes odour discrimination and the olfactory map possible. Most receptor genes are held in heterochromatin; LHX2, LDB1 and EBF1 occupy intergenic enhancers that coalesce into an interchromosomal super-enhancer driving one allele, after which a feedback signal from accumulated receptor protein in the endoplasmic reticulum locks out the rest. Trafficking is the second bottleneck: the receptor transport proteins RTP1 and RTP2, with weaker help from REEP1, escort receptors out of the ER to the cell surface.

Paracetamol is among the most widely taken analgesic and antipyretic drugs, and its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion determine both its safety at therapeutic doses and its lethality in overdose. Most of an oral dose is inactivated in the liver by glucuronidation through UGT1A enzymes, notably UGT1A1, UGT1A6 and UGT1A9, and by sulfonation through cytosolic sulfotransferases such as SULT1A1, with conjugates pumped out of hepatocytes by ABCC and ABCG2 efflux transporters into bile and blood for renal clearance. A minor fraction is oxidised by CYP2E1 to the reactive electrophile NAPQI, which glutathione S-transferases and glutathione conjugation normally quench; the resulting conjugates are processed further by gamma-glutamyl transferases, dipeptidases and N-acyltransferases toward mercapturates. When conjugation capacity and glutathione are exhausted, NAPQI arylates protein thiols, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and centrilobular hepatic necrosis, the basis of acute liver failure from overdose.

RAS proteins cycle between an active GTP-bound state and an inactive GDP-bound state, and their intrinsic hydrolysis is far too slow to switch them off on its own; GTPase-activating proteins such as neurofibromin and the p120 family accelerate it. Certain oncogenic substitutions in HRAS, KRAS and NRAS, most notably at glycine 12, glycine 13 and glutamine 61, render the protein blind to GAP stimulation, so signalling by these GAP-insensitive RAS mutants persists regardless of upstream receptor input. The consequence is constitutive engagement of RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K effector arms, driving proliferation, survival and loss of growth-factor dependence. These are among the most frequent mutations in human cancer, prevalent in pancreatic, colorectal and lung carcinomas and melanoma, and they underlie resistance to therapies aimed at receptor tyrosine kinases upstream of RAS.

RAS proteins are membrane-anchored switches that relay growth factor receptor input to the MAPK and PI3K cascades, and they are only "on" while bound to GTP. Signaling by RAS GTPase mutants covers the oncogenic forms of the three human RAS genes, KRAS, NRAS and HRAS, in which substitutions at hotspot residues such as glycine 12, glycine 13 and glutamine 61 cripple the intrinsic hydrolysis of GTP and blunt the response to GTPase-activating proteins. The switch therefore stays loaded with GTP and continues to recruit RAF and PI3K effectors without an upstream signal, driving proliferation, survival and altered metabolism independent of receptor occupancy. These mutations are among the most frequent events in pancreatic, colorectal and lung carcinoma and in melanoma, and they predict resistance to therapies aimed at receptors upstream of RAS, which is why the mutant proteins and their immediate effectors are pursued as drug targets.</description>

Passage through the G1 restriction point depends on D-type cyclins binding CDK4 or CDK6, and blocking those kinases with drugs is the basis of a now-standard class of anti-cancer therapy. Palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib occupy the ATP pocket of the kinases, leaving RB1 unphosphorylated so that E2F-dependent transcription stays off and cells arrest in G1 rather than committing to DNA replication. Because CCND1, CCND2 and CCND3 sit where mitogenic and oncogenic growth signalling converges, tumours that amplify cyclin D or lose upstream restraint are especially dependent on this step; intact RB1 is generally needed for the drugs to work, and its loss is a common route to resistance. The effect is mainly cytostatic, though senescence-like changes and altered immune recognition of the tumour also follow from sustained CDK4/6 inhibition.

Gastrulation converts a single-layered epiblast into the three germ layers, and germ layer formation at this stage sets out the body plan: everything from notochord and heart to gut endoderm traces back to cells that ingress through the primitive streak. NODAL signalling through SMAD2, SMAD3 and SMAD4, with the chromatin reader TRIM33, acts together with BMP4 and WNT-driven beta-catenin/TCF7-LEF1 input to position the streak posteriorly and to switch on the first mesendoderm transcription factors, TBXT and EOMES. These, with FOXH1, MIXL1 and GSC, specify mesoderm and definitive endoderm while shutting down the pluripotency network of POU5F1, SOX2 and NANOG. Mesoderm emerges by epithelial-mesenchymal transition; endoderm uses a partial, more plastic version. Failure of streak formation arrests the embryo before any organ lineage exists.

Autophagy normally destroys intracellular pathogens by delivering them to lysosomes, and SARS-CoV-2 blunts this defence while exploiting the membranes it generates. Viral accessory proteins ORF3a and ORF7a localize to late endosomal, lysosomal and trans-Golgi membranes and interrupt autophagic flux by separate routes: ORF7a raises lysosomal pH, while ORF3a prevents autophagosomes from fusing with lysosomes, so autophagosomes pile up with cargo undegraded; the viral M protein additionally drives mitophagy. The host machinery targeted here is the membrane tethering and fusion apparatus, including the HOPS subunits VPS11, VPS16, VPS18, VPS33A, VPS39 and VPS41, the regulator UVRAG, and LC3B, which marks the stalled autophagosomes. Interfering with fusion protects viral replication organelles from lysosomal degradation, dampens delivery of viral components for antigen presentation and innate sensing, and links this step of infection to lysosomal biogenesis and the broader control of endolysosomal traffic.

During SARS-CoV-2 infection, viral nonstructural proteins commandeer the host gene expression apparatus, suppressing cellular protein synthesis while viral mRNAs continue to be translated. This shutoff blunts the infected cell's ability to mount an interferon and antiviral response, and contributes to the mismatch between viral replication and innate immune control seen in COVID-19. Two host machines are targeted here. The small ribosomal subunit, represented by the full complement of 40S proteins together with RPSA and RACK-associated components, is blocked by nsp1, which lodges in the mRNA entry channel and prevents loading of capped cellular transcripts. In parallel, nsp16 engages U1 and U2 snRNA at their splice-site and branchpoint recognition elements, interfering with spliceosome function; the Sm core proteins and the SMN-Gemin assembly complex that builds and delivers these snRNPs are consequently implicated. Additional viral proteins impair targeting of nascent proteins to membranes.

Atorvastatin lowers circulating LDL cholesterol by inhibiting HMG-CoA reductase in the liver, and how much of the drug reaches that target is set by the absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination steps collected here. Because the drug is highly bound to plasma proteins and heavily cleared before it enters the systemic circulation, its bioavailability is low and its effect depends on hepatic exposure. Sinusoidal organic anion transporters encoded by SLCO1B1, SLCO1B3 and SLCO2B1 carry it into hepatocytes, where CYP3A4 hydroxylates it and UGT1A3 drives lactonization to inactive lactone, which paraoxonases PON1 and PON3 can hydrolyse back to active hydroxy acid. Efflux pumps ABCB1 and ABCC2 return drug to the gut lumen and bile, the main elimination route. Variation in SLCO1B1 raises plasma exposure and statin myopathy risk.

Ribavirin ADME describes how the antiviral nucleoside analog ribavirin is taken up, activated and cleared in humans, which determines both its efficacy against hepatitis C, respiratory syncytial virus and viral haemorrhagic fevers and its dose-limiting toxicity. Because the drug is a prodrug, its activity depends entirely on host nucleoside handling: concentrative and equilibrative nucleoside transporters carry it across intestinal and hepatocyte membranes, adenosine kinase performs the first phosphorylation, and nucleoside diphosphate kinases complete conversion to the active triphosphate, while 5'-nucleotidase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase and adenosine deaminase run the competing catabolic route of dephosphorylation and de-ribosylation. Trapping of phosphorylated drug inside erythrocytes, which lack the enzymes to reverse it, gives the very long half-life and the characteristic haemolytic anaemia; ITPA variants that relieve accumulated triphosphate reduce that risk, making this pharmacogenetics as much as metabolism.

Ribavirin is a guanosine analogue prodrug used against hepatitis C, respiratory syncytial virus and some viral haemorrhagic fevers, and its absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination determine both its antiviral potency and its main toxicity. Because the drug must be phosphorylated to the triphosphate to act, it depends on host nucleoside salvage machinery rather than any viral enzyme. Concentrative and equilibrative nucleoside transporters carry it across intestinal and cell membranes, adenosine kinase performs the first phosphorylation, and nucleoside diphosphate kinases complete the conversion to the active triphosphate; 5'-nucleotidase, purine nucleoside phosphorylase, adenosine deaminase and the inosine triphosphatase ITPA oppose or divert this flux. Accumulation of phosphorylated drug in erythrocytes, which lack dephosphorylating capacity, explains the long body half-life and the dose-limiting haemolytic anaemia, and variation in ITPA modifies that risk.

Cells survive oxidative and electrophilic insult largely because a single transcription factor is released from constant destruction, and this is the switch that does it. Under basal conditions KEAP1, acting with CUL3 and RBX1 as a ubiquitin ligase, marks NFE2L2 for proteasomal degradation; oxidation or adduct formation on KEAP1's reactive cysteines disables that targeting, so newly made NFE2L2 accumulates, partners with small MAF proteins and drives antioxidant response element genes. The resulting transcriptome spans glutathione synthesis, thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin recycling, heme catabolism through HMOX1, quinone reduction by NQO1, cystine import via SLC7A11, and drug efflux, together with pentose phosphate and NADPH-generating enzymes. SQSTM1 links the same axis to autophagy. Weak output contributes to neurodegenerative, cardiovascular, metabolic and airway disease, whereas constitutive activation through KEAP1 loss lets tumours reprogram metabolism and resist chemotherapy.

Hybrid N-glycans are a distinct branch of Golgi N-glycan maturation, and the reaction that defines them is the transfer of a bisecting GlcNAc onto the core mannose of the growing glycan by the branching enzyme MGAT3. Because this bisected structure is no longer a substrate for the mannosidase that trims the remaining mannose arms, the modification locks the glycan into a hybrid form rather than allowing it to proceed to a fully complex, multiply branched one. The same addition blocks the further branching enzymes and the core fucosyltransferase, so the relative levels of MGAT3 and the competing complex-branching activity set the balance between hybrid and complex glycan output in a given tissue. This matters because the bisecting GlcNAc changes glycoprotein behaviour on cell surfaces, altering receptor signalling, adhesion, and lectin recognition, and shifts in it are a recurring feature of tumour cell glycosylation.

N-glycan antennae elongation in the medial/trans-Golgi builds the branched, terminally decorated sugar chains that give secreted and cell-surface glycoproteins their mature identity, determining receptor half-life, cell adhesion, immune recognition and the clearance of circulating hormones. After a committed GlcNAc is added to the alpha1,3 branch, the pathway forks: a bisecting GlcNAc placed by MGAT3 blocks further mannose trimming and yields hybrid structures, while Golgi alpha-mannosidases with MGAT2 open the route to complex N-glycans. Additional branches from MGAT4 and MGAT5 enzymes are then extended by beta1,4-galactosyltransferases and capped by sialyltransferases such as ST6GAL1, with core fucosylation by FUT8 and sulfation adding further variation. The resulting diversity tunes lectin binding and growth-factor receptor signalling; loss of individual transferases causes congenital glycosylation disorders, and altered branching accompanies tumour invasion.

Glycoproteins leaving the Golgi carry branched N-linked sugars whose outer arms are built here, in the medial and trans compartments. This elaboration converts simple oligomannose structures into the hybrid and complex N-glycans that determine protein half-life, receptor clustering, cell adhesion and recognition by lectins of the immune system; loss of branching enzymes causes congenital glycosylation disorders, and altered branching is a hallmark of tumour cell surfaces. Alpha-mannosidase II enzymes trim mannose residues, after which GlcNAc transferases including MGAT2, MGAT4 family members and MGAT5 add antennae, MGAT3 adds a bisecting GlcNAc that blocks further branching, and FUT8 attaches core fucose. Beta-1,4-galactosyltransferases cap the branches, and sialyltransferases such as ST6GAL1 and ST3GAL4 terminate them with sialic acid, with sulfation and fucosylation generating further diversity. Glycoprotein hormone subunits are among the substrates matured this way.

After a glycoprotein's N-glycan is committed to the complex or hybrid class, its branches are built out and capped, and this antennae elongation step determines the final sugar structures that decorate the cell surface and secreted proteins. Those terminal structures are what lectins, selectins and galectins actually read, so the pathway shapes cell adhesion, receptor residency time and immune recognition rather than any single metabolic output. In the Golgi, branching N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases add further antennae to the core, galactosyltransferases of the B4GALT family extend each arm with galactose, and sialyltransferases cap them — ST6GAL1 placing α2,6-linked sialic acid and ST3GAL4 α2,3-linked, with ST8SIA enzymes able to add polysialic acid. Altered branching, particularly through MGAT5, is a long-standing feature of tumour cell behaviour and metastasis, and defects in these steps cause congenital glycosylation disorders.

SARS-CoV-2 does not simply replicate inside a cell; several of its structural and accessory proteins bind host signalling hubs and bend them toward viral advantage, shaping survival of the infected cell, cytokine output and how virions are trafficked. Three such hijackings are captured here. The viral membrane protein engages PDPK1, the kinase that phosphorylates the activation loop of AKT1, AKT2 and AKT3, so pro-survival PKB/Akt signalling downstream of PI3K is blunted. The nucleocapsid protein binds the 14-3-3 family of phosphoserine-reading adaptors, including YWHAZ, YWHAE and SFN, which govern its nucleocytoplasmic shuttling and oligomerisation. The accessory 3a protein associates with caveolin-1, a scaffold of membrane caveolae, implicating it in viral entry and in trafficking of structural proteins. Together these interactions illustrate how a respiratory virus rewires kinase cascades and membrane organisation to control its own life cycle and the host inflammatory response.

Branched, complex N-glycans on secreted and membrane proteins arise from a committed set of reactions that begin once alpha-mannosidase II trims the last two mannoses from a hybrid intermediate, a step blocked if a bisecting GlcNAc has already been added. Because the mannosidases MAN2A1 and MAN2A2 cannot act on bisected structures, their relative activity decides whether a tissue makes hybrid or complex glycans. Trimming licenses MGAT2 to build the second antenna, after which core fucosylation by FUT8, outer-arm fucosylation, and sulfotransferase modification diversify the finished glycan; a lysosomal fucosidase reverses fucose addition during turnover. The glycoprotein hormone alpha subunit and luteinizing hormone beta appear as physiological acceptors whose sulfated and fucosylated glycans set circulatory half-life and receptor signalling. Loss of core fucosylation alters growth factor and immune receptor function, and these structures underlie much of the glycan change seen in cancer.

Vitamin A cannot be synthesised by animals, so it must be absorbed from diet as carotenoids or retinyl esters and delivered to tissues that need it for vision, epithelial differentiation and transcriptional control through retinoic acid receptors. This pathway covers that uptake, esterification and distribution. Pancreatic lipase and colipase release retinyl esters from dietary fat, carotenoid cleavage enzymes such as BCO1 and BCO2 generate retinal, and reductases including RDH11 and aldo-keto reductases interconvert retinal and retinol; LRAT re-esterifies retinol for storage. Intracellular and plasma binding proteins RBP1, RBP2 and RBP4, the latter circulating with transthyretin, keep these hydrophobic molecules soluble. Delivery rides on the chylomicron and lipoprotein system, with apolipoproteins, lipoprotein lipase anchored by GPIHBP1 and heparan sulfate proteoglycans, and clearance through LDL receptor family members. Deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia; excess retinoid is teratogenic.

Prednisone is an orally administered glucocorticoid prodrug, and its absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion determine how much active hormone reaches glucocorticoid receptors in inflamed tissue. The pivotal step is interconversion with the active steroid prednisolone: a reductase in liver and adipose cells generates the active form, while the opposing oxidative enzyme in kidney and colon converts it back, so tissue-specific expression of these two enzymes sets local glucocorticoid exposure. Circulating drug travels bound to albumin and corticosteroid-binding globulin, oxidative metabolism by a major hepatic cytochrome P450 produces 6beta-hydroxy derivatives, an aldo-keto reductase yields 20-dihydro metabolites, and UDP-glucuronosyltransferases conjugate these for urinary excretion; an efflux transporter limits intestinal and tissue uptake. Variation in these steps underlies differences in anti-inflammatory response, drug interactions with P450 inhibitors, and steroid side-effect burden.

NF- erκB controls the transcriptional programmes of inflammation, innate and adaptive immune activation, proliferation and survival, so its output must be switched on only as long as a stimulus lasts. Regulation of NF-kappa B signaling covers the brakes and modulators acting at the IKK complex, whose catalytic subunits CHUK and IKBKB together with the regulatory IKBKG phosphorylate IκB proteins and release NF-κB for nuclear entry. Here the emphasis is on restraint of Toll-like receptor-driven activation: TRAF6- and TRAF2-dependent ubiquitin chains built from the polyubiquitin precursors provide the scaffolding signal, deubiquitinases such as USP14 and USP18 and the RNA-binding suppressor N4BP1 oppose it, and NLRC5, NLRX1, LRRC14 and IKBIP interfere with IKK assembly or activity. Loss of this tuning yields chronic inflammation, tissue damage and a permissive state for tumour development.

Innate immune recognition at the cell surface — by TLR5, TLR10 and IL-1-family receptors, plus damage signals such as HMGB1, S100 proteins and AGER ligands — is converted into inflammatory gene expression through the MyD88 cascade initiated on the plasma membrane. This is how macrophages and epithelial cells detect bacterial flagellin or tissue injury and respond with cytokines, chemokines and antimicrobial peptides; loss of MyD88 or IRAK4 leaves children susceptible to pyogenic bacterial infection, while chronic activation drives inflammatory disease. Receptor-bound MyD88 nucleates a Myddosome with IRAK4, IRAK1 and IRAK2, engaging the E3 ligase TRAF6 and its ubiquitin-conjugating partners to build polyubiquitin chains that activate the TAK1–TAB complex. TAK1 then drives the IKK complex to degrade IκB and release NF-κB, and feeds the JNK, p38 and ERK modules toward AP-1, CREB and MEF2 targets, with Pellino ligases, phosphatases and A20-like inhibitors setting the limits.

Vitamin B12 cannot be made by human cells, so the whole body depends on a relay of binding proteins that carry dietary cobalamins from the stomach to the distal ileum and deliver them into enterocytes. Loss of any step causes B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia and demyelinating neuropathy, since the vitamin is required as methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Salivary and gastric haptocorrin (TCN1) shields the vitamin from acid, pancreatic proteases such as trypsin and chymotrypsin degrade it in the duodenum, and gastric intrinsic factor (CBLIF) takes over as carrier. The cubilin–amnionless receptor complex then endocytoses intrinsic factor-bound cobalamin at the ileal brush border, and lysosomal export via LMBRD1 and the ABCD4 transporter releases the vitamin into the cytosol. Mutations in cubilin or amnionless underlie hereditary selective B12 malabsorption with proteinuria.

Vitamin B12 absorbed in the gut has to reach every tissue that needs it, and this pathway covers the carrier proteins and receptors that move cobalamins from the enterocyte into blood, into target cells, and back out of the glomerular filtrate. The cargo is handled with broad specificity, so methyl-, adeno- and cyanocobalamin all travel the same route. Transcobalamin II binds cobalamin in circulation and delivers it to cells through the CD320 receptor, with clathrin-coat adaptor LDLRAP1 supporting endocytic uptake; haptocorrin carries a separate plasma pool; megalin (LRP2) reclaims filtered transcobalamin-cobalamin in the proximal tubule. Within the lysosome, LMBRD1 and the ABCD4 transporter release cobalamin to the cytosol for conversion into the cofactors used by methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Defects cause inherited B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anaemia, methylmalonic aciduria and neurological damage.

Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) during gastrulation is the step that turns the epiblast into a body plan: cells in the primitive streak lose their epithelial character, detach from their neighbours and the basement membrane, and ingress to form mesoderm, while an incomplete version of the same program generates definitive endoderm. Without it no mesoderm forms and embryogenesis fails. FGF, WNT, NODAL and BMP signals converge on the posterior streak, where the transcription factors TBXT and EOMES switch on SNAI1; SNAI1 then represses E-cadherin, occludin and claudins, dismantling adherens and tight junctions so cells can move and adopt an N-cadherin mesenchymal program. Cytoskeletal and polarity regulators coordinate the actual ingression. The same transcriptional circuit is reactivated pathologically in carcinoma cells, where it underlies invasion and metastasis.

Gastrulation requires that epiblast cells in the primitive streak stop behaving as an epithelium and leave it, and this epithelial-mesenchymal transition is how mesoderm is generated; an incomplete version of the same programme delivers definitive endoderm. Posterior signals, prominently FGF acting through FGFR1 along with WNT, NODAL and BMP, converge on the primitive streak transcription factors EOMES and TBXT, which switch on SNAI1. SNAI1 then represses the genes that hold the epithelium together, including E-cadherin, occludin and claudins, so that junctions dissolve, cells detach from the basement membrane and ingress, and a mesenchymal expression programme with N-cadherin takes over. Without it the germ layers cannot be laid down. The same transcriptional switch is redeployed in carcinoma cells, where TGF-beta-driven loss of E-cadherin underlies invasion and metastasis, making this early developmental step a template for tumour cell dissemination.

During gastrulation the primitive streak produces mesodermal subsets with distinct fates, and the lateral plate mesoderm is the population that goes on to build heart, limbs, blood, and the linings of the body cavity and gut. Its induction depends on Hedgehog signals, SHH and IHH, arriving from the adjacent endoderm to switch on the forkhead factor FOXF1, which marks the tissue once specified. FOXF1 then drives BMP4 expression, and BMP4 with FOXF1 turns on GATA4; BMP4 sustains FOXF1 while GATA4 reinforces its own transcription and that of BMP4, creating a self-maintaining loop that locks in lateral identity before downstream differentiation genes are engaged. Because this territory gives rise to cardiac and vascular progenitors, disturbance of the loop underlies congenital heart and diaphragm defects, and the same signals are used to derive these lineages from pluripotent stem cells.

Gastrulation is the step that turns a simple two-layered early embryo into a three-layered body plan, generating the mesoderm and endoderm alongside ectoderm and thereby specifying the founders of muscle, blood, gut, skin and nervous system. Failure at this stage is embryonic lethal, and its regulators reappear in birth defects and in tumour cell invasion. Epiblast cells at the posterior primitive streak, where NODAL/SMAD, BMP, FGF and WNT signals converge, switch on TBXT, EOMES and MIXL1 and undergo epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, losing CDH1 and claudin/occludin junctions through SNAI1 and ZEB2 while endoderm-bound cells only partially do so before re-epithelialising as SOX17/FOXA2 gut progenitors. Notch-RBPJ with MESP2, TBX6 and HES7 times somitic mesoderm segmentation; SOX2, OTX2 and PAX genes pattern the retained ectoderm. Proteasome subunits enforce the rapid turnover of these transcription factors and signalling effectors that makes lineage switching irreversible.

Gastrulation converts the single-layered epiblast of the early embryo into the three germ layers "" ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm "" from which every tissue of the body is later built, and it establishes the anterior-posterior and medial-lateral coordinates along which those tissues are patterned. Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak, a posterior site specified by converging NODAL/SMAD, BMP, FGF and WNT signalling, and lose their epithelial character through an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition driven by SNAI1 and ZEB2 with loss of CDH1, claudin and occludin junctions. Streak cells switch on TBXT, EOMES and MIXL1 as pluripotency factors such as POU5F1 and NANOG are resolved into lineage programmes: SOX17 and FOXA2 for endoderm, TBX6 and MSGN1 for paraxial mesoderm, SOX2 and ZIC factors for neuroectoderm. Notch components with a segmentation clock, Hedgehog signals from axial mesoderm, Hippo effectors and proteasomal turnover of regulators shape the output. Failure produces embryonic lethality or axial and laterality malformations.

Oxidative and electrophilic stress is met by a transcriptional programme that rebuilds the cell's antioxidant and detoxification capacity, and the nuclear phase of NFE2L2 action is where that programme is written. Once freed from KEAP1-directed ubiquitination and proteasomal turnover, NFE2L2 enters the nucleus, dimerises with small MAF proteins such as MAFG and MAFK, and occupies antioxidant response elements together with coactivators CREBBP and EP300. The genes switched on cover glutathione synthesis (GCLC, GCLM), thioredoxin and peroxiredoxin recycling, NQO1 and heme oxygenase, cystine uptake via SLC7A11, NADPH supply through the pentose phosphate enzymes G6PD and PGD, drug efflux transporters, and subunits of the proteasome itself. BACH1 competes for the same elements as a repressor, while GSK3B and beta-TrCP provide a second route to NFE2L2 degradation. Constitutive activation, often through KEAP1 loss, gives tumours chemoresistance and a metabolic advantage.

Vitamin B12 taken up from the diet is not usable as such; cobalamin metabolism converts it into the two active cofactors cells need, adenosylcobalamin for the mitochondrial matrix and methylcobalamin for the cytosol. Only two human enzymes depend on them: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which routes propionyl-CoA from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol and branched-chain amino acids into the citric acid cycle, and methionine synthase, which remethylates homocysteine and so links folate turnover to methylation capacity. Processing enzymes dealkylate and reduce the incoming cobalt, a chaperone and an ATP-dependent adenosyltransferase deliver and build the mitochondrial cofactor, and a reductase reactivates methionine synthase when its cofactor oxidises. Defects at individual steps produce methylmalonic acidaemia, homocystinuria or both together, with acidosis, developmental delay and neurological damage in infancy.

Cadherin-11, an adhesion molecule of mesenchymal and osteoblastic cells, is controlled here at every level from transcription to protein partnership. Its output matters for skeletal formation, mesodermal stem cell fate decisions, heart and brain development, and wound repair, while excess activity drives synovial fibroblast invasion in rheumatoid arthritis, tissue fibrosis, and tumour cell migration. Transcription factors including HOXC8, ZEB2, SNAI1, FOXF1, HEYL, BHLHE22 and ILF3 act directly on the gene, linking its expression to epithelial-mesenchymal transition programmes and to growth factor and hormone cues such as TGF-beta. Post-transcriptional control comes through microRNAs, notably miR-200c-3p and miR-451a, acting with Argonaute and TNRC6 silencing machinery. At the membrane, the cytoplasmic tail binds p120, beta-, gamma- and alpha-catenin to build adherens junctions, while angiomotin and the extracellular ANGPTL4 fragment couple it to migration and healing responses.

Regulation of Homotypic Cell-Cell Adhesion governs how much cadherin is present at a cell's surface to bind identical cadherins on its neighbours, and thereby sets the strength of adherens junctions holding an epithelium together. Loss of this control is the core of epithelial-mesenchymal transition: when E-cadherin expression falls, cells detach, become motile and invasive, a step central to development, wound healing and tumour metastasis. Cadherin ectodomains form calcium-dependent trans dimers across the intermembrane space, while their cytoplasmic tails recruit alpha-, beta- and p120-catenin, plakoglobin and vinculin to anchor the junction to actin. Regulation here is largely transcriptional and post-transcriptional: SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST repressors recruit HDAC1/2, LSD1 and Polycomb complexes to silence CDH1, microRNAs including miR-200c act through Argonaute complexes, and glycosylation, proprotein convertase processing, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation and Src/Fyn phosphorylation tune the mature protein.

Cells of the same type stick to one another through calcium-dependent cadherin dimers that bridge apposed membranes, and control over homotypic cell-cell adhesion determines whether an epithelium stays sealed or a cell detaches and migrates. E-cadherin and its relatives link through catenins -- beta-catenin, alpha-catenin, p120 and plakoglobin -- to actin and vinculin, so adhesion strength is read out as cytoskeletal tension at adherens junctions. Much of the regulation shown here is upstream of the junction itself: transcriptional repression of cadherin genes by SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST factors acting with histone deacetylases, LSD1 and Polycomb components, microRNA-mediated silencing through Argonaute complexes, plus biosynthetic maturation by N-glycosylation and signal peptidase machinery, proprotein convertase cleavage, cathepsin and ADAM-mediated shedding, and ubiquitin-proteasome turnover. Loss of this control underlies epithelial-mesenchymal transition, developmental patterning defects and carcinoma invasiveness.

Messenger RNAs bearing premature stop codons are destroyed before they can yield truncated proteins, and this branch of nonsense-mediated decay operates on transcripts that lack an exon junction complex downstream of the termination site. It acts as a quality-control filter on the transcriptome, clearing mRNAs from nonsense and frameshift mutations as well as normal transcripts with unusually long 3' UTRs, and so shapes the severity of many genetic diseases depending on whether a mutant message survives. Recognition occurs at the terminating ribosome, where the release factors eRF1 and eRF3 assemble with the small and large subunit proteins; poly(A)-binding protein and UPF1 compete for eRF3, so a distant poly(A) tail favours UPF1 loading and commits the mRNA to decay. Cap-binding and initiation components link the event to the first round of translation, after which UPF1 phosphorylation recruits degradation activities.

Messenger RNAs carrying a premature stop codon are destroyed rather than translated, and this surveillance route is the version of that quality control triggered when a spliced exon junction lies downstream of the terminating ribosome. It protects cells from truncated, potentially dominant-negative proteins and sets the severity of many nonsense-mutation diseases, since whether a transcript escapes or is degraded determines how much product remains. Exon junction complexes containing eIF4A3, Magoh, Y14/RBM8A and CASC3 are laid down during splicing and normally stripped off by the first round of translation; one left behind recruits UPF2 and UPF3 and thus UPF1 to release factors at the stalled ribosome. SMG1, with SMG8 and SMG9, phosphorylates UPF1, which then engages the endonuclease SMG6 or the SMG5-SMG7 pair, feeding the transcript to decapping and exonucleolytic decay, with phosphatase subunits reversing the switch.

Fatty acids and several amino acids are broken down inside mitochondria, and inherited defects in that route cause the group of disorders known as diseases of mitochondrial beta oxidation. The example captured here is methylmalonic aciduria, which follows loss of methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (MMUT) or of MMAA, the accessory GTPase that delivers and repairs its adenosylcobalamin cofactor. The mutase normally isomerises methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, the step that feeds propionyl-CoA derived from odd-chain fatty acids, cholesterol side chains, and isoleucine, valine, methionine and threonine into the citric acid cycle. When it fails, methylmalonic acid and related organic acids accumulate, producing metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, failure to thrive, encephalopathy and renal damage, often provoked by catabolic stress. Because MMAA handles cofactor chemistry, some patients respond to vitamin B12 supplementation while MMUT-null patients do not.

Propionyl-CoA arises from the breakdown of odd-chain fatty acids, branched-chain amino acids such as valine and isoleucine, cholesterol side chains, and gut bacterial fermentation, and it must be converted to succinyl-CoA to enter the citric acid cycle. Diseases of propionyl-CoA catabolism arise when the final mitochondrial step of that route fails: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which isomerises L-methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA, depends on adenosylcobalamin, and MMAA is the accessory GTPase that loads and protects this cofactor on the enzyme. Loss of either protein causes methylmalonic acidaemia, in which methylmalonic acid and propionyl-CoA-derived metabolites accumulate, provoking metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and renal damage, typically in infancy and worsened by protein intake or catabolic stress. MMAA defects are often responsive to vitamin B12 supplementation, whereas mutase deficiency generally is not, which links this anaplerotic step to cobalamin handling and to amino acid and lipid catabolism more broadly.

CDH11 encodes OB-cadherin, an adhesion molecule of osteoblasts, fibroblasts and mesenchymal tissues that contributes to skeletal development, tissue stiffening and fibrosis, and to the invasive behaviour of some tumours. Its message is held in check after transcription by microRNAs, chiefly miR-200c-3p and miR-451a, which pair with the CDH11 transcript and lower its protein output. The silencing is executed by an RNA-induced silencing complex: an Argonaute protein carries the guide microRNA, a TNRC6 scaffold recruits deadenylation and decapping activity, and the helicase MOV10 assists remodelling of the target mRNA. Setting cadherin-11 levels this way tunes how strongly mesenchymal cells adhere and migrate, linking microRNA control to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, joint and bone biology, and fibrotic or metastatic disease when the repression is lost.

Bacterial toxin secretion is the step that turns a harmless gut inhabitant into a pathogen: a commensal that acquires a toxin gene together with the machinery to export it becomes capable of disrupting host physiology directly. In enterobacteria such as E. coli, the relevant genes commonly sit on plasmids or within proviruses, so virulence is transferable between strains rather than fixed by taxonomy. Heat-labile enterotoxins are AB5-type heterohexamers exported across the outer membrane by a type II secretion system, whereas the small heat-stable enterotoxins leave through an efflux pump built around the TolC pore. Once delivered, heat-labile toxin raises cyclic AMP by activating adenylate cyclase and heat-stable toxin activates guanylate cyclase C; both drive ion channel opening, fluid loss and secretory diarrhoea. Extraintestinal strains additionally export proteases whose host targets remain poorly defined.

The intermediate mesoderm is the strip of embryonic mesoderm that gives rise to the entire urogenital system — gonads, nephric ducts, ureteric epithelium and metanephric mesenchyme — so its specification determines whether kidneys and reproductive tracts form at all, and defects here underlie renal agenesis and urogenital malformation. It is carved out along the medial-lateral axis by graded BMP signalling, high in lateral plate and low in paraxial mesoderm, while Wnt, FGF and retinoic acid gradients set its position along the head-to-tail axis. OSR1 and LHX1 mark the territory first, followed by the paralogous transcription factors PAX2 and PAX8, which act in a mutually reinforcing loop with the earlier factors. FOXC1 and FOXC2 expressed in neighbouring paraxial mesoderm repress LHX1 and OSR1 and so confine the domain. The same cues are used to direct human pluripotent stem cells toward kidney lineages in vitro.

NFE2L2 (NRF2) is the transcription factor that switches on antioxidant and detoxification genes, so how fast it is destroyed sets the cell's capacity to handle oxidative and electrophilic stress. Alongside the better-known KEAP1-CUL3 route, a second disposal route operates through the SCF ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1, RBX1 and the substrate receptor BTRC. GSK3B phosphorylates a DSGIS motif in the Neh6 domain of NFE2L2, after priming phosphorylation of nearby serines, creating the phosphodegron that BTRC recognises; polyubiquitination then targets NFE2L2 to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here. Because PI3K/AKT signalling inhibits GSK3B, this branch couples growth-factor and insulin signalling to stabilised NFE2L2 and heightened stress-response output, and its loss in tumours contributes to the constitutive NRF2 activity that supports chemoresistance.

CDH11, or OB-cadherin, is a classical cadherin of mesenchymal tissues — osteoblasts, fibroblasts and synovial cells — and its regulation determines how strongly those cells adhere to one another versus how readily they migrate. Adhesive function depends on the cytoplasmic tail recruiting catenins: p120 catenin stabilises the cadherin at the surface, while beta-catenin or plakoglobin link through alpha-catenin to the actin cytoskeleton of adherens junctions. Competing interactions steer the same molecule toward motility. Binding of angiomotin to the C-terminus promotes migration and has been tied to tumour cell invasiveness, and the extracellular region engages the C-terminal fragment of angiopoietin-like 4 during wound healing, an interaction a shorter spliced membrane-bound isoform can compete for. Shedding by ADAM metalloproteinases provides a further route to disassembling adhesion. Related cadherins act in comparable junctional contexts, and CDH11 activity is prominent in synovial fibroblast behaviour in inflammatory arthritis.

Regulation of CDH11 gene transcription controls expression of OB-cadherin, the adhesion molecule that lets osteoblasts, fibroblasts and mesenchymal cells recognise and bind one another. Its output determines bone matrix formation, mesenchymal condensation during development, and the fibroblast-to-myofibroblast conversion that drives tissue fibrosis and synovial invasion in arthritis; loss of CDH11 weakens skeletal mineralisation and blunts fibrotic remodelling. Transcription is tissue-restricted, active in bone, heart, brain, lung and placenta but not kidney, liver or skeletal muscle, and is set by a small set of direct regulators: HOXC8 and FOXF1 acting in skeletal and mesenchymal patterning, the epithelial-mesenchymal transition factors ZEB2 and SNAI1, the Notch effector HEYL, ILF3, SP1, and the BHLHE22-PRDM8 repressor complex in neurons. Growth factors and hormones, TGF-beta in particular, feed into these factors, and CDH11 in turn modulates TGF-beta signalling as a feedback loop.

CDH11 encodes OB-cadherin, an adhesion molecule of osteoblasts, fibroblasts and mesenchymal tissues that also appears in heart, brain, placenta and lung, and its transcriptional control determines how much of this adhesive capacity a cell displays. The level matters: CDH11 induction accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, fibroblast activation in fibrosis and synovial invasion in arthritis, and it participates in bone matrix formation. Direct activators include HOXC8, ZEB2, FOXF1, HEYL and the RNA/DNA-binding factor ILF3, with SP1 supplying basal promoter activity and SNAI1 linking expression to the EMT programme; BHLHE22 acts with its partner PRDM8 as a repressive complex in neural contexts. Growth factors and hormones, TGF-beta family ligands in particular, feed into these factors, and because CDH11 itself modulates TGF-beta responses the arrangement can form a self-reinforcing loop during tissue remodelling.

BRCA2 delivers RAD51 to resected DNA ends so that broken chromosomes can be repaired by homologous recombination, and it cannot do this job unless it is stable and properly localized to the nucleus. The small acidic protein SEM1, also called DSS1, binds the BRCA2 DNA-binding domain and provides exactly that support, acting as a chaperone-like partner that protects BRCA2 from degradation and promotes its nuclear accumulation and engagement with single-stranded DNA. Cancer-associated missense changes in BRCA2 that disrupt this interface leave the protein unstable or mislocalized, so recombination repair fails, cells fall back on error-prone end joining, and genomic instability accumulates. Loss of this binding is one route by which inherited and somatic BRCA2 variants drive breast, ovarian and pancreatic tumours, and it underlies the sensitivity of such tumours to PARP inhibition and crosslinking agents.

Regulation of Expression and Function of Type II Classical Cadherins controls where and when the type II classical cadherins are made and how they hold cells together, an adhesion code used mainly in the nervous system to sort neurons into circuits and to bundle motor axons, and in mesenchymal and endothelial tissues via CDH11 and VE-cadherin. These cadherins bind through strand swapping, in which conserved tryptophans in the first extracellular repeat dock into a partner's hydrophobic pocket, producing homotypic and selective heterotypic pairs whose binding preferences define distinct specificity subgroups. Adhesive strength depends on cytoplasmic partners such as beta-catenin, plakoglobin, p120 and alpha-catenin linking the complex to actin. Expression is set transcriptionally by factors including SOX10, SNAI1, ZEB2 and PRDM8, and post-transcriptionally by microRNAs acting through Argonaute-containing silencing complexes. Misregulation contributes to epithelial-mesenchymal transition, tumour invasion and defective neural wiring.

Type II classical cadherins are calcium-dependent adhesion receptors whose five-repeat ectodomains pair by strand swapping, docking conserved tryptophans from the first repeat into a partner's hydrophobic pocket via an intermediate X dimer. Because members bind selectively within defined specificity subgroups, both homotypically and heterotypically, they act as an adhesive code that sorts cells and wires neuronal circuits; CDH5 instead seals endothelial junctions, and CDH11 mediates mesenchymal and osteoblast adhesion. Regulation of their expression and function determines how much adhesive receptor reaches the surface and how long it stays there. Transcriptional control involves lineage and epithelial-mesenchymal factors such as SOX10, SNAI1, ZEB2, PRDM8 and BHLHE22, while microRNAs acting through Argonaute and TNRC6 silencing complexes tune transcript levels, and ADAM metalloproteinases shed ectodomains. Cytoplasmic tails couple to α-, β-, p120-catenin and plakoglobin, linking adhesion to the actin cytoskeleton and to junctional signalling that influences proliferation and tumour invasiveness.

Regulation of CDH1 Expression and Function governs how much E-cadherin an epithelial cell displays at its surface, and therefore whether that cell stays anchored to its neighbours in a polarized sheet. E-cadherin trans-dimers, linked through alpha-, beta- and p120-catenins to the actin cytoskeleton, build adherens junctions; losing them is a defining step of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and germline CDH1 loss underlies hereditary diffuse gastric cancer while sporadic silencing accompanies invasive carcinoma broadly. Control operates at every level: transcriptional repression by SNAI1/2, ZEB1/2 and TWIST factors recruiting HDAC, LSD1 and Polycomb complexes, microRNA-mediated silencing through Argonaute effectors, co-translational translocation, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase cleavage in the secretory pathway, endocytic trafficking, and ubiquitin-proteasome and cathepsin-dependent degradation. Src- and CK2-mediated phosphorylation of the cytoplasmic tail tips this balance toward junction disassembly and motility.

E-cadherin (CDH1) is the adhesion receptor that holds polarized epithelial sheets together, and the control of its abundance and activity decides whether a cell stays epithelial or converts to a migratory mesenchymal state. Because loss of CDH1 permits invasion, this regulation underlies its behaviour as a tumour suppressor: germline loss-of-function mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer, and silencing accompanies epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in many carcinomas. Transcription is repressed by SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST factors recruiting histone deacetylases, LSD1 and Polycomb components, while KLF4 and other factors favour expression; microRNAs and Argonaute-containing complexes add post-transcriptional control. The mature protein is made through signal peptide cleavage, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase processing, then anchored to actin through beta-catenin, alpha-catenin, p120 and vinculin at adherens junctions. Kinases such as SRC and casein kinase 2, HECT-type ubiquitin ligase CBLL1, endocytosis, cathepsins and the proteasome drive its turnover.

Type I classical cadherins — E-, N-, P-, R- and M-cadherin — are calcium-dependent adhesion receptors whose homotypic trans-dimers hold epithelia and other tissues together, and their levels are controlled at nearly every step from transcription to degradation. This regulation matters because loss of E-cadherin releases cells from adherens junctions, licenses epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and invasion, and underlies hereditary diffuse gastric cancer. Transcriptional repressors including SNAI1/SNAI2, ZEB1/ZEB2 and TWIST recruit histone deacetylases, the LSD1 demethylase and Polycomb components to silence the CDH1 promoter, while microRNAs and the RNA-induced silencing machinery restrain the transcript. Newly made cadherin passes through signal peptidase, N-glycosylation and proprotein convertase processing before reaching the surface, where catenins (CTNNB1, CTNNA1, CTNND1, JUP) link it to actin and vinculin; Src- and CK2-dependent phosphorylation, ubiquitination and proteasomal or cathepsin-mediated turnover set junction stability.

Cadherin-19 is a classical type II cadherin whose expression marks Schwann cell precursors and migrating neural crest, and the control of its expression and function links transcriptional identity in that lineage to the physical adhesion between cells. At the plasma membrane it behaves like other classical cadherins, engaging alpha-, beta-, gamma- and delta-catenin (CTNNA1, CTNNB1, JUP, CTNND1) to couple homotypic cell-cell contacts to the actin cytoskeleton in adherens junctions. Upstream, the transcription factor SOX10 binds the CDH19 promoter and drives its expression, and loss of CDH19 slows sacral neural crest migration during formation of the enteric nervous system. The RNase ZC3H12A induces CDH19 transcription in endothelial cells stimulated by the chemokine CCL2, tying it to angiogenesis. CDH19 levels are altered in several tumours, with reported oncogenic and tumour-suppressive effects depending on the cancer type.

E-cadherin is the adhesion molecule that holds epithelial sheets together, and transcriptional control of the CDH1 gene sets whether a cell stays epithelial or converts to a migratory mesenchymal state. Loss of CDH1 expression is a hallmark of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, used normally in development and wound healing and hijacked during tumour invasion and metastasis. Positive regulators including ARID1A, FOXA2, FOXJ2, KLF4, KLF9, RB1, SP1 and TFAP2A bind the promoter to sustain expression, while repressors SNAI1, SNAI2, TWIST1/2, ZEB1, ZEB2, WT1, ZBTB33 and ZNF217 shut it off, typically downstream of TGF-beta, WNT and NF-kappaB signalling. Repression is enforced chromatin-wise through recruited corepressors and enzymes: HDAC1/2, the demethylase KDM1A, CTBP1/2, the Polycomb components EZH2, SUZ12 and EED, and nucleosomal histones, whereas SWI/SNF activity also shapes CDH1 exon inclusion.

E-cadherin holds epithelial cells together at adherens junctions, and how much of it sits at the cell surface decides whether an epithelium stays polarized and cohesive or loses contact and becomes invasive. Regulation of CDH1 function operates largely by controlling its stability: beta-catenin and plakoglobin compete for the same site on the cadherin tail, and binding by one of them is needed for surface delivery, while p120 catenin binds separately and protects against turnover and supports the antiparallel, calcium-dependent trans-dimers that bridge opposing cells. Alpha-catenin joins indirectly and, with vinculin and actin, couples the junction to the cytoskeleton. Src-family kinases phosphorylate the complex, promoting ubiquitination by HAKAI and clathrin-mediated endocytosis, after which cadherin is degraded by lysosomal cathepsins or the proteasome. Loss of this cadherin underlies epithelial-mesenchymal transition and diffuse gastric and lobular breast carcinoma.

Regulation of CDH1 mRNA translation by microRNAs describes how small RNAs silence E-cadherin, the adhesion molecule that holds epithelial sheets together and marks the epithelial state. Loss of E-cadherin loosens cell-cell junctions and is a defining step in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, invasion and metastasis, so post-transcriptional control of its message directly influences tumour behaviour. Mature miR-9 family members and miR-10b base-pair with the CDH1 transcript within an Argonaute-containing silencing complex, where TNRC6 scaffolding proteins and the helicase MOV10 enforce translational repression and decay. The MYC and MYCN oncoproteins drive transcription of the miR-9 genes, linking proliferative oncogenic signalling to dismantling of epithelial adhesion. Additional microRNAs, including miR-23b, miR-106a, miR-155 and miR-503, have been reported to target the same message, making CDH1 a convergence point for microRNA control of epithelial identity.

E-cadherin, encoded by CDH1, holds epithelial cells together at adherens junctions, and lowering its abundance is one of the decisive steps by which an epithelial cell becomes migratory and invasive. One route to that loss bypasses transcription entirely: microRNAs base-pair with the CDH1 message and silence it post-transcriptionally, with miR-9 family members and miR-10b the best supported examples. The silencing is carried out by the canonical machinery, in which an Argonaute protein loaded with the guide microRNA recruits a TNRC6 scaffold and associated factors such as the RNA helicase MOV10 to repress translation and destabilise the target. Because MYC and MYCN drive miR-9 expression, oncogenic transcription factor activity is linked to junctional dissolution, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and metastatic spread, making this a translational control node in tumour progression.

E-cadherin is the adhesion molecule that holds epithelial sheets together, and silencing its gene is the decisive step in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, occurring normally in development and wound healing and pathologically as tumours become invasive and metastatic. Transcriptional repression of CDH1 is carried out by a well-defined set of sequence-specific factors — SNAI1 and SNAI2, ZEB1 and ZEB2, TWIST1 and TWIST2, FOXQ1, TCF3 and TCF12, WT1, TGIF2, ZBTB33 and ZNF217 — which bind E-box and related elements in the promoter and recruit chromatin-modifying corepressors. Those effectors include the CtBP proteins, TLE1, class I deacetylases HDAC1 and HDAC2, the histone demethylase KDM1A, and the Polycomb PRC2 core of EZH2, SUZ12 and EED, so the outcome is heritable histone deacetylation and methylation across the locus. Upstream, TGF-beta, WNT, prostaglandin and NF-kB signalling induce these repressors, linking inflammatory and developmental cues to loss of epithelial adhesion.

E-cadherin is the adhesion molecule that holds epithelial sheets together and defines the epithelial state, so the transcription factors that switch its gene on set whether a cell stays epithelial or drifts toward a migratory, mesenchymal phenotype. Positive regulation of CDH1 transcription therefore sits at the heart of epithelial integrity, adherens junction formation and the suppression of invasion and metastasis; loss of CDH1 expression is a hallmark of epithelial-mesenchymal transition and of diffuse gastric and lobular breast cancers. Direct activators acting at the CDH1 promoter include the chromatin remodelling subunit ARID1A, forkhead factors FOXA2 and FOXJ2, the Kruppel-like factors KLF4 and KLF9, SP1, TFAP2A and the retinoblastoma protein RB1, which cooperates with TFAP2A rather than acting only as a cell cycle brake. These inputs oppose the repressive arm of the same promoter, exemplified by ZEB2.
