Degradation of CDH1 removes E-cadherin from the cell surface, dismantling the adherens junctions that hold epithelial sheets together. This post-translational loss of E-cadherin is one of the earliest steps in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, preceding transcriptional silencing of the gene, and it underlies the loss of cell-cell adhesion, apical-basal polarity and contact inhibition seen in invasive carcinoma. Two routes are described: MDM2 ubiquitinates E-cadherin for proteasomal destruction, while CBLL1 (Hakai) tags it for clathrin- and dynamin-dependent internalisation and cathepsin-mediated lysosomal breakdown. Src-family kinases including SRC and FYN phosphorylate the cadherin-catenin complex to license this ubiquitination, releasing alpha-, beta- and p120-catenin; freed beta-catenin can then feed into Wnt-responsive transcription. The pathway therefore links junction turnover to cell motility, wound repair and tumour progression.

E-cadherin holds epithelial cells to their neighbours, and its removal from the cell surface is one of the earliest steps by which an epithelium loosens and cells become migratory. Degradation of CDH1 describes the post-translational arm of that loss, preceding the transcriptional silencing seen later in epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and it matters for wound healing, for morphogenesis, and for the invasive behaviour of carcinomas in which E-cadherin is lost. Two ubiquitin ligases are implicated: MDM2 routes E-cadherin to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits is represented here, while CBLL1 promotes ubiquitin-dependent internalisation and lysosomal destruction involving clathrin machinery and cathepsins. Src-family kinase phosphorylation of the junctional complex — catenins, p120, plakoglobin — licenses this turnover, tying adherens junction stability to growth factor and kinase signalling.

E-cadherin is the adhesion receptor that holds epithelial sheets together, and it only works once it has been correctly matured on its way to the cell surface. The maturation route described here takes the CDH1 precursor from the endoplasmic reticulum to the plasma membrane: signal peptidase removes the signal sequence, the oligosaccharyltransferase complex transfers high-mannose glycan to asparagine residues, glucosidases and calnexin supervise folding, protein O-mannosyltransferases add a second class of glycan, and proprotein convertases such as FURIN cleave the prodomain in the trans-Golgi so that mature cadherin can engage in homotypic adhesion. Beta-catenin and plakoglobin associate with the cytoplasmic tail early, coupling the receptor to the actin cytoskeleton and to casein kinase 2 phosphorylation. Defective glycosylation or trafficking reduces surface cadherin and intercellular adhesion, a change seen in carcinoma cells as they lose epithelial character.

Regulation of NPAS4 gene expression controls the level of an activity-dependent transcription factor that neurons use to translate electrical activity into lasting changes in synaptic wiring. NPAS4 is induced by Ca2+ entering through NMDA receptors and L-type channels, so its abundance tracks how strongly a neuron has been firing; the protein then shapes inhibitory input onto excitatory cells, supporting circuit plasticity, contextual memory formation and protection against neurodegenerative stress. Induction is opposed by repressors acting at the promoter, including REST and the Ca2+-binding regulator KCNIP3/DREAM, while SRF and glucocorticoid signalling through NR3C1 tie expression to activity and stress hormones. Argonaute proteins with TNRC6 scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10 impose miRNA-mediated control on the transcript. The same calcium-linked regulation operates in pancreatic beta cells, and chronic stress, isolation, ageing or viral infection lower expression.

NPAS4 is an activity-dependent transcription factor whose induction couples neuronal firing to changes in synaptic wiring, and the control of its expression is how calcium entry becomes a lasting change in circuit behaviour. Transcription rises within minutes of calcium influx through NMDA receptors and L-type channels, driven by factors including SRF and the calcium-sensitive repressor KCNIP3/DREAM, and is held down by REST in non-neuronal contexts; glucocorticoid signalling through NR3C1 links chronic stress to reduced hippocampal levels. Argonaute proteins with their TNRC6 scaffolds and the RNA helicase MOV10 place the transcript under microRNA-mediated post-transcriptional control as well. The output matters for excitatory-inhibitory balance, plasticity and contextual memory formation, and NPAS4 loss accompanies neurodegeneration and age-related memory impairment. The same calcium-driven regulation operates in pancreatic beta cells.

NPAS4 is a neuron-specific transcription factor induced within minutes of activity that tunes inhibitory synapse number onto excited neurons, and the control of NPAS4 gene transcription is how that homeostatic brake is set. Calcium entry during neuronal stimulation drives transcription, with SRF acting as an activity-dependent activator at the promoter and PI3K/AKT signalling contributing, while calcium-free KCNIP3 (DREAM) occupies the promoter and holds it silent in the resting state. REST keeps the gene off in non-neuronal cells and can act in either direction in neurons, limiting the duration of the response. Stress imposes a second layer: glucocorticoid-bound NR3C1 binds upstream response elements and represses induction, and histone deacetylase activity and promoter CpG methylation state further gate the locus. Loss of this regulation disturbs excitatory-inhibitory balance, memory formation, and stress-related and neurodegenerative processes in the hippocampus.

NPAS4 is an activity-dependent transcription factor made in neurons after depolarisation, where it shapes the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses onto a cell; because its protein must appear quickly and disappear again, how much of its mRNA is translated is tightly controlled. Here that control is exerted by microRNAs acting on the unusually conserved NPAS4 3'UTR, with miR-224 and miR-203 among the species shown to repress reporter expression through it. Silencing is carried out by the RNA-induced silencing complex: an Argonaute protein loaded with the guide microRNA, scaffolded by a GW182-family partner (TNRC6A, TNRC6B or TNRC6C) that recruits deadenylation and decay machinery, with the RNA helicase MOV10 assisting on structured targets. Loss of this restraint disturbs experience-driven synaptic scaling, memory formation and seizure thresholds.

NPAS4 is an activity-induced transcription factor that couples neuronal excitation to changes in gene expression, and through it to the balance of excitatory and inhibitory synapses on a stimulated neuron. It matters for experience-dependent plasticity, contextual memory formation, protection of neurons after seizure or ischaemic injury, and for insulin gene expression in stressed pancreatic beta cells. Because its basic helix-loop-helix domain cannot bind DNA alone, NPAS4 dimerizes with ARNT, ARNT2 or BMAL1 and recruits coactivators such as CREBBP, with MAPK1/MAPK3 signalling and nuclear export machinery shaping its activity and short half-life. Target genes span neuronal differentiation and maturation (CDK5 with its activator CDK5R1, RBFOX3, RET), synaptogenesis and synaptic transmission (BDNF, IQSEC3, PLK2, SYT10, FOS), and metabolic and circadian outputs including NAMPT. It is also expressed in endothelium, where it has been linked to angiogenesis.

Defects of Coagulation cascade collects the inherited failures of blood clotting, the molecular basis of haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, afibrinogenaemia and the platelet disorder Bernard-Soulier syndrome, as well as gain-of-function variants of factors V and IX that tip the balance toward thrombosis. Normal haemostasis depends on a proteolytic relay in which factors VIII, IX, X and V assemble on activated platelet surfaces to generate thrombin, which converts fibrinogen into the fibrin mesh of a clot; von Willebrand factor and the GPIb-IX-V receptor complex tether platelets to injured vessel wall. Loss of any component gives spontaneous joint, mucosal or surgical bleeding, while loss of the protein C/protein S anticoagulant arm gives thrombophilia. Also represented are the post-translational steps clotting factors require, including vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation and tyrosine sulfation, and phospholipid scrambling by ANO6 that exposes the procoagulant membrane.

Blood clotting depends on a relay of plasma proteases and cofactors that converts fibrinogen to fibrin at a site of vessel injury, and this grouping collects the inherited defects of that cascade. Loss-of-function changes in factor VIII or factor IX cause haemophilia A and B, fibrinogen chain mutations give afibrinogenaemia and dysfibrinogenaemia, and von Willebrand factor defects impair platelet adhesion through the GPIb-IX-V receptor complex, whose subunits are themselves mutated in Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Failures of post-translational processing matter as much as the factors: vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation by GGCX licenses calcium-dependent membrane binding, and tyrosine sulfotransferases modify factor VIII and related substrates. The balance runs both ways, since protein C and protein S defects, and gain-of-activity variants of factor V and factor IX, tip the system toward thrombophilia rather than bleeding. Scrambling of membrane phospholipid by ANO6 supports procoagulant surface exposure on platelets.

Fibrin formation is the final structural step of blood coagulation, converting soluble plasma fibrinogen into the insoluble meshwork that seals a wounded vessel and gives a clot its mechanical strength. Thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides from the fibrinogen chains, releasing monomers that self-assemble into protofibrils and then thick fibers in a three-dimensional network; activated factor XIII, a transglutaminase, covalently cross-links the fibers in a calcium-dependent manner so the clot resists premature mechanical and enzymatic breakdown. Platelet integrin αIIbβ3 binds the network, linking aggregation to clot retraction and stability. The same module carries the brakes: antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and other serpins neutralize thrombin, while protein C restrains upstream cofactors, so fibrin deposition stays local. Deficiency of fibrinogen or factor XIII causes bleeding and poor wound healing, whereas loss of the inhibitory arm predisposes to thrombosis.

Initiation of coagulation cascade is the trigger step of blood clotting: when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor to plasma, a small burst of thrombin is generated on the surface of tissue factor-bearing cells such as fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, committing the system to clot formation. Without it bleeding goes unchecked, while inappropriate tissue factor exposure on activated macrophages, apoptotic cells, tumour cells or shed extracellular vesicles drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation in cancer and sepsis. Tissue factor is held in a cryptic state until phosphatidylserine exposure, sphingomyelin hydrolysis and thiol-disulfide exchange decrypt it; it then binds factor VII/VIIa with high affinity and the complex activates factors IX and X. Antithrombin, tissue factor pathway inhibitor, protein S and cell-surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans including syndecans and glypicans restrain the reaction, keeping initiation local to damaged vessel wall.

Blood clotting begins when injury or inflammation exposes tissue factor to plasma, and this initiation phase produces the first small burst of thrombin that primes the rest of the cascade. Tissue factor (F3) sits on fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells and pericytes, normally held in a cryptic, low-activity state; phosphatidylserine exposure and thiol-disulfide rearrangement convert it to its procoagulant form, where it binds factor VII/VIIa with high affinity and the complex cleaves factors IX and X to their active proteases. Cofactors FV and FVIII, von Willebrand factor and prothrombin carry the signal forward, while TFPI, antithrombin and protein S restrain it, and heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans, glypicans and perlecan provide the surface on which inhibition is accelerated. Unrestrained or ectopic tissue factor activity, including on tumour- and sepsis-derived vesicles, drives thrombosis and disseminated intravascular coagulation; deficiency of FVIII or FIX causes haemophilia.

Blood clotting must be confined to the site of injury, and this is the braking system that keeps it there. Losing it produces thrombosis and consumptive coagulopathy, while losing too much of it produces bleeding; the same components are the targets of anticoagulant therapy. Tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks the initiation complex of tissue factor, factor VIIa and factor Xa. Thrombin bound to endothelial thrombomodulin switches specificity and activates protein C, which with protein S degrades the cofactors factor Va and factor VIIIa. Serpins including antithrombin, heparin cofactor II, protein C inhibitor and protein Z-dependent inhibitor trap thrombin and factor Xa irreversibly, accelerated by heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans, glypicans and perlecan. ADAMTS13 trims von Willebrand factor multimers so platelet adhesion via the GPIb-IX-V complex does not run away, as it does in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

Blood clotting at a site of vessel injury is described here in its cell-based form, in which coagulation factors assemble on the membranes of tissue factor-bearing cells and activated platelets rather than in free solution. The output is a fibrin-stabilised platelet plug that stops haemorrhage; loss of individual factors causes haemophilia and related bleeding disorders, while unchecked activity produces pathological thrombosis. Tissue factor with factor VIIa generates the first trace of thrombin, which then amplifies the response by activating factors XI, VIII and V and, through the platelet thrombin receptor, recruiting and degranulating platelets that expose phosphatidylserine. Membrane-bound tenase and prothrombinase complexes produce the thrombin burst that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, crosslinked by factor XIII. Counterbalancing regulators — tissue factor pathway inhibitor, thrombomodulin with protein C and protein S, and heparan sulfate-bound antithrombin — confine the reaction to the wound, alongside von Willebrand factor and its protease ADAMTS13 governing platelet adhesion.

Amplification and propagation of coagulation cascade is the explosive middle of blood clotting, in which trace thrombin made during tissue factor-dependent initiation feeds back to generate a burst of thrombin on the activated platelet surface and convert fibrinogen to a stable fibrin clot. Without it, haemostasis fails and bleeding disorders such as haemophilia A and B follow, while unrestrained activity produces thrombosis. Thrombin activates factors XI, VIII and V, assembling the tenase (FIXa:FVIIIa) and prothrombinase (FXa:FVa) complexes on phosphatidylserine exposed by scramblase activity, so that prothrombin cleavage accelerates enormously. Platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V and von Willebrand factor tether platelets to the injury site and support their procoagulant conversion. Counterbalancing anticoagulants -- antithrombin, heparin cofactor II, protein C with protein S, and protein C inhibitor -- confine the burst to the site of vessel damage.

Once tissue factor has generated a trace of thrombin at a wound, the amplification and propagation phases turn that trace into a burst large enough to clot blood. Thrombin feeds back to activate factors XI, VIII and V on the activated platelet surface, where the tenase complex (FIXa with FVIIIa) makes FXa and the prothrombinase complex (FXa with FVa) cleaves prothrombin, so fibrinogen is converted to cross-linked fibrin and the platelet plug is stabilised. Phosphatidylserine exposure, which requires the scramblase ANO6, and von Willebrand factor binding through the GPIb-IX-V receptor provide the procoagulant membranes and platelet adhesion. Antithrombin, heparin cofactor II and the protein C/protein S system restrain the burst; loss of factor VIII or IX causes haemophilia, while defective inhibition predisposes to thrombosis.

Nearly every eukaryotic mRNA, histone messages aside, is finished at its 3' end by an endonucleolytic cut followed by addition of a poly(A) tail, and mRNA polyadenylation is that maturation step. The tail determines whether a transcript is exported, translated efficiently and protected from decay, and because most genes carry several polyadenylation sites, the choice among them sets 3' UTR length and thus which microRNAs and RNA-binding proteins can act on the message. Site selection depends on recognition of the AAUAAA hexamer and flanking elements by the cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor, whose CPSF3 subunit performs the cut, together with the downstream-element-binding CSTF subunits, the UGUA-recognizing NUDT21-CPSF6/7 heterotetramer, and CLP1-PCF11. PAPOLA then builds the tail, its length controlled by nuclear PABPN1. The reaction is physically coupled to RNA polymerase II transcription, cap binding, spliceosomal components and termination by XRN2, linking 3' end formation to the rest of gene expression.

Mucin-type O-glycans on secreted and membrane mucins are capped by sialic acid, and this terminal step decides how long a chain grows, what charge it carries, and which lectins can read it. Sialylation gives mucus its dense negative charge and hydration, protects epithelial surfaces of the gut, airway, eye and salivary glands, and blocks further elongation or branching of Core 1 and Core 2 structures. Sialyltransferases of the ST3GAL family add α2,3-linked sialic acid to galactose, while ST6GALNAC enzymes act on the GalNAc of the core, generating sialyl-Tn and related short antigens; ST6GAL1 contributes α2,6 linkages. The acceptor substrates are heavily repeated mucin apoproteins such as MUC1, MUC2, MUC5AC and MUC16. Shifts in this terminal sialylation produce the truncated, hypersialylated O-glycans typical of carcinomas and alter mucosal barrier function and immune recognition.

Amyloid fiber formation covers the conversion of soluble human proteins into rigid, cross-beta-sheet fibrils that deposit in tissue and cause amyloidosis, including the plaques of Alzheimer's disease, Lewy pathology in Parkinson's disease, islet deposits in type 2 diabetes, and systemic deposits of transthyretin, serum amyloid A, immunoglobulin light chain-like fragments and beta-2 microglobulin. The pathway includes the proteolytic events that generate aggregation-prone peptides, notably cleavage of the amyloid precursor protein by BACE1, ADAM10 and the gamma-secretase complex (nicastrin, presenilin enhancer, APH1), along with trafficking adaptors and sortilin-related receptor SORL1 that route the precursor. Other members are intrinsically aggregating proteins such as alpha-synuclein, islet amyloid polypeptide, cystatin C, gelsolin and lysozyme, plus chaperone-like and stabilizing partners including apolipoprotein E, serum amyloid P component and heparan sulfate proteoglycan. Oligomeric intermediates, rather than mature fibrils, are thought to drive membrane damage and neurotoxicity; ubiquitin and parkin-linked ubiquitination reflect attempted clearance of these aggregates.

This is the entry and immediate post-entry phase of SARS-CoV-2 infection, the step that determines which tissues the virus can infect and the point at which antiviral entry inhibitors act. The spike glycoprotein engages ACE2 on the cell surface, with heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as syndecans, glypicans and perlecan acting as attachment factors that concentrate virions, and neuropilin-1 binding the furin-processed spike to boost uptake. Fusion requires proteolytic priming: the surface serine protease TMPRSS2 and the proprotein convertase furin cleave spike at the plasma membrane, while endosomal cathepsin L supports an alternative endocytic route. Once the genome reaches the cytoplasm, translation of the large open reading frames yields polyproteins that are processed into non-structural proteins forming the replication-transcription complex on remodelled membranes. Accompanying ESCRT-III subunits, VPS34 complex components and autophagy factors reflect the membrane trafficking and vesicle-shaping machinery the virus co-opts.

Late in the SARS-CoV-2 replication cycle, newly translated structural proteins are folded, modified and assembled with encapsidated genomic RNA in the secretory pathway before virions bud into ERGIC-derived compartments and are released. The genes here describe how host machinery is conscripted for that maturation. Oligosaccharyltransferase subunits such as STT3A/STT3B and RPN1/RPN2, the calnexin-glucosidase folding cycle, mannosidases and Golgi glycosyltransferases build the extensive N- and O-glycan shield on spike, which masks epitopes and shapes receptor engagement. The receptor ACE2 and the proteases TMPRSS2 and furin determine priming and entry of the resulting particles. ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases S-acylate spike cysteines to support membrane fusion, while kinases, ubiquitin and SUMO components, arginine methylation and ADP-ribosyltransferases modify viral and host proteins, the PARPs representing an interferon-induced arm that the virus counters. Blocking these steps limits production of infectious progeny, a therapeutic aim in COVID-19.

WDR5 is a scaffolding hub that nucleates chromatin-modifying assemblies, and this pathway covers how those complexes are built. WDR5 joins RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 to form the WRAD module that licenses and positions the six KMT2 methyltransferases (KMT2A-D, SETD1A, SETD1B), which deposit mono-, di- and trimethylation on histone H3 lysine 4 at active promoters and enhancers. Complex-specific partners diversify targeting: MEN1 and the protease TASP1 with KMT2A/B, KDM6A, NCOA6, PAXIP1 and PAGR1 with KMT2C/D, and CXXC1 with WDR82 in the SET1 complexes. WDR5 also sits in the GCN5/PCAF-ATAC and KAT8-NSL acetyltransferase complexes, linking H3K4 methylation to histone acetylation. This machinery sets Hox gene expression during embryonic patterning and lineage specification; germline loss causes chromatinopathies such as Kabuki and Wiedemann-Steiner syndromes, and KMT2A rearrangement drives mixed lineage leukemia, making the WDR5 interface a drug target.

Serine metabolism supplies the L-serine that cells use as a precursor for nucleotides, phospholipids, sphingolipids and one-carbon units, and that the brain uses to make the neurotransmitters glycine and D-serine. Because serine crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, neural tissue depends on local synthesis, and loss of the biosynthetic enzymes causes congenital microcephaly, seizures and psychomotor retardation that can be mitigated by early serine supplementation. The route branches from glycolysis at 3-phosphoglycerate, with PHGDH oxidising it, PSAT1 transferring an amino group from glutamate, and PSPH releasing free serine; serine dehydratase activity returns carbon to pyruvate when serine is in excess. Serine racemase generates D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, while serine incorporators feed serine into sphingolipid and phosphatidylserine synthesis at the membrane, linking amino acid supply to lipid biogenesis and synaptic signalling.

Serine metabolism supplies the brain and dividing cells with L-serine, a precursor for nucleotides, phospholipids, sphingolipids and the neurotransmitters glycine and D-serine, and a donor of one-carbon units for folate-dependent methylation. Synthesis branches from glycolysis: 3-phosphoglycerate is oxidised by PHGDH, transaminated by PSAT1 using glutamate as the amino donor, and dephosphorylated by PSPH to release free serine. Serine racemase generates D-serine, the co-agonist at NMDA receptors, while serine dehydratase enzymes catabolise serine to pyruvate and ammonia and set the balance between supply and disposal. The SERINC proteins incorporate serine into membrane lipids during their synthesis. Loss of the biosynthetic enzymes causes congenital microcephaly, seizures and severe developmental delay that respond to dietary serine if begun early, and PHGDH is frequently amplified in tumours dependent on serine for growth.

GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the central nervous system, and its receptors set the brake that keeps excitatory circuits from running away; loss of this restraint produces seizures, and the same receptors are the targets of benzodiazepines, barbiturates, general anaesthetics and baclofen. Activation works through two receptor families. Ionotropic pentamers assembled from alpha, beta, gamma, rho and theta subunits form ligand-gated chloride channels that shift membrane potential within milliseconds, clustered at synapses with the help of collybistin. Metabotropic signalling through a GABBR1/GABBR2 heterodimer recruits Gi/Go heterotrimers, whose alpha subunits suppress adenylate cyclase and cAMP-dependent PKA activity while the released beta-gamma pair inhibits presynaptic calcium entry and opens inwardly rectifying Kir3 potassium channels, hyperpolarising the cell. Mutations in the channel subunits cause inherited epilepsy syndromes.

Slow, sustained inhibition in the nervous system depends on metabotropic GABA B receptors, which damp neuronal excitability over hundreds of milliseconds rather than the millisecond timescale of ionotropic GABA channels. This tone sets seizure threshold, modulates pain and spasticity, and is the target of baclofen; its loss contributes to epilepsy and disordered pain signalling. The receptor is an obligate heterodimer in which GABBR1 binds the transmitter and GABBR2 couples to heterotrimeric G proteins. The released Gi/Go alpha subunits inhibit adenylate cyclase, lowering cAMP and reducing downstream kinase activity, while the freed beta-gamma dimer opens inwardly rectifying potassium channels of the KCNJ family, hyperpolarising the membrane. Presynaptically the same signalling restrains transmitter release, making these receptors both autoreceptors and heteroreceptors that tune synaptic gain across many circuits.

Regulation of Complement cascade keeps an amplifying, self-sustaining immune proteolytic system aimed at pathogens and away from healthy tissue. Because C3 activation feeds back to generate more C3 convertase, and because the alternative pathway ticks over continuously through spontaneous C3 hydrolysis, host surfaces must be actively protected; loss of this control causes atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, C3 glomerulopathy and age-related macular degeneration. Regulators built from tandem complement control repeats — factor H, CD46, CD55 and CR1, with C4BP and the factor H-related proteins — act in two ways: accelerating decay of C3 and C5 convertases, and serving as cofactors for factor I cleavage of C3b and C4b. C1 inhibitor restrains the classical initiating proteases, carboxypeptidases inactivate the C3a and C5a chemoattractants, and CD59 blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex. Pathogens subvert this system by capturing plasma regulators onto their surfaces.

Complement is destructive by design and self-amplifying, so host tissue survives only because its activation is continuously restrained. This regulation keeps the inherent positive feedback of C3 cleavage and the constant low-grade tickover of the alternative pathway from turning on healthy cells, while still allowing opsonisation of pathogens and clearance of dead cells, debris and oxidative damage. Membrane-anchored and plasma regulators of complement activation work in two ways: they accelerate irreversible decay of the C3 and C5 convertases, as decay accelerating factor CD55 does, and they serve as cofactors for factor I-mediated cleavage of C3b and C4b, the role of factor H, membrane cofactor protein CD46, complement receptor 1 and C4b-binding protein. C1 inhibitor blocks the classical pathway proteases and CD59 caps membrane attack complex assembly. Loss of these brakes underlies atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, macular degeneration and hereditary angioedema; many microbes evade attack by capturing host regulators.

Attachment of SUMO to proteins of the nuclear envelope controls where those proteins sit and therefore how traffic across the envelope and the mechanics of the lamina behave. The best-understood case is RANGAP1, whose modification by SUMO1 through the conjugating enzyme UBE2I creates the binding surface that docks it, with RANBP2, at the cytoplasmic face of the nuclear pore; anchoring it there sets up the steep RanGTP gradient across the envelope that gives nucleocytoplasmic transport its direction. SUMOylation of lamin A likewise affects its behaviour at the inner nuclear membrane, and mutations that disturb the modified site are associated with cardiomyopathy, while modification of the pore-associated nucleoporin NUP153 has no assigned consequence. As a branch of the wider SUMO conjugation system, this is post-translational targeting rather than degradation: a reversible mark that localises rather than destroys its substrates.

The axial skeleton and skeletal muscle trace back to paraxial mesoderm, the trunk tissue that ingresses through the primitive streak and then buds off somites at regular intervals. Its specification depends on graded signalling: BMP4 from lateral plate mesoderm is buffered by notochord-derived NOG so that paraxial fate arises at low BMP activity, while WNT3A acting through beta-catenin and LEF1, FGFR1 signalling, and TBXT switch on TBX6 and MSGN1. These two transcription factors reinforce one another, drive epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and turn on NOTCH components including DLL1, DLL3, NOTCH1 and the RBPJ/MAML coactivator complex, feeding the segmentation clock in which HES7 and LFNG oscillate. Somite boundaries are set by a loop between TBX6 and MESP2 with RIPPLY2, resolved by proteasomal degradation of TBX6 — hence the prominent proteasome subunits here. Failure of this segmentation programme produces vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis.

Ciprofloxacin ADME traces how a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic is absorbed, distributed, metabolised and excreted, which determines both its efficacy against susceptible urinary, respiratory, gastrointestinal and bone infections and its liability for tendon, nerve and CNS toxicity. Because the drug is neither highly soluble nor highly permeable at intestinal pH, its handling depends less on passive diffusion than on carrier proteins: organic cation and anion transporters mediate hepatic and renal tubular uptake, an organic anion transporting polypeptide contributes to intestinal and hepatic entry, and the efflux pump ABCG2 drives secretion back into the gut lumen and bile. Albumin binding sets the free fraction in plasma. Most of the dose leaves unchanged by the renal and biliary routes, with only a minor fraction oxidised or sulfated, so transporter competition and renal impairment dominate exposure and dosing decisions.

Ciprofloxacin, a broad-spectrum fluoroquinolone antibiotic, is handled by the body largely through transport rather than metabolism, and this disposition route explains both its tissue concentrations and its drug interactions. Absorption occurs mainly in the upper small intestine, where the drug's poor permeability makes uptake and efflux carriers decisive; the remainder of a dose is excreted essentially unchanged by the kidney and, to a lesser extent, the intestine and bile, with only a minor fraction converted to oxo- and sulfo-metabolites. An organic anion transporting polypeptide mediates cellular uptake, organic cation and organic anion transporters of the solute carrier family move the drug across renal tubular and hepatic membranes, and the ATP-driven efflux pump ABCG2 exports it into gut lumen and bile. Albumin binding limits the free plasma fraction. Variation in these carriers shifts exposure and underlies the tendon, nerve and central nervous system toxicities that now restrict prescribing.

Formation of axial mesoderm is the early embryonic step that builds the notochord and its anterior derivatives from cells ingressing at the front of the primitive streak. It matters because the notochord is the embryo's midline organiser: it stiffens the body axis, patterns neural tube, somites and gut through Sonic Hedgehog and related signals, and later persists as the nuclei pulposi of the intervertebral discs, whose failure underlies disc degeneration and, in rare cases, chordoma. NODAL signalling through SMAD2/3 cooperates with the pioneer factor FOXH1, with TBXT expressed before streak formation, and with TEAD factors held in check by Hippo signalling via YAP1; together they activate FOXA2, which drives notochord-specific targets including NOTO and SHH. WNT input through beta-catenin with TCF/LEF partners contributes to axial specification, linking morphogen gradients to midline cell fate.

Early in gastrulation, cells ingressing at the anterior primitive streak form the axial mesoderm, or chordamesoderm, the midline tissue that becomes the prechordal plate, head process and notochord. This midline is the embryo's organizing rod: it stiffens the body axis, patterns neural tube and somites through secreted Sonic Hedgehog, and later persists as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc, whose degeneration underlies disc disease. NODAL signalling through SMAD2 and SMAD3 cooperates with the pioneer factor FOXH1, with TEAD factors and their coactivator YAP1 released from Hippo restraint, and with the mesodermal factor TBXT to switch on FOXA2, which in turn drives notochord genes such as NOTO and SHH. WNT input via CTNNB1 with LEF1 and TCF7 positions this programme along the axis, coupling germ layer specification to midline identity.

After fertilization the embryo must stop living off the mother's supplies and start running its own genome; this handover is the maternal-to-zygotic transition. It sets the stage for totipotency and the first lineage decisions, and its failure is a cause of early embryonic arrest and infertility. Three coupled events define it: maternally stored mRNAs are deadenylated and destroyed through CCR4-NOT machinery with BTG4 and ZFP36L2 licensing decay, plus uridylation by TUT4/TUT7 and exonucleolytic clearance; paternal chromatin is remodelled as protamines PRM1/PRM2 give way to oocyte-supplied histones via NPM2 and the HIRA chaperone; and DNA methylation is erased through TET3 oxidation with base excision repair while repressive histone marks are stripped by KDM4E, KDM6A/B and related demethylases. The resulting permissive chromatin permits zygotic genome activation, in which DPPA2/DPPA4 and DUX4 induce ZSCAN4, LEUTX, TPRX1 and transcription from endogenous retroviral LTRs, and newly made products complete degradation of the maternal transcriptome.

The stress-responsive transcription factor NFE2L2 (NRF2) is best known for switching on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also reshapes central carbon metabolism, and its control of tricarboxylic acid cycle genes is one arm of that metabolic reprogramming. Here NFE2L2 drives expression of IDH1 and ME1, two NADPH-generating dehydrogenases that link citrate and malate metabolism to reductive biosynthesis and to regeneration of glutathione and thioredoxin. The effect is to couple the cell's response to oxidative and electrophilic stress with the supply of reducing equivalents and of carbon skeletons for lipid and nucleotide synthesis. In tumours with constitutive NFE2L2 activation, typically through loss of its KEAP1-dependent degradation, this same wiring supports anabolic growth and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, making TCA-linked gene regulation a point where redox homeostasis and proliferative metabolism meet.

The stress-responsive transcription factor NFE2L2 is best known for switching on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also sets the tone of inflammatory gene expression, and this arm of its activity links redox state to immune signalling. Acting at antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with a small MAF partner, NFE2L2 recruits the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300 to remodel chromatin at target promoters, among them the monocyte chemoattractant CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Output is context-dependent: NFE2L2 can drive such genes directly while also restraining NF-kB-driven inflammation indirectly, partly through heme oxygenase-1. Loss of this control contributes to chronic inflammatory and oxidative-stress-associated disease, including airway and vascular inflammation, and explains why NFE2L2 activators are pursued as anti-inflammatory as well as cytoprotective agents.

When reactive oxygen species or electrophiles accumulate, the transcription factor NRF2 escapes degradation, enters the nucleus and switches on a battery of cytoprotective genes; this arm of the antioxidant response is what allows cells to survive oxidative and xenobiotic insult, and its loss sensitises tissues to inflammation, chemical injury and degeneration, while its constitutive activation in tumours confers drug resistance. NRF2 binds antioxidant response elements as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins, with BACH1 acting as a competing repressor and the acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300 supplying coactivator function. The induced programme spans glutathione synthesis and recycling (GCLC, GCLM, GSR), cystine import through SLC7A11, glutathione transferase-mediated phase II conjugation, quinone reduction by NQO1, heme catabolism by HMOX1, and thioredoxin- and peroxiredoxin-based peroxide removal. ATF4 coupling links this response to integrated stress signalling.

Cells meeting oxidative stress need NADPH, and the transcription factor NRF2 supplies it by turning up the pentose phosphate pathway. Acting with a small MAF partner at antioxidant response elements, and recruiting the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, NRF2 induces glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase in the oxidative branch, plus transketolase and transaldolase in the non-oxidative branch. The result reroutes glucose away from glycolysis toward NADPH production, which regenerates reduced glutathione and thioredoxin, and toward ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. This coupling of redox sensing to central carbon metabolism supports survival during electrophilic and oxidant challenge, and is exploited by tumours: constitutive NRF2 activation sustains the reducing power and biosynthetic precursors that proliferating cancer cells require, and contributes to chemotherapy and radiation resistance.

NRF2, encoded by NFE2L2, is best known as the stress-responsive transcription factor that switches on antioxidant and detoxification genes, but when it is constitutively stabilised — as in tumours with KEAP1 loss or NFE2L2 mutation — the same factor drives a pro-tumorigenic transcriptional programme. This arm of NRF2 output supports cancer cell survival, growth-factor autonomy and resistance to chemotherapy and radiation, and its activation marks aggressive lung and other epithelial cancers. Acting as a heterodimer with small MAF proteins such as MAFK and recruiting the coactivators CREBBP and EP300, with SP1 contributing to promoter occupancy, NRF2 induces anti-apoptotic BCL2 and BCL2L1, mitogens including AREG, EGF and PDGFA, and components of NOTCH1 signalling. The result couples cytoprotection to proliferation and developmental signalling, so that a defence pathway becomes a driver of tumour progression rather than a barrier to it.

The transcription factor NRF2 (NFE2L2) does more than defend cells against oxidative and electrophilic stress: by driving expression of drug efflux transporters it also sets how much of a xenobiotic a cell retains. This arm of its programme, in which NFE2L2 regulates multidrug resistance-associated enzymes and transporters, explains why tumours with constitutive NRF2 activity survive chemotherapy that should kill them. NFE2L2 partners with a small Maf protein such as MAFK on antioxidant response elements and recruits the coactivators CREBBP and EP300 to acetylate histones and open those promoters. Among the induced targets are ATP-binding cassette pumps: ABCC1 and ABCC3, which export glutathione and drug conjugates, and ABCG2, a broad efflux pump, alongside ABCF2, linked to platinum resistance in ovarian cancer. The same circuitry that provides cytoprotection in normal tissue therefore becomes a liability in treated cancer.

NRF2 is best known as the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, but it also converges on the transcriptional arm of the endoplasmic reticulum stress response, and this branch describes its control of ER-stress-associated targets. The central output is ATF4, a stress-induced transcription factor that lets cells survive hypoxia, amino acid limitation and accumulation of unfolded protein by turning on adaptive metabolic and chaperone genes; under sustained stress the same factor tips the balance toward apoptosis. ATF4 also drives serine and glycine biosynthesis, one reason tumour cells including non-small cell lung cancer depend on it. Transcription here requires NRF2 heterodimerised with a small MAF partner on antioxidant response elements, together with the histone acetyltransferase coactivators CREBBP and EP300, linking redox sensing to proteostasis and to cancer cell stress tolerance.

Enhancers must be marked before the genes they control can be switched on, and the MLL3 and MLL4 complexes provide that mark: KMT2C or KMT2D, with the shared core subunits ASH2L, RBBP5, WDR5, DPY30, PAXIP1, PAGR1 and the H3K27 demethylase KDM6A, monomethylates histone H3 lysine 4 at tens of thousands of enhancers across the genome. Full enhancer activation also needs p300/CBP-mediated H3K27 acetylation, recruited through these complexes, so priming and activation are coupled. Recruitment is largely by nuclear receptors and their coactivators, and the accompanying adipogenic programme illustrates the output: PPARG and RXRA with NCOA and Mediator subunits drive lipid droplet, lipolysis and fatty acid genes such as FABP4, PLIN1, ADIPOQ and LPL, opposed by NCOR1/2, HDAC3 and SIRT1. KMT2C and KMT2D are among the most frequently mutated genes in cancer, and germline loss causes Kabuki and related developmental syndromes.

NFE2L2 (NRF2) is the master transcription factor for antioxidant and detoxification genes, and how much of it a cell makes sets the ceiling on its stress defences; tumours that raise it gain resistance to oxidants and chemotherapy, while too little leaves tissues vulnerable to oxidative and electrophilic injury. Beyond the familiar control of NRF2 protein stability, transcription of the gene itself is regulated, and this is where antioxidant capacity is wired into other signalling routes. MYC, the NF- innerB subunit p65 with p50, and the NOTCH1 intracellular domain act at its promoter, and NRF2 with its small MAF partner feeds back on its own gene, while CREBBP and EP300 supply histone acetyltransferase and coactivator function. The result couples proliferative, inflammatory and developmental signals to the size of the cellular antioxidant response.

The embryo begins life transcriptionally silent, relying on maternal mRNA and protein; zygotic genome activation is the switch by which the newly formed embryonic genome starts transcribing for itself, and without it development arrests within the first few cleavages. It follows extensive epigenetic remodelling of both pronuclei, including DNA demethylation and changes in histone methylation and acetylation, and proceeds in a minor wave at the one-cell stage and a major wave around the eight-cell stage in humans. DUX4, whose expression is promoted by DPPA2 and DPPA4, binds promoters of early embryonic genes such as ZSCAN4, LEUTX, DUXA and KDM4E and recruits coactivators including CREBBP and EP300 to activate them; it also drives bidirectional transcription from endogenous retroviral long terminal repeats and pericentric satellite repeats, the latter contributing to chromocenter formation. Clearance of maternal transcripts by the uridylyltransferases TUT4 and TUT7 accompanies the handover to embryonic control.

The exocrine pancreas — the acinar cells that make digestive enzymes and the duct cells that carry them to the duodenum — arises from multipotent progenitors in the foregut-derived pancreatic buds, and this set captures the extracellular niche that guides those lineage decisions. Fibrillar and network collagens, the full complement of laminin chains, fibronectin and vitronectin build the basal lamina and interstitial matrix against which budding epithelium branches, polarises and differentiates, while FGF7, FGF10, FGF2, FGF4 and EGF act as mesenchyme-derived growth signals that sustain progenitor proliferation and tubulogenesis. Correct apical–basal orientation of acinar cells around a lumen and the single-layered ductal epithelium both depend on this matrix–receptor dialogue. The same programme is relevant to disease: loss of normal acinar or ductal identity, together with remodelled collagen-rich stroma, accompanies acinar-to-ductal metaplasia and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

An oocyte enters fertilization loaded with transcripts it made during oogenesis, and clearing them on schedule is what allows the embryo to switch from maternal to its own gene products. M-decay is the arm of this clearance carried out by factors the mother already stored in the egg, as opposed to later degradation driven by zygotic products; when it fails, oocytes arrest, zygotes stall at early cleavage and fertility is lost. Two adaptors set the timing: ZFP36L2 acts in the maturing oocyte and BTG4 after fertilization, each recruiting the multisubunit CCR4-NOT deadenylase, whose CNOT7/CNOT8 and CNOT6/CNOT6L nucleases shorten poly(A) tails and commit messages to decay. BTG4 links the complex to poly(A)-binding protein and the eIF4 cap-binding machinery, coupling translation to turnover. In parallel, DICER1-derived endogenous siRNAs guide AGO2 to slice complementary maternal mRNAs. Oocyte-specific factors such as NOBOX, ZP2 and PADI6 mark the transcripts and cellular context involved.

After fertilization the embryo must dismantle the stockpile of messages it inherited from the oocyte, and zygotic decay is the arm of that clearance carried out by factors the zygotic genome itself switches on. Timely removal of maternal transcripts allows the embryo to hand control of gene expression to its own genome; when it fails, transcript levels stay abnormal, development stalls and infertility follows. Mechanistically, partially deadenylated maternal mRNAs held in a closed-loop translation complex with cap-binding and poly(A)-binding proteins are tagged at their 3' ends with untemplated uridines by the terminal uridylyltransferases TUT4 and TUT7, whose expression is induced in the zygote. The uridine tail recruits PABPN1, which in turn brings in the 3'-to-5' exoribonuclease DIS3L2 to destroy the transcript, linking deadenylation, uridylation and exonucleolytic decay into one maternal-to-zygotic transition programme.

Respiratory syncytial virus is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and hospitalisation in infants, and this pathway traces its life cycle in airway epithelium together with the host responses it triggers and subverts. Attachment involves cell-surface glycosaminoglycan-bearing proteins — syndecans, glypicans, perlecan — alongside candidate entry receptors such as IGF1R, CX3CR1 and EGFR, followed by endocytic uptake through RAB5-marked early endosomes; the fusion glycoprotein requires furin cleavage and signal peptidase processing for maturation, and chaperones including HSP90 and HSPA8 support viral protein folding and polymerase activity. Sensing by cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 via MAVS, by endosomal Toll-like receptors, and by PKR and OAS drives IRF3 activation, type I interferon production and ISG15 conjugation, while Mediator complex subunits and CBP/p300 mediate the transcriptional output. Viral antagonism of this interferon arm underlies the severity and reinfection typical of RSV disease.

Respiratory syncytial virus begins infection by sticking to the luminal surface of the airway epithelium and fusing its envelope with the host membrane, a step that determines its tropism for ciliated epithelial cells and underlies bronchiolitis in infants. Attachment is mediated largely by the viral G protein binding cell-surface glycosaminoglycans on syndecans, glypicans and other heparan sulfate proteoglycans such as perlecan and agrin, along with the chemokine receptor CX3CR1 on airway cells; nucleolin, EGFR and IGF1R have been implicated as cofactors for fusion and uptake, with RAB5 GTPases supporting early endosomal trafficking of internalised virions. The host protease furin cleaves the F precursor into its fusion-competent form, while CD14, LY96 and TLR4 represent recognition of the virus at the cell surface rather than entry itself. Efficiency of these interactions shapes viral load and disease severity.

Assembly and release of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) virions is the final step of the RSV replication cycle, in which newly made genomes and viral proteins are packaged into filamentous virions that bud from the apical surface of ciliated airway epithelium and spread infection through the respiratory tract. Progeny virions form when the nucleoprotein-coated negative-sense genome, together with the L/P polymerase and the M2-1 processivity factor, is bridged to the matrix protein layer beneath a lipid envelope studded with the fusion, attachment, and small hydrophobic proteins; the last forms a pentameric ion channel that delays death of the infected cell. Budding depends on host membranes and cytoskeleton, and on the HSP90 chaperones, whose folding activity supports viral polymerase and glycoprotein maturation, making them a point at which host chaperone function can be targeted to limit virion production.

The final step of respiratory syncytial virus replication is the packaging of new genomes and the release of infectious particles from the infected cell. RSV assembles at the apical surface of ciliated airway epithelium, where viral filaments form: the negative-sense genome coated by nucleoprotein and bound by the polymerase and its phosphoprotein cofactor is bridged by M2-1 to a matrix layer that in turn supports an envelope carrying the fusion, attachment and small hydrophobic proteins. Budding depends on cooperation between these viral proteins, host membranes and the cytoskeleton, and the requirement here is for host cytosolic HSP90 chaperone activity, which supports folding and stability of the viral polymerase and structural proteins. Blocking this chaperone step limits production of progeny virions, making it a host-directed target in bronchiolitis and other severe RSV disease of infants and the elderly.

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) genome replication, transcription and translation is the intracellular phase of infection by the leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, in which the virus copies its negative-sense RNA genome and expresses its eleven proteins entirely from host resources. The viral polymerase complex, built from the large catalytic subunit and its phosphoprotein cofactor, reads a template that stays encapsidated by nucleoprotein, and switches between making mRNAs and making full-length antigenome depending on regulatory viral factors. Everything shown here is the host contribution the virus subverts: casein kinase 2 and protein phosphatase 1 set the phosphorylation state of the phosphoprotein that governs elongation, HSP90 and HSPA8 chaperone polymerase assembly, importin and exportin move viral proteins across the nuclear envelope, and signal peptidase and furin process the envelope glycoproteins. Blocking these steps is the basis of antiviral strategies against RSV.

Respiratory syncytial virus carries a negative-sense RNA genome that must be copied and expressed entirely by virally encoded machinery, and the host proteins gathered here are the ones that machinery borrows. RSV genome replication, transcription and translation depend on the viral polymerase large subunit and its phosphoprotein cofactor acting on nucleoprotein-coated RNA, with a processivity factor and a regulator that switches synthesis between mRNA and antigenome. Host casein kinase 2 subunits and protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits set the phosphorylation state of the phosphoprotein that licenses transcript elongation, HSP90 and HSPA8 chaperone polymerase assembly, and importin beta and exportin 1 move viral proteins in and out of the nucleus. Signal peptidase subunits and furin process the envelope glycoproteins, furin cleaving the fusion protein into its active form. This biology underlies bronchiolitis in infants and is where antiviral polymerase inhibitors act.

After fertilization the embryo must erase the chromatin states it inherited from egg and sperm and build one capable of supporting its own transcription; these chromatin modifications during the maternal to zygotic transition accomplish that reprogramming. Both pronuclei lose DNA methylation, by different routes: in the paternal genome cytosine deamination and base excision repair, aided by TET3-mediated oxidation of 5-methylcytosine, replace modified bases with unmodified cytosine, while in the maternal genome DPPA3 blocks TET3 recruitment and displaces UHRF1 so that DNMT1-dependent maintenance methylation fails and demethylation occurs passively through cleavage divisions. In parallel, histone demethylases of the KDM5 and KDM6 families trim inherited H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, opening developmental loci. The result is the progressively accessible chromatin that permits zygotic genome activation, before methylation and repressive marks are re-imposed around implantation; failure impairs preimplantation development and imprint handling.

Sperm package nearly all of their DNA with protamines rather than histones, achieving extreme compaction at the cost of a transcriptionally silent, epigenetically bare genome. Immediately after fertilization the male pronucleus must be rebuilt into ordinary chromatin using histones supplied by the oocyte, and this protamine-to-nucleosome exchange is what makes the paternal genome decondense, become permissive for transcription, and participate in the first embryonic divisions. The kinase SRPK1 phosphorylates PRM1 and PRM2, which promotes their removal by nucleoplasmin NPM2 and recruits the histone chaperone HIRA; HIRA then deposits the replacement-independent variant H3.3 together with core H2B and H4 histones, H2AX, and the oocyte-specific linker histone H1-8. Arginine methylation of H3.3 by METTL23 supports its incorporation. The reprogrammed chromatin established here sets the paternal epigenome inherited by the embryo, and defects contribute to fertilization failure.

When a vessel wall is injured, platelets must catch onto exposed subendothelial collagen before they can aggregate and seal the breach; defects in this adhesion step produce bleeding disorders on one hand and pathological thrombosis on the other. Von Willebrand factor bridges collagen to the platelet glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex, whose subunits are encoded by GP1BA, GP1BB, GP9 and GP5, and this tethering under high shear allows platelets to decelerate and stick. Loss-of-function mutations in the receptor subunits cause Bernard-Soulier syndrome, while VWF mutations underlie von Willebrand disease; conversely, failure of the metalloprotease ADAMTS13 to cleave ultralarge von Willebrand multimers leaves hyperadhesive strings that trap platelets in the microvasculature, as in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. The collagen chains COL1A1 and COL1A2 supply the adhesive substrate, linking primary haemostasis to matrix composition.

During gastrulation, epiblast cells ingressing through the anterior primitive streak become definitive endoderm, the germ layer that gives rise to the gut tube and its derivative organs including liver, pancreas, thyroid and lung epithelium. Its specification is driven by high NODAL signalling, which acts through SMAD2 and SMAD3 with SMAD4 to induce EOMES, MIXL1 and goosecoid; EOMES in turn switches on FOXA2, SOX17 and the GATA4/GATA6 pair that define endodermal identity and license later organ-specific programmes. Unlike prospective mesoderm, these progenitors retain E-cadherin rather than switching to N-cadherin, avoiding a full epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition and instead remodelling adhesion so they can intercalate into an epithelial sheet; CDH1 together with the chemokine receptor CXCR4 is the usual way the population is isolated. WNT input via CTNNB1 and TCF7L2 patterns the streak alongside brachyury. Directing stem cells through this step is the starting point for making hepatocytes and insulin-producing beta cells.

The earliest step in building a brain is the specification of the anterior neural plate, the rostral epiblast territory that will fold into a neural tube and give rise to forebrain and midbrain; failure of neural tube closure produces spina bifida and related congenital defects of the central nervous system. Anterior character depends on BMP signalling being held off by inhibitors from the anterior visceral endoderm, after which OTX2, ZIC2 and POU-domain factors including POU3F1 and POU5F1 act on an upstream enhancer to switch on SOX2 in the neuroepithelium. SOX1, PAX6, ZEB2 and ZNF521 accompany this transition from pluripotency, as NANOG and POU5F1 expression is resolved. The sharp limit with the posterior neural plate is set by reciprocal repression between high anterior OTX2 and posterior GBX2, fixing the midbrain-hindbrain boundary and the regional identity of later brain development.

Somitogenesis is the periodic segmentation of the embryo's paraxial mesoderm into somites, the blocks of tissue that later give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis; its failure produces congenital vertebral malsegmentation such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Segment size and timing follow a clock-and-wavefront logic: an oscillator running in presomitic mesoderm cells intersects a slowly regressing determination front set by opposing WNT/FGF and retinoic acid gradients. The oscillator is built from Notch signalling with negative feedback, in which HES7 represses its own transcription and LFNG glycosylates Notch to damp DLL1/DLL3-dependent activation through RBPJ. Where the wave meets the front, TBX6 with MSGN1 licenses MESP2 expression, which sets rostrocaudal polarity, induces EPHA4 for boundary formation, and drives RIPPLY2 to extinguish TBX6 and reset the cycle. Rapid proteasomal turnover of these short-lived regulators keeps the oscillations sharp.

Somitogenesis is the periodic segmentation of the vertebrate embryo's paraxial mesoderm into somites, the blocks of mesenchyme that give rise to vertebrae, ribs, skeletal muscle and dermis; its failure produces congenital vertebral malformations such as spondylocostal dysostosis. Segment size and spacing arise from a clock-and-wavefront arrangement, in which a molecular oscillator in presomitic mesoderm meets gradients of WNT, FGF and retinoic acid signalling that set the determination front. The oscillator is built from Notch-pathway negative feedback: HES7 represses its own transcription, and the glycosyltransferase LFNG, induced through NOTCH1/RBPJ, feeds back to dampen Notch, with DLL1 and DLL3 ligands shaping the response. At the front, TBX6 and MSGN1 drive MESP2, which turns on EPHA4 for boundary formation and RIPPLY2 to extinguish TBX6. Rapid proteasomal turnover keeps these short-lived regulators oscillating.

Human cells are the battlefield for bacterial disease, and this collection of bacterial infection pathways covers how pathogens attach to host surfaces, force their way in, deliver toxins, and dodge immune clearance. The consequences are clinical: tetanus and botulism from clostridial neurotoxins, anthrax, diphtheria, enterotoxigenic diarrhoea, tuberculosis and listeriosis. Anthrax toxin receptors ANTXR1 and ANTXR2 with the protease furin allow toxin entry, while diphtheria toxin exploits the HBEGF precursor and ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EEF2 to shut down translation. Clostridial neurotoxins bind synaptic vesicle proteins such as SV2 isoforms and synaptotagmins and cleave SNAP25, VAMPs and syntaxins, abolishing neurotransmitter release. Listeria subverts E-cadherin, MET and the endocytic and ubiquitin machinery to invade epithelial cells, and the extensive laminin and collagen IV repertoire reflects adhesion to basement membranes. Host defence appears as TLR2 sensing, guanylate-binding proteins, inflammatory caspase activity and nitric oxide production.

Human parasitic infection pathways describe how a parasite attaches to host cells, gets inside them, and then blunts the immune response that should clear it; the current content centres on Leishmania, a sandfly-borne flagellate that infects skin and mucosa and can spread to liver, spleen and bone marrow as often-fatal visceral disease. The genes trace the macrophage side of that encounter: complement C3 and its receptor plus Fc gamma receptors opsonise and bind the promastigote, Src-family and Syk/BTK kinases with VAV and DOCK/ELMO exchange factors activate CDC42 and RAC1, and WASP/WAVE with the ARP2/3 complex drives the actin remodelling of phagocytic cup formation and uptake. Downstream, NLRP3 inflammasome assembly with caspase-1, IL1B, IL18 and gasdermin D, purinergic and adenosine receptor signalling through adenylate cyclase and PKA, NF-kB and MAPK activation, and IL10 output determine whether the phagocyte kills the parasite or becomes its permissive niche.

This collection maps how human viruses take over the cells they infect, covering the shared life-cycle steps of SARS coronaviruses, influenza, HIV and human cytomegalovirus: attachment and entry, genome replication and viral protein synthesis, assembly and release, and subversion of host defences. It matters because these steps define the pathology of flu, COVID-19, AIDS and congenital or opportunistic CMV disease, and because nearly every step is a drug target. Entry factors such as ACE2 with the proteases TMPRSS2, furin and cathepsin L, along with CD4 and the coreceptors CCR5 and CXCR4, set tropism. Downstream, the virus borrows host RNA polymerase II and Mediator, the spliceosome, cap and polyadenylation machinery, ribosomes, N-glycosylation and secretory traffic, nuclear pore transport, ubiquitin-proteasome and ESCRT budding components. Against this, innate sensors, interferon signalling, restriction factors and MHC antigen presentation are engaged and actively antagonised.

Skin, hair and eye colour depend on a melanocyte transcriptional programme driven by the M-isoform of MITF, which switches on the enzymes and structural proteins that build and move melanosomes. Loss of this output causes hypopigmentation and deafness syndromes, while its reactivation sustains the differentiated state of melanoma cells. MITF binds M-box elements in the promoters of the melanin-synthetic enzymes tyrosinase, TYRP1 and DCT, and of melanosome components such as MLANA, PMEL and GPR143; it also drives RAB27A, MYO5A and melanophilin, the machinery that tethers and transports pigment granules toward the cell periphery for transfer to keratinocytes. Transcription requires partners and coactivators — SOX10, TFAP2A, LEF1 with beta-catenin, CREB1, IRF4 — and remodelling of target promoters by BAF/SWI-SNF chromatin complexes, linking pigmentation gene expression to Wnt and stress-kinase signalling inputs.

Melanocytes depend on the transcription factor MITF-M not only to build pigment but to stay alive, and this branch of its output is the survival programme: MITF drives anti-apoptotic targets including BCL2, BCL2A1 and the IAP family member BIRC7, so melanoblasts survive migration and colonisation of the skin during development and melanocytes persist afterwards. Loss of this activity causes pigment cell death and depigmentation phenotypes, while its persistence in melanoma supports tumour cell survival and resistance to therapy. MITF also induces DICER1, linking it to microRNA processing, and one of its own targets, the TRPM1 intronic microRNA miR-211, acts with Argonaute proteins and TNRC6 scaffolds in silencing complexes to shape downstream gene expression. Repressive input comes through POU3F2 and the SIN3A-HDAC1 corepressor, tuning how much survival signal the lineage receives.

Toll-like receptor 7 senses single-stranded RNA and guanosine-containing nucleosides in endosomes, a system built to detect viral genomes but also capable of reacting to self-derived nucleic acids released by dying or activated host cells. When that discrimination fails, self RNA and guanosine metabolites become damage-associated ligands that drive sustained type I interferon production and autoantibody-generating B cell responses. This is a recognised route into systemic lupus erythematosus: polymorphisms raising TLR7 expression increase disease risk, and the gain-of-function variant Y264H, which binds endogenous guanosine ligands with heightened affinity, was found in a lupus patient. The broader theme is the difficulty of keeping innate sensing of damage signals confined to controlled tissue repair rather than chronic autoimmune inflammation, a boundary also crossed in rheumatoid arthritis and atherosclerosis. Receptor compartmentalisation and ligand availability are the checkpoints that fail here.

Type I interferon production downstream of Toll-like receptor sensing depends on two related kinases, TBK1 and IKKε, which phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7 and license them to enter the nucleus and switch on interferon-β and related antiviral genes. How strongly and how long these kinases fire determines whether a cell mounts a protective antiviral response or drives damaging inflammation, so their activity is tuned rather than simply switched on. Here TLR4 with its co-receptors CD14 and MD-2 signals through the TRIF adaptors TICAM1 and TICAM2 to TRAF3, which builds K63-linked polyubiquitin chains that promote TBK1 and IKKε activation; the scaffold TANK and the autophagy receptor optineurin bind TBK1 and modulate its output. Loss of this control contributes to interferonopathy and autoimmunity, while optineurin mutations link the same kinase to neurodegeneration.

The melanocyte master regulator MITF-M does not simply promote growth; its target gene output shifts with its own activity level, and the cell cycle genes it controls explain why. At intermediate activity MITF drives proliferation by inducing mitotic and G1/S machinery including CDK2, cyclin D1, cyclin B1, CDC25B and PLK1, plus the receptor tyrosine kinase MET; when activity falls, cells dedifferentiate, slow their cycle and become invasive, and when it rises too far the CDK inhibitors p21 and p16 impose arrest. This rheostat behaviour is central to melanocyte biology and to melanoma, where phenotype switching between proliferative and invasive states tracks MITF levels independently of pigmentation output. Wnt-responsive TCF/LEF factors with beta-catenin feed into the same promoters, while TBX2 and the SIN3A-HDAC1 corepressor set the repressive side of the balance.

Regulation of MITF-M-dependent genes involved in DNA replication, damage repair and senescence describes how the melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, beyond pigmentation, sustains the machinery that copies and protects the genome. This link explains why melanocytes and melanoma cells tolerate proliferation without accumulating lethal damage, and why lowering MITF levels drives replication stress, DNA damage and entry into senescence rather than simple growth arrest. MITF-M binds promoters of replication and repair genes including the MCM helicase subunits MCM2 and MCM5, the ligase LIG1, the homologous recombination factor BRCA1, and the telomerase catalytic subunit TERT, coupling lineage identity to S-phase competence and chromosome stability. The outcome of MITF loss depends on context: depletion accompanied by ATF4-driven translational reprogramming yields reversible arrest instead of senescence, a switch relevant to melanoma phenotype-switching and drug tolerance.

MITF-M is the melanocyte-specific master transcription factor, and beyond pigmentation it directs a set of target genes that keep proliferating melanocytes and melanoma cells genomically stable. Through this arm of its programme it drives replication and repair machinery, including the MCM2 and MCM5 subunits of the replicative helicase, the DNA ligase LIG1 that seals nicks during replication and repair, the homologous recombination and damage-response factor BRCA1, and the telomerase catalytic subunit TERT for chromosome end maintenance. Losing MITF by RNA interference allows DNA damage to accumulate and pushes cells into senescence, whereas MITF suppression driven by ATF4 and translational reprogramming produces a reversible cell cycle arrest without senescence. The pathway therefore links lineage identity to replication licensing, genome integrity and proliferative lifespan, and is central to how melanoma cells switch between proliferative and invasive, dedifferentiated states.

Growth hormone from the pituitary sets lean body mass, driving longitudinal bone growth, muscle and cartilage anabolism and lipolysis while exerting insulin-like effects on amino acid and glucose transport, protein synthesis and lipogenesis. Loss of growth hormone receptor function causes severe postnatal growth failure with high circulating hormone, and excess signalling underlies acromegaly; the axis also influences metabolic, cardiac, immune and brain function and lifespan. Hormone binding to the preformed dimeric receptor activates the associated kinase JAK2, which phosphorylates receptor tyrosines to recruit STAT5A/STAT5B along with STAT1 and STAT3 for transcription of growth-promoting genes, while Lyn and the insulin receptor substrates IRS1/IRS2 feed into ERK and metabolic signalling. Negative control is built in: CISH and SOCS proteins bind phosphorylated sites, PTPN1 and PTPN6 dephosphorylate the receptor and kinase, and ADAM17 sheds receptor ectodomain to limit surface availability. Prolactin and its receptor share this signalling architecture.

Primordial germ cells are the founders of the entire gamete lineage, set aside from somatic tissue in the early embryo and later giving rise to oocytes and sperm; failure of their specification or migration leaves the gonad without germ cells, causing infertility, while their aberrant persistence underlies germ cell tumours. In human and primate embryos, BMP4 from extraembryonic tissue acts on transiently competent epiblast-like cells, and EOMES-driven induction of SOX17 together with TFAP2C and PRDM1 locks in germ cell identity while shutting down mesendodermal and other somatic programmes. SOX17 activates, PRDM1 represses, and the pair maintain expression of POU5F1 and NANOG without SOX2. PRDM1, with its cofactor CBFA2T2, silences DNA methylation machinery so that, with TET2, the genome undergoes extensive demethylation and epigenetic resetting. CXCR4 and PDPN support the migration of these cells to the genital ridge, and NANOS3 sustains their survival.

When TLR3 detects double-stranded RNA in endosomes, it signals through the adaptor TRIF to the kinases TBK1 and IKKε, which phosphorylate the transcription factors IRF3 and IRF7 and drive type I interferon production — the antiviral output that limits early viral replication and shapes downstream immunity. This branch concerns how that kinase step is restrained and tuned rather than simply switched on. K63-linked polyubiquitination of TBK1 and IKKε, supported by the ubiquitin precursors and the E3 ligase TRAF3, promotes assembly of active signalling complexes, while the adaptor TANK and the ubiquitin-binding autophagy receptor optineurin associate with TBK1 to modulate its activity and interferon induction. Because interferon responses are damaging when sustained, this layer of control sets the amplitude and duration of the response; its imbalance contributes to interferonopathies and to impaired antiviral defence, and optineurin mutations also link this kinase to neurodegeneration.

Respiratory syncytial virus, a leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants, carries a negative-sense RNA genome that must first be copied into messenger RNAs before any viral protein can be made. Its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, built from the large subunit L with the phosphoprotein cofactor P acting on the nucleoprotein-encased genome, starts at the 3' end and produces ten capped and polyadenylated mRNAs in a gradient of decreasing abundance, with M2-1 conferring processivity and M2-2 governing the switch from transcription to genome replication. The products include the envelope attachment and fusion glycoproteins and the nonstructural proteins that blunt interferon signalling and apoptosis in the infected airway epithelium. The host chaperone HSPA8 is recruited to support this process, illustrating the virus's dependence on cellular protein-folding machinery; blocking transcription halts the entire replication cycle.

Respiratory syncytial virus is the leading cause of infant bronchiolitis and pneumonia, and its entire protein repertoire is produced by host ribosomes reading the ten subgenomic mRNAs made by the viral polymerase. Translation of these messages yields eleven proteins, because the M2 mRNA carries two overlapping reading frames and alternative start codon use on the G and SH mRNAs generates a secreted attachment protein and a truncated SH. The products cover every stage of the replication cycle: nucleoprotein rings that encapsidate genomic RNA, the large polymerase subunit with its phosphoprotein cofactor, M2-1 as a transcription processivity factor and M2-2 as the switch between transcription and genome replication, and the envelope-embedded attachment and fusion glycoproteins that mediate entry. The nonstructural NS1 and NS2 proteins act together to blunt interferon responses and apoptosis, making this step of viral gene expression the origin of both particle assembly and immune evasion.

After human respiratory syncytial virus proteins are translated, they must be cleaved, glycosylated, phosphorylated and trafficked before infectious virions can be built, and the maturation of hRSV A proteins is carried out almost entirely by borrowed host machinery. Signal peptidase subunits process the fusion and attachment glycoproteins as they enter the secretory pathway, and the proprotein convertase furin cleaves the F precursor to generate the fusion-competent form that drives entry and syncytium formation, making it the target of neutralising antibodies and antiviral design. Casein kinase 2 subunits phosphorylate viral phosphoprotein, nucleoprotein, matrix and M2-1, while protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits reverse these marks, the cycling being required for oligomerisation and transcriptional function. Importin beta and exportin 1 shuttle matrix and M2-1 through the nucleus before they act as scaffolds at the plasma membrane assembly site.

The kidney and much of the male reproductive tract descend from a single epithelial tube, and this pathway covers how that nephric duct is carved out of intermediate mesoderm. Cells of the nephrogenic cord epithelialise in response to signals from adjacent somites and surface ectoderm, forming the duct of the pronephros and then the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, from whose caudal end the ureteric bud emerges to branch into the adult metanephric kidney. Positional cues from retinoic acid acting via HOXB4 set where this occurs, while PAX2 and PAX8 with LHX1 mark early renal progenitors; LHX1 and GATA3 sustain each other in a self-reinforcing loop that drives duct differentiation and switches on targets such as EMX2, ID4, nephronectin and the receptor tyrosine kinase RET. RET responds to GDNF from metanephric mesenchyme, and nephronectin engages integrin alpha8beta1, coupling duct to mesenchyme. Failure here produces renal agenesis and other congenital urinary tract anomalies.

The kidney arises from intermediate mesoderm, and this developmental programme covers the whole sequence from specification of renal progenitors through nephric duct formation, ureteric bud outgrowth and branching, to the induction of nephrons that will filter blood. Its failure underlies congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract, the leading cause of chronic kidney disease in children, and its steps are the template for growing kidney organoids in vitro. A self-reinforcing transcription factor module including PAX2, PAX8, LHX1, GATA3 and EMX2 marks the earliest renal lineage, with HOX genes and paraxial FOXC1/FOXC2 setting its rostral-caudal position and boundaries. Reciprocal signalling then drives morphogenesis: mesenchymal GDNF acting through RET and GFRA1, nephronectin binding integrin alpha8/beta1, and canonical Wnt signalling in which WNT9B induces WNT4 to epithelialize pre-tubular aggregates while SIX2 and SALL1 hold a progenitor pool in the cap mesenchyme.

The permanent kidney begins when a single outgrowth, the ureteric bud, sprouts from the nephric (Wolffian) duct into the adjacent metanephric mesenchyme; that bud goes on to form the ureter, branches to build the collecting duct tree, and induces nephrons at its tips. Getting the number and position of buds right determines final nephron endowment, and errors produce renal agenesis, duplex or multicystic dysplastic kidneys and other congenital urinary tract anomalies. Budding depends on reciprocal signalling: nephronectin secreted by the duct engages integrin alpha8/beta1 on the mesenchyme to switch on GDNF, which acts through the RET receptor tyrosine kinase and its co-receptor GFRA1 on duct cells and induces WNT11. Transcription factors including PAX2, EYA1, SIX1/SIX2, SALL1 and posterior HOX11 paralogues specify the competent mesenchyme, while SLIT2-ROBO2, BMP4 with its antagonist gremlin, and FOXC1/FOXC2 restrict budding to one site.

Cytotoxic T cells can only see what is inside a cell if that cell's own proteins are destroyed and sampled, and this route supplies the peptides. Foreign, mutated, misfolded and short-lived host proteins are tagged with lysine-48-linked polyubiquitin chains and fed to the 26S proteasome, whose products are trimmed and loaded onto MHC class I for surface display; the yield is poor, with thousands of degraded molecules per stable complex. Tagging requires a ubiquitin-activating enzyme, one of many conjugating enzymes, and a ligase drawn from RING, HECT and cullin-RING families including SCF and anaphase-promoting complexes, which set substrate specificity. The proteasome itself combines a proteolytic core of alpha and beta subunits with an ATPase-containing regulatory particle, and cytosolic peptidases further process released fragments. The same machinery underlies general protein quality control, cell cycle progression and immune surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells.
