Every nucleated cell continuously advertises samples of its internal protein content on MHC class I molecules, and CD8+ T cells read that display to detect viral infection, intracellular bacteria or tumour-derived proteins and kill the cell that shows them. Loss of the pathway allows infected and transformed cells to escape cytotoxic surveillance, which is why many viruses and tumours target its steps. Antigenic peptides arise from ubiquitin-dependent degradation by the 26S proteasome, reflected here in the ubiquitin-activating and conjugating enzymes and the large families of cullin-RING, F-box, HECT and TRIM ligases that mark substrates. Peptides are pumped into the endoplasmic reticulum by the TAP1/TAP2 transporter, trimmed by aminopeptidases such as ERAP1 and ERAP2, and loaded onto the HLA heavy chain-beta2-microglobulin dimer with help from tapasin, calreticulin and PDIA3 before secretory transport to the surface. Cross-presentation and phagocytic uptake routes are also represented.

Every nucleated cell displays fragments of its internal proteins on MHC class I molecules so that cytotoxic T cells can detect infection or malignancy, and this pathway covers how those molecules are built and charged with peptide before they reach the surface. A newly made heavy chain is folded with help from calnexin, BiP and the thiol oxidoreductase ERp57, pairs with beta-2-microglobulin, and then joins the peptide loading complex built around tapasin and calreticulin. TAP1/TAP2 pump proteasome-derived peptides into the ER, where ERAP1 and ERAP2 trim them to the right length for binding. Only stably loaded trimers are released, packaged into COPII vesicles by SAR1B, SEC23/24 and SEC13/31 for transport through the Golgi. Loss of TAP or tapasin leaves surface MHC class I scarce and immune surveillance blunted, a route tumours and viruses exploit to escape.

Kinesins are ATP-driven motors that walk along microtubules, and they are how a cell moves cargo and reshapes its own cytoskeleton. Most step toward microtubule plus ends, carrying vesicles, mitochondria, mRNA granules and signalling receptors outward along axons and dendrites, while other families depolymerise microtubule ends or crosslink and slide antiparallel filaments. This underlies mitotic spindle assembly and elongation, chromosome congression at kinetochores, central spindle formation and the final cleavage of the cytokinetic furrow, along with intraflagellar transport in cilia. The set pairs the motor domains with their light chains and adaptors and with the alpha- and beta-tubulins that form the track itself. Loss of function causes hereditary spastic paraplegia and axonal neuropathy, microcephaly, congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles and oocyte maturation failure; spindle kinesins are anti-mitotic drug targets.

Nephron development builds the kidney's filtering unit -- glomerulus, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule and connecting segment -- from mesenchymal progenitors, and sets the number of nephrons a person is born with, a count that is never increased and whose deficit predisposes to hypertension and chronic kidney disease. WNT9B from the ureteric bud tip induces progenitors to aggregate and switch on WNT4, driving a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into renal vesicles, while SIX2-positive neighbours instead self-renew to keep the progenitor pool alive. The vesicle is polarised from the outset: WT1 marks the proximal pole and represses PAX2 to permit podocyte formation, whereas LHX1, POU3F3 and HNF1B pattern distal segments and switch on Notch ligands DLL1, JAG1 and LFNG, with HNF1B also activating IRX1/IRX2 in the intermediate limb. Mutations in HNF1B or PAX2 cause human renal hypodysplasia.

The nephron is the filtering and reabsorbing unit of the kidney, running from glomerulus through proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal segments to the collecting duct, and its formation during fetal life sets the number of nephrons a person will ever have. Nephron development begins where ureteric bud tips meet metanephric mesenchyme: WNT9B from the bud induces progenitors to aggregate and express WNT4, driving a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition into renal vesicles, while a self-renewing progenitor pool is maintained in parallel. The vesicle is polarized from the outset, with WT1 acting proximally to repress PAX2 and permit podocyte formation, and LHX1 and POU3F3 specifying distal segments and loop elongation. HNF1B then activates Notch components DLL1, JAG1 and LFNG plus IRX1/IRX2 as the comma- and S-shaped bodies form, and HNF4A supports proximal tubule identity. Defective versions of this programme underlie congenital kidney malformation and reduced nephron endowment.

Platelets arise as cytoplasmic fragments shed by megakaryocytes, and this programme covers the factors that drive megakaryocyte development and platelet production, from cytokine-driven expansion of progenitors through endomitotic polyploidisation to proplatelet extension. Its failure produces thrombocytopenia and defective haemostasis, while its dysregulation underlies myeloproliferative disease. Thrombopoietin receptor signalling runs through JAK2 with SH2B adaptors, of which SH2B3 acts as a brake on proliferation. Lineage identity is set by GATA1 and GATA2 with their ZFPM (FOG) cofactors, RUNX-associated and ETS partners, and NFE2 with small MAF proteins controlling terminal maturation and platelet release; MYB restrains thrombopoiesis, and KDM1A-containing CoREST/Sin3-HDAC complexes shape the chromatin context. Proplatelet formation and organelle trafficking depend on tubulins, notably megakaryocyte-restricted TUBB1, on kinesin motors, actin capping proteins, and Rho-family GTPases with their DOCK activators.

Formation of the posterior neural plate is the step in early embryogenesis that lays down the neuroepithelium destined to become hindbrain and anterior spinal cord, as distinct from the anterior neural plate that yields forebrain and midbrain. It matters because this sheet must be specified and then folded into a closed tube; incomplete closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida, the commonest congenital malformation of the central nervous system. Posterior neural fate arises largely from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors near the primitive streak, in which WNT3A and FGF8 signalling drives SOX2 expression through a posterior-specific enhancer, while TBX6 diverts sister cells to paraxial mesoderm. Regional identity is then fixed by mutual repression between GBX2 posteriorly and OTX2 anteriorly, which sharpens the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, with SOX1, ZEB2, POU3F1 and ZNF521 accompanying commitment to neural progenitor character.

Early in development the dorsal epiblast thickens into the neural plate, the sheet that folds into the neural tube and becomes the entire central nervous system; incomplete closure produces neural tube defects such as spina bifida. Formation of the posterior neural plate specifies the caudal half of that sheet, which gives rise to the hindbrain and anterior spinal cord, and it is built differently from the anterior half: rather than arising directly from epiblast, its caudal portion derives from bipotent neuromesodermal progenitors in which WNT and FGF signalling, via WNT3A and FGF8, drive SOX2 through a dedicated posterior enhancer while TBX6 pulls sister cells toward paraxial mesoderm. Regional identity is then fixed by mutual transcriptional repression between GBX2 posteriorly and OTX2 anteriorly, setting the midbrain-hindbrain boundary, with SOX1, ZEB2 and POU3F1 accompanying commitment to neural fate.

Respiratory syncytial virus infection proceeds with little or no type I interferon, because the virus actively dismantles the sensing pathway that should detect it. The host arm represented here is the cytosolic RNA-sensing route: RIG-I and MDA5 detect viral RNA, signal through the mitochondrial adaptor MAVS, and activate IRF3 with the CREBBP/EP300 coactivators to transcribe IFN-beta and the IFN-alpha genes, which then act back through IFNAR1/IFNAR2, JAK1, TYK2 and STAT2 to arm neighbouring cells. RSV nonstructural proteins NS1 and NS2 reach mitochondria and nucleus to engage these components, aided by TRIM25-dependent ubiquitin steps and a cullin-5/RBX1/elongin ubiquitin ligase that directs host factors for degradation, while the nucleoprotein sequesters MDA5 and blocks PKR-driven translational shutdown. The result is blunted innate alarm, permissive replication, and the severe bronchiolitis seen in infants.

Respiratory syncytial virus enters through airway epithelium, and the outcome of infection is decided by how the host senses the virus and how the virus blunts that sensing. This is the front line of bronchiolitis in infants, and excessive or misdirected responses here underlie the wheezing and asthma risk that can follow. Attachment uses cell-surface heparan sulfate proteoglycans — syndecans, glypicans, perlecan — and lectins, while the viral G protein subverts the fractalkine receptor CX3CR1 to misdirect immune cell trafficking. Cytosolic RIG-I and MDA5 signalling through MAVS, together with Toll-like receptors and their accessory proteins CD14 and LY96, converges on IRF3 and type I interferon production; secreted IFN-alpha/beta then act via IFNAR1/2, JAK1, TYK2 and STAT2 to induce PKR, OAS2 and ISG15 conjugation. Viral nonstructural proteins counter these steps, exploiting cullin-RING ubiquitin ligases, and the Mediator complex links infection to reprogrammed host transcription.

PKR-mediated signaling is the cell's innate response to double-stranded RNA, the hallmark of viral replication, and its main output is a rapid shutdown of protein synthesis. The interferon-inducible kinase EIF2AK2 (PKR) shifts from monomer to dimer on binding dsRNA or activating partners such as PRKRA/PACT and the ISG15 conjugation machinery, autophosphorylates, and then phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eIF2, blocking the GDP-to-GTP exchange needed for cap-dependent initiation. This places PKR alongside the other arms of the integrated stress response, and inhibitors including the co-chaperone DNAJC3/P58IPK, protein phosphatase 2A subunits, the RNA-editing enzyme ADAR and a non-coding vault RNA restrain it. Beyond translational control, PKR substrates and partners extend to the IkappaB kinase complex and NF-kappaB activation, MAP2K6 and p38 signalling, CDK1-dependent G2 arrest, DHX9-associated RNA metabolism, tau phosphorylation, apoptosis and p53, linking antiviral defence to inflammation and neurodegeneration.

Cadherins hold cells together by binding partners on the neighbouring cell surface, and the specificity of those bonds determines which cells sort together into a tissue. CDH11, an osteoblast cadherin also expressed in mesenchymal cells and synovial fibroblasts, forms trans dimers with itself and with a narrow group of relatives, CDH8 and probably CDH24, so that cells bearing these molecules adhere selectively to one another. Binding through the extracellular domains is coupled inside the cell to the catenins: beta-catenin or the related plakoglobin binds the cadherin tail, alpha-catenin links the complex toward the actin cytoskeleton, and p120 catenin regulates cadherin stability at the surface. Adhesion of this kind supports skeletal and connective tissue architecture, and CDH11 activity contributes to synovial invasion in inflammatory arthritis and to mesenchymal behaviour in tumours.

Human respiratory syncytial virus copies its negative-sense RNA genome through a full-length positive-sense antigenomic intermediate, the step that amplifies viral genomes for packaging into new particles in infected airway epithelium and underlies bronchiolitis in infants and severe lower respiratory disease in the elderly. Synthesis is carried out by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, whose catalytic L subunit works with the phosphoprotein P, with M2-1 acting as a processivity factor; nascent genomic and antigenomic RNAs must be encapsidated by nucleoprotein N, which shields them from degradation given their lack of a 5' cap and poly(A) tail. Replication follows primary transcription, and accumulating M2-2 shifts the polymerase from transcription toward genome synthesis. The host contribution here is chaperone-based: cytosolic HSP90 isoforms stabilise and support folding of the large L polymerase subunit, making viral genome amplification dependent on host proteostasis and a target for chaperone inhibitors.

Between the future brain and the future skin, a strip of ectoderm is set aside that will become the neural crest and the cranial placodes; specifying this neural plate border is what allows vertebrates to build a peripheral nervous system, craniofacial skeleton, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, lens, inner ear and olfactory epithelium. The territory is defined positionally by intermediate levels of BMP and FGF with a graded WNT input, so that BMP4, FGF4 and WNT3A acting through beta-catenin and TCF7L1 place cells between neural and epidermal fates rather than in either. Within that domain a combination of transcription factors, including GBX2, TFAP2A and its paralogues, PAX3, PAX7, MSX1, DLX5 and ZIC1, cross-regulate into a self-reinforcing border identity while pluripotency factors are resolved. No single gene marks the border; failure here underlies neurocristopathies and craniofacial malformation.

Mitochondria transcribe both strands of their circular genome, so every mRNA has a complementary antisense partner and the organelle must actively dispose of surplus and double-stranded RNA as well as set the lifetime of each transcript. Controlled turnover of mitochondrial RNA keeps the thirteen respiratory chain mRNAs and the two rRNAs at appropriate levels and prevents accumulation of duplex RNA that would otherwise leak to the cytosol and trigger interferon responses. Degradation is carried out by a degradosome in which the SUPV3L1 helicase unwinds structured or duplex RNA and feeds single strands to the PNPT1 3'-to-5' exonuclease; the short products are finished off to mononucleotides by REXO2. GRSF1 resolves G-quadruplexes, while the SLIRP:LRPPRC complex and the FASTK family of RNA-binding proteins protect or select particular transcripts. Imbalance here compromises oxidative phosphorylation and underlies inherited mitochondrial disease.

When antigen binds surface IgM or IgD on a mature B cell, the receptor complex converts that recognition event into intracellular second messengers that decide whether the cell proliferates, differentiates or dies — the initiating step of antibody responses and the checkpoint that enforces tolerance to self. Immunoglobulin heavy and light chain variable regions provide the binding specificity, while the associated CD79A/CD79B chains carry the tyrosine motifs phosphorylated by Src-family kinases such as LYN, FYN and BLK. This recruits and activates SYK, which builds signalosomes on the adaptors BLNK, PIK3AP1 and CD19; BTK and PI3K-generated PIP3 then activate PLCG2, splitting PIP2 into diacylglycerol and IP3. IP3 opens ER receptors ITPR1-3, and store depletion drives STIM1 to gate ORAI and TRPC1 channels for sustained calcium entry. CD22 and PTPN6 dampen the output; loss of BTK or SYK signalling causes agammaglobulinaemia, and chronic activation of this route sustains B cell lymphomas.

Antigen recognition by a mature B cell converts binding of its surface immunoglobulin into proliferation, survival and differentiation, and this receptor signalling is what allows humoral immunity to be antigen-specific while also enforcing tolerance against self-reactive clones. Membrane IgM and IgD paired with the CD79A/CD79B heterodimer present ITAM motifs that Src-family kinases LYN, FYN and BLK phosphorylate, recruiting and activating SYK; scaffolds including BLNK, CD19 and PIK3AP1 then assemble a signalosome containing BTK, PI3K, VAV1 and PLCG2. Phospholipase C gamma 2 generates inositol trisphosphate and diacylglycerol, emptying ER calcium stores through IP3 receptors and triggering STIM1-gated ORAI entry, while calcineurin activates NFAT, RasGRP proteins engage RAS, and PKC-beta drives the CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 complex to IKK-dependent NF-kappaB activation with proteasomal destruction of IkB. Tonic signalling sustains B cell survival; dysregulation underlies lymphomas and autoimmunity, and SYK and BTK are drug targets.

Mitochondrial DNA is transcribed as long polycistronic precursors, and the thirteen respiratory chain mRNAs plus the two rRNAs must be cut out, matured and held at the right abundance before they can be translated. The FASTK family of RNA-binding proteins carries out much of that post-transcriptional control, determining how much of each transcript survives. All family members share FAST_1, FAST_2 and RAP domains and act inside the organelle, but their effects differ by target: FASTK protects the MT-ND6 mRNA, which lacks flanking tRNAs and so escapes canonical excision, from the mitochondrial degradosome; FASTKD2 associates with 16S rRNA; TBRG4 stabilises and helps process several heavy-strand mRNAs including MT-CO1 and MT-ND5; FASTKD5 binds 12S rRNA and lowers levels of a defined subset. Because their targets encode subunits of complexes I, III, IV and the ATP synthase, imbalance here translates directly into oxidative phosphorylation deficiency and mitochondrial disease.

Ion channel transport covers the proteins that move ions across membranes, either passively through gated pores or actively using ATP, and it sets the electrical and chemical gradients on which excitability, secretion and volume regulation depend. Without it nerves cannot fire, muscle cannot contract or relax, epithelia cannot absorb salt and water, and organelles cannot be acidified. The set spans sodium-potassium and calcium pumps that build gradients, V-type ATPases that acidify lysosomes and the osteoclast ruffled border, P4-type flippases, chloride channels and anoctamins, acid-sensing and TRP cation channels responding to temperature, touch and irritants, epithelial sodium channels, and ryanodine receptors releasing calcium from sarcoplasmic reticulum stores. Regulatory layers are included: calmodulin and CaMKII, phospholamban and sarcolipin restraining SERCA, and WNK kinases with SGK1 and NEDD4L controlling channel abundance. Mutations here cause cystic-fibrosis-like secretory defects, myotonia, osteopetrosis, Wilson and Menkes disease, and channelopathies of heart and nerve.

Mitochondria keep their own proteome in order using a set of ATP-dependent proteases inherited from their bacterial ancestry, and this degradation system both clears damaged protein and sets the level of key regulators. Without it, unfolded, unassembled and oxidatively damaged subunits accumulate, respiratory complexes and the mitoribosome fail to assemble correctly, and neurons are the first cells to suffer — loss of SPG7 causes spastic paraplegia, AFG3L2 mutations cause ataxia, and HTRA2 is linked to parkinsonism. LONP1 and the CLPX–CLPP complex unfold and digest matrix substrates such as TFAM, aconitase and dehydrogenases of the citrate cycle; the membrane-anchored AFG3L2 and YME1L1 hexamers face the matrix and intermembrane space respectively. Proteolytic processing also sets mitochondrial shape, since OMA1 and YME1L1 cleave OPA1 to shift the balance between fusion and fission, and controls lipid transfer by PRELID1 and STARD7.

Signaling by TGFBR3 describes how betaglycan, a transmembrane proteoglycan co-receptor without kinase activity of its own, shapes the cell's response to TGF-beta family ligands. It matters because betaglycan sets ligand sensitivity: it captures TGF-beta isoforms and presents them to TGFBR2 so that a signalling complex with TGFBR1 can form and activate SMAD3/SMAD4, while sequestering inhibin and modulating activin and BMP responses. It is abundant in normal tissue and lost in many carcinomas, where its downregulation removes a brake on invasion and marks it as a tumour suppressor; it also contributes to FGF2/FGFR co-receptor function. The pathway includes its own regulation, by myogenic and other transcription factors, by microRNA silencing through Argonaute-containing complexes, and by ectodomain shedding via matrix metalloproteinases and gamma-secretase, which converts membrane betaglycan into a soluble ligand trap.

Betaglycan, the type III TGF-beta receptor encoded by TGFBR3, is a transmembrane proteoglycan with no kinase activity that works as a co-receptor, capturing TGF-beta family ligands and presenting them to the signalling type II and type I receptors so that a SMAD2/3-SMAD4 transcriptional response can be mounted. It also binds activin and inhibin subunits and BMPs, and stabilises FGF2:FGFR complexes, so it can either promote or dampen a given ligand's output. Its abundance is set transcriptionally, by factors including SP1, myogenic regulators of the MyoD/myogenin family and E-protein partners, retinoid receptors with EP300, and post-transcriptionally by Argonaute-TNRC6 microRNA silencing; the ectodomain is shed by membrane metalloproteinases restrained by TIMPs, and gamma-secretase components process the remaining stub. Loss of TGFBR3 is common in carcinomas, where it behaves as a tumour suppressor, and it has been linked to inflammatory disease and Alzheimer's.

TGFBR3, also called betaglycan, is a co-receptor that binds TGF-beta ligands (notably TGF-beta2) and inhibin and presents or sequesters them, so the chemistry that modifies it sets how strongly a cell responds to TGF-beta family signals. Its post-translational regulation begins with glycosaminoglycan-decorated maturation and delivery to the plasma membrane, after which membrane-tethered matrix metalloproteinases such as MMP14 and MMP16 shed the ectodomain to release a soluble form that acts as a ligand trap; TIMP1 and TIMP2 restrain that cleavage. The retained membrane stub is then cut within the lipid bilayer by gamma-secretase, whose catalytic presenilins act with nicastrin, APH1 and PSENEN. Loss of betaglycan and shifts in the balance of shed versus intact receptor alter growth control, angiogenesis and epithelial differentiation, and reduced expression accompanies progression in breast, prostate and ovarian cancers.

Betaglycan (TGFBR3) is a co-receptor that tunes how much TGF-beta signal reaches the cell, and its dosage determines whether TGF-beta acts as a growth suppressor or is lost in tumour progression; reduced betaglycan expression accompanies epithelial cancers and increased invasiveness. Lacking kinase activity itself, TGFBR3 binds TGF-beta1 and TGF-beta2 and presents ligand to the signalling receptor pair, improving capture of the low-affinity TGF-beta2 isoform so that TGFBR2 can recruit and phosphorylate TGFBR1. Regulation runs in both directions: ligand-bound betaglycan is phosphorylated by the type II receptor, which recruits beta-arrestin and drives co-internalisation of the receptor complex, downregulating surface receptor levels, while the scaffold GIPC1 binds the betaglycan tail and stabilises it at the membrane to sustain signalling. Shed soluble ectodomain sequesters ligand extracellularly. The pathway therefore sets the gain of TGF-beta control over proliferation, differentiation and matrix production.

TGFBR3 expression governs how much betaglycan, the type III TGF-beta receptor, a cell displays, and thereby sets the sensitivity of that cell to TGF-beta, activin and BMP ligands. Betaglycan presents ligand to the signalling receptors and can also be shed to act as a soluble trap, so its abundance tunes growth inhibition, epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cell migration; loss of expression is a recurrent feature of carcinoma progression. Control operates at two levels. Transcription is driven by Sp1 together with retinoic acid receptor heterodimers, SMAD3/SMAD4, and the myogenic program of MYOD1, MYF5, MYOG and E-protein partners, with EP300 as coactivator and HELLS, KLF16 and MYCN acting as repressive inputs. Post-transcriptionally, miR-23b, miR-27b and let-7 loaded into Argonaute-TNRC6 silencing complexes limit translation of the transcript, linking receptor levels to microRNA-mediated repression.

TGFBR3, or betaglycan, is the most abundant TGF-beta receptor on many cell surfaces; it presents ligand to the signalling type I/II receptor pair and, when shed, acts as a soluble ligand trap, so how much of it a cell makes sets the gain of TGF-beta family signalling. Control of TGFBR3 expression operates at two levels. Transcriptionally, Sp1 together with retinoic acid receptors RARA/RXRA, the myogenic bHLH factors MYOD1, MYF5, MYF6 and MYOG with their E-protein partners TCF3, TCF4 and TCF12, and SMAD3/SMAD4 acting with the EP300 coactivator converge on the promoter, while chromatin regulators such as the HELLS remodeller and the KLF16 zinc finger, and the oncoprotein MYCN, modulate output. Post-transcriptionally, miRNAs including miR-23b, miR-27b and let-7 direct Argonaute-TNRC6 silencing complexes to the transcript. Loss of betaglycan is a recurrent feature of carcinoma progression.

Betaglycan, the type III TGF-beta receptor encoded by TGFBR3, is best known as a co-receptor for TGF-beta superfamily ligands, but it also binds fibroblast growth factor 2 and shapes how cells respond to it. This cross-talk matters because FGF2 acting through FGFR1 drives proliferation, angiogenesis and differentiation decisions, and TGFBR3 levels are frequently lost in carcinomas, where the switch between growth-suppressive TGF-beta input and growth-promoting FGF input is altered. Here TGFBR3 acts positively rather than as a ligand sink: its short cytoplasmic tail engages the scaffolding adaptor GIPC1, and the resulting FGF2-TGFBR3-GIPC1 assembly enhances FGF2 signalling and downstream MAPK output, with GIPC1 influencing receptor trafficking and surface retention. The arrangement illustrates how a non-signalling co-receptor can redirect an unrelated growth factor pathway, linking TGF-beta and FGF systems in differentiation and tumour biology.

Activin signalling drives follicle-stimulating hormone production, gonadal function and a range of growth and differentiation responses, and it is held in check partly at the level of ligand presentation. Betaglycan, the type III TGF-beta receptor encoded by TGFBR3, acts as the accessory receptor that makes inhibin an effective antagonist: it binds the inhibin alpha subunit and captures the type II activin receptor ACVR2A, sequestering it so that activin dimers built from the beta-A subunit cannot assemble a productive signalling complex. The same mechanism restrains bone morphogenetic protein responses through the type II BMP receptor. Because betaglycan availability sets how strongly inhibin can oppose activin, this arm of regulation shapes pituitary-gonadal feedback and ovarian and testicular cell behaviour, and its loss removes a brake on activin-driven proliferation implicated in gonadal tumour formation.

Dengue virus, a mosquito-borne flavivirus with four serotypes, causes the most common arthropod-transmitted viral disease worldwide, ranging from silent infection through dengue fever to hemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome, the severe forms being favoured by antibody-dependent enhancement during secondary infection with a heterologous serotype. This describes the full replication cycle of the enveloped positive-strand RNA virus in human cells and the host machinery it commandeers. Attachment and uptake use lectins and phosphatidylserine receptors such as CD209, CLEC5A and the TAM kinases AXL and MERTK, followed by clathrin-mediated endocytosis and low-pH fusion. The polyprotein is translated at the endoplasmic reticulum and processed by signal peptidase and by furin during maturation, with heavy reliance on chaperones, the oligosaccharyltransferase complex and ER membrane remodelling for replication-organelle formation and virion assembly. Viral proteins also subvert host spliceosome, mRNA 3'-end processing and nuclear transport factors, and blunt innate sensing through cGAS-STING, RIG-I-like receptor and interferon signalling; egress proceeds via ESCRT components, while complement activation contributes to pathology.

Glycosphingolipid biosynthesis elaborates ceramide into the glycolipids that populate the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, where they organize lipid rafts, provide blood group and tumour-associated carbohydrate antigens, and serve as receptors for toxins and pathogens. The committed step is glucosylceramide synthesis by UGCG, while UGT8 makes galactosylceramide, the precursor of sulfatide via the sulfotransferase GAL3ST1 — lipids that dominate myelin, so this route underlies insulation of axons. Sequential galactosyl-, N-acetylgalactosaminyl- and N-acetylglucosaminyltransferases build the lacto-, globo- and ganglio-series cores, and sialyltransferases including ST3GAL5 and ST8SIA5 add the sialic acids that define gangliosides, with fucosyltransferases generating H and related antigens. Loss of ganglioside synthesis causes infantile epilepsy and hereditary spastic paraplegia, and shifts in these glycans accompany oncogenic transformation and modulate growth factor receptor signalling at the cell surface.

Glycosphingolipids built in the Golgi and displayed at the plasma membrane must eventually be taken apart, and this lysosomal catabolic route is where that happens. Gangliosides and related lipids reach the late endosome, bud inward on intraluminal vesicles, and are stripped sugar by sugar: sialidases remove N-acetylneuraminic acid, beta-galactosidase and the beta-hexosaminidase A/B subunits trim the remaining glycan, and glucocerebrosidase, galactosylceramidase, sphingomyelinases and acid ceramidase complete breakdown to sphingosine and fatty acid. Because the substrates sit in a membrane, the hydrolases depend on lipid-binding cofactors, notably the saposin precursor prosaposin and the GM2 activator protein, which present the lipid to the enzyme; cathepsin A stabilises a sialidase-galactosidase complex, and sulfatase maturation factors activate the arylsulfatases. Loss of any enzyme or cofactor causes lysosomal lipid storage and the sphingolipidoses, including Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Fabry, Krabbe, metachromatic leukodystrophy and Niemann-Pick disease, with prominent neurodegeneration.

Damage to mitochondria must be reported to the rest of the cell, and this stress-response route is how the organelle tells the cytosol and nucleus to slow down and rebuild. Loss of inner membrane potential, blocked proton flux or failure to import proteins activates the inner membrane protease OMA1, which cleaves DELE1 so that a C-terminal fragment escapes to the cytosol, oligomerizes, and switches on the kinase EIF2AK1 (HRI). That kinase phosphorylates the alpha subunit of eIF2, shutting down bulk translation while favouring mRNAs with upstream open reading frames that encode ATF4, ATF5 and CHOP, so chaperones and metabolic genes are induced. It is one arm of the integrated stress response, restrained by the YME1L1 protease and the prohibitin-stomatin scaffold of the inner membrane, and its adaptive output helps tumour cells survive harsh conditions.

When misfolded proteins accumulate inside mitochondria, cells mount a retrograde stress response that raises mitochondrial folding and proteolytic capacity, restoring the organelle's ability to carry out oxidative phosphorylation rather than letting damaged proteins poison it. The mitochondrial unfolded protein response is read out in the nucleus: reactive oxygen species and stalled precursor proteins in the cytosol trigger oxidation of DNAJA1, which displaces HSF1 from HSP70 chaperones so HSF1 can trimerize and drive chaperone genes; ATF5, normally imported into mitochondria, accumulates and redirects to the nucleus to reinforce that programme. In parallel, AKT1 phosphorylates estrogen receptor alpha to induce HTRA2 and NRF1, while SIRT3-dependent deacetylation of FOXO3 raises antioxidant defences such as SOD2 and catalase. The induced effectors include the matrix chaperonin HSPD1/HSPE1, mortalin, and the LONP1 protease. Chronic failure contributes to neurodegeneration and age-related mitochondrial decline.

Fat cells are made by a transcriptional programme in which the nuclear receptor pair PPARG and RXRA, once bound by lipid ligands, switches on the genes of lipid uptake, storage and droplet formation. Here that switch is coupled to chromatin: the related histone H3K4 methyltransferases KMT2C and KMT2D, with their shared complex subunits ASH2L, RBBP5, WDR5, DPY30, PAXIP1, PAGR1, NCOA6 and the H3K27 demethylase KDM6A, are recruited to PPARG:RXRA sites and deposit activating marks, while Mediator, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators are exchanged for NCOR1/NCOR2-HDAC3 corepressors. The output genes define the adipocyte — adiponectin, FABP4, CD36, perilipins, LPL, DGAT2, SCD, PNPLA2 and LIPE — and also drive thermogenic brown fat and hepatocyte triglyceride synthesis. Loss of the methyltransferase activity blocks adipogenesis and protects against diet-induced hepatic steatosis, the first step toward fatty liver disease, steatohepatitis and cirrhosis.

LTK is a receptor tyrosine kinase closely related to ALK, and this pathway covers the oncogenic signalling it drives when its kinase activity is deregulated in tumours. Under normal conditions LTK's job is poorly defined, but it is overexpressed in leukaemia, high expression in early-stage non-small cell lung cancer tracks with metastatic risk, and a CLIP1-LTK fusion has been found in a small subset of lung adenocarcinomas. Fusion of the kinase domain to a coiled-coil partner promotes constitutive dimerisation and autophosphorylation, so that signalling proceeds without ligand. The downstream output runs through the canonical growth-factor routes: ERK1/ERK2 activation driving proliferative gene expression, and class IA PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits generating PIP3 for survival signalling. Because the kinase domain closely resembles that of ALK, such tumours are candidates for ALK inhibitor therapy.

Signaling by LTK describes ligand activation of leukocyte tyrosine kinase, a receptor closely related to ALK and, like it, a receptor for the small secreted cytokines ALKAL1 and ALKAL2. The pathway supports neuronal differentiation and cell survival, promoting neurite outgrowth in responsive cells, and has been implicated in regulating secretory traffic between the ER and Golgi; oncogenic LTK fusions drive a subset of non-small cell lung cancers, making it a candidate kinase target. Ligand binding to the extracellular EGF-like and glycine-rich modules drives receptor dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation, creating docking sites for SHC1, GRB2-SOS1, IRS1 and the p85 regulatory subunits of PI3K, so that RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT arms are engaged together. The kinase TNK2 and ubiquitin-mediated receptor downregulation shape the duration of the response.

Leukocyte tyrosine kinase is a receptor tyrosine kinase of the insulin receptor superfamily and the closest relative of ALK, with which it shares the small secreted cytokines ALKAL1 and ALKAL2 as activating ligands. Signalling through LTK has been linked to neurite outgrowth and cell survival, and to control of secretory traffic between the ER and Golgi; fusion proteins involving the kinase occur in non-small cell lung cancer, placing it alongside ALK as an oncogenic driver. Ligand binding to the extracellular glycine-rich and EGF-like modules drives trans-autophosphorylation of the cytoplasmic kinase domain, creating docking sites for SHC1, GRB2 and IRS1 and thereby engaging the SOS1-Ras-MAPK route, with recruitment of class IA PI3K catalytic and regulatory subunits feeding the survival arm. TNK2 participates as an associated cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase in the downstream response.

Nearly half the human genome consists of transposable elements, and keeping endogenous retroelements such as LINE1, Alu and endogenous retrovirus LTRs transcriptionally quiet protects the genome from insertional mutation, recombination and inappropriate activation of nearby genes, while still allowing their controlled use as regulatory DNA during early embryogenesis and germ cell specification. Silencing is imposed chiefly through repressive chromatin: KRAB zinc finger proteins recognise particular element families and recruit the TRIM28 scaffold, which assembles the histone H3K9 methyltransferase SETDB1 together with its partner ATF7IP, the EHMT1/EHMT2 methyltransferases, and the NuRD deacetylase complex built around HDAC1/2, MTA and CHD4. The HUSH components TASOR, MPHOSPH8 and PPHLN1 read LINE1 RNA and seed heterochromatin, SWI/SNF remodellers and histones supply the nucleosomal context, and in germ cells PIWIL4 with SPOCD1 and DNMT3A/3L directs DNA methylation. Loss of this control causes retroelement derepression, innate immune activation and developmental failure.

Brown and beige adipocytes burn fatty acids and glucose to make heat rather than ATP, supporting non-shivering thermogenesis and influencing whole-body energy balance; the same browning of white fat contributes to wasting in cancer-associated cachexia. The gene programme behind these cells is set at the level of transcription: EBF2, PRDM16 and the coactivators PPARGC1A and PPARGC1B work with the nuclear receptors PPARG, PPARA and RXRA to switch on thermogenic targets, chief among them UCP1, which short-circuits the mitochondrial proton gradient so respiration releases heat. Other outputs of the programme include CIDEA, DIO2, ELOVL3 and COX7A1, marking lipid handling, local thyroid hormone activation and mitochondrial build-up. BMP7 with SMAD1 and SMAD4 commits precursors to the brown lineage, while nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase components including CHD4, MTA proteins, HDAC1 and HDAC2 shape chromatin permissive for these genes.

Adipogenesis is the developmental program by which precursor cells become fat cells, generating the tissue that stores and releases energy for the whole body and, in its brown and beige forms, burns substrate to make heat. Its output determines fat mass distribution, insulin sensitivity and thermogenic capacity; when it fails or is misdirected, the result is lipodystrophy, ectopic lipid deposition and metabolic disease. Commitment runs through a transcriptional cascade in which C/EBP factors induce PPARG, which with RXRA drives the mature adipocyte program — lipid handling and secretion by FABP4, CD36, LPL, PLIN1, ADIPOQ and leptin. Brown and beige identity is imposed by PRDM16, EBF2 and PGC-1 coactivators, activating UCP1, CIDEA and DIO2. Much of the gene list is coregulatory machinery: the Mediator complex, p300/CBP and NCOA coactivators, and NuRD and NCOR/HDAC corepressors that keep the program off until BMP, TGF-beta and Wnt cues permit differentiation.

Adipogenesis is the differentiation of precursor cells into fat cells, the storage depot and endocrine organ that buffers systemic energy supply; when it fails or is overwhelmed, lipid spills into liver and muscle and insulin resistance follows, while its extremes produce lipodystrophy or obesity. The programme is transcriptional at heart: CEBPB and CEBPD initiate, then PPARG with its RXRA partner and CEBPA lock in the mature state, driving the lipid-handling machinery of white adipocytes such as FABP4, CD36, LPL, PLIN1, GLUT4 and the hormones leptin and adiponectin. Coactivators and Mediator subunits, acetyltransferases CREBBP and EP300, and repressive NCOR/HDAC and NuRD complexes tune this output; WNT and TGF-beta signals restrain it. A parallel branch specified by PRDM16, EBF2 and PPARGC1A yields thermogenic brown and beige cells expressing UCP1, CIDEA and DIO2 for heat production.

Roughly half the human genome is retroelement-derived, and keeping those sequences transcriptionally silent is the job of the KRAB zinc finger protein family, the largest group of transcription regulators encoded by our genome. Each KRAB-ZFP uses its zinc finger array to recognise a particular class of transposable element, and the family has expanded in step with retroelement invasion, an evolutionary arms race in which younger elements are bound by fewer factors. Silencing is executed through the scaffold TRIM28, which binds the KRAB domain, is SUMOylated via UBE2I and SUMO2, and recruits effectors: the histone H3K9 trimethyltransferase SETDB1 with its partner ATF7IP, heterochromatin protein HP1, and the NuRD deacetylase complex built on HDAC1/2, MTA and CHD3/4 subunits. The resulting heterochromatin protects genome stability, especially in early embryos and germ cells, and its loss permits retrotransposition, aberrant transcription and innate immune activation.

Retrotransposons and integrated retroviral DNA are transcriptionally silenced by the Human Silencing Hub, a three-subunit complex of MPP8, Periphilin and TASOR that keeps young LINE-1 elements, some HIV proviruses and other intronless foreign sequences switched off. This surveillance protects genome stability and limits insertional mutagenesis, and it is also why therapeutic transgenes and viral vectors are often epigenetically shut down. Recognition works partly through nascent transcripts bound by Periphilin and partly by reading existing H3K9 trimethylation, after which the methyltransferase SETDB1 with its partner ATF7IP, together with EHMT1/EHMT2, marks surrounding nucleosomes; the chromatin remodeller MORC2 compacts the locus. Components of the nuclear RNA exosome targeting complex, including MTREX, ZCCHC8 and RBM7, link the silenced transcripts to degradation. Long exons of host genes are sensitive, while introns confer protection, making transcript architecture the discriminating signal for self versus non-self DNA.

Brown and beige adipocytes burn substrate to make heat rather than store it, and EBF2 is the transcription factor that marks preadipocytes committed to that fate and drives the thermogenic gene programme. It partners with the adipogenic nuclear receptors PPARG and RXRA and the coactivator NCOA1 to switch on PRDM16, UCP1, PPARA, PPARGC1A, CIDEA, DIO2 and ELOVL3, giving the cell uncoupled mitochondrial respiration and futile energy expenditure. Commitment is contested: ZNF423 binds EBF2 and blocks it to favour white adipocyte differentiation, while BMP7 acting through SMAD1 and SMAD4 relieves that block and pushes cells toward the brown/beige lineage. Chromatin context matters too, with NuRD-type remodelling and deacetylase components such as CHD4, MBD3, MTA proteins and HDAC1/2 shaping target accessibility. Because thermogenic capacity influences whole-body energy balance, this circuit is of interest in obesity, insulin resistance and cachexia-associated fat browning.

Transposable elements are a standing threat to germline genome integrity, and piRNA-guided silencing of endogenous retroelements is how germ cells keep them quiet across generations. Short PIWI-interacting RNAs, generated from transposon and non-coding transcripts and amplified by successive rounds of cleavage, load onto PIWI proteins and find their targets by base-pairing with nascent or mature transcripts, triggering either co-transcriptional or post-transcriptional repression. In the transcriptional arm represented here, PIWIL4 engages nascent retroelement RNA and, through SPOCD1 and C19orf84, recruits de novo DNA methylation machinery including DNMT3A and its cofactor DNMT3L, together with nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase activity and BAF-type chromatin remodellers acting on the surrounding histones. This imprinting of methylation during the perinatal window of germ cell reprogramming establishes lasting retroelement repression; its loss derails spermatogenesis, and SPOCD1 mutations cause male infertility.

Glycosphingolipids and gangliosides are made on Golgi membranes but must reach the plasma membrane, endosomes and lysosomes where they organise lipid rafts, present cell-surface recognition determinants and support neuronal membrane function. Getting them there is only partly a matter of vesicle budding, endocytosis and exocytosis: dedicated lipid transfer proteins move individual glycosphingolipid molecules through the cytosol, uncoupling lipid distribution from the vesicular traffic that carries proteins. Soluble and membrane-tethered glycolipid transfer proteins, including GLTP, the ceramide-1-phosphate carrier CPTP and the Golgi-associated FAPP2 (PLEKHA8), extract glycolipids at one bilayer and deliver them to another, while extended synaptotagmins act at endoplasmic reticulum-plasma membrane contact sites and ARF1 supports Golgi vesicle formation. CLN3 links this lipid handling to lysosomal function, and its loss causes juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, underscoring how sphingolipid distribution matters in neurons.

Sphingolipid catabolism dismantles ceramides and their phosphorylated derivatives, returning their carbon to general lipid metabolism and, just as importantly, clearing signalling lipids that would otherwise accumulate. Ceramide and sphingosine-1-phosphate act in opposition on cell survival, proliferation and lymphocyte trafficking, so the enzymes that degrade them set the balance between growth and death signals. Alkaline ceramidases hydrolyse ceramide to sphingosine and free fatty acid; phosphatases acting on sphingosine-1-phosphate and on lipid phosphates reverse the kinase step, and sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase performs the only irreversible exit from the sphingolipid pool, cleaving it to hexadecenal and phosphoethanolamine. Fatty aldehyde dehydrogenases then oxidise the resulting long-chain aldehyde; loss of that activity causes Sjögren-Larsson syndrome with ichthyosis and neurological disease, while lyase deficiency produces nephrotic syndrome and adrenal insufficiency. Skin barrier formation and immune cell egress both depend on this flux.

Enhanced cleavage of VWF variant by ADAMTS13 describes a molecular basis of type 2A von Willebrand disease, in which mutant von Willebrand factor is destroyed too readily by its own regulatory protease and platelet plug formation fails. Normally the metalloprotease ADAMTS13 trims VWF multimers by cutting the Tyr1605-Met1606 bond in the A2 domain, a site exposed only when shear forces unfold that domain, so that ultra-large multimers are kept in check and microvascular thrombosis is avoided. Missense substitutions such as Y1584C, I1568N and G1579R destabilise the A2 fold and expose the scissile bond prematurely, accelerating proteolysis and depleting the high-molecular-weight multimers that tether platelets to exposed collagen I at sites of vessel injury. The result is a mucocutaneous bleeding phenotype, illustrating how haemostasis depends on balanced VWF multimer turnover.

Von Willebrand factor circulates as long multimers that capture platelets at sites of vessel injury, and their size is trimmed by the plasma metalloprotease ADAMTS13, which cuts a single Tyr-Met bond in the A2 domain only when shear force unfolds it. Certain von Willebrand disease missense variants, including Y1584C, I1568N, G1579R and G1631D, destabilise that domain so the scissile bond is exposed too readily; the resulting enhanced cleavage of the VWF variant strips high-molecular-weight multimers from plasma and produces a bleeding phenotype of the type 2A kind. The same protein also carries collagen-binding sites that tether it to subendothelial type I collagen, the step that presents VWF to flowing blood and generates the tension needed for proteolysis. This regulated degradation sets the balance between haemostasis and thrombosis, with loss of ADAMTS13 activity causing the opposite disorder, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

Platelets stick to injured vessel wall because the GPIb-IX-V complex on their surface catches von Willebrand factor that has unfurled on exposed subendothelial collagen, the first tethering step of haemostasis under arterial shear. Gain-of-function variants in GP1BA, which encodes the ligand-binding GPIbα subunit, raise the receptor's affinity for VWF so that binding occurs spontaneously rather than only at sites of damage. The result is platelet-type von Willebrand disease: circulating VWF multimers and platelets are consumed together, leaving large platelets in reduced numbers and mucocutaneous bleeding despite an intact clotting cascade. The other complex members GP1BB, GP9 and GP5 assemble with GPIbα in the receptor, while type I collagen chains provide the immobilised surface on which VWF is presented. The disorder is clinically mimicked by VWF variants with the reciprocal defect, and distinguishing them guides treatment.

Von Willebrand factor is secreted as ultra-large multimers that are hyperactive in capturing platelets, and the plasma metalloprotease ADAMTS13 trims them to safe sizes by cutting a single bond in the shear-exposed A2 domain. When an ADAMTS13 variant cannot perform that cleavage, uncleaved multimers persist and string platelets into microvascular thrombi, producing thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with its consumptive thrombocytopenia, haemolysis and ischaemic organ damage; the same failure arises from acquired autoantibodies against the enzyme. Loss-of-function substitutions and truncations that are still secreted normally illustrate that catalytic competence, not protein availability, is what is lost. Collagen I chains appear here because VWF binds subendothelial collagen at sites of vessel injury, the step that unfolds the A2 domain and exposes the scissile bond, linking this proteolysis to haemostatic control at the platelet-vessel wall interface.

When a vessel wall is injured, circulating von Willebrand factor must anchor to newly exposed subendothelial collagen so that flowing platelets can be captured and a plug can form under high shear. This event describes the failure of that first attachment: loss-of-function mutations in the collagen-binding A3 domain of VWF leave the protein unable to engage fibrillar collagen type I, whose triple helix is built from the COL1A1 and COL1A2 chains. The result is type 2M von Willebrand disease, a qualitative defect in which VWF is present at normal or near-normal levels with an essentially intact multimer pattern, yet platelet adhesion and collagen binding are impaired. Patients bleed from mucosal surfaces and after trauma or surgery, illustrating that primary haemostasis depends not on VWF abundance but on its ability to bridge collagen and the platelet surface.

Platelet capture at a site of vascular injury depends on von Willebrand factor bridging exposed subendothelial collagen to the platelet receptor complex GPIb-IX-V, the only interaction fast enough to tether platelets out of flowing blood under high shear. Missense substitutions in the A1 domain of VWF, such as S1358N, S1387I, S1394F and Q1402P, weaken binding to the GPIbα subunit, so platelets fail to adhere and roll on damaged vessel wall and the initial haemostatic plug does not form. This defective engagement underlies a form of von Willebrand disease presenting as mucocutaneous bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia and prolonged bleeding after surgery or trauma. The partners involved define the axis: collagen I chains as the anchoring matrix, multimeric VWF as the adhesive bridge, and GP1BA with GP1BB, GP9 and GP5 as the receptor whose ligation also initiates platelet activation signalling.

Pleiotrophin and midkine are secreted heparin-binding growth factors that promote neurite outgrowth, cell growth and survival, and this pathway represents their historically proposed action as activating ligands for the receptor tyrosine kinase ALK. Binding was reported to trigger receptor autophosphorylation and recruitment of IRS, SHC, phospholipase C and PI3 kinase adaptors, feeding into the growth and anti-apoptotic signalling that makes ALK a driver oncogene in neuroblastoma and lymphoma. The claim has been difficult to reproduce, and ALKAL1/ALKAL2 are now recognised as the physiological ALK ligands, so the ligand role here is best regarded as provisional. Both cytokines do act robustly through the receptor-type phosphatase PTPRZ1, whose inhibition raises substrate tyrosine phosphorylation, which places this biology in the wider context of midkine and pleiotrophin control of neural development, tissue repair and tumour growth.

Fat cell formation requires that enhancers near lipid-handling genes be switched on at the right moment, and the MLL3 (KMT2C) and MLL4 (KMT2D) methyltransferase complexes are what license them. These complexes deposit mono- and dimethylation on histone H3 lysine 4 at enhancers bound by the adipogenic transcription factors CEBPB, CEBPA and PPARG with its partner RXRA, and their loss blocks the accompanying H3K27 acetylation, Mediator recruitment and RNA polymerase II loading, so preadipocytes fail to differentiate. Complex subunits such as ASH2L, RBBP5, WDR5, DPY30, PAXIP1, NCOA6 and PAGR1 support catalysis and target selection, while p300/CBP, the NCOA coactivators and the opposing NCOR/HDAC3/SIRT1 repressors tune output. The genes switched on define the mature adipocyte: PLIN1, FABP4, ADIPOQ, LPL, CD36 and lipolytic enzymes. This chromatin control underlies white and brown fat development and diet-induced hepatic steatosis.

The alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex carries out one of the rate-limiting steps of the citric acid cycle, converting 2-oxoglutarate, coenzyme A and NAD+ into succinyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH. Because it sits at the branch point where carbon leaving the cycle feeds glutamate and amino acid metabolism, its flux sets how much reducing power reaches the respiratory chain and how much nitrogen handling the mitochondrion can support. The complex is a large assembly: a core of DLST subunits bearing lipoamide arms, decorated with OGDH dimers that decarboxylate the substrate, DLD dimers that reoxidise dihydrolipoamide and pass electrons to NAD+, and an accessory subunit (KGD4/MRPS36) that stabilises E3 binding. It is also a notable source of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and loss of DLD or DLST activity produces encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and tumour-associated metabolite accumulation.

When platelets are strongly activated, phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine must move from the inner to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, creating the negatively charged surface on which the tenase and prothrombinase complexes assemble and thrombin is generated. Anoctamin-6 (TMEM16F) is the calcium-activated phospholipid scramblase that performs this collapse of lipid asymmetry, and loss-of-function variants such as the truncating R419* and W407Lfs*5 alleles abolish it. Platelets from these individuals activate, aggregate and secrete normally but fail to expose procoagulant lipid or shed phosphatidylserine-bearing microvesicles, so coagulation factor complexes cannot be efficiently nucleated. The result is Scott syndrome, a rare recessive bleeding disorder with normal routine clotting times yet impaired thrombin generation and serious post-traumatic or post-surgical haemorrhage. This defect illustrates how much of haemostasis depends on membrane lipid movement rather than on proteolytic cascade components alone.

The citric acid cycle enzymes do not work as made: several require cofactor insertion, assembly factors, or covalent modification before they can turn, and this maturation and regulatory layer sets how much flux the cycle can carry. Aconitase and succinate dehydrogenase both depend on iron-sulfur clusters built by the mitochondrial scaffold machinery, with a cysteine desulfurase, frataxin, and the ISCU/ISCA carriers supplying and transferring the clusters; succinate dehydrogenase additionally needs dedicated SDHAF chaperones for flavinylation and for loading its iron-sulfur subunit into the membrane complex. Citrate synthase is trimethylated on a single lysine by CSKMT, a modification opposed by oxaloacetate, and the deacetylase SIRT3 tunes several of these enzymes according to nutrient state. Loss of individual factors causes mitochondrial disease, paraganglioma, or Friedreich ataxia, placing this step upstream of oxidative energy metabolism rather than within it.

The melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation genes: it also sets how much oxidative metabolism a melanocyte or melanoma cell runs. By inducing PPARGC1A, the coactivator that coordinates mitochondrial biogenesis and respiratory gene expression, MITF pushes cells toward oxidative phosphorylation rather than glycolysis, and this axis helps explain why some melanomas survive targeted BRAF inhibition while low-MITF, low-PPARGC1A tumours are more invasive and drug-tolerant. MITF also raises expression of SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase that couples metabolic state to transcription and, through deacetylation of substrates including the p300 acetyltransferase, supports proliferation and opposes senescence. Together these targets make MITF a node linking lineage identity to cellular energetics, oxidative stress tolerance and melanoma phenotype switching.

Regulation of MITF-M dependent genes involved in invasion describes how the melanocyte master transcription factor MITF controls whether a pigment cell stays put or moves, a switch that governs melanoblast migration in development and metastatic spread in melanoma. MITF-M, the melanocyte-specific isoform, activates targets that remodel adhesion and the actin cytoskeleton: the adhesion molecule CEACAM1, the formin DIAPH1 that drives actin filament elongation and a rounded, less invasive morphology, and GMPR, which lowers GTP available to Rho-family GTPases and thereby damps membrane protrusion. MITF also feeds into epithelial-mesenchymal transition programmes through factors such as SNAI2. The result is the phenotype-switching behaviour characteristic of melanoma, in which high MITF favours proliferation and differentiation while low MITF licenses an invasive, migratory state, linking transcriptional identity directly to cell motility and metastatic potential.

The melanocyte master transcription factor MITF, in its melanocyte-specific M isoform, does more than drive pigmentation: it sets how mobile and invasive a melanocytic cell is. Through targets such as the adhesion molecule CEACAM1, the actin-nucleating formin DIAPH1 and the purine-metabolic enzyme GMPR, MITF tunes cell-cell adhesion and the state of the actin cytoskeleton, and it also feeds into epithelial-mesenchymal-transition programmes via SNAI2. This matters most in melanoma, where cells switch between an MITF-high proliferative, differentiated state and an MITF-low invasive state; the level of MITF activity therefore helps determine whether tumour cells divide locally or migrate and metastasise, and it influences response to targeted therapy. The same transcriptional control underlies normal melanoblast migration during development, linking lineage identity to motility rather than treating them as separate programmes.

Cellular responses to mechanical stimuli describes how cells sense physical force — blood flow, tissue stretch, matrix stiffness, touch, skeletal loading — and convert it into chemical signalling that changes gene expression, growth and behaviour. It underlies endothelial adaptation to laminar versus turbulent shear stress and the nitric oxide production that sets vascular tone, osteocyte responses to mechanical load and bone remodelling, and tactile sensation in Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles; its failure contributes to atherosclerosis at branch points, hypertension, disuse bone loss and touch insensitivity. Force is detected by mechanically gated channels such as PIEZO1 and TRPV4, by integrins and their adhesion plaques with talin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase, and by junctional and G protein-coupled receptors. Signals are then amplified through PI3K-AKT-mTOR, adenylate cyclase and PKA, NF-κB, purinergic ATP release via pannexin, and YAP-mediated transcription.

Cells continuously read the physical forces around them — blood flow shear, tissue stretch, matrix stiffness, touch — and convert them into chemical signals, and this conversion is what allows endothelium to align with laminar flow, osteocytes to remodel bone under load, and sensory structures to register mechanical contact. Force-gated channels such as PIEZO1 and TRPV4 admit calcium, while integrins (ITGA5, ITGAV, ITGB1) coupled through talin, vinculin and focal adhesion kinase transmit tension from fibronectin and the matrix into the cytoskeleton. Downstream, PI3K–AKT–mTOR complexes, adenylyl cyclase and PKA, NF-κB subunits, and the transcriptional coactivator YAP1 translate the stimulus into changes in gene expression, growth and survival; PECAM1, CDH5 and eNOS carry the endothelial arm toward vasodilation. Purinergic release through pannexin and P2 receptors amplifies the response, and NLRP3 links excessive force to inflammation. Disturbed mechanotransduction contributes to atherosclerosis at flow-disturbed sites, fibrosis and disuse bone loss.

Regulation of FXIIa and plasma kallikrein activity restrains the contact activation and kallikrein-kinin systems, the plasma proteolytic cascades that link surface-triggered coagulation to bradykinin release, complement activation and fibrinolysis. Restraint matters because unchecked activity produces bradykinin-driven swelling and pathological thrombosis: loss of C1 inhibitor, the serpin encoded by SERPING1, causes hereditary angioedema, and this same inhibitor accounts for the great majority of factor XIIa neutralisation in plasma. Alpha-2-macroglobulin traps plasma kallikrein by a distinct caging mechanism, and the two together dominate its inhibition; histidine-rich glycoprotein competes for the negatively charged surfaces that nucleate assembly. Factor XII, prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen form the reciprocal activation loop being controlled, assembled on endothelial and leukocyte receptors including gC1qR, cytokeratin 1 and the urokinase receptor, which localise the cascade to vessel walls and inflamed tissue.

The contact activation system generates factor XIIa and plasma kallikrein, proteases that link blood clotting to inflammation by cleaving kininogen to release bradykinin, feeding back to activate each other, and touching complement and fibrinolysis as well. Restraint of FXIIa and plasma kallikrein activity keeps this amplifying loop from running away: C1 inhibitor, encoded by SERPING1, is the dominant brake on FXIIa and a major inhibitor of kallikrein, alpha-2-macroglobulin traps kallikrein in a covalent complex, and histidine-rich glycoprotein limits assembly of the system. Loss of C1 inhibitor causes hereditary angioedema, in which unchecked kallikrein activity produces bradykinin-driven vascular leak and episodic swelling. Assembly is surface-dependent, with prekallikrein and factor XII delivered by high-molecular-weight kininogen to endothelial and cell-surface partners including the C1q-binding protein, cytokeratin 1 and the urokinase receptor.

Endothelial cells lining arteries read the mechanical force of blood flow, and steady laminar shear stress triggers a protective response: release of vasodilatory nitric oxide and elongation of the cells along the flow axis. This is the atheroprotective arm of flow sensing, and its loss at branch points and curvatures, where flow is disturbed, permits inflammation and plaque formation. Force is detected by the mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 at the apical surface and by a junctional complex of PECAM1, VE-cadherin and VEGFR2. Calcium entry through PIEZO1 and TRPV4 activates calpain, which cleaves talin and vinculin to remodel the cytoskeleton, and opens pannexin channels releasing ATP onto the P2Y2 receptor. Convergent PI3K-AKT, PDPK1-PKN2 and adrenomedullin-driven cAMP/PKA signalling phosphorylate eNOS, raising nitric oxide output that relaxes underlying smooth muscle through cGMP.

Bone adapts to the loads placed on it because osteocytes, buried in mineralized matrix, sense fluid flow through their lacunae and canaliculi and convert it into chemical signals. Mechanical load activates signaling by PIEZO1 and integrins in these cells, and the result is release of anabolic mediators such as prostaglandin E2 and ATP that instruct osteoblasts and osteoclasts on the bone surface; loss of this sensing underlies disuse osteopenia and contributes to age-related bone loss. Membrane stretch opens PIEZO1 to admit calcium and sodium, voltage-gated channel subunits including CACNA1H amplify the calcium rise, and cytosolic calcium opens PANX1 to export ATP, which acts back on P2RX7 to propagate calcium waves. In dendrites, alphaV:beta3 integrins engaging matrix, together with perlecan and osteopontin, signal through PI3K to AKT1, which phosphorylates ITGA5 and connexin 43 to permit hemichannel release.

MITF-M is the master switch that turns a neural crest-derived precursor into a melanocyte rather than a neuron or Schwann cell, and control of its expression and activity determines pigmentation, melanoblast migration and survival, and, when deregulated, melanoma behaviour. Before commitment, FOXD3, SOX2 and SNAI2 hold the melanocyte-specific promoter silent, with ZIC1, PAX3 and SOX9 upstream and HDAC1 contributing to relief of repression. In committed melanoblasts PAX3 and SOX10 bind the promoter, reinforced by WNT/beta-catenin with LEF1, endothelin signalling through EDNRB, KIT ligand, and melanocortin input via MC1R and cAMP-driven CREB. Once expressed, MITF-M feeds back to extinguish FOXD3 and SOX2, locking in fate. Its protein output is further tuned by MAPK, GSK3B and AKT phosphorylation, SUMO1/UBE2I conjugation, ubiquitin-mediated turnover, 14-3-3 binding, XPO1-dependent export and SIRT1/CBP-p300 acetylation, which shifts occupancy at differentiation target promoters.

Melanocytes owe their identity to a single master transcription factor, and MITF-M-dependent gene expression is the programme it runs. It specifies melanocyte fate in the developing neural crest and sustains pigment production in skin, hair and eye; loss of function causes hypopigmentation and deafness syndromes, while its amplification and rewiring in melanoma switch cells between proliferative, pigmented and invasive states. MITF binds E-box and M-box elements as a dimer and, with SOX10, TFAP2A, LEF1/TCF partners and the BRG1/BAF chromatin remodelling complex, activates the melanin synthesis enzymes tyrosinase, TYRP1 and DCT, melanosome structural and transport proteins including PMEL, MLANA, RAB27A, MYO5A and melanophilin, and the vacuolar ATPase subunits that acidify lysosome-related organelles. It also tunes cell cycle and survival genes such as CDK2, CCND1 and BCL2, and represses adhesion, matrix and EMT genes, with the MITF-embedded microRNA miR-211 adding a further regulatory layer.

Malate-aspartate shuttle moves reducing equivalents from the cytosol into mitochondria without moving NADH itself, regenerating the cytosolic NAD+ that glycolysis, serine synthesis and glutamate metabolism depend on while feeding electrons to the respiratory chain. Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters via the oxoglutarate carrier in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate; matrix MDH2 regenerates NADH, and transamination by the GOT1/GOT2 pair exports aspartate through the calcium-sensitive aspartate-glutamate carriers AGC1 and AGC2. Because glutamate import is proton-coupled and effectively irreversible, the proton-motive force keeps the cycle running in one direction. The shuttle also sets aspartate availability for nucleotide and protein synthesis. Its failure starves the cytosol of NAD+ and the brain of aspartate and glutamate for neurotransmission, and mutations in the carriers and mitochondrial glutamate transporters cause early infantile epileptic encephalopathy and citrin deficiency.

Cytosolic NADH cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so the malate-aspartate shuttle moves its reducing equivalents indirectly, keeping the cytosol oxidized enough for glycolysis to continue while delivering electrons to the respiratory chain. Cytosolic malate dehydrogenase reduces oxaloacetate to malate, which enters in exchange for 2-oxoglutarate via the dicarboxylate carrier SLC25A11; inside, MDH2 regenerates NADH. Transaminases GOT1 and GOT2 interconvert aspartate and glutamate on either side, and the aspartate-glutamate carriers SLC25A12 and SLC25A13 co-import a proton, making the cycle unidirectional and driven by the proton-motive force. Glutamate carriers SLC25A18 and SLC25A22 feed the amino acid arm. Loss of any step starves the cytosol of NAD+ and limits aspartate, serine and glutamate supply; in the brain this presents as early infantile epileptic encephalopathy, and carrier defects also cause citrin deficiency with hyperammonaemia.

The melanocyte transcription factor MITF-M is best known for driving pigmentation genes, but it also runs a second programme that builds and acidifies the degradative compartments of the cell. Its targets here are essentially the whole vacuolar H+-ATPase, both the membrane-embedded V0 sector and the cytosolic V1 ATP-hydrolysing sector, plus an accessory subunit; together these pump protons to acidify lysosomes and endosomes, which is a precondition for hydrolase activity, cargo degradation, receptor recycling and melanosome maturation. The same output supports autophagic flux when melanoma cells are starved of nutrients, giving them a route to recycle their own material and survive stress. MITF also induces the lysosomal acid ceramidase ASAH1, which clears ceramide and thereby links sphingolipid handling to proliferation and drug resistance in melanoma. This places lysosome biogenesis alongside differentiation in the MITF-controlled repertoire.

Protein lipoylation builds the lipoyl cofactor inside mitochondria and attaches it to the handful of enzymes that cannot run without it: the E2 subunits of pyruvate, 2-oxoglutarate, 2-oxoadipate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenases, plus the glycine cleavage system. It therefore sits upstream of oxidative energy metabolism, amino acid catabolism and one-carbon supply, and its failure produces severe lactic acidosis with combined dehydrogenase deficiency; loss of the carrier protein GCSH additionally causes hyperglycinemia and epileptic encephalopathy. Octanoyl groups from mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, carried on the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1, are transferred by LIPT2 onto GCSH; the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS then inserts two sulfurs using iron-sulfur clusters supplied through NFU1, with FDX1 providing electrons; LIPT1 finally relays the lipoyl group to the acceptor lysines of DLAT, DLST and DBT.

Five mitochondrial redox enzymes work only if one of their subunits carries a covalently attached lipoyl arm, and protein lipoylation is how that arm is built and installed. It supplies the pyruvate, 2-oxoglutarate, 2-oxoadipate and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes, linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and driving amino acid catabolism, and it equips the glycine cleavage system. Octanoate delivered by the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1 is loaded onto the carrier GCSH by LIPT2, the radical-SAM enzyme LIAS inserts two sulfurs using iron-sulfur clusters supplied with help from FDX1 and NFU1, and LIPT1 transfers the finished lipoyl group to the E2 subunits DLAT, DLST and DBT. Loss of any step produces severe lactic acidosis with combined dehydrogenase deficiency, and GCSH defects additionally cause hyperglycinemia with epileptic encephalopathy.

Lysine, hydroxylysine and tryptophan are broken down through a common route that converts 2-oxoadipate to glutaryl-CoA, and the mitochondrial alpha-oxoadipate dehydrogenase complex catalyses that step. It links amino acid catabolism to the final stages of degradation that feed acetyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, and it supplies NADH to the respiratory chain. Three enzymes act in sequence: DHTKD1, the substrate-specific E1 component, decarboxylates 2-oxoadipate and loads the glutaryl group onto the lipoyl arm of DLST; DLST transfers it to coenzyme A; and DLD, the shared dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase also used by pyruvate and 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, reoxidises the lipoamide using NAD+. Architecturally, DHTKD1 dimers dock onto a 24-mer DLST core. Loss of DHTKD1 causes 2-aminoadipic and 2-oxoadipic aciduria, while DLD deficiency impairs several dehydrogenase complexes at once.

Leucine, isoleucine and valine are disposed of by a committed, irreversible step in the mitochondrial matrix: once transaminated to their branched-chain alpha-ketoacids, the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex oxidatively decarboxylates them and attaches coenzyme A, yielding isovaleryl-CoA, alpha-methylbutyryl-CoA and isobutyryl-CoA plus CO2 and NADH, which feed onward to acyl-CoA dehydrogenation and eventually the TCA cycle. This sets the rate at which dietary branched-chain amino acids are catabolised rather than reused for protein synthesis or signalling. The complex is built like other ketoacid dehydrogenases, with a decarboxylating E1 heterotetramer from BCKDHA and BCKDHB, a lipoyl-bearing E2 transacylase encoded by DBT, and the shared dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase DLD that reoxidises lipoamide using NAD+. Loss of E1 or E2 function causes maple syrup urine disease, in which accumulated amino acids and keto acids produce encephalopathy and neurodegeneration, while DLD defects also impair pyruvate oxidation and present with lactic acidosis.

SLC15A4:TASL-dependent IRF5 activation is the branch of endosomal Toll-like receptor signalling that turns nucleic acid sensing into type I interferon and pro-inflammatory cytokine transcription. It gives immune cells, particularly plasmacytoid dendritic cells and B cells, their interferon response to viral RNA and CpG DNA, and its overactivity by self nucleic acids drives systemic lupus erythematosus, making the transporter and its adaptor attractive drug targets. SLC15A4, a proton-coupled histidine and oligopeptide transporter, doubles as a scaffold on the endolysosomal membrane, docking TASL on the cytosolic face. After TLR7, TLR8 or TLR9 engagement, TASL is phosphorylated and its pLxIS motif recruits IRF5, which the IKK complex catalytic subunit IKKβ phosphorylates; IRF5 then homodimerises and enters the nucleus. This positions the pathway as a spatially restricted, lysosome-anchored counterpart to the STING and MAVS routes to interferon induction.

Endosomal Toll-like receptors that sense nucleic acids need a dedicated route to switch on interferon gene transcription, and this is it: a lysosomal transporter doubling as a signalling scaffold delivers IRF5 to the kinase that activates it. SLC15A4, a proton-coupled histidine and oligopeptide transporter, anchors the adaptor TASL on the cytosolic face of endolysosomes, where TASL is phosphorylated and captures IRF5 through a pLxIS motif. The IKK complex, with IKBKB as the relevant catalytic subunit, then phosphorylates IRF5, which homodimerizes and moves to the nucleus to drive type I interferon and pro-inflammatory cytokine genes. The output shapes plasmacytoid dendritic cell and B cell responses to viral RNA and DNA. When self nucleic acids trigger it, chronic interferon production follows, and both SLC15A4 and IRF5 are genetically linked to systemic lupus erythematosus, making the axis a drug target.

Blood flow is not uniform along the arterial tree, and endothelial cells read the difference. Where flow is turbulent, oscillatory or disturbed instead of smoothly laminar instead of quiescence the cells mount an inflammatory response, which is why curved segments and branch points of arteries are the sites where atherosclerotic plaque forms. The mechanosensitive cation channel PIEZO1 opens under disturbed shear and admits calcium, activating the calpain protease complex that cleaves vinculin at the link between integrins and actin. Fibronectin-engaged integrins such as ITGA5:ITGB1 recruit PP2A and PDE4D, lowering cAMP and dephosphorylating YAP1 so it enters the nucleus; focal adhesion kinase PTK2 drives NF- cob tiny B activation through CHUK and RELA, while IKBKE-STAT1 signalling induces NLRP3. The output is sustained endothelial inflammation and atherosclerosis-prone activation.

Response of endothelial cells to shear stress describes how the cells lining blood vessels sense the frictional force of flowing blood and translate it into vessel tone, cell shape, and inflammatory state. It explains why arterial regions of steady high flow stay atheroprotected while branch points and curvatures with disturbed or sluggish flow become sites of atherosclerotic plaque. All flow types open the mechanosensitive channel PIEZO1, admitting calcium that activates calpain-2 and remodels the submembrane cytoskeleton so cells elongate along the flow axis. Steady laminar flow additionally engages VEGFR2, purinergic P2RY2 and adrenomedullin signalling through PI3K-AKT to phosphorylate eNOS, raising nitric oxide and driving vasodilation. Disturbed flow instead works through integrin alpha5-beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP loss, PP2A-dependent YAP1 activation and FAK-driven NF-kB nuclear entry, switching on pro-inflammatory transcription and adhesion molecule expression.

Endothelial cells lining blood vessels continuously read the frictional drag of flowing blood, and how they respond to shear stress determines whether a vessel segment stays quiescent and dilated or turns inflamed and atherosclerosis-prone. Flow is sensed at the apical membrane and at junctional and adhesion complexes: the mechanosensitive cation channels PIEZO1 and TRPV4 admit calcium, activating the calpain-2 protease that remodels submembrane cytoskeleton so cells elongate and align with the flow axis. Steady high-volume laminar flow signals through VEGFR2, ATP-released P2RY2, and adrenomedullin acting on CALCRL/RAMP2 to raise cAMP and activate PI3K-AKT, which phosphorylates eNOS to generate nitric oxide and vasodilation. Disturbed or low flow instead engages integrin alpha5/beta1, PDE4D-mediated cAMP hydrolysis, focal adhesion kinase, and PP2A-dependent YAP1 activation, driving NF-kB-dependent inflammatory gene expression, inflammasome priming, and leukocyte recruitment at branch points and curvatures.

The conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by the mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is the committed, irreversible step linking glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Without it, glucose-derived carbon cannot be burned aerobically, lactate accumulates, and patients present with congenital lactic acidosis, encephalopathy and Leigh-like neurodegeneration, since the brain depends heavily on glucose oxidation. The complex is built from many copies of a few subunits: the E1 heterotetramer (PDHA1 or its testis-specific counterpart PDHA2, with PDHB) performs thiamine-dependent oxidative decarboxylation, the E2 transacetylase DLAT carries the acetyl group on a lipoamide arm and transfers it to coenzyme A, and the flavoenzyme E3 (DLD) reoxidizes lipoamide while reducing NAD+. PDHX anchors E3 to the E2 core. Defects in PDHA1 and PDHX are the most frequent causes of complex deficiency, and flux through the reaction is further tuned by phosphorylation of E1.

Pyruvate sits at the junction between glycolysis and mitochondrial oxidation, and its fate — burned in the TCA cycle, reduced to lactate, or returned toward gluconeogenesis — is set by the control layer described here.
