The decisive switch is phosphorylation of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex: four kinases (PDK1-PDK4) inactivate the E1 subunits PDHA1/PDHB, while the phosphatases PDP1 and PDP2 with their regulatory subunit restore flux, so that fuel choice tracks nutrient supply, insulin, hypoxia and exercise. Lactate dehydrogenase A and the pyruvate kinase M isoform govern the glycolytic exit favoured by proliferating and tumour cells, malic enzyme feeds pyruvate from malate with NADPH output, and SIRT4 adds mitochondrial deacylation-dependent restraint. A CTLH/GID-type ubiquitin ligase assembly with ubiquitin itself provides degradative control of gluconeogenic enzymes. Loss of this regulation produces lactic acidosis and the encephalopathy of pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency.

Cytochrome c oxidase, the terminal enzyme of the respiratory chain, transfers electrons from cytochrome c to oxygen and pumps protons; complex IV assembly is the stepwise construction of this enzyme in the inner mitochondrial membrane. It matters because the mature complex requires far more proteins than it contains: three mitochondrially encoded core subunits, eleven nuclear-encoded subunits, and a large set of factors that insert heme a, the CuA and CuB copper centres, and bound phospholipids. Copper delivery runs through soluble and membrane metallochaperones such as COX17, SCO1 and SCO2, while COX15 supplies heme a and translational activators like TACO1 ensure core subunit synthesis. Subunit paralogues and hypoxia-responsive members permit tissue- and oxygen-tuned versions of the enzyme, and some factors also govern supercomplex formation. Loss of any subunit or assembly factor produces cytochrome c oxidase deficiency, typically presenting as Leigh syndrome and other infantile encephalomyopathies.

Loss-of-function mutations in DBT cause MSUD2 describes how defects in the dihydrolipoamide branched-chain transacylase subunit cripple the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex and produce maple syrup urine disease type 2. This complex performs the committed, irreversible step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism, oxidatively decarboxylating their transaminated keto acids so that the carbon skeletons can enter the TCA cycle. DBT forms the E2 core to which the E1 heterotetramer of BCKDHA and BCKDHB and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase attach, and its lipoyl domain shuttles the acyl group between them; losing it destabilises the entire assembly. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids then accumulate in blood and brain, causing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidotic crises and, untreated, neurological damage or death. It illustrates how one scaffold subunit determines the activity of a whole multienzyme complex.

The branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex commits leucine, isoleucine and valine to oxidative breakdown, and mutations that destroy the integrity of its E2 core subunit cause the maple syrup urine disease subtype known as MSUD2. The complex is built from E1 decarboxylase subunits, the dihydrolipoyl transacylase E2 component encoded by DBT, and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase; E2 carries the lipoyl groups that accept the acyl intermediate and pass reducing equivalents on, so loss of functional DBT stalls the whole complex regardless of intact E1. Branched-chain amino acids and their ketoacids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine, encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and risk of cerebral oedema. Management relies on dietary restriction of these amino acids, placing this step at the centre of branched-chain amino acid catabolism and nitrogen handling.

Maple Syrup Urine Disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which performs the oxidative decarboxylation step in catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine in the mitochondrial matrix and feeds acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the Krebs cycle. When this step fails, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate, producing the characteristic sweet-smelling urine along with neonatal feeding failure, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death unless dietary intervention follows newborn screening. The complex is built around a 24-mer transacylase core (DBT) decorated by the E1 decarboxylase tetramers of BCKDHA and BCKDHB and by DLD, the E3 dehydrogenase also shared with pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation of the E1 beta subunit, with PPM1K dephosphorylation activating the complex, linking amino acid disposal to nutrient state.

Maple syrup urine disease is the inborn error of metabolism that follows loss of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, the mitochondrial machine performing the second, committed step of leucine, isoleucine and valine catabolism. Without it, branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids accumulate in blood and urine, producing the characteristic sweet odour along with poor feeding, lethargy, encephalopathy, seizures, coma and death in the classic neonatal form; milder intermediate and stress-triggered intermittent forms reflect higher residual activity. The complex is built from an E1 decarboxylase made of BCKDHA and BCKDHB dimers, a DBT transacylase core, and the shared DLD dehydrogenase, and requires thiamine diphosphate, lipoamide, FAD and NAD+. Flux is set by reversible phosphorylation, with the phosphatase PPM1K activating the complex. Because DLD also serves pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, its loss causes broader, lethal lactic acidosis. Newborn screening enables dietary intervention.

Leucine, isoleucine and valine are degraded by a shared route that begins with transamination and oxidative decarboxylation and then splits into three acyl-CoA oxidation arms, and inherited defects along it produce some of the best-known inborn errors of metabolism. Loss of the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex subunits, its E3 component or the dihydrolipoyl transacylase causes maple syrup urine disease, with ketoacid accumulation, encephalopathy, acidosis and neonatal death if untreated; the kinase and phosphatase that reciprocally inactivate and reactivate the complex set flux through it. Downstream lesions in isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, the two subunits of methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase, the leucine pathway hydratase, and the valine pathway enzymes including a short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase and hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase give distinct organic acidurias, some with basal ganglia injury. Clinical management rests on dietary restriction because the toxicity comes from the accumulated intermediates rather than the missing products.

Branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine are degraded by a mitochondrial multienzyme complex whose first, committed step is oxidative decarboxylation of their transaminated keto acids. That reaction is carried out by the E1 heterotetramer built from BCKDHA and BCKDHB subunits docked onto the DBT transacylase core. Severe loss-of-function mutations in either E1 subunit disrupt subunit interfaces or the hydrophobic core, so the complex fails to assemble and branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase activity is lost. Branched-chain amino acids and their keto acids then accumulate in blood, urine and brain, producing classic maple syrup urine disease with its characteristic sweet-smelling urine, neonatal encephalopathy, cerebral oedema and, untreated, death; management depends on lifelong dietary restriction. Mutations at BCKDHA define MSUD type 1A and those at BCKDHB type 1B, the latter accounting for roughly a third of cases.

Complex III, the cytochrome bc1 reductase, passes electrons from ubiquinol to cytochrome c while pumping protons, and its assembly is the stepwise route by which that enzyme is built from a mitochondrially encoded core and ten or so nuclear-encoded subunits. Without it oxidative phosphorylation stalls at the middle of the respiratory chain, producing the infantile encephalopathy, liver failure, tubulopathy and lactic acidosis of complex III deficiency. Cytochrome b synthesis is chaperoned by dedicated factors including UQCC1-UQCC3 and LYRM7, cytochrome c1 and the peripheral subunits are added in defined order, and the Rieske protein UQCRFS1 is inserted last, requiring the AAA-ATPase BCS1L for its maturation. Because UQCRFS1 carries a [2Fe-2S] cluster, the mitochondrial iron-sulfur assembly machinery, with NFS1, ISCU, frataxin and their chaperones, feeds directly into this pathway; TTC19 acts later in turnover of cleaved Rieske fragments.

Loss-of-function mutations in DLD cause MSUD3/DLDD describes an inherited metabolic disease in which the shared E3 subunit of several mitochondrial keto acid dehydrogenase complexes fails, blocking the oxidative decarboxylation steps that feed the citric acid cycle. DLD serves as dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase built from BCKDHA, BCKDHB and DBT, so its loss has pleiotropic consequences: lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, alpha-keto acids and plasma branched-chain amino acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because branched-chain catabolism is impaired, the condition is grouped with maple syrup urine disease, but the phenotype is broader and reflects a general failure of mitochondrial fuel oxidation. Affected individuals are frequently compound heterozygotes, and residual enzyme activity measured in vitro predicts clinical severity poorly.

Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase is the shared E3 subunit of three mitochondrial alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complexes, so recessive loss-of-function mutations in it disable branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and pyruvate dehydrogenase at once. The resulting deficiency presents with lactic acidosis, accumulation of pyruvate, branched-chain amino acids and urinary alpha-keto acids, and progressive neurological deterioration, sometimes with liver involvement. Because the branched-chain complex is affected, the condition is classed with maple syrup urine disease, but its pleiotropic biochemistry sets it apart from defects in the complex's own catalytic subunits, the E1 alpha and beta chains and the E2 transacylase. Mechanistically the E3 component reoxidizes the lipoamide arm after decarboxylation, passing electrons to NAD+; without it, oxidative decarboxylation stalls and both amino acid catabolism and entry of carbon into the citric acid cycle fail. Compound heterozygosity is common and residual activity predicts severity poorly.

Proteasome assembly builds the cell's principal protein-destroying machine, the multisubunit complex that carries out ubiquitin-dependent regulatory and quality-control degradation. Without it, cyclins and transcription factors are not cleared on schedule, misfolded proteins accumulate, and antigenic peptides are not generated for MHC class I presentation. Dedicated chaperones (PSMG1-4, POMP) template the heteroheptameric alpha and beta rings of the barrel-shaped proteolytic core, whose catalytic beta subunits mature by autolytic propeptide removal; ATPase (PSMC) and non-ATPase (PSMD) subunits with ADRM1 and SEM1 then form the regulatory particle that recognises polyubiquitinated substrates, deubiquitinates them, and unfolds and threads them into the core. Subunit swapping generates tissue-specific variants: the immunoproteasome and thymoproteasome shape peptide repertoires for cytotoxic T cell recognition and thymic positive selection, while PSMA8-containing spermatoproteasomes serve spermatocyte differentiation. PSME activators and the inhibitor PSMF1 tune output, including stress-induced turnover of oxidised proteins.

Nearly all regulated protein destruction in the cytosol and nucleus passes through the proteasome, and building that machine correctly is what proteasome assembly accomplishes. Seven distinct alpha and seven distinct beta subunits must be placed in the right order into four stacked rings to form the barrel-shaped 20S proteolytic core, a task guided by dedicated chaperones (PSMG1-4) and the maturation factor POMP; the ATPase base and lid subunits then stack on as the 19S regulatory particle, which recognises ubiquitylated substrates, strips their chains and feeds unfolded polypeptides into the core. Alternative caps and subunit swaps generate specialised forms: the PSME1/PSME2 activator and the interferon-inducible beta subunits produce immunoproteasomes that shape peptides for MHC class I presentation, PSMB11 supports thymic positive selection, and PSMA8 with PSME4 serves spermatogenesis. PSMF1 restrains core activity. Defective assembly causes proteotoxic stress and inflammatory proteasome-associated syndromes.

Circadian clock is the cell-autonomous 24-hour timekeeper that schedules gene expression, metabolism, sleep-wake behaviour and cell division, with the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus entrained by light acting as master pacemaker over peripheral tissue clocks; its disruption underlies sleep phase disorders, metabolic syndrome and altered drug responses. Timing arises from a negative transcription-translation feedback loop: BMAL1 paired with CLOCK or NPAS2 drives E-box-dependent transcription of PER and CRY genes, whose protein products accumulate, are phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 delta/epsilon and CDK5, re-enter the nucleus and shut off their own activators. Overnight, SCF complexes using beta-TrCP, FBXL3 and FBXL21 direct PER and CRY to the proteasome, restarting the cycle. A reinforcing loop through RORA/RORC and REV-ERB tunes BMAL1 output, while coactivators, HDAC3/NCOR and SIRT1 couple the oscillator to lipid and NAD+ metabolism via PPARA, PGC-1alpha, NAMPT and SREBF1.

Nearly every tissue keeps its own 24-hour time, and this cell-autonomous oscillator is what sets the daily schedule for sleep and waking, hormone release, and fuel use; its disruption by shift work, mutation or mistimed feeding predisposes to metabolic syndrome, sleep phase disorders and altered drug responses. A transcription-translation feedback loop lies at the core: BMAL1 paired with CLOCK or NPAS2 drives E-box-dependent transcription of PER and CRY genes, whose protein products accumulate, are phosphorylated by casein kinase 1 delta and epsilon, re-enter the nucleus and shut off their own activators. Overnight, SCF-type ubiquitin ligases using BTRC or FBXL3 mark PER and CRY for proteasomal destruction, restarting the cycle. A reinforcing loop through ROR activators and the repressor NR1D1 tunes BMAL1 expression, while SIRT1, coactivators and corepressors couple the clock to NAD+ status and to lipid programmes via PPARA, CPT1A and SREBF1.

3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency is an inherited block in the breakdown of leucine, and the most common organic aciduria detected by newborn screening, at roughly one in fifty thousand births. The normal enzyme is a mitochondrial biotin-dependent carboxylase built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries the covalent biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity; together they convert 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA at the fourth step of leucine catabolism. Recessive mutations that destabilise either subunit or prevent its biotinylation stall the route, so 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine accumulate and are excreted. Outcomes range widely, from lifelong absence of symptoms in most carriers of the biochemical phenotype to neonatal metabolic crisis with severe neurological damage in a small minority, linking amino acid catabolism to mitochondrial energy supply.

Leucine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a biotin-dependent carboxylation step, and loss of that step defines 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, the most common organic aciduria found by newborn screening at roughly one in 50,000 births. The enzyme converts 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA as the fourth reaction of leucine catabolism, and is built from an alpha subunit encoded by MCCC1, which carries a covalently attached biotin needed for ATP-dependent carboxylation, and a beta subunit encoded by MCCC2, which supplies carboxyltransferase activity. Recessive mutations in either subunit destabilise the complex, impair catalysis, or block biotinylation, so leucine-derived intermediates spill over into 3-hydroxyvaleric acid and 3-methylcrotonylglycine. Outcomes vary widely: most affected individuals remain mildly affected or asymptomatic, while a small fraction present in the neonatal period with metabolic decompensation and severe neurological injury.

Interferon responses must be switched off as well as on, and this is the braking arm: a set of interferon-stimulated genes that feed back to dampen the antiviral programme they were induced by. Products such as IFI44, IFI44L, IFI6 and IFI27 restrain signalling downstream of the cytosolic RNA sensors RIG-I and MDA5, limiting type I interferon production and the inflammatory output of the IKK complex, so that virus clearance does not tip into tissue damage or autoinflammation. A parallel branch is ISG15 conjugation, where UBA7, UBE2L6 and the ligase HERC5 modify targets including the RIG-I regulator TRIM25, tuning sensor activity. Several members also intersect with endoplasmic reticulum stress and the unfolded protein response through ATF6, PERK and BiP, linking secretory-pathway strain to the magnitude and duration of innate immune signalling in infected cells.

Whether a tumour or an immune cell displays the checkpoint ligand PD-L1 on its surface is decided largely after the protein is made, and this post-translational control of PD-L1 sets how strongly PD-1 on T cells can be engaged to dampen their killing. Loss of the restraining arm stabilises PD-L1 and favours immune evasion; excess degradation strips the brake and permits autoimmunity. N-linked glycosylation by the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, with STT3A/STT3B and the branching enzyme B3GNT3, is required for correct folding and trafficking, while phosphorylation by GSK3B and casein kinase 2 marks the protein for ubiquitin-dependent turnover through cullin-RING ligases including SPOP-CUL3 and SKP1-CUL1-BTRC, ER-associated degradation components such as SEL1L, DERL and VCP, and the 26S proteasome. AMPK subunits and JAK1 add further modification-dependent tuning, and each step is a candidate handle for improving checkpoint blockade.

PD-L1 is the ligand that engages PD-1 on T cells and switches off their killing response, so how much of it a cell makes sets the threshold between tolerance and autoimmunity, and in tumours between immune clearance and immune escape. Control of PD-L1 translation places that decision partly after transcription: microRNAs including miR-34a/b/c, the miR-200 family members miR-200b, miR-200c and miR-429, miR-148a/miR-152, miR-93 and let-7 pair with the 3' UTR of the CD274 transcript and reduce its stability and translational output. The repression is executed by RNA-induced silencing complexes built from Argonaute proteins with GW182 scaffolds (TNRC6A-C) and the helicase MOV10. Loss of these microRNAs raises surface PD-L1 on tumour and stromal cells, contributing to checkpoint-mediated T cell exhaustion and shaping responsiveness to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.

PD-L1 is the ligand that shuts down T cells through the PD-1 receptor, dampening T cell receptor and costimulatory signalling to keep immune responses self-limiting and prevent autoimmunity; tumours exploit the same brake to escape cytotoxic T cells, which is why antibodies against this axis became mainstream cancer therapy. How much PD-L1 reaches the cell surface is set at every layer, and those layers are what this regulation comprises. Interferon-driven JAK1-STAT1 signalling, NF-kB, HIF1A and EPAS1 under hypoxia, MYC, AP-1 factors, Wnt-beta-catenin with TCF/LEF, and YAP/TAZ-TEAD all act on the CD274 promoter, while Polycomb (EZH2, SUZ12, EED) and MLL-WDR5 complexes with core histones supply the epigenetic setting. Several microRNAs, including miR-34 and miR-200 family members acting through Argonaute complexes, restrain the transcript. Post-translationally, N-glycosylation by the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, CSNK2 and GSK3B phosphorylation, ERAD components, and SPOP-CUL3 and SCF ubiquitin ligases feeding the proteasome determine PD-L1 stability.

PD-L1 is the ligand that engages PD-1 on T cells to damp their activation, and how much of it a cell displays is set largely at the level of CD274 transcription. In healthy tissue this restraint maintains immune tolerance and limits collateral damage during inflammation; in tumours the same promoter is driven hard, cloaking cancer cells from cytotoxic T cells and determining who responds to checkpoint blockade. Interferon and cytokine signals act through STAT1, STAT3 and IRF1, while oncogenic and stress inputs converge via MYC and MYCN, NF-kB subunits, AP-1 factors, HIF1A and EPAS1 under hypoxia, NRF2, Wnt-driven beta-catenin with TCF/LEF partners, and YAP/TAZ with TEAD factors. Access to the locus is gated chromatin-wise by the activating COMPASS/MLL complex with WDR5 and RBBP5, the p300/CBP and BRD4 acetylation readers and writers, and the opposing PRC2 repressor built on EZH2, EED and SUZ12.

Human-specific partial duplicates of NOTCH2, the NOTCH2NL genes (NOTCH2NLA, NOTCH2NLB, NOTCH2NLC and NOTCH2NLR) encode secreted, truncated Notch-like proteins whose expression is thought to have contributed to the evolutionary enlargement of the human cortex. Three copies sit in the 1q21.1 region and one near NOTCH2 on 1p12; they are functional only in humans, existing as pseudogenes in other great apes. During corticogenesis they modulate Notch signalling in radial glia, delaying the differentiation of neural progenitors and thereby prolonging the proliferative phase that expands the progenitor pool, acting in concert with neighbouring, co-expressed NBPF genes. The clinical stakes are clear: copy-number loss or gain across 1q21.1 produces microcephaly or macrocephaly with neurodevelopmental disease, and a GGC repeat expansion in the NOTCH2NLC 5' untranslated region causes neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease. Expression is not confined to brain, with neutrophil-associated transcription also reported.

Loss of branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase activity leaves the cell unable to brake catabolism of leucine, isoleucine and valine, and the resulting shortage of these amino acids causes a neurological disorder with impaired intellectual development, microcephaly and autistic features. Normally the kinase phosphorylates serine residues on the E1 alpha subunit of the branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, switching off the irreversible oxidative decarboxylation step that commits branched-chain ketoacids to degradation; this sets how much of the dietary supply is spared for protein synthesis and neurotransmitter-related metabolism. When the kinase is inactivated, the complex, built from the E1 alpha and beta subunits with the E2 transacylase and the shared E3 dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, runs unrestrained, and branched-chain amino acids fall in plasma, tissue and urine. It is the mirror image of maple syrup urine disease, and symptoms respond to dietary branched-chain amino acid supplementation.

Branched-chain amino acids from dietary protein are disposed of by oxidative decarboxylation of their ketoacid derivatives, a committed and irreversible step performed by the mitochondrial branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase complex built from BCKDHA and BCKDHB (E1), DBT (E2) and the shared DLD (E3). The products feed acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, and when the complex fails, leucine, isoleucine and valine and their ketoacids accumulate to neurotoxic levels, producing the encephalopathy, ketoacidosis and characteristic sweet-smelling urine of maple syrup urine disease. Complex activity is switched off by inhibitory phosphorylation of the E1 beta subunit and switched back on by the mitochondrial phosphatase PPM1K, which removes that mark. A frameshift truncating PPM1K destabilises the phosphatase, leaves the dehydrogenase locked in its phosphorylated inactive state, and causes a mild, variant form of the disease that is corrected by restoring wild-type phosphatase.

Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells only see peptides that a proteasome has already cut to the right length, and this route generates them without ubiquitin tagging or ATP. The 20S core particle, built from seven alpha and seven beta subunits, is capped instead by the PA28 activator formed from PSME1 and PSME2, which lacks a ubiquitin receptor and so admits intrinsically disordered or oxidatively damaged proteins directly for cleavage. In immune cells and under interferon-gamma or TNF stimulation, the constitutive catalytic subunits PSMB5, PSMB6 and PSMB7 are replaced by PSMB8, PSMB9 and PSMB10, shifting cleavage specificity toward hydrophobic and basic C-termini that fit MHC class I binding grooves. The output feeds antigen presentation, surveillance of virus-infected and tumour cells, and disposal of misfolded protein during stress.

Antimicrobial resistance describes how bacteria, viruses and parasites survive drugs meant to kill them, and it is among the most pressing public health problems because it strips standard therapy of effect and turns routine infections into untreatable ones. In enterobacteria, treatment relies on beta-lactams, aminoglycosides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones, and each is defeated by a small repertoire of strategies: enzymatic degradation or chemical modification of the drug, active efflux out of the cell, alteration of the target so the drug no longer binds, and rerouting of metabolism through a bypass pathway. Resistance to antiseptics and disinfectants relies similarly on efflux, target modification and biofilm formation. These traits may be intrinsic, arise by mutation, or spread by horizontal gene transfer, and growth within a consortium such as a biofilm adds tolerance mechanisms unavailable to single cells.

Assembly of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex builds a mechanical bridge from the actin cytoskeleton, through the plasma membrane, to laminins and other basement membrane components, so that contracting muscle fibres can transmit force without tearing their own sarcolemma. Its core is dystroglycan, whose heavily O-glycosylated extracellular chain binds laminins, agrin and perlecan, while its transmembrane chain binds dystrophin or the related utrophin, which in turn engage actin. A sarcoglycan-sarcospan ring stabilises the membrane face, and syntrophins and dystrobrevins dock on the cytoplasmic side, recruiting signalling enzymes and clustering ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors. Loss of dystrophin causes Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, and sarcoglycan mutations cause limb-girdle dystrophies and cardiomyopathy. Similar complexes in non-muscle tissues, including Schwann cells and brain, support membrane stability, mechanotransduction and receptor organisation.

Each mitochondrion must copy its own 16.6 kb circular genome, and in the strand-asynchronous (strand-displacement) mode the heavy strand is copied well before the light strand, each from its own origin. Because this genome encodes core respiratory chain subunits plus the rRNAs and tRNAs needed to make them, failures here cause mitochondrial DNA depletion or deletion syndromes such as progressive external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and hepatocerebral disease. The mitochondrial RNA polymerase POLRMT lays down short RNA primers at the origins, the TWNK helicase unwinds duplex DNA ahead of polymerase gamma (POLG with its POLG2 accessory subunits), and SSBP1 coats the displaced parental strand. Maturation requires RNASEH1 to remove primer RNA, MGME1 and EXOG to trim the resulting 5' flaps, the mitochondrial ligase III isoform to seal nicks, and TOP3A to decatenate the two finished daughter genomes.

Slow, sustained inhibition in the nervous system depends on metabotropic GABA-B receptors, which damp neuronal excitability over seconds rather than milliseconds and set the tone against which fast synaptic transmission operates. The receptor is an obligate heterodimer: GABBR1 binds GABA while GABBR2 couples to heterotrimeric Gi/Go proteins. The released Galpha subunits inhibit adenylate cyclase isoforms and lower cAMP, while the Gbeta-gamma pair acts membrane-delimited on effector channels, opening inwardly rectifying potassium channels of the Kir3/GIRK family to hyperpolarise the postsynaptic membrane and suppressing presynaptic voltage-gated calcium entry to reduce transmitter release. This signalling underlies baclofen's antispastic action and is targeted in spasticity, epilepsy, pain and addiction; loss or gain of receptor function is associated with epileptic encephalopathy and disordered inhibitory balance.

Leucine, once its carbon skeleton is broken down, passes through a mitochondrial hydratase step that converts 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA to 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA, feeding the amino acid's carbons into ketone body and acetyl-CoA production. The enzyme AUH carries out this fifth reaction of leucine catabolism, and loss-of-function mutations that destabilise or inactivate it cause the autosomal recessive disorder 3-methylglutaconic aciduria. Blocking the step backs up the pathway, so 3-methylglutaconic acid, 3-methylglutaric acid and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid accumulate and spill into the urine, where they serve as the diagnostic signature. Clinical severity is unpredictable, ranging from an incidental biochemical finding to metabolic acidosis, encephalopathy and coma, a spread that reflects how much residual enzyme activity remains and how heavily a given tissue depends on leucine oxidation for energy.

Leucine catabolism proceeds through a mitochondrial flavoenzyme, isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase, which dehydrogenates isovaleryl-CoA to 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA while reducing FAD; loss of this single step causes isovaleric acidemia, one of the classic organic acidemias. Blocked flux backs up isovaleryl-CoA, which is diverted into isovaleric acid, 3-hydroxyisovalerate, isovalerylglycine and isovalerylcarnitine that accumulate in blood and urine and give affected infants the characteristic odour of sweaty feet. Presentation ranges from neonatal metabolic crisis with vomiting, lethargy, acidosis, hyperammonaemia and seizures to a milder intermittent or nearly asymptomatic course, with poor correlation between mutation and severity. Because the defect lies in branched-chain amino acid breakdown feeding acetyl-CoA into the citric acid cycle, catabolic stress and protein load provoke decompensation, and management rests on leucine restriction plus glycine and carnitine conjugation to clear the accumulated acyl groups.

Beta-ketothiolase deficiency, also called alpha-methylacetoacetic aciduria, is an inherited error of branched-chain amino acid and ketone body metabolism caused by loss of the mitochondrial enzyme ACAT1. Normally ACAT1 performs the thiolytic cleavage of 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA into propionyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA, the final step of isoleucine catabolism, and also handles acetoacetyl-CoA during ketone body utilisation. Mutations that destabilise the protein or abolish its activity cause isoleucine intermediates and their organic acid derivatives to accumulate in blood and urine, the diagnostic hallmark. Affected children typically present between six and eighteen months with ketoacidotic crises, vomiting, lethargy and occasionally coma, often provoked by infection or fasting; neonatal onset is unusual. As in other branched-chain metabolic disorders, genotype predicts severity poorly, and management rests on avoiding catabolic stress.

Short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase deficiency is an inborn error of mitochondrial metabolism caused by loss-of-function mutations in ECHS1, the hydratase that adds water across the double bond of short-chain enoyl-CoA intermediates. The enzyme serves two converging routes: the hydration step of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation, and the degradation of branched-chain amino acids, where its preferred substrate is the valine-derived methylacrylyl-CoA and it also acts on the leucine intermediate 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA while binding but barely turning over the isoleucine-derived tiglyl-CoA. When the enzyme is absent, reactive methylacrylyl-CoA and related acyl-CoA species accumulate and damage mitochondrial proteins, producing a Leigh-like encephalopathy with basal ganglia lesions, epilepsy, cardiac involvement and severe developmental and neurological regression. The disorder illustrates how a single hydratase step links amino acid catabolism to cellular energy supply and to metabolite detoxification in the brain.

Valine breakdown in mitochondria passes through a reactive thioester intermediate, and the loss of the hydrolase that clears it defines 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA hydrolase deficiency, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. HIBCH normally catalyses the fifth step of valine catabolism, hydrolysing 3-hydroxyisobutyryl-CoA to free 3-hydroxyisobutyrate and coenzyme A so the pathway can continue toward methylmalonate semialdehyde and eventually succinyl-CoA. When the enzyme is defective, the unhydrolysed acyl-CoA accumulates and, like the upstream intermediates that build up in ECHS1 deficiency, behaves as a reactive electrophile that modifies cysteine residues in proteins such as those of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. The clinical result is a Leigh-like encephalopathy: psychomotor regression, developmental delay, neurodegeneration and symmetrical basal ganglia lesions. It illustrates how a single branched-chain amino acid catabolic step protects the brain's energy metabolism from its own intermediates.

WDR5 sits at the centre of a family of chromatin-modifying machines that write the marks distinguishing active promoters and enhancers from silent chromatin. Together with RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 it forms the WRAD module that licenses and positions the H3K4 methyltransferases KMT2A-D, SETD1A and SETD1B; the MLL1/2 complexes act mainly at promoters, while MLL3/MLL4 with UTX and PAXIP1 monomethylate H3K4 at tens of thousands of enhancers. WDR5 also joins GCN5/PCAF acetyltransferase complexes and the KAT8-NSL complex, linking methylation to histone acetylation. These activities set the timing and amplitude of developmental transcription, and the presence of PPARG, CEBPA, RXRA, Mediator subunits, coactivators and lipid-droplet and lipolysis genes shows the output concretely: enhancer priming during adipogenesis and the fat-cell gene programme. Mutation of the MLL genes is a recurrent driver in leukaemia and many solid tumours.

Dengue virus encodes a single polyprotein, and it is the host cell that turns that chain into functional structural and non-structural proteins. Maturation of DENV proteins therefore describes a hijacking of ordinary secretory-pathway quality control: signal peptidase subunits cleave the nascent chain at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, the oligosaccharyltransferase complex with its STT3A and STT3B catalytic subunits and accessory MAGT1/TUSC3 adds N-glycans to prM, E and NS1, and BiP, calnexin, calreticulin and protein disulfide isomerases fold and oxidise the products. Further host enzymes add other marks — N-myristoyltransferase, prolyl 4-hydroxylase, ubiquitin and SUMO conjugation machinery — while importins and exportin 1 carry capsid and NS5 between cytoplasm and nucleus. The matured non-structural proteins assemble replication factories on ER membranes where virions bud into the lumen, making these host activities determinants of infectivity and candidate antiviral targets.

Trichromatic colour vision depends on three cone opsins whose absorption spectra are compared by retinal circuits; loss of function of the medium-wavelength cone pigment removes the green-sensitive channel and so degrades the red-green comparison at the first step of phototransduction. OPN1MW encodes a G protein-coupled visual pigment in which 11-cis-retinal is isomerised by light, triggering transducin activation, cGMP hydrolysis and closure of cyclic nucleotide-gated channels to hyperpolarise the cone. When the pigment is absent, mislocalised or spectrally shifted by mutation or by unequal recombination within the tandem X-linked opsin array, the result is deuteranopia or deuteranomaly, the commonest inherited colour vision defect in men. More damaging alleles destabilise the cone itself, producing X-linked cone dystrophy with progressive loss of photopic acuity while rod-driven night vision remains intact.

Rod and cone pigments are regenerated by a retinoid recycling loop between photoreceptors and the retinal pigment epithelium, and loss of RDH5 function breaks the dehydrogenase step within it. RDH5 is an NAD+-dependent retinol dehydrogenase of RPE microsomes that interconverts retinol and retinal, working on substrate delivered and shuttled by the cellular retinaldehyde-binding protein RLBP1; the retinal product is returned to photoreceptor opsins to reconstitute light-sensitive visual pigment. When the enzyme is defective, chromophore is regenerated too slowly after a bleach, producing fundus albipunctatus, an autosomal recessive stationary night blindness marked by delayed dark adaptation and scattered yellow-white deposits at the level of the retina or pigment epithelium. The condition illustrates how visual phototransduction depends not only on the signalling cascade in the outer segment but on the metabolic supply of its chromophore.

Loss of RDH12 function breaks a protective step in the retinoid cycle that supports visual phototransduction. In photoreceptor inner segments, this NADP(H)-dependent retinol dehydrogenase reduces all-trans-retinal released from bleached rhodopsin, and 11-cis-retinal, to the corresponding retinols, which are then returned to the pigment epithelium for regeneration of chromophore. Because free retinaldehydes are reactive aldehydes that form adducts and drive oxidative damage, clearing them keeps rods and cones viable through repeated cycles of light exposure. When the enzyme is absent or catalytically dead, retinal accumulates and photoreceptors degenerate: biallelic mutations cause Leber congenital amaurosis type 13, one of the commonest causes of congenital blindness, and a recessive retinitis pigmentosa in which rods are lost first and cones follow. The defect illustrates how retinoid detoxification, rather than signalling itself, limits photoreceptor survival.

Regenerating visual pigment requires that all-trans-retinol released from bleached photoreceptors be trapped in the retinal pigment epithelium as retinyl esters, and lecithin retinol acyltransferase performs that esterification, transferring an acyl group from phosphatidylcholine onto retinol delivered by cellular retinol-binding protein. When LRAT function is lost, retinol cannot be stored or committed to the downstream isomerisation step that regenerates 11-cis-retinal, so the visual cycle stalls and rod and cone chromophore supply fails. The consequence in humans is defective phototransduction presenting as Leber congenital amaurosis type 14, an autosomal recessive juvenile-onset retinal dystrophy with severe early visual loss, nystagmus and profoundly abnormal retinal responses. The same reaction underlies retinoid storage more generally, linking photoreceptor maintenance to vitamin A handling and making this step a point at which dietary or pharmacological retinoid supply is considered therapeutically.

Defective visual phototransduction due to OPN1SW loss of function describes the failure of the blue-sensitive cone photopigment and the loss of blue-yellow colour discrimination that follows. Human trichromacy depends on three cone opsins with distinct spectral peaks, and downstream retinal circuits compare their outputs to construct colour; when the short-wavelength pigment encoded by OPN1SW is disabled, the roughly 420 nm channel drops out and the perceptual comparison becomes impossible, producing tritanopia. Missense substitutions in this opsin are inherited dominantly and are thought to misfold or mistraffic the pigment in the cone outer segment, so that light absorption no longer activates the transducin-driven cascade that hyperpolarises the cell. The condition is rare relative to red-green defects, is not progressive in the way retinal degenerations are, and illustrates how a single G protein-coupled receptor defines an entire sensory channel.

Blue-cone opsin is the visual pigment that gives short-wavelength sensitivity to the eye, and its loss produces tritan colour vision deficiency, in which blue and yellow become hard to distinguish. Trichromatic vision depends on comparing the light captured by three cone classes with peak sensitivities near 420, 530 and 560 nm; the short-wavelength pigment supplies one of those channels, and downstream retinal circuits cannot reconstruct it when the pigment is faulty. Missense substitutions in OPN1SW misfold or destabilise the opsin so that it fails to initiate the phototransduction cascade in blue cones, and the resulting defect is inherited dominantly and is much rarer than the red-green deficiencies. The consequence is selective loss of blue spectral sensitivity rather than reduced acuity, since rod and long-wavelength cone phototransduction remain intact.

Defective visual phototransduction due to STRA6 loss of function describes what happens when cells can no longer take up circulating vitamin A, cutting off the supply of retinoid needed both to build the eye during development and to regenerate visual pigment afterwards. Retinol travels in blood bound to retinol-binding protein 4, stabilised as a complex with transthyretin, and STRA6 is the membrane receptor that recognises that complex and channels retinol into target cells for conversion to retinyl esters and ultimately 11-cis-retinal, the chromophore of rhodopsin. Loss of STRA6 function starves retinoic acid signalling in the developing embryo, producing syndromic microphthalmia (Matthew-Wood syndrome) with anophthalmia, cardiac, pulmonary and diaphragmatic malformations, and in surviving tissue leaves photoreceptors unable to sustain the visual cycle, causing blindness.

Vitamin A reaches the eye bound to retinol-binding protein 4, which circulates in complex with transthyretin, and cells take up that retinol through the membrane receptor STRA6. Loss of STRA6 function breaks this uptake step, and the retinoid supply needed both for embryonic patterning and for regenerating the visual chromophore 11-cis-retinal fails. The consequence is defective visual phototransduction together with a severe developmental syndrome: microphthalmia or anophthalmia with blindness, frequently accompanied by diaphragmatic, pulmonary and cardiac malformations, described as Matthew-Wood syndrome. The pathway therefore links plasma retinol transport to retinoic acid signalling in the developing eye and to the retinoid cycle that sustains rod and cone pigment. It illustrates how a single receptor-mediated transport event, rather than an enzymatic defect, can limit access to an essential dietary cofactor.

Loss of function in OPN1LW removes the long-wavelength-sensitive (red) cone opsin and with it one of the three channels on which human colour vision depends. The gene encodes the G protein-coupled visual pigment of red cones, which absorbs a photon, isomerises its retinal chromophore and activates transducin to trigger the cascade that closes cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and hyperpolarises the photoreceptor. Without a functional pigment, red cones cannot signal: patients have protanopia, and when the neighbouring green opsin is also lost the result is blue cone monochromatism, an X-linked cone dysfunction in which vision relies on rods and short-wavelength cones alone, with reduced acuity, nystagmus, photophobia and myopia from birth. The defect illustrates how cone-specific opsin expression, rather than the shared downstream phototransduction machinery, sets spectral discrimination.

Photoreceptor outer segments regenerate visual pigment after every photon capture, and the retinoid cycle they run leaves behind reactive aldehyde intermediates that must be cleared. ABCA4, an ATP-binding cassette transporter confined to rod and cone outer segment discs, performs that clearance by flipping retinal-phosphatidylethanolamine adducts from the lumenal to the cytoplasmic face of the disc membrane so all-trans-retinal can be reduced and recycled. When the transporter is lost through mutation, unflipped adducts condense into bisretinoids that accumulate as lipofuscin in the underlying retinal pigment epithelium, poisoning the cells that support photoreceptors. The result is Stargardt disease type 1, an autosomal recessive juvenile macular degeneration that presents in the first two decades with progressive irreversible central vision loss and delayed dark adaptation; related ABCA4 defects also cause cone-rod dystrophy and retinitis pigmentosa. The pathway illustrates how a single transport step protects visual phototransduction from its own chemistry.

The final stage of the dengue virus replication cycle, in which newly made positive-sense genomes are packaged with the capsid, prM and envelope proteins at the endoplasmic reticulum and the resulting immature particles are matured and released. This step determines how many infectious virions an infected cell exports, and blocking it is one way to limit viral spread and the vascular leak that drives severe dengue. Budded particles traffic through the secretory route, where ER-Golgi transport machinery and the retrieval receptor KDELR1 and the Arf activator GBF1 support membrane flow; the proprotein convertase furin then cleaves prM in the acidic trans-Golgi, converting spiky immature particles into smooth mature virions with E:M heterodimers, and exocytosis completes release. Host factors including nucleolin, YBX1 and the ESCRT component TSG101 are co-opted for assembly and egress, illustrating how the virus borrows normal secretory and membrane-budding pathways.

Dengue Virus-Host Interactions describes how dengue virus proteins, once made and processed in the cytosol, ER and ERGIC, spread to other cellular compartments and seize host machinery, and how that seizure produces the vascular leak and immune dysregulation of dengue fever and dengue hemorrhagic fever. Secreted NS1 circulates in blood, binds glycosaminoglycan-bearing proteoglycans, complement components and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4, and disrupts endothelial junctions before cells are even infected. Inside the cell, the capsid protein and NS5 enter the nucleus, where NS5 engages the spliceosome, the RNA polymerase II transcription and 3'-end processing apparatus and heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins, reshaping host mRNA output. The NS2B3 protease cleaves innate sensing adaptors including STING and MAVS to blunt interferon induction, while other viral proteins tune autophagy, mTOR complexes and apoptosis to favour replication.

Dengue virus encodes only ten proteins and must therefore borrow host machinery and disarm host defences, and this collection captures the physical and functional contacts it makes across compartments. The consequences are clinical: secreted NS1 circulating in blood engages complement components and pattern-recognition receptors such as TLR4 and CLEC5A, and together with nuclear NS5 it perturbs endothelial junction proteins including ZO-1, contributing to the vascular leak of dengue haemorrhagic fever. The viral NS2B3 protease and NS5 blunt innate sensing by acting on the STING/MAVS/RIG-I axis and on STAT2, so interferon induction and signalling both fail. Extensive interactions with spliceosomal, hnRNP, SR protein, RNA polymerase II and 3' end processing factors, and with autophagy and mTOR complex components, show how host gene expression, membrane remodelling and metabolism are redirected to support replication, while nuclear capsid and NS5 also modulate apoptosis.

Dengue virus begins infection by sticking to the surface of skin keratinocytes, dendritic cells and macrophages and then being swallowed into an endosome, and this attachment and entry step sets which tissues the virus can reach and how severe the resulting febrile or haemorrhagic disease becomes. The viral envelope glycoprotein E, stabilised during assembly by prM and matured by furin cleavage, engages a broad set of attachment factors: the lectin CD209 on dendritic cells, the mannose receptor MRC1, ribosomal protein RPSA, and heparan sulfate displayed on syndecans, glypicans, agrin and perlecan. The virion also exposes phosphatidylserine and exploits apoptotic mimicry, binding TIM-family receptors such as HAVCR1 and TIMD4 directly and TAM kinases AXL, MERTK and TYRO3 indirectly through the bridging ligands GAS6 and PROS1. Clathrin adaptor AP-2 subunits then drive endocytosis, and endosomal acidification triggers E-mediated membrane fusion and genome release.

Dengue virus carries a positive-sense RNA genome that host ribosomes translate directly into a single polyprotein, and the same molecule is then copied through a negative-sense intermediate to make new genomes. Both steps are hijacked host biology, which is why the genes here are cellular rather than viral: cap-dependent initiation factors and poly(A)-binding protein for translation, signal peptidase and the oligosaccharyltransferase complex for cleaving and glycosylating the polyprotein as it threads back and forth across the ER membrane, ER chaperones and disulfide isomerases for folding, and importin/exportin carriers that traffic viral proteins through the nucleus. Reticulon and related membrane-shaping and lipogenic factors help invaginate the ER into the replication vesicles that shelter the replication complex, while ubiquitin, VCP and XRN1 set the turnover of viral protein and RNA. Blocking these host dependencies is a route to antiviral therapy for dengue fever.

Dengue virus survives in humans partly by blunting the immune responses that would otherwise clear it, and this pathway collects the host factors it engages to do so. The consequences are clinical: interference with complement regulation and interferon induction shapes viral load, vascular leak and the severity of dengue fever and shock syndrome. Viral nonstructural proteins bind classical-pathway and regulatory complement components, including C1q, C4 and the C4b-binding protein subunits, alongside mannose-binding lectin and soluble modulators such as clusterin and vitronectin. In parallel, sensing and signalling through the cytosolic RNA sensors MDA5 and MAVS, the DNA-sensing cGAS-STING axis, and downstream STAT2 and TRIM25 is disabled or redirected, with the PAF1 transcription elongation complex and HSP90 chaperones also recruited. Impaired antigen presentation and antigenic variation extend the same evasion to adaptive immunity, contributing to antibody-dependent enhancement on reinfection.

Dengue virus manipulates the death of the cells it infects, timing apoptosis to its own advantage: early killing is held off so replication and particle assembly can finish, while later cell death aids spread and contributes to the vascular leak, liver and brain injury seen in dengue haemorrhagic fever and shock syndrome. The host machinery recruited here spans autophagy initiation and mTOR signalling — the class III PI3K complex with BECN1, PIK3C3, PIK3R4 and ATG14, the reticulophagy receptor RETREG1, and both mTORC1 and mTORC2 through RPTOR, RICTOR, MLST8 and MAPKAP1 — alongside death and inflammatory regulators such as DAXX, RIPK1 and the NF-κB inhibitors NFKBIA and NFKBIB. Viral capsid and the NS2B:NS3 protease complex engage host factors to promote apoptosis, whereas NS1 sustains autophagic flux to keep the infected cell alive, linking membrane remodelling, nutrient sensing and cell-survival signalling to viral fitness and disease severity.

The mammary gland is the organ that defines mammals, and its construction proceeds in stages: embryonic placode and bud formation, ductal elongation and branching at puberty, and alveolar differentiation for milk production during pregnancy and lactation. Charting the developmental lineages of this tissue traces how surface ectoderm gives rise to bipotent mammary stem cells and then to ductal luminal cells, milk-secreting alveolar lactocytes, and the contractile myoepithelial sheath that expels milk in response to oxytocin. Hormonal cues act largely through paracrine growth factors from epithelium and surrounding mesenchyme: FGF10 positions and initiates the placode, EGF-family ligands including amphiregulin and TGFA drive estrogen-dependent ductal outgrowth, and prolactin instructs alveolar secretory differentiation. WNT, NOTCH and Hedgehog signalling pattern these choices. The same lineage hierarchy underlies breast cancer subtypes, which resemble arrested stages of this programme.

The exocrine pancreas, which makes up most of the organ's mass, is built from tubuloacinar glands whose acinar cells synthesise and store the digestive zymogens released into the duodenum; loss of this compartment produces exocrine insufficiency and maldigestion, and its transformation underlies pancreatic adenocarcinoma. This developmental lineage traces how acinar cells arise: definitive endoderm formed at gastrulation is patterned along anterior-posterior, dorsal-ventral and medial-lateral axes into dorsal and ventral foregut endoderm, which passes through duodeno-pancreatic and hepato-pancreatic intermediates to generate multipotent pancreatic progenitors in the two pancreatic buds. Branching morphogenesis then segregates tip from trunk domains and establishes the apical-basal polarity on which the acinar-ductal unit depends. Tip progenitors commit to a pro-acinar and then acinar fate, acquiring expanded endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi, apically clustered secretory granules, tight junctions at the lumen and attachment to basal lamina.

Pancreatic ductal cells form the single-layered epithelium that lines the branching duct tree and carries acinar secretions and bicarbonate to the gut; their developmental lineage traces back through bipotent trunk progenitors, which also yield endocrine progenitors, to the multipotent pancreatic progenitors of the early bud. Duct shape changes with calibre, from cuboidal to high columnar, and apical cilia and microvilli mark the mature cell. The genes here are the matrix side of that programme: fibrillar collagens together with fibronectin and vitronectin build the interstitial stroma around growing ducts, while the laminin chains and their assembled trimers, with collagen IV-type partners, form the basement membrane that polarises the epithelium and positions trunk progenitors for duct versus endocrine choice. Adhesion to this matrix via integrin engagement guides branching morphogenesis, and disturbed duct identity underlies cystic disease and ductal adenocarcinoma with its dense desmoplastic matrix.

In melanocytes and melanoma cells the transcription factor MITF-M controls pigmentation and proliferation, but it also acts as a direct repressor of genes governing extracellular matrix organization, focal adhesion and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and this arm of its programme sets whether a cell proliferates or switches to an invasive, drug-resistant state. Loss or lowering of MITF-M releases adhesion and matrix targets such as the integrin subunit ITGA2, the focal adhesion scaffold paxillin, the matrix components EDIL3 and peroxidasin, and the plasminogen activator inhibitor SERPINE1, alongside phenotype-switch regulators including ZEB1, SOX2 and the cadherin pair CDH1 and CDH2. The result is cytoskeletal remodelling, altered attachment to matrix and a mesenchymal-like, migratory character. Because high MITF-M marks proliferative melanoma and low MITF-M marks quiescent invasive cells, this repressive output links a lineage transcription factor to metastatic behaviour and to resistance against targeted therapy.

Iron is scarce in host tissues, and enterobacteria growing under iron limitation can bypass siderophore-based uptake by stripping iron from host heme instead. Human hemoglobin, the alpha and beta globin chains of the erythrocyte oxygen carrier, is the reservoir exploited in this heme assimilation route: secreted SPATE-family serine proteases such as EspC and Hbp cleave hemoglobin and liberate heme, which TonB-dependent outer membrane receptors capture and translocate across the bacterial envelope. A periplasmic binding protein then delivers heme to an ABC transporter for passage into the cytosol, where the tetrapyrrole is degraded and its iron released for bacterial metabolism. The interaction matters for the host as a nutritional-immunity battleground, since hemolysis and hemoglobin proteolysis convert an oxygen transport protein into a growth substrate, contributing to the virulence of uropathogenic and enteric Escherichia coli and related organisms.

Lymphocyte activation has to be braked as well as triggered, and co-inhibition by BTLA is one of the brakes that keeps T cell responses proportionate and preserves peripheral tolerance. BTLA is an inhibitory receptor on T cells, B cells and dendritic cells whose ligand is HVEM (TNFRSF14), a tumour necrosis factor receptor family member displayed broadly on lymphoid and myeloid cells. Ligation phosphorylates tyrosine motifs in the BTLA tail, which dock the SH2-domain phosphatases SHP-1 and SHP-2 (PTPN6, PTPN11); these strip phosphate from proximal T cell receptor signalling intermediates and so blunt activation, with the adaptor GRB2 also recruited to the same site. Loss of this restraint favours autoimmunity and chronic inflammation, while tumours exploit it to evade T cell attack, placing BTLA alongside CTLA-4 and PD-1 as an immune checkpoint of therapeutic interest.

Once a T cell has been activated through its antigen receptor, a second wave of costimulation sustains and shapes the response, and ICOS provides it. Unlike CD28, which naive T cells carry constitutively, ICOS appears only after activation, and its engagement by ICOSLG on antigen-presenting cells drives survival, cytokine output and differentiation — most visibly the generation of T follicular helper cells that license germinal centre reactions and high-affinity antibody. Loss of this axis in humans produces common variable immunodeficiency with poor antibody responses, while excess costimulation feeds autoimmunity. Mechanistically the receptor recruits class IA phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase heterodimers — catalytic p110 subunits with regulatory p85-family partners — generating PIP3 and activating AKT more strongly than CD28 does, linking costimulatory input to metabolic and transcriptional programmes of effector and helper T cells.

The luminal epithelial lineage of the mammary gland comprises the inner cell layer of ducts and the milk-secreting alveolar cells, and it arises postnatally from unipotent luminal progenitors that expand during puberty and pregnancy. This programme builds the ductal tree and the terminal ductal lobular units, and the hormone-receptor-positive and -negative progenitor compartments within it are the presumed cells of origin for major breast cancer subtypes. Fate choice between ductal and alveolar destinies depends on Notch and steroid hormone receptor signalling, while the progenitors retain enough plasticity to revert toward a stem-like state when the microenvironment changes. The epidermal growth factor receptor ligands represented here, amphiregulin, EGF and TGF-alpha, act as the paracrine link between systemic oestrogen signalling and local epithelial proliferation, driving ductal elongation and branching morphogenesis alongside fibroblast growth factor cues that shape duct architecture.

Milk-secreting alveolar cells arise during pregnancy from hormone receptor-negative luminal progenitors of the mammary gland, the alternative fate to the ductal epithelium that lines the gland's branching ducts. This lineage decision is what allows lactation: without alveolar commitment and expansion there is no secretory compartment to synthesise and release milk. Fate choice is set by the interplay of Notch, WNT and hormone receptor signalling, with loss of Notch input pushing progenitors toward alveolar identity, and prolactin acting through its receptor and downstream STAT signalling to drive alveolar differentiation and milk protein production. Neighbouring myoepithelial cells contribute by modulating Notch ligand availability. After weaning, most alveolar cells are cleared by involution, but a surviving pool of alveolar precursors self-renews and reconstitutes the secretory tissue in later pregnancies, linking this programme to mammary stem cell hierarchy and to breast cancer subtype origins.

The basal layer of the mammary epithelium supplies its own committed progenitors, and the myoepithelial lineage arising from them gives the gland its contractile capacity: spindle-shaped cells wrapped around ducts and alveoli that squeeze milk toward the nipple in response to oxytocin, so that lactation fails without them. These cells sit between luminal cells and the basement membrane, which they help deposit, and their continuous sheath also acts as a barrier restraining luminal outgrowth. Specification toward this fate is driven by strong EGF receptor stimulation, and the ligands represented here — amphiregulin, EGF and TGF-alpha — are the inputs that set that signal intensity during ductal morphogenesis and organoid differentiation. Myoepithelial progenitors are normally unipotent, but after loss of luminal cells, EGFR together with Notch and Wnt signalling licenses them to regenerate the luminal compartment.

PD-L1 on a cell surface tells approaching T cells to stand down, so how much of it survives is a decision about immune tolerance, and tumours that keep it high escape T cell killing. This route sets that level by destroying the protein: the constitutively active kinase GSK3B phosphorylates PD-L1 on nearby threonine and serine residues, which blocks its glycosylation and creates a phosphodegron recognised by the beta-TrCP substrate receptor of an SCF ubiquitin ligase built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1. Polyubiquitin chains assembled from the ubiquitin precursors then commit PD-L1 to the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core and regulatory subunits carries out degradation. Growth factor signalling through EGFR or WNT inactivates GSK3B and thereby stabilises PD-L1, linking oncogenic proliferative signals to immune checkpoint expression and to responsiveness to checkpoint blockade.

SPOP-mediated proteasomal degradation of PD-L1(CD274) sets how much of the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 a cell displays, and therefore how effectively tumour cells escape cytotoxic T cell attack. PD-L1 is a short-lived protein: the substrate adaptor SPOP delivers it to a CUL3-RBX1 cullin-RING ligase, which polyubiquitinates it for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle, ATPase and lid subunits together with ubiquitin executes the final step. The rate-limiting control is on SPOP itself. Cyclin D1-CDK4 phosphorylates SPOP at Ser-6, promoting binding by 14-3-3 gamma, which sequesters SPOP away from the ligase complex and stabilises PD-L1; casein kinase 2 contributes further phosphoregulation. This links cell cycle machinery directly to tumour immune evasion and explains why SPOP mutation or CDK4/6 inhibition alters checkpoint blockade responsiveness.

How much PD-L1 a tumour cell displays determines how effectively it silences cytotoxic T cells, and one route controlling that level is ubiquitin-dependent turnover of the protein by a cullin-RING ligase. SPOP acts as the substrate-recognition adaptor within a CUL3:RBX1 complex, marking PD-L1 for destruction by the 26S proteasome, whose core particle, regulatory ATPases and ubiquitin receptors are all represented here alongside ubiquitin itself. Cyclin D1:CDK4 opposes this by phosphorylating SPOP at Ser-6, creating a binding site for 14-3-3 gamma that sequesters SPOP away from the ligase; casein kinase 2 subunits contribute further phosphorylation input. Loss of SPOP function, common in prostate and endometrial cancer, stabilises PD-L1 and reduces tumour immune surveillance, which links cell cycle kinase activity and CDK4 inhibitor therapy to checkpoint blockade responsiveness.

Human chromatin is transcribed far more extensively than its protein-coding output requires, and nuclear RNA decay is what clears the surplus: enhancer and promoter upstream transcripts, long non-coding RNAs, abortive transcripts, and the discarded by-products of rRNA and mRNA processing. Without it, misfolded or misassembled RNA-protein complexes accumulate and aberrant transcripts escape into the cytoplasm. Degradation runs mainly through the barrel-shaped RNA exosome, whose nine-subunit core is coupled to the exonucleases DIS3 and EXOSC10, plus the 5'-3' exonuclease XRN2 and the decapping enzyme DXO, which also strips NAD and other metabolic caps. Substrate choice comes from targeting adaptors built around the helicase MTREX: NEXT for capped non-polyadenylated species, PAXT for polyadenylated ones, and nucleolar TRAMP for pre-rRNA spacer fragments.

Blood clotting is switched off in part by activated protein C, which cuts factor Va at arginine 534 and destroys the cofactor that accelerates thrombin generation. Missense variants at this site — factor V Leiden (R534Q) and factor V Bonn (A540V) — resist that cleavage, so factor Va persists, the prothrombinase complex with factor Xa stays active, and thrombin production continues unchecked. This activated protein C resistance is the commonest inherited thrombophilia and predisposes carriers to deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, with risk amplified by oestrogen exposure, pregnancy or surgery. Protein S serves as the cofactor for protein C in this reaction. Loss of cleavage also removes non-activated factor V's role as a cofactor helping inactivate factor VIIIa, compounding the procoagulant shift, and the Bonn variant's tighter factor Xa binding further shields the cleavage site.

Blood clotting has to be switched off as well as on, and activated protein C does much of the switching off by cleaving factor Va, the cofactor that accelerates thrombin generation. Cleavage at R534 and R334, the latter assisted by protein S, dismantles the prothrombinase complex and limits clot propagation. Missense substitutions in factor V near the R334 site, including the Cambridge and Liverpool variants, leave the cofactor resistant to this particular cut, so factor Va activity persists longer than it should. The result is activated protein C resistance and a prothrombotic tilt in the haemostatic balance, associated with venous thromboembolism in carriers. This is an inherited thrombophilia mechanism of the same kind as the more common factor V Leiden defect, arising from loss of a regulatory proteolytic step rather than from overproduction of a procoagulant.

Factor V circulates as a procofactor and, once activated, accelerates thrombin generation on platelet surfaces; the brake on that reaction is activated protein C, which with its cofactor protein S cleaves activated factor V at defined sites to shut it down. Variants of factor V that alter or remove those cleavage sites, such as the common R534Q substitution and rarer changes at R334 and nearby residues, leave the activated cofactor resistant to inactivation. The result is inherited activated protein C resistance and defective factor V as a cause of thrombophilia: a persistent tilt of coagulation toward thrombin production that raises lifetime risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, particularly with pregnancy, oral contraceptives, surgery or immobility. It illustrates how haemostasis depends less on clotting enzymes themselves than on the timely proteolytic termination of their cofactors.

Tumour cells evade T cell killing by displaying PD-L1 on their surface, and this route explains how energy stress removes it. When ATP falls and AMP rises, the AMPK heterotrimer of catalytic alpha, regulatory beta and nucleotide-binding gamma subunits is allosterically activated and phosphorylates PD-L1 (CD274). One phosphorylation site causes defective mannose trimming and abnormal glycosylation, trapping PD-L1 in the endoplasmic reticulum, where lectin-like recognition by OS9 and ERLEC1, the SEL1L-derlin retrotranslocation machinery, the RNF5/RNF185 ubiquitin ligases and the VCP ATPase deliver it to the 26S proteasome. Phosphorylation at a second site breaks the stabilising interaction with CMTM4 and diverts PD-L1 to lysosomal destruction instead. The result links metabolic state to immune checkpoint abundance, and it rationalises why AMPK agonists such as metformin can enhance antitumour immunity by stripping this inhibitory ligand from the cell surface.

PD-L1(CD274) glycosylation and translocation to plasma membrane describes how the immune checkpoint ligand PD-L1 is matured and delivered to the cell surface, where it engages PD-1 on T cells and enforces immune tolerance. Tumours exploit this route to escape cytotoxic killing, and the modifications it installs determine how much PD-L1 a cell displays and how well checkpoint-blocking antibodies recognise it. In the endoplasmic reticulum the oligosaccharyltransferase complex, with catalytic STT3A or STT3B, attaches N-glycans at three asparagines; this shields PD-L1 from GSK3B-directed proteasomal turnover. IL-6-activated JAK1 both phosphorylates PD-L1 and promotes STT3A recruitment, linking inflammation to checkpoint output. In the Golgi, B3GNT3 extends the glycans and MIB2 adds K63-linked ubiquitin, after which PD-L1 reaches the plasma membrane. The pathway sits at the interface of secretory protein quality control and adaptive immune regulation.

PD-L1 can only restrain T cells if it reaches the cell surface in a stable, correctly modified form, and this route describes how the immune checkpoint ligand CD274 is glycosylated and translocated to the plasma membrane. Tumour cells exploit it to engage PD-1 on T cells and enforce immune tolerance, which is why the modifications here influence responses to checkpoint blockade. In the ER, the oligosaccharyltransferase complex — catalytic STT3A or STT3B with RPN1, RPN2, DDOST, DAD1 and accessory subunits — attaches N-glycans to asparagines in the PD-L1 extracellular domain, blocking GSK3B-directed proteasomal degradation. IL-6-activated JAK1 both phosphorylates PD-L1 and promotes recruitment of the glycosylation machinery. Further elongation by the Golgi glycosyltransferase B3GNT3 and K63-linked ubiquitination by the ligase MIB2 complete maturation before surface delivery, where PD-L1 and the related ligand PDCD1LG2 engage PD-1.

Expression of BMAL (ARNTL), CLOCK, and NPAS2 describes how the positive limb of the circadian clock is itself transcribed, setting the amplitude and phase of daily rhythms in sleep, feeding, hormone release and metabolism. The BMAL1:CLOCK heterodimer, with NPAS2 substituting for CLOCK, drives diurnal gene expression; loss of this arm flattens behavioural and metabolic rhythms and predisposes to metabolic disease. Their promoters carry ROR response elements contested by activating retinoid-related orphan receptors RORA/B/C and the repressive nuclear receptor NR1D1 (REV-ERBα). RORs recruit coactivators such as EP300, NCOA proteins and PPARGC1A, while heme-bound NR1D1 brings NCOR1, TBL1X and HDAC3 to silence the same sites. Because RORs sense oxysterols, NR1D1 senses heme, and SIRT1 and PPARα couple in nutrient status, this secondary feedback loop links the clock directly to cellular metabolism.

The positive limb of the mammalian circadian clock depends on transcription of the activators BMAL1 (ARNTL), CLOCK and its partial substitute NPAS2, whose heterodimers drive rhythmic daytime gene expression throughout the body. How much of these activators a cell makes sets the amplitude and phase of everything downstream, from sleep-wake behaviour to rhythms in glucose and lipid handling; loss of the loop flattens circadian output and is linked to metabolic disturbance. Their promoters carry ROR response elements contested by the retinoid-related orphan receptors RORA, RORB and RORC, which recruit coactivators such as EP300, NCOA1/2 and PPARGC1A to activate, and by REV-ERBα (NR1D1), which recruits NCOR1 with HDAC3 and the TBL1X adaptors to repress. Because the RORs bind oxysterols and NR1D1 binds heme, and because SIRT1 and CREB-regulated coactivators feed in, this secondary feedback loop ties clock gene expression to metabolic state.

The daytime arm of the molecular circadian clock: once phosphorylated and imported into the nucleus, the BMAL1:CLOCK heterodimer (or BMAL1:NPAS2) binds E-box elements and switches on thousands of rhythmic genes, setting the phase of sleep-wake behaviour, feeding, hormone release and much of metabolism. Activation requires coactivators, including CREB-binding protein and the histone methyltransferase KMT2A, which open chromatin at target promoters in a time-of-day-dependent way. Crucially, the targets include the genes encoding its own repressors, PER1-3 and CRY1/2, so activation builds the delayed negative feedback that generates a ~24 hour period; a secondary loop through the nuclear receptors RORA/RORC and REV-ERBα (NR1D1) reciprocally tunes BMAL1 and CLOCK transcription, while DBP, BHLHE40 and CIPC add further feedback. Disruption produces arrhythmia, altered sleep timing and metabolic disease.

The circadian clock keeps daily rhythms in metabolism, sleep and hormone output aligned with the light cycle, and this step is where its central activator complex is switched on and timed for destruction. Once phosphorylated BMAL1:CLOCK heterodimers occupy E-box elements in target promoters, CLOCK acetylates its partner BMAL1 and itself becomes hyperphosphorylated; that modification raises transcriptional output while also marking CLOCK for proteolysis, so activation is inherently self-limiting. Coactivators including CREBBP and the histone methyltransferase KMT2A are recruited at these promoters, and the genes switched on include the repressors PER1-3, CRY1 and CRY2 and the nuclear receptors NR1D1 and RORA, which feed back to close the transcription-translation loop. Post-translational timing of this sort sets the roughly 24-hour period, and its disruption shifts sleep timing and metabolic rhythms.

The negative limb of the circadian clock: a complex of cryptochromes CRY1/CRY2, period proteins PER1-3 and the casein kinases CSNK1D/CSNK1E docks onto the BMAL1:CLOCK activator while it sits on E-boxes, shutting off the transcription it had switched on hours earlier. This delayed feedback is what makes the oscillator oscillate rather than settle at a steady output, setting the roughly 24-hour timing of sleep and wake, hormone release, and metabolic gene expression in essentially every tissue. Mechanistically the repressor complex brings kinase activity to CLOCK (or its paralogue NPAS2), and the resulting phosphorylation evicts the heterodimer from DNA, ending the activating phase. Coactivators such as CREBBP and KMT2A and the counter-regulators NR1D1 and RORA tune the amplitude of each cycle. Mutations in the kinases or period genes shift human sleep phase, and clock disruption is tied to metabolic disease.

Phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of BMAL1 (ARNTL) and CLOCK is the activation step that licenses the positive limb of the circadian clock, converting newly made transcription factors in the cytosol into a nuclear heterodimer competent to drive rhythmic gene expression. Everything downstream of the clock -- the daily cycling of period and cryptochrome genes, sleep-wake timing, feeding rhythms and the rhythmic control of hepatic and metabolic gene programmes -- depends on this dimer reaching chromatin on schedule. Casein kinase 2 phosphorylates BMAL1 while CDK5 modifies CLOCK; these marks promote heterodimerization and nuclear import, and they also set the tempo, since altering the phosphorylation sites lengthens or shortens period and can destabilize the proteins. NPAS2 substitutes for CLOCK as BMAL1's partner in some tissues. Such post-translational control links kinase activity and metabolic state to the phase of the clock.

The core positive limb of the circadian clock is built in the cytosol and must be phosphorylated before it can act in the nucleus. Newly made CLOCK is phosphorylated by CDK5, while casein kinase 2, through its catalytic CSNK2A1 subunit with the regulatory CSNK2B partner, phosphorylates BMAL1; the modified proteins then heterodimerize and move into the nucleoplasm, where the dimer drives transcription of period and cryptochrome genes and sets the pace of the roughly 24-hour feedback loop. NPAS2 can substitute for CLOCK in this partnership. Such modifications tune both the timing and amplitude of clock output and mark the proteins for eventual turnover, linking the oscillator to metabolic state. Disruption of this step flattens rhythmic gene expression and contributes to sleep, mood and metabolic disturbance.

The negative limb of the circadian clock depends on a bulky repressor assembly being built in the cytosol and delivered to the nucleus on a schedule, and this is the step that does it: newly made Cryptochrome and Period proteins are phosphorylated and translocate as a CRY:PER:kinase complex. Its timing sets the roughly 24-hour period of behaviour, sleep, and metabolic gene expression, and mutations that alter it shift human sleep phase, as in familial advanced sleep phase attributed to casein kinase I delta and to PER2. CDK5 marks PER2 for CRY1 binding; casein kinase I delta and epsilon join the complex and phosphorylate PER and CRY, with casein kinase 2 subunits contributing and protein phosphatase 1 catalytic subunits opposing these marks to tune stability and nuclear entry. Once nuclear, the complex silences BMAL1:CLOCK-driven transactivation, closing the transcriptional feedback loop.

Defective GALM causes GALAC4 describes the metabolic block that arises when galactose mutarotase loses function, producing type IV galactosemia. GALM is the cytosolic epimerase that interconverts beta-D-galactose and alpha-D-galactose, and only the alpha anomer can be phosphorylated by galactokinase, the first committed step of the Leloir pathway that funnels dietary galactose into glucose-1-phosphate and onward into glycolysis and glycoprotein synthesis. Without this anomeric conversion, galactose and its derivatives accumulate in blood and tissues. Affected individuals are usually mildly affected, with raised galactose levels, transient cholestasis and cataracts from lens galactitol accumulation, but severe cases extend to kidney, liver and brain injury. Because newborn screening detects elevated galactose, this defect is part of the differential diagnosis alongside classic galactosemia caused by loss of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase or the epimerase, and it is managed by dietary galactose restriction.
