Dietary galactose enters catabolism only in its alpha anomer, and galactose mutarotase is the cytosolic epimerase that interconverts beta-D-galactose to alpha-D-galactose so that galactokinase can phosphorylate it, the first committed step of the Leloir pathway. Loss-of-function mutations in GALM cause type 4 galactosemia, the mildest and most recently recognised form of the disease: affected individuals typically show raised blood galactose with transient cholestasis and cataracts, the lens opacities reflecting accumulation of galactose and its reduction product galactitol, while severe cases extend to liver, kidney and brain injury. Because the defect sits upstream of galactokinase rather than at the classical galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase step, toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation is limited, which explains the comparatively benign course and the need to distinguish this condition from classic galactosemia in newborn screening.

Bacterial colonization of a host begins with irreversible attachment to a surface, the step that converts motile bacteria into a sedentary, matrix-encased community far more resistant to host defenses and antibiotics before it eventually releases new motile cells again. Represented here from the host side, the attachment substrates are the extracellular matrix and epithelial molecules that adherent bacteria engage: type IV collagen networks and the laminin heterotrimers of basement membranes, fibrillar type V collagen, fibronectin, the epithelial adhesion molecule EpCAM, and uroplakin of the urothelial surface. Adhesins such as curli fibres and Ag43 bind these ligands, while the maturing biofilm matrix is built largely of polysaccharides including cellulose and colanic acid. The interaction matters clinically in catheter-associated and recurrent urinary tract infection, where exposure of basement membrane after epithelial damage offers high-affinity anchoring sites and seeds persistent, treatment-refractory colonization.

The circadian clock keeps time because its repressors are destroyed on schedule, and the timed degradation of CRY and PER proteins sets the length of the roughly 24-hour cycle. CRY1/2 and PER1/2/3 accumulate to shut off BMAL1:CLOCK-driven transcription; clearing them at night permits a new round of transcription the next morning, and altering their stability lengthens or shortens behavioural period, as seen in familial sleep phase disorders. Recognition is by cullin-RING ligases built on CUL1, SKP1 and RBX1: the beta-TrCP proteins BTRC and FBXW11 capture phosphorylated PER in the cytosol, while FBXL3 targets nuclear CRY and a related F-box protein opposes it in a cytosolic pool. Polyubiquitinated substrates are then processed by the 26S proteasome, whose core and regulatory subunits make up most of the machinery here, linking timekeeping to regulated proteolysis and to sleep, metabolic and hormonal rhythms.

Nucleosomes block access to DNA, and ATP-dependent chromatin remodelers use ATP hydrolysis to slide, eject, restructure or exchange them so that transcription factors, polymerases and repair machinery can reach the underlying sequence. This determines which genes a cell can express, and mutations in the subunits are among the most common genetic lesions in cancer and in developmental syndromes affecting brain, heart and craniofacial formation. All classes share a SWI2/SNF2-family translocase — SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 in BAF/PBAF complexes, CHD paralogs, SMARCA5-type enzymes — surrounded by accessory subunits such as ARID1A, SMARCB1, SMARCC1/2 and the DPF and BCL7 proteins that read histone marks and confer target specificity. CHD3/CHD4 assemble with HDAC1/2, MTA and MBD proteins into repressive complexes, linking remodelling to histone deacetylation. Tissue-specific subunit swapping, as in muscle differentiation driven with MYOD1, and coupling to spliceosomal and elongation factors extend the output to lineage identity and co-transcriptional RNA processing.

Genes encoding the ATP-dependent SWI/SNF chromatin remodelers, machines that use ATP hydrolysis to slide, evict or restructure nucleosomes and so open enhancers and promoters to transcription factors. Their output is cell identity: lineage-specific subunit swapping drives neural, muscle and immune differentiation programmes, and loss of remodelling leaves regulatory DNA inaccessible. Every complex is built around the catalytic ATPase SMARCA2 or SMARCA4 together with actin and actin-like subunits, a SMARCC dimer base, SMARCD and BCL7 paralogs, while distinguishing subunits define three assemblies: canonical BAF with ARID1A/B and SMARCB1, polybromo-containing PBAF with PBRM1, ARID2 and BRD7, and non-canonical BAF built on BRD9 and BICRA. Subunit mutations are among the commonest in human cancer, including SMARCB1 loss in rhabdoid tumours and SS18 fusion in synovial sarcoma, and germline variants cause neurodevelopmental syndromes.

Two families of nuclear receptors compete at the same DNA sequence, and the balance between them sets the daily rhythm of metabolic gene expression. Retinoid-related orphan receptors and the heme-sensing receptor REV-ERBA both bind ROR response elements, but with opposite consequences: the RORs recruit coactivators such as EP300, CREBBP, the NCOA proteins and PPARGC1A to drive transcription, while NR1D1 pulls in the NCOR1 corepressor together with HDAC3 and the TBL1X/TBL1XR1 subunits to shut it down. The genes they control are those of lipid and fatty acid handling, including CPT1A, ELOVL3 and targets shared with PPARA/RXRA and SREBF1, so this axis couples the circadian clock to fuel oxidation, lipogenesis and bile acid metabolism. Disruption perturbs sleep-wake behaviour, cerebellar development and lipid homeostasis, and RORC additionally underlies a lymphocyte differentiation programme.

Canonical BAF is the most abundant of the mammalian SWI/SNF chromatin remodellers, and its stepwise assembly determines which genes a cell can keep accessible. Built around an ATPase subunit, SMARCA4 or SMARCA2, together with SMARCC scaffolds, SMARCB1, SMARCD and SMARCE1, actin and actin-like subunits, and BCL7 proteins, the complex acquires its identity from ARID1A or ARID1B and a DPF acetyl-lysine reader, with SS18 or SS18L1 completing the particle. Using ATP hydrolysis to slide and evict nucleosomes, cBAF opens enhancers, sustains lineage-specific transcription programmes, and counteracts polycomb-mediated silencing, though in mammals it supports both activation and repression. Assembly is ordered, so loss of a core module destabilises the whole complex. These subunits are among the most frequently mutated in human cancer: ARID1A in carcinomas, SMARCB1 in rhabdoid tumours, and SS18 fusion in synovial sarcoma.

Chromatin must be opened before transcription factors can reach their sites, and the polybromo-BAF complex is one of the ATP-dependent remodellers that does this. Its stepwise assembly produces a machine that slides and evicts nucleosomes at promoters and enhancers, coupling signals to gene expression during differentiation, development and DNA damage responses. A shared core of SMARCC scaffolding subunits, SMARCB1, actin and ACTL6A, BCL7 proteins and the SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 ATPase is combined with subunits that define this variant rather than the canonical one: ARID2 in place of ARID1A/B, plus PBRM1, BRD7 and PHF10, whose bromodomains and PHD fingers read acetylated and modified histones to direct targeting. Subunits of this family are recurrently mutated in cancer, with PBRM1 loss characteristic of clear cell renal carcinoma and SMARCB1 loss of rhabdoid tumours, making assembly integrity a tumour suppressive function.

Embryonic stem cells use a specialised version of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodelling machinery, and its assembly into the esBAF complex is what keeps their chromatin permissive for pluripotency. The complex opens nucleosome-packed promoters and enhancers so that the core pluripotency factors can bind and self-renewal genes stay on; losing it drives stem cells out of the undifferentiated state, and forced expression of its subunits can push fibroblasts toward pluripotency. Compositionally it is defined by what it lacks as much as what it holds: SMARCA4/BRG1 provides the ATP-dependent remodelling activity while the paralogue SMARCA2 is excluded, and BCL11A and BCL11B are characteristic members. Assembly proceeds modularly, with a core of SMARCC and SMARCD proteins, SMARCB1 and SMARCE1 built around actin and ACTL6A before the ARID1A-containing module and the ATPase join.

Chromatin remodelling complexes of the SWI/SNF family use ATP to slide and evict nucleosomes so that transcription factors can reach DNA, and the non-canonical BAF complex is one of three distinct assemblies built from this shared parts list. It is defined by what it lacks and what it uniquely gains: no SMARCB1, SMARCE1, ARID or DPF subunits, but obligatory BRD9 together with BICRA or BICRAL, assembled around an ATPase core of SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 with SMARCC, SMARCD, BCL7, actin and ACTL6A modules. The bromodomain of BRD9 reads acetylated histones and helps target the complex to CTCF-bound sites, linking it to insulator function and genome organisation. Because synovial sarcoma fusions involve SS18 and rhabdoid tumours lose SMARCB1, cancers retaining this complex become dependent on it, making BRD9 degradation a therapeutic strategy in those tumours and in some leukaemias and prostate cancer.

Neural stem cells and the neurons they produce use chromatin remodelling complexes of different composition, and the switch between them helps decide when a progenitor stops dividing and becomes a neuron. The progenitor form, built around ACTL6A, SS18 and the BAF45 subunits DPF2 or PHF10, sustains multipotency and proliferation; on cell cycle exit these subunits are exchanged for ACTL6B, SS18L1 and DPF1 or DPF3 to give the neuronal complex, which supports dendritic outgrowth and the transcriptional programme of a post-mitotic neuron. Both share an ATPase core of SMARCA4 or SMARCA2 with SMARCB1, SMARCC and SMARCD subunits and ARID1A or ARID1B, using ATP-dependent nucleosome repositioning to open lineage genes. Mutations in these subunits cause intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental syndromes, and the same core is a recurrent tumour suppressor target.

The contact system feeds into clotting when factor XII autoactivates on a surface: FXIIa converts factor XI to XIa, and plasma kallikrein, generated from prekallikrein bound to high molecular weight kininogen, can also activate factor IX directly, so this FXIIa- and kallikrein-dependent route amplifies fibrin formation while linking coagulation to kinin-driven inflammation. It is not needed for ordinary haemostasis — people lacking factor XII or prekallikrein do not bleed — yet it drives pathological thrombus growth, and factor XII deficiency is associated with protection from venous thrombosis while C1 inhibitor deficiency raises thrombotic risk. That dissociation makes the system an attractive antithrombotic target. Assembly occurs at the platelet surface, where the GPIb-IX-V complex provides a docking platform that concentrates these zymogens; by contrast, factor XI loss does cause bleeding, placing FXI at the junction of the contact and canonical cascades.

Blood-brain barrier breakdown lets fibrinogen, normally kept within the circulation, leak into brain parenchyma, where it can encounter amyloid beta peptides derived from APP. The interaction of aggregated β-amyloid with fibrinogen links the plaque pathology of Alzheimer's disease to its vascular component: the two proteins co-assemble, and the resulting fibrin clots are structurally abnormal and unusually resistant to fibrinolysis. Persistent clots promote occlusion of small cerebral vessels, hypoperfusion, and inflammation, aggravating neuronal injury independently of plaque burden itself. The three fibrinogen chains, encoded by FGA, FGB and FGG, form the circulating hexamer that thrombin converts to fibrin, so the same molecules that normally seal a wound become a substrate for amyloid-driven aggregation in the extravascular brain. This helps explain cerebral amyloid angiopathy and the vascular contribution to cognitive decline in dementia.

Amyloid beta fibrils do more than accumulate in plaques; their negatively charged surface acts as an activating scaffold for the contact system of plasma, and this is where that link begins. Factor XII, encoded by F12, binds aggregated APP-derived Aβ peptides and undergoes autoactivation to FXIIa, the trigger step for two downstream arms: cleavage of prekallikrein to kallikrein, which liberates bradykinin from high molecular weight kininogen, and activation of factor XI, feeding intrinsic-pathway thrombin generation. The consequence in Alzheimer's disease is a prothrombotic, proinflammatory vascular state, with raised kallikrein activity and cleaved kininogen in cerebrospinal fluid and plasma tracking with cognitive decline, and FXII and bradykinin detectable within plaques themselves. Because activation depends on the aggregated surface, antibodies that clear Aβ plaques also blunt this contact activation, connecting amyloid pathology to cerebrovascular dysfunction and neuroinflammation.

The thirteen mRNAs encoded by mitochondrial DNA, all of them subunits of the oxidative phosphorylation machinery, are chemically tailored after transcription before they can be translated efficiently, and this modification step sets how much respiratory chain protein a mitochondrion makes. Nuclear-encoded enzymes do the work: a mitochondrial poly(A) polymerase adds short adenylate tails (~40-50 residues) that stabilise the transcripts, a pseudouridylation module built around RPUSD3, RPUSD4 and TRUB2 isomerises specific uridines in cytochrome c oxidase messages, and TRMT61B installs N1-methyladenosine, which stalls the mitoribosome and dampens translation. RNA-binding partners including LRPPRC, SLIRP, FASTKD2 and NGRN organise the transcripts into granules and govern their stability and handling. Loss of these activities lowers mitochondrial translation and respiratory capacity, and mutations in components such as the poly(A) polymerase or LRPPRC cause inherited ataxia and infantile mitochondrial disease.

The pancreas begins as two buds of foregut endoderm, and this developmental lineage traces how definitive endoderm formed at gastrulation is patterned along the body axes and directed into multipotent pancreatic progenitor cells that will later give rise to acinar, ductal and islet endocrine cells, including insulin-producing beta cells. Dorsal foregut endoderm passes through a duodeno-pancreatic intermediate state and ventral endoderm through a hepato-pancreatic or pancreato-biliary one, with signals from surrounding mesenchyme and notochord deciding pancreatic rather than hepatic or biliary fate. The growth factors here act as those instructive cues: fibroblast growth factors including FGF10 from the mesenchyme sustain progenitor proliferation and expansion of the buds, alongside FGF2, FGF4, FGF7 and EGF. Failure of this specification step underlies pancreatic agenesis and neonatal diabetes, and the same cues are used to make beta cells from stem cells in vitro.

Mitochondria run their own translation machinery, and when a mitoribosome stalls — on a damaged tRNA, or on an mRNA that runs out before a stop codon appears — the trapped ribosome, its peptidyl-tRNA and its unfinished polypeptide must be cleared. This ribosome-associated quality control keeps the small pool of mitoribosomes available for synthesis of the respiratory chain subunits encoded by mitochondrial DNA, so its failure shows up as impaired oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial disease. Recognition begins with splitting of the 55S ribosome into its 39S and 28S subunits, a separated state stabilised by MALSU1 together with MIEF1 and the acyl carrier protein NDUFAB1. An MTRFR–MTRES1 pair then occupies the vacant A site and the peptidyl-tRNA anticodon stem to hydrolyse and eject the nascent chain and spent tRNAs, while MRPL58 handles non-stop messages by reaching into the empty mRNA channel to release the peptide.

CHD chromatin remodelers use ATP to slide, assemble, space and edit nucleosomes, setting how accessible DNA is to transcription, splicing and repair machinery. Nine human CHD ATPases read methylated histone tails through paired chromodomains and translocate DNA, and their loss is developmentally catastrophic: CHD7 mutations cause CHARGE syndrome, CHD8 is among the strongest autism risk genes, and CHD4-containing complexes are required for proliferation and genome stability. The gene list reflects the complexes these ATPases work within: CHD3, CHD4 and CHD5 anchor distinct nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase complexes with HDAC1/2, MTA1-3, RBBP4/7, MBD2/3 and GATAD2 subunits, coupling remodeling to histone deacetylation and gene repression. Other partners connect the family to transcription elongation through the PAF1 complex, to histone chaperoning via FACT, to U2 snRNP and spliceosomal components, and to lineage transcription factors such as MYOD1, IKZF family members and beta-catenin-driven WNT targets.

NuRD complex assembly builds a chromatin remodeler that is unusual in coupling two activities in one machine: ATP-dependent nucleosome sliding by a CHD3, CHD4 or CHD5 ATPase, and histone deacetylation by HDAC1 or HDAC2. The resulting complex sets the accessibility and acetylation state of target promoters and enhancers, and through this controls lineage commitment, stem cell differentiation, DNA damage responses and metabolic gene programs such as hepatic gluconeogenesis. Assembly nucleates on a core of HDAC1/2 with MTA1/2/3 and the histone chaperones RBBP4/7, onto which MBD2 or MBD3, GATAD2A/B and CDK2AP1/2 are added; paralog choice generates compositionally distinct complexes with different targets. Recruitment to chromatin comes mainly from transcription factors, including Ikaros family and nuclear receptor partners, plus reader proteins such as ZMYND8 and PWWP2A. Originally viewed as purely repressive, NuRD also activates transcription, and its misregulation contributes to cancer and developmental disorders.

Chromatin remodelling and histone deacetylation are usually separate jobs; the NuRD complex does both in one machine, sliding nucleosomes with a CHD3/CHD4/CHD5 ATPase while HDAC1 or HDAC2 strips acetyl groups from nearby histone tails. Assembly of this complex is what licenses that dual activity: a nucleating core of HDAC1/2 with MTA1/2/3 and the histone-binding WD40 proteins RBBP4/7 recruits MBD2 or MBD3, GATAD2A/B and CDK2AP1/2, and paralogue choice at each position generates complexes with distinct targets. Recruitment to genes comes largely through transcription factors and chromatin readers, including Ikaros-family zinc fingers, nuclear receptors, ZMYND8 and PWWP2 proteins, and can repress or activate transcription. The outputs shape stem cell differentiation, lymphoid and neural development, DNA damage responses and metabolic gene programmes such as gluconeogenic PCK1, FBP1 and G6PC1, and its subunits are recurrently mutated in cancer.

Antibody affinity maturation depends on deliberately mutating the immunoglobulin variable regions of germinal centre B cells, and this is the pathway that does it. After T follicular helper cells deliver CD40 ligand and IL21, STAT3 and AP-1 factors drive BCL6, which blocks plasma cell commitment by repressing PRDM1 and silences damage checkpoints including TP53, CDKN1A, ATR and CHEK1 so that mutated cells keep dividing; BACH2 with PAX5 and MLL3/4 components reinforces the germinal centre state. NF-kappaB subunits induce AICDA, the cytidine deaminase that converts deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine in single-stranded DNA exposed at stalled RNA polymerase II complexes, where SUPT5H and elongation, Paf1 and chromatin remodelling machinery localise its activity to the heavy and light chain loci. Uracil excision by UNG or MutSalpha mismatch recognition then recruits error-prone polymerases eta, iota, zeta and REV1 via ubiquitinated PCNA, fixing point mutations that selection converts into higher-affinity antibodies. Dysregulated targeting contributes to B cell lymphoma.

Antibody diversity is generated after a B cell has already made a working receptor, and immunoglobulin maturation covers that second stage: class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation in germinal centres, which convert a low-affinity IgM response into high-affinity IgG, IgA or IgE. Without it, humans have hyper-IgM syndromes and cannot mount durable protective antibody responses. The variable and constant gene segments of the heavy, kappa and lambda loci provide the substrate; activation-induced deaminase AICDA deaminates cytidine in switch regions and variable exons, and the resulting uracil is processed by uracil-DNA glycosylase, mismatch repair factors such as MSH2/MSH6, and translesion polymerases including POLH and REV1 to yield mutations or double-strand breaks. Transcription through the loci by RNA polymerase II with elongation and chromatin remodelling complexes licenses this targeting, while CD40, IL4 and IL21 signals from follicular helper T cells and MHC class II antigen display drive selection, with BCL6 and PRDM1 governing the germinal centre and plasma cell fates.

Affinity selection of immunoglobulins is the germinal centre reaction that converts a repertoire of randomly generated B cell receptors into high-affinity antibodies, and it is the reason vaccination and repeated infection yield progressively better protection. In the light zone, B cells test their receptors against antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells via FCGR2B, CR1 and CR2, and high-affinity clones physically extract antigen using non-muscle myosin IIa and the actin and microtubule machinery, then process it through cathepsins and present peptides on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells. CD40L, IL4 and IL21 rescue those cells from apoptosis and return them to the dark zone, where BCL6, PAX5 and AICDA-driven somatic hypermutation, coupled to error-prone polymerases and mismatch repair, diversify the immunoglobulin variable regions for another round of selection. Failure distorts antibody quality and underlies immunodeficiency, autoantibody production and germinal-centre-derived lymphoma.

Antibody responses improve over days to weeks because germinal center B cells are repeatedly tested for how tightly their receptors bind antigen, and only the best binders survive. This affinity selection of immunoglobulins is what converts a low-affinity naive repertoire into high-affinity, class-switched antibody, and its failure underlies poor vaccine responses, immunodeficiency, and, when selection is subverted, autoantibodies and B cell lymphoma. Antigen held as immune complexes on follicular dendritic cells via complement receptors CR1/CR2 and FCGR2B is extracted by high-affinity receptors using non-muscle myosin IIa, then processed by cathepsins and presented on MHC class II to follicular helper T cells, whose CD40L, IL4 and IL21 grant survival. Selected cells cycle back for AICDA-driven hypermutation, requiring mismatch repair, translesion polymerases and BCL6-centred transcriptional control.

Mammary glands arise from non-neural surface ectoderm, and the mammary stem cells derived from that ectoderm are the founders of the ductal tree, capable of regenerating a functional gland and of giving rise to both luminal and myoepithelial progeny. This developmental lineage traces that transition, from embryonic surface ectoderm to basal-residing mammary stem cells (also described as bipotent progenitors), which in the adult human breast are rare and concentrated in the ducts of terminal ductal lobular units. Their behaviour underlies placode and bud formation, pubertal ductal outgrowth, pregnancy-associated remodelling, and, when misregulated, the stem-like compartments implicated in breast cancer. FGF10 signalling through its epithelial receptor is one of the better-conserved inputs generating and maintaining these cells, acting alongside Wnt/beta-catenin, Hedgehog, Notch and ovarian hormone signalling in mammary specification.

Alpha-dystroglycan links muscle and nerve cells to their basement membrane, but only if it carries matriglycan, a long linear glucuronic acid-xylose polysaccharide built on threonines in its mucin-like domain. This sugar is the actual laminin-binding element of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, so its loss uncouples the cytoskeleton from the extracellular matrix and produces the alpha-dystroglycanopathies " congenital and limb-girdle muscular dystrophies that in severe forms add brain malformations, seizures and eye defects. It is also the entry receptor exploited by Lassa and other arenaviruses. Construction proceeds stepwise through a Core M3 trisaccharide, addition of two ribitol-phosphate units by CRPPA, FKTN and FKRP, a xylose-glucuronate primer laid down by RXYLT1 and B4GAT1, and finally chain elongation by the bifunctional glycosyltransferases LARGE1 and LARGE2, with nucleotide-sugar transporters supplying the Golgi lumen.

Assembly of the ChAHP complex brings the chromatin remodeller CHD4 together with the neuroprotective transcription factor ADNP, or its paralogue ADNP2, and an HP1 family chromobox protein such as CBX1 or CBX3, giving CHD4 a role distinct from its better-known service in NuRD remodelling complexes. The complex binds nucleosomal chromatin, recognises specific sequence motifs through ADNP, and represses target genes while silencing repetitive SINE and endogenous retroviral elements, so it contributes both to transcriptional programmes and to keeping transposable elements quiescent. ADNP2-containing assemblies act largely in heterochromatin maintenance. Loss or mutation of ADNP causes Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome, a neurodevelopmental disorder with intellectual disability and autistic features, placing this chromatin-repressive activity upstream of neuronal differentiation and genome stability. The accompanying core histones represent the nucleosome substrate on which the complex is recruited and acts.

The NuRD complex couples ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling to histone deacetylation, and it is directed to particular genes largely by the sequence-specific transcription factors it binds. This targeting is how a general chromatin-compacting machine produces gene-specific repression: it silences lineage-inappropriate programmes during development, shapes lymphocyte differentiation, and restrains genes whose misexpression drives leukaemia. A CHD3/CHD4/CHD5 helicase provides remodelling activity, HDAC1 and HDAC2 strip acetyl groups from nucleosomal histones, MTA and GATAD2 subunits scaffold the assembly, RBBP4/RBBP7 and the methyl-CpG-binding MBD2 or MBD3 read histones and DNA, and multiple histone-binding domains let the complex engage adjacent nucleosomes. Partners represented here include Ikaros-family zinc fingers, nuclear receptors such as NR2F2 and NR2C2, the reader ZMYND8, and PHF6, mutated in intellectual disability and T-cell leukaemia. Repressed targets include gluconeogenic genes such as PCK1, G6PC1 and FBP1.

Naive CD4+ T cells commit to the T helper 1 fate when antigen receptor engagement coincides with interferon gamma and interleukin-12, and the resulting Th1 cells drive immunity against intracellular bacteria and viruses by secreting IFNG and TNF to arm macrophages; too much of this programme underlies organ-specific autoimmunity and chronic inflammation, too little leaves mycobacterial infection uncontrolled. The lineage-defining transcription factor TBX21 (T-bet) is induced in two waves: first through STAT1 downstream of IFNG together with calcium-dependent NFATC1, then reinforced after TBX21 raises IL12RB2 and IL-12 signals through STAT4. With RUNX3, TBX21 amplifies IFNG expression in a feedback loop, while sequestering RUNX1 to block RORC-driven Th17 differentiation and repressing IL4 to exclude the Th2 option. It also switches on the Th1 phenotype itself, including the chemokine receptor CXCR3, CCL3, and TPST2, which supports trafficking into inflamed tissue.

CHD1 and CHD2 are monomeric ATP-dependent chromatin remodellers of CHD subfamily I that slide and space nucleosomes at transcriptionally active genes, keeping promoters and gene bodies accessible to the transcription machinery. Each combines tandem chromodomains that read trimethylated histone H3 lysine 4 with a central SNF2-family ATPase motor and a C-terminal DNA-binding module, so the enzymes are recruited to marks of active chromatin and then reorganise the histones they find there; both have been linked to deposition of the replication-independent variant H3.3. Their activity is coupled to elongation and co-transcriptional RNA processing, reflected here by the PAF1 elongation complex, the FACT histone chaperone, and U1/U2 snRNP and SF3 splicing components, and to differentiation programmes driven by MYOD1, MYOG and E-protein partners. Loss of CHD2 causes epileptic encephalopathy, and CHD1 loss is recurrent in prostate cancer.

Subfamily III of the CHD chromatin remodellers "— CHD6, CHD7, CHD8 and CHD9 —" uses ATP-dependent nucleosome remodelling to set how accessible genes are to transcription, and their loss has developmental consequences: CHD7 mutation causes CHARGE syndrome, while CHD8 disruption is one of the strongest single-gene risks for autism spectrum disorder. All four share tandem chromodomains and a SNF2-family ATPase, plus C-terminal BRK, SANT and DNA-binding modules that distinguish them from other CHD proteins; the BRK domain has been linked to association with the insulator factor CTCF. Their targets are nucleosomal histones, and the accompanying partners indicate the promoters they act on: CHD8 restrains beta-catenin-driven Wnt output at genes such as AXIN2 and the DKK and NKD antagonists, cooperates with p300/CBP and the WDR5-containing methyltransferase machinery, and participates in NFE2L2-MAFK control of oxidative stress genes including NQO1. Related activities extend to proliferation control and DNA damage repair.

The CHD3, CHD4 and CHD5 subfamily of ATP-dependent chromatin remodellers repositions nucleosomes to close chromatin and silence transcription, and it does most of this work inside larger assemblies rather than alone. The best known is the nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase complex, which couples remodelling by CHD4 to histone deacetylation by HDAC1 and HDAC2, with MTA scaffolds, the histone chaperones RBBP4 and RBBP7, methyl-CpG-binding MBD2 or MBD3, and GATAD2 subunits; a related ADNP-containing assembly and a ZMYND8/ZNF-based module direct the remodeller to different chromatin marks. Through these complexes the subfamily controls lineage decisions, Ikaros-dependent lymphocyte gene programmes, repression of gluconeogenic genes, DNA damage responses and nucleosome turnover involving variants such as H2AX and H2A.Z. Mutations in CHD4 cause a congenital intellectual disability syndrome, while CHD5 loss is implicated in neuroblastoma and other tumours.

KMT2D is the catalytic subunit of a histone H3 lysine 4 methyltransferase complex that marks enhancers for active transcription, and heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in it are the leading cause of Kabuki syndrome, a developmental disorder with characteristic long palpebral fissures, skeletal anomalies, intellectual disability and postnatal growth deficiency; some KMT2D variants instead give a syndrome of branchial arch defects, choanal atresia, hearing loss and hypothyroidism. Catalysis requires assembly with the core scaffolding module made of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30, which stimulates methyl transfer and stabilises the enzyme on chromatin. Disease-associated substitutions and truncations disrupt this interaction or the SET domain itself, so enhancers in neural crest, craniofacial and neuronal lineages fail to acquire H3K4 methylation and the transcriptional programmes of embryonic patterning and growth are under-activated, linking an epigenetic writer directly to congenital malformation.

Loss of Function of KMT2D in MLL4 Complex Formation in Kabuki Syndrome describes how disease-causing mutations in the histone methyltransferase KMT2D break assembly of the MLL4 complex that deposits H3K4 methylation at enhancers. This modification licenses enhancer activity during development, so its loss disrupts transcriptional programs in neural, craniofacial, cardiac and immune tissues, producing the intellectual disability, distinctive facial features, heart defects and immunodeficiency of Kabuki syndrome. Catalysis requires KMT2D's C-terminal SET and adjacent WIN, FYRN/FYRC, PHD and zinc-finger modules to engage the four-subunit WRAD platform of WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30, which stimulates methyltransferase activity. Missense changes in this region weaken WRAD binding, while truncating alleles trigger nonsense-mediated decay of KMT2D mRNA and cause haploinsufficiency. Both routes converge on reduced enhancer H3K4 methylation, placing the disorder among chromatin-modifier developmental syndromes.

KMT2D is the histone H3 lysine 4 methyltransferase of the MLL4 complex, depositing the mono- and trimethyl marks that keep developmental enhancers and promoters poised for transcription. Its catalytic activity depends on assembly with the four-subunit WRAD module — WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L and DPY30 — which docks onto the C-terminal region containing the WIN and SET domains; the SET domain alone is a poor enzyme without these partners. Missense changes in that region, found in people with Kabuki syndrome, weaken WRAD binding and so impair methyltransferase output, while truncating alleles trigger nonsense-mediated decay of the transcript and produce haploinsufficiency. The result is a congenital disorder of chromatin regulation marked by distinctive facial features, intellectual disability, growth delay, skeletal and cardiac anomalies, illustrating how quantitative loss of enhancer H3K4 methylation disrupts the transcriptional programmes of embryonic development.

T cell differentiation traces bone marrow-derived progenitors through the thymus, where double-negative stages assemble a T cell receptor, become double positive for CD4 and CD8, and are selected into naive single-positive CD4+ or CD8+ cells; peripheral antigen and cytokine cues then drive CD4+ cells into helper subsets. This programme supplies the adaptive immune repertoire, and its miswiring underlies immunodeficiency, allergy, autoimmunity and T cell leukaemia. Lineage identity is set by master transcription factors paired with cytokine-driven STAT signalling: TBX21 with STAT4 and IL12 receptor signalling for interferon gamma-producing Th1 cells, GATA3 with STAT6 downstream of IL4 for Th2 cells secreting IL4, IL5 and IL13, and IRF4, MAF, BATF and RUNX factors shaping other fates. Notch signalling through RBPJ and MAML coactivators drives early thymocyte commitment, while histone deacetylase complexes, NuRD, Polycomb rings and MLL/WDR5 methyltransferase modules lock these choices into chromatin.

Airway epithelium, brain ependyma, oviduct and developing kidney depend on multiciliated cells, which carry hundreds of motile cilia that sweep mucus, cerebrospinal fluid and oocytes; when the transcriptional programme that builds them fails, the result is reduced generation of multiple motile cilia, mucus stasis, chronic airway infection and hydrocephalus. The pathway describes how a cell is licensed to override once-per-cycle centrosome duplication and amplify centrioles into basal bodies. A hierarchy runs from the geminin-family proteins GEMC1 and MCIDAS, which partner with E2F4/E2F5 and TFDP1 rather than acting as DNA-binding factors themselves, through TP73 and MYB to effectors FOXJ1 and RFX2/RFX3 that switch on axonemal and dynein genes. A variant cell cycle involving cyclin CCNO, DEUP1-based deuterosomes, Notch-Delta lateral inhibition selecting which progenitors differentiate, GRHL factors, and miR-34/449 families acting through Argonaute-containing silencing complexes to damp Notch and cell-cycle transcripts complete the circuit.

Plasma contact activation links surface-triggered proteolysis to inflammation, vascular permeability and coagulation, and its failures produce swelling attacks and vascular injury rather than simple bleeding. On negatively charged surfaces, factor XII autoactivates, converts prekallikrein to kallikrein, and kallikrein liberates bradykinin from high-molecular-weight kininogen; C1 inhibitor, encoded by SERPING1, is the principal brake on both proteases. When that brake is lost, or when factor XII itself is mutated, unrestrained bradykinin release dilates postcapillary venules and causes hereditary angioedema. Aggregated amyloid beta from APP supplies an activating surface in Alzheimer disease, coupling this cascade to neuroinflammation, prothrombotic change and cognitive decline. Contact factor deficiency prolongs aPTT without causing bleeding, so the system contributes to pathological thrombus formation more than to normal haemostasis.

Cytosolic lipopolysaccharide from Gram-negative bacteria is sensed directly by caspase-4, whose activation constitutes the non-canonical inflammasome arm of innate immunity. This is how a cell that has been invaded, or that has taken up bacterial outer membrane vesicles, commits to pyroptosis and alerts its neighbours; loss of the response permits unchecked intracellular bacterial replication, while excessive activation drives endotoxic shock and sepsis. Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding proteins GBP1-GBP4 form a coat on bacteria and pathogen-containing vacuoles that exposes LPS and recruits caspase-4, which oligomerizes, self-cleaves, and then cuts gasdermin D to generate membrane pores, and processes pro-IL-18 into its mature, secreted form. Calmodulin and the serine protease inhibitor SERPINB1 act as modulators of assembly and caspase activity, and bacterial effectors that chemically modify caspase-4 illustrate how tightly pathogens must restrain this route.

Gram-negative bacterial lipopolysaccharide that reaches the cytosol is sensed directly by inflammatory caspases, and caspase-5 is one of the two human sensors that respond. Assembly of the caspase-5 inflammasome converts this detection into pyroptosis, an inflammatory form of cell death that destroys the infected cell's replicative niche and releases alarm signals; it underpins host defence against intracellular Gram-negative bacteria and contributes to septic shock when LPS is abundant. Caspase-5 is barely expressed at rest and is strongly induced by LPS through NF-κB and by interferons through JAK-STAT, mainly in monocytes and other immune-rich tissues. LPS binding to its CARD drives oligomerisation, autoprocessing into an active heterotetramer, and cleavage of gasdermin D, whose N-terminal fragment forms membrane pores. It also matures pro-IL-18 for release, while its cleavage of pro-IL-1β yields an inactive product.

Ribosomes stall when they encounter damaged nucleotides, strong mRNA structure, long polylysine stretches, or a missing stop codon, and ribosome-associated quality control is how the cell clears those jams and destroys the incomplete protein they produce. Without it, aborted nascent chains accumulate and aggregate, a burden linked to neurodegeneration in animals lacking listerin. The ubiquitin ligase ZNF598 marks small-subunit proteins eS10 and uS20 on collided ribosomes, licensing the ASCC2:ASCC3:TRIP4 helicase complex to split the stalled 80S; non-stop stalls are instead recognised by PELO:HBS1L with the ATPase ABCE1 driving subunit separation. The 60S subunit retains the peptidyl-tRNA, where NEMF adds a C-terminal alanine tail that exposes lysines for K48 ubiquitination by LTN1, CRL2-KLHDC10 or RCHY1. ANKZF1 cleaves the tRNA, VCP with UFD1:NPLOC4 extracts the chain for proteasomal degradation, and both subunits return to translation.

Hurler syndrome is the severe end of mucopolysaccharidosis I, a lysosomal storage disease caused by loss of alpha-L-iduronidase, the enzyme encoded by IDUA that strips non-reducing terminal alpha-L-iduronic acid residues during stepwise lysosomal breakdown of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate. Because these sugar chains are turned over constantly from cartilage, cornea, skin, blood vessels and the extracellular matrix generally, blocking one step in chondroitin/dermatan sulfate degradation halts the whole sequential route and leaves partially digested chains accumulating in lysosomes, with excess excreted in urine. The resulting multisystem disease includes coarse facial features, skeletal dysplasia and short stature, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac valve and airway involvement, and progressive neurological decline, with milder Hurler-Scheie and Scheie forms reflecting residual enzyme activity. The pathway underlies enzyme replacement and hematopoietic transplant strategies that supply functional iduronidase.

MPS II - Hunter syndrome (CS/DS degradation) describes the lysosomal step that fails in Hunter syndrome, an X-linked disorder of glycosaminoglycan turnover that affects mainly boys. Iduronate-2-sulfatase removes the 2-sulfate group from L-iduronate residues in dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin, and this desulfation must occur before the downstream exoglycosidases can continue stepwise degradation of the chain. When the enzyme is deficient or absent, partially degraded glycosaminoglycans accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body and spill into urine. The consequences are systemic: hepatosplenomegaly, thickened heart valves and reduced cardiac function, airway obstruction, joint stiffness and skeletal deformity, and in severe forms progressive neurological deterioration and death in childhood. Milder forms preserve cognition and allow survival into adulthood. The pathway situates lysosomal catabolism of extracellular matrix polysaccharides within normal tissue remodelling.

Hunter syndrome is the X-linked lysosomal storage disease that results when the degradation of chondroitin/dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate stalls at a single sulfatase step. Iduronate-2-sulfatase normally removes the 2-sulfate group from L-iduronate residues in dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin, and this removal must happen before the downstream exoglycosidases and sulfatases can continue trimming the glycosaminoglycan chain. Loss of that one activity blocks the whole sequential pathway, so undegraded fragments accumulate in lysosomes throughout the body and spill into urine. The consequences are multisystem: hepatosplenomegaly, thickened cardiac valves, airway obstruction, joint stiffness and skeletal dysostosis, and in severe forms progressive neurological decline and death in childhood, while attenuated forms allow survival into adulthood. Because males carry a single copy of the gene, affected individuals are almost exclusively boys.

MPS VII - Sly syndrome (CS/DS degradation) describes the failure of lysosomal beta-glucuronidase and the block it imposes on stepwise breakdown of glycosaminoglycans. GUSB removes terminal glucuronic acid residues from chondroitin sulphate, dermatan sulphate and heparan sulphate as these long sugar chains are dismantled one sugar at a time by a relay of exoglycosidases and sulfatases; when the enzyme is absent, degradation stalls and partially digested chains accumulate in lysosomes throughout connective tissue, liver, spleen, bone and brain. The consequence is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease with a broad spectrum of severity, from non-immune hydrops fetalis and perinatal death to hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, coarse facial features and cognitive impairment in those surviving to adulthood. It illustrates how turnover of extracellular matrix proteoglycans depends on complete lysosomal catabolism, since a single missing step arrests the whole sequence.

Mucopolysaccharidosis VII, or Sly syndrome, is the lysosomal storage disease that follows loss of beta-glucuronidase activity during the stepwise breakdown of chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate. Glycosaminoglycan chains from turnover of extracellular matrix and cell surface proteoglycans are degraded inside the lysosome by sequential removal of terminal sugars and sulfate groups; GUSB performs the step that releases terminal glucuronic acid residues, and without it the partially digested chains accumulate in lysosomes of liver, spleen, bone, cartilage and brain. The consequences are strikingly variable, from non-immune hydrops fetalis and perinatal death to milder disease compatible with survival into adulthood, with hepatosplenomegaly, dysostosis and skeletal deformity, coarse facial features and differing degrees of cognitive impairment. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the defect illustrates how a single missing glycosidase can stall an entire catabolic route.

Hyaluronan is a large glycosaminoglycan that fills the extracellular matrix of joints, skin and connective tissue, and it must be continually broken down as well as made. Lysosomal hyaluronidase 1 performs the degradative step, cleaving the linkages between N-acetylglucosamine and glucuronate within internalized hyaluronan chains so that the resulting oligosaccharides can be processed to monosaccharides by exoglycosidases. When HYAL1 activity is lost, hyaluronan accumulates in serum and tissues and causes mucopolysaccharidosis IX, or Natowicz syndrome: periodically painful soft-tissue masses around the joints, acquired short stature and erosion of the hip, with joint mobility and intelligence spared. The disorder belongs to the lysosomal storage diseases, in which failure of a single step in glycosaminoglycan catabolism leaves partially degraded substrate trapped in the lysosome, and it is the mildest and rarest of that group.

Lysosomal turnover of glycosaminoglycans proceeds by stepwise removal of terminal sugars, and this step is the removal of terminal galactose by acid beta-galactosidase (GLB1) during chondroitin and dermatan sulfate breakdown. When GLB1 activity is lost, undegraded keratan sulfate accumulates inside lysosomes, producing mucopolysaccharidosis IVB, or Morquio B disease: an autosomal recessive storage disorder marked by skeletal dysplasia, short stature, corneal clouding and raised urinary keratan sulfate, but with normal intelligence and no central nervous system disease. The same enzyme also cleaves galactose from gangliosides and glycoproteins, so different mutations in GLB1 instead cause GM1 gangliosidosis with neurodegeneration, making the clinical outcome a function of which substrates remain accessible to residual activity. The pathway situates skeletal and connective-tissue matrix recycling within lysosomal catabolism.

Guanylate binding proteins are interferon-gamma-inducible, dynamin-related GTPases that carry out cell-autonomous defence inside infected cells, attacking pathogens that hide in vacuoles or in the cytosol. Their loss leaves cells unable to restrict organisms such as Salmonella, Shigella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Toxoplasma, and blunts the inflammatory response to cytosolic bacteria. GBP1 binds GTP, dimerizes and hydrolyses it stepwise to GMP, and a prenyl anchor added by farnesyl- or geranylgeranyltransferase subunits lets it insert into pathogen membranes, where it oligomerizes and recruits GBP2, GBP3 and GBP4 into a dense coat. The coat damages bacterial membranes, blocks actin-based bacterial motility, and licenses caspase-mediated non-canonical inflammasome activation with pyroptosis and IL-1 family cytokine release. Regulation runs through PIM1 phosphorylation and 14-3-3 sigma sequestration in the cytosol. GBP2 and GBP5 additionally restrict enveloped viruses by interfering with furin-dependent maturation of viral glycoproteins.

When a ribosome stalls and is split, the large subunit is left holding an incomplete nascent chain still attached to tRNA, and ribosome quality control is the salvage operation that destroys that chain and frees the subunit for reuse. Without it, aborted polypeptides accumulate and aggregate, a burden linked to neurodegeneration in animals lacking the ligase LTN1. NEMF recognises the obstructed 60S subunit, adds C-terminal alanine tails that push buried lysines out of the exit tunnel and themselves act as degrons, and recruits LTN1, which with its partner TCF25 attaches lysine-48 polyubiquitin; CRL2-KLHDC10 and RCHY1 provide alternative ubiquitination routes. ANKZF1 cleaves the tRNA to release the peptide, and the VCP ATPase with its UFD1-NPLOC4 adaptor ratchets the ubiquitinated chain out of the tunnel and delivers it to the 26S proteasome.

Ribosomes that translate an mRNA lacking a stop codon run to the 3' end and stall with no release factor able to act, and this rescue route clears them so that the trapped subunits and nascent chain can be recycled. Recognition falls to a complex of PELO with the GTPase HBS1L, paralogues of the normal termination factors eRF1 and eRF3, which occupy the A site of ribosomes carrying little or no mRNA beyond the P site. GTP hydrolysis releases HBS1L and uncovers a binding surface on PELO for the ATPase ABCE1, whose ATP-driven conformational change splits the ribosome into 40S and 60S subunits, leaving peptidyl-tRNA on the large subunit for downstream degradation. Together with no-go and ASCC-mediated rescue, this surveillance keeps the pool of translating ribosomes free of dead-end complexes and feeds aberrant transcripts and their products toward decay.

When a ribosome stalls in the middle of a message — on damaged nucleotides, strong structure, or a run of poly-lysine AAA codons — trailing ribosomes crash into it, and this branch of ribosome-associated quality control recognises the collision and takes the stalled ribosome apart. Without it, aberrant mRNAs are translated repeatedly and incomplete, aggregation-prone nascent chains accumulate, a burden that neurons tolerate poorly. The E3 ligase ZNF598 senses the collided interface and, with UBE2D enzymes and ubiquitin, marks 40S proteins eS10 and uS10; K63-linked chains on uS10 are read by ASCC2, recruiting the ribosome quality control trigger complex, whose ASCC3 helicase pulls on the mRNA to split 40S from 60S. The peptidyl-tRNA stays with the 60S for downstream degradation, while the faulty mRNA is released and destroyed. Collision sensing also feeds the ribotoxic stress MAPK response.

Organic anions — lactate, urate, citrate, bile acids, prostaglandins, thyroid hormone, sulfate conjugates and most acidic drugs — cannot cross membranes unaided, and this family of solute carriers moves them across the plasma membrane and the inner mitochondrial membrane. The transport sets renal handling of urate and citrate, hepatic uptake of bile acids and xenobiotics for clearance, and the export of lactate from glycolytic tissue. Monocarboxylate carriers of the SLC16 family, which need the chaperone basigin for surface delivery, shuttle lactate, pyruvate and ketone bodies, while SLC16A2 imports thyroid hormone into neurons and its loss causes severe X-linked psychomotor retardation. Organic anion transporters of the SLC22 and SLCO groups govern proximal tubule secretion and hepatocyte uptake, making them principal determinants of drug disposition and interactions; SLC22A12 variants alter serum urate and gout risk. Dicarboxylate and citrate carriers link this transport to intermediary metabolism and lipogenesis.

Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 catalyses the first and rate-limiting step of the urea cycle in the liver mitochondrial matrix, condensing ammonia, bicarbonate and two ATP into carbamoyl phosphate so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea. Loss-of-function variants in CPS1 cause an autosomal recessive deficiency in which ammonia accumulates, presenting as catastrophic neonatal hyperammonaemia or as later crises provoked by catabolic stress, infection or protein load; untreated episodes produce cerebral oedema and irreversible neurological injury. The enzyme requires allosteric activation by N-acetylglutamate, so truncating mutations upstream of the C-terminal activator-binding domain abolish activity, while missense changes in the bicarbonate and carbamate phosphorylation domains or the integrating domain that channels carbamate between active sites destabilise folding and reduce catalysis. Severity tracks with residual activity, linking this single enzymatic step to whole-body nitrogen homeostasis.

Nitrogen from amino acid breakdown leaves the body as urea, and the urea cycle only runs if its first enzyme is switched on by an allosteric activator. N-acetylglutamate synthase makes that activator in the mitochondrial matrix, condensing acetyl-CoA with glutamate to give N-acetylglutamate, the obligatory cofactor of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I. Loss-of-function variants in NAGS abolish activator production, so carbamoyl phosphate is never formed and the cycle cannot begin. The result is N-acetylglutamate synthase deficiency, a rare recessive urea cycle disorder presenting with hyperammonemia, vomiting, lethargy, seizures and encephalopathy, often in the newborn period, with low citrulline and risk of permanent neurological damage or death if untreated. It is distinctive among urea cycle defects in responding to carbamylglutamate, a stable analogue of the missing activator that restores flux.

Nitrogen from amino acid breakdown is disposed of as urea by the liver, and inherited failures of that route make up the urea cycle disorders. The cycle spans two compartments: mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, dependent on its allosteric activator N-acetylglutamate, condenses ammonia with bicarbonate, ornithine transcarbamylase makes citrulline, and after ornithine/citrulline exchange across the inner membrane by SLC25A15, cytosolic argininosuccinate synthetase and lyase build and cleave argininosuccinate to arginine, which arginase hydrolyses to urea while regenerating ornithine. Loss of any step or of the transporter allows ammonia to accumulate, producing neonatal or later-onset hyperammonemic encephalopathy with lethargy, vomiting, seizures and lasting neurological damage, together with the characteristic metabolite signatures of citrullinemia, argininosuccinic aciduria, argininemia or HHH syndrome. The same reactions also supply arginine and link nitrogen excretion to aspartate and fumarate metabolism.

The urea cycle spans two compartments, so ornithine made in the cytosol must be carried into mitochondria and the citrulline made there must be carried out. SLC25A15 is the mitochondrial inner-membrane antiporter that performs this exchange, and loss-of-function variants in it cause hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome. Without transport, ornithine accumulates in the cytosol while the matrix is starved of it, leaving carbamoyl phosphate to condense with lysine into homocitrulline and stalling nitrogen disposal; ammonia rises, producing episodic encephalopathy, protein intolerance, spastic paraparesis and developmental impairment. A related carrier, SLC25A2, overlaps in function and partially buffers the defect, which helps explain the variable age of onset and severity. The biology sits at the intersection of amino acid metabolism, mitochondrial solute transport and detoxification of waste nitrogen, and the resulting disorder is managed like other urea cycle defects.

ARG1 variants cause hyperargininemia describes the loss-of-function mutations in arginase 1 that break the last step of the urea cycle and produce an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism. Arginase 1 is a cytosolic, manganese-dependent enzyme most abundant in liver and present at lower levels in kidney, where it hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, both disposing of waste nitrogen and regenerating the ornithine that keeps the cycle turning. When the enzyme is deficient, arginine accumulates in blood and tissues and patients develop spastic paraparesis, progressive neurological impairment and developmental delay; unlike other urea cycle defects, severe hyperammonemia is uncommon, so the phenotype is attributed largely to arginine and its guanidino derivatives. The pathway therefore links hepatic amino acid catabolism and nitrogen excretion to neurological health, and underlies dietary arginine restriction as treatment.

The final step of the urea cycle is carried out by cytosolic arginase 1, which hydrolyses L-arginine to urea and L-ornithine, completing nitrogen disposal and regenerating the ornithine that re-enters the cycle. The enzyme is most abundant in liver, with lower activity in kidney and red cells. Loss-of-function variants in ARG1 cause arginase 1 deficiency, or hyperargininemia, an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism in which plasma and cerebrospinal arginine accumulate. Affected children typically present after infancy with progressive spastic paraparesis, developmental regression, seizures and growth failure, a neurological course distinct from the other urea cycle disorders because severe hyperammonemia is uncommon. Treatment relies on protein restriction and nitrogen-scavenging agents. This biology links amino acid catabolism and ureagenesis to arginine availability for nitric oxide and polyamine synthesis.

Argininosuccinate synthase carries out the third step of the urea cycle, joining citrulline to aspartate in an ATP-dependent condensation to form argininosuccinate, and it is the point at which loss-of-function variants produce type 1 citrullinemia. The enzyme works in the cytosol of hepatocytes, with lower activity in kidney, and its output feeds both nitrogen disposal as urea and the endogenous supply of arginine for downstream uses such as nitric oxide synthesis. Missense changes typically destabilise folding or the citrulline and aspartate binding sites, while nonsense, frameshift and splice-site variants remove the protein altogether; the common G390R allele is recurrent among more than a hundred catalogued mutations. The result is hyperammonemia with raised plasma citrulline, glutamine and orotic acid and low arginine, and in severe neonatal presentations lethargy, vomiting, seizures, coma and death from ammonia-driven encephalopathy.

Ornithine transcarbamylase catalyses the second step of the urea cycle, transferring a carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate onto ornithine to make citrulline, and this reaction is how the liver and small intestine commit waste nitrogen to disposal as urea. Loss-of-function variants in the X-linked gene cause ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the commonest urea cycle disorder, in which ammonia accumulates and produces encephalopathy, coma and lasting neurological injury; severe alleles present in the newborn period, milder ones later in life or only under catabolic stress. The enzyme is made as a precursor whose N-terminal leader directs it into mitochondria, where the mature subunits assemble into a homotrimer with three active sites. Mutations act by disrupting mitochondrial targeting, trimer assembly, or the motifs that bind ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate and cap the active site during catalysis.

Argininosuccinate lyase performs the fourth step of the urea cycle, splitting argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea and so that the cycle's arginine supply is regenerated. Loss-of-function variants in the gene encoding this homotetrameric enzyme cause argininosuccinic aciduria, a recessive urea cycle disorder in which argininosuccinate accumulates and ammonia is not cleared. Severe neonatal presentations bring hyperammonemia, encephalopathy and respiratory alkalosis, while milder late-onset disease may declare itself only under catabolic stress or infection. Because the active site is formed at subunit interfaces, different mutant alleles can partially complement one another within a tetramer and leave residual activity, which helps explain the wide clinical spectrum. Beyond ammonia detoxification, the reaction also supplies arginine for nitric oxide synthesis, a likely contributor to the hypertension and neurological features seen in patients.

Ornithine transcarbamylase catalyses the second step of the urea cycle inside mitochondria, condensing carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to make citrulline so that waste nitrogen can be disposed of as urea. The enzyme is encoded in the nucleus and made on cytosolic ribosomes, so it must be imported: a 33-residue N-terminal leader sequence directs the precursor across the mitochondrial membranes and is proteolytically removed on arrival. Variants that alter this leader are a recognised cause of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common inherited urea cycle disorder and X-linked in inheritance. Such mutations can destabilise the transcript, lower protein levels, and prevent correct mitochondrial targeting and maturation, leaving the mature enzyme absent from the matrix. The result is hyperammonaemia with orotic aciduria, and in severe neonatal presentations encephalopathy, illustrating how a failure of protein targeting alone can disable an entire metabolic route.

Ornithine transcarbamylase performs the second step of the urea cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, condensing ornithine with carbamoyl phosphate to form citrulline and thereby committing waste nitrogen to disposal as urea. Amino acid substitutions in the main chain of the enzyme underlie ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, the most common inherited urea cycle disorder and the only X-linked one. When the enzyme cannot process carbamoyl phosphate, ammonia accumulates in blood, producing encephalopathy, cerebral oedema, coma and death in severely affected newborns. Mutations fall along a severity gradient: those striking catalytic or substrate-binding residues abolish activity and present neonatally, while changes at surface or domain-interface positions leave partial function and surface later, often triggered by protein load, illness or catabolic stress. The pathway connects hepatic nitrogen handling to neurological health, and management relies on nitrogen scavengers and dietary protein restriction.

Gut pathogens such as Shigella and enteropathogenic or enterohemorrhagic E. coli inject type III secretion effectors that disarm the host's cytosolic response to lipopolysaccharide, and this is how enterobacterial factors antagonize host defense. The pathway centres on caspase-4, the human sensor that binds LPS reaching the cytosol and triggers pyroptosis, a lytic death that destroys the pathogen's replicative niche and releases inflammatory signals including processed interleukin-18. Guanylate-binding proteins, induced by interferon and loaded onto bacterial surfaces in a ubiquitin-dependent manner, expose LPS for detection and amplify caspase-4 activation. Effectors defeat this step directly: OspC3 ADP-riboxanates caspase-4 to abolish its protease activity, while NleF inserts its C-terminus into the active site of caspase-4 and of the apoptotic caspases 8 and 9. The result is a silenced epithelium that tolerates intracellular bacterial persistence.

SLC-mediated bile acid transport groups solute carrier proteins that move bile acids and related amphipathic solutes across membranes, activity that sustains the enterohepatic circulation by which conjugated bile acids are secreted, reabsorbed in the ileum and reclaimed by hepatocytes. Efficient recovery of this pool is what allows dietary fat and fat-soluble vitamins to be emulsified and absorbed, and limits the accumulation of cytotoxic bile acids in liver and gut. The sodium-dependent carriers here are the same family that handles choline: SLC10A6 transports sulfated steroids and bile acid conjugates, while the SLC44 choline-like transporters and the high-affinity neuronal choline transporter SLC5A7 supply choline for phosphatidylcholine and acetylcholine synthesis. The shared theme is sodium-coupled uptake of small charged metabolites, linking bile salt handling to membrane lipid supply and cholinergic neurotransmission.

Bile acids and structurally related amphipathic solutes cross plasma and organelle membranes only with help from solute carriers, and this grouping collects the SLC-mediated bile acid transport steps together with the closely related choline-transporting members of the same superfamily. SLC10A6 belongs to the sodium/bile acid cotransporter family and imports sulfoconjugated steroids and bile acids into peripheral tissues, where local desulfation can regenerate active hormone, linking this transport to steroid availability rather than to hepatic bile flow alone. The SLC44 choline transporter-like proteins and the high-affinity, hemicholinium-sensitive carrier SLC5A7 move choline into cells; SLC5A7 supplies presynaptic cholinergic neurons with substrate for acetylcholine synthesis, and its loss causes congenital myasthenic syndrome with impaired neuromuscular transmission. Collectively these carriers set intracellular supply of bile acid conjugates and choline for membrane lipid synthesis, neurotransmission and enterohepatic and steroid handling.

Cells and epithelia must move chloride, bicarbonate, sulfate, phosphate and iodide across membranes, and this family of solute carriers does that work. Their output sets intracellular chloride and pH, drives fluid secretion and absorption in gut, airway and kidney, reclaims filtered phosphate, and concentrates iodide in thyroid for hormone synthesis. Cation-chloride cotransporters of the SLC12 group load or extrude chloride and thereby determine whether GABA responses are inhibitory or excitatory in neurons, while also mediating salt reabsorption targeted by loop and thiazide diuretics. Bicarbonate transporters of the SLC4 family and the SLC26 anion exchangers pair with carbonic anhydrase chemistry to buffer pH and secrete bicarbonate, and SLC34 carriers handle sodium-dependent phosphate uptake. Loss of individual members produces Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, congenital chloride diarrhoea, Pendred syndrome deafness with goitre, distal renal tubular acidosis, and hereditary phosphate wasting with rickets.

Oncogenic SRC activation drives STAT3 phosphorylation, but the strength of that signal depends on how much cadherin survives, making this a dose-dependent rather than a switch-like route to transformation. Activated SRC raises RAC1 activity and IL6 secretion, which engages the gp130 receptor subunit IL6ST to phosphorylate STAT3; at the same time SRC downregulates cadherin-11 and E-cadherin, and cadherins are needed to maintain IL6ST at the surface. Intermediate SRC levels leave enough cadherin for robust STAT3 activation, while very high levels strip cadherin and abolish it, so inhibiting SRC in such cells can paradoxically restore STAT3 phosphorylation. The gene complement reflects this: adherens junction components and catenins, Rho-family GTPase exchange factors and GTPases that feed RAC1, cathepsins and ubiquitin that degrade cadherin. The loop matters for interpreting SRC-directed cancer therapy and for tumour cell survival signalling.

Epithelial cells sense when they have reached confluence, and one consequence is that the transcription factor STAT3 switches on. Homophilic engagement of E-cadherin between neighbouring cells, and equivalently of the mesenchymal cadherins CDH11 and N-cadherin, raises the levels and activity of the Rho-family GTPases RAC1 and CDC42 by sparing them from ubiquitin-proteasome degradation; exchange factors such as TIAM1 and VAV2 and the DOCK1-ELMO1 module feed this step, while HACE1-directed ubiquitination and the 26S proteasome oppose it. Active RAC1/CDC42 drive NF-kB-dependent transcription of IL6-family cytokines, which act back on the same cells through IL6R and gp130 to engage JAK1/JAK2/TYK2 and SRC, phosphorylating STAT3 on tyrosine-705 for dimerization, nuclear entry and transcription of proliferation and survival genes. The circuit links adherens junction assembly, anchored by catenins and the actin cytoskeleton, to autocrine growth signalling, and its persistent activation supports tumour cell survival and immune evasion.

Amino acids cannot cross membranes unaided, and this family of solute carrier transporters moves them across the plasma membrane and into organelles, supplying substrates for protein synthesis, nitrogen handling, neurotransmission and redox defence. The carriers differ in driving force and specificity: sodium-coupled glutamate and neutral amino acid transporters of the SLC1 group clear synaptic glutamate and take up glutamine and cysteine; SLC38 members handle glutamine flux between astrocytes, neurons, liver and placenta; heteromeric exchangers pair the heavy chains SLC3A1 or SLC3A2 with light chains such as SLC7A9, SLC7A5 or SLC7A11 to swap cationic, large neutral or aromatic amino acids, with SLC7A11 importing cystine for glutathione synthesis. Proton-coupled SLC36 and SLC6 members support intestinal and renal reabsorption. Loss of individual carriers causes cystinuria, Hartnup disorder and lysinuric protein intolerance, and leucine uptake through SLC7A5 feeds mTORC1 nutrient sensing.

Small peptides left over from protein digestion or lysosomal proteolysis must be moved across membranes intact, and this family of solute carriers does that work. In the small intestine and kidney proximal tubule, a proton-coupled peptide transporter takes up di- and tripeptides from the lumen, recovering dietary nitrogen efficiently and also carrying peptide-like drugs such as beta-lactam antibiotics and ACE inhibitors, which makes it a determinant of oral drug absorption. Related carriers sit on lysosomal and endosomal membranes of immune cells, where peptide and histidine export helps deliver bacterial products to innate sensors and supports Toll-like receptor signalling. A cystine-specific lysosomal exporter belongs here too; its loss traps cystine in lysosomes and causes cystinosis, with renal tubular failure. Together these transporters link digestion, lysosomal turnover, and innate immune recognition.

Caspase-4 is the human sensor that detects cytosolic bacterial lipopolysaccharide and converts that detection into inflammatory cell death, and the cleavage events described here are how it does so. Its principal substrate is gasdermin D: proteolysis separates the pore-forming N-terminal fragment from the C-terminal domain that otherwise restrains it, and the freed fragment oligomerises in the plasma membrane to cause pyroptosis. The same pores provide the exit route for interleukin-18, which caspase-4 processes directly into its mature, receptor-activating form; pro-IL-1β is a poorer substrate, and cleavage within its pro-domain can yield an inactive product rather than the active cytokine. This arm of the non-canonical inflammasome underlies host defence against Gram-negative intracellular bacteria, and its overactivation contributes to sepsis and endotoxic shock. Caspase-3 links the same gasdermin substrate to apoptotic proteolysis, which inactivates rather than activates pore formation.

Cytosolic lipopolysaccharide from invading Gram-negative bacteria is sensed directly by inflammatory caspases, and caspase-5 is the human protease that converts that detection into pyroptotic death and cytokine release. Its defining substrate is gasdermin D, cleaved within the linker to free an N-terminal fragment that oligomerises in the plasma membrane as a pore; loss of the autoinhibitory C-terminal domain is what permits this. The resulting pores lyse the infected cell and provide the conduit through which mature interleukin-1 family cytokines leave it. Caspase-5 also processes pro-IL-18 at its prodomain to the active cytokine using a bivalent recognition mode, while its cleavage of pro-IL-1 inside the prodomain yields an inactive product, so substrate preference shapes which inflammatory signals are amplified. This arm of innate immunity drives fever, neutrophil recruitment and, when unrestrained, septic shock.

Antibody affinity maturation depends on deliberately mutating immunoglobulin variable regions in germinal centre B cells, and this error-prone, non-canonical use of mismatch repair supplies most of the mutations that appear at A:T base pairs. Canonical repair would restore the original sequence; here the same machinery is subverted to diversify it. The MSH2:MSH6 heterodimer recognises the G:U mismatches left by AID-mediated cytosine deamination, converts to a sliding clamp upon ATP binding, and recruits MLH1:PMS2, whose endonuclease nicks the DNA. EXO1 then resects a short single-stranded gap that is refilled not by high-fidelity replicative polymerases but by translesion synthesis enzymes such as POLH, POLI and the REV1-REV3L complex, loaded via ubiquitinated PCNA and the RFC clamp loader. Loss of MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 skews the mutation spectrum and narrows the antibody repertoire, contributing to immunodeficiency.

Antibody affinity maturation depends on germinal center B cells deliberately mutating their own immunoglobulin variable regions, and one route to those mutations is an error-prone version of base excision repair. After AID-generated deoxyuridine is excised by the nuclear uracil-DNA glycosylase UNG, the resulting abasic site is handled by APEX2 rather than the usual APEX1: it nicks the strand and widens the lesion into a short single-stranded gap. Ubiquitinated PCNA, loaded with the replication factor C clamp loader and the polymerase delta accessory subunits, then recruits translesion polymerases eta and iota together with REV1 and the REV3L-MAD2L2 complex, which fill the gap inaccurately and install transversions at G and C and a share of the mutations at A and T. The output is the diversified B cell repertoire that high-affinity antibody responses require; the same low-fidelity synthesis, misdirected, contributes to lymphomagenesis.

Interferon-inducible guanylate-binding protein 1 coats intracellular bacteria and parasite vacuoles, recruiting caspase-4 and driving pyroptotic death of the infected cell; because that response is destructive, its intensity has to be restrained, and this pathway describes the brakes on GBP-mediated host defense. Caspase-1 cleaves GBP1 at Asp192, generating fragments that can no longer decorate cytosolic Salmonella, recruit caspase-4, or trigger pyroptosis, a negative feedback loop that limits inflammatory cell death during bacterial infection but is not engaged against Toxoplasma, so regulation is pathogen-specific. In parallel, the kinase PIM1 phosphorylates GBP1 at Ser156, creating a binding site for the 14-3-3 protein sigma encoded by SFN, which holds GBP1 in the cytosol away from pathogen membranes. GTP binding allosterically breaks the PIM1 complex, coupling nucleotide state to release. Loss of this tuning shifts the balance toward excessive inflammation and tissue damage.

Circulating monocytes arise in the bone marrow from myeloid progenitors, egress to the blood in a CCR2-dependent manner, and survive there only a day or two before either dying or entering tissues to become monocyte-derived macrophages and dendritic cells. Their differentiation sustains innate defence: classical CD14-high monocytes phagocytose and kill bacteria, non-classical CD16-high monocytes patrol the vasculature and respond to nucleic acids and viruses, with an intermediate antigen-presenting state between them. The two cytokines represented here set the fate and tone of this output: macrophage colony-stimulating factor drives survival, proliferation and mononuclear phagocyte differentiation through its receptor CSF1R, while interferon gamma from T and NK cells licenses classical activation, raising antigen presentation and antimicrobial capacity. Too little of this axis leaves monocyte and macrophage compartments depleted; excess drives the inflammatory monocyte influx seen in atherosclerosis, autoimmunity and chronic infection.

The first half of cholesterol synthesis runs from cytosolic acetyl-CoA to lanosterol, the first sterol-ring intermediate, and everything downstream — cholesterol itself, bile acids, steroid hormones, vitamin D — depends on it. The route also supplies isoprenoid branch products such as farnesyl and geranylgeranyl diphosphate used to lipid-anchor Ras and Rho GTPases, and dolichol and ubiquinone precursors. Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase and HMG-CoA synthase build HMG-CoA, HMG-CoA reductase reduces it to mevalonate in the rate-limiting and sterol-feedback-controlled step that statins block, and successive kinases and a decarboxylase generate isopentenyl diphosphate, which isomerases and prenyltransferases condense into squalene via farnesyl diphosphate synthase and squalene synthase. Squalene epoxidase then oxidizes squalene and lanosterol synthase cyclizes the epoxide. Enzymes act in the cytosol and on the endoplasmic reticulum membrane; inherited deficiency of mevalonate kinase causes periodic fever syndromes.

Cholesterol is made from lanosterol by two classic routes, and tracer work in mice and human cells shows that much tissue flux actually takes a hybrid path: the Bloch intermediate zymosterol is reduced at the C24 double bond by DHCR24 to zymostenol, which is then finished by the last three steps of the Kandutsch-Russell route. EBP isomerises the sterol double bond, SC5D introduces the C5 desaturation, and DHCR7 reduces the C7 bond to yield cholesterol. This modified sequence predominates in skin, preputial gland and brain, tissues with heavy local demand for cholesterol in membranes, myelin and barrier lipids, since circulating lipoprotein cholesterol crosses poorly into brain. Loss of the terminal enzymes causes recognisable malformation syndromes -- DHCR7 deficiency underlies Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, and EBP mutation causes chondrodysplasia punctata -- reflecting both cholesterol shortage and accumulation of bioactive precursor sterols.

When blood contacts a negatively charged surface — polyphosphate from activated platelets, extracellular DNA and histones, phosphatidylserine, collagen, or artificial materials — factor XII autoactivates and cleaves plasma prekallikrein to kallikrein, which reciprocally activates more FXII and liberates bradykinin from high-molecular-weight kininogen. This contact-driven activation of the plasma kallikrein-kinin system controls vascular tone, permeability, smooth muscle contraction and pain, and links contact activation to coagulation, fibrinolysis and complement. Assembly occurs largely on endothelial surfaces, where kininogen docks through receptors including C1QBP, uPAR and cytokeratin 1 in a zinc-dependent manner, and where prolylcarboxypeptidase can activate prekallikrein independently of FXIIa. Restraint is imposed by C1 inhibitor, alpha-2-macroglobulin and histidine-rich glycoprotein; loss of C1 inhibitor causes unopposed bradykinin generation and hereditary angioedema, the clearest demonstration of why this cascade must be held in check.

Presynaptic inhibition depends on shutting down calcium entry at the nerve terminal, and this is one of the main routes by which it happens: metabotropic GABA-B receptors, built from the GABBR1 and GABBR2 heterodimer, release Gbeta/gamma subunits that bind and inhibit voltage-gated calcium channels directly, without a diffusible second messenger. Less calcium influx means fewer synaptic vesicles fuse and fewer are recruited to release sites, so neurotransmitter output falls.
