The same liberated Gbeta/gamma dimers open inwardly rectifying potassium channels of the Kir3/GIRK family, hyperpolarizing the membrane and reinforcing the same inhibitory outcome postsynaptically. Together these actions set the gain of inhibitory tone in the brain, and the pathway is the target of baclofen in spasticity as well as a contributor to seizure susceptibility, nociception and the control of neuronal excitability generally.

Repair of DNA double-strand breaks must be switched off as well as on, and this pathway describes how the break response is damped by destroying the proteins that organize it. The BRCA1-BARD1 heterodimer, which drives homologous recombination and end resection, is polyubiquitinated by Cullin4-RBX1-DDB1 ubiquitin ligase complexes using DCAF8L1 or DCAF8L2 as substrate receptors, and the tagged proteins are then degraded by the 26S proteasome, whose full complement of core particle, ATPase and lid subunits is represented here along with ubiquitin itself. Limiting BRCA1-BARD1 levels restrains recombination, influences the choice between repair routes, and tunes how long checkpoint signalling persists after damage. Because BRCA1-BARD1 loss underlies hereditary breast and ovarian cancer, ubiquitin-dependent turnover of these factors also shapes genome stability and the sensitivity of tumour cells to agents that create double-strand breaks.

Most quiescent human cells extend a single non-motile primary cilium from the mother centriole, and this antenna is where Hedgehog, WNT, calcium, G protein-coupled receptor and receptor tyrosine kinase signals are received and interpreted; its loss produces the ciliopathies, from polycystic kidney disease and nephronophthisis to retinal degeneration, obesity and skeletal and brain malformation. Assembly of the 9+0 axoneme begins with conversion of a centriole into a basal body, docking of vesicles and exocyst-dependent membrane delivery, and construction of a transition zone whose MKS and NPHP components gate entry. Anterograde intraflagellar transport by kinesin-2 with IFT-B and retrograde transport by cytoplasmic dynein-2 with IFT-A then ferry tubulin and cargo along the axoneme, while the BBSome sorts membrane receptors such as SMO and somatostatin receptor 3. Because tubulin turns over at the tip, the same machinery maintains the organelle after it is built.

Assembly of the 9+2 motile cilia builds the beating cilia that line the airways, brain ventricles, and reproductive tract, where their coordinated strokes clear mucus, circulate cerebrospinal fluid, and move gametes. Beyond the nine microtubule doublets and central pair, motile axonemes require dynein arms, radial spokes, and nexin links, and multiciliated cells must first amplify hundreds of centrioles through deuterosomes. The genes here represent the transcriptional and post-transcriptional program that licenses this fate: GMNC and MCIDAS relieve Geminin-mediated restraint and partner with E2F4/E2F5 and TFDP1 to drive centriole amplification through DEUP1 and CCNO, while FOXJ1, RFX2/RFX3, MYB, TP73, and Grainyhead factors switch on axonemal and motility genes. Notch signalling limits how many progenitors adopt this fate, and miR-34/449 families acting through Argonaute complexes reinforce the commitment. Failure produces primary ciliary dyskinesia, with chronic airway infection, laterality defects, and infertility.

Motile cilia of the 9+2 type — nine microtubule doublets around a central pair, equipped with dynein arms, radial spokes and nexin links — beat rhythmically to clear mucus from the airways, drive cerebrospinal fluid flow in the brain ventricles, and move eggs along the oviduct; when their assembly fails the result is primary ciliary dyskinesia, with chronic airway infection, situs defects and infertility. The genes here largely cover the front end of that programme: the transcriptional and centriole-amplification decisions that let a single epithelial cell build hundreds of cilia. GMNC and MCIDAS, acting with E2F4/E2F5 and TFDP1, license multiciliate differentiation and deuterosome-mediated centriole duplication via DEUP1 and CCNO, while FOXJ1, RFX2/RFX3, MYB, TP73 and Grainyhead factors drive axonemal and motility gene expression. Notch signalling restrains the fate, and miR-34/449 families with Argonaute and TNRC6 partners relieve that repression.

When a naive CD4+ T cell meets antigen on a dendritic cell in the presence of the right cytokines, it can commit to the T helper 2 fate, the arm of adaptive immunity that defends against helminths and drives allergic inflammation, asthma and IgE class switching. IL2-driven STAT5 dimers open the IL4 locus and induce IL4R, and IL4 signalling then generates STAT6 dimers that switch on GATA3, the master regulator whose expression is reinforced by NFATC2 downstream of the T cell receptor and by Notch receptors acting through RBPJ and Mastermind-like coactivators. Commitment is largely a chromatin problem: GATA3 and STAT6 act at a locus control region within the RAD50 gene beside the clustered IL4, IL5 and IL13 genes, recruiting histone acetyltransferases such as CREBBP/EP300 and MLL-type methyltransferase complexes while HDAC, NuRD, NCoR and Polycomb complexes restrain the alternative programmes.

Germinal center B cells survive and mature only if they can show helper T cells what antigen their receptor has captured, and this is the machinery that converts captured antigen into MHC class II-bound peptide. Antigen bound by the B cell receptor is internalized and delivered along microtubules to late endosomal, multivesicular compartments, a step supported here by tubulins, kinesins, the dynein-dynactin complex and the Rab7 effector RILP, which positions and fuses these vesicles. Inside them, a family of cathepsin proteases together with the thiol reductase IFI30 unfolds and digests antigen, while HLA-DM exchanges the invariant chain CLIP fragment for antigenic peptide on HLA-DR, -DP and -DQ; HLA-DO tunes that editing. Efficient presentation determines which clones receive T cell help, drive affinity maturation and class switching, and it also shapes autoimmune and allergic responses.

The islets of Langerhans arise during development from duct-like bipotent trunk progenitors of the pancreas, and this step describes their passage into a committed endocrine mid-progenitor state that still retains the capacity to make alpha, beta, delta, gamma and epsilon cells. Whether a trunk progenitor takes the ductal or the endocrine route is decided largely by its mechanical environment, which is why the matrix proteins dominate here. Fibronectin and vitronectin engage integrin alpha5beta1, promote cell spreading and sustain a YAP1-NOTCH mechanosignalling axis that represses endocrine commitment, while fibrillar collagens and laminins favour confinement, relieving that repression so NEUROG3 can rise and progenitor markers such as SOX9 and ONECUT1 fall. EGF signalling likewise restrains NEUROG3 induction. Understanding these cues underpins efforts to direct stem cells toward insulin-producing beta cells for diabetes therapy.

The urea cycle disposes of nitrogen as urea, and here it is shut down deliberately: p53 tetramers occupy the promoters of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1, ornithine transcarbamylase and arginase 1 and repress their transcription. The consequence is a rise in intracellular ammonia rather than its clearance, and that ammonia boosts translation of ornithine decarboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme of polyamine biosynthesis. Polyamines in turn support the nucleic acid and protein synthesis that proliferating cells require, so this arm of p53 activity links nitrogen handling to growth metabolism and is one of the ways a tumour suppressor can be co-opted to favour proliferation. It illustrates how transcriptional control of hepatic and intestinal ammonia-detoxifying enzymes feeds back on amino acid catabolism, and it frames urea cycle gene expression as a metabolic decision point rather than a fixed housekeeping function.
